pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Volume & Vibrations

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 4 Sound):** Pupils should find patterns between the volume of a sound and the strength of the vibrations that produced it. (Volume is taught alongside, but kept distinct from, pitch.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS 4-PS4-1, partial):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-1]." Loudness is the everyday face of amplitude; the formal amplitude–loudness link is named at MS-PS4. There is no standalone elementary NGSS performance expectation for volume, so this topic is UK-anchored with 4-PS4-1 as the nearest conceptual bridge.

- **Operational details:** Children investigate that the SIZE of a vibration — how far the object moves — sets how loud the sound is, while keeping it separate from pitch (how FAST it vibrates). Anchor in canonical demos where the vibration is made visible: rice or salt grains scattered on a drum skin jump higher when you hit harder; a ruler twanged off a desk swings in a bigger arc and sounds louder; a plucked elastic band or guitar string blurs more widely on a strong pluck. The teaching move is predict–do–measure: predict which will be louder, vary ONLY the force, then describe the pattern in their own words — 'bigger/stronger vibration → louder sound; smaller/gentler vibration → quieter sound.' Crucially, contrast a louder-but-same-pitch change against a higher-but-same-volume change so the two variables are felt as independent. Introduce 'amplitude' informally as 'the size of the vibration' so the Year 4 pattern lands on the right word for later wave work.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can, with a real sound-maker, vary the force and reliably state and demonstrate the loud↔big-vibration / quiet↔small-vibration pattern, and can keep volume distinct from pitch when both are in play. Mastery is an articulated, demonstrated pattern from their own manipulation — not a quantitative amplitude measure (Tier C).
bestPractices: Make the vibration VISIBLE: rice/salt on a drum skin, a blurred plucked band, or a twanged ruler's arc — so children literally see 'bigger movement' before they name it as louder.
Use predict–do–measure, changing only the force applied while holding the sound-maker fixed, so the volume–vibration-strength pattern is isolated as a fair test.
Explicitly and repeatedly separate volume (size of vibration) from pitch (speed of vibration) by demoing each while the other is held constant — the single most important discrimination at this age.
Have children articulate the pattern in their own words and in both directions (harder hit → bigger vibration → louder; gentler → smaller → quieter) rather than only recognising it.
Seed the word 'amplitude' informally as 'the size/size-of-swing of the vibration' to pre-load the Year 5 amplitude–wavelength model without demanding measurement now.
keyRepresentations: Drum with rice/salt grains — grains bounce higher for louder sounds (amplitude made visible on a horizontal surface).
Twanged ruler over a desk edge — arc width maps directly to loudness while length (pitch) is held fixed.
Plucked elastic band / guitar string — the blur envelope of the vibrating string widens with a stronger pluck.
A two-control mental model: one dial for 'how hard' (volume) and a separate dial for 'how fast/short' (pitch), shown as independent.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing volume with pitch — thinking a louder sound is automatically higher, or that turning something 'up' changes the note; the two must be dissociated explicitly.
Believing hitting/plucking HARDER makes a HIGHER pitch (rather than a louder sound of the same pitch).
Thinking volume is a property of the object alone rather than of how strongly it is made to vibrate.
Assuming the sound's loudness at the ear equals the vibration's strength regardless of distance (distance-fading is a separate, later idea).
Treating 'amplitude' as the height/size of the object instead of the size of its back-and-forth movement.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9 (UK Year 4 Sound; conceptual bridge to NGSS 4-PS4-1): children find the pattern that, for the same sound-maker and listening position, a bigger vibration (larger SIZE) usually makes a LOUDER sound, while keeping this distinct from pitch (how fast the object vibrates). The central difficulty is dissociating volume from pitch, so activities make the vibration visible, change only the striking/plucking force in a fair test, have children articulate the pattern in both directions, and contrast a louder-same-pitch change against a higher-same-volume change. 'Amplitude' is seeded informally as 'the size of the vibration' to pre-load later wave work. Work here is Tier A (concrete/observational): an articulated, demonstrated pattern from the child's own manipulation, not a quantitative amplitude measure.

activities.title: Rice on the drum: hit harder, watch and listen
feedback: Listen for high/low separately from loud/quiet. On the same drum, changing strike strength mainly changes loudness, and the note may stay roughly the same. If a child hears a pitch change, report that observation rather than declaring it impossible; use a controlled audio comparison to isolate the two qualities.
If the child says louder but gives no mechanism ('more sound', 'more energy'): direct attention to the rice — it jumps HIGHER for the louder sound, so louder means a bigger movement of the skin.
If the child treats loudness as 'sound stuff coming out': reframe loudness as the SIZE of the vibration of the skin, not an amount of material leaving the drum.
When correct: 'Yes — bigger vibration, louder sound, and the note stayed about the same.' Ask them to repeat it as a rule in their own words.
activities.rationale: Rice movement gives a visible, qualitative sign of the drum skin's motion. Predicting and testing moderate strikes on the same drum can help learners relate stronger vibration to louder sound while listening separately for pitch; rice bounce height is not a direct measurement of vibration amplitude. This is a research-informed proposed activity, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should find patterns between the volume of a sound and the strength of the vibrations that produced it, and between pitch and features of the object producing the sound.

Volume/loudness corresponds to the size (amplitude) of the vibration while pitch corresponds to how fast the object vibrates (frequency); the two are commonly confused and should be taught as independent, with the vibration made visible (e.g. rice on a drum).
learnerActions: Scatter a few grains of rice or salt on a drum skin (or stretched clingfilm/foil over a bowl).
Predict out loud: when I hit harder, will the rice jump higher or lower, and will the sound be higher, lower, louder, or quieter? Say WHY before hitting.
Hit the drum gently, then hit the SAME drum much harder, keeping everything else the same.
Describe what you saw (how high the rice jumped) and what you heard (how loud, and whether the note sounded higher or lower).
State the pattern in your own words in BOTH directions: 'harder hit → bigger vibration → louder sound' and 'gentler hit → smaller vibration → quieter sound.'
activities.intendedInsight: For the same drum and listening conditions, a larger vibration usually produces a louder sound. Compare pitch separately: striking harder may mainly change loudness, but do not treat an observed pitch change as impossible.

activities.title: Twanged ruler and plucked band: arc width and blur
feedback: If the child changes the overhang or string length between tries: remind them to change ONLY the force, or the test is not fair and pitch may change too.

Listen to high/low separately from loud/quiet. Fixed length helps control the comparison, but real instruments can couple amplitude and frequency; use the controlled audio examples if an isolated comparison is needed.

When correct: confirm that 'wider swing/blur → louder, about the same note' and connect it back to the rice-on-the-drum rule — the same pattern within each sound-maker, seen across different sound-makers.
activities.rationale: Seeing the same volume–vibration-size pattern across several sound-makers (drum, ruler, band) supports transfer and reinforces that loudness depends on how strongly the object is made to vibrate, not on the object alone.
sourceClaims: Volume/loudness corresponds to the size (amplitude) of the vibration while pitch corresponds to how fast the object vibrates (frequency); the two are commonly confused and should be taught as independent, with the vibration made visible (e.g. rice on a drum).
learnerActions: Hold a ruler firmly over the edge of a desk so part of it overhangs, keeping the overhang length FIXED.
Twang it gently, then twang it hard; watch how wide the arc is and listen to how loud it is.
Do the same with a plucked elastic band or guitar string: pluck softly, then strongly, and watch how much more widely the string blurs.

Say what stayed roughly the same and what changed. With moderate plucks and fixed length and tension, the note may stay approximately the same while the swing and loudness change; report any differences actually observed.
Describe the observed swing and loudness. With a fixed ruler or band and moderate plucks, a wider swing usually sounds louder while the pitch may stay roughly the same; report any pitch change too.
activities.intendedInsight: With the same ruler or band and the same listening position, a wider swing (a bigger vibration) usually sounds louder. The overhang length of the ruler, and the length and tension of the band or string, mainly set pitch, so these are held fixed.

activities.title: Two separate controls: compare amplitude and frequency
feedback: Compare the prepared same-note sounds first, changing only level. Then compare the roughly loudness-matched higher and lower notes. Ask which quality changed in each case; do not assume that changing a real instrument’s length or tension leaves its loudness unchanged.
If the child still merges the two: slow down and do one change at a time, naming aloud which variable is changing and which is held constant.
When correct: 'You've shown they are two separate dials.' Introduce 'amplitude' informally as 'the size of the vibration' that sets loudness.
activities.rationale: Controlled comparisons let learners attend separately to vibration amplitude and frequency, addressing the volume/pitch confusion. A model can vary these properties independently; real instruments and perceived loudness can involve additional factors, so the audio examples and listening conditions must be chosen deliberately. This is a research-informed proposed activity, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should find patterns between the volume of a sound and the strength of the vibrations that produced it, and between pitch and features of the object producing the sound.

Volume/loudness corresponds to the size (amplitude) of the vibration while pitch corresponds to how fast the object vibrates (frequency); the two are commonly confused and should be taught as independent, with the vibration made visible (e.g. rice on a drum).
learnerActions: Use a controlled wave model and prepared audio comparisons to distinguish vibration size from vibration frequency. For the loudness comparison, use the same note and listener position; for the pitch comparison, use sounds matched roughly in perceived loudness.
Keep frequency fixed in the model and increase amplitude: observe the wider vibration trace and hear the same note played more loudly at a comfortable level.

Change frequency in the model while keeping the trace amplitude fixed. Compare higher and lower notes using audio matched roughly for loudness; notice that higher pitch does not necessarily mean louder sound.

Explain which feature changed in each comparison: the size of the vibration or the number of vibrations each second. Do not use whisper-versus-shout throat feeling as a measure of vibration amplitude.

State the rules separately: for the same sound and listening conditions, a larger vibration amplitude usually gives a louder sound; more vibrations each second gives a higher pitch. Real instrument changes can affect both, so check what is actually held constant.
activities.intendedInsight: Volume and pitch are two different qualities that can be changed separately in a controlled model: for the same note and listening conditions, loudness mainly depends on the SIZE of the vibration, while pitch depends on how FAST it vibrates. Changing loudness need not change the note, and changing the note need not change loudness.

activities.title: Sort and predict: which change makes it louder?
feedback: A higher note is not automatically louder. For a same-note comparison at the same listener position, increasing amplitude usually increases loudness; compare prepared audio carefully rather than judging unrelated sounds by a picture alone.
If sorting mixes the categories: re-test each change one at a time against a real instrument to decide which quality it alters.
When correct, ask the child to state the general rule that guided the sort.
activities.rationale: Deliberate contrasting of volume-changes against pitch-changes, including a plausible higher-pitch distractor that tempts the louder=higher confusion, sharpens the discrimination that pupils most struggle with. Treat this as checking and consolidating the pattern rather than as the first exposure to it.
sourceClaims: Volume/loudness corresponds to the size (amplitude) of the vibration while pitch corresponds to how fast the object vibrates (frequency); the two are commonly confused and should be taught as independent, with the vibration made visible (e.g. rice on a drum).
learnerActions: Sort prepared controlled examples into changes in loudness, changes in pitch, both, or depends on conditions. For real shortening or tightening, describe what was measured or heard rather than assuming only one quality changes.
For a 'predict which will be louder' prompt, choose and justify your answer in terms of which produces the bigger vibration BEFORE testing it.

Watch out for a tricky option that is HIGHER in pitch but is NOT actually louder — a change that only raises the note can tempt you into calling it 'louder'; decide carefully whether each change affects volume, pitch, or neither.

For pictures representing the same frequency, sound-maker and listening conditions, predict the order from smaller to larger vibration amplitude, then compare the corresponding sounds. State what was held constant.
Check your predictions against a real sound-maker where possible.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can discriminate changes that affect volume from those that affect pitch, and can justify loudness predictions by the size of the vibration — and recognise that a higher note is not automatically louder.

activities.title: Talk it through with a drummer
feedback: Ask the learner to describe both qualities actually heard. On the same drum a softer strike mainly reduces loudness and may leave pitch roughly unchanged; use same-note controlled audio if needed, rather than declaring every pitch difference impossible.
Praise explanations that link loudness to vibration SIZE and keep pitch separate; prompt for the two-directional rule if only one direction is given.
Use this as a reflective wrap-up, not as a substitute for hands-on hitting, plucking and listening.
activities.rationale: Spoken, responsive discussion is valuable for eliciting and naming ideas and surfacing the volume/pitch confusion. Because loudness is something to hear and manipulate, talk works best after a hands-on experience rather than as the primary means of building the perceptual pattern.
learnerActions: After hands-on work, explain to a questioner (real partner or an in-role 'percussionist/sound engineer') what happens to the note and the loudness when you hit softer.
Answer the probe: 'If I hit softer, does the NOTE change or just the loudness?' and justify with what you saw and heard.
Respond when the questioner pushes back on a wrong answer, revising your explanation.
Name 'amplitude' as 'the size of the vibration' and use it correctly in a sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Children consolidate and articulate the volume–vibration-size pattern and the volume/pitch distinction in their own words, catching any remaining confusion.

constraints: Distinguish volume from pitch using controlled comparisons. Hold frequency fixed when exploring amplitude; use roughly loudness-matched sounds when comparing pitch. A real instrument change can affect both qualities, and observed differences should be discussed rather than marked impossible.

For the real-instrument strength comparison, keep length, tension, material and listener position fixed and use moderate strikes or plucks. When length or tension changes, recheck both pitch and loudness; fixed force alone does not hold loudness constant.
Have children articulate the pattern in both directions (harder → bigger → louder; gentler → smaller → quieter), not just recognise it.
Mastery here is Tier A: an articulated, demonstrated pattern from the child's own manipulation — not a quantitative amplitude measurement (which is a later, Tier C goal).
Introduce 'amplitude' only informally as 'the size of the vibration'; do not demand measurement now.

A labelled drum/rice/ruler image can illustrate the pattern and support vocabulary. It does not itself let a learner vary linked sound and vibration, so offer manipulation or controlled audio examples when that is the intended task.

A quiz or sort can teach, practise and check the distinction. Ask for a reason and, where useful, test a prediction with a controlled sound comparison; selection alone does not show how the learner explained it.
A higher-pitched sound is not automatically louder; keep any 'which is louder?' judgement tied to vibration size, not to pitch.
Loudness at the ear also depends on distance (distance-fading), which is a separate, later idea; do not conflate the vibration's strength with how loud it seems far away.

An optional model may vary frequency and amplitude independently, with prepared audio comparisons matched as needed for the intended judgement. Label it as a controlled illustration; changing a real string’s length or tension at fixed force does not guarantee unchanged loudness.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Earlier model reviews missed coupled-variable assumptions and an invalid whisper-versus-shout amplitude example. Subsequent agent editorial corrections distinguish controlled audio/models from real instruments and do not claim this establishes educational effectiveness.

The original row rated a 3D rendering 'poor' and a 2D interactive 'ideal' as the primary artefact. These are catalog fit preferences, not established pedagogical laws; they have been reframed as proposals with stated affordances/limits rather than universal claims. No claim is made that only a screen playground can teach this.

The original claimed the conversation format 'cannot deliver' the perceptual pattern and that a static image 'cannot let loudness and vibration size co-vary'. The genuine, narrowly scoped limit (recognition/talk alone does not substitute for hands-on manipulation and listening) is retained; the stronger universal phrasing has been softened.

The original louder-versus-higher distractor needed clearer controlled conditions. The revised comparisons use same-note amplitude examples or roughly loudness-matched pitch examples; they do not rank unrelated sounds by amplitude alone.

Only learning guidance was revised. Original pedagogy and assessment fields remain unchanged and may contain the same coupled-variable or whisper assumptions; reconcile those separately before publishing or using them as an authoritative task specification.
Source claims are preserved verbatim and attached only where they support the stated teaching principle; activities carrying [] are reasonable extensions not directly backed by a listed claim.

assess.poeTask: Put rice on the drum skin. Predict what happens to the rice, and to the sound (higher/lower/louder/quieter), when you hit the drum harder. Say why first, then hit it and explain what you saw and heard.
probeDeeper: Put rice on the drum skin. Hit gently, then hard — what do you notice about how high the rice jumps, and how does that connect to how loud it is?
Does hitting the drum harder change how HIGH the note is, or how LOUD it is? Which one?
A whisper and a shout — which one makes your throat vibrate with bigger movements?
assess.correctAnswer: The harder hit is LOUDER (not higher). Hitting harder makes the drum skin vibrate with BIGGER movements, and the bigger/stronger the vibration, the louder the sound. The pitch (how high or low) stays about the same — only the loudness changed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Volume and pitch collapsed: 'hitting harder makes it higher'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Independent moves — vary hitting force (volume) on the same drum so pitch is fixed, then change the drum's tension/size (pitch) at a fixed force; prove louder is not higher.
errorPatterns.distractor: The harder hit sounds higher.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the louder sound as higher-pitched

errorPatterns.pattern: Loudness not linked to vibration SIZE: knows harder = louder but treats loudness as 'more sound' with no mechanism
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make amplitude visible — rice on the drum jumps higher for a harder hit; louder means a bigger vibration.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says louder but attributes it vaguely to 'more energy/more sound' with no reference to how big the movement is

errorPatterns.pattern: Volume as a substance: 'loudness is how much sound stuff comes out'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe loudness as the SIZE of the vibration, not an amount of substance leaving the drum.
errorPatterns.distractor: Louder means more sound stuff is coming out of the drum.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about volume as an amount of sound-material being emitted

responseLevels.gap: Describes the louder sound as higher (volume = pitch), or can give no link between loudness and the vibration.
responseLevels.full: Reports the harder hit as LOUDER (not higher), explains it by bigger/stronger vibrations while pitch stays put, and transfers the vibration-size idea (rice jumping higher, whisper vs shout).
responseLevels.partial: Knows harder hits are louder and can demonstrate it, but doesn't connect loudness to the SIZE of the vibration, or still muddles louder with higher.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You hit a drum gently, then hit the SAME drum much harder. How is the second sound different — is it higher, lower, louder, or quieter — and what is different about how the drum skin is moving? Explain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This is the mirror of pitch — children collapse 'louder' into 'higher'. Changing only the hitting force (same drum) should leave pitch put, so a child with the concept reports louder and ties it to bigger vibrations, while the conflater says 'higher'. Whether they attribute loudness to vibration SIZE (amplitude), not speed, is the tell.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 13–14 years

- **Topic:** Motors & the Motor Effect

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics, 'Magnetism'):** 'the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only)'. [The full motor effect — force direction by the left-hand rule and F = BIL — sits at KS4 'Magnetism and electromagnetism'.]

- **Standards — US (NGSS, MS Forces & Interactions — MS-PS2-3):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-3] — the clarification explicitly names electric motors (e.g. the effect of the number/strength of magnets on the speed of an electric motor); DCI PS2.B. [The perpendicular force-direction geometry extends into HS-PS2.]

- **Operational details:** [No standalone operational prose preceded the markers in the source summary.]

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational, age 13-14, the KS3→KS4 boundary). The hardest leap in the domain: a current-carrying conductor placed in an external magnetic field experiences a force that is PERPENDICULAR to BOTH the current and the field (a genuinely 3D relationship), and reversing either the current or the field reverses the force — the basis of the electric motor and the loudspeaker. At KS3 this stays at 'predict the direction the wire is pushed and that reversing current or field reverses it' (D.C. motors, principles only); the left-hand rule and quantitative F = BIL belong to KS4. Honest stance (IOP/Oak): predict and observe the motion; explaining the underlying field-interaction mechanism is beyond this level — don't substitute a hand-wavy wrong model.
bestPractices: Sequence predict → observe → reconcile, but only AFTER pupils have enough theory — research shows real apparatus can otherwise trigger 'gut-feeling' reversion to force-along-the-field thinking.
Let pupils discover the direction-dependence empirically by reversing the current and reversing the magnets BEFORE the left-hand rule is introduced as a summary.
Explicitly SEPARATE the two rules pupils conflate: 'the field produced by a current' versus 'the force on a current in a field'.
Pre-empt the electrostatics import — directly confront 'opposites attract' reasoning applied to current-carrying wires; magnetism is not electrostatics.

Teach the perpendicular 3D relationship deliberately (force ⊥ both current and field; maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the field, zero when along it) using a physical three-axis prop or hand.

Use the classic demo — a stiff copper wire or foil strip between slab (Magnadur) magnets on an iron yoke — then connect the same force on the two sides of a coil to the turning motor and to the loudspeaker cone; be honest that the deeper 'why' is left for later.
keyRepresentations: A wire between magnet poles with three mutually-perpendicular arrows: current, field (N→S) and force
Side-by-side reverse-current and reverse-field cases showing the force flip
A physical three-axis hand/prop modelling force ⊥ (current, field)
A coil in a field → turning effect → motor with a split ring; a loudspeaker cone driven by the force
The left-hand rule shown as a SUMMARY introduced after the empirical direction-dependence (KS4)
commonMisconceptions: Importing 'opposites attract' from electrostatics to current-carrying wires (Singh).
Expecting the wire to be pushed TOWARD a pole (along the field) rather than perpendicular to it (Singh).
Believing the force and the field point in the SAME direction — a gut-feeling error, strongest when shown real apparatus (Singh).
Mixing up the 'field from a current' rule and the 'force on a current' rule (Singh).
Treating the multi-step reasoning (field, then force) as a single guess, and memorising outcomes (e.g. 'opposite currents repel') without being able to reason them (Singh).
Thinking the explanation of HOW the two fields interact is required at this level — it is deliberately out of scope (Oak/IOP).

learn.summary: For ages 13–14 (KS3→KS4 boundary), learners build the motor effect: a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force that is perpendicular to BOTH the current and the field, and reversing either the current or the field reverses the force. The lead activity is a predict → observe → reconcile cycle on a motor-effect bench (physical demo or live simulation) with independent reverse-current and reverse-field controls, so each cause is isolated and the direction pattern (later named the left-hand rule) is discovered rather than handed down. Complementary activities attack the non-intuitive 3D perpendicularity, drill direction prediction, and label motor/loudspeaker parts. At KS3 the goal is to predict and observe the motion and connect it to the motor and loudspeaker; the quantitative F = BIL and a full field-interaction explanation belong to KS4 and later.

activities.title: Motor-effect bench: predict, run, reconcile
feedback: If a learner predicts the wire is pulled toward a pole: run it so they see the sideways kick (impossible for simple attraction), and name the force as perpendicular to both current and field.
If they expect 'nothing changes' when the current reverses: isolate the reverse-current control and let them watch the kick flip — this is the direct test that it is not ordinary magnetic attraction.
If they predict a flip when BOTH inputs are reversed: have them reason that two reversals cancel, then demonstrate the wire jumping the original way.
Confirm the discovered pattern before introducing the left-hand rule, so the rule reads as their finding, not an imposed trick.
activities.rationale: Independent reverse-current and reverse-field controls isolate each cause of the force's direction, and letting pupils discover the direction-dependence empirically before the left-hand rule is introduced as a summary addresses documented misconceptions (attraction-to-a-pole, force-along-the-field). Predicting before switching surfaces gut-feeling reasoning so it can be confronted. Efficacy of this proposed sequence is research-informed but not independently validated here.
sourceClaims: There is a force on a current-carrying wire at right angles to both current and field; maximum when perpendicular, zero when the wire lies along the field; reversing current or field reverses the force; demonstrate with slab magnets on a yoke and a stiff wire/foil, reversing current and magnets before introducing the left-hand rule; honestly admit the field-interaction explanation is beyond the syllabus.

Documented student misconceptions: importing 'opposites attract' from electrostatics to current-carrying wires; expecting deflection toward a pole rather than perpendicular; treating force and field as parallel (gut-feeling, worse with real apparatus); mixing up the field-from-current and force-on-current rules; fragile multi-step reasoning and memorised-without-reasoning outcomes.
KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only).
learnerActions: View a straight wire hanging between a north and a south pole, seen end-on (use real slab/Magnadur magnets on an iron yoke with a stiff copper wire or foil strip, or a live end-on simulation).
BEFORE switching on, predict which way the wire will move and say why.

Run it and observe: from rest the wire kicks SIDEWAYS, perpendicular to both the current and the field — either out of the gap or deeper into it, depending on the current and field directions — not toward either pole.
Use an independent reverse-current control: flip only the current and observe the kick reverse.
Use an independent reverse-field control: flip only the magnets and observe the kick reverse again.
Flip BOTH current and field together and predict first — observe that the kick returns to the original direction.
After several (current, field) → force rounds, state the pattern you found in your own words; then meet the left-hand rule as a summary of that pattern.

'Roll the wire up' into a coil and observe that, because the current flows in opposite directions along the two sides, they feel forces in opposite directions, which together turn the coil (a motor; a split ring reverses the current every half turn so it keeps turning the same way); see how a changing current drives a cone in a loudspeaker.
activities.intendedInsight: The force on a current-carrying wire is perpendicular to both the current and the field; reversing either input reverses the force while reversing both restores it; a wire that is free and initially at rest therefore starts to move in the direction of that force, and the same force turns a motor coil and moves a loudspeaker cone.

activities.title: Orienting the three axes: force ⊥ both current and field
feedback: If a learner draws the force parallel to the current or to the field, point back to the three-axis prop and have them physically set the third perpendicular axis.
Reinforce the max-when-perpendicular / zero-when-parallel cases by having them rotate the wire relative to the field and report when the force shrinks to nothing.
activities.rationale: The central hurdle is the non-intuitive 3D geometry that students struggle to visualise; a reorientable three-axis model lets learners see the perpendicularity directly. This is a scaffold for the perpendicularity insight and is best used after the 2D direction-dependence is secure. A 3D model offers a different view from the 2D bench; neither is claimed to be universally necessary.
sourceClaims: There is a force on a current-carrying wire at right angles to both current and field; maximum when perpendicular, zero when the wire lies along the field; reversing current or field reverses the force; demonstrate with slab magnets on a yoke and a stiff wire/foil, reversing current and magnets before introducing the left-hand rule; honestly admit the field-interaction explanation is beyond the syllabus.

Documented student misconceptions: importing 'opposites attract' from electrostatics to current-carrying wires; expecting deflection toward a pole rather than perpendicular; treating force and field as parallel (gut-feeling, worse with real apparatus); mixing up the field-from-current and force-on-current rules; fragile multi-step reasoning and memorised-without-reasoning outcomes.
learnerActions: Work with three mutually-perpendicular axes representing current, field (N→S), and force — using a physical three-axis hand/prop, or a 3D model you can reorient and view from any angle.
Set the current axis and the field axis in space, then identify the force on the third, perpendicular axis.
Rotate the viewpoint to confirm the force stays perpendicular to both regardless of how you look at it.
Explore the special cases: the force is maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the field, and zero when the wire lies along the field.
activities.intendedInsight: The force is always perpendicular to both the current and the field; when the wire is at right angles to the field (where the force is largest), current, field and force are all mutually perpendicular — a genuinely three-dimensional relationship that a single flattened view can hide.

activities.title: Predict the force direction and separate the two rules
feedback: If a learner gives the force along the field toward a pole and says reversing the current makes no difference, treat it as the attraction misconception: return to the bench's reverse-current test.
If they recite a memorised outcome (e.g. 'opposite currents repel') without being able to reason it, have them rebuild the field-then-force steps rather than quoting the result.
If they confuse the two rules, ask explicitly 'is this the field a current makes, or the force a current feels?' before they answer.
activities.rationale: Prediction, reverse-input, and step-sequencing tasks drill the direction-dependence and force the two commonly-conflated rules apart. Note this is recognition/short-answer practice: it can check and strengthen reasoning but does not by itself elicit the independent construction that the hands-on bench does.
sourceClaims: Documented student misconceptions: importing 'opposites attract' from electrostatics to current-carrying wires; expecting deflection toward a pole rather than perpendicular; treating force and field as parallel (gut-feeling, worse with real apparatus); mixing up the field-from-current and force-on-current rules; fragile multi-step reasoning and memorised-without-reasoning outcomes.
learnerActions: Given a current direction and a field direction, predict which way the force pushes the wire.
Answer reverse-current and reverse-field tasks: state how the force direction changes when only one input flips, and when both flip.
Sequence the reasoning: first identify the field, THEN apply the force rule — do not treat it as a single guess.
Match a motor and a loudspeaker to the motor-effect principle they rely on.
Distinguish 'the field produced by a current' from 'the force on a current in a field' when a question could invite either.
activities.intendedInsight: Direction of the force follows reliably from the current and field via multi-step reasoning, and the 'field from a current' rule is not the same as the 'force on a current' rule.

activities.title: Label the arrows, the motor and the loudspeaker
feedback: Confirm correct arrow labels against the left-hand-rule card.
If a learner cannot say why the coil keeps turning, prompt them toward the split ring's role in maintaining rotation past half a turn.
activities.rationale: A labelling summary consolidates vocabulary and the motor/loudspeaker application. It is a companion to the bench, not a replacement: a static labelled image shows the arrangement but cannot animate the kick or the reversals, so direction-dependence should be discovered first on the bench and only reviewed here.
sourceClaims: KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only).
learnerActions: Label the three arrows on a wire-between-poles diagram: current, field (N→S), and force.
Label the parts of a D.C. motor (coil, magnets, split ring) and a loudspeaker (coil, magnet, cone).
Use a left-hand-rule reference card to check the arrow directions.
Explain in a sentence how the force on the coil's two sides produces rotation, and how a changing current moves the cone in and out.
activities.intendedInsight: The same perpendicular force appears in a diagram, a motor and a loudspeaker; the parts and arrow directions can be named and connected to the principle.

constraints: KS3 scope: predict the push direction and that reversing current or field reverses it, and grasp the motor/loudspeaker principle. The left-hand rule is formally KS4 content; at this boundary it may be previewed only as a summary of the pattern pupils have already found. The quantitative F = BIL belongs to KS4.
Be honest that explaining HOW the two magnetic fields interact to produce the force is deliberately out of scope at this level — do not substitute a hand-wavy or wrong mechanism.

Sequence predict → observe → reconcile only AFTER pupils have enough background that a force is expected; real apparatus shown too early can trigger gut-feeling reversion to force-along-the-field thinking.
Directly confront the imported 'opposites attract' electrostatics reasoning: the force on current-carrying wires is not electrostatic attraction.
The labelling activity is a static summary scaffold: a static image can show the arrangement but cannot animate the reversals, so it should follow the hands-on bench rather than lead.

The 3D-axis activity is a scaffold scoped to the perpendicularity insight; use it after the 2D direction-dependence is secure. A 2D view and a 3D model give different experiences; neither is asserted to be the only way to learn.
The prediction/reverse-input practice is recognition-style and checks reasoning; it does not substitute for independent hands-on construction of the effect.

Describe the wire's motion in terms of the force: a free wire initially at rest begins to accelerate and move in the force direction; do not state that a single force's direction is generally 'the direction of travel' in other contexts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two cited sources were marked unverified in the original row (IOP Spark/Oak on the motor effect, and Singh arXiv:1701.01523 on misconceptions); their claims should be re-checked before being relied upon as evidence.

Self-audit of the physics: reversing only current OR only field reverses the force, while reversing BOTH restores the original direction (two reversals cancel); the force is perpendicular to both current and field, not along either; from rest the free wire accelerates in the force direction. Retained as the core correct model.

The original framing that the conversation/persona artefact is categorically 'poor' and that a flattened 2D view 'cannot' address the 3D misconception was softened to narrow affordances: dialogue is ill-suited to building a manipulated direction relationship, and a static 2D view hides (rather than is universally incapable of teaching) the perpendicularity. No comparative efficacy claim beyond the sources is asserted.

The labelling activity's sourceClaims were reduced to the KS3 D.C.-motors statutory claim; the MS-PS2-3 'number/strength of magnets affects motor speed' claim was removed because it matches the topic but not that activity's teaching principle. MS-PS2-3 remains relevant context for the domain but is not built into an activity here.

Independent re-audit found the physics, initial conditions, causal logic, source-principle matches, and media affordance claims internally consistent; no new critical learner-facing errors were identified.

assess.poeTask: Set up a wire between the poles of a magnet so it can swing freely, and pass a current — it kicks. Ask students to predict which way it kicks and what happens when you reverse ONLY the current, and WHY, before switching. Predicting 'nothing changes, it's just attracted' versus 'it kicks the opposite way' reveals whether they see a current-in-a-field force or plain magnetic attraction.
probeDeeper: If you reversed the current AND swapped the magnet's poles at the same time, which way would the wire jump? Why?
In an electric motor, why does the coil keep turning the same way instead of jamming after half a turn?
A loudspeaker uses this effect — what is the current doing to make the cone move in and out?
Is the wire being 'attracted' to the magnet? What test would show it isn't?
assess.correctAnswer: The force is at right angles to BOTH the current and the field (not along either) — it pushes the wire perpendicular to the field lines and to the current direction. Reversing only the current reverses the direction of the force, so the wire jumps the other way. (Reversing the field alone also reverses it; reversing both leaves it unchanged.)

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The wire is just attracted to the magnet, like iron — the force pulls it toward a pole.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that reversing the current flips the wire's jump — impossible for simple attraction; establish that the force is perpendicular to both current and field.
errorPatterns.distractor: The wire is pulled toward the nearest magnet pole, the way iron is attracted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the force direction ALONG the field toward a pole and says reversing the current makes no difference.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The force points along the current (or along the field lines).'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use Fleming's left-hand rule and a clear three-direction demo; stress the three directions are mutually perpendicular.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws the force parallel to the current or to the field, not perpendicular to both.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Reversing BOTH the current and the magnet's poles reverses the force.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason it through (two reversals cancel) and demonstrate — the wire jumps the same way as at the start.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a flip when both inputs are reversed at once.

responseLevels.gap: Treats it as ordinary attraction — force toward a pole, reversing the current does nothing; or puts the force along the current/field.
responseLevels.full: Explains the force is perpendicular to both current and field, predicts the direction change for reversing current, field, or both, and applies the effect to a motor (with the split-ring maintaining rotation) and to a loudspeaker.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the wire feels a force and that reversing the current flips it, but can't state the perpendicular relationship, or gets the 'both reversed' case wrong — the reverse rules are recited, not reasoned.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A wire carrying a current sits between the poles of a magnet, and the wire suddenly jumps — it feels a force. Which way does the force push the wire, compared with the current and the magnetic field — and what happens to that push if I reverse ONLY the current?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who understands the motor effect says the force is PERPENDICULAR to both current and field and that reversing one input flips it. A student who thinks it's ordinary magnetic attraction says the wire is 'pulled toward' a pole (force along the field) and that reversing the current does nothing (a magnet 'just attracts metal'). The direction relationship and the reverse-one-input test are the discriminators.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5-7 (KS1/Grades K-2): how minibeasts move — crawling, flying, slithering, jumping, burrowing, swimming — and noticing body features that go with movement, especially counting LEGS (ants 6, spiders 8, woodlice many, worms/snails none) as a first, concrete grouping cue.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 Y1 'Animals, including humans' (identify and describe common animals; notice body parts); Y2 habitats. Working-scientifically: observing closely, identifying and classifying, gathering and recording simple data (a movement/leg tally).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 1-LS1-1 (external parts help animals survive/move); K-2 observation practices.
• Operational details — link FORM to FUNCTION at a simple level: wings → fly, many legs → crawl fast, no legs + muscles → slither, strong back legs → jump. Counting legs is the first classification hook (leads into the 7-9 'is it an insect?' work). Use slow-motion clips and real observation, and act movements out physically.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): names how a given minibeast moves (butterfly flies, snail slides). Tier B (age 6): counts legs on ant/spider and matches a body feature to a movement (wings→fly). Tier C (age 7): groups minibeasts by how they move and by leg number, and gives a form-function reason ('grasshoppers have big back legs so they can jump').
bestPractices: Link form to function explicitly — the body part (wings, many legs, strong back legs, no legs) explains the movement; this is the first form-function reasoning children do.
Use slow-motion video and real observation so children can actually see how a worm ripples or a bee beats its wings.
Have children act out the movements (crawl, slither, jump) — kinaesthetic enactment cements the vocabulary.
Introduce leg-counting as a concrete, countable classification cue (6 vs 8 vs many vs none), foreshadowing later insect grouping.
Record simple movement/leg data as a tally or pictogram to fold in early working-scientifically skills.
keyRepresentations: Animated movement clips paired with the movement word (flies, slithers, jumps, burrows, swims).
A leg-count tally chart grouping creatures by number of legs.
Feature-to-movement link cards (wings→fly, strong back legs→jump).
A sorting board with movement bins.
commonMisconceptions: 'All minibeasts crawl / move the same way' — missing the variety of movement.
'Spiders and insects are the same' — leg count (8 vs 6) is the first cue that they differ.
'Worms and snails have tiny legs' — children assume all creatures have legs; some move by muscle/foot.
'Movement isn't connected to body shape' — not yet linking wings/legs to how a creature moves.
Miscounting legs by counting antennae or by not counting both sides.

learn.summary: For ages 5-7 (KS1/Grades K-2): how minibeasts move (crawling, flying, slithering, jumping, burrowing, swimming) and the body features that go with each movement, with leg-counting (ant 6, spider 8, woodlouse many, worm/snail none) as a first concrete grouping cue. The core aim is form-to-function reasoning at a simple level: wings let a creature fly, strong back legs let it jump, no legs plus muscles let it slither. Children observe real movement, act it out, count legs, sort by way of moving, and record simple movement/leg data.

activities.title: Sort minibeasts by how they move, then count their legs
feedback: If a creature is sorted into the wrong movement bin, let it bounce or wobble back with a hint such as 'watch how it moves again'.

If a child gives the spider 6 legs like the ant, count together touching each leg: at this age, 6 legs is the cue for an insect and 8 legs for a spider (not an insect). Let the count, not the guess, settle it.
If a child miscounts the ant by including its feelers, point to the difference between legs (used for walking) and the antennae at the head.
If a child undercounts by looking at only one side, prompt them to count both sides of the body.
Where an animation is available, tapping each leg to add it to a running tally makes the count concrete; a static labelled picture with the legs numbered works too.
activities.rationale: Observing closely, identifying and classifying, and gathering simple data are core KS1 working-scientifically skills, and counting legs is a developmentally appropriate first classification cue toward distinguishing insects (6 legs) from spiders (8 legs). Seeing movement (via video, live observation, or animation) and physically tallying legs is intended to make the grouping concrete for this age.
sourceClaims: KS1 Y1 requires pupils to identify and describe common animals and their body parts; observing closely and classifying are core working-scientifically skills.
Counting legs is a developmentally appropriate first classification cue that leads toward distinguishing insects (6 legs) from arachnids (8 legs).
learnerActions: Watch each minibeast actually move — through slow-motion video, real observation, or an animation that plays when the creature is tapped (a grasshopper springs, a worm ripples and burrows, a bee lifts off).

Sort each creature into a way-of-moving bin by its main or most noticeable way of moving: flies / crawls / slithers / jumps / burrows / swims. Talk about creatures that move in more than one way (a grasshopper jumps but can also crawl and fly; an earthworm slithers on the surface and burrows underground; a bee flies but also crawls).

Count the legs on an ant (6) and a spider (8) by touching or tapping each leg one at a time and counting aloud; count both sides of the body so none are missed, and count only the walking legs — on the ant, do not count the two feelers (antennae) at the head as legs.
Place the ant and spider into different leg-number groups, and place worms/snails in a 'no legs' group.
Record the result as a simple tally or pictogram of how many legs each creature has.
activities.intendedInsight: Minibeasts move in different ways, and leg number (6 vs 8 vs many vs none) is a concrete, countable way to begin grouping them — foreshadowing later 'is it an insect?' work.

activities.title: Match the body feature to the movement
feedback: If a child treats leg number as a meaningless detail, ask them to act it out — walk like a six-legged ant, then wriggle like a legless worm on the carpet — so the count connects to the way of moving.

If a child cannot explain legless movement, watch a real worm (or clear video) on a damp surface and point out the body squeezing and stretching with no legs appearing; let the child 'inch' their own arm along a table to model muscle-driven motion.
Confirm correct links by replaying the movement: 'Yes — wings let the bee fly.'
activities.rationale: NGSS 1-LS1-1 expects Grade 1 pupils to learn that external parts help animals survive, grow and move, so explicitly linking a body part to its movement is the intended objective. Kinaesthetic enactment and responsive pictures are intended to help cement the vocabulary and the form-function link.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 students learn that animals have external parts that help them survive, grow and behave — including parts for movement (1-LS1-1).
learnerActions: Match a body-feature card to the creature and movement it enables: wings → fly (bee, butterfly), strong back legs → jump (grasshopper), many legs → crawl, no legs + muscles → slither.

Where an interactive picture is available, drag the feature onto the creature and watch the picture respond — give the grasshopper its big back legs and it can jump; remove the bee's wings and it can no longer fly.
Say or complete a reason sentence: 'Grasshoppers have big back legs SO they can jump'; 'Worms have no legs so they move by squeezing and stretching.'
activities.intendedInsight: How a minibeast moves comes from the body parts it has — the first form-to-function reasoning children do.

activities.title: Three minibeasts: count and explain (diagnostic)
feedback: Full understanding: gives 6/8/0 correctly AND explains the worm moves by squeezing and stretching with no legs, and transfers the idea to a new case such as the snail.
Partial: counts 6/8/0 correctly but lists them as separate facts — prompt 'how does the worm actually move with no legs?' to build the connection.

Gap: gives the same number for all three or insists the worm has tiny hidden legs — put a real or large-photo ant and spider side by side and count together, and watch a real worm move to show legless motion.
activities.rationale: A two-tier check — count the legs, then explain how the legless one moves — is intended to discriminate a child reasoning from observation (three different numbers, legless movement described) from one working from a vague 'all bugs are the same' picture who gives equal leg counts or claims hidden legs. The snail counterexample shows legless movement is varied, not a single trick.
learnerActions: Look at an ant, a spider, and an earthworm. Say how many legs each one has (6, 8, and 0).
Explain how the one with no legs gets around — the worm squeezes and stretches its body, its muscles pushing it along and tiny bristles gripping the soil.
Extend to a new case: predict whether a snail has legs and how it moves (it has no legs and glides on a muscular foot over slime — a different legless mechanism from the worm).
Consider a probe: 'A centipede — would you expect 6 legs, 8, or lots more? Why?' and 'If something has 6 legs, what might it be?'
activities.intendedInsight: Leg number and way of moving are connected, not memorised as separate facts; some creatures move with no legs at all, and different legless creatures (worm vs snail) can move differently.

constraints: Keep the activity concrete and countable at this age; leg-counting is the entry classification cue that later leads into 'is it an insect?' work — do not expect full insect-vs-arachnid taxonomy yet, and treat '6 legs = insect' as an age-appropriate first cue rather than a strict definition.

A tap-to-reveal or labelled garden scene teaches the movement vocabulary and highlights legs/wings well, but it does not itself run the sort or the count; pair labelling with an actual sorting and counting task so the form-function link lands.

A quiz (sort by movement, match feature↔movement, multiple-choice leg counts) can be used to assess or to practise, but recognition responses do not elicit independent construction — have children count aloud, act out movements, and give a reason sentence as well.
Real observation and slow-motion video of live creatures are valuable: children should see a worm ripple or a bee beat its wings, not only read labels.
When teaching legless movement, distinguish the worm's body squeeze-and-stretch from the snail's gliding on a muscular foot; do not let children generalise one mechanism to all legless creatures.
Guard against the common miscounting errors: counting an ant's antennae as legs, or counting only one side of the body.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all three listed sources were already marked verified:false in the source row. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'static image can't' phrasing was softened: a fixed or labelled image can still teach movement vocabulary; the distinct value of animation/observation is seeing the movement and running the count, stated as an affordance rather than a universal necessity.

The claim that conversation/dialogue is 'far weaker' and the concept is 'not dialogic' was not retained as a universal law; discussion and spoken explanation are in fact used in the diagnostic and reteach moves. No comparative efficacy of media is asserted because the sources do not establish it.
The 3D 'adds nothing / lower cost' framing was dropped as catalog cost-ranking, not a pedagogical fact; a 3D jump-arc or burrowing model could offer a different experience if available.
The reteach reference to a prerequisite micro-topic ID was omitted as an internal catalog identifier; the underlying reteach action (observe a real worm, model inching motion) is preserved.

Activity 3 sourceClaims set to [] because no source claim directly supports the two-tier diagnostic/discrimination principle; the leg-counting claim is retained in activity 1 where it directly supports grouping.
The antennae-miscount guard was scoped to the ant, since spiders have no antennae; the 'count both sides' guard remains general.
Woodlice are crustaceans with about 14 legs, kept as 'many' at this age; the simplification is noted rather than treated as exact.

probeDeeper: Point to the spider: 'Show me and count — is it really 8? What would make it an insect instead?'
'A snail has no legs either. Does it move the same way as the worm, or differently?' (foot gliding on slime vs body squeezing — a same-category, different-mechanism counterexample)
'A centipede — would you expect 6 legs, 8, or lots more? Why?'
'If something has 6 legs, what does that tell you about what kind of minibeast it might be?'
assess.correctAnswer: An ant has 6 legs, a spider has 8 legs, and an earthworm has 0 legs. The worm has no legs at all — it moves by squeezing and stretching its body (its muscles push it along, and tiny bristles grip the soil). Different minibeasts move in different ways: walking on legs, crawling, or wriggling.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks every minibeast has the same number of legs — gives the spider 6 like the ant, or says they all have 'lots of legs' ('they're all bugs, so they're all the same')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put a real (or large photo of an) ant and spider side by side and count together, touching each leg. Name the difference: 6 legs = insect, 8 legs = not an insect (spider). Let the count, not the guess, settle it.
errorPatterns.distractor: They all have 6 legs — they're all bugs
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assigns identical leg counts to ant and spider; cannot distinguish 6 from 8; treats 'minibeast' as one uniform kind

errorPatterns.pattern: Insists the worm (or snail) has tiny hidden legs because 'it moves, so it must have legs' — cannot picture legless movement
errorPatterns.nextMove: Watch a real worm (or a clear video) move on a damp surface. Point out the body squeezing and stretching — no legs appear. Let them feel their own arm 'inch' along a table to model muscle-driven, legless motion.
errorPatterns.distractor: The worm has tiny legs too small to see
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says the worm walks on little legs you can't see, or refuses to accept 0 legs

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts legs but treats the number as a meaningless detail — doesn't connect it to how the creature moves or what it is
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask them to act it out: walk like an ant, then wriggle like a worm on the carpet. Tie the number of legs to the way of moving so the count carries meaning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gets 6/8/0 correct but shrugs at 'how does the worm move?' — no link between body and motion

responseLevels.gap: Gives the same leg count for all three, or claims the worm has hidden legs; treats all minibeasts as one uniform kind of mover.
responseLevels.full: Gives 6/8/0 correctly AND explains that the worm moves by squeezing and stretching its body with no legs; transfers the idea to a new case (e.g. predicts a snail also has no legs and glides differently), showing legs-and-motion are connected, not just memorised.
responseLevels.partial: Counts the legs correctly (6, 8, 0) but lists them as separate facts — cannot explain how the legless worm actually moves, or connect leg number to way of moving.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three minibeasts: an ant, a spider, and an earthworm. How many legs does each one have? And how does the one with no legs get around?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has actually looked at and counted legs gives three DIFFERENT numbers (6, 8, 0) and can say the worm has none. A child working from a vague 'all bugs are the same' picture gives every creature the same number of legs, or insists the worm must have tiny hidden legs — because they reason 'it moves, so it must have legs' rather than from observation. Forcing the second-tier 'how does the legless one move?' exposes whether they can imagine leg-free motion at all.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 7–9 — classify ocean animals into major groups: fish (gills, scales), marine mammals (breathe air, warm-blooded, feed milk), and invertebrates (no backbone — jellyfish, octopus, crab, starfish).
• Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2): Y4 'recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways' and 'explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things' — marine animals are the exemplar set here.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 3-LS4 / grouping-by-observable-features reasoning; groups defined by shared traits, not habitat.
• Operational details: build on the 5–7 whale/dolphin work — now add INVERTEBRATE (no backbone) as a third group and formalise defining features. Teach a two-question classification key: (1) does it have a backbone? → if no, invertebrate; if yes, (2) gills+scales (fish) or breathes air+milk+warm-blooded (mammal). The backbone/no-backbone split is the big new idea and the main error source (children assume all animals have bones). Use varied, deliberately tricky exemplars (jellyfish, octopus, seahorse-which-IS-a-fish, dolphin, shark).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete, ~7–8): sorts clear cases into the three groups; Tier B (transitional, ~8–9): states a defining feature for each group and uses a simple key; Tier C (~9): classifies tricky cases (octopus, jellyfish, dolphin) by reasoning from features and justifies with the backbone test.
bestPractices: Teach classification as APPLYING A KEY (yes/no questions on observable features), not memorising which animal is in which box — keys are the Y4 curriculum skill and make reasoning transferable.
Foreground the backbone test as the first split: invertebrate vs vertebrate — most ocean animals are invertebrates, which surprises children and corrects 'all animals have bones'.
Use side-by-side defining-feature contrasts (gills vs lungs, scales vs smooth, backbone vs none) with real specimens/photos.
Deploy deliberately tricky exemplars (octopus, jellyfish, dolphin, shark, seahorse) so students confront that appearance and habitat don't decide the group — features do.
Have students BUILD/justify a classification, explaining the feature that placed each animal, not just the final bin.
keyRepresentations: A branching classification key (backbone? → gills or lungs?) the child follows
A three-column feature chart: FISH (gills, scales, eggs) / MAMMAL (lungs, warm-blooded, milk) / INVERTEBRATE (no backbone)
A Venn/sorting surface with tricky exemplars to place
Real-photo specimen cards with tappable feature evidence
commonMisconceptions: 'All animals have a backbone / bones' — so children miss that octopus, jellyfish, crab and starfish are invertebrates.
'It lives in the sea, so it's a fish' — habitat, not features, drives the (wrong) grouping (carried over from earlier).
'A whale is a fish because it's big and swims' / 'a dolphin is a fish because it has fins' — classifying by size or body shape.
'A jellyfish/starfish is a fish because the name says fish' — misled by naming.
'A shark is a mammal because it's smart/large' — over-extending the mammal category; sharks are fish (gills, no milk, cold-blooded).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, learners classify ocean animals into fish (gills, scales), marine mammals (breathe air, warm-blooded, feed milk) and invertebrates (no backbone — jellyfish, octopus, crab, starfish) by running a simple yes/no classification key on observable features rather than memorising which animal goes in which box. The central new idea is the backbone test: most ocean animals are invertebrates, which corrects the assumption that all animals have bones. Deliberately tricky exemplars (octopus, jellyfish, dolphin, shark, seahorse) force learners to classify by features, not by habitat, size, name or appearance.

activities.title: Run the two-question key on a mixed tank of sea creatures
feedback: If an octopus is placed with the fish, prompt: 'Check its backbone — does it have one?' to redirect it into invertebrates.
Reward answers that name the deciding feature ('gills', 'no backbone', 'breathes air and feeds milk') rather than just the final group.
When a shark is called a mammal because it is big or smart, show it breathes through gills and has scales and a backbone, so it stays a fish however large.

If the seahorse is set aside because it does not look like a typical fish or because its name has no 'fish', run the key on it: it has a backbone and breathes with gills, so it is a fish despite its unusual shape and name — note its body is covered in bony plates rather than ordinary scales, so feature (backbone and gills), not shape or name, decides.
If a learner routes every animal the same way, have them re-run question 1 (backbone?) separately for each animal so one shared trait (lives in the sea) stops driving the whole sort.
activities.rationale: The learning objective is the ACT of classifying by running a key, so learners should perform the key and get immediate feature-based feedback on each animal, including tricky cases that block the habitat/appearance/name shortcut. An interactive sorter that routes each animal from the features selected (tap yes/no on backbone, then gills vs lungs; the animal slides into its group) makes the mechanism live; a physical specimen tray with feature tags works similarly. This proposes the activity; it does not establish that one medium is uniquely effective.
sourceClaims: UK Lower KS2 Y4 science requires pupils to recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways and to explore and use classification keys to group, identify and name living things.

Fish, marine mammals and invertebrates are distinguished by defining features (gills vs air-breathing lungs; presence vs absence of a backbone); most animal species, including most marine animals, are invertebrates.
learnerActions: Face a tray or set of cards of mixed sea creatures (fish, dolphin, octopus, jellyfish, crab, starfish, shark, seahorse).
For each animal, answer question 1 first: 'Does it have a backbone?' If no, it is an invertebrate.
If yes, answer question 2: 'Breathes with gills (fish, usually covered in scales) or breathes air with lungs, warm-blooded, feeds milk (mammal)?'
Place the animal in fish, mammal or invertebrate, and say aloud which feature put it there.
Work through the whole tray and notice how many animals (jellyfish, crab, starfish, octopus) end up as invertebrates.
Deliberately try the octopus expecting 'fish', then let the backbone question redirect it to invertebrate.
activities.intendedInsight: Classification is the act of applying a key of yes/no questions about observable features; the first split is backbone vs no backbone, and most kinds of ocean animals are boneless invertebrates (in this tray, four of the eight animals are).

activities.title: Build and defend a three-column feature chart
feedback: If a dolphin is called a fish because it has fins, point out fins are not the test: a dolphin breathes air and feeds milk, so it is a mammal.
If a jellyfish or starfish is called a fish because its name contains 'fish', separate the name from the feature: check the backbone instead.
Prompt learners to state a feature for every placement, not just the correct bin.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or paper comparison chart with feature call-outs presents the defining criteria clearly and gives a reference; a scene where tapping an animal reveals its group plus evidence ('invertebrate — no backbone') makes the criteria concrete. This presents and organises the criteria; it does not by itself require the learner to run the key, so it pairs well after the sorter where learners perform the key themselves.
sourceClaims: Fish, marine mammals and invertebrates are distinguished by defining features (gills vs air-breathing lungs; presence vs absence of a backbone); most animal species, including most marine animals, are invertebrates.
learnerActions: Fill a three-column chart: FISH (gills, scales, typically lay eggs) / MAMMAL (lungs, warm-blooded, milk) / INVERTEBRATE (no backbone).
Set defining features side by side as contrasts: gills vs lungs, scales (most fish) vs skin with hair or fur (mammals, though dolphins have very little), backbone vs none.
For each animal, point to the exact feature evidence that places it, using real photos or specimens where possible.
Explain in your own words why a dolphin with fins is a mammal and a shark is a fish.
activities.intendedInsight: Each group is defined by shared traits you can observe and contrast, and naming the defining feature is what justifies a classification.

activities.title: Stump-the-classifier reasoning talk
feedback: When the reason is 'it swims' or 'it has fins', redirect to the breathing (gills vs lungs) or backbone test.
Accept answers that cite a specific feature; press for the feature whenever only a group name is given.
activities.rationale: Spoken Socratic probing can surface the criterion a learner is using and confront reasoning errors in the moment. It serves as a probe and discussion complement; the broader, repeated classification practice is better carried by the sorting activity. Its efficacy here is proposed, not tested.
learnerActions: Take Socratic questions one animal at a time: 'You tell me — does an octopus have a backbone?'
Justify each answer by naming the feature behind it, not the final group alone.

Answer discriminating probes: 'Two animals both live in the sea and both swim — can they still be in different groups? How?' and 'What one feature would you check first to tell a marine mammal from a fish?'
Explain why a shark is a fish and a dolphin is a mammal even though both are large sea swimmers.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who reasons from features can defend each placement and resist habitat, size, name and appearance shortcuts.

activities.title: Check and apply: sort and defend with a new animal
feedback: Correct answers: shark = fish (gills, scales, backbone); dolphin = marine mammal (breathes air with lungs, warm-blooded, feeds milk); jellyfish = invertebrate (no backbone at all).
If all three go into 'fish' justified by living in the sea, re-apply the feature gate: air or gills? backbone or none?

A strong response sorts all three correctly and applies the same criteria to a new animal such as an octopus; a partial response sorts most correctly but applies features unevenly (e.g. places shark and dolphin but cannot place the jellyfish, or names the group without the feature).
activities.rationale: A categorisation task plus feature questions and a tricky-case item is a direct check of every evidence goal: sort into the three groups, give defining features (gills vs lungs, backbone vs none), and classify at least two animals per group. The two-tier 'what feature?' question forces the criterion into the open, so a learner sorting by habitat or looks cannot reliably produce the correct sort. A recognition check confirms the group but does not by itself elicit a constructed, defended reason, so it is paired with the sort-and-explain task.
sourceClaims: Fish, marine mammals and invertebrates are distinguished by defining features (gills vs air-breathing lungs; presence vs absence of a backbone); most animal species, including most marine animals, are invertebrates.
learnerActions: Sort at least two animals per group into fish, marine mammals and invertebrates (e.g. shark and seahorse; dolphin and whale or seal; jellyfish and crab), and for each give the defining feature.
Answer a feature question such as 'Which feature makes it a mammal?' (breathes air / warm-blooded / feeds milk).
Classify a new or tricky case (octopus, shark) and state the reason.
Complete the diagnostic: sort a shark, a dolphin and a jellyfish and explain HOW you decided each — which is a fish, which a marine mammal, which an invertebrate, and what feature places each one.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct classification shows up as the right group AND the stated defining feature, especially for a new animal not practised before.

constraints: Groups are defined by shared traits (features), not by habitat; two animals can both live in and swim in the sea yet belong to different groups.
The backbone (invertebrate vs vertebrate) split is the main new idea and the main error source: children assume all animals have bones, so foreground it as the first question.
Teach keys as a transferable skill (yes/no questions on observable features), not as memorising which animal is in which box.

Keep deliberately tricky exemplars (octopus, jellyfish, dolphin, shark, seahorse-which-is-a-fish) so appearance, size and name cannot decide the group; resolve each introduced exemplar in feedback rather than leaving it unaddressed.
The seahorse is a vertebrate fish with a backbone and gills but is covered in bony plates rather than ordinary scales; resolve it with the backbone/gills test and do not assert typical scales for it.
A recognition or multiple-choice check confirms the group but does not by itself elicit the learner constructing and defending a feature-based reason; pair it with a sort-and-explain task.
A presented chart or tap-to-reveal scene shows the criteria but does not require the learner to run the key themselves; use it as reference alongside active sorting.
This builds on earlier (ages 5–7) whale/dolphin work; invertebrate is the newly added third group.
Egg-laying is a typical fish feature but not universal; do not use it as a decisive distractor, since some fish bear live young and some mammals lay eggs (not among the ocean exemplars here).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched and are marked verified:false in the source row.
Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions; no claim of tested effectiveness is made.

The source row claimed a 2D interactive 'makes that live' and 'cements transfer' and that 3D 'adds nothing'/'poor fit'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established comparative efficacy; this rewrite presents the interactive sorter as one concrete way to perform the key and omits the universal superiority/necessity framing.

The source states seahorses and sharks are fish and jellyfish/octopus/crab/starfish are invertebrates; these are consistent with standard biology. Note that seahorses, while fish, are covered in bony plates rather than ordinary scales, so the corrected feedback relies on backbone and gills.
Egg-laying is listed in the source's fish feature chart; kept as a typical, not absolute, feature and excluded from decisive learner questions.
'Warm-blooded'/'cold-blooded' is used at an age-appropriate level; it simplifies thermoregulation but is acceptable for ages 7–9.

probeDeeper: 'You called the shark a fish. Which exact feature proves it — and why isn't the dolphin in the same group?'
'An octopus — fish, mammal, or invertebrate? What's your reason?' (new invertebrate case)
'Two animals both live in the sea and both swim. Can they still be different groups? How?'
'What one feature would you check first to tell a marine mammal from a fish?'
assess.correctAnswer: Shark = fish (breathes through gills, has scales, has a backbone). Dolphin = marine mammal (breathes air with lungs at the surface, warm-blooded, feeds its babies milk). Jellyfish = invertebrate (has NO backbone at all). You decide by defining features — gills vs lungs, backbone vs no backbone — not by the fact that all three live in the sea.

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies by habitat — 'they all live in the sea, so they're all fish'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make features the gate: does it breathe air or use gills? does it have a backbone? Apply to each animal in turn so the sea-dwelling fact stops driving the sort.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're all fish, because they all live in the sea
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts all three in 'fish'; justifies by living in water

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a jellyfish (or octopus, starfish) is a fish because it lives in water and moves — doesn't recognise 'invertebrate'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce backbone as the test: feel your own spine, then note a jellyfish has none — it's an invertebrate. Sort a few no-backbone animals (crab, octopus, starfish) into that group.
errorPatterns.distractor: A jellyfish is a fish
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the jellyfish a fish; can't accept an animal with no backbone

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies by appearance — 'it has fins, so it's a fish' — so the dolphin gets miscalled a fish
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out fins aren't the test: a dolphin has fins but breathes air and feeds milk → mammal. Use the breathing and milk features, not the silhouette.
errorPatterns.distractor: A dolphin is a fish because it has fins
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: reason is 'it has fins/it swims', not gills/lungs or backbone

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by habitat or looks — calls all three fish, or the dolphin/jellyfish a fish; no feature-based reason.
responseLevels.full: Sorts all three correctly (fish/mammal/invertebrate) using defining features — gills vs lungs, backbone vs none — and applies the criteria to a new animal (e.g. octopus), showing classification by feature rather than by where it lives or what it looks like.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts most correctly and names a feature or two, but applies them unevenly — e.g. gets shark and dolphin right yet can't place the jellyfish, or gives the group without the defining feature.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Sort these three sea animals into groups and tell me HOW you decided each one: a shark, a dolphin, and a jellyfish. Which is a fish, which is a marine mammal, and which is an invertebrate — and what feature puts each where it belongs?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who can classify uses body features (gills/lungs, backbone/none) and gets all three right. A child who classifies by habitat calls them all fish because they live in water; a child who classifies by looks calls the dolphin a fish (it has fins) or the jellyfish a fish (it swims). The second tier ('what feature?') forces the criterion into the open — the correct sort depends on features, so a feature-free sorter can't reliably produce it.
