pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4), PROCEDURAL: using a dichotomous (branching yes/no) classification key to identify minibeasts — 'Does it have legs?' → 'How many?' → 'Does it have wings?' — and grasping WHY a fixed order of questions lets you identify a creature you've never seen.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' — explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name living things in local and wider environments.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 3-LS4 / classification practices (using tools and reasoning to identify and group organisms).
• Operational details — a key is a PROCEDURE: each question must split the remaining set into two, using an observable, unambiguous feature. Teach children both to FOLLOW a key and to BUILD one (choosing good splitting questions). The power idea: a key works on unfamiliar creatures because it asks about features, not names. Start with real specimens/photos and a small key (4-6 creatures).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): follows a given branching key to identify 4 minibeasts. Tier B (age 8): writes a yes/no question that separates two groups (e.g. 'Does it have six legs?'). Tier C (age 9): explains why a set order of questions works even for a creature never seen before, and builds a small key.
bestPractices: Have children both FOLLOW and BUILD keys — building forces them to choose good splitting questions and reveals the underlying logic.
Insist each question uses an observable, unambiguous feature that splits the set into two (avoid vague 'is it pretty?').
Start small (4-6 real specimens or photos) and grow the key gradually.
Make the narrowing visible — candidates eliminated at each step — so children see how questions reduce possibilities.
Draw out the big idea: a key works on unfamiliar creatures because it asks about features, not names.
keyRepresentations: A branching yes/no flowchart (dichotomous key).
A live candidate row that shrinks as questions are answered.
A build-a-key tree with forks the child fills in.
Feature-based splitting-question cards ('Does it have six legs?').
commonMisconceptions: 'A key identifies by name/appearance' — it works by asking about observable features, which is why it handles unknown creatures.
'Questions can be in any order' — the order structures the narrowing; a good key splits systematically.
'Any question will do' — a useful question must cleanly divide the remaining set into two.
'If I don't recognise the creature I can't identify it' — the key's whole point is identifying the unfamiliar.
Choosing subjective questions ('is it scary?') that don't reliably split organisms.

learn.summary: For ages 7-9 (Lower KS2 / Grades 2-4), this procedural topic teaches children to use a dichotomous (branching yes/no) classification key to identify minibeasts, and crucially to understand WHY a fixed order of feature-based questions can identify a creature they have never seen before, as long as that creature is one the key includes. It aligns to UK DfE KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (explore and use classification keys to group, identify and name living things) and loosely supports US NGSS life-science practices of observing and comparing traits. Learners both FOLLOW a given key and BUILD their own, choosing good splitting questions. The core insight: a key works on creatures you do not recognise, provided they are in the key, because it asks about observable features, not names. (The classic question 'Does it have six legs?' is used to separate insects from spiders in a small minibeast set, not as a full definition of 'insect'.)

activities.title: Identify a mystery minibeast by walking a key
feedback: If you name the creature by sight first and only use the key to justify your guess, cover the answers and read/answer each question aloud in order before naming anything — following the path is the rule, not the guess.

If you take the wrong branch after miscounting a feature (e.g. counting a spider as six legs), slow down: count each leg on the specimen or photo before answering. The key only works if you read the feature correctly.
Prompt to check understanding: 'You reached spider. Which answer along the way ruled out insect?'
Prompt for transfer: 'I hand you a creature you have never seen, but it is one of the creatures in our key. Why does going through the questions in order help more than just guessing?'
activities.rationale: KS2 Y4 requires pupils to explore and use classification keys to group, identify and name living things. Making the elimination visible — candidates dropping away at each yes/no — is a proposed way to help children feel why ordered feature-questions narrow the field, which is the conceptual heart of a dichotomous key.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 requires pupils to explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things in their local and wider environment.
Dichotomous keys identify organisms through a fixed sequence of paired either/or questions about observable features, enabling identification of unfamiliar specimens.
learnerActions: Use a small branching key (4-6 creatures) to identify a minibeast you cannot see all at once — you can only answer questions about it.
Trace the ONE mystery creature: 'Does it have legs?' → yes, so the legless candidates (e.g. worms, snails) drop out of a row of possibilities.
Continue the SAME creature: 'Six legs?' → no, eight; the insects fall away, leaving the arachnids. 'Two body parts?' → yes; the last card flips to reveal a spider.

Now, as a separate task, work through the key for at least four different minibeasts (e.g. ant, spider, woodlouse, snail): for EACH one, start at the top question and follow the branch that ITS own answers point to until you reach a name — different creatures take different branches.
For each identification, name which single answer along the way ruled out a wrong group (e.g. which answer ruled out 'insect').
activities.intendedInsight: A key identifies by asking about observable features in a set order; each answer narrows the remaining possibilities, so an ordered sequence of questions can pin down even a creature you have never met, as long as it is one of the creatures the key includes.

activities.title: Build your own key and test it
feedback: If you write a question that isn't a clean yes/no or doesn't separate the groups, test it on two known creatures — if everyone answers the same way, push toward countable/observable features (legs, wings, body parts).
Counterexample prompt: 'Could your question "Does it have wings?" put a wingless ant in the wrong group? How would you fix the key?'
If you can't say why order matters, walk one creature top-to-bottom and notice how each answer narrows the possibilities; starting in the middle skips the narrowing.

In a build-and-test tool, a question that fails to split the group cleanly can be flagged immediately so you can see what makes a good splitting question; this live flag is one helpful option, not the only way to learn it.
activities.rationale: Having children build as well as follow keys makes them choose good splitting questions, which surfaces the logic that a useful question must cleanly divide the remaining set using an observable feature. Testing the key on creatures from the set that the user does not already recognise shows how the tool handles the unfamiliar. Trying a creature from outside the set shows that a key can only name creatures it includes, and that a key can be extended with new branches.
sourceClaims: Dichotomous keys identify organisms through a fixed sequence of paired either/or questions about observable features, enabling identification of unfamiliar specimens.
learnerActions: Take a set of six minibeasts and build your own branching key, choosing the yes/no question at each fork.

Write questions that use an observable, unambiguous feature that cleanly splits the remaining group into two. For example, 'Does it have six legs?' separates insects from spiders in this set (yes: the six-legged insects / no: the eight-legged spiders, plus any other legged creatures without six legs, such as a woodlouse with 14 legs).
Test each question on two known creatures: do they give different answers? If a woodlouse and an ant give the same answer, that question won't split them — revise it.
Avoid subjective or vague questions ('Is it scary?', 'Is it pretty?', 'Is it big?') because different people answer them differently for the same creature.

Swap keys with a partner and use their key to identify creatures from their set without being told the names, fixing any fork where a creature gets stuck or mis-sorted. Then run a creature that is NOT in the set through a key: notice that it gets stuck or lands on a wrong name, because a key can only name creatures it includes. Extend the key by adding a new question and end point for it.
activities.intendedInsight: Building a key forces you to choose good splitting questions: each must have a clear yes/no answer and genuinely divide the remaining set, revealing the underlying logic of why a key is reliable.

activities.title: Reasoning practice: order and choice of questions
feedback: If you pick a question that both creatures would answer the same way, note that it does not separate them — look for a feature where they differ.
If you think any question can come first, show how starting in the middle skips earlier narrowing; the order structures how the possibilities shrink.

These recognition and ordering tasks check reasoning about key logic, but they do not by themselves require you to construct and traverse a working key — pair them with the follow and build activities.
activities.rationale: Selecting and ordering splitting questions targets the misconceptions that 'any question will do' and 'order doesn't matter'. Recognition and ordering tasks assess reasoning but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a working key.
learnerActions: Given two minibeasts, choose which of several questions best splits them apart, and explain why the others fail.
Put a set of jumbled key steps into a sensible order so the questions narrow systematically.
Explain in your own words why a fixed order of questions helps you identify a creature you have never seen (as long as it is in the key), rather than just guessing.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the best splitting question and ordering questions deliberately both depend on the same idea: good questions use clear, observable features and each one narrows the set.

constraints: Each question in a key must use an observable, unambiguous feature that splits the remaining set into two; avoid subjective questions ('is it pretty/scary?').
Start small (4-6 real specimens or photos) and grow the key gradually so the narrowing stays visible.
Draw out the big idea explicitly: a key works on creatures you do not recognise, as long as the key includes them, because it asks about features, not names.
Following a pre-made or tappable key is more passive; the deeper learning comes from traversing and especially building the branches. Use a tappable/reveal diagram as a scaffold, not the end goal.

Recognition-only tasks (multiple-choice, matching, ordering jumbled steps) assess reasoning about key logic but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a working key; include a build-and-test activity.

A 20-questions style dialogue can model the narrowing logic and is a legitimate alternative, but it makes the elimination less visible than a representation that shows candidates dropping away; treat it as a complement.
Reading features correctly (e.g. counting legs, spotting body parts) is a prerequisite — if a child miscounts, reteach insect/non-insect features before concluding the key is at fault.
Treat 'Does it have six legs?' as a feature that separates insects from spiders in the given set, not as a complete definition of an insect.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources are marked verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D interactive as 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing' and asserted a quiz 'can't let the child walk a live branch'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened to scoped statements about affordances (recognition tasks don't require construction; dialogue makes elimination less visible) rather than universal claims.

The 'each question halves the possibilities' phrasing in the legacy design notes is an idealisation — a key question splits the remaining set into two groups but not necessarily into equal halves. Activities say 'narrows/splits into two' rather than 'halves'.
The live-recolour/grey-out and drag-into-tree interactions are retained as optional concrete examples of how elimination and building can be made visible, not as mandatory mechanisms.
The original NGSS 3-LS4 alignment is retained in the summary alongside the KS2 Y4 reference.

The worked mystery walk uses 'worms' as a legless example while the four-creature diagnostic set is ant/spider/woodlouse/snail; legless examples illustrate the wider candidate pool and need not all appear in the specific diagnostic set.
'Does it have six legs?' is kept as a question that separates insects from spiders in this small set rather than as a universal definition of 'insect'.

probeDeeper: 'You reached "spider". Which answer along the way ruled out "insect"?'
'Test your new question on the woodlouse AND the ant — do they give different answers? If not, it won't split them.'
'I hand you a creature you've never seen. Why does going through the questions in order help more than just guessing?'
'Could your question "does it have wings?" put a wingless ant in the wrong group? How would you fix the key?' (counterexample forcing a robust feature)
assess.correctAnswer: The child starts at the first question of the key and answers each yes/no in order, following the branch its answer points to, until they reach a name — correctly identifying at least four minibeasts. When asked to extend the key, they write a question with a clear yes/no answer that genuinely separates the groups (e.g. 'Does it have six legs?' → yes: insect / no: not) and place it at a sensible branch point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Guesses the creature by sight first, then uses the key only to justify the guess — doesn't actually follow the branching
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cover the answers and require them to read and answer each question aloud in order before naming anything. Make following-the-path the rule, not the guess.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the minibeast before reaching that point in the key; skips questions; jumps branches

errorPatterns.pattern: Answers a key question wrongly because they miscount or mis-observe the feature (e.g. counts a spider as 6 legs)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slow down the observation step: count and touch each leg before answering. The key only works if the feature is read correctly — reteach the insect/non-insect features if needed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Takes the wrong branch after miscounting legs/body parts; ends at the wrong name

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes a splitting question that isn't a clean yes/no, or that doesn't actually separate the groups ('Is it scary?', 'Is it big?')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test their question on two known creatures: does everyone answer the same way? Push toward countable/observable features (legs, wings, body parts) with a definite yes/no.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Extension question is subjective or ambiguous; two children could answer it differently for the same creature

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't see why order matters — jumps around the key or thinks any question can come first
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that each answer NARROWS the possibilities; starting in the middle skips the narrowing. Walk one creature top-to-bottom to feel the funnel.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Starts in the middle of the key, or can't say why a set order helps with an unknown creature

responseLevels.gap: Guesses creatures by sight and can't follow the branching, or can't produce a yes/no splitting question at all.
responseLevels.full: Works the key systematically top-to-bottom to identify four+ minibeasts, authors a clean feature-based yes/no question that genuinely splits the groups and places it sensibly, AND explains that ordered questions narrow down an unknown creature — transferring the tool, not just running it.
responseLevels.partial: Follows the key to identify the given creatures but mechanically — can't explain why order matters, or writes a splitting question that is vague or doesn't cleanly separate the groups.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a simple branching key and four minibeasts to identify (e.g. ant, spider, woodlouse, snail). Work through the key out loud for each creature and tell me what each one is. Then I'll give you a creature that ISN'T on the key — make up a yes/no question that would split the insects from the spiders, and show me where it would go.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child WORK the key reveals whether they use it systematically — starting at the top, taking one question at a time, following the branch — or whether they jump straight to a guess and only use the key to confirm. Asking them to author a splitting question shows whether they understand a key is built from features with clean yes/no answers, not vague ones. Do not ask them to describe how a key works; set the task and watch the procedure.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — round decimals to any place using place-value understanding; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy'; Y5 round decimals with two places to the nearest whole number and to one decimal place.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.4 'Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place' and 4.NBT.A.3 round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
• Operational details: Round via NEARNESS on a number line — locate the number between the two candidate rounding points, find the midpoint, and decide which it is nearer. Derive the 'look at the next digit' rule FROM the midpoint (5-and-above is at/past halfway) rather than teaching it as an unexplained rule. Cover rounding both decimals (to dp) and large whole numbers (to nearest 10^k), and rounding for estimation (4.83×2.17 ≈ 5×2).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Round 3.46 to 1 dp.' Tier B: 'Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 and justify with the midpoint.' Tier C: 'Round 3.4567 to 2 dp and explain which digit decides it.'
bestPractices: Round as a nearness decision on a number line: mark the two candidate values, mark the midpoint, place the number, decide which it is closer to
Derive the next-digit rule from the midpoint (≥5 means at or past halfway → round up), rather than asserting it
Practise rounding decimals to a stated dp AND whole numbers to a stated place with the same nearness logic
Address the boundary/round-up cascade explicitly (rounding 3.798 to 2 dp → 3.80, and 9.96 → 10.0)
Connect rounding to estimation — round each factor to check a calculation — so rounding has a purpose beyond the drill
keyRepresentations: Number line with the two rounding candidates and a marked midpoint
Place-value chart to isolate the rounding place and the deciding next digit
'Rounding hill/valley' visual (nearer candidate is downhill) for the midpoint decision
Estimation strips pairing rounded factors with the exact calculation
commonMisconceptions: Rounding digit-by-digit / double rounding (3.4567 → 3.457 → 3.46 → 3.5) instead of one decision at the target place
'Always round 5 down' or inconsistent treatment of the exact-midpoint case
Truncating (chopping) rather than rounding (3.48 → 3.4 to 1 dp)
Forgetting the round-up cascade across a 9 (3.798 to 2 dp → 3.80, not 3.79 or 3.710)
Dropping the trailing zero that records the rounded place (writing 3.8 for 3.80 to 2 dp when the place must be shown)

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: round decimals to any place and whole numbers to a required degree of accuracy by treating rounding as a nearness decision on a number line. Learners locate the number between its two candidate rounding points, find the midpoint, and decide which it is nearer — deriving the 'look at the next digit' rule from the midpoint rather than memorising it. Work covers decimals to a stated number of places, large whole numbers to a stated place, carry/round-up cascades over a 9, placeholder zeros, the risk of double rounding, and rounding for estimation.

activities.title: Rounding as a nearness decision on a number line
feedback: If the learner chops instead of rounding (e.g. 3.4567 to 2 dp written as 3.45), have them look at the digit just past the cut: 6 ≥ 5 means 3.4567 is past the midpoint 3.455 and so is nearer 3.46. Place it between 3.45 and 3.46 to see which is closer. (To 1 dp, chopping would give 3.4, but the correct answer is 3.5.)

If they round digit-by-digit (double rounding), use 3.4547 to 2 dp to show why it fails: rounding to 3 dp first gives 3.455, which then rounds up to 3.46, but a single decision at the hundredths place (decider thousandths 4 < 5) gives 3.45. Double rounding changed the answer — compare the full number to the single midpoint for the target place.
When a carry crosses a 9 (3.798 → 3.80), confirm the trailing zero stays because '2 decimal places' means two digits after the point.
If they are unsure about the exact-midpoint case, reinforce that at the midpoint and beyond the number rounds up to the higher candidate.
activities.rationale: Deriving the next-digit rule from the midpoint gives the procedure a reason, directly targeting double-rounding and 'always round 5 down' errors; the 3.4547 contrast makes the double-rounding hazard observable because the two routes disagree. An interactive number line that auto-brackets candidates, marks the midpoint, lets the learner place the number, lights the nearer segment, and highlights the deciding digit can make the nearness judgement concrete; these interaction examples are optional ways to realise the mechanism, not requirements.
learnerActions: Pick a target precision (e.g. 1 decimal place) and draw a number line showing the two candidate values the number sits between — for 3.4567 to 1 dp, that is 3.4 and 3.5.
Mark the midpoint of the segment (3.45) clearly.
Place the number on the line (3.4567 lands just past the midpoint) and state which candidate it is nearer to.
State the rounded result (3.5) and point to the digit that decided it (the hundredths digit, 5, sits at/past halfway).
Repeat in whole-number mode: bracket 7,654,321 between 7,600,000 and 7,700,000, mark the midpoint 7,650,000, place the number, and round to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000).
Try a round-up cascade: place 3.798 to round to 2 dp between 3.79 and 3.80, see it is nearer 3.80, and write the trailing zero.

Compare two routes for rounding 3.4547 to 2 dp: round straight to 2 dp (decider is the thousandths 4, so 3.45) and also round to 3 dp first (3.455) then to 2 dp (3.46). Notice the answers differ — so make one decision at the target place, not a chain of roundings.
activities.intendedInsight: The midpoint IS the '5-and-above' rule: a number at or past halfway rounds up to the higher candidate. Rounding is one decision made at the target place by comparing nearness, not a digit-by-digit chop — and chopping or double rounding can give a different, wrong answer.

activities.title: Isolating the deciding digit with a place-value chart
feedback: If the learner gives 3.5 when 2 dp is asked, have them count decimal digits: 2 dp needs two, so the answer is 3.46.
If the wrong place is read for a large number, re-anchor on the chart: find the hundred-thousands column, then look one column to its right (the ten-thousands digit decides).
Keep the focus on the single decider digit, not on re-rounding digits further along.
activities.rationale: A place-value chart separates the target place from its decider, addressing wrong-precision errors and misreading places in large numbers. A static chart illustrates a case clearly; it is a scaffold that does not by itself let learners test arbitrary numbers or feel the boundary cascade.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.4: use place value understanding to round decimals to any place; 4.NBT.A.3 round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
learnerActions: Write the number in a place-value chart spanning the decimal point.
Circle the place you must round to and underline the single digit immediately beyond it — the decider.
Round 3.4567 to 2 dp (3.46) and say which digit decided it (the 6 in the thousandths).
Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000) and name the deciding digit (the ten-thousands digit, 5).
Count the digits after the point aloud to confirm you gave the asked-for precision (e.g. 2 dp means exactly two decimal digits).
activities.intendedInsight: Only the digit one place beyond the required accuracy decides the rounding; naming the target place prevents rounding to the wrong precision.

activities.title: Keeping placeholder zeros after a carry
feedback: If the learner writes 2.4 for 2.397 to 2 dp, point out it now shows only one decimal place; the correct answer is 2.40.
Distinguish this from a rounding mistake — the rounding was right, only the recorded precision is missing the zero.
For 9.96 → 10.0, confirm the whole-number carry still leaves a tenths place that must read 0.
activities.rationale: Carries that produce placeholder zeros are a distinct performance slip from the rounding decision itself, so they need their own targeted practice.
learnerActions: Round 2.397 to 2 dp. The hundredths carry gives 2.40 — write the final 0.
Explain why 2.4 would be wrong for '2 decimal places' even though the value looks the same.
Round 9.96 to 1 dp (10.0) and keep the tenths zero.
Check each answer by counting that it shows exactly the required number of decimal places.
activities.intendedInsight: A rounded answer must display the required place even when a carry produces a zero there; the trailing zero records the precision, so dropping it changes what the answer claims.

activities.title: Rounding to estimate a calculation
feedback: If the estimate is far from the exact answer, check whether each factor was rounded to a sensible place.
Encourage stating the chosen rounding place so the estimate's accuracy can be judged.
activities.rationale: Connecting rounding to estimation gives the skill a real use and reinforces the nearness idea across operations.
learnerActions: Round each factor of 4.83 × 2.17 to a convenient value (5 × 2) and compute the estimate (10).
Compare your estimate to the exact product once calculated (≈ 10.48) and say whether the estimate is reasonable.
Try estimating another product or sum by rounding each number first, and state which place you rounded to and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding has a purpose beyond drill: it gives quick, sensible estimates to check whether an exact calculation is plausible.

constraints: Multiple-choice, slider, and fill-in response formats can consolidate and check rounding outcomes (e.g. a truncation distractor of 3.4 for 3.48), but recognising a correct rounded value does not by itself show the learner is reasoning from the midpoint; pair outcome checks with working that reveals the method.
A static annotated number line illustrates a single rounding case but does not let the learner test arbitrary numbers or experience a boundary cascade; use it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.

Dialogue prompts (e.g. 'you rounded 3.4567 to 3.46 — walk me through why, not digit by digit') can surface double-rounding and truncation errors; the nearness decision can also be made where the number is placed and compared spatially.
Round in one decision at the target place; do not round digit-by-digit (double rounding) and do not truncate.
Treat the exact midpoint and above as rounding up to the higher candidate; avoid 'always round 5 down'.
Preserve trailing/placeholder zeros that record the required place (2.40, not 2.4; 10.0, not 10).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the Common Core claim as verified:false and the DfE claim as verified:true; confidence of the original row was 'high'. No new verification has been performed here.

Self-audit: 3.4567 to 2 dp = 3.46 (decider 6 ≥ 5); to 1 dp = 3.5 (candidates 3.4/3.5, midpoint 3.45). 3.4547 to 2 dp = 3.45 directly, but 3.455 then 3.46 by double rounding (illustrates the hazard). 2.397 to 2 dp = 2.40 (carry keeps placeholder zero). 7,654,321 to nearest 100,000: midpoint 7,650,000, value above it, rounds to 7,700,000 (decider ten-thousands digit 5). 3.798 to 2 dp = 3.80. 9.96 to 1 dp = 10.0. 4.83×2.17 ≈ 5×2 = 10 (exact ≈ 10.48). All consistent and checked.

The original row and recommendation wrote the 1-dp candidates as '3.40 and 3.50', displaying two decimal places for a one-decimal-place rounding; corrected in the learner action to '3.4 and 3.5' (midpoint 3.45) to avoid reinforcing a precision confusion.

Activity 1's sourceClaims were set to [] because its rationale is a number-line/midpoint-derivation teaching principle that neither curriculum claim directly supports (the claims establish the topic/standard, not that pedagogy). The place-value-chart activity retains the CCSS 'use place value understanding' claim, which does support its principle.
The original diagnostic listed '2.40 (keeping the final zero)' for rounding 2.397 to 2 dp, which is correct; retained as the placeholder-zero teaching point.
The non-preferred 3D option was dropped because the source itself only noted it adds nothing for a one-dimensional number-line task; no universal claim about 3D is asserted.

probeDeeper: Round 2.397 to 2 dp — why must you keep the 0 on the end?
Round 3.4547 to 3 dp first, then to 2 dp. Now round 3.4547 straight to 2 dp — same answer? (double-rounding)
Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 — which digit decides?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.46; 2.40 (keeping the final zero); 7,700,000 — deciding by the digit one place beyond the required accuracy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Truncates instead of rounding: chops 3.4567 to 3.45 rather than 3.46
errorPatterns.nextMove: Look at the digit just past the cut (6 ≥ 5 → round up). Place 3.4567 between 3.45 and 3.46 on a number line to see which is nearer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The kept digits are correct but never rounded up when the next digit is 5 or more.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero after a carry: writes 2.4 for 2.397 to 2 dp, so it no longer shows 2 decimal places
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach rounding — note that '2 dp' means two digits after the point, so the carried result is 2.40; the 0 must stay.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer to 2 dp has only one decimal digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds to the wrong precision — gives 1 dp when 2 dp is asked, or reads the wrong place for large numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the required place, then its decider digit; count decimal places explicitly. Reground with a place-value chart spanning the decimal point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 3.4567 comes back as 3.5, or the whole number is rounded to the wrong place.

responseLevels.gap: Truncates instead of rounding, or rounds to the wrong precision.
responseLevels.full: Rounds decimals to any number of places and whole numbers to any place, handling carries and placeholder zeros, and avoids double-rounding.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds simple cases but drops carried placeholder zeros or slips on the required number of places.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 3.4567 to 2 decimal places. Round 2.397 to 2 decimal places. Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000.' Watch whether they round or chop, and what they do at the carry.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 3.4567 distinguishes rounding from truncating (3.46 vs 3.45); 2.397 forces a carry that produces a placeholder zero the child must keep to show 2 dp (2.40, not 2.4); the whole-number item checks the same rule transfers to large places. Watching reveals which mechanism is running.

sources.claim: Y6 pupils round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy; Y5 round decimals to the nearest whole and to one decimal place.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9-11 (Upper KS2/Grades 4-6): threats to insects and conservation — populations are declining worldwide; causes include habitat loss, pesticides, light pollution (disrupting nocturnal insects) and climate change. Pollinator decline threatens our food. What children can DO: plant pollinator-friendly gardens, cut pesticide use, join citizen science (e.g. the Big Butterfly Count).
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 (environments can change and pose dangers to living things) and Y6 (human impact / interdependence); working-scientifically (evidence, citizen science data).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-4 (solutions to a problem caused by environmental change) and 5-ESS3-1 / MS-LS2-5 (human impact and protecting biodiversity/ecosystem services).
• Operational details — builds directly on the ecosystem-roles node: because insects do so much, their decline matters. Two halves: (a) understand the DRIVERS with evidence (link each threat to a mechanism — pesticides kill non-targets, light traps night-fliers, habitat loss removes food/shelter), and (b) AGENCY — concrete, realistic actions children can take, framed as efficacy not doom. Citizen science connects them to real data-gathering. Keep it evidence-based and avoid catastrophising.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): names three threats to insects. Tier B (age 10): explains why declining pollinators are a problem for our food. Tier C (age 11): links a specific threat to its mechanism and proposes two realistic conservation actions (and how citizen science helps).
bestPractices: Link each threat to a concrete mechanism (pesticides kill non-target insects; light lures night-fliers; habitat loss removes food/shelter).
Balance problem with AGENCY — give realistic, concrete actions and frame them as effective, not futile.
Keep it evidence-based and avoid catastrophising, which can disengage children.
Connect to real citizen science (e.g. butterfly counts) so children see how data reveals trends and how they can contribute.
Build on insects' ecosystem roles — decline matters BECAUSE of what insects do.
keyRepresentations: A neighbourhood with a live insect-population meter and threat toggles.
Threat-to-mechanism cards (light→trapped moths; spray→dead bees).
An action/design mode (wildflower strip, log pile, shielded lights).
A citizen-science counting task showing a trend over time.
commonMisconceptions: 'Fewer insects would be a good thing' — ignores their essential roles and the knock-on harm.
'Insect decline has no clear cause' — the drivers are known and specific.
'Nothing an individual does can help' — local action measurably supports insect populations.
'All pesticides only kill the target pest' — many harm beneficial insects too.
'Climate change doesn't affect tiny insects' — it shifts ranges, timing and survival.

learn.summary: For ages 9-11 (Upper KS2 / Grades 4-6): why insect populations are declining and what children can realistically do about it. The teaching has two linked halves: (a) understanding the DRIVERS and tying each to a concrete mechanism (pesticides kill non-target insects like bees; streetlights lure and trap night-fliers such as moths; habitat loss removes food and shelter; climate change shifts ranges, timing and survival), and (b) AGENCY — proposing realistic, cause-matched conservation actions framed as effective rather than futile. The discriminating idea, carried forward from insects' ecosystem roles, is WHY the decline harms people: pollinator loss means less fruit and vegetables, and fewer insects means less food for birds and other wildlife and less nutrient recycling. Keep it evidence-based and avoid catastrophising.

activities.title: Toggle the threats, then redesign for recovery
feedback: If a learner treats decline as causeless, revisit each toggle and ask them to name the mechanism aloud (e.g. 'light disrupts night insects like moths').

If an action is chosen without matching it to a threat, ask: 'Which threat does a wildflower strip fix, and which does it leave untouched?' (wildflowers add food/shelter but do not fix light pollution).
If a learner expects one action to solve everything, note that different threats need different fixes and that scale matters — see the collective-action discussion in the conversation activity.
activities.rationale: Turning both harm and remedy into levers the learner controls is intended to make the drivers and the efficacy of action reasoned rather than merely asserted; matching each action to a specific cause builds the integrated cause→consequence reasoning the topic targets. An optional live population indicator that rises and falls as toggles and actions change makes the mechanism concrete, but the core requirement is that the learner state mechanisms and match actions to causes — the indicator is a scaffold, not the lesson.
sourceClaims: Insect declines are driven by habitat loss, pesticide use, light pollution and climate change; pollinator loss threatens food production; citizen-science schemes like the Big Butterfly Count gather trend data.
Students generate and compare solutions to a problem caused by environmental change affecting organisms (3-LS4-4) and consider human impacts on biodiversity/ecosystems (5-ESS3-1, MS-LS2-5).
learnerActions: Starting from a healthy neighbourhood scene with an 'insect health' indicator, turn on one threat at a time and observe the stated mechanism: a bright streetlight lures moths to circle uselessly all night; a pesticide spray drifts and kills bees along with the target pests; paving over a meadow erases food and shelter.
After each threat, state in your own words WHY it lowers insect numbers (the mechanism), not just that numbers fall.
Switch to an action/design mode and intervene: sow a wildflower strip, build a log pile, shield or dim the lights, swap spraying for natural predators like ladybirds.
For each action you choose, say which specific threat it addresses — and name a threat it does NOT fix.
Explain why the population responds to your choices, so efficacy is reasoned, not just observed.
activities.intendedInsight: Insect decline is not mysterious: it has specific, identifiable causes with clear mechanisms, and concrete local actions can help when matched to the right cause.

activities.title: Count butterflies over several visits
feedback: If a learner judges the population from one count, ask what a single low count could be caused by (weather, time of day) and why repeating helps.
If a learner sees their own count as meaningless, explain that many people's counts combine into a dataset large enough to show national trends.
activities.rationale: Working scientifically with repeated observation and trend-reading is part of the standards, and connecting to a real scheme shows how evidence of decline is actually gathered and how individual contributions scale.
sourceClaims: Insect declines are driven by habitat loss, pesticide use, light pollution and climate change; pollinator loss threatens food production; citizen-science schemes like the Big Butterfly Count gather trend data.
learnerActions: Carry out a simple repeated 'count' of butterflies (or another insect) over several visits, keeping conditions as similar as possible (same place, same length of count, similar time of day, warm dry weather), and record each count.

Compare the counts and describe what they show (rising, falling, steady), remembering that a few visits in one year show short-term change caused by things like weather and season, not a long-term population trend.

Explain why repeating the count matters: a single count can mislead, repeated counts under similar conditions give a more reliable picture, and long-term trends come from comparing the same time of year across many years and many sites.
Connect this to real citizen-science schemes such as the Big Butterfly Count and describe how data from many people reveals large-scale changes scientists can act on.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated, standardised observations pooled from many people over many years turn single snapshots into evidence of trends, and ordinary people (including children) can contribute real data that scientists use.

activities.title: Ask a conservation scientist about your own situation
feedback: If a learner says nothing can be done, prompt them to recall how, in the simulation, actions matched to a threat raised the insect indicator, explain that real habitat improvements can help local insects, and ask them to name one action fitting their own space.
If a learner proposes an action that doesn't fit their situation, help them adapt it (balcony pots of pollinator-friendly plants rather than a meadow).
activities.rationale: A responsive dialogue can address a learner's specific circumstances and reasoning in a way a fixed scenario cannot, and is intended to counter the 'nothing I do helps' fatalism. This is a complementary mode, not a replacement for the hands-on mechanism and action work; its efficacy relative to other formats is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Pose an open, specific question to an in-role conservation scientist or entomologist, e.g. 'We only have a small balcony — what could I realistically do?'
Explain your reasoning about causes and actions so the expert can probe and extend it.
Respond when the expert gently challenges fatalism ('Is it hopeless?') by giving reasons that local action can contribute.
activities.intendedInsight: Conservation involves values and open, situation-specific decisions; realistic action exists even in constrained circumstances, and realistic local action can contribute, so defeatism is not the only reasonable response.

activities.title: Match threats to mechanisms and sort helpful from harmful actions
feedback: For a mismatched threat-mechanism pair, restate the mechanism and ask the learner to re-pair it.
If 'keep insects as pets indoors' is marked helpful, explain that this does not address habitat, pesticides or light and does not support wild populations.
If the food link is weak, bridge via pollination: fewer pollinators → less fruit and vegetables.
activities.rationale: Checks for knowledge and action-choices complement the construction tasks. Matching and sorting can verify classification of threats and actions but do not by themselves require the learner to independently construct and justify the cause→consequence→action chain, so pair them with the explanation and design activities. The decline-drivers claim is cited only to support the pollinator→food content being checked, not a comparative claim about task formats.
sourceClaims: Insect declines are driven by habitat loss, pesticide use, light pollution and climate change; pollinator loss threatens food production; citizen-science schemes like the Big Butterfly Count gather trend data.
learnerActions: Match each threat to its effect (e.g. light → trapped/disoriented moths; spray → dead bees; paving → lost food and shelter).
Sort proposed responses into genuinely helpful versus unhelpful or misdirected (e.g. planting wildflowers and reducing spray vs keeping wild insects as pets indoors).
Answer why declining pollinators matter for the food we eat, choosing and justifying the reason rather than only recognising it.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that threats map to specific mechanisms, that helpful actions target habitat/pesticides/light at scale, and that pollinator loss has a direct food consequence.

activities.title: Explore a before/after habitat and explain the links
feedback: If a learner only labels features, ask them to explain the consequence of each (why does losing the meadow reduce insects?).
Prompt them to state what would most improve the degraded scene and why.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal habitat scene informs and supports prediction and explanation. Because it does not simulate the population's response to the learner's own intervention, it works best as a scaffold toward the interactive toggle/redesign activity rather than a substitute for it; this is a narrow affordance of that specific format, not a claim that static images cannot teach.
sourceClaims: KS2 pupils learn that environments can change and this can pose dangers to living things (Y4) and study human impact and interdependence (Y6).
learnerActions: Examine a split scene of a healthy versus degraded habitat and reveal the threats and actions present in each.
For each revealed threat, state its mechanism and predict its effect on insects.
For each revealed action, say which threat it counters.
Explain why the degraded side supports fewer insects, connecting to food webs and pollination.
activities.intendedInsight: A habitat's condition is the sum of specific threats and actions, each with a traceable effect on insect populations.

constraints: Keep the framing evidence-based and avoid catastrophising; doom-laden framing can disengage children. Balance the problem with realistic, achievable actions presented as effective.

Each threat must be tied to a concrete mechanism, not left as a bare list (pesticides kill non-target insects; light lures/disrupts night-fliers; habitat loss removes food and shelter; climate change shifts ranges/timing/survival).
Build on insects' ecosystem roles: the decline matters BECAUSE of what insects do (pollination → food; prey → birds and wildlife; nutrient recycling).

Frame individual actions honestly: a single garden is part of a larger collective effort, not a total fix for a global problem. Avoid implying one action solves everything, and avoid the goal of preventing ALL insect deaths.

Recognition, matching and sorting tasks verify knowledge and choices; they do not by themselves require the learner to independently construct the cause→consequence→action explanation. Pair them with activities that demand that construction.

Before/after reveal scenes and conversation modes are complements to hands-on cause-and-action work, each with different affordances; none is presented as the only way to teach the topic, and no format is asserted as more effective than another.
Address the misconception that fewer insects is good by weighing the few nuisance species against the many essential ones and their services.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The three listed sources are marked verified:false in the row (DfE KS2 programmes of study; NGSS 3-LS4-4 / 5-ESS3-1 / MS-LS2-5; Butterfly Conservation / IPBES / insect-decline reviews). Standards citations and the general decline-drivers claim should be confirmed against primary documents before relying on them.

The legacy row rated 3D interactive 'poor' because it 'adds no conceptual value'; this universal dismissal has been dropped. 3D was simply not developed here as the concept is driver-and-action reasoning on a population rather than spatial exploration — no claim is made that 3D could never contribute.

The source's claim that a fixed scene 'can't run the population response' is retained only as a narrowly scoped affordance note (it does not simulate the learner's own intervention), not as a claim that fixed images cannot teach.

No comparative efficacy between the interactive model, conversation, quiz and reveal-image formats is established by the sources; the row's 'ideal/strong/possible' rankings are not asserted as evidence of effectiveness.

The recognition/sorting-vs-construction point and the 'dialogue addresses specific circumstances' point are agent pedagogical reasoning about task affordances, not source-verified efficacy; wording kept as intended/may rather than proven.

The row frames local action as 'effective'/that it 'measurably' helps; this anti-fatalism framing is preserved in qualified form, but its efficacy is not established by the verified:false sources and should be confirmed before being presented as settled evidence.

probeDeeper: 'You said fewer bites sounds good. What do bees and other pollinators do for the food on your plate — so what happens if they decline?'
'Light pollution mainly affects moths and other night insects. Why would streetlights be a threat to them?' (specific cause → mechanism)
'If your family planted wildflowers, which threat does that fix — and which threats does it NOT fix?' (forces matching action to cause)
'Would one family's garden be enough to reverse the decline? Why do lots of people need to act?'
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree — falling insect numbers are a serious problem, not good news. Causes include habitat loss (fewer wild places to live), pesticides (which poison insects), light pollution (which disrupts night insects like moths), and climate change. It matters for people because so much of our food depends on pollinating insects — fewer pollinators means less fruit and vegetables — and because insects feed birds and other wildlife and recycle nutrients. A family could help by planting wildflowers/pollinator-friendly plants, cutting pesticide use, leaving wild patches, turning off unnecessary lights, or joining a citizen-science count like the Big Butterfly Count.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees insects as pests — thinks fewer insects is a good thing, not a problem
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reconnect decline to services they value: fewer pollinators → less fruit; fewer insects → hungry birds. Weigh a few nuisance species against the many essential ones before judging the decline good.
errorPatterns.distractor: Agree — fewer insects means fewer bites and stings, so it's good for us
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees the decline is good (fewer bites/stings); no sense of loss

errorPatterns.pattern: Lists threats and actions but can't explain WHY the decline harms humans — facts without the causal link to food/ecosystems
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bridge with the roles from the previous topic: pollinators → our food; food source → birds/wildlife. Make each threat's consequence explicit rather than a standalone list.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: names habitat loss/pesticides and 'plant flowers' but can't say why it matters to people

errorPatterns.pattern: Suggests unrealistic or misdirected 'help' — e.g. keeping insects as pets indoors, or thinks one garden fixes a global problem, or that we should stop ALL insects dying
errorPatterns.nextMove: Steer toward habitat- and pesticide-focused, scalable actions (wildflowers, less spray, wild patches, citizen science). Frame small actions as part of a bigger collective effort, not a total fix.
errorPatterns.distractor: The best way to help is to catch insects and keep them safe indoors as pets
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Proposes actions that don't address habitat/pesticides/light, or over-claims that a single action solves it

responseLevels.gap: Welcomes the decline as good, or can't name any cause; sees no problem for people.
responseLevels.full: Explains the decline is a problem, links causes (habitat loss, pesticides, light pollution, climate) to consequences for food and wildlife via insects' roles, AND proposes a realistic, cause-matched action — integrated reasoning across the domain, not a memorised list.
responseLevels.partial: Names threats and a helpful action but as disconnected facts — can't explain WHY declining insects harm people (misses the pollination/food and food-web links), or matches actions loosely to causes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Scientists say insect numbers are falling fast around the world. A child says: 'Fewer insects just means fewer bites and stings — that's good for us, isn't it?' Do you agree? Explain what's causing the decline, why it's actually a problem for people, and one thing a family could do to help.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has integrated the domain links the CAUSES to the consequences via insects' ecological ROLES (pollination → food; food source → wildlife) and offers a realistic action. A child who still sees insects as pests welcomes the decline, or lists causes and actions as disconnected facts without explaining WHY fewer insects harms people. The second tier ('why is it a problem for people?') is the discriminator: it requires carrying forward the ecosystem-roles idea, not just naming threats.

sources.claim: Insect declines are driven by habitat loss, pesticide use, light pollution and climate change; pollinator loss threatens food production; citizen-science schemes like the Big Butterfly Count gather trend data.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten → Year 1). COMPARING TWO GROUPS — deciding which has more, fewer, or whether they are equal, using one-to-one MATCHING and/or counting. Builds the relational meaning of number and the vocabulary that later attaches to <, >, =.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'use the language of: equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least'; identify and represent/compare numbers with objects. Year 2 formalises comparison with the <, >, = signs to 100. EYFS 'Numerical Patterns' (compare quantities to 10).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.6 verbatim — 'Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies' (groups of up to ten). K.CC.7 then compares written numerals 1–10.
• Operational details: Teach TWO strategies — (1) MATCHING (pair objects one-to-one; a leftover = more, none left over = equal) and (2) COUNTING both and comparing the counts. Matching works before secure counting and directly confronts the length/spacing illusion. Stage the Piagetian conservation trap: a spread-out row of 5 vs a bunched row of 6 — 'longer' ≠ 'more'. Nail the vocabulary, especially 'fewer' (countable groups) and 'equal to'.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (4–5) matches two small groups one-to-one and says which has more/fewer or if equal. Tier B (5–6) compares groups to 10 by counting both, using 'more than / fewer than / equal to' correctly. Tier C (6) is not fooled when the larger group is bunched shorter than a spread-out smaller group; justifies by matching or counting.
bestPractices: Teach MATCHING first: line up and pair the two groups; the unmatched leftover shows 'more', a clean pairing shows 'equal' — a strategy that works before counting is secure.
Then connect to COUNTING: count both, the larger count = more; show the two strategies agree.
Deliberately confront conservation: compare a spread-out 5 with a bunched 6 so 'longer row' is caught out; demand a matching/counting justification, not a glance.
Drill precise language — 'fewer' vs 'less', 'equal to'; model full sentences ('7 is more than 5').
Show equal and unequal groups side by side and ask 'how could we make them equal?' (add or remove one — links to one-more/one-less).
keyRepresentations: Two rows lined up for one-to-one matching (connect-the-pairs; the leftover).
Two ten-frames side by side (empty cells show the gap).
Cube towers stood next to each other (taller = more; same height = equal).
A balance / see-saw image for 'equal to'.
commonMisconceptions: Length/spacing = number: judging the longer or more spread-out row as 'more' regardless of count (the classic conservation error).
Using 'bigger' / 'taller' loosely instead of comparing quantity; confusing 'fewer' with 'smaller objects'.
Comparing by which row 'ends further along' rather than by matching or counting.
Believing two groups can't be equal if the objects look different or are arranged differently.

learn.summary: For ages 4–6, teach children to compare two groups and decide which has more, fewer, or whether they are equal, using one-to-one matching and counting. The central challenge is the conservation-of-number trap: a longer or more spread-out row can look like 'more' even when it has fewer items. Matching one-to-one (and counting both groups) resolves the comparison and builds the vocabulary — 'more than', 'fewer than', 'equal to' — that later attaches to <, >, =.

activities.title: Match the two rows and find the leftover
feedback: If every object is paired and none is left over, the two groups are equal.
If one row has an object with no partner, that row has more and the other has fewer.
If you want to make the groups equal, add one object at a time to the smaller group or take one at a time away from the larger, checking the pairing again each time, until no object is left over.
When every object is identical (same-size cubes, same-weight objects), cube towers and a level balance are other ways to show 'equal': same height, or the see-saw sitting level.
activities.rationale: Matching one-to-one gives a direct, concrete meaning of more/fewer/equal that does not depend on secure counting, and sets up the comparison language. An interactive pairing (drag-to-pair or tap-to-match, with the leftover highlighted and a 'make it fair' add/remove control), towers of identical cubes, or a balance image with identical same-weight objects each make the relationship visible; keep groups to ten per K.CC.6.
sourceClaims: K.CC.6: 'Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies' (up to ten objects).
Year 1: 'use the language of: equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least'; Year 2 introduces the <, >, = signs and compares/orders numbers 0–100.
learnerActions: Set up two rows of objects and pair each object in the top row with one in the bottom row (draw a connecting line, or drag a string from each to its partner).
When one or more objects are left with no partner, say that row has MORE (and the other row has FEWER); when every object is paired, say the rows are EQUAL.

As an alternative, build the two groups as towers of identical cubes stood side by side (taller tower = more, same height = equal), or, using only identical objects of the same weight, use a balance/see-saw image to show two equal groups level each other.
Read off a full sentence about the two groups you built, using the frame '__ is more than __' or '__ is equal to __' with your own counts.
Use a 'make it fair' action: add or take away one object until every object pairs up and both rows read EQUAL.
activities.intendedInsight: Pairing objects one-to-one shows which group has more (a leftover) or whether they are equal (a clean pairing) — a strategy that works even before counting is secure.

activities.title: Count both groups and compare
feedback: If both strategies point to the same group (or both show the groups are equal), you can be confident in your comparison.
Remember 'fewer' is about how many items there are, not how big the items are — use identical objects and compare the counts.
If you count correctly but pick the wrong comparison word, slow down on the words 'more than', 'fewer than', 'equal to' — the counting itself was fine.
activities.rationale: Counting both groups connects the relational comparison to cardinality, and showing matching and counting agree strengthens confidence. Ten-frames side by side expose the gap between counts, and using identical objects isolates number from size so 'fewer' is not confused with 'smaller'.
sourceClaims: K.CC.6: 'Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies' (up to ten objects).
learnerActions: Count the objects in each group aloud.
Place the two groups in ten-frames side by side so the empty cells make the gap between the counts easy to see.
Compare the two counts: if one is larger, name that group as having 'more than' the other and the other as having 'fewer than'; if the counts match, say the groups are 'equal to' each other.
Check your answer against the matching method and notice the two strategies agree.
Practise the words 'fewer' and 'equal to' in full sentences, using identical objects so only the number differs.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting both groups and comparing the counts gives the same answer as matching; the larger count means more, and matching counts mean equal.

activities.title: The conservation trap: longer isn't always more
feedback: Spreading a row out makes it longer but does not add any objects — the count stays the same.
If a short bunched row of 6 beats a long spread-out row of 5, matching the strings or counting proves it: the longer look was misleading.
If you judged by length, line the two rows up one above the other, starting at the same end, and match one-to-one so the leftover object is visible, then count both aloud.
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the length/spacing illusion is the core conceptual work of this topic. Having the child commit to a prediction first and then check by matching/counting surfaces the misconception and provides the evidence to correct it. A spacing toggle that bunches or spreads a row stages this comparison concretely.
sourceClaims: Young children mis-judge which group has more by row length/spacing rather than number (conservation of number); one-to-one matching is the antidote.
learnerActions: Look at a spread-out row of 5 next to a bunched-together row of 6; before matching or counting, predict which has more and say why.
Then match the rows one-to-one (or count both) to check which actually has more — here the bunched row of 6 wins even though the spread-out row of 5 looks longer.
Take two equal rows, spread one out into a long line, and predict whether spreading changed how many there are — then check by matching or counting.
Explain in your own words why the longer-looking line does not always have more.
activities.intendedInsight: Spreading objects out or bunching them up does not change how many there are; the longer row is not necessarily the one with more.

constraints: Keep groups to no more than ten objects, consistent with K.CC.6.

A static labelled 'more/fewer/equal' picture can serve as a reference but does not let the child match, count, or rearrange to resolve a comparison; it is a reference scaffold, not a substitute for the child doing the matching.

Multiple-choice 'which has more?' items and categorising pairs into more/fewer/equal can check whether a child can pick the right comparison, but do not themselves require the child to construct the matching or justify it.
A fairness conversation ('who has more sweets — is that fair?') can frame the task and motivate the vocabulary; it does not itself settle the comparison, which is resolved by matching or counting.
Use identical objects when first teaching 'fewer' so children do not confuse 'more items' with 'bigger items'.

Expectations by stage: younger children match two small groups and say which has more/fewer or if equal; others compare groups to ten by counting both; the most secure are not fooled when the larger group is bunched shorter than a spread-out smaller group and justify by matching or counting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The conservation-of-number source is marked unverified (verified:false) in the original row; the copied claim that one-to-one matching is 'the antidote' to the length/spacing illusion is presented as a teaching proposal, not an established comparative result.

The original row asserted 3D depth 'only clutters' comparison and that comparison 'is settled by matching/counting, not talk'; these categorical medium claims have been dropped or softened to scoped affordance notes rather than universal claims about what media can or cannot teach.

Example number pairs differ across the original fields (5 vs 6 in the interactive, 6 vs 7 in the assessment); either works for the conservation trap as long as the shorter-looking row genuinely has more — both kept as illustrative, not canonical.
Ten-frames, cube towers, and the balance/see-saw image are drawn from the original keyRepresentations and offered as optional alternatives, not required tools.

assess.poeTask: Lay out two rows of 6, matched one-to-one, and agree together they are the same. Ask the child to PREDICT before you act: 'If I spread THIS row out into a long line, will it have more, fewer, or the same — and why?' They commit to a reason first; then spread it and check by matching/counting. 'The same, you didn't add or take any' is conservation; 'more, it's longer now' reveals the length-for-number misconception.
probeDeeper: Show me how you could match them up to check.
If I pushed Row A's counters close together like Row B, which would have more then?
How many more does Row B have?
Can you change them so the two rows are equal?
assess.correctAnswer: Row B has more — it has 7 and Row A has 6. I matched (or counted) them; the longer-looking line isn't always the one with more.

errorPatterns.pattern: length stands in for number — judges the longer or more spread-out row as 'more' regardless of count ('this one has more, it's longer')
errorPatterns.nextMove: line the two rows up end-to-end and match one-to-one so the leftover counter is visible; count both aloud; then squeeze/spread a row to show number doesn't change with length
errorPatterns.distractor: Row A has more because it's longer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: picks the visually longer Row A and, asked how, points to its length rather than a count

errorPatterns.pattern: 'more' taken as bigger or longer objects rather than more items
errorPatterns.nextMove: use identical objects and stress 'more' = greater number, established by matching one-to-one
errorPatterns.revealedBy: chooses the row with larger counters or the longer line even when items are identical

errorPatterns.pattern: counts both correctly but names the wrong one as 'more', or cannot yet use 'fewer'/'equal' precisely
errorPatterns.nextMove: scaffold comparison language on a number track (the later number is more); rehearse 'fewer' and 'equal' explicitly — do not reteach the counting itself
errorPatterns.revealedBy: accurate counts (6 and 7) but the comparison word is wrong or missing

responseLevels.gap: Chooses by appearance — the longer or more spread-out row 'has more' — and is not moved by matching or counting.
responseLevels.full: Determines more/fewer/equal by matching or counting even when appearance conflicts, explains the longer line isn't necessarily more, and uses the comparison language accurately.
responseLevels.partial: Counts both rows correctly but leans on the count alone; unsettled when appearance and number conflict, or cannot yet use 'fewer'/'equal' precisely.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two rows of counters. (Set up Row A as 6 counters spread out into a long line, and Row B as 7 counters bunched close together, so Row A LOOKS longer.) Which row has more counters — or are they the same? How can you be sure?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This pits appearance against number. A child who compares by number — matching one-to-one or counting both — finds Row B has more despite looking shorter. A child who compares by appearance picks the longer Row A ('it's more spread out'). The 'how can you be sure' tier forces the method: matching/counting versus looking-longer, which is exactly the conservation-of-number divide.

sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Kindergarten Counting & Cardinality (K.CC)

sources.source: DfE, National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Years 1–2, Number and place value)

sources.claim: Young children mis-judge which group has more by row length/spacing rather than number (conservation of number); one-to-one matching is the antidote.
