pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, using structure becomes a deliberate calculating tool: breaking 7×13 into 7×10 + 7×3 with the distributive property, using place value to explain why ×10 shifts every digit one place left (not 'add a zero'), and using the quadrilateral hierarchy (a square is a special rectangle) to carry properties down from category to subcategory. The teaching aim is that the child looks for a known structure before grinding a procedure. The area model is the workhorse: it makes the distributive split visible as two sub-rectangles, and CCSS MP7 names exactly this partitioning as the heart of the practice.
bestPractices: Model 7×13 on a partitioned area rectangle (7×10 and 7×3) so the split is seen, then connect it to the numeric decomposition
Teach ×10 as a place-value shift using a place-value chart (digits move one column left; a zero fills the emptied ones place) rather than the 'add a zero' rule, which breaks for decimals
Use overlapping property sets / a shape family tree so squares sit inside rectangles inside parallelograms, and reason 'a square must have… because it is a rectangle'
Prompt 'is there a number fact or shape fact you already know that this is like?' before any standard algorithm
keyRepresentations: Partitioned area model / grid for the distributive split
Place-value chart showing digits shifting left on ×10/×100
Shape hierarchy diagram (quadrilateral → parallelogram → rectangle → square)
Arrays and factor trees linking multiplication structure
commonMisconceptions: Uses 'multiplying by 10 adds a zero', which fails for decimals (2.5×10 read as 2.50)
Splits distributively but forgets to multiply the second part (7×13 = 7×10 + 3)
Refuses that a square is a rectangle because the names/looks differ, so properties don't transfer down the hierarchy
Treats each multiplication as needing the column algorithm, not looking for a decomposition that makes it easy

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, this topic develops the habit of looking for known mathematical structure before grinding a procedure: splitting a multiplication like 7×13 into 7×10 + 7×3 (distributive property), explaining ×10 as a place-value shift (digits move one column left) rather than 'add a zero', and using the quadrilateral hierarchy (a square is a special rectangle) to inherit properties from category to subcategory. The partitioned area model is the central representation, making the distributive split visible as two sub-rectangles. Activities centre on learners partitioning, justifying and generalising the structural move, not just reaching a correct answer.

activities.title: Split the rectangle: 7×13 from two easy facts
feedback: If a learner writes 7×10 + 3 = 73, point back to the rectangle: the second part is also 7 tall, so it is 7×3 = 21, not 3. Have them shade the missing 7×3 block.
If a learner reaches 91 only by the column algorithm, ask them to show the two sub-rectangles and name the two easy facts, so the structure is made explicit.
When a learner tries a second valid split (e.g. 11 and 2) and still gets 91, confirm that any split works because the ×7 is shared over the parts — the choice is just about which parts are easiest.
activities.rationale: The area model makes the distributive partition literally visible as two sub-rectangles and ties the picture to the numeric decomposition. CCSS MP7 gives this kind of distributive split (e.g. 7 × 8 = 7 × 5 + 7 × 3) as one example of 'using structure', alongside other examples. An interactive version where the learner drags the divider and watches the parts recompute and slide together is one proposed way to make the mechanism operate under the learner's hand, and a drawn, cut or folded paper rectangle may serve the same purpose; the relative effectiveness of either medium is not established by the cited sources. An array alongside the area model (the original row's arrays/factor-trees representation) could optionally reinforce the same structure.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes partitioning a product distributively (e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) as the basis of the distributive property
Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
learnerActions: Face 7×13 drawn as a rectangle 7 tall and 13 wide; mark where to cut the width to make a friendly 10 and 3
Cut the rectangle into a 7×10 part and a 7×3 part and work out each: 70 and 21
Combine the two parts (70 + 21 = 91) and state the matching number sentence: 7×13 = 7×10 + 7×3
Explain in your own words why BOTH parts have to be multiplied by 7 (both sub-rectangles are 7 tall)
Try a different cut of 13 (for example 11 and 2, giving 7×11 = 77 and 7×2 = 14) and check you still reach 91; say which cut was easiest and why
activities.intendedInsight: A multiplication that feels hard can be assembled from two multiplications you already know; the distributive property shares the ×7 across every part of the 13, which is why both parts must be multiplied.

activities.title: Why ×10 shifts digits, not 'adds a zero'
feedback: If a learner writes 2.5×10 = 2.50, show the chart: 2.50 is the same value as 2.5, so nothing has changed — ×10 must make it ten times bigger, which means shifting to 25.
Reinforce that for 36×10 = 360 the zero appears because the ones column is emptied, not because we 'add a zero' as a rule.
activities.rationale: A place-value chart exposes the structural reason behind the ×10 pattern and provides a built-in counterexample (the decimal case) to the shortcut. A live chart where digits slide one column on ×10/×100 can make the shift concrete, and a paper chart with movable digit cards can serve the same purpose; the relative effectiveness of the media is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
learnerActions: Place a number such as 36 in a place-value chart (tens and ones), then multiply by 10 and move each digit one column to the left, writing a 0 in the emptied ones place to read 360
Now push 2.5 through ×10 in the same chart: move each digit one column left to get 25, and notice that appending a zero would wrongly give 2.50 (the same value as 2.5)
State a rule in your own words: ×10 moves every digit one place left; 'add a zero' only looks right for whole numbers because a zero happens to fill the empty ones place
Repeat for ×100 (two columns left) with one whole number and one decimal
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by 10 (or 100) is a place-value shift of every digit; 'add a zero' is only a lucky special case for whole numbers and breaks for decimals.

activities.title: Nested shape families: a square is a special rectangle
feedback: If a learner denies that a square is a rectangle, use the nested sets: the square sits inside the rectangle set, so it must satisfy every rectangle property (four right angles).
If a learner claims every rectangle is a square, show a long thin rectangle as a counterexample — inheritance runs from the wider category to the narrower one, not back up.
activities.rationale: A shape family tree / nested property sets make the hierarchy visible and are intended to support reasoning by inheritance, which is the structural move for quadrilateral classification. Tappable property labels on a hierarchy diagram can serve as a reference; a sort by itself checks or teaches classification but does not itself elicit the learner's explanation, so pair the active sorting with a request to justify. The attached EEF claim supports using representations to expose structure in general and does not specifically evidence the nested-set method.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
learnerActions: Sort a set of quadrilaterals into nested property sets so squares sit inside rectangles, which sit inside parallelograms
For a given square, list what must be true of it just because it is a rectangle (e.g. it has four right angles) — without measuring
Complete sentences of the form 'A square must have … because it is a rectangle' and 'A square must have … because it is a parallelogram'
Decide and justify: is every rectangle a square? Explain why the inheritance runs one way down the hierarchy
activities.intendedInsight: Subcategories inherit the properties of the categories that contain them, so knowing 'a square is a rectangle' lets you carry rectangle properties down without re-checking; but the reverse is not guaranteed.

activities.title: 'What do I already know that this is like?' — probing and generalising
feedback: Listen for a structurally justified decomposition such as '7×13 is 7×10 plus 7×3, that's 70 and 21, so 91 — I can split the 13 because multiplying is shared out over the parts.' The justification, not the answer 91, is the target.
If the learner reaches 91 only by running the column algorithm in their head, that does not yet show structural insight — ask them to name the parts and why the split is valid.
If the learner cannot say why the split works, return to the area model activity before pushing generalisation.
activities.rationale: The answer 91 is reachable by the column algorithm with no structural insight; what discriminates is whether the learner decomposes and can justify the split, and whether they transfer the move to related products. Open probes are intended to elicit the justification that a scored answer would hide.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes partitioning a product distributively (e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) as the basis of the distributive property
learnerActions: Work out 7×13 mentally using a fact you already know instead of the written column method, then talk through how you split it and why that split is allowed
Answer: could you have split 13 a different way and still got 91? Which split was easiest and why?
Generalise: how is splitting 7×13 like splitting 6×13 or 7×23? Describe the structural move you reused
Before any standard algorithm on a new product, pause and ask 'is there a number fact or shape fact I already know that this is like?'
activities.intendedInsight: Using structure is a deliberate, transferable habit: decompose into known parts and justify the decomposition, rather than defaulting to a procedure.

constraints: The teaching aim is that the learner looks for a known structure before applying a standard procedure; reaching the correct numerical answer by the column algorithm does not demonstrate this objective.
Target the justification, not just the result: a distributive split must be explained as sharing the ×7 over both parts, and ×10 must be explained as a place-value shift.

Tap-to-reveal annotations on a pre-split area model or a shape hierarchy are useful as reference scaffolds, but they do not let the learner choose the split point or watch the parts recombine; use them to support, not replace, active partitioning.

Recognition or matching checks (e.g. 'which split makes 7×13 easy?') can confirm the structural move, but a correct selection can hide the reasoning; pair any such check with a request to explain why.
Avoid teaching 'multiply by 10 adds a zero' as a rule; use it only as a named special case for whole numbers alongside the place-value explanation.
Inheritance in the quadrilateral hierarchy runs from broader to narrower categories (a square inherits rectangle properties), not the reverse; make this directionality explicit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and medium/interaction choices are presented with proposed/may wording.

The legacy row rated dialogue ('conversation') and 3D as 'poor' with claims such as 'dialogue without the area model gives nothing to partition' and '3D adds load, not insight'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been reframed as narrow scaffold limits rather than universal laws; the open probes retained here use discussion productively once a visual model is available.

The original keyRepresentation 'arrays and factor trees linking multiplication structure' was not carried into any activity as a standalone task; it is noted as an optional reinforcement in activity 1 and could be reinstated to enrich the distributive-split work. Flagged as a substantive representation gap rather than silently dropped.

The EEF source claim is a general representation/structure statement; attaching it to the shape-hierarchy activity supports the 'use a representation to expose structure' principle but does not specifically evidence the nested-property-set approach — treated as topical support, not validation.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 7×13 = 7×10 + 7×3 = 70 + 21 = 91 (correct); alternative split 7×11 + 7×2 = 77 + 14 = 91 (correct). The common error 7×10 + 3 = 73 is retained only as an explicitly labelled misconception with a correction, never as a valid answer. 2.5×10 = 25 (correct); 2.50 is flagged as the wrong 'add a zero' outcome. 36×10 = 360, 6×13 = 78 and 7×23 = 161 by the same method (used only as generalisation prompts, not as stated answers).

probeDeeper: Ask 'you split 13 into 10 and 3 — could you have split it a different way and still got 91? which split was easiest and why?' to test flexible, purposeful structure use
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'does "add a zero" give the right answer for 2.5×10? why or why not?' to check the place-value structure beneath the rule
Ask 'a square is a rectangle — so what does that let you say about its angles without measuring?' to probe property inheritance in the hierarchy
Ask 'how is splitting 7×13 like splitting 6×13 or 7×23?' to see whether the distributive structure generalises
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a distributive decomposition justified structurally: '7×13 is 7×10 plus 7×3, that's 70 and 21, so 91 — I can split the 13 because multiplying is sharing out over the parts.' The justification, not the 91, is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Splits distributively but multiplies only the first part, giving 7×10 + 3 = 73, because the split is treated as chopping the number rather than sharing the ×7 over both parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the area model: both sub-rectangles are 7 tall, so the 3 must also be multiplied by 7; see the missing 7×3 block
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says '70 plus 3' or otherwise leaves the second part un-multiplied

errorPatterns.pattern: Relies on 'multiplying by 10 just adds a zero', which misfires on decimals and hides the place-value shift
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a place-value chart to shift every digit one column left; contrast the whole-number case where a zero happens to fill the ones place
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to explain ×10 or to do 2.5×10, the child appends a zero (2.50) instead of shifting digits

errorPatterns.pattern: Refuses that a square is a special rectangle, so shared properties don't transfer down the hierarchy
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort quadrilaterals into nested property sets so the square sits inside the rectangle set; reason that a square inherits rectangle properties
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'is a square a rectangle? so must it have four right angles?' the child denies the category link

responseLevels.gap: Reaches for the column algorithm or splits incorrectly (7×10+3), appends a zero for ×10, and won't accept the square-rectangle link
responseLevels.full: Chooses a distributive decomposition unprompted and justifies it via the area model, explains ×10 as a place-value shift, and reasons about inherited quadrilateral properties — applying 'what do I already know that this is like?' to new products and shapes
responseLevels.partial: Can carry out a distributive split or state a hierarchy fact when prompted, but cannot justify why the split is valid or transfers 'add a zero' unsafely to decimals

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 7 × 13 in your head, using a fact you already know instead of the written column method. Talk me through how you split it up and why that's allowed.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The answer 91 can be reached by the column algorithm with no structural insight. What discriminates is whether the child DECOMPOSES and can say why the split is valid. A child using structure partitions and justifies; a child without it either runs the algorithm mentally or splits wrongly (7×10+3).

sources.claim: Using structure includes partitioning a product distributively (e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) as the basis of the distributive property
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP7 'Look for and make use of structure'

sources.claim: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
sources.source: EEF, 'Improving Mathematics in Key Stages 2 and 3' guidance report (Recommendations 2 and 4)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 11–13; Seismic Waves & Earth's Interior (CONCEPTUAL): P-waves (compression, travel through solids AND liquids) vs S-waves (shear, blocked by liquids); the S-wave shadow zone on the far side of a quake; how seismologists use wave refraction/reflection and arrival times to INFER a layered Earth — solid inner core, liquid outer core, mantle, crust. This is a nature-of-science topic: knowing the unseen interior from indirect evidence.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS3 Chemistry 'Earth and atmosphere' gives 'the structure of the Earth'; KS3 Physics covers waves (transverse/longitudinal), giving the P=longitudinal/S=transverse vocabulary. Seismic-wave evidence for the core is GCSE-level in England. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS): no MS performance expectation names seismic waves/shadow zone directly (that sits at HS-ESS2 / physics wave PEs); the topic is anchored on the SEP/CCC of constructing explanations from evidence — MS-ESS2-2 'Construct an explanation based on evidence' (VERIFIED verbatim) supplies the inference-from-evidence framing. Specific seismic-wave standards here are knowledge-based (verified:false).
• Operational details — The teachable core is INDIRECT INFERENCE, not wave trivia. Build it as detective work: earthquakes send P and S waves in all directions; stations worldwide record which arrive and when; P always arrives first (faster), and there is a ring on the far side where S waves NEVER arrive — the S-wave shadow zone. Because S (shear) waves cannot pass through a LIQUID, that shadow is direct evidence of a liquid outer core; refraction bending of P waves reveals further layer boundaries and the solid inner core. Be precise: P = longitudinal/compression (push-pull along travel), S = transverse/shear (side-to-side). Prerequisite assumed: Measuring Earthquake Strength (energy travels as waves; seismometers). This topic feeds How Tectonic Plates Move (evidence for the layered engine) and KS3 'drawing conclusions from evidence'.
• Checkpoint — Tier C (formal/model-based): given seismograph records from stations around the globe, the child EXPLAINS the S-wave shadow zone as evidence of a liquid outer core and reconstructs the layered interior from the pattern of arrivals and absences — articulating that we map the unreachable interior indirectly, from how waves behave, not by digging.
bestPractices: Frame the whole topic as indirect inference/detective reasoning ('we cannot dig to the core, so how do we KNOW?') — the reasoning IS the learning objective, more than the wave taxonomy.

Make the shadow zone the hinge: show S waves stopping dead at the liquid outer core and the resulting far-side ring where no S arrives, then reason backwards from that absence to 'the outer core must be liquid'.

Nail the physical difference: S (shear/transverse) waves need a material that resists shape-change, which liquids don't provide, so they die in the liquid outer core; P (compression/longitudinal) waves pass through everything but bend (refract) at boundaries.
Use physical wave demos (slinky for longitudinal P; rope/shaken spring for transverse S) to embody the two wave types before applying them to the Earth.
Teach 'absence of data is data': the hole in the S-wave coverage is itself the evidence — a powerful nature-of-science habit that transfers to other inference topics.
Layer the evidence build-up: P-first arrivals → refraction/travel-time curves → S shadow zone → inner-core reflections, so the four-layer model is reconstructed step by step, not asserted.
keyRepresentations: Cross-section ray diagram: P and S rays fanning out from a quake focus, refracting at layer boundaries, with the S-wave shadow-zone ring shaded on the far side.
Slinky (longitudinal, P) vs shaken rope/spring (transverse, S): the canonical embodiment of compression vs shear.
Seismograph trace with P and S arrivals marked and the S-P time gap (which also gives distance to the quake).
Globe with seismometer stations: green where S arrives, grey shadow band where it never does — the reconstruct-the-core evidence map.
Layered-Earth cutaway (crust / solid mantle / liquid outer core / solid inner core) built up as each wave clue is added.
commonMisconceptions: 'S waves are just slower P waves.' — They are a different KIND of motion (shear/transverse vs compression/longitudinal); S being blocked by liquid is about wave type, not speed.

'The shadow zone means the waves were absorbed/used up.' — S waves are stopped because the liquid outer core cannot carry shear; P waves are refracted (bent) away, not destroyed — they reappear elsewhere.
'Seismic waves only travel along the surface.' — Body waves (P and S) travel THROUGH the Earth's interior; that through-travel is exactly what probes the layers.

'We know Earth's interior by drilling/sampling it.' — The deepest boreholes barely scratch the crust; the layered model is inferred almost entirely from seismic waves (plus meteorites, density, magnetism).
'The whole core is liquid' or 'the whole core is solid.' — The OUTER core is liquid (stops S), the INNER core is solid (revealed by reflected phases); conflating them loses the key evidence.
'A liquid outer core means a hollow or molten-through Earth.' — It is dense liquid iron–nickel under immense pressure, surrounded by solid mantle and a solid inner core, not a cavity or a lava sea.

learn.summary: Learners discover Earth's layered interior by reasoning from seismic-wave evidence, treating the S-wave shadow zone as positive evidence of a liquid outer core. The core objective is indirect inference ('we cannot dig to the core, so how do we KNOW?'), not wave vocabulary. Learners first embody the two body-wave types physically, then simulate a quake, place seismometers worldwide, read arrivals, and reconstruct the four-layer model (crust, solid mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core) step by step from P-first arrivals, refraction, the S shadow zone, and inner-core reflections.

activities.title: Feel the two kinds of wave: slinky (P) and shaken rope (S)
feedback: If a learner says 'S-waves are just slower P-waves', redirect: speed is not the point — S is a different kind of motion (shearing sideways), and that is why liquids affect them differently.
Reinforce: liquids flow and do not resist shape-change, so they cannot carry a shear (S) wave — hold this idea for the Earth model next.
activities.rationale: Embodying compression vs shear with physical demos grounds the abstract wave taxonomy before it is applied to the Earth, targeting the common 'S is a slow P' misconception directly through the motion itself.
sourceClaims: P-waves are longitudinal/compression and travel through solids and liquids; S-waves are transverse/shear and cannot travel through liquids, producing an S-wave shadow zone that evidences a liquid outer core; refraction and reflection of waves reveal the solid inner core, mantle, crust.
learnerActions: Push and pull one end of a stretched slinky along its length and watch the compression pulse travel through: this is a longitudinal P-wave (push-pull along the direction of travel).
Shake a rope or spring side to side and watch the sideways ripple travel along it: this is a transverse S-wave (side-to-side shearing across the direction of travel).
State in your own words how the two motions differ, and predict which type needs a material that resists being bent/sheared sideways.
activities.intendedInsight: P-waves are compression (push-pull) and S-waves are shear (side-to-side) — a difference of KIND of motion, not just speed. Shear motion requires a material that resists change of shape.

activities.title: Fire a quake and ring the globe with seismometers
feedback: If a learner says the missing S-waves 'faded out with distance' or the quake was 'too weak/far', point out that P-waves from the same quake DO arrive at far-side stations beyond about 140°, where S never arrives, so distance and strength cannot be the reason. S is selectively blocked, while P is only bent.
If a learner says 'the waves were absorbed/used up', clarify: P is refracted (bent) at boundaries and reappears elsewhere, not destroyed; S specifically cannot cross something on that path.

If a learner thinks seismic waves only travel along the surface, note that P and S are body waves that travel right THROUGH the Earth's interior — it is exactly this through-travel that lets them probe the hidden layers, rather than only skimming the surface.
activities.rationale: Letting learners generate and read the arrival pattern themselves sets up the key nature-of-science move: an absence in the data, contrasted against a present signal, becomes evidence. This supports constructing an explanation from evidence.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS2-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-2]' — supplies the evidence-based-explanation framing used to anchor inference of Earth's interior.

P-waves are longitudinal/compression and travel through solids and liquids; S-waves are transverse/shear and cannot travel through liquids, producing an S-wave shadow zone that evidences a liquid outer core; refraction and reflection of waves reveal the solid inner core, mantle, crust.
learnerActions: On a cross-section of the Earth, place an earthquake focus and send P and S waves outward in all directions; watch P arrive first (it travels faster) and the rays bend (refract) at layer boundaries.

Place seismometer stations all around the globe and read each trace, colour-coding stations where both P and S arrive (e.g. green), stations where P arrives but no direct S does (e.g. yellow), and stations where neither direct P nor direct S arrives (e.g. grey, roughly 104°–140° from the quake), to make the pattern visible.

Find all the far-side stations (beyond about 104° from the quake) that never record any direct S, and write down exactly what is present and what is absent there, noting where P is still recorded (beyond about 140°) and where direct P is also missing (about 104°–140°).
activities.intendedInsight: From the SAME earthquake, no station beyond about 104° from the quake records direct S, yet P still reaches many of those far-side stations (beyond about 140°), so the missing S cannot be explained by distance or fading. A separate, narrower P shadow zone (about 104°–140°) appears because P-waves are bent (refracted) at the core boundary, not stopped.

activities.title: Test the shadow zone: toggle the outer core solid vs liquid
feedback: If a learner claims a solid outer core would also give an S shadow zone, have them re-run the toggle and observe S-waves crossing a solid outer core — no S shadow appears.

Offer the analogy for 'can't we just know by looking inside?': spinning an egg tells you hard- from soft-boiled without opening it — seismic waves are our probe into a place we cannot visit; the deepest boreholes barely scratch the crust.
activities.rationale: A controlled 'what if this layer were solid?' manipulation isolates the causal link between liquid and the shadow zone, converting a pattern into justified inference and countering the 'unknowable interior' misconception.
sourceClaims: P-waves are longitudinal/compression and travel through solids and liquids; S-waves are transverse/shear and cannot travel through liquids, producing an S-wave shadow zone that evidences a liquid outer core; refraction and reflection of waves reveal the solid inner core, mantle, crust.
The layered-Earth model (crust, solid mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core) is inferred almost entirely from seismic-wave behaviour; the deepest boreholes barely penetrate the crust.
learnerActions: Switch the outer core from solid to liquid and back, and watch what happens to the S-waves at that boundary and to the far-side shadow band.
Record: with a liquid outer core, S-waves stop at the boundary and a far-side shadow zone appears; with a solid outer core, S-waves pass through and the S shadow zone disappears.
Reason backwards from the real data (an S shadow zone exists) to the conclusion: the outer core must be liquid, because only a liquid stops shear waves.
activities.intendedInsight: The ABSENCE of S on the far side is itself the evidence — it means shear waves hit a liquid layer. The shadow zone is a positive clue, not missing information.

activities.title: Reconstruct Earth's four layers from the data alone
feedback: If a learner says 'the whole core is liquid' or 'it's all lava inside', point to the evidence: S-waves cross the solid mantle and stop only at the outer core, and reflected and refracted waves reveal a separate inner core, which further evidence shows is solid. The layers are distinct.

If a learner says a liquid outer core means a hollow or molten-through Earth, clarify it is dense liquid iron–nickel under immense pressure, enclosed by solid mantle and a solid inner core — not a cavity or a lava sea.
Reinforce that S crossing the mantle is itself proof the mantle is solid — a useful counterexample check.
activities.rationale: Assembling the model from scratch forces genuine construction of an evidence-based explanation rather than recall of layer names, and sequencing the clues prevents the four-layer model from being merely asserted.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS2-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-2]' — supplies the evidence-based-explanation framing used to anchor inference of Earth's interior.
The layered-Earth model (crust, solid mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core) is inferred almost entirely from seismic-wave behaviour; the deepest boreholes barely penetrate the crust.

P-waves are longitudinal/compression and travel through solids and liquids; S-waves are transverse/shear and cannot travel through liquids, producing an S-wave shadow zone that evidences a liquid outer core; refraction and reflection of waves reveal the solid inner core, mantle, crust.
learnerActions: With the cutaway hidden, use only the pattern of what arrived where and when to rebuild Earth's structure layer by layer: P-first arrivals, refraction/travel-time bending, the S shadow zone, then a faint reflected phase.

Identify the mantle as solid (S-waves DO cross it), the outer core as liquid (S shadow zone), and the inner core as a separate region (its boundary is revealed by waves reflecting or refracting off it inside the liquid outer core), which further evidence, such as P-waves speeding up inside it, shows is solid.
Write a short explanation of how each clue pins down each layer, then compare your inferred model with the actual layered Earth.
Predict: what would far-side seismometers detect if the outer core were solid, and how is the solid inner core detected despite sitting inside a liquid?
activities.intendedInsight: The whole layered model (crust / solid mantle / liquid outer core / solid inner core) is reconstructed from indirect wave evidence, built up clue by clue — we map the unreachable interior by reasoning, not by digging.

activities.title: The detective story: discovering the inner core
feedback: If a learner treats the interior as 'just a guess', connect back to the toggle experiment: the conclusions follow from what the waves do and do not do.
Encourage naming the specific clue (shadow zone, reflected phase) rather than 'scientists figured it out'.
activities.rationale: A human history narrative can reinforce the nature-of-science theme as a complement to the hands-on reasoning; it enriches but does not itself provide the wave-manipulation and pattern-reading practice, which carries the core skill.
learnerActions: Read or listen to a short account of how seismologists read wiggly seismograph traces to deduce the interior, including how Inge Lehmann (1936) inferred an inner core from faint P-wave arrivals inside the P-wave shadow zone, and how later evidence showed that inner core is solid.
Discuss what made each discovery possible: which absence or faint arrival carried the information.
Explain why this counts as science even though no one has ever been to the core.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific knowledge of the unreachable interior is built from indirect, often subtle signals — including absences and faint reflections — and refined over time.

constraints: The central objective is indirect inference ('absence of data is data'), which must be built through learner reconstruction — recognition-only checks (matching wave type to motion, ordering arrivals, reading an S-P time gap whose size also indicates distance to the quake) can verify understanding but do not elicit the independent reconstruction and so should follow, not replace, the hands-on reasoning.
Be precise with wave types: P = longitudinal/compression (push-pull along travel); S = transverse/shear (side-to-side). S being blocked by liquid is about wave type, not speed.

Distinguish the three solid/liquid states clearly: solid mantle (S crosses it), liquid outer core (S shadow zone), solid inner core (reflected and refracted phases reveal its boundary; faster P-wave speeds inside it and later evidence indicate it is solid). Do not let learners collapse these into 'the core is liquid' or 'everything inside is molten'.

A static tap-to-reveal ray diagram or layered cutaway is a useful summary reference but cannot let learners test 'what if this layer were solid?' or reconstruct the interior from data; use it as a reference card after the reconstruction, not as the main reasoning vehicle.

A 3D globe can clarify the shadow zone as a spatial band wrapping the sphere and reflected phases bouncing off the inner core; however, the inference logic reads cleanly in a 2D cross-section and does not require depth perception, so 3D is an optional spatial enrichment, not a necessity.

Physical paper seismograph traces, a real slinky and rope, or a screen simulation each offer valid routes to the same reasoning; choose by available resources rather than assuming one medium is required.
Prerequisite assumed: energy travels as waves and seismometers record them (Measuring Earthquake Strength). This topic feeds evidence for how tectonic plates move.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Only the MS-ESS2-2 verbatim quotation is marked verified in the source row; the seismology content, DfE curriculum placement, and borehole-depth claim are marked verified:false and should be confirmed against current USGS/BGS and DfE materials before relying on specifics.

MS-ESS2-2 is literally about geoscience processes changing Earth's SURFACE; here it is used only to supply the 'construct an explanation from evidence' framing, as the source itself notes. The row acknowledges no MS NGSS performance expectation names seismic waves/shadow zone directly (that sits at HS-ESS2 / physics wave PEs) — treat the standard alignment as framing, not a direct topic match.

The original research framed a quiz as able to 'verify rather than build' the reasoning; retained as an ordering/scope point in constraints without asserting a universal law about what quizzes can teach.

Historical attribution of the inner-core discovery to Inge Lehmann is widely reported but was not in the verified source claims; the school-level phrasing that the inner core's solidity is 'revealed by reflections' simplifies a subtler inference (solidity was established by later work and normal-mode/density evidence). Present as background and confirm before emphasising.
Activity 2 simplifies P as arriving first 'everywhere'; in reality P also has a shadow zone (~103–143°). Retained at topic level, but confirm/qualify if precise arrival geometry is taught.

The 'seismic waves only travel along the surface' misconception corrective was absent from the candidate's feedback and was added to Activity 2 in this review to preserve all six original misconception correctives.

probeDeeper: P-waves reach the far side but S-waves don't, from the very same earthquake. Why does that rule out 'the waves just faded with distance'?
If the outer core were solid instead of liquid, what would seismometers on the far side detect — would there still be an S-wave shadow zone?
How can we tell the INNER core is solid if it sits inside a liquid outer core — what wave clue gives that away?
Counterexample: S-waves DO travel through the mantle. What does that tell you about whether the mantle is solid or liquid?
assess.correctAnswer: S-waves are shear waves that cannot travel through liquid; P-waves travel through both solid and liquid. The S-waves vanishing on the far side (the S-wave shadow zone) means they hit something liquid and were stopped — that is the evidence for a LIQUID outer core. The absence of the signal is itself the clue: nobody has drilled there, so we infer the interior indirectly from how the waves behave.

errorPatterns.pattern: No S-waves means the earthquake was too weak or too far, so the waves faded out before reaching there ('they ran out of energy').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out that P-waves DO arrive at the same far-side spot from the same quake, so distance cannot be the reason — only S-waves are selectively blocked.
errorPatterns.distractor: The S-waves lost their energy over the long distance and faded out before reaching the far side.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes the shadow zone to distance or fading, not to a liquid layer blocking shear waves.

errorPatterns.pattern: You can't really know what's inside the Earth because nobody has ever been there ('it's just a guess').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Frame indirect evidence — like telling a hard- from a soft-boiled egg by spinning it; the seismic waves are our probe into a place we cannot visit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the interior as unknowable and dismisses indirect evidence.

errorPatterns.pattern: The whole inside of the Earth is molten liquid ('it's all lava down there'), which is why S-waves are blocked.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the layered model from the wave evidence itself — S-waves DO cross the mantle (solid) and stop only at the outer core (liquid).
errorPatterns.distractor: The S-waves are blocked because the entire inside of the Earth is molten liquid rock.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Does not distinguish solid mantle, liquid outer core and solid inner core; says everything inside is liquid.

responseLevels.gap: Reads the missing S-waves as weak or distant waves or instrument failure, or claims the interior is unknowable; cannot distinguish P from S waves.
responseLevels.full: Explains that the S-wave shadow zone is direct evidence of a liquid outer core (shear waves stopped by liquid) while P-waves refract through, and that the layered interior is inferred indirectly; transfers to a new case, e.g. predicting what a solid outer core would show or how the solid inner core is detected.
responseLevels.partial: States that P-waves pass through solid and liquid while S-waves only pass through solid, and that a shadow zone exists, but cannot use the ABSENCE as positive evidence for a liquid outer core or assemble the layered structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On the far side of the Earth from a big earthquake, seismometers detect P-waves but no S-waves at all. What does this missing signal tell us about what is deep inside the Earth, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads 'no reading' as the waves fading with distance, an instrument fault, or nothing being there gives a different answer from one who treats the ABSENCE as positive evidence of a liquid layer. It separates reciting 'S-waves can't cross liquid' from using it to infer Earth's structure.

pedagogy.summary: Children begin to MEASURE elapsed time with tools — sand timers, stopwatches, counting seconds — to time real activities, and to record the result in simple units ('about 2 minutes'). The step is procedural and embodied: start the tool as the activity starts, stop it as it ends, read off the duration. The conceptual underpinning (from the prerequisite) is that duration is how long something lasts, independent of speed; children also begin to meet 1 minute = 60 seconds.
bestPractices: Time real, meaningful activities (how long to write your name, to tidy up) with a visible tool
Model starting and stopping the tool exactly AT the start and end of the event
Use sand timers first — duration is visible as the sand falls — before digital stopwatches
Introduce 1 minute = 60 seconds by counting seconds until a one-minute sand timer empties
Record informally ('about 2 minutes', 'a bit more than a minute') rather than demanding precision
keyRepresentations: Sand timers of known durations (1 minute, 3 minutes)
A stopwatch or large seconds display
A number line / counting track of seconds
A one-minute timer paired with a count to 60
commonMisconceptions: Judges duration by speed or by how much happened, not elapsed time (carried from comparing durations)
Starts or stops the tool out of step with the event
Reads the number currently showing as the duration, ignoring where timing started
Thinks 'a minute' and '60 seconds' are different amounts

learn.summary: Young children (around ages 5-6) learn to MEASURE elapsed time using tools — sand timers, stopwatches, counting seconds — to time real activities and record results in simple units ('about 2 minutes'). The core skill is procedural and embodied: start the tool exactly as the event begins, stop it exactly as it ends, then read off the duration. The conceptual underpinnings are that duration is how long something lasts from start to finish, measured with a tool rather than judged by how fast, effortful or busy the activity felt, and that 1 minute = 60 seconds, which is a genuine conceptual step because 60 is not a base-ten grouping.

activities.title: Time a real activity with start and stop aligned to the event
feedback: If the start or stop lagged or led the real event, replay it: count '3-2-1 start' together and stop on the final action. Focus on tightening the timing action; a timing slip on its own does not mean the child misunderstands duration.

If the spoken duration tracks effort ('it took ages because it was hard') but disagrees with the tool, bring attention back to the reading on the tool, then time two equally-effortful tasks that take different amounts of time so duration separates from effort.
Prompt reflection: 'You said about a minute — how do you know it was about a minute?' and 'If you had started the timer a bit late, would your answer be too much or too little?'
activities.rationale: Statutory Year 1 Measurement content asks pupils to measure and begin to record time in hours, minutes and seconds. Research locates the difficulty in measuring/recording elapsed duration rather than naming units (noting that the supporting figures come from Years 3-4 studies), so practising the act of timing a real event — starting and stopping in step — targets the hardest strand directly.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'measure and begin to record the following: ... time (hours, minutes, seconds)' (statutory Measurement content).

Duration is the weakest strand of children's time understanding in Years 3-4 (only ~50% full understanding vs ~60% for measurement/succession), and measuring duration using the hands of a clock is specifically among the challenging items — so measuring/recording elapsed time, not naming units, is where difficulty concentrates.
learnerActions: Pick a short, real activity to time (e.g. writing your name five times, tidying a small tray, building a block tower).

Choose the right tool: for an open-ended duration use a stopwatch or a seconds count/large seconds display; a fixed one-minute sand timer is best for checking whether something takes about a minute or comparing against its known span.
Hold the visible timing tool ready.
Count '3-2-1 start' and start the tool at the exact moment the activity begins.
Stop the tool the instant the activity finishes (on the last action).
Read off and say the duration in simple terms, e.g. 'about half a minute', 'about 40 seconds', 'a bit more than a minute'.
Repeat with a second activity and compare which took longer.
activities.intendedInsight: 'How long' is a quantity you can capture with a tool by aligning start and stop with the event, not a feeling guessed from how fast or how effortful the activity was.

activities.title: Build 1 minute = 60 seconds by counting a one-minute timer
feedback: If the child treats 'a minute' and '60 seconds' as different amounts, pair the two directly: count seconds in time with a seconds display while the one-minute timer empties so the same span is both about '60 seconds' and 'one minute'.
Probe: 'The sand timer ran out — how many seconds was that?' to check the minute is linked to a count of 60.
Note that a sand timer and a stopwatch may not match exactly depending on the tools; treat 'would it agree?' as something to observe and discuss, not a guaranteed result.
activities.rationale: Children reason about time with discrete whole-number thinking and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so 1 minute = 60 seconds is a real conceptual step. Counting seconds against a one-minute timer makes the grouping concrete rather than asserted.
sourceClaims: Children treat time with discrete whole-number reasoning and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so the relationship 1 minute = 60 seconds is a genuine conceptual step rather than an obvious fact.
learnerActions: Turn over a one-minute sand timer and count the seconds aloud (or follow a seconds display) until the sand runs out.

Notice that the count reaches about 60 as the minute ends, provided each number is paced to one second (e.g. by following a seconds display); young children counting freely often go faster and reach a higher number.
Say the relationship: 'one minute is the same as 60 seconds.'
Check with a second tool: 'If we used the stopwatch instead, would it agree?'
activities.intendedInsight: A minute and 60 seconds are the same amount of time, not two different amounts — the 60-grouping is something you can experience by counting it out.

activities.title: Compare two durations and read a growing span, not the end number
feedback: If the child reports the final stopwatch reading as 'how long it took' on a watch that was not started from zero, always zero or note the start, and use a bar that grows from the start so duration is its length.

OPTIONAL supportive display: a bar that grows as time passes and a 60-second ring that fills once per minute can make the accruing duration and the minute visible; a mis-timed start would visibly shorten or stretch the bar. These are illustrative aids, not required equipment — sand timers and a counting track of seconds work too.
activities.rationale: A common error is reading the number currently showing as the duration while ignoring where timing began. Representing duration as an accruing length from the start addresses this by making the span itself the thing being measured. This representation is a research-informed design proposal; no source directly tests it.
learnerActions: Time two different activities and record each duration ('about 20 seconds', 'about a minute').
Represent each duration as a length — e.g. a bar that grows FROM the start, or line up the two timings side by side.
Decide which activity took longer by comparing the lengths.
If using a stopwatch, note or zero the start first, so the duration is the span covered, not whichever number happens to show at the end.
activities.intendedInsight: Duration is the amount of time that elapsed between start and stop — represented as a length that grows from the start — not simply the number currently displayed.

constraints: This is a procedural, embodied skill: assess by WATCHING the child start and stop the tool with the event, not by asking them to recite the procedure or a fact. Reciting '1 minute = 60 seconds' is not by itself evidence they can measure.

Prefer sand timers first — duration is visible as the sand falls — before digital stopwatches; a fixed sand timer and a stopwatch give different experiences (checking a known span vs capturing an open-ended duration) and can be compared, with neither being universally necessary.
Record informally ('about 2 minutes', 'a bit more than a minute') rather than demanding precision at this age.

A recognition/ordering quiz (reading a stopwatch value, ordering activities by length) can check whether a child reads a duration, but does not elicit the act of measuring — starting and stopping in step with an event — which is the main objective.
A static labelled timer image can name the parts of a tool but does not let the child time an event or watch a duration accrue; use it as a scaffold, not as the performance itself.
Sand timers and stopwatches are concrete tools; a screen bar/ring display is one optional representation of the same idea, not a replacement for timing a real activity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'possible/poor' catalog-fit judgements included universal-sounding claims ('a fixed quiz cannot assess the ACT of measuring', '3D adds nothing', 'measuring is not an in-role dialogue'). These have been softened to scoped affordances/limits: a quiz can check reading a duration but not independent timing; a static image labels parts but does not show accrual. No comparative efficacy or necessity beyond these objective limits is asserted.

Activity 3 (compare durations / growing span) had no original sources[].claim directly supporting its end-number-error remedy or length representation; sourceClaims is [] and the rationale flags it as an untested design proposal.

Tool roles were clarified: a fixed one-minute sand timer is suited to checking/comparing a known span, while an open-ended activity duration is better captured with a stopwatch or seconds count — the original allowed both tools.
The elapsed-bar and 60-second ring were retained as OPTIONAL illustrative feedback, not as a mandatory mechanism.
Error-pattern reteach links in the source assessment metadata are left unchanged and are not reproduced as learner-facing content.
Research percentages come from Years 3-4 studies; the age-matched direction (elapsed-duration measuring is the hard strand) is retained but the figures are not specific to ages 5-6.

probeDeeper: 'You said about a minute — how do you know it was about a minute?'
'If you had started the timer a bit late, would your answer be too much or too little?'
'The sand timer ran out — how many seconds was that? If we used the stopwatch instead, would it agree?'
assess.correctAnswer: Starts the tool as the activity begins and stops it as it ends; reads and reports the duration in sensible units ('about half a minute', 'about 40 seconds'); counts roughly to 60 as the one-minute timer empties, showing a beginning grasp that 1 minute = 60 seconds.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports how long by how fast or how much happened rather than elapsed time — says the tidy-up 'took ages' because it was effortful, contradicting what the timer showed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bring attention back to the tool — read the bar/sand — and time two equally-effortful tasks that take different amounts, so duration is separated from effort and speed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The spoken duration tracks effort/speed and disagrees with the tool reading

errorPatterns.pattern: Starts or stops the timer out of step with the activity — begins timing late, or lets it run on after finishing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the procedure only — count '3-2-1 start' together and stop on the last action; do not reteach the concept of duration, just tighten the timing action.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watch the start/stop taps lag or lead the true start and end of the event

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the number currently on the stopwatch as the duration, ignoring where timing began
errorPatterns.nextMove: Always zero (or note) the start; use a bar that grows FROM the start so the duration is its length, not the end number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a stopwatch not started from zero, reports the end reading as 'how long it took'

responseLevels.gap: Guesses duration from effort or speed and cannot operate the tool in step with the event.
responseLevels.full: Independently starts and stops the tool with the event, reports the duration in sensible units, and shows a beginning grasp that 1 minute = 60 seconds, transferring to a new activity.
responseLevels.partial: Times an activity with help and reports a rough duration, but the start/stop drifts, or cannot yet link a minute to 60 seconds.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set a real timing task and WATCH (don't ask the child to explain the procedure): 'Here is a one-minute sand timer and a stopwatch. Time how long it takes you to write your name five times — start the timer as you begin and stop it as you finish, then tell me about how long it took. Then turn the one-minute sand timer over and count how many seconds go by until the sand runs out.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child START and STOP reveals whether they align the tool with the event rather than reporting whatever number shows; the sand-timer count reveals whether 'a minute' is connected to 60 seconds. Neither can be faked by reciting a fact.

sources.claim: Year 1 pupils should 'measure and begin to record the following: ... time (hours, minutes, seconds)' (statutory Measurement content).
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics, Year 1 Measurement (statutory), gov.uk

sources.claim: Duration is the weakest strand of children's time understanding in Years 3-4 (only ~50% full understanding vs ~60% for measurement/succession), and measuring duration using the hands of a clock is specifically among the challenging items — so measuring/recording elapsed time, not naming units, is where difficulty concentrates.
sources.source: Thomas, Clarke, McDonough & Clarkson (2023), 'Assessing students' understanding of time concepts in Years 3 and 4', Mathematics Education Research Journal

sources.claim: Children treat time with discrete whole-number reasoning and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so the relationship 1 minute = 60 seconds is a genuine conceptual step rather than an obvious fact.
sources.source: Earnest, Gonzales & Plant (2018), 'Time as a Measure', Journal of Numerical Cognition 4(1)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Earthquake Safety

- **Standards — UK (DfE, England):** Not a UK curriculum science/geography topic — earthquake drills are a Pacific-Rim/US life-skill rather than an England statutory standard. The closest UK home is PSHE/personal safety (following safety instructions, knowing a trusted adult), taught here as preparedness enrichment.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No NGSS PE covers safety drills (NGSS is science content, not preparedness). This is a preparedness/life-skill anchored on official emergency-management guidance — the internationally recommended response 'Drop, Cover, and Hold On' (USGS, FEMA/Ready.gov, Earthquake Country Alliance / Great ShakeOut).

- **Operational details:** The goal is a simple, rehearsable response, not understanding causes. Teach the three steps as a rhyme/routine — DROP to hands and knees, take COVER under a sturdy table (or against an interior wall away from windows if no table), and HOLD ON until the shaking stops — then tell a trusted adult. Ground the WHY in the key fact that most injuries come from falling and flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, shelves), not from the building collapsing, so getting low and covered protects your head and neck. Explicitly teach what NOT to do: do NOT run outside (windows and exterior walls are the most dangerous place), and standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings. Practise by rehearsing the moves — real muscle memory is the point (experts stress you react faster if you've actually practised). Keep it calm and matter-of-fact; name a trusted adult to tell.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/procedural, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can perform Drop, Cover, Hold On on cue, say why (falling objects), and name a trusted adult; they are NOT learning earthquake causes here. Confront the dangerous myths 'run outside' and 'stand in a doorway', and reassure that most buildings do not collapse.
bestPractices: Teach the three steps as a memorable routine/rhyme (Drop → Cover → Hold On) and rehearse them physically
Ground the WHY in the key fact: most injuries are from falling/flying objects, not collapse — so get low and cover head/neck
Explicitly teach the myth-busting 'do NOT run outside' and 'a doorway is not safest' with simple reasons
Keep the tone calm and matter-of-fact and reassure that most buildings do not collapse — preparedness, not fear
Always end the routine with 'tell a trusted adult' and have each child name theirs
Prioritise real physical practice (a drill) — experts note a fast response depends on having actually practised
keyRepresentations: A three-step Drop-Cover-Hold-On poster/routine
A room scene flagging safe spots (under a sturdy table; interior wall) vs danger (windows, exterior walls, tall shelves)
A simple 'falling objects' picture showing what the cover protects against
A 'do / don't' pairing (under table vs run outside / doorway)
commonMisconceptions: 'Run outside as fast as you can' — dangerous; windows and exterior walls are the most likely to hurt you; stay put and cover
'Stand in a doorway' — outdated advice; in modern buildings a doorway is no safer and you can't brace — under a table is safer
'The main danger is the building falling down' — most injuries are from falling/flying objects; most buildings don't collapse
'Just hide anywhere' — choose a sturdy cover and hold on; not all spots are equally safe
'The safest thing is to freeze and wait' — act immediately: drop, cover, hold on the moment shaking starts

learn.summary: Earthquake safety for ages 5–7: children over-learn a simple, rehearsable response — DROP to hands and knees, take COVER under a sturdy table (or against an interior wall away from windows if no table), HOLD ON until shaking stops, then tell a trusted adult. The teaching objective is embodied muscle memory via a real physical drill; an on-screen timed rehearsal is a useful primer and companion but is a scaffold that teaches the sequence and reasoning, not a substitute for actually practising the moves. The 'why' is grounded in a key fact: most injuries come from falling and flying objects, not building collapse. Act immediately rather than freezing, and choose sturdy cover rather than any spot. Myths to confront calmly: do NOT run outside, and a doorway is not safest in modern buildings. Keep the tone matter-of-fact and reassuring — preparedness, not fear.

activities.title: Classroom Drop-Cover-Hold-On drill (real practice)
feedback: If a child heads for the door or outside: model that exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; stay and take cover until shaking stops

If a child goes to a doorway: explain doorways are not stronger than other parts of a modern building, do not protect you from falling or flying objects, and a swinging door could hit you — under a sturdy table is safer
If a child freezes or stays standing: act immediately — drop, cover and hold on the moment shaking starts; waiting leaves you exposed to falling objects
If a child hides somewhere that is not sturdy: choose a sturdy table or desk — not all spots give the same protection from falling objects
If a child lets go or crawls out during a pause: hold on and stay put until it's fully over — shaking can pause and restart
activities.rationale: The objective is a procedural, decision-under-pressure routine that experts say depends on having physically practised. A teacher-led drill with a real desk rehearses the actual physical moves — the dropping, crawling and holding on — that on-screen tapping does not reproduce.
sourceClaims: The recommended response is Drop, Cover, and Hold On; the main danger is falling and flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, bookcases), not building collapse, so get low and protect your head/neck under a sturdy table or against an interior wall away from windows

Do NOT run outside — exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings; the 'triangle of life' advice is discredited and potentially dangerous; practising makes a fast response more likely
learnerActions: On a calm cue such as 'earthquake, drop!', physically DROP to hands and knees straight away rather than freezing
Crawl under a real, sturdy table or desk to take COVER, protecting head and neck
HOLD ON to a table leg and stay put until the teacher says the shaking has stopped
Practise staying under cover through a brief pause (shaking can start again) rather than crawling out early
When no table is available, practise moving against an interior wall away from windows and shelves and covering head/neck
After the all-clear, each child names a trusted adult they would tell, and says a short sentence they'd say
activities.intendedInsight: A fast, automatic safe response comes from having physically rehearsed the moves — act immediately, get low under sturdy cover, and protect the head and neck from falling and flying objects.

activities.title: On-screen rehearsal: the room starts to shake
feedback: Choosing to run to the window makes a lamp or vase topple harmlessly nearby (a near-miss, not scary), showing exactly why being low and covered matters
Choosing the doorway shows a gentle caption that a doorway is not the safest place in a modern building
Completing drop → cover → hold on confirms the correct sequence and offers a faster replay
activities.rationale: A timed rehearse-the-response scene teaches both the sequence and the reasoning, and primes the physical drill. Immediate consequence feedback (an object falling) makes the 'why' concrete. This is a digital primer that should point to real physical practice.
sourceClaims: The recommended response is Drop, Cover, and Hold On; the main danger is falling and flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, bookcases), not building collapse, so get low and protect your head/neck under a sturdy table or against an interior wall away from windows

Do NOT run outside — exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings; the 'triangle of life' advice is discredited and potentially dangerous; practising makes a fast response more likely
learnerActions: Watch a cosy room scene begin to shake, then act fast
Tap DROP so the character folds to hands and knees
Drag the character under a sturdy table to take COVER
HOLD ON as the room rattles, waiting until the shaking stops
Replay a few times to get faster at the sequence
After shaking stops, respond to the prompt 'tell a trusted adult'
activities.intendedInsight: The three steps happen in order and under time pressure; low-and-covered protects you because loose objects fall during shaking.

activities.title: Sequence and sort: safe vs not safe
feedback: If steps are out of order: re-show the routine — you get low first, then covered, then hold on until it's over
If 'run outside' is sorted as safe: exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place during shaking
If the 'why' is missed: the table protects your head and neck from falling and flying objects, which cause most injuries
activities.rationale: Sequencing and sorting assess knowledge of the steps and the myth-busting as a companion check. This format verifies recognition and recall of the procedure; it does not elicit the physical, timed response, so it complements rather than replaces the drill.
sourceClaims: The recommended response is Drop, Cover, and Hold On; the main danger is falling and flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, bookcases), not building collapse, so get low and protect your head/neck under a sturdy table or against an interior wall away from windows

Do NOT run outside — exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings; the 'triangle of life' advice is discredited and potentially dangerous; practising makes a fast response more likely
learnerActions: Put the three steps in order: Drop → Cover → Hold On
Sort action cards into 'safe' and 'not safe' (e.g. get under a sturdy table = safe; run outside / stand in a doorway = not safe)
Answer 'Why get under a table?' and choose the reason: to protect from falling objects
Explain in your own words why to move away from windows and shelves during shaking
activities.intendedInsight: Each safe or unsafe choice connects to a reason: get low under sturdy cover because falling and flying objects cause most injuries; don't run outside because moving during shaking can make you fall and the area near exterior walls and windows is the most dangerous place; and don't go to a doorway because in modern buildings it is no stronger than other places and does not protect you from falling or flying objects.

activities.title: Label the safe spots in the room
feedback: Tapping the window reveals that windows and exterior walls are the most dangerous place during shaking
Tapping under the sturdy table confirms it protects your head and neck from falling objects
The poster reinforces the order: drop, then cover, then hold on
activities.rationale: A labelled safe-spot scene teaches the decision and the reasons. It is a scaffold: a still, tappable image conveys where to go but cannot rehearse the timed, automatic response, so pair it with the physical drill.
sourceClaims: The recommended response is Drop, Cover, and Hold On; the main danger is falling and flying objects (TVs, lamps, glass, bookcases), not building collapse, so get low and protect your head/neck under a sturdy table or against an interior wall away from windows

Do NOT run outside — exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings; the 'triangle of life' advice is discredited and potentially dangerous; practising makes a fast response more likely
learnerActions: Explore a room scene and tap spots flagged safe or danger
Reveal why each spot is safe (under the sturdy table) or dangerous (by the window, near tall shelves, exterior wall)
Tap through a Drop-Cover-Hold-On poster where each of the three steps animates
Point to where you would go first if the ground started shaking
activities.intendedInsight: Builds the mental map of safe vs dangerous places and the three-step routine before or alongside rehearsing it.

activities.title: Coached walk-through with a calm helper
feedback: If a child suggests running outside: the helper gently explains it's safest to stay low and covered until shaking stops
If a child is anxious: the helper reassures that most buildings do not collapse and that practising helps you feel ready
Praise naming a trusted adult and a short, clear message to tell them
activities.rationale: A calm helper persona can coach the steps, address worries and secure the 'tell a trusted adult' habit. Talking through the steps supports recall and reassurance; it does not itself elicit the physical performance, so use it to supplement the drill.
sourceClaims: Do NOT run outside — exterior walls and windows are the most dangerous place; standing in a doorway is not recommended in modern buildings; the 'triangle of life' advice is discredited and potentially dangerous; practising makes a fast response more likely
learnerActions: Respond to a friendly safety helper who asks 'What would you do first if the ground shook?'
Talk through each step aloud as the helper coaches: drop, cover, hold on
Say who your trusted adult is and what you would tell them afterwards
Ask the helper any worries, and hear the reassurance that most buildings do not collapse
activities.intendedInsight: Rehearses recalling and explaining the routine and names a trusted adult, keeping the tone calm and reassuring.

constraints: The real learning objective is embodied muscle memory: a teacher-led physical drill with a real desk where children actually drop, cover and hold on is the primary activity. On-screen rehearsals, sorting tasks, labelled images and helper dialogue are scaffolds/primers that teach the sequence and reasoning but do not rehearse the physical moves.

Sequencing, sorting and choose-the-reason formats verify recognition and recall of the steps and myths; they do not elicit the fast, timed physical response, so do not treat them as proof a child can perform the drill under pressure.
Teach children to act immediately rather than freeze, and to choose a sturdy table/desk as cover — not just any spot, since not all spots give equal protection from falling objects.
Keep the tone calm and matter-of-fact throughout — this is preparedness, not fear. Always reassure that most buildings do not collapse.
Always end any rehearsal by naming a trusted adult to tell; have each child name theirs.
This topic teaches a rehearsable safety response only, not earthquake causes. Do not drift into explaining why earthquakes happen.
Teach 'hold on until the shaking fully stops' — shaking can pause and restart; leaving cover during a pause is unsafe.

Myths to confront with simple reasons: 'run outside' (moving during shaking can make you fall, and the area near exterior walls and windows is most dangerous), 'stand in a doorway' (not stronger in modern buildings and gives no protection from falling or flying objects), 'just hide anywhere' (needs sturdy cover) and 'freeze and wait' (act immediately). Avoid the discredited 'triangle of life' advice.
This is a preparedness/life-skill, not an England National Curriculum science/geography topic; its closest UK home is PSHE/personal safety. It is also not a stand-alone NGSS performance expectation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that most injuries come from falling/flying objects (not collapse) and the 'do not run outside / doorway not safest' guidance reflect the cited Earthquake Country Alliance (and USGS/FEMA-aligned) advice for typical modern, building-code-compliant structures. These recommendations can vary by building type and region; treat them as the standard guidance presented, not as universal across all structures.

The pedagogy's framing that the on-screen activities do not build true bodily reflex, and that physical practice is 'the point', is retained as the stated objective. The superiority of a physical drill over screen rehearsal for building reflex is an expert-stated rationale in the source material, not independently verified comparative efficacy here; it is presented as a narrow affordance (the drill rehearses the actual moves) rather than a proven head-to-head result.
The UK (PSHE) and US (not an NGSS performance expectation) standards framing comes from a source marked unverified in the row; retained as context, not as a verified claim.

probeDeeper: Why did you get under the table instead of standing by the window?
The shaking pauses for a second — do you get up now or stay put? Why?
After the shaking stops, who would you tell, and what would you say?
Why is running out of the door while it's still shaking not the safest choice?
assess.correctAnswer: The child immediately DROPS to hands and knees, takes COVER under the sturdy table (or against an interior wall away from windows and shelves), and HOLDS ON until the shaking stops — staying put rather than running outside or to a doorway — and afterwards says they'd tell a trusted adult.

errorPatterns.pattern: Runs outside as soon as the shaking starts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the words — model that the most dangerous place is next to exterior walls and windows; stay and take cover until shaking stops.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Heads for the door or outdoors the moment shaking begins.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stands in a doorway to be safe (outdated advice)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Doorways aren't safer in modern buildings; get down under a sturdy table.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Goes to a doorway instead of getting under cover.

errorPatterns.pattern: Freezes or stays standing near windows and shelves
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the drop-cover-hold sequence; falling and flying objects are the main danger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Stays upright beside hazards; doesn't drop or cover.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops and covers but lets go or crawls out before the shaking stops
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hold on and stay put until it's fully over — shaking can pause and start again.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Leaves cover during a pause in the shaking.

responseLevels.gap: Freezes, runs outside, or heads to a doorway/window; doesn't drop or take cover.
responseLevels.full: Promptly drops, covers under sturdy shelter away from windows and shelves, and holds on until shaking stops (not running out or to a doorway), and explains it's because of falling objects — naming a trusted adult to tell afterwards.
responseLevels.partial: Performs part of the sequence (e.g. drops and covers) but lets go early or hesitates about running outside, and can't fully explain why to stay away from windows.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Let's pretend the ground has just started shaking hard, right now. Show me exactly what you would do, from the moment you feel it until the shaking stops. (Set the room up with a sturdy table, a window, and some shelves.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can recite 'drop, cover, hold on' yet, when actually acting, run to the window or door or stand in a doorway. Watching the movements — and where they go — separates knowing the words from performing the safe procedure; running outside and heading for a doorway are the documented unsafe responses.
