pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Plate Boundaries — how plates pushing together (convergent), pulling apart (divergent), or sliding past (transform) create the forces that trigger earthquakes and volcanoes, and how mountains form where plates collide.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement):** In England this is KS2 **Geography** (physical geography: volcanoes and earthquakes; mountains), not KS2 science; the force mechanism is DfE **KS3**. Frame as the causal engine behind the hazard patterns.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** Boundary processes are middle-school content — **MS-ESS2-2** (geoscience processes over time-scales) and **MS-ESS2-3** (past plate motions); at elementary the anchor is **4-ESS2-2** (features cluster in bands along boundaries — DCI ESS2.B). This topic operationalises WHY the 4-ESS2-2 pattern exists. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisites 'Tectonic Plates' and 'Why Earthquakes Happen'. Deliver the three boundary MOTIONS and, crucially, map each to its RESULTS: convergent → collisions/subduction → mountains, deep quakes, explosive volcanoes; divergent → spreading → ridges, new crust, gentler volcanism; transform → grinding past → big earthquakes (usually no volcanoes). The load-bearing idea is that different motions produce DIFFERENT hazards — so boundary TYPE predicts what you get.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (early-formal, cause→effect modelling). Children can pair a motion with a result given a model but tend to think every boundary makes both volcanoes and quakes identically. Success = name the three boundary motions and explain which hazards/landforms each produces (esp. mountains at collisions, volcanoes where plates dive under or pull apart).
bestPractices: Teach motion-to-result as a small predictive rule set (three motions, each with its own signature landforms/hazards) rather than three isolated definitions.
Use hands-on plate models (foam blocks, hands, or biscuits/graham crackers with a soft filling) so pushing together, pulling apart and sliding are physically enacted before naming.
Make the collision→mountains link vivid (crumpling two sheets/rugs to raise a ridge) and the subduction→explosive-volcano link explicit (one plate dives, melts, magma rises).
Distinguish transform boundaries as the big-earthquake-but-usually-no-volcano case (e.g. San Andreas) to break the 'boundaries always do both' assumption.
Continually tie back to the map: place real boundary examples (Himalayas, Mid-Atlantic Ridge, San Andreas) so the abstract motions have real locations.
keyRepresentations: Three side-view boundary diagrams: convergent (collision/subduction), divergent (spreading ridge), transform (sliding)
Crumpling paper/rugs or colliding blocks to raise mountains (collision model)
Biscuit/graham-cracker-on-frosting model for pushing, pulling, sliding plates
A map linking each boundary type to real examples and its hazard signature
commonMisconceptions: Every plate boundary produces both volcanoes and earthquakes in the same way (the type of motion determines which hazards/landforms occur).
Mountains are pushed up by volcanoes only (many great ranges form by plate COLLISION crumpling crust, without volcanoes).
At divergent boundaries the plates leave a permanent empty gap (new crust forms from rising magma to fill the spreading gap).
Transform boundaries make volcanoes (they mainly cause earthquakes as plates grind past — usually no volcanism).
Boundaries are single thin lines with no width (they are zones where deformation, quakes and volcanism spread over a region).

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: how the three plate-boundary motions (convergent/pushing together, divergent/pulling apart, transform/sliding past) each produce different hazards and landforms, so the TYPE of motion predicts what you get. The load-bearing idea is that if everything else stays the same and only the motion changes, the results change: collisions build mountains, and where a denser ocean plate dives under another (subduction) you get volcanoes that are often explosive; spreading opens ridges with new crust, gentler volcanism and mostly smaller earthquakes; sliding can cause big earthquakes, usually with no volcano. Earthquakes happen at all three types. When plates push together, the kind of crust (ocean or continent) also affects what forms. Activities centre on enacting the motion and predicting the result before revealing it, then anchoring each rule to a real place (Himalayas, Mid-Atlantic Ridge, San Andreas). This operationalises WHY earthquakes and volcanoes cluster in bands along boundaries.

activities.title: Drive one boundary, three ways: predict then see the result
feedback: If a learner predicts the same outcome for all three motions, show the three results side by side (mountains or volcanoes / new crust / big earthquakes with no volcano) and ask what changed in the model — only the motion. Note that earthquakes happen at all three, but the landforms and volcanoes differ.
If a learner expects a volcano at the sliding boundary, point out the plates grind past without one diving under or pulling apart, so there is no path for magma — so you mainly get earthquakes.
If a learner thinks pulling apart leaves a permanent empty gap, highlight the magma welling up to fill the spreading gap and form new crust.
If a learner says mountains need volcanoes, replay the collision case where crust crumples upward into a range with no volcano.
activities.rationale: Treating motion→result as a small predictive rule set (three motions, each with its own signature), enacted and predicted before revealing, is intended to target the dominant misconception that all boundaries behave identically. A 'predict first' step is intended to prompt the learner to commit to the rule and to notice when their mental model mismatches the outcome. An interactive boundary where the result recomputes as the motion changes is intended to make the cause→effect link concrete; this is one medium that may help, not the only possible one, and its effectiveness here is a proposal rather than a tested result.
sourceClaims: The three plate-boundary types (convergent, divergent, transform) produce distinct hazards and landforms: collisions build mountains, subduction and spreading produce volcanoes, transform boundaries cause earthquakes.
learnerActions: Work with a single boundary between two plates that has a motion selector: PUSH (together), PULL (apart), SLIDE (past).
Before running each motion, write or say a prediction: 'If I push these plates together, I think I'll get ___.'

Run PUSH and watch the crust buckle and crumple upward into a mountain range; in a second case, where a denser ocean plate meets another plate, watch it dive under, heat up and release water so that rock above it partly melts, and a volcano (often explosive) grow.
Run PULL and watch a ridge crack open with magma welling up to make brand-new ground and gentle volcanism.
Run SLIDE and watch the plates lock, stress build, and SNAP into a big earthquake — with no volcano.
Attach real-place tags as you experiment: Himalayas (collision), Mid-Atlantic Ridge (spreading), San Andreas (sliding).
State the big insight in your own words: in this model, the same two plates give different results when only the way they move is changed (in real places, the kind of crust also matters).
activities.intendedInsight: Boundary TYPE (the kind of motion) predicts the hazard and landform; it is not that every boundary does the same thing. Convergent → mountains / subduction volcanoes / deep quakes; divergent → ridge, new crust, gentle volcanism, mostly smaller shallow quakes; transform → big earthquakes, usually no volcano. Earthquakes happen at all three; at convergent boundaries, the kind of crust decides whether you mainly get collision mountains or subduction volcanoes.

activities.title: Hands-on plate models with everyday materials
feedback: If the crumple model doesn't raise a ridge, push more slowly and firmly so the sheets buckle upward rather than slide flat.
If a learner can't explain the subduction volcano, trace the chain aloud: plate dives → heats up and releases water → rock above it partly melts → magma rises → volcano.
Ask the learner to match each physical model to a real place and its hazard signature.
activities.rationale: Physically enacting the three motions before naming them can ground the vocabulary in experienced action and make the collision and subduction mechanisms vivid. Tactile models and screen models offer different experiences; the hands-on version is a complement, not a substitute, for a driveable diagram, and neither is established by the sources as the required medium.
sourceClaims: The three plate-boundary types (convergent, divergent, transform) produce distinct hazards and landforms: collisions build mountains, subduction and spreading produce volcanoes, transform boundaries cause earthquakes.
learnerActions: Enact pushing together, pulling apart, and sliding past using foam blocks, your two hands, or biscuits/graham crackers resting on a soft filling (e.g. frosting).
Crumple two sheets of paper or two rugs by pushing them together to raise a ridge — model how collision crumples crust into mountains.

For subduction, push two blocks together and let one slide under the other; describe how the diving plate heats up and releases water, which makes the hot rock above it partly melt, feeding magma that rises to a volcano.
Name each motion only after you have physically done it, then predict what hazard or landform it would create.
activities.intendedInsight: The abstract motions become physical actions, and the collision→mountains and subduction→volcano links become something the learner has built with their hands before naming.

activities.title: Labelled cross-sections with reveal and drill-down
feedback: If a learner picks the wrong flap for 'mountains without volcanoes', contrast collision (crust crumples upward) with subduction (one plate dives and releases water, so rock above it partly melts to feed a volcano).
Reinforce that a cross-section is a slice through a boundary zone, which has width, not a single thin line.
activities.rationale: Labelled cross-sections cleanly present the motion→result mapping and serve as strong reference material. A fixed diagram is not manipulable like a driveable model, but with reveal and drill-down it still teaches the mapping and the subduction chain. Use it alongside the interactive and hands-on work rather than as a replacement for predicting-then-doing.
sourceClaims: The three plate-boundary types (convergent, divergent, transform) produce distinct hazards and landforms: collisions build mountains, subduction and spreading produce volcanoes, transform boundaries cause earthquakes.
learnerActions: Study three labelled side-view cross-sections: convergent (collision/subduction), divergent (spreading ridge), transform (sliding past).
Tap or lift a flap on each to reveal its motion, its hazards/landforms, and a real example.
Answer targeted reveal prompts such as 'Which boundary makes mountains without volcanoes?' (collision) before checking.
Drill into the subduction diagram to see one plate diving and releasing water at depth, rock above it partly melting, and magma rising.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference mapping of motion→result across all three boundary types, with the subduction mechanism made explicit.

activities.title: Consolidate and sort: match, categorize, sequence
feedback: Correct answer to the diagnostic: the friend is wrong — what happens depends on how the plates move. Push together (convergent) → mountains, and a plate can dive under, releasing water so that rock above it partly melts to feed volcanoes; pull apart (divergent) → magma rises to make new crust and volcanoes; slide past (transform) → mainly earthquakes, usually no volcanoes. Earthquakes can happen at all three, but the type of movement controls the landforms and whether volcanoes form.
If a learner gives one generic result for every boundary, place push/pull/slide outcomes side by side (mountains / new crust / earthquakes).
If a learner treats earthquakes/volcanoes as unrelated to plate movement, stress that the grinding, colliding and spreading AT boundaries is exactly what triggers them.
If a learner thinks collision mountains appear quickly or in one event, note that uplift is slow, happening over millions of years of continued pushing.

Probe deeper: What rises to fill the gap where plates pull apart, and what does it build? Why big earthquakes but usually no volcanoes where plates slide past? What forms when two plates push straight into each other? How long does a mountain range take to rise at a collision boundary?
activities.rationale: Matching, categorizing and sequencing consolidate the three-way structure and check that the learner can apply the rules to novel places. These tasks verify the rules rather than let the learner discover them, so they suit consolidation after the enactive and interactive work. A sort or match can check classification but does not itself elicit physical handling or a spoken explanation, so pair it with the diagnostic question, which discriminates learners who can list boundary types but still assume identical outcomes.
sourceClaims: The three plate-boundary types (convergent, divergent, transform) produce distinct hazards and landforms: collisions build mountains, subduction and spreading produce volcanoes, transform boundaries cause earthquakes.
learnerActions: Match each boundary type to its hazard/landform.
Categorize real places by boundary type: sort Himalayas (collision), Iceland/Mid-Atlantic Ridge (spreading), San Andreas (sliding).
Sequence a subduction chain in order: plate dives → heats up and releases water → rock above it partly melts → magma rises → volcano erupts.

Answer the diagnostic: 'At one place two plates push together; at another they slide past. A friend says it doesn't matter how plates meet — you get the same thing everywhere. Do you agree? What differs depending on HOW they meet?'
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall and correct application of the motion→feature rules, and explicit rejection of the 'same everywhere' idea by explaining what differs by motion type.

activities.title: Extension: 3D block model of subduction and collision
feedback: Ask the learner to point to where the diving plate releases water and the rock above it partly melts, and where magma rises, as they rotate the model.
Prompt: which view (3D block or 2D slice) helped you see the subduction depth, and which helped you read the labels?
activities.rationale: A rotatable 3D model can add a depth perspective on subduction and collision for learners who want it. This is an enhancement; 2D cross-sections are a standard and sufficient teaching form, so treat 3D as optional extension rather than required.
learnerActions: If available, manipulate a 3D plate-block model you can push, pull, and slide, and rotate to view from any angle.
Look along the depth of the model to see a subducting plate diving beneath another.
Compare the 3D depth view with the 2D cross-sections you used earlier and describe what each view shows more clearly.
activities.intendedInsight: Subduction and collision happen in three dimensions; a depth view can make the diving plate easier to picture, complementing the cross-section view.

constraints: Target age 9–11; checkpoint is early-formal cause→effect modelling (name the three motions and explain which hazards/landforms each produces).
Prerequisites assumed: 'Tectonic Plates' and 'Why Earthquakes Happen'.

Standards placement differs by system: in England, plate-boundary hazards and mountain formation sit in KS2 Geography with the force mechanism at KS3; in NGSS the boundary processes are middle-school (MS-ESS2-2, MS-ESS2-3), while grade-4 DCI ESS2.B covers the clustering pattern that this topic explains. Frame accordingly.

Address the key misconceptions explicitly: that every boundary makes both volcanoes and earthquakes identically; that mountains are made only by volcanoes; that divergent boundaries leave a permanent empty gap; that transform boundaries make volcanoes; and that boundaries are single thin lines rather than zones with width.

Matching/categorizing/sequencing tasks verify the rules but do not themselves elicit independent construction of the model or physical handling — use them after enactive and predictive work, not instead of it.
Paper, rug, biscuit/cracker and foam-block models are approximations of real crust; name what each stands for and don't treat the model's behaviour as identical to real rock.

Interactive 'predict then act', hands-on, reveal-flap and 3D examples are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; none is the single required medium, and the sources do not establish that any one is more effective than another.
State in learner-facing feedback that mountain uplift at collisions is slow, over millions of years of continued pushing, not a single fast event.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source row marks the USGS 'distinct hazards by boundary type' claim and the DfE KS2 geography placement claim as verified:false; treat these as unconfirmed. The NGSS placement claim is marked verified:true in the row but has not been re-checked here.

The original 'ideal' recommendation framed a driveable interactive as uniquely cementing the rules; this rewrite keeps the interactive as a strong option but does not assert it is the only medium that can teach, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

Non-preferred alternatives (cross-sections/interactive image, consolidation sort, 3D block model) are retained as separate activities with their stated pedagogical purposes; the 'conversation' format was judged a poor fit and is noted in omissions.

Simplifications to check with a subject reviewer: transform boundaries are described as 'usually no volcano', which matches the source's general rule but has exceptions in real settings; subduction volcanism arises from fluid-induced melting of the mantle wedge, simplified here as 'the diving plate melts' for this age group.
The NGSS standards-placement claim is used only for standards framing in the constraints/context, not as a sourceClaim supporting any activity's teaching principle.
Independent final review confirmed the three prior corrections are applied at their learner-facing locations and found no additional critical learner-facing errors.

Why do you get big earthquakes but not usually volcanoes where plates just slide past each other?
What forms when two plates push straight into each other?
How long does a mountain range take to rise at a collision boundary?

Where they push together (convergent) you get mountains, and one plate can slide under another and melt to feed volcanoes; where they pull apart (divergent) magma rises to make new crust and volcanoes; where they slide past (transform) you mainly get earthquakes. assess.diagnosticPrompt: At one place two plates are pushing together; at another they're sliding past each other. A friend says, 'It doesn't matter how the plates meet — you get the same thing everywhere.' Do you agree? What happens differently depending on HOW the plates meet at a boundary?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can list the boundary types yet think the result is the same everywhere. Asking what DIFFERS by movement type forces the movement→feature mapping; a child who says 'same everywhere' hasn't linked the mechanism to its outcome.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Relative Motion

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics — Motion):** Relative motion — trains and cars passing one another; describing an object's motion relative to a chosen reference point and recognising that the description depends on the observer's frame.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — Frames of Reference, extends HS-PS2 Motion and Stability):** Describing the motion of an object relative to a chosen reference frame; recognising there is no single privileged frame (foundational kinematics introduced at MS when describing motion, formalised at HS).

- **Operational details:** Relative motion is the idea that the apparent speed and direction of an object depend on the observer's own motion — there is no single 'true' motion, only motion measured relative to a chosen frame of reference. The central instructional habit to build is asking 'moving relative to what?' for every description of motion. The most powerful teaching tool is letting pupils SWITCH the observer's frame on the same scene (stand on the platform vs ride the train) and see how the description changes, supported by careful teacher language: words like 'see', 'appears', 'stationary' or 'standing still' used without naming a frame quietly reinforce the misconception that there is a privileged, absolute (usually Earth) frame. Quantitatively, relative speed is found by subtracting velocities when objects move the same way and adding them when they move towards/away from each other.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Relative motion is a threshold concept requiring the learner to decentre from their own frame: the milestone is internalising 'moving relative to what?' and accepting that there is no privileged, absolute (Earth) frame. At 11–12 this is early-formal — pupils can switch the observer on the same scene and see descriptions change, and begin the add/subtract relative-speed rule, but the intrinsic-motion intuition (and granting Earth a special status) persists well beyond this age and must be actively confronted.
bestPractices: Make 'relative to what?' a constant refrain; always name the frame, even when it is the Earth, to counter the belief that motion is absolute.
Let pupils switch frames on the SAME scenario (platform observer vs train passenger) rather than viewing a single fixed outcome — the comparison is where the concept lives.

Use the OpenStax embodied demo: a pupil stands as 'the background' while the teacher walks between them and the class; the class says 'to the right', the background pupil says 'to the left' — then state explicitly that the reference frame is the observer's viewpoint, not the background.
Use canonical everyday scenarios: two trains alongside each other, a passing car, a boat crossing a river; have pupils predict-observe-explain each observer's account.
Mind language: avoid bare 'it is moving / it is stationary'; model 'moving relative to the platform but stationary relative to the other train'.
For relative speed, build the add/subtract rule from concrete cases (two trains side by side at the same speed appear still to each other → subtract; trains approaching → add).
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side two-frame view: the same scene rendered from each observer's viewpoint
Train-alongside-train and platform scenario (the canonical relative-motion vehicle)
Labelled velocity arrows with explicit subscripts (e.g. 'train relative to platform', 'boat relative to water')
Number line for adding/subtracting velocities to get relative speed
The walk-across-the-room 'background vs viewpoint' demonstration
commonMisconceptions: Motion is intrinsic to an object — treating velocity/trajectory as a property the object 'has', not a quantity measured relative to a frame (Saltiel & Malgrange; ages 11 to university).
Distinguishing 'real' motion (dynamically caused) from 'apparent' motion ('just an optical illusion'), instead of all motion being frame-relative.
Granting the Earth a privileged or absolute frame of reference.
Treating the reference frame as the BACKGROUND/scenery of motion rather than the observer's viewpoint (OpenStax).
Treating a frame as fixed to and bounded by a concrete object ('a ball thrown can leave the reference frame'), with limited physical extent.
Assuming each observer is a separate frame even when observers are at rest relative to one another (they share a frame).

learn.summary: Relative motion for 11–12 year olds: the apparent speed and direction of an object depend on the observer's chosen frame of reference, so there is no single 'true' motion. The core instructional habit is to ask 'moving relative to what?' for every description, and the pivotal experience is switching the observer on the SAME scene (platform vs train passenger) so the description changes while nothing physical about the objects changes. Learners also build the quantitative rule: subtract the speeds for objects moving the same way, and add them for objects moving towards or away from each other in opposite directions; the same-speed same-direction case gives zero relative speed (one appears stationary). Guidance confronts persistent intuitions that motion is intrinsic, that the Earth is a privileged frame, that the reference frame is the background scenery rather than the observer's viewpoint, and that one view is the 'real' motion while another is a mere optical illusion.

activities.title: Switch the observer on the same train scene
feedback: If a learner says one train is 'really' moving, ask 'moving relative to what?' and have them re-describe it from the other train's viewpoint so each train becomes 'the mover' in turn.
When a learner reads motion off the scenery, point out the chosen frame is the observer's viewpoint, not the trees or ground; show that with two trains and no visible ground the view is symmetric.
For the same-speed, same-direction case, highlight that the relative speed reads zero, which is why Train B hangs still beside Train A's window.
For the oncoming case, draw attention to the larger relative speed and connect it to adding the speeds.
activities.rationale: The concept is that the same motion is described differently from a different frame, so letting learners change the observer and watch the apparent velocities recompute targets the 'motion is intrinsic' and 'Earth is the true frame' intuitions directly, and the scenery-vs-viewpoint feedback addresses the background misconception. Carrying the same reasoning to the passing car and boat-crossing-river cases shows the idea generalises. The frame toggle, apparent-velocity labels, subscripts and relative-speed readout are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
sourceClaims: Students treat motion as intrinsic rather than frame-relative; grant the Earth a privileged frame; treat frames as fixed to and bounded by concrete objects; many cannot apply a reference frame even after instruction.

Students assume a reference frame is the background of motion instead of the observer's viewpoint; the walk-across-the-room demo (background pupil sees 'left', class sees 'right') corrects this, concluding the frame is the viewpoint of the observer.
learnerActions: Watch a scene of two trains on parallel tracks beside a platform, with all objects at rest before the motion begins.

Choose a viewpoint — RIDE TRAIN A, RIDE TRAIN B, or STAND ON PLATFORM — and observe how the SAME physical motion is re-described from that viewpoint: e.g. riding Train A, the platform and scenery slide backwards and Train B (moving at the same speed and direction) appears frozen alongside; on the platform, both trains move.
For each viewpoint, read the apparent-velocity labels and relative-speed readout, which use explicit subscripts (e.g. 'Train B relative to Train A', 'train relative to platform').
Switch to an 'approaching/oncoming' setup and compare: two trains going the same way show a small relative speed; two oncoming trains show a large one.

Try the same frame-switch reasoning on other everyday scenarios — a car passing you on the road, or a boat crossing a river (its motion looks different relative to the water than relative to the bank) — to see the idea is not special to trains.
Before each switch, predict out loud what the chosen observer will see, then check against the scene.
State, in words, the frame for every description (e.g. 'Train B is stationary relative to Train A but moving relative to the platform').
activities.intendedInsight: The same motion looks different from different frames; nothing about the trains changes when you switch observers — only who is watching. Motion is always 'relative to' a chosen frame, not an intrinsic property, and the Earth/ground is just one frame among many.

activities.title: Walk-across-the-room: viewpoint vs background
feedback: If pupils equate the frame with the background, contrast the seated class (walker moving) with the pupil walking alongside (walker staying beside them): the background did not change, only the observer's motion did. If pupils cite the class and the background pupil saying 'right' versus 'left', point out that this is a difference in facing direction, not in frame.

For the side-by-side walkers, note that 'the other one looks stationary' (relative speed zero) surfaces the frame idea, whereas 'the same speed as we see them' reflects an absolute-motion assumption to be examined.
activities.rationale: This embodied demonstration gives learners a direct, physical experience of two observers in different states of motion describing one walk differently but equally validly, confronting the misconception that the frame is the background scenery and separating a genuine frame difference from a mere left/right facing difference. The predict-observe-explain structure makes each observer's account explicit.
sourceClaims: Students assume a reference frame is the background of motion instead of the observer's viewpoint; the walk-across-the-room demo (background pupil sees 'left', class sees 'right') corrects this, concluding the frame is the viewpoint of the observer.
learnerActions: One pupil stands still to act as 'the background'; the teacher (or another pupil) walks steadily between that pupil and the class, while a second pupil walks alongside the walker at the same pace as a moving observer.

The seated class describes the walker as moving across the room; the moving observer describes the walker as staying beside them. The background pupil may say 'to the left' where the class says 'to the right' only because they face the other way: they are at rest relative to the class, so they share the class's frame and agree the walker is moving at the same speed.
Compare the two descriptions of the exact same walk and discuss why they differ.
State explicitly that the reference frame is set by the observer's own motion, not by the background pupil, the scenery, or which way the observer is facing.
Extend: walk two pupils side by side at the same steady pace and have the class predict how fast each walker sees the OTHER moving, and why, before asking the walkers.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference frame is set by the observer's own motion, not by the background or scenery. Observers moving differently (the seated class and the pupil walking alongside) give different but equally valid descriptions of the same walk; observers at rest relative to each other share a frame, even if facing opposite ways makes their left/right words differ.

activities.title: Compute relative speed: add or subtract?
feedback: If a learner always adds the two speeds, test their rule on the same-speed same-direction case: adding would give double the speed, but the correct relative speed is zero because they appear stationary to each other — so same direction must subtract.
For the oncoming pair at 50 and 40, confirm the closing speed is 50 + 40 = 90; for the same-direction pair, the difference is 50 − 40 = 10.
Always ask which object the relative speed is measured relative to, so the number is tied to a frame.
activities.rationale: The add/subtract rule is best built from concrete cases rather than stated as a formula, and the same-speed same-direction 'appears stationary' result both anchors subtraction and connects back to the frame-toggle scene. A number line makes the add-vs-subtract contrast visual. Explicitly testing the faulty 'always add' habit against the zero-relative-speed case targets a documented error pattern.
learnerActions: Work through the same-direction case: two trains (or cars) travelling the same way at the same speed — compute the relative speed and confirm it is zero, so each appears stationary to the other.
Work through two cars driving side by side at the same 60 mph: state how fast each appears to move as seen from the other, and explain why it looks stationary.

Work through an oncoming case: two cars approach each other, one at 50 and one at 40 — compute how fast they close on each other (50 + 40 = 90), then redo it for both going the same way (50 − 40 = 10, closing if the faster is behind or separating if it is ahead).

Optionally use a number line: mark where each car is after one hour from where they started. In opposite directions the distance between them changes by both distances together (50 + 40 = 90), while in the same direction it changes only by the difference (50 − 40 = 10).
State the rule in your own words: same direction → subtract the speeds; towards or away in opposite directions → add the speeds.
Name the frame for each answer (e.g. 'relative to the other car').
activities.intendedInsight: Relative speed is found by subtracting the speeds when objects move the same way and adding them when they move towards or away from each other in opposite directions; the same-speed same-direction case gives zero relative speed (appears stationary).

activities.title: The ambiguous two-train departure
feedback: If a learner insists one train is 'really' moving regardless of frame, have them re-tell the scene from each frame so each train becomes 'the mover', and require the frame to be named every time.
If a learner reads the motion off the background scenery, strip the scenery away (two trains, no visible ground) to show the motion is symmetric.

If a learner tries to resolve the ambiguity by calling one view 'real' and the other 'just an optical illusion', clarify that neither description is a mere illusion: both are equally valid relative to their frames, so the fix is to name the frame, not to decide which view is the real motion.

Use the steady-straight-line train question to surface that, for steady straight-line motion and without an outside reference, no internal observation singles out one frame as 'truly' moving; changes in speed or direction can be felt, which is a separate idea.
activities.rationale: This diagnostic scenario discriminates between learners who treat motion as absolute (and privilege the ground/Earth or the scenery) and those who accept frame-relativity and resolve ambiguity by naming a frame. Working from both frames enforces the 'relative to what?' habit, and the optical-illusion feedback confronts the related 'real vs apparent motion' misconception (a pedagogy-level misconception, not drawn from a cited source).
sourceClaims: Students treat motion as intrinsic rather than frame-relative; grant the Earth a privileged frame; treat frames as fixed to and bounded by concrete objects; many cannot apply a reference frame even after instruction.
learnerActions: Consider: two trains sit side by side at a platform; yours begins to move smoothly, and looking only out of the window at the other train, it seems as though the OTHER train is sliding backwards.
Explain how the same view can mean either 'we are moving' or 'they are moving', and what decides which is true.
Resolve the ambiguity by naming a frame: relative to the platform/ground, whichever train's position changes is the mover; relative to the other train, each sees the other move.
Answer a paired question from two frames: 'You're on the train — is the platform moving?' answered from the train's frame AND from the platform's frame.

Discuss: is there any experiment inside a train moving at a steady speed in a straight line that could tell you you're moving, without looking outside? (Speeding up, braking or going round a bend can be felt, so keep the question to steady straight-line motion.)
activities.intendedInsight: Looking only at the other train, your train going forwards and their train going backwards look identical — the view is genuinely ambiguous. There is no single 'really moving' answer without saying relative to what.

activities.title: Check and consolidate frame reasoning
feedback: For 'same speed, same direction', the expected answer is that Train B appears stationary (relative speed zero); if a learner adds the speeds, revisit the subtract rule.
For the 'name the frame' prompts, treat any description without a named frame as incomplete, even when the frame is the Earth.
If a learner says two observers at rest relative to each other are separate frames, point out they share a frame because neither moves relative to the other.
activities.rationale: Frame reasoning and relative-speed arithmetic are readily assessable, so a focused check after the interactive work confirms transfer. It tests and consolidates the perspective shift rather than building it, so it should follow the switchable scene and embodied demo rather than replace them.
sourceClaims: After instruction over 2/3 of physics undergraduates and 1/3 of graduate students could not apply a reference frame to judge simultaneity; observers at rest relative to one another share a frame.
learnerActions: Answer: 'A passenger on Train A looks at Train B moving at the same speed and direction — what do they see?' and justify in terms of relative speed.
Use a slider or fill-in to give the relative speed for an approaching pair versus a same-direction pair, explaining the choice of add or subtract.
Match each observer (e.g. platform observer, Train A passenger, Train B passenger) to their correct description of a given motion.
Complete 'name the frame' prompts for several everyday descriptions, filling the blank in 'moving relative to ___'.
Decide whether two observers who are at rest relative to one another count as one frame or two, and explain.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can apply the 'relative to what?' habit and the add/subtract rule across new cases, and recognise that observers at rest relative to one another share a frame.

constraints: Always name the frame in descriptions of motion — even when it is the Earth — and avoid bare 'it is moving' or 'it is stationary'; teacher language using 'see', 'appears', 'stationary' without a named frame quietly reinforces the belief in a privileged absolute (Earth) frame.

The learning lives in the COMPARISON of frames on the same scenario (platform vs passenger); a single fixed outcome does not let learners see the description change, so provide a way to re-describe the same motion from more than one viewpoint.

A static two-panel 'from the platform / from the train' picture with tap-to-reveal can illustrate the contrast as a recap reference, but it does not let learners re-run the scene from a new viewpoint, so it works as a scaffold rather than the main route to the perspective shift.

A recognition-only quiz tests frame reasoning and relative-speed arithmetic but does not by itself elicit the learner's independent construction of a frame-switch; use it as a check after hands-on or interactive work.

Relative motion is a threshold concept at this age: intrinsic-motion intuition and granting Earth special status persist beyond 11–12 and must be actively and repeatedly confronted, not assumed fixed after one lesson.

Distinguish the chosen frame from the scenery/background — a frame is set by the observer's own state of motion (for example, riding with Train A or standing on the platform), not by what lies in the background, where the observer stands, or which way they face; a frame can be attached to an object such as a train, but it is not limited to that object's physical size.

For young learners, be precise about 'appears stationary': the same-speed same-direction case gives zero relative speed, which is why one object looks frozen beside the other — this is a frame effect, not the object being truly at rest in all frames.

Do not teach that one observer's description is the 'real' motion and another's is 'just an optical illusion': all frame-relative descriptions are equally valid, and ambiguity is resolved by naming a frame.

Treat the boat-crossing-river example qualitatively at this age: it is a vivid frame-switch illustration, but its full relative velocity involves perpendicular (vector) addition that goes beyond the add/subtract speed rule targeted here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three sources are marked verified:false in the row (the Alstein et al. 2021 review and Scherr et al. 2001); treat their claims as cited but not independently re-checked here.

Self-audit of arithmetic: oncoming cars at 50 and 40 close at 90 (50+40); same direction they close/separate at 10 (50−40); same-speed same-direction gives relative speed 0. These were checked and are consistent with the add/subtract rule.

The 'add when moving towards/away' phrasing is the original row's shorthand for opposite-direction motion; same-direction motion (including moving apart) subtracts. Feedback and summary tie each number to a named frame to keep this unambiguous.

The 'real vs apparent / optical illusion' misconception appears in the row's commonMisconceptions but in no sources[].claim, so it is confronted in Activity 4 feedback and the constraints without being attributed to a cited source.

The Scherr et al. claim was removed from the two-train departure activity because it concerns simultaneity and shared frames, not that activity's discrimination principle; it is retained only in the consolidation activity, which does address observers at rest sharing a frame.

The original 3D-interactive note ('3D adds cost without proportional gain') and conversation note ('dialogue cannot show' the recompute) are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they are softened: a spatial 3D frame-switch may genuinely help cases like spacecraft docking or overtaking where depth matters, and a Socratic interview ('tell me what you think the other driver sees') can usefully elicit and name intuitions as a reflective companion. These alternatives are preserved as options with stated affordances/limits rather than dismissed.

The original recommendation's claim that live state is 'the essence' and that only a frame toggle can make the idea 'click' has been scoped as a strong proposal with a stated affordance (switchable state makes the comparison explicit) rather than an assertion of unique necessity over other media.

The boat-crossing-river and passing-car scenarios from the original were restored into Activity 1 as alternative frame-switch examples so they are genuinely present, not merely listed; the boat case is kept qualitative because its quantitative treatment needs vector addition beyond this age band.

assess.poeTask: Walk two students side by side at the same steady pace across the room. Ask the class to predict how fast each walker sees the OTHER moving, and WHY, before asking the walkers. Predicting 'the same speed as we see them' (an absolute answer) versus 'the other one looks stationary' surfaces the frame idea — the same-speed pair appearing still to each other is the key observation.
probeDeeper: Two cars drive side by side at the same 60 mph. How fast does each appear to move as seen from the other, and why does it look stationary?
You're on the train — is the platform moving? Answer from the train's frame AND the platform's frame.
Two cars approach each other, one at 50 and one at 40. How fast do they close on each other? What if they were going the same way?
Is there any experiment inside a smoothly moving train that could tell you you're moving, without looking outside?
assess.correctAnswer: Motion is defined relative to a chosen frame of reference. Looking only at the other train, all you can see is that the gap is changing — your train going forwards and their train going backwards look identical. Which is 'really' moving depends on the frame: relative to the platform/ground, whichever train's position changes is the one moving; but relative to the other train, each sees the other move. There is no single 'really moving' without saying relative to what.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'One of the trains is REALLY moving and the other really isn't — there's a true answer without saying compared to what.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the student state the frame every time ('moving relative to what?'); switch frames on the same scene so each train is 'the mover' in turn.
errorPatterns.distractor: One train is really moving and the other really isn't — there's a single true answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Won't accept the view is ambiguous and picks a 'true' mover.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Whatever the background scenery is doing tells you who's moving — the mover is the one the trees go past.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the chosen frame from the scenery; on a featureless view (two trains, no ground) the motion is symmetric.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates the reference frame with the visible background rather than a chosen observer.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'To get the relative speed you always ADD the two speeds together.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Same direction -> subtract, opposite -> add; check with the same-speed same-direction case (relative speed zero -> appears stationary).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds speeds for two objects moving the SAME direction (should subtract).

responseLevels.gap: Insists one object is 'really' moving with no frame stated, or reads motion off the background scenery; adds or subtracts speeds by habit.
responseLevels.full: Explains motion as defined only relative to a chosen frame, resolves the ambiguous two-train view by naming the frame, and computes relative speed correctly for same-direction (subtract) and opposite (add) cases — including the same-speed-same-direction 'appears stationary' result.
responseLevels.partial: Says 'it depends on your point of view' and can compute a relative speed in one case, but doesn't consistently name the frame, or muddles same-direction versus opposite-direction relative speed — states the idea without applying it both ways.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two trains sit side by side at a platform. Yours begins to move smoothly and, looking only out of the window at the other train, it seems as though the OTHER train is sliding backwards. For a moment you can't tell which train is really moving. How can the same view mean either 'we are moving' or 'they are moving' — and what decides which is true?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Students treat motion as an absolute property and give the ground/Earth a privileged frame. A student who grasps relative motion says the view is genuinely ambiguous and resolves it only by naming a reference frame (ground versus the other train). A student with the misconception insists one train is 'really' moving regardless of frame, or reads the motion off the background scenery as if the scenery IS the motion.

sources.claim: Students assume a reference frame is the background of motion instead of the observer's viewpoint; the walk-across-the-room demo (background pupil sees 'left', class sees 'right') corrects this, concluding the frame is the viewpoint of the observer.
sources.source: OpenStax, Physics 2.1 — Relative Motion, Distance, and Displacement (Teacher Support)

sources.claim: Students treat motion as intrinsic rather than frame-relative; grant the Earth a privileged frame; treat frames as fixed to and bounded by concrete objects; many cannot apply a reference frame even after instruction.
sources.source: Alstein, Krijtenburg-Lewerissa & van Joolingen (2021), Phys. Rev. Phys. Educ. Res. 17, 023101 (review; incl. Saltiel & Malgrange 11-year-olds, Scherr et al.)

sources.claim: After instruction over 2/3 of physics undergraduates and 1/3 of graduate students could not apply a reference frame to judge simultaneity; observers at rest relative to one another share a frame.
sources.source: Scherr, Shaffer & Vokos (2001), 'Student understanding of time in special relativity', Am. J. Phys. 69, S24

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Friction & Surfaces

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 3 Forces and Magnets):** Compare how things move on different surfaces.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no discrete elementary PE; friction excluded from the K-PS2 boundary):** Friction is not assessed as a standalone elementary performance expectation — the K-PS2-2 assessment boundary explicitly excludes [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-2]; friction-as-a-force is treated qualitatively and connects to 3-PS2-1, then is formalised at MS-PS2.

- **Operational details:** Children compare how the SAME object moves across different surfaces (carpet, polished wood, sandpaper, ice) and discover that some surfaces produce more friction than others — rough surfaces slow things more than smooth. The key conceptual upgrade is to treat friction as a FORCE acting between two surfaces to oppose their motion, not merely as a property of 'rough things'. The Institute of Physics frames this for primary/lower-secondary as grip (friction that prevents sliding) and slip (friction that slows sliding, and warms the surfaces). Because friction can't be seen, it must be represented with force arrows ('forces spectacles'). The comparison is naturally a fair test: keep the object the same, change only the surface, measure how far it travels.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational).
bestPractices: Hands-on comparison: send the same object across at least three surfaces and measure distance travelled, keeping everything else the same (links to fair testing / pattern-seeking).
Name friction as a FORCE that opposes motion and represent it with an arrow pointing against the movement ('forces spectacles'), since friction is invisible (IOP).
Use the IOP grip/slip framing and a warming demonstration (rub hands together; feel a surface warm under sliding) to make the invisible force tangible — slip warms things, grip does not.
Foreground friction as the REASON things slow and stop, directly countering the 'force runs out' impetus idea.
Clean the variable: compare smoothness/roughness, and beware confounds — 'shiny' is not the same as 'low friction', and rolling must not be compared with sliding.
Discuss friction as both helpful (grip lets us walk, brakes work) and unhelpful (slows a sledge) so it isn't cast as simply 'bad'.
keyRepresentations: Multi-surface runway/ramp with one object and a distance scale
Force arrow opposing motion ('forces spectacles' — making the invisible friction visible)
Grip vs slip labelling of frictional forces (IOP)
Data table: surface ↔ distance travelled
Warming demonstration (rubbing hands / surfaces) to feel slip dissipating energy
commonMisconceptions: Friction is a phenomenon or a 'thing', not named/treated as a force (IOP).
Friction only acts when things move (slip) — or the mirror error, only when things are still (grip); both are partial views (IOP).
Friction is always bad/undesirable, ignoring that grip is what lets us walk and brake.
Things stop because the push/force 'runs out', rather than because friction pushes back (impetus link).
Confusing smoothness with shininess ('shiny = slippery'); and comparing rolling resistance with sliding as if they were the same.
Reasoning backwards from effect to cause — 'it took a long time to stop, so the friction must have been small' (IOP tripwire).

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds, teach friction as a FORCE between two surfaces that opposes sliding motion, not merely a property of 'rough things'. Central activity: send the SAME object across several surfaces (ice, polished wood, carpet, sandpaper) as a fair test, measure distance travelled, and represent the invisible friction with a force arrow pointing against the motion. Use the Institute of Physics grip/slip framing, connect slip to warming, and confront the 'push runs out' impetus idea plus the 'shiny = slippery' confusion. For grip (static friction), be clear it balances an applied push or a slope's pull — a still object with nothing pushing it has no horizontal friction. Includes consolidation sorting/ordering, an annotated real-world reference, and a two-tier diagnostic.

activities.title: Same object, different surfaces: a fair-test friction runway
feedback: If the object stops sooner on carpet than on polished wood, ask: what was the only thing you changed? The surface. So the surface is what made the difference.
If a learner changed the object or the push between runs, point out the test is no longer fair — reset and vary only the surface.
Praise predicting first: comparing your prediction to the measured distance is how a pattern ('rougher = stops sooner') emerges from your own trials rather than being told.
activities.rationale: Comparing one object across multiple surfaces with distance measured supports pattern-seeking and fair testing, and gives direct evidence that the surface is the causal variable. Representing the comparison with accumulated data makes the trend visible.
sourceClaims: Rough surfaces have more friction than smooth surfaces; lubricants reduce friction; sliding rough surfaces past each other has a warming effect (slip is dissipative, grip is not).
learnerActions: Set up a flat runway (physical track, or a screen simulation of one) and choose one object (e.g. a puck or wooden block) that you will NOT change between runs.
Before each run, predict how far the object will travel and mark your predicted stopping point.

Give the object the same push each time (e.g. release it from the same point on a small launch ramp or pull back a rubber band by the same amount, since hand flicks vary), send it across at least three different surfaces in turn (e.g. ice/very smooth, polished wood, carpet, sandpaper), repeat each run a few times, and keep everything else the same so only the surface changes.
Measure and record how far it travelled on each surface in a data table (surface ↔ distance), and build up a simple bar chart so the pattern becomes visible.
Order the surfaces from 'object travels furthest' to 'stops soonest' and describe the pattern in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing only the surface changes how far the same pushed object travels before it slows to a stop: rougher surfaces produce more friction and stop the object sooner. This is a fair test — keep the object and the push the same, change only the surface.

activities.title: Forces spectacles: drawing the invisible friction arrow
feedback: If a learner points the arrow the way the object is moving, ask which way the push that SLOWS it must point — against the motion.
If a learner calls friction 'the rough bits' or 'stickiness', re-voice it as a force: the surfaces rubbing push back on the object.
Linking arrow length to the measured stopping distance helps: the surface where it stopped soonest gets the longest backward arrow.
activities.rationale: Friction cannot be seen, so a force-arrow representation ('forces spectacles') makes it tangible and names it explicitly as a force opposing motion, addressing the phenomenon-not-force misconception.
sourceClaims: Many students see friction as a phenomenon rather than as a force; when two surfaces are in contact there is a force on each surface acting to stop them moving past one another.

The friction misconception has two mirror forms (friction only when moving / only when still); IOP teaches grip (prevents sliding, e.g. lets us walk) and slip (slows sliding and warms surfaces); friction can't be shown as a concrete entity so use force arrows; avoid reasoning backwards from effect to cause.
learnerActions: After a run, draw a force arrow on the moving object pointing BACKWARDS, against the direction it is sliding — this represents the friction slowing it.
Compare runs: draw a short arrow for a smooth surface and a longer arrow for a rough surface, matching 'more friction = longer arrow'.
Say out loud which way friction pushes and why the object slows: friction is a force from the surfaces acting against the sliding motion.
Optionally, in a screen simulation, toggle a 'forces spectacles' overlay that shows the opposing arrow growing longer on rougher surfaces, and watch a warming meter glow on the rough, sliding runs.
activities.intendedInsight: Friction is a force acting between two surfaces in contact, opposing their sliding. Though invisible, it can be represented by an arrow pointing against the motion; it is larger on rougher surfaces, which is why the object slows and stops sooner.

activities.title: Grip and slip, and the warming you can feel
feedback: If a learner says a still object never has friction: a block with nothing pushing it has no horizontal friction, but push it (or place it on a slope) and it still does not slide — static (grip) friction is balancing that push before any motion.
If a learner says friction is 'bad', ask how we would walk or stop a bike without it.
Feeling hands warm gives a direct sensation of slip dissipating energy — the screen can show a warming meter but cannot let you feel it.
activities.rationale: The grip/slip framing counters both mirror forms of the misconception (friction only when moving / only when still) and the 'friction is always bad' view; the warming experience grounds the energy aspect of slip. Scoping grip to an applied push or slope keeps the static-friction physics correct.
sourceClaims: The friction misconception has two mirror forms (friction only when moving / only when still); IOP teaches grip (prevents sliding, e.g. lets us walk) and slip (slows sliding and warms surfaces); friction can't be shown as a concrete entity so use force arrows; avoid reasoning backwards from effect to cause.
Rough surfaces have more friction than smooth surfaces; lubricants reduce friction; sliding rough surfaces past each other has a warming effect (slip is dissipative, grip is not).
learnerActions: Rub your hands together quickly and feel them warm up — notice that sliding (slip) between surfaces produces heat.
Discuss grip: push gently on a shoe (or block) resting on a path and notice it does NOT slide until you push hard — static (grip) friction is balancing your push before the object moves.

Sort example situations into grip (prevents sliding: walking without slipping, standing on a slope without sliding, a parked object on a slope held in place, brakes holding) and slip (slows an existing slide: a sledge stopping, a skidding object).
Discuss friction as both helpful (grip lets us walk and lets brakes work) and unhelpful (slows a sledge) so friction is not labelled simply 'bad'.
activities.intendedInsight: Friction has two faces. Grip (static friction) can act on a still object WHEN something pushes it or it rests on a slope — it balances that push up to the point the object starts to slide. Slip (sliding friction) slows an object already sliding and warms the surfaces. Friction is both helpful and unhelpful depending on the situation.

activities.title: Shiny is not the same as slippery (predict–observe–explain)
feedback: If a learner predicts the shiny foil will be slippery and is surprised, name the lesson: shiny but rough still grips — shininess was a distraction.
Keep the variable clean: compare smoothness vs roughness, and do not compare a rolling object with a sliding one as if they were the same.
If asked about tray vs glass, steer toward the surfaces in contact (how rough/smooth they are and what they are made of), not how they look; testing is the way to find out.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain contrast that deliberately crosses shininess with roughness separates the two, directly confronting the 'shiny = slippery' confusion and reinforcing roughness as the real cause.
sourceClaims: Rough surfaces have more friction than smooth surfaces; lubricants reduce friction; sliding rough surfaces past each other has a warming effect (slip is dissipative, grip is not).
learnerActions: Take two surfaces: crumpled-then-flattened kitchen foil (shiny but rough) and a sheet of matte-smooth card (dull but smooth).
Predict which lets the same block slide further, and say WHY before testing.
Slide the block on each with the same push and observe which surface lets it slide further; in most setups the block grips the crinkled shiny foil more and slides further on the smooth dull card.
Explain what your results suggest mattered (usually roughness, not shininess) and restate that friction is a force from the surfaces opposing motion.
Extra challenge: would a coin slide the same on a shiny metal tray and a shiny sheet of glass? Discuss what really decides it.
activities.intendedInsight: Shininess does not determine friction; what matters is the surfaces in contact: mainly how rough or smooth they are, and also what they are made of. 'Shiny = slippery' is a trap.

activities.title: Consolidate and check: sort, order, and explain
feedback: Full response: 'The block stops sooner on the rough carpet; the rough surface produces more friction — a force between block and surface acting against its motion; the smooth table has less friction so it slides further.'

If a learner says the block stopped because 'the push ran out' with no mention of the surface, re-run the same push on two surfaces so the only difference is the surface, forcing them to attribute the different distance to friction (reteach pushes-as-forces if the link is missing).
If a learner only says 'rough = slow, smooth = fast' as a surface property, push for the force language: the surfaces rubbing push back against the motion.

If a learner claims a pushed-but-still block has no friction, introduce grip (static): with nothing pushing there is no horizontal friction, but a shoe or block will not slide until pushed hard — static friction is balancing the push before movement.

Watch for backwards reasoning: 'it took a long time to stop, so friction was small' only holds if the test was fair (same object, same push, only the surface changed); otherwise ask what else could have changed, such as the push or the object.
activities.rationale: Ordering, categorising and explaining consolidate the pattern and are readily assessable, while the two-tier diagnostic discriminates the everyday view (push ran out / sticky / shiny) from the force view. These check and classify understanding but do not themselves generate the core insight or elicit the hands-on comparison.
sourceClaims: Many students see friction as a phenomenon rather than as a force; when two surfaces are in contact there is a force on each surface acting to stop them moving past one another.

The friction misconception has two mirror forms (friction only when moving / only when still); IOP teaches grip (prevents sliding, e.g. lets us walk) and slip (slows sliding and warms surfaces); friction can't be shown as a concrete entity so use force arrows; avoid reasoning backwards from effect to cause.
learnerActions: Order a set of surfaces by how far the object slides on each (furthest → stops soonest).
Sort everyday situations into friction that is helpful (walking, braking) versus unhelpful (slowing a sledge).
Match each surface to a grip or slip description.

Answer the diagnostic: 'I slide the same wooden block across a smooth table and across a rough carpet, giving the same push each time. On which surface does it stop sooner — and what about that surface stops it?' Give the mechanism, not just the outcome.
Reason about a still object: if you push gently on a block resting on a table but it does not move, is any friction acting on it? How could you tell (what happens as you push harder)?
activities.intendedInsight: A full understanding names friction as a FORCE between the two surfaces, acting opposite the motion and larger on rough surfaces, predicts the stopping order for a new pair of surfaces, and recognises that friction can also act on a still object being pushed or on a slope (grip/static friction balancing the push).

constraints: Keep the test fair: use the SAME object and the SAME push, change only the surface, and measure distance travelled.
Do not compare a rolling object with a sliding one as if equivalent — rolling resistance and sliding friction differ; keep the comparison to sliding.
Separate shininess from roughness deliberately (e.g. shiny-rough foil vs dull-smooth card); do not let learners treat 'shiny' as 'low friction'.

Address both mirror misconceptions: friction can act on a still object that is being pushed or on a slope (grip/static) as well as on a sliding one (slip); do not present it as only-when-moving or only-when-still. Also do not imply a free-standing object with nothing pushing it on a level surface has horizontal friction — it does not.
Present friction as both helpful and unhelpful, not simply 'bad'.

Sorting/ordering/matching and multiple-choice tasks consolidate and assess understanding but do not, on their own, produce the comparison that generates the insight; use them after hands-on or simulated trials.

An annotated static scene (shoe on ice vs path, brake on wheel, lift-the-flap friction facts) is a useful reference aid, but it cannot run the same-object-across-surfaces comparison; treat it as a recap, not the main investigation.
A screen simulation can show warming (a glowing meter) but cannot let learners feel heat; pair any simulation with real hands-rubbing/warming play.

A 2D runway fully captures the comparison and the arrow representation at this age; a 3D ramp would add realism but only use it if a 3D tilt/aim element is itself a learning goal, not as a substitute for the friction comparison.

Only infer friction from stopping distance inside a fair test (same object, same push, only the surface changed). Outside a fair test, avoid backwards reasoning from effect to cause (e.g. 'stopped slowly, so friction was small'), because a bigger push or a different object could explain the slow stop instead.
Role-play/open dialogue adds little for this specific objective: friction here is learned by comparing motion and visualising the opposing force rather than by talking in role.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three IOP sources carry verified:false in the source row (the grip/slip/drag sequence and the 'visualising grip and slip' page); treat their claims as cited but not independently re-checked here.

Force-direction care: friction opposes the direction of sliding and causes slowing; it is not the direction of travel and does not determine it. In these activities the object is given a push and then slows, so the opposing-arrow description is sound; if extending to objects that change direction, state the initial velocity explicitly.

Static-friction (grip) care: a still object with no applied push on a level surface has NO horizontal friction. Static friction only acts to balance an applied push or a slope's pull, up to the point the object starts to slide. The original assessment probe ('is there any friction on a still block right now?') was ambiguous on this and has been reframed to include a gentle push; the grip sort examples were also adjusted so each one (walking, standing on a slope, parked on a slope, braking) involves an actual push or slope. Do not teach that friction is always present on any still object.
The 'push runs out' idea is an impetus misconception to confront, not to teach; it appears only as an error pattern and in feedback, never as a correct explanation.

Source NGSS note: friction is excluded from the K-PS2-2 assessment boundary and is treated qualitatively at elementary, connecting to 3-PS2-1 and formalised at MS-PS2 — retained as standards context, not as a learner instruction.
The legacy row asserts 3D 'adds nothing' and that conversation has 'no value'; these have been softened to scoped trade-offs for this objective and age rather than universal laws.

assess.poeTask: Offer two surfaces: kitchen foil crumpled then flattened (shiny but rough) and a sheet of matte-smooth card. Ask the child to predict which lets the block slide further and WHY. Many predict the shiny foil (shininess = slippery); seeing the block grip the rough foil separates roughness from shininess as the real cause.
probeDeeper: Is friction pushing on the block? If so, which way?
The block is sitting still on the table. Is there any friction on it right now? How could you tell?
A shiny metal tray and a shiny sheet of glass — will a coin slide the same on both? What actually matters?
assess.correctAnswer: It stops sooner on the rough carpet. The rough surface produces more friction — a force between the block and the surface that acts against the block's motion and slows it; the smooth table has less friction so the block slides further.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The block stops because the push you gave it ran out, not because of the carpet.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the SAME push on two surfaces so the only difference is the surface — force the child to attribute the different distance to the surface. Reteach pushes as forces if the link is missing.
errorPatterns.distractor: The block stops because the push you gave it runs out — the surface doesn't matter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains stopping with no reference to the surface; friction plays no causal role.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Friction is only there when something is moving — a still block has no friction.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce grip (static) vs slip (sliding): a shoe won't slide until you push hard — friction is there before it moves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a stationary block on a table or gentle slope has zero friction and can't explain why it doesn't slide.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Shiny surfaces are always more slippery — friction is about shininess.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test shiny-rough vs dull-smooth so shininess and roughness are separated; keep only roughness as the variable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a shiny-but-rough surface (crumpled foil, glossy sandpaper) will be slippery.

responseLevels.gap: Attributes the difference to the push running out or to the surface being 'sticky/bumpy' with no force language, or claims shininess is what matters.
responseLevels.full: Explains friction as a force between the two surfaces that acts opposite to the block's motion and is greater on rough surfaces, predicts the stopping order for a new pair of surfaces, and recognises friction can also act on a still object (grip).
responseLevels.partial: Says the rough surface has more friction and stops the block sooner, but treats friction as a property of the surface or as only-when-moving — states 'rough = slow, smooth = fast' without describing friction as a force acting against the motion from the surfaces rubbing.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I slide the same wooden block across a smooth table and across a rough carpet, giving it the same push each time. On which surface does it stop sooner — and what is it about that surface that stops it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Tier 1 (rough stops it sooner) most 7-year-olds get from experience. Tier 2 divides: a child who understands friction names it as a FORCE opposing the motion, caused by the two surfaces rubbing; a child with the everyday view says the block 'ran out of push', calls the carpet 'sticky/bumpy' as a property rather than a force, or blames shininess. Same observation, different mechanism.

sources.claim: Many students see friction as a phenomenon rather than as a force; when two surfaces are in contact there is a force on each surface acting to stop them moving past one another.
sources.source: IOP Spark (Institute of Physics) — 'Many students see friction as a phenomenon, rather than as a force'

sources.claim: The friction misconception has two mirror forms (friction only when moving / only when still); IOP teaches grip (prevents sliding, e.g. lets us walk) and slip (slows sliding and warms surfaces); friction can't be shown as a concrete entity so use force arrows; avoid reasoning backwards from effect to cause.
sources.source: IOP Spark — 'How can you tell if there is friction', 'Friction', and 'A sequence to develop ideas about friction: grip, slip, drag'

sources.claim: Rough surfaces have more friction than smooth surfaces; lubricants reduce friction; sliding rough surfaces past each other has a warming effect (slip is dissipative, grip is not).
sources.source: IOP Spark — 'Visualising what happens at surfaces for grip and slip' (5-11)

pedagogy.summary: Children compare which of two objects is heavier by HEFTING (holding one in each hand) and by using a two-pan balance, learning that weight is felt and measured, not seen — size and appearance do not reliably tell you mass. The balance settles cases hefting can't. Language: heavy/light, heavier than, lighter than. (At this stage 'mass' and 'weight' are used interchangeably.)
bestPractices: Heft first (hands as scales), then confirm with a balance
Deliberately pair a small heavy object with a big light one so size cannot decide it — this is what breaks the 'bigger = heavier' assumption
Read the balance as 'the side that goes DOWN is heavier'
Use full comparative sentences: 'the tin is heavier than the box'
Keep it practical with real objects; move to ordering three items by pairwise balance comparisons
keyRepresentations: The two-pan balance (canonical model of comparison)
Hands as scales (hefting)
Deliberately mismatched pairs (small-heavy vs big-light)
commonMisconceptions: Bigger = heavier — judges mass by size or appearance
The taller/longer/fuller object is heavier (conflates mass with another attribute)
Misreads the balance — thinks the RAISED pan is the heavier side

learn.summary: Young children (about 4-6) compare which of two objects is heavier, first by HEFTING (holding one object in each hand) and then by confirming with a two-pan balance. The central aim is to challenge the 'bigger = heavier' assumption by deliberately pairing a small heavy object with a big light one, so size stops being a reliable guide. Children read the balance as 'the side that goes DOWN is heavier', use full comparative language (heavier than / lighter than), and progress to ordering three objects by pairwise comparison. At this stage 'mass' and 'weight' are used interchangeably. The curriculum frames this as a practical activity with real materials; screen or picture activities can support balance-reading and prediction but cannot deliver the felt sense of weight (no haptics).

activities.title: Heft then balance: feel it, then confirm
feedback: If the child picks the larger object, invite them to heft the pair with eyes shut, then let the balance decide — evidence over appearance. Repeat with more small-heavy/big-light pairs so size is repeatedly wrong.

If the child reads the balance backwards (raised pan = heavier), model with a known heavy-vs-light pair so they watch the heavy side drop; say 'the heavier side pushes DOWN' and let them press a pan to feel it fall.
When correct, prompt the reasoning: 'This one is smaller but you said it's heavier — how can something small be heavy?'
activities.rationale: For this age the embodied experience of feeling a small object press down is intended to do the conceptual work of challenging 'bigger = heavier'; the balance then provides shared, visible evidence that overrides appearance. The curriculum frames comparison of mass as a practical activity with real materials, moving from feeling to a balance.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils are taught to compare, describe and solve practical problems for mass/weight [heavy/light, heavier than, lighter than] and to 'measure and begin to record' mass/weight; at this stage mass and weight are used interchangeably.

NCETM Year 1 mastery mass tasks move from feeling ('sort three items lightest to heaviest by feeling them') to a balance with items 'quite similar in mass', and probe balance-reasoning ('which is heavier?', 'if you added a car to the teddy what would happen to the scales?', true/false from a balance picture) — designed so appearance/feel is unreliable and balance evidence decides.
Measurement Big Ideas frame it as comparison and equivalence conducted as a practical activity with real materials.
learnerActions: Hold one object in each hand (heft) and say which feels heavier — try this with eyes shut so appearance can't guide the choice.

Pair a small heavy object (a metal weight or pebble) with a big light object (an empty plastic box or inflated balloon), checked beforehand on the balance so the small item really is heavier (a small pebble can be lighter than a large box). Predict which is heavier before touching.
Place both on a two-pan balance and watch which pan goes down; say 'the ____ is heavier than the ____' in a full sentence.
Repeat with several deliberately misleading pairs (e.g. big cushion vs small tin of beans), checked beforehand so the small item really is heavier, so that size is repeatedly the wrong guide.
Press gently on one pan with a hand to feel that pushing down harder on one side makes that pan go down, just as a heavier object does.
activities.intendedInsight: Weight is felt and measured, not seen — a small object can be heavier than a big one, and the balance settles cases your eyes cannot.

activities.title: Order three objects by weight
feedback: If the child orders by look or by trial-and-error grabbing, scaffold with pairwise balance comparisons ('heavier than this one? lighter than that one?'). Systematic seriation is not expected at this age — it consolidates with practice, so do not drill an ordering rule.
Praise reasoning that uses the balance evidence to justify each placement.
activities.rationale: Ordering by successive pairwise balancing extends direct comparison and reinforces that weight evidence, not appearance, decides order. Developmentally, systematic seriation emerges gradually, so the task is scaffolded rather than drilled.
