pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9, What Causes Wind — the Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly, warm air rises because it is lighter, and cooler air flows in to take its place; that moving air is wind.
• Standards — UK (DfE): builds toward KS2 states/forces and KS3 atmosphere; at KS1/KS2 it sits within weather observation rather than a discrete statutory objective.
• Standards — US (NGSS): the convection mechanism is formalised later (MS-ESS2-6 role of unequal heating in atmospheric circulation; energy transfer in MS-PS3); at grade 3 it grounds 3-ESS2-1 weather description. State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach wind as a CONSEQUENCE of uneven heating and rising warm air, not a mysterious push; use the sea-breeze case (land heats faster than sea) as the canonical concrete example; make the invisible visible via effects (streamers, smoke) and a convection cross-section; keep 'warm air rises, cool air moves in' as the core causal chain.
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — state that the Sun heats the surface unevenly and define wind as moving air; Tier B — explain warm air rises and cool air flows in to replace it (a convection loop); Tier C — relate pressure differences to wind direction and strength.
bestPractices: Anchor to the sea breeze: land heats faster than the sea, air rises over the warm land, cooler sea air flows in — a concrete, everyday convection loop
Make wind visible through its effects (streamers, smoke traces, a pinwheel) since air itself is invisible
Teach the full causal chain 'uneven heating → warm air rises → cool air rushes in = wind' rather than a single fact
Use a convection cross-section (arrows up over warm, down over cool, sideways as wind) as the canonical model
Confront the idea that wind is created by trees/waves moving or comes from a fixed place — those are effects, not causes
keyRepresentations: Convection-loop cross-section: rising arrows over warm ground, sinking over cool, horizontal flow labelled 'wind'
Sea-breeze diagram (sun, warm land, cool sea, incoming breeze)
A heat dial that speeds/slows the rising air and the resulting sideways flow
Streamers/smoke traces revealing invisible moving air
commonMisconceptions: Wind is made by trees swaying, waves, or fans — those show or move air but the driver is uneven heating
Wind 'comes from' a fixed place or is a substance stored somewhere, rather than air flowing to replace risen warm air
Warm air sinks / cold air rises (reversed) — warm air is lighter and rises
Wind and the air are different things — wind IS moving air
Heating happens evenly, so there'd be no reason for air to move

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach wind as a consequence of uneven solar heating: the Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly, warm air is lighter and rises, and cooler air flows in to take its place — that moving air IS the wind. Anchor to the sea breeze (land heats faster than sea) as the canonical concrete example, make the invisible air visible through its effects (streamers, smoke, a pinwheel), and teach the full causal chain rather than a single fact. Confront the common belief that wind is 'made by' trees or waves, or that it is a special substance separate from air.

activities.title: Sea-breeze convection playground
feedback: If the learner says the trees or waves make the wind: trees and waves move BECAUSE of the wind — wind also blows over open sea where there are no trees or hills at all.
If the learner says warm air sinks: warm air is lighter and rises — think of the warmth you feel rising above a radiator, or a hot-air balloon climbing.
If the learner treats wind as separate from air: a fan or a wave of your hand turns still air into a breeze you can feel — wind IS air in motion.
When the breeze dies as the heat is turned down: point out that without uneven heating there is nothing to make the air move, so there is no wind from this cause.
When the night-time breeze reverses: the land is now cooler than the sea, so warm air rises over the sea and cooler land air flows out to replace it — the loop runs the other way.
activities.rationale: Wind causation is a convection mechanism; letting the child drive the heating and watch warm air rise while cooler air visibly flows in makes the abstract chain 'air moves to replace risen warm air' observable and controllable. The heat dial and reversible day/night cases let the learner test cause and effect rather than accept an asserted arrow.
sourceClaims: Uneven solar heating drives convection: warm air rises and cooler air moves in to replace it, producing wind; the sea breeze (land heats faster than sea) is the canonical example.
Children commonly attribute wind to moving objects (trees, waves) or treat it as a substance from a fixed source, rather than as air flowing due to heating differences.
learnerActions: Look at a cross-section showing the Sun, warm land, cool sea, and the air above
Warm the land using a Sun/heat control and watch a column of warm air rise over the land
Watch streamers (or smoke traces) reveal cooler sea air streaming sideways to fill the gap left by the risen warm air — and name that sideways flow as the wind
Turn the heat UP and observe the breeze strengthen; turn it DOWN and watch the breeze die away
Switch to a cool night where the land cools faster than the sea, and observe the breeze reverse direction; explain why
activities.intendedInsight: Wind is not a mysterious push and is not made by trees or waves — it is simply air moving to replace warm air that rose because the Sun heated the surface unevenly. Changing the heating changes the wind; removing the uneven heating stops it.

activities.title: Make the invisible air visible
feedback: If the learner thinks nothing is moving because they cannot see it: the streamer/pinwheel moves because invisible air is pushing against it.
Connect the observed flow to its cause: the air is moving toward where warm air has risen and left a gap.
activities.rationale: Because air is invisible, concrete indicators MAY help learners perceive that something is actually moving, which can support the shift from treating wind as a stored substance from a fixed source toward seeing it as air in motion. This perceptual benefit is an unvalidated proposal, not a source-established finding; source claim 3 is cited only because it documents the misconception this activity targets.
sourceClaims: Children commonly attribute wind to moving objects (trees, waves) or treat it as a substance from a fixed source, rather than as air flowing due to heating differences.
learnerActions: Use streamers, smoke traces, or a pinwheel to detect moving air you cannot see
Observe which way the indicators point and describe the direction and strength of the air movement
Relate what the indicators show back to warm air rising somewhere and cooler air flowing in
activities.intendedInsight: Air itself is invisible, but its movement can be detected through its effects — and those effects are evidence of air flowing, which is what wind is.

activities.title: Order the causal chain and explain the sea breeze
feedback: If the order is muddled: start from what the Sun does first (heats the surface unevenly) and follow what happens to the air step by step.
For the night case: the land is now the cooler surface, so the rising happens over the sea and air flows out from the land — the breeze reverses.

For the open ocean: wind still occurs because the Sun heats different parts of the Earth (sea, land, near and far) by different amounts, so air keeps moving, and that moving air can travel far across the ocean; trees and hills are not needed.
activities.rationale: Ordering the chain and explaining the sea breeze checks whether the learner can sequence and apply the mechanism; the night-time and open-ocean prompts discriminate genuine understanding from a memorised single fact. An ordering task checks that the learner can sequence the chain but does not by itself build dynamic intuition, so it works best after hands-on or observed exploration.
sourceClaims: Uneven solar heating drives convection: warm air rises and cooler air moves in to replace it, producing wind; the sea breeze (land heats faster than sea) is the canonical example.
learnerActions: Arrange the steps of the causal chain in order: uneven heating → warm air rises → cooler air moves in → wind
In your own words, explain why a breeze often blows from the sea onto the land on a hot afternoon
Predict and explain which way the breeze blows at night when the land cools faster than the sea
Decide whether there could be wind over the open ocean with no trees or hills, and say what causes it
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can state and apply the full chain of causes, not just recite that wind exists, and can use it to predict wind direction in new situations.

activities.title: Ask a weather expert why the wind blows
feedback: If the retelling drops a step, point to the missing link (what makes the air rise, or what fills the gap).
If the learner says equal heating would still make wind: with no uneven heating there is no reason for air to rise and be replaced, so there would be little or no wind from this cause.
activities.rationale: A spoken or written explanation lets the learner articulate the mechanism and tackle a counterfactual (equal heating), which targets the misconception that heating is even. This supports verbal reasoning alongside the observed model rather than replacing hands-on exploration; a narrated account alone does not let the learner see the loop in motion.
sourceClaims: Uneven solar heating drives convection: warm air rises and cooler air moves in to replace it, producing wind; the sea breeze (land heats faster than sea) is the canonical example.
learnerActions: Pose the question 'why does the wind blow?' and listen to or read an explanation that narrates uneven heating, rising warm air, and cooler air moving in
Retell the chain back and ask a follow-up, such as what would happen if the Sun heated everywhere equally
activities.intendedInsight: The same causal chain can be put into words and reasoned about in dialogue, reinforcing the explanation the learner has observed.

constraints: Target age is 7–9. Keep to 'uneven heating → warm air rises → cooler air moves in = wind' as the core chain; relating pressure differences to wind direction/strength is an extension (upper tier), not required for all learners.

A static labelled convection diagram names the parts but cannot show the air flowing; use it as a reference scaffold and pair it with moving indicators or an animated/manipulable model so the 'rushes in to replace' step is seen, not just asserted.
Step-ordering or matching tasks check that the learner can sequence the chain but do not on their own build the dynamic intuition of why air moves; use them after hands-on or observed exploration.
A 3D rendering of the convection cell is not required: the mechanism reads clearly in a 2D vertical cross-section. Offer 3D only if it adds clarity, not as a necessity.

Streamers, smoke, pinwheels and heat controls are offered as example mechanisms for revealing invisible flow and driving the heating; any means that makes the flow observable and the heating adjustable serves the same purpose.
Keep the direction of convection correct: warm air is lighter and RISES; cooler, denser air flows in. Watch for and correct the inverted 'warm air sinks' idea.

Keep the sea-/land-breeze reversal consistent: by day land heats faster so air rises over the land and sea air flows in; by night land cools faster so air rises over the warmer sea and land air flows out.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the listed sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
All three source claims are marked verified:false in the original row; treat the convection account, the NGSS grade mapping, and the misconceptions literature as unconfirmed citations.

The explanation 'warm air rises because it is lighter' is a simplified, age-appropriate account of buoyancy/density differences; it is correct at this level but omits that warm air is less dense. Acceptable for ages 7–9.

Original artefact ratings asserted that a 2D interactive is 'ideal', that 3D 'adds little', and that a static diagram 'cannot show' the flow; these are catalog preferences, not established efficacy claims, and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits here.
The claim about NGSS placement (MS-ESS2-6 vs 3-ESS2-1) is a standards-mapping note from the pedagogy field and was not used to make pedagogical-necessity claims.

Whether concrete flow indicators (streamers/pinwheels) improve understanding is an unvalidated pedagogical proposal; source claim 3 only establishes that the 'wind is a stored substance/moving-object' misconception exists, not that these indicators remediate it.

probeDeeper: At night the land cools faster than the sea. Which way would the breeze blow then — and why?
Where is the air going when it 'rises' over the warm land?
Could there be wind over the open ocean with no trees or hills anywhere? What causes it?
assess.correctAnswer: The Sun heats the land more than the sea; air over the warm land warms, becomes lighter and rises; cooler, denser air from over the sea flows in to take its place — that moving air is the wind. Wind is air moving because of uneven heating, from cooler/denser toward warmer/rising air.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Trees and waves make the wind by swishing about'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reverse it — trees move BECAUSE of wind; wind blows over open sea with no trees at all.
errorPatterns.distractor: The trees and waves swishing about push the air and make the wind.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names moving objects as the cause of wind

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Wind is its own special thing, not just moving air'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A fan or hand-wave turns still air into felt wind — wind IS moving air.
errorPatterns.distractor: Wind is a kind of invisible thing that isn't the same as air.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: can't say wind is air in motion

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Warm air sinks and cool air rises' — inverted convection
errorPatterns.nextMove: Warm air rises — show warmth above a radiator / a rising warm balloon.
errorPatterns.distractor: The warm air over the land sinks and pushes the breeze out to sea.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: gets the direction of rising air wrong

responseLevels.gap: Attributes wind to trees/waves or calls it a special substance.
responseLevels.full: Explains the sea breeze via uneven heating, rising warm air and cooler air flowing in, and predicts the reversed night-time land breeze.
responseLevels.partial: Says wind is moving air and heat is involved but cannot chain uneven heating → warm air rises → cooler air moves in, or gets the convection direction wrong.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: At the seaside on a hot afternoon a breeze often blows in from the sea onto the land. What makes the air move — what is wind, really?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks wind is 'made by trees/waves' or is special stuff cannot explain the sea breeze; only the uneven-heating → rising-air → air-moves-in model explains why the breeze blows from sea to land on a hot day.

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting fractions whose denominators are RELATED — one is a multiple of the other (1/3 + 1/6, 3/4 − 1/8, 2/5 + 3/10). The pivotal new idea is that unlike parts cannot be combined until they are the SAME size: you must rename one fraction as an equivalent fraction so both share a common unit (a common denominator), then count like parts as before. Because the denominators are related, only ONE fraction needs converting (1/3 = 2/6), which makes this the gentle bridge from same-denominator work to fully unlike denominators. The equivalence must scale numerator and denominator together — the heart of getting it right.
bestPractices: Establish the NEED for a common unit first (you can't add thirds and sixths as they are) using a representation that makes different-sized parts obvious, before any rule.
Exploit the related structure: spot that the larger denominator is already the common one, so only one fraction is renamed.
Insist that renaming scales BOTH numerator and denominator (1/3 → 2/6, not 1/6) — the commonest slip is changing only the denominator.
Use estimation to judge reasonableness (1/3 + 1/6 must be more than 1/3, so 2/9 can't be right).
Simplify the result and check it against a model; connect back to counting like units once the denominators match.
Choose representations that hold the unit constant (fraction strips, number lines); avoid ones (e.g. dot paper) shown to reinforce adding without a common denominator.
keyRepresentations: Two fraction strips with related partitions (thirds and sixths) overlaid so one must be re-partitioned to match
Number line where thirds are subdivided into sixths to align the two fractions
Fraction circles/area model showing 1/3 recut into 2/6 to give a common denominator (IES Fig 6)
Equivalence chain 1/3 = 2/6 shown as cutting each third in two (numerator doubles with denominator)
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the unlike denominators: 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9, combining numerators and denominators (NFER's 3/9-type error).
Renames the denominator without scaling the numerator: converts 1/3 to 1/6 and gets 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 — 'just inserts the larger denominator' (IES).
Forgets to simplify the result (leaves 3/6 rather than 1/2), or doesn't recognise the answer can be reduced.

learn.summary: Adding and subtracting fractions whose denominators are RELATED — one denominator is a multiple of the other (1/3 + 1/6, 3/4 − 1/8, 2/5 + 3/10). The central new idea: when you combine fractions by counting parts, the parts must be the same size, so one fraction is renamed as an equivalent fraction sharing a common unit (common denominator), after which like parts are counted as before. Because the denominators are related, only ONE fraction needs converting (e.g. 1/3 = 2/6), making this a gentle bridge from same-denominator work to fully unlike denominators. Renaming must scale numerator AND denominator together — the heart of getting it right.

activities.title: Align the strips: cut thirds into sixths to make a common unit
feedback: If a learner tries to add across (1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9): point to the strips — the pieces are different sizes, so there is nothing to count yet; the parts must be made the same size first.

If a learner changes only the denominator (1/3 → 1/6): show that cutting the one third-piece in two produces TWO sixth-pieces, not one, so the top number must double when the bottom doubles; 1/6 is visibly smaller than 1/3 on the strip.

If the sum is left as 3/6: ask 'is 3/6 finished, or can it be written with smaller numbers?' and confirm on the strip that 3/6 and 1/2 are the same length. Do not reteach the adding step — it is correct.
Estimation check: 1/3 plus a bit must be MORE than 1/3, so an answer less than 1/3 (2/9 is less than 1/3, since 1/3 = 3/9) cannot be right.
activities.rationale: The need for a common unit is felt when unlike parts will not combine by counting until one is re-partitioned; a strip or number-line model can force the re-partition and show the numerator scaling as the piece is cut. Representations that hold the unit (the whole) constant — fraction strips, number lines, fraction circles — cue the need for a common denominator; dot paper has been noted in the IES guide as reinforcing adding without one. The related structure means the larger denominator is already the common unit, so only one fraction is renamed, and renaming must scale numerator and denominator together.
sourceClaims: Students often fail to convert to a common denominator and instead just insert the larger denominator; the error reflects not understanding that different denominators are different-sized unit fractions and that adding requires a common unit. Use representations that cue the need for common denominators (fraction circles, Fig 6, 1/2 + 1/3 → sixths) and estimation; avoid representations (dot paper) that reinforce adding without a common denominator.

On different-denominator items only 54% of Year 6 were correct; a common error was adding both numerators and denominators (2/3 + ... → 3/9); NFER recommends practising common denominators where one denominator is a multiple of the other, working visually (rectangles split into thirds and sixths).
Generating equivalent fractions by scaling numerator and denominator together (a/b = na/nb) is prerequisite to finding common denominators.
learnerActions: Try to combine 1/3 and 1/6 using a thirds strip and a sixths strip laid together; notice the pieces are different sizes and do not line up as they are.
Cut each third-piece in half so each single third becomes TWO sixth-pieces; watch the label change 1/3 → 2/6 as the one piece splits into two and the numerator ticks 1→2.
Now that every piece is a sixth, combine: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6.
Simplify 3/6 to 1/2 and check on the strip that 3/6 and 1/2 are the same length.

Repeat the same cut-to-match process for 3/4 − 1/8 (recut quarters into eighths, giving 6/8 − 1/8 = 5/8) and 2/5 + 3/10 (recut fifths into tenths, giving 4/10 + 3/10 = 7/10), simplifying where possible.
activities.intendedInsight: When you add by counting parts, thirds and sixths must be made the same size first; cutting each third in two makes it two sixths (so the numerator doubles exactly as the denominator doubles), and only then do both fractions share one common unit and combine by counting like parts.

activities.title: Equivalence-and-combine practice that surfaces common errors
feedback: Selecting 2/9: the two denominators are not things to combine; they signal different-sized parts that must be made the same size first.
Selecting 2/6: the denominator was renamed but the numerator stayed at 1 — cutting each third in two makes TWO sixths, so the top doubles too.
If the chain is correct but left as 3/6: prompt for simplest form and confirm 3/6 = 1/2.
activities.rationale: Related-denominator sums and the equivalence step are scorable and can deliberately bait both the add-across and rename-denominator-only errors, surfacing the specific misconception for targeted feedback. A recognition/short-answer format is a useful diagnostic and practice companion; recognising a correct option is not the same as independently performing the re-partition, so it should sit alongside a task where the learner does the conversion.
sourceClaims: Students often fail to convert to a common denominator and instead just insert the larger denominator; the error reflects not understanding that different denominators are different-sized unit fractions and that adding requires a common unit. Use representations that cue the need for common denominators (fraction circles, Fig 6, 1/2 + 1/3 → sixths) and estimation; avoid representations (dot paper) that reinforce adding without a common denominator.

On different-denominator items only 54% of Year 6 were correct; a common error was adding both numerators and denominators (2/3 + ... → 3/9); NFER recommends practising common denominators where one denominator is a multiple of the other, working visually (rectangles split into thirds and sixths).
learnerActions: Complete the chain: 1/3 = __/6, so 1/3 + 1/6 = __/6 = __ (simplest form).
Choose the correct value of 1/3 + 1/6 from options that include the correct answer, 2/9 (the add-across error) and 2/6 (denominator renamed but numerator left at 1).
Match each fraction to its equivalent written over the common denominator (e.g. 1/3 ↔ 2/6, 3/4 ↔ 6/8).
Explain in words why only one of the two fractions needed changing.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking equivalence and combining in a scorable format can reveal whether the learner renames both numerator and denominator together and whether they look for a common unit at all; it does not by itself show they can carry out the re-partition unaided.

activities.title: Read a worked conversion, then perform your own
feedback: After the worked example, ask the learner to state why the numerator doubled; if they cannot, return to cutting each part in two on a strip.
If they can read but not reproduce the conversion, give another related pair and have them do the cut themselves.
activities.rationale: A static worked conversion can present one correct renaming as a reference anchor, but on its own it does not let the learner perform the re-partition that builds the understanding; it works best paired with a task where the learner does the conversion.
sourceClaims: Students often fail to convert to a common denominator and instead just insert the larger denominator; the error reflects not understanding that different denominators are different-sized unit fractions and that adding requires a common unit. Use representations that cue the need for common denominators (fraction circles, Fig 6, 1/2 + 1/3 → sixths) and estimation; avoid representations (dot paper) that reinforce adding without a common denominator.
learnerActions: Study a single worked conversion where 1/3 is shown recut as 2/6 over the common denominator, with the numerator and denominator both doubling.
Explain what happened to the top number and why.
Then perform the conversion yourself on a fresh related pair (e.g. rename 2/5 as tenths, giving 4/10) and complete the calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear worked example of renaming can anchor the 'scale both parts together' idea, but the learner must then carry out the re-partition themselves to secure it; reading a conversion does not by itself elicit producing one.

constraints: Establish the NEED for a common unit before any rule, using a representation that makes different-sized parts obvious (thirds and sixths cannot be counted together as they are).
Renaming must scale BOTH numerator and denominator together (1/3 → 2/6, not 1/6); the commonest slip is changing only the denominator.
Use estimation to judge reasonableness (1/3 + 1/6 must be more than 1/3, so 2/9 cannot be right).
Always simplify the result and check it against the model (3/6 → 1/2); connect back to counting like units once denominators match.

Prefer representations that hold the unit (the whole) constant — fraction strips, number lines, fraction circles. Dot paper has been noted (IES) as reinforcing adding without a common denominator, so avoid it for this objective.

Multiple-choice and fill-in items are useful for diagnosing and practising, but a recognition response does not by itself show the learner can independently perform the re-partition and combine; include a task where they carry out the conversion.

If paper fraction strips or circles are used as physical manipulatives, keep the represented whole constant and explicit each time pieces are cut, so the mathematical fraction — not the physical object — is what is combined; the slight thickness of real card is a negligible approximation of the ideal flat region it stands for.

Scope this to RELATED denominators (one a multiple of the other) so exactly one fraction is renamed; fully unlike denominators are a later step. Here the fractions are quantities being combined, so the common-unit requirement is about representing both portions on one whole — it is not a comparison of unit fractions.

One listed source (DfE National Curriculum, equivalent fractions a/b = na/nb) is marked verified:false in the row; it is used only as supporting context for the 'scale both parts together' principle and its prerequisite claim should be treated as unconfirmed.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2 ✓; 3/4 − 1/8 = 6/8 − 1/8 = 5/8 ✓; 2/5 + 3/10 = 4/10 + 3/10 = 7/10 ✓ (already simplest). The add-across error figures (2/9 for the first; 2/12 for 3/4 − 1/8, combining 4 and 8) are labelled only as errors, never offered as valid answers in any activity.

The original's fit-ranking language ('ideal', formats that 'only' assess, 3D/conversation 'add nothing') reflects a catalog ranking, not established comparative efficacy; it has been softened to affordance-and-limit statements. A static worked example can still teach the renaming idea even though it does not itself elicit the learner performing the cut.
Efficacy of all proposed activities is untested; wording uses 'can/may/intended' accordingly.

probeDeeper: When you changed 1/3 into sixths, what happened to the top number, and why?
A friend writes 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9. Is 2/9 bigger or smaller than 1/3? Can adding something to 1/3 give you less than 1/3?
Why did you only need to change ONE of the two fractions here?
Is 3/6 finished, or can it be written more simply? How do you know they're the same?
assess.correctAnswer: 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. 3/4 − 1/8 = 6/8 − 1/8 = 5/8. Rename one fraction to the common denominator (scaling numerator and denominator together), then combine like parts and simplify.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across the unlike denominators: '1 and 1 is 2 on top, 3 and 6 is 9 on the bottom, so 2/9' — treats the two denominators as things to combine.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use strips/circles that only combine when parts match: thirds and sixths can't be added until the third is recut into sixths. Add an estimation check — 1/3 + a bit must exceed 1/3, so 2/9 (which is less than 1/3) can't be right.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 2/9 (or 2/12 for the second, combining 4 and 8); no common denominator is sought.

errorPatterns.pattern: Renames the denominator but not the numerator: '1/3 becomes 1/6, so 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6' — just inserts the larger denominator.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the equivalence on a model: cutting each third in two makes the one piece become TWO sixth-pieces, so 1/3 = 2/6 — the top must double when the bottom doubles. Contrast 1/6 (too small) against 1/3 on the strip.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts 1/3 to 1/6 (numerator unchanged); the equivalent fraction is wrong before adding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Combines correctly but leaves the answer unsimplified: writes 3/6 (or doesn't reduce), not recognising 1/2.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach adding — it's correct. Prompt: 'is 3/6 finished, or can you write it with smaller numbers?' Check on the strip that 3/6 and 1/2 are the same length.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct unsimplified result (3/6); the operation is right, only the final simplest-form step is missing.

responseLevels.gap: Adds across (2/9) or renames the denominator without scaling the numerator (2/6); no common-unit reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Renames the necessary fraction (scaling numerator and denominator together), combines the like parts, simplifies (3/6→1/2), and explains that a common unit is needed to add; transfers to a fresh related-denominator pair.
responseLevels.partial: Converts to a common denominator and combines correctly for the straightforward case, but scales inconsistently, forgets to simplify, or can't say why only one fraction was changed — procedure without the equivalence reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing each step: 1/3 + 1/6, and 3/4 − 1/8. Give each answer in its simplest form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The denominators are related (6 is a multiple of 3; 8 of 4), so the child must convert exactly one fraction — revealing whether equivalence is understood. Add-across yields 2/9 / 2/12 (denominators combined), impossible if a common unit is sought. Renaming without scaling yields 2/6 (numerator left at 1). A correct solver converts 1/3→2/6 (numerator scales with denominator), combines the like parts, and simplifies. Watching the conversion step is the discriminator; the simplify step is a separate check.

sources.claim: Students often fail to convert to a common denominator and instead just insert the larger denominator; the error reflects not understanding that different denominators are different-sized unit fractions and that adding requires a common unit. Use representations that cue the need for common denominators (fraction circles, Fig 6, 1/2 + 1/3 → sixths) and estimation; avoid representations (dot paper) that reinforce adding without a common denominator.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K–8 (Siegler et al., 2010), Recommendation 3

sources.claim: On different-denominator items only 54% of Year 6 were correct; a common error was adding both numerators and denominators (2/3 + ... → 3/9); NFER recommends practising common denominators where one denominator is a multiple of the other, working visually (rectangles split into thirds and sixths).
sources.source: NFER Assessment Hub, 'What are the common mistakes when adding fractions?' (Emily Jones)

sources.claim: Generating equivalent fractions by scaling numerator and denominator together (a/b = na/nb) is prerequisite to finding common denominators.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum for England, Mathematics (Year 5)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: How Animals Have Babies, ages 5–7 — different animals have young in different ways: some LAY EGGS (birds, reptiles, fish, insects) and some give birth to LIVE YOUNG (most mammals); and babies may look like tiny adults or look very different from their parents (tadpole→frog, caterpillar→butterfly).
• Standards — UK: DfE KS1 Y2 'Animals, including humans' — "notice that animals, including humans, have offspring which grow into adults" (non-statutory examples: egg→chick→chicken, egg→caterpillar→pupa→butterfly, spawn→tadpole→frog).
• Standards — US: NGSS 1-LS3-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1]) and 3-LS1-1 later formalises life cycles (birth, growth, reproduction, death) with diverse patterns.
• Operational details: teach the two-way sort EGG-LAYERS vs LIVE-BEARERS with clear examples of each; then the second big idea — some babies are mini versions of the adult (a lamb, a chick soon feathers up) while others transform completely (tadpole→frog, caterpillar→butterfly), which is the surprising, engaging hook; keep it at 'how babies arrive and grow' — NO reproduction mechanism (that is much later and RSE-governed).
• Checkpoint: [Tier A] gives examples of animals that lay eggs AND animals that have live young, and describes at least one baby that looks very different from its parent (tadpole/frog or caterpillar/butterfly).
bestPractices: Build the core EGG vs LIVE-YOUNG sort with plenty of examples, deliberately including surprises that break the mammal=live, everything-else=egg shortcut (e.g. a shark that bears live young; a duck-billed platypus mammal that lays eggs) — kept as delightful curiosities, not rules to master.

Make the 'looks different' idea vivid with the two canonical transformations — tadpole→frog and caterpillar→(egg→)caterpillar→pupa→butterfly — as an animated 'grow the baby' reveal; the shock that a tadpole becomes a frog is the memorable moment.
Contrast 'mini-adult' babies (lamb, chick, kitten resemble their parents quickly) with 'transformer' babies (frog, butterfly) so children hold both patterns.
Use real photos/video of hatching and of young growing up; at 5–7 concrete imagery beats definitions.
Keep strictly to how babies ARRIVE (laid vs born) and GROW — do not stray into how reproduction happens; that is developmentally and curricularly later (and RSE-governed).
keyRepresentations: A two-bin sort: EGG-LAYERS (bird, fish, frog, lizard, insect) vs LIVE-YOUNG (dog, cow, human, whale).
Metamorphosis strips: spawn→tadpole→froglet→frog; egg→caterpillar→chrysalis→butterfly — the 'grow the baby' reveal.
A 'looks like / looks different' pairing board: baby beside adult (lamb–sheep look alike; tadpole–frog look different).
Real hatching / birth imagery as the concrete anchor.
commonMisconceptions: Believing ALL animals lay eggs, or that only birds/chickens lay eggs — missing that fish, reptiles, amphibians and insects lay eggs too.
Thinking every baby animal is just a smaller version of its parent — not expecting complete transformations like tadpole→frog or caterpillar→butterfly.
Assuming mammals never lay eggs and non-mammals never bear live young (the platypus and live-bearing sharks are real exceptions).
Thinking a caterpillar and its butterfly (or a tadpole and its frog) are different, unrelated animals rather than life stages of the SAME animal.
Conflating 'having babies' with human family framing; at this age it is simply 'laid as an egg or born live, then grows up'.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7 (How Animals Have Babies): children learn two big ideas — (1) different animals have young in different ways, some LAY EGGS (birds, and most fish, reptiles, amphibians and insects) and some give birth to LIVE YOUNG (most mammals); and (2) some babies look like miniature adults (lamb, chick, kitten) while others transform completely (tadpole→frog, caterpillar→butterfly) yet are still the SAME animal growing up. Teaching stays strictly on how babies ARRIVE (laid vs born) and GROW — not on reproduction mechanisms, which are developmentally later and RSE-governed. Activities combine an egg-layer vs live-bearer sort (with gentle surprises that break the mammal=live shortcut) and a 'grow the baby' metamorphosis sequence.

activities.title: Sort the animals: egg-layers or live-young?
feedback: If a child says only birds lay eggs: sort more animals together — many fish, frogs, lizards and insects lay eggs too; eggs are not just a bird thing.
If a child says a dog, cat or human lays eggs: contrast these live-birth mammals with the egg-layers using familiar examples.
When the platypus lays an egg or the shark bears live young, treat the giggle/surprise as the point: nature has exceptions, keep these as curiosities rather than rules to master.
Reinforce correct sorts by naming the group: 'Yes — the frog lays eggs in a pond; the cow has a live calf.'
activities.rationale: A concrete two-way sort with plenty of varied examples is intended to build the core distinction and to confront the common 'only birds lay eggs' and 'mammals never lay eggs' misconceptions. For 5–7s, hands-on sorting of familiar animals may be more accessible than definitions; a sort checks and practises classification but does not by itself elicit a child's own explanation.
learnerActions: Place or group animal pictures into two bins: EGG-LAYERS and LIVE-YOUNG.
Put the hen, an egg-laying fish (e.g. a salmon or goldfish), frog, an egg-laying lizard (e.g. a gecko) and a beetle into the egg-layers bin; put the dog, cow, whale and human into the live-young bin.
After sorting with familiar animals, meet a surprise: a platypus (a mammal that LAYS eggs) and a shark that bears LIVE young — discuss why these are delightful exceptions, not new rules to memorise.
Say aloud one animal that lays eggs and one animal that has live babies.
activities.intendedInsight: Many kinds of animals lay eggs — not just birds — and most mammals have live young; nature also has surprising exceptions, so the shortcut 'mammals are born, everything else lays eggs' doesn't always hold.

activities.title: Grow the baby: watch a creature transform
feedback: If a child calls the tadpole a different animal or a fish: walk through the sequence egg→tadpole→froglet→frog — it is one animal changing shape as it grows, not a new animal.
If a child expects every baby to look like its parent: contrast the lamb→sheep (same) pairing with the tadpole→frog (different) pairing so both patterns are held together.
Name the surprise when the frog or butterfly emerges — the moment one creature becomes something so different is a memorable anchor.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and watching the whole metamorphosis is intended to address the misconception that a caterpillar/tadpole and its adult are separate, unrelated animals, and that all babies are miniature adults. Advancing the stages oneself is intended to make the 'same animal, different form' idea vivid; pairing with mini-adult examples keeps both patterns in view.
sourceClaims: Children commonly think every baby animal is a miniature adult and that a caterpillar and butterfly are separate animals; using metamorphosis sequences directly addresses this.
Young [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1]; organisms have diverse life cycles all involving birth, growth, reproduction and death.
KS1 pupils should notice that animals, including humans, have offspring which grow into adults, with example sequences egg→chick, egg→caterpillar→pupa→butterfly, spawn→tadpole→frog.
learnerActions: Advance a life-cycle sequence step by step: spawn → tadpole → froglet → frog, watching legs sprout and the tail shrink.
Advance a second sequence: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly, watching the caterpillar eat, change into a chrysalis, and emerge as a butterfly.
After each transformation, decide and tag whether the grown-up 'looks the same' or 'looks different' from its baby.
Compare with a 'mini-adult' pairing: place a lamb beside a sheep and a chick beside a hen — these already look like small versions of their parents.
activities.intendedInsight: A tadpole IS a baby frog and a caterpillar IS a baby butterfly — the SAME animal at an early life stage. Some young change shape completely as they grow (metamorphosis) while others look like small versions of their parents from early on.

activities.title: Check and talk: same animal or different?
feedback: Target answer for the frog prompt: the tadpoles ARE baby frogs — the same animal at an early stage. As they grow they change (metamorphosis): they grow legs, lose the tail, and become frogs. They are not a different kind of animal and not fish.
If a child treats different-looking young as separate animals, this shows only partial understanding — return to the 'grow the baby' sequence to show it is one animal changing.
The 'what will happen as they grow' part is the key tell: a child who accepts that some young change form will predict the change rather than call the tadpole a fish.
activities.rationale: Matching, sequencing and categorisation are valid checks of the KS1 evidence, and the open discussion prompt helps distinguish a child who runs 'babies look like small versions of their parents' from one who accepts metamorphosis. Used during teaching, the talk may also surface and help repair misconceptions, not only measure them; matching/sequencing on their own assess recognition and ordering rather than a child's own explanation.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should notice that animals, including humans, have offspring which grow into adults, with example sequences egg→chick, egg→caterpillar→pupa→butterfly, spawn→tadpole→frog.
learnerActions: Match each baby to its grown-up (baby→adult pairing).
Put life-stage cards in the right order (e.g. order the tadpole→frog stages).
Categorise a fresh set of animals as egg-layers or live-young.

Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'A frog lays eggs in a pond, and out come tadpoles that look nothing like frogs. Are the tadpoles baby frogs, or a completely different animal? How do you know — and what will happen to them as they grow?'
Discuss: Does a kitten look like a small cat or completely different? Do ALL babies look like their parents? What will grow on the tadpole, and what will disappear, as it gets bigger?
activities.intendedInsight: Children can give examples of egg-layers and live-bearers, and recognise that a very different-looking baby (tadpole, caterpillar) is still the same animal, which will change as it grows.

constraints: Keep strictly to how babies ARRIVE (laid vs born) and GROW; do NOT teach reproduction mechanisms — that is developmentally and curricularly later and RSE-governed.
Present the platypus and live-bearing shark as delightful exceptions/curiosities, not as rules children must master.

A tap-to-reveal or lift-the-flap board reliably covers both ideas and is a good lighter-touch option, but a flap only shows the answer; where possible let children advance/sequence the metamorphosis themselves so the 'looks completely different' payoff is experienced, not just told.

Matching/sequencing/categorisation tasks are suitable as end checks but, on their own, assess recognition and ordering rather than eliciting a child's own explanation; pair them with the open 'same or different, and why' prompt for understanding.
Avoid human-family framing of 'having babies'; at this age it is simply 'laid as an egg or born live, then grows up'.
Use real photos/video of hatching and of young growing up as concrete anchors; at 5–7 concrete imagery supports the abstract idea.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all sources[].verified were false in the row and have NOT been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Activity 1 (egg-layer vs live-bearer sort) has sourceClaims=[]: no sources[].claim directly supports the egg-vs-live distinction or the 'only birds lay eggs'/'mammals never lay eggs' misconceptions; the available claims address growth/metamorphosis only.

Comparative efficacy wording from the row and earlier candidate ('concrete imagery beats definitions', interaction 'makes the idea vivid/unforgettable') was softened to may/intended wording, since no source establishes the comparative efficacy of any specific activity format.

The source row rated 3D as adding 'no conceptual value' and an in-role conversation as adding 'little'; these were scoped as fit judgements for this categorical/time-sequence topic and are not treated here as universal claims about those media. A spoken discussion of 'same animal or different' is in fact used as a teaching/check step above.

Source cites DfE KS1 and NGSS 1-LS3-1/3-LS1-1 and OpenLearn/Oak guidance; citations support the general principle and standards alignment but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity format.
Scientific content checked: tadpole→frog loses tail and grows legs; caterpillar→chrysalis→butterfly; platypus (monotreme) lays eggs; some sharks bear live young — all accurate as stated.

probeDeeper: What will grow on the tadpole, and what will disappear, as it gets bigger?
Name an animal that lays eggs and an animal that has live babies.
A caterpillar and a butterfly — are they the same animal or two different animals? Why?
Does a kitten look like a small cat, or completely different? Do ALL babies look like their parents?
assess.correctAnswer: The tadpoles ARE baby frogs — the same animal at an early stage of its life. As they grow they change (metamorphosis): they grow legs, lose the tail, and become frogs. They are not a different kind of animal and not fish.

errorPatterns.pattern: Babies always look like small versions of their parents — so a tadpole must be a different animal (or a fish).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the life-cycle sequence egg → tadpole → froglet → frog; it is one animal changing shape as it grows.
errorPatterns.distractor: The tadpoles are a different animal, because they don't look like frogs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the tadpole is not a frog, or calls it a fish, because it doesn't look like a frog.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only birds lay eggs.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort many animals into egg-layers (birds, fish, reptiles, frogs, insects) versus live-young; eggs are not just a bird thing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Surprised or doubtful that fish, reptiles and insects lay eggs; may say frogs give birth to live young.

errorPatterns.pattern: All animals have their babies the same way — e.g. mammals lay eggs too.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast live-birth mammals with egg-layers using familiar examples.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a dog, cat or human lays eggs, or that every animal gives live birth.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks all babies resemble their parents, so metamorphosing young must be 'different animals'; unsure that any non-birds lay eggs.
responseLevels.full: Knows egg-laying vs live-birth with examples across animal groups, and that some young change form (metamorphosis) while still being the same animal growing up.
responseLevels.partial: Knows some animals lay eggs and some have live young, but still treats very different-looking young (tadpole, caterpillar) as separate animals.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A frog lays eggs in a pond, and out come tadpoles that look nothing like frogs. Are the tadpoles baby frogs, or a completely different animal? How do you know — and what will happen to them as they grow?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A tadpole looks nothing like a frog, so a child running 'babies look like small versions of their parents' concludes it must be a different animal (often 'a fish'). Only a child who accepts that some young change form as they grow says 'same animal — it will change'. The 'what will happen' tier is the tell.

sources.claim: KS1 pupils should notice that animals, including humans, have offspring which grow into adults, with example sequences egg→chick, egg→caterpillar→pupa→butterfly, spawn→tadpole→frog.
sources.source: UK Department for Education — National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, KS1 Y2 'Animals, including humans' (statutory + non-statutory examples)

sources.claim: Young [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1]; organisms have diverse life cycles all involving birth, growth, reproduction and death.
sources.source: NGSS 1-LS3-1 / 3-LS1-1 (Next Generation Science Standards)

sources.claim: Children commonly think every baby animal is a miniature adult and that a caterpillar and butterfly are separate animals; using metamorphosis sequences directly addresses this.
