pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Herbivores, Carnivores & Omnivores

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 Animals including humans):** "identify and name a variety of common animals that are carnivores, herbivores and omnivores." Classifying familiar animals by what they eat, and giving a reason, is statutory in England.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no direct diet-label PE; nearest anchor K-LS1-1 / DCI LS1.C):** NGSS does not require the herbivore/carnivore/omnivore labels at K–2; DCI LS1.C states animals get their food from plants or other animals. The diet-category vocabulary is UK-driven; the US connection is 'where does this animal's food come from', which leads into food chains (later).

- **Operational details:** Teach the three labels by their meaning-in-the-word and by SORTING familiar animals with a stated reason ('the rabbit is a herbivore because it eats plants/grass'). Anchor each label to clear exemplars — herbivore: rabbit, cow, horse; carnivore: lion, shark, fox; omnivore: bear, pig, human, chicken — and make the OMNIVORE category central, as it is the one children over-simplify. Use evidence beyond the label: what the animal actually eats, and (as a bridge to KS2) clues like teeth shape (flat grinding teeth vs sharp pointed teeth). Connect to the child's own diet: humans eat both plants and meat, so we are omnivores. This node feeds directly into food chains and types of teeth.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–6, KS1 Y1). Children can define the three terms in their own words, sort at least six animals into the groups, and justify each with what the animal eats. Appropriate: familiar animals, diet as observable evidence, a light teeth-shape clue. NOT appropriate yet: trophic levels, producer/consumer terminology, energy flow. Watch the 'all big/fierce animals are carnivores' and 'omnivore = can't decide' misconceptions.
bestPractices: Teach the labels by sorting familiar animals into the three groups with a stated reason based on what each animal eats, not by rote definition.
Make the OMNIVORE category central and well-exemplified (bear, pig, human, chicken), because children over-simplify it or treat it as 'undecided'.
Use evidence beyond the label — the animal's actual food and a teeth-shape clue (flat grinding vs sharp tearing) — to bridge toward KS2 teeth and food chains.
Anchor to the child's own diet (we eat plants and meat, so humans are omnivores) to make the category personal and concrete.
Include deliberate surprises — fierce-looking herbivores (gorilla, hippo) and small carnivores (shrew) — to break the 'fierce means meat-eater' rule.
keyRepresentations: Three sorting groups: herbivore / carnivore / omnivore, with animal picture cards.
Animal→food evidence cards (rabbit–grass, lion–meat, bear–berries+fish) used to justify each sort.
Teeth-shape close-ups (broad flat molars vs sharp pointed canines) as diet clues.
The child's own dinner plate as the exemplar for 'omnivore'.
commonMisconceptions: 'Big, fierce or with big teeth = carnivore' — sorting gorillas, hippos or elephants as meat-eaters by appearance.
'Omnivore means the animal can't decide / eats anything including non-food' rather than 'eats both plants and animals'.
Assuming all farm/pet animals are herbivores, or that humans are herbivores/carnivores rather than omnivores.
Equating 'carnivore' with 'predator/hunter' only, missing scavengers and small insect-eaters.

learn.summary: For 5–6 year olds, teach the diet labels herbivore, carnivore and omnivore by sorting familiar animals into three groups and giving a reason based on what each animal actually eats, not by rote definition. Make the omnivore category central (bear, pig, human, chicken) because children over-simplify it, use the child's own mixed diet as the anchor example, and build in deliberate surprises (fierce-looking herbivores like gorilla/hippo, small carnivores like shrew) to break the 'fierce means meat-eater' rule. Diet is the rule; teeth shape (flat grinding vs sharp pointed) is a supporting clue that bridges toward later teeth and food-chain topics.

activities.title: Feeding-time sorting bench
feedback: When a learner drops the gorilla with the carnivores reasoning 'big and powerful', reveal its real meal of leaves, stems and fruit plus its broad, flat back teeth for grinding plants: the deciding evidence is what it actually eats, not its fierce appearance. (Gorillas also have big pointed canine teeth, so teeth are only a hint and the food decides.)
On placing 'human', show a meal of both salad and chicken — we eat plants and meat, so humans are omnivores — and let bear and pig join to confirm the 'eats both' meaning.
If a learner sorts by size or fierceness, offer counterexamples (elephant and cow are huge herbivores; a shrew is a small carnivore) and re-sort strictly by diet.
activities.rationale: The objective is to sort animals by diet WITH a reason. A drag-to-group bench with evidence revealed on drop lets the category be earned from evidence rather than guessed from appearance, and a food/teeth reveal is a proposed way to make the reasoning concrete. The revealed food and teeth close-ups are optional ways to make the mechanism vivid, not required machinery.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common animals that are carnivores, herbivores and omnivores'.

Diet classification can be evidenced by tooth shape — flat/broad teeth for grinding plants (herbivores) and sharp/pointed teeth for tearing meat (carnivores) — a clue used in primary teaching and the basis for the later 'types of teeth' topic.
learnerActions: Place each animal from a queue into one of three troughs: herbivore (leaves), carnivore (meat), or omnivore (both).
Start with easy cases — rabbit to plants, lion to meat — then meet the designed surprise: a gorilla.
After each placement, look at the revealed evidence (the animal's actual meal and/or a teeth close-up) and say the reason aloud: 'the rabbit is a herbivore because it eats grass'.
Sort 'human' and discover a plate of both salad and chicken, then place bear and pig alongside to define omnivore as 'eats both'.
activities.intendedInsight: An animal's diet group is decided by what it actually eats (and clued by its teeth), not by how big, fierce or scary it looks; omnivore means 'eats both plants and animals', not 'undecided'.

activities.title: Sort real picture cards in class
feedback: Accept a correct group placement, and when the learner has placed it, prompt 'what does it eat?' so the food-based reason is spoken as well as the group named.
Include a gorilla or hippo card so a fierce-appearance error can be surfaced and corrected with its actual plant diet.
activities.rationale: Physical picture-card sorting with evidence cards gives a hands-on version of the same sort-with-a-reason objective and lets a teacher hear the spoken justification. It complements the screen bench rather than replacing it; neither medium is required over the other.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common animals that are carnivores, herbivores and omnivores'.
learnerActions: Lay out picture cards of at least six familiar animals and three labelled hoops or trays: herbivore, carnivore, omnivore.
Match each animal to a 'what it eats' card (rabbit–grass, lion–meat, bear–berries+fish) and place it in the matching group.
Say a spoken reason for each decision based on the food, e.g. 'the bear is an omnivore because it eats berries and fish'.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying is a justified decision: each animal belongs in a group because of the food it eats, and that reason can be stated out loud.

activities.title: Who eats what — reveal scene
feedback: Confirm correct predictions by matching the revealed food to the label; for a missed prediction, point to the shown food as the deciding evidence.
Use the teeth close-up as a supporting clue, reminding learners the diet is the rule and teeth are the hint.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal scene is well suited to introducing the vocabulary and pairing each label with exemplars, food and a teeth clue. It is an introduction/exploration format: it does not itself require the learner to commit a sort and be corrected by evidence, so pair it with an activity that does.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common animals that are carnivores, herbivores and omnivores'.

Diet classification can be evidenced by tooth shape — flat/broad teeth for grinding plants (herbivores) and sharp/pointed teeth for tearing meat (carnivores) — a clue used in primary teaching and the basis for the later 'types of teeth' topic.
learnerActions: Tap an animal in a scene to reveal its diet group, food examples, and a close-up of its teeth.
Explore the reveals grouped by the three labels to meet exemplars of each category.
After exploring, predict a new animal's group before tapping to check.
activities.intendedInsight: Each label (herbivore, carnivore, omnivore) names a real group of animals with characteristic foods and teeth that you can observe.

activities.title: Guess the animal's diet from its day
feedback: Affirm an inference that cites the described food; if the learner guesses from the animal's identity or appearance, redirect to the meals actually described.
For omnivore cases, highlight that the day included both plant and animal foods.
activities.rationale: An in-role description that gives only the food evidence supports the reason-giving goal by removing appearance cues. Sorting many animals is handled more efficiently by direct manipulation, so use this for a few focused inference cases rather than a full sort.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common animals that are carnivores, herbivores and omnivores'.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a short first-person account from an animal describing only the kinds of food it usually eats ('Every day I spend the morning grazing on grass...').
Name the animal's diet group and say the reason drawn from the meals described.

Respond to a follow-up matched to the account: if the animal eats only one kind of food, say what other kind of food an omnivore would also eat; if the account already described both plant and animal foods, name it an omnivore and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: You can infer a diet category from evidence of what an animal usually eats, without seeing how the animal looks.

activities.title: Spot the surprise (checking questions)
feedback: Elephant is a herbivore because it eats only plants, even though it is huge; use this to counter the 'big = carnivore' rule.
A bear that eats berries and fish is an omnivore — it eats both plants and animals.

Confirm that people are omnivores because humans can eat, and usually do eat, both plants and meat; if a child eats no meat, accept that their own meals are plant foods while explaining that people as a group are omnivores. If they say humans aren't animals, establish that humans are animals.
For the same-size pair, the discriminating move is to ask what each one eats, not to compare their size.
If a learner picks 'eats meat' for the gorilla, reveal it eats leaves, stems and fruit — the correct reason is 'eats plants' (herbivore) — showing fierce looks do not decide diet.
activities.rationale: These prompts target the exact misconceptions (appearance-based sorting, omnivore as 'can't decide', humans excluded) and discriminate a diet-based sorter from an appearance-based one. They check classification and reasoning; recognition in a check does not by itself build the evidence-based reasoning, so combine with the construction activities above for teaching.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common animals that are carnivores, herbivores and omnivores'.
learnerActions: Answer: an elephant is enormous but eats only plants — what group is it in?
Answer: what do we call an animal, like a bear, that eats both berries and fish?
Answer: are you a herbivore, carnivore or omnivore, and how do you know?
Answer: two animals are the same size — can one be a carnivore and one a herbivore? How would you tell them apart?
For each animal shown, choose the reason that fits — 'eats plants', 'eats meat', or 'eats both' — including a gorilla, where 'eats meat' is the tempting-but-wrong fierce-appearance choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Size and fierceness do not determine diet group; you decide by what the animal eats, and humans are animals who are usually omnivores.

constraints: Appropriate for ≈5–6 (KS1 Y1): familiar animals, diet as observable evidence, and a light teeth-shape clue. Not yet appropriate: trophic levels, producer/consumer terminology, or energy flow.
Keep diet as the deciding rule; teeth shape is a supporting clue, not the rule by itself. Do not let learners judge group from looks or teeth alone.
Make the omnivore category central and well-exemplified (bear, pig, human, chicken); define it as 'eats both plants and animals', explicitly not 'undecided' or 'eats anything including non-food'.

Include deliberate counterexamples — fierce-looking herbivores (gorilla, hippo, elephant, cow) and small carnivores (shrew, insect-eaters) — so sorting by size/fierceness fails. Note that 'carnivore' includes scavengers and small insect-eaters, not only predators.

The reveal scene and the in-role dialogue introduce or probe the ideas but do not require the learner to commit a sort and be corrected; they are scaffolds to pair with an activity where the learner actually constructs and justifies a sort.
Checking questions assess classification and reasoning; recognition alone does not build the evidence-based reasoning, which the sorting activities develop.
The revealed food plates and teeth close-ups are optional ways to make the reasoning visible; they are examples of the mechanism, not mandatory components.

Diet classification is not a spatial concept, so clear 2D images plus food/teeth evidence are sufficient for this objective and a 3D model is not needed here; this is a design judgement for this objective, not a claim that 3D models cannot teach.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NGSS source claim (DCI LS1.C / K-LS1-1) is marked verified:false in the row: NGSS does not use the herbivore/carnivore/omnivore labels as a K–2 performance expectation; the diet-category vocabulary here is UK/DfE-driven. Treat the NGSS link as 'where an animal's food comes from' leading toward food chains, not as support for the labels.

The original recommendation phrased the gorilla reveal as the rule 'flips from fierce = meat-eater'; retained as a teaching move but framed as correcting an appearance-based error rather than any claim that only an interactive reveal can teach this.

The source row's claim that a 3D model 'adds no sorting insight' was treated as a design fit judgement, not a universal law; it is not asserted here that 3D cannot teach, only that diet classification is not spatial and 2D images plus food/teeth evidence suffice for this objective.
One listed misconception ('humans aren't animals, so aren't omnivores') references a reteach prerequisite (mt_zVLOm6U7bh) not reproducible here; handled via feedback that humans are animals.

The row lists 'fox' as a carnivore exemplar; red foxes are commonly omnivorous in reality. Retained as the row's exemplar for KS1 convention but flagged as an approximation that could be swapped for a clearer carnivore example.
Gorillas are predominantly folivorous herbivores; the herbivore classification used throughout is the appropriate KS1 simplification.

probeDeeper: An elephant is enormous but eats only plants. What group is it in?
What do we call an animal, like a bear, that eats both berries and fish?
Are you a herbivore, carnivore or omnivore? How do you know?
Two animals are the same size — can one be a carnivore and one a herbivore? How would you tell them apart?
assess.correctAnswer: The lion is a carnivore because it eats meat (other animals); the rabbit is a herbivore because it eats plants. You decide by WHAT the animal eats, not by its size or how scary it is — some big animals, like elephants and cows, are herbivores, and some small animals are carnivores.

errorPatterns.pattern: carnivores are the big, fierce, scary animals and herbivores the small, gentle ones (sorts by appearance, not diet)
errorPatterns.nextMove: give counterexamples — the elephant and cow are huge herbivores — and sort strictly by what each animal eats
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — a big scary animal is always a carnivore
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says a big scary animal is always a carnivore, or sorts by size and fierceness

errorPatterns.pattern: an animal that eats both plants and meat must go in one box only, not omnivore
errorPatterns.nextMove: introduce omnivore as the group for animals that eat both plants and animals
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot classify a bear or human that eats both

errorPatterns.pattern: humans aren't animals, so aren't omnivores
errorPatterns.nextMove: establish that humans are animals and most are omnivores, eating both plants and meat
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the probe denies humans fit any of the groups

errorPatterns.pattern: judges the group from looks or teeth alone without knowing the diet
errorPatterns.nextMove: keep the definition anchored to what the animal eats; teeth are a clue, but diet is the rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: guesses from appearance rather than the food eaten

responseLevels.gap: Sorts animals by size or fierceness rather than diet; cannot define the three groups.
responseLevels.full: Defines carnivore, herbivore and omnivore by diet, sorts six animals correctly with a diet-based reason for each, and handles counterexamples like large herbivores and omnivorous humans.
responseLevels.partial: Defines the groups and sorts obvious animals, but slips to appearance for tricky cases (big herbivores, omnivores) or can't justify each choice by diet.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A rabbit and a lion — which is the carnivore and which is the herbivore, and how do you know? Then tell me: is a big scary animal always a carnivore?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A young child who sorts by scariness or size says 'the big fierce one is the carnivore' as a rule; a child who sorts by diet correctly handles the big-herbivore counterexample. The second question is the discriminator.

sources.claim: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common animals that are carnivores, herbivores and omnivores'.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study (KS1)

sources.claim: Diet classification can be evidenced by tooth shape — flat/broad teeth for grinding plants (herbivores) and sharp/pointed teeth for tearing meat (carnivores) — a clue used in primary teaching and the basis for the later 'types of teeth' topic.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study (KS2 Y4 Animals including humans references teeth and digestive functions)

sources.claim: NGSS DCI LS1.C (K-LS1-1) states that all animals need food and obtain it from plants or other animals, which underpins where an animal's food comes from; NGSS does not use the herbivore/carnivore/omnivore labels as a K–2 performance expectation.

pedagogy.summary: The general case: adding and subtracting fractions with UNLIKE denominators where neither is a multiple of the other (2/3 + 5/4), and mixed numbers (3 1/4 − 1 3/5). Both fractions must now be renamed to a shared unit — a common multiple of the denominators (twelfths for thirds and quarters) — scaling BOTH numerators, then combining like parts. Mixed numbers add a further demand: in subtraction the fraction part of the minuend can end up smaller than that of the subtrahend, forcing a regroup across the whole (borrowing a whole, or converting to improper fractions). It is the culmination of the whole add/subtract strand: the same 'make the units the same, then count' idea, now with no shortcuts.
bestPractices: Reinforce that BOTH fractions must be renamed to a common unit; a common multiple of the denominators (often the product, sometimes the LCM) gives it.
Insist both numerators scale with their denominators (2/3 → 8/12, 5/4 → 15/12) — the multi-conversion is where partial-scaling slips appear.
For mixed numbers, teach two secure routes and let pupils choose: regroup/borrow a whole, OR convert to improper fractions first (often cleaner when a borrow is needed).
Use estimation and benchmarks to gate the answer (2/3 + 5/4 is more than 2, so 7/7 = 1 is impossible).
Verify with a visual model or number line, per the topic's own evidence; simplify and write mixed-number answers.
Keep units constant in representations; avoid manipulatives that encourage adding without a common denominator.
keyRepresentations: Two strips/number lines re-gridded to a common denominator (thirds and quarters → twelfths)
Area/fraction-circle model showing both fractions recut to the shared unit
Mixed-number bars showing a whole tile broken into the common unit to enable borrowing (1 whole → 20/20)
Improper-fraction conversion as an alternative route (3 1/4 = 13/4) laid beside the mixed form
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the unlike denominators: 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7, combining numerators and denominators.
Finds a common denominator but scales only one (or neither) numerator, or uses a wrong common denominator (2/3 = 2/12).

In mixed-number subtraction, subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger in each column regardless of position (does 12/20 − 5/20), never regrouping across the whole when the minuend's fraction part is smaller.

learn.summary: General case of adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators where neither denominator is a multiple of the other (e.g. 2/3 + 5/4), extended to mixed numbers (e.g. 3 1/4 − 1 3/5). Both fractions must be renamed to a shared unit — a common multiple of the denominators (twelfths for thirds and quarters) — which scales BOTH numerators, then like parts are combined. Mixed-number subtraction adds a further demand: the fraction part of the minuend can end up smaller than that of the subtrahend, forcing a regroup across the whole (borrow a whole) or a conversion to improper fractions. The unifying idea remains 'make the units the same, then count', now with no shortcuts.

activities.title: Shared-grid combiner: rename both fractions, then combine
feedback: If a learner writes 7/7 (adding tops and adding bottoms), re-partition both fractions on the strips and estimate first: 5/4 alone exceeds 1, so 2/3 + 5/4 must exceed 1, and 7/7 = 1 cannot be right.

If a learner finds the common denominator but leaves a numerator unscaled (e.g. writes 2/12 for 2/3), rebuild the equivalence on the model — one third cut into twelfths becomes FOUR twelfths, so 2/3 = 8/12 — and have them check both conversions before combining.
If the sum is left as 23/12, prompt converting to a mixed number and simplifying: 23/12 = 1 11/12.
Confirm with the estimate: 23/12 is more than 1 and a little less than 2, matching 'more than one (5/4) plus two-thirds'.
activities.rationale: Adding or subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions over a common unit; the add-across error and the 'use the larger denominator' error both come from not grasping this, and a chosen pair where neither denominator is a multiple of the other forces both numerators to scale, exposing partial-scaling slips. Estimation and benchmarks let learners judge reasonableness. A dynamic re-gridding model (strips that only align once a shared grid is chosen, with both numerators re-scaling as the grid is set) may make the re-unitising visible, but a fully worked static picture of 2/3 and 5/4 both shown as twelfths can also anchor the equivalence.
sourceClaims: Adding/subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions with a common denominator (a common unit fraction); the add-across error and the 'insert the larger denominator' error both stem from not grasping this. Teach with representations that cue the need for common denominators and use estimation to judge reasonableness.
The add-across error on different-denominator items is made mostly by lower- and middle-achieving pupils and remains common; visual work and staged conversion help.

Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators including mixed numbers by using equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator; using common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination is a Year 6 expectation.
learnerActions: Set up 2/3 + 5/4 on two strips or two number lines, one gridded in thirds and one in quarters, and notice they will not combine while the units differ.
Choose a shared unit (a common multiple of 3 and 4) and re-grid both strips into twelfths, re-tiling each fraction: 2/3 becomes 8/12 and 5/4 becomes 15/12.

State explicitly that cutting each third into four pieces turns 2/3 into 8/12 — the top is multiplied by the same factor as the bottom — and check the same for 5/4 (each quarter cut into three, so 5/4 = 15/12) before combining.
Combine the re-tiled pieces to get 23/12 and regroup into the mixed number 1 11/12.

Before computing, estimate: 5/4 is already more than 1, so adding a positive 2/3 makes the sum more than 1 (indeed more than 1.5). That already rules out answers like 7/7 = 1; the true sum lands just below 2 (23/12, just under 24/12).
activities.intendedInsight: Unlike fractions can only be combined once BOTH are rewritten over the same unit; each numerator scales by the same factor as its own denominator, and estimation gates whether a result is even possible.

activities.title: Mixed-number subtraction with a regroup across the whole
feedback: If a learner subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger regardless of position (e.g. does 12/20 − 5/20 and writes 7/20), model breaking one whole of the 3 into 20/20 so 3 5/20 becomes 2 25/20, then subtract; or convert both to improper fractions (65/20 − 32/20) to avoid the borrow.
If a learner is stuck because '5/20 minus 12/20 can't be done', show that the whole provides the extra twentieths: 2 25/20 − 1 12/20 = 1 13/20.
Check that the final answer is written as a simplified mixed number where appropriate.
Verify with the improper-fraction route: 65/20 − 32/20 = 33/20 = 1 13/20, matching the regroup route.
activities.rationale: Mixed-number subtraction where the fraction part becomes smaller after conversion forces a regroup across the whole; offering two secure routes — borrowing a whole, or converting to improper fractions — lets learners choose and builds understanding of why the borrow is needed. A bar model in which a whole tile breaks into the common unit can make the borrow concrete; the improper-fraction conversion laid beside the mixed form shows an equivalent clean alternative. This targets the common error of subtracting smaller-from-larger in each column without regrouping.
sourceClaims: Adding/subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions with a common denominator (a common unit fraction); the add-across error and the 'insert the larger denominator' error both stem from not grasping this. Teach with representations that cue the need for common denominators and use estimation to judge reasonableness.

Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators including mixed numbers by using equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator; using common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination is a Year 6 expectation.
learnerActions: Set up 3 1/4 − 1 3/5 and rename both fractions to a common denominator of twentieths: 3 5/20 − 1 12/20.
Notice that 5/20 is smaller than 12/20, so the fraction part cannot be taken directly — a regroup across the whole is needed.
Regroup one whole from the 3 into twentieths: break a whole tile into 20/20 so 3 5/20 becomes 2 25/20, then subtract to get 1 13/20.
As an alternative route, convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions first (3 1/4 = 13/4 = 65/20 and 1 3/5 = 8/5 = 32/20), subtract to 33/20, and convert back to 1 13/20.
Compare the two routes and decide which you find cleaner when a borrow is needed.
activities.intendedInsight: When the minuend's fraction part becomes smaller than the subtrahend's after finding a common denominator, you must regroup a whole into the common unit (or work with improper fractions) rather than subtracting the smaller fraction from the larger in each column.

activities.title: Explain and check with a model
feedback: Full understanding: renames both fractions to a real common denominator (scaling both numerators), combines, handles the mixed-number regroup, simplifies to a mixed-number answer, verifies with a model, and transfers to a new unlike-denominator pair including mixed numbers.

Partial understanding: finds a correct common denominator and adds unlike proper fractions reliably (23/12), but the mixed-number subtraction breaks down when a regroup is needed, or answers aren't simplified/converted — the procedure holds for the easy case but not the borrow.
Gap: adds across (7/7) or scales only one/neither numerator; in the mixed subtraction subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column and never regroups.
activities.rationale: A performance task in which neither denominator is a multiple of the other, and the mixed subtraction is built so the minuend's fraction part becomes smaller after conversion, discriminates whether equivalence, common-multiple choice, and regrouping are all in place. Asking learners to explain their choice of denominator and to test an absurd result against an estimate surfaces reasoning, not just answers.
sourceClaims: Adding/subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions with a common denominator (a common unit fraction); the add-across error and the 'insert the larger denominator' error both stem from not grasping this. Teach with representations that cue the need for common denominators and use estimation to judge reasonableness.

Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators including mixed numbers by using equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator; using common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination is a Year 6 expectation.
learnerActions: Work out 2/3 + 5/4 and 3 1/4 − 1 3/5, showing every step and giving each answer in simplest form as a mixed number where appropriate.
Explain how you chose the common denominator and why BOTH numerators changed when you did.
Answer the challenge: a friend says 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7 = 1 — but 5/4 on its own is more than 1, so can the total be exactly 1? Explain what went wrong.
For the subtraction, after reaching 3 5/20 − 1 12/20, explain what you do because you can't take 12/20 from 5/20 as it stands.
Verify 23/12 against the benchmark: confirm it is more than 1 (since 5/4 alone exceeds 1) and a little less than 2 — does that match adding 2/3 and 5/4?
activities.intendedInsight: A learner secure in this strand can rename both fractions to a genuine common denominator, handle a mixed-number regroup by either route, simplify, and verify a result against a benchmark estimate — not just execute steps.

constraints: Target age approximately 10–11 (Year 6); learners should already be able to generate equivalent fractions and convert between mixed and improper forms, since these are the enabling moves for the regroup.
A common multiple of the denominators gives the shared unit; the product always works and the least common multiple is sometimes tidier — do not teach that one specific denominator is required.
Both numerators must scale with their own denominators; the multi-conversion is where partial-scaling errors appear, so check both equivalences before combining.
Keep the unit constant within any representation and avoid manipulatives that let learners combine pieces without first establishing a common denominator.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-blank items (e.g. 2/3 + 5/4 with 7/7 as a distractor, or a mixed subtraction with the no-borrow answer as a distractor) can diagnose add-across, partial-scaling, and no-borrow errors, but recognising a correct option does not demonstrate independent construction of the renaming and regrouping; use alongside tasks where the learner carries out the full procedure.
A fully worked static picture can anchor one conversion or borrow but does not let the learner perform the re-gridding themselves; use it as a reference rather than the main activity.
Teach both the borrow-a-whole and convert-to-improper routes and let learners choose; the improper route is often cleaner precisely when a borrow would be needed.
Estimation benchmarks must be stated correctly: 2/3 + 5/4 is more than 1 (5/4 alone exceeds 1) and lands just below 2 (23/12); do not state it exceeds 2.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (DfE National Curriculum for England, Year 6) is marked unverified in the original row; the other two are marked verified. No new verification was performed here.

Corrected an arithmetic error inherited from the original row's bestPractices: it stated '2/3 + 5/4 is more than 2', but 23/12 ≈ 1.92 is less than 2. The valid benchmark that rules out 7/7 = 1 is that the sum exceeds 1 (because 5/4 alone exceeds 1). All learner-facing text now uses the 'more than 1, just below 2' benchmark.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 2/3 = 8/12 and 5/4 = 15/12, sum 23/12 = 1 11/12 (correct). 3 1/4 = 13/4 = 65/20, 1 3/5 = 8/5 = 32/20, 65/20 − 32/20 = 33/20 = 1 13/20; via regroup 3 5/20 → 2 25/20, minus 1 12/20 = 1 13/20 (consistent). The erroneous no-borrow answer 7/20 (from 12/20 − 5/20) is retained only as an error to diagnose, never as a valid answer.

Each of the two fractions must be renamed independently to the shared unit, and both numerators rescale by their own factor; this is a separate equivalence check per fraction, not a single rule applied once, and no 'denominator flip' reasoning is used.

probeDeeper: How did you decide what common denominator to use for 2/3 and 5/4 — and why did BOTH tops change?
A friend says 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7 = 1. But 5/4 on its own is more than 1 — can the total be exactly 1? What went wrong?
In 3 1/4 − 1 3/5 you reached 3 5/20 − 1 12/20. You can't take 12/20 from 5/20 as it stands — what do you do?
Check 23/12: is that more than 2 or less than 2? Does that match adding 2/3 and 5/4?

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across the unlike denominators: '2 and 5 is 7 on top, 3 and 4 is 7 on the bottom, so 7/7 = 1'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-partition both fractions to a shared unit on strips; estimate first — 5/4 is already more than 1, so 2/3 + 5/4 must exceed 1, and 7/7 = 1 can't be right.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7/7 (or similar) for the sum; denominators combined.

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds a common denominator but scales only one numerator (or none): '2/3 + 5/4, common denominator 12, so 2/12 + 15/12' — leaves 2 on top of the renamed 2/3.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild each equivalence on the model — thirds cut into twelfths turn ONE third into FOUR twelfths, so 2/3 = 8/12; the top scales by the same factor as the bottom. Check both conversions before combining.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct common denominator but a numerator left unscaled (2/12 for 2/3); the equivalence is incomplete.

errorPatterns.pattern: In the mixed-number subtraction, subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger regardless of position: does 12/20 − 5/20 in the fraction column and never regroups across the whole.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model regrouping a whole: break one whole of 3 1/4 into 20/20 so 3 5/20 becomes 2 25/20, then subtract; or convert both to improper fractions (65/20 − 32/20) to avoid the borrow. Reteach mixed↔improper conversion as the enabling move.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Fraction part of the answer is 7/20 (took 5 from 12 the wrong way) or the child is stuck because '5/20 minus 12/20 can't be done'.

responseLevels.gap: Adds across (7/7) or scales only one/neither numerator; in the mixed subtraction subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column and never regroups.
responseLevels.full: Renames both fractions to a genuine common denominator (scaling both numerators), combines, handles the mixed-number regroup (by borrowing or converting to improper fractions), simplifies to a mixed-number answer, and can verify with a model; transfers to a new unlike-denominator pair including mixed numbers.
responseLevels.partial: Finds a correct common denominator and adds unlike PROPER fractions reliably (23/12), but the mixed-number subtraction breaks down when a regroup across the whole is needed, or answers aren't simplified/converted — the procedure holds for the easy case but not the borrow.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing your steps: 2/3 + 5/4, and 3 1/4 − 1 3/5. Give each answer in simplest form, as a mixed number where appropriate.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Neither denominator is a multiple of the other (3 and 4; 4 and 5), so the child can't convert only one fraction — both numerators must scale, exposing partial-scaling errors. The mixed-number subtraction is built so the minuend's fraction part becomes SMALLER after the common denominator (5/20 vs 12/20), forcing a regroup across the whole; a child who subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column reveals the borrowing gap. Add-across yields 7/7 = 1, absurd since 5/4 alone exceeds 1. Watching the steps shows whether equivalence, common-multiple choice, and regrouping are all in place.

pedagogy.summary: This is the CAUSAL explanation of Moon phases at primary grain, building on the earlier observational topic (that the Moon's shape changes over ~a month). Three linked ideas: (1) the Moon orbits Earth roughly once every 28-30 days; (2) the Moon makes NO light of its own — it reflects sunlight, so the Sun always lights up one half of it; (3) phases are caused by how much of that lit half we can see from Earth as the Moon moves around us. The crucial and hard idea is that phases are NOT the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon — they are a viewing-angle effect. Teach with a lit ball orbiting the child's head so the child sees the lit fraction change from their own vantage point.
bestPractices: Use the classic ball-and-lamp model: a single lamp (Sun) lights one half of a ball (Moon) at all times; the child holds the ball at arm's length and slowly turns around, watching how much of the lit half faces them — reproducing new, crescent, half, gibbous, full from their own point of view.
Make the reflected-light idea explicit and testable first: half the Moon is ALWAYS lit by the Sun; what changes is only how much of that lit half we see — not how much is lit.

Directly confront the Earth's-shadow misconception: show that in most phases the Earth is not between the Sun and Moon at all, so its shadow is not on the Moon; reserve Earth's shadow for the separate rarer event (a lunar eclipse), which is NOT the cause of ordinary phases.
Link the phase cycle to the orbit period the child already met: one trip of the Moon around Earth ≈ one month ≈ one full phase cycle, connecting motion to appearance.
Couple the space view (Moon orbiting Earth, lit half fixed toward the Sun) with the Earth view (what the Moon looks like tonight) so the child maps position-in-orbit to shape-in-the-sky.
keyRepresentations: Ball (Moon) + single lamp (Sun) + child's head (Earth) — the canonical phases model seen from the child's own viewpoint
Half-lit sphere: the Sun always lights exactly one hemisphere of the Moon (fixed toward the Sun)
Coupled dual view: overhead space view of the Moon at 8 orbit positions PLUS the matching Earth-view shape for each position
Phase wheel / strip: new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning … mapped around the orbit
The terminator on the Moon (the line between its lit and unlit halves) as the boundary we see cutting across the disc
commonMisconceptions: Believing phases are caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon (the single most common and persistent error) — rather than by our changing view of the lit half.
Thinking the Moon produces its own light, rather than reflecting the Sun's.
Believing clouds, or an object passing in front, cover the Moon to make the phases.
Thinking only part of the Moon is lit at any time (not realising a full hemisphere is always lit; what changes is our viewing angle).
Confusing the ordinary monthly phase cycle with a lunar eclipse (which IS Earth's shadow, but rare) — merging two different phenomena.
Assuming the Moon is only visible at night, or that a new moon means the Moon has 'gone away'.

learn.summary: Teaches the causal explanation of Moon phases for ages 7-9: the Moon orbits Earth about once a month, makes no light of its own but reflects sunlight (so one half is always lit by the Sun), and the phases we see are caused by how much of that lit half faces us from Earth as the Moon moves around us. The central, hard idea is that phases are a viewing-angle effect, NOT the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon (that rarer event is a lunar eclipse). The canonical activity is a lit ball (Moon) orbiting the child's head (Earth) under a single lamp (Sun) so the child watches the lit fraction change from their own vantage point; screen models and a reference diagram support and extend this.

activities.title: Ball-and-lamp: orbit the Moon around your own head
feedback: If a learner says part of the Moon has 'gone', ask them to find the dark half with their finger — it is still there, just turned away from them.
If they say the light changes, pause the ball: the lamp still lights about one half, the same amount as before; only the learner's viewing angle changed.

Prompt: can you make a thin crescent by holding the ball ALMOST between you and the lamp, just off to one side? Note that if the ball is directly between you and the lamp you see only its dark side — a new moon — and nudging it aside reveals a thin bright sliver. Where is the bright side pointing now?

If a shadow creeps across the ball at the 'full' position, that is your own head's shadow — raise the ball a little so it misses. It is not the cause of the phases; the lit half always stays facing the lamp, which is why we keep the ball above our shadow.
activities.rationale: Phases depend on the relationship between Sun-light direction, the Moon's orbital position, and the Earth viewpoint; moving the Moon and watching the visible lit fraction change makes the cause-to-appearance link concrete from the child's own vantage point. Raising the ball avoids the learner's head casting a shadow that could be mistaken for the cause.
sourceClaims: The ball-and-lamp model viewed from the learner's own vantage point is the canonical method for teaching Moon phases as a viewing-angle effect.

The Moon shines by reflected sunlight and its phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth; the Earth's-shadow explanation of phases is a well-documented, persistent misconception distinct from a lunar eclipse.
learnerActions: In a darkened room, shine a single lamp (the Sun) on a ball (the Moon); notice one half of the ball is always bright and the other half dark.
Hold the ball at arm's length and slightly above head height (so your own shadow does not fall on it), stand with your head as Earth, and slowly turn all the way around so the ball orbits your head.

As you turn, watch how much of the bright half you can see and name the views you pass through: all of it (full), half the disc lit (quarter), a thin sliver (crescent), or none at all (new) — these appear at different points as you rotate, not only at the quarter-turns.
Say aloud for one position: 'The Moon is still fully half-lit by the lamp — I am just seeing more / less of the bright side from here.'
Point to where the dark side is pointing when you see a crescent, to confirm nothing is covering the Moon.
activities.intendedInsight: Phases are caused by our changing view of the always-half-lit Moon as it orbits, not by anything covering or shadowing it.

activities.title: Does the Moon make its own light?
feedback: If the learner expected the ball to stay lit, connect it to the lamp-off result: no Sun, no reflected light, no glow.
Reinforce: the Moon shines by bouncing back the Sun's light, like a brightly lit wall, not by making its own light like a lamp.
activities.rationale: Addresses the misconception that the Moon is its own light source with a model: the ball, like the Moon, makes no light of its own, so switching off the lamp shows what happens to an object that only reflects light. A switchable light source (lamp or an on/off control in a screen model) makes this dependence visible. It models the Moon's dependence on the Sun rather than testing the real Moon.
sourceClaims: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight and its phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth; the Earth's-shadow explanation of phases is a well-documented, persistent misconception distinct from a lunar eclipse.
learnerActions: Put the ball where you can see its bright and dark halves.
Predict what happens to the ball if the lamp is switched off.
Switch off the lamp and observe: the ball goes dark, or only stays dimly visible from any other light leaking into the room, because it makes no light of its own.
Explain in a sentence where the Moon's glow comes from, using the word 'reflect'.
activities.intendedInsight: The Moon produces no light of its own; it shines only by reflecting the Sun's light, so with no Sun there is nothing to see.

activities.title: Where is Earth's shadow really? Separating phases from eclipses
feedback: If a learner explains a crescent as Earth's shadow, trace the shadow direction with them and show it misses the Moon entirely.
Clarify: a lunar eclipse only happens at certain full-moon line-ups, not every month, so it cannot be the monthly phase cause.
A 'show Earth's shadow' toggle (in a screen model) or a torch casting the real shadow (with the ball) can make the shadow direction visible for each position.
activities.rationale: The Earth's-shadow belief is the most common and persistent phase misconception; having the learner locate where the shadow actually falls lets them rule it out themselves, rather than being told it is wrong.
sourceClaims: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight and its phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth; the Earth's-shadow explanation of phases is a well-documented, persistent misconception distinct from a lunar eclipse.
learnerActions: For an ordinary crescent or half phase, work out where the Sun is, where the Moon is, and where Earth's shadow would stretch (straight away from the Sun).
Check whether Earth's shadow actually falls on the Moon in that position — in ordinary phases it points off into empty space, nowhere near the Moon.
Describe the special, rare line-up when Earth is EXACTLY in line between the Sun and the full Moon, so the shadow does reach the Moon — name this a lunar eclipse.
Write one sentence stating what causes ordinary phases and one sentence stating what causes a lunar eclipse, keeping them separate.
activities.intendedInsight: In ordinary phases Earth's shadow does not touch the Moon, so phases cannot be caused by it; Earth's shadow on the Moon is a separate, rare event (a lunar eclipse).

activities.title: Map position in orbit to shape in the sky (coupled dual view)
feedback: If the learner memorises the sequence without the cause, ask them to justify a shape by pointing to where the lit half faces.
Link back to the ball-and-lamp: the overhead space view is the same situation seen from above instead of from the learner's eyes.
activities.rationale: Coupling the space view (lit half fixed toward the Sun) with the Earth view (tonight's shape) lets the learner map orbit position to appearance and ties the phase cycle to the orbit period. A draggable Moon with a live-updating Earth-view window makes the mapping dynamic; stepping the model works as an alternative.
sourceClaims: UK National Curriculum Year 5 (Earth and space) requires pupils to 'describe the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth'.

The Moon shines by reflected sunlight and its phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth; the Earth's-shadow explanation of phases is a well-documented, persistent misconception distinct from a lunar eclipse.
learnerActions: Look at an overhead 'space view' showing the Moon at several positions around Earth, with its lit half always facing the Sun.
For a chosen orbit position, predict the shape you would see from Earth before checking the matching 'tonight's sky' Earth-view.

Drag or step the Moon around the orbit and watch the Earth-view shape change: full when the Moon is on the far side from the Sun, thinning to a crescent as it swings towards the Sun, vanishing at new moon.

Connect the repeating phases to the Moon’s motion around Earth: a full phase cycle is about a month. The orbital period relative to the stars is slightly shorter than the phase cycle because Earth is also moving around the Sun.
activities.intendedInsight: The Moon’s position relative to the Sun and Earth determines the phase seen from Earth. Both the orbital period and phase cycle are roughly a month, but they are not exactly the same period.

activities.title: Fly to Earth's surface and look up (spatial extension)
feedback: If the shapes seem to disagree, return to the space view and check which part of the lit half is turned towards the Earth viewpoint.
activities.rationale: The Sun-Earth-Moon geometry is genuinely spatial, and moving between a space view and a stood-on-Earth view can strengthen the link between orbit position and observed shape. This enriches the 2D mapping; the essential cause-to-appearance idea is already carried by the ball-and-lamp and the dual view.
sourceClaims: UK National Curriculum Year 5 (Earth and space) requires pupils to 'describe the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth'.
learnerActions: Using a 3D model, orbit the camera to view the Sun-Earth-Moon system from space, keeping the Moon's lit hemisphere always facing the Sun.
Drop the camera down to stand on Earth's surface and look up at the Moon for the current orbit position.
Compare the shape you see looking up with the lit half shown in the space view, and explain why they match.
activities.intendedInsight: Standing on Earth and looking up connects the Moon's orbital position directly to the shape you would actually see in the sky.

activities.title: Reference diagram and recap of the 8 phases
feedback: Use this as a recap after the hands-on work, not as the first teaching: a static diagram shows the pattern but does not let the learner test why the visible fraction changes, so return to the ball or dual view if a learner recites names without the cause.
If a learner labels the full-moon position 'eclipse', remind them an eclipse needs the special Sun-Earth-Moon line-up.
activities.rationale: A labelled static diagram is a useful reference and consolidation for the sequence and vocabulary, and reveal-the-label prompts aid recall; because it does not recompute the visible fraction as the learner moves the Moon, it best supports review after the mechanism has been built.
learnerActions: Study a labelled diagram of the eight phase positions around the orbit: new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.
Reveal or state the name and Earth-view shape for each position.
On the full-moon position, note that it is usually a full phase and only a lunar eclipse at the rare special alignment, keeping phase and eclipse distinct.
Order the phases into the correct cycle and say which way the lit part grows (waxing) and shrinks (waning).
activities.intendedInsight: The named phases form a repeating cycle around the orbit, and the full-moon position is normally just a phase, not an eclipse.

activities.title: Check and explain: two-tier phase questions
feedback: Full understanding: the Moon reflects sunlight (always half-lit), phases are the changing amount of that lit half we see as it orbits monthly, and ordinary phases are separate from the rare lunar eclipse.

Partial: knows the Moon reflects sunlight and orbits Earth but still reaches for Earth's shadow or cannot say why the lit amount we see changes — return to the ball-and-lamp and the shadow-direction task.
Gap: attributes phases to Earth's shadow and/or thinks the Moon makes its own light — reteach reflected light and the orbit-position-to-shape mapping.
activities.rationale: A two-tier true/false-with-why question discriminates because the shadow explanation sounds plausible and is stated confidently by those who hold it, while the 'why' tier also surfaces the self-light misconception. This checks understanding rather than building the spatial-causal idea, so it belongs alongside the hands-on activities. Note that recognising a correct answer in options does not, by itself, demonstrate the learner can produce the explanation, so the 'why' tier matters.
sourceClaims: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight and its phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth; the Earth's-shadow explanation of phases is a well-documented, persistent misconception distinct from a lunar eclipse.
learnerActions: Answer whether this statement is right: 'The crescent happens because Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon' — then explain WHY in your own words.
Choose what causes Moon phases from options that include the Earth's-shadow idea as a tempting wrong answer, and justify your choice.
Match each orbit position to the shape seen from Earth, and put the phases in order.

Answer the probes: where does the Moon's glow come from if it makes no light? At a thin crescent, is the rest of the Moon gone or just not lit towards us? How is a lunar eclipse different from a crescent? How long is one orbit and phase cycle?
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to reject the shadow explanation and give the reflected-light, viewing-angle reason shows understanding rather than only memorised phase names.

constraints: This causal topic builds on observations that the Moon’s phases repeat about monthly. Use about a month at this age without equating the exact periods: the orbit relative to the stars is about27.3days, while the phase cycle is about29.5days; children need not memorise these precise figures here.

Keep the single light source fixed so that about one half of the Moon is always lit. With a nearby lamp it is slightly less than half, but the lit amount stays the same as the ball moves. The lesson is undermined if learners think the amount LIT changes rather than the amount SEEN.

In the hands-on ball-and-lamp, have learners raise the ball slightly above their own head so their head's shadow does not fall on it at the full position, which would otherwise mimic and reinforce the Earth's-shadow misconception.

Address the Earth's-shadow misconception by having learners locate where the shadow actually falls, and clearly name the lunar eclipse as the separate, rare shadow event — do not let the two phenomena merge.
A static diagram supports recap and vocabulary but does not let learners vary the viewing angle themselves, so use it after the hands-on or dynamic work, not as the primary teaching.

A quiz checks facts and confronts the misconception but does not itself build the spatial-causal understanding; pair it with construction/explanation activities. Recognising a correct option is not the same as producing the explanation.
3D fly-to-surface views are enriching for the spatial link but are not required; the cause-to-appearance mapping is fully carried by the ball-and-lamp plus a space-view/Earth-view pairing.

Interactive features named here (draggable Moon, live Earth-view window, show-shadow toggle, Sun on/off switch) are optional ways to make the mechanism visible; equivalent hands-on versions with a ball, lamp and torch work too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources are marked verified:false in the original (the NGSS/misconception claim and the ball-and-lamp pedagogy-consensus claim); treat their support as unverified. Only the DfE National Curriculum Year 5 claim is marked verified:true.

Original source claims support the teaching principles (reflected light, viewing-angle cause, shadow misconception, curriculum coverage) but do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any specific medium; efficacy wording is kept as 'may/can/intended'.

The original framing that a conversation/in-role format 'cannot make the viewing-angle effect felt' and that 3D 'adds nothing essential' has been softened to scoped affordance claims, not established universal limits.

Original lists the standard 28-30 day orbit figure and 'about a month' for the phase cycle; the sidereal orbital period (~27.3 days) and synodic phase cycle (~29.5 days) differ slightly. At this age 'about a month' is acceptable, but note the distinction if precision is later needed.

Added a practical safeguard to the ball-and-lamp activity: raise the ball above head height so the learner's own shadow does not fall on it at the full position (otherwise it can be mistaken for Earth's shadow and reinforce the very misconception being addressed).

The reference-diagram activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because its rationale concerns the recall/consolidation affordance of a static diagram, which none of the available source claims directly supports (the DfE claim is about describing Moon movement, a topic-level match only).

The original 'terminator' representation and the 'Moon only visible at night' misconception are not separately carried into these activities; the underlying always-half-lit idea and the 'gone away' belief are retained. Add them if fuller coverage is wanted.
One error-pattern entry references a reteach prerequisite id; this is internal routing metadata and is not reproduced in learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: If the Moon makes no light of its own, where does its glow come from?
When we see a thin crescent, where is the rest of the Moon — gone, or just not lit towards us?
How is a lunar eclipse different from an ordinary crescent phase?
How long does the Moon take to go once around the Earth and back to the same phase?
assess.correctAnswer: No — Earth's shadow is not what causes the ordinary phases. The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight, so the half of the Moon facing the Sun is always lit. As the Moon orbits Earth (about once a month), we see different amounts of that lit half from where we stand — sometimes all of it (full), sometimes a sliver (crescent), sometimes none (new). That changing VIEW of the lit half, not Earth's shadow, makes the phases. (Earth's shadow does fall on the Moon occasionally — but that is a rare, separate event called a lunar eclipse.)

errorPatterns.pattern: the Moon's phases are caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a lamp and a ball: the lit half always faces the lamp, and walking the ball around 'Earth' reproduces every phase with NO shadow involved; name the rare eclipse as the real shadow event.
errorPatterns.distractor: The phases happen because the Earth's shadow covers up part of the Moon.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child explains the crescent or half moon as Earth's shadow covering part of the Moon

errorPatterns.pattern: the Moon makes its own light / glows by itself
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a ball in a single beam — one side bright, one dark; the Moon shines only by bouncing back the Sun's light.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Moon shines because it makes its own light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats the Moon as a light source rather than a reflector of sunlight

errorPatterns.pattern: at new moon the Moon has gone away or disappeared
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Moon is still there — its lit side is facing away from us, so the side we see is dark; it hasn't gone anywhere.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child thinks the Moon leaves the sky at new moon

responseLevels.gap: Attributes phases to Earth's shadow and/or thinks the Moon makes its own light.
responseLevels.full: Explains the Moon reflects sunlight (always half-lit), that phases are the changing amount of that lit half we see as it orbits monthly, and separates ordinary phases from the rare lunar eclipse.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the Moon reflects sunlight and orbits Earth, but still reaches for Earth's shadow to explain the phase shapes, or can't say why the lit amount we see changes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Some people think the Moon's phases — like the thin crescent — happen because the EARTH'S shadow falls on the Moon and hides part of it. Is that right? If not, what really causes the phases? And does the Moon make its own light? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The Earth's-shadow explanation is the single most common phase misconception and sounds plausible, so a child who holds it states it confidently. A child who understands the geometry rejects the shadow and explains phases as seeing different amounts of the always-lit half as the Moon orbits. The 'why' tier also catches the belief that the Moon is its own light source.
