pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Fossilised Dinosaur Dung / Coprolites (ages 7–9): a coprolite is fossilised dung (droppings turned to rock), and palaeontologists cut them open to find plant fragments, seeds, bones, or fish scales inside — direct evidence of what a dinosaur actually ATE.
• Standards — UK (DfE): 'working scientifically' (gather and interpret evidence to answer a question); builds on the trace-fossil category and herbivore/carnivore classification.
• Standards — US (NGSS): grade-3 3-LS4-1 (fossils as evidence of organisms and their behaviour — here, diet).
• Operational details — Coprolites are TRACE fossils (record of an activity: eating/digesting). The teaching value is that they give DIRECT dietary evidence, complementing the INDIRECT clue of tooth shape: teeth suggest what an animal COULD eat; coprolite contents show what it DID eat. Contents reveal diet — seeds and plant cell walls → herbivore; crushed bone → a bone-crunching carnivore (famously a T. rex coprolite full of bone); fish scales → a fish-eater. Address the 'ick' factor by framing it as prized evidence. Note the challenge: it's often hard to be sure WHICH dinosaur produced a given coprolite.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7): says a coprolite is fossilised dung and it tells us what a dinosaur ate. Tier B (~8): links contents (seeds vs bone) to plant- vs meat-eater. Tier C (~9): explains coprolites give direct diet evidence (vs teeth as indirect) and notes it's often uncertain which animal produced one.
bestPractices: Frame coprolites as prized DIRECT evidence of diet to convert the 'ick' reaction into scientific curiosity.
Contrast direct (coprolite contents = what it DID eat) with indirect (tooth shape = what it COULD eat) evidence — a clean lesson in evidence strength.
Have children read contents to a conclusion (seeds→plants; bone→meat; scales→fish), practising inference.
Flag the identification problem — you often can't be certain which species left a coprolite — to model honest uncertainty.
Use the memorable real case (a large bone-filled Cretaceous coprolite attributed to a T. rex) to make it concrete.
keyRepresentations: A 'slice and examine' view: a coprolite cross-section with visible seeds, bone bits, or scales under a lens.
A contents → diet inference card (seeds→herbivore, bone→carnivore, scales→fish-eater).
Side-by-side 'teeth clue (could eat)' vs 'coprolite clue (did eat)'.
A magnifier tool revealing microscopic plant/bone fragments.
commonMisconceptions: 'A coprolite is a body fossil / a stomach' — it's fossilised dung, a trace fossil recording feeding.
'Coprolites are worthless/just gross' — they are direct, high-value evidence of diet.
'Teeth already tell us exactly what it ate' — teeth show capability; coprolites show actual meals.
'We always know which dinosaur made a coprolite' — attribution is often uncertain.
'All dung fossils look the same inside' — contents differ (plants, bone, scales) and that's the whole point.

learn.summary: Children (ages 7–9) learn that a coprolite is fossilised dung — a trace fossil that records an animal's feeding — and that cutting one open can reveal contents (seeds and plant fibres, crushed bone, or fish scales) that give DIRECT evidence of what the animal that produced it actually ate, at least in that meal (mostly the tougher, less-digested parts survive). The central idea is contrasting this with the INDIRECT clue of tooth shape: teeth suggest what an animal COULD eat, while coprolite contents show what it DID eat. Learners practise reading contents to a diet conclusion (seeds→plant-eater, bone→meat-eater, scales→fish-eater), and also meet the honest limit that it is often uncertain WHICH animal produced a given coprolite.

activities.title: Slice and examine: read the coprolite's contents
feedback: If a learner reads seeds/plant fibres: confirm this points to a plant-eater (herbivore) — those are undigested parts of plants it swallowed.
If a learner reads crushed bone or scales: confirm this points to a meat- or fish-eater — those are the remains of prey, NOT pieces of the dinosaur's own skeleton.
If a learner thinks the bones are the dinosaur's own body: clarify that dung contains what was eaten and passed through; the bones belonged to the prey.
If a learner says dung cannot become a fossil: explain dung can be mineralised and preserved like other trace fossils, and the hardened contents are exactly what makes it useful evidence.
activities.rationale: The objective is an investigation — open, examine, deduce — so an examine-and-infer task where the learner selects evidence and states a conclusion is intended to build the reasoning rather than just name it. Dragging finds into an analysis panel and showing the reasoning is an optional way to make the inference visible. This is a proposed, untested design.
learnerActions: Receive a lumpy grey 'coprolite' specimen and the explanation that it is fossilised dinosaur dung turned to rock.
Open the specimen and sweep a magnifier across the cut face to find embedded contents — seeds and shredded plant fibres in one specimen, splinters of crushed bone in another, fish scales in a third.

Collect each find (optionally by dragging items into an analysis panel) and state the diet verdict it supports: seeds/plant fibres → plant-eater; crushed bone → bone-crunching meat-eater; fish scales → fish-eater.
Write or say the reasoning: 'the contents are the remains of what the animal ate, so this dinosaur was a ___.'
activities.intendedInsight: The things preserved inside fossilised dung are the remains of an animal's meals, so reading those contents lets you infer what the dinosaur actually ate.

activities.title: Teeth clue vs dung clue: could eat vs did eat
feedback: If a learner says teeth already tell us exactly what it ate: point out teeth show capability; the coprolite shows the actual meal, which can confirm or refine the tooth clue.
If a learner treats both as equally direct: note that one shows a preserved meal (direct) while the other is inferred from body shape (indirect).
activities.rationale: Contrasting a preserved meal (which the source identifies as direct dietary evidence) with a structural clue gives children a concrete, age-appropriate lesson in evidence type and strength. A paired comparison panel contrasting the two clues is an optional presentation that keeps the comparison explicit.
sourceClaims: Coprolites (fossilised dung) are trace fossils whose contents — plant fragments/seeds, bone, or fish scales — provide direct evidence of diet; a large bone-rich Cretaceous coprolite has been attributed to Tyrannosaurus rex. Attribution to a specific producer is often uncertain.
learnerActions: Look at an animal's teeth beside the contents of a coprolite thought to come from that kind of animal, presented side by side.
Say what the teeth suggest the animal COULD eat (capability) and what the coprolite shows it ACTUALLY ate (its real meals).
Explain in their own words why the coprolite is direct evidence of diet while the teeth are an indirect clue.
activities.intendedInsight: Tooth shape suggests what an animal was capable of eating, but coprolite contents are direct evidence of what it really ate — a comparison of indirect versus direct evidence.

activities.title: Whose dung was it? Modelling honest uncertainty
feedback: If a learner insists we always know which dinosaur made a coprolite: explain that attribution to a specific producer is often uncertain, even when the diet is clear.
Praise a learner who distinguishes the confident claim (diet) from the uncertain one (producer) — that is how real scientists report findings.
activities.rationale: Deliberately leaving attribution ambiguous models honest uncertainty and separates a well-supported inference (diet) from an under-determined one (species), a core 'working scientifically' habit. The source directly notes that attribution to a specific producer is often uncertain.
sourceClaims: Coprolites (fossilised dung) are trace fossils whose contents — plant fragments/seeds, bone, or fish scales — provide direct evidence of diet; a large bone-rich Cretaceous coprolite has been attributed to Tyrannosaurus rex. Attribution to a specific producer is often uncertain.
learnerActions: Examine a coprolite with clear contents (e.g. the famous large bone-filled Cretaceous specimen attributed to T. rex) and confidently state the DIET it shows.
Then try to name exactly which animal produced it, and notice how hard that is.
Say out loud what we can be sure of (the diet) and what remains uncertain (the exact producer), and why 'we're not sure' is a valid scientific answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Even strong evidence leaves some questions open: coprolite contents can firmly reveal diet while the exact animal that produced the dung often stays uncertain.

activities.title: Check: match contents to diet and explain the evidence
feedback: Correct answer for bone/scales: a meat- or fish-eater — the bones and scales are remains of its food preserved in its fossilised droppings; the contents are direct evidence of diet.
Correct answer for leaves/seeds: a plant-eater (herbivore).
If a learner cannot reason from contents to diet or thinks the contents are the animal's own body, return to the slice-and-examine activity before re-checking.
activities.rationale: Matching and short-answer items check the inference. They confirm whether a learner can classify contents→diet but do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing and justifying the inference, so they are intended to be used after the hands-on examination rather than instead of it.
learnerActions: Match coprolite contents to the diet they imply: seeds/plant fibres → plant-eater; crushed bone → meat-eater; fish scales → fish-eater.
Answer: 'What does crushed bone inside a coprolite tell us about the dinosaur that made it?' and explain how you know.
Transfer the reasoning to a new case: a coprolite full of chewed leaves and seeds — what kind of dinosaur made it?
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to map contents onto a diet, and explain why, confirms the inference transfers to new specimens.

activities.title: Optional: palaeontologist hands over a specimen
feedback: Prompt deeper if the learner states a diet without naming the evidence: 'Which contents led you to that?'
If the learner is over-confident about the producer, ask what else could have made dung with those contents.
activities.rationale: A Socratic exchange fits the inference and gives practice in justifying and qualifying a claim. It is offered as an alternative with a different purpose (verbal reasoning and confidence) and is intended to complement, not replace, the hands-on examination where the inference is intended to be constructed.
learnerActions: Take a coprolite from an expert who asks, 'What did this animal eat, and how sure are you?'
Describe the contents you can see and reason aloud toward a diet.
Respond to follow-up prompts about how confident you are and whether you can tell which animal made it.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the inference and your confidence to a questioner strengthens the reasoning and the habit of qualifying claims.

constraints: Matching/recognition tasks can check that a learner classifies contents→diet, but recognition alone does not elicit the learner producing and justifying an inference; they are best used after the hands-on examination.
Attribution of a coprolite to a specific species is often uncertain; do not ask learners to name the exact producer as if determinable — ask what diet the contents show and what remains uncertain.
The slice-and-examine specimens model ideal evidence; frame the 'ick' factor as prized evidence and handle sensitively for this age group.
The hands-on examination design and any efficacy/sequencing wording are proposed, not empirically tested.
reviewNotes: This guidance was rewritten by an agent from the original row without fresh source verification; the single source is marked verified:false, so the T. rex attribution and contents-as-diet claims remain unverified here.
All activities are proposed/unvalidated designs; efficacy is stated with intended/may/proposed wording and should not be read as tested.

probeDeeper: If a coprolite was full of chewed-up leaves and seeds instead, what kind of dinosaur made it?
Why is fossilised dung sometimes better evidence of diet than the shape of an animal's teeth?
How could scientists be fairly sure the coprolite came from a dinosaur and not some other animal?
assess.correctAnswer: It was a meat-eater — it ate animals and fish. The crushed bones and scales inside are the remains of its food, preserved in its fossilised droppings (a coprolite). The contents are direct evidence of what the dinosaur ate.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dung is too soft or gross to fossilise: 'poo can't turn into a fossil, so this isn't real evidence.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that dung can be mineralised and preserved like other trace fossils; the hardened contents are exactly what makes it useful.
errorPatterns.distractor: Dung can't become a fossil, so this can't tell us anything real.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies a coprolite is a genuine fossil, or refuses to draw any conclusion from it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the contents as the animal's own body: 'the bones inside are pieces of the dinosaur's own skeleton.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify that dung contains the remains of what was eaten and passed through — the bones belonged to the prey, not the dinosaur.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bones inside are pieces of the dinosaur's own skeleton.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes the bones and scales to the coprolite-maker rather than to its food.

errorPatterns.pattern: Denies diet can be read from droppings: 'you can't tell what an animal ate from its poo.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Walk through the inference: seeds mean plants eaten, bones mean animals eaten — the contents ARE the diet.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States that dung reveals nothing about diet even when contents are described.

responseLevels.gap: Denies dung can fossilise, or says a coprolite reveals nothing about the animal.
responseLevels.full: Reads the contents as ingested food to infer diet (bones/scales mean carnivore) AND transfers the reasoning to the leaves-and-seeds case for a herbivore.
responseLevels.partial: Knows a coprolite is fossilised dung but cannot reason from its contents to the diet, or thinks the contents are the animal's own body.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Scientists cut open a fossilised lump of dinosaur dung and find crushed bones and fish scales inside. What can they tell about the dinosaur that made it, and how do they know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands says the stuff inside is what the animal ate, so it was a carnivore. A child who doesn't thinks dung cannot become a fossil at all, or reads the bones inside as the dinosaur's own skeleton.

sources.claim: Coprolites (fossilised dung) are trace fossils whose contents — plant fragments/seeds, bone, or fish scales — provide direct evidence of diet; a large bone-rich Cretaceous coprolite has been attributed to Tyrannosaurus rex. Attribution to a specific producer is often uncertain.
sources.source: Natural History Museum (UK) / published coprolite research (e.g. Chin et al.) — coprolite education resources

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Science Can Be Revised

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 / KS3 Working Scientifically):** Pupils should recognise that scientific ideas change and develop over time, identify evidence used to support or refute ideas or arguments, and understand (into KS3) that scientific methods and theories develop as earlier explanations are modified to take account of new evidence and ideas. Provisionality is presented as a strength of science, not a weakness.

- **Standards — US (NGSS Nature of Science, grades 3–5/6–8):** 'Scientific knowledge is open to revision in light of new evidence' — an explicit Nature-of-Science understanding: scientific explanations are subject to revision and improvement as new evidence and better instruments become available, and this openness is what makes scientific knowledge durable and self-correcting.

- **Operational details:** The child grasps that scientific knowledge is the BEST CURRENT explanation given the available evidence — provisional, not final — and that it can and should be revised when better evidence arrives (people once thought the Sun orbited the Earth; better observations overturned it). Crucially they see this as science working AS INTENDED, not failing: ideas earn their place by surviving tests, and are updated (not merely discarded) when new evidence doesn't fit. This distinguishes 'we're not sure, so anything goes' from 'this is our best-supported explanation, held open to revision'. It rests on the habits of changing your mind with evidence and seeking alternatives, and connects to authority: an idea holds because of evidence, not because an expert asserted it.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional, meta-understanding). This reframes 'science' from a fixed body of facts to a self-correcting process. Success = the child explains, with a concrete historical example, that scientific ideas are revised when new evidence arrives, and articulates why this openness is a strength rather than a weakness — while distinguishing provisional-but-best-supported from mere opinion.
bestPractices: Ground provisionality in concrete historical revisions (geocentric→heliocentric, fixed continents→plate tectonics, spontaneous generation→germ theory) rather than abstract assertion.
Frame revision explicitly as a STRENGTH — science self-corrects — to counter the intuition that changing an idea means science was 'wrong' or unreliable.
Distinguish 'provisional but best-supported by evidence' from 'just an opinion / anything goes', so provisionality isn't mistaken for relativism.
Show old ideas as reasonable given the evidence of their time, so revision is upgrading, not ridiculing past scientists.
Connect to evidence-over-authority: ideas hold because of evidence, not because an expert said so.
Have children identify what NEW evidence forced a change, tying revision to specific observations or instruments.
keyRepresentations: Timeline of an idea being revised as evidence accumulates
Old explanation / breaking evidence / revised explanation triptych
A balance or 'best-supported' meter tipping as evidence is added
Gallery of famous overturned ideas across different sciences
Provisional-but-evidence-based vs opinion contrast card
commonMisconceptions: Thinking that if science changed its mind, it must have been 'wrong' and can't be trusted.
Believing scientific knowledge is a fixed, finished set of facts.
Confusing 'provisional / open to revision' with 'just a guess' or 'anything goes'.
Assuming ideas change because of a powerful person's opinion rather than new evidence.
Viewing past scientists as foolish rather than reasonable given their evidence.
Thinking a well-established theory is beyond all possibility of revision.

learn.summary: For learners aged 9–11, build the meta-understanding that scientific knowledge is the best current explanation given available evidence — provisional, not final — and that revising ideas when better evidence arrives is science working as intended, a strength rather than a failure. The central worked case is the shift from a geocentric to a heliocentric model, driven by specific observations (retrograde/looping motion of Mars, phases of Venus, Jupiter's moons). Learners should drive a revision themselves by feeding evidence into an accepted model and seeing it strain and be replaced, hear the human/affective side through in-role dialogue, survey a gallery of recurring revisions across sciences, and crucially distinguish 'best-supported but open to revision' from 'just an opinion / anything goes'. Past scientists should be shown as reasonable given their evidence, not foolish, and ideas as holding because of evidence, not authority. The replacement model is itself presented as a new best-current explanation, still open to future revision — not a final, perfect answer.

activities.title: The 'Best Idea So Far' machine: overturn a model with evidence
feedback: When an observation doesn't fit, highlight the strain on the old model (e.g. the extra circle bolted on for Mars' retrograde loop) so the learner feels the model being pushed, not just told it is wrong.

After revising, show the heliocentric model re-explaining the observations gathered in this activity, reinforcing that a revised idea must account for the old evidence as well as the new — while itself staying open to revision.
Frame the moment of revision with a 'strength' cue — science self-corrected — rather than an 'error' or 'failure' cue.

On the final sort, if a learner labels a best-supported explanation as 'just an opinion', prompt them to point to the evidence behind it; if they treat an opinion as settled science, ask what evidence would test it.
activities.rationale: Provisionality is abstract until a learner drives the revision themselves. Having the learner add evidence and watch the accepted explanation strain and be replaced makes revision a mechanism they experience rather than a story they are told. Grounding it in a concrete historical revision, and ending with an explicit provisional-vs-opinion discriminator, targets both the misconception that revision means science was unreliable and the misconception that provisional means 'anything goes'. Framing the new model as itself still revisable keeps the lesson consistent with the provisional-not-final objective.
sourceClaims: DfE Working Scientifically requires pupils to recognise that scientific ideas change over time and (KS3) that theories develop as earlier explanations are modified to take account of new evidence.
NGSS Nature of Science states that scientific knowledge is open to revision in light of new evidence — explanations are revised and improved as new evidence and instruments become available.
learnerActions: Start with the accepted model: Earth sits still at the centre and everything circles it — note that at first it seems to work, so you accept it.

Feed observations into the model one at a time from an evidence tray and judge for each whether the current model fits it or not: 'Mars sometimes loops backwards across the sky' (the geocentric model needs an awkward extra circle to cope), 'Through a telescope, Venus shows phases like the Moon' (a model with Venus circling Earth cannot fit the full set of phases), 'Through his telescope, Galileo saw four moons orbiting Jupiter, not Earth' (another mismatch with 'everything circles Earth').
Watch mismatches accumulate until a REVISE option becomes available; choose to revise, swapping in the Sun-centred model.
Re-test the revised Sun-centred model against each of these earlier observations and confirm that it now accounts for all three.
Note that the Sun-centred model is itself a new best-current explanation — stronger because it fits more evidence, but still open to further revision, not a final perfect answer.
At the end, sort statements into 'this is our best-supported explanation, open to revision' versus 'that's just an opinion', so provisional is never mistaken for 'anything goes'.
activities.intendedInsight: Revision is an evidence-driven mechanism: the old idea was the best explanation for the evidence people HAD, and when better evidence arrived science did not collapse — it upgraded and became stronger. The new model earns its place by accounting for the observations the old one could AND the ones it could not, while itself remaining a best-current explanation open to revision.

activities.title: Interview a scientist who lived a revision
feedback: Keep the figure welcoming of challenge and anchored to specific observations, redirecting if the conversation drifts into opinion or bare storytelling.
When the learner asks a sharp evidence question, have the figure reward it by explaining exactly which observation forced the change.
activities.rationale: This nature-of-science idea has a strongly human, narrative side. In-role dialogue can build the affective understanding — openness as strength — vividly. It complements rather than replaces the hands-on machine because dialogue does not let the learner mechanically drive the model's revision; keeping it evidence-focused prevents it becoming mere anecdote.
learnerActions: Take the role of an interviewer and question a historical or expert figure at the moment an accepted worldview is crumbling (e.g. an astronomer as the geocentric picture breaks down).
Challenge the figure: ask why they are changing a belief they once held, and what specific evidence turned them.
Press for evidence, not just anecdote — ask 'what did you observe?' and 'why didn't the old idea fit?'
Ask whether being shown to be mistaken means they failed, and listen to them explain why revising an idea in light of evidence is the point of science, not a defeat.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing your mind in the light of evidence is honest and is what science is for; this builds the affective sense that openness to revision is a strength, told from inside a real human change of view.

activities.title: Gallery of overturned ideas
feedback: For each exhibit, make explicit what NEW observation or instrument (or, where applicable, a reinterpretation of existing evidence) forced the change, tying revision to concrete evidence.
Reinforce that each revised idea was an upgrade that explained more, framing past scientists as reasonable for their time.
activities.rationale: A reveal-based gallery is an efficient, memorable way to establish that revision is the norm across sciences and to drill the recurring triptych structure. It supports rather than leads because it shows the pattern but does not let the learner drive a revision.
learnerActions: Move through examples of scientific revision: Earth-centred to Sun-centred models, fixed continents to plate tectonics, and spontaneous generation to the explanation that new organisms come from existing living organisms.
For each exhibit, reveal in order: the old explanation, then the new evidence that broke it, then the revised explanation.
Read for each a note on why the change strengthened science, and look for the common pattern across all three.
activities.intendedInsight: Revision is normal and recurring across all of science, not a one-off embarrassment in one field; the same old-idea -> breaking-evidence -> revised-idea pattern repeats.

activities.title: Astronomy close-up: how the old and new models explained retrograde motion differently
feedback: Connect the apparent loop back to the relative motion of Earth and Mars (Earth overtaking Mars) rather than to a single central, still Earth.
Keep the scope to the astronomy example and relate it back to the general lesson that a wider body of evidence, not retrograde motion alone, supported the change.
activities.rationale: An orbital model can illustrate this particular comparison by making Earth’s and Mars’s relative motion visible. Relate the observation and competing explanations back to the broader evidence-and-revision question; no comparative effectiveness of the orbital model and other media is established here.
learnerActions: Examine how Mars appears to loop backwards when viewed from Earth. Compare how an Earth-centred model uses epicycles to represent this observation with how a Sun-centred model explains it through the relative motions of Earth and Mars.
Compare how the Sun-centred arrangement, with Earth also moving, explains the apparent loop as a viewing effect of two moving bodies.

Explain how both models account for the apparent loop, and describe how Earth overtaking Mars provides the Sun-centred account. Consider this alongside the other observations in the activity rather than treating retrograde alone as decisive proof.
activities.intendedInsight: Different models can account for the same observation in different ways. Here the Sun-centred arrangement explains Mars’s apparent backward loop through relative motion, while Earth-centred models used epicycles; judging the models involves a wider body of evidence.

activities.title: Explain and sort: check the understanding
feedback: Full response: explains past scientists reasoned soundly from their evidence, that revision on new evidence is a strength, and that current ideas are provisional-but-best — and transfers this to a fresh example.

Partial response (e.g. only 'we got better telescopes'): acknowledge that new instruments did matter in this case, then discuss how the SAME evidence can sometimes support a new explanation without new tools (a reinterpretation, not just a new machine), and ask why revision is a strength rather than just a fact.

Gap response ('old scientists were stupid', or 'science is proven and won't change', or 'they keep changing it so you can't trust it'): reteach with a case where a 'certain' idea changed (continents don't move -> plate tectonics), and walk through why the geocentric view was reasonable given that the Sun really does appear to cross the sky.
activities.rationale: An open explanation elicits the independent reasoning this meta-understanding requires; matching and sorting items check the evidence–idea links and the provisional-vs-opinion distinction. Scored recognition items can confirm the links but do not by themselves build the felt sense of an explanation being remade by evidence, so this follows the constructive activities.
learnerActions: Answer 'why did scientists change this idea?' for a revision you have met, naming the specific evidence that forced the change.
Match old ideas to the evidence that revised them.
Sort statements into 'best current explanation (evidence-based, open to revision)' versus 'just an opinion / anything goes'.

Respond in writing to the prompt: 'Long ago most people, including most scientists, were sure the Sun moved around the Earth; now we say the Earth moves around the Sun. Does that mean the old scientists were foolish? And might what scientists tell us today change too? Explain your thinking.'
activities.intendedInsight: Demonstrate that you can hold BOTH that the old view was reasonable for its evidence AND that current views remain open to revision, while keeping provisional distinct from mere opinion.

constraints: Target age 9–11; this is transitional meta-understanding, reframing 'science' from a fixed body of facts to a self-correcting process. Success = the learner explains, with a concrete historical example, that scientific ideas are revised when new evidence arrives and why this openness is a strength, while distinguishing provisional-but-best-supported from mere opinion.

Ground provisionality in concrete historical revisions: Earth-centred to Sun-centred models, fixed continents to plate tectonics, and spontaneous generation to life arising from existing organisms, rather than relying only on abstract assertions.
Show old ideas as reasonable given the evidence of their time, so revision is upgrading past scientists, not ridiculing them.
Always distinguish 'provisional but best-supported by evidence' from 'just an opinion / anything goes' so provisionality is not mistaken for relativism.

Present a revised model as a new best-current explanation that is itself still open to revision, not a final or perfect answer; do not imply the heliocentric model instantly and perfectly explained everything, and keep any 'fits the evidence' claim scoped to the specific observations presented.
Avoid proof language ('proven', 'proves it') when describing how ideas change; science offers best-current explanations shown to fit evidence, not final proof.
Connect to evidence-over-authority: ideas hold because of evidence, not because an expert asserted them.

Aim to include at least one case where the SAME evidence is reinterpreted without new instruments (distinct from the telescope-driven geocentric/heliocentric case), so learners do not conclude that revision happens ONLY because of better machines/telescopes; a concrete age-appropriate example should be sourced, as none was verified here.
The reveal gallery and the interview build the pattern and the affective side but do not let the learner drive a revision; use them to support, not replace, the evidence-driven activity.

Recognition-only responses (matching, sorting, multiple choice) confirm links but do not by themselves elicit the independent explanation that demonstrates this understanding; pair them with an open explanation task.
The spatial/orrery-style astronomy activity is scoped to the geocentric/heliocentric example only; it is a narrow vehicle for the general provisionality concept.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and both listed sources carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Both cited claims support the general principle that scientific ideas are revised in light of new evidence; they do NOT establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular activity format proposed here, so efficacy language is kept as proposed/may/intended.

The original recommendation describes the model-revision via an interactive 2D artefact; it has been rendered medium-independently as learner actions (feed evidence, test fit, revise, re-test). Optional interactive details (evidence tray, 'doesn't fit' flags, revise action, strength meter, contrast panel) are retained as illustrative examples, not mandatory mechanisms.

The source assessment attributes the geocentric model's difficulty with Mars to retrograde/looping motion handled by extra epicycles — historically standard and retained; no arithmetic or physics error was found requiring correction.

Softened the source's framing that a scored quiz 'can't build the felt sense' into a narrowly scoped objective limit (recognition items do not by themselves elicit independent construction) rather than a universal 'quiz only assesses' claim.

Corrected a learner-facing idealisation: an earlier draft implied the heliocentric model instantly and perfectly re-explained ALL prior evidence cleanly. Scoped this to the three observations used in the activity and added that the new model is itself a revisable best-current explanation, consistent with the provisional-not-final objective.
Removed 'proven wrong' proof language from the interview activity because the assessment explicitly targets the myth that science delivers final proof; reworded to 'shown to be mistaken'.

Historically, phases of Venus refuted the pure Ptolemaic Earth-centred model but were consistent with hybrid (e.g. Tychonic) models; retained at an age-appropriate level as 'the Earth-centred model cannot fit the full set of phases'. The telescope-driven nature of this case is why the 'same evidence reinterpreted without new tools' point should be illustrated with a separately sourced example rather than this one.

The feedback and constraint calling for a same-evidence-reinterpretation case were kept as a design intent; no concrete age-appropriate example was verified here, so the partial-response feedback now discusses the general possibility rather than naming an unverified case.

probeDeeper: You say today's ideas might change — can you give an example of something scientists believe now that could turn out different?
If a scientist runs an experiment and gets a result nobody expected, what should she do — hide it, or tell people? Why?
Here's a tricky one: if science can always change, does that mean anyone's idea is as good as a scientist's? Where is the line?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning holds that the old scientists reasoned honestly from the evidence they had — the Sun does appear to cross the sky — and were not foolish: their idea was the best explanation for the evidence available. It sees revision as a strength of science, not a failure: ideas change because new evidence, or a better interpretation of the same evidence, arrives, and today's ideas are 'the best so far', still open to revision if evidence demands. It rejects both 'they were just stupid' and 'science is now finished and certain'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Science proves things and delivers final, certain truth ('it's a fact now, it can't change').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Offer a case where a 'certain' idea changed — continents don't move, then plate tectonics; name that science gives best-current-explanations, never final proof.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says current scientific ideas are proven or certain and will not change.

errorPatterns.pattern: When scientists change their minds it means they were wrong before, so science can't be trusted ('they keep changing it, so how do we know anything?').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe: revising in the light of evidence is what makes science trustworthy, not what breaks it; contrast with a belief that never checks itself.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats revision as evidence of unreliability or incompetence.

errorPatterns.pattern: The old scientists were simply stupid or ignorant, not reasoning from the evidence they had.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Walk through the geocentric evidence — the Sun really does appear to move — so the child feels why it was reasonable; separate 'wrong in hindsight' from 'foolish'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses past scientists rather than seeing they explained the evidence available to them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ideas change only because we got better machines or telescopes, never because scientists re-thought the same evidence.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give a case of reinterpretation without new tools; discuss how the same evidence can support a new explanation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes all revision to new technology, ignoring reinterpretation and argument.

responseLevels.gap: Holds a fixed-truth or distrust stance — 'science is proven and won't change', or 'they keep changing it so you can't trust it', or 'the old ones were stupid'.
responseLevels.full: Explains that past scientists reasoned soundly from their evidence, that revision on new evidence is a strength of science, and that current ideas are provisional-but-best — connecting the parts into a coherent view of how knowledge grows, and transferring to a fresh example.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts that ideas can change but explains it thinly — e.g. only 'we got better telescopes' — without seeing revision as evidence-driven and a strength, or without granting that the old view was reasonable.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Long ago, everyone — including scientists — was sure the Sun moved around the Earth. Now we say the Earth moves around the Sun. Does that mean the old scientists were bad at science, or foolish? And does it mean that what scientists tell us today might change too? Explain your thinking.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks knowledge is fixed truth says either 'the old ones were wrong and stupid' or 'science can't change now, it's proven'. A child who thinks changing your mind means science is unreliable says 'so we can't trust scientists'. Only a child who grasps provisional-but-evidence-based reasoning can hold both that the old view was reasonable AND that current views may still change — a combination neither naive stance can produce.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Physical vs Chemical Changes

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry & Physics 'Matter'):** Chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms; the difference between chemical and physical changes; conservation of mass in changes of state and chemical reactions.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-2):** Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.

- **Operational details:** The dividing line: a PHYSICAL change alters form or state but makes NO new substance and is usually reversible (melting, dissolving, shaping) — the same particles, just rearranged in space; a CHEMICAL change REARRANGES ATOMS into new substances with different properties, usually hard to reverse (burning, rusting, cooking). The particle-level story is the key upgrade from KS2's observational reversible/irreversible work: in a physical change existing molecules stay intact and only move; in a chemical change bonds break and new bonds form, so the atoms regroup into different molecules. Diagnose a chemical change by evidence (new substance signalled by colour change, gas, heat/light, precipitate) AND by comparing properties before and after (MS-PS1-2). Conservation of mass holds in BOTH (atoms are neither created nor destroyed). Guard the overlap with reversible/irreversible: not all physical changes are trivially reversible in practice, but none make new substances.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child classifies a change as physical or chemical using property-change evidence and the atom-rearrangement idea, and explains that mass is conserved in both because atoms are only regrouped.
bestPractices: Define the split at the particle level: physical = intact molecules rearranged; chemical = bonds break and atoms regroup into new substances.
Diagnose chemical change by evidence (new substance: colour, gas, heat/light, precipitate) AND by comparing properties before and after.
Stress conservation of mass in BOTH change types — atoms are only rearranged.
Use ambiguous cases (dissolving = physical) to sharpen the 'no new substance' criterion.
Connect to KS2 reversible/irreversible while upgrading it with the atom-rearrangement mechanism.
keyRepresentations: A macro event synced to a particle window (molecules intact vs atoms regrouping)
A before/after property comparator
A conserved-mass balance readout across the change
Contrasting exemplars: melting/dissolving (physical) vs burning/rusting (chemical)
commonMisconceptions: A change is chemical whenever the appearance changes (colour, state).
Mass changes during a chemical reaction (atoms created or destroyed).
Dissolving is a chemical change because the solid 'disappears'.
Physical changes are always easily reversible and chemical ones never.
New atoms are created in a reaction, rather than existing atoms being regrouped.

learn.summary: Learners distinguish physical from chemical changes using a particle-level criterion — in a physical change existing particles stay intact and only rearrange in space; in a chemical change bonds break and atoms regroup into new substances. They diagnose chemical change by observable evidence (colour change, gas, heat/light, precipitate) AND by comparing properties before and after, and they explain that mass is conserved in BOTH types because atoms are only rearranged, never created or destroyed — provided all atoms involved (including any gas taken from or released to the surroundings) are counted. Ambiguous cases (dissolving, melting) sharpen the 'no new substance' rule against a weaker 'reversibility' or 'appearance' test.

activities.title: Change classifier: macro stage synced to a particle window
feedback: If a learner labels dissolving chemical because the solid disappeared, point to the particle window: the same particles dispersed among the water particles and can be recovered by evaporation — no new substance formed, so the change is physical.

If a learner expects mass to change in the burning case, return to the particle window and count atoms before and after: the magnesium combines with oxygen from the air, and every atom (magnesium and oxygen) is still present, just regrouped, so the total mass of the closed system is conserved — on an open bench balance the collected solid product is heavier than the original magnesium (if none escapes as smoke) precisely because it has gained that oxygen.
If a learner relies on 'reversible vs irreversible', note that this often correlates but is not the definition; the robust test is whether a new substance formed.

Confirm correct reasoning by having the learner name what the particle view showed: intact particles of the same substance rearranging (physical) versus bonds breaking and new substances forming (chemical).
activities.rationale: The physical/chemical distinction is defined at the particle level, and the key KS3 upgrade from observational reversible/irreversible work is the atom-rearrangement mechanism. A synced macro-and-particle view with a property comparator and a mass readout makes the defining feature — whether the substance stays the same or atoms regroup — directly observable, and the dissolving case targets the common 'looks different so it's chemical' error.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms; difference between chemical and physical changes; conservation of mass
Students judge change type by appearance and think mass changes in reactions; the atom-rearrangement view and property comparison correct this
learnerActions: Trigger melting wax: observe the macro stage turn liquid, and in the particle window watch the same wax molecules loosen and slide while staying whole.
Check the before/after property panel ('same substance') and the mass-balance readout; label the change physical.

Trigger burning magnesium: observe the macro stage flare white, and in the particle window watch magnesium atoms combine with oxygen atoms drawn from the surrounding air into a new white compound (magnesium oxide).

Check the property panel ('new substance, new properties') and confirm that when every atom — including the oxygen taken from the air — is counted, the closed-system mass balance still holds; note that on an open bench balance the solid product would weigh more than the original magnesium, provided all of the product is collected, because it has gained that oxygen; label the change chemical.

Classify a dissolving case: observe the solid seem to disappear on the macro stage while the particle window shows the same particles dispersing among the water particles, not new substances forming; label it physical despite the changed appearance.
For each case, state the rule you used: did the particles stay as the same substance (physical) or did atoms regroup into new substances (chemical)?
activities.intendedInsight: The only difference that matters is whether the substance's particles stayed the same or atoms regrouped into new substances; mass is conserved either way because atoms are only rearranged (counting every atom involved, including any gas exchanged with the surroundings). A changed appearance (state, colour, a solid 'disappearing') is not by itself evidence of a chemical change.

activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain: dissolving versus displacement
feedback: If a learner predicts dissolving makes a new substance, note that a solution is a recoverable mixture — the solid can be recovered by evaporation unchanged, so no new substance formed.

If a learner says mass changes in a sealed reaction, re-anchor on atom conservation: in a sealed flask no atoms enter or leave, so the same atoms are present before and after and total mass is unchanged.
For baking a cake, accept evidence-based answers that cite new substances (gas from raising agents, browning, irreversible texture) as signs of chemical change, rather than a reversibility claim.
activities.rationale: Predict-Observe-Explain makes the learner commit to a rule before seeing the result, surfacing reliance on appearance or reversibility. Contrasting dissolving (physical) with a displacement reaction (chemical) targets an appearance-based classifier, which may wrongly call dissolving chemical. A reversibility rule happens to classify both correctly, so reliance on it is revealed only through the learner's stated explanations.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-PS1-2: analyse and interpret data on properties before and after interaction to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred
Students judge change type by appearance and think mass changes in reactions; the atom-rearrangement view and property comparison correct this
learnerActions: Before observing, predict for adding blue (hydrated) copper sulfate crystals to warm water whether a NEW substance will form, and explain why.
Before observing, predict for dropping an iron nail into copper sulfate solution whether a NEW substance will form, and explain why.

Observe both: the blue copper sulfate crystals dissolve (blue solution, crystals recoverable by gentle evaporation/crystallisation, no new substance); the iron nail turns copper-coloured and the blue fades (a new substance forms).
Compare each prediction with what happened, and revise any rule that relied on reversibility or appearance rather than 'was a new substance made?'.

Answer probes: why is dissolving sugar physical but rusting chemical? What signs show a new substance has formed? Does total mass change in a sealed flask, and why not? Is baking a cake physical or chemical, and what is your evidence?
activities.intendedInsight: Pre-observation reasoning exposes whether a learner classifies by 'new substance formed?' or by a weaker reversibility/appearance test. The dissolving case is the key discriminator: its dramatic appearance change tempts an appearance-based classifier to call it chemical even though no new substance forms, whereas the displacement reaction genuinely is chemical — so committing to a rule before observing reveals which criterion the learner is actually using.

activities.title: Classify and justify the rule
feedback: If the learner classifies solely by reversibility and stumbles on reversible chemical changes or hard-to-reverse physical ones, shift the criterion to 'new substance made?' and show a reversible chemical change alongside an awkward-to-reverse physical one.
If dissolving is placed in the chemical pile, note that dissolving makes a recoverable mixture; the sugar is unchanged, so no new substance → physical.
If melting or boiling is called chemical, use the particle picture to show the same particles rearrange — still the same substance.
Credit full reasoning only when the rule is 'new substance made?', signs are named, and mass conservation is justified by atoms being regrouped.
activities.rationale: Asking for the rule, not just the sort, is the discriminator: all three sorted items (melting, dissolving, rusting) are classified the same way by a reversibility rule and a new-substance rule, so the sort alone cannot tell the two apart. Only cases such as reversible chemical changes or hard-to-reverse physical changes separate them, so requiring the stated rule, plus such follow-up cases, reveals which criterion the learner holds. This is a check/assessment activity best paired after the exploratory sim.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-PS1-2: analyse and interpret data on properties before and after interaction to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred
learnerActions: Sort three changes into physical and chemical: (a) ice melting to water, (b) sugar dissolving in tea, (c) a nail rusting.
State the RULE used — what has to happen for a change to count as chemical.
Interpret before/after property data for further cases to decide whether a chemical reaction occurred.
For a chemical change occurring in a sealed flask, state whether total mass changes and justify using atom conservation.
activities.intendedInsight: A robust classifier rests on 'was a new substance made?' (often signalled by colour change, gas, temperature change, or precipitate, though these signs alone are not proof, since boiling releases gas and some dissolving changes temperature or colour), not on 'is it reversible?'. State changes and dissolving stay physical because the same substance is preserved, and mass is conserved in chemical changes because atoms are only regrouped.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal contrast panel (consolidation)
feedback: Prompt the learner to say explicitly whether any new substance appears in the 'after' picture; if none does, the change is physical.
If a learner conflates a state change with a new substance, point to identical particles in both pictures.
activities.rationale: A reveal-and-describe panel consolidates the vocabulary and the particle contrast. It is a scaffold: fixed pictures support recognition and verbalisation but do not let the learner trigger changes, watch bonds break and reform, or test their own classifications, so it complements rather than replaces the interactive sim.
learnerActions: Reveal paired before/after particle pictures for a physical change (same particles, rearranged) and a chemical change (bonds broken, new substances formed).
Describe in your own words what stayed the same and what changed at the particle level for each.
Match each revealed example to the evidence that signals a new substance (or its absence).
activities.intendedInsight: Static particle pictures let learners rehearse and verbalise the same-substance-versus-regrouped-atoms contrast and connect it to observable evidence.

constraints: Define the split at the particle level: physical = same substance's particles rearranged; chemical = bonds break and atoms regroup into new substances.
Diagnose chemical change by evidence (new substance: colour, gas, heat/light, precipitate) AND by comparing properties before and after.

Stress conservation of mass in BOTH change types — atoms are only rearranged, never created or destroyed; when a gas is exchanged with the surroundings (e.g. magnesium gaining oxygen from the air), it must be counted, so an open bench balance can still show a change in the mass of the solid.
Use ambiguous cases (dissolving, melting) to sharpen the 'no new substance' criterion against reversibility- or appearance-based tests.
Connect to KS2 reversible/irreversible while upgrading it with the atom-rearrangement mechanism; note that not all physical changes are trivially reversible in practice, but none make new substances.

The tap-to-reveal contrast panel is a recognition/verbalisation scaffold: it does not let learners trigger changes or test classifications, so it supports but does not substitute for the interactive investigation.

A classification task with fixed response options checks sorting and data interpretation but does not by itself elicit the learner's independently generated rule or reasoning; pair it with a task that asks for the justification.

Mass-conservation and property examples (wax melting, magnesium burning, iron/copper sulfate displacement) depend on the specified setup; present them as the stated scenarios rather than universal outcomes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled a 2D interactive 'ideal' and rated 3D and conversation 'poor' as catalog fit judgements. These are framed here as fit-for-purpose proposals: a 2D particle view suits a particle-rearrangement concept, but this does not establish that 3D or dialogue 'add nothing' or 'cannot teach' the idea. The comparative-efficacy framing in the original has been softened.

The original claim that a static image 'cannot animate bonds breaking/forming or let the child test and classify' is retained only as a scope note (the panel supports recognition/verbalisation), not as a universal 'static art cannot teach' law.
Two of three sources are marked verified:false in the row (NGSS MS-PS1-2 and the BEST diagnostics claim); evidence strength has not been upgraded here.

The POE displacement example (iron nail in copper sulfate) and magnesium burning involve reagents that require appropriate supervision/safety in a real classroom; the row does not specify safety handling.

Magnesium burning is the classic case where an open-air demonstration shows the solid gaining mass; conservation of total mass only holds literally when the oxygen taken from the air is included. The activity now states this explicitly rather than implying no mass change.

Dissolving copper sulfate (the POE physical example) separates the ionic solid into ions in solution rather than keeping intact molecules; it is still a physical change by the recovery/no-new-substance test, but the generic 'particles disperse' wording is preferred over 'molecules stay intact' for ionic solutes.

In this POE pair a strict reversibility classifier happens to label both cases correctly; it is specifically the appearance-based classifier that mislabels dissolving, which is why the activity frames the dissolving case as the discriminator.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: add a spatula of copper sulfate to warm water (dissolves — physical) and, separately, drop an iron nail into copper sulfate solution (displacement — chemical, nail goes copper-coloured, blue fades). Ask the child to predict, for each, whether a NEW substance forms and WHY, before observing. A 'reversibility/appearance' classifier predicts wrongly. The pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Sugar dissolving looks permanent-ish and rusting looks permanent — so why is one physical and one chemical?
Name the signs you'd look for that tell you a NEW substance has formed.
A chemical reaction happens in a sealed flask — does the total mass change? Why not?
Is baking a cake physical or chemical? What's your evidence?
assess.correctAnswer: Physical: melting ice and dissolving sugar (no new substance — same stuff rearranged, reversible). Chemical: rusting (a NEW substance, iron oxide, forms). The rule: a CHEMICAL change makes one or more NEW substances (signalled by colour change, gas, temperature change, or a precipitate); a physical change makes none. Full marks rest the rule on 'new substance made?', not on 'is it reversible?'.

errorPatterns.pattern: reversibility is the whole test ('if you can undo it, it's physical; if you can't, it's chemical')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shift the criterion to 'new substance made?'. Reversibility often correlates but isn't the definition — show a reversible chemical change and an awkward-to-reverse physical one.
errorPatterns.distractor: Rusting is chemical only because you can't undo it, and the others are physical because you can.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: classifies solely by whether it can be reversed; stumbles on reversible chemical changes or hard-to-reverse physical ones

errorPatterns.pattern: dissolving is a chemical change because 'the sugar reacts with the water / turns into something new'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Dissolving makes a mixture, recoverable by evaporation; the sugar is unchanged. No new substance → physical. Reconnect to conservation and recovery.
errorPatterns.distractor: Dissolving is chemical, because the sugar turns into a new substance in the tea.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: puts dissolving in the chemical pile, treating the solution as a new substance

errorPatterns.pattern: a change of state (melting/boiling) is chemical because 'it turned into something different'
errorPatterns.nextMove: State changes rearrange the SAME particles — still water, no new substance. Use the particle picture to show identity is preserved.
errorPatterns.distractor: Melting is chemical, because a solid turning into a liquid is a new substance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: labels melting/boiling chemical because the appearance/state changed

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by reversibility alone or by appearance; mislabels dissolving or melting as chemical; no 'new substance' criterion.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by whether a new substance formed, names the observable signs, keeps state changes and dissolving as physical using the particle/recovery argument, and explains mass is conserved in a chemical change — transferring to novel cases (baking, reversible reactions).
responseLevels.partial: Sorts the three correctly and states 'new substance = chemical', but leans on reversibility as backup and can't handle a reversible chemical change or justify via conservation of mass — rule stated, not yet robust.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three changes: (a) ice melting to water, (b) sugar dissolving in tea, (c) a nail rusting. Sort them into 'physical change' and 'chemical change'. Then the important part: explain the RULE you used — what has to happen for a change to count as chemical?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two rule separates a child who classifies by 'was a new substance formed' from one who uses 'reversible = physical' as the whole test. Dissolving (reversible, physical) fits both rules, but rusting isn't easily reversed AND some chemical changes seem reversible — so only the 'new substance' rule classifies robustly. Asking for the rule, not just the sort, is the discriminator.
