pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Animal Classification Vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'Living things and their habitats'):** 'recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways' and 'explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things in their local and wider environment' — this is the statutory home of vertebrate/invertebrate and the group names (mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian, fish, insect). The life-cycle terms (metamorphosis, larva, pupa, gestation, complete vs incomplete metamorphosis) are seeded here and consolidated at Y5: 'describe the differences in the life cycles of a mammal, an amphibian, an insect and a bird.'

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-LS1-1):** honest note — NGSS has NO taxonomy-naming performance expectation, so there is no US anchor for 'vertebrate/invertebrate/mammal…' as named categories. The nearest PE, 3-LS1-1 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS1-1] share a common set: birth, growth, reproduction, death'), supports the LIFE-CYCLE half of this vocabulary (metamorphosis, larva, pupa) but not the classification-group naming, which is UK-curriculum-driven.

- **Operational details:** This is a LANGUAGE node — the job is precise, correctly-applied terminology, not new phenomena. Two vocabulary clusters live here: (1) grouping words — vertebrate/invertebrate as the top split, then the five vertebrate classes plus insect/arachnid within invertebrates; (2) life-cycle words — offspring, gestation, larva, pupa, metamorphosis, and the complete-vs-incomplete contrast. Teach each word anchored to the OBSERVABLE feature that defines it (backbone; feathers; scales-and-lay-eggs-on-land vs moist-skin-and-water-eggs; six legs vs eight) rather than by habitat or size. Introduce terms in contrasting pairs so the discriminating attribute is felt (frog=amphibian vs lizard=reptile; butterfly=complete vs grasshopper=incomplete). Use the words immediately in sorting and comparing tasks — a term is only learned when the child deploys it to justify a placement.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child sorts real/pictured organisms and NARRATES the placement using the target word and the feature that licenses it ('a whale is a mammal because it breathes air and feeds milk, even though it lives in water'), and contrasts a complete metamorphosis (egg→larva→pupa→adult) with an incomplete one (egg→nymph→adult) using the terms correctly.
bestPractices: Anchor every group word to its DEFINING OBSERVABLE FEATURE, not habitat or size — mammal = fur/hair + feeds young milk + breathes air; bird = feathers + beak; reptile = dry scales + eggs on land; amphibian = moist skin + eggs in water; fish = gills + fins; insect = 6 legs + 3 body parts; arachnid = 8 legs + 2 body parts. Feature-first defeats the habitat trap.

Introduce terms in minimal-contrast pairs so the discriminating attribute is salient (frog vs lizard for amphibian/reptile; butterfly vs grasshopper for complete/incomplete metamorphosis; whale vs shark for mammal/fish).
Make children USE the word to justify a sort ('I put it here BECAUSE it has a backbone') — productive use, not just recognition, is what fixes technical vocabulary.
Teach vertebrate/invertebrate as the top-level split first (has a backbone / no backbone), then nest the finer groups inside — a two-level hierarchy the child can hold.

Pair the life-cycle vocabulary with a physical sequence to order (egg, larva, pupa, adult), and explicitly contrast complete (four distinct stages, a pupa) with incomplete (nymph resembles a small adult, no pupa) so 'metamorphosis' is tied to the degree of change.
Use exemplars AND non-exemplars (a bat is a mammal not a bird; a penguin is a bird not a fish; a spider is not an insect) to draw the category boundary sharply.
keyRepresentations: A two-level branching tree/Carroll-or-Venn diagram: first branch vertebrate vs invertebrate, then the class names as leaves — the canonical model for how the words nest.
A classification key (yes/no questions on observable features) that outputs a group name — the DfE Y4 canonical tool and the reason the vocabulary exists.
A labelled 'feature card' per group pinning the word to its 1–2 defining features (backbone, feathers, moist skin, 6 legs…).
A life-cycle wheel/strip showing egg→larva→pupa→adult (complete) beside egg→nymph→adult (incomplete), with each stage labelled by its term.
A sorting mat with header labels (the group words) that children populate with organism cards.
commonMisconceptions: Classifying by HABITAT not features — 'a whale/dolphin is a fish because it lives in the sea', 'a penguin is a fish because it swims' — the dominant error; must be countered with feature-first sorting.
Thinking every small crawling animal is an 'insect' (spiders, woodlice, centipedes) — insect is specifically 6 legs + 3 body parts; a spider is an arachnid (8 legs).
Believing a bat is a bird (it flies) rather than a mammal (fur, feeds milk) — flight is not a class-defining feature.
Treating 'metamorphosis' as any growth/change, rather than the specific staged transformation with a larva and (in complete metamorphosis) a pupa.
Assuming ALL insects have a pupa — grasshoppers, crickets and true bugs undergo INCOMPLETE metamorphosis (nymph, no pupal stage).

Confusing 'amphibian' and 'reptile' — assuming anything that lives near water/land or looks lizard-like is the same group; the split is moist skin + water eggs (amphibian) vs dry scales + land eggs (reptile).

learn.summary: Learners aged 7–9 build precise animal-classification vocabulary (vertebrate/invertebrate; mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian, fish; insect, arachnid) and life-cycle vocabulary (offspring, gestation, larva, pupa, nymph, metamorphosis, complete vs incomplete). This is a LANGUAGE objective: the goal is binding each term to the relevant observable features of the chosen examples (backbone; fur+milk; feathers; dry scales in typical reptiles; moist skin in typical amphibians; gills+fins in typical fish; adult insect6 true legs+3 body regions vs typical adult arachnid8 legs+2 body regions) rather than by habitat or size, and then USING the words to justify sorts and compare life cycles (including a frog's amphibian metamorphosis and a mammal's cycle against an insect's). Activities move from a feature-reveal gallery (fix meaning) to productive sorting, key-building and life-cycle comparison (prove meaning), with a dialogue 'mystery animal' variant for feature-question practice.

activities.title: Feature-reveal classification gallery and life-cycle strip
feedback: When a group is revealed, confirm the shared feature in words the child can reuse: 'all three are mammals because they feed their young milk and have hair or fur at some stage of life.'
For a myth-prone case, state the feature that overrides the habitat/appearance guess: 'a whale lives in the sea but breathes air and feeds milk, so it is a mammal, not a fish.'

On the life-cycle strip, contrast explicitly: 'the butterfly has a pupa stage — that is complete metamorphosis; the grasshopper has no pupa, just a nymph that grows into the adult — that is incomplete metamorphosis.'
activities.rationale: For a vocabulary objective the first task is anchoring each term to its defining observable feature; an authored reveal that links word↔feature and co-highlights exemplars across different habitats makes the feature-first rule salient and pre-empts the dominant habitat-based error. Showing complete and incomplete life cycles together surfaces the discriminating attribute (presence/absence of a pupa).
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 statutory: 'recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways' and 'explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things in their local and wider environment' — the statutory home of vertebrate/invertebrate and group vocabulary.

Children commonly classify by habitat rather than defining features (e.g. whale/dolphin called a fish because it lives in the sea; classify by where an animal lives), so teaching must foreground feature-based sorting.
learnerActions: Look at a spread of familiar animals arranged on a two-level branching tree: first split is 'has a backbone' (vertebrate) vs 'no backbone' (invertebrate), then the group names sit as leaves below.

Reveal a group word (e.g. 'mammal') and see every member of that group highlight together — e.g. the whale, the bat AND a pet dog light up at once — while a callout names the shared defining features: 'has hair or fur at some stage of life (a whale has only a few bristly hairs) and feeds its young milk'.

Reveal an individual animal to see a one-line 'because…' that busts a habitat/appearance myth: 'a whale is a mammal even though it lives in the sea'; 'a bat is a mammal, not a bird'; 'a penguin is a bird, not a fish'; 'a spider is an arachnid — 8 legs, not an insect'.

On a life-cycle strip, step through egg → larva → pupa → adult and see each stage name itself; directly above or below, step through egg → nymph → adult so complete and incomplete metamorphosis sit side by side as a visible contrast.
Use a lift-the-flap style question such as 'Is a spider an insect?' and reveal the reasoned answer: 'No — 8 legs, so it's an arachnid.'
activities.intendedInsight: A classification word tracks a defining body feature (such as a backbone, feathers, or feeding young milk), not where an animal lives or whether it flies or swims. Seeing a sea creature and a flying creature light up as the SAME group makes 'the word follows the feature' concrete, and placing complete beside incomplete metamorphosis ties 'metamorphosis' to a degree of change (a pupa/rebuild vs a nymph that resembles a small adult).

activities.title: Sort, justify, and build a classification key
feedback: On a wrong placement, prompt back to the feature, not the answer: 'check the feature — how many legs does it have? does it have a backbone?'
Reward a justification that names the licensing feature: 'yes — 6 legs and 3 body parts, so insect is right.'
For the spider distractor: 'count the legs — an adult with 8 legs and 2 body parts is an arachnid, not an insect.'
activities.rationale: Sorting cards under group headers and building/using a yes/no key matches the DfE Y4 expectation to explore and use classification keys, and requires productive use of the vocabulary with immediate, feature-focused feedback, which supports learning technical terms. Exemplar/non-exemplar pairs draw category boundaries sharply.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 statutory: 'recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways' and 'explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things in their local and wider environment' — the statutory home of vertebrate/invertebrate and group vocabulary.

Children commonly classify by habitat rather than defining features (e.g. whale/dolphin called a fish because it lives in the sea; classify by where an animal lives), so teaching must foreground feature-based sorting.
learnerActions: Drag or place organism cards first onto 'vertebrate'/'invertebrate' mats, then into the finer group bins (mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian, fish; insect, arachnid). Use only insects and arachnids as invertebrate cards, or add an 'other invertebrate' bin for animals such as snails, worms or crabs.
Say or write the reason for each placement using the group word AND its feature: 'I put the whale under mammal BECAUSE it breathes air and feeds its young milk.'

Build and then use a yes/no classification key out of feature questions ('Does it have a backbone?', 'Does it have feathers?', 'How many legs?') so that answering the questions names the animal's group.
Deliberately place exemplars and non-exemplars: confirm a bat as a mammal (not a bird), a penguin as a bird (not a fish), and a spider as NOT an insect (an arachnid, 8 legs).
activities.intendedInsight: A technical term is only truly learned when the child deploys it to justify a decision; building a key makes the defining features the engine of naming.

activities.title: Compare life cycles and narrate the change
feedback: If the child calls a grasshopper nymph a 'larva': 'larva and pupa belong to the butterfly's complete metamorphosis; the grasshopper's gradually-changing young is a nymph — re-tell it with the right word.'
If 'metamorphosis' is used for a puppy or a child growing: 'that is getting bigger, not changing body form — metamorphosis is a change in shape.'
If 'incomplete' is read as 'something went wrong': 'incomplete just means fewer stages and no pupa — the grasshopper is a perfectly complete, finished adult.'
For the frog, confirm: 'the tadpole turning into a frog is a big change in body form — that is metamorphosis too, even though we use the complete/incomplete labels only for insects.'

For the mammal comparison, confirm the terms: 'yes — gestation is the time the baby grows inside the mother, and a puppy or kitten is born with the same basic body form as its parents, so it grows and develops without changing body form the way the butterfly does.'
activities.rationale: Pairing the life-cycle vocabulary with a physical sequence to order, and contrasting insect complete vs incomplete metamorphosis, an amphibian's metamorphosis, and a mammal's cycle, ties 'metamorphosis' to the degree of change, covers the gestation/offspring and amphibian requirements in the objective's evidence list, and targets the specific interference errors (over-generalising 'larva', equating metamorphosis with any growth, misreading 'incomplete').
sourceClaims: DfE Y5 statutory: 'describe the differences in the life cycles of a mammal, an amphibian, an insect and a bird' — where metamorphosis/larva/pupa vocabulary is consolidated.
learnerActions: Order the stage cards for a butterfly: egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa (chrysalis) → adult.
Order the stage cards for a grasshopper: egg → nymph (a small wingless version of the adult) → adult.
Narrate both insect stories aloud using the correct term at each stage, reserving 'larva' and 'pupa' for the butterfly and 'nymph' for the grasshopper.
State which insect cycle is complete metamorphosis and which is incomplete, and say WHY (the pupa/body-rebuild stage is present or absent) — keeping the complete/incomplete labels for insects.

Describe a frog's life cycle to show metamorphosis in an amphibian: egg → tadpole (lives in water, has gills and a tail) → adult frog (has legs and lungs, usually no tail, and can live on land, though many frogs stay in or near water) — a dramatic change in body form, so 'metamorphosis' is not an insect-only word.

Describe a dog’s or cat’s life cycle using gestation, the period the young develop inside the mother before birth, and offspring, the young produced. Compare that selected live-bearing mammal with the butterfly’s larva–pupa–adult transformation; some mammals lay eggs, so do not present live birth as universal.
Sort growth examples into 'changes body form' (metamorphosis) vs 'just gets bigger' (e.g. a kitten becoming a cat) to separate metamorphosis from ordinary growth.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Metamorphosis' names a change in body FORM, not just size; in insects, complete metamorphosis has four distinct stages including a pupa, while incomplete metamorphosis has a nymph that resembles a small adult and no pupa ('incomplete' means fewer stages, not defective). Metamorphosis also happens in amphibians — a frog changes body form from a gilled, tailed, water-living tadpole into a legged adult with lungs that can live on land — so the word is not insect-only. A live-bearing mammal's cycle such as a dog's or cat's (gestation, birth of offspring, then growth) differs again: precise words let the child compare these kinds of change.

activities.title: Mystery-animal feature dialogue (variant practice)
feedback: Confirm a correct group with its reason: 'yes — backbone plus feathers means bird.'
Gently redirect a habitat-based guess: 'swimming doesn't decide the group — ask about the backbone, the skin or the legs.'
activities.rationale: A feature-question dialogue maps naturally onto the classification-key logic and forces productive use of the discriminating vocabulary. It is a useful variant, though without visible animals the word↔feature anchoring is weaker, so it supplements rather than replaces the gallery and sorting tasks.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 statutory: 'recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways' and 'explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things in their local and wider environment' — the statutory home of vertebrate/invertebrate and group vocabulary.
learnerActions: Question an in-role 'mystery creature' using only feature questions: 'Do you have a backbone?', 'Do you have feathers?', 'How many legs do you have?'
Use the answers to propose the animal's group and state the reason: 'You have a backbone and feathers, so you are a bird.'
When tempted to guess by habitat ('you must be a fish because you swim'), re-ask a feature question instead and revise the guess.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming a group is a matter of asking the right feature questions in turn — the same logic as a classification key — so the discriminating vocabulary becomes a tool for reasoning, not a label to recall.

constraints: Use relevant features of selected examples rather than habitat alone: mammals feed young milk and have hair at some life stage; birds have feathers; typical reptiles have dry scales; typical amphibians have moist skin; typical fish have gills and fins. Many reptiles lay eggs on land and many amphibians lay eggs in water, but these are not universal definitions. Use adult insects for the six-true-legs/three-body-regions comparison and typical adult spiders for eight legs/two body regions; larval forms may look different.
Teach vertebrate/invertebrate as the top-level split first, then nest the five vertebrate classes and insect/arachnid inside — a two-level hierarchy the child can hold.

Introduce terms in minimal-contrast pairs (frog vs lizard for amphibian/reptile; butterfly vs grasshopper for complete/incomplete metamorphosis; whale vs shark for mammal/fish) so the discriminating attribute is salient.
Include non-exemplars (bat is a mammal not a bird; penguin is a bird not a fish; spider is an arachnid not an insect) to draw boundaries sharply.

A reveal/gallery fixes the meaning but does not by itself show whether the child can deploy the word; always follow with productive use (sorting with justification, key-building, or narrating a life cycle).

Recognition-only responses (tapping, matching, multiple choice) can check correct use but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and justification that this objective targets; use them as checks, not as the whole learning.
Not all insects have a pupa: grasshoppers, crickets and true bugs undergo incomplete metamorphosis (nymph, no pupal stage); 'incomplete' means fewer stages, not defective.

Scope the complete/incomplete labels to insects; amphibians (e.g. frogs) also undergo metamorphosis — a dramatic change in body form from tadpole to adult — so 'metamorphosis' should not be taught as an insect-only word.

Cover the mammal life-cycle terms gestation (young developing inside the mother before live birth) and offspring (young produced), comparing a mammal's cycle with an insect's, per the objective's evidence requirement.

The US NGSS has no performance expectation naming vertebrate/invertebrate or the class names; the classification-naming half is UK-curriculum-driven, while the life-cycle half aligns with NGSS 3-LS1-1. Keep this scope distinction when stating standards alignment.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles, not the efficacy of any specific activity here.

Source marks two citations as unverified (NGSS 3-LS1-1 and the Oak National Academy 'Animal groups' lesson); the habitat-misconception and NGSS-scope claims rest on these unverified sources and should be re-checked.

The original 3D-interactive entry asserted that classification vocabulary gains 'nothing' from 3D; this comparative/necessity claim is not established by catalog ratings and has been dropped rather than restated as a universal law. 3D rendering is simply not the most direct route for a categorical vocabulary objective here.

The original framed the tap-to-reveal image as uniquely delivering the 'click-moment' and the quiz as scoring 'rather than teaching'; these comparative-efficacy claims are catalog-fit rankings, not established findings, and have been softened to describe affordances and sequencing instead.

Amphibian metamorphosis (frog tadpole→adult) has been added to activity 3 to meet the evidence item on amphibian life cycles; 'gestation' and 'offspring' are addressed via the mammal-vs-insect comparison but still receive lighter treatment than the classification and metamorphosis vocabulary, and teachers may wish to add a dedicated mammal- or bird-focused task to deepen coverage.

probeDeeper: What do you call the young grasshopper — and why isn't it a larva?
You said 'metamorphosis' — does a kitten going to a cat count? Why or why not?
What is inside the chrysalis doing that a moulting grasshopper is not?
Use 'vertebrate' and 'invertebrate' to tell me where the butterfly and a frog each belong.
assess.correctAnswer: The butterfly goes through complete metamorphosis: egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa (chrysalis) → adult, with the body completely rebuilt. The grasshopper goes through incomplete metamorphosis: egg → nymph (a small wingless version of the adult) → adult, moulting as it grows, with no pupa stage. The child uses larva, pupa and nymph correctly for the right animal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Every baby insect is a 'larva' ('the young grasshopper is a larva too')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two stories: 'larva' and 'pupa' belong to complete metamorphosis; the gradually-changing young is a 'nymph'. Have the child re-tell using the right word for each.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls a grasshopper nymph a larva, using 'larva' as a general word for insect young

errorPatterns.pattern: Metamorphosis just means growing up or getting bigger
errorPatterns.nextMove: Metamorphosis is a change in body FORM, not just size. Sort examples into 'changes shape' vs 'just gets bigger'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses 'metamorphosis' for a puppy or a human growing, i.e. any growth

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Incomplete metamorphosis' means the animal is unfinished or something went wrong
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe: 'incomplete' means fewer stages (no pupa), not defective. The grasshopper is a perfectly complete adult.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads the everyday meaning of 'incomplete' into the term, thinking the grasshopper failed to finish

responseLevels.gap: Uses the terms loosely or interchangeably — 'larva' for any baby insect, 'metamorphosis' for any growth — with no tie to real stages.
responseLevels.full: Narrates both life cycles with the right vocabulary in place — larva/pupa for complete metamorphosis, nymph for incomplete — and contrasts the two kinds of change accurately.
responseLevels.partial: Uses some terms correctly for the butterfly but misapplies larva/pupa to the grasshopper, or can label stages but not compare the two life cycles.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell me the story of how a butterfly grows up, and then how a grasshopper grows up, using the words that describe each kind of change. Which one goes through complete metamorphosis — and what would you call the grasshopper's kind of change instead?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The test is correct USE inside the narrative, not a recited definition. A child with the vocabulary reserves 'larva' and 'pupa' for the butterfly and calls the young grasshopper a 'nymph'. A child who only memorised words misapplies them — giving the grasshopper a larva or a pupa — revealing the terms aren't tied to the real stages.

sources.claim: DfE Y4 statutory: 'recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways' and 'explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things in their local and wider environment' — the statutory home of vertebrate/invertebrate and group vocabulary.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS1 & KS2), Year 4 'Living things and their habitats'

sources.claim: DfE Y5 statutory: 'describe the differences in the life cycles of a mammal, an amphibian, an insect and a bird' — where metamorphosis/larva/pupa vocabulary is consolidated.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study, Year 5 'Living things and their habitats'

sources.claim: NGSS 3-LS1-1 covers life cycles (birth, growth, reproduction, death) but NGSS has no performance expectation requiring vertebrate/invertebrate or class-name taxonomy — the classification-naming half of this vocabulary is UK-curriculum-driven.
sources.source: NGSS 3-LS1-1, Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

sources.claim: Children commonly classify by habitat rather than defining features (e.g. whale/dolphin called a fish because it lives in the sea; classify by where an animal lives), so teaching must foreground feature-based sorting.
sources.source: Oak National Academy, KS2 'Animal groups' lesson (five vertebrate groups; classify by features not habitat)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** States of Matter Vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE, formal home Y4 'States of matter'; introduced informally earlier):** England's statutory treatment sits in Year 4 — "compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases." The non-statutory guidance supplies the child-friendly descriptors this vocabulary node teaches: "solids hold their shape; liquids form a pool not a pile; gases escape from an unsealed container," and pupils "observe water as a solid, a liquid and a gas." At ages 5–7 there is no KS1 statutory states content, so this is early, informal vocabulary-building that seeds the Y4 objective.

- **Standards — US (NGSS, honest gap):** NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to naming the three states; the nearest is DCI PS1.A ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]', anchoring 2-PS1-1) and 2-PS1-4 on reversible/irreversible heating/cooling changes. State-naming is treated as embedded vocabulary rather than a discrete PE.

- **Operational details:** Build the three category words from OBSERVABLE BEHAVIOUR, not definitions: a solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container (forms a pool not a pile), a gas spreads out to fill whatever holds it. Use water as the anchor substance seen in all three states (ice, water, steam/vapour) so the SAME material carries the vocabulary. Introduce 'change of state' as the word for what happens when ice melts or water boils. Sort plentiful everyday examples and talk through borderline cases (is sand a solid? is it still a solid when it 'pours'?). Deliberately name a gas children can feel but not see (air in a balloon) to start dislodging 'gas isn't really stuff'.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can correctly sort everyday substances as solid, liquid or gas and give a behaviour reason for each, use the three words accurately in description, and use 'change of state' to describe ice melting or water boiling.
bestPractices: Define each state by observable behaviour ('keeps its shape' / 'forms a pool not a pile' / 'fills its container'), not abstract definitions.
Use water as the through-line — ice, water, steam — so one familiar material demonstrates all three states and the change-of-state word.
Sort many real examples and talk through tricky cases (sand, powder, honey) to test the behaviour rule rather than surface looks.
Introduce a felt-but-unseen gas (air in a balloon, bubbles) early to begin challenging 'gas is not stuff'.
Handle everyday 'gas' language carefully — clarify the science sense versus natural gas/petrol so the word doesn't mislead.
Keep 'change of state' concrete and reversible (melting/freezing water) at this age; avoid heating that causes burning/cooking (a chemical change).
keyRepresentations: Water shown in three states (ice cube, glass of water, steam) as the anchor example
Behaviour cards: 'keeps its shape' / 'flows, takes the shape of its container' / 'spreads to fill the space'
A three-bin sort (solid / liquid / gas) of everyday substances
A balloon or bubbles to make an invisible gas tangible
A simple melt/boil before-after pair introducing 'change of state'
commonMisconceptions: Gases are not matter / are weightless — rooted in 'seeing is believing' since most gases are invisible (a very common and persistent idea).
A 'solid' must be hard and rigid, so powders and sand (which pour) get miscalled liquids.
Thinking of a liquid as anything that pours, conflating flow with the liquid state.
The everyday meaning of 'gas' (fuel) crowding out the physical-state meaning.
Treating steam/water vapour as something other than water, or as 'hot air', rather than water in its gas state.

learn.summary: Early (ages 5–7) informal vocabulary-building for the three states of matter — solid, liquid, gas — anchored to OBSERVABLE BEHAVIOUR rather than abstract definitions: a solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container (forms a pool not a pile), a gas spreads out to fill whatever holds it. Water is the through-line (ice, water, steam) so one familiar material carries all three words plus 'change of state'. It deliberately makes an invisible gas tangible (air in a balloon) to begin unseating 'gas is not stuff'. This seeds the later UK Year 4 objective; at this age there is no KS1 statutory states content, and NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to naming the three states. (Steam, meaning water vapour, is the gas state and is invisible; the white cloud seen above a kettle is tiny drops of liquid water that form as the steam cools, so it should not be presented as the gas.)

activities.title: Tap-to-name the three states in a kitchen scene
feedback: When a learner taps an item, state the name AND the behaviour reason together ('LIQUID — it flows and takes the shape of the cup'), so the word is always tied to behaviour rather than appearance.

On the balloon, reinforce that the air spreads to fill the balloon and takes up space — a gas is a real material, not 'nothing'. (You can also feel it is really there by gently squeezing a sealed balloon, but the key point is that a gas fills and takes up space, not that it 'pushes'.)
On the water trio, name that ice, water and steam are all the same water in different states.
activities.rationale: This is a language node: attaching three category words to observable behaviours for early, pre-reading learners suits tap-to-reveal with audio and picture support (no reading required). Using water as one anchor material lets all three words and 'change of state' hang on something already known, consistent with the curriculum descriptors. Optional details such as lift-the-flap melting/boiling and a tappable balloon make the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'States of matter' statutory: 'compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases'; non-statutory descriptors 'solids hold their shape; liquids form a pool not a pile; gases escape from an unsealed container'; observe water as solid, liquid, gas.
learnerActions: Explore a home/kitchen scene and tap everyday items to hear each one's state and the behaviour reason, e.g. tap the ice cube → 'SOLID — it keeps its shape'; tap the juice → 'LIQUID — it flows and takes the shape of the cup'; tap the kettle → 'When water boils it becomes steam, a GAS you can't see — it spreads out into the air. The white cloud is tiny water drops made as the steam cools.'

Visit a dedicated water trio panel showing the SAME water as hard ice, runny liquid, and invisible steam (water vapour) shown as spreading arrows or a dotted cue, with audio explaining that you can't see the gas itself.
Open a 'melting' and a 'boiling' flap on the water panel to hear that the move between states is called a 'change of state'.
Tap the balloon in the corner to hear 'the air inside is a GAS — it fills the balloon up'.
activities.intendedInsight: Three new category words attach to familiar things through how they behave (shape and container), and the SAME water can be solid, liquid or gas (the gas, steam or water vapour, is invisible), with 'change of state' naming the move between them; a gas (air) really is stuff that spreads out to fill its container.

activities.title: Sort real substances into solid / liquid / gas bins
feedback: For sand/sugar/salt placed as liquid: zoom in on a single grain — it is a hard solid that keeps its shape; the PILE pours only because the grains slide past each other.
For a damp sponge called 'a liquid': re-anchor to behaviour — the sponge keeps its shape (solid) even though it is wet.
When an item behaves as sorted, confirm using the behaviour phrase ('yes — it spreads to fill the jar, so it's a gas').
activities.rationale: Sorting many real examples and talking through tricky cases tests the behaviour rule rather than appearance, and the self-checking 'watch it behave' actions make the defining behaviours observable. Repeated hands-on sorting is reported to support conceptual change at this age. This does slightly more than a bare naming task, which is appropriate for the borderline cases. A sort of this kind can teach and check classification but does not by itself elicit the child's spoken explanation, so the checkpoint below adds spoken use.
sourceClaims: Elementary states-of-matter misconceptions are partly developmental; steam/water vapour confused with 'hot air'; powders/solids confusion; hands-on repeated activities needed for conceptual change.
learnerActions: Drag or place plentiful everyday substances into three bins labelled solid, liquid and gas.

For a chosen item, trigger a short 'watch it behave' action — a liquid pouring and taking the shape of a cup, a solid holding its shape, a gas (shown with a coloured animation cue, since most gases are invisible) spreading to fill a jar — and check the sort against the behaviour.
Discuss borderline cases out loud: Is sand a solid when it 'pours'? What about honey, sugar, salt, or a damp sponge?
Use a mini melt/boil before-after pair to practise the words 'change of state'.
activities.intendedInsight: The defining test is BEHAVIOUR (keeps its shape / flows and takes its container's shape / spreads to fill the space), not surface looks, size, smell or wetness; tricky cases like pourable powders are still solids because each grain keeps its shape.

activities.title: Use the words like a scientist (checkpoint)
feedback: Expected: rock = solid (hard, keeps its shape); milk = liquid (runny, flows, takes the shape of its container); the air = gas (spreads out, fills the balloon); sand = tiny solid grains (each grain keeps its shape, though the pile pours).
'Change of state' = the same material in a different state, e.g. ice (solid) melting to water (liquid) on heating, or water freezing back.

If the learner says the balloon has 'nothing' or 'just air': make the gas tangible as a demonstration — squeeze the sealed balloon or fan the air onto a face so it can be felt; this shows the gas is really there and takes up space, filling its container (the 'push' you feel is the trapped air, not the definition — the point is a gas is a real material that fills the space).
If 'solid' is taken to mean strong/big, 'gas' only petrol/fumes, or 'liquid' any wet thing: re-anchor each word to BEHAVIOUR (shape and container), not size, smell or wetness.
Listen for the words used correctly in context ('fills its container', 'keeps its shape'), not merely recited; naming the trio alone (recitation) is not enough.
activities.rationale: The sand and air cases discriminate meaningful use from recitation: sand pours yet is solid, and gas is invisible yet real. Listening for USE exposes loose everyday usage a definition would hide. Keep 'change of state' concrete and reversible (melting/freezing water); avoid heating that causes burning/cooking, which is a different kind of change. The misconception that a gas is 'not matter' is well attested, which is why the air case is included (source verification status noted in reviewNotes).
sourceClaims: 'Gas has no mass / gas is not matter' is a common, persistent misconception rooted in the 'seeing is believing' principle because most gases are invisible; everyday 'gas' language and 'empty' containers reinforce it.
learnerActions: Name whether each of several things is solid, liquid or gas AND describe HOW it behaves: a rock, milk, the air in a balloon, and sand.
Explain what 'change of state' means, using ice as the example (ice melting to water, or water freezing back), including what happens to ice on a warm day.

Answer probing questions: Is the air in the balloon solid, liquid or gas — how can you tell it's really there? Sand pours like a drink — is sand a liquid? Look closely at one grain. Is toothpaste a solid or a liquid — what makes it hard to decide?
activities.intendedInsight: Correct, meaningful USE of the behaviour-vocabulary in context (including tricky cases) shows genuine understanding, not recitation of the three words.

constraints: Define each state by observable behaviour ('keeps its shape' / 'forms a pool not a pile' / 'fills its container'), not abstract definitions.
Keep 'change of state' concrete and reversible (melting/freezing water) at this age; avoid heating that causes burning or cooking, which is a different (chemical) kind of change.
Handle everyday 'gas' language carefully — distinguish the science sense (a state of matter) from natural gas/petrol/fumes so the word doesn't mislead.

All materials should be picture + audio with no reading required for ages 5–7; recognition/sorting and tap-to-reveal are supportive scaffolds that can teach and check classification, but they do not by themselves elicit the child's spoken use, so the checkpoint requires the child to USE the words aloud in context.

A linear quiz (categorization, matching, picture multi-select) can assess and score the vocabulary and may be used during teaching with heavy audio support, but it checks recall rather than building the behaviour-based categories; it is a supporting scaffold, not the core activity.

A tactile real-world version (handling real ice/water, real sand, a real balloon) and a screen scene offer different experiences; where safe, real substances can strengthen behaviour-based reasoning. Use adult supervision for any boiling/steam.

The 'air can be felt' balloon demonstration shows a gas is really there and takes up space; present it as a hands-on demo, not as a formal pressure explanation, and do not define a gas as 'something that pushes'.

Present steam (water vapour) as the gas state: it is invisible and spreads out into the air, and it is the same water as the ice and liquid. Do not call the visible white cloud above a kettle a gas; at this age simply say it is tiny water drops made when the steam cools.

This is early, informal vocabulary-building: at ages 5–7 there is no KS1 statutory states content, and NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to naming the three states (nearest is PS1.A observable-property classification and 2-PS1-4 on reversible/irreversible heating/cooling). State-naming is embedded vocabulary, not a discrete standard.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: no arithmetic claims present. The 'sand pours but is solid' and 'air in a balloon is a gas' reasoning is internally consistent; the single-grain explanation and tangible-balloon demonstration are retained as the key discriminators.

The claim that air 'pushes back' / a gas 'can be felt to resist' is a pressure effect for a sealed/inflated balloon, not a general definition of a gas; it is framed only as a tangible demonstration that a gas is really there and takes up space, and the definitional language is 'spreads to fill / takes up space' in every learner-facing item.

One source (Victorian DoE Science Continuum / RSC Beyond Appearances) is marked verified:false in the row; the misconception it supports is widely attested, but its verification status is unconfirmed here and no fresh verification was performed.

Visible 'steam' is partly condensed water droplets, not pure water vapour; treating it as the gas state is an age-appropriate simplification carried over from the original and flagged as an approximation rather than re-verified.

The original row rated conversation and 3D artefacts 'poor' with comparative/necessity claims ('adds no naming power', '3D adds nothing'); these are not established by catalog ratings and have been dropped rather than propagated. Spoken use of the vocabulary is instead retained within the checkpoint as a narrow objective (recognition alone does not elicit production).
Minor concrete detail: the original's 'bubbles' example was collapsed into the balloon demonstration; it could be restored as an additional felt-but-unseen gas example.

probeDeeper: Is the air in this balloon a solid, liquid or gas — and how can you tell it's really there?
Sand pours like a drink — so is sand a liquid? Look closely at one grain.
Is toothpaste a solid or a liquid? What makes it hard to decide?
Say what happens to ice on a warm day using the words 'change of state'.
assess.correctAnswer: Rock = solid (hard, keeps its shape); milk = liquid (runny, flows, takes the shape of its container); the air = gas (spreads out, fills the balloon); sand = tiny solid grains (each grain keeps its shape, though the pile pours). 'Change of state' = when ice (solid) melts to water (liquid) on heating, or water freezes back — the same material in a different state.

errorPatterns.pattern: Air/gas is 'nothing' — won't call the air in the balloon a gas or a material; treats gas as empty space.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make gas tangible: squeeze the sealed balloon, fan the air onto a face, feel it resist — a gas fills its container and can be felt, so it is a real material.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the balloon has 'nothing' or 'just air' rather than a gas that fills it and pushes back.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Sand is a liquid because it pours' — uses flows/liquid for a pourable solid.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Zoom on a single grain: it is a hard solid that keeps its shape; the PILE pours only because the grains slide past each other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Classifies sand (or sugar, salt) as a liquid because the pile pours.

errorPatterns.pattern: Everyday clash — 'solid' taken to mean strong/big, 'gas' only petrol or smelly fumes, 'liquid' any wet thing.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor each word to BEHAVIOUR (shape and container), not to size, smell or wetness.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls a heavy object 'more solid'; reserves 'gas' for fumes; calls a damp sponge 'a liquid'.

responseLevels.gap: Uses solid/liquid/gas loosely by size or wetness; denies air is a gas; cannot use the behaviour-words.
responseLevels.full: Uses the state names and behaviour-vocabulary (keeps its shape / flows / fills its container) correctly in context including tricky cases, and uses 'change of state' accurately for melting and freezing.
responseLevels.partial: Names the three states for clear cases and uses some behaviour-words, but slips on tricky cases (sand as liquid, gas as 'nothing').

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'I'll name some things and I want you to tell me, like a scientist, whether each is a solid, a liquid or a gas — and describe HOW it behaves using proper words: a rock, milk, the air in a balloon, and sand.' Then: 'Now tell me what “change of state” means, using ice as your example.' Listen for the words used correctly, not recited.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The sand and air cases test whether the child uses the behaviour-words meaningfully rather than reciting the trio: sand pours yet is solid, and gas is invisible yet real. Listening for USE ('fills its container', 'keeps its shape') exposes loose everyday usage a definition would hide.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Interpret negative numbers in real contexts (temperature, sea level, bank balance) and count forwards and backwards through zero with positive and negative whole numbers; place negatives on a number line and begin to find simple intervals (−4°C rises 7° → 3°C). Extends 'count back through zero' into using and reasoning with negatives.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): integers and their contexts are formalised in Grade 6 (6.NS.5-7); this is the pre-formal contextual foundation.
• Operational details — Ground negatives in multiple contexts (thermometer, sea level, money) and use the number line to count and to find intervals by 'counting the gap' through zero rather than by rules. Reinforce ordering (−4 < −1) and the meaning of the gap between a negative and a positive (the interval spans zero). Keep it count/interval based; defer formal signed arithmetic.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): places negatives on a line and reads a sub-zero temperature. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): counts through zero and finds a simple rise/fall interval across zero. Tier C (age 10, extending): reasons about intervals spanning zero in context and orders mixed positive/negative sets confidently.
bestPractices: Use several contexts (temperature, sea level, money) so 'negative' is meaningful, not abstract.
Find intervals by counting the gap along the number line THROUGH zero, not by memorised sign rules.
Reinforce ordering across zero (−4 < −1 < 0 < 2) with the line.
Make the zero crossing explicit: the interval from −4 to 3 is 4 up to zero, then 3 more.
Keep to counting/intervals in context; defer formal negative arithmetic to later years.
keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line spanning negatives and positives
Vertical thermometer / sea-level scale
Number line 'gap counting' for intervals across zero
Real contexts: temperature change, floors/lifts, bank balance
Ordering strip mixing negatives and positives
commonMisconceptions: Ordering negatives by magnitude (−4 > −1).
Counting the interval across zero wrongly (forgetting the zero step or double-counting it).
Treating a negative as just its digit (ignoring sign).
Believing you 'can't go below zero'.
Applying whole-number intuitions (bigger digit = bigger) to negatives.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: interpret negative whole numbers in real contexts (temperature, sea level, bank balance), place them on a number line, order mixed positive/negative sets, count forwards and backwards through zero, and find simple intervals that cross zero by counting the gap through zero (e.g. −4°C rising 7° reaches 3°C). Keep the work count- and interval-based in context; defer formal signed arithmetic to later years. Core misconceptions to confront: ordering negatives by magnitude (believing −4 > −1) and miscounting when crossing zero.

activities.title: Count the gap through zero on a thermometer/number line
feedback: If the learner lands on 11, pause: starting at −4 is to the LEFT of (below) zero, so counting 7 steps right/up only reaches 3. Contrast with starting at +4, where 7 steps reach 11.

If the learner lands on 2, check whether they counted the starting value −4 as a jump or counted zero twice; if they land on 4, check whether they skipped zero (jumping straight from −1 to 1). Count the jumps aloud together: −4→−3→−2→−1→0 is exactly four jumps, then 0→1→2→3 is three more; reaching zero takes one jump of its own, so zero is counted once, never skipped and never repeated.
When counting backwards from 3, check that after 0 comes −1, then −2 — the count continues below zero rather than stopping at 0.
When the learner splits the count as '4 up to zero, then 3 more = 7 steps total, landing on 3', confirm they have read the interval positionally rather than by a rule.
For −4°C rising 7°, the interval is 7 degrees (4 up to zero, then 3 more) and the landing value is 3°C.
activities.rationale: Grounding negatives in multiple real contexts and finding cross-zero intervals by counting the gap on the number line (before formal signed arithmetic) makes the zero crossing concrete and directly targets the magnitude-ordering and double-counting errors; counting both forwards and backwards through zero matches the stated standard.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
Intervals across zero should be found by counting the gap on the number line through zero, in multiple contexts, before formal signed arithmetic.
learnerActions: Set a starting value in a real context, e.g. the temperature is −4°C, marked on a vertical thermometer or horizontal number line.
Apply a change, e.g. 'it rises by 7 degrees', and move a marker one step at a time, saying each value aloud: −4 → −3 → −2 → −1 → 0, then 1 → 2 → 3.
Deliberately split the count into two parts: how many steps up to reach zero (4), then how many steps beyond zero (3), and record the landing value (3°C).
Count backwards through zero as well: start at 3 and step down in ones — 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2 — saying what comes after 0, so you can move both forwards and backwards across zero.

Switch the SAME line into a different context — sea-level depth or a bank balance — keep the start and change equivalent, and notice the number behaves identically even though it means something different.
State in words where you crossed zero and why the total rise is 7 even though you land on 3.
activities.intendedInsight: An interval that spans zero is found by counting the gap along the line through zero — so many steps up to zero, then so many more beyond — not by a sign rule; you can count both forwards and backwards across zero, and negatives in different contexts behave the same positionally.

activities.title: Order and place mixed negatives and positives
feedback: If the learner places −4 as larger than (to the right of) −1, show both on the line: −4 sits further left/lower, so it is the smaller (colder) value; −7°C is colder than −3°C for the same reason.
Tie the feedback to the context: colder, lower, or more in debt all correspond to being further left on the line and therefore a smaller number.
Correct order smallest to largest: −4, −1, 0, 2, 5.
activities.rationale: Reinforcing ordering across zero with a concrete left-is-less experience confronts the seductive −4 > −1 magnitude error that the research flags as a common misconception.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
learnerActions: Arrange a mixed set such as −4, −1, 0, 2, 5 from smallest to largest on a number line.
Place a single value such as −3 at its correct spot on a labelled line.
Decide which of two values is colder/lower/more in debt, e.g. 'Which is colder, −7°C or −3°C?', and justify using position on the line.
Explain why −4 is smaller than −1 even though 4 is a bigger digit than 1, referencing left-is-less on the line.
activities.intendedInsight: On the number line, further left (colder / lower / deeper in debt) means smaller, so −4 < −1 < 0 < 2 < 5 — the size of the digit does not decide the order for negatives.

activities.title: Explain the context (optional spoken/role-play extension)
feedback: Prompt the learner to justify answers by referring to the number line or scale, not just a figure, especially when a change crosses zero.
If a change does not actually cross zero (e.g. −30 m rising to −18 m), confirm that too — not every rise or fall passes through zero.
Keep answers interval/count based; avoid introducing formal signed-arithmetic rules at this stage.
activities.rationale: A character or role-play can motivate multiple real contexts and generate interval questions; the interval reasoning itself is still best grounded on the number line, so this is offered as a contextual extension rather than the primary mechanism.
learnerActions: Take on a role such as a submarine pilot describing depths below sea level, or a weather presenter describing temperature changes.

Pose and answer questions like 'We were at −30 m and rose 12 m — where are we now?' (−18 m, still below the surface) and 'It was −3°C and rose 8° — how warm now?' (+5°C, passing up through zero), and explain the crossing of zero where it happens.
Reason aloud about which depth/temperature is higher or lower and how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Negatives describe real quantities (depth, temperature, balance); talking through changes rehearses counting through zero in meaningful situations, while noting that not every change actually crosses zero.

constraints: Use several contexts (temperature, sea level, money) so 'negative' is meaningful rather than abstract.
Find intervals by counting the gap through zero on the line, not by memorised sign rules; make the zero crossing explicit (e.g. −4 to 3 is 4 up to zero, then 3 more).
Support counting both forwards and backwards through zero, including stepping down below zero into the negatives.
Keep to counting and intervals in context; defer formal signed arithmetic to later years (US formalises integers in Grade 6; this is the pre-formal contextual foundation).

Ordering and placing tasks (ordering a set, placing on a line, fill-in-the-blank, multiple choice) can assess placement, ordering and simple cross-zero intervals, including the magnitude trap, but selection/recognition responses do not by themselves show the learner can count through zero and construct the reasoning aloud — pair them with the learner explaining their method.

A static thermometer or context poster is a useful reference and can introduce negative readings, but it cannot let the learner step through a changing value; use it as a scaffold alongside an activity where the learner actually counts the gap.
The 1D number line/scale is the natural representation for this topic; a 3D model is not needed here (this is a representation preference for this content, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing).
The role-play/spoken extension is optional and supplementary; do not treat it as a replacement for working on the number line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source assessment lists distractor 'It is 2°C' while revealedBy says 'Answer is 2 or 4 (an off-by-one at the zero crossing)'. Both off-by-one outcomes (2 and 4) are plausible miscounts; feedback here addresses landing on 2 or 4 rather than asserting a single wrong value.

The original source labelled the 3D representation 'poor' with 'negatives live on a 1D line/scale; 3D adds nothing'. The comparative/necessity 'adds nothing' assertion is not established by the cited sources, so it has been reframed as a representation preference for this topic rather than a universal law.

Arithmetic checked: −4°C rising 7° = 3°C (four steps to zero, three beyond). Sign-stripping error gives 11 (4+7). Off-by-one at zero gives 2 or 4. Counting backwards from 3 through zero gives 3,2,1,0,−1,−2. Role-play examples: −30 m +12 m = −18 m (no crossing); −3°C +8° = +5°C (crosses zero). These are internally consistent and retained for diagnostic feedback.
The CCSS Grade 6 claim and the NCETM guidance claim were marked verified:false in the source; treat their status as unverified in any downstream use.

probeDeeper: Show −4 rising by 7 on a number line — where do you cross zero?
Which is colder, −7°C or −3°C? How does the line show it?
Count backwards from 3 in ones — what comes after 0?
assess.correctAnswer: 3°C. Count up 7 from −4: four steps reach 0, then three more reach 3 — you pass through zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the sign and treats −4 as 4: −4 + 7 = 11
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put −4 on a number line to the LEFT of zero; count 7 steps right and see you only reach 3. Contrast with starting at +4.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is 11°C.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 11°C.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts across zero — stops at 0, or counts 0 twice
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the jumps aloud on the line: −4→−3→−2→−1→0 is four jumps, not five; zero is a point you pass, not a step you repeat.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is 2°C.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 2 or 4 (an off-by-one at the zero crossing).

responseLevels.gap: Strips the sign (−4 + 7 = 11) or cannot count through zero.
responseLevels.full: Interprets negatives in context and counts through zero accurately (−4 + 7 = 3), reasoning from number-line position.
responseLevels.partial: Places negatives correctly and orders them, but miscounts by one when crossing zero.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'The temperature is −4°C and it rises by 7 degrees. What is it now, and how did you work it out?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads negatives positionally counts up through zero and lands on 3; a child who strips the sign computes 4 + 7 = 11, and one who mishandles zero stalls at 0 or double-counts it. The reason tier reveals how they treat the crossing of zero.

sources.claim: Year 5 pupils should 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 5 Number & place value)

sources.claim: Integers, their ordering and real-world contexts are formalised in Grade 6 (6.NS.5-7).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, The Number System, Grade 6

sources.claim: Intervals across zero should be found by counting the gap on the number line through zero, in multiple contexts, before formal signed arithmetic.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7–9; understand how energy/nutrients flow through a rainforest food web — producers (plants) → primary consumers (herbivores) → secondary consumers (predators) — and that decomposers (fungi, insects) break down dead material and recycle nutrients back to the soil.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (construct and interpret food chains; identify producers, predators and prey) — the exploratory age-7 lead-in to that Y4 node.
• Standards — US: NGSS 5-LS2-1 (matter/energy movement among plants, animals, decomposers, environment) and 5-PS3-1 (energy from food traces back to the Sun).
• Operational details — build the chain in the correct DIRECTION with arrows meaning 'energy flows TO': Sun → kapok leaves → leaf-cutter ant → anteater → jaguar. Introduce the three roles with clear tests: producer MAKES its own food (photosynthesis), consumer EATS others, decomposer BREAKS DOWN the dead. Show the web (many interlinked chains) not just one chain, and close the loop with decomposers returning nutrients to the soil for producers. Emphasise arrow direction as the classic error.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (7): build a 3-level chain producer→herbivore→predator with arrows the right way. Tier B (8): explain the decomposer's role in returning nutrients to soil. Tier C (9): use producer/consumer/decomposer correctly and predict a knock-on effect when one species is removed from the web.
bestPractices: Insist on correct arrow direction — arrows point TO the eater, showing where energy flows — as this is the classic error.
Teach the three roles by test, not label: producer MAKES food, consumer EATS others, decomposer BREAKS DOWN the dead.
Move from a single chain to an interconnected WEB so interdependence is visible.
Close the loop: decomposers return nutrients to soil for producers — the recycling that leads into the Y5/6 nutrient-cycling topic.
Use remove-a-species reasoning to reveal knock-on effects and the fragility of the web.
keyRepresentations: A directional food chain Sun→plant→herbivore→predator with energy-flow arrows.
A multi-strand food WEB linking several chains.
Role cards/icons: producer (leaf+sun), consumer (mouth), decomposer (fungus).
A closed nutrient loop: dead matter → decomposers → soil → roots.
commonMisconceptions: 'Arrows point to who eats / to the prey' — arrows show energy flow, pointing toward the consumer.
'Decomposers are just rubbish/dead things' — they are active organisms that recycle nutrients.
'Big predators are producers because they're at the top' — confusing trophic position; only plants are producers.
'Removing one animal doesn't matter' — webs are interdependent; one loss can cascade.
'Energy is recycled like nutrients' — nutrients cycle, but energy flows one way from the Sun and is lost as heat.

learn.summary: For learners aged 7–9, build understanding of a rainforest food web: energy flows from producers (plants) to primary consumers (herbivores) to secondary consumers (predators), while decomposers (fungi, insects) break down dead material and recycle nutrients back to the soil. Core teaching goals are correct arrow direction (arrows mean 'energy flows TO the eater'), defining the three roles by test rather than label, moving from a single chain to an interconnected web, and reasoning about knock-on effects when a species is removed. A build-and-perturb activity is the lead approach, with a labelled reference web and sequence/matching tasks as complementary supports. Energy flows one way from the Sun and is lost as heat; only nutrients cycle.

activities.title: Build the web, then pull a thread
feedback: If an arrow points from the eater to its food, prompt: 'The arrow means energy flows TO — which way does the food (energy) go?' and let the learner flip it toward the eater.
If the learner builds a chain with no decomposers, prompt them to add fungi/insects that break down the dead material and return nutrients to the soil, closing the loop.
If the learner treats a plant as an eater or gives it a food source, remind them plants are producers that make their own food from sunlight and start the chain.

After removing the ants, draw attention to the fading anteater (in this model the ants are its only food) and then the thinning jaguar (it has lost the anteater it preys on here), so the cascade along the chain is seen rather than just stated. Mention that real anteaters and jaguars have other food too.
activities.rationale: A build-and-perturb system lets the learner construct chains, test arrow direction, and watch a cascade when a species is removed; it is intended to make the 'arrows = energy flow' rule and web interdependence experienced rather than only memorised. Live recomputation when a species is removed targets the common belief that removing one animal doesn't matter. This supports KS2 Y4 construction/interpretation of food chains and NGSS 5-LS2-1 energy/matter movement. Efficacy relative to other media is not established here.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey
Energy flows from producers to consumers and decomposers recycle nutrients from dead material back into the soil; arrows in a food chain denote the direction of energy/matter flow
learnerActions: Assemble a rainforest food web by placing the energy source and organisms: sunlight (the Sun), kapok leaves, a leaf-cutter ant, an anteater, a jaguar, and fungi on the forest floor.
Draw energy-flow arrows between them in the correct direction, starting Sun → kapok leaves → leaf-cutter ant → anteater → jaguar.
When you draw an arrow the wrong way (e.g. from the anteater TO the ant), respond to the prompt 'which way does the FOOD (energy) go?' and flip it to point toward the eater.
Connect the dead jaguar and fallen leaf litter to the fungi, and the fungi back to the soil and roots, closing the nutrient loop.

Remove the leaf-cutter ants from the web and observe what happens in this simplified model to the anteater (which eats the ants) and then the jaguar (which eats the anteater), so the cascade along the chain is visible. In a real rainforest, these animals also eat other food, so the effect would usually be smaller.
Explain in your own words why pulling out one species affects the others.
activities.intendedInsight: Producers, consumers and decomposers are not just a list of labels — they are connected to each other. Energy flows one way from the Sun toward each eater and is not recycled, while nutrients cycle back through decomposers to the soil for plants to reuse. Removing one species can affect others that depend on it, and the effect can pass along a chain.

activities.title: Label the web: roles and who eats whom
feedback: If a learner calls a top predator a 'producer' because it is at the top, apply the test: does it make its own food? In this web only the plants do, so the jaguar is a consumer.
If the learner thinks decomposers are 'just rubbish or dead things', clarify they are active organisms that recycle nutrients back into the soil.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference diagram supports vocabulary and layout and works alongside the construction activity. On its own it lets a learner read and identify roles but does not elicit testing of arrow direction or observing a cascade, so it is best used as a companion reference rather than a replacement for building.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey
learnerActions: Explore a labelled rainforest web diagram where tapping an organism reveals its role (producer, consumer or decomposer) and what eats it.
Use each role's TEST to justify the label: producer MAKES its own food by photosynthesis, consumer EATS others, decomposer BREAKS DOWN the dead.
Trace at least one full chain through the web and read the layout of the many interlinked chains.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary (producer, consumer, decomposer) and web layout become a clear reference, defined by what each organism DOES rather than just a name or its position in the diagram.

activities.title: Order the chain and sort the roles
feedback: If a chain is ordered with a predator before its prey, ask what each organism eats and rebuild from the producer outward.
If an arrow is reversed, re-state that arrows point to the eater because they show where energy flows.

A sorting-and-ordering task can check classification and sequence, but it does not itself show interdependence — follow with the build-and-perturb activity to see how the sorted organisms connect and depend on each other.
activities.rationale: Sequence and matching tasks map directly onto the evidence statements and give a clean check of ordering and vocabulary. Such a task assesses recognition and ordering but does not display the interdependence cascade, so it complements rather than replaces construction.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey
learnerActions: Order a scrambled set of organisms into a correct chain (producer → herbivore → predator), placing an arrow at each link pointing toward the eater.
Sort a mixed set of rainforest organisms into producers, consumers and decomposers.
State for each sorted organism the test that justifies its group (makes food / eats others / breaks down the dead).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to order a chain with correct arrows and categorise organisms by role confirms the vocabulary and sequencing are secure.

constraints: Insist on correct arrow direction: arrows point TO the eater, showing where energy flows. This is the classic learner error and should be checked explicitly.
Teach the three roles by test, not label: producer MAKES food, consumer EATS others, decomposer BREAKS DOWN the dead.
Move from a single chain to an interconnected web so interdependence is visible, and close the loop with decomposers returning nutrients to the soil for producers.

Keep the consumer and decomposer roles distinct in the removal cascade: in this simplified model, removing a consumer (the leaf-cutter ant) can propagate along the chain (anteater, then jaguar). In a real rainforest the effect is usually smaller, because anteaters eat many kinds of ants and termites and jaguars hunt many prey. In this web the fungi, not the leaf-cutter ants, are the decomposers that recycle dead leaf litter.

Distinguish nutrient cycling (nutrients return to the soil and are reused) from energy flow (energy flows one way from the Sun and is lost as heat; it is not recycled). Avoid implying energy is recycled.

A tap-to-reveal reference diagram and sequence/matching tasks support vocabulary and ordering; by themselves they do not elicit testing of arrow direction or experiencing a cascade, so use them alongside construction, not instead of it.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 7) build a 3-level chain producer→herbivore→predator with arrows the right way; Tier B (age 8) explain the decomposer's role in returning nutrients to soil; Tier C (age 9) use producer/consumer/decomposer correctly and predict a knock-on effect when one species is removed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both cited sources carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two listed sources were not re-fetched; citations support the teaching principles (chain construction, energy/matter flow direction, decomposer recycling) but do not establish that these specific activities were tested or that any one medium is superior.

The original 3D and conversation 'poor fit' judgements (e.g. '3D adds nothing', concept 'better done than discussed') were catalog-preference rankings and are not carried as universal claims; a relational web fits a 2D build, but necessity of any one medium is not established.
Efficacy phrasing ('FELT rather than memorised') was softened to intended-effect wording, since comparative efficacy is not established by the sources.

The original recommendation described leaf litter 'piling up unrecycled' when the leaf-cutter ants were removed. Because leaf-cutter ants are consumers rather than the litter's recyclers, this is ecologically misleading and has been removed from the learner-facing cascade; decomposer fungi remain the litter recyclers in the closed-loop step. The learner-facing cascade is now the clean ant → anteater → jaguar chain.

probeDeeper: What do we call a plant's role in a food chain — producer, consumer or decomposer?
What would happen to the forest if all the decomposers disappeared?
Build me a rainforest chain with at least three links, using an arrow each time.
If the caterpillars all vanished, what happens to the birds that eat them, and to the leaves? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: The arrow points FROM the leaf TO the caterpillar. The arrow shows which way the energy (food) flows — from the thing being eaten to the eater — so it always points towards the animal doing the eating: leaf → caterpillar → bird, and so on. Decomposers like fungi and insects then break down dead things and return the nutrients to the soil for plants to use again.

errorPatterns.pattern: the arrow points to the food/prey — 'it points at what gets eaten'
errorPatterns.nextMove: the arrow means 'energy flows to'; it points to the EATER, from food to feeder
errorPatterns.distractor: From the caterpillar to the leaf, because the arrow points at its food
errorPatterns.revealedBy: draws the arrow from the caterpillar to the leaf

errorPatterns.pattern: decomposers are ignored / not part of the web — 'fungi aren't in the food chain'
errorPatterns.nextMove: add decomposers returning nutrients to the soil, closing the loop
errorPatterns.revealedBy: builds a chain with no decomposers or role for dead material

errorPatterns.pattern: plants get their food by eating, like animals — doesn't see plants as producers
errorPatterns.nextMove: plants are producers; they make their own food from sunlight and start the chain
errorPatterns.revealedBy: places a plant as a consumer or gives it a food source

responseLevels.gap: Points the arrow at the food; treats plants as eaters; no decomposers.
responseLevels.full: Draws arrows from food to eater to show energy flow, builds a 3+ level chain using producer/consumer/decomposer correctly, and explains decomposers recycling nutrients to the soil.
responseLevels.partial: Builds a chain and mostly points arrows correctly but can't explain they show energy flow, or omits decomposers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a food chain we draw an arrow between a leaf and a caterpillar that eats it. Which way should the arrow point — from the leaf to the caterpillar, or from the caterpillar to the leaf? Draw it, and then tell me WHY it points that way.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the arrow points to the food ('the caterpillar wants the leaf') reverses it; the concept child knows the arrow tracks energy flow toward the eater. The reason-tier forces the energy-flow meaning.

sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England — Science programme of study, Y4 'Living things and their habitats'

sources.claim: Energy flows from producers to consumers and decomposers recycle nutrients from dead material back into the soil; arrows in a food chain denote the direction of energy/matter flow
