pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 9–11 (META) — scientists study the ocean with submarines, remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), satellites and diving; much of the deep ocean remains unexplored, and it is hard to explore because of darkness, crushing pressure and sheer vastness.
• Standards — UK (DfE): 'working scientifically' — how scientists use tools and evidence; the nature and limits of scientific knowledge.
• Standards — US (NGSS/NOS): Nature of Science — science uses instruments to extend the senses; scientific knowledge is open to revision as tools and evidence improve.
• Operational details: this is a META topic about HOW WE KNOW and the FRONTIER of knowledge. Cover: (1) the toolkit — crewed submersibles, ROVs, satellites, sonar mapping, diving — and what each is for; (2) why the deep is so hard (no light, extreme pressure, huge area, no radio through water); (3) how MUCH is unknown — with an important accuracy nuance: the seafloor is ~fully mapped at coarse satellite resolution but only ~29% at high resolution, and humans have directly SEEN <0.001% of the deep seafloor. Crucially, the popular line 'we know more about the Moon than the ocean' is an OUTDATED, contested claim — a superb chance to teach map-vs-see-vs-understand and critical source evaluation rather than repeat a myth.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~9): names ≥2 exploration tools and says most of the deep ocean is unexplored; Tier B (~10): explains why exploring is hard (dark/pressure/vast); Tier C (~11): distinguishes mapping from directly seeing, and critically evaluates the 'more than the Moon' claim rather than accepting it.
bestPractices: Teach the toolkit by matching each instrument to the problem it solves (ROV = eyes without risking people; sonar = mapping shape without light; satellite = broad surface/coarse seafloor; submersible = humans on site).

Make the difficulty concrete: below ~1000 m there is no sunlight, pressure is hundreds of times the surface, radio/light don't travel through water, and the area is planet-sized — so exploration is slow and costly.
Teach the map–see–understand distinction explicitly: ~100% coarsely mapped, ~29% high-resolution mapped, <0.001% directly seen — different senses of 'explored'.

Treat 'we know more about the Moon than the ocean' as a CLAIM TO EXAMINE, not a fact: it dates to the 1950s, predates Moon landings, and experts say it conflates map/see/understand — a model lesson in evaluating sources.
Frame the unknown as exciting and revisable: knowledge grows as tools improve (high-res mapping rises every year), reinforcing that science is provisional.
keyRepresentations: A tool–job matching board (ROV / submersible / sonar / satellite / diver → what each does)
A 'three kinds of explored' bar: coarsely mapped ~100% | high-res mapped ~29% | directly seen <0.001%
A 'why it's hard' panel (darkness, pressure, vastness, no radio through water)
A claim-evaluation card examining 'more than the Moon' (origin, map vs see vs understand)
commonMisconceptions: 'We've explored most of the ocean' — vs directly seeing far less than 1% of the deep seafloor.
Uncritically accepting 'we know more about the Moon than the ocean' as a current fact — it is outdated and conflates mapping, seeing and understanding.
'Mapped = explored/seen' — conflating a coarse satellite map with direct visual observation.
'Satellites can photograph the deep seafloor' — not knowing light/radio don't penetrate deep water, so sonar/ROVs are needed.
Thinking scientific knowledge is fixed — rather than growing and being revised as tools and evidence improve.

learn.summary: Ages 9–11 META topic on HOW we explore the ocean and the LIMITS of what we know. Learners (1) match exploration tools (crewed submersible, ROV, sonar, satellite, diver) to the problem each solves; (2) explain why the deep is hard — darkness below ~1000 m, pressure hundreds of times the surface, planet-sized vastness, and radio/light not travelling through deep water; and (3) distinguish three senses of 'explored' — coarsely mapped (~100%), high-resolution mapped (~29%), and directly SEEN (<0.001%) — then critically evaluate the slogan 'we know more about the Moon than the ocean' rather than accepting or dismissing it. The peak activity is an in-role dialogue with an ocean explorer who both answers and probes the child's thinking; concrete ROV-sim and tool-matching activities build the factual grounding.

activities.title: Interview an ocean explorer (in-role dialogue)
feedback: If the learner repeats the Moon line as plain fact, open it up: what exactly is being compared — high-resolution maps? direct observation? total understanding? Ask how they would check it rather than marking it right or wrong.

If the learner assumes 'closer = easier to study', discuss the real barriers: darkness, crushing pressure, vastness, and light and radio not travelling far through water (sound does, which is why sonar works) — and how ROVs, sonar and satellites get around them.

If the learner thinks the ocean is basically finished being explored, share that only a small fraction of the seafloor is mapped at high resolution and new species are found regularly; frame exploration as ongoing.
activities.rationale: A META 'how do we know' goal with a contested claim suits open, unscripted dialogue, which affords adaptive back-and-forth — Socratic follow-ups tuned to the child's own answers — that a fixed artefact cannot provide and that may better support examining what 'explored' and 'know' mean. This is a design proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: The popular claim that 'we know more about the Moon than the deep ocean' is outdated (dating to the 1950s, before Moon landings) and misleading — it conflates mapping and imaging with understanding; experts argue we understand a great deal about the deep sea, though much remains to be discovered.

Humans have directly seen less than 0.001% of the deep ocean seafloor (an area about the size of Rhode Island), even though the entire seafloor is mapped at coarse satellite resolution and only ~29% at high resolution — so most of the deep ocean remains unexplored.
learnerActions: Interview someone in the role of a deep-sea explorer fresh from a submersible dive: ask what it looks like out the porthole a kilometre down, what happens as pressure rises, and how much of the deep sea has actually been seen.
Respond when the explorer turns a question back: 'People love saying we know more about the Moon than the ocean — is that even true? What do you mean by "know"?'
State, in your own words, the difference between mapping the shape of the seafloor, SEEING it with your own eyes, and UNDERSTANDING it.
Say what evidence you would check (e.g. how much seafloor is mapped at high resolution) before repeating the Moon claim.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Explored' has several meanings — coarsely mapped, high-resolution mapped, and directly observed are different; we have directly seen a tiny fraction of the deep seafloor; and the catchy 'more than the Moon' line is an old, contested claim to interrogate, not a fact to store.

activities.title: Pilot an ROV descent and tally what you've seen
feedback: If the learner expects to light up a wide area, point to the narrow headlamp cone and sonar strip — light does not travel far through deep water, so coverage is slow.
If the learner is surprised how little the running tally shows, connect it to the <0.001% directly-seen figure: the ocean floor is enormous relative to what any mission can observe.
activities.rationale: A running coverage bar and live pressure/headlamp cues can make the vastness and hazards felt firsthand rather than merely stated; these interaction examples are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required. The sim grounds the facts but, being closed, does not host the open critical evaluation of the knowledge-claim.
sourceClaims: Scientists explore the ocean with crewed submersibles, ROVs, satellites, sonar mapping and diving; the deep ocean is difficult to explore because of darkness, extreme pressure, its vast size, and because light/radio do not travel through deep water.

Humans have directly seen less than 0.001% of the deep ocean seafloor (an area about the size of Rhode Island), even though the entire seafloor is mapped at coarse satellite resolution and only ~29% at high resolution — so most of the deep ocean remains unexplored.
learnerActions: Descend a simulated ROV/submersible: manage a limited headlamp cone in the darkness, watch a pressure gauge climb as you go deeper, and use sonar to map a narrow strip of seafloor.
Watch a running bar that shows how little of the vast floor you have covered after a full dive.
Describe afterwards why this makes exploration slow and costly, naming darkness, pressure, and vastness as reasons.
activities.intendedInsight: The difficulty of deep-sea exploration becomes concrete: no sunlight, rising pressure, and a planet-sized area mean each dive reveals only a tiny strip, so direct observation of the deep seafloor stays vanishingly small.

activities.title: Match the tool to the job
feedback: If the learner says satellites photograph the deep seafloor, explain that light and radio do not travel through deep water, so sonar and ROVs are needed for the deep.
If the learner treats a coarse satellite map as the same as 'seen', contrast ~100% coarsely mapped with <0.001% directly observed.
activities.rationale: Matching instruments to the barriers they overcome builds the toolkit and the map–see–understand distinction cheaply; a tappable panel with a 'what it does' reveal and a claim-evaluation flap on the Moon comparison can make this concrete. Presentation is clear but static, so pair it with dialogue for the critical-evaluation goal.
sourceClaims: Scientists explore the ocean with crewed submersibles, ROVs, satellites, sonar mapping and diving; the deep ocean is difficult to explore because of darkness, extreme pressure, its vast size, and because light/radio do not travel through deep water.

Humans have directly seen less than 0.001% of the deep ocean seafloor (an area about the size of Rhode Island), even though the entire seafloor is mapped at coarse satellite resolution and only ~29% at high resolution — so most of the deep ocean remains unexplored.
learnerActions: Match each tool to the problem it solves: ROV = eyes on site without risking people; sonar = mapping shape with sound instead of light; satellite = broad surface view and coarse seafloor mapping worked out indirectly from tiny bumps in sea-surface height; crewed submersible = humans on site; diver = shallow, hands-on work.
Explain why a satellite cannot photograph the deep seafloor and what is used instead.
Place three labels on a 'three kinds of explored' bar: coarsely mapped ~100%, high-resolution mapped ~29%, directly seen <0.001%.
activities.intendedInsight: Each instrument extends a different sense and addresses a specific barrier; 'mapped' (especially coarsely) is not the same as 'directly seen', and satellites cannot image the deep because light/radio do not penetrate deep water — their coarse seafloor maps are worked out indirectly from the shape of the sea surface.

activities.title: Check your facts and examine the Moon claim
feedback: For the Moon item, do not treat flat acceptance OR flat rejection as the goal: credit reasoning that asks what 'know more' measures and names evidence to check.
If a difficulty item is missed, revisit which barrier each tool addresses from the matching activity.
activities.rationale: Recognition items faithfully check factual recall of tools and difficulties as a companion. Selected-response items confirm recall but do not, on their own, elicit the independent critical reasoning the dialogue targets.
sourceClaims: The popular claim that 'we know more about the Moon than the deep ocean' is outdated (dating to the 1950s, before Moon landings) and misleading — it conflates mapping and imaging with understanding; experts argue we understand a great deal about the deep sea, though much remains to be discovered.
learnerActions: Match each tool to its job.
Answer multiple-choice items on why deep-sea exploration is hard (darkness, pressure, vastness, light and radio signals not travelling far through water).
Answer an item that distinguishes 'mapped' from 'directly seen'.

Without giving a true/false verdict, say what 'we know more about the Moon than the ocean' would need to compare (high-resolution maps, direct observation or understanding), and why it should be examined rather than simply accepted or rejected.
activities.intendedInsight: Factual checks (tools, difficulties, mapped-vs-seen) can confirm the evidence goals, while the Moon item is used to prompt critical examination rather than a simple right/wrong store.

constraints: Treat 'we know more about the Moon than the ocean' as a CLAIM TO EXAMINE, not a fact to state and not a myth to flatly dismiss: it dates to the 1950s (before Moon landings) and conflates mapping, seeing and understanding.

Keep the saved research snapshot’s estimates distinct: roughly100% of the seafloor coarsely mapped, roughly29% mapped at high resolution, and less than0.001% of the deep seafloor directly seen. These have different coverage definitions and are time-sensitive estimates; attach their source dates and check updated figures before presenting them as current.
Recognition/quiz items confirm recall of tools and difficulties but do not elicit the independent, critical reasoning about the knowledge-claim; use the dialogue for that.
The ROV sim conveys difficulty vividly but is closed and cannot host open critical evaluation; pair it with discussion.
Keep the Moon-claim discussion unmarked: the aim is to interrogate it, not to award a right/wrong score for accepting or rejecting it.

A 3D descent is atmospheric but optional — the META learning (tools, limits of knowledge, evaluating a claim) does not depend on 3D space; interaction examples (headlamp cone, pressure gauge, coverage bar, claim flap) are illustrative, not mandatory.

Treat the difficulty/toolkit claim as provisional.

probeDeeper: When someone says we 'know more' about the Moon, what exactly do you think is being counted — and could that be measured a different way?
The Moon is 380,000 km away and the deep sea floor is a few km down. Why might the near one still be harder to explore?
If you read this claim in a book from 20 years ago, would you trust it's still true today? What might have changed?
Scientists can't just look at the deep sea — name a tool they use instead, and what problem it gets around.
assess.correctAnswer: There is no single right answer to score — listen for the QUALITY of the reasoning. Strong responses (a) unpack what the claim actually means (it's about how much of each has been MAPPED/imaged at high resolution and directly observed, not literally 'everything about the Moon'); (b) explain why closeness doesn't equal ease — the deep ocean is dark, crushingly high-pressure, vast and hard to send signals through, so we explore it with submarines, ROVs, satellites and sonar rather than just looking; (c) treat the slogan critically — ask what 'know more' is being measured, notice it's a memorable comparison that can be out of date, and say they'd check a reliable source (how much seafloor is mapped at high resolution) before repeating it. The point is not to accept OR dismiss the slogan, but to interrogate it.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'We know everything about the Moon and nothing about the sea' — takes the catchy slogan literally.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Open it up: what exactly has been compared — high-resolution MAPS? Discuss that the slogan is a memorable shorthand about observation coverage, not literal total knowledge, and can date quickly. Don't award a right/wrong mark; push them to say how they'd check it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Repeats the line as a plain fact; doesn't ask what 'know more' is measuring or notice it's about mapping/imaging.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'If it's closer, it must be easier to study' — assumes proximity equals accessibility.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss the real barriers — darkness, pressure, vastness, signals not travelling well through water — and how we get round them with ROVs, sonar and satellites. Keep it a discussion of how scientists know, not a graded answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puzzled that the nearby ocean is less mapped than the Moon; treats distance as the only barrier to knowledge.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Scientists have basically finished exploring the ocean' — assumes the map is complete.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Share that only a small fraction of the seafloor is mapped at high resolution and new species are found regularly; frame exploration as ongoing and open-ended.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes most of the ocean is already known; surprised that most of the deep sea is unexplored.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts or rejects the slogan flatly; treats distance as the only factor; asks nothing about what 'know more' means.
responseLevels.full: Unpacks what the claim measures (mapping/observation coverage, not literal knowledge), explains why proximity ≠ accessibility with real barriers and the tools that address them, treats the slogan as a datable comparison, and names evidence they'd check before repeating it.
responseLevels.partial: Gives a sensible reason the deep sea is hard (dark, pressure) OR notes the slogan is a simplification, but doesn't both interrogate the claim AND say how to check it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: People often say 'we know more about the surface of the Moon than about the deep ocean floor', even though the ocean is right here on our own planet. What do you think that claim really means — and how could that even be true when the ocean is so much closer to us than the Moon? What would you want to check before you believed it, or repeated it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This is surfaced for discussion, not marked right/wrong. Weak reasoning takes the slogan at face value ('the Moon's just easier to see') or rejects it flatly; strong reasoning asks what is being measured, distinguishes 'mapped/observed' from 'known', and names what evidence would settle it. It probes whether a child can evaluate a scientific claim rather than simply store it.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** What happens when things collide

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** no general KS2 'energy' topic (energy enters at KS3), so no direct UK primary statutory match; nearest UK home is KS2 'Working scientifically' (asking questions, making and testing predictions) and forces work on collisions/changes in motion.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NATIONAL (NGSS): 4-PS3-3 (verbatim) '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3]'; clarification '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3]'; DCI PS3.B '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; assessment boundary excludes quantitative measurements of energy. NGSS-anchored. Sits directly on 'Speed and energy' (faster = more kinetic energy).

- **Operational details:** Children ask questions and predict outcomes about the energy changes when objects collide: energy transfers from one object to another (one speeds up, the other slows), and some energy also goes to the surroundings as sound and a little warming. Strictly qualitative and observational — no momentum, no calculations; the emphasis (per NGSS) is on the energy change [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3].

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 9-10).
bestPractices: Lead with predict-then-observe: before each collision the child predicts what will happen to BOTH objects ('which speeds up? which slows? will there be a sound?'), then runs it and compares — the gap is where the energy-transfer idea forms.

Use clean, watchable collisions — a rolling marble hitting a stationary one (Newton's-cradle / boules style), a fast ball hitting a slow one — so the transfer (giver slows, receiver speeds up) is directly visible.

Make the surroundings audible/visible: name the BANG and any warming as energy that left the moving objects — 'the click you hear is some of the energy leaving as sound' — which seeds conservation without the formal law.
Keep attention on energy/speed change, not force (the NGSS clarification is explicit): describe what happens to each object's motion and where the energy went, not how hard they pushed.
Vary the incoming speed and connect back to 'speed and energy': a faster striker transfers more (knocks the target further, louder click), reinforcing more-speed-more-energy.
keyRepresentations: Two-ball collision: a moving ball striking a stationary one (giver slows/stops, receiver moves off) — the canonical transfer picture.
Before/after speed arrows on each object (long arrow = fast, short = slow) showing motion handed from one to the other.
A 'where did the energy go?' tally: into the other object (motion) + a bit to the surroundings (sound + slight warming).
Everyday anchors: snooker/pool break, bumper cars, a kicked ball striking another, skittles/bowling.
commonMisconceptions: 'The energy just disappears when things stop after a crash' — the central energy-is-lost error; it transferred to the other object and to the surroundings (sound, warming), it didn't vanish.
Thinking only ONE object changes — children watch the target and ignore that the striker slowed down too.
Treating the sound of the collision as separate/irrelevant rather than as energy carried away from the moving objects.
Reasoning about which object 'wins' or 'pushes harder' (forces) instead of how the energy/speed changes — the NGSS clarification steers away from force talk here.
'The bigger/heavier object always keeps moving and the small one always stops' — outcome depends on speeds and masses together; predict-then-test surfaces the surprises.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: children ask questions and predict outcomes about the energy changes when objects collide. When objects collide, energy can transfer from one to another (often one speeds up while the other slows, though in a head-on crash both may slow or stop). Some energy also leaves the moving objects to the surroundings as sound and a little warming (and into squashing when objects deform), so it is redistributed, never destroyed. Keep everything qualitative and observational (NGSS 4-PS3-3): no momentum, no calculations, and emphasis on the energy change [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3] forces. The core predict-then-observe cycle and 'where did the energy go?' bookkeeping can run as a live screen simulation, with real marbles/physical collisions, or as reference/assessment companions; each is described below with its affordances and limits.

activities.title: Collision lab: predict, run, and track where the energy goes
feedback: If a learner says the energy 'disappeared', point to the target that moved off and the 'surroundings' bar: whether the striker slowed, stopped, or bounced back, 'the click you hear is some of the energy leaving as sound' — it moved, it didn't vanish.
If a learner watches only the target and ignores the striker, replay and ask them to describe what happened to the striker's speed too.
When a faster striker knocks the target further with a louder click, name it: more incoming speed carried more energy to transfer.
activities.rationale: A live predict-then-test interaction where the learner sets the speed, commits a prediction, then sees per-object motion arrows and energy bars update makes the transfer visible and answers 'where did the energy go?' directly. Optional interaction cues — speed sliders, size/mass toggle, before/after motion arrows (long = fast, short = slow), motion bars handing energy across, and a small surroundings bar gaining the sound+warming share — make the energy-bookkeeping mechanism concrete and let surprises (e.g. a lighter striker rebounding) emerge from the child's own prediction. Keep it bars-and-arrows, never numbers, to stay inside the qualitative Tier-A boundary.
sourceClaims: 4-PS3-3 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3]'); clarification emphasises energy change due to speed change, NOT forces; DCI PS3.B '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; boundary excludes quantitative energy.
Children commonly believe energy 'disappears' when colliding objects stop, and attend to only one object; the sound/warming of a collision is energy carried to the surroundings.
learnerActions: Choose incoming speed in a simulation, or release the same marble from different heights on a fixed ramp and observe its speed before a stationary target. Keep objects,surface and collision alignment unchanged for the speed comparison; explore a mass toggle separately.
COMMIT a prediction before running: say what each object will do ('the red one will stop, the blue one will shoot off') AND predict whether there will be a sound.

Observe both objects. In a nearly elastic,head-on equal-mass model with one target initially still, the striker nearly stops as the target moves off; with different masses or materials it may continue or rebound. Record the actual outcome rather than requiring every real collision to match one ideal case.
Watch the energy bookkeeping: the striker's motion-bar shrinks as the target's grows, and a small 'surroundings' bar lights up for the sound and slight warming, so the total is visibly accounted for.

Vary incoming speed while keeping the same objects,alignment and surface. A faster incoming object carries more kinetic energy; observe how much reaches target motion,sound,deformation or warming, rather than guaranteeing a particular loudness or travel distance.
activities.intendedInsight: When things collide, energy doesn't disappear when the striker slows: it moves into the other object and some escapes to the surroundings as sound and a little warming. More incoming speed means more energy transferred.

activities.title: Watch real clean collisions and name where the energy went
feedback: Track the changed motion and listen for sound or look for deformation. Warming may be too small to detect by touch,so do not require a child to feel it; use the labelled model to discuss possible internal-energy changes.
If a learner thinks the still marble 'can't gain energy', have them predict and watch the struck marble shoot off: energy was transferred to it, which is why it moves.
Name the BANG explicitly as energy that left the moving objects, seeding conservation without the formal law.
activities.rationale: Clean, watchable physical collisions make the transfer (giver slows, receiver speeds up) directly visible and let learners use their own ears for the sound share. The head-on case is a strong challenge to the 'energy disappears' idea, clearest with squashy balls that visibly stop and squash (any thud is sound energy, and warming may be too small to feel); with hard marbles that rebound, motion remains and the click still evidences some energy leaving. Physical objects give a tactile, audible experience; this complements the screen model rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Children commonly believe energy 'disappears' when colliding objects stop, and attend to only one object; the sound/warming of a collision is energy carried to the surroundings.

4-PS3-3 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3]'); clarification emphasises energy change due to speed change, NOT forces; DCI PS3.B '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; boundary excludes quantitative energy.
learnerActions: Roll one marble into a stationary one (Newton's-cradle / boules style) and watch the giver slow or stop while the receiver moves off.

Use two identical balls of equal mass approaching head-on at equal speeds. Predict their motion before testing: hard,nearly elastic balls tend to rebound,while soft sticky clay balls may join and stop near the collision point. The materials and conditions matter; do not generalise this outcome to unequal masses.
Close your eyes during the head-on crash and listen: what do you HEAR? Discuss what that sound tells you about where the energy went.

Make a 'where did the energy go?' tally for each collision: any motion that remains or is passed to the other object + some to the surroundings (sound you hear, plus possible slight warming that may be too small to feel) + any squashing (deformation). For sticky clay balls that stop, most of the motion energy goes into squashing and warming rather than motion.
Try everyday anchors — snooker/pool break, bumper cars, a kicked ball striking another, skittles/bowling — and describe the transfer each time.
activities.intendedInsight: When objects rebound,some energy remains as motion; when soft objects stop and deform,more of the initial motion energy becomes internal energy or deformation. Sound may carry some energy to the surroundings. Account for all these destinations rather than treating lost motion as destroyed energy.

activities.title: Predict outcomes and trace the energy (check/assess companion)
feedback: If a learner says energy disappeared,compare the motion before and after,list any sound or deformation,and discuss possible internal-energy changes. Rebounding objects retain motion energy; any warming may be too small to feel. Include the surroundings when accounting for the total.
If a learner predicts the outcome from size alone, remind them the outcome depends on BOTH speed and mass — a fast small object can carry more energy than a slow big one; vary both.
If a learner says the still marble can't gain energy, point back to the struck object shooting off as evidence of transfer.
activities.rationale: Prediction and matching formats map naturally onto the standard's 'predict outcomes' verb and surface whether a learner tracks energy to all destinations. These formats are used to check and consolidate; on their own they assess recognition and prediction rather than eliciting the hands-on predict-then-run cycle, so pair them with Activity 1 or 2.
sourceClaims: 4-PS3-3 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3]'); clarification emphasises energy change due to speed change, NOT forces; DCI PS3.B '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; boundary excludes quantitative energy.
learnerActions: Predict post-collision motion: for a given collision, choose what happens to ball B (and to the striker).
Match 'energy went to →' with the destinations: the other object (motion) / sound / warming / squashing (deformation).
Order a set of collisions using the same objects by how much energy the striker brings in (e.g. by incoming speed).
Answer the counterexample: two identical marbles, one still; the moving one stops and the still one goes off at the same speed — did energy disappear, and where did it go?
Answer: after any collision, is the total energy more, less, or the same as before, and where would you look for the 'missing' bit?
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can predict outcomes and name all the destinations of the energy, including the surroundings and deformation share, confirming they track energy rather than treat it as lost — the TOTAL energy, including the surroundings, is the same before and after; motion energy is shared between the objects and partly changed into sound, warming or squashing.

activities.title: Before/after reference scene (optional companion)
feedback: Use the flaps to confirm answers after a learner has predicted, rather than revealing them first.
activities.rationale: A static before/after scene with tappable flaps is a fair reference and vocabulary aid. Because it is fixed it cannot deliver the prediction-then-result cycle that builds the idea, so treat it as a companion to the interactive or physical collisions, not a substitute.
learnerActions: Open a before/after collision illustration with tappable 'what happened to each object' and 'where did the energy go' flaps.
Use it to review the canonical two-ball transfer picture and the surroundings share after doing the live or physical activity.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear before/after picture consolidates the vocabulary of transfer and the destinations of the energy as a reference.

constraints: Keep it strictly qualitative and observational: no momentum, no calculations, bars-and-arrows rather than numbers (NGSS assessment boundary excludes quantitative energy).
Keep attention on the energy/speed change and where the energy went, NOT on force or which object 'pushed harder' — the NGSS clarification is explicit on this.
Always attend to BOTH objects: children tend to watch the target and miss that the striker slowed too.
Outcome depends on speed and mass together; avoid 'the bigger/heavier object always keeps moving' — vary both and use predict-then-test to surface surprises.

For an ideal elastic,head-on collision into a stationary target,an equal-mass striker stops,a lighter striker rebounds,and a heavier striker continues. Real materials,rotation,friction and alignment change outcomes; label the model and accept actual observations rather than enforcing its exact prediction.

For the head-on 'both stop' demonstration use squashy/inelastic balls (modelling clay); hard, elastic marbles rebound rather than stop. In either case the click and any warmth/squashing show energy transferred, not destroyed — do not present 'equal marbles stop dead' as the only correct head-on outcome.
Recognition/matching formats check prediction and vocabulary but do not elicit the independent predict-run-observe construction; pair them with hands-on or live collisions.
The static before/after scene is a reference scaffold: it cannot run the prediction-then-result cycle and should follow, not replace, active collisions.

Label the screen simulation as a simplified model. Real marbles or clay allow observing motion,sound and sometimes deformation; slight warming may not be detectable by touch. Model bars represent energy accounting,not a direct measurement or proof that every predicted channel was observed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists the IOP Spark children's-ideas claim as verified:false; the related 'energy disappears / only one object' misconception guidance should be treated as plausible but unverified.

Original error corrected: the original assessment stated two identical marbles colliding head-on at equal speeds 'both stop dead'. For elastic marbles the realistic outcome is to rebound; stopping dead requires inelastic (squashy) objects. Learner-facing text was corrected to hold for either outcome and to use squashy balls where 'stop and squash' is intended, preserving the robust point that sound/warmth/squashing show energy was transferred, not destroyed.

Added correction: the original 'striker stops' picture holds only for equal masses; a lighter striker rebounds off a heavier stationary target. Activity 1 text widened to slow/stop/bounce-back so the mass toggle does not produce a stated outcome that is false.

Comparative efficacy of the live simulation versus physical marbles or the reference scene is not established by the sources; descriptions of fit were softened to affordances/limits, not claims of necessity.

The original row framed force talk as to be avoided per the NGSS clarification; this is a standards-scoping choice for this grade band, retained as a constraint rather than a universal claim that forces are irrelevant to collisions.

assess.poeTask: Set up the head-on case: ask the child to predict what happens when two marbles of equal speed collide head-on — will they bounce back, stop, or pass through — and WHERE the energy goes, before rolling them. The 'energy disappears' child expects it simply gone when they stop; a tracking child predicts the energy leaves as the audible click and slight warmth. Then collide them and listen.
probeDeeper: In the head-on crash, close your eyes — what do you HEAR? What does that sound tell you about where the energy went?
Predict: a fast marble hits a slow, heavy ball. What happens to each, and why?
Counterexample: two identical marbles, one still. The moving one stops and the still one goes off at the same speed. Did energy disappear? Where did it go?
After any collision, is the total energy more, less, or the same as before? Where would you look for the 'missing' bit?
assess.correctAnswer: In the first, the moving marble transfers its kinetic energy to the still one, which speeds off. In the head-on crash both stop, but the energy isn't gone — it's transferred to sound (the click), a little heat, and momentarily squashing the marbles; it moved out of motion into other forms. Energy is transferred, never destroyed, in both.

errorPatterns.pattern: When both objects stop, the energy has just disappeared ('they cancelled out and the energy's gone').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Listen for the sound and feel for warmth; the energy left the kinetic store into sound and thermal — stopping isn't destroying.
errorPatterns.distractor: Both marbles stop, so their energy cancelled out and disappeared.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't name where the energy went when the motion stops.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only the moving object has energy; the still one has none to do anything with ('the still marble is just in the way').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Energy is TRANSFERRED to the struck object — that's why it moves; predict and watch the struck marble shoot off.
errorPatterns.distractor: The still marble can't gain any energy, so it shouldn't move at all.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Doesn't expect the struck object to gain energy and move off.

errorPatterns.pattern: The heavier or bigger object always wins the collision, whatever the speeds ('big always beats small').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Outcome depends on BOTH speed and mass — a fast small object can carry more energy than a slow big one; vary both.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the outcome from size alone, ignoring speed.

responseLevels.gap: Says energy disappears when objects stop; thinks only the moving object has energy, or that size alone decides.
responseLevels.full: Tracks kinetic energy transferring between objects and, when motion stops, into sound/heat/deformation (never destroyed), and predicts outcomes using both speed and mass.
responseLevels.partial: Knows energy transfers between colliding objects and predicts simple cases, but says energy is lost when both stop, or ignores sound and heat.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A moving marble hits a still marble and stops; the still one shoots off. Then two marbles crash head-on and BOTH stop dead. In the second case it looks like the energy just vanished. Where did the energy go in each collision?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'both stopped, so the energy disappeared' differs from one who tracks the energy into sound/heat/deformation. The reason tier separates 'energy vanished' from 'energy transferred to sound and heat'.

pedagogy.summary: Orbital mechanics for ages 12-13 should be taught conceptually, not algebraically. The central, counter-intuitive idea is that an orbit is CONTINUOUS FREEFALL: a satellite is always falling toward the planet, but it moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it just as quickly, so it keeps missing. Newton's cannonball thought experiment is the canonical bridge — fire a cannonball faster and faster from a mountaintop until it falls all the way around. From there, build two more ideas: a GRAVITY ASSIST (a spacecraft steals a tiny bit of a planet's orbital motion in a close flyby to gain speed for free), and the conceptual heart of the ROCKET EQUATION — because a rocket must carry the fuel it hasn't burned yet, the fuel needed grows explosively (exponentially) as you demand more speed change, which is why getting to space is so hard. Keep it about momentum-versus-gravity balance and 'falling sideways', reserving the maths for later.
bestPractices: Lead with the paradox 'astronauts are not weightless because there's no gravity — they are in constant freefall', to confront the dominant misconception head-on
Use Newton's cannonball as the spine: increase launch speed step by step so the child sees crash → suborbital arc → circular orbit → ellipse → escape emerge from one variable
Frame orbit as a tug-of-war between sideways momentum and gravity's inward pull: too slow and you spiral in, too fast and you fly away, just right and you circle
Teach gravity assist as borrowing motion from a moving planet — a slingshot that costs the planet an imperceptible amount and gives the craft a lot
Convey the rocket equation qualitatively with a 'fuel to carry fuel' spiral: each extra bit of speed needs disproportionately more propellant because you must lift the unburned fuel too
Separate the two forces cleanly — thrust changes the orbit, gravity shapes it — so children don't think engines must fire continuously to stay up
keyRepresentations: Newton's cannonball diagram: a mountaintop cannon with a family of paths from crash to full orbit to escape
'Falling but missing' picture: the straight-line path the object would take without gravity vs the curved orbit, with the ground curving away
Momentum-vs-gravity vector picture: forward velocity arrow plus inward gravity arrow producing a curved path
Gravity-assist trajectory: a spacecraft's bent path speeding up as it swings past a moving planet
Rocket 'fuel-carrying-fuel' staging bar showing propellant mass ballooning as target speed rises
commonMisconceptions: 'There's no gravity in space, that's why astronauts float' — gravity in low orbit is nearly as strong as on the ground; they float because they and their ship are falling together
'Rockets need to keep their engines on to stay in orbit' — once at orbital speed, no thrust is needed; the craft coasts in freefall indefinitely
'Orbits are perfect circles' — most are ellipses; a circle is just the special case of exactly the right speed
'Going up is the hard part of reaching orbit' — the real challenge is going sideways fast enough; altitude alone gives you a suborbital hop that falls back down
'A gravity assist gets energy from nothing' — the craft borrows orbital momentum from the planet, which loses an unmeasurably tiny amount in exchange
'More speed just needs proportionally more fuel' — because you must carry the fuel you haven't burned, required fuel rises exponentially with desired speed change

learn.summary: Conceptual (non-algebraic) orbital mechanics for ages 12-13. The core, counter-intuitive idea: an orbit is CONTINUOUS FREEFALL — a satellite is always falling toward the planet, but it moves sideways so fast that the curved ground falls away beneath it just as fast, so it keeps missing. Newton's cannonball thought experiment is the canonical bridge (fire faster from a mountaintop: crash → suborbital arc → circular orbit → ellipse → escape, all from one speed variable). Build two further ideas: a gravity assist (a spacecraft borrows a tiny amount of a planet's orbital momentum in a close flyby to gain speed), and the qualitative heart of the rocket equation (because a rocket must carry fuel it hasn't burned yet, propellant needed rises steeply/exponentially as demanded speed change increases). Frame throughout as momentum-versus-gravity and 'falling sideways', reserving maths for later.

activities.title: Newton's cannonball: one speed dial from crash to escape
feedback: If the ball crashes, you are going too slow — its path curves down into the ground faster than the ground curves away; increase the speed.

At the circular-orbit setting, point out that the straight-line overlay shows the ball steadily dropping below where it 'should' be — that drop IS the falling, and the sideways motion is why it never arrives.

If the ball escapes, it had too much sideways speed (at or above escape speed) for gravity to bend its path into a closed loop — gravity still acts and keeps slowing it, but can't curve the path back around.
Connect back to astronauts: a person inside this orbiting ball would float, not because gravity is gone, but because they are falling together with it.
activities.rationale: The relationship is dynamic and single-variable; letting a learner vary one speed and watch the trajectory morph makes 'falling sideways' something observed rather than asserted. The straight-line overlay makes Newton's first law and the continuous bending by gravity concrete.
sourceClaims: An orbiting object is always falling toward the planet but moving sideways fast enough that it never hits — a balance (tug-of-war) between momentum and gravity; too much momentum and it escapes, too little and it crashes
Without gravity an orbiting object would fly off in a straight line (Newton's first law); gravity continuously bends that straight-line path into the orbit
Newton's cannonball thought experiment (fire faster and faster from a mountaintop until the projectile orbits) is the canonical conceptual bridge for orbit-as-freefall
learnerActions: Stand a cannon on a mountaintop above a round planet and set a single SPEED value, then fire and watch where the projectile goes.
At low speed, observe the cannonball arc down and crash into the ground; raise the speed and watch the arc get longer but still fall back.

Keep raising the speed until you find the setting where the ball curves downward exactly as fast as the planet's surface curves away, so it sweeps all the way around into a circular orbit (and would come back and hit the cannon from behind).
Push past that setting to see the circle stretch into an ellipse, then push higher still to watch the ball escape and not return.

Compare the orbit against a faint 'no-gravity straight line' overlay showing the path the ball would take with gravity switched off, and note how far it 'falls away' from that straight line each second.
State in your own words why the orbiting ball is still falling even though it never hits the ground.
activities.intendedInsight: Orbiting is just falling and continuously missing the ground: one launch speed, varied smoothly, produces crash, circular orbit, ellipse and escape; gravity bends the would-be straight-line path into the orbit.

activities.title: The momentum-vs-gravity tug-of-war
feedback: If a learner invokes an outward (centrifugal) force balancing gravity, redirect: gravity is the only force here; it bends the straight-line sideways motion into a curve, and that curve is the orbit.

Too slow: gravity curves the path down into the ground, so it falls back and crashes. Faster than circular speed but below escape speed: the path still closes, but stretches into an ellipse. At or above escape speed: gravity can't curve it enough to close the loop. Just right for a circle: the curve exactly follows the planet's surface shape.
Note that gravity sets how the path accelerates (curves), not the direction the ball is currently travelling — the ball keeps moving sideways while gravity pulls it inward.
activities.rationale: Naming and drawing the two influences confronts the common 'balanced outward force' misconception directly and reinforces that only gravity acts on the ball in flight in this idealised model.
sourceClaims: An orbiting object is always falling toward the planet but moving sideways fast enough that it never hits — a balance (tug-of-war) between momentum and gravity; too much momentum and it escapes, too little and it crashes
Without gravity an orbiting object would fly off in a straight line (Newton's first law); gravity continuously bends that straight-line path into the orbit
learnerActions: For a chosen launch, sketch or identify two arrows at the projectile: a forward (sideways) velocity arrow and an inward arrow pointing at the planet's centre for gravity.
Predict, before firing, whether a given speed will crash, circle, stretch into an ellipse or escape, and justify using the two arrows.

Explain why 'too slow' falls back and crashes, why a bit faster than circular speed stretches the orbit into an ellipse, why 'much too fast' (at or above escape speed) flies away, and what 'just right' for a circle means.
State explicitly that gravity is the only force acting on the ball in flight (in this idealised model) — there is no outward force holding it out.
activities.intendedInsight: An orbit results from sideways momentum plus a single inward gravitational pull that continually curves the path; there is no real outward force balancing gravity.

activities.title: Gravity assist: borrowing a planet's motion
feedback: If a learner says the assist 'creates' energy, clarify: it is a transfer — the planet's orbital motion is the source, and its loss is unmeasurably small because it is enormously more massive.
Note that the net speed gain depends on the planet moving; a flyby of a stationary body returns the craft at the same speed it arrived (in that body's frame) and gives no net boost.
activities.rationale: Seeing the speed readout change during a timed flyby makes the momentum transfer tangible; the navigator dialogue adds mission-level reasoning about why routes are chosen.
learnerActions: Time a close flyby of a spacecraft past a MOVING planet and watch a speed readout before and after the encounter.
Experiment with the timing/geometry of the flyby to make the craft gain speed, and describe what happened to its path.
Explain where the extra speed comes from — the craft borrows a tiny share of the planet's orbital momentum, while the planet loses an unmeasurably tiny amount.
Optionally, discuss with a mission navigator planning a probe to Jupiter why it might slingshot past Venus and Earth first instead of flying straight there.
activities.intendedInsight: A gravity assist is not free energy from nothing: a spacecraft exchanges momentum with a moving planet during a close flyby, gaining useful speed while the planet's change is imperceptible.

activities.title: Fuel to carry fuel: why rockets are mostly propellant
feedback: If a learner expects 'more speed just needs proportionally more fuel', have them compare two Δv settings and read off how disproportionately the fuel grows.
Reinforce the loop: more fuel adds more mass, which needs yet more fuel to move — this compounding is why the growth is so steep.
activities.rationale: Letting the learner drive the Δv and watch propellant balloon conveys the exponential intuition without algebra, directly targeting the proportional-fuel misconception.
sourceClaims: The rocket equation implies propellant needed rises exponentially with desired velocity change because a rocket must carry unburned fuel — taught here qualitatively
learnerActions: Set a target speed change (Δv) and watch the required propellant amount build up.

Increase the target Δv in steps and observe that the propellant needed grows faster than in proportion — doubling the demand always takes more than double the fuel, and far more than double once the Δv is large.
Explain in your own words why this happens: the rocket must lift and accelerate the fuel it hasn't burned yet, so extra fuel also needs its own fuel to be carried.
Describe why this means getting to orbit is hard and why large rockets are mostly fuel by mass.
activities.intendedInsight: Because a rocket carries its unburned fuel, the propellant needed rises steeply (exponentially) with the demanded speed change — the qualitative heart of the rocket equation.

activities.title: Consolidate and predict
feedback: For 'astronauts float': the correct reason is that they and the ship are falling together in continuous freefall, not that gravity is gone (gravity in low orbit is still about 90% of surface strength).

For engines: once at orbital speed in the idealised vacuum model nothing slows the sideways motion, so no thrust is needed to stay in orbit — thrust changes an orbit, it does not hold the craft up. (Real very low orbits have slight atmospheric drag, so craft such as the ISS need occasional reboosts.)
activities.rationale: Prediction and explanation tasks check the ideas after the interactive exploration; this is consolidation, not first exposure, since it tests rather than generates the insight.
sourceClaims: An orbiting object is always falling toward the planet but moving sideways fast enough that it never hits — a balance (tug-of-war) between momentum and gravity; too much momentum and it escapes, too little and it crashes
learnerActions: Order a set of launch outcomes (crash, suborbital arc, circular orbit, ellipse, escape) from slowest to fastest launch speed.
Set the speed that produces a circular orbit and justify the choice.
Answer 'why do astronauts float?' and explain why it is freefall, not absent gravity.
Explain why a spacecraft already at orbital speed does not need its engines running to stay up.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can apply the falling-sideways model to new cases: predicting outcomes by speed, and explaining floating and engine-off coasting.

constraints: Keep the treatment conceptual, not algebraic: momentum-versus-gravity and 'falling sideways', reserving the Tsiolkovsky maths for later.
Lead with the paradox that astronauts float because they are in constant freefall, not because gravity is absent; low-orbit gravity is still strong (around 90% of surface value).
Separate the two forces cleanly: thrust changes an orbit; gravity shapes it. Avoid implying engines must fire continuously to stay in orbit.
Avoid introducing a real outward (centrifugal) force: gravity is the only force bending the straight-line sideways motion into the orbit in this model.
An ordering/prediction task checks understanding but does not generate the 'aha' of seeing an orbit emerge; use it to consolidate after exploration, not as first exposure.

A static annotated cannonball diagram can name the paths and label the freefall idea, but a fixed picture cannot show speed continuously morphing the trajectory; treat it as a reference scaffold, not a substitute for the dynamic exploration.

A 3D view better conveys inclination and the out-of-plane geometry of transfers and slingshots; the clean 2D plane is clearer for the straight-line-versus-curve comparison, so 3D is proposed as an extension after the 2D intuition is built. Neither is universally required.

A navigator/engineer dialogue can motivate route choices and mission reasoning; seeing the counter-intuitive geometry in motion may help learners grasp it, so dialogue is proposed alongside the moving model rather than as a replacement for it.
Where a slingshot or orbit model uses an idealised, frictionless vacuum, state that it is a model; real missions involve additional factors such as atmospheric drag during launch.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched this session. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two source claims are marked unverified in the original row: the Newton's-cannonball framing (classic Newtonian mechanics, not confirmed against a fetched page) and the exponential rocket-equation claim (Tsiolkovsky, not confirmed against a fetched page). They are standard physics-education content but were not independently verified here.

The '90% of surface gravity' figure and '~8 km/s' orbital speed come from the row's assessment fields and are consistent with standard low-Earth-orbit values; they were not re-verified against a source this session.

The original phrased orbit as a 'balance'/'tug-of-war' between momentum and gravity; this is a useful intuition but can be misread as implying a real outward force. Activities explicitly correct this by stating gravity is the only force acting on the ball in flight (idealised model), consistent with the row's own centrifugal-force error pattern. Source claim[0] is retained as an exact copy and keeps the looser 'balance' wording.

The original's 'too slow and you spiral in' phrasing is imprecise for a frictionless two-body model: an under-speed launch follows an ellipse that crosses the surface and crashes rather than spiralling inward (which would require drag/orbital decay). Corrected to 'falls back and crashes' in the activity and feedback.

Self-audit of logic: a resultant (gravity) force sets acceleration/curvature, not the current direction of travel — the cannonball keeps moving sideways while gravity pulls it inward; the straight-line overlay and an explicit feedback note make this clear rather than implying gravity 'drags' the ball straight down. No arithmetic claims were asserted in learner-facing tasks.
One medium-efficacy constraint was softened from an unqualified necessity claim to proposed/may wording, since relative medium effectiveness is untested here.

probeDeeper: Roughly how strong is gravity at the Space Station's height compared with the ground — near zero, or almost as strong?
If gravity is still pulling the Station down, why doesn't it hit the Earth?
What would happen to the Station if you could magically switch gravity off?
Why doesn't a spacecraft in orbit need to keep burning fuel to stay up?
assess.correctAnswer: There is still strong gravity at the Station's height — about 90% as strong as at Earth's surface — so it hasn't escaped gravity at all. The Station IS falling toward Earth constantly; it just moves sideways so fast (about 8 km per second) that as it falls, the curved Earth keeps curving away beneath it and it keeps 'missing' the ground. That continuous falling-while-missing IS an orbit (Newton's cannonball). The astronauts float because they are in the same continuous freefall as the Station, falling together — not because gravity is gone. No engine thrust is needed to stay in orbit, because nothing slows the sideways motion in the vacuum.

errorPatterns.pattern: the Station floats because there's no gravity that high up, or it has escaped Earth's gravity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Gravity is about 90% as strong at that height; the Station is falling, not gravity-free — reconnect to gravity acting across space to hold the Moon and planets.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Station stays up and astronauts float because there is no gravity at that height.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child attributes orbit and floating to absent or escaped gravity

errorPatterns.pattern: you have to keep the engines firing constantly to stay in orbit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Once at orbital speed the Station coasts in freefall — no thrust needed, since nothing in the vacuum slows its sideways motion.
errorPatterns.distractor: A spacecraft has to keep its engines running the whole time to stay in orbit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child thinks continuous thrust holds the spacecraft up

errorPatterns.pattern: orbit is where Earth's gravity and some outward force exactly balance
errorPatterns.nextMove: There is no outward force — gravity is the ONLY force, continually bending the straight-line sideways motion into a curve; that curve IS the orbit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child invokes a real outward (centrifugal) force balancing gravity

responseLevels.gap: Says there's no gravity in orbit, that it's escaped or balanced, or that engines hold it up.
responseLevels.full: Explains orbit as continuous freefall — strong gravity plus fast sideways motion so it keeps missing Earth — that astronauts float because they fall with the Station, and that no thrust is needed once at orbital speed.
responseLevels.partial: Knows gravity is still present and the Station is 'falling', but can't articulate the sideways-motion 'keeps missing Earth' mechanism, or still invokes a balancing force.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Astronauts on the Space Station float around, and the Station keeps circling Earth without its engines running. Is that because there's no gravity that high up, or because the Station has escaped Earth's gravity? If neither, what is actually keeping it up — and why doesn't it just fall down? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'no gravity in space' idea persists even among older students. A child who holds it says the Station floats because gravity is gone or has been escaped or balanced. A child who understands orbital motion says gravity is still strong and the Station is in continuous freefall, moving sideways fast enough to keep missing Earth. The 'why' tier forces the falling-sideways model.

pedagogy.summary: Dividing a whole number by a unit fraction is the MEASUREMENT (quotitive) meaning of division: 4 ÷ 1/5 asks 'how many one-fifths fit inside 4 wholes?' — each whole holds 5, so 4 hold 20. The whole pedagogical battle is that the answer is BIGGER than the number you started with, which collides head-on with the whole-number intuition that 'dividing makes smaller'. Teach it by physically fitting unit-fraction pieces along a number line or ribbon, reason with estimation ('5 ÷ 5/6 is a bit more than 5 because 5/6 is nearly 1'), and cement it with the inverse check 20 × 1/5 = 4 — never as a rote rule.
bestPractices: Lead with the 'how many fit' question on a length model — lay 1/5 ribbons or number-line jumps across 4 wholes and count them to 20 — so the quotient is something the child physically counts, not computes
Confront 'division makes smaller' head-on: predict the count first, then fit the pieces and see it exceed the dividend; discuss WHY (small divisor → many copies)
Use estimation to police reasonableness (IES: 5 ÷ 5/6 ≈ just over 5) so an answer of 0.8 for 4 ÷ 1/5 is caught as absurd
Always tie back to the inverse: 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20 because 20 × 1/5 = 4 — the multiplication just learned justifies the division
Have children invent a story context ('how many 1/4-cup scoops in 6 cups?') so the measurement structure is owned, not memorised
keyRepresentations: Number line partitioned into fifths with jumps counted across 0–4
Ribbon/tape model: unit-fraction lengths laid end-to-end inside the whole (IES Fig 8 style)
Array of unit-fraction pieces filling the dividend
The inverse equation 20 × 1/5 = 4 written beside the count
commonMisconceptions: Quotient must be smaller than the dividend, so 4 ÷ 1/5 'can't' be 20 (whole-number over-generalisation that division shrinks)
Divides by the denominator instead: 4 ÷ 1/5 read as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 (treats the unit fraction as its denominator)
Confuses with multiplication: computes 4 × 1/5 = 4/5 (imports the more-familiar operation)
Treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers rather than 1/5 as one quantity

learn.summary: Dividing a whole number by a unit fraction is the measurement (quotitive) meaning of division: 4 ÷ 1/5 asks 'how many one-fifths fit inside 4 wholes?' Each whole holds 5 fifths, so 4 wholes hold 20. The central challenge is that the quotient is BIGGER than the dividend, which collides with the whole-number intuition that 'dividing makes smaller'. Teach it by physically fitting unit-fraction pieces along a length model, using prediction then counting, estimation to police reasonableness, and the inverse check 20 × 1/5 = 4 — never as a rote rule.

activities.title: How many fit? Predict then count on a length bar
feedback: If a learner predicts 'fewer than 4 because dividing shrinks', treat it as the teachable moment: lay the tiles and count to 20 together, then name the principle — a small divisor means many copies fit.
If a learner reads 4 ÷ 1/5 as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8, rebuild what 1/5 IS (one part of a whole split five ways) and re-ask 'how many of THOSE fit in 4?'
If a learner computes 4 × 1/5 = 4/5, separate the two questions explicitly: '4 × 1/5 means four fifths; 4 ÷ 1/5 means how many fifths in four', and model both on the same bar.
activities.rationale: The measurement/quotitive meaning is made concrete by fitting unit-fraction pieces into the dividend and counting them, with a length/ribbon or number-line model. Prediction-first surfaces the 'division shrinks' misconception so it can be confronted directly.
sourceClaims: Division of a whole/number by a fraction is the measurement/quotitive question 'how many of the divisor fit in the dividend' (e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = how many 1/4s in 1/2), modelled with ribbons or a number line; dividing by a fraction can yield a quotient LARGER than the dividend, a key gap for students and teachers; estimation (5 ÷ 5/6 is a little more than 5) polices reasonableness

The misconception that operations shrink/grow numbers predictably (e.g. that multiplying/dividing must make numbers larger/smaller) and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers interfere with computational understanding and must be confronted directly
learnerActions: Take a 4-unit strip/bar and a stack of 1/5 tiles (ribbon lengths or number-line jumps work equally well).
BEFORE placing any tile, write down a prediction of how many 1/5 tiles will fit, and a one-sentence reason.
Lay the 1/5 tiles end-to-end across the bar, counting as you go: 5 fill the first whole, 10 the second, and so on until you reach 20.
Compare the count (20) with your prediction, and discuss why the answer is bigger than 4.
Repeat with a different piece size (e.g. 1/2 gives 8, 1/10 gives 40) and describe how the size of the piece drives the count.
activities.intendedInsight: When the piece is small, many copies fit, so dividing a positive whole number by a fraction between 0 and 1 produces a count larger than the dividend. The quotient is something you can physically count, not a trick.

activities.title: Estimate first to catch absurd answers
feedback: If a learner cannot say whether the answer grows or shrinks, return to the 'how many fit' question with a concrete piece.
Praise reasoning that ties the estimate to the piece size relative to 1 whole (e.g. 'the piece is nearly a whole, so a bit more than 5').
activities.rationale: IES recommends estimation to police the reasonableness of fraction computations, which directly guards against the counterintuitive-result errors.
sourceClaims: Division of a whole/number by a fraction is the measurement/quotitive question 'how many of the divisor fit in the dividend' (e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = how many 1/4s in 1/2), modelled with ribbons or a number line; dividing by a fraction can yield a quotient LARGER than the dividend, a key gap for students and teachers; estimation (5 ÷ 5/6 is a little more than 5) polices reasonableness
learnerActions: Before computing, estimate whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the dividend, and roughly how big.
Work an example like 5 ÷ 5/6: reason that because 5/6 is nearly 1 whole, the answer is a little more than 5.
Check a worked answer for reasonableness: decide whether 0.8 could possibly be the answer to 4 ÷ 1/5, and explain why not.
State a rule of thumb: dividing by a piece smaller than 1 gives more copies than the number of wholes.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimation acts as a reasonableness check: an answer of 0.8 for 4 ÷ 1/5 is immediately caught as absurd because many small fifths must fit in 4 wholes.

activities.title: Prove it with the inverse multiplication
feedback: If a learner cannot form the inverse, prompt: 'If 20 fifths make up 4, what multiplication says that?'
If the inverse product does not rebuild the dividend, revisit the count rather than accepting the quotient.
activities.rationale: Using the multiplication–division relationship to explain and verify the quotient is a core standard-aligned goal and avoids rote rule use.
sourceClaims: Interpret and compute quotients of whole numbers by unit fractions (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20) using visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division; explain why the quotient is larger
learnerActions: After counting 20 fifths in 4 wholes, write the matching multiplication: 20 × 1/5 = 4.
Explain in words how the multiplication just learned justifies the division answer.
Gather or redraw the 20 fifths into 4 wholes to show the multiplication rebuilding the original dividend.
Apply the same check to a fresh case, e.g. verify 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24 by showing 24 × 1/4 = 6.
activities.intendedInsight: Division by a unit fraction and the related multiplication are inverse statements about the same quantity, so the multiplication check confirms the division.

activities.title: Invent and solve a measurement story
feedback: If a learner's story does not match a 'how many small pieces fit in a whole amount' structure, help reshape it before solving.
Draw out the prediction step: a learner who expects fewer scoops has surfaced the shrink misconception, which the count then resolves.
activities.rationale: Creating and solving a story context cements the quotitive 'how many fit' measurement meaning; a measuring/cooking persona can pose the prediction challenge, though the counting itself benefits from a visual or physical surface.
sourceClaims: Division of a whole/number by a fraction is the measurement/quotitive question 'how many of the divisor fit in the dividend' (e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = how many 1/4s in 1/2), modelled with ribbons or a number line; dividing by a fraction can yield a quotient LARGER than the dividend, a key gap for students and teachers; estimation (5 ÷ 5/6 is a little more than 5) polices reasonableness
learnerActions: Invent a real context for a whole ÷ unit-fraction, e.g. 'how many 1/4-cup scoops are in 6 cups?' or 'how many 1/3-cup scoops in this jug?'
Before counting, predict out loud whether there will be more or fewer scoops than the number of whole cups, and say why.
Solve the story by counting the pieces and state the answer with its meaning.
Match several division expressions (e.g. 6 ÷ 1/4, 4 ÷ 1/5) to the correct 'how many … in …' story.
activities.intendedInsight: Owning the measurement structure through a self-made context makes the 'how many fit' meaning transferable rather than memorised.

activities.title: Check your understanding (prediction, count, and reasoning)
feedback: If a learner picks an answer smaller than the dividend, return to fitting pieces and the piece-size-drives-count principle.
If a learner picks a denominator-division distractor (e.g. treating 6 ÷ 1/4 as 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5), rebuild what the unit fraction is.
If the number is right but the reason is missing or rote, treat it as partial and probe the 'why bigger than the dividend' explanation.
activities.rationale: Recognition and ordering items can test the counterintuitive 'bigger answer' and the divisor-vs-denominator error; requiring the reason guards against rote recall passing as understanding. Selecting answers checks the misconception but does not by itself elicit the independent construction and explanation developed in the earlier activities.
sourceClaims: The misconception that operations shrink/grow numbers predictably (e.g. that multiplying/dividing must make numbers larger/smaller) and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers interfere with computational understanding and must be confronted directly
learnerActions: Answer 'how many 1/5 fit in 4?' using a number-line count or slider, giving 20.

Answer a multiple-choice item for 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24, ruling out derivable distractors such as 1.5 (from the denominator-division error 6 ÷ 4) and a value smaller than the dividend (from the 'division shrinks' misconception).
Order several whole ÷ unit-fraction quotients by size to expose the 'answer must be smaller' misconception.
For any answer, add a sentence saying WHY it is bigger than the dividend; a correct number without a correct reason is incomplete.
activities.intendedInsight: A genuine grasp of the measurement meaning produces both the right quotient AND a 'how many fit' justification; recalling a number alone is not sufficient.

constraints: Lead with the 'how many fit' measurement question on a length model; the quotient should be something the child physically counts, not a rule they apply.
Confront 'division makes smaller' directly: predict first, then fit pieces and see the count exceed the dividend, then discuss why (small divisor → many copies).
Always tie back to the inverse check (20 × 1/5 = 4); do not teach an invert-and-multiply rule without this meaning.

A static number-line image showing 4 wholes cut into fifths with 20 countable segments supports the meaning well, but does not let the learner vary the divisor to test the pattern; use it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.

Recognition/multiple-choice items can check the misconception but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and explanation; pair them with activities that require counting and justifying.

Optional interactive supports (e.g. dragging 1/5 tiles into a bar with a running counter, a divisor dial that swaps 1/4, 1/3, 1/10 and shows the count change, an inverse panel animating 20 fifths fusing into 4 wholes, a contrast switch to the partition case 1/3 ÷ 4) make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful examples, not required.
Keep the model one-dimensional ('how many lengths fit'); adding 3D depth risks implying volume and is not needed for this concept, though this is a design judgement, not a proven limitation.
Distinguish 4 ÷ 1/5 (how many fifths in four) from both 4 ÷ 5 (dividing by the denominator) and 4 × 1/5 (four fifths); model the contrasts explicitly.
