pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, strategic tool use begins as CHOOSING among familiar concrete tools (cubes, counters, fingers, ten frame) and being able to say WHY that tool helps this problem. The point is not fluent tool use but the dawning judgement that a tool is FIT for a purpose: a ten frame organises and shows the gap to ten; fingers are quick for small numbers but run out; cubes can be joined and split. Teach the choice explicitly — offer a genuine choice rather than prescribing one — and press for the reason, because the reason is where the practice lives.
bestPractices: Offer a real choice of tools rather than handing one over, then ask 'why did you pick that?' so the rationale becomes visible and assessable (EEF: clear rationale for the tool)
Use the ten frame to make 'how many to ten' structural, not just a mat to put counters on — the aim is to reveal structure, not merely reach an answer
Name each tool's limitation in play — 'fingers run out past ten', 'a ten frame only holds ten' — so children begin weighing fit rather than habit
Keep tools as thinking aids and model solving a small, known fact WITHOUT a tool afterwards, so reliance does not set in (EEF: manipulatives are a temporary scaffold)
Value the explanation as much as the answer — a child who solved it but cannot say why the tool helped has not yet met this practice
keyRepresentations: Ten frame (rows of five/ten expose the gap to ten)
Cubes / multilink (joinable and splittable)
Counters
Fingers
Five frame
commonMisconceptions: Reaches for the same familiar tool (usually fingers) every time regardless of whether it fits — e.g. fingers for 8+7
Uses the tool to get an answer but cannot say why it helped — treats it as a ritual, not a thinking aid (EEF)
Becomes reliant on the tool and cannot attempt even a small, known fact without it (EEF)
Thinks the ten frame is just somewhere to put counters, missing that its rows of five and ten show structure

learn.summary: For 5-6 year-olds, strategic tool use begins as CHOOSING among familiar concrete tools (cubes, counters, fingers, ten frame, five frame) and being able to say WHY that tool fits THIS problem. The learning lives in the reason, not fluent handling. Offer a genuine choice rather than prescribing a tool, let a tool's limitation be felt in action (using fingers to show both parts of 8+7 runs past ten), and press for a fit-reason tied to the numbers. Keep tools as temporary scaffolds and model solving a small known fact without a tool so reliance does not set in.

activities.title: The tool tray: 8 + 7 and 3 + 2
feedback: If fingers are chosen for 8+7 and used to show both parts, let the count pass ten so the limitation is felt rather than told, then ask what else the tray offers.

After solving, ask why this tool and strategy helped. Accept a reason tied to the numbers or representation, including a valid counting-on explanation with fingers. If the child tried to show all15 objects simultaneously, discuss that specific ten-finger limitation and compare it with the ten frame.
If the ten frame is filled correctly but the reason is only 'because you're meant to', ask what the frame SHOWS: 'how many empty spaces to ten?'
For 3+2, confirm fingers fit well here, so the choice genuinely depends on the numbers.
activities.rationale: Strategic tool choice is a doing-then-justifying act; letting a limitation bite in action and then prompting for the reason makes the fit-judgement visible and assessable, and the ten frame is used to expose structure (the gap to ten) rather than just reach an answer. 8+7 is chosen deliberately because it crosses ten, so trying to show every object at once on fingers really does run out (although counting on with fingers can still work), while 3+2 contrasts so children see the choice depends on the numbers.
sourceClaims: Proficient students consider available tools and make sound decisions about when each tool might be helpful, recognising both the insight to be gained and the tool's limitations

Manipulatives are just tools; they need a clear rationale, should reveal mathematical structure rather than just get pupils to an answer, and should act as a temporary scaffold removed as understanding grows — avoid pupils becoming reliant on them
learnerActions: Face the problem 8 + 7 with a tray offering cubes, counters, a ten frame, and fingers; pick a tool and use it to solve.
If you choose fingers and try to show 8 and then 7 more, notice you pass ten and run out of fingers before you reach the answer.

Try the ten frame instead: place 8 (nearly filling one frame), then split the 7 — 2 completes the first ten, and the remaining 5 go beside the full frame (or into a second frame), giving 'fill to ten, then five more — fifteen.'
Say why your chosen tool helped: e.g. 'it shows the gap to ten' or 'the fingers ran out'.
Now solve 3 + 2 and decide which tool fits — discover that fingers work perfectly here, so the best choice depends on the numbers, not on a favourite.
activities.intendedInsight: Choose a tool and strategy because they help with the particular problem. Showing all15 objects at once on one finger each exceeds ten fingers, but counting-on with fingers can still solve8+7. A ten frame offers another useful structure: the gap to ten. Accept a valid strategy when the learner explains how it helps.

activities.title: The puzzled friend who always uses fingers
feedback: If the child names the same tool for every problem and can't say why it suits this one, pose paired problems where one tool fits one and fails the other.
Press for a reason tied to the numbers ('they cross ten') rather than 'I just like cubes'.
If the child can recall 8+7 without a tool, treat that as healthy scaffold removal — do not insist they return to a tool.
Value the explanation as much as the answer; a child who solved it but can't say why the tool helped has not yet met this practice.
activities.rationale: A responsive dialogue pulls the fit-reason into spoken words and lets a contrasting problem test whether the reasoning is about fit or habit; a recognition item does not by itself elicit that spoken justification. The 'without a tool' probe checks that the scaffold can be removed as understanding grows.
sourceClaims: Proficient students consider available tools and make sound decisions about when each tool might be helpful, recognising both the insight to be gained and the tool's limitations

Manipulatives are just tools; they need a clear rationale, should reveal mathematical structure rather than just get pupils to an answer, and should act as a temporary scaffold removed as understanding grows — avoid pupils becoming reliant on them
learnerActions: Talk with an in-role friend or puppet who says 'I always use my fingers — would that work here?' for 8 + 7.

Justify or correct the friend: explain why fingers run out when you try to show every object for a total over ten, and which tool or strategy fits better (e.g. a ten frame, or counting on from 8 with fingers).
Respond when the friend poses a contrasting small problem (like 3 + 2) to test whether your reason is about fit or just habit.
Answer probing questions: 'What does the ten frame show you that a loose pile of counters doesn't?' and 'If you had 12 + 5, what would you reach for instead?'

Answer 'Can you do 8 + 7 now without any tool — what happened in your head?'; if you know it or can work it out mentally, that shows the tool can be set aside once the fact is secure, and if not, it is fine to still use a tool.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the fit-reason into words — distinguishing choosing a tool because it suits the numbers from grabbing a favourite out of habit — is the heart of the practice at this age, and a tool can be set aside once a fact is secure.

activities.title: Meet the tools (warm-up)
feedback: Confirm each tool's purpose and limit as the child names them.
Note that naming limits here is only a warm-up — the real learning is choosing and using a tool on a problem, so follow this with the tool tray.
activities.rationale: An introductory tap-to-reveal can name what each tool does and its limit, but it primes rather than teaches the choice because the child does not yet pick or feel a limitation in action; use it before the hands-on bench.
learnerActions: Explore a shelf of tools — cubes, counters, ten frame, five frame, fingers — and reveal for each what it is 'good for' and when it 'runs out'.

Name a purpose and a limit for each approach: fingers can show up to ten objects at once, and can also track counting-on steps; a single ten frame holds ten counters and shows the gap to ten; cubes can be joined and split.
Then move on to choosing and using a tool on a real problem.
activities.intendedInsight: Each tool has an affordance and a limit; knowing these in advance primes children to weigh fit when they later choose for a real problem.

constraints: The goal at this age is the dawning judgement that a tool is FIT for a purpose, not fluent tool use — value the fit-reason as much as the answer.
Keep tools as temporary scaffolds: model solving a small, known fact without a tool afterwards so reliance does not set in.

A child who insists on a tool for a fact they genuinely already know (e.g. 2+1) is likely showing reliance on the scaffold rather than a conceptual gap — gently invite them to try without the tool to build confidence, and only revisit counting if the fact turns out not to be secure.

A 'meet the tools' reveal and a single 'which tool is best?' recognition item can introduce or feed into the work, but they do not elicit the child choosing, using, and justifying a tool, so they are not the main vehicle. A lucky pick on a recognition item can score full marks without revealing the reasoning.

Compare3+2 and8+7 and ask what each tool or strategy makes easier. Directly showing every object on one finger runs out above ten, but a child may use fingers successfully for counting-on; accept a correct method with a clear fit-reason rather than requiring one tool to fail.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The 'fingers run out past ten' claim assumes the direct-representation model standard at 5–6 (showing 8 fingers and then 7 more exceeds ten). Under a counting-on strategy a child need not literally run out; the limitation is retained as valid for the assumed model and this assumption should be made explicit in delivery.

The legacy row claimed '3D adds nothing' for these tools; this has been softened to the narrow point that these tools and the counting they support are planar and concrete, so a 3D handling layer adds cost without a stated fit benefit — not a universal law that 3D cannot teach here.

The legacy row framed a scored quiz as unable to teach the WHY. This is retained only as the objective limit that recognition-only items do not elicit independent justification, not as a claim that quizzes can never support this learning.
Arithmetic check: 8 + 7 = 15 (fill one ten frame with 8, then 2 from the 7 reaches ten, remaining 5 gives fifteen); 3 + 2 = 5; 12 + 5 = 17. These are consistent across the activities.
The 'do 8+7 without a tool' probe is represented in activity 2 to carry the scaffold-removal principle at the learner-facing level, consistent with the preservation audit.

probeDeeper: Would fingers work well for 3 + 2? Why is that different from 8 + 7?
What does the ten frame show you that a loose pile of counters doesn't?
If you had 12 + 5, would you still use fingers — what would you reach for instead?
Can you do 8 + 7 now without any tool — what happened in your head?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child noticing fingers run out past ten (a limitation) and that the ten frame helps because it shows 'fill to ten, then the rest', and for a fit-REASON tied to the numbers rather than 'I just like cubes'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches for the same familiar tool every time by comfort, not fit — 'I always use my fingers' — even when the numbers cross ten
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pose paired problems (3+2 then 8+7) where the same tool fits one and fails the other, and make the finger limitation visible; ask which tool the numbers call for.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the same tool for every problem including 8+7 and cannot say why it suits this one

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the tool as a ritual — fills the ten frame correctly but says only 'because you're meant to', with no link to what it shows
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what the frame SHOWS ('how many empty spaces to ten?'); link the action to the structure rather than accepting the correct answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Solves with the frame but the justification is procedural, not about the gap to ten

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot attempt even a small, known fact without a tool — reaches for counters for 2+1
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a scaffolding lapse, not a gap: briefly withhold the tool for facts they know to build confidence — do NOT reteach counting or the tool.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists on a tool for facts already known, showing reliance rather than a conceptual gap

responseLevels.gap: Uses a tool or names a favourite but gives no fit-reason, or cannot work without it, and does not notice that fingers run out past ten.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, matches the tool to the problem (ten frame for crossing ten), names the finger limitation, explains what the frame reveals (the gap to ten), and would switch tools for a smaller problem where fingers fit.
responseLevels.partial: Chooses a sensible tool and, when prompted, says the ten frame 'shows ten', but the reason is about the tool in general rather than why it fits THIS problem, and the finger limitation is not raised spontaneously.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's 8 + 7. One child worked it out on their fingers, another used the ten frame. Which tool helped more for THIS problem, and why? What could go wrong with using fingers here?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who merely uses tools names a favourite; a child who chooses strategically points to the PROBLEM (the numbers cross ten) and to the tool's fit or limitation. 8+7 is chosen deliberately to cross ten so the finger limitation is real, not hypothetical — a 3+2 problem would not separate the two children.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7; simple, true stories of brave polar explorers — Scott and Amundsen racing to the South Pole, and Shackleton bringing every one of his men home after his ship Endurance was crushed by ice.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 History 'the lives of significant individuals in the past' (explorers as significant people) links with science of cold environments; supports Y2 habitats/cold-places context.
• Standards—US: NGSS is not the primary anchor (this is largely historical/character content); connects loosely to K-2 engineering/needs-in-environments and to CCSS ELA narrative comprehension.
• Operational details: keep it story-shaped and emotionally concrete — courage, teamwork, and never giving up. Amundsen reached the Pole first; Scott reached it too but died on the way back; Shackleton's greatest 'success' was that he lost his ship yet saved all 27 men. Focus on the human qualities (endurance, leadership, care for the team) rather than dates.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) name one thing that made polar exploration hard (freezing cold, no food, thick ice); Tier B (6) retell one explorer's story in a sentence; Tier C (7) explain why Shackleton is remembered as brave even though he never reached his goal (he kept all his men alive).
bestPractices: Tell it as narrative — a beginning, a danger, and an ending — not a list of facts or dates, which young children won't retain
Use the powerful reframing that 'brave' and 'successful' aren't the same: Shackleton failed his mission but succeeded as a leader by saving everyone
Anchor the danger in things a 5-year-old feels: bitter cold, hunger, darkness, and being far from home
Show real photographs (Frank Hurley's Endurance images) so children grasp these were real people, not a fairy tale
Connect to the child's own experience of persevering when something is hard, keeping the emotional lesson accessible
keyRepresentations: Illustrated story-map of a route to the South Pole with key story beats marked
Before/after pictures of the Endurance whole, then trapped, then sinking
Portrait cards of Scott, Amundsen and Shackleton with one memorable fact each
A simple 'what they packed' picture (dogs, sledges, tents, warm furs) showing how they survived
commonMisconceptions: Being brave means always winning — Scott and Shackleton are heroes despite not achieving their goals
Explorers went alone — these were teams who depended on each other
It happened long, long ago in a made-up way — these are real people from about 100 years ago with real photographs
They could just call for help — there were no phones, planes or rescue; they had to save themselves
Reaching the Pole was the only thing that mattered — getting the team home mattered just as much

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, help children KNOW and feel a few vivid, true stories of polar explorers: Amundsen reaching the South Pole first, Scott reaching it but dying on the return, and Shackleton losing his ship Endurance yet bringing all of the Endurance crew home. Teach it as narrative with a beginning, danger and ending, anchoring the hardship in things a young child can feel (bitter cold, hunger, darkness, being far from home) and surfacing the reframe that 'brave' and 'successful' are not the same thing. This fits the UK KS1 History aim of teaching the lives of significant individuals in the past (explorers), alongside a cold-environments science context.

activities.title: Three explorers, three stories (illustrated narrative with reveals)
feedback: If a child thinks it is a made-up fairy tale, show real photographs (e.g. Frank Hurley's images of the Endurance) so they grasp these were real people.
They could not simply telephone for immediate help from their remote camp. Shackleton and companions made a dangerous boat journey to seek help, then returned by ship to rescue the men left behind.
If a child thinks explorers went alone, point to the whole crew in the camp and lifeboat: they depended on each other.
Affirm the reframe: Shackleton 'failed' his mission but succeeded as a leader because every man of the Endurance crew came home.
activities.rationale: Young children tend to retain story shape and emotional beats better than dates or lists, so the content is delivered as a self-paced narrative with pictures carrying the load. Tap-to-reveal beats and lift-the-flaps are intended to make the twist (goal missed, everyone saved) the memorable moment. These interaction examples are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required.
learnerActions: Look at a wide wintry picture of the ship Endurance trapped in white pack ice under a low sun.

Reveal the story in order: Endurance is crushed and sinks; the crew camps on the ice and reaches Elephant Island in boats; Shackleton and a small party sail through rough seas to South Georgia to seek help; a rescue ship later returns for the men left behind.
Reveal Shackleton's outcome: 'He brought all the men of the Endurance crew home — not one was lost.'

For Scott, Amundsen and Shackleton, ask whether they reached the South Pole: Amundsen reached it first; Scott reached it but died on the return; Shackleton did not reach it on the Endurance expedition, but all members of the Endurance party survived.
(Optional) Reveal a 'what they packed' picture — dogs, sledges, tents and warm clothing such as furs and wool — to show how the explorers tried to survive the cold.
Talk about a time you kept going when something was really hard, and connect it to the explorers' endurance.
activities.intendedInsight: These were real people from more than 100 years ago who faced real danger as a team; being brave is not the same as winning — Shackleton never reached his goal but kept every member of the Endurance crew alive.

activities.title: Talking with Shackleton (spoken role-play extension)
feedback: Encourage the child to put the courage and teamwork in their own words rather than just naming facts.
If the dialogue stalls, offer a gentle prompt such as 'What did the crew eat?' or 'Why didn't they give up?'
activities.rationale: Spoken role-play may make the human qualities emotionally concrete and is intended to give practice retelling, but open dialogue is demanding for the youngest children and the topic spans three explorers, so this suits an extension rather than the core first encounter. This is an untested proposal, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Pretend to talk with a warm, friendly Shackleton and ask how he kept his men going when the ship was lost.
Ask him what the hardest and coldest moments were, and how the team helped each other.
Say back in your own words one thing Shackleton did to bring everyone home.
activities.intendedInsight: Leadership and care for the team — not reaching the goal — are what make Shackleton remembered as brave.

activities.title: Who did what? (sorting to firm up recall)
feedback: If a child muddles who did what, re-sort the three cards slowly, saying each explorer's one memorable fact aloud.

If a child says Amundsen 'just got lucky', compare choices: his skilled use of dog sleds and skis and careful supply planning versus Scott's reliance on ponies, motor sledges that broke down, and men pulling heavy sledges themselves — preparation and choices mattered a lot (though weather and other factors played a part too).
If a child calls Shackleton's trip 'just a disaster', refocus on the outcome that made it legendary: the ship was lost but every crew member came home alive.
activities.rationale: A light matching/recall check helps keep the three explorers straight, which children commonly confuse. The sort/match step confirms recall but does not by itself capture the courage in the story, so it is paired with a short explanation prompt and supports rather than replaces the narrative work.
learnerActions: Sort three portrait cards — Amundsen, Scott, Shackleton — each with one memorable fact.
Match each explorer to his story: Amundsen (first to the Pole), Scott (reached it, died returning), Shackleton (ship crushed, saved all of the Endurance crew).
Name at least one thing that made polar exploration hard: freezing cold, running short of food, or thick ice.
Say in one sentence why Shackleton is remembered as brave even though he never reached his goal.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can keep the three stories distinct and tie each explorer to his outcome, while still holding onto the point that getting the team home mattered as much as reaching the Pole.

constraints: Keep it story-shaped and emotionally concrete; focus on human qualities (endurance, leadership, care for the team) rather than dates.
Anchor danger in things a 5-year-old feels: bitter cold, hunger, darkness, being far from home.

The sorting/matching step itself confirms recall of who did what; it does not by itself elicit the child retelling or feeling the courage, so pair it with an explanation prompt, which is the aim of the topic.
Open spoken role-play is demanding for the youngest children; use it as an extension with prompts, not as the first encounter.
A pack-your-sledge or plan-the-route mini-game can show survival choices but risks turning a human-courage story into a logistics game for this age — use sparingly if at all.
Use real photographs to make clear these are real people, not a fairy tale.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; both sources are marked verified:false in the row and were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Standards link: DfE KS1 History 'the lives of significant individuals in the past' (explorers) justifies teaching this topic; it is retained in the summary rather than as an activity sourceClaim, since it supports the topic's inclusion, not any activity rationale's teaching principle.

Activity sourceClaims were set to [] because the only relevant source claim states the historical facts, which underpin the content and the correct sort answers but do not support the pedagogical principle asserted in each rationale (narrative retention; recall-check). The factual basis is recorded here and in the preservation audit's uncertain list instead.

The original 'possible' quiz and 2D mini-game alternatives are preserved as a recall-check activity and a constraint note respectively, because they carry distinct pedagogical purposes even though the row ranked them below the narrative.
The row's 3D 'poor' rating is retained only as the reasonable observation that there is no strongly spatial concept here; it is not asserted that 3D 'adds nothing' as a universal law.

Historical specifics (Amundsen first Dec 1911; Scott died returning; the survival of the Endurance crew) rest on unverified sources; confirm dates and the exact crew count (the candidate says 27, but 28 is commonly cited, including a stowaway) before publishing to young learners.

The 'Amundsen won by planning, not luck' framing is pedagogically sound but is a simplification; weather and other factors also contributed. Keep the preparation message without overstating it as the sole cause.

probeDeeper: Why do you think Amundsen's careful planning helped him more than just being lucky?
Shackleton lost his ship. Why do people still call him a hero?
What kind of things would make a journey to the South Pole so dangerous?
Which explorer reached the Pole first, and which one saved his whole crew?
assess.correctAnswer: It wasn't just luck: Amundsen won because he PLANNED carefully — using dog sleds and preparing well — while Scott's journey was far harder and he tragically died returning. And Shackleton's story, although his ship was crushed, is famous as amazing because he got EVERY one of his men home ALIVE through an incredible rescue journey. So it's a story of courage, planning and endurance, not just luck or disaster.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Amundsen just got lucky' — attributes success to chance, not preparation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare choices: Amundsen's dogs and careful supply planning vs the much harder route Scott took; success came from preparation.
errorPatterns.distractor: Amundsen only reached the Pole first because he was lucky.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says winning was luck; can't name planning, dogs, or preparation.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Shackleton's expedition was just a failure because the ship sank' — judges only by the ship, missing the rescue.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refocus on the outcome that made it legendary: the ship was lost but every crew member was brought home alive.
errorPatterns.distractor: Shackleton's trip was a complete disaster with nothing good about it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls it a disaster; doesn't mention that all the men survived.

errorPatterns.pattern: Muddles who did what — mixes up Scott, Amundsen and Shackleton.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort three simple cards: Amundsen (first to Pole), Scott (reached it, died returning), Shackleton (ship crushed, saved all his men).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes the wrong story to the wrong explorer.

responseLevels.gap: Recalls outcomes as luck/disaster; can't explain why or muddles the explorers.
responseLevels.full: Tells the three stories, credits Amundsen's planning for his success, and identifies Shackleton's bringing every man home alive as the reason his 'failed' expedition is celebrated.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the basic stories but frames Amundsen's win as luck or Shackleton's as pure failure, missing the planning / all-survived points.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Long ago, brave explorers tried to reach the South Pole. Amundsen from Norway got there first; Scott from Britain arrived later and sadly died on the way back; and Shackleton's ship the Endurance got crushed by the ice. A friend says 'Amundsen only won because he got lucky, and Shackleton's trip was a total disaster.' Do you think it was just luck — and was Shackleton's story only a disaster, or is there something amazing in it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who only remembers 'who won/who died' agrees it was luck and calls Shackleton a failure; a child who grasped the point credits planning for Amundsen and names Shackleton's all-survived rescue as the triumph. The two-part question separates outcome-recall from understanding why things happened.

sources.source: DfE National Curriculum, History KS1

sources.claim: Amundsen reached the South Pole first (Dec 1911); Scott's party reached it and died returning; Shackleton's Endurance was crushed by ice yet all 27 crew survived

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Building shade from the sun

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** no KS1 'energy' content, so no direct UK science statutory match; the design-make-evaluate element lives in KS1 Design & Technology, and the testing reasoning in KS1 'Working scientifically' (performing simple tests; gathering and recording data to answer a question).

- **Standards — US NATIONAL (NGSS):** K-PS3-2 (verbatim) '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]' (an engineering PE, asterisked); clarification examples — umbrellas, canopies, tents; SEP '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-2]'. NGSS-anchored. Builds directly on 'Sunlight warms things up'.

- **Operational details:** An ENGINEERING-DESIGN topic: children use simple [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2] (umbrella, canopy, tent, parasol) that REDUCES [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-2], then test it by comparing the shaded spot with an unshaded one (relative warmer/cooler). The science is the prior observation (sun warms surfaces); the task is design→build→test, kept qualitative — no degrees, no materials-science theory.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/procedural, age 5-6, pre-readers).
bestPractices: Frame a real problem the child cares about: 'the slide / the sandpit / our toy gets too hot in the sun — can you build something to keep it cool?' so the build has a purpose.
Run a genuine design loop at a 5-6 level: choose materials, build a shade, TEST by feeling/measuring the shaded vs sunny spot, then improve one thing (bigger? thicker? angled to block the sun?).
Make the test a fair comparison without the jargon: same object, one spot shaded by the structure and one left in the sun, checked at the same time — cooler under the shade is the evidence it worked.
Let material choice matter: compare a see-through/mesh cover with a solid opaque one so children notice that blocking the sunlight (not just covering) is what cools the area.
Connect cause to design: because the SUN warms the area (prior topic), the structure works by getting between the sun and the area — position and coverage matter, not just size.
keyRepresentations: The problem object (hot slide / sandpit / a chocolate or ice cube to protect) plus a build kit of cloths, card, sticks, pegs.
A design-loop at picture level: think → build → test (feel/measure) → make it better.
A shaded-vs-sunny comparison of the same spot, with warm/cool faces as the result.
Real exemplars: umbrella, canopy, tent, parasol, sun-sail — things that get between the sun and the ground.
commonMisconceptions: 'Any cover works the same' — a see-through or holey cover still lets the sun warm the area; blocking the sunlight is what matters (opacity/coverage).
'Shade makes cold' — carried from the prior topic; the structure doesn't make cold, it stops the sun reaching and warming the area.
Thinking the structure must be big or tall rather than POSITIONED to block the sun's path to the area.
Treating the first build as finished — missing that testing and improving (iteration) is the task.
Judging success by looks ('it's a nice tent') rather than by the evidence (is the shaded spot actually cooler than the sunny one?).

learn.summary: For children aged 5–6, build-and-test a shade structure that reduces the warming effect of sunlight on a spot (aligned to NGSS K-PS3-2 engineering design). The central learning is a hands-on design loop: choose materials, build a cover (umbrella/canopy/tent/parasol), position it between the sun and a target spot, then test by comparing the shaded spot with an unshaded one at the same time. Key insight: blocking the sunlight (opacity and position), not just covering, is what keeps the area cooler. Check which cover works by looking at the shadow or bright patch on the ground — never by looking toward the sun. An on-screen design bench and reference/check activities support the loop and fair-comparison logic, but the real outdoor build-and-test is what the standard requires.

activities.title: Build, position and test a real shade
feedback: If sunlight still lands on the spot: 'Is your spot still in a bright patch of sunlight? Move your cover until your spot is in its shadow — shade is wherever the light is blocked.'
If the child declares success without comparing: 'How do you know it's cooler? Let's check a covered spot and a sunny spot side by side at the same time and feel/measure both.'

If a see-through or thin cover is used: 'Put each cover over the spot and look at the GROUND — which one still shows a bright patch, and which casts a dark shadow? Then test which cover keeps the spot coolest compared with a sunny spot. (Never look up at the sun through the cover.)'

If the build is treated as finished after one try: 'Change just one thing — maybe make it bigger or use a thicker cloth — and test again, comparing the shaded and sunny spots to see if it gets cooler.'
activities.rationale: K-PS3-2 calls for [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]. This activity includes choosing and assembling real materials, testing their coverage, and revising the build. Comparing matched shaded and unshaded spots after the same elapsed time provides evidence about reduced warming.
sourceClaims: K-PS3-2 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]'); clarification examples umbrellas, canopies, tents; SEP '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-2]'.
Young children commonly think any cover works the same and that shade 'makes cold'; blocking the sunlight (opacity/position) is what reduces warming.
learnerActions: Start from a real problem the child cares about: 'the slide / sandpit / our toy gets too hot in the sun — can you build something to keep it cool?'

Offer a kit — cloths, card, sticks, pegs — and ask the child to choose a material and build a cover (umbrella, canopy, tent, parasol) over a target spot (a thermometer, a toy, or something to keep cool such as a chocolate or ice cube on the ground).
Have the child place the cover so it sits BETWEEN the sun and the spot; look at the ground and move the cover until the target spot is in the cover's shadow instead of bright sunlight.

Set up a fair comparison: two of the same kind of spot that start out alike, one shaded by the structure and one left in the sun, then check both after the same time has passed, by careful feel or with a relative thermometer.
Improve one thing and re-test (bigger? thicker/more opaque? angled to block the sun's path?), then judge success from the evidence: is the shaded spot cooler than the sunny one?
activities.intendedInsight: A shade works by getting between the sun and the area and blocking the sunlight; you can tell it worked because the shaded spot is cooler than a matching sunny spot checked at the same time, not because it looks nice.

activities.title: On-screen shade-design bench (companion for the design loop)
feedback: When an open net still lets light reach the spot: 'The sun is coming through the holes, so that spot keeps warming — compare it with the solid cover over the same time.'
When the solid cover keeps the spot cooler: 'Over the test the covered spot stayed cooler while the bare spot kept warming — your shade blocked the sunlight.'
Using the results strip: 'Look back at your marks — which build kept the spot coolest?'
activities.rationale: An interactive design bench rehearses the design-loop and the fair-comparison logic on screen and makes the blocking-vs-covering idea visible through an open cover that lets light through. It is a companion to, not a replacement for, the physical build-and-test the standard requires.
sourceClaims: K-PS3-2 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]'); clarification examples umbrellas, canopies, tents; SEP '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-2]'.
Young children commonly think any cover works the same and that shade 'makes cold'; blocking the sunlight (opacity/position) is what reduces warming.
learnerActions: Show a toy on a sunny slide (or a spot on a play area) and a kit of covers — cloth, open net, card — that the child can drag over the spot, resize and position relative to the sun.

Run a 'sun test' over time with two probes that start alike, one covered and one uncovered: across the test the uncovered spot keeps warming (warm face) while the covered spot stays cooler (cool face), so the difference grows over elapsed time rather than appearing instantly.
Use a 'change one thing' control and a persistent results strip that keeps each test's hit/miss mark on screen, so a pre-reader can read their own evidence and judge 'did it work?'.

Have the child try an open see-through net first and watch it still let light reach the spot so the spot keeps warming, then swap to a solid opaque cloth and re-test over the same time to see the covered spot stay cooler (note a tight weave may only partly reduce warming).

Keep all prompts picture + audio and all temperature language relative (warmer/cooler, no degrees); read which build worked from the shadow under the cover and the two probes, not by looking toward the sun.
activities.intendedInsight: Blocking the sun's light — not merely covering — is what keeps the spot cooler, and the structure must sit between the sun and the area; you confirm it by comparing covered and uncovered probes over the same time across repeated tests.

activities.title: Explore real shade exemplars (reference)
feedback: 'Where does this umbrella block the sun? Which patch of ground stays in the shadow and cool?'
'What do the tent, canopy and umbrella all do to the sunlight?'
activities.rationale: Exemplar scenes build the concept with familiar objects and picture+audio support, but they are reference material: a picture cannot deliver the design, build or test actions that are the core of this engineering topic.
sourceClaims: K-PS3-2 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]'); clarification examples umbrellas, canopies, tents; SEP '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-2]'.
learnerActions: Share a tappable or picture scene of real shade structures — umbrella, tent, canopy, sun-sail — and reveal the cooler area beneath each with 'this blocks the sun so it's cooler underneath' in picture + audio.
Ask the child to point out where each structure sits relative to the sun and which patch of ground it keeps in shadow.
Connect to the prior idea that the sun warms the area: because the sun warms the ground, a structure helps by getting between the sun and the spot.
activities.intendedInsight: Real shade structures all work in the same way — they get between the sun and the ground to block the light and cast a shadow — so position and coverage matter, not just size.

activities.title: Quick check — which cover keeps it coolest? (recognition)
feedback: If the see-through cover is chosen as coolest: 'Look at the ground under each cover — the sun still makes a bright patch under the see-through one. Which cover casts a dark shadow on the ground?'
If correct: 'Yes — that cover blocks the sun and casts a dark shadow, so the spot stays cooler.'
activities.rationale: A short picture+audio check can confirm the blocking-vs-covering idea, but recognition-only questions do not elicit the independent design-build-test-improve work that is the objective, so use it only alongside the build activity.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly think any cover works the same and that shade 'makes cold'; blocking the sunlight (opacity/position) is what reduces warming.
learnerActions: Pose a picture + audio question such as 'which shade keeps it coolest?' or 'is the spot under the umbrella warmer or cooler?' comparing a see-through cover with a solid one.
Ask the child to match a shade structure to the cooler shaded area beneath it, looking at which cover casts a dark shadow on the ground.
Keep temperature language relative (warmer/cooler) and provide adult/audio support for pre-readers.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid, well-positioned cover casts a dark shadow and keeps the spot cooler than a see-through or poorly placed one.

constraints: This is an engineering-design (procedural) topic for ages 5–6: the required learning is designing, building and testing a real structure with tools and materials, kept qualitative — no degrees and no materials-science theory.
Keep the test a fair comparison without jargon: same object/spot, one shaded and one in the sun, checked at the same time; cooler under the shade is the evidence it worked.

Observe shade safely by looking at the cast shadow or bright patch on the GROUND; never ask a child to look toward the sun or hold material up to their eyes to see whether they can see the sun through it.
Shade reduces warming over time rather than instantly cooling an already-hot surface; compare the shaded and unshaded spots over the same elapsed time, not a magic instant drop.
Open see-through/net covers let light through, but a tightly woven cover may only partly reduce warming; compare actual outcomes rather than assuming mesh always fails and opaque always succeeds.

On-screen benches, exemplar scenes and quizzes are scaffolds/companions for the design loop and comparison logic; they do not substitute for the physical build-and-test and the genuine cool of a real shaded patch, so pair them with the real outdoor activity.
Recognition-only questions check understanding but do not demonstrate independent design, build or iteration.
Address the 'shade makes cold' idea: the structure does not make cold, it stops the sun reaching and warming the area.
Address the 'any cover works' idea: a see-through or holey cover still lets the sun warm the spot; opacity and position matter.
Emphasise positioning over size: the cover must intercept the sun's path to the spot; a tall or large structure that is not in the sun's path to the spot still lets light land on it.
Treat iteration as part of the task: change one thing and re-test rather than stopping at the first build; judge success by evidence, not by looks.
Needed for the real activity: a shade-building kit (cloths, card, sticks/pegs) and a sunny spot to test shaded vs unshaded by hand or with a relative thermometer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The IOP Spark source on children's ideas (any cover works the same; shade 'makes cold') is marked unverified in the source row; treat the misconception framing as guidance pending verification.

The original assessment error-pattern nextMove instructed holding candidate materials 'up to the sun' to see through them; corrected across the guidance to a ground-shadow check for child safety, since looking toward the sun is unsafe for young children.

Mesh/open-cover outcomes depend on weave and setup; the original row framed a mesh cover as simply 'failing' — softened to an open net letting light through while noting a tight weave may only partly reduce warming.

The original row asserts '3D adds handling burden for young children' and that an in-role dialogue 'doesn't develop the engineering task'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established efficacy findings; a 3D build or a conversation could still support motivation or explanation. Narrowed accordingly and not stated as universal laws.

The original recommendation leaned on a specific digital bench as the primary vehicle; corrected emphasis so the real hands-on build-and-test is primary and the bench is a companion, consistent with the row's own catalog-gap note.

Outdoor testing results depend on real conditions (cloud, time of day, sun's movement); keep comparisons same-time and same-spot, and note the shade may not cover the spot later as the sun moves (per the assessment probes).

probeDeeper: Show me where the sunlight is still getting through — can you change your shade so it doesn't?
How will you prove your shade made it cooler, and that it wasn't just cooler there anyway?
It's cloudy now — will your shade still make much difference? Why or why not?
If the sun moves across the sky, will your shade still cover the spot this afternoon?
assess.correctAnswer: Builds a cover that physically blocks the sunlight from reaching the spot — positioned between the sun and the target, opaque enough to cast real shade — then tests by comparing the temperature or feel of the shaded spot against an unshaded spot, judging it worked if the shaded one is cooler.

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a structure but doesn't place it to block the sun's path — a wall beside the spot, or a roof full of gaps ('it's a shelter' but light still lands on the spot).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child look for the bright patch on the ground and move the cover until that patch is gone; shade is wherever the light is blocked.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watching where the cover goes — sunlight still reaches the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Declares it worked without comparing to an unshaded spot ('it's cooler, I just know').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Set up two spots side by side — one covered, one not — and compare by touch or thermometer; scaffold the fair comparison rather than reteaching shade.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Skips the test or offers no control comparison when asked to show how they'll check.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses a see-through or very thin material and expects full shade ('the clear plastic will shade it').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hold candidate materials up to the sun and pick the one you can't see through; test which casts the darkest shadow.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The material lets light through and the target stays bright.

responseLevels.gap: Builds a structure that doesn't block the light (gaps, wrong position, transparent), or claims success with no comparison.
responseLevels.full: Positions an opaque cover to intercept the sun's light so the target is fully shaded, then tests by comparing the shaded and unshaded temperature or feel and judges effectiveness on that evidence.
responseLevels.partial: Blocks the sunlight and produces shade, but tests loosely — no clear comparison to an unshaded spot, or can't say what 'worked' should look like.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are cloth, card, sticks and pegs. Make something that will keep this spot of ground (with a thermometer or toy on it) cooler in the sunshine. Set it up, then show me how you'll check whether it worked. [Watch: does the child place the cover BETWEEN the sun and the spot, block the light fully, and compare the shaded spot with a sunny one to test?]
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates a child who grasps that shade means blocking the sun's path (places the cover to intercept the light and checks against a sunny control) from one who builds a decorative 'house' without blocking the light, or declares success with no comparison.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Separating Mixtures (KS2)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y5 Properties & changes of materials):** Pupils should be taught to use knowledge of solids, liquids and gases to decide how mixtures might be separated, including through filtering, sieving and evaporating.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-PS1-3):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-3] — the basis for choosing a separation method that exploits a difference in property.

- **Operational details:** This is a PROCEDURAL 'choose the method that fits the property' node. The key move is REASONING FROM A PROPERTY DIFFERENCE to a separation technique: sieving separates by particle SIZE (big bits caught, small bits through); filtering separates an INSOLUBLE solid from a liquid (solid trapped, liquid passes); evaporating recovers a DISSOLVED solid from a solution (liquid leaves as vapour, solid stays); a magnet pulls out a magnetic component. Teach with multi-component mixtures that demand a SEQUENCE (e.g. sand + salt + water → filter out sand, then evaporate to recover salt), so the child plans an order. Connect back to properties (solubility, particle size, magnetism) so method choice is justified, not memorised. Distinguish filtering (insoluble) from evaporating (dissolved) — the classic confusion.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). Given a described mixture, the child selects and ORDERS separation techniques and justifies each by the property difference it exploits.
bestPractices: Reason from a PROPERTY DIFFERENCE to the method (particle size → sieve; insolubility → filter; solubility → evaporate; magnetism → magnet), not by rote.
Use multi-component mixtures (sand + salt + water) that force pupils to plan an ORDERED sequence.
Distinguish filtering (removes insoluble solids) from evaporating (recovers dissolved solids), the classic confusion.
Connect each method back to the underlying property so choices are justified.
Let a mis-chosen method visibly fail so the property-dependence is felt.
keyRepresentations: A separation planner routing a mixture through sieve/filter/evaporate/magnet stations
Property tags on each component (soluble / insoluble / magnetic / grain-size)
The canonical sand+salt+water sequence (filter then evaporate)
Apparatus diagrams (filter funnel, evaporating dish) linked to what each separates
commonMisconceptions: Filtering can separate a dissolved solid from its solution (it passes straight through).
Sieving and filtering are the same technique.
Evaporating destroys the dissolved solid rather than leaving it behind.
Any mixture can be separated by a single step, ignoring the need for a sequence.
The order of steps does not matter.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 9–10 learn to separate mixtures by reasoning from a PROPERTY DIFFERENCE to a technique: particle size → sieve; insolubility → filter; solubility → evaporate; magnetism → magnet. The central skill is planning an ORDERED sequence for multi-component mixtures (e.g. sand + salt + water: filter out insoluble sand, then evaporate the filtrate to recover dissolved salt) and justifying each step by the property it exploits — not reciting a recipe. A persistent confusion to address directly is filtering (removes insoluble solids) versus evaporating (recovers dissolved solids).

activities.title: Plan an ordered separation for sand + salt + water
feedback: If a learner evaporates first and ends with dry salt crystallised through the sand, don't just correct the order — ask: 'Which of these is dissolved in the water and which is just mixed in but not dissolved?' Rebuild the plan from insoluble vs dissolved, and point out they would now have to add water and begin again.

If a learner expects the filter to catch the salt too, demonstrate safely by evaporating a small drop of the filtrate to leave a tiny visible salt residue: the salt passed straight through, so filters catch undissolved bits, not dissolved substances. Reconnect to what dissolving means. (Do not taste lab substances.)

If a learner correctly executes filter-then-evaporate but explains it only as a remembered recipe, prompt: 'What is different about sand and salt that lets us use these two steps?' so the justification rests on solubility.
activities.rationale: The target is a procedural planning-and-doing task: pick a technique, apply it, observe what separates, decide the next step. Working through a multi-component mixture with an ordered plan — and seeing a mis-ordered attempt send them backwards — makes the property→method reasoning and the need for sequence explicit and testable. Letting a wrong order produce a visibly spoiled interim result ties the choice to the property it depends on.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5: use knowledge of solids, liquids and gases to decide how mixtures might be separated, including through filtering, sieving and evaporating
NGSS 5-PS1-3: identify materials by properties — the property differences that separation methods exploit
Children confuse filtering (removes insoluble solids) with evaporating (recovers dissolved solids); separation choice should follow from the property difference
learnerActions: Start with one beaker holding sand + salt + water and the goal: recover a clean, dry pile of sand AND a clean, dry pile of salt, separated from each other.
Before acting, tag each component with its relevant property: sand = insoluble solid, salt = dissolved (soluble) solid, water = liquid.
Choose an order of techniques from available stations/apparatus (sieve, filter funnel, evaporating dish, magnet) and carry it out.
Filter first: observe that the insoluble sand stays on the filter paper while the salty water passes through; rinse and dry the sand.

Then evaporate the filtered salt-water: observe the water level falling as the water leaves as invisible water vapour (any visible 'steam' is tiny droplets formed as the vapour cools), and salt crystals remaining behind once the water has gone.

Deliberately try the wrong order (evaporate before filtering) and observe the result: the water leaves and you are back to a dry sand-and-salt mixture with the salt crystallised among the grains — there is no simple DRY way to separate them, so you would have to add water again and start over.
State, for each step, which property difference it exploits.
activities.intendedInsight: The order matters because each method depends on a specific property difference: the insoluble sand must be filtered out first. If the water is evaporated too early, the dissolved salt crystallises among the sand grains, leaving a dry mixture with no simple way to separate the two solids — you would have to re-dissolve and start over, wasting the step. Method choice follows from properties, not memory.

activities.title: Transfer: choose a method for a new mixture by its property
feedback: If a learner picks a method by recall of a past activity rather than the property, ask: 'What is different about these two substances that we can take advantage of?' so the choice is driven by magnetism, solubility, or particle size.
Confirm when a learner correctly links iron filings + sand to a magnet and can say why the magnet works on iron but not sand.
activities.rationale: Matching mixtures to methods and justifying by property difference checks whether method selection has become property-driven rather than recipe-bound, and probes transfer to a mixture the learner has not drilled.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-PS1-3: identify materials by properties — the property differences that separation methods exploit
learnerActions: Face a different mixture, e.g. iron filings mixed with sand, and decide how to separate it.
Name the property difference being exploited (here, magnetism: iron is magnetic, sand is not) and choose the matching method (a magnet).
Try other new mixtures (e.g. gravel + sand needing a sieve for particle size; a dissolved solid needing evaporation) and justify each method by the property difference.
Explain why a method would fail if the property it relies on were absent (e.g. a magnet does nothing for two non-magnetic solids).
activities.intendedInsight: A separation method is chosen because of a specific property difference between components; the same reasoning transfers to any mixture, so the learner is not bound to one memorised sequence.

activities.title: Apparatus reference: what each tool separates and why
feedback: If a learner says the sieve and filter are the same, contrast them: a sieve separates by particle size (large bits caught, small bits through), while a filter separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.
If a learner says evaporating destroys the salt, clarify that the water leaves as vapour and the dissolved solid stays behind.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or labelled diagram of each apparatus with what it separates and why is a useful reference and supports the vocabulary and property links. It is a support that complements, not replaces, actually planning and testing a sequence — on its own it does not let the learner plan an order or discover a mis-chosen method failing.
learnerActions: Study each piece of apparatus — sieve, filter funnel, evaporating dish, magnet — and state what it separates (large bits from small; insoluble solid from liquid; dissolved solid from solution; magnetic from non-magnetic).
For each, name the property that makes it work and sketch or label where each component ends up.
Link each tool back to the mixtures it would suit.
activities.intendedInsight: Each separation tool exploits one property difference, and knowing which property each relies on is what makes it possible to plan a correct sequence.

activities.title: Explain and defend the plan (discussion probes)
feedback: A full response executes filter-then-evaporate in order, justifies the sequence from 'sand insoluble / salt dissolved', recognises the filtrate still holds salt, and can choose a method for a new mixture by naming the property it exploits.
A partial response carries out the steps correctly for this mixture but explains it as a remembered recipe and cannot justify the order by solubility or transfer it.
A gap response uses the wrong order or a single method, ends unable to separate salt from sand, and cannot name the property being used.
activities.rationale: Spoken justification distinguishes genuine property-based reasoning from recipe recall, and the probes target the exact decision points (order, purity of filtrate, transfer, property named) where a weak mental model shows. Discussion checks reasoning after doing; it does not by itself show whether a method physically separates the mixture.
learnerActions: After separating, answer: 'Why did you filter before evaporating and not the other way round? What would go wrong if you swapped them?'
Answer: 'The water that came through the filter — is it pure, or is something still in it? How do you know?'
Answer: 'If it were iron filings mixed with sand instead, what would you use, and why?'
Answer: 'Which property of each substance is each of your steps taking advantage of?'
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying the sequence aloud reveals whether the learner understands the property basis of each step or is reproducing a remembered recipe.

constraints: Discussion/justification is used to check and deepen understanding after doing; it should not replace the empirical step of actually applying a method and observing what separates.

A labelled apparatus diagram is a reference support: it builds vocabulary and property links but does not by itself let a learner plan a sequence or experience a mis-ordered attempt failing. Pair it with a planning-and-doing task.
Assess by watching the ORDER the learner chooses and what they do at each stage; do not tell them the sequence, or the task stops discriminating the mental model.
Real filtering-and-evaporating apparatus is a valuable hands-on complement; any on-screen planner is a model of that process.
Follow safe practice for gentle heating during evaporation. Do NOT taste lab substances; show that salt passed through the filter by evaporating a small drop of filtrate to leave a visible residue.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the Royal Society of Chemistry claim as verified:false; the misconception framing (filtering vs evaporating confusion) rests on that unverified source and should be confirmed before relying on it as established.

The original row asserted a conversation format 'cannot show whether a method actually separates' and that 3D 'adds cost without insight'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical facts; dialogue is retained here as a justification/check activity with its role scoped (checks reasoning after doing) rather than as a universal limit.

The original 'let a mis-chosen method visibly fail' and wrong-order failure are retained as productive-failure learning moments; they assume a safe demonstration or model environment and should be supervised in a real lab.

Reviewer correction: the original row described the wrong-order result as salt 'fused together and no clean way to split them'. Evaporating first is in fact recoverable by re-dissolving, filtering, then evaporating again; the learner-facing text now states the learner is sent back a step and must start over, rather than implying permanent fusion.

Reviewer correction: a 'taste the filtrate' suggestion inherited from the assessment was replaced with the safe evaporate-a-drop observation, as tasting lab substances is unsafe to model for this age.

Reviewer correction: a feedback prompt described insoluble sand as 'floating'; sand sinks/suspends and is undissolved, so the wording was changed to contrast 'dissolved' with 'mixed in but not dissolved' to avoid reinforcing a misconception.

probeDeeper: Why did you filter before evaporating and not the other way round? What would go wrong if you swapped them?
The water that came through the filter — is it pure or is something in it? How do you know?
If it were iron filings mixed with sand instead, what would you use, and why?
Which property of each substance is each of your steps taking advantage of?
assess.correctAnswer: Filter FIRST: the sand stays on the filter paper (insoluble), the salt-water solution passes through into the beaker. Rinse/dry the sand. Then EVAPORATE the filtered solution so the water leaves and dry salt is recovered. The critical move is filtering before evaporating — the child must exploit that sand is insoluble and salt is dissolved.

errorPatterns.pattern: evaporates first, before filtering ('boil off the water, then I've got the solids')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't just correct the order — ask 'which of these is dissolved and which is just floating?'; rebuild from the property (insoluble vs dissolved), then let them re-plan.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: heats the whole mixture first, ending with salt caked into the sand — cannot then separate them

errorPatterns.pattern: expects filtering to catch the dissolved salt too ('the filter paper stops everything')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Taste/evaporate a drop of the filtrate to show salt passed through — filters catch undissolved bits, not dissolved substances. Reconnect to what dissolving means.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: surprised the filtrate is salty; treats filtering as removing all solids including dissolved ones

errorPatterns.pattern: chooses a method by memory of an activity, not by the property being exploited
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — prompt 'what's different about these two substances that we can use?' so the choice is driven by properties (magnetism, solubility, particle size), not by recall.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: can recite 'filter then evaporate' for THIS setup but picks wrongly when the mixture changes (e.g. iron filings + sand)

responseLevels.gap: Wrong order or single method (evaporates the lot, or filters and stops); ends unable to separate salt from sand; can't name the property being used.
responseLevels.full: Executes filter-then-evaporate in the right order, justifies the sequence from 'sand insoluble / salt dissolved', recognises the filtrate still holds salt, AND selects an appropriate method for a new mixture by naming the property it exploits.
responseLevels.partial: Carries out filter-then-evaporate correctly for this mixture but explains it as a remembered recipe — can't justify the order by solubility or transfer to a different mixture.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child a beaker holding a mixture of sand and salt in water, with filter paper + funnel, an empty beaker, and an evaporating dish over gentle heat available. Say: 'Get me back a clean pile of dry sand AND a clean pile of dry salt, both separated from each other. Show me your steps.' Watch the ORDER they choose and what they do at each stage — do not tell them the sequence.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The task is discriminating because a wrong mental model produces a wrong ORDER. A child who hasn't linked 'salt is dissolved, sand isn't' to a separation strategy evaporates first (fusing salt into the sand, ruining both) or tries to filter out the dissolved salt. Watching the sequence, not asking about it, is what exposes the model — this is why it is a performance task.
