pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Current, voltage, and what they measure

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** KS3 Physics, 'Electricity and electromagnetism / Current electricity' — statutory wording 'electric current, measured in amperes, in circuits, series and parallel circuits, currents add where branches meet and current as flow of charge' and 'potential difference, measured in volts, battery and bulb ratings; resistance, measured in ohms, as the ratio of potential difference (p.d.) to current' (verified by fetch).

- **Standards — US National (NGSS):** there is NO middle-school performance expectation covering DC-circuit current/voltage analysis — circuits are not an NGSS MS topic — so this topic is UK-ANCHORED (the nearest NGSS contact, MS-PS2-3, concerns electromagnet/motor force strength, not circuit quantities). State the UK anchor honestly and note NGSS does not cover it at MS.

- **Operational details:** This topic QUANTIFIES the circuit by naming two distinct quantities that beginners notoriously fuse. Current is the RATE OF FLOW OF CHARGE (amperes, measured by an ammeter placed IN SERIES); potential difference / voltage is the ENERGY TRANSFERRED PER UNIT CHARGE (volts, measured by a voltmeter placed IN PARALLEL across a component). The single most important teaching job is to separate these three things — charge (the stuff that flows), current (how fast it flows), and voltage/energy (what the cell gives each bit of charge and what each component takes) — because almost every later electricity error comes from blurring them. The most effective route is a concrete transport model (a moving loop of 'charge' that the cell energises and that drops energy at components) so 'current is the same all the way round' and 'voltage is a difference ACROSS something' become visible rather than asserted.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional / early-formal, ~11–12). At KS2 the child watched 'more cells → brighter bulb' qualitatively.
bestPractices: Separate the three ideas explicitly and keep saying them: CHARGE is the stuff that flows, CURRENT is how fast it flows (rate of flow of charge, amperes), VOLTAGE is the energy each unit of charge carries/delivers (energy per charge, volts). Most errors are a collapse of these into one 'electricity'.

Use a transport/loop model so current-is-conserved is seen, not told: a moving loop of charge (the rope-loop kinaesthetic, or an animated charge ring) where every part moves together — push anywhere and the whole loop moves — makes 'current is the same all the way round a series circuit' immediate and kills the current-used-up error.

Model voltage as energy GIVEN to charge by the cell and TAKEN from charge by components: charges leave the cell 'loaded' and 'unload' energy at the bulb. This grounds 'energy per charge' and explains why voltage is always measured ACROSS two points, not at one point.

Drill the meter rules with the reason, not as a ritual: an ammeter goes IN SERIES because it counts the charge passing through (it must be in the flow); a voltmeter goes IN PARALLEL because it compares the energy of charge on either side of a component (it measures a difference across).

Treat analogies with explicit caveats: the water-circuit / central-heating model (pump = cell, flow rate = current, pressure/push = voltage) helps, but flag where it breaks (water can leak; charge cannot leave the wire; the pipe is always full). Pair it with the rope loop, which is strong for current but silent on energy.

Contrast 'the battery provides voltage, the circuit determines the current' — the cell does not push out a fixed current; current depends on what the charge meets around the loop. This pre-empts 'the battery supplies X amps no matter what'.

Anchor in measurement: have pupils predict, then read, ammeters at several points (all equal in a series loop) and voltmeters across the cell and across each component (they share out), so the abstract definitions are tied to instrument readings.
keyRepresentations: The moving charge-loop / rope-loop model — a continuous loop that all moves together when pushed anywhere; current = how fast the loop moves (same everywhere in series), with the cell as the hand doing the pushing.
Charges as energy carriers — little parcels leave the cell 'full' and 'empty out' energy at each component, making voltage = energy per charge and a DIFFERENCE across a component.
Ammeter-in-series vs voltmeter-in-parallel circuit diagram — the ammeter in the line of flow, the voltmeter bridging across a component, each annotated with what it counts.
The water-circuit / central-heating analogy (with caveats) — pump = cell, flow rate = current (A), pressure/push = potential difference (V).
A multi-point readout circuit — several ammeters around a series loop reading identically, and voltmeters across cell and components showing the pd sharing out.
commonMisconceptions: Current is 'used up' as it goes round — carried over from KS2; in a series circuit the current is the SAME everywhere, and an ammeter reads identically before and after the bulb (the bulb takes energy, not charge).
Conflating current and voltage — saying 'voltage flows through' the circuit; voltage is not a flow, it is the energy per charge / a difference across two points, while current is the flow.
Treating voltage as a property of a single point rather than a difference ACROSS two points — hence the voltmeter must straddle a component, not sit at one spot.
Believing the battery delivers a fixed current regardless of the circuit — the cell sets the voltage; the current depends on the whole loop (and its resistance).
Thinking charge is created or consumed — charge is conserved and simply circulates; the cell transfers energy to it, it does not manufacture or destroy the charge.
Putting the ammeter in parallel or the voltmeter in series — a symptom of not knowing that one counts through-flow (series) and the other measures a difference across (parallel).
Assuming more current automatically means more voltage — they are distinct quantities; their relationship depends on resistance (the next topic).

learn.summary: Help 11–12 year-olds separate three ideas they tend to fuse into one 'electricity': CHARGE (the stuff that flows), CURRENT (how fast it flows — rate of flow of charge, amperes, measured by an ammeter IN SERIES), and VOLTAGE/potential difference (energy transferred per unit charge, volts, measured by a voltmeter IN PARALLEL across a component). Centre the work on a circuit model with visibly flowing charge, measurement at multiple points, and predict-then-check tasks so that 'current is the same all the way round a series loop' and 'voltage is a difference across something' are seen and measured rather than asserted. This topic is UK-anchored (KS3); NGSS has no equivalent middle-school expectation for DC-circuit current/voltage analysis.

activities.title: Two ammeters around one bulb: does current get used up?
feedback: If you predicted a smaller reading after the bulb, look again: both ammeters read the same, apart from tiny differences due to meter accuracy (e.g. 0.3 A before AND 0.3 A after). Current is not consumed.
What the bulb 'uses' is energy — that is where the 'using up' belongs, not in the current.
Moving the ammeter to any point in a single series loop gives the same reading; swapping the bulb for a buzzer does not change that the current is equal on both sides.

Adding a second identical bulb in series makes the current SMALLER everywhere than it was with one bulb (there is now more for the moving charge to pass through), but the reading is still equal at every point around the loop.
activities.rationale: The current-used-up/attenuation error is a persistent, widely reported difficulty. A predict-then-measure task with two meters makes the equal readings confront the prediction directly, and the committed pre-observation reason is the diagnostic. A moving-charge model makes conservation visible rather than told.
sourceClaims: The current-used-up / attenuation error and the current–voltage conflation are documented, persistent difficulties best addressed with a transport model (rope loop / moving charge) showing current is the same all the way round and voltage as energy per charge measured across a component.
learnerActions: Build (physically or in a circuit simulation) a single-cell, single-bulb series loop with one ammeter just BEFORE the bulb and an identical ammeter just AFTER it.
Before closing the switch, predict whether the second meter will read less than, equal to, or more than the first — commit to a specific value and write down your reason.
Close the switch and read both meters.
In a sim with visibly flowing charge, watch the dots stream round and note how quickly the dots pass a point (their speed) as a picture of the current.
Move one ammeter to a different point in the loop and read it again; try replacing the bulb with a buzzer and check whether the pattern holds.
Add a second identical bulb in series and read the ammeter again anywhere in the loop, saying what happened and why.
activities.intendedInsight: In a series circuit the current is the same all the way round: an ammeter reads the same before and after the bulb (within the accuracy of the meters). The bulb takes ENERGY, not charge — charge is conserved and simply circulates.

activities.title: Charges leave full, arrive empty: voltage as energy per charge
feedback: '3 V across the bulb' means each coulomb (unit) of charge transfers 3 joules of energy as it passes through the bulb.
Voltage is always a difference ACROSS two points — that is why a voltmeter bridges a component; a reading 'at one point' has no meaning on its own.
The cell gives energy to charge; the bulb takes energy from charge. The charge itself keeps flowing round — it is not made or destroyed.
Watch the energy of the charges drop across the component where the voltmeter reads a value: that is the energy being transferred there.
activities.rationale: Treating voltage as a flow, or as a property of a single point, is a core misconception. Grounding voltage as energy-per-charge and showing it as a difference across a component (with the cell loading and components unloading energy) explains the across-vs-through distinction physically.
sourceClaims: The current-used-up / attenuation error and the current–voltage conflation are documented, persistent difficulties best addressed with a transport model (rope loop / moving charge) showing current is the same all the way round and voltage as energy per charge measured across a component.
learnerActions: In the circuit model, snap a voltmeter ACROSS the cell and read it; then snap a voltmeter ACROSS the bulb and read it.
In a sim that shades charges by energy, watch charges leave the cell 'full/bright' and arrive back 'empty/dim' after unloading energy at the bulb.
Explain in your own words what a reading of, say, '3 V across the bulb' tells you about each bit of charge that passes through it.
Try connecting a voltmeter to a single point in the main line and describe what goes wrong or why it makes no sense.
Explain WHERE you would connect a meter to measure voltage and why there, rather than in the main line of flow.
activities.intendedInsight: Voltage (potential difference) is the energy transferred per unit charge — the energy the cell gives each bit of charge and the energy each component takes from it. Because it is a difference between two points, a voltmeter must straddle (go across) a component, not sit at one point.

activities.title: Where does each meter go, and why?
feedback: Correct placements: ammeter IN SERIES (in the line of flow, counting charge through), voltmeter IN PARALLEL (across a component, measuring the energy transferred per unit charge between those two points).
If both meters end up 'in the flow', that is the placement-confusion error: only current is measured through; voltage is measured across two points.
A voltmeter wrongly put in series tends to stop/choke the flow; an ammeter put across a component short-circuits it — the consequence tells you the rule.
Blanks: current is the rate of flow of CHARGE; voltage is energy per CHARGE.
activities.rationale: Placement errors are a symptom of not distinguishing through-flow (series) from difference-across (parallel). Tying placement to the reason, and letting wrong placements show their consequence, makes the rule meaningful rather than a ritual. Sorting/matching items surface the current-vs-voltage conflation directly, though they check recognition rather than producing an explanation.
sourceClaims: The current-used-up / attenuation error and the current–voltage conflation are documented, persistent difficulties best addressed with a transport model (rope loop / moving charge) showing current is the same all the way round and voltage as energy per charge measured across a component.
learnerActions: Sort a set of statements into two columns: 'about current' and 'about voltage' (e.g. 'measured in amperes', 'energy per charge', 'the same all the way round a series loop', 'a difference across a component', 'measured by a meter in series', 'measured by a meter in parallel').
Match each quantity to its unit and its instrument and its placement: current–ampere–ammeter–in series; voltage–volt–voltmeter–in parallel.
Look at circuit diagrams and spot the wrongly-placed meter (e.g. a voltmeter put in series, or an ammeter put across a component).
Try, in a sim that allows wrong placements, putting a voltmeter in series and an ammeter across a component, and describe the consequence you observe.
Fill in: 'current is the rate of flow of ___; voltage is energy per ___.'
Explain the reason behind each placement rule rather than reciting it.
activities.intendedInsight: An ammeter goes in series because it must be in the flow to count the charge passing through; a voltmeter goes in parallel because it compares the energy of charge on either side of a component — it measures a difference across. Sorting and matching can check whether the vocabulary and rules are recognised, but on their own they do not elicit the reasoning for WHY current stays constant while voltage drops; pair them with build/predict/measure and explanation.

activities.title: Currents add where branches meet
feedback: Check: the two branch readings should add up to the main-line reading where the branches meet.
Changing the cell voltage changes the size of the currents, but the branch currents still add to the main-line current.
This is the KS3 phrase 'currents add where branches meet' in action — charge splitting between paths, not disappearing.
activities.rationale: 'Currents add where branches meet' is explicit statutory KS3 content and reinforces charge conservation in a parallel context, extending the series-conservation insight. Measuring and summing branch currents makes the rule empirical rather than asserted.
sourceClaims: KS3 'Current electricity' statutory wording: electric current measured in amperes, in series and parallel circuits, currents add where branches meet, current as flow of charge; potential difference measured in volts; resistance measured in ohms as the ratio of p.d. to current.
learnerActions: Build (or simulate) a circuit with one branch point so the main line splits into two parallel paths and then rejoins.
Read the current in the main line and in each branch, and compare the main-line reading with the sum of the branch readings.
Adjust a slider for cell voltage (or add a cell) and re-read all the currents, describing what changes and what stays related.
State in your own words the rule for how branch currents relate to the main current where branches meet.
activities.intendedInsight: Where branches meet, the currents add: the current in the main line equals the sum of the currents in the branches. Current is conserved — it divides and recombines but is not lost.

activities.title: The battery sets the voltage; the circuit sets the current (analogy with caveats)
feedback: 'The battery supplies X amps whatever the circuit' is wrong: add more to the loop and the current changes even though the cell is the same.
Good analogy mapping: pump→cell, flow rate→current (A), pressure/push→voltage (V).

Where the water model breaks: a cut pipe spills water, but a broken wire does not spill charge — the current just stops; and the water picture does not show energy per unit charge well. (The wire being always 'full' of charge is a way the model fits, like a full sealed pipe — so don't picture charge draining away.)
More current does not automatically mean more voltage; they are distinct, and how they relate depends on resistance, which comes next.
activities.rationale: The 'fixed current from the battery' belief and the 'more current means more voltage' error both stem from not treating current and voltage as distinct quantities set by different things. Dialogue that probes predictions, plus an analogy used WITH stated limits, pre-empts these. The water/central-heating analogy is strong for current and pressure but silent/misleading on energy and leakage, so caveats matter.
sourceClaims: The current-used-up / attenuation error and the current–voltage conflation are documented, persistent difficulties best addressed with a transport model (rope loop / moving charge) showing current is the same all the way round and voltage as energy per charge measured across a component.
learnerActions: Discuss with a partner or an in-role 'electrician' the claim 'the battery always pushes out the same number of amps no matter what' — decide whether it is true and justify your view.
Use a water-circuit / central-heating picture: pump = cell, flow rate = current, pressure/push = voltage. Map each electrical quantity to its water counterpart.

List at least two places where the water analogy BREAKS (e.g. a cut pipe spills water, but a broken wire does not spill charge — the flow just stops; the water picture does not clearly show energy carried per unit charge). Note that 'the pipe/wire is always full' is where the analogy WORKS, not where it breaks.
Predict what happens to the current when you add more components to the loop, then check with meters.
State the summary rule: the cell provides voltage; the current depends on the whole loop (and, later, its resistance).
activities.intendedInsight: A cell does not force out a fixed current. It sets the voltage; the current that results depends on the whole circuit. Analogies help but have limits that must be named.

constraints: This topic is UK-anchored (KS3 Physics, Current electricity). NGSS has no middle-school performance expectation for DC-circuit current/voltage analysis; state the UK anchor honestly and do not imply NGSS coverage at this level.

Keep saying the three ideas explicitly and repeatedly: charge is the stuff that flows, current is how fast it flows (amperes), voltage is energy per charge (volts). Most errors collapse these into one 'electricity'.

Analogies (water circuit, rope loop) must carry explicit caveats: the rope loop shows current/conservation well but is silent on energy; the water model handles flow and pressure but breaks on leakage and on energy per charge. Never present an analogy as the full story.

Recognition and matching tasks (sorting statements, matching quantity–unit–instrument, spotting a mis-placed meter) check vocabulary and rules but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or reasoning about WHY current stays constant while voltage drops; pair them with build/predict/measure tasks and explanation.

A static labelled circuit diagram is a useful reference layer for vocabulary and correct meter placement, but it cannot display charge flowing at a rate, energy being delivered, or equal readings around a loop; use it as a pre-activity reference, not as the demonstration of conservation.
Predictions describe how an existing situation changes; have learners commit a value and reason BEFORE switching on so the equal readings can confront the prediction.
Allowing 'wrong' meter placements in a simulation is a learning-by-consequence device; make sure the consequence (choked flow / short) is visible and discussed, not left to chance.

Adding components such as bulbs or buzzers in series reduces the current everywhere in a single loop while keeping it equal at every point (an ideal ammeter or a closed switch added in series has negligible effect); voltage/current relationships via resistance are a later topic and should not be pre-asserted here beyond this observation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's artefact-fit entries assert strong comparative/necessity claims ('Nothing static can show flow-rate conservation', '3D adds no purchase', a conversation 'targets the misconception through dialogue' but is 'weakly served by talk'). These comparative-efficacy and necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits in constraints rather than propagated as laws.
The IOP Spark source supporting the transport-model/misconception claim is marked verified:false in the row; treat that claim's support as unconfirmed.

The 'battery sets voltage / circuit sets current' principle in the final activity is physically sound but is not directly stated by any cited source claim; the attached IOP claim supports only the related current–voltage conflation strand ('more current means more voltage').
Specific current/voltage VALUES used in activities (e.g. 0.3 A, 3 V) are illustrative only and should be set by the actual circuit; do not present them as fixed outcomes.

The legacy reasoning is physically sound for this topic (series current conserved; voltage as energy per charge measured across; currents add at junctions; cell sets voltage, circuit sets current; added series components lower the current). No conceptual error required correction, but the quantitative relationship of current to voltage depends on resistance, a later topic that should not be pre-asserted here.

assess.poeTask: Build a series circuit with an ammeter just before the bulb and an identical ammeter just after it. Before closing the switch, ask the child to predict whether the second meter will read less than, equal to, or more than the first — commit to a value and a reason. Then switch on and read both. The current-consumed model predicts the 'after' meter reads lower; the equal readings force a rethink toward charge conservation, and the pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I add a second identical bulb in series, what happens to the ammeter reading anywhere in the loop — and why?
The voltmeter across the bulb reads 3 V. In your own words, what does '3 volts' tell us about each bit of charge that passes through?
Suppose I move the ammeter to the other side of the bulb — would you expect a different reading? What if the component were a buzzer instead of a bulb?
Where would you connect a meter to measure the voltage, and why there rather than in the main line?
assess.correctAnswer: The current is the same before and after the bulb — an ammeter reads the same on both sides. What the bulb 'uses' is energy: the voltage (potential difference) across the bulb drops because energy is transferred there. Current is the rate at which charge flows (amperes); voltage is the energy carried per unit charge (volts).

errorPatterns.pattern: Current-consumed model: 'the bulb uses up the current, so there's less current after it than before' — expects the ammeter to read lower on the far side.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put two ammeters, one each side of the bulb, and show equal readings; name what does drop (voltage/energy) so the child has somewhere to put the 'using up'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The current is smaller after the bulb because the bulb uses some of it up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tier-2 reasoning that has the current diminishing as it goes round, or predicting a lower reading on the ammeter after the bulb.

errorPatterns.pattern: Current/voltage conflation: uses 'current' and 'voltage' as two words for the same 'electricity' — 'the voltage flows through and gets used up, which is the same as the current dropping'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two with the analogy of rate-of-flow (amps, how much charge passes per second) versus energy-per-charge (volts); measure each with its own meter in its own place.
errorPatterns.distractor: The voltage flows through the bulb and gets used up, which is the same thing as the current dropping.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tier-2 explanation swaps the terms freely, or treats amps and volts as measuring the same thing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ammeter/voltmeter placement confusion: puts both meters in the main line, or expects a voltmeter in series and an ammeter across the bulb.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie placement to meaning: current is measured THROUGH (in series), voltage is measured ACROSS two points (in parallel) because it is a difference between them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked (in follow-up) to place meters, connects the voltmeter in series or reasons that both meters go 'in the flow'.

responseLevels.gap: Says the current is used up in the bulb (smaller after it), or uses 'current' and 'voltage' interchangeably; would put both meters in the line.
responseLevels.full: Explains current as the conserved rate of charge flow (the same before and after the bulb) and voltage as the energy transferred per unit charge (which drops across the bulb), uses this to justify meter placement, and transfers the reasoning to a new component — coordinating the two quantities rather than listing them.
responseLevels.partial: Knows current is measured in amps and voltage in volts, and that an ammeter goes in series while a voltmeter goes in parallel, but recites these as separate facts — cannot say WHY current stays the same while voltage drops, or treats current and voltage as two names for the same 'electricity'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A single bulb is lit by one cell. Does the electric current get smaller after it has passed through the bulb, or is it the same all the way round the circuit? Explain your reasoning — and say what, if anything, the bulb actually 'uses up'.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the current-consumed model, or conflating current with voltage, must predict the current is smaller after the bulb. The correct reasoner keeps current constant everywhere and moves the 'using up' onto energy/voltage. It is very hard to answer 'same all the way round, energy is what's transferred at the bulb' without the charge-flow-plus-energy model, and easy to get it wrong for the intuitive reason.

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10 arguments become genuinely multi-step and start reaching toward proof: a child proves 3/4 > 2/3 not by drawing two bars and eyeballing them but by converting to a common denominator (9/12 vs 8/12) and stating why that settles it, and critiques a peer's long multiplication by finding a misaligned partial product and explaining the place-value consequence. The practice now spans three arenas at once — fractions, angles, calculation — and the SMP3 demand sharpens: an argument must be a connected logical progression, and a critique must name the flawed step AND offer why the correct method works. This is the empirical-to-deductive transition Hoyles & Küchemann document as slow and fragile: children will still offer 'I tried it and it worked' as proof, and the teaching job is to make them feel the gap between a convincing example and a watertight general reason.
bestPractices: Demand a general reason, not a confirming example: after a child checks 3/4 > 2/3 with a picture, ask 'would that convince someone who couldn't see your drawing?' and push toward the common-denominator argument
Use deliberately flawed peer work across all three arenas (a misaligned partial product, a mis-added angle, a wrong common denominator) and require 'which step and why', per SMP3's explain-the-flaw
Teach the tear-and-arrange angle demonstration as an argument, not a fact to memorise — the arrangement into a straight line IS the reasoning that the three angles sum to 180°
Introduce the counter-example as a tool: one case that breaks a claim disproves it, whereas any number of confirming cases does not prove it (the asymmetry Hoyles & Küchemann flag)
Insist on because/therefore connectives linking each step to the next so a list of true facts becomes a valid chain
keyRepresentations: Common-denominator conversion (3/4=9/12, 2/3=8/12) as the engine of a size argument
Column/grid long-multiplication layout for locating a misaligned partial product
Tear-and-rearrange triangle (three corners meeting on a straight line) as a visual proof of the 180° angle sum
A because/therefore chain frame connecting givens to conclusion
commonMisconceptions: Treating a confirming example (or a careful drawing) as a proof of the general claim
Comparing fractions by whichever has the bigger numerator or bigger denominator rather than by a common referent
Critiquing by answer-agreement — 'the total's wrong' — without locating the misaligned step or explaining the place-value error
Believing the tear-and-arrange result is a lucky fact of that one triangle rather than a general property

learn.summary: For children aged 9-10, this guidance supports the empirical-to-deductive transition in mathematical reasoning (SMP3): constructing multi-step arguments and critiquing others' reasoning across fractions, angles, and calculation. The core teaching objective is to make learners feel the gap between a convincing example (or careful drawing) and a watertight general reason, and to critique flawed work by naming the specific broken step AND explaining why the correct method works - not merely noticing the answer is wrong. Dialogue with a skeptic is proposed as a strong vehicle because the defining moves are dialogic, while constructed-argument workspaces, annotated correct-vs-flawed comparisons, and limited recognition warm-ups each have a distinct, more limited role noted below.

activities.title: Convince the skeptic without a picture
feedback: If the learner offers more examples or a neater drawing, ask: 'How many would it take before you were CERTAIN? Is there any number that would make it a proof?'
If the learner converts to twelfths, revoice their chain back: 'so 3/4 is 9/12, 2/3 is 8/12, 9 is more than 8 - and that holds whatever you drew.'
Name success as locating a reason that covers every case at once, not as getting the right verdict.

If the learner senses the drawing isn't enough but stalls, scaffold: 'you're right it's not settled - what could you turn both fractions into so they're easy to compare?' and let them complete the chain.
activities.rationale: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates at this age and the shift to deductive reasoning is slow; a skeptic who accepts only a because-chain targets the empirical-proof habit and exercises argument construction (one half of SMP3). A dialogic format may respond to the child's over-reliance on examples in real time.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements; if there is a flaw in an argument, explain what it is; distinguish correct logic from flawed.

Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the empirical→deductive transition is slow and fragile; a general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false, whereas confirming examples cannot establish a general truth.

The describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder: convincing may be confident but incomplete, whereas justifying is a correct, complete because/therefore chain; recognising that specific examples do not constitute watertight proof is a key developmental step.
learnerActions: State a claim, e.g. 3/4 > 2/3, and offer your first justification however you like (a drawing is fine to start).

When challenged ('your drawing looks close - how do I know you didn't just draw it that way? Convince me without the picture'), reach for a general reason: convert to a common denominator - 3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, and 9/12 > 8/12.
State explicitly why this reason settles it for ANY representation, not just your drawing.
Respond to repeated pressing ('but ALWAYS?') and refuse to let 'I tried it and it worked' count as proof.
Try the same argument on a fresh pair, e.g. 5/8 versus 2/3, to test whether your method generalises (work out the common-denominator comparison rather than guessing).
activities.intendedInsight: A confirming example or a careful drawing can persuade, but a reason that holds independent of any picture is what actually settles a general claim.

activities.title: Find the broken step in a long multiplication
feedback: If the learner only says 'the total's wrong', redirect: 'which step caused it, and what did the misalignment do to the place value of that partial product?'
Confirm success when the learner links the misaligned column to the partial product sitting in the wrong place value.

A column/grid layout makes the misaligned partial product easier to locate; nudging a partial product in and out of column alignment can make the place-value cost felt (optional illustration, not required).
activities.rationale: Critiquing multi-step work by locating the flawed step and explaining why the correct method works is the critique half of SMP3. Using deliberately flawed work targets this directly rather than rewarding mere answer-agreement.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements; if there is a flaw in an argument, explain what it is; distinguish correct logic from flawed.
learnerActions: Examine a worked long multiplication in which one partial product has been shoved one column to the right of where it belongs (misaligned).
Identify WHICH step is wrong, not just that the final total is off.

Explain the place-value consequence: the partial product for the next higher-place digit should sit one column further LEFT than the previous partial product (or, equivalently, end in a placeholder zero). Shoved one column to the right, it lands in a place value that is too low, so it is added into the wrong columns and contributes only one tenth of its true value.
State what the correct alignment should be and why that fixes the value.
activities.intendedInsight: A valid critique names the flawed step and explains the underlying place-value error, which is deeper than noticing answer-disagreement.

activities.title: Tear and rearrange: from evidence to a reason why ALL triangles have angles summing to 180 degrees
feedback: If the learner treats the result as specific to their triangle, prompt: 'would this happen for a long thin triangle too? Try one and watch what the corners do.'

Name success as telling apart what the demonstration shows (strong evidence of about 180 degrees for the triangles tried) and a general reason that covers every triangle, not just reporting the 180 degree sum.

A draggable triangle that keeps re-forming the straight line as you deform it can make the pattern vivid (optional), but it is still a series of examples. Note the approximation: tearing and placing corners is imprecise, so a paper demonstration can only look close to a straight line. The exact 180 degree result is about the idealised mathematical triangle and is established by a general argument.
activities.rationale: Teaching the demonstration as evidence that motivates a general argument, rather than as a fact to memorise or as a proof in itself, connects a visual action to a general geometric claim. It also counters the belief that the result is coincidental for one triangle, and stays consistent with the point that confirming examples alone do not prove a general claim.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements; if there is a flaw in an argument, explain what it is; distinguish correct logic from flawed.
learnerActions: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them so their vertices meet at a point along a straight edge.
Observe that the three angles together appear to form a straight line (about 180 degrees, within the precision of the tearing).

Treat the arrangement as evidence, not yet a proof: the corners appearing to meet on a straight line suggests that the three angles sum to 180 degrees. A torn paper triangle is only one approximate example, so ask what general reason would make this happen for every triangle.

Repeat with a differently shaped triangle (or deform a draggable on-screen triangle) and see that the corners again appear to form a straight line. Note that each successful case makes the claim more convincing, but more cases on their own still do not prove it for every triangle.

State the general claim that the angles of ANY triangle sum to 180 degrees, and explain the general reason (with teacher support): draw a line through one corner parallel to the opposite side. The other two angles reappear at that corner as equal (alternate) angles, so the three angles together fill a straight line, which is 180 degrees. This reason does not depend on the triangle's shape.
activities.intendedInsight: Tearing and rearranging corners convincingly suggests that a triangle's angles sum to 180 degrees, and repeating it builds confidence. But only a general reason (such as the parallel-line argument) shows that it holds for ALL triangles; examples alone are not a proof.

activities.title: Counter-examples and the asymmetry of proof
feedback: If the learner holds 'bigger denominator wins', have them test it on 1/4 versus 1/3 (equal numerators, larger denominator) and watch it fail; if they hold 'bigger numerator wins', have them test it on 3/8 versus 1/2 (differing numerators) and watch that fail - match the test case to the rule they actually hold.
Reinforce the connectives: ask the learner to join their true statements with 'because' and 'therefore' so the argument reads as a chain, not a list.

Distinguish an incorrect comparison rule (a false belief about fraction size) from a reasoning gap; if the learner misranks fractions, revisit comparison via a common denominator or a benchmark before judging their reasoning.
activities.rationale: Introducing the counter-example as a tool teaches the logical asymmetry between refutation and confirmation, a developmental step flagged as key; insisting on because/therefore connectives turns true facts into a valid chain. The 1/4 vs 1/3 case holds the numerator fixed to break the bigger-denominator rule, while the 3/8 vs 1/2 case has both parts differing and is used to break the bigger-numerator rule (3 > 1, yet 3/8 < 4/8 = 1/2). These vary different quantities to refute different single-component rules; this is not a denominator rule 'flipping'. Fractions remain comparable as numbers throughout.
sourceClaims: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the empirical→deductive transition is slow and fragile; a general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false, whereas confirming examples cannot establish a general truth.

The describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder: convincing may be confident but incomplete, whereas justifying is a correct, complete because/therefore chain; recognising that specific examples do not constitute watertight proof is a key developmental step.
learnerActions: Consider a claim such as 'the fraction with the bigger denominator is always bigger' or 'the fraction with the bigger numerator is always bigger'.
Test the bigger-denominator claim where the numerator is held fixed: compare 1/4 and 1/3 - the denominator 4 is larger, yet 1/4 is smaller than 1/3, so that claim fails.

Test the bigger-numerator claim on a case where the numerators actually differ: compare 3/8 and 1/2 - the numerator 3 is larger than 1, yet 3/8 is smaller than 1/2 (since 1/2 = 4/8), so that claim fails too.
State each breaking case as a counter-example that disproves the rule.
Articulate the asymmetry: one counter-example disproves a general claim, but any number of confirming examples does not prove it.
Build a because/therefore chain linking the givens to the conclusion so a list of true facts becomes a connected argument.
activities.intendedInsight: One counter-example is enough to refute a general claim, whereas confirming examples alone never establish one - and each step of an argument should be linked by because/therefore.

constraints: Do not accept a correct verdict (e.g. agreeing 3/4 > 2/3) as evidence of reasoning; a child can be right for the wrong reason via a single-component comparison rule. The discriminating act is explaining WHY examples don't settle it and producing the general reason.

Fixed-answer or 'spot the misaligned step' recognition tasks can serve as a warm-up but do not elicit a constructed general justification or a flaw explained in the child's own words; a score on such a task is not evidence of the reasoning practice, and recognition formats can inadvertently reward the confirming-example habit. Recognition alone does not elicit production.

Annotated correct-vs-flawed comparisons with tap-to-reveal explanations can seed critique talk but do not themselves respond to a child's over-reliance on examples or capture a constructed chain; use them to launch discussion, not as the assessment.

A single confirming example or drawing is a starting point for talk, not a proof; always push toward a reason that holds independent of the representation. Fractions remain comparable as numbers; the common-whole caveat applies only to comparing represented portions within a drawing.
Separate two distinct causes of wrong fraction comparisons: a faulty comparison rule (reteach comparison) versus a reasoning-articulation gap (scaffold and scribe); treat them differently.

Paper-corner tear-and-arrange uses physical cutouts as an imprecise, concrete approximation of idealised angles; a draggable on-screen triangle is a model of the same relationship. Both offer repeated examples that make the pattern vivid, but neither proves the general claim by itself, and neither is universally required.

Optional interaction examples (draggable triangle re-forming the straight line, nudging partial products in/out of column alignment, linked fraction/angle/multiplication tools) are illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory features. Comparative claims that one medium uniquely teaches, or that another 'cannot', are not established by the sources.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research, re-reviewed independently without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original row's confidence was 'high' and its sources were marked verified; this review does not re-verify them and does not upgrade or downgrade that status.

Arithmetic confirmed: 3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, 9 > 8, so 3/4 > 2/3; 1/4 < 1/3; 3/8 < 1/2 (= 4/8); 5/8 = 15/24 and 2/3 = 16/24, so 5/8 < 2/3 (the 5/8 vs 2/3 pair is used only as a generalisation test, with no answer asserted in the activity).

Long-multiplication critique: a partial product belonging to a higher-place digit should be shifted one column to the LEFT; if instead shoved one column to the right it lands in a place value that is too low, so that partial product contributes too little. The source gives no concrete numeric example and describes this only as the 'wrong place value', so the net total direction is not asserted (an earlier candidate claim that the misalignment 'inflates the total' was incorrect - rightward columns are lower place values - and has been removed).

The original framed a 'doubting Thomas'/skeptic persona and claimed dialogue uniquely targets both halves of SMP3 and 'directly attacks' the empirical-proof habit; comparative necessity claims, or that other formats 'cannot' teach, are not established by the source citations and have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances and limits.

Counter-example wording was tightened: 1/4 vs 1/3 holds the numerator fixed to break the bigger-denominator rule, while 3/8 vs 1/2 is a case where both numerator and denominator differ (used to break the bigger-numerator rule, since any numerator-rule counter-example must vary both parts). This is a fair test of single-component rules, not a denominator rule 'flipping'.

probeDeeper: 'How many examples would it take before you were CERTAIN? Is there any number that would make it a proof?'
'Turn both fractions into twelfths for me — now what does that let you say, for sure?'
'A classmate says 3/4 > 2/3 because 4 is bigger than 3. Is that a good reason? Test it on 1/4 and 1/3.'
'Would your common-denominator argument still work for 5/8 versus 2/3? Show me.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that confirming examples/drawings do not constitute a general proof, and offering (or reaching for) a common-denominator argument (3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, 9/12 > 8/12) as the reason that settles it independently of any picture.

errorPatterns.pattern: Empirical proof scheme: treats confirming examples or a careful drawing as proof — 'I tried it and it worked, so it's true.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront the asymmetry: 'How many pizzas would you have to try to be SURE? Could there ever be one where it's different?' Then co-build the common-denominator reason and name it as the kind of argument that covers every case at once.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses the classmate ('yes, that settles it') and, asked to show it themselves, offers another example or a neater drawing rather than a general reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares fractions by a single component — bigger numerator or bigger denominator wins — so any 'reason' given rests on a faulty comparison rule.
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a false belief about fraction size, not an argument-skill gap — reteach comparison via a common denominator or a benchmark using bars. Do not accept the correct verdict as evidence of reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child justifies 3/4 > 2/3 with '4 is bigger than 3' or '3 is bigger than 2' rather than by a common referent; may get the right verdict for the wrong reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Senses that 'drawings can be misleading' matters and rejects the example-proof, but cannot yet articulate the common-denominator reason — reasoning outruns the ability to state it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT read as not-knowing. Scribe/revoice: 'you're right it's not settled — what could you turn both fractions into so they're easy to compare?' Let the child complete the chain; the discriminating instinct is already there.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'no, that's not really a proof' or 'you need a proper reason' but stalls when asked to give one; may gesture toward twelfths without completing the chain.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts the examples/drawing as settling it and offers only more examples when asked to show it themselves.
responseLevels.full: Recognises confirming examples don't prove the claim AND produces a common-denominator (or benchmark) argument that settles it independent of any picture, explaining why that reason covers every case — and spontaneously applies the same 'examples aren't proof' stance to a new comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Is uneasy with the example-proof or gives the correct verdict, but justifies by a single-component rule or an unexplained drawing; can describe a comparison but not a reason that generalises.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate says: 'I checked and 3/4 is bigger than 2/3 — I drew them and the 3/4 bar looked longer, and I tried it with a pizza too, so it's definitely true.' Do you think that settles it? How would YOU show whether 3/4 is bigger than 2/3, and would your way convince someone who says drawings can be misleading?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has crossed toward deductive reasoning is uneasy with 'I drew it and tried a pizza' and reaches for a reason that holds regardless of the drawing; a child still in the empirical-proof scheme is fully satisfied by the examples and sees nothing to add. The prompt separates them because it explicitly offers the empirical justification as 'settled' — a correct reasoner pushes past it, an empirical reasoner endorses it. Reasoning right for the wrong reason is hard here: agreeing 3/4 > 2/3 is easy, but explaining WHY the examples don't settle it and producing the common-denominator reason is the discriminating act.

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, repeated reasoning matures into working the multiplication tables as a web of derivable facts and checkable patterns: noticing all multiples of 4 are even and using that to CHECK an answer, deriving 8×7 from 8×5 + 8×2, and describing the rule of a growing sequence ('add 50 each time') to predict onward. The MP8 emphasis on 'maintaining oversight… evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results' becomes concrete here: a pattern (multiples of 4 are even) is not just noticed but used as a reasonableness check. Teaching should build tables from known facts and pattern, not rote alone, and always ask 'does that answer look sensible given the pattern?'
bestPractices: Derive harder table facts from anchor facts (×5 and ×2 to reach ×7) using an array split, so the table is a network not a list to memorise
Explicitly use pattern as a check: 'a multiple of 4 must be even — is your answer even?' to build reasonableness monitoring
Have children describe the rule of a growing sequence and predict several terms ahead, then verify
Surface and test near-generalisations ('all multiples of 4 are even — are all even numbers multiples of 4?') to sharpen what the rule does and doesn't claim
keyRepresentations: Arrays / area model split for deriving ×7 from ×5 + ×2
Multiplication grid highlighting column/row patterns (evens, digit patterns)
Number line with equal repeated steps for growing sequences (+50)
Hundred square shading multiples to reveal their pattern
commonMisconceptions: Skip-counts or guesses harder facts instead of deriving them from known ones (8×5 + 8×2)
Splits the derivation wrongly (8×5 + 2, forgetting to multiply the 2 by 8)
Accepts an unreasonable answer because the pattern check (multiples of 4 are even) isn't applied
Over-generalises a pattern from a few cases without testing, or reverses it wrongly (thinks every even number is a multiple of 4)

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, turn multiplication tables from a memorised list into a web of derivable facts and checkable patterns. Children derive a harder fact (8×7) from anchor facts they own (8×5 + 8×2 = 40 + 16 = 56) using an array split, use a pattern as a reasonableness check (multiples of 4 and 8 are even — is my answer even?), and describe/test the rule of a growing sequence ('add 50 each time') to predict onward terms. The core habit is deriving AND self-checking, plus probing what a pattern does and does not claim.

activities.title: Split an array to derive a hard fact
feedback: If a child skip-counts 8, 16, 24… or recalls insecurely: show the array split into 8×5 and 8×2 so the two anchor facts are visible to combine.
If a child computes 8×5 + 2 = 42 (forgetting to multiply the 2 by 8): return to the array — the second block is also 8 tall, so it is 8×2 = 16, not 2. This is a scaffolding nudge, not a full reteach.
Correct target: 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 = 40 + 16 = 56 (and equivalently 8×8 − 8 = 56).
activities.rationale: Deriving facts from known facts and using arrays that reveal structure supports reasoning over rote recall; a splittable/foldable array makes the decomposition something the child acts on.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Face 8×7 shown as an array 8 rows tall and 7 wide.
Cut the 7 into 5 and 2 (drag a divider, fold a paper array, or draw a line) so the array cleaves into an 8×5 block and an 8×2 block.
Read off 8×5 = 40 and 8×2 = 16, then combine the two blocks to get 56.

Try a different way to reach the same answer: 8×8 − 8 = 64 − 8 = 56 (take one group of 8 away from eight 8s). Compare which way you prefer and why — this uses one fewer group of 8, which is a different idea from cutting the 7 into 5 and 2.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'hard' table fact can be assembled from facts you already own; the array makes the decomposition (distributive idea) visible rather than relying on recall or skip-counting, and the 8×8 − 8 route is a distinct alternative strategy (adjusting from a near fact), not another split of the 7.

activities.title: Use a table pattern as a reasonableness check
feedback: If a child has no test when asked to check: practise 'multiples of 4/8 are even; is yours?' and connect it back to the shaded grid.

If a child accepts an odd number as a multiple of 4: point to the shaded multiples of 4 (a single column or row on a multiplication grid, a staggered pattern on a 10-wide hundred square) — no odd number is shaded.
A product that is odd cannot be a multiple of 4 or 8; a product well outside the 40–64 range for 8×7 should prompt a recheck — then confirm the exact value by the derivation.
activities.rationale: Maintaining oversight by evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results is central to MP8; a shadeable grid makes the pattern visible so it can be used as a live check.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Shade the multiples of 4 (and of 8) on a multiplication grid or hundred square and observe that every one is even.
State the pattern as a check: 'a multiple of 4 must be even — is my answer even?'
Apply the check to a proposed product: given a candidate like an odd 'multiple of 4', decide whether it can be right and say why.
Estimate before computing: 'roughly how big should 8×7 be — between which two facts I know?' (between 8×5=40 and 8×8=64).
activities.intendedInsight: A noticed pattern is not just an observation — it becomes a tool you use to catch your own errors and judge whether an answer looks plausible (this check shows an answer is plausible, e.g. even and within range, not that it is exactly right).

activities.title: Describe and test a sequence rule
feedback: If a child only continues one step: ask them to state the rule explicitly first, then jump ahead using it.
Check predictions against equal repeated steps on the number line; a term that breaks the constant step signals an arithmetic slip.
activities.rationale: Describing the regularity in repeated reasoning and using it to predict, then checking, is the sequence form of MP8.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
learnerActions: Given a growing sequence (e.g. steps of +50 along a number line), describe the rule in words: 'add 50 each time'.
Predict several terms ahead — e.g. the term after 350 (400), and the one after that (450) — then verify by stepping along the number line.
Say how sure you are and how you could check a predicted term.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly stated rule lets you predict beyond what you can see and then verify, which is the predict-and-check habit in a sequence context.

activities.title: Test the limits of a pattern (don't over-reverse it)
feedback: If a child says 18 (or 6) is a multiple of 4 because it is even: offer the counterexample and ask them to list actual multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12, 16…) to see 6 and 18 are absent.
Correct distinction: 'multiple of 4 ⇒ even' holds, but 'even ⇒ multiple of 4' is false.
activities.rationale: Surfacing and testing near-generalisations guards against over-generalising a pattern from a few cases or reversing it wrongly; this is recognising precisely what the mathematical structure does and does not entail.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'all multiples of 4 are even' and agree it is true.
Now test the reverse: 'is every even number a multiple of 4?' Try 6 — it is even but not a multiple of 4.
State precisely what the rule claims and what it does not (every multiple of 4 is even, but not every even number is a multiple of 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A true pattern often does not reverse; testing a near-generalisation with a counterexample sharpens exactly what a rule does and doesn't claim.

activities.title: Check understanding with targeted questions
feedback: Include an '8×5 + 2' distractor for the split: the correct combination is 8×5 + 8×2, so the second term is 16, not 2 (giving 56, not 42).
For the sorting task, an even number that is not a multiple of 4 (like 6) tests whether the child over-reverses the pattern.
Pair each selection with a 'why' so recognition is backed by reasoning, not guessing.
activities.rationale: At this age, well-designed questions can probe the derivation and reasonableness-checking content when paired with a justification step; note this checks recognition and stated reasoning, not independent construction, so pair it with open construction tasks.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
learnerActions: Answer 'which known facts can you combine to make 8×7?' and explain why your choice works.
Sort a set of numbers into multiples of 4 and not-multiples-of-4, including an even non-multiple to catch over-generalising.
Spot the unreasonable answer: given candidate products, identify one that breaks a pattern (e.g. an odd 'multiple of 8') and say which pattern it breaks.
activities.intendedInsight: Questions can check both the derivation route and the pattern-as-check habit, including whether a child is fooled by a plausible wrong split; this checks recognition and stated reasoning, not whether the child can construct the derivation unprompted.

constraints: Build tables from known facts and visible pattern, not rote memorisation alone; always ask 'does that answer look sensible given the pattern?'

Arrays and grids should be things the child acts on (cut, fold, shade) so the derivation and pattern are visible; a pre-split array or fixed shaded grid with tap-to-reveal annotations can illustrate and reference the method but does not let the child choose the split or test their own candidate answer against the pattern — treat it as a scaffold.

Recognition/selection questions check whether a child can identify a correct split or sort numbers, but do not by themselves require the child to construct a derivation unprompted; pair with a spoken or written 'why' and with open construction tasks.
Open discussion alone supplies nothing to split or shade; pair talk with an array, grid, or number line (a practical pairing, not a claim that talk cannot support reasoning).
These are flat number-and-pattern ideas; a 3D presentation is not needed and may add load — this is a practical note for this topic, not a universal claim about 3D.
Pattern-as-check establishes that an answer is plausible (e.g. even, within a range), not that it is exactly correct; keep both the derivation and the check.
Keep the 8×5 + 8×2 array split distinct from the 8×8 − 8 near-fact route; both reach 56 but they are different strategies (decomposition vs. adjusting from a known neighbour).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic): 8×5=40, 8×2=16, 40+16=56; alternative 8×8−8 = 64−8 = 56; both confirmed. Estimation bound 'between 8×5=40 and 8×8=64' is correct for 8×7=56. Sequence +50 from 350 gives 400 then 450.

Self-audit (pattern logic): 'all multiples of 4 are even' is true; its reverse is false (6 and 18 are even but not multiples of 4); 18 is not a multiple of 4. The '8×5 + 2 = 42' error is a genuine common slip and is used only as a diagnosed misconception, never offered as a correct option.

The original claims that 'open talk supplies nothing' and '3D adds load, not insight' were softened to scoped practical notes; catalog fit rankings are not evidence of comparative efficacy or necessity.

sourceClaims are exact copies of this row's two sources; neither establishes that any specific activity here was empirically tested, nor that questioning is a superior assessment method. Source 2 is retained for the near-generalisation activity only as structure-level support, not as direct evidence for converse-testing.

Editor correction: activity 1's alternative route (8×8 − 8) was reworded into child-friendly language and kept clearly distinct from the 5+2 array decomposition (a near-fact adjustment, not a split of the 7).

probeDeeper: Ask 'could you also get 8×7 from 8×8 minus 8? which route do you prefer and why?' to test flexible reuse of anchor facts
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'all multiples of 4 are even — so is every even number a multiple of 4? what about 6?' to check the child does not over-reverse the pattern
Ask 'your sequence adds 50 each time — what will the term after 350 be, and the one after that? how sure are you?' to probe rule-based prediction
Ask 'without working it out exactly, roughly how big should 8×7 be — between which two facts you know?' to surface reasonableness monitoring
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for deriving 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 = 56, AND a reasonableness check such as '56 is even, and multiples of 8 (or 4) are even, so it looks right', or noticing it lies between 8×5 and 8×8. The derivation plus the self-check is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Skip-counts or guesses 8×7 rather than deriving it from the known 8×5 and 8×2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Split an array into 8×5 and 8×2 so the derivation is visible; connect it to the distributive idea they can see
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts 8, 16, 24… or recalls insecurely rather than combining the two anchor facts

errorPatterns.pattern: Splits the derivation wrongly — computes 8×5 + 2 (forgets to multiply the 2 by 8)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the array: the second block is 8 tall too, so it is 8×2=16, not 2; a scaffold not a reteach
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives 42, having added 2 rather than 8×2

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not apply a pattern as a reasonableness check, accepting an odd or wildly-off product; or over-generalises (thinks every even number is a multiple of 4)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Practise pattern-as-check ('multiples of 4/8 are even; is yours?') and test the reverse claim with counterexamples (6 is even but not a multiple of 4) so the rule's limits are clear
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to check, the child has no test, or claims 18 is a multiple of 4 because it is even

responseLevels.gap: Skip-counts or guesses harder facts, mis-splits derivations, and applies no reasonableness check; patterns noticed but not used
responseLevels.full: Derives 8×7 from known facts, checks it against a pattern (even/between anchors), and states and tests a sequence rule — maintaining oversight of reasonableness and transferring the derive-and-check habit unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Derives a fact from anchors or states a pattern when prompted, but does not spontaneously check reasonableness or test/limit a generalisation

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You're sure that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16. Use those to work out 8 × 7 without counting up in eights. Then — how could you quickly check your answer looks sensible?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reaching 56 by skip-counting shows no repeated-reasoning insight; deriving it from anchor facts AND checking it against a pattern does. A child with the habit both decomposes and monitors reasonableness; a child without either counts up or accepts an answer with no check.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11; understand the CAUSES (cattle ranching — the biggest Amazon driver — plus soy, palm oil, logging, mining) and the SCALE of deforestation (~10 million hectares/year), and its impact on biodiversity, climate and indigenous peoples.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (land use, economic activity, distribution of natural resources) and Science Y6 'human impact on environments'; leads to KS3 'Earth and atmosphere'.
• Standards — US: NGSS 5-ESS3-1 and MS-ESS3-3/-4 (human activities affecting Earth's systems; managing human impact).
• Operational details — teach causes as an ECONOMIC chain (demand → land cleared for a cash crop/pasture → forest lost), naming cattle as the Amazon's largest single driver. On scale, the taxonomy's '~10 million hectares/year' is essentially right: FAO FRA 2025 gives GROSS deforestation of 10.9 Mha/year (2015–2025), down from 17.6 Mha in the 1990s; teach it as 'about the size of a country like Portugal/Iceland every year, though the rate is now falling'. Distinguish for stronger pupils: gross deforestation (~10.9 Mha) vs NET forest change (~4.1 Mha after regrowth), and 'deforestation' (permanent) vs temporary tree-cover loss (fire/logging that regrows). Link three impacts: biodiversity (habitat gone), climate (stored carbon released), indigenous peoples (homes and rights lost).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (9): name three causes. Tier B (10): state the ~10 million ha/year scale and explain two impacts. Tier C (11): trace a driver (beef/soy/palm) to forest loss and distinguish gross vs net loss or permanent vs temporary clearance.
bestPractices: Frame causes as an economic chain: demand → land cleared for a product → forest lost, with cattle named as the Amazon's biggest single driver.
Make the scale concrete by comparing ~10 Mha/year to a familiar country's area, and note the rate is now falling (avoid a doom-only framing).
Distinguish gross deforestation from net loss, and permanent deforestation from temporary tree-cover loss that regrows, for higher-attaining pupils.
Tie each impact to a mechanism (habitat destroyed → biodiversity; carbon released → climate; land taken → indigenous peoples).
Use up-to-date figures (FRA 2025) rather than older round numbers, and cite the source.
keyRepresentations: A land-use map/dashboard with drivers (cattle, soy, palm, logging, mining) and live forest/biodiversity/carbon meters.
A scale comparison: 10 Mha ≈ the area of a named country, shown against a map.
Before/after satellite imagery of a cleared region.
A driver→product→forest-loss flow chain.
commonMisconceptions: 'Deforestation is mostly people chopping wood for firewood' — the big drivers are commercial cattle, soy, palm oil, logging and mining.
'The whole rainforest will be gone next year' — the scale is huge but it is a percentage per year, and the rate is currently falling.
'Tree-cover loss and deforestation are the same' — some loss (fire, selective logging) regrows; deforestation is permanent land-use change.
'It only harms animals' — it also releases carbon (climate) and displaces indigenous communities.
'Trees just grow back quickly' — cleared rainforest on thin soil often does not recover its biodiversity.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, this guidance teaches the CAUSES of rainforest deforestation as an economic chain (demand → land cleared for a cash product → forest lost), with cattle ranching named as the Amazon's single largest driver, alongside soy, palm oil, logging and mining. It teaches the SCALE (gross deforestation ~10–11 million hectares worldwide per year, made concrete by comparison to a familiar country's area, with the note that the rate is currently falling) and links three impacts via their mechanisms: habitat loss → biodiversity, carbon release → climate, land taken → indigenous peoples. A manipulable land-use model is the lead activity; a reveal infographic, a sort-and-estimate practice task, an optional 3D flythrough, and (deferred) stakeholder dialogue are preserved as alternatives with distinct purposes.

activities.title: Land-use control panel: build the forest loss from ordinary demands
feedback: When a learner clears only one driver, point out which drivers they haven't yet accounted for and that cattle is the single biggest Amazon driver.
When the running total approaches the scale figure, anchor it to the country-area comparison and clarify that ~10 million ha/year is the WORLDWIDE annual total, not the loss of one region alone.

When regrowth/protection is toggled, highlight two separate ideas: protection reduces how much is cleared each year (gross loss), and regrowth makes net loss smaller than gross loss. Add that the real worldwide deforestation rate is high but has slowed in recent decades, so avoid a 'gone next year' reading.

If a learner treats all cleared land as permanently lost, use the regrowth toggle to distinguish temporary tree-cover loss (fire, selective logging) from permanent land-use change; add that cleared rainforest on thin soil often does not recover its original biodiversity even where some regrowth occurs.
activities.rationale: A drivers→consequences system is well suited to a manipulable model where cause-and-effect allocation is visible: allocating land and seeing forest, biodiversity, carbon and community meters respond may build a systems intuition that static facts alone do not. Live meters and the gross-vs-net toggle are concrete mechanisms intended to make the economic chain and the scale trend felt, not just stated. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention; the live-meter and toggle examples are illustrative, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Global GROSS deforestation is 10.9 million hectares per year for 2015–2025, down from 17.6 million ha/year in 1990–2000; net forest loss is about 4.12 million ha/year after accounting for forest expansion

Tropical primary rainforest loss was about 4.3 million hectares in 2025 (a record 6.7 Mha in 2024); cattle ranching is the largest single driver of Amazon deforestation, with soy, palm oil, logging and mining also major causes
learnerActions: Play the role of a developer on a map of a rainforest region: allocate patches of land to cattle pasture to meet beef demand, then add soy and palm plots, then logging and mining.
Watch linked meters recompute live as you clear land — forest area falls, a biodiversity/species meter drops, a CO2-released gauge climbs, and a marker shows a displaced community.

Play a year-timeline forward and watch the forest visibly shrink while a running total ticks upward; note that the worldwide annual total is about 10 million hectares a year, so the regional model shows how such demands accumulate.
Compare that worldwide annual total to a familiar country's area (e.g. roughly the size of Portugal or Iceland).

Switch on a second set of controls — regrowth and protected areas — and watch protected areas reduce how much forest is cleared each year (gross loss), while regrowth makes NET loss smaller than gross loss; note that the real worldwide deforestation rate has slowed over recent decades but is still high.
activities.intendedInsight: Deforestation is not random destruction but the sum of ordinary DEMANDS — beef, soy, palm, timber, minerals — each trading a patch of irreplaceable forest for a product; the totals are staggering yet changeable, and gross loss differs from net loss once regrowth is counted.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal driver infographic with before/after and scale comparison
feedback: If a learner expects firewood-gathering to dominate, reveal the commercial driver shares to correct it.
Reinforce that cattle ranching is the largest single Amazon driver when learners rank the causes.
activities.rationale: A reveal infographic delivers the causes and the scale statistic memorably and may support learners who need the facts anchored before modelling trade-offs. It conveys shares and mechanism clearly, though it does not itself let pupils explore the trade-offs a manipulable model can.
sourceClaims: Global GROSS deforestation is 10.9 million hectares per year for 2015–2025, down from 17.6 million ha/year in 1990–2000; net forest loss is about 4.12 million ha/year after accounting for forest expansion

Tropical primary rainforest loss was about 4.3 million hectares in 2025 (a record 6.7 Mha in 2024); cattle ranching is the largest single driver of Amazon deforestation, with soy, palm oil, logging and mining also major causes
learnerActions: Tap each driver hotspot (cattle, soy, palm oil, logging, mining) to reveal its share and the mechanism by which it clears forest.
Swipe a before/after satellite pair of a cleared region to see the change directly.
Study a scale visual showing '≈10.9 Mha worldwide per year = an area this big' set against a map of a familiar country.
activities.intendedInsight: In the Amazon and many tropical regions the major drivers are commercial land uses producing for national and export markets (not mainly firewood), and the annual worldwide scale is enormous but comparable to a real country's footprint.

activities.title: Sort the causes and estimate the annual scale
feedback: On the firewood distractor, redirect to the large commercial drivers clearing land for profit and export.
On the slider, give the real figure and the country-area comparison rather than only marking right/wrong.

For the regrowth-vs-ranch item, confirm that under the common definition used for the ~10 million ha figure, permanent conversion to farmland is deforestation while temporary loss that regrows is not, so not all tree-cover loss is permanent — and note thin-soil rainforest often does not recover its original biodiversity.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, estimation and mechanism-matching map cleanly onto the three evidence points and give clean practice and checking. A sort or match can teach and check classification but does not by itself elicit independent construction of the economic chain, so pupils are also asked to state the chain in their own words.
sourceClaims: Global GROSS deforestation is 10.9 million hectares per year for 2015–2025, down from 17.6 million ha/year in 1990–2000; net forest loss is about 4.12 million ha/year after accounting for forest expansion

Tropical primary rainforest loss was about 4.3 million hectares in 2025 (a record 6.7 Mha in 2024); cattle ranching is the largest single driver of Amazon deforestation, with soy, palm oil, logging and mining also major causes
learnerActions: Sort a set of cards into the main commercial drivers of Amazon and tropical deforestation (cattle, soy, palm, logging, mining) versus minor causes like 'villagers gathering firewood'.
Use a slider to estimate how many hectares of forest are lost worldwide each year, then compare your estimate against the real figure (~10–11 million ha/year gross worldwide).
Answer short questions matching each impact to its mechanism: habitat loss → biodiversity, carbon release → climate, land taken → indigenous peoples.
Decide whether two scenarios are both 'deforestation': a patch logged that regrows over 30 years versus a patch turned permanently into a cattle ranch — and explain why.
State the driver→product→forest-loss chain in your own words for one driver.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can identify the dominant commercial drivers, place the annual worldwide scale, and distinguish permanent deforestation from temporary tree-cover loss that regrows.

activities.title: Optional: 3D flythrough over cleared vs intact forest
feedback: If learners focus only on the visual drama, link it back to which demands drove the clearance and to the scale figures from the other activities.
activities.rationale: A 3D flythrough may make the contrast between cleared and intact forest visceral. The drivers-and-quantities learning is also carried by the 2D map/model, so this is an optional enrichment rather than the core, and is practical only where a reusable terrain asset already exists. No claim is made that 3D is more or less effective than the 2D model; efficacy is untested.
learnerActions: View or navigate a 3D flythrough that passes over cleared land beside intact rainforest to see the contrast directly.
Relate what you see to the drivers and quantities studied in the other activities — which demands drove this clearance, and how it adds to the annual total.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing cleared versus intact forest in 3D can make the loss vivid, while the core learning remains the drivers and quantities behind it.

activities.title: Optional: competing stakeholders (deferred extension)
feedback: Where learners cast one group as the sole cause, surface the chain of demand connecting consumers, producers and land clearance.
activities.rationale: Multi-stakeholder dialogue may surface competing motives, but that debate belongs to a downstream 'Futures & Trade-Offs' topic; at this stage the goal is understanding causes and scale, so keep this as an optional extension rather than the core.
learnerActions: Hear from or role-play a rancher, a logger and a conservationist, each stating their motives for and against clearing forest.
Identify the competing demands and trade-offs behind a single cleared patch.
activities.intendedInsight: Behind forest loss sit real people with competing economic motives; deforestation decisions involve trade-offs, not simple villains.

constraints: Core objective is understanding causes (as an economic demand chain) and scale, plus linking three impacts to mechanisms — not stakeholder debate, which is a later topic.

Sort/estimate/match formats can teach and check classification and recall, but recognition-only tasks do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the economic chain; have learners state the driver→product→forest-loss chain in their own words.

The reveal infographic, sort/estimate task and 3D flythrough are scaffolds; they do not let learners explore trade-offs the way the manipulable model does, and no medium is asserted as universally superior.
Avoid a doom-only framing: state that the rate is high but currently falling, and distinguish gross deforestation from net loss and permanent deforestation from temporary tree-cover loss.
Present the ~10 million ha/year figure as approximate and as a WORLDWIDE annual total, and cite up-to-date sources rather than older round numbers.
Address the misconception that 'trees just grow back': cleared rainforest on thin soil often does not recover its original biodiversity, even where some regrowth occurs.
