Figure reconciliation: the pedagogy/evidence state '~10 million hectares/year' while FAO FRA 2025 gives gross ~10.9 Mha/year (2015–2025) and net ~4.12 Mha/year; these are consistent if '10 million' is read as the approximate GROSS worldwide figure. Activities use '~10–11 million ha/year gross' and explicitly contrast net loss to avoid conflating the two.
The ~10 million ha/year figure is global; the lead model depicts one rainforest region, so feedback explicitly clarifies the total is worldwide to avoid implying a single region loses that amount.

The WRI/Global Forest Watch source (cattle as largest Amazon driver; tropical primary forest loss figures) is marked verified:false in the row; the DfE curriculum source is also verified:false. Country-area comparisons (Portugal/Iceland) are approximate illustrations of scale, not precise equivalences; present them as rough visual anchors.

probeDeeper: Which single activity clears the most Amazon rainforest?
About how much forest is lost worldwide each year?
Name two different kinds of harm deforestation causes beyond losing trees.
A patch is logged and grows back over 30 years; another is turned into a permanent cattle ranch. Are both 'deforestation'? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: No — firewood-gathering is not the main cause. Most large-scale deforestation is commercial: clearing land for cattle ranching (the biggest driver in the Amazon), soy and palm oil plantations, logging for timber, and mining — clearing huge areas for profit and export. Roughly 10 million hectares of forest are lost worldwide each year, harming biodiversity, the climate, and indigenous communities.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A lot of people think rainforests are mostly cut down by poor villagers gathering firewood. Is that the main cause of large-scale deforestation? Tell me yes or no, then tell me what the biggest causes really are and WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child blaming small-scale firewood or local poverty misidentifies the driver; the concept child names the big COMMERCIAL, export-driven causes (cattle/soy/palm/logging/mining) and the global scale. The reason-tier forces the profit-and-scale reasoning.

pedagogy.summary: Two shapes are SIMILAR when one is a scaled copy of the other: corresponding angles are equal and every pair of corresponding sides is in the SAME ratio (the scale factor). Solving similar-shape problems means (1) finding the scale factor from a known pair of corresponding sides, then (2) multiplying (to enlarge) or dividing (to reduce) the other sides by it. The pedagogical crux is that enlargement is MULTIPLICATIVE, not additive: every side is multiplied by the SAME factor, so the shape keeps its proportions. Children must resist adding a constant to each side (which distorts the shape) and, when area comes in, must learn that a length scale factor k multiplies AREA by k².
bestPractices: Establish 'same shape, sides in the same ratio, equal angles' as the definition of similar before any calculation; contrast a genuine enlargement with a stretched (distorted) copy.
Find the scale factor first from a matched pair of corresponding sides (new ÷ old), then apply it to every other side — make 'multiply by the SAME number' explicit.

Confront the additive error directly: show that adding the same amount to each side changes the shape (a 2×5 rectangle + 4 to each side is 6×9, no longer similar), whereas multiplying keeps it similar.
When perimeter/area appear, build the k² result from a diagram: doubling the sides of a rectangle makes FOUR copies fit inside, so area ×4 not ×2 (MAP Enlargements).
Use a ratio table / double number line pairing corresponding sides so the constant multiplier is visible across all pairs.
keyRepresentations: Ratio table pairing corresponding sides (old side | new side), scale factor as the column multiplier
Overlaid/nested shapes on a grid showing the enlargement from a centre
Area grid showing k² tiling (double sides → four sub-rectangles)
The scale-factor arrow (×k) applied to every corresponding side
commonMisconceptions: Additive enlargement — adding the same amount to each side instead of multiplying by the scale factor (distorts the shape; the classic Hart/CSMS rectangle error).
Treating 'similar' as 'roughly the same shape' or as 'congruent/identical', not checking that all sides share one ratio.
Believing that doubling the lengths doubles the area (area actually scales by k²; MAP Enlargements documents this as a persistent error).
Applying the scale factor to only one side, or using new÷old for one pair and old÷new for another (inconsistent direction).

learn.summary: Similar shapes are scaled copies: corresponding angles are equal and every pair of corresponding sides shares one ratio (the scale factor). Learners find the scale factor from a known matched pair (new ÷ old), then multiply the other sides by that same factor (a factor greater than 1 enlarges; a factor less than 1, such as 1/3, reduces — equivalently, when reducing you can divide by the enlargement factor). The pedagogical crux is that enlargement is MULTIPLICATIVE, not additive — adding a constant to each side generally distorts the shape (e.g. any non-square rectangle; a square or equilateral triangle is an exception) — and that a length scale factor k scales area by k² (and volume by k³ for solids).

activities.title: Enlargement studio: grab, scale, and compare with additive mode
feedback: If you scaled only one side: ask whether the new shape is still the same shape — overlay it and check that EVERY corresponding side grew by the same multiplier.

If additive mode looked 'about right', overlay it on the original's diagonal: a true enlargement stays on the diagonal; the additive copy of a non-square rectangle slides off it, showing distorted proportions.
When you predicted area, compare your guess with the tiled count: doubling sides gives four tiles (×4), tripling gives nine (×9) — area follows k².
activities.rationale: Live manipulation with a locked aspect ratio plus a contrasting additive mode may make the multiplicative nature of enlargement observable, so the documented additive error becomes visible rather than merely asserted. The tiling overlay builds the k² area result from a concrete diagram. The additive mode, ratio table, diagonal check and tiling overlay are optional illustrative mechanisms, not the only way to teach this.
sourceClaims: Students apply inappropriate ADDITIVE strategies to multiplicative scaling situations (adding a constant rather than multiplying by a scale factor) — a documented error in proportional-reasoning classroom trials.

Doubling the length and width of a rectangle multiplies its area by 4, not 2; for similar shapes the area scale factor is the square of the scale factor (k²) and the volume scale factor is k³ — documented as a persistent student misconception (treating price/area as scaling linearly).
learnerActions: Work on a grid with a non-square rectangle or triangle whose aspect ratio is locked. Drag a corner to enlarge it and watch a live scale-factor readout while every side multiplies by the same factor and the angles stay unchanged; for a rectangle enlarged from a fixed corner, notice the dragged opposite corner moves along the original's diagonal, showing it is the same shape.
Fill a ratio table alongside (old side | new side for each pair) and check that the same column multiplier appears for every pair of corresponding sides.

Flip to an 'additive mode' that instead ADDS your chosen number to each side of the non-square rectangle; observe it stretch lopsided and fall off the original's diagonal — it is no longer similar. Compare directly with the multiplicative result.
Turn on a grid-tiling overlay: with a scale factor of 2, see FOUR copies of the original tile the new shape; with a factor of 3, nine copies fit — connect this to area × k².
If a scaling touches only one side, use the flag that highlights the unchanged side and correct it so every corresponding side is scaled.
activities.intendedInsight: Enlargement multiplies every corresponding side by the SAME factor, preserving shape and angles; adding the same amount to each side of a non-square rectangle distorts it. Because the shape grows in two dimensions, area scales by k², not by k.

activities.title: Confront the additive error on paper
feedback: Compare the two ratios as numbers: 6/9 (= 2/3) does not equal 2/5, so the additive version is not a true enlargement.
If unsure, draw both shapes to scale and overlay a corner — the similar one nests exactly along the diagonal.
activities.rationale: Explicitly performing and comparing the additive versus multiplicative transformation targets the classic Hart/CSMS rectangle error. Worked on paper this needs no device and makes the ratio check the decider.
sourceClaims: Students apply inappropriate ADDITIVE strategies to multiplicative scaling situations (adding a constant rather than multiplying by a scale factor) — a documented error in proportional-reasoning classroom trials.
learnerActions: Take a 2×5 rectangle. Add 4 to each side to get a 6×9 rectangle, and draw both. Check whether the side ratios match: 2:5 versus 6:9 — they do not, so the shapes are not similar.
Now enlarge the same 2×5 rectangle by a scale factor, multiplying each side by 3 to get 6×15, and confirm 2:5 and 6:15 are the same ratio.
State in your own words why 'add the same to each side' changes the shape while 'multiply each side by the same number' keeps it.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a constant to every side changed the proportions of the 2×5 rectangle (as it does for any non-square rectangle); multiplying every side by a common factor always keeps corresponding sides in a single ratio and preserves the shape.

activities.title: Solve and judge similar-shape problems
feedback: If you wrote 21, you added the 12 difference; instead find the factor (×3) and apply it — the correct missing side is 27 cm.
If you said the area is 3× bigger, tile it: a factor of 3 fits nine copies, so area is ×9 (54 → 486 cm²).

On a reduction, sense-check direction: the answer should be SMALLER than the side you began with, so divide by the enlargement factor (e.g. ÷3) or, equivalently, multiply by the new ÷ old factor (e.g. ×1/3).
Keep new ÷ old consistent — do not use new ÷ old for one pair and old ÷ new for another.
activities.rationale: These items make the scale factor, the additive distractor, the direction-of-application slip and the area-scaling error separately assessable. Watching the working (e.g. 27 via ×3 versus 21 via +12) reveals which strategy a learner used; recognition items alone would not elicit this production. Pair it with the manipulation activities so the rule is understood, not just recognised.
sourceClaims: Pupils should solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found (Year 6 ratio and proportion).

Doubling the length and width of a rectangle multiplies its area by 4, not 2; for similar shapes the area scale factor is the square of the scale factor (k²) and the volume scale factor is k³ — documented as a persistent student misconception (treating price/area as scaling linearly).
learnerActions: Given a rectangle 6×9 enlarged so 6→18, find the scale factor (18 ÷ 6 = 3) and the missing side (9 × 3 = 27 cm). Beware of adding the difference 12 to get 21 — that is the additive error, not a valid answer.
Find the scale factor between two similar triangles from a matched pair of side lengths, keeping new ÷ old consistent for the comparison.

Judge whether two given shapes are similar by testing EVERY pair of corresponding sides for the same ratio, not by appearance, and by checking that corresponding angles are equal (for triangles, matching side ratios are enough; for other polygons they are not, e.g. a square and a non-square rhombus). One mismatched ratio means not similar.

For a REDUCTION (e.g. 18 back to 6), decide first whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the side you start from; then divide by the enlargement factor (÷3), which is the same as multiplying by the new ÷ old factor (6 ÷ 18 = 1/3).
On an area follow-up for the 6×9→18×27 rectangle, reason that area scales by k² = 3² = 9 (54 cm² → 486 cm²), not by 3.
activities.intendedInsight: Problem solving means finding the scale factor from a known pair, applying it in the correct direction to every side, checking similarity by shared ratio, and using k² for area.

activities.title: Optional extension: scaling a solid to feel k² and k³
feedback: If you expected volume to double when edges double, count the unit cubes: eight small cubes fit, so volume is ×8 (2³).
Keep the core objective in view — this 3D view is an extension beyond the 2D similar-shapes task.
activities.rationale: A solid-scaling sandbox may give a concrete feel for how area and volume grow with dimension, complementing the 2D work. This is explicitly optional and exceeds the stated 2D objective; it should not replace the primary 2D activities.
sourceClaims: Doubling the length and width of a rectangle multiplies its area by 4, not 2; for similar shapes the area scale factor is the square of the scale factor (k²) and the volume scale factor is k³ — documented as a persistent student misconception (treating price/area as scaling linearly).
learnerActions: Enlarge a cube or cuboid with a slider and watch surface area grow by k² and volume by k³.
Fill the enlarged solid with unit cubes to count that doubling every edge of a cube gives 2³ = 8 times the volume, and relate the growing faces to k² area.
Return to a flat similar-shapes problem and restate: length ×k, area ×k², and for solids volume ×k³.
activities.intendedInsight: Scaling length by k scales area by k² and, for solids, volume by k³ — the same multiplicative idea extended by dimension.

constraints: Establish the definition — same shape, equal angles, ALL corresponding sides in one ratio — and contrast a true enlargement with a stretched copy BEFORE any calculation.
Find the scale factor first from a matched pair (new ÷ old), then apply the SAME factor to every other side; make 'multiply by the same number' explicit.

A static nested-shapes diagram with tap-to-reveal '×k per side' and 'area ×k²' can consolidate the rule as a reference card, but does not let the learner manipulate and watch the additive distortion occur; use it after, not instead of, hands-on work.

Multiple-choice/recognition items (e.g. choosing which pair is similar) assess discrimination but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of finding and applying a scale factor; include fill-in and show-your-working tasks for production.
Keep the direction of division consistent (new ÷ old) within a comparison, and sense-check whether the answer should be larger or smaller before computing.
The 3D solid-scaling activity is an optional extension that goes beyond the 2D similar-shapes objective and must not be the main teaching artefact.

Illustrative interface features (locked aspect ratio, live scale-factor readout, additive-mode toggle, diagonal check, tiling overlay, ratio table, single-side flag) are examples of the learning mechanism, not mandatory requirements.

The additive-mode distortion demonstration should use a non-square rectangle, since a square keeps its shape under equal additions; present the additive result (e.g. 21) only as a flagged error, never as a valid answer option.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying principle, not the specific activity designs.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic): 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 9 × 3 = 27 are correct; the additive distractor 21 comes from 9 + 12 where 12 = 18 − 6. For a scale factor of 3, nine copies tile the area (3² = 9) and area 6×9 = 54 cm² becomes 486 cm² (18×27=486=54×9). Volume for a doubled edge is 2³ = 8, correct. In Activity 2, 2+4=6 and 5+4=9 (additive, not similar: 2/5≠2/3); 2×3=6 and 5×3=15 (multiplicative, similar: 2/5=6/15).

The original design used a scale-factor-2 tiling example showing FOUR copies (2²=4), while the worked problem uses factor 3 giving nine copies (3²=9); both are internally consistent and kept distinct to avoid conflating the example with the problem.

Activity 1 keeps the enlargement studio's aspect ratio locked; otherwise a free corner-drag would change width and height independently and distort the shape, contradicting the same-factor/angle-preserving behaviour.

The additive-mode 'falls off the diagonal' behaviour holds for non-square rectangles; a square would remain similar under equal additions, so the demonstration is scoped to non-square cases and treated as an illustrative affordance, not an invariant law.

The original artefact framing asserted a conversation 'cannot exercise' the skill and that 3D 'overshoots'; these are softened to scoped limits (in-role dialogue is a poor fit for this spatial-procedural practice; 3D is an optional extension) rather than universal pedagogical laws.

The double-number-line representation from the original was folded into the ratio-table scaffold rather than dropped; centre-of-enlargement detail was not emphasised as it exceeds the stated scale-factor objective.

probeDeeper: Is your enlarged rectangle the SAME shape as the original — how could you check that all the sides grew in the same way?
What is the scale factor here, and what does it mean to say the sides are 'in the same ratio'?
Now think about AREA: the original is 6×9 = 54 cm². What is the area of the enlarged one — is it 3 times bigger? (counterexample forcing the k² idea: it is 9 times bigger.)
If instead I SHRANK the rectangle so the 18 went back to 6, what would you do to the other side — multiply or divide, and by what?
assess.correctAnswer: 27 cm. The scale factor is 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so every side is multiplied by 3: the 9 cm side becomes 9 × 3 = 27 cm.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive enlargement — adds the constant difference (here +12) to each side instead of multiplying by the scale factor
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'is the new rectangle the SAME shape as the old one?' Draw both and overlay — the additive version is distorted. Rebuild on a ratio table: every side ×3. Reteach multiplicative missing-value ratio.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 9 + 12 = 21, having taken the 18−6 = 12 increase from the known side and added it to the other; no scale factor computed

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 'similar' as 'roughly the same shape' or 'congruent', not checking that all sides share one ratio
errorPatterns.nextMove: Restate the definition: same shape, equal angles, ALL sides in the same ratio. Test each side pair — one mismatched ratio means not similar. Reteach the vocabulary of ratio/proportion/scale.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When judging whether two given shapes are similar, decides on appearance ('they both look like rectangles') without comparing side ratios, or assumes similar means identical

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes doubling the lengths doubles the area (ignores that area scales by the square of the scale factor)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tile the enlarged rectangle with copies of the original on a grid — a scale factor of 3 fits 9 copies. Establish length ×k → area ×k². Reteach area of rectangles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On an area follow-up, says the enlarged rectangle's area is 3× (or 2×) the original instead of 3² = 9×; treats area like a length

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds the scale factor correctly but applies it in the wrong direction (multiplies when reducing, or divides when enlarging)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: ask 'is the answer meant to be bigger or smaller than the side you started from?' before computing, as a sense-check on the direction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes the factor as 3 but on a REDUCTION problem multiplies anyway, giving a bigger shape when it should be smaller

responseLevels.gap: Adds the constant difference to the other side (21), or judges similarity by appearance; does not find or apply a scale factor.
responseLevels.full: Finds the scale factor (×3), applies it to give 27, explains that all corresponding sides share that ratio so the shape is preserved, correctly reasons that area scales by k² (×9), and handles a reduction by dividing — transferring the method to an unfamiliar shape.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the scale factor and the missing side correctly for lengths, but slips on area (says ×3 not ×9) or cannot reliably judge whether two new shapes are similar — the multiplicative rule is not yet secure across cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a rectangle 6 cm by 9 cm. I enlarge it so the 6 cm side becomes 18 cm, and the new rectangle is similar to the old one. Work out the length of the other side. Show your working.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning multiplicatively finds the scale factor (×3) and applies it to the other side, giving 27 — a value only that method produces. A child using the additive strategy sees the 6→18 side grew by 12 and adds 12 to the other side, giving 21. The two children produce different numbers by different routes, and watching the working (not asking them to state a rule) shows immediately which they used.

sources.claim: Doubling the length and width of a rectangle multiplies its area by 4, not 2; for similar shapes the area scale factor is the square of the scale factor (k²) and the volume scale factor is k³ — documented as a persistent student misconception (treating price/area as scaling linearly).
sources.source: Shell Centre / Mathematics Assessment Project (MAP), 'Evaluating Statements About Enlargements' teacher guide (Common Issues + whole-class introduction)

sources.claim: Students apply inappropriate ADDITIVE strategies to multiplicative scaling situations (adding a constant rather than multiplying by a scale factor) — a documented error in proportional-reasoning classroom trials.
sources.source: Shell Centre / Mathematics Assessment Project (MAP), 'Proportion and Non-Proportion Situations' (Grade 7)

sources.claim: Pupils should solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found (Year 6 ratio and proportion).
sources.source: UK National Curriculum, Mathematics programmes of study

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Electromagnets

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics, 'Magnetism'):** 'the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only)'.

- **Standards — US (NGSS, MS Forces & Interactions — MS-PS2-3):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-3] — the clarification statement explicitly names 'the effect of the number of turns of wire on the strength of an electromagnet' (DCI PS2.B; assessment of quantitative questions limited to proportional reasoning).

- **Operational details:** The new idea: magnetism can be CREATED by an electric current — a current-carrying wire has a circular field; coiling the wire adds the loops' fields into a bar-magnet-like field (solenoid); a soft-iron core concentrates it. Its defining feature is that it can be switched ON/OFF and varied, unlike a permanent magnet. Pupils INVESTIGATE the three strength factors (current, number of turns, soft-iron core) as a controlled fair test — qualitative/proportional reasoning, NOT quantitative field-strength calculation.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B→C (early-formal, age 12-13).
bestPractices: Build the idea in the sequence single wire → coil → cored coil: a current makes a circular field around a wire; coiling adds each loop's field; a soft-iron core greatly strengthens it.
Foreground the defining advantage — an electromagnet is switchable on/off and adjustable in strength — and anchor it in real uses (scrapyard crane, relay, MRI, maglev).

Investigate the three factors as a controlled fair test: change current OR turns OR core while holding the others constant; measure strength by paperclips lifted (or a force meter); take repeat readings.
Vary current safely with 0/1/2/3 cells in series rather than a power pack (which overheats the wire); demonstrate if needed.
Insist on precise language: 'turns' are loops added to ONE coil (not 'more coils'), and the wire must be INSULATED so the current goes round every turn rather than shorting across touching turns.
Use a SOFT-iron core (magnetises and demagnetises instantly) and explain why steel (a 'hard' magnetic material) is wrong — it would stay magnetised and not switch off.
keyRepresentations: Single straight wire with a circular field shown by plotting compasses around it
Coil/solenoid with a bar-magnet-like field; the classic nail-and-coil electromagnet
Fair-test results table: factor varied vs strength (paperclips lifted)
Cells-in-series to step the current; turns counted compactly along one core
Real-device images: scrapyard crane, relay, MRI, maglev
commonMisconceptions: 'Turns' means 'number of coils' — turns are loops on a single coil (Oak).
A magnetic field is the same as the electric field around a charged object — a charged balloon does NOT deflect a compass, but a current-carrying wire does (Oak).
Bare/uninsulated wire is needed for the coil — insulated wire is needed so the current loops each turn (Oak).

Faulty causal stories for why paperclips fall off when switched off ('the magnetism returns to the power pack', 'the wire overheated', 'the clips repel') — the cause is simply no current = no field (Oak).
Any metal core (e.g. copper) will strengthen it — it must be ferromagnetic soft iron; ties to the wider 'all metals are magnetic' error (Oak).
Confusing the MEASURE of strength (paperclips held) with a CAUSE of strength.

learn.summary: Learners aged 12–13 build and investigate an electromagnet to understand that magnetism is created by an electric current, that the magnet can be switched on/off and varied (unlike a permanent magnet), and that its strength depends on current, number of turns on a single coil, and a soft-iron core. The core sequence is a controlled fair-test investigation (change one variable at a time, measure strength by paperclips lifted, take repeats) using qualitative/proportional reasoning rather than quantitative field calculation. A hands-on coil-winding kit with a force meter is the fullest form; a live-state interactive bench is a strong digital stand-in, with diagnostic questions, a labelled reference image, and an optional coil-winding sandbox as supporting layers.

activities.title: Electromagnet test bench: isolate what changes the strength
feedback: When current stops, the current-produced coil field stops. A suitable soft-iron core usually loses most induced magnetisation, unlike a harder magnetic material that retains more; inspect the actual result rather than treating retained clips as proof that current was not the field’s source.

Switching off stops the current-produced coil field; it does not send magnetism back to the supply or make the clips repel. Compare the actual switch-off result, allowing for small residual core magnetism.

Compare measured strength with soft iron and copper or no core. Soft iron supplies substantial ferromagnetic strengthening in this chosen apparatus, while copper does not; the current-carrying coil still has a field in every case, and whether it lifts a clip depends on its strength and the setup.
If a learner says 'more coils' instead of 'more turns': turns are extra loops added to ONE coil; count them along the single core.
If two variables were changed in one run, point out you cannot tell which caused the change — repeat with only one varied.

Soft iron is chosen because it magnetises readily and typically retains little magnetisation after the applied field is removed. Harder magnetic materials such as steel can retain more, making clean switch-off less effective; test the actual core rather than promising instant complete demagnetisation.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable bench lets learners isolate each of the three factors and witness the switch-off drop, directly confronting the named causal misconceptions (stored magnetism, any-metal core, voltage vs current) while practising fair-test logic. The strength relationships and the fair test are well captured in a 2D live-state model; a real kit adds the enquiry craft of winding, noisy measurement and repeat readings.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-3: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-3]; clarification explicitly cites the effect of the number of turns of wire on the strength of an electromagnet; DCI PS2.B — electromagnetic force sizes depend on currents/magnetic strengths and distances.

A current in a wire makes a magnetic field; coiling adds the loops' fields; a soft-iron core strengthens it and lets it switch on/off (steel would stay magnetised). Strength rises with more turns, greater current, and a soft-iron core. Named misconceptions: turns vs coils; magnetic vs electrostatic field (charged balloon doesn't deflect a compass); needing bare wire; faulty reasons for clips falling; copper core working. Vary current safely with cells, not a power pack.
KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only).
learnerActions: Build the electromagnet: wind insulated wire around a soft-iron nail and connect it to cells so it picks up paperclips.
Before switching off, predict out loud what will happen to the dangling paperclips the instant the circuit is broken, and WHY.

Switch the current off and observe how many paperclips fall or remain. The current-produced coil field disappears; a suitable soft-iron core usually loses most induced magnetism, but residual core magnetism or sticking can leave some clips attached.
For the current test, keep turns and core fixed and use teacher-approved current-limited settings. Measure the current and record paperclips lifted at each setting, with repeat readings.

For the turns test, keep the core fixed, add turns to the same coil, and check the measured current stays fixed using the approved controls; otherwise note current as a confounding change. Record repeat strength measurements.

For the core test, hold measured current and turns fixed and compare soft iron, copper, wood and no core. Record the actual paperclip counts or compass response. The current-carrying coil produces a field without iron; soft iron normally strengthens it substantially, while copper and wood do not provide that ferromagnetic strengthening. Do not predetermine that the core-free coil cannot lift a clip.
Each run, change only ONE variable; if more than one is changed, note it as a confounded run that cannot show a single cause.
Optionally overlay plotting compasses or a compass near the coil to show the solenoid's bar-magnet-like field.
activities.intendedInsight: Current produces the coil’s magnetic field, which can be controlled by switching or changing the current. A soft-iron core strengthens the field and usually retains little magnetisation after switch-off. Strength depends on current, turns and core material; changing one measured variable at a time helps isolate a cause.

activities.title: Build the idea: single wire → coil → cored coil, and real uses
feedback: If a learner claims a single straight wire has no field: a compass placed near a straight current-carrying wire deflects (Oersted); coiling just concentrates the field.

If a learner treats the magnetic field as the same as the field around a charged object: a static charge produces no magnetic field, while a current produces a steady circular magnetic field round the wire. Any slight pull of the needle towards a charged balloon is electrostatic attraction, not magnetism.
If a learner thinks bare wire is needed: the wire must be INSULATED so current goes round every turn instead of shorting across touching turns.
For real uses, tie each example back to current-based control — the crane drops its load by cutting the current, while devices such as MRI and maglev rely on strong current-controlled fields.
activities.rationale: Building the concept in the single wire → coil → cored coil sequence grounds why each stage increases strength and separates magnetic from electrostatic effects, while real-device anchoring makes the current-controlled advantage memorable. A labelled reference image with tap-to-reveal parts and a real-uses gallery supports vocabulary but, being static, cannot run the fair test or show the switch-off drop, so it complements rather than replaces the bench.
sourceClaims: A current in a wire makes a magnetic field; coiling adds the loops' fields; a soft-iron core strengthens it and lets it switch on/off (steel would stay magnetised). Strength rises with more turns, greater current, and a soft-iron core. Named misconceptions: turns vs coils; magnetic vs electrostatic field (charged balloon doesn't deflect a compass); needing bare wire; faulty reasons for clips falling; copper core working. Vary current safely with cells, not a power pack.
KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: the magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets, D.C. motors (principles only).
learnerActions: Hold plotting compasses around a single straight current-carrying wire and observe the circular field around it. Compare with a charged balloon: a static charge produces no steady magnetic field. A strongly charged balloon can still tug the needle slightly by electrostatic attraction, but it does not make the steady circular pattern around the wire that the current does.
Coil the wire and observe how the loops' fields add to make a bar-magnet-like field (a solenoid).
Add a soft-iron core and observe the field strengthen.

Match real devices to magnetism CREATED and CONTROLLED by an electric current — scrapyard crane, relay, MRI, maglev — explaining the control each relies on: the crane and relay most clearly switch the magnet on and off, while MRI and maglev depend on strong, current-controlled fields that can be set or varied.
Explain in your own words why a scrapyard crane can pick up AND drop a car just by switching the current, while a simple permanent magnet cannot be switched off to release it.
activities.intendedInsight: Magnetism can be CREATED by a current; coiling concentrates it and a soft-iron core strengthens it, and the defining advantage over a permanent magnet is being switchable and adjustable. A magnetic field (from current) is distinct from the electric field around a static charge.

activities.title: Diagnose causes and vocabulary: why did the clips fall?
feedback: Stopping current removes the current-produced coil field, which is why a suitable soft-iron electromagnet usually releases its load. Magnetism is not returned to the supply, and the clips do not drop because they suddenly repel; real cores may retain a little magnetisation.

A soft-iron (ferromagnetic) core increases strength; a copper core (like no core) does not give that strengthening. It leaves only the coil's own field, which is usually much weaker but may still lift clips if the current and turns are large enough.
On voltage vs current: field strength is set by the current through the coil; adding cells raises current (and voltage together), so credit the current rather than voltage alone.
A core-free coil with current still produces a field. Soft iron strengthens that field and usually loses most induced magnetisation after disconnection, though some residual magnetism may remain.
Distinguish the MEASURE of strength (paperclips held) from a CAUSE of strength (current, turns, core).
activities.rationale: Diagnostic questions that reuse the documented faulty-cause distractors give precise retrieval and formative assessment of the targeted misconceptions. These check understanding rather than build the investigation, so they are best used alongside the hands-on/interactive work rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: A current in a wire makes a magnetic field; coiling adds the loops' fields; a soft-iron core strengthens it and lets it switch on/off (steel would stay magnetised). Strength rises with more turns, greater current, and a soft-iron core. Named misconceptions: turns vs coils; magnetic vs electrostatic field (charged balloon doesn't deflect a compass); needing bare wire; faulty reasons for clips falling; copper core working. Vary current safely with cells, not a power pack.
learnerActions: Answer a diagnostic question on why the paperclips fall off when the current stops, choosing between faulty-cause explanations ('magnetism returns to the power pack', 'the wire overheated', 'the clips repel') and the correct 'no current = no current-produced coil field (a soft-iron core keeps only a little residual magnetism)'.

Sort proposed changes into those that DO and DON'T increase strength (e.g. more current, more turns, soft-iron core vs copper core); and address 'voltage-only' reasoning by noting that strength is set by the current through the coil (adding cells raises both voltage and current together).
Fill in the key vocabulary: turns, insulated, soft iron.
Predict whether a coil with current but NO iron core would still deflect a compass, and whether the nail stays magnetic after disconnection, then justify each answer.
activities.intendedInsight: The current produces the coil field; turns are loops of insulated wire on one coil. A soft-iron core is a useful strengthening material with low retained magnetisation, but the core-free coil still produces a field and may lift clips if sufficiently strong.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain and probing discussion
feedback: If a learner expects the nail to stay strongly magnetic, test it after switch-off: a soft-iron nail usually keeps only a little residual magnetism, while a steel nail may keep more. If a learner expects a bare coil to do nothing, run the bare coil (or a straight current-carrying wire near a compass) to show current alone makes a field; the soft-iron core amplifies it.
If a learner credits voltage not current: current is the rate of flow of charge, and the field depends on the current through the coil.
If a learner denies a straight wire has any field: the Oersted demo shows a compass deflecting under a straight current-carrying wire.
Full response: field produced by current (switchable), core concentrates but isn't the source, and strength relates to current, turns and core — applied to the crane picking up and dropping a car.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain cycle with targeted probes is a strong way to elicit and confront the specific errors documented here, especially the discriminating 'remove the core' test. It is a teaching and assessment routine rather than a quantitative investigation and pairs naturally with the bench work.
sourceClaims: A current in a wire makes a magnetic field; coiling adds the loops' fields; a soft-iron core strengthens it and lets it switch on/off (steel would stay magnetised). Strength rises with more turns, greater current, and a soft-iron core. Named misconceptions: turns vs coils; magnetic vs electrostatic field (charged balloon doesn't deflect a compass); needing bare wire; faulty reasons for clips falling; copper core working. Vary current safely with cells, not a power pack.
learnerActions: Predict what happens to the paperclips the instant the battery is disconnected, and WHY, before carrying it out.
Predict whether the coil ALONE (nail removed) can deflect a nearby compass, then test it.

Answer probing questions: would the core-free coil still affect a compass and why; name one change that strengthens it and one that doesn't and why; why can a scrapyard crane pick up AND drop a car; what actually produces the field — the metal, the battery, or the moving charge?

Explain that current produces the coil field and switching current off removes that contribution; a soft-iron core strengthens the field and usually retains little magnetisation. Relate measured strength to current, turns and core material.
activities.intendedInsight: Committing to a prediction then testing it surfaces the 'iron-is-the-magnet' and 'voltage-not-current' ideas and pins the field to the moving charge; learners should be able to transfer the reasoning to real devices like a scrapyard crane.

constraints: Keep reasoning qualitative/proportional: investigate how strength depends on current, turns and core, not quantitative field-strength calculation (consistent with the age range and MS-PS2-3's proportional-reasoning limit).

Use a teacher-approved low-voltage, current-limited classroom circuit and its instructions. Cells and power supplies can both overheat a low-resistance coil; adding cells is not inherently safe. Keep practical tests brief, disconnect between readings and stop if wire or cells warm.
Use INSULATED wire so current goes round every turn instead of shorting across touching turns; count 'turns' as loops on a single coil, not 'more coils'.

Use a suitable soft-iron core to demonstrate substantial strengthening and usually little retained magnetisation after switch-off. Steel may retain more magnetisation. Copper and wood lack the ferromagnetic strengthening of soft iron, but a current-carrying core-free coil still produces a field and can lift clips if current, turns and geometry suffice; observe actual strength rather than hardcoding a no-lift outcome.
Fair testing requires changing only one variable at a time with repeat readings; a confounded run (two variables changed) cannot attribute a change to a single cause.

A static labelled image supports vocabulary and real-use anchoring but cannot run the fair test or show the switch-off drop, so the causal and investigative learning needs the hands-on kit or the live interactive bench. A 3D coil-winding sandbox adds spatial/building experience but the strength relationships are captured in 2D; treat it as optional enrichment, not the core teacher.

A real coil-winding plus force-meter kit adds enquiry craft (winding, noisy measurement, repeats) that a simulation only models; where feasible accompany or precede the digital bench with the physical investigation.
Distinguish the MEASURE of strength (paperclips held or force-meter reading) from the CAUSES of strength (current, turns, core).
Field strength is set by the current through the coil; attribute strength to current (adding cells raises current and voltage together), not to voltage alone.
Anchor real uses to current-created, current-controlled fields: the crane and relay clearly switch on/off, while MRI and maglev rely on strong controllable fields rather than routine on/off toggling.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The Oak National Academy source is marked verified:false in the row; treat its specific misconception list and safety guidance as informative but unverified. The DfE and NGSS sources are marked verified:true.

Claims in the legacy recommendation that a static image 'cannot teach' the causal/investigative content, that no conversation persona can advance the investigation, and that the live sim is uniquely suited have been softened to scoped affordances/limits; comparative efficacy or necessity is not established by the source claims here.

The statement that a bare coil (no core) 'still works' as a magnet is physically sound (a current-carrying solenoid produces a field), but ensure in practice the current/turns are sufficient for an observable compass deflection; a weak coil field may be hard to detect otherwise — hence the detectability is now qualified in the activity text.

Whether 'voltage does not affect strength' was imprecise in the original candidate: the field depends on current, and adding cells raises current and voltage together, so the teaching point is that current is the direct cause — reflected in the sort and feedback.

MRI/maglev are retained among real uses but reframed as current-controlled fields rather than simple on/off examples, since an MRI magnet is not routinely switched on and off; the crane and relay remain the clearest on/off illustrations.

assess.poeTask: Build the coil-and-nail electromagnet lifting paperclips. Ask students to predict what happens to the clips the instant you disconnect the battery, and WHY, before doing it — then predict whether the coil ALONE (nail removed) can deflect a nearby compass. Predicting the nail 'stays a magnet' or the bare coil 'does nothing' reveals the iron-is-the-magnet idea; the observations pin the field to the current.
probeDeeper: If you removed the iron nail and had just the coil with current flowing, would it still affect a compass? Why?
Name one change that would make the electromagnet stronger and one that wouldn't help, and say why.
Why can a scrapyard crane use an electromagnet to pick up AND then drop a car, when a permanent magnet couldn't?
What actually produces the magnetic field here — the metal, the battery, or the moving charge?
assess.correctAnswer: The magnetism comes from the electric current flowing in the coil — a current produces a magnetic field. Stop the current and the field disappears, so the nail is no longer magnetised and the clips fall. Without the iron nail the coil alone still makes a (weaker) magnetic field when current flows; the iron core just concentrates and strengthens it — it is not the source.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The iron nail is really the magnet — the coil and battery just wake it up.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run the bare coil (or hold a compass near a straight current-carrying wire) to show current alone makes a field; the soft-iron core only amplifies it.
errorPatterns.distractor: The iron nail is really the magnet; the current just switches it on.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects the nail to stay magnetic after disconnection, and says a coil with no core wouldn't be magnetic at all.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It's the voltage that makes it magnetic, not the current.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach current as the rate of flow of charge; the field depends on the current through the coil.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes field strength solely to voltage and can't name current as what matters.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A straight current-carrying wire has no field — you need it coiled to get any magnetism.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the Oersted demo: a compass under a straight current-carrying wire deflects; coiling just concentrates the field.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that a single straight wire deflects a nearby compass.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the iron core is the magnet (expects it to stay magnetic, or nothing without the core), or attributes strength only to voltage.
responseLevels.full: Explains the field is produced by the current (so it vanishes when current stops, hence switchable), the iron core concentrates but doesn't cause it, and relates current, turns and core material to strength — transferring to why a scrapyard crane uses an electromagnet.
responseLevels.partial: Lists the three factors (current, turns, core) and says it switches on and off, but treats these as separate facts — can't explain that the CURRENT is the source (so the field goes when current stops) or that a bare coil still works.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I wrap a coil of wire around an iron nail and connect it to a battery — it picks up paperclips. When I disconnect the battery, the paperclips drop off. Why does the nail lose its magnetism when the current stops — and would it still work if I took the iron nail out and left just the coil?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The switch-off behaviour separates 'the current is the source' from 'the iron is the magnet'. A student who thinks the iron core is the magnet expects it to stay magnetic (or can't explain why the clips drop) and expects nothing without the core. A student who understands electromagnetism attributes the field to the current, so it vanishes when current stops and a bare coil still works. Tier 2 (remove the core) is the clincher.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 13–14 years

- **Topic:** Effects of Drugs & Alcohol

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Health):** "the effects of recreational drugs (including substance misuse) on behaviour, health and life processes."

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No specific MS performance expectation; substance-effect content is handled in US health education rather than NGSS science. This is UK-led. (US/UK divergence.)

- **Operational details:** Children classify common recreational drugs by their effect on the nervous system — depressants (slow it, e.g. alcohol), stimulants (speed it up, e.g. nicotine, caffeine) and hallucinogens (distort perception) — and explain specific effects of alcohol (liver damage, impaired judgement/reactions) and tobacco (lung disease, cancer, cardiovascular harm). They distinguish physical dependence (the body adapts and needs the drug) from psychological dependence (craving), and connect drug effects to the body systems they act on. The move that matters is mechanistic and non-moralising: a drug is a chemical that changes how a body SYSTEM works, with short-term behavioural effects and long-term health consequences.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal). Extends KS2 'diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle affect the body'; a mature health topic. A child is secure when they can classify a drug as depressant/stimulant/hallucinogen, name a specific organ effect of alcohol and of tobacco, and distinguish physical from psychological dependence.
bestPractices: Frame drugs mechanistically and non-judgementally — a chemical that changes how a body system works — rather than moralising, which improves both accuracy and engagement.
Anchor classification (depressant/stimulant/hallucinogen) to the nervous-system effect, then attach specific organ harms for alcohol and tobacco.
Separate physical from psychological dependence explicitly, as pupils routinely conflate them.
Use accurate, age-appropriate, non-sensational information and attend to safeguarding and pupils' personal contexts.
Connect effects to the body systems already studied (nervous, circulatory, respiratory, liver) so it consolidates prior learning.
keyRepresentations: Body-map of organ-specific effects (liver, lungs, brain, heart)
Depressant / stimulant / hallucinogen classification chart tied to nervous-system effect
Physical vs psychological dependence comparison
Reaction-time / behaviour change illustration for depressants vs stimulants
commonMisconceptions: Thinking alcohol is a stimulant because it can make people lively — it is a depressant.
Believing dependence is only physical (missing psychological dependence/craving).
Assuming legal drugs (alcohol, tobacco) are therefore harmless.
Thinking harm is only immediate, missing long-term/cumulative organ damage.
Treating all illegal drugs as identical rather than having different classes and effects.

learn.summary: Learners (ages 13–14) study how recreational drugs act on the body as chemicals that change how a body SYSTEM works — framed mechanistically and non-judgementally. Core tasks: classify drugs as depressants (slow the nervous system, e.g. alcohol), stimulants (speed it up, e.g. nicotine, caffeine) or hallucinogens (distort perception); attach specific organ harms to alcohol (liver damage/cirrhosis, impaired judgement and reactions) and tobacco (lung disease and cancer, cardiovascular harm); and distinguish physical dependence (body adapts, withdrawal) from psychological dependence (craving/compulsion). A body-map reveal activity, a probing in-role dialogue, a classification check, and an optional reaction-time model each address different facets. All content must be age-appropriate, non-sensational and safeguarding-aware.

activities.title: Tappable body-map of drug effects with myth-busting flaps
feedback: If a learner classes alcohol as a stimulant from the initial 'confidence', the flap corrects: early disinhibition comes from depressing self-control, but overall alcohol slows the nervous system, so it is a depressant — point to its effect on reaction times.
If a learner thinks 'depressant' means 'makes you sad', clarify that here it means it slows (depresses) nervous-system activity, which is not the same as low mood.

If a learner assumes legal drugs are harmless, the reveal shows alcohol's liver damage and tobacco's lung cancer and cardiovascular harm: whether a drug is legal depends partly on history, culture and regulation, so being legal does not mean being safe.
activities.rationale: Attaching specific effects to specific organs and classifying drugs by nervous-system effect is a clear reveal-and-sort task; lift-the-flap predictions directly surface the common safety and classification misconceptions. A static authoritative illustration supports safeguarding-friendly, non-sensational delivery. The tap-to-reveal and flap interactions are suggested mechanisms to make the content concrete, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Recreational drugs can be classified as depressants (e.g. alcohol), stimulants (e.g. nicotine) or hallucinogens by their effect on the nervous system; alcohol harms the liver and brain and tobacco harms the lungs and cardiovascular system, and dependence may be physical or psychological.
learnerActions: Tap an organ on a body diagram to reveal the specific effect: liver → 'alcohol is broken down here; heavy use scars it (cirrhosis)'; lungs → 'tobacco smoke damages airways and causes cancer'; brain → 'depressants slow nerve signals, stimulants speed them up'; heart → tobacco's cardiovascular harm.
Use a side panel to sort each named drug (alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, a hallucinogen) into depressant / stimulant / hallucinogen by its nervous-system effect.

Open lift-the-flap myth-busters and predict the answer before revealing: 'Is alcohol a stimulant?' → 'No — it is a depressant that slows you down, which is why it impairs reactions.' / 'Can you be dependent without physical withdrawal?' → 'Yes — psychological dependence (craving) is real.'
activities.intendedInsight: A drug is a chemical that changes how a specific body system works. It can cause short-term changes in behaviour and, for some drugs (especially with heavy or long-term use), long-term organ damage. Effects vary with the drug, the dose and the person, so drugs are not simply 'good' or 'bad'.

activities.title: In-role conversation with a GP or addiction nurse
feedback: If a learner dismisses psychological dependence as 'not real' addiction, the responder distinguishes withdrawal-based physical dependence from craving/compulsion-based psychological dependence, noting both are powerful and real.
Responses should remain non-judgemental, safeguarding-aware and sensitive to pupils' personal contexts.
activities.rationale: A dialogue can ask open questions and probe a learner's reasoning on behaviour and dependence, which a static map does not; the body-map presents the defined organ-effects and classification content as a visual reveal, so these activities are complementary rather than ranked. Comparative efficacy of the dialogue format is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Ask an in-role GP or addiction nurse age-appropriate questions about how alcohol and tobacco affect the body, why dependence develops, and how to make safe choices.
Explain your own reasoning about a scenario (e.g. why someone might keep using a drug they know is harmful) and have it probed Socratically.
Work through why physical dependence (withdrawal symptoms) differs from psychological dependence (craving, compulsion) in a real question-and-answer exchange.
activities.intendedInsight: Behaviour, decision-making and dependence can be explored through responsive dialogue that probes a learner's reasoning, complementing the factual organ-effect core.

activities.title: Classification and drug→organ check
feedback: For a wrong classification, re-anchor to the nervous-system effect: does the drug slow signals (depressant), speed them up (stimulant) or distort perception (hallucinogen)?
For a dependence item, remind: physical = body adapts and withdrawal appears; psychological = craving/compulsion.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and matching items check the factual core. These confirm recall and matching rather than eliciting independent explanation, so pair with the dialogue and body-map for reasoning.
sourceClaims: Recreational drugs can be classified as depressants (e.g. alcohol), stimulants (e.g. nicotine) or hallucinogens by their effect on the nervous system; alcohol harms the liver and brain and tobacco harms the lungs and cardiovascular system, and dependence may be physical or psychological.
learnerActions: Categorise named drugs as depressant, stimulant or hallucinogen.
Match each drug to the main organ(s) it harms (e.g. alcohol → liver/brain; tobacco → lungs/heart).
Answer items distinguishing physical from psychological dependence.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall of the classification and specific organ harms, and of the physical/psychological dependence distinction.

activities.title: Optional reaction-time / synapse mini-model
feedback: If a learner expects alcohol to 'speed you up', the model shows a lengthened reaction time, reinforcing that a depressant slows signalling.
activities.rationale: A dynamic model can make the slow/speed mechanism concrete, but most of the syllabus is organ effects, classification and dependence, so this is a supporting option rather than the primary teach. It is a simplified illustration, not a measured physiological result.
sourceClaims: Recreational drugs can be classified as depressants (e.g. alcohol), stimulants (e.g. nicotine) or hallucinogens by their effect on the nervous system; alcohol harms the liver and brain and tobacco harms the lungs and cardiovascular system, and dependence may be physical or psychological.
learnerActions: Explore a simple model of nervous-system signal transmission where a depressant lengthens reaction time and a stimulant shortens it.
Compare the modelled reaction time for a depressant versus a stimulant and connect it to real behaviour (e.g. why alcohol impairs reactions).
activities.intendedInsight: Makes the mechanism felt: 'depressant' and 'stimulant' describe slowing or speeding of nervous-system signalling, which drives the behavioural effects.

constraints: Frame drugs mechanistically and non-judgementally — a chemical that changes how a body system works — not moralising.
Use accurate, age-appropriate, non-sensational information; attend to safeguarding and pupils' personal contexts.
Separate physical from psychological dependence explicitly, since learners routinely conflate them.
Connect effects to body systems already studied (nervous, circulatory, respiratory, liver) to consolidate prior learning.
Classification and matching items confirm recall and sorting; they do not by themselves elicit independent explanation of mechanism or dependence — pair with explanation/dialogue tasks.
The reaction-time model is a simplified representation of nervous-system signalling, not a measured physiological result.
This is UK-led (DfE KS3); there is no specific NGSS MS performance expectation, as US substance-effect content sits in health education.
No activity format is asserted as superior or necessary; medium choices are proposed affordances pending efficacy evidence.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (BBC Bitesize KS3 claim) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its classification/organ-harm specifics as unverified secondary material.

Sources establish curriculum requirements and general classification/harm facts but do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any one activity format; relative 'best teach', 'faster' and 'efficient' judgements have been reduced to affordances.
Safeguarding: delivery must be adapted to the class context; the dialogue activity in particular needs a trusted, age-appropriate, non-sensational responder.

probeDeeper: If alcohol makes people feel confident, why does it actually slow reaction times and impair judgement?
Alcohol and tobacco are legal but heroin is not — does that ranking match how harmful they are? Why might law and harm not line up?
How is being physically dependent on a drug different from being psychologically dependent?
What specific long-term damage do alcohol and tobacco do to particular organs?
assess.correctAnswer: Alcohol is a depressant: it slows down the nervous system, giving slower reactions, impaired judgement and slurred speech, even though people feel less inhibited at first. 'Depressant' means it depresses (slows) nervous-system activity — not that it makes you sad. Being legal does not make it safe: alcohol causes liver damage and many deaths, and tobacco (also legal) causes lung cancer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Alcohol is a stimulant because it makes people lively and confident
errorPatterns.nextMove: The early 'confidence' comes from depressing self-control; overall alcohol slows the nervous system, so it's a depressant. Use reaction-time evidence.
errorPatterns.distractor: Alcohol is a stimulant — it gives you energy and confidence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Classifies alcohol as a stimulant from the initial disinhibited feeling

errorPatterns.pattern: Legal drugs like alcohol and tobacco aren't really drugs or aren't dangerous
errorPatterns.nextMove: Alcohol and nicotine are drugs; legality reflects history and regulation, not safety. Both cause major, well-documented harm.
errorPatterns.distractor: Alcohol and tobacco aren't really drugs because they're legal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says only illegal substances are harmful drugs

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Depressant' means it makes you feel sad or depressed
errorPatterns.nextMove: In this context 'depressant' means it slows nervous-system activity; it is not the same as low mood.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads the everyday meaning of 'depressed' into the drug category

errorPatterns.pattern: You can't really get addicted without physical dependence
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish physical dependence (withdrawal symptoms) from psychological dependence (craving, compulsion); both are powerful and real.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses psychological dependence as 'not real' addiction

responseLevels.gap: Classifies drugs by surface feelings and assumes legal means safe; can't define the categories.
responseLevels.full: Categorises drugs by their effect on the nervous system, argues that legality doesn't equal safety with organ-specific harms, and distinguishes physical from psychological dependence.
responseLevels.partial: Places some drugs in the right category and knows alcohol/tobacco are harmful, but slips on the depressant label or on separating legality from safety.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Alcohol is legal and is often described as a way to 'loosen up' and feel more confident, so some people assume it's a stimulant and basically harmless. Which category does alcohol actually belong to — depressant, stimulant, or hallucinogen — and does being legal make it safe? Explain what 'depressant' really means here.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the categories classifies by effect on the nervous system and separates legality from safety. A child who reasons from surface feelings calls alcohol a stimulant, or assumes 'legal' means 'not a dangerous drug'.

sources.claim: DfE KS3 Biology requires teaching 'the effects of recreational drugs (including substance misuse) on behaviour, health and life processes'.
