pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Speed and energy

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** there is NO general 'energy' topic at KS2 — energy enters at KS3 — so there is no direct UK primary statutory match; the nearest UK home for the reasoning is the KS2 'Working scientifically' skills (using evidence/observations to construct explanations) and forces work on what changes an object's motion.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** 4-PS3-1 (verbatim) '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-1]'; DCI PS3.A '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-1]'; assessment boundary excludes quantitative speed measures and any precise/quantitative definition of energy. This topic is therefore NGSS-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Strictly qualitative: more speed → more effect (more damage, pushes things farther, louder bang), and the name 'kinetic energy' / 'energy of motion'. NO formulas, no ½mv², no quantitative speed measures — the win is an evidence-based explanation, not a calculation. It sits on 'Naming types of energy' (kinetic vocabulary) and feeds collisions and, later, the KS3 kinetic energy store.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 9-10) — children use evidence to build the explanation that a moving object has energy and that the faster it moves the more energy it has.
bestPractices: Build the idea from evidence the child gathers: roll a ball at different speeds into a row of skittles / a sand pit / a block and have them observe that the faster ball knocks over more, pushes farther, makes a bigger dent — 'more speed, more effect' IS the evidence for 'more energy'.
Control the variable: use the SAME object so only speed changes; this both isolates speed and quietly models fair testing (mass effects are a separate, later idea).
Name it precisely — 'kinetic energy' or 'energy of motion' — and tie the word to the observation, so the term labels a thing they've seen, not an abstraction.
Keep it qualitative and comparative ('faster → more', 'slower → less'); the assessment boundary explicitly excludes measuring speed or quantifying energy at this age.
Distinguish energy from force/speed in talk: the fast ball HAS more energy (shown by what it can do), rather than 'carries a force' — heading off the impetus idea that a moving thing contains a push.
keyRepresentations: A launch-and-hit set-up: same ball at low/medium/high speed into skittles or a block, with the result (how far / how many) as the visible evidence.
A simple 'energy meter' or bar that grows as the chosen speed increases — linking speed to amount of kinetic energy.
A comparison strip: slow vs fast trial side by side with their outcomes, for 'which had more energy, and how do you know?'.
Everyday anchors: a gentle vs hard kick of a football; a slow vs fast bumper car; wind turbines spinning faster in stronger wind.
commonMisconceptions: 'Only living things / engines have energy' — a rolling ball or blowing wind is not seen as having energy; the damage/movement evidence counters this.
Confusing energy with the force or 'push' the object carries (impetus) — the moving object HAS energy (it can do something), it does not contain a stored push that 'runs out'.
Treating speed and energy as the same thing rather than speed being the EVIDENCE for how much kinetic energy there is.
'A heavier object always has more energy' — mass matters too, but it is deliberately held constant here; don't let it smuggle in (kept for later).
'A stationary object has no energy at all' — it may have stored/potential energy; here we only claim it has no KINETIC energy.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, help children use evidence they gather to explain that a moving object has energy (kinetic energy / energy of motion), and that the faster it moves the more energy it has. Keep it strictly qualitative and comparative ('faster → more effect, more energy'): no formulas, no ½mv², no speed or energy measurements. Build the explanation from observed effects (knocks over more, pushes farther, makes a bigger dent/louder bang) while holding the object the same so only speed varies. Name the term precisely and tie it to what children have seen, and separate 'has energy' from 'carries a push' to head off the impetus idea.

activities.title: Launch-and-hit bench: build the speed→energy explanation from your own trials
feedback: If a learner can predict the damage from the speed alone before firing, prompt them to put the rule into words and name the evidence: 'which shot had more energy, and how do you know?'

If a learner says the fast ball has 'more force' or 'more push', separate the words: the push is what acts during contact; the energy is what the moving ball carries and hands over — more speed means more energy to give.
If a learner thinks only the heavier ball matters, point out it was the SAME ball every trial, so only speed changed, yet the effect grew — so speed alone increased the energy here.

If a learner says a still ball already 'has the speed energy stored inside', note that kinetic energy exists only while moving; a still ball has none of it (though a raised ball can store another kind of energy).
activities.rationale: The NGSS performance expectation asks children to use evidence to construct the explanation, so the child should generate the evidence through controlled trials rather than just be told the rule. Holding the object constant isolates speed and quietly models fair testing while keeping mass (a later idea) out of the pattern.
sourceClaims: 4-PS3-1 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-1]'); DCI PS3.A '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-1]'; assessment boundary excludes quantitative speed measures and any precise/quantitative definition of energy.
learnerActions: Use the SAME ball every time and change only its launch speed (a slider or a fixed ramp released from a low vs high start).

Choose one target (a row of skittles, a loose block, or a sand pit), set it up the same way and in the same place for every trial, fire the ball at it, and record the outcome each trial: how many fell, how far the block moved, how big the dent.
Run several trials ordered slow → medium → fast and lay the outcomes side by side as a results strip.
After a few shots, PREDICT the result of the next speed before firing, then fire to check.
State the explanation in words and point to your evidence: 'the faster it moves, the more energy it has — I know because it knocked over more / pushed it farther.'
Say the term out loud for what the moving ball has: 'kinetic energy' or 'energy of motion'.
activities.intendedInsight: A moving object has kinetic energy; the faster it moves the more energy it has, and comparing the size of the effect on the same target is the evidence for which shot had more energy. Keeping the same object and the same target setup isolates speed as the cause.

activities.title: Swap the evidence: same rule, different effect
feedback: If a learner treats one effect (e.g. toppling) as the only sign of energy, show that distance pushed and loudness also grow with speed — all are evidence of more energy.
Reinforce naming: in each case the faster ball had more kinetic energy, shown by a bigger effect.
activities.rationale: Seeing the same qualitative rule across different outcomes supports transfer and keeps the claim about energy rather than one particular effect.
learnerActions: Repeat the fast-vs-slow comparison but change what the ball hits: a sand crater to dent, a block to shove, or a buzzer/plate that sounds louder on a harder hit.
For each target, decide which speed produced the bigger effect and say what that tells you about the energy.
Compare across targets: check whether the same rule ('faster → more energy') shows up as more damage, more distance, AND a louder bang in your own results.
activities.intendedInsight: The relationship between speed and energy is general: it shows up in many kinds of evidence, not just one toppling task, so the explanation is about the moving object's energy rather than one specific effect.

activities.title: Predict-and-check: ramp roll into dominoes (diagnostic reasoning)
feedback: A full response: more speed → more kinetic energy → more energy transferred to the dominoes (object held constant), and the child transfers the reasoning to a new case (e.g. where the energy went).
A partial response names more energy and more dominoes but can't connect it to energy TRANSFER, or slips into force or mass language — prompt gently toward 'what did the moving object hand over?'

A gap response explains only via 'more force/push' or claims a still object has kinetic energy — reteach the distinction between a contact push and carried energy, and that kinetic energy exists only while moving.
activities.rationale: Asking for the prediction AND the reason discriminates a speed→force story from a speed→energy→effect story, matching the standard's emphasis on evidence-based explanation.
sourceClaims: Children commonly attribute energy only to living/engine-driven things and confuse a moving object's energy with a 'push' it carries (impetus).
learnerActions: Roll the same object down a ramp from a low start, then from a high start (a higher start, on the same ramp, means it is moving faster at the bottom) into a row of dominoes/blocks.
BEFORE the fast roll, predict how many will move compared with the slow roll, AND say why.
Run the roll and compare your prediction with the result.
Answer the follow-ups: 'It's the same object both times — what does that let you rule out, so what's left?' and 'Where did the fast object's energy go after it hit?'
Consider a still object on the table that knocks nothing down: what does that say about whether a motionless object has kinetic energy?
activities.intendedInsight: The reason matters: a speed→energy explanation predicts more effect because faster means more energy; the sameness of the object rules out mass, leaving speed as the cause, and a motionless object has no kinetic energy.

activities.title: Name it and reference it: everyday anchors
feedback: If a learner only recognises the label but can't justify it, send them back to a trial so the word stays tied to observed effect.
Confirm correct, precise use of 'kinetic energy' or 'energy of motion' tied to a stated piece of evidence.
activities.rationale: A labelled static scene names the vocabulary and offers a frozen fast-vs-slow comparison as a reference layer; it supports naming but does not itself supply the live speed→effect evidence that drives the explanation, so it works best alongside the hands-on work. Recognising a label does not by itself show a learner can produce the explanation.
learnerActions: Point to everyday cases — a gentle vs hard kick of a football, a slow vs fast bumper car, wind turbines spinning faster in stronger wind — and say which has more energy of motion and how you can tell.
For a labelled picture of a fast cyclist, strong wind, or hard kick, reveal and read the label 'more speed → more energy of motion' to fix the vocabulary.
Use this as a reference to check your words after the hands-on trials, not as a substitute for them.
activities.intendedInsight: The term 'kinetic energy' / 'energy of motion' labels something they have observed in the world, not an abstraction detached from evidence.

constraints: Keep everything qualitative and comparative; the assessment boundary explicitly excludes measuring speed and quantifying energy at this age — no formulas or ½mv².
Hold the object (mass) constant so only speed varies; mass also affects energy but is deliberately kept for a later topic and must not smuggle into the pattern here.

Ordering trials by speed or choosing 'which knocks over more' in a recognition format can check the rule but does not, on its own, have the child GENERATE and explain the evidence; pair any recognition task with hands-on trials and a spoken/written explanation.

A labelled static picture is a vocabulary/reference scaffold: it can name kinetic energy and show a frozen comparison but cannot deliver the live speed→effect evidence, so it should support rather than lead the lesson.
Distinguish 'has energy' from 'carries a push': the moving object HAS energy it can transfer, it does not contain a stored push that runs out.
Claim only that a MOTIONLESS object has no KINETIC energy; it may still store other energy (e.g. if raised up), so avoid saying a stationary object has 'no energy at all'.

In England there is no general energy topic at KS2 (energy enters at KS3); the primary reasoning here is anchored on Working Scientifically skills, so treat this as NGSS-aligned enrichment for a UK primary setting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the NGSS/DfE claims as verified and the IOP Spark misconception claim as unverified (verified:false); treat the impetus/'only living things have energy' claim (used in the ramp-into-dominoes activity) as plausible but unconfirmed here.

Self-audit: 'a higher start means the object is moving faster at the bottom' assumes the same ramp/object and negligible added complications; this is a reasonable qualitative setup for this age and is kept as a comparative (not quantitative) claim.

Self-audit: the original correctly notes kinetic energy depends on both speed and mass; mass is intentionally held constant, so claims here are limited to 'more speed → more energy for the same object' and should not be generalised to 'faster always beats heavier'.

assess.poeTask: Roll the same object down a ramp from a low start, then from a high start (a higher start means it's moving faster at the bottom), into a row of blocks. BEFORE the second roll ask the child to predict how many blocks will move compared with the slow roll, AND why. The reason is diagnostic: a speed→energy child predicts more because faster = more energy, while a force-only or 'same object, same effect' child can't justify a difference. Then run it.
probeDeeper: It's the same marble both times. What does that let you rule out as the reason — so what's left?
Where did the fast marble's energy GO after it hit the dominoes?
Counterexample: a marble sitting still on the table knocks down no dominoes. What does that tell you about whether a still object has kinetic energy?
Would a slow bowling ball or a fast marble do more to the dominoes? What two things does the energy of motion seem to depend on?
assess.correctAnswer: The faster marble has more kinetic energy (energy of motion). The faster something moves, the more energy it carries, so it transfers more energy to the dominoes and knocks more of them down. It's the same marble, so the only difference is speed, and more speed means more energy.

errorPatterns.pattern: The fast marble has more force/push, not more energy ('it hits harder because it's got more force').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the words — force is the push during contact; energy is what the moving marble carries and hands over; more speed means more energy to give.
errorPatterns.distractor: The fast marble has more force pushing it along, and that's what knocks the dominoes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the effect with 'force/push/power' and never uses energy, or treats force and energy as the same thing.

errorPatterns.pattern: A still object already 'has speed energy' stored inside, ready to go ('the energy is in it waiting').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Kinetic energy exists only while MOVING; a still marble has none of it, though it may store another kind of energy if it is raised up.
errorPatterns.distractor: The marble had the energy stored inside it the whole time, even before it moved.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes kinetic energy to a stationary marble.

errorPatterns.pattern: It's the heaviness that matters and speed makes no real difference ('you just need a heavier ball').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out it's the SAME marble both times — only speed changed — so speed alone increased the effect.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ignores speed as the variable even though mass is held constant.

responseLevels.gap: Explains the effect only as 'more force/push', or says a still object has kinetic energy; doesn't link speed to energy.
responseLevels.full: Explains more speed → more kinetic energy → more energy transferred to the dominoes (holding the marble constant), and transfers the reasoning to a new case such as a bowling ball vs a marble, or where the energy went.
responseLevels.partial: Says the faster marble has more energy and knocks down more, but can't connect it to energy TRANSFER to the dominoes, or slips into force language or mass confusion.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You roll the same marble into a line of dominoes twice: once slowly, once fast. The fast marble knocks down far more dominoes. Why does the faster marble knock down more — what's different about it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who says the fast marble has more 'force/push' but never links it to energy, or who imagines it is somehow heavier or stronger, differs from one who says more speed = more kinetic energy = more energy transferred. The reason tier separates a speed→force story from a speed→energy→effect story.

pedagogy.summary: Year 6 (age 10–11) pupils convert between standard units using DECIMAL notation to up to three decimal places, moving in both directions (smaller↔larger), and can explain the mm–cm–m–km (and g–kg, ml–l) relationships as powers of 10. This is the decimal extension of Year 5 conversion: the same 'reason from unit size, move the digits' method, now with the decimal point in play. The load-bearing hazard is decimal place value — the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut fails (3250 g ÷ 1000 is 3.25 kg, not 325), and children who think 'the point is the decimal' misplace digits.
bestPractices: Convert by moving the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point (×/÷ by 10/100/1000), explicitly rejecting 'add a zero' and 'move the point' — use true/false error-spotting (0.45÷10 = .45?) to confront the shortcut (NCETM Spine 2.29).
Keep the unit-size reasoning from Year 5 ('larger unit → fewer → divide') so direction is reasoned, not guessed.
Make the powers-of-10 STRUCTURE explicit: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km — so a conversion is one multiplication/division by a power of ten, and mixed chains compose.
Use a place-value chart extended to thousandths so pupils can state the value of each digit before and after, and place holder zeros correctly.
Include a reasonableness check (should the number get bigger or smaller?) to catch direction and decimal-placement errors.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart extended to thousandths (digits slide, point fixed)
Powers-of-10 ladder mm×10→cm×100→m×1000→km
Double number line for the two units
Gattegno chart for ×/÷ by powers of 10
commonMisconceptions: 'Add/remove a zero' with decimals: 3250 g → '325 kg', or 0.45 km → '45 m' / '4.5 m'.
Reverses the multiply/divide direction, giving an answer orders of magnitude out (0.45 km → 0.00045 m).
'The point is the decimal' — mis-values digits after the point or treats 0.45 as the whole number 45.
Cannot articulate the powers-of-10 relationship, so treats each conversion as an isolated fact.

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils (age 10–11) convert between standard measurement units using decimal notation to up to three decimal places, moving in both directions (smaller↔larger), and explain the mm–cm–m–km (and g–kg, ml–l) relationships as powers of ten. This extends Year 5 conversion with the decimal point now in play: the method stays 'reason from unit size, then move the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point', using ×/÷ by 10/100/1000. The load-bearing hazard is decimal place value — the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut fails (3250 g ÷ 1000 = 3.25 kg, not 325), and children who think 'the point is the decimal fraction' misplace digit values.

activities.title: Move the digits, keep the point still (place-value conversion)
feedback: If a learner answers 325 kg for 3250 g, they removed zeros instead of moving digits three places. Rebuild it on the chart: 3250 ÷ 1000 moves each digit three places right, giving 3.25 — count the places, do not delete symbols.

If a learner answers 4.5 m or 45 m for 0.45 km, name the error precisely: 4.5 m is a one-place shift (as if ×10), and 45 m is a two-place shift (as if ×100). Both are wrong; 0.45 × 1000 moves digits three places left to 450 m. Have them name the value of the 4 (four tenths) and the 5 (five hundredths) first, then shift three places.
If an answer is wildly out (e.g. 0.00045 m or 3 250 000 kg), the multiply/divide direction was reversed. Re-reason from unit size before trusting the result.
If a learner treats 0.45 as the whole number 45, rebuild decimal place value: each column to the right is ten times smaller, so 0.45 is four tenths and five hundredths.
activities.rationale: Converting by moving digits across a fixed point directly confronts the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut, which fails for decimals; pairing it with explicit unit-size reasoning keeps direction reasoned rather than guessed, and the equal-value check (3.250 = 3.25) addresses holder-zero confusion. The 5 cm→0.05 m case instances the same method on a shorter chain.
sourceClaims: Convert measures by moving the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point via ×/÷ by 10/100/1000; the guide embeds 'add/remove a zero' as FALSE statements for decimals (0.45÷10 = .45; 25.34×10 = 25.340) to expose the misconception.
Grade 5 pupils convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given system, with the parenthetical example 'convert 5 cm to 0.05 m', using decimal notation.
UK DfE Year 6 pupils solve problems involving conversion of units using decimal notation up to three decimal places, converting length/mass/volume/time from a smaller unit to a larger and vice versa.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart extended to thousandths. Write 3250 g in it, then convert to kilograms by sliding every digit three places to the RIGHT (dividing by 1000) while the decimal point stays fixed, landing on 3.25 kg; note that a holder zero is inserted only where place value demands it.
Before moving, state the unit-size reason aloud: 'Kilograms are the bigger unit, so there will be FEWER of them — I divide.' Then check the direction of the digit shift matches.
Convert the reverse case 0.45 km to metres (×1000), sliding digits three places LEFT to get 450 m; state that metres are smaller, so there are MORE.

Convert 5 cm to 0.05 m (÷100), sliding each digit two places to the right — a shorter example of the same digit-movement method with decimal notation; say why metres are the larger unit so there are fewer.
Confirm that 3.250 kg and 3.25 kg name the same quantity — the trailing zero after the last significant digit does not change the value.
Do a reasonableness check each time: 'Should this number get bigger or smaller?' and reject any answer that is orders of magnitude out.
activities.intendedInsight: A conversion moves the SAME digits across a FIXED decimal point; the point does not move. Converting to a larger unit gives fewer of them (divide, digits move right); converting to a smaller unit gives more (multiply, digits move left). 3250 g and 3.25 kg are one quantity; 3.250 equals 3.25.

activities.title: Spot the false shortcut (error-spotting with decimals)
feedback: If a learner accepts 0.45 ÷ 10 = .45, show on the chart that dividing by ten moves each digit one place right: 0.45 → 0.045. Nothing was divided in '.45'.
If a learner accepts 25.34 × 10 = 25.340, point out that 25.340 equals 25.34 (same value). Multiplying by ten gives 253.4 — digits move one place left.
activities.rationale: True/false error-spotting on carefully chosen decimal cases makes the failure of the zero shortcut explicit and forces articulation of digit movement and place value.
sourceClaims: Convert measures by moving the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point via ×/÷ by 10/100/1000; the guide embeds 'add/remove a zero' as FALSE statements for decimals (0.45÷10 = .45; 25.34×10 = 25.340) to expose the misconception.
A common decimal misconception is thinking 'the point is the decimal fraction'; place value must extend so each column to the right is ten times smaller, and holder zeros are understood.
learnerActions: Judge true or false and explain: 'Is 0.45 ÷ 10 = .45?' Correct it to 0.045 by moving each digit one place right.
Judge true or false: 'Is 25.34 × 10 = 25.340?' Explain that appending a zero after the last decimal does NOT multiply by ten; the correct answer is 253.4, with digits moving one place left.
For each false statement, state the correct conversion and justify it with the value of each digit and the direction of movement.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or removing a zero is not the same as multiplying or dividing by a power of ten once decimals are involved. ×/÷ by 10, 100, 1000 moves the digits by one, two, or three places; the zero trick coincidentally works for some whole numbers but misvalues decimals.

activities.title: Climb the powers-of-ten ladder (composing conversions)
feedback: If a learner cannot say why 1 km = 1000 m, walk the ladder rung by rung (m → ×10 → tens of metres → ×10 → hundreds → ×10 → 1000 m) so the ×1000 is seen as 10×10×10.
If a learner treats g–kg differently from m–km, point out both are ÷1000 (or ×1000) — the same power-of-ten structure applies.
activities.rationale: Making the powers-of-ten structure explicit lets conversions be reasoned and composed rather than memorised, which supports transfer across length, mass and volume.
sourceClaims: UK DfE Year 6 pupils solve problems involving conversion of units using decimal notation up to three decimal places, converting length/mass/volume/time from a smaller unit to a larger and vice versa.
A common decimal misconception is thinking 'the point is the decimal fraction'; place value must extend so each column to the right is ten times smaller, and holder zeros are understood.
learnerActions: Build a ladder stating each relationship: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km. For each rung, say whether you multiply or divide and by what power of ten.
Hop along the ladder to compose a chain, e.g. mm → cm (÷10) → m (÷100) → km (÷1000), and recognise that any single conversion is one multiplication or division by a power of ten.
Optionally use a Gattegno chart (rows for powers of ten) to see each conversion as a single ×/÷ by a power of ten — moving along a row, or jumping rows for the larger steps.
Explain in words why 1 km is a thousand metres and not a hundred, using the powers-of-ten structure rather than reciting it as an isolated fact.

Transfer the same structure to mass (g–kg) and volume (ml–l) to show the method is general across metric units, not tied to length. Then contrast with time (e.g. 2.5 h = 150 min, not 250 min) to see that time units use factors of 60 and 24, not powers of ten.
activities.intendedInsight: The metric system is built on powers of ten, so every metric conversion is a single ×/÷ by a power of ten and mixed chains compose; knowing the structure removes the need to memorise each conversion separately. Time units are not decimal (60 s = 1 min, 60 min = 1 h, 24 h = 1 day), so time conversions use those factors instead of powers of ten.

constraints: Reject 'add/remove a zero' and 'move the decimal point' as methods; teach movement of the DIGITS across a point that stays fixed.
Keep unit-size reasoning ('larger unit → fewer → divide; smaller unit → more → multiply') so direction is reasoned, not guessed, and pair it with a reasonableness check.

A fixed reference ladder of powers of ten can show the relationships but does not let a learner move digits or check direction themselves; use it alongside an activity where the learner performs the transformation (chart, writing, or spoken step-by-step), not as the only medium.

Matching, fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice items (including true/false decimal cases) can probe direction and the add-a-zero error precisely, but recognition responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the conversion; include tasks where the learner produces the converted value and justifies it.
Ensure a holder zero is inserted only where place value requires it (e.g. 0.045), and that trailing zeros after the last significant decimal (3.250 vs 3.25) are recognised as equal value.

An extended place-value chart to thousandths, a double number line between the two units, and a Gattegno chart for ×/÷ by powers of ten are useful supports but are scaffolds; learners should also reason and state values without them to show secure understanding.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3250 g ÷ 1000 = 3.25 kg (digits move three places right); 0.45 km × 1000 = 450 m (three places left); 5 cm ÷ 100 = 0.05 m (two places right); 0.45 ÷ 10 = 0.045 (one place right); 25.34 × 10 = 253.4 (one place left, NOT 25.340). All checked and consistent with the source's intended corrections. The misconception answers (325 kg, 45 m, 4.5 m, 25.340, 0.00045 m, 3 250 000 kg) appear only as errors to correct, never as valid answers.

The original source frames an interactive place-value slider as 'ideal' and a static image/3D/dialogue as 'poor' for this topic. These are catalog fit rankings, not established comparative efficacy; this rewrite retains the digit-movement mechanism as a concrete support while softening claims that other media 'cannot teach' the concept. A static ladder, Gattegno chart, and spoken/written reasoning can also support the objective.
The Gattegno chart from the original keyRepresentations is retained as an optional scaffold in the powers-of-ten activity and the scaffold constraint.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum) carries verified:false in the row; treat its claim with appropriate caution pending verification.

probeDeeper: 'Kilograms are bigger than grams — so should the number of kg be bigger or smaller than 3250? Does 3.25 fit?'
'Is 3.250 kg the same as 3.25 kg? How do you know?'
'You wrote 0.45 km = ___ m. What is the 4 worth, and the 5? Now move them.'
'Explain to me why 1 km is a thousand metres and not a hundred — using powers of ten.'
assess.correctAnswer: 3250 g = 3.25 kg (÷1000, 'kg bigger → fewer'); 0.45 km = 450 m (×1000); explains 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km, each step a ×/÷ by a power of ten, digits moving across a fixed point.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Add/remove a zero' with decimals — divides 3250 by 1000 by deleting zeros ('325 kg'), or multiplies 0.45 by 1000 by appending/one-step zeros ('45 m' or '4.5 m').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Move digits three places on a place-value chart with the point fixed; use true/false items (0.45÷10 = .45? 25.34×10 = 25.340?) to show the zero shortcut fails for decimals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer has the wrong number of decimal places; zeros were added/removed rather than digits moved three places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the multiply/divide direction — gives an answer orders of magnitude out (0.45 km → 0.00045 m, or 3250 g → 3 250 000 kg).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason from unit size first ('metres smaller → more → multiply') and add a reasonableness check before trusting the answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The result is far bigger/smaller than sensible; no unit-size reasoning offered.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The point is the decimal' — mis-values digits after the point, treating 0.45 as the whole number 45 or misreading thousandths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild decimal place value: each column right is ten times smaller; state the value of each digit in 0.45 (four tenths, five hundredths) before converting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digit values after the point are wrong; 0.45 handled as 45; three-decimal-place answers misplaced.

responseLevels.gap: Adds/removes zeros, reverses direction, or mis-values decimal digits; answers orders of magnitude out.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions with correct decimal placement (digits move, point fixed), handles up to 3 dp, and explains the ×/÷ powers-of-10 structure linking mm–cm–m–km — transferring across length, mass, volume and time.
responseLevels.partial: Converts a friendly case correctly but slips on three decimal places or on the reverse direction, or converts but cannot explain the powers-of-10 relationship.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to think aloud through three tasks: (1) 'Convert 3250 g to kilograms.' (2) 'Convert 0.45 km to metres.' (3) 'Explain how mm, cm, m and km are related using powers of 10.' Watch the direction choice, where the decimal point ends up, and whether the powers-of-10 structure is understood — not just the final numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil with secure decimal place value moves the digits the right number of places in the right direction (3.25 kg; 450 m) and explains the ×10 chain; a pupil relying on 'add/remove a zero' produces 325 kg or 45 m, and one who thinks 'the point is the decimal' mis-values 0.45. Digit-movement understanding versus zero-shortcut diverge precisely on these decimal cases.

pedagogy.summary: Children model shapes two ways: BUILDING them from components (sticks/straws as edges, clay balls/connectors as vertices) and DRAWING them. The procedural work turns attribute knowledge into action — knowing a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners means reaching for 3 sticks and 3 balls and joining them into a CLOSED loop; building a cube means coordinating 12 edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces into a genuine 3-D frame rather than a flat square. It is the doing counterpart of the informal-analysis topic, and it exposes whether a child truly holds a shape's structure. Best taught by naming the attributes and counting the parts before building, insisting on closure, and drawing straight sides on supportive grids.
bestPractices: Name the attributes first and count the components before building ('a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners, so 3 sticks and 3 balls'), then check the finished shape against a real one.
Insist every corner is joined so the figure is CLOSED; an open V is not yet a triangle.
For the cube, build one square face then raise vertical edges to a second square, so children feel a solid is more than a single face (6 faces, not 1).
Support accurate drawing with dotted paper, geoboards or a straight edge, marking each side as it is drawn.
Ask for a non-prototypical version (a long thin triangle, a tall rectangle) so building/drawing is driven by attributes, not a single remembered picture.
keyRepresentations: Sticks/straws (edges) and clay balls/connectors (vertices) for building frames
Geoboard and dotted paper for constructing straight-sided closed figures
A real triangle/cube to compare the built model against
One square face raised into a cube frame to show the 2-D→ 3-D step
commonMisconceptions: Uses the wrong number of components — grabs 4 sticks for a triangle, or the wrong count of straws/connectors for a cube — not matching parts to the shape's attributes.
Leaves the figure OPEN or makes wobbly/curved sides, so the corners don't join into a closed shape.
Builds a cube flat as a single square or a laid-out cross, not raising it into a closed 3-D frame.
Draws only the prototypical wide, horizontal rectangle (or rounds the corners) and cannot draw a tall or tilted one.

learn.summary: Children model shapes two ways: BUILDING them from components (sticks or straws as edges, clay balls or connectors as vertices) and DRAWING them. This procedural work turns attribute knowledge into action — knowing a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners means reaching for 3 sticks and 3 balls and joining them into a CLOSED loop; building a cube means coordinating 12 edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces into a genuine 3-D frame rather than a flat square. It is the 'doing' counterpart of describing and analysing shapes, and it exposes whether a child truly holds a shape's structure. Teach by naming the attributes and counting the parts before building, insisting on closure, and supporting straight drawn sides with grids or a straight edge.

activities.title: Build a triangle from counted components
feedback: If the child grabs 4 sticks, pause and re-count against the named attributes: 'how many sides does a triangle have? So how many sticks?'
If an open 'V' is left, point out the corners do not all join: an open V is not yet a triangle — close the loop.
If sides are wobbly or curved, support straight sides and ask whether a triangle's sides are straight.
For the non-prototypical build: 'Good — a long thin one is still a triangle because it still has 3 straight sides and 3 corners.'
activities.rationale: A polygon is a closed 2-D figure of straight sides meeting at vertices; counting each side and vertex and insisting on closure matches the structure children must coordinate when building. Producing a non-prototypical triangle checks whether the build is attribute-driven rather than copied from a single image.
sourceClaims: A polygon is a closed 2-D shape made of straight sides meeting at vertices; children should count each side/vertex once and are supported by marking each as they go — grounds the 'closed, right number of straight sides' requirement when drawing/building.
learnerActions: Name the attributes aloud first: 'a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners, so I need 3 sticks and 3 balls.'
Count out exactly 3 sticks and 3 clay balls before joining anything.
Join the sticks at the balls into a CLOSED loop so every corner meets.
Check the finished model against a real triangle.
Then make a different triangle — a long thin one — so the build is driven by the attributes, not one remembered picture.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's attributes tell you which parts to gather and how to join them; a triangle must be a closed figure of 3 straight sides meeting at 3 corners, and many different triangles satisfy that.

activities.title: Draw a rectangle (and a non-canonical one)
feedback: If corners are rounded, point out that a rectangle has square corners where two straight sides meet, not curves.
If there is a gap, show the figure is not yet closed and the last corner needs joining.
If only the wide horizontal version is produced, challenge: 'Can you draw a tall thin rectangle?' and confirm it still counts because it is closed, with four straight sides and four square corners.
activities.rationale: Dotted paper, geoboards and a straight edge support accurate straight-sided closed figures; marking each side as it is made helps children track the count. Asking for a non-prototypical rectangle targets the common misconception of drawing only the wide horizontal case. The 'closed, four straight sides and four square corners' description is a deliberately simple age-5-6 working definition rather than a full formal one.
sourceClaims: A polygon is a closed 2-D shape made of straight sides meeting at vertices; children should count each side/vertex once and are supported by marking each as they go — grounds the 'closed, right number of straight sides' requirement when drawing/building.
learnerActions: Draw a recognisable rectangle on dotted paper or a geoboard, marking each side as it is made.
Use a straight edge to keep each of the four sides straight and join the four corners so the figure is closed.
Then make a tall rectangle (longer than it is wide) or a tilted one, not only the wide horizontal version.
activities.intendedInsight: A rectangle is a closed figure with four straight sides and four square (not rounded) corners; a tall or tilted rectangle is just as valid as the familiar wide one.

activities.title: Build a cube frame: from one square to a solid
feedback: If straws are laid flat into a single square or a cross/plus shape, show that a cube rises into 3-D — build one square, then raise vertical edges to a second square on top.
If the edge or vertex count is wrong, re-count together against a real cube: 'how many square faces should a cube have? Not 1 — find all six squares.'
Confirm success by checking the frame has 12 edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces (the six square openings) and stands as a solid (an optional screen tally may show the same).
activities.rationale: Properties of 3-D shapes are faces (each a 2-D shape), edges (straight lines where two faces meet) and vertices (corners where edges meet); a cube has 6 square faces. Handling and marking real solids supports getting these counts right, and the hardest step is coordinating this structure while raising a flat face into a solid — so building one square then raising it directly targets the 'a cube is not just a square' misconception. Note that a stick-and-ball frame is a skeleton: its 6 'faces' are the square openings the edges enclose, not solid surfaces. The built frame (real sticks and balls, which have slight thickness) and any on-screen frame are MODELS of the mathematical cube, whose edges and vertices are ideal and thicknessless; the structure (12 equal edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces), not the material, defines the shape.
sourceClaims: Properties of 3-D shapes are the faces (each a 2-D shape), edges (straight lines where two faces meet) and vertices (corners where edges meet); a cube has 6 square faces — grounds the edge/vertex/face structure a child must coordinate when building a triangle (3 edges/3 vertices) or a cube from components.

3-D shapes can be described and sorted by their properties (faces, edges, vertices); handling and marking real solids supports getting these counts right — supports checking a built cube frame against the correct edge/vertex count.
learnerActions: Using sticks that are all the same length, build one square face first from 4 sticks and 4 balls.
Raise 4 vertical sticks from the corners of that square (adding 4 more balls at their tops).
Cap them with a second square on top, so the flat face lifts into a solid frame.
Count the finished frame: 12 edges (sticks), 8 vertices (balls) and the 6 square faces — in a skeleton frame these are the six square openings the edges enclose.
Compare against a real cube and check the counts match.
activities.intendedInsight: A cube is more than a single square: it is a 3-D frame of 6 square faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, built by raising one face to a second.

constraints: Building and drawing are active production tasks: the learner must assemble components or draw the figure, not just recognise or tap a finished picture.
Closure is a required outcome, not a stylistic preference: an open figure (an unjoined V, a rectangle with a gap) does not yet count as the shape.

Checking whether a drawing is closed, with four straight sides and four square corners, can confirm the rectangle task, but it does not let a child build a frame or verify edge/vertex counts — use it only as a complement to hands-on building.

Physical sticks-and-balls and clay are central; an optional on-screen snap-together builder (with a live edge/vertex/face tally that only 'sets' when the frame closes, and an open shape that refuses to set) can make closure and counting feel concrete, but is a complement to real materials, not a replacement. Treat both the screen frame and the physical frame as models of the mathematical solid — real sticks and balls have slight thickness, while the ideal cube's edges and vertices are thicknessless.
The cube step (2-D face raised into a 3-D solid) is the hardest to coordinate and benefits most from genuine 3-D handling; a flat picture or 2-D-only tool makes this step harder to feel.
A real triangle and a real cube should be available to compare the built models against.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The 'four straight sides and four corners' rectangle description is a simplified age-5-6 working definition; it does not, by itself, distinguish a rectangle from other quadrilaterals. It is retained for age-appropriateness, with 'square corners' used to rule out rounded ones; fuller right-angle formalism is deliberately deferred.

A stick-and-ball cube is a wireframe with no solid surfaces: its '6 faces' are the square openings bounded by the edges. This modelling approximation is now stated in the cube activity and feedback, not only here.

Original materials describe clay 'balls' and stick 'edges' as approximations of ideal vertices and edges. Real sticks and balls have thickness; the built frame models the mathematical solid rather than being it — stated in the cube activity and constraints as well as here.

The source framed a 3-D interactive as the single 'ideal' and other media as 'poor'/'possible'. Comparative-efficacy and necessity claims are not established by the available sources, so this rewrite presents hands-on building and optional screen models as complementary rather than ranking them.
The original 'adds nothing' dismissal of in-role/conversation formats is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been removed.

probeDeeper: How many sticks did you use? How many corners (balls)? Is that right for a triangle?
Is your shape closed — do all the corners join up?
Can you make a triangle a different way — a long thin one?
Your cube — how is it different from just one square? How many square faces should it have?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) A closed triangle — 3 sticks joined at 3 balls. (2) A recognisable rectangle — a closed figure with four roughly-straight sides and four corners (longer than wide is fine). (3) A cube frame of 12 straws (edges) and 8 connectors (vertices) forming 6 square faces. The child selects the right number of parts and closes the shape, using its attributes to guide the build.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong number of components — grabs four sticks for a triangle, or the wrong count of straws/connectors for a cube — not matching parts to the shape's attributes.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the attributes first ('a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners → 3 sticks, 3 balls') and count the parts before building; compare the finished model against a real shape.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The built shape has the wrong number of sticks (edges) or balls (vertices) for the named shape.

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the figure OPEN or makes wobbly/curved sides, so the corners don't join into a closed shape.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: check that every corner is joined so the shape is closed, and support straight sides with a straight edge or dotted paper.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The sticks don't meet to close the loop; the drawn rectangle has a gap or curved, wandering sides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a cube flat as a single square or a laid-out cross, not raising it into a closed 3-D frame.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build one square face, then show it needs vertical edges rising to a second square on top; count that a cube has 6 faces, not 1, and 12 edges.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For the cube, lays straws flat into a square or a plus-shape rather than building up into a solid frame.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the wrong number of components, leaves figures open, or lays a cube flat as a single square; drawings are rounded or unrecognisable.
responseLevels.full: Selects the correct number of sticks/balls or straws/connectors from the shape's attributes, closes the figure with roughly straight sides, builds a genuine 3-D cube frame (12 edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces), and can produce a non-prototypical version (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Builds and draws recognisable shapes for the familiar prototypical case (a wide rectangle, one triangle) but miscounts components on the cube, leaves gaps, or cannot build/draw a non-canonical version (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three tasks and watch how the child works: (1) 'Use these sticks and balls to make a triangle.' (2) 'Draw a rectangle.' (3) 'Now build a cube with these straws and connectors.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Building and drawing are direct performances of attribute knowledge: a child who knows a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners reaches for 3 sticks and 3 balls and joins them into a closed loop, while one who does not adds extra parts, leaves the figure open, or makes a non-rigid shape. The cube build in particular reveals whether the edge/vertex/face structure is held or whether the child collapses a solid into a single flat square. Watching the making — not asking about it — shows which.
