pedagogy.summary: This topic has two linked strands: automatic recall of addition and subtraction facts to 20 (so 7+8 and 15−8 come without calculating) and derivation of related facts to 100 by scaling and using known bonds (6+4=10 → 60+40=100; 5+5=10 → 35+5=40). Recall is built from secure make-ten strategy plus spaced retrieval, not speed drills; derivation is built by treating tens as units, so a known bond reappears at a larger scale.
bestPractices: Build automaticity from strategy, then retrieval: secure make-ten within 20 first, then space low-stakes recall practice so facts move to memory (DfE: emphasis on practice aids fluency)
Teach fact families so + and − are learned together (7+8=15, 15−8=7, 15−7=8) and the inverse is available
Derive decade facts by scaling a known bond: 6+4=10 becomes 60+40=100 because six tens plus four tens is ten tens
Use the same visual at two scales (ten-frame counters vs ten-rods) to show 6+4 and 60+40 are one picture
Avoid timed pressure that induces anxiety; keep finger/strategy use welcome while retrieval matures
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame / double ten-frame (make-ten)
Fact-family triangle (shows the three related facts)
Bead string / Rekenrek
Base-ten ten-rods (scaling a bond to tens)
Number bonds part-whole diagram
commonMisconceptions: Recall not automatic — still counting on fingers every time for 7+8
Failing to scale the bond: knowing 6+4=10 but giving 60+40=10 or 70 or 700
Treating addition and subtraction as unrelated, so 15−8 is re-counted despite knowing 7+8=15
Applying a derived pattern blindly (e.g. 35+5=40 but then 35+50=40)

learn.summary: Two linked goals for ages 6–7: automatic recall of addition and subtraction facts to 20 (so 7+8 and 15−8 come without calculating) and derivation of related facts to 100 by scaling and using known bonds — 6+4=10 → 60+40=100 by scaling the bond to tens, and 5+5=10 → 35+5=40 by using the ones bond inside a larger number. Recall is built from a secure make-ten strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval rather than speed drills; derivation is built by treating tens as units so a known bond reappears at a larger scale.

activities.title: Same bond, bigger units: scaling 6+4 to 60+40
feedback: If a child gives 60+40=10, 70 or 700, show 6+4 and 60+40 with the same picture at two scales (counters then ten-rods) and name that six tens plus four tens is ten tens = 100.
If a child says 35+50=40, slow down and count the tens being added: adding five tens to 35 gives 85, while adding five ones gives 40. Keep both comparisons visible side by side.
When a child derives correctly, ask 'how did you know that?' so the scaling or ones-bond reasoning is spoken, not just the answer.
activities.rationale: Using the same visual at two scales makes 'derive' concrete: a known within-ten bond is reused at the scale of tens by unitising. A manipulable or scalable model lets the learner see the identical make-ten action produce 10 and then 100; a fixed two-scale picture can also show this relationship.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.
Recall of pairs that make ten supports calculation, and known facts are extended by unitising tens so a within-ten bond is reused at the scale of tens.
learnerActions: Complete 6+4 on a ten-frame by sliding four counters in to fill all ten; confirm this is a known, secure bond making 10.
Switch the counters to tens: let each counter become a ten-rod (or restate each counter as 'one ten') so the same full frame now reads 100.
Say aloud what changed: 'six tens plus four tens is ten tens, which is 100' — the gesture and picture are identical, only the unit changed.
Repeat the tens-scaling with another known bond: 5+5=10 → 50+50=100 (five tens plus five tens is ten tens).
Separately, derive 35+5 by using the ones bond 5+5=10: 30 + (5+5) = 40, so here the 5 is added as five ones, not scaled to tens.
Deliberately contrast 35+5=40 with 35+50=85: in 35+50 you are adding five tens, not five ones, so the answers differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Deriving a decade fact like 60+40 is scaling a known bond, not memorising a new fact: six tens plus four tens is ten tens = 100. A different move is using a bond inside a larger number — 35+5 uses the ones bond 5+5=10 to give 40. Which unit you add (ones vs tens) decides the result, so 35+5=40 and 35+50=85 are different.

activities.title: Fact-family triangle: one trio, both operations
feedback: If a child re-counts 15−8 straight after giving 7+8=15, lay out the fact family 7, 8, 15 and show the same three numbers make both facts.
Prompt: 'If 7+8=15, what subtraction facts do you already know without working them out?'
A tap-to-reveal triangle is good reference for the inverse link but does not by itself build recall speed; pair it with retrieval practice.
activities.rationale: Teaching fact families makes the inverse explicit so + and − are learned together and the inverse is immediately available. This supports the misconception where subtraction is treated as a separate unknown fact.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.
learnerActions: Lay out the three numbers 7, 8 and 15 on a fact-family triangle (part–part–whole).
Cover one corner and read off the fact it reveals: cover 15 to get 7+8=15 and 8+7=15; cover 7 to get 15−8=7; cover 8 to get 15−7=8.
State explicitly: because 7+8=15, you already know 15−8 and 15−7 without re-counting.
Build a second family (e.g. 6, 9, 15, giving 6+9=15, 9+6=15, 15−6=9, 15−9=6) and name all its related facts the same way.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition and subtraction are the same relationship between three numbers; knowing one fact hands you the inverse, so 15−8 need not be re-counted once 7+8=15 is known.

activities.title: Spaced, untimed retrieval to build automatic recall
feedback: If a child counts on fingers for 7+8 every time with no drop in effort on a second asking, do NOT impose timed drills or penalise finger use — keep practising the make-ten strategy and spaced recall without the clock.
For a derive prompt like '6+4=10, so 60+40=?', if a wrong value such as 10, 70 or 700 is chosen, return to the two-scale picture and re-establish six tens plus four tens = 100.
Ask 'which of those did you just know, and which did you have to work out?' to make the recall/calculation distinction visible to the learner.
activities.rationale: Recall is built from a secure make-ten strategy then moved to memory by spaced low-stakes practice; timed pressure can induce anxiety and is avoided. A self-paced fill-in or choice format can exercise retrieval and check the derive insight, but repeated spaced practice, not a single check, is what builds automaticity.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.
Recall of pairs that make ten supports calculation, and known facts are extended by unitising tens so a within-ten bond is reused at the scale of tens.
learnerActions: Practise recalling facts to 20 in short, low-stakes sessions spread over days (e.g. 7+8, 15−8, 6+4, 9+4), rather than one long timed drill.
Mix in derive-a-fact prompts such as '6+4=10, so 60+40=?' and '5+5=10, so 35+5=?', choosing or writing the answer.
After each prompt, say which ones you just knew and which you had to work out.
Keep finger and make-ten strategy use welcome; the aim is that repeated facts need less effort each time, not beating a clock.
activities.intendedInsight: Automaticity grows from secure strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval; a fact becomes 'known' when recalling it needs noticeably less effort on later encounters.

activities.title: Playful recall talk: 'how did you know that?'
feedback: Spoken back-and-forth gives retrieval practice but does not by itself build the make-ten strategy or the scaling insight; pair it with the ten-frame and two-scale work.
If a child cannot explain how they knew a fact, return to the relevant model (ten-frame or fact-family triangle) before more recall practice.
activities.rationale: A conversational recall routine offers extra retrieval opportunities and surfaces thinking, complementing the manipulative and the fact-family work without replacing the strategy-building they provide.
learnerActions: Trade quick spoken recall prompts back and forth with a partner or adult (flashcard-style), e.g. one asks 7+8, then 15−8, then 6+4.
For each answer, the asker follows up with 'how did you know that?' — did you just know it, make ten, or use the inverse?
Keep it low-stakes and untimed; celebrate strategy explanations as much as correct answers.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising recall and the reasoning behind it reinforces both the facts and the strategies (make-ten, inverse, scaling) that generate them.

constraints: Do not use timed drills or penalise finger/strategy use; automaticity is to grow from a secure make-ten strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval.

A tap-to-reveal fact-family triangle is a reference scaffold for the inverse relationship; it does not exercise retrieval speed or the scaling derivation, so pair it with practice and the two-scale model.
A fill-in or choice retrieval format can check the derive insight and give recall practice, but a single check does not build automaticity; genuine fluency needs repeated spaced practice over time.
Recognition/choice responses alone do not elicit independent construction of a derived fact; include prompts where the child states or writes the answer and explains the scaling.
A conversational recall routine is a supplementary retrieval vehicle; it does not directly build the make-ten strategy or the scaling insight.

Keep the ones-vs-tens distinction explicit (35+5=40 by adding five ones vs 35+50=85 by adding five tens) so the derived pattern is not applied blindly, and keep scaling to tens (60+40) distinct from using a ones bond inside a number (35+5).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched, and activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit arithmetic check: 6+4=10 and 60+40=100 (six tens + four tens = ten tens) are correct; 5+5=10, 50+50=100, 35+5=40 are correct; 35+50=85 is correct. The original source field left 35+50 only as a 'why not same answer?' probe without stating the value; the correct value 85 has been added so the contrast is taught, not left ambiguous.

Scaling (60+40, 50+50) and using a ones bond inside a larger number (35+5) are kept as two distinct derivation types; the summary and intendedInsight were adjusted so 35+5 is not mislabelled as a scaling case.

The legacy claim that '3D adds nothing' and that number facts 'are not spatial' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it has been dropped rather than asserted. Ten-frames and base-ten rods are themselves spatial supports for these facts.

The legacy framing that a scalable tool 'turns derive into it's the same fact' overstates necessity; a fixed two-scale picture can also show the relationship, so the activity keeps the model affordance without claiming one medium is uniquely required.
The original bead string / Rekenrek representation was not carried into these activities; it remains a valid make-ten manipulative if an implementer wishes to add it.

probeDeeper: You knew 6 + 4 = 10 — how does that help you with 60 + 40?
If 7 + 8 = 15, what subtraction facts do you already know without working them out?
You said 35 + 5 = 40. What about 35 + 50 — same answer? Why not?
Which of those did you just know, and which did you have to work out?
assess.correctAnswer: 15, 7, 10, 100, 40. Fluent: 7+8 and 15−8 recalled (or via make-ten) without counting; 60+40 derived by scaling 6+4 (six tens + four tens = ten tens = 100); 35+5 derived from 5+5=10 → 40.

errorPatterns.pattern: Recall not yet automatic — counts on fingers for 7+8 and 15−8 every time, no faster on a second asking
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT impose timed drills or penalise finger use — automaticity grows from spaced, low-stakes retrieval built on a secure make-ten strategy, not speed pressure. Keep practising strategy and recall without the clock.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct answers but visible counting each time; no drop in effort when the same fact recurs

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to scale the bond — 'six and four is ten, so sixty and forty is ten' (or 70, or 700)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 6+4 and 60+40 with the same picture at two scales (counters then ten-rods); name that six tens plus four tens is ten tens, which is 100.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 60+40 the answer ignores that each number is a group of tens; the bond isn't reused at the ten-scale

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverse not linked — answers 7+8=15 instantly but re-counts 15−8 as if it were a separate, unknown fact
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay out the fact family 7, 8, 15 and show the same three numbers make both facts, so knowing one hands you the other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No drop in effort on 15−8 despite having just given 7+8=15

responseLevels.gap: Counts out every fact including 7+8; gives 60+40 as 10 or 70; treats + and − as unrelated.
responseLevels.full: Instant recall of facts to 20 and their inverses, derives 60+40=100 and 35+5=40 by scaling and using known bonds, and explains the link.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls within-20 facts but cannot yet derive the scaled facts, or derives 60+40 only with prompting; the inverse link is emerging.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Rapid-fire, watching for hesitation and finger-counting: ask 7 + 8, then 15 − 8, then 6 + 4; then 'use 6 + 4 to tell me 60 + 40', then 'what's 35 + 5?'. Note which come instantly and which are counted out.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Speed and effort on 7+8 and 15−8 separate recall from calculation. 60+40 separates a child who scales the known bond from one who says 10 or 700. 15−8 separates a child who uses the inverse of 7+8 from one who re-counts despite just answering 7+8.

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.

pedagogy.summary: Probabilities sum to one captures a structural truth: when you list ALL the possible outcomes of a trial, their probabilities must total 1. This lets a child find a missing probability, or the probability of an event NOT happening, by subtracting from 1 (P(not A) = 1 − P(A)) rather than counting every unfavourable outcome. The concept rests on the outcomes being both mutually exclusive and exhaustive — covering the whole of what can happen, with no overlap.
bestPractices: Model the whole of possibility as a bar of length 1 partitioned among the outcomes, so 'the rest of the bar' IS the complement
Establish that the list must be exhaustive (covers everything) and mutually exclusive (no overlaps) before the sum-to-1 argument applies
Teach P(not A) = 1 − P(A) as a shortcut, contrasting it with the slower count-all-the-others method on the same problem
Use spot-the-error tables whose probabilities don't total 1, and ask what must be wrong
Link back to calculating simple probabilities so children see favourable + unfavourable together exhaust the outcomes
keyRepresentations: Unit bar (length 1) partitioned into outcome segments
Complete outcome table with probabilities totalling 1
P(not A) shown as the remaining part of the whole
Spinner whose sectors fill the entire disc
commonMisconceptions: Ignoring the sum-to-1 constraint and assigning a missing outcome an arbitrary or 'equal' value by analogy to another
Treating 'not A' as a single other outcome rather than everything except A, or thinking P(not A) equals P(A)
Adding probabilities of overlapping or non-exhaustive events and still expecting them to total 1
Adding fractions without a common denominator when totalling probabilities

learn.summary: Teach that when you list ALL the possible outcomes of a trial — with no overlaps and nothing left out — their probabilities must total exactly 1. This lets a learner find a missing probability, or the probability of an event NOT happening, by subtracting from 1 (P(not A) = 1 − P(A)) instead of counting every unfavourable outcome. The reasoning only holds when the outcomes are mutually exclusive (no overlap) and exhaustive (cover everything).

activities.title: Fill the unit bar: the leftover IS the missing probability
feedback: If the learner says green = 1/6 'like blue': add the given segments (1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3) and point to the strip still unfilled — the missing value is whatever completes the whole to 1, not a copy of another outcome.
If segments overshoot the bar or leave a gap: these probabilities don't total 1, so the list is impossible — check it covers everything with no overlap.
If 'not red' is named as just blue or just green: highlight the whole rest of the bar — 'not red' means every outcome except red (blue AND green together).
activities.rationale: Partitioning a unit whole makes both sum-to-1 and the complement concrete: the remaining segment is literally the missing or complementary value, and an over- or under-filled bar flags an impossible set. This directly targets the misconception of assigning an 'equal' value by analogy.
sourceClaims: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).
Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Take a bar exactly one unit long that stands for everything that can happen when you draw a counter from a bag of red, blue and green counters.
Set red to one-half of the bar and blue to one-sixth, marking those segments.
Before being told, work out what must fill the remaining strip and state it: green = 1 − (1/2 + 1/6) = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3.
Mark 'P(not red)' by highlighting the entire rest of the bar (blue and green together) and give its value as 1 − P(red) = 1/2.
State in words why green could NOT be a free choice and why 'green must be 1/6 like blue' is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The whole of possibility has length 1; once some outcomes are placed, the leftover segment IS the missing probability, and 'not red' is the whole rest of the bar — everything except red — not a single other colour.

activities.title: Spinner that fills the whole disc
feedback: If the prediction ignores the total (e.g. guesses arbitrarily or copies a colour): add the known sectors and show how much of the disc is still empty — that gap is the missing probability.
If the fraction sum is slipped: rewrite with a common denominator (1/2 = 3/6, 1/3 = 2/6, so together 5/6; the rest is 1/6) before subtracting from 1.
activities.rationale: A full disc reinforces exhaustiveness visually and gives a second representation of the same structural truth, supporting learners who grasp area more readily than a linear bar; representing the full set of outcomes directly addresses the sample-space misconception.
sourceClaims: Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Look at (or draw) a spinner whose coloured sectors must fill the entire disc with no gap and no overlap.
Given red = one-half and blue = one-third, predict the remaining sector's probability (yellow) before it is revealed: 1 − (1/2 + 1/3) = 1/6.
Check the revealed sector really is a sixth of the disc.
Tap or mark each sector in turn and track the running total as it reaches exactly 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A spinner's sectors are another model of the whole-equals-1 idea: because the sectors must fill the disc, the last sector's size (and probability) is forced by the others.

activities.title: Complement shortcut versus counting the others
feedback: If the learner thinks P(not A) equals P(A): contrast the two methods — 'not 3' on a die is five outcomes out of six (5/6), clearly not the same as P(3) = 1/6.
If 'not A' is treated as a single other outcome: list what 'not A' actually contains and show it is every outcome except A.
If the learner struggles with the compound case: note that 'red or blue' already covers two of the three exhaustive colours, so green is simply whatever is left of the whole — 1 − 3/4 = 1/4.
activities.rationale: Running the slow count-all-the-others method alongside the subtraction shortcut on the same problem makes the equivalence explicit and justifies why the shortcut works, rather than presenting it as a rule to memorise.
sourceClaims: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).
learnerActions: Calculate P(not rolling a 3) on a fair six-sided die two ways: first by subtracting, 1 − 1/6 = 5/6; then by counting all the other outcomes (1,2,4,5,6) and adding their probabilities (five sixths).
Compare the two methods, note they give the same answer, and that subtracting from 1 is faster when there are many unfavourable outcomes.
For the counter bag, find P(not red) as 1 − P(red) = 1/2 and confirm it matches blue + green (1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2).

Extend to a compound complement: a different bag of red, blue and green counters has P(red or blue) = 3/4; find P(green) = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4, since each counter is exactly one of the three colours and the three colours exhaust the bag.
activities.intendedInsight: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) is a shortcut for 'everything except A', and it equals the sum of all the other outcomes because together they fill the whole; the same subtraction works when the known part is a compound event like 'red or blue'.

activities.title: Spot the impossible table
feedback: If a learner accepts 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/6: show the sum is 5/6, not 1, so one value must change — there is no rule forcing green to match blue.
If the learner cannot add the fractions: use a common denominator (1/2 = 3/6) before totalling, giving 3/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 5/6.
activities.rationale: Error-spotting forces the learner to apply the constraint actively rather than restate it, and directly confronts the equiprobability-by-analogy misconception.
sourceClaims: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).
learnerActions: Examine probability tables and decide which are impossible because the values do not total 1 (e.g. a table listing 1/2, 1/6 and 1/6 for three colours).
Add the values, compare the total with 1, and explain exactly what is wrong.
Correct one impossible table by finding the value that would make it total 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A complete list of outcomes that does not total 1 cannot be right. Checking the sum is a necessary test, but it is not enough on its own: a valid probability distribution also needs every value to be between 0 and 1, and the outcomes must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

activities.title: When the sum-to-1 argument does NOT apply: overlapping events
feedback: If a learner adds overlapping events' probabilities and is satisfied the total is 1: show that P(even or prime) is really 5/6, because outcome 2 was counted in both 'even' and 'prime' — reaching 1 here is a coincidence, not a valid use of sum-to-1.
If a learner thinks the rule never applies to dice: clarify it does apply to a complete list of distinct single outcomes (1–6), just not to overlapping compound events.
activities.rationale: Making the conditions explicit prevents over-generalising the rule. 'Even' and 'prime' sharing 2 on a die is a documented student error, so naming the overlap condition — and showing that its naive sum equals 1 by coincidence while the true union is 5/6 — guards against it.
sourceClaims: The addition/sum-to-1 argument only holds for mutually exclusive events; applying it to overlapping events (e.g. 'even' and 'prime' on a die, which share 2) is a documented student error.
Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Consider rolling a fair die and the events 'even' and 'prime'. List the outcomes for each: even = {2,4,6}, prime = {2,3,5}.
Notice that 2 belongs to both, so the events overlap and are NOT mutually exclusive.

Add P(even) = 3/6 and P(prime) = 3/6 and notice the total comes to 1 — then find the true chance of 'even or prime': the combined outcomes are {2,3,4,5,6}, which is 5/6, not 1. The naive sum reached 1 only by counting outcome 2 twice.
Explain why adding probabilities of overlapping events double-counts the shared outcome, so the total does not give P(even or prime), even when the arithmetic happens to land on 1.
Contrast with the counter-bag colours, which are mutually exclusive (a counter is exactly one colour) and exhaustive, so there the probabilities genuinely total 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Sum-to-1 and the complement shortcut only hold when the listed events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive; with overlapping events, adding probabilities double-counts shared outcomes, and the total — even if it coincidentally equals 1 — does not represent the combined event.

activities.title: Socratic challenge: do your outcomes cover everything?
feedback: If the learner cannot justify the total: return to the bar or disc model where the whole visibly equals 1.
If the learner asserts equal likelihood by habit: ask what evidence fixes each value — the total constraint, not similarity to another colour.
activities.rationale: Prompting for the conditions and the justification surfaces whether the learner is actually using the constraint and targets the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely; this works best alongside a filled-whole representation rather than in isolation.
sourceClaims: Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Respond to prompts such as 'Do your outcomes cover everything, with no overlap?' and 'What do they add up to?'
Defend or revise a claim like 'so green must be 1/6 too' by appealing to the sum-to-1 constraint.
Explain in your own words why all the outcomes must add to exactly 1 — not more and not less.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the exhaustive-and-mutually-exclusive conditions and the total-equals-1 constraint strengthens reasoning beyond pattern-matching.

constraints: The sum-to-1 argument and P(not A) = 1 − P(A) require the listed outcomes to be mutually exclusive (no overlap) AND exhaustive (cover everything); establish both conditions before applying the rule.
Do not present 'each outcome is equally likely' as a default; the sum-to-1 constraint, not sameness between outcomes, fixes a missing value.

Adding probabilities of overlapping events (e.g. 'even' and 'prime' on a die) double-counts shared outcomes; the resulting total does not represent the combined event even when it coincidentally equals 1 (here P(even)+P(prime)=1 but the true P(even or prime)=5/6). This is a condition failure, not a sum-to-1 counterexample.
Totalling probabilities given as fractions requires a common denominator; a wrong total here is an arithmetic lapse, not a probability misconception, and should be scaffolded separately.

A static tap-to-reveal partitioned bar or disc can show a complete set totalling 1 but does not let the learner test an incomplete or overlapping list; use it as a display scaffold, then move to a task where the learner constructs or corrects a list.

Choosing the impossible table from options can check whether a learner applies the constraint but does not by itself show the learner can independently construct a valid distribution; pair it with a construction task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit: every fraction sum and outcome set was re-derived — green = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3; spinner yellow = 1 − 5/6 = 1/6; P(not 3) = 5/6 (matches counting 1,2,4,5,6); impossible table 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 5/6 ≠ 1; compound complement P(green) = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4; overlap P(even)+P(prime) = 3/6 + 3/6 = 1 while the true union {2,3,4,5,6} = 5/6. All consistent, and the overlap activity makes the coincidence explicit rather than claiming the sum fails to reach 1.

The legacy entry rated a 3D interactive 'poor' on the basis that '3D adds nothing'; this ranking is not an established pedagogical law and has been dropped rather than restated as a universal claim. Sum-to-1 is well modelled in 1D/2D, but no claim is made that a 3D medium could add nothing.

The legacy 'possible' static-image and conversation formats are preserved as the tap-to-reveal scaffold and the Socratic activity respectively, with their narrow observable limits placed in constraints rather than asserted as 'cannot teach' claims.
The tempting wrong answer '1/6 — green is one colour, the same as blue' is retained only as a misconception to confront in feedback, never offered as a correct option.

assess.poeTask: Show a spinner divided into unequal sectors you have pre-measured: red is one-half, blue is one-third, yellow is one-sixth. Cover the yellow sector. Say: 'The red part is a half and the blue is a third. Before I uncover the last colour, predict the probability of yellow — and explain how you got it.' A child ignoring sum-to-1 guesses arbitrarily or says 'a third, like blue'; the sum-to-1 reasoner predicts 1 − (1/2 + 1/3) = 1/6. Uncover the sector and check it really is a sixth of the disc. The reason given BEFORE uncovering is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: What is P(not red) for this bag? How did you get it — by adding colours or by taking red from the whole?
If I told you the three probabilities were 1/2, 1/6 and 1/6, what would be wrong with that?
Why do all the outcomes have to add up to exactly 1, and not more or less?
Suppose a bag had red, blue and green but you were told P(red or blue) = 3/4 — what is P(green)?
assess.correctAnswer: P(green) = 1/3. All the outcomes must total 1, so P(green) = 1 − (1/2 + 1/6) = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3. The classmate is wrong: there is no rule that each colour is equally likely — the sum-to-1 constraint, not sameness with blue, fixes the missing value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the sum-to-1 constraint and assigns the missing outcome an arbitrary or 'equal' value by analogy ('green is 1/6, the same as blue')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the given probabilities and show they don't yet reach 1; the missing value is whatever completes the whole, so subtract from 1 rather than copy another outcome
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/6 — green is one colour, the same as blue.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives P(green) = 1/6 or reasons that the colours must be equally likely, without checking the total

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 'not A' as a single other outcome, or thinks P(not A) equals P(A), rather than everything except A
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show P(not red) as the whole rest of the bar (blue and green together) = 1 − P(red); 'not red' is every outcome except red, not a single one
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up 'what is P(not red)?' names just one colour, or gives 1/2 as if 'not red' mirrors red

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the fractions without a common denominator when totalling
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the common-denominator step (1/2 = 3/6, so 3/6 + 1/6 = 4/6); this is an arithmetic lapse, not a probability misconception
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 1/2 + 1/6 as 2/8 or similar, then subtracts wrongly

responseLevels.gap: Assigns the missing probability with no regard to the total; cannot find P(not A) except by trying to list every other outcome, often wrongly
responseLevels.full: Uses sum-to-1 to find the missing probability (1/3) and P(not A) = 1 − P(A), justifies by the outcomes being exhaustive and mutually exclusive, and spots tables that cannot be right because they don't total 1
responseLevels.partial: Knows outcomes should total 1 and can find a missing value in the simplest cases, but copies another outcome's value, mishandles 'not A', or slips on the fraction arithmetic — states the rule without applying it reliably

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A bag holds red, blue and green counters. P(red) = 1/2 and P(blue) = 1/6. A classmate says P(green) must be 1/6 as well, 'because green is just one colour, the same as blue'. Ask the child: is the classmate right? What is P(green), and why? Take the answer, then ask them to explain the reasoning fully (Tier 2).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The sum-to-1 reasoner subtracts the known probabilities from 1; the surface reasoner copies blue's value or assumes the colours are equal; a complement-confused child mishandles what 'the rest' means. The Tier-2 explanation reveals whether the total-equals-1 constraint was actually used.

sources.claim: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).
sources.source: Third Space Learning — Mutually Exclusive Events

sources.claim: The addition/sum-to-1 argument only holds for mutually exclusive events; applying it to overlapping events (e.g. 'even' and 'prime' on a die, which share 2) is a documented student error.
sources.source: Third Space Learning — Mutually Exclusive Events

sources.claim: Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
sources.source: Bryant & Nunes, Children's Understanding of Probability: A Literature Review (Nuffield Foundation, 2012)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers, with the unknown in any position (8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □). Ages 6–7, a procedural target resting on the meaning of '=' and the inverse relationship.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'solve one-step problems... including missing number problems such as 7 = □ − 9' and Y2 'solve problems with addition and subtraction... and missing number problems'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.8 'Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers. For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of 8 + ? = 11, 5 = □ − 3, 6 + 6 = □.'
• Operational details: vary the unknown's POSITION deliberately (result unknown, change unknown, start unknown, answer-on-left) so the child cannot rely on 'add the two numbers I see'. Solve by choosing the inverse move and reading '=' as balance, not by keyword. Bar/part-whole models externalise which quantity is missing.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — solves 6 + 6 = □ and 8 + ? = 11. Tier B (age 7) — solves answer-left and subtraction-position forms (5 = □ − 3) correctly. Tier C (age 7+) — chooses the inverse operation for the unknown position and checks the answer by substituting back.
bestPractices: Systematically vary the unknown position (a+b=□, a+□=c, □+b=c, and answer-left forms) so pupils build a flexible method, not a keyword habit.
Represent each equation on a bar / part-whole model first to see which quantity is unknown before calculating.
Teach solving-by-inverse explicitly: convert □ + 9 = 14 into 14 − 9.
Insist on substituting the answer back to check the equation balances.
Use non-standard forms (5 = □ − 3) early to defeat the left-to-right 'answer-comes-next' reading.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / part-whole diagram with the unknown segment shaded
Pan balance with an unknown mass on one side
Empty number line for count-on / inverse jumps
Fact-family triangle to pick the needed operation
Equation cards with the box in varied positions
commonMisconceptions: Adding the two visible numbers regardless of the box's position (8 + ? = 11 → 19).
Reading answer-left forms as backwards (5 = □ − 3 → writes 2, i.e. 5 − 3).
Always subtracting or always adding by keyword rather than by the unknown's role.
Not checking the solution by putting it back into the equation.
Treating '=' as 'work out the total' so a box before '=' is confusing.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year olds find the unknown whole number in addition/subtraction equations where the unknown appears in any position (8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □). The target is a flexible method built on reading '=' as 'both sides balance' and choosing the inverse move, not an 'add the two numbers I can see' habit. Vary the unknown's position deliberately (result, change, start, answer-on-left) and insist on checking by substituting the answer back.

activities.title: Balance the unknown with counters
feedback: If the child writes 2 for 5 = □ − 3: show that □ − 3 must equal 5, so starting from 5 we add back the 3 that was taken away, giving □ = 8 (5 + 3 = 8). Try more answer-left forms.
If the child adds the two visible numbers (8 + ? = 11 → 19): point to the bar — 11 is the whole, 8 is one part, the box is the missing part, found by 11 − 8 = 3.
Live true/false balance feedback as counters are added lets the child self-correct before stating an answer.
Praise explicitly when the child checks by substituting back, e.g. 'you put 3 back and 8 + 3 does make 11'.
activities.rationale: A missing-number target is procedural and benefits from repeated practice with immediate feedback across varied positions. A balance or part-whole representation externalises which quantity is missing and makes '=' mean balance rather than 'compute the total', which is intended to address the answer-left misread. Note that a physical two-pan balance shows addition most naturally; the subtraction form 5 = □ − 3 is modelled by filling the box and removing 3, an approximation of the equation. Optional interactions such as a slider, draggable counters, or a live beam that tips make the balancing mechanism concrete; they are helpful examples, not required.
sourceClaims: Varying the position of the unknown (result/change/start unknown) changes problem difficulty, and children commonly add the two visible numbers regardless of position.
1.OA.8 requires determining the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation, with the examples 8 + ? = 11, 5 = □ − 3, 6 + 6 = □.
learnerActions: Set out an equation with a box, e.g. 5 = □ − 3, on a two-pan balance or bar model where one side already shows 5.
Add or remove counters in the box until both sides match: too few and the box side is too light, too many and it tips down.
State the value that makes both sides balance (for 5 = □ − 3 the box must hold 8, because □ − 3 has to equal 5).
Repeat with the unknown in every position: 8 + ? = 11, □ + 6 = 12, 6 + 6 = □.
Check each solved equation by putting the found number back in and confirming both sides match.
activities.intendedInsight: The box holds whatever value makes the two sides equal; '=' means balance, so an answer-on-left form like 5 = □ − 3 is not 'backwards' — it is the same balancing task. One balancing method works for every position.

activities.title: Solve by the inverse, then check
feedback: If the child only guesses and checks repeatedly: prompt the inverse move via the fact family — 'the whole is 11, one part is 8, so the missing part is 11 − 8' — to build efficiency. The concept need not be re-taught here.
If the wrong operation is chosen, return to a bar model to re-identify which quantity is unknown before computing.
Reinforce that the check (substituting back) is part of the method, not an optional extra.
activities.rationale: Choosing the inverse for the unknown's position is the efficient method the standard targets; a fact-family representation helps pupils map position to operation. Trial-and-error can give correct answers but does not build the intended fluency, so prompting the inverse addresses a genuine performance gap.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.8 requires determining the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation, with the examples 8 + ? = 11, 5 = □ − 3, 6 + 6 = □.
Y1–Y2 pupils solve missing-number problems such as 7 = □ − 9 and problems with addition and subtraction.
learnerActions: Given □ + 9 = 14, convert it to the inverse: 14 − 9, and compute □ = 5.
Given 8 + ? = 11, use 11 − 8 = 3 rather than guessing and testing values.
Use a fact-family triangle (whole 14; parts 9 and 5) to pick the operation needed for the unknown's position.
Substitute the answer back and confirm the sentence is true.
Practise a mixed set covering result-unknown, change-unknown, start-unknown and answer-left forms.
activities.intendedInsight: Once you know which quantity is the whole and which is a part, you can go straight to the answer with the inverse operation instead of slow trial-and-error.

activities.title: Explain your move (strategy talk)
feedback: If the child says they 'added the two numbers', probe where the box sits and what '=' requires, then re-model on a bar.
Note that for 5 = □ − 3 and □ − 3 = 5 the answer is the same (□ = 8), because both say the box minus 3 equals 5; discuss why.
Accept any correct reasoning the child can justify; press for the inverse when they rely only on guessing.
activities.rationale: Discussion is a supporting diagnostic that reveals strategy, not just answers; it may complement rather than replace hands-on practice with feedback. It is especially useful for catching the left-to-right 'answer-comes-next' reading, though talk alone does not provide the repeated solving practice a procedural target needs.
sourceClaims: Varying the position of the unknown (result/change/start unknown) changes problem difficulty, and children commonly add the two visible numbers regardless of position.
learnerActions: Solve a varied-position equation aloud, e.g. 5 = □ − 3, then explain how you decided what to do.
Answer probes: 'Which of these could you check with an addition, and how?' and 'What if it were □ − 3 = 5 instead of 5 = □ − 3 — would the answer change?'
Show how you'd check that your answer to 8 + ? = 11 makes the sentence true.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the reasoning surfaces whether a child is using a keyword/positional habit or genuinely reasoning from which quantity is missing.

activities.title: Anchor each position to an operation (worked bar models)
feedback: Use the diagram to correct an added-the-two-numbers error by showing the box is a part, not the whole.
A fixed worked example can anchor the mapping, but pupils still need to then solve fresh items themselves to build fluency.
activities.rationale: A static annotated bar model is a useful anchor for connecting position to operation. On its own it does not provide practice with feedback, so pair it with solving fresh items; it is a scaffold toward the balancing/inverse practice rather than a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Study a worked part-whole/bar diagram for each unknown position (result, change, start, answer-left) with the missing segment highlighted.
Reveal, for each, which operation finds the missing part and why (whole − part = part; part + part = whole).
Then solve matching fresh equations and verify by substitution.
activities.intendedInsight: Each position maps to a specific inverse move once you identify the whole and the parts; the diagram makes that mapping visible.

constraints: Systematically vary the unknown's position (a+b=□, a+□=c, □+b=c, and answer-left forms) so pupils build a flexible method, not a keyword habit.
Introduce non-standard forms (5 = □ − 3) early to counter the left-to-right 'answer-comes-next' reading.
Read '=' as 'both sides balance', not 'work out the total'; a box before '=' is legitimate.
Insist on checking by substituting the found value back into the equation.

Fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice practice (e.g. choosing the inverse calculation that solves □ + 9 = 14, with '2' as a wrong option for 5 = □ − 3) is useful for spaced retrieval and checking fluency, but recognition/selection does not itself require the child to construct and reason through the balancing move, so pair it with constructed solving.
Worked static diagrams anchor the position→operation mapping but do not themselves provide practice with feedback; follow them with fresh items to solve.
Trial-and-error can produce correct answers but does not build the intended inverse-method fluency; prompt the inverse once accuracy is secure.
Keep the wrong-answer value '2' (from 5 − 3) only as an incorrect option; the correct answer to 5 = □ − 3 is 8.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels a numeric/non-spatial '3D adds nothing' claim; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped rather than asserted. A 2D balance/bar is proposed on its affordances (making balance and the missing part visible), not as the uniquely necessary medium.

Self-audit of arithmetic and logic: 8 + ? = 11 → 3; 5 = □ − 3 → 8 (box minus 3 equals 5, so box = 5 + 3 = 8); 6 + 6 = □ → 12; □ + 9 = 14 → 5; □ + 6 = 12 → 6. The answer-left value '2' (from 5 − 3) is the misconception value and must only appear as a wrong option, never as a correct answer.

Representational caveat: a two-pan balance models addition most directly; the subtraction form 5 = □ − 3 is handled by filling the box and removing 3, which approximates the equation rather than weighing it literally. This is stated in Activity 1 so the scaffold's limit is visible to the teacher.
Noted and preserved the clarification that 5 = □ − 3 and □ − 3 = 5 have the same solution (□ = 8); the source probe asks pupils to consider this.

The standards claims (DfE; CCSS 1.OA.8) attached to Activities 1–2 ground the objective (determining the unknown across positions); they do not empirically establish that the inverse method or the balance representation is more effective than alternatives. Efficacy wording is kept as intended/proposed.

Source 'verified' flags are mixed (DfE true; CCSS and Cognitively Guided Instruction false in the row); confidence was legacy 'high'. No fresh verification performed, so no confidence upgrade is claimed.

probeDeeper: How did you decide what to do for 5 = □ − 3?
Which of these three could you check using an addition, and how?
What if it were □ − 3 = 5 instead of 5 = □ − 3 — would the answer change?
Show me how you'd check that your answer to 8 + ? = 11 makes the sentence true.
assess.correctAnswer: ? = 3; □ = 8; □ = 12. Watch for the child using the inverse (11 − 8 = 3; 5 + 3 = 8) on the first two and adding directly on the last, and for correct handling of the answer-left/subtraction-position form.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the two visible numbers regardless of the box's position — 8 + ? = 11 becomes 8 + 11 = 19 in the box.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model on a bar: 11 is the whole, 8 a part; the box is the missing part, found by 11 − 8. Re-establish what '=' constrains.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 19 (or otherwise combines the two shown numbers) for a change-unknown item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the answer-left form as backwards — 5 = □ − 3 solved as 5 − 3 = 2.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Balance model: □ − 3 must weigh the same as 5, so □ = 8; practise more answer-left forms.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 2 in the box for 5 = □ − 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Solves only by slow trial-and-error / counting, never using the inverse to go straight to the answer.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — prompt the inverse move via the fact-family triangle; build efficiency.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Guesses values and checks repeatedly rather than computing 11 − 8 directly.

responseLevels.gap: Combines the two given numbers regardless of the box's position (e.g. 19, 2); standard result-unknown may be right by habit only.
responseLevels.full: Solves all three fluently, selecting the inverse operation for the unknown's position and verifying by substituting the answer back into the equation.
responseLevels.partial: Solves result-unknown and change-unknown forms but stumbles on the answer-left/subtraction-position item, or solves all only by slow trial-and-error without using the inverse.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these three and write the missing number in each box, working at the table while I watch: 8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three items place the unknown differently — change-unknown, start-of-a-subtraction with the answer on the left, and result-unknown. A child running an 'add the two numbers I can see' habit produces tell-tale wrong values (19 for the first, 2 for the second) while getting the standard third right. Watching HOW they solve, not just the answers, separates a flexible inverse method from a keyword habit.

sources.claim: Y1–Y2 pupils solve missing-number problems such as 7 = □ − 9 and problems with addition and subtraction.

sources.claim: 1.OA.8 requires determining the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation, with the examples 8 + ? = 11, 5 = □ − 3, 6 + 6 = □.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 1 Operations & Algebraic Thinking

sources.claim: Varying the position of the unknown (result/change/start unknown) changes problem difficulty, and children commonly add the two visible numbers regardless of position.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Drawing conclusions from evidence — quantitative conclusions & error analysis (KS3)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils to "interpret observations and data, including identifying patterns and using observations, measurements and data to draw conclusions", to "present reasoned explanations, including explaining data in relation to predictions and hypotheses", and to "evaluate data, showing awareness of potential sources of random and systematic error". This topic operationalises hypothesis-referenced, quantitative conclusions plus formal error evaluation.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 4 Analyzing & Interpreting Data, grades 6–8):** the progression requires students to "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-1] phenomena", to "apply concepts of statistics and probability… to distinguish between correlation and causation", and to "consider limitations of data analysis (e.g. measurement error) and seek to improve precision." SEP 6 adds constructing explanations referencing the hypothesis.

- **Operational details:** Builds on constructing tables/graphs with best-fit lines (prerequisite mt_YHsUhi4Prc) and KS2 causal/trust reporting (mt_nyPMkeHlVJ, mt_AstzvYDU2m). Three step-ups: (1) identify the pattern/trend using SPECIFIC VALUES from a graph or table; (2) write a conclusion that explicitly references the HYPOTHESIS, states whether the prediction was supported, and quotes NUMERICAL evidence; and (3) distinguish a SYSTEMATIC error (shifts all readings the same direction — e.g. an uncalibrated zero) from a RANDOM error (unpredictable scatter), and propose a targeted procedural improvement for each. Feeds forward to full structured report-writing with peer review (dependent mt_ThTbUuNb3p).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/quantitative). A learner who can quote specific values to state a trend, write a hypothesis-referenced conclusion with numerical evidence, and correctly distinguish systematic from random error with a targeted improvement for each has met the bar.
bestPractices: Anchor the systematic-vs-random distinction in the DATA SIGNATURE: systematic error shifts every reading the same way (the whole line offset/parallel), random error scatters points either side of the trend — teach pupils to diagnose the type from how the data looks, then trace it to a cause.
Require conclusions to close the loop to the hypothesis explicitly ('the prediction was supported: as X increased, Y increased from __ to __'), quoting numbers, not just 'it went up'.

Match each error type to its remedy: systematic → recalibrate/zero the instrument or fix the method; random → repeat and average / use a more precise instrument — so 'evaluate' produces targeted improvements, not generic 'be more careful'.

Use best-fit lines and anomalies from the graphing prerequisite: anomalies off the line flag random error or mistakes; a line that misses the origin when it should pass through it flags systematic error.
Distinguish precision from accuracy explicitly — tight scatter (precise) can still be systematically wrong (inaccurate) — connecting to the parallel KS3 precision/accuracy topic.
keyRepresentations: A data-signature contrast: systematic error (whole line offset/parallel) vs random error (scatter about the line)
A hypothesis-referenced conclusion frame: 'The prediction was (not) supported — as IV increased, DV changed from __ to __'
An error-type → cause → targeted-improvement table
A best-fit graph with an anomaly circled and an offset (zero-error) line shown
A precision-vs-accuracy target diagram (tight-but-off vs spread-but-centred)
commonMisconceptions: Conflating systematic and random error, or thinking any large/anomalous reading is 'systematic' — not recognising systematic error as a consistent directional shift affecting all readings.
Writing a qualitative conclusion ('it increased') without quoting specific values or referencing the hypothesis.
Believing repeating readings fixes ALL error — repeats reduce random error but do NOT remove a systematic error (a miscalibrated instrument stays wrong however many times you read it).
Equating precision with accuracy — assuming tightly clustered readings must be correct.
Proposing vague improvements ('be more careful', 'do it again') instead of remedies targeted to the specific error type.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13 (KS3 / NGSS grades 6–8): draw quantitative, hypothesis-referenced conclusions from data and evaluate investigations by distinguishing systematic error (shifts every reading the same direction) from random error (scatter about the trend), proposing a targeted fix for each. The anchoring insight is that repeating and averaging reduces random scatter but leaves an additive systematic offset untouched — a miscalibrated instrument stays wrong however many times it is read. A systematic zero-offset preserves the per-unit slope but shifts the whole line off its intercept, so it must be corrected before judging a through-origin (proportionality) claim. Conclusions must quote specific numerical values and state whether the prediction was supported, not merely say 'it went up'.

activities.title: Error bench: inject each error type and watch the data respond
feedback: If a learner proposes repeating readings to remove a constant offset: show that averaging tightens scatter but leaves the offset exactly where it was — a consistent bias is fixed by calibration/zeroing or by subtracting the known offset, not by repeats.

If a conclusion says only 'it increased': prompt for two real values and an explicit statement of whether the prediction held (e.g. 'as the load increased, extension rose from __ to __, supporting the prediction').

If a learner rejects a relationship outright because all the numbers are offset: explain that a systematic offset moves every point by the same amount, preserving the per-unit slope but shifting the line off the origin — so rather than rejecting the relationship, correct or subtract the offset and re-test (for a proportionality hypothesis, check whether the corrected line now passes through the origin).
If a learner proposes a vague fix ('be more careful'): ask them to name the error type first, then give the remedy that specifically addresses it.
activities.rationale: The distinction between systematic and random error is defined by how the error moves the data, so letting a learner inject each type and observe the graph respond — then see averaging act differently on each — makes an abstract typology visible and diagnosable. KS3 Working Scientifically requires evaluating data with awareness of random and systematic error, and NGSS SEP 4 requires considering measurement-error limitations to improve precision. The interactive mechanism is a proposed, unvalidated way to make this concrete.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Working Scientifically requires interpreting observations and data to identify patterns and draw conclusions, presenting reasoned explanations relating data to predictions and hypotheses, and evaluating data with awareness of random and systematic error.

NGSS SEP 4 at grades 6-8 requires analysing/interpreting data to provide evidence for phenomena, applying statistics to distinguish correlation from causation, and considering limitations such as measurement error to improve precision.
learnerActions: Start from a clean results graph with a best-fit trend line.

Use a systematic-error control (e.g. a zero-offset slider) that shifts the ENTIRE line parallel — every point moved the same way, like a balance that was never zeroed — and observe that the per-unit slope is preserved while the whole line moves off its original intercept.

Note that for a through-origin (proportionality) claim this intercept shift matters: the offset must be corrected (recalibrated or subtracted) before checking whether the line passes through the origin.
Use a random-error control (e.g. a scatter dial) that jitters points above and below the true trend.

Run a 'repeat and average' action and watch random scatter shrink toward the trend line. If an offset is also switched on, the averaged points settle on the offset line, not the true line, so the systematic offset stays put however many repeats you run.

State, for each error type, the targeted fix: recalibrate/zero the instrument (or subtract the known offset) for systematic error; take repeats and average (or use a more precise instrument) for random error.
Write a conclusion that quotes at least two specific values from the graph and states explicitly whether the hypothesis/prediction was supported.
activities.intendedInsight: Systematic and random error are diagnosed by how they move the data — an offset of the whole line versus scatter about it — and each demands a different remedy. Averaging defeats random error but is powerless against a miscalibrated instrument; a systematic zero-offset leaves the slope intact but shifts the intercept, so it must be corrected before a proportionality claim can be tested.

activities.title: Classify, match, and conclude from data signatures
feedback: If a learner labels a single anomalous reading as 'systematic': clarify that a systematic error is a consistent directional shift affecting ALL readings, whereas a lone off-line point signals random error or a one-off mistake.
If a learner picks a conclusion without numbers: contrast it with one quoting values and a hypothesis statement, and explain why the quantitative version meets the bar.
If a learner matches 'repeat readings' to a systematic case: reconnect to the bench insight that repeats cannot remove a consistent bias — recalibrate or subtract the offset instead.
activities.rationale: Classification, matching to remedies, and selecting hypothesis-referenced quantitative conclusions give focused practice and quick diagnosis of misclassification. A sort/select format can check recognition of error type and of good conclusions, but it does not itself elicit a learner-constructed written conclusion or show how data behaves under repeated measurement, so it works best alongside the interactive bench and a constructed write-up.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Working Scientifically requires interpreting observations and data to identify patterns and draw conclusions, presenting reasoned explanations relating data to predictions and hypotheses, and evaluating data with awareness of random and systematic error.
learnerActions: Examine several datasets or graphs and classify each as showing systematic error (here, a zero-offset shifting the whole line parallel) or random error (scatter either side of the trend).
Match each error type to its targeted remedy: systematic → recalibrate/zero, subtract the known offset, or fix the method; random → repeat and average or use a more precise instrument.
Read a specific value off a graph (e.g. using a slider or gridline) and use it in a conclusion.
From a set of candidate conclusions, select or construct the one that is quantitative and hypothesis-referenced, rejecting qualitative 'it went up' versions and ones that ignore the prediction.
Identify an anomaly sitting off the best-fit line, and distinguish it from a line that fails to pass through the origin when it should (a systematic zero-error signature).
activities.intendedInsight: Error type is read from the data's signature, and 'evaluate' means proposing a remedy matched to that specific signature — not a generic improvement.

activities.title: Mentor probe: diagnose and defend an error claim
feedback: Praise responses that name the error type, justify it from the data signature, and attach the matching remedy.
Where a learner falls back on 'repeat it' as a catch-all, redirect to which errors repeats actually address and which they cannot.

If a learner treats a constant per-unit step as automatic proof of proportionality, point out that a systematic offset gives a constant step yet moves the line off the origin, so the offset must be corrected before any proportionality verdict.
activities.rationale: A mentor dialogue can probe reasoning and press for numerical evidence and error diagnosis, which complements the bench; a conversation alone cannot show the data responding to repeats, so it is best used as a follow-up to hands-on work. Efficacy of this dialogue is not independently verified.
learnerActions: Present your conclusion and have a mentor/examiner press for the specific numerical evidence behind it.
Respond to a diagnostic prompt such as: 'Your line doesn't pass through the origin when it should — what kind of error is that, and would repeating fix it?'

Answer follow-ups like: 'By how much does the reading change per unit — and does a constant step, on its own, establish strict proportionality (through the origin) or only a linear trend?', 'Would ten repeat readings remove a constant 2 cm zero-offset? Why or why not?', and 'If the readings instead scattered randomly by ±0.5 cm with no consistent offset, what would you do differently?'
Explain how a systematic error changes a graph compared with a random error.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner can articulate, under questioning, why a systematic offset is fixed by calibration/subtraction rather than repeats, why a constant per-unit step shows linearity but proportionality additionally requires passing through the origin, and can defend a conclusion with numbers tied to the hypothesis.

constraints: Classification/matching and multiple-choice formats assess recognition of error type and conclusions; they do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a written conclusion or show how data behaves under repeated measurement. Pair them with constructed written conclusions and the interactive bench.

A static contrast diagram (systematic offset vs random scatter) is a useful reference, but a fixed image cannot show the offset-vs-scatter behaviour changing or the averaging effect; treat it as a supporting reference, not the main vehicle. This is a narrow affordance limit, not a claim that static or other media cannot teach the concept.

Interactive controls (offset slider, scatter dial, repeat-and-average action, value-reading slider) are suggested ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative options, not mandatory implementations, and their effectiveness is untested.
Conclusions must include specific numerical values and an explicit hypothesis/prediction verdict; a qualitative 'it increased' does not meet the standard.

Error remedies must be matched to error type: systematic → recalibrate/zero, subtract the known offset, or fix method; random → repeat and average / more precise instrument. Generic 'be more careful' is insufficient.

A systematic zero-offset preserves the per-unit slope but shifts the intercept; for a strict proportionality (through-origin) hypothesis the offset must be corrected before judging whether the relationship holds — do not teach that an offset leaves proportionality intact.
Distinguish precision from accuracy where relevant: tightly clustered (precise) readings can still be systematically wrong (inaccurate).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the row. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no human review or empirical effectiveness is claimed.

CAUTION — the saved diagnostic dataset is internally inconsistent and could not be corrected because it lives in an unmodifiable source field. It states load 1–5 N give extension 2.0, 4.1, 5.9, 8.0, 10.1 cm with 'every reading about 2 cm too high', but these readings have a best-fit intercept of ≈0 and a constant extension/load ratio ≈2, so they already pass through the origin and show NO 2 cm offset. A genuine +2 cm zero-offset on proportional data would read 4, 6, 8, 10, 12; subtracting 2 cm from the given data yields 0, 2.1, 3.9, 6.0, 8.1 (line y≈2·load−2, intercept −2), which is linear but NOT through the origin and so NOT strictly proportional — it therefore cannot both carry a 2 cm systematic offset AND support the stated proportionality hypothesis. The teaching points (repeats cannot cure an additive systematic offset; an offset shifts the intercept and must be corrected before testing proportionality) remain sound independent of these specific numbers, and the learner-facing activities above avoid presenting the flawed numbers, using a learner-injected or generic offset instead.

If a concrete worked example is wanted without the source inconsistency, a sound substitute is a dataset that genuinely displays the offset, e.g. loads 1–5 N reading 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 cm where the true proportional values are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 cm; this is offered only as an illustrative option, not as verified source data.

The source claims establish curriculum requirements (what pupils must be able to do) but do NOT establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular medium; the original row's 'poor fit' ratings asserting a static image 'can't teach this' and that the task 'is not spatial' were softened to scoped affordance limits rather than universal claims.

Original row framed the interactive bench as 'ideal' and other formats by catalog fit ranking; these product/fit rankings were removed and the alternatives retained as complementary activities with distinct pedagogical purposes.

'Systematic error = whole-line parallel offset' is retained as the row's deliberate zero-offset teaching model; note that a multiplicative/gain systematic error would instead change the slope. This nuance is kept out of learner text to preserve the intended KS3 scope.

Independent re-audit: the three prior corrections (reviewNote flagging the dataset, the slope-vs-proportionality distinction in actions/feedback/constraints, and reclassifying the dataset into preservationAudit.uncertain) were re-checked occurrence-by-occurrence and confirmed consistent across summary, insights, actions, feedback, constraints and notes; no new contradictions or unsupported categorical claims were found.

probeDeeper: By how much does extension change per newton? Does that constant step support 'proportional'?
Would taking ten repeat readings remove the 2 cm offset? Why or why not?
Suppose instead the readings scattered randomly by ±0.5 cm with no consistent offset — what would you do differently?
How does a systematic error change a graph compared with a random error?
assess.correctAnswer: A strong response describes the trend quantitatively (extension rises by about 2 cm per 1 N — a linear, proportional pattern), concludes that this supports the hypothesis while quoting numbers, and identifies the constant 2 cm offset as a SYSTEMATIC error (it shifts every reading in the same direction) fixed by zeroing/checking the ruler or subtracting the offset — NOT by repeating. It contrasts this with RANDOM error (scatter in both directions) reduced by taking repeats and means, and ties each proposed fix to the error type it addresses.

errorPatterns.pattern: Repeats-fix-everything: proposes taking more repeat readings to remove the constant 2 cm offset.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Repeats average out random scatter but leave a consistent bias untouched; fix systematic error by calibration/zeroing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Suggests repeats/means as the fix for a systematic error.

errorPatterns.pattern: Qualitative conclusion without numbers: 'extension goes up as load goes up' with no values and no reference to proportionality or the hypothesis.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold quoting the per-newton step and stating explicitly whether the proportional prediction holds.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The conclusion lacks quantitative reference or a statement about whether the prediction was supported.

errorPatterns.pattern: Offset misread as invalidating the trend: concludes the hypothesis is wrong because the numbers are all off.
errorPatterns.nextMove: A systematic offset shifts all points equally — the proportional relationship (the slope) is preserved; only the intercept moves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects a genuinely proportional trend because of the constant offset.

responseLevels.gap: Describes the trend only qualitatively, or proposes 'repeat it' as a blanket fix, mistaking the systematic offset for random error.
responseLevels.full: States the quantitative trend, concludes with numerical reference to the hypothesis, correctly classifies the 2 cm offset as systematic (fixed by calibration, not repeats) versus random scatter (reduced by repeats/means), and ties each fix to its error type.
responseLevels.partial: Quotes values and references the hypothesis, and knows the terms systematic and random, but can't cleanly match each error type to the improvement that addresses it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's data from a spring experiment: as load increased 1–5 N, extension rose 2.0, 4.1, 5.9, 8.0, 10.1 cm — but every reading looks about 2 cm too high because the ruler wasn't zeroed. Describe the trend using values, say whether it supports the hypothesis 'extension is proportional to load', and identify whether the 2 cm offset is a systematic or random error and how you'd fix it — versus how you'd handle readings that just scatter a bit. Talk me through it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The systematic-vs-random distinction is the discriminator: a student can offer 'repeat the readings' as a catch-all, which does nothing for a systematic offset. Only one who understands the difference targets the offset with a zeroing/calibration fix and reserves repeats for random scatter. It also flushes the 'more repeats fix everything' habit.
