pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Balanced & Unbalanced Forces

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Lower KS2 Working Scientifically):** Setting up simple practical enquiries and comparative/fair tests; making systematic and careful observations and, where appropriate, taking accurate measurements; the underlying balanced/unbalanced-force content sits in Year 5 Forces.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-PS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-1] (assessment is qualitative and relative, one variable — number, size or direction — at a time, with gravity addressed as a downward pull).

- **Operational details:** This is a working-scientifically (procedural) topic mapped almost verbatim to NGSS 3-PS2-1: children PLAN and CONDUCT a fair-test investigation that provides evidence of how balanced and unbalanced forces affect an object's motion. The procedural core is variable control — change ONE variable (the number, size, or direction of forces) while keeping everything else the same — together with considering the NUMBER OF TRIALS (repeating readings). At 8-9 the force science stays qualitative and relative (bigger/smaller push, not measured newtons) and gravity is treated simply as a downward pull. The concept under the procedure: balanced forces (equal in size, opposite in direction) produce no change in motion; unbalanced forces change motion. Canonical contexts are tug-of-war (isolate force strength), motion across different surfaces (friction), and parachute canopy area.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational).
bestPractices: Frame the investigation around ONE testable question with a single independent variable (e.g. does a bigger push on one side change the motion?) and control the rest
Explicitly teach the two markers of a fair test — control variables AND consider the number of trials (repeat readings) — not just the slogan 'fair test' (NGSS SEP; Oak)
Model an investigation first, then release pupils to design their own (gradual release)
Require pupils to use their RESULTS as evidence to decide balanced vs unbalanced, rather than asserting the answer in advance
Keep it qualitative and relative at this age (no force measurement); treat gravity as a downward pull (NGSS assessment boundary)
Use tug-of-war as the canonical balanced↔unbalanced context; surface-friction and parachute area as alternatives; make predictions evidence-based, expecting trend-based reasoning
keyRepresentations: Fair-test planning frame / variable table: change one · measure · keep the same
Force-arrow diagram on the object — equal opposite arrows (balanced) vs unequal arrows giving a resultant (unbalanced)
Tug-of-war setup with a results table showing repeated trials
commonMisconceptions: 'Balanced forces' means there are NO forces / nothing is acting (balanced means equal and opposite, not absent)
Over-defaulting to 'fair test' as a slogan without grasping WHY only one variable may change (AKSIS: fair tests dominate primary practicals)
Changing more than one variable at once, or not repeating readings
Treating a prediction as a guess rather than reasoning from prior knowledge/evidence
The 'motion implies force' backbone — a moving object is thought to carry a force in its direction of travel
If a parachute/air-resistance context is used: that all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape

learn.summary: Procedural goal for 8–9 year-olds: plan and conduct a fair-test investigation that provides evidence of how balanced and unbalanced forces affect an object's motion. The craft is variable control (change exactly one of force number/size/direction, hold the rest constant), repeating readings, and then reading messy results to decide when forces are balanced (equal, opposite, no change in motion) versus unbalanced (motion changes). Science stays qualitative and relative (bigger/smaller pushes, not measured newtons); gravity is treated simply as a downward pull. The core experience should be a real hands-on investigation; a virtual investigation bench teaches the variable-control logic and is a strong complement but does not replace physically handling apparatus and real data.

activities.title: Run a real fair-test tug: how does the size of the pull change the motion?
feedback: If a learner labels the setup 'unbalanced' the instant any pull is applied while the trolley is still not moving: point out the trolley isn't moving, so the pull is being balanced by friction (or the held string) — that is balanced; unbalanced is when the motion CHANGES.

If a learner insists a steadily rolling trolley must have unbalanced forces: don't overload at this age — note that steady, unchanging motion is also balanced, and the constant-velocity case is deepened later.

If a learner changes two things at once (e.g. adds pulling mass AND swaps in a heavier trolley): rebuild so only the pulling force varies; ask 'which one caused the change?' so the need for one variable is felt.

If a learner treats balanced/unbalanced as separate memorised facts ('balanced = still, unbalanced = moving'): return them to their own trial — a still trolley with the pull cancelled = balanced; motion changing = unbalanced.
activities.rationale: The objective is procedural working-scientifically skill, so the learner must physically plan, run, repeat, and reason from real (messy) measurements rather than only recognise answers. Keeping it qualitative and relative matches the stated age expectation. The small-pull-held-still case is modelled with friction as an age-appropriate idealisation.
sourceClaims: The standard is to [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-1], [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4]; assessment is qualitative and relative (not quantitative force size), [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-1]), with gravity addressed as a downward pull.

A fair test is where only one variable is changed to see its effect; scientists control variables when planning fair tests; the working-scientifically skill is planning, carrying out and reviewing a fair-test investigation (in an air-resistance context).
learnerActions: Set up a wheeled trolley at rest on a table, a string over a pulley at the table edge, a small pot you can add identical masses to, plus a metre ruler and stopwatch.
Choose ONE thing to change — the size of the pulling force (add masses one at a time) — and list everything you will keep the same: same trolley, same surface, same starting point.
Predict, using what you already know, what will happen as the pull grows, and say why (reason from prior knowledge, not a blind guess).
Run each setting at least three times, recording distance travelled in a set time (or speed) in a results table.

Point to a moment when the trolley was NOT changing its motion (for example, a setting where the pull was too small to move it, if your data has one) and say what the forces were doing; point to a moment when the motion WAS changing (for example, the trolley speeding up after starting from rest).
Use your own data to conclude whether a bigger pulling force produces a bigger change in motion.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing only one variable and repeating readings lets you read results as evidence: if the trolley starts at rest and a small pull leaves it still, that pull is balanced by friction, so the forces are balanced (no change in motion); once the pull is bigger than the friction the forces become unbalanced and the trolley starts to move and speed up toward the pull, and a bigger unbalanced force makes a bigger change in motion.

activities.title: Virtual investigation bench: lock the variables and see why only one may change
feedback: If the learner changes more than one variable: the bench flags the confound and asks which change caused the effect, so the one-variable rule is experienced rather than recited.
If the learner says balanced means 'no forces at all': show the two equal arrows still present on the still cart — balanced means equal and opposite, not absent.
Live recolouring of the arrows and a results table that updates each trial can make the balanced↔unbalanced transition visible; offer these as optional supports, not required steps.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable model lets a learner isolate a variable, lock the rest, and observe the cause-effect of changing it, which supports control-of-variables reasoning. It is offered as a complement to real apparatus, not a substitute, because the hands-on enquiry craft is itself the goal; its comparative efficacy over other media is not established here.
sourceClaims: A fair test is where only one variable is changed to see its effect; scientists control variables when planning fair tests; the working-scientifically skill is planning, carrying out and reviewing a fair-test investigation (in an air-resistance context).
learnerActions: On a virtual tug-of-war or cart-with-pushers bench (cart starting at rest), pick ONE independent variable (e.g. the force on the left); the bench keeps the others the same by default (same cart, same surface, same number of pulls), though you can unlock them to test what happens if you change more than one.
Run the trial three times and watch a results table fill in; note that with equal, opposite forces the two arrows match and the cart stays still.
Nudge one force bigger and observe the cart, starting from rest, begin to move toward that force; connect the unequal arrows (a resultant) to the motion changing.
Deliberately try to change two things at once and respond to the bench's prompt ('you changed the surface AND the force; which one caused it?').
State from the table when forces were balanced (equal, opposite, no change in motion) and when unbalanced.
activities.intendedInsight: The variable-control logic can be experienced, not just stated: equal and opposite forces produce no change in motion; an unequal pair produces a resultant that changes motion (here, from rest, the cart starts moving toward the larger force); and changing two things at once makes the cause unreadable.

activities.title: Sort and sequence the fair-test reasoning (retrieval companion)
feedback: If a scenario with a still object under a small pull is marked unbalanced: remind that while motion is unchanging the forces cancel — balanced.
If only the slogan 'fair test' is given without naming the controlled variables: ask which specific things must be held the same and why.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, categorising and targeted questions can consolidate the procedural reasoning and vocabulary. This is a retrieval/consolidation aid: it checks and rehearses reasoning but does not itself elicit independent design and execution of an investigation, which the performance task must still provide.
learnerActions: Put the steps of a fair test in order: question with one variable → decide what to change, measure, and keep the same → run repeated trials → read results → conclude.
Categorise described scenarios as balanced (no change in motion) or unbalanced (motion changing), including a still object held by a small pull cancelled by friction.
Answer 'which variable should you change, and which must stay the same?' prompts for a given question.
Explain in a sentence why repeating readings matters.
activities.intendedInsight: Fair-test reasoning can be rehearsed: one variable changes, the rest are controlled, readings are repeated, and balanced/unbalanced is judged by whether motion changes.

activities.title: Labelled tug-of-war reference scene (vocabulary scaffold)
feedback: If the learner thinks the balanced state has no forces: point to the two equal arrows still shown — balanced means they cancel, not that they are gone.
Tap-to-reveal arrow states can make the contrast concrete; treat this as a reference, not a replacement for running trials.
activities.rationale: A fixed labelled scene supports vocabulary and set-up recognition. Because it is static it does not run trials or show the cause-effect of changing a variable, so it is a scaffold toward, not a substitute for, the live bench and the real investigation.
learnerActions: Study a labelled tug-of-war or cart scene; tap to reveal the force arrows in a balanced state (equal, opposite) and an unbalanced state (unequal, resultant).
Use a 'change one / keep the same' overlay to name the independent variable and the controlled variables for a chosen question.
Say aloud which state shows no change in motion and which shows motion changing.
activities.intendedInsight: Builds the set-up vocabulary and the look of balanced versus unbalanced force arrows before and alongside running a real test.

constraints: Keep the force science qualitative and relative at this age (bigger/smaller push, not measured newtons); treat gravity simply as a downward pull.

Balanced forces mean no CHANGE in motion (equal and opposite), which includes steady, unchanging motion — not necessarily being at rest. Avoid teaching 'balanced = still' as a rule; the constant-velocity case is deepened later.
Balanced does not mean no forces are acting; it means the forces cancel. A still object under a small pull cancelled by friction is balanced.

When a trolley starts at rest, an unbalanced pull makes it begin to move and speed up toward that pull; state the at-rest starting condition wherever 'speeds up' is claimed, and describe the resultant as changing motion rather than as the current direction of travel.
Change exactly one variable (number, size or direction of forces) and hold the rest constant; repeat readings to build the number-of-trials habit.

The learning objective is the hands-on enquiry craft: the performance task requires physically planning, running, repeating and reasoning from real data. The virtual bench, the sort/sequence companion, and the labelled scene are complements/scaffolds and do not on their own satisfy the procedural goal.
Recognition-only sorting and sequencing can rehearse and check reasoning but do not elicit independent design and execution of an investigation.
Treat predictions as evidence-based, trend-based reasoning from prior knowledge, not blind guesses.
The wheeled-trolley 'held still by friction under a small pull' is an age-appropriate simplification; present it qualitatively and do not over-formalise the friction mechanism at this age.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's '3D adds nothing' and 'static image cannot show cause-effect' claims and the 'only a live bench teaches the logic' framing were softened to scoped affordances/objective limits; catalog fit rankings and product/artefact-type labels were removed.

One source (AKSIS/PSTT enquiry guidance) was marked verified:false in the row. It directly backs the evidence-based/trend predictions and repeated-readings points and is retained only there; it was removed from the sort/sequence activity's sourceClaims because it does not support that activity's consolidation-via-sorting principle.

Self-audit of the force/motion logic: 'unbalanced when motion changes', 'balanced can include steady motion', 'a still trolley under a friction-cancelled pull is balanced', and 'from rest an unbalanced pull makes it start moving and speed up toward the pull' are internally consistent; 'balanced = stationary only' is treated as a misconception, not taught. No arithmetic or geometric claims required correction.

The friction model for a wheeled trolley held still under a small pull is an idealisation (rolling/axle resistance presented as friction); it is stated qualitatively in the activity and flagged here, not over-specified for the age group.

probeDeeper: Point to a time when the trolley wasn't changing its motion. What were the forces doing then?
What did you change, and what did you keep the same? Why does that matter?
When you added more mass to the pot, what happened — and does that make the forces more balanced or more unbalanced?
The trolley is sitting still with the string pulling gently. Balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: Changes only the pulling force (adds masses one at a time), keeps the trolley, surface and start point the same, and measures the effect on motion (distance in a set time, or speed), repeating readings. Reads the results as: while the trolley stays still and a small pull is cancelled by friction, the forces are balanced (no change in motion); once the pull is bigger than friction the forces are unbalanced and the trolley speeds up. Concludes a bigger unbalanced force makes a bigger change in motion.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'If a force is pulling it, the forces must be unbalanced — even before it moves.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out the trolley isn't moving, so the pull is being cancelled (by friction / the held string) — that is balanced; unbalanced is when the motion CHANGES.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels the setup unbalanced the moment a pull is applied, while the trolley is still not moving.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Balanced forces means the object has to be completely still — it can't be balanced if it's moving.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't overload at this age — note that steady, unchanging motion is also balanced, and deepen the constant-velocity case at KS3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists a trolley rolling steadily must have unbalanced forces.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'I'll add more pulling mass AND use a heavier trolley to make it interesting.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild so only the pulling force varies; keep the trolley and surface the same.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Changes two things between trials, so the motion changes for mixed reasons.

responseLevels.gap: Runs the setup but changes more than the force, or calls any situation with a force 'unbalanced'; can't connect results to balanced vs unbalanced.
responseLevels.full: Controls variables, measures the effect of force size with repeats, and reads the results relationally — identifies balanced (no change in motion, forces cancel) and unbalanced (motion changing, net force) moments in the actual trial and concludes a bigger unbalanced force makes a bigger change.
responseLevels.partial: Runs a fair-ish test and sees bigger pull -> more motion, and can define balanced and unbalanced, but treats them as separate facts ('balanced = still, unbalanced = moving') without reading their OWN moments — still trolley = pull cancelled = balanced; motion changing = unbalanced.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a wheeled trolley on the table, a string running over a pulley at the table's edge, a small pot you can add identical masses to, and a metre ruler and stopwatch. Plan and run a FAIR test to find out how the size of the pulling force changes how the trolley moves. Set it up, take your measurements, then use your results to point out a moment when the forces on the trolley were BALANCED and a moment when they were UNBALANCED.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because it is a procedure, you WATCH rather than ask about it. The discriminator is whether the child (a) controls variables so only force size changes and (b) reads 'no change in motion' as balanced and 'motion changing' as unbalanced. A child who labels the setup unbalanced the instant any pull is applied (even while it sits still), who thinks balanced means only-stationary, or who changes trolley mass and pull together, reveals the gap even if the measuring is fine.

sources.claim: The standard is to [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-1], [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4]; assessment is qualitative and relative (not quantitative force size), [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-1]), with gravity addressed as a downward pull.
sources.source: NGSS 3-PS2-1 (Next Generation Science Standards, official)

sources.claim: A fair test is where only one variable is changed to see its effect; scientists control variables when planning fair tests; the working-scientifically skill is planning, carrying out and reviewing a fair-test investigation (in an air-resistance context).
sources.source: Oak National Academy — Air resistance (plan) KS2 lesson

pedagogy.summary: Finding a non-unit fraction of a quantity is a two-step operator procedure: divide the whole by the denominator to find one equal part (the unit fraction), then multiply that part by the numerator. The teaching goal at age 8-9 is fluency and reliable structure — children already know unit fractions of sets, so the new work is coordinating the divide-then-multiply sequence and interpreting worded problems ("3/8 of 24 sweets") into that structure. Best taught by making the two steps explicit and visible before compressing them, and by grounding the procedure in the meaning of the denominator (how many equal shares) and numerator (how many shares we take).
bestPractices: Make the two steps explicit: ring-fence 'divide by the denominator to get one part' as step 1, then 'multiply by the numerator' as step 2, before letting children compress it — many errors are a collapsed or reversed sequence, not arithmetic slips.

Anchor the procedure in the fraction-as-operator meaning: the denominator says how many equal groups to split into, the numerator says how many of those groups to take. This lets children self-check which number divides and which multiplies.

Use bar models / arrays: draw the whole as a bar, partition into 'denominator' equal parts, shade 'numerator' of them, and read off the total — the model makes the divide-then-multiply visible and catches the 'divide by numerator' error.
Sequence from unit to non-unit: confirm 1/8 of 24 = 3 first, then 3/8 = 3 x 3 = 9, so the new step (multiply by numerator) is isolated against secure ground.
Include a plausibility check: a proper fraction of a quantity must be smaller than the whole (9 red sweets out of 24), which catches multiply-the-whole errors.
Vary the worded contexts (sweets, money, measures, sets of people) so children practise translating language into the divide-then-multiply structure rather than pattern-matching one phrasing.
keyRepresentations: Bar model partitioned into denominator equal parts with numerator shaded (whole labelled, one part labelled)
Array / equal groups (24 counters in 8 groups of 3; take 3 groups)
Double number line: 0 ... whole on top, 0 ... fraction on bottom, marking one part then stepping along
Written two-step record: 24 ÷ 8 = 3, then 3 × 3 = 9
commonMisconceptions: Divides by the numerator instead of the denominator (3/8 of 24 read as 24 ÷ 3)
Stops after one step — finds the unit fraction (24 ÷ 8 = 3) and gives that as the answer without multiplying by the numerator
Multiplies the whole by the numerator (24 × 3) giving an answer larger than the whole
Multiplies numerator and denominator into the whole in the wrong order or muddles which is which under worded-problem load

learn.summary: Finding a non-unit fraction of a quantity (e.g. 3/8 of 24) is a two-step operator procedure for 8-9 year olds: divide the whole by the denominator to find one equal part, then multiply that part by the numerator. Children already know unit fractions of sets, so the new work is coordinating the divide-then-multiply sequence, grounding it in the meaning of numerator and denominator, and translating worded problems into that structure. Make the two steps explicit and visible before compressing them.

activities.title: The fraction-of machine: divide to build parts, then take them
feedback: If a learner takes 3 single sweets rather than 3 groups, pause: '3/8 means 8 equal shares - how many shares do you take, and how big is each share?' This shows the learner is treating the numerator as a number of single items and ignoring the denominator. Note that the answer (3) matches the size of one share here, so watch the action, not just the answer.

If a learner tries to make 3 groups instead of 8, use a meaning-based prompt (24 does divide evenly by 3, so the partition alone will not flag the error): 'Does the bottom number tell how many groups, or the top? /8 means 8 equal groups.'
If a learner stops after making 8 groups of 3 and reports '3', prompt: 'That is 1/8. The question asks for 3/8 - how many of those groups do we take?'

If a learner produces a number bigger than 24, ask the plausibility check: 'Can 3/8 of 24 be more than 24? A proper fraction of an amount is smaller than the whole.' Then rebuild the divide-first step.
When correct, confirm: dividing built the parts (24 ÷ 8 = 3) and selecting took 3 of them (3 × 3 = 9).
activities.rationale: Letting the child perform and see both steps, with a bar model shown alongside tying the actions to the written record, isolates the load-bearing skill (the sequence) and surfaces the two canonical errors in the action itself. Live partitioning, selecting groups, and a running total are optional interaction examples that make the divide-then-multiply mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.
Finding fractions of quantities is taught as divide-then-multiply, developing from unit-fraction-of-a-set to non-unit fractions; children should solve worded problems in varied contexts.
learnerActions: Set up the problem '3/8 of 24 sweets': start with 24 sweets to share.
Split the 24 sweets into equal groups, where the number of groups is fixed by the denominator (8 groups of 3).
Now take the numerator's worth of those groups: take 3 of the 8 groups and count the total (9).
Record the two steps in writing alongside the action: 24 ÷ 8 = 3, then 3 × 3 = 9.
Repeat with new fractions and new contexts (e.g. 3/5 of 20 pounds, 2/3 of 18 people) so the structure, not one phrasing, is practised.
activities.intendedInsight: The procedure is two distinct actions with two distinct results: dividing by the denominator builds the equal parts, and multiplying by the numerator (selecting that many groups) takes them. Children can self-check which number divides (how many equal shares) and which multiplies (how many shares to take).

activities.title: Isolate the new step: from unit fraction to non-unit fraction
feedback: If the learner re-divides when the numerator changes, point out the groups of 3 already exist - only the number of groups taken changes.
If the learner can do 3/8 but stalls on 5/8, they may be pattern-matching the last answer rather than using the structure; walk back to 'how big is one group?'
Praise explanations that reference meaning ('8 says make 8 equal shares, 3 says take 3 of them') over recited rules.
activities.rationale: Sequencing from unit to non-unit isolates the new multiply step against secure ground and builds the fraction-as-operator meaning rather than a rote rule.
sourceClaims: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.
Finding fractions of quantities is taught as divide-then-multiply, developing from unit-fraction-of-a-set to non-unit fractions; children should solve worded problems in varied contexts.
learnerActions: First confirm the unit fraction on secure ground: find 1/8 of 24 (= 3).
Then isolate the new step: 'That is one group. For 3/8, how many groups do we take?' Take 3 groups to get 9.
Try the same whole with a different numerator: 5/8 of 24 re-uses the groups of 3 and takes 5 (= 15); notice you do NOT re-divide.
Explain in your own words why the denominator divides and the numerator multiplies.
activities.intendedInsight: The division step is shared across all eighths of 24; only the numerator (how many groups to take) changes. This separates the secure prior skill from the genuinely new multiply-by-numerator step.

activities.title: Bar models and arrays: making divide-then-multiply visible
feedback: If a learner partitions into the numerator's parts, compare: 'Which number tells how many equal parts to cut? The bottom (denominator).'
If a learner shades all parts or more than the whole, revisit: the shaded amount is part of the bar, so it cannot exceed 24.

A tap-to-reveal worked example (reveal the partition, then reveal which parts are taken and the total) can serve as a pre-teach, but it shows one case and does not let the child perform the procedure across varied quantities, which fluency requires.
activities.rationale: Bar models, arrays and number lines represent the operator structure concretely and catch the characteristic errors; a single revealed worked example is a useful scaffold but limited to one case.
sourceClaims: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.
learnerActions: Draw the whole as a bar labelled 24; partition it into the denominator's number of equal parts (8 parts), label one part (3).
Shade the numerator's number of parts (3 parts) and read off the shaded total (9).
Build the same with counters: arrange 24 counters as 8 groups of 3, then ring 3 groups.
Use a double number line: amount (0 to 24) on top and fraction (0 to 1, marked in eighths) on the bottom, so 1/8 lines up with 3 and 8/8 lines up with 24. Mark one part, then step along to 3/8 (9).
activities.intendedInsight: The model makes the divide-then-multiply structure visible: partitioning is the division, shading/selecting is the multiplication. Reading the total off the model catches the divide-by-numerator error (wrong number of parts) and the multiply-the-whole error (answer must fit inside the bar).

activities.title: Varied worded problems and plausibility checking
feedback: If a learner computes 24 x 3 = 72, ask 'Can part of 24 be bigger than 24?' before rebuilding the divide-first step.
If a learner solves sweets but stalls on money, highlight that the structure is identical: divide the amount by the denominator, multiply by the numerator.

Scored practice can check fluency and capture the two-step structure: on a 0-24 slider an answer of 3 (stopping after one step) is a selectable error, while a free-entry answer can additionally surface an answer of 72 (multiplying the whole), and a fill-in-the-blanks format (24 ÷ ☐ = ☐, ☐ × ☐ = ☐) shows which step goes wrong. Recognising a correct option, however, does not show the child can independently construct the steps - pair it with doing.
activities.rationale: Worded problems in varied contexts are curriculum expectations; a plausibility check catches the multiply-the-whole error; talking a problem through may support translating worded language into the structure and should accompany, not replace, the independent practice a procedural skill requires.
sourceClaims: Finding fractions of quantities is taught as divide-then-multiply, developing from unit-fraction-of-a-set to non-unit fractions; children should solve worded problems in varied contexts.
learnerActions: Solve worded problems across contexts: sweets (A bag has 24 sweets, 3/8 are red - how many red?), money (3/5 of 20 pounds), measures (cm), and sets of people (2/3 of 18).
For each, write the two lines of working and name which number divides and which multiplies.
Before accepting an answer, run the plausibility check: a proper fraction of an amount must be smaller than the whole (9 red sweets out of 24 is reasonable; 72 is not).
Optionally talk a problem through aloud with a partner or in-role 'shopkeeper' who poses 'fraction of my stock' problems, explaining each step.
activities.intendedInsight: Translating varied language into the same divide-then-multiply structure prevents pattern-matching one phrasing, and the plausibility check guards against multiply-the-whole errors.

constraints: Keep the two steps explicit and ring-fenced before compressing them: many errors are a collapsed or reversed sequence, not arithmetic slips.
Anchor the procedure in meaning - denominator = how many equal groups, numerator = how many groups taken - so children can self-check which number divides and which multiplies.
A revealed/worked static example shows one case and cannot let the child perform the procedure across varied quantities; use it as a pre-teach, not the main practice.

Recognition-only response formats (selecting a correct option) can assess fluency and surface specific errors but do not elicit independent construction of the two steps; include tasks where the child builds or writes the procedure.
Talking a problem through supports translating worded language into the structure but should accompany, not replace, repeated independent doing for a procedural skill.

Do NOT rely on a visible remainder to flag the divide-by-numerator error in '3/8 of 24': 24 divides evenly by 3, so making 3 groups gives 8-per-group with no remainder. Use a meaning-of-denominator prompt instead.

Watch out for the diagnostic coincidence in '3/8 of 24': the group size (3) equals the numerator (3), so an answer of 3 could mean the child took 3 single counters (treating the numerator as a count of items and ignoring the denominator) or stopped after finding one group (1/8). Neither is divide-by-numerator confusion, which shows up as making 3 groups of 8. Watch what the child actually does, and also use a problem where group size and numerator differ (e.g. 3/4 of 24, group size 6) so these errors can be told apart.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (National Curriculum in England programmes of study) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

The source row's own diagnostic note is self-contradictory: it states the design avoids numerator equal to group size, then states 24 deliberately gives group size 3 and numerator 3. The latter is correct for '3/8 of 24'.

The original 'fraction-of machine' design-note feedback claiming the division visibly stalls (trays won't divide evenly) when a child divides by the numerator does not hold whenever the numerator also divides the whole (as with 3 and 24); it was corrected to a meaning-based prompt in the activity feedback, not relying on a visible remainder.

Claims that a 2D interactive is uniquely 'ideal' or that 3D 'adds nothing', or that doing is inherently superior to talking, are catalog/efficacy judgements not established by the sources; reframed as affordances and qualified limits without asserting necessity or comparative superiority.

probeDeeper: Once they answer, ask 'how did you know to make 8 groups and not 3?' — listen for the denominator meaning, not a recited rule.
'Show me 1/8 of the 24 first — now how do you get to 3/8?' isolates whether the second step is understood or lucky.
Counterexample: 'What if I'd asked for 5/8 of 24 instead?' — a child with the structure re-uses the groups of 3 and takes 5 (=15); a child who pattern-matched the last answer stalls.
'Could your answer be bigger than 24? Why not?' surfaces whether the plausibility check is available.
assess.correctAnswer: 9. The child splits the 24 into 8 equal groups (24 ÷ 8 = 3 in each), then takes 3 of those groups (3 × 3 = 9).

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by the numerator: reads '3/8 of 24' as 24 ÷ 3 and makes 3 groups (or takes just 3 counters), giving 8 or 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the meaning of the denominator: it says how many equal shares. Rebuild with 'how many equal groups does /8 mean?' before touching the numerator.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child makes 3 groups instead of 8, or grabs 3 counters straight away — using the top number as the divisor

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops after one step: finds the unit fraction (24 ÷ 8 = 3) and offers 3 as the answer, not multiplying by the numerator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach division of sets — scaffold the second step only: 'that's 1/8; the question asks for 3/8 — how many of those groups?' Point back at the numerator's job.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child correctly makes 8 groups of 3 then reports '3' — the division is right but the second step is dropped

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the whole by the numerator: computes 24 × 3 = 72, giving an answer larger than the starting quantity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trigger the plausibility check first ('can 3/8 of 24 be more than 24?'), then rebuild the divide-first step with the bar model.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child produces a number bigger than 24 with no partitioning, or multiplies before dividing

responseLevels.gap: Cannot coordinate the two steps: divides by the numerator, or multiplies the whole, or produces the unit-fraction-only answer and cannot get further even with the numerator pointed out.
responseLevels.full: Reliably divides by the denominator then multiplies by the numerator, explains each step by the meaning of the fraction, transfers to a new fraction and a new context (money, measures), and checks the answer is smaller than the whole.
responseLevels.partial: Executes both steps for the practised case (makes 8 groups, takes 3, gets 9) but treats them as a memorised recipe — cannot explain why the denominator divides, or stalls when the fraction changes to 5/8 or the context changes to money.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 24 counters. Find 3/8 of them. Do it however you like, and I'll watch — you don't need to tell me the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the teacher WATCHES the procedure rather than asking about it, the two canonical breakdowns show themselves in the child's actions: a child who divides by the numerator makes 3 groups; a child who stops after one step makes 8 groups but reports 3; only a child who has the divide-then-multiply structure makes 8 groups AND takes 3 of them. 24 is chosen so 3/8 divides evenly (no remainder to mask the error) and the numerator (3) differs from the group size (also 3) is avoided — deliberately 24 gives group size 3 and numerator 3, so watch that they take 3 GROUPS not 3 counters: taking 3 counters instead of 3 groups is the exact tell for divide-by-numerator confusion.

sources.claim: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Protecting Eyes from Sunlight

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 3 Science, Light):** recognise that light from the sun can be dangerous and that there are ways to protect their eyes. (Non-statutory guidance: pupils should be warned that it is not safe to look directly at the sun, even when wearing dark glasses.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No NGSS performance expectation covers sun/eye safety — this is a UK-specific health-and-safety objective rather than a physics PE; in US schemes it sits under health/safety education, not the NGSS waves strand. (NGSS waves PEs concern how light behaves, e.g. 1-PS4-2/3, not eye safety.)

- **Operational details:** The load-bearing message is a non-negotiable safety RULE plus its reason. Lead by eliciting and explicitly challenging the dominant misconception — that it is safe to look at the Sun if it is cloudy or if you are wearing sunglasses — and correct it directly: NEVER look straight at the Sun, even with dark glasses. Give an age-appropriate why: the eye's lens focuses sunlight to a point on the retina (like a magnifying glass), which can burn the light-sensitive cells, and instruments (binoculars/telescopes) make it far worse. Separate EYE protection (sunglasses for general brightness/UV; never staring at the Sun; safe indirect viewing via a pinhole projector) from SKIN protection (sunscreen, clothing, shade). UV beads support a fair test of which sunglasses block the most UV — useful evidence for 'ways to protect', but reinforce that blocking UV is NOT the same as making it safe to stare. Model accurate language (the Sun APPEARS to move) to avoid seeding astronomy misconceptions.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). At 7–8 success is stating the rule (never look at the Sun, even with sunglasses, even when cloudy), giving a simple reason (it can damage the eyes), and naming ways to protect eyes (and, distinctly, skin). This is safety knowledge plus a simple cause; the optics of focusing/retinal detail is teacher background, not a pupil expectation.
bestPractices: Lead by eliciting then explicitly refuting the key misconception that the Sun is safe to look at when cloudy or through sunglasses — the rule is NEVER look directly at the Sun, even with dark glasses.
Give an age-appropriate reason (the eye focuses sunlight onto the retina and can burn it; instruments make it worse) so the rule is understood, not just imposed.
Distinguish eye protection (sunglasses, never staring, safe indirect viewing) from skin protection (sunscreen, clothing, shade) — they are different needs.
Use UV-sensitive beads to fair-test which sunglasses/sun creams block the most UV — hands-on evidence for 'ways to protect' — while stressing that blocking UV ≠ safe to look at the Sun.
Provide a safe indirect way to observe the Sun (pinhole/box projector) rather than ever direct viewing.
Model accurate language ('the Sun appears to move across the sky') to avoid reinforcing Sun/Earth astronomy misconceptions; reinforce that all skin tones need UV protection.
keyRepresentations: A clear 'NEVER look at the Sun — even with sunglasses' rule card
A simple eye diagram: sunlight focused by the lens onto the retina (why it harms)
UV-sensitive beads used to fair-test different sunglasses / sun creams
A pinhole / box projector for safe indirect Sun viewing
An eye-protection vs skin-protection sorting display
commonMisconceptions: It is safe to look at the Sun on a cloudy day (cloud removes the danger).
Wearing sunglasses (or 'dark enough' glasses) makes it safe to look directly at the Sun.
The Sun is only dangerous on hot/bright summer days.
If it doesn't feel hot or look painfully bright, the Sun isn't harmful to the eyes.
Only some skin tones need protection from UV, rather than everyone.
Sunglasses protect the eyes the same way for staring as for general brightness (conflating UV protection with safe direct viewing).

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds, teach the non-negotiable safety rule that you must NEVER look directly at the Sun — even through sunglasses, even on a cloudy day — paired with a simple, age-appropriate reason (the Sun is so bright it can permanently damage the light-sensitive cells inside the eye). Lead by surfacing then directly refuting the central misconception that sunglasses or cloud make it safe to stare. Separately build the 'ways to protect' half of the objective: naming eye protections (sunglasses for general brightness/glare, shade, hat, and safe indirect viewing via a pinhole/box projector) distinct from skin protections (sunscreen, clothing, shade, hat), and optionally testing which sunglasses block the most UV using UV-sensitive beads — while stressing that blocking UV is not the same as making direct viewing safe. The focusing/retinal optics is teacher background; the pupil expectation is the rule, a simple cause, and named protections.

activities.title: The Sun-and-eye safety scene: naming the 'but I've got sunglasses' excuse
feedback: If a learner says sunglasses make staring safe: sunglasses reduce glare for comfort and block some UV, but they never make direct Sun-gazing safe — the safe move is not to look at all.
If a learner says a cloudy or dim-looking Sun is safe to view: don't judge safety by how bright it happens to look; the Sun is still dangerously intense through thin cloud or haze.
Affirm the pinhole/box projector answer: watching the projected image of the Sun on a surface lets you observe it without ever pointing your eyes at the Sun.
activities.rationale: Fixed, authoritative safety content with a named-and-answered misconception suits a pre-authored tap-to-reveal scene, where the sunglasses flap lets the child's own 'but I've got sunglasses' objection be surfaced and corrected rather than drifting toward 'so when IS it okay?'. The animated reveal is intended to make the simple mechanism (light gathering to a point inside the eye) more concrete for young learners without requiring them to master the optics; this is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 3 statutory: recognise that light from the sun can be dangerous and that there are ways to protect their eyes; non-statutory guidance warns pupils that it is not safe to look directly at the sun, even when wearing dark glasses.

Key misconception that it is safe to look at the Sun when cloudy or when wearing sunglasses (it is never safe); UV-sensitive beads support fair tests of sunglasses/sun creams; eye protection should be distinguished from skin protection; conceptual change requires hands-on, repeated experience and explicit correction.
learnerActions: Look at an illustration of a child outdoors under the Sun and predict aloud or in writing: 'Is it ever safe to look straight at the Sun?'
Reveal the Sun-to-eye path: light gathers through the eye's lens to a tiny point inside the eye — caption 'the Sun can damage the inside of your eye for ever — never look straight at it.'
Reveal the sunglasses flap after stating your own thought 'but I've got sunglasses': 'sunglasses dim the brightness and block some UV — but they do NOT make it safe to stare at the Sun.'
Reveal the cloud: 'still not safe on a cloudy day — the Sun is still dangerously bright through thin cloud or haze.'

Reveal the pinhole/box projector: the safe way to watch the Sun is by looking at its projected image on a surface, never at the Sun itself and never by holding anything up to your eyes toward the Sun.
activities.intendedInsight: Looking directly at the Sun is never safe, and the common reasons children think it becomes safe — such as wearing sunglasses or the Sun looking dim behind cloud — are each wrong; there is a separate safe way to observe the Sun indirectly.

activities.title: UV-bead fair test: which sunglasses block the most UV?
feedback: Praise a controlled comparison: if the beads started uncoloured, matched, and were in the same light at the same time, with only the sunglasses changed, then differences in the beads are fair evidence about UV blocking.
If a learner concludes the best UV-blocking glasses make it safe to stare: separate 'protects your eyes generally' from 'lets you look at the Sun' — the rule to never look directly still holds.
Reminder for the outdoor set-up: observe the beads on the ground or table, never look up at the Sun and never hold sunglasses up to your eyes toward the Sun to test them.
activities.rationale: A hands-on UV-bead comparison provides evidence for the 'ways to protect' half of the objective and is intended to give practice in fair-test reasoning, while the explicit caution prevents the dangerous over-extension from UV protection to safe direct viewing. This is a proposed supporting activity and must never let a child experience looking at the Sun.
sourceClaims: Key misconception that it is safe to look at the Sun when cloudy or when wearing sunglasses (it is never safe); UV-sensitive beads support fair tests of sunglasses/sun creams; eye protection should be distinguished from skin protection; conceptual change requires hands-on, repeated experience and explicit correction.
learnerActions: Set out UV-sensitive beads and watch THE BEADS change colour in sunlight (or a UV source) — keep your eyes on the beads, never on the Sun.

Using fresh beads that have been kept out of sunlight (not the beads already coloured in the first step), put a matching set of beads under each pair of sunglasses (or under clear plastic spread with sun cream), plus one uncovered set to compare. Lay them out side by side in the same light at the same time, keeping everything else the same, and observe how much each set changes colour.
Record which item lets the beads change least, i.e. which blocks the most UV, and discuss what makes this a fair test (same beads, same light, change only the sunglasses).
State explicitly: blocking the most UV is NOT the same as making it safe to look straight at the Sun.
activities.intendedInsight: There are testable, evidence-based 'ways to protect' — the test can show whether some sunglasses block more UV than others (and how dark a lens looks does not tell you how much UV it blocks) — but blocking UV helps protect eyes from UV exposure and does not permit staring at the Sun.

activities.title: Eyes vs skin: sorting protections and checking the rule
feedback: If a learner equates the Sun with a lamp: the Sun is vastly more intense than ordinary household lamps and, unlike them, can cause permanent eye damage — so never look directly at it.
If a learner tries to place 'shade' in only one group: shade legitimately protects both eyes and skin, so it belongs in both.
Reinforce that everyone, of every skin tone, needs UV protection.
activities.rationale: Categorising and short rule-checks reinforce and assess the safety knowledge and the eyes-vs-skin distinction. A sort-and-check task can confirm the rule and vocabulary but does not by itself require the learner to construct the reasoning aloud, so it is paired with the spoken explanation prompts for the cloudy-day and torch cases.
sourceClaims: Key misconception that it is safe to look at the Sun when cloudy or when wearing sunglasses (it is never safe); UV-sensitive beads support fair tests of sunglasses/sun creams; eye protection should be distinguished from skin protection; conceptual change requires hands-on, repeated experience and explicit correction.
learnerActions: Sort protection actions into 'protects eyes' (sunglasses, never staring, safe indirect viewing) and 'protects skin' (sunscreen, clothing); note that 'shade' and 'a sun hat' are shared items that belong in BOTH groups, so this sort allows an item to go in two places.
Answer short check questions: Is it safe to look at the Sun while wearing sunglasses? (No.) Is it safe on a cloudy day? (No.)
State the rule in your own words and give one simple reason, then name at least two ways to protect your eyes outside on a very bright day.
Discuss the torch question: why is a quick glance at a torch different from a glance at the Sun?
activities.intendedInsight: Eye protection and skin protection meet different needs (with shade and a sun hat helping both); the Sun is far more intense than any ordinary household light, so we must never look directly at it, whereas a quick accidental glance at an ordinary torch is unlikely to harm your eyes (though we still should not stare into torches).

activities.title: Ask the eye doctor: why can't I look at the Sun?
feedback: Keep the message fixed: the answer is always 'never look directly, even with sunglasses' — do not negotiate exceptions.
If instruments come up: binoculars and telescopes concentrate the Sun's light and make direct viewing far more dangerous, never safer.
activities.rationale: A role-play with an authoritative persona may be engaging and may motivate the 'why'; because the message is a non-negotiable safety rule for young children, any dialogue should deliver the fixed answer and avoid open-ended drift toward exceptions, so keep it tightly scripted or use it after the rule is secure. The persona's core 'never, even with sunglasses' message is supported by the curriculum/misconception sources; the 'instruments make it worse' detail rests on the Ogden Trust source, which is marked unverified in the row.
sourceClaims: Key misconception that it is safe to look at the Sun when cloudy or when wearing sunglasses (it is never safe); UV-sensitive beads support fair tests of sunglasses/sun creams; eye protection should be distinguished from skin protection; conceptual change requires hands-on, repeated experience and explicit correction.

The eye's lens is about four times as powerful as a magnifying glass and focuses sunlight to a point on the retina that can burn the light-sensitive cells and cause permanent damage; the effect is worse through unfiltered cameras/telescopes/binoculars; safe observation uses indirect methods such as projection.
learnerActions: Pose a child's questions to an optometrist/eye-doctor persona: 'Why can't I look at the Sun?' and 'What if I wear sunglasses?'

Hear the authoritative answer: the Sun is so intensely bright it can permanently damage the light-sensitive cells inside the eye; sunglasses reduce glare but do not make looking safe; instruments like binoculars or telescopes make it far worse.
Repeat the rule back in your own words and name the safe indirect way to watch the Sun (looking at its projected image on a surface, never directly).
activities.intendedInsight: An expert confirms the same single rule and reason, reinforcing that there are no exceptions and that instruments increase the danger.

constraints: The load-bearing outcome is a non-negotiable safety rule plus a simple reason: NEVER look directly at the Sun, even with dark glasses, even on a cloudy day — because it can permanently damage the eyes.

No activity may ever invite, simulate, or rehearse a child looking directly at the Sun, nor ask whether a child can see the Sun through a cover or hold any material up to the eyes toward the Sun; provide only safe indirect viewing (a pinhole/box projector that shows a projected image on a surface, or observing UV beads on the ground/table).
Blocking UV (by sunglasses or sun cream) is not the same as making direct viewing safe; keep 'protects your eyes generally' separate from 'lets you stare at the Sun' whenever UV testing is discussed.

The optics of the lens focusing light onto the retina is teacher background to justify the rule, not a pupil expectation; pupils are expected to state the rule, give a simple reason, and name protections. The Ogden Trust 'four times a magnifying glass' figure is unverified and is teacher background only, never a pupil-facing fact.

A sort-and-check task can confirm the rule and vocabulary but does not by itself elicit independent spoken/written explanation; pair it with prompts that ask learners to explain the cloudy-day and torch cases in their own words.
Model accurate language ('the Sun appears to move across the sky') to avoid seeding Sun/Earth astronomy misconceptions, and state that all skin tones need UV protection.
This is a statutory objective in the England national curriculum Year 3 science programme (Light unit); it has no direct NGSS performance-expectation equivalent.
Shade is a protection that helps both eyes and skin; where protections are sorted, allow it to belong to both groups.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles or delivered content, not the efficacy of any specific activity or format.

The Ogden Trust claim (lens ~four times a magnifying glass; worse through cameras/telescopes/binoculars; indirect projection is safe) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the quantitative 'four times' detail as teacher background only and do not present it to pupils as a fact to learn. The broad 'instruments make direct viewing worse' caution is retained as a safety-positive message, but its specific source is unverified.

No source directly supports the persona/role-play pedagogy as such; the Ogden and misconception claims cited on that activity support the delivered factual content and the fixed safety message, not a claim that a persona format is more effective than another medium.

The row's claim that a 3D or open-dialogue format would 'dramatise' or risk rehearsing looking at the Sun is a design caution, not an established comparative fact; it is reframed here as a narrowly scoped safety constraint (no activity should simulate direct Sun-gazing) rather than a universal law about media.
Legacy confidence was recorded as 'high'; this rewrite does not independently re-verify that rating.

probeDeeper: Name two ways to protect your eyes outside on a very bright, sunny day.
A torch and the sun are both light sources — why is it OK to glance at a torch but never at the sun?
It's cloudy and the sun looks dim behind the clouds — is it safe to look straight at it now? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: No. Sunglasses cut down brightness and glare, but they do NOT make it safe to look straight at the sun — you should never look directly at it, because the sun is so intensely bright it can permanently damage your eyes even through sunglasses. Protect your eyes with shade, a hat, and by not looking at it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Protection equals permission: 'sunglasses (or squinting) make it safe to look right at the sun'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sunglasses reduce glare for comfort but never make direct sun-gazing safe; the safe move is not to look at all. Separate 'protects your eyes generally' from 'lets you stare at the sun'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — dark sunglasses make it safe to look right at the sun.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says yes — sunglasses make direct looking safe

errorPatterns.pattern: Dimness equals safe: 'on a cloudy or hazy day, or at sunset, you can look at the sun'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The sun is still dangerously bright through thin cloud or haze; don't judge safety by how bright it happens to look.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's fine to look at the sun when it's cloudy or the sun looks dim.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a cloudy/hazy day or a low, dim-looking sun is safe to look at

errorPatterns.pattern: Sun is just a big lamp: 'you can glance at a torch, so a quick look at the sun is OK too'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The sun is vastly more intense than any artificial light and, unlike them, can cause permanent damage — even a brief direct look is unsafe.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates the sun with household lights; thinks a brief glance is harmless

responseLevels.gap: Thinks sunglasses, squinting, cloud, or a dim-looking sun make it safe to look directly at the sun, or treats the sun like an ordinary lamp.
responseLevels.full: States that looking directly at the sun is never safe and can permanently damage eyes; that sunglasses/hat/shade reduce brightness but don't permit staring; and explains the sun is far more intense than artificial light — transferring to the cloudy-day and torch cases.
responseLevels.partial: Knows you shouldn't stare at the sun and can name a protection, but still believes some condition (sunglasses, cloud) makes direct looking safe.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Your friend puts on dark sunglasses and says 'Now it's safe for me to look straight at the sun.' Is your friend right? Explain what you would tell them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Children know sunglasses 'protect' their eyes, so they over-extend that to 'sunglasses make the sun safe to stare at'. The prompt forces the decision of whether protection equals permission to look. A child with the concept refuses to look directly even with sunglasses; a child without it treats protection as a green light.

pedagogy.summary: This extends line plots to eighth-inch precision and, crucially, USES the plotted data for computation — finding the difference between the longest and shortest specimen, or totalling all the measurements — which requires adding and subtracting fractions with like and related denominators. Two skills are fused: build an accurate 1/8 scale, and operate on the fractions read from it. It is best taught by generating data, plotting to the nearest 1/8, then posing genuine questions answerable only from the plot (difference, total, redistribution), with the eighth scale showing equivalence (2/8 = ¼, 4/8 = ½) so common denominators are visible on the axis itself.
bestPractices: Measure to the nearest 1/8 inch with a subdivided ruler and scale the axis into equal eighths
Make equivalence visible on the scale — mark that 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½ — so common denominators for later arithmetic are seen, not just computed
Pose real difference and total problems that can only be answered by reading positions and adding fractions
Stress that a stack of Xs contributes its value once per X (three Xs at 3/8 add 3/8 three times) — multiplicity matters when totalling
Keep the one-X-per-case rule and connect eighths back to quarters and halves
keyRepresentations: A ruler subdivided to eighths
A number line in eighths showing equivalence (2/8 = ¼, 4/8 = ½)
Fraction bars for adding and subtracting like denominators
The plot itself used as a data source for computation
commonMisconceptions: When asked for a total length, adding or counting the Xs (frequency) instead of summing the measured values
Adding fractions by adding numerators AND denominators (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16)
Spacing eighths unequally or not seeing 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½, so scales don't line up and common denominators are missed
Counting a value only once when several Xs are stacked on it while totalling

learn.summary: Grade 4 measurement line plots at eighth-inch precision, fused with using the plotted data for fraction arithmetic. Learners measure specimens to the nearest 1/8 inch, build an equal-interval eighth scale, plot one X per object, then answer genuine questions that require adding and subtracting fractions with like/related denominators: the difference between longest and shortest, and the total length of everything. The key insight comes when totalling over stacks: three Xs at 3/8 contribute 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8, so frequency (how many Xs) and value (how much length) diverge. Marking 2/8 = 1/4 and 4/8 = 1/2 on the axis makes common denominators visible, so 1/2 − 3/8 becomes 4/8 − 3/8 right on the scale.

activities.title: Build-then-compute an eighth-inch line plot
feedback: If the learner gives the number of objects as the 'total', point to a stack of three at 3/8 and ask 'how much length is here?', holding 'how many objects' apart from 'how much length'.
If the learner adds each distinct axis value only once while ignoring stack height, show that each X on the stack contributes its value again (three Xs at 3/8 give 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8).
If the learner writes 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16, reteach fraction addition as joining same-size parts: the denominator (the size of the part) stays the same, so 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8.
If ticks are mis-spaced or 1/2 − 3/8 is attempted without a common denominator, overlay quarter and half ticks on the eighth scale and use a fraction strip to find the common denominator (1/2 = 4/8).
activities.rationale: The standard asks learners both to make a line plot in fractions of a unit and to solve addition/subtraction problems using that plot, so building and computing should be fused rather than separated. Posing a total over stacked Xs directly targets the documented frequency-vs-value confusion.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.

Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (count / stack height) with the value of the variable; the confusion persists after instruction and appears in dot plots. This underlies totalling a plot by counting Xs rather than summing values.
learnerActions: Measure several real objects (e.g. seedlings or paper strips) to the nearest 1/8 inch using a ruler subdivided into eighths; include some objects that share a length.
Draw a number line marked in equally spaced intervals that each represent 1/8 inch, and plot one X per object at its measured value.
Mark where 2/8 lines up with 1/4 and where 4/8 lines up with 1/2 directly on the axis.
Find longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions, converting to a common denominator on the scale (e.g. 1/2 − 3/8 = 4/8 − 3/8 = 1/8).
Find the total length of all objects by adding each object's value with multiplicity — a stack of three Xs at 3/8 contributes 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8, not '3'.
Predict how the total changes if one more object at 1/2 is added, then check (the total rises by 1/2 = 4/8).
activities.intendedInsight: An accurate eighth scale makes equivalences (2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2) and common denominators visible, and totalling over a plot means summing measured values with multiplicity — which is different from counting Xs.

activities.title: Compute from a given plot: difference and total
feedback: If the answer equals the count of Xs, revisit the distinction between how many Xs and how much length.
If a non-standard sum appears (e.g. denominators added, giving 6/16), reteach that same-size parts are joined with the denominator unchanged, so 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8.
Confirm correct work by checking the common-denominator conversion against the axis ticks (e.g. 1/2 reads as 4/8).
activities.rationale: When the plot is given, the operate-on-data half of the skill — solving addition and subtraction of fraction problems from line-plot data — can be exercised in a focused, checkable way. This is a scaffold that isolates computation; it does not exercise constructing the scale or measuring to the nearest 1/8.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.

Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (count / stack height) with the value of the variable; the confusion persists after instruction and appears in dot plots. This underlies totalling a plot by counting Xs rather than summing values.
learnerActions: From a pre-drawn eighth-scale plot, state the longest and shortest values and compute longest − shortest over a common denominator.
Compute the total length, taking care that a stack of several Xs at one value contributes that value once per X.
Choose which of several candidate totals is correct, and explain why the count of Xs is NOT the total length.
activities.intendedInsight: Given an accurate plot, the difference and total are determined by reading positions and adding/subtracting fractions correctly, keeping multiplicity in mind.

activities.title: Reveal equivalence on the eighth scale (reference scaffold)
feedback: Confirm when the learner names an equivalence correctly; prompt 'what else is this the same as?' to surface 2/8 = 1/4.
If a stack's total is read as the number of Xs, reveal the repeated-value sum to contrast count with length.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference can make equivalence and stack contribution concrete and label positions, supporting the fuller build-and-compute work. As a reference it does not exercise measuring to the nearest 1/8 or performing the computations independently, so it supports rather than replaces the main activity.
learnerActions: Tap or point to a position on an eighth-scale line and read off its equivalent (2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2).
Tap a stack of Xs to reveal its combined contribution to the total (e.g. three Xs at 3/8 reveal 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8).
Name where 1/4 and 1/2 sit and what else each is the same as.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same point on an eighth scale, and a stack's contribution is its value repeated once per X.

constraints: Learners must construct the scale themselves and measure to the nearest 1/8 inch; a given-plot or tap-to-reveal task isolates computation or shows equivalence but does not exercise building an accurate eighth scale or measuring.
Scale-building should be assessed through actual construction; recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of an equal-interval scale.
Keep the one-X-per-case convention, and ensure eighth intervals are drawn equally spaced so quarter/half ticks line up.
The total must be computed by summing measured values with multiplicity, not by counting Xs; keep frequency and value explicitly distinct.

Adding fractions that have the same denominator keeps the denominator unchanged (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8); adding denominators (giving 6/16) is an error. When denominators are related but different (e.g. 1/2 and 3/8), first rewrite them with a common denominator (1/2 = 4/8) before adding or subtracting.

An interactive panel showing live arithmetic (e.g. selecting a stack to lay out 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8) or overlaying quarter/half ticks is an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required tool; the same reasoning can be done with a ruler, drawn number line and fraction strips.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted that a static image and a scale-blind quiz 'cannot' build the fusion of multiplicity and fraction addition, and that a spatial dimension or dialogue 'adds nothing'. These are catalogue-fit judgements, not established necessity claims; here they are softened to scoped affordances/limits (given-plot tasks isolate computation; tap-to-reveal is a reference).

The cited standard (4.MD.B.4) supports making the plot and solving add/subtract problems from it, but does not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular interactive or reference format; no efficacy claim is made, which is why the reference activity carries no sourceClaims.

The Kaplan et al. source documents persistent frequency-vs-value confusion in histograms/dot plots; its transfer to line-plot totalling is plausible and used to justify the total-over-stacks probe, but the source does not test this specific activity.
'Redistribution' appears in the source pedagogy as a third question type but is not separately operationalised here; difference and total are the operationalised computations.

Fresh independent review: fraction arithmetic (1/2 − 3/8 = 1/8; three at 3/8 = 9/8; +1/2 = +4/8; 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8) verified; no categorical medium-superiority claims remain in summary, insights, actions, feedback or constraints.

probeDeeper: You have three Xs at 3/8 — how much length is that altogether, and why isn't it just 3?
To find longest minus shortest you need ½ take away 3/8 — how do you make those two comparable?
Where is ¼ on your eighth scale? What else is it the same as?
If I added one more object at ½, how would the total change?
assess.correctAnswer: Builds an equal-interval eighth-inch scale, plots one X per object, finds longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions over a common denominator, and totals by adding each object's value WITH multiplicity (a stack of three at 3/8 contributes 3/8 three times), recognising 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½.

errorPatterns.pattern: When asked for total length, adds or counts the Xs (frequency) instead of summing the measured values
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to a stack of three at 3/8 and ask 'how much length is here?'; hold apart 'how many objects' from 'how much length'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the number of objects as the 'total', or adds each distinct axis value once while ignoring stack height

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds fractions by adding numerators and denominators (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach fraction addition as joining same-size parts using fraction bars, denominator unchanged
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Non-standard sums when totalling or differencing the measurements

errorPatterns.pattern: Spaces eighths unequally or doesn't see 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½, so scales don't line up and common denominators are missed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay quarter and half ticks on the eighth scale to show equivalence; use a fraction strip to find the common denominator
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Mis-spaced ticks, or subtracting ½ − 3/8 without converting to a common denominator

responseLevels.gap: Cannot build an accurate eighth scale or cannot operate on the fractions; totals by counting Xs or adds denominators.
responseLevels.full: Builds an equal-interval eighth scale showing equivalence, plots one X per case, and computes both difference and total correctly — summing values with multiplicity and using common denominators — transferring to an added data point.
responseLevels.partial: Builds and reads the plot and can do one operation (e.g. the difference) but mishandles multiplicity in totals or needs prompting to find a common denominator; lists values without combining them correctly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler marked in eighths and several objects, some sharing a length. Say: 'Measure each to the nearest eighth inch, plot them, then tell me the difference between the longest and shortest, and the total length of all of them.' Watch the scale-building, and especially watch how they handle stacks of more than one X when totalling, and how they subtract the two fractional positions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for a TOTAL over stacks forces the child to separate frequency (count of Xs) from value (length) AND to add fractions correctly. A child running the bar-graph habit totals by counting Xs; a child adding numerators and denominators produces a specific wrong sum. Each error shows a different, diagnosable signature in both the plot and the arithmetic — which asking about the procedure would not reveal.
