pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–7; Storm Safety (CONCEPTUAL/safety, 0.007): basic thunderstorm safety — during thunder and lightning go indoors or into a car, stay away from trees and water; storms can be frightening but there are ways to stay safe.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 weather observation + PSHE 'keeping safe'; storm safety is PSHE/personal-safety content rather than a KS1 science statutory bullet. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS): relates to K-ESS3-2 (prepare for and respond to severe weather; NOT fetched this session, verified:false). The science of thunder/lightning is the 7-9 topic; here the payload is the SAFETY RULES and emotional reassurance.
• Operational details — Two payloads: (1) a small set of clear, correct safety rules — get inside a building or car; stay away from tall trees, open ground, and water (pools, ponds, the sea); (2) reassurance — storms are loud and can be scary but are natural, and following simple rules keeps you safe. Teach WHY going indoors is safest in child terms (lightning is more likely to hit tall/open/wet things; a building or car protects you). Avoid myths (a tree is NOT shelter; don't stand under it). Keep it calm and empowering, not fear-inducing. Prerequisite: Types of Weather (storms); feeds Thunder & Lightning (7-9, the science). Evidence: state ≥2 thunderstorm safety rules; explain why indoors is safest; describe storms as natural events you can be safe in.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/procedural + emotional): the child states at least two thunderstorm safety rules, explains that going indoors (or into a car) is safest, and frames storms as natural events they can stay safe during — knowing the right action and feeling reassured rather than frightened.
bestPractices: Teach a SHORT, memorable rule set (inside a building or car; away from trees, open ground and water) — few rules, clearly correct, rehearsed.
Pair each rule with a child-level WHY (lightning tends to hit tall, open or wet things, so we go inside where it's protected) so rules are understood, not just recited.
Bust the dangerous 'shelter under a tree' myth explicitly — a tree is one of the LEAST safe places in a storm.

Handle FEAR directly and calmly: name that thunder is loud and can feel scary, explain thunder is just the sound (it can't hurt you), and emphasise that knowing what to do helps you feel safe and in control.
Rehearse the safe response as a simple decision ('storm coming → go inside') through role-play/scenario, since rehearsal makes recall likelier when it matters.
Keep the physics minimal here (why lightning is dangerous) and defer the thunder-lightning science to the 7-9 topic; this topic is about action and reassurance.
keyRepresentations: A safe/unsafe place sorter: building, car (safe) vs under a tree, open field, swimming pool (unsafe).
A simple 'storm coming → go inside' action sequence/flow.
Calm reassurance scene: a child safe indoors watching a storm through the window, 'thunder is just a loud sound'.
Rule cards with matching why-icons (tall tree = lightning target; car/building = protected).
commonMisconceptions: 'Shelter under a tree to stay dry/safe' — a dangerous myth; trees are among the worst places in a thunderstorm.
'Thunder can hurt you' — thunder is only the SOUND; the danger is lightning, and being indoors protects you.
'Water is fine to be in/near during a storm' — pools, ponds and the sea are unsafe; get out and away from water.
'If you can't see rain it's safe' — lightning can strike from a storm that's still some distance away; go in when you hear thunder.
'Storms are out to get you / are a punishment' — animistic fear; storms are natural, and simple rules keep you safe.

learn.summary: Thunderstorm safety for ages 5–7: children learn a short, correct set of safety rules (go inside a building or a hard-topped car; stay away from tall trees, open ground, and water such as pools, ponds and the sea), each paired with a child-level reason (lightning tends to hit the tallest thing around, and being on open ground or in or near water leaves you exposed; a building or hard-topped car carries lightning around you into the ground), plus calm emotional reassurance that storms are natural and following simple rules helps keep you safe. The core activity is rehearsing the decision 'hear thunder → go inside', complemented by a safe/unsafe place sort to confirm the rules. This is PSHE/personal-safety content; the thunder/lightning science is a later topic.

activities.title: Storm scenario: choose where to go
feedback: Safe choice: 'You're inside and safe — now you can watch the storm from indoors, a little way back from the window.'
Tree choice: 'A tall tree is one of the riskiest places in a storm because lightning tends to hit the tallest thing — let's get inside instead.'
Water/open-ground choice: 'Open ground and water aren't safe in a storm — head for a building or a car.'
Keep every corrective message calm and empowering, never frightening.
activities.rationale: Safety is a set of decisions, so letting a child make and rehearse the choice with immediate, kind feedback lets them actively enact the response rather than only hear a list; this is intended to build recall and a sense of control. Rehearsing the response as a simple decision is intended to make it more likely to be recalled when it matters. (Efficacy here is a research-informed proposal, not a validated result.)
sourceClaims: Thunderstorm safety: go indoors (a substantial building) or into a hard-topped car; avoid tall isolated trees, open areas, and water; 'when thunder roars, go indoors'; wait before going back out.
learnerActions: Watch or imagine a storm rolling in — dark clouds gather and a rumble of thunder sounds.
Choose where to go: a house, a car, under a big tree, an open field, or beside a swimming pool.
When you choose a safe place (house or car), see yourself safe and cosy indoors, watching the storm from a little way back from the window.
When you choose an unsafe place, read the kind, un-scary prompt explaining why it is risky (e.g. 'a tall tree is one of the riskiest places — let's get inside instead') and try again.
Repeat the 'hear thunder → go inside' decision several times until it feels familiar.
activities.intendedInsight: Staying safe in a storm is a decision you can make and rehearse: go indoors or into a car, and the right action becomes familiar so you feel in control rather than frightened.

activities.title: Safe place / unsafe place sort
feedback: Correct sort: confirm the rule and its reason, e.g. 'Right — a building protects you because if lightning hits it, the building carries the lightning around you and down into the ground.'
Tree placed as safe: 'A tree shelters you from rain but NOT from lightning — it's actually one of the least safe places.'
activities.rationale: Categorising places checks the rule set and surfaces the dangerous 'shelter under a tree' myth, distinguishing rain-shelter logic from lightning safety. A sort can check and reinforce this classification; the 'say the reason aloud' step is added because the sort alone does not elicit the child's own explanation.
sourceClaims: Thunderstorm safety: go indoors (a substantial building) or into a hard-topped car; avoid tall isolated trees, open areas, and water; 'when thunder roars, go indoors'; wait before going back out.
learnerActions: Sort places and things into 'safe in a storm' and 'not safe in a storm'.
Safe: inside a building, inside a hard-topped car.
Unsafe: under a tall tree, in an open field, in or beside a swimming pool, pond or the sea.
For each one, say the reason aloud — e.g. 'a tall tree is unsafe because lightning tends to hit tall things'.
activities.intendedInsight: A tree is for rain shelter, not storm safety; the safe places are indoors or a car, and open or wet places are dangerous.

activities.title: Calm reassurance: thunder is just a sound
feedback: 'Thunder is just a loud noise — it can't hurt you, but it tells you lightning is near. The danger is lightning, and being inside keeps you safe.'
'Storms are natural. There are safe places to go — buildings and hard-topped cars — so you can act and stay safe.'
If a conversational persona is used, keep it strictly bounded to correct, calm storm-safety guidance.
activities.rationale: Handling fear directly and calmly — naming that thunder is loud, explaining it is only a sound, and emphasising agency — addresses the emotional reassurance goal alongside the safety rules. A caring persona may help the fear dimension but needs careful guard-railing for an anxious young child.
learnerActions: Look at a scene of a child safe indoors, watching a storm from inside.
Hear or read the message that thunder is just a loud sound — it can't hurt you, but hearing it means lightning is near; the thing to stay away from is lightning, and being indoors protects you.
Talk about how storms are natural events, not something out to get you, and that knowing what to do helps you feel safe.
Optionally ask a caring, reassuring character a worry such as 'is thunder going to hurt me?' and talk through what to do.
activities.intendedInsight: Storms can feel scary because they are loud, but thunder is only the sound; following simple rules helps keep you safe, so you can feel in control.

activities.title: What should you do? quick check
feedback: Correct: confirm and extend — 'Yes, go indoors or to a car, and stay away from tall trees and water.'

Partial (knows to go in but not why): add the reason — 'Lightning tends to hit tall things out in the open, and a building or hard-topped car carries the lightning around you into the ground, so inside you're protected.'
activities.rationale: A targeted question confirms the two-rules evidence target and the reasoning behind going indoors; used here during teaching as a check, not only as end assessment. Recognising the right choice checks knowledge of the rule but does not by itself guarantee the child can act on it, which is why the scenario rehearsal is the core activity.
sourceClaims: Thunderstorm safety: go indoors (a substantial building) or into a hard-topped car; avoid tall isolated trees, open areas, and water; 'when thunder roars, go indoors'; wait before going back out.
learnerActions: Answer: 'What should you do when you hear thunder?' — choosing 'go inside a building or car' over unsafe options.
Explain in your own words why indoors is safer than being out in the open.
Name one more thing to stay away from (tall trees, open ground, or water).
activities.intendedInsight: You can state at least two thunderstorm safety rules and say why indoors is safest.

constraints: Keep the rule set short, clearly correct and rehearsed; pair every rule with a child-level reason so rules are understood, not just recited.
Keep the tone calm, empowering and never fear-inducing; corrective feedback must reassure, not frighten.
Keep physics minimal here (only why lightning is dangerous); defer the thunder/lightning science to the later 7–9 topic.
This is a safety-rehearsal scaffold, not a substitute for a real safety conversation with a trusted adult — the digital rehearsal supports that conversation, it does not replace it.
A static reveal or reference scene can present the rules and reassurance but describes the action rather than exercising it; pair it with an activity where the child enacts the decision.
If a conversational persona is used with an anxious young child, bound it strictly to correct, calm storm-safety guidance.
Where an indoor reassurance scene is shown, keep the child a little way back from windows and doors in line with lightning-safety guidance; being inside is the key safety point.
Prerequisite: Types of Weather (storms). This feeds the later Thunder & Lightning science topic.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims for NGSS K-ESS3-2 and NWS/CDC lightning guidance were marked verified:false in the original (not fetched this session); treat as legacy, not freshly confirmed.

Independent review refined the indoor reassurance image so the child watches from a little way back from the window, consistent with the lightning-safety 'stay away from windows and doors' point; the cosy indoor image was preserved rather than removed.

Safety messaging: 'wait before going back out' appears in the original safety source but was not foregrounded in the legacy activities; consider adding a 'stay inside until the storm has passed' beat for completeness. The '30 minutes after last thunder' specifics are not stated in the source and should not be invented.

One source note said lightning can strike from a storm still some distance away ('if you can't see rain it's safe' misconception); this nuance may be advanced for 5–7 but is correct and could be gently included ('go in when you hear thunder, even if it's not raining yet').
Claims that the scenario rehearsal builds recall are untested here and are stated as intended/proposed rather than asserted as established fact.

probeDeeper: Why is being indoors or in a car safer than being out in the open?
Name one more place or thing to stay away from in a thunderstorm.
Are storms something to be terrified of, or something we can stay safe in — what makes the difference?
assess.correctAnswer: No — a tall tree is one of the most dangerous places to be in lightning, because lightning tends to strike the tallest thing around. You should go indoors or into a car, and stay away from trees and water. That keeps you away from where lightning is most likely to hit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Tree as safe shelter — 'stand under a tall tree in a storm'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish rain shelter from lightning safety: lightning hits the tallest thing, so a tall tree is dangerous; head indoors or to a car instead.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — stand under the tall tree, it will shelter you.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses the tree because it shelters from rain, ignoring lightning

errorPatterns.pattern: Underestimates lightning — 'a storm is just rain, you only get wet'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name lightning as electricity that can be dangerous, so a thunderstorm is more than getting wet — it's a reason to get inside.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats a thunderstorm as only a rain problem, not a lightning danger

errorPatterns.pattern: Nowhere is safe / panic — 'you'll get hit no matter what'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reassure with agency: storms are natural and there ARE safe places — indoors and cars are safe; you can act to stay safe.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sees storms as hopeless danger with no safe action

responseLevels.gap: Chooses the tree or another exposed spot; treats a storm as only rain or as hopeless danger.
responseLevels.full: Rejects the tree, chooses indoors/car, explains lightning strikes the tallest or most exposed things, adds staying away from water and tall objects, and frames storms as natural events you can be safe in.
responseLevels.partial: Knows to go indoors but can't say why, or gives one safety rule without the reason that lightning hits tall things.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A big thunderstorm with lightning starts while you're playing in the park. A child says, 'Let's stand under that big tall tree to stay safe.' Is that a good idea? What should you do instead, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands lightning safety rejects the tree and heads for indoors or a car. A child using everyday 'tree = shelter' logic picks the tree — the tell — targeting the specific documented error rather than a vague 'be careful'.

sources.claim: Thunderstorm safety: go indoors (a substantial building) or into a hard-topped car; avoid tall isolated trees, open areas, and water; 'when thunder roars, go indoors'; wait before going back out.

pedagogy.summary: Children need fluent, usable knowledge that 1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and tenths/hundredths have partner percentage and decimal forms, and — crucially — must DEPLOY those equivalences to solve problems (25% off £40; 20% of 60). The skill is procedural: recognise which landmark equivalent applies, convert to the handiest form, and compute. Good teaching anchors the equivalents to a hundred-grid or bar so 'per cent = per hundred' stays concrete, and builds a benchmark toolkit (50% = half, 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100, 25% = ÷4) that children combine to reach any of the target percentages rather than memorising isolated facts.
bestPractices: Teach percentages of amounts via landmark benchmarks — 50% (halve), 10% (divide by 10), 1% (divide by 100), 25% (quarter) — and combine them (e.g. 20% = double 10%), so the child reasons rather than recalls a rule.
Ground every equivalent on a hundred-grid or bar model: 1/5 shaded is 20 of 100 squares = 20% = 0.2, keeping 'per cent means per hundred' visible.
Rehearse the recall set (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and /10, /25 denominators) as a connected web, deriving 2/5 and 4/5 from 1/5 rather than as separate facts.
Always require the child to interpret the answer in context — '25% off £40' means find the DISCOUNT (£10) then the SALE PRICE (£30), not just compute 25% of 40.
Move between all three forms in problems so the child chooses the easiest tool: 1/5 of 60 is fastest as 60 ÷ 5, while 20% of 60 might be found as double-10%.
keyRepresentations: Hundred-grid (10×10) with a fraction shaded, read simultaneously as fraction, hundredths-decimal and percentage
Bar model / percentage bar marked at 0, 25, 50, 75, 100% aligned with the whole amount
Double number line: amount on top, percentage on the bottom, for scaling to any percentage
Benchmark toolkit table: 50% = ÷2, 25% = ÷4, 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100 with worked combinations
commonMisconceptions: Base-neglect: treats a percentage as a fixed amount independent of the whole — '25% off means £25 off' or '20% of 60 is 20'.
Denominator-as-decimal / faulty equivalent: converts 1/5 to 0.5 (copies the 5) or thinks 1/5 = 15%.
Rote 'divide by 100' with no meaning: divides by 100 and stops, or divides by the wrong number (e.g. by 20 for 20%).
Solves '25% off' by finding 25% and forgetting to subtract, giving the discount as the sale price.

learn.summary: Children build fluent, usable knowledge that landmark fractions (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and tenths/hundredths) have partner percentage and decimal forms, and — crucially — deploy those equivalences to solve problems (25% off £40; 20% of 60). The core is procedural: recognise which landmark applies, convert to the handiest form, and compute. Ground every equivalent on a hundred-grid or bar so 'per cent = per hundred' stays concrete, and build a benchmark toolkit (50% = halve, 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100, 25% = ÷4) that children combine to reach any whole-number target percentage rather than memorising isolated facts. Always require interpreting the answer in context (discount vs sale price).

activities.title: Live percentage bar over a settable amount
feedback: If the learner expects £10 for 25% of both £40 and £80, pause on the two bars side by side: the same 25% shades a different amount because the whole differs.
If the learner reports £10 as the sale price, prompt: 'that's how much comes off — what does the coat cost now?' and show discount-then-remaining on the bar (£40 − £10 = £30).
When they build 20% from two 10% blocks, highlight that 10% of 60 = 6 so 20% = 12, connecting the combination to the arithmetic.
activities.rationale: Acting on a model where the whole is settable is intended to make base-dependence felt and to let learners rehearse benchmark combinations with immediate feedback; the settable whole is meant to make base-neglect hard to sustain. The live recompute and sale-price readout are optional, proposed interaction examples that make the discount-vs-remaining distinction concrete; their comparative efficacy over other formats is not established.
sourceClaims: Base-neglect — treating a percentage as an absolute quantity rather than a proportion of the whole — is a documented, persistent student error in percentage problems.
Percentages of amounts are best taught via benchmark percentages (50%, 10%, 1%, 25%) that students combine, grounded on hundred-grid and bar models.
learnerActions: Set the whole amount to £40 on a percentage bar and move a marker to 25%; read off the shaded amount (£10) and a separate sale-price readout (£30), so discount and remaining stay distinct.
Build 20% of 60 by stacking two 10% benchmark blocks (10% of 60 = 6, so 20% = 12), watching the arithmetic appear as you combine them.
Keep the marker at 25% but change the whole from £40 to £80 and observe the pounds answer change from £10 to £20 — the same percentage, a different amount.
Try each target percentage two ways where possible (e.g. 1/5 of 60 as 60 ÷ 5, and 20% of 60 as double 10%) and compare.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage is a proportion of the whole, not a fixed amount: changing the whole changes the pounds answer. Benchmark percentages (50%, 10%, 1%, 25%) can be combined to reach any whole-number target percentage, and the discount is a different quantity from the sale price.

activities.title: Hundred-grid reference for landmark equivalents
feedback: If a learner writes 1/5 = 0.5, point to the grid: five equal parts of 100 is 20 each, so 1/5 = 20 hundredths = 0.2, not 0.5.
If a learner writes 1/5 = 15%, recount the shaded squares to confirm 20 of 100 = 20%.
Reinforce that 2/5 is just two of the 1/5 blocks (40 squares) rather than a new fact to memorise.
activities.rationale: A hundred-grid keeps 'per cent = per hundred' visible and consolidates the landmark equivalents and conversions. This is a reference/consolidation scaffold: a tap-to-reveal grid cannot by itself vary the whole or compute a percentage of a chosen amount, so it supports but does not replace the problem-solving work.
sourceClaims: Percentages of amounts are best taught via benchmark percentages (50%, 10%, 1%, 25%) that students combine, grounded on hundred-grid and bar models.
learnerActions: Shade 1/5 of a 10×10 hundred-grid and count the squares (20 of 100), then read it simultaneously as 1/5 = 20 hundredths = 0.2 = 20%.
Shade 1/4 to reveal 25 squares = 25% = 0.25, and 3/4 to reveal 75 squares = 75% = 0.75.
Contrast 1/5 (20 squares) with 1/2 (50 squares) to check against the 'copy the denominator digit' habit (1/5 is not 0.5 or 15%).
Derive 2/5 and 4/5 from 1/5 by counting 40 and 80 squares, building the recall set as a connected web rather than separate facts.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Per cent means per hundred': the fraction, hundredths-decimal and percentage are three readings of the same shaded quantity on a hundred-grid, and related fractions (2/5, 4/5) derive from 1/5.

activities.title: Fluency and context-step rehearsal
feedback: If a learner selects £10 as the sale price, confirm the discount is right but ask what remains: £40 − £10 = £30.
If a learner selects £25, revisit per-cent-means-per-hundred: 25% of £40 is a quarter of 40 = £10, not £25.

If a learner writes 60 ÷ 100 or 60 ÷ 20 and presents it as 20% of 60, connect the divisor to the fraction: 1% = ÷100 (so 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6 is one per cent), then 20% = 20 of those = 12; or 20% = 1/5 = ÷5, not ÷20.
If a learner can only reach an answer one way, prompt a benchmark route (e.g. 10% then double) to build flexibility.
activities.rationale: The evidence statements (20% of 60; convert 3/4; sale price of a 25%-off £40 item) can be rehearsed as scored items, efficiently practising the recall set and catching the forgot-to-subtract and rote-divisor errors. Recognition/matching items rehearse and check fluency but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a method, so pair them with the model and explanation work.
learnerActions: Match the three equivalent forms: 1/5 ↔ 20% ↔ 0.2 and 3/4 ↔ 75% ↔ 0.75.
Complete fill-in-the-blank computations such as '20% of 60 = __' and '1/5 of 60 = __'.
Answer a contextual item: a shop offers 25% off a £40 item — what is the sale price? Watch for the trap of £10 (that is the discount, not the price) and £25 (base-neglect, '25% off = £25').
Explain, for at least one item, a second route to the same answer (e.g. 20% of 60 via 10% of 60 doubled).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of the equivalents must combine with the context subtract-step: finding the discount is not the same as finding the sale price.

constraints: Always require interpreting the answer in context: '25% off £40' means find the discount (£10) then the sale price (£30), not just compute 25% of 40.
Teach percentages of amounts via combinable benchmarks (50% halve, 10% ÷10, 1% ÷100, 25% ÷4), e.g. 20% = double 10%, so children reason rather than recall an isolated rule.
Ground every equivalent on a hundred-grid or bar so 'per cent means per hundred' stays visible; connect the divisor to the fraction (20% = 1/5 = ÷5), not to the percentage number.
Address base-neglect directly by varying the whole: 25% of £40 vs 25% of £80 gives different pounds for the same percentage.

A static/tap-to-reveal hundred-grid is a reference scaffold for the recall set; it does not let the learner vary the whole or compute a percentage of a chosen amount, so it is not sufficient on its own for the problem-solving evidence.
Matching and multiple-choice items check recognition and fluency but do not elicit independent construction of a method; use them alongside tasks where the learner builds and explains a calculation.
A shopping role-play can motivate the context, but the calculation and model-manipulation must be where the doing happens, not just talked about.

Distinguish the forgot-to-subtract error (calculation correct, interpretation incomplete — scaffold the re-read, do not reteach percentages) from genuine misconceptions (base-neglect or faulty equivalents — reteach the meaning).

probeDeeper: You found the £10 — so what does the coat cost now? Why?
How did you know 1/5 is the same as 20%? Show me on the grid.
If the coat had been £80 instead of £40, would the 25%-off amount be the same? Why not?
Quick one: what's 20% of 60 a different way — can you get it from 10% of 60?
assess.correctAnswer: 25% of £40 = £10 (a quarter of 40), so the sale price is £40 − £10 = £30. 1/5 = 20% = 0.2, and 1/5 of 60 = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 (equivalently 20% of 60 = 12).

errorPatterns.pattern: Base-neglect: 'it's 25% off so that's £25 off' or '20% of 60 is 20' — treats the percentage as a fixed amount not tied to the whole.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to per-cent-means-per-hundred on a bar: 25% of £40 vs 25% of £80 side by side so the same percent gives different pounds; rebuild the calculation as a quarter of the actual amount.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes £25 (or a sale price of £15) for the coat, or gives 20 for 1/5 of 60; the number equals the percentage figure regardless of the amount.

errorPatterns.pattern: Faulty equivalent: converts 1/5 to 0.5 (copies the denominator digit) or thinks 1/5 = 15%, then computes with the wrong value.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild 1/5 on a hundred-grid: five equal parts of 100 is 20 each, so 1/5 = 20 hundredths = 0.2 = 20%; contrast with 1/2 to break the copy-the-digit habit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States 1/5 = 0.5 or 1/5 = 15%, or finds 1/5 of 60 as 30 (used 0.5); the conversion itself is wrong before any arithmetic.

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets the context subtract-step: finds 25% of £40 = £10 correctly but gives £10 as the sale price.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach percentages — the calculation is right. Prompt re-reading: 'that's how much comes off; what does the coat cost now?' Model discount-then-remaining on a bar. Scaffold, don't re-teach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct discount (£10) written as the final answer; child computed the percentage but didn't interpret 'off'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rote 'divide by 100' with no meaning: divides by 100 and stops, or divides 60 by 20 taking the '20' as the divisor.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the benchmark meaning: 1% = ÷100 (so 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6 is ONE per cent), then 20% = 20 of those = 12; or 20% = 1/5 = ÷5. Connect the divisor to the fraction, not the percentage number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 60 ÷ 100 or 60 ÷ 20 = 3 and presents it as 20% of 60; procedure applied without tracking what the numbers mean.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the percentage as a fixed amount (£25 off, 20% of 60 = 20) and/or converts 1/5 wrongly (0.5, 15%); cannot connect the fraction, percentage and decimal forms to a calculation.
responseLevels.full: Computes the sale price (£10 off → £30) with the subtract-step, states 1/5 = 20% = 0.2, uses it to get 1/5 of 60 = 12, and can reach the same result a second way (e.g. via 10%), showing flexible, meaning-based use of the equivalents.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls the equivalents and can compute 25% of £40 = £10 and 1/5 of 60 = 12, but stumbles on interpreting the context (gives the discount as the sale price) or can only do it one way without deriving via benchmarks — knows the parts but doesn't reliably assemble them in a problem.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A coat costs £40 and there is 25% off. Work out the sale price and show your method. Then tell me the percentage and the decimal that are equal to 1/5, and use that to find 1/5 of 60.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the method, not asking about it, exposes the two things that separate real fluency from surface performance: whether the child SUBTRACTS to reach the sale price (vs stopping at the £10 discount) and whether they use a correct equivalent for 1/5 (vs 0.5/15% or dividing by the wrong number). Requiring both a discount problem and a fresh conversion-and-use in one task means a child can't pass on a single memorised fact.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7; Earth has a North Pole and a South Pole — the two coldest places on the planet — found at the very top and very bottom of a globe, as far from the middle (the Equator) as you can get. (Highest-centrality node in the domain — the spatial anchor everything else hangs on.)
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 Geography 'name and locate the world's continents and oceans' and locational knowledge (poles, Equator); links KS1 science of cold environments.
• Standards—US: NGSS K-ESS2/K-ESS3 (weather/environment) plus early geography standards; foundational spatial vocabulary for later Earth science.
• Operational details: this is a globe/locational topic — the poles are the top and bottom points, the Equator is the warm belt around the middle, and 'far from the Equator = cold'. Use a real globe or ball the child can turn to find both poles. Build the simple rule: middle = hot, top and bottom = cold. This spatial frame underpins later work on climate, seasons, and Arctic-vs-Antarctic.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) point to the top of a globe and say 'North Pole' (and bottom = South Pole); Tier B (6) show the Equator around the middle and say it is warm there; Tier C (7) explain that the poles are cold because they are as far as possible from the warm Equator.
bestPractices: Use a real, turnable globe or ball so 'top' and 'bottom' are physical and spatial, not just words on a flat map
Pair every 'pole' with the Equator so children build the middle-hot / ends-cold contrast, not just two dots
Beware the flat-map distortion — on many wall maps the poles are smeared along the top and bottom edges; a globe shows them as single points
Give the coldness a cause children can hold: the poles are the furthest places from the warm middle of the Earth
Connect to the animals topics — the North Pole end is where polar bears live, the South Pole end is penguins — so location links to life
keyRepresentations: Turnable globe with North Pole (top), South Pole (bottom), and Equator (middle) clearly marked
Hot-middle / cold-ends colour band from red Equator to blue poles
Flat-map-vs-globe comparison to correct the smeared-poles distortion
Simple 'how far from the middle?' arrow from Equator up to a pole
commonMisconceptions: The poles are two objects/sticks you could touch — they are just the top and bottom points of the spinning Earth
The North Pole is a country or a piece of land — it sits on a frozen ocean, not solid ground
On a flat map the poles are long strips along the top and bottom — on a globe each pole is a single point
It's cold everywhere far from home — the SPECIFIC reason the poles are coldest is that they are furthest from the warm Equator
North Pole and South Pole are the same place — they are opposite ends of the Earth

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: Earth has a North Pole (top) and a South Pole (bottom), among the coldest places on the planet, sitting as far as possible from the warm Equator that belts the middle. The core spatial pattern is 'middle = hot, top and bottom = cold' (in general), and the simple cause children should hold is that the Sun's warmth is strongest around the middle and weakest at the top and bottom, where the poles are furthest from the warm middle. Use a turnable globe or ball so top and bottom are physical and spatial, always pairing each pole with the Equator so the hot-middle/cold-ends contrast is built rather than two isolated dots.

activities.title: Find the poles on a turnable globe
feedback: If the child points to the side of the globe for a pole, cue 'North = top, South = bottom' with an up/down gesture and have them point again.
If a child confuses the two poles, anchor North to the top and South to the bottom and practise pointing to each in turn.
Praise using the globe to turn and locate, not just naming from memory.
activities.rationale: A turnable globe makes 'top' and 'bottom' physical and spatial rather than words on a flat page, and pairing each pole with the Equator builds the middle-hot/cold-ends contrast at the right grain for this age.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils name and locate the world's continents and oceans and use basic locational knowledge including poles and Equator
learnerActions: Hold and turn a real globe or ball; point to the very top and say 'North Pole', then the very bottom and say 'South Pole'.
Run a finger around the middle band (the Equator) and say 'warm here'.
Say the simple rule out loud: 'middle is hot, top and bottom are cold.'
activities.intendedInsight: The poles are the top and bottom points of the Earth, and the Equator is the warm belt around the middle — a single spatial frame, not three unrelated facts.

activities.title: Why are the poles so cold?
feedback: If a child says the poles are warm, use a globe coloured from a red-hot Equator to icy-blue caps so the hot stripe and cold ends are visible.

If a child says the poles are cold because the top of the Earth is closest to the Sun or to cold space, note that the whole Earth is roughly the same distance from the Sun; the poles are cold because the Sun's warmth is weakest at the top and bottom, furthest from the warm middle where it is strongest.
If a child locates the poles and knows they are cold but can't say why, re-trace the 'how far from the middle?' arrow and ask again.
activities.rationale: Giving coldness a cause a young child can hold ('the Sun warms the middle most, and the poles, furthest from the warm middle, get the least warmth') turns label-recall into a usable spatial idea and targets the common 'closer to the Sun' muddle. The deeper low-angle-sunlight reason comes later; here distance from the warm middle is a clue to weaker sunshine, not a cause on its own.
sourceClaims: The North and South Poles are the Earth's axial endpoints, the regions furthest from the Equator, and among the coldest places on Earth
learnerActions: With a finger on the warm Equator, trace an arrow outward to a pole and say the pole is the furthest place from the warm middle.
Answer: 'Are the poles the hottest or the coldest places on Earth?' and explain why in your own words.
Move a finger from the North Pole down towards the Equator and say whether it gets warmer or colder along the way.
activities.intendedInsight: The poles are so cold because the Sun's warmth is weakest at the top and bottom of the Earth, as far as possible from the Equator, where it is strongest. They are not random cold spots, and they are not cold because of being nearer to or further from the Sun.

activities.title: Drag-to-spin exploration (optional interactive scaffold)
feedback: On tapping the top, confirm 'North Pole — top of the world, freezing cold; polar bears live in the icy Arctic around it'; on the bottom, 'South Pole — bottom of the world, freezing cold; penguins live on the icy coasts of Antarctica, far from the Pole itself'; on the middle, 'the Equator — the warm middle, as far from the poles as you can get'.
If the child only taps labels without noticing the colour band, prompt them to look at how colour changes from middle to ends.
activities.rationale: A drag-to-spin globe with live recolouring makes the location and the hot-middle/cold-ends pattern concrete through the child's own action, and the animal labels link the polar regions to life. Tapping-to-reveal labels is an interaction example, not a required product.
learnerActions: Drag to spin a globe, stopping to tap the top, the bottom, and the middle band.
Watch a hot-to-cold colour band shift from red at the Equator to blue at the caps as you look from middle to ends.
Lift a flap or reveal panel asking 'Why are the poles so cold?' and read the arrow tracing from warm middle out to a pole.
activities.intendedInsight: Actively rotating to find and tap each pole, with live colour feedback from hot middle to cold ends, reinforces where the poles are and why they are cold.

constraints: Use a real, turnable globe or ball so top and bottom are physical and spatial, not words along the top and bottom of a flat map.
Always pair each pole with the Equator so children build the hot-middle/cold-ends contrast rather than memorising two isolated dots.

Beware flat-map distortion: on many wall maps the poles are smeared along the top and bottom edges, whereas on a globe each pole is a single point. A globe or a flat-map-vs-globe comparison helps correct this.

Point-and-say or hot-or-cold recognition tasks check the vocabulary but presume the globe picture is already understood; they do not by themselves show the child can explain the 'furthest from the warm middle' cause.

Keep the causal story age-appropriate: 'the Sun warms the middle most and the top and bottom least, so the poles, furthest from the warm middle, are coldest' is the target. Distance from the Equator does not cause the cold by itself, and the low-angle-sunlight explanation is for later and should not be introduced here.
The North Pole sits on frozen ocean, not solid land, and is not a country — worth clarifying if a child treats it as a place you stand on land.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources remain marked verified:false. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Scientific note preserved from the source: the real reason the poles are colder involves sunlight striking at a low, slanting angle and the whole Earth being roughly equidistant from the Sun. 'Farthest from the warm Equator' is a simplified, age-appropriate framing, not the full physical cause; it should not be presented to older learners as the complete explanation.

The objective describes the poles as 'the two coldest places on the planet'. This is an acceptable simplification for ages 5–7 but is not strictly accurate: the North Pole region is milder than interior Antarctica and some high-latitude land areas. It is kept only as the stated age-appropriate objective, never offered as a comparison choice in a learner question.

The source frames a 2D labelled globe as 'ideal' and 3D/drag-to-spin as alternatives; this is a catalog preference, not evidence of comparative efficacy. All formats are retained here as options without asserting one teaches better.

The 'closer to the Sun at the top' idea appears both as a misconception to correct and is implicitly guarded against; ensure feedback corrects it rather than reinforcing any 'top of the Earth' spatial-height intuition.
The polar bear / penguin life link is present in the interactive activity's reveal labels, matching the source recommendation and the best-practice animal-topic connection.

probeDeeper: The middle of the globe (the Equator) is warm. As you move your finger up towards the North Pole, does it get warmer or colder — and why?
Is the North Pole closer to the Equator or to the South Pole? Which is warmer?
If you lived exactly on the Equator, would you need a big winter coat? What about at the North Pole?
Are the two poles the two hottest or the two coldest places on Earth?
assess.correctAnswer: The child points to the top (North Pole) and bottom (South Pole) of the globe and says the poles are much COLDER than the Equator. The reason a young child should give: the poles are as far as you can get from the Equator (the warm middle of the Earth), so they get the least warmth from the Sun and are the coldest places on the planet. (The deeper reason — sunlight hitting at a low, slanting angle — comes later; here, 'farthest from the warm middle' is the target.)

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The North Pole is cold because the top of the Earth is closest to the Sun / space' — muddles 'top' of the globe with nearness to the Sun.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that the whole Earth is roughly the same distance from the Sun; the poles are cold because they are farthest from the warm middle (Equator) where the Sun's warmth is strongest.
errorPatterns.distractor: The poles are cold because the top and bottom of the Earth stick out closest to cold space.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the poles are cold (or hot!) because of being nearest/farthest from the Sun by being at the top/bottom.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The poles are the warmest places' or no sense that poles=coldest — hasn't linked poles to extreme cold.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a globe with a warm-middle/cold-ends colour band; the Equator is the hot stripe, the poles the icy caps.
errorPatterns.distractor: The poles are the hottest places because they are at the very top and bottom.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Guesses the poles are warm, or can't say how they compare to the Equator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses which pole is which / top vs bottom — a placement slip.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor 'North = top, South = bottom' with a simple up/down cue on the globe; practise pointing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to North for South or vice versa, or puts a pole on the side.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably locate the poles, or thinks they are warm / gives an unrelated reason.
responseLevels.full: Locates North (top) and South (bottom) poles, states they are the coldest places, and explains it as being farthest from the warm Equator — and can reason that moving toward the middle gets warmer.
responseLevels.partial: Locates both poles and knows they are cold, but can't say why — or gives the 'closer to the Sun at the top' reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Point to the North Pole and the South Pole on this globe. Now tell me: is it hotter or colder at the poles than where the Equator is drawn round the middle — and WHY do you think the poles are the way they are?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has only memorised the labels can point to the poles but gives a wrong or no reason (e.g. 'colder because they're closer to the Sun at the top'); a child with the idea both locates them AND links cold to being farthest from the warm Equator. Asking 'why' separates label-recall from understanding.

sources.claim: KS1 pupils name and locate the world's continents and oceans and use basic locational knowledge including poles and Equator
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum, Geography KS1 (locational knowledge)

sources.claim: The North and South Poles are the Earth's axial endpoints, the regions furthest from the Equator, and among the coldest places on Earth
sources.source: National Geographic Education — geographic poles and the Equator

pedagogy.summary: Moon phases are the single most misconceived topic in school astronomy. The child must build a working Sun-Earth-Moon geometric model in which the Moon is always half-lit by the Sun, and a phase is simply how much of that lit half we happen to see from Earth as the Moon orbits over ~29.5 days. The decisive move is to separate two things children conflate: phases (an every-month consequence of viewing geometry) and eclipses (rare alignments where one body's shadow falls on another). Teach phases first, purely as 'which fraction of the sunlit side faces us', then treat solar (Moon between Sun and Earth) and lunar (Earth between Sun and Moon) eclipses as the special cases when the three bodies line up. Kinaesthetic modelling — each child holding a ball ('Moon') at arm's length and turning while a lamp acts as the Sun — is the best-evidenced route because it puts the child at Earth's viewpoint and lets them literally see a crescent become gibbous become full as they rotate.
bestPractices: Run the ball-and-lamp (or head-as-Earth) kinaesthetic model where each child holds a polystyrene ball at arm's length and slowly turns: they watch the lit fraction facing them grow and shrink, experiencing the full phase cycle from the Earth-centred viewpoint

Insist on the two-viewpoint discipline: show the God's-eye view (Moon orbiting a lit Earth, always half-illuminated) AND the Earth-based view (what a person actually sees in the sky) side by side, and repeatedly translate between them

Teach phases and eclipses as separate ideas in that order; explicitly contrast 'phases happen every month from geometry' with 'eclipses are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted, so alignment is uncommon'
Name and sequence the phases with the waxing/waning vocabulary tied to the geometry (waxing = lit part growing as the Moon moves toward the far side of Earth from the Sun)
Directly confront the Earth's-shadow misconception by asking children to locate where Earth's shadow points relative to the Sun, and show that in most phases the Moon is nowhere near it
keyRepresentations: Sun-Earth-Moon orbital diagram showing the Moon always half-lit, with eight positions round the orbit and the matching Earth-view phase drawn beside each
The ball-and-lamp physical model (child's head = Earth, ball = Moon, single bright lamp = Sun)
Phase strip / circular sequence: new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent
Eclipse alignment diagram distinguishing umbra/penumbra and the straight-line Sun-Moon-Earth (solar) vs Sun-Earth-Moon (lunar) arrangements
commonMisconceptions: Phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon (the dominant misconception; actually that is a lunar eclipse, which is rare)
Phases are caused by clouds, or by planets/other bodies blocking the Moon
The Moon is only present in the sky at night, or the far side is permanently dark ('dark side of the Moon')
A solar and a lunar eclipse are the same event, or an eclipse happens every month (fails to account for the Moon's tilted orbit)
The Moon does not rotate / the phase is a fixed property of the Moon rather than of the viewing geometry

learn.summary: Help 11-12 year-olds build a working Sun-Earth-Moon geometric model in which the Moon is always half-lit by the Sun, and a phase is simply how much of that lit half we see from Earth as the Moon orbits over roughly 29.5 days. The decisive teaching move is to separate two ideas learners routinely conflate: phases (an every-month consequence of viewing geometry) and eclipses (rare alignments where one body's shadow falls on another). Teach phases first, purely as 'which fraction of the sunlit side faces us', then treat solar (Moon between Sun and Earth) and lunar (Earth between Sun and Moon) eclipses as the special cases when the three bodies line up. Kinaesthetic modelling, linked orbit/sky views, a labelled phase reference, and sequencing/matching checks each contribute a distinct part of this learning.

activities.title: Ball-and-lamp phase cycle (head as Earth)
feedback: If you predicted 'my head's shadow makes the dark part', that is the common Earth's-shadow misconception. Look at the crescent position: the ball is on the lamp's side of your head, so your head's shadow falls behind you, far from the ball, yet most of the ball facing you is dark. That dark part is the ball's own unlit side. At the full position, raising the ball slightly keeps it just above your head's shadow, so it looks fully lit.
If the ball never looks 'full' as you turn, check you are holding it slightly above head height so your own head doesn't block the lamp each time.
Waxing means the lit part is growing as the Moon moves toward the side of your head away from the lamp; waning means it is shrinking.
activities.rationale: Putting the learner physically at Earth's viewpoint lets them see a crescent become gibbous become full by rotating, directly experiencing phases as viewing geometry. The predict-then-turn structure surfaces the Earth's-shadow misconception so it can be confronted with what is actually observed.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS1-1 asks students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS1-1] and eclipses of the sun and moon; models may be physical, graphical, or conceptual.

The belief that Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon is a widespread and persistent student misconception, distinct from the actual cause (changing Sun-Earth-Moon viewing geometry).
learnerActions: In a darkened room, use a single bright lamp as the Sun and hold a polystyrene ball on a stick at arm's length as the Moon, held slightly above head height, with your own head as the Earth.

Before turning, PREDICT with a reason: as you slowly turn the ball around your head, will it go through crescent → half → full, and what makes the dark part? Commit to your prediction out loud or in writing.
Slowly turn on the spot and watch the lit fraction of the ball facing you grow and shrink through the full cycle.

When the ball looks 'full', deliberately look for where your head's (Earth's) shadow points and check whether it passes just below the raised ball (it should if the lamp is at about head height or higher).
Name each phase as it appears using waxing/waning vocabulary tied to the geometry (waxing = the lit part growing).
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun always lights half the Moon; a phase is how much of that lit half we see from Earth as the viewing angle changes. The dark part of a crescent is the Moon's own unlit side, not Earth's shadow — and at the 'full' position your head's shadow passes just below the raised ball and misses it entirely, so no shadow is dimming it.

activities.title: Linked orbit view and sky view
feedback: At full Moon, if you expected Earth's shadow to darken the Moon, notice the full Moon still shows its fully lit face. Earth's shadow does extend toward the Moon's side of the sky (opposite the Sun), but the tilted orbit usually carries the Moon just above or below it, so no eclipse happens most months.
If you think an eclipse should happen every month, use the tilt control: in most months the Moon rides slightly high or low of the line-up, so the shadow misses.

A crescent in the sky view corresponds to the Moon being roughly between you and the Sun, so mostly its unlit side faces you — and Earth's shadow, which always points away from the Sun, is then on the far opposite side of the sky, nowhere near the Moon.
activities.rationale: The core idea is a live geometric relationship: as orbital position changes, the visible fraction of the sunlit side changes. Linking a top-down orbit panel to the Earth-based sky panel lets learners watch the phase morph in real time and test the shadow misconception by manipulation. A free-viewpoint 3D version can additionally make the orbital tilt and eclipse rarity vivid by letting the learner tilt the orbital plane and see the shadow miss Earth; it offers a different spatial experience and may add control complexity for this age group.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS1-1 asks students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS1-1] and eclipses of the sun and moon; models may be physical, graphical, or conceptual.

The belief that Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon is a widespread and persistent student misconception, distinct from the actual cause (changing Sun-Earth-Moon viewing geometry).
learnerActions: Work with two linked views side by side: a top-down Sun-Earth-Moon diagram where you move the Moon around its orbit of a fixed, brightly lit Earth, and a synchronized view of how the Moon would appear from Earth.
In the top-down view keep in mind the Moon is always half-lit toward the Sun; move it step by step around the orbit.
At each position, read off the matching Earth-view phase and say why that fraction is visible.
Park the Moon at the 'full' position, then trace where Earth's shadow points relative to the Sun and notice it extends toward the Moon's side of the sky.

Use a 'line up the three bodies' challenge that arranges them in a row to show eclipse geometry, and a tilt control that lifts the Moon's orbit slightly high or low to show how the shadow usually misses.
Keep translating between the two viewpoints: the God's-eye orbit and what a person actually sees in the sky.
activities.intendedInsight: Coupling the orbit view to the sky view shows the phase morph continuously and lets learners test the Earth's-shadow account against what they actually see — it does not fit, most clearly for a crescent. At full Moon the lit face is turned fully toward us; Earth's shadow does point to the Moon's side of the sky (away from the Sun), but the Moon's tilted orbit usually carries it just above or below the shadow, which is why most full Moons are ordinary, not lunar eclipses. For a crescent, by contrast, the Moon is near the Sun's direction so Earth's shadow is on the far opposite side, nowhere near the Moon — the dark part is simply the Moon's own unlit side.

activities.title: Phase-wheel reference and 'why this phase?'
feedback: If you cannot explain 'why this phase', return to the linked orbit/sky view and find the matching orbital position.
Check that you place a solar eclipse with the Moon between Sun and Earth, and a lunar eclipse with Earth between Sun and Moon.
activities.rationale: A static labelled diagram cannot show the continuous morphing or let the learner manipulate the geometry, but it is a useful reference and consolidation layer for naming the eight phases and recording the umbra/penumbra and alignment facts.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS1-1 asks students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS1-1] and eclipses of the sun and moon; models may be physical, graphical, or conceptual.
learnerActions: Study a labelled phase sequence: new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent.
For each phase, lift a flap or reveal the answer to 'why this phase?' and relate the sky appearance to the Moon's orbital position.
Compare the phase wheel to an eclipse alignment diagram that distinguishes umbra and penumbra and the straight-line Sun-Moon-Earth (solar) versus Sun-Earth-Moon (lunar) arrangements.
Use this as a consolidation reference after the hands-on and linked-view work.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming and ordering the phases consolidates the cycle, and placing the phase wheel beside the eclipse diagram keeps the two ideas distinct: monthly phases from viewing angle versus rare shadow-casting alignments.

activities.title: Sequence, match and distinguish check
feedback: Correct ordering with reasons tied to orbital position shows the mechanism; ordering by rote alone should be revisited with the linked views.

If you call a crescent a 'partial eclipse', recall that the dark part of a crescent is the Moon's own unlit side seen at an angle (the bright sliver is part of its sunlit half), while an eclipse is a real shadow cast during a rare line-up.
If you expect a monthly eclipse, recall the tilted orbit usually carries the Moon just above or below the alignment, so the shadow misses.
activities.rationale: Recognition and matching tasks assess whether learners can apply the model but do not by themselves build the geometric intuition, so they work best after the hands-on and interactive work. Adding a short reasoning requirement surfaces residual misconceptions.
learnerActions: Put the eight phases in correct order from new Moon through full and back.
Match each top-down orbital position to the phase seen from Earth.
Given a described or drawn alignment, decide whether it is a solar eclipse (Moon between Sun and Earth) or a lunar eclipse (Earth between Sun and Moon).
In reasoning, explain why a crescent is NOT a partial eclipse, and why an eclipse does not happen every month.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to sequence phases, pair positions to views, and separate solar from lunar eclipses demonstrates the outcome of the geometric model; the reasoning items check whether the mechanism, not just the labels, is held.

constraints: Teach phases before eclipses, and keep them explicitly distinct: phases are a monthly consequence of viewing geometry; eclipses are rare alignments where a shadow actually falls, rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's.
Maintain the two-viewpoint discipline: present the God's-eye orbit view (Moon always half-lit) and the Earth-based sky view together and keep translating between them.

At full Moon, do not teach that Earth's shadow 'points away' from the Moon: the full Moon sits near the anti-solar point where Earth's umbra points, and it is usually not eclipsed only because the Moon's orbit is tilted. Use the crescent as the clean case where Earth's shadow is genuinely far from the Moon.

The sequence/matching/distinguish check tests the outcome but does not build spatial intuition on its own; place it after modelling. A static phase wheel is a reference and consolidation aid, not a substitute for seeing the phase morph or manipulating the geometry.

Approximate the phase cycle (new Moon to new Moon, the synodic month) as about 29.5 days; the Moon's orbit measured against the stars (the sidereal month) is about 27.3 days. The legacy '~28-day cycle' is only a rough approximation, and these figures should not all be presented as exactly correct.

The ball-and-lamp model needs a genuinely darkened room and a single bright source to read the lit fraction clearly; hold the ball slightly above head height so the learner's own head does not repeatedly block the lamp.
Avoid the 'dark side of the Moon' framing: the far side is not permanently dark, and the Moon is present in the daytime sky too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The legacy source for the Earth's-shadow misconception (Baxter / IOP-SPARK) is marked unverified in the row; treat the misconception's prevalence claim as reported, not independently confirmed here.

The orbital period is cited inconsistently in the source: the pedagogy states ~29.5 days while the assessment and descriptor state ~28 days. Activities use ~29.5 days and flag the discrepancy; a reviewer should settle on one figure (the synodic month is about 29.5 days).

The original recommendation and assessment describe Earth's shadow at full Moon as 'stretching off in the opposite direction', which is geometrically imprecise: a full Moon lies near the anti-solar point where Earth's umbra actually points, and it is usually not eclipsed because of the ~5 degree orbital tilt. Corrected in the activities and constraints; the crescent is used as the clean 'shadow is far away' demonstration.

The source's claim that linking the two views causes the Earth's-shadow misconception to 'collapse' and that an in-role conversation 'cannot deliver the aha' are catalog preference assertions; softened here to narrowly scoped affordances (manipulable linked views let learners test the shadow idea; a 3D model offers a different spatial experience). No comparative-efficacy claim is asserted.
The assessment field references a reteach prerequisite id for the phase-eclipse conflation; routing/prerequisite logic was not altered and is outside this learning-guidance rewrite.

assess.poeTask: In a darkened room use a single bright lamp as the Sun and give the child a ball on a stick as the Moon, with their own head as the Earth. Ask them to PREDICT with a reason: as you slowly turn the ball around your head, will it go through crescent → half → full, and what makes the dark part? Many predict their own head's (Earth's) shadow falls on the ball. Have them commit, then turn: the lit portion they see grows and shrinks purely with the angle to the lamp, and at 'full' their head's shadow misses the ball entirely. The pre-turn reason is diagnostic — predicting 'my shadow makes the dark part' is the Earth's-shadow misconception.
probeDeeper: If the phases were the Earth's shadow, how often would they happen — and could we ever see a full Moon?
How much of the Moon is lit by the Sun at any moment? So why don't we always see a full Moon?
What is actually different between a crescent Moon and a lunar eclipse?
assess.correctAnswer: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon; phases are how much of that lit half we can SEE from Earth as the Moon orbits us — set by the changing angle between Sun, Earth and Moon. The dark part of a crescent is the Moon's own unlit side, not the Earth's shadow. The Earth's shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse, which is rare.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the phases are the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon' (the dominant Moon-phase misconception)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Couple an orbit-view with a sky-view and park at full Moon: the Earth's shadow points AWAY into space; the dark part is the Moon's own unlit side seen at an angle.
errorPatterns.distractor: The dark part is the Earth's shadow cast onto the Moon.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes the dark part of the Moon to the Earth's shadow

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Moon makes its own light and gets covered up / dims itself' (Moon as light source; blocking)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Moon shines only by reflected sunlight and half is always lit; phases are about our viewing angle, not the Moon changing its own light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: talks about the Moon's own light being blocked or the Moon dimming itself

errorPatterns.pattern: 'phases and eclipses are the same thing' (phase–eclipse conflation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Phases happen monthly (viewing angle); eclipses are rare alignments where a shadow really is cast, rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's.
errorPatterns.distractor: A crescent Moon is a partial eclipse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls a crescent a 'partial eclipse,' or says an eclipse should happen every month

responseLevels.gap: Attributes phases to the Earth's shadow, or thinks the Moon makes and loses its own light.
responseLevels.full: Explains phases as the changing amount of the always-half-lit Moon visible from Earth as it orbits, explicitly rejects the Earth's-shadow account (the shadow points away at full Moon), sequences the ~28-day cycle, and distinguishes solar from lunar eclipse; transfers.
responseLevels.partial: Knows phases come from the Sun–Earth–Moon arrangement and reflected light but still can't rule out the shadow, or conflates phases with eclipses.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Many people think the dark curved part of a crescent Moon is the Earth's shadow falling on it. What actually makes the Moon look like a crescent, a half, or full? … Explain your reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both the shadow account and the geometry account 'explain' a crescent, so tier one is silent — the reasoning tier separates them. A child citing the Earth's shadow reveals the dominant misconception; one citing the changing viewing angle of the always-half-lit Moon has the mechanism. If shadow were the cause, a 'phase' would appear whenever Earth's shadow fell, and a full Moon could never happen.
