pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Magnetic Fields

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics, 'Magnetism'):** 'magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion'; 'magnetic fields by plotting with compass, representation by field lines'; 'Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation'.

- **Standards — US (NGSS, MS Forces & Interactions — MS-PS2-5):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-5] (qualitative evidence; DCI PS2.B — forces that act at a distance can be explained by fields that extend through space and can be mapped by their effect on a test object).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal, age 11-12). The leap from KS2 is from an observable attract/repel RULE to an abstract FIELD MODEL: the magnetic field is the region of space around a magnet where it exerts a force, represented by directed field lines (north-seeking → south-seeking, never crossing, closer spacing = stronger), and REVEALED — not created — by a plotting compass or iron filings. Qualitative only; includes Earth-as-a-magnet, the compass, and navigation. No quantitative field strength.
bestPractices: Start with a plotting COMPASS, not iron filings: the compass reveals field DIRECTION (the needle lies along the line, pointing north-seeking → south-seeking), which pupils need before the filings' clumped strength pattern.

Keep returning to the core idea that the field is the space where a force acts — iron filings and compasses only PROBE that space, they don't make the field 'more real'; stress the field is 3D, not merely the flat textbook pattern.
Don't assume the pattern is obvious: explicitly model drawing field lines (continuous, arrowed north→south, never crossing, spacing showing strength) and guide pupils on what to look for.
Scaffold the representation: draw small magnets → small compasses → omit the compass box and leave just an arrow, so the field-line abstraction is built up.

Treat the compass as a tiny magnet that aligns with Earth's field for navigation; the fact that Earth's geographic-north magnetic pole is really a magnetic south pole is enrichment, not essential at KS3.
Elicit pupils' own sentence on what 'magnetic field' means to surface wrong-track thinking, and carefully separate magnetic from gravitational and electric fields.
keyRepresentations: Plotting compass moved step-by-step around a bar magnet to trace a single field line
Bar-magnet field diagram: arrowed lines north→south, symmetrical, non-crossing, spacing = strength
Compass → arrow symbol progression for representing field direction
Iron-filings pattern (shape and strength) shown alongside the compass (direction)
Earth drawn as a bar magnet with a compass needle aligning to it (navigation)
commonMisconceptions: 'The field IS the iron filings / lines' — the lines are a representation; the field is a continuous region of force filling 3D space (IOP).
'The field exists only at the poles' or 'lines come out of the centre of the magnet' (Oak).
Drawing field lines that cross, or that have no direction/arrows.
Conflating the magnetic field with the gravitational or electric field because all 'act at a distance' (IOP; Bradamante & Viennot).
'Magnets need air/a medium to work' — the force acts through a vacuum (IOP).
Pole-labelling/reversal errors in attraction-repulsion diagrams (KS3 assessment analysis); carried-over 'all metals are magnetic / aluminium is magnetic'.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12, build the leap from the KS2 attract/repel rule to the abstract FIELD MODEL: a magnetic field is the region of space around a magnet where it exerts a force, revealed (not created) by a plotting compass or iron filings, and represented by directed field lines running north-seeking → south-seeking, continuous, never crossing, with closer spacing meaning stronger. Treatment is qualitative only (no field-strength numbers) and includes Earth-as-a-magnet, the compass and navigation. The anchor activity is a hands-on/screen field-MAPPING task where learners probe the space with a compass and assemble field lines themselves; a drawing/prediction activity assesses the examined competency; a reference layer consolidates vocabulary; and a narrowly scoped 3D exploration addresses the real 'field is only the flat pattern' misconception.

activities.title: Map the field with a plotting compass
feedback: If arrows appear only near the poles: ask the learner to test positions directly out to the side and below/above the magnet. The needle lines up with the magnet's field there too, which shows the field surrounds the magnet in all directions, getting weaker with distance.

If field lines are drawn crossing or without arrows: remind that each point has one needle direction, so lines cannot cross and must carry an arrow (pointing the way the needle's north-seeking end points, from the magnet's north pole toward its south pole).
If the learner says 'there's no field between my lines': have them drop the compass into a gap — it still deflects, so the field is continuous and the lines are just a representation.
If densest lines are drawn at the centre of the bar: compare with the iron-filings pattern, which clumps at the POLES — closer lines mean stronger field.
activities.rationale: Reading a field as a directed map revealed by a probe is a build-and-recompute task; letting learners stamp compass directions that knit into field lines and superpose a second magnet makes the abstract field something constructed and manipulated, directly confronting 'field only at the poles' and 'the lines aren't real'. Starting with the compass (direction) before iron filings follows the recommended teaching order. This can be done at a real bench with a bar magnet, plotting compass and iron filings, or with a screen model offering the same probe-and-stamp interaction; a live-recomputing screen model adds the second-magnet reshaping and compass/iron-filings view toggle as optional ways to make the mechanism visible.
sourceClaims: The field is the space around a magnet where it exerts a force; iron filings/plotting compasses only reveal direction and strength, they don't make it more real; the field exists in 3D, not just the 2D textbook pattern; start teaching with a compass (direction) before iron filings; field patterns are far from obvious to pupils and must be explicitly modelled.

KS3 lesson names 'the field only exists at the poles' as the common misconception, addressed by plotting field lines around the whole magnet; field lines run north-seeking to south-seeking, are continuous, do not cross, and spacing represents strength.

MS-PS2-5: conduct an investigation [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-5] even though not in contact (qualitative); DCI PS2.B — forces at a distance explained by fields that extend through space and can be mapped by their effect on a test object.
KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion; magnetic fields by plotting with compass, representation by field lines; Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation.
learnerActions: Place a plotting compass far from any magnet and note that it settles pointing north.

Position a bar magnet, then move the compass step-by-step to many positions around it; at each position draw a small arrow pointing the way the needle's NORTH-SEEKING end points — this is the field direction, running outward from the magnet's north pole toward its south pole.
Join the arrows to trace continuous field lines, working outward from one pole and around to the other.

Deliberately place the compass out to the SIDE of the magnet (not just near the poles) and record which way the needle points compared with when the magnet was absent. Near the magnet the needle lines up with the magnet's field, but with some magnet orientations that direction can match its original northward direction, so also try turning the magnet.
Overlay or compare an iron-filings pattern on the same magnet, noting that filings show shape/strength while the compass shows direction — two readings of one field.
Bring a second magnet nearby and re-map a few points to see how the whole pattern changes (like poles push lines apart, opposite poles link them).
activities.intendedInsight: The field is a continuous region of force filling the space all around the magnet, not something that exists only at the poles or only where a line is drawn; the compass and filings merely PROBE it. Direction and strength are two readings of one invisible field.

activities.title: Draw, predict and apply the field-line rules
feedback: Predicting 'nothing, it always points north' vs 'it swings to line up with the nearer, stronger field' reveals whether the learner sees the needle as a magnet responding to a field — use iron filings afterward to make the field visible.
For lines without arrows: each line has a direction (the way a compass's north-seeking end points, from the magnet's north pole to its south pole); add arrows and re-check.
For crossed lines: two directions at one point is impossible, so redraw so lines never meet.
For pole-labelling errors: the end where lines emerge is north; cross-check with needle directions nearby.
activities.rationale: Producing and predicting (not just recognising) exercises the examined KS3 competency — 2D field-line drawing, compass direction, and pole labelling. The predict-observe-explain prompt surfaces whether the needle is understood as a magnet responding to a field. Recognition-only multiple-choice items can check the rules but do not by themselves elicit independent drawing, so construction tasks are included.
sourceClaims: KS3 lesson names 'the field only exists at the poles' as the common misconception, addressed by plotting field lines around the whole magnet; field lines run north-seeking to south-seeking, are continuous, do not cross, and spacing represents strength.
KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion; magnetic fields by plotting with compass, representation by field lines; Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation.
learnerActions: Trace a field line through a marked point on a bar-magnet diagram, and at several marked positions draw the direction a compass needle would point.
Predict which way a compass will swing when placed at a given point near the magnet, then check against a plotted pattern.
Decide whether drawn field lines obey the rules: Do any cross? Do they carry arrows? Does spacing show strength?
Label the poles of a magnet from an unlabelled field pattern.
Predict-and-explain (predict, observe, explain): a compass far from magnets points north; predict what happens as a bar magnet is brought alongside it, and WHY, before testing.
activities.intendedInsight: Field-line drawing is a precise skill governed by rules (continuous, arrowed north→south, never crossing, spacing = strength), and the learner can predict a compass's behaviour from the field rather than treating it as a passive pointer.

activities.title: Earth as a magnet and the compass for navigation
feedback: If the learner says the needle is pulled toward the North Star, 'the cold', or 'north as a place': introduce Earth as a giant magnet with a field the needle aligns to, and deflect the needle with a bar magnet to prove the needle is itself magnetic.

Full understanding connects needle-as-magnet with Earth's field; a partial response states separate facts (Earth has a field; poles attract/repel) without explaining why the same end always points north.
The geographic-north/magnetic-south detail is enrichment; do not treat confusion about it as a core error at this stage.
activities.rationale: Earth's magnetism, the compass and navigation are statutory KS3 content and the standard explanation for 'why the needle points north'. Treating the compass as a tiny magnet aligning with Earth's field unifies the pole rule with the field model. Spoken discussion of the transfer questions supports reasoning but the objective is the explanation, not dialogue for its own sake.
sourceClaims: KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion; magnetic fields by plotting with compass, representation by field lines; Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation.
learnerActions: Draw the Earth as a bar magnet with a compass needle aligning to its field.
Explain why a compass needle's SAME end always turns to point north, in terms of the needle being a tiny magnet aligning with Earth's field.
Reason about transfer: if you took the compass to Australia, would the same end still point north? Why?

Discuss the enrichment point: the Earth's magnetic pole near geographic north behaves like a magnetic south-type pole, so the needle's north pole is attracted to it (opposites attract) — flagged as enrichment, not required.
activities.intendedInsight: A compass works because the needle is itself a small magnet that aligns with Earth's magnetic field (when away from other magnets and iron), which is why the same end consistently points (magnetic) north and the compass can be used for navigation.

activities.title: Reference layer: the field-line rules at a glance
feedback: Treat this as a companion to the mapping bench: a finished diagram tells the learner the rules but does not let them probe with a compass or watch the pattern build, so use it after or alongside active mapping.
Tap-to-reveal regions can confirm rule-by-rule understanding; return to the compass whenever a learner doubts that the field fills the space.
activities.rationale: A tidy, labelled reference with tap-to-reveal explanations gives a reliable vocabulary and rule layer. Because it is fixed it cannot be probed, so it is positioned as a consolidation companion to the active mapping rather than the primary teacher — a fixed example can still teach the rules but cannot reproduce the field-as-revealed discovery.
sourceClaims: KS3 lesson names 'the field only exists at the poles' as the common misconception, addressed by plotting field lines around the whole magnet; field lines run north-seeking to south-seeking, are continuous, do not cross, and spacing represents strength.
learnerActions: Consult a finished, labelled bar-magnet field diagram and reveal, region by region, the rules: lines run N→S, closer spacing = stronger, field strongest at the poles.
Reveal the Earth/compass link: Earth acts like a bar magnet and the compass needle aligns with its field.
Use this as a vocabulary and rule check-reference alongside the mapping activity.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the correct vocabulary and the field-line rules as a quick reference to support, not replace, hands-on probing.

activities.title: The field in three dimensions (narrow complement)
feedback: If a learner believes the field is only the flat pattern they drew on the table: have them hold the compass a short distance above the magnet and watch it still respond to the magnet, showing the field extends in all directions.
Keep this scoped to the 3D-nature point; the examined drawing, direction and navigation skills are fully served in 2D.
activities.rationale: The field genuinely is three-dimensional and 'the field is only the flat pattern' is a named misconception, so moving a probe through the surrounding space can address the 3D-nature point. This is proposed as a narrow complement, not the primary teacher, since the examined competencies are served in 2D; a physical exploration around a real magnet or a 3D screen model can both show the volume, each offering a different experience.
sourceClaims: The field is the space around a magnet where it exerts a force; iron filings/plotting compasses only reveal direction and strength, they don't make it more real; the field exists in 3D, not just the 2D textbook pattern; start teaching with a compass (direction) before iron filings; field patterns are far from obvious to pupils and must be explicitly modelled.
learnerActions: Move a compass or sensor through the space around a magnet at different heights and positions — above, below and to the sides — not just in the flat tabletop plane.

Record how the needle responds at each height and position close to the magnet (the effect weakens with distance), concluding the field occupies a VOLUME around the magnet, not only the flat textbook pattern.
Relate the 3D volume back to the 2D field-line diagram, recognising the diagram as one slice through the full field.
activities.intendedInsight: The magnetic field is genuinely three-dimensional — it surrounds the magnet in every direction — and the familiar 2D field-line diagram is one plane through that volume.

constraints: Keep treatment strictly qualitative at this stage: no numerical field-strength values.
Start with a plotting compass (direction) before iron filings (shape/strength); both only PROBE the field and do not make it 'more real'.
Field lines are a representation, not physical strings or the field itself; the field is a continuous region of force filling 3D space, present in the gaps between drawn lines.

Field-line rules to enforce: continuous, arrowed in the direction a compass's north-seeking end points (north-seeking → south-seeking, i.e. out of the magnet's north pole into its south pole), never crossing, closer spacing = stronger, field strongest at the poles (not the centre of the bar).
Carefully separate the magnetic field from gravitational and electric fields even though all 'act at a distance'; the magnetic force acts through a vacuum and does not need air/a medium.
Watch for carried-over errors: 'all metals are magnetic' / 'aluminium is magnetic', and pole-labelling/reversal mistakes in attraction–repulsion diagrams.
The Earth's geographic-north magnetic pole behaving as a magnetic south-type pole is enrichment, not essential at this level.
A fixed/labelled diagram is a reference scaffold: it cannot be probed with a compass and does not reproduce the field-as-revealed discovery, so pair it with active mapping.
Recognition-only items (e.g. rule multiple-choice) can check understanding of rules but do not elicit independent construction of a field diagram; include drawing/prediction tasks for that.

A persona/dialogue format does not itself elicit the compass-probing and field-line drawing that build and read a field map (those require hands-on or screen construction); discussion can still support reasoning about explanations such as why the needle's same end points north.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four sources (IOP Spark; Oak National Academy) are marked verified:false in the source row; claims attributed to them (including the 3D-nature misconception and the field-line rules) should be re-checked before relying on them as established.

The original recommendation asserted that the mapping bench conveys the field 'exactly what a static diagram cannot convey'. This comparative-necessity claim is not established by the sources; it has been softened to a scoped affordance (fixed diagrams cannot be probed) rather than a universal law.

The source's framing that a quiz 'only assesses' and that 3D is uniquely necessary for the 3D point were softened: production/prediction tasks can teach, and both physical and screen 3D exploration can address the 3D-nature misconception.

Enrichment detail retained from the source: Earth's geographic-north magnetic pole is actually a magnetic south-type pole. This is a correct standard statement but can confuse at KS3; flagged as enrichment only.

The 'conversation' artefact was judged a poor fit in the source; its narrow point — that a dialogue format does not itself elicit the probing/drawing needed to construct a field map — is preserved as a constraint, without claiming dialogue cannot support related reasoning.

The field-direction/arrow convention was clarified in Activity 1 so the arrow points the way the compass's north-seeking end points (out of the magnet's north pole toward its south pole); an earlier ambiguous '(north-seeking end → south-seeking end)' phrasing could have been read as drawing the arrow the wrong way.

assess.poeTask: Place a plotting compass far from any magnet — it points north. Ask students to predict what happens as you slowly bring a bar magnet alongside it, and WHY, before doing it. Predicting 'nothing, it always points north' versus 'it swings to line up with the nearer, stronger field' reveals whether they see the needle as a magnet responding to a field; iron filings then make the field visible.
probeDeeper: Is there a magnetic field in the space between two field lines you've drawn? How do you know?
If you took the compass to Australia, would the same end still point north? Why?
Earth's magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole — is it a magnetic north or a magnetic south pole? How can you tell from the compass?
Where around the bar magnet is the field strongest, and how would iron filings show it?
assess.correctAnswer: The Earth has its own magnetic field. The compass needle is a tiny magnet that lines up with that field, so its north-seeking (north) pole always turns toward Earth's magnetic north. The same end points north because it is that end's north pole being pulled along the field toward Earth's magnetic north (which is actually a magnetic south-type pole, so opposites attract).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The needle points north because it's pulled toward the North Star / the cold / true north as a place.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce Earth as a giant magnet with a field the needle aligns to; deflect the needle with a bar magnet to prove the needle is itself magnetic.
errorPatterns.distractor: The needle is pulled toward the North Star, the coldest place on Earth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names a non-magnetic cause; no mention of Earth's field.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Field lines are real strings, and there's only a field where I've drawn a line.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a plotting compass / iron filings to show the field is continuous everywhere around the magnet; lines are a representation, their direction = force on a north pole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says there is no field in the gaps between drawn lines; treats the lines as physical objects.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The field is strongest in the middle of the magnet, between the poles.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iron filings show the field concentrated at the POLES; closer lines mean a stronger field.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws the densest field lines at the centre of the bar.

responseLevels.gap: Explains the compass by a non-magnetic cause (North Star, cold, 'north is up'), or thinks field lines are physical strings with nothing between them.
responseLevels.full: Explains the needle as a small magnet aligning with Earth's magnetic field so its north pole points to magnetic north, draws the field (with direction, strongest at the poles) as a representation of a continuous field, and transfers to navigation and other locations.
responseLevels.partial: States the pole rule and that Earth has a field, and can draw a bar-magnet field pattern, but treats these as separate facts — e.g. draws lines without direction, or can't say why the needle's same end points north (doesn't connect needle-as-magnet with Earth's field).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A compass needle settles pointing north wherever you put it in the room. What is making the needle point that way — and why does the SAME end always end up pointing north?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student with the field model attributes the alignment to the EARTH'S magnetic field acting on the needle-magnet everywhere in the room. A student without it invokes the needle being 'attracted to the North Pole/North Star' or 'to the cold', or thinks it only works near another magnet. Tier 2 — why the SAME end — forces them to treat the needle as a magnet with poles interacting with a field, not a passive pointer.

sources.claim: KS3 'Magnetism' statutory content: magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion; magnetic fields by plotting with compass, representation by field lines; Earth's magnetism, compass and navigation.
sources.source: DfE — National curriculum in England: science programmes of study (KS3 Physics, Magnetism)

sources.claim: MS-PS2-5: conduct an investigation [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-5] even though not in contact (qualitative); DCI PS2.B — forces at a distance explained by fields that extend through space and can be mapped by their effect on a test object.
sources.source: NGSS — Topic: MS. Forces and Interactions

sources.claim: The field is the space around a magnet where it exerts a force; iron filings/plotting compasses only reveal direction and strength, they don't make it more real; the field exists in 3D, not just the 2D textbook pattern; start teaching with a compass (direction) before iron filings; field patterns are far from obvious to pupils and must be explicitly modelled.
sources.source: IOP Spark — Many students are unable to accurately represent a magnetic field using field lines; Representing magnetic fields in practice

sources.claim: KS3 lesson names 'the field only exists at the poles' as the common misconception, addressed by plotting field lines around the whole magnet; field lines run north-seeking to south-seeking, are continuous, do not cross, and spacing represents strength.
sources.source: Oak National Academy (KS3) — The magnetic field of a bar magnet

pedagogy.summary: Children solve multi-step word problems set in real measurement contexts — distance, time, capacity, mass, money — using the four operations on quantities that are often fractions or decimals, and represent the situation with a diagram (a number line or bar model) before computing. The heart of the topic is not the arithmetic but the MODELLING: reading the situation, choosing a representation that captures the relationships, attending to units (converting where needed), and checking the answer is reasonable in context. It is best taught by having students build a visual representation before they calculate, monitor their own problem-solving steps, and compare strategies — and by explicitly refusing the keyword habit ('altogether means add').
bestPractices: Teach students to draw a visual representation — number line or bar/strip diagram — that links the quantities BEFORE writing an equation (IES/WWC Recommendation 3, strong evidence); gains are largest when students design and refine their OWN representation
Give self-monitoring prompts ('What is the problem asking?', 'Does my answer make sense?') and model thinking aloud (IES/WWC Recommendation 2, strong evidence)
Insist on unit-checking: convert to a common unit before operating (95 cm → 0.95 m) and label the answer's unit and money symbol
Estimate first to bound the answer, then check the computed result against that estimate for reasonableness
Expose several strategies and compare them on worked examples (IES/WWC Recommendation 4); never teach keyword shortcuts — require modelling the situation
keyRepresentations: Number-line diagram with a measurement scale
Bar / strip (Singapore) model showing part-whole relationships
A labelled part-whole diagram linking known and unknown quantities
A conversion table for units within a system (km/m/cm, kg/g, l/ml, hr/min)
commonMisconceptions: Keyword plucking — grabbing the numbers and applying the operation a keyword cues, with no model of the situation
Operating across mixed units without converting (adding 0.75 m and 95 cm as if the same unit)
Treating time as base-ten (handling 1 hr 45 min as 1.45; carrying at 100 rather than 60)
Misaligning decimal points or dropping/mixing the money symbol (writing $5.7, or $0.50¢)
Computing with no diagram or estimate, so an unreasonable answer goes unchecked

learn.summary: Grade 4 learners (ages 9–10) solve multi-step measurement word problems — distance, time, capacity, mass, money — using the four operations on quantities that are often fractions or decimals. The core skill is MODELLING, not bare arithmetic: read the situation, build a visual representation (number line or bar/strip diagram) that captures the relationships, convert mixed units to a common unit, sequence the operations, label units and money symbols, check the answer is reasonable, and transfer the approach when a quantity changes. The habit to refuse is keyword plucking ('altogether means add'); learners who design their own representation before computing are the target.

activities.title: Build the model before you compute
feedback: If a learner writes a bare equation straight from a keyword cue, cover the numbers and ask them to retell the situation in their own words and draw it before any calculation.

For the flour example, splitting 2500 g (2.5 kg) into 4 gives 625 g (0.625 kg) per tub; after removing 150 g the tub holds 475 g (0.475 kg). Confirm the diagram shows four equal parts and one marked-off segment, and ask the learner to point to where the 150 g sits on the diagram.
If the answer comes out wildly off-scale (e.g. 0.006 kg or 6000 kg per tub), prompt: 'Roughly how big should each tub be? Does your answer match your estimate?'
If kg and g are combined directly, ask: 'Can you subtract these as they are? Why or why not?' and have them convert to one unit first.
For the transfer check, confirm 3 kg ÷ 4 = 0.75 kg per tub, which is 0.125 kg more than the 0.625 kg from the 2.5 kg bag; the diagram structure (4 equal parts) is unchanged — only the whole changed.
activities.rationale: Teaching learners to build and refine their own visual representation before writing an equation is supported as improving problem-solving achievement, with the largest gains when learners design their own representation. Building the model (rather than reading a finished one) is the active ingredient the diagram-first task targets.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to use visual representations improves problem-solving achievement (STRONG evidence); students who visually represent the information before writing an equation are more effective, and gains are largest when students design their own representations. Assisting students to monitor and reflect on the problem-solving process also has STRONG evidence. Genuine problem solving is non-routine and is NOT the execution of memorised shortcuts such as key words.

Grade 4 standard: use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit; represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.
learnerActions: Read a multi-step measurement problem, e.g. 'A 2.5 kg bag of flour is shared equally into 4 tubs, then 150 g is taken from one tub — how much is left in that tub?'
Before writing any equation, draw a bar/strip diagram or number line that shows the quantities and how they relate (the whole 2.5 kg, the 4 equal parts, the 150 g removed)
Convert to a common unit where needed (150 g = 0.15 kg, or 2.5 kg = 2500 g) and note the conversion explicitly

Let the structure of your diagram tell you the operations: splitting the bar into 4 equal parts IS the ÷4 (each part = 2500 g ÷ 4 = 625 g = 0.625 kg), and marking off 150 g from one part IS the subtraction (625 g − 150 g = 475 g = 0.475 kg). Working in grams keeps the numbers whole, because 0.625 kg is in thousandths and Grade 4 decimal work usually stops at hundredths.
Estimate roughly first, then check the computed answer against that estimate and label the unit

Test transfer: if the same bag had been 3 kg instead of 2.5 kg shared into 4 tubs, predict whether each tub holds more or less and by how much before computing — the same partition-then-subtract model still applies
activities.intendedInsight: The diagram generates the operations, so you never have to guess an operation from a keyword; partitioning a bar is division and marking off a segment is subtraction. Checking against an estimate catches off-scale answers, and the same model transfers when a quantity changes (e.g. a 3 kg bag still partitions into four equal parts).

activities.title: Convert units before operating
feedback: If a learner writes 0.75 + 95 = 95.75 or 2.5 − 150, point out that metres and centimetres (or kilograms and grams) are different sizes and must be matched first.
Check that 0.75 m + 1.2 m + 0.95 m is computed as 2.9 m, with all three already in metres.
For time, verify that 09:20 + 1 hr 45 min = 11:05 by adding 45 min to 20 min = 65 min = 1 hr 5 min, carrying the hour, then adding the journey hours — not by treating 1.45 as a decimal.
activities.rationale: The standard explicitly requires expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit (e.g. 0.75 m = 75 cm, 2.5 kg = 2500 g); converting to the smaller unit also keeps numbers whole. Converting to a larger unit (95 cm = 0.95 m) is also valid. A common unit-handling error is operating across mixed units without converting, so an explicit convert-first step addresses a frequent breakdown.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit; represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.
learnerActions: Given quantities in mixed units (e.g. 0.75 m, 1.2 m and 0.95 m; or 95 cm alongside 0.75 m), identify that they cannot be combined until expressed in one unit
Use a conversion table within a system (km/m/cm, kg/g, l/ml, hr/min) to rewrite every quantity in a common unit (95 cm → 0.95 m)
Only then add, subtract, multiply or divide, and label the result with the correct unit
Treat time carefully: 1 hr 45 min is NOT 1.45; minutes carry at 60, not 100 (e.g. leaving 09:20 and travelling 1 hr 45 min arrives at 11:05)
activities.intendedInsight: Operations are only valid between quantities expressed in the same unit; converting first prevents combining unlike units, and time is base-60, not base-10.

activities.title: Self-monitor and compare strategies
feedback: Prompt reflection with 'Before you calculate, roughly what should the answer be? About how big?' and 'Does this make sense?'
When comparing strategies, confirm the learner can say why both a bar model and a number line lead to the same ÷4-then-subtract sequence.

A tap-to-reveal annotated worked example can teach how a bar maps to the equation and is useful for exposition and reference, but it does not itself let the learner build or revise their own representation; follow it with a problem where the learner constructs the diagram themselves.
activities.rationale: Self-monitoring prompts and reflection on the problem-solving process are supported teaching moves directly backed by the quoted source. Comparing valid strategies may also support flexible problem solving (from the original's IES Recommendation 4 best practice), though the quoted source claim directly supports only the self-monitoring component. An annotated worked example supports exposition but cannot substitute for learner-built representation.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to use visual representations improves problem-solving achievement (STRONG evidence); students who visually represent the information before writing an equation are more effective, and gains are largest when students design their own representations. Assisting students to monitor and reflect on the problem-solving process also has STRONG evidence. Genuine problem solving is non-routine and is NOT the execution of memorised shortcuts such as key words.
learnerActions: At the start, ask yourself 'What is the problem asking?' and restate the goal before choosing a representation
After solving, ask 'Does my answer make sense?' and compare it to your up-front estimate
Solve a problem, then view or discuss an alternative strategy for the same problem (e.g. a bar model vs. a number-line path) and explain how each maps to the same operations
Explore a worked example where each diagram segment is annotated with the quantity it stands for and the operation the structure implies — use this for reference, then build your own on a new problem
activities.intendedInsight: Monitoring your own steps and comparing different valid representations can deepen understanding of why the operations follow from the situation, rather than from a cue word.

constraints: The target skill is modelling plus computing: learners must build their own representation, not only read or tap a finished one. Annotated worked examples and reveal-the-segment displays are exposition/reference scaffolds and should be followed by learner-constructed diagrams.

Fill-in-the-blank, slider and draw-the-jump response formats can assess computation and unit handling, but a sequence that only scores the final number cannot see whether the learner modelled the situation or plucked a keyword — so pair any such checks with observation of the build.

Interactive supports such as dragging quantities onto a bar or number line, partitioning a bar into equal parts, a unit strip that snaps g↔kg or cm↔m, and flags for off-scale answers are useful ways to make the model concrete and provide feedback; they are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required tooling.
Refuse keyword shortcuts ('altogether means add', 'left means subtract'); require a model of the situation before an equation.
Insist on unit-checking (convert to a common unit before operating) and on labelling the answer with its unit and money symbol (avoid $5.7 or $0.50¢).
Treat time as base-60: 1 hr 45 min is not 1.45, and minutes carry at 60.
A fixed/static annotated example can still teach how a bar maps to an equation; it simply cannot be manipulated by the learner — scope its role to exposition rather than claiming it cannot teach.
Include transfer: once a model works, vary a quantity (e.g. 2.5 kg → 3 kg) and have the learner predict whether and by how much the result changes using the same model.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general teaching principles, not that these specific tasks were tested.

The original worked example ('2.5 kg split into 4 = 0.625 kg each') is arithmetically correct (2.5 ÷ 4 = 0.625). After removing 150 g (0.15 kg) from one tub, that tub holds 0.475 kg; the source stated the per-tub value but not the final remaining amount, so 0.475 kg has been added for completeness and should be confirmed.

The time example (leave 09:20, travel 1 hr 45 min) was listed in the source evidence without a stated answer; 11:05 is supplied here and flagged as an added computation. The source's own misconception list warns against treating 1 hr 45 min as 1.45, which this activity corrects explicitly.

The transfer figures (3 kg ÷ 4 = 0.75 kg per tub; 0.125 kg more than 0.625 kg) were computed here from the original's transfer probe and responseLevels 'full' criterion, which left the numbers unstated; they should be confirmed.

The compare-strategies element of Activity 3 reflects the original's 'expose several strategies' best practice (IES Recommendation 4), but the quoted source claim directly supports only the visual-representation and self-monitoring principles, not the compare-multiple-strategies recommendation; wording has been qualified accordingly.
Source claims about 'strong evidence' and 'verified' flags are copied from the legacy row and were not independently re-checked in this rewrite.

probeDeeper: Before you calculate — roughly what should the answer be? About how big?
You have kilograms and grams here — can you subtract them as they are? Why or why not?
Show me on your diagram where the 150 g is.
If the bag had been 3 kg instead of 2.5, would each tub be more or less — and by how much?
assess.correctAnswer: Draws a representation (bar or number line) that captures the relationships, converts to a common unit (2.5 kg = 2500 g, or 150 g = 0.15 kg), applies the operations in the right sequence (÷4 then subtract), labels the answer with its unit, and can say why the size of the answer is reasonable.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword plucking — writes an equation straight from a number-plus-keyword cue ('shared → divide everything', 'left → subtract the two numbers') with no model of the situation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cover the numbers and ask them to retell the situation in their own words and draw it first; require a model before any calculation
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces a bare equation using all the numbers once in the keyword-cued operation, with no diagram and often the wrong structure for a multi-step problem

errorPatterns.pattern: Operates across mixed units without converting — combines quantities in different units as if the same
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach relative unit sizes and convert to a common unit before operating, using a conversion table
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes e.g. 2.5 − 150, or adds 0.75 m + 95 cm as 95.75, ignoring that kg≠g and m≠cm

errorPatterns.pattern: Computes without checking reasonableness — can do the arithmetic but omits estimating or sense-checking, so an off-scale answer stands
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold an estimate-first and a 'does this make sense?' step; do not reteach the arithmetic — the computation is held, the monitoring lapses
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces an answer wildly off-scale (each tub 0.006 kg, or 6000 kg) with no estimate and no diagram to check it against, and does not flag it

responseLevels.gap: Grabs numbers and applies a keyword-cued operation with no model; combines mixed units without converting; cannot say whether the answer is reasonable.
responseLevels.full: Models the situation with a diagram, converts to a common unit, sequences the operations correctly, labels units and money symbols, and checks the answer against an estimate — transferring the approach when a quantity is changed.
responseLevels.partial: Represents and computes single steps but the chain breaks — converts OR models but not both, or reaches a correct number without checking reasonableness; can list the steps but not justify the operations from the situation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child two multi-step measurement problems that mix units and involve a fraction or decimal — e.g. 'A 2.5 kg bag of flour is shared equally into 4 tubs; then 150 g is taken from one tub. How much is left in that tub?' Say: 'Show your thinking with a diagram, then solve it.' Provide blank paper and watch: do they draw a number line or bar that models the situation BEFORE calculating, do they convert kg and g to a common unit, and do they check the answer is reasonable?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'show your thinking with a diagram' demand on a mixed-unit multi-step problem separates a modeller from a keyword-plucker and a converter from a non-converter: the plucker writes a bare equation using every number once in the cued operation, the non-converter combines kg and g directly, and the unmonitored child leaves an off-scale answer standing. Watching the build — not asking about the method — makes each visible.

sources.claim: Grade 4 standard: use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit; represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 4.MD.A.2

sources.claim: Teaching students to use visual representations improves problem-solving achievement (STRONG evidence); students who visually represent the information before writing an equation are more effective, and gains are largest when students design their own representations. Assisting students to monitor and reflect on the problem-solving process also has STRONG evidence. Genuine problem solving is non-routine and is NOT the execution of memorised shortcuts such as key words.
sources.source: Woodward et al. (2012), IES/WWC Practice Guide 'Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8' (NCEE 2012-4055)

pedagogy.summary: This Year 5 topic builds the heliocentric model: the Sun (a star) at the centre with the planets, including Earth, orbiting it; the Moon orbiting Earth while Earth orbits the Sun; and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies. It is best taught with physical/enacted models the children move themselves, establishing sphericity explicitly and distinguishing the two nested orbits (Moon–Earth, Earth–Sun), while bridging the deep geocentric intuition using the history of ideas (Ptolemy → Copernicus).
bestPractices: Use kinesthetic/physical models children enact — be the Earth orbiting a lamp 'Sun' while a partner 'Moon' orbits you — because manipulating the model beats watching a demonstration.
Establish sphericity explicitly (the Sun, Earth and Moon are balls, not discs) using globes and real photos, since many children hold a flat-disc or flat-sky model.
Distinguish the two nested orbits clearly: the Moon orbits Earth, and Earth (with all the planets) orbits the Sun — the common confusion is what orbits what.
Bridge from the geocentric intuition to the heliocentric model using the story of ideas (Ptolemy, Alhazen, Copernicus), which makes the counter-intuitive model credible.
Handle scale honestly — flag that diagrams compress sizes and distances hugely and are not to scale.
Keep 'rotation causes day and night' as the linked next step; here concentrate on the orbital model and sphericity.
keyRepresentations: A heliocentric model — Sun-centred with the planets' orbits, Earth among them.
A nested-orbit diagram: Moon → Earth, Earth (and planets) → Sun.
Physical enactment: a child as the orbiting/spinning Earth around a lamp Sun, a partner as the Moon.
A globe plus light source, and photos showing the Sun, Earth and Moon as spheres.
A 'not to scale' caption or scale strip.
commonMisconceptions: The Sun orbits or goes around the Earth (the geocentric model), or everything orbits Earth.
The Sun, Earth and Moon are flat discs rather than spheres.
The Moon orbits the Sun directly, rather than orbiting Earth while both orbit the Sun.
The Sun is somehow different from 'a star'.
Planets are close together and similar in size (a scale error from diagrams); Pluto is still a planet.

learn.summary: Year 5 'Earth and space': build the heliocentric model — the Sun (a star) at the centre with Earth and the other planets orbiting it, the Moon orbiting Earth while Earth orbits the Sun, and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies. The core difficulty is the deep geocentric intuition and the nested two-orbit system (Moon to Earth, Earth to Sun), plus a flat-disc reading of the bodies. Teach it with enacted/physical models children move themselves, a top-down orbit model they run and compare against observation, explicit sphericity evidence, and the history of ideas (Ptolemy's Earth-centred model, Alhazen's critique of it, and Copernicus's Sun-centred model).

activities.title: Be the Earth, the Moon and the Sun — enact the nested orbits
feedback: If the Moon child drifts off to circle the lamp instead of their Earth, stop and re-tether: 'The Moon stays with its Earth — it loops you while you loop the Sun.'
If a child says the Sun moves round the Earth, ask them to name who is standing still at the centre and who is walking around whom.
Check the pair can state what orbits what before swapping roles.
activities.rationale: Upper-primary children are becoming ready for a heliocentric perspective but typically still hold a geocentric model; physically manipulating a model the child enacts is recommended, and curriculum guidance recommends using a model of the Sun and Earth. Any claim that enactment outperforms watching a demonstration is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Early-elementary children typically hold a geocentric (Earth-centred) model and struggle with sphericity and nested orbits; upper-elementary pupils become ready for a heliocentric perspective, so physical models the child manipulates are recommended.

DfE Year 5 non-statutory guidance recommends pupils learn how ideas about the solar system developed — how the geocentric model gave way to the heliocentric model via Ptolemy, Alhazen and Copernicus — and use a model of the Sun and Earth.
learnerActions: In a group of three, place a lamp or ball as the Sun. One child is the Earth and walks a slow circle around the Sun.
The 'Moon' child circles the 'Earth' child continuously WHILE the Earth keeps walking its orbit around the Sun, so both motions happen at once.
Pause and say aloud: 'The Moon goes around the Earth, and the Earth (with the Moon) goes around the Sun.'
Swap roles so every child has been the Moon that must keep looping its Earth while the Earth travels.
activities.intendedInsight: The Moon orbits Earth while the Earth–Moon pair together travel round the Sun — two simultaneous, nested orbits, not the Moon circling the Sun directly.

activities.title: Run and compare a top-down solar-system model
feedback: If the child reads the toggle as 'both are equally fine', ask them to point to what each arrangement shows for the planets' paths and which one accounts for them more simply (the Moon circles Earth in both).
If they say the Moon circles the Sun, slow the slider right down and have them trace the Moon's path relative to the Earth, not the Sun.

Note honestly that an Earth-centred picture can look like it fits everyday sunrise and sunset, so the real comparison rests on the planets' changing positions the model shows; the Moon staying with Earth happens in both arrangements, so it does not decide between them.
Reinforce: 'The Sun is at the centre; the Earth is one of the planets, and the Sun is a star.'
activities.rationale: The nested-orbit relationship and the geocentric-versus-heliocentric contrast are largely planar, so a top-down model the child runs and scrubs makes the two simultaneous motions and the comparison visible and controllable. A fixed diagram can show the layout but cannot be run or compared interactively by the learner.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 statutory 'Earth and space' requires pupils to describe the movement of the Earth and other planets relative to the Sun; the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth; and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies.

DfE Year 5 non-statutory guidance recommends pupils learn how ideas about the solar system developed — how the geocentric model gave way to the heliocentric model via Ptolemy, Alhazen and Copernicus — and use a model of the Sun and Earth.
learnerActions: Run a top-down view: the planets glide around the Sun while the Moon circles the Earth. Use a time slider to speed up, slow down or scrub the motion.
Watch specifically for the Moon looping the Earth AT THE SAME TIME as the Earth loops the Sun, and describe this nesting in your own words.
Flip a toggle to an Earth-centred arrangement (Sun and everything circling the Earth) and compare it with the Sun-centred one.

Compare the two using concrete things the model shows: notice that the Moon circles the Earth in both arrangements, so look at the planets. In which arrangement do the planets' paths, including times when a planet seems to drift backwards across our sky, come out more simply? Explain your choice.
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun-centred model, with the Moon still orbiting Earth, accounts for the planets' observed motions more simply; together with later observations, this is why it replaced the earlier Earth-centred model.

activities.title: Spheres, not discs — gather the evidence
feedback: If a child still describes them as circles or plates, return to a photo and the lit globe and ask what a flat disc would look like from the side.
Note that round pictures in books are flat drawings of round balls — distinguish the drawing from the body it represents.
activities.rationale: Many children hold a flat-disc or flat-sky model, so sphericity should be established explicitly with globes, photographs and observable evidence rather than assumed.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 statutory 'Earth and space' requires pupils to describe the movement of the Earth and other planets relative to the Sun; the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth; and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies.

Early-elementary children typically hold a geocentric (Earth-centred) model and struggle with sphericity and nested orbits; upper-elementary pupils become ready for a heliocentric perspective, so physical models the child manipulates are recommended.
learnerActions: Handle a globe lit by a single light source and describe how light falls on a ball versus a flat disc.
Look at real photographs of the Sun, Earth and Moon taken from space and state whether each is a ball or a flat circle.

List evidence that the bodies are spheres: photos from space of all three; for Earth, the curved shadow it casts on the Moon during a lunar eclipse and ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon; for the Moon, the curved edge between its lit and dark parts as its phases change.
Say the conclusion in full: 'The Sun, Earth and Moon are approximately spherical.'
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun, Earth and Moon are approximately spherical bodies, not flat discs drawn on a flat sky.

activities.title: Name and order the planets; test what-orbits-what
feedback: A matching answer that sends the Moon around the Sun shows the nesting has flattened — return to the enactment or the slowed model.
If a learner places Earth at the centre with the Sun orbiting, revisit the run-and-compare model and anchor 'the Sun is at the centre, Earth is one of the planets.'
This task checks understanding rather than teaching it: follow up wrong choices by returning to the enactment or the model, not just by marking them.
activities.rationale: Matching, ordering and a geocentric/heliocentric choice surface whether the learner coordinates the two orbits and can defend Sun-at-centre; such tasks check recall and discrimination and do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing or enacting the model.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 statutory 'Earth and space' requires pupils to describe the movement of the Earth and other planets relative to the Sun; the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth; and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies.
learnerActions: Name the planets in order out from the Sun and state that they all orbit the Sun.
Match each body to what it orbits: Moon to Earth; Earth and the other planets to the Sun.
Answer a geocentric-vs-heliocentric choice: which arrangement has the Sun at the centre, and why is it the accepted one?
Sort pictures or statements into 'sphere' versus 'flat disc' for the Sun, Earth and Moon.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the model: Sun at the centre as a star, planets orbiting it in order, the Moon orbiting Earth, all three bodies spherical.

activities.title: Interview Copernicus — why move the Sun to the centre? (optional history companion)
feedback: If the conversation drifts into biography only, steer back to 'what does each model account for, and which does it more simply?'
Keep this as a companion to the orbit model, not a replacement for running and comparing it.
activities.rationale: The history of ideas bridges the geocentric intuition to the heliocentric model and is recommended in the non-statutory guidance; it teaches why the idea changed more than the mechanics of the model, so it supports rather than replaces the orbit work.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 non-statutory guidance recommends pupils learn how ideas about the solar system developed — how the geocentric model gave way to the heliocentric model via Ptolemy, Alhazen and Copernicus — and use a model of the Sun and Earth.
learnerActions: In role, or questioning a peer in role as Copernicus, ask: 'Why isn't the Earth at the centre?'
Draw out that placing the Sun at the centre accounted for the observed motions more simply than the earlier Earth-centred model.

Connect the story to the model: Ptolemy set out a detailed Earth-centred model, Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham) criticised problems in Ptolemy's model, and Copernicus proposed putting the Sun at the centre; later observations by others helped it become accepted.
activities.intendedInsight: The counter-intuitive heliocentric model became accepted because it accounted for observations more simply and was supported by later observations (such as Galileo's telescope discoveries) — the history makes the model credible.

constraints: Core statutory goals: describe Earth and the other planets moving relative to the Sun; the Moon moving relative to the Earth; and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies.
Address the common confusions directly: the Sun orbiting the Earth (geocentric), the Moon orbiting the Sun directly (flattened nesting), and the bodies as flat discs.

Handle scale honestly: diagrams and models compress sizes and distances hugely and are not to scale — flag this with a 'not to scale' caption or scale strip rather than implying planets are close together or similar in size.
Anchor that the Sun is a star and the Earth is a planet like the others.
Keep 'rotation causes day and night' as the linked next step; here concentrate on the orbital model and sphericity.

A top-down or flat screen model represents the orbits on a plane; use rotating-globe imagery or 3D/physical balls to make clear the bodies themselves are spheres. A 3D free viewpoint can help learners feel the nesting in space but is an enhancement, not a requirement — the core orbital relationship is largely planar.

When contrasting geocentric and heliocentric arrangements, keep the comparison age-appropriate and honest: a simple Earth-centred picture can appear to fit daily sunrise/sunset, so rest the comparison on the planets' changing positions (for example, planets sometimes appearing to drift backwards across the sky), which a Sun-centred model explains more simply. Note that the Moon orbits Earth in both arrangements, so the Moon's motion alone does not decide between them. Do not claim the Earth-centred model fits nothing.

Matching, ordering and multiple-choice tasks check recognition and discrimination; they do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing or enacting the nested motions, so pair them with enactment or a runnable model.
If Pluto arises, use current convention (Pluto is a dwarf planet); do not present 'Pluto is still a planet' as correct.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (IOPSpark / NSTA geocentric-model guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the readiness and 'physical models the child manipulates are recommended' claims as unverified.

The original best-practice phrasing 'manipulating the model beats watching a demonstration' asserts comparative efficacy the cited sources do not establish; it has been removed from activity rationales and replaced with a recommendation to use/enact a model, qualified as unverified.

The row's framing of a static diagram as unable to teach the nested motion has been narrowed to an observable affordance/limit (a fixed diagram shows layout but cannot be run or compared interactively), not a categorical 'cannot teach' claim.

Pluto's status (the row notes 'Pluto is still a planet' as a misconception) is a classification point; present current convention that Pluto is a dwarf planet, and keep the focus on the orbital model.

The child-facing contrast between Earth-centred and Sun-centred models is simplified for Year 5. Historically, a simple geocentric view superficially matches daily sunrise/sunset and epicyclic geocentric models matched naked-eye observations fairly well; the activity has been reworded to rest the comparison on the fuller set of motions the model shows rather than implying the Earth-centred picture fits nothing.

probeDeeper: If you stood on the Moon, what would you see going around you — and what would you BOTH be going around?
How would you persuade someone who thinks the Sun goes round the Earth that it's actually the other way?
Is the Earth the centre of the solar system? If not, what is — and how do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: The Moon orbits the Earth; the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun — so the Moon circles the Earth while the pair together travel round the Sun, which sits at the centre. The Earth is a planet like the others, and the Sun is a star.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Sun goes round the Earth' (geocentric model, reinforced by sunrise/sunset language)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run a Sun-centred model beside an Earth-centred one and test which matches what we see; anchor 'the Sun is at the centre, Earth is one of the planets.'
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun orbits the Earth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: places the Earth at the centre with the Sun orbiting it

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Moon orbits the Sun directly' (flattens the nested two-orbit system)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the Moon tethered to the Earth, the Earth–Moon pair travelling together round the Sun; act it out with three children.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Moon orbits the Sun directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: draws or describes the Moon circling the Sun rather than the Earth

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Sun, Earth and Moon are flat circles / discs' (2-D reading of the bodies)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sphericity evidence — photographs from space, the round shadow Earth casts on the Moon, ships dipping below the horizon.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes them as circles or plates rather than balls

responseLevels.gap: Geocentric (the Sun orbits the Earth), or describes the bodies as flat; cannot say what orbits what.
responseLevels.full: Coordinates the nested system — Moon round Earth, Earth and planets round the Sun at the centre — states the Sun, Earth and Moon are spheres, and can justify heliocentric over geocentric; transfers to another planet-and-moon pair.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the planets orbit the Sun but flattens the nesting (sends the Moon round the Sun) or cannot coordinate the two simultaneous motions; states sphericity only when prompted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell me the path of the Moon: what does the Moon go around, and what does THAT thing go around? … Now, how do you know the Earth travels round the Sun and not the other way?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A geocentric child puts the Earth at the centre with the Sun going round it — the reason tier surfaces this. A child who has only memorised 'planets orbit the Sun' may still send the Moon straight round the Sun, missing the nesting. Correct reasoning coordinates two simultaneous orbits and can defend Sun-at-centre.
