pedagogy.summary: Direct proportion means two quantities keep a CONSTANT RATIO: as one is multiplied by k, so is the other, and their graph is a straight line THROUGH THE ORIGIN (y = kx). Inverse proportion means the PRODUCT is constant: as one is multiplied by k, the other is divided by k (xy = c, a curve). The pedagogical heart of the topic is (1) making the multiplicative structure of direct proportion explicit against merely additive change, and (2) resisting the 'illusion of proportionality' — the reflex to treat every relationship as directly proportional. Children must learn to ASK whether doubling one quantity really doubles the other, or halves it, or does neither.
bestPractices: Contrast three situations side by side — directly proportional (4 pens £6 → 10 pens £15, line through origin), inversely proportional (workers vs time to dig a hole; taps filling a bucket), and neither (phone plan £15/month + £0.20/min: linear but NOT proportional because the line misses the origin). Sorting situations into these three bins is the key discrimination.

Use the 'if one is zero the other is zero' test for direct proportion, and the 'doubling one halves the other' test for inverse — make the defining property a checkable question, not a memorised label.
Build direct proportion from ratio tables and double number lines so unit rate (cost per pen) is visible; scale up by multiplying, never by adding a constant difference.

Graph both: direct proportion is a straight line through the origin; inverse is a smooth decreasing curve. Reading the origin behaviour off a graph is a fast diagnostic of which (if either) relationship holds.
Delay the formulae y=kx and xy=c until the ratio-table and product-constancy reasoning is secure, so children reason about structure rather than substituting into a triangle.
keyRepresentations: Ratio table / double number line (direct proportion — scale columns by multiplying)
Graph through the origin (direct: straight line) vs decreasing curve (inverse)
Product-constant table for inverse proportion (e.g. speed×time = distance held fixed)
Three-bin sorting mat: directly proportional | inversely proportional | neither
commonMisconceptions: Illusion of proportionality — treating every relationship as directly proportional, applying y=kx to situations that are linear-but-not-proportional (phone plan with a fixed charge) or inverse.
Confusing direct and inverse: expecting 'twice as fast' to mean 'twice the time' rather than half the time.
Additive rather than multiplicative scaling: going from 4 pens to 8 pens by adding the same amount to the cost instead of doubling it.
Believing any straight-line graph shows direct proportion, ignoring whether it passes through the origin.

learn.summary: Direct proportion means two quantities keep a constant ratio: multiply one by k and the other is multiplied by k, so the graph is a straight line through the origin (y = kx). Inverse proportion means the product is constant: multiply one by k and the other is divided by k (xy = c, a decreasing curve). The core learning goals are (1) making the multiplicative structure of direct proportion explicit, distinct from merely additive change, and (2) resisting the 'illusion of proportionality' — the reflex to treat every relationship as directly proportional. Learners should habitually ASK whether doubling one quantity really doubles the other, halves it, or does neither.

activities.title: Proportion lab: drive one quantity, watch the other
feedback: Direct scenario: 'You multiplied pens by 2.5 and the cost multiplied by 2.5 too — the ratio (cost per pen) stayed the same at £1.50, and the line runs straight through (0,0). That is direct proportion.'

Phone-plan scenario: 'You doubled the minutes but the bill did not double — it landed below your guess. The £15 fixed charge is added whatever you do, so at 0 minutes the bill is £15, not £0, and the line misses the origin. This is linear but not proportional.'

Inverse scenario: 'Halving the taps doubled the fill time. Here the bucket's volume is fixed and each tap has the same flow, so the number of taps and the fill time always multiply to the same constant (with one tap taking 60 s, taps × time = 60 s). That constant product, not just one falling as the other rises, is what makes it inverse proportion, and its graph is a curve, not a line.'

If a prediction treats every scenario as doubling: 'Before predicting, ask: if I set this quantity to zero, is the other zero too? That one check separates true proportion from a plan with a fixed charge.'
activities.rationale: Predicting then observing a live recompute makes the multiplicative structure visible and surfaces the illusion of proportionality precisely where it breaks. Contrasting the three scenarios side by side turns the defining property into a checkable question rather than a label. A ratio table shown alongside the graph keeps unit-rate reasoning visible while scaling by multiplication.
sourceClaims: Direct proportion: graph is a straight line through the origin, doubling one quantity doubles the other, and if one quantity is zero the other is zero; children fail to recognise when quantities vary in direct proportion and confuse direct with inverse situations.

A situation such as a phone plan with a fixed monthly charge plus a per-minute rate is linear but NOT proportional (the line does not pass through the origin); students over-apply proportional reasoning ('the numbers dictate the operation').
Distinguishing ratio from proportion and reasoning multiplicatively (unit rate, scaling) rather than additively is the core of proportional reasoning.
learnerActions: Work with three switchable scenarios: pens & cost (4 pens £6 → 10 pens £15, directly proportional); taps filling a bucket or workers digging a hole (inversely proportional); and a phone plan of £15/month + £0.20/min (linear but NOT proportional).
Before changing anything, PREDICT where the next point will land on the graph and what the paired value should be — write or say the prediction and your reason first.
Change quantity A (e.g. with a slider or by choosing a new value) and watch quantity B recompute, with the point plotting live on a graph while a ratio table fills in alongside.

In the phone-plan scenario, double the minutes while predicting the cost will also double; observe that the plotted point lands below your prediction and the traced line clearly does NOT pass through the origin.
In the inverse scenario, halve the number of taps and observe the fill time double, with the curve bending away from the straight line you expected.

Apply two quick tests out loud: 'if one quantity is zero, is the other zero?' (a first check for direct proportion; it is needed but not enough by itself, so also confirm that the ratio stays constant) and 'does doubling one halve the other, keeping the product the same?' (inverse-proportion test).
activities.intendedInsight: Quantity B's response to driving quantity A reveals the structure: in direct proportion the ratio holds (and the line goes through the origin), in inverse proportion the product holds (one goes down as the other goes up), and in linear-but-not-proportional situations a fixed charge means the line misses the origin so doubling fails. Proportionality is a property to test, not a default to assume.

activities.title: Sort situations into direct, inverse, or neither
feedback: If a not-through-origin line is picked as direct proportion: 'Check the start: does this line pass through (0,0)? A line with a fixed starting value is linear but not proportional. Direct proportion must begin at the origin.'

If a ratio table is completed by adding a constant difference: 'From 4 pens to 8 pens you doubled the pens, so double the cost (£6 → £12) rather than adding the same gap. Scale by multiplying — cost per pen stays constant.'

If a 'twice as fast means twice the time' answer appears: 'Picture the taps filling a bucket: more taps means LESS time, not more. One quantity falling as the other rises is not enough on its own, though. It is inverse proportion only if their product stays constant, as taps × time does here.'
activities.rationale: The additive-scaling error and the 'any straight line is proportional' error make sharp, diagnostic distractors, so sorting and selection tasks directly target the known misconceptions. These response formats check discrimination; pair them with the hands-on lab so learners also construct and drive the relationships, not only recognise them.
sourceClaims: Direct proportion: graph is a straight line through the origin, doubling one quantity doubles the other, and if one quantity is zero the other is zero; children fail to recognise when quantities vary in direct proportion and confuse direct with inverse situations.

A situation such as a phone plan with a fixed monthly charge plus a per-minute rate is linear but NOT proportional (the line does not pass through the origin); students over-apply proportional reasoning ('the numbers dictate the operation').
learnerActions: Sort six real-world situations into three bins: directly proportional, inversely proportional, or neither.

For each, justify the placement with a test: for direct proportion, check that the ratio stays constant (so doubling one doubles the other, and zero gives zero); for inverse, check that the product stays constant (so doubling one halves the other). 'Zero gives zero' alone is not enough: a square's side and its area both start at zero, but they are not proportional.
Choose which of several graphs shows direct proportion, deliberately comparing a straight line through the origin against a straight line that misses the origin.
Complete a ratio table for a directly proportional situation by multiplying (scaling columns), and check whether an answer found by adding a fixed difference gives the same result.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying situations and matching them to graphs forces the discrimination that defines the topic: not every straight line is proportional (it must pass through the origin), and additive scaling is not the same as multiplicative scaling.

activities.title: Reference triptych: three graphs, three tests
feedback: 'The through-origin straight line is the only one of the three showing direct proportion — equal multiplying of both quantities. The offset line is linear but not proportional; the curve shows a constant product (inverse).'
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated reference teaches the recognition cues and supports consolidation. It does not let learners drive a quantity and watch the other respond, so it works best as a reference card after the hands-on lab rather than as the first encounter.
sourceClaims: Direct proportion: graph is a straight line through the origin, doubling one quantity doubles the other, and if one quantity is zero the other is zero; children fail to recognise when quantities vary in direct proportion and confuse direct with inverse situations.
learnerActions: Study a labelled set of three graphs side by side: a straight line through the origin (direct), a smooth decreasing curve (inverse), and a straight line that misses the origin (linear but not proportional).
Reveal, for each graph, its defining property — 'does the line start at (0,0)?' for the lines and 'does the product stay the same?' for the curve.
Use the triptych as a consolidation reference while classifying new situations, checking origin behaviour as a fast first diagnostic.
activities.intendedInsight: For straight-line graphs, origin behaviour is a quick diagnostic: through the origin means direct proportion, and missing the origin means linear but not proportional. A decreasing curve should prompt a check of whether the product stays constant, because not every decreasing curve shows inverse proportion.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain with two taps
feedback: Correct reasoning: 'Sam is wrong. Because of the fixed £15, at 0 minutes the bill is £15, not £0, so the relationship does not pass through the origin. Doubling the minutes only doubles the £0.20-per-minute part: 100 min costs £35, but 200 min costs £55 — less than double £35, which would be £70.'
If 'Sam is right, double is double': 'What does Sam pay if he makes NO calls this month? The £15 at zero minutes shows the line misses the origin, so doubling cannot apply to the whole bill.'

If the bill is said to go DOWN as minutes rise: 'Here more minutes means more cost — both rise together, so it is not inverse. Inverse proportion needs one to fall as the other rises AND their product to stay constant, like taps × fill time.'
If a fixed amount is added again for extra minutes: 'Recompute the variable part: 200 × £0.20 = £40, plus the fixed £15 = £55. The £15 stays put while only the per-minute part scales.'
Counterexample check: 'If there were no £15 charge, just £0.20 per minute, THEN Sam would be right — that version is directly proportional, a line through the origin.'
activities.rationale: Requiring a prediction and a reason before observing makes the diagnostic hinge on reasoning, not just the numerical answer, so the fixed-charge structure is hard to get right for the wrong reason. The taps case and the phone-plan case together separate inverse proportion from linear-but-not-proportional.
sourceClaims: A situation such as a phone plan with a fixed monthly charge plus a per-minute rate is linear but NOT proportional (the line does not pass through the origin); students over-apply proportional reasoning ('the numbers dictate the operation').

Direct proportion: graph is a straight line through the origin, doubling one quantity doubles the other, and if one quantity is zero the other is zero; children fail to recognise when quantities vary in direct proportion and confuse direct with inverse situations.
learnerActions: PREDICT: One tap fills a bucket in 60 seconds. If you open a SECOND tap of the same flow, how long to fill the same bucket? Write your time AND your reason before testing.
OBSERVE: in the idealised model (each tap gives the same constant flow, the bucket volume is fixed, nothing overflows), two taps fill it in 30 seconds.

EXPLAIN: why the naive 'still 60' or '120 seconds' prediction is wrong — twice the taps gives HALF the time because taps and time are inversely proportional: the bucket's volume (total water) is fixed and each tap has equal flow, so the number of taps × the fill time stays constant, meaning doubling the taps halves the time.

Then tackle the phone-plan question: a plan costs £15/month plus £0.20 per minute. Sam says 'if I talk for twice as many minutes, my bill will be twice as big.' Decide whether Sam is right and explain how you know.

Probe deeper: What would Sam pay for 0 minutes, and what does that say about proportionality? Work out the bill for 100 minutes and for 200 minutes — is the second exactly double the first? What if the plan had no £15 charge — would Sam be right then? And is 'twice as many taps' the same kind of relationship as the phone bill?
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before observing exposes the illusion of proportionality: a learner who truly grasps direct proportion tests the origin ('what happens at zero?') and sees that the fixed charge breaks the doubling rule, while a learner running the reflex answers 'twice the bill' automatically.

constraints: Delay the formulae y = kx and xy = c until ratio-table and product-constancy reasoning is secure, so learners reason about structure rather than substituting into a memorised triangle.
Scale direct-proportion tables by multiplying, never by adding a constant difference.
Build direct proportion from ratio tables and double number lines so the unit rate (e.g. cost per pen) stays visible.

Selection and sorting tasks check whether a learner can discriminate the three families, but recognition-only responses do not require the learner to construct or drive a relationship; pair them with the hands-on predict-and-drive work.
The fixed reference triptych shows cues and supports consolidation but cannot let a learner vary one quantity and watch the other respond; treat it as a reference, not the first encounter.

When using the taps/inverse example, state the idealisation (equal constant flow per tap, fixed bucket volume, no overflow) and be precise that the constant product is taps × time (equal to the one-tap fill time, 60 s), not the volume itself.

Optional interaction examples (a slider driving a value, a live-plotting point, a ratio table filling alongside, tap-to-reveal properties) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory; the essential requirements are prediction-before-observation and side-by-side contrast of the three families.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit of arithmetic: phone plan £15 + £0.20/min gives 100 min → £15 + £20 = £35 and 200 min → £15 + £40 = £55; £55 is less than double £35 (which would be £70), confirming non-proportionality. Pens: 4 → 10 is ×2.5 with cost £6 → £15 (ratio £1.50/pen held). These figures are consistent across the activities and the source's assessment.

Independent re-audit of the taps/inverse claim: the original source phrasing 'their product, the total water, is fixed' is imprecise. What is fixed is the bucket's volume; given equal flow per tap, t = 60/n so the number of taps × the fill time is the constant 60 s (equal to the one-tap fill time), not the volume. The learner-facing text avoids equating the product with the volume.
The idealisation behind the taps example (equal constant flow, fixed volume, no overflow) is stated in the activity and constraint.

The source's artefact-fit entries asserted that in-role dialogue 'adds no persona-grounded value' and that 3D 'adds a dimension the concept does not have.' These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; they have been dropped rather than propagated as universal claims. The planar, tabular/graphical nature of the relationship is retained as a design rationale without claiming other media cannot teach it.

assess.poeTask: PREDICT: One tap fills a bucket in 60 seconds. If you open a SECOND tap of the same flow, how long to fill the same bucket? Write your time and WHY before testing. OBSERVE: two taps fill it in 30 seconds. EXPLAIN: the naive 'still 60' or '120' prediction is violated — twice the taps gives HALF the time because the taps and time are INVERSELY proportional (their product, total water, is fixed), not directly proportional. The stated reason before observing is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: What would Sam pay for 0 minutes? What does that tell you about whether the bill is proportional to the minutes?
Work out the bill for 100 minutes and for 200 minutes — is the second exactly double the first? Why not?
What if the plan had NO £15 monthly charge, just £0.20 a minute — would Sam be right THEN? (counterexample: this version IS directly proportional, line through origin.)
Now think about filling a bucket: if you use twice as many taps, does it take twice as long, or half as long? Is that the same kind of relationship as the phone bill?
assess.correctAnswer: Sam is wrong. The bill is NOT directly proportional to the minutes because of the fixed £15 charge: at 0 minutes the bill is £15, not £0, so the relationship does not pass through the origin. Doubling the minutes doubles only the £0.20-per-minute part, not the whole bill — e.g. 100 min costs £35, but 200 min costs £55, which is less than double.

errorPatterns.pattern: Illusion of proportionality — 'twice the minutes, twice the bill', treating every relationship as directly proportional and ignoring the fixed £15 charge
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what does Sam pay if he makes NO calls this month?' — the £15 at zero minutes exposes that the line misses the origin, so doubling can't apply to the whole bill. Sort more situations by the zero test.
errorPatterns.distractor: Sam is right — if the minutes double then the bill doubles too
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'Sam is right' and, when asked, says 'because double is double' without ever considering the cost at zero minutes

errorPatterns.pattern: Confusing inverse with direct — thinking 'twice as many minutes' might HALVE something, misreading which quantity grows
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two families explicitly: here more minutes means MORE cost (both rise), so it is not inverse; inverse is when one rises as the other falls. Contrast with a taps-filling-a-bucket case.
errorPatterns.distractor: Sam is wrong — doubling the minutes actually halves part of the bill
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about the bill going down or getting smaller when minutes increase, conflating this with a 'twice as fast, half the time' situation

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive scaling — adds a fixed amount to the bill for the extra minutes rather than reasoning multiplicatively about the per-minute rate
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to a ratio table for the per-minute part only; show the variable part scales multiplicatively while the £15 stays put. Reteach unit-rate scaling on the pens&cost case.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to find the bill for 200 minutes having been told 100 minutes, adds the same £20 gap again instead of recomputing 200×£0.20+£15

responseLevels.gap: Says Sam is right ('double is double') or reasons only additively; does not consider the cost at zero minutes and cannot distinguish proportional from non-proportional situations.
responseLevels.full: States Sam is wrong BECAUSE the £15 fixed charge means the relationship does not pass through the origin, so doubling the minutes does not double the whole bill; confirms with 100→£35, 200→£55, and correctly identifies that removing the fixed charge would make it directly proportional while a bucket-and-taps case is inverse.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises something is off or can compute 100 vs 200 minutes, but explains it as arithmetic ('I just worked it out') without articulating the origin/fixed-charge structure, and cannot reliably sort a new situation into direct / inverse / neither.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A phone plan costs £15 each month plus £0.20 for every minute you call. Sam says: 'If I talk for twice as many minutes, my bill will be twice as big.' Is Sam right? Explain how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who truly grasps direct proportion tests the origin ('what happens at zero minutes?') and sees the fixed charge breaks the doubling rule — they cannot be talked out of it. A child running the illusion of proportionality hears 'twice the minutes' and answers 'twice the bill' automatically; the fixed charge is invisible to them. The two children give different answers AND different reasons, and the fixed-charge structure makes it hard to be right for the wrong reason.

sources.claim: Direct proportion: graph is a straight line through the origin, doubling one quantity doubles the other, and if one quantity is zero the other is zero; children fail to recognise when quantities vary in direct proportion and confuse direct with inverse situations.
sources.source: Shell Centre / Mathematics Assessment Project (MAP) Classroom Challenge, 'Proportion and Non-Proportion Situations' (Grade 7)

sources.claim: A situation such as a phone plan with a fixed monthly charge plus a per-minute rate is linear but NOT proportional (the line does not pass through the origin); students over-apply proportional reasoning ('the numbers dictate the operation').
sources.source: Shell Centre / Mathematics Assessment Project (MAP) Classroom Challenge, proportional-reasoning lessons

sources.claim: Ratio and proportion in the national curriculum: solve problems involving direct and inverse proportion including graphical and algebraic representations.
sources.source: UK National Curriculum, Mathematics programmes of study (KS3)

sources.claim: Distinguishing ratio from proportion and reasoning multiplicatively (unit rate, scaling) rather than additively is the core of proportional reasoning.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 or 100,000, using the same number-line nearness / midpoint reasoning applied to a chosen larger place — e.g. 456,782 to the nearest 10,000 is 460,000. Extends rounding to higher places and to boundary/cascade cases (950,500 to nearest 100,000).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'round any number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.3 'use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place'.
• Operational details — Keep the number-line/midpoint meaning central but scale it to large bounding multiples; identify the rounding place and the single decider digit to its right (ignore the rest). Rehearse the target place selecting the bounding multiples, the halfway convention, and cascade cases where rounding up rolls a 9 over. Link explicitly to estimating large calculations.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): rounds a six-digit number to the nearest 10,000 using a landmarked line. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): rounds to any specified place and explains via the decider digit / nearer multiple. Tier C (age 10, extending): handles cascade/boundary cases (950,500→1,000,000) and uses rounding to estimate sums.
bestPractices: Scale the number-line/midpoint model to large bounding multiples; keep 'nearer multiple' as the meaning.
Identify the rounding place and the SINGLE decider digit to its right; the rest are irrelevant.
Make explicit that the requested place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 10,000 → bound by ten-thousands).
Rehearse the halfway convention and cascade cases (950,500 to nearest 100,000).
Link to estimating large sums/differences and checking reasonableness.
keyRepresentations: Number line with large bounding multiples and midpoint
Place-value chart marking the rounding digit and decider digit
0-1,000,000 line rescaled per target place
Estimation contexts (populations, budgets)
'Rounding hill' midpoint image scaled up
commonMisconceptions: Looking at the wrong decider digit or rounding to the wrong place.
Successive/chained rounding across places instead of one decision.
Truncating (always down) or always up.
Cascade errors (950,500 to nearest 100,000 mishandled).
Losing place value in the unchanged trailing digits (they become zeros).

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 or 100,000. Keep the number-line 'nearer multiple' meaning central but scale it to large bounding multiples: identify the rounding place, read the single decider digit immediately to its right, zero everything after the rounding place, and handle halfway and cascade/boundary cases (e.g. 950,500 → 1,000,000). Link to estimating large sums and checking reasonableness.

activities.title: Scaled rounding bench: drag across the midpoint
feedback: If a learner reads a column other than the one immediately to the right of the rounding place: mark the target place and its single decider digit on a labelled six-digit place-value chart and look only at that digit.

If the rounded answer keeps later digits (e.g. 456,782 → 456,000 or keeps the 782): on the number line point out the answer must be a multiple of the target place, so everything after it becomes zero.
If a learner rounds step-by-step across several places instead of making one decision: return to the single decider digit for the chosen place only.
Reinforce correct work by having them say 'nearer to ___ than to ___, so it rounds to ___.'
activities.rationale: A draggable marker between large bounding multiples with a visible midpoint makes the nearness decision concrete and lets the decider-digit rule be derived rather than memorised; dragging across the midpoint and watching the result flip, plus watching trailing digits collapse to zero, ties the procedure to meaning. A place selector that rescales the line shows how the requested place chooses the bounds.
sourceClaims: Large-number rounding uses the same number-line/midpoint meaning scaled up; cascade cases and single-decider-digit reasoning are key.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
Year 5 pupils should 'round any number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000'.
learnerActions: Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000: place it on a number line between the bounding multiples 450,000 and 460,000, with the midpoint 455,000 flagged.
Decide which multiple it is nearer and state the rounded value (460,000); check it against the midpoint.
Change the target place to nearest 100,000 so the line rescales to the bounding multiples 400,000 and 500,000 (midpoint 450,000), and round 456,782 again (it is past the midpoint, so 500,000).
After each decision, write out the rounded number and confirm every digit after the rounding place is now zero.
Explain which single digit you used to decide (the one immediately to the right of the rounding place) and why the rest are irrelevant.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding a large number is the same nearness decision scaled up: the requested place chooses the two bounding multiples and the midpoint, the one decider digit settles the decision, and all trailing digits become zeros.

activities.title: Cascade and boundary cases
feedback: If the boundary case is not carried (950,500 → 900,000): walk only the single carry rather than reteaching the whole rule — 9 hundred-thousands rounding up becomes 1,000,000. Rehearse near the boundary on a number line.
If a learner is unsure at the exact midpoint: state and apply the agreed halfway convention (conventionally round up) and name it aloud.
activities.rationale: Cascade cases are the common failure point and need targeted rehearsal at the boundary; animating or tracing the roll from 9 to the next place makes the carry visible.
sourceClaims: Large-number rounding uses the same number-line/midpoint meaning scaled up; cascade cases and single-decider-digit reasoning are key.
learnerActions: Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000, placing it between 900,000 and 1,000,000 with the midpoint 950,000 flagged.
Decide whether it rounds up (it is just past the midpoint) and work the carry explicitly: 9 hundred-thousands rounding up = 10 hundred-thousands = 1,000,000.
Try a case that sits exactly on a midpoint (e.g. 950,000 to the nearest 100,000), state the convention you are using (round half up), and give the result (1,000,000).
Explain in your own words what happens when rounding up rolls a 9 over into the next place.
activities.intendedInsight: When rounding up at a 9, the carry rolls into the next higher place; the rounded value can gain a digit (950,500 → 1,000,000), and this is still a single rounding decision, not chained rounding.

activities.title: Round to estimate a large sum
feedback: If a learner computes the exact sum instead of estimating: ask them to round each number first, then add the rounded values.
If estimates are far off: discuss whether the chosen place was appropriate for the numbers involved.
Confirm a correct estimate such as 400,000 + 200,000 = 600,000 and relate it back to the rounding decisions made.
activities.rationale: Linking rounding to estimation of large, meaningful quantities gives the procedure a purpose and reinforces place-value reasoning; this is an explicit curriculum aim in the original pedagogy, though no source claim speaks directly to estimation.
learnerActions: Estimate 387,412 + 214,560 by rounding each addend to a sensible place before adding — for example, treat the numbers as two town populations you want a quick combined total for.
Round each number (e.g. to the nearest 100,000: 400,000 and 200,000) and add to get about 600,000.
State why the estimate is reasonable and how it could be used to check a full calculation (e.g. a budget total or population count).
Try estimating to a different place and discuss how the choice of place affects how close the estimate is.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding supports quick, sensible estimates of large real quantities (populations, budgets) and a reasonableness check on exact answers; the chosen rounding place trades precision for simplicity.

activities.title: Consolidation: round to any specified place
feedback: If a rounded value is not a multiple of the target place, it is wrong — re-check that trailing digits are zeroed.

If a learner always rounds down (truncates) or always rounds up regardless of the digits: compare the number to the midpoint and read the decider digit — rounding up and rounding down each happen depending on that digit, not by habit.
For cascade traps, confirm the carry rolled into the next place correctly.
Use the decider-digit explanation as the mark of secure understanding rather than a correct answer alone.
activities.rationale: Practice with varied place targets, halfway and cascade cases consolidates the rule and surfaces the common misconceptions for feedback. This activity emphasises applied practice; items that only require selecting an answer check recognition and should be paired with learners stating their reasoning to elicit the procedure.
sourceClaims: Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
learnerActions: Given a six-digit number and a target place, state the two bounding multiples, the midpoint, the decider digit, and the rounded value.
Work a mixed set that includes a cascade trap (e.g. 950,500) and a halfway case.
Match several numbers to their rounded values for a stated place, and spot any that are not clean multiples of the target place.
Choose the place, then round — justify the bounding multiples the place implies.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding to any place up to 100,000 becomes fluent and self-checked: the answer is always a clean multiple of the target place.

constraints: Keep 'nearer multiple' as the meaning; the requested place chooses the two bounding multiples (nearest 10,000 → bound by ten-thousands).
Use only the single decider digit immediately to the right of the rounding place; the remaining digits are irrelevant to the decision and become zeros.
Make one rounding decision per task; do not round step-by-step across successive places (chained rounding is an error).
State and apply a halfway convention explicitly (conventionally round up) and name it when at an exact midpoint.
Rounding direction depends on the decider digit relative to the midpoint; do not always round down (truncate) or always round up.

A static scaled 'rounding hill' or poster is a useful reference but does not itself require the learner to act on the decision; pair it with a task where the learner makes and justifies the rounding decision.
Selected-response items (multiple choice, matching) check recognition; to elicit the procedure, also require the learner to construct or explain the rounding decision.

Number-line nearness is a one-dimensional model, so a flat line with bounding multiples and a midpoint is sufficient and no 3D representation is needed for this objective; this is a scoped sufficiency note, not a claim that other media cannot teach it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked values: 456,782 → 460,000 (nearest 10,000; decider digit 6 → up; bounds 450,000/460,000, mid 455,000) and → 500,000 (nearest 100,000; decider digit 5 → up; bounds 400,000/500,000, mid 450,000); 950,500 → 1,000,000 (nearest 100,000; decider digit 5 → up, carry rolls 9→10 hundred-thousands); estimate 387,412 + 214,560 ≈ 400,000 + 200,000 = 600,000. All consistent.

The original recommendation's '400,000–500,000' for nearest 100,000 are the correct bounding multiples for 456,782, and the rounded value is 500,000 (decider digit 5). There is no original error here.

The original fit judgements ('open dialogue adds little'; conversation/3D as poor fit) are catalog verdicts, not established pedagogy; retained only as narrowly scoped affordance notes (planar model suffices here; selected-response checks recognition), not as universal superiority claims.
Halfway convention (round-half-up) is a stated convention; alternative conventions exist and the choice should be made explicit to learners.
CCSS 4.NBT.3 and the NCETM source are marked verified:false in the row; claims are retained as cited without fresh verification.

probeDeeper: Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000 — what happens when rounding up passes 900,000?
Is 456,782 nearer 450,000 or 460,000? Show it on a number line.
How did rounding each number help you estimate 387,412 + 214,560 quickly?
assess.correctAnswer: 460,000; 1,000,000; and about 400,000 + 200,000 = 600,000 — deciding by the digit one place to the right of the rounding place, zeroing everything after it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong column to decide — not the digit immediately to the right of the target place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the target place and its 'decider' (one to the right); look only at that. Reground with a labelled place-value chart for six-digit numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounding to the nearest 10,000, the child inspects the units or the ten-thousands digit itself rather than the thousands digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails the carry when rounding up rolls into a higher place: 950,500 → 900,000 instead of 1,000,000
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole rule — walk the single carry: 9 hundred-thousands rounding up = 10 hundred-thousands = 1,000,000. Rehearse near the boundary on a number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The boundary case is not carried up to the next place.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the target digit but leaves later digits unchanged (456,782 → 456,000 or keeps the 782)
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a number line show the answer must be a multiple of 10,000, so everything after the ten-thousands becomes zero.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounded value is not a clean multiple of the target place.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the wrong decider column or leaves trailing digits; rounded value isn't a clean multiple.
responseLevels.full: Rounds to any place up to 100,000 accurately including boundary carries, zeroes trailing digits, and rounds sensibly to estimate sums.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds clear cases but mishandles the carry into a new place or which column to read for higher places.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000. Now round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000. Then estimate 387,412 + 214,560 by rounding first.' Watch which column they use to decide and what happens at the boundary.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 456,782 checks the child finds the correct decider column among many digits and zeros the rest; 950,500 forces a carry that rolls up into a new place (900,000 → 1,000,000); the estimate checks they round each addend to a sensible place before adding. Watching the columns used exposes the mechanism.

sources.claim: Year 5 pupils should 'round any number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000'.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 5 Number & place value)

sources.claim: Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Number & Operations in Base Ten, Grade 4

sources.claim: Large-number rounding uses the same number-line/midpoint meaning scaled up; cascade cases and single-decider-digit reasoning are key.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Fair testing — using results to predict and re-test

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils are taught to use "test results to make predictions to set up further comparative and fair tests" (verbatim), alongside "reporting and presenting findings from enquiries, including conclusions, causal relationships and explanations". This is the point where an enquiry stops being a one-off and becomes an iterative line of enquiry.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 + SEP 4, grades 3–5):** SEP 3 at 3–5 covers planning fair tests with controlled variables; SEP 4 (Analyzing & Interpreting Data) at 3–5 adds "use data to evaluate and refine design solutions" and comparing/contrasting data to make sense of a phenomenon. Using results to generate a testable prediction and a follow-up investigation bridges these two practices.

- **Operational details:** Builds on drawing conclusions and making predictions (prerequisite mt_7VrR1GzhrN) and independently planning enquiries with variable control (prerequisite mt_ArVBEpMAPk); soft-linked to the reasoning habit of describing a pattern as a rule and testing it in new cases (mt_hbe_kdE_7C). The distinctive skill is EXTRAPOLATION-AND-TEST: reading the trend in one set of results, using it to make a specific prediction for a NEW value or condition ('if thinner wire conducted better, an even thinner one should conduct better still'), then designing a fresh fair test to check that prediction. The reasoning link (why the results imply the prediction) must be made explicit. Feeds forward to presenting findings with causal explanations (dependent mt_nyPMkeHlVJ).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). A learner who can read a trend in results, turn it into a specific testable prediction for a new value, design a follow-up fair test to check it, and articulate the reasoning connecting the original data to the new prediction has met the bar.
bestPractices: Teach prediction as reading the trend, not guessing: pupils point to the pattern in the existing results ('as X increased, Y increased') and extend it to a new, unmeasured value — the prediction is evidence-based, not a hunch.
Distinguish interpolation (a value between tested points) from extrapolation (beyond them) and flag that extrapolated predictions are less certain and precisely why they must be TESTED, not assumed.
Make the reasoning link explicit and spoken/written: 'I predict… BECAUSE the results showed…' — the justification is the assessed skill, not just the prediction itself.
Design the follow-up as a genuine fair test in its own right (one variable changed, the rest controlled, repeat readings) so the new question is answered validly.
Model science as an iterative cycle — results raise the next question — rather than a single linear experiment that 'finishes' at a conclusion.
keyRepresentations: A results table/graph with the trend arrow extended to a predicted new value (interpolation vs extrapolation marked)
The sentence frame 'I predict ___ because the results showed ___'
An enquiry cycle: question → fair test → results → prediction → new fair test
A line graph where pupils extend the line of best fit to read off a prediction
A prediction-then-test comparison card (predicted value vs measured value)
commonMisconceptions: Making a prediction as a random guess rather than reading it off the existing trend in the data.
Treating an extrapolated prediction as a proven fact instead of a claim that still needs its own fair test.
Assuming a pattern continues indefinitely beyond the tested range (e.g. that a trend never levels off or reverses) without checking.
Skipping the reasoning link — stating a prediction without connecting it to the specific results that motivate it.
Believing an experiment 'ends' at its conclusion, rather than that good results generate the next testable question.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, teach the extrapolation-and-test cycle in fair testing: read the trend in an existing set of results, use it to make a specific, testable prediction for a NEW untested value or condition, design a fresh fair test to check that prediction, and explicitly state the reasoning that connects the original data to the prediction. The distinctive skill is turning a one-off experiment into an iterative line of enquiry, while learning that an extrapolated prediction is a claim to be tested, not a proven fact.

activities.title: Predict a new point, then run the test to check it
feedback: If the learner predicts a value already tested, ask 'which value haven't we tried yet? what would you expect there?' to push past the collected points.
If the learner skips the justification, prompt them to complete 'I predict ___ because the results showed ___' before the test runs.
If the prediction is vague ('it'll just go further'), scaffold a specific value or range and a clear fair follow-up set-up.
When a surprising case makes the trend level off, highlight that this is exactly why extrapolated predictions must be tested, not assumed.
If the learner treats the matched prediction as proof the pattern holds forever, discuss that a few points can't guarantee the trend never levels off or reverses.
activities.rationale: The target skill is a cycle — read a trend, commit to a prediction for a new value, then actually test it and compare predicted-vs-measured. An interactive investigation where the learner extends a trend, records reasoning, and then runs a new test can make both the power and the limits of extrapolation concrete. A reasoning field required before the test runs keeps the justification explicit. This proposes an interactive medium as a good fit for showing the predicted-vs-measured moment; a static reference graph can still support the reasoning but cannot show the live follow-up test. Efficacy of the specific mechanism is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to use test results to make predictions to set up further comparative and fair tests.

NGSS SEP 3 (fair tests, controlled variables) and SEP 4 (analyzing and interpreting data to make sense of phenomena and refine solutions) at grades 3-5 together underpin using results to predict and re-test.
learnerActions: Study a graph of results from a completed fair test (e.g. sugar dissolving faster in warmer water, or distance a car rolls from three ramp heights).
Point to the trend in the data in words ('as temperature increased, dissolving got faster') before predicting anything.
Extend the trend line to a temperature/height you never tested and lock in a specific predicted value for that new condition.
Type or say the reasoning: 'I predict ___ BECAUSE the results showed ___' — before any test is run.
Run a fresh fair test at that new value, keeping everything else the same and taking repeat readings, and place the measured point on the graph next to your prediction.
Compare predicted vs measured: discuss when the point lands on your extended line, and what it means when a case makes the trend level off or change instead.
activities.intendedInsight: Good data lets you make an evidence-based prediction for conditions you have not yet tested, but an extrapolated prediction is a claim that must be checked with its own fair test — the pattern may not continue indefinitely, so science is a loop where each result raises the next question.

activities.title: Interpolation vs extrapolation: where is the prediction, and how sure are we?
feedback: If the learner can't distinguish the two, show that interpolation sits inside the measured range while extrapolation reaches past it into untested territory.
If the learner rates an extrapolated prediction as certain, ask what could make the trend level off or reverse past the last tested point.
If a prediction is chosen that merely restates existing data, point out it does not reach beyond the evidence already gathered.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing interpolation from extrapolation and matching predictions to their justifications sharpens the reasoning link and the sense of uncertainty. Selection and sequencing tasks can check whether the learner can identify a well-justified prediction and order the enquiry cycle, but they do not elicit the learner constructing and running their own follow-up test, so they work best as support alongside a hands-on investigation.
learnerActions: On a results graph, mark predictions that fall BETWEEN tested points (interpolation) and predictions that fall BEYOND the tested range (extrapolation).
For each prediction, state whether it is interpolation or extrapolation and rate how certain you can be, explaining why extrapolated predictions carry more uncertainty.
Choose which of several written predictions is best justified by the given data, and explain what makes the others weaker (guess, restated data, or unsupported leap).
Sequence the enquiry cards into the cycle: question → fair test → results → prediction → new fair test.
Say why an extrapolated prediction in particular must be tested rather than assumed.
activities.intendedInsight: Predictions between tested points are generally more secure than predictions beyond the tested range; naming which kind a prediction is tells you how much it needs checking, and an extrapolated prediction especially must be tested because the pattern might not continue.

activities.title: Justify and defend your prediction in dialogue
feedback: If the learner only restates the result, ask them to name an untried value and what they expect there.
If the follow-up design isn't clearly fair, ask what must be kept the same and what will be changed.
If the learner treats the pattern as already proven, discuss that a pattern from a few points might not continue and a further test guards against over-generalising.
activities.rationale: An in-role dialogue can push the learner to justify a prediction from evidence and defend a follow-up design, exercising the explicit reasoning link that is the core assessed skill. This spoken/written justification complements, rather than replaces, actually running the follow-up test to check the prediction, which may or may not support it.
learnerActions: Answer a mentor's question: 'What does this data make you predict for a value you haven't tried — and why that value?'
Explain how your prediction follows FROM the observed pattern, not from a hunch.
Describe how you would set up the follow-up test so it is fair and actually checks your prediction (one variable changed, the rest controlled, repeat readings).
Respond to the challenge: 'What if the trend stops or levels off past a certain point — how would your test reveal that?'
Explain how making an evidence-based prediction differs from simply repeating what you already found.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and defending the evidence-to-prediction reasoning out loud is the core assessed skill; a prediction without its justification and a fair plan to check it is incomplete.

constraints: Builds on prerequisites: drawing conclusions and making predictions, and independently planning enquiries with variable control (one variable changed, the rest controlled, repeat readings).

The prediction must reach a NEW, untested value or condition (interpolation between points or extrapolation beyond the range), not restate a value already measured; the core target skill is extrapolating beyond the tested range and then testing.
The reasoning link must be made explicit in speech or writing ('I predict ___ because the results showed ___'); the justification is the assessed skill, not just the prediction.
The follow-up must be a genuine fair test in its own right, designed to check the specific prediction.

Selection, matching and sequencing tasks can check whether a learner can identify a well-justified prediction and order the enquiry cycle, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the learner independently constructing a prediction and running their own follow-up test; use them as support, not as the whole objective.
A reference graph can support the reasoning, but on its own it cannot show the learner's own follow-up test or the predicted-vs-measured comparison.
Keep examples honest to real science: an extrapolated pattern may level off or reverse, so do not present the trend as guaranteed to continue indefinitely.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted that a static image 'cannot teach' the skill and that '3D adds nothing'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited standards; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. A fixed graph can still support the reasoning even though it cannot be manipulated or run a live test.

The claim that the interactive loop 'can't be conveyed statically' is a design preference, not an established comparative-efficacy finding from the sources; treat it as a rationale for medium choice, not proof.

The two cited sources support that the standards require using results to predict and set up further fair tests; they do NOT establish that any particular activity format or medium was tested or is most effective.

Independent re-audit: the previously flagged 'optional/required' contradiction in activity 1's reasoning field is resolved — the field is consistently described as required before the test runs. No further learner-facing contradictions or unsupported categorical modality claims were found.

probeDeeper: What exactly would you predict for a height you haven't tried — and why that?
How would you set up the new test so it's fair and actually checks your prediction?
What if the car stopped going further past a certain height — how would your test reveal that? Does the pattern have to continue forever?
How is making a prediction different from just repeating what you already found?
assess.correctAnswer: A strong response uses the pattern in the results to make a specific, testable prediction for a NEW, untried value ('an even higher ramp will roll even further, maybe about X'), and designs a fair follow-up test to check it (new height, everything else kept the same). It explains that the prediction comes FROM the observed pattern, and that a further test is needed because the pattern might not continue (it could level off) — treating the prediction as something to test, not something already proven.

errorPatterns.pattern: Restates existing data instead of extrapolating: predicts one of the heights already tested, or just repeats 'higher rolls further' with no new value.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'which height haven't we tried yet? what would you expect there?' to push the prediction past the collected points.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The prediction doesn't reach beyond the data already gathered.

errorPatterns.pattern: Pattern treated as proven: 'we already know it, so there's nothing left to check' — sees no need for a follow-up test.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss that a pattern from a few points might not continue; a further test guards against over-generalising.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses the further test as unnecessary because the rule feels certain.

errorPatterns.pattern: Prediction not testable: offers a vague 'it'll go further' with no value and no follow-up design.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold specificity (a value or range) and a fair follow-up set-up that would confirm or refute it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The prediction lacks a specific value/range or any plan for how to check it.

responseLevels.gap: Restates a result already collected, or offers a vague 'it'll go further' with no new value and no follow-up test.
responseLevels.full: Extends the observed pattern into a specific, testable prediction for an untried value, designs a fair follow-up test to check it, and explains that the prediction follows from the pattern yet still needs testing because the pattern might not hold — connecting evidence, inference, and next enquiry.
responseLevels.partial: Makes a prediction for a new value and knows a further test is needed, but the prediction is loosely linked to the pattern, or the follow-up test isn't clearly fair or aimed at checking it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You tested how far a car rolls from three ramp heights and found: the higher the ramp, the further the car rolls. A friend asks, 'So what should we try next?' Using your results, what would you predict for a ramp height you haven't tried yet — and what new test would you set up to check whether your idea holds? Talk me through your thinking.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the idea generates a prediction that goes BEYOND the data (a new, untried value) and sees the need to test it. A child who doesn't merely restates a result already collected, or treats the pattern as proven and sees no reason for a further test. The tell is whether the prediction extends past the evidence and is framed as checkable.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Objects vs Materials

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 'Everyday materials'):** Pupils should be taught to "distinguish between an object and the material from which it is made." The non-statutory guidance frames Year 1 as a time to "explore, name, discuss and raise and answer questions about everyday materials so that they become familiar with the names of materials and properties such as: hard/soft; stretchy/stiff; shiny/dull; rough/smooth; bendy/not bendy; waterproof/not waterproof; absorbent/not absorbent; opaque/transparent."

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-1, partial anchor):** There is no NGSS performance expectation dedicated to the object/material distinction; it is a UK-led foundation. The nearest DCI is PS1.A: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]," which underpins 2-PS1-1 ("[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]").

- **Operational details:** Teach through hands-on sorting of real classroom objects: name each object (chair, cup, spoon, window) and then ask the separate question "what is it MADE OF?" Make the two questions visibly distinct so children stop treating the object's name and its material as the same word. Use the canonical Oak National demonstration of three identical water bottles — one plastic, one glass, one metal — to show one object made from different materials, and a spoon that could be metal, wood or plastic to show the same. Extend to objects made from more than one material (a pencil = wood + graphite + metal + rubber). Keep talk grounded in touch-and-look evidence, not definitions.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). Given a real object, the child can name it AND separately name the material it is made from, and can give an example of one object (e.g. a cup) made from two different materials — showing the object and its material are held apart in thought.
bestPractices: Ask the two questions separately and explicitly — "What is this?" (object) then "What is it made of?" (material) — so children learn the words 'object' and 'material' name different things; the everyday sense of 'material' as only cloth/fabric is a known blocker to overcome.
Use plentiful real objects to handle and sort, not pictures alone; concrete exploration is the KS1 norm and lets children reason from touch and sight.
Show the same object in different materials side by side (three water bottles: plastic, glass, metal) so children abstract that the object stays the same while the material changes.
Present objects made from more than one material (a pencil, a shoe, a window frame) to break the 'one object = one material' rule.
Use comparison of two same-material examples of different shape/size (per Hardy et al. 2020) to help children attend to material kind rather than to size, weight or shape.
Elicit ideas first with questioning or Concept Cartoons before correcting, treating a misconception as 'a concept in embryo' rather than simply wrong.
keyRepresentations: Real everyday objects to handle: chair, cup, spoon, window, pencil, shoe
The 'same object, different material' trio — three identical water bottles in plastic, glass and metal
Sorting mats / frequency tables that pair each object with its material
A two-column 'object | material' talk frame that keeps the two ideas visibly separate
One-object-many-materials exemplars (a pencil labelled wood + graphite + metal + rubber)
commonMisconceptions: Children conflate the object with the material, treating 'rock' or 'chair' as if the name of the thing and the name of the stuff are one and the same (an explicit KS1 statutory hurdle).
'Material' means only fabric/cloth — so children think building materials, glass or water are not 'materials'.
An object can only be made from one material (a pencil is 'wood', ignoring the graphite, metal ferrule and rubber).
A given object is always made from the same material — e.g. 'all spoons are metal', 'all cups are the same'.
When reasoning about objects, children fixate on salient surface features (size, weight, shape) rather than material kind, even though they can usually name the material (Hardy et al. 2020).

learn.summary: For 5–6 year olds, teach the object/material distinction (UK KS1 Y1 'Everyday materials') through hands-on naming and sorting of real objects: name the thing, then separately ask 'what is it MADE OF?'. The core insight is that the same kind of object can be made from different materials (three bottles of the same kind, one plastic, one glass, one metal), and that one object can be made from several materials (a typical pencil with an eraser = wood + graphite core + metal + rubber). Keep talk grounded in touch-and-look evidence, not definitions, and overcome the everyday blocker that 'material' means only cloth.

activities.title: Two questions: 'What is it?' then 'What is it made of?'
feedback: If a child answers 'What is this?' with a material ('it's the metal one' / 'it's wood'), hold up two different objects made of the same material (a wooden spoon and a wooden block): 'same stuff, different things' — then name object and material separately for each.

If a child says the metal spoon 'isn't made of a material' or that 'material' means cloth, broaden the word explicitly: 'material means whatever something is made of — wood, metal, glass, plastic and cloth are all materials', then re-sort the tray naming each material.
Praise answers that keep the two words apart: 'Yes — the OBJECT is a spoon, and the MATERIAL is metal.'
activities.rationale: KS1 statutory requirement is to distinguish an object from the material it is made from, and the non-statutory guidance frames Year 1 as a time to explore, name and discuss real everyday materials. Asking the two questions separately targets the known blocker that children treat the thing's name and its stuff as one word, and that 'material' is taken to mean only fabric.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y1 statutory requirement: pupils taught to 'distinguish between an object and the material from which it is made'; non-statutory property vocabulary list (hard/soft, shiny/dull, etc.).
Documented KS1 misconceptions: children confuse object with material; 'material' taken to mean only fabric; objects thought to be one material only or always the same material.
learnerActions: Handle real classroom objects (cup, spoon, pencil, shoe on a tray; touch and look at a chair and a window frame where they are).
For each object, first answer out loud 'What is this?' (name the object), then answer the separate question 'What is it made of?' (name the material).
Use a two-column 'object | material' talk frame or sorting mat so the two answers are placed in visibly different spots.

Sort the objects into material bins (wood, plastic, metal, glass, fabric, rubber/other), saying the object name and material name for each as you place it; an object made of more than one material (e.g. a pencil or a shoe) can go in more than one bin, or be talked through part by part.
activities.intendedInsight: The name of a thing and the name of the stuff it is made from are two different words answering two different questions; 'material' means whatever something is made of — wood, metal, glass, plastic and cloth are all materials.

activities.title: Same object, different material
feedback: If a child insists a spoon 'is always metal' or that an object can only be one material, let them handle real examples of the same object in several materials (plastic/glass/metal cup; wooden/plastic/metal spoon) and re-state object vs material for each.
When a child offers their own example of an object made from a different material, confirm the move: 'Right — it's still a cup, but the material has changed.'
activities.rationale: Side-by-side comparison of the same object in different materials helps children abstract that object identity holds while material varies, breaking the 'a given object is always made from the same material' misconception. This is the canonical Oak National three-bottle demonstration.
sourceClaims: Documented KS1 misconceptions: children confuse object with material; 'material' taken to mean only fabric; objects thought to be one material only or always the same material.
learnerActions: Examine three bottles that look like the same object but are made of different materials — one plastic, one glass, one metal — handling and looking at each.
Answer the pair of questions: 'Are these the same object?' (yes, all bottles) and 'Are they the same material?' (no — plastic, glass, metal).
Do the same with a spoon that could be metal, wood or plastic.
Suggest a fresh example of one object that could be made from more than one material (e.g. a cup, a chair).
activities.intendedInsight: The same object can be made from different materials — the object stays the same while the stuff changes.

activities.title: One object, many materials
feedback: If a child names only the most obvious material (a pencil is 'wood'), prompt: 'Look again — what is the pointy bit made of? What is the pink end made of?' until all the materials are found.
Confirm the rule-break: 'A pencil isn't just wood — it's wood AND graphite AND metal AND rubber.'
activities.rationale: Presenting objects made from more than one material breaks the 'an object can only be made from one material' misconception, which the source lists as a documented KS1 hurdle.
sourceClaims: Documented KS1 misconceptions: children confuse object with material; 'material' taken to mean only fabric; objects thought to be one material only or always the same material.
learnerActions: Look closely at a pencil and find each separate part: the wooden body, the graphite core, the metal ferrule, the rubber eraser.
Name the material of each part, discovering this pencil is made from several materials (four here: wood, graphite, metal, rubber), not one.
Try the same with a shoe or a window frame, listing every material you can find in it.
If using a sorting activity, place a multi-material object (the pencil) into more than one material bin — 'this one needs more than one bin!'
activities.intendedInsight: One object can be made from more than one material, so you cannot assume 'one object = one material'.

activities.title: Attend to material, not size or shape
feedback: If a child groups objects by size or shape instead of material, draw attention back: 'These two are different sizes — but what are they both MADE of?'
Reinforce when the child names the shared material across different shapes/sizes.
activities.rationale: Hardy et al. (2020) found that comparing two same-material standards helps young children induce 'material kind' and reduces reliance on size, shape and weight; children can often name a material yet still reason from surface features. Note the study's context was a float/sink task with preschoolers, not this exact classroom activity.
sourceClaims: Comparing two same-material standards helps preschoolers induce 'material kind' for float/sink and reduces reliance on size/shape/weight; children can name materials yet still reason from surface features; adding labels gave no benefit beyond the two-object comparison.
learnerActions: Compare two objects made of the same material but different in shape or size (e.g. a wooden spoon and a wooden block, or a small and a large wooden item).
Say what is the SAME about them (the material) even though they look different.
Then compare two objects of the same shape but different material, and say what is DIFFERENT (the material).
activities.intendedInsight: What something is made of is a different question from how big, heavy or what shape it is; the material kind can stay the same even when size and shape change.

activities.title: Check-up: point, name, and transfer
feedback: Full grasp looks like: reliably naming object and material separately AND offering a fresh unprompted example that the same object can be built from different materials.
Partial grasp looks like: naming object and material for a single item when prompted, but not yet seeing that the SAME object can be made from different materials — treating each item in isolation.

Gap looks like: using one word for both ('it's wood'), giving a material when asked for the object, or insisting an object is always one fixed material. Reteach with the same-material/different-object pair, then same-object/different-material examples.
activities.rationale: The two-spoons stimulus keeps the kind of object the same while the material differs (real spoons may also differ in colour, size or shape), so it focuses attention on the object/material distinction; a child who conflated them answers 'which is the object?' with a material word or insists a spoon must be one material. These are assessment prompts from the source, used here during teaching as a self-check, not only as a scored test.
learnerActions: Point to any object in the room and say both the object name AND the material it is made from.
Given a wooden spoon and a metal spoon, point to the OBJECT, then say what MATERIAL each is made from, then answer 'Could I make this same spoon out of something else?'

Compare a teddy and a wooden train: say whether they are the same OBJECT (no — a teddy and a train) and whether they are the same MATERIAL (no — one is fabric, one is wood), keeping the two questions apart.

Answer a probing question such as: 'If I melted this plastic cup into a blob, is it still a cup? Is it still plastic?' (the object can stop existing while the material stays) — use this as a talking point, not a strict right/wrong test.
Discuss: 'Could a spoon be made of glass? Why might we not choose glass for a spoon?'
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who holds the distinction separates the thing (and its job) from the stuff it is made of, and can transfer the idea to fresh examples and to cases where the object changes but the material persists.

constraints: Keep all talk grounded in touch-and-look evidence from real objects, not definitions; concrete handling and sorting is the KS1 norm at this age.
Pre-readers need heavy audio/spoken scaffolding; avoid reading-dependent tasks.
Elicit children's ideas first (questioning or Concept Cartoons) before correcting, treating a misconception as 'a concept in embryo' rather than simply wrong.

A picture-only or tap-to-reveal screen scene is a useful scaffold for the two-question move and the same-object/different-material contrast — for example a material-swap/re-skin surface where a bottle stays the same bottle while its skin changes (turning see-through for glass or shiny for metal) — but it is not a substitute for handling and sorting real objects; recognition/matching responses do not by themselves elicit the independent naming and fresh-example production that signals full grasp.
A linear scored matching/sorting quiz can assess the distinction but does not by itself build it; use such formats as a check-up alongside hands-on exploration.

There is no NGSS performance expectation dedicated to the object/material distinction; it is a UK-led foundation. The nearest DCI is PS1.A ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]'), underpinning 2-PS1-1.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the cited sources were marked verified:false in the original row (NGSS 2-PS1-1 and the Oak National / STEM Learning misconceptions list); treat claims drawn from them as unconfirmed.

The Hardy et al. (2020) finding comes from a float/sink task with preschoolers and concerns inducing 'material kind'; it supports attending to material over surface features but does not directly establish efficacy for this specific KS1 object/material naming activity. Note also the source's point that adding labels gave no benefit beyond the two-object comparison.

Original row framed an interactive tap-to-reveal image as the primary 'teacher' and rated conversation and 3D as 'poor'; these are catalog-format preferences, not established pedagogical laws. This rewrite preserves the hands-on priority but does not assert that any single medium uniquely teaches or that 3D 'adds nothing'.

The 'melt the plastic cup into a blob' probe assumes the melted plastic remains the same material; for a thermoplastic this is roughly true, but it glosses over whether a child cleanly distinguishes 'is it still a cup?' from 'is it still plastic?' — use it conversationally, not as a strict right/wrong test.

The check-up activity's sourceClaims was set to [] because the original DfE claim supports the distinction as an objective but does not directly support the assessment-discrimination (two-spoons stimulus) rationale of that activity; no original claim directly backs that design point.

probeDeeper: If I melted this plastic cup down into a blob, is it still a cup? Is it still plastic? (object can stop existing while the material stays)
Point to anything in the room and tell me both the object AND the material it's made of.
Here's a teddy and a wooden train — are they the same OBJECT? Are they the same MATERIAL?
Could a spoon ever be made of glass? Why might we not choose glass for a spoon?
assess.correctAnswer: The OBJECT is the spoon (the thing, what it's for); the MATERIALS are wood and metal (the stuff each is made of). Yes — the same object (a spoon, a cup, a chair) can be made from different materials.

errorPatterns.pattern: Object and material are the same thing — the child answers 'what is the object?' with the stuff it's made of ('it's the metal one', 'it's wood') and has no separate word for the thing versus the stuff.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront directly: hold up two DIFFERENT objects made of the SAME material (wooden spoon + wooden block) — 'same stuff, different things' — then two same objects of different material, naming object then material each time.
errorPatterns.distractor: This one isn't a spoon, it's just metal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to point to the OBJECT, names a material instead; uses one word to cover both.

errorPatterns.pattern: An object can only ever be one material — 'a spoon is metal, that's what a spoon is'; denies you could make the same object from something else.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show real examples of one object in several materials (plastic/glass/metal cup; wooden/plastic/metal spoon); let the child handle them and re-state object vs material for each.
errorPatterns.distractor: You can't make that spoon out of anything else — a spoon is always metal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the idea that the same spoon/chair/cup could be made from a different material.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Material' means only cloth or fabric — the child reserves the word for soft textile-type stuff and won't call wood, metal or glass a 'material'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Broaden the word explicitly: 'material means whatever something is made of — wood, metal, glass, plastic and cloth are all materials'; sort a tray naming the material of each.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked the material of the metal spoon, says it isn't made of a material / 'material' is what clothes are made of.

responseLevels.gap: Uses a single word for both the thing and the stuff ('it's wood'); when asked for the object, gives a material; insists an object is always one fixed material.
responseLevels.full: Reliably distinguishes the object (what it is / its job) from the material (what it's made of), AND transfers the idea: states the same object can be built from different materials and offers a fresh example unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Names the object and the material separately for a single item when prompted, but does not yet grasp that the SAME object can be made from different materials — treats each item in isolation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a wooden spoon and a metal spoon on the table. Say: 'Both of these are spoons. Point to the OBJECT — then tell me what MATERIAL each one is made from. And could I make this same spoon out of something else?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two-spoons stimulus is identical in object but differs only in material, so it isolates the object/material distinction. A child who has conflated the two answers the 'which is the object' question with a material word ('it's wood') or insists a spoon must be one particular material; a child who holds the distinction separates the thing-and-its-purpose from the stuff and readily agrees the same object could be made from something else.
