pedagogy.summary: Children measure in standard units and then calculate with the measures — adding and subtracting lengths (m/cm/mm), masses (kg/g) and volumes (l/ml). The governing rule is that you can only add or subtract measures that are in the SAME unit, and the answer keeps that unit. At Year 3 the arithmetic is done within a single unit (250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml); systematic conversion between units (mm–cm–m) comes later, so mixed-unit sums are not yet expected.
bestPractices: Establish 'same unit before you calculate' — line up like units, add, and carry the unit into the answer.
Model length calculations on a number line / tape so adding lengths is combining distances and subtracting is finding a gap.
Always write the unit in the answer; treat a bare number as incomplete.
Keep arithmetic within one unit at this stage; delay formal mm–cm–m conversion (it belongs to a later unit-conversion topic).
Use real measuring-then-calculating tasks (ribbon needed, juice combined) so the operation has a purpose.
keyRepresentations: A number line / tape diagram for combining and comparing lengths
Aligned columns of like units (all in ml, or all in cm) before adding
A measuring bench: measure two quantities, then combine them
An answer frame that always includes the unit (____ ml, ____ cm)
commonMisconceptions: Adds or subtracts across different units as if they were the same number (2 m + 30 cm = 32).
Drops the unit from the answer (250 ml + 400 ml = 650).
Muddles compound units, e.g. reads 3 cm 5 mm as 35 or adds 3 + 5 — not yet knowing 10 mm = 1 cm.
Applies the wrong operation — adds when the problem asks for a difference, or vice versa.

learn.summary: Year 3 children calculate with standard-unit measures: adding and subtracting lengths (m/cm/mm), masses (kg/g) and volumes/capacities (l/ml). The governing rule is 'same unit before you calculate': you only add or subtract measures expressed in the same unit, and the answer keeps that unit (250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml). Arithmetic stays within a single unit at this stage; systematic mm–cm–m conversion comes later, so mixed-unit sums are not yet expected. A number line / tape model makes combining (stacking) versus differencing (finding the gap) concrete, and every answer must carry its unit.

activities.title: Measure-and-combine bench with a number line
feedback: If the learner writes a bare number (e.g. 650), ask: 'What unit belongs on this answer, and why does it matter?' Treat a measurement answer without a unit as incomplete.

If the learner adds across units (2 m + 30 cm = 32), ask: 'Is 2 metres the same size as 2 centimetres? What has to be true before you can add them?' Line both up on one common scale (2 m lines up as 200 cm) so the mismatch is visible; the goal here is to recognise that the units must match, not to carry out the full conversion, which is a later-stage skill.

If the learner picks the wrong operation, ask: 'Does this problem want you to put the amounts together, or find how much more one is than the other?' and rebuild it on the number line (combine = stack/mark to total, difference = gap).

If the learner muddles a compound unit (writes 3 cm 5 mm as 35 cm, or adds 3 + 5 to get 8), keep the task within a single unit for now; full mm–cm conversion belongs to a later stage. (Note that 35 mm is a correct value for 3 cm 5 mm, so do not mark it as wrong.)
activities.rationale: Representing add/subtract on tape or number-line diagrams follows established measurement progressions where combining and differencing are modelled on a line with equal unit spacing; measuring-then-calculating gives the operation a real purpose. An optional live mechanism — marking measured amounts on the line and a running answer box that always carries the unit — may make the combining idea and the same-unit requirement concrete, but is not the only possible setup.
sourceClaims: Second graders add two lengths to obtain the length of the whole and subtract one length from another to find the difference; length add/subtract problems are represented with tape or number-bond diagrams and equations with a symbol for the unknown, and a number line diagram is a measurement model where consecutive whole numbers are one unit apart.
Unit size is critical in measurement and the unit must always be considered ('what are you counting?' -> the length-units), so a measurement answer is meaningful only with its unit.
Year 3 pupils measure, compare, add and subtract lengths (m/cm/mm), mass (kg/g) and volume/capacity (l/ml) using standard units.
learnerActions: Measure two real quantities of the SAME kind — e.g. two lengths of ribbon in cm, or two beakers of juice in ml (250 ml and 400 ml), or two masses in g.

Combine the two measures on a number line / tape: place lengths end to end to read the total (e.g. 25 cm + 40 cm = 65 cm), or mark the two volumes along the scale to reach the total (250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml). Write the answer WITH its unit (65 cm; 650 ml).
Switch to a subtraction task: use the same number line to find the difference between the two measures as the gap between them.
Decide for each worded problem whether you are combining the amounts (stack them / mark to the total) or finding how much more one is than the other (find the gap).

Meet the mixed-unit case: a 2 m length and a 30 cm length. Try to total them and notice you cannot simply write 32 — line both up on one common scale (2 m lines up as 200 cm) and say what has to be true (same unit) before adding.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding measures means combining amounts and subtracting means finding a gap; a measurement answer is only meaningful with its unit; and you can only add or subtract measures that are in the same unit.

activities.title: Same-unit calculation check with targeted wrong-answer options
feedback: For the option that drops the unit: 'The arithmetic is right, but what is missing? A measurement answer needs its unit.'

For the option that adds across units: 'Why can't 2 m and 30 cm just be added as 2 + 30? What would make them addable?' Line them up on one common scale (2 m lines up as 200 cm) so the units clearly differ; actually converting and totalling is a later-stage skill, not expected now.
If the learner answers correctly, ask them to generalise: 'What is the rule for when two measures CAN be added together?'
activities.rationale: Short checks that target the specific error patterns (dropping the unit, adding across units) are strongly discriminating for whether the same-unit rule is understood. This format can test and make the rule explicit; recognising a correct option is not the same as producing unit-bearing work, so it complements rather than replaces the number-line sense built on the bench.
sourceClaims: Unit size is critical in measurement and the unit must always be considered ('what are you counting?' -> the length-units), so a measurement answer is meaningful only with its unit.

The systematic relationship among length units (km, m, cm, mm) and conversion between them is placed in Grade 4 (4.MD.1), not Grade 3; expressing larger units in smaller units reinforces place value. This means at the earlier stage children work within a single unit and full mm–cm–m conversion is not yet expected.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in-the-blank sums within one unit, writing the unit in the answer (e.g. 250 ml + 400 ml = ___ ml).
Choose the correct result from options that include one that drops the unit and one that adds across units (e.g. for 2 m + 30 cm, recognise that '32' is wrong).
Explain in words why the across-unit option is wrong before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: The same-unit rule and the unit-bearing answer can be stated explicitly and recognised in others' work, not just produced on the bench.

activities.title: Reference number-line diagram of a length addition
feedback: Prompt: 'Point to where the total ends on the line — what number is it, and what unit?'
Prompt: 'If this were a subtraction, which part of the picture would be the gap you measure?'
activities.rationale: A fixed diagram cannot be manipulated and does not let the child measure across varied cases or meet the same-unit trap by recomputing, so it works best as a reference or worked example alongside active tasks. It can still clarify the combining idea and unit placement.
sourceClaims: Second graders add two lengths to obtain the length of the whole and subtract one length from another to find the difference; length add/subtract problems are represented with tape or number-bond diagrams and equations with a symbol for the unknown, and a number line diagram is a measurement model where consecutive whole numbers are one unit apart.
learnerActions: Study a labelled number line / tape showing two lengths placed end to end and the total read off the scale.
Trace along the line to see where the first length ends and the second begins, and where the total sits.
Describe in your own words why the total is found by combining distances, and identify where the unit appears in the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked tape/number-line picture shows the combining idea and anchors the vocabulary, as a reference to support the active measure-and-calculate work.

constraints: Keep all arithmetic within a single unit at this stage; delay formal mm–cm–m (and kg–g, l–ml) conversion to a later unit-conversion topic. The mixed-unit trap is used only to reveal that units must match, not to have the child compute a converted total.
Always require the unit in the answer; treat a bare number as an incomplete answer.

Keep length examples (ribbon in cm/mm), capacity examples (juice in ml) and mass examples (in g) coherent — do not label a volume as a 'length' or carry a length action over to a capacity or mass result.
The fill-in/selection check tests and states the same-unit rule but does not by itself build number-line sense; pair it with the measure-and-combine activity.
The reference diagram is a worked example: it cannot let the child measure varied cases or recompute at the same-unit trap, so use it to support, not replace, hands-on measuring and calculating.

Optional interaction examples (marking measured amounts on a line, a subtraction 'gap' mode, a running unit-bearing answer box, lining up mismatched units on one common scale) illustrate the mechanism; they are suggestions, not mandatory features.

When a child muddles a compound unit (e.g. writes 3 cm 5 mm as 35 cm, or adds 3 + 5 to get 8), do not drill conversion now; keep calculations within one unit and let compound-unit fluency arrive with the later conversion topic.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Original inconsistency: the source recommendation text conflated capacity and length examples ('measures two lengths of ribbon (250 ml and 400 ml of juice...)'). 250 ml and 400 ml are capacities (juice/beakers), not lengths of ribbon; ribbon is measured in cm/mm. Activities now keep length (cm), capacity (ml) and mass (g) examples distinct.

Arithmetic checked: 250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml is correct; 25 cm + 40 cm = 65 cm is correct; 2 m + 30 cm is NOT 32 (2 m = 200 cm, so a converted total would be 230 cm). The mixed-unit item is retained only as a deliberate error to recognise, never as a valid answer; the full conversion to 230 cm is a later-stage skill and is not presented to the child as expected Year 3 work.

The mass strand (kg/g) is named in the objective and evidence but was not exemplified by a dedicated activity; a two-masses-in-g version of the measure-and-combine bench has been offered so this strand can be covered.
The last source (UK National Curriculum, Year 3 measurement) is marked verified:false in the row; the Year 3 scope claim rests on this unverified source and should be confirmed on review.

Original fit field framed some claims as universal ('3D adds nothing', dialogue unsuitable because the skill is 'a watched performance'). These are not established by the cited sources and have been omitted; a conversation or worked demonstration can still support this skill even if it is not the primary vehicle.

probeDeeper: What unit should be on your answer of 650? Why does it matter?
You wrote 2 m + 30 cm = 32 — is 2 metres the same size as 2 centimetres? What has to be true before you can add them?
Show me this addition on the number line — where does the total end up?
Does this problem want you to put the amounts together, or find how much more one is than the other? How can you tell?
assess.correctAnswer: The child adds/subtracts measures that are in the same unit, keeps the unit in the answer (650 ml; 7 cm), chooses the operation that fits the problem, and — faced with the mixed-unit item — recognises the units must match first rather than adding 2 + 30 to get 32.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds/subtracts across different units as bare numbers: treats unlike units as like, e.g. 2 m + 30 cm = 32, or 1 kg + 200 g = 201.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on a common unit before calculating; show both quantities on one scale so the mismatch is visible; return to attending to the unit when measuring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Combines the digits of measures in different units without matching them; answer has no coherent unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the unit from the answer: computes correctly but writes a bare number (250 ml + 400 ml = 650).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat a measurement answer without a unit as incomplete; build the habit of writing the unit every time; the calculation itself is sound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Right arithmetic, no unit on the result; supplies it only when asked.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compound-unit muddle: reads or combines mixed compound units wrongly, e.g. writes 3 cm 5 mm as 35 or adds 3 + 5, not yet knowing 10 mm = 1 cm.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill mm–cm conversion now — systematic conversion belongs to a later stage; keep calculations within a single unit and let compound-unit fluency come with the conversion topic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the two parts of a compound measure as one number, or adds them; expected before unit conversion is taught.

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong operation: adds when the problem asks for a difference, or subtracts when it asks for a total.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Represent the problem on a number line/tape (combine = stack, difference = gap) so the operation follows the model; comprehension, not calculation, is the issue.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct arithmetic but the operation does not match the question's structure.

responseLevels.gap: Adds across different units as bare numbers, or routinely omits the unit, or picks the wrong operation.
responseLevels.full: Calculates with measures in a common unit, carries the unit into every answer, chooses the operation from the problem structure, and recognises that unlike units must be made the same before adding or subtracting.
responseLevels.partial: Adds/subtracts correctly within a single unit and usually keeps the unit, but is caught by the mixed-unit item or an unfamiliar compound unit — the same-unit rule is not yet explicit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give real quantities to measure and combine: e.g. two lengths of ribbon and two beakers of water, plus a written problem ('250 ml + 400 ml = ?') and a deliberately mixed-unit one ('2 m + 30 cm = ?'). Say: 'Measure these and work out the totals and the difference.' Watch whether they keep like units together, carry the unit into the answer, and choose the right operation.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands calculating with measures produces unit-bearing answers and pauses at the mixed-unit sum; a child who does not writes 650 without a unit, or 2 m + 30 cm = 32, or applies the wrong operation — each visible in the written work.

sources.claim: Second graders add two lengths to obtain the length of the whole and subtract one length from another to find the difference; length add/subtract problems are represented with tape or number-bond diagrams and equations with a symbol for the unknown, and a number line diagram is a measurement model where consecutive whole numbers are one unit apart.
sources.source: Common Core Progressions — K–5 Geometric Measurement (2012), Grade 2 (2.MD.5–6) (ISBE mirror)

sources.claim: The systematic relationship among length units (km, m, cm, mm) and conversion between them is placed in Grade 4 (4.MD.1), not Grade 3; expressing larger units in smaller units reinforces place value. This means at the earlier stage children work within a single unit and full mm–cm–m conversion is not yet expected.
sources.source: Common Core Progressions — K–5 Geometric Measurement (2012), Grade 4 (4.MD.1) (ISBE mirror)

sources.claim: Unit size is critical in measurement and the unit must always be considered ('what are you counting?' -> the length-units), so a measurement answer is meaningful only with its unit.
sources.source: Common Core Progressions — K–5 Geometric Measurement (2012), Grade 2 (ISBE mirror)

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils measure, compare, add and subtract lengths (m/cm/mm), mass (kg/g) and volume/capacity (l/ml) using standard units.
sources.source: UK National Curriculum — Mathematics, Key Stage 2 Measurement

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** How We See Objects

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 6 Science, Light):** use the idea that light travels in straight lines to explain that objects are seen because they give out or reflect light into the eye; explain that we see things because light travels from light sources to our eyes or from light sources to objects and then to our eyes.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 4-PS4-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-2]. (Assessment boundary: does NOT include knowledge of specific colours [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-2].)

- **Operational details:** The target model is the one-way light path: source → object → (reflected) → eye. The dominant obstacle is the extramission belief that something travels OUT of the eye to see — an ancient, intuitive and empirically robust misconception that ordinary telling and even reading rarely dislodge (learners assimilate 'light reflects to the eye' into their existing 'I look out and it brightens the object' frame). So elicit first with diagnostics ('My eye', 'Dark room'), then teach REFUTATIONALLY: name the wrong idea and contrast it ('in real life nothing comes out of your eyes — unlike Superman'). Build and draw the full journey with arrowed rays, and use a physical receiver model (string/wool tracing source→object→eye; a webcam or camera obscura as an eye that light ENTERS). Pair it with diffuse reflection — all surfaces, not just shiny ones, scatter light into the eye — so everyday objects qualify as senders. Expect fragility: gains are often short-lived, so revisit and re-test over time rather than treating one lesson as sufficient.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Although the age sits in upper-KS2, the defining demand is conceptual change: the child must abstract an invisible, directional light path and actively overturn a deeply held intuition (eyes reach out / image flies into the eye whole). This is a threshold concept — mastery means correctly modelling and explaining source→object→eye and rejecting any 'out of the eye' arrow, with the understanding holding up on delayed re-testing, not just immediately after teaching.
bestPractices: Elicit the child's existing model first with diagnostic probes (e.g. 'draw how you see this book') before teaching — extramission must be surfaced to be challenged.
Teach refutationally: explicitly name the wrong idea ('nothing comes out of your eyes — you are not Superman') and contrast it with the correct path, rather than only presenting the right answer.
Build and draw the FULL journey with arrowed rays: light source → object → reflected → eye; insist every ray has a direction arrow.
Use a physical 'receiver' model so the eye is visibly something light ENTERS: a webcam or camera obscura, or string/wool tracing the path from source to object to eye.
Connect to diffuse reflection — ALL surfaces (dull as well as shiny) scatter light into the eye — so that everyday non-luminous objects count as senders of light.
Revisit and re-test over weeks: refutational gains on extramission are often short-lived, so one lesson is not enough.
keyRepresentations: Arrowed ray diagram: source → object → (reflected ray) → eye
String or wool physically tracing the light path from lamp to object to eye
Camera obscura or a webcam used as a model 'eye' that light enters to form an image
Three-holes-in-card or a tube lined up so light only reaches the eye along a straight path
commonMisconceptions: Extramission: the eye sends something out (rays/'visual feelers') to see the object.
Light travels both ways — into the eye from luminous things but out of the eye toward non-luminous things.
Seeing just requires light to 'land on' and brighten the object; the reflected-into-the-eye step is missing.
A whole image or picture of the object flies intact into the eye.
Once eyes 'adjust', we can see in complete darkness.
Only shiny surfaces reflect light into the eye, so dull objects are seen by some other means.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, teach that we see a non-luminous object because light travels from a source to the object, reflects off it, and then enters the eye (source → object → eye, one way only). Light sources such as lamps are seen by light travelling directly from them into the eye. The central obstacle is the intuitive extramission belief that something leaves the eye to 'reach out' and see. Surface this belief first with diagnostic drawing/probes, then teach refutationally — name and reject the wrong idea and build the full arrowed ray path — and connect to diffuse reflection so dull everyday objects count as light senders. Because gains often revert, revisit and re-test over time.

activities.title: Make yourself able to see it: route the light path
feedback: If you drew an arrow out of the eye: in real life nothing comes out of your eyes to see — you are not Superman. An outgoing arrow does nothing; see whether the object actually becomes visible from it.
If the lamp lights the mug but you stop there: lighting the object is not enough. Ask where the light goes next — it must bounce off the mug and travel INTO the eye.
When lamp → mug → reflected ray → eye is complete, the object becomes visible in the model: the reflected light arriving at the eye is what lets you see it.

Lamp off → in the model (or a completely dark room) the mug cannot be seen: with no light to reflect, nothing reaches the eye. In a real dim room you may still see it faintly, because light from other sources still reflects off it.
Dull matt object still visible: dull surfaces scatter light into the eye too, so everyday non-shiny objects are seen the same way.
activities.rationale: Conceptual change on extramission needs the wrong idea to fail visibly rather than simply be contradicted. Having the learner route light and watch an 'out of the eye' arrow do nothing, while the completed source→object→eye chain makes the object spring into view, makes the refutation experiential. An optional live-recolour cue (grey silhouette snapping to full colour when the chain completes) and a lamp-off toggle make the mechanism concrete, and the webcam-style receiver idea and the dull-surface swap come from the misconception review. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Extramission and related vision misconceptions: students describe light going from the eye to objects, light going both ways, or an image entering the eye; diagnostics ('My eye', 'Dark room') surface the belief; recommended models include a webcam as an eye that receives light, and reflection from any surface (not just shiny) links to seeing non-luminous objects.
learnerActions: In an on-screen model of a dark scene with a hidden object (e.g. a mug on a table), take on the goal: 'make yourself able to see it.' (In this model the rays you draw control what can be seen; in real life, drawing arrows does not change what you see.)
First try your own intuition: draw an arrow pointing FROM the eye toward the mug, and notice what happens.
Place a movable lamp and draw a light ray from the lamp to the mug; check whether that alone is enough.
Complete the full chain: lamp → mug → reflected arrow → eye, with a direction arrow on every ray.
Toggle the lamp off and describe what happens to the mug and why.
Swap the shiny mug for a dull matt object and check whether it can still be seen; explain why.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing is not the eye reaching out; it is light arriving AT the eye after bouncing off the object. If no light reaches the object or no reflected light reaches the eye, the object cannot be seen. Shiny surfaces reflect light mostly in one direction, like a mirror, and dull surfaces scatter it in many directions, so both can send light to the eye.

activities.title: Elicit and refute: 'How do you think you can see this book?'
feedback: If you say your eyes send out rays or 'reach' the book: name the idea explicitly — nothing leaves your eyes; that only happens with cartoon superheroes. The eye catches light; it does not send it.
If you draw arrows both ways: keep the incoming ray but remove the outgoing one — the eye contributes no light, it only receives.
If you stop at 'the light lights up the book': ask what happens to that light next — it must reflect from the book into your eye for you to see.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue is useful for surfacing the belief and naming it refutationally before correcting it, which matches the elicit-first guidance. It pairs well with the hands-on routing task; on its own, dialogue surfaces and challenges the belief but does not provide the felt failure of a wrong light path. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Extramission and related vision misconceptions: students describe light going from the eye to objects, light going both ways, or an image entering the eye; diagnostics ('My eye', 'Dark room') surface the belief; recommended models include a webcam as an eye that receives light, and reflection from any surface (not just shiny) links to seeing non-luminous objects.

Oak Year 6 'Reflected light' teaches the journey of light source→object→eye, recommends explicit teaching of light rays plus demonstrations and diagram practice, and names the misconception that light shines OUT of our eyes.
learnerActions: Before any teaching, draw or describe how you see a nearby object such as a book ('draw how you see this book').
Answer a Socratic optician/vision-scientist persona who asks what you think travels, and in which direction, when you look at the book.
When prompted, decide whether anything leaves your eye, and justify your answer.
Re-draw the path after the discussion, adding a direction arrow to every ray.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting your own theory into words exposes the hidden extramission assumption so it can be named and replaced with the one-way source→object→eye path.

activities.title: Physical receiver model: the eye is something light ENTERS
feedback: If light reaching the model eye makes an image but no image forms when the path is blocked: this shows light must travel into the eye for seeing to happen.
If the holes/tube only let you see along a straight line: this demonstrates light travels in straight lines from object to eye.
Connect back: whatever the surface — lamp, apple, dull mug — the light ends its journey by entering the eye.
activities.rationale: A concrete receiver model makes the abstract, invisible, directional light path tangible and shows the eye receiving rather than emitting light; string/wool makes the straight-line path physical. These media give a different, complementary experience from screen models. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Extramission and related vision misconceptions: students describe light going from the eye to objects, light going both ways, or an image entering the eye; diagnostics ('My eye', 'Dark room') surface the belief; recommended models include a webcam as an eye that receives light, and reflection from any surface (not just shiny) links to seeing non-luminous objects.

Oak Year 6 'Reflected light' teaches the journey of light source→object→eye, recommends explicit teaching of light rays plus demonstrations and diagram practice, and names the misconception that light shines OUT of our eyes.
learnerActions: Use string or wool to physically trace the light path from the lamp to the object and then to the eye position.
Observe a camera obscura or a webcam used as a model 'eye', noticing that an image forms only because light enters it.
Line up three holes in cards (or a tube) so light reaches the eye only along a straight path, and check what happens when one card is shifted out of line.
State in your own words which way the light must be travelling for the image to form.
activities.intendedInsight: Because an image only forms when light goes INTO the model eye (camera/webcam/obscura), the eye must be a receiver of light, not a sender; light also travels in straight lines along the traced path.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: block the line of sight
feedback: If you predicted you'd still see it because it's lit: notice you can't. The card blocks the path between the apple and your eye, so in the light model the apple's reflected light can no longer reach your eye. The apple-to-eye leg of the path is essential.
Closing your eyes: the light still reaches the apple, so your eye is not making or needing to send the light — it only catches it.
Pitch-black room: no light means nothing to reflect into your eye, so waiting never lets you see — eyes do not generate sight in true darkness.

Eye like a camera: both form an image from light that enters them; neither sends light out. (Keep to the image-forming comparison; do not extend into retinal or cellular detail, which is outside this topic's scope.)
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain test with the line-of-sight card gives a surprising, checkable outcome that targets the 'light stops at the object' and extramission patterns directly, and the darkness probe heads off the 'eyes adjust to see in the dark' error. Refutational diagnostic items are evidence-informed; this remains a proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Extramission and related vision misconceptions: students describe light going from the eye to objects, light going both ways, or an image entering the eye; diagnostics ('My eye', 'Dark room') surface the belief; recommended models include a webcam as an eye that receives light, and reflection from any surface (not just shiny) links to seeing non-luminous objects.
Extramission beliefs are robust against ordinary education; refutational interventions produce gains that often revert, so the idea must be revisited over time.
learnerActions: Look at a brightly lit toy or apple you can clearly see.
Predict: if a card is slid between the object and your eye while the object stays fully lit, will you still see it? Say why before testing.
Slide the card and observe the result.

Explain what this shows: the space between the object and your eye must be clear. Then, using the lamp-off and dark-room evidence as well, explain why scientists say the light travels from the object into your eye.
Answer follow-up probes: does the light still reach the object if you close your eyes? Could you ever see it by waiting in a truly pitch-black room? How is your eye like a camera?
activities.intendedInsight: The object is still fully lit, yet blocking the space between object and eye stops you seeing it, so the path from object to eye must be clear. Put together with the fact that you cannot see anything without a light source (even with your eyes open), this supports the model that light travels FROM the object INTO the eye, and seeing does not 'make' the light.

activities.title: Delayed re-check: sequence, draw, and refute
feedback: Correct sequence should be source first, then object, then eye — the eye is always the final receiver.
If you say something leaves the eye: nothing does; only light arriving at the eye lets you see.
A complete drawing needs the reflected ray from object to eye, not just light landing on the object.
If an earlier correct answer has slipped back to an eye-out arrow, that's not unusual — this idea can revert, so re-teach and re-test.
activities.rationale: A fixed check tests the model rather than building it against a stubborn intuition, so it is used as a companion rather than the main teaching, and especially as the delayed re-test the research calls for because refutational gains often revert. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Extramission beliefs are robust against ordinary education; refutational interventions produce gains that often revert, so the idea must be revisited over time.
learnerActions: Sequence the three steps of the journey into the correct order: source → object → eye.
Answer a refutational check such as 'Does anything leave your eye when you see something?' and justify your choice.
Draw the complete ray path for a new everyday object, with a direction arrow on every ray.
Revisit this check days or weeks later to confirm the idea has held.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to re-sequence, reject the outgoing-eye arrow, and draw the full path on a delayed test shows the model has genuinely replaced the intuition rather than been temporarily memorised.

constraints: Keep within the standards' assessment boundary: do not teach specific colours reflected/seen, [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-2].
Elicit the learner's existing model before teaching; extramission must be surfaced before it can be challenged.

Teach refutationally — name the wrong idea and contrast it with the correct path — rather than only presenting the right answer, because learners otherwise assimilate 'light reflects to the eye' into their existing 'I look out' frame.
Insist every ray carries a direction arrow and that the full chain source → object → (reflected) → eye is completed, not stopped at the object.
Explicitly include diffuse reflection so dull surfaces, not only shiny ones, count as senders of light into the eye.
Expect fragility: gains on extramission are often short-lived, so plan to revisit and re-test over weeks; one lesson is not sufficient.
A fixed sequencing/drawing check mainly assesses the model and should accompany, not replace, the experiential refutation.
The camera/webcam/obscura is a model of the eye as a light receiver; it is an approximation and is not intended to teach retinal or cellular detail.
Physical receiver models (string, obscura, hole-cards) and screen models offer different, complementary experiences; neither is presented here as the only possible route.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four cited sources were marked verified:false in the source row (the Oak National Academy 'Reflected light' page and the Winer/Cottrell extramission-persistence research); treat the persistence-of-gains and specific lesson-design claims with corresponding caution.

The source material contains several catalog-style comparative claims (e.g. that telling/reading cannot dislodge extramission, that 3D 'adds nothing', that static presentation is 'precisely' what research shows learners absorb without change, and that felt failure is a 'sharper corrective than persuasion'). These were softened to narrowly scoped proposals with stated affordances; the exact sources here do not establish such comparative efficacy or necessity.

The research-backed claim is that ordinary education and refutational interventions often revert over time; the stronger phrasing that 'telling and reading rarely dislodge' is retained only as an instructional caution, not as a proven universal law. The summary and feedback were qualified to 'often/can revert' accordingly.
The 'how is your eye like a camera?' probe is a useful image-forming analogy but must not be extended into retinal/cellular mechanism, which is outside the assessment boundary.

The NGSS 4-PS4-2 claim supports the objective/model content rather than the specific teaching-principle rationales in individual activities, so it is reflected in the summary/objective rather than appended as per-activity sourceClaims support.

The Winer/Cottrell persistence claim is scoped to activities about revisiting/delayed re-testing (the POE and delayed-re-check activities); it was not retained on the initial routing activity, whose rationale has no delayed-re-test component.

assess.poeTask: Show a brightly lit toy the child can clearly see. Predict: if I slide a card between the toy and your eye (the toy stays fully lit), will you still see it? Say why before we try. Then slide the card and explain what it proves about the direction light travels.
probeDeeper: If she closes her eyes, does the light still reach the apple? What does that tell you about whether seeing 'makes' the light?
Slide a card between the apple and her eye — the apple is still brightly lit but she can't see it now. Which way must the light have been travelling?
Suppose we sealed every window and turned off every light so the room was truly pitch black — could she ever see the apple by waiting? Why not?
How is your eye like a camera taking a picture?
assess.correctAnswer: Light travels from a source (the lamp or sun) to the apple, reflects (bounces) off the apple, and then travels into her eye. Her eye receives the light — nothing comes out of her eye.

errorPatterns.pattern: Extramission: 'my eyes send something out to the apple so I can see it' — the tell is arrows drawn FROM the eye, or 'I look at it and that's how I see it'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refutational teaching — name and reject it explicitly ('nothing leaves your eyes, that's only Superman'); build the full source-object-eye path with arrowed rays; model the eye as a receiver (camera / webcam / camera obscura). Revisit repeatedly because the gain reverts.
errorPatterns.distractor: Her eyes send out rays to the apple, and that lets her see it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws or describes rays going from the eye to the object, or a beam that reaches out; treats seeing as the eye doing something active to the object

errorPatterns.pattern: Light stops at the object: 'the light just lights the apple up and then she sees it' — no light needs to travel from apple to eye
errorPatterns.nextMove: Complete the third leg of the path; use the 'block the line of sight' test — slide a card between apple and eye and she can no longer see it, proving light must travel FROM the apple INTO the eye.
errorPatterns.distractor: Light shines on the apple to light it up, and then she just sees it — nothing needs to go from the apple to her eye.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws light source to apple but omits the third leg (apple to eye); says lighting the object is enough for sight

errorPatterns.pattern: Two-way seeing: light reaches the apple AND the eye also reaches out — a simultaneous exchange
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refute the outgoing eye-arrow specifically while keeping the correct incoming ray; the eye contributes nothing to the light, it only catches it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws arrows in both directions between eye and object

responseLevels.gap: Describes or draws light (or 'looking') coming OUT of the eye, or says she sees the apple simply because it is lit, with no light entering the eye.
responseLevels.full: Traces the complete one-way path source-object-eye with the eye as receiver, AND transfers it: explains why the card in the line of sight blocks vision and why total darkness prevents sight, both from 'light must reflect into the eye'.
responseLevels.partial: Names the pieces — light source, apple, eye — and knows light must be present, but leaves the path incomplete or cannot commit to a direction (e.g. lights the object but omits apple-to-eye, or still says the eye 'looks at' it).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A girl is looking at an apple sitting on a table in a well-lit room. Explain what has to happen with the light for her to see the apple — trace the light's journey from start to finish.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the intuitive extramission model describes or draws something leaving the eye and going TO the apple (or a two-way 'looking' beam); the correct model has light going one way only, source to object to eye, with the eye as a pure receiver. Asking for the direction of the journey forces the mechanism out into the open, where telling and even reading the right answer usually fail to.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 11–13 (KS3) — contrast photosynthesis (energy from sunlight) with chemosynthesis (energy from oxidising chemicals like hydrogen sulphide); hydrothermal-vent communities where chemoautotrophic bacteria are the producers supporting tube worms, giant clams and vent crabs with NO sunlight; what this implies for the origin of life; why NASA studies vents as analogues for possible life on Europa and Enceladus.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS3): biology 'photosynthesis as the key process for food production' and cellular respiration/energy — chemosynthesis as an alternative producer pathway; nutrition and food webs.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS1-6 (role of photosynthesis in cycling matter/energy) and MS-LS2-3 (energy flow through an ecosystem) — extended to a non-photosynthetic base.
• Operational details: the core is the PRODUCER-ENERGY-SOURCE contrast — both photosynthesis and chemosynthesis fix carbon into food, but one is powered by light and the other by chemical energy (oxidising H2S from vent fluid). Bacteria are the base of a vent food web independent of the Sun. The big-idea tail is genuinely open/speculative: vents as a candidate cradle for life's origin, and as Earth analogues guiding the search for life on icy ocean moons — questions science is still debating.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~11, concrete): states vent bacteria make food from chemicals, not light; Tier B (transitional): contrasts photosynthesis and chemosynthesis by energy source and builds a vent food web with bacteria as producers; Tier C (formal, ~13): explains why vents inform origin-of-life and astrobiology (chemical energy + water ± sunlight), evaluating the reasoning behind Europa/Enceladus missions.
bestPractices: Teach chemosynthesis by direct contrast with the already-known photosynthesis: same job (producers making food/fixing carbon), different energy source (chemical vs light) — an analogy that scaffolds the new idea.
Make bacteria the visible PRODUCERS at the base of the vent food web, correcting the assumption that producers must be green/plants.
Use a real vent community (chemoautotrophic bacteria → tube worms/clams → crabs) so energy flow from a chemical source is concrete.
Frame the origin-of-life and astrobiology material as OPEN questions with evidence and reasoning to weigh, not settled facts — model scientific argumentation.
Connect explicitly to the 9–11 deep-sea topic ('life without sunlight') and to KS3 photosynthesis to bind the sequence together.
keyRepresentations: A side-by-side photosynthesis vs chemosynthesis comparison (inputs, energy source, product)
A vent food-web diagram with chemoautotrophic bacteria as producers
A vent cross-section: mineral-rich fluid → bacteria → tube worms/clams/crabs
An astrobiology analogue panel: Earth vent ↔ Europa/Enceladus subsurface ocean
commonMisconceptions: 'All producers photosynthesise / all food chains start with sunlight' — the key misconception chemosynthesis overturns.
'The vent's HEAT is the energy source for the food web' — conflating heat with the chemical energy bacteria actually oxidise.
'Producers must be plants/green' — not recognising bacteria as producers.
'Chemosynthesis is just photosynthesis in the dark' — missing that the energy source is fundamentally chemical, not light.
Treating origin-of-life/alien-ocean claims as proven rather than as reasoned, evidence-based hypotheses.

learn.summary: Ages 11–13 (KS3; NGSS MS-LS1-6, MS-LS2-3): teach chemosynthesis by direct contrast with the already-known photosynthesis — both are producers fixing carbon from CO2 into food, but one is powered by light and the other by chemical energy (oxidising hydrogen sulphide, H2S, from vent fluid). Build a hydrothermal-vent food web where chemoautotrophic bacteria are the producers at the base, supporting tube worms, giant clams and vent crabs with no sunlight as the energy source. Then weigh the open, still-debated questions: could life have begun at vents, and why do agencies like NASA study vents as analogues for possible life on icy ocean worlds such as Europa and Enceladus? Key targets include correcting 'all producers are green plants / all food chains start with sunlight', distinguishing chemical energy from the vent's heat, and distinguishing an energy source from a food source.

activities.title: Build a vent food web on a different power source
feedback: If a learner keeps the Sun at the base: no sunlight reaches a deep vent — point to exactly where sunlight enters the ENERGY path. If you can't, the producers' energy must be something else. (Some marine snow does drift down, and the oxygen in seawater comes from photosynthesis at the surface, but the vent's PRODUCERS build food using chemical energy, not light.)

If a learner picks the vent's heat as the food energy: heat is not what the bacteria capture to build food. They oxidise a chemical (H2S) and use that chemical energy — line up heat vs chemical energy explicitly.

If a learner says bacteria 'eat' or 'feed on' H2S: just as plants don't eat sunlight, vent bacteria don't eat H2S — they use its chemical energy to synthesise their own food from CO2. Keep CO2 as the carbon source.

If a learner calls it 'photosynthesis in the dark': both processes build food (sugar) from CO2, but the energy input differs — light for photosynthesis, chemical for chemosynthesis. Same kind of food made, fundamentally different fuel (and different by-products: photosynthesis releases oxygen, while H2S oxidation produces sulfur or sulfate).
activities.rationale: Assembling and running two contrasting webs is intended to make the producer-energy contrast and the energy flow explicit and manipulable, rather than asserted. Choosing a base that fails (sunlight in the dark) and one that works (chemical energy) targets the misconception that all food chains start with sunlight. A side-by-side comparison panel scaffolds the new idea onto the known photosynthesis case. Linked sunlit/vent builders, a selectable base energy source, and a vent cross-section showing fluid feeding the bacteria are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Chemosynthesis lets bacteria at hydrothermal vents produce food using chemical energy (e.g. oxidising hydrogen sulphide) instead of sunlight, forming the base of a vent food web that supports tube worms, clams and crabs with no sunlight.
learnerActions: First build (or label) a familiar sunlit web: Sun → phytoplankton/plants → consumers, and mark where the energy enters.
Now build a hydrothermal-vent food web set in permanent darkness. Try to place the Sun at the base and notice it cannot power this web — no sunlight reaches kilometres down.

Choose the base's actual energy source from options including 'sunlight', 'the vent's heat', and 'chemical energy (oxidising hydrogen sulphide, H2S)'. Select the chemical-energy option so chemoautotrophic bacteria become the producers.
Extend the web: bacteria → tube worms / giant clams → vent crabs, and trace the energy flow from the chemical source upward.
Set the two webs side by side and fill a comparison table: inputs, energy source, and product (food/organic matter from CO2) for photosynthesis vs chemosynthesis.
activities.intendedInsight: Photosynthesis is not the only way to build a food web. Producers do the same job — making food by fixing carbon from CO2 — but can be powered either by light (photosynthesis) or by chemical energy from oxidising H2S (chemosynthesis). Bacteria, not green plants, are the producers at a vent, and the community's energy source is chemical, not the Sun.

activities.title: Reason with an astrobiologist: did life begin at vents, and where else might it be?
feedback: If a learner treats origin-of-life or alien-life claims as proven: these are reasoned, evidence-based hypotheses still being debated — distinguish what is observed from what is inferred.

If a learner dismisses the moons because 'there's no sunlight': that's the point — vent communities show sunlight isn't required as the energy source, so the relevant question is whether chemical energy, water and minerals are present.
Push for the mechanism of the analogy: name what Earth vents and the moons' suspected environments have in common (chemical energy + water ± minerals) rather than just asserting they are similar.
activities.rationale: The open tail of this topic is genuine unsettled scientific argument, well suited to in-role dialogue where a learner may probe reasoning and weigh evidence and uncertainty. This is intended to model scientific argumentation and frame speculative material honestly as hypotheses. Dialogue is a companion to the mechanism work, not a replacement for building the food web.
sourceClaims: Hydrothermal vents are studied as analogues for possible habitats on icy ocean worlds (Europa, Enceladus) and are relevant to hypotheses about the origin of life, because they combine chemical energy, water and minerals.
learnerActions: Take on the question in role: ask and answer 'Why look at hydrothermal vents to search for life beyond Earth?' and 'Could life have begun at vents?'

Set out the reasoning: if life needs chemical energy, water and minerals — which vents supply without sunlight as the energy source — then sunless environments elsewhere are not automatically lifeless.
Apply the analogy to Europa and Enceladus: these icy moons may have subsurface oceans and hydrothermal chemistry but no sunlight; discuss what makes them candidates and what remains unknown.
State explicitly which parts are established (vent communities exist and run without sunlight as their energy source) and which are open hypotheses (origin of life at vents; life on ocean moons).
Weigh at least one piece of evidence for and one source of uncertainty before giving a tentative, reasoned position.
activities.intendedInsight: Vents reshape the search for life because they show a food web can run on chemical energy and water rather than light. Whether life began at vents, and whether ocean moons host life, are genuine open scientific questions to be argued from evidence and uncertainty — not settled facts.

activities.title: Explore and interrogate a vent cross-section
feedback: Producer check: the producers here are bacteria, not plants and not animals — producers need not be green.
Energy vs carbon check: the energy source is chemical (H2S oxidation); the carbon source is CO2. Keep these distinct.
If a learner expects a sunlight input in the energy path: there is none — trace the arrows and confirm the base's energy is chemical, not light.
activities.rationale: A clear tappable exposition presents the vent anatomy, the two-process comparison and the astrobiology analogue cheaply and accessibly. It does not itself let a learner build and run the alternative-energy web, so it works best as support alongside the builder rather than as the construction task.
sourceClaims: Chemosynthesis lets bacteria at hydrothermal vents produce food using chemical energy (e.g. oxidising hydrogen sulphide) instead of sunlight, forming the base of a vent food web that supports tube worms, clams and crabs with no sunlight.
learnerActions: Explore a labelled vent scene: mineral-rich fluid rising, bacterial mats, tube worms, giant clams and vent crabs — tracing which organism depends on which.
Open a photosynthesis/chemosynthesis comparison showing inputs, energy source and product aligned for each.
Examine an Earth-vent ↔ Europa/Enceladus analogue panel and state what the two settings share.
Answer short checks: name the producer at a vent; name its energy source (oxidising H2S) and its carbon source (CO2); and explain why the community survives with no sunlight as its energy source.
activities.intendedInsight: A vent community is a complete food web whose base producers are bacteria powered by chemical energy, with no sunlight as the energy source; the same comparison that defines photosynthesis clarifies how chemosynthesis differs.

activities.title: Check and discriminate the concept
feedback: Gap response (insists the base energy traces to the Sun; claims sunlight seeps down or that drifting detritus feeds the WHOLE community): re-establish chemosynthesis as a genuinely independent energy pathway — the producers' energy is from vent chemicals, not light.

Partial response (says 'chemosynthesis' but can't name H2S oxidation as the energy source or keep CO2 as the carbon source): press for the mechanism — what is oxidised for energy, and where does the carbon come from?
Full response: bacteria oxidise H2S for energy to build food from CO2, cleanly contrasted with photosynthesis, placed at the base of the web, and transferred to astrobiology reasoning.
Asking 'how do the bacteria capture it?' forces the mechanism rather than just the label — require the energy step, not a one-word answer.
activities.rationale: A two-tier diagnostic that asks both the judgement (is the Sun the source?) and the mechanism (how is energy captured?) is designed to discriminate a learner who over-generalises photosynthesis from one who holds the concept. Recognition and short-answer items check the contrast but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction the builder provides.
sourceClaims: Chemosynthesis lets bacteria at hydrothermal vents produce food using chemical energy (e.g. oxidising hydrogen sulphide) instead of sunlight, forming the base of a vent food web that supports tube worms, clams and crabs with no sunlight.
learnerActions: Answer a two-tier diagnostic: given giant tube worms and clams thriving around bacteria in permanent darkness, decide whether sunlight is the energy source the producers capture — and if not, state what is and how the bacteria capture it.

Give the full answer: chemoautotrophic bacteria oxidise H2S (using oxygen dissolved in seawater) for energy and use it to build food from CO2; tube worms, clams and crabs depend on those bacteria; the energy the producers capture is chemical energy from vent fluid (from reactions in the Earth's crust), not sunlight.
Compare a leaf and a vent bacterium: what is the same (both build food from CO2) and what differs (light energy vs chemical energy)?
Predict: if a vent stopped emitting hydrogen sulphide, what happens to the tube worms, and why?
Contrast the two energy sources, identify the vent producer, and reason about how far the Europa/Enceladus analogue holds and what remains unknown.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure understanding means naming chemosynthesis, identifying the oxidised chemical (H2S) as the energy source, keeping CO2 as the carbon source, and transferring the idea to origin-of-life and ocean-world reasoning — not merely using the word 'chemosynthesis' as a label.

constraints: Scaffold onto prior knowledge: introduce chemosynthesis as a contrast with the already-taught photosynthesis, and connect to the earlier deep-sea 'life without sunlight' topic.
Keep energy source distinct from carbon source throughout: bacteria oxidise H2S for ENERGY and fix CO2 as their CARBON; never let learners conclude bacteria 'eat' H2S.
Keep chemical energy distinct from the vent's heat; heat is not the food energy the bacteria capture.
Producers need not be green or plants — bacteria are the producers at a vent; address this explicitly.
Frame origin-of-life and Europa/Enceladus material as open, evidence-based hypotheses under active debate, never as settled fact.
State the vent's sunlight-independence as being about the ENERGY SOURCE (chemical, not light); do not overclaim that no surface-derived material of any kind reaches the deep sea.

Tappable/exposition and recognition items check and present the concept but do not themselves elicit independent construction of the alternative-energy food web; use them alongside the builder rather than as the only task.
A 3D vent dive can add atmosphere but the conceptual payload (energy-source contrast, food web, astrobiology reasoning) is not spatial; do not treat immersion as required for the learning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; both sources carry verified:false and have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both cited sources (NOAA Ocean Exploration; NASA Ocean Worlds) are listed as verified:false in the source row; treat the science claims as plausible but unconfirmed in this rewrite.
The origin-of-life and ocean-moon (Europa/Enceladus) material is inherently speculative in the source and should be taught as open argument; do not present it as established.
The source's astrobiologist-dialogue and food-web-builder descriptions are proposed designs; retained as options with their stated affordances and limits, not as evidence of efficacy.

Scientific nuance held outside learner text: the vent community is independent of sunlight for its ENERGY SOURCE (correct, and the taught objective), but aerobic vent chemosynthesis commonly uses dissolved oxygen ultimately generated by surface photosynthesis. Beyond KS3 scope; learner-facing statements are scoped to the energy source to stay accurate without overclaiming total sunlight-independence.

Also beyond scope but noted for accuracy: some drifting detritus (marine snow) does reach deep water, so the correction to learners targets 'the base/whole community traces to the Sun', not the stronger false claim that nothing from the surface ever arrives.

probeDeeper: You said energy traces to the Sun. A vent has run in total darkness for thousands of years — point to exactly where the Sun enters that food web. If you can't, what does that imply?
What's the same, and what's different, between a leaf and a vent bacterium in how each gets its energy and its carbon?
Why would NASA send missions to icy moons with no sunlight but suspected hot vents on the seabed — what are vents telling them?
If a vent stopped emitting hydrogen sulphide tomorrow, what would happen to the tube worms, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: No — vent communities are independent of sunlight. Their base is CHEMOSYNTHESIS, not photosynthesis: chemoautotrophic bacteria get energy by oxidising chemicals (especially hydrogen sulphide, H2S) streaming from the vent, and use that energy to build food (organic matter) from CO2. Tube worms, clams and vent crabs then depend on those bacteria. So the ultimate energy source is chemical energy from the Earth's interior, not the Sun. This is why vents matter for ideas about the origin of life and why agencies like NASA study them as analogues for possible life on ocean worlds such as Europa and Enceladus, where there is no sunlight but there may be hydrothermal chemistry.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All food energy on Earth ultimately comes from the Sun' — treats photosynthesis as the only possible base of any food web.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish chemosynthesis as a genuinely independent pathway: the energy comes from vent chemicals, not light. Contrast the two energy sources side by side.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun — all food energy starts with photosynthesis, so it must reach the vent somehow.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists the Sun must be involved somewhere; claims sunlight seeps down or that detritus from above feeds the whole vent community.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Chemosynthesis and photosynthesis are basically the same, just in the dark' — blurs the energy source.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line them up: both build food from CO2, but photosynthesis uses LIGHT energy while chemosynthesis uses CHEMICAL energy (oxidising H2S). Same product, different energy input.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same process — the bacteria just do photosynthesis in the dark.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes bacteria 'photosynthesising without light', or can't say what differs between the two processes.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The bacteria eat the chemicals like food' — confuses an energy source with a food source.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify producer logic: like plants don't 'eat' sunlight, vent bacteria don't 'eat' H2S — they use its chemical energy to synthesise their own food from CO2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the bacteria 'feed on' hydrogen sulphide as if it were a meal, not that they use it to MAKE food from CO2.

responseLevels.gap: Insists all energy traces to the Sun; cannot name a non-light energy source or conflates the two processes.
responseLevels.full: Explains chemosynthesis mechanistically (bacteria oxidise H2S for energy to build food from CO2), contrasts it cleanly with photosynthesis, places it at the base of the vent web, and transfers the idea to origin-of-life / ocean-world astrobiology reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: Knows vent life doesn't use sunlight and can say 'chemosynthesis', but treats it as a label — can't identify H2S oxidation as the energy source or keep CO2 as the carbon source.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: At a hydrothermal vent, kilometres down in permanent darkness, giant tube worms and clams flourish around bacteria — with no sunlight ever reaching them. A student says 'the energy must still trace back to the Sun somehow, because photosynthesis is where all food energy on Earth begins'. Is the Sun the ultimate energy source for a vent community? If not, what is, and how do the bacteria capture it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who over-generalises photosynthesis insists the energy must trace to the Sun and cannot name the chemical source; a student with the concept names chemosynthesis, identifies the oxidised chemical (H2S) as the energy source, and keeps CO2 as the carbon source. Asking 'how do the bacteria capture it' forces the mechanism, not just the label.
