pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9-11 (Upper KS2/Grades 4-6): adaptation and natural selection in insects — the peppered moth (dark forms survived better on soot-darkened trees), stick insects evolving to look like twigs, ant-mimicking spiders. The key idea: adaptations arise over MANY GENERATIONS through natural selection, NOT within one insect's lifetime.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y6 'Evolution and inheritance' — identify how animals and plants are adapted to suit their environment and that adaptation may lead to evolution.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-3 and especially MS-LS4-4/MS-LS4-6 (natural selection, changes in trait frequency over generations) — the peppered moth is the flagship school example.
• Operational details — the load-bearing and hard-won idea is that selection acts on EXISTING variation across a population over generations: individuals don't change to fit; rather, better-camouflaged individuals survive and leave more offspring, so the population shifts. Confront the Lamarckian 'the moth turned dark because of the soot / because it needed to' error directly. The peppered moth is ideal because the environmental change (Industrial Revolution soot, then clean-air recovery) and the frequency shift are documented.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): retells the peppered moth story and which colour survived when. Tier B (age 10): explains that the better-camouflaged moths survived and bred more, shifting the population. Tier C (age 11): explains that adaptation happens over generations via selection on existing variation, not by an individual changing in its lifetime.
bestPractices: Confront the Lamarckian misconception head-on — individuals don't change to fit; the population's mix shifts as survivors breed.
Use the peppered moth precisely because its environmental change and frequency shift are documented and reversible (soot then clean air).
Emphasise that selection acts on EXISTING variation already present in the population.
Make generations explicit — the change is across many generations, not one lifetime.
Connect the abstract mechanism to multiple examples (stick insect, ant-mimic spider) so it's a general principle.
keyRepresentations: A generational selection sim with a live population-ratio graph.
Before/after habitat panels (lichen tree vs sooty tree) with moth visibility.
A 'follow one individual' tag showing it never changes colour.
Adaptation-to-function cards (twig shape→hide; ant-mimicry→fool predators).
commonMisconceptions: 'The moth turned dark because of the soot / because it needed to' — the Lamarckian error; individuals don't change to fit.
'Adaptation happens within one insect's lifetime' — it occurs across generations.
'The moths chose to camouflage' — selection is not a conscious decision.
'The environment creates the new trait' — variation pre-exists; the environment selects among it.
'Evolution has a goal / strives toward perfection' — it's differential survival and reproduction, not purpose.

learn.summary: Teach natural selection in insects (ages 9-11) using the peppered moth: adaptation arises across MANY GENERATIONS as selection acts on EXISTING variation in a population, NOT by an individual changing within its lifetime. The load-bearing goal is to confront the Lamarckian error ('the moth turned dark because of the soot / because it needed to') by showing that it is which moths survive and breed that changes, not the moths themselves. A generation-by-generation selection model (toggling sooty vs clean environments and tracking the colour ratio, with a 'follow one moth' probe) is intended to make the mechanism visible; discussion, sequencing, and matching activities extend and check it; a static before/after scene is a useful scaffold with the limit that it cannot show the generational shift unfolding.

activities.title: Run the generational selection model: watch the population shift, not the individual
feedback: If a learner says the moths 'turned dark', point to the 'follow one moth' tag: that individual kept its colour the whole time — what changed is which moths survived to breed.
When the environment is toggled clean again and the ratio reverses, ask the learner to explain the reversal using survival of existing variants, not moths 'repainting' themselves.
If the learner expects an instant flip, slow the model down one generation at a time so they see the shift build up as more survivors of one colour reproduce.
Prompt: 'Where did the dark moths come from before the trees got sooty?' to surface that variation existed before the environment changed.
activities.rationale: A runnable generation-by-generation model is intended to let learners see trait frequency track the environment while an individual-tracking probe shows no individual changes, addressing the Lamarckian and 'change within one lifetime' misconceptions. The live ratio graph, environment toggle, and follow-one-moth probe are optional concrete mechanisms that make the abstract mechanism observable, not required implementations.
sourceClaims: The peppered moth (Biston betularia) shift toward melanic forms during industrial pollution and back after clean-air legislation is a documented example of natural selection.
Natural selection leads to predominance of certain inherited traits in a population and changes in trait frequency over generations (MS-LS4-4/MS-LS4-6); 3-LS4-3 covers differential survival.
learnerActions: Start with a pale-lichen tree and a moth population that is mostly light with a few dark moths (variation that already exists).

Each round, let a bird eat the moths it can most easily SEE; on the pale tree the dark moths stand out and are eaten, the survivors breed, and read the colour ratio off a live population graph as the next generation appears.
Slide the environment into the Industrial Revolution so soot blackens the bark; now the LIGHT moths are the visible ones. Run several more generations and watch the graph flip toward mostly dark.
Slide the air clean again and run more generations to watch the ratio reverse back toward pale.
Use a 'follow one moth' tag on a single individual across the rounds and confirm it NEVER changes colour — only which moths survive to breed changes.
State in your own words what changed: the population's mix of colours, not any single moth's colour.
activities.intendedInsight: Adaptation is selection acting on pre-existing variation across generations: better-camouflaged individuals survive and leave more offspring, so the population's trait frequency shifts. An adult moth's inherited wing colour stays the same for its whole adult life.

activities.title: Explain the reversal and transfer to other animals (stick insects and ant-mimicking spiders)
feedback: A correct explanation says: variation already existed; the better-camouflaged variant survived and reproduced more, so over many generations the population's common colour/shape changed; no individual transformed itself.

If a learner explains the stick insect as 'growing twiggy on purpose' or because it 'needed to', remove intention: by chance some were already more twig-like, and those survived more — nothing wanted or planned anything.

If the learner keeps the explanation only at the peppered-moth example, ask them to re-run the structure (variation → differential survival → inheritance over generations) on the spider to check for transfer.
activities.rationale: Transfer to the reversal case and to other insects distinguishes rote retelling from understanding of the mechanism, and the reversal is a strong counterexample to the idea that organisms change themselves to fit.
sourceClaims: The peppered moth (Biston betularia) shift toward melanic forms during industrial pollution and back after clean-air legislation is a documented example of natural selection.
learnerActions: Explain, in writing or aloud, why pale moths became common again after air pollution fell (for example through clean-air laws) and trees got cleaner — using survival of existing variants, not moths changing themselves.
Answer: 'Could ONE adult moth, in its own life, change its wing colour from pale to dark to hide better? So what actually changed — the moth, or the population?'
Apply the same reasoning to a stick insect: did one stick insect grow twiggy on purpose, or did twig-like ones survive better over generations? Explain using differential survival and inheritance.
Apply it again to ant-mimicking spiders: explain how looking like an ant could help an individual survive and pass on that appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: The same mechanism — differential survival of pre-existing variation, inherited across generations — explains the reversal and generalises to many camouflage and mimicry adaptations; it is not a one-off story about moths.

activities.title: Socratic discussion to surface and correct the Lamarckian idea
feedback: If the learner uses intentional language ('they knew they had to blend in'), point out that variation already existed by chance and the environment only affected which variant survived more — no moth wanted or planned anything.
If the learner compresses the change into one season or one moth, ask them to tally colour across several generations so inheritance over time becomes explicit.
activities.rationale: Responsive discussion can elicit and challenge intuitive teleological and Lamarckian reasoning that multiple-choice recognition may leave hidden. Discussion complements the model rather than replacing its demonstration of the mechanism.
learnerActions: Discuss the question 'Did the moth decide to change colour?' and defend your answer.
Respond to follow-ups that probe intention and timescale, e.g. 'Did the moths change because they needed to?' and 'Did this happen to one group of moths in a single summer?'
Restate the mechanism without using words like 'turned', 'changed to fit', or 'adapted itself'.
activities.intendedInsight: Natural selection is a filter acting on variation, not a conscious choice or a need-driven transformation, and it unfolds over many generations rather than within one lifetime.

activities.title: Check understanding: sequence, contrast, and match
feedback: For the contrast question, the correct answer is that dark moths survived better; reject the 'turned dark' option and ask the learner to explain why in terms of survival and breeding.
If a match is made without a survival reason, ask 'how does this adaptation help the insect survive and leave offspring?'
activities.rationale: Sequencing, targeted contrast, and matching check whether the learner can apply the mechanism; note that selecting among given options checks recognition and does not by itself show the learner can independently construct the explanation, so pair with the open explanation task.
learnerActions: Order the peppered-moth events into the correct selection story (clean trees with mostly pale moths → soot darkens bark → dark moths better hidden → dark survivors breed more → population becomes mostly dark → clean air returns → pale moths favoured again).
Answer a contrasting question: 'Did the moth turn dark, or did dark moths survive better?' and justify the choice.

Match each animal to the function of its adaptation (stick insect's twig shape → hide from predators; ant-mimicking spider's ant-like look → fool predators; peppered moth's dark colouring on sooty bark → camouflage). Note that the spider is an arachnid, not an insect.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the distinction between individual change and population shift, and connect adaptations to the survival function they serve.

activities.title: Read the before/after habitat scene (scaffold)
feedback: If the learner says the panel 'shows the moths changing', clarify that each panel is a snapshot of a population at one time; the shift between them happens across generations of survival and breeding, which this static scene does not itself show.
Prompt the learner to then run or recall the generational model to see the change actually unfold.
activities.rationale: A before/after annotated scene makes the camouflage-to-background link concrete and is a helpful entry scaffold, but its limit is that it shows two static states rather than the generational mechanism connecting them.
learnerActions: Study a two-panel scene — an industrial sooty tree and a recovered clean tree — each with its moth population.
Tap or point to reveal which moths are easiest for a predator to see in each panel.
Describe which colour is better hidden in each environment and predict which would survive more there.
activities.intendedInsight: Camouflage depends on the match between the moth's colour and its background, which sets up why selection favours different colours in different environments.

constraints: Keep the central distinction explicit throughout: the population's mix of traits changes across generations; individuals do not change their own colour to fit.
Confront the Lamarckian misconception directly ('turned dark because of the soot / because it needed to'), the teleological 'wanted/needed to' error, and the 'within one lifetime' error.
Make inheritance across many generations explicit — survivors pass their colour to offspring, and the shift builds up over generations.
Emphasise that variation pre-exists the environmental change; the environment selects among existing variants rather than creating the new trait.

Recognition-only tasks (multiple choice, matching, sequencing) check whether a learner can identify the correct mechanism but do not elicit independent construction of the explanation; pair them with an open explanation or discussion task.

The static before/after scene is a scaffold: it shows camouflage states but not the generational selection process, so do not treat it as a substitute for working through the generation-by-generation shift.

Live-graph, environment-toggle and follow-one-moth probes are illustrative optional mechanisms; the required learning is the mechanism itself, which can be reached through other media (e.g. a physical generation-by-generation tally).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source listed all three cited claims as verified:false; treat the curriculum alignments (DfE KS2 Y6; NGSS 3-LS4-3, MS-LS4-4/6) and the peppered-moth documentation as legacy unverified references.

The original row asserted that a non-spatial concept means '3D adds no conceptual value' and that a static telling 'can't' make the idea felt; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances and limits rather than universal laws.
Efficacy wording in the summary and the first activity's rationale was softened to intended/proposed phrasing because the interactive model and other activities are unvalidated.

The peppered-moth story is a standard school example; the real-world history (Kettlewell's and later Cook & Saccheri studies) involves nuance the source simplifies. Keep learner explanations at the age-appropriate level (differential survival of existing variation over generations) and avoid overstating experimental detail not supported by the cited references.

Tiered checkpoints (retell / explains survival-and-breeding shift / explains over-generations selection on variation) are preserved conceptually; exact age-tier labels are from the source and were not independently validated.

Several activity sourceClaims were set to [] because the cited claims support only the topic or curriculum content, not the specific teaching principle in those rationales (assessment methodology and scaffold affordance); no new source verification was performed.

probeDeeper: 'Could ONE moth, in its own life, change from pale to dark to hide better? So what actually changed — the moth, or the population?'
'Where did the dark moths come from in the first place, before the trees got sooty?' (variation exists before selection)
'When factories closed and trees got clean again, pale moths became common once more. Explain that using survival, not moths repainting themselves.' (reversal counterexample)
'A stick insect looks just like a twig. Did one stick insect grow twiggy on purpose, or did twig-like ones survive better over generations?'
assess.correctAnswer: It's not right — individual pale moths did NOT turn dark. What happened is natural selection over generations: moths already varied (some pale, some dark). On sooty trees the dark moths were better camouflaged, so more of them survived and had young; pale moths were spotted and eaten more. So over many generations the dark colour became common — the POPULATION changed because the survivors passed on their colour, not because any single moth changed itself.

errorPatterns.pattern: Lamarckian: thinks individual moths changed their own colour to match the sooty trees during their lifetime ('they turned dark to hide')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stress that a single moth is born its colour and keeps it for life — it cannot repaint itself. Track two colour variants across several generations: only the PROPORTIONS change, because survivors pass colour on. Contrast 'the moth changed' with 'which moths survived changed'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The pale moths turned dark so they could hide on the sooty trees
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the shift as moths transforming themselves; uses 'turned', 'changed to fit', 'adapted itself'

errorPatterns.pattern: Teleological/need-driven: thinks the moths changed because they NEEDED to or WANTED to survive ('they knew they had to blend in')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Remove intention: variation already existed by chance; the environment just decided which variant survived more. No moth wanted or planned anything. Selection is a filter, not a wish.
errorPatterns.distractor: The moths changed because they needed to survive on the dark trees
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: explains change as driven by the moth's need or intention rather than by survival of existing variants

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the change happened fast, within one moth or one season, not over many generations
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put time in: each generation passes colour to the next; the shift builds up over many generations of more dark survivors reproducing. Use a simple generation-by-generation tally.
errorPatterns.distractor: It all happened to one group of moths in a single summer
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks as if the population flipped in a single lifetime; no sense of inheritance across generations

responseLevels.gap: Explains the change as individual moths turning dark to fit the trees (Lamarckian), or as the moths wanting/needing to change.
responseLevels.full: Explains natural selection cleanly: variation already existed, dark moths survived and reproduced more on sooty trees, so over generations the population became mostly dark — individual moths did not change — AND transfers it (e.g. explains the reversal when trees cleaned up, or the stick insect, the same way).
responseLevels.partial: Mentions survival and camouflage but muddles the mechanism — e.g. says the survivors were better hidden yet still implies moths changed themselves, or leaves out that it happens over generations through inheritance.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: During the Industrial Revolution, tree trunks near factories got covered in dark soot, and over time dark peppered moths became far more common than pale ones. A child explains it like this: 'The pale moths turned dark to hide on the sooty trees.' Is that the right explanation? Tell me what actually happened, and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This is the classic Lamarckian error. A child who understands natural selection explains it as differential SURVIVAL of existing variation across GENERATIONS — the population shifts. A child with the intuitive (Lamarckian) idea says the moths changed themselves to fit, or 'needed to' change and so did, within their own lifetime. The second tier ('why?') is where the two split: same observation, opposite mechanism. An individual moth cannot change its colour to match soot; only the mix of the population can change over time.

sources.claim: KS2 Y6 pupils identify how animals and plants are adapted to suit their environment and that adaptation may lead to evolution.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS2 Y6 Evolution and inheritance)

sources.claim: Natural selection leads to predominance of certain inherited traits in a population and changes in trait frequency over generations (MS-LS4-4/MS-LS4-6); 3-LS4-3 covers differential survival.
sources.source: NGSS MS-LS4-4, MS-LS4-6 and 3-LS4-3 Biological Evolution

sources.claim: The peppered moth (Biston betularia) shift toward melanic forms during industrial pollution and back after clean-air legislation is a documented example of natural selection.
sources.source: Natural History Museum / peer-reviewed peppered-moth studies (Kettlewell; Cook & Saccheri) (general reference)

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting mixed numbers with like denominators has two viable routes: operate on the whole-number and fraction parts separately, or convert both to improper fractions. The separate-parts route exposes the two signature difficulties — in addition the fraction parts can sum past a whole (2 3/5 + 1 4/5 → 3 + 7/5 needs regrouping to 4 2/5), and in subtraction the minuend's fraction can be smaller than the subtrahend's, forcing a borrow (4 2/6 − 1 5/6: regroup 4 into 3 + 6/6). The convert-to-improper route sidesteps the borrow entirely, which is exactly why it is worth teaching as the fallback. Teach both, let the awkward subtraction MOTIVATE the improper method, and keep the denominator a fixed unit throughout.
bestPractices: Teach BOTH methods and let a subtraction that needs regrouping (4 2/6 − 1 5/6) motivate why converting to improper fractions is often cleaner
Make the borrow physical: exchange one whole for its equivalent in the common unit fraction (1 = 6/6) before subtracting the fraction parts
In addition, always check whether the fraction parts crossed a whole and regroup (7/5 → 1 2/5) so the answer is a proper mixed number
Estimate with the whole numbers first (2 3/5 + 1 4/5 is between 3 and 5, near 4½) to police the result
Hold the denominator as a fixed unit — fifths add to fifths — to block the add-across error carried over from whole-number habits
keyRepresentations: Number line: jump the whole numbers, then the fraction parts, crossing whole boundaries
Bar model with whole tiles plus fraction tiles; a whole tile that shatters into b unit-fractions for the borrow, or b fraction tiles that fuse into a whole
The regroup written as 4 = 3 + 6/6 (or the improper rewrite 26/6)
Improper-fraction form beside the mixed form for comparison
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the fraction parts (3/5 + 4/5 → 7/10), applying whole-number addition to numerator and denominator
Subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column and never borrows (4 2/6 − 1 5/6 → 3 3/6, taking |2−5|=3)
Leaves an improper fraction part in the answer (3 7/5) instead of regrouping to 4 2/5
Miscounts when converting mixed to improper (2 3/5 → 10/5 then forgets the +3/5, or writes 5/5)

learn.summary: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators (ages 9–10). Two routes are worth teaching: (a) operate on whole-number and fraction parts separately, which exposes the two signature difficulties — in addition the fraction parts can sum past a whole (2 3/5 + 1 4/5 → 3 + 7/5, regroup to 4 2/5), and in subtraction the first fraction can be smaller than the second, forcing a borrow (4 2/6 − 1 5/6: regroup 4 into 3 + 6/6); and (b) convert both to improper fractions, which sidesteps the borrow and is worth teaching as the cleaner fallback. Let the awkward subtraction motivate the improper method, keep the denominator a fixed unit throughout, and always tidy an improper fraction part back into a proper mixed number.

activities.title: Trade a whole for unit fractions: make the borrow and carry physical
feedback: If you take |2 − 5| = 3 and write 3 3/6, you subtracted the smaller fraction from the larger without exchanging. Trade one whole for 6 sixths first so you have 8 sixths to subtract from — or convert both to improper fractions (26/6 − 11/6).
If you write 3/5 + 4/5 as 7/10, you added the denominators too. Three fifths and four fifths is seven fifths: the size of the part does not change when you join same-size parts.
If you leave 3 7/5, check: is 7/5 more than a whole? Tidy it into the whole-number part to get 4 2/5. Your addition itself was correct.
activities.rationale: Making the regroup a felt exchange of one whole for its unit fractions targets the add-across and never-borrow misconceptions directly and keeps the denominator as a fixed unit. Locked fraction tiles make the add-across error impossible during the manipulation; the number line offers a parallel view of the same crossing.
sourceClaims: The add-across misconception (adding numerators AND denominators) is a central, documented error in fraction addition/subtraction, arising from misapplying whole-number addition and failing to treat the denominator as the size of the part.

Same-denominator addition items are answered correctly by the large majority (~92%) but a minority of lower-attaining pupils add both numerator and denominator; concrete materials and 'which is bigger' reasoning support remediation.
learnerActions: Work the subtraction 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 using whole tiles and fraction tiles that are locked to sixths so you cannot change the denominator.
Try to take away 5 sixths when you only have 2 — notice you are stuck. Break one whole tile into 6 sixths (the borrow), so you now have 8 sixths, and finish: 8/6 − 5/6 = 3/6, leaving 2 3/6 = 2 1/2.
Work the addition 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 the same way: gather the fifths, and when 5 fifths collect, fuse them into a fresh whole tile, giving 4 2/5.

Optionally model the same two problems on a number line: jump the whole numbers first, then the fraction parts, and watch a jump cross a whole boundary — the same regroup seen as a different representation.
Write each exchange as a number sentence: 4 = 3 + 6/6, and 7/5 = 1 + 2/5.
Say aloud whether the carry and the borrow are the same exchange running in opposite directions.
activities.intendedInsight: Borrowing is not a mysterious digit-move: it is literally trading one whole for its equivalent in the common unit fraction (1 = 6/6), and carrying is the reverse — fusing a whole-worth of unit fractions back into one whole. The denominator stays fixed because fifths only join with fifths.

activities.title: The improper-fraction fallback, side by side
feedback: If your two methods disagree, check the improper conversion: 2 wholes of fifths is 10/5, and you still add the 3/5 on top.
If you write 2 3/5 as 10/5, you forgot to add the 3/5 — it should be 13/5.

Standards expect pupils to add and subtract mixed numbers by replacing each with an equivalent (improper) fraction and/or by using properties of operations, so being fluent in both routes is the goal.
activities.rationale: The subtraction that needs a borrow is the natural motivation for the improper method; running both side by side lets learners compare and self-check. Miscounting during conversion is a known error to guard against.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction' (4.NF.B.3c). In England, adding/subtracting mixed numbers using equivalent fractions is a Year 6 objective.
learnerActions: Rewrite 4 2/6 and 1 5/6 as improper fractions (26/6 and 11/6), subtract to get 15/6, then convert back: 15/6 = 2 3/6 = 2 1/2.
Do the same subtraction by the separate-parts borrow method and check both answers match.
When converting 2 3/5 to improper, count carefully: 2 wholes is 10/5, plus 3/5 is 13/5 — do not drop the +3/5 or stop at 5/5.
Decide which method you found cleaner for the subtraction, and explain why converting to improper removed the borrow.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting to improper fractions avoids the borrow entirely, so it is a reliable fallback when the subtraction needs regrouping; both methods give the same answer when done carefully.

activities.title: Estimate first to police the answer
feedback: If your answer is far from the estimate, re-check for a missed borrow or for added denominators. Separately, check that the fraction part is proper; an untidied part like 3 7/5 has the right value but still needs regrouping to 4 2/5.
3 7/5 is not a tidy mixed number because 7/5 is more than a whole; regroup it to 4 2/5.
activities.rationale: Estimating with the whole numbers and then adjusting for the fraction parts gives learners an independent reasonableness check against value errors such as a missed borrow or added denominators. The proper-fraction check covers un-regrouped answers, which have the correct value.
learnerActions: Before computing 2 3/5 + 1 4/5, estimate using the whole numbers: the sum is between 3 and 5, and since both fraction parts are large, near 4 1/2.
Compute the exact answer and check it sits close to your estimate.

Repeat for 4 2/6 − 1 5/6: whole-number subtraction gives about 3, but because 2/6 is less than 5/6 the fraction part pulls the answer down by about a half, so expect a result between 2 and 3, around 2 1/2 — then confirm 2 1/2 is reasonable.
For each result, ask: is the fraction part proper (numerator less than denominator)? If not, regroup.
activities.intendedInsight: An estimate that starts with the whole numbers and then adjusts for the fraction parts catches value errors such as a missed borrow (3 3/6 instead of about 2 1/2) or added denominators (3 7/10 instead of about 4 1/2), because a wrong answer no longer sits near the estimate. An un-regrouped answer like 3 7/5 has the correct value (it equals 4 2/5), so an estimate cannot catch it; the separate proper-fraction check does that job.

activities.title: Study a worked carry and a worked borrow
feedback: If you cannot say where the extra sixths came from, trace them back to the one whole you broke apart: 1 = 6/6.
A worked example shows the steps but does not let you trigger the exchange on your own numbers — pair it with hands-on or written practice on fresh problems.
Matching mixed numbers to improper forms checks recognition; it does not by itself show you producing every regrouping step, so follow it with a problem you solve in full.
activities.rationale: A worked carry-and-borrow pair with revealable steps supports meaning-making; it is a scaffold, not independent practice, because the learner does not initiate the regroup on their own numbers.
learnerActions: Read a worked addition showing 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 with the step 7/5 revealed as 1 + 2/5, and explain in your own words why the whole-number part becomes 4.
Read a worked subtraction showing 4 rewritten as 3 + 6/6, and answer: why change the 4 into 3 and 6 more sixths?
Match each mixed number to its improper form (e.g. 4 2/6 ↔ 26/6).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading and explaining the regroup steps consolidates the meaning behind the exchange, even without acting it out yourself.

constraints: Lock the denominator as a fixed unit so fifths add to fifths; this blocks the add-across error carried over from whole-number habits.
Always check whether fraction parts crossed a whole and regroup so answers are proper mixed numbers (7/5 → 1 2/5).

Worked-example or revealable-step formats support meaning but do not let the learner trigger the exchange on their own numbers — treat them as scaffolds and follow with independent construction on fresh problems.

Recognition and matching tasks (mixed-to-improper, choosing the right answer) can check understanding but do not elicit the learner's own step-by-step regrouping; include tasks where the learner shows every step.
Teach both methods; do not present the improper route as the only correct one — the separate-parts route is where the borrow and carry become meaningful.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 = 4 2/5; 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 = 2 3/6 = 2 1/2 (improper: 26/6 − 11/6 = 15/6 = 2 1/2); 2 3/5 = 13/5. The subtraction's fraction parts give 2/6 − 5/6 = −3/6 = −1/2, so the answer sits about half a whole below the whole-number estimate of 3 (hence around 2 1/2). All consistent. The wrong answers 3 3/6, 3 7/5 and 7/10 appear only as errors to diagnose, never as valid options.

The original quiz design listed answer choices 2 1/2 and 2 3/6 together, which are equal (both correct); this ambiguous multiple-choice set was not reproduced as a learner question — only the genuine distractor 3 3/6 is used, as an error to diagnose.

The original source claimed the topic is 'planar' so '3D adds nothing' and that 'talk cannot enact the borrow'; these are catalog-format judgements, not established facts, and have been dropped rather than asserted. Spoken explanation and physical fraction pieces can both support this learning; no comparative necessity is claimed here.
The number-line representation from the original is included as an optional alternative view in the first activity.

probeDeeper: In the subtraction, why did you turn the 4 into a 3 — where did the extra sixths come from?
Estimate 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 before finishing — should it be above or below 4? How do you know?
Could you do the subtraction by turning both into improper fractions instead? Try it and see if you get the same.
Is 3 7/5 a tidy way to leave a mixed number — why or why not?

errorPatterns.pattern: Never borrows in subtraction: subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger in each column regardless of order — 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 → 3 3/6, taking |2−5| = 3 sixths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the exchange physical — trade one whole for 6/6 so there are 8 sixths to subtract from — or switch to improper fractions (26/6 − 11/6), which removes the borrow altogether
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 3 3/6 (or 3 1/2); the working shows 5/6−2/6 with no exchange of a whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across the fraction parts: 3/5 + 4/5 → 7/10, adding numerators AND denominators
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to fifths as a fixed unit — three fifths and four fifths is seven fifths — on a locked bar; re-establish joining same-size parts before regrouping
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The fraction part of the sum has a changed denominator (7/10 rather than 7/5); the whole numbers may be added correctly

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the answer with an improper fraction part: 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 → 3 7/5, not regrouping the 7/5 into 1 2/5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach — prompt 'is 7/5 more than a whole? then tidy it into the whole-number part'; the child already added correctly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer written as 3 7/5 (numerator ≥ denominator in a mixed number); the addition itself is sound

responseLevels.gap: Adds across the fraction parts, or never borrows (3 3/6); the denominator is not held as a fixed unit and regrouping is absent.
responseLevels.full: Solves both via a chosen method (separate parts with borrow/carry, or convert to improper), regroups the answer to a proper mixed number, estimates reasonableness with the whole numbers, and transfers to a new mixed-number add/subtract.
responseLevels.partial: Handles cases with no crossing and no borrow, but fails the regrouping subtraction or leaves an improper fraction part; can compute by one method but has no whole-number estimate to check against.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing every step: first 2 3/5 + 1 4/5, then 4 2/6 − 1 5/6.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items are engineered to force the two signature moves: the sum crosses a whole (fraction parts 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5), so a child who does not regroup leaves 3 7/5; the subtraction needs a borrow (2/6 < 5/6), so a child who subtracts column-by-column takes |2−5| and lands on 3 3/6. Watching the METHOD — not just the answer — reveals which happened, and the add-across error shows up immediately as a changed denominator. A child who regroups both ways, or who converts to improper fractions and gets 4 2/5 and 2 1/2, has the idea; the specific wrong answer names the specific fault.

In England, adding/subtracting mixed numbers using equivalent fractions is a Year 6 objective.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–7 (LANGUAGE): read and write numbers to at least 100 in WORDS — extending the number-word vocabulary to decade words and two-word compounds (fifty-seven), mapping word↔numeral↔quantity.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'read and write numbers to at least 100 in numerals and in words'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.3 'read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form' (the 0–100 word range sits within this).
• Operational details — building on words to twenty, the child learns the DECADE words (twenty, thirty ... ninety) and the hyphenated compound structure 'tens-word + ones-word' (fifty-seven = 57). The English pattern above twenty is regular and tens-first (unlike the teens), so the main work is (i) the decade spellings, (ii) the fifteen/fifty, thirteen/thirty confusions, and (iii) hyphenation and word↔numeral order.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): read 'fifty-seven' and write 57. Tier B (6–7): write 'eighty-three' when shown 83. Tier C (7): read and write all decade words and compound words to 100 correctly, spelling and hyphenating them.
bestPractices: Teach the DECADE words as a set (twenty…ninety) and their link to the tens digit, then the regular compound rule 'decade-word + ones-word' (sixty-four) — above twenty the words are tens-first and regular, a helpful contrast with the teens.
Drill the sound-alike traps directly: thirteen/thirty, fifteen/fifty, etc. — pair each with its numeral and a quantity so meaning disambiguates the near-identical words.
Always connect word ↔ numeral ↔ quantity (read 'seventy-two' → write 72 → show ~72 on a line) so the words carry meaning, not just spelling.
Address orthography explicitly: the hyphen in compounds (forty-five), the tricky spellings (forty not fourty, ninety), coordinating with spelling/handwriting teaching.
Practise both directions and across decade boundaries (seventy-nine → eighty) to cement the compound structure.
keyRepresentations: Decade-word chart (20–90) linked to the tens digit and to bundles of tens.
Word-building frame: [decade word] + [ones word] → compound (sixty + four → sixty-four) beside 64.
Triple-match cards: numeral ↔ word ↔ quantity/number-line position.
Sound-alike contrast pairs (thirteen|thirty, fifteen|fifty) each with a set/numeral.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing '-teen' and '-ty' words by sound and spelling (fifteen vs fifty, thirteen vs thirty).
Misspelling irregular decades (forty as 'fourty', ninety as 'ninty').
Omitting the hyphen or writing compounds as one/many words incorrectly.
Transposing compound numbers back to numerals (writing 'forty-two' as 24) — carrying over the teen ones-first habit.
Writing decade words with extra zeros from the spoken parts (fifty-seven → 507).

learn.summary: For ages 6–7: reading and writing numbers to at least 100 in words, extending from number words to twenty into the decade words (twenty, thirty … ninety) and two-word hyphenated compounds (fifty-seven). The central work is mapping word ↔ numeral ↔ quantity, learning commonly misspelled decade words (forty drops the u of four; ninety keeps the e of nine), fixing the hyphen, and untangling the sound-alike '-teen'/'-ty' pairs (fifteen/fifty, thirteen/thirty). Above twenty the English words follow a regular tens-first pattern (decade word, then ones word), a useful contrast with the teens, although some decade stems (twenty, thirty, fifty, forty) are spelled irregularly.

activities.title: Build compound number words from decade + ones parts
feedback: If a learner writes 'eighty-three' as 803, show that eighty-three means 8 tens and 3 ones: build it and place the 3 into the ones column of a tens/ones frame so it does not trail after 80.
If the compound is run together or missing the hyphen, point to the two parts (decade word + ones word) and show the hyphen joins exactly those two words.
If the order is reversed (writing 'forty-two' as 24), re-read the word tens-first: 'forty' is the tens, '-two' is the ones, so the tens digit comes first (42).
If a decade word is misspelled ('fourty', 'ninty'), flag the correct spelling (forty, ninety) and keep it visible as a reference.
activities.rationale: Composing the word from decade and ones parts and mapping it to both numeral and quantity makes the regular tens-first structure explicit and keeps the words meaningful rather than rote spellings. An optional on-screen builder where tiles snap to the numeral and a number-line position can make this mapping concrete, but the same can be done with word-part cards and a drawn line.
sourceClaims: Number words above twenty are regular tens-first compounds; the persistent difficulties are the -teen/-ty sound-alikes and irregular decade spellings (forty, ninety).
learnerActions: Choose a decade-word part (e.g. 'sixty') and a ones-word part (e.g. 'four') and join them into the compound word 'sixty-four', writing it with the hyphen.

Write the numeral64 beside sixty-four and locate it on a0–100 line. Optionally join on-screen tens and ones word tiles so the compound immediately links to its numeral and line position, with a reverse round asking the learner to assemble or spell the word for83.
Work the reverse direction: shown the numeral 83, say and then correctly spell the word 'eighty-three'.
Write seventy-eight, seventy-nine, eighty, eighty-one, then ninety-nine and one hundred. Notice when a decade changes, when a hyphenated compound is used, and how100 is written.
activities.intendedInsight: For numbers from21 to99 with a nonzero ones digit, the English word is a tens-first compound, such as sixty-four. Exact tens use the decade word alone, and100 is one hundred; connect each form to its numeral and quantity.

activities.title: Sound-alike contrast: '-teen' versus '-ty'
feedback: If a learner uses fifteen and fifty interchangeably, contrast them directly: fifty = 5 tens; fifteen = 1 ten and 5 ones. Say them slowly, stressing -ty vs -teen, and pair each with its base-ten model.
If reading 76 drifts toward a teen word, re-anchor on the tens: seventy is 7 tens, then the ones word -six follows, giving seventy-six.
activities.rationale: The -teen/-ty confusion is a persistent difficulty noted in teaching guidance; attaching each word to its numeral and a concrete quantity disambiguates by meaning. A listen-and-repeat prompt (optional tap-to-hear audio) can help learners hear the ending difference.
sourceClaims: Number words above twenty are regular tens-first compounds; the persistent difficulties are the -teen/-ty sound-alikes and irregular decade spellings (forty, ninety).
learnerActions: Take a minimal pair such as fifteen/fifty and read both aloud, stressing the ending (-teen vs -ty).
Beside each word, write its numeral (fifteen = 15, fifty = 50) and show a matching quantity or base-ten model (fifteen = 1 ten and 5 ones; fifty = 5 tens).
Repeat with thirteen/thirty and other pairs, each time pairing word, numeral and quantity so meaning separates the near-identical sounds.
Answer a quick 'fifteen or fifty?' decision with the set of objects visible, choosing by quantity rather than guessing.
activities.intendedInsight: The '-ty' word names a number of tens (fifty = 5 tens) while the '-teen' word is a teen (fifteen = 1 ten and 5); linking each to a quantity removes the guesswork from the near-identical sounds.

activities.title: Use number words in a real read-and-write task
feedback: If the numeral comes out as 803 (or similarly 507 for fifty-seven), name the error (concatenating the spoken parts as full digits) and rebuild using a tens/ones frame so the ones digit sits in the ones place.
If teen and decade are swapped, return to the contrast pair with quantities before retrying.
Confirm success when the learner produces both directions correctly: 'seventy-six' for 76 and 83 for 'eighty-three'.
activities.rationale: Using the words in a live read/write task, rather than defining them, surfaces the specific slips (teen/decade confusion and the concatenation error) and shows real fluency across both directions. A short matching or fill-the-blank set (e.g. match 'seventy-two' to 72, spell the word for 45) consolidates afterward but checks recognition rather than independent production.
learnerActions: Given a label showing the numeral 76, write the words for a new label a customer could read ('seventy-six'), ordered correctly and hyphenated.
Given the word 'eighty-three' on a card, read it and write the numeral (83).
Check a friend's work: they wrote 803 for 'eighty-three' — decide whether it is right and explain what went wrong.
Compare 40 and 14 (and 'ninety' vs 'nineteen'): read each aloud and write each the other way to confirm you can move both directions.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who has the system can move fluently in both directions — word to numeral and numeral to word — without concatenating the spoken parts or confusing teen and decade words.

constraints: Teach the decade words (twenty…ninety) as a set linked to the tens digit before drilling compounds, so compounds are built on an understood base.
Always connect word ↔ numeral ↔ quantity; spelling practice alone does not guarantee the words carry meaning.

Address orthography explicitly: the hyphen in compounds, and the commonly misspelled decade words forty (irregular: drops the u of four, not 'fourty') and ninety (regular: keeps the e of nine, not 'ninty'); coordinate with spelling/handwriting teaching.

Matching provided words to numerals checks recognition; independent spelling requires a response in which the word is not supplied. A free-writing or open fill-in task can elicit that production, especially when the learner also explains its quantity.

A static decade-word chart with tap-to-hear audio is a useful reference wall but does not rehearse active spelling/production or sound-alike discrimination; treat it as support, not the main practice.
Practise both directions and across decade boundaries (seventy-nine → eighty) to cement the compound structure.

assess.correctAnswer: Writes 'seventy-six' (decade word + ones word, correctly ordered and hyphenated) and writes 83 for 'eighty-three'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the -ty decade word with the -teen word: reads/writes 'fifteen/50' or 'fifty/15' interchangeably
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the pair explicitly (fifty = 5 tens; fifteen = 10 and 5). Say them slowly, stressing -ty vs -teen, and pair each with its base-ten model.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Communities Protecting Resources — how communities use science ideas to protect Earth's resources and environment

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 6, Working scientifically / Living things and their habitats):** report and present findings from enquiries, including conclusions and causal relationships, and identify scientific evidence used to support or refute ideas — here applied to real environmental-protection efforts.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-ESS3-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS3-1].

- **Operational details:** This is an OBTAIN-AND-COMBINE-INFORMATION topic: the skill is gathering evidence about real solutions and explaining the SCIENCE that makes each work, then seeing how individual and community action combine. Anchor in three concrete, contrasting real examples so the child generalises across cases rather than memorising one — e.g. solar panels/wind (convert sunlight or moving air into electricity, cutting fossil-fuel burning), recycling and composting (returning materials and nutrients to use instead of landfill), and habitat restoration / reforestation or wetland protection (rebuilding the ecosystem services a place provides). For EACH, the load-bearing step is naming the underlying science idea, not just the action: 'solar panels convert sunlight to electricity, so less coal is burned, so less CO₂ released'. Then draw the scaling insight: one household helps a little, but a whole community (a town scheme, a school, a council policy) multiplies the effect — collective action is why these work. Keep it evidence-based and hopeful: pupils compare sources, weigh how well each solution works, and see that science informs real choices people make together.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/relational). Pupils this age can hold a multi-step causal chain (action → science mechanism → environmental benefit) and reason about aggregation (individual × many = community effect), but still lean on concrete named cases. Success = three real examples described, the science idea behind each explained, and an account of how individual and community efforts combine.
bestPractices: Use three contrasting real examples (energy, materials, habitat) so pupils generalise the pattern rather than memorising a single case.
For each example, insist pupils name the underlying SCIENCE idea, not just the action — e.g. 'sunlight → electricity → less coal burned'.
Make the individual→community scaling explicit: show that a small action × many people is what produces a measurable effect.
Have pupils obtain and COMBINE information from more than one source, comparing how well solutions work — mirroring the standard's evidence skill.
Keep the framing solution-focused and hopeful so pupils leave with agency rather than eco-anxiety.
Connect at least one example to the pupils' own community or school so the abstraction becomes personally actionable.
keyRepresentations: An illustrated community map dotted with real protection projects (solar roofs, wind turbine, recycling centre, restored wetland, orchard)
Action → science-mechanism → benefit causal chains for each example
A 'one household vs whole town' scaling comparison (small effect multiplied)
Evidence-comparison table: solution, how it works, how much it helps
Before/after images of a restored habitat or a switched-to-renewable town
commonMisconceptions: Thinking naming the action ('they recycle') counts as explaining it, without the science mechanism behind why it helps.
Believing one person's actions are pointless because they're tiny — missing that collective scaling is the whole point.
Assuming renewable/clean solutions have no costs or trade-offs, or work everywhere equally.
Confusing recycling (returning materials to use) with simply throwing things away 'nicely'.
Thinking environmental protection is only governments' job, not something communities and individuals do together.
Treating a single success story as proof a solution works everywhere, without comparing evidence across cases.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: pupils obtain and combine information about how communities use science ideas to protect Earth's resources, across three contrasting real cases (energy, materials, habitat). The load-bearing skill is naming the underlying science mechanism behind each action (not just the action), and reasoning about how individual actions scale when many people combine them to community-level effects. Primary approach: an in-role interview where pupils probe 'why does it work?' and hear real mechanisms plus honest numbers. Supporting approaches include a browsable project map, a scaling comparison, and recognition-style matching, each with stated affordances and limits.

activities.title: Interview the people doing the protecting
feedback: If the pupil just repeats the action ('they recycle'), ask 'what does recycling actually do to the materials, and why is that better than landfill?' to force the mechanism.
If the pupil says solar is good because it's 'clean and green', ask 'where does the electricity come from if there are NO panels?' to supply the fossil-fuel comparison.
If the pupil gives a cost reason ('the electricity is free'), acknowledge the saving, then ask specifically what happens to the air or pollution when less fossil fuel is burned.

If the pupil thinks a cloudy week makes the panels useless, ask whether they still help overall across a year: panels produce less in cloudy weather but still generate some electricity, and over a year their total output can replace electricity that would otherwise come from burning fossil fuels.
If the pupil dismisses effort as pointless ('one town is too small to matter'), build from one to many: revisit how individual solutions add up when a whole community combines them.
Reinforce when the pupil both traces a full causal chain AND notes how many efforts combine.
activities.rationale: The topic is fundamentally about gathering and combining information from people doing real protection work and reasoning about their choices; an open, evidence-seeking spoken exchange lets the learner obtain evidence and probe the mechanism directly, and responsive questioning can surface and address slogan-only thinking.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-ESS3-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS3-1].
Year 6 pupils should report and present findings including causal relationships and identify scientific evidence used to support or refute ideas.
Solar photovoltaic and wind generation convert sunlight and moving air into electricity, displacing fossil-fuel combustion and reducing CO₂ emissions.
learnerActions: Take on the role of a reporter and interview a community-project lead in role — e.g. a solar-co-op organiser, a reforestation ranger, a recycling-scheme coordinator.
Ask the blunt, evidence-seeking question: 'Does putting panels on roofs really make a difference? How does it actually help?'

Record the mechanism the character gives, e.g. 'sunlight becomes electricity, so power stations need to burn less fossil fuel such as coal or gas (where the local electricity comes from them), so less CO₂ goes up — here's how many homes we've switched.'
Respond to the character's flip-question — 'one roof is tiny, so why do we sign up whole streets at once?' — and explain in your own words why many people combining the same small action matters.
Interview at least two more leads (reforestation ranger, recycling coordinator) and note the same shape of argument: a science mechanism paired with collective action.
After the interviews, compare how well each solution works and where it might have costs or trade-offs.
activities.intendedInsight: Protecting resources means pairing a science mechanism (e.g. sunlight → electricity → less fossil fuel burned) with collective action; the science idea is only half the story, and the power comes from many people combining the same action.

activities.title: Map the community's protection projects
feedback: If the pupil names the action without the science idea, reopen that hotspot and ask them to state the mechanism before continuing.
If the pupil treats recycling as 'throwing things away nicely', clarify that recycling returns materials to use instead of landfill.
Prompt the pupil to compare the 'how much does it help?' flaps across projects rather than treating one success story as proof it works everywhere.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal map presents and combines several worked examples with their mechanisms in one browsable place, supporting the obtain-and-combine half of the standard. Note this is a fixed presentation: it shows cross-links but does not dynamically model scaling, so pair it with an activity that makes aggregation explicit.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-ESS3-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS3-1].
learnerActions: Browse an illustrated community map with hotspots: solar rooftops, a wind turbine, a recycling centre, a restored wetland, a community orchard.
Tap each hotspot to reveal three things: the action, the science idea behind it, and a lift-the-flap 'how much does it help?'
Follow cross-links that show how separate efforts add up across the town.
For each project, say the underlying science mechanism aloud or in writing before moving on — e.g. 'sunlight → electricity → less fossil fuel (such as coal or gas) burned in power stations'.
Connect at least one project to your own school or neighbourhood: what could happen here?
activities.intendedInsight: Several contrasting worked examples (energy, materials, habitat) share the same pattern — an action backed by a science mechanism that produces an environmental benefit — so the learner generalises rather than memorising one case.

activities.title: One household versus the whole town
feedback: If the pupil concludes one person's action is worthless, point back to the gauge after town-wide adoption and ask what changed and why.
If the pupil assumes the numbers are exact, remind them these magnitudes are illustrative, not precise predictions.
Reinforce when the pupil links the multiplied gauge movement to the idea of combined community effort.
activities.rationale: Letting pupils toggle household-versus-town adoption and watch a shared meter move can make the individual-vs-community scaling felt. Because this topic is about combining real information rather than simulating a system, keep magnitudes honest and illustrative so the model does not imply invented precision.
learnerActions: Start with a single household adopting solar, recycling, or restoration and note the small effect on a shared resource/emissions gauge.
Toggle to town-wide adoption and watch the same gauge move further, making the multiplied effect visible.
Explain in your own words why 'a small action × many people' is what produces a measurable effect.
State one honest limit or trade-off for the solution you explored (e.g. it may not work equally everywhere).
activities.intendedInsight: Individual actions are small but not pointless; collective scaling is the whole reason these solutions work at the community level.

activities.title: Match the action to its science idea
feedback: For a wrong match, restate the action and ask 'what does this physically do, and why does that help the environment?'

If the pupil miscategorises an energy source, revisit what 'renewable' means: a source that is naturally replenished on human timescales (like sunlight or wind), versus fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) that took millions of years to form and are used up much faster than they can be replaced. Burning fossil fuels also releases CO₂, but burning is not what makes a source non-renewable.
If the pupil tries to force recycling, composting or reforestation into the renewable-vs-fossil sort, clarify these are resource-protection actions, not ways of generating electricity.
activities.rationale: Matching action-to-mechanism checks the core understanding efficiently. This is a recognition-only format: it can confirm whether the mechanism link is known but does not elicit the independent evidence-gathering and combining the standard centres on, so treat it as a check rather than the main teaching, and use it alongside the interview.
learnerActions: Match each action (solar panels, recycling, reforestation, wind turbine, composting) to the science idea that explains why it helps.
Answer a question on why combining many people's actions at community scale produces a measurable effect that a single household's action alone cannot.

Sort only the energy-generation examples into renewable (e.g. solar, wind) versus non-renewable/fossil-fuel (e.g. coal, gas, oil); note that recycling, composting and reforestation protect resources in other ways and are not energy sources, so they do not belong in either energy category.
activities.intendedInsight: Each protective action is backed by a specific science mechanism, and many people's actions combining at community scale multiply the effect; among energy sources, renewables are naturally replenished while fossil fuels take millions of years to form and run out, and burning them also releases CO₂.

constraints: Pupils must name the underlying SCIENCE idea for each example, not just the action — the mechanism is the load-bearing step.
Use three contrasting real examples (energy, materials, habitat) so pupils generalise rather than memorising a single case.
Pupils should obtain and COMBINE information from more than one source and compare how well solutions work.
Keep the framing solution-focused and hopeful so pupils leave with agency rather than eco-anxiety.
Connect at least one example to the pupils' own community or school so the abstraction becomes personally actionable.
The project map is a fixed presentation: it browses worked examples but does not dynamically model scaling — pair it with an activity that makes aggregation explicit.
The scaling dashboard's magnitudes must be honest/illustrative, not presented as precise predictions, because the topic is about combining real information, not simulating a system.
The matching quiz is recognition-only: it checks whether the mechanism link is known but does not elicit independent evidence-gathering or construction of an explanation.
Keep the renewable-versus-fossil sort to energy sources only; recycling, composting and reforestation are resource-protection actions, not energy-generation methods.
Treat success stories carefully: a single case is not proof a solution works everywhere; compare evidence across cases.
Renewable/clean solutions have costs and trade-offs and do not work everywhere equally — present this honestly.
Frame collective action as individual actions combining and multiplying, not as community action being superior to or replacing individual effort.

Two of the three cited sources (NGSS 5-ESS3-1 and the EPA renewable/CO₂ claim) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE Year 6 claim is marked verified:true. Do not treat any as independently re-checked here.

The scaling-dashboard activity depends on numeric gauges that were flagged in the source as potentially 'inventing tidy numbers'; keep magnitudes clearly illustrative and avoid asserting specific emissions figures that are not sourced.

The intermittency feedback (panels still help overall across a year despite cloudy periods) is a qualitative restoration of the source's assessment probe; no cited source quantifies it, so keep it qualitative.

The '3D adds nothing' judgement from the source was dropped as a catalog-fit opinion, not a pedagogical law; a spatial model is simply not required for this evidence-focused topic, but this is not a universal claim about 3D media.

The matching activity's NGSS source claim was removed because the obtain-and-combine standard does not support a recognition-only check as a teaching principle; the claim supported only the topic, not the method.

probeDeeper: Where does the electricity come from if there are no solar panels — and why is that worse for the environment?
Give me a second, different example of a community protecting a resource, and tell me the science behind it.
It's cloudy for a whole week — do the panels still help overall? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: The panels convert sunlight into electricity, so the town needs less electricity made by burning fossil fuels. Burning less coal, oil or gas means less pollution and less carbon dioxide released — and that is what helps the environment. It works because many schools, homes and communities are doing the same thing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Slogan without mechanism — 'solar panels help because they're clean and green'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask the follow-up 'where does the electricity come from if there are NO panels?' to force the fossil-fuel comparison that supplies the mechanism.
errorPatterns.distractor: Solar panels help because they are made of clean, green materials.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asserts an environmental benefit but cannot say what the panels do or why it helps; no link to displacing fossil fuels

errorPatterns.pattern: Economic reason mistaken for environmental — 'they help because the electricity is free'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate cost from environment: acknowledge the saving, then ask specifically what happens to the AIR or to pollution when less fossil fuel is burned.
errorPatterns.distractor: They help the environment because the electricity becomes free.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the benefit as saving money rather than as reducing pollution or fossil-fuel use

errorPatterns.pattern: Agency dismissal — 'one town's panels are too small to matter, so it doesn't really help'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build from one to many: revisit that individual solutions add up and communities combining efforts is how the difference is made.
errorPatterns.distractor: One town's panels are far too small to matter, so it doesn't really help.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses the effort as pointless against a global problem, missing how individual and community actions combine

responseLevels.gap: Calls the panels 'good' or 'green' with no mechanism, or thinks they store/make sunshine; no environmental chain.
responseLevels.full: Gives the full causal chain (sunlight to electricity replaces fossil-fuel electricity, so less pollution) and applies the same reasoning to a second community example, noting how many efforts combine.
responseLevels.partial: States that panels turn sunlight into electricity AND that this helps, but lists these without connecting the chain to burning fewer fossil fuels, or cannot supply a second example.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A town puts solar panels on the school roof and says it is helping the environment. Explain what the solar panels actually do, and why that helps the environment.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands says the panels displace fossil-fuel electricity and traces the chain to less pollution. A child with only a slogan says solar is 'clean' or 'green' with no mechanism, or gives an economic reason (free electricity) that isn't an environmental one — neither reaches the fossil-fuel chain the correct answer names.
