pedagogy.summary: This is the PROCEDURAL partner to the Angle Sum Rules concept: the child treats angle measure as ADDITIVE (a whole angle equals the sum of its non-overlapping parts, CCSS 4.MD.7) and turns an angle diagram into an EQUATION with a symbol for the unknown, then solves it. The move that matters is representing 'the parts share a fixed whole' as arithmetic — 65° + x° = 180° on a straight line, or 120° + 90° + x° = 360° at a point — and solving by subtraction. Taught well it is not a new fact but a disciplined routine: read the configuration to fix the whole (180° or 360°), write the equation, solve, and sanity-check the answer against the diagram. The diagram is a source of GIVEN facts, not something to remeasure.
bestPractices: Make the equation explicit every time: write 65 + x = 180 (or 120 + 90 + x = 360), name the whole first, then solve — so the reasoning is visible and checkable rather than a mental leap to an answer.
Anchor the whole to the configuration before any arithmetic: straight line → 180°, point → 360°; decide which BEFORE computing, so a point problem is never solved with 180°.
Use a bar/part-whole model of the fixed whole with the unknown as a labelled segment, connecting the algebraic symbol to the shared-whole picture.
Insist the diagram gives facts, not measurements: the answer comes from the marked angles and the rule, NOT from putting a protractor on the printed (often not-to-scale) figure.
Separate a reasoning error (wrong whole, non-additive) from an arithmetic slip (mis-subtracting from 180) when marking — they need different help.
Progress from one unknown on a line, to one unknown among several at a point, to decomposition (two parts making a named whole).
keyRepresentations: Equation with a symbol for the unknown: 65 + x = 180, 120 + 90 + x = 360
Bar / part-whole model of the fixed whole (180° or 360°) with the unknown as a labelled segment
The straight line (180°) and the full point (360°) as the two 'wholes' to subtract from
Decomposition diagram: a large angle split into marked parts that sum to it
commonMisconceptions: Subtracts from the wrong whole — uses 180° at a point or 360° on a straight line because the configuration was not identified first.
Treats angle measure as non-additive — tries to measure the unknown on the diagram instead of computing it from the others.
Reads the diagram as if it were to scale — assumes two angles that 'look equal' are equal (e.g. an isosceles-looking triangle), or measures the printed unknown, rather than using the marked values.
Arithmetic slip when subtracting from 180°/360° (e.g. 180 − 145 gives 45 instead of 35) — the angle reasoning is sound but the subtraction fails.

learn.summary: Learners treat angle measure as additive (a whole angle equals the sum of its non-overlapping parts, CCSS 4.MD.7) and turn an angle diagram into an equation with a symbol for the unknown, then solve by subtraction. The disciplined routine is: read the configuration to fix the whole (straight line = 180°, point = 360°, or a decomposition whole that is either named or found by adding the parts), write the equation, solve, and sanity-check the answer against the diagram. The diagram supplies given facts from its marked values; it is not to be remeasured with a protractor, and it may be drawn not to scale.

activities.title: Name the whole, then build and solve the equation
feedback: If the equation uses the wrong whole (e.g. 120 + 90 + x = 180 for angles at a point, or 360 on a straight line), this is a reasoning error: go back and re-name the whole from the configuration. Sort several diagrams by which whole applies before computing again.

If the equation is correct but the final number is off (e.g. writing 180 − 145 = 45 when the correct result is 35), this is an arithmetic slip, not an angle error: redo the subtraction carefully with a number line or column method; the geometry is already sound.
If no equation appears and a protractor is reached for, point back to the marked values: the other angles plus the rule fix the answer, so cover the figure and solve from the numbers alone.
activities.rationale: Making the equation and the chosen whole explicit every time keeps the reasoning visible and checkable, and lets a reasoning error be separated from an arithmetic slip — which need different help. Anchoring the whole to the configuration before computing prevents solving a point problem with 180°.
sourceClaims: Angle measure is additive: an angle decomposed into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts; students solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram, using an equation with a symbol for the unknown (4.MD.7).

In diagnostic data on finding a missing angle, some wrong answers are genuine misconceptions (e.g. subtracting from 360 instead of 180) while the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip in subtracting from 180 by students who knew the rule; another group wrongly assumed the triangle was isosceles because it looked that way — so reasoning errors and arithmetic slips must be distinguished, and 'not drawn to scale' framing helps.
learnerActions: Look at each diagram and first decide and state the whole before any arithmetic: a straight line split by a ray is a half turn (180°); angles meeting at a point make a whole turn (360°); for a decomposed angle, either the whole is named and you find a missing part, or the parts are marked and you add them to find the whole.
For a straight line with one angle marked 65° and the other marked x, write the equation 65 + x = 180, then solve to get x = 115°.
For angles round a point marked 120°, 90° and x, write 120 + 90 + x = 360, then solve to get x = 150°.
For a large angle decomposed into two marked parts, 35° and 40°, write 35 + 40 = w with a symbol for the whole, then solve to get w = 75°.
After solving, check the answer back against the fixed whole (do all the parts add to 180° or 360°, or to the stated decomposition whole?).
activities.intendedInsight: An unknown angle is determined by the marked angles and the fixed whole, so it can be computed with an equation rather than measured. Choosing the correct whole (180° vs 360° vs a decomposition whole) is the first decision, not an afterthought.

activities.title: Part-whole bar model linking the symbol to the shared whole
feedback: If the segments overflow or underfill the bar, the parts do not sum to the chosen whole — recheck either the whole or the arithmetic.
If a learner can fill the bar but not write the matching equation, pair each step: 'the gap' becomes '180 − 65', and 'parts fill the whole' becomes '65 + x = 180'.
activities.rationale: A part-whole/bar model connects the algebraic unknown to the shared-whole picture, supporting learners who treat angle measure as non-additive by showing parts recombining to the whole and a missing part found by subtraction.
sourceClaims: The Progressions develop unknown-angle problems from angle additivity: decomposing an angle and recombining the parts, then finding a missing part by subtraction from the whole.

Angle measure is additive: an angle decomposed into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts; students solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram, using an equation with a symbol for the unknown (4.MD.7).
learnerActions: Draw or use a bar representing the fixed whole (e.g. a bar labelled 180° for a straight line, or 360° for a point).
Fill the bar with the known angles as labelled segments, leaving a gap for the unknown.
Label the remaining gap as x, and read off that x is what is left when the known parts are taken from the whole.
Connect this to the equation: the gap in the bar is 180 − 65, which is the same as solving 65 + x = 180.
Optionally, use a live model where solving the subtraction makes the x segment snap to exactly fill the bar, so the 'parts complete the whole' idea is visible.
activities.intendedInsight: The algebraic symbol x corresponds to a concrete missing segment of a fixed shared whole; subtraction finds the gap that completes the whole.

activities.title: Decompose and recombine a concrete angle
feedback: If a learner still reaches for a protractor on the missing part, revisit the recombination: since the parts provably sum to the whole, the missing part is fixed by subtraction and does not need measuring.
If the two parts don't sum to the stated whole, check which part is mismarked rather than assuming the rule failed.
activities.rationale: Decomposing and recombining a concrete angle makes additivity tangible before it is used in reverse to find a missing part — the development route described in the K–5 Progressions.
sourceClaims: The Progressions develop unknown-angle problems from angle additivity: decomposing an angle and recombining the parts, then finding a missing part by subtraction from the whole.
learnerActions: Take a concrete angle (e.g. a cut paper wedge, or an angle built from two strips) and split it into two marked parts.
Add the two parts to confirm they equal the whole angle (e.g. 35° + 40° = 75°).
Reverse the process: cover one part and find it by subtracting the known part from the whole.
State in words that non-overlapping parts that exactly fill the angle always sum to the whole, so a missing part can be computed rather than measured.
Note that the paper wedge or strips are physical approximations with slight thickness; the mathematical angle being reasoned about is the idealised figure they represent.
activities.intendedInsight: Angle measure is additive: parts sum to the whole, and reversing this gives a missing part by subtraction. This directly addresses the belief that an unknown angle must be measured.

activities.title: Not-to-scale diagram: reason from marked values, not appearance
feedback: If the answer is close to the printed size rather than 115°, the learner measured or trusted appearance — redo it from the marked values with the figure covered.
If an answer is justified by 'they look the same', point out that only marked or equal-labelled angles can be assumed equal.
activities.rationale: Diagnostic data shows learners who read diagrams as to-scale (e.g. assuming an isosceles-looking triangle) make reasoning errors; 'not drawn to scale' framing and solving from marked values counter this.
sourceClaims: In diagnostic data on finding a missing angle, some wrong answers are genuine misconceptions (e.g. subtracting from 360 instead of 180) while the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip in subtracting from 180 by students who knew the rule; another group wrongly assumed the triangle was isosceles because it looked that way — so reasoning errors and arithmetic slips must be distinguished, and 'not drawn to scale' framing helps.
learnerActions: Work a diagram labelled 'not drawn to scale' where the printed unknown angle looks smaller than the given 65° angle (for example, drawn acute) but must still equal 115° by the rule.
Cover the figure and solve from the marked numbers and the fixed whole alone (65 + x = 180, x = 115°).
Only then reveal the drawing and notice the picture was misleading.
Discuss a case where two angles 'look equal' but are not marked equal, and explain why you cannot assume equality from appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: A diagram carries stated facts, not scale: answers come from the marked values and the rule, not from measuring the printed figure or assuming look-alike angles are equal.

activities.title: Mixed practice: choose the whole each time
feedback: If one whole is applied to every diagram regardless of configuration, sort the diagrams by which whole applies before solving.
If an impossible answer slips through (e.g. parts exceeding the whole), use the sanity-check step to catch it.
Writing the relationship two ways (65 + x = 180 vs x = 180 − 65) shows flexible understanding; if only one form is possible, revisit the part-whole model.
activities.rationale: Varied configurations force the learner to select the whole and expose a wrong-whole error; requiring a written equation reveals whether the additive structure is understood and distinguishes arithmetic slips from reasoning errors. This volume of varied, feedback-rich practice is how the routine is mastered.
sourceClaims: In diagnostic data on finding a missing angle, some wrong answers are genuine misconceptions (e.g. subtracting from 360 instead of 180) while the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip in subtracting from 180 by students who knew the rule; another group wrongly assumed the triangle was isosceles because it looked that way — so reasoning errors and arithmetic slips must be distinguished, and 'not drawn to scale' framing helps.

Angle measure is additive: an angle decomposed into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts; students solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram, using an equation with a symbol for the unknown (4.MD.7).
learnerActions: Work a mixed set that includes a straight-line single-unknown case, a point case with several angles and one unknown, and a decomposition case (adding two marked parts to find the whole, e.g. 35 + 40 = 75°, or finding a missing part from a named whole).
For each item, write the equation first, labelling the whole, before giving a number.
Try writing the same relationship two ways for one diagram, e.g. 65 + x = 180 and x = 180 − 65, to show they describe the same additive structure.

Sanity-check each result: plug the answer back and confirm the parts add to the stated whole (e.g. for two 100° angles and x at a point, 100 + 100 + 160 = 360); ask whether the answer is even possible (e.g. a result of 180° or more for one of two angles on a straight line, or a zero or negative result, means the whole or a value was misread).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means choosing the correct whole for each configuration rather than applying one habitual routine, and verifying the answer against the fixed whole.

constraints: This is a procedural skill: learners must actually set up and solve their own equations across varied diagrams, not just watch a labelled worked example. A reveal-the-answer picture can illustrate a worked example but does not let the learner construct and solve, so it is only a scaffold toward independent solving.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. completing 65 + x = ___, or choosing whether to subtract from 180 or 360) give useful scorable practice and can be used during teaching, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves show independent equation setup; pair them with tasks where the learner writes the whole equation.

Always distinguish a reasoning error (wrong whole, treating measure as non-additive) from an arithmetic slip (mis-subtracting from 180 or 360) when giving feedback — they require different remediation.
Insist that the diagram supplies stated facts, not measurements; include at least one deliberately not-to-scale diagram so measuring or assuming look-alike angles are equal is caught.
Progress from one unknown on a line, to one unknown among several at a point, to decomposition (adding parts to find the whole, or finding a missing part from a named whole).
Physical angle cut-outs and strips are approximations with real thickness; use them to demonstrate additivity, but the represented angle is the idealised figure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic in the source: 65 + x = 180 → x = 115° ✓; 120 + 90 + x = 360 → x = 150° ✓; 35 + 40 = 75° ✓; 100 + 100 + x = 360 → x = 160° ✓. The illustrative slip 180 − 145 has correct result 35; the value 45 is the deliberately-wrong slip used in feedback to model an arithmetic error, never offered as a learner answer. No errors were propagated into learner-facing correct answers.

The original material asserted that a 3D environment 'gains nothing' and that dialogue cannot deliver this skill; these catalog-style necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been reframed as scoped observations about affordances (procedural fluency needs learner-constructed solving and feedback-rich practice) rather than universal laws.

Activity 5's decomposition wording was corrected to match the worked example (whole found by adding) and activity 1's two sub-cases, resolving a minor internal inconsistency carried from the original 'named whole' progression phrasing.

probeDeeper: 'You wrote 65 + x = 180. Why 180 and not 360 here?' — listen for 'it's a straight line, a half turn' versus a memorised default.
Counterexample: 'This diagram is not drawn accurately. If I told you nothing looks the right size, could you still find x? How?' — checks reliance on the rule over appearance.
'If the two given angles at the point were both 100° instead, what would x be — and is that even possible?' (100+100+x=360 → 160; probes whether they sanity-check against the fixed whole).
'Show me a different equation for the same diagram' — e.g. x = 180 − 65 vs 65 + x = 180 — tests flexible understanding of the additive relationship.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) writes 65 + x = 180 and solves x = 115°; (2) writes 120 + 90 + x = 360 and solves x = 150°; (3) writes 35 + 40 = 75°. Uses the marked values and the correct whole for each configuration, and does NOT try to measure the printed (not-to-scale) angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts from the wrong whole — uses 180° for the angles-at-a-point diagram (or 360° on the straight line) because the configuration wasn't identified first.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish 'name the whole first': straight line = half turn 180°, point = whole turn 360°; sort diagrams by which whole applies before any arithmetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 120 + 90 + x = 180, or gives a point answer that's 180° short; may apply one whole to every diagram regardless of shape.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the diagram as to-scale — measures the printed unknown with a protractor, or assumes two angles that 'look equal' are equal, instead of computing from the marked values.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinforce that diagrams carry stated facts, not scale; cover the figure and solve from the numbers alone, then reveal that the drawing was misleading.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the not-to-scale diagram gives a value close to the printed size rather than 115°; or justifies an answer with 'they look the same'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats angle measure as non-additive — doesn't believe the unknown is determined, so reaches for a protractor rather than writing an equation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Decompose-and-recombine a concrete angle to show parts sum to the whole, then reverse it to find a missing part by subtraction; frame the whole as fixed and shared.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot start without measuring; produces no equation even though the other angles are given.

errorPatterns.pattern: Arithmetic slip — sets up the correct equation but mis-subtracts from 180°/360° (e.g. 180 − 145 = 45 rather than 35).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the subtraction (number line / column method); no angle reteaching needed — the geometry is held, the arithmetic slipped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equation is correct and the method sound, but the final number is off by a computation error, often consistent across items.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot set up or solve: no equation, wrong whole, or measures the diagram; answers bear no reliable relation to the marked angles.
responseLevels.full: Writes and solves the correct equation for line, point and decomposition, choosing the right whole each time, ignores misleading scale by using marked values, sanity-checks the result against the fixed whole, and any error is a clean arithmetic slip rather than a reasoning failure.
responseLevels.partial: Solves the standard single-unknown-on-a-line case and can state 'they add to 180', but is derailed by the point configuration (wrong whole), the not-to-scale diagram (measures/assumes equal), or produces an answer without an equation — applies one routine rather than choosing the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three diagrams in front of the child. (1) A straight line split by one ray, one angle marked 65°, the other x. (2) Angles round a point marked 120°, 90° and x. (3) A large angle decomposed into two marked parts, 35° and 40°, asking for the whole. Say: 'Find each unknown, and write down the equation you used to get it.' Make diagram (1) deliberately NOT to scale so the printed x looks bigger than 65°. Watch how they set up and solve — do not prompt the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three configurations force the child to choose the whole (180° vs 360°) rather than apply one habit, so a wrong-whole error is exposed. The not-to-scale diagram separates a child who reasons from the rule from one who measures or trusts appearance. Requiring the written equation shows whether the additive structure is understood or the answer was guessed, and it distinguishes an arithmetic slip (equation right, number wrong) from a genuine reasoning error.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; multiply and divide mentally drawing on known facts, related facts and place-value adjustments (40×60 via 4×6; 7×15 via 7×10+7×5; 360÷9 via 36÷9).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 3.OA.7/3.OA.5 (strategies) and 5.NBT.1–2 (place-value scaling) applied to mental calculation.
• Operational details — this extends Y4 mental strategy to LARGER numbers via three moves: (1) scale a known fact by place value (40×60 = (4×6)×100 = 2400; 360÷9 = (36÷9)×10 = 40); (2) partition and use the distributive law (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5 = 105); (3) derive from a near/related fact. The recurring danger with (1) is the 'append zeros' shortcut applied without place-value understanding — keep it grounded as scaling. Encourage flexible CHOICE of strategy and comparing methods; the aim is efficiency and flexibility, not one prescribed route.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): scale a known fact (30×40 via 3×4). Tier B (age 9–10): use partitioning for 7×15 and place-value scaling for 360÷9. Tier C (age 10): choose and justify the most efficient mental strategy for a mixed set and explain the place-value scaling.
bestPractices: Scale known facts by place value (4×6 → 40×60) understood as ×100, not 'append zeros', so it survives decimals.
Teach partitioning via the distributive law (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5) with an area-model backing.
Use the ×÷ inverse and related facts to derive division mentally (360÷9 from 36÷9).
Foster flexible strategy CHOICE — compare methods for the same calculation and discuss which is most efficient.
Verbalise the chosen strategy and check reasonableness against an estimate.
keyRepresentations: Known-fact-scaled-by-place-value chains (4×6 → 40×60 = 2400)
Area/partition model for distributive mental multiplication (7×15)
Place-value chart — the scaling behind ×÷ by tens/hundreds
Number line / derived-fact links for division
commonMisconceptions: 'Appending zeros' without place-value understanding, misfiring on decimals or miscounting zeros (40×60 as 240 or 24000).
Partitioning incorrectly (7×15 = 7×10 + 5, dropping the second multiplication).
Not using the inverse/related facts for division, computing from scratch.
Fixating on one strategy rather than choosing the most efficient.
Losing a place value in ÷ scaling (360÷9 as 4 rather than 40).

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, mentally multiply and divide larger numbers by drawing on known facts, related facts and place-value adjustments: scale a known fact by place value (40×60 = (4×6)×100 = 2400; 360÷9 = (36÷9)×10 = 40), partition using the distributive law (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5 = 105), and derive from related facts. The goal is flexible, efficient strategy CHOICE and reasoning about place value — not a single prescribed route, and not a 'just append zeros' trick.

activities.title: Scaling studio: watch the known fact grow
feedback: If a learner gives 240 for 40×60: ask 'what is a ten times a ten?' Guide to 4 tens × 6 tens = 24 hundreds = 2400 — both numbers contributed a ten, so two zeros.
If a learner gives 24000: have them recount — only one hundred factor arises from tens×tens, so the known fact 24 is scaled by 100, giving 2400 (24000 would be scaling by 1000).
If a learner gives 360÷9 = 4: prompt 'you found 36÷9 = 4; 360 is ten times 36, so the answer is ten times bigger — 40.'
If the digit-sliding helps, confirm: 'the digits moved two places left; each place to the left is worth ten times more, so two places is ×10×10 = ×100.'
activities.rationale: Grounding ×÷ by tens/hundreds as place-value scaling of a known fact keeps the method correct for decimals and helps guard against miscounted zeros, a common misconception at this stage.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts.
Scaling known facts by place value and distributive partitioning are efficient mental strategies; teach flexible strategy choice, not 'append zeros'.
Mental strategies build on properties (3.OA.5) and fluency (3.OA.7) with place-value scaling (5.NBT.1–2).
learnerActions: Take 40×60 and name the known fact hiding inside it (4×6=24).
Place 24 on a place-value chart and scale it by ×100, watching the digits slide two columns to the left to make 2400 — because a ten times a ten makes a hundred, and both numbers contributed a ten.
Explain in units: '4 tens × 6 tens = 24 hundreds = 2400', so the answer has two zeros, not one.
Try the same scaling move on a division: link 360÷9 to the known fact 36÷9=4, then scale by ×10 to get 40.
Contrast with a tricky case where a naive 'add a zero' rule would mislead (e.g. a decimal such as 0.4×60, which is 24, not 240) to feel why scaling by place value is the reliable idea.
Optionally use a live place-value chart where the digits visibly shift columns, rather than zeros simply appearing, to make the scaling felt.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying/dividing by tens and hundreds scales a known fact by place value; tens×tens makes hundreds, so the number of zeros follows from the place-value reasoning, not from a memorised 'append a zero' rule.

activities.title: Partition to make it friendly
feedback: If a learner writes 7×15 = 7×10 + 5 = 75: point to the area model — the second tile is 7×5, not 5. Both parts must be multiplied by 7.
If a learner stalls trying to recall 7×15 whole: prompt 'split 15 into 10 and 5 — which of those are easy to multiply by 7?'
If both tiles are computed but added wrong, have them re-add 70 + 35 and compare to the estimate.
activities.rationale: Partitioning via the distributive law with an area-model backing gives a reliable derived-fact route and directly corrects the common error of dropping the second multiplication.
sourceClaims: Scaling known facts by place value and distributive partitioning are efficient mental strategies; teach flexible strategy choice, not 'append zeros'.
Y5 pupils multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts.
learnerActions: Take 7×15 and split 15 into friendly parts: 10 and 5.
Compute 7×10 = 70 and 7×5 = 35, then add: 70 + 35 = 105. State both multiplications explicitly so the second part is not dropped.
Back the partition with an area model: a rectangle 7 wide split into a 7×10 tile and a 7×5 tile, whose areas sum to the whole.
Say the full reasoning aloud and check it against an estimate (7×15 is a little over 100).
activities.intendedInsight: The distributive law lets you break a hard factor into friendly parts and multiply each part, then recombine — so you only need facts you already know.

activities.title: Two routes, same answer: choosing the friendliest
feedback: If both routes give different answers, help locate the slip by re-stating the known fact in each route.
If a learner always uses the same method, ask them to find a second route and compare effort — reinforce that either is correct and efficiency can depend on the numbers.
Praise explicit justification of a choice ('I used scaling because 36÷9 is a fact I know').
activities.rationale: Comparing methods for the same calculation builds flexibility and efficiency, the stated aim of mental calculation at this level.
sourceClaims: Scaling known facts by place value and distributive partitioning are efficient mental strategies; teach flexible strategy choice, not 'append zeros'.
learnerActions: Take 7×15 and solve it two different ways: (a) partition into 7×10 + 7×5, and (b) factor-scaling (15 = 3×5, so 7×15 = (7×5)×3 = 35×3, or 7×3×5 = 21×5).
Confirm both routes land on 105.
Discuss which route felt quicker for this calculation and why.
Repeat the compare-methods habit on a mixed set and justify the most efficient choice for each item.
Optionally present the same calculation in more than one worked form side by side so the alternatives can be compared directly.
activities.intendedInsight: Mental maths is about selecting the friendliest of several valid routes to the same answer, not following one prescribed procedure.

activities.title: Explain-aloud diagnostic and quick checks
feedback: Full response: mentally combines a known fact with correct place-value or partitioning adjustments across × and ÷, explaining the reasoning.
Partial: derives some facts (e.g. 7×15) but mishandles place-value scaling in 40×60, or needs prompting for the division link — revisit the scaling studio.
Gap: appends wrong zero-counts, has no derived-fact strategy, or defaults to a written algorithm — return to known facts and the scaling/partition models.
If the method is right but a single arithmetic slip occurs, do not reteach: have the learner re-state the known fact and re-apply the adjustment; this often lets them self-correct on recheck.
activities.rationale: Listening to the spoken strategy (especially on 40×60) is intended to help distinguish genuine place-value understanding from a memorised zero-count; the quick checks are recognition/fill-in/spot-the-error items, so they consolidate and verify a chosen method but do not by themselves elicit independent strategy construction. Efficacy is not established by this rewrite.
learnerActions: Do 40×60, 7×15 and 360÷9 in your head while explaining your reasoning aloud for each.
Answer a few quick checks to consolidate: choose the quickest way to do 7×15 among options; complete 40×60 = (4×6)×□; find the error in a worked solution where zeros were miscounted.
For each check, re-state the known fact at the core and the place-value or partitioning adjustment you applied.

Answer and justify the probe prompts: how many zeros does 40×60 have and why two not one? how did you break up 15? what small division fact hides inside 360? if you know 4×6=24, what else can you work out quickly?
activities.intendedInsight: A correct mental method pairs a known-fact core with a correct place-value or partitioning adjustment, and you can verify your answer by explaining and estimating.

constraints: Keep ×÷ by tens/hundreds grounded as place-value scaling of a known fact, not 'append zeros' — the latter can lead to miscounted zeros (e.g. when the known fact already ends in zero, as in 50×40 = 2000) and fails on decimals.
When partitioning, require BOTH parts to be multiplied (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5), not 7×10 + 5.

Recognition/fill-in-the-blank and spot-the-error checks consolidate and verify a chosen strategy but do not by themselves elicit independent strategy construction; pair them with explain-aloud production.
Tap-to-reveal strategy cards anchor the methods but let the learner see rather than try alternatives; use them as a reference scaffold, not as the main practice.
A coaching dialogue ('what known fact helps? is there a quicker route?') can rehearse strategy selection but will not on its own build mental speed or show the place-value scaling visually.
Live-updating place-value charts, draggable area tiles and side-by-side worked routes are optional interaction examples to make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.

assess.correctAnswer: 2400 (4×6 = 24, then ×100 because tens×tens); 105 (7×10 + 7×5 = 70 + 35); 40 (36÷9 = 4, then ×10). The teacher listens for a known-fact core plus a place-value or partitioning adjustment, done mentally.

pedagogy.summary: At age 13-14 children meet bivariate data: they describe the RELATIONSHIP between two variables shown on a scatter graph as positive, negative or no correlation, draw a line of best fit, and use it to make predictions. Conceptually the load-bearing ideas are three. First, correlation is about a TREND across the cloud of points — the strength is how tightly the points cluster around a line, not how steep the line is. Second, and most important, correlation is NOT causation: two variables can rise and fall together because one causes the other, because a third (confounding) variable drives both, because of reverse causation, or by coincidence — so a correlation alone never proves that changing one will change the other. Third, people tend to see the correlation they EXPECT ('illusory correlation'), over-reading a relationship when they believe a causal story and under-reading one that surprises them. Teaching should ground correlation in real, meaningful pairs (temperature vs ice-cream sales), constantly ask 'what could explain this link besides cause?', and separate strength-of-correlation from steepness-of-line.
bestPractices: Ground correlation in real bivariate contexts (temperature vs ice-cream sales, revision time vs test score) and describe the TREND in words before naming positive/negative/none
Confront correlation-vs-causation head-on with classic confounded pairs (ice-cream sales and drownings; firefighters at a fire and damage) and ask what third variable could drive both
Distinguish the STRENGTH of correlation (how closely points hug a line) from the STEEPNESS/gradient of the line — a steep line is not a strong correlation
Name the four explanations for a correlation — direct cause, common cause (confounder), reverse cause, coincidence — so 'not causation' becomes a set of alternatives, not a slogan
Read the correlation FROM the data, guarding against seeing a relationship just because one is expected (illusory correlation)
Treat 'no correlation' (no trend) as distinct from 'negative correlation' (a real, downward relationship), not as the same 'no/bad' idea
keyRepresentations: Three canonical scatter clouds side by side: positive, negative, and no correlation
A real confounded pair (ice-cream sales vs drownings) with the hidden common cause (hot weather) made explicit
Two scatters with the same gradient line but very different scatter, to separate strength from steepness
A line of best fit through a point cloud, used to read a predicted value within the data range
commonMisconceptions: Treating correlation as proof of causation — assuming that because two variables move together, one must cause the other
'Illusory correlation' — seeing or overstating a relationship because a causal link is expected, and dismissing one that isn't
Confusing the strength of correlation with the steepness of the line (thinking a steeper line means stronger correlation)
Treating negative correlation as 'no correlation' (or as 'bad'), rather than as a genuine downward relationship

learn.summary: For ages 13–14, this guidance teaches bivariate data on scatter graphs: describing the trend between two variables as positive, negative, or no correlation; drawing a line of best fit and using it to predict within the data range; and, most importantly, separating correlation from causation. Three load-bearing ideas: (1) correlation is a trend across a cloud of points, and strength means how tightly points cluster around a line, NOT how steep the line is; (2) correlation is not causation — co-variation can arise from direct cause, a common cause (confounder), reverse cause, or coincidence; (3) people tend to see the correlation they expect ('illusory correlation'), over-reading expected links and under-reading surprising ones. Activities ground every example in real, meaningful pairs and repeatedly ask 'what else could explain this link?' A live scatter sandbox with a confounder slider is the primary proposed mechanism; a Socratic sceptic, a scorable check, a static annotated gallery, and a predict-observe-explain task are preserved as distinct complementary approaches.

activities.title: Scatter sandbox: tighten the cloud, then toggle a confounder
feedback: If a learner stretches the cloud vertically so the line gets steeper and the spread grows in proportion, point out the read-out did not change: strength depends on how tightly points cluster around the line compared with the size of the trend, not on the gradient by itself.
When the temperature slider makes ice cream and drownings rise together, prompt: 'Neither of these causes the other — what is making both go up?' to surface the common cause (hot weather).
If a learner names a direct cause for a confounded pair, ask them to check whether a single third factor could be driving both before concluding one causes the other.
activities.rationale: Correlation is a felt property of a cloud of points and its trend. Manipulating the cloud and toggling a confounder may let a learner SEE strength-vs-steepness and common-cause directly, making the abstract ideas concrete. These are proposed interaction examples (live strength read-out, draggable points, temperature slider), not mandatory mechanisms; a static annotated image could illustrate the same labelled cases without live manipulation.
sourceClaims: 'Correlation' refers to co-variation/association between two quantitative variables and does NOT necessarily imply a cause-and-effect relationship — merely the existence of co-variation
KS3 pupils describe simple mathematical relationships between two variables (bivariate data) in observational and experimental contexts and illustrate using scatter graphs
learnerActions: Drag points on a scatter graph and watch a live 'strength' read-out and a best-fit line update as you move them.

Stretch the whole cloud vertically (scale every y-value by the same factor) so the trend line gets steeper and the spread around it grows in proportion, and notice that the strength read-out stays the same; then pull the points closer to the line without changing its steepness and watch the strength increase.

Move a single 'temperature' slider and watch it simultaneously push ice-cream sales UP and beach-swimming/drownings UP, so a strong positive correlation appears between ice cream and drownings even though neither causes the other.
Turn the temperature slider back down and watch both variables fall together, showing that in this model, where temperature is built in as the common cause, the hidden variable drives both.

For fresh correlated pairs, use a 'what else could explain this?' prompt to name any plausible confounder, and decide which of four explanations seems most plausible for each pair, giving a reason: direct cause, common cause, reverse cause, coincidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Strength of correlation is how closely points hug the line, not how steep the line is; and a real, strong correlation can exist between two variables when a hidden third variable drives both — so correlation alone never proves causation.

activities.title: Argue it out with a sceptical scientist
feedback: If a learner accepts the causal claim, prompt them to look for a third variable that could drive both quantities.
If a learner denies any link ('they're unrelated'), affirm that the correlation is genuinely real and redirect them to explain WHY correlated things need not be causally connected.
Reward answers that name a specific plausible confounder and state that co-variation alone does not establish causation.
activities.rationale: Judging causal claims is fundamentally reasoning, and a Socratic partner can press a learner on WHY a correlation need not be cause and surface their own causal assumptions — including the expected causal stories that drive over-reading of a link. This discussion complements, and does not replace, work with actual scatter data: a conversation cannot by itself verify plotting a graph or reading a trend, so it should be paired with the data tool.
sourceClaims: 'Correlation' refers to co-variation/association between two quantitative variables and does NOT necessarily imply a cause-and-effect relationship — merely the existence of co-variation

'Illusory correlation' (Chapman & Chapman): people hold beliefs about how two variables relate that create the impression of an empirical contingency, and they overestimate the association when they believe a causal link exists between the variables
learnerActions: Respond to a character who presents tempting causal claims drawn from correlations, e.g. 'Towns with more churches have more crime — so do churches cause crime?' or 'More firefighters are sent to bigger fires and there is more damage — so should we send fewer firefighters?'
For each claim, explain in your own words what ELSE could account for the link besides one variable causing the other, and try to name the confounding common cause (e.g. town population; fire size).
When pressed, state whether the correlation is real, and separately whether the causal claim follows from it.
activities.intendedInsight: Correlation-vs-causation is an argument you can make: a real link can be explained by a confounder, reverse cause, or coincidence, so you must give a reason rather than accept the causal story.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain: the firefighters data
feedback: A written reason of 'yes, fewer firefighters → less damage' reveals reading correlation as causation: introduce the confounder (fire size) explicitly, name the four explanations — direct cause, common cause, reverse cause, coincidence — and, if the learner has misread correlation itself, revisit what 'correlation' means (a trend/co-variation, not a cause).
A 'no, because they're unrelated' answer misses that the variables ARE genuinely correlated; affirm the real link and ask for the common cause.
A full answer names the confounder (fire size / summer weather) and states that variables moving together does not by itself establish that one causes the other.
activities.rationale: Requiring the reason BEFORE the reveal makes the task diagnostic: it distinguishes a learner who read correlation as causation from one who already holds the concept. Transfer to a fresh pair checks that the reasoning generalises rather than being memorised for one example.
sourceClaims: 'Correlation' refers to co-variation/association between two quantitative variables and does NOT necessarily imply a cause-and-effect relationship — merely the existence of co-variation
learnerActions: Study data in which the number of firefighters sent to a fire is strongly positively correlated with the amount of damage caused.

Before any discussion, WRITE your prediction and your REASON for this question: 'If the fire service sent FEWER firefighters to each fire, would there be less damage?' Commit to both prediction and reason first.
Then observe the lurking variable — the SIZE of the fire — which drives both the firefighters sent and the damage, and compare it against your written reason.
Finally, transfer the reasoning to a fresh pair: explain what could cause BOTH ice-cream sales and drownings to rise and fall together.
activities.intendedInsight: A correlation can be fully real yet not show the effect of one variable on the other, because a confounding variable (fire size; hot weather) drives both measured quantities — so changing one variable need not change the other in the way the correlation suggests (sending fewer firefighters would likely mean more damage, not less).

activities.title: Scorable check: type, strength, and causal claims
feedback: If a learner picks the steeper-but-more-scattered graph as 'stronger', show the two scatters again and point to how tightly the points hug the line, not the gradient.
If a learner labels a clear downward trend 'no correlation', contrast the three cases: positive (up together), negative (one up as the other down), none (no trend at all).
On the causal item, require the 'why' tier: a correct 'no' must be backed by a plausible confounder or other non-causal explanation, not by denying the link.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and comparison items give a scorable check, and a two-tier causal item can catch the causation misconception and the shallow-'no' error at the 'why' tier. A recognition check confirms discrimination but does not by itself elicit the independent construction of an explanation, so pair it with the predict-observe-explain and discussion tasks.
sourceClaims: 'Correlation' refers to co-variation/association between two quantitative variables and does NOT necessarily imply a cause-and-effect relationship — merely the existence of co-variation
KS3 pupils describe simple mathematical relationships between two variables (bivariate data) in observational and experimental contexts and illustrate using scatter graphs
learnerActions: Sort scatter graphs into positive, negative, or no correlation, each anchored in a real context.

Compare two scatters for strength, drawn on the same axes, including a pair where one has a steeper line but points widely scattered around it and the other a gentler line with points hugging it closely (so the gentler one clearly has the stronger correlation) — choose which shows the STRONGER correlation.
Answer a two-tier causal item: first 'Does this correlation prove X causes Y?' and then 'Why / why not?', explaining your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: You can reliably identify correlation type, judge strength by clustering rather than gradient, and reject an unwarranted causal claim with a stated reason.

activities.title: Annotated scatter gallery (reference)
feedback: Use the same-gradient/different-scatter pair to confirm that strength is about clustering, by revealing which is more tightly clustered.
For the confounded pair, reveal the common cause and restate that the link is real but not causal.
activities.rationale: A static annotated gallery can label the correlation types and flag a confounded pair as a reference, but it cannot let a learner manipulate the cloud or toggle a confounder to watch a spurious correlation arise. It is best used for reference and consolidation alongside the interactive and reasoning activities, not as the sole means of teaching the concept.
learnerActions: View three canonical scatter clouds side by side — positive, negative, and no correlation — and reveal each one's correlation type.
Examine a confounded pair (ice-cream sales vs drownings) and reveal the hidden common cause (hot weather).
Compare two scatters that share the same gradient line but have very different amounts of scatter, and view a line of best fit used to read a predicted value within the data range.
activities.intendedInsight: The three correlation types, the strength-vs-steepness distinction, and a worked confounded example can be recognised and named as reference points.

constraints: Ground every example in a real, meaningful bivariate pair (temperature vs ice-cream sales; revision time vs test score; firefighters vs fire damage) and describe the trend in words before naming positive/negative/none.
Treat 'no correlation' (no trend) as genuinely distinct from 'negative correlation' (a real downward relationship); do not let either be read as 'no/bad'.
Keep strength (how tightly points hug the line) separate from steepness/gradient of the line throughout; a steep line is not a strong correlation.
Frame 'not causation' as a set of alternatives — direct cause, common cause (confounder), reverse cause, coincidence — not as a slogan to recite.
When a learner misreads correlation as causation, besides naming the confounder also revisit the meaning of 'correlation' itself if needed.

The Socratic conversation cannot verify plotting or reading a trend; pair it with actual scatter data. The recognition/quiz check confirms discrimination but does not elicit independent construction of an explanation; pair it with the predict-observe-explain and discussion tasks.
The static gallery is for reference and consolidation; it cannot provide the live manipulation of cloud or confounder that may make strength-vs-steepness and spurious correlation concrete.
Line-of-best-fit predictions should stay within the data range (interpolation), as reflected in the stated evidence.

Interactive examples (live strength read-out, draggable points, temperature/confounder slider, tap-to-reveal) are illustrative proposed mechanisms, not mandatory; the same concepts can be approached with other media.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated or tested interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any activity's effectiveness.

The source rated a 3D interactive as adding nothing because bivariate correlation is 2D; this reflects that a third spatial dimension is not needed at this level, not an established universal claim, so it was omitted rather than asserted as a law.

The claim that live manipulation teaches strength-vs-steepness and common-cause 'in a way words cannot' was softened to a scoped affordance: the interactive may make these concrete, but a static gallery and verbal reasoning can still teach the same ideas.

sourceClaims attached to activities support the underlying principles (co-variation is not causation; illusory correlation; KS3 bivariate expectations); they do not certify that the specific sandbox, conversation, POE, or quiz designs were empirically tested. The illusory-correlation claim's attachment to the Socratic activity is a migration judgement based on that activity surfacing expected causal stories.

The illusory-correlation idea (over-reading expected links, under-reading surprising ones) is well-motivated by the Chapman & Chapman citation but is only lightly operationalised in the activities; a reviewer may wish to strengthen tasks that deliberately present a surprising-but-real correlation to test under-reading.

assess.poeTask: Show the class data in which the number of firefighters sent to a fire is strongly positively correlated with the amount of damage caused. Ask each pupil to PREDICT, writing their REASON first: 'If the fire service sent FEWER firefighters to each fire, would there be less damage?' Have them commit to prediction + reason before any discussion. THEN reveal/observe the lurking variable — the SIZE of the fire — which drives both the firefighters sent and the damage. The reason stated before the reveal is the diagnostic part: a pupil who predicted 'yes, fewer firefighters → less damage' has read the correlation as causation, while one who predicted 'no, because bigger fires cause both' already holds the concept.
probeDeeper: 'What could cause BOTH ice-cream sales and drownings to go up at the same time?' — elicits the confounding common cause
'If two things are correlated, what are all the ways that could happen besides one causing the other?' — pushes for common cause / reverse cause / coincidence
Counterexample: 'Data shows the more firefighters sent to a fire, the more damage there is — so should we send fewer firefighters? Why not?' — a fresh confounded pair (fire size)
'Here is a scatter with a steep line but points scattered all over, and here is one with a gentle line but points hugging it — which shows the stronger correlation?' — probes strength vs steepness
assess.correctAnswer: Tier 1: No. Tier 2: because correlation is not causation — a third, confounding variable (hot/summer weather) drives BOTH ice-cream sales and how many people swim (and so drown); the two are linked through a common cause, not because one causes the other. A full answer names the confounder and states that variables moving together does not by itself establish that one causes the other.

errorPatterns.pattern: Correlation implies causation: because the two variables move together, concludes that one must cause the other
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce the confounder explicitly — hot weather drives both — and name the four possible explanations for a correlation (direct cause, common cause, reverse cause, coincidence); a link is not a cause; reteach the meaning of 'correlation' via the vocabulary prerequisite
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — since ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together, buying more ice cream must cause more drownings
errorPatterns.revealedBy: At tier 1 the child says 'yes, more ice cream causes more drownings' (or that the correlation proves a causal link), rather than looking for another explanation

errorPatterns.pattern: Shallow 'no': denies causation but by claiming the variables are unrelated, missing that they ARE genuinely correlated (just not causally)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Affirm the correlation is real, then supply the common cause: the job is to explain WHY correlated things needn't be causally linked, not to deny the link
errorPatterns.distractor: No — ice cream and drowning have nothing to do with each other; the pattern is just a coincidence
errorPatterns.revealedBy: At tier 2 the child says 'they have nothing to do with each other', failing to explain the real co-variation via a common cause

errorPatterns.pattern: Strength confused with steepness: judges the strength of a correlation by how steep the line is rather than how closely the points cluster around it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two: strength is how tightly points hug the line; show two scatters with the same gradient but different scatter, and a shallow line with tight points
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up comparing two scatters the child calls the one with the steeper line 'more correlated' even though its points are more scattered

errorPatterns.pattern: Negative correlation read as 'no correlation': treats a downward relationship as the absence of correlation (or as 'bad'), not as a genuine negative relationship
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the three cases — positive (up together), negative (one up as the other down), none (no trend) — so 'negative' is a real relationship and 'none' means no trend at all
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shown a clear downward trend the child says 'there's no correlation' because the points go down, reserving 'correlation' for upward trends

responseLevels.gap: Reads correlation as proof of causation (says the ice cream causes the drownings), or cannot describe the type of correlation on a scatter
responseLevels.full: Describes the correlation and, faced with a causal claim, rejects it by naming a plausible confounder (or reverse cause/coincidence) and explaining that co-variation alone does not establish causation — transferring the reasoning to a fresh correlated pair
responseLevels.partial: Describes positive/negative/no correlation on a scatter and may recite 'correlation isn't causation', but cannot identify the confounding common cause or explain WHY a correlation can arise without one variable causing the other — states the rule without applying it

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Pose the claim, then ask for the reason. Tier 1: 'Across the year, ice-cream sales and the number of people who drown at the beach rise and fall together — they are strongly positively correlated. Does buying more ice cream CAUSE more drownings?' Tier 2: 'Explain your reasoning — how do you account for the fact that they go up and down together?' Read it aloud and listen; do not offer options.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two tiers together defeat guessing. A child who thinks correlation proves cause answers 'yes' at tier 1. A child who answers 'no' for a shallow reason ('they're not connected') is caught at tier 2 — they miss that the two ARE genuinely correlated, just not causally. Only a child who identifies a common cause and articulates co-variation-without-causation gives the right answer for the right reason.

sources.claim: 'Correlation' refers to co-variation/association between two quantitative variables and does NOT necessarily imply a cause-and-effect relationship — merely the existence of co-variation
sources.source: Batanero, Godino, Vallecillos, Green & Holmes (1994), 'Errors and difficulties in understanding elementary statistical concepts' (Section on correlation/association)

sources.claim: 'Illusory correlation' (Chapman & Chapman): people hold beliefs about how two variables relate that create the impression of an empirical contingency, and they overestimate the association when they believe a causal link exists between the variables
sources.source: Batanero et al. (1994), citing Chapman & Chapman

sources.claim: KS3 pupils describe simple mathematical relationships between two variables (bivariate data) in observational and experimental contexts and illustrate using scatter graphs
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS3 Statistics)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Understand that 100 is a bundle of ten tens (just as a ten is ten ones) — unitising climbs one level. Ten ten-rods fuse into one hundred-flat; 100 becomes a single countable unit.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): work in the number system to 1000; 'recognise the place value of each digit in a three-digit number (hundreds, tens, ones)' (this concept is its prerequisite unit).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.1a '100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a hundred'; foundation for 2.NBT.1.
• Operational details — Re-run the exact bundling story one order of magnitude up, using base-ten flats: count ten tens-rods, physically stack/overlay them onto one hundred-flat, and name the new unit. Stress the self-similar pattern (10 ones→1 ten; 10 tens→1 hundred) so children see place value as a repeating ×10 structure, not a list of separate facts.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): builds 100 from ten tens-rods and says 'ten tens make one hundred'. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): explains 100 = 10 tens = 100 ones and treats a hundred-flat as one unit. Tier C (age 8, extending): articulates the repeating ×10 pattern and predicts the next unit (ten hundreds = one thousand).
bestPractices: Re-tell the SAME unitising story up a level with base-ten flats: ten tens-rods physically become one hundred-flat, mirroring ten ones → one ten.
Name the pattern explicitly: 'each new place is ten of the one before' — make the ×10 self-similarity the headline, not an incidental.
Hold three equivalent views of 100 together: 100 ones (a flat of little squares), 10 tens (ten rods), 1 hundred (one flat) — same quantity, different unit.
Anticipate the next rung (ten hundreds = a thousand) so the pattern is felt as open-ended.
Use the hundred-square (10×10 grid) as the bridge image between 'ten tens' and 'a hundred'.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten hundred-flat (10×10) vs ten tens-rods vs 100 unit-cubes — three views of 100
Hundred-square (10×10 grid) showing ten rows of ten
Gattegno / place-value chart adding the hundreds column
Bundled straws: ten bundles-of-ten wrapped into one bundle-of-hundred
0-1000 number line with hundred markers
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 100 is 'ten' with zeros, not literally ten tens or a hundred ones.
Failing to see the repeating ×10 structure — treating hundreds as an unrelated new idea.
Confusing a hundred-flat with a ten-rod (not tracking which unit is which).
Believing 100 ones and 10 tens are different amounts rather than the same quantity re-unitised.
Counting the little squares one-by-one instead of trusting the unit (no unitising).

learn.summary: For ages 7-8: understand that 100 is a bundle of ten tens, just as a ten is ten ones. The core proposed experience is watching ten ten-rods fuse into one hundred-flat, mirroring the earlier ten-ones-to-one-ten move, so children are intended to experience place value as a repeating ×10 structure rather than a list of separate facts. Hold three equivalent views of 100 together (100 single cubes, 10 rods, 1 flat), and foreshadow the next rung (ten hundreds make a thousand).

activities.title: Fuse ten tens into one hundred on an exchange bench
feedback: When the ten rods snap into one flat, confirm: 'Ten tens just became one hundred — the same move as ten ones becoming one ten, one level up.'
On the three-views toggle, point out the counter never moves: 'Still 100 — same amount, just re-unitised into a different unit.'
If a child treats the flat as unrelated to the rods, re-run the fuse and split slowly so they see the flat come apart into exactly ten rods.
Prompt the prediction: 'If ten tens make a hundred, what do you think ten hundreds make?'
activities.rationale: Performing the fuse/split action is intended to make unitising felt rather than merely stated, and re-running the same story one magnitude up is intended to surface the repeating ×10 structure. The merge animation together with a counter that stays steady at 100 is intended to make the equivalence concrete. Offered as a proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Place value is a self-similar ×10 structure; teaching should surface the repeating unitising pattern across ones/tens/hundreds.
100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred' (2.NBT.1a).
learnerActions: First re-bundle ten single ones into one ten-rod as a familiar recap, naming what happened: 'ten ones make one ten'.
Gather ten ten-rods into a staging tray; as the tenth rod lands, watch the ten rods merge into a single 10×10 hundred-flat.
Say aloud the pattern that connects the two moves: 'ten of the last unit always makes one of the next'.
Use a 'three views' toggle to flip the same hundred between 100 loose cubes, 10 rods, and 1 flat, while a counter stays steady at 100.
Look at a dimmed 'next level' shelf showing ten flats waiting to become a thousand-cube, and predict what comes next.
activities.intendedInsight: 100 is literally ten tens (and a hundred ones); each new place is ten of the one before, so place value is a self-similar ×10 pattern that keeps going.

activities.title: Bundle physical materials: ten tens into one hundred
feedback: If a child counts the rods and says 'ten', count the ones inside one rod (10), then skip-count the rods in tens to 100, naming 'ten tens, one hundred'.
If a child says 'twenty', distinguish 'ten AND ten' (which is 20) from 'ten LOTS of ten' (which is 100), then skip-count all ten rods to 100.
Reinforce by removing the materials and asking them to say '100 is ten tens' from memory.
activities.rationale: Base-ten equipment is genuinely 3D (cube→rod→flat→large cube), so handling real pieces or straw bundles can support unitising, and the hundred-square grid gives a stable bridge image. Offered as consolidation alongside the interactive fuse, not as evidence that any one medium is superior.
sourceClaims: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred' (2.NBT.1a).
learnerActions: Lay out ten ten-rods (or ten bundles-of-ten straws) and skip-count them: 10, 20, 30 … 100.
Physically stack or wrap all ten together and name the new unit: 'one hundred'.
State the three views in words: 100 ones, 10 tens, 1 hundred — the same quantity.
Overlay ten rods onto a 10×10 hundred-square grid to see ten rows of ten make the hundred.
activities.intendedInsight: A hundred built from real materials is the same quantity whether seen as 100 ones, 10 tens, or 1 hundred; the hundred-square bridges 'ten tens' and 'a hundred'.

activities.title: Match and complete the three views of 100
feedback: For 'ten tens = ___', accept 100 (or '1 hundred' / '100 ones', which name the same amount); for '100 = ___ tens', the answer is 10. If a child writes 100 for the number of tens, point back to the ten rods that made the flat.
If a child picks an option that is not equal to 100, lay the views side by side and count the tens together.
Ask the child to justify a correct match aloud so equivalence is reasoned, not guessed.
activities.rationale: Consolidation that checks the equivalence after the construction work. Recognition and fill-in confirm the stated equivalence but do not by themselves elicit the independent act of unitising, so they follow the hands-on activities.
sourceClaims: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred' (2.NBT.1a).
learnerActions: Match each representation to the others: 100 ↔ 10 tens ↔ 100 ones.
Complete 'ten tens = ___' and '100 = ___ tens'.
Choose which option is the same amount as 100 from a set of choices.
Explain in one sentence why each view is still 100.
activities.intendedInsight: The three views of 100 are equivalent, and the ×10 pattern can be stated, not just built.

constraints: The fuse/split construction should come before matching or fill-in tasks: recognition and completion check equivalence but do not elicit the independent act of unitising.

A static side-by-side reference (flat beside ten rods and 100 cubes with tap-to-reveal equivalences) is a useful anchor for the three views but does not let the child perform the fuse/split; use it to support, not replace, the hands-on move.

Paper, card, straw bundles and base-ten blocks have real (slight) thickness; a 2D screen flat is an idealised picture of the hundred-flat. Treat both as representations of the same quantity and name which unit each piece stands for.
Keep the 'next level' shelf (ten flats → thousand-cube) as an optional teaser to show the pattern is open-ended; do not require mastery of 1000 at this stage.

Diagnostic: show ten tens-sticks and ask what the bundled block is called, how many single ones it is, and how the child knows — the reason reveals ten-tens structure versus rote counting. Discriminating follow-up probes: 'How many single ones are there altogether in ten tens, and how could you be sure without counting them all?'; 'If I take one ten away, how many ones are left in the block now?'; 'Both 10 and 100 use the digits 1 and 0 — how are they different?'
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (CCSS-M 2.NBT.1a and NCETM Primary Mastery) are marked unverified in the source row; the DfE Year 3 claim is marked verified. Comparative efficacy of any one medium is not established by these citations.
The DfE Year 3 claim is a curriculum/necessity statement about the objective rather than direct support for a specific teaching principle, so it is not used in activity sourceClaims.

The source row claimed 3D handling 'adds manipulation friction without insight' and that dialogue 'adds little'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established facts; physical base-ten work is retained as a genuine activity and spoken reasoning (skip-counting aloud, justifying matches) is used within tasks.

Efficacy language in the summary and the interactive activity's rationale was softened to intended/proposed wording because the activities are unvalidated; an invented 'recolouring' visual not present in the original design notes was removed, keeping only the source's merge animation and steady counter.

Self-audit of arithmetic: ten tens = 100 ones (10 groups of 10); '10' tens (not 100) completes '100 = ___ tens', while '100' ones completes 'ten tens = ___'. 'Ten and ten' (20) differs from 'ten lots of ten' (100). These were checked; no erroneous value is left in any question or answer.

probeDeeper: How many single ones are there altogether in ten tens? How could you be sure without counting them all?
If I take one ten away, how many ones are left in the block now?
Both 10 and 100 use the digits 1 and 0 — how are they different?
assess.correctAnswer: One hundred. It is 100 ones altogether, because ten tens is 10 groups of 10, which makes 100.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the sticks rather than their value: 'there are ten sticks so it's ten'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the ones inside one stick (10), then skip-count the sticks in tens: 10, 20 … 100. Name the new bundle 'one hundred = ten tens = a hundred ones'.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's ten.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts 1–10 across the sticks and answers 'ten'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds two tens instead of taking ten of them: 'ten and ten is twenty'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish 'ten AND ten' from 'ten LOTS of ten'. Skip-count all ten sticks in tens to 100.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's twenty.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 'twenty', treating 'ten tens' as 10 + 10.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches 100 only by counting every one, with no sense of the ten-tens structure
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the count — attach language to it: each time say '10, 20, 30 … that's ten tens, one hundred'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child laboriously counts all ones to 100 but cannot say '100 is ten tens' when asked again with sticks removed.

responseLevels.gap: Answers 'ten' (counts sticks) or 'twenty' (adds), showing no hundred-as-ten-tens unit.
responseLevels.full: Names the bundle 'one hundred', states it is ten tens and one hundred ones, and moves between the nested units (ones ⇄ tens ⇄ hundred).
responseLevels.partial: Reaches 100 but only by counting all the ones; cannot articulate that a hundred is ten tens.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show ten tens-sticks laid out. Ask: 'If I bundle all ten of these sticks together into one block, what is that block called, and how many single ones is it altogether? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has built the nested unit says 'a hundred' and knows it is 100 ones; a child counting only the visible sticks says 'ten' (counts the sticks, not their value), and an additive thinker says 'twenty' (10 + 10). The reason tier reveals whether they reach 100 by the ten-tens structure or by rote.

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in a three-digit number (hundreds, tens, ones), which depends on treating 100 as a unit.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 3 Number & place value)

sources.claim: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred' (2.NBT.1a).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Number & Operations in Base Ten, Grade 2

sources.claim: Place value is a self-similar ×10 structure; teaching should surface the repeating unitising pattern across ones/tens/hundreds.
