pedagogy.summary: Comparing decimals is a place-value skill, not a digit-counting one: the digit in the highest place decides the size, so you compare tenths first, then hundredths, then thousandths — exactly as with whole numbers you compare from the left. The whole difficulty is that decimals invite false analogies with whole numbers. Two opposite faulty rules dominate: 'longer-is-larger' (0.45 > 0.5 'because 45 > 5', treating the tail as a separate whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger' (0.4 > 0.87, either because 0.4 is read like 1/4 versus 1/87, or from the partial truth 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'). Both give correct answers on tidy same-length pairs, so RAGGED decimals (different numbers of places) are essential to expose them. Teach comparison through place-value reasoning and a length model, and establish that annexing zeros (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) does not change value.
bestPractices: Compare from the highest place value: line up the points, compare tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths — and reason aloud ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, which is less than 4 tenths').
Use ragged decimals deliberately (0.4 vs 0.38, 0.5 vs 0.45, 0.9 vs 0.11) because same-length pairs let faulty rules pass undetected.
Establish annexing zeros as value-preserving: 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700, so you may fill to equal length to compare — but only after the meaning is understood, never as a rote substitute.
Use a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) or a number line where size is shown by length, which is conceptually clearer than area/volume blocks, so 0.38 is visibly shorter than 0.4.

Name the misconception to be resisted (metacognitive approach) and show correct and incorrect comparisons side by side, since the error is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, not only missing knowledge.
Avoid teaching 'add zeros then compare as whole numbers' as the primary method — rules unsupported by place-value understanding are forgotten and mask the misconception.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with decimals aligned on the point
Number line (with zoom) for locating and comparing ragged decimals
Linear Arithmetic Blocks / length model where size = length
10×10 hundredths grids shaded for each decimal to compare area
Side-by-side correct vs incorrect comparison cards for discussion
commonMisconceptions: Longer-is-larger: judging the decimal with more digits as larger (0.45 > 0.5, 0.311 > 0.4), treating the tail as a whole number.
Shorter-is-larger (fraction-thinking): 0.4 > 0.87 because 0.4 is read as 1/4 and 0.87 as 1/87 ('sharing among fewer gives more').
Shorter-is-larger (tenths>hundredths): 0.4 > 0.87 from the over-applied partial truth that a tenth is bigger than a hundredth.
Believing annexing a zero changes value (0.7 ≠ 0.70).
Comparing digit-by-digit from the right, or comparing the fractional parts as isolated whole numbers regardless of place.

learn.summary: Comparing decimals is a place-value skill, not digit-counting. You compare from the highest place: any whole-number part first, then tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths, until the digits differ, reasoning aloud ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, which is less than 4 tenths'). The core difficulty is false analogy with whole numbers, producing two opposite faulty rules: 'longer-is-larger' (claiming 0.45 > 0.5 'because 45 > 5', treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger' (claiming 0.4 > 0.87, from reading 0.4 as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87, or from over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'). Both faulty rules give correct answers on tidy same-length pairs, so RAGGED decimals (different numbers of places) are essential to expose them. Teach through place-value reasoning and a length model, and establish that annexing zeros (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) does not change value.

activities.title: Order ragged decimals against a length model
feedback: If the learner ranks 0.312 or 0.38 as largest ('more digits'), draw the bars: 0.38 is plainly shorter than 0.4, and 0.312 is shortest. Say in place value: '0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths.'

If the learner picks the shorter decimal as larger using a sharing/fraction analogy on 0.4 vs 0.87 ('like 1/4 vs 1/87'), separate decimal place value from denominator size: 0.4 is four tenths, 0.87 is eight tenths and seven hundredths, so 0.87 is larger; show both lengths.
If the learner says 'tenths beat hundredths so 0.4 > 0.87', compare from the left: 0.87 already has more tenths than 0.4, so it wins before hundredths matter.

If the learner ranks 0.405 above 0.45 because '405 > 45', line up the points: both have 4 tenths, then 0.45 has 5 hundredths while 0.405 has 0 hundredths, so 0.45 is larger — the extra digits in 0.405 are thousandths, not a bigger whole number.
If the learner says 0.7 and 0.70 differ, show seven tenths equals seventy hundredths and the two lengths are identical.
When the learner reasons highest-place-first and justifies in place-value words, confirm the method and extend to a new thousandths case, for example ordering 3.142, 3.14, 3.2.
activities.rationale: Two opposite, documented misconceptions dominate decimal comparison, and both pass on same-length pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model and place-value reasoning are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'. Predicting-then-checking against visible length is intended to confront the longer-is-larger error at the moment the whole-number rule breaks. The main set already exposes longer-is-larger but can hide shorter-is-larger, so 0.4 vs 0.87 is needed to surface shorter-is-larger, while 0.9 vs 0.11 and 0.45 vs 0.405 give further checks on longer-is-larger.
sourceClaims: Two opposite, well-documented misconceptions dominate decimal comparison — 'longer-is-larger' (more digits taken as larger, treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger', the latter with two sub-types: confusing decimals with fractions (0.4 read as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87) and over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'. Faulty strategies can yield correct answers on tidy pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) and place-value reasoning ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths') are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'.
learnerActions: Before using any model, predict the order of ragged decimals from smallest to largest and say why, e.g. for 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5.
Represent each decimal as a bar or length drawn to a common scale (for example a Linear Arithmetic Block / bar model), then check your predicted order against the lengths.

State the correct order (0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5) and justify it in place-value language: 0.312 and 0.38 both have 3 tenths, so they are smaller than 0.4 (4 tenths) and 0.5 (5 tenths); among the 3-tenths numbers, 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths).

Also compare the counterexample ragged pairs 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.9 vs 0.11, and 0.45 vs 0.405: predict first, then check each against the length model and in place-value words. These pairs deliberately trip both faulty rules — for example 0.45 vs 0.405 tempts longer-is-larger (405 looks bigger than 45), yet 0.45 (4 tenths 5 hundredths) is larger than 0.405 (4 tenths 0 hundredths 5 thousandths); and on the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 set a shorter-is-larger learner can still land the right order.
Locate the decimals on a number line and, where helpful, zoom between 0.3 and 0.4 to see 0.38 and 0.312 separated in the hundredths.
Compare 0.7 with 0.70 (optionally using an annex-zero toggle or shading) and explain why trailing zeros do not change the value.
activities.intendedInsight: The decimal with more digits is not automatically larger, and the one with fewer digits is not automatically larger either; size is decided by the highest place where the digits differ. A length/number-line model shows that more digits need not mean more length (0.38 is shorter than 0.4, but 0.87 is longer than 0.4). Annexing trailing zeros gives decimals the same number of decimal places without changing their value.

activities.title: Name and resist the whole-number rule (correct vs incorrect cards)
feedback: If the learner cannot name why a wrong card is wrong, re-read both decimals in place-value words and point to where the comparison first decides (the highest differing place).
Praise explicit self-monitoring ('I nearly counted the digits — but I compared tenths first').
If the learner only identifies the right answer without naming the faulty rule, prompt: which rule would make someone pick the wrong card here?
activities.rationale: The greater-digits misconception reflects an overgeneralisation of whole-number knowledge and is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, so metacognitive approaches that name the misconception and present correct/incorrect examples side by side are recommended.
sourceClaims: The 'greater number of digits means greater magnitude' misconception is among the most common in decimal comparison and reflects an overgeneralisation of whole-number knowledge; it is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, so metacognitive approaches that name the misconception and present correct/incorrect examples side by side are recommended. Longer-is-larger declines with age while shorter-is-larger persists into adulthood.
learnerActions: Look at side-by-side comparison cards, one clearly labelled correct and one clearly labelled wrong, e.g. '0.45 > 0.5' (labelled wrong) beside '0.45 < 0.5' (labelled correct).
Say out loud which faulty rule produced the wrong card ('longer-is-larger: it counted 45 against 5') and explain why it fails here.
Write or state the place-value reason the correct card holds (0.5 is 5 tenths; 0.45 is 4 tenths 5 hundredths; 5 tenths is more).
Before answering each new pair, flag the rule you must NOT use, then compare correctly.
activities.intendedInsight: The error is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, not only missing knowledge; naming the misconception and inspecting clearly-labelled correct/incorrect examples side by side helps a learner catch and override it.

activities.title: Show equivalence and area with hundredths grids
feedback: If the learner thinks 0.38 covers more than 0.4 because '38 > 4', count tenths columns: 0.4 fills four full columns (40 squares), 0.38 fills three columns and part of a fourth (38 squares).
If the learner denies 0.7 = 0.70, overlay or count: 7 tenths = 70 hundredths cover the same squares.
On the aligned chart, if the learner compares from the right, redirect to the highest place first.
activities.rationale: Grids and an aligned place-value chart are useful references for area comparison and for making annexing-zeros equivalence concrete; however such references need to be paired with practice across many ragged cases with feedback rather than used alone.
learnerActions: Shade 0.4 and 0.38 each on a 10×10 hundredths grid and compare the shaded areas.
Shade 0.7 on one grid and 0.70 on another, and explain why seven tenths fills the same area as seventy hundredths.
Use an aligned place-value chart (points lined up) to read each decimal digit by digit, starting from tenths, and state which decimal is larger and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals can be compared by area as well as by length, and both representations show that annexing a zero (0.7 = 0.70) preserves value while more digits need not mean more size. (Note: the source synthesis treats length as the clearest magnitude model for this topic; the grid is a complementary reference.)

constraints: Use ragged decimals deliberately (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.38, 0.5 vs 0.45, 0.9 vs 0.11, 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.45 vs 0.405); same-length pairs let both faulty rules pass undetected and should not be the only practice.
On the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 ordering set a shorter-is-larger learner can still reach the right order, so include at least one pair (such as 0.4 vs 0.87) that directly exposes shorter-is-larger.
Teach 'annexing zeros is value-preserving' (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) only after the meaning is understood, never as a rote substitute for place-value reasoning.
Avoid teaching 'add zeros then compare as whole numbers' as the primary method; rules unsupported by place-value understanding are forgotten and can mask the misconception.

A length model or number line (where size is shown by length) is the recommended visual here; the source synthesis prefers length over volume/3D models for this topic. This is a stated preference for showing decimal magnitude, not a universal claim that other media cannot teach.

A static aligned chart or single shaded grid is a reference/scaffold: it may support reading or checking a comparison but does not by itself provide the repeated ragged-case practice with feedback that builds the comparison skill.

Multiple-choice/ordering/true-false questions with distractors built from longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger can diagnose which faulty rule a child uses, but recognising the right option does not by itself build place-value insight; pair any quizzing with construction and justification.
Scope: Year 5 expectation is to read, write, order and compare numbers with up to three decimal places; extend from hundredths to thousandths deliberately.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked examples: 0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5 is correct; 0.312 and 0.38 share 3 tenths, and 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) < 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths); 0.4 and 0.5 have 4 and 5 tenths. 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700 is correct (seven tenths = seventy hundredths). 0.87 > 0.4, 0.9 > 0.11, and 0.45 > 0.405 are correct. Ordering 3.142, 3.14, 3.2 gives 3.14 < 3.142 < 3.2. Grid counts: 0.4 = 4 columns = 40 squares; 0.38 = 38 squares. No arithmetic errors found.

Coherence fix applied: feedback referring to 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.9 vs 0.11 and 0.45 vs 0.405 now has matching learnerActions in Activity 1, because the main ordering set 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 can be ordered correctly by a shorter-is-larger learner and therefore does not reveal that misconception on its own.

Source verification is mixed in the original row: the SMART/Victoria synthesis claim is marked verified; the Durkin & Rittle-Johnson / Roell et al. / Steinle & Stacey synthesis claim and the DfE National Curriculum claim are marked unverified. The Durkin-synthesis claim is reused as a sourceClaim because it directly supports the metacognitive-naming principle, but its verification status was not upgraded here.

The original artefact wording asserting that a conversation or 3D model offers 'no spatial gain' and that a static picture 'cannot' teach has been softened to scoped affordances/limits; comparative necessity is a catalog preference, not established efficacy.
The length-over-volume preference is carried from the source synthesis as a recommendation for this topic, not as proof that volume/3D representations cannot teach decimal comparison.

probeDeeper: You placed 0.38 relative to 0.4 — which has more tenths? Does having more digits always mean bigger?
A friend says 0.9 is smaller than 0.11 because 11 is more than 9. What would you tell them?
Is 0.5 bigger or smaller than 0.45? What about 0.5 and 0.500?
How could you use this number line to check your whole order is right?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5. Reasoning by place value: 0.312 and 0.38 have 3 tenths (smaller), and 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths); 0.4 and 0.5 have 4 and 5 tenths. 0.7 = 0.70 — seven tenths equals seventy hundredths; the trailing zero does not change the value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer-is-larger: 'more digits means bigger — 0.38 is more than 0.4 because 38 is bigger than 4', treating the digits after the point as a whole number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the length model — 0.38 is shorter than 0.4 — and reason in place value: '0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths'. Use ragged decimals; name and inhibit the whole-number rule. Reteach comparison of same-length decimals first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ranks 0.312 and/or 0.38 as the largest; orders by digit count rather than by tenths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shorter-is-larger (fraction-thinking): 'the shorter one is bigger — 0.4 beats 0.87 because sharing among 4 gives more than among 87', reading 0.4 as 1/4 and 0.87 as 1/87.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate decimal place value from denominator-size reasoning: 0.4 is four tenths, 0.87 is eight tenths and seven hundredths, so 0.87 is bigger; show both on the length model. Reteach decimal comparison from place value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the shorter decimal as larger and justifies with a sharing/denominator analogy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shorter-is-larger (tenths>hundredths): 'tenths are bigger than hundredths, so 0.4 is bigger than 0.87' — over-applying a partial truth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare place by place from the left: 0.87 has more tenths than 0.4, so it wins before hundredths matter; grids/length model make it visible. Reteach highest-place-first comparison.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct on pure tenth-vs-hundredth cases but wrong when the hundredths total exceeds the tenths gap (0.4 vs 0.87); may also mis-order fractions by denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Annexing a zero changes the value — '0.7 and 0.70 are different, 0.70 is bigger (or smaller)'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 7 tenths = 70 hundredths on a grid and equal lengths on the line; trailing zeros fill to equal length without changing size. Reteach place-value equivalence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the tier-2 question, denies 0.7 = 0.70.

responseLevels.gap: Orders by number of digits (longer- or shorter-is-larger) or compares the tails as whole numbers; denies 0.7 = 0.70. Ragged decimals are mis-ordered.
responseLevels.full: Orders ragged decimals correctly by comparing the highest place value first, justifies in place-value language ('0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths'), knows 0.7 = 0.70, and transfers the method to thousandths and to counterexample pairs like 0.9 vs 0.11.
responseLevels.partial: Compares same-length decimals correctly but slips on ragged decimals, or reaches the right order by annexing zeros without explaining place value — executes a rule without the highest-place-first reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put these in order from smallest to largest and show me how you decided: 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5. Then tell me — is 0.7 the same size as 0.70, and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These are RAGGED decimals, so faulty rules cannot hide. A longer-is-larger child ranks 0.312 or 0.38 as largest ('more digits'). A shorter-is-larger child ranks 0.4/0.5 as largest for the wrong reason and mis-orders 0.312 vs 0.38, or claims 0.4 > 0.5-style errors on other pairs; watching the justification reveals whether it is the fraction-analogy or the tenths>hundredths route. The 0.7 vs 0.70 tier catches the belief that annexing a zero changes value. Same-length pairs would let every faulty rule pass — these do not.

sources.claim: Two opposite, well-documented misconceptions dominate decimal comparison — 'longer-is-larger' (more digits taken as larger, treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger', the latter with two sub-types: confusing decimals with fractions (0.4 read as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87) and over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'. Faulty strategies can yield correct answers on tidy pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) and place-value reasoning ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths') are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'.
sources.source: Mathematics Developmental Continuum P–10 (Victoria/SMART), 'Comparing Decimal Numbers', synthesising Steinle & Stacey's longitudinal decimal research (3,000+ students, Grades 4–10)

sources.claim: The 'greater number of digits means greater magnitude' misconception is among the most common in decimal comparison and reflects an overgeneralisation of whole-number knowledge; it is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, so metacognitive approaches that name the misconception and present correct/incorrect examples side by side are recommended. Longer-is-larger declines with age while shorter-is-larger persists into adulthood.
sources.source: Durkin & Rittle-Johnson (2015), Learning and Instruction; Roell, Viarouge, Houdé & Borst (2017), PLOS ONE; Steinle & Stacey longitudinal studies (via web research synthesis)

sources.claim: Pupils should read, write, order and compare numbers with up to three decimal places (Year 5 statutory content).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics Programmes of Study, Year 5 Fractions (including decimals and percentages)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8 (META). Solve number and practical problems using place value to 1000 — e.g. 'how many tens in 340?', money in pounds and pence, or 'my number has 4 hundreds and 7 ones and no tens, what is it?'. Applying three-digit place value flexibly, not learning it.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'solve number problems and practical problems involving these ideas' (three-digit place value).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT / 2.MD.8 apply place value and use it in money and measurement contexts; problem-solving with base-ten reasoning.
• Operational details — Pose varied problems that reward partitioning, 'how many tens/hundreds', missing-digit clues and real contexts (money, measures). Model with part-whole/bar models and place-value counters; think aloud then hand reasoning to the child. Emphasise flexible partitioning (340 = 34 tens = 3 hundreds 4 tens) and inverse/missing-value reasoning.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): solves a one-step place-value problem with a model. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): answers 'how many tens in 340' and missing-digit clues, explaining the strategy. Tier C (age 8, extending): tackles multi-step/real-context problems and reasons flexibly about non-canonical partitions.
bestPractices: Pose genuine problems (how-many-tens, missing-digit clues, money/measures) that reward place-value reasoning, not routine recall.
Model with part-whole / bar models and place-value counters, thinking aloud, then transfer the explaining to the child.
Stress flexible partitioning: 340 is 3 hundreds 4 tens AND 34 tens AND 300 + 40 — choose the useful view.
Use money as a natural place-value context (£/10p/1p mirror hundreds/tens/ones).
Include missing-value / inverse problems to build reasoning beyond direct calculation.
keyRepresentations: Part-whole and bar models for problem structure
Place-value counters and H|T|O chart
Money (pounds/tens of pence/pence) as a place-value context
0-1000 number line for jump/benchmark reasoning
Arrow cards for flexible partitioning
commonMisconceptions: Only seeing canonical partition (340 = 300 + 40) and missing '34 tens'.
Counting in ones instead of using place-value structure.
Mishandling internal zeros in problem numbers (407).
Inverse-blindness on missing-digit/missing-number clues.
Not mapping money/measure contexts onto place-value columns.

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, solve number and practical problems using three-digit place value to 1000, applying it flexibly rather than first learning it. The central objective is flexible re-unitising: seeing that the SAME number can be decomposed many equivalent ways (340 = 3 hundreds 4 tens = 34 tens = 300 + 40) and choosing the view that fits the problem. Children work 'how many tens/hundreds' questions, missing-digit clues (4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones give 407), and money/measure contexts, explaining and checking their reasoning.

activities.title: Place-value problem workbench: re-unitise to answer
feedback: If the child gives only the canonical partition (340 = 3 hundreds 4 tens), prompt: 'Can you exchange each hundred for ten tens? How many tens altogether now?'
When the child exchanges correctly, confirm that 34 tens and 3 hundreds 4 tens are the same number seen two ways.
If the child counts in ones, redirect to the place-value structure: 'Use the hundreds and tens rather than counting each one.'
For 'how many hundreds in 680?', accept 6 hundreds (with 8 tens left over) and discuss why this count is not a whole re-unitising like 340 to 34 tens.
activities.rationale: A manipulable problem bench lets the child physically partition, regroup and read off answers, making the re-unitising move visible rather than guessed. Live recomputation (hundred-flats visibly breaking into ten tens-rods) is intended to make the equivalence concrete. This is one suitable, proposed approach for a problem-solving (META) topic; physical base-ten pieces or arrow cards serve the same purpose without a screen.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'solve number problems and practical problems' involving three-digit place value.
Flexible (non-canonical) partitioning and re-unitising underpin place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Read a problem card such as 'How many tens are in 340?'
Build 340 with place-value pieces (three hundred-flats, four tens-rods) or arrow cards.
Exchange each hundred-flat for ten tens-rods on an exchange pad and watch 340 reassemble as 34 tens-rods, then read off the answer: 34 tens.
Repeat for another number (e.g. how many tens in 350? how many hundreds in 680?) and say which decomposition you used.
Name the strategy you used each time ('I re-unitised the hundreds into tens').
activities.intendedInsight: The same number can be re-unitised into equivalent decompositions; you pick the view that answers the question, and you can check by rebuilding the original number.

activities.title: Money and measures as place-value columns
feedback: If the child doesn't connect pounds to hundreds, lay the money beside place-value counters so the one-to-one mapping is visible.
For £4.07, check the internal zero: 'There are no 10p coins here — how do we show that in the tens column?'
Confirm answers by rebuilding: '407 pence — can you make that back into pounds and pence?'
activities.rationale: Money is a natural, real context where place-value columns transfer directly, and it surfaces the internal-zero case (£4.07 = 407p). Real contexts reward place-value reasoning over routine recall.
sourceClaims: Place-value reasoning is applied in problem contexts including money and measurement (2.NBT / 2.MD.8).
learnerActions: Solve a money problem such as '£4.07 = how many pence?' using a money tray (pounds, 10p, 1p).
Counting the amount in pence, map pounds onto hundreds (£1 = 100p), 10p onto tens, and 1p onto ones, lining them up in place-value columns.
Work a small shopping total using the same columns you used for whole numbers.
State how the money columns mirror hundreds/tens/ones.
activities.intendedInsight: Money (pounds / 10p / 1p) mirrors the hundreds/tens/ones structure, so a shopping total is solved with the identical place-value reasoning.

activities.title: Missing-digit and missing-value clues
feedback: If the child writes 47 for 'four hundreds, no tens, seven ones', ask: 'Where do the hundreds go? What holds the tens place when there are none?'
For inverse problems, prompt 'what is the number made of?' before any calculation.
Confirm by reading the built number aloud and checking it matches every part of the clue (34 tens and no ones gives 340; 34 tens make 340).
activities.rationale: Missing-digit and inverse problems build reasoning beyond direct calculation and are intended to address inverse-blindness and mishandling of internal zeros, both common difficulties.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'solve number problems and practical problems' involving three-digit place value.
learnerActions: Read a clue such as 'I have 4 hundreds, 0 tens and 7 ones — what number am I?' and build the number (407).
Honour the placeholder: put no tens pieces in the tens column but keep the column, and write a 0 digit there when recording, so the number is written correctly as 407, not 47.
Work an inverse/missing-value problem, e.g. '__ tens make 340' or 'a number has 34 tens and no ones — what is it?'
Explain how you knew where each digit belonged.
activities.intendedInsight: Place value is a two-way tool: you can reason backwards from a description to the number, and internal zeros act as placeholders that must be honoured.

activities.title: Talk-it-through: how did you decide?
feedback: If the child insists '350 IS 3 hundreds and 5 tens, that's it', model several equivalent builds of 350 with base-ten pieces (exchange a hundred for ten tens) and name each as the same number seen differently.
If the child reaches for a taught calculation first, don't supply a procedure — ask 'what is 350 made of?' so composition drives the method.
Treat this as eliciting reasoning, not scoring: surface the thinking rather than grading it.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning suits a META topic for eliciting strategy. At 7-8, pairing talk with an external model (pieces, arrow cards) is usually more productive than sustained talk alone, so keep manipulatives available during the discussion. A dialogue can elicit and probe reasoning but does not by itself build the hands-on re-unitising move.
sourceClaims: Flexible (non-canonical) partitioning and re-unitising underpin place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Respond to a riddle or problem and explain, step by step, how you worked it out.

Answer probes such as: 'How many tens are in 350? Is there more than one way to see that?', 'Could 350 also be 35 tens — how would you check?', 'What did you already know about how numbers are built that helped you decide?'
Test whether the same thinking helps for 'how many tens are in 352' and say what changes.
Justify your chosen decomposition and check it by rebuilding the number.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate why a chosen decomposition fits — and to check it — shows place value is held as a flexible strategy, not a single fixed label.

activities.title: Consolidation problems and worked reference
feedback: For a fill-in or multiple-choice item, if wrong, send the child back to build the number and re-unitise rather than restating the answer.
Use the worked example to prompt the next reasoning step, not to supply the result.
Encourage the child to explain the strategy after answering, as the evidence asks for ('explain the strategy used').
activities.rationale: Structured items and a worked-example anchor support consolidation and self-correction. Recognition and recall items assess and reinforce but do not by themselves elicit the independent re-unitising and explanation; use them alongside, not instead of, hands-on construction.
learnerActions: Answer a mix of items: 'how many tens in 340?', '£4.07 = __ pence', 'which number has 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones?', and match each problem to its useful partition.
Attempt a multi-step word problem in a real context (e.g. money).
Use a worked example of a how-many-tens problem as a reference: step through the reasoning when stuck, rather than copying the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Varied practice consolidates flexible partitioning and lets the child recognise which decomposition a given problem rewards.

constraints: Target the actual objective — flexible re-unitising and problem solving — not routine recall of 'hundreds, tens, ones'.

Recognition-only items (multiple choice, matching) assess and consolidate but do not by themselves elicit the independent re-unitising and explanation that are the goal; pair them with construction and spoken reasoning.
A worked example is a reference, not varied problem practice; it cannot replace the child working new problems.
Keep money/measure mappings honest: pounds / 10p / 1p mirror hundreds/tens/ones, and the internal-zero case (£4.07 = 407p) must be handled explicitly.
Honour placeholders: a clue like '4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones' must build 407, not 47.

Physical base-ten pieces, arrow cards and screen models all make re-unitising visible; none is uniquely necessary. On-screen live recolouring/exchange is an optional way to show the move, not a requirement.
The evidence expects the child to explain the strategy, so build explanation into every activity.

Where a 'how many hundreds/tens' question does not re-unitise to a whole count (e.g. 680 as hundreds gives 6 hundreds and 8 tens over), treat the remainder honestly rather than forcing a clean single number.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research, not fresh source verification. Sources were NOT re-fetched; activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists one US-standards claim and one NCETM claim as verified:false; treat their support as unconfirmed.

The original recommendation framed the interactive bench as the single ideal and rated 3D as having 'no payoff'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy or necessity claims; alternatives (physical manipulatives, dialogue, quiz, worked example) are preserved here as legitimate approaches with different purposes.
Efficacy-leaning wording in rationales was softened to proposed/intended/narrow-affordance language, as these activities are unvalidated and were not re-verified.

Self-audit checks: 340 = 34 tens (3 hundreds = 30 tens, + 4 tens = 34 tens) is correct; 350 = 35 tens is correct; 352 = 35 tens with 2 ones remaining; £4.07 = 407 pence is correct; '4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones' = 407 is correct; '34 tens and no ones' = 340 is correct; 680 as hundreds = 6 hundreds with 8 tens remaining. No arithmetic errors found in the migrated examples.

probeDeeper: How many tens are in 350? Is there more than one way to see that?
Could 350 also be 35 tens — how would you check?
What did you already know about how numbers are built that helped you decide?
Does that same way of thinking help for 'how many tens are in 352'? What changes?
assess.correctAnswer: Not scored. A rich response recognises 350 can be viewed in several equivalent ways (3 hundreds 5 tens, OR 35 tens, OR 350 ones) and that you choose the view that fits the problem — and can check by rebuilding the number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a number has only ONE correct decomposition ('350 IS 3 hundreds and 5 tens, that's it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model several equivalent builds of 350 with base-ten pieces (exchange a hundred for ten tens) and name each as the same number seen differently.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child rejects 35 tens as a way to see 350, or cannot regroup to suit the question.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches for a taught calculation without first asking what the number is made of
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't supply a procedure — prompt 'what is 350 made of?' first, so place-value reasoning drives the choice of method.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child hunts for an operation to 'do' rather than reasoning about the number's composition.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the number as having one fixed decomposition; looks for a procedure without reasoning about composition.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously views a number in whichever equivalent decomposition fits the problem, justifies it, and checks by rebuilding.
responseLevels.partial: Regroups when prompted but doesn't yet treat flexible decomposition as a general problem-solving move.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Someone tells you 350 is made of 3 hundreds and 5 tens. Is that the only way to see what 350 is made of, or are there others? If you got a problem like “how many tens are in 350?”, how would you decide what the number is really made of? Talk me through it.' Surface the thinking — don't grade it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe surfaces whether the child sees place value as a flexible tool — a number can be decomposed many ways and you pick the useful one — or as a single fixed label. That stance, not one answer, is what solving place-value problems depends on.

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils should 'solve number problems and practical problems' involving three-digit place value.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 3 Number & place value)

sources.claim: Place-value reasoning is applied in problem contexts including money and measurement (2.NBT / 2.MD.8).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2

sources.claim: Flexible (non-canonical) partitioning and re-unitising underpin place-value problem solving.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 7–9 — understand ocean animals have adaptations for their environment: streamlined bodies for fast swimming, camouflage to hide, blubber to stay warm in cold seas, tentacles/suckers to catch prey.
• Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2): Y4 links to habitats/environment; the adaptation–evolution strand is formalised at Y6 'identify how animals and plants are adapted to suit their environment in different ways and that adaptation may lead to evolution'. At 7–9 keep it at structure–function ('this body part helps it do this job').
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-3 (organisms can only survive in habitats where their needs are met) and 4-LS1-1 (internal/external structures support survival) — the structure-serves-a-function anchor.
• Operational details: the core cognitive move is CONNECTING an adaptation to the specific CHALLENGE it solves (cold → blubber; predators → camouflage; catching prey → tentacles/suckers; moving fast → streamlined shape). Teach it as problem→solution matching, not a feature list. Guard against purpose/intent language ('the fish WANTED to be fast') — frame as 'this shape helps it survive here'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7–8): names ≥3 adaptations; Tier B (~8–9): explains how each helps the animal survive; Tier C (~9): given a new challenge (freezing water / hunting in the dark), predicts a plausible adaptation and justifies it — reasoning from challenge to feature.
bestPractices: Teach adaptation as PROBLEM → SOLUTION: name the environmental challenge first (cold, predators, catching food), then show the body feature that answers it — the connection IS the learning objective.
Use compare-and-contrast pairs (blubbery seal in cold seas vs sleek tuna built for speed) so form follows the specific challenge, not a generic 'good body'.
Predict-then-check: pose a challenge ('how would you survive freezing water?') and let students propose features before revealing the animal's real adaptation.

Explicitly avoid teleological wording — model 'this camouflage helps it hide, so it survives and has young' rather than 'it wanted to blend in' (pre-empts the intent misconception ahead of Y6 evolution).
Anchor with vivid, verifiable exemplars: whale/seal blubber, octopus/flatfish camouflage, octopus suckers, shark/tuna streamlining.
keyRepresentations: A challenge→adaptation matching board (cold / predators / prey / speed → feature)
Compare pairs: streamlined swimmer vs blubbery insulator, side by side
A 'build-a-survivor' design surface where features are chosen to meet a stated challenge
Labelled anatomy call-outs tying each feature to the job it does
commonMisconceptions: Teleology/intent: 'the animal chose/wanted/tried to grow' the feature — adaptations framed as deliberate rather than as survival advantages.
'An animal can change its body within its lifetime to fit new conditions' — confusing individual change with population adaptation over generations.
Listing features without linking them to a challenge (naming 'blubber' but not why cold seas require it).
'One super-animal could have every adaptation' — missing that adaptations involve trade-offs and suit specific environments.
Assuming camouflage/adaptations are for the animal's comfort rather than survival (avoiding predators, catching food).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach ocean-animal adaptations as a problem→solution match: name the environmental challenge first (cold, predators, catching prey, moving fast), then connect the body feature that answers it (blubber, camouflage, tentacles/suckers, streamlined shape). The learning objective IS the connection between challenge and feature, not a list of features. Keep framing at structure–function ('this body part helps it do this job here') and avoid intent/teleology and within-lifetime-change wording ahead of later evolution work.

activities.title: Survive the sea: equip an animal to meet a challenge
feedback: If a thin-skinned animal is sent into cold water, show it weakening and prompt: what feature would slow the body's heat from escaping? (blubber as insulation).
If a brightly coloured animal is spotted by predators, prompt: what feature would help it hide? (camouflage).
When a learner tries to add every feature to one animal, highlight that real animals are suited to particular seas and ask which feature best fits THIS challenge.
Reinforce correct links by restating the pairing as 'this feature helps because it solves [this challenge]', not as a feature the animal wanted.
activities.rationale: Adaptation can be built as a live challenge→feature match with visible consequences, which is intended to make the structure–function link concrete and to support predict-then-check. Compare-and-contrast across several seas foregrounds that form follows the specific challenge rather than a generic 'good body'. Immediate cause–effect per feature (e.g. a cold tank draining a thin-skinned animal's warmth) is an illustrative design example, not a required mechanism, and the comparative advantage of this builder over the other activities is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: NGSS 3-LS4-3 and 4-LS1-1 establish that organisms survive where their needs are met and that internal/external structures support survival, growth and reproduction — the structure-serves-function basis of adaptation.
learnerActions: Read a stated habitat challenge, e.g. a freezing polar ocean full of predators, or fast-moving prey to catch.
Choose features to fit onto a bare animal from a set: a layer of blubber, a streamlined shape, camouflage skin, suckered arms.
Predict, before checking, which features will help the animal survive this specific challenge and say why.

Run the outcome and observe the consequence of each choice: a thin-skinned animal weakens in cold water until blubber is added; a brightly coloured animal is spotted and chased until camouflage is used; a boxy body misses prey a streamlined one catches.
Solve several different seas (cold, predator-heavy, hunting), noticing that no single animal can carry every possible adaptation.
Given a brand-new environment (e.g. freezing water or hunting in the dark), predict a plausible adaptation and justify it from the challenge.
activities.intendedInsight: Each adaptation answers a SPECIFIC environmental challenge; no single animal carries every possible adaptation (there is no all-purpose 'super-animal'). Learners reason from a problem to the body feature that solves it, and can transfer this reasoning to a new challenge.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal: what challenge does this feature solve?
feedback: Confirm a correct link by restating it as challenge→feature, e.g. 'cold seas → blubber keeps the seal's own heat in'.
If a learner only names the feature, prompt them to finish 'this helps because…' and name the challenge it solves.
activities.rationale: A guided labelling/reveal activity is intended to teach structure–function and is low cost. It is suited to exposition but mainly presents the pairings rather than letting learners test choices against challenges, so pair it with the active builder and transfer prediction above.
sourceClaims: NGSS 3-LS4-3 and 4-LS1-1 establish that organisms survive where their needs are met and that internal/external structures support survival, growth and reproduction — the structure-serves-function basis of adaptation.
learnerActions: Explore labelled animals (seal, octopus, tuna, flatfish) and select a body feature to reveal the challenge it solves and how.
For each feature, read or state the pairing, e.g. 'blubber — slows body heat from escaping, so the seal stays warm in freezing seas'.
Say out loud, in a 'this helps because…' sentence, what problem each feature answers before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Specific body features map to specific survival jobs: blubber insulates against cold, camouflage hides from predators, suckers catch and hold prey, streamlining lets a swimmer move fast.

activities.title: Blubber-glove investigation: insulation, not heat
feedback: If a learner says the fat heated the hand, point to the result: the fat was room temperature yet the insulated hand stayed comfortable longer, so the fat trapped the body's own heat rather than making heat.

If a learner says a seal grew blubber because it felt cold, separate one animal's life from change across many generations: an animal inherits its features from its parents (some, like a seal pup's blubber, build up as it grows), and better-suited animals survive and pass their features on. (Full natural selection comes later; here just block 'it changed itself because it needed to'.)
When a learner names a second adaptation, ask them to pair it with the specific challenge it solves (streamlined → swim fast to catch food or escape; camouflage → hide from predators).
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check physical investigation targets the 'fat is warm' misconception by showing room-temperature fat slowing heat loss, and the follow-up prompts separate individual change from adaptation across generations and reinforce feature→challenge pairing. Keep exposure to iced water brief and safe.
learnerActions: Predict which hand will stay comfortable in a bowl of iced water: a hand inside an empty bag, or a hand inside an identical bag surrounded by solid fat/shortening. Say why before trying.

Dip both hands briefly and compare how well each keeps its warmth. Usually the fat-covered hand stays comfortable longer while the hand in the empty bag soon gets uncomfortable, even though the fat was never warmer than the hand. Exactly how it feels depends on how thick the fat is, how well it covers the hand, how cold the water is and how long the hands stay in.
Explain the result: the fat did not make heat; it slowed the body's own heat from escaping into the cold water — this is what blubber does for a seal.

Discuss follow-up puzzles: why a polar seal has blubber but a fast tuna is streamlined instead; where blubber comes from (seals inherit the ability to build blubber from their parents, and many pups are born quite thin and put it on by drinking rich milk; a seal does not grow blubber because it felt cold); and what challenge an anglerfish's glowing lure might solve.
activities.intendedInsight: Blubber is not itself warm and does not generate heat; it insulates by slowing heat loss. Different animals have different adaptations because they face different challenges.

activities.title: Ask a marine biologist: justify an adaptation
feedback: Prompt the learner to tie any proposed feature back to the specific challenge it answers.
If reasoning stalls, offer a simpler contrast (cold vs needing speed) to re-anchor the challenge→feature logic.
activities.rationale: Spoken dialogue can deepen curiosity and surface a learner's reasoning. It supplements rather than replaces the hands-on challenge→feature practice; the builder additionally affords repeated structured practice across several challenges. Comparative efficacy of either medium is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Pose or respond to a survival puzzle, e.g. 'how might an animal survive the cold, or hunt in the dark?'
Propose a plausible adaptation and justify it by naming the challenge it solves.
Respond to follow-up questions that probe the reasoning (why this feature and not another for this environment).
activities.intendedInsight: Adaptations can be reasoned about from a challenge, and explaining the link out loud consolidates the problem→solution understanding.

activities.title: Enrichment: streamlined vs boxy in moving water
feedback: If a learner attributes the difference to size or colour, redirect attention to how water moves around the shape.
Connect back: streamlining answers the SPEED challenge, one of several different challenges different animals face.
activities.rationale: The speed case is mildly spatial and a flow comparison can make 'why shape aids speed' concrete for that single adaptation. It is niche enrichment; it is not required to meet the broad structure–function objective, which spans all four adaptations.
learnerActions: Compare how water flows around a streamlined body versus a boxy one and observe which moves more easily.
Explain why a streamlined shape helps a fast swimmer catch prey or escape predators.
activities.intendedInsight: A streamlined shape reduces resistance in water, which helps an animal move fast — one specific solution to the challenge of speed.

constraints: Keep the level at structure–function ('this body part helps it do this job here'); the adaptation→evolution strand is formalised later (UK Y6), so do not require evolutionary mechanism at 7–9.
Avoid teleological/intent wording ('the fish wanted to be fast', 'it chose/tried to grow a feature'); model 'this feature helps it survive here'.

Explicitly block the within-lifetime-change idea: animals inherit their features from their parents (some inherited features, such as a seal's blubber, develop as the young animal grows); an animal does not grow a new feature because it needs it. Adaptations build up across generations because better-suited animals survive and pass them on. Full natural selection is taught later.
State blubber as insulation (slows heat loss), never as a heat source; a correct activity must not let 'fat is warm / the blubber heats the seal' stand as acceptable.

The reveal/labelling activity presents pairings and does not require learners to construct choices; use it alongside the builder and transfer prediction, which elicit independent reasoning. Recognition of a pairing does not by itself show the learner can produce the challenge→feature link.

Simulation consequences (a cold tank draining warmth, a predator spotting an uncamouflaged animal) are illustrative examples of a mechanism, not mandatory features of any single tool, and are not evidence that the builder is superior to the other activities.

Guard against the 'one super-animal has every adaptation' idea by using several different seas and compare-contrast pairs so form follows the specific challenge; note that real animals carry several adaptations, so the point is that no animal carries every possible one.
Treat the blubber-glove result as a comparison of relative heat retention under fair, safe, brief conditions; do not state a guaranteed sensation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and both cited sources were already marked verified:false. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original emphasised consequence-driven simulation as 'ideal'; comparative efficacy over the labelling, dialogue, or investigation approaches is not established by the cited standards, so these are kept as complementary options rather than ranked, and activity rationales use qualified (intended/can/may) wording.

The blubber-glove investigation's sensations ('stays comfortable' vs 'aches') depend on fat thickness, coverage, water temperature and timing; treat the comparison as a demonstration of relative heat retention rather than a guaranteed sensation, and keep exposure brief and safe.
The source material references a prerequisite/reteach identifier for the Lamarckian error; it concerns an external topic link and is not reproduced here as it is not learner-facing guidance.

The UK KS2 source claim supports the topic/standard context but not the specific challenge→feature teaching principle, so it was not attached as a sourceClaim to any activity; the NGSS structure-serves-function claim is retained where it supports the principle.

assess.poeTask: Blubber-glove test: have the child PREDICT which hand will stay comfortable in a bowl of iced water — a bare hand, or one sealed inside a bag surrounded by solid fat/shortening — and say WHY before trying. Then dip both. The insulated hand stays comfortable while the bare hand aches, even though the fat was never 'warm'. This forces the split between 'fat is warm' (it wasn't) and 'fat traps the body's own heat in' — which is what blubber does for a seal.
probeDeeper: 'If blubber isn't warm itself, how does it keep the seal warm in freezing water?'
'A polar seal has blubber; a fast tuna is streamlined instead. Why do these two animals have DIFFERENT adaptations?' (feature→challenge contrast)
'Did one seal grow its blubber because it felt cold, or were seals born with it? Where does the blubber come from?' (blocks Lamarckism)
'Pick a deep-sea anglerfish's glowing lure — what challenge might THAT solve?'
assess.correctAnswer: Blubber is not itself 'warm' and does not make heat — it INSULATES: a thick fatty layer slows the seal's body heat from escaping into the cold water, so the seal stays warm. Another adaptation: a streamlined body lets a fast swimmer (tuna, dolphin) slip through water to catch prey or escape predators; camouflage helps an animal hide from predators; tentacles or suckers help catch and hold prey. Each adaptation solves a particular challenge — cold, predators, or catching food.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks blubber is 'warm' / makes heat, rather than slowing heat loss
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe as a coat/insulation: the seal makes its own body heat; blubber just stops it escaping into cold water. Fat traps heat in, it doesn't create it.
errorPatterns.distractor: The blubber is warm and heats the seal up
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the fat heats the seal up; treats blubber as a heat source

errorPatterns.pattern: Lamarckian: thinks the animal grew or changed its body during its own life because it wanted/needed to survive
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish a single animal's life from adaptation across generations: an animal is born with its features; adaptations build up over many generations because better-suited animals survive and pass them on. (Full natural selection comes later — here, just block 'it changed itself'.)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Probe: says the seal 'grew blubber because it was cold' / the fish 'made itself streamlined'

errorPatterns.pattern: Names an adaptation but can't connect it to the challenge it solves (feature floats free)
errorPatterns.nextMove: For each named feature, finish the sentence 'this helps because...': camouflage → hide from predators; streamlined → swim fast to catch food/escape. Tie every feature to a challenge.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says 'camouflage' or 'streamlined' but can't say what problem it solves

responseLevels.gap: Thinks blubber makes heat / is warm, or that the animal changed its own body because it wanted to; can't link any feature to a challenge.
responseLevels.full: Explains blubber insulates (slows heat loss, doesn't make heat), pairs at least one other adaptation with the challenge it addresses (cold/predators/food), AND resists the idea that an animal changes itself during its life — treating adaptations as fitted solutions.
responseLevels.partial: Says blubber keeps the seal warm and names another adaptation, but describes blubber as 'warm' rather than insulating, or lists features without connecting each to the specific challenge it solves.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A seal has a thick layer of blubber (fat) under its skin. A child explains: 'The blubber keeps the seal warm because fat is warm.' Is that the right way to explain it? Tell me what the blubber actually does. Then pick another ocean-animal adaptation and say what challenge it helps the animal deal with.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands adaptation says blubber slows heat LOSS (insulation) and can pair a second feature with the specific challenge it addresses. A child with the 'fat is warm' idea thinks blubber generates heat; a child with the Lamarckian idea says the seal grew blubber because it wanted/needed to be warm. The second tier (feature→challenge) checks whether adaptations are understood as solutions to challenges rather than as magic or wishes.

sources.claim: NGSS 3-LS4-3 and 4-LS1-1 establish that organisms survive where their needs are met and that internal/external structures support survival, growth and reproduction — the structure-serves-function basis of adaptation.
sources.source: NGSS Performance Expectations 3-LS4-3, 4-LS1-1

sources.claim: UK KS2 science treats adaptation to environment (Y6: how animals and plants are adapted to suit their environment, which may lead to evolution).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (Year 6 Evolution and inheritance)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–6 (LANGUAGE): read and write the number WORDS one–twenty, and connect each word to its numeral and quantity. This is the vocabulary/orthography layer over numerals 0–20.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): supports K.CC/1.NBT number-name work; reading/writing number names in words is a Grade 1–2 literacy-of-number expectation aligned to 2.NBT.3 (read/write numbers using number names).
• Operational details — many number words are irregular sight words (one, two, eight) or phonically awkward, and the teens are doubly tricky: 'eleven'/'twelve' give no clue to ten-and-one, and 'thir-teen'/'fif-teen' hide their tens+ones structure and say the ones part first. The child decodes/blends the word, recognises irregular ones by sight, and maps word↔numeral↔quantity. Crosses into phonics (blending) and sight-word reading.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): read 'twelve' and identify it as 12; match numeral cards to word cards. Tier B (5–6): write the word form of a given number 1–20. Tier C (6): read and write all the words fluently including the irregular/teen forms, spelling them correctly.
bestPractices: Explicitly link WORD ↔ NUMERAL ↔ QUANTITY (three-way matching) so the word is read for meaning, not just decoded as text; builds on secured numerals 0–20 (prerequisite mt_fR0UtsSREU).
Treat irregular number words as SIGHT words (one, two, four, eight, twelve) taught alongside phonically decodable ones (six, ten) — coordinate with the phonics/high-frequency-word programme.

Give the teens special attention: 'eleven'/'twelve' are opaque and must be memorised; 'thirteen–nineteen' say the ones-word first (thir, four, fif...) then '-teen' — pair with a ten-frame to keep the ten-and-ones meaning attached.
Use number-word washing lines, labels around the room, and books/rhymes so the words are met in reading and writing repeatedly, not just in a maths drill.
Practise both directions — read a word to make/point to the quantity, AND write the word for a given numeral — to prevent word-recognition without production (or vice versa).
keyRepresentations: Triple-match cards: numeral (13) ↔ word (thirteen) ↔ ten-frame/quantity.
Number-word washing line 0–20 above the numeral track for constant reference.
Colour/segment cues on teen words (thir·teen, four·teen) highlighting the ones-part + '-teen'.
Word-and-numeral labelling of classroom objects and calendar for incidental exposure.
commonMisconceptions: Reading a number word as text without linking it to a quantity or numeral.
Spelling confusions: four/for, eight, nine→'nighn', and the many silent/irregular letters.
Teen/decade word muddles by sound: 'thirteen' vs 'thirty', 'fifteen' vs 'fifty'.
Assuming all number words are phonically regular and mis-decoding the irregular ones (one, two, eight).
Reversing the teen meaning because the word says the ones first (thir-teen → thinking 3 then 1 → 31).

learn.summary: For ages 5–6, learners read and write the number words one–twenty and connect each word to its numeral and its quantity (a three-way word↔numeral↔quantity mapping with a spelling/production component). Many number words are irregular sight words (one, two, eight, twelve). Some teen words are opaque ('eleven' and 'twelve' give no clue to ten-and-one or ten-and-two), and others say the ones-part first ('thir-teen', 'fif-teen'), so teaching should keep the ten-and-ones meaning attached while building sight-word recognition and correct spelling. Practise both reading (word→quantity) and writing (numeral→word) directions. A wider 0–20 reference range (washing line, chart) can support this, while the production target is the words one–twenty.

activities.title: Word–numeral–quantity triple match
feedback: If a learner says or writes 31 for 'thirteen' (31 is not one of the 0–20 cards), compare the quantities directly: building 31 would need three full tens and one more, whereas thirteen is one ten and three ones. Seeing the quantities can help the learner notice that 31 is far too big and correct the mistake.
When a match is correct, restate the three-way link aloud: 'thirteen — that's the numeral 13 and this many: ten and three.'
For the opaque words 'eleven' and 'twelve', confirm by sight and set out the matching quantity rather than expecting the word to sound out.
activities.rationale: Linking word↔numeral↔quantity and structure-linked sight-word teaching build reading for meaning on top of secured numerals 0–20, and acting on the quantity can help a learner notice and correct an error in an opaque or reversed teen word. A linked quantity frame makes the ten-and-ones structure visible; dragging onto numeral and frame are optional ways to make the mapping concrete.
sourceClaims: Many number words are irregular sight words and the teens are opaque (eleven/twelve) or say the ones-part first, so they need dedicated sight-word and structure-linked teaching.
learnerActions: Hear or read a number word such as 'thirteen'.
Place or drag that word card onto its numeral (13).
Place it onto a ten-frame or set showing one full ten plus three.
Match across the number words one–twenty (with 0–20 available as reference), including a playful pairs/memory game over the words.
Also work the reverse direction: given a numeral or a quantity, find and say the matching word.
activities.intendedInsight: The number word carries meaning: it names a specific numeral AND a specific quantity, so the word must be read for meaning, not just decoded as text.

activities.title: Build-the-word: spell the number for a numeral
feedback: Flag the four/for and 'thirteen'/'thirty' traps as they happen, contrasting the two spellings with their quantities.

If a young learner spells phonetically (e.g. 'fiveteen', 'elevin', 'nighn' for nine), treat it as normal early spelling: keep showing the correct written form and let spelling mature rather than marking it as a maths failure.
Praise correct production of irregular forms specifically, since these cannot be sounded out.
activities.rationale: Practising the writing/production direction prevents word-recognition without spelling (or vice versa), which the objective to read AND write the words requires. Treating phonetic invented spellings as developmentally normal avoids penalising expected early-years errors while still exposing correct forms.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words.
Many number words are irregular sight words and the teens are opaque (eleven/twelve) or say the ones-part first, so they need dedicated sight-word and structure-linked teaching.
learnerActions: Look at a shown numeral (for example 13).
Use letter tiles, tracing, or handwriting to build or write the matching word ('thirteen').
Check the spelling against a reference wall, correcting classic traps like four/for and thirteen/thirty.
Spell several words one–twenty, returning to the irregular and teen forms for extra practice.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a number word and producing its correct written form are different skills; learners need to spell the word, not only recognise it.

activities.title: Teen zone: keep ten-and-ones visible
feedback: If a learner reads 'thirteen' as 31, re-point to the full ten plus three ones: the word means one ten and three, not three tens and one.
Contrast minimal pairs by sound and quantity: 'thirteen' vs 'thirty', 'fifteen' vs 'fifty', matching each to counters.
Confirm 'eleven' and 'twelve' by sight, since their letters give no clue to the quantity.
activities.rationale: Showing the ones-part + '-teen' beside a ten-frame for thirteen to nineteen, and pairing the opaque words eleven and twelve with their ten-and-ones frames, helps keep the ten-and-ones meaning attached to the teen words, directly targeting the known reversal and sound-alike confusions. Segment cues and the linked frame are concrete ways to show structure, not the only possible format.
sourceClaims: Many number words are irregular sight words and the teens are opaque (eleven/twelve) or say the ones-part first, so they need dedicated sight-word and structure-linked teaching.
learnerActions: Segment each teen word from thirteen to nineteen beside its quantity: thir·teen, four·teen, fif·teen, and so on.
Place each segmented word next to a ten-frame showing one full ten plus the ones part.
Memorise 'eleven' and 'twelve' as sight words paired with their ten-and-ones frames.
Say the word slowly and match it to the quantity, noticing that the ones-word comes first (thir-) but the quantity is ten-and-three.
activities.intendedInsight: The teens name ten-and-ones even though the word is opaque ('eleven'/'twelve') or says the ones-part first; keeping the structure visible helps prevent the reversal 'thir-teen → 31'.

activities.title: Number words in real reading and writing
feedback: If the wrong quantity appears after reading a word (e.g. 20 or 2 counters for 'twelve'), reteach the irregular word as a sight word alongside its numeral.
If a learner reads or writes the wrong member of a minimal pair (twelve/twenty), place the two words side by side with their quantities and say each slowly.
Confirm success when the learner acts on the word correctly and produces the word form, not merely when they recite a sequence.
activities.rationale: Encountering number words in authentic reading and writing (labels, lists, rhymes, washing lines) gives repeated meaningful exposure, and acting on a written word can expose genuine decoding of irregular words in context rather than recitation.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words.
learnerActions: Read a short real instruction, e.g. 'buy twelve eggs', and set out that many counters, then write the numeral.
Label a box of 15 crayons with the number WORD.
Meet number words on a washing line 0–20, on classroom labels, and in books/rhymes repeatedly, not just in a maths drill.
Read a word to make or point to the quantity, and write the word for a given numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Number words are used to act in the world: reading one to do something and producing a word label shows real command beyond reciting.

activities.title: Reference wall: tap-to-hear number words 0–20
feedback: Encourage using the wall to self-check a spelling or a minimal-pair confusion rather than guessing.
Point out the highlighted ones-part + '-teen' when a word from thirteen to nineteen is in doubt; for eleven and twelve, point to the matching ten-and-ones quantity instead.
activities.rationale: A static numeral–word–quantity chart with optional tap-to-hear audio is a strong always-available reference for the words; however it supports recognition and recall and does not by itself have the child write/spell the words, which is half the objective, so pair it with production practice.
learnerActions: Use a 0–20 chart showing each numeral, its word, and a matching quantity.
Tap an entry to hear the word spoken and see the teen structure highlighted.
Return to the wall to check spelling and meaning while reading or writing elsewhere.
activities.intendedInsight: A consistent reference linking numeral, word and quantity supports recall of sight words and teen structure during other tasks.

constraints: Reading/recognition and matching tasks support consolidation but do not by themselves elicit independent spelling; include writing/production of the words to cover the full objective.
A reference chart or tap-to-hear wall supports recall but does not have the learner construct or spell the words; it is a scaffold, not the whole objective.
Build on secured numerals 0–20 as a prerequisite before layering the word forms.

Coordinate irregular number words (one, two, four, eight, twelve) with the phonics/high-frequency sight-word programme; do not assume all number words are phonically regular, and note that some (six, ten) are decodable.
Phonetic/invented spellings (fiveteen, elevin, nighn) in early writers are developmentally normal and should not be marked as maths failures; keep exposing correct forms as spelling matures.
Practise both directions (word→quantity and numeral→word) so recognition does not develop without production or vice versa.
The read/write production target is the words one–twenty; a wider 0–20 range may appear on reference displays as context.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources (CCSS 2.NBT.3 alignment and the NCETM sight-word/structure guidance) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their claims as legacy and unconfirmed.

The 'self-correcting ten-frame' and segment-cue mechanisms are reasonable design proposals; the source material does not establish their comparative efficacy or that any one format uniquely teaches the mapping. They are offered as options, not necessities.
Reading '31' for 'thirteen' is the ones-first reversal; the corrective is to contrast ten-and-three with three-tens-and-one, preserved and surfaced in feedback.

Activity 1's source citation uses the sight-word/structure claim, which directly supports structure-linked teaching; the standard claim is cited in activities 2 and 4 where it directly supports read/write-in-words.
Original reference range is 0–20 (washing line/chart); the objective's production target is one–twenty, so zero is retained only as reference context, not as a required written-word target.

probeDeeper: Read this word for me: fifteen — now put out that many.
Write the word that means 12.
Which word says 20 and which says 12? Show me each with counters.
assess.correctAnswer: Reads 'twelve' and sets out 12, writes 12; labels the box 'fifteen'. Uses the word correctly in the task, not just recites it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Guesses the irregular word from its first letters/shape: reads 'twelve' as 'twenty' or 'two'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat number words as sight words: build automatic recognition of the irregular ones (one, two, twelve, eleven) alongside their numerals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sets out the wrong quantity after reading the word (20 or 2 for twelve).

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses similar-sounding words (twelve/twenty, thirteen/thirty-ish) when reading or writing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the pair side by side with their quantities; say them slowly and match each to counters.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads or writes the wrong member of a minimal pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: Spells the word phonetically/invented (fiveteen, elevin) when writing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark it as a maths error or drill it as failure — it is normal early spelling; keep exposing the correct written forms and let spelling mature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The word is readable but non-standard.

responseLevels.gap: Misreads irregular number words so the wrong quantity is produced; cannot write the correct word.
responseLevels.full: Reads any number word 1–20 to act on it and writes the correct word form, distinguishing minimal pairs in context.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes most words but confuses look-/sound-alike pairs or invents spellings.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a real task. 'This shopping list says buy twelve eggs — read it and put out that many counters, then write the numeral.' Then: 'Label this box of 15 crayons with the number WORD.' Watch them read a number word to act, and produce the word form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Acting on a written number word (put out twelve) and producing a word label exposes real use: a child who only recites can't reliably decode an irregular word in context or spell the correct one, while the minimal pairs (twelve/twenty, fifteen/fifty-ish) reveal confusions a definition task would hide.

sources.claim: Year 1 pupils read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 1, Number and place value)

sources.claim: Pupils read and write numbers using base-ten numerals and number names, a literacy-of-number expectation formalised by Grade 2.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 2.NBT.3 (building on K.CC)

sources.claim: Many number words are irregular sight words and the teens are opaque (eleven/twelve) or say the ones-part first, so they need dedicated sight-word and structure-linked teaching.
