pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** What uses electricity at home

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS2 Year 4 Electricity, statutory):** 'identify common appliances that run on electricity.'

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** National (NGSS): no direct grade-3/4 performance expectation for naming electrical appliances; the nearest energy strand is 4-PS3-2 (energy transferred by electric currents), which this topic only foreshadows. This topic is therefore UK-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Children name and sort everyday appliances by whether they run on electricity and, within that, whether the power comes from the mains (wall socket) or from a battery. No circuit theory, no current, no quantities; the cognitive work is categorisation and safety awareness, not mechanism. The teaching aim is a clean mental sort — mains vs battery vs not-electric — plus the safety habit that mains sockets are dangerous and only batteries are for exploring.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 8-9).
bestPractices: Start from the child's own home: have them name devices in the kitchen, lounge and bedroom, then sort into 'runs on electricity' vs 'does not' (a candle, a wind-up toy, a bicycle are not-electric foils).

Make the mains-vs-battery distinction explicit and physical — show a plug going into a wall socket vs a battery sliding into a torch — because it underpins both the later circuit work (batteries are what you build with) and the safety message (sockets are not).

Embed electrical safety as a non-negotiable: mains sockets, plugs and cables are never for experimenting; only battery-powered circuits are safe to build. This is a statutory expectation in the surrounding curriculum.
Use sorting and odd-one-out tasks rather than explanation; at this age the learning is reliable categorisation, surfaced and corrected through many quick examples.
Surface edge cases that build flexible thinking: a phone has a battery AND charges from the mains; a car runs on fuel but has electric lights — discuss rather than mark wrong.
keyRepresentations: A labelled scene of a home (kitchen/lounge/bedroom) with tappable appliances — the canonical 'spot the electrical things' picture.
A two-way sort: mains (plug + socket icon) vs battery (cell icon) vs not-electric.
Side-by-side icon pair: a plug entering a wall socket; a battery entering a torch — the mains/battery contrast.
A simple safety symbol/flag attached to mains items ('grown-up only, never poke').
commonMisconceptions: 'Anything that moves or makes noise uses electricity' — children over-include wind-up toys, clockwork and friction-driven things; foils are needed to break this.
'Battery things aren't really electricity' — some children reserve the word for the mains; the battery torch and the wall lamp both use electricity.
'Plugging in charges it up forever' — confusion between charging a battery and being powered while plugged in; not resolved here but worth noting for later.
Treating gas appliances (gas hob, gas fire) as electrical because they are kitchen/heating devices.
Believing the socket itself is 'the electricity' rather than a supply the appliance draws from.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year olds learning what uses electricity at home (UK KS2 Year 4: 'identify common appliances that run on electricity'). The learning goal is a clean three-way mental sort — mains (wall socket) vs battery vs not-electric — anchored in children's own homes, plus the safety habit that mains sockets/plugs/cables are never for experimenting and only battery-powered things are safe to explore. The work is categorisation and safety awareness, not circuit theory, current, or quantities. Deliberate foils (a candle, a wind-up/clockwork toy, a gas hob) break the misconception that anything moving, noisy, or switch-on uses electricity.

activities.title: Spot the electrical things in a home scene
feedback: When a child says a plain wind-up or clockwork TOY uses mains/battery electricity: it moves, but it has no plug and no battery — it stores energy in a wound-up spring and is not electric. (A wind-up RADIO is a different case: it has a small generator and does make its own electricity — see the two-tier check activity.)

When a child calls a gas hob electric because it's in the kitchen and makes heat: trace the energy source — its heat comes from burning gas to make a flame (some hobs use a small electric spark just to light it); contrast with a glowing electric heating element. 'Looks electric, but its heat comes from gas.'

When a child won't call a battery torch electric: both the torch and a wall lamp use electricity — a battery is a portable energy store that supplies electricity when it is connected; mains electricity comes into the home through the socket from power stations and other generators.
On every mains item, reinforce: sockets, plugs and cables are never for experimenting — grown-up only.
activities.rationale: At this age reliable categorisation is built and corrected through many quick concrete examples starting from the child's own home; a tap-to-reveal home scene delivers the power-source fact and the safety flag on every mains item together, with foils to break over-inclusion.
sourceClaims: Year 4 Electricity statutory requirement: 'identify common appliances that run on electricity'; pupils taught to construct simple series circuits and about electrical safety.
Children commonly over-attribute 'uses electricity' to any moving/noisy device and under-attribute it to battery devices; sorting with foils addresses this.
learnerActions: Walk through a labelled home picture (kitchen, lounge, bedroom) and name the devices you see.
Tap or point to each device and say whether it runs on electricity, and if so whether its power comes from the mains (wall socket) or from a battery.

For each device, reveal or state a short fact: e.g. toaster — 'Mains: I plug into the wall. Wall sockets are grown-up only, never poke them'; torch — 'Battery: safe for you to open and explore'; candle or wind-up clock — 'No electricity at all.'
Explain for each item how you can tell — does it have a plug and lead to a socket, or does it carry a battery inside?

Discuss the deliberate foils: a gas hob (may look electric, but its heat comes from burning gas; some use a small electric spark only to light it) and a clockwork/wind-up toy (moves but isn't mains/battery electric).
activities.intendedInsight: The sort isn't simply 'electric or not' but THREE piles — mains, battery, not-electric — and the mains pile is exactly the dangerous one you must never build with, so the only things safe to experiment with are the battery ones.

activities.title: Sort the appliances into three bins
feedback: A wrong drop prompts: 'does it have a plug or a battery?' before retrying.
Edge-case cards (phone, car) open a short 'both!' / 'neither, really' explainer rather than being marked right or wrong.
If a child sorts only by 'has a plug', point out the battery torch is still electric, and a gas hob gets its heat from burning gas even though some are plugged in for a spark igniter.
activities.rationale: A drag-to-sort bench makes categorisation active and self-correcting and doubles as quick formative assessment; immediate right/wrong feedback helps build the sort, not just test it.
sourceClaims: Children commonly over-attribute 'uses electricity' to any moving/noisy device and under-attribute it to battery devices; sorting with foils addresses this.
learnerActions: Take a set of appliance cards and place each into one of three labelled bins: Mains, Battery, Not electric.
For a wrong placement, use the hint 'does it have a plug or a battery?' and try again.

Handle edge-case cards (a phone, a car) by discussing rather than scoring: a phone has a battery AND charges from the mains; a petrol or diesel car burns fuel to move but uses a battery for its electric lights, while an electric car runs on a big battery.
Name at least ten appliances and place them, then say aloud the rule you used to sort.
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting by energy source (mains vs battery vs not-electric) is an active, self-correcting way to build and firm up the mental model, and edge cases show the piles aren't always clean-cut.

activities.title: Odd-one-out and power-source matching
feedback: If the odd-one-out is chosen by looks alone, ask which energy source each one uses.
For a wrong match, restate: mains items have a plug/lead to a wall socket; battery items carry their energy inside with no plug.
activities.rationale: Odd-one-out and matching cleanly check the sort. Note that recognition tasks like these assess and firm up the model more than they build it, so use them alongside the exploratory scene and the sorting bench.
learnerActions: Given a small group of appliances, pick the odd one out (e.g. the one that does not run on electricity) and say why.
Match each device to its power source (mains socket icon vs battery/cell icon).
Answer 'which of these run on electricity?' and justify the choice by energy source, not just by appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: Quick recognition tasks let a learner check and firm up the mains/battery/not-electric sort across many examples.

activities.title: Ask the electrician: why and what's safe
feedback: The character always returns to the rule: wall sockets are grown-up only, never poke them.

For 'is the gas cooker electric?' the answer traces the energy source: it cooks with heat from burning gas, not electricity (some have a small electric spark or light, but that is not what cooks the food).
activities.rationale: In-role dialogue can reinforce the safety habit and answer 'why?' questions. The core target skill is silent sorting, so treat this as a supplement rather than the main vehicle.
sourceClaims: Year 4 Electricity statutory requirement: 'identify common appliances that run on electricity'; pupils taught to construct simple series circuits and about electrical safety.
learnerActions: Pose questions to an in-role 'electrician' character, e.g. 'is the toaster electric?' or 'why can't I poke the socket?'
Ask 'where does the electricity come from?' for a mains item and for a battery item, and compare the answers.
Restate the safety rule in your own words: mains sockets, plugs and cables are never for experimenting; only battery-powered circuits are safe to build.
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through 'why' reinforces the safety habit and the idea that mains and battery are both electricity from different supplies.

activities.title: Two-tier check: four things, which use electricity and how?
feedback: Full answer: the battery torch and mains fridge use electricity; the gas cooker gets its cooking heat from burning gas (some have a small electric spark to light it); the wind-up radio makes its own electricity because winding it turns a small generator, so it can work with no plug (some models store that electricity in a built-in rechargeable battery). Mains items have a plug/lead to a socket; battery ones carry energy inside with no plug.

Gap pattern ('no plug, no electricity'): sort by energy source, not plug — a battery is a portable energy store that supplies electricity, and the wind-up radio generates its own with a small generator.
If the gas cooker is labelled electric: its cooking heat comes from burning gas to make a flame (any electric spark only lights it); contrast with a glowing electric heating element.

If the torch is denied as electric: both mains and a battery supply electricity to make things work; mains electricity comes through the socket from power stations and other generators, while a battery is a portable energy store that supplies electricity when it is connected.
activities.rationale: A two-tier diagnostic with a reason tier discriminates children who equate 'has a plug' with 'uses electricity' (they miss the wind-up radio and may include the gas cooker) from those who reason about the energy source.
learnerActions: Look at four things: a torch that takes batteries, a gas cooker, a wind-up radio, and a fridge plugged into the wall.
Say which ones use electricity to work.
For the ones that do, say how you can tell which get their electricity from the mains and which from a battery.

Answer deeper probes: how can a wind-up radio with no battery and no plug still use electricity? When a phone is plugged in, is it mains or battery, and what's happening to the battery? Name three things at home that make heat — which get that heat from electricity and which from burning something? If the power cut off in your street, which of the four things would still work, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying by electrical energy source (mains vs battery vs self-generated) — rather than by 'has a plug' — is what separates a surface sort from real understanding, and extends to new cases like a power cut or a phone charging.

constraints: No circuit theory, current, or quantities at this stage; the cognitive work is categorisation and safety awareness, not mechanism.
Electrical safety is non-negotiable and a statutory expectation: mains sockets, plugs and cables are never for experimenting; only battery-powered circuits are safe to build.

Recognition tasks (odd-one-out, matching) assess and firm up the model more than they build it, so pair them with other activities; the interactive drag-to-sort bench, by contrast, is active and self-correcting and does help build the sort as well as check it.
The in-role electrician dialogue is a useful supplement for 'why' and safety, not the main vehicle, since the target skill is silent sorting.
Edge cases (phone that is both battery and mains-charging; car that runs on fuel but has electric lights) should be discussed rather than marked right/wrong.
'Plugging in charges a battery forever' / the confusion between charging and being powered while plugged in is not resolved at this level but is worth flagging for later.

A flat labelled scene teaches the categorisation adequately; a 3D navigable house adds navigation cost without teaching the sort better, so a spatial/3D treatment is not needed here (this is not a claim that 3D cannot teach).
Distinguish a plain wind-up/clockwork toy (mechanical, not electric) from a wind-up radio (has a small generator and does produce electricity); do not let one blanket rule cover both.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (IOP Spark / SPT children's ideas about electricity) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its misconception claim as indicative, not confirmed.

The learner-level phrasings 'a battery is a portable store of electrical energy' and the wind-up radio 'makes its own electricity' are age-appropriate simplifications (a battery stores chemical energy converted to electrical current; a wind-up device stores elastic/mechanical energy driving a small generator). Kept as the original row stated them, but flagged so reviewers can decide how precise to be for this age.
The US NGSS mapping notes no direct grade-3/4 performance expectation for naming electrical appliances (nearest is 4-PS3-2, only foreshadowed); this topic is UK-anchored.
Product/artefact-type names, fit rankings, and quiz-step vocabulary from the source were removed; the underlying tasks and feedback were preserved.

The DfE statutory claim is mapped to activities that concretely deliver its safety message; it is a curriculum/convention source, not evidence that any proposed activity is effective or superior to another medium.

probeDeeper: The wind-up radio has no battery and no plug. How can it still be using electricity?
A phone can run while plugged in AND unplugged. Is it mains or battery — and what's happening to the battery when it's plugged in?
Name three things at home that make heat: which get that heat from electricity and which from burning something?
If the power cut off in your street, which of your four things would still work, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: The battery torch and the mains fridge use electricity; the gas cooker burns gas, not electricity; the wind-up radio makes its own electricity from a spring you wind, so it uses electricity but needs no battery or plug. Mains appliances have a plug/lead to a wall socket; battery ones carry their energy inside a battery and have no plug.

errorPatterns.pattern: Anything with a plug or that you switch on uses electricity, and anything without a plug doesn't ('no plug, no electricity').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort by ENERGY SOURCE, not by plug — mains, battery, wind-up/other; show that a battery is a portable store of electrical energy.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only the fridge uses electricity, because it's the only one plugged into the wall.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the wind-up radio isn't electrical and can't classify battery devices.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gas and electric appliances are the same because both switch on and both make heat ('it's all electric really').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the energy source — gas burns a fuel to make a flame; contrast that with a glowing electric heating element.
errorPatterns.distractor: The gas cooker uses electricity, because you turn it on to make heat like the others.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels the gas cooker as electric.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mains and battery electricity are two completely different things, not both electricity ('battery isn't real electricity').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Both deliver an electric current to make the device work; mains comes from a power station through the socket, a battery is a portable store of the same thing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Won't call the torch electric, or treats battery power as a separate kind of thing.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by 'has a plug' alone; calls the gas cooker electric or the wind-up/battery device non-electric.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by electrical energy source — mains vs battery vs self-generated — explains that gas burns fuel rather than using electricity, and applies it to a new case such as a power cut or a phone charging.
responseLevels.partial: Names many electrical appliances and knows some run on batteries, but can't consistently sort by energy SOURCE (misses the wind-up radio, or lumps the gas cooker in).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at these four things: a torch that takes batteries, a gas cooker, a wind-up radio, and a fridge plugged into the wall. Which ones use electricity to work, and how can you tell which get their electricity from the mains and which from a battery?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who equates 'has a plug' with 'uses electricity' misses the wind-up radio and may wrongly include the gas cooker; the reason tier separates 'plugged in = electric' from 'the energy source is an electric current'.

sources.claim: Year 4 Electricity statutory requirement: 'identify common appliances that run on electricity'; pupils taught to construct simple series circuits and about electrical safety.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, KS2 Year 4 Electricity

sources.claim: Children commonly over-attribute 'uses electricity' to any moving/noisy device and under-attribute it to battery devices; sorting with foils addresses this.
sources.source: IOP Spark / SPT — electricity teaching guidance (children's ideas about electricity)

pedagogy.summary: Understanding positive and negative numbers as quantities with opposite DIRECTIONS about a meaningful zero, and operating on them using number-line reasoning. The number line (or thermometer / floors-in-a-building / bank balance) is the central representation: a number's sign is its direction from zero and its magnitude is its distance. Adding a positive moves right/up, adding a negative moves left/down, and subtracting a negative reverses that to move right — so 'subtracting a negative is the same as adding' is derived from direction, not memorised. The recurring difficulty is distinguishing the two meanings of the minus symbol: the sign OF a number versus the operation of subtraction.
bestPractices: Anchor every idea on a number line / thermometer where zero is a real reference (freezing point, ground floor, break-even), not 'nothing'
Keep magnitude (distance from zero) and sign (direction) as separate ideas - counter 'bigger digit = bigger number' for negatives
Use directed-journey language: adding a negative is a move in the negative direction; subtracting a negative reverses direction
Distinguish the operation minus from the negative sign explicitly (colour, gesture, or bracket: 4 + (-7))
Derive 'subtract a negative = add' on the line (removing a debt / turning to face the other way) rather than stating a rule
keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line spanning zero (arrows for direction and length)
Vertical thermometer / floors of a building / sea level
Bank balance and debt (money owed as negative)
Two-colour counters (zero pairs) for combining opposites
commonMisconceptions: Orders negatives by magnitude - thinks -7 > -3 because 7 > 3
Conflates the negative sign with the subtraction operation ('two minuses', reads 4 + (-7) as 4 - 7 or 4 + 7 arbitrarily)
Believes numbers 'stop' at zero, so cannot count or move through zero
Thinks subtracting always makes smaller and adding always makes bigger (fails for negatives)
Treats 'subtract a negative' as more negative rather than as reversing direction

learn.summary: Positive and negative numbers are quantities with opposite DIRECTIONS from a meaningful zero (freezing point, ground floor, break-even), where sign is direction and magnitude is distance. On a number line, adding a positive moves right/up, adding a negative moves left/down, and subtracting a negative reverses direction to move right/up — so 'subtracting a negative is the same as adding' is derived from the direction of travel, not memorised as a sign rule. The central difficulty is distinguishing the two meanings of the minus symbol: the sign OF a number versus the operation of subtraction. Learners should both READ arrows/journeys and PRODUCE their own for new signed calculations, including moves straight through zero.

activities.title: Operate a directed number line: fire and flip the arrow
feedback: If the 1 - (-3) arrow is drawn moving LEFT to -2 ('subtracting a negative makes it more negative'): model on the line and with debt — subtracting a negative reverses direction (removing a -3 is adding 3); walk the arrow flip physically.
If 4 + (-7) is drawn rightward or read as 4 - 7 or 4 + 7: separate 'negative seven' (a directed quantity) from 'subtract' (a move) using brackets, colour and gesture for the two roles.
If the arrow halts at zero: continue the thermometer/lift below zero and count aloud through it (2, 1, 0, -1, -2).
activities.rationale: An operable line where the learner chooses the calculation and watches direction (sign) and length (magnitude) makes the structure of the move the object of attention, rather than a sign rule applied by habit. NCETM advises examining the STRUCTURE of the calculation rather than teaching sign rules; standards frame p+q as a distance |q| from p in a direction set by the sign, and p-q as adding the additive inverse. The through-zero journey for 4 + (-7) (passing 2, 1, 0, -1, -2 on the way to -3) covers an interval across 0 (7 units from 4 to -3), which links to the Year 6 statutory wording on intervals across zero; the 1 - (-3) journey does not cross zero. This is a research-informed design proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative' and 'understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p - q = p + (-q)', representing these on a horizontal or vertical number line (7.NS.A.1b, 1c).

Hart (1981)/CSMS records that when subtracting a positive integer many students 'simply subtract the numerals and then attempt to determine the sign for the answer', and when subtracting a negative use the rule 'two negatives make a positive'; the misconception is rooted in prior experience that 'addition makes larger and subtraction makes smaller', which breaks down for negatives. NCETM advises examining the STRUCTURE of the calculation rather than teaching sign rules.
Year 6 pupils 'use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across 0' (Year 6 Number - number and place value, verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Enter 4 + (-7): start a marker at 4 and draw/trace an arrow 7 units LEFT, landing on -3 — state that the negative sign IS the leftward direction and the 7 is how far.
Enter 1 - (-3): show that the arrow subtraction would send LEFT instead FLIPS to point RIGHT, landing on 4; compare with adding 3 (1 + 3 = 4) and confirm you land in the same place.
Say in words why the arrow reversed: removing a -3 (e.g. clearing a debt of 3) is the same as adding 3.

Replay both journeys vertically on a thermometer/lift mode: for 4 + (-7), count aloud straight down through zero (4, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3); for 1 - (-3), count up from 1 (2, 3, 4) and notice that this journey stays above zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Signed addition and the direction-reversal of subtracting a negative become visible: 'two minuses make a plus' is a direction reversal you can see, not a spell to recall. Numbers do not stop at zero.

activities.title: Zero in context and the two minus signs
feedback: If zero is described as 'nothing': re-anchor on a real context where below-zero values exist (temperature, basement floors, debt).
If the two minus signs are conflated: name 'negative seven' (a directed quantity) separately from 'subtract' (a move), and re-read the calculation aloud with that distinction.
activities.rationale: A fixed reference display supports reading direction, zero-in-context and the sign/operation distinction. It is a reference scaffold: it does not animate a calculation the learner chooses, so it complements rather than replaces the operable line, and it does not by itself show the learner can produce a move.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across 0' (Year 6 Number - number and place value, verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: On a labelled reference line/thermometer, point to a value and state both its sign (direction from zero) and its distance from zero.
Switch contexts (temperature, floors of a building, bank balance) and say what zero means in each (freezing point, ground floor, break-even — not 'nothing').
For a written calculation like 4 + (-7), mark which minus is the negative SIGN of a number and which (if any) is the subtraction OPERATION; use brackets/colour to keep them apart.
activities.intendedInsight: Zero is a meaningful reference point, and the minus symbol carries two distinct meanings that must be read, not guessed.

activities.title: Place, order and interpret signed calculations
feedback: If -7 is placed to the RIGHT of -3 (ordering by magnitude, treating -7 as greater): use the thermometer/line — left of zero is less, and the further left the smaller; contrast -7 and -3 directly.
If the given arrow's calculation is misread: separate direction (sign) from length (magnitude) explicitly and re-read the endpoints.
activities.rationale: Placing, ordering and reading signed calculations target the 'bigger digit = bigger number' error directly and rehearse separating sign from magnitude. The interpret action reads an interval across zero, which the Year 6 statutory wording supports; the ordering focus rests on the separated-ideas teaching principle rather than on that claim. Include a deliberate magnitude-ordering contrast such as -7 versus -3.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across 0' (Year 6 Number - number and place value, verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Place -7 and -3 on a number line and state which is smaller, explaining via position (the further left, the smaller).
Order a set of negatives from least to greatest.

Interpret a given arrow (e.g. starting at -3, ending at 2): state the calculation it shows (-3 + 5 = 2, or the difference 2 - (-3) = 5, an interval across 0) and what its direction and length tell you.
Decide and justify which way 1 - (-3) moves before drawing it.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering by position (not by digit size) and reading an arrow's direction and length consolidate that magnitude and sign are separate ideas.

activities.title: Talk through the two meanings of minus
feedback: If the learner says subtracting always sends you left: revisit 1 - (-3) on the line and the debt model to show the reversal.
If the two minuses are described as the same thing: re-draw the calculation distinguishing the directed quantity from the move.
activities.rationale: A probing discussion can surface the two-meanings-of-minus confusion and whether the learner reasons about direction or guesses; it works best alongside the line, where the directional insight is seen, rather than in place of it. Discussion can elicit explanation but does not itself show the learner can construct an arrow for a new calculation.
sourceClaims: Hart (1981)/CSMS records that when subtracting a positive integer many students 'simply subtract the numerals and then attempt to determine the sign for the answer', and when subtracting a negative use the rule 'two negatives make a positive'; the misconception is rooted in prior experience that 'addition makes larger and subtraction makes smaller', which breaks down for negatives. NCETM advises examining the STRUCTURE of the calculation rather than teaching sign rules.
learnerActions: Answer: what is the difference between the minus in 'negative three' and the minus in 'subtract three'?
Explain which way your arrow for 4 + (-7) went and why.
Answer: does subtracting always send you left? What did 1 - (-3) do, and why?
Explain, using the line, which is bigger, -7 or -3.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the two roles of the minus symbol and justifying arrow direction surfaces and tests understanding beyond a correct final answer.

constraints: Anchor every idea on a number line/thermometer/floors/balance where zero is a real reference (freezing point, ground floor, break-even), not 'nothing'.
Keep magnitude (distance from zero) and sign (direction) as separate ideas; counter 'bigger digit = bigger number' for negatives.
Use directed-journey language: adding a negative moves in the negative direction; subtracting a negative reverses direction (right/up on the chosen axis).
Explicitly distinguish the subtraction operation from the negative sign using colour, gesture, or brackets, e.g. 4 + (-7).
Derive 'subtract a negative = add' on the line (removing a debt / turning to face the other way) rather than stating it as a rule.
A fixed reference poster/line supports reading sign, magnitude and zero-in-context but does not animate a learner-chosen operation; use it to complement, not replace, learner production of arrows.

Recognition/placement tasks (ordering, selecting a direction) do not by themselves show the learner can PRODUCE an arrow for a new signed calculation; include tasks where the learner constructs the move themselves.
Two-colour counters (zero pairs) are a useful alternative representation for combining opposites and may be offered alongside the line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and legacy 'verified'/'confidence' flags are not independently confirmed. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a genuine third spatial dimension as adding nothing over a 2D vertical thermometer/lift. This is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it is framed here only as a scope note (directed number is one-dimensional, so a vertical 2D thermometer/lift already represents that single directed axis) rather than a universal 'adds nothing' claim.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 4 + (-7) = -3 (7 left of 4); 1 - (-3) = 4 (reverse to move 3 right from 1, matching 1 + 3); -3 + 5 = 2 and 2 - (-3) = 5 — all consistent across the source fields and retained as stated.
The debt analogy ('removing a -3 is the same as adding 3') is a model of direction reversal, not a proof; present it as an illustration alongside the line.

Activity 3's single source claim directly supports its interval-across-zero interpret action; the ordering/magnitude focus rests on the separated-ideas teaching principle rather than on that statutory wording. The Year 6 claim on activity 1 supports the through-zero counting action, not the sign/magnitude-separation principle.

probeDeeper: What is the difference between the minus in 'negative three' and the minus in 'subtract three'?
Your arrow for 4 + (-7) went which way, and why that way?
Does subtracting always send you left? What did 1 - (-3) do - and why?
On the line, which is bigger, -7 or -3, and how does the line show it?
assess.correctAnswer: Interpret: the arrow shows -3 + 5 = 2 (it points right/positive, so something is added; its length 5 is the amount, matching the distance from -3 to 2) - equivalently the difference 2 - (-3) = 5. Translate: 4 + (-7) starts at 4 and moves 7 LEFT to -3; 1 - (-3) reverses direction to move 3 RIGHT (subtracting a negative), landing on 4. Distinguishes the negative sign (direction/position) from the subtraction operation (a move).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Subtracting a negative just makes it more negative' - draws 1 - (-3) moving LEFT, landing on -2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model on the line/with debt: subtracting a negative reverses the direction (removing a -3 is the same as adding 3); walk the arrow flip physically.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The translate step: the 1 - (-3) arrow points the wrong way

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates the negative sign with the subtraction operation - reads 4 + (-7) as 4 - 7 done arbitrarily, or as 4 + 7, unsure which minus is which
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explicitly separate 'negative seven' (a directed quantity) from 'subtract' (a move); use brackets, colour, and gesture for the two roles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Misreads the calculation the given arrow shows, or draws 4 + (-7) rightward

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude, so places -7 to the RIGHT of -3 on the line
errorPatterns.nextMove: Thermometer / left-of-zero-is-less; the further left, the smaller; contrast -7 and -3 directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endpoints placed wrongly; -7 treated as greater than -3

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes numbers 'stop' at zero, so an arrow crossing zero confuses or is halted there
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a thermometer/lift that continues below zero; count aloud through zero (2, 1, 0, -1, -2).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Arrow stops at 0, or the child cannot continue a move through zero

responseLevels.gap: Orders negatives by size, cannot cross zero, or draws arrows in the wrong direction; treats the two minus signs as the same thing.
responseLevels.full: Interprets and produces arrows for adding and subtracting both positive and negative numbers, articulates subtracting a negative as reversing direction (equivalent to adding), and transfers to a new case moving through zero.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a given arrow correctly and places integers on the line, but cannot reliably PRODUCE an arrow for adding a negative or subtracting a negative - knows the pieces but cannot translate a new signed calculation onto the line.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First, INTERPRET: here is a number line with an arrow that starts at -3 and ends at 2. What calculation does this arrow show, and what do its direction and length tell you? Then, TRANSLATE: on the number line, draw an arrow to show 4 + (-7) and say where you land; then draw one for 1 - (-3) and say where you land.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reading the given arrow forces separating direction (sign) from length (magnitude). Producing an arrow for adding a negative (move left) versus subtracting a negative (move right) reveals whether the child understands subtracting-a-negative as a direction reversal or is guessing - and a child who conflates the operation minus with the negative sign draws 4 + (-7) or 1 - (-3) in the wrong direction. Interpreting then producing catches the child who can read a diagram but cannot build one for a new signed calculation.

pedagogy.summary: This topic connects a sky observation to Earth's orbit: some constellations (e.g. Orion, Leo) are seen only in particular seasons, while a few near the pole (Ursa Major/the Plough, Cassiopeia) are visible year-round. The reason seasonal ones come and go is that at night we look OUTWARD, away from the Sun, into space — and as Earth travels around its orbit through the year, 'away from the Sun' points at a different patch of stars each season. A constellation like Orion is 'missing' in summer because it is then up in the DAYTIME sky, on the Sun's side, its faint light lost in daylight. The two moves are (1) name and recognise a few constellations, and (2) explain seasonal visibility by Earth's ORBIT (not its daily spin).
bestPractices: Start from recognisable patterns the child can name and re-find — Orion (with its belt), the Plough/Big Dipper, Leo, Cassiopeia — before explaining why some change with the season; recognition first, mechanism second.

Use a top-down orbit model: place Earth at the four seasons around the Sun; at each position, shade the NIGHT side (facing away from the Sun) and show which constellations lie in that outward direction — those are tonight's stars.
Make the 'behind the Sun' idea explicit: a summer constellation isn't gone, it's in the daytime sky on the far side of the Sun, so sunlight hides it — it returns to the night sky half a year later.

Distinguish the two Earth motions carefully: the nightly east-to-west drift of stars is the daily SPIN; the slow change of WHICH constellations are up at night across months is the yearly ORBIT. Keep these causes separate, as children routinely merge them.

Contrast seasonal vs circumpolar: constellations near Polaris (Plough, Cassiopeia) circle the pole and stay visible all year, while those around the celestial equator/ecliptic are seasonal — this explains why the child's familiar Plough is always there but Orion is not.
keyRepresentations: Top-down orbit diagram: Sun in the centre, Earth at four seasonal positions, night-side arrow pointing outward to that season's constellations
Coupled dual view: orbit position (bird's-eye) beside the night-sky view a child on Earth would actually see at midnight
Constellation recognition cards: Orion, Ursa Major/Plough, Leo, Cassiopeia with their star-join patterns
A 'behind the Sun' highlight showing a summer constellation lost in the daytime side of the sky
Circumpolar circle around Polaris (always-visible stars) vs the seasonal band
commonMisconceptions: Attributing seasonal star changes to Earth's daily SPIN (day/night) rather than its yearly ORBIT — conflating the two motions.
Thinking the constellations themselves move away or change shape seasonally, rather than our night-time viewing direction changing as Earth orbits.
Believing a 'missing' constellation has disappeared or been destroyed, not realising it is in the daytime sky (on the Sun's side) and lost in sunlight.
Assuming ALL constellations are seasonal, missing that circumpolar ones (Plough, Cassiopeia) stay visible all year from mid-northern latitudes.
Confusing the cause of seasonal star visibility with the cause of the seasons themselves (axial tilt) — they are different, orbit-related but distinct.
Thinking stars are joined by real lines or that a constellation is a single object rather than a pattern of stars at very different distances.

learn.summary: Children first recognise and name a few star patterns (Orion with its belt, the Plough/Big Dipper — a star pattern within the constellation Ursa Major — Leo, Cassiopeia), then explain why some are seasonal: at night we look OUTWARD, away from the Sun, into space, and as Earth travels around its orbit through the year 'away from the Sun' points at a different patch of stars each season. Seen from the Northern Hemisphere, a constellation like Orion is 'missing' in summer because it is then up in the DAYTIME sky, on the Sun's side, its faint light lost in daylight. Key moves: (1) recognition first, then (2) explain seasonal visibility by Earth's ORBIT, carefully distinguished from the daily SPIN, and contrasted with circumpolar stars near Polaris that stay visible all year from mid-northern latitudes.

activities.title: Drag Earth round its orbit and watch tonight's sky change
feedback: If a learner says Orion 'disappeared' or 'moved away', point to the orbit view: Orion is still there but on the daytime side, lost in the Sun's glare; the night side simply faces away from it in summer.
If a learner credits the daily spin, use the toggle: the spin sweeps the same stars across each night; it is the orbit that swaps the cast across months.
If a learner thinks the stars move around us, highlight that the distant stars stay put while Earth's changing orbital position changes which way we look at night.
activities.rationale: Seasonal visibility is a relationship between Earth's orbital position and which stars the night side faces. A coupled, continuously recomputing model is proposed to let the child discover that the change tracks the orbit and watch a summer constellation cross onto the Sun's daytime side — the step intended to make the cause click. Recognition precedes mechanism.
sourceClaims: Grade-5 standard: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-2]', with examples including [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-2]'.
Seasonal constellations are hidden when they lie in the daytime sky (Sun's side); circumpolar constellations near Polaris remain visible year-round — standard observational-astronomy explanation.
learnerActions: Study two linked views side by side: a bird's-eye (top-down) view of Earth orbiting the Sun, and the night sky a child on Earth would actually see at midnight.

Slowly move Earth around its year-long loop. On the orbit view the night side (facing away from the Sun) is shaded; watch the night-sky window swap in which named constellations are up in the night sky for each position.

Find Orion shining high in the southern midnight sky in (northern-hemisphere) winter; then move Earth toward summer and watch how, as Earth moves, the Sun comes to lie in Orion's direction as seen from Earth, so Orion ends up on Earth's day side and fades out of the night-sky window, with a label noting 'now up in the daytime — hidden by the Sun'.
Use a 'spin vs orbit' toggle: see that the daily spin only slides the SAME stars east-to-west across the night, while the yearly orbit changes WHICH constellations are there at all.
Notice that the Plough/Cassiopeia, near the pole (Polaris), stay visible all year from mid-northern latitudes while Orion comes and goes.
activities.intendedInsight: The stars didn't go anywhere — WE moved around the Sun, so at night we face a different part of space. The yearly orbit (not the daily spin) changes which constellations are up at night, and a 'missing' summer constellation is really in the daytime sky on the Sun's side.

activities.title: Four-season orbit diagram with reveal cards
feedback: If a learner cannot yet re-find a pattern, revisit the star-join picture and a memorable feature (e.g. Orion's belt of three) before linking to the season.
Reinforce that the summer-hidden constellation is revealed as still present but daytime-side, not gone.
activities.rationale: A labelled four-season diagram with reveal patches plus recognition cards is intended to teach naming and the seasonal arrangement. It presents four discrete snapshots but cannot be swept continuously, so pair it with the continuous model when possible.
sourceClaims: Grade-5 standard: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-2]', with examples including [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-2]'.
Seasonal constellations are hidden when they lie in the daytime sky (Sun's side); circumpolar constellations near Polaris remain visible year-round — standard observational-astronomy explanation.
learnerActions: Look at a labelled orbit diagram with the Sun at the centre and Earth at four seasonal positions.
Reveal, for each of the four positions, that season's constellations and a night-side arrow pointing outward into space.
Reveal a constellation to see its name and star-join pattern (Orion, Ursa Major with its Plough pattern, Leo, Cassiopeia).
Open the reveal on a summer-hidden Orion to read 'it's in the daytime sky now'.
Compare the four snapshots to notice which constellations change season-to-season and which (circumpolar) stay.
activities.intendedInsight: Across the four seasons, Earth's night side points outward in different directions, so different constellations are overhead — and the ones that lie toward the Sun in a given season are up in the daytime instead.

activities.title: Stand on Earth and advance the date (immersive view)
feedback: If the first-person view feels disorienting, return to the top-down orbit view and re-link the date to Earth's position; the causal point lives in the orbit, with the sky view as the observed consequence.
activities.rationale: An immersive 'stand and look up' view may build engagement and connect the abstract orbit to lived sky-watching. It is offered as an optional complement; the essential insight is already carried by the top-down orbit plus a sky window, and immersion is not required to grasp the cause.
learnerActions: Take a first-person 'look up from Earth' view of the night sky.
Advance the date forward through the months and watch which constellations are visible change.
Relate the immersive view back to the top-down orbit position so the ground-view change connects to Earth's movement around the Sun.
activities.intendedInsight: From the ground, the visible constellations change through the year; this is the same orbit effect seen from a different vantage, reinforcing that our changing position changes what we face at night.

activities.title: Check recognition and reasoning
feedback: For a spin answer, reteach the distinction: daily spin = same stars rise/set each night; yearly orbit = which constellations are on the night side across seasons.
For 'Orion is gone' answers, reteach that it is on the daytime side, hidden by sunlight, and gradually returns to the night sky, being best seen about half a year later.
activities.rationale: Recognition and the orbit reason can be checked after teaching. A fixed set of recognition/reasoning items can verify what has been learned and can surface the spin/orbit confusion; the orbital-viewing intuition, by contrast, may be more directly supported by the continuous model.
learnerActions: Match each constellation to its name (Orion, Ursa Major with its Plough pattern, Leo, Cassiopeia).
Answer: 'Why do we see different constellations in different seasons?' choosing the orbit explanation over the daily-spin distractor.

Sequence the seasonal constellations (e.g. Orion, Leo) by the season in which they are best seen in the evening sky, and note that circumpolar ones (Plough, Cassiopeia) are visible in every season from mid-northern latitudes.
Explain in your own words where Orion is during summer.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate naming and articulate the orbit-based reason, separating it from the daily-spin explanation.

constraints: Recognition first, mechanism second: let children name and re-find patterns before explaining seasonal change.

Keep the two Earth motions separate: nightly east-to-west drift is the daily SPIN; the slow change of which constellations are up at night across months is the yearly ORBIT. Children routinely merge these.

Make the 'behind the Sun' idea explicit: a constellation hidden in summer is not destroyed or gone — it is in the daytime sky on the Sun's side, so sunlight hides it; it gradually reappears (first before dawn) and is best placed in the night sky about half a year later.

Contrast seasonal vs circumpolar: from mid-northern latitudes, constellations near Polaris (Plough, Cassiopeia) circle the pole and stay visible all year, but which constellations are circumpolar depends on observer latitude; keep them visible in any model so the child's familiar Plough being 'always there' is explained.

Distinguish this orbital cause of star VISIBILITY from the axial-tilt cause of the SEASONS themselves — both orbit-related but different; per NGSS 5-ESS1-2 the causes of seasons are outside the grade-5 boundary and the orbital explanation here is enrichment beyond the observational pattern.
Clarify that constellation lines are not real: a constellation is a pattern of stars at very different distances, not a single joined object.

The four-snapshot diagram is a scaffold: it shows discrete seasons but cannot be swept continuously, so it does not by itself show a constellation crossing from night into daytime. A recognition/reasoning check can verify naming and surface the spin/orbit confusion but does not by itself build the orbital-viewing intuition.
The stated age range is 9–11; teaching the orbital cause goes beyond the grade-5 observational core and should be treated as age-appropriate enrichment.

Interactive examples (draggable Earth, linked sky window, spin/orbit toggle, tap-to-reveal, advancing the date) are illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory; the same ideas can be taught with physical or drawn orbit models.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source claim (circumpolar/daytime-hiding observational explanation) is marked unverified in the row; treat the circumpolar and 'behind the Sun' framing as standard pedagogy rather than independently verified here.

The legacy row asserted that talk/conversation 'cannot deliver' the payoff and that a quiz 'can't build' the intuition. These are softened: narration and recognition checks can support teaching of this spatial topic even if a dynamic model may more directly show the orbital change; comparative necessity is not established by the source claims.

Circumpolar visibility depends on observer latitude (described for mid-northern latitudes); which constellations are circumpolar changes with latitude, so present the Plough-always-visible claim as latitude-dependent.
The orbital-visibility cause and the axial-tilt cause of seasons are distinct; ensure learners do not conflate them, as the pedagogy notes this is a common error.
Efficacy wording was further softened (e.g. 'reliably teaches' → 'is intended to teach'; 'confirms learning' → 'can verify') because the proposed activities are untested.

probeDeeper: In summer, where exactly is Orion — gone, or up in the sky at a time we can't see it?
What's the difference between why stars rise and set each NIGHT and why we see different ones each SEASON?
If Earth stopped orbiting and just span in one place, would the night-time constellations still change through the year?
Are the constellations moving around us, or are we moving around the Sun?
assess.correctAnswer: Orion hasn't moved or gone anywhere — in summer it is still there, but it's up in the sky during the DAYTIME, on the same side as the Sun, so the Sun's glare drowns it out and we can't see it at night. As Earth travels around the Sun through the year, our night side faces different directions in space, so at night we look out at different constellations in different seasons. In winter our night side faces toward Orion; in summer our night side faces the opposite way, so Orion is only 'up' in the daytime.

errorPatterns.pattern: constellations disappear or move away in the seasons they aren't visible ('Orion has left')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show with an orbit model that Orion is still there but on the daytime side, lost in the Sun's glare; the night side simply faces away from it in summer.
errorPatterns.distractor: Orion isn't visible in summer because it has moved away to a different part of space.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child says the out-of-season constellation is gone or has travelled elsewhere

errorPatterns.pattern: we see different constellations because the Earth SPINS to face them, or because of weather/clouds
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the daily spin (same stars rise and set each night) from the yearly orbit (which constellations are on the night side at all across the seasons).
errorPatterns.distractor: We see different constellations in different seasons because the Earth spins around to point at them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child attributes the seasonal change to the daily spin or to weather rather than the yearly orbit

errorPatterns.pattern: the stars themselves orbit the Earth or move around us with the seasons
errorPatterns.nextMove: The distant stars are effectively fixed; it is Earth's changing position in its orbit that changes which way we look at night.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child has the distant stars doing the moving rather than Earth changing position

responseLevels.gap: Says the out-of-season constellations disappear or move away; may blame spin or weather.
responseLevels.full: Names several constellations and explains that Earth's orbit makes our night side face different directions across the year, so an out-of-season constellation (e.g. Orion) is still there but up in the daytime.
responseLevels.partial: Knows different constellations appear in different seasons and names some, but explains it vaguely or reaches for the daily spin instead of the orbit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: We can see the constellation Orion clearly on winter nights, but not on summer nights. Has Orion moved away or disappeared by summer — or is it still there somehow? Tell me WHY we can't see it in summer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks stars come and go seasonally says Orion has left. A child who understands Earth's orbit says Orion is still there but on the day side, hidden by the Sun, and links which constellations we see at night to which way our night side faces as Earth orbits. The 'why' tier separates 'the stars go away' from 'we face a different direction'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Find 1000 more or less than a number by recognising that only the thousands digit changes (4,562 → 5,562 / 3,562), extending the 10-more/100-more pattern to the next place — unless a boundary forces a roll-over (9,500 + 1000 = 10,500).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): count in multiples and find 1000 more or less than a given number (place-value fluency).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): generalises 2.NBT.8 (±10/±100) into the thousands place; 4.NBT.1 place-value relationships.
• Operational details — Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart so +1000 steps the thousands digit while others hold; connect to counting in 1000s on a number line. Contrast +10, +100, +1000 side by side so the child tracks which column responds. Teach the roll-over boundary explicitly. Demand the 'which digit changes' reasoning.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): finds 1000 more/less with no boundary, using a chart. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): does it mentally, naming the thousands digit as the one that changes. Tier C (age 9, extending): handles roll-overs (9,500+1000) and generalises to numbers beyond 10,000.
bestPractices: Extend the established pattern: +1000 steps the thousands digit, others unchanged — keep asking 'which digit?'.
Contrast +10 / +100 / +1000 side by side so the child locates the responding column.
Use a Gattegno / place-value chart so one digit visibly changes per operation.
Teach roll-over boundaries (9,500 + 1000) as the interesting case.
Insist on place-value reasoning, not counting on, and generalise beyond 10,000.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (thousands row)
Th|H|T|O place-value counters (add/remove one 1000)
0-10,000 number line with ±1000 hops
Side-by-side ±10/±100/±1000 comparison
Base-ten thousand-cubes for the concrete move
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (stepping hundreds instead of thousands).
Boundary errors at 9,000s / crossing 10,000.
Counting on in smaller steps instead of jumping the place.
Confusing 1000 more with 100 more.
Assuming only one digit ever changes, mishandling roll-over.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: find 1000 more or less than a four-digit number by recognising that normally only the thousands digit changes (4,562 → 5,562 or 3,562), extending the earlier +10/+100 pattern into the next place. The key exceptions are boundary crossings: adding 1000 when the thousands digit is 9 regroups into the ten-thousands place (9,500 + 1000 = 10,500), and subtracting 1000 can remove or reduce a higher digit (1,562 − 1000 = 562; 10,500 − 1000 = 9,500). Learners should justify which digit changes, not count on in smaller steps, and generalise beyond 10,000, where crossings such as 19,500 + 1000 = 20,500 change the ten-thousands digit too.

activities.title: Digit-stepper: which column responds to +1000?
feedback: If the learner expects the hundreds or ones to change, show only the thousands digit ticking and ask them to re-state which column a thousand lives in.
If they confuse 1000 more with 100 more (e.g. answer 4,662), run +100 and +1000 side by side so the differing columns are visible.
Reinforce correct predictions by having the learner say the thousands digit aloud before and after the press.
activities.rationale: Acting on the number and watching a single column respond makes 'which digit changes' concrete and self-correcting; side-by-side comparison with +10/+100 locates the responding column. An interactive stepper is one effective medium, but a place-value chart with counters or a labelled number line can carry the same comparison.
sourceClaims: Mentally adding/subtracting a power of ten changing a single place generalises the Grade 2 ±10/±100 standard.
learnerActions: Start from a four-digit number such as 4,562 shown in a place-value chart or on a number line.
Press +1000 (and −1000) and observe which digit moves: the thousands digit ticks 4→5 for +1000 (giving 5,562) or 4→3 for −1000 (giving 3,562) while hundreds, tens and ones stay locked.
Before each press, predict the result and name the digit that will change; then check against what moves.
Compare +10, +100 and +1000 side by side on the same starting number, saying which column each operation drives.
Use a 0–10,000 number-line view to see ±1000 as equal hops along the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting 1000 normally changes only the thousands digit, extending the same place-value logic that governs +10 and +100.

activities.title: The roll-over: when a place fills up
feedback: If the answer is 0,300 or stays 9,300, point out that the thousand must be carried; walk through 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands = 10,300.
If the answer is 19,300, check that they added exactly one thousand, not ten thousand.
Treat the boundary as a short targeted rehearsal of the single roll, not a re-teach of the whole idea.
activities.rationale: Boundary cases are where place-value reasoning is genuinely tested, so making the carry explicit addresses the common 9,000s/10,000-crossing error directly.
sourceClaims: Boundary roll-overs are the key teaching case for more/less across places.
learnerActions: Start from a boundary number such as 9,500 or 9,300.
Press +1000 and watch the thousands digit pass 9: it rolls 9→0 while a carry moves left, opening a new ten-thousands column (9,500 → 10,500; 9,300 → 10,300).
State in words why the number gains a digit: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands.
Rehearse just the single roll in reasoning: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands, so 9,300 + 1000 = 10,300 — not 0,300, not 9,300, not 19,300.
Try numbers beyond 10,000 to confirm the same place-value rule continues, including crossings such as 19,500 + 1000 = 20,500 and 10,500 − 1000 = 9,500.
activities.intendedInsight: When the thousands digit passes 9, the 'only one digit changes' pattern has a principled exception: the place fills up and regroups into the ten-thousands place (opening a new place for 9,500 → 10,500, or raising an existing ten-thousands digit for 19,500 → 20,500); the reverse crossing happens when subtracting (10,500 − 1000 = 9,500).

activities.title: Scored fluency and boundary checks
feedback: For a plain-case slip, ask which single digit should have moved.
For a boundary slip, redirect to the single-roll rehearsal (9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands).
Note: scored practice confirms fluency but does not by itself build the conceptual 'which digit' reasoning — pair it with the stepper/chart activities.
activities.rationale: Mixed plain and boundary items discriminate between a learner who only handles the easy case and one who regroups correctly across the thousands boundary.
learnerActions: Answer fill-in items such as '1000 more than 4,562 = __' and '1000 less than 4,562 = __'.
Answer which-digit-changes questions for ordinary cases.
Tackle boundary items deliberately, e.g. 9,500 + 1000 and 9,300 + 1000, writing the full regrouped answer.
Use a slider on a 0–10,000 line to land exactly 1000 away from a given point.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure, quick retrieval of 1000 more/less, including the regrouping boundary, confirms the place-value reasoning is fluent.

constraints: Demand place-value reasoning ('which digit changes, and why') rather than counting on in 1000s.
A static annotated chart is a useful reference but does not let the learner perform the transformation; pair any static image with an action (counters, stepper, or spoken prediction).

Recognition-only items (multiple choice 'which digit changes?') confirm identification but do not elicit independent construction of the answer; include fill-in and boundary items that require producing the regrouped number.
Scored quizzes assess and rehearse fluency; they do not substitute for the comparison work that builds the underlying concept.
Teach the roll-over boundary explicitly as the key case, and generalise to numbers beyond 10,000.
Timed/fluency modes are optional for securing speed, not a prerequisite for understanding.

probeDeeper: Which digit changes when you find 1000 more? Does any other digit move?
9,300 + 1000 — does it become a five-digit number? Why?
1000 less than 4,562 — did the hundreds/tens/ones change at all?
assess.correctAnswer: 5,562; 3,562; 10,300 — changing only the thousands digit, and rolling into a new place when it passes 9.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adjusts the wrong place — changes the hundreds (or another digit) instead of the thousands
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the thousands column; add one thousand-block and watch only that column change (unless it overflows).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 1000 more than 4,562 comes out as 4,662 or 4,563.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to roll into a new place: 9,300 + 1000 → 0,300 or stays 9,300 or gives 19,300
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole idea — rehearse the single roll: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands = 10,300.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The boundary case is malformed or not carried to ten-thousands.

responseLevels.gap: Adjusts the wrong place or cannot cross the thousands boundary.
responseLevels.full: Finds 1000 more/less for any number, changing only the thousands digit and regrouping into a new place when needed.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the plain case but stumbles when the thousands digit rolls past 9.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask quickly and watch the method: '1000 more than 4,562? ... 1000 less than 4,562? ... 1000 more than 9,300?' The last one crosses into the ten-thousands — watch what happens.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 4,562 checks the plain case (only the thousands digit moves); 9,300 + 1000 forces a roll from 9 thousands into ten-thousands, exposing whether the child regroups or malforms the number. Watching the working shows which digit they touch.
