pedagogy.summary: At 8-9 the reasoning practice turns outward: children stop merely explaining their own method and begin CRITIQUING someone else's, and they string more than one fact into a chain ('since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48'). Two moves define the level — building a multi-step argument, and diagnosing why a peer's method fails, not just that its answer is wrong. This is the SMP3 'construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others' pairing made age-appropriate: arguments still lean on concrete referents (fraction bars, place-value equipment) but now demand a because/therefore link between steps. It is best taught not as a solo skill but through structured talk — analysing a deliberately flawed worked example, agreeing whether an argument 'makes sense', and being asked 'which STEP is wrong and why?' rather than 'is the answer right?'
bestPractices: Give children a peer's WRONG-but-plausible worked example (e.g. a column subtraction where the exchange was mis-recorded) and ask them to locate the faulty STEP and say why it breaks — not to redo it and compare answers
Model and require because/therefore connectives so a chain of facts becomes an argument ('since… and… therefore…'), scribing the child's spoken chain when their reasoning outruns their writing
Use 'convince me / convince a doubter' talk routines so an assertion is pushed into a justification; treat 'it just is' as the start, not the end
Anchor arguments in a shared representation (fraction bar, base-ten blocks) both parties can point at, so a critique targets the reasoning and not the person
Teach that finding one clear error and explaining it is worth more than re-solving — error analysis is the practice, per SMP3's 'distinguish correct logic from flawed logic and explain the flaw'
keyRepresentations: Fraction bars / area models for size arguments (more equal parts ⇒ smaller pieces, so 1/3 > 1/5)
Place-value equipment or a written column layout for locating an exchange error
A because/therefore sentence frame turning a list of facts into a chain
Derived-fact number strings (6×10, 6×2 ⇒ 6×8) shown as a linked sequence, not isolated facts
commonMisconceptions: 'It's wrong because the answer's different from mine' — judges a peer's argument by answer-agreement rather than by finding the flawed step
Checking one example and treating the rule as proved for all cases
Restating the method louder instead of giving a reason why it works
Believing a longer fraction/denominator names a bigger piece (1/5 > 1/3)

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, reasoning turns outward: children stop merely explaining their own method and begin critiquing someone else's, and they chain multiple facts into a single argument ('since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48'). Two moves define this level — building a multi-step because/therefore argument, and diagnosing WHY a peer's method fails (which step broke, not just that the answer differs). Arguments still lean on concrete referents (fraction bars, place-value equipment) but now require a because/therefore link between steps. Best taught through structured talk — analysing a deliberately flawed worked example, agreeing whether an argument 'makes sense', and asking 'which STEP is wrong and why?' rather than 'is the answer right?'

activities.title: Convince-me dialogue: catch the broken step
feedback: Name whether the faulty step was correctly located, not whether an answer matches: 'Yes — that flip is the broken line. Now tell me why flipping isn't allowed.'
If the child only announces the right answer ('it's 25'), redirect: 'Don't tell me the right answer yet — show me the first line where their thinking stops being okay, and say why that line breaks.'

If the child senses the error but cannot articulate it, revoice/scribe: offer 'you can't do that because…?' and let the child complete it; point at base-ten equipment so the reason has something to attach to. The reasoning is present even when the telling lags — do not treat this as not-knowing.

If the child agrees you can 'just do 6 take 1' because 'you always take the little one from the big one', this is a genuine false belief about the algorithm: build 71 with base-ten equipment, try to remove 6 ones, and force the exchange before returning to the argument skill.
activities.rationale: The level's core — constructing a chain and critiquing another's — is intrinsically dialogic. An in-role partner that asserts a flawed argument and asks the child to find and explain the broken step exercises SMP3's critique half, and 'how do you know?' pressure pushes the child's own assertions into because-clauses in real time. Children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so eliciting and scribing is appropriate rather than judging by fluency.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.

Reasoning develops along a describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder, and children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so a teacher must elicit and scribe the reasoning rather than judge it by fluency of telling.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a plausible-but-wrong worked chain, e.g. a partner says: 'I did 71 minus 46. I couldn't do 1 take 6, so I did 6 take 1, that's 5, then 7 take 4 is 3, so 35.'
Point to the EXACT line where the thinking first goes wrong (the digit-flip), rather than re-solving and comparing totals.
Say WHY that line breaks, grounded in place value: 'you can't flip the digits; the 1 is really part of 71, so you exchange a ten to make 11, and 11 take 6 is 5.'
When challenged with 'how do you know?' or 'why does exchanging fix it?', keep going until the objection becomes a because-chain.
Then construct a correct chain aloud for 71 − 46, starting from what 71 really is (giving 25).
activities.intendedInsight: Critiquing someone else's error forces your own reasoning to become explicit: a vague 'that's not right' can be turned, under questioning, into a because-chain you did not know you had.

activities.title: Build-an-argument workspace: chain the facts, mark the flaw
feedback: Report whether the flaw was correctly located, not whether a final answer matches.
If the child's chain lists facts without connectives, prompt: 'What word joins these two so the second follows from the first?'
If the marked step is wrong, ask the child to read each line aloud and test whether it genuinely follows from the one before.
activities.rationale: A build-an-argument workspace lets the child assemble a chain and mark the exact faulty step, making the 'which step, and why' move concrete and productive. Dragging/snapping tiles and tapping the broken step are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not required. This complements rather than replaces talk.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Assemble fact tiles ('6×10=60', '6×2=12') into a because/therefore sequence and write the linking reason, e.g. 'since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48.'
In a separate flawed worked example (a column subtraction with a mis-recorded exchange), tap or mark the single broken step and write or pick why it fails.
Check your own chain reads as 'since… and… therefore…', not just a list of true facts side by side.
activities.intendedInsight: A string of true facts only becomes an argument when because/therefore links them; locating 'which step, and why' is a concrete, repeatable move.

activities.title: Fraction-bar size argument: 1/3 > 1/5
feedback: Accept the chain only when it links the number of parts to the size of each part, not just 'the bar looks bigger'.
If the child believes a bigger denominator means a bigger piece, return to the shared bar split from the same whole and count/compare the actual pieces before re-stating the argument.
Treat 'it just is' as the start of a justification, not the end: ask 'convince a doubter'.
activities.rationale: Anchoring an argument in a shared representation lets a critique target the reasoning rather than the person, and directly addresses the common belief that a larger denominator names a bigger piece. For unit fractions the numerator is fixed at 1, so the comparison varies only the number of equal parts of the same whole. Concrete referents are age-appropriate for constructing arguments at this stage.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Using fraction bars or an area model showing the same whole split into 3 and into 5, state and justify which piece is bigger.
Build the chain: 'more equal parts means smaller pieces, so fifths are smaller than thirds, therefore 1/3 > 1/5.'
When a classmate claims '1/5 is bigger because 5 is bigger than 3', find and explain the flaw using the shared bar both of you can point at.
activities.intendedInsight: Splitting the same whole into MORE equal parts makes each part SMALLER, so a unit fraction with the larger denominator is the smaller number — and a representation both parties can point at keeps a critique about the reasoning, not the person.

activities.title: When is a check really a proof? Convince a doubter
feedback: Draw out that 'it works in one example' is evidence to explore, not a proof; ask what a doubter could still object to and what would be needed to be sure for every case.
For the inverse check, point out that 35 + 46 = 81, not 71 — so a careful exact check actually reveals 35 is wrong. 'Close to' only hints at plausibility; it does not prove the answer is right.
If the child treats one checked case as settling a general claim, offer a claim where a second case breaks it, and discuss what changed.
activities.rationale: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates at this age and the shift to deductive justification is slow and fragile; explicitly surfacing that checking examples does not prove a general claim targets a documented developmental step. The 'close to' inverse-check prompt extends this to verifying a single computation and is an agent-added illustration, conservatively framed as a proposal rather than a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates in this age range and the transition to deductive justification is slow and fragile; recognising that checking examples does not prove a general claim is a key developmental step.

Reasoning develops along a describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder, and children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so a teacher must elicit and scribe the reasoning rather than judge it by fluency of telling.
learnerActions: Given a general claim and a single example that fits it, decide whether checking that one example proves the claim for all cases.
Explain why one confirming example is not a proof, and what would be needed to be convinced for every case.
Evaluate a weak check such as: 'A classmate says 71 − 46 = 35 is fine because 35 + 46 is close to 71. Is that a good way to check? What does it actually tell you?'
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence that falls short of a complete argument — a single confirming example, or an approximate 'close to' check — does not establish or verify a claim; distinguishing 'it works here / it's roughly right' from 'it must always work / it is exactly right' is a key step toward justification.

activities.title: Compare-and-annotate launch: sound vs flawed argument
feedback: After the reveal, ask the child to re-explain the flaw without the annotation open.
Move promptly from recognising the flaw to constructing or critiquing a new one, so the productive half is exercised.
activities.rationale: A static correct-vs-flawed pair with tap-to-reveal annotations can seed critique and model reasons, but it shows arguments rather than eliciting the child's own chain or responding to their reasoning; treat it as a launch for talk, not as the assessment. Tap-to-reveal is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Study a side-by-side pair of worked arguments for the same problem — one sound, one with a hidden error.
Tap each step to reveal the reason it does or does not follow, then say in your own words which argument holds and where the other breaks.
Use this only as a springboard: afterwards, construct your OWN correct chain or critique a fresh flawed example aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a correct and a flawed argument side by side can seed critique and vocabulary for 'why a step follows', but reading annotations is only a starting point for producing your own argument.

constraints: The productive half of this practice — constructing a multi-step argument and explaining a flaw in the child's own words — requires construction and talk; a scored fixed-answer format can test RECOGNISING a correct argument or spotting a flagged flawed step, but a 'spot the flawed step' multiple-choice item should be used only as a warm-up and its score should not be treated as evidence of the reasoning practice.

Static compare-and-annotate pairs are scaffolds: they can show and label arguments but cannot elicit the child's own chain or respond to their reasoning. Follow them immediately with construction or critique.

Error analysis is the practice: finding one clear faulty step and explaining it is the goal, not re-solving and comparing answers. Keep critique pointed at the shared representation so it targets the reasoning, not the person.
Scribe/revoice a child whose reasoning outruns their words; do not judge reasoning by fluency of telling or score it.

Distinguish an argument-skill gap from a prerequisite gap: if a child endorses 'always take the smaller from the larger', reteach the column-subtraction exchange concept with base-ten equipment before expecting critique of that algorithm.

This guidance is medium-flexible: a live partner, scribed classroom talk, paper worked examples, or a screen workspace can all carry it. Interaction examples (tile snapping, tapping a step, tap-to-reveal) are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 71 − 46 = 25 (correct in the source). The flawed worked example's '35' is explicitly the peer's error to be critiqued, never presented as a valid answer. The exchange explanation (1 becomes 11, 11 − 6 = 5; tens become 6, 6 − 4 = 2, giving 25) is sound and preserved. Note also 35 + 46 = 81 ≠ 71, so the classmate's 'close to 71' inverse check would in fact expose the error; this is surfaced in the weak-evidence activity's feedback.

Self-audit of derived-fact chain: 6×8 = 60 − 12 = 48 is correct (6×10=60, 6×2=12). Note a wording inconsistency in the source: pedagogy and the first evidence item present the chain as 'since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48', but the third evidence item phrases it as 'since 6×8=48 and 6×2=12, then 6×10=60 so 6×8=60−12=48', which assumes the conclusion (6×8=48) as a premise — a circular/garbled ordering. Activities use the sound forward direction (6×10 and 6×2 ⇒ 6×8); the circular phrasing was not propagated.

Self-audit of fraction claim: 1/3 > 1/5 is correct and justified by more equal parts of the same whole meaning smaller pieces; both are unit fractions so only the number of parts varies. No 'denominator rule flips' language is used; same-whole scoping applies to comparing represented portions, while the fractions remain comparable as numbers.

The original labelled a conversation artefact 'ideal' and 3D 'poor/adds nothing'. Those are catalog fit rankings, not established pedagogical laws, and have been removed; the dialogic and workspace activities are presented as complementary options with stated affordances and limits rather than a universal 'only talk teaches this' claim.
Internal identifiers (microTopic and reteach-prerequisite IDs) were stripped from the guidance; the exchange prerequisite is retained conceptually only.

Activity 4 blends example-based generalisation (supported by Hoyles & Küchemann) with critique of an approximate single-computation 'close to' check; the 'close to' strand is an agent extension and is not directly supported by a cited source, though it is conservatively framed and its exact-check correction (35+46=81≠71) is mathematically sound.

probeDeeper: 'Show me the exact line where the thinking first goes wrong — put your finger on it.'
'Why can't you just swap it round and do 6 take away 1? What would you have to do instead?'
'A different classmate says 71 − 46 = 35 is fine because 35 + 46 is close to 71. Is that a good way to check? What does it actually tell you?'
'Now build me a correct chain for 71 − 46 out loud — start with what 71 really is.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child locating the specific faulty STEP (flipping 1−6 into 6−1 instead of exchanging a ten) AND giving a reason grounded in place value (the 1 is part of 71, so you take a ten to make 11, then 11−6=5), rather than just announcing that 35 is the wrong answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges the peer's argument by answer-agreement, not by the reasoning: 'it's wrong because I got 25' — re-solves and compares totals without ever locating or explaining the faulty step.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect from answer to step: 'Don't tell me the right answer yet — show me the first line where their thinking stops being okay, and say why that line breaks.' Model once on a different flawed example.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child announces the correct answer or redoes the calculation but cannot point to WHICH step is wrong or WHY; treats 'different answer' as the whole critique.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts the smaller-from-larger step as fine — shares the bug: agrees you can 'just do 6 take 1' because 'you always take the little one from the big one.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a genuine false belief about the algorithm — confront it with base-ten equipment: build 71, try to remove 6 ones, force the exchange. Reteach the exchange concept, not the argument skill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses the flipped subtraction, or hesitates only about the final total, treating column subtraction as digit-by-digit with the smaller digit always subtracted.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees something is wrong and objects, but the objection stays at 'that's not right' — reasoning outruns communication, no because-clause emerges even though the child clearly senses the flaw.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as not-knowing. Scribe/revoice: offer 'you can't do that because…?' and let the child complete it; point at base-ten blocks so the reason has something to attach to. The reasoning is present; only the telling lags.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Frowns, says 'no you can't do that' or 'it doesn't work like that' but cannot yet articulate the place-value reason when asked 'why not?'

responseLevels.gap: Only evaluates the answer ('it's 25, so they're wrong') or redoes the sum; cannot locate the faulty step or gives no reason.
responseLevels.full: Pinpoints the flipped-subtraction step AND explains the place-value reason it fails (the 1 stands for part of 71, so a ten must be exchanged to make 11−6=5), then reconstructs a correct because/therefore chain — and transfers the 'find the broken step and say why' move to a new flawed example unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Locates the wrong step (the digit-flip) but explains it as 'that's not the rule' or restates the correct procedure without the place-value reason; can describe the steps but not why the flawed one breaks.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is how a classmate worked out 71 − 46. They wrote: '1 take away 6 — I can't, so I'll do 6 take away 1, that's 5. Then 7 take away 4 is 3. So the answer is 35.' Is their thinking okay? Talk me through what they did, step by step, and tell me where — if anywhere — it goes wrong and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who genuinely constructs and critiques arguments identifies the exact broken step and explains the place-value reason it fails; a child who only checks answers will say 'it's wrong, it should be 25' (or redo the sum) without ever naming which step broke or why — same surface verdict, completely different reasoning. Because the error is a real, well-documented one (the 'always take smaller from larger' / smaller-from-larger bug), a child reasoning correctly and one reasoning by answer-agreement give observably different responses.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9-11 (Upper KS2/Grades 4-6): insect communication and behaviour — the bee WAGGLE DANCE (tells hive-mates the direction and distance to flowers), ant PHEROMONE trails, firefly light flashes, cricket chirps, and the monarch butterfly MIGRATION across continents. How insects 'talk' without words.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4/Y5 living things and animal behaviour contexts; working-scientifically (interpreting how signals carry information).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 4-LS1-2 (animals sense, process and respond to information) and 3-LS2-1 (group behaviour); communication as information transfer.
• Operational details — the unifying idea is that a SIGNAL carries INFORMATION: the waggle dance encodes two variables (angle to the sun = direction; duration = distance); pheromone trails are chemical messages that build up and fade; flashes are species-specific codes. The waggle dance is the star because it's a decodable, two-variable code — genuinely astonishing. Migration adds navigation over vast distance across generations. Avoid over-anthropomorphising (bees don't 'talk' with intent/words).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): names three ways insects communicate. Tier B (age 10): explains what the waggle dance conveys (direction AND distance). Tier C (age 11): explains how a signal encodes information (angle=direction, length=distance) and describes the monarch migration's remarkable distance/navigation.
bestPractices: Centre the idea that a signal carries INFORMATION — the waggle dance encodes two variables at once (direction and distance).
Let children decode AND produce signals so the code is understood from both ends.
Show pheromone trails as chemical messages that build up and fade, not permanent paths.
Avoid over-anthropomorphising — insects signal, they don't 'talk' with words or intent.
Use the monarch migration to add scale and navigation, connecting behaviour to survival.
keyRepresentations: A waggle-dance decoder linking angle→direction and duration→distance.
An ant pheromone-trail that strengthens with traffic and fades over time.
A firefly flash-pattern matcher (species-specific codes).
A monarch migration map across a continent.
commonMisconceptions: 'Bees talk / have a language like ours' — they signal information, without words or conscious intent.
'The waggle dance only shows direction' — it encodes distance too (via duration).
'Ant trails are permanent roads' — they are chemical signals that evaporate unless reinforced.
'All fireflies flash the same' — patterns are species-specific codes.
'One butterfly makes the whole migration round-trip' — the monarch migration spans multiple generations.

learn.summary: For ages 9-11, this topic builds the idea that insect communication is a SIGNAL carrying INFORMATION that changes another insect's behaviour, without words. The star example is the honeybee waggle dance, which encodes two variables at once: the angle of the straight 'waggle run' gives direction (on the vertical comb in the dark hive, the run's angle from straight up stands for the flowers' angle from the sun's direction), and the duration of the waggle run gives distance. Supporting examples include ant pheromone trails (chemical messages that build up with traffic and fade unless reinforced), firefly flash patterns (species-specific codes), and cricket chirps. The monarch butterfly migration adds scale and navigation across generations, and is deliberately used as a contrast — remarkable behaviour that is NOT communication. Children should both DECODE and PRODUCE signals so the code is understood from both ends. Avoid over-anthropomorphising: insects signal, they do not 'talk' with words or conscious intent.

activities.title: Decode and perform the waggle dance
feedback: When the heading matches the dance angle and the set distance matches the waggle duration: 'You landed on the flowers — you read both parts of the code.'
When the direction is right but distance is wrong: 'Right way, wrong distance — the LENGTH of each waggle run tells you how far, not just the angle.'
When the angle is misread: 'You went the wrong way — the ANGLE of the straight waggle run from straight up on the comb is the angle to fly measured from the sun's direction.'
When producing the dance: 'Check both variables — does your dance angle point toward the patch, and does your waggle length match how far it is?'
activities.rationale: Letting children decode AND produce the signal makes 'a signal carries information' concrete and reveals the two-variable structure (angle=direction, duration=distance) that a single-fact statement hides. An interactive encode/decode loop lets learners test and correct their reading; a fixed diagram can show the key but cannot provide this trial-and-correction. Efficacy of the specific interactive format is a proposal, not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: The honeybee waggle dance encodes direction (angle relative to the sun) and distance (waggle-run duration) to a food source; ants use pheromone trails; monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres.
KS2 pupils study animal behaviour within living things and their habitats and interpret how information/signals function.
learnerActions: Watch a forager bee perform a waggle dance: a straight 'waggle run' tilted at an angle, then a loop back, repeated over and over.

Read the two pieces of information: use the ANGLE of the straight run from straight up on the comb to work out the direction to the flowers (that same angle measured from the sun's direction), and use how LONG each waggle run lasts to judge the distance.
Set your heading at the dance's angle measured from the sun's direction and set a distance from the waggle duration, then 'fly out' to try to reach the flower patch.
If you overshoot, fall short, or head the wrong way, watch the bee dance again and adjust your reading.
Then swap roles: given a flower patch in a chosen position, perform the correct dance (right angle, right waggle length) so hive-mates could find it.
activities.intendedInsight: The little dance is a real message that carries TWO pieces of information at once — which direction and how far — a decodable code, not just excited wiggling. Producing the dance as well as reading it shows the code works from both ends.

activities.title: Lay an ant trail that strengthens and fades
feedback: If a learner treats the trail as permanent: 'Watch again with no ants using it — the trail fades. It only stays while ants keep reinforcing it.'
If a learner says it is not communication because there are no words: 'The chemical IS the message — it changes where other ants go, so it carries information.'
activities.rationale: Showing the trail build up and fade targets the 'ant trails are permanent roads' misconception directly and broadens 'communication' to a chemical channel. A dynamic strengthen/fade behaviour makes the temporary, reinforced nature visible in a way a still picture of a path does not.
sourceClaims: The honeybee waggle dance encodes direction (angle relative to the sun) and distance (waggle-run duration) to a food source; ants use pheromone trails; monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres.
Animals receive information through senses, process it, and respond in ways that aid survival, including in groups (4-LS1-2, 3-LS2-1).
learnerActions: Draw a scent (pheromone) trail between the nest and a food source.
Watch what happens as more ants travel the trail — notice it strengthens with traffic.
Stop the traffic and observe the trail fade over time.
Explain in your own words why a trail is NOT a permanent road and what information it carries to other ants.
activities.intendedInsight: A pheromone trail is a chemical message: it carries 'food this way', builds up when reinforced by traffic, and evaporates when not — so it is a signal, not a fixed path.

activities.title: Match firefly flash patterns to species
feedback: If a learner assumes all fireflies flash the same: 'Compare two patterns — the timing differs. The pattern is a code that usually identifies the species.'
If the pattern is reproduced incorrectly: 'Check the timing and order of the flashes — that sequence is what carries the message.'
activities.rationale: A light channel reinforces that communication is any signal that carries information, and addresses the 'all fireflies flash the same' misconception. Reproducing the pattern adds a production step rather than recognition alone. No cited source directly addresses firefly signalling, so this activity is an extrapolation from the general signal-carries-information principle.
learnerActions: Observe different firefly flash patterns (timing and sequence of flashes).
Reproduce a given species' flash pattern.
Match a flash pattern to the species that uses it, and explain who the signal is for and why (finding a mate).
activities.intendedInsight: Flashes are species-specific codes — a signal using light. Different species use different patterns, so the pattern itself carries meaning to the right receiver.

activities.title: Navigate the monarch migration — and ask: is this communication?
feedback: If a learner says one butterfly makes the whole round-trip: 'The journey spans several generations — different butterflies complete different legs.'
If a learner calls migration a form of communication: 'Ask: is one monarch sending a signal to change another's behaviour? Migration is travelling and navigating, not signalling.'
activities.rationale: Using migration as a deliberate non-example (a counterexample) prompts learners to apply the definition of communication rather than memorise a list, and adds scale/navigation connecting behaviour to survival.
sourceClaims: The honeybee waggle dance encodes direction (angle relative to the sun) and distance (waggle-run duration) to a food source; ants use pheromone trails; monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres.
learnerActions: Trace the monarch butterfly migration across a continent-spanning map, following the route over thousands of kilometres.
Describe what makes the journey remarkable in terms of distance and navigation.
Note that the full round-trip spans multiple generations — one butterfly does not complete it alone.
Decide and justify: is migrating the same as communicating, or is it something different?
activities.intendedInsight: Migration is a remarkable navigational behaviour, but it is NOT communication — it does not pass information to another insect to change its behaviour. This contrast sharpens the definition of communication.

activities.title: Explain what the waggle dance does (diagnostic discussion)
feedback: If a learner says the bee is just excited/random: 'Move the food and the dance angle and length change with it — a meaning that reliably maps to location is information, not excitement.'

If a learner says the bee flies off and the others just follow behind: 'The other bees read the dance INSIDE the hive, then fly out on their own. The information is transmitted, not demonstrated by leading — telling where is different from guiding there.'

If a learner says insects can't communicate because they can't talk: 'Communication is any signal carrying information — chemical trails, light flashes, chirps, and the dance all change another insect's behaviour without words.'
activities.rationale: A two-tier discussion (what the dance does, then what information and why it is communication) discriminates a signal-with-meaning from a meaningless wiggle and targets the three main misconceptions directly with contrastive moves.
sourceClaims: The honeybee waggle dance encodes direction (angle relative to the sun) and distance (waggle-run duration) to a food source; ants use pheromone trails; monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres.
KS2 pupils study animal behaviour within living things and their habitats and interpret how information/signals function.
learnerActions: Consider the claim: 'When a honeybee finds flowers, it just gets excited and wiggles about.' Decide whether that is right.
Explain what the waggle dance actually does, what information it carries, and why that counts as communication.
Answer a follow-up: HOW does one dance show BOTH direction AND distance — what part of the dance carries each?
Explain whether an ant's chemical trail and a firefly's flash also count as communication, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Communication is a signal that carries information and changes another animal's behaviour. The dance is not mere excitement: the angle encodes direction and the waggle duration encodes distance, and hive-mates decode it inside the hive before flying out on their own.

constraints: Centre the idea that a SIGNAL carries INFORMATION; keep the two-variable structure of the waggle dance (angle=direction, waggle duration=distance) explicit.
Avoid over-anthropomorphising: insects signal, they do not 'talk' with words or conscious intent. Use 'the dance carries information' rather than 'the bee says'.
Present pheromone trails as chemical messages that build up with traffic and fade unless reinforced — not permanent roads.
Treat firefly patterns as species-specific; do not imply all fireflies flash identically.
Use migration as a non-example of communication and make clear the round-trip spans multiple generations, not one individual.
A tap-to-reveal annotated scene or a static waggle-dance key can explain each method but does not provide the decode/produce loop; treat it as a scaffold, not the core activity.

Recognition/matching and multiple-choice checks can assess decoding but do not, on their own, elicit independent production of a signal; include a production step (performing the dance, reproducing a flash pattern, laying a trail).
An in-role 'forager bee' narration can introduce the dance, but learners still need to decode the two variables themselves, not just be told the answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

All three source claims are marked verified:false in the source row; confidence was legacy-labelled 'high', but the efficacy and necessity of any specific interactive format are not established by the cited sources.

The firefly flash-pattern activity is not directly supported by any cited source claim (the behaviour claim covers only bees, ants and monarchs); sourceClaims set to [] and the activity flagged as an extrapolation.

Self-audit: the von Frisch waggle-dance description (angle relative to the sun = direction; waggle-run duration = distance) is stated consistently across the source and retained as-is; no arithmetic or force/motion content required correction.

The original rationale asserted 'no static image can' convey that a signal carries information and that interactive decode 'teaches far better'; these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not supported by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped scaffold/affordance statements.

Activity[0]'s second sourceClaim (KS2 'interpret how information/signals function') is retained because the activity enacts interpreting a signal; it supports the interpret/decode act, not the untested efficacy of the interactive format, which remains qualified.

The monarch-as-non-example framing is pedagogically useful, but monarch navigation mechanisms are summarised at a child-appropriate level; the sources cite only migration distance, not navigation-mechanism detail.

probeDeeper: 'You said the dance tells the others where the flowers are. HOW does one dance show both the direction AND how far? What in the dance carries each part?'
'An ant lays a chemical trail instead of dancing. Is that communication too? What information does the trail carry?' (different channel, same idea)
'A firefly flashing a pattern — who is it signalling to, and what for?'
'A monarch butterfly migrates thousands of miles alone. Is migrating the same as communicating, or something different?' (counterexample: remarkable behaviour that is NOT communication)
assess.correctAnswer: It's not just excitement — the waggle dance is communication. Through the direction and length of the waggle, the bee tells its hive-mates WHERE the flowers are: the angle of the dance shows the direction (relative to the sun) and the length/duration of the waggle shows the distance. Other bees read this and fly to the food. It counts as communication because one bee is deliberately passing useful information that changes what the other bees do — even though there are no words.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the dance is just random movement or excitement, carrying no information
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that the dance is systematic: change the food's location and the dance angle/length changes too. A meaning that reliably maps to location = information, not excitement.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the bee is just excited and wiggling about
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the bee is excited/happy/wiggling for no reason; can't say the dance means anything

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the bee physically leads the others to the flowers rather than encoding location in the dance
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out the other bees decode the dance INSIDE the hive and then fly out on their own. The information is transmitted, not demonstrated by leading. Separate 'telling where' from 'guiding there'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bee flies off and the others simply follow behind it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says the bee flies out and the others just follow it; misses that the dance itself tells them where before they leave

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks insects communicate the way humans do — with sounds/words meaning things — and misses non-word channels (chemical trails, light, vibration)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Broaden 'communication' to any signal that carries information: ant pheromone trails (chemical), firefly flashes (light), cricket chirps (sound), bee dance (movement). Each changes another insect's behaviour without words.
errorPatterns.distractor: Insects can't really communicate because they can't talk
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes communication must be 'talking'; struggles to count pheromone trails or firefly flashes as communication

responseLevels.gap: Says the dance is just excitement/random, or thinks insects can't communicate because they can't talk.
responseLevels.full: Explains the waggle dance encodes direction and distance to food, that hive-mates decode it and act on it, and defines communication as a signal carrying information — transferring to other channels (pheromone trails, flashes) AND distinguishing migration (not communication), showing the concept rather than memorised examples.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the waggle dance means something and lists other examples, but can't say what information it carries (direction + distance) or why a signal counts as communication — separate facts without the 'carries information that changes behaviour' idea.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: When a honeybee finds a good patch of flowers, it goes back to the hive and does a 'waggle dance'. A child says: 'The bee is just excited and wiggling about.' Is that right? Tell me what the waggle dance actually does, what information it carries, and why that counts as communication.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands insect communication says the signal CARRIES INFORMATION that changes another insect's behaviour — and can name what the waggle encodes (direction + distance). A child with a shallow view says the bee is just excited/random, or that it 'shows' the others by leading them, missing that the dance itself encodes direction and distance. The second tier (what information, why communication) separates a signal-with-meaning from a meaningless wiggle.

pedagogy.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a fraction (and by a whole number), understood as 'a fraction OF a fraction': (a/b) × (c/d) takes a/b of c/d, computed as (a×c)/(b×d) and written in simplest form. The area model makes it visible — shade c/d of a square one way, then a/b of that the other way, and the overlap is the product. The key realisations are that you multiply straight across (no common denominator, unlike addition) and that the product of two proper fractions is SMALLER than either factor, because you are taking part of a part.
bestPractices: Read the product as 'of': 2/3 × 4/5 is two-thirds OF four-fifths, and model it as a fraction of a fraction.
Use the area/'redefine the unit' model (IES Fig 7): shade one fraction vertically, the other horizontally, the crosshatch is the product over the b×d grid.
Establish that you multiply numerators and denominators directly — explicitly contrast with addition, which needs a common denominator, to block the imported rule.
Use estimation/benchmarks so a product smaller than both factors is expected (1/2 of 1/2 is 1/4), refuting 'multiplication makes bigger'.
Simplify products and, where possible, simplify before multiplying; convert improper products to mixed numbers.
Fold in the whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) as c/d with d = 1.
keyRepresentations: Area model: unit square partitioned b×d, one fraction shaded each way, product = overlapping tiles
'Fraction of a fraction' bar: take c/d of the whole, then a/b of that piece
Number line for the fraction × whole case
Equation (a×c)/(b×d) aligned with the shaded grid count
commonMisconceptions: Leaves the denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3), over-generalising the common-denominator rule from addition to multiplication (IES).
Seeks a common denominator before multiplying, importing the addition procedure unnecessarily.
Believes the product must be bigger than the factors, so distrusts a smaller answer.
Computes the product but leaves it unsimplified (6/12 rather than 1/2).

learn.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a fraction, understood as 'a fraction OF a fraction': (a/b) × (c/d) takes a/b of c/d, computed as (a×c)/(b×d) and written in simplest form. An area model makes it visible — shade c/d of a unit square one way, a/b of that the other way, and the overlap is the product. The key realisations: you multiply straight across (no common denominator, unlike addition), and the product of two nonzero proper fractions is SMALLER than either factor, because you are taking part of a part. The whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) folds in as c/d with d = 1: 2/3 of 4 means splitting 4 into 3 equal parts and taking 2 of them, which equals four copies of 2/3. For a whole number greater than 1, the product is larger than the fraction factor (for 1 it is equal, for 0 it is 0).

activities.title: Two-way area shader: a fraction of a fraction
feedback: If the overlap puzzles the learner, point to the two striped strips: the crosshatch is the region that is BOTH two-thirds and four-fifths-shaded — a smaller block inside both.
When a product like 6/12 appears, prompt: 'Can 6/12 be written with smaller numbers?' and check on the grid that 6/12 and 1/2 cover the same region.

A running 'is the answer bigger or smaller than each factor?' readout (where available) shows that for two PROPER fractions, taking part of a part gives a product smaller than either; note that the whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) instead grows beyond the fraction factor 2/3, because it is repeated copies rather than a part of a part.
activities.rationale: A fraction of a fraction is exactly the two-way-shaded area model; partitioning both ways and highlighting the overlap makes 'product = crosshatched tiles' and 'smaller than each proper factor' concrete and manipulable. Letting the learner build and vary the shading, rather than view a finished picture, is where the understanding is constructed.
sourceClaims: Students often leave the denominator unchanged in fraction multiplication (e.g. 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3) by over-generalising the addition procedure; teach the conceptual basis with the area model ('redefine the unit', Fig 7: 1/4 of 2/3) and unit fractions, showing 1/2 × 1/2 = half of a half = 1/4, so the product is smaller than either factor.

Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction, interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b parts, find area of a rectangle with fractional sides by tiling, and write products in simplest form.
learnerActions: Shade 4/5 of a unit square with vertical stripes.
Shade 2/3 of the square with horizontal stripes, over the same region.
Watch the square rule itself into a 3×5 grid of fifteenths; count the crosshatched overlap (8 tiles) and read the product as 8/15.
Repeat for 3/4 × 2/3: see the overlap as 6 tiles out of 12, then use a simplify step to collapse 6/12 to 1/2 on the same picture.
Say each product in words using 'of': '2/3 × 4/5 is two-thirds OF four-fifths.'

Fold in a whole-number case: model 2/3 × 4 (as 2/3 × 4/1) using four unit squares, splitting each into thirds and shading 2/3 of each (equivalently, splitting the 4 wholes into 3 equal parts and taking 2), and read off 8 thirds = 8/3 = 2 2/3; optionally show the same on a number line, jumping 2/3 four times to land on 8/3.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying two proper fractions means taking a part of a part; the crosshatched overlap sits plainly INSIDE both striped regions, so the product is smaller than either proper factor, and the b×d grid gives the denominator automatically (no common denominator needed). The whole-number case is different: 2/3 × 4 is four copies of 2/3, so 8/3 is larger than 2/3.

activities.title: Contrast multiplication with the addition rule
feedback: If the learner keeps a denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 → 2/3), model on the grid that 2/3 of 1/3 is a small block — 2/9 of the whole (2 tiles of 9), not 2/3.

If the learner hunts a common denominator first, ask which operation this is and whether equal-sized parts are needed to combine (that is addition); show the grid gives fifteenths automatically from 3×5 for 2/3 × 4/5.
activities.rationale: The leave-the-denominator and seek-a-common-denominator errors come from importing the addition schema. Explicitly contrasting the two operations on the same visual blocks the imported rule rather than just correcting the symbol manipulation.
sourceClaims: Students often leave the denominator unchanged in fraction multiplication (e.g. 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3) by over-generalising the addition procedure; teach the conceptual basis with the area model ('redefine the unit', Fig 7: 1/4 of 2/3) and unit fractions, showing 1/2 × 1/2 = half of a half = 1/4, so the product is smaller than either factor.
learnerActions: Work out 2/3 × 1/3 on the area grid: shade 1/3 one way, take 2/3 of it the other way, and count the overlap — 2 tiles out of 9, i.e. 2/9.
State explicitly: the answer is NOT 2/3; two-thirds OF one-third is smaller than one-third.

Compare side by side with an addition problem that needs re-partitioning (e.g. 2/3 + 4/5): notice addition needs same-sized parts (a common denominator) before you can combine, while multiplication splits the unit BOTH ways and the b×d grid supplies the denominator.
Explain in words why you do not need a common denominator to multiply.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication and addition of fractions run different procedures: addition needs a common denominator to combine like-sized parts; multiplication multiplies across because you are partitioning the unit in two directions.

activities.title: Compute and simplify (practice and self-check)
feedback: For a product that keeps an original denominator (e.g. 8/5 or 8/3 written for 2/3 × 4/5), point back to the grid: the tiles are fifteenths because the square was split 3×5, so the answer is 8/15.
For a correct but unsimplified answer (6/12), do not reteach the multiplication — it is right; only prompt for simplest form.
Use the benchmark 1/2 of 1/2 = 1/4 to confirm that a smaller-than-both answer is expected for two proper fractions, not an error.
activities.rationale: A scorable practice set can deliberately bait the leave-denominator and need-common-denominator errors and can isolate whether the simplifying step is secure. Recognition/fill-in items consolidate and diagnose; they check fluency rather than building the initial 'part of a part' concept, so they follow the construction activities.
sourceClaims: Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction, interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b parts, find area of a rectangle with fractional sides by tiling, and write products in simplest form.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in-the-blank items of the form '2/3 × 4/5 = __/__ = __ (simplest form)'.
Answer a multiple-choice item for 2/3 × 1/3 where '2/3' (denominator left unchanged) is offered as a tempting wrong answer, and choose/justify the correct 2/9.
Finish a problem that yields 6/12 and reduce it to 1/2 as a required step.
Estimate before computing: predict whether each product is bigger or smaller than its factors.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency: multiply numerators and denominators directly, always put the result in simplest form, and expect the product of two proper fractions to be smaller than each factor.

constraints: Read every product as 'of' first (2/3 × 4/5 = two-thirds OF four-fifths) and model it before computing symbolically.
Explicitly contrast with addition: multiplication multiplies straight across and needs no common denominator; raise this whenever a learner tries to find one.
Always put products in simplest form, and where possible simplify before multiplying; convert improper products to mixed numbers (8/3 = 2 2/3).
The practice items check fluency and bait known errors; they do not by themselves build the 'part of a part' meaning, so pair them with the area-model construction rather than substitute for it.

A static finished picture (e.g. tapping to reveal 8/15 on a pre-shaded square) can serve as a reference anchor, but it does not let the learner build the shading or vary the factors, which is where the understanding forms — use it as a supplement, not the main activity.
The area model is planar; a flat grid is the natural representation here and a 3D rendering is not needed for this objective.

The claim 'product is smaller than either factor' is scoped to two nonzero proper fractions; when a proper fraction multiplies a whole number greater than 1, the product (e.g. 2/3 × 4 = 8/3) is smaller than the whole number but larger than the proper fraction factor.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15 (correct); 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2 (correct); 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/9 (correct); 2/3 × 4 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 (correct). The original row's next-move text said '2/3 of 1/3 is a small block, one-ninth of the whole': that is imprecise — 2/3 OF 1/3 = 2/9 (2 tiles of 9), while 1/9 would be 1/3 of 1/3. Activities use the corrected value 2/9 for 2/3 × 1/3; the mistaken 1/9 is recorded here only, never offered as a learner option.

The 'smaller than either factor' narrative is scoped to proper fractions throughout; activity[0] mixes proper×proper with the whole-number case, so the readout feedback now explicitly flags that 2/3 × 4 = 8/3 grows beyond 2/3 because it is repeated copies.

The original keyRepresentations list includes a number line for the fraction × whole-number case; it is retained as an optional scaffold in the whole-number action (2/3 jumped four times to 8/3) so the distinct representation is not lost.
CCSS/DfE source is marked verified:false in the row; treat it as a standards-alignment reference rather than evidence of efficacy.
Source claims cite the teaching principle (area model, multiply across, simplest form); they do not establish that the specific interactive shader described has been empirically tested.

probeDeeper: Say 2/3 × 4/5 in words using 'of' — what are you taking a part of? Show it on an area picture.
A friend says 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3. But two-thirds OF one-third — is that bigger or smaller than 1/3? Can it be 2/3?
Do you need a common denominator to multiply? How is that different from adding?
Is 6/12 finished? Write it as simply as you can — how do you know it's the same amount?
assess.correctAnswer: 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15. 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2. Multiply numerators and denominators directly (no common denominator), then simplify.

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the denominator unchanged: '2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3' or keeps a shared denominator in the answer — imports the addition (common-denominator) rule into multiplication.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model on the area grid: 2/3 of 1/3 is a small block, one-ninth of the whole — not 2/3. Contrast explicitly: addition needs a common denominator, multiplication does not; here you split the unit BOTH ways (b×d).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Product keeps one of the original denominators unchanged; for 2/3 × 4/5 may write 8/5 or 8/3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds a common denominator before multiplying, converting 2/3 and 4/5 to fifteenths and then mis-combining — applies the addition setup to a multiplication.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what operation this is and whether it needs equal-sized parts to combine (no — that's addition). Multiply across; show the grid gives fifteenths automatically from 3×5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rewrites both fractions over a common denominator as a first step for a multiplication; often then adds or muddles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies correctly but leaves the answer unsimplified: writes 6/12 and stops.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach multiplying — it's correct. Prompt: 'can 6/12 be written with smaller numbers?' Check on the grid that 6/12 and 1/2 are the same region.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct unsimplified product (6/12); the operation is right, only simplest form is missing.

responseLevels.gap: Leaves the denominator unchanged or seeks a common denominator (importing the addition rule); products don't come from multiplying across.
responseLevels.full: Computes (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd, simplifies (6/12 → 1/2), justifies with an area or 'fraction of a fraction' model, recognises the product of proper fractions is smaller than each; transfers to a new pair including a whole number.
responseLevels.partial: Multiplies across correctly for the straightforward case but forgets to simplify, or can't justify with an area model / explain why the product is smaller — procedure without meaning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing how (a picture is fine): 2/3 × 4/5, and 3/4 × 2/3. Give each answer in its simplest form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Multiplying straight across contrasts with the addition habit: a child who leaves the denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 → 2/3) or hunts a common denominator reveals they're running the addition procedure. 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 is chosen to require simplifying, isolating whether that final step is secure. Both products are smaller than their factors, probing whether the child accepts 'a fraction of a fraction is smaller'. Watching the method shows which operation's schema is running.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9, Weather vs Climate — weather is what the atmosphere is doing now/today (changes hour to hour); climate is the typical long-term pattern of weather in a place averaged over many years.
• Standards — UK (DfE): the distinction sits across KS1/KS2 science (Y1 Seasonal changes) and KS2 geography (hot/cold areas relative to Equator and poles; climate zones).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-ESS2-1 'represent data… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]' (note: assessment boundary excludes climate change) and 3-ESS2-2 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-2]'. State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach the difference as a matter of TIMESCALE and AGGREGATION — climate is the long-run average, weather is a single sample; use the maxim 'climate is what you expect, weather is what you get'; build from many days of real weather data settling into a stable average; directly pre-empt the 'a cold day disproves warming' conflation (kept age-appropriate, not full climate-change teaching).
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — sort statements as weather or climate and give an example showing one cold day doesn't change the climate; Tier B — explain climate as a multi-year average and compare two places; Tier C — reason about trends vs variability and why single events are weak evidence.
bestPractices: Use the anchor phrase 'climate is what you expect, weather is what you get' and return to it repeatedly
Show aggregation directly: accumulate many days of a place's weather and watch a running average settle into its climate band — make the timescale visible
Contrast two places with the same day's weather but different climates to separate the single sample from the long-run pattern
Explicitly address the misconception that one unusually cold (or hot) day changes or disproves the climate/trend
Keep climate-change specifics light at this age per the 3-ESS2-1 assessment boundary — focus on the weather/climate distinction itself
keyRepresentations: A scatter of daily weather points with a running-average line settling into a stable climate band
A wide vs narrow time-window slider (few days = weather, many years = climate)
Side-by-side 'today' snapshot vs 'typical year' summary for the same place
A sorting mat: statements dropped into WEATHER vs CLIMATE columns
commonMisconceptions: 'A cold day (or snowstorm) means the climate isn't warming' — confusing one weather sample with the long-term trend
Weather and climate are synonyms / interchangeable words
Climate is just 'the weather somewhere far away or exotic' rather than the long-run average of any place's weather
Climate never changes / weather is totally random — both are patterns at different timescales

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, distinguish weather (what the atmosphere is doing now/today, changeable hour to hour) from climate (the typical long-run pattern of weather in a place, averaged over many years — roughly 30). The core idea is TIMESCALE and AGGREGATION: climate is the long-run average, weather is a single sample. Use the anchor phrase 'climate is what you expect, weather is what you get', build climate from many days of real weather data settling into a stable average, and directly address the belief that one unusually cold (or hot) day changes or disproves the climate. Keep climate-change specifics light at this age, focusing on the weather/climate distinction itself.

activities.title: Watch a climate form from many days of weather
feedback: If a learner says the climate changed when the freezing day was added, point them back to the running-average line: ask how far it actually moved compared to how far a single point jumped.
If a learner calls the narrow few-day window 'climate', ask them how many years of data the window is covering, and whether a handful of days can reveal the typical pattern.
When the second town forms a different band from its own weather, ask: could both towns have the same weather on one day but still have these different climates? (Yes.)
Reinforce with the anchor phrase: 'climate is what you expect, weather is what you get'.
activities.rationale: The concept is aggregation across a timescale, which becomes concrete when learners accumulate samples and watch a running average settle. Making the running mean and an adjustable time window visible turns the abstract 'long-term average' into something a child can watch form, and the single record-day demonstration targets the trend-vs-sample misconception directly. Swapping to a second town extends this to comparing climates in different regions — a different place averages its own weather into a different stable band.
sourceClaims: A persistent public/student misconception conflates a single cold-weather event with the long-term climate trend; climate is best framed as the multi-year average pattern of weather.
NGSS 3-ESS2-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-2].'
learnerActions: Step forward through a town's daily weather, one day at a time — a jittery mix of hot and cold days plotted as daily temperature points (rain can be tracked on a separate chart).
Watch a running-average line gradually settle into a steady band as more and more days accumulate.

Narrow a time window to just a few days and describe what you see (scattered, hard to predict = WEATHER); widen it to many years and describe how the long-run average and the usual seasonal pattern become steady and predictable (= CLIMATE).
Drop in one unusually freezing record-day and watch how much (or how little) the many-year average moves.
Switch to a second town and watch a different climate band form from its own weather, then compare the two towns' climates.
Say out loud, in your own words, why one cold day does not change the climate.
activities.intendedInsight: Climate is the long-run average of many days of weather; a single day is just one sample, so one cold or hot day barely shifts the multi-year average and cannot by itself tell you the climate.

activities.title: Today vs a typical year, side by side
feedback: If a learner treats the two panels as the same kind of thing, ask which one could change by tomorrow and which would stay roughly the same for years.
Prompt for the timescale: climate needs many years (about 30) of averaged data, not a single day.
activities.rationale: A side-by-side snapshot-vs-summary comparison states the distinction clearly and supports learners who are not ready to reason about an accumulating average. It is a scaffold: it labels the difference and presents a 'typical year' summary of conditions, but does not itself show the aggregation over time that drives the concept, so it works best as a lead-in to or support for the accumulating-average activity.
sourceClaims: NGSS 3-ESS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]'; assessment boundary explicitly does not include climate change.
learnerActions: Look at a 'today' snapshot for a place (one day's weather) next to a 'typical year' summary for the same place.
Reveal labels and state which panel shows weather and which shows climate, and why.
Explain what you would need to collect — and over how long — to describe the climate of your own town.
activities.intendedInsight: Weather is a single-day snapshot of the atmosphere; climate is a summary of the typical pattern built from many years of such snapshots.

activities.title: Sort statements: weather or climate?
feedback: For the trap item, if a learner says one hot day shows the climate is warming, respond: that is weather — one day's state of the atmosphere; climate is the average over many years, so a single day cannot show the trend.
If a learner sorts 'It is raining right now' as climate, ask whether that statement could be true today and false tomorrow — if so, it is weather.
Model the correct example: a desert can have a rainy day and still have a desert climate, because its climate is the average over many years.
activities.rationale: A categorization task plus a targeted trap item maps closely onto the teaching objective — sorting weather vs climate and testing the trend-vs-sample misconception. This is a recognition/categorization format, so it can check whether the learner applies the distinction but does not by itself elicit an extended independent explanation; pair it with a spoken or written justification to capture reasoning.
sourceClaims: A persistent public/student misconception conflates a single cold-weather event with the long-term climate trend; climate is best framed as the multi-year average pattern of weather.
learnerActions: Drag or write statements into two columns, WEATHER and CLIMATE (e.g. 'It is raining right now', 'Summers here are usually hot and dry', 'It snowed yesterday', 'This region is hot all year round').
Answer a trap item: a single record-hot (or record-cold) day — does that one day change the climate? Choose and justify.
Give your own example that shows one cold day doesn't change the overall climate.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding whether each statement is about a single moment or a long-run average checks that the learner separates a single sample from the aggregated pattern, including rejecting the claim that one extreme day changes the climate.

activities.title: Question a climate expert about a cold snap
feedback: If a learner accepts the cold snap as proof, restate: one day is weather; to say anything about climate you need long-run averages and trends.
Affirm that two towns can share one day's weather yet differ in climate, and that a desert staying a desert through a rainy day shows climate is the long-run average.
activities.rationale: A question-and-answer exchange can directly target the key 'one cold day' misconception and give practice articulating reasoning. Discussion can clarify the distinction, while the accumulating-average activity more directly shows the aggregation intuition; the two are complementary rather than interchangeable.
sourceClaims: A persistent public/student misconception conflates a single cold-weather event with the long-term climate trend; climate is best framed as the multi-year average pattern of weather.
learnerActions: Pose the question: 'Today there's a sudden cold snap — is that proof there's no warming?' and predict the answer before reading the reply.
Discuss follow-ups: 'Could two towns have the same weather today but different climates?' and 'A desert has a rainy day — has its climate stopped being a desert climate?'
Summarise, in your own words, what evidence would actually tell us about a place's climate.
activities.intendedInsight: Single weather events are weak evidence about climate; describing climate requires many years of averaged data and attention to trends, not individual days.

constraints: Target age 7–9; keep climate-change specifics light, consistent with the NGSS 3-ESS2-1 assessment boundary that excludes climate change — focus on the weather/climate distinction itself.

The side-by-side 'today vs typical year' snapshot is a scaffold: it labels the distinction but does not show aggregation over time, which is the heart of the concept. Use it to introduce or support, not as the whole lesson.

The sorting/categorization and multiple-choice formats are recognition tasks: they can check whether a learner applies the distinction but do not by themselves elicit extended independent explanation. Pair them with spoken or written justification.
State climate as roughly a 30-year average of weather for this age; avoid implying climate never changes or that weather is purely random — both are patterns at different timescales.

Interaction examples (daily-weather scatter, running-average line, time-window slider, dropping in a record day, swapping towns) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
