pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare with >, =, < on place-value meaning.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 read/write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparison and ordering of decimals to three places.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.3 — 'Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths. (a) Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form... (b) Compare two decimals to thousandths based on the meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, < symbols.'
• Operational details: Read decimals as fractions of the whole ('five and sixty-two thousandths', not 'five point zero six two') to keep place meaning audible. Build expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers (3×(1/10)+9×(1/100)+2×(1/1000)). Compare by aligning place value left-to-right, using equalising trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) to defeat the 'longer-is-larger' error.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Write five and sixty-two thousandths as a numeral.' Tier B: 'Compare 0.372 and 0.38 and justify.' Tier C: 'Write 347.392 in expanded form with unit fractions.'
bestPractices: Read decimals using place-value names ('sixty-two thousandths') rather than digit-by-digit 'point zero six two', so the meaning stays audible
Build expanded form with explicit unit-fraction multipliers (×1/10, ×1/100, ×1/1000) to bind each digit to its place
Compare left-to-right by place value, and equalise decimal length with trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) to expose 'longer-is-larger' as false
Use a thousandths grid / decimal place-value chart so 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 are seen as nested tenths-of-tenths
Move fluently among numeral, words and expanded form in both directions
keyRepresentations: Decimal place-value chart Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths
Thousandths grid (10×10×10 nesting) or 1000-cube partition of the unit
Three-pane numeral ↔ words ↔ expanded-form translator
Number line to hundredths/thousandths for comparison; trailing-zero alignment tool
commonMisconceptions: 'Longer decimal is larger' (0.372 > 0.38 because it has more digits)
'Shorter decimal is larger' (over-correcting to 'fewer digits = closer to whole')
Reading 0.062 as 'point zero sixty-two' and losing the thousandths meaning
Treating the decimal part as a whole number after the point (comparing 372 vs 38)
Misplacing digits in expanded form — attaching 1/10 to the hundredths digit

learn.summary: Learners aged 10–11 read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, and compare with >, =, < based on place-value meaning. The central hurdle is the 'longer-is-larger' error (judging 0.372 > 0.38 because it has more digits). Guidance centres on place-value alignment, equalising with trailing zeros, naming decimals by their place ('sixty-two thousandths') to keep place meaning audible, and building expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers.

activities.title: Align and compare on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner picks 0.372 as larger because '372 > 38', line the decimals up tenths-under-tenths and compare the tenths first (3 vs 3, equal), then the hundredths (7 vs 8), so 0.372 < 0.38. Padding to 0.380 shows equal-length strings so the digit-count argument disappears.
If the grid shading surprises them — the 'shorter' 0.38 shades MORE squares than the 'longer' 0.372 — ask them to restate why: 0.380 > 0.372 because the deciding place (hundredths) has 8 > 7.
Reinforce by naming the deciding place aloud: 'they are equal in the tenths, so the hundredths decides.'
activities.rationale: Comparison to thousandths depends on place-value alignment. Aligning columns, padding trailing zeros and identifying the first differing place makes the >,=,< decision follow from meaning rather than memorised rules, and directly targets the 'longer-is-larger' misconception. A grid and a number line give two further views of the same magnitude relationship.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Write two decimals into aligned Ones . tenths . hundredths . thousandths rows, e.g. 0.372 and 0.38.
Pad the shorter decimal with a trailing zero so both have the same length: 0.38 becomes 0.380.
Compare left-to-right, place by place: tenths match (3 = 3), then at the hundredths the 7 and 8 differ, so 0.372 < 0.380.
State the comparison with the correct symbol and say which place decided it.
Shade each value on a thousandths grid (380 squares vs 372 squares) and check which covers more area.
Optionally, mark both decimals on a number line to hundredths/thousandths to see their relative positions as a second representation of the same comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: The length of a decimal does not determine its size; comparison is decided by the first place where the digits differ, read left-to-right. Trailing zeros make equal-length strings without changing value (0.38 = 0.380).

activities.title: Write spoken decimals keeping placeholder zeros
feedback: If a learner writes 5.62 for 'five and sixty-two thousandths', ask which place the word 'thousandths' names (the third place). The 2 must sit there, so 62 becomes 062: 5.062.
Check the reverse: ask them to read 5.62 and 5.062 aloud and notice these are different numbers (sixty-two hundredths vs sixty-two thousandths).
activities.rationale: Reading digit-by-digit ('point zero six two') hides place meaning. Naming the place of the final digit forces correct placement and surfaces the need for placeholder zeros, addressing the dropped-zero error.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Read a decimal aloud using place-value names: 'five and sixty-two thousandths' rather than 'five point zero six two'.
Write 'five and sixty-two thousandths' as a numeral, anchoring the last digit in the named place: 'thousandths' means the 2 sits in the third decimal place.
Fill the places: 062 occupies tenths–hundredths–thousandths, giving 5.062.
Explain where the placeholder 0 goes and why it cannot be dropped.
Translate in both directions: given 5.062, say the words; given the words, write the numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming a decimal by its place ('thousandths') tells you which column the last digit must occupy; a placeholder zero may be needed so the digits land in the correct places. 5.062 ≠ 5.62.

activities.title: Build expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers
feedback: If a learner writes 3×10 or 3×1 for the tenths digit, extend the ×10-to-the-left / ÷10-to-the-right pattern through the point: the place right of ones is 1/10, so the tenths digit is multiplied by 1/10.
If a digit is attached to the wrong unit fraction (e.g. 1/10 given to the hundredths digit), re-read the chart left-to-right naming each place in turn.
activities.rationale: Expanded form with explicit unit-fraction multipliers binds each digit to its place and prevents expanding decimal digits with whole-number multipliers. A static labelled number with revealed place values is a useful anchor but does not itself perform the comparison alignment, so pair it with the comparison activity.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Tap or point to each digit of a number such as 347.392 and name its place and value.
Write the expanded form binding each digit to its place: 3×100 + 4×10 + 7×1 + 3×(1/10) + 9×(1/100) + 2×(1/1000).
Say what each digit is worth, e.g. 'the 9 is worth 9 hundredths, 9×(1/100)'.
Extend the ×10 pattern rightward through the decimal point: each place is one tenth of the place to its left (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000).
Check a tricky case: the tenths digit is multiplied by 1/10, NOT by 10 or 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Expanded form makes each digit's value explicit. Decimal places continue the base-ten pattern to the right with unit-fraction multipliers (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000), one tenth of the place to the left.

activities.title: Argue and justify a comparison (discussion)
feedback: If the learner argues from digit count, redirect to the tenths-under-tenths alignment and ask which place first differs.
Accept a correct answer only with a place-value justification, not just the right symbol.
activities.rationale: A discussion that baits and corrects the 'longer-is-larger' error can usefully surface a learner's reasoning, though learners should still manipulate aligned place values to resolve the comparison. Treat talk as a complement to the alignment work, not a replacement.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38, and prove it?'
Make a claim and justify it by aligning place values, not by counting digits.
Defend the claim against the 'longer-is-larger' bait by padding to 0.380 and comparing the hundredths.
Put the comparison into a sentence: '0.38 is bigger because they are equal in the tenths but 8 hundredths beats 7 hundredths.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain a comparison in words — citing the first differing place — demonstrates place-value understanding rather than rule-following.

activities.title: Check and order several decimals
feedback: For a comparison item, mark a digit-count answer wrong and prompt a place-value re-check with padded zeros.
For the ordering item, have the learner write all values to the same number of places first (0.300, 0.290, 0.305, 0.310), then order the aligned strings.
For the fill-in item, confirm the placeholder zero lands in the tenths place (5.062, not 5.62).
activities.rationale: Comparing, writing from words and ordering mixed-length decimals checks the key skills and misconceptions. This verifies understanding built through manipulation and discussion; it does not by itself build the alignment intuition.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Compare 0.372 and 0.38 and choose >, = or <, rejecting any answer based purely on digit count.
Complete 'five and sixty-two thousandths = ___' with the correct numeral (5.062).
Order four decimals of unequal length (e.g. 0.3, 0.29, 0.305, 0.31) by padding to equal length and comparing left-to-right, giving 0.29 < 0.3 < 0.305 < 0.31.
Explain each placement rather than only giving the final order.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading, writing and comparing decimals can be verified across numeral and word forms and by ordering, including deliberately mixed-length cases that expose the 'longer-is-larger' trap.

constraints: Read decimals with place-value names ('sixty-two thousandths') rather than digit-by-digit 'point zero six two', so the place meaning stays audible.
Equalise decimal length with trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) when comparing; this exposes 'longer-is-larger' as false without changing value.
Watch for over-correction to 'shorter-is-larger' (fewer digits = closer to the whole); length alone decides nothing — only the first differing place does.
5.062 is not 5.62: keep placeholder zeros when a spoken place name requires the final digit to sit further right.

A static labelled number with revealed place values anchors reading and expanded form but cannot carry out the padding/alignment that resolves comparisons; use it alongside the comparison activity, not instead of it.
Recognition or multiple-choice checks verify the skill but do not require the learner to construct alignment reasoning independently; include tasks where they write and justify.

Grid shading, column-highlight tools and a number line to hundredths/thousandths are illustrative, complementary supports for the comparison mechanism, not required equipment; the reasoning can also be carried out on paper by writing values to equal length.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original row's 'quiz' companion and 'conversation' options were retained as the check/ordering activity and the discussion activity respectively, with product and fit-ranking vocabulary removed.
The source keyRepresentations listed a 'number line to hundredths/thousandths for comparison'; it is reinstated as an optional comparison representation in Activity 1 and the constraints.

The source claimed decimal notation is 'planar and symbolic' so '3D adds no explanatory power' for this topic; this is a reasonable scoping judgement for comparison/notation but is not an established universal law, so it is not asserted as one here.

The original framing that an interactive comparator uniquely makes comparison 'felt, not memorised' is softened: alignment, grid and trailing-zero reasoning can also be done on paper; the interactive example is one concrete medium.
The second CCSS-M source is marked unverified in the row (verified:false); its claim is retained as stated but not treated as independently confirmed.

probeDeeper: Line up 0.372 and 0.38 by place — which is bigger and why?
Write sixty-two thousandths on its own — where does the 0 go?
In 347.392, what is the 9 worth?

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Longer decimal is larger': says 0.372 > 0.38 because 372 > 38 / it has more digits
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align by place (tenths under tenths); compare tenths first (3 vs 8). Pad with a zero (0.380) to see equal-length strings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The decimal with more digits is chosen regardless of place value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero in a spoken decimal: writes 5.62 for 'five and sixty-two thousandths'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the last digit in the named place: 'thousandths' means the 2 sits in the third place, so 062 fills tenths–hundredths–thousandths → 5.062.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sixty-two thousandths is placed in the tenths/hundredths instead of hundredths/thousandths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expanded form mishandles the fractional places: writes 3×10 or 3×1 for the tenths instead of 3×(1/10)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend the ×10 pattern rightward through the point: each place is 1/10 of the one to its left (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Decimal digits are expanded with whole-number multipliers.

responseLevels.gap: Uses 'longer-is-larger', drops placeholder zeros, or expands decimals with whole-number multipliers.
responseLevels.full: Reads, writes (numerals/words/expanded) and compares decimals to thousandths by place value, keeping placeholder zeros.
responseLevels.partial: Reads/writes tidy decimals but slips on comparisons of unequal length or on spoken thousandths.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch across forms. 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38? Line them up to decide. Write “five and sixty-two thousandths” as a decimal. Then write 347.392 in expanded form.' Watch the comparison reasoning and the placeholder zero in the thousandths write.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 0.372 vs 0.38 is the classic 'longer-is-larger' trap — a child comparing digit-strings picks 0.372. 'Sixty-two thousandths' needs a placeholder zero in the tenths (5.062), catching the child who writes 5.62. Expanded form checks each decimal place carries its unit fraction.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Fast & Slow Earth Changes

- **Standards — UK (DfE, England):** No direct KS1 science statement; the 'slow change' strand (rock worn away by wind/water) is developed in KS2 science (Y3 Rocks; erosion) and KS2 Geography, and 'fast change' (volcanoes/earthquakes) sits in KS2 Geography. At 5–7 teach via KS1 'Working scientifically' (comparing, using information sources) as enrichment.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** Direct anchor — **2-ESS1-1**: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1].' Clarification: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1].' Assessment boundary: does NOT include quantitative measurements of timescales. CCC [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1, 2-ESS2-1].' SEP: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1].

- **Operational details:** The big idea is that Earth's surface is always changing — but at very different speeds. Some changes are sudden (a volcanic eruption or earthquake reshapes land in moments); others are so slow (wind and water wearing rock into sand over very long times) you can't watch them happen. Teach by CONTRASTING paired examples from photos/footage and sorting events into 'fast' and 'slow', then confronting the hardest part for young children: slow changes are REAL changes even though we can't see them happening — use before/after pairs (a smooth pebble was once a rough rock; a cliff that has retreated). Honour the assessment boundary: compare fast vs slow qualitatively, never quantify years. This topic ties the batch together (volcano/earthquake = fast; erosion = slow).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can give an example of a fast change and a slow change and say which is which; they are NOT expected to quantify timescales. Confront two misconceptions: 'the Earth never changes / has always looked the same', and 'only dramatic fast events count as change' (slow wearing-away is change too).
bestPractices: Teach through paired contrasts (a fast example beside a slow one) so the RATE difference is the focus, not the events in isolation
Make time the variable children control, so 'you can't watch slow change happen' is experienced, not just stated
Use before/after pairs (rough rock → smooth pebble; cliff retreated) to prove slow changes are real changes
Provide a simple fast/slow sorting task to meet the 'compare and classify' evidence directly
Honour the assessment boundary — keep it qualitative (fast vs slow), never quantify years
Draw the fast examples from this batch (eruption, earthquake) and the slow from erosion, tying the topics together
keyRepresentations: Two scenes under one shared time slider (fast scene vs slow scene)
Fast/slow sorting bins with event cards (eruption, earthquake, erosion, pebble-smoothing)
Before/after image pairs showing slow change has really happened
A simple 'rock → sand' sequence for wearing-away over long time
commonMisconceptions: 'The Earth never changes / has always looked exactly the same' — the surface is always changing, just often too slowly to see
'Only big dramatic events (eruptions/quakes) are changes' — slow wearing-away by wind and water is change too
'If you can't see it happen, it isn't really happening' — slow changes are real; before/after evidence shows it
'Slow changes are small changes' — given long enough, slow processes carve valleys and wear mountains down
'Fast changes build the land and slow changes only destroy it' — both build and wear down (keep simple: both reshape the land)

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach that Earth's surface is always changing but at very different speeds: some changes are quick (earthquakes can reshape land in moments, and volcanic eruptions can change it within hours or days) and some are so slow (wind and water wearing rock into sand) that you cannot watch them happen. The core work is contrasting a fast example beside a slow one so the difference in RATE is the focus, sorting events into 'fast' and 'slow', and using before/after evidence to prove slow changes are real changes. Keep everything qualitative — compare fast vs slow, never quantify years (per the NGSS assessment boundary).

activities.title: Same nudge, different world: a shared time control over two scenes
feedback: When the tiny nudge erupts the left scene but barely touches the right, prompt: 'Same nudge — why did one change so much and the other hardly at all?'
If the child stops dragging too soon on the slow scene, encourage: 'Keep going — slow changes need a LOT of time. Watch what happens to the rock if you keep cranking time forward.'
Once the pebble has rounded, affirm: 'The rock really did change — it just took a long, long time. That is a slow change, and it is still a real change.'
activities.rationale: A shared time control lets learners compare how much two modelled scenes change during the same elapsed time. The linked scenes and optional slider provide one proposed way to explore the crosscutting idea that things may change slowly or rapidly; their effectiveness has not been independently evaluated.
sourceClaims: CCC Stability and Change for this PE: 'Things may change slowly or rapidly'; DCI ESS1.C: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1]'
learnerActions: Look at two scenes placed side by side that share ONE time control (for example a slider or scrubber the child drags).
Give the time control the tiniest nudge and watch the left scene: a volcano erupts or an earthquake strikes, reshaping the land very quickly.
Now expect the right scene to change the same way — but notice the cliff barely moves with that same small nudge.
Keep dragging time on and on for the right scene until the cliff slowly wears back and a rough rock gradually rounds into a smooth pebble.
Say out loud which change was fast and which was slow, and agree that BOTH really changed the land.
activities.intendedInsight: Some Earth changes are sudden and some are so slow you cannot watch them happen, yet both are real changes to the land. The felt asymmetry — the same action causing wildly different amounts of change — makes the difference in rate experiential rather than just stated.

activities.title: Sort the changes: fast bin or slow bin
feedback: For these represented examples, the eruption and earthquake change the land rapidly; the cliff wearing-away, pebble smoothing and gradual dune buildup occur over a much longer time. Other instances can differ: use the conditions and time context shown.
If a slow card is called 'not a real change': 'It changes slowly, but it still changes — a rough rock really did become a smooth pebble.'
If a card is misplaced, ask: 'Would that happen in a day, or over many, many years?'
activities.rationale: Sorting can teach and check classification. Ask learners to justify a card using its described change and elapsed-time context; optionally pair the sort with the shared-time model to compare amounts of change over the same interval.
sourceClaims: 2-ESS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1]'; clarification names volcanic explosions and earthquakes (quick) and erosion of rocks (slow); assessment excludes quantitative timescales
learnerActions: Take event cards showing a sudden eruption, a sudden earthquake, gradual cliff wearing-away, gradual pebble smoothing and gradual sand-dune buildup. Use each card’s described conditions and time context, rather than assuming every instance of a process has the same speed.
Place each card into a 'fast' bin or a 'slow' bin.
For at least one card, say why it goes where it goes ('the eruption changed the land quickly, so it's fast').
Answer a 'Which change is slow?' question and a reinforcement question: 'Are the slow changes still real changes to the land?'
activities.intendedInsight: In these card examples, the eruption and earthquake are fast changes, and the wearing-away and dune buildup are slow changes. Both kinds genuinely reshape the land. Classifying events can check whether a child compares quick and slow changes.

activities.title: Before and after: proving slow change is real
feedback: When a difference is found: 'Good spotting — that part of the cliff is gone now. Something like waves, water or wind slowly wore it away.'
If the child says the slow pair looks 'the same', point to a specific difference: 'Look here — is this edge in the same place in both pictures?'
Reinforce: 'We didn't see it move, but the two pictures are different — so it really did change.'
activities.rationale: Before/after pairs address the misconception that 'if you can't see it happen, it isn't really happening' by supplying observable evidence of slow change. A still pair cannot by itself convey how fast or slow the change was, which is why pairs are tagged fast/slow and paired with the time-control activity; this is a scaffold for the 'real change' idea, not a substitute for experiencing rate.
sourceClaims: 2-ESS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1]'; clarification names volcanic explosions and earthquakes (quick) and erosion of rocks (slow); assessment excludes quantitative timescales
learnerActions: Look at paired before/after images — for example a cliff that has retreated, or a rough rock that has become a smooth round pebble; alongside a fast pair such as land before and after an eruption.
Tap or point to each spot that is different and name what changed.

Use the source’s time context, such as moments later or a long time later, to tag each pair as fast or slow. If no elapsed-time context is available, state that the images show a change but do not establish its speed.
For the slow pair, answer: 'How do we know this really changed if we never watched it happen?'
activities.intendedInsight: Even when we cannot watch a change happen moment to moment, comparing a 'before' and an 'after' is evidence that the change is real. Slow changes leave proof behind.

activities.title: Talk it through: is a wearing-away cliff still changing?
feedback: If the child says water is too soft to change rock: 'Think of a smooth round pebble — it started rough. What made it smooth? Moving water tumbled it against sand and other stones again and again, over a very long time.'
If the child still doubts that gentle forces matter, point to everyday proof: 'Look at worn-down stone steps — many feet treading over many years wore the hard stone away. Slow, but real.'
If they deny the cliff is changing: 'It changes too slowly to watch, but photos taken a long time apart would look different — so it really is changing.'
Affirm fresh correct examples: 'Yes, that's another slow change — nicely spotted.'
activities.rationale: Asking the child to generate and justify their own examples moves beyond recognition into independent explanation, targeting the crux misconception that only dramatic events count as change. Spoken dialogue can support this reasoning; for this age the hands-on sort-and-time activities may deliver the rate contrast more concretely, so talk is best used to probe and extend understanding. This is a proposed use, not an efficacy-tested one.
learnerActions: Respond to prompts such as 'Can you think of a fast change to the land? A slow one?'
Explain whether a cliff that is slowly wearing away is still changing, and why.
Give a fresh example of each kind of change in your own words.
Answer the probe: 'If you photographed a cliff today and again a long time from now, would they look the same?'
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the idea into your own words — naming examples and defending that a slow, gentle process genuinely changes the land — consolidates and reveals understanding. Recognition in a sort does not by itself show a child can produce and explain examples; this activity targets that production.

constraints: Keep all comparisons qualitative: compare fast vs slow and 'a long time' vs 'a moment', but never ask children to quantify timescales in years — the NGSS 2-ESS1-1 assessment boundary excludes quantitative measurement of timescales.
Draw fast examples from eruptions and earthquakes and slow examples from erosion/wearing-away, so the topic ties to the wider volcanoes & earthquakes material.

A sorting/classification task can check whether a child compares quick and slow changes, but does not by itself elicit the felt sense of how different the rates are; use it alongside, not instead of, an activity where the child controls time.

Before/after pairs show that change occurred. Include qualitative elapsed-time context to compare rates; an undated pair alone does not establish speed. A shared time-control model is an optional additional representation.
Keep 'both build and wear down' simple: say both kinds of change reshape the land, rather than assigning 'building' only to fast events and 'destroying' only to slow ones.
Target the key misconceptions explicitly: that the Earth never changes, that only dramatic events count as change, that unseen slow change isn't real, and that slow changes are only small.
Keep the slider/panel, sort and dialogue as proposed, complementary scaffolds; do not present any one medium as the only route to understanding or as proven more effective than another.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a side-by-side time-control interactive as 'ideal' and dialogue and 3D as 'poor/possible'; those are catalog fit rankings, not evidence of comparative efficacy. The activities here are preserved as complementary proposals with their affordances and limits stated, rather than ranked.

The claim that erosion wears rock into sand, that cliffs retreat, and that pebbles and stone steps are smoothed/worn by water or use over long time is standard primary-science content consistent with the cited NGSS clarification; actual rates depend on rock type and conditions, but since the topic stays qualitative no quantitative claim is made or needed.
One source (DfE KS2 placement) is marked verified:false in the row; the UK curriculum placement note is retained only as context and not relied on for the US-anchored teaching objective.

The original assessment probe phrased the thought experiment as 'again in fifty years'; it was kept as a qualitative 'a long time from now' framing to avoid implying a timescale measurement, while still matching the original intent. Either phrasing is a hypothetical, not a quantification the child must produce.

The 2-ESS1-1 'several sources' claim was removed from activity 1 because its core assertion supports the evidence/classify tasks (activities 2–3) rather than activity 1's experiential-rate principle, which the CCC claim directly supports.

probeDeeper: Which took longer to happen — the volcano changing the land, or the cliff wearing away?
If you photographed the cliff today and again in fifty years, would they look the same?
Can you think of another fast change and another slow change to the land?
A pebble on the beach is smooth and round. What made it that shape — something fast or something slow?
assess.correctAnswer: The volcano is a fast change (it can reshape the land in a day); the cliff wearing away is a slow change (it takes many years). And yes — even gentle water and wind really do wear away solid rock, but so slowly that we can't watch it happen.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only big dramatic events change the land; gentle water or wind can't change solid rock
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show worn stone steps or a smooth round pebble — slow change adds up over very many years.
errorPatterns.distractor: The waves can't really change solid rock — only the volcano changes the land.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the cliff isn't really changing, or that water is too soft to wear rock.

errorPatterns.pattern: If you can't see it moving, nothing is happening ('the cliff looks the same, so it's not changing')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a photo now with one from long ago; the change is real but too slow to see moment to moment.
errorPatterns.distractor: Nothing is happening to the cliff — it looks the same.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates 'can't watch it change' with 'not changing at all'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Landforms like mountains and cliffs were always exactly as they are now
errorPatterns.nextMove: The land has a history and keeps changing — sometimes fast, sometimes slow.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the land was ever different in the past.

responseLevels.gap: Can't sort fast vs slow, or denies that gentle/slow processes change the land at all.
responseLevels.full: Sorts quick vs slow with examples AND explains that slow processes really do change the land over long time even though we can't watch it, giving a fresh example of each.
responseLevels.partial: Labels the volcano fast and the cliff slow but treats the slow change as 'not really happening', or can't explain the difference.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A cliff by the sea slowly wears away as waves hit it, year after year. A volcano can change the land in a single day. Which change is fast and which is slow — and can something as gentle as water really change solid rock?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The crux is whether the child accepts that a slow, gentle process genuinely changes rock over long time. Sorting fast vs slow is easy; a child who thinks only dramatic events change the land will deny the slow one counts — so affirming the gentle change is real is what separates them.

pedagogy.summary: The key distinction is APPARENT brightness (how bright a star LOOKS from Earth) versus ACTUAL/intrinsic brightness (how much light it truly gives off). The Sun looks overwhelmingly the brightest star only because it is by far the CLOSEST — it is an ordinary medium-sized star, not the biggest or most luminous in the universe. Brightness falls off steeply with distance, so a nearby modest light can outshine a distant powerful one. The canonical anchor is the torch-up-close vs distant-floodlight comparison: the floodlight is far more powerful, yet the near torch looks brighter. Teaching this untangles 'looks brightest' from 'is most powerful' and sets up later work on stellar distance and magnitude.
bestPractices: Separate the two meanings of 'bright' explicitly and give each a label — apparent (how bright it looks from here) vs actual/intrinsic (how much light it really pours out) — and keep using both terms so children don't collapse them.

Lead with the torch-vs-floodlight demonstration: hold a small torch close and shine a powerful lamp from across the room; the torch looks brighter though the lamp is stronger — distance, not power alone, sets how bright something looks.

Make the argument evidence-based (the NGSS framing): the Sun looks far brighter than any night-time star, and we know it is enormously closer — so its extreme apparent brightness is explained by its nearness, not by it being the most powerful star.
Correct the 'Sun is special/biggest' idea directly: the Sun is a fairly average star; many stars we see as faint dots are far larger and more luminous but look dim because they are light-years away.
Connect to everyday distance-brightness experience (car headlights approaching, a candle across a field) so the inverse relationship 'farther = looks dimmer' is grounded before applying it to stars.
keyRepresentations: Torch-close vs distant-floodlight comparison (the canonical model)
A distance slider: the same star dragged nearer looks brighter, dragged farther looks dimmer, while its actual output is unchanged
Two-star setup: a small near star and a huge far star tuned to the SAME apparent brightness — revealing looks can't tell you power without distance
Label pair on every star: 'how bright it looks' (apparent) vs 'how much light it makes' (actual)
Scale reminder that the Sun is one ordinary star, vastly closer than the next-nearest star
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the Sun is the biggest or most powerful star in the universe, rather than an average star that merely looks brightest because it is closest.
Believing a star that LOOKS brighter must actually be giving off more light — conflating apparent with actual brightness and ignoring distance.
Assuming the dim dots of night-time stars are small or weak, when many are far larger and more luminous than the Sun but extremely distant.
Thinking brightness does not depend on distance (that a light looks equally bright however far away it is).
Believing stars we see are all at the same distance (a 'dome of stars'), so their apparent brightness reflects their true output.
Confusing 'the Sun is close, so it's small' — nearness is about how bright/large it LOOKS, not its true size.

learn.summary: Children aged 9-11 learn that the Sun looks far brighter than any other star only because it is by far the CLOSEST star, not because it is the biggest or most powerful. The core distinction is between apparent brightness (how bright a star LOOKS from Earth) and actual/intrinsic brightness (how much light it truly gives off). How bright a star looks depends on BOTH its true power AND its distance, so a nearby modest light can outshine a distant powerful one. The canonical anchor is the near torch vs distant floodlight: the floodlight is far more powerful, yet the near torch looks brighter.

activities.title: Distance dial: dim the Sun to just another dot
feedback: When the Sun fades to a speck: 'The Sun isn't the most powerful star — it's just the closest. Its actual light output never changed; only its distance did.'
When the giant is dragged closer and blazes: 'A more powerful star only looked dim because it was so far away. Distance, not power alone, sets how bright a star looks.'
If a learner expects the output meter to change as distance changes: 'The light a star truly makes stays the same wherever it is — it is only how bright it LOOKS to us that changes with distance.'
activities.rationale: Apparent brightness is a relationship between true output and distance, so letting the learner vary distance while a fixed output readout stays put can make that relationship concrete rather than merely asserted. A live distance control and a separate fixed-output meter make the two meanings of 'bright' visible at once.
sourceClaims: Grade-5 standard: 'Support an argument that differences in the apparent brightness of the sun compared to other [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-1] Earth', with the core idea that [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-1] to Earth.

Apparent brightness (how bright a star looks) depends on both its intrinsic luminosity and its distance; a nearer, less luminous source can outshine a distant, more luminous one — the basis of the torch-vs-floodlight analogy and of astronomical magnitude.
learnerActions: Start with a scene showing the blazing Sun beside a tiny faint dot labelled 'a giant star, far away'.
Drag the Sun's DISTANCE control outward and watch its apparent brightness dim steadily until it becomes just another pale speck in the star field.
Notice that the separate 'actual light output' meter for the Sun does NOT change while you move it.
Take the distant giant star and drag ITS distance control closer until it blazes brighter than the Sun ever looked.
State in your own words why the giant looked dim at first even though it is more powerful.
As an everyday on-ramp, switch to a torch-and-floodlight version and rehearse the same idea: a near torch that looks brighter than a far floodlight that is really much stronger.
activities.intendedInsight: Apparent brightness is a relationship: it changes with distance while a star's actual light output stays fixed. 'Looks brightest' is not the same as 'is most powerful' — distance has to be taken into account.

activities.title: Two stars tuned to look equally bright
feedback: If a learner guesses the two are equally powerful because they look the same: 'They only LOOK the same. The giant is far away, so even a huge output arrives looking as faint as the near star — distance evens out the look, not the real power.'

If a learner assumes both stars are the same distance away: 'Stars are not fixed on one sky-dome at equal distance — they lie at wildly different distances, which is exactly why how bright they look cannot be read as how powerful they really are.'
On reveal: 'Same apparent brightness, very different actual brightness. That is why astronomers must know a star's distance before judging its true power.'
activities.rationale: Setting a near modest source and a distant powerful source to the same apparent brightness targets the misconception that a brighter-looking star must emit more light. Contrasting two stars at once isolates the role of distance in the relationship and confronts the 'all stars at equal distance' idea.
sourceClaims: Apparent brightness (how bright a star looks) depends on both its intrinsic luminosity and its distance; a nearer, less luminous source can outshine a distant, more luminous one — the basis of the torch-vs-floodlight analogy and of astronomical magnitude.
learnerActions: Place a small, near star (like the Sun: medium output) beside a huge, distant star.
Adjust the distant giant's distance until both stars LOOK equally bright on screen.
Predict which star is actually more powerful before revealing the outputs.
Reveal each star's 'actual light output' and compare it with how bright each one looks.
Explain why 'looks equally bright' tells you nothing about power until you know each star's distance.
activities.intendedInsight: Looks alone cannot reveal a star's true power; you need to know its distance too. Two stars can look identical yet pour out vastly different amounts of light, because stars sit at wildly different distances from us.

activities.title: Torch vs floodlight: predict, observe, explain
feedback: If the prediction was 'the stronger one always looks brighter': 'The near torch looked as bright as, or brighter than, the stronger lamp. How bright a light LOOKS depends on distance as well as power.'
If the prediction was 'the near one might win because it's closer': 'Exactly — being close can make a weaker light look brighter than a stronger, far one.'
Connect back: 'This is why the Sun looks brightest of all stars: it is the nearest, not the most powerful.'
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain task with real lights grounds the inverse distance-brightness relationship in everyday experience before applying it to stars, and the reason given BEFORE observing is diagnostic of whether the learner has separated true power from distance.
sourceClaims: Apparent brightness (how bright a star looks) depends on both its intrinsic luminosity and its distance; a nearer, less luminous source can outshine a distant, more luminous one — the basis of the torch-vs-floodlight analogy and of astronomical magnitude.
learnerActions: Before anything is switched on, look at a small dim torch set close to where you sit and a much brighter lamp placed far across the room.
PREDICT which light will LOOK brighter from your seat, and say WHY.
Switch both on and observe: the weaker near torch can look as bright as or brighter than the powerful distant lamp.
Compare what actually happened with your prediction and revise your reasoning if needed.
Answer: which light is really more powerful, and which one LOOKS brighter from here?
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday lights obey the same rule as stars: how bright something looks depends on both its power and its distance. A prediction of 'the stronger one always looks brighter' shows power and distance have not yet been separated.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal: closest, not biggest
feedback: On tapping the Sun: 'The Sun looks brightest because it's the closest star. In true power it is a fairly ordinary star, and many stars give off far more light.'
On tapping a faint dot: 'This faint dot is really a giant, more powerful than the Sun. It looks dim only because it is enormously far away.'
activities.rationale: A labelled reveal scene reinforces the 'closest, not biggest' content point and keeps the apparent/actual label pair in front of the learner, which may help prevent collapsing the two meanings of 'bright'.
sourceClaims: Grade-5 standard: 'Support an argument that differences in the apparent brightness of the sun compared to other [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-1] Earth', with the core idea that [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-1] to Earth.
learnerActions: Tap the Sun in a star scene and read why it looks brightest ('closest to us').
Tap a faint dot and discover it is actually a giant star, just very far away.
Open the torch/floodlight pair and decide which is more powerful versus which looks brighter.
For each star shown, read the paired labels 'how bright it looks' (apparent) and 'how much light it makes' (actual) and say how they differ.
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun is a fairly ordinary medium-sized star that looks brightest only because it is nearest; many faint dots are far larger and more luminous but look dim because they are light-years away.

activities.title: Check: why does the Sun look brightest?
feedback: If 'most powerful' is chosen: 'The Sun looks brightest because it's nearest, not because it's strongest. It's a fairly ordinary star; some faint-looking stars are far more powerful.'

If a faint dot is ranked low in true power purely from its look: 'A faint-looking star can be a powerful giant that is simply very far away — you can't read true power straight off how bright it looks.'
On the distance estimate: 'The farther a star is, the dimmer it looks, even though the light it makes is unchanged.'
activities.rationale: A linear check is useful for confirming the apparent/actual distinction and the torch-vs-floodlight reasoning after teaching. It verifies recall and discrimination but does not itself build the felt distance-brightness relationship, so it works best following the interactive work.
learnerActions: Answer 'Why does the Sun look brightest?' choosing between 'because it's the closest star' and 'because it's the most powerful star', and justify your choice.
Match star cards to their apparent brightness and their actual brightness, noticing where the two disagree.
Estimate, using a distance slider, how a star's apparent brightness changes as it is moved farther away.
Answer: could a star that looks like a faint dot actually be giving off more light than the Sun, and how?
activities.intendedInsight: Checks whether the learner can hold apparent and actual brightness apart and reason with distance, after the relationship has been explored.

constraints: Keep both terms in use throughout — apparent (how bright it looks from here) and actual/intrinsic (how much light it really pours out) — so learners do not collapse them into one idea of 'bright'.
Treat the inverse-square relationship qualitatively at this age: 'farther = looks dimmer, with true output unchanged'. Do not require numeric brightness calculations.

A tap-to-reveal or labelled static scene can state and reinforce the distinction, but it cannot let the learner vary distance themselves; pair it with a manipulable version or a hands-on torch/floodlight activity so the distance-brightness relationship is explored, not just asserted.

A linear check (multiple choice, matching, a single slider estimate) confirms the distinction and reasoning but does not build the felt relationship; use it after exploration, not as the sole experience.

The real-light demonstration depends on room setup: the near torch must be dim and close and the far lamp powerful and distant enough that the near torch can genuinely look as bright or brighter. Check the arrangement actually produces this before the predict step.

A flythrough or 3D view of the Sun fading into a star field can reinforce distance and is atmospheric, but is not required to grasp apparent vs actual; the relationship is most cleanly isolated with a controlled distance change.
An in-role astronomer or dialogue can state the distinction but cannot by itself deliver the hands-on dimming-with-distance experience; if used, pair it with manipulation or demonstration.

If apparent size is discussed alongside brightness, keep apparent angular size and apparent brightness as separate ideas; do not merge them even though the source wording says the Sun 'appears larger and brighter' because it is closer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NGSS 5-ESS1-1 source is marked verified in the row; the astronomy-education source on apparent vs absolute magnitude / inverse-square is marked unverified. Evidence strength has not been re-checked here.

Original source wording says the Sun 'appears larger and brighter' because it is closer. Apparent angular SIZE and apparent BRIGHTNESS are distinct phenomena; the pedagogy also flags the misconception 'close, so it's small'. Activities here focus on brightness; keep apparent size and apparent brightness as separate ideas rather than merging them.

Legacy entries asserted '3D adds spectacle without being needed' and that a static image 'can only assert' the relationship, framed as near-universal claims. These have been softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints; the comparative necessity claims are not established by the source material.

The original 'possible/poor' rankings for quiz, 3D and conversation formats were catalog fit ratings; the underlying pedagogical points (checks confirm but don't build the relationship; dialogue states but doesn't demonstrate) are preserved as constraints without the ranking vocabulary.
The 'dome of stars' / all-stars-at-equal-distance misconception from the pedagogy and assessment error patterns is addressed in the two-star activity feedback; efficacy of that treatment is untested.

Activity 5's sourceClaims were set to [] because its rationale concerns the limits/placement of a linear check — a methodological claim no sources[].claim directly supports (the claims support the topic, not the method).

assess.poeTask: Set a small, dim torch close to where the children sit and a much brighter lamp far across the room. Before switching either on, ask them to PREDICT which will LOOK brighter from their seats, and to say WHY. Then switch both on: the weaker torch, being close, can look as bright as or brighter than the powerful distant lamp. The reason a child gives BEFORE seeing it is the diagnostic part — 'the stronger one always looks brighter' reveals they haven't yet separated true power from distance, while 'the near one might win because it's closer' shows they have.
probeDeeper: Could a star that looks like a faint dot actually be giving off more light than the Sun? How?
What two things together decide how bright a star LOOKS to us?
If you moved the Sun ten times farther away, would it still look the brightest star?
Why does a nearby torch look brighter than a distant floodlight, even though the floodlight is stronger?
assess.correctAnswer: No. The Sun looks brightest only because it is by far the CLOSEST star to us. It's actually a fairly ordinary, medium-sized star; many of the faint dots we see at night are really far more powerful than the Sun but look dim because they are enormously farther away. How bright something LOOKS (apparent brightness) depends on both its true power AND its distance — just as a torch held close looks brighter than a powerful floodlight far down the street, even though the floodlight gives off much more light.

errorPatterns.pattern: the Sun is the brightest and most powerful star in the universe ('that's why it looks so bright')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate apparent from actual brightness: the Sun looks brightest because it's nearest and is only average in true power; some night stars far outshine it in reality.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun really is the most powerful, brightest star — that's why it looks so bright to us.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child reads 'looks brightest' as 'is the greatest', ignoring distance

errorPatterns.pattern: a star that looks fainter must be giving off less light than one that looks brighter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the torch-near versus floodlight-far demonstration: a faint-looking star can be a powerful giant that is simply very far away.
errorPatterns.distractor: A star that looks dimmer than the Sun must be giving off less light than the Sun.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child ranks true power straight off apparent brightness, leaving distance out

errorPatterns.pattern: all stars are the same distance away (fixed on one sky-dome), so how bright they look shows their real power
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stars lie at wildly different distances — which is exactly why how bright they look can't be read as how powerful they are.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child assumes stars sit at equal distance, so apparent brightness = true power

responseLevels.gap: Says the Sun is the most powerful star because it looks brightest — no separation of apparent from actual brightness.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes apparent from actual brightness, explains the Sun only looks brightest because it's nearest (an average star), and that apparent brightness depends on true power AND distance — transferring it to the torch/floodlight case.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the Sun looks brightest because it's closest, but cannot clearly say a faint-looking star could be more powerful, or leaves distance out of 'how bright it looks'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The Sun looks far brighter to us than any star in the night sky. Does that mean the Sun is the most powerful, brightest star there is — giving off more light than all the others? Tell me WHY, or why not.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who conflates 'looks brightest' with 'is most powerful' says the Sun is the greatest star. A child who separates apparent from actual brightness says the Sun only looks brightest because it's nearest, and that a faint-looking star can be more powerful. The 'why' tier forces the apparent/actual distinction and the role of distance.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Controlling variables — hypotheses & full experimental design (KS3)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils to "ask questions and develop a line of enquiry based on observations of the real world…", to "make predictions using scientific knowledge and understanding", and to "select, plan and carry out the most appropriate types of scientific enquiries to test predictions, including identifying independent, dependent and control variables, where appropriate", alongside applying "sampling techniques" and evaluating risks. This topic operationalises hypothesis-led full experimental design.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3, grades 6–8):** the 6–8 progression requires students to "plan an investigation individually and collaboratively, and in the design: identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed to do the gathering, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim." The 9–12 band adds directional hypotheses specifying "what happens to a dependent variable when an independent variable is manipulated" — previewed here.

- **Operational details:** Builds directly on upper-KS2 planning with variable control (prerequisite mt_ArVBEpMAPk); parallels the general planning and structured-reasoning habits (soft links mt_QR3vxbN1o4, mt_WKxX-b86Vr). The step-up is fourfold: (1) writing a TESTABLE HYPOTHESIS in the form 'I predict that [IV] will affect [DV] because [scientific reasoning]' — a prediction with a mechanism, not a bare guess; (2) formally naming the independent, dependent, and at least three control variables; (3) planning repeat readings and an appropriate SAMPLE SIZE for reliability; and (4) a RISK ASSESSMENT identifying hazards and control measures. Feeds forward to writing full structured reports with peer review (dependent mt_ThTbUuNb3p).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/quantitative). A learner who can write a reasoned testable hypothesis linking an IV to a DV, identify the IV, DV and at least three controls, plan repeat readings and sample size, and identify relevant hazards with control measures has met the bar. Distinguishing systematic vs random error and evaluating precision come at the next step (mt_3jmBpEepYX, mt_auJqTemMpI).
bestPractices: Teach the hypothesis as prediction-plus-mechanism: the 'because…' clause carrying scientific reasoning is what separates a hypothesis from a guess and is the assessed core — model strong vs weak 'because' clauses.

Formalise the KS2 change/measure/keep-same language into independent / dependent / control variables now, explicitly bridging from the pupils' prior vocabulary so the terms attach to an already-understood idea.
Make control-variable identification demanding — require at least three, and justify each — because at KS3 the plausible confounds multiply and 'what else could affect the result?' is the key habit.
Introduce sample size and repeat readings as reliability tools with a reason (spotting anomalies, reducing the effect of random error, enabling a mean) rather than as a ritual 'do it three times'.
Embed risk assessment as routine professional practice (hazard → who/what is at risk → control measure), normalising safety planning as part of every KS3 investigation design.
keyRepresentations: The hypothesis frame 'I predict that [IV] will affect [DV] because [reasoning]'
An IV / DV / control-variables table (with ≥3 named controls, each justified)
A full planning template: hypothesis → variables → method → repeats & sample size → risk assessment → recording
A risk-assessment grid (hazard | risk | control measure)
A predicted results sketch-graph showing the expected IV–DV relationship before data collection
commonMisconceptions: Writing a hypothesis as a bare prediction with no 'because' / mechanism, or as a non-testable statement of opinion.
Confusing independent and dependent variables, or mislabelling a control variable as the independent variable.
Treating 'repeat three times' as a rule without understanding that repeats and sample size exist to improve reliability and expose anomalies.
Naming only one or two obvious control variables and missing subtler confounds that would invalidate the result.
Seeing risk assessment as a bureaucratic add-on rather than an integral part of designing a valid, safe investigation.
Thinking a hypothesis that turns out wrong means the investigation failed — a refuted hypothesis is a valid, informative result.

learn.summary: Learners aged 11–12 design a full, hypothesis-led investigation (KS3 / NGSS SEP 3): a testable hypothesis with a mechanism ('because…'), named independent/dependent/≥3 control variables, planned repeats and sample size, and a hazard-with-control-measure risk assessment. The core is coordinating this design with the epistemic distinction between validity (controlling variables so the IV's effect is what is measured) and reliability (consistency across repeats). The proposed primary approach is a design-and-run studio in which poor design is intended to produce visibly untrustworthy data; supporting approaches include variable/hypothesis classification tasks and a Socratic supervisor dialogue.

activities.title: Design studio: build it, then run it
feedback: If a control is omitted, show that the result cannot be attributed to the IV alone — name the uncontrolled variable as the confound.

If only one trial is run, show how a single freak reading drags the conclusion; as repeats increase, show the mean settle so the pattern becomes more reliable (repeats improve reliability, but only a controlled design makes it valid).
If a hazard is skipped, raise a safety flag naming the hazard and a suitable control measure.
If the 'because' clause is missing, prompt: what mechanism explains why the IV would change the DV?
If the data differs from the predicted sketch, note that a refuted prediction is still a valid, informative result, not a failed investigation.
activities.rationale: Full experimental design is a generative, multi-part construction task where each choice has consequences for validity and reliability; running the design is intended to make those abstract principles concrete and let learners feel the cost of a missing control or too-small a sample. The cited standards require planning investigations that identify IV/DV/controls, tools, recording and sufficient data.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Working Scientifically requires selecting, planning and carrying out the most appropriate types of scientific enquiries to test predictions, including identifying independent, dependent and control variables, using sampling techniques, and evaluating risks.

NGSS SEP 3 at grades 6-8 requires planning an investigation that identifies independent and dependent variables and controls, the tools needed, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim; 9-12 adds directional hypotheses relating DV changes to IV manipulation.
learnerActions: Write a testable hypothesis in the form 'I predict that [IV] will affect [DV] because [scientific reasoning]', e.g. 'I predict warmer water will speed up dissolving BECAUSE particles move faster and collide more often'.
Assign the independent variable, the dependent variable, and name at least three control variables, justifying for each why it would otherwise affect the DV.
Before running, sketch the predicted IV–DV relationship as a graph showing the expected pattern.
Set the number of repeat readings and the sample size.
Complete a risk-assessment grid: hazard | who/what is at risk | control measure.
Run the planned (simulated) investigation and inspect the data it returns, comparing it with your predicted-results sketch.
Deliberately leave one control out (e.g. don't fix water volume), re-run, and compare how interpretable the results are.
Run a single trial versus many repeats and watch how an anomaly affects the mean.
activities.intendedInsight: Validity and reliability are properties you build into a plan: an uncontrolled variable makes results muddied and unattributable (a validity problem), while too few repeats let one anomaly swing the mean (a reliability problem). More repeats do NOT rescue a confounded design.

activities.title: Sort, judge and match (variable and hypothesis practice)
feedback: For a mislabelled variable, re-check: 'is this the one thing I deliberately change (IV), the thing I measure (DV), or something else that would otherwise affect the DV?' — if it is something else that could affect the DV, it should be controlled.
For a bare prediction such as 'more concentration = faster' chosen as a hypothesis, point to the absent 'because' / mechanism.
For a mismatched hazard, show the specific control measure that reduces that risk.
activities.rationale: Classifying variables, judging whether a hypothesis is testable and reasoned, selecting adequate sample size, and matching hazards to controls exercise the curriculum-required skill of identifying IV/DV/control variables against clear criteria. This builds and checks the component skills, though on its own it does not let the learner feel reliability consequences in live data.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Working Scientifically requires selecting, planning and carrying out the most appropriate types of scientific enquiries to test predictions, including identifying independent, dependent and control variables, using sampling techniques, and evaluating risks.
learnerActions: For an acid-concentration-affects-reaction-rate scenario (e.g. hydrochloric acid reacting with marble chips), sort the quantities (concentration, rate/time, temperature, volume, surface area, same apparatus) into independent / dependent / control.

From several hypotheses — including the bare prediction 'more concentration = faster' and the reasoned 'increasing concentration will increase the rate BECAUSE more particles per volume means more frequent collisions' — choose which are both testable AND carry scientific reasoning, and say what is wrong with the rest.
Match named hazards to appropriate control measures.
Set repeats/sample size for the scenario and justify the choice (spotting anomalies, enabling a mean, reducing the effect of random error).
activities.intendedInsight: Variable roles, hypothesis quality, hazard control and sample-size adequacy can each be judged against clear criteria; a hypothesis needs a mechanism, and a control is something that would otherwise affect the DV.

activities.title: Supervisor challenge dialogue
feedback: Push on any vague mechanism until the reasoning is explanatory, not merely directional.
When a confound is overlooked, ask what else varies that could change the DV.
Separate validity from reliability explicitly if the learner swaps or merges them.
activities.rationale: A supervising-scientist persona can pressure-test hypothesis reasoning and control identification Socratically. It is a proposed supplement, best used after the studio, since dialogue alone cannot execute the design to demonstrate validity and reliability in data.
learnerActions: Present a hypothesis and plan to a lab-supervisor persona.
Respond to Socratic challenges: 'Is that testable?', 'What else could affect your DV?', 'Is three repeats enough — and what does that fix?', 'Are your results valid, reliable, or both?'.
Revise the 'because' clause and the control-variable list in response to the questioning.
activities.intendedInsight: Pressure-testing the reasoning behind a hypothesis and hunting for subtler confounds can strengthen the 'because' clause and surface missed controls.

constraints: The assessed core is the 'because…' mechanism clause: a hypothesis must be a reasoned, testable prediction, not a bare directional guess or a statement of opinion.
Require at least three genuine control variables, each justified as something that would otherwise affect the DV; naming only one or two obvious controls misses subtler confounds.
Treat repeats and sample size as reliability tools with a reason (spotting anomalies, reducing the effect of random error, enabling a mean), not a ritual 'do it three times'.

Keep validity and reliability distinct: controls → validity (the right thing is measured); repeats → reliability (consistent readings); accuracy → closeness to the true value. More repeats do not make a confounded design valid.
Embed risk assessment as routine design practice (hazard → who/what is at risk → control measure), not a bureaucratic add-on.
A refuted hypothesis is a valid, informative result; a hypothesis turning out wrong does not mean the investigation failed.

The classification/matching tasks and reference plans build or check components but do not themselves let learners experience reliability consequences in live data; the dialogue cannot run the experiment. A labelled reference of a completed plan is a reference, not the main teaching activity.
Formalise the KS2 change/measure/keep-same language into independent/dependent/control variables, bridging explicitly from prior vocabulary.
Distinguishing systematic vs random error and evaluating precision belong to a later step, not this one.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted a 'static image cannot support' this skill and that design reasoning 'is not spatial'. These are presented as narrowly scoped affordance observations (a fixed reference plan cannot be reconfigured and run), not as universal laws; a labelled reference plan can still support learning as a reference.

The 'poor fit' claims for image-only and 3D formats were catalog comparisons; retained only as the limitation that those formats do not support constructing and running a plan, without asserting comparative efficacy.
The UK DfE source is marked verified:false in the row; the standards claim is retained as cited but not independently confirmed here.
The relative strength of the studio over the classification and dialogue formats is a design proposal, not a tested-efficacy finding.

Self-audit: the worked example particle-collision mechanisms (warmer water → faster particle motion → faster dissolving; higher concentration → more particles per volume → more frequent collisions → faster rate) are scientifically consistent and retained as illustrative hypotheses, not as the only acceptable answers.

probeDeeper: Why does your hypothesis include a 'because'? What would be missing without it?
You take three close repeats but left temperature uncontrolled — are your results reliable? Are they valid? Can they be one without the other?
If a classmate got very consistent results from a test that changed two variables at once, would you trust their conclusion? Why or why not?
How does your number of repeats or sample size affect how much you trust the pattern?
assess.correctAnswer: A strong plan states a reasoned hypothesis ('increasing concentration will increase the rate BECAUSE more particles per volume means more frequent collisions'), correctly assigns the independent variable (concentration) and dependent variable (rate/time), names at least three genuine controls (temperature, volume, same apparatus, surface area…), plans repeats (e.g. three runs, take a mean) and an adequate sample, and identifies hazards with control measures. Crucially it distinguishes VALIDITY (controlling variables so the test actually measures the effect of the IV) from RELIABILITY (consistency across repeats), and treats the hypothesis as a testable prediction with a mechanism, not a guess.

errorPatterns.pattern: Validity/reliability conflation: thinks taking more repeats makes a confounded test valid, or calls a well-controlled test 'reliable' as if the words were interchangeable.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate them explicitly: controls → validity (the right thing is measured); repeats → reliability (consistent readings); accuracy → closeness to the true value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The valid-vs-reliable explanation swaps or merges the two ideas.

errorPatterns.pattern: Hypothesis as bare prediction: 'more concentration = faster' with no mechanism or 'because'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the 'because…' with a particle-collision mechanism so the hypothesis is explanatory, not just directional.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The stated hypothesis predicts an outcome but gives no scientific reasoning.

errorPatterns.pattern: Weak or mislabelled variables: lists fewer than three genuine controls, or names the dependent variable as something to control.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Three-column IV/DV/control sort; check each control is something that would otherwise affect the DV.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The variable list is short, or assigns the wrong role to a variable.

responseLevels.gap: Gives a bare prediction with no mechanism, lists too few or muddled variables, or treats 'more repeats' as what makes a test valid.
responseLevels.full: Produces a complete, reasoned plan (mechanistic hypothesis, correct IV/DV, at least three justified controls, repeats and sample size, hazards with controls) and cleanly distinguishes validity (control → right thing measured) from reliability (repeats → consistency) and accuracy — coordinating design and epistemic reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: Writes a reasoned hypothesis and identifies IV/DV/controls and repeats, but conflates validity with reliability, or can't fully justify the sample size and controls.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You're planning an experiment on whether the concentration of a sugar solution affects how fast a reaction happens. Talk me through your full plan: your hypothesis and the reasoning behind it, which variable you change, which you measure, at least three you must control, and how many readings or repeats you'd take and why. Then explain the difference between making your results VALID and making them RELIABLE.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The valid-vs-reliable distinction is the discriminator: a student can list controls and repeats yet conflate the two — thinking more repeats fix a confounded design, or calling a well-controlled test 'reliable'. A strong response ties controls to validity and repeats to reliability, and gives the hypothesis a mechanism rather than a bare prediction.
