pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, repeated reasoning becomes explicit generalisation WITH justification: noticing that every fraction equivalent to 1/2 has a numerator half its denominator, seeing 3×4=12, 3×40=120, 3×400=1200 as one scaling pattern and saying WHY, and naming 'derive from a known fact' (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as a general strategy rather than a one-off. CCSS MP8 stresses moving from noticed repetition to a general method while checking reasonableness. Teaching should press beyond 'I see a pattern' to 'why must it happen, and will it always?' — grounding the scaling pattern in place value and the fraction pattern in a visual model.
bestPractices: Lay out a scaling chain (3×4, 3×40, 3×400) and ask the child to explain WHY the product scales by 10 each time using place value, not just append zeros
Show families of equivalent fractions on a bar/number line so the numerator-half-denominator rule for 1/2 is seen to hold and can be tested
Name the derive-from-known-facts move as a reusable general strategy and ask the child to describe it in their own words
Insist on a test case for any stated rule ('does it still work for 3×4000? for 4/8?') to separate a justified generalisation from a guess
keyRepresentations: Place-value scaling chain (×10 shifts) for 3×4 → 3×40 → 3×400
Fraction wall / number line for families of equivalent fractions
Array / area-model split for deriving ×7 from ×5 + ×2
Multiplication grid showing column patterns
commonMisconceptions: Uses 'add a zero' for ×10 scaling with no place-value reason, so it fails on decimals
Notices a pattern but treats it as coincidence, unable to say why it must hold or whether it always will
Over-generalises the 1/2 rule to other fractions, or applies it without testing
Derives a fact but does not recognise the derive-from-known-facts move as a general strategy for other facts

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, press repeated reasoning into justified generalisation: not just noticing that 3×4=12, 3×40=120, 3×400=1200 scale by ten, but saying WHY (place value shifts the digits one place) and testing whether a rule always holds. Similarly, families of equivalent fractions (1/2, 2/4, 3/6) reveal a numerator-half-denominator pattern that should be tested on new cases, not trusted on sight. Name 'derive from a known fact' (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as a reusable strategy the child can describe in their own words. The target is the justification and the extension, not just correct numbers.

activities.title: Scaling machine with a 'why' window
feedback: If the child only says 'add a zero', show the scaling on a place-value chart so the digits visibly shift one column, and contrast a decimal case where 'add a zero' gives the wrong answer: 1.2 × 10 is 12, but writing a zero on the end gives 1.20, which is still 1.2. Use the chart to show that 3×0.4 = 1.2 is a tenth of 12 because the digits shift one column right

If the child gives 120 and 1200 but shrugs at 'will it always work?', don't just assert the rule — ask 'why does times-ten make it ten times bigger?' and work the next case (3×4000 = 12000) together so a justified generalisation forms
Affirm reasoning that connects the shift to place value and confidently extends to 3×4000 for the same reason
activities.rationale: CCSS MP8 stresses moving from noticed repetition to a general method while evaluating reasonableness; grounding the scaling in place value (rather than 'add a zero') supplies the justification and reveals why it generalises. An interactive scaling tool lets the child produce cases and test an extension live, but a place-value chart or written scaling chain achieves the same reasoning on paper.
sourceClaims: MP8: students move from repeated calculations to general methods and shortcuts, and evaluate the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts, recognise/use structure, and explain why patterns hold using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Start from 3×4 = 12, then produce 3×40 and 3×400 by scaling up by ten each step
For each step, explain WHY the product gets ten times bigger using place value (40 is ten times 4, so the answer is ten times bigger; the digits shift one place left) rather than saying 'add a zero'
Predict 3×4000 and state whether the same reason guarantees it will work, then check
Now test the idea going the OTHER way: 0.4 is a tenth of 4, so is 3×0.4 a tenth of 12? Work it out and explain why the place value, not an added zero, decides this
activities.intendedInsight: The product scales by ten BECAUSE place value shifts the digits one column, so the pattern must keep working (including for 3×4000). Reasoning from place value (not just appending zeros) also handles decimal cases like 3×0.4 = 1.2 — here 0.4 is a tenth of 4, so the product is a tenth of 12, with the digits shifting one column right. The add-a-zero shortcut cannot explain this, and it gives wrong answers for decimals (1.2 × 10 is 12, not 1.20).

activities.title: Equivalent-fraction family tester
feedback: If the child claims a fraction is equivalent to 1/2 on the verbal rule alone when it isn't, check it on the fraction wall/number line (same whole) so the mismatch is visible
If the child says 5/9 is equivalent because 5 is roughly half of 9, prompt them to compare 5/9 and 1/2 exactly on the bar and see they don't line up
Affirm when the child tests a candidate fraction (e.g. confirms 4/8 lines up, 5/9 does not) rather than trusting the rule outright
activities.rationale: EEF guidance recommends explaining why patterns hold using representations that reveal structure; a bar/number line makes the equivalence testable and guards against over-generalisation. A live generator makes testing immediate, but a drawn fraction wall supports the same checking.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive facts from known facts, recognise/use structure, and explain why patterns hold using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Line up 1/2, 2/4, 3/6 on a fraction bar or number line (same whole) and notice that each numerator is half its denominator
State the candidate rule 'a fraction equals 1/2 when the numerator is half the denominator'
Invent a new fraction and test whether the rule holds by checking it against the bar/number line, not by eyeballing
Try a trap case: is 5/9 equivalent to 1/2 because 5 is 'about half' of 9? How could you be sure?
activities.intendedInsight: A noticed rule must be tested before it is trusted; the numerator-half-denominator pattern for 1/2 can be confirmed on a model, and over-applying it (e.g. to 5/9) is caught by checking rather than guessing.

activities.title: Derive-from-known-facts as a named strategy
feedback: If the child treats 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 as a single trick for one fact, ask them to describe it as a general approach and apply it to a new fact
Use an array/area model split into 8×5 and 8×2 parts so the child sees why the parts add to the whole
Watch for the common wrong split 8×5 + 2 (adding 2 instead of 8×2 = 16, which gives 42 not 56); check the split against the model
activities.rationale: EEF recommends deriving facts from known facts and recognising structure; naming the strategy and transferring it to a new fact turns a single derivation into a general method, consistent with MP8's move from repetition to general strategy. An area/array model makes the factor split visible.
sourceClaims: MP8: students move from repeated calculations to general methods and shortcuts, and evaluate the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts, recognise/use structure, and explain why patterns hold using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Work out 8×7 from facts you already know: 8×5 = 40 and 8×2 = 16, then add to get 56
Explain why splitting 7 into 5 + 2 lets you reuse known facts (an array or area model split into an 8×5 part and an 8×2 part)
Describe the move in your own words as a general strategy for any hard table fact
Try the same strategy on another fact (e.g. 6×7 or 9×6) and say which known facts you'd lean on
activities.intendedInsight: Deriving an unknown fact by splitting a factor and reusing known facts is a reusable general strategy, not a one-off; the child should recognise and name it so they can apply it to other facts.

activities.title: Prove it holds every time
feedback: If the child treats a pattern as coincidence and won't commit to whether it always holds, ask 'why must it happen?' and test the next case together
Praise a reason grounded in structure (place value, the fraction model) over 'it just works'
activities.rationale: MP8 emphasises expressing regularity as a general method and checking reasonableness; insisting on a reason and a test case is how a child moves from 'I see a pattern' to 'it must always happen'.
sourceClaims: MP8: students move from repeated calculations to general methods and shortcuts, and evaluate the reasonableness of results
learnerActions: After extending a scaling chain or stating a fraction rule, answer: how could you convince someone the pattern works every time, not just for these three cases?
Produce a test case for any stated rule ('does it still work for 3×4000? for 4/8?') and report what you find
Distinguish a justified generalisation ('it must, because place value shifts') from a guess ('it just seems to')
activities.intendedInsight: A pattern noticed is not a pattern proven; a reason it must hold, plus a fresh test case, separates a reliable generalisation from a coincidence.

activities.title: Check your generalisation (quick questions)
feedback: If the child picks 5/9 as equivalent to 1/2, send them back to the fraction model to test it
If the child selects 8×5 + 2, point out the second part must be 8×2 = 16, not 2 (so the total is 56, not 42)
Always ask the 'why does it work?' follow-up; a correct pick without a reason is not yet a generalisation
activities.rationale: Recognition questions can check whether a generalisation has formed, but selecting an answer is not the same as constructing a justification; pairing every item with a 'why' step keeps the focus on reasoning. This supplements, not replaces, the construct-and-test activities.
learnerActions: Continue the scaling chain: given 3×4=12 and 3×40=120, give 3×400 and 3×4000
Pick which fractions are equivalent to 1/2 from a set that includes near-misses (e.g. 5/9)
Choose the correct derivation of 8×7 and reject the wrong split 8×5 + 2 in favour of 8×5 + 8×2 = 56
For each choice, say WHY it is correct, not just which answer
activities.intendedInsight: Selecting correct continuations and derivations, paired with a stated reason, confirms the child is generalising with justification rather than pattern-matching.

constraints: The learning target is the justification and the extension, not just correct products or correct fraction picks; accept an answer only when the child can say WHY and whether it always holds.

Recognition/selection questions can check whether a generalisation exists but do not elicit the child's own construction or justification; always pair them with a 'why does it work?' step and treat them as a supplement to construct-and-test work.

A static annotated scaling chain or fraction wall can show and explain the pattern, but cannot let the child generate and test new cases; use it as a reference scaffold, not as the place where testing happens.

Discussion on its own supplies no concrete case or model for the child to test a generalisation against; pair any talk with numbers, a place-value chart, a fraction model, or an array so claims can be checked.
'Add a zero' is an unjustified shortcut that misfires on decimals; require a place-value reason instead.
Scaling chains and fraction families are flat relationships, so a 3D representation is not needed to show their structure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic checked: 8×5=40, 8×2=16, 40+16=56 (8×7); 3×40=120, 3×400=1200, 3×4000=12000, 3×0.4=1.2; the wrong split 8×5+2=42 is only ever presented as an error to reject, never as a valid answer.

Place-value reasoning for ×10 (digits shift one place left on whole numbers) is sound; 3×0.4 is the scaling-DOWN direction (0.4 is a tenth of 4, so the product is a tenth of 12 = 1.2), which is where the 'add a zero' shortcut fails — the activity now flags this is the opposite direction rather than the same leftward shift.
The 5/9 case is a genuine non-equivalence (5 is not half of 9), used to prompt checking rather than eyeballing; 4/8 is a confirming case (4 is half of 8).

The non-preferred 'conversation' and '3D' entries were low-fit in the source; their genuine affordance limits are preserved as narrowly scoped constraints without asserting any universal 'only X can teach this' claim.

probeDeeper: Ask 'you scaled 3×4 up by tens — does the same idea work going the other way, 3×0.4? why or why not?' to test the limits of the generalisation
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'is 5/9 equivalent to 1/2 because 5 is about half of 9? how could you be sure?' to check the child tests rather than eyeballs
Ask 'you got 8×7 from 8×5 + 8×2 — could you describe that as a general trick for any hard table fact?' to see if the strategy is generalised
Ask 'how could you convince someone the pattern works every time, not just for these three?' to surface justification
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for 120 and 1200 with a place-value justification ('40 is ten times 4, so the answer is ten times bigger; the digits shift a place') and confidence it extends to 3×4000 = 12000 for the same reason. The WHY and the extension, not just the numbers, are the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'add a zero' with no place-value reason, so cannot justify why the product scales and it would misfire on decimals
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the scaling on a place-value chart so digits shift one column; contrast a decimal case where 'add a zero' fails
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked why, the child says only 'you add a zero' and cannot connect it to ×10 or place value

errorPatterns.pattern: Notices the pattern but treats it as a coincidence, unable to say it must always hold
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT just assert the rule; ask 'why does times-ten make it ten times bigger?' and test the next case together so a justified generalisation forms
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives 120 and 1200 but, asked 'will it always work?', shrugs or won't commit to 3×4000

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises the equivalent-fraction pattern (applies the 1/2 numerator-half-denominator rule to fractions it doesn't fit) without testing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Check the claim on a fraction wall/number line; test candidate fractions rather than trusting the verbal rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child claims a fraction is equivalent to 1/2 on the rule alone when it isn't, or won't test

responseLevels.gap: Produces the products by 'add a zero' but cannot justify, treats patterns as coincidence, and over-applies fraction rules without testing
responseLevels.full: Extends the scaling chain with a place-value justification, states the derive-from-known-facts move as a general strategy, and tests fraction generalisations — explaining WHY a rule must hold and transferring it unprompted
responseLevels.partial: States the pattern and can extend it when prompted, but justifies weakly ('you add a zero') and does not reliably test whether a rule always holds

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You know 3 × 4 = 12. What are 3 × 40 and 3 × 400? Explain WHY the pattern works — and would it still work for 3 × 4000?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The products can be produced by 'adding a zero' with zero understanding. What discriminates is the place-value reason and whether the child is sure it generalises. A child with repeated-reasoning insight explains why it must scale and extends confidently; one without recites 'add a zero' and cannot justify or is unsure about 3×4000.

sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP8 'Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning'

sources.claim: Pupils should derive facts from known facts, recognise/use structure, and explain why patterns hold using representations that reveal the structure

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Resultant Forces

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics — Forces):** Using force arrows in diagrams, adding forces in 1 dimension, balanced and unbalanced forces (DfE expresses the resultant as 'adding forces in 1 dimension'); 'forces being needed to cause objects to ... change their speed or direction of motion'.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS2-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-2] (the sum of the forces is the resultant; emphasis [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-2]; assessment limited to [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-2] one variable at a time).

- **Operational details:** At 11-12, a resultant (net) force is taught as the single force equivalent to all the forces acting on an object. When the forces are balanced the resultant is zero, so there is no CHANGE in motion — the object is either stationary OR moving at constant velocity; an unbalanced resultant causes acceleration in its own direction. Teach vector addition starting collinear (combine along one line) before moving to head-to-tail addition for non-collinear forces. The persistent battles are 'no resultant means it must be stationary', 'a bigger force makes it go faster' (rather than change faster), and drawing the resultant as an extra arrow added to the free-body diagram instead of the equivalent that replaces the others.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal).
bestPractices: Start collinear: combine forces along a single line (tug-of-war / number line) before introducing 2D vectors
Use head-to-tail (or parallelogram) arrow addition for non-collinear forces; never add the magnitudes as scalars unless they are along the same line
Use predict-observe-explain with cognitive conflict — especially the constant-velocity case where forces are balanced yet the object keeps moving
Stress that the resultant points in the direction of the CHANGE in motion, not necessarily the direction of motion
Show the resultant REPLACING the individual forces (the equivalent), not drawn as an additional arrow alongside them
Tie 'resultant = zero' explicitly to BOTH stationary and steady-speed cases
keyRepresentations: Free-body diagram of arrows, with the resultant shown separately as the single equivalent
Tug-of-war / number line for collinear addition
Head-to-tail vector triangle (or parallelogram) for non-collinear addition
commonMisconceptions: No resultant force means the object must be stationary (ignores constant velocity)
A bigger force makes an object go faster — conflating force with speed rather than with acceleration (rate of change)
The resultant is read as an extra/additional force acting on the body (Gunstone et al.)
The direction of the resultant equals the direction of motion (it should be the direction of CHANGE of motion)
Adding non-collinear vectors as scalars, or using a 'bisector' shortcut for the resultant direction
Motion implies a force in the direction of travel (the impetus backbone misconception)

learn.summary: For 11–12 year-olds, teach resultant (net) force as the single force equivalent to all forces on an object: a zero resultant means NO CHANGE in motion (stationary OR constant velocity), while a non-zero resultant causes acceleration in its own direction. Confront three stubborn errors — 'no resultant means stationary', 'bigger force means faster' (rather than changing motion faster), and reading the resultant as an extra arrow added to the forces rather than the equivalent that replaces them. A single force's direction is the direction of the CHANGE in motion, not automatically the direction of travel. Build vector addition collinear-first (along one line) before head-to-tail addition for non-collinear forces.

activities.title: Force-arrow playground: balanced forces that keep gliding
feedback: If you predicted the moving crate would stop when forces are balanced: balanced forces give a zero resultant, meaning no CHANGE — an already-moving object keeps its steady speed. Here friction is treated as negligible, so no other horizontal force is present to slow it.

If you expected the crate to reach a fixed fast speed and stay there while the rightward arrow stays longer: a constant unbalanced force pointing along the motion keeps accelerating the crate, so its speed keeps climbing for as long as that force acts.
If you read the resultant as an additional push: notice the overlay replaces the original arrows — it is their single combined effect, not an extra force.

For the angled case (crate starting from rest): the resultant is built head-to-tail; it is not the bisector of the two arrows, and it is not found by adding their lengths as plain numbers. Starting from rest, the crate accelerates along the resultant; if it were already moving in another direction, an angled resultant would curve its path rather than instantly align travel with the force.
activities.rationale: The decisive cases — balanced forces producing constant velocity, and a sustained unbalanced force along the motion making speed keep rising — are dynamic relationships that a live model lets the learner size arrows for and watch drive motion in real time, surfacing the 'balanced = stationary' and 'bigger force = faster' errors. A linked live resultant arrow and head-to-tail mode make the combination mechanism concrete. The model treats horizontal friction as negligible so the drawn arrows represent all horizontal forces; each prediction is tied to a stated initial motion.
sourceClaims: A zero resultant force corresponds to no change in motion — either stationary or constant velocity; an unbalanced resultant causes acceleration in its direction; the resultant points in the direction of the change of motion, not necessarily of motion.
Forces must be combined as vectors (head-to-tail or parallelogram); adding magnitudes as scalars is only valid when collinear, and the 'bisector' direction is a common error.
learnerActions: Set the crate moving steadily to the right. In this model horizontal friction is treated as negligible, so the only horizontal forces acting are the arrows you draw.
On the already-moving crate, place two equal and opposite horizontal force arrows and adjust their lengths so they are exactly balanced (zero resultant).
Predict what the already-moving crate will do BEFORE releasing: will it stop, slow down, or keep moving at the same speed? State your reasoning.
Observe the crate: with balanced forces (zero resultant) it keeps gliding to the right at a steady speed rather than stopping.

Now make the RIGHTWARD arrow longer than the leftward one, so the resultant points right — the same direction the crate is already moving — and watch it accelerate; keep that arrow stretched and notice its SPEED keeps climbing for as long as the unbalanced force acts along the motion.
View an overlay showing a single resultant arrow that REPLACES the separate arrows (not drawn in addition to them).

Switch to the non-collinear mode: this clears the previous motion and sets the crate at rest. Place two arrows at an angle, join them head-to-tail to build the resultant geometrically, then watch the crate accelerate from rest along that resultant direction.
activities.intendedInsight: A zero resultant means no change in motion — which includes continuing to move at a steady speed, not only being at rest. A sustained unbalanced resultant keeps changing the motion; when it points along the direction of travel the speed keeps climbing, showing that force governs CHANGE of motion rather than speed itself. The resultant is the single equivalent of the combined forces, and for non-collinear forces it is found by head-to-tail (vector) addition. This model assumes negligible horizontal friction, so the drawn arrows are the only horizontal forces.

activities.title: Combining forces and judging the direction of change
feedback: For 30 N right and 20 N left, the resultant is 10 N to the right — you subtract opposing magnitudes only because they lie on the same line.
For a car that is moving forwards and braking, the resultant points BACKWARDS (opposite the motion), because the motion is changing by slowing down.
If you placed the resultant along the direction of travel for a slowing object: the resultant follows the direction of CHANGE, not the direction of motion.
A zero resultant can still have several forces present — they simply cancel; it does not mean there are no forces.
activities.rationale: Retrieval through construction, direction-judgement, and categorisation rehearses the 'bigger force = faster' and 'balanced = stationary' distractors and the 'resultant along the motion' error. Recognition and multiple-choice items assess and rehearse but do not by themselves elicit the felt confrontation of balanced-yet-moving, so pair them with the hands-on model.
sourceClaims: Forces must be combined as vectors (head-to-tail or parallelogram); adding magnitudes as scalars is only valid when collinear, and the 'bisector' direction is a common error.
Common student errors include treating the net force as an additional force on the body and believing a larger force produces a greater speed rather than greater acceleration.

A zero resultant force corresponds to no change in motion — either stationary or constant velocity; an unbalanced resultant causes acceleration in its direction; the resultant points in the direction of the change of motion, not necessarily of motion.
learnerActions: Drag arrows head-to-tail (or along a number line for collinear cases) to construct the resultant, then draw or state its direction and size.
For collinear forces, calculate the resultant: e.g. 30 N right and 20 N left gives 10 N to the right.
Answer multiple-choice items on which way the resultant points for an object that is stated to be speeding up, slowing down, or turning, and justify the choice from the stated initial motion.
Categorise described situations as balanced (zero resultant, no change in motion) or unbalanced (non-zero resultant, motion changes).
Decide whether a zero resultant means there are no forces on the object, and explain.
activities.intendedInsight: Collinear forces combine by signed addition along the line; non-collinear forces need head-to-tail construction. The resultant points in the direction of the CHANGE in motion — which can be opposite to the current direction of travel when an object is slowing down. A zero resultant does not mean there are no forces; it means the forces balance.

activities.title: Tug-of-war predict–observe–explain
feedback: If you predicted 'lots of force, so it should move' or 'the stronger side's force is left over': equal and opposite pulls cancel to a zero resultant regardless of how hard each side pulls.
Skydiver at steady speed: weight down and air resistance up are equal, so the resultant is zero — yet she IS moving, at a constant speed. Zero resultant means no change, not stopped.
Braking car that is moving forwards: the resultant points backwards (opposite the forward motion) because the car is slowing down.
activities.rationale: A moving-but-steady case forces the split between 'moving' and 'changing motion', directly addressing the dominant 'zero resultant means stationary' misconception and the 'leftover force' idea. Predict-observe-explain with cognitive conflict is well suited to the constant-velocity case.
sourceClaims: A zero resultant force corresponds to no change in motion — either stationary or constant velocity; an unbalanced resultant causes acceleration in its direction; the resultant points in the direction of the change of motion, not necessarily of motion.
Common student errors include treating the net force as an additional force on the body and believing a larger force produces a greater speed rather than greater acceleration.
learnerActions: Set up two students to pull a rope tied to a central marker; they will both pull hard and adjust until the marker holds still.
Before the pulling starts, predict: if both students pull hard and the marker is held still, what is the resultant on the marker? Does a big pull on each side mean a big resultant? Say WHY.
Observe that the marker can be held still even under large pulls, then explain in terms of the resultant why, while it stays still, the two pulls must be equal and opposite.
Discuss the skydiver case: during a steady (terminal-velocity) fall, state the resultant and whether she is moving.
Discuss a braking car that is still moving forwards: state which way the resultant points and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Large equal and opposite pulls still give a zero resultant; the size of the individual forces does not add up to a 'big leftover'. A zero resultant means no change in motion, so a steadily falling skydiver has a zero resultant yet is still moving, and a forwards-moving braking car has a backward resultant while still moving forwards.

activities.title: Free-body diagram reference with the resultant as equivalent
feedback: If you drew weight, air resistance AND a separate resultant all acting at once: the resultant replaces the combined forces — show it on its own, not as an extra force.

A balanced free-body diagram (arrows cancel to a zero resultant) implies no change in motion; it does not by itself tell you whether the object is at rest or moving steadily — the skydiver at terminal velocity (weight balanced by air resistance) and a book sitting still (weight balanced by support from the table) both have zero-resultant diagrams, even though one is moving and the other is not.
activities.rationale: A static labelled diagram is a useful reference for naming forces and practising the resultant-as-equivalent idea. Because it is static it cannot itself show balanced forces producing steady motion, so it supports but does not replace the dynamic model; treat it as a reference scaffold.
sourceClaims: Common student errors include treating the net force as an additional force on the body and believing a larger force produces a greater speed rather than greater acceleration.
learnerActions: Reveal, one at a time, the labelled forces on a chosen object (e.g. a book resting on a table, or a skydiver).
Identify each force's direction and relative size from its arrow.
Reveal the resultant drawn separately as the single equivalent arrow, and confirm it is NOT added alongside the individual forces.
State what a static diagram does and does not tell you: it fixes the force balance, but a zero resultant alone does not reveal whether the object is at rest or moving steadily.
activities.intendedInsight: A free-body diagram shows all forces as arrows; the resultant is their single equivalent, drawn on its own rather than as an extra arrow among the originals. For a supported object such as a book on a table, the downward weight and the upward support from the table balance. A static snapshot shows the force balance but not, by itself, whether a zero-resultant object is stationary or moving at constant velocity.

constraints: Build vector addition collinear-first (combine along a single line, e.g. tug-of-war or number line) before head-to-tail addition for non-collinear forces.
Only add force magnitudes as plain numbers when the forces are collinear; otherwise use head-to-tail (or parallelogram) construction. The bisector of two arrows is NOT the resultant direction.

When describing speeding up, slowing down, or turning, always state the object's initial motion: the resultant sets the CHANGE in motion and may point opposite to the current direction of travel (e.g. a braking car still moving forwards). A resultant pointing along the existing motion makes the object speed up in a straight line (more generally, it speeds up whenever the resultant has a part along the motion); starting from rest it accelerates along the resultant, but an angled resultant on an already-moving object curves the path rather than instantly aligning travel with the force.
Tie 'zero resultant' explicitly to BOTH the stationary case and the constant-velocity case; never present zero resultant as meaning stopped.

In the dynamic crate model, state that horizontal friction is treated as negligible so the drawn arrows are the only horizontal forces; two balanced arrows then give a zero resultant and constant velocity. This is a stated model, not a universal requirement.

Recognition and multiple-choice items assess and rehearse but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a resultant or the felt balanced-yet-moving confrontation; pair them with hands-on construction and the dynamic model.

The static free-body diagram is a reference scaffold: being static it cannot display balanced forces producing steady motion, and a zero-resultant diagram alone does not distinguish rest from constant velocity.
3D vector work is deferred; at this stage the curriculum works in a plane and planar vectors carry resultants fully — treat 3D as later extension, not as adding conceptual content now.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the listed sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Sources in the original row are marked verified:false; evidence strength and effectiveness are not established here.

The source attributing the 'net force as an additional force' and 'bigger force = faster speed' errors is credited to Gunstone et al. / Education Victoria; original attribution retained but not re-checked.

Checked the collinear example: 30 N right minus 20 N left gives 10 N right — consistent and retained. The skydiver terminal-velocity case correctly implies a zero resultant while still moving — retained as stated.

The original crate recommendation did not state the crate's initial motion or friction model, and described the non-collinear crate as 'veering off precisely along' the resultant while already moving; these have been corrected to state the initial motion, declare a negligible-friction model, and start the non-collinear case explicitly from rest, since a resultant sets acceleration (not velocity) and only a from-rest object travels exactly along it.
The non-collinear mode is an explicit motion reset (crate placed at rest) so the from-rest claim does not silently contradict the earlier moving-right setup.

assess.poeTask: Have two students pull a rope tied to a central marker, adjusting until the marker holds still though both pull hard. Ask the class to predict the resultant on the marker, and whether a big pull on each side should mean a big resultant, and WHY, before revealing it isn't moving. Predicting 'lots of force, so it should move' or 'the stronger side's force is left over' reveals the balanced=stationary and leftover-force ideas; a standstill under large equal pulls makes a zero resultant concrete.
probeDeeper: Earlier in her fall she was speeding up. What was the resultant force then, and which way did it point?
A car brakes to a stop while still moving forwards. Which way does the resultant force point — forwards or backwards? Why?
Two people push a box: 30 N right and 20 N left. What's the resultant, and what does the box do?
If the resultant is zero, does that mean there are no forces on the object?
assess.correctAnswer: The resultant force is zero — weight down and air resistance up are equal and opposite, so they balance. She IS moving (falling fast), but at a steady speed: a zero resultant means no CHANGE in motion, which can be either stationary or constant velocity. A zero resultant does not mean stopped.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'She's moving, so the resultant can't be zero — something must be winning.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A zero resultant means no CHANGE in motion — constant velocity counts; revisit steady-motion cases repeatedly.
errorPatterns.distractor: The resultant can't be zero — she's still falling, so weight must be winning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses a zero resultant for a moving object.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A bigger resultant force means a faster speed.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The resultant sets the CHANGE in motion (acceleration/direction of change), not the speed; a fast object can have a zero resultant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads a large resultant as 'going fast' rather than 'changing motion quickly'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The resultant is an EXTRA arrow you add on top of the other forces.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The resultant REPLACES the individual forces — it's their single combined effect, drawn on its own, not added to them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws weight, air resistance AND a separate resultant all acting at once.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The resultant force always points the way the object is moving.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The resultant points in the direction of the CHANGE in motion — e.g. backwards when the object is slowing down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a decelerating or turning object, draws the resultant along the motion.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks a zero resultant means stationary, or reads a bigger resultant as a bigger speed; draws the resultant as an extra arrow among the others.
responseLevels.full: Treats force as a vector, combines collinear forces into a single resultant that REPLACES them, and links a zero resultant to no change (rest or constant velocity) and a non-zero resultant to a change in the direction it points — transferring to skydiver, braking and tug scenarios.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates resultants of collinear forces and states 'balanced = no change', but can't apply it to a moving-but-steady case, or muddles the resultant's DIRECTION (points it along the motion) — rules stated, not connected to motion.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A skydiver falls and, for a while, falls at a STEADY speed (terminal velocity) — not speeding up. Two forces act on her: her weight downwards and air resistance upwards. What is the resultant force on her during this steady fall — and is she moving?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The recurring error is 'zero resultant means stationary'. A moving-but-steady case forces the split: a student who understands says the resultant is zero AND she is still moving (no change), whereas a student with the misconception either denies the resultant can be zero (because she's moving) or insists she must be stopped. It also exposes 'motion needs a net force'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Add and subtract a two-digit number and ones (36 + 7, 52 − 4), mentally and with concrete/pictorial support, bridging through a multiple of ten. Ages 6–7.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'add and subtract numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally, including: a two-digit number and ones'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.4 add within 100 including a two-digit and a one-digit number, using place value and the relationship between addition and subtraction; extended by 2.NBT.5.
• Operational details: the key skill is bridging the tens boundary — partition the ones to reach the next (or previous) decade, then add/subtract the rest (36 + 7 → 36 + 4 = 40, + 3 = 43; 52 − 4 → 52 − 2 = 50, − 2 = 48). Ground in base-ten blocks and the number line so the new ten is seen forming. Contrast with cases that don't cross a ten (43 + 5) so children bridge only when needed.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds ones without crossing a ten (43 + 5) and with blocks when crossing. Tier B (age 7) — bridges 36 + 7 and 52 − 4 mentally via the decade. Tier C (age 7+) — explains why the tens digit changes and chooses to bridge only when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
bestPractices: Teach bridging explicitly: partition the ones to land on the decade, then add/subtract the remainder.
Use base-ten blocks so ten ones visibly regroup into a new ten (and vice versa when subtracting).
Use the empty number line to show the two-part jump to and past the decade.
Mix bridging and non-bridging items so children decide when a boundary is crossed.
Connect the mental bridging steps to later column methods (regrouping).
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (ones regrouping into a ten)
Empty number line with a jump to the decade then on
Ten-frames / partially filled frames showing the ones
Hundred square (move along a row, drop to next row at the boundary)
Part-whole splitting the ones (7 as 4 + 3)
commonMisconceptions: Adding the ones digits and ignoring the new ten (36 + 7 → 33 or '313').
Counting on/back in ones and slipping by one at the tens boundary.
Failing to change the tens digit when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
Bridging when it isn't needed, or not bridging when it is.
For subtraction, stopping at the decade (52 − 4 → 50) or miscounting past it.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 add and subtract a two-digit number and ones by bridging through a multiple of ten: partition the ones to land on the decade, then add or subtract the remainder (36 + 7 → 36 + 4 = 40, + 3 = 43; 52 − 4 → 52 − 2 = 50, − 2 = 48). Core activities use a manipulable number line and base-ten blocks — with ten-frames and a hundred square as alternative views — so the new ten is seen forming and the tens digit updates for a visible reason, with mixed bridging and non-bridging items (43 + 5) so children decide when a boundary is actually crossed. Fluency practice, a static anchor image, and a narrate-your-method conversation are retained as complementary approaches with distinct purposes.

activities.title: Bridge the decade on a number line with a base-ten mat
feedback: If the answer keeps the original tens digit (e.g. 36 + 7 → 33 or '313'), show the ten ones regrouping into one new ten on the mat and re-run the jump through 40 so the tens digit visibly changes.
If the answer is one off (e.g. 42 or 44), point out counting single steps across the boundary; partition the ones to land exactly on 40 first, then add the rest.
For subtraction, if the child stops at 50 or lands on 49/47, model bridging back to 50 first, then taking the remaining 2 to reach 48.
For a non-bridging item like 43 + 5, confirm that the ones do not cross a decade so no bridge is needed, reinforcing when bridging applies.
activities.rationale: Bridging is a two-part jump, and a manipulable number line plus a regrouping mat lets the child reach the decade and then complete the jump while seeing ten ones become a new ten; ten-frames and a hundred square offer the same structure in other concrete/pictorial forms. Live feedback can catch the count-in-ones slip and the ignore-the-new-ten error as they occur. Non-bridging items prevent over-applying the strategy.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils add and subtract a two-digit number and ones using concrete, pictorial and mental methods.
1.NBT.4 covers adding within 100 including a two-digit and a one-digit number using place value, with regrouping of ten ones into a ten.
Bridging through ten by partitioning is a core mental strategy; digit-separation errors (ignoring the regrouped ten) are common.
learnerActions: Work 36 + 7 by first jumping from 36 to the next decade (40), then completing the jump with the remaining ones (to 43).
On a base-ten mat, watch four loose ones combine with the existing ones to make a whole new ten-stick as the jump reaches 40, so the tens digit change has a visible cause.
Switch to subtraction mode for 52 − 4: jump back to the decade first (52 − 2 = 50), then take the remaining 2 to reach 48.
Mix in non-bridging items such as 43 + 5 and decide for each item whether the ones cross a decade before choosing to bridge.

Optionally view the same bridging in another representation: a ten-frame filling up to a complete ten of ones, or a hundred square where you move along a row and drop to the next row as you cross the decade, so the new ten is seen forming in more than one way.
State out loud which decade you bridge through and why the tens digit does or does not change.
activities.intendedInsight: When adding makes the ones fill up to a whole ten, a new ten is formed and the tens digit increases by one; when subtracting takes away more ones than there are, a ten is broken into ones and the tens digit decreases by one (52 − 4 = 48). Partitioning the ones to reach the decade makes this regrouping explicit for both addition and subtraction.

activities.title: Fluency practice: fill in, draw the jump, choose the decade
feedback: If a learner picks the results distractor that ignores the regrouped ten (e.g. 33 for 36 + 7), return to a regrouping representation to show why the tens digit must change and re-run the jump through 40.
If the drawn jump skips the decade stop, prompt the learner to mark the decade first, then the remainder.
Confirm correct recognition when a non-bridging item is answered without an unnecessary bridge.
activities.rationale: A fixed practice sequence consolidates the method and surfaces the characteristic errors through targeted distractors, but it cannot provide the live regrouping feedback of the manipulative, so it is best used after the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: Bridging through ten by partitioning is a core mental strategy; digit-separation errors (ignoring the regrouped ten) are common.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in results such as 36 + 7 = ___ mentally or with a jotting.
Draw the two-part bridging jump on an empty number line to show reaching the decade and then continuing.
Choose which decade you bridge through for a given calculation, with decade options as the choices (for 36 + 7 the decade is 40).
In a separate results question, identify the correct total, where a distractor such as 33 for 36 + 7 reflects the ignore-the-new-ten error (keeping the original tens digit).
Include at least one non-bridging item so you practise recognising when no bridge is needed.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the bridging strategy is understood, spaced and varied practice builds fluency in partitioning the ones and updating the tens digit accurately.

activities.title: Anchor image: a worked bridging number line
feedback: If the learner cannot say why the jump pauses at 40, highlight that the first jump completes a ten and point to the labelled new ten.
Prompt the learner to connect the picture back to doing their own jump on the manipulative.
activities.rationale: A static worked number line anchors the appearance of bridging and labels the regrouped ten. It supports understanding of the structure, though the count itself still needs to be rehearsed in a doing activity; treat this as a reference rather than practice of the procedure.
learnerActions: Study a number line showing 36 → 40 → 43 with the regrouped ten labelled, revealing each step in turn.
Describe in your own words why the jump stops at 40 before continuing to 43.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear worked picture shows what a bridging jump looks like and names the new ten, giving a reference model for the two-part method.

activities.title: Narrate your method: how did you get across the ten?
feedback: If the explanation describes counting single steps, guide the child to describe partitioning the ones to reach the decade first.
If the child cannot justify why the tens digit changes, revisit the regrouping of ten ones into a new ten.
Confirm reasoning when the child correctly identifies that a non-bridging item needs no bridge.
activities.rationale: A talk-through surfaces the child's method and misconceptions, complementing the hands-on and practice activities; it is a way to assess and reinforce the procedure being practised, though recognition in talk does not by itself guarantee independent production.
learnerActions: Work a bridging item and a non-bridging item, then explain aloud how you got across the ten (or why you did not need to).
Answer questions such as 'Why does the tens digit change here?' and 'For 43 + 5, did you need to cross a ten? How do you know?'
Show 52 − 4 on the number line and say where you stopped on the way.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the decade step and the reason the tens digit changes reveals whether the child is partitioning to bridge or merely counting in ones.

constraints: Ground the strategy in base-ten blocks and the number line (with ten-frames or a hundred square as alternative representations) so the new ten is seen forming (and un-forming when subtracting) before expecting mental calculation.
Always mix bridging and non-bridging items (e.g. 43 + 5) so children learn to bridge only when the ones cross a decade and do not over-apply the strategy.
A fixed practice sequence consolidates fluency but does not provide live regrouping feedback; use it after hands-on manipulative work.
A static worked image anchors what bridging looks like but does not rehearse the count; it is a reference, not a substitute for doing the procedure.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 6) adds ones without crossing a ten and with blocks when crossing; Tier B (age 7) bridges 36 + 7 and 52 − 4 mentally via the decade; Tier C (age 7+) explains why the tens digit changes and chooses to bridge only when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
Connect the mental bridging steps to later column methods (regrouping) as children progress.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source labels CCSS 1.NBT.4 and the NCETM claims as unverified; do not treat the standards-alignment or misconception-frequency claims as independently confirmed.

The legacy source asserted '3D adds nothing' for this 1-D number-line skill; this comparative/necessity claim is not established by the evidence and has been omitted rather than propagated. A 3D representation is simply not the focus here, not proven worthless.

The legacy source implied a static image 'can't rehearse' the count and that a quiz 'can't give live feedback'; these have been softened to stated-affordance limits (reference vs. practice; delayed vs. live feedback) rather than universal laws.
The ten-frame and hundred-square representations, and the part-whole partitioning of the ones, from the original keyRepresentations are retained within the core activity.

Fixed the fluency activity so the 'which decade?' choice offers decade options while the ignore-the-new-ten distractor (33) belongs to a separate results item; the original design notes had conflated these into one incoherent question.

probeDeeper: How did you get across the ten in 36 + 7?
Why does the tens digit change here?
For 43 + 5, did you need to cross a ten? How do you know?
Show me 52 − 4 on the number line — where did you stop on the way?
assess.correctAnswer: 43; 48; 48. Watch for bridging through the decade on the first two (36 + 4 = 40, + 3 = 43; 52 − 2 = 50, − 2 = 48) and a straightforward ones-addition on the third, which does not cross a ten.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the ones and ignores the new ten — 36 + 7 becomes 33 (keeps the 3 tens) or '313'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Base-ten blocks: ten ones regroup into a new ten; bridge via 40 and watch the tens digit change.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer keeps the original tens digit; ones handled as if isolated.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts on/back in ones and slips by one crossing the tens boundary (36 + 7 → 42 or 44).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Partition the ones to land on the decade first, then add the rest; track on the number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is one off; observed counting single steps through the decade.

errorPatterns.pattern: For subtraction, stops at the decade or miscounts past it (52 − 4 → 50 or 49/47).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bridge back to 50 first (− 2), then take the remaining 2; model on the number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 50, 49 or 47.

responseLevels.gap: Adds/subtracts the digits with no regard to place, or cannot get across the tens boundary.
responseLevels.full: Bridges through the decade by partitioning the ones, updates the tens digit correctly, and recognises when no bridge is needed.
responseLevels.partial: Reaches answers by counting in ones across the boundary — slow and error-prone — without partitioning to bridge.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out — mentally or on the number line — and talk me through each: 36 + 7; 52 − 4; 43 + 5.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two items cross a tens boundary and one does not. A child with place-value bridging partitions the ones to hit the decade and updates the tens digit; a child treating the digits separately gives the tell-tale 33 for 36 + 7, and a count-in-ones child slips by one at the boundary. The non-bridging item checks they don't over-apply bridging.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Naming types of energy

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England)):** HONEST NOTE: there is NO general 'energy' topic anywhere in KS1 or KS2 — energy as a strand first appears at KS3. Primary physics is organised as Light, Sound, Forces, Electricity (Y4/Y6), etc. So this 7–9 'name the types of energy' topic has NO direct UK primary anchor; the nearest UK contact is incidental (e.g. Y2 'seeds and bulbs have a store of food inside them'). The vocabulary becomes statutory only at KS3 ('energy changes and transfers'). (Verified by fetch of gov.uk KS1–KS3 science programmes of study.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS, grade 4, PS3 'Energy'):** NGSS itself deliberately AVOIDS cataloguing 'forms of energy', but its grade-4 DCI PS3.A (Definitions of Energy) states '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]' and '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]', and 4-PS3-1 relates an object's energy to its speed. So the closest national anchor is the grade-4 PS3.A definitions and 4-PS3-1/-2 (qualitative; assessment boundary excludes quantitative energy), NOT a formal 'list the forms of energy' expectation. (Verified by fetch of nextgenscience.org 4-PS3-2 and the MS.Energy DCIs.)

- **Operational details:** Energy here is a NAMING / vocabulary topic (LANGUAGE type): the child attaches everyday energy words to concrete, observable examples they can point to. Keep it phenomenon-anchored — NO joules, NO quantification, NOT the formal stores-and-pathways model (that is Tier B, mt_Jvg_r4yWaY). The one forward-looking move that matters at this age is planting 'STORED vs being TRANSFERRED', which the topic's own evidence asks for and which the later KS3 model depends on.

The child learns to name kinetic (movement), potential/elastic (stretched/raised), thermal (hot), light, sound, electrical and chemical energy, and to describe simple energy changes in familiar devices (a torch, a toaster, a wind-up toy). The single most important pedagogical decision is how to handle 'types of energy' and 'energy transformation' language: modern physics teaching (IOP/SPT) has deliberately MOVED AWAY from cataloguing 'forms of energy' and from 'transformation', because it later treats light, sound and electric current as PATHWAYS (energy on the move) rather than stores, and because 'forms/transformation' language seeds the misconception that energy is a substance that changes into different stuff. At 7–9 the everyday words are still the accessible on-ramp and should be taught — but framed so they do not have to be un-taught later: anchor each word to a concrete example, and sort words into 'STORED / waiting' (chemical in a battery or food, elastic in a spring, movement in a ball) versus 'ON THE MOVE / being transferred' (light, sound, heat, electric current). Introduce 'energy is transferred / moves from here to there' rather than entrenching 'changes form'.

Best taught through tap-and-name work on rich familiar scenes, with examples AND non-examples to fence each word, plenty of talk (not worksheets), and repeated exposure across many devices.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete / observational, ≈7–9).
bestPractices: Anchor every energy word to a concrete, observable example the child can point to (moving ball = movement/kinetic; battery or food = chemical store; torch = light; drum = sound; hot drink = thermal; stretched spring = elastic) — vocabulary from phenomena, not dictionary definitions.

From the very start, sort the words into 'STORED / waiting' versus 'ON THE MOVE / being transferred' — this delivers the topic's own 'distinguish stored from transferred' evidence and is forward-compatible with the KS3 stores-and-pathways model.
Use examples AND non-examples to fence each word (a still ball has no movement energy; a switched-off torch gives no light), the way effective vocabulary instruction (Frayer) does.
Say 'energy is transferred / moves from here to there' rather than entrenching 'changes form / transformation' — don't build the substance-changing idea that later teaching has to undo (IOP).
Give multiple exposures across many familiar devices (torch, toaster, wind-up toy, remote) and teach through talk and description, not worksheets.
Explicitly include STORED energy in things at rest (a battery, a stretched spring, raised object) so children don't conclude only moving or living things 'have energy'.
keyRepresentations: A rich familiar scene (kitchen/playground) with taggable energy sources — ball, battery, torch, drum, hot drink, stretched spring
A two-column sort: 'STORED / waiting' vs 'ON THE MOVE / being transferred'
Frayer-lite word cards (drawing-based for young): word + meaning + example + non-example
A start→end snapshot of one device (wind-up toy: energy stored in the spring → movement of the toy)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking only living or moving things 'have energy', so a still spring, raised object or battery at rest has none — missing stored energy.
Treating light, sound and electric current as the same kind of 'stuff' as chemical or movement energy, rather than as energy on the move — the seed of the later store-vs-pathway error.
Reading 'energy transformation' as energy literally changing into a different substance.
Confusing energy with the object or fuel itself, or with force, 'power', or temperature (loose everyday usage).
Believing energy gets 'used up' and disappears (planted early by 'the battery ran out') — it is the fuel/battery that is used up, the energy is transferred elsewhere.

learn.summary: Help 7–9 year-olds name everyday types of energy — kinetic (movement), elastic (stretched or wound), gravitational/potential (raised), thermal (hot), light, sound, electrical and chemical — by anchoring each word to a concrete, observable example they can point to. The single most important move is to sort these words into 'STORED / waiting (or doing)' (chemical in a battery or food, elastic in a stretched or wound spring, gravitational energy in a raised object, thermal energy in a hot drink, movement/kinetic in a moving ball) versus 'ON THE MOVE / being transferred' (light, sound, heat flowing from hotter to cooler things, electric current), and to describe simple devices with 'energy is transferred / moves from here to there' rather than 'changes form'. This plants the stores-and-transfer distinction that later schooling builds on, without joules or quantification. Note: in England's national curriculum this age band has no formal primary energy topic (energy appears at KS3; other UK curricula such as Scotland's differ) and NGSS grade 4 gives qualitative definitions only, so this is vocabulary anchored to phenomena, not a formal 'list the forms of energy' expectation.

activities.title: Tap-and-name a busy familiar scene
feedback: If a child names an object or a force where an energy type belongs ('the battery is energy', 'the push is the energy'), separate them: the battery is the object, chemical is the energy it stores (just as a spring is an object and elastic is the energy it stores); the push is a force, not a type of energy.
If a child says only moving or living things have energy, point to the battery at rest and the stretched spring: these store energy while completely still.
Confirm a correct tag by restating it with its store/on-the-move label so the discriminator is reinforced.
activities.rationale: This is a vocabulary/naming topic, so word knowledge tied to concrete phenomena (term → meaning → example → non-example, in the spirit of Frayer vocabulary instruction) suits it. Anchoring words to observable examples rather than dictionary definitions keeps it phenomenon-based and age-appropriate. No source in the row directly addresses this vocabulary-instruction method, so no source claim is attached.
learnerActions: Look at a rich familiar scene (kitchen or playground) containing taggable energy sources: a ball flying, a battery in a remote, a torch shining, a drum sounding, a steaming kettle or hot drink, a stretched spring, a wind-up toy.

Point to each object and say its energy word, a one-line kid-friendly meaning, and a matching everyday example (moving ball = movement/kinetic; battery or food = chemical store; torch = light; drum = sound; hot drink or kettle = thermal; stretched spring = elastic; ball on a high shelf = raised/gravitational store).

For each object answer 'is this energy waiting, or on the move?' and then say the fuller sentence, e.g. 'The battery STORES chemical energy; when the torch is on, that energy is on the MOVE as light.'
Use the non-examples too: a still ball has no movement energy; a switched-off torch gives no light.
activities.intendedInsight: Each everyday energy word names something you can point to in a real scene, and a hidden meaning + example + non-example fences exactly what each word does and does not cover.

activities.title: Sort the scene: STORED / waiting vs ON THE MOVE
feedback: If a child treats light, sound or electric current as the same kind of 'stuff' as chemical or movement energy, re-sort it into 'on the move' and say 'this is energy travelling, not stored'.
If a child says 'energy changes into' different stuff, re-voice it as 'the energy is transferred / moves from here to there' so the substance-changing idea is not built in.
Praise a correct column placement by naming why: 'Yes — a stretched spring holds energy even when nothing is moving, so it is stored.'
activities.rationale: Delivering the 'distinguish stored from transferred' objective from the start is forward-compatible with the later stores-and-pathways model, and avoiding 'forms/transformation' language avoids seeding the misconception that energy is a substance that changes into different stuff.
sourceClaims: Modern physics teaching (IOP/SPT) deliberately moves away from 'forms of energy' and 'energy transformation' language, treating light, sound and electric current as PATHWAYS by which energy is transferred rather than stores/forms; 'forms/transformation' framing can seed the idea that energy is a substance that changes into different stuff.
learnerActions: Take every energy word from the scene and place it in one of two columns: 'STORED / waiting (or doing)' or 'ON THE MOVE / being transferred'.

Put chemical (battery, food), elastic (stretched or wound spring), a raised object (ball on a high shelf) and the thermal energy of a hot drink into STORED because the energy waits there even when nothing moves; put the moving ball's movement/kinetic energy there too, as energy an object has while it is doing something; put light, sound, heat flowing out from a hot thing to cooler surroundings, and electric current into ON THE MOVE.

After sorting the whole scene, say what pattern you notice — light, sound, heat flowing out of hot things and electric current tend to land in 'on the move', while chemical, elastic, gravitational, thermal (in a hot thing) and movement sit in 'stored or doing'.
Say two sentences for one device: a labelling sentence ('A moving ball has ___ energy') and a transfer sentence ('The battery stores chemical energy and transfers it to the torch as light').
activities.intendedInsight: Some energy is stored and waiting in things that can be completely still (including the thermal energy of a hot drink), movement is energy an object has while it is doing something, and light, sound, heat flowing from hotter to cooler things and electric current are energy on the move being transferred from one place to another — energy 'moves from here to there' rather than turning into a different substance.

activities.title: Watch the energy move through a device
feedback: If a child says the energy is 'used up' or 'gone' when the toy stops, ask 'where did it GO?' and explain that it spreads out as heat (and a little sound) into the floor, gears and air — usually too little warming to feel. The spring unwinds and transfers its stored energy to the toy's movement, and in a battery-powered toy it is the battery's chemical store that runs down; in neither case does the energy itself vanish, it is transferred elsewhere.
If a child uses 'energy' with no type, model the frame '___ energy is stored in ___ and is transferred so that ___ now has ___ energy' and ask them to name the type at each stage.
Confirm a correct narration by restating the transfer chain: elastic stored → kinetic → heat and sound to the surroundings.
activities.rationale: Several target words are dynamic and relational, so seeing a battery's stored energy travel to a bulb, or a spring's energy launch a toy, makes 'transferred' and 'on the move' observable rather than merely defined. Devices should be qualitative at this age because quantitative energy is outside the grade-4 expectation.
sourceClaims: NGSS grade-4 DCI PS3.A: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; energy is present in moving objects, sound, light, heat; 4-PS3-1 relates energy to an object's speed; assessment boundary excludes quantitative measurements of energy. NGSS does not require cataloguing 'forms of energy'.

Modern physics teaching (IOP/SPT) deliberately moves away from 'forms of energy' and 'energy transformation' language, treating light, sound and electric current as PATHWAYS by which energy is transferred rather than stores/forms; 'forms/transformation' framing can seed the idea that energy is a substance that changes into different stuff.
learnerActions: Watch or act out one device from start to end: wind up a toy and release it, or switch on a torch, keeping attention on where the energy starts and where it goes.

For the wind-up toy: say that winding stores elastic energy in the spring; releasing transfers that stored energy to the toy so it now has movement (kinetic) energy; all the while, rubbing in the gears and between the wheels and floor, and pushing through the air, transfers energy away to the surroundings as heat (and a little sound); once the spring has unwound, nothing keeps refilling the movement energy, so the toy slows and stops.
For the torch: say the battery stores chemical energy; when switched on, that energy is on the move along the wire and leaves the torch mostly as light, with some as heat (the bulb gets warm).
Mark out loud the 'store' and the 'on the move' moment for each device, keeping it qualitative with no numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Dynamic words like 'transfer' and 'kinetic' name something you can watch happen: stored energy being transferred so an object starts moving, and energy travelling out of a device, so the words describe a process not just a label.

activities.title: Retrieval practice: match, sort and complete sentences
feedback: Picture-led with minimal reading for 7–8 year-olds; if a match is wrong, return to the concrete example and the store/on-the-move label rather than giving the answer outright.
If a child labels a static object correctly but cannot say the IN and OUT energy of a device, step back to the watch-it-move activity to rebuild the transfer idea.
activities.rationale: Brief retrieval practice such as matching, categorising and sentence completion strengthens and checks recall of the vocabulary; it works best after the words have first been introduced and anchored in the scene and device work, and recognising a word is not the same as independently producing it in a narrative, so a spoken explain-back is also needed for production.
learnerActions: Match each energy word to a picture of its everyday example.
Sort a fresh set of words into 'stored' versus 'being transferred'.
Complete sentences about familiar devices, e.g. 'A moving ball has ___ energy' and 'The battery stores ___ energy, and the torch gives out ___.'
For a torch and a toaster, name the energy that goes IN and the useful energy that comes OUT of each.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall of which word fits which example, and which column each word belongs to, consolidates the vocabulary after it has been built.

activities.title: Explain it back to an 'energy detective'
feedback: Keep turns very short and spoken for this age; if reading or typing becomes the barrier, do it as talk rather than written work.
If the child names a type correctly, name it back and extend with 'and where does that energy go next?' to practise the transfer chain.
activities.rationale: Light explain-it-back practice supports a vocabulary topic by prompting the child to produce the words in context; at 7–9 it should be audio-led because reading and typing can limit written versions, and it works as enrichment alongside, not instead of, the naming work.
learnerActions: Answer short spoken prompts about a scene or device, e.g. 'Point to where the energy is stored here', 'Is the torch's light stored or on the move?', 'Where was the car's energy a moment BEFORE you let it go?'
For a ball sitting still on a high shelf, say whether it has any energy stored, what type, and how you could release it.
Explain, in your own words, the energy story of a device, with the listener naming your idea back to you.
activities.intendedInsight: Saying where energy is stored and where it goes, out loud and in your own words, strengthens and checks the vocabulary beyond simply recognising it.

constraints: Keep it qualitative: no joules, no numbers, no quantification of energy — this is naming vocabulary anchored to phenomena, not the formal measurement model.

In England's national curriculum this age band has no formal primary 'energy' topic (energy as a strand first appears at KS3; other UK curricula such as Scotland's differ) and NGSS grade 4 provides qualitative definitions only, not a 'list the forms of energy' expectation; treat the vocabulary as an accessible on-ramp, not a required curriculum list.
Prefer talk, description and repeated exposure across many familiar devices (torch, toaster, wind-up toy, remote) over worksheets.

Frame everything as 'energy is transferred / moves from here to there', not 'changes form / transformation' or 'becomes a different energy', so the substance-changing idea does not have to be un-taught later.
Always include stored energy in things at rest (battery, stretched spring, raised object) so children do not conclude that only moving or living things have energy.

Movement/kinetic energy belongs with the stores as 'stored or doing' (energy an object has while it moves); a raised object has gravitational stored energy and a wound spring has elastic stored energy — keep these three examples distinct.

Matching/sorting/sentence-completion strengthen and check recall but do not by themselves elicit the child independently narrating a transfer; use the spoken explain-back or device narration for that.

A fixed scene can label each energy word well but cannot show movement happening; pair it with a device that can be acted out or animated so dynamic words (transfer, kinetic) are also seen in motion. Neither is universally required — they offer different experiences.
The everyday 'forms' words are taught here as the accessible on-ramp; the later stores-and-pathways model is a separate, more advanced treatment and is out of scope at this age.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source material at times pairs 'transfer' and 'transform' as acceptable (e.g. the assessment correct answer and one error-pattern move accept 'transform'), while the pedagogy and the IOP source explicitly advise avoiding 'transformation'/'becomes' to prevent the substance-changing misconception. This rewrite resolves the tension toward 'transfer / moves from here to there' in all learner-facing actions and feedback, including the device sentence frames; reviewers should confirm this is the intended stance.

The 'STORED vs ON THE MOVE' sort is pedagogically useful but is a simplification: thermal/heat is placed as 'on the move' (heating/radiating) although a hot drink also holds a thermal store, and kinetic/movement is placed with the stores as 'stored or doing'; whether a given example is best called a store or a transfer can be context-dependent, and the two-column framing is a scaffold for the later model, not a complete account. The child-facing 'tend to land in' pattern is a scaffold observation, not a universal law.

The original pedagogy's STORED-column example list ('movement in a ball') blurs kinetic with the truly-waiting stores; this rewrite keeps movement in the left column but labels it 'stored or doing' and keeps the moving ball, raised object and wound spring as distinct examples. Reviewers may wish to decide whether kinetic should sit in its own middle category.

Activity 1's sourceClaims were set to [] because no source in the row directly supports the vocabulary-instruction (Frayer/phenomenon-anchoring) principle it rests on; the standards claims support context, not that teaching method.

The claim that this topic has no direct UK primary anchor and that NGSS avoids cataloguing forms is drawn from the row's standards notes; the underlying standards pages were not re-verified in this rewrite.

probeDeeper: You said it has kinetic energy when it races. Where was that energy a moment BEFORE, when the car was wound up but not yet let go?
When it stops you said the energy is gone. If I touch the floor where the wheels rubbed, might I feel anything — and what would that tell you about where the energy went?
Compare a torch and a toaster: name the energy that goes IN and the useful energy that comes OUT of each.
A ball sitting still on a high shelf — does it have any energy stored? What type, and how could you release it?
assess.correctAnswer: Winding the key stores elastic (potential) energy in the spring. When released, that stored energy is transferred and becomes kinetic energy — the energy of motion — as the car races. As the car rubs on the floor the energy is transferred away as heat (and a little sound) to the surroundings, so it slows and stops. The story uses 'stored' and 'transfer/transform' and names elastic → kinetic → heat/sound correctly.

errorPatterns.pattern: Says the energy is 'used up' or 'disappears' when the car stops ('the energy runs out and is gone').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'where did it GO?' and introduce that it spreads out as heat to the floor and air — energy moves, it doesn't vanish (foreshadows conservation).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the slowing as energy vanishing rather than being transferred to heat in the floor and air.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'energy' as one all-purpose word without naming a type, or talks about it like a fuel/substance ('it's got energy in it').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the sentence frame '___ energy is stored in ___ and is transferred to ___ energy'; insist on naming the type at each step of the story.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot say WHICH type of energy at each stage; treats energy as a single fluid.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the energy TYPE with the object or the force ('the push is the energy', 'the battery is energy').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort cards separating the object (spring) from the energy it stores (elastic), and the 'push/force' from the 'energy'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names an object or a force where an energy type belongs.

responseLevels.gap: Uses 'energy' as one undifferentiated word, or says it is 'used up'/gone; cannot attach a type to a stage of the story.
responseLevels.full: Narrates the sequence — elastic/chemical stored → kinetic → heat/sound dissipated to the surroundings — using 'stored' and 'transfer/transform' correctly, and transfers the pattern to a new device such as a torch or toaster.
responseLevels.partial: Names some energy types correctly in isolation (battery = chemical, moving car = kinetic) but cannot narrate the TRANSFER through the story, or says the energy disappears at the end.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a wind-up toy car: you turn the key, let go, and it races across the floor, then slows and stops. Tell me the story of the toy using energy words — where the energy is stored to begin with, what type it becomes when the car races, and what happens to it as the car slows down.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has only memorised a word list can label a static object ('a battery has chemical energy') but in a running narrative misuses the terms — calling motion just 'energy' with no type, or saying the energy 'runs out and disappears'. Correct use threads stored → kinetic → dissipated through the story.

sources.claim: Modern physics teaching (IOP/SPT) deliberately moves away from 'forms of energy' and 'energy transformation' language, treating light, sound and electric current as PATHWAYS by which energy is transferred rather than stores/forms; 'forms/transformation' framing can seed the idea that energy is a substance that changes into different stuff.
sources.source: Institute of Physics, Spark / SPT — 'What's wrong with forms of energy?' and 'pathways and stores'

sources.claim: There is no general 'energy' topic at KS1 or KS2 in England (primary physics is Light, Sound, Forces, Electricity at Y4/Y6); energy as a strand first appears at KS3.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study (gov.uk)

sources.claim: NGSS grade-4 DCI PS3.A: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; energy is present in moving objects, sound, light, heat; 4-PS3-1 relates energy to an object's speed; assessment boundary excludes quantitative measurements of energy. NGSS does not require cataloguing 'forms of energy'.
