pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Predicting Motion Patterns

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS2 Working Scientifically):** Recording data and findings in tables and graphs, taking repeat readings, identifying patterns and relationships, and using results to make predictions to set up further tests — set within Year 5 forces (gravity, air/water resistance, friction).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-PS2-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-2] (Science & Engineering Practices: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Crosscutting Concept: Patterns).

- **Operational details:** This is a procedural 'working scientifically' skill at the heart of primary science: pattern-seeking. Children make repeated measurements of an object's motion under varied conditions (e.g. distance a toy car rolls from different ramp heights), look for a relationship in the data ('the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls'), and then use that pattern to PREDICT motion in a new, untested case — and test the prediction. The defining feature, distinguishing pattern-seeking from a fair test, is that the focus is on identifying a relationship across many readings (and often some variables can't be fully controlled). Prediction is integral: children use their own collected data to justify how things might behave in a related situation or to generalise, then turn that into a new 'big question'. Good practice grounds this in hands-on apparatus, organised recording (tables → graphs), repeat readings, and the explicit 'what do you notice?' move that surfaces the trend.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). At 8–9 this sits in the concrete-operational band: children reason from apparatus they can handle and readings they take themselves, and the developmental milestone is moving from a single observation to a generalisable trend ('the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls') and using that trend to predict an untested case. The threshold to watch is treating a prediction as an evidence-based inference rather than a guess, and accepting that pattern-seeking — where some variables cannot be fully controlled — is still real science alongside the fair test.
bestPractices: Frame the enquiry with a 'big question' ('does a steeper ramp make the car roll further?') and let children handle real apparatus — ramps, toy cars, metre rules, stopwatches.

Record measurements systematically in a table, then plot them (bar/line/scatter as appropriate) so the pattern becomes visible; take repeat readings for reliability (upper-KS2 working scientifically).
Use the 'what do you notice?' prompt to elicit the relationship from the data, rather than stating it for the children (Science-Sparks; Ogden Trust).
Make prediction explicit and evidence-based: use the established pattern to predict an UNTESTED condition, then run it and compare — 'predict, then test' (Ogden Trust).

Name the enquiry type honestly as pattern-seeking and don't default everything to a fair test; pattern-seeking often serves as a preliminary enquiry that generates predictions and new questions (PSTT; Ogden Trust).
Build measurement progression — accurate lengths (to the nearest mm/cm), times in seconds — and discuss variables that cannot be controlled and how they might affect the data.
keyRepresentations: Ramp-and-car apparatus (height/gradient as the changed condition; distance rolled as the measure)
Data table pairing the condition with the measured motion (e.g. ramp height vs distance)
Line/scatter graph revealing the trend across readings
The 'big question' framing the enquiry
A prediction marker on the graph/number line for an untested condition, later checked against the actual reading
commonMisconceptions: Thinking one reading is enough — not repeating measurements, so noise is mistaken for pattern.
Believing only 'fair tests' produce trustworthy science, so pattern-seeking feels 'not real science' (AKSIS: fair tests dominate >50% of practical work).
Treating a prediction as a guess rather than an inference justified by the collected data/pattern.
Expecting an exact value rather than a trend-based prediction ('about this far / further than before').
Not separating the condition being changed from the quantity being measured when recording.
(Content) believing all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape (Oak National Academy).

learn.summary: Pattern-seeking for 8–9 year-olds: children take repeated measurements of an object's motion under varied conditions (classically, how far a toy car rolls from different ramp heights), organise the readings into a table and graph, identify the relationship (e.g. 'the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls', for the heights tested), and then use that pattern to predict motion in an untested case — before testing the prediction. The pedagogically ideal vehicle is a real hands-on investigation where children do the measuring, repeat readings, and meet genuinely uncontrollable variables themselves; an on-screen ramp-and-car simulation is intended to rehearse the data→pattern→prediction reasoning as an alternative but does not build real-apparatus measurement craft. The core objective is that a prediction is an evidence-based inference anchored in collected data, not a guess, and that pattern-seeking is real science alongside the fair test.

activities.title: Hands-on ramp-and-car pattern investigation
feedback: If a prediction is made without reference to the data, ask: 'Show me on your results why you predicted that distance' and require the prediction to sit on the trend.
If a near miss is treated as failure, introduce repeat readings and a 'close enough / within range' judgement — predictions from patterns are trend-based, not exact.
If more than one thing is changed between trials (e.g. moving the start point or adding a push), rebuild the test so only ramp height changes: same release point, no push.
If only one reading is taken per height, scaffold a second and third reading and compare, so noise is not mistaken for pattern.

If the changed condition and the measured quantity are muddled in recording, prompt the child to label one column 'ramp height' (what we change) and another 'distance rolled' (what we measure), so the pattern can be read cleanly.
When a self-discovered trend correctly foretells a motion never measured, name that moment explicitly: the data predicted the result.
activities.rationale: Pattern-seeking is a distinct 'working scientifically' enquiry where children identify relationships in data (sometimes with variables that cannot be fully controlled) and form evidence-based predictions; grounding it in real apparatus, systematic recording, repeat readings and an explicit 'predict then test' move is intended to develop the measurement craft and the inference discipline at the heart of the skill.
sourceClaims: Pattern-seeking enquiries involve measurements where variables can't easily be controlled; children form evidence-based predictions from their data to generalise and to create new 'big questions'; often a preliminary enquiry leading to fair/comparative tests.

Pattern-seeking is a distinct enquiry approach — 'identify patterns and look for relationships in enquiries where variables are difficult to control' — alongside fair testing, research, observation over time, classifying and problem solving.

A ramp/toy-car set-up investigates how distance travelled is affected by gradient and surface; record distance for several gradients and notice what happens; fair testing should not be the default enquiry type.

Year 5 statutory forces content (gravity, air/water resistance, friction, mechanisms) with upper-KS2 working-scientifically skills: plan enquiries controlling variables where necessary, take repeat readings, record in tables/graphs, use results to make predictions.
learnerActions: Start from a 'big question': 'Does a steeper ramp make the car roll further?'
Set up real apparatus — a ramp you can prop at different heights, a toy car, a metre rule, and (optionally) a stopwatch.
Release the car from the SAME start point each time, raising the ramp in steps, and measure the distance it rolls for each height.

Take repeat readings (at least two or three) at each height, and record all readings systematically in a table that keeps the changed condition (ramp height) and the measured quantity (distance rolled) in separate labelled columns.
Plot the results on a graph (bar, line, or scatter as appropriate) so the trend across readings becomes visible.
Use 'what do you notice?' to state the relationship in your own words (e.g. 'for the heights we tried, the steeper the ramp, the further it rolls').

PREDICT, THEN TEST: for a ramp height you have NOT tried, use the pattern to predict the roll distance (best between your measured heights; if beyond them, only a little and with more caution), mark it, then run that height and compare the car's actual stop to your prediction.
Judge success by how close the actual distance is to the predicted trend, not by an exact hit, and raise a new 'big question' the enquiry suggests.
activities.intendedInsight: A pattern found across many readings can be used to make and justify a prediction about an untested, related case; a prediction grounded in your own data is an evidence-based inference, not a guess.

activities.title: On-screen ramp-lab simulation (data→pattern→prediction)
feedback: When the self-discovered trend correctly foretells where the car stops, surface that this is the payoff: a pattern you found predicted motion you never measured.
If the child expects the car to land exactly on their marker, point to the repeat-run scatter and reframe the prediction as 'about this far, within a range'.
If the child predicts before accumulating enough points, prompt them to run more heights until the trend is clear.
activities.rationale: A 2D interactive with live state and instant data capture can hold the full data→pattern→prediction loop, with a linked table/graph updating per run, repeat-run scatter, and a predict-then-compare marker making the mechanism concrete. This is proposed as an alternative to hands-on work for rehearsing the reasoning, not as a replacement for real measurement practice.
sourceClaims: Pattern-seeking enquiries involve measurements where variables can't easily be controlled; children form evidence-based predictions from their data to generalise and to create new 'big questions'; often a preliminary enquiry leading to fair/comparative tests.

A ramp/toy-car set-up investigates how distance travelled is affected by gradient and surface; record distance for several gradients and notice what happens; fair testing should not be the default enquiry type.
learnerActions: Use a ramp-and-car sandbox: a slider sets ramp height; tap RELEASE and the car rolls while the distance is auto-measured.
Watch each run drop a point onto a growing table and scatter graph beside the track; after a few runs a trend becomes visible.
Deliberately repeat runs at the same height to see the slight scatter, so reliability is felt rather than assumed.

Take a PREDICT challenge: set the ramp to a height you haven't tried, mark where you think the car will stop on the track, then release and compare the car's actual stop to both your marker and the trend.

Notice the small run-to-run variation the simulation includes (e.g. a gentle random nudge standing in for real-world wobble), which is why repeat runs differ slightly and predictions are 'about this far' rather than exact.
activities.intendedInsight: The reasoning core of pattern-seeking — accumulate readings, spot the trend, predict an untested case, then check — can be rehearsed and made visible when live data capture links each run to a growing graph.

activities.title: Pattern-use consolidation questions
feedback: Flag over-precise answers: the data supports a trend-based estimate, not an exact distance.
If a 'not supported' statement is placed under 'pattern shown', ask which reading in the data would back it up.
activities.rationale: Pattern-use is cleanly assessable and useful for consolidation; this is proposed to check that a prediction is anchored to a trend rather than invented. It exercises pattern-USE and does not, on its own, develop the investigate-measure-predict craft.
learnerActions: Given a described or shown trend, predict the distance at a new ramp height (e.g. choose a value along a slider or number line consistent with the pattern).
Order a set of results by ramp height to see the trend as a sequence.
Choose which conclusion the data supports, rejecting an over-precise option that claims an exact value the data cannot justify.
Sort statements into 'pattern shown by the data' vs 'not supported by the data'.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a trend and extrapolating a reasonable (not over-precise) prediction can be checked and reinforced once the investigate-measure-predict experience has been had.

activities.title: Finished-results graph with reveal (supporting scaffold)
feedback: If the child only names points without a relationship, prompt 'what do you notice as the height increases?'
activities.rationale: A static image can display and annotate a finished trend, which supports reading relationships. It shows the product rather than running the measure→accumulate→predict→test process, so it is a scaffold toward, not a substitute for, the investigation.
learnerActions: Study a finished results graph (ramp height vs distance rolled) and tap to reveal labels for axes, readings, and the trend.
Describe the relationship shown and point to where an untested height would fall on the trend.
activities.intendedInsight: A completed graph can help children read a trend and locate where a new case sits, as preparation or support for doing the full loop themselves.

constraints: The target skill is PROCEDURAL: children must actually measure, record, identify a trend and make-and-test a prediction — recognition-only responses do not elicit this independent construction.

Hands-on measurement with real apparatus supports repeat-reading discipline, accurate length/time measurement, and confrontation with genuinely uncontrollable variables; an on-screen simulation does not provide this real-world apparatus-handling.

Keep the fair-test control explicit: same release point and no extra push, changing only the ramp height, so ramp height is the only factor deliberately changed (small run-to-run variation from the car, surface or aim will still occur).
Keep the changed condition (ramp height) and the measured quantity (distance) clearly separated when recording.
Predictions should be trend-based (a value between measured ones, or a little beyond them with extra caution, 'about this far'), judged by closeness to the trend, not by an exact hit.

Name the pattern-seeking aim honestly: finding and using a relationship across several ramp heights. Recognise that this ramp investigation also uses fair-test controls (one changed factor), so it is not a pattern-seeking enquiry in the sense of variables that cannot be controlled. Pattern-seeking often serves as a preliminary enquiry generating predictions and new questions.
A finished-results graph and consolidation questions are scaffolds/checks and do not, by themselves, provide the measure-accumulate-predict-test loop.
A 3D version would only be worthwhile if spatial set-up (aiming, 3D track shapes) were itself the learning goal; the investigative reasoning here lives in the 2D data and trend.
An in-role conversation (e.g. with a scientist about spotting patterns) could motivate but does not itself provide the measure-and-predict practice.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Several source claims are marked unverified in the original row (PSTT enquiry approaches; Science-Sparks/Science Fix; National Curriculum programmes of study). The AKSIS finding that fair tests dominate >50% of practical work is cited via Science-Sparks/Science Fix and is unverified here; treat as context, not an established effect size.

The original listed one content misconception ('all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape') that is not directly exercised by the ramp-roll pattern-seeking activities; it is retained as pedagogy context but not built into a learner action.
The original 'not separating the condition being changed from the quantity being measured' misconception is surfaced in the hands-on activity's recording step and feedback.

Original framing claimed a static image 'cannot run' the loop, that 3D 'adds nothing', and that dialogue 'cannot deliver' practice; these are kept as narrowly scoped affordances/limits (a graph shows the product and supports reading; a conversation can motivate) rather than universal laws, since the cited sources do not establish comparative efficacy.

No empirical evidence establishes that hands-on, the simulation, or predict-then-test sequencing is more effective than other media; comparative wording has been kept to 'intended/proposed/alternative' throughout.

The error-pattern referencing a fair-test control prerequisite (reteachPrerequisiteId mt_3WMADSy0mA in the source assess field) is preserved as feedback guidance; the pedagogy/assess fields themselves are left unchanged.

probeDeeper: Show me on your results why you predicted that distance.
How many times did you measure at each height, and why?
If the car rolls a few centimetres short of your prediction, was the prediction wrong? How would you decide?
What did you keep the same every time, and why does that matter?
assess.correctAnswer: Releases the car from the same start point each time, raises the ramp in steps, measures the roll distance for each height (repeating readings), notices the pattern 'higher ramp -> further roll', predicts a new height's distance consistent with that trend (interpolating or extrapolating), then tests it by measuring — judging success by closeness to the prediction, not an exact hit.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'I'll just guess how far — I don't need the earlier measurements for that.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask the child to point on their own results to what makes them expect that distance; require the prediction to sit on the pattern.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Makes the prediction without referring to the trend in the data just collected.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It has to land exactly on my predicted number or my prediction was wrong.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce repeat readings and a 'close enough / within range' judgement — predictions from patterns are trend-based, not exact.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats a near miss as failure and doesn't allow for measurement variation.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'I'll change the ramp height AND give the car a push each time.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the test so only ramp height changes: same release point, no push. Reteach fair-test control if it's missing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Alters the start position or adds a push between trials, so distance changes for mixed reasons.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'One measurement per height is enough — I won't repeat any.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a second and third reading and compare — don't reteach the whole method.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Takes a single reading per height, so noisy data hides the trend.

responseLevels.gap: Collects a few distances but the prediction is a guess unlinked to the data, or changes more than one thing so no clean pattern emerges.
responseLevels.full: Controls the release and measures consistently with repeats, identifies the trend across heights, uses it to predict a specific distance for an untried height, tests it, and judges success by closeness to the trend — transferring the pattern to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Measures roll distance at several heights and states 'higher = further', but predicts loosely (just 'more') or expects an exact value — lists results and a pattern without using the trend to place a specific, testable prediction for a new height.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a ramp you can prop at different heights, a toy car, and a metre ruler. Investigate how the ramp height changes how far the car rolls across the floor. Take the measurements you need, find the pattern, then use it to predict how far the car will roll from a height I choose that you haven't tried — and test your prediction.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because this is a procedure, you WATCH rather than ask about it. The discriminator is whether the child's prediction is anchored in their OWN measured pattern (they point to the trend and give a value between or beyond measured ones) versus a guess unconnected to the data, and whether they control the release and measure consistently. A child who predicts before gathering a pattern, changes two things at once, or expects an exact number reveals that pattern-based reasoning is absent even if individual measurements are fine.

pedagogy.summary: This is the conceptual definition that underpins all percentage work: a percentage is a number of parts PER HUNDRED — a standardised proportion — which is why it can be written equivalently as a fraction (out of 100) and a decimal (45% = 45/100 = 0.45), why the same percentage of different wholes gives different amounts (it is relative to its base, not an absolute quantity), and why percentages can exceed 100% (150% = one and a half times the whole). Standardising 'out of 100' is precisely what makes percentages useful for COMPARING proportions with different totals. Teaching should ground the definition in the 100-grid, hammer the three-way fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence, and repeatedly confront the intuition that a percentage names a fixed amount rather than a proportion of a whole.
bestPractices: Define percentage on a 100-grid: shade 45 of 100 cells — 45% = 45/100 = 0.45 = the shaded proportion; the grid makes 'per hundred' literal.
Stress that a percentage is RELATIVE to its whole: 50% of a small quantity and 50% of a large quantity are different amounts — percentage is a proportion, not a fixed number.
Drill the three-way conversion (fraction ↔ decimal ↔ percentage) in both directions, watching decimal placement (7% = 0.07, not 0.7).
Introduce percentages over 100% deliberately (a 100-grid plus part of a second grid; 150% = 1.5 = one and a half wholes) so 100% is understood as 'the whole', not a ceiling.
Teach 'express A as a percentage of B' as A/B × 100, tying it back to proportion (A out of B, restated out of 100).
Use side-by-side comparison tasks (which class did better: 18/25 or 70/100?) so standardising to 'per hundred' is seen to be the point of percentages.
keyRepresentations: 100-grid (each cell = 1%), shaded to show a percentage as a proportion
Fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence triple (45% = 45/100 = 0.45)
Two differently-sized bars/quantities with the same percentage shaded (relative-to-whole)
A 100-grid plus a partial second grid to show >100% (150% = 1.5 wholes)
'A out of B, restated out of 100' bridge for expressing one quantity as a percentage of another
commonMisconceptions: Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount (50% is 'the same amount' regardless of the whole), not as a proportion of its base
Believes percentages cannot exceed 100% (100% is seen as a maximum rather than 'one whole')
Mis-converts between forms: 7% → 0.7 (decimal misplacement), or 0.45 → 4.5%
Confuses 'A as a percentage of B' with 'B as a percentage of A', or which quantity is the whole (the base)

learn.summary: A percentage is a number of parts per hundred — a standardised proportion — so it can be written equivalently as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal (45% = 45/100 = 0.45). Because a percentage is relative to its whole (base), the same percentage of different wholes gives different amounts, and percentages can exceed 100% (150% = one and a half wholes). Standardising 'out of 100' is what makes percentages useful for comparing proportions with different totals. Teaching grounds the definition in a 100-grid, drills the three-way fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence, and repeatedly confronts the intuition that a percentage names a fixed amount rather than a proportion of a whole.

activities.title: Shade a 100-grid to define 'per hundred'
feedback: If a learner writes 7% = 0.7, point back to the grid: 7 cells out of 100 is 7 hundredths = 0.07; 0.7 would be 70 out of 100 cells.
If a learner thinks the grid cannot be exceeded, give a second grid and ask them to shade 150 cells in total across the two, naming it as one and a half wholes.
Confirm when all three forms (45%, 45/100, 0.45) are matched to the same shaded region.
activities.rationale: Grounding the definition on a 100-grid makes 'per hundred' literal and ties the fraction and decimal forms to a single visible proportion; a second partial grid shows >100% concretely. Curriculum framing treats fractions, decimals and percentages as different ways of expressing proportions.
sourceClaims: Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').

Translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty; a documented error is converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (treating a small percent as a large decimal, e.g. 7% → 0.7).
learnerActions: On a 10×10 grid (100 cells, each cell = 1%), shade 45 cells and write the result three ways: 45% = 45/100 = 0.45.
State in your own words what '45 out of 100' means by pointing at the shaded and unshaded parts of the grid.
Shade a second grid partly to show more than one whole: fill one full grid and 50 cells of a second, and write 150% = 1.5 = one and a half wholes.
Convert a small percentage carefully: shade 7 cells and record 7% = 7/100 = 0.07 (watch that it is 0.07, not 0.7).
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage literally means parts per hundred, so it is the same quantity expressed as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal; 100% is 'one whole', not a ceiling, and percentages can go beyond it.

activities.title: Same percentage, different wholes — 50% of two bags
feedback: If a learner predicts 'the same, because it's 50% of each', have them compute 50% of each whole (10 vs 20) and shade half of each: half of a larger whole is more.

If a learner says 'Bag B gives 20 more, because it has 20 more sweets', compute both halves — the gap is 10, not 20. The halves differ by 50% of the difference in the wholes; reason from 'half of each', not the raw total gap.
If a learner insists 100% must always beat 50%, return to the trap comparison: 100% of 10 = 10 is fewer than 50% of 40 = 20, because the percentages sit on different wholes.
Confirm when the learner both gets 'different amounts' AND justifies it by 'half of each whole, and the wholes differ'.
activities.rationale: The percentage-as-absolute misconception is the central error for this topic; predicting then computing and shading the same percentage on two different wholes directly confronts it, and the trap comparison blocks the shortcut '100% always beats 50%' by showing 50% of a larger whole exceeding 100% of a smaller one. A separate check distinguishes a correct 'no' reasoned proportionally from a 'no' reasoned from the raw total gap.
sourceClaims: Bassan Cincinatus & Sheffet (2016), a peer-reviewed study, documents the percentage-as-absolute misconception: learners treat a percentage as a fixed number added/subtracted regardless of its base — assuming '32% bigger' implies '32% smaller' the other way, and that 32% of one amount equals 32% of a different amount. It states 'a 32% value of one initial amount is not equal to a 32% value of another initial amount — it is important to find out from which whole the percentage is calculated', and that a price +20% then −20% does NOT return to the original.

Per the article abstract (personally fetched), percent is a 'privileged proportion' whose 'extremely concise language has lost its explicit referents, has misleading additive terminology for multiplicative meanings, and has multiple uses for the preposition of', and it 'forms a bridge between real-world situations and mathematical concepts of multiplicative structures' — explaining why learners default to additive schemas. (Abstract verified; full text paywalled.)
learnerActions: Predict first: Bag A has 20 sweets and Bag B has 40 sweets. If you take 50% of each, will you get the same amount from both, or more from one — and why? Write your reason before checking.
Compute 50% of each: 50% of 20 = 10, 50% of 40 = 20.
Shade half of two bars (or grids) sized to represent 20 and 40, and compare the shaded amounts.
Explain in one sentence why the same percentage gave different amounts.

Check a trap comparison: is 100% of a small 10-sweet bag more or fewer sweets than 50% of Bag B (40 sweets)? Compute both (10 and 20): 50% of the larger bag gives MORE than 100% of the smaller bag — so '100% always beats 50%' is false, because each percentage acts on its own whole.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage is a proportion of its own whole (50% = half of whatever the whole is). Because the wholes differ, equal percentages give different amounts, so a percentage is not a fixed absolute quantity; a larger whole's 50% can even exceed a smaller whole's 100%.

activities.title: Convert fluently between fraction, decimal and percentage
feedback: If 0.45 is written as 4.5%, re-anchor: 0.45 = 45/100 = 45%; 4.5% would be 0.045.
If 7% is converted to 0.7, re-anchor to 7/100 = 0.07.
Confirm when conversions are correct in both directions, including a value over 100%.
activities.rationale: Fluent two-directional conversion, with attention to decimal placement, is a documented difficulty and a stated curriculum requirement. Recognition/matching is a useful check of whether a learner can identify equivalent forms, but it does not by itself show they can produce a conversion; so matching is paired with learner-produced conversions.
sourceClaims: Translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty; a documented error is converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (treating a small percent as a large decimal, e.g. 7% → 0.7).

Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').
learnerActions: Match each percentage to its decimal and its fraction-out-of-100 (e.g. 45% ↔ 0.45 ↔ 45/100; 7% ↔ 0.07 ↔ 7/100; 150% ↔ 1.5 ↔ 150/100).
Go in both directions: given 0.08, write the percentage (8%); given 3/100, write the percentage (3%) and decimal (0.03).
Place a given value on a number line that passes 100%, locating 150% at one and a half wholes.
Explain the decimal-placement rule: converting a percent to a decimal divides by 100, moving two places, so a small percent becomes a small decimal (7% → 0.07).
activities.intendedInsight: The three forms are interchangeable notations for the same proportion; converting reliably in both directions depends on tracking the 'out of 100' divisor and decimal place.

activities.title: Express one quantity as a percentage of another, and compare
feedback: If a learner reports 18/25 as the loser without converting, have them compute 18/25 = 72/100 = 72%, which beats 70%.
If a learner confuses 'A as a % of B' with 'B as a % of A', mark which quantity is the whole in each phrasing and recompute both.
Confirm when the learner identifies the base correctly and uses A/B × 100.
activities.rationale: Expressing one quantity as a percentage of another and comparing via a common 'out of 100' base are explicit curriculum goals; confusing which quantity is the base is a listed misconception, so direction is checked deliberately.
sourceClaims: Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').
learnerActions: Write 'A as a percentage of B' as A/B × 100, and say aloud 'A out of B, restated out of 100'.
Compare two results: one class had 18 out of 25 pass, another 70 out of 100. Convert 18/25 to a percentage (72%) and decide which class did better.
Explain why percentages make this comparison easy: both are restated out of the same total, 100.
Check direction: is 'A as a percentage of B' the same as 'B as a percentage of A'? Try A=10, B=40 (10/40×100 = 25% vs 40/10×100 = 400%) and state which quantity is the whole each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Standardising to 'per hundred' lets you compare proportions with different totals; the base (the 'of B' quantity) is the whole, and swapping A and B changes the question and the answer.

constraints: Keep the base explicit at all times: every percentage is 'of' some whole; when amounts are involved, state the whole before computing.

Matching and multiple-choice checks confirm recognition of equivalent forms but do not, on their own, show the learner can produce conversions or justify the proportional reasoning; pair them with learner-constructed answers and spoken/written explanations.

A static shaded 100-grid is a strong, honest picture of the 'per hundred' definition and the equivalence triple; to let a learner test that the SAME percentage yields different amounts on different wholes, they need to act on at least two different wholes themselves (compute, shade, or physically share), whether with paper grids/bars or an interactive model.

Optional interactive supports — a grid whose fraction and decimal update as cells are shaded, a side-by-side panel shading the same percentage on two differently-sized bars, a drag-past-100% mode onto a second grid, and an 'A as % of B' tool that restates A/B out of 100 — make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same learning can be reached with paper grids, drawn bars, or shared counters.
Distinguish the diagnostic prediction step from the explanation: the reason given BEFORE observing is what reveals the absolute-vs-proportion view.
Do not teach '100% always beats 50%': supply a counterexample, e.g. 100% of a 10-sweet bag (10) is fewer than 50% of a 40-sweet bag (20), so 50% of a larger whole can exceed 100% of a smaller one.
Percentages compare proportions directly because each one is restated out of a common whole of 100. Comparing the actual amounts still needs each whole: 50% of 40 (20) is more than 100% of 10 (10).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Scope gap: the objective/evidence includes 'calculate percentage increases and decreases', but no activity builds this (only percentages >100% are represented). The original learn field likewise did not build it, so the rewrite is faithful, but this target is NOT covered and should not be read as taught. The Bassan '+20% then −20%' content is cited for the percentage-as-absolute principle in Activity 2, not for a change-calculation task.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 50% of 20 = 10 and 50% of 40 = 20 (difference 10, not 20); the trap comparison 100% of 10 = 10 is fewer than 50% of 40 = 20; 18/25 = 72% > 70%; 10/40 = 25% and 40/10 = 400%; 7% = 0.07, 45% = 0.45, 0.45 = 45% (not 4.5%), 150% = 1.5, 0.08 = 8%, 3/100 = 0.03 = 3% — all verified consistent.

Trap-comparison restored to the source form: '100% of a 10-sweet bag (10) vs 50% of Bag B (40) = 10 vs 20', which vividly shows 50% of a larger whole exceeding 100% of a smaller one. An equal-case variant reusing only Bags A and B (100% of 20 vs 50% of 40 = 20 vs 20) is also mathematically valid and refutes '100% always beats 50%'; reviewers may prefer it for setup economy.

The second misconception ('reaches no by raw total difference') is subtle: the halves differ by 10, which is 50% of the 20-sweet difference in the wholes — preserved in Activity 2 feedback as stated in the source.

The 'conversation/tutor' alternative and the 'per-hundred static grid' explainer from the source are preserved as approaches within activities and constraints rather than as separate ranked artefacts; comparative-efficacy phrasing was softened because the cited sources do not establish one medium as superior.
Source claims are marked 'verified' in the legacy row, but no re-verification occurred here; evidence strength should not be read as freshly confirmed.

assess.poeTask: Show the child two chocolate bars of clearly different sizes — a small one and a large one. Say you will give them 50% of each. PREDICT before breaking anything: will they get the same amount of chocolate from both, or more from one — and WHY? (A child answering 'the same, because it's 50% of each' is treating the percentage as absolute; the reason given before observing is the diagnostic part.) OBSERVE: break each bar in half — the large bar's half is visibly much more chocolate. EXPLAIN: 50% means half of EACH bar's own whole; because the wholes differ, the halves differ — a percentage is a proportion of its base, not a fixed amount.
probeDeeper: 'Write 50% as a fraction and as a decimal' — checks the parts-per-hundred equivalence (1/2, 0.5), and watch for decimal slips.
'Can you ever have more than 100% of something? Give me an example' — surfaces whether 100% is understood as 'the whole' rather than a ceiling.

Counterexample: 'Bag C has 10 sweets — is 100% of bag C more or fewer sweets than 50% of bag B?' — 100% of 10 (=10) equals 50% of 40 (=20)? No: 10 vs 20 — a child who reasons proportionally computes both; an absolute-view child assumes 100% always beats 50%.
'In one class 18 out of 25 passed; in another 70 out of 100 passed — which did better, and why are percentages useful here?' — tests standardising to 'per hundred' for comparison.
assess.correctAnswer: No. 50% of bag A is 10 sweets and 50% of bag B is 20 sweets. A percentage is a proportion of its OWN whole (50% means half of whatever the whole is), so because the bags have different totals, the same percentage gives different amounts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Percentage-as-absolute: 'Yes, 50% is 50%, so you get the same number of sweets from each bag' — treats the percentage as a fixed amount, not a proportion of the whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with the two bags: compute 50% of each (10 and 20) and shade half of each on a grid; a percentage is half of ITS whole, and the wholes differ. Rebuild percentage as a proportion of the base.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — 50% is 50%, so you get the same number of sweets from each bag
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 'yes, the same', or computes only one bag and assumes it holds for both; the percentage is treated as an absolute quantity

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches 'no' by the raw difference in totals rather than by proportion: 'bag B gives 20 more, because it has 20 more sweets'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute both halves (10 and 20, a gap of 10, not 20): the percentage acts on each whole, so the difference in the results is 50% of the difference in the wholes. Anchor to 'half of each'.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — bag B gives 20 more sweets, because it has 20 more sweets than bag A
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the halves differ by 20 (the difference in the bags) instead of 10; reasons from the absolute gap, not 50% of each whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes percentages cannot exceed 100% (100% is a maximum, so 150% is impossible or meaningless)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 100% = one whole (the full grid); 150% = one and a half wholes on a grid-plus-half-grid. Percentages describe proportions that can exceed the whole (e.g. prices rising to 150% of the original).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked (probe) about 150%, child says 'you can't have more than 100%' or caps it at 100

responseLevels.gap: Treats a percentage as a fixed amount ('50% is the same in both'), or insists percentages cannot exceed 100%; cannot connect percentage to a fraction/decimal of the whole.
responseLevels.full: Defines percentage as parts per hundred / a proportion of its whole, so equal percentages of different wholes give different amounts; converts fluently among fraction, decimal and percentage; interprets and uses percentages greater than 100%; and standardises 'out of 100' to compare proportions with different totals.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises the amounts differ and can compute 50% of each for the practised case, but explains it by the raw difference in totals rather than 'a proportion of each whole', or is shaky on ↔fraction/decimal conversion or on percentages over 100%.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Bag A has 20 sweets and bag B has 40 sweets. Is 50% of bag A the same amount of sweets as 50% of bag B? And — this is the important part — how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The prompt forces the relative-vs-absolute distinction and, via the second tier, the REASON. A child who understands percentage as a proportion of the whole says 'no' and explains it by the different wholes; a child holding the absolute view says 'yes, 50% is 50%'. Crucially the tier-two reason also separates a child who reaches 'no' for the RIGHT reason (proportion of each whole) from one who reaches 'no' for a wrong reason (e.g. 'B has 20 more sweets so its half is 20 more') — hard to answer correctly without the proportional idea.

sources.claim: Bassan Cincinatus & Sheffet (2016), a peer-reviewed study, documents the percentage-as-absolute misconception: learners treat a percentage as a fixed number added/subtracted regardless of its base — assuming '32% bigger' implies '32% smaller' the other way, and that 32% of one amount equals 32% of a different amount. It states 'a 32% value of one initial amount is not equal to a 32% value of another initial amount — it is important to find out from which whole the percentage is calculated', and that a price +20% then −20% does NOT return to the original.

(Abstract verified; full text paywalled.)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 12–13; Supervolcanoes & Volcanic Winter (CONCEPTUAL): calderas such as Yellowstone and Toba as supervolcanoes that can erupt thousands of km³ of ash; how sulphur-dioxide aerosols injected into the STRATOSPHERE scatter incoming sunlight and cause a volcanic winter (global cooling); the Toba catastrophe theory and giant eruptions interacting with ice ages; and the CONTRAST in scale and climate impact between a supereruption and an ordinary eruption.
• Standards — UK (DfE): links KS3 Chemistry 'Earth and atmosphere' (composition/structure; the carbon/atmosphere system) and KS3 Geography (tectonic hazards, climate). Supervolcano/climate-forcing specifics are enrichment above the statutory KS3 core. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS, ANCHOR): MS-ESS2-2 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-2]' (VERIFIED verbatim) — clarification: processes 'usually behave gradually but are punctuated by catastrophic events', at large and small scales — supereruptions are the archetypal catastrophic punctuation. MS-ESS3-2 (forecasting hazards) frames the risk side. Climate-forcing/aerosol specifics are knowledge-based (verified:false).
• Operational details — TWO payloads. (1) SCALE: a supereruption is not 'a bigger eruption' — it is orders of magnitude larger (VEI 8; thousands of km³ vs <1 km³), leaving a collapse CALDERA, not a cone; the intuition to build is logarithmic, non-linear scale. (2) CAUSAL CLIMATE CHAIN: the killer is not ash or lava reach but SO2 → sulphate aerosols in the stratosphere → reflect/scatter sunlight → global surface cooling for years (volcanic winter). Be precise it is sulphate aerosols (not CO2, not ash) that cool, and that they must reach the STRATOSPHERE to persist and spread globally. Use Toba (~74 ka) and its debated bottleneck, and the historical Tambora 1815 'year without a summer' as a smaller verified analogue. Prerequisites assumed: Hazard Assessment, Monitoring Volcanoes, Seismic Waves (imaging the magma chamber). Highest-centrality node in the domain.
• Checkpoint — Tier C (formal/model-based): the child EXPLAINS the supereruption→stratospheric-SO2→aerosol-scattering→global-cooling chain and CONTRASTS a supereruption with an ordinary eruption on a non-linear scale — attributing the cooling to sulphate aerosols reaching the stratosphere, not to ash or CO2, and recognising the event as rare-but-catastrophic (MS-ESS2-2 punctuation).
bestPractices: Lead with the non-linear SCALE contrast: put an ordinary eruption and a supereruption on a LOG axis of erupted volume so the child feels 'thousands of times bigger', not 'a bit bigger' — and show the collapse caldera vs cone as the structural signature.

Build the climate chain as an explicit causal sequence: magma's dissolved SO2 → blasted into the stratosphere → forms sulphate aerosols → scatter/reflect sunlight → surface cools for years → volcanic winter.

Be precise about the cooling agent: sulphate AEROSOLS cause the cooling (short-lived, years); ash falls out fast and volcanic CO2 is a minor long-term warmer — do not let 'ash blocks the sun' or 'CO2' displace the real mechanism.
Insist on the STRATOSPHERE condition: only aerosols that reach the stratosphere persist and spread globally; tropospheric injections rain out locally — this is why supereruption plume height matters.
Anchor with a verified historical analogue (Tambora 1815 → 1816 'year without a summer') to make the abstract climate forcing concrete, then scale up to Toba/Yellowstone.
Treat the Toba catastrophe/bottleneck theory as a genuine, contested hypothesis (evidence for and against) rather than settled fact — model how science weighs a dramatic but debated claim.
keyRepresentations: Log-scale volume comparison: a single dot for an ordinary eruption vs a vast block for a VEI-8 supereruption (thousands of km³) — the scale-shock rep.
Caldera-vs-cone cross-section: emptied magma chamber collapsing into a broad caldera, contrasted with a built-up stratocone.
Causal-chain diagram: SO2 → stratospheric sulphate aerosols → sunlight scattered → global temperature drop → volcanic winter.
Global temperature-anomaly graph before/during/after a supereruption (years-long dip and recovery), with Tambora 1816 as a labelled real data point.
Ash-fall and aerosol-spread map: local/regional ash blanket vs the hemispheric-to-global reach of the stratospheric aerosol veil.
commonMisconceptions: 'A supervolcano is just a bigger normal volcano.' — It is orders of magnitude larger (VEI 8), erupts from a huge shallow magma chamber, and leaves a collapse caldera rather than a cone; the difference is non-linear, not incremental.
'The global cooling comes from ash blocking the sun.' — Ash falls out within days–weeks; the years-long cooling is caused by sulphate AEROSOLS from SO2 in the stratosphere scattering sunlight.
'Volcanoes mainly warm the climate (CO2).' — On short timescales the dominant climate effect of a big eruption is COOLING via sulphate aerosols; volcanic CO2 is small compared with human emissions.
'Yellowstone is overdue and will definitely erupt soon.' — 'Overdue' misreads recurrence intervals (long-run averages, not schedules); a supereruption is very low-probability in any given year.
'The aerosols and cooling last a long time / permanently.' — Stratospheric sulphate aerosols persist for a few years then settle out; the climate recovers — the winter is severe but temporary.
'The Toba bottleneck is a proven fact.' — It is a debated hypothesis; genetic and archaeological evidence is mixed — a good example of contested science, not settled history.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13: build two coupled ideas about supervolcanoes — (1) the NON-LINEAR scale gap between an ordinary eruption and a VEI-8 supereruption (thousands of km³ vs <1 km³, a collapse caldera rather than a cone), and (2) the causal CLIMATE CHAIN by which sulphur dioxide injected into the stratosphere forms sulphate aerosols that scatter sunlight and cause a multi-year 'volcanic winter' that then recovers. Learners should attribute the cooling to stratospheric sulphate aerosols — not ash, not CO2 — and treat the Toba bottleneck hypothesis as contested science. Anchored by the historical 1815 Tambora / 1816 'year without a summer' analogue and framed by MS-ESS2-2's gradual-processes-punctuated-by-catastrophe idea.

activities.title: Turn the eruption dial: from cone to caldera on a log scale
feedback: If a learner calls a supervolcano 'just a bigger normal volcano', point to the log axis: from about VEI 2 upward each VEI step is about ten times more material, so the gap is non-linear — thousands of times or more, not incremental.
If they expect a taller mountain at the top end, show that the emptied chamber causes collapse into a caldera — reaching for 'where did the mountain go?' is the intended jolt.
Reinforce correct reasoning that reads the log axis as leaping by thousands rather than adding a little.
activities.rationale: A manipulable log-scale volume control with a caldera-vs-cone contrast makes the orders-of-magnitude leap felt rather than merely stated, directly serving MS-ESS2-2's framing of catastrophic punctuation at varying spatial scales.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS2-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-2]'; clarification states many geoscience processes usually behave gradually but are punctuated by catastrophic events.

Supereruptions (VEI 8) eject thousands of km³ of material and form collapse calderas (Yellowstone, Toba); volcanic winter is caused by sulphur-dioxide-derived sulphate aerosols reaching the stratosphere and scattering sunlight, cooling the surface for years.
learnerActions: Work with an eruption-size control (a dial or slider) whose erupted-volume axis is drawn as a LOG scale, and record what the volcano looks like at ordinary scales versus when pushed toward VEI 8.
Notice and describe the structural change at the top end: the mountain does not simply grow taller — the emptied magma chamber collapses into a broad caldera tens of kilometres across.

Compare an ordinary eruption (<1 km³) against a supereruption (thousands of km³) using a side-by-side 'ghost' reference, and state in your own words how many times bigger it is, not just 'a bit bigger'.

Write one sentence explaining why each step up the VEI scale (from about VEI 2 upward) means roughly ten times more material, so a VEI-8 eruption like Toba or Yellowstone's largest is thousands of times (or more) bigger than an ordinary eruption.
activities.intendedInsight: A supervolcano is not an ordinary volcano scaled up a little; erupted volume differs by orders of magnitude (a logarithmic scale), and the structural signature is a collapse caldera, not a built-up cone.

activities.title: Build the volcanic-winter causal chain
feedback: If a learner names ash as the cooling agent, remind them ash is heavy and settles within days to weeks and only regionally; sustained global cooling needs something that reaches and lingers in the stratosphere — sulphate aerosols.

If a learner predicts warming from eruption CO2, compare magnitudes and timescales: eruption CO2 is small and slow, while the aerosol cooling is fast and strong, so the short-term net effect is cooling.
If a learner thinks the cooling is permanent, note that stratospheric sulphate aerosols settle out after a few years and the climate recovers — the winter is temporary.
Reinforce reasoning that ties the global reach specifically to the plume penetrating the stratosphere.
activities.rationale: Rendering the chain as an explicit, manipulable sequence with coupled map-and-graph feedback lets learners isolate the mechanism (vary SO2, vary plume height) and discover that stratospheric aerosols — not ash or CO2 — drive the cooling. The SO2/aerosol/stratosphere specifics are knowledge-based and were not re-verified this session.
sourceClaims: Supereruptions (VEI 8) eject thousands of km³ of material and form collapse calderas (Yellowstone, Toba); volcanic winter is caused by sulphur-dioxide-derived sulphate aerosols reaching the stratosphere and scattering sunlight, cooling the surface for years.
learnerActions: Assemble, in order, the causal sequence as an explicit chain: dissolved SO2 in the magma → blasted high into the STRATOSPHERE → forms sulphate aerosols → scatter/reflect incoming sunlight → global surface cooling for a year or two → recovery.

Using linked panels (an aerosol-spread world map and a global temperature-anomaly graph that respond together), observe how a stratospheric injection blooms a pale aerosol veil across the globe and drives the temperature graph into a multi-year dip that then recovers.
Run two contrasts: turn the SO2 amount down and watch the cooling weaken or vanish; keep the plume LOW (tropospheric only) and watch the aerosols rain out locally with no global winter.

State explicitly which ingredient caused the cooling and why ash and CO2 did not: ash falls out within days to weeks and only regionally; eruption CO2 is small and warms only slightly over long timescales.
activities.intendedInsight: The years-long global cooling is caused by sulphate aerosols formed from SO2 that must reach the stratosphere to persist and spread worldwide — the cooling is severe but temporary, and is not due to ash or CO2.

activities.title: Calibrate on Tambora, then scale up to Toba and Yellowstone
feedback: A full response explains stratospheric SO2 forming sulphate aerosols that reflect sunlight for a year or two while ash rains out and CO2 stays minor short-term, and transfers to the Hawaiian-vs-explosive or eruption-vs-factory cases.

A partial response names SO2 or aerosols and knows supervolcanoes are larger but cannot say WHY aerosols cool or why the log-scale difference matters — prompt for the reflecting/lingering-in-the-stratosphere step.
For the Hawaiian counterexample, steer toward explosiveness and SO2 plume height (whether SO2 reaches the stratosphere) rather than lava volume as what governs climate impact.
activities.rationale: Anchoring an abstract mechanism in a historical case, then scaling up and testing transfer, supports robust explanation under MS-ESS2-2. The Tambora and Toba details are general knowledge not re-verified this session.
sourceClaims: The 1815 Tambora eruption caused the 1816 'year without a summer' (Northern Hemisphere cooling and crop failures) — a historical analogue for volcanic-winter climate forcing.
MS-ESS2-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-2]'; clarification states many geoscience processes usually behave gradually but are punctuated by catastrophic events.
learnerActions: Study the 1815 Tambora eruption and the 1816 'year without a summer' as a real, labelled data point on the temperature-anomaly graph, and describe the Northern-Hemisphere cooling and crop failures that followed.

Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'Volcanoes pour out ash, CO2 and sulphur dioxide — which of these cooled the planet after Tambora, and how did it cool rather than warm?' Give both the agent and the reason.

Scale the reasoning up from Tambora to Toba (~74 ka) and Yellowstone, describing how a much larger supereruption could reach up and cool the entire planet, and connect this to how a cooling pulse could interact with an ice age (snow and ice reflecting still more sunlight).

Tackle the transfer counterexamples: why a typical Hawaiian-style lava eruption usually has little global cooling effect even when it produces a lot of lava, compared with a smaller explosive eruption that blasts SO2 into the stratosphere; and why a factory and a supervolcano emitting the same CO2 would differ in short-term effect.
activities.intendedInsight: A smaller historical analogue makes the abstract climate forcing concrete and transferable; the same mechanism scaled up explains how a rare supereruption can be a planet-wide catastrophic punctuation.

activities.title: Weigh the Toba bottleneck as contested science
feedback: If a learner states the Toba bottleneck as proven, note the evidence is mixed and the claim is contested — a model case of how science handles dramatic but unsettled ideas.
If a learner says Yellowstone will 'definitely erupt soon', correct the 'overdue' framing: recurrence intervals are averages, not countdowns, and any given year's probability is very low.
Reward answers that cite specific evidence on both sides rather than asserting a verdict.
activities.rationale: A role-play debate suits the contested-science dimension and the probability misconception, which are argumentation goals rather than quantitative-mechanism goals; it supplements, and does not replace, the manipulable scale and mechanism work. The contested status of the Toba hypothesis is general-literature knowledge not re-verified this session.
sourceClaims: The Toba catastrophe / human genetic bottleneck (~74 ka) is a debated hypothesis with mixed genetic and archaeological support, not settled fact.
learnerActions: Take on the role of a volcanologist or climate scientist and debate the question 'Is the Toba catastrophe / human genetic bottleneck real?', laying out evidence for and against.

Separate what is well-supported (the eruption's scale and the aerosol-cooling mechanism) from what is debated (whether it caused a human population bottleneck ~74 ka), citing the mixed genetic and archaeological picture.
Discuss why 'Yellowstone is overdue' is a misreading: recurrence intervals are long-run averages, not schedules, and a supereruption is very low-probability in any given year.
Conclude with a short written statement distinguishing a dramatic-but-debated hypothesis from settled fact, and how scientists weigh such claims.
activities.intendedInsight: Science distinguishes robust mechanisms from contested historical inferences; the Toba bottleneck is a genuine, debated hypothesis, and 'overdue' misreads probability.

activities.title: Check the key discriminations
feedback: Flag 'ash blocked the sun for years' as incorrect: ash settles within days to weeks and regionally only, so it cannot drive multi-year global cooling.
Flag 'eruption CO2 warmed the planet' as importing climate-change teaching — compare magnitudes and timescales, since the short-term net effect is cooling.

Treat such checks as confirmation of discriminations already built through manipulation and explanation; recognition items confirm specific discriminations but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own construction of the mechanism.
activities.rationale: Targeted recognition items usefully confirm the specific discriminations (agent, order, structure, probability), but recognition alone does not elicit independent construction of the explanation, so place these after the manipulable and explanatory activities.
learnerActions: After building the mechanism, answer short items that discriminate the cooling agent: choose sulphate aerosols (not ash, not CO2) as the cause of multi-year global cooling and justify the choice.
Put the causal-chain steps into the correct order and match the caldera to the supereruption and the cone to an ordinary eruption.
Explain why plume height into the stratosphere matters, and correct the statement 'Yellowstone is overdue so it will erupt soon.'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can reliably distinguish the real cooling mechanism and the structural/scale signatures from common distractors.

constraints: The sulphate-aerosol/SO2/stratosphere mechanism, the Tambora and Toba details, and the DfE/KS3 context are knowledge-based claims not re-fetched this session (verified:false); only the MS-ESS2-2 wording is marked verified. The 1815 Tambora eruption and the 1816 'year without a summer' are well-established history and may be taught as a real historical analogue; keep the size and duration of the cooling stated approximately rather than as precise figures.

Be precise that the cooling agent is sulphate AEROSOLS from SO2, that they must reach the STRATOSPHERE to persist and spread globally, and that the cooling is severe but temporary (a few years, then recovery) — do not let 'ash blocks the sun' or 'CO2 warms' displace the mechanism.

Keep VEI explicitly logarithmic: from about VEI 2 upward each step is roughly ten times more erupted material (the lowest steps differ by even more); avoid describing a supereruption as merely a larger ordinary eruption.

A static scale-comparison poster or labelled causal-chain graphic is a useful summary/reference after the manipulable work, but on its own it cannot let a learner vary the eruption or watch the temperature respond, where the scale intuition and mechanism become clear.

A 3D caldera fly-over or plume-through-layers view adds spatial scale intuition and awe at higher cost; it is a supplement for footprint/plume-height, not a replacement for the 2D causal-chain and log-scale manipulation.
Recognition-only items verify discriminations but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own explanation of why aerosols cool or why the log scale matters — use them after construction.
Treat the Toba bottleneck as a contested hypothesis and 'Yellowstone overdue' as a probability misreading; do not present either as settled fact.
Prerequisites assumed: Hazard Assessment, Monitoring Volcanoes, and Seismic Waves (imaging the magma chamber).

probeDeeper: Why does it matter that the sulphur dioxide reaches the STRATOSPHERE — what happens to gas and ash that only reach the lower atmosphere?
Counterexample: a huge Hawaiian lava eruption pours out far more lava than an explosive one but barely cools the climate. Why?
If a supervolcano and a factory released the same mass of CO2, why would the supervolcano still cool the planet in the short term while the factory warms it?
How could a single eruption's cooling deepen an ice age — what's the feedback with snow and ice reflecting even more sunlight?
assess.correctAnswer: Sulphur dioxide did it. SO2 injected into the stratosphere reacts to form tiny sulphate aerosol droplets that spread around the globe and reflect/scatter incoming sunlight back to space, cooling the surface for a year or two. Ash falls out within days to weeks (too heavy to linger and only regional), and although CO2 is a warming gas the amount from even a giant eruption is small next to the aerosol cooling — so the short-term net effect is cooling.

errorPatterns.pattern: The ash cloud blocked out the sun and that's what cooled everything ('the sky went dark from ash').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ash is heavy and settles within days to weeks and only regionally; global multi-year cooling needs something that reaches the stratosphere and stays — sulphate aerosols.
errorPatterns.distractor: The thick ash cloud blocked out the sun for years and cooled the whole planet.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names ash as the cooling agent.

errorPatterns.pattern: Volcanoes release CO2, so a giant eruption warms the planet through the greenhouse effect ('more CO2 means hotter').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare magnitudes and timescales — eruption CO2 is small and slow, the sulphate aerosol cooling is fast and strong; separate the short-term cooling from any tiny long-term CO2 nudge.
errorPatterns.distractor: The CO2 from the eruption added to the greenhouse effect and warmed the planet.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts warming from eruption CO2, importing climate-change teaching.

errorPatterns.pattern: A supervolcano is just a bigger version of a normal volcano — a bit more lava ('same thing, scaled up a little').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the log scale explicitly — each VEI step is roughly ten times more material; Toba and Yellowstone are hundreds to thousands of times an ordinary eruption.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot grasp that the VEI scale is logarithmic — thousands of cubic kilometres, orders of magnitude beyond an ordinary eruption.

responseLevels.gap: Says ash blocked the sun, or that eruption CO2 warmed the planet; treats a supervolcano as a slightly bigger ordinary one.
responseLevels.full: Explains stratospheric SO2 forming sulphate aerosols that reflect sunlight for a year or two while ash rains out and eruption CO2 stays minor short-term, and grasps VEI as a logarithmic scale; transfers to a new case such as Hawaiian lava versus an explosive eruption, or eruption versus factory CO2.
responseLevels.partial: Names sulphur dioxide or aerosols and knows supervolcanoes are much larger, but cannot explain WHY sulphate aerosols cool (reflecting sunlight from the stratosphere, lingering while ash falls out) or why the logarithmic scale difference matters.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: After the 1815 Tambora eruption, 1816 became 'the year without a summer' and crops failed across the Northern Hemisphere. Volcanoes pour out ash, CO2 and sulphur dioxide. Which of these cooled the planet, and how did it cool it rather than warm it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who says 'ash blocked the sun' or 'CO2 warmed it via the greenhouse effect' gives a different answer from one who identifies stratospheric sulphate aerosols reflecting sunlight. The reason tier separates 'dust blocks light' from 'sulphate droplets high in the stratosphere scatter sunlight and linger'.
