pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Compare and order numbers to 1000 with >, =, < by reasoning from the highest place down: compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones. Directly extends the two-digit 'tens-first' rule to a three-place, most-significant-digit-first procedure.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'compare and order numbers up to 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.4 'compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits, using >, =, and < symbols'.
• Operational details — Generalise 'compare the biggest place first' to three columns using aligned builds and a place-value chart; only drop to the next column when the current column ties. Stress-test with same-hundreds pairs (352 vs 358), digit-swap traps (352 vs 325) and different-length comparisons (99 vs 100). Move from pairs to ordering sets and to number-line placement.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): compares three-digit numbers with different hundreds using a build. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): orders a set to 1000 and states 'hundreds first, then tens, then ones'. Tier C (age 8, extending): resolves same-hundreds and mixed-length cases and justifies via place value, not digit count.
bestPractices: Generalise the rule to 'compare the highest place first, move down only on a tie' — same reasoning as two-digit, one more column.
Align builds/columns so the child scans hundreds→tens→ones and sees where the decision is made.
Use same-hundreds pairs (352/358) and digit-swaps (352/325) so the ordering can't be done by eyeballing.
Include mixed-length comparisons (99 vs 100) to defeat 'more digits sometimes / bigger ones digit' errors via place value.
Progress pair → ordered set → number line to connect comparison with magnitude.
keyRepresentations: Aligned base-ten builds / place-value counters in H|T|O columns
0-1000 number line for magnitude placement
>, =, < symbols (open side to the larger)
Place-value comparison chart scanning left-to-right
Ordered card rails (smallest→largest)
commonMisconceptions: Comparing ones or the biggest single digit instead of hundreds first (358 > 372 because 8 > 2).
'More digits = bigger' misapplied, or failing 99 vs 100 by digit count reasoning done wrongly.
Not descending to the next column when the hundreds tie.
Reversing the symbol or binding it to page order.
Ignoring internal zeros when comparing (305 vs 350).

learn.summary: Ages 7-8 compare and order numbers up to 1000 using >, =, < by reasoning from the highest place down: compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones, descending a column only when the current one ties and stopping at the first place where the digits differ. This extends the two-digit 'tens-first' rule to three places. Core practice uses aligned place-value builds with a left-to-right scan, trap pairs (same-hundreds, digit-swap, mixed-length, internal-zero), set ordering, and number-line placement.

activities.title: Scan the places left-to-right with two aligned builds
feedback: If a learner judges 358 > 372 because 8 > 2, point back to the hundreds: 3 hundreds vs 3 hundreds tie, so move to the tens where 5 < 7, so 358 < 372.
When the hundreds tie (352 vs 358), prompt: 'Hundreds are equal, so which place decides next?' then compare the tens, then the ones.
For 99 vs 100, align by place: 100 has 1 hundred while 99 has 0 hundreds, so 100 is larger. The extra digit matters because it stands for a higher place.
For 305 vs 350, highlight the internal zero: hundreds tie, then compare the tens (0 vs 5), so 305 < 350.
If the reasoning is right but the symbol is reversed, re-anchor: the open side faces the larger number; read the whole statement aloud to check.
activities.rationale: Comparison to 1000 is a left-to-right decision procedure; acting on aligned builds and scanning H→T→O makes visible where the decision is settled and generalises the known two-digit rule by adding one column.
sourceClaims: Compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens and ones digits, using >, =, < (2.NBT.4).
Comparison generalises as a most-significant-digit-first procedure; mixed-length and same-leading-digit cases target common errors.
learnerActions: Build or view two numbers (e.g. 352 and 358) as aligned base-ten builds or counters in H | T | O columns.
Place a >, =, or < card between them, with the open side facing the larger number.
Work left to right: decide at the hundreds first; only if the hundreds tie, move to the tens; only if the tens tie, move to the ones. Stop at the first place where the digits differ.
Say aloud which place settled the decision and why.
Repeat with trap pairs: same-hundreds (352 vs 358), digit-swap (352 vs 325), and mixed-length (99 vs 100).
Then order a set of 4-5 numbers smallest to largest and place numbers on a 0-1000 number line.
activities.intendedInsight: When the numbers are lined up by place, the comparison is always decided at the first (highest) place where the two numbers differ; move down to the next place only on a tie. A bigger ones digit does not by itself make a number larger. A whole number with more digits (and no leading zeros) is larger because it reaches a higher place, as when 100 has a hundred and 99 does not.

activities.title: Consolidation: choose the symbol, order a set, make it true
feedback: If a trap pair is answered by the ones digit, re-run the left-to-right scan from the hundreds.
After ordering a set, ask the learner to justify one adjacent pair by naming the deciding place.
On the number line, check that placement agrees with the symbol choice — larger numbers sit further right.
activities.rationale: Comparison and ordering map directly to scorable item formats, which are well suited to consolidating and checking the procedure once the scan is understood. This format exercises the rule rather than first scaffolding it.
learnerActions: Choose the correct >, =, or < for pairs including trap cases such as 358 vs 372 and 305 vs 350.
Order a set of five numbers up to 1000 from smallest to largest.
Fill a blank to make a comparison statement true (e.g. choose a tens digit that makes '3_6 > 352' true).
Place a given number on a 0-1000 number line (slider or marked rail).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent, reliable application of hundreds-first comparison across varied pairs and sets, connecting comparison to magnitude on a number line.

activities.title: Annotated worked reference for the scan
feedback: Prompt the learner to name the first place that differs in each annotated example.
After reading, ask them to predict and then check a new pair using the same steps.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated example gives a stable reference for the procedure and vocabulary; it supports but does not replace practice across many varied pairs, which develops fluency.
learnerActions: Step through a static annotated comparison such as 352 vs 358: see 'hundreds equal → look at the tens → 5 = 5 tie → look at the ones → 8 > 2, so 358 is larger'.
Read the caption that states the rule: compare the highest place first; move down only on a tie; stop at the first place that differs.
Re-state the rule in your own words before trying fresh pairs.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference model of the left-to-right scan and the stopping condition that learners can return to.

activities.title: Convince-me: rebut a wrong comparison
feedback: If the learner only restates the answer, ask them to name which place proves it and why the ones digit does not decide.
Accept any correct justification that identifies the first differing place and the correct order.
activities.rationale: Articulating and defending the reasoning surfaces whether the learner understands the stopping condition rather than reciting a surface rule. The underlying skill is procedural, so pair this with hands-on comparison practice.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who claims 358 > 372 'because 8 is bigger than 2'.
Explain why the claim is wrong, using the hundreds-then-tens reasoning, and state the correct comparison.
Construct a short justification: 'Hundreds tie, so look at the tens; 5 < 7, so 358 < 372.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify a comparison in words — not just get the symbol right — strengthens the place-value reasoning behind the procedure.

constraints: UK DfE National Curriculum, Year 3: 'compare and order numbers up to 1000'. US CCSS-M 2.NBT.4: compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens and ones digits using >, =, <.

Include same-hundreds pairs (352/358), digit-swap traps (352/325) and mixed-length comparisons (99/100) so learners cannot order by eyeballing or by the ones digit. For mixed-length pairs, link the extra digit to the higher place it represents.
Progress from single pairs to ordering a set to number-line placement to connect comparison with magnitude.
Right-align numbers by place before comparing; include internal-zero cases (305 vs 350).
A static annotated reference models the procedure but does not substitute for practice across many varied pairs; use it as a scaffold.

Scorable item formats (choose-the-symbol, order-the-set, fill-the-blank, number-line slider) are well suited to consolidation and checking; they exercise the procedure and do not by themselves scaffold the initial left-to-right scan.
The 'convince-me' dialogue targets justification; because the skill is procedural, keep it paired with hands-on comparison practice rather than using it alone.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

CCSS-M 2.NBT.4 and the NCETM claim are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE Year 3 claim is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is carried over as-is and not independently confirmed here.

Per-activity sourceClaims were trimmed to retain a claim only where it directly supports that activity's teaching principle. The DfE claim is topic/objective-level and was removed from all per-activity lists (it remains cited in constraints as the standard). The NCETM/CCSS claims were retained only on activity 1, whose rationale is the comparison procedure itself; activities 2-4 were set to [] because their rationales concern medium/method affordances (consolidation formats, reference model, dialogue justification) that the retained claims do not directly establish, even though those activities use the same comparison content.

The legacy '3D adds nothing' universal for magnitude ordering is not established by the source evidence and was dropped; 'not proposed in 3D here' is not the same as 'impossible'. Ordering is well represented in 2D/number-line form.

Legacy 'ideal'/'self-correcting'/'engineered moment of insight' framing implied the interactive bench uniquely achieves the effect; this has been softened to an observable affordance (a visible left-to-right scan) without asserting superiority over other media.

Assessment-field examples (254 vs 245 turns on the tens; 73 among 137/307/370) were checked and are consistent with hundreds-then-tens-then-ones reasoning, but were not independently re-verified against sources.

probeDeeper: Which place did you compare first — and why the hundreds?
254 and 245 — which is bigger, and how did you decide?
Where does 73 go among the three-digit numbers, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 254 > 245; order 73, 137, 307, 370; comparing hundreds first, then tens, then ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares from the ones, or by a bigger digit anywhere, instead of hundreds-first: judges 254 vs 245 by the ones (says 245 is bigger)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare place by place from the hundreds; stop at the first place that differs (tens: 5 > 4).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The same-hundreds pair is ordered by the ones digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misorders 2- and 3-digit numbers by digit-count or first glance: places 73 above 137
errorPatterns.nextMove: Right-align by place; a number reaching the hundreds beats one that stops at tens. Line them up in columns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 73 is ordered as if larger than a three-digit number, or numbers aren't aligned by place.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the < / > symbol despite correct reasoning
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor: the open side faces the larger number. Read the statement aloud to check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says which is bigger correctly but writes the symbol the wrong way round.

responseLevels.gap: Compares from the ones or by digit-count; symbol may be reversed.
responseLevels.full: Compares hundreds-then-tens-then-ones, orders numbers to 1000 reliably, and records with >, =, < correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Orders clearly different numbers but errs on same-hundreds pairs or mixed-length sets.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch them compare and order. 'Put a symbol between 254 and 245. Now order these smallest to largest: 307, 370, 73, 137. Tell me which place you looked at first.' The 254/245 pair turns on the tens, and 73 tests mixing 2- and 3-digit numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 254 vs 245 share hundreds and differ only at the tens, so a ones-first comparer picks wrongly; including 73 checks whether the child aligns by place rather than counting digits. Watching where they start (hundreds) exposes the method.

pedagogy.summary: The area model makes the distributive property visible: a rectangle a×(b+c) split by a single line becomes two sub-rectangles a×b and a×c whose areas SUM to the whole. It is a representational bridge from area to symbolic multiplication — the same picture that shows 6×13 = 6×10 + 6×3 later underwrites partial products and long multiplication. It rests on spatial structuring (seeing the region as rows and columns) and on area being additive, both established earlier.
bestPractices: Start concrete: tile a rectangle, then physically cut it into two sub-rectangles and match each piece to a product and the whole to a×(b+c)
Always translate BOTH ways — read a given model into an equation, AND draw a model for a given equation — since the topic is representational fluency, not just computing
Split at a friendly number (the ten): 6×13 → 6×10 + 6×3, so the model becomes a calculation strategy
Keep the repeated factor visible on BOTH sub-rectangles (both parts are still 'a' units tall) to pre-empt the drop-the-factor error
Show that different splits of the same rectangle all recompose to the same total (additivity)
keyRepresentations: A partitioned rectangle / area model split into two labelled regions
The open array (regions labelled by dimensions, tiles not all drawn)
The aligned equation a×(b+c) = a×b + a×c written beside the picture
Row-strip cutouts for children still building the row/column structure
commonMisconceptions: Distributes to only one addend: 6×(10+3) = 6×10 + 3 (drops the ×6 on the second part)
Adds the side lengths instead of the region areas (6 + 13, or 10 + 3)
Cannot place the split so the two parts recompose to the whole — a spatial-structuring difficulty
Computes the two sub-areas but forgets to add them into the whole

learn.summary: Builds representational fluency between a partitioned rectangle (area model) and the distributive equation a×(b+c) = a×b + a×c. The same picture that shows 6×13 = 6×10 + 6×3 later underwrites partial products and long multiplication. Rests on spatial structuring (seeing a region as rows and columns) and on area being additive, both built earlier. Learners should translate BOTH ways — read a model into an equation and draw a model for an equation — and keep the repeated factor visible on both sub-rectangles.

activities.title: Cut the rectangle, keep the factor
feedback: If a piece is labelled just '3' instead of '3×4', point to its height: it is still 3 rows tall, so its area is 3×4, not 3.
If side numbers are added (e.g. 4+2) instead of areas, tile one sub-rectangle and count the squares inside to contrast a length (edge) with a region (area).
If the two sub-areas are found but not added, ask: 'You found the two parts — now what is the WHOLE rectangle worth?'
activities.rationale: Starting concrete with tiling and physical cutting grounds the additive, decomposition structure of area before symbols; keeping the height visible on both pieces pre-empts the drop-the-factor error.
sourceClaims: Students learn that the area of a 12-by-5 rectangle can be found either by 12×5 or by adding two products, e.g. 10×5 and 2×5, illustrating the distributive property; they use composition/decomposition, spatial structuring and addition of area measurements to investigate arithmetic properties with area models.

Area work rests on spatial structuring — seeing a region as rows and columns of squares; this is the key hurdle, needs many array activities, and incomplete arrays are where children struggle; row-strip cutouts and drawing/joining unit marks scaffold it.
learnerActions: Tile a 3×(4+2) rectangle (3 rows of 6 tiles), then physically cut it along the grid line between the first 4 columns and the last 2 columns, making two sub-rectangles.
Match each piece to its product (3×4 and 3×2) and match the whole uncut rectangle to 3×(4+2).
Say out loud how tall BOTH pieces are (still 3 rows), confirming the repeated factor appears on each part.
Recompose the pieces and check the two areas sum to the whole.
activities.intendedInsight: A rectangle a×(b+c) split by one line across its (b+c) side, at the point between b and c, becomes two sub-rectangles a×b and a×c whose areas SUM to the whole; the repeated factor 'a' stays on both parts.

activities.title: Split at the ten to make a hard fact easy
feedback: If the learner writes 6×13 = 6×10 + 3, point out the second region is still 6 rows tall, so it is 6×3 = 18, not 3.
If an awkward split appears to give a different total, re-tile or re-count: a correct split always recomposes to the same whole.
Prompt flexibility: 'Is one split easier to compute? Does choosing it change the answer?'
activities.rationale: Making the split a visible choice shows the model is a calculation strategy, not a trick, and demonstrating that different splits recompose to the same total reinforces area additivity. Moving from fully tiled to an open array previews partial products. A draggable split line that relabels regions and assembles the equation live is one optional way to make the choice and recomposition vivid.
sourceClaims: Students learn that the area of a 12-by-5 rectangle can be found either by 12×5 or by adding two products, e.g. 10×5 and 2×5, illustrating the distributive property; they use composition/decomposition, spatial structuring and addition of area measurements to investigate arithmetic properties with area models.
learnerActions: On a 6-by-13 rectangle on a grid, place one vertical split line under the '10'.
Label the two regions with their products (6×10 = 60 and 6×3 = 18) and write the matching equation 6×13 = 6×10 + 6×3 = 78 beside the picture.
Once comfortable, re-label the same partition as an open array — mark each region by its dimensions (6×10 and 6×3) without drawing every tile — as a step toward purely symbolic partial products.
Try a different split of the same rectangle (e.g. 6×7 and 6×6) and check the total is still 78.
Explain why splitting at the ten makes the calculation easier even though any valid split gives the same total.
activities.intendedInsight: Splitting at a friendly number (the ten) turns a hard product into two known facts; the split is a strategy the learner chooses, and different valid splits all recompose to the same total (additivity).

activities.title: Read it and draw it both ways
feedback: If the produced model shows 5×12 = 5×10 + 2, the second region is 5 rows tall → 5×2, not 2; the factor 5 belongs on both parts.
If the regions are read as loose squares or edge numbers, return to tiling one region and counting its area.

If the drawn regions overlap, leave gaps, or have widths that don't add to 12, offer row-strip cutouts or a pre-drawn grid and let the learner find where 12 = 10 + 2 falls before adding the equation on top. If the learner cuts across the 5 instead (e.g. 2×12 + 3×12), accept it as a valid split that still totals 60, then ask them to also try splitting the 12 so both pieces keep the factor 5.
activities.rationale: The topic is representational fluency, not just computing, so both the reading direction and the independent constructing direction are needed; a learner who draws 5×12 = 5×10 + 2 exposes the distributive misconception in their own diagram. A matching / fill-the-blank / find-the-error / draw-the-split response format can be used during teaching as well as for checking.
sourceClaims: Students learn that the area of a 12-by-5 rectangle can be found either by 12×5 or by adding two products, e.g. 10×5 and 2×5, illustrating the distributive property; they use composition/decomposition, spatial structuring and addition of area measurements to investigate arithmetic properties with area models.
Discussions must clearly distinguish the attribute of area from other attributes, notably length — grounding the error of adding side lengths instead of region areas.
learnerActions: Given a rectangle split into a shaded 6×10 region and a 6×3 region, state the multiplication each shaded part stands for and what they make together.
Given 5×12, draw your own area model, choose where to split it, and write the matching equation (e.g. splitting at the ten: 5×12 = 5×10 + 5×2 = 50 + 10 = 60).
Keep the factor 5 on BOTH sub-rectangles and recompose to the whole.
Examine a worked example such as '6×13 = 6×10 + 3', find the error, and say what was forgotten.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means moving in both directions: reading a given model into an equation AND constructing a model for a given equation, keeping the common factor and recomposing to the whole.

activities.title: Reveal the parts, then the whole
feedback: If the learner stops after naming the two parts, ask what the whole rectangle is worth so they complete the recomposition.
If the whole is given as one region's value (e.g. 60, the 6×10 region, offered as the answer to 6×13), point to the second shaded region (6×3 = 18) that has not yet been added in.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal static model supports reading each region as a product and makes the 'remember to add the parts' step explicit; its limit is that pre-baked content cannot let the learner choose and draw their own split, so it is a scaffold toward independent production. Lift-the-flap / tap-to-reveal on each region is one optional way to stage the reveal.
learnerActions: On a static split area model of 6×13, reveal the left region's product (6×10 = 60), then the right region's (6×3 = 18).
Reveal the whole rectangle's value (6×13 = 78) and state in words that it is the two parts added.
Re-tell the chain: two parts → added → whole.
activities.intendedInsight: The whole area equals the sum of the two sub-areas; revealing them in sequence makes the 'add the parts' step explicit.

constraints: Translate in BOTH directions: reading a model into an equation alone is not sufficient; learners must also construct a model for a given equation.
Keep the repeated factor on BOTH sub-rectangles to pre-empt the drop-the-factor error (6×13 = 6×10 + 3).
Distinguish the attribute of area (region/tiles inside) from length (edges) to prevent adding side lengths instead of region areas.
A static tap-to-reveal model is a scaffold: it supports reading regions as products but does not by itself elicit the learner's own choice of split or independent drawing.

Do not impose the equation on a partition the learner cannot yet see: if they cannot place a split that recomposes to the whole, give row-strip cutouts or a pre-drawn grid and coordinate with array practice first.
Interactive examples (a draggable split line, live relabelling, running products, lift-the-flap) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms.
Recognition/reveal-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a model; include at least one task where the learner draws and writes their own split.
The area model is planar for this objective; this does not establish that other media cannot teach it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Confirmed the incomplete-recomposition feedback in the reveal activity is consistent with its 6×13 setup: 60 is the 6×10 region offered as the whole, not a wrong claim about 5×12.
Restored the open array as an optional intermediate representation in the split-at-the-ten activity, since it was a named representation in the original research.

The original marked 3D and conversation media as 'poor'; those catalog comparisons are softened to the objective point that the area model is planar for this objective, without universal-necessity or medium-superiority claims.
The Year 4 National Curriculum age-placement claim is flagged verified:false in the row; treated as unverified and not used as a sourceClaim.

probeDeeper: 'Why did you split the 12 into 10 and 2, and not into 6 and 6? Is one easier — and does it change the answer?'
'Here's a model split into 6×10 and 6×3, but someone wrote 6×13 = 6×10 + 3. What did they forget?' (surfaces the drop-the-factor error on a fresh case)
'Show me on the picture where the ×6 is hiding in BOTH parts.'
'Could you split 5×12 a different way and still get 60? Show me.' (tests flexibility and additivity)
assess.correctAnswer: Interpret: the left region is 6×10 = 60, the right is 6×3 = 18, and together they are the whole rectangle, so 6×13 = 6×10 + 6×3 = 78. Produce: draws a 5×12 rectangle split into 5×10 and 5×2, writes 5×12 = 5×10 + 5×2 = 50 + 10 = 60, with the split at the ten and the factor 5 kept on BOTH sub-rectangles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Distributes to only one addend — reads or writes 6×13 = 6×10 + 3, labelling the second region just '3' instead of '6×3' (drops the repeated factor)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to tiles: show the second sub-rectangle is still 6 (or 5) rows tall, so its area is 6×3 not 3; label the repeated side on BOTH regions.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the produce tier writes 5×12 = 5×10 + 2, or in the interpret tier names the second part '3' rather than '6×3'

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the side lengths instead of the region areas — reads the whole as 6 + 13, or the parts as 10 + 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a length (an edge) with a region (the tiles inside); tile one sub-rectangle so the child counts area, not edges.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sums edge numbers rather than the shaded areas; answer looks like a perimeter or a length total

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot place a split that recomposes to the whole — the drawn split line doesn't correspond to 10+2, fragments the repeated factor, or they can't partition at all
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT impose the equation on top of a partition they can't yet see; give row-strip cutouts or a pre-drawn grid and let them find where 12 = 10 + 2 falls — this coordinates with array practice and self-corrects.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the produce tier draws overlapping/unequal regions, a split that doesn't total 12, or a horizontal cut that breaks the ×5

errorPatterns.pattern: Splits correctly but forgets to recompose — computes the two sub-products and stops, offering one region as 'the answer'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'You found the two parts — now what is the WHOLE rectangle worth?' — a prompt to complete, not a reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Finds 5×10 = 50 and 5×2 = 10 but doesn't add them, or gives 50 as the answer to 5×12

responseLevels.gap: Reads the regions only as loose squares or as edge numbers; when asked to produce a model, cannot partition or drops the common factor (writes 5×10 + 2).
responseLevels.full: Interprets each region as a product AND independently chooses a friendly split, keeps the repeated factor across both regions, and recomposes to the whole (5×12 = 5×10 + 5×2 = 60), transferring the move to a new product.
responseLevels.partial: Reads both regions as products and can draw a split, but treats the two facts as separate — lists 5×10 and 5×2 without joining them into 5×12, or can only work from a split that is handed to them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show an area model of 6 × 13: a rectangle split by one line into a shaded 6×10 region and a differently-shaded 6×3 region. FIRST (interpret): 'This picture shows 6 × 13. Point to the two parts — what multiplication does each shaded part stand for, and what happens when you put them together?' THEN (translate/produce): 'Now here is 5 × 12. Draw an area model that splits it to make it easier to work out, and write the matching equation.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The interpret tier catches whether the child sees each region as a PRODUCT (not just loose squares or edge numbers); the produce tier catches whether they can choose a useful split AND keep the common factor across both parts. A child who draws 5×12 = 5×10 + 2 exposes the distributive misconception in their own diagram — a translation task makes the error visible without having to ask about it.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including using the distributive law, integer scaling problems, and harder correspondence (n×m combinations) problems.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including using the distributive law to multiply two-digit numbers by one digit, integer scaling problems and harder correspondence problems such as n objects are connected to m objects'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.2/4.OA.3 — multiplicative comparison and multistep word problems (including which operation and interpreting remainders); 3.OA.8 two-step problems; correspondence combinations connect to the multiplication principle of counting.
• Operational details — this is the APPLICATION topic that ties three distinct multiplicative structures together: (1) distributive-law calculation (14×6 = 10×6 + 4×6) as a mental/written strategy; (2) SCALING — 'three times as tall/heavy', a multiplicative (not additive) comparison; (3) CORRESPONDENCE / combinations — 3 breads × 4 fillings = 12 sandwiches, where multiplication counts pairings. Children must identify which structure a problem has and choose operations; the bar model and a systematic table/tree are the key tools. The recurring pitfall is reading scaling additively and mis-organising correspondence.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): solve a one-step scaling problem and a small correspondence problem with support (2×3). Tier B (age 8–9): use the distributive law on 14×6 and solve a correspondence problem by systematic listing/table. Tier C (age 9): solve a multi-step multiply-and-add problem, choosing operations and justifying with a bar model.
bestPractices: Teach the three structures explicitly and by name — distributive calculation, scaling (times-as-many), correspondence (combinations) — so children recognise which they face rather than key-word guessing.
Use the bar model as the shared representation for scaling and multiply-and-add, making the multiplicative comparison visible against an additive one.
For correspondence, build systematic organisation — a grid/table or tree diagram — so children see why you multiply the two counts rather than add them.
Contrast scaling with addition directly ('3 times as tall' vs '3 m taller') using the same numbers so the multiplicative meaning is felt.
Progress from one-step to genuinely multi-step problems, requiring an estimate and an operation choice, and checking answers for reasonableness.
keyRepresentations: Bar model — scaling and multiply-and-add (unit bar × scale factor; combine bars)
Systematic table / grid — correspondence combinations (rows×columns = pairings)
Tree diagram — correspondence (each bread branches to each filling)
Distributive split (area/partition) — 14×6 as 10×6 + 4×6
commonMisconceptions: Reading scaling additively — 'three times as tall as 15 m' answered as 15+3 rather than 15×3.
Adding the two counts in a correspondence problem (3+4=7 sandwiches) instead of multiplying.
Unsystematic listing of combinations, so some pairings are missed or duplicated.
Applying the distributive split incorrectly (14×6 = 10×6 + 4, dropping the second multiplication).
Relying on key words instead of the problem's structure, choosing the wrong operation in multi-step problems.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: solving multiply-and-add problems across three distinct multiplicative structures — (1) the distributive law as a calculation strategy (14×6 = 10×6 + 4×6 = 60+24 = 84); (2) scaling / multiplicative comparison ('3 times as tall as 15 m' = 45 m, NOT 15+3 = 18); and (3) correspondence / combinations (3 breads × 4 fillings = 12 sandwiches). The central aim is for learners to identify which structure a problem has and choose operations accordingly, rather than guessing from key words. Bar models and systematic tables/trees are the shared tools; the recurring pitfalls are reading scaling additively and adding the two counts in correspondence problems.

activities.title: Correspondence combinations: pair every bread with every filling
feedback: If a learner answers 7 (adding the counts), show the grid or tree: there are more than 7 cells to fill. Name it explicitly — '4 sandwiches for EACH of the 3 breads'.
If pairings are missed or duplicated, point to the empty or repeated cells and work row by row so each bread is paired with all 4 fillings exactly once.
Confirm correct reasoning by linking the completed grid back to 3 rows × 4 columns = 12.
activities.rationale: The multiplicative structure in correspondence problems is hidden, so children most often add (3+4=7). Building the pairings systematically in a grid or tree reveals why the total is a product. A draggable grid that auto-fills as each bread is paired, with a visible counter settling on 12, makes the 3×4 structure concrete — but a paper table or tree diagram achieves the same organisation. (Optional interactive: show empty cells remaining if a learner tries to add rather than pair.)
sourceClaims: Bar models and systematic tables/tree diagrams support scaling and correspondence problems; scaling should be contrasted with additive comparison to prevent the additive misconception.
learnerActions: Work with a concrete set-up of 3 kinds of bread and 4 kinds of filling (cards, drawings, or a draggable grid).
Systematically pair each bread with each filling, recording every sandwich in a table whose rows are breads and columns are fillings, or a tree where each bread branches to all 4 fillings.
After completing the pairings, count the filled cells and state the total as a number sentence: 3 × 4 = 12.
Explain in words why it is 3×4 and not 3+4: 'each of the 3 breads makes 4 sandwiches.'
Predict then check: 'If there were 5 fillings instead of 4, how many sandwiches now?' (3 × 5 = 15).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication counts pairings. When n objects each connect to m objects, the total number of combinations is n×m, not n+m. A systematic grid or tree makes every pairing visible so none are missed or duplicated.

activities.title: Scaling vs adding: 'times as tall' against 'taller by'
feedback: If a learner answers 18 for 'times as tall', show that they added the multiplier; 'times as tall' means making copies — lay out three 15 m bars and count.
Reinforce by asking the learner to re-read the phrase and decide: copies (×) or an amount extra (+)?
Confirm 3 × 15 = 45 m and have them point to the three stacked bars.
activities.rationale: Directly contrasting the scaling and additive readings with identical numbers targets the common additive-scaling error. The bar model makes the multiplicative comparison visible. (Optional interactive: a bar that stretches ×n beside a faint '+n' bar so 45 towers over 18.)
sourceClaims: Bar models and systematic tables/tree diagrams support scaling and correspondence problems; scaling should be contrasted with additive comparison to prevent the additive misconception.
4.OA.2/4.OA.3 require multiplicative comparison and multistep word problems including choosing operations; correspondence problems connect to the multiplication counting principle.
learnerActions: Draw or build a bar representing a 15 m building.
Make the tower '3 times as tall' by building three copies of the 15 m bar stacked end to end, and compute 3 × 15 = 45 m.
Alongside it, build a second comparison: '3 m taller than 15 m' = 15 + 3 = 18 m.
Place the two results side by side and describe the difference between 'times as tall' (multiplicative) and 'taller by' (additive).
State which phrase means multiply and which means add, using the same numbers so the contrast is felt.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Times as many/tall/heavy' is a multiplicative comparison (copies of the original), fundamentally different from 'more than / taller by', which is additive. The same numbers give very different answers (45 vs 18).

activities.title: Distributive law: split, multiply both parts, recombine
feedback: If a learner gives 60 or 64 (only the 10 multiplied, or 4 added without multiplying), return to the area model: the 4-strip must also be multiplied by 6, giving 24, before adding.
Note that the two partial products here are 60 and 24, which sum to 84; check both are present.
If the set-up is right but the arithmetic slips, do not reteach the structure — have the learner recompute and estimate to catch the slip.
activities.rationale: A frequent error is splitting the distributive calculation but multiplying only one part (14×6 = 10×6 + 4). The area/partition model shows both strips must be multiplied and combined. Self-audit: 10×6=60 and 4×6=24 sum to 84; the partial products are 60 and 24.
learnerActions: Split 14 into 10 + 4.
Multiply BOTH parts by 6: 10 × 6 = 60 and 4 × 6 = 24.
Add the two partial products: 60 + 24 = 84.
Use an area/partition model — a rectangle split into a 10-strip and a 4-strip, both ×6 — to show both pieces are included.
Check the result is reasonable (e.g. 14×6 is a bit more than 10×6 = 60, and less than 15×6 = 90).
activities.intendedInsight: The distributive law lets you multiply a two-digit number by splitting it, but every part of the split must be multiplied by the second factor and then added. Dropping a partial product gives a wrong answer.

activities.title: Which structure is it? Classify and choose the operation
feedback: If a learner relies on a key word and picks the wrong operation, ask what the problem is really doing — making copies (scaling), counting pairings (correspondence), or splitting a calculation (distributive)?
For multi-step problems, check the estimate against the final answer for reasonableness.
Praise justifications that name the structure and match it to a representation, not just correct numbers.
activities.rationale: Progressing from one-step to multi-step problems and requiring operation choice plus an estimate builds the habit of structural reasoning over key-word matching. Classification and matching number-sentence tasks are good for checking recognition, but should accompany, not replace, building the intuition with bars and grids — recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the pairings or the comparison.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.2/4.OA.3 require multiplicative comparison and multistep word problems including choosing operations; correspondence problems connect to the multiplication counting principle.
learnerActions: Read a mix of word problems and sort each into its structure: distributive calculation, scaling (times-as-many), or correspondence (combinations) — and some multi-step multiply-and-add problems.
For each, write the number sentence before computing, justifying why that operation fits the structure.
Tackle at least one genuinely multi-step problem that needs an operation choice and a combine step; estimate first, then compute and check for reasonableness.
Explain your choice using a bar model (for scaling/multiply-and-add) or a table/tree (for correspondence).
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing operations should come from recognising the problem's structure, not from hunting for key words. The same operation (multiplication) appears in three disguises; identifying the structure drives the correct set-up.

activities.title: Talk it through: what is this problem really asking?
feedback: If the learner is unsure, redirect to a quick table or drawing to ground the discussion in visible pairings.
When they say 'one more filling gives 3 more sandwiches (one per bread)', confirm they are reasoning about the structure, not a memorised rule.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue supports problem-parsing habits and surfaces a learner's thinking. It complements, rather than replaces, the manipulable bars and grids where the structures are most clearly seen.
learnerActions: With a partner or adult playing a sandwich-shop owner, discuss a correspondence problem aloud: 'How many different sandwiches can I make?'
Answer probing questions: 'Are we making copies, or pairing options? If I add one more filling, how many MORE sandwiches — and why that many?'
Articulate the reasoning in your own words before writing a number sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Parsing a word problem aloud — distinguishing 'times as many' from 'how many pairs' — builds the habit of interpreting structure before computing.

constraints: Classification and multiple-choice tasks verify whether a learner recognises structure but do not require them to construct the pairings or the comparison themselves; pair them with building activities.

Static worked panels (a scaling bar, a filled grid, a distributive split) are useful anchors for recognising structure, but they do not let the learner build the pairings or experience the multiplicative-vs-additive contrast dynamically; treat them as reference scaffolds.
Paper/card cards and cutouts are good concrete stand-ins for breads and fillings; a screen grid is an alternative, not a requirement.
Discussion activities develop parsing habits but should be grounded in a visible table, tree, or bar so reasoning stays concrete.

Incorrect answer options in any check (e.g. 18 for '3 times as tall as 15 m', 7 for correspondence, 60/64 for the distributive split) must target the real misconceptions; do not offer arithmetically incoherent options as plausible answers.

Differentiate by readiness: less-confident/younger learners can start with a smaller correspondence set (e.g. 2×3) and a one-step scaling problem with support, progressing to the distributive calculation with systematic listing and then to multi-step multiply-and-add problems justified with a bar model.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 14×6 = 10×6 + 4×6 = 60 + 24 = 84 (correct); the partial products are 60 and 24. 3×15 = 45 (correct); '3 m taller' = 18. 3×4 = 12 correspondence (correct); 3×5 = 15 for the 5-fillings extension. No arithmetic errors found.

The source's distributive error-pattern notes answers of '60 or 64' for splitting only one part — 60 (forgetting 4×6 entirely) and 64 (adding 4 un-multiplied) are both coherent error accounts and are preserved as diagnostic feedback, not as valid answers.

sourceClaims were pruned where an exact-copy claim supported only the curriculum topic rather than the activity's teaching principle: the DfE claim is not used on the correspondence activity (NCETM retained as the principle support) and the distributive activity has [] because no source[].claim directly supports the 'multiply both parts' area-model principle.

The CCSS-M 4.OA claim is retained on the scaling and classify activities on the basis of direct content overlap (multiplicative comparison; multistep problems with operation choice); its role as partly curriculum-scope and its verified:false status are flagged as uncertain rather than treated as established efficacy.
The original checkpoint tiering (Tier A age 8, Tier B, Tier C age 9) was folded into a differentiation constraint rather than dropped.

The legacy source's catalog-fit comparisons (3D 'adds cost', quiz 'verifies rather than builds') were softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements; no comparative-efficacy or medium-superiority claim is asserted beyond the objective point that recognition-only tasks do not elicit independent construction.
One source claim (CCSS-M 4.OA) and the NCETM guidance claim are marked verified:false in the source; treat their support as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: For the sandwiches, why do you multiply 3 by 4 instead of adding them?
In 14 × 6, did you multiply BOTH the 10 and the 4 by 6?
'3 times as tall as 15 m' — how is that different from '3 m taller'?
If there were 5 fillings instead of 4, how many sandwiches now?
assess.correctAnswer: 84 (10×6 + 4×6 = 60 + 24); 45 m (3 × 15); 12 sandwiches (3 × 4). The teacher watches for splitting both parts in the distributive item, multiplying for scaling, and recognising the correspondence problem as a product of the two option-sets, not a sum.

errorPatterns.pattern: adds instead of multiplying on the correspondence problem (3 + 4 = 7 sandwiches)
errorPatterns.nextMove: make a systematic grid/table of bread × filling so all 12 pairings are visible; name it as '4 sandwiches for EACH of the 3 breads'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 7; child sums the two option-sets rather than pairing every bread with every filling

errorPatterns.pattern: splits only one part in the distributive method (10×6 = 60, forgets 4×6) giving 60 or 64
errorPatterns.nextMove: use the area model — both the 10-strip and the 4-strip must be multiplied by 6 and added.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: distributive answer missing a partial product

errorPatterns.pattern: reads scaling additively — '3 times as tall as 15' as 15 + 3 = 18
errorPatterns.nextMove: build three copies of the 15 m height; 'times as tall' means copies, not 'taller by'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: scaling answer of 18 (added the multiplier)

errorPatterns.pattern: correct set-up, arithmetic slip in a partial product or product
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach structure; have the child recompute and estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right method, wrong number

responseLevels.gap: adds on the correspondence problem, splits one part in distributive, or reads scaling additively.
responseLevels.full: recognises and correctly sets up multiplication across distributive, scaling and correspondence problems, justifying why each is a product, and checks the results.
responseLevels.partial: handles the familiar distributive/scaling items but adds on correspondence, or needs prompting to see the multiplicative structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three problems to solve while you watch the method: (distributive) 'Work out 14 × 6 by splitting 14 into 10 and 4'; (scaling) 'A model tower is 3 times as tall as a 15 m building — how tall is the model?'; (correspondence) 'There are 3 kinds of bread and 4 kinds of filling. How many different sandwiches can you make?' Watch how they set up each — especially whether they multiply for correspondence rather than add.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Correspondence problems are where children most often add (3 + 4 = 7) instead of multiplying, because the multiplicative structure is hidden. Watching all three problem types shows whether the child recognises multiplication across distributive, scaling AND correspondence structures — the same operation wearing three disguises.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Controlling variables (planning enquiries)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils are taught to "plan different types of scientific enquiries to answer questions, including recognising and controlling variables where necessary" (verbatim). Non-statutory guidance adds that upper-KS2 pupils should "recognise when and how to set up comparative and fair tests and explain which variables need to be controlled and why." This is the central experimental-design skill of the primary phase.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 Planning & Carrying Out Investigations):** the 3–5 progression is "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS2-1, 4-PS3-2, 5-PS1-3, 5-PS1-4]"; the overarching practice framing asks students to decide "which variables should be treated as results or outputs, which should be treated as inputs and intentionally varied… and which should be controlled, or kept the same across trials." This topic (ages 9–11) sits at that 3–5 core and previews the 6–8 shift to naming independent/dependent variables.

- **Operational details:** The hub of the primary experimental-design spine (highest centrality in its band). Builds on setting up simple fair tests (prerequisites mt_qgb76wHN2X, mt_eoPcc4nrBE) and identifying patterns/using evidence (mt_CVywzrjT_c). Two linked competencies: (1) CHOOSING THE RIGHT ENQUIRY TYPE for a question — fair test, observing over time, pattern-seeking, identifying/classifying, or research — rather than defaulting to fair testing; and (2) within a fair test, INDEPENDENTLY identifying the variable to change (independent), the variable to measure (dependent), and the variables to control, and explaining WHY control matters for a valid result. Feeds forward to prediction-driven re-testing and KS3 hypothesis-led full design (dependents mt_5PgQB0QkWi, mt_Ae56umVlTT).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). A learner who can independently plan an investigation identifying the change/measure/control variables, choose an appropriate enquiry type for a given question, and explain why controlling variables is essential for a valid result has met the bar. Formal hypothesis wording, sample size and risk assessment are the KS3 tier (mt_Ae56umVlTT).
bestPractices: Teach enquiry-TYPE selection explicitly against the five named types, using questions that are NOT best answered by a fair test (e.g. 'how does the moon's shape change over a month?' → observing over time; 'do taller children have longer arms?' → pattern-seeking) so pupils stop reflexively reaching for a fair test (the AKSIS over-default).

Move pupils from teacher-set to self-planned: give the question and have them decide the variables and the enquiry type, then justify their choices — planning independence is the assessed step-up from earlier fair-testing.

Require the 'why control?' justification for each controlled variable ('we keep the water amount the same because otherwise we couldn't tell if temperature or water amount caused the change') — controlling variables is understood, not just listed.
Introduce the input/output/kept-same language (independent/dependent/control in child-friendly form) as a bridge to the KS3 vocabulary, without over-formalising at this age.
Use a planning proforma (question → enquiry type → variable to change → to measure → to control → prediction → how to record) so the full plan is visible before any doing.
keyRepresentations: A five-enquiry-type selector (fair test / observe over time / pattern-seek / classify / research) matched to question types
An independent – dependent – control variable planner (the formalising of change/measure/keep-the-same)
A planning proforma from question through to recording method
A 'which variables must we control, and why?' annotated set-up
A decision flow: what kind of question is this → which enquiry answers it best
commonMisconceptions: Defaulting to a fair test for every question, including ones better answered by observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying or research (the AKSIS over-default persists into upper KS2).
Listing controlled variables without understanding why control is necessary — not connecting uncontrolled variables to invalid, uninterpretable results.
Confusing the independent (changed) and dependent (measured) variables, or thinking the thing you measure is something you set.
Believing 'more variables changed = a better/bigger experiment', missing that changing more than one destroys attribution.
Thinking planning is a formality to rush past, rather than the step that determines whether the results can answer the question at all.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: pupils learn to plan scientific enquiries by choosing the right enquiry type for a question and, within a fair test, assigning each factor as the variable to change (independent), measure (dependent), or keep the same (control), and justifying why control makes a result valid. The central active experience is designing a plan and seeing how an uncontrolled variable makes a result impossible to interpret. Supporting activities assess variable roles and enquiry-type matching and probe pupils' justifications. Alternatives include categorisation-and-matching questions and a Socratic plan-interrogation; a labelled reference image is a scaffold only.

activities.title: Design the plan, then run it: make a confound wreck your experiment
feedback: When key variables are left uncontrolled: 'More than one thing differed here (light, water, AND pot size) — you can't tell which caused the change. Lock the others so only the light varies.'

When a learner changes several factors deliberately: 'Varying more things at once does not make a better test — with light, water and pot all different, no single cause can be pinned down. Change exactly one.'

When the plan isolates a single variable: 'Only light differs among the things you controlled now, so a growth difference can more fairly be linked to light — though plants vary naturally, so repeating with several plants makes the answer more trustworthy.'

When 'fair test' is chosen for 'How does the Moon's appearance change over a month?': 'Nothing is being compared under controlled conditions here — this question asks you to watch how the Moon looks change over time. Pick the enquiry type that matches the question.'
When asked why a specific control matters: 'Say which rival explanation keeping the pot size the same rules out — control exists to make the cause attributable, not just to tidy things up.'
activities.rationale: Planning with variable control is a generative design decision; letting a learner build a plan, run it, and see an uncontrolled variable undermine the result is intended to make the necessity of control concrete rather than stated. A live planner-and-runner with a type-selector lets the mismatch between question and enquiry type show itself. This is proposed to address the reported AKSIS over-default to fair testing, the belief that changing more variables makes a bigger experiment, and the common failure to connect uncontrolled variables to uninterpretable results.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires planning different types of scientific enquiries to answer questions, including recognising and controlling variables where necessary; guidance adds pupils should explain which variables need controlling and why.

NGSS SEP 3 at grades 3-5 requires investigations that control variables, with the practice framing asking students to decide which variables are outputs, which are intentionally varied inputs, and which are controlled/kept the same across trials.
Primary pupils over-default to fair testing rather than selecting from the five enquiry types (observing over time, pattern seeking, classifying, comparative/fair testing, research).
learnerActions: Take a real question (e.g. 'Do plants grow taller with more sunlight?') and plan an investigation before doing anything.
Choose one enquiry type from the five: fair/comparative test, observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying/identifying, or research.
Sort each factor into 'change' (the one input you vary), 'measure' (the output/result), and 'keep the same' (controls).

Run the plan. If you left factors uncontrolled — e.g. the sunny plant also got more water and a bigger pot — observe how the result comes back ambiguous: 'light, water and pot size all differed, so we can't say which caused the growth.'
Fix the plan by keeping every other factor you can the same so only one is changed, re-run, and compare how a cleaner plan gives an answer you can more fairly put down to that one change.
Notice that changing several factors at once does not make a 'bigger or better' experiment — it only destroys your ability to attribute the effect to any one cause.

Try a question that is NOT best answered by a fair test (e.g. 'How does the Moon's appearance (its phase) change over a month?') and see that choosing 'fair test' misfires — observing over time fits better.
activities.intendedInsight: Controlling variables is not a rote rule: it removes rival explanations so a difference in results can be attributed to the one thing you changed. Changing more than one factor does not make the experiment stronger — it makes the cause unknowable. Different questions need different enquiry types, so a fair test is not always the right tool.

activities.title: Sort the variables and match the enquiry type
feedback: If independent and dependent are swapped: 'You set the amount of light; you measure the height. The thing you measure is an outcome, not something you choose.'
If a control is listed without reason: 'Which alternative explanation would differ if you did NOT keep this the same? That's why it's controlled.'

If every question is matched to 'fair test': 'Check whether the question compares conditions, watches change over time, looks for a pattern, sorts things into groups, or needs looking up — match the type to the question.'
activities.rationale: Matching questions to enquiry types, assigning variable roles, and justifying control map onto categorisation and multiple-choice formats, which can check and consolidate the planning evidence statements. This format assesses understanding but does not itself let a learner run their own flawed plan and see the consequence, so it complements rather than replaces the design-and-run activity.
sourceClaims: Primary pupils over-default to fair testing rather than selecting from the five enquiry types (observing over time, pattern seeking, classifying, comparative/fair testing, research).
learnerActions: Categorise a list of factors in a given investigation into independent (change), dependent (measure), and control (keep the same) roles.
Match several questions to their best-fitting enquiry type among the five named types.
Answer 'why must we keep X the same?' by naming the rival explanation it rules out.
activities.intendedInsight: Pupils can distinguish the thing you set from the thing you measure, and can pick an enquiry type fit to the question — the knowledge that underpins independent planning.

activities.title: Interrogate the plan: what else might be affecting your result?
feedback: If a hidden confound is missed: 'You changed the light, but did the two plants also start at different heights? Name every way they differ.'
If the justification is a bare rule: 'Keeping the pot size the same removes which possible cause? Tie the control to the explanation it eliminates.'
activities.rationale: A Socratic interrogation exercises the justification skill and probes for hidden uncontrolled variables and wrong enquiry-type choices. It pairs well AFTER the design-and-run planner, but on its own does not execute the investigation to show whether the plan is valid, so it is a complement rather than the primary teach.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires planning different types of scientific enquiries to answer questions, including recognising and controlling variables where necessary; guidance adds pupils should explain which variables need controlling and why.
learnerActions: Present a draft investigation plan to a 'scientist' partner or mentor.
Respond to probing questions such as 'What else might be affecting your result?' and 'Which rival explanation does each control rule out?'
Revise the plan to remove hidden uncontrolled variables and to confirm the enquiry type fits the question.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and defending a plan can surface hidden confounds and push the 'why control?' reasoning to become explicit.

constraints: Planning independence is the assessed step-up: move pupils from teacher-set to self-planned investigations where they decide the variables and enquiry type and justify their choices.
Require a 'why control?' justification for each controlled variable, tied to a specific rival explanation it rules out, not just a list of things kept the same.
Introduce input/output/kept-same (independent/dependent/control) language in child-friendly form as a bridge to KS3 vocabulary without over-formalising at this age.
A planning proforma (question → enquiry type → variable to change → to measure → to control → prediction → how to record) helps make the full plan visible before any doing.
Formal hypothesis wording, sample size and risk assessment belong to the later (KS3) tier, not here.

Categorisation and multiple-choice questions can check and consolidate variable-role and enquiry-type knowledge, while a labelled reference image can only illustrate or label it; neither elicits a learner constructing and running their own plan, so keep them as assessment or scaffold rather than the main teach.
A labelled reference image of variable types is a reference scaffold only — it cannot let the child construct and test a plan.

Experimental-design logic is not inherently spatial, so a 3D/spatial representation is not required here; its conceptual value for this skill is unestablished rather than categorically absent, and it should not be ruled out as harmful either.
Changing more than one variable at once is not a 'bigger/better' experiment — it prevents attributing the result to any single cause; keep exactly one input varied.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the AKSIS over-default claim (fair-test-by-default) as unverified (verified:false); treat statements about pupils over-defaulting to fair testing — including the sourceClaims that cite it in activities 1 and 2 — as a reported finding, not confirmed here.

Legacy entries asserted that 'a static image cannot teach this', '3D adds no conceptual value', and that only the live planner makes control 'felt'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limitation statements. A fixed image can still serve as a reference even though it cannot be manipulated.

The confounded-plant diagnostic (different light AND water AND pot size) is sound as written: the point is precisely that multiple simultaneous differences prevent attribution. Feedback wording states all three stated confounds consistently.

The original commonMisconception that 'more variables changed = a bigger/better experiment' was previously only addressed implicitly; it is now explicitly named in activity 1 so the substantive point is preserved.

probeDeeper: Which things must be kept the same here, and what alternative explanation does each one rule out?
If the sunny plant had the SAME water and pot and still grew taller, what could you now conclude?
Someone asks whether the class gets taller through the year — is a fair test the right enquiry, or would observing over time fit better?
Why does changing only one thing let us trust the answer, when changing several doesn't?
assess.correctAnswer: No — more than one thing differs (light, water, pot size), so you can't tell which caused the taller plant; the test is confounded. A strong response says you must keep water, pot size, soil, plant type and starting height the same, changing ONLY the light, so that any difference in growth can be attributed to light alone. It frames controlling variables as what makes the result VALID — it removes rival explanations — and may name this as a fair/comparative enquiry rather than, say, observation over time.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts the confounded conclusion: 'yes, it was the sunlight — the sunny one grew taller'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Highlight the two other differences (water, pot); ask which one caused it — establish that with three differences you can't tell.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endorses the causal claim without noticing the extra differences.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rule without reason: knows to 'keep everything the same' but can't say why, or keeps irrelevant things constant while missing the real confounds.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie each control to a specific rival explanation it removes — control exists to make the cause attributable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States the control rule but can't tie it to ruling out alternative causes, or mis-targets what to control.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fair-test-by-default (AKSIS): treats every question as a fair test even when observation-over-time or pattern-seeking would fit better.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Review the five enquiry types; match the question to the appropriate type before planning controls.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked about a different question type, still reaches for a fair test.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts the confounded conclusion, or recites 'keep things the same' without linking it to trusting the result.
responseLevels.full: Identifies the confounds, specifies which variables to control and why each removes a rival explanation, frames variable-control as what makes a conclusion valid, and matches the question to the appropriate enquiry type.
responseLevels.partial: Spots that more than one thing differs and knows to control variables, but can't fully justify why (in terms of ruling out alternative causes) or mis-selects the enquiry type.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A student wants to know if plants grow taller with more sunlight. They put one plant on a sunny windowsill and another in a dark cupboard — but they also water the sunny one more and use a bigger pot for it. After two weeks the sunny plant is taller. Can they be sure it was the sunlight? Talk me through what's wrong with the test, what needs to be kept the same, and why that matters for trusting the answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the concept spots that several differences make the cause unknowable and justifies control in terms of ruling out alternative explanations. A child without it either declares the conclusion safe ('sunlight, obviously') or recites 'keep things the same' as a rule without connecting it to why the conclusion would otherwise be untrustworthy.
