sources.claim: Gravity always attracts and acts on anything with mass, and reaches far beyond the Earth's surface; it is independent of the Earth's magnetic field (children often conflate gravity with magnetism).
sources.source: IOPSpark — Differentiating between gravity and magnetism

sources.claim: The 'heavier falls faster' intuition is documented from early childhood and resembles pre-Newtonian (Aristotelian) physics, persisting across ages and into teacher populations.
sources.source: Potvin et al. (2023) and falling-bodies misconception literature

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 7–9 — coral reefs are built by tiny living animals called coral polyps (reefs are not rock), reefs host more species than almost any other ocean habitat, and are called the 'rainforests of the sea'.
• Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2): Y4 'recognise that environments can change and that this can sometimes pose dangers to living things' and habitats/food-chain strands — the reef as a super-rich habitat and later a threatened one.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-3/3-LS4-4 (habitats and environmental change) and 2-LS4-1/biodiversity framing — the reef as the ocean's biodiversity hotspot.
• Operational details: three ideas — (1) coral is a colony of tiny living ANIMALS (polyps), not a plant and not rock; the hard reef is the limestone they build; (2) reefs are astonishingly biodiverse — a small area holds a huge variety of life; (3) the 'rainforests of the sea' analogy captures both the biodiversity and the reef-as-structure-that-shelters-others. The polyp-is-an-animal fact is the key surprise; the biodiversity is the wonder. (Bleaching/threats are the KS3 dependent — keep light here.)
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7–8): states coral is made by tiny living animals, not rock; Tier B (~8–9): describes a reef as one of the most life-packed habitats; Tier C (~9): explains the rainforest analogy (huge biodiversity + a structure that houses countless other species).
bestPractices: Lead with the counter-intuitive core fact — coral is a living ANIMAL (a polyp), not a plant or a rock — using close-up footage of polyps feeding to make it vivid and believable.
Zoom across scales: single polyp → colony → whole reef, so children see how tiny builders make a giant structure over long time.
Make biodiversity concrete with a 'how many species can you spot?' count in one reef patch, then compare to a barer seabed — richness is felt by contrast.
Unpack the rainforest analogy explicitly on two grounds: (a) exceptional variety of life, (b) the reef, like a forest, is a physical structure that provides homes/food for everything else.
Connect to prior habitat and food-web learning — the reef is a habitat and the base structure of a dense web.
keyRepresentations: A zoom sequence: coral polyp → coral colony → whole reef
A close-up of a polyp (tentacles, mouth) labelled 'a tiny living animal'
A biodiversity 'spot-the-species' reef scene vs a bare seabed for contrast
A side-by-side reef ↔ rainforest analogy panel (variety + structure that shelters others)
commonMisconceptions: 'Coral is a rock / a stone' — not knowing the reef is built by living animals (only the limestone skeleton is hard).
'Coral is a plant' — misled by its branching, flower-like, rooted appearance.
'A reef is one big creature' — rather than a colony of many tiny polyps (and a whole community).
'Reefs are colourful decorations' — missing that they are the most biodiverse marine habitat and shelter for countless species.
Taking 'rainforests of the sea' as being about greenery/plants rather than about biodiversity and structure.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny living ANIMALS called polyps (the hard reef is the limestone skeleton they build — made by living animals, not just lifeless rock, and not a plant); reefs are among the most biodiverse marine habitats; and they are called 'rainforests of the sea' because of both their variety of life and their role as a living structure that shelters countless other species. The counter-intuitive 'coral is alive — it's an animal' fact is the key surprise; the biodiversity is the wonder. Keep bleaching/threats light at this stage.

activities.title: Zoom from reef to a single living polyp
feedback: If a learner says the reef 'isn't alive' or is 'just rock the fish live on', show or describe a close-up of a polyp's tentacles feeding and name the animal vs its limestone house — like a snail is alive but its shell is hard.

If a learner says coral 'makes its own food from sunlight like a plant' or calls it seaweed, clarify: tiny algae living inside the coral use sunlight, but the coral itself is an animal that also catches prey — a partnership, not a plant. Contrast with true seaweed. (Bring this detail in only when the plant idea is raised; the core message stays 'coral is an animal'.)
If a learner thinks a reef is one big creature, remind them it is a colony of many tiny polyps forming a whole community.
activities.rationale: Leading with the close-up of a feeding polyp and a scale reveal from reef to single animal targets the dominant misconceptions (coral is a rock / a plant / one big creature) directly, letting children see an animal behaviour that a rock never shows.
sourceClaims: Coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny living animals called coral polyps, which secrete a hard calcium-carbonate skeleton; coral is an animal, not a plant or rock.
learnerActions: Start with a view of a whole busy reef, then step inward: reef → one branch of coral → a single polyp with its ring of tentacles and a mouth.
Name what you see at the smallest scale: a tiny living animal, not a rock or a stone.
State in your own words how billions of these tiny animals, each building a hard limestone cup around itself, add up to the giant reef structure over long time.
Explain what tells you a polyp is an animal and not a plant (it has a mouth and catches drifting food with stinging tentacles; seaweed has no mouth or tentacles and makes its food from sunlight).
activities.intendedInsight: The hard reef is the limestone skeleton that colonies of tiny living animals (polyps) build; coral is an animal, not a rock or a plant.

activities.title: Count the species: reef versus bare seabed
feedback: If the learner undercounts, prompt them to look for hidden and small animals (in crevices, on the coral surface), not just the large fish.
Reinforce that the point is the number of DIFFERENT kinds of living things, not just how many animals total.
activities.rationale: Richness is abstract until felt by contrast; a hands-on spot-and-tally against a sparse seabed makes biodiversity concrete for this age.
sourceClaims: Coral reefs are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth — occupying a tiny fraction of the ocean yet supporting about a quarter of all marine species — which is why they are called 'rainforests of the sea'.
learnerActions: Explore one reef scene and tap or point to each different creature; keep a running tally of how many distinct species you can spot.
Do the same count on a bare patch of seabed and compare the two tallies.
Say in a sentence what the contrast shows about how much variety of life a small reef area holds.
activities.intendedInsight: Reefs are among the most biodiverse habitats in the ocean — a tiny area holds a huge variety of life, felt most strongly by contrast with a barer habitat.

activities.title: Unpack the 'rainforests of the sea' analogy
feedback: If a learner explains the nickname by bright colours or plants, reframe to the huge number of different living things sheltered, and to the reef-as-structure idea — point back to the species tally and the living build from the zoom activity.
Encourage connecting to earlier habitat and food-web learning: the reef is both a habitat and the base structure of a dense web of life.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating the two grounds of the analogy prevents the common misreading of the phrase as being about greenery, and ties biodiversity to structure.
sourceClaims: Coral reefs are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth — occupying a tiny fraction of the ocean yet supporting about a quarter of all marine species — which is why they are called 'rainforests of the sea'.
learnerActions: Look at a side-by-side comparison of a reef and a rainforest.
List two reasons the names match: (a) exceptional variety of life, and (b) both are physical living structures that provide homes and food for everything else.
Explain why the nickname is NOT mainly about colour or greenery/plants.
activities.intendedInsight: The analogy captures biodiversity AND the reef as a living structure that shelters other species — like a forest provides homes for forest animals.

activities.title: Grow a reef over time (optional dynamic model)
feedback: If the learner thinks the reef appeared all at once, highlight the time-lapse: reefs build up slowly from countless tiny animals.
Connect the climbing species counter back to the reef-versus-bare-seabed comparison, noting that more varied structure tends to support more kinds of life.
activities.rationale: A time-lapse builder adds time and the tiny-builders-make-a-giant-structure sequence that a static scene cannot show, though the core facts do not require it.
sourceClaims: Coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny living animals called coral polyps, which secrete a hard calcium-carbonate skeleton; coral is an animal, not a plant or rock.
learnerActions: Seed a few polyps and watch (or step through) as they divide and secrete limestone, building structure over time.
Watch a species counter climb as the growing structure attracts more animals.
Say how this shows that tiny builders make a giant structure, and that a larger, more complex structure tends to provide homes for more kinds of animals.
activities.intendedInsight: Tiny living builders make a giant structure over long time; in this model a larger, more complex structure tends to offer more homes, so biodiversity tends to increase as the reef grows.

activities.title: Check your understanding
feedback: For a 'rock' or 'plant' answer, return to the polyp close-up and the animal-feeding evidence.
For an analogy answer based on colour, redirect to variety of life and structure-that-shelters-others.
activities.rationale: Short justify-your-answer questions can confirm coverage of the three evidence goals as a companion check; recognition questions confirm knowledge but do not by themselves elicit the fuller explanation produced in the construction activities, so justification is required here.
learnerActions: Answer: is coral a rock, a plant, or an animal? Justify your choice.
Compare the variety of life on a reef with that on a bare seabed and say which is more biodiverse.
Explain in a sentence why reefs are called the 'rainforests of the sea'.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state and justify all three core ideas: polyp-is-an-animal, reef biodiversity, and the analogy.

activities.title: Meet a talking coral polyp (optional spark)
feedback: Use the polyp's answers to reinforce: the animal is the polyp, the hard part is the house it builds.
If the role-play drifts, bring it back to the three core facts with the close-up and the species tally.
activities.rationale: A character voice can spark wonder and motivate questions; the three core facts and the scale reveal are presented in the visual activities, so this dialogue is offered as a complement rather than the main carrier of those facts.
learnerActions: Interview a polyp character (or a reef biologist) who explains in role: 'I'm an animal!', how its colony built the reef over a long time, and how it catches food while staying fixed in one place, using its moving tentacles.
Ask your own wonder questions and compare the answers to what you learned from the zoom and counting activities.
activities.intendedInsight: A polyp's first-person account can make the 'it's alive and it's an animal' surprise memorable and invite curiosity.

constraints: Keep bleaching and reef threats light at this stage; the detailed threat/cause reasoning is a later (KS3) dependent.

The 'coral has algae living inside it that use sunlight' detail appears in the assessment answer and explains why reefs grow in shallow sunlit water; it is advanced for the 7–9 state-the-facts goal — introduce only as an extension, and only when a learner raises the plant/sunlight idea, and do not let it replace the core 'coral is an animal' message.

Recognition questions (is it a rock/plant/animal?) confirm knowledge but do not by themselves elicit the independent explanation; pair them with activities where the child states and justifies the ideas.

Optional interaction examples (tap-to-name, zoom drill-down, reef↔seabed toggle, species counter, linked analogy panel, time-lapse builder, character dialogue) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory; the learning can be delivered with pictures, counting on paper, or discussion.
The 3D swim-through and the dynamic builder are enrichment; the learning goals do not hinge on spatial navigation or on time-lapse mechanics.
The structure→biodiversity link in the optional builder is a general ecological idea, not a figure established by the cited sources; keep it qualified ('tends to') and model-descriptive.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; the two NOAA sources were marked verified:false in the original and have NOT been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source assessment states reef-building corals 'house tiny algae inside their body that make food from sunlight'. This is biologically accurate (zooxanthellae) but is a notable step beyond the stated 7–9 evidence goals; verify age-appropriateness before foregrounding it.
The claim that reefs support 'about a quarter of all marine species' comes from the cited NOAA source and has not been independently re-verified here.

The 'more structure brings more biodiversity' relationship in the optional 'grow a reef' model is a general ecological generalisation and is not directly asserted by either cited source; it is kept qualified and presented as what the model shows.

The original framed the interactive image as the uniquely ideal medium and other media as lesser; this rewrite preserves the alternatives as genuinely useful without asserting comparative efficacy, which the sources do not establish.

probeDeeper: You said it's alive — what would we expect to see a living coral DO that a rock never does?
Reefs only build up in shallow, clear, sunny water. Why would an animal 'need' sunlight — unless something living inside it does?
If the water got so cloudy that no sunlight reached the coral, what do you predict would happen to it, and why?
A sea anemone in a rock pool and a coral polyp are close cousins. What is the one big difference between them?
assess.correctAnswer: A coral is a living thing — the hard reef is made by huge colonies of tiny animals called polyps, each like a minute sea anemone in a little cup of limestone it builds around itself. It doesn't chase food: it catches tiny drifting plankton with stinging tentacles, and (in reef-building corals) it also houses tiny algae inside its body that make food from sunlight, which is why reefs grow in shallow, sunlit, warm water. The rock is what the animals build, not the animal itself.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Coral is a rock / a stone you find in the sea' — treats the hard reef as non-living because it is hard and doesn't move.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a close-up video of extended polyp tentacles feeding at night; name the polyp as the animal and the limestone as its skeleton/house — the same way a snail is alive but its shell is hard.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's a colourful rock on the seabed — rocks aren't alive, so coral isn't either.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the reef isn't alive, or that it's 'just rock that fish live on'; surprised that anything animal-like is involved.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Coral is a plant / seaweed' — because it is fixed in place, branching and colourful, so it must be like a plant growing up from the bottom.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish: the ALGAE living inside the coral do use sunlight, but the coral itself is an animal that also catches prey — a partnership, not a plant. Contrast with true seaweed nearby.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's a plant — it's fixed down and branches like one, so it grows from the seabed like seaweed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says coral 'makes its own food from sunlight like a plant' with no mention of the animal, or calls it a kind of seaweed.

errorPatterns.pattern: '"Rainforest of the sea" means it is pretty/full of plants' — reads the phrase as about colour or vegetation rather than biodiversity.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe: like a rainforest, a reef packs an enormous VARIETY of species into a small space; count the different animals visible in one photo.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the nickname by the bright colours, not by the huge number of different living things it shelters.

responseLevels.gap: Calls coral a rock or a plant; denies it is an animal, or cannot say how a fixed thing could feed.
responseLevels.full: Explains that the reef is built by colonies of tiny animal polyps that both catch plankton and host sunlight-using algae, and uses that to explain why reefs grow in warm shallow sunlit seas and why 'rainforest of the sea' means biodiversity — transferring the idea to predict what harms a reef.
responseLevels.partial: Knows coral is a living animal and that reefs are rich in life, but treats these as separate facts — can't connect the polyp's feeding (plankton + algae partners) to why reefs need shallow sunlit water.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a photo of a coral reef, all knobbly and colourful. I tell you a coral reef is alive — it is built by thousands of tiny animals. Is that true, and if a coral is an animal, how does it eat and grow when it never moves around like a fish does?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks coral is a rock or a plant will say it isn't really alive, or that it 'grows like a plant from the seabed', and cannot explain feeding by an animal that stays put. A child with the concept separates the living polyp from the limestone it secretes and gives a plausible non-chasing way to eat (catching plankton / algae partners). Asking HOW a fixed animal eats is the discriminator — a rock/plant view has no answer to it.

sources.claim: Coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny living animals called coral polyps, which secrete a hard calcium-carbonate skeleton; coral is an animal, not a plant or rock.
sources.source: NOAA National Ocean Service — What is coral / are corals animals or plants?

sources.source: NOAA — Coral reef ecosystems / value of coral reefs

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Grouping Living Things (by observable features)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'Living things and their habitats'):** pupils recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-LS4-1 context):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1]; classifying by observable characteristics underpins pattern-finding across organisms (US delays formal taxonomy, so DfE is the primary anchor).

- **Operational details:** The central idea is that grouping is a CHOICE of criterion, not a fixed truth: the same set of organisms can be grouped many valid ways (by habitat, body covering, diet, number of legs, has-a-backbone), and the SAME organism lands in different groups depending on the criterion used. Pupils must (a) group a set by at least two different criteria, (b) state the criterion they used, and (c) recognise a group can be re-cut a different way. This is the conceptual seed of classification and, later, of variation — it teaches that categories are tools we impose to make sense of diversity.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete moving to relational). Pupils sort concrete/pictured organisms and articulate their criterion; the relational step is realising the SAME organism regroups under a new criterion. Success = groups one set two different ways and explains why the same animal moved groups.
bestPractices: Make the CRITERION explicit every time — always ask 'what rule are you grouping by?' so pupils see the rule, not the piles, is the point.
Have pupils group the SAME set at least two different ways so they experience that groups are not fixed.
Use a criterion that visibly moves one organism between groups (a frog: 'lives in water' vs 'has no fur') to make the choice-not-truth idea concrete.
Let pupils invent their own criteria and test them for consistency — ownership of the rule deepens the concept.
Introduce the vertebrate/invertebrate and animal-group vocabulary as ready-made criteria without letting them crowd out free grouping.
keyRepresentations: Sorting mat / bins with a selectable criterion header
The same organism shown in two different groups under two criteria (highlighted moving)
Feature cards per organism (covering, legs, diet, backbone) — the attributes to group by
Carroll/Venn-style two-way sort for a single criterion pair (e.g. has wings / lays eggs)
commonMisconceptions: Believing each organism has one 'correct' group it truly belongs to, rather than grouping being a choice of criterion.
Grouping by superficial similarity (colour, size) and treating that as equivalent to biologically meaningful features.
Thinking that if an animal moves groups the animal itself has changed, rather than the criterion changing.
Assuming 'lives in water' means 'is a fish' — conflating habitat with classification group.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, teach that grouping living things is a CHOICE of criterion, not a fixed truth: the same set of organisms can be validly grouped many ways (habitat, body covering, diet, number of legs, has-a-backbone), and the SAME organism lands in different groups depending on the rule used. The core learner work is to (a) group a set by at least two different criteria, (b) state the criterion used each time, and (c) recognise that one organism regroups when the criterion changes. This seeds classification and, later, variation. The central activity is an active re-sort; the alternatives support pre-teaching the attributes to sort by, checking placements, and defending a chosen rule in discussion.

activities.title: Multi-criteria sorting bench: group the same set two ways
feedback: If a learner treats one grouping as the 'real' one, show two valid groupings of the same set side by side using criteria they actually applied (e.g. by body covering; by diet) and ask which rule each pile follows — both are legitimate.
If a learner says the animal 'changed' when it moved piles, point back to the single organism and ask: 'What about the frog is different now? Or did only our rule change?'
If a learner sorts sensibly but cannot name the rule, ask 'What is the same about everything in this pile?' to surface the criterion already in use — scaffold, don't reteach.
If a learner sorts by colour or size, contrast that with fur/backbone and ask which features tell you more about the animals themselves.
activities.rationale: Grouping-as-choice is felt through active re-sorting of one set under successive rules; physically or on-screen dragging the same animals into new piles is intended to make the criterion, not the piles, the object of attention. A selectable criterion header and highlighting one organism as it moves between sorts make the mechanism concrete. A free-choice mode gives the learner ownership of the rule.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'Living things and their habitats' requires pupils to recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways.
Grouping by observable characteristics is the foundational classification skill; the same organism can belong to different groups depending on the criterion chosen.
learnerActions: Take a tray of 8–12 familiar organisms (pictured or on cards) and sort them into groups under one chosen rule, e.g. body covering: fur / feathers / scales / bare skin.
State out loud or write the rule you are grouping by before you start each sort.

Now change the criterion to 'what it eats', then to 'how many legs', then to 'lives in water or not', and re-sort the SAME animals each time; watch which animals leave one pile and join a different one.

Track one organism across the sorts you actually perform, e.g. a frog: under the body-covering sort it sits in the 'bare skin' pile, but under a 'lives in or near water' habitat sort it joins the fish (many adult frogs also spend time on land, so agree the rule's wording first) — note that the frog itself did not change, only the rule did.
As an extension, try a two-way (Carroll or Venn) sort that crosses two criteria at once, e.g. 'has wings' against 'lays eggs', and notice that where one organism lands depends on both rules together.
In a 'make your own group' mode, invent your own rule, sort by it, and check that every animal in a pile really shares that feature (test your rule for consistency).
activities.intendedInsight: Groups are not fixed labels stuck to each creature; a group is a tool we impose by choosing a criterion. The same organism belongs to different groups depending on the feature we sort by.

activities.title: Feature reveal: pre-teach the attributes you can sort by
feedback: If a learner cannot find a feature to group by, prompt them to compare two animals' feature cards and spot a shared attribute.
If a learner only notices colour/size, draw attention to covering, legs, diet and backbone as the biologically meaningful attributes.
activities.rationale: An annotated set where each organism reveals its features pre-teaches the sortable attributes so the later re-sort is about choosing rules, not discovering facts. This is a reference/pre-teach step: it supplies the attributes but does not itself let the learner experience grouping as a choice.
learnerActions: Look at each organism in the set and name its features: body covering, number of legs, diet, and whether it has a backbone.
Make a feature card for each organism recording those attributes (e.g. tapping a pictured organism to reveal a card, or writing one by hand).
Before sorting, predict which feature would put two particular animals in the same group and which would split them.
activities.intendedInsight: Before you can group by a rule, you need to know each organism's features — some you can see (body covering, number of legs) and some you find out (diet, whether it has a backbone) — and these attributes are what the rules act on.

activities.title: Check and defend: place, justify, and relate groupings
feedback: If a learner sorts a bat with birds because it flies, contrast flight (shared by unrelated animals) with fur/milk, and ask which features a bat shares with a dog that a robin does not.
If a learner insists each animal has one correct box, show the bat in both 'can fly' (with robin, butterfly) and 'feeds its young milk' (with dog, whale) and point out both sorts are valid.

If a learner concludes a whale 'is a fish', clarify that grouping it with fish only reflects the 'lives in water'/shape criterion, while breathing air and feeding its young milk group it with mammals and reflect how the animals are really related.
If a learner can't say why a placement is right, ask 'What rule did you use to decide?'
activities.rationale: Placement items and a 'defend your grouping' discussion let you check whether the learner can both sort and articulate the criterion, and whether they accept one organism in two groups. These check and extend the idea; recognition/placement alone does not, by itself, surface the criterion-is-a-choice insight, so pair it with the active re-sort and justification talk.
learnerActions: Place given organisms into vertebrates/invertebrates (or another named pair), then state the criterion that pair uses.
Use a two-way (Carroll/Venn) grid for a single criterion pair, e.g. 'has wings' and 'lays eggs', and explain why a chosen animal lands in its cell.

Answer: 'Does a whale go with the fish or with the dog? What does it depend on?' and explain your reasoning — grouping a whale with fish reflects only a 'lives in water'/body-shape criterion, while grouping it with the dog reflects 'breathes air / feeds its young milk', so the answer depends on the rule you choose.
Place the SAME animal into two different correct groups under two different criteria and say why each placement is right.
Discuss: 'Is there a wrong way to group these animals, or just different ways?' and 'Which grouping tells you more about how the animals are really related — can fly or feeds milk? Why?'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to place organisms correctly AND name the criterion, and to show one organism fits two groups, demonstrates that grouping depends on the chosen feature rather than a single hidden truth; some features (feeds milk) also reflect how animals are actually related.

constraints: Make the CRITERION explicit every time — always ask 'what rule are you grouping by?' so the rule, not the piles, is the focus.
Have learners group the SAME set at least two different ways so they experience that groups are not fixed.
Choose at least one criterion that visibly moves one organism between groups (e.g. a bat: 'can fly' puts it with birds, but 'has fur' puts it with dogs) to make choice-not-truth concrete.
Let learners invent their own criteria and test them for consistency to build ownership.
Introduce vertebrate/invertebrate and animal-group vocabulary as ready-made criteria without letting them crowd out free grouping.

Guard against conflating habitat with classification (e.g. 'lives in water' means 'is a fish') and against treating superficial similarity (colour, size) as equivalent to biologically meaningful features.

The feature-reveal step is a pre-teach scaffold: it supplies attributes but does not let the learner perform the re-sort that reveals grouping as a choice. Recognition/placement items check sorting but do not require independent construction of a new criterion; pair them with the active re-sort and a spoken or written justification. None of these media is asserted as universally superior to the others.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source claim (that grouping by observable characteristics is foundational and the same organism can belong to different groups) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its evidential weight cautiously even though it aligns with the verified DfE standard.

The original row asserted that a 3D medium 'adds nothing' and that sorting is 'better done by hand than described'. These are unproven catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and are not reproduced as universal claims. Hands-on dragging, on-screen dragging and spoken justification each offer different, complementary affordances with no proven superiority established here.

The whale example is treated as a criterion-dependent case (fish by habitat/shape vs mammal by fur/milk); ensure learners are not left believing a whale is a fish — the point is that the GROUP depends on the chosen feature, while fur/milk reflects how the animals are actually related.
The frog-tracking step follows the frog across criteria the learner actually applies (body covering and habitat), keeping the activity internally coherent.
The Carroll/Venn two-way sort (e.g. has wings / lays eggs) from the original representations was restored; it had been dropped in an earlier candidate.
Activity[0] feedback was adjusted so the two side-by-side groupings reference criteria run in that activity (body covering, diet) rather than 'flight', which is only used in the bat assessment case.

probeDeeper: Group these three by ONE feature, then re-group the same three by a DIFFERENT feature.
Does a whale go with the fish or with the dog? What does it depend on?
Is there a 'wrong' way to group these animals, or just different ways?
Which grouping tells you more about how the animals are really related — 'can fly' or 'feeds milk'? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: A bat is a mammal. But which GROUP it lands in depends on the criterion you sort by: group by 'can fly' and the bat joins the robin and butterfly; group by 'has fur / feeds milk' and it joins the dog and whale. The same organism belongs to different groups depending on the feature chosen — there is no single fixed grouping.

errorPatterns.pattern: Surface-similarity sorting — 'it flies like a robin, so a bat is a bird.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast flight (shared by unrelated animals) with fur/milk; ask which features a bat shares with a dog that a robin does not.
errorPatterns.distractor: A bat is a bird, because it flies like the robin.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assigns the bat to birds on the basis of flight alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Each animal has one correct group' — grouping is fixed, so you must pick the single right box.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show two valid groupings side by side (by flight, by fur); both are legitimate — the group depends on the sorting rule, not on one hidden truth.
errorPatterns.distractor: A bat can only be in one group — you have to pick the one right group for it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists the bat can only go in one group and there is a single right answer to which.

errorPatterns.pattern: Groups sensibly but cannot state the criterion — 'they just go together.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: ask 'what is the same about everything in this pile?' to surface the criterion already in use.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sorts correctly yet cannot name the feature the grouping is based on.

responseLevels.gap: Assigns one fixed group by surface features and rejects the idea of multiple groupings.
responseLevels.full: Groups by two or more criteria, names each criterion, and explains that the same organism belongs to different groups depending on the feature chosen, transferring the idea to the whale case.
responseLevels.partial: Groups by two criteria when prompted but treats one grouping as the 'real' one, or cannot state that the same organism moves between groups.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'A bat, a robin and a butterfly can all fly. But a bat, a dog and a whale all have fur or feed their babies milk. So which group does the bat belong in — and could it belong to more than one group? Explain how you decided.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks each animal has one 'true' group, or who sorts by surface resemblance ('it flies, so it's a bird'), cannot accept the bat in two different groupings. A child who understands grouping-by-criterion explains that the group changes with the feature you sort by — the whole point of this topic.

pedagogy.summary: Whole numbers are fractions too. Any whole number n equals n/1 (n wholes, each in one piece), and a fraction whose numerator is a multiple of its denominator equals a whole number (4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 6/3 = 2). This grows from a/b as iteration of 1/b: b copies of 1/b make one whole (b/b = 1). The number line unifies it — 4/4 and 1 are the same point — and the idea connects to division (a/b = a ÷ b).
bestPractices: Build b/b = 1 by iterating the unit fraction b times (four quarters fill exactly one whole).
Introduce n/1 as 'n wholes, each left in one piece' — a denominator of 1 means 'not cut'.
Use the number line to land 4/4 on 1 and 8/4 on 2.
Sort fractions into 'equals a whole number' vs 'not' (6/3, 8/4 vs 5/2).
Connect informally to division: 6/3 = 6 ÷ 3 = 2.
keyRepresentations: Number line (4/4 on 1, 8/4 on 2)
Iterating unit fractions to complete a whole (b/b = 1)
Area model with the whole fully shaded
Fraction-as-division link (a ÷ b)
commonMisconceptions: 'A fraction can't be a whole number / can't equal 1' — fractions are always 'parts', always less than one
Thinking 4/4 is a little less than 1, or reading it as 'four'
n/1 puzzling — treating a denominator of 1 as meaningless or as zero
Reading 8/4 as separate digits rather than as 2

learn.summary: Helps 8–9 year-olds see that whole numbers are fractions too: any whole number n equals n/1, and a fraction whose numerator is a multiple of its denominator equals a whole number (4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 6/3 = 2, 6/1 = 6). The core insight grows from iterating a unit fraction — b copies of 1/b make one whole, so b/b = 1 — and is unified on the number line, where 4/4 and 1 sit at the same point. The idea connects informally to division (a/b = a ÷ b). It is designed to address the misconception that fractions are always 'parts' less than one.

activities.title: Iterate quarters until a fraction lands on a whole number
feedback: If the marker is placed short of 1 for 4/4: lay the four quarter pieces end to end — they fill exactly one whole with nothing missing and nothing left over, so 4/4 sits exactly on 1, not before it.
If 8/4 is read as 'eight' or as separate digits: count the quarters as you stack — it takes four to reach 1 and four more to reach 2, so 8/4 lands on 2.
Prompt: 'How many quarters do you need to make exactly one whole? What fraction is that?' to reinforce b/b = 1.
activities.rationale: b copies of the unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built by iterating 1/b; placing whole numbers and fractions on the same number line lets 4/4 and 1 be seen as the same point, countering the idea that fractions are always less than one. Live iteration makes the moment of completion visible; a static families chart or an area model can also show b/b = 1 for recall but do not show the completion unfolding.
sourceClaims: b copies of a unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built from unit fractions; number lines should place whole numbers, proper and improper fractions together so that e.g. 4/4 and 1 occupy the same point; treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception.
learnerActions: Starting from 0 on a number line, add one quarter piece at a time and read the running total: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 …
As the fourth quarter is added, check where the marker lands and name the fraction there (4/4) and the whole number at that point (1).
Keep stacking quarters past one whole and find where 8/4 lands (on 2), noticing it took eight quarters — two full wholes' worth.
Say in your own words how many quarters make exactly one whole, and complete b/b = 1 for quarters (4/4 = 1).
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction can land exactly on a whole number: four quarters compose one whole, so 4/4 IS 1, and 8/4 IS 2. This happens whenever the numerator is a multiple of the denominator.

activities.title: A denominator of 1 means 'not cut': writing whole numbers as fractions
feedback: If a denominator of 1 seems meaningless or like zero: a cut into 1 piece leaves the whole intact, so 5/1 is five whole, uncut bars — not nothing.
If the child cannot write 5 as a fraction: ask how many pieces each whole is cut into when it is left whole (one), then the numerator counts the wholes: 5/1.
Check placement: 5/1 should sit on the 5 mark, confirming 5/1 = 5.
activities.rationale: Expressing whole numbers as fractions (3 = 3/1) and recognising fractions equivalent to whole numbers are stated Year 3 expectations in the cited curriculum; framing a denominator of 1 as 'in one piece' addresses the specific n/1 confusion where a denominator of 1 seems meaningless.
sourceClaims: In Year 3 (age 8–9) pupils recognise fractions equivalent to whole numbers and begin to express whole numbers as fractions.
learnerActions: Work with whole, uncut bars and read a denominator of 1 as 'the whole is left in one piece'.
Write the number 5 as a fraction (5/1) and explain that it means five wholes, each uncut.
Place 5/1 on a number line at 5, and 3/1 at 3, checking they land on the whole-number marks.
Explain what the bottom number 1 is telling you when you write 3 = 3/1.
activities.intendedInsight: A denominator of 1 is meaningful: it says the whole has not been cut, so n/1 is simply n wholes. Every whole number can be written as a fraction.

activities.title: Sort fractions: whole number or not?
feedback: If 5/2 is called a whole number 'because 5 and 2 are both whole numbers': 5 ÷ 2 is not exact — 5 is not a multiple of 2 — so 5/2 lands at 2½, between the whole numbers, not on one.
If 6/3 is mishandled: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 exactly, and three thirds make one whole so six thirds make two wholes; 6/3 lands on 2.
Prompt: 'Is 5/2 a whole number? Where does it land, and what does that tell you?'
activities.rationale: Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception; relating a/b to a ÷ b and testing the multiple relationship generalises beyond the single case b/b = 1 to a·b/b. Sorting and matching tasks are suited to checking and consolidating classification once the completion idea has been built; a sort by itself does not elicit the child building a whole or explaining why.
sourceClaims: b copies of a unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built from unit fractions; number lines should place whole numbers, proper and improper fractions together so that e.g. 4/4 and 1 occupy the same point; treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception.
learnerActions: Decide for each of 6/3, 8/4 and 5/2 whether it equals a whole number, and sort them into 'equals a whole number' vs 'not'.
For each, test whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, using division: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 8 ÷ 4 = 2, 5 ÷ 2 is not a whole number.
Place 5/2 on a number line to show it lands at 2½, between 2 and 3.
Match 8/4 to the whole number 2 and explain how you knew.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction equals a whole number exactly when the numerator is a multiple of the denominator; a/b can be read as a ÷ b. Having both digits be whole numbers (as in 5/2) does not make the fraction a whole number.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: where does 4/4 land?
feedback: If the prediction was 'before 1' because 'a fraction is always less than one': the four quarters fill exactly one whole with nothing left over, landing on 1 — so a fraction CAN equal a whole number.
Confirm the generalisation: this works whenever the numerator is a multiple of the denominator (4/4, 8/4, 6/3), not just for this one case.
If the reason given before observing was correct, ask the child to predict where 8/4 lands to extend the rule.
activities.rationale: The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part: a child who thinks fractions are always parts less than one predicts before 1, and iterating the quarters directly contradicts that belief by landing exactly on 1. Predict-then-check with a reason is proposed to surface the misconception rather than only assess the answer.
sourceClaims: b copies of a unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built from unit fractions; number lines should place whole numbers, proper and improper fractions together so that e.g. 4/4 and 1 occupy the same point; treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception.
learnerActions: Before doing anything, PREDICT with a reason whether 4/4 lands before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 on a number line, and state your reason out loud or in writing first.
Then iterate four 1/4-jumps from 0 (or build four quarters) and observe where you land.
Compare what happened to your prediction, and revise your reason if needed.
State the general rule you now believe about whether a fraction can equal a whole number.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before observing surfaces the belief 'fractions are always parts less than one'; building four quarters that fill exactly one whole and land on 1 contradicts it.

constraints: Multiple-choice, matching and slider tasks (e.g. 'which equal whole numbers: 6/3, 8/4, 5/2?', matching 8/4 → 2, placing 4/4 on a line, filling in 5 = ?/1) are suited to classifying and recall once the idea is built, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit the child constructing the whole by iteration or explaining why; pair them with building or explanation.

A static reference (tap 4/4 → 'four quarters = one whole = 1', flip-to-reveal 8/4 = 2) can support recall of b/b = 1 families but does not show the completion of a whole unfolding; use it as a reference alongside the iteration activity, not as a replacement.

An area model with the whole fully shaded (e.g. four shaded quarters filling one square) is another valid representation of b/b = 1 alongside the number line and the stacked/length model; use whichever makes 'four quarters compose one whole' concrete for the child.

Paper or card quarter pieces have slight real thickness and are a physical model of the ideal mathematical idea; treat the stacked pieces as a way of composing one whole, and keep the exact number-line point as the mathematical meaning.
Ensure the child generalises beyond the single memorised case b/b = 1 to a·b/b (e.g. 8/4, 6/3); accepting 4/4 = 1 alone is partial understanding.
Use the fraction-as-division link (a/b = a ÷ b) informally at this age, as a test for whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, not as a formal algorithm.
Treat fractions as numbers that share one number line with the whole numbers; the task is to compare and place their values, not to require redrawing a common whole.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The first listed source (IES/WWC Practice Guide) is marked verified:true in the row; the second (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified:false. The Year 3 curriculum claim used in activity 2 should be treated as unconfirmed in this rewrite.

The predict-then-check routine in activity 4 is a design proposal; the cited sources support that iteration on a number line refutes the 'less than one' belief, but do not establish the comparative effectiveness of reason-before-observing.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 6/3 = 2, 6/1 = 6, and 5/2 = 2½ (between 2 and 3) are all correct and retained. No arithmetic errors found.
The area model representation listed in the source's key representations is carried as an alternative representation constraint alongside the number line and length model.

The non-preferred 3D-interactive and conversation catalog entries were dropped as ranking judgements, not pedagogical laws; a denominator of 1 and the fraction-as-division idea could in principle also be discussed verbally as support, so no categorical 'only building teaches' claim is asserted.

Independent re-audit confirms no 'denominator flips' comparison, no categorical modality claim, and that the physical-cutout thickness/ideal-figure distinction is stated in the activity-facing constraints, not only in a reviewer note.

assess.poeTask: Ask the child to PREDICT, with a reason, whether 4/4 lands before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 on a number line. The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part — a child who thinks fractions are always 'parts less than one' predicts before 1. Then iterate four 1/4-jumps from 0 (or build four quarters): they fill exactly one whole and land on 1, refuting 'a fraction must be less than 1'.
probeDeeper: How many quarters do you need to make exactly one whole? What fraction is that?
Where does 8/4 go on the line — and why is it the same place as 2?
Is 5/2 a whole number? Where does it land, and what does that tell you?
Write the number 3 as a fraction. What does the bottom number 1 mean?
assess.correctAnswer: 4/4 = 1 — four quarters make one whole, so it lands exactly on 1. Whole numbers: 6/3 = 2 and 8/4 = 2 (the numerator is a multiple of the denominator: 6÷3 = 2, 8÷4 = 2). 5/2 is not a whole number (5 is not a multiple of 2; it lands at 2½, between 2 and 3).

errorPatterns.pattern: Fractions are always parts / always less than 1 — '4/4 is a bit less than 1, it's still a fraction'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iterate four quarters to fill exactly one whole; land 4/4 on the 1 mark; name b/b = 1
errorPatterns.distractor: 4/4 is a little less than 1 — it's a fraction, not a whole number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 4/4 short of 1; denies a fraction can equal a whole number

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — 'if both digits are whole numbers the fraction is a whole number', so 5/2 counts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Relate a/b to a ÷ b and to iterating on the line; test whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator
errorPatterns.distractor: 5/2 is a whole number because 5 and 2 are both whole numbers
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls 5/2 a whole number, or cannot see 8/4 = 2

errorPatterns.pattern: n/1 confusion — a denominator of 1 seems meaningless, so cannot write 5 as 5/1
errorPatterns.nextMove: A denominator of 1 means the whole is in one piece, so 5/1 is five wholes; place 5/1 on the line at 5
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot express a whole number as a fraction, or misreads 5/1

responseLevels.gap: Believes fractions are always less than 1; places 4/4 before 1; reads 8/4 and 5/2 by their separate digits.
responseLevels.full: Places 4/4 on 1 and explains b copies of 1/b make a whole; identifies 6/3 and 8/4 as whole numbers (numerator a multiple of the denominator / a ÷ b) and 5/2 as not; writes a whole number as n/1.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts 4/4 = 1 but cannot reliably identify 6/3 and 8/4 as whole numbers or explain n/1 — knows the single case b/b = 1 without generalising to a·b/b.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 4/4 equal to 1, or less than 1? Put a dot where 4/4 goes on this 0-to-2 number line and explain why it lands there. Then: which of these are whole numbers — 6/3, 8/4, 5/2 — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands b/b = 1 and a/b as iteration places 4/4 on 1 and identifies 6/3 and 8/4 as whole numbers. A child who believes fractions are always less than 1 puts 4/4 short of 1; a whole-number-bias child mishandles 6/3 or calls 5/2 a whole number by reading the digits separately.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2). Using addition to find the total in rectangular arrays (up to 5×5) and writing an equation expressing the total as a sum of EQUAL ADDENDS — the array-to-repeated-addition bridge.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'solve problems … using … arrays, repeated addition …'; recorded with × signs as tables develop (Y2–Y3).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 'use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends'.
• Operational details: read the array by ROWS — each row is an equal addend — and write 4+4+4 (three rows of four), then connect to 3×4. Emphasise the addends are EQUAL (that's what makes it a multiplication situation). This formalises the array as the pivot between addition and multiplication.
• Checkpoint: array → equal-addend equation. Tier A (7): count an array's total by adding rows. Tier B (7–8): write the equal-addend equation (4+4+4=12) for a 3-row array. Tier C (8): write both the addition and the multiplication for an array and explain the addends must be equal.
bestPractices: Read the array row by row so each row becomes one equal addend, then write the repeated-addition equation — making 'sum of equal addends' concrete before the × symbol.
Stress that the addends must be EQUAL: contrast an array (equal rows) with a ragged arrangement (unequal rows) that is NOT a multiplication situation.
Bridge to the × symbol by pairing the equal-addend equation with the multiplication (4+4+4 alongside 3×4), so children see multiplication as the shorthand.
Read the same array by columns too, foreshadowing commutativity (three 4s or four 3s).
Keep arrays within 5×5 and physically buildable, so the structure (rows/columns) is clear and countable.
keyRepresentations: Rectangular array read row-by-row (each row = one equal addend)
Repeated-addition equation (4 + 4 + 4 = 12)
Paired addition/multiplication (4+4+4 ↔ 3×4)
Ragged (unequal-row) non-example for contrast
commonMisconceptions: Adding UNEQUAL groups and still writing it as a single multiplication (missing the equal-addends requirement).
Counting every object individually rather than adding equal rows.
Confusing the number of rows with the number in each row when writing the equation.
Not connecting the repeated-addition equation to the multiplication (seeing them as separate).
Miscounting by losing track of which rows have been added (no systematic row-by-row approach).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2): use addition to find the total of objects in a rectangular array (up to 5×5) and write an equation expressing the total as a sum of EQUAL addends, then bridge to the multiplication fact. The core insight is that each row of the array contributes one equal addend, so reading an array row by row turns it into repeated addition (4+4+4=12) and then into 3×4. Equality of the rows is what makes it a multiplication situation, so a ragged (unequal-row) arrangement serves as the key non-example.

activities.title: Sum the rows: build the equal-addend equation from an array
feedback: If the child writes 3+4 (rows plus row-size): shade one row to show it holds 4, then show that same 4 repeats for every row → 4+4+4. Name clearly that 'number of rows' and 'amount in each row' are two different things; the equation adds the row-amount once per row.

If the child gives the correct sum but justifies it only as 'because it makes 12': cover the rows one at a time so each shows the same 4, and name that the rows being equal is exactly what lets you add 4 repeatedly instead of counting every dot.

If the child insists on counting every dot and distrusts the shortcut: do NOT force the shortcut. Let them verify by counting a few arrays so repeated addition earns their trust over several examples.

For the ragged arrangement: confirm that because the rows are not equal you cannot write one repeated-equal-addend equation, so it is not a multiplication situation — this is the point of the contrast.
activities.rationale: Assembling 4+4+4 row by row makes 'sum of equal addends' concrete before the × symbol, and pairing it with 3×4 presents multiplication as shorthand for adding equal rows. Reading by columns previews commutativity (three 4s vs four 3s), and the ragged non-example isolates the equal-addends requirement that defines a multiplication situation.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems using arrays and repeated addition, recorded with multiplication signs as tables develop.
2.OA.4 use addition to find the total in rectangular arrays (up to 5×5) and write an equation expressing the total as a sum of equal addends.
learnerActions: Look at a 3×4 array (3 rows, 4 dots in each row) and point to one row to establish that it holds 4 dots.
Add the array one row at a time, saying and writing the running total: 4, then 4+4, then 4+4+4 = 12 — one addend per row.
After writing 4+4+4=12, write the matching multiplication 3×4=12 and say which number tells how many rows and which tells how many are in each row.
Read the same array by columns instead and write it as 3+3+3+3 (four 3s), noticing you get 12 again.
Now try a ragged arrangement where one row has 4 and another has 5; attempt to write a single equal-addend equation and explain why it will not form.
activities.intendedInsight: Each equal row of an array is one equal addend, so adding the rows gives the total; the multiplication fact is just the shorthand for adding equal rows, and this only works when the rows are equal.

activities.title: Draw an array for a given equation
feedback: If the number of rows and the amount per row get swapped, have the child count the addends in the equation (how many 5s? four) and match that to the number of rows drawn.
If rows are drawn unequal, point out that the equation uses the same number each time, so every row must hold the same amount.
activities.rationale: Constructing an array from a given equation requires producing structure rather than recognising it, strengthening the array↔equation bridge in both directions.
learnerActions: Given the equation 5+5+5+5, draw a rectangular array that matches it (four rows of five, or equivalently five columns of four).
Say aloud which part of the equation is the number of rows and which is the amount in each row.
Write the multiplication fact for your array (4×5 or 5×4) and check the total matches 20.
Explain why your drawing shows equal rows and how that connects back to the repeated addition.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can move in both directions — from array to equation and from equation to array — which shows they understand the equal-groups structure rather than just reading one off the other.

activities.title: Match and complete: array ↔ equal-addend equation ↔ multiplication
feedback: If a learner picks the unequal-addend distractor, draw the arrangement that equation would represent and shade its rows to show they are not equal, so it does not match the equal-rows array and cannot be written as one repeated-equal-addend equation.
If the addition and multiplication are seen as unrelated, place 4+4+4 beside 3×4 and count: three rows, four in each — the multiplication summarises the addition.
activities.rationale: Fill-in and matching tasks check the bridge crisply and surface whether a child still confuses adding equal rows with adding unequal groups. These are checks of recognition and completion; they confirm understanding but do not by themselves require independent construction, so pair them with the drawing and build-the-equation activities.
learnerActions: For a shown array, fill in the blanks of the equal-addend equation (__ + __ + __ = __).
Write the matching multiplication fact for the same array.

From a set of candidate equations, choose the one that matches a given equal-rows array; include a distractor that uses unequal addends (e.g., 3+4+5), which would correspond to a ragged arrangement and does not match.
Explain why the unequal-addend distractor cannot represent the equal-rows array as a single equal-addend equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and completing the correct equal-addend equation (and rejecting an unequal-addend distractor) confirms the array-to-repeated-addition bridge and the equal-addends requirement.

constraints: Keep arrays within 5×5 and physically buildable (counters, dots, or drawn grids) so rows and columns stay clear and countable.
Emphasise throughout that the addends must be EQUAL; always contrast the array with a ragged, unequal-row arrangement that is NOT a multiplication situation.

Matching/fill-in tasks assess recognition and completion; they do not on their own elicit independent construction of an array or equation, so include at least one task where the child builds an array from an equation or assembles the equation from scratch.

A static labelled array (tap- or lift-to-reveal addends and the × fact) is a useful reference and shows the bridge, but does not let the child build the sum row by row or test the equal-addends requirement dynamically; treat it as a scaffold, not a replacement for building.
Do not push the repeated-addition shortcut on a child who still needs to count every object to trust it; let repeated addition earn trust through several verified examples.

If optional on-screen interaction is used (tapping a row to drop its value into a running equation, a 'fold'/combine action collapsing 4+4+4 into 3×4, a rotate control to read by columns, a ragged-array mode), these are illustrative mechanisms to make the bridge visible, not required tooling.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The second listed source (CCSS-M 2.OA.4) is marked verified:false in the row; the exact-claim citations are carried over as-is and their verification status is unchanged.

Activity 2 (equation→array drawing) corresponds to the row's evidence item 'Draw a rectangular array to model a given repeated-addition equation', but no cited source claim directly supports the reverse-construction principle, so its sourceClaims is [] (topic-aligned, not evidence the reverse task is required).

Planar vs 3D: the original row asserts '3D adds nothing' and that dialogue 'adds little unique value'. These are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the sources; they have been dropped as universal laws. Arrays are naturally planar, so a flat representation fits the content, but no claim is made that other media cannot teach it.

Arithmetic self-check performed: 4+4+4=12 and 3×4=12 are correct; reading the same 3×4 array by columns gives 3+3+3+3=12 (four 3s), consistent with the commutativity preview. The 5+5+5+5 drawing example corresponds to 4×5=20. The Activity 3 distractor 3+4+5 sums to 12 (same total, unequal addends), a valid equal-addends discriminator.
The misconception '3+4' is handled as a clear conceptual error: the activity feedback corrects it (row-count vs row-size) rather than presenting it as a valid alternative.

Activity 3's equation-matching distractor is an unequal-addend equation (not a loosely described 'arrangement'), so the choice set stays internally consistent; its feedback draws and shades the represented ragged arrangement to show the rows are unequal.

probeDeeper: Which number in 4 + 4 + 4 is the amount in a row, and which tells how many rows?
Draw an array for 5 + 5 + 5 + 5.
If one row had 4 and another had 5, could you still add the same number each time?
How would you write this array as a multiplication?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — every row has the same number, 4, and there are 3 rows, so the total is 4 added three times. Equal rows let you add the row-amount repeatedly instead of counting every dot.

errorPatterns.pattern: adds the dimensions, not the equal rows — writes something like 3 + 4 (row-count plus row-size) instead of repeated equal addends
errorPatterns.nextMove: shade one row (4), then show it repeats 3 times → 4 + 4 + 4; distinguish the number of rows from the amount in each row
errorPatterns.distractor: 3 + 4 works because there are 3 rows and 4 in each.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: an addition that isn't repeated equal addends

errorPatterns.pattern: agrees the sum but not the reason — accepts 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 yet justifies only 'because it makes 12', not because the rows are equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: cover the rows one at a time to show each contributes the same 4; name equality as what licenses repeated addition
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct sum with no equal-rows reason

errorPatterns.pattern: counts by ones only — insists you must count every dot; repeated addition feels untrustworthy
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT push the shortcut — let the child verify by counting a few times so repeated addition earns trust; the shortcut is adopted with experience
errorPatterns.revealedBy: won't accept 4 + 4 + 4 without counting to confirm

responseLevels.gap: Can only get the total by counting every object; can't connect it to repeated addition.
responseLevels.full: Explains repeated addition works because every row holds the same number, and moves between array, equal-addends sum, and multiplication.
responseLevels.partial: Writes or accepts the repeated-addition equation but doesn't ground it in the rows being equal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at this array — 3 rows with 4 dots in each row. Sam counted the dots one by one and got 12. Priya wrote 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 without counting them all. Is Priya's way correct, and why does adding 4 three times work for this array?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the array's equal-groups structure explains that repeated addition works BECAUSE the rows are equal. A child without it accepts 12 as 'the count' but can't say why 4 + 4 + 4 matches, or writes an addition that ignores equal rows (e.g. 3 + 4). The 'why does adding 4 three times work' tier forces the equal-addends reasoning.
