pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Pushes & Pulls

- **Standards — UK (DfE — no discrete KS1 forces unit; first statutory at Year 3):** England has no Key Stage 1 forces programme of study — 'forces as pushes or pulls' is first statutory at Year 3 (KS2). At 5–6 push/pull is met informally through play and EYFS 'Understanding the World', alongside the statutory KS1 Working Scientifically skills (observing closely, performing simple tests).

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-PS2-1; DCI PS2.A):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-1] (assessment limited to relative strengths OR directions, not both at once, and excludes non-contact pushes/pulls such as magnets). DCI PS2.A: [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-1, K-PS2-2].

- **Operational details:** At ages 5-6, forces are introduced concretely as PUSHES and PULLS: actions that can start an object moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, or change its direction. Children compare a gentle push with a strong push on the same object (bigger push → bigger change) and notice that an object tends to move in the direction it is pushed or pulled. The teaching is overwhelmingly hands-on — children act on real objects and describe what happens. Crucially, this is where the lifelong 'impetus' misconception is seeded (the idea that a moving thing carries a 'force' inside it that runs out), so even at this age good teaching frames a push/pull as something ONE thing does to ANOTHER, and gently introduces that things stop because something pushes back (friction), not because the push 'runs out'.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational).
bestPractices: Lead with hands-on play: push/pull toy cars, balls, trolleys, doors, swings, drawers — children feel and cause the effect before naming it.
Use precise words from the start — push, pull, force — and narrate effects ('your push made it speed up / change direction').
Predict-then-do: 'Which way will it go? What if you push harder?' then act and compare — building evidence for strength and direction effects.
Compare systematically: same object, vary ONE thing (gentle vs strong; push from different sides) so the effect of strength and of direction is isolated.
Start from children's own ideas as 'anchoring conceptions' to build on, rather than just correcting wrong statements (sense-making conversation).
Begin to counter the impetus seed: when something rolls to a stop, attribute it to a push-back from the ground/air (friction), not to force 'running out'.
keyRepresentations: Real manipulable objects (the primary 'representation' at this age — balls, cars, trolleys)
Push/pull picture sorts (classify everyday actions)
Simple direction arrows showing which way the push/pull acts (seed of the force-arrow representation)
Before/after motion pictures (object at rest → moving; fast → slow)
commonMisconceptions: Only living/animate things can push or pull (a table or wall can't exert a force).
There is only a force if you can see movement — a push that doesn't visibly move something 'isn't a force'.
Impetus seed: a moving object has 'force' or 'go' stored inside it that gradually runs out, which is why it stops (MOSART; RESPeCT Grade 3).
Force is the same as the object's energy / a property the object owns, rather than an interaction between two objects.
A bigger push makes something go faster and faster forever (constant push → ever-increasing or fixed speed confusion, in seed form).

learn.summary: Help 5-6 year-olds experience that a push or pull is a force one thing does to another that can start, stop, speed up, slow down, or turn an object, and that a bigger push makes a bigger change. From rest, a push strong enough to move a free object such as a ball starts it moving in the direction it is pushed, while a sideways tap on an already-moving ball bends its existing path in the direction the tap pushes. Centre real hands-on play with objects, predict-then-do comparisons that vary one thing at a time, and begin to attribute stopping to a push-back from the ground/air (friction) rather than a force 'running out'. Screen or picture activities act as complements and light checks, not replacements for physical play.

activities.title: Flick-and-push play: feel a bigger push make a bigger change
feedback: When a child says 'it went faster', reflect the cause: 'Your bigger push made it speed up more.'
If a child thinks every push is the same, line up two identical balls at rest, tap one and shove the other, race them, and let them see strength map to speed before naming it.

If a child says the heavy and light ball move the same with the same push, repeat the same gentle push on two similar-sized balls and watch together. When the lighter ball goes faster or further, name it: 'The same push makes a bigger change to the lighter ball.'
When something rolls to a stop on the floor or carpet, say the ground (or carpet/air) is pushing back and rubbing against it to slow it, rather than the push 'running out'.
(Optional screen cue) A soft coast-to-stop with a 'the ground pushes back' prompt can quietly reinforce that things stop because something opposes them.
activities.rationale: The concept is cause-and-effect on motion, so children should act on real objects and immediately observe the response; varying one thing (gentle vs strong, same push on heavy vs light, or push direction) isolates each effect. An interactive screen version can let a child vary strength and direction and see the object respond, but it complements rather than replaces physical play.
sourceClaims: Forces cause changes in motion; if an object is moving no force is needed to keep it moving, but a force is needed to stop it or change direction; objects don't contain force and can't run out of it; everyday stopping is due to friction. Build on children's intuitive 'anchoring conceptions' rather than simply correcting.
learnerActions: Push and pull real objects (balls, toy cars, trolleys, a door, a drawer) and say out loud what happened: did it start, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction?
With two identical balls at rest, tap one gently and shove the other hard at the same time; watch which travels faster and further.

With the same gentle push (for example, the same flick from the same spot), compare a heavier ball and a lighter ball of about the same size (for example, a solid rubber ball and a hollow plastic ball), and notice how far and fast each goes. The same push usually changes the lighter ball's motion more.

Push a ball from different sides and notice that, from rest, it moves off in the direction you pushed it; once it is rolling, give it a sideways tap and watch its path bend in the direction the tap pushes it.
Predict before acting: 'Which way will it go? What happens if I push harder?' Then do it and compare with your prediction.

(Optional screen companion) In a tap-and-flick play space, drag a stretchy aimer back further to push harder and release to send a ball off; set up a side-by-side 'gentle vs strong' race on identical balls and watch the hard-pushed one go faster and further.
activities.intendedInsight: A push or pull is a force that changes how an object moves; a stronger push makes a bigger change to the motion. From rest, a push strong enough to move a free object such as a ball starts it moving in the direction it is pushed, while a sideways tap on an already-moving ball bends its existing path in the direction the tap pushes.

activities.title: Compare smooth vs rough: why things stop
feedback: If a child predicts 'the same because I pushed the same', point to the carpet stopping the ball sooner and name the rough surface rubbing as the cause.
If a child explains continued rolling by a push 'stored inside', gently point to the floor/carpet rubbing as what slows it; expect this idea to come back and revisit it on slippery vs rough floors.
When a cushion slows the already-rolling ball, name it: 'The cushion pushed back against the ball and slowed it — that push changed its motion.'
activities.rationale: Comparing the same push on two surfaces sets up friction as an observable cause of stopping (both surfaces here have appreciable friction, which is why the ball slows and stops) and begins to counter the 'impetus' idea that a moving object carries a force that runs out. Formal inertia is not taught at this age.
sourceClaims: Elementary students believe a moving object contains a force given by an outside source and stops when that force 'runs out'; force is wrongly seen as a property inside the object rather than an interaction between two objects.

Forces cause changes in motion; if an object is moving no force is needed to keep it moving, but a force is needed to stop it or change direction; objects don't contain force and can't run out of it; everyday stopping is due to friction. Build on children's intuitive 'anchoring conceptions' rather than simply correcting.
learnerActions: Give one ball the same push on a smooth floor and then on a rough carpet.
Before each roll, predict which will travel further and say why.
Watch the carpet ball stop sooner and talk about what was different between the two surfaces.
Try to slow a ball that is already rolling toward you without catching it (for example, hold a cushion in its path).
activities.intendedInsight: Things slow and stop because a surface (or air) rubs against them and pushes back — friction — not because the push is used up inside the object.

activities.title: Pushes slow and turn, not just start
feedback: If a child says a push can only make things go or go faster, demonstrate a cushion pushing against an already-rolling ball (slowing) and a sideways tap on a rolling ball (bending its path), and name both as the push changing the motion.
Reinforce by asking the child to narrate each effect in their own words.
activities.rationale: Children often think a push can only start or speed up motion; demonstrating slowing and turning as the same force broadens their idea of what a force does. This addresses a documented misconception for this age.
sourceClaims: Forces cause changes in motion; if an object is moving no force is needed to keep it moving, but a force is needed to stop it or change direction; objects don't contain force and can't run out of it; everyday stopping is due to friction. Build on children's intuitive 'anchoring conceptions' rather than simply correcting.
learnerActions: Take a ball that is already rolling and find a way to slow it down before it arrives (hold a cushion in its path).
Give a ball that is already rolling a sideways tap and watch its path bend in the direction the tap pushes it.
Say which of these a push can do: start it, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, change its direction — and show an example of each with a real object.
activities.intendedInsight: A push or pull is the same kind of force whether it starts, speeds up, slows, stops, or turns an object; slowing and turning are the force acting, not something different.

activities.title: Name pushes and pulls around us
feedback: Confirm correct sorts and, for mistakes, mime the action together to decide whether you are pushing away or pulling toward.
When predicting direction for an object at rest, link it back: 'If the push is strong enough and nothing holds it in place, it starts to move the way the push points.'
activities.rationale: Picture sorts and scene labelling are good vocabulary companions and a light check of direction prediction, but they do not let a child feel that a harder push makes a bigger change, so they supplement physical play rather than carry the core idea. Reading load is a real constraint at 5-6, so use audio or adult support.
learnerActions: Sort picture cards of everyday actions into PUSH and PULL (with an adult reading or audio support).
Look at a playground or home scene and point out where someone is pushing and where someone is pulling (for example, pulling a child on a swing, pushing a trolley).
For a pictured object at rest about to be pushed, point which way it will start to move.
Use the words push, pull, and force as you describe what is happening.
activities.intendedInsight: Pushes and pulls happen all around us; naming them and reading the direction of the force builds the vocabulary that supports the hands-on experiences.

constraints: Keep the teaching overwhelmingly hands-on with real objects; screen and picture activities complement, not replace, physical push/pull play.
Picture sorts and recognition activities can support vocabulary and direction prediction, but do not elicit the child independently producing and feeling a push; pair them with physical play.
Reading load is a real constraint at 5-6; use audio support or an adult reader for any picture-sort activity.
Do not teach formal inertia or Newtonian terminology; frame everything concretely as what one thing does to another.
Frame a push/pull as something ONE thing does to ANOTHER object, and attribute stopping to a push-back (friction), to avoid seeding the 'force runs out' / 'force stored inside' misconception.
The 'impetus' idea is expected to return; plan to revisit and gently re-challenge it across contexts rather than expecting a single correction to settle it.

A push strong enough to move a free object at rest, such as a ball, starts it moving in the push direction (objects on a hinge or track, like a door or drawer, can only move the way they are guided); a sideways tap on an already-rolling ball bends its existing path in the direction the tap pushes (away from the tapping hand) — do not imply a single side push instantly makes travel point exactly in the push direction. State the object's starting motion (at rest or already rolling) whenever predicting an effect.
The smooth/rough coasting comparison models surfaces with appreciable friction, which is why the ball slows and stops; name that rubbing as the cause rather than a used-up push.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled the 3D 'knock-over-the-blocks' option as adding 'production cost without conceptual gain' and the conversation format as unable to deliver the experience; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have not been carried in as universal claims. Tactile 3D or spatial play can be worthwhile if that experience is itself a goal.

The claim that 'live recompute is the whole point' and that a static scene 'cannot' teach the strength effect is a catalog preference; retained only as a narrowly scoped affordance (interactive feedback makes the effect vivid), not as proof that static media cannot teach it.
Two of the three sources (MOSART and RESPeCT Grade 3) are marked verified:false in the row; treat the impetus/friction claims as plausible but not independently confirmed here.

The 'correctAnswer' in the assessment frames a strong push as what makes a ball reach the target 'quickly'; this is fine as an age-appropriate speed/direction link, but note that at this age children should reason about changes to motion rather than steady-state speed.

The same-push heavy-vs-light comparison is taught in the conventional age-appropriate form (the lighter object moves more for the same push); it is a simple demonstration, not a friction-controlled result.

Summary and the first activity's intendedInsight originally stated unconditionally that the push direction sets the direction of travel; this has been scoped to starting an object from rest (with a sideways tap bending a moving object's path) to match the physics and the stated constraints.

assess.poeTask: Give one ball the same push on a smooth floor and on a rough carpet. Before rolling, ask the child to predict which travels further and WHY. Many predict 'the same, because I pushed the same' or 'it stops when the push runs out'; seeing the carpet ball stop sooner sets up friction (the ground rubbing) as the cause rather than a used-up push.
probeDeeper: If you push it only gently, will it still reach me? What will be different?
Now it's rolling toward me — show me a way to slow it down before it arrives, without catching it.
A heavy football and a light beach ball each get the same push — will they move the same? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Give it a hard/strong push in my direction. A stronger push makes it speed up more, so a hard push makes it go faster than a gentle one; the push is the force that starts it moving and sets how fast it goes.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'How hard you push doesn't change anything — a little tap and a big shove make it roll the same.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up two identical balls, tap one gently and shove the other, and race them so the child SEES strength map to speed, then name it.
errorPatterns.distractor: It doesn't matter how hard you push — the ball rolls the same either way.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In tier 2 the child cannot say a stronger push gives more speed; treats every push as equivalent.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The ball keeps rolling because the push is still inside it, and it stops when the push runs out.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't teach formal inertia; point to the floor/carpet rubbing (friction) as what slows it, and revisit on a slippery vs rough floor. Expect this idea to return and challenge it repeatedly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains continued motion by a force stored in the ball rather than the hand's push having ended.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A push can only make something go or go faster — it can't slow something down or turn it.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate a cushion pushing against a rolling ball (slowing) and a sideways tap (turning); name both as the push changing the motion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to slow or steer a rolling ball, says you can only stop it by grabbing it, or that a push can't change direction.

responseLevels.gap: Says only 'push it' with no link between how hard the push is and how the ball moves, or claims the push amount is irrelevant; may say a push can't slow or turn things.
responseLevels.full: Explains that a push or pull is a force that changes motion and that a bigger force makes a bigger change — a strong push speeds it up more, an opposing push slows it, a sideways push turns it — and predicts direction from the direction of the push, transferring to a new object.
responseLevels.partial: Knows a harder push makes it go faster and can aim the push toward the target, but treats a push only as 'making it go' — lists effects (start, faster) without seeing slowing and turning as the same force acting.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: This ball is sitting still on the floor. If you want it to roll over to me quickly, what would you do to it — and why does doing that make it go fast instead of slow?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tell is in the 'why'. A child who grasps that a force changes motion connects a HARDER push to MORE speed and aims the push toward the target. A child who thinks the amount of push doesn't matter, that you must push repeatedly, or that only certain 'strong' things can make it move gives the same first answer ('push it') but a reason that shows no force-to-effect link. Both children say 'push it'; only the reason separates them.

sources.claim: Students think a force is needed to keep an object moving at constant speed (a constant force gives constant speed); the correction is that at constant speed the forces add to zero. These intuitive ideas must be challenged repeatedly across many contexts.
sources.source: IOP Spark (Institute of Physics) — 'Many students think that a force is needed to keep an object moving with a constant speed'

sources.claim: Elementary students believe a moving object contains a force given by an outside source and stops when that force 'runs out'; force is wrongly seen as a property inside the object rather than an interaction between two objects.
sources.source: Harvard-Smithsonian MOSART — elementary physical-science misconceptions; BSCS/RESPeCT Grade 3 Forces module

sources.claim: Forces cause changes in motion; if an object is moving no force is needed to keep it moving, but a force is needed to stop it or change direction; objects don't contain force and can't run out of it; everyday stopping is due to friction. Build on children's intuitive 'anchoring conceptions' rather than simply correcting.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 13–14 — appreciate the infinite nature of the sets of integers, rational and real numbers; position numbers on a number line; distinguish rational from irrational numbers.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): develops the number system — rational numbers, the reals, and the distinction of irrationals (e.g. √2, π) — and the density/infinity of number sets.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 8.NS.A.1 (know numbers that are not rational are irrational; every rational has a terminating or repeating decimal, and conversely) and 8.NS.A.2 (approximate irrationals and locate them on a number line).
• Operational details: A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers and its decimal either TERMINATES or REPEATS; an irrational number's decimal neither terminates nor repeats (√2, π). Contrast the countable infinity of integers/rationals with the idea that between ANY two numbers lie infinitely many more (density). Locate irrationals approximately on the line via their decimal expansions. Distinguish 'infinite decimal' (can be rational, e.g. 0.333…) from 'irrational'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 13): 'Is 0.75 rational? Give its fraction.' Tier B: 'Explain why √2 is irrational, not just "it has lots of decimals".' Tier C: 'Name a number between 0.12 and 0.13, then argue there are infinitely many.'
bestPractices: Define rational as expressible as a ratio of integers, tied to terminating OR repeating decimals; irrational as neither terminating nor repeating
Guard against 'infinite decimal = irrational' — 0.333… is infinite yet rational (1/3); the test is repetition, not length
Use density concretely: repeatedly find a number between two numbers to show infinitely many lie between any pair
Locate irrationals (√2 ≈ 1.414…, π ≈ 3.1415…) approximately on a number line while keeping their exact symbolic form
Give canonical irrational examples (√2, π, non-repeating constructed decimals) and canonical rationals (fractions, terminating/repeating decimals)
keyRepresentations: Zoomable number line demonstrating density (always another number between two)
Decimal-expansion classifier: terminating / repeating (rational) vs non-terminating-non-repeating (irrational)
Set nesting diagram: integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ reals, with irrationals filling the gaps
Fraction ↔ decimal conversions showing why some terminate and some repeat
commonMisconceptions: Believing any number with infinitely many decimals is irrational (0.333… is rational)
Thinking √2 or π 'equal' their rounded decimals (1.414, 3.14)
Assuming there is a 'next' number after a given one, or a smallest gap on the line
Confusing 'irrational' with 'very large' or 'undefined' rather than non-repeating-non-terminating
Thinking there are finitely many numbers between two close decimals like 0.12 and 0.13

learn.summary: For ages 13–14: build the distinction between rational and irrational numbers from the decimal signature (terminating OR repeating = rational; non-terminating AND non-repeating = irrational) and develop the idea of density — that infinitely many numbers lie between any two distinct numbers. The guidance aims to counter the 'infinite decimal = irrational' and 'discrete line' misconceptions, and to keep irrationals (√2, π) in their exact symbolic form while locating them approximately on a number line.

activities.title: Decimal-signature classifier: repetition, not length, decides
feedback: If a learner calls 0.333… irrational 'because it goes on forever', have them find and box the repeating 3 and write it as 1/3 — length is not the test; a repeat means rational.
If a learner calls √9 irrational 'because of the root sign', have them evaluate √9 = 3, a ratio of integers, and contrast with √2 whose value is not any such ratio; the symbol does not decide it.
If a learner treats 1.414 as 'equal to' √2, show the expansion continuing past those digits and keep the exact √2 pinned alongside the approximation.
activities.rationale: Classifying by decimal signature is intended to address the most common misconceptions (infinite-means-irrational, root-sign-means-irrational) and connects the fraction definition to its decimal behaviour. A streaming classifier that highlights a repeating block may make the repetition test concrete. If it reports 'no repeating block found', that only describes the digits shown, so irrationality must come from proof. This is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: 8.NS.A.1/A.2: rational numbers have terminating or repeating decimals (and conversely), irrational numbers do not; approximate irrationals and locate them on a number line.
KS3 pupils develop the number system to include rationals, reals and the distinction of irrational numbers, and reason about the density/infinity of number sets.
learnerActions: For each, write out or stream the decimal expansion and decide whether it TERMINATES or REPEATS. For √2 and π, note that a finite list of digits can never show that a decimal does NEITHER: some rationals have very long repeating blocks (1/97 repeats only after 96 digits). We know √2 and π are irrational because it has been proved, so their decimals never terminate or repeat.
Mark the repeating block when there is one (e.g. box the 3 in 0.3̅, or the 142857 in 1/7) and write the equivalent fraction.
State a rule in your own words for deciding rational vs irrational, then test it against √9 = 3 and 0.333…
Keep √2 and π written exactly as symbols, noting that 1.414… and 3.14… are only approximations.
Locate √2 and π approximately on a number line (e.g. √2 just past 1.4, between 1 and 2; π between 3 and 4) using their decimal approximations, while keeping the exact symbol pinned alongside.
activities.intendedInsight: A number is rational exactly when it can be written as a ratio of two integers — which shows up as a terminating OR repeating decimal. The deciding feature is whether the digits settle into a repeat, not how many digits there are: 0.333… is endless yet rational (=1/3). √2 is proved to be irrational, so its expansion never repeats. Checking a finite number of digits could never establish that on its own.

activities.title: Squeeze another number in: density of the line
feedback: If a learner says 'none' or a small finite count lie between two close fractions, walk through the averaging process twice. Then argue that averaging any two distinct numbers always gives a new number strictly between them, so the process never terminates and the count is infinite.
If a learner imports 'consecutive neighbours' from whole numbers, contrast finding the number after 5 (which is 6) with trying to find the number right after 0.12 — no such number exists.
Confirm when a learner articulates that the squeezing process has no end and therefore infinitely many numbers lie in any interval.
activities.rationale: Repeatedly constructing an in-between number makes density an action the learner performs rather than a fact to accept, and is intended to address the consecutive-number carryover. A zoomable number line that names a between-number then zooms to offer another is an optional interaction example that may make the 'well never runs dry' idea vivid; it is not the only way to teach density.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils develop the number system to include rationals, reals and the distinction of irrational numbers, and reason about the density/infinity of number sets.
learnerActions: Name two close numbers, e.g. 0.12 and 0.13 (or 1/4 and 1/3).
Find a number strictly between them — averaging the two is one reliable method (e.g. 0.125).
Now find a number between THAT one and the upper end, and again, and again.
Argue why this process can never run out, and conclude how many numbers lie between the original pair.
Explain why there is no 'next' number after a given one, unlike the integers.
activities.intendedInsight: Between any two distinct numbers there are infinitely many others, so the number line is dense: there is no smallest gap and no 'next' number. This contrasts with the discrete, consecutive structure of the integers.

activities.title: Dialogue: why √2 cannot be a fraction
feedback: If a learner justifies √2's irrationality only by 'it has lots of decimals', redirect to the structural argument that no integer ratio can equal it.
If a learner claims a number comes 'right after' 0.12, ask them to name it, then name one between 0.12 and their answer — surfacing density.
Acknowledge that the full proof-by-contradiction is challenging; partial reasoning that grasps 'no integer ratio works' is valuable progress.
activities.rationale: This philosophically rich topic (what infinity means, why √2 is not a fraction, whether there is a next number) suits Socratic dialogue that can probe and challenge intuitions. Dialogue is offered as a complementary approach to the manipulatives, each exposing different facets; it is not claimed to be superior to or necessary over hands-on classification.
learnerActions: Work through the classic argument: suppose √2 = a/b in lowest terms, and reason about whether a and b can both be chosen with no common factor.
Respond to Socratic prompts about what would have to be true of a² and b², and where a contradiction arises.
Then tackle the intuition probe: 'Is there a number right after 0.12?' and explain your answer.

Try to write π as a fraction of two whole numbers (e.g. 22/7 or 355/113) and check that these are only approximations. Note that mathematicians have proved π is irrational, though the proof is beyond this level, which is why its decimal never terminates or repeats.
activities.intendedInsight: Some numbers genuinely cannot be written as a ratio of integers — this is a provable fact, not just 'it has lots of decimals'. Engaging with the proof-by-contradiction and the 'no next number' question deepens understanding of what irrationality and density actually mean.

activities.title: Reference anchor: nested number sets
feedback: If a learner places √9 among the irrationals, have them evaluate it (=3) and move it into the integers/rationals.
If a learner cannot place 0.333…, have them recall its fraction (1/3) and place it with the rationals.
activities.rationale: A set-nesting diagram is a useful static reference that organises the vocabulary and relationships. Note its limit: a fixed diagram anchors structure but does not by itself demonstrate density or classify expansions dynamically, so pair it with the active tasks above.
learnerActions: Study a nested-sets diagram: integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ reals, with irrationals filling the gaps in the reals.
For each region, note example numbers and their decimal signature (terminating / repeating / non-repeating).
Place given numbers into the correct region and justify the placement by the rational/irrational test.
activities.intendedInsight: The number systems nest: every integer is rational, every rational is real, and irrationals occupy the reals that are not rational. This gives a map for where any number sits.

activities.title: Consolidation: sort and justify
feedback: Recognition sorting confirms classification but does not by itself show independent reasoning — require a stated justification for each item.
If a learner picks the wrong item, ask them to name the decimal signature that justifies each option before re-choosing.
activities.rationale: Sorting and selected-response items cleanly assess the decimal-signature distinction and make good consolidators AFTER the concept is constructed. Treat selected-response as a check that follows construction; requiring a justification keeps it from being pure recognition.
sourceClaims: 8.NS.A.1/A.2: rational numbers have terminating or repeating decimals (and conversely), irrational numbers do not; approximate irrationals and locate them on a number line.
learnerActions: Sort a mixed set (e.g. 0.333…, √2, 3/8, 0.25, √9, π) into rational vs irrational.
Choose which of a list is irrational and explain the reason, not just the choice (e.g. 'which is irrational: 0.333…, √2, 3/8, 0.25?').
Given a repeating decimal, write the equivalent fraction.
For a classification you make, state the decision rule you applied.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the concepts are built, fluent classification and fraction-recovery confirm that the learner applies the repetition/ratio test rather than surface cues.

constraints: Keep irrationals in exact symbolic form (√2, π); treat 1.414… and 3.14… as approximations, never as equal to the exact value.
The decision test is repetition/terminability (equivalently, expressibility as a ratio of integers), NOT how long or 'messy' the decimal looks — 0.333… is rational.
The root symbol does not determine irrationality: √9 = 3 is rational while √2 is irrational; evaluate the value.
A static nested-sets diagram is a reference scaffold: it anchors vocabulary and structure but does not demonstrate density or dynamically classify expansions, so it should accompany active tasks.
Selected-response/sorting tasks are consolidators that follow concept-building; pair them with required justifications so they elicit reasoning rather than recognition alone.

Tier the challenge: age-13 checkpoint 'Is 0.75 rational? Give its fraction'; mid 'Explain why √2 is irrational, not just that it has lots of decimals'; stretch 'Name a number between 0.12 and 0.13, then argue there are infinitely many.'
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'conversation' entry's proof-by-contradiction for √2 is mathematically standard but demanding for ages 13–14; it is retained as an exploratory dialogue with the caveat that partial reasoning is acceptable, and is not asserted as more effective than the manipulative approaches.

The original claims that a dialogue can probe intuitions 'in ways a manipulative cannot' and that '3D adds nothing' were catalog fit-rankings; these have been softened or dropped — the 3D option was omitted as it carried no distinct learning action and risked implying spurious structure on a one-dimensional topic.

The pedagogy's contrast between the countable infinity of integers/rationals and the density of the reals is an advanced nuance; this rewrite develops density but does not separately treat countability — add it only if learners are ready.
The two reteach prerequisite IDs and one null in the source error patterns are internal references not reproduced in learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: What is the actual test for whether a decimal is rational — length, or something else?
Give me a number between 1/4 and 1/3 — now one between THAT and 1/3.
Is √16 rational or irrational? How do you decide?
Can you write π as a fraction of two whole numbers? Why does that matter here?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.333... is rational — it equals 1/3, a ratio of two integers, and a repeating decimal is always rational. There are infinitely many numbers between 1/4 and 1/3 (indeed between any two distinct numbers).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Non-terminating decimal = irrational' — calls 0.333... irrational because it never ends.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish repeating (rational: 0.333...=1/3, 0.142857...=1/7) from non-repeating-non-terminating (irrational: π, √2); the test is the pattern, not the length.
errorPatterns.distractor: Irrational — it goes on forever.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child cites 'goes on forever' as proof of irrationality, ignoring the repeat.

errorPatterns.pattern: Consecutive-number / discreteness carryover — thinks there are no (or only a few) numbers between 1/4 and 1/3, as if fractions have 'next' neighbours like integers.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find a number between (e.g. average them), then between that and 1/3, and again — show the process never stops, so infinitely many lie between; the line is dense.
errorPatterns.distractor: None — they're right next to each other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 'none', 'one', or a small finite count for numbers between the two fractions.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Irrational = anything with a root or a messy decimal' — calls √9 irrational, or thinks all surds are irrational.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Evaluate √9 = 3 (rational) versus √2 (irrational); the root symbol does not decide it — whether the value is a ratio of integers does.
errorPatterns.distractor: √9 is irrational because it's a root.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child labels √9 (=3) or a rounded decimal as irrational on sight of the root sign.

responseLevels.gap: Equates infinite/root with irrational; treats the line as discrete (finite numbers between fractions).
responseLevels.full: Classifies by whether a value is a ratio of integers (repeating/terminating = rational; non-repeating-non-terminating = irrational), gives correct examples, and explains that infinitely many numbers lie between any two distinct numbers.
responseLevels.partial: Can classify clear cases but relies on 'goes on forever' or the root sign as the test, or is unsure about density between fractions.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 0.333... (the 3 repeating forever) rational or irrational? And how many numbers are there between 1/4 and 1/3? Explain both.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the rational/irrational distinction knows 'goes on forever' is not the test — REPEATING or terminating means rational, only non-repeating-non-terminating is irrational — and grasps the density of the number line. A child equating 'infinite decimal' with 'irrational', or importing whole-number 'consecutive' thinking, answers differently and reveals the misconception in the reason.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils develop the number system to include rationals, reals and the distinction of irrational numbers, and reason about the density/infinity of number sets.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** The Particle Model

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter' — Particle model & Physical changes):** The differences in arrangements, in motion and in closeness of particles explaining changes of state, shape and density, the anomaly of ice-water transition; atoms and molecules as particles; density differences between solids, liquids and gases. (DfE KS3 Chemistry: properties of states in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-4):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-4] (qualitative molecular-level models).

- **Operational details:** This is the FULL KS3 particle model: using arrangement, spacing and motion to EXPLAIN properties, not just depict them. Targets: (1) compressibility — only gases compress because only they have large empty gaps; (2) density — gases are far less dense because the same particles are spread through much more space; (3) the ice-water anomaly — water is unusual because its solid (ice) is LESS dense than its liquid (particles lock into an open, spaced structure on freezing), which is why ice floats. Also gas pressure as particle collisions with container walls. Build each explanation from a particle diagram/sim and reason from it. This node assumes fluent particle diagrams (prereq) and extends the introductory model. Keep qualitative; formal kinetic theory and gas laws are later.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child uses particle arrangement/spacing/motion to explain compressibility AND relative density across states, and explains why ice floats via the open structure of solid water — without treating individual particles as changing size or property.
bestPractices: Derive each property (compressibility, density, floating ice) FROM particle arrangement/spacing, rather than stating it alongside a diagram.
Contrast the three states on the same screen so density and compressibility differences are read from spacing.
Treat the ice-water anomaly as a deliberate 'exception that proves the model' — the open lattice explains why ice floats.
Introduce gas pressure as particle collisions with the walls, keeping it qualitative.
Reinforce that particles keep their size and identity; only spacing, pattern and motion change.
keyRepresentations: A three-state particle sim with a compression piston
A per-box particle counter as a density meter
A water-freeze mode showing the open, spaced ice lattice growing in volume
A wall-collision counter representing gas pressure
commonMisconceptions: Solids are denser because their particles are 'bigger/heavier', not because they are closer packed.
All solids are denser than their liquids (missing the water/ice anomaly).
Liquids compress noticeably like gases.
Gas pressure comes from particles pushing on each other rather than colliding with the walls.
Particles expand or change on heating rather than moving faster and spreading.

learn.summary: Learners aged 11–12 use the particle model (arrangement, spacing and motion) to EXPLAIN — not just depict — compressibility, relative density, and the ice-water anomaly, keeping particle size and identity fixed. The core activity derives each property from a manipulable particle model: compress each state, count particles per box (a qualitative count-based density proxy for one substance across states) to compare density, and freeze water to watch it lock into an open, spaced lattice that takes up more room (so ice floats). Alternatives include a reveal-panel summary companion, a matching/sequencing check, a predict-observe-explain syringe task, and an optional 3D ice-lattice view. Gas pressure is introduced qualitatively as particle collisions with container walls. Formal kinetic theory and gas laws are deliberately left for later. The density ordering solid > liquid > gas is the typical pattern, with water deliberately treated as the exception (ice less dense than liquid water).

activities.title: Particle explainer: derive compressibility, density and floating ice from a model
feedback: If a learner says the gas particles get squashed smaller: in this model the particles keep the same size — what changes is the space between them. Redraw before/after with same-size dots and smaller gaps.

If a learner says gases are less dense because their particles are smaller or lighter: the particles are the same; a gas simply spreads the same particles through much more space, so fewer sit in each box.

If a learner predicts ice sinks or says it is denser because it is solid: water is the anomaly — its particles lock into a MORE open arrangement when frozen, so ice is LESS dense and floats; contrast with the usual solid-denser pattern.

If a learner attributes expansion on heating to particles growing: particles don't grow — for most substances they move faster and spread further apart, so the substance takes up more room while each particle stays the same size (liquid water between 0 °C and about 4 °C is an exception: it contracts when heated); anchor to 'same particles, more space'.
If a learner treats the per-box count as the actual density: clarify it is a qualitative proxy showing more particles in the same space means denser, not a literal measurement.
activities.rationale: Explaining density, compressibility and the ice anomaly each involve manipulating particle spacing and reading off the consequence, so a model the learner can compress, count and freeze is proposed to turn each abstract explanation into an observed cause-and-effect. Research cited for this topic (marked unverified in the source row) reports that students struggle to explain density/compressibility via spacing and often think particles themselves change, with the ice-water anomaly a key explanatory target. The NGSS claim is relevant to the freeze/state-change step rather than to the compression and density derivations.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter/Particle model': arrangement/motion/closeness of particles explain changes of state, shape and density, the anomaly of ice-water transition; atoms and molecules as particles; density differences between states
NGSS MS-PS1-4: develop a qualitative molecular-level model predicting/describing changes in particle motion, temperature and state
Students struggle to explain density/compressibility via spacing and often think particles themselves change; the ice-water anomaly is a key explanatory target
learnerActions: Squeeze a piston on a solid, then a liquid, then a gas in a particle simulation; observe that only the gas yields noticeably while a callout shows its empty gaps closing and the close-packed states barely move.
State in your own words why only gases compress much — because only they have large empty spaces between particles to remove, not because particles shrink.

Use a per-box particle counter to compare how many particles fill the same box in each state of the same substance; read off that a gas has far fewer particles in the same space, so it is far less dense. Treat this count as a qualitative, count-based proxy for density (valid for one substance across states), not a literal mass/volume measurement.
Cool liquid water and watch the particles snap into an OPEN, spaced lattice that visibly takes up MORE room; see the resulting ice float on liquid water.
Explain why water is the odd one out — its solid is LESS dense than its liquid because particles lock into an open, spaced structure on freezing — and connect this to why ponds freeze top-down.
Switch to a gas-pressure mode that counts particle hits on the container walls, and describe gas pressure as the result of those collisions with the walls.
activities.intendedInsight: The same model — particles of fixed size whose spacing, pattern and motion change — explains compressibility, relative density across states, and the anomalous floating of ice. The explanation is read off the arrangement, not asserted alongside a picture.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: syringe of air vs syringe of water
feedback: Full understanding: uses particle spacing to explain compressibility, low gas density, AND ice floating, keeping particles fixed in size throughout — the model transfers across all three phenomena.

Partial: explains compressibility by inter-particle space for the gas/liquid case but can't yet extend spacing to density or the anomalous expansion of water — one application, not the model; re-run the density and freeze challenges.

Gap: explains compression by shrinking particles or gas 'disappearing' and can't link density or floating ice to arrangement; redraw same-size dots with changing gaps and reconnect to the particle diagram.
For oil: like water, a liquid is close-packed with little inter-particle space, so it barely compresses — the reason rests on spacing, not on the specific substance.
activities.rationale: Probing the mechanism rather than the fact is intended to discriminate understanding, because the same inter-particle-space idea underlies compressibility, density and anomalous expansion. A hands-on syringe prediction makes the learner commit to a causal account before seeing the result. The DfE claim supports the represented properties rather than independently validating the discrimination point.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter/Particle model': arrangement/motion/closeness of particles explain changes of state, shape and density, the anomaly of ice-water transition; atoms and molecules as particles; density differences between states
learnerActions: Before pushing, predict which sealed plunger will push in and how far: a syringe of air (plunger out) or a syringe of water (plunger out), and say WHY in terms of particles.
Push both plungers: observe that air compresses markedly while water barely moves.

Explain the result: in a gas the particles are far apart with empty space between them, so pushing brings them closer (you compress the SPACE, not the particles); in a liquid the particles are already touching (close-packed but disordered), so there is almost no space to remove.

Answer follow-ups: When you squash the air, what gets smaller — the particles or the gaps? Draw it. Using particles, why is a gas much less dense than a solid? What must be different about how particles are arranged in ice so it floats? If it had been oil instead of water, compressible or not, and why the same as water?
activities.intendedInsight: The pre-observation reasoning about space between particles — not the observation itself — is intended to be the diagnostic that separates understanding spacing from thinking particles get squashed or the gas 'disappears'.

activities.title: Spacing-explains-property reveal panel (consolidation companion)
feedback: If a learner reads the flap text without linking it to the picture, ask them to point to the exact spacing difference that causes the property.
For the ice panel, prompt: which arrangement has particles spread into more space — the liquid or the solid — and how does that set the density?
activities.rationale: A static reveal panel is a useful summary and reference after manipulation; because it cannot be compressed, frozen or measured, it consolidates rather than derives the explanations, so it works best paired with the simulation.
learnerActions: Study a contrasting panel showing particle spacing for solid, liquid and gas side by side.
Reveal the 'why it compresses / why it's less dense / why ice floats' flaps and restate each explanation in your own words, pointing to the spacing that causes it.
Open the key panel contrasting ordinary liquid water with its open ice lattice and explain why the open structure makes ice less dense.
activities.intendedInsight: Having the three states and their explanations visible together is intended to consolidate that one spacing-based model accounts for all three properties.

activities.title: Match and order: properties to particle explanations
feedback: If typical density ordering is wrong, return to the per-box counter: more particles in the same space means denser.
If a learner extends solid > liquid > gas to claim ice must sink, re-surface the anomaly: ice floats because its solid arrangement is more open, not because solids are always denser.
If a learner matches 'floats' to 'is solid', re-surface the anomaly: ice floats because its solid arrangement is more open, not simply because it is solid.
activities.rationale: Matching and sequencing are apt checks when the target is explanation-from-model, but as recognition formats they do not by themselves require the learner to construct an explanation, so they belong after the derivation work; the density-ordering step is scoped to the typical pattern so it does not contradict the water anomaly.
learnerActions: Match each property (compressible, dense, floats) to the particle-arrangement explanation that causes it.
Order the three states by density for a typical substance (solid > liquid > gas) and justify the order from particle spacing.
Then flag water as the deliberate exception: explain why ice (solid water) is LESS dense than liquid water, so it does not fit the usual solid-denser pattern.
Work through this after the simulation so the matching tests explanation-from-model, not recall of labels.
activities.intendedInsight: Pairing a property with its spacing-based cause, ranking the typical states by density, and recognising water as the exception checks that the learner reasons from the model rather than reciting a blanket rule.

activities.title: Optional 3D view of the open ice lattice
feedback: If the 3D view distracts from the spacing point, return to the 2D diagram, which conveys the anomaly adequately.
activities.rationale: The curriculum works from 2D particle diagrams and a 2D simulation conveys spacing and the anomaly adequately, so a 3D view is an optional cameo offered when the open structure is hard to read in 2D — a different spatial experience, not a required one.
learnerActions: If the open structure is hard to read in 2D, rotate a 3D packing view of the ice lattice to see how particles sit in a more open, spaced arrangement than in liquid water.
Compare the 3D open lattice with the close-packed arrangement and connect the extra space to lower density.
activities.intendedInsight: Density and the ice lattice are genuinely spatial, so seeing the open structure in three dimensions may make the 'more open means less dense' link clearer for some learners.

constraints: Keep everything qualitative: formal kinetic theory and gas laws are for later study.
Reinforce throughout that particles keep their size and identity; only spacing, pattern and motion change — never depict particles shrinking, growing, or 'disappearing'.
This node assumes learners are already fluent with particle diagrams; it extends the introductory model to explanation.
Treat the ice-water case as the deliberate anomaly: the typical pattern is solid denser than liquid, but do not let learners generalise 'all solids are denser than their liquids'.
Introduce gas pressure only as particle collisions with the container walls, not as particles pushing on each other.

Reveal panels, matching and sequencing are recognition/consolidation formats: they do not by themselves require the learner to construct an explanation, so use them after the derivation activity, not instead of it.

A flat screen simulation or diagram represents three-dimensional particle arrangements; name it as a model of the real spatial packing rather than the packing itself, and treat per-box particle counts as a qualitative count-based density proxy (valid for one substance across states), not a literal density measurement.

A child who thinks particles get squashed predicts both compress. Push both: air compresses markedly, water almost none. The pre-observation reasoning about space between particles is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: When you squash the air, what exactly gets smaller — the particles or the gaps? Draw it.
A gas is much less dense than a solid. Using the particles, why?
Ice floats on water. What must be different about how the particles are arranged in ice?
If it had been a syringe of oil instead of water — compressible or not? Why the same as water?
assess.correctAnswer: In a gas the particles are far apart with empty space between them, so pushing brings them closer — you're compressing the SPACE, not the particles. In a liquid the particles are already touching (close-packed, just disordered), so there's almost no space to remove — hence it barely compresses. The reason rests on SPACING between particles, and on the particles themselves not shrinking.

errorPatterns.pattern: the particles themselves get squashed/smaller when you compress a gas
errorPatterns.nextMove: Particles are incompressible — what changes is the space between them. Redraw before/after: same-size dots, smaller gaps. Reconnect to the particle diagram.
errorPatterns.distractor: The air particles get squashed smaller when you push the plunger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains compression as shrinking particles rather than closing the gaps between them

errorPatterns.pattern: heating makes each particle expand, which is why things expand when heated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Particles don't grow — they move faster and take up more room, so spacing increases. Anchor to 'same particles, more space'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes thermal expansion to particles growing rather than moving more and spacing out

errorPatterns.pattern: ice sinks / ice is denser because it's solid ('solids are always denser than their liquid')

responseLevels.gap: Explains compression by shrinking particles or gas 'disappearing'; can't link density or floating ice to arrangement.

responseLevels.partial: Explains compressibility by inter-particle space for the gas/liquid case, but can't yet extend the spacing idea to density or the anomalous expansion of water — one application, not the model.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You can squash a sealed syringe full of air to half its size, but a sealed syringe full of water barely moves at all. Using what you know about particles, why can you compress the gas but not the liquid? Give me the picture in your head, then the reason.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who explains compressibility by inter-particle SPACE from one who thinks the particles themselves are being squashed or that the gas 'disappears'. The same error surfaces with density and anomalous expansion — so probing the mechanism, not the fact, is what discriminates.
