pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Vocabulary for rock types & geological processes

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Science, Year 3 Rocks + upper-KS2 working scientifically):** Pupils use and apply the correct technical vocabulary for rock types (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic) and processes (erosion, weathering, deposition, sediment, strata, permeable, impermeable, fossil).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 4-ESS/MS-ESS2 vocabulary strand):** Name and correctly use rock-type and Earth-process terms when explaining how rocks form and how landscapes change.

- **Operational details:** This is a LANGUAGE node knitting the rocks/earth cluster together. Each rock TYPE must be pinned to how it forms — igneous (cooled from molten magma/lava), sedimentary (layers of sediment pressed together, where fossils are found), metamorphic (existing rock changed by heat and pressure). Each PROCESS word must be pinned to what it does and its place in a sequence — weathering (rock broken down in place) → erosion (broken pieces carried away) → deposition (pieces dropped/laid down); plus sediment, strata (layers), and the permeable/impermeable pair (lets water through vs not). The commonest error is treating weathering and erosion as synonyms; teach them as distinct, ordered stages. Anchor every term to an image or process animation, not a definition list, and have children USE the words to explain a formation.
bestPractices: Pin each rock-type word to its FORMATION story (igneous=cooled magma, sedimentary=pressed layers, metamorphic=heat+pressure), not just a label.
Teach weathering → erosion → deposition as three DISTINCT, ordered stages, explicitly contrasting the perennially-confused weathering vs erosion.
Attach process words to visuals/animations of the process, then have children narrate a formation using the terms in sequence.
Introduce paired opposites together (permeable vs impermeable) so the contrast defines each.
Assess by application — the child explains how a named rock/landform formed using the terms correctly — not by matching definitions alone.
keyRepresentations: A rock-type triptych (igneous / sedimentary / metamorphic) each with its formation image.
A weathering→erosion→deposition process strip to sequence.
Labelled strata diagram with 'sediment', 'strata', 'fossil' callouts.
A permeable vs impermeable water-drip comparison image.
Word–process matching cards with example landscapes.
commonMisconceptions: 'Weathering and erosion mean the same thing' — conflating breaking-down-in-place with transport-away.
'Igneous/sedimentary/metamorphic are just names' — not connecting each to its formation process.
'Fossils are found in any rock' — not knowing they form in sedimentary rock.
'Deposition is the same as erosion' — not seeing it as the later dropping-off stage.
'Permeable and impermeable are about hardness' — rather than whether water passes through.
'Sediment and sedimentary rock are the same' — missing that loose sediment must be compacted/cemented into rock.

learn.summary: Vocabulary node for ages 9–11 on rock types (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic) and geological processes (weathering, erosion, deposition, plus sediment, strata, permeable/impermeable, fossil). The teaching goal is not matching definitions but pinning each term to how it forms or what it does, and having children USE the words to narrate a formation in correct sequence. The two highest-priority targets: keep weathering (breakdown in place) and erosion (transport away) as distinct ordered stages, and distinguish loose sediment from compacted/cemented sedimentary rock.

activities.title: Tour a geology scene and name what you see
feedback: Prompt to separate the confusable pair: 'Did the rock break where it sat, or get carried somewhere? Weathering breaks; erosion carries.'
If a learner says the loose sand is already 'sedimentary rock', point out that loose sediment must be compacted and cemented over long time before it becomes rock.
Reinforce that fossils are typically found in sedimentary rock, because organisms get buried in settling layers of sediment that are later compacted and cemented into rock.
activities.rationale: Anchoring each term to an image of the process or formation, rather than a definition list, and placing weathering/erosion/deposition as separate labelled points makes the confusable distinction visible. Optional lift-the-flap 'weathering or erosion?' prompts and highlighting the shared-versus-different attribute when contrasting a pair make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Weathering (breakdown in place) and erosion (transport of material) are distinct, commonly confused processes; deposition is the subsequent laying-down; the three rock types are defined by formation.
DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils use vocabulary for rock types and formation; upper KS2 applies erosion/weathering/deposition terminology.
learnerActions: Study a rich labelled geological scene showing a volcano oozing lava, a banded cliff of layered rock, a swirl of folded metamorphic rock, and a river cutting through the landscape.

Reveal each term in its natural home: the cooling lava is 'igneous — cooled from molten rock'; the cliff bands are 'sedimentary — layers of sediment pressed together and cemented over a long time, where fossils are typically found', with the layers labelled 'strata' and the loose material 'sediment'; the folded rock is 'metamorphic — existing rock changed by heat and pressure'.

Follow the river to three separate points and name them in order: weathering (rock crumbling in place), then erosion (broken pieces carried off), then deposition (pieces dropped and settling downstream).
Say aloud, for each rock type, one sentence about how it forms using the correct term.
activities.intendedInsight: Each rock-type word carries a formation story, and weathering/erosion/deposition are three different points along one journey, not synonyms.

activities.title: Tell the story of a rock
feedback: If weathering and erosion are swapped (e.g. 'the rock eroded into bits' for breaking, or 'it weathered downstream' for moving), have the child re-tell with weathering in the breaking slot and erosion in the carrying slot.
If the settling stage is skipped (jumping from 'carried away' straight to 'became rock'), prompt: 'what happens when the river slows and drops its load?' and name deposition.
If 'sediment' and 'sedimentary rock' are used interchangeably, distinguish loose sediment from rock formed by compaction and cementation over long time.
activities.rationale: Asking for the words used inside a story, rather than defined in isolation, exposes the common weathering↔erosion swap and the omission of deposition: a child can recite definitions yet still misorder or conflate the terms when narrating. Assessment by application targets correct placement, not recitation.
sourceClaims: Weathering (breakdown in place) and erosion (transport of material) are distinct, commonly confused processes; deposition is the subsequent laying-down; the three rock types are defined by formation.
DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils use vocabulary for rock types and formation; upper KS2 applies erosion/weathering/deposition terminology.
learnerActions: Narrate the journey of a rock high on a mountain that ends up as a pebble on a beach and, millions of years later, as a new layer of rock.
Use the words weathering, erosion, deposition, sediment and sedimentary rock each in its correct place and in correct order.
On request, extend to igneous and metamorphic rock and to how fossils form.
Answer follow-up probes: 'When the river slows and drops its load, what is that called?' and 'Is a heap of loose sand already sedimentary rock — what has to happen first?'
activities.intendedInsight: Correct vocabulary shows up in correct use: the terms must be deployed in a coherent, ordered account of formation, not merely recited as definitions.

activities.title: Sort, sequence and complete
feedback: For a sorting error, point back to the formation story (igneous = cooled molten rock (magma or lava), sedimentary = layers of sediment compacted and cemented, metamorphic = existing rock changed by heat and pressure).
For a sequence error, re-run the river journey: broken in place, carried away, dropped and settled.
For a cloze error, check whether the chosen word names a breakdown, a transport, or a laying-down.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, ordering, matching and cloze give clear checkpoints on naming and sequencing. These support recognition and ordering but, on their own, do not require the learner to construct a narrative; pair them with the story task for independent production.
learnerActions: Sort named rocks and examples into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.
Put the three stages weathering → erosion → deposition into correct order.
Match each term to its process image or short meaning.
Complete the blanks in a short rock-formation paragraph using the correct terms.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct categorisation and sequencing are concrete checks that each term is pinned to its formation or role and that the ordered stages are kept distinct.

activities.title: Pair the opposites: permeable vs impermeable
feedback: If a learner says a rock is impermeable 'because it is hard', redirect to the actual test: does water pass through it or not?

Reinforce the contrast by asking which rock lets water soak right through to the other side and which does NOT let water pass through — the test is whether water passes through, not how hard the rock is.
activities.rationale: Paired opposites are defined by their contrast, so presenting them together with a visible water-through-versus-blocked comparison grounds the distinction in an observable behaviour rather than a guessed property.
learnerActions: Compare two water-drip scenes side by side: one rock that lets water pass through and one that does not.
Name the one that lets water through as 'permeable' and the one that blocks it as 'impermeable'.
Explain in your own words that these terms are about whether water passes through, not about how hard the rock is.
activities.intendedInsight: Introducing the paired opposites together lets the contrast define each word, and heads off the error of linking permeability to hardness.

constraints: Assess by application: the child explains how a named rock or landform formed using the terms correctly, not by matching definitions alone.
Weathering → erosion → deposition must be taught as three distinct, ordered stages, explicitly contrasting the perennially confused weathering versus erosion.
Each rock-type word must be pinned to its formation story, not treated as a bare label.
Loose sediment and sedimentary rock are different: sediment must be compacted and cemented over long time to become rock; do not let the terms be used interchangeably.
Fossils are typically found in sedimentary rock; avoid implying they form in any rock type (and note that not every sedimentary rock contains fossils).
Permeable versus impermeable is about whether water passes through, not about hardness; teach the pair together so the contrast defines each.
Sorting, sequencing, matching and cloze check recognition and ordering but do not by themselves elicit independent narration; use the story task to require construction.

Real rock samples and a stream-table demonstration are a valuable hands-on complement; the labelled scene is a scaffold that shows the terms in context, not a replacement for handling real material where available.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched and both carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source row listed a dialogue/role-play format and a 3D format as poor fit with absolute claims ('3D adds no vocabulary benefit', chat 'would simply recite definitions'). These comparative-efficacy claims are not established by the evidence here and have been dropped rather than restated as universal laws; a spoken retelling (the story task) is retained as a production activity because narration is exactly the stated objective.
The animated process-builder (drag terms onto stages of an eroding-then-depositing river) is preserved as an optional engagement variant of the sequencing task, not as a required mechanism.

The original permeable feedback contrasted 'stay wet inside' with 'let water drain away', which was potentially backwards; it has been reframed to the passage-of-water test, with impermeable described as 'does not let water pass through' rather than 'keeps water out' to avoid implying the rock stays dry.

Fossils-in-sedimentary-rock is stated as the standard age-appropriate teaching; the simplification (not every sedimentary rock contains fossils; some fossils occur in altered/other contexts) is noted here and in the audit rather than asserted as a universal rule to learners.
Permeable/impermeable teaching is a pedagogy choice consistent with the node's representations; neither cited source claim directly supports it, so sourceClaims for that activity is left empty.

probeDeeper: You said the rock 'weathered' — did it break where it sat, or get carried somewhere? Which word fits?
Between the pebble on the beach and the new rock layer, what has to happen to all that sediment?
Now use 'igneous' and 'metamorphic' in one sentence each about how that kind of rock forms.
Is a heap of loose sand already 'sedimentary rock'? What has to happen for it to become rock?
assess.correctAnswer: A recount that uses the terms correctly and in sequence: the rock is broken down by weathering, the pieces are carried away by erosion, they are dropped and settle (deposition) building up as sediment, which over long time compacts and cements into sedimentary rock.

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps weathering and erosion ('the rock eroded into bits' for breaking; 'it weathered downstream' for moving)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it — weathering breaks, erosion carries; have them re-tell with each word in its correct slot.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses erosion for breaking-in-place, or weathering for transport.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits deposition — jumps from 'carried away' straight to 'became rock', dropping the settling stage
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — 'what happens when the river slows and drops its load?' and name deposition.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No deposition step; sediment appears without ever being dropped.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'sediment' and 'sedimentary rock' interchangeably — loose sediment is already 'rock'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish loose sediment from compacted and cemented rock formed over long time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the loose sand or pebbles 'sedimentary rock' before any compaction.

responseLevels.gap: Can't deploy the terms in the story, or uses them at random.
responseLevels.full: Narrates weathering → erosion → deposition → sediment → sedimentary rock, each used correctly and in order, and extends the vocabulary to igneous/metamorphic and to fossils on request.
responseLevels.partial: Uses some terms correctly but swaps weathering/erosion or drops deposition — the sequence isn't fully intact.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell me the story of a rock high on a mountain that ends up as a pebble on a beach, and then, millions of years later, as a new layer of rock. As you tell it, use the words weathering, erosion, deposition, sediment and sedimentary rock in the right places.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for the words used in a story rather than defined exposes the common swap of weathering↔erosion and the omission of deposition — a child can recite definitions yet still misorder or conflate the terms when narrating. Listening for correct placement, not recitation, is the test.

sources.claim: DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils use vocabulary for rock types and formation; upper KS2 applies erosion/weathering/deposition terminology.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study — Year 3 Rocks

sources.claim: Weathering (breakdown in place) and erosion (transport of material) are distinct, commonly confused processes; deposition is the subsequent laying-down; the three rock types are defined by formation.
sources.source: USGS / National Geographic Education — weathering, erosion, deposition and rock types

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Classification Keys (dichotomous keys)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'Living things and their habitats'):** pupils explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things in their local and wider environment.

- **Standards — US (context):** aligns with pattern-based classification of organisms by observable characteristics; the US standards do not name dichotomous keys, so DfE is the primary anchor.

- **Operational details:** A PROCEDURAL topic. A classification (dichotomous) key is a sequence of yes/no questions about OBSERVABLE features that narrows a set of organisms down to a single identity, one binary split at a time. Two skills: (a) FOLLOW a key — answer each question about an unknown organism and follow the branch until named; (b) BUILD a key — choose good discriminating questions that split a set roughly in half and never leave ambiguity. Good questions are binary, observable, and unambiguous ('Does it have a backbone?' not 'Is it big?'). The key is a tool that makes grouping-by-features systematic and repeatable.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B. Following a key is concrete (Tier A); building a valid key for 6–8 organisms is the relational step (Tier B) because the child must anticipate how each question partitions the whole set. Success = follows a branching key to a correct ID and builds a consistent yes/no key for a small set.
bestPractices: Teach following a key before building one — experiencing the narrowing logic makes the design constraints obvious.
Insist questions be binary, observable and unambiguous; contrast a good question ('Does it have a backbone?') with a bad one ('Is it big?') to make the standard concrete.
Use local, real organisms in a field context so the key is a genuine identification tool, not an abstract puzzle.
When building, have pupils test their key by running every organism through it — a valid key sends each to a unique endpoint.
Aim for splits that roughly halve the set so the key is efficient, and show what goes wrong when a question separates only one organism at a time.
keyRepresentations: Branching (dichotomous) tree diagram with a yes/no question at each node
Live 'remaining candidates' set that shrinks as each question is answered
Two-column split table (organisms that answer yes | organisms that answer no)
A worked key for a familiar set (minibeasts / leaves) as the model to imitate
commonMisconceptions: Writing non-binary or vague questions ('What colour is it?', 'Is it nice?') that don't cleanly split the set.
Thinking a key identifies by matching a picture rather than by answering questions about features.
Believing there is only one 'correct' key for a set, rather than many valid keys built from different questions.
Building a key that leaves two organisms in the same endpoint (unresolved) and not noticing the ambiguity.

learn.summary: Children aged 8–9 learn dichotomous classification keys as a procedure: a sequence of yes/no questions about observable features that narrows a set of organisms down to a single identity, one binary split at a time. Two skills are developed — FOLLOWING a key (concrete) and BUILDING a valid key for 6–8 organisms (the harder relational step that requires anticipating how each question partitions the whole set). Teach following before building, use real local organisms, and make good questions concrete by contrasting a binary observable question ('Does it have a backbone?') with a vague one ('Is it big?'). Note that a good question must be binary and observable AND must actually divide the particular set being keyed.

activities.title: Follow a branching key to name a mystery organism
feedback: If the child names the creature first and works backwards, cover the endpoints and require answering each question on the specimen before moving on — this is a discipline lapse, not a gap in understanding the concept of a key.

If the child answers on overall 'looks like' resemblance, point back to the exact feature the question names (e.g. wings), have them locate it on the specimen before choosing a branch, and reground the idea of grouping by observable features.
If the child reaches a correct single endpoint feature-by-feature, confirm that reading each question and checking the real feature is exactly how a key works.
activities.rationale: Following a key is concrete and naturally comes first; experiencing the narrowing logic makes the later design constraints obvious. Using local, real organisms keeps the key a genuine identification tool rather than an abstract puzzle. The shrinking candidate strip is an optional device that makes the elimination mechanism visible.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'Living things and their habitats' requires pupils to explore and use classification keys to help group, identify and name a variety of living things in their local and wider environment.
learnerActions: Receive a mystery minibeast (or leaf) and a branching yes/no key with 6–8 candidate organisms.
Read the first question (e.g. 'Does it have legs?'), check the actual feature on the specimen, and take the matching branch — do not skip ahead to guess a name.
Continue answering each question in order ('More than six legs?', 'Does it have wings?') and track which candidates remain after each split.
Stop when a single organism is left: that is the identification, provided the specimen is one of the organisms the key covers (check it against the endpoint's description).
Optionally use a live 'remaining candidates' strip that shrinks from all the key's creatures (6–8) to one as each answer is given, so the narrowing is visible.
activities.intendedInsight: A key identifies an organism by answering questions about its observable features one split at a time, not by matching it to a picture; each yes/no answer eliminates candidates until exactly one remains.

activities.title: Build your own yes/no key from a jumble of organisms
feedback: If the child writes subjective or non-splitting questions ('Is it pretty?', 'Is it scary?', 'Is it a bug?'), model recasting each to a binary observable feature and test it with two checks: 'could two people disagree on the answer?' and 'does it split the pile roughly in two?'.

If a question is binary and observable but sends every or almost every organism down one branch (for example 'Does it have a backbone?' with a set of all invertebrates, which sends every organism to 'no'), point out that it does not usefully divide this set, and ask for a feature on which these organisms genuinely differ.
If two organisms share an endpoint, highlight that they are unseparated and ask what new observable feature distinguishes them.
Prompt: 'Could two people using your key ever get different answers to the same question? Which question?' — use disagreement as the signal to fix a question.
If a question separates only one organism at a time, note the key becomes long and inefficient; aim for splits that roughly halve the set.
activities.rationale: Building a valid key is the relational step the curriculum asks for: the child must anticipate how each question partitions the whole set. Immediate feedback that flags an unresolvable or non-splitting branch lets the child discover the design constraints themselves. A two-column split table and live validation (flagging ambiguous splits and organisms that can't be separated) are optional interactions that make the standard concrete, but a child can also test a key on paper by hand-running each organism.
sourceClaims: A dichotomous classification key uses a series of binary (yes/no) questions about observable features to identify an organism; good questions are unambiguous and split the set cleanly.
learnerActions: Take 6–8 organisms and arrange them into a branching tree, authoring one yes/no question at each fork.
Choose questions that are binary and observable, that are unambiguous, and that actually divide the remaining set — ideally roughly in half.
Optionally use a two-column split table at each question (organisms answering yes | organisms answering no) so the partition is visible before committing to it.
Test the key by running every organism through it: a valid key sends each creature to its own unique endpoint.

Deliberately try a vague question such as 'Is it big?' and notice that different people may answer it differently for the same creature (big compared with what?), so the same organism can be sent down different branches and the key gives inconsistent results.

Rewrite the vague question as a binary observable feature that genuinely splits THIS set — e.g. 'Does it have wings?' or 'More than six legs?' for a minibeast set, or 'Does it have a backbone?' only when the set mixes vertebrates and invertebrates — then re-test. (A feature that sends every organism down the same branch, like 'Does it have a backbone?' for an all-invertebrate set, does not split the set.)
activities.intendedInsight: A key's questions must be binary, observable and unambiguous, and must divide the actual set so every organism reaches a unique endpoint; discovering that people disagree on a vague or subjective question, or that a non-splitting question leaves organisms unseparated, shows WHY such questions fail, not just that keys exist.

activities.title: Study and annotate a worked key, then stress-test it
feedback: If the child believes there is only one correct key, show a second valid key for the same organisms built from different starting questions.
If the child thinks a key matches pictures, re-emphasise that each branch answers a question about a feature, not an image.

Prompt: 'Follow your key with a creature you've never seen — it will still reach one endpoint, but is that endpoint really this creature? If not, where would a new question be needed?' to show that reaching an endpoint is not the same as a correct identification.
activities.rationale: An annotated worked key is a strong exposition scaffold that shows the structure of a dichotomous key before building. It is a pre-teach model to imitate; on its own it cannot catch the child's own bad question, so it should precede, not replace, the follow and build activities. The 'many valid keys' point is a pedagogical observation, not a source-derived claim.
sourceClaims: A dichotomous classification key uses a series of binary (yes/no) questions about observable features to identify an organism; good questions are unambiguous and split the set cleanly.
learnerActions: Examine a pre-built key for a familiar set (minibeasts or leaves), revealing at each branch the question and which organisms go left and right.
Describe aloud the STRUCTURE: every node is one yes/no question; every path leads to a single named organism.
Discuss whether there is only one 'correct' key, and try writing a different first question that still cleanly splits the same set.
Challenge the key: if a brand-new creature arrived that fits none of the endpoints, decide where a new question or branch would be added to fix it.
activities.intendedInsight: Many valid keys can be built from the same set using different questions; a key is a flexible tool, and it can be extended or repaired when a new organism does not fit any existing endpoint.

activities.title: 'Guess my organism' 20-questions warm-up
feedback: If questions are vague ('Is it nice?'), reflect that the answer didn't help eliminate anyone, and ask for an observable feature instead.
Praise questions that roughly halve the remaining candidates and connect this to efficient keys.
activities.rationale: A spoken 'guess my organism' game models the narrowing logic through dialogue and is an engaging warm-up. It builds intuition for binary questioning but does not render the branching tree the child needs to build, so it supports rather than replaces the build activity.
learnerActions: Play a Socratic '20 questions' game: an adult (or peer) thinks of one organism and the child asks yes/no questions to identify it.
Keep a running list of candidate organisms and cross off those eliminated by each answer.
After the game, notice which questions eliminated the most candidates and discuss why binary, feature-based questions worked better than vague ones.
activities.intendedInsight: Narrowing a set by asking good yes/no questions is the same logic a key automates; question quality determines how quickly the set shrinks.

constraints: Teach following a key before building one so the narrowing logic is experienced before the design constraints are required.

Questions in a valid key must be binary, observable and unambiguous AND must actually divide the particular set; contrast a good question ('Does it have a backbone?') with a vague one ('Is it big?'), and note that even a good binary feature fails if it sends every organism down one branch (e.g. backbone with an all-invertebrate set).
Use local, real organisms in a field context so the key is a genuine identification tool, not an abstract puzzle.

Building a key is the relational step (requires anticipating how each question partitions the whole set) and is harder than following; expect self-made keys to contain some ambiguous or redundant questions at first.

A quiz or recognition task (e.g. 'which branch does this organism take?', 'which question best splits this set?') can check the follow skill and probe judgement, but recognition-only items do not elicit the independent construction of a key; building must be done by actually authoring questions.

The annotated worked key and the 20-questions game are scaffolds with narrow limits: the worked key cannot catch a child's own bad question, and the dialogue game cannot render a branching tree to build; neither replaces the build activity.
Distinguish a discipline lapse (guessing the endpoint then back-filling) from a genuine conceptual gap — the former needs the endpoints covered, not reteaching of what a key is.
Emphasise that many valid keys exist for one set; avoid implying a single 'correct' key.
When curating the 6–8 organisms, ensure each pair differs on at least one observable binary feature so a clean key is achievable.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claim that 'a key is a logical/branching structure, not a spatial one; 3D adds nothing' is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; it has been omitted rather than asserted. A branching structure can be represented in several media.

The source claim about dichotomous keys using binary observable questions is marked verified:false in the source row; its exact wording is cited but should be treated as unverified guidance pending confirmation.

'Does it have a backbone?' is a valid binary observable question only when the set includes both vertebrates and invertebrates; for an all-invertebrate minibeast set it does not split the set, so activities were adjusted to require a feature that genuinely divides the chosen organisms.

The valid-key check (unique endpoint per organism) assumes organisms are genuinely distinguishable by observable features in the chosen set; when curating organisms, ensure each pair differs on at least one observable, binary feature so a clean key is possible.
The two-column split table was retained from the original keyRepresentations as an optional build aid.
The 'many valid keys exist / repairability' insight in the worked-key activity is a pedagogical point and is not asserted as source-verified.

probeDeeper: Why did you choose 'has wings?' as a question rather than 'is it pretty?'
Follow your key with a creature you've never seen — does it still reach exactly one answer?
Could two people using your key ever get different answers to the same question? Which question?
If a brand-new creature arrived that fits none of your endpoints, how would you fix the key?
assess.correctAnswer: Following a key: reads each question, checks the actual feature on the specimen, and takes the correct branch in order until one organism remains — without skipping to a guessed name. Building a key: chooses observable, unambiguous yes/no features (e.g. 'Has wings?', 'More than six legs?') that divide the set, with each question narrowing the group so every organism ends at its own unique endpoint.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes subjective or non-splitting questions — 'Is it pretty?', 'Is it scary?', 'Is it a bug?' — that can't be answered objectively or don't divide the group.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model recasting each question to an observable, binary feature; test it with 'could two people disagree on the answer?' and 'does it split the pile roughly in two?'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The self-made key contains questions two people could answer differently, or that send most organisms down one branch.

errorPatterns.pattern: Follows the key by guessing the endpoint — names the creature first, then works backwards (confirmation).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cover the endpoints; require answering each question on the specimen before moving on. This is a discipline lapse — do not reteach the concept of a key.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States the answer before working through the branches, then justifies it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the printed feature and answers on overall 'looks like' — sorts by surface resemblance instead of the specific feature the question names.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point back to the exact feature the question names and have them locate it on the specimen; regroup on grouping-by-observable-features.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers a question ('Does it have wings?') based on general impression rather than checking the actual structure.

responseLevels.gap: Questions are subjective or fail to split the set; follows a key by guessing rather than testing features.
responseLevels.full: Follows any key rigorously feature-by-feature AND builds a key of observable binary questions that uniquely identifies every organism, and can repair it for a novel specimen.
responseLevels.partial: Follows a given key correctly step by step, but the self-made key contains some ambiguous or redundant questions, or does not cleanly separate every organism.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child pictures of 6–8 minibeasts (or leaves) and two jobs to DO while you watch. First: 'Use this branching key to name this unknown creature — show me each step as you go.' Then: 'Now make your own yes/no key so a friend could identify any one of these six creatures.' Watch how they choose questions and follow branches; do not explain the method or supply features.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching rather than asking reveals whether the child genuinely tests each discriminating feature and reads both branches, versus jumping to a familiar name and back-filling; and whether their self-made key uses objective binary features that actually split the set, versus vague or subjective questions that leave organisms unseparated.

sources.source: UK DfE National Curriculum, Science programmes of study: key stages 1 and 2

pedagogy.summary: This is an early pattern-recognition and sky-orientation topic: children learn that people have picked out patterns among the stars and given them names (constellations), starting with the easily found Big Dipper / the Plough, and that the two 'pointer' stars at the end of its bowl lead the eye to the North Star (Polaris). At 5–7 the aim is recognising and re-finding a simple shape in the star field and understanding that a constellation is a named pattern people imagined — not a physical group of stars joined together. Best practice is lots of playful pattern-spotting (connect-the-dots, matching a shape card to the sky) and, if possible, real stargazing or a planetarium/app, because finding the Plough for yourself is memorable. Two accuracy points to hold lightly: the stars in a constellation are not actually near each other in space (they only look like a pattern from Earth — introduce gently), and the North Star is useful because it marks north, an early hook into navigation. Keep it recognition-and-naming, not astrophysics.
bestPractices: Make it hands-on pattern-spotting: connect-the-dots the Big Dipper, then find the same shape hidden in a busy star-field — recognition through repetition
Use the pointer trick concretely: draw the line from the two bowl-end stars to Polaris so children can 'find north' themselves, giving the pattern a purpose
If at all possible, observe the real night sky or use a planetarium/star app, since spotting the Plough first-hand is what makes it stick
Teach 'constellation = a pattern of stars people named' with a few cultural examples, so children see the shapes are imagined/story-based, not drawn in the sky
Gently note the stars in a pattern are not really joined or close together — they just line up into a shape when we look from Earth — without labouring the distance idea
keyRepresentations: A connect-the-dots Big Dipper / Plough (seven stars) — the canonical first pattern
The 'pointer stars → North Star' line drawn across the sky
A shape/outline card overlaid on a star field to practise matching pattern to sky
A star map or planetarium view of the night sky for finding the pattern
commonMisconceptions: The stars in a constellation are close together / physically joined in space (they only appear as a pattern from Earth; they can be hugely different distances away)
The constellation lines are really drawn/visible in the sky (the lines are imaginary aids; people invented the patterns and names)
The North Star is the brightest star in the sky (it is not especially bright; it is useful because it sits above the north pole)
Constellations are fixed pictures that look obviously like their names (they are loose patterns that take imagination to see)
The star patterns are in exactly the same place all night / all year (they appear to move; deeper seasonal change is a later topic)

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, this is a star-pattern recognition and sky-orientation topic. Children learn that people have picked out patterns among the stars and given them names (constellations and smaller star patterns), starting with the Big Dipper / the Plough. Strictly, the Plough is part of a bigger constellation called the Great Bear, and it is easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere. They practise re-finding that seven-star saucepan shape in a busy star field, use the two 'pointer' stars at the end of the bowl to find the North Star (Polaris), and come to understand that a constellation is a named pattern people imagined, not a group of stars joined together. Keep it recognition-and-naming, not astrophysics.

activities.title: Connect the dots to find the Plough, then find it again
feedback: If the child joins the wrong stars, show the correct saucepan outline lit up alongside their attempt and let them compare the shapes.
When they re-find the Plough in the busier field, confirm: 'Yes — that's the same saucepan shape, just with more stars around it.'
If they struggle to find it again, briefly re-show the outline, then hide it and invite another try, so the skill builds through repetition.
activities.rationale: Early star-pattern work is about recognising a simple shape in the star field and re-finding it. Active construction (joining the dots) plus a 'find it again' round with distractor stars gives recognition practice with feedback, and real sky or planetarium viewing may make the pattern more memorable. Scoped to night-visible patterns like the Big Dipper, in line with the cited standard.
sourceClaims: 1-ESS1-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-1]) frames early work with star patterns; its clarification limits star-pattern work to those visible at night, matching simple constellation-spotting like the Big Dipper.
learnerActions: Look at a night-sky scene scattered with stars and join seven of them, dot-to-dot, into the saucepan shape of the Big Dipper / the Plough
Say or hear the name once the shape is built
Then look at a busier star field and point out (or re-join) the same Plough shape hidden among many more stars, proving you can re-find it yourself
If possible, go outside on a clear night or use a planetarium/star app and try to spot the real Plough in the sky
activities.intendedInsight: A constellation is a pattern you can learn to recognise and re-find; the Big Dipper is the easiest first pattern to pick out.

activities.title: Use the pointer stars to find north
feedback: If the child extends the line in the wrong direction, re-highlight the two bowl-end stars and show the straight line running off them to Polaris.

If the child says you find Polaris because it is the brightest, gently correct: 'It isn't the brightest — we find it by following the pointer stars, and it's useful because, from our half of the world, it stays almost still in the north.'
activities.rationale: Giving the pattern a purpose (finding north) is intended to make it more meaningful and is an early hook into navigation. Drawing the pointer line concretely lets children find north for themselves. Addresses the common misconception that Polaris is spotted by being the brightest star.
learnerActions: Starting from the built Plough, draw or trace a line from the bottom pointer star through the top pointer star (the two stars at the end of the bowl furthest from the handle), and keep going out past the top of the bowl
Follow that line to a lone star and name it the North Star (Polaris)
Say what the pattern is useful for: it helps you find which way is north
activities.intendedInsight: The two end-of-the-bowl stars 'point' to the North Star, so the pattern has a real job — it helps you find north. For people in the Northern Hemisphere, Polaris is useful because it marks north and barely moves, not because it is the brightest star.

activities.title: Are the stars really joined up there?
feedback: If the child says the stars are joined or clustered close together, explain they are not touching: they are huge distances apart, at different distances from us, and only appear to line up from Earth — some are further away than others.
If the child treats the connecting lines or figure as physically drawn in the sky, say the lines are imaginary aids people added, and different cultures drew different pictures in the same stars.
Affirm a correct answer: 'Right — it only looks like a saucepan from where we stand; it's a pattern people named, not stars stuck together.'
activities.rationale: Targets two core misconceptions: that constellation stars are physically joined/close, and that the lines are really drawn in the sky. Introduce the distance idea gently, without labouring it, and use cultural examples so children see the shapes are imagined and story-based. Whether a prediction-then-reveal moment produces durable conceptual change is a design proposal, not an established result.
sourceClaims: A constellation is a named pattern of stars as seen from Earth; the component stars are typically at very different distances and are not physically associated — a common point of confusion for learners who assume the pattern is a real grouping.
learnerActions: Guess whether the seven Plough stars are really joined together or close to each other in space
Reveal the answer (for example by lifting a flap, tapping, or being told the explanation)
Talk about how different cultures looked at the same stars and imagined different pictures and names
activities.intendedInsight: The connecting lines are imaginary — people joined the dots and named the picture. The stars are actually enormous distances apart and only line up into a shape when seen from Earth; from another viewpoint the pattern would fall apart.

activities.title: Quick check: match, name and point
feedback: For a wrong match, re-show the saucepan outline and the correct name together.
For the pointer question, re-highlight the two bowl-end stars and the line they make to Polaris.
activities.rationale: Recognition of the Plough and the pointer-star fact are cleanly checkable in a short check. This confirms recall and recognition; on its own it does not elicit the independent re-finding practice or the reasoning about why stars only appear joined, so pair it with the construction and reveal activities.
learnerActions: Pick which pattern is the Big Dipper from a few options
Match the pattern to its name
Show or say which way the pointer stars point (trace a path or choose an answer)
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the Plough and recalling the pointer-to-North-Star fact are things you can now do.

constraints: Keep the topic to recognition and naming of simple night-visible patterns, not astrophysics; for Northern Hemisphere learners the Big Dipper (part of the Great Bear) is the usual first pattern, but it and Polaris are low or not visible from much of the Southern Hemisphere.
Introduce the 'stars are actually far apart' idea gently — do not labour the distance concept at this age.
Seasonal and nightly apparent motion of star patterns is a later topic; for now treat the pattern as a shape to recognise.

A dot-to-dot or matching check confirms recognition and recall but does not by itself show the child can re-find the pattern in a real busy sky or explain why the stars only appear joined — include the construction and reasoning activities for that.

A flat star map or screen scene shows the pattern as seen from Earth, which is the goal here; a 3D star model (which spreads the 'joined' stars far apart) is a worthwhile later extension for the distance idea but adds complexity that works against simple recognition at this stage. Treat any outline/connecting lines on a screen as an imaginary aid, not a real feature of the sky.
Real stargazing or a planetarium/app is valuable where available because first-hand spotting may be especially memorable, but it is not required to teach the recognition skill.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One listed source (Royal Museums Greenwich / NASA Space Place constellations explainer) is marked unverified in the row; the distance/line-of-sight claim it supports is scientifically standard but the citation itself was not re-checked.
The claim that a reveal/lift-the-flap 'moment of insight' defeats the 'joined stars' misconception is a design hope, not an established efficacy finding; treat as a proposal.
Claims that first-hand/real-sky spotting is especially memorable are inherited pedagogy, now phrased with 'may', and are not independently verified here.

Narrow affordance of the open-dialogue alternative (from the original's 'poor fit' note): open dialogue alone cannot present the visual star pattern and is reading-heavy for ages 5–7, so it is weak as the sole medium here — this is a scoped limitation, not a claim that dialogue teaches nothing.

Optional interaction examples (tap-to-light stars, lift-the-flap reveal, drag-to-join lines, extend pointer line) are retained as concrete ways to make the mechanism vivid, not as mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: Why do you think people in different parts of the world named different pictures in the very same stars?
How can the Big Dipper help you find the North Star?
If you flew far off to another star, would the Big Dipper still look like a saucepan?
Are all the stars in the pattern the same distance away from us?
assess.correctAnswer: They just look like a pattern from where we stand. The stars are not joined and are actually enormous distances apart — some far behind others — but from our viewpoint on Earth they happen to line up into a shape that people long ago named. A constellation is a pattern of stars that people have named, not a bunch of stars stuck together.

errorPatterns.pattern: the stars in a constellation are joined together or clustered close in space
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the stars sit at very different distances and only line up into the shape when seen from Earth; from another viewpoint the pattern would fall apart.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the Big Dipper stars are joined together, close to each other in space.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child says the Big Dipper stars are linked, or all near each other

errorPatterns.pattern: the constellation is a real picture drawn up in the sky ('the lines are really there')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain the lines are imaginary — people joined the dots and gave the pattern a name; different cultures drew different pictures in the same stars.
errorPatterns.distractor: The shape is really drawn up in the sky for everyone to see.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats the connecting lines or the pictured figure as physically present in the sky

errorPatterns.pattern: the North Star is the brightest star in the sky ('that's how you find it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Polaris is useful because it marks north and barely moves, not because it is brightest; use the Dipper's pointer stars to find it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child says you spot Polaris because it is the brightest

responseLevels.gap: Says the stars are joined or that the constellation is a real picture drawn in the sky.
responseLevels.full: Explains the constellation is a line-of-sight pattern named by people, that the stars are actually huge distances apart, and can use the Dipper's pointer stars to locate Polaris.
responseLevels.partial: Calls it a pattern but cannot explain that the stars are far apart or that people named it — or thinks Polaris is found by being brightest.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The seven stars of the Big Dipper (the Plough) make a shape like a saucepan. Are those stars really close together and joined up in space — or do they just LOOK like a pattern from where we stand on Earth? Tell me which, and WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who pictures the constellation as a real connected object, or a picture physically drawn in the sky, says the stars are joined. A child who understands it is a chance line-up seen from Earth and named by people says they only look that way. The 'why' tier separates 'a picture in the sky' from 'a pattern from our viewpoint'.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** The Circulatory System

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y6 'Animals, including humans'):** "identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood"; and "describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans".

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE at this band):** NGSS treats the circulatory system as one of the interacting subsystems that transport materials in MS-LS1-3 (middle school); there is no US elementary PE naming heart/vessels/blood. Treat as UK-led and note US placement one band later.

- **Operational details:** Children learn the circulatory system as a TRANSPORT loop: the heart (a muscular double pump) pushes blood through vessels — arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, capillaries are tiny vessels where exchange happens — and blood carries oxygen, nutrients and water to cells and carries waste (like carbon dioxide) away. Key structural facts: the heart has left and right sides; blood makes a round trip (body→heart→lungs to collect oxygen→heart→body). Keep 'double circulation' simple at KS2 (blood passes through the heart twice per loop) — chambers/valves detail and full double-circuit belong to KS3. Connect to the linked Y6 idea that nutrients and water are transported in the blood, and to diet/exercise's effect on the heart.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional). A Y6 child can name heart, blood vessels (artery/vein/capillary) and blood and state their jobs, and describe blood as the body's transport system; the transitional stretch is grasping that blood CIRCULATES in a continuous loop (not a one-way trip that gets 'used up') and that the heart pumps to the lungs AND the body.
bestPractices: Anchor the system in the child's own body: find your pulse, feel the heartbeat, feel it quicken after exercise — so 'the heart pumps blood' is a felt fact before it is a diagram.
Teach it as a continuous LOOP rather than a start-to-end journey, using a closed circuit so children see blood is recirculated and refreshed, not used up.
Name the vessels by DIRECTION (arteries away from the heart, veins back to it, capillaries for exchange) so the labels carry function, not just position.
Keep double circulation simple at KS2 (blood passes through the heart on the way to the body and again after the lungs); defer chambers, valves and the full double circuit to KS3.
Link explicitly to the paired Y6 statement that nutrients and water are transported in the blood, and to diet/exercise effects on the heart, so the strand coheres.
Use colour convention carefully (red = oxygen-rich, blue = oxygen-poor) while flagging the myth that venous blood is literally blue.
keyRepresentations: A closed-loop circulation diagram (heart–lungs–body) with directional arrows and red/blue colouring
A labelled heart showing left/right sides and the connecting great vessels
A vessel comparison (artery thick-walled, vein with valves, capillary one-cell thin) tied to function
An animated blood 'parcel' carrying oxygen/nutrients out and CO2/waste back
A pulse-finding / heart-rate activity linking felt heartbeat to the pumping model
commonMisconceptions: Thinking blood travels one way and gets 'used up', rather than circulating in a continuous refreshed loop.
Believing the heart is on the far left of the chest or is heart-shaped, rather than roughly central and fist-sized.
Assuming blood in veins is actually blue (it is dark red); the blue is only a diagram convention and skin/vein appearance.
Confusing arteries and veins, or thinking arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood (the pulmonary artery does not).
Thinking the heart is a single pump with one path, missing that it sends blood both to the lungs and to the body.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year olds learning the human circulatory system (UK DfE Y6; note NGSS places this at middle school, MS-LS1-3, with no US elementary performance expectation naming heart/vessels/blood). The core objective: name the main parts (heart, arteries, veins, capillaries, blood), describe their functions, and grasp that blood CIRCULATES in a continuous refreshed loop (e.g. body→heart→lungs→heart→body) rather than travelling one way and being 'used up'. Anchor the abstract model to the child's own body (pulse, heartbeat, quickening after exercise), name vessels by direction so labels carry function, and keep double circulation simple (blood passes through the heart on the way to the body and again after the lungs); chambers, valves and the full double circuit are for later (KS3).

activities.title: Drive the circulation loop
feedback: If a learner thinks the blood ends its journey at the body, prompt: trace the blue blood back — which vessels return it to the heart, and where does it go next to collect more oxygen?
When the parcel changes colour at the lungs, highlight: this is the moment the same blood is refreshed and reused, not replaced.
If a learner says arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood, note that the route to the lungs carries oxygen-poor blood away from the heart — direction, not oxygen content, defines an artery.
Point out the red/blue colouring is a diagram convention: oxygen-poor blood is dark red, not literally blue.
activities.rationale: Circulation is a dynamic loop; letting the child drive the pump and watch a parcel complete the circuit, change colour at the lungs, and both deliver and collect materials makes 'blood circulates and is refreshed' concrete. A rest/exercise toggle ties the heart's pumping to the Y6 diet-and-exercise strand. Colour change, vessel labels and a speed toggle are concrete interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms.
sourceClaims: For KS2: the heart pumps blood around the body; arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, capillaries are tiny vessels; blood transports oxygen, nutrients and water and removes waste such as carbon dioxide.

DfE Y6 statutory requirements: 'identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood'; and 'describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans'.
learnerActions: Power a circulation-loop model by repeatedly tapping/pumping the heart so a surge of bright-red (oxygen-rich) blood flows out through the arteries to the body.

Follow a single blood 'parcel': watch it drop off oxygen, nutrients and water and collect carbon dioxide/waste at the body cells, turn blue (oxygen-poor), flow back through the veins to the heart, get pumped to the lungs, release the carbon dioxide and pick up oxygen so it flushes back to red, then start the loop again.
Tap each vessel to label it: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, capillaries are the tiny vessels where exchange with cells happens.
Toggle a 'rest vs run' control to make the heart beat faster and the flow speed up, then relate this to how your own heart behaves during exercise.
activities.intendedInsight: Blood goes ROUND in a continuous, closed loop and is refreshed at the lungs — it is not consumed on a one-way trip. As it circulates it both delivers (oxygen, nutrients, water) and collects (carbon dioxide, waste). The heart pumps blood both to the lungs and to the body; vessel names describe direction and function.

activities.title: Feel your own pump (pulse and prediction)
feedback: If a learner expects a steady stream, connect the throb they feel to each push of the heart.
If the pulse quickens after exercise, prompt: why would the body move blood faster when muscles are working harder?
Reinforce that any on-screen pump model mirrors their own beating heart.
activities.rationale: Anchoring the model in the child's own body makes the pumping action tangible before it is a diagram, and the predict-then-feel sequence surfaces reasoning. This uses real physical investigation (pulse-finding) as a concrete medium alongside any screen model.
sourceClaims: For KS2: the heart pumps blood around the body; arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, capillaries are tiny vessels; blood transports oxygen, nutrients and water and removes waste such as carbon dioxide.
learnerActions: Find your pulse at the wrist or neck. Before feeling it, predict: does blood leave the heart in a smooth steady stream or in pushes, and why?
Feel the throb with each heartbeat and compare it to your prediction.
Do star jumps or run on the spot, then feel your pulse again and describe what changed.
State in your own words what the heartbeat is doing to the blood and why exercise changes it.
activities.intendedInsight: The heart pumps blood in beats to drive it around the loop; 'the heart pumps blood' becomes a felt fact, and the rate rises with exercise to move more blood (and oxygen) to working muscles.

activities.title: Name the parts and bust the myths
feedback: If a learner says blood only carries oxygen, prompt them to add nutrients, water and the waste (carbon dioxide) it collects.
If a learner confuses arteries and veins, return them to direction: away from the heart = artery, back to the heart = vein.
For the blue-blood myth, clarify oxygen-poor blood is dark red; blue is only how diagrams, and sometimes skin/veins, can appear.
activities.rationale: Naming parts and functions and directly addressing the listed misconceptions consolidates the vocabulary and corrects durable errors. Flap-style 'why does blood keep going round?' and 'what does blood carry?' reveals are concrete interaction examples. A matching/true-false task can check classification but does not by itself elicit extended explanation, so pair it with reasoning in the learner's own words.
sourceClaims: DfE Y6 statutory requirements: 'identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood'; and 'describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans'.

For KS2: the heart pumps blood around the body; arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, capillaries are tiny vessels; blood transports oxygen, nutrients and water and removes waste such as carbon dioxide.
learnerActions: Match each part (heart, artery, vein, capillary, blood) to its job.
Explain why blood keeps going round instead of stopping, and list what blood carries (oxygen, nutrients and water delivered to cells; carbon dioxide and other waste carried away from them).
Decide whether this statement is true: 'the blood in your veins is blue' — and explain your answer.

Locate roughly where the heart sits (near the middle of the chest behind the breastbone, tilted slightly to the left, about fist-sized), correcting the idea that it is on the far left or heart-shaped.
activities.intendedInsight: Each vessel's name carries its function; blood is a two-way carrier (delivers and collects); the blue colouring is only a convention, and the heart's real position and size differ from common myths.

activities.title: Order the journey and check understanding
feedback: If a learner says the heart makes new blood, separate 'pump' from 'produce': the heart moves blood; blood cells are made in bone marrow.
If the described path has no return, prompt them to trace blood back through the veins — it's a closed circuit, not an open one.
If capillaries are omitted so the loop has a gap, point out capillaries join arteries to veins and are where oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged with cells.
If only oxygen is named, prompt them to add nutrients, water and the carbon dioxide/waste the blood also carries.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and probing questions assess whether the loop is truly understood and target the specific error patterns (heart makes blood; one-way open path; blood only carries oxygen; missing capillaries). Ordering and selection consolidate but do not by themselves elicit independent construction, so pair them with explanation in the learner's own words.
sourceClaims: For KS2: the heart pumps blood around the body; arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, capillaries are tiny vessels; blood transports oxygen, nutrients and water and removes waste such as carbon dioxide.
learnerActions: Put the blood's route in order: body → heart → lungs (collect oxygen) → heart → body.

Answer: if blood isn't used up, how does the same blood keep delivering oxygen all day? By what route does it get from your toes back to your heart? Besides oxygen, what else is it carrying as it passes your toes? Where does it pick up fresh oxygen?
Choose the correct statement and explain why 'blood only travels one way and gets used up' is wrong.
Describe the heart's job as pumping (not making) blood, noting blood cells are produced in bone marrow.
activities.intendedInsight: The route forms a closed, continuous loop; the heart pumps and does not manufacture blood; capillaries link arteries to veins where exchange happens.

activities.title: Enrichment: explore the heart in three dimensions
feedback: Keep the focus on 'two destinations' rather than full chamber-and-valve anatomy.
If chambers/valves come up, note these are explored in more detail at a later stage (KS3).
activities.rationale: A 3D heart model is optional enrichment that may help visualise left/right sides and vessel connections; at this band the core target remains the transport loop and part functions, so this supplements rather than replaces the loop activity.
learnerActions: Examine a rotatable/cutaway model of the heart to see the left and right sides and how the great vessels connect.
Relate the left/right sides to the idea that the heart pumps blood to the lungs AND to the body.
activities.intendedInsight: The heart is a genuinely three-dimensional muscular double pump with left and right sides feeding two destinations (lungs and body).

constraints: Keep double circulation simple at KS2: blood passes through the heart on the way to the body and again after the lungs. Defer chambers, valves and the full double circuit to KS3.

The target objective is the continuous transport LOOP and part functions; the 3D heart model and any in-role conversation ('talk to a cardiologist') are enrichment/motivational options, not substitutes for driving or tracing the loop.
Red/blue colouring is a diagram convention only — flag explicitly that oxygen-poor (venous) blood is dark red, not literally blue.

Ordering, matching and multiple-choice tasks consolidate and can check vocabulary and route, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent explanation; have learners also state the loop and functions in their own words.
Link explicitly to the paired Y6 statement that nutrients and water are transported in the blood, and to diet/exercise effects on the heart, so the strand coheres.
NGSS has no US elementary performance expectation naming heart/vessels/blood; treat as UK-led and note US placement one band later (MS-LS1-3).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources (BBC Bitesize; NGSS MS-LS1-3) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat unverified claims accordingly.

The original artefact rationales asserted comparative claims such as 'a static picture cannot' animate circulation and that dialogue 'wouldn't teach the loop as efficiently'. These comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

Conceptual check: the guidance correctly distinguishes pumping from producing blood (bone marrow makes blood cells) and names vessels by direction (arteries = away from the heart regardless of oxygen content, e.g. the pulmonary artery). No arithmetic, force, fraction or shade-investigation issues arise in this topic.

Fix applied in this review: water added to activity 1's delivered materials (action and insight) to match the cited BBC claim and the DfE 'nutrients and water are transported' statement, which had been dropped from the preferred activity.

assess.poeTask: Have students find the pulse at the wrist or neck and, before feeling it, PREDICT whether blood leaves the heart in a smooth steady stream or in pushes, and why. Feeling the throb with each heartbeat reveals the heart pumping in beats to drive blood around the loop.
probeDeeper: If blood isn't used up, how does the same blood keep delivering oxygen all day?
By what route does blood get from your toes back to your heart?
Besides oxygen, name something else the blood is carrying as it passes your toes.
Where does the blood pick up fresh oxygen before heading out again?
assess.correctAnswer: The blood is not used up. After delivering oxygen it returns to the heart through the veins, is pumped to the lungs to pick up more oxygen, and circulates again in a continuous loop. The heart's job is to pump blood, not to make it — blood cells are produced in bone marrow.

errorPatterns.pattern: The heart makes new blood to replace blood that gets used up
errorPatterns.nextMove: The heart pumps; blood recirculates and is not used up; blood cells are made in bone marrow. Separate 'pump' from 'produce'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The heart makes new blood to replace the blood that gets used up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the heart produces blood rather than pumping it

errorPatterns.pattern: Blood flows out to the body and is used up — it doesn't come back
errorPatterns.nextMove: Veins return blood to the heart; it's a closed circuit. Trace blood out through arteries and back through veins.
errorPatterns.distractor: The blood is used up delivering oxygen and doesn't return to the heart.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a one-way, open path with no return to the heart

errorPatterns.pattern: Blood only carries oxygen
errorPatterns.nextMove: Blood also carries dissolved nutrients, carbon dioxide and other wastes; it both delivers and collects.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Omits nutrients, carbon dioxide and waste when saying what blood transports

errorPatterns.pattern: Arteries and veins aren't joined — blood somehow jumps between them
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tiny capillaries link arteries to veins and are where oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged with cells.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Leaves out capillaries, so the loop has a gap

responseLevels.gap: Thinks blood is used up and/or made by the heart; no idea of a returning loop.
responseLevels.full: Describes a continuous closed loop — arteries out, capillaries exchanging, veins back, lungs to reoxygenate — with the heart pumping (not making) blood that carries oxygen, nutrients and wastes.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the heart pumps blood carrying oxygen but describes an open path (no return) or omits nutrients/waste and capillaries.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Blood leaves your heart and travels all the way out to your toes. What happens to that blood after it has delivered oxygen to your toes — does it get used up so the heart has to make new blood, or does something else happen? And what is the heart's actual job in all this?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands circulation describes a closed, continuous loop with blood returning and being reused. A child without it thinks blood is consumed and remade, or that the heart manufactures blood.
