pedagogy.summary: Fluent addition and subtraction within 100 means computing accurately AND selecting an efficient strategy for the particular numbers, rather than running one algorithm for everything. Children partition into tens and ones, compensate, use known facts, and exploit the inverse relationship. Fluency is built on secure single-digit recall and strategy-based adding within 100; the goal is flexible, justified computation, not speed alone.
bestPractices: Teach a repertoire and the judgement to choose: partitioning for 46+37, counting-up/finding-the-difference for near numbers like 71−68, compensation for numbers near a ten
Use the inverse relationship to check (add the answer back) and to solve missing-number problems
Partition the subtrahend into tens and ones for two-digit subtraction, decomposing a ten where the ones are insufficient (NCETM Spine 1.16)
Contrast two methods on the same calculation and ask which was quicker and why, to build strategic flexibility
Keep concrete/pictorial support (base-ten, number line) available so regrouping stays meaningful, not a memorised digit ritual
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (compose/decompose a ten for regrouping)
Number line (count-up for finding a difference between close numbers)
Part-whole / partitioning jottings (70+13=83)
Bar model (comparison subtraction)
Hundred square (jumps of tens and ones)
commonMisconceptions: Smaller-from-larger subtraction bug: in 83−25 doing 5−3 in the ones column, answer 62
Partitioning correctly but dropping or mis-recombining the regrouped ten (46+37 → 73)
Applying one written method rigidly even when the numbers make a mental strategy far quicker (column-subtracting 71−68)
Treating addition and subtraction as unrelated, so the inverse is not used to check

learn.summary: Fluent addition and subtraction within 100 means computing accurately AND choosing an efficient strategy for the particular numbers, not running one algorithm for everything. Learners partition into tens and ones, compensate near a ten, use known facts, count up to find a difference between close numbers, and exploit the inverse to check. The target is flexible, justified computation, built on secure single-digit recall. The core activity places the same calculation on two tools so the learner feels why the smart method depends on the numbers; supporting activities add strategy-selection practice, a worked strategy reference, and spoken justification.

activities.title: Same calculation, two tools: feel which method fits the numbers
feedback: If the borrow and the count-up look equally fast to you, count the steps in each: counting up from 68 to 71 covers a difference of just three, while the borrow takes several steps. Closeness of the numbers is the signal to count up.
If 46+37 came out as 73, show exactly where the extra ten went: 6+7 makes 13, which is one ten and three. That one ten joins the 70 to make 80, and the 3 ones make the total 83.
If you reached for the same written method on every pair, pause first and read the numbers: are they close (count up), near a ten (compensate), or a known fact you can just recall?
activities.rationale: Presenting the identical calculation on a number line and a base-ten workspace side by side lets the learner directly compare strategies on the same numbers, which is the comparison that strategy selection depends on. Auto-composing/decomposing a ten keeps the regroup visible so it is not reduced to a memorised digit ritual. Optional timing/animation of both methods and drag-to-count on the number line make the efficiency gap concrete; these are illustrative supports, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Two-digit subtraction is done by partitioning the subtrahend into tens and ones (decomposing a ten where needed), and strategy choice varies with the numbers — e.g. counting up from 67 to find 94−67, or counting back for 64−25.

Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100, use the inverse relationship to check calculations, and partition numbers in different ways (e.g. 23 = 20+3 and 10+13) to support subtraction.
learnerActions: Take 71 − 68 and first work it on a base-ten column workspace: there are not enough ones, so decompose a ten, cross out, and carry through the several steps of the borrow.
Now work the same 71 − 68 on a number line: count up from 68 to 71 and see the difference is just three.
Place the three-hop count-up beside the multi-step borrow and say which was quicker and why.
Switch to 46 + 37 on the base-ten side: combine 40+30 and 6+7, compose the thirteen ones into one ten and three, and add that ten in so the total is 83, not 73.
Finish by looking at a fresh pair of numbers and stating, before you start, which method you will use and why.
activities.intendedInsight: The efficient method depends on the numbers: when the numbers are close, counting up the difference beats a columnar borrow; regrouping must be composed or decomposed deliberately so the extra ten is never silently dropped.

activities.title: Check with the inverse and solve missing-number problems
feedback: If adding the answer back does not return to the start, either the subtraction or the checking addition has an error—often a dropped or mis-recombined ten; rework both with place-value support.
If you treated the missing-number problem as unrelated to subtraction, notice that 46 + ? = 83 is answered by 83 − 46 = 37.
activities.rationale: Using the inverse to check and to solve missing-number problems targets the common gap of treating the two operations as unrelated, and is named directly in the Year 2 curriculum.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100, use the inverse relationship to check calculations, and partition numbers in different ways (e.g. 23 = 20+3 and 10+13) to support subtraction.
learnerActions: After computing 83 − 25, add your answer back to 25 and confirm it returns to 83.
Given a missing-number problem such as 46 + ? = 83, use subtraction (83 − 46) to find the unknown, then add back to check.
State in words how addition and subtraction undo each other for the pair you just solved.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition and subtraction are inverse operations, so adding an answer back is a reliable self-check and lets you turn a missing-number problem into the operation you find easier.

activities.title: Match the calculation to the smartest strategy (selection practice)
feedback: If you chose 62 for 83 − 25, you likely did 5 − 3 in the ones column; you cannot take 5 from 3, so 83 must give up a ten (becoming 70 + 13) first, giving 58. Check by computing 62 + 25, which comes to 87, not 83.
If you matched a slow method to close numbers like 71 − 68, reconsider: close numbers signal counting up the difference.
activities.rationale: A selection/matching task with 62 offered as the tempting wrong answer rehearses strategy choice and catches the smaller-from-larger bug. This format checks and reinforces selection rather than building flexibility through sustained varied doing, so it supplements, not replaces, the two-tool work.
sourceClaims: The 'smaller-from-larger' subtraction error is a classic, systematic buggy algorithm — the child subtracts the smaller digit from the larger within each column regardless of position (the '437−284=253' pattern). In Brown & Burton's 1325-student data it was used by 54 students; such bugs are stable, not careless (~40% of students consistently buggy).

Two-digit subtraction is done by partitioning the subtrahend into tens and ones (decomposing a ten where needed), and strategy choice varies with the numbers — e.g. counting up from 67 to find 94−67, or counting back for 64−25.
learnerActions: Across a mixed set of additions and subtractions, pair each calculation with the most efficient strategy (partition, compensate near a ten, count up the difference, or recall a known fact).
For 83 − 25, choose the correct answer (58) and explain why 62 is wrong.
Say aloud what feature of the numbers made you pick that strategy.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading the numbers first—how close they are, whether they sit near a ten, whether a fact is known—tells you which method is efficient before you compute.

activities.title: Worked strategy reference to consult
feedback: If the reference method differs from yours, identify which numbers triggered it—that trigger is the point to remember.
Use the reference to locate a slip (e.g. a dropped ten) rather than to replace doing the calculations yourself.
activities.rationale: A static reveal-the-method chart displays worked examples clearly but cannot exercise the choosing itself, so it is a reference scaffold alongside active practice, not a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Reveal, for each calculation type, its most efficient method and a short reason: partitioning for 46 + 37, counting up for 71 − 68, compensation for numbers near a ten.
Compare a worked example with your own jotting on a similar pair to see whether your recombination kept the regrouped ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Each strategy has a signature of numbers it suits; a worked example makes the method and its justification explicit.

activities.title: Justify your method aloud
feedback: If you cannot give a reason beyond 'that's how I always do it', look again at the numbers for a feature (closeness, nearness to a ten, a known fact) that favours a particular method.
If prompted to try counting up and it proves faster, note that for next time.
activities.rationale: Spoken justification prompts a learner to articulate strategy choice, which supports metacognition; on its own it cannot supply the volume of varied practice fluency needs, so it accompanies the computational activities.
learnerActions: After solving a pair, explain to a partner or adult why you chose your method for those particular numbers.
Respond to a prompt such as: 'You borrowed for 71 − 68—can you see a quicker way to find the gap between 68 and 71?' and try the alternative.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify a strategy choice out loud consolidates the habit of reading the numbers before computing.

constraints: Fluency is a doing skill: recognition, matching, and tap-to-reveal reference formats check or display strategy but do not by themselves build flexible computation; keep substantial varied practice of actually computing.
Keep concrete/pictorial support (base-ten blocks, number line, hundred square, and bar model for comparison subtraction) available so regrouping stays meaningful rather than a memorised digit ritual.
The smaller-from-larger bug is stable and systematic, not careless; confront it with place-value regrouping and an inverse check (62 + 25 = 87 ≠ 83) rather than simply marking it wrong.
Spoken justification alone cannot supply the volume of practice needed; use it to consolidate choice, not to replace computation.
Timing/animation, drag-to-count, and auto-exchange are optional supports that make the efficiency gap and the regroup visible; they are illustrative, not mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (NCETM Spine 1.16) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its strategy-choice examples (count up for 94−67, count back for 64−25) as unverified.

Arithmetic self-checked: 46+37 = 83 (40+30=70, 6+7=13, 70+13=83; 73 is the dropped-ten error); 83−25 = 58 (62 is the smaller-from-larger bug; 62+25=87≠83); 60−24 = 36; 71−68 = 3; missing-number 46+?=83 gives 37. The diagnostic correctAnswer string '83, 58, 36, 3' matches these.

Legacy claims that '3D adds no explanatory power' and that dialogue 'cannot supply the volume of varied practice' were softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements; they were catalog fit rationales, not established comparative-efficacy findings.
Legacy claim that a coded surface offering the same pair on two tools is where 'fluency clicks' is retained as a design rationale, not as a claim of demonstrated necessity or verified effectiveness.
The assessment's 60−24 and the 83−45 probe variant are not given a dedicated activity; consider adding practice that exercises those if full coverage of the diagnostic set is wanted.

probeDeeper: For 71−68 you took away by borrowing — is there a quicker way to see the gap between 68 and 71?
Add your answer to 25 to check 83−25 — does it come back to 83?
You partitioned 46 and 37 into tens and ones — show me exactly where the extra ten in the answer came from.
What if it were 83 − 45 instead of 83 − 25 — would your method still work? Try it and see.
assess.correctAnswer: 83, 58, 36, 3. Fluent work: 46+37 by partitioning (70+13=83); 83−25 by regrouping or counting up; 60−24 as 60−20−4 or by counting up from 24; 71−68 should trigger counting up (68→71 = 3) rather than columnar borrowing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger subtraction bug — 'eighty-three take twenty-five: five take three is two', answering 62 regardless of column order
errorPatterns.nextMove: Go back to place-value regrouping with base-ten blocks: 83 must give up a ten to make enough ones (as 70+13) before the ones can be taken. Confront by checking 62+25.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ones column of 83−25 is done as 5−3 with no decomposition of a ten; answer 62

errorPatterns.pattern: Partitions correctly but loses the regrouped ten — '46 and 37: seventy and thirteen… seventy-three'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the recombination, don't reteach the method: have the child compose the 13 into 'one ten and three' and add that ten to the seventy. This is a lapse, not a missing concept.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct partial sums (70 and 13) but the final recombination drops the extra ten, giving 73 instead of 83

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches for the same written method regardless of the numbers — column-subtracts 71−68 with full borrowing instead of counting up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the algorithm; put the count-up and the borrow side by side on the same pair and ask which was quicker and why, building the habit of looking at the numbers first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Works 71−68 with a multi-step borrow, showing no sensitivity to how close the numbers are

responseLevels.gap: Smaller-from-larger or dropped-ten errors; answers are unreliable whenever regrouping is needed.
responseLevels.full: Efficient and accurate on all four, selects the method to suit the numbers (counts up for 71−68, partitions for 46+37), keeps regrouping correct, and checks using the inverse.
responseLevels.partial: Accurate with one preferred method (e.g. always partitions) but does not adapt to the numbers; slow or stumbles where counting up would be far easier; needs prompting to check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set these four one at a time and watch the child work each, letting them choose their own method and jot: 46 + 37, then 83 − 25, then 60 − 24, then 71 − 68. Pay particular attention to which method they reach for on 71 − 68.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 83−25 exposes the smaller-from-larger bug (a child doing 5−3 answers 62). 71−68 separates a child with strategic flexibility, who notices the numbers are close and counts up, from one who mechanically column-subtracts everything. 46+37 exposes a dropped regroup (answer 73). Together they distinguish accurate-and-flexible from accurate-but-rigid from buggy.

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100, use the inverse relationship to check calculations, and partition numbers in different ways (e.g. 23 = 20+3 and 10+13) to support subtraction.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1, Year 2)

sources.claim: Two-digit subtraction is done by partitioning the subtrahend into tens and ones (decomposing a ten where needed), and strategy choice varies with the numbers — e.g. counting up from 67 to find 94−67, or counting back for 64−25.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery PD, Spine 1 Segment 1.16

sources.claim: The 'smaller-from-larger' subtraction error is a classic, systematic buggy algorithm — the child subtracts the smaller digit from the larger within each column regardless of position (the '437−284=253' pattern). In Brown & Burton's 1325-student data it was used by 54 students; such bugs are stable, not careless (~40% of students consistently buggy).
sources.source: Brown & Burton, 'Diagnostic Models for Procedural Bugs in Basic Mathematical Skills', Cognitive Science 2(2), 1978 (full text: ERIC ED159036)

pedagogy.summary: Two-step contextual problems where the child must plan before computing: identify the two steps and their order, choose an appropriate method (mental or written) for each step given the numbers, and justify the choices. The intellectual work is structuring the situation, not arithmetic — so the enemy is the KEYWORD strategy ('altogether' means add, 'left' means subtract), which collapses on comparison and multi-step structures. Bar-model representation of the whole problem before any calculation is the central pedagogy.
bestPractices: Represent the whole problem with a bar model BEFORE computing — structure first, numbers second
Explicitly plan the two steps and their order; name the intermediate quantity so it is not mistaken for the answer
Directly discredit keyword-spotting with problems where the keyword misleads (a 'more than' comparison that needs subtraction)
Choose method per step by the numbers (a near-multiple mentally, an awkward pair on paper)
Check the final answer for reasonableness against the story
keyRepresentations: Bar model (comparison and aggregation)
Part-whole diagram
Empty number line / jottings
Two-box 'step 1 -> step 2' planner
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy — picks the operation from a word ('altogether', 'more than') rather than the situation
One-step-only — solves the first step and offers the intermediate quantity as the final answer
Wrong order of steps, or choosing operations from the numbers present rather than the story
Uses a written method where a mental one is efficient, or vice versa
Does not notice an implausible answer

learn.summary: Year 4 two-step addition and subtraction problems in context, where the real work is structuring the situation before computing: identify the two steps and their order, name the intermediate quantity, choose a mental or written method per step based on the numbers, and check the answer for reasonableness. The central aim is to beat the keyword strategy (treating 'altogether' as always add, 'more than' as always add, 'left' as always subtract), which collapses on comparison and multi-step problems. Representing the whole problem (e.g. with a bar model) before any calculation is the core move.

activities.title: Model the structure before you compute (bar-model planner)
feedback: If a learner answers 425 (340+85) on the sticker problem: ask 'who has more, Sam or Kim, and how do you know?' Draw the comparison so they see Kim must be found by subtraction first.
If a learner answers 247 on the apple problem: re-read and underline what is actually asked, and mark BOTH steps so the second (the delivery) is not dropped.
If a learner adds all the numbers in sight or does the steps in the wrong order: narrate the story in order, mapping each event to one operation.

Prompt: 'If it said Sam has 85 FEWER than Kim, would you still subtract to find Kim — or add?' to test whether they are modelling rather than word-spotting (here, fewer would mean Kim is larger, so you would add).
activities.rationale: Representing a problem's underlying structure visually before writing an equation focuses attention on the relationships between quantities, and keyword shortcuts are an explicitly discouraged substitute for reasoning. A tool or drawing that cannot 'close' the total until the unknown is found may make the two-step dependency visible; a static annotated version can show the structure but does not let the learner plan a fresh problem.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils solve addition and subtraction two-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why.

Problem solving 'is not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; students who represent a problem's underlying structure visually (strip/bar diagrams) before writing an equation are more effective, because well-chosen representations focus attention on the relationships between quantities rather than surface story context. STRONG evidence rating.
The keyword strategy fails on comparison and multi-step structures; bar/strip modelling of problem structure before computing supports correct operation choice.
learnerActions: Before writing any calculation, draw or build a bar model of the whole story showing which quantities are known and which are unknown.
Work the trap problem: 'Sam has 340 stickers. That is 85 more than Kim. How many stickers do they have altogether?' First decide who has MORE — Sam or Kim.
Notice that the 'altogether' total cannot be found yet because Kim is unknown; find Kim first by 340 - 85 = 255, then add 340 + 255 = 595.

Then work the aggregation problem: 'A shop has 415 apples. In the morning it sells 168. In the afternoon a delivery brings 230 more. How many are there now?' Model it, then compute 415 - 168 = 247, then 247 + 230 = 477.
Name the intermediate quantity out loud (e.g. '247 is the apples after the morning, not the final answer').
activities.intendedInsight: The operation comes from the structure of the situation, not from a keyword. 'More than' can require subtraction (to find the smaller unknown quantity) before any adding, and a two-step problem has an intermediate value that is not the final answer.

activities.title: Talk me through your plan: justify each step and method
feedback: If the learner picks a written method where a mental one is efficient (or vice versa): ask what makes these particular numbers easy or hard, and compare the two methods on that step.
Praise plans that name the intermediate quantity and give a reason for each method choice, not just correct arithmetic.
If a reason is 'because the word said so', press for a reason based on what the story is actually doing.
activities.rationale: The objective explicitly requires explaining why chosen operations and methods are appropriate, so producing a justification (spoken or written) exercises exactly that; a recognition-only task does not itself elicit a produced justification.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils solve addition and subtraction two-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why.
learnerActions: State the two steps and their order before computing anything.

For each step, choose a mental or written method based on the numbers (e.g. adding a multiple of ten like +230 can easily be done mentally; a pair that needs exchanging, like 415 - 168, may be better written for many learners, though some may compensate mentally, e.g. 415 - 170 + 2) and say why.
Answer a questioner who keeps asking 'why that operation?', 'which step first and why?', 'why did you do that one in your head?'
Defend or revise your plan when challenged.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding which operations and methods to use — and being able to justify them — is itself the skill, not just getting a number. Method choice should fit the specific numbers.

activities.title: Ordering and method checks (with a keyword trap)
feedback: For a trap item, after the answer, reveal the comparison structure and show why the keyword misled.
For a method item, confirm by comparing how awkward the computation would be each way.
activities.rationale: Selection items can check ordering and method choice quickly and surface keyword reliance, but as recognition tasks they do not themselves require the learner to construct a plan or model independently — pair them with the modelling and justification activities above.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils solve addition and subtraction two-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why.
learnerActions: Given a two-step problem, put the two operations in the correct order.
Choose the better method (mental or written) for a specified step and give the reason.
Answer at least one item deliberately designed as a keyword trap, where 'more than' or 'altogether' points to the wrong first move.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering the steps and matching a method to the numbers are distinct decisions; keywords are not a reliable guide to either.

activities.title: Reasonableness pause
feedback: If an implausible magnitude is accepted without pause, prompt 'roughly what should we expect here, and does this fit?' and build the habit of a reasonableness check — this is about noticing, not re-teaching the arithmetic.
activities.rationale: Checking reasonableness against the story guards against both word-spotting and dropped steps by catching errors the computation alone does not reveal.
learnerActions: After reaching a final answer, estimate roughly what size answer the story should produce, then check the result against that expectation.

For the apple problem, reason about the net change: the shop sold 168 but a larger delivery of 230 arrived, so the final count should be a little MORE than the 415 it started with (477 fits); an answer far larger — such as adding all three numbers (813) — or far smaller (e.g. 247, which drops the delivery) would signal an error.
If the answer does not fit the expected size, re-examine the plan (not just redo the arithmetic).
activities.intendedInsight: A final answer must be sense-checked against the situation; a magnitude that does not fit what the story should produce signals a planning or structuring error.

constraints: The learning target is situation structure and method choice, not arithmetic fluency alone; the arithmetic should be within reach so attention stays on planning.
Do not teach keyword rules ('altogether means add', 'more than means add', 'left means subtract'); these are the misconception this topic targets.
A static annotated worked problem can illustrate the two-step structure but does not let a learner plan or model a new problem — treat it as an exposition scaffold, not the main task.
Selection/ordering items are recognition tasks and do not by themselves elicit an independently constructed plan or model; use them alongside construction and justification, not instead of them.

A tool that physically blocks keyword-adding (e.g. a total bar that will not close until the unknown part is found) is an optional mechanism to make the dependency visible; a drawn bar model on paper serves the same purpose.
The intermediate quantity must be named and distinguished from the final answer so it is not reported as the solution.

The reasonableness check must use expected magnitude for the specific story; do not teach that 'more than the starting amount' is automatically implausible, since in the apple problem the correct answer (477) is legitimately more than the 415 start because the 230 delivery outweighs the 168 sale (net +62).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: apple problem 415 - 168 = 247, then 247 + 230 = 477 — correct; adding all three (415+168+230) = 813. Sticker problem: Kim = 340 - 85 = 255, then 340 + 255 = 595 — correct. The named keyword-trap error value (340+85 = 425) and the dropped-step value (247) are presented only as learner errors to diagnose, never as valid answers.

The original row's performance error pattern gives 'more apples than started, after a net change' as an example of an implausible magnitude, but for this apple problem the correct answer (477) genuinely exceeds the 415 start because the 230 delivery outweighs the 168 sale (net +62). The reasonableness activity has been corrected to anchor on expected magnitude rather than 'more/fewer than started'.

One source (Cognitively Guided Instruction / Singapore model method / NCETM bar-model guidance) is marked verified:false and 'not fetched this session' in the original row; its claim is retained but should not be treated as independently confirmed.

The original design note asserts a bar-model tool 'can refuse a keyword-driven mis-structuring' and marks 'the moment situation-modelling beats word-spotting'; this is a plausible design claim but comparative efficacy/necessity is not established by the cited sources, so it is framed here as an optional mechanism rather than a proven one.
The original artefact rating '3D adds nothing' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been omitted rather than restated as universal.

probeDeeper: What is the question actually asking for - the apples after the morning, or at the very end of the day?
In the sticker problem, who has more, Sam or Kim? How do you know?
If it said Sam has 85 FEWER than Kim, would you still subtract to find Kim - or add?
Which step did you do in your head and which on paper, and why that choice?
assess.correctAnswer: Problem 1: 415 - 168 = 247, then 247 + 230 = 477 (two steps, right order; the subtraction likely written, the +230 can be mental). Problem 2: recognises 'more than' does NOT simply mean add - Kim has 340 - 85 = 255, then 340 + 255 = 595 altogether. Explains why each operation fits the story.

errorPatterns.pattern: Word-spots: 'more than means add, altogether means add everything' - does 340 + 85, or adds all the numbers, and stops
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the bar - who has MORE, Sam or Kim? Build the comparison model so the child sees Kim must be found by subtraction. Attack keyword reliance directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Problem 2 answer of 425 (340+85) or an all-numbers sum; no comparison is modelled

errorPatterns.pattern: Solves only the first step and gives the intermediate quantity as the final answer (e.g. 247 apples, forgetting the delivery)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-read and underline what is actually asked; mark BOTH steps on the bar so the second is not dropped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Problem 1 answer of 247

errorPatterns.pattern: Picks operations from the numbers present or in the wrong order rather than from the story sequence
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act out or narrate the story in order; each event maps to one operation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 415 + 168 first, or an arbitrary order

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts an implausible answer without checking it against the story
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'does that make sense - more or fewer than we started with?' Build a reasonableness pause; do not reteach the arithmetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports a magnitude that cannot be right (e.g. more apples than started, after a net change) without pause

responseLevels.gap: Grabs numbers and one operation, driven by keywords; produces no two-step plan.
responseLevels.full: Models both problems with a bar, sequences the two steps correctly including the comparison, chooses a method per step, and checks reasonableness; transfers correctly to a 'fewer than' variant.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the straightforward two-step problem but is misled by the 'more than' comparison, or answers the intermediate value; can list steps but does not model the situation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Read this aloud and watch the child PLAN before computing: 'A shop has 415 apples. In the morning it sells 168. In the afternoon a delivery brings 230 more. How many apples are there now?' Ask 'what are the steps, and how will you do each one?' Then give a second problem where the keyword misleads: 'Sam has 340 stickers. That is 85 more than Kim. How many stickers do they have altogether?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Problem 2 contains 'more than' and 'altogether' - a keyword solver adds 340 + 85 and stops, or adds all the numbers in sight. A child who models the situation finds Kim by subtraction first, then adds. Meanwhile the two-step structure of Problem 1 catches the child who reports the intermediate 247 as the answer. Together they separate situation-modelling from word-spotting and one-step shortcutting.

pedagogy.summary: Here the fixed-whole idea generalises from lines and points to CLOSED SHAPES: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, of a quadrilateral to 360°, and of any polygon to (n−2)×180° — because every polygon can be cut into (n−2) triangles. The child uses these sums to find a missing angle by subtraction, and for a REGULAR polygon divides the sum equally among the vertices (regular hexagon: 720° ÷ 6 = 120°). The central pedagogical danger is teaching '180° in a triangle' as an isolated fact to memorise; taught well, the triangle sum is DERIVED (torn corners laid on a straight line, or a triangle's angles rearranged to 180°) and the quadrilateral/polygon sums are built by partitioning into triangles — so the whole family hangs together and, crucially, the sum is seen to be INDEPENDENT of the triangle's size.
bestPractices: Derive the triangle sum, don't just state it: tear off the three corners and fit them onto a straight line (180°), or fold them to a point on the base — so 180° is a thing the child has seen happen, not a number to recall.

Build the quadrilateral (360°) and polygon sums by PARTITIONING into triangles — a quadrilateral is two triangles, an n-gon is (n−2) triangles — connecting every polygon back to the triangle rather than memorising separate facts.

Confront size-dependence directly: show that stretching a triangle bigger, or drawing it with longer sides, leaves the angle sum at 180° — many children (and adults) intuitively expect the angles to grow with the triangle.
Use 'not drawn to scale' problems and non-isosceles-looking triangles so children compute from given angles rather than assuming equal angles from appearance.
For regular polygons, separate the two steps clearly: find the total angle sum, THEN divide by the number of (equal) vertices — don't conflate the sum with a single interior angle.
Treat finding a missing angle as subtraction from the known sum, writing the calculation, and sanity-checking (a triangle angle can't exceed 180°).
keyRepresentations: Torn-corners demonstration: three triangle corners rearranged onto a straight line = 180°
Polygon partitioned into triangles: quadrilateral = 2 triangles (360°), n-gon = (n−2) triangles
Angle-sum table: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°
Regular polygon: total sum ÷ number of vertices = one interior angle (hexagon 720° ÷ 6 = 120°)
A stretchable triangle whose angle sum stays 180° as its size changes
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° rather than 180° (documented in diagnostic data), so subtracts from the wrong total.

Believes the angle sum (or a missing angle) depends on the triangle's SIZE — expects a bigger/longer triangle to have larger angles; contradicts the constant 180° sum (documented in children and adults).
Assumes a triangle is isosceles or equilateral because it looks that way on a not-to-scale diagram, so wrongly takes two angles as equal.
Knows '180° in a triangle' only as a disconnected fact and cannot extend it to a quadrilateral or polygon (does not partition into triangles).
For a regular polygon, reports the total angle sum as if it were a single interior angle (forgets to divide by the number of vertices).

learn.summary: Learners find unknown angles in triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons using angle-sum properties — but with the triangle's 180° DERIVED (not merely recalled), the quadrilateral/polygon sums BUILT by partitioning into (n−2) triangles, and the crucial fact that the angle sum is INDEPENDENT of the triangle's size made visible rather than asserted. Activities span a hands-on/manipulable derivation of 180° and size-invariance, a partition-to-build-larger-sums task, scorable missing-angle practice (including 'not drawn to scale' and 360°-distractor items), and a two-step regular-polygon calculation (total sum ÷ vertices). The central danger addressed throughout is teaching '180° in a triangle' as an isolated memorised fact.

activities.title: Torn corners make a straight line (deriving 180°)
feedback: If the corners fill the line with no gap or overlap, the angles make a straight angle, 180°. Paper shows this up to small imperfections, and the exact value is the ideal geometric result.
Tearing and folding should give the same result: both arrange the three angles along a straight line.
Try a very differently-shaped triangle: if its corners still fill a straight line, the 180° result is not specific to one triangle.
A paper cutout has slight thickness and torn edges, so expect tiny imperfections; the screen model shows the idealised exact fit for the ideal (zero-thickness) plane figure.
activities.rationale: Deriving the triangle sum by physically rearranging corners onto a straight line — whether by tearing or by folding to a point on the base — connects it to 'angles on a straight line = 180°' and makes 180° an observed outcome rather than a disconnected fact, the pedagogy's central correction. Both paper and an optional drag-and-snap screen model make the mechanism concrete; efficacy relative to simply stating the rule is proposed, not tested.
sourceClaims: Year 5 primary lesson: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, derived from angles on a straight line; a common misconception is that pupils know this only as a disconnected fact, so the recommended approach is to relate the triangle to the quadrilateral by partitioning shapes into triangles.
learnerActions: Cut or tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them side by side so their vertices meet at a single point — observe that together they fill a straight line (180°), with no visible gap or overlap apart from small paper imperfections.

Alternatively derive the same result by using the longest side as the base: fold the top corner down so it touches the base at the foot of the height, then fold the other two corners in to meet it at that point — they again fill a straight line along the base.
Repeat either method with a differently-shaped triangle (e.g. a long thin one and a squat one) and confirm the three corners again fill a straight line.
On a drag-and-drop screen model, drag the three corner-wedges onto a straight line so they snap to fill 180°, with a banner reading the running sum.
activities.intendedInsight: The three interior angles of ANY triangle rearrange to lie on a straight line, so they sum to 180° — this is something you can see happen (by tearing or by folding the corners), not a number to recall.

activities.title: Does the sum change when the triangle changes size?
feedback: If you predicted the sum would grow but it stayed 180°, that is exactly the intuition this task is designed to surface and correct.

Stretching or squashing changes side lengths and individual angles, and simply enlarging the same shape keeps every angle the same. Either way the three angles total 180° (paper measurements may be off by a degree or two).
Making a triangle bigger does NOT make its angles bigger — an enlarged copy of a triangle has exactly the same angles. Work from the given angles, not from how big the triangle looks.
activities.rationale: Both children and educated adults intuitively expect a triangle's angles to scale with its size; confronting this prediction directly, then showing the sum hold constant under reshaping, targets a documented and persistent misconception. An optional live vertex-drag with a sum readout calculated from the current angles (an idealised model) makes the invariance experienceable; its advantage over simply asserting the rule is proposed, not demonstrated.
sourceClaims: Children (6–7) and even educated adults intuitively judge a triangle's missing third angle as scaling with the triangle's overall size — predicting a larger angle when the base is longer — in direct contradiction with Euclid's proposition 32 that the internal angles of a triangle sum to a constant regardless of size; the error reflects mental simulation rather than use of the angle-sum rule, and formal schooling did not predict accuracy.
learnerActions: Predict, before testing: 'If I make this triangle much bigger or stretch it long and thin, will the angle sum get bigger?' Write down your prediction.
Make the triangle larger, then longer and thinner, then squat and wide — on a screen model drag a vertex to reshape it; on paper draw each new triangle.

Each time, re-check the angle sum: read the live sum readout on the screen model, or (on paper) tear or fold the corners of each new triangle, or measure its three marked angles, and record the total.
Compare your prediction with what actually happened to the sum.
activities.intendedInsight: The angle sum stays 180° no matter how big, small, long or stretched the triangle is — side length does not change the angle sum, even though many people expect bigger triangles to have bigger angles.

activities.title: Build the polygon sums by cutting into triangles
feedback: Check: your number of triangles should always be two fewer than the number of sides.
If the quadrilateral gives 360° as two triangles of 180°, you have connected it to the triangle rather than memorised a separate fact.
If you can state WHY a quadrilateral is 360° ('it is two triangles'), you understand the partition, not just the number.
activities.rationale: Partitioning into triangles turns a set of separate memorised sums into one connected system and directly addresses the misconception of knowing '180°' only as an isolated fact that cannot be extended. A tap-to-partition screen mode can make the triangle count visible.
sourceClaims: Year 5 primary lesson: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, derived from angles on a straight line; a common misconception is that pupils know this only as a disconnected fact, so the recommended approach is to relate the triangle to the quadrilateral by partitioning shapes into triangles.
learnerActions: Draw a diagonal inside a quadrilateral to split it into two triangles (in a dented, non-convex quadrilateral, use the diagonal that stays inside); conclude its angle sum is 2 × 180° = 360°.
Partition a convex pentagon (3 triangles) and a convex hexagon (4 triangles) from one vertex, counting the triangles each time.
Record results in an angle-sum table: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°.
State the pattern in words and as a rule: an n-gon splits into (n−2) triangles, so its angle sum is (n−2) × 180°.
activities.intendedInsight: Every simple polygon's (one with no crossing sides) angle sum is built from triangles: an n-sided polygon divides into (n−2) triangles, so its interior angles sum to (n−2) × 180° — the whole family connects back to the triangle.

activities.title: Missing-angle practice, including 'not drawn to scale'
feedback: If you subtracted from 360° for a triangle and got 230°, that exceeds 180° — a sign the wrong total was used; a triangle is 180°.
If a figure looks isosceles but the marked angles differ, trust the numbers: 'not drawn to scale' means both appearance AND measuring the drawing are unreliable — only the marked angles are correct.
Writing the subtraction and checking it is reasonable guards against both the wrong-total error and arithmetic slips.
activities.rationale: Scorable number-entry and multiple-choice practice efficiently rehearses the procedure and catches two documented errors — subtracting from 360° and assuming isosceles from appearance. On a not-to-scale figure, measuring the drawing returns the misleading drawn angles, so only the marked values work. Diagnostic data also notes that the most common wrong answer can be an arithmetic slip by students who DO know the rule, so writing and checking the calculation matters. This practice can check and rehearse the procedure but cannot itself stage the size-invariance discovery, which the manipulable tasks above provide.
sourceClaims: Diagnostic-question data: a documented wrong answer is that angles in a triangle add up to 360° (students subtract from 360 rather than 180); another group assumes the triangle is isosceles because it looks that way; the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip by students who knew the 180° rule — so reasoning errors must be separated from computation errors.
learnerActions: Find a triangle's third angle given two angles by subtracting from 180° (e.g. 180 − (70 + 60) = 50°); write the calculation.
Find a quadrilateral's missing angle by subtracting the three known angles from 360°.
Answer an item deliberately drawn roughly isosceles though it is NOT to scale: compute only from the marked angles, not from how the figure looks and not by measuring the drawing with a protractor.
Sanity-check each answer (each triangle angle must be more than 0° and less than 180°; the three sum to exactly 180°).
activities.intendedInsight: Missing angles are found by subtracting known angles from the correct total (180° for a triangle, 360° for a quadrilateral), using the MARKED values rather than the picture's appearance or a protractor reading of a not-to-scale drawing.

activities.title: Regular polygons: find the sum, THEN share it out
feedback: If you stopped at 720°, that is the TOTAL of all six angles, not one angle — you still need to divide by 6.
Labelling 'total sum' versus 'one angle' keeps the two steps from collapsing together.
Check scale: one interior angle of a hexagon (120°) should be far smaller than the full 720° total.
activities.rationale: A documented error is reporting the total polygon sum as if it were a single interior angle; explicitly separating the sum step from the divide-equally step addresses this without needing to reteach the sum. An optional regular-polygon panel showing sum ÷ vertices makes the share-equally step concrete.
learnerActions: For a regular hexagon, first find the total interior-angle sum (4 triangles × 180° = 720°).
Then, because all six interior angles of a regular hexagon are equal, divide: 720° ÷ 6 = 120° for one interior angle.
Write the two steps separately and label which number is the TOTAL sum and which is ONE angle.
Repeat for another regular polygon (e.g. regular pentagon: 540° ÷ 5 = 108°).
activities.intendedInsight: For a regular polygon there are two distinct steps: find the total angle sum, then divide equally among the (equal) vertices to get one interior angle — the total sum is not itself a single angle.

constraints: '180° in a triangle' must be derived (e.g. torn corners on a straight line, or corners folded to the foot of the height on the longest side) and connected to the other polygon sums by partitioning into triangles — not taught as an isolated fact to memorise.
Scorable multiple-choice/number-entry practice rehearses and catches distractors but cannot by itself stage the size-invariance discovery; pair it with a manipulable or hands-on reshaping task.
Paper/card triangle cutouts have slight thickness and torn edges; treat them as physical approximations of the ideal zero-thickness plane figure. Label any screen model as an idealisation.

A static picture or table can seed the 180° fact and the angle-sum table but cannot let the learner reshape a triangle to experience the sum staying constant; use it as a scaffold, not a replacement for manipulation.

'Not drawn to scale' problems require computing from marked angles only; do not infer equal angles from an isosceles-looking figure, and do not measure the drawing with a protractor to get the angles.
Separate genuine reasoning errors (wrong total, size-dependence, isosceles assumption) from mere arithmetic slips when interpreting a wrong answer.
Interior-angle sums here concern plane polygons; a 3D setting is not required and could be confused with solid angles.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row framed a 3D or conversation artefact as adding 'no conceptual gain' or being unable to teach the discovery; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limitation statements in constraints rather than universal laws.
sourceClaims are limited to claims that directly support each principle; the regular-polygon two-step activity has no directly supporting source claim and is marked [].
Arithmetic self-checked: 180−(70+60)=50; wrong-total 360−130=230; quadrilateral 2×180=360; pentagon 3×180=540, 540÷5=108; hexagon 4×180=720, 720÷6=120 — all consistent with the source row.

Edits in this independent review: clarified the size-invariance check method in activity 2 (read the screen sum readout, or tear/fold/measure each fresh paper triangle) because re-tearing the corners of an already-drawn or on-screen triangle is not coherent; retained the earlier restorations of the fold-to-a-point derivation (activity 1) and the 'measuring a not-to-scale drawing misleads' point (activity 4).

probeDeeper: 'You said the missing angle is 50°. If I stretched this triangle to twice as wide but kept these two angles the same, what would the third angle be now?' — counterexample targeting size-dependence (it stays 50°).
'How could you use triangles to work out the angle sum of this hexagon?' — probes whether the polygon sum is derived by partition or just recalled.
'This quadrilateral — why 360° and the triangle only 180°? What's the connection?' — listens for 'a quadrilateral is two triangles'.
'The drawing makes these two angles look equal. Are they? How can you be sure without measuring?' — tests reliance on marked values over appearance.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) third angle = 180 − (70+60) = 50°, using the triangle sum 180°; (2) missing = 360 − (sum of the three), using the quadrilateral sum 360°; (3) one interior angle = 720° ÷ 6 = 120°, having found the hexagon's angle sum (4 triangles × 180°). Computes from the marked/derived sums, not from appearance, and divides the sum for the regular polygon.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° — subtracts the two known angles from 360 instead of 180.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-derive 180° by tearing the corners onto a straight line; contrast triangle (180°) with quadrilateral (360°) and show the quadrilateral is TWO triangles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the triangle's third angle as 360 − (70+60) = 230°, or explains 'a triangle is 360°'; often the rest of the working is correct.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the angle sum depends on the triangle's size — expects a bigger or longer-sided triangle to have a larger third angle / larger sum.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the same angles on triangles of very different sizes, and reshape one triangle while the 180° sum holds; make explicit that side length does not change the angle sum.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges the missing angle by how big or stretched the triangle looks rather than computing 180 − known; says a wider triangle 'must have a bigger angle there'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes the triangle is isosceles/equilateral from its appearance — takes two angles as equal because the not-to-scale drawing looks that way.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinforce 'not drawn to scale': compute only from marked angles; show a case where the equal-looking angles are provably unequal from the numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Splits the remaining angle equally, or asserts two angles are equal, with no marking to justify it; relies on how the figure looks.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the polygon's total angle sum as a single interior angle — for the regular hexagon gives 720° (the sum) instead of dividing by 6.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two-step structure: total sum, THEN ÷ number of equal vertices; no reteaching of the sum needed — the final division was dropped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Finds 720° correctly but stops there, or writes 720° as 'the angle'; the sum step is right, the share-equally step is missing.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find missing angles reliably: uses the wrong total, judges by appearance or size, or cannot get beyond the triangle; no method for the quadrilateral or hexagon.
responseLevels.full: Computes missing angles in triangle, quadrilateral and regular polygon; derives the polygon sums by partitioning into triangles and divides for a regular polygon; recognises the sum is independent of size; and uses marked values rather than appearance — the 180° rule is a connected tool, not an isolated fact.
responseLevels.partial: Finds a triangle's missing angle using 180° in the standard case, but treats the sums as separate memorised facts — defeated by the regular hexagon (can't partition or forgets to divide), misled by the not-to-scale/isosceles-looking triangle, or shows size-dependence when the shape is stretched. Lists the sums without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three figures with angles marked (not to scale). (1) A triangle with two angles 70° and 60°, third unknown — draw it looking roughly isosceles though it isn't. (2) A quadrilateral with three angles marked, one unknown. (3) A regular hexagon, asking for one interior angle. Say: 'Work out each missing angle, and tell me how you got it.' Watch the method — which total they use, whether they partition, whether they trust the picture — without prompting the rules.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Spanning triangle, quadrilateral and regular polygon separates a child who holds a connected system (all sums built from triangles) from one who has a single memorised fact and no way to reach the hexagon. The not-to-scale, isosceles-looking triangle catches trust-the-picture reasoning. Asking 'how did you get it' exposes the 360°-for-a-triangle error and the size-dependence intuition, and separates a genuine reasoning error from a mere arithmetic slip.

sources.claim: Year 5 primary lesson: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, derived from angles on a straight line; a common misconception is that pupils know this only as a disconnected fact, so the recommended approach is to relate the triangle to the quadrilateral by partitioning shapes into triangles.
sources.source: Oak National Academy, 'Angles in triangles' (KS2/Year 5)

sources.claim: Diagnostic-question data: a documented wrong answer is that angles in a triangle add up to 360° (students subtract from 360 rather than 180); another group assumes the triangle is isosceles because it looks that way; the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip by students who knew the 180° rule — so reasoning errors must be separated from computation errors.
sources.source: Craig Barton / Eedi, 'Angles in a Triangle: Guess the Misconception'

sources.claim: Children (6–7) and even educated adults intuitively judge a triangle's missing third angle as scaling with the triangle's overall size — predicting a larger angle when the base is longer — in direct contradiction with Euclid's proposition 32 that the internal angles of a triangle sum to a constant regardless of size; the error reflects mental simulation rather than use of the angle-sum rule, and formal schooling did not predict accuracy.
sources.source: Hart, Dillon, Marantan, Cardenas, Spelke & Mahadevan (2018), 'The statistical shape of geometric reasoning', Scientific Reports 8:12906

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–11 years (wide span — an early observational seed that is revisited and formalised at Y6)

- **Topic:** Offspring resemble parents (resemblance with variation)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y6 'Evolution and inheritance'):** 'recognise that living things produce offspring of the same kind, but normally offspring vary and are not identical to their parents' — the exact dual idea: like their parents (same kind, shared features) yet not identical.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 1-LS3-1):** '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1, 1-PS4-2, 2-PS1-3].' This is introduced early (grade 1) in the US, matching the age-6 start of this topic.

- **Operational details:** The whole concept is a TENSION held together: offspring RESEMBLE their parents (so we can tell whose baby it is) AND VARY from them and from each other (so no two are identical). Teach both halves at once through direct comparison — look at a parent and its young and name the shared inherited features (a foal has its mother's coat pattern, a sunflower seedling grows the parent's flower colour), then look across a litter/group and name the differences. The productive activity is MATCHING young to parents using resemblance, which forces the child to use shared features as evidence, immediately followed by spotting that the match isn't a perfect copy. Use plants as well as animals so 'resemblance' isn't animals-only. At the younger end keep it purely observational ('they look alike'); toward Y6 connect it to the word 'inherited' and to variation feeding survival advantage. Avoid any genetic mechanism.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (early) → Tier B (by Y6). The child matches offspring to the correct parent using named shared features AND identifies at least one way the offspring differs — holding 'like but not identical' together, with examples from both a plant and an animal.
bestPractices: Teach both halves together — resemblance AND variation — via side-by-side parent/offspring comparison; teaching only 'they look like their parents' breeds the identical-copy error.
Use MATCHING young-to-parent as the core task: it makes children cite shared inherited features as evidence, then immediately notice the match is imperfect.
Include plant examples (seedlings resembling the parent plant's flower/leaf) alongside animals so resemblance is seen as general.
Point explicitly at variation WITHIN a litter/group (siblings differ from each other), not just offspring-vs-parent.
Keep it observational and mechanism-free, especially at the younger end; connect to the term 'inherited' and to survival advantage only as the child approaches Y6.
keyRepresentations: A parent × offspring comparison panel with shared features highlighted and differences flagged.
A 'match the baby to its parent' family set (animals and plants).
A litter/sibling line-up showing variation among offspring of the same parents.
A shared-feature checklist (coat pattern, ear shape, petal colour) used as matching evidence.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking offspring are identical copies / clones of a parent, missing the 'vary and are not identical' half.
Believing a baby resembles ONLY one parent (all mum or all dad) rather than a mix, and can't vary from both.
Assuming resemblance applies to animals but not plants.
Expecting babies to look like miniature adults in every species (missing that some young look very different, e.g. caterpillar/tadpole — resemblance emerges by adulthood).
Attributing resemblance to the environment ('they look alike because they live together') rather than inheritance.
Thinking differences between siblings mean they aren't really 'the same kind'.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–11 build the dual idea that offspring resemble their parents yet are not identical, through direct side-by-side comparison. The core task is matching young to the correct parent using named shared features (coat pattern, ear shape, petal colour), then immediately spotting at least one way the young differs. Plants are used alongside animals so resemblance is seen as general, and a sibling line-up makes within-group variation visible. Keep it observational and mechanism-free at the younger end — describe features as 'coming from the parent' rather than naming genetics — and introduce the word 'inherited' and the link to variation feeding survival advantage only toward Year 6.

activities.title: Match the family yard
feedback: On a correct match, highlight the shared feature used so the resemblance evidence is explicit; with younger children keep this observational ('same coat pattern — this came from the parent'), and introduce the word 'inherited' for that shared feature only as the child approaches Year 6.
On a wrong match, gently point to a mismatched feature so the child re-checks the evidence rather than just guessing again.
When the child names a difference, affirm that resemblance plus difference together is the normal pattern — 'like but not a copy'.
If the child treats differences as odd or wrong, reassure that every young differs a little; that variation is expected, not a mistake.

If the child thinks young look alike because they live in the same place, point out that features like coat pattern or petal colour come from the parents the young came from; living in the same place does not make them share those features (though surroundings can affect things like size).
activities.rationale: Doing the matching forces the child to cite shared features as evidence, and the immediate 'spot the difference' step confronts the identical-copy error in the same breath. Asking for several shared features meets the evidence aim of describing at least three inherited features. A sibling line-up makes variation within a group concrete, and the plant lane prevents resemblance being read as animals-only. Dragging/placing and the live feature highlight are optional ways to realise the comparison, not the only way; the matching task may teach and check classification but should be paired with the child naming features and differences so it also elicits explanation.
sourceClaims: DfE Y6 statutory: 'recognise that living things produce offspring of the same kind, but normally offspring vary and are not identical to their parents'.
NGSS 1-LS3-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1, 1-PS4-2, 2-PS1-3]' — introduced at grade 1, matching the early age start.
Children commonly think offspring are identical copies of a parent, or resemble only one parent, and may attribute resemblance to shared environment rather than inheritance.
learnerActions: Match a jumbled pen of young (foals, puppies, and a plant lane of young plants grown from the parents' seeds) to the parent each one most resembles by dragging or placing them.

When you place a young correctly, name the shared feature you used as evidence (e.g. 'same coat pattern', 'same petal colour'); across the whole set, try to name at least three different shared features (such as eye colour, petal colour, fur type).
Right after each correct match, tap or state ONE way that young differs from its parent (a white paw, a different patch of colour, a different tail shape).
Look at a line-up of five puppies from the same mum and dad and point out how each one is a little different from the others.
Do the same for the plant lane: match young plants that have grown true leaves or flowers to the parent plant by flower colour or leaf shape, then name a difference.
activities.intendedInsight: Offspring are like their parents (so you can tell whose young it is from shared features that came from the parent) but not identical copies — and siblings vary from each other too. This holds for plants as well as animals.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal family portrait
feedback: Confirm each shared feature as one the young got from its parent and each flagged feature as an individual difference; use the word 'inherited' toward Year 6 while staying observational ('came from the parent') with younger children.
Prompt the child to state both halves ('like … but different in …') rather than only naming the similarity.
activities.rationale: A guided tap-to-reveal portrait cleanly displays shared features and differences and serves as a strong reference, especially for children who need the comparison modelled before doing it themselves. Its limit is that resemblance is presented already identified rather than being worked out by the child, so it supports but does not replace the active matching task.
sourceClaims: DfE Y6 statutory: 'recognise that living things produce offspring of the same kind, but normally offspring vary and are not identical to their parents'.
Children commonly think offspring are identical copies of a parent, or resemble only one parent, and may attribute resemblance to shared environment rather than inheritance.
learnerActions: Look at a parent-and-young portrait (e.g. a mare and foal, or a parent plant and a young plant grown from its seed) and tap a feature on the young.
See the matching feature light up on the parent, and read that it is a feature the young got from its parent.
Tap across a litter or seedling group to see each one flagged as a little different — 'variation'.
Say in your own words which features are shared and which are individual differences.
activities.intendedInsight: Shared features connect young to parent, while flagged differences show the young is not a perfect copy — a clean reference view of resemblance-with-variation.

activities.title: Check: like but not identical
feedback: If the child says young should be identical and treats differences as odd, compare several offspring against both parents to establish resemblance-plus-difference as the normal pattern.
If the child attributes every feature to the one parent shown, introduce the second parent as another source of features so the young is a blend of both.

If the child denies plant offspring resemble the parent plant, show young plants grown from the parent's seeds that, once grown, share the parent's leaf shape or flower colour with some variation, paralleling the animal case.
If the child insists young always look like small adults, give examples where young look very different (caterpillar, tadpole) yet are still that species' offspring.
If the child says the resemblance is because they live together, redirect to the parents as the source of the shared features.
activities.rationale: Matching and short reasoning items surface whether the child reads similarities and differences as connected (a mix from both parents) or as unrelated observations. Choosing a correct match alone (recognition) does not show the child can independently articulate the idea, so pair it with a spoken or written explanation. This checks the conclusion; it does not by itself build the insight, so it should follow the observational comparison work.
sourceClaims: DfE Y6 statutory: 'recognise that living things produce offspring of the same kind, but normally offspring vary and are not identical to their parents'.
Children commonly think offspring are identical copies of a parent, or resemble only one parent, and may attribute resemblance to shared environment rather than inheritance.
learnerActions: Match babies to parents and explain the feature that justified each match.
Answer whether siblings from the same parents are identical or varying, and give a reason.
Find the 'odd one out' difference within a litter or seedling group.

Respond to a reasoning prompt: a puppy has its mother's floppy ears and brown fur, but a differently shaped tail and a white patch she lacks — are the puppy and its mum exactly the same, or not, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: A child who holds the idea can name both the inherited similarities and the individual differences, and (toward Year 6) explain that young animals, and plants grown from seed, usually get a mix of features from two parents rather than being a copy of one.

constraints: Teach both halves together — resemblance AND variation — via side-by-side parent/offspring comparison; teaching only 'they look like their parents' breeds the identical-copy error.

Keep the work observational and mechanism-free, especially at the younger end; describe features as 'coming from the parent' and introduce the word 'inherited' and the link to survival advantage only as the child approaches Year 6. Avoid any genetic mechanism.

Include plant examples (young plants grown from the parent's seeds that, once they have true leaves or have flowered, resemble the parent's leaf shape or flower colour) so resemblance is not read as animals-only.
Point explicitly at variation within a litter or group (siblings differ from each other), not only offspring-vs-parent.
Address the 'young look like miniature adults' error: some young look very different (caterpillar, tadpole) yet are the same species' offspring, with resemblance emerging by adulthood.

Address the environment misconception: features such as coat pattern, ear shape or petal colour come from the parents the young came from; living in the same place does not make young share those features (although surroundings can affect things like size or health).
Reassure that differences between siblings do not mean they are not 'the same kind'; variation within a kind is expected.

The tap-to-reveal portrait and the check are a scaffold and an assessment respectively: they present or test resemblance already identified and, on their own, do not build the insight that comes from the child doing the matching and difference-hunting.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. choosing a correct match) do not by themselves show the child can independently articulate resemblance-with-variation; pair with a short spoken or written explanation.
Pair the activity with a first-hand anchor such as real family photos or a class-pet litter where available.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row (NGSS 1-LS3-1 wording and the OU OpenLearn misconception claim); treat their exact wording as unconfirmed pending review.

The original 'persona/conversation adds no perspective' and '3D adds nothing over 2D' judgements were catalog fit rankings, not established pedagogical facts; they are omitted rather than asserted as universal claims.

The source states young 'inherit a mix from both parents'; at the youngest end this should stay observational ('like their parents, but a little different') and not be framed as a genetic mechanism — it is retained only as a reasoning target toward Year 6.
The caterpillar/tadpole example is preserved as in the original; it illustrates young that look unlike the adult (metamorphosis), not a claim about resemblance 'emerging' through any mechanism.

probeDeeper: Which of the puppy's features do you think came from its dad — and how could we find out?
A sunflower's seeds grow into new sunflowers. Do they look exactly like the parent flower, or a bit different?
A tadpole doesn't look like a frog at all. Is it still the frog's offspring? How do you know?
If two puppies come from the same mum and dad, will they be identical to each other? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The puppy resembles its parents because it inherits features from them (floppy ears, brown fur), but it isn't identical — it inherits a mix from both parents and has its own variations (tail shape, white patch), so offspring are similar to parents but not exact copies.

errorPatterns.pattern: offspring are exact miniature copies of a parent ('the puppy should look just like its mum')
errorPatterns.nextMove: compare several offspring with both parents; establish resemblance plus individual differences as the normal pattern
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says they should be identical and treats the differences as odd

errorPatterns.pattern: young always look like small adults, so a very different-looking baby 'isn't really the offspring'
errorPatterns.nextMove: give examples where young look very different (caterpillar, tadpole) yet are still that species' offspring
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the probe insists young always resemble the adult form

errorPatterns.pattern: the puppy resembles only its mother (the other parent is ignored)
errorPatterns.nextMove: introduce the second parent as a source of features; the puppy is a blend of both
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes every feature to the one parent shown

errorPatterns.pattern: plants don't inherit from parents the way animals do
errorPatterns.nextMove: show seedlings resembling the parent plant's flower colour and leaf shape with variation, paralleling animals
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked about seeds and flowers, denies that plant offspring resemble the parent plant

responseLevels.gap: Says offspring should be exact copies, or that the differences mean it isn't really the parent's young.
responseLevels.full: Explains offspring resemble parents through inherited features yet differ because they inherit a unique mix, giving both animal and plant examples and handling young that look unlike the adult.
responseLevels.partial: Names inherited similarities and notices differences, but as separate observations — cannot explain that inheriting a mix from both parents produces resemblance-with-variation, or extend it to plants and very-different-looking young.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A puppy has floppy ears and brown fur just like its mother — but its tail is a different shape and it has a white patch she doesn't have. Are the puppy and its mum exactly the same, or not? Explain why a puppy looks like its parents but isn't a perfect copy.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A young child who thinks babies are miniature copies of one parent cannot account for the differences; a child holding resemblance-with-variation names both the inherited similarities and the individual differences. The reason tier surfaces 'it should be the same' versus 'it's a mix from both parents'.
