pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Rainforest Animals (ages 7–9): the most species-rich habitat on Earth, structured in vertical LAYERS (forest floor, understory, canopy, emergent) each home to different animals with layer-matched adaptations.
• Standards — UK (DfE): extends KS1 'Living things and their habitats' and Y4 grouping/adaptation; the layer structure introduces the idea that ONE habitat contains many micro-environments.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 2-LS4-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1] different places); 3-LS4-3 (survival in a habitat) — rainforest biodiversity is the flagship case of 'many kinds in one place'.
• Operational details: anchor the four layers with signature animals and layer-linked adaptations — canopy (howler monkeys, sloths, toucans, tree frogs: gripping hands/tails, gliding, bright colours); understory (jaguars climbing, snakes, insects: camouflage, ambush); forest floor (tapirs, ants, decomposers: foraging, burrowing); emergent (harpy eagle, large birds/bats: flight above the trees). Establish that rainforests grow near the equator, are warm and wet all year, and hold more species than any other land habitat.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~7–8): name the layers and one animal in each. B (transitional, ~8–9): explain one adaptation that suits an animal to its layer (e.g. prehensile tail for canopy life). C (formal, ~9): explain WHY rainforests hold so many species (warm, wet, year-round, many niches/layers).
bestPractices: Teach the forest as a vertical stack, not a flat scene — build the four layers bottom-to-top so pupils grasp light and food changing with height and animals matched to each level.
Tie each adaptation to its layer's demand (prehensile tails and gripping feet for the canopy; camouflage and ambush for the dim understory; decomposing/foraging on the floor).
Use the biodiversity hook concretely — 'a single rainforest tree can hold more ant species than the whole UK' — to make 'most species-rich' vivid rather than abstract.
Connect to warmth-and-water availability so pupils reason about WHY so much life is possible here, linking back to what plants/animals need.
keyRepresentations: A cross-section of the rainforest showing the four stacked layers with signature animals placed in each.
A light gradient down the layers (bright emergent → dark floor) explaining why canopy life differs from floor life.
Adaptation close-ups: a prehensile tail gripping a branch, a sloth's hook-like claws, a tree frog's sticky toe pads.
A 'species pile-up' comparison bar: rainforest vs other habitats to show sheer diversity.
commonMisconceptions: 'The rainforest floor is where most animals live' — the canopy holds the greatest abundance and diversity; the floor is dim and comparatively sparse.
'Rainforest and jungle are the same everywhere' — the structured layers create very different living conditions within one forest.
'Rainforests are hot deserts of trees' / it rains all the time — they are warm and consistently wet, but the defining traits are year-round warmth and high rainfall.
'Bright colours help animals hide' — many rainforest colours are warnings (poison) or signals, not camouflage.
'All rainforest animals live in trees' — each layer, including the floor, has its own specialised residents.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach that a tropical rainforest is not one flat scene but a vertical stack of four layers — forest floor, understory, canopy, and emergent — each with different light, food, and space, and animals whose bodies are matched to their layer. Build the layers bottom-to-top, tie each adaptation to its layer's demands, and help children reason why so many species can live in one warm, wet, year-round habitat (the most species-rich land habitat on Earth, with the canopy the richest layer — a widely taught generalisation here drawn from unverified references). Core activities centre on matching animals to layers by their adaptations; supporting activities include a labelled cross-section to explore, a predict-reveal about which layer is busiest, a categorisation/matching check, and an optional field-biologist curiosity hook.

activities.title: Stock the rainforest: match animals to their layers
feedback: When a match is correct, narrate why it works: 'The monkey's gripping tail holds on to branches as it climbs through the sunny canopy, where fruit and fresh leaves grow.'

When a mismatch is tried, show the consequence: 'On the dark floor the monkey's gripping tail has no branches to hold, and it is far from the fresh leaves and fruit growing up high — it would struggle; a tapir foraging in the litter does well here instead.'
If a child treats placement as interchangeable ('they could swap'), return to one layer's light and food and ask what that animal would eat or grip there.
activities.rationale: Layer-matching is a construction task rather than recognition: children build the adaptation→layer relationship by placing animals and reasoning about the consequence, which directly targets the 'floor is busiest' and 'animals could swap places' misconceptions. A filling 'diversity meter' as niches are correctly occupied is an optional device to make 'most species-rich' concrete.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests occur near the equator, are warm and wet year-round, are structured into forest floor / understory / canopy / emergent layers, and hold more species than any other land habitat, with the canopy the richest layer.
Many different kinds of living things live in different places; some organisms survive well in a given habitat — rainforest is the flagship high-diversity case.
learnerActions: Work with a vertical cross-section from the dark forest floor up to the sunlit emergent layer, with each layer labelled by its light level and food (fruit and leaves high up; litter and decomposers on the dim, damp floor).

Place animals into the layer where their body suits them: a howler monkey or prehensile-tailed creature and a sloth with hook-like claws into the canopy; a tapir, decomposers, and a ground-hunting jaguar on the forest floor; a camouflaged ambush animal such as a snake into the dim understory; a harpy eagle or large bat in the emergent layer. (Jaguars also climb into the understory, so the sim should accept that placement too.)
For each placement, say WHY the animal fits — name the adaptation (gripping tail, hooked claws, camouflage, strong flight) and the layer demand it meets.
Try a deliberate mismatch (e.g. put the gripping-tailed monkey on the floor, or the tapir up in the canopy) and describe what would go wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: An animal's body and its layer are a matched pair: adaptations such as a prehensile tail or hooked claws make an animal thrive in one layer and struggle in another. A rainforest packs in so much life precisely because its stacked layers create many different homes in one warm, wet place.

activities.title: Explore the four-layer cross-section
feedback: Prompt the child to say, for an animal they reveal, what it finds in its layer that it couldn't find elsewhere.
Reinforce that the canopy — not the floor — holds the greatest abundance and diversity (the commonly taught generalisation).
If a child thinks bright colours help animals hide, note that many rainforest colours (e.g. poison dart frogs) are warning signals, not camouflage.
activities.rationale: A rich, labelled cross-section conveys the vertical stack and light gradient well and lets a child explore structure before being asked to build it; a tap-to-reveal layer with a lift-the-flap 'why here?' card is an optional way to make exploration active. This is a scaffold for the matching task — it shows the structure but does not itself let the child test placement or its consequences.
sourceClaims: Rainforest layers extend KS1/KS2 habitat and adaptation content by showing one habitat containing many micro-environments.

Tropical rainforests occur near the equator, are warm and wet year-round, are structured into forest floor / understory / canopy / emergent layers, and hold more species than any other land habitat, with the canopy the richest layer.
Many bright rainforest colours are warning (aposematic) signals of toxicity rather than camouflage.
learnerActions: Study a tall cross-section of the rainforest built bottom-to-top: forest floor, understory, canopy, emergent.

Reveal the signature animals in each layer and, for each, a 'why here?' note linking its body to the layer (prehensile tail gripping a branch, a sloth's hook-like claws, a tree frog's sticky toe pads).
Trace the light gradient from the bright emergent top to the dark floor and connect it to why canopy life differs from floor life.
Compare a 'species pile-up' of a rainforest against another habitat (including a local temperate wood) to see the sheer difference in number of kinds of animals.
activities.intendedInsight: One habitat contains many micro-environments stacked vertically; light and food change with height, and this structure is why the rainforest supports so many kinds of life.

activities.title: Predict then reveal: which layer is busiest?
feedback: Treat a 'forest floor' prediction as the expected starting point, then use the reveal to prompt revision rather than marking it simply wrong.
Draw out that removing canopy trees removes the fruit, leaves, and space the canopy animals depend on.
If the child says the rainforest is cold or rains without ever stopping, locate the equator on a globe and establish warm and wet year-round (rain most days but warm), not cold.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain cycle directly confronts the common 'the floor is where most animals live' misconception by making the child commit before the reveal. Prompts about the toucan's food and the effect of logging push toward causal, layer-specific reasoning.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests occur near the equator, are warm and wet year-round, are structured into forest floor / understory / canopy / emergent layers, and hold more species than any other land habitat, with the canopy the richest layer.
learnerActions: Look at a labelled rainforest cross-section or photo and predict which layer holds the most animals, saying why BEFORE any reveal.
Compare the prediction with the answer: scientists think the canopy, not the forest floor, is home to the most kinds of rainforest animals.

Discuss why the canopy is richest — bright light, fruit, and leaves up top — and why the floor is dim, with fewer plants growing and fewer kinds of animals, even though it is busy with decomposers and insects.
Answer follow-up prompts: 'What does a toucan find high up that it couldn't find on the floor?' and 'If all the tall canopy trees were cut down, what would happen to the toucan?'
activities.intendedInsight: Most children expect the floor to be busiest; surfacing and then revising that prediction makes the canopy's richness and its dependence on light and food memorable.

activities.title: Sort and match check
feedback: For a sorting error, revisit that layer's light and food and ask which animal body features would help there.
For the species-richness question, reinforce the combination of warmth, constant moisture, and many layered niches.
Flag the 'bright colours = hiding' choice and correct it to warning signals where relevant.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and adaptation-matching can check classification directly and surface the 'floor is busiest' and 'bright = hiding' errors. A sort checks rather than builds the layer intuition and does not by itself elicit the child's full explanation, so it is best used after the matching and exploration activities.
sourceClaims: Many different kinds of living things live in different places; some organisms survive well in a given habitat — rainforest is the flagship high-diversity case.
Many bright rainforest colours are warning (aposematic) signals of toxicity rather than camouflage.
learnerActions: Sort a set of rainforest animals into their correct layers.
Match adaptations to the layer demand they meet (gripping tail → canopy; camouflage and ambush → dim understory; foraging/decomposing → floor; strong flight → emergent).
Answer a short question on why rainforests hold so many species (warm, wet, year-round, many niches across stacked layers).
activities.intendedInsight: The child can categorise animals by layer and connect adaptations to layer demands, and can state why the habitat is so species-rich.

activities.title: Optional: canopy biologist curiosity hook
feedback: Use the child's questions to connect back to why the canopy — being high, bright, and fruit-rich — holds so much life.
Redirect to the cross-section if curiosity turns to how the layers themselves differ.
activities.rationale: An in-role biography can feed curiosity about how the treetops are studied. It is a motivational supplement: the conversation can spark interest but does not itself convey the vertical layer structure, which the cross-section shows directly; any comparative advantage over other media is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Hear or read a short in-role account from a field biologist describing a canopy walkway and how scientists study the treetops.
Pose a question about how researchers reach and observe canopy animals that are hard to see from the ground.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientists study the rainforest in layers too; the hard-to-reach canopy requires special methods, which reinforces that it is a distinct, species-rich world.

constraints: Build the forest as a vertical stack bottom-to-top (floor → understory → canopy → emergent); teaching it as a flat scene loses the light-and-food-by-height idea at the heart of the topic.
Tie every adaptation to its layer's specific demand rather than listing adaptations in the abstract.
The sort/match check verifies classification but does not build the layer intuition or elicit the child's full explanation; use it after hands-on matching and exploration, not as the first encounter.
The cross-section exploration is a scaffold: it shows the layered structure but does not let the child test placements or consequences, which the matching activity provides.
The field-biologist conversation is an optional curiosity hook, not the primary means of teaching the spatial layer structure.
Keep the distinction that bright rainforest colours are often warning signals, not camouflage, so children do not generalise 'bright = hiding'.
Establish that rainforests are warm and wet year-round near the equator — not cold and not under constant non-stop storms.

Keep the jaguar consistent across activities: present it primarily as a forest-floor ground hunter (matching the assessment) while allowing the understory, and never mark one of these defensible placements wrong.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all sources[].claim entries remain marked verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that the canopy is the richest rainforest layer is widely cited but the original sources are listed as unverified; 'canopy holds the majority of rainforest life' is presented as the commonly taught generalisation.

The 'diversity meter', tap-to-reveal, lift-the-flap, and drag-to-place devices are retained as optional interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms. A 3D fly-through of the layers could convey scale and light but is a nice-to-have, not needed for the core adaptation/layer logic.

Legacy material asserted 3D 'adds nothing to the core logic' and that spatial content is 'better shown than talked through'; these comparative claims are not established by the sources and have been rendered as affordance/limit statements (including in the cross-section and conversation rationales) rather than universal claims.

The original is internally inconsistent about the jaguar: the pedagogy places it in the understory ('jaguars climbing') while the assessment treats it as a forest-floor ground hunter. Both are ecologically defensible. To prevent a learner-facing contradiction with the predict-reveal and diagnostic tasks, the matching sim now treats the floor as the jaguar's primary placement and also accepts the understory; the exact canonical layer is left to the source.

assess.poeTask: Show a labelled rainforest cross-section (or photo). Ask the child to predict which layer holds the most animals and to say why BEFORE revealing. Most children pick the forest floor; reveal that the canopy holds the majority of rainforest life — then discuss why (light, fruit, leaves up top).
probeDeeper: You said the toucan lives high up. What does it find up there that it couldn't find on the floor?
If we cut down all the tall canopy trees, what would happen to the toucan?
Rainforests have more kinds of animals than almost anywhere on Earth. Why do you think so many different animals can live in one forest?
Is a rainforest hot or cold? How do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: The rainforest has layers with different conditions. The canopy at the top is bright and full of fruit, leaves and most of the animals, so a fruit-eating, tree-climbing bird like the toucan lives there. The forest floor is dark, damp and open, where a big ground hunter like the jaguar can prowl and stalk prey. Different layers offer different light, food and space, so different animals are suited to each.

errorPatterns.pattern: The rainforest is the same all the way through — animals just pick a favourite tree ('they could swap places')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Revisit the four layers with a cross-section picture; walk from floor upward naming the light and food at each level before re-placing the animals.
errorPatterns.distractor: They could swap places — the rainforest is the same all the way up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places toucan and jaguar interchangeably; cannot say how the floor differs from the canopy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rainforests are cold and it rains without stopping
errorPatterns.nextMove: Locate the equator on a globe; establish hot and wet (rain most days but warm), not cold.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the rainforest as cold or under constant storm; unsure it sits near the equator.

errorPatterns.pattern: A rainforest is just like the woods near my house
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare species counts of a local wood versus a rainforest; introduce 'more kinds of animals than almost anywhere on Earth'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates local temperate woodland with a tropical rainforest; surprised by how many species it holds.

responseLevels.gap: Names a rainforest animal or two but treats the forest as one undifferentiated place; can't say why toucan and jaguar live at different heights, or thinks a rainforest is just like local woods.
responseLevels.full: Explains that layers differ in light, food and living space (bright fruit-rich canopy vs dark open floor), places a new animal in the right layer with a reason, knows rainforests are hot and wet near the equator, and that they hold more species than almost any habitat.
responseLevels.partial: Lists the layers (floor, understory, canopy) and places some animals, but describes the layers only as 'higher up' without saying how light, food and space differ, so can't fully explain why each animal fits its layer or place a new animal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two rainforest animals: a toucan and a jaguar. The toucan spends its days high up in the treetops; the jaguar lives down on the forest floor. Why don't they just live in the same place? What is different about the top of the rainforest and the bottom?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who only knows 'animals live in the rainforest' says the two could live anywhere or 'they just like different trees' — no account of why each fits its height. A child who grasps layering names the difference in light, food and space between canopy and floor. Because the second tier demands a specific reason each animal matches its layer, it is hard to be right for the wrong reason.

sources.claim: Rainforest layers extend KS1/KS2 habitat and adaptation content by showing one habitat containing many micro-environments.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS1 'Living things and their habitats'; KS2 Y4)

sources.claim: Many different kinds of living things live in different places; some organisms survive well in a given habitat — rainforest is the flagship high-diversity case.
sources.source: NGSS 2-LS4-1; 3-LS4-3

sources.claim: Tropical rainforests occur near the equator, are warm and wet year-round, are structured into forest floor / understory / canopy / emergent layers, and hold more species than any other land habitat, with the canopy the richest layer.
sources.source: Standard biome reference (e.g. National Geographic Education 'rainforest'); natural-history sources on rainforest stratification

sources.claim: Many bright rainforest colours are warning (aposematic) signals of toxicity rather than camouflage.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Reducing Human Impact

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-ESS3-3):** '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-3].'

- **Standards — UK (no direct KS1 statutory line; links to KS2 'recognise that environments can change and that this can sometimes pose dangers to living things'):** early environmental-care is addressed in England via PSHE/enrichment at this age rather than statutory science; the science destination is the KS2 human-impact strand. Note the divergence honestly — this is a US-led early expectation.

- **Operational details:** Children identify simple, concrete ways humans harm the LOCAL environment (litter, wasting water, air pollution, damaging habitats) and COMMUNICATE solutions that reduce that harm (bin/recycle litter, turn off taps, plant trees, walk instead of drive), explaining how each helps the land, water, air, or living things. The verb is COMMUNICATE — propose and share a solution — so cause (problem) is paired with an action (solution) and a benefit.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, solution-oriented). Success = naming at least three local human impacts, proposing a matching solution for each, and saying which part of the environment (land/water/air/living things) it protects — problem paired to action paired to benefit, communicated clearly.
bestPractices: Keep it LOCAL and concrete — the child's own park, street, pond — not abstract global problems, at this age.
Pair every problem with a doable solution AND a benefit ('bin the litter → the pond is clean → fish are safe').
Emphasise the COMMUNICATE verb: let children share/present their solution, not just identify it.
Frame children as capable helpers (agency), avoiding eco-anxiety or blame.
Use before/after contrast so the value of a solution is visible.
keyRepresentations: A before/after local scene (messy → cared-for).
Problem→solution→benefit cards linking a harm to an action to what it protects.
Category icons for land / water / air / living things.
A simple 'my plan to help' the child assembles and shares.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking problems are too big for a child to help with (no sense of agency).
Naming a solution without connecting it to WHAT it protects.
Believing 'throwing litter in any bin' and 'recycling' are the same, or that waste simply disappears.
Seeing environmental care as only about animals, missing land/water/air.
Treating the solution as magic rather than a cause with an effect.

learn.summary: For 5–6-year-olds: identify concrete, LOCAL ways humans harm the environment (litter, wasting water, air pollution, damaged habitats), pair each harm with a doable solution, and COMMUNICATE how that solution protects the land, water, air, or living things. Success is naming at least three local impacts, proposing a matching solution for each, saying which part of the environment it protects, and sharing a simple plan — problem paired to action paired to benefit. Keep the emphasis on the cause→effect mechanism (not instant magic) and frame children as capable helpers to avoid eco-anxiety.

activities.title: Heal the local scene (before/after)
feedback: When a fix is applied, show the matching recovery (litter binned → pond clears → fish return; flowerbed replanted → birds and insects return) and name the part of the environment it protects, so the benefit is concrete rather than abstract.
Make clear the scene is sped up: in real life a place takes time to recover, so children focus on the cause→effect link rather than treating the fix as instant magic.
If a child names a solution without a benefit, prompt: 'And how does binning the litter help the fish in the pond?'
Close by having the child share their assembled plan, exercising the 'communicate a solution' skill, not just identifying it.
activities.rationale: The standard's verb is COMMUNICATE: propose and share a solution, pairing problem to action to benefit. A before/after local scene makes the cause→effect link visible and keeps the task concrete and local for this age, and the recovery links each solution to what it protects in one move.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-ESS3-3: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-3].'
learnerActions: Look at a messy local park/pond scene containing several concrete problems: dropped litter, a running tap, a smoky car, a trampled flowerbed.
Tap each problem to choose a fix — bin and recycle the litter, turn off the tap, walk instead of drive, replant the flowerbed.

Watch that part of the scene recover as a direct result of the choice — the pond gradually clears and fish return after the litter is gone; birds and insects come back once the flowerbed is replanted. The scene speeds this up to show the link; in real life recovery takes time.
Notice which part of the environment each fix protects — land, water, air, or living things — surfaced as the scene heals.
Assemble the fixes you chose into a simple 'my plan to help', then say or present it to someone.
activities.intendedInsight: A solution works through a cause→effect mechanism: removing this harm leads to this improvement and protects this part of the environment. The scene shows recovery sped up, but the point is the link (litter removed → cleaner water → safer home for fish), not instant magic. Children are capable helpers whose choices improve a real local place.

activities.title: Spot the problems, lift the solution
feedback: Confirm the problem→solution→benefit link calmly as each flap is revealed.
Prompt the child to name which of land, water, air, or living things is protected.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal / lift-the-flap scene communicates problem→solution→benefit in an age-appropriate, low-anxiety way. Its limit is that the improvement is pre-authored rather than caused by the child's own choices, so use it as a calmer scaffold alongside the interactive before/after scene.
learnerActions: Tap each problem in a local scene to reveal the harm it causes.
Lift a flap to show a matching solution and what part of the environment it protects.
Say the pairing aloud: problem → solution → benefit.
activities.intendedInsight: Each of these local harms can be paired with a doable fix, and each fix protects at least one part of the environment.

activities.title: Match and sort the fixes
feedback: Correct mismatches by returning to what the harm does and what the fix changes.
For sorting, prompt the child to justify the category: 'What does the clean pond give the fish?'
activities.rationale: Matching, categorisation and picture selection check the problem→solution→benefit pairing and are easy to score at this age. These are recognition-style tasks: they confirm the pairing but do not let the child see the recovery or construct and communicate their own plan, so pair them with a construction/sharing task.
learnerActions: Match each harm to the solution that reduces it (litter → bin/recycle; running tap → turn off tap; smoky car → walk; trampled flowerbed → replant).

Sort each fix by the part or parts of the environment it protects — land, water, air, or living things — knowing that some fixes protect more than one (binning litter protects land, water and the animals).
Pick a picture answer when asked which fix helps a given part of the environment.
activities.intendedInsight: Problems and solutions pair up, and each solution protects at least one part of the environment — often more than one.

activities.title: Tell the ranger your plan
feedback: When the child names a fix only, the ranger asks how it helps, prompting the benefit.
Affirm plans that link action to a protected part of the environment; gently prompt for the missing piece when it is absent.
activities.rationale: Because the standard's verb is COMMUNICATE, telling a plan to a listener who asks how each idea helps directly exercises the communicate-a-solution skill. For 5–6-year-olds an open dialogue is harder to scaffold than a visual fix-the-scene, so it complements the interactive scene rather than leading.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-ESS3-3: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS3-3].'
learnerActions: Tell a friendly park-ranger listener your clean-up plan for the local park.
Answer the ranger's follow-up questions, e.g. 'And how does that help the fish?' or 'Which part of the park does that protect?'
Revise or add to your plan after the questions.
activities.intendedInsight: Communicating a solution means not just naming a fix but explaining how it helps and what it protects.

activities.title: Does the litter just go away? (diagnostic discussion)
feedback: If a child says the rain or wind will wash it away or it just rots, ask what a plastic bottle looks like after a year outside, and establish that litter like plastic bottles and packets stays and builds up — and rain or wind only moves it somewhere else, such as into the pond.

Use the apple-core-vs-plastic-bottle comparison to surface that a natural scrap rots away quite quickly while a plastic bottle stays for a very long time — so plastic litter is a bigger, longer-lasting problem (while noting we still shouldn't drop either).
If a child says it only matters because it looks untidy for people, reconnect to the animals: the park is their home — ask how a bird or hedgehog might be harmed by a bottle or packet.
If a child says one little packet is too small to hurt anything, ask what happens if everyone thinks that, building from one to many to show the total.

A full answer connects the harm to the solution's mechanism (binning/recycling keeps the habitat clean so animals have a safe home) and transfers to a second example such as saving water or planting a tree. A partial answer names a harm and a solution but treats them as separate facts; a gap answer denies the problem or only says it looks messy — prompt these toward the mechanism.
Frame the child as a capable helper throughout, so the discussion builds agency rather than worry.
activities.rationale: This two-tier diagnostic discriminates children who understand human impact (yes AND it harms living things' home) from those who think rubbish disappears on its own or only object that it looks messy. Comparing an apple core with a plastic bottle surfaces the persistence-of-waste idea.
learnerActions: Consider: some people drop crisp packets and drink bottles on the ground in the park instead of using the bin. Is that a problem for the plants and animals that live there? Why?
Explain what a plastic bottle might look like after a whole year outside.
Think about whether one dropped apple core would be the same as a dropped plastic bottle — is it? Why or why not?
Say what might happen if everyone in the park thought one little packet was too small to matter.
Explain how putting rubbish in the bin or recycling it helps the animals' home.
activities.intendedInsight: Litter such as plastic bottles and packets does not just vanish — it stays a long time, can trap or be eaten by animals, and can wash into soil and water where plants and animals live. A plastic bottle persists far longer than a natural scrap like an apple core, which rots away much sooner (though dropping any litter is still unkind to the park). Binning or recycling keeps their home clean and safe; this protects living things, not just human tidiness.

constraints: Keep it LOCAL and concrete — the child's own park, street, pond — not abstract global problems at this age.
Pair every problem with a doable solution AND a benefit ('bin the litter → the pond is clean → fish are safe').
Emphasise the COMMUNICATE verb: let children share or present their solution, not just identify it.
Frame children as capable helpers (agency); avoid eco-anxiety or blame.
Use a before/after contrast so the value of a solution is visible.

Show any scene recovery as sped-up/representational and make clear real-world recovery takes time and fair conditions, so children learn the cause→effect mechanism rather than treating a solution as instant magic.

Keep each shown recovery matched to a fix that is actually available in the scene (e.g. replanting the flowerbed brings back birds/insects); do not depict a recovery caused by a fix the child cannot choose.
The lift-the-flap scene is a calmer scaffold; its improvement is pre-authored rather than caused by the child's choices, so it does not by itself show the child their choices cause recovery.

Matching, sorting and picture-selection are recognition tasks that score the pairing but do not elicit the child constructing and communicating an original plan; pair them with a construction/sharing task.

Watch for key misconceptions: problems feel too big to help with; naming a solution without saying what it protects; treating 'any bin' and 'recycling' as the same or thinking waste disappears; seeing care as only about animals and missing land/water/air; treating the solution as magic rather than a cause with an effect.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that a spatial/3D treatment 'adds nothing' for this age is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; it has been dropped rather than asserted. A 3D scene is simply not needed here because the target skill is a problem→solution→benefit link, not a spatial task.

Standards divergence noted honestly: NGSS K-ESS3-3 is a US-led early expectation; England has no direct KS1 statutory science line (environmental care is addressed via PSHE/enrichment at this age), with the KS2 'environments can change and pose dangers to living things' strand as the science destination. One source (NGSS) is marked verified:false in the original row.

The original design's scene recovery is depicted as effectively instantaneous; this has been qualified to sped-up/representational to avoid reinforcing the 'solution as magic' misconception. Real recovery depends on material, setting and elapsed time.

The original recommendation attributed returning birds to a planted tree, but the scene's only planting fix is replanting the trampled flowerbed; recovery has been realigned to the replanted flowerbed so the shown effect matches an available fix. Tree-planting remains a valid general solution in the objective but is not a tappable fix in this scene.

The diagnostic's 'correct answer' asserts litter can wash into soil and water and harm animals — reasonable at this level, but specifics (how long a given plastic persists, exact harms, how fast organic scraps break down) depend on material and setting; keep claims qualitative and avoid overstating absolutes.
Original response levels (gap/partial/full) have been folded into the diagnostic's intendedInsight and feedback rather than listed separately.

probeDeeper: If it's a problem, what is one thing we could do about it?
How does putting the rubbish in the bin actually help the animals in the park?
What if it was one apple core instead of a plastic bottle — is that the same? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes. The litter doesn't go away by itself — it stays for a long time, can trap or be eaten by animals, and can wash into the soil and water where plants and animals live. It spoils the home they need. Putting rubbish in the bin or recycling it keeps their home clean and safe.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rubbish vanishes — 'it's fine, the rain or wind will wash it away' or 'it just rots and disappears'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront the persistence of waste: ask what a plastic bottle looks like after a whole year outside; establish that most litter stays and builds up.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's not a problem — the rubbish will just wash or blow away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says it is not a problem because the litter will go away on its own

errorPatterns.pattern: Anthropocentric — 'it only matters because it looks untidy for people'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reconnect to the animals' needs: the park is the animals' home; ask how a bird or hedgehog might be harmed by a bottle or packet.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's only a problem because it looks untidy for people.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Frames litter purely as a human eyesore, with no mention of harm to plants or animals

errorPatterns.pattern: Scale dismissal — 'one little packet is too small to hurt anything'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what happens if everyone in the park thinks that; build from one to many to show the total.
errorPatterns.distractor: One little packet is far too small to hurt anything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts a single item as harmless, missing that litter accumulates

responseLevels.gap: Says it is not a problem, or only that it looks messy; cannot say why it harms plants or animals.
responseLevels.full: Connects the harm to the solution's mechanism (binning or recycling keeps the habitat clean so animals have a safe home) and can transfer to a second example such as saving water or planting a tree.
responseLevels.partial: Says litter harms animals and offers a solution (use the bin, recycle) but treats them as separate facts — cannot explain HOW the solution protects the animals, land or water.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Some people drop their crisp packets and drink bottles on the ground in the park instead of using the bin. Is that a problem for the plants and animals that live in the park? Why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands human impact says yes AND explains it harms the living things' home. A child who lacks the idea either thinks the rubbish disappears on its own, or only objects that it 'looks messy' for people — an answer with no reference to plants and animals needing a clean habitat.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Heating experiments and Q = mcΔT

- **Standards:** This topic STRADDLES KS3→KS4 (UK) and MS→HS (US).

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** the EXPERIMENTAL skills — planning, measuring temperature change over time with thermometer and stopwatch, plotting and interpreting graphs, and evaluating sources of error — are KS3 'Working scientifically' together with the KS3 heating/thermal-equilibrium content; but the quantitative apparatus of this topic, 'specific heat capacity' and Q = mcΔT-type calculation, is KS4 statutory ('calculating energy changes involved on heating, using specific heat capacity', under KS4 Physics 'The structure of matter') — the term and the calculation do not appear at KS3 (verified by fetch).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** MS-PS3-4 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS3-4]' is the strong middle-school anchor — but its assessment boundary explicitly states '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS3-3, MS-PS3-4]', which places the quantitative Q = mcΔT calculation at HS (HS-PS3). So the PRACTICAL and the relationship are MS/KS3; the calculation is HS/KS4 (verified by fetch).

- **Operational details:** This is a PROCEDURAL topic: the child plans and runs a heating experiment, records temperature against time, plots a temperature–time graph and reads its gradient as a rate, applies Q = mcΔT, and — the maturity marker — evaluates sources of error and proposes improvements. It builds on efficiency/conservation (prereq) and demands genuine quantitative reasoning plus experimental design, so it sits at the top of the energy ladder. The conceptual core under the procedure is specific heat capacity c — the idea that different materials (and different masses) need different amounts of energy for the same temperature rise — which is precisely what separates temperature from energy. The best teaching keeps the maths anchored to a real (or realistically simulated) measurement: heat a known mass with a known energy input, watch the temperature climb, and reconcile the energy you put in with the temperature change you got — then notice the books don't balance because energy leaked to the surroundings, which is the doorway to error evaluation.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational / quantitative, ~12–14).
bestPractices: Keep the equation tied to a measurement: run an actual (or faithfully simulated) heating — known mass, known energy in from an immersion heater / joulemeter, temperature logged over time — so Q = mcΔT describes something the child watched happen, not an abstract formula.

Build the temperature–time graph as the central record: plot temperature against time, read the GRADIENT as the heating rate, and use the graph (not just a single reading) to reason about the experiment — explicitly naming that the line shows rate, it is not a picture of anything going 'uphill'.

Make specific heat capacity concrete BEFORE the algebra: add the same energy to equal masses of water, oil and aluminium and compare the temperature rises — c is 'how stubborn a material is to heat', the energy needed per kilogram per degree.

Run Q = mcΔT in more than one direction — find the energy for a given rise, find the temperature rise for a given energy, and (the payoff) work back to a measured c and compare it with the true value to expose experimental error.

Centre error evaluation as the main intellectual task, not an afterthought: the measured c almost always comes out too HIGH because some input energy escaped to the surroundings, so less reached the substance than you counted — have the child name the loss and propose fixes (lid, insulation/lagging, start below and end above room temperature, account for the container).

Distinguish temperature from thermal energy at every step: a bigger temperature rise does not by itself mean more energy was supplied — it depends on mass and material (c). This is the misconception the whole practical exists to break.

Treat the heating rate as variable, not constant: as the substance warms, the temperature difference with the room grows and losses increase, so the temperature–time line bends — a hook into why insulation and a lid matter.

Be explicit about which parts are KS3/MS (designing, measuring, graphing, evaluating error — do these firsthand) versus KS4/HS (the c value and the Q = mcΔT number), so the quantitative layer extends rather than replaces the practical skill.
keyRepresentations: The temperature–time graph — temperature on the y-axis, time on the x-axis; gradient = heating rate; a flattening curve as losses grow; any plateau flagged as energy going elsewhere (e.g. a change of state) rather than raising temperature.

The Q = mcΔT relationship laid out so the child can navigate it both ways (Q = mcΔT, c = Q / (mΔT)), with each symbol tied to a measured quantity (energy in, mass on a balance, temperature change on the thermometer).

The immersion-heater / joulemeter apparatus diagram — energy input source, the substance, thermometer and stopwatch — with arrows showing useful heating of the substance versus energy lost to the surroundings (a Sankey-style split).
A same-energy comparison of materials — equal masses of water, oil and aluminium reaching different temperatures — making c a visible property of the material.

An energy-accounting strip: electrical energy supplied = energy raising the substance + energy lost to surroundings (+ to the container), making 'why is my measured c too high?' a balance you can see.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing temperature with heat / thermal energy — the deepest error this practical targets: the same energy gives different temperature rises depending on mass and material, so temperature change alone does not measure energy supplied.
Assuming a bigger temperature rise always means more energy was supplied — it depends on m and c; a small mass or a low-c material rises faster for the same energy.
Ignoring energy lost to the surroundings — treating all the electrical energy as reaching the substance, which makes the measured specific heat capacity come out too high.

Reading the temperature–time graph as a picture / path rather than a relationship — thinking a steeper or 'higher' line means the substance physically went up, instead of reading the gradient as the rate of heating (the same graph-as-picture trap seen with motion graphs).
Expecting the heating rate to stay constant — as the substance warms, losses to the cooler room grow, so the line bends; the rate is not fixed.
Muddling the variables in Q = mcΔT — e.g. using total temperature instead of the CHANGE ΔT, or swapping mass and capacity; ΔT is a difference, not a final reading.
Treating specific heat capacity as 'how hot something gets' rather than how much energy each kilogram needs per degree — a property of the material, independent of how much you have.
Thinking a plateau on the graph means 'no energy is being supplied' — during a change of state energy is still going in, it is just not raising the temperature.

learn.summary: Learners (ages 12–13) plan and run a heating experiment, record temperature against time, plot and read a temperature–time graph, apply Q = mcΔT in more than one direction, and evaluate real sources of error. The conceptual heart is that different materials need different amounts of energy per kilogram for the same temperature rise (specific heat capacity c, a property of the material), and that a larger mass needs more energy for the same rise; together these separate temperature from thermal energy. Standards note: the practical skills and the energy/mass/temperature relationship are KS3/MS (UK KS3 'Working scientifically'; NGSS MS-PS3-4), while the term 'specific heat capacity' and the Q = mcΔT calculation are KS4/HS. The quantitative layer should extend, not replace, firsthand measurement. The firsthand bench practical is the primary evidence; a virtual lab may be a strong teacher of the relationship, graph-reading and error logic but remains a digital fallback for the hands-on skill.

activities.title: Hands-on heating practical: measure energy and evaluate error
feedback: If a learner expects input to equal Q, prompt them to identify where energy goes besides the water — air, beaker, evaporation — so the experiment is less than 100% efficient and input exceeds Q.
If a learner plugs in the final temperature, point to both the start and final readings and have them subtract before substituting: ΔT = final − start.
If the thermometer bulb is not fully immersed or is read at an angle, ask what error that introduces and have them correct the technique.
Ask: 'Your measured input is bigger than the Q you calculated — is that a mistake or expected, and why?' to surface loss reasoning.
activities.rationale: This is a PROCEDURAL topic whose stated evidence is firsthand use of apparatus, planning, and evaluating genuine (un-modelled) error — including thermometer lag and uneven heating that a simulation cannot fully reproduce. Centring error evaluation as the main intellectual task, anchored to a real measurement, targets the temperature-vs-energy misconception directly.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-PS3-4 asks students to plan an investigation into the relationships among energy transferred, type of matter, mass, and change in average kinetic energy (temperature) of the sample; its assessment boundary explicitly states [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS3-3, MS-PS3-4], placing the quantitative calculation at HS.

Confusing temperature with thermal energy, ignoring energy lost to the surroundings (making a measured specific heat capacity too high), and reading a temperature–time graph as a picture rather than a rate are documented difficulties best tackled by tying Q = mcΔT to a real measurement and centring error evaluation.
learnerActions: Set a known mass of water (weighed on a balance) in a beaker with an immersion heater/joulemeter, thermometer and stopwatch.
Switch on and record the temperature at regular time intervals while noting the energy supplied (power × time, or the joulemeter reading).
Compute ΔT as the CHANGE (final minus start, not a single reading) and calculate Q = mcΔT.

Compare the electrical energy you put in with the Q you calculated; it is usually larger, so explain why, and if it is not, look for measurement problems such as thermometer lag or heat gained from the room.

Name specific losses (heat to the air, the beaker, evaporation) and propose and, if possible, test improvements (lid, insulation/lagging, starting below and ending above room temperature, accounting for the container).
Read the thermometer at eye level with the bulb fully immersed, and note where lag or uneven heating could introduce error.
activities.intendedInsight: The electrical energy supplied is more than the Q reaching the substance because real experiments lose energy to the surroundings; naming and reducing those losses is the core evaluative skill, and ΔT is a difference, not a final reading.

activities.title: Virtual heating lab with modelled heat loss
feedback: When measured c is too high, prompt the learner to ask where the missing energy went before adding insulation.
If the learner expects a constant rate, point to the bending line: as the substance warms, the temperature difference with the room grows and losses increase.
If the learner confuses the gradient with a path going 'uphill', relabel it as rate of heating and separate the graph-as-relationship from a picture of motion.
If the learner reads a flat plateau as 'no energy is being supplied', explain that during a change of state energy is still going in — it is just not raising the temperature.
activities.rationale: A coded virtual lab can model heat loss that scales with the growing temperature difference, turning error evaluation into something diagnosed and fixed; live point-by-point plotting makes the gradient-as-rate reading concrete, and a plateau at the boiling point can be shown to distinguish a change of state from loss-driven bending or gradual levelling-off. Offered as a strong teacher of the relationship and error logic and the best available digital stand-in, not a replacement for the bench practical.
sourceClaims: Confusing temperature with thermal energy, ignoring energy lost to the surroundings (making a measured specific heat capacity too high), and reading a temperature–time graph as a picture rather than a rate are documented difficulties best tackled by tying Q = mcΔT to a real measurement and centring error evaluation.
learnerActions: Choose a substance (water, oil or aluminium), set its mass on a balance, and switch on a joulemeter-fed immersion heater delivering known energy.
Watch a temperature–time graph auto-plot point by point as the thermometer and stopwatch log readings over time.
Compute Q from power × time and use Q = mcΔT (and c = Q/(mΔT)) to find the measured c — noticing it reads HIGH.
Toggle on a lid, insulation and lagging and re-run, observing the temperature–time line climb straighter and the measured c slide toward the true value.
Read the gradient of the line as the heating rate, and explain why the line bends (curves) as the substance warms and losses to the cooler room grow.

If the simulation is taken to a change of state (e.g. water reaching boiling), note the flat PLATEAU and explain that energy is still being supplied there but is going into the change of state rather than raising the temperature.
activities.intendedInsight: Energy leaks to the surroundings make a measured c come out too high; reducing losses pulls it toward the true value, so 'sources of error → improvements' becomes a visible cause-and-effect rather than a memorised list. A bending line signals growing losses (which can level the line off gradually below the boiling point), while a flat plateau at the melting or boiling point signals a change of state where energy enters without raising temperature.

activities.title: Same energy, three materials
feedback: If a learner treats c as 'how hot something gets', re-anchor it as energy per kilogram per degree — a fixed property of the material.

If a learner says the hottest sample must have received the most energy, remind them the energy was identical and the difference is c (aluminium has the lowest c, so it rises most; water the highest c, so it rises least).
activities.rationale: Making specific heat capacity concrete before (or alongside) the algebra, by comparing temperature rises for the same energy, directly attacks the temperature-vs-energy and 'bigger rise = more energy' misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Confusing temperature with thermal energy, ignoring energy lost to the surroundings (making a measured specific heat capacity too high), and reading a temperature–time graph as a picture rather than a rate are documented difficulties best tackled by tying Q = mcΔT to a real measurement and centring error evaluation.
learnerActions: Give equal masses of water, oil and aluminium the identical energy input, side by side.
Record and compare the different temperature rises reached by each material.
Work back to a measured c for each and relate it to how 'stubborn to heat' the material is.
State in your own words why a bigger temperature rise does not by itself mean more energy was supplied.
activities.intendedInsight: Specific heat capacity is a property of the material (energy needed per kilogram per degree), independent of how much you have; with the same energy and the same mass, a lower-c material rises more, so temperature change is not the same as energy supplied.

activities.title: Socratic debrief on the result
feedback: If the learner cannot say where energy went, list candidate sinks (air, beaker, evaporation) and ask which they could reduce.
If the learner uses a final reading as ΔT, have them mark start and end and subtract.
activities.rationale: An in-role partner or physicist can drive error-evaluation reasoning through questioning, complementing the measurement work; dialogue supports the evaluative skill but does not by itself carry the quantitative measuring and graphing, so it works best as a debrief around the practical or virtual lab.
learnerActions: Predict what c you expect before computing it, then compare with the measured value.
Answer a lab-partner's questions: 'Your value for c is bigger than the textbook's — where did the missing energy go?'
Explain what lagging would change, and whether ΔT is the change or the final reading.
Justify your reasoning about why the input exceeds Q.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating where energy was lost, and distinguishing ΔT from a final reading, consolidates the evaluative reasoning behind the measurement.

activities.title: Calculation and graph-reading practice
feedback: For a ΔT error, confirm ΔT = final − start and have them recompute.
For a 'too high c' item, confirm the cause is energy lost to the surroundings so less reached the substance than was counted.
Keep numbers friendly so arithmetic does not obscure the physics.
activities.rationale: Retrieval and checking items consolidate the quantitative layer, but are a check rather than the primary teacher; the firsthand practical and the relationship-building activities must precede them.
learnerActions: Apply Q = mcΔT both directions: find Q for a given rise, find ΔT for a given energy, and back out c from measured values.
Read the heating rate from the gradient of a temperature–time graph.
Answer 'why did the measured c come out too high?' and justify (energy lost to surroundings).
Sort changes by whether they raise or lower the temperature rise for a fixed energy (e.g. more mass, higher-c material → smaller rise).
Spot the slip of using the final temperature instead of ΔT.
activities.intendedInsight: The calculations, gradient-reading and error-identification are well-defined skills that also surface the temperature-vs-energy and ΔT-vs-final-temperature misconceptions.

constraints: The firsthand bench practical is the primary evidence for this PROCEDURAL topic: handling apparatus, coping with thermometer lag and uneven heating, and confronting genuine un-modelled error. A virtual lab cannot deliver this experimental-design-and-execution skill and should sit alongside, not instead of, a real practical.

A static labelled apparatus diagram and annotated graph are a useful pre-lab reference for the setup and equation parts, but cannot run the experiment, grow the graph, or model the heat loss that drives the error reasoning.
Dialogue/Socratic debrief supports the evaluative reasoning but does not by itself develop the quantitative measuring and graphing; use it as a complement.
Recognition/retrieval items (quiz) check calculation and graph-reading but do not elicit independent planning, apparatus handling, or firsthand error evaluation.
Keep ΔT explicitly as a change (final − start), never a single reading; keep each symbol in Q = mcΔT tied to a measured quantity.

Treat the heating rate as variable: the temperature–time line bends as losses grow, so avoid presenting a fixed constant rate. Distinguish this loss-driven bending, which can level off gradually below the boiling point when losses approach the power input, from a flat plateau at the melting or boiling point, which signals a change of state where energy is supplied but does not raise temperature.
Separate the KS3/MS skills (designing, measuring, graphing, evaluating error — done firsthand) from the KS4/HS quantitative layer (the c value and the Q = mcΔT number).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that a measured c 'almost always comes out too high' and that electrical input exceeds Q assumes the dominant error is heat loss to the surroundings; this holds for typical immersion-heater water-heating setups but depends on apparatus and conditions (e.g. heater self-heating, calorimeter inclusion). Presented as the expected outcome, not a universal law.

The source for the IOP/misconception claim is marked verified:false in the row; treat the misconception guidance as documented difficulty rather than independently confirmed here. The IOP claim argues for tying the equation to a REAL measurement, so it only partially supports the virtual-lab activity (via its error-evaluation emphasis); the virtual lab is framed as a qualified digital stand-in, not evidenced as superior to real measurement.

The 'same energy, three materials' and virtual-lab heat-loss and plateau behaviours describe a modelled simulation; real materials (especially aluminium as a solid vs water as a liquid) involve contact/heating-method differences, so firsthand results may differ from the idealised side-by-side comparison.
The original 'poor' rating of 3D framing is retained only as a design preference (apparatus and graph are well served in 2D); it is not asserted that 3D 'adds nothing' as a general principle.

probeDeeper: Is your thermometer fully in the water and read at eye level — what error creeps in if not?
You raised 200 g by 10 °C and 400 g by 10 °C. Which needed more energy, and what part of Q=mcΔT tells you?
Your measured input is bigger than the Q you calculated. Is that an experimental mistake, or expected — and why?
What does the GRADIENT of your temperature-time graph tell you, and why does the line start to flatten?
assess.correctAnswer: Sets up the heater in the water, records temperature at time intervals, computes ΔT (the rise, not the final temperature) and Q = m c ΔT. Explains the electrical energy supplied exceeds Q because some heat is lost to the surroundings, the beaker and evaporation. Plots temperature against time and reads the gradient as the rate of temperature rise (steeper = faster heating), flattening as losses grow.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats temperature and heat energy as the same thing ('the temperature IS the energy').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Temperature is how hot; Q is the energy transferred — the same temperature rise needs more energy for more mass (that's the m in the equation).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about the reading as if it were the energy; surprised that mass matters in Q=mcΔT.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the final temperature (or the starting one) as ΔT instead of the CHANGE ('ΔT is 80 because it ended at 80').
errorPatterns.nextMove: ΔT = final minus start; mark both readings and subtract before substituting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watching the substitution — plugs a single reading, not the difference, into Q=mcΔT.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes all the electrical energy supplied goes into the water, so measured input should equal Q ('they must match').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Identify losses — to air, the beaker, evaporation; that's why the experiment isn't 100% efficient and input exceeds Q; suggest insulation and a lid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Doesn't expect or can't explain input > Q; ignores heat loss.

responseLevels.gap: Confuses temperature with heat, uses the final temperature as ΔT, or assumes input equals Q (ignores losses).
responseLevels.full: Measures ΔT and reads the thermometer correctly, applies Q=mcΔT, explains input > Q through heat loss to the surroundings (with improvements), and interprets the temperature-time gradient as the heating rate.
responseLevels.partial: Runs the practical and applies Q=mcΔT to the numbers, but mishandles ΔT or thermometer technique, or can't explain why input exceeds Q.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Plan and run a quick experiment to measure the energy needed to raise this beaker of water's temperature, using the heater, thermometer and stopwatch. Record your readings, use Q = mcΔT, and tell me why your measured energy input is more than the Q you calculate. Then show me the temperature-time graph and what its gradient means. [Watch: thermometer immersed and read at eye level; ΔT is the CHANGE not the final; readings at intervals; recognises heat lost to surroundings so input > Q; reads gradient as rate.]
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the practical separates a child who measures ΔT correctly, immerses and reads the thermometer properly, and accounts for heat loss (input > Q), from one who confuses temperature with heat, uses the final temperature as ΔT, or assumes all input energy entered the water.
