pedagogy.summary: Year 2–Grade 2 (age 7–8) pupils solve one-step LENGTH word problems within 100 using addition and subtraction, REPRESENTING the situation with a drawing (such as a ruler drawing or bar) and an EQUATION that uses a symbol for the unknown number. The pedagogy is about modelling: the child should build a picture of the problem structure (whole/parts, or comparison) and read the number sentence off that picture — including missing-addend forms like 18 + □ = 45 — rather than grabbing the two numbers and applying an operation cued by a keyword. (This maps CCSS 2.MD.B.5 almost verbatim, with 2.MD.B.6 adding the number-line-from-0 model.)
bestPractices: Model the situation before calculating — use a bar model or a ruler/number-line drawing to show the whole and its parts (or the two lengths being compared), so the operation follows from the structure, not from a keyword.

Teach the symbol-for-the-unknown explicitly: write 45 − 18 = □ AND 18 + □ = 45 for the same rope, showing both describe the same picture and that '=' means 'has the same value as', not 'the answer comes next'.
Deliberately include comparison ('12 cm longer') and missing-addend ('how much was cut off?') problems, not just result-unknown take-aways, so keyword strategies break down.
Represent lengths from 0 on a number line with equally spaced points, and show sums/differences as jumps (2.MD.B.6).
Insist on units in the answer (cm) and on a drawing that matches the numbers, so the model and the equation stay tied to the quantity.
keyRepresentations: Bar model (whole split into known part + unknown □)
Ruler / number-line drawing with jumps from 0
Equation with a symbol for the unknown (□ or ?)
Comparison bars stacked to show 'how much longer'
commonMisconceptions: Chooses the operation from a keyword ('longer'/'altogether' → add; 'cut off'/'left' → subtract) without modelling the situation, so comparison and missing-addend problems are miscalculated.
Writes the answer where the unknown symbol should go, reading '=' as 'the answer is' rather than 'has the same value as', so cannot represent 18 + □ = 45 before solving.
When drawing/using a ruler, counts the marks or starts at 1 instead of 0, so the represented length is off by one.
Drops the unit or draws a picture that doesn't match the quantities.

learn.summary: Year 2 / Grade 2 (age 7–8) pupils solve one-step length word problems within 100 using addition and subtraction, representing each situation with a drawing (such as a ruler or bar drawing) and an equation that uses a symbol (□ or ?) for the unknown — including missing-addend forms like 18 + □ = 45. The core skill is modelling: the child builds a picture of the problem structure (whole and parts, or two lengths compared) and reads the number sentence off that picture, rather than grabbing the two numbers and applying an operation cued by a keyword. This maps CCSS 2.MD.B.5, with 2.MD.B.6 adding the length-from-0 number-line model.

activities.title: Build a bar or ruler model, then read the equation off it
feedback: If the child writes the answer where the □ should go (e.g. writes 27 instead of keeping □ in 18 + □ = 45), point back to the drawing: 'Which piece don't we know yet? That piece is the box — keep the box until the very end.'
If only one form is offered, prompt: 'Can you write it a different way — an adding sentence with a box — that means the same thing?' and check it against the same bar.
If the unit is dropped, ask 'How long — in what?' so the answer reads 27 cm.
activities.rationale: CCSS 2.MD.B.5 names drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown as the target representation; writing both the subtraction and the missing-addend form on one picture is intended to build a relational reading of '=' as 'has the same value as'.
sourceClaims: Grade 2 pupils use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths given in the same units, e.g. by using drawings (such as drawings of rulers) and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

Elementary children generally read '=' operationally — as a signal to carry out the calculation before it and write the total after — rather than relationally as 'is the same value as'. Given 8 + 4 = □ + 5, across 145 sixth-graders every child answered 12 or 17 and almost none the correct 7; the pattern held from grade 1 to 6 and did not improve with age. Building a relational view via true/false and open number sentences (unknown in varied positions) enabled first/second graders to answer correctly (14 of 16 in a pilot class).
learnerActions: Read a result-unknown story, e.g. 'A rope is 45 cm long. I cut off 18 cm. How long is it now?'
Draw a bar (or ruler line) labelled 45, mark off the 18 cm that was cut, and mark the leftover piece with a □ to show it is the length you do not yet know.
Write a number sentence that matches the drawing, using a symbol for the unknown: 45 − 18 = □ AND 18 + □ = 45.
Solve and label the answer with its unit: 27 cm.
Show the two equations against the same drawing and explain why both describe one picture.
activities.intendedInsight: The unknown is a visible piece of the bar or ruler you can point to before you know its number, so the equation is a description of the picture — not a guess triggered by a word like 'cut off'.

activities.title: Model comparison stories with stacked bars
feedback: If the child adds simply because they saw 'longer', ask them to show the 12 on the two stacked bars first, then decide: 'Is the piece we don't know the whole ribbon, or the gap?'
If the bars don't start level, re-align them at 0 so the overhang is read correctly.
Prompt: 'This story says 12 cm longer — where is the 12 in your picture?'
activities.rationale: Comparison and missing-addend structures are where keyword strategies fail; modelling the structure lets the correct operation follow from the picture. Problem semantics (Compare, Add To with unknown start, Take From with unknown change) do not map reliably onto surface words.
sourceClaims: CGI classifies add/subtract word problems by semantic structure (Add To, Take From, Put Together/Take Apart, Compare) crossed with which quantity is unknown (result/change/start; difference/bigger/smaller). Keyword mapping breaks down on non-result-unknown structures: a 'take from' story with an unknown change is solved by adding (5 − ? = 3), an 'add to' story with unknown start by subtracting (? + 3 = 5), and Compare 'more/fewer' wording does not reliably signal the operation — so children must model the structure, not cue on a word.

Genuine mathematical problem solving is non-routine and is NOT the execution of memorised shortcuts such as key words; teaching students to build a visual representation of the problem before writing an equation has strong evidence for improving problem-solving achievement.
learnerActions: Read a comparison story, e.g. 'Sam's ribbon is 30 cm. Mia's is 12 cm longer. How long is Mia's?'
Draw two bars stacked so they start level; make Mia's bar stick out past Sam's, and mark the extra gap as 12 cm.
Point to where the 12 cm sits in the picture (the overhang), not just the word 'longer'.
Write the matching equation with a symbol for the unknown total and solve: 30 + 12 = □, so □ = 42 cm.
Compare a 'how much longer?' version where the gap itself is the unknown, and show the gap is what the □ marks this time.
activities.intendedInsight: In a comparison the operation comes from where the lengths line up and which piece of the drawing is unknown. The word 'longer' always points to the overhang (the difference). Whether you add or subtract depends on whether the unknown is the longer bar, the shorter bar or the overhang itself.

activities.title: Lengths from 0 on a number line, with jumps
feedback: If the count gives the number of marks rather than intervals, ask the child to point to the first space and count spaces: 'The length is the ground you cover, not the fence posts.'
If a measurement begins at the '1' instead of 0, re-set the start to 0 and re-read.
Confirm the jump lands on the expected number and relate it back to the equation with the □.
activities.rationale: CCSS 2.MD.B.6 asks pupils to represent lengths from 0 on a number line and show sums and differences as jumps; a documented error is counting marks or starting from the wrong point.
sourceClaims: Grade 2 pupils represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line diagram with equally spaced points, and represent whole-number sums and differences within 100 on a number line.

When using a ruler/number line to model length, children count marks and treat them as the units, or read from the wrong start point rather than accumulating length from 0 — an off-by-one representation error.
learnerActions: Draw a number line with equally spaced points and label the start point 0.
Place a length by counting the intervals (spaces) from 0, not the marks, so a length of 18 cm ends at the mark labelled 18 after 18 intervals, rather than by counting 18 marks (which lands short).
Show a sum or difference as a jump along the line (e.g. jump back 18 from 45, landing on 27).
Say aloud where each length begins and ends, confirming it accumulates from 0.
activities.intendedInsight: Length accumulates from 0, and it is the intervals (the spaces between marks) that count — starting from 1, or counting marks instead of spaces, gives a length that is off by one.

activities.title: Check your equation and answer against the picture
feedback: For an open sentence like 18 + □ = 45, if the child writes 45 (the whole) or 63 (adding both numbers), return to the bar: 'The box is the missing piece, not the whole rope — 18 and the box together make 45.'
If a matched pair is solved with the same operation for both, ask which piece is unknown in each drawing.
Reinforce that selecting a correct sentence from options is a check — the main goal is to build and label your own model and equation.
activities.rationale: Open number sentences with the unknown in varied positions are intended to build the relational view of '=' and let pupils verify that the written equation genuinely describes the modelled structure; selecting a correct sentence checks, but does not itself elicit, independent construction.
sourceClaims: Elementary children generally read '=' operationally — as a signal to carry out the calculation before it and write the total after — rather than relationally as 'is the same value as'. Given 8 + 4 = □ + 5, across 145 sixth-graders every child answered 12 or 17 and almost none the correct 7; the pattern held from grade 1 to 6 and did not improve with age. Building a relational view via true/false and open number sentences (unknown in varied positions) enabled first/second graders to answer correctly (14 of 16 in a pilot class).
learnerActions: After solving, respond to short checks: choose the number sentence that matches a given drawing; complete an open sentence such as 18 + □ = 45; state the answer with its unit; and draw the matching jump on a number line.
Re-tell which piece of the drawing the □ stood for and why the operation fits the structure.

Try a matched pair that share a keyword but have different structures (e.g. one 'how much longer' difference-unknown story and one 'longer' total-unknown story) and show why they need different operations.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct answer should be traceable back to the drawing: the symbol marks the unknown piece, the operation matches the structure, and the unit names the quantity.

constraints: The learning objective is for the child to construct the model and the equation, so recognition-only tasks (choosing a finished sentence, tapping to reveal a completed bar) check understanding but do not elicit the independent construction the standard requires; use them as checks or worked-example references, not as the main activity.

Deliberately include comparison and missing-addend problems alongside result-unknown take-aways, especially structures where a keyword points to the wrong operation (e.g. 'Mia's ribbon is 12 cm longer than Sam's. Mia's is 42 cm. How long is Sam's?', where 'longer' appears but you subtract). Keyword strategies often give the right operation on result-unknown items, and even on some comparison or missing-part items such as '12 cm longer, how long is Mia's?' or 'how much was cut off?'. So check the structure rather than assuming every comparison or missing-addend item will expose keyword use.
Insist on a drawing that matches the numbers and on units (cm) in the answer, so the model and equation stay tied to the quantity.
When a ruler or number line is used, start length from 0 and count intervals, not marks; otherwise represented lengths come out off by one.

A draggable on-screen builder (e.g. sliding a cutter along a 45 bar so the leftover segment is marked with a □, or stacking two comparison bars to reveal a 12 cm gap) makes the unknown concrete and can accept both 45 − 18 = □ and 18 + □ = 45; paper bar/ruler drawings achieve the same modelling and either medium is acceptable.
Keep problems to one step and within 100, with both lengths in the same unit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Worked example checked: for the rope, 45 − 18 = 27 cm and the equivalent 18 + □ = 45 gives □ = 27; for the ribbons, 30 + 12 = 42 cm. Likely wrong-answer slips to watch for include 45 + 18 = 63 (keyword-driven) and writing the answer where the □ belongs.

The original source material included framings such as '3D adds nothing spatial' and a dialogue format having no value for this topic; these catalog-style comparative judgements are not treated as established and have been reframed as narrow scope notes (recognition tasks check rather than construct; a manipulable builder and paper drawings each support modelling). No claim of one medium being universally necessary is asserted.

The original assessment field wrote the ribbon work as a chained equation '30 + 12 = □ = 42 cm'; this run-on use of '=' conflicts with the relational-equality goal and has been corrected to '30 + 12 = □, so □ = 42 cm' in the guidance. The original slip is recorded here only, not in any learner-facing prompt.
The assessment field's partial/full response levels and diagnostic prompts were used to inform activity feedback but were not altered in the original row.

probeDeeper: 'Show me on your drawing which part is the number we don't know.'
'Can you write it a different way — as an adding sentence with a box — that means the same thing?'
'This story says "12 cm longer". Draw Sam's and Mia's ribbons — where is the 12?'
'If the rope had been 45 cm and it is now 27 cm, how much was cut off? Same picture — which piece is missing now?'
assess.correctAnswer: For the rope: draws a bar/ruler showing 45 split into 18 and an unknown, writes 45 − 18 = □ (or 18 + □ = 45) and gets 27 cm. For the ribbons: models 30 with 12 more, writes 30 + 12 = □ = 42 cm. Chooses each operation from the STRUCTURE, represents the unknown with a symbol, and labels cm.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword-driven operation choice — picks the operation from a surface word ('cut off' → subtract, 'longer'/'more' → add) without modelling, so a comparison or missing-addend problem gets the wrong operation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the structure first — bar model of whole and parts, or stacked comparison bars — and read the operation off the picture; contrast two problems with the same keyword but different structures.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies an operation that matches a word but not the situation (e.g. 45 + 18 because a number 'sounds like adding', or can't handle 'how much was cut off?').

errorPatterns.pattern: Operational view of '=' — writes the answer where the unknown symbol should go and reads '=' as 'the answer is', so cannot represent 18 + □ = 45 before solving.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build meaning for '=' as 'has the same value as' using a balance and true/false number sentences; model the unknown as a box in the picture first, then transcribe the equation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses or fails to write an equation with the unknown as a symbol; only writes a completed 'sum = answer' string after solving mentally.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ruler-representation error — when drawing or using a ruler to model the length, counts the marks or starts at 1 instead of 0, so the represented/measured length is off by one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish that length accumulates from 0 and that it is the INTERVALS (spaces), not the marks, that count; represent the story on a number line starting at 0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A ruler drawing whose count of marks (not intervals) gives the length, or a measurement that begins at the '1' or the ruler's edge rather than 0.

responseLevels.gap: Grabs the two numbers and applies a keyword-cued operation with no model; writes the answer in place of the unknown; ruler drawing counts marks or starts at 1.
responseLevels.full: Models the situation (bar/ruler/number line from 0), chooses the operation from the structure not keywords, represents the unknown with a symbol, solves within 100, labels cm, and transfers across take-away, comparison and missing-addend variants.
responseLevels.partial: Solves a simple result-unknown take-away by subtracting and can draw a picture, but a comparison ('12 cm longer') or missing-addend ('how much was cut off?') derails the operation choice, or the unknown is written as the answer rather than a symbol.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give two length stories and watch how the child represents and solves them. First: 'A rope is 45 cm long. I cut off 18 cm. How long is it now? Draw something to show the problem and write a number sentence with a box for the number you don't know.' Then a comparison: 'Sam's ribbon is 30 cm. Mia's is 12 cm longer. How long is Mia's? Show me.' Watch the model, the operation choice, the use of a symbol for the unknown, and the unit.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who models the structure handles both the take-away and the 'longer' comparison correctly and can place a □ for the unknown; a keyword-reliant child adds for 'longer' but may subtract or add wrongly on the missing-addend/comparison, and writes the answer where the box belongs. Modelling-from-structure and keyword-cueing diverge exactly on the comparison and missing-addend items.

sources.claim: Grade 2 pupils use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths given in the same units, e.g. by using drawings (such as drawings of rulers) and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 2.MD.B.5

sources.claim: Grade 2 pupils represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line diagram with equally spaced points, and represent whole-number sums and differences within 100 on a number line.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 2.MD.B.6

sources.claim: When using a ruler/number line to model length, children count marks and treat them as the units, or read from the wrong start point rather than accumulating length from 0 — an off-by-one representation error.
sources.source: Gómezescobar, A. (2026), 'Ruler by Steps', Early Childhood Education Journal 54(3), citing Clements et al.

sources.claim: Elementary children generally read '=' operationally — as a signal to carry out the calculation before it and write the total after — rather than relationally as 'is the same value as'. Given 8 + 4 = □ + 5, across 145 sixth-graders every child answered 12 or 17 and almost none the correct 7; the pattern held from grade 1 to 6 and did not improve with age. Building a relational view via true/false and open number sentences (unknown in varied positions) enabled first/second graders to answer correctly (14 of 16 in a pilot class).
sources.source: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter (1999), 'Children's Understanding of Equality: A Foundation for Algebra', Teaching Children Mathematics 6(4), 232-236

sources.claim: CGI classifies add/subtract word problems by semantic structure (Add To, Take From, Put Together/Take Apart, Compare) crossed with which quantity is unknown (result/change/start; difference/bigger/smaller). Keyword mapping breaks down on non-result-unknown structures: a 'take from' story with an unknown change is solved by adding (5 − ? = 3), an 'add to' story with unknown start by subtracting (? + 3 = 5), and Compare 'more/fewer' wording does not reliably signal the operation — so children must model the structure, not cue on a word.
sources.source: Idaho SDE, 'Cognitively Guided Problem Types' chart (based on Carpenter, Fennema, Franke, Levi & Empson, Children's Mathematics: Cognitively Guided Instruction, Heinemann 1999; NRC 2009; CCSS 2010)

sources.claim: Genuine mathematical problem solving is non-routine and is NOT the execution of memorised shortcuts such as key words; teaching students to build a visual representation of the problem before writing an equation has strong evidence for improving problem-solving achievement.
sources.source: Woodward et al. (2012), IES/WWC Practice Guide 'Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8' (NCEE 2012-4055)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten → Year 1). THE CARDINALITY PRINCIPLE — the last number word said when counting a set tells HOW MANY (its numerosity), and that total is unchanged by rearrangement or the order counted. The bridge from counting-as-reciting to counting-as-quantity; prerequisite for +1, comparison, number representation and all early addition/subtraction (centrality 0.97).
• Standards — UK (DfE): EYFS 'Number' ELG (deep understanding of number to 10). NC Year 1 'count, read and write numbers to 100' and 'given a number, identify 1 more and 1 less' presuppose cardinality; the language 'equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least' is Year 1.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.4b verbatim — 'Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.' K.CC.4 heads this as 'connect counting to cardinality.'
• Operational details: 'How many?' and 'give me N' are the canonical assessments — a child who RECOUNTS when asked 'how many?' has not grasped it (Thompson). Confront arrangement-invariance: count, then spread out / bunch up / recount in a different order → same total. Subitising small sets (≤5) supports instant cardinality. Use the Bermejo 'start counting at three' probe to distinguish TRUE cardinality from last-word parroting.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (4–5) after counting ≤5 answers 'how many?' with the last word without recounting, and gives-N for N≤5. Tier B (5–6) knows rearranging a counted set of ≤10 doesn't change the total, without recounting. Tier C (6) sees the total is unchanged when counted from a different starting object/order and isn't fooled by spreading the set out (early conservation).
bestPractices: Emphasise the last word's DOUBLE job — it names the final object AND tells the whole set's size (Thompson); mark the shift with stress/gesture: '…four, five — FIVE altogether!'
Use 'give me N' tasks (child counts out a subset) as the strongest cardinality check — harder and less gameable than 'how many?'.
Confront arrangement-invariance directly: count, then move/scatter the same objects and ask 'how many now?'; the child who must recount reveals the gap.
Probe with the Bermejo trick — ask the child to start counting 5 objects from 'three'; answering 'seven' (last word) rather than 'five' exposes last-word parroting, not cardinality.
Build subitising (instant recognition of ≤5) with dot cards, dice and ten-frames so small quantities are known as wholes, reinforcing number = amount.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame / five-frame (the filled frame shows the total as a stable whole).
Dot / dice / domino patterns for subitising (cardinality without counting).
The 'count → cover it → how many?' routine (forces recall of the total, not a recount).
A numeral card placed beside a counted set (numeral ↔ quantity).
commonMisconceptions: Recounting when asked 'how many?' — treating the count as a performance rather than something that yields a total (the diagnostic error).
Last-word parroting without meaning — repeating the final word said even when the count started at the wrong number (Bermejo: counts 5 from 'three', answers 'seven').
Believing rearranging or spreading out a set changes how many there are (pre-conservation; length/spacing mistaken for quantity).
Thinking the last number names only the last OBJECT, not the whole set.

learn.summary: Help children aged 4–6 grasp the cardinality principle: the last number word said when counting a set tells how many objects there are (its total), and that total does not change when the objects are rearranged or counted in a different order. This is the bridge from counting-as-reciting to counting-as-quantity and underpins +1/−1, comparison and early addition/subtraction. Useful checks include 'how many?' answered without recounting, 'give me exactly N', and arrangement/order-invariance probes.

activities.title: Count, scatter, re-ask: the total that stays put
feedback: If the child says the same number without recounting and explains 'you didn't add or take any away', affirm: that reasoning is conservation of number.
If the child insists on recounting after rearrangement, rearrange back and forth while asking each time 'did I add any or take any away?' to surface that nothing changed.

If the child says 'fewer, it's a smaller pile' or 'more, it's spread out', lay out a second matching set in the original arrangement and pair each moved object one-to-one with an object in that set, so the child can see none are left over and the quantity is the same.
Mark the shift from naming the last object to naming the whole set with stress and gesture on the total: '…four, five — FIVE altogether!'
activities.rationale: Directly confronting arrangement-invariance (count, then move the same objects and re-ask) targets the diagnostic error of recounting and the pre-conservation belief that spreading/bunching changes quantity. A persistent visible total makes the invariance concrete.
sourceClaims: Cardinal principle: the final number name tells the numerosity of the set, not just names the last object; a child who recounts when asked 'how many?' has not grasped it. Bermejo et al. (2004): asked to count five objects starting from 'three', many children answer 'seven' (the last word said) — showing last-word repetition ≠ cardinal understanding.
K.CC.4b: 'Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.'
learnerActions: Count a small set of objects aloud (start with 5, e.g. five toy ducks or cars) and say the total: '…four, five — five altogether!'
Place or keep visible a total badge/numeral card showing the count beside the set.
Now move the same objects around: bunch them in a corner, spread them out in a ring or long line — without adding or removing any.

Before recounting, say how many there are now and explain why (if the total card is still showing, ask why the card still matches the set, so the answer is reasoned rather than simply read off the card).
Check by recounting together only if needed, and notice the total is the same.
activities.intendedInsight: Moving objects around cannot change how many there are; the total is a fixed property of the set, so you do not need to recount after rearranging.

activities.title: Give me exactly N (count-out task)
feedback: If the child counts past the requested number or hands over too few, gently restart and emphasise stopping at the target word.
If the child cannot stop at the requested amount, return to 'count then say the total' tasks before retrying count-out.

Count-out is harder and less gameable than 'how many?'; consistent success across several requests, including larger numbers such as 5 or more, is strong evidence of cardinality rather than of last-word repetition.
activities.rationale: 'Give me N' tasks require the child to use the number word as a target quantity, which recognition or last-word repetition cannot easily fake (though a correct answer with a very small N can come from knowing small numbers rather than general cardinality), so they complement the 'how many?' check. (The supporting source establishes the cardinality principle these tasks draw on, not the method's measured effectiveness.)
sourceClaims: Cardinal principle: the final number name tells the numerosity of the set, not just names the last object; a child who recounts when asked 'how many?' has not grasped it. Bermejo et al. (2004): asked to count five objects starting from 'three', many children answer 'seven' (the last word said) — showing last-word repetition ≠ cardinal understanding.
learnerActions: From a heap or big box of objects, count out exactly a requested number (e.g. 'give me exactly 5 cars', 'give me exactly 4').
Stop as soon as the requested amount is reached, rather than counting the whole heap.
Check the handed-over set by recounting together.
activities.intendedInsight: A number word is a stop-signal for a specific quantity: knowing 'five' means being able to produce a set of exactly five, not just reciting up to five.

activities.title: Start counting from three (parroting trap)
feedback: If the child answers 'seven', recount normally from one together and compare: the set had five objects both times.
If the child answers 'five', acknowledge they are tracking the actual quantity, not the last word spoken.
Use this as a diagnostic probe, not a correction exercise — the goal is to focus attention on what the final number means.
activities.rationale: The Bermejo 'start at three' probe distinguishes true cardinality from last-word parroting, which a simple 'how many?' after a normal count may not expose.
sourceClaims: Cardinal principle: the final number name tells the numerosity of the set, not just names the last object; a child who recounts when asked 'how many?' has not grasped it. Bermejo et al. (2004): asked to count five objects starting from 'three', many children answer 'seven' (the last word said) — showing last-word repetition ≠ cardinal understanding.
learnerActions: Lay out 5 objects. The adult asks the child to count them but to START saying 'three' on the first object, then 'four', 'five', 'six', 'seven'.
Afterwards ask: 'So how many objects are there really?'
Discuss why the answer is still five even though the last word said was 'seven'.
activities.intendedInsight: The correct total (five) is a property of the set, not just whatever word you happen to say last; answering 'seven' may mean the child is repeating the last word rather than finding how many (or may reflect confusion about the unusual instruction).

activities.title: Count from the other end (order-irrelevance)
feedback: If the child predicts a different number for a different starting point, do NOT mark it wrong — let them count both ways carefully (touching each object once) and discover the totals match; if they get different totals, recount slowly together to find the skipped or double-counted object.
Genuine order-irrelevance develops late, so build it through repeated hands-on experience rather than correction.
activities.rationale: Order-irrelevance develops late and is built through repeated experience, so letting the child count both ways and discover that the totals match is preferable to correcting a prediction; premature marking-wrong does not accelerate the understanding.
sourceClaims: K.CC.4b: 'Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.'
learnerActions: Count a line of objects left-to-right and say the total.
Count the same line right-to-left (or starting from a middle object) and say the total again.
Compare: as long as each object is counted exactly once, the total is the same whichever object you start from and whatever order you count in.
activities.intendedInsight: The total does not depend on which object you count first or the order you count in.

activities.title: Subitising small sets as wholes
feedback: If the child counts one-by-one on a quick flash, shorten the exposure and start with 2 or 3 before building to 5.
After covering the set, if the child wants to uncover and recount, prompt 'you already counted — how many were there?' to encourage recall of the total.
activities.rationale: Subitising and the cover-and-recall routine may support cardinality by presenting small sets as stable wholes and prompting recall of a total rather than a recount. The supporting source frames subitising as part of a developmental progression toward number sense, but that source is unverified, so this is a qualified proposal.
sourceClaims: Subitising and comparing magnitudes support number sense in early years as part of a developmental progression toward cardinality.
learnerActions: Briefly show dot cards, dice faces, domino patterns or a five-frame (or a ten-frame filled only partly) showing small quantities (≤5) and say how many without counting one-by-one.
Match a numeral card to a set to link the symbol to the quantity.
Use the 'count → cover it → how many?' routine: count a set, cover it, then recall the total from memory instead of recounting.
activities.intendedInsight: Small quantities can be recognised instantly as whole amounts, reinforcing that a number names an amount, and the total can be recalled rather than re-derived.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: will bunching change how many? (assessment companion)
feedback: 'The same, because you didn't add or take any away' is the target conservation reasoning — affirm it.
'Fewer, it's a smaller pile' or 'more, it's spread out' signals number is not yet conserved; rearrange back and forth asking 'did I add or take any away?' and use one-to-one matching.

'You'd have to count them again to know' signals the child does not yet trust that rearranging leaves the total unchanged; rearrange back and forth asking 'did I add or take any away?', and add count-out tasks and the cover-and-recall routine.
activities.rationale: Asking the child to commit to a prediction and a reason BEFORE observing makes the diagnostic distinction between conservation reasoning and appearance-based judgement explicit.
sourceClaims: K.CC.4b: 'Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.'
learnerActions: Show 5 cars in a line and agree there are 5.
Before anything is moved, PREDICT: 'If I bunch these into a pile, will there be more, fewer, or the same — and why?' Commit to a reason first.
Then bunch them and count together to check against the prediction.
Afterwards answer: 'How could you have known it would still be 5 without counting?'
activities.intendedInsight: The reason given before observing reveals understanding: 'the same, because you didn't add or take any' shows conservation; 'fewer, it's a smaller pile' does not.

constraints: Target standards: EYFS 'Number' ELG (deep understanding of number to 10); CCSS-M K.CC.4b and K.CC.4 ('connect counting to cardinality'); NC Year 1 '1 more/1 less' and the language 'equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least' presuppose cardinality.
A child who RECOUNTS when asked 'how many?' after a completed count may not yet have grasped cardinality — this is a key diagnostic sign, best confirmed with give-N and other probes.

Progression checkpoints: Tier A (4–5) answers 'how many?' with the last word without recounting and gives-N for N≤5; Tier B (5–6) knows rearranging a counted set of ≤10 does not change the total without recounting; Tier C (6) sees the total is unchanged when counted from a different start/order and is not fooled by spreading out (early conservation).
Order-irrelevance and conservation develop late; build them through experience and do not mark a child wrong for predicting a different total before they have discovered otherwise.

A static labelled scene ('5 counted, 5 altogether') can serve as a reference but cannot by itself animate the rearrange-and-recheck that demonstrates invariance; use it alongside hands-on rearrangement.

Multiple-choice or slider-style response formats ('how many altogether?', 'same or different total?', give-N via slider) can serve as an assessment companion; recognition-only responses do not themselves elicit the independent count-out production that most strongly evidences cardinality.
A screen 'persistent total badge' or live recolouring/dragging is one optional way to make invariance visible; physical objects a child can move by hand serve the same purpose and are equally valid.
Keep sets small to preserve focus on the small-set quantity; avoid cluttered or busy displays that distract from the quantity itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One listed source (IES/WWC 'Teaching Math to Young Children', WWC 2014-4005, on subitising supporting number sense) is marked verified:false in the row; the subitising activity relies on it, so treat that supporting claim and the activity as unconfirmed.

The give-N activity's sourceClaim supports the underlying cardinality principle (final word = numerosity), not the measured effectiveness or superiority of the count-out method itself; 'strong evidence' is a design judgement, not fresh efficacy data.

The original row framed a non-spatial/3D medium as 'poor' and asserted cardinality is non-spatial; this comparative/necessity framing has been softened to affordance-based focus/clutter notes rather than treated as an established pedagogical law.

Self-audit: counting/quantity examples (5 objects; give-N for N≤5; start-at-three yielding 'three, four, five, six, seven' = 5 words for 5 objects, with 'seven' as the parroting error and five as the true total) were checked and are internally consistent; 'seven' is presented only as the error to expose, never as a correct total.

assess.poeTask: Show 5 cars in a line and agree there are 5. Ask the child to PREDICT before you act: 'If I bunch these into a pile, will there be more, fewer, or the same — and why?' They commit to a reason first; then bunch them and count together to check. The reason given before observing is the diagnostic part — 'the same, because you didn't add or take any' is conservation; 'fewer, it's a smaller pile' is not.
probeDeeper: Give me exactly 5 cars from this big box.
If I spread them out in a long line, how many now?
What if you counted them starting from that end instead — how many?
How do you know it's still 5 without counting?
assess.correctAnswer: Still 5 — I already counted them and I didn't add any or take any away, so bunching them up doesn't change how many.

errorPatterns.pattern: last-word parroting — gives the final count word when asked 'how many' but doesn't treat it as the total; recounts when asked again, or cannot count out a requested amount
errorPatterns.nextMove: play 'so how many?' games — count, then immediately ask the total and hide the set; add count-out tasks ('give me exactly 4') so the number becomes a stop-signal for a quantity
errorPatterns.distractor: You'd have to count them again to know.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: after the rearrangement insists on recounting, or (Bermejo count-out test) cannot 'give me exactly 5' from a heap without counting past or short

errorPatterns.pattern: number not conserved — thinks bunching up or spreading out changes how many ('fewer now, it's a small pile' / 'more, it's spread out')
errorPatterns.nextMove: rearrange back and forth while the child watches, each time asking 'did I add or take any away?'; pair with one-to-one matching to show the quantity is preserved
errorPatterns.distractor: There are fewer now because the pile is small.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: states a different number after rearrangement, pointing to how the arrangement looks

errorPatterns.pattern: order-irrelevance not yet held — thinks counting from the other end, or in a different order, could give a different total
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT mark wrong; let the child count from both ends and discover the totals match — genuine order-irrelevance develops late, so build it through experience, not correction
errorPatterns.revealedBy: asked 'what if you started from that end?', predicts a different number or insists you must start from one particular end

responseLevels.gap: Recounts the set every time it is rearranged, or changes the total based on how the arrangement looks — treats 'how many' as something to re-derive, not a fixed property.
responseLevels.full: States the total is unchanged because nothing was added or removed, counts out an exact quantity on request, and accepts that counting order does not matter.
responseLevels.partial: Answers 'how many' with the last count word and holds the total under a small rearrangement, but cannot count out a given quantity on request, or is unsure whether starting from the other end changes it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 5 toy cars in a row. Count them for me. (Child counts to 5.) Good — so how many cars are there? Now watch, I'll bunch them into a pile. Without counting again, how many cars are in the pile now — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the cardinality principle treats the last count word as a fixed property of the whole set, so answers '5' immediately and justifies by conservation (nothing added or removed). A last-word parroter recounts the pile or gives a new number — for them '5' was an echo of the last word, not the set's total. A child lacking conservation says there are now more/fewer because the pile 'looks different'. The 'without counting again... how do you know' tier separates knowing the total from re-deriving it.

sources.claim: Cardinal principle: the final number name tells the numerosity of the set, not just names the last object; a child who recounts when asked 'how many?' has not grasped it. Bermejo et al. (2004): asked to count five objects starting from 'three', many children answer 'seven' (the last word said) — showing last-word repetition ≠ cardinal understanding.
sources.source: Ian Thompson, 'The Principal Counting Principles' (NCETM article, Stanford PreK-Math mirror)

sources.claim: K.CC.4b: 'Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.'
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Kindergarten Counting & Cardinality (K.CC)

sources.claim: Year 1: 'given a number, identify 1 more and 1 less'; use the language of 'equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most, least' — statutory goals that presuppose cardinality.
sources.source: DfE, National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 1, Number and place value)

sources.claim: Subitising and comparing magnitudes support number sense in early years as part of a developmental progression toward cardinality.
sources.source: IES/What Works Clearinghouse practice guide, 'Teaching Math to Young Children' (WWC 2014-4005)

pedagogy.summary: At age 11-13 pupils move from recognising shapes to DERIVING and justifying their properties — the interior angles, diagonals, symmetry and side relationships of triangles, quadrilaterals and circles — and to reasoning about how the shapes relate. The signature idea is hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification: a square is a special case of BOTH a rectangle and a rhombus because it possesses all their defining properties and more. The dominant obstacle, robustly documented, is the prototype phenomenon and partition thinking: pupils who can state definitions still judge by the prototypical picture, so they deny that 'a square is a rectangle' (rectangles are 'long'/slanted parallelograms look a certain way), and even when they accept one direction they miss the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram ⇒ square ⊆ parallelogram). For circles, properties are relational and multiplicative — diameter = 2 × radius, circumference = π × diameter — with π a constant ratio independent of the circle's size. Effective teaching derives properties by construction and measurement, works from hierarchical (not partition) definitions, and uses dynamic shapes so pupils see one shape become a special case of another without losing the general properties.
bestPractices: Derive properties rather than assert them: have pupils construct, fold, measure and mark to establish (e.g.) that a parallelogram's diagonals bisect each other, distinguishing this from a rectangle's equal diagonals
Teach hierarchical (inclusion) definitions explicitly and contrast them with partition definitions (de Villiers): a square counts as a rectangle because it meets every rectangle property
Use dynamic shapes to defeat prototype/partition thinking: drag a rectangle until all sides are equal and note that 'square' switches on while 'rectangle' never switches off
Target the opposing-direction and transitive inclusions directly (every square is a rhombus AND a parallelogram; not every rectangle is a square) with always/sometimes/never tasks
For circles, establish diameter = 2r and circumference = πd by measuring several circles, so π emerges as a constant ratio independent of size
keyRepresentations: Dynamic quadrilateral with live name-tags (parallelogram/rectangle/rhombus/square) that light up as properties are met
Quadrilateral hierarchy Venn diagram / family tree
Fold-and-measure derivations of diagonal and symmetry properties
Circle with labelled radius, diameter and circumference and a circumference ÷ diameter ≈ 3.14 readout
Property tables comparing triangles/quadrilaterals for always/sometimes/never reasoning
commonMisconceptions: Partition/prototype classification: denying that a square is a rectangle (or a rhombus) because the shapes 'look different' or a rectangle 'must have two long and two short sides'
One-directional / non-transitive inclusion: accepting square ⊆ rhombus but not square ⊆ parallelogram, or thinking a rectangle cannot share square properties
Judging properties by appearance rather than derivation — e.g. assuming a parallelogram's diagonals are equal (confusing it with a rectangle)
Confusing radius and diameter, or believing π (circumference ÷ diameter) depends on the size of the circle
Treating each named shape as an isolated category with no overlapping membership

learn.summary: For learners aged 11-13, the goal is to move from recognising triangles, quadrilaterals and circles to DERIVING and justifying their properties (interior angles, diagonals, symmetry, side relationships) and reasoning about how shapes relate hierarchically. The signature idea is class-inclusion classification: a square is a special case of BOTH a rectangle and a rhombus because it has all their defining properties and more. The documented core obstacle is prototype/partition thinking — pupils who can state definitions still judge by the prototypical picture, denying 'a square is a rectangle', and often miss the opposing-direction and transitive inclusions (square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram ⇒ square ⊆ parallelogram). For circles, properties are relational: diameter = 2 × radius and circumference = π × diameter, with π a constant ratio independent of the circle's size. Effective teaching derives properties by construction and measurement, builds from hierarchical (not partition) definitions, and uses dynamic (or adjustable) shapes so a learner can watch one shape become a special case of another without losing the general properties, with hands-on construction, measurement and comparison supporting the same ideas.

activities.title: Morph a rectangle into a square and watch inclusion persist
feedback: If a learner says the shape 'stopped being a rectangle' when it became a square, ask: which rectangle property did it lose? (It kept four right angles and opposite sides equal/parallel, so it is still a rectangle.)
If a learner insists the shapes 'look different', redirect to checking the square against EVERY rectangle property one by one rather than judging by overall appearance.
activities.rationale: Prototype/partition thinking is robustly documented: learners who know definitions still deny 'a square is a rectangle'. Watching one shape acquire a more general class's name-tags while keeping the general tag makes inclusion visible rather than asserted. The continuous morph requires a dynamic geometry tool (or an adjustable model such as a linkage/geoboard) with name-tags that light up as each shape's properties are met; a set of physical cutouts can support a compare-across-shapes version (holding a long rectangle beside a square and checking shared properties) but cannot show the live transformation, and a static family-tree/Venn reference can support the idea but cannot display the morph itself.
sourceClaims: Hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification means more particular concepts form subsets of more general ones (de Villiers 1994); most learners nevertheless reason by prototype/partition even when they know definitions, denying e.g. that a square is a rectangle ('parallelograms are slanted'), and struggle with the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (accepting square⊆rhombus but not square⊆parallelogram) — a static, inflexible concept image blocking hierarchical reasoning (Fujita 2012 levels; van Hiele informal-deduction level is where class inclusion is understood).

KS3 statutory: pupils 'derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other plane figures (for example, equal lengths and angles) using appropriate language and technologies', 'identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections', and know circle parts and that circumference = π × diameter.
learnerActions: Start with a 'long' rectangle and list which names currently fit it: note that, of the names parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and square, only 'rectangle' and 'parallelogram' apply (it is also a quadrilateral).
Change the shape by moving its corners/sides until all four sides are equal, keeping the four right angles.
Observe that 'rhombus' and 'square' now apply too — while 'rectangle' never stopped applying.
Say in your own words why the square never stopped being a rectangle: it kept every rectangle property and simply gained the extra property of four equal sides.
activities.intendedInsight: A square is a special case of a rectangle (and of a rhombus): it satisfies every defining property of the more general class and adds more, so it belongs to both classes at once.

activities.title: Derive diagonal and symmetry properties by folding and measuring
feedback: If a learner claims a parallelogram's diagonals are equal, ask them to measure both diagonals of a clearly non-rectangular parallelogram — they differ. Equal diagonals belong to the rectangle, not the general parallelogram.
Praise justifications that cite a fold or measurement ('I measured both halves and they matched, so the diagonals bisect') over 'it looks like it'.
activities.rationale: A common error is attributing the wrong property to the wrong class by appearance (e.g. giving a parallelogram equal diagonals by confusing it with a rectangle). Construction and measurement give learners a reliable method to establish and distinguish properties. Paper/card cutouts are approximations with real thickness; treat them as stand-ins for the ideal zero-thickness plane figures.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other plane figures (for example, equal lengths and angles) using appropriate language and technologies', 'identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections', and know circle parts and that circumference = π × diameter.
learnerActions: Construct or cut out a parallelogram, a rectangle and a rhombus (paper/card approximations of the ideal flat figures).

Draw the diagonals; fold and measure to test: do the diagonals bisect each other? Are they equal in length? Do they meet at right angles? Also fold along each diagonal and along each line joining midpoints of opposite sides to test which are lines of symmetry.

Record for each shape which diagonal and symmetry properties hold, e.g. a parallelogram's diagonals bisect each other but are NOT generally equal, whereas a rectangle's diagonals ARE equal and a rhombus's diagonals meet at right angles; a non-square rectangle's lines of symmetry join midpoints of opposite sides (its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry), a non-square rhombus's lines of symmetry are its diagonals, and a parallelogram that is neither has no line of symmetry.
State each property as something you checked by construction/measurement, not something you guessed from the picture.
activities.intendedInsight: Properties should be derived and verified, not read off appearance; different classes have genuinely different diagonal/symmetry properties, which is how you can tell them apart and justify inclusion.

activities.title: Measure several circles to let π emerge as a constant ratio
feedback: If a learner predicted the ratio would be larger for bigger circles, point to their own table: the ratios should be roughly the same for every circle, close to 3.14 apart from measuring error, with no trend by size — the true ratio is fixed, so π is a constant, not size-dependent.
If radius and diameter are confused, have them lay the radius against the diameter and confirm the diameter spans twice the radius across the centre.
Note that small measuring errors make the ratios differ slightly; the pattern 'a bit more than 3 every time' is the point, not a perfectly identical decimal.
activities.rationale: Measuring several circles and comparing the ratio lets π be felt as an invariant rather than memorised, directly confronting the misconception that π depends on circle size. A resizable circle with a live circumference ÷ diameter readout held near 3.14 is an optional model that reinforces the same invariance when physical objects aren't available.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other plane figures (for example, equal lengths and angles) using appropriate language and technologies', 'identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections', and know circle parts and that circumference = π × diameter.
learnerActions: Collect several circular objects of different sizes (tins, lids) and some string or tape.
Before measuring, PREDICT how many times the diameter will fit around the circumference, and say WHY — in particular, predict whether the answer changes with the size of the circle.
Wrap and measure the circumference, then measure the diameter, for each object.
Compute circumference ÷ diameter for each and compare: the ratio should come out a little more than 3 (close to 3.14, within measuring error) each time, regardless of the circle's size.
Also check that the diameter is twice the radius (d = 2r) and state circumference = π × diameter in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Radius, diameter and circumference are related multiplicatively: d = 2r and C = πd, where π is a constant ratio (≈ 3.14) that does NOT depend on the size of the circle.

activities.title: Always / sometimes / never and the inclusion chain
feedback: If a learner accepts 'a square is a rhombus' but denies 'a square is a parallelogram', walk the chain: a square is a rhombus, every rhombus is a parallelogram, so a square is a parallelogram.
If a learner answers 'a rectangle is a square' as always true, show a long rectangle: it lacks four equal sides, so it is a rectangle but not a square — hence only sometimes.
Encourage justification by which properties are present/absent rather than by appearance.
activities.rationale: Targeting the opposing-direction and transitive inclusions directly addresses the documented one-directional/non-transitive error. Always/sometimes/never items (phrased in singular form so each verdict is well defined), categorisation and matching assess inclusion well, and prototype distractors ('a square is not a rectangle because it looks different') probe the core misconception. Used in teaching, these response formats can also surface reasoning for discussion, though a selection item alone does not elicit a learner's own justification.
sourceClaims: Hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification means more particular concepts form subsets of more general ones (de Villiers 1994); most learners nevertheless reason by prototype/partition even when they know definitions, denying e.g. that a square is a rectangle ('parallelograms are slanted'), and struggle with the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (accepting square⊆rhombus but not square⊆parallelogram) — a static, inflexible concept image blocking hierarchical reasoning (Fujita 2012 levels; van Hiele informal-deduction level is where class inclusion is understood).
learnerActions: Decide for each statement whether it is always, sometimes or never true, and justify by properties: 'A square is a rectangle', 'A rectangle is a square', 'A square is a rhombus', 'A square is a parallelogram'.
Trace the inclusion chain square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram and explain why it follows that a square is a parallelogram (transitive reasoning).
Explain why 'a square is a rectangle' is always true but 'a rectangle is a square' is only sometimes true — the two directions are different.
Build or complete a family-tree / Venn diagram of parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and square, placing each shape in every class it belongs to.
activities.intendedInsight: Inclusion has a direction and is transitive: the more special shape belongs to the more general classes, but not the reverse; chaining inclusions lets you conclude square ⊆ parallelogram.

activities.title: 'Convince me a square is a rectangle' — a reasoning dialogue
feedback: Reward arguments that answer an objection with a property check rather than restating the conclusion.
If the learner concedes to a prototype objection, ask which rectangle property the square actually fails — it fails none.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue that repeatedly asks 'does a square have every property a rectangle needs?' and offers prototype counter-claims can surface and challenge partition reasoning and rehearse justification. It complements, and does not replace, the hands-on derivation and the dynamic morph activities, which can make the inclusion idea visible more directly.
sourceClaims: Hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification means more particular concepts form subsets of more general ones (de Villiers 1994); most learners nevertheless reason by prototype/partition even when they know definitions, denying e.g. that a square is a rectangle ('parallelograms are slanted'), and struggle with the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (accepting square⊆rhombus but not square⊆parallelogram) — a static, inflexible concept image blocking hierarchical reasoning (Fujita 2012 levels; van Hiele informal-deduction level is where class inclusion is understood).
learnerActions: Take the position that a square IS a rectangle and argue it to a partner or teacher who keeps pushing back with prototype objections ('but rectangles are long', 'they look different').
For each objection, answer by checking the square against a specific defining property of a rectangle (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel).
Conclude with a property-based statement: a square has every rectangle property and adds four equal sides, so it is a special rectangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A convincing justification of inclusion is built from checking defining properties, and it withstands appearance-based objections.

constraints: Build from hierarchical (inclusion) definitions and explicitly contrast them with partition definitions; a partition definition (e.g. 'a rectangle must have two long and two short sides') is the source of the core misconception and should be surfaced and corrected, not used.

Properties should be explored by construction, folding and measurement, then stated as checked for the shapes tested (within measuring accuracy) and, where possible, justified by reasoning from the definitions so they hold in general — avoid letting learners assert properties from appearance alone.

Paper/card cutouts have real thickness and are approximations of ideal zero-thickness plane figures; a flat screen is also a model. Distinguish the represented ideal shape from its physical or pictured representation.
Measurement of real circles yields ratios near 3.14 with small variation from measuring error; the invariance ('always a bit more than 3') is the learning point, not a perfectly identical decimal.

A static hierarchy/Venn reference is a useful support but cannot display a shape morphing while inclusion persists, and a fixed cutout cannot morph; pair either with a dynamic or adjustable model (or a deliberate compare-across-shapes activity) so inclusion is experienced, not only read.
Recognition-only response formats (picking the right option) do not by themselves elicit a learner's own justification; require them to state property-based reasoning in their own words.

When using always/sometimes/never, phrase items in singular form ('a rectangle is a square') so the verdict is well defined; a universally quantified statement is simply true or false, not 'sometimes'.

Optional interactive features — draggable corners, live name-tags that light up as properties are met, a diagonals overlay toggle, a resizable circle with a fixed C÷d readout — make the mechanism concrete when available, but are not mandatory; paper, string and construction tools serve the same objectives.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The legacy row rated 3D as adding 'nothing essential'. These are plane figures plus one circle ratio, so 2D/physical work is well matched; this is a scope judgement, not evidence that a 3D representation could not help any learner.

The legacy claims that the square/rectangle question 'cannot be answered correctly from the picture alone' and that a static image 'cannot teach' inclusion are comparative claims not established by the cited sources; retained only as the narrow, true point that a static reference and a fixed cutout cannot display the continuous morph, while a dynamic/adjustable model can.

Corrected the morph activity and summary: a fixed paper cutout cannot continuously morph a rectangle into a square, so the continuous transformation is credited to dynamic geometry/adjustable models, with cutouts supporting comparison instead.

The always/sometimes/never activity uses singular-form statements so each a/s/n verdict is well defined; universally quantified statements ('every rectangle is a square') are simply true or false and were not used in learner-facing items.
The objective lists triangle interior angles, but like the original row no dedicated triangle angle-sum derivation activity is included; this is a scope gap to flag, not an introduced error.

Self-audit of mathematical content: d = 2r, C = πd, π ≈ 3.14 constant across sizes, parallelogram diagonals bisect but are not generally equal, rectangle diagonals equal, rhombus diagonals perpendicular, and the inclusion chain square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram are all internally consistent and used as stated; no arithmetic or geometric error found to correct.

assess.poeTask: Give the child several circular objects (tins, lids) and string or tape. Ask them to PREDICT how many times the diameter will fit around the circumference — and to say WHY — BEFORE measuring. Then wrap and measure each: the ratio is always a little more than 3 (π), for every size of circle. Whether they predicted the ratio would depend on the circle's size is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Is every rectangle a square? Why is that direction different from 'every square is a rectangle'?
List the properties of a parallelogram — are its diagonals equal? How could you CHECK rather than guess?
A square is a rhombus and a rhombus is a parallelogram — so is a square a parallelogram? How do you know?
For a circle, how do the radius, diameter and circumference relate — and which stays about 3 times another no matter how big the circle is?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes to both. A square IS a rectangle because it has every defining property of a rectangle — four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel — and simply adds the extra property that all four sides are equal, so it is a special rectangle. A square IS a rhombus because it has the rhombus's defining property of four equal sides, adding right angles, so it is a special rhombus. The reasoning must be property-based inclusion (the square satisfies all the properties of the more general class), not 'they look different'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Partition/prototype classification — denies a square is a rectangle because rectangles are 'long' (two long, two short sides) or the shapes simply 'look different'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach hierarchical vs partition definitions; check the square against EVERY rectangle property; drag a rectangle dynamically until it becomes a square while its rectangle properties persist
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides, so a square is not a rectangle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no, a square isn't a rectangle' and justifies it by appearance or by a length restriction on rectangles

errorPatterns.pattern: One-directional / non-transitive inclusion — accepts an easy inclusion (square is a rhombus) but not the transitive or opposing-direction one (square is therefore a parallelogram), or thinks a rectangle cannot share square properties
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the inclusion chain explicit (square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram) and reason transitively; use a Venn/family tree and always/sometimes/never tasks to distinguish the two directions
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On follow-up says a square is a rhombus but denies it is a parallelogram, or accepts every square is a rectangle yet insists a rectangle can never be 'square-like'

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges properties by appearance rather than derivation — e.g. asserts a parallelogram's diagonals are equal (confusing it with a rectangle)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the pupil derive the property by construction/measurement and compare classes (parallelogram diagonals bisect but are not equal; rectangle diagonals are equal)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States a property (equal diagonals, right-angle diagonals) from how the figure looks, without constructing or measuring, and attributes the wrong property to the wrong class

responseLevels.gap: Classifies by appearance/prototype, denies a square is a rectangle, states properties only by looking, and treats each shape as an isolated category.
responseLevels.full: Reasons hierarchically from definitions and properties (a square satisfies all rectangle AND all rhombus properties, so is a special case of both), handles opposing-direction and transitive inclusions, derives and verifies properties (parallelogram diagonals bisect; C = πd, d = 2r), and transfers the reasoning to a new shape.
responseLevels.partial: Lists correct properties of each shape and may accept the easier inclusions (square ⊆ rhombus), but cannot handle the opposing-direction or transitive inclusions, or derive/verify a property rather than assert it — knows the parts without the relational hierarchy.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Answer each with yes or no, then explain: Is a square a rectangle? Is a square a rhombus? Use the properties of these shapes in your reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who reasons hierarchically from properties answers yes-and-yes and justifies by property inclusion; a pupil reasoning from the prototype answers 'no' because the shapes look different or 'a rectangle must be long'. The square/rectangle question is the classic separator of hierarchical from partition/prototype thinking — it cannot be answered correctly from the picture alone.
