pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Animal Nutrition

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y3 'Animals, including humans'):** "identify that animals, including humans, need the right types and amount of nutrition, and that they cannot make their own food; they get nutrition from what they eat".

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE):** No US elementary PE names food groups; the closest idea, that animals get materials and energy from food, sits within 5-PS3-1 / LS1.C ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS3-1]... and the energy'). Treat as UK-led.

- **Operational details:** The organising contrast is heterotroph vs autotroph in child terms: plants MAKE their own food (using light); animals CANNOT and must EAT it. From there children learn two separate things: foods are sorted into the FOOD GROUPS of a local healthy-eating guide (in the UK, the Eatwell Guide's five groups: fruit and vegetables; starchy carbohydrates; proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads), and foods supply NUTRIENTS the body needs (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and fibre, plus water), most foods supplying several. The body needs the RIGHT TYPES and the RIGHT AMOUNTS (not just 'more is better') — a variety of foods from each food group in roughly the guide's proportions, balanced over a day or week. Consequences of imbalance make it concrete (too little calcium → weak bones; too little of a vitamin → illness). Keep it at the level of sorting foods into the guide's food groups and naming the main nutrients and their jobs; never call nutrients 'food groups'. Detailed nutrient chemistry is KS3.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). A Y3 child can sort foods into the Eatwell Guide's food groups, name the main nutrients and what they do, and state that animals must eat while plants make their own food; the conceptual stretch is 'right types AND amounts' — that a balanced variety, not a single favourite food, keeps the body healthy.
bestPractices: Lead with the plant-vs-animal contrast (plants make their own food from light; animals cannot and must eat) because it is the load-bearing idea that distinguishes animal nutrition and sets up food chains.

Teach nutrients by FUNCTION not just name (carbohydrates for energy, protein for growth/repair, fats for energy/warmth, vitamins & minerals for health, fibre to keep the gut working, water for everything), separately from food groups, so children learn that food groups are groups of foods on a healthy-eating guide while nutrients are what those foods supply.
Make 'right types AND amounts' concrete with consequences (too little calcium → weak bones; too little vitamin C → illness; too much sugar → unhealthy) rather than an abstract 'balance'.

Use real or pictured foods children eat: sort them into the Eatwell Guide's food groups and build meals in roughly the guide's proportions (fruit and vegetables and starchy foods the biggest parts, oils and spreads small), balanced over a day, connecting to their own diet.

Distinguish food groups from nutrients: a single food (e.g. an egg or a glass of milk) sits in one food group but supplies several nutrients, and mixed dishes such as pizza combine several food groups — avoid matching each food to one nutrient.
Link forward to digestion (how the body gets the nutrients out of food) and to food chains (why animals must eat other organisms).
keyRepresentations: An Eatwell Guide plate showing the proportions of the five food groups (fruit and vegetables; starchy carbohydrates; proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads), with foods high in fat, salt and sugar outside the main groups
Food-group sorting cards (foods → the five Eatwell food groups), with a 'mixed foods' pile for dishes such as pizza or sandwiches
A plant-vs-animal contrast panel: plant with sun → 'makes its own food'; animal with mouth → 'must eat food'
A nutrient function strip pairing each nutrient (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, plus water) with what it does for the body
Consequence cards linking a missing nutrient to a health effect (calcium→bones, vitamin C→scurvy)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking animals (or humans) can make their own food or 'get energy from the sun' like plants — the core misconception this topic must correct.
Believing 'more food is always better' or that one favourite food can be a whole diet, missing 'right amounts' and variety.
Assuming each food supplies just one nutrient, rather than most foods supplying several (e.g. milk supplies protein, fat and calcium).

Calling nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins) 'food groups' — food groups are groups of foods on a healthy-eating guide such as the Eatwell Guide, and each food supplies several nutrients.
Confusing 'healthy = expensive/special food' rather than balance across ordinary foods.
Thinking only 'unhealthy' people need to worry about nutrition, rather than everyone needing the right types and amounts.

learn.summary: Animal nutrition for 7–8 year-olds (UK DfE Y3 'Animals, including humans'). The load-bearing idea is that plants MAKE their own food using light while animals CANNOT and must EAT to get energy and nutrients. From there children sort foods into the food groups of a local healthy-eating guide (in the UK, the Eatwell Guide's five groups), learn separately which nutrients foods supply and what each does for the body (energy, growth/repair, warmth, health, gut function; water for hydration), recognising that most foods supply several nutrients, and grasp that the body needs the RIGHT TYPES and RIGHT AMOUNTS — a variety of foods from each food group in roughly the guide's proportions over a day or week, not a single favourite or simply 'more'. Consequences of imbalance (weak bones without calcium, illness without vitamin C) make this concrete. The core proposed activity is a build-a-balanced-plate task with a responsive balance meter, complemented by a real classroom food-sort and a plant-vs-animal contrast that also links to food chains; alternatives (reveal poster, sorting consolidation, nutritionist dialogue) are kept for their distinct purposes.

activities.title: Build a balanced plate with a live balance meter
feedback: If the plate is piled with only sweets or cakes: 'Lots of energy from sugar, but very little for growth or health — these foods sit outside the main food groups; your body needs foods from the main groups too.' If it is piled with only one non-sugary food, name which food group it comes from, what nutrients it gives and which food groups are still missing.
If variety and proportions are good: meter settles green and the cartoon body perks up — 'Right types and right amounts.'

When a deficiency pop-up appears (e.g. too little calcium over time → weak bones), explain that calcium is a mineral (a nutrient) found in foods from the dairy and alternatives group such as milk, cheese and yoghurt, and let the child add one of those foods.
If two equal-sized plates score differently, draw attention to WHY: 'Same amount of food, but one has a healthy variety.'
activities.rationale: The objective is sorting foods into the guide's food groups and balancing amounts, which is a sortable, buildable task. A live balance meter is intended to make 'right types AND amounts' something the child notices through the recompute rather than a stated rule. The parallel real-food sort connects to the child's own diet as recommended in best practice.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory requirement: 'identify that animals, including humans, need the right types and amount of nutrition, and that they cannot make their own food; they get nutrition from what they eat'.

The Eatwell Guide divides the foods and drinks we consume into five main food groups (fruit and vegetables; potatoes, bread, rice, pasta and other starchy carbohydrates; beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads) and shows how much of what we eat overall should come from each; choosing a variety of foods from each group helps provide the wide range of nutrients the body needs, combination foods such as pizzas and sandwiches contain several food groups, and balance can be achieved over a day or a week.

Foods provide a range of nutrients with different roles in the body — carbohydrates (energy), protein (growth and repair), fats, and vitamins and minerals (health) — alongside fibre and water; most foods provide several nutrients.
learnerActions: Drag on-screen food cards onto an Eatwell-style plate divided into the five food groups while a health/balance meter responds to what you add (in the classroom, do a parallel hands-on sort using real packets and pictures of your own meals).
Pile the plate with only cakes and sweets and read the meter: it swings to 'too much sugar — not enough for growth', with a cartoon body looking sluggish.

Now swap in foods from the main food groups — fruit and vegetables, a starchy food such as bread or rice, a protein food such as beans, eggs or fish, and a dairy food such as yoghurt — with water to drink; watch the meter settle into the green as the body perks up.
Compare two plates with the SAME total amount of food but different variety, and say which scores healthier and why.
When a nutrient is missing, read the consequence pop-up (e.g. too little calcium over a long time → weak bones; too little vitamin C over a long time → illness) and add a food that fixes it.
activities.intendedInsight: It is the right TYPES and AMOUNTS together — a variety of foods from each food group in roughly the guide's proportions — that keep the body healthy, not quantity alone; the same total food scores differently depending on its variety.

activities.title: Plant makes food vs animal must eat
feedback: If the child says the dog can feed on sunlight: contrast directly — plants make their own food using light; animals cannot do this and must eat.
Correct answer: the dog cannot make food; it must eat, and its energy comes from the food it eats.
On the food chain: both the cow and the lion get their energy from food (grass, then the cow); the energy in bread began in a plant that captured sunlight.
Clarify a common slip: plants DO get nutrition — they just make their own rather than eating it, so saying 'plants get no nutrition' is wrong.
activities.rationale: This heterotroph/autotroph contrast is the core misconception to correct and the idea that sets up food chains. A responsive toggle is intended to make the 'make vs eat' distinction observable, and the food-chain question links the energy animals eat back to plants.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory requirement: 'identify that animals, including humans, need the right types and amount of nutrition, and that they cannot make their own food; they get nutrition from what they eat'.
NGSS frames the idea that food provides animals with the materials and energy they need within 5-PS3-1 / LS1.C, rather than a food-groups PE.
learnerActions: Watch or act out two side-by-side cases: a plant in sunlight whose food bar fills on its own, and an animal whose hunger bar only refills when you feed it.
Toggle sunlight on and off: the plant's food bar fills only when light is on, while the animal's hunger bar does not respond to sunlight at all.
Feed the animal a meal and watch its hunger bar refill, then say in your own words why the animal needed the food.
Answer: 'Can a dog just sit in the sun and make its own food like a sunflower?' and explain where the dog's energy actually comes from.
Trace a food chain: a cow eats grass and a lion eats the cow — say how each gets its energy, and where the energy in a slice of bread first came from (the plant, which captured it from the sun).
activities.intendedInsight: Animals cannot make their own food and must eat (plants or other animals) to get energy and nutrients; plants make their own food using light, and in food chains like these the energy animals eat traces back to plants.

activities.title: Reveal-the-job nutrients and food-groups poster (scaffold)
feedback: When a nutrient flap is revealed, restate its job in child terms and ask for a food that supplies it, then ask which food group that food belongs to.
On the myth-buster flap: reinforce that animals must eat; plants make their own food using light, but animals cannot.
If a child matches a food to just one nutrient, note that many foods (e.g. an egg) supply several nutrients; if a child calls a nutrient a 'food group', point back to the Eatwell plate.
activities.rationale: A reveal poster names nutrients and their jobs, shows the Eatwell food groups as a separate panel, and includes the plant-vs-animal myth-buster. It is a naming/revealing scaffold: it does not itself let the child actively balance amounts or experience the consequence of imbalance, so it supports but does not replace the build-a-plate task.
sourceClaims: Foods provide a range of nutrients with different roles in the body — carbohydrates (energy), protein (growth and repair), fats, and vitamins and minerals (health) — alongside fibre and water; most foods provide several nutrients.

The Eatwell Guide divides the foods and drinks we consume into five main food groups (fruit and vegetables; potatoes, bread, rice, pasta and other starchy carbohydrates; beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads) and shows how much of what we eat overall should come from each; choosing a variety of foods from each group helps provide the wide range of nutrients the body needs, combination foods such as pizzas and sandwiches contain several food groups, and balance can be achieved over a day or a week.
learnerActions: Tap or lift each flap of a nutrients poster to reveal the nutrient and its job (carbohydrates for energy, protein for growth/repair, fats for energy/warmth, vitamins & minerals for health, fibre for the gut, water for everything).
Tap each section of an Eatwell plate panel to reveal the food group's name and two example foods.
Open a myth-buster flap: 'Can animals make their own food like plants?' and read the answer.
Name a food you ate recently, say which food group it belongs to and which nutrients it supplies.
activities.intendedInsight: Each nutrient has a job in the body; food groups sort foods on a healthy-eating guide, and each food supplies several nutrients.

activities.title: Sort-and-match consolidation
feedback: For a mis-sort, point back to what kind of food it is and where the Eatwell Guide places it (e.g. beans go with proteins, cheese with dairy and alternatives, potatoes with starchy foods).
For 'why can't a cat make its own food?': reinforce that animals must eat; plants make food using light, but animals cannot.
If the child accepts 'humans make food from sunlight', re-run the plant-vs-animal contrast.
activities.rationale: Sorting, matching and single-answer questions check the objectives and rehearse the reasoning. On their own they do not build the quantitative balancing intuition, so they follow the active build task rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: The Eatwell Guide divides the foods and drinks we consume into five main food groups (fruit and vegetables; potatoes, bread, rice, pasta and other starchy carbohydrates; beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads) and shows how much of what we eat overall should come from each; choosing a variety of foods from each group helps provide the wide range of nutrients the body needs, combination foods such as pizzas and sandwiches contain several food groups, and balance can be achieved over a day or a week.

Foods provide a range of nutrients with different roles in the body — carbohydrates (energy), protein (growth and repair), fats, and vitamins and minerals (health) — alongside fibre and water; most foods provide several nutrients.
learnerActions: Sort a set of food cards into the Eatwell Guide's five food groups, using a 'mixed foods' pile for dishes such as pizza that combine several groups.
Match each nutrient (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, plus water) to its function, and name a food that supplies several of them (e.g. milk or an egg).
Answer 'why can't a cat make its own food?' and explain in a sentence.
Spot and reject a wrong claim such as 'humans make food from sunlight'.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate sorting foods into food groups, linking nutrients to their functions, and the reason animals cannot make their own food.

activities.title: Ask-a-nutritionist curiosity dialogue
feedback: For 'only chips': name what is missing (growth, health) and what too much of one thing does.
For 'is more always better?': emphasise right amounts, not just quantity.
For 'why can't I make my own food?': animals must eat; plants make their own food using light, but animals cannot.
activities.rationale: An in-role dialogue can motivate the balance idea through the child's own curiosity. It is a motivational complement; for the core sorting/balancing objective, actively building a plate may be a more direct route.
learnerActions: Ask a nutritionist/'body' character questions such as 'What happens if I only eat chips?', 'Is more food always better?' and 'Why can't I make my own food?'.
Predict the answer before revealing it, then compare.
Use the answer to plan one change to a one-sided plate.
activities.intendedInsight: A one-sided or over-large diet causes problems; the body needs variety and the right amounts, and animals must eat to get nutrients.

constraints: Keep at the level of sorting foods into a local guide's food groups and naming the main nutrients and their jobs; detailed nutrient chemistry is KS3 and out of scope.
The reveal poster is a naming/revealing scaffold: it does not let a child actively balance amounts or experience the consequence of imbalance, so pair it with the active build task.
Sort/match/single-answer questions consolidate and check recall and reasoning but do not by themselves build the quantitative balancing intuition.
Keep food groups and nutrients distinct: food groups are groups of foods on a healthy-eating guide; nutrients are what foods supply, and most foods (e.g. an egg) supply several.

Plate proportions follow the food groups of a local guide (Eatwell: fruit and vegetables and starchy foods the largest parts, oils and spreads small), balanced over a day or week — never equal shares of nutrients.
Keep 'right types AND amounts' concrete via consequences (calcium→bones, vitamin C→illness, too much sugar→unhealthy) rather than an abstract 'balance'.
Use real or pictured foods the children actually eat so sorting connects to their own diet; keep the physical sort distinct from the on-screen responsive meter.
A balance meter is an illustrative teaching device, not a clinical nutrition assessment; thresholds are simplified for learning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The British Nutrition Foundation claim is marked verified:false and now states only nutrient roles; food-group statements cite the NHS Eatwell Guide, which was fetched and checked during the October 2026 nutrition review.
Self-audit: 'plants get no nutrition' is a listed misconception — guidance clarifies plants DO get nutrition by making their own food, so no learner-facing action asserts plants are nutrition-free.
Self-audit: the balance-meter thresholds and 'green/sluggish' outcomes are pedagogical simplifications, not measured nutritional facts; framed as a teaching device in constraints.
The source assessment's probeDeeper food-chain and energy-origin questions have been incorporated into the plant-vs-animal activity to preserve the forward link to food chains.

The original 3D 'poor-fit' entry asserted a 3D scene 'adds cost without insight'; this reflects an internal catalog ranking rather than an established pedagogical law and was dropped rather than propagated as a universal claim.

Nutrition review (October 2026): corrected the teaching text, sorting cards, activities, constraints and assessment so that carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and fibre are taught as nutrients, not 'food groups'. Foods are classified with the Eatwell Guide's five food groups, nutrients and their functions are taught separately (most foods supply several), and plate proportions follow the guide's food groups over a day or week. Learning aims, the plant-vs-animal activity and the dialogue are unchanged.

probeDeeper: Where did the energy in a slice of bread originally come from?
Name some different food groups — does it matter if you only ever ate one of them?
A cow eats grass and a lion eats the cow. Do both get their energy from food? How?
Why can't you live on sunlight and water the way a sunflower does?
assess.correctAnswer: No — animals like the dog cannot make their own food; they must EAT food (plants or other animals) to get energy and nutrients. Only plants can make their own food using sunlight. The dog's energy comes from the food it eats, which is why animals must find and eat food to survive.

errorPatterns.pattern: animals can make their own food like plants (e.g. from sunlight)
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast plants (make their own food using light) with animals (must eat); only plants photosynthesise
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — sitting in the sun gives the dog energy just like a plant
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the dog can make food by sitting in the sun

errorPatterns.pattern: food just fills you up; it doesn't give energy
errorPatterns.nextMove: link food to energy — animals get all their energy from what they eat
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies that food is the energy source

errorPatterns.pattern: all foods are the same, or one food provides everything
errorPatterns.nextMove: introduce the main food groups and that eating a variety of foods from each provides the range of nutrients the body needs
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the probe cannot name different food groups or what the nutrients in them do

errorPatterns.pattern: plants don't need nutrition because they don't 'eat'
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify plants DO get nutrition — they just make their own food rather than eating it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says plants get no nutrition

responseLevels.gap: Says animals can make their own food, or that food gives no energy; cannot name food groups.
responseLevels.full: Explains that animals cannot make their own food and must eat to get energy and nutrients (unlike plants), names the main food groups and the main nutrients they supply, and describes consequences of too much or too little of a nutrient.
responseLevels.partial: Names food groups and knows animals eat, but as separate facts — cannot clearly contrast animals (must eat) with plants (make their own food), or link food to energy and the effect of imbalance.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A plant can sit in the sunshine and make its own food. Can a dog do the same — just sit in the sun and make its own food? Explain why or why not, and where a dog's energy actually comes from.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks animals can make food like plants, or that sunlight feeds animals, answers 'yes'; a child who knows animals must eat while plants make their own food says no and locates the dog's energy in its food. The reason tier is decisive.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** What Is an Earthquake

- **Standards — UK (DfE, England):** Not a KS1 science topic; England places earthquakes in the **KS2 Geography** programme of study ('volcanoes and earthquakes', ages 7–11). At 5–7 teach as enrichment supported by KS1 'Working scientifically' (observing, describing, using simple sources).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No K–2 PE names earthquakes directly; the anchor is **2-ESS1-1** ('… Earth events can occur quickly or slowly'), whose clarification names 'earthquakes, which happen quickly' — an earthquake is a canonical fast Earth event. CCC [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1, 2-ESS2-1].'

- **Operational details:** At 5–7 an earthquake is 'a sudden shaking of the ground'. Two ideas to secure: (1) it is the GROUND ITSELF that shakes (not just objects, not an explosion), and (2) earthquakes vary in strength — from so weak you barely notice, to strong enough to knock things over. Because a real earthquake can't be shown live, the felt experience is best simulated: shake a scene and let children see cups rattle, pictures tilt, shelves wobble. Connect to body experience ('imagine the whole floor wobbling like jelly'). Keep the CAUSE (rocks breaking/moving underground, releasing energy) for the 7–9 'Why Earthquakes Happen' topic; here, describe WHAT it is and what it feels like. Address the Hollywood image early: the ground shakes, it does not usually 'open up and swallow' people.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can describe an earthquake as sudden ground shaking and say it can be strong or weak; they are NOT yet expected to explain the underground cause. Confront the 'giant crack swallows everything' myth and the idea that only objects (not the ground) move.
bestPractices: Simulate the felt experience (a scene that shakes) because a real earthquake can't be shown live — the concept is sensory
Make the WHOLE scene shake, floor included, so children grasp it is the ground moving, not just objects on it
Teach the strong–weak range explicitly with a simple intensity label ('barely felt' → 'very strong')
Tie to the body ('the floor wobbles like jelly') to make 'what it feels like' concrete and meet the evidence
Confront the 'ground opens and swallows people' myth directly with reassurance that shaking settles
Defer the underground cause (rocks breaking, energy released) to the 7–9 'Why Earthquakes Happen' topic
keyRepresentations: A shaking room scene with a strength dial (gentle → strong)
An intensity scale in words/faces ('barely felt' to 'very strong')
Everyday objects as shake-indicators (swinging lamp, rattling cup, sliding books)
A whole-scene wobble (including the floor/ground) to show the ground itself moves
commonMisconceptions: 'The ground opens up and swallows people/cars' — the ground shakes and settles; wide swallowing fissures are a movie myth
'Only the objects shake, not the ground' — it is the ground itself moving, which is why everything on it shakes
'An earthquake is an explosion/bomb underground' — it is shaking caused by rock movement (cause taught later), not a blast
'All earthquakes are huge and destructive' — most are weak; strength ranges from barely noticeable to very strong
'Earthquakes only happen far away / to other people' — they occur in many places, some regions much more than others

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach that an earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground that can be strong or weak. Secure two core ideas: (1) it is the GROUND ITSELF that shakes, not just the objects on it, and (2) earthquakes range in strength from barely felt to very strong. Keep the underground cause (rocks breaking and releasing energy) for the later 7–9 topic; here focus on WHAT an earthquake is and what it feels like. Directly confront the film myth that the ground 'opens up and swallows' people, reassuring that the shaking settles. The central activity lets children control a shaking scene so the felt, variable-intensity idea becomes experiential; supporting activities add naming, a recall check, and a reassuring personal account.

activities.title: Shake the room: feel strong and weak
feedback: When the floor shakes with everything else, point out: 'See how the ground moves, not just the cup — that is why everything wobbles at once.'
At the low setting: 'This is a weak earthquake — you might barely notice it. Real earthquakes can be this gentle.'
At the high setting: 'This is a strong one — things slide and tilt, but the ground shakes and then settles; it does not open up and swallow things.'
If a child expects the ground to split open, reassure: 'The ground shakes side to side and up and down, and may crack a little, but it does not open into a chasm that swallows people.'
activities.rationale: The target concept is a felt, dynamic intensity ('sudden shaking, strong or weak'), and a scene the child controls lets them experience the same event across the whole range under their own hand. Making the floor shake together with the objects makes 'it is the ground that moves' visible, and shows objects move because they rest on the moving ground. The strength dial, word/face readout, and body captions are optional supports that make the idea concrete. Because a real earthquake cannot be shown live, a controllable simulation is a reasonable stand-in; it may make the felt range more experiential than a still image, though this comparison is a design judgement rather than an established finding.
sourceClaims: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground; the ground rarely opens into a fissure that swallows people (a common myth)
learnerActions: Slide a strength dial from 'gentle' to 'strong' and watch the whole room respond
At the gentle end, notice a teacup and a hanging lamp just tremble
Nudge the dial higher and watch books slide, pictures tilt, and the shelf rattle
Notice that the FLOOR shakes too, along with everything else, so you can see it is the ground itself moving
Read the intensity label as it changes ('barely felt' → 'very strong') and say aloud what you would feel in your body at each setting
activities.intendedInsight: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground that can span from barely felt to very strong; because the ground itself moves, everything resting on it moves with it.

activities.title: Name what is happening in the shaking scene
feedback: 'The lamp swings because the ground under the whole room is moving.'
If a child says only the objects move: 'The shelf rattles because the ground it stands on is shaking — when the ground moves, everything resting on it moves with it.'
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal scene can name visible effects and connect them to the underlying ground shaking. It is a useful naming and labelling support; a still or lightly animated scene conveys the strong/weak dimension less directly than a scene the child can actively intensify, so it works best alongside the controllable simulation.
learnerActions: Look at a scene of a shaking room and tap points such as the rattling shelf or swinging lamp
Read the one-line fact each tap reveals about what is happening
Say in your own words what an earthquake is doing to the room and to the ground
activities.intendedInsight: The signs of an earthquake (rattling, tilting, sliding) all happen because the ground is shaking.

activities.title: How strong, and what is an earthquake?
feedback: If the 'explosion' description is chosen: 'An earthquake is the ground shaking, not a blast or bomb. We will learn later what makes the ground shake.'
When the ordering is correct: 'Yes — from barely felt to very strong, earthquakes come in many strengths, and most are weak.'
activities.rationale: Short checks help confirm the definition and the weak→strong ordering. Recognition and ordering confirm recall but do not themselves deliver the felt experience of variable shaking, so use this after children have experienced the shaking rather than as a first encounter.
learnerActions: Read a described scene and set a strength slider to show how strong that earthquake was
Say what an earthquake is and choose the best description, rejecting an 'explosion underground' description
Put three earthquakes in order from weakest to strongest
activities.intendedInsight: An earthquake is ground shaking (not an explosion), and earthquakes can be ordered from weak to strong.

activities.title: Someone who felt an earthquake
feedback: 'The ground felt like it was wobbling like jelly, and then it stopped — the shaking does not go on forever; it settles.'
If a child seems worried: 'The shaking does not last forever, and the ground does not open up and swallow people.'
activities.rationale: A personal account can add vividness and reassurance and tie the concept to body experience. It works best as an optional add-on to the hands-on shaking activity rather than the main route to the concept for this age.
learnerActions: Listen to a friendly character describe feeling a small earthquake
Ask or choose questions like 'Was it scary?' and 'What did you do?'
Talk about what you would feel and do if the ground wobbled like jelly under your feet
activities.intendedInsight: An earthquake is something people feel in their bodies; a weak one can be barely noticeable, and the shaking settles.

constraints: Teach only WHAT an earthquake is and what it feels like at this age; defer the underground cause (rocks breaking, energy released) to the later 7–9 'Why Earthquakes Happen' topic.

Earthquakes are a KS2 Geography topic in England, and in the US NGSS K–2 standards they appear only as an example (the grade 2 standard 2-ESS1-1 gives earthquakes as an Earth event that happens quickly), so treat this as enrichment supported by observing and describing.

Directly address the 'ground opens and swallows people/cars' film myth with reassurance that the shaking settles; the ground shakes and may crack a little but does not form chasms that swallow people.

Make the whole scene (floor included) shake so children grasp that the ground itself moves, not just objects on it; objects move because the ground under them moves, though some (like sliding books or a swinging lamp) slide, tip or swing rather than moving exactly together with the floor.
The controllable simulation is a stand-in because a real earthquake cannot be shown live; it represents the felt experience rather than being an actual earthquake.
Recognition and ordering checks confirm recall but do not by themselves give the felt experience of variable shaking; use them after hands-on experience, not instead of it.

Interaction examples (strength dial, word/face intensity readout, tap-to-reveal points, swinging lamp, rattling cup, sliding books) are illustrative ways to make the idea concrete, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent editorial review: the prior correction of the activity-2 causal framing to simultaneity is sound, and no categorical medium-superiority claims remain; the remaining uncertainties are evidence-level, not learner-facing errors.
Source row marks the NGSS 2-ESS1-1 claim as verified; the DfE KS2 Geography placement claim and the USGS earthquake-basics/myth claim are marked unverified in the original.
The original stated a static picture 'cannot' convey shaking and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established facts, and have been softened to narrowly scoped trade-offs.
The 'earthquakes only happen far away / to other people' misconception from the source is not addressed in these activities and is left for a future extension.
'Most earthquakes are weak' is retained from the source; confirm it fits the local/regional context when used.

probeDeeper: If an earthquake was very weak, what might it feel like — could you even notice it?
Does the ground stay open after an earthquake, or does the shaking just stop?
What would you feel in your body if you were standing up during a strong earthquake?
Is a tiny trembling of the ground still an earthquake, or does it have to be huge to count?
assess.correctAnswer: No — that's a film exaggeration. In a real earthquake the ground shakes suddenly, side to side and up and down; it doesn't split open into a chasm that swallows people. The shaking can be so weak you barely notice it, or strong enough to be frightening.

errorPatterns.pattern: The ground opens into a huge crack and swallows people and cars
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront the film myth — the ground shakes and may crack a little, but big openings that swallow people don't happen; reassure them.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the ground opens up and swallows people.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a chasm that people fall into and disappear.

errorPatterns.pattern: Every earthquake is huge and knocks everything down (doesn't know they vary in strength)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Most earthquakes are so weak we don't even feel them; introduce a strength range from barely-felt to very strong.
errorPatterns.distractor: An earthquake always shakes so hard it knocks buildings down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes all earthquakes are catastrophic; no idea that most are weak.

responseLevels.gap: Believes the ground opens and swallows people; equates an earthquake with a chasm.
responseLevels.full: Describes an earthquake as sudden ground shaking that ranges from barely-felt to very strong, rejects the swallowing/chasm myth, and can say what the shaking would feel like.
responseLevels.partial: Says an earthquake is the ground shaking but still thinks it always opens the ground or is always huge.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a film, the ground rips open into a giant crack during an earthquake and people fall in. Does that really happen in an earthquake? What does an earthquake actually do to the ground?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can define an earthquake as 'the ground shaking' (first tier) yet still believe the ground opens and swallows people. Asking what actually happens to the ground forces 'shaking, not a chasm' — a child holding the myth describes the ground opening up and people falling in.

sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England — Geography KS2 programme of study (gov.uk)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–10 years

- **Topic:** Testing Materials for Uses

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Y5 'Properties and changes of materials'):** Pupils should be taught to "give reasons, based on evidence from comparative and fair tests, for the particular uses of everyday materials, including metals, wood and plastic." This sits within Working Scientifically at upper KS2: "planning different types of scientific enquiries... including recognising and controlling variables where necessary" and "reporting and presenting findings from enquiries... including conclusions, causal relationships."

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-2 → 3-5-ETS1-3):** 2-PS1-2 — "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-2]." The fair-test SEP is developed at grades 3–5 in 3-5-ETS1-3: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4]." DCI PS1.A: "Different properties are suited to different purposes." CCC: Cause and Effect.

- **Operational details:** Shift from asserting suitability to EVIDENCING it. Teach the fair-test structure explicitly: one question, one thing changed (the material), one thing measured (the outcome), everything else kept the same. Model the variable-control move — same size sample, same force, same amount of water — because uncontrolled variables are the commonest failure. Have children measure a comparable outcome (how much water passes through each fabric; how far each material bends under the same weight; which insulates a warm cup longest) and then write the reason-from-evidence sentence: 'plastic is best for a raincoat BECAUSE in our test least water passed through it.' Emphasise that the CONCLUSION must cite the data, not prior belief.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (procedural / early-quantitative). The child can design a fair test that changes only the material and controls the other variables, record comparable results in a table, and state an evidence-based reason for a material's use that explicitly refers to the results.
bestPractices: Teach the fair-test skeleton explicitly — change ONE variable (material), measure ONE outcome, keep everything else the same — and rehearse identifying the variable to control.
Make variable control the focus: same sample size, same force, same volume of water, because uncontrolled variables are the classic source of unfair results.
Require the conclusion to cite the evidence ('...because in our test...'), breaking the habit of concluding from prior belief.
Use a genuine, decision-worthy question (best material for a lunchbox / umbrella / cup cosy) so the test has a real purpose.
Record comparable, ideally measurable, outcomes in a table so results can be compared fairly rather than judged by eye.
Discuss reliability lightly — repeat a trial, note odd results — to introduce the idea that evidence can be more or less trustworthy.
keyRepresentations: The fair-test planning frame: question / change / measure / keep-the-same
A variables checklist (what must stay the same for the test to be fair)
A results table comparing the same outcome across materials
A 'claim — evidence — reasoning' sentence scaffold for the conclusion
Worked example: waterproofing test (fixed water volume poured on same-size fabric squares)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a test is fair while leaving variables uncontrolled (different sample sizes, different forces), so the comparison is invalid.
Changing more than one thing at once and being unable to attribute the result to the material.
Drawing the conclusion from prior belief or expectation rather than from the data collected.
Confusing a fair test with simply 'trying things out' — no controlled comparison, no measured outcome.
Treating a single trial as certain, with no sense that a result might need repeating or could be unreliable.

learn.summary: Children aged 7–10 learn to evidence (not just assert) which everyday material best suits a use by designing and running a fair test: change one thing (the material), measure one outcome, keep everything else the same, then write a conclusion that cites the data. The central objective is planning, controlling variables, measuring, and reasoning from results — ideally with real materials and measurement — and transferring that fair-test logic to a new property. Interactive simulations and consolidation/assessment tasks are supporting scaffolds around that doing-and-measuring core.

activities.title: Run a real fair test: which fabric makes the best raincoat?
feedback: If sample sizes, water amounts or holding methods differ between materials, the comparison is unfair: point to exactly what differs and re-run with those variables matched.

If the child concludes before testing or explains away a surprising result, ask them to quote the measured number that supports their claim (e.g. 'the cup under the paper collected the most water: 30 ml'), using whatever their own table shows.
If 'best' is judged by how a material looks or feels, agree the measured outcome in advance so the result is an observation, not an impression.
Prompt reflection: 'What did you keep the same, and why does that matter?' and 'If someone said your test wasn't fair, what would they point to?'

Probe trust in evidence: if the result surprises the child, ask 'Do you trust the test or your first guess, and why?' — a fair, measured result is better evidence than a guess, and repeating the trial to check it gives similar numbers makes it more trustworthy still.

Probe transfer: 'Would this same waterproofing test also tell us which coat is warmest? Why not?' to check the child separates the property actually tested from other properties a material might have.
activities.rationale: The target skill is procedural and data-driven: designing a controlled comparison, measuring a comparable outcome, and reasoning from the evidence. Real materials and a measuring jug let children feel the difference between a guess and a conclusion, and make variable control a concrete action rather than a definition. Uncontrolled variables and concluding from belief are the classic failure points, so the activity foregrounds both, and a transfer probe checks that the reason is tied to the specific property tested.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Y5 statutory requirement: 'give reasons, based on evidence from comparative and fair tests, for the particular uses of everyday materials, including metals, wood and plastic'; upper-KS2 WS controlling variables and evidence-based conclusions.
NGSS 2-PS1-2 (analyze data to find best-suited material) and 3-5-ETS1-3 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3]...'); DCI PS1.A; CCC Cause and Effect.
Common working-scientifically errors: uncontrolled variables making a test unfair, changing more than one variable, concluding from belief rather than data.
learnerActions: Pose a decision-worthy question, e.g. 'Which material — nylon, cotton or paper — makes the best raincoat?'
Set up the comparison yourself: cut same-size squares of each fabric, stretch each over an identical cup or tray.

Before testing, agree out loud what will be measured (how much water soaks through / reaches the tray beneath) and what must stay the same (square size, how it is held, the time, the amount of water).
Pour the SAME measured amount of water (e.g. one level cupful) on each square, catching and measuring what passes through (ml collected).
Record each result in a table so the materials can be compared by number, not by eye.

Write the conclusion with a claim–evidence–reasoning frame, using your own results, e.g. if nylon let the least water through: 'Nylon was the most waterproof material we tested, so it is the best choice for keeping rain out, BECAUSE in our test only 2 ml passed through it, compared with more through the cotton and paper.'
Repeat at least one trial and note any odd result to discuss whether the evidence can be trusted.
activities.intendedInsight: A conclusion about a material's use should be earned from a controlled, measured comparison — changing only the material and keeping everything else the same — not asserted from prior belief.

activities.title: Fair-test bench simulation with a fairness check
feedback: When the fairness indicator flags an uncontrolled variable, the message is that the result cannot be trusted until that variable is matched — fix it and re-run.
Once variables are controlled, the clean per-material measurement is the evidence the conclusion must cite.
If the sentence builder is completed without reference to the measured number, prompt the child to insert the actual data.
activities.rationale: A simulated test bench lets a child repeatedly set up and correct controlled comparisons and see the consequence of (not) controlling variables, making fair testing a felt procedure. The live 'fairness meter' and automatic measured outcomes are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they support, but do not replace, hands-on testing with real materials.
sourceClaims: Common working-scientifically errors: uncontrolled variables making a test unfair, changing more than one variable, concluding from belief rather than data.
learnerActions: Choose a question for a test bench, e.g. most waterproof fabric, strongest bag material, or best cup insulator.
Set each variable yourself: deliberately leave sample sizes or amounts uneven first and see what happens.

Watch an optional 'fairness meter' flag the setup red when more than one variable differs, then fix it — lock every sample to the same size and apply the same measured input — and watch it turn green.
Run the test and read the comparable measured result for each material (ml through, mass held before tearing, or °C lost) collected into a table.

Use a sentence builder to complete a claim–evidence–reasoning conclusion from the data, e.g. 'Nylon was the most waterproof BECAUSE only 2 ml passed through it, less than through any other material we tested.'
activities.intendedInsight: Controlling variables is what turns a comparison from unfair to trustworthy; only a controlled test yields a clean number you can reason from.

activities.title: Spot the unfair test and sort the variables (consolidation/check)
feedback: For a wrong 'fair test' choice, point to the variable left uncontrolled: 'both squares must be the same size or the comparison proves nothing.'
If a variable is mis-sorted, re-ask which single thing is deliberately different between the materials (the one changed) versus what is read off (the one measured).
Note that getting the right material for the wrong reason (e.g. by belief) still fails the goal: the justification must cite a tested property.
activities.rationale: Recognition and categorisation tasks are efficient for checking understanding of the fair-test structure and for consolidating vocabulary. They can verify knowledge about fair testing but do not themselves elicit the child running and controlling a test, so they belong alongside, not instead of, a run-and-measure activity.
sourceClaims: Common working-scientifically errors: uncontrolled variables making a test unfair, changing more than one variable, concluding from belief rather than data.
learnerActions: Decide 'Which test is fair?' between options, including one unfair option where a variable is left uncontrolled, and say what makes the unfair one invalid.
Sort variables into three buckets: the one to change (the material), the one to measure (the outcome), and those to keep the same.
Put the steps of an enquiry into order: question → change one thing → measure → record → conclude from the data.
Match materials to evidence-based uses, justifying each match with a tested property.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising fair vs unfair tests and classifying variables consolidates the structure of a controlled comparison and the habit of concluding from evidence.

activities.title: Label the parts of a fair test (structure reference)
feedback: If a child confuses the changed and measured variables, restate: the material is the one thing we choose to change; the outcome is what we read off to compare.
Use the sample results table to show that 'best' is decided by the recorded numbers, not by appearance.
activities.rationale: A labelled worked example consolidates the structure and gives a reference for the claim–evidence–reasoning sentence. It is a static scaffold: it cannot let the child manipulate variables or generate data, so it should precede or support the hands-on and simulated activities rather than stand alone.
learnerActions: Study an annotated fair-test diagram and identify the changed variable, the controlled variables, and the measured outcome.
Reveal each element's role (why it is changed, controlled, or measured).
Reveal a finished results table and read off how the winning material is identified from the numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: A fair test has distinct parts — one changed variable, several controlled variables, and one measured outcome — that together make a comparison trustworthy.

activities.title: A character sets the design brief (optional framing)
feedback: If the plan changes more than one thing, remind the child that only the material should differ so the result can be attributed to it.
Check the plan names a measurable outcome before any testing begins.
activities.rationale: Dialogue can motivate and frame the problem with a real purpose, but on its own it does not deliver the manipulation or the measured data this procedural objective requires. It is a framing device that should hand off to an activity where the child actually controls variables and measures an outcome.
learnerActions: Receive a decision-worthy design brief from a character, e.g. 'Help me pick the best material for a lunchbox / umbrella / cup cosy.'
Restate the brief as a testable question and plan what to change, measure, and keep the same before moving to a real or simulated test.
activities.intendedInsight: A genuine, purposeful question gives the test a reason to exist and clarifies what counts as 'best'.

constraints: The core objective requires the child to plan, control variables, measure a comparable outcome, and state an evidence-based conclusion — recognition-only tasks (multiple choice, sorting, labelling) can check understanding but do not elicit this independent construction and must not replace a run-and-measure activity.
A real bench with actual materials and a measuring jug is the intended hands-on experience; the simulation is a complementary scaffold, not a substitute.

The 'fairness meter', live red/green feedback, drag-to-set variables, and automatic measured outputs are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory mechanisms.
The labelled diagram is a static reference: it cannot let the child manipulate variables or generate evidence, so use it to consolidate structure, not to teach the procedure.
Dialogue framing can pose the brief but does not on its own supply the manipulation or data; it must hand off to doing and measuring.
Conclusions must cite the measured data ('...because in our test...'), not prior belief; engineer or allow surprising outcomes so children practise trusting evidence over expectation.
Use a genuinely decision-worthy question (lunchbox / umbrella / cup cosy) so controlling variables has a real purpose.
Introduce reliability lightly (repeat a trial, note odd results); do not overstate certainty from a single trial.
Include a transfer check (e.g. whether the waterproofing test also shows which coat is warmest) so the child ties the conclusion to the specific property tested, not to the material in general.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source efficacy and comparative claims are not re-checked here. One legacy source (STEM Learning misconceptions) was marked unverified in the original row; its claim is retained only as a general pedagogy principle, not as established evidence.

The original row asserted that 3D 'adds no conceptual value' and that a quiz 'verifies rather than builds' the procedure. These have been softened: the task is procedural and data-driven, so a clear 2D or physical bench is sufficient, but no universal claim of 3D's uselessness is made; recognition tasks are described by their objective limit (they do not elicit independent construction) rather than by a blanket ranking.

Measured example values (e.g. '2 ml passed through') are illustrative placeholders; actual results depend on materials, water volume, and setup and should come from the child's real measurements, not be pre-stated as outcomes.

The example uses nylon as the winning fabric to match the original recommendation; the original assessment used 'plastic' — either is acceptable, provided the conclusion is read from the child's own data rather than fixed in advance.

probeDeeper: What did you keep the same for all three materials? Why does that matter?
If someone said your test wasn't fair, what would they point to?
Your result surprised you — do you trust the test or your first guess, and why?
Would this same test also tell us which coat is warmest? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Pours the SAME amount of water on equal pieces held the same way for the same time, catches/observes what soaks through, and concludes plastic is most waterproof CITING the result ('least water got through') tied to the real use (a raincoat).

errorPatterns.pattern: Unfair test — changes more than one thing at once (different amounts of water, different-sized pieces, different times) so the comparison proves nothing.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with a 'what did we keep the same?' checklist and re-run; the fair-test procedure needs anchoring, not the concept of properties.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot say what was kept the same; several variables differ between the materials.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conclusion asserted from prior belief, not evidence — decides 'plastic wins' before testing and ignores a surprising result.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hide the material labels or engineer a surprising outcome, and insist the claim quote the measured result ('the tray under the paper had the most water').
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States the answer before or regardless of the data; explains away a result that disagrees.

errorPatterns.pattern: Measures the wrong thing or nothing — judges 'best' by how a material looks or feels rather than by an outcome.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Agree BEFORE running what will be measured (how much water reaches the tray beneath) so the result is an observation, not an impression.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No quantity or observation recorded; 'this one looks the most waterproof'.

responseLevels.gap: 'Tests' by guessing or a single look; changes several things at once; concludes from prior belief.
responseLevels.full: Controls the key variables, measures an outcome, and gives an evidence-based reason linking the tested property to the real-world use — transferring the fair-test logic to a new property.
responseLevels.partial: Runs a comparison and reaches a sensible conclusion, but leaves a variable uncontrolled or doesn't tie the result explicitly to the use.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'You want to find which material makes the best rainy-day coat: cotton, plastic or paper. Set up a test to compare how waterproof they are. Show me how you keep it FAIR, how you'll measure, then tell me which to use and why.' Watch the whole thing, don't coach.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching exposes whether the child controls variables — the heart of a fair test — or changes several things at once, and whether the conclusion is drawn from the measured RESULT or asserted from prior belief. A child who 'already knows plastic wins' can run an unfair test and still name the right material for the wrong reason; the process, not the answer, is the evidence.

pedagogy.summary: This is the shared LANGUAGE of geometric diagrams: a small square means exactly 90°, single and double tick marks mean 'these lengths are equal to each other' (a second, independent equal pair uses double ticks), matching arc marks mean equal angles, arrows mean parallel, and three-letter notation ∠ABC names the angle whose vertex is the MIDDLE letter, B. Fluency is two-way — reading a marked diagram to extract the given information, and producing correct marks when drawing. Crucially the marks encode relationships that are NOT to be read from the picture's appearance: a geometric diagram is a carrier of stated facts, not a scale drawing.
bestPractices: Teach each mark as a statement of a relationship — a tick pair asserts equal lengths, an arc pair asserts equal angles, a square asserts 90° — true regardless of how the picture looks.
Drill the three-letter rule with the vertex in the middle: ∠ABC is the angle at B; point to B first, then trace the two arms BA and BC.
Practise both directions: read a marked diagram aloud ('these two sides are equal, this angle is a right angle') AND mark up a plain diagram to encode given facts.
Stress 'not to scale' — use diagrams whose appearance contradicts the marks so pupils learn to trust the marks over the drawing.
Use double ticks for a second, different pair of equal lengths so pupils see that single versus double distinguishes independent equalities.
keyRepresentations: The mark key: small square = 90°, single/double ticks = equal lengths, single/double arcs = equal angles, arrows = parallel
A triangle or quadrilateral fully marked up and read as a set of statements
∠ABC with B highlighted as the vertex and BA, BC as the arms
A deliberately 'not to scale' diagram whose marks override its look
commonMisconceptions: Reads ∠ABC as the angle at the first (or last) letter rather than the middle letter (the vertex)
Reads tick marks as a measurement or length value rather than 'equal to each other', or treats single and double ticks as equal to one another
Treats the marks as decoration and judges lengths, angles and right angles from the diagram's appearance (assumes it is drawn to scale)
Thinks the small square is just 'a corner' rather than exactly 90°, or misses that unmarked features are unknown

learn.summary: Teach the shared language of geometric diagram markings as statements of relationships, not pictures: a small square asserts exactly 90°, a matching pair of single tick marks asserts 'these two lengths are equal to each other', a second independent equal pair uses double ticks, matching arc marks assert equal angles, and arrows assert parallel lines. Three-letter notation ∠ABC names the angle whose vertex is the MIDDLE letter (B), with arms BA and BC. Fluency runs in two directions — reading a marked diagram to extract the given facts, and adding correct marks when drawing. Critically, a geometric diagram carries stated facts and is not a scale drawing: the marks override the picture's appearance.

activities.title: Mark up a plain figure, then read a 'not to scale' one
feedback: If the learner labels ∠ABC using an arm letter (A or C), rehearse the rule: the middle letter is always the vertex — point to B first, then trace arms BA and BC. An optional interactive can light up the wrong angle when the wrong letter is tapped, making the mismatch visible.

If the learner reads a ticked side as a measurement (e.g. '1 unit') or treats a single-ticked and double-ticked side as equal, restate each mark as a relationship within its own pair and show that double ticks mark a separate, independent equal pair.
If the learner calls a marked-equal pair unequal because one looks longer, insist the marks are the authority on a not-to-scale diagram.

When producing a diagram, check that every stated fact carries its mark and that equal marks are never left on just one side — a stated right angle needs a square, and equal sides need matching ticks on EVERY side in the equal group (both sides of a pair, or all sides if more than two are equal).
activities.rationale: The topic requires fluency in both reading and producing marks, so an activity that has the learner construct marks on a plain four-sided figure and then interpret a not-to-scale marked figure is intended to exercise both directions. A quadrilateral is used for the marking step so the single-tick pair and the independent double-tick pair can both be shown. Using appearance-contradicting diagrams targets the documented error of judging a figure by its look rather than its marked givens. (Proposed design; not empirically validated here.)
sourceClaims: Pupils use conventional markings for parallel lines and right angles (Year 5) and conventional markings and labels for lines and angles (Year 6); at KS3 they describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations for points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines and right angles, and use the standard conventions for labelling the sides and angles of triangle ABC. Misreading these conventions (e.g. the ∠ABC vertex or a tick pair) is therefore a violation of an explicitly stated convention.

A common misconception is trying to MEASURE angles on a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'When the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure the missing angles using a protractor. We need to use angle facts to calculate the missing angle.' The page also lists 'pairing up the incorrect angles in an isosceles triangle' as a common error — both cases of judging a diagram by its appearance rather than its stated/marked information.

Pupils frequently infer that a triangle is isosceles (and pair up 'equal' base angles) from how the diagram LOOKS rather than from the tick/arc markings — a documented children's-ideas error of trusting appearance over the marks that carry the given information.

Students with an accurate conception of angle read the additivity of angle measure from a diagram and solve for unknown angles using the MARKED given information (right angles and benchmark angles are marked in diagrams), i.e. the marks are the authoritative carriers of the givens.
learnerActions: Starting from a plain quadrilateral (a four-sided figure gives room to show two independent equal-side pairs without overlap), add a small square to the corner stated to be right-angled.

Add a single pair of tick marks to one pair of sides stated to be equal, and a double pair of ticks to a different, independent pair of equal sides — a four-sided figure is needed so the two pairs do not share a side.
Label a stated angle in three-letter notation by identifying its vertex: point to the vertex B first, then trace the two arms BA and BC, so the middle letter B names the angle ∠ABC.
Switch to reading: on a deliberately not-to-scale marked diagram where one side LOOKS longer but carries the matching tick, state which sides are equal from the marks, not the picture.
State aloud what each mark means as a relationship (e.g. 'these two sides are equal to each other', 'this angle is exactly 90°').
activities.intendedInsight: The marks, not the drawing, tell you the truth about a diagram, and the middle letter of three-letter notation is always the vertex.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal the mark key (reading scaffold)
feedback: Confirm correct readings; where the learner's prediction differs from the reveal, name the relationship the mark asserts.
Highlighting the equal sides together reinforces that ticks mean 'equal to each other', not a measurement value.
activities.rationale: Reading conventional markings correctly is an explicit curriculum requirement, and misreading them is a convention violation; a reveal-based tool is intended to build the interpretation half of the skill by linking each symbol to a highlighted feature. It is a scaffold: it supports reading marks but does not ask the learner to produce marks, so it must be paired with construction practice. Its instructional effect is proposed, not empirically validated here.
sourceClaims: Pupils use conventional markings for parallel lines and right angles (Year 5) and conventional markings and labels for lines and angles (Year 6); at KS3 they describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations for points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines and right angles, and use the standard conventions for labelling the sides and angles of triangle ABC. Misreading these conventions (e.g. the ∠ABC vertex or a tick pair) is therefore a violation of an explicitly stated convention.
learnerActions: Tap the small square to reveal 'this angle is exactly 90°'.
Tap a tick pair and see the two equal sides highlight together.
Tap ∠ABC and see the vertex B with its arms BA and BC light up.
Say each meaning aloud before revealing it, then check against the reveal.
activities.intendedInsight: Each symbol in the mark key encodes a specific relationship that can be read off a diagram reliably.

activities.title: Match and select: check interpretation and light production
feedback: If the learner selects the angle at A for ∠ABC, re-state the middle-letter rule and have them trace arms BA and BC from B.
If a single-ticked and double-ticked side are matched as equal, clarify that double ticks denote a separate, independent equal pair.
Choosing 'the angle at point A' for ∠ABC reveals the middle-letter misread; redirect to the vertex B.
activities.rationale: Selection and matching tasks are intended to check interpretation and limited production, and the ∠ABC item specifically targets the middle-letter misconception that source 1 identifies as a convention violation. Recognition tasks are efficient checks but do not require the learner to construct a full marked diagram, so they complement rather than replace hands-on marking.
sourceClaims: Pupils use conventional markings for parallel lines and right angles (Year 5) and conventional markings and labels for lines and angles (Year 6); at KS3 they describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations for points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines and right angles, and use the standard conventions for labelling the sides and angles of triangle ABC. Misreading these conventions (e.g. the ∠ABC vertex or a tick pair) is therefore a violation of an explicitly stated convention.
learnerActions: Answer 'Which angle is ∠ABC?' by selecting the angle at vertex B, not the angle at A or C.
Match each mark (square, single tick pair, double tick pair, arc pair, arrows) to its meaning.
Mark the equal sides on a figure by selecting/drawing the pair that carries matching ticks.
On a not-to-scale item, identify equal sides from the marks even when one side looks longer.
activities.intendedInsight: Both interpreting marks and identifying where marks belong can be checked explicitly, including the middle-letter vertex rule.

activities.title: Probe diagram authority and unmarked features
feedback: Reinforce that two equally-ticked sides are equal regardless of apparent length.
∠BCA has vertex C, so it is a different angle from ∠ABC (vertex B).
If the learner assumes an unmarked corner is a right angle because it looks square, point out that only a drawn square asserts 90°; unmarked features are unknown.
activities.rationale: These prompts target the specific misconceptions of trusting appearance, misplacing the vertex, confusing single/double ticks, and assuming unmarked features. Reasoning about what the diagram does and does not state is intended to deepen the 'marks over appearance' principle.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is trying to MEASURE angles on a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'When the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure the missing angles using a protractor. We need to use angle facts to calculate the missing angle.' The page also lists 'pairing up the incorrect angles in an isosceles triangle' as a common error — both cases of judging a diagram by its appearance rather than its stated/marked information.

Pupils frequently infer that a triangle is isosceles (and pair up 'equal' base angles) from how the diagram LOOKS rather than from the tick/arc markings — a documented children's-ideas error of trusting appearance over the marks that carry the given information.
learnerActions: Answer: 'This side LOOKS longer than that one, but both carry a single tick — which is actually longer?' (Answer: they are equal.)
Show ∠BCA on the same diagram and decide whether it is the same as ∠ABC or a different angle.
Decide what mark to add for a second pair of equal sides so no one confuses it with the first pair (double ticks).
Answer: 'This corner has no square drawn on it — can you be sure it's a right angle? How would the diagram tell you?' (You cannot assume it; unmarked features are unknown.)
activities.intendedInsight: Marks are authoritative, three-letter names with different middle letters (vertices) denote different angles (though reversing the outer letters, as in ∠ABC and ∠CBA, names the same angle), and an unmarked feature is not a stated fact.

constraints: Cover BOTH directions: reading marked diagrams AND producing marks when drawing. A reading-only reveal tool is a scaffold and does not assess production; pair it with construction tasks.

Recognition and matching tasks check interpretation and light production but do not require constructing a complete marked diagram, so include a production task where the learner draws the square and adds matching ticks in pairs.
Use deliberately not-to-scale diagrams whose appearance contradicts the marks so learners practise trusting the marks over the picture.

Always add equal marks to every member of an equal group, so at least two sides are marked and never just one (e.g. both sides of an equal pair, or all three sides of an equilateral triangle); a stated right angle must carry a drawn square; unmarked features must be treated as unknown.

Reserve double ticks for a second, independent equal pair, and make clear single- and double-ticked sides are NOT equal to each other. Demonstrating two independent equal-side pairs needs a figure with at least four sides (a quadrilateral), not a triangle.

This notation is a convention of 2-D diagrams; a 3-D environment is not required for this objective. Paper-and-pencil marking is an acceptable medium for the production half alongside any interactive tool.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and their efficacy wording is intended/proposed only.

The original row's recommendation described marking two independent equal-side pairs on a TRIANGLE; a triangle has only three sides, so two disjoint equal pairs cannot both be marked. Corrected to a quadrilateral for the marking step so the single- and double-tick pairs are coherent. Logged as an original-row error.

The legacy row claimed a 3-D environment 'has nothing to add' and that open dialogue cannot deliver this skill. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; softened to narrowly scoped notes that 2-D marking (including on paper) suffices for this objective and that spoken discussion can support reasoning about marks even if it is not the primary production medium.

Self-audit: verified that ∠ABC has vertex B (middle letter) and ∠BCA has vertex C (a different angle) — consistent throughout. Verified that matching single ticks mean equal lengths and that single vs double ticks denote distinct independent pairs, with single- and double-ticked sides NOT equal to each other. No arithmetic claims present.

Source 1 is cited in the reading/matching activities only to support the convention-reading principle and the fact that misreading a convention is a violation; it is not evidence that any particular interaction format is effective.

probeDeeper: This side LOOKS longer than that one, but they both have a single tick — which is actually longer?
Show me ∠BCA on the same diagram — is that the same angle as ∠ABC or a different one?
If I add a second pair of equal sides, what mark should I use so no one confuses them with the first pair?
This corner has no square drawn on it — can you be sure it's a right angle? How would the diagram tell you?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the small square as 'this angle is exactly 90°', the tick marks as 'these two sides are equal in length', and identifies ∠ABC as the angle at vertex B (the middle letter); and on the plain diagram draws a small square in a corner to denote 90° and adds a matching pair of tick marks to two sides to denote equal lengths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads ∠ABC as the angle at A (or C) instead of the vertex B ('ABC, so it's at A')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the rule explicit and rehearse it — the middle letter is always the vertex; point to it first, then trace the two arms.
errorPatterns.distractor: The angle at point A
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to the wrong vertex for ∠ABC, or names an angle using an arm letter rather than the vertex letter

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads tick marks as a measurement or length value, or treats single- and double-ticked sides as equal to each other, rather than 'equal within their own pair'
errorPatterns.nextMove: State each mark as a relationship ('these two are equal to each other') and use double ticks for a separate, independent equal pair.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a ticked side is '1 unit', or claims a single-ticked and a double-ticked side are equal

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the marks and judges lengths, angles and right angles from how the diagram looks (assumes it is drawn to scale)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use deliberately not-to-scale diagrams where the marks contradict the appearance, and insist the marks are the authority.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a not-to-scale diagram, calls a marked-equal pair unequal because one looks longer, or calls an unmarked corner a right angle because it looks square

errorPatterns.pattern: When drawing, omits or misplaces the marks — states a right angle but adds no square, or ticks only one side of an equal pair
errorPatterns.nextMove: Check that each stated fact carries its mark, and that equal marks are added in pairs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The produced diagram does not encode the stated facts (missing square, a single tick on only one side)

responseLevels.gap: Judges lengths, angles and right angles from the diagram's appearance; misreads the vertex in ∠ABC; treats marks as decoration or as measurements.
responseLevels.full: Reads a marked diagram as a coherent set of stated relationships (trusting the marks over appearance), identifies ∠ABC by its middle-letter vertex, and produces diagrams that correctly encode given facts with square, tick and arc marks, transferring to a new figure (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Reads individual marks correctly in isolation (a square = 90°, a tick pair = equal) but misplaces the vertex in three-letter notation, is swayed by appearance on a not-to-scale diagram, or omits marks when producing a diagram (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a triangle marked with a small square at one corner, single tick marks on two of its sides, and one angle named ∠ABC. First (read): 'What does the small square tell you? What do the tick marks tell you? Which angle is ∠ABC — point to it.' Then (produce): 'On this second plain diagram, mark a right angle with the correct symbol, and show that two of its sides are equal in length.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking the child both to READ the marks and to PRODUCE them catches the pupil who can recite a meaning but mislabels the vertex or marks equal lengths as measurements. The ∠ABC item specifically catches the middle-letter misread, and requiring production (draw one) is the interpret-translate discriminator — recognition alone hides the gap.
