pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 12–14; Hazard Assessment & Evacuation (CONCEPTUAL, META/decision-under-uncertainty): probabilistic hazard assessment (eruption recurrence intervals, fault slip rates); how observatories monitor deformation/gas/seismicity to set alert levels; WHY communities stay near hazards (fertile volcanic soil, poverty, cultural/ancestral ties); and the ethics, politics and SOCIAL-JUSTICE dimensions of who bears risk and who decides to evacuate.
• Standards — UK (DfE): the science of hazards/monitoring links KS3 (Earth structure, waves); the risk/vulnerability/social-justice dimension is cross-curricular — KS3 Geography (natural hazards, why people live in risky places, responses) and Citizenship/PSHE. Not a KS3 science-only topic. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS, ANCHOR): MS-ESS3-2 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2]' — clarification (VERIFIED verbatim): some hazards (volcanic eruptions, severe weather) are preceded by phenomena allowing reliable predictions, but earthquakes 'occur suddenly and with no notice, and thus are not yet predictable'; data can include locations, magnitudes, and frequencies. DCI ESS3.B (mapping hazard history to forecast; mitigation) is knowledge-based here (verified:false). Builds on 4-ESS3-2 (VERIFIED earlier) generate-and-compare mitigation solutions.
• Operational details — TWO intertwined payloads. (1) QUANTITATIVE: probability is not prediction — recurrence intervals and slip rates give a likelihood/return period, not a date; a '1-in-100-year' event can happen next year; alert levels translate monitoring data into staged decisions. Be precise that volcanoes often give warning signs while earthquakes do NOT (per MS-ESS3-2). (2) HUMAN/ETHICAL: evacuation is a decision under uncertainty with real costs — a false alarm has economic and trust costs; a missed evacuation costs lives; people stay for rational reasons (livelihood, poverty, culture), and disaster risk falls unequally (social justice). Prerequisite assumed: Earthquake-Resistant Design (mitigation framing). This topic feeds Supervolcanoes and Mass Extinctions (scaling the assessment up).
• Checkpoint — Tier C (formal/model-based + reasoned judgement): given monitoring data and a probabilistic assessment, the child WEIGHS an evacuation decision — distinguishing probability from certainty, articulating the cost asymmetry of false-alarm vs missed-warning, and accounting for WHY people stay and who bears the risk — reaching a justified position rather than a single 'correct' answer.
bestPractices: Separate probability from prediction explicitly: a recurrence interval / slip rate gives a likelihood or return period, NOT a date — practise reading '1-in-N-year' correctly (it does not mean 'safe for N years').
Use MS-ESS3-2's own distinction: volcanoes and severe weather usually give precursors (so alerts are possible), earthquakes strike without notice (so preparedness, not prediction, is the defence).
Teach the decision as a cost-asymmetry problem: false alarm (economic loss, eroded trust, 'cry wolf') vs missed warning (deaths) — there is no cost-free choice, only trade-offs.

Take the 'why do people stay?' question seriously and non-judgementally: fertile soil and livelihoods, poverty and lack of alternatives, deep cultural/ancestral ties — staying is often rational, not ignorant.

Foreground social justice: vulnerability is unequally distributed; the poorest and most marginalised typically bear the greatest disaster risk and have the fewest options — use real cases to make this concrete.

Ground it in authentic decisions and roles (observatory scientist, mayor, resident, aid agency) so students reason WITH the uncertainty and the human stakes rather than treating hazard as a purely technical problem.
keyRepresentations: Recurrence-interval / probability timeline: return periods and the (mis)reading of '1-in-100-year' — the core quantitative literacy rep.
Alert-level ladder (e.g. green→yellow→orange→red) mapping monitoring signals (deformation, gas, seismicity) to staged actions.
Decision matrix of the evacuation call: rows = evacuate / don't, columns = eruption happens / doesn't, cells = the four outcomes and their (asymmetric) costs.
Vulnerability map: overlay of hazard zone with population, poverty, and infrastructure — showing risk = hazard × exposure × vulnerability, not hazard alone.
Stakeholder panel: scientist / official / resident / aid worker viewpoints on the same evacuation call, exposing the value conflicts.
commonMisconceptions: 'Scientists can predict exactly when a volcano/earthquake will strike.' — Assessment yields probabilities and (for volcanoes) precursor-based alerts; earthquakes are not yet predictable — probability is not a date.
'A 1-in-100-year event won't happen for 100 years / just happened so we're safe.' — Return periods are long-run averages; the event can occur in any year, including consecutive years.
'People who live in hazard zones are just ignorant or foolish.' — They usually stay for rational reasons (livelihood, poverty, culture); dismissing this misreads the whole risk problem.
'The safe choice is always to evacuate.' — Evacuation has real costs (economic, health, trust); false alarms erode compliance with future warnings — the decision is a genuine trade-off.
'Natural disasters affect everyone equally.' — Risk is socially uneven; the poorest and most marginalised bear disproportionate exposure and have the fewest means to prepare or recover.
'Monitoring/technology removes the risk.' — It reduces and informs, but cannot eliminate uncertainty; decisions must still be made without knowing the outcome.

learn.summary: For ages 12–14, this topic teaches hazard assessment and evacuation as a judgement under uncertainty with competing human values. Two intertwined payloads: (1) a quantitative strand — probability is not prediction: recurrence intervals and fault slip rates give a likelihood or return period, not a date; observatories translate ground deformation, gas emissions and seismicity into staged alert levels; volcanoes and severe weather usually give precursors (so alerts are possible) while earthquakes strike without notice; and (2) a human/ethical strand — evacuation carries asymmetric costs (a false alarm brings economic loss and eroded trust; a missed warning costs lives), people stay near hazards for rational reasons (livelihood, poverty, culture), and disaster risk falls unequally. The core activity is an in-role deliberation reaching a defensible position rather than a single correct answer, supported by quantitative risk-literacy practice.

activities.title: The evacuation call: reasoning in role under uncertainty
feedback: If the learner treats the decision as having a single correct answer, probe: 'What would change if you had to answer to the 40,000 people either way?'

If the learner dismisses residents as ignorant or foolish, redirect: 'What rational reasons might someone have to stay — livelihood, poverty, ancestral ties? Does staying make the risk their own fault?'
If the learner says the safe choice is always to evacuate, ask them to name who bears the cost of a false alarm versus a missed warning, and whether those are the same people.
If the learner speaks as if the scientist can predict the eruption, prompt them to restate the data as a probability with warning signs, not a prediction of when.

If the learner judges a false-alarm outcome as proof the scientists failed, separate the quality of a decision from its luck: a sound call given the available information can still be followed by no eruption.
activities.rationale: The defining payload is weighing evidence and competing values with no single correct answer. An open, unscripted dialogue affords interactive probing and lets the learner articulate and defend a position in real time — an observable affordance a static artefact lacks — though this reflects catalog fit rather than demonstrated comparative efficacy, so other media are not claimed to be incapable of building the skill. The MS-ESS3-2 distinction (volcanoes forewarned, earthquakes sudden) and the socially uneven nature of disaster risk give the role-play its authentic content.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS3-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2].' Clarification: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2] allowing reliable predictions, but earthquakes occur suddenly with no notice and are not yet predictable; data can include locations, magnitudes, and frequencies.

Disaster risk is socially uneven (risk = hazard × exposure × vulnerability); communities stay near hazards for fertile soil, livelihood, poverty, and cultural ties; evacuation decisions carry asymmetric false-alarm vs missed-warning costs.
learnerActions: Take the role of a volcano-observatory scientist briefing a mayor: the monitoring data is ambiguous — gas emissions and tremor are rising, but could fizzle out. State out loud whether to recommend evacuation and justify it.

Respond when the mayor presses back in role: 'If I evacuate 40,000 people and nothing happens, I've wrecked the harvest, cost millions, and no one will believe the next warning — are you sure?' Articulate that this is a probability, not a prophecy.
Face a lifelong resident who refuses to leave — this volcanic soil feeds their family and their grandparents are buried here. Engage their reasons seriously rather than dismissing them.
Hear an aid worker point out that it is usually the poorest, with nowhere to go, who die; factor equity into the position you defend.
Weigh the false-alarm cost (economic loss, eroded trust, 'cry wolf') against the missed-warning cost (lives) explicitly, naming that there is no cost-free choice.
Reach and defend a justified position, acknowledging you might be wrong either way.
activities.intendedInsight: Hazard assessment is not a calculation that outputs an answer; it is a judgement made under irreducible uncertainty, shaped by fairness and human stakes. One can make a good decision given the available information and still have an unlucky outcome.

activities.title: Risk dashboard: probability is not prediction
feedback: If the learner assumes a '1-in-100-year' event is 'safe for 100 years' or 'overdue' after 100 years, point to the repeated-trial tally: the event can appear in any run, including consecutive ones.
If the learner picks an alert level that ignores rising precursors, ask which monitoring signal they relied on and what it implies for staged action.
If the learner reads a false-alarm run as proof the scientists failed, revisit the tally: judge the policy over many runs, not one outcome.
activities.rationale: A simulation with repeated trials can model the numbers and the cost asymmetry so the probability-not-prediction lesson may land statistically; it is intended to pair with the dialogue rather than replace it, because reducing the ethical and social-justice deliberation to a payoff score would misrepresent the part that should not be a single number.
sourceClaims: Probabilistic hazard assessment uses recurrence intervals and fault slip rates to express likelihood/return period (not a date); observatories translate deformation, gas and seismicity into staged alert levels.

MS-ESS3-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2].' Clarification: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2] allowing reliable predictions, but earthquakes occur suddenly with no notice and are not yet predictable; data can include locations, magnitudes, and frequencies.
learnerActions: Read a recurrence-interval / probability readout and a set of monitoring signals (deformation, gas, seismicity) that climb over time.
Set an alert level (e.g. green → yellow → orange → red) by mapping the monitoring signals to staged actions.
Make an evacuation call, then see a simulated outcome reveal whether the event actually came that run.
Repeat the call across many runs and watch a running tally accumulate false alarms versus missed warnings, so the cost asymmetry is felt statistically rather than argued abstractly.
Toggle a vulnerability-map overlay (hazard zone with population, poverty and infrastructure) to see that exposure and vulnerability, not hazard alone, shape who is at risk.
activities.intendedInsight: A '1-in-100-year' figure is a long-run average and an annual likelihood, not a countdown; with imperfect prediction and the same monitoring information, lowering the alert threshold to cut missed warnings raises false alarms, and raising it does the reverse, so the best alert policy manages their asymmetric costs (better monitoring can reduce both, but not to zero).

activities.title: Reading the probability and the alert ladder (factual check)
feedback: For the gambler's-fallacy answer ('overdue, so much more likely now'), use a coin-flip analogy: within this lesson's constant-annual-chance model, a run of tails doesn't make heads 'due'; a recurrence interval averages many unequal gaps, not a timer. (Some real fault models do let probability change with elapsed time, so this is a modelling simplification.)

For 'a 1-in-100 chance is so small it basically won't happen', separate probability from consequence: risk needs both, and compounding a small annual chance over a lifetime shows why preparing is rational.
For confusion between hazards, restate that eruptions and severe weather are often forewarned while earthquakes are not yet predictable, so earthquake defence is preparedness, not a date.
activities.rationale: A scored factual check suits misconception-critical knowledge (probability reading, signal-to-alert mapping, the volcano-vs-earthquake distinction), but it should stay on the factual layer; scoring the 'should you evacuate?' judgement would wrongly imply a single right answer, so that judgement belongs to the dialogue.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS3-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2].' Clarification: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2] allowing reliable predictions, but earthquakes occur suddenly with no notice and are not yet predictable; data can include locations, magnitudes, and frequencies.

Probabilistic hazard assessment uses recurrence intervals and fault slip rates to express likelihood/return period (not a date); observatories translate deformation, gas and seismicity into staged alert levels.
learnerActions: Interpret statements like 'a 1-in-100 chance each year': decide whether elapsed time since the last event raises this year's chance. As a modelling assumption for this probability-literacy lesson, treat the annual chance as roughly constant and independent of elapsed time, so it does not rise simply because time has passed.
Match monitoring signals (ground deformation, gas, seismicity) to the appropriate alert level on the ladder.

Identify which hazards usually give precursors (volcanoes, severe weather) versus which strike without notice (earthquakes), and state the consequence for how each is managed (forecasting and alerts plus preparedness vs preparedness alone).
Use a tap-to-reveal vulnerability map or alert-level ladder as a reference for what each alert level means and what makes a community vulnerable.
activities.intendedInsight: Core probability literacy and monitoring facts underpin the judgement work: a return period is an average, not a schedule, and alert levels are a translation of data into staged action.

constraints: Separate probability from prediction explicitly: a recurrence interval or slip rate gives a likelihood or return period, not a date; '1-in-N-year' does not mean 'safe for N years'.

Treat each year's probability as roughly constant and independent of elapsed time as a modelling assumption for the probability-literacy lesson; the event is not 'saving up' and is not made more likely simply because time has passed. (Real geophysical hazards can show clustering and stress transfer, so independence is a simplification, not a physical law.)
Risk combines probability with consequence: a low annual probability is not negligible when the consequence is severe, so preparation can be rational even at low odds.

Use the MS-ESS3-2 distinction: volcanoes and severe weather usually give precursors (alerts possible), earthquakes strike without notice (preparedness, not prediction, is the defence). This verbatim clarification is a verified source; the broader mapping-to-forecast DCI detail was recorded as not re-verified.
Take 'why do people stay?' seriously and non-judgementally — fertile soil, livelihoods, poverty, cultural and ancestral ties — rather than framing residents as ignorant.
Foreground that disaster risk is socially uneven: the poorest and most marginalised typically bear the greatest exposure and have the fewest options; use real cases where possible.

The evacuation judgement should NOT be scored as if there is one correct answer; keep scoring to the factual probability-and-monitoring layer. The outcome of the dialogue is a defensible justified position.
A static vulnerability map or alert ladder is a useful reference for the components but does not by itself exercise the decision-making; use it to support, not replace, the deliberation.

The simulated repeated-trial tally and vulnerability overlay are illustrative mechanisms to make probability and exposure concrete; they are optional and should not flatten the ethical deliberation into a payoff score.
A good decision made under uncertainty can be followed by an unlucky outcome; judge warnings by the information available at the time, not solely by what happened afterwards.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four source claims (observatory/recurrence-interval mechanics; social-unevenness of risk and asymmetric evacuation costs) are marked verified:false in the row and attributed to material not fetched this session; treat the specific monitoring and disaster-risk details as unverified.
The MS-ESS3-2 clarification text is marked verified in the source; the DCI ESS3.B mapping-to-forecast detail was recorded as knowledge-based (verified:false).

The original diagnostic framing ('about a 1-in-100 chance each year, and on average erupts roughly every 100 years') is internally consistent, but learners may conflate the annual probability with the average interval; keep the two framings distinct when posing such prompts.

The source asserts individual years are 'roughly independent'; for real geophysical hazards this is a simplification (clustering and stress transfer can occur), so present independence as a modelling assumption for the probability-literacy lesson rather than a physical law. This qualification is also surfaced in the relevant activity and constraint, not only here.

Claims that an open dialogue is 'uniquely able' to teach the judgement and that a fixed artefact 'cannot' build the skill reflect catalog fit ranking, not established comparative efficacy; these have been reduced to affordance-based phrasing (interactive probing/real-time defence) without asserting other media are incapable.

Activity 1's intended insight was tightened: the trade-off (not the simultaneous occurrence of both error types) is what cannot be escaped under imperfect prediction, since an always-evacuate or never-evacuate policy eliminates one error type at the cost of inflating the other.

probeDeeper: Why might people keep living right beside an active volcano even after they understand the risk — and does that make the risk 'their own fault'?
An official orders an evacuation and the eruption never comes. Was that a bad decision? How would you judge it without knowing the future?
Earthquakes still can't be predicted to a day, but eruptions often give warning signs. What's the difference, and why does it change how each hazard is managed?
Who bears the cost of a false alarm, and who bears the cost of a missed warning — are they the same people?
assess.correctAnswer: The newspaper is wrong. A 1-in-100 annual chance is a probability, not a countdown — the volcano is not 'saving up' an eruption, and this year's risk is still about 1-in-100 no matter how long it has been. 'Every 100 years on average' is a long-run average across many unequal gaps, not a due date; each year is roughly independent.

errorPatterns.pattern: It's been 100 years, so the eruption is 'overdue' and much more likely now ('it's been building up / saving up').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a coin-flip analogy — a run of tails doesn't make heads 'due'; a recurrence interval is an average of many unequal gaps, not a timer.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — 100 years have passed, so a big eruption is overdue and very likely this year.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the risk rises simply because time has passed since the last eruption.

errorPatterns.pattern: A 1-in-100 chance is so small it basically won't happen, so there's no need to prepare ('the odds are tiny').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate probability from consequence (risk needs both); compound the annual chance over a lifetime and discuss why preparing is rational even at low annual odds.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — 1-in-100 is so small it basically won't happen, so nobody needs to prepare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses a low annual probability as negligible and ignores the huge consequence.

errorPatterns.pattern: If they evacuate and nothing erupts, the scientists were simply wrong and 'cried wolf' ('a false alarm proves they failed').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Weigh the missed-warning cost (lives) against the false-alarm cost (disruption); a good decision under uncertainty can still have an unlucky outcome.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges a warning purely by its outcome rather than by the decision given the information available.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the recurrence interval as a schedule ('overdue'), or dismisses the low probability as 'won't happen'; judges warnings only by their outcome.
responseLevels.full: Explains annual probability as roughly constant and independent of elapsed time, combines probability with consequence to justify preparation, weighs the asymmetric costs of acting under uncertainty, and applies it to a new case such as why an earthquake can't be dated while an eruption may be forewarned.
responseLevels.partial: Explains that 1-in-100 is a probability and 'every 100 years' an average, and lists monitoring signs and reasons people stay, but cannot combine probability with consequence to justify the evacuation decision or weigh false-alarm against missed-warning costs.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A volcano observatory says a volcano has 'about a 1-in-100 chance of a major eruption each year, and on average it erupts roughly every 100 years. The last big eruption was 100 years ago.' A newspaper prints: 'Scientists say the volcano is now overdue and will erupt this year.' Is the newspaper right, and how should we understand that '1-in-100 each year'?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the 'overdue' / gambler's-fallacy model answers 'yes, it's due' — a different answer from one who treats the annual probability as roughly constant and independent of elapsed time. The reason tier separates '100 years passed so it must be now' from 'probability isn't a schedule'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — recognise that a digit represents 10× the place to its right and 1/10 the place to its left (the ×10/÷10 place-value relationship, now extended in BOTH directions across the decimal point).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'recognise the place value of each digit in numbers with up to 3 decimal places' and multiply/divide by 10/100/1000; the reciprocal ÷10 direction underpins Y6 decimal work.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.1 — 'Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.'
• Operational details: Treat place value as a single self-similar structure that continues seamlessly through the decimal point — each step left is unitising (×10), each step right is partitioning (÷10). Contrast digits of equal face value in different places (the 4 in 0.4 vs 0.04 vs 4000) so the child articulates the multiplicative, not additive, gap. Use a Gattegno/place-value chart where a digit physically slides between columns and its value recomputes.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'The 4 in 0.4 is ten times the 4 in ___.' Tier B: 'Explain why the 6 in 6000 is a million times the 6 in 0.006.' Tier C: 'A digit moves two places right — what happens to its value and why?'
bestPractices: Present place value as one continuous ×10/÷10 chain that runs unbroken through the decimal point — do not teach whole-number and decimal place value as separate systems
Use a Gattegno chart or place-value slider so a digit physically moves between columns and its value visibly recomputes (×10 left, ÷10 right)
Contrast the SAME face-value digit sitting in different places (4 in 4000 vs 0.4 vs 0.04) and require a multiplicative statement ('ten times', 'one tenth of'), never 'bigger/smaller'
Anchor the ÷10 direction in concrete partitioning — one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth — before abstracting to the rule
Vary the non-example: ask why moving a place is NOT 'add a zero' when decimals are involved, exposing the multiplicative meaning
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (digit slides between columns, value scales ×10 or ÷10)
Place-value chart spanning millions to thousandths with the decimal point fixed and digits mobile
Arrow/relationship cards labelling adjacent columns '×10 →' and '← ÷10'
Base-ten / Dienes extended to decimal flats-longs-units where the 'one' can be reassigned
commonMisconceptions: Believing 'moving a place left just adds a zero' — a rule that breaks for decimals (0.4 → 4, not 0.40)
Treating the decimal point as moving rather than the DIGITS moving relative to a fixed point
Thinking the gap between places is additive (0.4 is '0.36 more than' 0.04) rather than multiplicative (ten times)
Assuming longer decimals are always larger, ignoring place value (0.004 seen as bigger than 0.4)
Losing the self-similar structure at the decimal point — seeing tenths as unrelated to ones

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: understand that each place in a number is worth ten times the place to its right and one tenth of the place to its left, and that this ×10/÷10 structure continues unbroken through the decimal point. The core goal is for a learner to state multiplicative relationships ('ten times', 'one tenth of') between the same digit sitting in different places, and to justify them by position rather than by face value or decimal length.

activities.title: Slide the same digit across the places
feedback: If a learner says the two 4s are 'the same because both are 4', redirect to position: the digit is identical but the places differ, so the worth differs — ask them to read each value aloud (four tenths vs four hundredths).
If a learner counts a single move as ÷100 or ÷2, have them count the columns crossed: tenths to hundredths is ONE step, so ÷10; show 0.004 to illustrate what two steps (÷100) would look like.
Reinforce correct multiplicative language: accept 'ten times' / 'one tenth of', and gently reject 'bigger/smaller' or 'add a zero' as the explanation.
activities.rationale: The concept is a transformation of value by place, so performing the move and reading the recomputed value makes the multiplicative gap concrete rather than merely stated. An optional live readout and a proportional magnitude bar that is ten times longer per leftward step can make the multiplicative (not additive) gap visible.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1: a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as the place to its right and 1/10 of the place to its left.
The Gattegno chart is a canonical representation for building the ×10/÷10 place-value relationship across whole numbers and decimals.
learnerActions: Work on a place-value chart with columns from millions down to thousandths and a fixed decimal point.
Take a single digit, for example a 4, and place it in the tenths column so it reads 0.4.
Move the same 4 one column to the left to read 4, then 40, then 400, then 4000; each move, say aloud 'ten times as much' and write the ×10 relationship.

Before moving right, split one tenth into ten equal parts and check that each part is one hundredth (and one hundredth into ten parts gives thousandths). Then move the same 4 one column to the right from 0.4 to 0.04 to 0.004; each move, say aloud 'one tenth of' and write the ÷10 relationship.
Park the same 4 three columns apart (for example 4000 and 4, or 4 and 0.004 — each three steps, so ×1000) and state how many times larger one is than the other.
Finish the sentence: '0.4 is ten times 0.04; 0.04 is one tenth of 0.4.'
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's worth changes multiplicatively (×10 each step left, ÷10 each step right) according to its place; the decimal point stays fixed while the digit moves, and the same self-similar rule runs through the decimal point.

activities.title: Why isn't it just 'add a zero'?
feedback: If a learner insists 'add a zero' works, show 0.4 → 4: adding a zero gives 0.40, which is still four tenths, not four.
Confirm understanding when the learner states the rule as '×10 when moving left, ÷10 when moving right' and can apply it to a decimal example.
activities.rationale: Directly contrasting a tempting but faulty shortcut with the multiplicative rule surfaces and addresses the common 'add a zero' misconception.
sourceClaims: Y5 requires recognising the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places and multiplying/dividing by 10, 100 and 1000.
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'moving a digit one place left just adds a zero.'
Test it on whole numbers: 4 → 40 (works) and then on a decimal: 0.4 → 4 (not 0.40).
Explain in your own words why 'add a zero' fails for decimals but ×10 always works.
Write a corrected rule that holds for both whole numbers and decimals.
activities.intendedInsight: The underlying operation is multiply/divide by ten, not a digit-appending trick; 'add a zero' is a surface pattern that breaks for decimals, exposing the multiplicative meaning.

activities.title: Compare across many places and across zero
feedback: If a learner ranks the 4 in 0.04 as larger because it comes 'further along', use the number line to show 0.04 sits close to zero while 0.4 is near halfway.
If a learner cannot bridge 6,000 and 0.006, have them step through the places one at a time, tagging each ×10 (six steps), to reach a million-fold difference.
activities.rationale: Spanning many places and crossing the decimal point counters the 'longer decimal is larger' and 'face value' errors, and a number line makes the shrinking rightward value visible.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1: a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as the place to its right and 1/10 of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Compare the 6 in 6,000 with the 6 in 0.006: count how many ×10 steps separate the two places (six steps).
State and justify how many times larger the 6 in 6,000 is (6,000 is 0.006 × 1,000,000).
Place 0.4 and 0.04 on a 0–1 number line (0.4 near the middle, 0.04 close to zero) to see the value shrinking to the right.
Explain which stays the same and which changes when a digit moves place — the digit, or its worth.
activities.intendedInsight: The place-value relationship holds across several steps and across the decimal point; value decreases to the right and increases to the left, regardless of decimal length.

activities.title: Explain and defend your reasoning
feedback: A full response states the ten-times / one-tenth relationship, justifies it by positional value, and applies it in both directions and across several places.
A partial response can order the values and say one is smaller but cannot justify the exact ÷10 factor or muddles it; prompt the learner to count places and name the single ×10/÷10 step.
If the learner says one tenth of a tenth is a twentieth or a tenth, have them partition one tenth into ten equal parts to see each part is a hundredth.
activities.rationale: Requiring a justified comparison rather than a memorised ranking discriminates true positional understanding from surface rules, and asking the learner to explain the partitioning met earlier (one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth) checks that the ÷10 direction rests on concrete meaning rather than a memorised rule.
learnerActions: Answer the prompt: 'Look at the 4 in 0.4 and the 4 in 0.04. How do their values compare, and why?'
Answer a deeper probe: 'Why does moving one place to the right divide the value by ten and not some other number?'
Explain, with reasons, why the 6 in 6,000 is a million times the 6 in 0.006.
Anchor the ÷10 direction in partitioning: explain why one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the exact ÷10/×10 relationship by position — not just order the values — is what demonstrates genuine place-value understanding.

constraints: Present whole-number and decimal place value as ONE continuous ×10/÷10 chain running through the decimal point, not two separate systems.
Require multiplicative language ('ten times', 'one tenth of'); do not accept 'bigger/smaller' or 'add a zero' as the explanation of the relationship.

Recognition-only tasks (for example choosing from multiple options or filling a blank) can consolidate and assess the rule but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own justification; include tasks where the learner states and defends the relationship.

A static annotated chart with reveal cards is a useful reference, but it tells rather than lets the learner perform the slide; treat it as a scaffold, not a substitute for the learner moving a digit and reading the recomputed value.
Partitioning (one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth) should be established concretely before abstracting to the divide-by-ten rule.
Keep worked examples arithmetically exact: columns N apart differ by a factor of 10^N (three columns apart is ×1000, two columns apart is ×100).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit confirmed: 0.4 = 0.04 × 10 and 0.04 = 0.4 ÷ 10; 6,000 vs 0.006 differ by six ×10 steps (a factor of 1,000,000); one tenth of one tenth = one hundredth; three columns apart = ×1000 and two columns apart = ×100. The example pairs 4000 and 4, and 4 and 0.004, are genuinely three steps apart and consistent with the ×1000 framing.

The original claim that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing' and 'risks implying value scales with physical size' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; a spatial model could still be used — it is simply not required here.

The original framing that manipulation is 'necessary' while dialogue is merely 'possible' reflects catalog fit ranking, not demonstrated comparative efficacy; both a manipulable chart and a Socratic exchange are retained as legitimate approaches serving different purposes.
CCSS-M 5.NBT.A.1 and the NCETM Gattegno-chart claim were marked unverified in the source row; treat their support as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: Why does moving one place to the right divide the value by ten and not some other number?
How does the 6 in 6,000 compare to the 6 in 0.006 — how many tens apart are they?
If I move the 4 in 0.4 one place LEFT instead, what happens to its value?
What stays the same and what changes when a digit moves place — the digit, or its worth?
assess.correctAnswer: The 4 in 0.04 is worth one-tenth of the 4 in 0.4 (0.04 = 0.4 ÷ 10). A digit one place to the right is worth ten times less, because each place is a tenth of the place to its left.

errorPatterns.pattern: Face value — 'they're the same, both digits are 4', ignoring position.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with place-value counters or a Gattegno chart: slide the 4 from tenths to hundredths and show its worth divides by ten; the digit is the same but its place is not.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same — both digits are 4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says equal value and justifies by the digit alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer-decimal-is-larger / places grow to the right — thinks the 4 in 0.04 is worth more because it is 'further along'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place 0.4 and 0.04 on a 0–1 line (0.4 near halfway, 0.04 close to zero) so the shrinking value to the right is visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 in 0.04 is bigger because it comes further along.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks 0.04's 4 as the bigger value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Right direction, wrong factor — says the 0.04 four is a hundredth (or half) of the other, not a tenth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the places moved: tenths→hundredths is ONE step, so ÷10; contrast with 0.004 to show what ÷100 would look like.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 in 0.04 is one hundredth of the other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child knows it is smaller and moved one place, but names ÷100 or ÷2.

responseLevels.gap: Compares by the digit or by decimal length; cannot say one value is a tenth of the other.
responseLevels.full: States the ten-times / one-tenth relationship between adjacent places, justifies it by positional value, and applies it in both directions and across several places (e.g. 6,000 vs 0.006).
responseLevels.partial: States the 0.04 four is smaller and can order them, but cannot justify the exact ÷10 relationship or muddles the factor.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at the 4 in 0.4 and the 4 in 0.04. How do their values compare, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands positional value says one is a tenth of the other and can say why (the place, not the digit, carries the value). A child stuck on face value says 'same, both are 4'; a child with the longer-is-larger error says the 0.04 one is bigger. The REASON separates true place-value understanding from a memorised comparison.

sources.claim: Y5 requires recognising the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places and multiplying/dividing by 10, 100 and 1000.

sources.claim: 5.NBT.A.1: a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as the place to its right and 1/10 of the place to its left.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Number & Operations in Base Ten Grade 5

sources.claim: The Gattegno chart is a canonical representation for building the ×10/÷10 place-value relationship across whole numbers and decimals.

pedagogy.summary: Children reflect and translate a shape on a squared grid, give the image's coordinates, and articulate that the moved shape is congruent to the original — same size and shape, only its position (and, for reflection, its sense) has changed. The pedagogical heart is that a transformation is a rule for where every point goes, not a vague 'slide it over': reflection sends each vertex perpendicularly across the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side, and translation sends every vertex the same distance in the same direction. Congruence is the invariant that makes both trustworthy.
bestPractices: Build reflection from the point rule, not 'flip it': for each vertex, draw the line to the mirror, note it is PERPENDICULAR to the mirror, count the squares to the line, then count the same number of squares beyond it — the image vertex lands there. Assemble the image vertex by vertex.

Explicitly avoid the language 'straight across' or 'straight down' even for vertical/horizontal mirrors; say 'perpendicular to the mirror line' so the idea generalises when mirror lines later slope (NCETM KS3 6.3).

Draw attention to 'sense': after a reflection the shape reads the mirror-image way round (a clockwise vertex order becomes anticlockwise). This is what distinguishes a true reflection from a shape that has merely been slid across.

Establish translation as 'every point moves the same' — model it by moving ONE vertex '5 right, 2 up', then checking every other vertex followed the identical move; the shape's orientation and sense are unchanged.
Make congruence explicit and testable: trace the original onto tracing paper and lay it over the image to confirm same size and shape; name the word 'congruent'.
Keep coordinate reading disciplined — state the image coordinates as (across, up), guarding against the x-y reversal that surfaces whenever coordinates re-enter.
keyRepresentations: Squared/coordinate grid with a vertical (then horizontal) mirror line
Perpendicular 'joining lines' from each object vertex to its image vertex, crossed at right angles by the mirror line
Tracing paper laid over object and image to demonstrate congruence
A translation vector shown as a 'staircase' arrow (e.g. 5 right then 2 up) applied identically to every vertex
commonMisconceptions: Reflecting by sliding the shape across the mirror unchanged, so its sense is not reversed (translate-instead-of-flip).
Placing the image the wrong distance from the mirror — not equidistant — often by miscounting or letting the shape touch the line.
Believing the shape changes size or becomes a 'different shape' once moved, rather than staying congruent.
Reversing the image coordinates (writing y before x) when reporting where the shape landed.

learn.summary: Year 5 learners reflect and translate a scalene shape on a squared/coordinate grid, state the image coordinates as (across, up), and justify that the moved shape is congruent — same size and shape, with only its position (and, for reflection, its sense) changed. The core idea is that a transformation is a precise rule for where every point goes: reflection sends each vertex perpendicularly across the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side, and translation sends every vertex the same distance in the same direction. Congruence is the invariant that makes both trustworthy.

activities.title: Build a reflection vertex by vertex using the perpendicular-equidistant rule
feedback: If the image reads the same way round as the original (sense not reversed), it is not a reflection. It was most likely slid (or possibly turned) rather than reflected. Rebuild it one vertex at a time using the perpendicular lines so the reversal emerges from the rule. Avoid 'straight across/down' language; say 'perpendicular to the mirror line'.
If the square-counts from the mirror differ between an object vertex and its image, or the image touches the mirror line, recount perpendicular to the line on each side and make the two counts equal.

If coordinates come out as (up, across) — e.g. a corner at (5,3) reported as '(3,5)' while the plotted point is correct — re-anchor 'across first, then up' and recheck one corner together against the grid.
activities.rationale: Teaching reflection from the perpendicular point-rule, and explicitly avoiding 'straight across/down' language, targets the documented misconception that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane and generalises to sloping mirror lines later. Using a scalene shape makes the reversal of sense observable; of the two transformations in this unit, only reflection reverses sense.
sourceClaims: A common reflection misconception is that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane rather than moving perpendicular to the mirror; the remedy is to teach that every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line and to avoid 'straight across/down' language.

Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segments joining object and image vertices (lines joining equivalent points are parallel and the mirror is perpendicular to them).
A recurring coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair (writing/reading the second value before the first); teaching should reinforce reading across before up.
learnerActions: Start with a scalene triangle on a squared grid and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right (choose scalene so a reversal of sense is visible).

For each vertex in turn, draw the line from the vertex to the mirror line that meets the mirror at a right angle (perpendicular to the mirror line); with this vertical mirror it runs along a horizontal grid line. Check the right angle rather than assuming it.
Count the squares from the vertex to the mirror along that perpendicular, then count the SAME number of squares beyond the mirror and mark the image vertex there.
Repeat for every vertex, then join the image vertices to complete the reflected shape.

Compare the vertex order: check that the image reads the mirror-image way round (a clockwise order of corners becomes anticlockwise) — this reversed 'sense' is what makes it a true reflection rather than a slide.
State the coordinates of each image corner as (across, up), reading across first then up.
activities.intendedInsight: A reflection is produced point by point: every line joining an object vertex to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line, and the image vertex is the same distance beyond the mirror as the object is in front. Because this reverses the vertex order, the shape's sense flips — distinguishing a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.

activities.title: Translate every point by the same vector and contrast it with reflection
feedback: If only part of the shape moves, or vertices move by different amounts, re-apply the single vector to each vertex in turn until every corner has shifted identically.
If a learner claims the translated shape has 'turned', check the vertex order against the original: a translation leaves it reading the same way round.
Prompt: 'Is your translated triangle congruent to the reflected one as well as to the original? How do you know?' — both transformations preserve size and shape.
activities.rationale: Modelling translation as 'every point moves the same' and directly contrasting it with reflection isolates the invariant (orientation/sense preserved) that separates the two transformations. The curriculum expects Year 5 pupils to translate shapes and recognise the result is congruent.
sourceClaims: Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Take the original triangle and set a single translation rule, e.g. '5 squares right, 2 squares up', shown as a staircase arrow.
Apply that identical move to ONE vertex first, then check that every other vertex has to follow the exact same move.
Complete the translated shape and confirm its orientation and sense are unchanged (it reads the same way round as the original).
Place the reflected shape and the translated shape side by side and describe the felt difference: the slide keeps sense, the flip reverses it.
Report the translated image coordinates as (across, up).
activities.intendedInsight: A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, so orientation and sense are unchanged — the opposite of reflection, which reverses sense. Both leave the shape congruent to the original.

activities.title: Test congruence by tracing and overlaying
feedback: If a learner says the moved shape is bigger, smaller, or 'different', lay the tracing directly over the image (turning it over for a reflection) to show the exact match, then name 'congruent'.
For a reflected image the tracing must be flipped over to match — note that this flip IS the reversed sense, and the shape is still congruent.
If a learner can overlay correctly but resists the word, restate: position changed, size and shape did not — that is what congruent means.
activities.rationale: A direct physical match makes congruence testable rather than asserted, targeting the misconception that moving a shape changes it. Tracing paper or a card cutout is a concrete approximation of the ideal flat figure, which has zero thickness; the demonstration is about the mathematical shape represented, not the physical copy.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Trace the original triangle onto tracing paper (or cut out a card copy, noting that real paper/card has slight thickness and only approximates the ideal zero-thickness flat figure it represents).

Lay the tracing directly over the translated image and confirm an exact match in size and shape; for the reflected image, turn the tracing paper OVER to make it match — this flip is itself the reversed sense, and the size and shape are still identical.
Say aloud that the moved shape is congruent to the original: only its position (and, for the reflection, its sense) has changed, not its size or shape.
Answer the challenge 'Is it a new, different triangle now?' — about the mathematical shape represented — by pointing to the exact overlay match.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection and translation change where a shape is (and reflection changes which way round it reads) but never its size or shape; the technical word for this sameness is 'congruent'.

activities.title: Diagnostic performance task: reflect, translate, and justify
feedback: Watch how the image is built rather than explaining the rule first; a block-shunted image reading the same way round signals a slide-instead-of-reflect error to reteach via the perpendicular rule.

Full response: each reflected vertex perpendicular and equidistant with sense reversed, every translated vertex moved identically, coordinates as (across, up), congruence justified by matching/tracing, and correct transfer when the mirror line or vector changes.

Partial response: carries out both transformations and may name congruence but treats each as a remembered procedure — cannot say WHY the image sits where it does or transfer to a mirror in a new position; reteach the point rule explicitly.
If coordinates are reversed, re-anchor 'across first, then up' and check one vertex together.
activities.rationale: A watch-the-build performance task discriminates genuine understanding of the point rule from imitation, because the two documented misconceptions (unreversed sense; unequal distance from the mirror) show up in how the image is constructed. Probing the perpendicular relationship and congruence surfaces reasoning rather than recall.
sourceClaims: A common reflection misconception is that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane rather than moving perpendicular to the mirror; the remedy is to teach that every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line and to avoid 'straight across/down' language.

Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segments joining object and image vertices (lines joining equivalent points are parallel and the mirror is perpendicular to them).
Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Given a squared grid showing a scalene triangle and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right, reflect the triangle in the mirror line and state the coordinates of the reflected corners as (across, up).
Back with the original, translate it 5 squares right and 2 squares up, and describe the move made.
Explain whether the new triangle is the same as the first and how you know, using tracing/overlay and the word congruent.

Answer probes: What is the relationship between the line joining a corner to its image and the mirror line? If the mirror moved one square further right, what would happen to the reflected triangle? If a friend slid the triangle across without turning it, is that a reflection, and how can you tell?
activities.intendedInsight: Holding the perpendicular-equidistant rule produces an image that is both the correct distance AND reversed in sense; merely sliding produces the wrong sense (and often the wrong distance). Watching HOW the image is assembled — perpendicular vertex by vertex, or shunted as a whole block — separates understanding from imitation, and the congruence question separates learners who see the shape as invariant from those who think moving changes it.

constraints: Use a scalene shape so the reversal of sense is visible; a symmetric shape can hide whether a learner reflected or merely slid.
Say 'perpendicular to the mirror line' rather than 'straight across/down', even for vertical or horizontal mirrors, so the rule generalises to sloping mirror lines later.
Report image coordinates as (across, up), guarding against the x-before-y / y-before-x reversal.
When using tracing paper to check a reflection, the tracing must be turned OVER to overlay the image; the shape remains congruent and that flip is the reversed sense.

Discrete-item checks (choosing the correctly reflected image among a slid-across distractor and a not-equidistant distractor, filling in image coordinates, true/false on congruence) can diagnose the two misconceptions but, because nothing recomputes, they check rather than build the felt rule; use them alongside, not instead of, construction.

A pre-annotated worked diagram that reveals the perpendicular joining lines, the equal square-counts and the label 'congruent' can illustrate the rule but does not let a learner test their own placement, which is the core skill; treat it as a scaffold, not the assessment.

A live grid where dragging a vertex or the mirror line recomputes the image (with faint perpendicular joining lines, live square-counts that turn green when the two sides match, a sense badge that flips when the reflection is correct, a settable translation arrow applied to all vertices at once, and a ghost of the original for congruence) can make the invariants concrete; these interaction and feedback examples are optional ways to expose the mechanism, not mandatory.

Tracing paper or a card cutout is a concrete approximation of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) figure; use it to demonstrate congruence of the represented mathematical shape while distinguishing that shape from the physical copy.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One legacy source claim (National Curriculum, Year 5 reflect/translate/congruence) was marked verified:false in the row and is cited in Activities 2, 3 and 4; it directly supports the congruence principle and is the only curriculum source for it, but its evidential status is unconfirmed, so treat its citation accordingly.

The legacy entry framed a 3D rendering and an in-role dialogue as 'poor' for this planar skill. Those are catalog-fit judgements, not universal laws: a planar grid is well suited to square-counting and depth is not used here, but no claim of universal impossibility is made. These alternatives were not carried forward as activities because they do not let the learner construct and verify a reflection; their underlying affordances are noted only as scaffolds/limits.

Legacy phrasing such as 'cannot let the child TEST their own placement' and 'adds nothing' was softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; the exact sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

The row's evidence statement gives a '3 units right, 2 units up' translation example, whereas the diagnostic and these activities use '5 right, 2 up'; the activities follow the diagnostic consistently.

probeDeeper: Point at one object vertex and its image and ask: 'What can you tell me about the line joining these two corners and the mirror line?' (listen for perpendicular / equal distance, not 'it's across from it').
'If I moved the mirror line one square further right, what would happen to your reflected triangle?' (tests that the image is defined by distance from the mirror, not a fixed spot).
Counterexample: 'Your friend slid the triangle straight across to here without turning it round — is that a reflection? How can you tell?' (listen for sense/orientation reversal being absent).
'You translated it 5 right and 2 up. Is the translated triangle congruent to the reflected one as well as to the original? How do you know?' (congruence is preserved by both transformations).
assess.correctAnswer: The child places each reflected vertex perpendicularly opposite its original at an equal number of squares beyond the mirror line, so the image is equidistant and its sense is reversed (a scalene triangle visibly reads the other way round); reports the image coordinates as (across, up); translates by moving every vertex 5 right and 2 up together; and states the moved shape is congruent — same size and shape — checking by matching or tracing, understanding only position (and, for the reflection, orientation/sense) changed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflects by sliding the whole shape across the mirror without reversing it, so its sense is unchanged ('I just moved it over to the other side')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the line from one vertex to the mirror, show it meets the mirror at a right angle, count the squares and count the same beyond; repeat per vertex so the reversed sense emerges from the rule. Avoid 'straight across' language.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The image reads the SAME way round as the original (vertex order not reversed) — for a scalene triangle the 'point' faces the same direction; the child moves the shape as one block rather than vertex by vertex.

errorPatterns.pattern: Places the image the wrong distance from the mirror — not equidistant — often letting the shape touch the line or miscounting one side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count squares perpendicular from each vertex to the line, then step the identical count to the far side; mark both counts and compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Square-counts from mirror differ between object and image; image sits closer to or on the mirror line.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the shape changes size or becomes a different shape once moved, so it is no longer 'the same' ('it's a new triangle now')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the original and lay it over the image to show an exact match; name 'congruent' — position (and sense) changed, size and shape did not.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the moved shape is bigger/smaller or 'different'; cannot justify sameness or resists the word congruent.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the reported image coordinates, giving the up-value before the across-value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'along the corridor then up the stairs': read across first, then up; check one vertex together against the grid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States a landed vertex as (up, across) — e.g. calls (5,3) '(3,5)' — while the plotted point is actually correct.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place a correct image: slides the shape across with unchanged sense or at an unequal distance, and treats the moved shape as changed or 'new'. Coordinates may also be reversed.
responseLevels.full: Builds both images from the point rule — each reflected vertex perpendicular and equidistant across the mirror with sense reversed, every translated vertex moved identically — reports image coordinates as (across, up), and justifies congruence by matching/tracing, transferring correctly when the mirror line or vector is changed.
responseLevels.partial: Can carry out a reflection and a translation and may name congruence, but treats each as a remembered procedure — e.g. reflects correctly in a vertical mirror yet cannot say WHY the image sits where it does (perpendicular, equidistant), or reports the steps without connecting them to the shape staying congruent. Lists the moves but cannot explain how the point rule forces the image, nor transfer to a mirror in a new position.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child a squared grid showing a scalene triangle and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right. Now, back with the original, translate it 5 squares right and 2 squares up and describe the move you made. Last, tell me: is your new triangle the same as the first one, and how do you know?' Set the task and WATCH how the image is built — do not explain the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the perpendicular-equidistant rule produces an image that is both the right distance AND reversed in sense; a child who merely 'slides it across' produces an image that is the wrong sense (and often the wrong distance), so watching HOW the image is assembled — vertex by perpendicular vertex, or shunted whole — separates real understanding from imitation. The congruence question further separates children who see the shape as invariant from those who think moving it changes it.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11. Relative dating from rock layers — reading the sequence of strata to tell what is older or younger without knowing exact ages — taught by ordering layers with the law of superposition and handling real-world disruptions.
• Standards — UK (DfE): Y3 Rocks (fossils are found in rock; how fossils form) and Y6 Evolution & inheritance (fossils inform us about the past); KS2 working-scientifically. Leads to KS3 Earth's structure and geological time.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-ESS1-4 (construct an explanation from rock-strata evidence for how the geologic time scale organises Earth's ~4.6-billion-year history). Superposition is foundational.
• Operational details: teach the law of superposition (undisturbed layers: deeper=older, higher=younger); original horizontality; and correlating layers between sites with index fossils. Then complicate it: folding/tilting, faults, and intrusions/unconformities that break the simple rule, so children READ the story rather than assume.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (concrete, ~9): in an undisturbed cliff, say which layer formed first (the bottom). Tier B (transitional, ~10): order several layers oldest→youngest and use a matching fossil to line up two separated outcrops. Tier C (formal, ~11): explain how a tilt, fault or intrusion disturbs the order, and how you'd still work out the sequence of events.
bestPractices: Start from the intuitive core (bottom layer settled first) before adding vocabulary like 'superposition'.
Move quickly from single-cliff ordering to correlating TWO sites with index fossils, so children see why fossils matter for dating.
Deliberately introduce disturbed sequences (tilt, fault, intrusion) so 'deeper=older' is understood as a rule with conditions, not an absolute.
Frame the task as reconstructing a SEQUENCE OF EVENTS, not just stacking layers — deposition, then deformation, then erosion.
Distinguish relative dating (order) from absolute dating (numeric age) so children don't conflate the two.
keyRepresentations: A labelled strata cliff cross-section with oldest at the bottom.
Two separated outcrops linked by a shared index fossil (correlation line).
A block diagram showing a fault or igneous intrusion cutting across layers.
An unconformity (wavy contact) marking missing time.
An events-timeline strip translating a cross-section into ordered happenings.
commonMisconceptions: 'The bottom layer is always oldest, no matter what' — tilting, folding and faulting can overturn or rearrange sequences.
'Rock layers tell you exact ages in years' — relative dating gives order only, not numeric age.
'A gap in layers means nothing happened' — an unconformity represents missing/eroded time.
'Layers formed at the slope they're now tilted to' — by original horizontality, they formed flat and were tilted later.
'Matching rock type proves same age' — correlation relies on index fossils/markers, since similar rock can form at different times.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, teach relative dating as reading a sequence of rock strata: order layers by the law of superposition (undisturbed: deeper = older, higher = younger), correlate layers between separated sites using index fossils, then handle real-world disruptions (tilting/folding, faults, intrusions, unconformities) so the rule is understood with its conditions. The core objective is reconstructing a SEQUENCE OF EVENTS from the evidence — for example deposition, then deformation, then erosion, with features that cut across layers being younger than those layers — and distinguishing relative dating (order) from absolute dating (a number of years).

activities.title: Build the cliff, then correlate two sites, then read the disruptions
feedback: If a layer is placed against the evidence (e.g. a younger layer below an older one in an undisturbed stack), flag it immediately and ask the learner to re-check what 'deposited first' means.
When the learner draws the correlation line, confirm that the shared index fossil — not the rock type — is what links the two bands, since similar rock can form at different times.

If the learner keeps reading 'deeper = older' straight off current height after the beds are tilted or folded, prompt: 'These layers were flat when they formed and were tilted or folded later, so current height on its own may not give the order — and if a fold has turned them right over, the sequence can even be reversed. How would you work out which layer was deposited first here?'

If the learner reads an exact number of years off a layer's position, respond: 'The layers tell you the ORDER (which is older/younger). A number of years needs a different method, such as radiometric dating.'
activities.rationale: Relative dating is a spatial-sequencing-and-reasoning skill, so learners benefit from actually ordering and correlating layers and then confronting disturbed sequences, rather than only naming the rule. Immediate feedback on misplaced layers makes superposition and its exceptions concrete. Starting from the intuitive core (bottom settled first) before adding the word 'superposition', and moving quickly to correlating two sites with index fossils, shows why fossils matter for dating.
sourceClaims: By the law of superposition, in an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock layers the oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest at the top.

MS-ESS1-4 expects students to construct an explanation from rock-strata evidence for how the geologic time scale organises Earth's ~4.6-billion-year history; index fossils allow correlation of strata between distant locations.
learnerActions: Arrange labelled sediment layers (e.g. sand, mud, ash) into the order they were deposited, and check them against the law of superposition — the deepest layer settled first, so bottom = oldest, top = youngest.

Look at a second outcrop a valley away with no obvious link; find the SAME distinctive index fossil appearing in a band of each cliff and draw a correlation line connecting those bands, so two separate cliffs tell one shared story.

Introduce complications one at a time: tilt the beds onto their side, push a sheet of magma (an igneous intrusion, which cools underground) up through the layers, or cut a fault across them — then reconstruct the ORDER OF EVENTS from the evidence: layers must exist before they can be tilted, and anything that cuts across layers (a fault or an intrusion) is younger than the layers it cuts. For example: layers deposited, THEN tilted, THEN cut by an intrusion — but if a fault breaks through the intrusion, the fault came last.

Identify an unconformity (a buried erosion surface — often uneven, or with layers at different angles above and below it) and state that it represents a gap in the record where rock was eroded away or never deposited, not 'nothing happened'.
State explicitly whether your reading gives an order only or an exact age in years.
activities.intendedInsight: Rocks record a sequence of happenings you read like a diary, not just a stack you count from the bottom. Superposition (deeper = older) holds for undisturbed layers; tilting, faulting and intrusions can reorient, rearrange or cut across layers, so you must reconstruct the sequence of events rather than assume the simple rule. Index fossils let you line up distant outcrops, and relative dating gives order only — not a numeric age.

activities.title: Annotated strata cliff: vocabulary and the basic reading
feedback: Confirm the bottom layer formed first in an undisturbed cliff, and connect the revealed label back to the idea that sediment settles layer on layer.
When the unconformity is revealed, emphasise that the gap means time is missing, not that nothing happened.
activities.rationale: A richly annotated cross-section teaches the core vocabulary and the basic reading clearly. This is a scaffold for the building/ordering activity: a fixed annotated image presents the labels and story but does not itself let the learner practise ordering or handle disruptions interactively, so it works best as a lead-in or reference, not as the whole lesson.
sourceClaims: By the law of superposition, in an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock layers the oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest at the top.
learnerActions: Examine a labelled strata cliff cross-section and reveal, for each band, its relative age position and any index fossils it contains.
Reveal the meaning of the marked erosion-surface contact line: 'unconformity — a gap in the record where rock was eroded away or never deposited'.
Say, in your own words, which layer formed first and why.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary of strata reading — superposition, index fossil, unconformity — attached to a concrete labelled cross-section, so the basic 'bottom-is-oldest' reading and its key terms are secure before ordering and disruption practice.

activities.title: Check the reading: order, matching and which-formed-first
feedback: If the order is reversed, re-show the deposition picture: sediment settles layer on layer, so the bottom was laid down first and is oldest.
If a match is made on rock type rather than the shared fossil, note that similar rock can form at different times, so correlation relies on index fossils/markers.
activities.rationale: Ordering and matching tasks test the reading efficiently and reveal specific errors. This format checks and consolidates recognition/reading; it does not by itself build the event-sequence reasoning or let learners construct and manipulate disrupted strata, so pair it with the building activity.
sourceClaims: By the law of superposition, in an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock layers the oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest at the top.

MS-ESS1-4 expects students to construct an explanation from rock-strata evidence for how the geologic time scale organises Earth's ~4.6-billion-year history; index fossils allow correlation of strata between distant locations.
learnerActions: Put five labelled layers into order oldest → youngest.
Answer which layer formed first in a given undisturbed cliff.
Match a shared index fossil across two columns — e.g. link layer B at site 1 to layer D at site 2 — to show the two outcrops correlate.
activities.intendedInsight: Checks whether the learner can read a sequence and use index fossils to correlate sites, surfacing confusions such as reversing the order or relying on rock type instead of fossils.

activities.title: Optional extension: rotate and slice a 3D geological block
feedback: Prompt the learner to connect what the slice reveals back to the order of events: which came first — the layers, the fault, or the intrusion?
activities.rationale: For the disruption cases, a rotatable, sliceable block can clarify how a fault or tilt sits in space. This is an enhancement, not a requirement: the core superposition reasoning works fully in a 2D cross-section, and a 3D model is one way to add spatial clarity for learners who want it.
learnerActions: Rotate a geological block model to view the strata from different angles.
Slice the block along a chosen plane to expose the internal layers and a fault surface.
Describe how the tilt or fault reads differently when seen in three dimensions versus a flat cross-section.
activities.intendedInsight: Strata are genuinely three-dimensional; viewing and slicing a rotatable block can make a tilt or fault surface easier to see for the disruption cases.

constraints: The annotated cross-section is a scaffold: a fixed image presents labels and the story but does not let learners practise ordering or interactively handle disruptions — pair it with a build/order activity.
Ordering and matching checks assess reading/recognition; they do not by themselves require learners to construct the full event sequence or manipulate disrupted strata.
Keep relative dating (order) clearly separate from absolute dating (numeric age); learners should know a number of years needs a different method such as radiometric dating.

Teach 'deeper = older' as a rule with conditions (undisturbed layers), and deliberately include tilted/faulted/overturned sequences so it is not taken as absolute; note that tilting/folding reorients layers (order preserved but current height misleads) while an overturned fold can reverse the sequence.
Treat the 3D block as an optional spatial aid, not a necessity; do not imply the 2D reasoning is insufficient.
Correlation between sites should rely on index fossils/markers, not matching rock type, since similar rock can form at different times.

Talk and narration can support reasoning about the event sequence, but on their own they do not elicit the hands-on ordering and correlation practice this objective targets; this is an observable affordance limit, not a claim that discussion is inferior to other media.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources remain marked verified:false and were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels one interactive medium 'ideal' and dialogue 'poor'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established comparative efficacy. The rewrite keeps the pedagogical purposes (interactive ordering vs. vocabulary scaffold vs. recognition check vs. 3D extension) without asserting one medium is universally necessary or superior.

Geological accuracy for the disruption cases: simple tilting and non-overturned folding preserve the depositional order (only the current vertical reading is affected), whereas an overturned fold can reverse the sequence. Introduce the simple undisturbed case first, then tilted, and only later overturned examples, so 9–11 learners are not confused.
Age figures in the geologic-time claim (~4.6 billion years) are stated as in the original source and not independently re-verified here.

probeDeeper: If the rock layers had been folded so they're now tilted or even flipped over, could the 'bottom' layer still be the youngest?
What extra information would you need to say a fossil is '150 million years old' rather than just 'older'?
Why does the oldest layer end up at the bottom in the first place?
assess.correctAnswer: The fossil in the deeper, lower layer is older, because sediment layers build up with the oldest at the bottom and the youngest on top. But the layers only tell you the ORDER (which is older or younger), not an exact age in years — you'd need another method, such as radiometric dating, for an actual number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reading the layers tells you the exact age in years.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish relative dating (order) from absolute dating (a number); the strata give sequence, not years.
errorPatterns.distractor: The layers tell you exactly how many millions of years old the fossil is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States an exact age (e.g. 'millions of years') straight from the layer position.

errorPatterns.pattern: The top layer is oldest because it 'formed first' or has been there longest.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the deposition picture — sediment settles layer on layer, so the bottom was laid down first and is oldest.
errorPatterns.distractor: The fossil in the top layer is older, because the top formed first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reverses the order, calling the upper fossil the older one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rock layers are always flat and undisturbed, so lower always equals older.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show folded/faulted strata; position tells age only when the layers haven't been rearranged.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists lower is older even when the strata are clearly tilted or overturned.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the top layer is oldest, or reads an exact age straight off the layers.
responseLevels.full: Orders fossils by layer (lower = older), states relative dating gives order not an exact age, and recognises that folding or faulting can complicate the sequence.
responseLevels.partial: Knows lower layers are older but conflates relative with absolute dating (thinks it gives a number of years), or assumes strata are never disturbed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a cliff, one fossil is found in a deep low layer of rock and another in a high layer near the top. Which fossil is older — and does looking at the layers tell you exactly how many years old it is? Explain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who confuses relative with absolute dating claims the layers give an exact age. A child who understands says lower means older (order only) and that a number of years needs a different method.
