pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Conservation of Mass

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry & Physics 'Matter'):** Conservation of mass in changes of state and chemical reactions; conservation of material and of mass, and reversibility, in melting, freezing, evaporation, sublimation, condensation and dissolving. (Bridged from KS2 change work.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-PS1-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-2] (heating, cooling, mixing, dissolving), the total weight of matter is conserved.

- **Operational details:** The principle: matter is neither created nor destroyed in a physical or chemical change — the TOTAL mass of a closed system is the same before and after. Teach it as a MEASURED law: weigh the whole system before and after a change (dissolve, mix, melt) and read the unchanged balance. The particle model supplies the WHY (the same particles are still there, just rearranged), which is why this sits just after 'matter is made of particles'. The hardest case is a change where something seems to vanish or appear: dissolved sugar (invisible but still weighed), and — as a bridge to reactions — a gas produced or consumed (mass only appears lost because gas escaped an OPEN container; seal it and mass holds). Stress 'account for the WHOLE system, including any gas'. Keep chemical-reaction conservation light at this age; the water-and-dissolving cases are the core.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal, quantitative). The child predicts and confirms that total mass is unchanged across a change, explains a 'disappearing' case (dissolved solid; escaped gas) by appeal to the whole system and to particles not being destroyed.
bestPractices: Teach conservation as a MEASURED law: weigh the whole system before and after and read the unchanged balance.
Use the particle model to supply the WHY — the same particles persist, only rearranged.
Confront the apparent-loss cases directly: dissolved solid (invisible but weighed) and gas escaping an OPEN container.
Resolve the open-container case by SEALING the system so the gas is counted.
Insist pupils account for the whole system, including any gas produced or absorbed.
keyRepresentations: A balance with before/after readouts on a sealed system
An open-vs-sealed toggle for a gas-producing reaction
A particle overlay showing the same particles rearranged, none destroyed
Dissolving as the invisible-but-still-weighed case
commonMisconceptions: Mass is lost when a solid dissolves because you can't see it.
Mass is destroyed when a gas is given off (forgetting the escaped gas has mass).
Burning destroys matter, so the ash weighs the same as nothing was added.
A change that makes something look bigger/smaller must change the mass.
Mass and volume are the same thing (a puffed-up product must weigh more).

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, investigate conservation of mass by accounting for a whole system before and after a change. A covered dissolving investigation and a sealed melting-ice investigation can provide real measurements for mixing and for a change of state caused by heating or cooling; prepared experimental data or a clearly labelled model can extend the comparison to gas-producing reactions in open and closed systems. In physical changes the material is still present; in chemical reactions atoms are rearranged into different substances rather than created or destroyed. Distinguish conserved mass from a balance reading affected by escaping matter, leaks, evaporation, condensation on the outside of a cold container, instrument precision or changing air buoyancy. Keep the chemical-reaction explanation introductory.

activities.title: Mass detective: track the whole system
feedback: If a learner expects dissolved sugar to become weightless, connect the before/after readings to the material remaining in solution. Readings that agree within measurement precision support that account.

If the open reaction seems to violate conservation, identify the gas that left the weighed system. A decrease can reflect escaped gas, but do not claim every change in reading is exactly the gas mass without considering other losses and measurement effects.

If the learner says nothing changed, distinguish appearance from substance: sugar dispersed during dissolving; a chemical reaction forms new substances by rearranging atoms. Neither requires matter to disappear.

For an expanding balloon or bag, explain that greater displaced air increases the upward buoyant force, so an unchanged total mass need not produce an exactly unchanged apparent balance reading. Do not respond by sealing the reaction in an improvised rigid pressure vessel.

Always identify the whole system and what crosses its boundary. Any real gas-producing demonstration must follow an established, supervised school protocol and an appropriate risk assessment; otherwise use prepared data or a model.
activities.rationale: A before/after dissolving measurement lets learners generate evidence while tracking material that becomes invisible. Prepared gas-reaction data can contrast open and closed boundaries without requiring an improvised pressurised experiment. A labelled model or particle overlay may support explanation, but its conserved total follows from its design and is not independent experimental proof. These are proposed activities, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3: conservation of mass in changes of state and chemical reactions; conservation of material and mass and reversibility in melting/freezing/evaporation/sublimation/condensation/dissolving
NGSS 5-PS1-2: measure and graph to show total weight of matter is conserved regardless of change type (heating/cooling/mixing/dissolving)
Students think mass is lost when a gas escapes an open container or when a solid dissolves; sealing the system and accounting for gas resolves it
learnerActions: Place water and sugar, initially separate but both inside the same covered container, on a balance and record the whole-system reading.
Without adding or removing material, mix until the sugar dissolves. Reweigh the covered container in the same position, allowing any movement of the balance to settle.

Compare the readings within the balance’s resolution and explain why invisible dissolved sugar is still present. If readings differ, consider spills, evaporation, material left outside the weighed system or measurement variation before drawing a conclusion.

Use a particle picture or optional overlay to show sugar particles dispersed through the water rather than destroyed. Then test a change of state: weigh an ice cube sealed in a bag or covered container, let it melt at room temperature, wipe off any condensation that forms on the outside, and reweigh. Explain why the water's mass stays the same within the balance's resolution even though its state changed.
Use prepared experimental observations or a labelled model of an open vinegar-and-bicarbonate reaction. Predict what happens as gas leaves the weighed system, then inspect the data or model output.

Compare with prepared data or a model of a closed system that retains the gas. An optional flexible bag or flask-with-balloon illustration shows how gas can remain within the system; it is not a home procedure for sealing a gas-producing reaction in a rigid vessel.

Explain the distinction: total mass is conserved when all material is included, while a measured balance reading may change if matter escapes or if the apparatus expands and displaces more air. A model illustrates its built-in assumptions rather than supplying new experimental evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Dissolved material retains its mass. Chemical reactions rearrange atoms into products, including gases, without destroying the atoms. A closed system retains the material; an open weighed container can lose material as gas leaves. Balance readings must be interpreted with the measurement conditions.

activities.title: Consolidate: where did the mass go?
feedback: If the learner cannot say where material went, identify it explicitly: dissolved sugar remains in the liquid; escaped gas has left the weighed container; trapped gas remains part of a closed system.

A worked diagram can support explanation and review. Ask the learner to interpret fresh measurements or data too, and distinguish a schematic constant mass from a claim that every real balance reading must be identical.
activities.rationale: A before/after diagram with optional explanation flaps offers a worked example and a chance to compare the learner’s account with a material-tracking explanation. It does not establish an experimental result by itself; this is a proposed companion to measurements or prepared data.
learnerActions: Study before/after measurement data or diagrams for dissolving and open-versus-closed gas-producing reactions. Identify whether each display represents real measurements, idealised data or a model.
Reveal a 'where did the mass go?' explanation flap and check it against your own reasoning.

For the open reaction, explain why escaping gas can lower the reading. State which material must be included in a closed-system comparison, and why a flexible expanding apparatus can complicate the balance reading.
Account for every bit of matter in the change by naming where it ended up (in solution, as trapped gas, etc.).
activities.intendedInsight: Conservation requires accounting for material and system boundaries. Invisible dissolved material remains present, and gas has mass; apparent measurement changes need an explanation based on what was weighed and how it was measured.

activities.title: Predict and justify the balance reading
feedback: If the numerical prediction has a weak reason, ask which material is where and whether gas remains inside the system.

If a learner predicts less total mass in the closed model, ask where any atoms would have gone. If they predict a small decrease in a real expanding-balloon balance reading, discuss buoyancy and measurement effects instead of automatically marking it wrong.

Require an explanation for an open-system decrease that tracks escaping matter rather than claiming that gas disappears or has no mass. Consider additional measurement effects if the data require them.
activities.rationale: Prediction plus explanation can reveal whether a learner tracks material and distinguishes the system from its measured reading. Compare predictions with actual dissolving measurements or prepared gas-reaction data; model output is a conditional illustration. No effectiveness claim is established for this task design.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-PS1-2: measure and graph to show total weight of matter is conserved regardless of change type (heating/cooling/mixing/dissolving)
learnerActions: Before revealing the data, predict the total mass for a closed dissolving system and an idealised closed gas-reaction model. Separately predict what a real balance might show, noting measurement precision and whether the apparatus expands.
Choose, from options, the correct explanation for why an OPEN fizzing reaction appears to lose mass.
Justify each prediction by naming the system boundary, the material present and any material that can leave. For a chemical reaction, refer to atoms rearranging into new products, including gas.
activities.intendedInsight: A useful prediction distinguishes conserved total mass from an instrument reading and is supported by tracking material, including gas, rather than by reciting a slogan.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: compare open and closed system data
feedback: If the learner says the wax or tablet is used up and gone, distinguish a starting substance being consumed from its atoms disappearing. Trace those atoms into products, and include oxygen entering a combustion system.

If the learner says gas has no mass, use reliable prepared measurements or an appropriate established classroom demonstration to show that gases contribute mass. Avoid treating inflation of a flexible balloon as a direct mass measurement without considering displaced air.

If the learner thinks dissolved sugar adds no mass, account for the known sugar added to the same initial water amount and check for spills or evaporation. The dissolved material remains in the system.

A full explanation predicts conserved total mass for a closed system, traces atoms into products, tracks escaped gas in an open system, and separates the principle from measurement artefacts. For physical dissolving, the sugar disperses rather than vanishing.
activities.rationale: The contrast between a recited conservation rule and an explanation that tracks atoms, products and boundaries can be explored through prediction and data interpretation. The candle and dissolving extensions test transfer to different changes. Real measurements, idealised data and model outputs must be identified separately; these proposals have not been empirically validated.
sourceClaims: Students think mass is lost when a gas escapes an open container or when a solid dissolves; sealing the system and accounting for gas resolves it
learnerActions: Use a prepared measurement record of an effervescent tablet reacting with water in an open vessel. Before viewing the later readings, predict their trend and explain where the produced gas can go.
Compare with prepared data from an established supervised closed-system protocol, or use a clearly labelled idealised model. Do not improvise a stopper-on rigid-flask reaction.

Observe the records or model outputs. For a closed system, explain conserved total mass; if real readings differ, inspect the apparatus, expansion, possible leakage and measurement precision instead of assuming matter was destroyed.

Use a flexible-bag or flask-with-balloon illustration to explain that retaining gas accounts for the material. Label expansion and its possible buoyancy effect on the balance; no exact unchanged reading is guaranteed.

Transfer the explanation to a diagram of a candle burning: identify oxygen entering and gaseous products leaving an open system, rather than treating wax alone as the whole system. Explain why a sealed-jar scenario differs without performing a sealed combustion experiment.
For water and sugar, compare equal initial water amounts before and after adding a known sugar mass without losing material. Explain why dissolved sugar adds mass even though it is no longer visible.
activities.intendedInsight: Atoms persist through the chemical reactions and are rearranged into products: an effervescent reaction produces gas and dissolved products; wax burning consumes oxygen and produces gases. The total mass of all inputs and outputs is conserved. Open-vessel readings omit escaping material, while closed-system readings still require attention to measurement conditions.

constraints: Target age 10–11; keep chemical-reaction conservation light — water, dissolving, and a simple gas-producing reaction are the core cases.
Always require learners to account for the WHOLE system, including any gas produced or absorbed; this is the crux that resolves the apparent-loss cases.

Distinguish the changes accurately: combustion (wax burning) is not the same as an effervescent tablet reacting in water; both conserve mass but by different reactions, so do not label the fizzing tablet as 'burnt'.

Do not improvise a sealed rigid-vessel gas-producing reaction. Use prepared data or a clearly labelled model for the closed-gas comparison unless an adult is following an established supervised school protocol with appropriate apparatus and risk assessment. A flexible bag or balloon can illustrate gas retention, but expansion changes air buoyancy and can alter the apparent balance reading.

Worked diagrams, explanation flaps, data tables and models may support interpretation. Distinguish their stated or built-in results from measurements the learner makes; no single format is a necessary first teaching method.
Predict-only or recognition-only responses do not show whether a learner can trace the matter through the change; require an explanation that names where the matter went.

Ask for an account of the material and system boundary, not just a slogan. Distinguish physical changes, in which material can disperse or change state, from chemical changes, in which atoms rearrange into different substances.

Interpret observations within instrument resolution and experimental conditions. Total mass conservation does not require an identical balance display when a flexible container expands, gas leaks, material evaporates, or temperature and air currents affect the reading.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The saved research used categorical medium preferences. This guidance retains distinct affordances—physical measurements, worked diagrams, prediction checks and optional models—without claiming that one format is necessary or that these activities are proven effective.
The original claim that a sim 'delivers the law and its key caveat' and similar strong efficacy wording has not been empirically established by the cited sources; retained as proposals only.
One source ('Students think mass is lost...' ACS/RSC guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unverified in any downstream use.

Editorial repair distinguishes conserved mass from a changing apparent balance reading, atoms from molecules in chemical reactions, and physical observations from built-in model results. Gas-reaction comparisons use prepared data or a model unless an established supervised protocol is available.

The factual audit correctly raised the buoyancy effect of expanding flexible apparatus, but its proposed capped-bottle procedure was not adopted. This guidance removes improvised sealed rigid gas-reaction instructions and exact-reading guarantees. No fresh source verification was performed.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: put a fizzing tablet and water in a flask, first with the stopper OFF, then a fresh one with the stopper ON, each on a balance. Ask the child to predict each reading over time and WHY. A 'matter destroyed / gas weightless' model predicts a drop in both. Open drops (gas escapes); sealed stays constant. The pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I did the SAME candle burning in the OPEN air on the balance, would the reading change? Why is that different from the sealed jar?
The wax turned into gas — does that gas weigh anything? How could we prove it?
Dissolve sugar until it vanishes: is the beaker heavier, lighter, or the same? Why?
If matter is never destroyed, where exactly did every bit of the wax end up?
assess.correctAnswer: In the SEALED jar the total reading stays the SAME: matter isn't destroyed — the wax turns into gases (carbon dioxide and water vapour) that are still inside the jar, so the total mass is conserved. The reason must invoke 'the gas is still there and has mass', not just 'nothing changed'.

errorPatterns.pattern: burning destroys matter, so mass is lost ('the wax is used up and gone')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track the atoms: wax + oxygen → CO2 + water vapour, all still in the sealed jar. Weigh a sealed reaction to show no drop. Confront the 'used up' idea directly.
errorPatterns.distractor: It goes down, because the wax is burnt away and gone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts the reading drops; can't say where the wax went

errorPatterns.pattern: gases have no mass / weigh nothing ('it's only gas now, so it weighs less')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Weigh a sealed syringe/flask of gas vs vacuum, or an inflated vs deflated ball — gas has mass. Then re-run the conservation argument.
errorPatterns.distractor: It goes down, because gas doesn't weigh anything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: accepts gas forms but says gas is weightless, so predicts a drop

errorPatterns.pattern: dissolved solid stops contributing to weight because you can't see it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Weigh water, add sugar, weigh again — heavier by the sugar. Invisible isn't weightless; link back to dissolving conservation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: for the dissolving case, says sugar-water weighs the same as plain water

responseLevels.gap: Predicts a change in the sealed jar because matter is destroyed or gas is weightless; can't track where the wax went.
responseLevels.full: Predicts 'same' in the sealed jar AND explains by tracking matter (wax→gases still present, gases have mass), correctly distinguishes the open system (gas leaves), and applies conservation to dissolving — invisible is not weightless.
responseLevels.partial: States 'mass is conserved / matter isn't destroyed' and predicts 'same' for the sealed jar, but can't explain the OPEN-air case (gas escapes) or apply conservation to dissolving — the principle is recited, not traced through the matter.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I weigh a lit candle sitting on a balance in a sealed jar. As it burns, wax disappears. Does the reading on the balance go down, up, or stay the same while it burns in the sealed jar? Then the key part: explain WHY, using where the matter goes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason distinguishes a child who tracks matter through the change (wax→invisible gases that still weigh something, trapped in the jar) from one who believes burning/dissolving destroys matter or that gases are weightless. The sealed jar is chosen precisely so a 'matter is destroyed' model predicts a DROP.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: The inverse relationship between addition and subtraction — addition and subtraction 'undo' each other, so a known sum yields three related facts and a subtraction can be checked by adding back. Ages 6–7, building on unknown-addend and fact families.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction and use this to check calculations and solve missing number problems'. Reappears in KS2 for checking with larger numbers.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 1.OA.4 (subtraction as unknown addend) and 1.OA.6 relationships; supports 2.NBT/3.NBT checking by inverse. Inverse operations are the explicit mechanism for solving □ + 9 = 14 and verifying answers.
• Operational details: teach through the fact family / part-whole triangle — one whole and two parts generate 2 additions and 2 subtractions. Use inverse deliberately for TWO jobs: (a) checking (15 + 7 = 22, so 22 − 7 should give 15) and (b) solving missing-number equations (□ + 9 = 14 → □ = 14 − 9). Emphasise it is a relationship between operations, not a new procedure.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — given 6 + 4 = 10 states 10 − 4 = 6 and 10 − 6 = 4. Tier B (age 7) — solves □ + 9 = 14 by subtracting and checks a subtraction by adding back. Tier C (age 7+) — explains that addition undoes subtraction and uses inverse to check a calculation with two-digit numbers.
bestPractices: Anchor on the fact-family triangle / part-whole model so all four related facts come from one whole and two parts.
Make 'checking by the inverse' a routine habit after every calculation, not an add-on.
Use inverse explicitly to convert a missing-number equation into a calculation the child can do (□ + 9 = 14 → 14 − 9).
Keep the SAME three numbers while flipping the operation, so the child sees one relationship rather than four separate facts.
Contrast with situations where inverse reasoning is misapplied, e.g. reminding that order matters in the subtraction facts (10 − 6 vs 6 − 10).
keyRepresentations: Fact-family / part-whole triangle (one whole, two parts, four facts)
Bar model with the whole and two parts, read as add or subtract
Empty number line showing a forward jump and its reversing backward jump
Balance model where adding then subtracting the same amount returns to start
Cuisenaire rods showing a+b and the reverse whole−a
commonMisconceptions: Treating the four fact-family facts as unrelated things to memorise separately.
Believing subtraction facts can also be reversed freely (10 − 6 = 6 − 10), over-extending the 'undo' idea.
Checking a sum by repeating the SAME operation rather than using the inverse.
Solving □ + 9 = 14 by adding 9 and 14, not recognising subtraction as the inverse move.
Thinking 'undoing' requires a different, brand-new procedure rather than the operation they already know.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year-olds see that addition and subtraction undo each other, so one known sum (e.g. 15 + 7 = 22) generates all four related facts, lets you check a calculation by reversing it, and lets you solve a missing-number equation (□ + 9 = 14) by subtracting. The core aim is to treat these as ONE relationship between operations, not four separate facts to memorise. Builds on fact families and part-whole/unknown-addend ideas.

activities.title: Do and undo it on a number line (with a fact-family triangle)
feedback: If the learner recomputes the subtraction from scratch, point back to the triangle: the whole (22) and two parts (15, 7) already give the subtraction — read it off rather than counting again.
If the learner writes 15 − 7 = 22 or similar, mark on the bar/triangle which number is the whole: you can only take a part away FROM the whole, and 15 and 7 are both parts.

If the learner checks 15 + 7 = 22 by just adding 15 + 7 again, point out that repeating the same calculation can repeat the same mistake. Reversing it (22 − 7 = 15) is a real check, in the same way that adding the parts back (15 + 7) checks the subtraction 22 − 7 = 15.
When the backward jump lands exactly on 15, name it: 'the subtraction undid the addition.'
activities.rationale: A reversible forward/backward action makes 'undo' literal and ties all four facts to a single whole-and-parts structure, directly targeting the misconception that related facts are unrelated. The number-line and triangle are one way to realise this; equivalent reversing can be shown on paper, on a balance model, or with Cuisenaire rods, and none of these media is required over the others.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations and solve missing-number problems.
Fact families and the inverse relationship are taught via part-whole structures; children commonly treat related facts as separate and check by repeating rather than reversing.
learnerActions: Start at 15 on a number line and make a forward jump of +7, landing on 22.
Before reversing, predict out loud where a backward jump of 7 will land and why.
Make the backward jump of −7 and confirm you return exactly to 15.
Say in your own words why the subtraction lands back on the start: it is the same jump run in reverse.
Fill in a fact-family triangle with the whole (22) and the two parts (15 and 7), then write all four facts: 15 + 7 = 22, 7 + 15 = 22, 22 − 7 = 15, 22 − 15 = 7.
Check a subtraction by adding the parts back: verify 22 − 7 = 15 by computing 15 + 7.

(Optional) Show the same reversing with another model: a balance that returns to its start after you add then subtract the same amount, or Cuisenaire rods laid as 15 + 7 and then the whole with one part removed.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction reverses addition over the SAME three numbers, so taking one part from the whole returns the other part; one sum gives four related facts and a built-in way to check.

activities.title: Solve a missing number by reversing
feedback: If the learner adds 9 and 14, remind them that the box plus 9 already makes 14, so you need to take 9 away from 14 to find the box.
Praise a correct check that substitutes the answer back into the original equation (5 + 9 = 14).
activities.rationale: Turning the equation into a doable subtraction shows inverse operations as the mechanism for solving, not a brand-new procedure.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations and solve missing-number problems.
Understanding subtraction as an unknown addend (1.OA.4) and part-whole/fact-family relationships underpins using inverse operations to solve and check.
learnerActions: Look at □ + 9 = 14 and decide what operation would find the missing part.
Explain why subtracting (14 − 9) finds the box: addition and subtraction undo each other.
Compute □ = 14 − 9 = 5 and check by putting it back: 5 + 9 = 14.
Try one or two more missing-number equations, each solved by the inverse and then checked by adding back.
activities.intendedInsight: A missing-addend equation becomes a calculation you can already do by using the inverse operation, and the answer can be confirmed by reversing again.

activities.title: Explain WHY adding back proves a subtraction
feedback: If the learner says 15 − 7 = 22, steer to the whole: 22 is the whole; you subtract a part from the whole, so valid subtractions are 22 − 7 and 22 − 15.
If the learner only recites facts without saying the operations undo each other, ask them to point to the jump that reverses the addition.
Accept a justification that names 22 as the whole and explains the returned part.
activities.rationale: A justification prompt exercises the conceptual 'explain' goal and lets a learner confront the over-generalisation that any pair of the three numbers reverses.
sourceClaims: Fact families and the inverse relationship are taught via part-whole structures; children commonly treat related facts as separate and check by repeating rather than reversing.
learnerActions: Given 22 − 7 = 15, explain how you could be sure it is right WITHOUT redoing the subtraction.
Discuss the difference between reversing (adding the parts back) and simply repeating the same subtraction.
Respond to the claim that 'subtraction undoes too, so 15 − 7 = 22' and explain why that is wrong using which number is the whole.
State a DIFFERENT true subtraction from the same three numbers (22 − 15 = 7) and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking works because addition reverses subtraction over the same whole and parts; the 'undo' idea applies to taking a part from the whole, not to any rearrangement of the three numbers.

activities.title: Match and consolidate related facts
feedback: For a choice that repeats 15 + 7, explain that a genuine check reverses the operation; an inverse check is 22 − 7 = 15 (or 22 − 15 = 7).
For a mismatched subtraction, return to the whole-and-parts triangle.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fill-in tasks consolidate the four related facts and the inverse check; on their own they confirm familiarity but recognition alone does not require the learner to produce and feel the do-and-undo action.
learnerActions: Match one sum (15 + 7 = 22) to its three related facts.
Fill in blanks in missing-number equations such as □ + 9 = 14, solving by the inverse.
Choose which calculation correctly checks 15 + 7 = 22, distinguishing an inverse check (22 − 7 = 15 or 22 − 15 = 7) from a decoy that just repeats the same addition.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall and recognition of the four related facts and the correct inverse check, reinforcing the single relationship.

constraints: Keep the SAME three numbers while flipping the operation so the learner sees one relationship, not four isolated facts.
Make 'check by the inverse' a routine habit after calculating, in line with the objective, rather than an optional afterthought.

Distinguish the whole from the parts explicitly: subtractions take a part from the whole (22 − 7, 22 − 15); a part minus a part (15 − 7) is NOT one of this fact family's four facts (15 − 7 = 8 is a valid operation but a different problem).
Emphasise that subtraction does not reverse 'freely' — order matters, so do not over-extend the undo idea to 15 − 7 = 22.

A fixed/static fact-family picture with tappable corners can anchor the four facts and the checking idea, but it does not let the learner perform the reversing action; it can support rather than stand in for do-and-undo work.

Recognition and matching tasks can check recall of the four related facts and the correct inverse check, but recognition alone does not elicit independent production or the felt experience of reversing; pair them with reversing and explanation work rather than relying on them alone, without mandating a particular medium or strict ordering.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's correctAnswer field contains self-corrected scratch text ('22 − 6... no — 22 − 15 = 7'); the two valid related subtractions are 22 − 7 = 15 and 22 − 15 = 7. This rewrite uses only the corrected forms and never offers the scratch value as an option.

The original listed a '3D adds nothing' judgement for this numeric relationship; this is a catalog fit opinion, not an established pedagogical law, so it is omitted from learner-facing guidance. A third spatial dimension is simply not needed here, but no universal-necessity claim is made either way.
Two source claims (CCSS-M grade 1; Carpenter et al. CGI) were marked unverified in the original; retained as cited where they support a principle, without upgrading their confidence.

The interactive number-line/triangle, 'undo'/'check' controls, tappable corners, linked panes, balance model, and Cuisenaire rods are optional concrete examples of the same reversing mechanism, not mandatory tooling; the reversing and checking can equally be done on paper. No claim is made that any one medium teaches this better than another.

assess.poeTask: Predict what happens if you start at 15, jump forward 7 on a number line, then jump back 7. Say where you'll land and why BEFORE you move. Then do it — what does landing back on 15 tell you about how adding and subtracting 7 are related?
probeDeeper: Why does taking 7 away from 22 have to give 15 back?
Which of your three numbers is the whole, and how does that decide the subtractions?
If I made a mistake and wrote 22 − 7 = 16, how would the inverse show me I was wrong?
Can you also make a DIFFERENT true subtraction from these three numbers? What is it?
assess.correctAnswer: 22 − 7 = 15 (or 22 − 6... no — 22 − 15 = 7). Either 22 − 7 = 15 or 22 − 15 = 7. Explanation: subtraction undoes addition, so taking back one part from the whole must return the other part — the three numbers form one whole (22) and two parts (15 and 7).

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the facts as separate — recomputes a subtraction from scratch rather than reading it off the relationship.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the fact-family triangle: one whole and two parts generate all four facts; practise reading them off without recalculating.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Starts counting/calculating a subtraction instead of deriving it from 15 + 7 = 22.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Subtraction undoes too, so 15 − 7 also works' — over-extends reversal and offers an invalid subtraction from the wrong pair.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the bar model, mark which number is the whole (22) — you can only take a part FROM the whole; 15 and 7 are both parts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 15 − 7 = 22 or similar, subtracting a part from a part or expecting the whole as the answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'To check it, do 15 + 7 again' — checks by repeating the same operation rather than the inverse.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast repeating (same errors reappear) with reversing; establish adding-back as the check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to check, re-adds the two numbers instead of subtracting.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a valid related subtraction, or recomputes with no sense of relationship; may give 15 − 7.
responseLevels.full: States a valid subtraction, identifies 22 as the whole, and justifies it by inverse reasoning ('subtraction undoes addition, so the part comes back'), and can use it to check or solve a missing-number equation.
responseLevels.partial: Produces a correct related subtraction but justifies it by calculating, or lists the facts without saying the operations undo each other; doesn't reliably identify the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I worked out that 15 + 7 = 22. Using only those three numbers, tell me a subtraction that must also be true — and explain how you know it is true without working it out from scratch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has memorised facts separately, or who thinks checking means redoing, will either recompute or offer an invalid rearrangement (e.g. 15 − 7). A child who holds the inverse relationship names a valid subtraction immediately and justifies it by 'undoing' rather than by calculating — the 'without working it out' clause is what forces the relational justification.

pedagogy.summary: This is a vocabulary/naming topic: children learn the eight planets in order from the Sun and the core space nouns (planet, star, sun, moon, satellite, orbit, solar system, galaxy, universe, asteroid, comet), and use them correctly to describe what is in the sky. It is best taught by pairing each word with a vivid canonical image and one defining feature, using a memorable mnemonic for planet order, building the load-bearing verb 'orbit' (what goes round what), and explicitly separating the confusable categories — the Sun is a star (not a planet), the Moon is not a planet, stars make their own light while planets shine by reflection.
bestPractices: Anchor each term to a canonical image plus one defining feature — a star makes its own light; a planet orbits a star and shines by reflected light; a moon orbits a planet; a comet trails a tail.
Teach planet order with a mnemonic (e.g. 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming') and repeated ordering practice, since naming the eight in order is the headline evidence.

Build the nested 'orbit' idea early — moons orbit planets, planets orbit the Sun (a star), the solar system sits within a galaxy — because 'orbit' is the word every later Earth-and-space topic depends on.
Explicitly separate confusable categories: the Sun IS a star, the Moon is NOT a planet, a 'shooting star' is not a star, and asteroids are small/irregular not planets.
Flag that pictures are not to scale (planets are not really crammed together or the same size) so the vocabulary does not smuggle in a scale misconception.
Keep the focus on naming and correct use at this age — defer mechanisms (why things orbit, phases) to later topics.
keyRepresentations: An ordered row of the eight planets out from the Sun, with the Sun labelled as a star.
A nested-orbit picture: Moon → Earth, planets → Sun, solar system within a galaxy within the universe.
Word–picture cards pairing each vocabulary term with an image and one distinguishing feature.
A mnemonic strip for planet order.
commonMisconceptions: The Sun is a planet (it is a star) — or, conversely, the Sun is not a star at all.
The Moon is a planet, rather than a satellite orbiting Earth.
Stars and planets are the same, and a 'shooting star' (a meteor) is a star.
Pluto is still the ninth planet — it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Planets are all similar in size and packed close together, a scale error picked up from diagrams.

learn.summary: A space-vocabulary/naming topic for ages 5–8: learn the eight planets in order from the Sun and the core space nouns (planet, star, sun, moon, satellite, orbit, solar system, galaxy, universe, asteroid, comet), and use them correctly to describe what is in the sky. Anchor each word to a canonical image plus one defining feature, lock in planet order with a mnemonic and ordering practice, build the load-bearing verb 'orbit' (what goes round what), and explicitly separate confusable categories — the Sun is a star (not a planet), the Moon is a satellite (not a planet), stars make their own light while planets shine by reflected light. Keep the focus on naming and correct use; defer mechanisms (why things orbit, phases) to later topics.

activities.title: Tap-through solar-system scene with category badges
feedback: When the Sun is tapped, confirm it is a STAR at the centre of our solar system, not a planet.

At the two-dot night-sky panel, name which is a planet and which is a star and give the test: one makes its own light, the other only reflects it (this is revealed by the panel, not judged by looking).
When zooming out, name each nested level in order (solar system, then galaxy, then universe) so the move outward matches the words.
activities.rationale: A naming/vocabulary topic pairs each term with a canonical image and one defining feature; tap-to-reveal lets a child meet each word with its picture and category. The two-dot comparison is intended to make the star/planet distinction clear through the reveal rather than merely stated; it is not a criterion a young child can reliably judge visually.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 non-statutory guidance states the Sun is a star at the centre of our solar system with 8 planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), that Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and that a moon is a body that orbits a planet.
A common category confusion is that the Sun/Moon are treated as fixed or miscategorised and that children conflate stars and planets; correcting category vocabulary is a documented teaching need.
learnerActions: Explore a single richly labelled solar-system scene where tapping each body reveals its name, one memorable feature, and a category badge: planet / star / moon / asteroid / comet.
Tap the Sun to lift a flap that declares 'I'm a star, not a planet'.
Use a lift-the-flap that contrasts how a moon differs from a planet (a moon — also called a natural satellite — orbits a planet; a planet orbits the Sun).
Tap a comet to reveal its name and its defining feature — an icy body that grows a glowing tail when it comes near the Sun — so every target word has a picture-and-feature anchor.
Follow a zoom-out drill-down that travels outward: solar system → Milky Way galaxy → universe, so the nesting words land as places you move out through.
Tap two look-alike dots in a night-sky panel; the panel reveals that one is a planet (shines by borrowed, reflected light) and the other a star (makes its own light).
activities.intendedInsight: Each space word belongs to a specific kind of object, and the key distinction the whole vocabulary hinges on — a star makes its own light, a planet shines by reflected light — is made clear through the tap-reveal comparison of two look-alike dots; it is not something a child can simply judge by eye.

activities.title: Order the planets and sort sky objects
feedback: Snap a planet into place when it is in the correct position; on a wrong placement, say which planet should come next out from the Sun.
When an object is mis-sorted, restate the sorting test for the correct bin (e.g. 'a moon orbits a planet, so the Moon goes in the moon bin, not the planet bin').
activities.rationale: Active naming and sorting with immediate feedback directly rehearse the two evidence goals (order the planets; distinguish planet/star/moon/asteroid); a mnemonic supports recall of the sequence. Placement and sorting rehearse recognition and sequencing; they do not by themselves demonstrate spontaneous correct use.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 non-statutory guidance states the Sun is a star at the centre of our solar system with 8 planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), that Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and that a moon is a body that orbits a planet.
learnerActions: Drag the eight planets into correct order outward from the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), using a mnemonic such as 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming' as a memory aid.

Sort a set of sky objects into bins by category: makes its own light (star), a big, round world that orbits the Sun and shines by borrowed light (planet), orbits a planet (moon), a small rocky body that orbits the Sun, often lumpy in shape (asteroid).
Repeat the ordering until the sequence is secure.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming the eight planets in order and placing each sky object in the right category are the two headline skills, rehearsed through active placement with feedback.

activities.title: Build the nested 'orbit' idea with hands and narration
feedback: If 'orbit' is used to mean 'near' or 'next to', ask the child to show the circling motion with a hand and re-state what goes around what; give more move-and-narrate practice rather than drilling dictionary definitions.
If the Sun is called a planet, contrast light-MAKER (star) with light-BORROWER (planet) and sort a few objects by that test.

If a star and planet, or moon and star, are confused, sort sky objects three ways: makes its own light (star), a big, round world that orbits the Sun and shines by borrowed light (planet), orbits a planet (moon).
activities.rationale: 'Orbit' is the load-bearing verb every later Earth-and-space topic depends on; it is sometimes acquired before its full meaning attaches, so the circling sense is best built through move-and-narrate use rather than recited definitions. This developmental point comes from the assessment notes, not from a cited source.
learnerActions: Show 'orbit' with a hand — move one fist around another and say what is going around what.
Narrate the nesting: the Moon orbits the Earth; the planets orbit the Sun (a star); the solar system sits within a galaxy, within the universe.

Answer probe questions: 'Is the Sun a planet, or something else?'; 'What does the Moon orbit — the Earth or the Sun?' (it orbits the Earth, and travels around the Sun together with the Earth); 'If I said Mars is a moon, would that be right? Why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: 'Orbit' means travelling around, not being near or next to — and the going-around relationships are nested (moon→planet, planet→Sun).

constraints: Keep the focus on naming and correct use at this age; defer mechanisms (why things orbit, phases of the Moon) to later topics.
Diagrams are not to scale — planets are not really the same size or crammed close together. State this explicitly so the vocabulary does not smuggle in a scale misconception.
Pluto is a dwarf planet (reclassified in 2006), not the ninth planet; a 'shooting star' is a meteor, not a star.

Do not drill dictionary definitions of 'orbit'; the goal is correct use in running speech, not reciting definitions. Reciting the planet mnemonic without being able to point-and-apply is rote-without-use.

Sorting bins and drag-to-order give recognition and sequencing practice; they do not by themselves show the child can use the words correctly in spontaneous description — pair with narration where the child walks the model outward and names each body and its motion.
An orbiting 3D model can convey the spatial sense of 'orbit', but naming is fully served in 2D; treat 3D as an optional engagement aid, not a requirement for this naming goal.

Open conversation/role-play does not by itself drill a fixed term set or the planet sequence; for early readers it may be better suited to consolidating vocabulary after the terms have been introduced than to first establishing them.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (IOPSpark teaching-and-learning issues) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim about documented category confusion as unconfirmed.

The source row's 3D-interactive note asserts '3D adds scale and cost without extra naming payoff' and the conversation note asserts an 'open dialogue is the wrong vehicle'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

The 'light-borrower vs light-maker' sorting test is a sound heuristic for star/planet; the original recommendation also cited planets 'wandering', but this is not reliably perceptible to young learners at a single glance, so it is dropped from the learner-facing two-dot panel and the star/planet distinction there is revealed by the interactive reveal rather than by eye.

Activity 3's 'orbit' rationale derives from the assessment's developmental error pattern, not from either cited source; sourceClaims left empty rather than citing the IOPSpark category-confusion claim, which concerns star/planet conflation, not the meaning of 'orbit'.

The original best practices paired 'comet' with the feature 'trails a tail'; that pairing has now been added to the tap-through scene so every target term has a canonical image+feature anchor. Whether 'comet' should also carry its own sorting-bin/badge category alongside planet/star/moon/asteroid is a design judgement not resolved by the source row.

probeDeeper: You said Jupiter orbits the Sun — show me 'orbit' with your hand. What is moving around what?
Is the Sun a planet, or something else? How is it different from Earth?
The Moon — does it go around the Sun, or around us? How do you know?
If I said 'Mars is a moon,' would that be right? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: In running speech the child names the planets Mercury→Neptune in order, uses 'orbit' for the going-around motion (planets orbit the Sun; the Moon orbits the Earth), calls the Sun a star, a satellite a 'moon', and applies 'asteroid' correctly — reserving each term for the right object rather than reciting definitions.

errorPatterns.pattern: treats the Sun as a planet — 'the Sun is the biggest planet' — because it is a big ball in space
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast light-MAKER (star) with light-BORROWER (planet): the Sun makes its own light, planets only reflect it; sort a few objects by that test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: labels the Sun a planet while walking the model outward

errorPatterns.pattern: uses 'orbit' to mean 'near/next-to' rather than 'travelling around' — a word acquired before its full meaning attaches
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill dictionary definitions; give more move-and-narrate practice ('show me orbit with your hand — what goes around what?') so the circling sense attaches through use.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the Moon 'orbits' beside the Earth, or applies 'orbit' to a body's position rather than its motion

errorPatterns.pattern: stars and planets are the same, just dots — 'a moon is a little star'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort sky objects three ways: makes its own light (star), borrows light and orbits the Sun (planet), orbits a planet (moon).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls a star a planet or a moon a star while pointing

responseLevels.gap: Recites planet names (often via a mnemonic) but mislabels object types — calls the Sun a planet, uses 'orbit' for position, cannot distinguish star, planet and moon.
responseLevels.full: While describing the model names Mercury→Neptune in order, uses 'orbit' correctly for both planets-round-Sun and Moon-round-Earth, and cleanly distinguishes star, planet, moon and asteroid — transferring the words to a new object when asked 'what would you call…?'
responseLevels.partial: Names the planets in order and uses 'orbit' for the Sun–planet motion, but slips on one relation (e.g. the Moon orbiting the Sun) or one category (asteroid vs planet).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a picture of the Sun with lots of things around it. Walk me from the Sun outwards and tell me the story of our solar system — point to each thing, tell me what it is and how it moves.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the words but not the concepts mislabels while narrating — calls the Sun a planet, says the Sun 'orbits' Earth, or uses 'orbit' to mean 'is near'. A child with secure vocabulary uses each term for the right object and reserves 'orbit' for the circling motion. Reciting the planet mnemonic while being unable to point-and-apply reveals rote-without-use, which a 'define X' question would miss.

pedagogy.summary: By Year 5 children move from counting squares to using formulae: area of a rectangle = length × width, perimeter = 2 × (length + width), with AREA in square units (cm², m²) and PERIMETER in linear units (cm, m). They apply these both ways (e.g. find a missing side from area and one dimension), compare areas, and estimate the area of irregular shapes on a cm² grid by counting whole and part squares. The central risk is that the formulae are learned instrumentally and area and perimeter get confused; the antidote is to keep each formula anchored to its meaning — area as the number of unit squares covering the surface, perimeter as the distance around the edge.
bestPractices: Keep area tied to covering unit squares and perimeter to the distance around even once formulae are used, so the two are not conflated (relational, not merely instrumental).
Teach area = l × w as an array of unit squares (rows × columns) and perimeter as 2×(l+w); label every answer with correct units (cm² vs cm).
Work both directions: give the area and one side and find the other (area 48 m², length 8 m → width 6 m); express missing-measure problems algebraically, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20.
Estimate irregular area on a cm² grid by counting whole squares and combining part-squares (count a part square if it is at least half), and treat the result explicitly as an estimate.
Use grids, tiles and cut-and-fit activities alongside the formulae so children can see where l × w comes from.
keyRepresentations: cm² grid / squared paper
Unit-square array (rows × columns)
Rectangle with labelled length and width
String-around-the-edge model for perimeter
Algebraic missing-measure equation (e.g. 4 + 2b = 20)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses area and perimeter — uses one formula for the other, or gives the distance around when asked for the covered surface.
Overgeneralises 'area = length × breadth' and reports the answer in linear units (cm) instead of square units (cm²).
When estimating irregular area, counts only whole squares and ignores part-squares (or counts every touched square as a whole).

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils move from counting squares to applying area = length × width and perimeter = 2 × (length + width) for rectangles (including squares), used both forwards and to find a missing side, with area labelled in square units (cm², m²) and perimeter in linear units (cm, m). They also estimate the area of irregular shapes on a cm² grid by counting whole and part squares, treating the result as an estimate. The central risk is instrumental learning that confuses area and perimeter or reports area in linear units; the antidote is keeping each formula anchored to meaning — area as unit squares covering the surface, perimeter as distance around the edge. Activities below range from a hands-on/grid manipulation intended to make the two quantities visibly distinct, through a tap-to-reveal formula scaffold, to a checking quiz, each with its own purpose and limits.

activities.title: Grid playground: reshape a rectangle and watch area and perimeter move apart
feedback: If you used one formula for both, or got the same number by mixing up the methods: shade the whole surface for area (count squares) and run a finger around the edge for perimeter (count length) — rebuild area as covering unit squares before using l × w again. (Getting the same number is not wrong in itself: a 4×4 square really has area 16 cm² and perimeter 16 cm, and the units are still different.)
If you labelled the area in cm instead of cm²: point to one covering square — because area counts squares, it is measured in square units; keep the multiplication, just fix the unit.

For the blob: agree one rule — either 'count a part-square as one if it is at least half, ignore smaller parts' or 'pair up part-squares that together make about one whole' — use it consistently, and say your answer could be a little more or less because it is an estimate.
To check that the two really differ: reshape 6×4 into 12×2 — the area stays 24 cm² but the perimeter changes (from 20 cm to 28 cm), showing they are not the same thing.
activities.rationale: Keeping area tied to covering unit squares and perimeter to distance around — with both counts visible as the shape changes, so one can stay fixed while the other moves — is intended to support relational rather than instrumental understanding and to address the confusion of the two. Live, side-by-side counters in two units (an optional interaction example) can make the distinction concrete; the same can be achieved with physical squared paper, tiles and a finger-trace. Calculating areas and perimeters of rectangles and estimating irregular areas reflect the Year 5 statutory expectations; working backwards to a missing side reflects the non-statutory guidance.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: 'calculate and compare the area of rectangles (including squares), including using standard units, square centimetres (cm²) and square metres (m²), and estimate the area of irregular shapes'; 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: missing-measure problems can be expressed algebraically, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20.

Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae are taught together without conceptual grounding; they overgeneralise A = l × b to non-rectangles ('most children respond to the word area by saying length times breadth'); they hold instrumental rather than relational understanding (Skemp). Recommendation: shift from teaching formulae to cm² grids and fitting/cutting/folding/counting activities.
learnerActions: On cm² paper (physical squared paper or an on-screen grid), draw or drag the corners of a rectangle and, as it changes shape, keep two counts — tallied by hand on paper or shown live on screen: the squares filling the inside (area, in cm²) and the units traced around the outline (perimeter, in cm).
Compare a 6×4 rectangle (24 cm², 20 cm) with other shapes you make, saying aloud which count is 'squares covering it' (area) and which is 'steps around it' (perimeter).
Switch to a 'missing side' task: with the area fixed at 48 cm² and the length given as 8 cm, find the width (6 cm); then try area 48 m² with length 8 m → width 6 m.
Switch to an 'irregular blob/pond' task: shade whole squares and part-squares on the grid and combine them to estimate the blob's area, stating that it is an estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: Area and perimeter are different quantities with different units: area counts the unit squares covering a surface (cm²); perimeter measures the distance around the edge (cm). One can stay the same while the other changes as a shape is reshaped.

activities.title: Build l × w from an array of unit squares, then express a missing side algebraically
feedback: If you cannot explain why l × w gives area: rebuild the array — each row has 'length' squares and there are 'width' rows, so the total squares = length × width.
If a missing side is wrong: check with the array (does your width, times the length, give the stated area?) or substitute back into your equation.
Always re-check units at the end: a surface answer is square units, an around-the-edge answer is linear units.
activities.rationale: Deriving l × w from a unit-square array is intended to keep the formula meaningful, and reversing it (and expressing it algebraically) matches the Year 5 non-statutory guidance and the worked examples. Tiles/cut-and-fit alongside the formula can show where it comes from rather than relying on instrumental recall.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: 'calculate and compare the area of rectangles (including squares), including using standard units, square centimetres (cm²) and square metres (m²), and estimate the area of irregular shapes'; 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: missing-measure problems can be expressed algebraically, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20.

Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae are taught together without conceptual grounding; they overgeneralise A = l × b to non-rectangles ('most children respond to the word area by saying length times breadth'); they hold instrumental rather than relational understanding (Skemp). Recommendation: shift from teaching formulae to cm² grids and fitting/cutting/folding/counting activities.
learnerActions: Cover a labelled rectangle with unit-square tiles (or draw the array on squared paper) and count the squares by rows × columns to see where length × width comes from.
Compute the perimeter of the same rectangle as 2 × (length + width), and label each answer with its unit (cm² for area, cm for perimeter).
Find a missing dimension: given area 48 m² and length 8 m, work back to width 6 m; calculate the area of a square with side 7.5 cm (56.25 cm²).
Write a missing-measure problem as an equation, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20, and solve for b.
activities.intendedInsight: The area formula is a shortcut for counting rows × columns of unit squares, and a missing side can be found by reasoning backwards from the area (or as an equation), while perimeter adds the edge lengths.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal formula reference (scaffold)
feedback: Prompt the learner to state which revealed quantity is 'squares covering it' and which is 'distance around', so the formula stays linked to meaning.
Ask the learner to pick the correct unit before revealing it, so they are not just reading the answer.
activities.rationale: A fixed labelled rectangle with tap-to-reveal facts conveys the formulae and units but cannot show area and perimeter varying as the shape changes, so it supports recall rather than building the conceptual distinction. Useful as a reference, best paired with a grid activity.
learnerActions: On a static labelled rectangle, tap the length and width to reveal l × w (area) and 2 × (length + width) (perimeter).
Note the unit each answer takes — cm² for area, cm for perimeter — and say why they differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Recall the two formulae and the correct unit for each as a memory and reference aid.

activities.title: Checking quiz: area, perimeter, missing side and estimate with a units check
feedback: If a units item is wrong, send the learner back to the meaning: area counts covering squares (square units); perimeter measures distance (linear units).

If the blob estimate ignores part-squares or counts every touched square whole, remind them of the agreed part-square rule (either 'at least half counts as one' or pairing part-squares into about one whole) and to apply it consistently.
If area and perimeter are swapped, re-link each formula to its meaning before retrying.
activities.rationale: These tasks map cleanly onto selected-response and slider formats with a units check, making it a useful instrument for checking accuracy and spotting unit confusion. Recognition/selection responses verify application but do not elicit the independent construction and reshaping reasoning of the grid activity, so this complements rather than replaces it.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: 'calculate and compare the area of rectangles (including squares), including using standard units, square centimetres (cm²) and square metres (m²), and estimate the area of irregular shapes'; 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: missing-measure problems can be expressed algebraically, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20.
learnerActions: Compute the area and the perimeter of a labelled rectangle, then answer a units question (is the area cm or cm²?).
Find a missing width when given the area and the length.
Estimate the area of a gridded blob, including part-squares.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirm that the learner can apply both formulae accurately, choose correct units, and estimate an irregular area.

constraints: Label every answer with correct units: area in square units (cm², m²), perimeter in linear units (cm, m).

Treat irregular-area counting as an estimate; agree one explicit rule for part-squares — either count a part-square as one if it is at least half and ignore smaller parts, or pair part-squares that together make about one whole — and apply it consistently.
The tap-to-reveal reference supports recall of the formulae and units but cannot show area and perimeter changing as a shape is reshaped; use it alongside, not instead of, grid manipulation.

The checking quiz confirms accurate application and unit choice but its recognition/selection responses do not require the learner to construct and reshape figures or reason about why the two quantities differ.

Keep the formulae anchored to meaning (array of unit squares for area, distance around for perimeter) so they are not learned purely instrumentally; avoid overgeneralising l × w to non-rectangular shapes.

Live counters, dragging corners and a slider estimate are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; physical squared paper, tiles and finger-tracing achieve the same purpose and neither is mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any activity was tested.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 8×3 = 24 cm² and 2×(8+3) = 22 cm (diagnostic rectangle); 6×4 = 24 cm² and 2×(6+4) = 20 cm; reshaping 6×4 to 12×2 keeps area 24 cm² (12×2) but changes perimeter to 2×(12+2) = 28 cm — area stays, perimeter changes. Missing-side example: area 48 m², length 8 m → width 6 m (48/8). Square side 7.5 cm → area 56.25 cm². All consistent.

The original row framed the 3D and conversation formats as adding 'no insight'/not applicable; this is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, so it has been omitted rather than asserted as a universal limit. No claim is made that only a dragging grid can teach this distinction.

The 'at least half' counting rule and pairing of part-squares is a reasonable convention for estimation but is an approximation, not an exact method; it is presented explicitly as yielding an estimate.

Efficacy wording in activity rationales was softened to intended/can register because no source proves the proposed activities were tested; affordances (e.g. tap-to-reveal cannot show variation; recognition does not elicit construction) are stated as narrow limits, not medium-superiority claims.

probeDeeper: Point to the part of the rectangle that is its area, and trace the part that is its perimeter — how are they different?
You found area 24 and perimeter 22. If I stretched this into a 12 cm by 2 cm rectangle, would the area stay 24? Would the perimeter stay 22?
Why is the area measured in cm² but the perimeter in cm?
For the blob, how sure are you of your number — could it be a little more or less, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: Computes area 24 cm² (8×3) and perimeter 22 cm (2×(8+3)), keeps the two distinct with correct units, and estimates the blob's area by counting whole squares plus part-squares (roughly counting halves), presenting it as an estimate.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses area and perimeter — uses the wrong formula, or reports the same number for both.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the meanings physically: shade the surface (area = squares) versus run a finger around the edge (perimeter = length). Rebuild area as covering unit squares before returning to the formula.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 2×(8+3) when asked for area, or 8×3 when asked for perimeter, or gives one figure for both.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports area in linear units (overgeneralising 'length × breadth' without the square-unit meaning).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect cm² to one covering square: area counts squares, so it is measured in square units. Do not reteach the multiplication itself — only the unit meaning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels the area '24 cm' or omits units / mislabels perimeter as cm².

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles part-squares when estimating irregular area — counts only whole squares, or counts every touched square as a whole.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Agree a rule (a part square counts if it is at least half) and pair up part-squares into wholes; frame the result explicitly as an estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ignores part-squares (answer too small) or counts each touched square fully (answer too large), and does not present it as an estimate.

responseLevels.gap: Confuses area and perimeter or applies l×w indiscriminately; units missing or wrong; cannot estimate the irregular area meaningfully.
responseLevels.full: Finds area (24 cm²) and perimeter (22 cm) with correct units, keeps the concepts distinct, estimates the irregular area sensibly from whole and part squares, and explains area as covered squares versus perimeter as distance around.
responseLevels.partial: Computes area and perimeter correctly for the rectangle but muddles units, or handles the rectangle yet cannot estimate the blob's part-squares; runs the formulae without keeping the two meanings distinct.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a rectangle labelled 8 cm by 3 cm drawn on cm² paper and, on the same grid, an irregular blob. Say: 'Find the area of the rectangle, then its perimeter, then estimate the area of the blob — and label each answer with its units.' Then WATCH: which operation they use for each, whether they keep area and perimeter distinct, whether area is cm² and perimeter cm, and how they treat the blob's part-squares.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Setting area, perimeter and an estimate side by side forces the child to keep the two concepts and their units apart; a child with only instrumental knowledge reveals it in the doing — cross-applying a formula, dropping or swapping units, or being unable to handle part-squares — not in what they say about it.

Y5 non-statutory: missing-measure problems can be expressed algebraically, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20.
