pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Greenhouse Gas Science for ages 11–12 — WHY certain gases warm the planet, at the molecular level: short-wave solar in, long-wave infrared out, and the specific gases that trap the outgoing IR.
• Standards — UK: KS3 chemistry 'Earth and atmosphere' (composition of the atmosphere; carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases; human impacts) and KS3 physics 'Energy' / 'Waves' (the electromagnetic spectrum; infrared radiation). Builds toward GCSE combined-science climate content.
• Standards — US: NGSS MS-ESS3-5 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-5]) and MS-PS4-2 (waves; how the EM spectrum interacts with matter). DCI ESS3.D, PS4.B.
• Operational details: anchor on the two-radiation idea (Sun sends mostly visible/short-wave; Earth re-emits invisible thermal IR) BEFORE naming gases; use a photon-and-molecule model so 'trapping' is the molecule absorbing an IR photon and re-emitting in all directions, not a solid lid; contrast IR-active gases (CO2, CH4, H2O, N2O — three-or-more atoms, vibrations change the dipole moment) with IR-transparent N2/O2 (symmetric diatomics); layer in potency/GWP only after the mechanism is felt.
• Checkpoint: [Tier B] child can explain that the atmosphere is transparent to incoming sunlight but partly opaque to Earth's outgoing infrared, and that only certain molecules absorb that IR; [Tier C] child can say WHY (dipole-changing vibrations; symmetric diatomics don't absorb) and rank CO2 vs CH4 by concentration-vs-potency.
bestPractices: Separate the two radiations first: sunlight arrives mostly as short-wavelength visible/near-IR (~0.1–4 µm); Earth, being cool, re-radiates long-wavelength thermal infrared (~4–30 µm). The atmosphere treats these two bands completely differently — that asymmetry IS the greenhouse effect.

Model 'trapping' as absorb-and-re-emit-in-all-directions, not reflection off a barrier: a CO2 molecule catches an outgoing IR photon, jiggles, and re-emits — half of that goes back down. Repeated many times, this slows heat's escape and raises surface temperature.

Explicitly contrast IR-active vs IR-inactive molecules: gases with three or more atoms (CO2, CH4, H2O, N2O, O3) have vibrations that change the molecule's dipole moment and so absorb IR; symmetric diatomics N2 and O2 — 99% of the air — do not, which is why trace gases matter so much.

Distinguish the NATURAL greenhouse effect (keeps Earth ~+33 °C warmer; without any GHGs Earth's surface would average ≈ −18 °C / 255 K) from the ENHANCED effect (extra CO2/CH4 from burning fossil fuels and agriculture). The mechanism is good and necessary; the problem is the amplification.

Introduce potency vs abundance carefully: CH4 traps far more heat per molecule than CO2 but is present in much smaller amounts and is shorter-lived — use Global Warming Potential to compare fairly over a stated time horizon rather than saying one gas is simply 'worse'.
keyRepresentations: Photon-and-molecule diagram: incoming yellow short-wave arrows pass straight through the gas layer; outgoing red IR arrows get caught by CO2/CH4 molecules that vibrate and re-emit in all directions.

Two-band spectrum picture: the Sun's emission curve (peaking in visible) beside Earth's emission curve (peaking in thermal IR ~10 µm), with the atmospheric 'absorption bands' shaded to show where GHGs block outgoing IR (and the 8–15 µm atmospheric window where it escapes).
Molecular ball-and-spring models: symmetric O2/N2 stretching (no dipole change → IR-transparent) vs bending/asymmetric-stretch of CO2 (dipole change → IR-active).
GWP comparison bars: heat trapped per molecule (CH4 ≫ CO2) alongside atmospheric concentration (CO2 ≫ CH4), showing why both matter.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole — believing warming is caused by holes 'letting extra heat in'. These are distinct: ozone depletion is about UV and CFCs in the stratosphere; the greenhouse effect is about IR absorption by GHGs in the troposphere.
Thinking GHGs 'reflect' heat back like a mirror or form a solid 'blanket/lid'. The real mechanism is absorption and omnidirectional re-emission of infrared by individual molecules.
Assuming the most abundant gases (nitrogen, oxygen) must be the greenhouse gases. In fact N2 and O2 are IR-transparent; the trace gases (CO2 ~0.04%, CH4 far less) do the trapping.
Believing the greenhouse effect is inherently bad. The natural effect is essential for life; the concern is the human-caused ENHANCEMENT.
Treating 'CO2 is the problem' as the whole story and ignoring methane, or conversely thinking methane's higher potency makes CO2 unimportant — missing the concentration × potency × lifetime picture.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: understand WHY certain gases warm the planet at a molecular level. Separate the two radiations first (short-wave sunlight in, long-wave infrared out), model 'trapping' as a molecule absorbing an IR photon and re-emitting it in all directions (not a reflecting lid), contrast IR-active gases (CO2, CH4, H2O, N2O — three-or-more atoms whose vibrations change the dipole moment) with IR-transparent symmetric diatomics N2/O2, distinguish the natural greenhouse effect from the human-enhanced one, and compare gases by potency × abundance × lifetime. A causal photon-and-molecule investigation is proposed to lead; categorisation, dialogue, and reference diagrams consolidate. All activities are proposed, research-informed approaches whose effectiveness has not been validated.

activities.title: Photon-and-molecule energy-balance investigation
feedback: If a learner expects added N2/O2 to warm the surface: point out the outgoing IR photons passed straight through — symmetric diatomics have no dipole change when they vibrate, so they cannot absorb IR at all, not even 'a little'.

If a learner describes the molecule 'reflecting' or 'bouncing' the photon like a mirror: highlight that the molecule absorbs the photon, vibrates, then re-emits in a random direction — only some of that goes downward; it is absorb-and-re-emit, not reflection off a barrier.

If a learner thinks the gases trap incoming sunlight: replay the short-wave arrows passing through to the ground untouched, and contrast with the outgoing IR that gets caught — trapping acts on the OUTGOING infrared.

If a learner concludes CO2 at ~0.04% is too tiny to matter: show the thermometer climbing as a small number of CO2 molecules are added, and that stripping all GHGs drops the modelled surface toward 255 K.

If a learner says methane's higher potency makes CO2 unimportant (or vice versa): use the comparison mode to show that total effect depends on potency per molecule AND how many molecules are present AND how long each persists, compared over a stated GWP time horizon.

If a learner treats the ~+33 °C rise as the whole human problem: distinguish it from the smaller human-enhanced increment — the natural effect is essential; the concern is the extra warming humans add on top.
activities.rationale: The target understanding is a dynamic causal chain (photon absorbed → molecule vibrates → re-emitted in all directions → surface warms). This activity is a proposal designed so learners may grasp that chain more readily by driving the model and watching temperature respond than by reading an asserted outcome; its effectiveness has not been validated. Separating the two radiation bands before naming gases, and modelling trapping as omnidirectional re-emission, are intended to target the most common misconceptions.
sourceClaims: For a molecular vibration to absorb infrared energy the motion must change the molecule's dipole moment; all molecules with three or more atoms meet this criterion, while symmetric diatomics N2 and O2 (and monatomic Ar) do not absorb IR — so the trace gases CO2, H2O, CH4, N2O and O3 are the greenhouse-active constituents.

Incoming solar radiation is dominated by short wavelengths (~0.1–4 µm, peaking in the visible) while Earth re-radiates thermal infrared (~4–30 µm, peaking near 10 µm); the atmosphere is largely transparent to the incoming short-wave but absorbs much of the outgoing long-wave, with an 8–15 µm atmospheric window through which some IR escapes.

Without its greenhouse gases Earth's surface would average roughly 255 K (about −18 °C); the natural greenhouse effect raises it by about 33 °C to a habitable mean, and human emissions of CO2 and CH4 enhance this effect.
learnerActions: Start with air made only of N2 and O2: watch the Sun emit short-wave photons that pass straight through the gas layer and warm the ground, and watch the ground re-emit red infrared photons that escape to space while a surface thermometer sits low.

Drag a few CO2 molecules into the air and observe what happens when an outgoing IR photon meets one: the molecule bends/jiggles (its bonds flexing in a mode that changes its dipole) and re-emits the photon in a random direction — roughly half the time back toward the ground.
Add more CO2 (and try CH4, H2O) and record how the surface thermometer and an 'escaping to space' counter change.
Swap the added gas for extra N2 or O2 and note that outgoing IR passes through untouched — nothing changes.

Toggle 'strip all greenhouse gases' and observe the modelled surface temperature fall toward about 255 K (−18 °C); then toggle to air containing greenhouse gases and see it rise to a habitable mean (≈ 288 K / +15 °C). The ~+33 °C jump is the NATURAL greenhouse warming; present-day air carries this natural effect plus a smaller human-enhanced increment on top. Present all figures as model outputs, not precise measurements.

In a comparison mode, match a few CH4 molecules against many CO2 molecules to feel potency per molecule versus abundance; write one sentence explaining why both a highly potent trace gas and an abundant weaker one matter. Note the comparison depends on a stated GWP time horizon.
activities.intendedInsight: Warming happens because the atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming short-wave sunlight but partly opaque to Earth's outgoing infrared: only molecules whose vibrations change their dipole moment absorb and re-emit that IR (the main greenhouse gases CO2, CH4, N2O and H2O all have three or more atoms), sending some back down and slowing heat's escape. Symmetric N2/O2 — 99% of the air — do not absorb IR, which is why trace gases dominate the effect. The natural effect is essential; human emissions enhance it.

activities.title: Two-band spectrum and molecular-vibration reference
feedback: If a learner reads the bars as 'CH4 is simply worse than CO2': note that potency per kilogram (or per molecule) is only one axis; CO2's far larger concentration and emissions (and much longer persistence) mean it contributes more of the human-enhanced warming than CH4 — compare fairly using a stated GWP time horizon.
If a learner cannot locate where IR escapes: direct them to the 8–15 µm atmospheric window on the spectrum.
If a learner thinks all vibrations absorb IR: contrast the symmetric O2/N2 stretch (no dipole change) with CO2's bending mode.
activities.rationale: Static spectra, molecular models, and GWP bars name and consolidate the discriminations after the mechanism is felt. They assert relationships rather than letting the learner cause them, so they are proposed as reference companions rather than the primary route to the causal insight; a fixed diagram can still teach the relationships even though it cannot be manipulated.
sourceClaims: Incoming solar radiation is dominated by short wavelengths (~0.1–4 µm, peaking in the visible) while Earth re-radiates thermal infrared (~4–30 µm, peaking near 10 µm); the atmosphere is largely transparent to the incoming short-wave but absorbs much of the outgoing long-wave, with an 8–15 µm atmospheric window through which some IR escapes.

For a molecular vibration to absorb infrared energy the motion must change the molecule's dipole moment; all molecules with three or more atoms meet this criterion, while symmetric diatomics N2 and O2 (and monatomic Ar) do not absorb IR — so the trace gases CO2, H2O, CH4, N2O and O3 are the greenhouse-active constituents.
learnerActions: Study a two-band spectrum picture: the Sun's emission curve peaking in the visible beside Earth's emission curve peaking in the thermal IR near 10 µm, with atmospheric absorption bands shaded and the 8–15 µm window where IR escapes marked.
Use ball-and-spring molecular models to compare the symmetric stretch of O2/N2 (no dipole change → IR-transparent) with the bending and asymmetric stretch of CO2 (dipole change → IR-active).

Read GWP comparison bars showing warming per kilogram emitted over the stated time horizon (CH4 ≫ CO2) alongside atmospheric concentration (CO2 ≫ CH4), note the stated GWP time horizon, and explain in your own words why both gases matter.
Label a photon-and-molecule diagram: incoming short-wave arrows passing through, outgoing IR arrows caught by CO2/CH4 and re-emitted in all directions.
activities.intendedInsight: The asymmetry between how the atmosphere treats short-wave in and long-wave out is what produces the greenhouse effect, and it traces back to which molecular vibrations change the dipole moment. Potency and abundance are separate axes that must be combined (with lifetime) to judge a gas's overall contribution.

activities.title: 3D vibrational-mode inspector for CO2
feedback: If a learner assumes every vibration absorbs IR: show the symmetric stretch of CO2, whose dipole does not change, as a mode that does not absorb, contrasted with the bending mode that does.

If a learner thinks 3D viewing changes the planetary story: clarify that the whole-planet energy balance is a flat photons-in/photons-out flow; the 3D view adds detail at the single-molecule scale and complements rather than replaces the 2D account.
activities.rationale: A 3D molecule viewer offers a different view of the dipole-change idea than a flat ball-and-spring picture, since it can be rotated to show the bending motion in both perpendicular directions. It is proposed as a supplementary inspector; the planetary energy-balance story that carries the learning is conveyed clearly in 2D.
sourceClaims: For a molecular vibration to absorb infrared energy the motion must change the molecule's dipole moment; all molecules with three or more atoms meet this criterion, while symmetric diatomics N2 and O2 (and monatomic Ar) do not absorb IR — so the trace gases CO2, H2O, CH4, N2O and O3 are the greenhouse-active constituents.
learnerActions: Rotate and view a CO2 molecule in three dimensions to see its vibrational modes: symmetric and asymmetric stretch (atoms moving along the molecule's straight line) and bending (which can happen in two perpendicular directions).
Identify which modes change the molecule's dipole moment (and therefore absorb IR) and which do not.
Relate what you see back to why CO2 absorbs outgoing infrared while symmetric N2/O2 do not.
activities.intendedInsight: Viewing a molecule's vibrational modes in 3D shows how its atoms move, and only modes that change the dipole moment absorb infrared — making the abstract 'dipole change' criterion concrete.

activities.title: Sort, sequence and explain: consolidating the discriminations
feedback: If a learner sorts N2/O2 as IR-active: remind them symmetric diatomics have no dipole change on vibration and absorb no IR.

If a learner conflates greenhouse and ozone: ozone depletion is about CFCs destroying stratospheric ozone so more UV reaches the ground; the greenhouse effect is greenhouse gases absorbing outgoing IR, mostly in the lower atmosphere — different radiation and a different process (although CFCs and ozone are themselves also greenhouse gases).
If a learner orders the sequence with absorption on the incoming sunlight: the absorption step acts on the OUTGOING infrared from the surface.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, sequencing, and short-answer items are intended to help consolidate distinctions and surface residual misconceptions once the causal model is built. These recognition and recall formats can check understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent causal reasoning the investigation is intended to build, so they are best used as follow-up.
sourceClaims: For a molecular vibration to absorb infrared energy the motion must change the molecule's dipole moment; all molecules with three or more atoms meet this criterion, while symmetric diatomics N2 and O2 (and monatomic Ar) do not absorb IR — so the trace gases CO2, H2O, CH4, N2O and O3 are the greenhouse-active constituents.

Without its greenhouse gases Earth's surface would average roughly 255 K (about −18 °C); the natural greenhouse effect raises it by about 33 °C to a habitable mean, and human emissions of CO2 and CH4 enhance this effect.
learnerActions: Categorise gases as IR-active (CO2, CH4, H2O, N2O) or IR-transparent (N2, O2) and justify each placement by its molecular structure.

Put the mechanism in order: Sun → short-wave radiation → surface warms → emits infrared → infrared absorbed by GHG molecules → re-emitted in all directions → some returns to the surface → surface warms further (heat escapes to space more slowly).
Answer short questions: why do trace gases matter so much? how is the greenhouse effect different from the ozone hole? which radiation is actually trapped?
Estimate Earth's surface temperature with greenhouse gases versus with none, and explain the gap (≈ +33 °C natural effect; ≈ 255 K / −18 °C without GHGs, as modelled figures).
Distinguish the natural greenhouse effect from the enhanced effect and state what drives the enhancement (burning fossil fuels, agriculture).
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall and discrimination of the key categories, sequence, and distinctions: IR-active vs IR-transparent, incoming vs outgoing radiation, greenhouse vs ozone, natural vs enhanced.

activities.title: Ask-the-climate-scientist dialogue to untangle misconceptions
feedback: If the learner says N2/O2 trap 'a little' heat: steer them to the dipole-change criterion — symmetric diatomics do not absorb IR at all.
If the learner blames the ozone hole: separate the two — stratospheric UV/CFC chemistry versus tropospheric IR absorption.
If the learner treats water vapour as a direct human emission: discuss why its atmospheric amount responds to temperature, making it a feedback rather than a lever humans set directly.
activities.rationale: Dialogue suits a topic dense with persistent misconceptions because it lets learners voice and test their reasoning. It supports the mechanism rather than demonstrating it operating, so it is proposed as a follow-up to an investigation where the learner has already seen the process.
sourceClaims: Roughly 80% of students conflate the greenhouse effect with stratospheric ozone depletion, believing warming comes from 'holes letting heat in'; effective teaching explicitly separates the IR-absorption (troposphere) mechanism from UV/CFC ozone chemistry (stratosphere).
learnerActions: Pose the questions that puzzle you to a climate-scientist role (real teacher, peer-in-role, or a guided prompt), e.g. 'Why don't nitrogen and oxygen trap heat if they're 99% of the air?' and 'Isn't warming just the ozone hole letting heat in?'
Explain back, in your own words, why only certain molecules absorb IR and how greenhouse warming differs from ozone depletion.
Probe the follow-ups: is water vapour a human 'switch' like CO2 or a feedback? Is the greenhouse effect itself the problem, or its enhancement? What does 'potent' mean for methane?
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and defending the mechanism through dialogue can expose and help repair the misconception-heavy areas of this topic — abundance vs IR-activity, greenhouse vs ozone, natural vs enhanced, potency vs amount.

constraints: Establish the two-radiation asymmetry (short-wave in, long-wave IR out) BEFORE naming gases; layer in potency/GWP only after the absorb-and-re-emit mechanism is understood.
Model 'trapping' as a molecule absorbing an IR photon and re-emitting in all directions (so some returns toward the surface), not as reflection off a mirror or a solid blanket/lid.
Be explicit that N2 and O2 do not absorb IR at all (no dipole change on vibration) — avoid implying they trap heat 'just less' than CO2.

Distinguish the natural greenhouse effect (essential; ≈ +33 °C, surface ≈ 255 K without GHGs rising to ≈ 288 K/+15 °C) from the smaller human-enhanced increment; the mechanism is not inherently bad — the amplification is the concern.
Compare gases by potency per molecule AND concentration AND lifetime using a stated GWP time horizon; do not label one gas simply 'worse'.

Static spectra, GWP bars and labelled diagrams assert relationships and serve as references; they do not let the learner cause the process. Categorisation/sequence/short-answer formats consolidate and check discriminations but do not by themselves elicit independent causal construction.

The 3D vibrational-mode viewer and the live sim (dragging molecules, surface thermometer, escaping-to-space counter, GHG-strip toggle, GWP comparison mode) are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory tools; equivalent paper, ball-and-spring, or role-play versions can serve the same purpose.

Temperature values (255 K / −18 °C; +33 °C natural effect; ≈ 288 K/+15 °C habitable mean) are standard modelled figures from the cited energy-balance source; present them as model outputs, not precision measurements.
Efficacy of all activities here is untested; present them as proposed approaches using may/intended wording rather than as proven methods.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Several sources carry verified:false in the original row (UK KS3 curriculum statement, NGSS MS-ESS3-5/MS-PS4-2, and the '~80% of students conflate greenhouse with ozone' misconception statistic). The 80% figure (and its embedded 'effective teaching' assertion) and the standards mappings should be checked against primary sources before being cited as established.

The original framed a static image as able only to 'assert, not let the child cause' the mechanism and 3D as adding little; these have been softened to affordance/limit statements. A fixed diagram can still teach the relationships even though it cannot be manipulated.

The sim's binary toggle (no GHGs vs air with GHGs) is a simplification: the ~+33 °C jump is the natural greenhouse effect, while present-day air additionally includes a smaller human-enhanced increment. Keep the natural-vs-enhanced distinction explicit so the toggle is not read as showing only the natural effect.
Potency vs abundance reasoning depends on a stated GWP time horizon and gas lifetime; the GWP bars/comparison should specify the time horizon to avoid implying a single fixed 'CH4 vs CO2' ratio.

Comparative efficacy wording ('learners grasp best by…', 'effective for consolidating', 'the reasoning the investigation builds') in the candidate was downgraded to proposed/intended/may language, since no empirical effectiveness has been established for these activities.

Self-audit: the dipole-change criterion, the short-wave/long-wave band assignment, the 255 K / +33 °C / ≈288 K figures, and the natural-vs-enhanced distinction align with the cited ACS material; no arithmetic or physics errors were found requiring correction in learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: Water vapour is a greenhouse gas too. Why does that make it a feedback rather than a direct human 'switch' like CO₂?
Without any natural greenhouse effect Earth would average about −18°C instead of +15°C. So is the greenhouse effect itself the problem, or its enhancement?
Methane is present in far smaller amounts than CO₂ but is called more 'potent.' What does potent mean here?
assess.correctAnswer: The Sun's energy arrives mainly as short-wave radiation, which passes through; Earth's surface warms and re-emits long-wave infrared. Greenhouse-gas molecules (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) have bonds that vibrate at infrared frequencies with a changing dipole, so they absorb and re-emit that outgoing IR; symmetrical N₂ and O₂ have no dipole change when they vibrate, so they don't absorb IR. So greenhouse gases trap outgoing infrared, not incoming sunlight — and it's molecular structure, not abundance, that matters.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks greenhouse gases block incoming sunlight, that all air gases trap heat, or conflates the effect with the ozone hole.
responseLevels.full: Explains the short-wave-in/long-wave-out model, attributes IR absorption to molecular vibration (dipole change) that symmetrical N₂/O₂ lack, distinguishes natural from enhanced greenhouse effect, and reasons about potency versus abundance — transferring to methane or water vapour.
responseLevels.partial: Knows CO₂/methane trap heat and that the effect can be enhanced, but can't distinguish short-wave in from long-wave out, or can't say why N₂/O₂ don't absorb IR.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The atmosphere is nearly 99% nitrogen and oxygen, yet these gases play almost no part in the greenhouse effect, while CO₂ at under 0.05% does. pedagogy.summary: This is the vocabulary foundation for the whole ratio-and-proportion strand: children must use ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole and 'out of' precisely, and grasp the central distinction that a RATIO compares part to part (3 red : 2 blue) while a PROPORTION compares a part to the whole (3 out of 5 are red = 3/5). Because these words are used loosely in everyday speech and are often taught as an inseparable phrase ('ratio and proportion'), the teaching goal is to differentiate them through repeated use in concrete contexts — mixing paint or squash, recipes, sharing — rather than through memorised definitions. Language precision here prevents the classic error of reading a part-to-part ratio as if it were a part-to-whole fraction.
bestPractices: Introduce terms through a concrete mixing/sharing context (e.g. squash: '1 part concentrate to 4 parts water') and the 'for every' phrasing before any notation — 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water' makes part-to-part audible.

Contrast ratio and proportion side by side on the SAME situation: 'the ratio of concentrate to water is 1:4' vs 'the proportion that is concentrate is 1 out of 5' — so children hear part-to-part against part-to-whole.

Attach each term to a representation: ratio → two coloured bars side by side; proportion/percentage → one bar (the whole) with a shaded part; scale → an enlargement pair. Language and picture reinforce each other.
Use 'out of' deliberately as the bridge to fractions and percentages: 3 out of 5 = 3/5 = 60%, all describing the same proportion.
Elicit and require the vocabulary in pupils' own explanations (talk moves) rather than accepting a right numeric answer with vague words — the objective IS the language.
Draw scale/equivalent language from enlargement examples ('every length is 3 times as big — a scale factor of 3') so 'scale' and 'equivalent' are grounded in action.
keyRepresentations: Two side-by-side coloured bars (part-to-part) contrasted with one part-shaded whole bar (part-to-whole / proportion)
'For every ___ there are ___' sentence frame linking language to the ratio
Squash/paint mixing jugs or coloured counters (concrete part-to-part)
A double-headed 'same proportion' triple: fraction 3/5 = 60% = 3 out of 5
An enlargement pair of shapes labelled with the scale factor
commonMisconceptions: Uses 'ratio' and 'proportion' interchangeably, as if they mean the same thing
Reads a part-to-part ratio as a part-to-whole fraction: hearing 'red to blue is 2:3' and saying '2/3 are red' (should be 2/5)
Treats 'proportion' only as everyday 'a large proportion' (a vague amount) rather than a comparison of part to whole
Confuses 'scale' / 'scale factor' with a difference (adds a fixed amount) rather than a multiplicative enlargement

learn.summary: Language foundation for ratio and proportion (ages 9–11): children must use ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole and 'out of' precisely, and grasp the central distinction that a RATIO compares part to part (3 red : 2 blue) while a PROPORTION compares a part to the whole (3 out of 5 are red = 3/5 = 60%). Because these words are used loosely in everyday speech and are often taught as the inseparable phrase 'ratio and proportion', the objective is to differentiate them through repeated use in concrete mixing/sharing/recipe contexts rather than through memorised definitions. The payoff is preventing the classic error of reading a part-to-part ratio as if it were a part-to-whole fraction.

activities.title: Squash-mixing bench: one mixture, two descriptions
feedback: If a child writes the proportion as '1 out of 4', point to the single whole-bar: it visibly shows five parts in the whole, not four, so the 4 cannot be the whole — count all parts first (1 + 4 = 5), then name the proportion as 1 out of 5.

If a child gives the same numbers for both (e.g. 1:4 for the ratio AND '1 out of 4' for the proportion), have them re-describe each from its own picture using the matching word: the twin-bar for ratio, the whole-bar for proportion.
When both frames are correct, prompt the 'say it another way' link: 1 out of 5 = 1/5 = 20%, all naming the same proportion.

When the recipe is scaled to 2 concentrate and 8 water, work it through: the ratio 2:8 is equivalent to 1:4, and to find the proportion count the whole first (2 + 8 = 10), so the proportion that is concentrate is 2 out of 10 = 1 out of 5 — unchanged from the 1:4 mixture even though the numbers grew.
activities.rationale: A LANGUAGE objective is met when the child manipulates a situation and NAMES what changes; showing part-to-part and part-to-whole pictures simultaneously lets the learner attach each term to a distinct representation and makes the wrong denominator visibly contradicted rather than corrected by a rule. The live twin-bar/whole-bar pairing and the completion frames are offered as a concrete mechanism for this language work, not as the only possible medium.
sourceClaims: Ratio compares part to part while proportion compares a part to the whole; the 'for every' phrasing and simple pictures (rectangles/counters) are recommended for first teaching, and proportion is related to fractions.
learnerActions: Build a mixture by adding whole 'parts' of concentrate and water into a jug (for example 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water).

As each part is added, read two pictures that update together: a twin-bar showing concentrate beside water (part to part) and a single stacked bar showing the whole mixture with the concentrate shaded (part to whole).
Complete two sentence frames about the SAME mixture: 'the RATIO of concentrate to water is __ : __' and 'the PROPORTION that is concentrate is __ out of __'.
Then 'say it another way': express the proportion as a fraction, a percentage and an 'out of' phrase (for 1 part in 5: 1/5 = 20%).
Change the recipe and say whether the ratio and the proportion change.
activities.intendedInsight: The same mixture is described two different ways depending on which picture you read: for 1 concentrate to 4 water, the 1 sits against the 4 in the twin-bar (ratio 1:4) and against the whole of 5 parts in the single bar (proportion 1 out of 5). Ratio compares part to part; proportion compares part to whole; the whole = the sum of the parts.

activities.title: 'For every' spoken frame before notation
feedback: If the child jumps straight to '1 out of 5' when asked 'for every', redirect: 'for every' compares the two amounts to each other (1 to 4), not to the whole.
If the child says 'for every 1 there are 5', count the water parts only (4) — the whole (5) is a separate idea named by proportion, not by the 'for every' comparison.
activities.rationale: Grounding language in 'for every' speech before notation is explicitly recommended for first teaching and keeps part-to-part distinct from part-to-whole from the start.
sourceClaims: Ratio compares part to part while proportion compares a part to the whole; the 'for every' phrasing and simple pictures (rectangles/counters) are recommended for first teaching, and proportion is related to fractions.

At upper KS2 percentages, decimals and fractions are taught as different ways of expressing proportions; pupils meet ratio informally via 'for every' and unequal sharing, and 'scale factor' describes multiplicative enlargement.
learnerActions: Describe a mixture aloud using 'for every' before any colon notation: 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water'.
Then translate the spoken frame into the ratio 1:4.
State separately how much of the WHOLE drink is concentrate: 1 out of 5.
Repeat with coloured counters or paint instead of squash to hear the same structure in a new context.
activities.intendedInsight: 'For every ___ there are ___' makes part-to-part audible before symbols are introduced, so the ratio notation is read as a comparison of parts rather than copied as a rule.

activities.title: In-role recipe talk that requires precise words
feedback: If the child swaps the terms, the partner asks which comparison they mean and points back to the two amounts (part to part) versus the whole (part to whole).
Accept a correct numeric answer only when it is paired with the matching word; the goal is the language, not just the number.
activities.rationale: A responsive partner can require precise term use and gently challenge everyday blurred usage; this targets the language objective through genuine use rather than recited definitions. Offered as one route; a human conversation partner serves the same purpose.
learnerActions: Describe recipes and drink orders to an in-role partner (for example a smoothie-bar owner), using 'ratio' and 'proportion' correctly.
When the partner challenges a loose statement — 'you said proportion; did you mean part to part or part to whole?' — re-say it with the matching word.
Explain a part-to-part comparison and a part-to-whole comparison for the same order.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct USE of the vocabulary in unscripted dialogue is the actual objective; being asked to clarify loose usage forces the part-to-part vs part-to-whole reference to become explicit.

activities.title: Sort and complete: ratio vs proportion across contexts
feedback: If a child reads 'red to blue is 2:3' as '2/3 are red', count the whole: 2 + 3 = 5 parts, so 2 out of 5 are red — the 3 is the other part, not the whole.
If a statement is miscategorised, ask: does it compare two parts to each other (ratio) or a part to the whole (proportion)?
activities.rationale: A scored sorting and fill-in set can check whether the child selects the right term and distinguishes part-to-part from part-to-whole across contexts; it checks recognition and discrimination but does not by itself require the child to generate descriptions unprompted, so pair it with the spoken/building tasks.
sourceClaims: Ratio compares part to part while proportion compares a part to the whole; the 'for every' phrasing and simple pictures (rectangles/counters) are recommended for first teaching, and proportion is related to fractions.
learnerActions: Sort statements about mixtures, recipes and beads into 'this is a ratio' vs 'this is a proportion'.
Fill in sentence frames: 'the ratio of red to blue is __ : __' and 'the proportion that is red is __ out of __'.
For a described situation such as 'red to blue is 2:3', state what proportion are red (2 out of 5) and explain why '2/3 are red' is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Across varied contexts the same structural distinction holds: the ratio uses the part counts; the proportion uses the whole (sum of the parts).

activities.title: Labelled mixing glossary (reference scaffold)
feedback: Reveals the correct label on tap; because it does not require the child to produce or choose the word, use it as a glossary alongside, not instead of, tasks that demand use.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal labelled example is a useful reference, but a LANGUAGE objective is met by using the words, which a reveal-only artefact does not require; hence it is a support, not the main activity.
learnerActions: On a worked mixing example, tap the concentrate to reveal 'part', tap the jug to reveal 'whole', and tap the pair to reveal 'ratio 1:4 / proportion 1 out of 5'.
Use it to look up which word names which comparison while doing the building or talking tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each term is anchored to a concrete feature of the mixture: parts, the whole, and the two comparisons built from them.

activities.title: Scale factor from an enlargement pair
feedback: If a child says the shape got '2 cm bigger' on each side, check a second length that was a different length on the original shape (e.g. a 1 cm side and a 2 cm side enlarged by 3 become 3 cm and 6 cm, adding 2 cm and 4 cm): the added amount differs between those sides while the multiplier stays the same — scale factor is the multiplier. (If every side starts the same length, as in a square, the added amounts will match, so compare sides of different original lengths.)
Confirm by checking that each length of the new shape equals the matching original length times the scale factor.
activities.rationale: Grounding 'scale' and 'equivalent' in an enlargement action connects the words to a multiplicative relationship, addressing the common confusion of scale with additive difference.
sourceClaims: At upper KS2 percentages, decimals and fractions are taught as different ways of expressing proportions; pupils meet ratio informally via 'for every' and unequal sharing, and 'scale factor' describes multiplicative enlargement.
learnerActions: Compare an original shape with its enlargement and find how many times bigger every length is ('every length is 3 times as big').
State the scale factor as that multiplier ('a scale factor of 3') and check it is multiplicative, not an added amount.
Describe a reduction the same way (for example a scale factor of 1/2).
activities.intendedInsight: 'Scale'/'scale factor' names a multiplicative enlargement or reduction — every length is multiplied by the same number — not a fixed amount added on.

constraints: The objective is linguistic and relational: require the vocabulary in the child's own explanations rather than accepting a correct number with vague words.
Introduce terms through a concrete mixing/sharing context and 'for every' speech before any colon notation.

Reveal-only labelled examples and sort/fill-in tasks are scaffolds: they support recognition and reference but do not by themselves require the child to generate correct descriptions unprompted; pair them with building and spoken tasks.
Keep ratio and proportion contrasted on the SAME situation so the part-to-part vs part-to-whole difference is heard and seen, not memorised.
The whole used for a proportion is the SUM of the parts (1 concentrate + 4 water = 5), so the proportion that is concentrate is 1 out of 5, not 1 out of 4.

Scaling the amounts (e.g. 1:4 to 2:8) leaves the ratio equivalent (2:8 = 1:4) and the proportion unchanged once the whole is recomputed (2+8=10, so 2 out of 10 = 1 out of 5); use this to test real command of the language.
'Scale factor' is multiplicative (every length times the same number), not an added difference.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's '3D adds nothing' judgement about this being spatial-only has been removed as a universal claim; a spatial model is simply not the proposed route here, which is a narrow design choice, not an established law.

Independent re-audit confirmed the scaled-mixture feedback is now correct: for 2:8 the whole is 2+8=10 and the proportion of concentrate is 2 out of 10 = 1 out of 5 (unchanged), derived rather than carried as a fixed denominator; no residual '1 out of 10' error remains.

Self-audit of central numbers: 1 concentrate to 4 water gives ratio 1:4 and proportion 1 out of 5 = 1/5 = 20% (concentrate); water is 4 out of 5 = 4/5 = 80%. 'red to blue is 2:3' gives 2 out of 5 red, not 2/3. Scale factor 3 and reduction 1/2 are multiplicative. All consistent.
Coverage note: the vocabulary terms 'relative size' and 'unequal' from the stated objective are only lightly exercised; consider an explicit task if full vocabulary coverage is required.

probeDeeper: 'Say the same thing as a fraction and as a percentage' — checks the 'out of'/proportion link to 3/5, 60% style equivalence.

Counterexample: 'If I made it 2 cups concentrate to 8 cups water, would the ratio change? Would the proportion that is concentrate change?' — a child with the language sees ratio 2:8 = 1:4 and proportion still 1 out of 5 (unchanged); a child without it thinks bigger numbers mean a different drink.
'Point to what the ratio compares, and what the proportion compares' — forces the part-to-part vs part-to-whole reference to be made explicit.
'A recipe says the ratio of sugar to flour is 2:3 — what proportion of the mixture is sugar?' checks transfer of the whole = 2+3 = 5 idea to a new context.
assess.correctAnswer: The RATIO of concentrate to water is 1:4 (or 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water') — a part-to-part comparison; and the PROPORTION of the drink that is concentrate is 1 out of 5 (1/5, 20%) — a part-to-whole comparison. The two numbers (4 vs 5) differ because ratio compares part to part and proportion compares part to whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'ratio' and 'proportion' as if identical: 'the proportion of concentrate to water is 1:4' — applies part-to-part language to a part-to-whole comparison and vice versa
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with the twin picture: 'ratio compares these two bars; proportion compares this part to the whole bar' — have the child re-describe each from its own picture, using the matching word.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child swaps the terms freely, or uses only one of them for both comparisons; the everyday blurred usage carries over

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the part-to-part ratio as a part-to-whole fraction: gives the proportion as '1 out of 4' (using the water count as the whole) instead of 1 out of 5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the single whole-bar: count all the parts in the whole drink (5) before naming the proportion. Reinforce 'out of' = out of the whole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child keeps the 4 as the denominator for the proportion, not seeing that the whole is 1+4=5 parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 'proportion' only in its vague everyday sense ('a big proportion is water') rather than as a numerical part-to-whole comparison
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the precise sense: 'proportion means how many parts out of the whole — how many of the 5 parts are water?' Bridge to fraction/percentage (4/5, 80%).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a qualitative amount ('mostly water') and cannot attach a number-out-of-the-whole to 'proportion'

responseLevels.gap: Uses ratio and proportion interchangeably or vaguely; cannot separate the part-to-part comparison from the part-to-whole one; gives the same numbers for both.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously and correctly uses ratio (part-to-part), proportion (part-to-whole) and 'out of' across new contexts, connects proportion to fraction and percentage, and recognises that scaling the amounts leaves the ratio and the proportion unchanged.
responseLevels.partial: Uses the terms correctly for the practised squash example and can state the ratio 1:4, but slips when the context changes (recipe, beads), or lists the terms without reliably matching ratio→part-to-part and proportion→part-to-whole, or needs prompting to find the whole (5).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a jug of orange squash made with 1 cup of concentrate and 4 cups of water. Tell me about this drink using the words 'ratio' and 'proportion' — describe how much concentrate there is compared with the water, and how much of the whole drink is concentrate.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The context forces the child to USE both words about the same situation, so the part-to-part vs part-to-whole distinction shows itself in whether they say 1:4 for the ratio but 1 out of 5 for the proportion. A child who has the language keeps the two comparisons separate; a child who does not either uses the words interchangeably or gives the same denominator for both (1:4 and '1 out of 4'), revealing the part-to-part-as-part-to-whole confusion. Because it asks for USE, not a definition, it distinguishes real command of the vocabulary from a recited gloss.

pedagogy.summary: Venn diagrams organise outcomes into regions defined by set membership: elements outside both circles, in one circle only, and in the overlap (intersection). Students learn to CONSTRUCT the diagram (fill the intersection FIRST, then subtract to find the 'only' regions, then account for the 'neither' universal-set remainder) and to INTERPRET it (read region frequencies and translate them into probabilities over the correct denominator). The intersection A∩B is 'in both', the union A∪B is 'in either', and probability is always the region count over the total number in the universal set (unless a conditional restricts the denominator). Systematic listing and the product rule generate the full outcome set that the diagram then organises.
bestPractices: Fill the INTERSECTION first, then subtract it from each set total to get the 'only-A' and 'only-B' regions — this prevents double-counting the overlap
Always place the 'neither' elements inside the rectangle (universal set) but outside both circles, and check all regions sum to the total
Name each region in words before writing set notation — 'likes both', 'likes cricket but not football' — then attach A∩B, A∪B, A only
Compute probability as region-frequency ÷ universal-set total; only restrict the denominator when the question conditions on a subset
Use systematic listing / the product rule to build the complete outcome set, then sort it into the diagram so favourable ÷ total rests on genuine outcomes
keyRepresentations: Two-circle Venn diagram inside a labelled rectangle (universal set)
Three-circle Venn diagram for three-set problems (seven internal regions)
Intersection-first fill order: overlap, then 'only' regions by subtraction, then 'neither'
Two-way table as an alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions
commonMisconceptions: Confusing intersection and union — shading 'in either' when asked for 'in both', or vice versa
Double-counting the overlap — adding the two circle totals for A∪B without subtracting A∩B
Forgetting the 'neither' region, so the diagram's regions do not sum to the universal-set total
Using a circle total (or the whole universal set) as the denominator for a probability that is actually conditional on a restricted subset

learn.summary: Students learn to CONSTRUCT a Venn diagram (fill the intersection first, then subtract to find the 'only' regions, then account for the 'neither' remainder inside the universal-set rectangle) and to INTERPRET it (read region frequencies and translate them into probabilities over the correct denominator). A∩B is 'in both', A∪B is 'in either', and probability is region-count over the universal-set total unless a conditional restricts the denominator. Systematic listing and the product rule generate the full outcome set the diagram then organises. The discriminating skill is construction on a fresh case, which exposes intersection/union confusion and wrong-denominator errors that reading a pre-labelled diagram can hide.

activities.title: Build a two-circle Venn from student data, then shade and read probabilities
feedback: If a learner shades both whole circles for A∪B, point out the overlap has been counted twice and the running total passes 30 — the middle six can only be counted once, so the union count is A + B − A∩B.

If they shade the entire cricket circle (14) for 'cricket but NOT football', return to region naming: the overlap is 'both'; 'cricket but not football' is the cricket circle MINUS the overlap — the crescent only (8).
If they write P(cricket only) = 8/14, ask 'out of how many students altogether?' — an unconditional probability is over the whole 30, so 8/30.
If they answer 'the probability is 8' (a count), restate that a probability is a part of the whole between 0 and 1 — the region count over the total: 8 out of 30 is 8/30.
On the conditional, if they keep 30 as the denominator, ask who is being considered now — only the cricket-lovers, so the denominator is 14, not 30.
activities.rationale: Venn regions are spatial partitions of the outcome set; constructing the diagram from raw data (intersection-first, then subtraction, then 'neither') prevents double-counting and makes the correct denominator concrete. Construction on a fresh description is the move that distinguishes genuine understanding from parroting region labels.
sourceClaims: On a Venn diagram the intersection A∩B is the region 'in both sets' and the union A∪B is 'in either set'; to find the union you cannot simply add the two circle totals because that double-counts the overlap, and a conditional probability restricts the denominator to the relevant subset rather than the whole universal set.
learnerActions: Place 30 student tokens into a two-circle Venn (football / cricket) inside a rectangle; fill the intersection first (likes both), then the 'only' crescents (by subtracting the overlap from each set total when only totals are given), then the 'neither' region outside both circles — e.g. 12 football-only, 6 both, 8 cricket-only, 4 neither.
Check that all regions sum to 30 before reading anything off.
Name each region in words BEFORE writing notation: 'likes both' = A∩B, 'football only' = A only, 'likes either' = A∪B, 'neither' outside both.
Shade 'likes cricket but NOT football' (the cricket-only crescent, 8 students) and write its probability as 8/30 = 4/15 over the total of 30.
Shade A∪B and find its COUNT two ways: by adding region counts (12 + 6 + 8 = 26), and by checking 18 + 14 − 6 = 26 to see why the overlap is subtracted; the probability is then 26/30.
Switch to a conditional: 'among the cricket-lovers, what fraction also like football?' — identify the new denominator (14, all who like cricket) and compute 6/14.
activities.intendedInsight: The overlap counts once, so the union COUNT is A + B − A∩B; and the denominator is the whole universal set unless a question conditions on a restricted subset, in which case the denominator shrinks to that subset.

activities.title: Generate the full outcome set, then sort it into the diagram
feedback: If a probability looks wrong, check whether every outcome was listed — a missing outcome changes both the region count and the total.

If the learner struggles to coordinate regions with individual outcomes, have them tag each listed outcome with its region before counting, so region totals are built from real outcomes rather than guessed.
activities.rationale: Research highlights that children's core difficulty is coordinating aggregated regions with the underlying equally-likely outcomes; building the outcome set first and sorting it addresses that directly.
sourceClaims: Correctly enumerating and counting outcomes over unions and intersections requires representing the complete set of outcomes systematically (tables, grids, Venn diagrams); the difficulty children face is coordinating aggregated regions with the underlying equally-likely outcomes.
learnerActions: For a combined-events scenario, use systematic listing or the product rule to enumerate every possible outcome before sorting.
Place each enumerated outcome into the correct Venn region (or a two-way table as an alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions).

Confirm that favourable ÷ total rests on the genuine, fully-listed outcomes, and that those listed outcomes are equally likely (e.g. ordered pairs from a fair coin and a fair die, not just the possible totals of two dice). Then count the region, count the universal set and form the fraction.
Compare the Venn diagram and a two-way table of the same data to see that both encode the four regions (both, A only, B only, neither).
activities.intendedInsight: Probabilities read off a diagram are only trustworthy when the complete set of equally likely outcomes has been enumerated and sorted correctly; the diagram organises outcomes but does not create them.

activities.title: Explain why the overlap is not counted twice (reasoning talk)
feedback: If a learner adds the two circle totals for the union, ask them to point to who gets counted twice and why that inflates the total.
If they say adding 'neither' students changes no probabilities, remind them the universal-set total grew, so every probability over the whole set changes even though the circle counts did not.
activities.rationale: Dialogue can probe why the overlap is not double-counted and why denominators shift, but the core skill is constructing and reading the spatial diagram, so talk is best used alongside construction, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: On a Venn diagram the intersection A∩B is the region 'in both sets' and the union A∪B is 'in either set'; to find the union you cannot simply add the two circle totals because that double-counts the overlap, and a conditional probability restricts the denominator to the relevant subset rather than the whole universal set.
learnerActions: Justify each region count aloud: how many like football altogether (18, not 12), how many like cricket altogether (14), how many like both (6).

Explain in your own words why the number who like football OR cricket is 12 + 8 + 6 = 26 — and NOT 18 + 14 = 32 — because the 6 who like both are already included in each circle total; the probability is then 26/30.

State what changes and what stays the same if four more 'neither' students join: the universal-set total rises to 34, so every probability taken over the universal set changes, while the region counts for football and cricket stay fixed (and a probability taken only among cricket-lovers, like 6/14, is unaffected).
activities.intendedInsight: Verbal justification surfaces the double-counting logic and the role of the denominator, reinforcing the construction skill rather than replacing it.

activities.title: Interpretation and sorting practice (scaffold)
feedback: If a learner selects 6/18, ask what the denominator should be — the universal-set total of 30, not a circle total.
If they select the bare count 6, restate that a probability is a fraction of the total: 6/30.
activities.rationale: Tap-to-reveal and sorting tasks teach the region vocabulary and interpretation efficiently, but they are recognition-level: they do not require the learner to construct a diagram from raw data or decide a denominator on a fresh case. Use them before, not instead of, the construction activity.
sourceClaims: On a Venn diagram the intersection A∩B is the region 'in both sets' and the union A∪B is 'in either set'; to find the union you cannot simply add the two circle totals because that double-counts the overlap, and a conditional probability restricts the denominator to the relevant subset rather than the whole universal set.
learnerActions: On a pre-authored Venn, reveal region labels: tap the overlap for 'likes both — 6 students — A∩B', a circle-only crescent for 'football only — 12', outside for 'neither — 4'; answer 'What fraction like both?' → 6/30.
Sort described students into the four regions (drag-to-region sorting).
Match region names (A∩B, A∪B, A only) to shaded pictures.
Read a probability off a completed diagram, watching for a wrong-denominator option such as 6/18 (circle-total denominator) or an unnormalised count such as 6.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising region meanings and reading probabilities off a completed diagram builds the vocabulary that construction then applies.

constraints: Fill the intersection first, then subtract to get the 'only' regions, then place 'neither' inside the rectangle but outside both circles — and check all regions sum to the universal-set total.

When one member of the universal set is chosen at random (each equally likely), compute probability as region-frequency ÷ universal-set total; restrict the denominator only when the question conditions on a subset.
Keep probabilities and counts distinct: a union COUNT may exceed 1 (e.g. 26), but the probability is that count over the total (26/30) and always lies between 0 and 1.

Recognition and sorting tasks (tap-to-reveal, matching, categorization, multiple choice) assess and build vocabulary but do not elicit independent construction of a diagram from raw data or an independently chosen denominator; keep a genuine construct-from-description task in the sequence.
A completed/pre-authored Venn is a scaffold: it teaches what each region means but cannot test whether the learner can build a diagram or choose the correct denominator on a new case.

Interactive features (drag tokens into regions, tap-to-shade with live set-notation and probability recompute, a conditional mode that greys out the rest and switches the denominator, a flag when the union overlap is selected twice) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative, not required.
A two-way table is a valid alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions; do not treat the circle layout as the only representation.
Three-circle Venn diagrams (seven internal regions) extend the same logic for three-set problems.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic on the worked example (30 students: 12 football-only, 6 both, 8 cricket-only, 4 neither): football total 12+6=18, cricket total 8+6=14, union 12+8+6=26 = 18+14−6, neither 4, grand total 18+8+4=30 (or 12+6+8+4=30) — all consistent. P(cricket only)=8/30=4/15 and P(both)=6/30=1/5 check out. The conditional P(football | cricket)=6/14 uses denominator 14 (all cricket-lovers), which is correct.

The union work distinguishes the union COUNT (26) from its probability (26/30). The original assessment probe ('What is P(likes football OR cricket)? ... do you add 12 + 8 + 6, or 18 + 14?') had conflated the count with the probability; this is kept distinct in the learner-facing actions.

The original source row claimed a 3D representation 'adds nothing' to a flat categorical partition. This is a catalog-style universal claim not established by the cited sources; it has been dropped rather than propagated. A flat partition is well-suited here without asserting a third dimension is universally useless.
The original also framed dialogue as something 'talk alone cannot deliver'; rescoped to a narrow point that verbal justification complements, rather than replaces, construction.
Original assessment distractor '6/18' uses a circle-total denominator (football total 18); retained as a diagnostic distractor, not as a valid answer.

The Bryant & Nunes claim was removed from Activity 1's sourceClaims (it supports the systematic-enumeration principle of Activity 2, not Activity 1's construction/double-counting principle) and retained where it directly applies.

probeDeeper: You said the middle is 6 — if I ask how many like football ALTOGETHER, is it 12 or 18? Why?
What is P(likes football OR cricket)? Talk me through it — do you add 12 + 8 + 6, or 18 + 14? Why can't you just add the two circle totals?
Suppose I only look at the students who like cricket — among THEM, what fraction also like football? What's the denominator now, and why did it change?
If four more students who like neither sport joined, which probabilities would change and which would stay the same?
assess.correctAnswer: Tier 1 (interpret): the middle region is the intersection — students who like both football AND cricket — 6 students, so P(both) = 6/30 = 1/5. Tier 2 (construct): shades ONLY the cricket-only crescent (the part of the cricket circle outside the overlap), 8 students, and writes P = 8/30 = 4/15 over the universal-set total of 30.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses intersection and union when shading — shades the whole cricket circle (overlap included) for 'cricket but NOT football', or the reverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to region-by-region naming: the overlap is 'both'; 'cricket but not football' is the cricket circle MINUS the overlap — shade the crescent only
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the construct move, shades the entire cricket circle (14) rather than the cricket-only crescent (8), or shades the overlap when 'only' was asked

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses a wrong denominator — divides by a circle total (or, for a conditional, by the whole universal set) instead of the total in the correct set
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'out of how many?' — an unconditional probability is over the whole 30; only a conditional ('among cricket-lovers') restricts the denominator to that subset
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes P(cricket only) = 8/14 (cricket-circle denominator) instead of 8/30, or on a conditional keeps 30 as the denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports a region frequency as the probability — writes P = 8 or P = 6, not a fraction of the total
errorPatterns.nextMove: A probability is a part of the whole between 0 and 1 — the region count over the universal-set total; 8 students out of 30 means 8/30
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'the probability is 8' or 'the probability is 6', giving a count rather than count/total

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably name the overlap as 'both', shades union when intersection is asked, or reports counts instead of probabilities; construction fails
responseLevels.full: Constructs the region accurately (cricket-only crescent), writes the probability over the correct denominator (8/30 = 4/15), computes A∪B by subtracting the double-counted overlap, and shifts the denominator correctly when a question is conditional — transferring the region logic to a new description
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a labelled diagram correctly and reads P(both) off it, but the construct move slips — shades the whole circle for a 'not' region, or uses a circle total as the denominator; can name regions but cannot yet coordinate 'only', union, and the correct denominator on a fresh case

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a completed two-circle Venn inside a rectangle: 12 in 'football only', 6 in the overlap, 8 in 'cricket only', 4 outside both (30 students total). FIRST ask: 'Point to the middle region — what does it mean, and how many students like BOTH sports? What is the probability a random student likes both?' THEN hand them a blank Venn and this fresh description and ask them to CONSTRUCT it and answer: 'Shade the region for students who like cricket but NOT football, and write the probability as a fraction.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting a given region is easier than constructing one: a child can parrot 'the middle is both' yet still shade the whole cricket circle (including the overlap) for 'cricket but NOT football', or divide by a circle total instead of 30. The construct move is the discriminator — it exposes intersection/union confusion and denominator errors that reading a labelled diagram hides.

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting within 1000 extends the compose/decompose-a-ten idea to a second boundary — composing a hundred from ten tens and decomposing a hundred into ten tens. It is taught concretely and pictorially (base-ten blocks, place-value counters, drawings) BEFORE the compact column algorithm, so that 'carrying' and 'borrowing' across two columns are understood as exchange, not digit rituals. The DfE places this in Year 3 as the conceptual foundation for formal columnar methods.
bestPractices: Work concrete→pictorial→written for the SAME calculation so the recording mirrors the exchange (NCETM Spine 1.17: strategies across the hundreds boundary combine bridging-ten with unitising)
Make both boundaries explicit: ten ones → one ten, and ten tens → one hundred; and the reverse for subtraction
Use place-value counters or base-ten on a H-T-O mat so an exchanged unit physically moves one column left/right
Deliberately include 'exchange across a zero' cases (e.g. 402−137) since these are the hardest and most error-prone
Check with estimation and the inverse operation (DfE Year 3)
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (ones, ten-rods, hundred-flats) on a place-value mat
Place-value counters on a H-T-O grid
Part-whole / partitioning drawings (256 = 200+50+6)
Number line for count-up subtraction across hundreds
Expanded written layout bridging to compact columns
commonMisconceptions: Smaller-from-larger subtraction across any column (e.g. ones done as larger-minus-smaller)
Failing to compose a hundred: ten or more tens left in the tens place (170+80 recorded with 15 in the tens column)
Borrow-across-zero errors: decomposing when the adjacent column is 0 (402−137) done incorrectly
Treating each column independently with no exchange, so carried/borrowed units vanish

learn.summary: Year 3 learners add and subtract within 1000 by extending the compose/decompose-a-ten idea to a second boundary: ten tens make a hundred, and a hundred can be broken back into ten tens. Taught concretely then pictorially then in writing for the SAME calculation, so 'carrying' and 'borrowing' across two columns are understood as exchange, not digit rituals. Across-a-zero subtraction (e.g. 402−137) is the hardest, most error-prone case and deserves deliberate attention.

activities.title: Double exchange on a place-value mat: 256 + 167
feedback: If twelve tens are left sitting in the tens column, prompt: 'You have twelve tens — can you swap ten of them for a hundred? Show me on the mat.' Physically swap ten ten-rods for one hundred-flat and watch it slide to the hundreds column.
If a carried unit disappears, point back to the rod/flat that moved and ask where its mark is in the written record.
Check with estimation: 260+170 is about 430, so 423 is reasonable.
activities.rationale: Working concrete→pictorial→written for one calculation lets the recording mirror the physical exchange; making BOTH boundaries explicit (ten ones→one ten and ten tens→one hundred) addresses the compose-a-hundred misconception directly.
sourceClaims: Strategies for calculating across the tens boundary combine with unitising to calculate across the hundreds boundary; exchange (ten ones for one ten, ten tens for one hundred) is the unifying structure.

Year 3 pupils add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal written methods, add/subtract mentally, estimate and use inverse operations to check, and apply partitioning related to place value (e.g. 146 = 100+40+6, 146 = 130+16).
learnerActions: Lay out 256 and 167 with base-ten blocks (or place-value counters) on a H-T-O mat.
Combine the ones: 6+7=13. Exchange ten ones for one ten and move that ten into the tens column (leave 3 ones).
Combine the tens: 5+6+1(carried)=12 tens. Exchange ten tens for one hundred and move it into the hundreds column (leave 2 tens).
Combine the hundreds: 2+1+1(carried)=4. Read the result: 423.
Record the matching written steps beside the blocks — first in an expanded layout, then in compact columns — so each written mark names a physical exchange.
activities.intendedInsight: Carrying across two columns is the same exchange move repeated at a second boundary: ten ones become one ten, and ten tens become one hundred.

activities.title: Cascade across a zero: 402 − 137
feedback: If the child does 7−2 ('seven take two is five') instead of exchanging, return to decomposition within 100 first (the same move one column up), then rebuild 402−137 so a unit must be broken open before subtracting.

If the child fabricates a digit (9 or 0) at the zero column without decomposing, model the two-step cascade with blocks: a hundred becomes ten tens, THEN a ten becomes ten ones. Slow it down and have the child narrate each step.
Compare: 'What if it were 452−137 instead of 402−137 — which is easier, and why?' to surface why the zero is the hard part.
activities.rationale: Across-a-zero cases are deliberately included because they are the hardest and expose borrow-across-zero and smaller-from-larger bugs; building and narrating the cascade shows why the procedure works rather than rehearsing a ritual.
sourceClaims: Borrow-across-zero and smaller-from-larger are classic systematic subtraction bugs.

Year 3 pupils add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal written methods, add/subtract mentally, estimate and use inverse operations to check, and apply partitioning related to place value (e.g. 146 = 100+40+6, 146 = 130+16).
learnerActions: Build 402 with blocks on the mat (4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones).
Try to subtract the ones (2−7): there aren't enough, and there are no tens to borrow — notice the empty tens column.
Break one hundred into ten tens (now 3 hundreds, 10 tens, 2 ones).
Break one of those tens into ten ones (now 3 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones). This is 402 written as 300+90+12.
Narrate each exchange aloud before recording it, so the two-step cascade is spoken and written in order.
activities.intendedInsight: When a column is empty you cannot borrow directly; you must first decompose the next higher unit to fill it, then decompose again — a cascade, not a one-step borrow.

activities.title: Annotated worked example: reveal each exchange step
feedback: If a prediction is wrong, ask the learner to redo the step with physical blocks before moving on, since this format shows the exchange but does not let the child perform it.
Reinforce naming: 'ten tens is one hundred, exactly as ten ones is one ten.'
activities.rationale: A step-revealing worked example gives a reference model and prompts prediction, but it is a scaffold: it does not let the child perform the double regroup, so it should follow or accompany hands-on work.
learnerActions: Study a worked addition and a worked across-zero subtraction with each exchange step hidden until requested.
Before revealing, predict what happens to a pile of ten tens, or where a borrowed ten in an empty column comes from.
Reveal the step (e.g. the tens pile becoming one hundred and some tens; the zero column being fed from a decomposed hundred) and compare it with your prediction.
Explain in your own words why the unit moved one column over.
activities.intendedInsight: Each written exchange step corresponds to a specific regrouping of units; a step-by-step reference makes the structure of the double regroup visible.

activities.title: Consolidation practice with across-zero and compose-a-hundred checks
feedback: If '15 tens' is left uncomposed, return to the mat and swap ten ten-rods for one hundred-flat.
If an across-zero answer is wrong, rebuild that one with blocks and narrate the cascade.
Use estimation to flag unreasonable answers before checking the detail.
activities.rationale: Practice consolidates and catches borrow-across-zero and compose-a-hundred errors; it rehearses the skill rather than building the initial exchange insight, so it belongs after concrete and pictorial work.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal written methods, add/subtract mentally, estimate and use inverse operations to check, and apply partitioning related to place value (e.g. 146 = 100+40+6, 146 = 130+16).
Borrow-across-zero and smaller-from-larger are classic systematic subtraction bugs.
learnerActions: Work a mixed set of three-digit additions and subtractions, including several across-a-zero subtractions.
For 170+80, choose the correct result and explain why '15 tens' (a two-digit entry in the tens column) is wrong — ten of those tens must become a hundred (250).
Fill in the decomposition of 402 as 300+90+12 and use it to complete 402−137.
Check each answer by estimating and, where possible, by the inverse operation.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recording still depends on composing a hundred and decomposing across a zero; checking with estimation and inverse catches slips.

constraints: Work concrete→pictorial→written for the SAME calculation so the written recording mirrors the physical exchange.
Make both boundaries explicit in both directions: ten ones↔one ten and ten tens↔one hundred.
Deliberately include across-a-zero subtraction (e.g. 402−137); do not treat it as an afterthought.
A step-revealing worked example is a reference scaffold: it shows exchange steps but does not let the child perform the double regroup, so pair it with hands-on work.
Practice items consolidate and diagnose errors but rehearse rather than build the exchange insight; use them after concrete and pictorial work, not instead of it.
Place-value counters or base-ten blocks on a labelled H-T-O mat should be arranged so an exchanged unit physically moves one column, and the written record should name that move.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The Brown & Burton (1978) / VanLehn (1990) source on subtraction bugs is marked unverified in the original row; treat the borrow-across-zero / smaller-from-larger bug framing as plausible but unconfirmed here, even though its claim text is cited to support the relevant rationales.

Arithmetic self-audit: 256+167 → ones 13 (carry 1), tens 5+6+1=12 (carry 1), hundreds 2+1+1=4 → 423 ✓. 402−137 → 402 as 300+90+12; 12−7=5, 90−30=60, 300−100=200 → 265 ✓. 170+80=250, and leaving '15 tens' (15 in the tens column) is the error to avoid ✓.

The original rated conversation 'poor' with the claim talk 'cannot supply the repeated hands-on exchange'; narrated explanation is included here as a supporting move within hands-on activities rather than asserted as incapable of teaching. The original 3D 'poor' rating is noted but not framed as a universal law.

The original claim that the animated across-zero case 'is exactly the case that defeats children on paper' is softened to 'hardest and most error-prone'; no comparative efficacy of any one medium over another is asserted.

Activity 3 (annotated worked example) carries sourceClaims [] because its rationale is a pedagogical scaffold-limitation claim that no original source directly supports; the underlying exchange mathematics is nonetheless consistent with the NCETM unitising claim cited elsewhere.

probeDeeper: You had twelve tens in 256+167 — can you swap some of those for a hundred? Show me on the mat.
For 402 − 137 there were no tens to take from — where did you get them?
Check 256+167 by estimating first: roughly 260+170 is about 430 — is your answer close?
What if it were 452 − 137 instead of 402 − 137 — which is easier, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 423 and 265. For 256+167: ones 6+7=13 (compose a ten), tens 5+6+1=12 (compose a hundred), hundreds 2+1+1=4 → 423. For 402−137: no tens to give ones, so decompose a hundred into ten tens then a ten into ten ones (402 as 300+90+12), 12−7=5, 90−30=60, 300−100=200 → 265.

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger across a column — in 402−137 does 7−2 in the ones ('seven take two is five') rather than exchanging
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to concrete decomposition within 100 first (this exchange is the same move one column up), then rebuild 402−137 with blocks so the child must break a unit open before subtracting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ones (or tens) column is done as larger-digit-minus-smaller regardless of which is on top; no decomposition attempted

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to compose a hundred — leaves ten or more tens in the tens place (records '12' in the tens column of 256+167)
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the mat, physically swap ten ten-rods for one hundred-flat and watch it move into the hundreds column; name that ten tens is one hundred, exactly as ten ones is one ten.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens total reaches twelve but no hundred is composed; the written answer has a two-digit entry in one column

errorPatterns.pattern: Borrow-across-zero error — in 402−137 tries to take a ten from the empty tens column, so writes 9 or 0 there without first decomposing a hundred
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the two-step cascade with blocks: a hundred becomes ten tens, THEN a ten becomes ten ones. Slow it down and have the child narrate each exchange before recording.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child stalls or fabricates a digit at the zero column; the hundred is never decomposed to feed the tens

responseLevels.gap: Columns handled independently; leaves twelve tens uncomposed, or stalls/fabricates at the zero, or does smaller-from-larger; answers unreliable when a boundary is crossed.
responseLevels.full: Composes a ten and a hundred, decomposes across a zero, records the exchanges, relates the drawing to the written method, and checks with estimation or the inverse.
responseLevels.partial: Exchanges correctly with blocks in front of them but cannot yet carry it into a written record, or manages the single exchange in 256+167 but not the across-zero decomposition in 402−137.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child base-ten blocks (or place-value counters) and paper and set two calculations to work with the apparatus and record: 256 + 167, then 402 − 137. Watch what happens at each column, and especially at the zero in 402.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 256+167 forces exchange at BOTH the ten and hundred boundaries; a child who leaves twelve tens in the tens place, or drops a carry, is exposed. 402−137 requires decomposing across a zero — the classic borrow-across-zero bug and smaller-from-larger both surface here, and neither can be faked by treating columns independently.
