pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Coral Bleaching & Acidification (ages 12–13): two distinct human-driven threats to reefs, one thermal (bleaching) and one chemical (acidification), both traced from atmospheric CO2 and rising temperature to reef collapse.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS3 biology — relationships in an ecosystem, and the interdependence of organisms; KS3 chemistry — the carbon cycle and combustion of fossil fuels adding CO2; builds on KS2 Y6 adaptation/interdependence.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS2-4 (construct an argument that changes to physical/biological components of an ecosystem affect populations); MS-ESS3-3/MS-ESS3-5 (human impacts and factors causing rise in global temperatures); MS-LS2-1 (resource availability limits populations).
• Operational details — Separate the two mechanisms explicitly so they are not conflated. BLEACHING: coral is an animal in mutualism with zooxanthellae (photosynthetic algae in its tissue that give it colour and most of its food); heat stress makes coral expel the algae, turning it white and starving it — reversible if brief, fatal if prolonged. ACIDIFICATION: ~25–30% of emitted CO2 dissolves into seawater, forming carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions coral needs to build its calcium-carbonate skeleton — so growth slows and skeletons can dissolve. Reefs host ~25% of marine species, so reef loss is a habitat-loss cascade. End on evaluating responses (emissions cuts vs local restoration/heat-tolerant coral).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete, ~11–12): can state that too-warm water makes coral turn white and that this harms it. Tier B (transitional, ~12–13): explains bleaching as coral expelling its algae partner and links extra CO2 to more acidic water that weakens skeletons. Tier C (formal, ~13): distinguishes the thermal mechanism from the chemical (carbonic acid, ↓pH, ↓carbonate) and reasons about why reef loss propagates to ~25% of marine species and which interventions target which cause.
bestPractices: Teach the two threats as SEPARATE mechanisms with a shared root cause (emissions) — do not let students merge 'hot' and 'acidic' into one vague 'pollution' story; contrast them side by side.
Anchor bleaching in the mutualism first: students must know the coral animal depends on the algae for colour AND food before 'expelling the algae' means anything.

Make the reversible-vs-fatal threshold explicit — brief stress recovers, prolonged stress kills — so students grasp why the DURATION and frequency of marine heatwaves matter, not just peak temperature.

Connect the chemistry to the biology causally: CO2 → carbonic acid → ↓pH → fewer carbonate ions → harder to build/maintain CaCO3 skeleton; keep the chain visible rather than stating 'acid dissolves coral'.
Close with argument/evaluation (NGSS MS-LS2-4): which interventions address which cause, and why local fixes (shade, restoration) cannot solve a global chemistry problem.
Use real bleaching-event imagery/data (e.g. Great Barrier Reef events) so the phenomenon is grounded in evidence, not abstraction.
keyRepresentations: Coral polyp cutaway showing zooxanthellae living inside the tissue — the mutualism made visible.
Healthy → bleached → dead colour sequence, paired with a coral energy/food meter to show starvation.
The acidification chain as a labelled flow: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 (carbonic acid) → ↓pH → ↓carbonate ions → weak/dissolving skeleton.
A pH scale/readout falling as CO2 rises, with the ~0.1-unit shift (~30% more acidic) marked.
A reef-dependence panel: the reef structure as habitat for ~25% of marine species, thinning as structure is lost.
commonMisconceptions: 'Bleached coral is dead coral' — bleaching is a stress response; brief bleaching can recover if the algae return, though prolonged bleaching is fatal.
'Coral is a plant' or 'coral bleaches because it loses its own colour' — coral is an animal; most of its colour and food come from the symbiotic algae it expels.
'Bleaching and acidification are the same thing' — one is thermal (heat expels algae), the other chemical (CO2 lowers pH and carbonate); they have different mechanisms and different fixes.
'Acidification means the ocean is turning into acid' — seawater stays slightly alkaline; it is becoming LESS alkaline / more acidic (lower pH), which is enough to reduce carbonate availability.
'Cooling the water or shading reefs would fix everything' — that can relieve bleaching but does nothing for acidification, which only falls with reduced CO2.

learn.summary: Students aged 12–13 learn to distinguish two separate human-driven threats to coral reefs that share one root cause (rising CO2 from burning fossil fuels): thermal bleaching (heat stress makes coral expel its symbiotic algae, losing colour and most of its food) and chemical acidification (dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowers pH, reduces carbonate ions, and weakens/dissolves calcium-carbonate skeletons). The core insight is that these are DIFFERENT mechanisms needing different fixes, with reef loss cascading to the ~25% of marine species that depend on reef structure. Activities build from anchoring the coral–algae mutualism, through a two-lever reef model where learners drive temperature and CO2 and observe distinct failures, to argument/evaluation of which interventions address which cause.

activities.title: Drive the reef: two levers, two different failures
feedback: If a learner merges 'hot' and 'acidic' into one vague 'pollution' effect, point to the two separate controls: show that moving only temperature changes colour/food while moving only CO2 changes pH and skeleton.
If a learner says bleached means dead, replay the quick-recovery run: colour returns when heat eases soon, so brief bleaching can recover while prolonged bleaching is fatal.

If a learner expects cooling to fix everything, point to the toggle result: cooling reversed recoverable bleaching but left the acidification damage, so a local/temperature fix cannot solve a global chemistry problem.
When a learner correctly separates the two chains and names CO2 as the shared root, affirm that identifying one cause behind two different attacks is the key idea.
activities.rationale: Two coupled cause→effect chains become concrete when learners drive the inputs and watch a living reef respond, letting the reversible-then-fatal threshold and the mechanism-specific fixes be experienced rather than told. The linked panels (food/energy meter, pH readout, carbonate tokens, species panel) make each mechanism visible; these are illustrative interaction examples, not required implementations.
sourceClaims: Coral bleaching occurs when heat-stressed corals expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae (algae), losing colour and their main energy source; corals can recover if stress is brief but die if it is prolonged. Reefs support around a quarter of marine species.

Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions available to marine calcifiers such as corals, impairing their ability to build and maintain calcium-carbonate skeletons/shells.
learnerActions: Work with a reef model that has two separate controls: water temperature and atmospheric/dissolved CO2.
Raise the TEMPERATURE and describe what happens: zooxanthellae drain out of the polyps, the coral turns white, and a coral food/energy meter falls.
Hold the heat high and observe the coral die; then, in a fresh run, ease the heat back quickly and watch colour return — state in your own words why duration matters, not just peak temperature.

Separately raise the CO2 and describe the different failure: a pH readout falls, carbonate-ion tokens the coral needs to build its skeleton become scarce, growth stalls, and skeleton edges pit and dissolve.
Watch a linked species panel: reef-dependent fish and invertebrates thin out as the reef structure is lost (~25% of marine species).
Test restoration levers (cut emissions, shade/cool the water, plant heat-tolerant coral) and record which lever repairs which failure.

Toggle 'cool the water' after bleaching and acidification have both appeared: note that bleaching recovers — provided the heat stress was not already prolonged to the point of death — while the acidification damage does not budge, and explain what this reveals.
activities.intendedInsight: Bleaching is a reversible-until-it-isn't stress response driven by heat, while acidification is a chemical attack on the skeleton driven by CO2; they are two distinct threats from the same emissions, and only cutting CO2 addresses both.

activities.title: Inside the polyp: anatomy and the two mechanisms
feedback: If a learner calls coral a plant, redirect to the cutaway: coral is an animal that houses algae which photosynthesise and supply most of its energy.
If a learner writes 'acid dissolves coral', ask them to restore the intermediate steps (carbonic acid, lower pH, fewer carbonate ions) so the causal chain stays visible.

If a learner mislabels which state goes with which threat, clarify that the bleached coral is a stressed LIVE animal whose white skeleton shows through transparent tissue after heat-driven algae loss, whereas the pitted/dissolving skeleton is caused by acidification reducing carbonate.
activities.rationale: A clear cutaway and a labelled chemistry chain teach the anatomy and both mechanisms cleanly. This is a strong anchor and consolidation support; because a fixed diagram shows before/after states rather than learner-driven threshold behaviour, pair it with the driven model for the reversible-then-fatal insight.
sourceClaims: Coral bleaching occurs when heat-stressed corals expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae (algae), losing colour and their main energy source; corals can recover if stress is brief but die if it is prolonged. Reefs support around a quarter of marine species.

Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions available to marine calcifiers such as corals, impairing their ability to build and maintain calcium-carbonate skeletons/shells.
learnerActions: Examine a cutaway of a coral polyp and identify the zooxanthellae living inside its tissue; state in your own words that these algae give the coral its colour AND most of its food.

Compare three states side by side — a healthy coloured polyp, a bleached polyp (still a live animal whose transparent tissue reveals the white skeleton beneath after the algae are expelled), and a coral whose skeleton is pitted/dissolving from acidification — and say which threat produced each.
Follow a labelled chemistry chain and fill in the missing steps: CO2 + H2O → carbonic acid (H2CO3) → lower pH → fewer carbonate ions → harder to build/maintain the CaCO3 skeleton.
Write a one-sentence contrast: how the thermal mechanism differs from the chemical mechanism.
activities.intendedInsight: The coral is an animal in mutualism with photosynthetic algae; losing those algae starves it and reveals the white skeleton through its still-living tissue (bleaching), while a separate chemistry chain (CO2→carbonic acid→↓pH→↓carbonate) physically weakens its skeleton (acidification).

activities.title: Does acid attack something hard? Predict–Observe–Explain
feedback: If a learner predicted the hard shell was safe, use the fizzing to surface and name the 'hard things are safe from acid' intuition.
If a learner concludes the ocean is 'turning into acid', correct conservatively: seawater remains slightly alkaline; it is becoming less alkaline (lower pH), which is enough to reduce carbonate ions.

If a learner treats vinegar and seawater as equivalent, restate the caveat: the ocean is far weaker and slower, stays slightly alkaline, and mainly works by lowering carbonate ions so skeletons are harder to build and maintain. It shares the acid–carbonate chemistry but does not visibly fizz like vinegar.
activities.rationale: A concrete predict–observe–explain with a shell or calcium-carbonate chalk in vinegar exposes the 'hard things are safe' intuition and grounds the acid–carbonate reaction in a visible phenomenon before mapping it to the much milder ocean case.
sourceClaims: Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions available to marine calcifiers such as corals, impairing their ability to build and maintain calcium-carbonate skeletons/shells.

Ocean acidification: the ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of emitted CO2; surface-ocean pH has fallen about 0.1 unit since the industrial era, equivalent to roughly a 30% increase in acidity (hydrogen-ion concentration).
learnerActions: Before observing, write a prediction with a reason: could a weak acid damage something as hard as a seashell or coral skeleton? Most people expect 'no, it's too hard'.

Observe a clean shell or a piece of natural chalk or limestone (calcium carbonate) placed in vinegar; note the immediate fizzing (carbon dioxide gas being released) as the surface is attacked and slowly dissolves. Note: many blackboard chalks are calcium sulfate and will not fizz, so check the material first.
Explain the link to ocean acidification: CO2 makes seawater more acidic, attacking the same calcium carbonate that corals and shellfish build.

State the important caveat in your own words: vinegar is far stronger than seawater, so the ocean effect is much slower and gentler. The shared chemistry is that acid reacts with carbonate, but in the ocean this mainly lowers the number of carbonate ions, making skeletons harder to build and easier to wear away, rather than visibly fizzing them away. Seawater stays slightly alkaline and becomes LESS alkaline, not an actual acid.
activities.intendedInsight: Hard calcium-carbonate structures are not safe from acids; a mildly more acidic ocean is enough to reduce carbonate availability and attack skeletons over time.

activities.title: Interview a reef scientist: trade-offs and evaluation
feedback: If a learner claims shading or restoration can save reefs alone, ask them to trace acidification's cause: lowering water temperature does not remove the extra dissolved CO2, so it cannot reverse the CO2-driven fall in seawater pH.
If a learner cannot name what links warming and acidification, return to the shared root: fossil-fuel CO2 both traps heat and dissolves into seawater.
Credit arguments that explicitly pair an intervention with the cause it addresses and acknowledge trade-offs and uncertainty.
activities.rationale: Open, values-laden evaluation (NGSS MS-LS2-5, evaluating competing solutions for maintaining biodiversity, building on MS-LS2-4) is best handled through argument and discussion once the mechanisms are understood; a responsive interview format lets learners weigh trade-offs a mechanistic model cannot adjudicate.
sourceClaims: Coral bleaching occurs when heat-stressed corals expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae (algae), losing colour and their main energy source; corals can recover if stress is brief but die if it is prolonged. Reefs support around a quarter of marine species.
learnerActions: Interview (in role-play or with a knowledgeable persona) a marine biologist who has surveyed a bleaching event; ask what they saw and why some reefs recover while others do not.
Pose the evaluation questions: is restoration worth it? Should effort go to cutting emissions or to engineering heat-tolerant coral? What has already been lost?
Argue, using the two-mechanism model, why local fixes such as shade, cooling, or restoration help bleaching but cannot solve acidification.
State which interventions target which cause, and why reducing CO2 is the only lever that addresses both.
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluating responses requires matching each intervention to the mechanism it affects; because acidification only eases with reduced CO2, local-only measures are insufficient on their own.

activities.title: Sort and sequence: consolidate the two chains
feedback: If a learner misorders the chain, have them check that each step is caused by the one before (CO2 before carbonic acid, lower pH before fewer carbonate ions).
If a learner miscategorises a symptom, ask whether temperature or CO2 produced it.
If a learner matches cooling to acidification, point out that cooling does not remove the extra dissolved CO2, so it cannot reverse acidification.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, categorisation, and matching can check and consolidate the two-mechanism distinction and the causal chains after the model and chemistry work. This sorting task confirms classification but does not itself elicit the learner-driven, felt model, so use it after the interactive and diagram activities.
sourceClaims: Ocean acidification: the ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of emitted CO2; surface-ocean pH has fallen about 0.1 unit since the industrial era, equivalent to roughly a 30% increase in acidity (hydrogen-ion concentration).
learnerActions: Sequence the acidification chain in order: CO2 → carbonic acid → lower pH → fewer carbonate ions → weak/dissolving skeleton.
Categorise a mix of symptoms and causes as either bleaching (thermal) or acidification (chemical).
Match each intervention to the cause it addresses (e.g. shading/cooling → bleaching only; cutting emissions → both).
Estimate how much of emitted CO2 the ocean absorbs (~25–30%) and connect that to why ocean pH has fallen about 0.1 unit since the industrial era.
activities.intendedInsight: The two threats have distinct causal chains and distinct fixes; placing each step and symptom in the right chain confirms the learner can keep them separate while recognising the shared CO2 root.

activities.title: Fly through a changing reef (optional immersive view)
feedback: If a learner treats the fly-through as explaining WHY the reef changed, redirect them to the two-lever model and chemistry chain for the mechanism; the fly-through shows the scale of the outcome.
If a learner attributes all the damage to a single cause, ask them to separate the whitening (heat/algae loss) from the structural erosion (CO2/carbonate loss).
activities.rationale: A 3D swim-through can convey scale and the visceral sense of loss that a diagram or dial cannot. Because the concept is chemical/physiological rather than spatial, treat this as an optional engagement/context layer used alongside — not instead of — the driven two-lever model, which may carry the mechanism more efficiently.
learnerActions: Take an optional 3D fly-through over a reef transect and scrub time forward under a combined warming-and-acidifying scenario, watching the reef whiten and erode.
Describe the scale and extent of loss across the transect in your own words.

Connect what you see back to the two mechanisms learned elsewhere: the whitening is heat-driven expulsion of algae, while the crumbling/eroding structure reflects CO2-driven weakening of the skeleton.
activities.intendedInsight: An immersive fly-through may convey the scale and felt sense of reef loss; because the concept is chemical/physiological rather than spatial, this view is less suited to conveying the underlying mechanisms, which are better reached through the two-lever model and chemistry chain. Treat it as a context/engagement layer rather than the primary teacher of mechanism.

constraints: Teach bleaching and acidification as SEPARATE mechanisms with a shared root cause (emissions); do not let learners merge 'hot' and 'acidic' into one vague 'pollution' story.
Anchor bleaching in the mutualism first: learners must know the coral animal depends on the algae for colour AND food before 'expelling the algae' means anything.
Make the reversible-vs-fatal threshold explicit: brief heat stress can recover, prolonged stress kills, so duration and frequency of marine heatwaves matter, not just peak temperature.
Keep the acidification chain visible (CO2 → carbonic acid → ↓pH → fewer carbonate ions → weakened CaCO3 skeleton) rather than collapsing it to 'acid dissolves coral'.

Present bleaching as a stressed LIVE coral whose white skeleton shows through transparent tissue after algae loss — distinct from acidification physically pitting/dissolving the skeleton; do not conflate 'bleached' with an exposed or dead skeleton.
State accurately that seawater stays slightly alkaline and is becoming less alkaline (lower pH); do not say the ocean is 'turning into acid'.
In the vinegar demonstration, make clear vinegar is far stronger than seawater: the demo shows the mechanism, not the ocean's rate or magnitude.

The fixed diagram shows before/after states, not learner-driven threshold behaviour; the sort/sequence task confirms classification rather than eliciting the driven model; the 3D fly-through is better suited to conveying scale than mechanism. Use them alongside, not instead of, activities where learners drive and observe change.
Treat the two-lever model's linked panels, readouts, and tokens as illustrative examples of the learning mechanism, not mandatory features or product requirements.

Local measures (shade, cooling, restoration, heat-tolerant coral) can relieve recoverable bleaching but do not address acidification, which only eases with reduced CO2; present this as the evaluation payoff.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NOAA coral-bleaching source (claim on zooxanthellae expulsion, recovery vs death, and reefs supporting ~a quarter of marine species) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat the ~25% figure and recovery claims as from an unverified source pending review.

The ~25–30% CO2 absorption and ~0.1 pH-unit / ~30% acidity-increase figures come from a source marked verified:true, but exact figures should be confirmed against current NOAA wording before publication.

The original artefact notes asserted a 3D swim-through 'adds atmosphere, not understanding' and that a static image 'can only show before/after'; these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the source evidence and have been softened throughout to scoped affordances with may/less-suited wording. The 3D alternative is retained as an optional activity to preserve the distinct alternative.

No arithmetic or force/motion content required correction; the chemistry chain, the slightly-alkaline framing, and the reversible-only-if-brief bleaching logic were checked and the cooling-toggle action was qualified so no dead/prolonged-bleached coral is implied to revive.

assess.poeTask: Ask the student to PREDICT, with a reason stated first, whether a weak acid could damage something as hard as a seashell or a piece of coral skeleton — most expect 'no, it's too hard'. Drop a clean shell/chalk (calcium carbonate) into vinegar and OBSERVE the immediate fizzing as it is attacked and slowly dissolves. Then EXPLAIN the link to ocean acidification — CO2 makes seawater more acidic, which attacks the same calcium carbonate corals and shellfish build — while noting vinegar is far stronger than seawater, so the ocean effect is slower but works the same way. The pre-observation reason exposes the 'hard things are safe from acid' intuition.
probeDeeper: If a bleached coral can sometimes recover, what does that tell you about whether 'bleached' means 'dead'?
Warming causes bleaching; acidification dissolves skeletons. What single human activity is behind BOTH — and how does one cause produce two different attacks?
Why does losing microscopic algae threaten to starve an animal that can also catch plankton with its tentacles?
Cutting local pollution helps a reef a bit, but scientists say it won't save reefs alone. Given the root cause, why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Bleaching isn't a chemical whitening and the coral isn't necessarily dead. Reef-building corals live in mutualistic symbiosis with tiny photosynthetic algae (zooxanthellae) inside them, which give the coral both colour and most of its food. When water gets too warm, the stressed coral EXPELS the zooxanthellae; without them it loses its colour (you see the white skeleton through clear tissue) and starves — it can recover if conditions ease soon, or die if not. Acidification is a different mechanism: extra CO2 dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid, lowering the pH and making it harder for corals to build (and easier to dissolve) their calcium carbonate skeletons. But the two threats share ONE root cause — rising CO2 from burning fossil fuels drives BOTH the warming that causes bleaching and the acidification that attacks skeletons.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Bleaching means the coral was chemically whitened / is definitely dead' — reads 'bleach' literally.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe: the white is the coral's own skeleton showing through once it expels its coloured algae under heat stress; it's stressed/starving, and may recover if the heat passes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the heat bleaches the coral white like bleach on fabric, and a white reef is a dead reef.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says heat 'whitens' the coral like household bleach, or that a bleached reef is always dead; no mention of algae being expelled.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Warming and acidification are unrelated problems' — misses the shared CO2 root.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace both back to fossil-fuel CO2: it traps heat (→ warming → bleaching) AND dissolves into seawater (→ carbonic acid → acidification). One cause, two attacks.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're separate coincidental problems that happen to be harming reefs at the same time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the two as coincidental; can't name what links them; surprised both stem from CO2 emissions.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The coral just makes its own food / the algae are unimportant guests' — misunderstands the mutualism.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish mutualism: the zooxanthellae photosynthesise and supply most of the coral's energy; lose them and the coral starves even if unharmed directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Doesn't see why losing the algae matters; thinks the coral animal feeds itself entirely by catching prey.

responseLevels.gap: Treats bleaching as literal whitening/death and warming and acidification as unrelated; no role for zooxanthellae.
responseLevels.full: Explains bleaching as heat-driven expulsion of symbiotic zooxanthellae (recoverable or fatal), explains acidification as CO2→carbonic acid lowering pH and attacking CaCO3 skeletons, unifies both under rising fossil-fuel CO2, and reasons about why local-only measures are insufficient.
responseLevels.partial: Can describe bleaching as algae loss AND describe acidification chemistry, but as two separate facts — doesn't connect them to a shared CO2 root or link reef loss to wider biodiversity.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A bleached reef is bone-white; nearby, other corals are struggling to build their skeletons at all. A student says 'the heat literally bleached the coral white like bleach does to a T-shirt, and the acid problem is a totally separate thing that just happens to be going on too'. Is a bleached coral 'dead and bleached white', and are warming and acidification two unrelated problems? Explain what actually turns the coral white and what the two threats have in common.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student with the naive view treats 'bleaching' as literal whitening/death and sees warming and acidification as coincidental; a student with the concept explains bleaching as loss of symbiotic zooxanthellae under heat stress AND identifies CO2 as the common root of both threats. Asking 'what do the two have in common' is the key discriminator — the naive model has no shared cause.

sources.claim: Ocean acidification: the ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of emitted CO2; surface-ocean pH has fallen about 0.1 unit since the industrial era, equivalent to roughly a 30% increase in acidity (hydrogen-ion concentration).
sources.source: NOAA — Ocean Acidification (Education / Ocean & Coasts resource collection)

sources.claim: Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions available to marine calcifiers such as corals, impairing their ability to build and maintain calcium-carbonate skeletons/shells.
sources.source: NOAA Climate.gov — Ocean acidification explainer

sources.claim: Coral bleaching occurs when heat-stressed corals expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae (algae), losing colour and their main energy source; corals can recover if stress is brief but die if it is prolonged. Reefs support around a quarter of marine species.
sources.source: NOAA — What is coral bleaching? (National Ocean Service)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–7 years

- **Topic:** Simple Food Chains

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'):** 'describe how animals obtain their food from plants and other animals, using the idea of a simple food chain, and identify and name different sources of food.'

- **Standards — US (no direct K-2 NGSS food-chain PE):** US introduces feeding relationships informally at K-2 (LS2.A: animals depend on plants/other animals for food) but formalises food chains/energy flow later at grade 5 (5-LS2-1, 5-PS3-1). Food chains as an explicit KS1 topic are UK-led — note the divergence honestly.

- **Operational details:** Children build the first big idea in ecology: energy/food passes along a chain that ALWAYS starts with a plant (producer, which makes its own food) and flows to animals (consumers) that eat it and each other. They draw a three-link chain with ARROWS and read the arrow as 'is eaten by / energy flows to'. The arrow direction is the crux — it points from the eaten to the eater, tracking the flow of food-energy, not the act of eating.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, first causal chain). Success = drawing a 3-organism chain that starts with a plant, using arrows the correct way round, and using 'producer' and 'consumer' correctly — not reversing the arrows or starting a chain with an animal.
bestPractices: Establish the arrow convention explicitly and early: the arrow means 'is eaten by / energy flows to', pointing from food to feeder.
Insist every chain STARTS with a plant (producer) and elicit why (only plants make their own food).
Use local, familiar organisms first (grass→rabbit→fox) before exotic ones.
Draw and read chains both ways — build one, then interpret a given one — to consolidate direction.
Link to prior herbivore/carnivore knowledge so consumer roles make sense.
keyRepresentations: A three-link chain with directional arrows (plant→herbivore→carnivore).
Producer/consumer labels attached to links.
An 'is eaten by' arrow key.
Familiar organism cards to arrange into a chain.
commonMisconceptions: Drawing arrows the wrong way (pointing from the eater to the food).
Starting a food chain with an animal instead of a plant.
Thinking the arrow means 'eats' rather than 'energy/food flows to'.
Believing plants get their food by eating, like animals, rather than making it.
Treating the top predator as the 'start' or most important, rather than the producer.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7, children learn that a simple food chain shows food-energy passing along a sequence that always starts with a plant (a producer that makes its own food) and flows to animals (consumers). The crux is the arrow convention: the arrow means 'is eaten by / energy flows to' and points from the food to the feeder. Activities span building and drawing a three-link chain, interpreting a given labelled chain, checking structure through ordering and matching, and talking through an organism's place in the chain including what happens if the producer is lost. Aligns with UK DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'.

activities.title: Build and arrow a three-link food chain
feedback: If a learner starts the chain with the fox, ask 'Where does the fox's food come from?' and trace back link by link until a plant appears — that is where the chain begins.

If an arrow points the wrong way (from the eater to the food), rename the arrow out loud as 'is eaten by / food goes to' and walk the food-energy from grass into the rabbit into the fox so the arrowhead follows the food.
If a learner is reluctant to begin with grass ('grass isn't really food'), point out that the rabbit's food IS the grass, so the plant is the food source where the chain must start.
Confirm success when the learner draws grass→rabbit→fox with forward arrows, names producer and consumer correctly, and can say why a plant comes first.
activities.rationale: Constructing the chain and the arrows themselves (rather than only recognising a finished one) makes the arrow-direction rule and the plant-first rule a decision the child must make, surfacing the two common reversals so they can be corrected in the moment.
learnerActions: Arrange organism cards (grass, rabbit, fox) into the correct order, left to right.
Draw an arrow between each pair of organisms, pointing from the one that is eaten to the one that eats it.
Say aloud what each arrow means: 'is eaten by / the food and energy pass to the next animal.'
Label each link as 'producer' (the plant) or 'consumer' (each animal).
Explain why the chain must begin with the plant: the grass makes its own food, but the rabbit and fox must eat to get theirs.
activities.intendedInsight: Every food chain starts with a plant that makes its own food, and arrows track food-energy flowing from the eaten to the eater.

activities.title: Interactive chain reference: read the roles and the arrow
feedback: Reinforce the arrow key each time: the arrowhead points to whoever eats.
If a learner reads the arrow as 'eats', restate it as 'is eaten by / food goes to' and have them re-read the chain in that direction.
activities.rationale: A clean labelled reference consolidates the vocabulary and the arrow key. This is a reading/interpretation scaffold rather than independent construction, so it supports but does not replace the building task.
learnerActions: Study a labelled grass→rabbit→fox chain.
Tap or point to each organism to reveal its role: 'I eat… / I am eaten by…' and whether it is a producer or consumer.
Tap or point to each arrow to reveal that it means 'is eaten by / energy flows to'.
Retell the chain in your own words, naming producer and consumer and reading each arrow correctly.
activities.intendedInsight: The arrow carries a fixed meaning ('is eaten by / energy flows to') and each organism has a role (producer or consumer) that stays consistent across the chain.

activities.title: Order the chain and choose the starting rule
feedback: For ordering errors, ask what each animal's food is and trace back to the plant.
For the 'starts with' item, confirm plants make their own food so they are the source everything else depends on.
For arrow-direction items, restate the arrow as 'is eaten by'.
activities.rationale: Ordering, selection and matching efficiently check the structure of the chain. These response formats confirm recognition of the rule; they do not require the learner to draw arrows live, so pair them with the building activity for independent construction.
learnerActions: Put a scrambled set of organisms (grass, rabbit, fox) into the correct chain order.
Answer: 'What does every food chain start with?' and choose the plant/producer.
Answer an arrow-direction item: which way does the arrow point between two organisms?
Match each organism to its label: 'producer' or 'consumer'.
activities.intendedInsight: A food chain has a fixed structure — producer first, then consumers — and the arrow direction and role labels can be identified reliably.

activities.title: Talk through an animal's place in the chain
feedback: If the learner cannot name what comes before an animal, prompt 'what is its food?' and connect that to the previous link.
Steer every trace-back to the producer so the plant-first idea is reinforced through talk.
For the 'what if the grass died out' prompt, help the learner reason that the rabbit would lose its food and the fox in turn would lose the rabbit — the chain depends on the producer.
activities.rationale: A spoken walk-along the chain can reinforce the 'before/after' relationships and the chain's dependence on the producer through dialogue. For this age, pair it with building or seeing the chain drawn, since an abstract spoken sequence can be harder to hold than a visible chain.
learnerActions: Take the part of one animal in the chain (e.g. the rabbit).
Answer: 'What do I eat?' and 'Who eats me?'
Name what comes before you (your food) and after you (your eater) in the chain.
Trace the whole chain back to the plant that makes its own food.
Consider what would happen to the fox if all the grass died out, and explain how the whole chain depends on the plant at the start.
activities.intendedInsight: Each animal sits between what it eats and what eats it; following those links backwards always reaches a plant, and because every animal ultimately depends on the producer, losing the plant affects the whole chain.

constraints: Establish the arrow convention explicitly and early: the arrow means 'is eaten by / energy flows to', pointing from food to feeder.
Insist every chain starts with a plant (producer) and elicit why — plants make their own food, while animals have to eat other living things.
Use local, familiar organisms first (grass→rabbit→fox) before exotic ones.
Build chains both ways: construct one, then interpret a given one, to consolidate arrow direction.
Link to prior herbivore/carnivore knowledge so consumer roles make sense.

Reading/interpretation activities (labelled reference, ordering, matching) confirm recognition but do not require the learner to construct arrows independently; include at least one task where the learner draws the chain and arrows themselves.
Spoken walk-throughs support relational understanding but should accompany, not replace, a visible or drawn chain at this age.

Address the common misconceptions directly: reversed arrows, starting with an animal, reading the arrow as 'eats', believing plants eat for their food rather than making it, and treating the top predator as the start/most important.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The building activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because the DfE KS1 standard supports the objective/topic but does not directly evidence the construction-surfaces-reversals rationale; the curriculum alignment is noted here instead.

The source noted a US/UK divergence: NGSS introduces feeding relationships informally at K-2 but formalises food chains and energy flow at grade 5 (5-LS2-1, 5-PS3-1); explicit KS1 food-chain teaching is UK-led. Adjust expectations for US learners accordingly.

The original claim that '3D adds nothing over a flat builder' was a catalog fit comment, not an established pedagogical law; it has been softened/omitted. A food chain is commonly represented as a flat directional sequence, which is sufficient for this objective, but this does not prove other media cannot help.

The original 'bench checks flow / animates food flowing backwards and is rejected' describes an optional interactive mechanism; retained as an example of corrective feedback, not as a required mechanism.

The dependency/knock-on reasoning (what happens if the producer is lost) comes from the saved assessment's probeDeeper and full-response level; it has been reinstated as an extension in the dialogue activity to preserve that assessment depth.
The comparative claim that a spoken sequence is harder to hold than a visible chain is kept only in qualified form and is not independently verified.

probeDeeper: If the arrow means 'is eaten by', who is eaten by the fox in your chain?
Where does the grass get its own food from?
Could a food chain ever start with a fox? Why not?
What would happen to the fox if all the grass died out?
assess.correctAnswer: Arrows point grass → rabbit → fox, and an arrow means 'is eaten by' / the food and its energy pass to the next animal. The chain starts with grass because a plant is a producer — it makes its own food using sunlight, so it is the source of food and energy that everything else depends on; animals are consumers and cannot make their own food.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The arrow shows who eats who, so it points from the fox to what it eats' — reads the arrow as 'eats' and reverses the whole chain.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rename the arrow out loud as 'is eaten by / food goes to'; walk energy from grass into the rabbit into the fox so the arrowhead follows the food.
errorPatterns.distractor: The arrows should point from the fox to the rabbit to the grass, to show who eats who.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws fox → rabbit → grass, or says the arrow 'points to its dinner'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The chain starts with the biggest, strongest animal' — puts the top predator first.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what the fox's energy ultimately came from; trace back until you reach the thing that makes its own food — the plant — and start there.
errorPatterns.distractor: The chain should start with the fox, because it is the biggest and strongest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Begins the chain with the fox; treats 'first' as most powerful rather than the food source.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Food chains start with an animal — grass isn't really food' — does not see the plant as the producer/food source.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish plants as producers that make food; the rabbit's food IS the grass, so the plant is where the chain must begin.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reluctant to begin with grass; says food chains start with 'something that eats'.

responseLevels.gap: Reverses the arrows or starts the chain with an animal; cannot say what the arrow means.
responseLevels.full: Draws correct direction, explains the arrow as food/energy passing to the eater, justifies the plant-first rule by producers making their own food, and predicts a knock-on effect if the producer is lost.
responseLevels.partial: Draws the chain grass-first with forward arrows but explains the arrow only as 'eats', or cannot say why a plant must come first.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'A rabbit eats grass, and a fox eats the rabbit. I want you to draw this as a food chain with arrows, and tell me what each arrow means. Then tell me: why must the chain start with the grass and not with the fox?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the arrow means 'eats' draws them backwards (fox → rabbit → grass). A child who thinks the 'biggest, strongest' animal comes first starts with the fox. Only a child using the food-source/energy-flow idea puts the plant first with forward-pointing arrows — the two errors give visibly different drawings.

sources.claim: DfE KS1 Year 2: 'describe how animals obtain their food from plants and other animals, using the idea of a simple food chain, and identify and name different sources of food.'
sources.source: UK Department for Education, National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS1)

sources.claim: NGSS formalises food chains and energy flow at grade 5 (5-LS2-1 movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers; 5-PS3-1 energy in food once came from the sun), not at K-2.
sources.source: NGSS, 5-LS2 / 5-PS3 (Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Subtraction as an unknown-addend problem — understanding that 10 − 8 = ? is the same question as 8 + ? = 10, so subtraction can be solved by finding the missing part / counting on. Ages 6–7, a key bridge from take-away to the additive structure.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): supports Y1–Y2 'represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts' and 'recall and use addition and subtraction facts', where subtraction facts are derived from known addition bonds; underpins missing-number problems like 7 = □ − 9.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.4 'Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem. For example, subtract 10 − 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.'
• Operational details: reframe the take-away picture as a missing-part picture on a part-whole model — whole known, one part known, find the other part. Encourage counting on from the subtrahend to the minuend, especially when the parts are close (12 − 9 by counting up 9→10→11→12). This is the efficiency insight, not just an alternative.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — given 9 + □ = 13, matches it to 13 − 9 and finds 4. Tier B (age 7) — chooses to count on for 12 − 9 because the numbers are close, and explains why. Tier C (age 7+) — states that every subtraction can be rewritten as an addition with a missing part and uses it to solve/check.
bestPractices: Anchor on the part-whole model: subtraction reveals a missing PART when the whole and one part are known.
Teach counting-up (shopkeeper's method) explicitly as the efficient strategy when subtrahend and minuend are close.
Pair each subtraction with its unknown-addend twin (13 − 9 = ? ↔ 9 + ? = 13) so the equivalence is repeatedly seen.
Use missing-number equations in varied positions to force the additive reading rather than a take-away action.
Delay pure take-away drilling; contrast 'how many are left' with 'how many more to reach' so difference/missing-part meanings are established.
keyRepresentations: Part-whole (cherry) diagram with the missing part as the unknown
Bar model: total bar with one part shaded and the gap to find
Empty number line showing a count-on jump from subtrahend to minuend
Double ten-frame with one frame filled and the gap to ten visible
Fact-family triangle linking the whole and its two parts
commonMisconceptions: Believing subtraction can only mean 'take away / count back', so refusing to count up.
Not seeing 8 + ? = 10 and 10 − 8 = ? as the same question.
Counting back inefficiently for close numbers (12−11 counted back eleven steps) and making errors.
Confusing which quantity is the whole and which is a part in the part-whole model.
Treating the answer to 8 + ? = 10 as 10 (writing the whole) rather than the missing part.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year-olds understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem: 12 − 9 = ? asks the same question as 9 + ? = 12 — find the missing PART of a known whole. Anchor the equivalence on a part-whole model, teach counting up from the subtrahend when the numbers are close, and repeatedly pair each subtraction with its addition twin. A linked part-whole/number-line display can make the 'same gap, two routes' insight concrete; dialogue draws out the justification; matching and missing-number tasks consolidate; a static part-whole picture (with a double ten-frame and fact-family triangle as further representations) anchors both equations against one diagram.

activities.title: Two routes, one gap: linked part-whole and number line
feedback: When both routes land on the same gap, say: 'Taking away and counting up reached the same number — because they are the same question asked two ways.'
If the child gets 4 on 12 − 9 by counting back including the start (or by counting up starting on 9), replay the count-up: 9→10→11→12 is three jumps; count them together on the line.
If the child writes the whole (12) as the missing addend, point to the gap on the bar: 'We already know this part is 9; we are looking for the piece that fills the rest up to 12.'
activities.rationale: Showing the same situation two ways at once — take-away and count-on landing on one gap — can make the unknown-addend equivalence visible from a single action, and close-number cases let the child feel why counting up is often more efficient. Dragging to remove, hopping up the line, and the two equations updating together are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.

Missing-addend problems are conceptually harder than take-away and children often solve subtraction by counting back even when counting up is more efficient; deriving subtraction from known addition facts is a documented strategy.
Y1–Y2 pupils represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts and solve missing-number problems, deriving subtraction facts from addition bonds.
learnerActions: Look at a part-whole bar with whole 10 and known part 8, and a number line beside it.
First try to count BACK from the whole by the known part (back 8 from 10) to find the missing part; notice this is fiddly for some pairs.
Then start at the known part (8) and hop UP to the whole (8→9→10), counting the jumps to find the gap.
See both routes highlight the SAME gap of 2, and read the two printed sentences 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10 together.
Repeat with a close-number case such as 12 − 9: count back nine steps, then instead start at 9 and hop up 9→10→11→12 (three easy jumps), and see 12 − 9 = 3 printed above 9 + 3 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: A subtraction and its unknown-addend twin ask the same question — the missing part of a whole — and counting up from the subtrahend is often the shortcut, especially when the numbers are close.

activities.title: Explain why counting up works
feedback: If the child says the two are 'different sums', put 12 as the whole and 9 as a known part on a part-whole model and show the single missing part answers BOTH questions.
Affirm reasoning that names the missing part: 'Yes — the number you add to 9 to reach 12 is the same as the number left when you take 9 from 12.'
activities.rationale: The equivalence is a reasoning insight, so inviting the child to explain why counting up works and to state the addition twin targets the conceptual 'understand as' objective. Responsive spoken discussion lets a tutor probe the justification directly; recognition-only tasks would not elicit this spoken justification.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
learnerActions: Solve a close-number subtraction such as 12 − 9 using whatever method you choose.
Answer aloud: 'You could take 9 away — but is there a quicker way to get from 9 up to 12?'
State the matching addition sentence (9 + ? = 12) for the subtraction.
Explain in your own words why 12 − 9 and 9 + ? = 12 are the same question.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the equivalence — not just produce the number — shows the child reads subtraction additively rather than only as take-away.

activities.title: Match, fill, and choose the quicker route
feedback: For 9 + □ = 13: the missing part is 4, not 13 — 13 is the whole; underline the gap being asked for.
For the 'quicker route' choice, affirm counting up for 12 − 9 because 9 and 12 are close (three jumps) while counting back nine steps invites errors.
If the child reverses whole and part, restate: the whole is the total; the two parts add to it.
activities.rationale: Matching, missing-number and strategy-choice tasks consolidate an already-built idea. A fixed sequence of items consolidates and checks recognition and strategy choice rather than letting the child freely toggle representations, so it is best used after the linked model and paired with an explanation prompt.
sourceClaims: Y1–Y2 pupils represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts and solve missing-number problems, deriving subtraction facts from addition bonds.

Missing-addend problems are conceptually harder than take-away and children often solve subtraction by counting back even when counting up is more efficient; deriving subtraction from known addition facts is a documented strategy.
learnerActions: Match each subtraction to its unknown-addend twin, e.g. 13 − 9 ↔ 9 + □ = 13.
Fill in the missing addend: 9 + □ = 13 (answer 4), then write the matching subtraction 13 − 9 = 4.
Decide which is quicker for 12 − 9 — counting up or counting back — and give a reason.
Given a known fact such as 8 + 5 = 13, write a subtraction you can now answer straight away.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the pairing of subtraction with its addition twin and the strategic choice of counting up when numbers are close.

activities.title: One diagram, both equations (anchor)
feedback: Point at the gap: 'This is the part we are finding — it completes 8 up to 10.'
If the child names the whole as the answer, re-point to the known part and the gap.
On the ten-frame, the empty cells show the same gap (2 empty cells when 8 of 10 are filled); on the triangle, the whole sits apart from its two parts.
activities.rationale: A static part-whole picture can present both equations against one diagram and reveal the missing part, which anchors the equivalence; a double ten-frame and fact-family triangle offer the same structure in other forms. It does not let the child act out take-away and count-on as the same gap, so use it as an anchor or for learners who need a settled reference rather than as the primary builder.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
learnerActions: Look at a part-whole diagram with a tappable whole and one known part.
Tap or lift a flap to reveal the missing part.
Read both equation forms shown side by side against the same diagram, e.g. 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10.
Name which number is the whole and which are the parts.

Compare the same whole and parts in other representations — a ten-frame with 8 cells filled and the gap of 2 to ten visible (use a double ten-frame for wholes above 10, e.g. 9 filled plus 3 more to reach 12), and a fact-family triangle linking the whole and its two parts — and read how each shows the missing part.
activities.intendedInsight: Both the subtraction and its addition twin describe the same part-whole picture, and the answer is the missing part.

constraints: Target ages 6–7; this bridges take-away toward the additive structure of subtraction.

The static part-whole picture and the matching/missing-number tasks consolidate or anchor; they do not let the child freely toggle between the take-away and count-on views, which the linked model provides.

Matching and multiple-choice items check recognition and strategy choice; they do not by themselves elicit the child's own spoken or written justification of why the two questions share an answer — pair them with an explanation prompt.

Teach counting up explicitly as the efficient strategy when subtrahend and minuend are close; do not present it as universally faster — for a pair like 12 − 3, counting back three is quicker, so prompt strategy choice by how near the numbers are.
Delay pure take-away drilling; contrast 'how many are left' with 'how many more to reach' so both difference and missing-part meanings are established.

Watch the count-up step count: 9→10→11→12 is three jumps; starting the count on the subtrahend itself (or counting back including the start) produces an off-by-one error (answer 4). This is a procedural slip, not a conceptual one — model the count rather than reteaching the concept.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the DfE National Curriculum claim as verified:true and the CCSS 1.OA.4 and Cognitively Guided Instruction claims as verified:false; these flags were not re-checked here.
The double ten-frame (gap-to-ten) and fact-family triangle representations from the original keyRepresentations are preserved in the anchor activity.

The recommendation narrative for 12 − 9 uses a gap of 3 (9→10→11→12), while the worked example for 10 − 8 uses a gap of 2 (8→9→10); both are arithmetically correct. Confirmed 9 + 3 = 12 and 8 + 2 = 10, and 9 + 4 = 13.

The off-by-one answer of 4 for 12 − 9 arises from miscounting the up-jumps (counting the start) or counting back including the start; handled as a strategy/counting fix, not a conceptual reteach, consistent with the source.

probeDeeper: You found 3. In this story, is 3 a part or the whole? How do you know?
What's your evidence that 9 + 3 and 12 − 9 have the same answer?
What if it were 12 − 3 instead? Would counting up still be the quick way, or would counting back be quicker — and why?
If I tell you that 8 + 5 = 13, what subtraction could you answer straight away?
assess.correctAnswer: 3 — and explains that 12 − 9 asks the same question as 9 + ? = 12: the number you add to 9 to reach 12 is the same as the number left when you take 9 from 12, so both give 3. Often solved by counting up from 9.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Subtraction just means take away, so it isn't an adding question' — gets 3 by counting back but insists 12−9 and 9+?=12 are different, unrelated sums.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place on a part-whole model: put 12 as the whole and 9 as a known part, and show the single missing part answers BOTH questions; do not drill more take-away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: solves the subtraction yet cannot connect it to the addition, or calls them 'different sums'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The answer to 9 + ? = 12 is 12' — writes the whole (or adds the visible numbers) instead of the missing part.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the part-whole diagram to name which piece is the whole and which is the unknown part; point at the gap that is being asked for.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked the addition twin, says 12 (the total) rather than 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back for close numbers and slips by one (starts the count on 9 rather than the first step), giving 4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — model counting UP for close numbers and prompt strategy choice by how near the numbers are; check the count with fingers or a number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 4; on watching, counts '9, 10, 11, 12' as four steps or counts back including the start.

responseLevels.gap: Solves only by counting back (or not at all) and treats 12−9 and 9+?=12 as unrelated; cannot state the matching addition.
responseLevels.full: Explains that 12−9 and 9+?=12 ask the same thing (the missing part of a whole), chooses to count up when the numbers are close, and uses a known addition fact to answer a new related subtraction.
responseLevels.partial: Gets 3 and, when prompted, can state 9+3=12, but treats it as a separate fact — cannot explain why the two questions share an answer and does not transfer to a new pair.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a subtraction: 12 − 9. Work out the answer. Then tell me how this is the same as the addition 9 + ? = 12.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds only a take-away conception can still reach 3 by counting back, but stalls or denies the link on the second tier — they cannot say why 9 + ? = 12 gives the same result. A child with the unknown-addend concept answers the 'why' immediately and frequently prefers counting up because the numbers are close. The REASON tier separates the two even when both produce the numeric answer.
