pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Force & Motion Vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 5 Forces & KS3 Motion and Forces):** Vocabulary spans Year 5 forces and KS3 'Motion and forces' — force arrows, adding forces in 1 dimension, balanced and unbalanced forces, moment as the turning effect of a force, and 'forces being needed to cause objects to stop or start moving, or to change their speed or direction of motion (qualitative only)'. Terms such as resultant, moment, lever and mechanical advantage are KS3-level.

- **Standards — US (no standalone NGSS PE; embedded across PS2 + CCSS literacy):** Force-and-motion vocabulary is embedded across NGSS PS2 Motion and Stability (3-PS2, MS-PS2) rather than being a discrete performance expectation, and is supported by the CCSS literacy-in-science standards for domain-specific vocabulary (e.g. RST.6-8.4).

- **Operational details:** This is a Tier-3, subject-specific vocabulary (LANGUAGE) topic: balanced/unbalanced forces, resultant force, acceleration, deceleration, speed, moment, lever, fulcrum, mechanical advantage — used to explain and predict how forces affect motion. It is best taught with explicit vocabulary instruction: select a small number of high-leverage concept words, define and contextualise them, have pupils actively process them (examples, non-examples, characteristics, a drawing), and provide multiple exposures across contexts. The Frayer Model is the canonical graphic organiser, though it demands some abstraction, so at the primary end it is adapted (a drawing in place of characteristics; synonyms/antonyms). The distinctive challenge of THIS word set is that most terms name a relationship or a dynamic effect (acceleration, deceleration, resultant, moment) rather than a concrete object — so each word must be pinned to the phenomenon it labels, and crisp NON-examples are needed to fence off the everyday-vs-scientific drift.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal).
bestPractices: Select a few high-leverage concept words to teach in depth (Frayer is time-intensive) — resultant, balanced/unbalanced and acceleration anchor this set — rather than every term

Use explicit instruction: give a student-friendly definition, contextualise it in a sentence, and supply examples AND non-examples to sharpen the concept's boundary (acceleration vs deceleration vs constant speed; resultant vs an extra force)
Make it discussion-centred and actively processed (Frayer / drawing), not a glossary look-up worksheet
Provide multiple exposures across varied contexts; revisit and refine the organiser over a unit; add terms to a vocabulary wall and require pupils to use them in speech and writing
Anchor each term to the phenomenon it names — tie the word to a seen motion or force effect — because these are relational, not concrete, nouns
Explicitly contrast everyday and scientific meanings (speed/force used loosely; 'moment' is not an instant of time; 'mechanical advantage')
keyRepresentations: Frayer Model graphic organiser (term · definition · characteristics or picture · examples · non-examples)
Vocabulary wall with each term anchored to a motion image or force-arrow diagram
Word-to-phenomenon pairing card linking the term to the effect it labels
commonMisconceptions: Using 'speed' and 'acceleration' interchangeably — speed is how fast; acceleration is how fast the speed is changing; deceleration mis-described as 'negative speed'
'Resultant force' treated as an extra/additional force rather than the net combined effect of the forces
'Balanced forces' read as meaning there are no forces acting
Everyday-vs-scientific drift: 'force', and especially 'moment' (mistaken for an instant of time) and 'mechanical advantage'
Treating a word as learned once a definition is copied, without applying it to explain or predict (the topic's evidence demands application)
Confusing lever / fulcrum / moment — which part is the pivot, which is the turning effect

learn.summary: Portable guidance for teaching Tier-3 force-and-motion vocabulary (balanced/unbalanced forces, resultant force, speed, acceleration, deceleration, moment, lever, fulcrum, mechanical advantage) to 9–11 year olds. The distinctive challenge is that most of these words name a relationship or a dynamic effect rather than a concrete object, so each term must be pinned to a visible phenomenon and fenced off from everyday meanings with crisp non-examples. Guidance favours explicit vocabulary instruction (student-friendly definition, contextualised sentence, examples AND non-examples, active processing, multiple exposures) and productive use in speech and writing, not glossary copying. Note that a resultant force sets the change in motion (acceleration), not the current direction of travel.

activities.title: Pin each word to a scene, then fence it with a non-example
feedback: If a learner says acceleration means 'going fast', contrast a fast STEADY speed (no acceleration) with a slow speeding-up (acceleration): acceleration means the speed is increasing, deceleration means it is decreasing, and steady speed (however fast) is neither.
If a learner treats 'resultant' as an extra force, re-show the two unequal pulls and the single combined arrow — the resultant is the net effect of the forces already there, not an additional one.

If a learner says 'balanced forces' means there are no forces, point to a tug-of-war where both sides pull equally and it stays at a standstill: two real pulls are acting, they just cancel to a zero resultant. (Equal pulls give balance and zero resultant; unequal pulls give a net resultant.)
If a learner confuses lever/fulcrum/moment, label the pivot (fulcrum), the bar (lever) and the turning effect (moment) separately on the see-saw.
activities.rationale: Effective vocabulary instruction selects a few central concept words and teaches them in depth with explicit definition, contextualisation, active processing and multiple exposures; non-examples sharpen the concept's boundary. Anchoring each relational term to a visible phenomenon addresses the specific difficulty that these words name effects, not objects.
sourceClaims: Effective vocabulary instruction selects a few central concept words and teaches them in depth via explicit definition, contextualisation, active processing and multiple exposures; the Frayer Model (term + definition + characteristics + examples + non-examples) operationalises this, is taught through modelling and gradual release, must be discussion-centred (not a worksheet look-up), uses non-examples to sharpen the concept's boundary, and is revisited over time.

The Frayer Model requires a degree of abstraction and is most effective at upper-elementary level and above; for younger primary children it is adapted (e.g. a drawing in place of characteristics, synonyms/antonyms for examples/non-examples).
learnerActions: Study one rich force-and-motion scene containing a cart that is speeding up, a see-saw, and a tug-of-war.
For each key term, state a student-friendly meaning in your own words, point to the part of the scene it labels, give one example, and give one non-example.
For 'fulcrum', identify the see-saw pivot and say why it is not the load and not the effort — it is the point the lever turns on.

For 'acceleration', show several positions of the cart taken at equal time intervals, with the gaps between them getting progressively larger so the increasing speed is visible (not merely that the cart is fast), and contrast it with 'deceleration' (gaps shrinking, slowing down) and 'constant speed' (equal gaps, no change).

For 'resultant', look at a tug-of-war in which one side pulls harder than the other, draw the single combined arrow that shows the net, and explain that it is not an extra pull but the net of the two.

Build a Frayer-style organiser for 2–3 high-leverage words (term, meaning, a drawing, examples, non-examples); at the primary end, use a drawing in place of 'characteristics' and synonyms/antonyms for examples/non-examples.
activities.intendedInsight: Each abstract term becomes learnable when tied to something you can see AND to a non-example that fences off the usual confusion: acceleration is not just 'fast', a resultant is not an added force, and balanced does not mean no forces.

activities.title: See the dynamic words happen
feedback: If a learner labels the steady-speed stage 'accelerating', point out the speed is not changing, so there is no acceleration during that stage.

If a learner expects the object to instantly travel in the push direction, explain that a resultant sets how motion changes, not an instant jump: from rest the object starts moving in the resultant's direction and builds up gradually, and an object that is already moving keeps its motion while the resultant gradually bends its path or speeds/slows it.
When introducing the resultant, start the object from rest where possible so the link between resultant direction and the change in motion is cleanest.
activities.rationale: Seeing an effect enacted gives additional, varied exposures and ties a dynamic word to the phenomenon it labels. This is proposed as a companion to the static scene; the goal remains word knowledge, so watching an animation supplements rather than replaces explicit instruction.
sourceClaims: Effective vocabulary instruction selects a few central concept words and teaches them in depth via explicit definition, contextualisation, active processing and multiple exposures; the Frayer Model (term + definition + characteristics + examples + non-examples) operationalises this, is taught through modelling and gradual release, must be discussion-centred (not a worksheet look-up), uses non-examples to sharpen the concept's boundary, and is revisited over time.
learnerActions: Watch the cart start from rest and speed up, then move at a steady speed, then slow to a stop; name the stage with 'acceleration', 'constant speed' and 'deceleration' as each happens.

Combine two arrows of different sizes and directions acting on an object that starts from rest, and watch the single resultant arrow that results; describe which way it points and how the object's motion changes from rest.
Contrast a steady glide (constant speed, no acceleration) with a speeding-up motion (acceleration) and say what is different about the speed in each.
activities.intendedInsight: The relational, dynamic terms (acceleration, deceleration, resultant) are clearer when you watch the effect they name unfold, not just read a definition — and the resultant sets how the motion changes, not an instant jump to the push direction.

activities.title: Consolidate with retrieval across varied contexts
feedback: For a sorting error, re-ask whether the speed is changing: changing speed is accelerating or decelerating; unchanging speed is constant.
If a learner can select the right word but cannot use it in a sentence, prompt them to say the same idea in their own words so recognition becomes production.
activities.rationale: Multiple exposures across varied contexts and revisiting over time are core to the recommended vocabulary approach. Matching and categorising check recognition; note the objective limit below.
sourceClaims: Effective vocabulary instruction selects a few central concept words and teaches them in depth via explicit definition, contextualisation, active processing and multiple exposures; the Frayer Model (term + definition + characteristics + examples + non-examples) operationalises this, is taught through modelling and gradual release, must be discussion-centred (not a worksheet look-up), uses non-examples to sharpen the concept's boundary, and is revisited over time.
learnerActions: Match each term to its student-friendly definition.
Sort short motion descriptions or clips into 'accelerating', 'decelerating' or 'constant speed'.
Complete sentences by choosing and inserting the correct term, then read the full sentence aloud.
Revisit the vocabulary over the unit, adding each term to a vocabulary wall anchored to a motion image or force-arrow diagram, and use the words again in later lessons.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated retrieval in different contexts strengthens word knowledge and the ability to recognise where each term belongs.

activities.title: Explain it back and use the words to describe real cases
feedback: Expected accurate use: at rest and at steady speed the forces are balanced (zero resultant, no change in motion); pushing off from rest, forces are unbalanced with a resultant forwards causing acceleration; braking while moving forwards, unbalanced with a resultant backwards causing deceleration; 'speed' is how fast, and acceleration (speeding up) is distinguished from deceleration (slowing).

If steady speed is called 'unbalanced' because 'it's moving', correct it: steady speed means no change in motion, so the forces are balanced with zero resultant — reserve 'unbalanced' for changing motion.
If 'balanced' is used only for a stationary object, model using 'balanced' for BOTH the at-rest stage and the constant-speed stage.

If 'moment' is treated as an instant of time, re-anchor it to the turning effect of a force on a lever; if 'mechanical advantage' or 'force' drifts to an everyday meaning, contrast the everyday and scientific senses explicitly.
activities.rationale: Productive use — speaking and writing with the terms — gives extra exposures and reveals whether the vocabulary is owned. Assessing use in context discriminates genuine word knowledge from recitation.
sourceClaims: Effective vocabulary instruction selects a few central concept words and teaches them in depth via explicit definition, contextualisation, active processing and multiple exposures; the Frayer Model (term + definition + characteristics + examples + non-examples) operationalises this, is taught through modelling and gradual release, must be discussion-centred (not a worksheet look-up), uses non-examples to sharpen the concept's boundary, and is revisited over time.
learnerActions: Explain a chosen term in your own words to a partner and justify an example you pick.
Use 'moment', 'lever' and 'fulcrum' to describe how a see-saw works.
Explain why a longer spanner helps turn a tight bolt, using the word 'moment'.
Give a sentence using 'mechanical advantage' about a bottle opener or a wheelbarrow.

Talk through a whole journey — waiting at rest, pushing off and speeding up, then steady speed, then braking to a stop — saying at each stage whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced and what the resultant force is doing.
activities.intendedInsight: A word is only truly learned when it does real work in explaining and predicting, not when a definition has been copied.

constraints: Select a few high-leverage words to teach in depth (resultant, balanced/unbalanced and acceleration anchor this set) rather than attempting every term at once; in-depth organisers are time-intensive.
Anchor each term to the phenomenon it names, because these are relational or dynamic words, not concrete nouns.
Always include crisp non-examples to fence off everyday-vs-scientific drift (acceleration ≠ 'fast'; resultant ≠ an extra force; balanced ≠ no forces; 'moment' ≠ an instant of time).
Keep instruction discussion-centred and actively processed; a glossary look-up worksheet alone is insufficient.

Matching and categorising check recognition; they do not by themselves elicit independent production, so include speaking and writing tasks that require the learner to construct sentences and explanations.
The Frayer Model demands some abstraction; at the primary end adapt it (a drawing in place of characteristics; synonyms/antonyms for examples/non-examples).

When describing changing motion, remember a resultant force determines the change in motion (acceleration), not the current direction of travel: start from rest or describe how an existing path changes rather than saying a side push makes the object instantly travel in the push direction. Balanced forces mean no change in motion, which includes steady-speed movement, not only rest.

For the tug-of-war prop, make it explicit which configuration is shown: equal opposing pulls give balanced forces with a zero resultant (a standstill), while unequal pulls give a visible net resultant toward the stronger side.

A lift-the-flap or tap-to-reveal scene, an animation that enacts a word, and a vocabulary wall are useful presentation options, not mandatory mechanisms; choose the medium that best supports explicit instruction and repeated use.

When illustrating acceleration with a moving object, ensure the representation shows the speed CHANGING (e.g. increasing gaps between positions taken at equal time intervals), not merely a fast object, to avoid reinforcing the acceleration = 'fast' confusion.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the general teaching principle, not the specific tasks here.

The legacy worked example stating that at steady speed the forces are balanced with zero resultant is physically correct for 1-D motion and has been preserved; ensure learners understand 'balanced' applies to both rest and constant-speed stages, as the misconception data flags the constant-speed-is-unbalanced error.

One supporting source on Frayer adaptation for younger children is marked unverified (verified:false) in the original row; treat its adaptation guidance as practitioner practice rather than established efficacy.

The original scene used a tug-of-war and a speeding cart; to avoid internal inconsistency the guidance distinguishes equal pulls (balanced, zero resultant) from unequal pulls (net resultant), and specifies starting from rest for the arrow-combiner so a resultant is not read as instantly redirecting an already-moving object. The intended original tug-of-war configuration is not certain.

No comparative-efficacy or necessity claims across presentation media were asserted; the original ranked some presentations as weaker or unsuitable and stated a 3D environment 'adds nothing', but exact sources do not establish such comparisons, so these were dropped or softened to scoped options while retaining the genuine objective limit that recognition tasks do not elicit independent production.

probeDeeper: Use the words 'moment', 'lever' and 'fulcrum' to describe how a see-saw works.
Here's a spanner on a tight bolt — tell me why a longer spanner helps, using 'moment'.
Give me a sentence using 'mechanical advantage' about a bottle opener or a wheelbarrow.
The car slows as it reaches the corner — which word fits, acceleration or deceleration? Use it in a sentence.
assess.correctAnswer: Uses the terms in the right places: at rest and at steady speed the forces are BALANCED (zero RESULTANT, no change in motion); pushing off, the forces are UNBALANCED with a resultant forwards causing ACCELERATION; braking, unbalanced with a resultant backwards causing DECELERATION. Uses 'speed' for how fast, and distinguishes acceleration (speeding up) from deceleration (slowing).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Going along at a steady speed means the forces are unbalanced — it's moving, so something's winning.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Steady speed = no change = balanced (zero resultant); reserve 'unbalanced' for changing motion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels constant-speed motion 'unbalanced'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Balanced forces means nothing is moving' — uses 'balanced' only for a stationary object.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model using 'balanced' for BOTH the at-rest and the constant-speed stages.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies 'balanced' only to the object at rest, not to the steady-speed stage.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It's accelerating' used to mean 'it's going fast', not that its speed is changing.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a fast STEADY speed (no acceleration) with a slow speeding-up (acceleration); acceleration = changing speed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses 'acceleration' for a high steady speed, or swaps 'speed' and 'acceleration'.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the terms loosely or wrongly — 'balanced' only for still objects, 'acceleration' to mean fast, 'resultant' avoided — reaching for everyday words instead of the technical ones.
responseLevels.full: Deploys the vocabulary accurately across the whole journey and new contexts — balanced/unbalanced matched to no-change/change, resultant for the net effect, acceleration vs deceleration for speeding up vs slowing, and moment/lever/fulcrum/mechanical advantage for machines.
responseLevels.partial: Uses several terms correctly in familiar sentences but slips in a less-scripted context — e.g. mislabels steady speed as unbalanced, or can define but not deploy 'moment/fulcrum' in a fresh scenario.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch this journey: a cyclist waits at the lights, pushes off and speeds up, then rides along at a steady speed, then brakes to a stop. Talk me through the whole journey using the right force-and-motion words — at each stage tell me whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced and what the resultant force is doing.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This is about USE, not definitions. A child who owns the vocabulary maps each term to the right stage (unbalanced -> accelerating at the start, balanced at steady speed). Errors show as misused terms: calling steady speed 'unbalanced', using 'acceleration' to mean 'fast', or using 'resultant force' loosely. Listen for whether the words do real work in the description, not whether a definition can be recited.

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7 the modelling cycle becomes explicit at both ends: represent a measurement or money problem with a number sentence, bar model, or diagram, AND interpret the numerical answer back in context ('15 cm means the ribbon is 15 centimetres long') (CCSS MP4). Bar models now carry two-step and comparison structures. The defining new demand — and the one teachers most often skip — is the return trip: a bare '5' is not an answer to 'how much is left?'; the answer is '5p change'. This is exactly where 'suspension of sense-making' (CDE) does its damage: children compute and stop, without asking whether the number is reasonable or what it means. The CDE guide warns that stripping problems down to numbers and keywords ('take away means subtract') actively reinforces the habit; the remedy is to reason about the situation first and always interpret and sense-check the result.
bestPractices: Insist on the return trip: every numerical answer is interpreted in context with its unit ('5p change', '15 cm long') — the interpret-in-context half of MP4
Reason about the situation before computing; resist keyword-stripping, which the CDE guide identifies as a cause of suspension of sense-making
Use bar models to expose two-step and comparison structure so the child models the relationships, not just grabs numbers (NCETM)
Build the reasonableness check: 'could you have MORE money after spending some?' — sense-check the answer against the situation
Ask 'what does this number mean here?' at the end of every problem, not just 'what's the answer?'
keyRepresentations: Part-whole and comparison bar models for two-step problems
Number sentence with units attached to the quantities
Number line for measurement/money jumps
Simple diagrams of the situation (coins, ribbon lengths)
commonMisconceptions: Stops at a bare number without interpreting it in context or attaching a unit
Grabs the numbers and applies the operation a keyword suggests, without modelling the situation
Doesn't sense-check — accepts an answer that can't be true in the situation (change larger than the money paid)
Reports the wrong quantity (gives the total when the question asks for what's left)

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, this topic develops the full mathematical modelling cycle: represent a money or measurement word problem with a number sentence, bar model, or diagram, AND complete the 'return trip' by interpreting the numerical answer back in context with its unit ('5p change', '15 cm long') and checking whether it is reasonable. The defining new demand is that a bare number is not an answer; the remedy to 'suspension of sense-making' is to reason about the situation before computing and always interpret and sense-check the result afterwards.

activities.title: Model a shop story, then make the return trip
feedback: If the child stops at a bare '5': ask 'five what? what is that for Sam?' — the calculation is right, only the interpretation needs prompting.
If the child endorses 35: 'you gave 20p and want 35p back — can you get more money by spending some?' Let them catch and reject the impossibility, then state the real change as '5p change'.
Direct feedback at the interpretation and the sense-check, not only at whether the arithmetic was correct.
activities.rationale: Building and then being required to interpret and sense-check makes the situation-answer link explicit; an optional live reasonableness gate (a slider or thumbs that flags impossible answers such as change > amount paid) and a required 'what does it mean?' step make the return trip concrete rather than skippable.
sourceClaims: MP4: represent a situation with an equation/diagram and interpret the mathematical result in the context of the situation, reflecting on whether it makes sense.

Suspension of sense-making leads students to compute without checking realism; stripping problems to numbers and keywords reinforces this, and problem-specific supports (explain why the answer makes sense, draw it, consider a contrasting answer) promote reasoning — whereas a general 'these are tricky' warning does not.
learnerActions: Read a shop story, e.g. 'Sam has 20p in his purse and buys a sticker costing 15p. How much change does he get?'
Build a bar model of the situation: 20 as the whole, split into a 15 part and a mystery (change) part; or write a matching number sentence.
Work out the missing part to land on 5.
Complete a mandatory 'what does your 5 mean?' step: attach the unit and quantity, finishing the sentence '5p change'.
Pass a reasonableness check before the answer is accepted: decide whether a candidate answer could possibly be true in the story (e.g. flag that change greater than the amount paid is impossible).
activities.intendedInsight: A calculation is not finished when the number appears; it is finished when the number is read back into the story and checked for whether it could possibly be true. You cannot end up with MORE money after spending some.

activities.title: Argue with the shopkeeper: catch the impossible change
feedback: Keep this dialogic and unscored — the aim is reasoning and interpretation, not a mark.
If the child accepts 35p untroubled, prompt them to picture the purse: 'show me how Sam could end up with more than 20p.'
Praise rejecting the impossible answer AND naming the unit of the real one ('5p change').
activities.rationale: Saying what an answer means and defending its reasonableness is naturally dialogic; a partner offering a bare or impossible number lets the child practise interpreting and sense-checking, which the CDE guide names as problem-specific supports. This is a proposed activity; the dialogic format's effectiveness is not independently verified.
sourceClaims: Suspension of sense-making leads students to compute without checking realism; stripping problems to numbers and keywords reinforces this, and problem-specific supports (explain why the answer makes sense, draw it, consider a contrasting answer) promote reasoning — whereas a general 'these are tricky' warning does not.
learnerActions: Talk with a shopkeeper character (role-played by a partner, teacher, or on-screen character) who offers a plausible-sounding but impossible answer: 'You gave me 20p for a 15p sticker, so your change is 35p, right?'
Decide out loud whether 35p can be right, and explain why change cannot be larger than the money paid.
State the correct change in context ('5p change') and justify it.
Respond to a follow-up: 'If the sticker cost 25p, could Sam buy it with his 20p? How do you know?'
activities.intendedInsight: Defending why an answer does or does not make sense out loud strengthens the reasonableness habit; a contrasting impossible answer provokes the check that compute-and-stop skips.

activities.title: Bar models for part-whole and comparison problems
feedback: If the child adds the two numbers because a keyword suggested it, pause before any operation and model the situation on the bar first (e.g. 20 as the whole, 15 as a part).
Check that each number on the bar carries a unit and matches a real quantity in the story.
Ask 'what does this number mean here?' at the end, not just 'what's the answer?'
activities.rationale: Drawing part-whole and comparison bar models, and number-line models, for one-step and comparison problems builds the habit of modelling the relationships before computing, then attaching units and interpreting the result (NCETM/MP4).
sourceClaims: Bar models expose two-step and comparison structure so children model the relationships in a situation rather than grabbing numbers.
MP4: represent a situation with an equation/diagram and interpret the mathematical result in the context of the situation, reflecting on whether it makes sense.
learnerActions: Draw a part-whole bar model for a word problem, labelling which part is the known quantity, which is the whole, and which is the unknown.
Use a comparison bar model to show two quantities side by side for a comparison problem (e.g. one ribbon longer than another).
Use a number line to represent money or measurement jumps when that fits the story better.
Attach units to each quantity on the model and to the final answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Bar models expose the structure of a situation — including part-whole and comparison relationships — so the child models the relationships rather than grabbing numbers and applying a keyword operation.

constraints: Every numerical answer must be interpreted in context with its unit ('5p change', '15 cm long') — the interpret-in-context half of MP4 is the core objective, not an optional extra.
Reason about the situation before computing; resist keyword-stripping ('take away means subtract'), which the CDE guide identifies as a cause of suspension of sense-making.

A static worked example (story, bar, answer, and a 'what it means' flap) can illustrate the return trip but does not let the child model or sense-check for themselves; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.

Recognition-only scored items check getting the number rather than interpreting it in context or judging reasonableness, and can reward the compute-and-stop habit; a short 'is this answer reasonable?' item can still be useful during teaching, but keep the modelling and interpretation work open and constructive.

A reasonableness gate, slider, or shopkeeper character are optional ways to make the sense-check concrete, not mandatory mechanisms; the required learning is the interpretation and the check themselves.

Where a learner shows number-grabbing errors, reteach by modelling the real situation on a bar before any operation; this connects to the prerequisite skill of representing the situation rather than grabbing numbers/keywords (CDE).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic checked: 20p - 15p = 5p change is correct; 20 + 15 = 35 is the keyword-grabbing error and must only ever appear as the impossible candidate to be rejected, never as a valid answer.

The source's claim that scored/quiz items only test getting the number and reward compute-and-stop was softened: a response format can be used reasonably during teaching, so it is framed as a limitation of recognition-only items rather than a universal law.
The 3D 'poor fit' entry carried no teaching content (money/measurement modelling here is not spatial), so it was omitted rather than converted into guidance.

An internal prerequisite/catalog ID present in the source has been removed from learner-facing text; only the pedagogical reteach move it pointed to is retained, and its identifier was not re-verified.

Independent re-audit confirms the three previously logged issues (internal ID in a constraint, internal ID in a preservation entry, and blended rationale in the bar-model activity) are resolved at every occurrence; no catalog IDs, fit labels, or quiz-step vocabulary remain in learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: 'Sam only had 20p. Can his change be 35p? Why not?'
'What should the answer be — and 5 WHAT?'
'Draw me a bar for this: which part is the 20, which is the 15, which is the change?'
'If the sticker cost 25p, could Sam buy it with his 20p? How do you know?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting 35 as impossible (you can't have more money after spending), finding 5, and interpreting it as '5p change', not a bare number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Number-grabbing / keyword operation: adds the two numbers (or applies the operation a word suggests) without modelling the situation — gets 35.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the situation on a bar (20 as the whole, 15 as a part) before any operation; reteach representing the real situation rather than grabbing numbers/keywords (CDE).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses 35, justifying it by 'there's a 20 and a 15'; cannot say why change should be less than 20.

errorPatterns.pattern: Suspension of sense-making: doesn't check the answer against the situation — accepts a number that can't be true (change bigger than the money paid).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the habit of asking 'could this be true here?'; use contrasting/impossible answers to provoke checking (CDE problem-specific supports).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches 35 (or any impossible value) and is untroubled; no reasonableness check.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bare number, no interpretation: finds 5 but doesn't say it is 5p of change.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the return trip: 'five what? what is that for Sam?'; the calculation is right, the interpretation needs prompting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers '5' and stops; asked what it means, restates '5'.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts 35 (or another impossible value); no sense-check and no interpretation.
responseLevels.full: Rejects 35 as impossible because change can't exceed the money paid, finds 5, interprets it as '5p change', and can locate the quantities on a bar — transferring the reasonableness check to a new case unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Rejects 35 or finds 5, but not both fully — e.g. computes 5 without noticing 35 is impossible, or says 'it should be less' without interpreting '5p change'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Sam has 20p. He buys a sticker that costs 15p. A friend worked it out and said the answer is 35. Does 35 make sense as Sam's change? Talk me through it — what should the answer be, and what does that number mean for Sam?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who models and sense-checks rejects 35 because change can't exceed the money you had, and interprets the answer with its unit and meaning; a child who computes-and-stops or keyword-adds accepts 35 or gives '5' with no meaning. The impossible candidate answer is the hinge: sense-making children reject it instantly, compute-and-stop children don't. Hard to reject it for the wrong reason; hard to accept it if you're really picturing the situation.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9; why the poles have extreme seasons — Earth's axis is tilted ~23.5°, so as Earth orbits the Sun each pole spends half the year tilted TOWARD the Sun (continuous daylight, warmer summer) and half tilted AWAY (continuous darkness, bitter winter); this tilt also drives sea ice expanding in winter and retreating in summer and triggers animal migration and breeding.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 Y5 'Earth and space' (Earth's rotation to explain day/night; movement relative to the Sun) extended to axial tilt and seasons.
• Standards—US: NGSS 5-ESS1-2 (patterns of daylight from Earth's motion); MS-ESS1-1 (Earth-Sun model for seasons) foreshadowed.
• Operational details: the key move is that seasons come from the TILT, not from Earth being nearer/further from the Sun. Model Earth orbiting with its axis pointing a FIXED direction, so at one point in the orbit the North Pole leans sunward (Arctic summer, midnight sun) and six months later leans away (Arctic polar night). Tie it to consequences: sea ice grows/shrinks with the seasons and animals migrate and breed on that cycle. This is the 'why' behind the 5–7 midnight-sun/polar-night phenomenon.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (7) say Earth is tilted and that's why we have seasons; Tier B (8) explain that a pole tilted toward the Sun has summer/long days and tilted away has winter/long nights; Tier C (9) explain that the tilt (not distance to the Sun) drives the extreme polar seasons and the yearly sea-ice and animal cycles.
bestPractices: Model the axis pointing a FIXED direction all the way round the orbit, so the same tilt produces opposite seasons on opposite sides of the Sun
Confront the distance misconception directly — Earth is actually slightly closer to the Sun in northern winter; it's the TILT that matters
Use a torch-and-tilted-globe demo so children see the toward-Sun pole bathed in light for a full turn (midnight sun)
Link cause to consequences pupils can picture: sea ice expanding/retreating, animals migrating and breeding on the seasonal cycle
Connect back to the 5–7 midnight-sun/polar-night phenomenon as the effect this tilt explains
keyRepresentations: Orbit diagram: Earth at four positions, axis fixed, showing which pole leans sunward
Tilted-globe-and-torch demo with the sunlit pole staying lit through a full spin
Toward-Sun / away-from-Sun pole close-ups labelled summer/midnight-sun and winter/polar-night
Seasonal sea-ice extent animation paired with a migration/breeding calendar
commonMisconceptions: Seasons happen because Earth moves closer to and further from the Sun — it's the axial TILT, not distance
The whole Earth is hot in summer and cold in winter at once — opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons
The axis tips back and forth toward the Sun — it points a fixed direction; Earth's position in orbit changes which pole leans sunward
The Sun goes out in polar winter — that pole is tilted away, so the Sun stays below the horizon
Seasons and sea-ice/animal cycles are unrelated — the same tilt drives the extreme seasons AND the yearly ice and migration cycles

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, explain why the poles have extreme seasons: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5° and points in a FIXED direction as Earth orbits the Sun, so each pole spends half the year leaning toward the Sun (continuous daylight, comparatively warmer summer) and half leaning away (continuous darkness, bitter winter). The seasons come from the tilt, not from Earth's changing distance to the Sun. The same tilt drives sea ice expanding in winter and retreating in summer, and animal cycles of migration and breeding. The preferred build is a 2D orbit a child can drag to see which pole is lit, with linked day/night and sea-ice responses; a 3D fly-around orbit, a tap-to-reveal static diagram, a torch-and-globe demonstration, and targeted multiple-choice checks are offered as alternatives with different purposes, none claimed to be superior.

activities.title: Drag Earth around the Sun with a fixed tilt
feedback: If a learner thinks closer-to-Sun means summer, point to the distance toggle and to a real fact: Earth is actually slightly closer to the Sun in January, during northern winter. The small change in distance does not cause the seasons — the tilt does.
If a learner thinks the axis tips back and forth, replay the loop and highlight that the axis arrow stayed pointing the same way; only Earth's position in the orbit changed which pole leans sunward.
When a pole leans toward the Sun, confirm: long daylight and warmer summer, and the sea-ice gauge shrinks; when it leans away, long darkness and winter, and the sea-ice gauge grows.
If a learner says the Sun goes out in polar winter, clarify the Sun is still shining — that pole is tilted away so the Sun stays below the horizon.
activities.rationale: The target is a spatial cause-and-effect mechanism, so letting the child operate the orbit and see the lit pole, day-clock and sea-ice gauge respond makes the tilt-not-distance causal link concrete, and the distance toggle challenges the distance misconception directly. The linked day-clock and sea-ice gauge are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required components.
sourceClaims: Earth's ~23.5° axial tilt, with the axis fixed in direction through the orbit, causes seasons and the polar cycles of continuous summer daylight and winter darkness — not variation in Earth-Sun distance
learnerActions: Grab Earth and drag it all the way around a glowing Sun, noticing that the axis stays locked pointing the same direction for the whole loop.
Watch a spotlight show which pole is bathed in sunlight as Earth moves.

Drag Earth to the position where the North Pole leans into the light and observe a day-clock spinning a full 24 hours with the Sun never setting (Arctic summer, midnight sun) while a sea-ice gauge shrinks.
Drag Earth to the opposite side where the North Pole leans away and observe the Sun never rising, the polar-night scene darkening, and the sea-ice gauge growing.
State in your own words which pole has summer at each position and why.

Use a 'blame the distance?' toggle that briefly moves Earth slightly nearer and further and notice that, in this simplified model, the seasons do not change. In real life, the small change in distance has only a minor effect and is not what causes the seasons.
activities.intendedInsight: The SAME fixed tilt produces summer on one side of the orbit and winter on the other; it is the tilt (combined with orbital position), not distance to the Sun, that makes a pole swing between endless day and endless night.

activities.title: Fly around the orbit in 3D to find the sunward-leaning pole
feedback: If the learner loses track of the tilt direction while rotating the view, pause and trace the axis arrow — it points the same way regardless of your viewpoint.
Confirm that the pole tilted toward the Sun has summer and endless daylight, and the pole tilted away has winter and endless night.
activities.rationale: A 3D fly-around may build spatial intuition by showing the tilt from angles a flat diagram cannot, and is offered as a richer alternative; a well-built 2D orbit conveys the same causal story at lower cost, so 3D is a valuable option rather than a requirement. Comparative efficacy between these formats is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Move your viewpoint around a 3D Earth-Sun orbit to look at the tilted axis from different angles.

At each of four orbital positions, identify which pole is leaning toward the Sun and which is leaning away. Notice that at the two in-between (equinox) positions, neither pole leans toward the Sun, and both poles get some day and some night.
At the two positions where one pole leans fully toward the Sun, describe how the lit pole experiences continuous daylight and the dark pole continuous night.
activities.intendedInsight: Earth-Sun geometry is genuinely three-dimensional; viewing the tilt from different angles can build spatial intuition for why one pole is bathed in light while the other is in darkness.

activities.title: Four-position orbit diagram with tap-to-reveal labels
feedback: If a learner expects both poles to be warm at once, point out that at the summer and winter positions one pole leans toward the Sun while the other leans away, so opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons. At the two in-between positions, neither pole leans toward the Sun.
Reinforce that the axis arrow points the same direction in all four positions; it is Earth's place in the orbit that changes.
activities.rationale: A labelled static diagram makes the four key orbital positions visible and is useful for consolidation or low-tech settings; because it does not animate the continuous link between orbital position, tilt and sunlight, pair it with hands-on or interactive modelling where possible.
learnerActions: Look at an orbit diagram showing Earth at four positions with its axis drawn in a fixed direction.
Tap each position to reveal whether the North Pole leans toward the Sun, away from it, or neither (sideways to the Sun, at the spring and autumn positions), and the season it causes.
Match each position to 'summer/midnight-sun', 'winter/polar-night' or 'spring/autumn (in-between, with sunrise and sunset)' for the North Pole.
activities.intendedInsight: At different points in the same orbit, the fixed tilt leaves one pole leaning sunward (summer) and later leaning away (winter).

activities.title: Torch-and-tilted-globe demonstration
feedback: If a learner tips the globe to point at the torch each time, stop and reset: the axis must keep pointing the same direction; only your position around the torch changes.
Confirm that the pole in continuous light is having summer and the pole in continuous shadow is having winter.
activities.rationale: A physical torch-and-globe demonstration lets children see the toward-light pole bathed in light for a full turn, which may make the midnight-sun effect tangible. The globe and torch are approximations of the real Earth and Sun and should be kept distinct from the bodies they represent.
learnerActions: Tilt a globe so its axis points a fixed direction, then carry it around a torch standing in for the Sun, keeping the tilt pointing the same way the whole time.
Spin the globe at the position where one pole leans toward the torch and watch that pole stay in the light through a full spin (midnight sun).
Carry the globe to the opposite side and spin it again to see that pole stay in shadow (polar night).
Describe what season each pole is having at each position.
activities.intendedInsight: A pole tilted toward the light source stays lit even as Earth spins, giving continuous daylight; a pole tilted away stays dark, giving continuous night.

activities.title: Check understanding: tilt vs distance and which pole has summer
feedback: If a learner picks 'closer in summer', counter with simultaneity: when the north has summer the south has winter though both are at similar distance from the Sun — so it must be the tilt.
If a learner says the Sun is just brighter/hotter in summer, note the Sun's output is steady; what changes is how directly and how long its light reaches a place, because of the tilt.
Credit answers that link the tilt to sea ice growing in winter and shrinking in summer, or to animals migrating and breeding on the seasonal cycle.
activities.rationale: Short recognition checks can confirm the model has taken hold and surface the distance misconception, but recognition alone does not elicit independent construction of the explanation, so use them after the operable activities rather than to teach.
learnerActions: Answer which-pole-has-summer questions for given orbital positions.
Decide whether tilt or distance explains the seasons, using the fact that opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time.
Explain how the same tilt links to sea ice spreading in winter and shrinking in summer, and to animal migration or breeding on the yearly cycle.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who understands credits the axial tilt (not distance) and can connect the seasonal cycle to at least one consequence such as sea-ice change or animal behaviour.

constraints: Model the axis pointing a FIXED direction all the way round the orbit; do not let the axis tip toward and away from the Sun, which seeds the 'wobbling axis' misconception.
Confront the distance misconception directly: Earth is actually slightly closer to the Sun during northern winter, so it is the tilt, not distance, that matters.

Tie cause to consequences children can picture: sea ice expanding/retreating and animals migrating and breeding on the seasonal cycle (meets the requirement to connect to at least one animal behaviour).
Connect back to the midnight-sun / polar-night phenomenon as the effect this tilt explains.

Recognition-only multiple-choice checks do not elicit independent construction of the explanation; use them to confirm, not to build, understanding — they are not claimed to be superior to the other formats.
A static diagram does not animate the continuous link between orbital position, tilt and sunlight; treat it as a consolidation scaffold and pair with hands-on or interactive modelling.
Globes, torches and screen orbits are approximations of the real Earth and Sun; keep the represented bodies distinct from the models.
Make clear the Sun does not go out in polar winter — the pole is tilted away so the Sun stays below the horizon.

The distance toggle's 'nothing changes' result is an age-appropriate idealisation; Earth's distance to the Sun does vary slightly through the year, but that small effect is dominated by and distinct from the tilt.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The three listed sources are marked verified:false in the row; curriculum and NASA/Royal Museums Greenwich references support the tilt-causes-seasons principle but do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular medium.

sourceClaims were kept only on the 2D drag activity, because that activity directly demonstrates and tests the sourced tilt-not-distance principle via the distance toggle; they were set to [] on the 3D, static-diagram, torch-globe and check activities, whose rationales concern medium choice, viewpoint, tangibility or check timing, which no source claim supports.
Legacy fit rationales asserting a static image 'can't animate' the dynamic link and that open dialogue is 'poorly served' were reframed as scoped observable limits, not universal pedagogical laws.

The row's distance point is physically sound for a 7–9 audience: both hemispheres are at similar Sun distance at a given time and Earth is actually slightly nearer the Sun in northern winter; this was retained as the key counter to the distance misconception.

probeDeeper: When it's summer at the North Pole, what season is it at the South Pole — and are they different distances from the Sun right then?
If distance caused seasons, both poles would be warm at the same time. Are they? What does that tell you?
Which way is a pole tilted during its months of endless daylight — toward or away from the Sun?
How does the same tilt explain sea ice spreading in winter and shrinking in summer?
assess.correctAnswer: No — seasons are NOT caused by the Earth getting closer to or farther from the Sun. They are caused by the TILT of the Earth's axis (about 23.5°). As the Earth orbits the Sun, each pole spends half the year tilted TOWARD the Sun — giving continuous daylight and the warmer polar summer — and half tilted AWAY — giving continuous darkness and bitter winter. (In fact both hemispheres are at similar distances from the Sun at the same time, and it's the tilt, not distance, that gives one summer while the other has winter.) The same tilt drives sea ice growing in winter and shrinking in summer, and animal behaviours like migration and breeding.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Seasons are caused by Earth's distance from the Sun (closer=summer)' — the classic distance misconception.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Counter with simultaneity: when the north has summer the south has winter, though both are the same distance from the Sun. It must be the TILT, not distance.
errorPatterns.distractor: In summer the Earth is much closer to the Sun, and in winter it's much farther away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains summer/winter by the Earth moving nearer/farther from the Sun.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The Earth's tilt changes back and forth through the year' — thinks the axis wobbles rather than pointing steadily.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model it: the axis stays pointed the same direction all year; it's the POSITION in orbit that puts a given pole toward or away from the Sun.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Earth tips toward the Sun in summer and tips away in winter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the Earth tilts toward the Sun then tilts the other way; doesn't grasp a fixed axis pointing the same way while orbiting.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The Sun is just brighter/hotter in summer' — attributes seasons to the Sun changing, not Earth's geometry.
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Sun's output is steady; what changes is how directly and for how long its light reaches a given place, due to the tilt.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the Sun gives out more heat in summer.

responseLevels.gap: Attributes seasons to the Earth's distance from the Sun, or to the Sun changing.
responseLevels.full: Explains seasons by the fixed ~23.5° axial tilt — a pole tilted toward the Sun gets continuous daylight/summer, tilted away gets continuous dark/winter — rejects the distance idea using opposite-hemisphere seasons, and links the tilt to the sea-ice cycle.
responseLevels.partial: Mentions the tilt but can't explain how toward/away in orbit gives months of light or dark, or still lets distance creep in.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The poles have extreme seasons — a summer of endless daylight, a winter of endless dark. A student says 'that's because in summer the Earth is much CLOSER to the Sun, and in winter it's much farther away.' Is it distance from the Sun that causes the seasons? If not, what does — and why does that give a pole months of daylight then months of dark?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This targets the classic, robust 'distance causes seasons' misconception. A student holding it credits closeness/farness; a student with the concept credits the axial tilt and can explain toward/away producing months of light or dark. The counter (both hemispheres at similar distance, yet opposite seasons) is decisive.

sources.claim: KS2 Y5 pupils use the idea of Earth's rotation and movement relative to the Sun to explain day/night and related phenomena
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum, Science Y5 'Earth and space'

sources.claim: Students represent Earth's motion to explain patterns of daylight and, later, seasons via axial tilt
sources.source: NGSS 5-ESS1-2 and MS-ESS1-1

sources.claim: Earth's ~23.5° axial tilt, with the axis fixed in direction through the orbit, causes seasons and the polar cycles of continuous summer daylight and winter darkness — not variation in Earth-Sun distance

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, using structure extends place value to three digits (adding hundreds changes only the hundreds digit), turns the multiplication/division link into a fact-deriving tool (6×4=24 gives 4×6, 24÷4 and 24÷6), and makes shape classification property-based (sort by number of sides, right angles, parallel lines rather than by look). The teaching aim is a habit: before computing or naming, ask 'what do I already know that this is like?' CCSS MP7 marks this as the run-up to the distributive property (7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) and to reasoning about geometric figures by their structure.
bestPractices: Use a single array to show a whole fact family at once (6 rows of 4) so 6×4, 4×6, 24÷4 and 24÷6 are read off one structure, not learned as four separate facts
Use a three-digit place-value machine / arrow cards and predict-then-check which column moves when adding 100, 10 or 1
Classify shapes with property checklists and overlapping sets (sides, right angles, parallel pairs) so classification survives rotation and odd examples
Ask 'which fact that you already know helps here?' to build the transfer habit rather than fresh computation
keyRepresentations: Rectangular array / area model for the multiplication-division fact family
Three-digit place-value apparatus and arrow cards
Property checklists and Venn-style overlapping shape sets
Distributive splits (7×8 as 7×5 + 7×3) shown on a partitioned array
commonMisconceptions: Treats multiplication and division as unrelated, recomputing 24÷4 from scratch despite knowing 6×4
When adding 100 to a three-digit number, changes the wrong column or mis-carries
Classifies shapes by orientation/appearance (a rotated square becomes a 'diamond'; only a 'pointing-up' triangle is a triangle)
Thinks a derived fact must be checked by counting because facts feel separate rather than connected

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, build the habit of looking for structure before computing or naming: ask 'what do I already know that this is like?' Three strands: (1) read a whole multiplication/division fact family off one array (6×4, 4×6, 24÷4, 24÷6 from the same 6 rows of 4); (2) use three-digit place value so adding 100/10/1 changes only the matching column, barring a carry into the next place; (3) classify shapes by properties (sides, right angles, parallel pairs) so the classification survives rotation. This is the run-up to the distributive property (7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) and to reasoning about figures by structure.

activities.title: One array, four facts
feedback: If the child pauses to count or skip-count for the divisions, return to the one array and physically read all four facts from it (rows, columns, sharing, grouping) so the single structure is seen to hold them all; name division as undoing multiplication.
If they treat 24÷4 as unrelated to 6×4, cover a factor on the array they just built and ask 'how many fours are hidden here?' so the quotient is read, not recalculated.
Probe scaling: 'you knew 6×4 — does that also help with 6×8, or 60×4? how?' to check the structural link transfers.
Counterexample check: 'division undoes multiplication — so does 24÷5 come out as neat as 24÷4? why not?' to test understanding beyond the slogan.
activities.rationale: A single manipulable array makes the shared structure of a fact family visible as the child acts, supporting the deriving habit rather than four separately memorised facts; well-chosen representations such as arrays expose structure and can later be faded.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, using well-chosen representations (e.g. arrays, place-value apparatus) that expose structure and are then faded
Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Lay out 24 counters as 6 rows of 4 and state the multiplication it shows (6×4=24).
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn and read it again as 4 rows of 6; say why 6×4 and 4×6 are the same 24 dots seen two ways.
Cover one factor: with 24 shared into 4 rows, read off how many are in each row (6) to get 24÷4; then read 24÷6 the same way.
Say in your own words how knowing 6×4=24 means you already know 24÷4 and 24÷6 without counting.
Try a second fact family (e.g. 5 rows of 3) and derive all four facts from the single array.
activities.intendedInsight: One rectangular array holds a whole fact family; multiplication and division are the same structure read different ways, so a known product gives the related quotients without recomputing.

activities.title: Partition to derive a harder product
feedback: If the parts don't recombine, re-count each sub-array (7×5 and 7×3) separately before adding, and check the split covers all 8 columns with none missing.
Audit the arithmetic together: 35+21=56; if a child suggests another total, recount one part on the array rather than accepting the number.
Ask them to split the same product a second way (e.g. 7×4 + 7×4, where each part is 28 and the total is again 56) and confirm it reaches the same total, reinforcing that the whole is conserved.
activities.rationale: Showing the distributive split on a partitioned array connects the fact-deriving habit to standard structural reasoning named in the practice standards.
sourceClaims: Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Take a product you don't know by heart, e.g. 7×8, and lay it as 7 rows of 8.
Split the 8 columns into 5 and 3, drawing a line through the array.
Work out the two easier parts (7×5=35 and 7×3=21) and add them (35+21=56).
State the rule you used: 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3, then try splitting a different product your own way.
activities.intendedInsight: A large product can be built from easier known products by partitioning the array — this is the distributive property seen concretely.

activities.title: Predict which column moves
feedback: If the child names or alters the wrong column when adding 100, predict-then-check on the place-value machine and watch only the hundreds count move.
If a carry occurs (e.g. adding 100 to 970 → 1070), treat it explicitly: the hundreds column fills and rolls into thousands — note this is still the hundreds place acting, not a random digit changing.
Probe directly: 'which digit changes when I add 100 to 470, and which stay the same? why those?'
activities.rationale: Predict-then-check with place-value apparatus makes the column structure something the child reasons about rather than a procedure to copy; such representations expose structure and can be faded.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, using well-chosen representations (e.g. arrays, place-value apparatus) that expose structure and are then faded
learnerActions: Using a three-digit place-value apparatus or arrow cards, build a number such as 253 (or 470).
Before adding, predict out loud which digit will change and which will stay the same when you add 100.
Add one hundred-flat (or spin the +100 wheel) and check: for 253 and 470 only the hundreds count moves, with no carry.

Repeat for +10 and +1, each time predicting first, then stating why only that one column changed (true for 253 or 470; if the column being added to holds a 9, notice that a carry also changes the next place).
activities.intendedInsight: Place value is structured by columns; adding 100 changes only the hundreds, 10 only the tens, and 1 only the ones, unless the addition causes a carry into the next place (e.g. 259+1=260, 295+10=305, 970+100=1070).

activities.title: Classify by properties, not by how it looks
feedback: If the child says a rotated square is a 'diamond' and no longer a square, or that only a point-up triangle is a triangle, run the property checklist while rotating the shape so they see the properties are unchanged by orientation.
If they justify by appearance, ask 'count the sides and right angles — did any change when it tilted?' to redirect to properties.
Include odd and rotated examples deliberately so classification does not depend on a standard pose.
activities.rationale: Property checklists and overlapping sets make classification depend on structure rather than orientation, addressing the common misconception that a rotated square becomes a 'diamond' and is no longer a square; recognising significant structure in figures is the aimed-for habit.
sourceClaims: Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Pick a shape and run a property checklist: count the sides, mark the right angles, find any parallel pairs.
Classify it from the checklist (e.g. square: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles, 2 pairs of parallel sides — also a rectangle).
Rotate the shape 45° and re-run the checklist; confirm the same properties, so the classification does not change.
Sort several shapes into overlapping sets (e.g. 'has a right angle', 'has parallel sides') and place a rotated square and an upside-down triangle correctly.
Justify one classification aloud by citing properties, not orientation.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's class comes from its properties (sides, angles, parallel lines), which stay the same under rotation — a tilted square is still a square; calling it a 'diamond' does not make it a different shape (a square is also a special rhombus).

constraints: The teaching aim is the transfer habit 'which fact that I already know helps here?' — reaching the right numbers is not enough; the child should explain why one fact yields the others.

A fixed reference diagram of a fact family or distributive split can annotate and explain, but cannot be rotated or re-covered by the learner; a manipulable array lets the child test that a turned array re-reads and that covering a factor reveals a quotient. Use static diagrams as support, not as the sole route to the deriving habit.

Matching or derive-the-answer tasks (from 6×4=24, give 24÷6) can check whether facts are treated as connected, but a correct answer may be a recomputed one; always pair with 'which known fact did you use?' to distinguish deriving from recalculating.

Carrying is an exception to 'only one column changes': when adding 100/10/1 causes a carry, the named column fills and rolls into the next place. Address this explicitly rather than teaching 'the other columns never change'.

Fact families and three-digit place value are quantitative; 2D shape classification by property needs the 2D figure and its properties. These do not require 3D models, though a 3D context is not forbidden where genuinely useful.

Optional interaction examples (tap to highlight 6×4, rotate the array to read 4×6, cover a factor to reveal a division, a predict-then-check place-value wheel, live recolouring of a checklist while rotating a shape) make the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general principles rather than proving any specific task was tested.

The original claimed adding 100 'only changes the hundreds digit'; this holds except when a carry occurs. The summary, Activity 3 and the constraints now qualify the generalisation, and the child predicts and checks, so it is not taught as absolute.

The original artefact notes asserted a dialogue 'lacks the array and columns the child needs' and that these topics 'do not need 3D'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established necessity claims; softened to scoped affordances/limits in constraints.
Arithmetic self-audit: 6×4=24; 24÷4=6; 24÷6=4; 5×3=15; 7×5=35, 7×3=21, 35+21=56 (=7×8); alternative split 7×4+7×4 = 28+28 = 56; 970+100=1070. All checked and consistent as used in activities.
Source claims as written describe general guidance (recognise/use structure; use and fade representations) and do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular artefact type.

probeDeeper: Ask 'you knew 6×4 — does knowing 6×4 also help with 6×8, or 60×4? how?' to test whether the structural link scales to new facts
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'you said division undoes multiplication — so does 24÷5 come out as neat as 24÷4? why not?' to check the child understands the relationship, not a slogan
Ask 'which digit changes when I add 100 to 470, and which stay the same? why those?' to probe the place-value structure directly
Rotate a square 45° and ask 'is it still a square? how can you be sure?' — a structural thinker checks sides and angles, not the tilt
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child deriving all three from the one fact and explaining the link: 4×6 is the same array turned round; 24÷4 asks how many fours in 24 (six), 24÷6 asks how many sixes (four) — division undoes the multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats multiplication and division as unrelated operations, recomputing 24÷4 from scratch despite just stating 6×4=24
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to one array and physically read all four facts from it (rows, columns, sharing, grouping) so the single structure is seen to hold them all; name division as undoing multiplication
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child pauses to count or skip-count for the divisions rather than reading them off the known fact

errorPatterns.pattern: When adding hundreds, changes the wrong column (253+100 alters tens or ones) because three-digit place-value structure is insecure
errorPatterns.nextMove: Predict-then-check on a three-digit place-value machine; add one hundred-flat and watch only the hundreds count move
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked which digit changes when adding 100 to a three-digit number, the child names or alters the wrong column

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies shapes by orientation or appearance — a rotated square becomes a 'diamond', or only checks how it looks rather than its sides/angles/parallel lines
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run a property checklist (sides, right angles, parallel lines) while rotating the shape so the child sees the properties are unchanged by orientation
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to justify a classification, the child cites how the shape looks or which way it points rather than counting sides/right angles/parallel pairs

responseLevels.gap: Recomputes divisions from scratch, mis-places the changing digit when adding hundreds, and classifies shapes by look; each task handled in isolation
responseLevels.full: Reads all four facts off the one array and explains the inverse relationship, predicts and justifies which digit changes, and classifies by properties despite rotation — and reuses 'what do I already know that this is like?' on new problems unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Derives the related facts or names the right column/property when prompted, but cannot clearly explain why one fact gives the others or reverts to counting under pressure

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You know that 6 × 4 = 24. Without counting anything out, what does that tell you about 4 × 6, and about 24 ÷ 4 and 24 ÷ 6? How does the one fact give you the others?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reaching the numbers is easy; the discriminating content is the EXPLANATION of why one fact yields the others. A child using structure narrates the array/inverse relationship; a child without it treats each as a separate fact to recompute or recall, or gets the divisions but cannot say why they follow.

sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP7 'Look for and make use of structure'
