pedagogy.summary: Equivalent fractions are different names for the same amount: holding the whole constant, splitting each part into more (smaller) pieces multiplies both numerator and denominator without changing the quantity, so 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9. The load-bearing insight, best seen on a fraction wall or bar, is that MORE pieces each SMALLER can total the same amount — which directly confronts the whole-number bias that '4/6 must be more than 2/3 because 4 > 2'. Teach the multiplicative structure with diagrams before any 'times top and bottom' rule.
bestPractices: Build equivalence by SPLITTING each part of a fixed bar (2/3 → split each third in two → 4/6) so the shaded amount visibly never changes
Use a fraction wall / stacked bars so equal rows align and equivalents line up
Confront the additive error explicitly — show that '+1 to top and bottom' (2/3 → 3/4) shifts the shaded amount
Confirm on a number line that equivalent fractions land on the SAME point
Compare shaded AREAS of identical wholes, never different-sized wholes, when judging equivalence
keyRepresentations: Fraction wall / stacked equal-length bars (canonical equivalence reference)
A single bar re-partitioned by splitting each part (2/3 → 4/6)
Number line with dual labelling (thirds above, sixths below) showing the same point
Area model (identical rectangles shaded to the same amount)
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — 4/6 judged more than 2/3 'because 4 > 2 and there are more pieces'
Different numbers must mean different amounts (denies equivalence)
Makes 'equivalents' by ADDING the same number to top and bottom (2/3 → 3/4)
Compares shaded amounts across different-sized wholes
Thinks changing only the numerator or only the denominator keeps the value

learn.summary: Equivalent fractions are different names for the same amount. Holding the whole constant, splitting each part into more (smaller) pieces multiplies both numerator and denominator without changing the quantity, so 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9. The load-bearing insight, best seen on a fraction wall or bar, is that MORE pieces each SMALLER can total the same amount, which confronts the whole-number bias that '4/6 must be more than 2/3 because 4 > 2'. Teach the multiplicative structure with diagrams before any 'times top and bottom' rule.

activities.title: Split each part of a fixed bar (2/3 becomes 4/6)
feedback: If the child says the second bar has more chocolate, lay the 2/3 bar directly over the 4/6 bar so the shaded lengths coincide; the pieces are smaller but the shaded strip is identical.

If the child changes only the numerator or only the denominator and expects the same amount, shade that fraction on an identical bar and compare: the shaded length differs, so both parts must be multiplied by the same number.
If the child offers 3/4 as equal to 2/3, shade 3/4 on an identical bar and align it with 2/3: the shaded length is clearly longer, so adding is not the same as splitting.
Prompt: 'Did the amount of chocolate change when you drew the splitting lines? What changed and what stayed the same?'
Reinforce: both the number of parts and the number shaded were multiplied by the same number, so the fraction's value did not change.
activities.rationale: Making and watching the split while the shaded length stays fixed lets equivalence be felt as 'same amount, more cuts', and directly contrasts changing one part, and the additive error, with the multiplicative structure. An interactive version (a 'split every part into ___' control that cleaves each part live while the symbol updates 4/6, 6/9, with an 'add 1 to top and bottom' button that visibly shifts the strip) may make the mechanism more concrete, but drawing the splits on paper serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.
learnerActions: Shade two of three equal parts of a bar to show 2/3.
Split every third into two equal pieces by drawing a line through each part; count that four of six parts are now shaded and write 4/6.
Describe what happened to the length of shaded strip: it did not grow or shrink, there are just more lines.
Keep splitting to generate the family: split each part into three for 6/9, into four for 8/12; each time check the shaded strip stays the same length.

Test changing only one number: on an identical bar change only the bottom number (2/3 to 2/6) or only the top number (2/3 to 3/3) and shade it; check that the shaded amount changes, so changing just one part does NOT make an equivalent fraction.
Try the trap: add one to the top and one to the bottom (2/3 to 3/4) and shade 3/4 of an identical bar; compare the shaded length with the original 2/3.
activities.intendedInsight: Splitting each part (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) makes more, smaller pieces that cover exactly the same amount; for fractions like 2/3, changing only one of the two numbers, or adding one to each, shifts the amount, so neither is a way to make an equivalent fraction.

activities.title: Fraction wall: which rows line up
feedback: If the child reads only the numbers, redirect attention to where each bar ends relative to the shared vertical line.
Ask: 'These have different numbers but reach the same line. What does that tell you about the amount?'
If the child cannot see why rows align, connect back to splitting: a third split into two gives two sixths, which is why 2/3 and 4/6 reach the same line.
activities.rationale: The fraction wall is the canonical static reference for equivalence; tapping or tracing a row shows which fractions align. It shows the result rather than generating the split-each-part mechanism, so pair it with the splitting activity.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.
learnerActions: Use a fraction wall of stacked equal-length rows (halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, ninths) and find where rows end at the same vertical line.
Identify equivalents by alignment: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6, and 2/3 = 4/6.
Explain in words why two fractions that reach the same line are equal (they cover the same length of the identical whole).
Check a non-example: does 2/3 line up with 3/4? Note it does not, so they are not equivalent.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction wall is a reliable reference: fractions that cover the same length of the identical whole name the same amount, regardless of how many pieces.

activities.title: Same point on the number line
feedback: If the child expects two different points, count the sixths across to 4/6 and the thirds across to 2/3 and show the marks fall together.
Ask: 'If they are at the same point, how much of the distance from 0 to 1 does each cover?'
Connect to the bar: the same length on the bar becomes the same point on the line.
activities.rationale: Showing equivalents coinciding at one point addresses whole-number bias, where a child compares numerators and denominators separately, by making magnitude the object of attention. Dual labelling (thirds above, sixths below) makes the shared point concrete.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias leads students to compare fractions by their separate numerators/denominators (e.g. thinking 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators); the guide recommends showing equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude/point using number lines and dividing a 0-1 line into halves and quarters so 1/2 and 2/4 coincide.
learnerActions: Draw a number line from 0 to 1 and mark thirds above it (1/3, 2/3).
On the same line, mark sixths below it (1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6, including 4/6 against 2/3).
Place 2/3 and 4/6 and check whether they land on the same point or different points.
Repeat with 1/2 and 2/4 (marking halves and quarters) to confirm they coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude and land on the same point of a number line, independent of how the line is partitioned.

activities.title: Sort, match and complete equivalents
feedback: If 3/4 is placed with the equivalents, ask the child to shade 3/4 and 2/3 on identical bars and compare the lengths.
For a missing-value error, return to splitting: 2/3 with each part split into two gives 4/6, so the numerator is 4.
Note: these matching and completion tasks check classification and completion; they do not by themselves build the multiplicative structure, so use them after the diagram work above.
activities.rationale: Recognition and completion tasks assess equivalence and can catch the additive error, but they test rather than construct the underlying structure. Keep them as consolidation, not as the primary teaching.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.
learnerActions: Match pairs of equivalent fractions (for example 1/2 with 2/4, 2/3 with 4/6), justifying each with a quick diagram.
Complete the missing value: 2/3 = __/6, and explain how the splitting gives the answer.
Sort a set into 'equivalent to 2/3' and 'not equivalent', deliberately including the additive trap 3/4, and explain why 3/4 does not belong.
When comparing shaded amounts, always use identical-sized wholes, never different-sized wholes.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying and completing equivalents consolidates the idea; the additive trap, together with a required explanation, checks whether the child multiplies both parts rather than adding.

activities.title: Predict, overlay, explain (diagnostic)
feedback: If the prediction is '4/6 is more because 4 > 2', after overlaying the bars, split each third in front of the child to show four smaller sixths covering the same length.
If the child says the two 'just look the same', push for the mechanism: each third was split in two, so the amount could not change.
If the child denies they can be equal because the numbers differ, show them landing on the same number-line point and name both as one amount.

A full response states 2/3 = 4/6, justifies by holding the whole constant and splitting each part, rejects the additive error, generates another equivalent, and confirms the same point on a number line. A partial response agrees the shaded amounts match but explains it only as 'they look the same' or by counting, without the split-each-part mechanism. A gap response says the fraction with bigger numbers is more or denies equivalence is possible.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task with a required reason surfaces whole-number bias, no-equivalence and additive misconceptions even when a rehearsed child guesses 'same'. Comparing only identical wholes keeps the portion comparison valid; the number-line step confirms shared magnitude.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.

Whole-number bias leads students to compare fractions by their separate numerators/denominators (e.g. thinking 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators); the guide recommends showing equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude/point using number lines and dividing a 0-1 line into halves and quarters so 1/2 and 2/4 coincide.
learnerActions: Look at two identical bars held apart: one shaded 2/3, one shaded 4/6.
Predict whether 4/6 shades MORE than, LESS than, or the SAME as 2/3, and state a reason BEFORE checking.
Slide the second bar onto the first and observe whether the shaded regions coincide.
Respond to a claim: 'Mia says 4/6 is more because 4 > 2 and there are more pieces.' Explain why she is wrong.
Generate one further fraction equal to 2/3 using a diagram and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: The stated reason, not just the final answer, reveals whether the child holds the whole constant and compares the shaded amount, or falls into whole-number or additive thinking.

constraints: When comparing represented portions (shaded areas or bar lengths), always use identical-sized wholes; comparing shaded amounts across different-sized wholes invalidates the equivalence judgement. As numbers on a number line, equivalent fractions remain comparable and coincide at one point.
Teach the multiplicative structure (splitting each part, multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) with diagrams BEFORE introducing any 'times top and bottom' rule.

Both numerator and denominator must be multiplied by the same number: for fractions less than one, such as 2/3, adding one to each (2/3 to 3/4) or changing only one of the two numbers shifts the shaded amount and does not make an equivalent fraction. (Adding one to each keeps the amount the same only when the fraction is a whole, e.g. 3/3 to 4/4, so it is not a valid rule.)
Matching, sorting and fill-in-the-blank tasks consolidate and check classification/completion but do not on their own build the underlying structure; use them after diagram-based construction.
A fraction wall shows which fractions align but does not itself demonstrate the split-each-part mechanism; pair it with active splitting.
Suitable for ages 7-8 (small denominators); the goal is recognising and showing equivalence with diagrams, not symbolic manipulation in isolation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original catalog rated a conversation/persona format as 'adds little' and a third dimension as 'decorative' for this planar area/length idea. These were catalog fit judgements and are not asserted here as universal claims: a discussion may still support reasoning and a 3D model is simply not needed for a planar length/area concept; the stated objective is diagram-based construction of equivalence.

Arithmetic check: 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9 = 8/12 (multiplying both parts by 2, 3, 4); 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. The additive trap 2/3 to 3/4 is correctly presented as NOT equivalent (3/4 = 0.75 > 2/3 approximately 0.667). No numerical errors found.

The source pedagogy also listed the misconception that changing only the numerator or only the denominator preserves value; this is now explicitly addressed in the splitting activity (e.g. 2/3 to 2/6), alongside the additive trap.

The IES source claim quotes the student misconception 'thinking 3/8 > 3/5' (in reality 3/8 < 3/5); it is retained verbatim only as a description of the misconception in sourceClaims and is never offered to a learner as a valid comparison.
The source row referenced internal prerequisite reteach ids for the whole-number and no-equivalence misconceptions; these are internal identifiers and have been omitted from learner-facing guidance.

sourceClaims are exact copies of this row's sources[].claim, cited only where they support the stated teaching principle (showing/recognising with diagrams; number-line magnitude). Citation does not establish that any specific activity was empirically tested or human-reviewed.

assess.poeTask: Show the two fractions un-overlaid: a bar shaded 2/3 and an identical bar shaded 4/6, held apart. Ask the child to predict whether 4/6 shades MORE than, LESS than, or the SAME amount as 2/3, and to say why before checking. A whole-number-biased child predicts '4/6 is more, because 4 > 2'. Then slide the second bar onto the first — the shaded regions coincide exactly. The pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Draw a line splitting each of the three parts of the first bar in half. What fraction is shaded now, and did the amount of chocolate change?
Is 2/3 the same as 3/4? Someone got 3/4 by adding one to the top and one to the bottom — what would you say?
Find another fraction equal to 2/3 using a diagram. How do you know it's equal?
On a number line from 0 to 1, would 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point or different points? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: They are equal — 2/3 = 4/6. The same amount of chocolate is shaded on both bars; the second bar just has each third split into two, so four smaller sixths cover exactly the same length as two thirds. Mia is wrong: more pieces are each smaller, so the total amount is the same.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — the fraction with bigger numbers/more pieces is judged to be more (4/6 > 2/3 because 4 > 2 and 6 > 3)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the two identical bars so the shaded lengths coincide; split each third to generate the sixths in front of the child so the amount is seen not to change
errorPatterns.distractor: 4/6 is more, because 4 is more than 2 and it has more pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 4/6 is more chocolate and points to the larger numbers or the greater number of shaded pieces

errorPatterns.pattern: No-equivalence — different numbers must name different amounts, so 2/3 and 4/6 'can't be the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 2/3 and 4/6 landing on the same point on a number line and covering the same length on the wall; name both as one amount
errorPatterns.distractor: They must be different — the two fractions have different numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists they must differ because the fractions are written with different numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive equivalence — makes 'equivalents' by adding the same number to top and bottom (2/3 = 3/4)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast +1-to-each (shifts the shaded strip) with split-each-part (leaves it fixed); establish that both parts must be MULTIPLIED
errorPatterns.distractor: 2/3 = 3/4 — I added one to the top and one to the bottom.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Generates an equivalent by +1 to each, or agrees 2/3 = 3/4

responseLevels.gap: Says the fraction with bigger numbers is more (4/6 > 2/3), or denies that two differently-written fractions can be equal.
responseLevels.full: States 2/3 = 4/6 and justifies by holding the whole constant and splitting each part (multiplicative), rejects the additive error, generates a further equivalent, and confirms on a number line that they share the same point.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees 2/3 and 4/6 shade the same amount when shown the diagram, but explains it as 'they just look the same' or by counting, without the split-each-part mechanism; may still make equivalents by adding, or falter when the whole isn't drawn.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two identical chocolate bars. The first is split into three equal parts with two of them shaded (2/3). The second is split into six equal parts with four of them shaded (4/6). Mia says 4/6 is more chocolate, because 4 is more than 2 and there are more pieces. Is she right? How much of each bar is shaded, and WHY are they the same or different?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-biased child says 4/6 > 2/3 'because 4 > 2 / more pieces'. Correct reasoning holds the identical whole constant and compares shaded amount, recognising that splitting each part (multiplying numerator AND denominator) leaves the amount unchanged — the reason (tier 2) exposes the bias and the additive error even when a rehearsed child guesses 'same'.

sources.claim: Whole-number bias leads students to compare fractions by their separate numerators/denominators (e.g. thinking 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators); the guide recommends showing equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude/point using number lines and dividing a 0-1 line into halves and quarters so 1/2 and 2/4 coincide.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Newton's Third Law

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** The UK KS3 national curriculum frames forces as 'arising from the interaction between 2 objects' and covers 'opposing forces and equilibrium' but names the laws explicitly only at KS4.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NGSS MS-PS2-1 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-1]', limited to 1-D vertical/horizontal interactions; engineering-integrated); DCI PS2.A states the equal-and-opposite pair for interacting objects.

- **Operational details:** At 12-13 pupils meet Newton's Third Law: for any pair of interacting objects, the force A exerts on B is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force B exerts on A — and crucially these two forces act on DIFFERENT bodies. This is the hardest of the three laws (one two-tier study found ~68.5% holding a misconception, and performance is reliably worse in gravitational than in contact contexts).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational/quantitative). The key cognitive move at this age is to identify the TWO bodies in the interaction and resist treating the pair as forces on one object that 'cancel'. Frame the law as a single INTERACTION between two bodies (A on B, B on A) rather than 'action then reaction' — the action/reaction wording implies a false time sequence and drives the same-body error (IOP; Taber).
bestPractices: Frame the law as a single INTERACTION between two bodies (A on B, B on A), not sequential 'action then reaction' — the words imply a false time order and feed the same-body error (IOP; Taber)

Teach the three diagnostic features of a true pair: they act on TWO DIFFERENT bodies, are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, and are the SAME type of force (both gravitational, or both contact)

Explicitly contrast a third-law pair with balanced forces on ONE body — book on a table: weight + table's push both act on the book (balanced, NOT a pair); the partner to the book's weight is the book's gravitational pull on the Earth
Use kinaesthetic demos so students FEEL both bodies get a force (trolleys, skateboards, metre-rule pull; back-to-back force-meters that stay equal even during acceleration)
Deliberately address the gravity-context version (performance is worse there) as well as contact pushes
Resolve 'the bigger/active object pushes harder' with equal-force/different-effect cases (bug & windscreen; different accelerations come from different masses via N2)
keyRepresentations: Two separate free-body diagrams side by side, one per body, each showing its half of the pair on a different object
The 'swap and reverse' test (A↔B) to locate the partner force
Book / table / Earth three-bodies diagram separating the interaction pairs from the balanced forces on the book
commonMisconceptions: Pairing the two forces on the SAME body and concluding they cancel — conflating a third-law pair with balanced forces (the central error; Taber)
During acceleration the 'active' pusher exerts the bigger force ('Blue pushes Green harder to start the motion') — reported in ~100% of incoming students and very stubborn
The more massive object exerts more force (forces are equal; different EFFECTS come from different masses)
'Action' then 'reaction' implies a time sequence (B responds after A), rather than simultaneous forces
Third-law forces 'cancel out' (they act on different bodies, so can never cancel on one body)
Greater difficulty identifying the partner force in gravitational interactions than in contact pushes

learn.summary: Newton's Third Law for ages 12–13: every force is one half of an interaction between TWO objects — if A pushes or pulls B, then B pushes or pulls A with an equal-magnitude, opposite-direction force of the same type. The decisive learner moves are to name the two different bodies in each pair, to see the pair stays equal even during acceleration and for very different masses, and to distinguish a third-law pair (two bodies) from balanced forces on one body. This is the hardest of Newton's laws; the central misconception is fusing a third-law pair with balanced forces on a single object and concluding they 'cancel'. Frame the law as one simultaneous interaction, not sequential 'action then reaction'.

activities.title: Matched force-meters: the pair stays equal
feedback: If you predicted the harder/active pusher's meter reads more: look again — the readings stay matched even as you push harder and even while the carts speed up together. The interaction force on each object is equal.

Name the object each reading belongs to: the measured interaction force acts on cart A one way and on cart B the opposite way — one force per object. Because they act on different objects they form a genuine third-law pair, not two forces on one body.

A static picture can show the two arrows, but watching the readings stay equal while you push harder is what directly tests the 'active object pushes harder' idea; if you only have a diagram, reason explicitly about what the sensors would read during acceleration. Any small difference between real readings comes from instrument limitations (precision, zeroing or calibration, or the sensors' own mass while accelerating). The interaction pair is equal in principle, and friction with the ground is a separate force that does NOT make the two readings unequal.
activities.rationale: The 'active/bigger object pushes harder during acceleration' idea is reported as common and stubborn; a live, equal-reading measurement during acceleration lets learners confront it directly. A prediction-first step surfaces the misconception before the evidence.
sourceClaims: Third-law pairs act on two different bodies, are equal and opposite, and are the same type of force; they do NOT cancel (each acts on a different body). 'Action/reaction' is misleading. Book-on-table involves three bodies (Earth, book, table): the book's weight pairs with the book's pull on the Earth, and the book-on-table push pairs with the table-on-book push — while the two forces ON the book merely balance.
learnerActions: Set two carts nose-to-nose with a push–pull force sensor on the front of each, touching (ordinary spring newton-meters only measure pulls; if that is all you have, hook two together and have one cart tow the other instead), and predict, before pushing, what each sensor will read when one cart pushes gently and when it pushes hard.
Make one cart push the other and read both sensors; then push harder and read again; then keep pushing so both carts speed up together, and read the sensors while they are accelerating.
Record whether the two readings are ever different, including while the carts are speeding up.
State in your own words which object each measured force acts on.
activities.intendedInsight: The two forces in an interaction are always equal in magnitude, even while the objects accelerate and even when one is doing the 'pushing' — so there is no 'stronger pusher'.

activities.title: Find the partner: two bodies, never the same one
feedback: If you placed both forces of a 'pair' on the same object, re-run the swap test: the partner of 'skater pushes wall' is 'wall pushes skater' — a different object. The skater is pushed away from the wall, and the wall is pushed away from the skater (in the direction of the skater's push).
Because the two forces act on different bodies, they cannot add up or cancel on one body; cancelling only happens between forces on the SAME body.
Optional highlight tools make the partner's object obvious, but the key check is verbal: name both objects every time.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating the two bodies and using the 'B on A' locating rule targets the same-body/cancellation error identified as central. Framing it as one interaction (not action-then-reaction) avoids implying a time sequence.
sourceClaims: Third-law pairs act on two different bodies, are equal and opposite, and are the same type of force; they do NOT cancel (each acts on a different body). 'Action/reaction' is misleading. Book-on-table involves three bodies (Earth, book, table): the book's weight pairs with the book's pull on the Earth, and the book-on-table push pairs with the table-on-book push — while the two forces ON the book merely balance.

A common alternative conception is misidentifying the action/reaction pair as both acting on the same body and concluding they cancel; the law concerns forces on a pair of bodies and so cannot explain why forces on a single body balance. Careful language matters; framing force as a single interaction between two bodies helps.
learnerActions: Watch a skater shove a wall and recoil, or push off a wall yourself, and name the two forces: the force on the wall and the force on the skater.
For each named force, apply the 'swap and reverse' test: if 'A acts on B', its partner is 'B acts on A' — state it aloud.
Use a highlight tool (optional) that greys out everything except the partner force on the OTHER body, and check it lands on a different object.
Decide whether the two forces in a pair could ever cancel each other, and explain why or why not.
activities.intendedInsight: A third-law pair always consists of forces on two different objects, so the pair can never cancel on a single object.

activities.title: Equal forces, unequal effects (bug vs windscreen)
feedback: If you said the heavier or faster object exerts the bigger force: the forces are equal. The bug and the windscreen push on each other equally.
The difference you observe is in acceleration: for the same force, a smaller mass gives a larger acceleration (a = F/m).
Keep 'bigger force' and 'bigger effect' as two separate questions — conflating them is exactly the misconception.
activities.rationale: Resolving 'the bigger/more massive object pushes harder' with an equal-force/different-effect case links N3 to N2 and addresses a documented misconception without asserting new empirical efficacy.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-1]' (examples: car collisions, meteor and space vehicle; assessment limited to 1-D vertical/horizontal interactions). DCI PS2.A: for any pair of interacting objects the force of the first on the second equals in strength the force of the second on the first, opposite in direction.
learnerActions: Consider a collision between a light object and a heavy object (e.g. a bug and a windscreen, or a small car and a truck); predict which experiences the bigger force.
Using a mass control (optional dial) or by reasoning, compare the forces on the two objects and then compare their accelerations.
Explain, using F = ma, why the lighter object changes its motion much more while the forces are equal.
Write one sentence separating 'which force is bigger' (neither — they're equal) from 'which object is affected more' (the lighter one).
activities.intendedInsight: Equal interaction forces produce different effects on different masses; the different accelerations come from the different masses (via F = ma), not from unequal forces (how much damage is done also depends on how fragile each object is).

activities.title: Book, table and Earth: pair vs balanced
feedback: If you called the table's push and the book's weight a pair: both act on the book, so they are balanced forces, not a pair.
The weight's partner is the book pulling the Earth up (both gravitational); the table-push's partner is the book pushing down on the table (both contact).
Use two checks for every candidate pair: different objects, and same type of force.
activities.rationale: The book/table/Earth case is the canonical setting where learners fuse balanced forces with a third-law pair; separating the interaction pairs from the one-body balance directly addresses the central error. A tap-to-reveal reference can support this, but a static version cannot show forces staying equal during acceleration, so pair it with the dynamic measurement activity.
sourceClaims: Third-law pairs act on two different bodies, are equal and opposite, and are the same type of force; they do NOT cancel (each acts on a different body). 'Action/reaction' is misleading. Book-on-table involves three bodies (Earth, book, table): the book's weight pairs with the book's pull on the Earth, and the book-on-table push pairs with the table-on-book push — while the two forces ON the book merely balance.

A common alternative conception is misidentifying the action/reaction pair as both acting on the same body and concluding they cancel; the law concerns forces on a pair of bodies and so cannot explain why forces on a single body balance. Careful language matters; framing force as a single interaction between two bodies helps.
learnerActions: Draw or reveal the three bodies in a book-on-table scene: Earth, book, table.
List the forces acting ON the book (its weight from the Earth, and the table's upward push) and state that these two balance because the book is at rest.
For the book's weight, find its third-law partner by the swap test (the book's gravitational pull up on the Earth).
For the table's push on the book, find its partner (the book's push down on the table).
Sort every named force into 'balanced forces on one body' versus 'third-law pair across two bodies', and check each pair is the same TYPE of force (both gravitational, or both contact).
activities.intendedInsight: The two forces on the book balance (same body) but are NOT a pair; each force's genuine partner acts on a different body and is the same type of force.

activities.title: Socratic 'am I pulling you?' questioning
feedback: If you described a delay or a sequence: the two forces happen at the same time — there is no first and second.
Notice you cannot pull the rule without it pulling back; the interaction is inherently two-sided.
Replacing 'action/reaction' with 'A on B / B on A' removes the false time-order cue.
activities.rationale: The questioning routine probes the simultaneity and mutuality of the interaction and supports language that avoids the sequence implication. It builds reasoning but does not provide the felt equality that a measured demonstration offers, so it complements rather than replaces the measurement activity.
sourceClaims: A common alternative conception is misidentifying the action/reaction pair as both acting on the same body and concluding they cancel; the law concerns forces on a pair of bodies and so cannot explain why forces on a single body balance. Careful language matters; framing force as a single interaction between two bodies helps.
learnerActions: With a partner or an in-role tutor, pull on opposite ends of a metre rule and answer: Which way am I pulling you? Which way are you pulling me?
Answer: Can I pull you without you pulling me back?
Relate your answers to the rule that the interaction is simultaneous — not 'my pull first, then your pull'.
Restate the law without using the words 'action' and 'reaction', using 'A on B' and 'B on A' instead.
activities.intendedInsight: Interaction forces are simultaneous and mutual; the 'action then reaction' wording wrongly implies a time order.

activities.title: Retrieval: sort pairs, match partners, apply
feedback: For any 'pair' you pick, confirm it passes both checks: two different objects AND the same type of force.
If you labelled two forces on one object a pair, they are balanced, not a pair.
For recoil, the gun pushes the bullet forward and the bullet pushes the gun back — equal forces, different objects.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorisation and applied items give retrieval practice and surface the same-body and 'pusher pushes harder' distractors. Recognition items assess discrimination but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and manipulate the interaction, so they are best used after the demonstration and reasoning activities.
sourceClaims: Third-law pairs act on two different bodies, are equal and opposite, and are the same type of force; they do NOT cancel (each acts on a different body). 'Action/reaction' is misleading. Book-on-table involves three bodies (Earth, book, table): the book's weight pairs with the book's pull on the Earth, and the book-on-table push pairs with the table-on-book push — while the two forces ON the book merely balance.
learnerActions: Match each named force to its partner on the OTHER body (e.g. 'rocket pushes gas down' ↔ 'gas pushes rocket up').
Categorise given force-pairs as 'third-law pair' or 'balanced forces on one body'.
Answer the book-on-table item: which forces form third-law pairs (there is more than one pair), and how do you decide?
For rocket propulsion and gun recoil, name both forces and the object each acts on.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can reliably identify third-law partners (different object, same type) and separate them from balanced forces across varied contexts.

constraints: Target age 12–13; this is the hardest of Newton's laws and the central misconception (fusing a third-law pair with balanced forces on one body) must be addressed explicitly, not assumed away.
Every third-law pair must satisfy two checks: the two forces act on DIFFERENT objects, and they are the SAME type of force (both gravitational, or both contact).
Avoid 'action then reaction' phrasing; use 'A on B' and 'B on A' to convey simultaneous, mutual forces.
Deliberately include a gravitational-context example (e.g. book/Earth), since learners find partner-finding harder there than in contact pushes.

Static tap-to-reveal diagrams are useful references but cannot show forces staying equal during acceleration; use them alongside, not instead of, a dynamic measurement that targets the 'active object pushes harder' idea.
Recognition/matching items assess discrimination but do not require independent construction of an interaction; follow them with tasks where learners name both objects and locate partners themselves.

Real newton-meters/force sensors are approximate instruments with limited precision; frame equal readings as evidence that the interaction forces are equal, treating any small difference as an instrument limitation (precision, zeroing/calibration, or the sensors' own mass during acceleration) rather than implying friction makes the pair unequal (friction is a separate force and does not affect the equality of the A-on-B / B-on-A pair).

NGSS MS-PS2-1 limits assessment to 1-D interactions; a planar treatment is sufficient and a 3-D representation adds handling cost without clear conceptual gain at this stage (a scoped observation, not a universal claim).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving these specific activities were tested.

The source cites a '~68.5% misconception' prevalence from a two-tier study and '~100% of incoming students' holding the 'active pusher pushes harder' idea; these figures are stated in the original pedagogy but are not attributed to a listed source[].claim, so they are reported here only as context, not as verified evidence, and are omitted from learner-facing text.

The Taber source (science-education-research.com) is marked verified:false in the row; claims drawn from it (language/framing, same-body cancellation error) are retained as pedagogical guidance but should be re-checked.

The original 'ideal' entry asserted the decisive facts 'do not survive a static treatment' and that a static image 'cannot' overturn the misconception; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, since catalog ratings do not establish such necessity claims.
The 3-D claim that it 'adds nothing' has been softened to a scoped observation tied to the 1-D standard and handling cost.

When describing collisions/recoil, note that equal forces coexist with different accelerations; any speeding-up/slowing description should reference the object's mass and initial motion rather than implying the resultant sets the current direction of travel.

Activity 1 was standardised to two linked newton-meters so the 'both meters read equal' comparison is coherent; the equal readings demonstrate the equal magnitude of the A-on-B and B-on-A interaction forces (treating the linking meter as approximately massless).

Corrected the measurement-limitation wording in Activity 1 feedback and the related constraint: third-law equality of the pair is exact, so any discrepancy in real readings is instrument precision/measurement noise; friction is a separate force and does not make the pair unequal. This avoids implying friction can unbalance a true third-law pair.

assess.poeTask: Hook two identical newton-meters (or force sensors) together and have two students pull — one gently, one hard. Ask the class to predict what each meter reads, and WHY, before they pull. Predicting the 'stronger' puller's meter reads more reveals the unequal-force idea; both reading the same, even during acceleration or with different-mass carts, is the surprise that establishes the equal pair.
probeDeeper: A truck and a small car collide head-on. Which experiences the bigger force — and why do they end up so differently damaged?
A rocket pushes hot gas downwards and rises. Name both forces in the pair and the object each one acts on.
For the two forces you called a pair — do they act on the same object or different ones? Could they ever cancel each other out?
assess.correctAnswer: The first student is right. A Third Law pair is two forces of the SAME type acting on DIFFERENT objects: the table pushes up on the book and the book pushes down on the table. The book's weight (Earth pulling the book) acts on the SAME object as the table's push — the book — so those two are BALANCED forces, not a pair; weight's actual pair is the book pulling the Earth up. To find a pair: state 'A acts on B', and its pair is always 'B acts on A' (same type, different objects).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The table's push up and the book's weight are the Third Law pair — they're equal and opposite.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on naming both objects for every force; a pair must act on two different objects, so weight and the table's push (both on the book) are balanced, not a pair.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the table's push up and the book's weight are the Third Law pair, equal and opposite.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Identifies two forces acting on the SAME object (the book) as a Third Law pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The action happens first, then the reaction happens back — there's a tiny delay.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Drop 'action/reaction' language: 'if A pushes B, B pushes A back equally AT THE SAME TIME' — the two forces are simultaneous.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a sequence, a delay, or a 'winner' between the two forces.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The bigger object pushes harder — a truck hits a car, so the truck's force is bigger.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The pair is always equal even for very different masses; the different DAMAGE comes from different accelerations (F = ma), not different forces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the forces in a collision are unequal (the bigger object wins).

responseLevels.gap: Calls any two equal-and-opposite forces a Third Law pair (including two forces on the same object), or describes action-then-reaction with a delay or winner.
responseLevels.full: Identifies pairs by naming 'A on B' and 'B on A' (same type, different objects, simultaneous, equal even for unequal masses), distinguishes them from balanced forces on one object, and applies this to rockets, recoil and collisions.
responseLevels.partial: States the law and gives an example, but can't reliably tell a Third Law pair from balanced forces — names forces without checking that a pair acts on two DIFFERENT objects and is the same type.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A book rests on a table. One student says: 'The table pushing up on the book and the book pushing down on the table are a Newton's Third Law pair.' Another says: 'No — the pair to the table's push up on the book is the book's WEIGHT.' Who is right, and how do you decide which two forces form a Third Law pair?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The classic error is fusing the Third Law pair with balanced forces. Both students name two equal-and-opposite forces, so tier 1 doesn't separate them — the METHOD in tier 2 does. A student who understands N3 checks the two OBJECTS (must differ) and the TYPE (same), correctly rejecting the weight/normal-force option because both act on the book. A student holding the misconception accepts any equal-opposite pair on the same object.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Gut Bacteria & Digestion

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Nutrition & digestion):** "the importance of bacteria in the human digestive system."

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No specific MS performance expectation on the gut microbiome; the beneficial-microbe idea sits loosely under matter cycling (MS-LS1-7 / ecosystem PEs). This is UK-led content. (US/UK divergence.)

- **Operational details:** Children explain that the gut is home to a huge community of bacteria (the microbiome), that MANY of these bacteria are beneficial rather than harmful, and that they do jobs human enzymes cannot — notably fermenting/breaking down dietary fibre the body cannot digest alone, and helping maintain a healthy gut environment (and making some vitamins). They describe what may happen when the microbiome is disrupted (e.g. by antibiotics or poor diet). The move that matters is overturning the 'all bacteria are germs' idea: here bacteria are partners in a mutualistic relationship, extending the body's digestive capability.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B→C. Builds on digestion & enzymes and on knowing unicellular organisms; a relatively modern, evidence-evolving topic. A child is secure when they can state one thing gut bacteria do that our own enzymes cannot, explain why that matters, and give a consequence of disrupting the microbiome.
bestPractices: Lead with the myth-correction — most gut bacteria are helpful partners, not germs — since this is the central conceptual shift.
Contrast what human enzymes CAN'T do (digest fibre) with what bacteria CAN, so the partnership is concrete.
Use the mutualism framing (both benefit) to connect to ecology/relationships between organisms.
Include disruption (antibiotics, poor diet) and its consequences so the microbiome's importance is felt.
Keep claims evidence-appropriate — the field is fast-moving; teach the well-established roles (fibre fermentation, gut health, some vitamin synthesis).
keyRepresentations: Gut scene showing the bacterial community in the large intestine
Two-track comparison: human enzymes vs bacterial fermentation on the same fibre
Mutualism diagram (bacteria get food/home; we get fibre broken down + gut health)
Before/after disruption panel (healthy diverse community vs depleted)
commonMisconceptions: Believing all bacteria are harmful germs, rather than mostly beneficial partners.
Thinking humans digest fibre themselves, rather than relying on gut bacteria to ferment it.
Assuming antibiotics only kill 'bad' bacteria and leave the helpful community untouched.
Thinking the microbiome is fixed rather than changing with diet.
Confusing gut bacteria with the pathogens that cause food poisoning.

learn.summary: For learners aged 12–13 (UK KS3 Biology: 'the importance of bacteria in the human digestive system'), the central goal is to overturn the 'all bacteria are germs' idea and understand the gut microbiome as a mostly beneficial, mutualistic community. Learners should name at least one thing gut bacteria do that human enzymes cannot (notably fermenting dietary fibre), explain why that matters, and give a consequence of disrupting the microbiome (e.g. by antibiotics or a fibre-poor diet). Guidance centres on an interactive 'tend the gut community' model that is proposed to make the partnership causal, supported by a reveal-based gut scene, an in-role scientist conversation for 'why' questions, and sorting/short-answer checks. Relative efficacy of these media is untested.

activities.title: Tend your gut community: two digestion tracks
feedback: If the learner feeds only low-fibre foods: point out the bacterial track has little to work on and gut health does not rise — highlight that fibre is the bacteria's fuel.
When the fibre slides untouched through the enzyme track: prompt 'Which track finally acts on this fibre, and what does that tell you about what your bacteria add?'
After the antibiotic/poor-diet crash: ask the learner to predict what a person might feel (e.g. upset stomach, diarrhoea) and why recovery depends on diversity returning.
Reinforce the myth-correction when it arises in play: most of these trillions of residents are helpful partners, not germs to be eliminated.
activities.rationale: The role of gut bacteria is a dynamic, ecological process; letting the learner act on the community and see consequences is proposed to make the mutualistic partnership causal rather than merely asserted, and may let the fragility and importance of the microbiome be experienced. Relative efficacy against other media is untested. Live recolouring, a rising/falling gut-health meter, food-selection controls and the parallel two-track comparison are offered as concrete interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms.
sourceClaims: The human gut hosts a large community of mostly beneficial bacteria that ferment dietary fibre humans cannot digest, help maintain gut health and synthesise some vitamins; disruption (e.g. by antibiotics) can impair these functions.
learnerActions: Feed a model gut by choosing foods: food first passes through the small intestine, where the body's own enzymes work, then reaches a model colon (large intestine) full of bacteria. Watch the two digestion tracks side by side.
Observe that the body's own enzymes break down starch, sugars and protein, but cannot digest dietary fibre. The fibre passes undigested through the small intestine into the large intestine.
Watch the bacterial community act on that same fibre, fermenting it, producing beneficial products, and raising a 'gut health' indicator.
Introduce a disruption — a course of antibiotics or a switch to a fibre-poor diet — and observe the community decline and gut health drop.

Restore fibre-rich foods and observe the model's gut health recover as bacterial diversity returns. In real people, recovery after antibiotics can be slow or incomplete, and it varies from person to person.
State in your own words why the two digestive systems complete each other.
activities.intendedInsight: Fibre, which the body's own enzymes cannot digest, is a major food source for the bacterial partners, so human enzymes and gut bacteria complement each other. The microbiome is mostly beneficial, and disrupting it can have real consequences for digestion.

activities.title: Lift-the-flap gut scene: name the roles, bust the myth
feedback: If the learner expects all reveals to say 'harmful', surface the contrast between a few disease-causing species and the many helpful residents.
Confirm correct naming: fibre fermentation is the headline role human enzymes cannot perform.
activities.rationale: A tap/lift-to-reveal scene is an efficient way to name roles and address the myth layer. It is a naming scaffold and does not itself show the ecological dynamics of feeding and disruption; the tap-to-reveal and flap panels are concrete interaction examples offered, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: The human gut hosts a large community of mostly beneficial bacteria that ferment dietary fibre humans cannot digest, help maintain gut health and synthesise some vitamins; disruption (e.g. by antibiotics) can impair these functions.
learnerActions: Tap the large-intestine community to reveal 'trillions of mostly helpful bacteria'.
Tap the fibre to reveal that bacteria ferment fibre that human enzymes cannot digest.
Open the flap 'Are gut bacteria harmful?' to reveal 'Most are helpful partners — we depend on them.'
Add a note of one further job (e.g. helping maintain a healthy gut environment or making some vitamins).
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can name what beneficial gut bacteria do and directly confront the 'all bacteria are harmful' idea.

activities.title: Ask the microbiome scientist (enrichment)
feedback: When a myth surfaces in a question, the scientist separates a few pathogens from the trillions of helpful residents rather than simply asserting the answer.
Keep claims evidence-appropriate: this is a fast-moving field, so emphasise well-established roles (fibre fermentation, gut health, some vitamin synthesis) and flag where science is still evolving.
activities.rationale: A responsive in-role conversation can follow a learner's questions and address 'why' and myths Socratically. It is valuable for the reasoning and myth layer; a dialogue can support, and need not replace, an interactive model intended to make the ecological dynamics felt. The relative efficacy of these media is untested.
learnerActions: Pose your own 'why' questions to an in-role gut-microbiome scientist, e.g. 'Why does my diet change my gut bacteria?' or 'What do probiotics do?'
Follow up on answers about what the bacteria do, why fibre matters, and what disrupts them.
Summarise one thing you learned that changed or confirmed your earlier idea.
activities.intendedInsight: The microbiome is an active, curiosity-rich research area; learners can pursue open questions and have their own ideas named and probed through dialogue.

activities.title: Check it: roles, what bacteria digest, disruption consequences
feedback: Full response: explains the microbiome is mostly beneficial, does jobs (fibre fermentation, crowding out pathogens) our enzymes can't, and predicts consequences of disruption.
Partial response: accepts gut bacteria can be helpful but cannot specify what they do (fibre breakdown) or what disruption causes — prompt for a specific job.

Gap response: treats all bacteria as harmful germs; reteach by contrasting a few disease-causing species with the trillions of helpful residents and showing fibre left undigested when bacteria are lost.
activities.rationale: Beneficial-vs-harmful sorting and 'what bacteria do that our enzymes can't' are clean items for surfacing the target misconceptions and confirming the specific knowledge. Recognition/sorting formats check classification but do not by themselves elicit extended independent explanation; the diagnostic prompt is included to draw out reasoning.
sourceClaims: The human gut hosts a large community of mostly beneficial bacteria that ferment dietary fibre humans cannot digest, help maintain gut health and synthesise some vitamins; disruption (e.g. by antibiotics) can impair these functions.
learnerActions: Sort roles/items into 'helpful' versus 'harmful' bacteria.
Answer: 'What do gut bacteria digest that we cannot?' (Answer: dietary fibre.)
Match each disruption (e.g. broad-spectrum antibiotics, fibre-poor diet) to a likely consequence (e.g. impaired digestion, diarrhoea, loss of diversity).

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: 'Adverts sell soap that kills 99.9% of all bacteria. Your large intestine is home to trillions of bacteria. Are those bacteria making you ill — and what would happen to your digestion if a strong course of antibiotics killed many of them?'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners demonstrate they can distinguish beneficial from harmful bacteria, identify fibre as what bacteria digest that we cannot, and predict consequences of disruption.

constraints: Lead with the myth-correction — most gut bacteria are helpful partners, not germs — as the central conceptual shift, and separate the few pathogens (e.g. food-poisoning species) from the resident microbiome.

Keep claims evidence-appropriate: the microbiome is a fast-moving research area; teach the well-established roles (fibre fermentation, maintaining gut health, synthesising some vitamins) and avoid overstating effects.
The reveal-based gut scene is a naming scaffold only; it does not demonstrate the feed/ferment/disrupt dynamics, so pair it with an interactive model or discussion for the causal story.
Sorting and multiple-choice items check recognition and recall; they do not by themselves require learners to construct an extended explanation, so include an open prompt for full-response reasoning.
The in-role scientist conversation is enrichment for 'why' questions; its answers should stay within established science and flag evolving areas rather than assert certainty.
Present the on-screen colon, tracks and meters as a model of real digestion, not a literal depiction; actual timings, populations and recovery vary by person, diet and medication.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source (British Nutrition Foundation, dietary fibre and gut bacteria) is marked verified:false in the row; the specific claims about vitamin synthesis and antibiotic-driven disruption rest on it and should be confirmed before being presented as settled fact.

The source row's '3D adds nothing' judgement for this topic was not carried over as a universal claim; it reflects a fit ranking, not established comparative efficacy. 3D was simply not proposed because the content is relational rather than spatial.

The original framing that the live model makes the partnership 'causal rather than asserted' and that other media cannot make dynamics 'felt' is a design preference, not demonstrated comparative efficacy; efficacy wording in the activity rationales has been softened to proposed/may/intended language accordingly.
The enrichment conversation activity carries no sourceClaims because its rationale concerns the dialogue medium (untested efficacy) rather than a factual claim the source substantiates.

NGSS has no specific middle-school performance expectation for the gut microbiome (the idea sits loosely under matter cycling / MS-LS1-7); this is UK-led content, which may affect portability to US contexts.

probeDeeper: If bacteria were all harmful, why would getting rid of your gut bacteria make your digestion worse, not better?
What can your gut bacteria do to your food that your own digestive enzymes cannot?
Why might someone get an upset stomach during a course of antibiotics?
How is a helpful gut bacterium different from a bacterium that causes food poisoning?
assess.correctAnswer: The gut bacteria are largely beneficial (a mutualistic microbiome): they break down dietary fibre that our own enzymes cannot digest and help keep harmful microbes out. Wiping them out — for example with broad-spectrum antibiotics — can disrupt digestion, cause diarrhoea, and let harmful species take over until the microbiome recovers.

errorPatterns.pattern: All bacteria are germs that make you ill
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate pathogens from the beneficial microbiome; most gut bacteria help us. Contrast a few disease-causing species with the trillions of helpful residents.
errorPatterns.distractor: The gut bacteria are germs — you'd be healthier if you killed them all.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the gut bacteria are harmful and you'd be healthier without them

errorPatterns.pattern: The human gut could digest everything on its own, without bacteria
errorPatterns.nextMove: Humans can't digest much dietary fibre; gut bacteria ferment it, releasing useful products. Their loss leaves fibre undigested.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims human enzymes handle all food, so bacteria are unnecessary

errorPatterns.pattern: The gut bacteria are an infection you caught
errorPatterns.nextMove: The microbiome is a resident community built up from birth and normally kept in balance, not an infection.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the microbiome as invaders that got in, rather than resident partners

responseLevels.gap: Treats all bacteria as harmful germs; sees no useful role for microbes in the gut.
responseLevels.full: Explains the microbiome is mostly beneficial, does jobs (fibre fermentation, crowding out pathogens) our enzymes can't, and predicts the consequences of disrupting it.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts that gut bacteria can be helpful but cannot say specifically what they do (fibre breakdown) or what disruption causes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Adverts sell soap that 'kills 99.9% of all bacteria' as if every microbe is the enemy. But your large intestine is home to trillions of bacteria. Are those bacteria making you ill — and what would happen to your digestion if a strong course of antibiotics wiped them out?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the microbiome sees these bacteria as helpful partners with a digestive job. A child holding 'all bacteria are germs' treats them as invaders that should be destroyed and cannot explain why losing them harms digestion.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Animal Body Groups

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 Animals including humans):** "describe and compare the structure of a variety of common animals (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals including pets)." This is the structure-comparison partner to naming the five groups — pupils move from naming to describing external body features and comparing them across groups.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 1-LS1-1 / DCI LS1.A, nearest anchor):** "all organisms have external parts... [they] use their body parts... to [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS1-1]." NGSS frames external parts by FUNCTION rather than by comparing across the five vertebrate classes, so the US link is structure–function, not the UK cross-group comparison.

- **Operational details:** Build directly on Naming Common Animals: now the child describes the external features (fur, feathers, scales, fins, wings, legs, tail, gills) and COMPARES two animals from different groups. Teach it as observation-and-comparison — lay a bird next to a fish and ask what each has, what's the same, what's different — so the group-defining features (feathers vs scales, wings vs fins) emerge from looking. Give precise body-part vocabulary and require it in comparisons. Keep the covering–group link explicit (feathers→bird, fur→mammal, scales→fish/reptile) because these coverings are the most reliable young-child cue. This directly seeds skeletons/muscles and the human-body-parts topics.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can describe key structural features of at least three groups, compare two animals noting two differences, and use body-part words correctly. Appropriate: external, visible features; direct side-by-side comparison. NOT appropriate yet: internal anatomy, skeletal detail, adaptation-as-function arguments. Watch for describing by colour/size rather than structural features, and for missing that reptiles AND fish both have scales (different kinds).
bestPractices: Stage direct side-by-side comparison (e.g. a bird next to a fish) and ask what each has, what is the same, and what is different, so group features emerge from observation.
Give and require precise body-part vocabulary (wings, fins, gills, feathers, scales, fur, beak, tail) in every description and comparison.
Anchor each group to its body covering (feathers→bird, fur→mammal, scales→fish/reptile), the most reliable cue for young children.
Move deliberately from naming (prior topic) to describing then comparing, keeping the same familiar exemplars.
Use real materials — feathers, scales, fur samples — and close-up images to make external structure tangible.
keyRepresentations: Two-animal side-by-side comparison layout with shared vs different features highlighted.
A five-group features chart (covering, limbs, how it moves) built up across animals.
Labelled animal diagrams tagging wings, fins, legs, tail, gills, feathers, scales, fur.
Body-covering sample cards (feather, fish scale, fur, reptile skin) matched to groups.
commonMisconceptions: Describing animals by colour, size or 'cuteness' rather than by structural features.
Assuming 'has scales' uniquely means fish — missing that reptiles also have (dry) scales.
Thinking all animals with four legs are the same group, or that 'has legs' distinguishes mammals.
Confusing wings as a bird-only feature — overlooking that bats (mammals) and insects also have wings.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, children describe and compare the external body structure of common animals across the five vertebrate groups (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals). The core objective is describe-AND-compare: moving from naming groups to describing external features (fur, feathers, scales, fins, wings, gills, legs, tail, beak) and comparing two animals from different groups side by side. The row treats body covering as the most reliable grouping cue for this age. A key point: group an animal by its body features, not by what it does (flying) or where it lives (in water).

activities.title: Side-by-side compare bench
feedback: When a child labels a part correctly, confirm it and link it to the group ('feathers — birds have these').
If a child says 'has scales' means fish, show the snake: reptiles have dry scales and no fins or gills, so compare further features before deciding the group.
If a child compares by colour or size ('the robin is small and brown'), redirect: 'those are colours and sizes — look at the body parts and coverings instead.'
activities.rationale: The objective is explicitly describe-and-compare, so staging an active side-by-side contrast where the child names, tags and compares features makes the comparison something performed and seen. Optional live highlighting (shared parts glow one colour, group-unique parts another) can make the shared-vs-different distinction concrete, but is one way to show it, not required.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'describe and compare the structure of a variety of common animals (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals including pets)'.

The five vertebrate groups are distinguished by external features/body coverings (mammal fur/hair, bird feathers, fish fins/scales/gills, reptile dry scaly skin, amphibian moist skin), which supports teaching structure comparison by these features.
learnerActions: Place two animals from different groups next to each other — e.g. a robin beside a goldfish.
Name what each animal has (feathers, wings, beak vs scales, fins, gills) and identify shared parts (eyes, tail).
Tag each body part by placing/dragging a word label (wing, fin, fur, scale, gill) onto the correct part of each animal.
Swap one animal for a snake and notice that the reptile ALSO has scales — but dry ones, with no fins — so 'has scales' alone is not enough to tell the group.
Build up a five-group feature chart (covering, limbs, and — as a described feature only — how it moves) as more animals are compared.
activities.intendedInsight: Group-defining features emerge from directly comparing the whole set of features between two animals, not from any single clue. Body covering (feathers→bird, fur→mammal, scales→fish/reptile) is treated as the most reliable cue, but scales appear in more than one group, so you compare the full feature set. Movement is described, but grouping is decided by body structure, not by how an animal moves.

activities.title: Explore a labelled animal and its coverings
feedback: Reinforce the correct body-part word each time ('that's the gill').
If vocabulary is vague ('the swimmy bits'), supply the precise word ('those are fins').
activities.rationale: Building descriptive vocabulary and the covering cue cleanly supports the comparison work; a single labelled picture teaches the words well but shows only one animal at a time, so pair it with an actual two-animal comparison for the compare half of the objective.
sourceClaims: The five vertebrate groups are distinguished by external features/body coverings (mammal fur/hair, bird feathers, fish fins/scales/gills, reptile dry scaly skin, amphibian moist skin), which supports teaching structure comparison by these features.
learnerActions: Examine a fully labelled animal from each group, revealing part names (feathers, wings, beak; fins, scales, gills; fur, legs, tail) and the group each covering signals.
Say aloud 'birds have feathers', 'fish have gills and fins', 'mammals have fur' as each part is revealed.
Compare two labelled animals using a 'what's the same / what's different?' prompt between them.
activities.intendedInsight: Precise body-part vocabulary and the covering→group link are the tools used in every comparison.

activities.title: Handle real coverings and sort features to groups
feedback: Confirm correct matches and name the covering; for a wrong match, place the real sample next to the labelled animal to compare textures.

For the compare prompt, accept any genuine structural difference (feathers vs moist skin; the robin has two wings and two legs while the frog has four legs and no wings; beak vs wide mouth) and redirect colour/size answers back to body structure.
activities.rationale: Real materials make external structure concrete, and sorting/matching checks the mapping directly. A sort or match can check the feature→group classification but does not itself stage the act of comparing two animals or elicit a spoken comparison, so it complements rather than replaces the comparison bench.
sourceClaims: The five vertebrate groups are distinguished by external features/body coverings (mammal fur/hair, bird feathers, fish fins/scales/gills, reptile dry scaly skin, amphibian moist skin), which supports teaching structure comparison by these features.
learnerActions: Handle real materials — feathers, fish scales, fur samples, close-up images of reptile skin — and match each to its group.
Sort feature cards under each group heading (feathers→bird, gills→fish, dry scales→reptile, fur→mammal, moist skin→amphibian).
Answer a short compare prompt: 'Name one body difference between a frog and a robin.'
activities.intendedInsight: Linking the tactile covering to the group makes external structure tangible and checks that the feature→group mapping is secure.

activities.title: Tricky cases: group by body, not by behaviour or habitat
feedback: If a child calls the bat (or a flying insect) a bird 'because it flies', regroup by covering: the bat has fur and feeds its young milk, so it is a mammal — compare feathers vs fur side by side.
If a child puts a whale or dolphin with fish 'because it swims', point to air-breathing, hair and feeding young milk: group by features, not habitat.
If a child denies a penguin or ostrich is a bird 'because it can't fly', show flightless birds still have feathers and wings — feathers make it a bird.
activities.rationale: The classic error at this age is grouping by behaviour or habitat rather than body structure. Confronting counter-cases (flying mammal, aquatic mammal, flightless bird) directly surfaces and corrects that error by forcing attention back to body features.
sourceClaims: The five vertebrate groups are distinguished by external features/body coverings (mammal fur/hair, bird feathers, fish fins/scales/gills, reptile dry scaly skin, amphibian moist skin), which supports teaching structure comparison by these features.
learnerActions: Consider: a bat flies and a robin flies, but only one is a bird — which one, and what body feature proves it?
Check the covering: the bat has fur and feeds its babies milk (mammal); the robin has feathers (bird). Group by feature, not by flight.

Decide whether a whale is a fish or a mammal by what you can check: whales breathe air through a blowhole and have no gills, have smooth skin rather than fish scales, have a few hairs (often only as babies) and feed their young milk, so they are mammals despite living in water.
Decide whether a penguin is a bird even though it can't fly: feathers make it a bird, not flight.
activities.intendedInsight: Animals are grouped by their body features (covering and parts), plus mammal traits like feeding young milk, not by what they do (flying) or where they live (in water). The bat is a mammal because it has fur and feeds its young milk; the whale is a mammal because it breathes air through a blowhole, has no gills or fish scales, and feeds its young milk; the penguin is a bird because it has feathers.

constraints: Keep to external, visible features and direct side-by-side comparison; internal anatomy, skeletal detail and adaptation-as-function arguments are not yet appropriate for this age.
Children should describe key structural features of at least three groups, compare two animals noting at least two differences, and use body-part words (wings, fins, legs, tail) correctly.
Watch for describing by colour, size or 'cuteness' rather than structural features, and redirect to body parts and coverings.
Watch for assuming all four-legged animals belong to one group, or that 'has legs' identifies mammals; redirect to body covering and the full feature set rather than a single part.
Make explicit that scales are not unique to fish — reptiles have dry scales too — so a single feature is not enough to assign a group.

The feature chart may record how an animal moves as a description, but grouping is decided by body structure (covering/parts), not by movement or habitat; keep this consistent with the tricky-cases message.

A sort, match or multiple-choice task can check the feature→group classification but does not by itself stage the act of comparing two animals or elicit a spoken comparison; include an actual two-animal comparison for the compare half of the objective.
A single labelled picture teaches vocabulary for one animal but does not display two animals side by side; pair it with a two-animal comparison.

An in-role dialogue is poorly suited to this observation-anchored comparison because it cannot visually display the two animals' features side by side; prefer a visual side-by-side for the comparison itself.

Optional feature highlighting (colour-coding shared vs group-unique parts) and drag-the-word labelling are illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory; the learning lever is the child's own naming and comparing.

A rotatable 3D view (turntable) may optionally help a child inspect one animal's covering and limbs from all sides (e.g. seeing a fish is streamlined or how a bird's wings fold), but clear 2D images convey the group features for this age, so treat 3D as a nice-to-have rather than the teaching lever.
Real-material handling and a screen/paper model offer different experiences; use both as complements rather than treating either as the only way to learn.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NGSS 1-LS1-1 source claim is flagged verified:false in the row (US standard frames external parts by function, not cross-group comparison); the UK KS1 describe-and-compare objective drives these activities. Not cited as support for comparison efficacy.
The row asserts body covering is 'the most reliable' young-child cue; preserved as stated pedagogy, not independently re-verified.

Amphibians (moist skin) are included in the group chart for completeness, though the row's exemplars emphasise bird/fish/reptile/mammal contrasts; ensure amphibian examples (e.g. frog) are available when comparing.
The row's diagnostic treats 'the bat is a bird because it flies' as the classic error; the tricky-cases activity resolves this by grouping on fur vs feathers rather than leaving it as a caveat.
The non-preferred conversation and 3D alternatives are retained only as qualified limits/affordances; their categorical dismissals from the row are removed as unsupported.

probeDeeper: What is the bat's body covered in, and what does that tell you about its group?
A penguin has feathers but can't fly — is it a bird? How do you know?
A whale lives in the sea its whole life — is it a fish or a mammal, and what would you check?
Name two animals in different groups and tell me one body difference between them.
assess.correctAnswer: The robin is the bird because it has feathers. The bat has fur, so it is a mammal. You tell the group from body covering (feathers, fur, scales), not from the fact that both can fly.

errorPatterns.pattern: If it flies it's a bird ('the bat has wings so it must be a bird')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Regroup by body covering: the bat has fur and feeds its babies milk, so it's a mammal. Compare feathers vs fur side by side.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bat is a bird because it has wings and flies.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the bat (or a flying insect) a bird because it flies and has wings

errorPatterns.pattern: If it lives in water it's a fish ('a whale swims in the sea so it's a fish')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Whales breathe air, have a little hair and feed young milk — mammals. Group by features, not habitat.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts whales or dolphins in the fish group because of where they live

errorPatterns.pattern: A bird has to be able to fly ('a penguin can't fly so it's not a bird')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Feathers make it a bird, not flight; show flightless birds with feathers and wings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that penguins or ostriches are birds because they don't fly

responseLevels.gap: Sorts animals by what they do or where they live (flies→bird, swims→fish) and cannot name a body feature for a group.
responseLevels.full: Uses body covering and structure (feathers, fur, scales, gills) to assign group, handles counter-cases (flightless bird, aquatic mammal), and gives a distinguishing feature for each group.
responseLevels.partial: Knows some group features (birds have feathers) but is pulled back to behaviour/habitat cues for tricky cases like bats or whales.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A bat flies through the air and a robin flies through the air, but only one of them is a bird. Which one is the bird — and what could you look at on their bodies to be sure?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who groups by body structure looks at feathers versus fur and answers correctly. A child who groups by what the animal does ('it flies, so it's a bird') calls the bat a bird — the classic behaviour-over-features error.
