pedagogy.summary: Children learn to compare and sort a mixed collection of 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects by their geometric PROPERTIES — number of sides, number/type of faces, flat vs curved surfaces, number of vertices — and to articulate the criterion they used. The procedural goal is a consistent, property-based sort: choosing one attribute, applying it to every item, and being able to re-sort the same collection a different way. It builds directly on knowing the properties (2-D sides, 3-D faces/edges/vertices) and pushes children off the van Hiele visual level, where they group by overall look, colour or size. Best taught with real shapes to handle, 'is/is not' two-set sorting, and 'guess my rule' games.
bestPractices: Sort a physical, mixed collection into two sets on an 'is / is not' criterion (e.g. has a curved surface / has no curved surface), then challenge children to re-sort the SAME set a different way.
Play 'guess my rule': present a set already sorted by someone else and have children infer the property used — this makes the criterion explicit.
Insist the rule is a geometric property; when a child groups by colour or size, restrict the set to one colour/size so appearance cannot be the criterion.
Hand children real solids to handle and mark faces/edges/vertices with a wipe-clean pen as they count, so a sort by 'number of faces' rests on an accurate count.
Model articulating the rule aloud ('all of these have a triangular face') and ask 'does EVERY shape in this group follow your rule?' to check consistency.
keyRepresentations: A mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes and 3-D solids plus everyday objects
Two sorting hoops / Carroll or Venn two-set frame labelled with an 'is / is not' criterion
Wipe-clean pen for marking faces/edges/vertices while counting
'Guess my rule' pre-sorted sets
commonMisconceptions: Sorts by a non-defining feature — colour, size or overall look — rather than a geometric property.
Groups shapes by holistic resemblance ('these look the same') and cannot state a single consistent rule, letting the rule drift mid-sort.
Miscounts sides, faces or vertices — losing track of where counting started — so shapes end up in the wrong group.
Can sort one way but cannot re-sort the same collection by a different property, or cannot infer the rule of a set sorted by someone else.

learn.summary: Children aged 6-7 learn to compare and sort a mixed collection of 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects by geometric PROPERTIES — number of sides, number/type of faces, flat vs curved surfaces, number of vertices — and to articulate the criterion used. The procedural goal is a consistent, property-based sort: choose one attribute, apply it to every item, then re-sort the SAME collection a different way. This builds on knowing the properties and pushes children off the van Hiele visual level, where they group by overall look, colour or size. Best taught with real shapes to handle, 'is / is not' two-set sorting, and 'guess my rule' games.

activities.title: Sort a real tray two ways on an 'is / is not' rule
feedback: If a child groups by colour, size or 'the pretty ones', restrict the collection to a single colour and size so appearance cannot be the criterion, forcing attention to a property.

When a placement breaks the chosen rule (e.g. a cone, which has a curved surface, dropped into 'no curved surface'), point to the mismatch and ask which property decides membership — the property, not the look.
Prompt consistency: 'Does every shape in this group follow your rule?' If membership drifts for a borderline shape, revisit the stated rule.

Watching a shape such as a triangular prism move to the other hoop when the rule changes — it has no curved surface but does have triangular faces, so it belongs in a different group under each rule — is the moment 'a sort needs one property' becomes concrete. (A cube would stay put, since it has neither a curved surface nor a triangular face.)
activities.rationale: 'Is / is not' two-set sorting with a required second re-sort of the same set targets the flexible, property-based sorting that distinguishes a child reading shapes by property from one grouping by overall look. Restricting colour/size removes appearance as a possible criterion.
sourceClaims: Children should sort shapes into two sets on 'is / is not' criteria and be able to guess a sorting rule from how shapes have been sorted; a common misconception is failing to recognise a shape in a different orientation, remedied by handling and rotating cut-outs.

Young children at the van Hiele visualization level group shapes holistically by appearance, colour and orientation rather than defining properties; the instructional goal is to analyse shapes by properties (e.g. number of sides), invariant to colour, size and orientation.
learnerActions: Take a physical, mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects.

Choose ONE geometric property as the rule (e.g. 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface') and place every item into one of two sorting hoops or a labelled two-set frame. Check that the rule makes sense for every item in the tray: a flat 2-D shape such as a circle has a curved side (edge) but no curved surface, so either agree how 2-D shapes are judged or pick a rule that fits both 2-D and 3-D items (e.g. 'has a curved edge or surface / has none').
Say the rule aloud ('all of these have a curved surface') and check: does EVERY shape in this group follow my rule?
Now scatter the SAME shapes and re-sort them by a different property (e.g. 'has a triangular face / has no triangular face'); notice which shapes move to a different hoop and why.
activities.intendedInsight: A sort rests on one geometric property held constant and applied to every item; the same collection can be grouped validly in more than one way depending on which property you choose.

activities.title: Guess my rule
feedback: If a child cannot state a single rule that every group member satisfies, model one aloud ('these all have a triangular face') and check each member against it.

If the inferred rule is a non-geometric feature such as colour or size, point to two members of the SAME group that differ in that named feature (e.g. two different colours) yet were grouped together, so the child sees appearance cannot be the rule and looks for the shared geometric property.
Confirm success when the child's continuation placements all satisfy the same stated property.
activities.rationale: Inferring someone else's rule separates a child who reads shapes by property from one who grouped by holistic resemblance; it makes the criterion explicit rather than letting it drift.
sourceClaims: Children should sort shapes into two sets on 'is / is not' criteria and be able to guess a sorting rule from how shapes have been sorted; a common misconception is failing to recognise a shape in a different orientation, remedied by handling and rotating cut-outs.
learnerActions: Look at a set someone else has already sorted into two groups, with the rule hidden.
Infer and state the geometric property that was used to make the two groups.
Continue the sort by placing a few more shapes into the correct group, keeping the rule constant.
Then set your own 'guess my rule' challenge for a partner.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the hidden criterion explicit forces attention onto defining properties and shows that a good sort rests on one rule every member satisfies.

activities.title: Count faces, edges and vertices accurately before sorting
feedback: If recounts give different totals, ask how to be sure each side/face is counted once and model marking each one as it is counted — scaffold the counting, do not reteach the whole topic.
If a shape lands in the wrong group, check whether its faces/vertices were miscounted rather than whether the rule was wrong.
activities.rationale: Miscounting sides, faces or vertices from losing track of the starting point is a known error that makes count-based sorts inconsistent; handling real solids and marking each feature addresses the difficulty of counting features from an image.
sourceClaims: 3-D shapes can be sorted by their properties (faces, edges, vertices; e.g. curved surface / no curved surface, 6-or-more vertices, no triangular faces); the stated common misconception is that children find it hard to count faces, vertices and edges from an IMAGE of a solid; remedy is to hand children real solids to handle and mark each feature with a wipe-clean pen as they count.

A common misconception is that children miscount sides or vertices because they lose track of where they started counting; the remedy is to ask how to count each side/vertex once and model marking each one as it is counted.
learnerActions: Hold a real solid and mark each face, edge or vertex with a wipe-clean pen as you count it, so you count each one exactly once.
Record the count, then use it as the sorting rule (e.g. 'sort solids by number of faces' or 'six or more vertices / fewer than six vertices').
Recount a solid a second way and check you get the same total; if not, find where you lost track.
Place each solid in the correct group based on the verified count.
activities.intendedInsight: A count-based sort is only as reliable as the count; marking each feature once prevents losing track and keeps the sort consistent.

activities.title: Inspect 3-D solids for flat vs curved surfaces
feedback: If a child decides from one view only, prompt them to turn the solid right over to check the other surfaces.
Confirm when the flat-vs-curved judgement matches every surface inspected (e.g. a cylinder has two flat circular faces and one curved surface).
activities.rationale: Handling and rotating solids helps children judge flat-vs-curved surfaces that are hard to read from a static image. An on-screen rotatable solid may supplement this for the 3-D portion, though the sorting action itself is a flat grouping task; efficacy relative to handling is untested here.
sourceClaims: 3-D shapes can be sorted by their properties (faces, edges, vertices; e.g. curved surface / no curved surface, 6-or-more vertices, no triangular faces); the stated common misconception is that children find it hard to count faces, vertices and edges from an IMAGE of a solid; remedy is to hand children real solids to handle and mark each feature with a wipe-clean pen as they count.
learnerActions: Pick up and rotate each solid to inspect every surface, feeling and looking for flat versus curved surfaces.
Sort the solids into 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface' based on what you found.
Explain for a tricky solid (e.g. a cylinder) which surfaces are flat and which are curved.
activities.intendedInsight: Rotating a solid to inspect all its surfaces reveals properties that a single view hides, supporting an accurate flat-vs-curved sort.

constraints: The skill is doing: placing shapes, testing a criterion, and re-sorting. A view-only tap-to-reveal illustration does not let the child perform or switch a sort, so it does not build the procedure on its own.

A fixed, scored categorization (sort by a GIVEN rule) can check sorting against a supplied criterion, but because the rule is provided it does not require the child to choose, articulate or switch the criterion; use it to check rather than to build the flexible re-sort.
Insist the rule is a geometric property; when a child groups by colour or size, restrict the set to one colour/size so appearance cannot be the criterion.
Require a SECOND, different sort of the same collection plus a 'guess my rule' inference — these are what best separate property-based sorting from grouping by overall look.

Paper or card cut-outs and real solids have slight thickness and can be held and turned; treat them as physical representations of the mathematical shapes, and ask children about the shape REPRESENTED, not whether the object can be picked up. A rotatable on-screen solid is a model that may supplement, not replace, handling where handling is available.

When naming a specific solid in an example, make sure it fits the property claimed (e.g. use a triangular prism/pyramid when illustrating 'has a triangular face', and only call a solid a cube when it is cube-shaped); do not assume a generic box is a cube.

An optional on-screen drag-into-two-loops sorter with a swappable rule tile and immediate feedback (a shape springing back with a red outline when it breaks the rule) can make the mechanism concrete; this is one possible interaction, not a required one, and its benefit over physical sorting is untested.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy 'poor / ideal / possible' artefact rankings and the claim that a conversation 'adds nothing' were catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical facts; they have been reframed as scoped affordances/limits (e.g. view-only media do not support the active sorting that is the objective). No claim of medium superiority is asserted beyond these narrow affordances.

The original research narrative used a CUBE as the shape that 'moves to the other hoop' when switching from 'has a curved surface' to 'has a triangular face'. A cube has neither a curved surface nor a triangular face, so under the natural relabelling it stays in the 'no' group for both rules and does not move. This has been corrected in the activity to a shape that genuinely moves (e.g. a triangular prism).
'Six or more vertices' as a sorting band is taken from the source example; confirm the solids provided actually make this discrimination meaningful for the specific collection used.
The first 'guess my rule' set must itself be sorted by a valid single geometric property, or the inference task is unsound; check the pre-sorted example before use.

probeDeeper: You put these together — tell me your rule. Does EVERY shape in this group follow it?
Can you sort exactly the same shapes a completely different way?
I'll add this shape [a large, differently-coloured triangle] — which group does it go in, and why?
Here is a set I sorted into two groups. What was my rule?
assess.correctAnswer: Sorts by a stated geometric property — e.g. 2-D shapes by number of sides, or 3-D solids by flat-vs-curved faces or number of faces/vertices — applies it consistently to every shape, articulates the rule ('these all have a curved surface'), re-sorts the same collection by a different property, and infers the property behind a set sorted by someone else.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sorts by a non-defining feature — colour, size or 'the pretty ones' — rather than a geometric property.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Restrict the collection to a single colour and size so appearance cannot be the criterion, forcing attention to a property; model a property rule aloud ('I'm putting all the ones with a curved surface here').
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The two groups differ by colour or size, not by sides/faces; when asked the rule, the child names a non-geometric feature.

errorPatterns.pattern: Groups by holistic resemblance ('these look the same') without an explicit criterion, and the rule drifts as more shapes are added.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Play 'guess my rule' with a pre-sorted set, then have the child continue that sort — modelling that a sort rests on one explicit property held constant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot state a single rule that every group member satisfies; membership changes when asked to justify a borderline shape.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts sides, faces or vertices because they lose track of where they started, so a count-based sort is inconsistent.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: ask how to be sure each side/face is counted once, and model marking each one with a wipe-clean pen as it is counted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Recounts give different totals; a shape lands in the wrong group because its sides/faces were miscounted.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by a non-geometric feature (colour, size) or by holistic resemblance, cannot state a consistent rule, or miscounts so the sort is wrong.
responseLevels.full: Sorts by a stated geometric property applied consistently to every shape, re-sorts the same collection by a different property, and infers the rule of a set sorted by someone else — treating number of sides / flat-vs-curved faces / number of vertices as the basis for grouping (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Sorts correctly by one property and states that rule, but cannot re-sort the collection a different way, applies the rule inconsistently to some shapes, or cannot infer the rule of a pre-sorted set (SOLO multistructural — one criterion, not coordinated).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a mixed tray of 2-D shapes and 3-D solids. Set the task and watch: 'Sort these into two groups so that everything in a group shares something. When you are done, tell me your rule.' Then: 'Now sort the same shapes a completely different way.' Finally, hand them a set you have already sorted and say: 'What was my rule?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the sort (rather than asking the child to describe sorting) reveals whether the criterion is a defining property applied consistently, or an appearance feature / a rule that drifts. Requiring a SECOND, different sort of the same shapes and a 'guess my rule' inference separates a child who reads shapes by property from one who grouped by overall look — the latter can rarely re-sort or name someone else's rule.

sources.claim: 3-D shapes can be sorted by their properties (faces, edges, vertices; e.g. curved surface / no curved surface, 6-or-more vertices, no triangular faces); the stated common misconception is that children find it hard to count faces, vertices and edges from an IMAGE of a solid; remedy is to hand children real solids to handle and mark each feature with a wipe-clean pen as they count.
sources.source: Oak National Academy — Find different ways to sort 3D shapes (KS1 / Year 2 Maths)

sources.claim: Children should sort shapes into two sets on 'is / is not' criteria and be able to guess a sorting rule from how shapes have been sorted; a common misconception is failing to recognise a shape in a different orientation, remedied by handling and rotating cut-outs.
sources.source: Oak National Academy — Explore, discuss and compare 2D shapes (KS1 / Year 1 Maths)

sources.claim: A common misconception is that children miscount sides or vertices because they lose track of where they started counting; the remedy is to ask how to count each side/vertex once and model marking each one as it is counted.
sources.source: Oak National Academy — Recognise and sort polygons (KS1 / Year 2 Maths)

sources.claim: Young children at the van Hiele visualization level group shapes holistically by appearance, colour and orientation rather than defining properties; the instructional goal is to analyse shapes by properties (e.g. number of sides), invariant to colour, size and orientation.
sources.source: NCETM — Early Years Shape and Space (common errors and approaches)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11y; find all factor pairs for numbers 1–100; identify common factors and common multiples of two numbers; use these to solve problems.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'identify multiples and factors, including finding all factor pairs of a number, and common factors of two numbers'; Y6 extends to common factors/multiples.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 (all factor pairs 1–100, factor vs multiple, prime/composite) and 6.NS.4 (common factors and multiples, GCF/LCM).
• Operational details — the concepts interlock: FACTORS divide into a number (found systematically in pairs, stopping at the square root); MULTIPLES are in a number's times table (infinite). COMMON factors/multiples are shared between two numbers — the intersection. The key discriminations are factor vs multiple (goes-into vs times-table) and the systematic search that guarantees completeness. Represent factors as rectangle dimensions and multiples as number-line hops; common factors/multiples as the overlap of two such sets (a Venn/two-column tool). This is the direct foundation for simplifying fractions (common factors), common denominators (common multiples), HCF/LCM and ratio.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): list all factor pairs of a number to ~50 systematically. Tier B (age 9–10): find common factors and the first common multiples of two numbers. Tier C (age 10–11): use common factors/multiples to solve a problem and explain factor-vs-multiple precisely.
bestPractices: Search factor pairs systematically (1,2,3… pairing each), stopping at the square root, using commutativity to know the set is complete.
Sharply distinguish factors (divide into the number; finite; rectangle side-lengths) from multiples (times table; infinite; number-line hops).
Represent common factors/multiples as the OVERLAP of two sets (two lists or a Venn diagram) so 'common' means shared.
Ground the work in problems — arranging rows, coinciding events (common multiples), sharing into equal groups (common factors) — not just listing.
Explicitly link to downstream use: common factors simplify fractions; common multiples give common denominators; both feed HCF/LCM and ratio.
keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array — factors as side lengths (factor rainbow for completeness)
Number line / multiplication-grid rows — multiples as skip-count hops
Two-set overlap / Venn diagram — common factors and common multiples
Factor and multiple lists side by side to spot the intersection
commonMisconceptions: Confusing factors with multiples (factor of 12 vs multiple of 12).
Missing factor pairs through unsystematic searching, especially middle ones and the number itself/1.
Thinking there is a 'largest multiple' or a 'smallest factor other than 1' confusion.
Treating 'common' loosely rather than as shared between BOTH numbers.
Forgetting 1 is a common factor of every pair, or that the numbers themselves are factors.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, build the interlocking ideas of factors (numbers that divide into a whole), multiples (a number's times table), and what two numbers share in common (common factors and common multiples). Learners search factor pairs systematically (pairing 1,2,3… and stopping near the square root), sharply distinguish factor from multiple, and treat 'common' as the overlap of two sets. Work is grounded in problems and linked downstream to simplifying fractions, finding common denominators, and later HCF/LCM and ratio. A manipulable sets-and-overlap tool is proposed as the core builder, with a two-tier probe and a static reference/quiz as complementary assessment and scaffolds.

activities.title: Factors-and-multiples explorer (three linked modes)
feedback: If a middle factor pair is missed (e.g. forgetting (4,9) of 36), prompt: 'Have you tried making a rectangle with 4 along one side?' and point to the gap in the rainbow.
If the child keeps checking past the square root, show that each new pair just repeats one already found — that is why you can stop near √N.
If the child slides a non-shared factor into the Venn overlap, ask: 'Is that number in BOTH lists?' and highlight the two source lists.
When the 6-hops and 8-hops coincide, name the meeting points: '24 is the first common multiple of 6 and 8; 48 and 72 are the next two.'
When the largest number in the overlap glows (12 for 24 and 36, and again for 36 and 48), name it as the highest common factor and ask how it could help simplify a fraction like 24/36.
activities.rationale: Direct manipulation and comparison of sets lets completeness and shared-ness be discovered rather than told; representing factors as rectangles and common factors/multiples as set overlaps supports the meaning of 'common' and is foundational for fractions and ratio. Live number-line hops make the first common multiple visible as a collision.
sourceClaims: Representing factors as rectangles and common factors/multiples as set overlaps supports completeness and the meaning of 'common', foundational for fractions and ratio.
learnerActions: Factor mode: for a chosen number N (e.g. 36), form every possible rectangle (array) of N counters and log each pair of side-lengths as a factor pair on a factor rainbow — e.g. (1,36), (2,18), (3,12), (4,9), (6,6).
Explain how you know you have found them all: pairs are logged from the outside in, and once you reach the square root the pairs repeat, so the set is complete.

Multiple mode: set one number line to skip-count in 7 and read off the first five multiples (7,14,21,28,35); then set two adjustable number lines to skip-count in 6 and 8, watch where the hops coincide, and record the first THREE common multiples (24, 48, 72) — the first collision is at 24.

Common mode: set two numbers (e.g. 24 and 36), pour each factor list into a two-set Venn diagram, slide the shared factors into the overlap, and identify the largest shared factor (12) as the highest common factor; then repeat with 36 and 48 (shared factors 1,2,3,4,6,12, highest common factor 12).
State in words what 'common' means here: a factor or multiple shared by BOTH numbers — the intersection of the two sets.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Common' literally means the overlap of two sets; completeness of a factor list comes from systematic pairing around the square root; and the first common multiple is the first place two skip-counts collide. Factors are finite and divide into a number (rectangle side-lengths), while multiples are infinite times-table hops.

activities.title: Factor detective: prove the list is complete
feedback: If the child stops arbitrarily, ask them to show that every remaining number to test would only repeat a pair already found.
If the child claims a shared factor without checking both numbers, ask them to point to it in each list.
Reinforce vocabulary when it slips: factors divide INTO the number; multiples are the number counted up.
activities.rationale: A Socratic 'have we found them all? what do these two numbers share?' builds the systematic-search habit and the meaning of 'common'. It complements the visual tool by forcing explicit justification.
learnerActions: For a given number, argue aloud or in writing that no factor has been missed: test divisibility in order (1, 2, 3, …) and pair each factor with its partner.
Justify why you can stop checking near the square root: if N = a×b, one of a or b is at most √N, so any larger factor has already appeared as a partner.
Identify what two chosen numbers share and defend your answer: which factors (and which early multiples) belong to BOTH?
activities.intendedInsight: Systematic searching plus the square-root stopping point guarantees a complete factor list, and 'common' must be justified as membership in both sets.

activities.title: Is it prime? Decide and justify the stopping point
feedback: If the child says '97 is prime because it is odd', counter: 9 is odd but 3×3 (not prime), and 2 is even but prime — parity does not decide primeness.
If the child calls 1 prime, restate the exactly-two-distinct-factors definition: 1 has only one factor.
If the child lists 97, 194, 291…, re-anchor: those are multiples of 97; primeness is about what divides INTO 97.
If the child checks every number up to 96, show that factors pair up so testing primes to ~10 suffices.
activities.rationale: Asking why a learner can stop checking exposes whether they understand that factors come in pairs around the square root — the deep idea — and distinguishes a reasoner from a guesser. Common errors (prime = odd, 1 is prime, confusing factors with multiples) are directly addressed with counterexamples.
learnerActions: Decide whether a given number (e.g. 97) is prime.
Test divisibility only by primes up to the square root (for 97: 2, 3, 5, 7, since √97 ≈ 9.8) and record the results.
Explain WHY you can stop at about 10: beyond √97 any factor would pair with one already checked.
Conclude using the definition: a prime has exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself); 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only one factor.
activities.intendedInsight: Primeness is about the NUMBER of factors, not about being odd; factor-pairing around the square root tells you when it is safe to stop checking.

activities.title: Static reference and checking quiz
feedback: For sorting errors, remind: factors divide into the number; multiples are in its times table.
For a wrong first-common-multiple choice, return to the two skip-counts and find the first collision (24 for 6 and 8).
Use the tap-to-reveal Venn to confirm which factors are truly shared.
activities.rationale: Listing all factors, first multiples, and common factors/multiples is crisply checkable with distractors targeting the classic factor-vs-multiple confusion; a static rainbow and Venn make completeness and overlap visible as a reference. A sort of this kind can check the factor/multiple classification but does not itself require the learner to perform the systematic search or vary the two numbers from scratch.
learnerActions: Study a factor rainbow of 36 and an adjacent Venn of the factors of 24 and 36, tapping to reveal the common factors.
Sort items into 'factor of 24' vs 'multiple of 24' to rehearse the core discrimination.
Fill in a missing factor pair of 36.
Choose the first common multiple of 6 and 8 from options and explain the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates and checks the factor/multiple distinction, completeness, and the meaning of overlap once the ideas have been built.

constraints: Target age 9–11; coverage: all factor pairs for numbers 1–100, common factors and common multiples of two numbers, and using these to solve problems, with prime/composite as a related discrimination.
Search factor pairs systematically (1,2,3… pairing each) and stop near the square root, using commutativity to confirm the set is complete.
Sharply distinguish factors (divide into the number; finite; rectangle side-lengths) from multiples (times table; infinite; number-line hops).
Treat 'common' strictly as shared between BOTH numbers (the intersection of two sets), not loosely.
Remember 1 is a common factor of every pair, the number itself is a factor, and there is no 'largest multiple'.
Define prime as exactly two distinct factors; 1 is neither prime nor composite.

Ground work in problems (arranging rows, coinciding events, sharing into equal groups), not just listing, and link explicitly to simplifying fractions (common factors), common denominators (common multiples), and later HCF/LCM and ratio.

The static rainbow/Venn and the quiz are scaffolds and checks: they let a learner read off or recognise answers but do not themselves require the learner to perform the systematic search or vary the two numbers. Use them after, or alongside, active construction.

The interactive examples (dragging counters into rectangles, adjustable number lines whose hops light up on coincidence, factor lists pouring into a Venn with the largest shared factor highlighted) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete; equivalent results can be reached with paper factor rainbows, two written multiple lists, and a hand-drawn Venn.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a 3D interactive 'poor' with the claim '3D adds cost without insight'; this universal claim is not established by catalog ratings and has been dropped rather than propagated. A manipulable 2D/physical set representation is proposed on its affordances, not on a claim that other media cannot teach the topic.

The legacy 'ideal/strong/possible/poor' fit rankings and the single 'recommended' format were catalog preferences; they are not treated as pedagogical laws. The static reference and quiz are preserved as genuine complementary tools with their stated scaffolding limits.

Worked example checked: factor pairs of 36 are (1,36),(2,18),(3,12),(4,9),(6,6) — correct and complete; √36 = 6, so (6,6) is the natural stopping pair. First five multiples of 7 are 7,14,21,28,35. First three common multiples of 6 and 8 are 24,48,72. Factors of 24 and 36 share 1,2,3,4,6,12 (HCF 12); factors of 36 and 48 share 1,2,3,4,6,12 (HCF 12). 97 is prime; testing primes up to √97 (≈9.8): 2,3,5,7 — correct stopping set.

Source 'claim' fields citing CCSS 4.OA.4/6.NS.4 and NCETM guidance are marked verified:false in the row; the DfE curriculum claim is marked verified:true. CCSS requirement claims and the DfE topic claim were removed from sourceClaims where they supported only coverage rather than the stated teaching principle; the NCETM representational claim is retained where it directly backs the principle, though it too is unverified. No efficacy or comparative-superiority claim is asserted for any proposed activity.

The diagnostic probe set (including 'Is 1 a prime number?', '9 is odd — is it prime?') and reteach prerequisite IDs belong to the assessment field and were not modified; relevant reasoning was surfaced into the prime activity's feedback without altering assessment design, and no internal IDs were carried into the learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: Why could you stop checking at about 10 instead of going all the way to 96?
Is 1 a prime number? Why or why not?
9 is odd — is it prime? What does that tell you about 'odd means prime'?
Find all the common factors of 24 and 36 — how do you make sure you get them all?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes, 97 is prime. A child reasoning correctly checks for factors other than 1 and 97 by testing divisibility by primes up to √97 (≈ 9.8) — 2, 3, 5, 7 — finds none divide it, and concludes it has exactly two factors. The key reasoning is WHY they can stop at ~10 (beyond that, a factor would pair with one already checked).

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks all odd numbers are prime (or all primes are odd) — calls 97 prime 'because it's odd', and would call 9 or 15 prime too
errorPatterns.nextMove: counterexample: 9 is odd but 3×3, so not prime; and 2 is even but prime. Primeness is about number of factors, not parity.
errorPatterns.distractor: 97 is prime because it is an odd number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: justification rests on oddness; child also calls 9, 15, 21 prime

errorPatterns.pattern: believes 1 is prime (or is unsure), miscounting factors
errorPatterns.nextMove: define prime as EXACTLY two distinct factors; 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child includes 1 as prime or reasons about factors including a phantom extra

errorPatterns.pattern: checks divisibility unsystematically and stops arbitrarily (or checks every number up to 96), not knowing the √n stopping point
errorPatterns.nextMove: show factors pair up (if 97 = a×b, one of them is ≤√97); so testing primes to ~10 suffices — that is why you can stop.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child either stops too early with no justification or laboriously tests far too many divisors

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses factors with multiples when justifying — lists multiples of 97 instead of testing its factors
errorPatterns.nextMove: re-anchor vocabulary: factors divide INTO 97; multiples are 97 counted up. Primeness is about factors.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child writes 97, 194, 291… rather than checking what divides 97

responseLevels.gap: equates prime with odd, thinks 1 is prime, or checks divisibility with no system; cannot justify certainty.
responseLevels.full: defines prime as exactly two factors, tests primes up to the square root systematically, justifies the stopping point via factor-pairing, and finds common factors/multiples reliably.
responseLevels.partial: correctly identifies 97 as prime by testing divisors but checks unsystematically or cannot explain the √n stopping point; shaky on the factor/multiple distinction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 97 a prime number? Decide, and then explain how you know for certain — what did you have to check, and how did you know when you could stop checking?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Many children think prime means 'odd', or check only a few small numbers unsystematically, or believe 1 is prime. Asking WHY they can stop checking exposes whether they understand that factors come in pairs around the square root — the deep idea. A guesser cannot justify certainty.

sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Years 5–6 Number — multiplication and division

sources.claim: 4.OA.4 requires finding all factor pairs 1–100 and distinguishing factors/multiples; 6.NS.4 requires common factors and multiples (GCF/LCM).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 4 & 6 (4.OA.B.4, 6.NS.B.4)

sources.claim: Representing factors as rectangles and common factors/multiples as set overlaps supports completeness and the meaning of 'common', foundational for fractions and ratio.
sources.source: NCETM factors, multiples and primes guidance

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Plant Cells vs Animal Cells

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Cells & organisation):** statutory — "the similarities and differences between plant and animal cells".

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS1-2):** the same 'develop and use a model... parts of cells contribute to the function' PE frames US coverage; NGSS has no separate plant-vs-animal comparison PE, so the comparison is taught as an application of the cell-parts model rather than as a standalone US requirement. The clarification statement lists chloroplasts and cell wall among the modelled parts, which anchors the plant-only distinction.

- **Operational details:** This is a compare-and-contrast / classification concept that sits directly on top of the 'Parts of Plant and Animal Cells' prerequisite. The core structure is a three-way sort: features shared by BOTH cell types (cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes), features found ONLY in plant cells (cell wall, permanent vacuole, chloroplasts), and — to sharpen the boundary — the fact that animal cells have none unique to them at KS3 level. Teach it with the two cells side by side, and drive every 'plant only' feature back to plant lifestyle: chloroplasts because plants make their own food by photosynthesis; cell wall and large vacuole because a stationary organism supports itself by internal turgor rather than a skeleton. Annotated comparative drawing is the classic output and doubles as the assessment.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional / early-formal). The child lists shared features, correctly identifies the plant-only trio AND justifies why plants need each (links structure to the plant's way of life), and can draw and annotate both cells. Not yet expected: specialised-cell adaptations, or exceptions such as non-green plant cells, though the better students should notice that not all plant cells are green.
bestPractices: Present the two cells side by side at all times so comparison is visual and simultaneous rather than sequential recall of two separate lists.
Anchor every plant-only feature to plant lifestyle — chloroplasts→makes own food, wall+vacuole→support without a skeleton — so the differences are reasoned, not memorised.
Use a Venn diagram or two-column 'both / plant only' sort as the organising representation, making the shared-vs-unique structure explicit.
Build directly on pupils' own annotated organelle work from the prerequisite so the comparison reuses known parts rather than introducing new ones.
Explicitly address that animal cells have no unique organelle at this level (they are the 'subset'), which pupils often find counter-intuitive.
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side labelled diagrams of a generalised plant cell and animal cell
Venn diagram / two-column sort: shared features vs plant-only features
A 'why does the plant need this?' column linking each unique part to plant lifestyle (photosynthesis, support)
Real onion-epidermis vs cheek-cell microscope images showing the actual presence/absence of wall and chloroplasts
commonMisconceptions: Thinking plant cells have a wall INSTEAD of a membrane — plant cells have both; the wall is an extra layer outside the membrane.
Believing every plant cell is green and packed with chloroplasts — many plant cells (roots, stems inside) have few or none.
Assuming animal cells must have some unique organelle to 'balance' the comparison — at this level animal cells share all their parts with plant cells.
Confusing the large permanent vacuole of plant cells with the small temporary vacuoles animal cells can have — treating them as identical.
Over-generalising 'plants are stiff because of the wall' to mean the wall alone — rigidity comes from the wall PLUS a full vacuole creating turgor.

learn.summary: Learners aged 11–12 compare plant and animal cells by actively sorting organelles into shared features and plant-only features, and justifying each plant-only part by linking it to the plant's way of life (photosynthesis and self-support). The core objective is a three-way distinction: features in BOTH cell types (cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes), features ONLY in plant cells (cell wall, permanent vacuole, chloroplasts), and the counter-intuitive point that at this level animal cells have no unique organelle. Keep both cells side by side so comparison is simultaneous, and close the loop by checking the model against real microscope images. Activities range from active construction (sorting and annotated drawing) to consolidation (classification and multiple-choice checks) and reveal-on-tap comparison scaffolds.

activities.title: Sort the organelles: both cells or plant only?
feedback: If a plant-only card is dropped onto the animal cell, point out that animals do not photosynthesise (no chloroplasts) and have no cellulose wall — only a flexible membrane — then ask the learner to move it back.
If the learner omits the membrane from the plant cell because it has a wall, correct that plant cells have BOTH: a cell membrane just inside the rigid cell wall; have them label both.

For a correct 'why?' answer on chloroplasts, affirm the link to the plant making its own food; for wall/vacuole, affirm the link to support without a skeleton (rigidity comes from wall PLUS a full vacuole creating turgor, not the wall alone).

When the microscope overlay is viewed, prompt the learner to confirm the wall in the onion image and its absence in the cheek image. Point out that the onion cells have no chloroplasts because onion bulb tissue is not green, which shows that not all plant cells have chloroplasts. Use a green leaf-cell image (for example pondweed) to confirm chloroplasts.
activities.rationale: A comparison is learned by actively making categorisation decisions rather than reading a finished table; constructing the sort turns abstract similarities/differences into choices the learner makes, and the plant-only trio emerges as a discovery. Requiring a structure-to-lifestyle justification makes the differences reasoned rather than memorised. The drag/drop, overlap region and microscope overlay are offered as one concrete way to make the mechanism visible, not as the only possible medium.
learnerActions: Work with a generalised plant cell and animal cell shown side by side, plus a bank of unlabelled organelle cards (cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, cell wall, permanent vacuole, chloroplasts).
Place each card where it belongs: onto both cells (a shared/overlap region), or onto the plant cell only.
As membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes are placed, notice the animal cell fills with these shared parts and then stops.
When placing each plant-only card (cell wall, big vacuole, chloroplasts), answer a 'Why does a plant need this and an animal doesn't?' prompt before it locks in.

Finally, overlay or view real onion-epidermis and cheek-cell microscope images and check your sort against what is actually visible: the onion cells show a cell wall but no chloroplasts (onion bulb tissue grows underground and is not green), while the cheek cells have no wall. If you have one, also look at an image of a green leaf cell (for example pondweed) to see chloroplasts.
activities.intendedInsight: The animal cell contains only features it shares with the plant cell; three structures — cell wall, permanent vacuole, chloroplasts — belong only to the plant, and each exists because of how a plant lives: chloroplasts because plants make their own food by photosynthesis; cell wall and large vacuole because a stationary organism supports itself by internal turgor rather than a skeleton.

activities.title: Annotated comparative drawing of both cells
feedback: Check that the membrane is present in the plant cell as well as the wall; a missing membrane signals the 'wall instead of membrane' misconception.
Check that chloroplasts, cell wall and permanent vacuole appear only on the plant cell and not on the animal cell.
Confirm each plant-only annotation ties to a plant need (food-making or support), not just a restated name.
activities.rationale: Annotated comparative drawing is a standard output for this objective and provides evidence of the learner's own construction, since it requires independent production rather than selecting from given options.
learnerActions: Draw a generalised plant cell and an animal cell side by side.
Label every structure, including the shared features and the plant-only features.
For the plant cell, label BOTH the outer cell wall and the cell membrane just inside it, and the large permanent vacuole.
Add a short 'why does the plant need this?' note next to each plant-only feature, linking it to photosynthesis or support.
Write a one-line statement of which features both cells share and which are unique to the plant.
activities.intendedInsight: Producing and annotating the two diagrams from memory consolidates the shared-versus-unique structure and forces the learner to place the membrane and wall correctly rather than recognising them on a pre-labelled image.

activities.title: Tap-to-compare the two cells (scaffold)
feedback: When a part has no counterpart (wall, vacuole, chloroplasts), the 'not present here' state confirms it is plant-only.
The lift-the-flap 'why?' ties each plant-only part to photosynthesis or support.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-compare pair presents shared and unique parts clearly with reveal-on-tap explanations and is quick to provide, but the comparison is pre-labelled for the learner rather than constructed by them, so use it to inform or to introduce the parts before the sorting and drawing activities build the reasoning.
learnerActions: View two static cells side by side.
Tap any part to highlight the SAME part in the other cell, or see 'not present here' when it has no counterpart.
Open a lift-the-flap 'why?' explanation for each plant-only feature.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a part and its counterpart (or its absence) highlighted at the same time makes the shared/unique boundary explicit and reveals why each plant-only feature exists.

activities.title: Categorisation check and targeted misconception questions
feedback: For an item claiming root cells contain chloroplasts: chloroplasts are found mainly in plant parts exposed to light (leaves, green stems); root cells growing underground usually have few or none and are not green. Contrast a leaf cell with a root-hair cell.
For an item that leaves out the membrane: plant cells have both a membrane and a wall, the wall sitting outside the membrane.

For the no-chloroplast cell: yes, it can still be a plant cell — not every plant cell has chloroplasts, so a cell with a cellulose wall and a permanent vacuole can still be plant tissue (for example a root cell).
activities.rationale: Plant-vs-animal sorting maps naturally onto a classification task, making a short set of classification and multiple-choice questions a low-cost consolidation and assessment of the same distinction; it checks the outcome rather than building the reasoning, so pair it with the construction activities.
learnerActions: Drag or classify a set of features into 'both cells' versus 'plant only'.
Answer multiple-choice items that directly target the 'wall instead of membrane' and 'all plant cells are green' misconceptions.
Answer: 'If you saw a cell with a wall and a big vacuole but no chloroplasts, could it still be a plant cell? Why?'
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates and checks the shared-versus-plant-only distinction and surfaces whether the learner over-generalises that all plant cells are green or drops the membrane when a wall is present.

activities.title: Spatial check: where the wall and vacuole sit (optional)
feedback: If the learner still treats the wall as replacing the membrane, point to the membrane visible just inside the wall in the model.
Reinforce that the large vacuole, not just the wall, contributes to the cell's firmness via turgor.
activities.rationale: The comparison itself is categorical and gains little from spatial manipulation, but rotating and peeling layers can make the outer-layer position of the wall and the bulk of the vacuole concrete for learners who hold the layering or vacuole-size misconceptions. Offered as an optional reinforcement, not a required step.
learnerActions: Rotate side-by-side 3D cell models and peel away layers.
Observe that the cell wall sits OUTSIDE the cell membrane, and that the permanent vacuole occupies a large volume inside the plant cell.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the wall as an outer layer (not a replacement for the membrane) and the vacuole as a bulky volume addresses two specific misconceptions about layering and size.

constraints: Build on learners' prior annotated organelle work so the comparison reuses known parts rather than introducing new ones.
Always present the two cells side by side so comparison is simultaneous rather than sequential recall of two separate lists.
Anchor every plant-only feature to plant lifestyle: chloroplasts → makes own food; wall + vacuole → support without a skeleton.
Explicitly address that animal cells have no unique organelle at this level (they are the 'subset'), which learners often find counter-intuitive.
Not every plant cell has chloroplasts: root cells and internal stem cells are not exposed to light and may have few or none. Do not teach 'all plant cells are green'.
Plant cells have BOTH a cell membrane and a cell wall; the wall is an extra outer layer, not a replacement for the membrane.
Rigidity comes from the wall PLUS a full vacuole creating turgor, not the wall alone; do not over-generalise 'plants are stiff because of the wall'.
The large permanent vacuole of plant cells is not the same as the small temporary vacuoles animal cells can have; do not treat them as identical.

Recognition and tap-to-compare scaffolds inform but do not by themselves elicit independent construction; use them to introduce or support, and reserve the sorting and annotated-drawing tasks for evidence that the learner can build the distinction themselves.
Not yet expected at this level: specialised-cell adaptations or exceptions beyond noting that not all plant cells are green.
Microscope images (onion epidermis vs cheek cell) are an evidence check to confirm the model against real observation; plant and animal cells here are generalised representations.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The DfE KS3 and NGSS MS-LS1-2 source claims establish that the plant-vs-animal comparison is a curriculum objective, but neither validates the efficacy of the specific activity methods (active sorting, annotated drawing, classification checks). sourceClaims were therefore set to [] on all activities rather than citing the claims as topic matches.

Ribosomes are listed among shared features in the operational notes but omitted from the assessment's 'correctAnswer' shared list; included here as shared, which is biologically correct (both cell types have ribosomes) and consistent with the pedagogy summary. Reviewer may confirm the intended shared-feature set for this age.
The source describes animal cells as having 'none unique to them at KS3 level'; this is framed as a level-appropriate simplification rather than a universal biological claim, and is retained as such.
Drag-and-drop, Venn overlap, lift-the-flap, 3D peel-away and microscope overlay are retained as concrete examples of interaction/feedback mechanisms, not as mandatory implementations.

The original rated an open in-role dialogue as poor-fit for this categorical objective; that is a scoped suitability judgement for this specific comparison task, not evidence that dialogue cannot teach, so it was omitted as an activity rather than asserted as a universal limit.

probeDeeper: Why would a root cell have no chloroplasts when a leaf cell is packed with them?
Does a plant cell have a membrane, a wall, or both — and where is each?
Which structures would you find in a human cheek cell that an onion cell also has?
If you saw a cell with a wall and a big vacuole but no chloroplasts, could it still be a plant cell? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Not every plant cell has chloroplasts. Root cells are underground with no light, so they have none and aren't green. Shared by both plant and animal cells: cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria. Only in plant cells: the cellulose cell wall, a permanent vacuole, and chloroplasts (in the parts exposed to light).

errorPatterns.pattern: Every plant cell has chloroplasts / all plant cells are green
errorPatterns.nextMove: Chloroplasts occur only where there is light (leaves, green stems); root cells have none. Contrast a leaf cell with a root hair cell.
errorPatterns.distractor: Every plant cell has chloroplasts, even the root cells underground.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims root cells photosynthesise or contain chloroplasts

errorPatterns.pattern: Plant cells have a cell wall instead of a membrane (no membrane)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Plant cells have BOTH: a cell membrane just inside the rigid cell wall. Label both on a diagram.
errorPatterns.distractor: Plant cells have a cell wall instead of a cell membrane.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Leaves the membrane out of a plant cell because it has a wall

errorPatterns.pattern: Animal cells also have chloroplasts and/or a cell wall
errorPatterns.nextMove: Animals don't photosynthesise (no chloroplasts) and have no cellulose wall; only a flexible membrane. Sort structures into a Venn diagram.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds plant-only structures to an animal cell

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably sort structures into shared vs plant-only; assumes all plant cells are green.
responseLevels.full: Separates shared features (membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria) from plant-only ones (wall, vacuole, chloroplasts) and explains why some plant cells lack chloroplasts.
responseLevels.partial: Lists plant-only structures but overgeneralises (all plant cells have chloroplasts) or drops the membrane when a wall is present.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Plant cells have chloroplasts to photosynthesise, so a student concludes 'every single plant cell must be green and full of chloroplasts.' Is that right — do a plant's root cells have chloroplasts? And give me one structure that BOTH plant and animal cells share, and one that only plant cells have.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who truly compares the cell types knows chloroplasts appear only in light-exposed cells (not roots) and can sort structures into shared versus plant-only. A child with a shallow rule assumes all plant cells are green, or thinks the wall replaces the membrane.

sources.claim: DfE KS3 Biology statutory content requires pupils to learn 'the similarities and differences between plant and animal cells'.
sources.source: DfE National curriculum in England: science programmes of study — Key stage 3 Biology (Cells & organisation)

sources.claim: NGSS MS-LS1-2 covers cell parts including chloroplasts and cell wall via developing and using a cell model; there is no separate NGSS plant-vs-animal comparison PE at middle school.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9, The Water Cycle — the Sun evaporates surface water into invisible vapour, which rises, cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as precipitation, repeating endlessly.
• Standards — UK (DfE): Y4 States of matter — 'identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and associate the rate of evaporation with temperature'; builds on Y1 Seasonal changes.
• Standards — US (NGSS): approached via grade-3 Earth's Systems (3-ESS2-1 typical seasonal weather) and matter/states; the full interacting-systems water cycle is formalised at Grade 5 (5-ESS2-1) and MS-ESS2-4 (sun + gravity drive the cycling of water). State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach as a continuous, Sun-driven loop with THREE named stages (evaporation, condensation, precipitation) but anchor the WHY (energy) not just the sequence; use discrepant-event demos (drying puddle; cold-can condensation with food-colouring to prove water didn't leak through) to confront the 'water disappears' and 'sweating' misconceptions; stress conservation — the same water changes form and place but is never lost.
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — name the three stages and state the Sun drives it; Tier B — explain evaporation/condensation as reversible state changes and rate rising with temperature; Tier C — trace runoff, transpiration and groundwater as part of one conserved global system.
bestPractices: Frame the cycle as a continuous loop with no beginning or end and no water lost — counter the memorised 'E-C-P' sequence by asking WHY each step happens (energy in, energy out)

Use discrepant-event demos: a drying puddle (water goes UP as invisible vapour, not into the ground) and condensation on a cold can with food-colouring added to the ice water (droplets are clear, so water did NOT seep through the wall)
Make invisibility explicit — water vapour is a clear gas you cannot see; steam and clouds are already-condensed liquid droplets, not the vapour itself
Have children draw-then-revise their own water-cycle diagram as formative assessment, then add missing arrows (evaporation from land/plants, not just oceans)
Connect rate to temperature with a fair test (warm vs cool water evaporating), aligning to the DfE Y4 objective
keyRepresentations: Closed-loop cycle diagram with labelled arrows (evaporate up, condense, precipitate down, flow back)
A single tracked water droplet/molecule journeying around the loop to make conservation concrete
Sun-as-engine icon driving the whole loop
Cross-section of land + sea + sky showing all evaporation sources, not a single ocean arrow
commonMisconceptions: 'The water disappears / soaks away' when a puddle dries — actually it becomes invisible water vapour in the air
'Condensation seeped through the cup' (the sweating model) — the water condensed FROM the air onto the cold surface
Clouds and steam ARE water vapour — actually both are visible LIQUID droplets; vapour is invisible
Water rises straight up into a waiting cloud, or a cloud scoops water and drops it elsewhere — vapour moves in all directions and clouds form by condensation
The cycle is only evaporation + condensation (omitting precipitation, runoff, groundwater, transpiration)

learn.summary: For learners aged 7–9, teach the water cycle as a continuous, Sun-driven loop in which the same water repeatedly changes form and place but is never lost. Anchor the WHY (energy in from the Sun, energy out as vapour cools) rather than only memorising the evaporation→condensation→precipitation sequence. Use discrepant-event demonstrations to confront the 'water disappears' and 'condensation seeped through the cup' misconceptions, and make the invisibility of water vapour explicit (clouds and the visible white 'steam' or mist above a kettle are tiny condensed water droplets or ice crystals, not the vapour itself).

activities.title: Sun-driven water-cycle model the learner controls
feedback: If the learner says the vapour 'disappears', show that in the follow-one-droplet view the tagged droplet is still there, just rendered faint — hidden as a clear gas, not gone.
If the learner says clouds ARE the vapour, point out the vapour is faint/near-invisible while the cloud is made of visible tiny water droplets (or ice crystals) that formed when the vapour cooled.
If the learner expects rain to be the end, run the droplet round again so they see it flow back and re-evaporate: the loop has no end.
If the learner thinks the water moves by itself, have them turn the Sun control down and notice the whole engine slow — the Sun is the driver.
activities.rationale: The target concept is a driven, conserved loop; letting the child act on the drive (the Sun control) and track one conserved droplet makes energy-drive, conservation and endlessness concrete rather than a memorised word order. A live heat control and the faint-vapour-then-visible-cloud rendering are intended to target the 'clouds are vapour' and 'water disappears' misconceptions named in the source misconception research. The controllable heat dial, faint-to-visible vapour rendering and droplet-tagging are illustrative mechanisms, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Children commonly think evaporated water 'disappears', that condensation 'seeped through' the cup, and that clouds/steam are water vapour rather than liquid droplets; understanding consolidates around age nine.
learnerActions: Over a land-and-sea scene, raise a Sun/heat control and watch puddles and sea surfaces give off vapour that rises, cools into clouds, and falls as rain that flows back to the sea.
Turn the Sun control down and observe the whole loop slow: evaporation slows, fewer clouds form, and rain becomes less — stating in your own words why.

Switch to a 'follow one droplet' view: tag a single glowing droplet and watch it evaporate, become near-invisible vapour, condense inside a cloud, fall as rain, and flow back to the start again — never disappearing.

Watch a drying puddle on a hard surface and describe out loud where the water goes (UP into the air as invisible vapour), rather than saying it just vanished. (On soil, some puddle water also soaks into the ground.)
activities.intendedInsight: The water cycle is an endless loop driven by the Sun's energy, and the same water is conserved — it only changes form (liquid↔invisible vapour) and place, never being used up or destroyed.

activities.title: Drying puddle and cold-can discrepant-event investigation
feedback: If the learner predicts the water is destroyed or 'used up', revisit with a covered dish: droplets usually appear on the underside of the lid when it is cooler than the water — hidden, not gone.
If the learner thinks the can's droplets came from inside, point to their clear colour versus the coloured water inside: coloured water cannot pass through and arrive clear.

When interpreting the result, note that droplets form readily on the cold surface in typical humid indoor air but fewer may appear in very dry air, so judge by what you actually observe rather than expecting a guaranteed outcome.
Reinforce that clouds and the white 'steam' (mist) you can see above a kettle are tiny condensed water droplets (clouds may also hold ice crystals); the vapour itself is a clear gas you cannot see.
activities.rationale: Discrepant events that contradict the learner's prediction are used to surface and challenge the specific, documented misconceptions (water disappears; condensation seeped through the cup). The food-colouring test gives a clear, checkable outcome that the condensed water came from the air.
sourceClaims: Children commonly think evaporated water 'disappears', that condensation 'seeped through' the cup, and that clouds/steam are water vapour rather than liquid droplets; understanding consolidates around age nine.
DfE Y4 States of matter: pupils should 'identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and associate the rate of evaporation with temperature'.
learnerActions: Before observing a puddle (or a shallow dish of water) left in a warm, sunny spot, predict and write down what will happen to the water and WHY.

Watch over time as it dries, then explain where the water went — into the air as invisible vapour. (Water in a dish cannot soak away, so it can only have gone into the air; a puddle on soil or grass can also lose some water by soaking into the ground.)
Add a few drops of food colouring to ice water in a can or cup, then watch for droplets forming on the OUTSIDE of the cold surface and check their colour.
Explain why any outside droplets are CLEAR, not coloured: the water condensed from the air onto the cold surface — it did not leak through the wall.
activities.intendedInsight: Evaporated water becomes invisible vapour in the air (it doesn't vanish), and 'sweating' on a cold surface is water condensing FROM the surrounding air, not water seeping through the container.

activities.title: Fair test: does temperature change how fast water evaporates?
feedback: If the learner changes more than one thing (amount of water, dish size, surface area, air flow or location), remind them a fair test keeps everything the same except the one variable being tested — here, temperature.
If the learner compares a sunny with a shaded dish and calls it a temperature test, point out that sunlight differs too; to test temperature alone, warm the water while matching the lighting.
Connect the result back to the whole cycle: more heat speeds evaporation, just as the Sun's warmth does on a hot day.
activities.rationale: A controlled comparison that isolates temperature (warm vs cool water under matched conditions) aligns with the DfE Y4 objective and gives the learner evidence that heat increases evaporation rate; a separate sun-vs-shade comparison surfaces the Sun as the energy source without being mislabelled a temperature-only test. The sun-vs-shade observation inspects the puddle on the ground, not the Sun itself.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 States of matter: pupils should 'identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and associate the rate of evaporation with temperature'.
learnerActions: Fill two similar open dishes with the same amount of water — one with warm water and one with cool water — keeping dish size, surface area, air flow and location the same so that only the water temperature differs.
Predict which will lose water faster and why.

Check them over time (e.g. mark or measure the water level) and compare which lost water faster, remembering that the warm water slowly cools towards room temperature, so the difference may be small and is clearest early on.
State your conclusion from what you observed: if the warmer dish lost more water, this supports the idea that higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation.

As a separate question about the Sun's role, compare a puddle in the sun with one in the shade (observing the puddles on the ground) and discuss which dries faster and why — remembering the puddles may also differ in size and depth.
activities.intendedInsight: Under matched conditions, warmer water evaporates faster, so the rate of evaporation rises with temperature. In everyday life a hot day speeds drying, and on a sunny day both the warmth and the direct sunlight raise the rate — the Sun's heat is what warms water and drives the cycle.

activities.title: Draw, revise and trace your own water-cycle diagram
feedback: If the diagram only shows an ocean arrow, prompt: where else does water evaporate from? (wet land, puddles, plants).
If the diagram is a one-way line ending at rain, ask how the fallen rain gets back up — close the loop.
If the Sun is missing, ask what provides the energy to lift the water as vapour.
Talking a droplet through 'where do you go next, and are you ever destroyed?' can surface conservation; keep it anchored to the real causes (heat drives it, cooling condenses it).
activities.rationale: Draw-then-revise works as formative assessment that exposes the learner's current model (often omitting precipitation, land/plant evaporation or the Sun), and constructing the labelled loop builds the conservation and endlessness intuition that recall alone does not. The droplet-narration is an optional way to voice conservation, not the primary causal explanation.
sourceClaims: Children commonly think evaporated water 'disappears', that condensation 'seeped through' the cup, and that clouds/steam are water vapour rather than liquid droplets; understanding consolidates around age nine.
learnerActions: Draw your own diagram of the water cycle from memory, labelling arrows for where water goes.
Compare it with a closed-loop cross-section showing land, sea and sky, then add any missing arrows — especially evaporation from land and plants, not just the ocean.
Draw the loop so it has no beginning and no end, and mark the Sun as the engine that drives it.
Optionally extend by adding runoff, groundwater and transpiration from plants as parts of one conserved system.
Explain to a partner, or to an imagined water droplet, where the water goes next and whether it is ever destroyed.
activities.intendedInsight: The water cycle is one continuous, conserved system — water evaporates from many sources (sea, land, plants), condenses, precipitates and flows back, driven by the Sun, with none lost.

constraints: Teach three named stages (evaporation, condensation, precipitation) but anchor WHY each happens (energy in from the Sun, energy out as vapour cools); do not let the learning reduce to memorising the E-C-P word order.

Make invisibility explicit: water vapour is a clear gas you cannot see; clouds and the visible white 'steam' (mist) above a kettle are tiny condensed water droplets or ice crystals, not the vapour itself.
Stress conservation: the same water changes form and place but is never lost, used up or destroyed.

A static labelled loop with tap-to-reveal names can teach vocabulary but cannot show the Sun-driven motion or conservation on its own; use it as a vocabulary scaffold alongside an activity that shows the loop moving and closing.

Recall-only sequencing or multiple-choice items (e.g. ordering evaporation→condensation→precipitation, or picking the Sun's role) can assess naming but do not by themselves build the loop/conservation intuition; use them to check vocabulary, not as the main teaching.
A richly rendered 3D landscape adds scenery but the cycle is conceptually a planar cross-section; extra depth is optional and not required for the causal insight.

Any evaporation-rate fair test must isolate temperature (match surface area, water amount, air flow and lighting); a sunny-vs-shaded comparison tests the Sun's role, not temperature alone, because sunlight differs between the two.
Shade/sun comparisons should observe the puddle or ground (or the drying water), never ask a child to look at or through a cover toward the Sun.

Tier expectations: naming the three stages and that the Sun drives it (introductory); explaining evaporation/condensation as reversible state changes with rate rising with temperature (intermediate); tracing runoff, transpiration and groundwater as one conserved global system (advanced).
Correct the 'vapour rises straight up into a waiting cloud / a cloud scoops and drops water elsewhere' picture: vapour moves in all directions and clouds form by condensation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated or tested interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (the DfE Y4 statement and the Beyond Penguins misconceptions page); the NGSS 3-ESS2-1 citation is marked verified but concerns seasonal weather representation rather than the water cycle directly, so it was not used to support water-cycle teaching claims.

The source notes the full interacting-systems water cycle is typically formalised later (around Grade 5 / middle school in NGSS); for ages 7–9 keep groundwater/transpiration as optional extension, consistent with the advanced tier.
No comparative efficacy or necessity claims are asserted for any medium; the interactive model, discrepant events, diagram and narration are complementary options with stated affordances and limits.

The food-colouring condensation demo assumes typical humid indoor air so droplets form on the cold surface; outcomes depend on actual humidity and temperature and should be presented as observed, not guaranteed.

The evaporation fair test isolates temperature (warm vs cool water under matched conditions); sun-vs-shade is kept as a separate question about the Sun's role because sunlight confounds a temperature-only test, and the everyday 'hot day' framing in the intendedInsight distinguishes warmth from direct sunlight.
The 'understanding consolidates around age nine' statement is from an unverified source and is reported as a claim, not established fact.

assess.poeTask: Put a little water in a clear sealed jar or zip-bag and stand it in a sunny window. Before observing, ask the child to PREDICT what happens to the water level and whether water appears on the lid, and to say WHY. The stated reason — the water evaporates and re-condenses and none can escape the sealed container — is the diagnostic part; a child who predicts the level simply drops with nothing on the lid still holds the 'water is used up' idea.
probeDeeper: Why does the puddle vanish faster on a hot sunny day than a cold cloudy one?
If you sealed the puddle under a clear plastic dome, where would the water end up, and why?
Does the same water fall as rain more than once, or is every raindrop brand new?
What would happen to the whole cycle if the Sun switched off?
assess.correctAnswer: The Sun's heat turned the puddle water into invisible water vapour (evaporation); it rose, cooled and condensed into cloud droplets; when the droplets grow heavy they fall back as rain (precipitation). The water isn't used up — it moves round a never-ending, Sun-driven loop.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The water just dried up and it's gone' — treats the puddle disappearing as the water being destroyed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Catch the vapour: a covered dish shows the water reappears as droplets — hidden, not gone.
errorPatterns.distractor: The heat destroys the water and it disappears for good.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot say where the water went; no link to later rain

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Clouds are made of smoke/steam/cotton, not the puddle's water' — severs cloud from the evaporated water
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link breath-on-cold-glass condensation to cloud droplets forming from the risen vapour.
errorPatterns.distractor: Rain comes from clouds, but clouds aren't made from the puddle's water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes clouds as unrelated stuff, can't close the loop to rain

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Rain falls and stops there' — runs the cycle as a one-way line, not a loop
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace one water molecule round the loop repeatedly until the cycle closes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Water goes down as rain and stops there; it doesn't go back up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot connect fallen rain back up to evaporation

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Water moves round by itself' — omits the Sun as the energy that drives the cycle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare drying rates of a shaded vs a sunny puddle to surface the Sun's role.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: never mentions the Sun/heat as the driver

responseLevels.gap: Says the water 'dried up and is gone'; cannot connect the puddle to later rain.
responseLevels.full: Explains the Sun heats water to vapour, which cools and condenses into cloud, falls as precipitation and evaporates again — a closed, Sun-driven loop with water conserved — and transfers this to a covered-dish or different-climate case.
responseLevels.partial: Names evaporation, condensation and precipitation as separate steps but cannot say the Sun drives them or that the same water is conserved and recirculated.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A puddle in the playground disappears on a sunny day. Where did the water go, and how could it end up falling as rain again later?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the water 'dried up and is gone' cannot connect the vanished puddle to future rain; only a child holding the conserved, Sun-driven cycle links the disappearance to rain returning.

sources.claim: Children commonly think evaporated water 'disappears', that condensation 'seeped through' the cup, and that clouds/steam are water vapour rather than liquid droplets; understanding consolidates around age nine.
