pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Grouping Species Using DNA / Cladistics (ages 13–14): organisms are classified by shared DERIVED characters (not overall similarity); phylogenetic trees are built from molecular data (DNA sequence alignment) and calibrated with the molecular clock; birds are a group WITHIN dinosaurs; convergent vs parallel evolution; horizontal gene transfer makes the 'tree' of life partly a web; classifications keep changing as new data arrive.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS3): 'the variation between species and between individuals', heredity and the genome (DNA), and classification; extends the traditional Linnaean grouping into evidence-based, evolutionary classification.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS4-2/MS-LS4-3 (anatomical and embryological/DNA similarities as evidence of evolutionary relationships); HS-LS4-1 horizon (evidence for common ancestry).
• Operational details: the key conceptual shift is grouping by SHARED DERIVED characters (synapomorphies) and common ancestry, not by looking alike — so a crocodile is more closely related to a bird than to a lizard, and 'reptiles' (excluding birds) is not a true clade. Teach how molecular data (aligning DNA/protein sequences; counting differences; molecular clock) build and date trees, and why more data revises classifications. Distinguish convergent evolution (unrelated lineages, similar traits from similar pressures — dolphin vs shark) from shared ancestry, and note horizontal gene transfer webbing the tree (esp. microbes). Read a cladogram: nodes = common ancestors, branching = shared-ancestry hypotheses.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~13): read a simple cladogram — identify which species share the most recent common ancestor. B (transitional, ~13–14): explain why grouping by shared derived characters/DNA can override grouping by resemblance (birds within dinosaurs; convergence misleads). C (formal, ~14): explain how molecular data build/date trees, why classifications change with new evidence, and how horizontal gene transfer complicates the tree.
bestPractices: Teach reading cladograms explicitly (nodes as common ancestors, branch points as shared-derived-character hypotheses) before building them — tree literacy is a documented stumbling block.

Confront convergence head-on: give look-alike but distantly related pairs (dolphin/shark, bird wing/bat wing/insect wing) so pupils learn resemblance can mislead and shared DERIVED characters/DNA arbitrate.
Use real reclassifications (birds nested within dinosaurs; whales within artiodactyls near hippos) to show classification as evidence-driven and revisable, not arbitrary or fixed.
Introduce molecular comparison concretely — more sequence differences ≈ longer since common ancestor — then add the molecular-clock caveat that rates vary, so trees are hypotheses.
keyRepresentations: A cladogram with labelled nodes (common ancestors) and synapomorphies marked on branches.
A DNA sequence-alignment panel where counting differences between species orders their relatedness.
A convergence vs homology contrast: dolphin/shark body shape (convergent) beside genuinely homologous limbs.
A 'tree becoming a web' diagram showing horizontal gene transfer links between branches (microbes).
A before/after classification showing birds moved inside the dinosaur clade.
commonMisconceptions: 'Things that look alike are most closely related' — convergent evolution produces similar traits in unrelated lineages; shared derived characters/DNA are the evidence.
'Higher/more advanced species evolved FROM the living species next to them on the tree' — tips are all modern; they share common ANCESTORS at the nodes, they don't descend from each other.
'Birds and dinosaurs are separate groups' — birds are a lineage within (theropod) dinosaurs.
'Classification is arbitrary or fixed forever' — it is an evidence-based hypothesis that changes as new (esp. molecular) data emerge.
'Evolution is always a branching tree' — horizontal gene transfer (especially in microbes) makes parts of the tree of life a web.
'The molecular clock is exact' — mutation rates vary across lineages/genes, so molecular dates carry uncertainty.

learn.summary: Cladistics for ages 13–14: group organisms by shared DERIVED characters (synapomorphies) and common ancestry, not by overall resemblance. Learners read and build phylogenetic trees from molecular data (DNA sequence alignment, counting differences), confront convergent evolution as a misleading resemblance, see that classification is an evidence-driven hypothesis that revises with new data (birds nested within dinosaurs; whales near hippos/artiodactyls), and meet horizontal gene transfer webbing the tree, plus the molecular clock with its rate-variation uncertainty.

activities.title: Build and revise a tree from character and DNA data
feedback: If a learner keeps a look-alike species on a resemblance-based branch after DNA is added, prompt: count the sequence differences again — assuming roughly comparable rates, fewer differences points to a more recent common ancestor, so where should this species attach?
When the tree reorganises, ask the learner to name the derived characters or DNA evidence that forced the move, so the revision is understood as evidence-driven, not arbitrary.
If a learner reads tips as 'more advanced', point out all tips are modern species that share ancestors at the nodes and do not descend from one another.
activities.rationale: Cladistics is fundamentally a constructive, data-driven inference: marking shared derived characters and counting molecular differences to assemble and revise a tree lets learners cause the reclassification rather than be told it. Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: an editable character/DNA-alignment matrix, a tree that redraws when molecular data are added, and a before/after showing birds moving inside the dinosaur clade when fossil skeletal characters are added. These are illustrative, not required.
sourceClaims: Cladistics groups organisms by shared derived characters (synapomorphies); phylogenetic trees are built from aligned molecular sequences and dated with the molecular clock (which has rate variation); birds are nested within theropod dinosaurs.
Anatomical similarities and DNA/molecular comparisons are used as evidence of evolutionary relationships and common ancestry.
learnerActions: Start with a small matrix of characters and DNA sequences for several species.
Mark which species share DERIVED characters and count sequence differences between pairs.
Group species by shared derived characters so a cladogram assembles, with common ancestors at the nodes and branch points as shared-ancestry hypotheses.

First build a tree using only overall appearance; then add molecular data and shared-derived-character data and observe which species move (e.g. DNA and mammalian features such as mammary glands move a dolphin placed beside sharks across to the mammals; fossil skeletal shared derived characters such as a wishbone and hollow bones place birds inside the dinosaurs, because no DNA is available from non-avian dinosaurs).
State in your own words why adding evidence changed the grouping.
activities.intendedInsight: Classification is a testable hypothesis about shared ancestry that changes as new (especially molecular) evidence arrives; grouping is decided by shared derived characters and DNA, not by appearance.

activities.title: The convergence challenge: when resemblance lies
feedback: If a learner cites the shared fin/streamlined shape as evidence of relatedness, respond: that shape evolved independently for swimming (convergence); it was not inherited from a common ancestor, so it should not group them.

If a learner treats bird and bat wings as evidence of close relatedness, distinguish the two levels: the underlying forelimb bones are homologous across tetrapods, but flight capability (the 'wing' function) evolved independently, so function alone does not group them.
Affirm reasoning that invokes homologous, inherited features plus DNA to place the dolphin with mammals rather than with fish.
activities.rationale: Confronting look-alike but distantly related pairs directly targets the 'things that look alike are most closely related' misconception and teaches learners to distinguish analogy from homology.
sourceClaims: Convergent evolution produces similar traits in unrelated lineages (misleading resemblance), and horizontal gene transfer, especially among microbes, makes the tree of life partly a web.
learnerActions: Examine a look-alike pair that are distantly related, e.g. dolphin vs shark/tuna body shape, and contrast this with homologous forelimbs — bird wing, bat wing, and a human arm (or whale flipper) are the same inherited tetrapod forelimb skeleton, even though flight in a bird and a bat evolved independently.
Decide whether the shared streamlined shape is inherited from a common ancestor or arose independently.
Check the grouping against DNA/molecular distance and name deep inherited (homologous) features the dolphin shares with mammals — mammary glands, three middle-ear bones.
Explain why a convergent trait is evidence AGAINST using it to group species.
activities.intendedInsight: Convergent evolution produces similar traits in distantly related lineages under similar pressures; shared derived homologies (characters inherited from a common ancestor), tested with DNA, are what arbitrate grouping.

activities.title: Dating nodes and the tree-becoming-web frontier
feedback: If a learner treats a molecular date as exact, prompt: rates vary, so the date is a best estimate with a range, not a fixed value.
If a learner says revising classifications means past scientists were wrong, reframe: schemes improve as new evidence (DNA, fossils) accumulates; revision is how evidence-based science works.
activities.rationale: Introducing molecular comparison concretely (more differences ≈ longer since common ancestor) with the explicit rate-variation caveat keeps trees framed as hypotheses, and horizontal gene transfer shows the genuine frontier of how life's history is shaped. Optional concrete controls: a molecular-clock slider showing an uncertainty band, and a toggle that draws horizontal-gene-transfer links.
sourceClaims: Cladistics groups organisms by shared derived characters (synapomorphies); phylogenetic trees are built from aligned molecular sequences and dated with the molecular clock (which has rate variation); birds are nested within theropod dinosaurs.
Convergent evolution produces similar traits in unrelated lineages (misleading resemblance), and horizontal gene transfer, especially among microbes, makes the tree of life partly a web.
learnerActions: Use molecular distance to order nodes in time — more sequence differences roughly means longer since the common ancestor, assuming comparable rates.
Apply a molecular-clock estimate to date a node, and note that estimates carry an uncertainty band because mutation rates vary across lineages and genes.
Add cross-branch links representing horizontal gene transfer (especially in microbes) and describe how they turn a purely branching tree into a partial web.
Explain why classification schemes keep being redrawn without this meaning earlier scientists were simply 'wrong'.
activities.intendedInsight: Molecular data can both build and date trees, but dates are hypotheses with uncertainty; horizontal gene transfer means ancestry is not always a clean branching tree.

activities.title: Read a cladogram explicitly before building
feedback: If a learner says one living tip evolved from a neighbouring living tip, correct: all tips are modern; they share common ancestors back at the nodes.
If a learner reads the tree as a primitive-to-advanced ladder, re-point to the branching structure: it shows shared ancestry, not a ranking.
activities.rationale: Tree reading is a documented stumbling block, so explicit reading practice (including the common-ancestor and 'descends from a neighbour' errors) is valuable groundwork before or alongside tree-building. A static labelled cladogram supports reading but does not by itself let learners build or revise a tree.
learnerActions: On a labelled cladogram, identify which two species share the most recent common ancestor.

Point to a node (branch point) and state what it represents (a hypothesised common ancestor); point to a derived character marked on the branch leading to that node and state what it represents (a shared derived character supporting the group that descends from that node).

Given a sequence table, order several species by molecular distance from a chosen reference species, treating fewer differences as a hypothesis of closer relatedness, assuming roughly comparable rates.
Answer: do the species at the tips descend from one another, or from shared ancestors at the nodes?
activities.intendedInsight: Tree literacy — nodes as common ancestors, branching as shared-ancestry hypotheses, tips as modern species sharing ancestors rather than descending from each other.

activities.title: Discussion extension: why do textbooks keep redrawing the tree of life?
feedback: Push learners to ground opinions in specific evidence types (shared derived characters, DNA/molecular distance, fossils) rather than general assertion.
If a learner frames revision as scientists being unreliable, reframe revision as the normal response to new data.
activities.rationale: A role-based discussion can deepen the 'classification is revisable' and 'tree-vs-web' ideas, but it supplements rather than replaces the constructive building/reading of trees from data.
learnerActions: Discuss, in the role of a systematist, why classifications keep changing and what counts as good evidence for moving a group.
Argue whether the 'tree of life' is better described as a tree or a web, citing horizontal gene transfer.

Explain how you would check a surprising claim (e.g. that birds belong within dinosaurs) using shared derived characters in fossil skeletons (e.g. wishbone, hollow bones, feathers preserved in some theropod fossils). Note that DNA can test how birds relate to living groups (their closest living relatives are crocodilians), but no DNA is available from non-avian dinosaurs.
activities.intendedInsight: Classification is an ongoing, evidence-based scientific debate, not a fixed set of labels.

constraints: A static, tappable cladogram supports tree-reading (identifying nodes and most-recent-common-ancestor) but does not let learners build or revise a tree from data, which is the core constructive skill of cladistics; treat it as a scaffold.

Multiple-choice and sequence tasks (read-the-cladogram, order by molecular distance, identify convergent look-alikes) assess interpretation and catch the 'look-alike = related' and 'descends from a neighbour' errors, but they test interpretation rather than the constructive, revise-with-data skill; use them for assessment, not as the only teaching.
Group by shared DERIVED characters (derived homologies) and DNA, never by overall resemblance or shared lifestyle; convergent traits are evidence against grouping, not for it.
Distinguish levels when using wings: the tetrapod forelimb skeleton is homologous, but flight (bird vs bat wing function) evolved independently, so function alone is not grouping evidence.
Present molecular-clock dates with uncertainty: mutation rates vary across lineages and genes, so dates are estimates, not exact; molecular-distance ordering assumes roughly comparable rates.
Frame classification as a testable, revisable hypothesis; revision reflects new evidence, not past error.
A role-play conversation is an optional extension; the central skill is building and reading trees from data.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all listed sources carry verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels birds as 'crown Avemetatarsalia' in one field while elsewhere (correctly) describing birds as nested within theropod dinosaurs; Avemetatarsalia is a much broader clade than theropods. Activities use 'birds nested within theropod dinosaurs' and avoid the 'crown Avemetatarsalia' phrasing; a specialist should reconcile the exact clade name.

The source distinguishes convergent from parallel evolution in the description but gives little operational detail on parallel evolution; activities focus on convergence vs homology, which is the better-supported discriminator here. Parallel evolution could be added if a reliable worked example is available.

The original 3D artefact rationale asserted '3D offers no conceptual gain'; this has been treated as a narrow design note (the content is data-driven inference, not spatial) rather than a universal claim about what 3D can teach.

Molecular distance ordering (more differences ≈ longer since common ancestor) is a useful heuristic but assumes roughly comparable rates; it is stated with the rate-variation caveat in both the build and dating activities and should not be taught as exact.

The source used bird/bat/insect wings as a convergence example; the homology contrast here uses a distinct-taxa vertebrate forelimb set (bird wing/bat wing/human arm or whale flipper) to avoid the earlier redundancy of pairing 'bat wing' with 'mammal forelimb' (a bat is a mammal). A specialist should confirm the preferred example set and the wording that separates forelimb homology from independently evolved flight.

probeDeeper: The dolphin's fin and the tuna's fin do the same job. Does that make them closely related? How would you check?
Birds are classified as a group within the dinosaurs. What evidence would place them there, despite how different a sparrow looks from a T. rex?
Why do classification schemes keep changing — does that mean scientists were simply 'wrong' before?
The 'tree of life' is sometimes called a 'web'. What could make ancestry a web rather than a purely branching tree?
assess.correctAnswer: No — grouping should be by shared DERIVED characters inherited from a common ancestor (homologies), not by overall resemblance. The dolphin's streamlined shape is convergent evolution: it arose independently for swimming and was not inherited from a fish ancestor. Dolphins share deep inherited features with mice — mammary glands, three middle-ear bones, and a common ancestor confirmed by DNA — so they group with mammals. Shared derived traits and DNA sequence data, not superficial similarity, decide the grouping, which is why the dolphin belongs with the mouse.

errorPatterns.pattern: Group organisms by how similar they look or how they live
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce homology versus analogy — group by shared derived characters from a common ancestor, tested with DNA, not by appearance.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — dolphins should go with sharks and tuna, because they look alike and both live in the sea.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Groups dolphin with fish, or bat with birds, on resemblance or shared lifestyle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Convergent evolution means the species are closely related because they ended up similar
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convergence is independent evolution of similar traits in unrelated lineages — it is evidence AGAINST using that trait to group them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cites the shared streamlined shape as evidence that dolphin and tuna are related.

errorPatterns.pattern: A phylogenetic tree ranks species from primitive to advanced, or one living species evolved from another living one
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trees show shared ancestry and branching, not a ladder; living species share common ancestors, they don't descend from one another.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads tree tips as 'more evolved', or says mammals evolved from living fish.

errorPatterns.pattern: Classification is fixed and just a matter of naming things
errorPatterns.nextMove: Present classification as a testable hypothesis about ancestry that changes as DNA and fossil data accumulate — e.g. birds nested within dinosaurs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Resists birds being classified within dinosaurs; treats groupings as arbitrary labels.

responseLevels.gap: Groups organisms by overall similarity or lifestyle (dolphin with fish), reads trees as primitive-to-advanced ladders, and treats classification as fixed naming.
responseLevels.full: Groups by shared derived characters from common ancestry (homology), tested with DNA/molecular data; distinguishes convergence/analogy from homology and explains why convergent traits mislead; reads trees as branching ancestry rather than a ladder; and treats classification as a data-revised hypothesis (birds within dinosaurs, tree-as-web via horizontal gene transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Knows the terms (shared characters, convergent evolution, phylogenetic tree) and can define them, but applies them inconsistently — still swayed by superficial resemblance in a new case, or unable to say why convergence argues against grouping — listing concepts without integrating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A dolphin and a tuna both have sleek, streamlined bodies and fins and live in the sea — a tuna looks far more like a dolphin than a mouse does. So should dolphins be grouped with sharks and tuna (fish) rather than with mice (mammals)? How do scientists actually decide?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student using overall similarity groups the dolphin with the fish. A student using cladistic reasoning invokes shared derived/homologous characters and common ancestry (backed by DNA) and names the fish-like shape as convergence. Distinguishing homology from analogy is the discriminator.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11; how climate change is affecting the poles — Arctic sea ice is shrinking fast (its September minimum is falling about 12–13% per decade), the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets are losing mass and raising sea level, permafrost is thawing and releasing methane (a powerful greenhouse gas), and these changes drive positive FEEDBACK LOOPS where melting causes more warming which causes more melting.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 Y6 links to human impact/environment; KS3 Chemistry 'Earth and atmosphere' (greenhouse gases, human impact on climate) and KS3 Biology (human effects on ecosystems).
• Standards—US: NGSS MS-ESS3-5 (factors causing rise in global temperatures) and MS-ESS2-6/MS-ESS3-3 (human impact; climate system); 5-ESS3-1 earlier.
• Operational details: the central, hardest idea is the positive feedback LOOP. Teach two flagship loops: (1) ice-albedo — bright ice reflects sunlight; melt exposes dark ocean/land that absorbs more heat, warming and melting more; (2) permafrost-carbon — thaw releases methane/CO2, adding greenhouse warming that thaws more permafrost. Distinguish sea-ice loss (floating, doesn't itself raise sea level) from land-ice loss (raises sea level). Poles warm faster than the global average (polar amplification). Keep it evidence-based and cause-and-effect, not doom.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (9) state that the poles are warming and ice is shrinking; Tier B (10) explain one feedback loop (dark water/land absorbs more heat than bright ice); Tier C (11) distinguish sea-ice from land-ice effects on sea level and explain how a feedback loop accelerates change.
bestPractices: Teach the feedback loop as a CYCLE the pupil can trace round (melt → darker surface → more heat absorbed → more melt), not a one-off effect
Explicitly separate floating sea ice (melting doesn't raise sea level) from land ice sheets (melting does) to fix a stubborn confusion
Use real, current data (sea-ice extent graphs) so the trend is evidenced, not asserted
Name polar amplification — the poles warm faster than the global average — and connect it to the feedbacks
Keep an agency framing (causes are human emissions; outcomes depend on choices) rather than fatalism
keyRepresentations: Ice-albedo loop diagram: bright ice reflects → melt → dark ocean absorbs → warmer → more melt
Permafrost-carbon loop: thaw → methane/CO2 released → more warming → more thaw
Arctic September sea-ice extent graph showing the downward trend
Split diagram: floating sea ice (no sea-level change) vs land ice (raises sea level)
commonMisconceptions: Melting Arctic sea ice raises sea level — floating ice melting barely changes it; land ice (Greenland/Antarctica) is what raises seas
The poles warm at the same rate as everywhere else — they warm faster (polar amplification)
A feedback loop is a single effect — it is a self-reinforcing cycle where the output feeds back to grow the cause
Permafrost is just frozen soil with no climate role — thawing it releases methane/CO2 that add further warming
It's too late / nothing affects it — the pace depends on human greenhouse-gas emissions and choices

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: how climate change affects the poles, centred on the hardest idea — positive feedback LOOPS. Learners trace two self-reinforcing cycles (ice-albedo and permafrost-carbon), distinguish floating sea ice (melting barely changes sea level) from land ice sheets (melting raises sea level), and connect these to polar amplification (the Arctic is warming much faster than the global average; warming across Antarctica is more uneven). The headline interactive proposal has learners operate a climate dashboard so the self-feeding nature of a loop becomes causal and visible; supporting activities build the loop via ordering/sorting, a scientist-style spoken explanation, and evidence reading from real sea-ice data. Framing stays evidence-based and cause-and-effect, with agency (human emissions and choices affect the pace) rather than doom.

activities.title: Run the polar climate dashboard (operate the feedback loop)
feedback: If the learner expects melting to stop the instant they stop touching the control: draw attention to the curl-back arrow — 'the dark water you exposed is now absorbing extra heat and melting more ice; that is the loop feeding itself, making the change bigger than your nudge alone.'

If the learner thinks melting the floating sea ice raised the sea level: point to the almost-unmoved floating-ice gauge versus the clearly rising land-ice gauge, and name that floating ice already displaces its own weight of water (Archimedes), so its melting barely changes sea level.
Reinforce the 'cut emissions' observation: the pace depends on human choices, not fate.
activities.rationale: Feedback loops are made concrete by operating them: letting the melt continue after the learner stops acting shows the self-amplifying dynamic, and parallel gauges make the sea-ice vs land-ice distinction visible. The live gauges, curl-back arrow, and emissions lever are interaction examples, not required technology; a paper loop or demonstration could serve the same end.
sourceClaims: The poles warm faster than the global average (polar amplification); ice-albedo and permafrost-carbon feedbacks accelerate polar warming; land-ice loss (not floating sea ice) raises sea level
learnerActions: Nudge a temperature control up one notch and watch a patch of bright sea ice melt into dark open ocean
Watch an albedo (reflectiveness) meter drop and an 'absorbed sunlight' reading rise as bright ice becomes dark water

Stop touching the control and observe that the exposed dark water keeps absorbing extra heat and melts some more ice — an arrow curls back to show melt causing more melt, so the total change ends up bigger than your single nudge alone would cause
Open a second panel: thaw permafrost, watch methane/CO2 puff out, push the temperature up, and thaw still more permafrost
Compare two gauges: melting the FLOATING sea ice barely moves the sea-level bar, but tipping meltwater off the Greenland LAND ice sheet clearly raises it
Pull a 'cut emissions' lever and see every loop slow down
activities.intendedInsight: A positive feedback loop is a self-reinforcing cycle: the output (melted ice / released methane) feeds back to strengthen its own cause, so a warming push leads to more warming and melting than it would on its own. Only land ice adds significant water to the sea; floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water, so its melting barely changes sea level.

activities.title: Build the loop from parts (label and order the cycle)
feedback: If the learner leaves the stages as a straight line: ask 'where does the last step — warming increases — lead?' and have them draw the return arrow from 'warming increases' back to 'ice melts', showing the cycle feeds itself rather than ending.

If the learner sorts a floating sea-ice statement into 'raises sea level': remind them floating ice already displaces its own weight (Archimedes), so only land-ice melt (Greenland/Antarctic sheets) adds water to the sea.

A correct sort or ordering shows the learner can recognise and arrange the loop structure; follow it by asking them to explain in their own words why the loop accelerates, since the sort alone does not elicit that explanation.
activities.rationale: Ordering and sorting let learners construct the loop structure and practise the sea-ice/land-ice distinction; these help build and check understanding but on their own test recognition rather than eliciting a full independent explanation.
learnerActions: Lay out the stages of the ice-albedo loop — bright ice reflects sunlight; ice melts; dark ocean is exposed; more heat is absorbed; warming increases — and arrange them into a closed circle rather than a straight line
Draw the return arrow from 'warming increases' back to 'ice melts' to show the cycle feeds itself
Repeat for the permafrost-carbon loop: thaw → methane/CO2 released → more warming → more thaw
Sort statements into 'raises sea level' (land-ice melt) and 'barely changes sea level' (floating sea-ice melt)
activities.intendedInsight: Assembling the cycle shows that the final step loops back to the first, which is what distinguishes a feedback loop from a one-off change.

activities.title: Explain it like a climate scientist
feedback: If the learner lists facts without closing the loop ('dark water absorbs heat, ice is shrinking, permafrost thaws'): ask them to connect each step to the next and back to the start.

For the 'stayed white' question: if the surface stayed bright and kept reflecting sunlight, the extra absorbed-heat step disappears, so the ice-albedo loop would no longer amplify the melting — some melting would still happen from greenhouse warming, but less. This shows albedo is what drives this particular loop.
If the learner says 'it's too late': redirect to the emissions idea — the pace depends on human greenhouse-gas choices.
activities.rationale: A scientist-style spoken explanation with responsive follow-ups probes the causal reasoning directly. Explanation and operating the loop address different aspects, so this complements rather than replaces the dashboard.
learnerActions: In your own words, explain to a listener why Arctic sea ice loss is bigger than warming alone would cause — say what happens AND why the loop makes the change bigger
Add permafrost thaw as a second reinforcing loop in your explanation
Answer a probing follow-up: 'Is there anything that would make it slow down on its own, or does the loop only push one way?'
Answer: 'What if the ocean under the ice had somehow stayed white — would the melting still speed up?' and justify your answer
activities.intendedInsight: Producing a spoken cause-and-effect explanation forces the learner to close the causal circle and transfer the loop idea to a new case, rather than listing facts.

activities.title: Read the evidence: sea-ice extent over time
feedback: If the learner points only to one dip: highlight the multi-decade downward slope beneath the year-to-year variation.
Anchor the figure: the September minimum is declining about 12–13% per decade relative to the 1981–2010 average over the satellite record (the verified NASA value is ~12.2%).
activities.rationale: Using real current data keeps the claim evidence-based. Reading an actual graph and selecting the trend builds the habit of grounding conclusions in measurement.
sourceClaims: Arctic sea ice September minimum extent is declining at about 12.2% per decade relative to the 1981–2010 average, measured over the satellite record since 1979
learnerActions: Study an Arctic September sea-ice extent graph covering the satellite record (since 1979) and describe the trend in your own words
State roughly how fast the September minimum is falling per decade and explain how you read it from the graph
Answer: 'What's your evidence that the ice is really shrinking, not just moving around from year to year?'
activities.intendedInsight: The downward trend is evidenced by measured data, not asserted; a long record distinguishes a real decline from year-to-year wobble.

constraints: Teach the feedback loop as a CYCLE the learner can trace round (melt → darker surface → more heat absorbed → more melt), not a one-off effect.
Explicitly separate floating sea ice (melting barely changes sea level) from land ice sheets (melting raises sea level); justify with displacement (floating ice already displaces its own weight).
Name polar amplification (the Arctic is warming much faster than the global average; Antarctic warming is more uneven) and connect it to the feedbacks.
Keep an agency framing — causes are human emissions and outcomes depend on choices — rather than fatalism.

Ordering/sorting checks and the sea-ice-vs-land-ice sort mainly confirm and help build the loop structure; they do not by themselves elicit a full independent explanation, so pair them with a spoken or written explanation task.

The dashboard interaction examples (albedo meter, curl-back arrow, sea-level gauges, emissions lever) are illustrative mechanisms to make the loop visible; they are not mandatory, and paper loop diagrams, demonstrations, or graphs can serve the same objectives.
Use the ~12–13% per decade figure for the satellite record relative to the 1981–2010 average; present it as measured data, not a prediction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Only one source (NASA Arctic sea-ice minimum, ~12.2% per decade) is marked verified; the curriculum-standard and polar-amplification/feedback claims are marked unverified in the source row. Treat the ~13% headline and polar-amplification statements as legacy claims, not independently confirmed here.
The description/objective uses '13% per decade' while the verified NASA claim states ~12.2%; retained learner-facing as '~12–13%' to span both without asserting a precise figure.

Original artefact notes contained universal-superiority phrasing ('a static image can't convey the runaway dynamic', '3D adds nothing', dialogue 'better traced by operating it'); these were rescoped to narrow affordances. A fixed diagram can still teach the loop's parts; a live model additionally shows the self-amplifying dynamic — neither is claimed universally necessary.
'Floating ice melting barely changes sea level' is the accurate statement (tiny salinity/density effects exist); kept as 'barely changes' rather than 'does not change' for precision at this age.

sourceClaims were re-checked verbatim against the original sources[].claim strings; only sources[0] and sources[3] directly support the activities they are attached to, and both are copied exactly (including the en-dash in '1981–2010'). No source was treated as evidence of empirical effectiveness or of any medium's superiority.

probeDeeper: You've told me melting makes more melting. Is there anything that would make it slow back down on its own, or does the loop only push one way?
Permafrost is frozen ground holding trapped methane and CO2. If it thaws, how could that join the same kind of loop?
What's your evidence that the ice is really shrinking, not just moving around from year to year?
What if the ocean under the ice had somehow stayed white — would the melting still speed up?
assess.correctAnswer: Bright white ice reflects most of the Sun's energy back to space; dark ocean absorbs it. When ice melts it uncovers dark water, which warms up and absorbs more heat, which melts more ice, which uncovers more dark water — a self-reinforcing feedback loop, so the warming and melting accelerate rather than staying steady. (Arctic September sea-ice is declining about 12% per decade.)

errorPatterns.pattern: melting is a one-off, steady change — 'it just melts a bit more each year because it's a bit warmer', with no loop
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw the loop as a circle (less ice -> darker surface -> more heat absorbed -> less ice) and contrast with a straight line
errorPatterns.distractor: The air just gets a little warmer each year, so a little more melts each year
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes linear/steady melting with no self-reinforcement

errorPatterns.pattern: melting sea ice raises sea level — confuses floating sea ice with land ice ('all that melting ice is what floods cities')
errorPatterns.nextMove: floating ice already displaces its own weight (Archimedes); only LAND ice (Greenland/Antarctic sheets) adds to the sea
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes sea-level rise to Arctic sea-ice melt

errorPatterns.pattern: the poles are remote bystanders — 'it's far away, it doesn't affect us'
errorPatterns.nextMove: link to albedo and ocean circulation and global sea level; the poles are a climate engine
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats polar change as local and irrelevant

responseLevels.gap: Says the ice is melting 'because it's hot' with no mechanism, or claims melting sea ice floods the land.
responseLevels.full: Explains a positive feedback loop (less ice -> darker surface -> more absorbed heat -> more melting), can add permafrost/methane as a second reinforcing loop, distinguishes sea-ice (floating) from land-ice (sea-level) effects, and transfers the loop idea to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Names bits — dark water absorbs heat, ice is shrinking, permafrost thaws — but lists them without closing the loop; can't explain why the rate accelerates.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In summer the sea ice near the North Pole melts, showing dark ocean underneath. The next summer, even more ice melts than the year before. Why does the melting speed up year after year instead of staying the same? Tell me what's happening, and then tell me WHY that makes it get faster.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child without the feedback idea treats melting as a one-off, steady 'it's just a bit warmer' process; the feedback child explains the LOOP — melting causes conditions that cause more melting. The reason-tier forces the causal circle, not just 'the Earth is warming'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–6: read and WRITE numerals 0–20 — connecting the spoken number, the quantity, and the written symbol. This is the most central node of the whole domain (centrality 0.59): the symbolic gateway everything else builds on.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words' and 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.3 'write numbers 0–20; represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0–20'.
• Operational details — the child must (i) recognise/name each numeral on sight, (ii) form each numeral legibly (a handwriting/motor skill), and (iii) map a numeral to a quantity and back. Rests on cardinality (a numeral names a total) and digit-formation. Watch the classic teen reversals and the say-it-as-you-hear-it trap (writing 'twelve' as 21, 'thirteen' as 31) that come from left-to-right speech vs place-value writing.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): read any numeral 0–20 shown. Tier B (5–6): write numerals 0–20 legibly from dictation, correct orientation. Tier C (6): shown a set of objects, write the matching numeral, and shown a numeral, make/point to that many.
bestPractices: Keep the numeral tied to QUANTITY at all times — read/write the symbol beside a set of objects, a ten-frame, or fingers — so 0–20 are symbols FOR amounts, not decorations; grounds in cardinality (prerequisite mt_dmNvjroCPT).

Treat numeral formation as an explicit motor skill: model stroke order, use sky-writing/sand/whiteboards, and directly address reversals (2, 5, 7, 9) and the b/d-style confusions with multisensory tracing.

Confront the teen 'hear-it-write-it' trap head-on: 'thirteen' SOUNDS like three-then-ten but is written 13 (ten then three) — pair the spoken word with a ten-frame showing a full ten and 3 more, and with the written 13.
Use frequent read↔write↔represent switching (numeral card → make the set; set → write the numeral; hear it → write it) so all three modes are linked, not siloed.
Include 0 deliberately as 'none' and as a written symbol — many children can count but hesitate to read or write zero.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame(s) beside the numeral (a full ten + extras for teens) linking symbol to a structured quantity.
Numeral formation cards with directional arrows / stroke-order guides for handwriting.
Number track / 0–20 washing-line pairing each numeral with its position and a matching set.
Numeral ↔ objects ↔ spoken-word matching cards (three-way correspondence).
commonMisconceptions: Digit reversals (2, 3, 5, 7, 9 written mirror-image) — a formation issue needing direct correction.
Teen transposition from speech: writing 'thirteen' as 31, 'fourteen' as 41 (hearing the ones first).
Reading a numeral without connecting it to a quantity (naming '7' but unable to make seven).
Confusing visually similar numerals (6/9, 2/5, 7/1) or omitting/misreading 0.
Treating a two-digit teen numeral as two separate single digits (reading 15 as 'one, five').

learn.summary: Children aged 5–6 learn to read and write numerals 0–20, connecting the spoken number word, the quantity, and the written symbol. This is a foundational symbolic skill requiring numeral recognition on sight, legible numeral formation (a handwriting/motor skill), and two-way mapping between a numeral and a quantity. Teaching keeps numerals tied to amounts, treats digit formation as an explicit motor skill, and directly confronts the teen 'hear-it-write-it' transposition trap (writing 'thirteen' as 31) and classic digit reversals.

activities.title: Numeral studio: trace, build the quantity, self-correct
feedback: If a digit is mirror-reversed (e.g. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 written backwards), treat it as a handwriting/formation issue, not a maths error — give stroke-order cues and multisensory tracing (sand, sky-writing) and let it resolve with practice.
If the written numeral doesn't match the set, recount the set together (one tag per object, the last word tells how many) and then write that numeral — don't reteach numeral forms.
When a quantity and its numeral are shown side by side, invite the child to point to 'the full ten and the extra ones' for teens so the symbol maps to the structure.
activities.rationale: Reading and writing numerals is an active symbol↔quantity mapping plus a tracing/formation skill. Keeping the numeral beside a structured quantity (ten-frame, fingers, counters) grounds it in cardinality, and read↔write↔represent switching prevents the modes from being siloed. A guided path makes stroke order and reversal correction concrete, but a fixed chart or paper tracing with adult feedback can serve the same purpose. No cited source directly establishes this pedagogy; it is a research-informed proposal.
learnerActions: Trace a numeral along a guided stroke-order path (start dot and directional arrows) on a whiteboard, in sand, by sky-writing, or on a coded surface that models stroke order.
As the numeral is formed, build or watch a ten-frame fill to that many (using a second ten-frame for 11–20), so the symbol is felt as a quantity rather than a squiggle.
Flip the task: tap/lay out a set of counters, then write or select the numeral that names how many.
Switch frequently between the modes — numeral card → make the set; set → write the numeral; hear it → write it — so reading, writing and representing stay linked.
activities.intendedInsight: A numeral is a symbol FOR a quantity, written and read, not a decoration; the three modes (spoken word, quantity, written symbol) are one connected idea.

activities.title: Hear it, write it: addressing the teen transposition
feedback: Writing a teen in spoken order (41 for 'fourteen', 71 for 'seventeen') is a normal transcription stage that fades as teen place value matures — do NOT drill it as careless or mark it repeatedly wrong. Keep modelling with a ten-and-ones frame.
Read a teen numeral back as a whole number ('fifteen'), not 'one, five', to counter reading a two-digit teen as two separate single digits.
Contrast visually similar numerals (6/9, 2/5, 7/1) by naming each beside its matching set when confusion appears.
activities.rationale: The spoken word order for teens conflicts with written place-value order, causing transposition errors; linking the numeral, the word, and a ten-structured quantity is a recognised way to mitigate this. Showing that 31 would demand three tens and one more gives the child a quantity-grounded self-check rather than a rule to memorise; the check depends on a display that visibly breaks for 31 and is a cue the child performs, not an automatic correction.
sourceClaims: Teen numbers are a known difficulty because the spoken word order (e.g. 'thir-teen') conflicts with the written place-value order, causing transposition errors; linking numeral, word and a ten-structured quantity mitigates this.
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken teen word, e.g. 'thirteen', and see two ten-frames: one FULL frame of ten and a second frame with 3 more.
Write the numeral by forming the ten digit first and then the ones digit: 1 then 3.
Check: if you write 31, the quantity would need three full tens and one more, which cannot match the single full ten and three extras shown.
Repeat with 'fourteen', 'seventeen', 'nineteen', pairing the spoken word, the ten-structured quantity, and the written numeral each time.
Include 0 deliberately — say 'none', show an empty frame, and read and write the symbol 0.
activities.intendedInsight: The words for 13–19 say the ones first ('thir-teen') but the numerals are written ten-then-ones (13); eleven and twelve do not follow this pattern. Pairing the word with a full-ten-plus-extras quantity shows why 13, not 31, is correct.

activities.title: Read-and-match reference wall and checks
feedback: Matching and multiple-choice checks confirm recognition but do not by themselves require the child to form a numeral — follow a correct match with an actual writing of the numeral.
If a child names a numeral but cannot make that many, return to building the set beside the symbol before moving on.
For a dictation check such as 'write fourteen, seventeen, twelve, nineteen', watch the teens especially, then ask the child to make a counted set (e.g. 16 counters) and write how many.
activities.rationale: Recognition and matching are cleanly assessable, and a tap-to-hear reference wall is a useful support, but recognition-only or matching-only responses do not elicit independent numeral formation, which is half the objective. These activities are best used to check and reinforce alongside, not instead of, actual writing.
learnerActions: Use a 0–20 number track or washing-line pairing each numeral with its position and a matching set; tap or point to a numeral to hear its name and reveal a matching ten-frame display (two frames for 11–20).
Match numeral cards to sets or ten-frames (three-way: numeral ↔ objects ↔ spoken word).
Given a shown or spoken quantity, pick or write the matching numeral, including deliberate 12/21-style distractors to probe the teen trap.
Trace a dictated numeral along a path to check formation.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and matching numerals to quantities is a distinct, checkable layer that should always reconnect the symbol to an amount and, where possible, to writing it.

constraints: Numeral writing (actual formation of each digit) is half the objective — matching, multiple-choice and tap-to-reveal reference activities test or support recognition but do not themselves require numeral formation and must not fully replace writing.
Always keep the numeral tied to a quantity (ten-frame, fingers, counters) so 0–20 are symbols for amounts, not decorations; grounds in cardinality (a prerequisite).
Treat digit reversals (commonly 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9) as a handwriting/formation issue needing stroke-order cues, not as a number error.
Treat teen transposition (41 for 'fourteen') as a normal developmental transcription stage; keep modelling the ten-and-ones structure rather than drilling or repeatedly marking it wrong.
Include 0 deliberately as 'none' and as a written symbol, since many children can count but hesitate to read or write zero.
A tap-to-hear numeral chart or number track is a useful reference but cannot capture the child forming numerals; use it as support alongside writing practice.

Stroke-order paths, reversal-blocking pens, live ten-frame fills and drag-to-match are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory, and paper, sand, whiteboards and counters with adult feedback can serve the same goals.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims for CCSS-M K.CC.3 and the NCETM teen-difficulty guidance were marked verified:false in the source row; treat their support as unconfirmed.

The original recommendation asserted an open in-role dialogue 'cannot teach numeral formation' and that a 3D environment 'adds nothing'. These are comparative/necessity claims not established by the sources; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (recognition vs formation) rather than universal laws. A fixed chart or non-interactive medium can still support recognition.

The claim that writing 31 for thirteen 'self-corrects' because the quantity would need three tens assumes a ten-frame display that visibly breaks for 31; this is a design-dependent cue, not an automatic correction, and is presented as a check the child performs.

sourceClaims were tightened so each cites only a claim that supports the activity's teaching principle. The NCETM teen-difficulty claim is retained for activity[1] (it directly supports linking numeral, word and quantity to reduce transposition). K.CC.3 was removed from activity[0] because it documents the curriculum objective rather than the activity's pedagogy (cardinality grounding and read↔write↔represent switching); activity[0] therefore has no directly supporting claim, and activity[2]'s recognition-vs-formation affordance likewise has none, so both use [].

probeDeeper: Write the number that comes after 12.
Show me 14 with counters, then write it — do they match?
Read this: 13. Now this: 12.
assess.correctAnswer: Reads all correctly; writes 14, 17, 12, 19; writes 16 for the set — with teens not reversed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes teen numbers in spoken order: 41 for 'fourteen', 71 for 'seventeen' (hears the ones word first)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill it as a careless mistake or mark it repeatedly wrong — it is a normal transcription stage that fades as teen place value matures. Keep modelling with a ten-and-ones frame.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dictated teens come out reversed while single digits and 'twelve/twenty' may be fine.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mirror-reverses individual digits (backwards 3, 7, or 5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat as handwriting, not maths — don't count it as a number error; give formation cues and let it resolve with writing practice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digits are recognisable but flipped left-right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes a numeral that doesn't match the counted quantity (miscounts the set)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach numeral forms — recount the set together (one tag per object, last word = how many) then write that.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The written numeral is off by one or two from the actual count of counters.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot read or write numerals 0–20 reliably, or the numeral doesn't match a counted set.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes all numerals 0–20 from sight and dictation and matches a numeral to a counted quantity.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes most, but teens are occasionally reversed or a digit mirror-formed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch the child read and write. 'Read these: 7, 13, 15, 11, 20. Now write these as I say them: fourteen, seventeen, twelve, nineteen.' Then: 'Here are 16 counters — write how many.' Watch the teens especially.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Dictating teens catches the transposition stage (41 for fourteen); a counted set checks the numeral is tied to quantity, not just copied. Watching the writing distinguishes a genuine gap from a normal formation/reversal stage.

sources.claim: Year 1 pupils read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words, and count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals.

sources.claim: Kindergarten pupils write numbers from 0 to 20 and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, K.CC.3

sources.claim: Teen numbers are a known difficulty because the spoken word order (e.g. 'thir-teen') conflicts with the written place-value order, causing transposition errors; linking numeral, word and a ten-structured quantity mitigates this.

pedagogy.summary: Proportional relationships are represented with double number lines (two parallel scales aligned at 0), ratio tables, and coordinate graphs — and the defining graphical signature is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN. The representational skills are (1) plotting proportional pairs and drawing that line, (2) explaining WHY it must pass through (0,0) — because zero of one quantity means zero of the other — and (3) reading off an unknown value from the line or table (if 3 kg costs £6, find 5 kg). The key idea to build is that the three representations show the SAME constant multiplier: the gap between rungs on a double number line, the column multiplier in a ratio table, and the gradient of the line are one and the same. The persistent error is thinking any straight line (or any rising graph) shows proportion, ignoring the origin.
bestPractices: Connect the three representations explicitly — double number line, ratio table, and graph — as views of one constant multiplier, moving between them on the same example.
Foreground the origin: ask 'what does it cost for 0 kg?' so pupils reason that a proportional graph MUST pass through (0,0), and use that as a test.
Align double number lines at 0 and keep the scales consistent, so equivalent ratios sit at matching positions.
Read unknowns both by scaling on the table/number line and by reading off the graph, checking the two agree.
Contrast a proportional line (through origin) with a straight line that misses the origin (e.g. a fixed charge plus a rate) so 'straight' alone is not mistaken for 'proportional'.
keyRepresentations: Double number line (two parallel scales aligned at 0)
Ratio table with a constant column multiplier
Coordinate graph: straight line through the origin (gradient = the rate)
Overlay contrasting a through-origin line with a not-through-origin line
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any straight line — or any rising graph — shows direct proportion, ignoring whether it passes through the origin.
Not aligning the double number line at 0, so equivalent ratios don't correspond.
Reading a graph as isolated points and being unable to interpolate an unknown, or swapping the axes when reading off.
Believing the graph need not start at (0,0) — missing that zero of one quantity means zero of the other.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 11–14 learn to represent direct proportion across three linked views — a double number line (two parallel scales aligned at 0), a ratio table in which every kg entry is multiplied by the same constant to give its £ entry, and a coordinate graph whose signature is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN. The core insight is that the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (e.g. 1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6), the kg-to-£ multiplier in each pair in the table, and the gradient of the line (£ per kg) are ONE AND THE SAME constant multiplier. Learners plot proportional pairs and draw the line, explain why it must pass through (0,0) (zero of one quantity means zero of the other), and read off unknowns (if 3 kg costs £6, find 5 kg → £10). The persistent error to confront is treating any straight or rising line as proportional while ignoring the origin.

activities.title: Linked board: one rate, three views that move together
feedback: If a drawn line misses (0,0), ask 'what does it cost for 0 kg?' — it must be £0, so the line has to start at the origin.
If the double number line is not aligned at 0, highlight that equivalent ratios then fail to sit at matching positions; realign at 0.
If axes are swapped when reading off, prompt: read UP from the weight on the x-axis to the line, then ACROSS to the cost on the y-axis.
When the fixed-charge toggle lifts the line off the origin, name it: still straight, but no longer proportional because 0 kg no longer costs £0.
activities.rationale: Plotting pairs, drawing the line, and reading off unknowns are direct-manipulation tasks; moving between the three views on one example is intended to make the shared multiplier concrete, and the fixed-charge contrast separates 'straight' from 'proportional'. Live linking and dragging are offered as examples of how to make the shared multiplier visible, not as the only possible medium.
sourceClaims: A directly proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin; properties include that doubling one quantity doubles the other and that if one quantity is zero the other is zero.

Pupils should use double number lines and ratio tables, and recognise that proportional relationships are represented by straight-line graphs through the origin, relating the multiplicative relationship to linear functions.
learnerActions: Enter or accept a rate such as 3 kg → £6 and watch a ratio table, a double number line, and a coordinate graph populate for the SAME example.
Plot the proportional pairs on the graph and draw the line; confirm it passes through the origin.
Drag a point to 5 kg and read £10 simultaneously on the table, the number line, and the graph.

Point to where the constant '×2' appears in each view: the gradient of the line (£2 per kg), the multiplier from each kg entry to its £ entry in the table (3 → 6, 5 → 10), and the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6).
Flip a 'fixed charge' toggle (e.g. add a standing £2) and observe the whole line lift OFF the origin while staying perfectly straight; state whether it is still proportional and why not.
activities.intendedInsight: All three representations encode the SAME constant multiplier, and the origin — not mere straightness — is the test of proportionality.

activities.title: Annotated proportion graph: reveal the origin, the rate, and a read-off
feedback: If the learner calls the not-through-origin line proportional, return to the origin: at 0 kg the fixed-charge line already costs £2, so it fails the origin test.
If the rate is misread, trace one unit along x and read the matching rise on y to recover the constant multiplier.
activities.rationale: A proportion graph is largely a fixed object; annotating it with tap-to-reveal on origin, gradient, and read-off, plus a contrasting line, is intended to rehearse the recognition cues at low cost. A fixed image here cannot be freely manipulated but can still surface these cues for inspection; it complements rather than replaces the interactive board.
sourceClaims: A directly proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin; properties include that doubling one quantity doubles the other and that if one quantity is zero the other is zero.
learnerActions: Examine a proportion graph and reveal, at the origin, that 'at 0 kg, cost is £0'.
Reveal along the line the constant multiplier (the rate, e.g. £2/kg).
Reveal at a chosen point its read-off (e.g. 5 kg → £10).
Compare a companion line that is straight but does NOT pass through the origin (a fixed £2 charge plus £2/kg) and decide, with reasons, that it is not proportional.
activities.intendedInsight: The recognition cues of a proportional graph are the origin crossing and a single constant rate; a straight line that misses the origin is a direct counterexample to 'straight means proportional'.

activities.title: Identify, read, and produce proportional lines
feedback: If a produced line misses (0,0), it is the key discriminator: recognition alone will not place the line; re-anchor using 'at 0 kg, cost £0'.
If an unknown is only found when the weight is an already-plotted point, stress that the line gives a value for EVERY weight, so interpolate between plotted points.
If axes are swapped during read-off, label both axes first, then read up-then-across.

If a £2/kg line is drawn as if it were separate from the given line, point out that equal rates give the SAME line through the origin; a genuinely different rate (e.g. £1/kg through (3,3)) gives a shallower distinct line.
activities.rationale: Identifying the proportional graph, reading off values, matching a table to a line, and drawing a new line are cleanly assessable, with 'any straight line' and axis-swap as sharp distractors. The draw step elicits independent construction, which recognition-only items do not.
sourceClaims: Pupils should use double number lines and ratio tables, and recognise that proportional relationships are represented by straight-line graphs through the origin, relating the multiplicative relationship to linear functions.
learnerActions: Choose which of several graphs shows direct proportion, where a straight not-through-origin line is a deliberate trap.
Given a ratio table, plot the points and draw the matching line through the origin.
Read an unknown off a line through (3,6) (e.g. find the cost of 5 kg → £10), stating which axis you read up from and which you read across to.

On the same axes, DRAW a line for a DIFFERENT fruit's price: note that a £2/kg fruit would COINCIDE with the given £2/kg line through (3,6), whereas a shallower £1/kg line passes through (3,3) — and check your line is anchored at the origin.
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting a point, interpolating an unknown, and independently producing an origin-anchored line together show whether the learner sees the graph as a constant-multiplier relationship rather than a picture.

constraints: Multiple-choice identification and tap-to-reveal items assess or rehearse recognition of cues; they do not by themselves elicit the independent production of an origin-anchored line, so include a draw/plot task for full mastery.
An annotated fixed graph cannot be freely manipulated; pair it with a task where learners plot, drag, or draw so the constant multiplier is explored, not just viewed.
Always keep double number lines aligned at 0 and scales consistent, or equivalent ratios will not correspond.
When introducing the fixed-charge contrast, state the setup explicitly (e.g. £2 standing charge plus £2/kg) so learners attribute the lifted line to the non-zero start, not to a changed rate.

When asking learners to draw a 'different' line, ensure the chosen rate is genuinely different from any line already on the axes (£1/kg, not £2/kg, against a given £2/kg line), so the task is coherent.

In-role dialogue and 3D manipulation were judged poor fits here: the relationship is inherently 2D (two quantities, one plane), and drawing/reading a graph is a visual-spatial task; these are design judgements for this topic, not universal rules.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic and geometry: at £2/kg, 3 kg → £6 and 5 kg → £10 are consistent; a £1/kg line through the origin passes through (3,3); the fixed-charge example (£2 + £2/kg) correctly gives £2 at 0 kg and so misses the origin. The original's note that a £2/kg drawn line coincides with the given (3,6) line has been preserved and the 'different rate' wording kept coherent (£1/kg used as the genuinely different, shallower line).

The source claims support the mathematical signature (straight line through the origin; zero maps to zero; use of double number lines and ratio tables) but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular interface (linked board, tap-to-reveal, drag). Efficacy of specific media is not asserted; medium wording has been kept to proposed/intended.
The original judgement that conversation and 3D 'add nothing' has been softened to a scoped design decision for this 2D topic rather than a universal law.

probeDeeper: What would this fruit cost for 0 kg? Where must the line be at x = 0, and why?
How did you find the cost of 5 kg from the line — which way did you read, and how do you know it isn't, say, £, from the other axis?

Here is a line that is straight but does NOT go through the origin (a fixed £2 charge plus £2/kg) — is THAT one directly proportional? How can you tell? (counterexample separating 'straight' from 'proportional'.)
Show me this same relationship as a ratio table — where is the '×2' that the graph's steepness shows?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 3 kg costs £6 (so this fruit is £2 per kg). (b) 5 kg costs £10 — read up from 5 on the x-axis to the line and across to £10. (c) A straight line through the origin passing through (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6)… — in fact the SAME line here, since £2/kg matches; if asked for, say £1/kg would be a shallower line through the origin, e.g. (3, 3).

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks any straight (or rising) line shows proportion; draws or accepts a line that misses the origin
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what does this fruit cost for 0 kg?' — it must be £0, so the line has to start at the origin. Contrast with a fixed-charge line that misses it. Rehearse the origin test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In (c) draws a line not through (0,0), or when shown a not-through-origin line calls it proportional

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the graph as isolated points and cannot interpolate an unknown, or swaps the axes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model reading up from the x-value to the line and across to the y-axis; the line gives a value for EVERY weight, not just plotted ones. Label axes before reading.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 5 kg, only answers if 5 is a plotted point, or reads across-then-up the wrong way giving the wrong coordinate

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not connect the graph to the double number line / ratio table — treats them as unrelated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put the three side by side for the same example; show the gradient, the column multiplier, and the number-line gap are the same number. Align the number line at 0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can read the graph but cannot say how the same relationship looks as a ratio table, or does not align the double number line at 0

responseLevels.gap: Misreads the axes or cannot interpolate; draws a line that misses the origin and treats any straight line as proportional.
responseLevels.full: Reads (3,6) as '3 kg for £6', interpolates 5 kg → £10 by reading the line, DRAWS a new proportional line through the origin, explains why it must pass through (0,0), and links the graph to the ratio table/double number line as the same constant multiplier.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets the given point and reads off 5 kg → £10 correctly, but draws a new line without anchoring it at the origin, or cannot translate the graph into a ratio table / double number line — recognition without full production or cross-representation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a graph: a straight line through the origin passing through the point (3, 6), where the x-axis is weight in kg and the y-axis is cost in pounds. (a) What does the point (3, 6) tell you? (b) Use the line to find the cost of 5 kg. (c) Now, on the same axes, DRAW the line for a different fruit that costs £2 per kg.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting a point, reading off an unknown, and then PRODUCING a proportional line all test whether the child sees the graph as a constant-multiplier relationship, not a picture. A child who has it reads (3,6) as '3 kg for £6', interpolates 5 kg → £10, and draws a new line THROUGH THE ORIGIN. A child who hasn't reads the axes the wrong way, cannot interpolate, or draws a line that misses (0,0). The 'now draw one' step is the discriminator — recognition alone won't produce a correct origin-anchored line.
