pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–8 years

- **Topic:** Habitat Vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'):** supports 'identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited... identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including microhabitats' — this LANGUAGE topic supplies the words (habitat, environment, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, woodland, ocean, desert, rainforest, pond) needed to describe those habitats.

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE; supports 2-LS4-1 / K-ESS3-1):** the vocabulary underpins 2-LS4-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1]' and K-ESS3-1 (needs–habitat relationship). NGSS has no standalone vocabulary PE — note honestly.

- **Operational details:** Children learn to NAME and USE the words for where living things live and what they need there, at two scales — habitat (woodland, pond, desert) and microhabitat (under a log, in a rock pool). They apply 'adapted to', 'conditions', and 'shelter' to justify why a given animal suits a given place. Vocabulary is taught in context (matching, describing real scenes), not as isolated definitions.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, vocabulary-in-use). Success = correctly using 'habitat' vs 'microhabitat' with an example of each, naming three contrasting habitats and what makes each distinctive, and explaining a match with 'conditions'/'shelter'/'adapted to' rather than just labelling.
bestPractices: Teach the words in context (matching and describing real scenes) rather than as isolated definitions to memorise.
Explicitly separate the two scales — habitat (the whole place) and microhabitat (a small habitat within it) — with a worked example of each.
Distinguish 'habitat' from 'home/shelter': the habitat is the whole place; the nest/burrow is only where it shelters.
Pair each habitat word with its defining 'conditions' (wet/dry, hot/cold, light/dark) so vocabulary carries meaning, not just labels.
Use local first-hand exploration (under logs, in ponds) so microhabitat vocabulary attaches to real experience.
keyRepresentations: A labelled habitat scene (woodland, pond, hedgerow, seashore) with tappable regions.
Habitat vs microhabitat scale pair (the woodland → the log within it).
Animal–habitat matching cards annotated with 'conditions' and 'adapted to'.
A conditions word-bank (wet, dry, hot, cold, dark, damp, sunny) applied to each place.
commonMisconceptions: Using 'habitat' to mean the animal's nest or home rather than the whole surrounding place.
Not grasping the microhabitat scale — treating 'under a log' as unrelated to the woodland it sits in.
Believing any animal can live in any habitat (ignoring conditions/suitability).
Confusing 'environment' and 'habitat' as identical, or using neither with precision.
Thinking only exotic places (jungle, desert) are habitats, not a local pond or hedge.

learn.summary: Help 6–8 year olds name and USE habitat vocabulary (habitat, environment, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, woodland, ocean, desert, rainforest, pond) in context rather than reciting definitions. Two scales matter: the whole habitat (woodland, pond, desert) and the microhabitat nested inside it (under a log, a rock-pool crevice). Children justify why an animal suits a place using 'conditions', 'shelter' and 'adapted to'. Teach through describing real scenes and matching, and anchor 'microhabitat' to first-hand local exploration where possible.

activities.title: Explore a labelled habitat scene and 'lift the log'
feedback: If a child calls the nest the 'habitat', point from the single nest out to the whole wood: the habitat is the whole place that holds many creatures; the nest is only its shelter.
If a child treats 'under the log' as unrelated to the woodland, trace the nesting physically — point from the log out to the whole wood — and say the microhabitat sits inside the habitat.
If a child names the place but not its conditions, prompt with 'The conditions here are ___ and ___' to attach words like wet, dry, dark, damp, sunny.
activities.rationale: Interactive labelled scenes with reveal-and-zoom make the habitat→microhabitat scale visible and let vocabulary attach to a pictured place rather than an abstract definition. The zoom from log to woodlice is an optional interaction example that makes the nesting concrete; a confusable-pair flap (habitat vs shelter) can target the common home/habitat slip. These are illustrative mechanisms, not required technology; a printed cross-section picture with a fold-out flap can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats' statutory includes identifying and naming plants and animals in their habitats including microhabitats, and that living things live in habitats to which they are suited.
learnerActions: Look at a cross-section countryside-to-coast picture holding woodland, pond, hedgerow and seashore.
Point to or tap each place, say its name, and state its conditions (a pond is wet; a wood is often shady and damp; a seashore is salty and windy; a hedgerow is sheltered and leafy).
Name one animal that lives in each place and say what it needs there (food, water, shelter, space).
'Lift the log' or zoom into a small damp, dark spot of woodlice and centipedes, and name it a microhabitat — a small habitat sitting inside the bigger woodland.
Compare the whole place (habitat) with one specific nest or burrow (shelter), saying aloud which word fits which.
activities.intendedInsight: A habitat is the whole place that supports many living things; a microhabitat is a smaller habitat nested within it; a shelter/nest is only the one spot where an animal hides. Each place has defining conditions that make it suit particular animals.

activities.title: Match animals to habitats and justify with conditions
feedback: For a wrong match, give a conditions hint: 'a cactus needs dry, sunny conditions — would a wet pond suit it?'
If a child sorts by size of animal rather than scale of place, re-focus on the place: is this the whole surrounding area, or a small spot within a larger one?
activities.rationale: Active matching with a required justification makes vocabulary productive and surfaces the suitability idea, countering the belief that any animal can live anywhere. Dragging cards and immediate conditions hints are optional interaction examples; paper cards work equally well.
learnerActions: Match living-thing cards (animals and plants) to habitat scenes (cactus, a plant→desert; crab→rock pool; fox→woodland; frog→pond).
For each match, add a 'why?' using 'conditions', 'adapted to' or 'shelter' (e.g. 'a cactus is adapted to dry, sunny conditions').
Test a deliberately wrong pairing (cactus→pond) and explain why the conditions do not suit it.
Sort a second set of cards into 'whole habitat' vs 'microhabitat inside it'.
activities.intendedInsight: Not every living thing can live in any place; a match is justified by the conditions a place offers and what the plant or animal is adapted to. The habitat/microhabitat sort reinforces the two scales.

activities.title: Describe a habitat aloud using the target words
feedback: If 'habitat' and 'microhabitat' are used interchangeably, make the nesting physical: point from the crack (microhabitat) out to the whole pool (habitat).

If 'conditions' means only 'the weather', scaffold with a frame — 'The conditions in a rock pool are ___ and ___' — to attach it to wet, salty, cold. Treat this as a word that needs exercise, not a misconception.
For the bird's nest question, accept that a nest is most precisely the bird's shelter, not the whole habitat; use it to re-separate shelter from the surrounding place.
Encourage transfer: ask the child to describe a second, contrasting habitat using the same words.
activities.rationale: A spoken-description task elicits spontaneous, contextual use and distinguishes a child who owns the words from one who can only recite. This is a teaching activity as well as a check; keep the focus on how words are used, not on definitions.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats' statutory includes identifying and naming plants and animals in their habitats including microhabitats, and that living things live in habitats to which they are suited.
learnerActions: Look at a rock pool or woodland picture.
Describe the place aloud: where a crab (or other animal) lives, what it is like there, and where it can hide.
Use whichever words fit while narrating: habitat, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, environment.

Answer follow-up prompts: point to a microhabitat inside the habitat; name the conditions that make a rock pool hard to live in; use 'environment' in a sentence about the seashore; decide whether a bird's nest is a habitat, a microhabitat or just a shelter, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Meaning is shown by correct USE in running description — naming the whole place as the habitat/environment, a crevice as a microhabitat within it, the specific conditions (wet, salty, cold, pounding waves), and the animal's shelter — not by reciting definitions.

activities.title: Meet an animal who describes its home
feedback: If the child names only the shelter, ask for the whole surrounding place too.
Prompt for at least one named condition before moving on.
activities.rationale: A talking-animal prompt offers a playful, responsive way to rehearse the words; it suits oral practice and motivation. It is an alternative with a different purpose — open prompting — complementing the anchored-visual work rather than replacing it.
learnerActions: Listen to or read an animal persona describing where it lives and asking 'where do I live, and why does it suit me?'
Name the animal's habitat and the conditions it needs.
Point out a microhabitat within the habitat where the animal might find shelter, and say how the microhabitat and the shelter differ from the whole habitat.
activities.intendedInsight: The same vocabulary can be rehearsed through dialogue, prompting a child to supply habitat, conditions and shelter for a described animal.

constraints: Teach the words in context (matching and describing real scenes), not as isolated definitions to memorise.
Explicitly separate the two scales — habitat (the whole place) and microhabitat (a small habitat within it) — with a worked example of each.
Distinguish 'habitat' from 'home/shelter': the habitat is the whole place; the nest or burrow is only where an animal shelters.
Pair each habitat word with its defining conditions (wet/dry, hot/cold, light/dark) so vocabulary carries meaning.
Use local first-hand exploration (under logs, in ponds) where possible so microhabitat vocabulary attaches to real experience; include local ponds and hedges, not only exotic places.

Recognition and matching tasks support vocabulary but do not by themselves elicit independent spoken or written use; include at least one task where the child produces running description with the target words.
Reveal/zoom/drag mechanisms and flaps are illustrative examples of interaction; printed pictures, fold-outs and paper cards can achieve the same goals.

Success criteria: correctly use 'habitat' vs 'microhabitat' with an example of each, name three contrasting habitats and what makes each distinctive, and explain a match using 'conditions'/'shelter'/'adapted to' rather than just labelling.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the NGSS 2-LS4-1 citation as unverified and notes NGSS has no standalone vocabulary performance expectation; this vocabulary supports but is not itself an NGSS PE. The NGSS claim was removed from activity sourceClaims because it supports the topic, not a specific teaching principle. Treat standards alignment as supportive context, not tested claim.

The retained DfE claim grounds the statutory curriculum content (naming in habitats including microhabitats, suitability); it justifies WHAT is taught but does not establish that any proposed interaction, medium or scaffold is effective or superior to another.

The legacy source asserted that open dialogue and a 3D world teach vocabulary less well than a labelled scene. These are catalog-ranking preferences, not established comparative efficacy; they have been softened to scoped affordance statements (dialogue suits oral rehearsal; navigation may add overhead without serving naming) and the dialogue activity is retained as a purposeful alternative.

The original 'is a bird's nest a habitat or a microhabitat?' probe implies a binary; a nest is most precisely a shelter, so graders should accept 'neither — a shelter'. This has been made explicit in the prompt and feedback.

probeDeeper: You used 'habitat' — can you point to a microhabitat inside it? Give me one.
What conditions make a rockpool a hard place to live?
Use 'environment' in a sentence about the seashore.
Is a bird's nest a habitat or a microhabitat? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Uses the terms accurately in running description: the rockpool/seashore is the habitat or environment; a crevice under a rock is a microhabitat within it; names the conditions (wet, salty, cold, pounding waves); identifies the crab's shelter (under a rock, in a crack). Meaning is shown by correct USE in context, not by reciting definitions.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'habitat' to mean the single home or den — 'the crab's habitat is its shell/hole'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the whole rockpool (habitat) with the one crack the crab hides in (its shelter/microhabitat); the habitat holds many creatures, not one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies 'habitat' to the exact spot one animal sits in rather than to the whole place that supports many organisms.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'habitat' and 'microhabitat' interchangeably — no sense that one is nested inside the other.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the nesting physical: point from the crack (microhabitat) out to the whole pool (habitat); microhabitat = a small habitat within a bigger one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the whole seashore a microhabitat, or a single crack a habitat, with no scale distinction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Avoids or empties 'conditions' — either doesn't use it, or uses it to mean only 'the weather'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with a frame — 'The conditions in a rockpool are ___ and ___' — to attach the word to wet/salty/cold; the concept is present, the word needs exercise. Do not treat as a misconception.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the scene vividly but never characterises it with 'conditions', or says only 'the weather is nice'.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the words as loose synonyms (habitat = home), avoids 'microhabitat' and 'conditions', or applies them wrongly.
responseLevels.full: Uses all the terms accurately and spontaneously in context, distinguishing habitat from microhabitat by scale and applying 'conditions' to specific physical features, then transfers the vocabulary to a second, contrasting habitat.
responseLevels.partial: Uses 'habitat' and 'shelter' correctly but blurs the habitat/microhabitat scale, or uses 'conditions' only vaguely.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a picture of a rockpool at the seaside (or a woodland). Say: 'Describe this place to me — where a crab lives, what it is like there, and where it can hide. As you talk, use whichever of these words fit: habitat, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, environment.' Listen for how the words are used, not for definitions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who only half-owns the words uses 'habitat' as a bare synonym for 'home', cannot separate habitat from microhabitat by scale, and skips or misuses 'conditions'. Correct use reveals the nested scale (a microhabitat sits inside the habitat) and applies 'conditions' to physical features — something a definition-reciter usually cannot do while narrating.

sources.source: UK Department for Education, National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS1)

sources.claim: NGSS 2-LS4-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1].'
sources.source: NGSS, 2-LS4 Biological Evolution: Unity and Diversity

pedagogy.summary: Expanding a single bracket applies the distributive law: the multiplier outside acts on EVERY term inside, and its sign travels with it. It is best taught through the area/grid model — a rectangle of width equal to the multiplier and length equal to the sum inside splits into one region per inside term, so 3(2x+5) is visibly 3×2x plus 3×5. The two persistent errors are distributing over only the first term (3(2x+5)→6x+5) and mishandling the sign of a negative multiplier; the area model and a substitution check defeat both.
bestPractices: Use the area/grid model: the multiplier is one side, each inside term a separate region, so every term must be multiplied.
Draw an arrow from the multiplier to EACH inside term to force full distribution.
Handle the sign explicitly — write −2(x−4) as (−2)×x + (−2)×(−4); a negative times a negative gives +8.
Check by substituting a value: 3(2x+5) and 6x+15 must agree at, say, x=1 (both 21).
Then combine with collecting like terms, e.g. 3 + 2(x+1) → 3 + 2x + 2 → 2x + 5, stressing that only the bracket is expanded first (order of operations).
keyRepresentations: Area/grid rectangle split into one region per inside term
Arrows fanning from the multiplier to each term
Number substitution check (evaluate both forms at x=1)
Signed-multiplier annotation (−2 × −4 = +8)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies only the first term inside: 3(2x+5) → 6x+5 (documented as 2(n+3)=2n+3 being judged correct).
Sign error with a negative multiplier: −2(x−4) → −2x−8 (fails to flip the second sign).
Confuses × with +: 3(2x+5) → 3+2x+5, or adds the outside number to the coefficient (3×2x → 5x).
Leaves the expression unexpanded or unsimplified after multiplying.

learn.summary: Teach expanding a single bracket as the distributive law: the multiplier outside acts on EVERY term inside, and its sign travels with it. An area/grid model makes this visible — a rectangle whose width is the multiplier and whose length is the sum inside splits into one region per inside term, so 3(2x+5) is seen as 3×2x plus 3×5. Target the two persistent errors directly: distributing over only the first term (3(2x+5)→6x+5) and mishandling the sign of a negative multiplier (−2(x−4)→−2x−8, instead of the correct −2x+8). A substitution check and factoring back give learners independent ways to verify.

activities.title: Split the rectangle: area model of a bracket
feedback: If only one region is multiplied: draw an arrow from the multiplier to EACH inside term — the multiplier's side borders BOTH regions, so both must be multiplied. 3(2x+5) = 3×2x + 3×5.

If the −4 keeps its sign (−2x−8): write the second product with brackets, (−2)×(−4) = +8, and connect to 'two negatives make a positive'. At x=0 this slip shows up (correct −2(0−4)=8, but −2x−8 gives −8); confirm at a non-zero value too, e.g. −2(1−4)=6 and −2×1+8=6.

If the outside number is added instead of multiplied (3+2x+5) or folded into the coefficient (3×2x=5x): rewrite as 3×(2x+5), and recall that a number against a bracket means multiply, not add; 3×2x means three lots of 2x, which is 6x.
activities.rationale: The area/grid model represents each inside term as a distinct region, making 'multiply everything inside' something learners can see and reconstruct rather than memorise. An optional interactive version (tapping the '+' to slice the length, regions auto-labelling their area, a toggle that recolours regions and flips signs when the multiplier becomes negative) makes the mechanism concrete, but the reasoning also works with a drawn and hand-labelled rectangle. This model is one effective route and need not be the only one.
sourceClaims: Students commonly mis-expand a single bracket by multiplying only the first term — e.g. judging 2(n+3)=2n+3 to be correct — whereas 2(n+3)=2n+6; the lesson uses area representations to address this distributive-law error.
learnerActions: Draw (or manipulate) a rectangle labelled width 3 and length (2x + 5).
Split the length at the '+' into two parts, producing two regions: a 3-by-2x region and a 3-by-5 region.
Label each region with its own area: 3×2x = 6x and 3×5 = 15.
Gather the two areas to write the total: 3(2x+5) = 6x + 15.

Now take a new example with a negative multiplier, −2(x−4), and split it into one part for each term inside the bracket. A length of −2 is not a real side length, so treat the grid as a signed diagram, not a literal area: write it as (−2)×x + (−2)×(−4), reasoning that a negative times a negative gives +8, so the result is −2x + 8.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the bracket as TWO regions answers 'why does the +5 not just come along unchanged?' — the multiplier covers every region, so every inside term must be multiplied, and the sign of a negative multiplier is applied to each term.

activities.title: Expand, then check by substitution
feedback: If both forms disagree at the chosen value, the expansion is wrong — re-check that every inside term was multiplied and that signs were handled.
If the check passes, note that agreement at one value is supporting evidence but not conclusive for a linear expression; test a second value and factor back to confirm the structure.
Avoid picking x=0 as the only check when a constant term could mask an error in the x-term — try a non-zero value such as x=1 or x=2, or use more than one value.
activities.rationale: A worked procedure with sign handling is consolidated by doing expansions and verifying them with feedback. Substitution and factoring back are genuine self-checking strategies learners can carry to any expansion. Scored fill-in or sort-the-terms tasks can give practice, provided they require learners to construct the expansion rather than only recognise a correct answer.
learnerActions: Expand 3(2x+5) and write the result (6x + 15).
Choose a value, say x=1, and evaluate both the original and the expansion: 3(2×1+5)=3×7=21 and 6×1+15=21 — they agree.
Expand −2(x−4) and check at x=1: −2(1−4)=−2×−3=6 and −2×1+8=6 — they agree.
Try to verify a second way by factoring the answer back to the bracket form.
Decide whether each expansion is correct, correcting any that disagree.
activities.intendedInsight: Substituting a value gives a learner an independent way to confirm or refute their expansion, so correctness is not dependent on the teacher's say-so; an expansion and its original must agree for every value.

activities.title: Expand within a larger expression (order of operations)
feedback: If the 3 is also multiplied by 2: point out that the 3 stands alone and is added, not part of the product 2(x+1); only 2 multiplies the bracket.
If terms are left uncombined (3 + 2x + 2): remind the learner to collect like constants, 3+2=5, giving 2x+5.
Confirm by substitution: at x=1, 3+2(1+1)=7 and 2(1)+5=7.
activities.rationale: Transferring expansion into a multi-term expression tests whether learners apply distribution selectively and then simplify, which is the National Curriculum expectation for manipulating algebraic expressions.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions by multiplying a single term over a bracket.
learnerActions: Take 3 + 2(x+1) and expand only the bracket first: 3 + 2x + 2.
Collect like terms to simplify fully: 2x + 5.
Explain why the +3 is not multiplied by 2 — only the term attached to the bracket is expanded first.
Check the simplified form by substituting a value into both the original and the final expression.
activities.intendedInsight: Only the multiplier attached to the bracket is distributed; other terms are combined afterwards by collecting like terms, respecting the order of operations.

constraints: Expansion with sign handling is a procedure built through practice with feedback; recognition-only tasks (choosing a correct answer from options) can diagnose errors but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an expansion — include tasks where learners write the full working.

A static labelled area diagram can show the split and support reasoning, but it does not let the learner carry out expansions across varied cases; pair any fixed diagram with learner-produced expansions to build fluency.
The area/grid model is inherently planar — the two dimensions represent multiplier and sum. Keep it in 2D; introducing a third dimension would misleadingly suggest volume.
The correct results to preserve are 3(2x+5) = 6x + 15 and −2(x−4) = −2x + 8 (NOT −2x−8). Any practice item or distractor must treat 6x+5 and −2x−8 as errors to be caught, never as acceptable answers.

When checking by substitution, prefer a non-zero value (e.g. x=1) or use more than one value so that a correct constant term cannot mask an error in the variable term; x=0 is acceptable only when the error being caught lives in the constant term.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists one citation as not verified (the CSMS/ICCAMS sign-error claim); treat its evidential strength as unconfirmed.

The legacy entry asserted that a third dimension 'adds nothing' and that dialogue is unsuitable; these have been softened to scoped claims (keep the model planar to avoid implying volume; a conversation alone may be less suited than practice with feedback for consolidating a multiplicative procedure, efficacy untested) rather than universal laws.

Self-audit on arithmetic and signs: 3×2x=6x, 3×5=15, total 6x+15 correct; (−2)×(−4)=+8 so −2(x−4)=−2x+8 correct; substitution checks 3(2×1+5)=21=6+15, −2(1−4)=6=−2×1+8, and 3+2(1+1)=7=2×1+5 verified. The legacy misconception example −2(x−4)→−2x−8 is retained only as an error to correct, never as a valid answer.

Editor adjustments: substitution checks harmonised to prefer non-zero values (removing an internal contradiction where x=0 was both used and discouraged); the self-check activity's sourceClaims set to [] because no source claim directly supports substitution/factoring as a verification strategy; the KS3 curriculum-necessity claim removed from the area-model activity's sourceClaims because it supports the topic only, not the area-model principle; single-value substitution reworded as supporting-but-not-conclusive evidence.

probeDeeper: Draw me a rectangle that shows why 3(2x+5) has two parts — what is each part's area?
In −2(x−4), what is −2 × −4, and how sure are you? (counterexample targeting the sign)
Is 3(2x+5) the same as 3×2x + 5? Put x=1 into both and check.
How could you convince someone your expansion is right — without me telling you? (expect: substitute a value, or factorise back)

errorPatterns.pattern: Distributes over the first term only — 3(2x+5) → 6x+5 — the second inside term is copied across unchanged (documented: students judge 2(n+3)=2n+3 to be correct).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the rectangle: the multiplier is one side and covers BOTH regions; draw an arrow from the 3 to each inside term. Show 3(2x+5) = 3×2x + 3×5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Only the first inside term is multiplied; the constant (or second term) appears unchanged in the answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sign error with a negative multiplier — −2(x−4) → −2x−8 — the sign of the second term is not flipped.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Write the multiplication with brackets and signs shown: (−2)×(−4) = +8; connect to two-negatives-make-a-positive; check by substituting x=0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second term keeps its inside sign, or a negative multiplier is applied to only the first term's sign; −2×−4 is written as −8.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses multiplication with addition — 3(2x+5) → 3+2x+5, or folds the multiplier into the coefficient as 3×2x = 5x.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish that a number against a bracket means multiply; rewrite 3(2x+5) as 3×(2x+5); check by substitution.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The outside number is added to inside terms, or coefficients are added rather than multiplied.

responseLevels.gap: Multiplies only the first term, or adds instead of multiplies; the second inside term is lost or unchanged so the expansion is wrong.
responseLevels.full: Distributes over every term with correct signs including negative multipliers, simplifies the result, checks by substitution or by factorising back, and transfers to 3 + 2(x+1)-type expressions where the bracket must be expanded before adding.
responseLevels.partial: Expands correctly with a positive multiplier over both terms, but slips on the negative multiplier's sign, or does not simplify/collect afterwards — the routine case works but a rule-exposing case fails.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child this card and say 'expand each of these, showing your working': 3(2x + 5), and then −2(x − 4). Say nothing about method. Watch whether the multiplier reaches BOTH inside terms, and how they handle the sign on the −4.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two cases isolate the two errors without any question being asked: 3(2x+5) → 6x+5 exposes distributing over the first term only, while −2(x−4) → −2x−8 exposes the negative-multiplier sign failure. A child who is sound multiplies both terms and gets +8 from two negatives; the written line tells the teacher which, if either, is missing.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions by multiplying a single term over a bracket.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS3)

sources.claim: Students commonly mis-expand a single bracket by multiplying only the first term — e.g. judging 2(n+3)=2n+3 to be correct — whereas 2(n+3)=2n+6; the lesson uses area representations to address this distributive-law error.
sources.source: Mathematics Assessment Project — 'Interpreting Algebraic Expressions' Classroom Challenge (assessment task, solutions & Common Issues)

sources.claim: Sign errors when a negative term is distributed over a bracket are a recurrent, documented algebra-manipulation difficulty.
sources.source: Küchemann/Hart CSMS tradition, as summarised in Hodgen et al. RME 11(2) (ICCAMS)

pedagogy.summary: Given two rules (e.g. 'start at 0, add 3' and 'start at 0, add 6'), the child generates both sequences, lines up CORRESPONDING terms (1st with 1st, 2nd with 2nd, …), and notices the relationship between the two is MULTIPLICATIVE: each Rule-B term is twice the corresponding Rule-A term — because the step 6 is twice the step 3 and both start at 0 — not merely 'more'. They form ordered pairs from corresponding terms, plot them in the first quadrant, and see the points fall on a straight line through the origin. It is a deliberate bridge from Grade 4/Year 5 pattern work toward proportional relationships (y = 2x) and functions. Crucially, pupils generate each pattern from a GIVEN rule; they are not required to guess a hidden rule.
bestPractices: Line the two sequences up in a two-row table so pupils compare column-by-column (corresponding terms), not within a single row
Press for a MULTIPLICATIVE description ('twice', '___ times as much') and an explanation of WHY — the step 6 is twice the step 3, and both start at 0
Explicitly contrast additive ('6 more') with multiplicative ('twice') using the corresponding pairs, showing the difference grows while the ratio stays constant
Form ordered pairs as (Rule-A term, Rule-B term), respecting the (x, y) order, and plot in the first quadrant
Notice the points lie on a straight line through the origin and connect this to y = 2x, previewing proportional reasoning
Keep both rules GIVEN — the task is to generate from the rules and then spot the relationship, not to infer a secret rule
Use tape/bar diagrams to make 'twice as much' visible
keyRepresentations: Two-row table of corresponding terms (positions aligned in columns)
The (x, y) ordered-pair notation drawn from corresponding terms
First-quadrant coordinate grid with points on a ray through the origin
Tape / bar diagram showing one quantity as twice the other
commonMisconceptions: Describes the relationship additively ('the second is 6 more') instead of multiplicatively ('twice') — defaulting to additive comparison, which only fits the first pair because the difference actually grows (3, 6, 9, …)
Compares term-to-term WITHIN one sequence (the +3 or +6 step) instead of between the corresponding terms of the two sequences
Reverses the ordered pair, plotting (6, 3) instead of (3, 6), or counting up-then-across
Tries to guess a single hidden rule underlying both sequences rather than generating each from its given rule
Assumes the 'twice' relationship comes from the steps alone, and keeps applying it even when the two sequences do not both start at 0

learn.summary: Pupils (age 10–11) generate two numerical sequences from two GIVEN rules (e.g. 'start at 0, add 3' and 'start at 0, add 6'), line up corresponding terms in a two-row table, and discover the relationship is multiplicative — each Rule-B term is twice the corresponding Rule-A term — because the step 6 is twice the step 3 and both start at 0. They explain why, contrast additive ('6 more') with multiplicative ('twice'), form ordered pairs (x, y) from corresponding terms, and plot them to see the points fall on a straight line through the origin (y = 2x). This bridges earlier pattern work toward proportional reasoning. Both rules are given; pupils are not asked to guess a hidden rule.

activities.title: Generate, align, and compare two sequences
feedback: If a pupil says 'B is 6 more than A', ask them to check a later pair — e.g. position 4, where A=9 and B=18, a gap of 9. The difference between corresponding terms is not constant but grows (3, 6, 9, 12…), so 'add 6' is not the relationship; the ×2 ratio, by contrast, stays constant — compare 'how many times' not 'how many more'.

If a pupil compares within one row (the +3 or +6 step), point to a single column (say position 3) and ask: 'what is B here, what is A here, how do they compare?' — the comparison is vertical across the two rows.
If a pupil hunts for a single hidden rule joining both sequences, remind them the rules are GIVEN: generate each sequence directly from its own rule, THEN look for the relationship between them.
Confirm the full reasoning: B is twice A at every corresponding position because 6 = 2×3 and both start at 0.
activities.rationale: Grade 5 pattern work asks pupils to generate two numerical patterns from given rules, examine relationships between corresponding terms, and prepare for proportional relationships. Distinguishing additive comparison (what is added) from multiplicative comparison (what factor multiplies) is a known conceptual hurdle, so explicitly contrasting the growing difference with the constant ratio targets the core discrimination.
sourceClaims: In Grade 5 (5.OA.3) students work with two numerical patterns that can be related, examine the relationships within sequences of ordered pairs and in first-quadrant graphs, and this prepares them for proportional relationships and functions; pupils generate a pattern from a GIVEN rule and are not required to infer or guess the underlying rule.

Additive versus multiplicative comparison (Grade 4): in an additive comparison the question is what amount would be ADDED to one quantity to get the other; in a multiplicative comparison the question is what FACTOR would multiply one to get the other; multiplicative Compare situations must be carefully distinguished from additive Compare problems.

CCSS 5.OA.B.3 canonical example: from 'Add 3' and 'Add 6' starting at 0, students observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other and explain informally why (because 6 is twice 3).
learnerActions: Write out the first six terms of Rule A (start at 0, add 3): 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15
Write out the first six terms of Rule B (start at 0, add 6): 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30
Line the two sequences up in a two-row table so position 1 sits above position 1, position 2 above position 2, and so on
For each column, compare Rule B's term with Rule A's term in the SAME position (vertical comparison across the two rows, not along one row)
State the relationship multiplicatively: 'B is twice (×2) A in every column' and explain why — Rule B adds 6, which is twice the 3 Rule A adds, and both start at 0
Check what happens to the difference between corresponding terms down the columns (6−3=3, 12−6=6, 18−9=9…): it is not constant but grows, while the ×2 ratio stays the same in every column
activities.intendedInsight: The two sequences are related by a constant factor (×2) at corresponding positions. 'B is 6 more' does not describe the relationship, because the difference between corresponding terms is not constant but grows (0, 3, 6, 9, …) — so no single 'add a number' rule fits every column. 'B is twice A' holds in every column instead, and here this works because the step 6 is twice 3 and both sequences start at 0.

activities.title: Make ordered pairs and plot them
feedback: If points sit on the wrong side of or below the intended line, check the (x, y) order: the first number moves across (Rule A, x), the second moves up (Rule B, y). Re-plot one pair together — e.g. ask the pupil to point to where (3, 6) goes and say which number moves across and which moves up.
If a pupil plots (6, 3) instead of (3, 6), re-establish the convention and re-plot.
Confirm that all points lie on one straight ray climbing through (0, 0), matching the constant ×2 in the table.
activities.rationale: Forming ordered pairs from corresponding terms and graphing them in the first quadrant is the explicit objective of this standard and the bridge to seeing a proportional relationship as a line through the origin. Respecting (x, y) order is a common error point worth rehearsing in the plotting itself.
sourceClaims: In Grade 5 (5.OA.3) students work with two numerical patterns that can be related, examine the relationships within sequences of ordered pairs and in first-quadrant graphs, and this prepares them for proportional relationships and functions; pupils generate a pattern from a GIVEN rule and are not required to infer or guess the underlying rule.
learnerActions: Turn each column into an ordered pair as (Rule-A term, Rule-B term): (0,0), (3,6), (6,12), (9,18)…
For each pair, use the first number to move ACROSS (x, Rule A) and the second number to move UP (y, Rule B)
Plot the first four pairs in the first quadrant of a coordinate grid
Describe the shape the points make, and notice they lie on a straight line through the origin
Connect this to y = 2x, linking the table, the pairs, and the line as one object
activities.intendedInsight: Corresponding terms of two proportional sequences form ordered pairs whose points lie on a straight line through the origin; the constant ×2 ratio is the same thing as the equation y = 2x and the slope of that ray.

activities.title: Test whether the ×2 depends on the starting number
feedback: If a pupil still says 'twice' after changing the start, work one column numerically: with A starting at 1, position 2 gives A = 4 and B = 6, and 6 is not 2×4 — the ratio is no longer constant.
Draw out the general point: the ×2 held cleanly because the starting numbers fitted it too (both were 0), not just because one step was twice the other.
activities.rationale: A listed misconception is assuming the 'twice' relationship comes from the steps alone and keeping it even when a changed starting number breaks it (e.g. A starting at 1 while B starts at 0). Varying the start deliberately exposes this and deepens understanding of the condition behind the proportional relationship.
sourceClaims: CCSS 5.OA.B.3 canonical example: from 'Add 3' and 'Add 6' starting at 0, students observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other and explain informally why (because 6 is twice 3).
learnerActions: Keep Rule B as 'start at 0, add 6' but change Rule A to 'start at 1, add 3' (1, 4, 7, 10, …)
Generate both sequences and line them up by position
Check each column: is B still exactly twice A now?
Explain what broke and why — the clean ×2 relationship relied on the starting numbers as well as the steps (in the original rules, both started at 0), not on the steps alone
activities.intendedInsight: The multiplicative relationship between corresponding terms comes from the steps AND the starting numbers; in the original rules both start at 0. When A starts at 1 but B starts at 0, 'twice' no longer holds in every column even though one step is still twice the other — so pupils should not assume 'twice' from the steps alone.

activities.title: Tape diagram for 'twice as much'
feedback: If a pupil focuses on the extra length (the gap) rather than the number of copies, redirect to 'how many A-tapes make a B-tape?' — the answer stays 2 in every column, while the extra length grows.
Confirm the two-copies structure matches the ×2 in the table and the slope of the line.
activities.rationale: A tape/bar diagram is a standard representation for making multiplicative comparison concrete and is specifically suggested as support for pupils defaulting to additive comparison. It offers a visual route to 'twice' alongside the numerical table.
sourceClaims: Additive versus multiplicative comparison (Grade 4): in an additive comparison the question is what amount would be ADDED to one quantity to get the other; in a multiplicative comparison the question is what FACTOR would multiply one to get the other; multiplicative Compare situations must be carefully distinguished from additive Compare problems.
learnerActions: For a chosen column (e.g. position 3: A = 6, B = 12), draw a tape/bar for the Rule-A term
Draw the Rule-B tape beside it and lay out how many copies of the A tape fit the B tape
Confirm the B tape is exactly two A tapes long, making 'twice as much' visible
Repeat for another column to check the two-copies relationship holds across positions
activities.intendedInsight: 'Twice as much' is a length/quantity relationship that can be seen directly: the larger bar is made of exactly two copies of the smaller, reinforcing multiplicative comparison over additive comparison.

activities.title: Check and sort: additive vs multiplicative, table-to-graph
feedback: If a pupil selects the additive answer ('B is 6 more than A'), return to a later column (e.g. position 4, where A=9 and B=18, a gap of 9) and show the difference between corresponding terms is not constant but grows, so 'add 6' does not describe the relationship — whereas ×2 holds in every column.
If a pupil reverses a plotted point, restate: first number across (x), second up (y).
Confirm correct matches by tracing one column from table to ordered pair to point on the line.
activities.rationale: Short checks (fill-in-the-blank, sort, match, plot) verify the skill and surface the common additive misconception ('B is 6 more') and the (y, x) reversal. These confirm mastery rather than build the generate-and-compare reasoning, so they belong after the construction activities.
learnerActions: Complete 'B term = __ × A term' for a given pair of sequences starting at 0
Given a described relationship, sort it as additive ('6 more') or multiplicative ('twice'), and say which one holds in every column
Match a two-row table to its correct straight-line graph
Plot a specified pair (e.g. (3, 6)) on the grid, deliberately avoiding the (6, 3) reversal
activities.intendedInsight: Pupils can apply the multiplicative relationship, choose it over the tempting additive description, and coordinate table, pairs, and graph correctly.

constraints: Keep both rules GIVEN; the task is to generate each sequence from its own rule and then find the relationship, not to guess a hidden rule.
Compare CORRESPONDING terms column-by-column (vertical, across the two rows), not term-to-term within a single sequence.

The clean ×2 relationship between corresponding terms depends on the starting numbers as well as the steps: here it works because 6 = 2×3 and both start at 0 (in general, Rule B's start must be twice Rule A's start). Do not present 'twice' as following from the steps alone.

The difference between corresponding terms is not constant — it grows (0, 3, 6, 9, 12…); do not present 'B is 6 more' as a true relationship that holds for a specific early pair. It coincides at most at a single column, and the honest contrast is 'difference grows' versus 'ratio stays ×2'.
Respect (x, y) order when forming and plotting pairs: Rule-A term across (x), Rule-B term up (y).

Recognition and sort/match/fill-in checks confirm the skill but do not, on their own, elicit the independent construction of generating two sequences and coordinating them into pairs and a graph; use them after construction.

A consolidation summary (a two-row table beside a pre-plotted line with the ×2 annotated and facts revealed on tap) can tidily review the result, but a fixed display does not let the learner generate the terms or watch the growing difference against the constant ratio themselves; treat it as a review aid, not the main task.

Optional interactive supports that make the mechanism concrete: taps that fill each row ('add 3' / 'add 6') with corresponding terms locked in columns; a toggle between a '+' view (drawing the growing difference 3, 6, 9…) and a '×' view (showing the constant ×2 in every column); auto-plotting each column as an ordered pair that lands on the ray through the origin; and a 'change the starting number' control to reveal that the ×2 breaks when the starts no longer fit it (e.g. A starts at 1 while B starts at 0), and holds only when B's start is twice A's start. These are illustrative, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source for the canonical 'Add 3 / Add 6, terms are twice the corresponding terms' example (CCSS 5.OA.B.3) is marked verified:false in the row; the two Progressions claims are marked verified:true. Treat the canonical-example claim as unverified.

Arithmetic self-check: Rule A 0,3,6,9,12,15 and Rule B 0,6,12,18,24,30; corresponding ratios all ×2; differences between corresponding terms are 0,3,6,9,12,15 (equal to Rule A's values), confirming the difference grows and is NOT constant. This means 'B = A + 6' coincides at exactly one column (A=6, B=12); the original row's phrasing that the additive claim is 'true only for the first pair' / 'fails from the second pair on' is arithmetically imprecise and was corrected in the guidance to 'the difference grows' with ×2 holding everywhere. The 'change the start' case A:1,4,7,10 vs B:0,6,12,18 correctly shows ×2 fails (e.g. 6 ≠ 2×4).

The original row's 3D and conversation 'poor' ratings carried universal phrasing ('adds nothing', dialogue 'does not build' the procedure). These catalog preferences were not propagated as pedagogical laws; the procedural, construction-based nature of the objective is instead captured in constraints without asserting any medium is universally incapable.

probeDeeper: You said B is 6 more than A. Check the pair at position 4 — is B still exactly 6 more? What is happening to the gap as you go down?
Why does B come out as twice A — what is it about the two rules that makes that happen?
What if Rule A started at 1 instead of 0 (1, 4, 7, …) while Rule B still started at 0 and added 6? Would B still be exactly twice A?
Point to where (3, 6) goes on the grid, and tell me which number moves you across and which moves you up.
assess.correctAnswer: A: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. B: 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. Each Rule-B term is TWICE (×2) the corresponding Rule-A term, because Rule B adds 6 each step which is twice the 3 that A adds, and both start at 0. Ordered pairs (0,0), (3,6), (6,12), (9,18) plotted give points on a straight line through the origin (y = 2x).

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares the two sequences additively — 'Rule B is 6 more than Rule A' — instead of multiplicatively ('twice')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up several corresponding pairs and ask 'is the gap the same or growing?'; the ×2 ratio is constant while the difference grows — compare 'how many times' not 'how many more', supported by a tape diagram
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the relationship as an added amount, usually read off the first pair; it fails later because the gap grows (3, 6, 9, 12)

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares WITHIN one sequence (the +3 or +6 step) rather than between the corresponding terms of the two sequences
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to a single column (say position 3): 'what is B here, what is A here, how do they compare?' — the comparison is vertical across the two rows, not horizontal
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer is about how one sequence grows down its own row, not how B relates to A at the same position

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the ordered pair — plots (6, 3) instead of (3, 6), or counts up-then-across
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish the convention: the first number moves you ACROSS (Rule A, x), the second moves you UP (Rule B, y); re-plot one pair together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points sit on the wrong side of / below the intended line; the (x, y) order is not respected

errorPatterns.pattern: Hunts for a single hidden rule connecting both sequences instead of generating each from its given rule
errorPatterns.nextMove: The rules are GIVEN — generate each sequence directly from its own rule, THEN look for the relationship between them; you are not hunting a secret rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Invents a rule or looks for 'the pattern' rather than applying the two rules as given, then comparing

responseLevels.gap: Cannot generate both sequences reliably from the rules, or describes only how one sequence grows; gives no relationship between corresponding terms; pairs and plot are missing or reversed.
responseLevels.full: Generates both, states B is twice A at every corresponding position and explains why from the steps (6 = 2×3, both start at 0), forms correctly ordered pairs, plots them on the ray through the origin, and recognises that the additive gap grows while the ×2 ratio stays constant — transferring to predict the relationship for a new pair or a changed start.
responseLevels.partial: Generates both sequences and lines them up, but describes the relationship additively ('6 more') or only for the first pair, and/or plots pairs mechanically without connecting the constant ×2 to the straight line — has the parts (two sequences, some pairs) but not the multiplicative structure joining them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Use two rules. Rule A: start at 0, add 3. Rule B: start at 0, add 6. Write out the first six numbers of each, lined up underneath one another. Then tell me how a number in Rule B compares with the number in the SAME position in Rule A — and why it works out that way. Finally, turn the first four matching pairs into points and plot them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the multiplicative structure says B is TWICE A in every position and explains it from the steps (6 = 2×3, both start at 0); the ×2 holds in every column. A child comparing additively says 'B is 6 more' — true only for an early pair, and decisively wrong because the DIFFERENCE grows (3, 6, 9, …), so 'plus 6' fails from the second pair on. Whether they compare corresponding terms across the two rows (vertical) or just read a within-row step (+3, +6) exposes the corresponding-terms confusion; and plotting (3,6) versus (6,3) exposes the ordered-pair order.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7 (highest-centrality node in the domain — the anchor the whole topic hangs on); a rainforest is a thick, tall forest in hot, wet places near the Equator where it rains almost every day, making a warm, damp world where huge numbers of plants and animals thrive.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' (habitats and how they provide for living things) and KS1 Geography (hot/cold places; the Equator).
• Standards—US: NGSS 2-LS4-1 (diversity of life in a habitat); K-ESS3-1 (organisms and their environment); K-ESS2-1 (weather patterns).
• Operational details: build the definition from THREE sticky features — HOT, WET (rains nearly every day), and near the EQUATOR (the warm middle of the Earth) — and the result: so many plants and animals that a rainforest is the busiest habitat on land. Distinguish it from woods children know at home (a rainforest is warmer, far wetter, evergreen, and packed with life). Seed the word 'habitat' as 'a home that gives living things what they need'.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) say a rainforest is a hot, wet, thick forest; Tier B (6) name the two conditions (hot + lots of rain) that make it; Tier C (7) explain that rainforests are near the warm Equator and are home to a huge number of plants and animals.
bestPractices: Anchor the definition on three memorable features (hot, wet, near the Equator) rather than a wordy description
Contrast with a familiar local wood so children feel what makes a rainforest different (warmer, wetter, greener all year, far more life)
Use vivid sensory imagery — dripping leaves, constant warmth, animal noise — to make 'warm and damp' concrete
Introduce 'habitat' gently as a home that meets living things' needs, connecting to later habitat work
Link 'near the Equator' to the warm middle of the globe, building the where-they-are idea for the next topic
keyRepresentations: Three-feature card: hot thermometer + rain cloud + globe with the Equator marked
Lush rainforest scene teeming with plants and animals to convey 'thrives'
Local-wood vs rainforest side-by-side comparison
Globe with a green rainforest belt around the warm middle
commonMisconceptions: A rainforest is just any big wood — it is specifically hot, extremely wet, and near the Equator
Rainforests are cold and dark like a spooky forest — they are warm and humid
It rains only sometimes — in a tropical rainforest it rains almost every day
Rainforests are empty and quiet — they hold more kinds of plants and animals than almost anywhere on land
Rainforests are found all over, including cold places — tropical rainforests cluster near the warm Equator

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, anchor the concept 'rainforest' on three memorable features — HOT, WET (rains almost every day), and near the EQUATOR (the warm middle of the Earth) — and the result: more kinds of plants and animals thrive there than almost anywhere on land. Contrast with a familiar local wood so children feel the difference (warmer, far wetter, green all year, far more life). Seed 'habitat' gently as 'a home that gives living things what they need'. The key insight is the combination: hot + wet + near the Equator makes the crowded green world, which also separates a rainforest from a hot, dry desert.

activities.title: Explore a rainforest scene and find its three features
feedback: If a child says only 'a big forest', prompt: is it hot? how often does it rain? where on the globe is it? Add the missing features.
If a child names the features as separate facts, ask them to join them: 'What do hot AND lots of rain together make happen to the plants?'
Reinforce correct answers by pointing back to the picture: the daily rain and constant heat are why the leaves are so green and the branches so crowded with life.

OPTIONAL interaction examples (not required): tapping the rain cloud could play a pattering shower; tapping a thermometer could reveal 'always hot'; tapping a globe could zoom to show the green equatorial belt; tapping the busy branches could reveal 'more kinds of plants and animals live here than almost anywhere on land'.
activities.rationale: A picture-first approach is proposed to fit 5–7: the definition is a small set of features plus a rich scene conveying 'thrives'. Making each feature discoverable in a concrete scene keeps the grain age-appropriate and ties the abstract conditions to visible consequences.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests occur in hot, very wet regions near the Equator with near-daily rainfall and exceptional biodiversity
KS1 pupils identify habitats and how they provide for living things and locate hot places and the Equator
learnerActions: Look closely at a lush rainforest picture full of parrots, monkeys, frogs and vines; describe what you see, and imagine what you would hear and feel if you were there (dripping leaves, warm damp air, animal noise).

Find and name the rain cloud, the thermometer, and the Equator on a small globe; say what each one tells you: it rains almost every day, it is always hot, and rainforests sit in a green belt around the warm middle of the Earth.
Say in your own words why so many plants and animals can live here.
Put the three features together: hot + lots of rain + near the Equator = a rainforest.
activities.intendedInsight: A rainforest is defined by three features working together (hot, very wet, near the Equator), and that combination is why it is the busiest habitat on land — not just any big wood.

activities.title: Compare a rainforest with the woods near you
feedback: If a child says a rainforest is the same as their local wood, revisit each feature one at a time (heat, rain, green-all-year, amount of life).
Praise answers that name a specific difference rather than 'it's bigger'; steer toward heat and constant rain as the key differences.
activities.rationale: Contrasting with a familiar habitat is proposed to make the defining features felt rather than memorised, and it addresses the common idea that a rainforest is just any big wood. The comparison also relates the greater abundance and variety of life to the hot, wet environment.
sourceClaims: Students observe the diversity of life in a habitat and relate organisms to their environment
learnerActions: Look at a local wood and a rainforest side by side.
List how they are different: which is warmer, which is wetter, which stays green all year, which has more kinds of plants and animals.
Use a lift-the-flap or fold-over card to answer 'How is this different from the woods near you?' and stack up: warmer, wetter, green all year, far more life.
Say one sentence that explains what makes a rainforest special compared to an ordinary wood.
activities.intendedInsight: A rainforest is not just any big woodland — compared with a typical cooler local wood, it is hotter, far wetter all year, green all year, and packed with far more kinds of life.

activities.title: Rainforest or desert? — telling hot-and-wet from hot-and-dry
feedback: If a child says a rainforest is dry and sandy because 'hot places don't get much rain', contrast a hot desert (hot, dry) with a rainforest (hot, wet, rains almost every day) and show it's the rain, added to the heat, that makes it green.

A full answer names water/rain as the difference AND connects the daily rain to the lush growth; a partial answer knows it's hot and rainy but treats those as separate facts; a gap answer says it's hot and dry or just 'a big forest' with no sense of constant rain.
If a child can't locate rainforests, point to the warm middle of the globe near the Equator.
Treat the 'if it stopped raining' question as reasoning practice: welcome sensible predictions (plants would dry out, less green) rather than grading a single correct fact.
activities.rationale: This diagnostic contrast surfaces the 'hot means dry' misconception and checks whether the child connects the defining conditions to the living result — the heart of the concept.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests occur in hot, very wet regions near the Equator with near-daily rainfall and exceptional biodiversity
learnerActions: Discuss: a hot desert is hot and a rainforest is hot — so why isn't a rainforest just a hot, dry place like a hot desert?
Name the one thing that makes the difference: WATER/rain. A rainforest is hot AND very wet; a hot desert is hot but dry.
Explain how you know: the near-daily rain, together with the year-round warmth, is why rainforest plants grow tall and thick and so many animals live there.

Wonder together about the probing questions (there is no single right answer — give your reasons): Why do the plants grow so tall and thick? Where on a globe would you look — top, bottom, or middle? What might happen if it stopped raining for a whole year?
activities.intendedInsight: It is the combination of heat AND lots of rain, near the Equator, that makes a rainforest lush — heat alone (as in a desert) does not.

constraints: Checkpoint tiers: a 5-year-old says a rainforest is a hot, wet, thick forest; a 6-year-old names the two conditions (hot + lots of rain) that make it; a 7-year-old explains rainforests are near the warm Equator and home to a huge number of plants and animals.
Introduce 'habitat' gently ('a home that meets living things' needs') — do not over-formalise it at this age.

Sorting tasks and feature multiple-choice questions can check the definition but should come after the picture/scene has built it; recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit the child's own explanation of the hot+wet combination.

A build-a-rainforest task (add heat and rain to a bare patch and watch green life appear) is a useful alternative for making the hot+wet→thriving link felt, but the primary goal here is recognising what a rainforest IS; keep the demonstration honest — real rainforest growth is gradual, not instant.

A guided 'stepping into the rainforest' chat can support vocabulary and engagement; for a definitional topic at this age we propose anchoring primarily on a concrete scene with contrast, using dialogue to supplement rather than replace it — this is a design preference, not an evidenced ranking of media.
Optional tap/flap interactions are illustrative examples to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features; the same learning can occur with a printed scene, a read-aloud, and a comparison card.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all three sources are marked verified:false in the row and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claims support general curriculum alignment and rainforest basics (topic/content accuracy); they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any one activity format. No necessity or 'only this teaches' claims should be inferred.
Activity 2's attached NGSS diversity claim supports the diversity-to-environment content within the comparison, not the pedagogical efficacy of the side-by-side contrast format itself.
The legacy entry rated 3D as 'poor' and dialogue as secondary; these were catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been reframed as scoped alternatives with stated purposes.

Simplification to watch: tropical rainforests are the hot, wet, near-Equator type described here; temperate rainforests exist in cooler regions. For this age the equatorial/tropical framing is appropriate, but 'all rainforests are near the Equator' is a simplification worth noting for an educator.
The 'if it stopped raining for a year' probe is an open prediction, not a question with one correct answer; it is framed as reasoning practice.

No substantive learner-facing factual errors or internal contradictions were found; corrections are limited to softening a comparative media-efficacy claim, scoping source claims to content support, growth-demonstration honesty, and educator-facing flags.

probeDeeper: Why do you think the plants grow so tall and thick in a rainforest?
Where on a globe would you look to find rainforests — near the top, the bottom, or the middle?
If it stopped raining in a rainforest for a whole year, what do you think would happen to it?
assess.correctAnswer: A rainforest is hot AND very wet — it rains almost every day, so it's warm and damp, and that's why so many tall thick plants and lots of animals can live there. A desert is hot but dry. It's the combination of heat and lots of rain, near the Equator, that makes a rainforest.

errorPatterns.pattern: hot places are dry like a desert — 'it's hot so it must be dry and sandy'
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast a desert (hot, dry) with a rainforest (hot, wet, rains daily); show it's the rain that makes it green
errorPatterns.distractor: It's dry and sandy, because hot places don't get much rain
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes a rainforest as dry/sandy or can't distinguish it from a desert

errorPatterns.nextMove: add the two defining features: hot and very wet all year, near the Equator

responseLevels.gap: Says a rainforest is hot and dry, or just 'a big forest', with no sense of constant rain.
responseLevels.full: Describes a rainforest as hot AND wet with near-daily rain near the Equator, and links that combination to why plants grow tall and thick and so many animals live there; contrasts it with a hot dry desert.
responseLevels.partial: Knows it's hot and rainy but treats those as two separate facts and can't say the combination near the Equator is what makes it lush.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A desert is hot and a rainforest is hot — so why isn't a rainforest just a hot, sandy place like a desert? What makes a rainforest different, and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'hot means dry' can't say what separates a rainforest from a desert; the child with the concept names WATER/rain as the difference. The reason-tier ('how do you know') surfaces whether they connect the daily rain to the lush growth.

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, repeated reasoning turns into deriving and rule-describing: using a known double to get a near-double (6+7 = 6+6+1 = 13), noticing that subtracting 10 always drops the tens digit by one, and stating a rule for a sequence ('add 5 each time, so the ones digit alternates 0, 5'). The MP8 habit is to notice the repeated step, articulate it as a rule, and use it to predict — while checking it actually holds. Teaching should make the known fact and the derived one adjacent (a double and its near-double side by side) and press for the rule in the child's words, then test it on a fresh case.
bestPractices: Put a doubles fact next to its near-double (6+6 and 6+7) so the '+1' adjustment is seen, not computed from scratch
Ask the child to state the rule ('what's happening each time?') and then test it on the next case to guard against a rule taken from too few examples
Use a hundred square / place-value cards so −10 visibly drops the tens digit each time
Record a sequence and its step so the repeating structure and its rule are both on show ('+5, +5, +5')
keyRepresentations: Doubles and near-doubles on ten-frames / cubes (double + 1)
Hundred square and place-value cards for ±10
Number line marked with equal repeated steps (+5)
Bead strings for repeated addition patterns
commonMisconceptions: Recomputes 6+7 from one, not seeing it as the known double 6+6 plus 1
Applies the near-double adjustment wrongly (adds 2, or doubles the larger number)
States a rule from one or two cases and assumes it holds without testing
Subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones instead of dropping the tens digit

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, this topic builds the habit of looking for and expressing regularity in repeated reasoning (MP8): deriving a near-double from a known double (6+7 = 6+6+1 = 13), noticing that subtracting 10 from a two-digit number drops the tens digit by one, and stating a sequence rule ('+5 each time starting from 5, so the ones digit alternates 5, 0') — then TESTING that rule on a fresh case rather than trusting it from one or two examples. Core teaching moves: place a known fact adjacent to the derived one so the adjustment is seen not recomputed, press for the rule in the child's own words, and always test the generalisation on a new case.

activities.title: Near-doubles builder: the double plus one
feedback: If the child counts up from 6 (or from 1) rather than referring to 6+6, put 6+6 and 6+7 side by side so the single extra cube is visible, and name 6+7 as 'the double and one more'.
If the child says 6+7=14 (added two) or doubles the 7, use the two rows to show exactly ONE cube was added — steady the adjustment; no need to reteach doubles.
Probe flexibility: 'you used 6+6 to get 6+7 — could you use 7+7 instead (one less than 14)? which double is handiest here?'
activities.rationale: Making the known fact and the derived one physically adjacent lets the '+1' be observed rather than computed, which is the derive-from-known-facts habit the guidance describes and keeps the derivation visible before fading support; repeating the adjustment across 6+7, 6+8 and 7+8 begins the repeated-reasoning shortcut.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
learnerActions: Set out two rows of 6 cubes (or two ten-frames of 6) and confirm the double: 6+6=12.
Add exactly ONE more cube to one row and say the new total: 6+7=13. State it as 'the double I know, and one more'.
Repeat for 6+8 ('two more than the double, so 14') and for another double you know, e.g. 7+7=14 so 7+8=15.
Say aloud which double you used and how many you adjusted by, before giving the total.
activities.intendedInsight: A near-double can be derived from an adjacent known double by adjusting, instead of counting up from one.

activities.title: State a rule, then test it
feedback: If the child announces 'it's add 5' after two terms and won't check, do not simply confirm or correct it — ask 'how could we be sure? test the next one' so the checking habit forms.
If a later term surprises the child, treat the surprise as the lesson: a rule from too few cases can be wrong; revise and re-test.
Ask 'your rule is add 5 — what will the ones digit of the next three terms be? how do you know?' to check the rule predicts, not just describes.
activities.rationale: Recording the sequence and its step together — on a number line or bead string as well as in writing — puts the repeating structure and its rule both on show (representations making the structure visible), and requiring a test on the next case guards against a generalisation drawn from too few examples.
sourceClaims: MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
learnerActions: Lay out the first few terms of a sequence (e.g. 5, 10, 15, 20) and say the repeating step out loud: '+5, +5, +5'. Optionally show the equal +5 jumps on a number line or bead string so the repeating structure is visible.
State the rule in your own words: 'each time we add 5'. Predict the NEXT term before extending.
Predict the ones digit of the next three terms (25, 30, 35) and say why ('they alternate 5, 0, 5').

TEST it: have the adult reveal the next term of the given sequence (e.g. uncover a hidden card or the next group on the bead string) and compare it with your prediction; if it does not match, revise the rule. Extending the sequence yourself with your own rule is not a test.
Then say how you could be sure a rule is right before trusting it.
activities.intendedInsight: A rule guessed from a couple of cases should be tested on fresh cases before we rely on it: a passing test makes us more confident (it does not prove the rule), while one failing case shows the rule needs revising — this is the MP8 discipline of checking a generalisation.

activities.title: Subtracting 10 on a hundred square — and bounding the rule
feedback: If the child subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones, use the hundred square to show the move is one whole row back (straight up on a square with 1 in the top row; straight down on a square numbered from the bottom) — the ones digit does not change.
Counterexample to bound the rule: 'you said take away ten drops the tens digit — does take away ONE do that to 45?' (45−1=44) to check the child limits the rule to −10.
Confirm by reading the place-value cards: the tens card goes down one, the ones card is untouched.
activities.rationale: A hundred square or place-value cards make the −10 move structural rather than counted, and testing whether −1 behaves the same teaches the child to bound a generalisation to its conditions and evaluate reasonableness.
sourceClaims: MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
learnerActions: On a hundred square (or with place-value cards), start at a two-digit number such as 45 and subtract 10; land on 35 and notice the tens digit dropped by one while the ones digit stayed the same.
Repeat from two or three other starting numbers to see the same pattern each time; state the rule: 'take away 10 drops the tens digit by one'.
Test the boundary: does taking away ONE do the same thing? Try 45−1 (which gives 44) and see it does not — so the rule is only for −10.
Say the rule in your own words AND what it does NOT cover.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting 10 from a two-digit number lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — and a good rule is stated with the conditions under which it holds.

activities.title: Check-in: which fact did you use?
feedback: A correct number alone does not show repeated-reasoning insight — follow up with 'which fact did you use?' because a scored blank does not reveal whether the rule was reasoned or guessed.
If the child recomputes from one, redirect to the adjacent known double before accepting the answer.
activities.rationale: Fill-in and sequence-continuation items can confirm a correct answer, but because scoring alone cannot reveal whether a derivation occurred or whether a rule was reasoned or guessed, pair every item with a 'how did you get it?' question. This is a check, best used after hands-on work; it verifies recall and continuation without by itself eliciting the child's reasoning.
learnerActions: Answer short derivation prompts such as '6+6=12, so 6+7=__' and 'continue the sequence 5, 10, 15, __'.
For each answer, say WHICH known fact or rule you used to get it, not just the number.
Try at least one where you explain how you'd check your answer is reasonable.
activities.intendedInsight: Getting the right number is not enough; the target is reusing a known fact or rule and being able to justify it.

constraints: This is a META/mathematical-thinking topic for ages 6-7: the goal is the derive-and-check habit, not just correct totals. Listen for reuse of a known fact and the adjustment, not just the answer 13.

Fill-in or sequence-continuation checks can show whether a correct answer was produced but cannot by themselves reveal whether a derivation occurred or whether a rule was reasoned, recalled or guessed; always pair with 'which fact did you use?' and treat them as a follow-up to hands-on building, not a replacement.

A static near-doubles card or annotated −10 column can illustrate the move for reference, but does not let the child adjust the quantity or test a self-stated rule; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main task.
Bound the −10 rule explicitly: it lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — this specific 'drop the tens by one' rule does not generalise to −1 or other amounts.
Do not confirm or correct a child's sequence rule for them when the aim is building the checking habit; prompt them to test the next case instead.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original recommendation leaned on a specific interactive 'near-doubles builder' and 'sequence machine' and rated conversation and 3D artefacts 'poor'. Those comparative/necessity ratings are catalog preferences, not established efficacy; the concrete affordances (live total update when a cube is added, a machine flagging a wrong predicted term) are preserved here as optional ways to make the mechanism visible, achievable with physical cubes, ten-frames, number lines, bead strings, hundred squares, or screen tools.

The original claims that '3D adds no structural information' and that 'open dialogue gives nothing concrete' were omitted as unsupported universal statements; spoken explanation of which fact was used is in fact central to assessing this reasoning habit, while a sort or fill-in check alone verifies classification/recall without eliciting that explanation.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 6+6=12, 6+7=13, 6+8=14, 7+7=14, 7+8=15, 45−10=35, 45−1=44 all check out; the sequence 5,10,15,20 continuing 25,30,35 has ones digits alternating 5,0,5. Independent re-review found no arithmetic or logic errors to correct.
The number-line (+5) and bead-string representations from the original keyRepresentations are retained as optional supports in the sequence activity.

Independent re-review adjusted only source attribution: the EEF visible-representation claim was added to Activity 2 because its rationale directly invokes representations making the repeating structure visible. No learner-facing error was found.

probeDeeper: Ask 'you used 6+6 to get 6+7 — could you use 7+7 to get 6+7 as well? which double is handiest?' to test flexible reuse of known facts
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'you said take away ten drops the tens digit — does taking away ten from 45 give 35? what about taking away ONE?' to check the child bounds the rule to −10
Ask 'your rule is add 5 — what will the ones digit of the next three terms be? how do you know?' to probe whether the rule predicts, not just describes
Ask 'how could you check your rule is right before trusting it?' to surface the MP8 habit of testing a generalisation
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child deriving from the known double: '6+7 is one more than 6+6, so 13; 6+8 is two more, so 14.' The reuse of the known fact and the adjustment, not just 13, is the target.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Put 6+6 and 6+7 side by side on ten-frames so the single extra cube is visible; name 6+7 as 'the double and one more'
