errorPatterns.pattern: Applies the near-double adjustment wrongly — adds two, or doubles the 7 instead of the 6
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with the two ten-frames to see exactly ONE cube was added; do not reteach doubles, just steady the adjustment
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says 6+7 = 14 (added 2) or 6+7 = 6+7+7

errorPatterns.pattern: States a sequence rule from one or two cases and assumes it holds without testing further
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT simply confirm or correct the rule; ask 'how could we be sure? test the next one' so the habit of checking a generalisation forms
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child announces 'it's add 5' after two terms and won't check, or is surprised when a later term breaks their rule

responseLevels.gap: Recomputes each sum from one, mis-adjusts near-doubles, and states rules without testing; each result treated as new
responseLevels.full: Independently derives from known facts (double ± 1, −10 drops the tens digit), states a sequence rule AND tests it on a fresh case, and predicts confidently — transferring the derive-and-check habit unprompted

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You know 6 + 6 = 12. Use that to work out 6 + 7 quickly, without counting from one. Then tell me how it would help with 6 + 8.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reaching 13 by counting up shows no repeated-reasoning insight; deriving it as 'the double plus one' does. A child using the structure adjusts the known fact and extends the idea to 6+8; a child without it recounts each sum from the start.

pedagogy.summary: Algebraic vocabulary (expression, equation, inequality, term, coefficient, factor) is best taught not as definitions to memorise but as language the child USES while doing and justifying maths. The load-bearing distinction is expression vs equation, which turns on the equals sign: an expression represents a value; an equation is a statement that can be true or false and therefore tested; an inequality uses <, >, ≤, ≥ instead. Teach the '=' relationally (sameness/balance) rather than operationally ('work out the answer'), and name terms/coefficients/factors on real expressions, including negative signs.
bestPractices: Contrast minimal pairs aloud: 2a+3 (expression) vs 2a+3=11 (equation) vs 2a+3<11 (inequality) — the child must say which is which and why, pointing to the =, <, or > as the deciding feature.
Use an Always/Sometimes/Never-true card sort so students must TEST statements by substitution rather than 'solve' them — this forces the relational meaning of the equals sign.
Insist on justification ('how do you know it's an equation and not an expression?') rather than accepting the label alone.
Teach '=' as balance/sameness (both sides name the same value), explicitly challenging the 'makes/gives the answer' reading, e.g. accept and discuss 7 = 3 + 4 and 3 + 4 = _ + 2.
Name terms, coefficients and factors on genuine expressions including signs, e.g. in 5x − 2y + 7 there are three terms, the coefficient of x is 5, of y is −2, and 7 is a constant.
keyRepresentations: Card sort into Expression / Equation / Inequality bins (and Always/Sometimes/Never true)
Balance scale for the equals sign as sameness
Colour-coded term boxes that isolate each term with its sign
Number line for representing inequalities
commonMisconceptions: Calls any algebra string an 'equation' and expects to 'solve' it, even with no equals sign (writes an expression when asked for an equation).
Reads '=' operationally ('= means work out the answer'), so rejects 8 = 3 + 5 or treats an equation as an instruction rather than a statement.
Conjoins terms / treats a letter as an object, so miscounts terms or reads 3a + 2b as a single quantity (or '5ab').
Treats an inequality as if it were an equation with a single answer, ignoring the range of values it describes.

learn.summary: Teach algebraic vocabulary (expression, equation, inequality, term, coefficient, factor) as language a learner USES while doing and justifying maths, not as definitions to memorise. The load-bearing distinction is expression vs equation, which turns on the equals sign: an expression names a value; an equation is a statement that can be true or false, so it can be tested by substitution; an inequality uses <, >, ≤, ≥ and is also a statement that can be tested; at this level it is typically true for a whole range of values (e.g. 2a + 3 < 11 for a < 4), though some inequalities are true for all values or for none. Teach '=' relationally (both sides name the same value / balance), explicitly challenging the operational 'work out the answer' reading, and name terms, coefficients and factors on genuine expressions including negative signs.

activities.title: Build an equation from an expression (card-sort workspace)
feedback: If a learner labels the bare 2a + 3 an equation and starts hunting for a value of a, put 2a + 3 and 2a + 3 = 11 side by side and ask: what changed, and what can you do now that you could not before? Draw out that the '=' is what creates a statement to test.
If a learner tries to 'solve' an inequality for a single answer, ask how many values of a make 2a + 3 < 11 true, and have them check several values to see it holds for a whole range (a < 4).

Optional interaction that makes the mechanism concrete: a greyed-out 'Test it' button that only lights once an '=' is present, and a truth-lamp that flips red↔green as a candidate value is slid in — these illustrate testability, they are not required for the lesson.
activities.rationale: A felt expression→equation transformation targets the documented error of writing/treating an expression as an equation, and substitution-based testing is intended to require the relational meaning of the equals sign rather than an operational 'find the answer' reading.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should use and interpret the vocabulary of expressions, equations, inequalities, terms and factors, and substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions.

In trials, students commonly write an expression (e.g. 'y+3') when asked for an equation, and fail to include a variable; the lesson requires them to TEST statements by substitution rather than assume, and highlights that some assume different letters must take different values.

Children frequently interpret the equals sign operationally ('do something / write the answer') rather than relationally (a statement that the two sides are equal), which underlies difficulty with equations.
learnerActions: Start with 2a + 3 sitting on its own and say aloud whether there is anything to 'test' or 'solve' — establish that it just names a value.
Drag an '=' and the number 11 alongside it to form 2a + 3 = 11, and say what has now changed.

Sort a set of six cards into Expression / Equation / Inequality bins (e.g. 2a + 3, 2a + 3 = 11, 2a + 3 < 11), pointing each time to the =, <, >, ≤ or ≥ as the deciding feature, or saying that no such sign is present for an expression.
Substitute candidate values of a into 2a + 3 = 11 to test whether the statement is true or false; confirm it is true only at a = 4.

Also do an Always / Sometimes / Never true card sort, TESTING each statement by substitution rather than trying to 'solve' it, and recognising that one counterexample rules out 'always' (and one true case rules out 'never'), but checking a few values alone cannot prove 'always' or 'never' — give a reason for those.
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign turns an inert value (expression) into a statement that can be true or false (equation) and therefore tested; an inequality is also a testable statement, and here (2a + 3 < 11) it is true across a whole range of values (a < 4) rather than at a single answer.

activities.title: Read '=' as balance and sameness
feedback: If a learner reads 2a + 3 = 11 as 'do 2a + 3 and the answer is 11', recast it as 'the two sides are the same value' and use the balance image to make sameness visible.
If a learner rejects 8 = 3 + 5 as 'the wrong way round', present it and 3 + 4 = ___ + 2 deliberately and discuss why both are legitimate statements about sameness.
activities.rationale: Addresses the well-documented operational reading of the equals sign by having learners accept and justify relationally-formatted equalities.
sourceClaims: Children frequently interpret the equals sign operationally ('do something / write the answer') rather than relationally (a statement that the two sides are equal), which underlies difficulty with equations.
learnerActions: Using a balance scale (physical or depicted), show that both sides of an equation name the same amount.
Judge and discuss statements written in unfamiliar orders, e.g. 7 = 3 + 4 and 3 + 4 = ___ + 2, deciding whether each is legitimate and what goes in the blank.
Explain to a partner why 3 + 4 = 7 and 7 = 3 + 4 are NOT different statements despite one looking 'backwards'.
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign asserts that both sides have the same value; it is not an instruction to 'produce the answer on the right', so reversed and two-sided equalities are perfectly valid.

activities.title: Name terms, coefficients and factors — keeping the signs
feedback: If a learner counts one or two terms in 5x − 2y + 7 or merges 3a + 2b, have them box each term with its sign and count the boxes; contrast with 3a + 2a to show when combining is valid.
If a learner gives the coefficient of y as 2 rather than −2, point to the minus sign immediately in front and have them read the term as a whole, sign included.
activities.rationale: Letter-as-object and conjoining of unlike terms are persistent interpretations among 11–16 year-olds; isolating each signed term and contrasting like with unlike terms targets these directly.
sourceClaims: Letter-as-object and the conjoining of unlike terms are persistent, well-documented interpretations of algebraic letters among 11–16 year-olds.
KS3 pupils should use and interpret the vocabulary of expressions, equations, inequalities, terms and factors, and substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions.
learnerActions: On 5x − 2y + 7, box each term WITH its sign and count the boxes (three terms).
State the coefficient of x (5) and of y (−2), being explicit that the minus sign belongs to the coefficient, and name 7 as the constant.
Contrast 3a + 2b (two terms, cannot be combined) with 3a + 2a (like terms that can) to resist conjoining and the '5ab' error.
On 2(a + 3), identify it as an expression whose factors are 2 and (a + 3), and state what would turn it into an equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Terms are the parts separated by + and − (each carrying its own sign); a coefficient is the number multiplying a letter, signs included; factors are what is multiplied together — and a letter stands for a number, not a labelled object, so unlike terms cannot be merged.

activities.title: Justify the word you chose ('convince me')
feedback: Accept a label only with a reason; if the reason is 'it just looks like one', redirect the learner to point to the =, <, or > AND say what it does to the statement.
If a learner cannot say what is missing from an expression, pair it with the matching equation so the added '=' and right-hand side are visible.
activities.rationale: Insisting on justification rather than the bare label is intended to surface whether the learner is relating the symbol to its meaning or merely matching surface features; spoken challenge can rehearse precise usage alongside the manipulation-based work.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should use and interpret the vocabulary of expressions, equations, inequalities, terms and factors, and substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions.
learnerActions: After labelling a card, answer 'how do you know it's an equation and not an expression?' by pointing to the deciding symbol and saying what it does.
Respond to a sceptical questioner who challenges sloppy usage, e.g. 'you called that an equation — convince me', and defend or correct the label.
Explain, for an expression you chose, what you would add to make it an equation and what you could then do that you cannot do now.
activities.intendedInsight: Precise algebraic language is a tool for reasoning: being asked to justify a label is intended to push the learner past surface pattern-matching to state what the deciding symbol (=, <, >) actually means — that an equals sign makes a testable statement of sameness, not just that a particular symbol is present.

constraints: This is a LANGUAGE objective for ages 11–12: the goal is precise USE and justification of vocabulary, not memorised definitions; always require the learner to say which category and why.

Categorization/matching/multiple-choice checks (sort statements into expression/equation/inequality; match term to coefficient; 'which change turns 2a+3 into an equation?') assess the distinction efficiently but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of an equation from an expression — use them after, not instead of, the build-and-test activity.

A static labelled 'anatomy' (tap the =, a term, a coefficient to reveal its name) works as a reference glossary but does not stage the expression↔equation transformation that carries the key insight; this is a limitation of a glossary-style reference, not an impossibility of static media.

Optional interactive features (greyed-out 'Test it' button, truth-lamp, value sliders, balance scale, colour-coded signed term boxes, number line for inequalities) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete; none is mandatory and they should not replace the learner's own stating and justifying.
A balance scale and value substitution are approximations of 'both sides name the same value'; keep the represented idea (sameness/testability) in focus rather than the prop.

All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles, not the tested effectiveness of any specific activity.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic checked): for 2a + 3 = 11, a = 4 is correct (8 + 3 = 11). For 2a + 3 < 11, the solution is a < 4, correct. In 5x − 2y + 7 there are three terms; coefficient of x = 5, of y = −2, constant = 7 — correct and signs preserved. 3 + 4 = 7 and 7 = 3 + 4 are the same relational statement — correct. 2(a + 3) has factors 2 and (a + 3).

Two source claims (Kieran 1981 on the operational/relational equals sign, and Hodgen et al. 2009 on letter-as-object/conjoining) carry verified:false in the original row; they are cited here to support teaching principles only, with no upgrade of their confidence or evidence status.

The original framing that 3D 'adds nothing' to a symbolic distinction has been softened to a scope note (a static or non-spatial representation can still teach the parts; manipulation additionally stages the transformation) rather than asserted as a universal law.
Removed the original claim that a static reveal 'cannot stage' the transformation, restating it as a limitation of a glossary-style reference rather than an impossibility.

Independent-review correction: activity 4's intendedInsight previously treated 'point to the =, <, > feature' as the goal while opposing it to 'surface appearance', which is contradictory because the symbol is itself a surface feature; reworded so justification goes beyond symbol-spotting to the symbol's relational meaning, consistent with the partial/full response levels.
Efficacy verbs ('forces', 'surfaces') in activity rationales/insights were softened to intended-effect wording to avoid asserting proven outcomes of untested proposals.

probeDeeper: You said this one is an expression — what would you have to add to make it an equation, and what could you then do that you can't do now?
Point to the terms in 5x − 2y + 7. How many are there, and what is the coefficient of x? Of y?
Your friend says 3 + 4 = 7 and 7 = 3 + 4 are different, because the second one is 'backwards'. What would you tell them? (counterexample probing the relational equals sign)
Is x + 2 > 10 an equation? If not, what is it, and how many values of x make it true?
assess.correctAnswer: 2a + 3 is an expression — it has no equals sign, so there is nothing to test; it just represents a value. 2a + 3 = 11 is an equation — a statement that can be true or false, so you can solve it (a = 4). 2a + 3 < 11 is an inequality — true for a range of values (a < 4). To turn the expression into an equation you set it equal to something.

errorPatterns.pattern: Calls an expression an equation and expects to 'solve' it — 'it's an equation, so a = something' — cannot say what is missing (documented as students writing expressions when asked for equations).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put the matched pair 2a+3 and 2a+3=11 side by side; ask what changed and what you can now do that you could not before. Establish that the '=' is what turns a value into a statement to test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels the bare 2a+3 an equation and starts trying to find a value of a, or cannot point to the equals sign as what an equation must have.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operational reading of the equals sign — '= means work out the answer' — so treats an equation as an instruction and is uneasy with 8 = 3 + 5 or 3 + 4 = _ + 2.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a balance scale: both sides name the same amount. Deliberately present 7 = 3 + 4 and 3 + 4 = _ + 2 and discuss why they are legitimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes 2a+3=11 as 'do 2a+3 and the answer is 11' rather than 'the two sides are the same'; rejects a reversed or two-sided equality as 'backwards' or 'wrong way round'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conjoins terms / treats letters as objects, so miscounts terms or reads 3a + 2b as one quantity (or '5ab').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Box each term WITH its sign; count the boxes. Contrast 3a+2b (two terms, cannot combine) with 3a+2a (like terms). Re-establish that a letter stands for a number, not a labelled object.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked how many terms are in 5x − 2y + 7, gives one or two, or merges 3a+2b; misreads the coefficient of y as 2 rather than −2 (drops the sign).

responseLevels.gap: Uses 'equation' as a catch-all for any string of algebra; cannot point to the equals sign as the distinguishing feature; tries to 'solve' an expression or reads '=' as 'gives the answer'.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes all three AND explains that the equals sign makes a statement that can be true or false (relational), identifies terms, coefficients and factors correctly including signs, and transfers to a new case — e.g. recognises 2(a+3) as an expression whose factor is 2, and states what would turn it into an equation.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly sorts expression/equation/inequality by spotting the =, <, > symbols, but cannot yet articulate WHY it matters (that an equation is a testable statement) or slips on terms/coefficients when negative signs are involved — lists the surface features without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three cards in front of the child: 2a + 3, then 2a + 3 = 11, then 2a + 3 < 11. Say: 'You and a partner are checking work. Your partner wrote 2a + 3 and called it an equation. Talk me through whether that's the right word, what you'd actually call each of these three, and what you could DO with each one.' Then listen — do not offer the words yourself.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the relational meaning of '=' names 2a+3 an expression, cites the MISSING equals sign, and says an equation is something you can test/solve. A child with the operational reading calls everything an 'equation to solve', tries to 'find a' from the bare expression, and cannot say what distinguishes the three — the same context separates the two reasoners because only correct use references the =, <, > signs as the deciding feature.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should use and interpret the vocabulary of expressions, equations, inequalities, terms and factors, and substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS3)

sources.claim: In trials, students commonly write an expression (e.g. 'y+3') when asked for an equation, and fail to include a variable; the lesson requires them to TEST statements by substitution rather than assume, and highlights that some assume different letters must take different values.
sources.source: Mathematics Assessment Project — 'Sorting Equations and Identities' Classroom Challenge (Common Issues table & activity)

sources.claim: Children frequently interpret the equals sign operationally ('do something / write the answer') rather than relationally (a statement that the two sides are equal), which underlies difficulty with equations.
sources.source: Kieran, C. (1981). Concepts associated with the equality symbol. Educational Studies in Mathematics, 12(3), 317–326.

sources.claim: Letter-as-object and the conjoining of unlike terms are persistent, well-documented interpretations of algebraic letters among 11–16 year-olds.
sources.source: Hodgen, Küchemann, Brown & Coe (2009). Children's understandings of algebra 30 years on. Research in Mathematics Education, 11(2).

pedagogy.summary: By upper KS2 children move from 'the heart pumps blood' to the double-loop circulatory system: a four-chambered pump (two atria receive, two ventricles push), one loop to the lungs to pick up oxygen and one loop to the body to deliver it, carried through arteries (away from heart, high pressure), veins (back to heart, valves), and capillaries (walls one cell thick where exchange happens). Blood itself is not a plain red liquid but a mixture — red cells carrying oxygen, white cells fighting infection, platelets for clotting, and plasma. Teach it as a JOURNEY a drop of blood takes, tracing the loop repeatedly until the double circuit and the reason for it (reload oxygen at the lungs, unload it at the body) become obvious. Ground the vessel types in things children can feel and see: the pulse in the wrist/neck is an artery, the blue-looking lines on the back of the hand are veins.
bestPractices: Trace a single drop of blood around the WHOLE double loop, out loud and repeatedly: body → vein → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs (drop O2 low, reload) → left atrium → left ventricle → body → repeat. The double loop only makes sense as a continuous circuit, not a labelled diagram.

Anchor vessel names to the body: find the pulse (an artery pushing), point out surface veins, and explain capillaries as the too-small-to-see meeting point where oxygen leaves and carbon dioxide is collected.

Colour-code by oxygen, not by vessel: blood reddens as it passes the lungs and darkens as the body uses the oxygen — so students see WHY two loops exist, rather than memorising 'arteries red, veins blue' (a misleading shorthand).

Separate the two ideas of 'what blood is made of' from 'where blood goes' — first build the four-part composition (red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma) with a jar-of-blood model, then set that mixture moving through the loop.
Use the child's own body as the manipulative: measure resting pulse, then link a faster pump to needing more oxygen delivered — previewing the circulation+breathing integration topic.
keyRepresentations: Double-loop circuit diagram (heart in the middle, lung loop on one side, body loop on the other) traced as a continuous path
Four-chamber cutaway of the heart with arrows showing receive-then-push (atria fill, ventricles pump)
Oxygen colour gradient — blood reddening at the lungs, darkening at the tissues — rather than fixed red/blue vessels
'Jar of blood' separation showing the four components layered (plasma, white cells/platelets, red cells)
The pulse as a felt representation of the heartbeat driving blood through an artery
commonMisconceptions: 'The heart makes blood' — it pumps blood, it does not manufacture it (blood cells are made in bone marrow).
'Blood is just red liquid' — missing that it is a mixture of cells, platelets and plasma, each with a job.
'Arteries are red and veins are blue' — vessels are not coloured; the shorthand refers to oxygen level, and deoxygenated blood is dark red, not blue. Veins only look blue through skin.
'Blood does one loop around the body' — missing the double circuit; children often think blood goes heart→body→heart and forget the separate lung trip to reload oxygen.
'The heart is on the left and heart-shaped' — it sits centrally behind the breastbone, tilted slightly left, and is a fist-sized muscular pump, not the symbolic shape.
'Capillaries are just tiny tubes' — missing that their one-cell-thick walls are the whole point: they are WHERE exchange happens.

learn.summary: Children aged 9–11 move from 'the heart pumps blood' to the double-loop circulatory system: a four-chambered pump (two atria receive, two ventricles push) driving one loop to the lungs to pick up oxygen and one loop to the body to deliver it, through arteries (away from heart, high pressure), veins (back to heart, with valves) and capillaries (walls one cell thick, where exchange happens). Blood is a mixture — red cells (oxygen), white cells (fight infection), platelets (clotting) and plasma. Teach it as a JOURNEY a drop of blood takes, tracing the circuit repeatedly until the double loop and its purpose become obvious: blood reloads oxygen at the lungs, comes back to the heart to be pumped out again, and unloads oxygen at the body. Ground vessel types in things children can feel: the wrist/neck pulse is an artery; the blue-looking lines on the back of the hand are veins. A driveable flow model is the primary vehicle; anatomy-labelling, a 3D heart for orientation, and a consolidation quiz are complementary scaffolds.

activities.title: Drive the double loop and follow one drop
feedback: If a learner traces only one loop (heart → body → heart), ask: when does the blood go back to the lungs to pick up more oxygen? Then re-run the model inserting the lung trip.
If a learner says the blood is 'used up' at the body, lock the camera on one drop and follow it all the way back to the heart to show the closed circuit.
When the colour change is noticed, prompt: why is going BACK to the lungs necessary — what happens to the blood there?
activities.rationale: Circulation is a dynamic flow process with a driving mechanism; letting the child drive the pump and watch the oxygen colour-gradient recompute is intended to make visible, in a way a static labelled diagram does not animate, why blood must visit the lungs between body trips and how it passes back through the heart in two loops. Colour-coding by oxygen (reddening at the lungs, darkening at the tissues) is intended to target the 'arteries red, veins blue' shorthand directly. This is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Tap or hold a beating-heart control so a drop of blood advances around the whole circuit: body → vein → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body → repeat.
Watch the blood flush bright red as it passes the lungs and darken as it threads the body's capillaries.
Turn on a 'follow one drop' option that locks the view onto a single cell for its full body → heart → lung → heart → body journey, and say out loud where it reloads and where it unloads oxygen.
Speed up the beat and notice delivery quickens, then link this to why exercise raises heart rate.
Trace the complete loop aloud, repeatedly, so it is experienced as one continuous circuit rather than a labelled diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: Blood must pass through the lungs to turn bright red (pick up oxygen) before going round the body again. In humans it then comes back to the heart to be pumped hard out to the body, so the circuit is two loops through the heart: heart → lungs → heart, then heart → body → heart. The same blood keeps circulating; it is never used up.

activities.title: Name the parts in context: heart cutaway and 'jar of blood'
feedback: If a learner says 'the heart makes blood', reframe: the heart is a pump, not a factory — blood cells are made in bone marrow; the heart moves blood.
If a learner calls capillaries 'just tiny tubes', highlight the one-cell-thick wall and ask where oxygen actually leaves the blood.
If a learner thinks blood is 'just red liquid', return to the jar model and ask what each separated layer does.
activities.rationale: This companion reference supports the anatomy-naming and blood-composition curriculum objectives: the curriculum requires naming the main parts and describing blood's components, and this scaffold directly serves that. It is strong for labelling but does not itself show flow or the double-loop logic, so it works best alongside the driveable model rather than as the primary artefact.
sourceClaims: Blood is composed of red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and plasma, each with distinct functions.
Y6 pupils should learn to identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood.
learnerActions: On a four-chamber heart cutaway, tap each chamber and say its job: atria receive (fill), ventricles push (pump).

Tap each vessel type in the flowing context and state its function: artery carries blood away from the heart (feel the pulse as it pushes), vein carries blood back with valves, capillary is the too-small-to-see meeting point where exchange happens — in the body's tissues oxygen leaves and carbon dioxide is collected, while in the lungs it is the other way round.

Explore a 'jar of blood' separation showing the four components in three layers — plasma on top, a thin layer of white cells and platelets together, red cells at the bottom — and match each component to its job (red: carry oxygen; white: fight infection; platelets: clotting; plasma: the liquid that carries everything).
Keep 'what blood is made of' as a separate step from 'where blood goes': build the four-part composition first, then set that mixture moving through the loop.
activities.intendedInsight: The named parts each have a function matched to their structure — capillaries' one-cell-thick walls are the whole point (that is WHERE exchange happens), not merely tiny tubes.

activities.title: Feel your own pump: pulse and the body as manipulative
feedback: If a learner says veins are blue and carry 'dirty' blood, ask whether blood heading TO the lungs is clean or dirty, and which vessel carries it — clarify veins only look blue through skin and deoxygenated blood is dark red, not blue.
If a learner draws the symbolic heart shape on the left, point to the breastbone and describe the real fist-sized muscular pump sitting centrally and tilted slightly left.
activities.rationale: Anchoring vessel names to sensations the child can feel and see is intended to make the abstract vocabulary concrete, and the pulse-after-exercise link bridges to the circulation+breathing integration topic. This is a proposed anchoring approach, not a validated one.
learnerActions: Find the pulse in your wrist or neck and feel it push — this is an artery.
Point out the blue-looking lines on the back of the hand: these are veins seen through the skin (the blood inside is not blue).
Measure your resting pulse by counting beats over a set time.
Do some brisk activity, measure the pulse again, and explain why a faster pump means more oxygen delivered to the body.
Locate where the heart really sits — centrally behind the breastbone, tilted slightly left, about fist-sized — not on the far left and not the symbolic heart shape.
activities.intendedInsight: The pulse is the felt heartbeat driving blood through an artery; when the body needs more oxygen the pump speeds up to deliver it, previewing how circulation and breathing work together.

activities.title: Brief 3D orientation: what shape and where the heart really is
feedback: If a learner expects the symbolic shape, compare it to the 3D muscle and name the difference.
Keep this to orientation only — return to the flat circuit model to reason about the loops, since the double-loop pathway is easiest to trace as a flat continuous circuit.
activities.rationale: A 3D view can usefully convey the heart's real shape and position (a known misconception), but the circulatory logic is a planar circuit; use 3D narrowly for anatomical orientation and not to teach the double loop, where the extra spatial dimension can obscure the path. This is a scoped suggestion, not evidence that 3D adds nothing in general.
learnerActions: Briefly view a 3D heart to see it is a chunky central muscle, not a flat symbolic shape, and to see its real position in the chest.
State in your own words where the heart sits and roughly how big it is.
activities.intendedInsight: The real heart is a fist-sized muscular pump sitting centrally behind the breastbone, correcting the symbolic 'heart shape on the left' picture.

activities.title: Consolidate and check: sequence, match, categorise
feedback: Recall-style sequencing and matching confirm vocabulary but do not by themselves show the flow intuition — pair any gaps with a return to the driveable model.
If a learner can list parts but cannot say what is exchanged where, send them back to trace one drop and narrate the pick-up/drop-off on each leg.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, matching and categorising are efficient for consolidating and assessing the naming objective after the model, but they check recall rather than building the flow intuition, so they belong after the driveable experience, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils should learn to identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood.
learnerActions: Put the double-loop stages in order: body → vein → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body.
Match each vessel type to its function (artery / vein / capillary).
Categorise the four blood components (red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma) by their jobs.
Answer the reasoning prompt: what would go wrong if blood went straight from the body back out to the body again without visiting the lungs first?
activities.intendedInsight: Sequencing, matching and categorising can confirm the named parts are recalled and connected to the reason the lung trip must come before the body trip; but these checks test recall, so they do not by themselves build the flow intuition.

constraints: Curriculum objective (ages 9–11): name the main parts of the circulatory system and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood — including the four chambers, the double loop, and the four blood components.

Colour the blood by oxygen level (reddening at the lungs, darkening at the tissues), NOT fixed 'arteries red, veins blue' — that shorthand is misleading; deoxygenated blood is dark red and veins only look blue through skin.
Keep 'what blood is made of' and 'where blood goes' as two separate build steps.
The labelling/cutaway and 'jar of blood' reference is a scaffold for naming parts; it does not demonstrate flow or the double-loop logic and should accompany, not replace, the flow model.
Use the 3D heart only for brief anatomical orientation (shape and position); it is not the tool for teaching the double loop.
Sequencing/matching/categorising tasks assess and consolidate recall; they do not on their own build the flow intuition, so run them after the model.

A conversation/in-role format is a weaker fit here: there is no central persona or open-ended debate in the mechanism, so an in-role chat may add little over driving and tracing the model — this is a fit judgement, not evidence that dialogue cannot teach.

The driveable model's interaction examples (tap/hold to beat, follow-one-drop camera lock, speed-up control, tap-a-vessel labelling, oxygen colour gradient) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory requirements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (British Heart Foundation claims on the four-chambered double circulation and on blood composition) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their specifics as unconfirmed pending re-check. Only the DfE curriculum claim is marked verified:true.

Activities 1, 3 and 4 have sourceClaims set to [] because their rationales concern the proposed medium/anchoring approach, which no source claim directly supports; the retained claims on activities 2 and 5 map to the naming/composition curriculum content those tasks teach, not to any proven efficacy of the interaction.

The original framing that driving the model is 'impossible on a static diagram and unnecessary in 3D' and that 3D 'adds nothing' has been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; catalog fit ratings do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

The capillary-exchange description ('oxygen leaves and carbon dioxide is collected') reflects systemic capillaries; the direction reverses at the lungs. This matches the original's KS2 simplification and is retained as such.

Self-audit: loop order, vessel functions (artery away/high pressure, vein back/valves, capillary one-cell-thick exchange), blood components, and heart position were checked for internal consistency and are coherent as stated; no arithmetic or force/motion claims were present. Grammar in activity 2's artery action ('as it pushing' → 'as it pushes') and the awkward activity 5 intendedInsight were corrected.

The reteachPrerequisiteId references and quiz-step vocabulary from the source have been dropped as internal identifiers; the underlying reteach moves (establish the closed circuit; insert the lung loop; heart-is-a-pump-not-a-factory) are preserved in activity feedback.

probeDeeper: What would go wrong if blood went straight from the body back out to the body again without visiting the lungs first?
People say veins are blue and carry 'dirty' blood. Is the blood going TO your lungs clean or dirty — and which vessel carries it?
Red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma — which of these is doing the oxygen-carrying on these trips?
assess.correctAnswer: Blood makes a double loop. On the trip to the lungs it drops off carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen; it returns to the heart, which pumps it out again on the second trip to the body, where it delivers oxygen and nutrients to the cells and collects their carbon-dioxide waste; then it returns to the heart to be sent to the lungs again. Two loops are needed so the blood is re-oxygenated at the lungs before being sent round the body — and the blood keeps returning, it is never used up.

errorPatterns.pattern: Blood flows out to the body and gets used up — it doesn't come back; it's a one-way path.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the closed circuit: the same blood returns to the heart to be reused; trace a full loop back to the start.
errorPatterns.distractor: The blood flows out to the body and is used up there, so the body makes new blood.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes blood ending at the body with no return; may say fresh blood is then made.

errorPatterns.pattern: There is only one loop — heart to body and back — the lungs aren't a separate trip.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insert the lung loop: blood must be re-oxygenated at the lungs between body trips; two loops, one heart.
errorPatterns.distractor: It only needs one loop — straight round the body and back to the heart.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a single body loop and omits the pulmonary (lung) loop.

errorPatterns.pattern: The heart makes or produces the blood.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe the heart as a pump, not a factory; blood is made in the bone marrow — the heart moves it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the heart creates blood rather than pumping it.

responseLevels.gap: Describes a single one-way path or blood being used up and not returning; may say the heart makes blood.
responseLevels.full: Explains the double loop as re-oxygenation at the lungs then delivery to the body, with the blood returning each time, naming what is picked up and dropped off on each leg — and reasons about skipping a loop.
responseLevels.partial: Knows there are two loops and names chambers and vessels, but can't say what is exchanged where — lists parts without explaining why the lung trip must come before the body trip.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Blood leaves your heart, and later the very same blood comes back to your heart again. Why does it need to make TWO different trips — one to your lungs and one to the rest of your body — instead of just one loop around? Explain what the blood picks up or drops off on each trip.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the classic single-loop or 'blood gets used up' model can't justify two trips or say the blood returns. Only a child who understands the double circuit can say what is exchanged at the lungs versus the body. The tier-two 'picks up or drops off on each trip' is precisely where the single-loop model collapses.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11; how polar oceans connect to the global climate system — cold, dense polar water sinks and drives thermohaline circulation (a global conveyor belt of currents); sea ice reflects sunlight back to space (the albedo effect), helping regulate Earth's temperature; and the Southern Ocean around Antarctica is one of the most productive marine ecosystems on Earth thanks to upwelling nutrients.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS3 Chemistry 'Earth and atmosphere' and KS3 Geography (global systems); KS2 Y5/Y6 human impact and Earth systems as build-up.
• Standards—US: NGSS MS-ESS2-6 (ocean circulation and its role in distributing heat/regulating climate) and MS-ESS2-4 (energy driving the water/ocean cycle); 5-ESS2-1.
• Operational details: three coupled mechanisms — (1) THERMOHALINE circulation: cold + salty = dense water that SINKS at the poles, pulling a global conveyor of currents that redistributes heat; (2) ALBEDO: bright sea ice reflects sunlight (cooling), so losing ice means more absorption (warming) — a climate regulator and a feedback; (3) Southern Ocean UPWELLING brings deep nutrients up, fuelling huge plankton/krill productivity. Emphasise that the poles are not remote bystanders — they are engines and thermostats of the whole climate system. Connect to the climate-change feedbacks and food-chain topics.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (9) state that polar oceans help control Earth's climate; Tier B (10) explain one mechanism (sinking cold water drives currents, OR ice reflects sunlight); Tier C (11) explain how sinking dense water, albedo, and upwelling link the poles to global heat distribution and productivity.
bestPractices: Teach the conveyor as a driven loop — cold, salty, dense water SINKS at the poles and pulls currents worldwide
Make albedo tangible: bright ice reflects, dark ocean absorbs; losing ice flips a cooler into a warmer state
Show upwelling as deep nutrients rising to feed surface plankton, linking physics to the food chain
Frame the poles as engines/thermostats of global climate, not passive faraway places
Cross-link to the climate-change feedback and polar-food-chain topics so the mechanisms reinforce each other
keyRepresentations: Global conveyor-belt map with cold dense water sinking at the poles
Albedo comparison: sunlight bouncing off bright ice vs absorbed by dark ocean
Density driver: temperature + salt → dense water sinking (a simple sink/float demo)
Southern Ocean upwelling diagram: deep nutrients rising to fuel plankton blooms
commonMisconceptions: The poles are remote and don't affect world climate — they drive ocean currents and regulate global temperature
Ocean currents are driven only by wind — sinking cold, salty (dense) polar water drives the deep global conveyor
Albedo is a minor detail — reflective ice is a key climate regulator, and losing it warms the planet further
Deep ocean water is lifeless — upwelling brings its nutrients up to fuel some of Earth's richest ecosystems
Warm water sinks — it is COLD, salty, dense water that sinks at the poles

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, learners connect polar oceans to the global climate system through three coupled mechanisms: (1) thermohaline circulation — cold, salty, dense water sinks at the poles and drives a global conveyor of currents redistributing heat; (2) albedo — bright sea ice reflects sunlight while dark ocean absorbs it, so losing ice shifts the system toward warming (a feedback); (3) Southern Ocean upwelling — deep nutrients rise to fuel large plankton/krill blooms. The throughline: poles are engines and thermostats of global climate, not remote frozen edges. The research entry recommends operating a model of the coupled loop and proposes this may give the richest learning; parts-based diagrams, ordering/density checks, and expert narration are useful companions or scaffolds with stated limits. Comparative efficacy of any one format is not established by the cited (unverified) sources.

activities.title: Run the polar engine room: drive the conveyor
feedback: If the learner makes water sink only by cooling, prompt: add salt and compare — cold AND salty gives the densest water and the strongest sinking.
If the learner says the conveyor keeps turning after sinking stops, replay the stall: in this model the deep loop is driven by the sinking, so stopping it stalls the currents.

When ice is removed and the modelled temperature climbs, ask what that does to nearby ice — draw out the feedback (more melting → darker ocean → more absorption). Keep these outputs framed as the model's behaviour, not exact real-world magnitudes.
After upwelling blooms plankton, ask where the nutrients came from, to connect deep water to surface productivity.
activities.rationale: Three coupled mechanisms may be easier to understand when operated so cause and effect are visible and connected; manipulating cooling/salinity, ice cover, and upwelling is intended to let learners trace the driving loop and the albedo feedback directly. The live conveyor, albedo meter, sunlight beam, and plankton bloom are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not required implementations. Efficacy of this format over others is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Students explain how ocean circulation distributes heat and regulates regional and global climate

Cold, dense polar water sinking drives thermohaline circulation; sea-ice albedo reflects incoming sunlight and helps regulate temperature; Southern Ocean upwelling makes it one of Earth's most productive marine regions
learnerActions: Chill and add salt to surface water at a modelled pole until it becomes dense and plunges downward; watch a colour-coded conveyor of warm and cold currents begin to turn around the whole globe as the sinking continues.
Stop the sinking (stop cooling or remove salt) and observe the modelled conveyor stall, then restart it to see that, in this model, the loop is driven by polar sinking.

Toggle a sea-ice dial: with ice present, a modelled sunlight beam bounces off the bright surface; remove the ice and watch the beam sink into dark ocean, an albedo meter drop, and the modelled temperature climb, visibly feeding back to melt more ice.
Switch on Southern Ocean upwelling and watch deep nutrients rise and bloom plankton that a krill-and-penguin food chain feeds on.
State in one or two sentences how cold + salt → dense → sinking → global currents, and how losing reflective ice shifts the system toward warming.
activities.intendedInsight: Polar oceans actively drive global heat distribution and regulate temperature: cold, salty, dense water sinking powers the conveyor; sea-ice albedo is a climate regulator with a warming feedback when ice is lost; and upwelling links ocean physics to a productive food chain.

activities.title: Density current demo: cold salty water sinks
feedback: If the learner predicts the water will just mix in or float on top, use the observed sinking to revise: denser water sinks beneath lighter water.
If the learner reasons on temperature alone, compare salty vs fresh cold water so salinity's contribution is visible.
Connect back: ask how sea-ice formation makes the leftover water saltier (salt is excluded as ice forms), boosting the sinking.
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain density demonstration is intended to surface the common 'warm water sinks' misconception and let learners build the density concept (cold AND salty) that underlies the conveyor. A concrete tank demo makes the abstract driving mechanism observable; its advantage over other formats is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Cold, dense polar water sinking drives thermohaline circulation; sea-ice albedo reflects incoming sunlight and helps regulate temperature; Southern Ocean upwelling makes it one of Earth's most productive marine regions
learnerActions: Predict, with a reason, what will happen when cold, salty, dyed water is gently poured into a clear tank of room-temperature plain water (will it mix in, float on top, or sink?).
Pour it in and observe what happens. If the water is salty enough and poured gently, the cold salty water should sink and spread along the bottom as a density current.
Explain how this models polar surface water sinking to drive the global conveyor.
Test a variation: discuss or try cold but FRESH (unsalted) water — would it sink as strongly? Use this to separate the roles of temperature and salinity.
activities.intendedInsight: Cold, salty water is denser than warm or fresher water, so it sinks beneath them. In the real ocean, this sinking in polar seas is a key physical driver of thermohaline circulation, alongside winds and mixing. Both temperature and salinity matter.

activities.title: Parts-based diagrams: conveyor, albedo, upwelling
feedback: After the conveyor map, ask what starts the loop (polar sinking) so the learner names the driver, not just the shape.
After the albedo panel, ask why losing ice warms rather than cools the surface, checking the reflect-vs-absorb logic.
After upwelling, ask whether deep ocean water is lifeless, to counter that misconception with the nutrient-rich reality.
activities.rationale: Clear tap-to-reveal diagrams teach the component parts and are a strong companion to a hands-on model. As a scaffold, fixed images present the steps but do not themselves let the learner drive the loop or watch the albedo feedback respond to their own actions, so pair them with the operable model or demo. This is an affordance limit, not a claim that images cannot teach.
sourceClaims: Cold, dense polar water sinking drives thermohaline circulation; sea-ice albedo reflects incoming sunlight and helps regulate temperature; Southern Ocean upwelling makes it one of Earth's most productive marine regions
learnerActions: Work through a global conveyor-belt map showing cold dense water sinking at the poles and following the currents it drives, revealing each step in order.
Compare an albedo panel: trace sunlight reflecting off bright ice versus being absorbed by dark ocean, and state what happens to temperature when ice is lost.
Study a Southern Ocean upwelling diagram showing deep nutrients rising to fuel plankton blooms, then describe the link from physics to the food chain in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Each mechanism — the driven conveyor, the albedo contrast, and nutrient upwelling — can be learned as a clear part before being assembled into the whole coupled system.

activities.title: Check and discuss: ordering and density questions
feedback: If a learner orders currents before sinking, point back to the driver: sinking comes first and pulls the loop.
If a learner picks warm/salty as densest, compare with cold/salty to show cold adds to density too — cold AND salty is the densest combination.
For the 'slowed conveyor' discussion, accept reasoned answers and probe for the link between sinking and heat transport to distant regions.
activities.rationale: Ordering and density questions are a strong companion check on whether the mechanisms are understood. Recognition- and ordering-style items can assess and reinforce the stated relationships but do not by themselves elicit the coupled-system explanation, so use them alongside the operable model or demo. The expert-narration/discussion option suits learners who benefit from spoken explanation and may work well alongside operating the system; its efficacy relative to other formats is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Students explain how ocean circulation distributes heat and regulates regional and global climate
learnerActions: Order the stages of the conveyor from polar sinking to warm currents reaching mid-latitudes.
Answer short questions on albedo (bright vs dark surfaces) and density (which water sinks: warm/fresh, warm/salty, cold/fresh, cold/salty).

Discuss with a partner or mentor: if polar sinking slowed or stopped, what might happen to a warm current that helps keep a place like Britain mild — and what's your evidence that polar water really sinks and travels deep?
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state and order the mechanisms and justify which water sinks (cold/salty is densest), then extend the reasoning to a 'what if the conveyor slowed' case.

constraints: Target age 9–11; UK links include KS3 Chemistry 'Earth and atmosphere' and KS3 Geography (global systems), built up from KS2 Y5/Y6 Earth-systems and human-impact content. US links include NGSS MS-ESS2-6 and MS-ESS2-4, built up from 5-ESS2-1.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age ~9) — state that polar oceans help control Earth's climate; Tier B (age ~10) — explain one mechanism (cold water sinking drives currents, OR ice reflects sunlight); Tier C (age ~11) — explain how sinking dense water, albedo, and upwelling together link the poles to global heat distribution and productivity.

Emphasise the correct direction: COLD, salty, dense water sinks at the poles. 'Warm water sinks' may appear only as a targeted misconception/distractor that is then corrected; never leave it standing as the correct answer.
Both temperature and salinity drive density; do not teach that temperature alone decides whether water sinks.

Static diagrams and ordering/density items are scaffolds or companion checks: they present or assess the mechanisms but do not themselves let the learner drive the loop or watch the feedback respond. Pair them with an operable model or a physical density demo; do not treat recognition-only responses as evidence of independent explanation. This is an affordance limit, not a claim that these formats cannot teach.

Expert narration/discussion supports learners who benefit from spoken explanation; it may work best alongside operating or demonstrating the coupled system and is not a required replacement for it. Its advantage over other formats is not established by the cited sources.
Keep model outputs (albedo meter, temperature climb, feedback) labelled as model behaviour rather than precise quantitative predictions.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all listed sources remain verified:false. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims cite UK/US curriculum standards and NOAA/British Antarctic Survey topic content; they support the scientific content taught but do NOT establish comparative efficacy of any one activity format, nor that these specific activities were tested. Format-preference statements are the original entry's recommendation, softened to proposed/may wording.

The original entry stated a static image 'can't show the driven loop' and that 3D adds limited value over a 2D map; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been reframed as scoped scaffold limits and affordances. The 3D option's whole-globe spatial affordance is noted but not reproduced as a separate activity.

The claim that losing sea ice 'warms the planet further' via feedback is a reasonable modelled relationship for this age, but real albedo/feedback magnitudes depend on conditions; model outputs are labelled as a model rather than precise predictions.
The feedback relationship 'sea-ice formation concentrates salt (brine exclusion), boosting sinking' is standard science presented at a simplified level appropriate for 9–11.

The deep conveyor is modelled as driven by polar sinking; wind-driven surface currents exist in reality but lie outside this model's scope — an acceptable age-appropriate simplification labelled as model behaviour.

assess.poeTask: Have the child predict, WITH A REASON, what will happen when you gently pour a cup of cold, salty, dyed water into a clear tank of room-temperature plain water. The naive prediction ('it'll just mix in' or 'it'll float on top') is the diagnostic part. Observe: the cold salty water sinks and spreads along the bottom as a density current — a model of polar water sinking to drive the conveyor.
probeDeeper: Why does forming sea ice make the water underneath saltier — where does the salt go?
If polar sinking slowed down or stopped, what might happen to the warm current that keeps Britain mild?
What's your evidence that water at the poles actually sinks and travels deep, rather than just staying put?
What if the polar water were cold but FRESH (no salt) — would it still sink as strongly?
assess.correctAnswer: It SINKS. Cold, salty water is denser (heavier for its size) than warm or fresher water, so it sinks to the deep ocean at the poles. This sinking drives a global conveyor belt of ocean currents (thermohaline circulation) that pulls warm surface water toward the poles — part of why places like Britain are milder than their latitude suggests. So the polar oceans act as an engine for the world's climate, not a remote backwater.

errorPatterns.pattern: warm water sinks / hot things go down — 'the cold water floats on top, the warm sinks'
errorPatterns.nextMove: density demo (cold dyed water sinks under warm); cold + salty = densest, so it sinks
errorPatterns.distractor: The warm water sinks and the cold water stays on top
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says warm water sinks or cold water rises

errorPatterns.pattern: salt doesn't change whether water sinks — only temperature matters
errorPatterns.nextMove: show salty water is denser than fresh; sea-ice formation concentrates salt, boosting the sinking
errorPatterns.revealedBy: ignores salinity and reasons on temperature alone

errorPatterns.pattern: the poles are remote bystanders — 'the polar ocean doesn't affect weather far away'
errorPatterns.nextMove: trace the conveyor belt from polar sinking to warm currents reaching mid-latitudes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies any global link

responseLevels.gap: Says warm water sinks, or that the polar ocean has nothing to do with distant weather.
responseLevels.full: Explains cold, salty (denser) water sinking at the poles as the driver of thermohaline circulation that carries heat globally (why Britain is mild), links sea-ice formation to salinity and albedo, and transfers to a new case (freshening slows the conveyor).
responseLevels.partial: Knows cold/salty water sinks OR that ocean currents move heat, but lists these separately — can't connect polar sinking to the global conveyor and remote climate.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: At the poles, surface seawater gets very cold and, as sea ice forms, the water left behind gets extra salty. What happens to that cold, salty water — does it stay at the surface or sink? Tell me which, and then tell me WHY, and what that has to do with warming places far away like Britain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding 'warm water sinks' or 'cold water rises' gets the direction wrong; the child with the density concept says cold+salty sinks and links it to global circulation. The reason-tier forces density (cold AND salty), not a warmth intuition, and connects to remote climate.

pedagogy.summary: A metacognitive topic: using rounding/estimation as an INDEPENDENT check on the reasonableness of a calculation, and judging the appropriate degree of accuracy for a context. Two ideas intertwine — (1) an estimate sets a ballpark that can DISPROVE an exact answer in seconds (if 47,832 + 23,156 is about 71,000, an answer of 3,988 must be wrong), and (2) the right level of accuracy depends on purpose (a stadium crowd is honestly '52,000'; a shop bill must be exact). The habit being built is 'is this answer sensible?', not another calculation.
bestPractices: Teach estimation as a CHECK done independently, before or after the exact calculation - never by repeating the exact method
Round to a level that keeps useful discrimination (nearest 1,000 for five-digit sums, not nearest 10,000)
Use deliberately wrong answers and ask 'how can you tell this is impossible without redoing it?'
Discuss real contexts where precision is spurious (crowd sizes, distances) vs essential (money, counts that must balance)
Frame accuracy as a decision with reasons, not 'more digits = better'
keyRepresentations: Number line showing the estimate as a bracket/ballpark around the true value
Rounded-vs-exact comparison ('about 71,000' beside 70,988)
Context cards (crowd / money / distance) ranking needed precision
Order-of-magnitude 'gauge' (is the answer in the right zone?)
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a good estimate should EQUAL the exact answer (so treats the small difference as an error)
Checks by recomputing exactly rather than estimating - defeating the purpose
Believes more accuracy is always better; cannot see when rounding is appropriate
Rounds to an unhelpful level (too coarse to discriminate, or too fine to be an estimate)
Treats the estimate itself as the required answer

learn.summary: Learners build the habit of asking 'is this answer sensible?' by using rounding/estimation as an INDEPENDENT check on a calculation, and by judging the level of accuracy a context actually needs. Two intertwined ideas: (1) an estimate sets a ballpark that can disprove an exact answer in seconds (if 47,832 + 23,156 is about 71,000, an answer of 3,988 must be wrong), and (2) the right precision depends on purpose (a stadium crowd is honestly '52,000'; a shop bill must be exact). The two ideas are one habit, not separate tricks, and the check is deliberately NOT a re-computation of the same sum.

activities.title: The estimate as a lie-detector: prove an answer wrong without redoing it
feedback: If a learner says 71,000 is 'wrong' because the exact answer is 70,988: an estimate is meant to be near, not equal; being close is exactly what you want, and its job is to catch big errors, not to match digit for digit.

If a learner reaches for the full algorithm to check: redoing the same method can easily repeat the same mistake (especially if it comes from how you do the method), so the error may go undetected; a quick, independent estimate can catch large errors that repeating the method might miss.

If a learner rounds a five-digit sum to the nearest 10,000: that grain is often too coarse to catch errors of a few thousand (50,000 + 20,000 = 70,000 would still expose 3,988, but would not show up an answer like 74,000 as suspicious) - match the rounding grain to the question, coarse enough to be quick but fine enough to still discriminate.
When an answer IS close to the estimate, note that 'close' does not guarantee correctness; the estimate rules out large errors, not small ones.
activities.rationale: Treating estimation as a check done independently of the exact method targets the core misconception of recomputing to verify, and the use of a deliberately wrong answer makes 'how can you tell without redoing it?' concrete; choosing between nearest 100 and nearest 1,000 practises matching the grain to the context.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy
Computational estimation is a distinct competence used to judge reasonableness (order-of-magnitude checking), and appropriate precision is context-dependent
learnerActions: Take a completed sum with its answer, e.g. 47,832 + 23,156 = 3,988.
Round each number to a useful grain (nearest 1,000: about 48,000 and about 23,000) WITHOUT recomputing the exact sum.
Add the rounded numbers to get a ballpark of about 71,000.
State whether the given answer is possible: 3,988 is nowhere near 71,000, so it must be wrong - perhaps a place-value, alignment or copying slip; the estimate shows that it is wrong, not why.
Decide, for a stated context, whether a nearest-100 or a nearest-1,000 estimate is the better grain, and justify which keeps enough discrimination to be a useful check.
Repeat with other answers, including one that is close to the estimate (e.g. 70,988) and judge whether 'close' is enough to trust.
Explain, in your own words, why this check catches the error faster than redoing the full algorithm.
activities.intendedInsight: An estimate is an independent order-of-magnitude check: it can PROVE an answer impossible in seconds without ever doing the exact calculation. An estimate is a deliberate ballpark, not a rival exact answer.

activities.title: Honest precision: choosing the right level of accuracy for the purpose
feedback: If a learner insists the exact figure is always best: ask who the figure is for and what they'll do with it; nobody counted every head in a crowd, so extra digits imply a certainty that doesn't exist.
If a learner accepts 'about 52 pounds' for a shop bill: money must balance exactly, so here precision is the point, not a preference.
If a learner rounds too coarsely or too finely: match the grain to the purpose - '50,000' may erase a meaningful difference, while rounding a crowd to the nearest 10 is pointlessly precise.
activities.rationale: Directly addresses the 'more accuracy is always better' misconception by framing accuracy as a justified choice across contrasting real contexts where precision is either spurious or essential.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy
Computational estimation is a distinct competence used to judge reasonableness (order-of-magnitude checking), and appropriate precision is context-dependent
learnerActions: Consider a context, e.g. a newspaper reporting a football crowd. Decide whether it should print '52,000' or '51,847', and say why.
Argue that a crowd figure is inherently approximate, so '52,000' communicates the scale honestly while '51,847' implies a false precision nobody actually counted.
Contrast with a shop totting up a customer's bill: decide whether 'about 52 pounds' is acceptable and explain why money (and any count that must balance) needs exactness.
Rank several context cards (crowd / money / distance / stock count) by how much precision each honestly needs, giving a reason for each.
Identify a case where rounding a crowd to '50,000' would be TOO rough - when might that coarse figure hide something that matters?
activities.intendedInsight: The right level of accuracy is a decision with reasons tied to purpose and audience - not 'more digits is always better'. Spurious precision can be misleading; appropriate rounding can be more honest.

activities.title: Convince the sceptic (spoken reasoning)
feedback: Reward reasoning that separates the ballpark role of the estimate from the exact answer, and that ties precision to purpose.
Press any claim that an estimate 'failed' because it wasn't equal, or that exactness is universally better.

If a learner treats estimate-checking and choosing accuracy as unrelated tricks, prompt them to see both as one question - 'is this number sensible for its purpose?' - so they can transfer the habit to a new context.
activities.rationale: Reasonableness and appropriate-accuracy judgements are genuinely dialogic; an in-role 'convince me' exchange exercises the justification directly, surfaces thinking for discussion, and targets the partial-level state of holding the two ideas apart.
sourceClaims: Computational estimation is a distinct competence used to judge reasonableness (order-of-magnitude checking), and appropriate precision is context-dependent
learnerActions: In role with a sceptical editor/partner, justify out loud why a proposed answer must be impossible, using only an estimate.
Argue, when challenged, why '52,000' is the honest figure to print for a crowd and why a bill demands exact pounds and pence.
Respond to follow-up challenges: 'Could an answer be close to your estimate and still be wrong?' and 'How close is close enough to trust?'
Explain how the estimate check and the accuracy choice are the same underlying habit - asking whether a number is sensible for its purpose.
activities.intendedInsight: Judging reasonableness and defending a level of accuracy is reasoning you can articulate and defend, not just a computed value; the two moves are one habit, not separate tricks.

activities.title: Quick checks: spot the impossible answer and sort by needed precision
feedback: For a correct selection, ask the learner to say how they knew without the exact sum.
A recognition response shows which option was chosen but does not by itself show the learner could build the estimate or justify the accuracy level, so always ask for the 'why'.
activities.rationale: Selection items make the curriculum skills (rounding to check, choosing accuracy) assessable, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent construction of an estimate or a justified accuracy choice, so pair them with brief reasoning.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy
learnerActions: Given an estimate, select which of several proposed answers is impossible (e.g. an answer near 4,000 when the estimate is about 71,000).
Sort contexts into 'needs an exact figure' vs 'a rounded figure is honest'.
For each choice, briefly state the reason rather than only choosing the option.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising impossible answers and matching precision to context are checkable skills; adding a short reason connects them to the underlying judgement.

constraints: Estimation must be taught as a CHECK performed independently of the exact method - never by repeating the exact calculation, which can easily repeat the same error (especially a misunderstanding of the method) and so may not catch it.

Round to a level that keeps useful discrimination (e.g. nearest 1,000 for five-digit sums, not nearest 10,000); choosing between nearest 100 and nearest 1,000 is itself a reasoned, context-dependent decision.
An estimate is a deliberate ballpark; being near the exact answer is correct, not an error. 'Close to the estimate' rules out large errors but does not guarantee the exact answer is right.
Accuracy is a decision justified by purpose and audience, not 'more digits = better'; both spurious precision and over-coarse rounding are wrong for their context.

Recognition/selection tasks confirm a choice but do not by themselves show the learner can independently generate an estimate or justify a precision level - pair them with spoken or written reasoning.

Scaffolds such as a gauge, dial, number-line bracket, or tap-to-reveal poster are aids to make the mechanism visible; the objective is the learner's own judgement, so fade them as learners articulate the reasoning unaided.
Treat estimate-as-check and accuracy-by-purpose as one connected habit; a learner who performs each in isolation but cannot link them has only a partial grasp.
Context-dependent precision claims (e.g. whether '50,000' is too rough) depend on the specific purpose and must be reasoned per case, not applied as a fixed rule.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 47,832 + 23,156 = 70,988 (exact); 48,000 + 23,000 = 71,000 (estimate) - consistent across the source. The impossible answers 3,988 and 3,421 each sit well over an order of magnitude below 71,000 and ~50,000 respectively, consistent with a place-value/alignment slip; retained as given.

The source's evidence line 'Identify that a calculated answer of 3,421 cannot be correct because the estimate gives approximately 50,000' names no addends, so the ~50,000 estimate cannot be independently checked here; used only as a generic 'order of magnitude out' illustration and kept out of any learner-facing option.

Interactive examples from the original (answer-checker 'bench', gauge swinging to a red IMPOSSIBLE zone, context dial for money/crowd/distance, number-line bracket, tap-to-reveal poster) are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory mechanisms.

Original 'poor fit' claim that a 3D/spatial treatment 'adds nothing' was not carried over as a universal law; the topic is simply judgement about number, so spatial manipulation is not the focus here.
The source's partial response level (treating estimate-as-check and accuracy-by-purpose as separate tricks) is addressed in the dialogic activity's actions and feedback.

Activity 4's cited curriculum claim supports naming the assessed skills only; the recognition-only limitation is stated as an objective affordance, not as claimed source-backed efficacy of any medium.

probeDeeper: Your estimate was about 71,000 and the real answer is 70,988 - does that small difference mean your estimate was wrong?
Could an answer be close to your estimate and still be wrong? How close is 'close enough' to trust it?
When would rounding a crowd to '50,000' be TOO rough - when might that hide something that matters?
For a shop totting up a customer's bill, would 'about 52 pounds' be an acceptable level of accuracy? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning rounds each number (about 48,000 + 23,000 = 71,000), so any answer near 4,000 is impossible - it is an order of magnitude out, probably a place-value or alignment slip - and this is spotted WITHOUT the exact sum. On accuracy: a crowd figure is inherently approximate, so '52,000' communicates the scale honestly and '51,847' implies a false precision nobody counted; but for money, or counts that must balance, exactness is the point. The right level of accuracy depends on the PURPOSE, not on having more digits.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a good estimate should equal the exact answer, so calls 71,000 'wrong' because the real answer is 70,988
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss: an estimate is a deliberate ballpark, not a rival answer; its job is to catch big errors, and being near (not equal) is exactly right.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Objects that the estimate 'doesn't match'; treats the estimate as a failed exact calculation

errorPatterns.pattern: Insists on recomputing the sum exactly to check it, rather than estimating
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss why an independent quick estimate catches errors that redoing the same method would just repeat; contrast the two as checks.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches for the full algorithm again when asked how to tell the answer is wrong

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes exact is always better - insists the newspaper print 51,847 and cannot see when rounding is appropriate
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss audience and purpose; surface spurious precision (nobody counted every head); contrast with a shop bill where exactness matters.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects '52,000' as 'not accurate enough' regardless of purpose

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds to an unhelpful level - checks a five-digit sum to the nearest 10,000 (losing all discrimination) or rounds a crowd to the nearest 10
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss matching the rounding grain to the question: coarse enough to be quick, fine enough to still tell a right answer from a wrong one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses a rounding grain that is far too coarse or too fine for the question

responseLevels.gap: Can only check by recomputing exactly; treats accuracy as 'more digits is better'; cannot use an estimate to judge an answer.
responseLevels.full: Uses the estimate as an independent order-of-magnitude check AND justifies the level of accuracy by purpose/audience, transferring to a new context (money exact, crowd rounded) and explaining why.
responseLevels.partial: Can produce an estimate and see 3,988 is wrong, OR can say a crowd figure is approximate - but treats these as separate tricks; lists the ideas without connecting estimate-as-check to accuracy-fits-purpose, and cannot choose the right grain for a new context.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A pupil works out 47,832 + 23,156 and writes 3,988. Without doing the exact sum yourself, how could you tell straight away that this answer must be wrong? Then a different question: if a newspaper reports the crowd at a football match, should it print '52,000' or '51,847' - and why? Talk me through your thinking on both.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who can only compute must redo the sum to judge it; strong reasoning uses the estimate as an independent order-of-magnitude check and recognises accuracy as purpose-dependent. This is surfaced for DISCUSSION - it reveals how the child thinks about number, not a single right/wrong mark.
