pedagogy.summary: Tree diagrams (and sample-space grids and systematic listing) generate the full set of equally-likely outcomes for single and combined events, from which theoretical probability is favourable ÷ total. Students list outcomes (e.g. the 36 ordered results of two dice), draw trees with probabilities on the branches, MULTIPLY along a path (the AND rule) and ADD across paths (the OR rule), and adjust probabilities for without-replacement (dependent) events. The recurring conceptual hazard is assuming aggregated outcomes — like the eleven dice totals — are equally likely.
bestPractices: Build the complete sample space first (grid or list), respecting ORDER, so favourable/total rests on genuinely equally-likely outcomes
Confront the two-dice trap head-on: the eleven totals 2–12 are NOT equally likely; there are 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes
Teach the AND rule (multiply along a branch) and OR rule (add across paths) explicitly, and the complement shortcut for 'at least one'
For without-replacement problems, recompute the second-level branch probabilities from the reduced situation (dependent events)
Leave fractions uncancelled until the end so common denominators are available for adding paths
keyRepresentations: Sample-space grid / two-way table (e.g. 6×6 for two dice)
Systematic ordered listing of outcomes
Probability tree with values on branches; multiply along, add across
Reduced-denominator second branches for dependent events
commonMisconceptions: Assuming aggregated outcomes are equally likely — treating the eleven totals of two dice as each 1/11 (equiprobability bias)
Ignoring order when listing — counting 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome, undercounting the sample space
Adding probabilities along a branch instead of multiplying (misapplying AND/OR)
Reusing the first-event probabilities on the second branch of a without-replacement (dependent) event

learn.summary: Students build complete, equally-likely sample spaces (ordered lists or grids) for single and combined events, then compute theoretical probability as favourable ÷ total. They draw probability trees, multiply along a single path (AND), add across separate, mutually exclusive complete paths (OR), use the complement for 'at least one', and recompute second-level branches for without-replacement (dependent) events. The central hazard is assuming aggregated outcomes — such as the eleven dice totals — are equally likely, when it is the 36 ordered outcomes that are equally likely.

activities.title: The two-dice grid: why totals are not equally likely
feedback: If a learner writes P(7) = 1/11: there are eleven possible totals, but they do not occur equally often. Count the shaded cells — seven has six ways, two has just one — so the totals cannot each be 1/11.

If a learner counts 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome (getting three ways to make 7, or 21 outcomes total): treat the dice as an ordered pair, first then second; (3,4) and (4,3) are genuinely different results, giving 36 outcomes and six ways to make 7.
Confirm success when the full grid is filled, six cells are identified for total 7, and the learner can say the ordered outcomes — not the totals — are what is equally likely.
activities.rationale: Theoretical probability only equals favourable ÷ total when the counted outcomes are genuinely equally likely; the two-dice grid makes the distinction between elemental equally-likely outcomes and aggregated events visible and countable.
sourceClaims: Children (and adults) show an equiprobability bias in the two-dice problem, assuming all the possible totals are equally probable; the difficulty is distinguishing elemental equally-likely outcomes from aggregated events, which requires representing the full sample space.
learnerActions: On paper or a 6×6 grid, write the total in every one of the 36 cells for (first die, second die), keeping the two dice as an ordered pair so 3+4 and 4+3 are separate cells.
Shade all cells where the total is 7 and count them (6 cells: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1), then shade cells where the total is 2 (1 cell: 1+1).
State P(total = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6 and P(total = 2) = 1/36.
Explain in a sentence why P(7) is NOT 1/11, referring to the 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes.
activities.intendedInsight: The 36 ordered (die1, die2) outcomes are equally likely; the eleven totals 2–12 are NOT, because different totals arise from different numbers of ordered outcomes.

activities.title: Trees: multiply along a path, add across paths
feedback: If a learner computes P(tail and 6) = 1/2 + 1/6: along a single path use the AND rule and multiply (1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12). Adding is only for OR across separate, mutually exclusive complete paths.
If a learner cancels fractions early and then struggles to add paths: keep denominators uncancelled until the end so paths can be added over a common denominator.
Confirm success when the learner multiplies along a path for a combined event and adds across separate paths for an 'or' event, and can say which operation goes with AND and which with OR.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating multiply-along (AND) from add-across (OR) addresses the common error of applying the wrong operation, and delaying cancellation keeps path addition tractable.
sourceClaims: In tree diagrams, probabilities on each set of branches sum to 1, you multiply along the branches for the AND rule (P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B)) and add across paths for OR; for dependent (without-replacement) events the second set of branch probabilities changes with the first outcome; and fractions should not be cancelled too early.
learnerActions: Draw a probability tree for a coin flip followed by a die roll, writing the probability on each branch and checking each set of branches sums to 1.
Find P(tail and 6) by multiplying along the single path: 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.
Find a two-path 'OR' probability by computing each separate complete path's product, then adding the path products together (the paths are mutually exclusive, so adding is valid).
Leave fractions uncancelled until the final step so paths share common denominators when added.
activities.intendedInsight: Along one path, combined events use AND and you multiply; across separate complete paths that each satisfy the question, you use OR and add. These are different operations for different situations.

activities.title: Without replacement: the second branch changes
feedback: If a learner keeps the original probabilities on the second branches: after removing a counter there are fewer counters in total and one fewer of the colour drawn — recompute each second branch from what is actually left.
Confirm success when every second-level branch reflects the reduced totals and the path product uses those updated values.
activities.rationale: Recomputing second-level branches from the reduced situation is the core procedure for dependent events and directly targets the misconception of reusing first-event probabilities.
sourceClaims: In tree diagrams, probabilities on each set of branches sum to 1, you multiply along the branches for the AND rule (P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B)) and add across paths for OR; for dependent (without-replacement) events the second set of branch probabilities changes with the first outcome; and fractions should not be cancelled too early.
learnerActions: Set up a bag problem, e.g. 3 red and 2 blue counters, and draw a tree for taking two counters without replacing the first.

Write the first-draw probabilities (3/5 red, 2/5 blue), then recompute each second-draw branch from the reduced situation — one fewer counter in total, and one fewer of whatever was drawn (e.g. after a red: 2/4 red, 2/4 blue).

If an optional tool offers a 'replace / don't replace' switch, toggle it and watch the second-level branch probabilities change (with no replacement) or stay the same (with replacement) to see the dependency.
Find a combined probability, e.g. P(two reds) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10, multiplying along the path with the updated second branch.
activities.intendedInsight: For dependent (without-replacement) events, the second draw's probabilities depend on the first outcome, so they must be recomputed from the reduced contents rather than reused.

activities.title: Drill and check: rules and the equiprobability trap
feedback: For the P(7) item, 1/11 is incorrect: counting ordered outcomes gives 6/36 = 1/6; 1/11 wrongly assumes the eleven totals are equally likely.
For the fill-in, the AND rule gives 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.
For the without-replacement item, the second branch uses the reduced totals; keeping the original values is the error to catch.
activities.rationale: Targeted recognition and fill-in items reinforce the rules and surface the equiprobability distractor; they consolidate procedures but do not by themselves require constructing a full fresh sample space, so they supplement — and do not replace — the construction activities. Efficacy of the format is proposed, not demonstrated.
learnerActions: Answer a short-answer item: P(total = 7) with two dice — write the fraction and justify it, explaining why the common answer 1/11 is wrong.
Complete a fill-in: P(tail and 6) = 1/2 × ___ = ___.
Solve a without-replacement item where the second branch must be recomputed, and explain why it differs from the first.
Where available, tap grid cells to reveal their totals or tap a tree path to reveal its product, using these only to self-check after you have reasoned.
activities.intendedInsight: Quick recognition and fill-in checks can reinforce the AND/OR rules and resurface the equiprobability trap, but learners should reason first and use any reveal only to confirm; such items check and consolidate the procedures and do not by themselves build a full fresh sample space.

constraints: Sample spaces must be built on genuinely equally-likely outcomes; for two dice that means the 36 ordered (die1, die2) pairs, not the eleven totals.
Order must be respected when listing: (3,4) and (4,3) are distinct outcomes; ignoring order undercounts the sample space.
For dependent (without-replacement) events, every second-level branch must be recomputed from the reduced contents; first-event probabilities cannot be reused.
The OR (add-across) rule applies only to separate, mutually exclusive complete paths; the AND (multiply-along) rule applies within a single path.
Leave fractions uncancelled until the end so paths can be added over a common denominator.

Short-answer, fill-in and tap-to-reveal items can reinforce and self-check the rules, but do not require a learner to independently construct a complete fresh sample space; pair them with construction tasks.

Tap-to-reveal grids/trees and a replace/don't-replace toggle are optional supports to make the mechanism visible; they are not required, and should be used after the learner has reasoned, not instead of reasoning.
Rolling physical or 3D dice can add realism and generate data, but the counting and branch arithmetic are carried by the grid and tree; feed any physical results back into the grid/tree.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: two-dice total 7 has six ordered ways (1+6,2+5,3+4,4+3,5+2,6+1) → 6/36 = 1/6; total 2 has one way (1+1) → 1/36; P(tail and 6) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12; without-replacement example P(two reds from 3R,2B) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10 (first draw 3/5 red, 2/5 blue). All consistent with the source row.
The '1/11' value appears only as a misconception to be corrected, never as a valid answer offered to learners.
The complement shortcut for 'at least one' is named in the pedagogy summary but is not given a worked activity here; a reviewer may wish to add one.

Activity 4 (drill) carries empty sourceClaims: the Nuffield equiprobability-bias claim documents the bias but its principle (resolving the bias requires building the full sample space) does not support a drill rationale that avoids full construction, and no source establishes the efficacy of recognition/fill-in drill.

Source claims cited support the underlying principles (tree rules; equiprobability bias) but do not establish that these specific activities or any particular interactive/toggle/tap-to-reveal feature were tested for efficacy; efficacy of any medium is therefore left as proposed/intended, not demonstrated.

probeDeeper: You flip a coin AND roll a die — what is P(heads and a 6)? Do you add or multiply the branch probabilities, and why?
Are the totals 2 to 12 equally likely? How many ways can you make 7, and how many ways to make 2?
If you draw two counters from a bag WITHOUT replacing the first, do the second-branch probabilities stay the same? Why not?
Why is 3+4 counted separately from 4+3 in the grid?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: builds the sample space of 36 equally-likely ordered (die1, die2) outcomes — via a grid or systematic list — finds 6 ways to total 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1) giving P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6, and 1 way to total 2 (1+1) giving P(2) = 1/36. The student recognises the 36 ordered outcomes are equally likely but the totals are not.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes aggregated outcomes are equally likely — treats the eleven totals 2–12 as each 1/11
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the 6×6 grid of the 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes; count how many make each total — seven has six ways, two has one — so the totals are not equally likely
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives P(7) = 1/11 (or P(2) = 1/11) without building the sample space of ordered outcomes

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores order when listing, undercounting the sample space
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat (die1, die2) as ordered pairs — 3+4 and 4+3 are different cells on the grid; there are 36 outcomes, six of which total 7
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome, giving 21 outcomes or only three ways to make 7

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds probabilities along a branch instead of multiplying (misapplies the AND rule)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Along a single path use the AND rule: multiply (1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12); adding is for OR across separate paths
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up combined event computes P(A and B) as P(A) + P(B) — e.g. P(tail and 6) = 1/2 + 1/6

errorPatterns.pattern: Reuses the first-event probabilities on the second branch of a without-replacement (dependent) event
errorPatterns.nextMove: For dependent events recompute the second branch from the reduced situation — one fewer item, and one fewer of whatever was drawn
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a 'draw two without replacing' probe, keeps the original probabilities on the second set of branches

responseLevels.gap: Assumes the totals are equally likely (P(7) = 1/11); no systematic sample space; adds branch probabilities for combined events
responseLevels.full: Builds the complete 36-outcome ordered sample space, counts favourable outcomes correctly (6 ways to 7 → 1/6), multiplies along branches and adds across paths, and recomputes probabilities for without-replacement events
responseLevels.partial: Builds some of the sample space and multiplies along branches for simple independent cases, but undercounts by ignoring order, or keeps probabilities fixed for without-replacement events — computes without a complete, ordered sample space

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child paper and this task: 'Two fair dice are rolled and the two numbers are added together. Work out the probability the total is 7. Then work out the probability the total is 2.' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they treat all totals 2–12 as equally likely or systematically build the 36-outcome sample space, whether they respect order when counting the ways to make 7, and how they express and simplify the answers.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates the student who lays out all 36 ordered outcomes and counts six ways to make 7 from one who assumes the eleven totals are equally likely (P(7) = 1/11), or ignores order and undercounts (three ways to 7, or 21 outcomes). The two-dice sample space is the classic exposer of assuming aggregated outcomes are equally likely.

sources.claim: In tree diagrams, probabilities on each set of branches sum to 1, you multiply along the branches for the AND rule (P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B)) and add across paths for OR; for dependent (without-replacement) events the second set of branch probabilities changes with the first outcome; and fractions should not be cancelled too early.
sources.source: Third Space Learning — Probability Tree Diagram

sources.claim: Children (and adults) show an equiprobability bias in the two-dice problem, assuming all the possible totals are equally probable; the difficulty is distinguishing elemental equally-likely outcomes from aggregated events, which requires representing the full sample space.
sources.source: Bryant & Nunes, Children's Understanding of Probability: A Literature Review (Nuffield Foundation, 2012)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Advanced Material Properties

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y5 Properties & changes of materials):** Compare and group together everyday materials on the basis of their properties, including hardness, solubility, transparency, conductivity (electrical and thermal), and response to magnets; give reasons, based on evidence from comparative and fair tests, for the particular uses of everyday materials.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-PS1-3):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-3] (including electrical and thermal conductivity, solubility, and response to magnetic forces).

- **Operational details:** This is a CONCEPTUAL/PROCEDURAL 'act to measure' node that goes beyond naming (see Material Properties Vocabulary) to QUANTIFYING and USING properties as evidence. The child runs the actual tests — build a circuit to check electrical conductivity, feel/measure how fast heat travels, scratch-test relative hardness, stir a solid into water to check solubility, bring a magnet near, shine light through for transparency — and records results in a properties table. Emphasise that each test isolates ONE property (a fair/comparative test: same amount, same conditions, one thing changed) and that the evidence gathered then JUSTIFIES a use ('copper for wires because it conducts electricity best in our test'). Keep electrical and thermal conductivity as separate measured columns. Density/floating can be touched as an emergent property but NGSS 5-PS1-3 does not require density.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal, quantitative). The child designs and runs a fair comparative test for a named property, tabulates results across several materials, and uses the table to argue which material best suits a given job.
bestPractices: Have children RUN each property test and record a measured result in a shared table, rather than being told the outcome.
Enforce fair/comparative testing: same quantity and conditions, one variable changed, so a result can be trusted.
Close the loop from evidence to use — require pupils to justify a material choice by citing their own table.
Treat electrical and thermal conductivity as separate measured columns to prevent the common fusion.
Bring the test that best discriminates materials to the front (conductivity, hardness) and keep quantities identical across specimens.
keyRepresentations: A multi-station property test bench (circuit, heat-travel, scratch-hardness, dissolve tank, magnet, light box)
A properties results table with materials as rows and tested properties as columns
A conductivity indicator (bulb brightness / reading) and a heat-travel colour gradient over time
A 'pick the material for the job' brief that forces evidence-based selection
commonMisconceptions: A material that conducts electricity is assumed to conduct heat identically (electrical and thermal conductivity fused).
'Hardness' is confused with strength or with being heavy.
A dissolved solid is thought to be destroyed rather than still present in solution.
'All metals are magnetic' — overgeneralising magnetism to non-ferrous metals like aluminium and copper.
A material's use is attributed to the object's name/tradition rather than to a measured property.

learn.summary: Children aged 9–11 learn advanced material properties (hardness, solubility, transparency, electrical and thermal conductivity, response to magnets) by running fair comparative tests, recording measured results in a table, and using that evidence to justify which material best suits a given job. The central aim is evidence-based reasoning: the measured property — not the object's name or tradition — decides the use. Electrical and thermal conductivity are kept as separate tested properties because children commonly fuse them.

activities.title: Materials test lab: run the tests, fill the table
feedback: If a learner reports 'it conducts' without saying which kind, prompt them to check the electrical column and the heat column separately — a material can score differently in each.
If results vary between pupils for the same material, ask whether the quantity and conditions were kept identical; an unfair test is the usual cause.
When a tile does not fit a prediction (e.g. aluminium not attracted to the magnet), treat the recorded result as the authority and update the table.
For the transparency test, remind learners to judge the light that lands on the surface behind the tile rather than looking toward the lamp or holding material up to the eyes toward a bright source.
activities.rationale: Children understand these properties by acting: running each test and watching a measured result appear lets them gather evidence and compare materials directly, which is the fair-test reasoning the standards demand. Isolating one property per test and keeping quantities/conditions identical is what makes a result trustworthy. Keeping electrical and thermal conductivity in separate columns targets a documented fusion. A hands-on classroom version with real circuits, real materials, and real measurements is an equally suitable way to do this work.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5 requires grouping by hardness/solubility/transparency/electrical+thermal conductivity/magnetism and giving evidence-based reasons from comparative and fair tests for uses of materials
NGSS 5-PS1-3: make observations and measurements to identify materials by properties incl electrical/thermal conductivity, solubility and response to magnetic forces; density is not included
Children fuse electrical and thermal conductivity and need them separated as distinct tested properties
learnerActions: Set up a specimen rack with tiles of different materials (e.g. copper, iron, aluminium, glass, wood, plastic, rubber, chalk).

At a circuit station, use a low-voltage battery circuit. Clip each tile into a gap in the circuit and observe whether the bulb lights (an optional conductivity reading makes this more concrete). Record conductor/insulator plus any measured value. Note that a simple bulb circuit usually cannot show differences between metals, because all the metal tiles light the bulb about equally.

At a heat station, stand one end of each tile (or same-sized strips) in the same amount of hot (not boiling) water, never in a flame, because wood, plastic and rubber can burn, melt or give off fumes. Time or watch how fast heat travels to the other end, for example with a heat-sensitive strip or a small blob of butter or wax at the far end. An optional colour-gradient-over-time display or timer can make heat travel visible. Record how fast heat moves.
At a scratch-hardness station, try scratching each material against the others to rank relative hardness; record the scratch order.

At a dissolve station, use small granular or powdered samples rather than the tiles. Include some soluble solids (e.g. salt, sugar) alongside insoluble ones (e.g. sand, powdered chalk). Stir the same measured amount of each into the same fixed amount of water at the same temperature, and record whether it dissolves (soluble/insoluble).
At a magnet station, bring a magnet near each tile and record whether it is attracted.

At a light/transparency station, shine light through each tile and record whether it is transparent, translucent or opaque — judge the light that passes through onto a surface placed behind the tile, and do not look toward the lamp or any bright source.

Handle the heat and circuit stations safely: use hot water rather than a flame for the heat test, and use only a low-voltage battery circuit for the electricity test (never mains). Work with adult supervision and a safe setup, and only check whether glass conducts electricity using a smooth-edged glass tile in that low-voltage circuit.

Enter every result into a shared properties table: materials as rows, tested properties as columns, keeping electrical and thermal conductivity in two separate columns and adding a transparency column.
For each test, keep the quantity and conditions the same and change only the material, so results can be trusted and compared.
activities.intendedInsight: Each property can be measured by an isolated fair test, and materials can be grouped and compared from the recorded evidence rather than from assumptions about what a material 'should' do.

activities.title: Pick the material for the job
feedback: If a learner picks a material by name/habit ('metal, because pans are metal'), ask which column of the table supports that and whether the job needs that property.
If they choose the overall 'best' material ignoring the job, point to a column where it fails the specific requirement (hot handle, safe case).
Accept any choice that is correctly justified by the right property column, even if it differs from the expected answer.
activities.rationale: Closing the loop from evidence to use requires pupils to justify a material choice by citing their own data. The tension between a material topping one column but failing another is what forces property-specific reasoning rather than name-based reasoning.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5 requires grouping by hardness/solubility/transparency/electrical+thermal conductivity/magnetism and giving evidence-based reasons from comparative and fair tests for uses of materials
learnerActions: Take a specific brief, e.g. 'choose the best handle for a hot pan' or 'choose the best core for an electromagnet'.
Sort or scan the completed properties table to find which materials score best on the property the job actually needs.

Notice when a material does well in one column but fails another. For example, copper conducts electricity well, yet a metal handle fails the heat-safety requirement because it conducts heat too well.

State a choice and justify it by citing the specific measured property from the table (e.g. 'plastic for the handle because it is an insulator and heat travelled slowly through it in our test', 'copper for the wire because it conducted electricity in our test').

Compare two metals for the same job (e.g. copper vs iron for a wire) and explain what the recorded results show. If the simple circuit showed no difference between them, say so, and note that other properties (e.g. bendiness, rusting) or measured conductivity readings would be needed to decide.
activities.intendedInsight: The right material depends on which measured property the job needs; evidence from your own table, not the object's name or tradition, justifies the choice.

activities.title: Predict-then-test the magnet (not all metals are magnetic)
feedback: If a learner predicts all four will stick, let the aluminium, copper and brass fail to stick first, then ask them to revise the rule.
If they still assert 'all metals are magnetic', ask them to name the metals that just failed the test.
Reinforce that the test, not the assertion, is the evidence: 'how would you know?' should be answerable by trying a magnet.
activities.rationale: 'All metals are magnetic' is a common overgeneralisation; a predict-observe-explain task exposes it because the prediction is made before the contradicting evidence arrives. This probes reasoning, not just the outcome.
learnerActions: Lay out an aluminium drinks can, a piece of solid copper (e.g. copper wire or pipe), a steel paperclip and a brass key. Avoid 'copper' coins: many, such as UK 1p and 2p coins made since 1992, are copper-plated steel and are attracted to magnets.
Before testing, predict which the magnet will pick up and write down WHY.
Test each one with the magnet and record what actually happens. If the objects really are aluminium, solid copper and solid brass, only the steel paperclip will be attracted.

Compare the prediction with the result and, if 'all metals are magnetic' was assumed, correct it: name the common magnetic metals (iron, most steels, nickel, cobalt) and the non-magnetic ones just tested (aluminium, copper, brass).
Answer a follow-up: name a metal a magnet will NOT pick up.
activities.intendedInsight: Being attracted to a magnet is a property of only some metals (mainly iron, most steels, nickel and cobalt), not a defining feature of all metals; a quick fair test settles it.

activities.title: Dissolving: gone or still there?
feedback: If a learner says the sugar/salt has 'gone' or been 'used up', point to the before/after mass or the recovered solid after evaporation.
Keep this brief here and signpost a fuller treatment of dissolving and solutions elsewhere.
activities.rationale: 'Dissolved means destroyed' is a documented misconception; comparing mass before/after and recovering the solid provides direct counter-evidence.
learnerActions: Dissolve a measured amount of a soluble solid (e.g. salt or sugar) into a fixed amount of water and note it seems to vanish.
Discuss whether the solid has been destroyed or is still present in the solution.

Where equipment allows, weigh the solid and water before mixing and the solution afterwards. Then recover the solid by letting the water evaporate from a salt solution in a shallow dish, to show it was present all along (sugar solutions tend to become sticky syrup rather than clean crystals).
Record 'soluble' in the properties table while noting the solid is not destroyed.
activities.intendedInsight: A dissolved solid is still present in the solution, not destroyed; dissolving changes how we see it, not whether it exists.

activities.title: Reference chart as a companion
feedback: If a learner relies only on the chart, redirect them to run the test and record their own result, since a fixed chart gives labels but cannot be re-measured or varied by the child.
Use the chart to settle terminology disputes, not to decide material choices in the 'pick the material' brief.
activities.rationale: A static reference chart is good for consolidating vocabulary and canonical results, but because it is fixed it cannot be re-measured or varied by the child; it is best as a companion to the hands-on testing rather than a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Use a tap-to-reveal or printed properties chart to confirm the correct vocabulary (conductor, insulator, soluble, transparent, magnetic) and canonical results after doing the tests.
Match each property word to the type of test that measures it.
Use the chart to check predictions before running a new test, then verify by testing.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidating the property vocabulary and canonical outcomes supports, but does not replace, gathering your own measured evidence.

constraints: Each test must isolate ONE property: same quantity, same conditions, only the material changed, so results can be trusted and compared.
Keep electrical and thermal conductivity as two separate measured columns; do not collapse them into a single 'conducts' result, because children commonly fuse them.
Pupils must justify material choices by citing their own recorded results, not the object's name or tradition.
Density/floating may be mentioned as an emergent property but is not required by NGSS 5-PS1-3.

A reference chart or categorise/match task consolidates vocabulary and checks classification already known but cannot provide the run-a-fair-test experience; use it as a companion, not the main activity.
Recognition or matching tasks can check classification and vocabulary but do not themselves elicit the independent evidence-gathering at the heart of this topic.
Define hardness operationally as resistance to scratching, kept separate from weight and from strength/toughness.

Heat and circuit tests involve hot water and electricity: a hands-on version needs appropriate adult supervision and a safe setup. Use a hot-water heat source, not a flame, because the samples include flammable and meltable materials. Use only low-voltage battery circuits, including when checking whether glass conducts electricity. State this safely in the activity itself.

For the transparency test, judge the light transmitted onto a surface behind the material; never look toward the lamp or a bright source or hold material up to the eyes toward a bright light. State this safe observation method in the relevant activity and feedback.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a conversation/dialogue format 'poor' and 3D as 'adds nothing'; these catalog-fit judgements were not carried over as universal claims. Discussion can usefully frame predictions and reasoning around measured evidence, and 3D or physical apparatus may offer a different experience — neither is asserted to be ineffective or unnecessary.

The source claimed a static image 'cannot let the child run the test' and so 'teaches the labels rather than the evidence-gathering'; softened to a narrowly scoped limit (a fixed chart cannot be manipulated or re-measured) rather than a universal claim that it cannot teach.
The Hardy et al. (2020) fusion claim is retained as support for the separate electrical/thermal columns but was not re-verified in this rewrite.

Heat-travel speed, scratch-hardness ranking, transparency and solubility outcomes depend on the specific materials, quantities and setup used; treat tabulated outcomes as results of the particular test performed, not fixed absolutes.

The interactive 'live reading / colour-gradient / magnet swings' details are retained as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory mechanisms; a real-materials version is an equally valid implementation.

assess.poeTask: Lay out an aluminium drinks can, a copper coin, a steel paperclip and a brass key. Ask the child to PREDICT which the magnet will pick up and WHY, before testing. Many predict all four ('they're all metal'). Test each: only the steel is attracted. The pre-test reasoning is the diagnostic part — the 'all metals are magnetic' rule is exposed the moment the aluminium and copper don't stick.
probeDeeper: The pan gets hot but the handle stays cool — what property difference explains that?
Name a metal a magnet will NOT pick up.
Is glass an electrical conductor or an insulator? How could we check safely?
Copper and steel are both metals — does it matter which you use for a wire? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Copper is a good electrical conductor (and thermal conductor) so it carries current / lets heat through; plastic is an insulator so the handle stays cool and safe to hold. NOT all metals are magnetic — only some (iron and steel, nickel, cobalt); you would test each with a magnet.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All metals are magnetic' — magnetism treated as a defining property of metal.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test aluminium, copper and brass with a magnet — no attraction — and name the few magnetic metals (iron/steel, nickel, cobalt).
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — all metals are magnetic, because being pulled by a magnet is what makes something a metal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says yes, all metals are magnetic; cannot name a non-magnetic metal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates thermal and electrical conductivity — uses one undifferentiated 'conducts' for both, so can't say WHY plastic suits a hot handle versus an electrical case.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a metal spoon getting hot in soup (thermal) with a wire carrying current (electrical); test each property separately and pair the word with its type.
errorPatterns.distractor: Copper is used because it conducts — heat and electricity are just the same conducting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a single 'it conducts' reason for both wire and handle, or can't separate heat from electricity.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Dissolved means destroyed' — a soluble solid that dissolves is thought to no longer exist.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Weigh before and after, and recover the solid by evaporation, to show it was still there all along (fuller treatment in Dissolving & Solutions).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the dissolved sugar/salt has gone / been used up.

errorPatterns.pattern: Hardness confused with heaviness or strength — calls the heaviest material the hardest.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define hardness operationally as resistance to scratching and test by scratch order; separate it from weight and from strength.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ranks 'hardest' by weight; conflates hard with strong/tough.

responseLevels.gap: Runs on 'metal = hard + conducts + magnetic' as one bundle; can't separate properties or cite test results.
responseLevels.full: Defines and tests each property distinctly, groups from results, and explains a real use by the specific property (electrical conductor vs insulator), accepting that metals vary — not all are magnetic.
responseLevels.partial: Tests and names some properties correctly but conflates electrical with thermal conduction, or still believes all metals are magnetic.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Copper is used for electrical wires, and a metal pan sits on the hob — but the pan's handle is plastic. Using the proper property words, explain why copper for the wire and plastic for the handle. Then tell me: are ALL metals magnetic, and how would you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Separating electrical from thermal conduction, and the 'not all metals magnetic' claim, distinguishes a child who holds the specific property concepts from one running on a 'metal = conducts + magnetic + hard' bundle. Tier-2's 'how would you know?' forces a test rather than an assertion.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Water Transport in Plants (investigation)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y3 'Plants'):** 'investigate the way in which water is transported within plants' — a working-scientifically, first-hand INVESTIGATION; the canonical method is coloured water drawn up a cut stem (celery, pale flower).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** honest note — no dedicated water-transport PE at this grade; it sits within plant-structure/function ideas (K-2-LS1-1 external structures) and later 5-LS1-1 (materials from water). This is primarily a UK Y3 investigation.

- **Operational details:** PROCEDURAL — the point is DOING and observing an investigation that makes an invisible process visible. Stand celery or a white carnation in coloured water; over hours the dye climbs and appears in the leaves/petals, evidencing that water travels UP from the cut base through the stem to the leaves and flowers. Slicing the stem afterwards reveals coloured dots/lines (the transport tubes), tying the observation to structure. The learning is threefold: (1) the OBSERVATION (colour reaches the top → water moved up); (2) the PATHWAY (roots/base → stem → leaves & flowers, an upward one-way route); (3) the METHOD itself — set up, wait, record over time, draw a labelled diagram of the path. Because it's slow and unseeable in real time, first-hand set-up plus time-lapse is ideal. Keep the mechanism simple: water moves up to the leaves (don't formalise xylem/transpiration — that's KS3). Guard against 'the stem sucks like a straw by mouth' — it's drawn up through fine tubes.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, procedural). The child describes/sets up the coloured-water investigation, observes and records that colour reaches the leaves/petals, and draws a labelled diagram showing water's path base → stem → leaves/flowers — concluding water is transported upward through the stem.
bestPractices: Do it first-hand — celery or a white flower in dyed water — because the whole value is watching an invisible transport process reveal itself over hours.
Record over TIME (photos/drawings at intervals) so the slow upward creep of colour is captured as evidence, not just an end result.
Cut and examine the stem afterwards to show the coloured tubes, linking the observation to the transport structure.
Trace the PATH explicitly — base/roots → stem → leaves and flowers — and have the child draw and label it.
Keep the mechanism age-appropriate (water moves up through tiny tubes to the leaves); do NOT introduce xylem/transpiration terminology (KS3).
Use a split-stem or two-colour variation to deepen the investigation (each half draws its own colour) as an extension.
keyRepresentations: A stem/celery with dye visibly risen into leaves/petals — the canonical evidence image.
A stem cross-section showing coloured transport tubes as dots/rings.
A labelled path diagram: water from the base up the stem to leaves and flowers.
A timed photo/drawing series showing the colour climbing.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking water moves DOWN or in all directions rather than being drawn upward from the base to the leaves.
Believing the stem 'sucks' water like drinking through a mouth, rather than water rising through fine tubes.
Assuming leaves get their water directly (e.g. from rain/air) rather than via transport up the stem.
Thinking the colour appearing in petals is the flower 'making' colour rather than dyed water arriving there.
Not connecting the observation to structure — missing that the stem contains tubes that carry the water.
Expecting the process to be instant rather than taking hours.

learn.summary: Water transport in plants for ages 7-8 (UK DfE Year 3 'Plants'): a first-hand, working-scientifically investigation in which children stand celery or a pale white flower in dyed water, watch the colour climb over hours, and slice the stem to see the tubes that carried it. The learning is threefold: the OBSERVATION (colour reaches the top, so water moved up), the PATHWAY (base/roots to stem to leaves and flowers, an upward route) and the METHOD itself (set up, wait, record over time, draw a labelled diagram). Keep the mechanism simple (water moves up through tiny tubes to the leaves) and do not formalise xylem/transpiration, which belong to later secondary science. A screen simulation can compress the slow process and let children run variations, but it is an untested scaffold paired with the real experiment, which supplies the actual evidence. In US NGSS there is no dedicated water-transport performance expectation at this grade; it sits near plant structure/function (1-LS1-1, 4-LS1-1) and plants' need for water (2-LS2-1, 5-LS1-1).

activities.title: Real coloured-water investigation (celery or white flower)
feedback: If the learner expects the colour to stay only at the base, point to the dye in the leaf veins or petals: water climbed all the way up. Trace the continuous path base to stem to leaf together.
If the learner expects the stem to get wet on the outside, cut it crossways and show the coloured dots inside: water travels inside through specific channels, not over the surface.
If the learner expects an instant result, prompt 'what will you look at, and when?' so they build in waiting and a before/after comparison; the process takes hours.
If the learner says the flower is 'making' the colour, remind them the beaker water was dyed and that same colour has now arrived in the petals: it was carried there.
activities.rationale: The whole value of this topic is watching an invisible transport process reveal itself over time with real materials; doing and observing it first-hand, recording over time, and inspecting the stem matches the procedural, working-scientifically aim of the standard and ties observation to structure.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory: 'investigate the way in which water is transported within plants'.

Children often think a stem 'sucks' water like a mouth or that leaves get water directly, rather than water rising through tubes from the base; the coloured-water investigation makes the upward path visible.
learnerActions: Stand a stick of white celery with leaves on, or a pale white carnation, in a beaker of water dyed a bright colour (e.g. red or blue).
Before leaving it, write or say your plan: what will you look at, and when? Set up a before/after comparison and take a first photo or drawing.
Over several hours (or leave overnight), record what you see at intervals with photos or drawings, so the slow upward creep of colour is captured as evidence, not just a final result.
When the colour has risen, point out where the dye ended up (in the leaf veins / petals) and describe which way the water travelled.
Cut across the stem with scissors or a knife (with adult help) and use a hand lens to find the coloured dots or lines inside, the tiny tubes that carried the water.
Draw and label a diagram showing the path of the water: base/roots to stem to leaves and flowers.
activities.intendedInsight: Water is drawn upward from the base of the plant, through fine tubes inside the stem, all the way up to the leaves and flowers. Watching dyed water appear at the top is the evidence that this invisible, slow process happens.

activities.title: Compress and vary the investigation on screen
feedback: When the colour reaches the petals: 'coloured water arrived here, it travelled up from the base.'
When the stem is sliced: 'these tiny tubes inside carried the water up.'

For the split-stem prediction: if the learner expects one uniform colour, show each half drew up its own colour, giving a two-tone flower, because each half's tubes carried the dye from the beaker it was standing in.
activities.rationale: The process is slow and hidden, so a time-compressing, variable simulation may make the climbing dye and internal tubes visible and let children run comparisons (different colours, split stem) that are hard with a single real specimen. This is an untested scaffold: it shows and lets them vary the process, while the real dyed plant remains the evidence that it is true.
sourceClaims: Children often think a stem 'sucks' water like a mouth or that leaves get water directly, rather than water rising through tubes from the base; the coloured-water investigation makes the upward path visible.
learnerActions: Choose a specimen (white carnation or celery) and a dye colour, place it in the water, and drag a time slider forward to compress hours into seconds as the colour creeps up the stem and blooms into the petals or leaf edges.

Use a 'slice the stem' action to reveal the coloured dots inside (for a carnation stem these sit in a ring; in a celery stalk they sit in a curved row near the outer, ridged edge), the tiny tubes that carried the water, linking what you saw to the plant's structure.
Try a split-stem mode: put each half of the stem in a different colour and predict, then check, that the flower comes out two-toned.
Complete a label step: mark the water's path base to stem to leaves on the diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: Water moves up from the base through internal tubes to the leaves and flowers; varying the set-up (colours, split stem) shows the same pathway behaves predictably.

activities.title: Reference diagram: trace the path and the tubes
feedback: If the learner names the path out of order, re-anchor at the base: water enters low and rises, so the base comes first and the leaves/flowers last.
If the learner cannot locate the tubes, direct attention to the coloured dots in the cross-section.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference diagram clearly shows the path and the tubes and is a useful consolidating reference; it presents a finished result rather than letting the child run the investigation, so it supports but does not replace the first-hand work.
learnerActions: Tap or point to the dyed petal and say what it tells you ('coloured water arrived here, it travelled up').
Tap or point to the stem cross-section and name what carries the water ('tiny tubes carry water up').
Tap or point to the base and say what happens there ('water enters here').
Using the diagram, retell the whole path in order: base/roots to stem to leaves and flowers.
activities.intendedInsight: A labelled picture of the dyed plant and stem cross-section fixes the pathway and the location of the transport tubes as a memory aid after the investigation.

activities.title: Check understanding of method and pathway
feedback: If a learner orders observation before set-up, remind them you cannot observe before you have set it up and waited.
If a learner says water moves down or in all directions, point back to the dye reaching the top leaves/petals as evidence of an upward route.
If a learner predicts a single colour for the split stem, explain each half carries up its own dye, so the flower usually shows two tones, often in different parts of the petals.
activities.rationale: Ordering, path-drawing and targeted questions check whether the method and pathway are understood; these consolidate rather than enact the investigation, so they follow the hands-on work rather than standing in for it.
learnerActions: Put the investigation steps in the right order (set up specimen in dyed water, record over time, observe the colour risen, slice the stem to see the tubes).
Draw the water's route on a plant outline from base to stem to leaves.
Answer: which way does water move through the plant, and where does the colour appear first and last?
Predict: if you split the stem and stand each half in a different colour, what will the flower look like?
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state the direction of movement (upward), the ordered pathway, and the role of the internal tubes, and can predict a variation.

constraints: This is a PROCEDURAL, first-hand investigation: the core learning is doing, waiting, observing and recording over time, so a real celery/carnation experiment should anchor the topic.
Keep the mechanism age-appropriate: water moves up through tiny tubes to the leaves. Do NOT introduce xylem or transpiration terminology, which belongs to later secondary science.
Guard against 'the stem sucks water like drinking through a mouth': water is drawn up through fine tubes, not sucked by a mouth.
The process takes hours; build in waiting and interval recording rather than expecting an instant result.

A screen simulation is an untested scaffold that compresses time and allows variations and a view of hidden tubes; it does not supply the first-hand evidence and should be paired with the real experiment.
A reference diagram and check-style questions present or review the finished result; they consolidate but do not substitute for setting up and observing the investigation.

Cross-section appearance depends on the specimen (carnation shows a ring of dots, celery a curved row of dots near the outer, ridged edge of the stalk); read the real cut as it actually appears rather than assuming a fixed pattern.
Cutting the stem needs adult supervision when a knife or scissors is used.
US NGSS has no dedicated water-transport performance expectation at this grade; this is primarily a UK Year 3 investigation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The OpenLearn source (misconceptions; coloured-water investigation makes the upward path visible) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its specific claims as unconfirmed even where cited in sourceClaims, including where it is reused for the simulation activity to identify the same misconception.

The source phrasing 'water was pulled all the way up' and references to vascular bundles reflect real xylem/transpiration mechanisms not taught at this level; activities deliberately keep to 'water moves up through tiny tubes' per the stated KS3 boundary. The fuller mechanism is noted here only for context.

The original recommendation leaned strongly on the simulation as 'ideal'; this rewrite retains it as a scaffold and restores the first-hand experiment as the primary activity, consistent with the PROCEDURAL type and the standard's working-scientifically intent.

The 'conversation adds nothing' and '3D adds nothing/adds cost without revealing anything' judgements from the source are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy claims, and have not been propagated as universal laws.

Cross-section appearance depends on the specimen: carnation (dicot) shows a ring of dots while celery shows scattered bundles; the on-screen 'ring of dots' is an approximation and the real cut should be read as it actually appears.

probeDeeper: Where exactly did the red water end up — and what does that tell you about the direction water travels?
When you cut the stem, what did you see inside? What are those coloured tubes for?
Which part of the plant took the water in first, and which got it last?
If you split the stem and stood each half in a different colour, what would you predict?
assess.correctAnswer: Stands the celery in the red water, waits, and observes the red colour travelling UP the stem into the leaves; cutting the stem reveals red-stained tubes (vascular bundles) running through it. Concludes water travels from the bottom (roots end) UP the stem to the leaves, through tubes inside the stem. A good performance sets it up as a tracked observation and reads the path from root-end to leaves.

errorPatterns.pattern: water stays in the roots/bottom and doesn't travel up to the leaves
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the red in the leaf veins — water climbs all the way up. Trace the continuous path base→stem→leaf together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: expects the red colour only at the base; surprised to find it in the leaves

errorPatterns.pattern: water soaks up the outside of the stem, not through tubes inside
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cut the stem crossways to reveal the red-stained tubes — water travels INSIDE through specific channels, not over the surface.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: doesn't cut/inspect the stem, or expects surface wetting rather than internal channels

errorPatterns.pattern: runs it as a one-off with no wait/observation plan (procedural lapse)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach transport — prompt 'what will you look at, and when?' so they build in waiting and a before/after comparison.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: expects an instant result, or doesn't leave time / doesn't plan what to look for

responseLevels.gap: Expects water to stay low or wet the outside; doesn't inspect the stem; can't trace a path.
responseLevels.full: Sets up a tracked observation, shows dye risen into the leaves and stained tubes inside a cut stem, and describes water travelling up through internal channels from the root-end to the leaves — predicting the split-stem two-colour result.
responseLevels.partial: Observes the colour rising and states water goes up, but doesn't connect it to internal tubes or lay out a clear root→stem→leaf path — result seen without the mechanism.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a stick of white celery (leaves on), a beaker of water dyed bright red, a knife/scissors and a hand lens. Say: 'Set this up to find out HOW water moves through the plant, leave it, then show me what you found and where the water went. You can cut the stem to look inside.' Watch how they set it up, what they observe, and how they trace the path — don't tell them what to expect.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Doing it (not describing it) reveals whether the child expects water to travel UP through internal tubes to the leaves, or holds that water just 'sits in the roots' / soaks the outside. The dyed water makes the invisible path visible; watching the setup and the where-did-it-go reading exposes the mental model.

pedagogy.summary: This topic teaches children to read rock layers (strata) as a record of time: layers are deposited over long periods with the oldest at the bottom (superposition), and fossils in different layers are evidence of organisms that lived at different times, so patterns in rock formations reveal how a landscape changed over millions of years. It is best taught with a built-up sediment model and real strata (e.g. the Grand Canyon), keeping to RELATIVE ordering of events rather than absolute dates or the detailed mechanism of rock formation.
bestPractices: Build superposition physically — lay down sediment layers over 'time' and bury objects/organisms in each — so the oldest-at-the-bottom rule is constructed, not asserted.
Use fossils as time-markers: different fossils in different layers show different organisms lived at different times; the order of layers gives the order of events.
Keep to RELATIVE time (which is older/younger, what happened before what), not absolute dates — matching the assessment boundary.
Read real, dramatic strata (canyon walls, cliff faces) so pupils apply the rule to genuine evidence of landscape change.
Have pupils construct an explanation of how a landscape changed over time FROM the pattern of layers and fossils, rather than being told the story.
Use correct vocabulary (sediment, strata, fossil, layer) established in the linked rocks topic, but keep the focus on the ordering inference.
keyRepresentations: A labelled strata cross-section with the oldest layer at the bottom.
A build-up-the-layers model (deposit sediment over time, bury an organism in each).
A fossil-in-layer timeline linking each fossil to its relative position/age.
A real canyon or cliff cutaway showing many layers.
commonMisconceptions: All rock layers formed at the same time, or the order of layers does not indicate time.
The youngest/oldest layer is at the top (reversing superposition).
Fossils are only dinosaur bones, or are just 'pictures in rocks', rather than remains of once-living organisms.
You can read the exact age of a layer directly by looking at it (confusing relative with absolute dating).
Landscapes are fixed — rather than the product of change recorded in the layers.

learn.summary: Children learn to read rock strata as a record of time: layers build up with the oldest at the bottom (superposition, which holds for layers that have not been folded, overturned or otherwise disturbed), and fossils in different layers are evidence of organisms that lived at different times, so patterns in the rock reveal how a landscape changed over long periods. The focus is the evidence-reading inference — ordering events and reconstructing landscape change from layers and fossils — kept to RELATIVE time (older/younger, before/after), never absolute dates or the detailed mechanism of rock formation.

activities.title: Build-up-the-layers time machine
feedback: If a learner orders the higher fossil as the earlier animal — e.g. reasoning 'it's been up there longest' — replay the build-up: each new layer lands ON TOP of the previous one, so the bottom layer formed first. Being higher means it arrived later, not earlier; oldest at the bottom, youngest at the top.
If a learner says all the layers and fossils formed together, emphasise that layers accumulate one atop another over long stretches of time, so different layers record different times.
Confirm correct reasoning by connecting a fossil's position to WHEN its organism lived: a lower fossil was buried longer ago, therefore that organism lived earlier.
Prompt for landscape change: a sea-creature fossil high on land shows that place was once underwater — so landscapes are not fixed but change over long time.
activities.rationale: The learning goal is an evidence-reading inference, which is served by having the child construct the layer order and perform the ordering reasoning rather than being told the story. Building superposition physically (laying sediment, burying organisms) makes the oldest-at-bottom rule something constructed and presents the common reversal and single-event misconceptions for correction.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-ESS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS1-1]' — boundary: relative time only, no mechanism of rock formation and no memorising layers; DCI ESS1.C: the presence and location of [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS1-1] formed.
Students commonly reverse superposition (thinking oldest is on top) and think fossils are only dinosaur bones; teaching the ordering with a build-up model addresses this.
learnerActions: Deposit sediment one layer at a time as 'time' passes, so each new layer settles on top of the last.
In each era, place/bury an organism in the layer being formed at that time (e.g. a trilobite early, an ammonite later).
Relate the build-up to a jar: pour in sand, then mud, then gravel, letting each settle before adding the next — the first poured ends up at the bottom, mirroring how the oldest layer sits lowest.
Cut into the resulting cliff/cross-section and read it back: order the buried fossils from earliest-lived to latest-lived.
State, in your own words, why the fossil in the lower layer must be older than the one above it.
Reconstruct how the landscape changed over time from the sequence of layers and the fossils in them.
activities.intendedInsight: The trilobite resting at the BOTTOM must be older than the ammonite above it, because its layer was deposited — and the organism buried — first. Undisturbed rock layers are a stack of time with the oldest underneath, so a landscape's history can be read from its layers.

activities.title: Read real strata and reconstruct the story
feedback: If the learner cannot connect a fossil's position to when its organism lived, point back to the build-up model: lower layer = buried earlier = organism lived earlier.
Reinforce landscape-change reasoning: ask what a sea fossil high on a hill tells you about that place long ago.
Keep answers to relative order (which came before which); if the learner reaches for exact ages, redirect — you cannot read an exact age off a layer just by looking at it.
activities.rationale: Applying the rule to real, dramatic strata lets pupils use the inference on authentic evidence and construct the explanation themselves, which is the stated objective. Transfer to a new cliff checks the ordering skill rather than recall of one example.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-ESS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS1-1]' — boundary: relative time only, no mechanism of rock formation and no memorising layers; DCI ESS1.C: the presence and location of [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS1-1] formed.
learnerActions: Examine a real, dramatic strata cross-section (a canyon wall or cliff face) with many visible layers that are flat-lying and not folded or overturned.
Identify which layers are older and younger using the oldest-at-the-bottom rule.
Match named fossils to the layers they appear in and order the organisms by relative time.
Write or say a short explanation of how this landscape changed over a long time, citing the layer/fossil pattern as evidence.
Transfer the reasoning to a second, unfamiliar cliff with undisturbed layers to check you can apply the rule to new evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: The ordering rule applies to genuine evidence: real rock formations whose layers have not been overturned record a sequence of events, and you can construct the landscape's history from the pattern of layers and fossils rather than memorising a told story.

activities.title: Labelled strata cross-section reference
feedback: Use this as a support when a learner is unsure of a term; then return them to building or reading a cliff so they perform the ordering themselves.

Correct 'fossils are only dinosaur bones' or 'just pictures in rock' — a fossil is the preserved remains or traces (such as imprints or footprints) of a once-living organism, from shells and plants as well as animals (often, over long time, the remains are gradually replaced by minerals; the full formation mechanism is covered in the linked prerequisite topic, so keep it brief here).
activities.rationale: A fixed, labelled reference consolidates vocabulary and the relative-age mapping. It is a scaffold: it displays the ordering rather than requiring the child to construct it, so it should accompany, not replace, the build-and-read activities.
learnerActions: Study a labelled strata cross-section with the oldest layer at the bottom.
Reveal, for a selected layer or fossil, its relative age and which organism it represents (e.g. tap or lift a panel).
Use it to check vocabulary: sediment, strata, fossil, layer.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference links each layer and fossil to its relative position and age, anchoring the vocabulary used when reasoning about order.

activities.title: Sequence and match check
feedback: If the higher fossil is picked as the earlier animal, this signals inverted superposition — revisit the build-up (new layers land on top, so the bottom is oldest).
If both animals are said to have lived at the same time, revisit that layers accumulate over long stretches of time, so different layers record different times.
A correct order can be selected without the underlying reason, so always pair the sequence with a 'how do you know?' to elicit and check the rule independently.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and matching are a natural fit for checking the ordering inference and surfacing the specific misconceptions. Requiring an explanation guards against a correct selection masking faulty reasoning; note that ordering well is evidence of the inference only when the reason is also produced.
sourceClaims: Students commonly reverse superposition (thinking oldest is on top) and think fossils are only dinosaur bones; teaching the ordering with a build-up model addresses this.
learnerActions: Order a set of layers from oldest to youngest.
Match each named fossil to the layer it belongs in.
Answer a short reasoning question on superposition, e.g. which of two fossils lived earlier and why.
Explain WHY, not just WHICH, so the rule you are using is visible.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering and matching reveal whether the learner is applying superposition correctly and connecting fossil position to time, or using an inverted/single-event rule.

constraints: Keep to RELATIVE time (older/younger, before/after); do not teach absolute dates. You cannot read an exact age off a layer just by looking at it.

Do not teach the detailed mechanism of rock formation or require memorising specific layer names, per the assessment boundary. (Year 3 linked work covers that fossils form when once-living things are trapped in rock — use it only to correct the 'fossils are just pictures/only dinosaur bones' idea, without making mechanism the focus here.)
A fixed labelled cross-section is a scaffold: it shows the order but does not require the child to construct or infer it, so pair it with building/reading activities rather than using it alone.
A sequence or matching task can be completed by selection without the underlying reasoning; require a 'how do you know?' to elicit the rule being used.
A fly-through 3D canyon can convey scale and atmosphere, but the ordering/reading skill is fully served in a 2D cross-section; treat immersive 3D as optional enrichment, not a requirement.
Interviewing or listening to a character (e.g. a palaeontologist) can add context, but the ordering inference is better performed by the child than narrated to them.
Use correct vocabulary (sediment, strata, fossil, layer) but keep the focus on the ordering inference, not terminology drill.
Optional interaction examples (scrubbable time, dragging fossils into order, tap/lift-to-reveal panels) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The DfE Year 3 'Rocks' claim and the general Earth-science misconceptions claim (including its assertion that a build-up model 'addresses' the reversal) were marked verified:false in the source; treat as unconfirmed, and read any efficacy wording as proposed/intended rather than demonstrated.

Self-audit of science logic: superposition (oldest at bottom, youngest on top) and reading fossil position as a record of relative time are internally consistent as stated across all activities; no superposition reversal or same-age slips remain. The jar analogy is framed as dry sequential pouring so first-poured sits lowest, avoiding density-settling confusion.

The reteach for the 'fossil = unchanged real bones' misconception concerns how fossils form (mineral replacement), which sits at the edge of this topic's relative-time boundary; it is kept light and deferred to the linked fossil-formation prerequisite topic.

The original 'moment of insight', the jar and sea-fossil-high-on-land examples, and the misconception/distractor content were preserved as activity actions and feedback; no conceptual error required correction, only boundary-scoping of the fossil-formation correction.
No comparative-efficacy or necessity claims (e.g. 'only doing teaches this', 'a static image cannot teach') are asserted; legacy framing was softened to scoped scaffold/limit statements.

probeDeeper: If you poured sand, then mud, then gravel into a jar, which ends up at the bottom — and which was poured first?
What does finding a sea creature's fossil in a cliff high on a hill tell you about that place long ago?
Someone says the higher fossil must be older because it's had longer up there. What's wrong with that?
assess.correctAnswer: The trilobite, in the lower layer, lived earlier: rock layers build up over time with the oldest at the bottom and the youngest on top, so a fossil in a lower layer was buried longer ago.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the top layer is the oldest — it's been sitting there longest' (inverted superposition)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build layers by dropping sediment — each new layer lands ON TOP, so the bottom formed first; oldest at the bottom, youngest at the top.
errorPatterns.distractor: The ammonite — the top layer is the oldest because it has been there longest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: picks the higher fossil (ammonite) as the earlier animal

errorPatterns.pattern: 'all the layers and fossils formed at the same time (one flood)' (single-event, no deep time)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Layers accumulate slowly, one atop another, over long stretches of time — different layers record different times.
errorPatterns.distractor: They lived at the same time — all the layers formed together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says both animals lived at the same time

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the fossil is the animal's actual body/bones, still there unchanged' (fossil = preserved remains, not mineralised)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach how fossils form: the remains are gradually replaced by minerals and turned to rock over long time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: talks about the real bones or skin still being present in the rock

responseLevels.gap: Inverts superposition (top = oldest) or says all fossils/layers are the same age.
responseLevels.full: Applies superposition to order the fossils, reads fossils as evidence of different organisms at different times, and infers landscape change over long time (e.g. a sea fossil high on land = once underwater); transfers to a new cliff.
responseLevels.partial: Knows oldest-at-the-bottom for layers but doesn't connect a fossil's position to WHEN the organism lived, or can't read landscape change from it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a cliff face you find a trilobite fossil in a low layer and an ammonite fossil in a higher layer. Which animal lived earlier — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with inverted superposition picks the higher (ammonite) as older, reasoning 'it's been up there longest.' A child who imagines all layers forming together says they lived at the same time. Correct reasoning uses oldest-at-bottom AND reads fossil position as a record of time. The why-tier exposes which rule the child is using.
