pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Ohm's Law: voltage, current, resistance

- **Standards:** This topic STRADDLES KS3→KS4 (UK); it is UK-anchored for the US.

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** KS3 'Current electricity' defines resistance as 'measured in ohms, as the ratio of potential difference (p.d.) to current', which is exactly R = V/I and licenses rearranging it — so the CALCULATION sits within KS3 reach; however the NAME 'Ohm's Law' appears NOWHERE in the National Curriculum at either key stage (it is a textbook/exam-board convention), and the GRAPHICAL exploration of current–voltage relationships for different components (I–V characteristics) is KS4 'exploring current, resistance and voltage relationships for different circuit elements, including their graphical representations' (all verified by fetch). So: the V=IR ratio and calculation = KS3; the named law and I–V graphs = KS4.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** no middle-school PE covers DC-circuit resistance/Ohm calculations, so this is UK-anchored.

- **Operational details:** This is a PROCEDURAL topic: given two of voltage, current and resistance, the child applies V = IR, rearranges it for the unknown, and explains that resistance OPPOSES current, naming the factors that change it (material, length, thickness). It builds directly on the previous topic's meanings of V and I; the new object is resistance, R, as the ratio that links them. The best teaching keeps the algebra tethered to meaning — resistance is how hard the circuit makes it for charge to flow, so for a fixed push (V) more resistance means less current, and for a fixed resistance more push means more current — rather than letting the formula triangle become a meaningless symbol-shuffle. A particle picture of resistance (charge colliding with a lattice; a longer wire = more collisions; a thicker wire = more lanes) makes the factors causal rather than memorised.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational / quantitative, ~12–13).
bestPractices: Build V = IR FROM the ratio definition the child already met: resistance is potential difference divided by current (R = V/I), so V = IR and I = V/R are the same relationship rearranged — derive it, don't drop it as a triangle.

Teach resistance as OPPOSITION to flow with a causal picture: charges collide with the vibrating lattice of the material; more collisions = more resistance = less current for the same voltage. This makes 'opposes current' mechanistic, not a slogan.

Make the factors predictable from the picture: a LONGER wire = more collisions on the way = more resistance; a THICKER wire = more parallel lanes = less resistance; different MATERIALS pack the lattice differently. Have pupils predict before checking.
Drill the proportional reasoning, not just substitution: for fixed R, doubling V doubles I; for fixed V, doubling R halves I. The relationships matter more than the arithmetic at this tier.

Use the formula triangle ONLY as a support after meaning is secure, and warn against it as a crutch — require a sentence of reasoning ('more resistance, same push, so less current') alongside any rearrangement.

Keep 'resistance opposes / reduces current' distinct from 'resistance uses up current' — resistance lowers the rate of flow everywhere in a series loop; it does not consume charge (the current is still the same all the way round, just smaller).

Flag honestly that real components aren't all 'ohmic': a filament bulb's resistance rises as it heats, so V and I are not simply proportional — but the graphical I–V treatment of that is the KS4 extension, kept qualitative here.
keyRepresentations: The ratio/relationship trio R = V/I, V = IR, I = V/R — shown as rearrangements of ONE relationship, each readable in words ('current is push divided by opposition').
Particle model of resistance — charges colliding with a lattice; longer wire = more collisions, thicker wire = more lanes, making the factors causal.
The V–I proportional relationship for a fixed resistor — double the voltage, double the current — introduced numerically/in words (the formal straight-line graph is the KS4 step).
The formula triangle (V over I and R) — a calculation support, explicitly labelled a crutch to be backed by reasoning.
A variable circuit picture — a battery slider (V) and a resistor slider (R) with a live ammeter (I) showing how changing one moves the current.
commonMisconceptions: Treating V = IR as a meaningless triangle to shuffle — substituting without knowing which quantity is the push, the flow, or the opposition.
Thinking resistance 'uses up' current — resistance REDUCES the current (everywhere in a series loop) but does not consume charge; the current is still the same all the way round, just smaller.
Believing a thicker wire has MORE resistance — it has LESS (more lanes for charge); thickness and length pull opposite ways.
Assuming current and voltage are always directly proportional — only when resistance is constant; a heating filament's resistance rises, so its V–I line bends (the KS4 caveat).
Confusing which quantity changes when — e.g. expecting changing the resistor to change the battery's voltage; the cell sets V, the circuit's R then sets I.
Mis-rearranging the equation — e.g. writing I = VR instead of I = V/R — from manipulating symbols without the proportional sense (more opposition must mean less current).
Equating 'Ohm's Law' with all components — it describes the constant-resistance (ohmic) case; not every component obeys a single straight-line relationship.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13, Ohm's Law (V = IR) is taught as ONE relationship linking voltage (the push), current (the flow) and resistance (the opposition). Current is proportional to voltage only while resistance stays constant. The relationship is derived from the ratio definition R = V/I rather than memorised as a formula triangle. The core learning is seeing how current responds when you change voltage or resistance, and understanding WHY via a particle picture of charges colliding with the lattice: in a longer wire each charge meets more collisions along the way, and a thinner wire has fewer parallel lanes for charge, so both give more resistance. Activities cover an interactive sandbox for cause-and-effect exploration, a retrieval set for calculation fluency, reference supports, and a Socratic debrief. Note the UK curriculum placement: the V=IR ratio and calculation sit at KS3, while the named 'Ohm's Law' and graphical I–V treatment are KS4 extensions kept qualitative here.

activities.title: Ohm's Law sandbox: change the push, change the opposition
feedback: When the learner predicts the current wrongly on a voltage change, point back to the proportional link: same resistance, twice the push, so twice the flow.
If a learner expects a thicker wire to have more resistance, show the particle view — a thicker wire offers more parallel lanes, so more charge gets through and resistance is lower.
Reinforce that the current still flows everywhere in the loop, just at a smaller rate: resistance reduces the flow, it does not use up or consume the charge.
If the learner assumes voltage and current are always proportional, use the filament mode to show the relationship bending once resistance changes with heating (kept qualitative; the graph is KS4).
Praise reasoning stated in words ('more opposition, same push, so less current') over silent slider-dragging.
activities.rationale: A manipulable sandbox with sliders and a live ammeter lets current respond to changes the learner makes, turning the equation from symbol-shuffle into observed proportional behaviour; the particle-view toggle supplies a mechanistic reason for the factor effects, and the optional filament mode previews the non-ohmic case. A fixed diagram can show the relationship but cannot let the learner test it interactively. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: The 'resistance uses up current', formula-triangle-without-meaning, and thicker-wire-more-resistance errors are documented difficulties best addressed by deriving V=IR from the ratio, drilling proportional reasoning, and a collision/particle picture of resistance and its factors.
learnerActions: Set a battery to 3 V across a resistor and read the current on a live ammeter.
Keeping the same resistor (constant resistance), drag the voltage to 6 V and watch the current double in real time — put twice the push in, get twice the flow.
Holding the voltage fixed, make the wire thicker and watch the current climb; lengthen it and watch the current fall.
Try a material swap to see that different materials give different resistance for the same size of wire.

Toggle a particle view that shows charges colliding with the lattice: observe that in a longer wire each charge meets more collisions along the way, and that a thinner wire has fewer parallel lanes for charge, so fewer charges get through per second.
Use a 'predict the ammeter, then reveal' mode: commit a value for the current before the meter is uncovered on each change.
Optionally switch on a filament mode where the resistance climbs as the wire heats, so the current no longer simply doubles when the voltage doubles — a qualitative preview of the KS4 non-ohmic case.
Read V = IR updating beside every move and say aloud which quantity is the push, which is the flow, and which is the opposition.
activities.intendedInsight: V = IR is a description of cause and effect the learner controls: for a fixed resistance, doubling the voltage doubles the current; for a fixed voltage, doubling the resistance halves the current. The factor effects (longer = more resistance, thicker = less resistance, material matters) become causal through the collision picture, not memorised. The optional filament mode shows that this neat proportionality holds only while resistance stays constant.

activities.title: Calculate and reason: V, I, R fluency set
feedback: For a rearrangement slip (multiplying when division is needed), have the learner re-derive from R = V/I and check against a proportional sentence.
If a learner picks I = VR, ask what should happen to current when resistance grows — the formula they chose makes current grow, which contradicts 'opposition reduces flow'.
When units are dropped, ask which quantity each number measures before accepting the answer.
activities.rationale: A scored, well-defined item set is a natural fit for checking calculation and rearrangement fluency and for surfacing the common errors. It verifies fluency but does not itself provide the manipulable experience of watching current respond, so it works best as a companion to the sandbox. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: The 'resistance uses up current', formula-triangle-without-meaning, and thicker-wire-more-resistance errors are documented difficulties best addressed by deriving V=IR from the ratio, drilling proportional reasoning, and a collision/particle picture of resistance and its factors.
learnerActions: Solve fill-in/numeric V=IR problems with friendly numbers: find I given V and R; find R given V and I; find V given I and R.
Answer proportional-reasoning questions such as 'voltage doubles, resistance stays the same — what happens to the current?' (it doubles).

Sort changes — longer wire / shorter wire / thicker wire / thinner wire — into 'more resistance' vs 'less resistance', and note that changing to a different material can give either more or less resistance depending on which material is used.
Spot the wrong rearrangement: identify that I = VR is incorrect and that I = V/R is right, explaining that more opposition must mean less current.
Write the correct unit beside each answer (volts, amperes, ohms) and say which unit belongs to which quantity.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can rearrange the single relationship for any unknown, attach correct units, and use proportional reasoning rather than rote substitution. Catching I = VR as wrong comes from the proportional sense, not from symbol-manipulation alone.

activities.title: Quick reference: the relationship and the particle picture
feedback: If a learner reaches for the formula triangle, require a sentence of reasoning alongside any rearrangement so the triangle stays a support, not a crutch.
activities.rationale: A tappable reference supports recall of symbols, units and factor effects. It cannot let current respond to a changed voltage or resistance, so it serves as reference beside the interactive work, not as the place where the proportional concept is first built. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Tap each symbol in R = V/I / V = IR / I = V/R to reveal its quantity, unit and plain-words meaning ('current is push divided by opposition').
Tap a longer or thinner wire in a labelled diagram to reveal 'more resistance', and a thicker wire to reveal 'less resistance'.
Use the reference alongside the sandbox or the calculation set as a memory aid, not as the main teacher.
activities.intendedInsight: The three forms R = V/I, V = IR and I = V/R are rearrangements of ONE relationship, each readable in words; the factor effects can be recalled with a labelled picture.

activities.title: Engineer debrief: what happens to the current if...?
feedback: Press for the mechanism: 'because resistance is opposition, halving it at the same voltage lets twice as much charge through per second, so the current doubles.'
If the learner says a big resistor stops current entirely, show that a large resistor still passes a small current — it reduces, not blocks.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue can probe and firm up reasoning after hands-on exploration, targeting the specific misconceptions. Talk alone does not let the learner manipulate voltage or resistance or watch the current respond, so it works best as a debrief around the sandbox rather than as the primary teaching of the quantitative relationship. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Respond to an engineer persona posing 'what happens to I if...' scenarios (e.g. 'you halved the resistance — what should the current do, and why?').
Explain the reason behind each prediction, not just the direction of change.
Correct, with guidance, the triangle-shuffle habit and the 'thicker wire = more resistance' error when they arise.
Articulate that resistance opposes and reduces current everywhere in a series loop but does not consume the charge.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can reason aloud about proportional changes and defend why, cementing 'resistance opposes, not consumes' and the inverse factor links.

constraints: Derive V = IR from the ratio definition the learner already met (R = V/I); do not introduce the formula triangle before meaning is secure, and when used require a sentence of reasoning alongside any rearrangement.
Keep 'resistance opposes/reduces current' distinct from 'resistance uses up current': current is the same all the way round a series loop, just smaller — charge is not consumed.
A large resistor reduces current but does not stop it entirely; a small current still flows.
Length and thickness pull opposite ways: longer wire = more resistance; thicker wire = less resistance. Do not conflate them.

Current and voltage are directly proportional ONLY when resistance is constant; a heating filament's resistance rises so its V–I line bends. Keep this qualitative — the graphical I–V treatment is a KS4 extension.

The static reference and the retrieval set are supports/checks: the reference cannot show current responding to change, and recognition/scored items verify fluency but do not by themselves provide the manipulable, mechanistic experience the sandbox gives.

Curriculum placement (UK): the V=IR ratio and calculation sit at KS3; the named 'Ohm's Law' and graphical I–V characteristics are KS4. There is no equivalent middle-school NGSS performance expectation, so this content is UK-anchored.

Interactive examples (sliders, live ammeter, particle-view toggle, material swap, filament mode, predict-then-reveal) are illustrative of the learning mechanism, not mandatory mechanisms or specific products.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The IOP Spark source backing the misconception/remediation claim is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its support as unconfirmed.

The source row framed a fixed page as something that 'cannot teach' the proportional core and stated '3D adds nothing' and 'weakly served by talk'; these comparative/necessity efficacy claims are not established by the evidence here and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (interactive manipulation lets current respond; a static reference supports recall; dialogue does not provide manipulation).
Checked the worked examples: (a) R = V/I = 6/2 = 3 Ω; (b) I = V/R = 3/12 = 0.25 A; (c) doubling length doubles resistance so current halves (0.5 A → ~0.25 A). These are consistent.

The assessment's part (b) uses 3 V across 12 Ω giving 0.25 A, while part (c) describes a wire carrying 0.5 A at 4 V — ensure learners are not confused by the reused 0.25 A value across different scenarios; both are internally correct.

probeDeeper: Talk me through how you got from V = IR to your formula for R — why does R end up on its own like that?
In part (b) you got 0.25 A. If I doubled the voltage to 6 V, what would the current be, and why?
Would a thick copper wire or a thin copper wire of the same length have more resistance — and what would that do to the current?
What are the units of each of your answers, and how do you know which unit goes with which?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) R = V/I = 6/2 = 3 Ω. (b) I = V/R = 3/12 = 0.25 A. (c) Doubling the length doubles the resistance, so for the same 4 V the current halves — to about 0.25 A (it goes down).

errorPatterns.pattern: Rearrangement slip: computes R = V×I, or I = R/V — muddles the formula triangle rather than isolating the unknown correctly.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with the V=IR triangle or a worked cover-up method, then have them re-derive R and I; check they can do the non-memorised rearrangement.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The written steps show the wrong operation (multiplying when division is needed), even though the child can state 'V = IR'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Resistance as a stopper: 'resistance stops the current — a big resistor means no current flows at all', so part (c) gives zero or 'none'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe resistance as opposition that reduces flow, tied to what current is (rate of charge flow); show a large resistor still passes a small current.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In part (c), or when asked what resistance does, predicts current is blocked entirely rather than reduced.

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverse-relationship error for resistance factors: thinks a longer (or thinner) wire lets MORE current through, or that doubling the length doubles the current.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the chain — longer wire → more resistance → (same V) less current; test with two wire lengths to make the inverse link concrete.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Part (c): predicts the current rises, or scales it the same way as the length instead of inversely.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot rearrange V = IR; multiplies when it should divide; or says a big resistor stops the current entirely.
responseLevels.full: Rearranges V = IR fluently with correct units and reasons about the relationship — doubling voltage doubles current, doubling length halves it — explaining resistance as opposition that reduces (not stops) current, and transferring to an unfamiliar variation.
responseLevels.partial: Substitutes and rearranges correctly for straightforward numbers and gives units, but stumbles when a factor changes (length or thickness) or when the required rearrangement isn't the memorised one — treating V = IR as a plug-in rule rather than a relationship.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these three on paper while I watch — show your steps and your units. (a) A 6 V battery drives 2 A through a lamp; find its resistance. (b) A 12 Ω resistor has 3 V across it; find the current through it. (c) A wire carries 0.5 A when 4 V is applied. You swap it for a wire of the same metal and thickness but twice as long — will the current go up or down, and roughly to what? Talk me through nothing in advance; just work, and I'll ask afterwards.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the working, not a description of it, reveals whether the child genuinely rearranges V = IR (rather than reciting it), tracks units, and treats resistance as opposition that reduces current. Rearrangement slips (multiplying instead of dividing), dropped units, and the 'longer wire lets more current through / resistance stops current' errors surface in the paper, where a verbal account would hide them.

sources.claim: KS3 defines resistance as 'measured in ohms, as the ratio of potential difference (p.d.) to current' (i.e. R = V/I); the phrase 'Ohm's Law' does not appear in the National Curriculum at any key stage, and the graphical current–voltage (I–V) treatment of different components is KS4 ('exploring current, resistance and voltage relationships for different circuit elements, including their graphical representations').
sources.source: DfE — National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS3 Current electricity; KS4 Physics Electricity)

sources.claim: DC-circuit resistance/Ohm calculations are not a middle-school NGSS performance expectation, so this content is UK-anchored.
sources.source: NGSS — MS.Forces and Interactions / MS.Energy (no MS DC-circuit PE)

sources.claim: The 'resistance uses up current', formula-triangle-without-meaning, and thicker-wire-more-resistance errors are documented difficulties best addressed by deriving V=IR from the ratio, drilling proportional reasoning, and a collision/particle picture of resistance and its factors.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–10 years

- **Topic:** Inheritance Vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y6 'Evolution and inheritance'):** supplies the language for 'recognise that living things produce offspring of the same kind, but normally offspring vary and are not identical to their parents' — offspring, variation, inherited, species are the words that make that statement sayable.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-LS3-1):** 'analyse and interpret data…[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS3-1]' — DCI LS3.A '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS3-1].' Honest note: NGSS's grade-3 assessment boundary EXCLUDES genetic mechanisms, so 'genetic' is used only loosely at this stage; keep to observable traits.

- **Operational details:** A LANGUAGE node — precise, correctly-applied terms, not new phenomena. The load-bearing DISTINCTION is inherited vs acquired: an inherited characteristic is passed from parent to offspring at birth (eye colour, petal colour, natural fur type); an acquired characteristic is gained during life (a scar, a learned skill, a pierced ear, a dog trained to sit) and is NOT passed on. Teach each term anchored to a sortable example, and teach the pair inherited↔acquired by CONTRAST because that boundary is where errors live. 'Variation' = differences within a species; 'trait/characteristic' = a single feature; 'offspring' = the young; 'species' = same kind that can breed; 'breed' = a variety within a species; 'environment' = surroundings that can also shape a feature. Make children USE the words to justify a sort ('a scar is acquired because you got it during your life, so puppies won't be born with it'). Keep 'genetic' informal at KS2 (no DNA/gene mechanism yet).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional). The child correctly sorts features into inherited vs acquired WITH a reason, uses 'variation' to describe within-species differences, and deploys offspring/species/trait accurately in a written description — the discriminating evidence being a correct inherited-vs-acquired justification.
bestPractices: Teach inherited vs acquired as a CONTRAST PAIR with sortable examples — the distinction (born-with vs gained-in-life, and only inherited passes on) is the crux and the commonest error.
Anchor every term to a concrete, sortable example rather than a dictionary definition; a word is learned when used to justify a placement ('inherited because…').
Use both plant AND animal examples (petal colour, seed type as well as eye colour, fur) so inheritance isn't seen as animals-only — and matches the NGSS 'non-human examples' emphasis.
Keep 'genetic' informal and mechanism-free at KS2 (no genes/DNA) to respect the NGSS assessment boundary and avoid over-reaching.
Distinguish 'variation' (differences within one species) from differences BETWEEN species, so the word isn't overstretched.
Surface the myth directly: acquired features (scars, learned tricks, dyed hair) are NOT inherited — test it with 'would the baby be born with it?'
keyRepresentations: A two-column sorting mat: INHERITED vs ACQUIRED, populated with feature cards (eye colour, scar, petal colour, learned trick).
A parent→offspring resemblance panel showing shared inherited traits plus visible variation.
A word↔example card set pinning each term (offspring, species, breed, variation, trait) to a picture.
A 'would the baby be born with it?' decision flow for testing inherited vs acquired.
commonMisconceptions: Believing acquired characteristics are inherited — e.g. a parent's scar, muscles, tan, or trained skill will show up in the offspring (the Lamarckian seed error).
Using 'variation' to mean differences BETWEEN species rather than WITHIN a species.
Treating 'trait/characteristic', 'gene' and 'DNA' as interchangeable, or expecting a genetic MECHANISM at this age.
Confusing 'species' and 'breed' — thinking different dog breeds are different species.
Thinking offspring are identical copies of a parent, missing the 'vary and are not identical' idea.
Assuming any feature an animal HAS is inherited, without checking whether it was gained during life.

learn.summary: Builds precise, correctly-applied inheritance vocabulary for 8–10 year-olds: inherited characteristic, acquired characteristic, variation, offspring, trait/characteristic, species, breed, environment (and 'genetic' used only informally, no DNA/gene mechanism at this stage). The load-bearing distinction is inherited (passed from parent to offspring; often visible at birth, but some inherited features, such as a Dalmatian's spots, a baby's final eye colour or a plant's petal colour, appear only as the young grow) versus acquired (gained during life through experience or surroundings, not passed on). It is taught by contrast with sortable plant AND animal examples and justified with the test 'Did it come from the parents, or did it happen to this individual during its life?' ('Would the baby be born with it?' is a useful first check for injuries and learned skills, but it is not proof.)

activities.title: Family album: tap a feature, name it, test whether it's passed on
feedback: When an inherited trait (coat colour, petal colour, eye colour) is named inherited: confirm 'inherited — it was passed from parent to offspring. Some inherited features show at birth; others, like a flower's petal colour, appear as the young grow.'

When a gained-in-life trait (scar, torn ear, learned trick, pierced ear, dyed hair) is tested: 'Acquired — it happened to this individual during its life (an injury, training or a choice), not something that came from the parents, so it is not passed on.'

If a learner calls a scar or learned skill 'inherited': ask 'Did it come from the parents, or did something happen during this animal's life to cause it?' and contrast it with an inherited trait beside it.

When differences across the litter are named: 'Variation — these are differences within one species. Dog-versus-cat differences can be called variation between species, but here we are comparing members of the same kind.'
activities.rationale: This is a language objective: the deliverable is binding each term to a clear example and nailing the inherited-vs-acquired boundary, which is where the commonest error lives. A viewable scene anchors each word to a picture and lets the 'came from the parents or happened during life?' test be applied to a specific feature. Plant and animal examples keep inheritance from seeming animals-only.
sourceClaims: DfE Y6 statutory: 'recognise that living things produce offspring of the same kind, but normally offspring vary and are not identical to their parents' — source of offspring/variation/inherited vocabulary.
NGSS 3-LS3-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS3-1]'; assessment boundary excludes genetic mechanisms and limits to non-human examples.
Distinguishing inherited from acquired characteristics is a persistent primary-age difficulty; children commonly believe acquired features (scars, learned skills) are passed to offspring.
learnerActions: Look at a scene of families: a dog with a litter of puppies, a plant with its seedlings, and a human family, each showing visible features.

Point to or tap a puppy's coat colour and say the term and definition: 'inherited characteristic — passed from parent to offspring' (optionally the matching colour on the parent lights up to make the link visible).
Point to or tap the parent dog's torn ear or a person's scar and apply the test: 'Would the baby be born with this? No — it was gained during life, so it is acquired and is not passed on.'
Compare several puppies across the litter and use 'variation — differences within the same species; they are not identical'.

Pin each remaining term to a picture you can see: offspring (the young, one or many), species (same kind that can breed together), breed (a variety within a species), environment (surroundings that can also shape a feature).
Answer a lift-the-flap check such as 'Is a learned trick inherited?' → 'No — acquired.'
activities.intendedInsight: Each vocabulary word attaches to a concrete example, and the invisible line between 'came from the parents' (inherited) and 'happened during this individual's life' (acquired) becomes visible and testable. Only inherited features are passed from parent to offspring, though the young can gain their own acquired features later.

activities.title: Sort the feature cards and justify each placement
feedback: Correct placement with a sound reason: affirm the reasoning, not just the answer ('Yes — and your reason is the key: gained during life, so not passed on').
Wrong drop: prompt the 'came from the parents, or happened during its life?' test rather than just revealing the answer, then let the learner re-place and restate the reason.

If 'variation' is used for a dog-versus-cat difference: accept it as variation between species, but explain that this round is about differences among individuals of the same species, and point back to the litter.
activities.rationale: Sorting with a stated reason makes the learner produce and apply the terms, giving the discriminating evidence (a correct inherited-vs-acquired justification). It complements the viewing activity: view to fix meaning, sort to prove command. Its effectiveness relative to other methods is a proposal, not an established result.
sourceClaims: Distinguishing inherited from acquired characteristics is a persistent primary-age difficulty; children commonly believe acquired features (scars, learned skills) are passed to offspring.
learnerActions: Take feature cards — eye colour, scar, petal colour, pierced ear, seed shape, natural fur type, a learned skill/trained trick — and place each into an INHERITED bin or an ACQUIRED bin.
Say aloud or write the reason for each placement, e.g. 'A scar is acquired because you got it during your life, so puppies won't be born with it.'
For any card you get wrong, ask 'Did it come from the parents, or did it happen during this individual's life?' and move it.
In a second round, sort examples of within-species VARIATION (e.g. different sizes and markings among the same litter or among seedlings of one plant).
activities.intendedInsight: Learners deploy the vocabulary to justify a decision, proving they own the inherited↔acquired boundary rather than just recognising definitions.

activities.title: Describe a dog and its puppies using the words
feedback: If the learner calls the mother the 'offspring' or hesitates over singular/plural: model 'offspring' for the young (one or many) across several sentences; this is settling usage, so do not over-correct.

If 'breed' and 'species' are swapped (a Labrador called a 'species'): clarify that a breed is a variety within a species, and that a trait is a single feature; have them use each in a contrasting sentence.
If a trait is called a 'type' or a 'species': name it a single characteristic/trait and re-separate the three words with examples.

If the learner says the environment changed the coat colour: that change is acquired (caused during life by the surroundings) and is NOT passed on to the puppies. Only coat colour that comes from the parents is inherited, even if it develops as the puppy grows (Dalmatians are born white and get their spots later). Do not let an environment-caused change be labelled inherited.
activities.rationale: A productive spoken or written description elicits independent construction and reveals whether the words are memorised labels or genuinely controlled. The probe questions target the exact boundaries where errors cluster (environment-caused change, acquired skills, within-species variation, breed vs species).
sourceClaims: DfE Y6 statutory: 'recognise that living things produce offspring of the same kind, but normally offspring vary and are not identical to their parents' — source of offspring/variation/inherited vocabulary.
learnerActions: Tell or write about a dog and its puppies using inherited, acquired, variation, and offspring as you go.
Describe one thing the puppies were born with and one thing an individual picked up during its life, using the right word for each.

Answer follow-up prompts: 'Could the environment change the coat colour at all — and what would you call that?'; 'One puppy learned to sit on command — inherited or acquired, and why?'; 'Use variation in a sentence about just the puppies, not comparing them to another animal'; 'What's the difference between the same breed and the same species?'
activities.intendedInsight: Correct use in a live, self-generated description — not a recited definition — shows genuine command, especially sorting traits that came from the parents (inherited) from those gained during life (acquired), and saying clearly whether 'variation' compares individuals of one species or different species.

constraints: Keep 'genetic' informal and mechanism-free at this age: no genes or DNA, and do not expect or teach a genetic mechanism; stay with observable traits (consistent with the NGSS grade-3 assessment boundary).
Use both plant and animal examples (petal colour, seed shape as well as eye colour, fur) so inheritance is not seen as animals-only; NGSS emphasises non-human examples.

Focus 'variation' on differences within one species (individuals of the same kind), which is the main use here. Note that scientists also talk about variation between species, so do not mark that use as wrong; just ask learners to say which kind of comparison they mean.

Distinguish species (same kind that can breed together) from breed (a variety within a species), and keep 'trait/characteristic' as a single feature. Treat 'species = can breed together' as an age-appropriate simplification, not a precise definition.
An environment-caused change to a feature is acquired and is not passed to offspring; do not let learners conclude environment-caused changes are inherited.

A viewing/tap-to-reveal scene fixes word↔example meaning but does not itself require the learner to produce the terms; pair it with sorting-with-reasons and a spoken/written description so learners actually deploy the vocabulary. It is not that viewing cannot teach — only that it does not by itself elicit production.

A spoken guessing dialogue can prompt productive use of the terms, but on its own it cannot show the features, which weakens word↔example anchoring; use it alongside a viewable example rather than as the sole method.

Recognition/matching and multiple-choice checks (e.g. matching term to definition, 'which is an acquired characteristic?' with a scar as a tempting wrong choice) can assess correct use but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the terms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and their relative effectiveness is untested.
The original source row marks the OpenLearn misconceptions claim as unverified (verified:false); treat the 'persistent primary-age difficulty' point as a reasonable but unconfirmed claim.

The original stated 'species = same kind that can breed'; this is an age-appropriate simplification (the biological species concept has known exceptions). Acceptable at this level but not a precise definition.

Environment can shape some features (e.g. nurture affecting size, sun affecting coat); the row notes this, and the probe about environment-caused colour change is retained with corrective feedback so learners do not conclude environment-caused changes are inherited.
The legacy row asserted that a spatial/3D treatment 'adds nothing'; this comparative claim is not established by the sources and has been reframed as a scope note rather than a universal law.
A stray off-topic fragment ('Fractions aside') was removed from the variation-scoping constraint; it was unrelated contamination, not part of the inheritance content.
The objective's 'explain what causes variation' is touched only via the environment probe; a dedicated prompt on causes of variation could be added if fuller coverage is wanted.

probeDeeper: You said the puppy inherited its coat colour — could the environment change that colour at all? What would you call a change like that?
One puppy learned to sit on command. Is that inherited or acquired? Why?
Use 'variation' in a sentence about just the puppies, not comparing them to another animal.
What's the difference between saying two dogs are the same breed and the same species?
assess.correctAnswer: The child uses each term correctly in a meaningful sentence: the puppies are the dog's offspring; they inherited traits such as coat colour (inherited characteristic); a scar or a learned trick is acquired (acquired characteristic); the puppies differ from one another in size and markings (variation).

errorPatterns.pattern: swaps 'inherited' and 'acquired' ('the puppy inherited its limp from the accident')
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor each word to a clear example — born-with = inherited, gained-in-life = acquired — and sort several traits together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: applies 'inherited' to a trait gained during life, or 'acquired' to a born-with trait

errorPatterns.pattern: uses 'variation' for differences between species rather than within one
errorPatterns.nextMove: restrict 'variation' to differences among individuals of the same species — the puppies among themselves
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the dog and the cat 'show variation'

errorPatterns.pattern: uses 'offspring' for the parent, or is unsure it can mean one or many
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not over-correct this settling usage; simply model 'offspring' for the young (one or many) across several sentences until it stabilises
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls the mother the offspring, or hesitates over whether 'offspring' is singular or plural

errorPatterns.pattern: treats 'trait', 'breed' and 'species' loosely (calls a breed a species, or a trait a 'type')
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify species versus breed, and that a trait is a single feature; use them in contrasting sentences
errorPatterns.revealedBy: labels a Labrador a 'species', or calls coat colour a 'species'

responseLevels.gap: Misapplies inherited/acquired, or uses 'variation' for between-species differences; the words function only as memorised labels.
responseLevels.full: Uses inherited, acquired, variation and offspring accurately and spontaneously in a described context, correctly assigning born-with versus gained-in-life traits and reserving 'variation' for within-species differences.
responseLevels.partial: Uses some terms correctly (offspring, trait) but confuses inherited with acquired, or over-extends 'variation' — applying the vocabulary inconsistently across examples.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell me about a dog and its puppies, using these words as you go: inherited, acquired, variation, offspring. Describe something the puppies were born with, and something one of them picked up during its life — and use the right word for each.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the words only as labels misapplies them — calling a scar 'inherited' or using 'variation' for the difference between a dog and a cat. Correct USE in a live context, not a recited definition, shows genuine command; the discriminator is whether inherited versus acquired is applied to the right examples.

pedagogy.summary: Read time and value axes together to solve line-graph comparison, difference and appropriate sum problems. Separate point height from change across equal time intervals; graph shape is not a literal picture of the situation. Temperature readings support trend interpretation and approximate interpolation under an explicit straight-line model. Period totals, such as monthly rainfall, can be compared and added but cannot be interpolated as rainfall at an intermediate date. Teach literal reads before combining values and interpreting trends.
bestPractices: Anchor the graph in a clear quantity, units and observation schedule; distinguish temperature observations from rainfall totals over periods.

Explicitly teach the three-part reading progression (Curcio): first READ THE DATA (lift a value straight off a point), then READ BETWEEN THE DATA (compare two points, find a difference, read an intermediate value), then READ BEYOND (predict the next day) — and name which you are asking for

Separate HEIGHT from CHANGE deliberately: pair 'which day was warmest?' (height) with 'which day did it warm up the most?' (steepest rise) on the same graph, so children cannot conflate the tallest point with the biggest jump
Trace vertically from a plotted point to the time axis, then horizontally from that same point to the value axis; say the paired reading.
Read an intermediate temperature from the segment as a straight-line estimate; distinguish this model assumption from what was measured.

Contrast a genuine time-series (temperature) with data that should NOT be joined into a line (favourite fruit) so children learn that joined lines suit values ordered in time, such as temperature readings or monthly totals, whereas unordered categories should not be joined
keyRepresentations: Temperature-over-a-week line graph (the canonical continuous time-series for this age)

A crosshair / ruler slid along the line to read plotted values and to estimate values between plotted temperature observations under a straight-line assumption (makes interpolation visible as an estimate)
Paired axes with a right-angle trace from point to time-axis and to value-axis
Two questions side by side on one graph — 'highest point' vs 'steepest climb' — to physically separate height from change
A rising / flat / falling segment triad annotated as increase / no change / decrease
commonMisconceptions: Graph-as-picture: reading the line's silhouette as a literal picture of the situation (a rising-then-falling temperature line 'is a hill/mountain', or a distance-time line read as the route travelled) rather than as a quantity plotted against time

Slope-height / height-for-difference confusion: when asked how much a quantity changed, naming the highest point rather than the steepest segment; treating a higher point as 'faster' or 'more increase'
Treating a line-based estimate as an exact unmeasured observation, or refusing any estimate because only the plotted points were measured.
Accepting or interpreting a joined line for categorical data (favourite pet) as if it showed a trend, or reading a scaled axis by counting squares rather than by the scale interval

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, solve comparison, sum and difference problems from line graphs. Read each point using both axes and the labelled scale; distinguish the highest observed value from the largest increase over equal time intervals. Use temperatures for reading and differences, and quantities that can meaningfully be added, such as monthly rainfall totals, for sum problems. Interpolated temperatures are estimates under a stated straight-line assumption, not additional measurements. Joining monthly rainfall totals does not reveal rainfall on intermediate dates.

activities.title: Read values and estimate between temperature observations
feedback: If you tap the tallest point for 'warmed up the most', that tells you the warmest day, which may or may not be where the biggest change happened — look instead for the segment that climbs most steeply across a single day.

If you read a value without tracing to both axes, pause: put your finger on the point, go straight down to read the day, then from the point go straight across to read the temperature, and say the pair.

The drawn segment passes smoothly through in-between values. Those are estimates assuming a straight-line change between readings; actual temperatures may have fluctuated differently, so this is not a record of every intervening temperature.
activities.rationale: Reading a time-series is a doing skill — lift a value, read between two values, find a difference, interpret a rise. Letting the learner act and the graph respond is intended to make interpolation and the slope-vs-height distinction concrete. A draggable/sliding read-out is one proposed way that may make the continuity of the segment visible; a ruler slid along a printed graph achieves a similar effect. Efficacy of the specific interaction is untested here.
sourceClaims: Slope-height confusion and related substitutions (height-for-slope, slope-for-height, height-for-difference, slope-for-curvature): students use the wrong graphical feature for the quantity asked; McDermott et al. found as many as half of students used height instead of slope to judge speed

KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Use a temperature-over-a-week line graph with observations at the same time each day and equal daily spacing. Slide a ruler, crosshair or finger along a segment to read a straight-line estimate between observations.

Slide between Monday and Tuesday and say aloud the values the line passes through — e.g. 14, 15, 16 degrees — noticing that the line gives estimated in-between values, not only the measured values at the plotted dots.

For each point, trace it back to BOTH axes: finger on the point, drop straight down to the time axis to read the day, then go back to the point and slide horizontally across to the value axis to read the temperature; say the paired coordinate.
Use a 'find the difference' move: mark two points and read the vertical gap between them (e.g. the rise from Tuesday to Wednesday).
Take on the challenge 'Which day did it warm up the MOST?' — then check whether the warmest day (tallest point) is the same as, or different from, the day of the steepest climb.
activities.intendedInsight: On this temperature graph, plotted points are observations and the connecting segments provide straight-line estimates between them. Compare rises over equal daily intervals to distinguish change from the temperature at a point.

activities.title: Separate HEIGHT from CHANGE on one graph
feedback: If you name the warmest day for 'warmed up the most', check the arrows — the longest upward arrow marks the biggest rise, which may not sit at the tallest point.
Correct justification sounds like 'it climbed 5 degrees from Monday to Tuesday', not 'that one is the highest'.
If height and steepest always seem to be the same day for you, try the tricky case where they come apart.
activities.rationale: Pairing a height question with a change question on the same graph targets height-for-difference confusion, a documented substitution error; comparing arrow lengths makes 'how much it changed' a visible, measurable quantity distinct from the tallest point.
sourceClaims: Slope-height confusion and related substitutions (height-for-slope, slope-for-height, height-for-difference, slope-for-curvature): students use the wrong graphical feature for the quantity asked; McDermott et al. found as many as half of students used height instead of slope to judge speed
learnerActions: On a single temperature line graph, answer 'Which day was warmest?' (height) and 'Which day did it warm up the most?' (steepest rise) — treat them as two different questions.
Draw a small vertical arrow for the change between each pair of consecutive days, pointing up for a rise and down for a fall, then compare the lengths of the upward arrows to find the biggest rise.
Justify your 'warmed up the most' answer by saying how far the line climbed across that one day, not by which point is highest.

Try a tricky case: a graph where a huge jump happens early in the week and the highest point is reached later by only a small rise, so the tallest point and the steepest segment are clearly on different days — identify each.
activities.intendedInsight: A higher observed temperature is not the same as a bigger increase. Over these equal one-day intervals, the largest rise has the steepest rising segment; with unequal intervals, compare changes and rates separately.

activities.title: Read the data, between the data, and beyond the data
feedback: For a difference question, report the gap (e.g. rose 3 degrees), not the two raw values; for a total/sum question, add the two read-off values and report the combined amount.

An intermediate point on the drawn temperature segment gives a straight-line estimate. Read it consistently with the axes and explain that the actual unmeasured value could differ; an exactly known temperature cannot be recovered from two daily observations alone.
A prediction is a reasoned guess from the trend; being off from the revealed value is fine — explain what the trend suggested.
activities.rationale: Curcio's three hierarchical levels structure the questions from literal lift to comparing/combining/finding differences to inference; this is where comparison, sum and difference problems from the graph live. Predict-then-reveal exercises reading beyond the data and makes the continuity of the line matter.
sourceClaims: Curcio's three hierarchical levels of graph comprehension — reading the data (literal lift), reading between the data (compare/combine/find differences), reading beyond the data (predict/infer) — students must read the data before they can read between or beyond it; framework adopted by NCTM for assessment

KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Read the data: lift a single value straight off a marked point (e.g. the warmest day's temperature).

Read between the data: compare two observed values, find their difference, and combine values only where the quantity makes a meaningful total, such as rainfall totals for March and May. Do not add daily temperatures as if they were a total temperature. On a temperature line graph, separately estimate an intermediate value under the straight-line assumption.

Read beyond the data: hide the final plotted day (e.g. Friday on a Monday-to-Friday graph), predict and place it from the earlier trend, then reveal the real value and compare — discuss why the prediction may differ.
Each time, name which kind of reading you are doing: reading a value, reading between, or predicting.
activities.intendedInsight: Graph comprehension has a progression — you must read a value before you can compare, combine or find differences between values, and only then predict or infer — and naming which you are doing clarifies the task.

activities.title: When should data be joined into a line? Continuous vs categorical
feedback: A point between two temperature observations has a time and a line-based estimate. The true temperature at that time was not measured by this graph and need not match the estimate.
If you would join favourite-fruit counts with a line, ask: what would a point halfway between apple and banana mean? There is no in-between fruit category — so the counts should not be joined.
activities.rationale: Contrasting temperature observations with unordered categorical counts may help learners explain when joining points supports a meaningful interpretation. Temperature interpolation remains a model-based estimate; this proposed comparison is not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Compare a genuine time-series (temperature across days) with categorical data (favourite fruit) and decide which should be drawn as a joined line and which should not.
Run a finger along a temperature segment, naming the estimates it passes through ('the line estimates about 15 here'); distinguish these from temperatures actually measured at the plotted points.
Explain why joining 'favourite fruit' counts into a line would be meaningless — there is no continuous quantity between the categories.
activities.intendedInsight: A line joining temperature observations can show a trend and support estimates under an explicit interpolation assumption. Joining unordered fruit categories does not create a meaningful intermediate category; use bars for those counts.

activities.title: Confront the graph-as-picture habit
feedback: Describing the silhouette ('it went up and over') is the picture trap — switch to values: 'on Wednesday it was 18, on Thursday it fell to 14'.
A falling segment means the quantity decreased (it got colder), not that something physically went downhill.
activities.rationale: The graph-as-picture error persists even when a learner can describe the changes verbally, so directly re-reading point-by-point and tracing to axes aims to break the habit of treating the silhouette as the situation.
sourceClaims: Graph-as-picture error: students treat the graph as a literal picture of the problem situation (drawing/reading a hill shape for a speed-vs-time graph over a hill), with two subtypes — global correspondence (whole scene matched to whole graph) and feature correspondence (a local visual feature matched to a graph feature); this occurs even when the student can describe the changes verbally
learnerActions: If you catch yourself describing the line as 'a hill' or 'the route it travelled', cover the whole line and expose one point at a time.
For each exposed point, answer 'What does THIS point tell us?' and trace it to both axes, reading a day and its temperature.
Re-read the whole graph as a set of day/temperature pairs rather than a shape or a scene.
activities.intendedInsight: The line is a quantity plotted against time, not a literal picture of the event; each point is a paired coordinate, and the overall shape summarises how the value changed, not a landscape.

activities.title: Check questions and reading the scale correctly
feedback: If your answer is off by a consistent factor (e.g. you say 6 where each square is 2 degrees and the real answer is 12), you counted squares instead of using the scale — relabel the interval and re-read.

The highest temperature and largest one-day rise can occur together or on different days. Compare consecutive values over equal daily intervals before deciding; do not automatically reject the highest point.
activities.rationale: Comparison, difference, sum and ordering questions give a scorable check of the reading procedure, but recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own interpolation or justification, so keep producing-and-explaining tasks too. Scale mis-reading is a counting slip, not a conceptual gap, and is addressed by labelling the scale interval first. Any illustration should be schematic rather than requiring an exact drawn quantity to be eyeballed.
sourceClaims: Curcio's three hierarchical levels of graph comprehension — reading the data (literal lift), reading between the data (compare/combine/find differences), reading beyond the data (predict/infer) — students must read the data before they can read between or beyond it; framework adopted by NCTM for assessment
learnerActions: Answer scorable items: choose the warmest day; estimate an intermediate temperature off a marked line (a sensible range is accepted); fill in 'the difference between March and May rainfall is ___ mm'; order months by rainfall.
Include one item that pairs 'highest point' against 'biggest rise' so you must distinguish height from change.
Before reporting any value, ask 'How much is each square worth here?' and label the scale interval, then read by the scale — not by counting squares as if each were one unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Targeted questions can check your reading skill, but you must read values by the axis scale interval, not by counting grid squares.

constraints: This topic assesses reading and solving problems from line graphs. Constructing a complete graph is developed separately in the later Line graphs topic (mt_HlNSurPVDp); do not require unrelated bar-chart tasks as evidence of this objective.

Always trace values back to BOTH axes (from the point, go vertically to the time axis to read the time, and horizontally from the point to the value axis to read the value) to counter reading the line as a shape rather than paired coordinates.

Deliberately pair a height question ('which day was warmest?') with a change question ('which day warmed up the most?') on the same graph so learners cannot conflate the tallest point with the biggest jump.

For temperature observations joined by straight segments, read intermediate estimates aloud and name the straight-line assumption. The line does not establish the exact path taken between observations. Do not interpolate monthly rainfall totals as rainfall on intermediate dates.

A labelled or tap-to-reveal graph can support a worked example. Ask the learner to read and explain new values before revealing answers when independent reading is the aim; paper tracing, discussion and digital controls are optional ways to organize this.

Recognition-only or pre-revealed items can confirm a classification or choice but do not themselves elicit the learner's own reading, difference-finding, combining/totalling, interpolation, or justification; include tasks where the learner produces and explains answers.
Scorable check items should use schematic illustrations and must not require eyeballing an exact drawn quantity that isn't readable from the scale.
Scale mis-reading is a counting slip to scaffold (label the interval, re-read), not a reason to reteach the whole graph concept.

For unordered categories such as favourite fruit, use bars rather than a joined trend line. Line graphs can also plot ordered period totals, but joining monthly totals does not supply rainfall amounts at intervening dates.

Where a point-only (intermediate-values-don't-exist) misconception appears, reteaching the continuous meaning may draw on the prerequisite micro-topic (continuous vs categorical data) rather than re-teaching the whole graph idea.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels conversation/persona and 3D treatments as poor fits, asserting a third spatial dimension 'conveys nothing' and that a conversational wrapper 'could not verify' reading. These are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the cited sources and are omitted as universal laws. Narrowly scoped, observable concerns remain worth noting: a time-series is a two-variable (time vs quantity) plot, so an added spatial dimension does not correspond to a variable here and may invite the graph-as-picture error; and a purely decorative conversational wrapper would still need a live graph to check reading. These are affordance observations, not proof that any medium 'cannot teach'.
The original feedback marked the tallest point wrong for biggest rise. This is not generally valid: the highest temperature and largest rise may coincide, so each graph must be checked.
One cited source (Oak National Academy KS2 line-graph guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as curriculum guidance of unconfirmed verification.

Draggable crosshair, live recolouring (steepest segment lighting up), and predict-then-drag are optional interaction examples that may make continuity and the height-vs-change distinction concrete; paper equivalents (sliding a ruler, drawing arrows) are acceptable, and these specific interactions are not required or proven mechanisms.
The original summary and evidence include SUM/total problems; a combine/total task was added to the read-between activity so this is genuinely delivered rather than only promised.
Taxonomy alignment repair after os-taxonomy PR #30 (2026-10-19). Sources were reused without being re-fetched. Activities are proposals, not empirically validated interventions.
The temporary bar-graph activities introduced to match the former description have been removed. PR #30 corrected the description to match the original line-graph evidence and assessment.

probeDeeper: Why is Friday warmest even though Monday–Tuesday has the biggest rise?
Could the actual temperature halfway between observations differ from 17°C? Explain the assumption behind the estimate.
Why can January and March rainfall totals be added, while daily temperatures are not a total temperature?
How would a value axis marked every 2°C change the way you read a point?
assess.correctAnswer: Friday is warmest at 19°C; Tuesday to Wednesday rises by 2°C; Monday to Tuesday has the largest daily rise, 4°C, although Friday is highest. Halfway between Tuesday noon and Wednesday noon the straight-line estimate is 17°C; the actual unmeasured temperature may differ. January plus March rainfall is 45 mm and February exceeds January by 15 mm. Wednesday to Thursday falls by 1°C, meaning the temperature decreased (it got colder), not that something went downhill. Both traces start at the plotted point: vertically to time and horizontally to value. Do not total daily temperatures or interpolate monthly rainfall totals as rainfall at an intermediate date.

errorPatterns.pattern: Graph-as-picture: reads the line's shape as a literal picture of the situation rather than a quantity over time ('it goes up like a hill then down the other side', or describes it as a route/mountain) instead of talking about temperature values on days
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront directly: cover the whole line and expose one point at a time, asking 'what does THIS point tell us?' and tracing it to both axes, until the child re-reads the line as a set of day/temperature pairs rather than a picture
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (6), or whenever asked to explain the line, the child narrates the silhouette ('it went up and over') and gestures the shape, rather than tying height at each day to a temperature value

errorPatterns.pattern: Height-for-difference (slope-height confusion): when asked how much the quantity CHANGED, names the highest point rather than the steepest segment; treats a higher point as 'more increase' or 'faster'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by putting 'highest point' and 'biggest jump' side by side on the same graph: mark the change between each pair of consecutive days with a little vertical arrow, and compare arrow lengths so the steepest rise is seen to differ from the tallest point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child points to the warmest day (same point as task 1) and says 'that one, it's the highest', instead of the day with the biggest jump from the day before

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses observed values with line-based estimates: either asserts an exact unmeasured temperature or cannot make an estimate even when the straight-line assumption is explicitly supplied.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate plotted observations from model estimates; mark the halfway position, read 17°C on the straight segment and explain that real temperatures could have varied differently.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims 17°C is a known observation, or refuses a line-based estimate after the interpolation assumption is made explicit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Scale mis-read: on task (1) or (2) counts grid squares as if each were one unit instead of reading the scale interval, giving a value or difference that is off by the scale factor
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach the graph idea: ask 'how much is each square worth here?' and have them label the scale interval before re-reading; the interpretation is sound, only the counting slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child locates the correct point and the correct pair, but the number they report is wrong by the scale factor (e.g. says 6 where each square is 2 degrees and the answer is 12)

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably read the axes or distinguishes neither point height nor daily change.
responseLevels.full: Reads values by the scale, distinguishes highest from largest rise, solves the rainfall sum/difference, explains a falling segment as a decrease in temperature and explains interpolation as an assumption-based estimate; transfers the procedure to another graph.
responseLevels.partial: Reads observed values and finds a difference, but needs support to compare increases, explain an estimate or select quantities that can be added.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give an equally spaced line graph of temperatures recorded at noon: Monday 12°C, Tuesday 16°C, Wednesday 18°C, Thursday 17°C, Friday 19°C. Ask the learner to (1) read the warmest day and value, (2) calculate the Tuesday-to-Wednesday change, and (3) identify the interval with the largest rise. (4) Ask for the estimated temperature halfway between Tuesday noon and Wednesday noon, explicitly assuming straight-line change. (5) Then show a line graph of monthly rainfall totals (January 20 mm, February 35 mm, March 25 mm); ask for January plus March and the February–January difference. (6) Return to the temperature graph and ask what the falling Wednesday-to-Thursday segment means. Watch the reading and calculations without supplying the answers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The fixed data deliberately separate the highest point (Friday) from the largest rise (Monday–Tuesday). Watching axis traces, scale reading and subtraction distinguishes sound graph reading from guessing by shape. The estimate requires an explicit assumption; a learner is not marked wrong for adding that the exact unmeasured value is unknown, provided they give the 17°C straight-line estimate. The rainfall questions check a meaningful sum and difference, and explaining the Wednesday-to-Thursday fall checks that a falling segment is read as a decrease rather than a picture.
