pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3). Recall and use multiplication AND division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables — the first fact set, built on the 2s/5s/10s skip counting.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables, including recognising odd and even numbers'; non-statutory 'connect the 2, 5 and 10 tables to each other' and 'use commutativity and inverse relations (4×5=20 and 20÷5=4)'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.7 'fluently multiply and divide within 100 … by end of Grade 3 know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers' (the 2s/5s/10s are the earliest-secured, from 2.OA skip counting).
• Operational details: derive rather than only chant — 10s from place value, 5s as half of the 10s, 2s as doubles. Crucially include the DIVISION facts and out-of-sequence recall (not just reciting). Use commutativity and the inverse to get four facts from one (2×5, 5×2, 10÷5, 10÷2).
• Checkpoint: quick recall + inverse. Tier A (6): recall 2s and 10s facts in order. Tier B (6–7): recall any 2, 5 or 10 fact out of order and its division fact. Tier C (7): explain that the 5s are half the 10s and state the full fact family for 5×4.
bestPractices: Build the three tables on structure, not rote: 10s from place value, 5s as exactly half of the matching 10s fact, 2s as doubles — so a forgotten fact can be re-derived.
Teach the DIVISION facts alongside the multiplication facts as fact families (5×4=20 → 20÷5=4, 20÷4=5), and use commutativity so learning one fact delivers its partner — halving the memory load.
Rehearse out of sequence and in mixed contexts once the count is secure, so recall is genuine fluency rather than a chant that only works from the start.
Exploit hundred-square and multiplication-square patterns (5s and 10s in columns, 2s in even columns) to make the facts a connected web — building on the skip-counting patterns already learned.
Connect the three tables to each other and to odd/even (the 2s table = even numbers) so the fact sets reinforce rather than compete.
keyRepresentations: Multiplication square / times-table grid (patterns and commutative symmetry)
Hundred square with 2s, 5s, 10s shaded (columns/even-number pattern)
Arrays for each fact (and the fact family)
Number line with equal jumps (bridge from skip counting)
commonMisconceptions: Being able to chant the table from the start but not recall a fact out of order — mistaking the chant for fluency.
Knowing the multiplication fact but not the corresponding division fact.
Treating 5×4 and 4×5 as separate facts to memorise (not using commutativity).
Confusing 'the 2 times table' with 'counting in 2s starting anywhere' — or muddling doubling with adding 2.
Not connecting 5s to 10s (missing that 5s are half the 10s), so each table is learned in isolation.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3): recall and USE multiplication AND division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, out of order and as fact families, built on structure rather than rote chanting. Derive 10s from place value, 5s as exactly half of the matching 10s fact, and 2s as doubles, so a forgotten fact can be re-derived. Teach division facts alongside multiplication (5×4=20 → 20÷5=4, 20÷4=5) and use commutativity so one learned fact delivers its partner. Connect the three tables to each other and to odd/even (the 2s = even numbers).

activities.title: Shade the table: derive the 5s from the 10s
feedback: If a child treats the 5s and 10s as unrelated, pair the two shaded columns side by side and ask 'what is half of 40?' to reveal 5×4 = 20.
If a child doubles wrongly or adds 2 instead, show 2×6 as two groups of 6 (or 6 doubled = 12), distinct from 6+2 = 8.
Reinforce the end-digit pattern as a self-check: 5s end in 5 or 0; 10s end in 0.
Optional live display: when the learner taps a grid cell, pop out the array for that fact and write its whole fact family so the derivation stays visible.
activities.rationale: Building facts on structure (place value, halving, doubling) lets a learner re-derive a forgotten fact and connects the tables rather than learning each in isolation; a visible, manipulable grid makes the 'half the 10s' relationship directly observable, and the number line links it to the skip-counting already secured.
sourceClaims: Y2: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, including odd/even; connect the tables and use commutativity and inverse relations.
Tables should be derived from structure (10s from place value, 5s as half of 10s, 2s as doubles) and learned with their division facts as fact families, not by rote chanting alone.
learnerActions: On a multiplication grid or hundred square, shade the 10s column (10, 20, 30, 40, 50…) and read them as place-value facts: 10×3 = 3 tens = 30.

Beside it, shade the 5s (5, 10, 15, 20, 25…) and line each 5s value up against the matching 10s value. On a multiplication grid this is the 5s column; on a hundred square the 5s fill two columns, the numbers ending in 5 and those ending in 0.
Notice and say aloud that each 5s value sits exactly halfway to the 10s value: 5×4 = 20 is half of 10×4 = 40.

Shade the 2s (on a multiplication grid, the 2s column; on a hundred square, every column ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8) and state that the answers in the 2s table are even numbers, and that 2×n is the double of n.
Pick one fact per table and write it as a derivation: '10×6 = 60, so 5×6 = 30 (half), and 2×6 = 12 (double of 6).'
Optionally, show the same facts as equal jumps on a number line (counting in 2s, 5s or 10s) to connect the shaded columns back to the skip-counting the child already knows.
activities.intendedInsight: The 2, 5 and 10 tables are a connected web, not three separate lists: 10s come from place value, 5s are half the matching 10s, 2s are doubles — so any fact can be rebuilt if forgotten.

activities.title: Four facts from one array: multiplication and its inverse
feedback: If division lags, return to the SAME array and count the rows/columns to show 20÷5 and 20÷4 directly.
If a child treats 5×4 and 4×5 as two separate things to memorise, rotate the array a quarter turn to show it is the same 20.
Use a fact-family triangle (20 at top, 5 and 4 below) so the child can cover any one number and state it from the other two.
activities.rationale: Fact families on a single array link multiplication with its inverse division and exploit commutativity, directly targeting the common gap where multiplication is fluent but division or the commutative partner is not.
sourceClaims: Tables should be derived from structure (10s from place value, 5s as half of 10s, 2s as doubles) and learned with their division facts as fact families, not by rote chanting alone.
Y2: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, including odd/even; connect the tables and use commutativity and inverse relations.
learnerActions: Build or look at an array for one fact, e.g. 5 rows of 4 (= 20).
Write the two multiplication facts the array shows using commutativity: 5×4 = 20 and 4×5 = 20.
Write the two division facts from the same array: 20÷5 = 4 and 20÷4 = 5.
Repeat for several 2/5/10 facts, each time producing the full fact family of four facts from one picture.
Say why 20÷5 = 4 'has to be' true given 5×4 = 20 (sharing 20 into 5 equal rows gives 4).
activities.intendedInsight: One array holds a whole fact family; using commutativity and the inverse means learning one fact delivers its partners, so division facts are not extra memorising.

activities.title: Mixed quick-recall, out of order, with a derive-it fallback
feedback: Correct answers for the prompts above: 5×3 = 15, 10×4 = 40, 2×7 = 14; 20÷5 = 4, 30÷10 = 3, 14÷2 = 7.
On a miss, respond with the array AND the derive-it prompt (find the ten fact and halve it; double for twos), not just the right number.

For a near-miss count error such as 5×3 answered as 20, note that 20 still ends in 0, so the basic end-digit check (5s end in 5 or 0) will not catch it. Use the derive-it route instead (10×3 = 30, half of 30 is 15), or the sharper pattern that 5 times an odd number ends in 5. Then re-count one step at a time to check. The correct answer is 15.
Do NOT drill under heavy time pressure if a child reconstructs by skip-counting; keep skip-counting as a backup while spaced, meaningful retrieval moves facts into memory.
Optional quick-fire mode: present facts in random order with instant array feedback on misses.
activities.rationale: Out-of-order mixed × and ÷ practice distinguishes true recall from skip-count reconstruction and exposes lagging division facts; pairing every miss with a structural derivation keeps fluency resting on recoverable structure.
sourceClaims: Y2: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, including odd/even; connect the tables and use commutativity and inverse relations.
learnerActions: Once skip-counting is secure, answer facts asked OUT of sequence, mixing × and ÷: 5×3, 10×4, 2×7, then 20÷5, 30÷10, 14÷2.
For each, notice whether you knew it instantly or had to count, and say which.
On any fact you did not just know, use the derive-it route aloud: for a 5s fact, find the matching 10s fact and halve it; for a 2s fact, double the number.
Keep skip-counting available as a backup check, not as the main method.
activities.intendedInsight: Genuine fluency is recall out of order (including division), not a chant that only works from the start; when memory fails, a structured derivation recovers the fact.

activities.title: Trade-a-fact oral rehearsal
feedback: Keep the derive-it prompt handy so a miss ends with a reconstructed fact, not just the answer.
If division is slower than multiplication, pair every × question with its ÷ inverse so the family is rehearsed together.
activities.rationale: Oral rehearsal adds low-stakes retrieval practice and reinforces fact families; a spoken partner does not itself display the shaded columns or arrays that make the halving relationship visible, so it works best alongside the grid and array tasks rather than replacing them.
sourceClaims: Tables should be derived from structure (10s from place value, 5s as half of 10s, 2s as doubles) and learned with their division facts as fact families, not by rote chanting alone.
learnerActions: Take turns with a partner: one asks a 2, 5 or 10 fact (× or ÷), the other answers, then they swap.
On a miss, the asker prompts the derivation: 'What's the ten fact? Now halve it' for 5s, or 'double it' for 2s.
Include inverse pairs deliberately, e.g. ask 5×6 then immediately 30÷5.
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken back-and-forth rehearsal gives extra meaningful retrieval and keeps the derive-it route verbal and quick.

constraints: Secure skip-counting in 2s, 5s and 10s is a prerequisite; if a child can only reconstruct every fact by counting from the start, strengthen that skip-counting first rather than drilling under time pressure.
Answer-giving/recall checks measure whether facts are fluent but do not by themselves build the structure; use them alongside the deriving and fact-family tasks, not in place of them.
A fixed poster or static grid is a good pattern reference but cannot run out-of-order recall practice or generate arrays on demand; combine it with spoken or interactive mixed-fact practice.
Out-of-order, mixed × and ÷ recall is the target; a chant that only works from the beginning of the table is not yet fluency.
Keep the halving relationship explicit: 5×n is half of 10×n (e.g. 5×4 = 20 is half of 40), and 2×n is the double of n, distinct from n+2.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic in prompts/feedback: 5×3 = 15, 10×4 = 40, 2×7 = 14, 20÷5 = 4, 30÷10 = 3, 14÷2 = 7, 5×4 = 20, 5×6 = 30, 2×6 = 12, 10×6 = 60 — all verified correct. The near-miss example '5×3 = 20' is presented explicitly as an error to correct (correct value 15), never as a valid option.
The source claim that '5s are half the 10s' and '2s are doubles' is mathematically sound and retained as the derivation backbone.

CCSS 3.OA.7 (verified:false) states the fluency objective but was not cited as method-level support for out-of-order practice; its comparative/efficacy weight should not be overstated. NCETM mastery guidance is also marked unverified in the row.

Original row asserted that a talking partner 'adds little' and that 3D 'adds no conceptual value'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been removed or recast as narrow affordance-and-limit statements.
The number-line-with-equal-jumps representation from the original row was restored as an optional action in the shading activity to preserve the stated bridge from skip counting.

probeDeeper: How did you work out 5 × 3 — did you know it or count it?
What's 5 × 6? How could 5 × 5 help?
Which of these tables feels easiest? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: 15, 40, 14; 4, 3, 7 — answered from memory (or by very rapid skip-count), with the division facts as secure as the multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: reconstructs every fact by skip-counting — to answer 5 × 3 counts '5, 10, 15' rather than recalling; accurate but slow
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill under time pressure — recall builds from repeated meaningful use; keep skip-counting as a backup while spaced retrieval moves facts into memory
errorPatterns.revealedBy: audible or finger counting-up before each answer

errorPatterns.pattern: division facts lag multiplication — fluent on 5 × 3 but stalls on 20 ÷ 5; the ÷ fact isn't linked to the same fact family
errorPatterns.nextMove: teach fact families on one array/triangle — 5 × 4 = 20, so 20 ÷ 5 = 4 and 20 ÷ 4 = 5
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quick on ×, slow or guessing on ÷

errorPatterns.pattern: near-miss count error — says 5 × 3 = 20 (miscounts a step) or muddles the 5s and 10s
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor the pattern (5s end in 5 or 0; 10s end in 0) and re-count to self-check
errorPatterns.revealedBy: an answer one step off, or a 5s/10s mix-up

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce the facts, or only by counting from the start each time with errors.
responseLevels.full: Answers 2/5/10 multiplication and division facts from memory (or near-instantly), using fact families to link × and ÷.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls 2s/5s/10s multiplication but reconstructs by skip-counting, or the division facts lag behind.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I'll ask some facts quickly — answer as fast as you can, and I'll watch whether you count to get there. 5 × 3? 10 × 4? 2 × 7? Now the division ones: 20 ÷ 5? 30 ÷ 10? 14 ÷ 2? (Watch whether recall is instant or reconstructed by skip-counting, and whether the division facts are as secure as the multiplication.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking multiplication and its inverse division side by side, and watching HOW the child answers, separates true recall from skip-count reconstruction, and reveals the common gap where multiplication is fluent but the matching division facts are not.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–8 years

- **Topic:** Modelling with Sketches

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-2-ETS1-2, Engineering Design):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-2]. This performance expectation pairs SEP 2 (Developing and Using Models) with the disciplinary idea ETS1.B (Developing Possible Solutions) and the crosscutting concept Structure and Function.

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Design & Technology / Working Scientifically):** Pupils generate, develop, model and communicate their ideas through talking, drawing and templates/mock-ups, and (in science) use observations and ideas to suggest answers — the same move of externalising a design idea as a sketch or model to show how it will work.

- **Operational details:** The child produces a sketch, drawing, or simple physical model of a solution to a given problem and — crucially — can explain how the SHAPE or structure of their design helps it do its job (a wide flat base so it won't tip; a curved roof so rain runs off; a hook shape so it can hang). The learning is the link between FORM and FUNCTION: a model is not just a picture but a way to show and think through how a design will work, and to communicate that idea to others. They relate the model back to the real-world problem it addresses, so the model is purposeful, not decorative. This sits at the 'developing possible solutions' stage of the engineering-design cycle, after defining/asking about the problem and before testing and comparing designs.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete). This is the child's first use of a model as a design-thinking and communication tool. Success = creates a sketch/model of a solution and explains how a specific shape or structural feature helps it function to solve the stated problem, connecting the model to the real problem.
bestPractices: Anchor every model to a given problem so it is a purposeful solution, not a decorative drawing.
Make the form–function link explicit: for each feature ask 'how does that shape help it work?'.
Use real objects whose shape obviously serves a function (boat hull, umbrella, spoon) as worked examples before children design their own.
Treat the sketch/model as a thinking-and-communication tool — something to show others how the design works and to improve.
Encourage labelling/annotation of features with their purpose, building explanatory vocabulary.
Allow iteration: let children change a shape and re-explain, so the model develops as their idea does.
keyRepresentations: Shape-to-function pairing (wide base → stable; sloped roof → sheds rain; point → cuts through)
Annotated sketch with feature labels explaining purpose
Real-object exemplars whose form serves a function
Design-cycle position: define → MODEL possible solution → test → compare
Model-to-problem link card (which real problem this solves)
commonMisconceptions: Treating the model as a picture to make pretty rather than a tool to show how a design works.
Not connecting the model to the problem it is meant to solve.
Being unable to say WHY a chosen shape helps the object function.
Thinking any shape will do — that form and function are unrelated.
Believing a model must look exactly like the finished object rather than illustrate the key idea.
Seeing the first sketch as final rather than something to test and improve.

learn.summary: For children aged 5–8, teach modelling as a design-thinking tool: a sketch, drawing, or physical model is a way to show and reason about HOW the shape or structure of a design helps it do its job, not a decorative picture. Anchor every model to a given problem, make the form–function link explicit ('how does that shape help it work?'), and let children iterate — change a shape, re-check, and re-explain. Use real objects whose form obviously serves a function as worked examples, and have children annotate features with their purpose.

activities.title: Shape Shop: build and test a shelter
feedback: If a flat roof lets water pool and drip through, prompt: 'What could you change about the roof shape so the water runs off instead of sitting there?'
When a child reshapes the roof into a slope and the rain runs off, affirm: 'You changed the SHAPE and that solved it — can you say why the slope helps?'
If a tower on a narrow base topples, ask: 'What shape of base would stop it wobbling?' and let them widen it and re-test.
If labels only name the goal ('stays dry'), ask them to name the feature that achieves it ('the sloped roof sends rain off the edge').
activities.rationale: Letting a child change a shape and immediately see whether it does the job makes the form–function link something they feel and can iterate on, then annotate into an explanation. An optional light physics/response check (water pooling vs running off, a wobble-test on a narrow base) and an annotate mode make the mechanism concrete; these are illustrative, not required. This supports the standard's call to develop a model illustrating how an object's shape helps it function.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-2-ETS1-2 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-2].
DfE KS1 Design & Technology requires pupils to generate, develop, model and communicate their ideas through talking, drawing, templates and mock-ups.
learnerActions: Read/hear the given problem: 'Design a shelter that keeps the toy animals DRY in the rain.'
Assemble a shelter from choosable parts — a base, walls, and a roof you can shape as flat, domed, or sloped — drawing or placing your solution.

Run a rain check: on a flat roof, watch whether water sits and pools (and, if the roof has gaps or leaks, drips through onto the animals); reshape the roof into a slope that overhangs the walls and run the rain again to see whether the water runs off the edge and away from the animals.
Try a stability challenge too: give a tall tower a narrow base, test it with a gentle nudge (it may wobble or topple), then widen the base and re-test to compare.
Label your finished design with why each shape helps, e.g. 'the roof is sloped so the rain runs off.'
activities.intendedInsight: It was not a fancier roof that kept the animals dry — it was the SHAPE: a slope sends water away, and a wide base helps keep a structure from tipping. Form does functional work, and a model lets you show and improve how a design works.

activities.title: Shape detectives: real objects whose shape has a job
feedback: If a child names only the object, redirect to the feature: 'Which part of the spoon lets it hold soup — what shape is it?'
Affirm form–function pairings in the child's own words: 'Yes — the hull comes to a point so it slices through the water.'
Bridge to making: 'Now you try — for your problem, what shape would do the job?'
activities.rationale: A gallery of pre-authored exemplars vividly teaches the form–function idea and builds explanatory vocabulary, priming the child to read designs. It is a reading/priming scaffold: because the examples are authored, the child does not create or adjust their own model here, so it should lead into a making activity rather than stand alone.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-2-ETS1-2 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-2].
learnerActions: Explore real objects whose shape serves a function — a boat's pointed hull, an umbrella's dome, a spoon's scoop.

For each, tap or point to the key shape-feature and reveal/say 'this shape helps because…' (the point cuts through water; the dome makes rain run off its edges, away from the person underneath; the scoop holds liquid).
Build vocabulary by naming the feature and the function it serves.
Then take your turn: pick a problem and start your own model, carrying over the 'this shape helps because…' move.
activities.intendedInsight: The shapes of made objects around us are usually chosen on purpose: the form of a designed object is tied to the function it serves, and you can read a design by asking what each shape is for.

activities.title: Design a squirrel-proof bird feeder (make-and-explain)
feedback: If the child draws a decorative, detailed picture (colours, patterns, a happy bird) with no stopping mechanism, refocus: 'Which part actually stops the squirrel? Draw just that part big.' Value the working feature over decoration.
If the model doesn't connect to the problem, ask: 'What would a squirrel try, and what about your shape stops it there?' Build the link one feature at a time.
If the child labels a wish ('no squirrels here') with no physical feature, ask: 'What SHAPE makes that happen?' and replace the label with a feature.
Probe deeper: 'Why did you make that part that shape rather than round/flat/wider?' and 'A real squirrel can jump and hang upside down — does your shape still work? What would you change?'
activities.rationale: Producing and justifying one's own model is the procedural skill the standard targets; watching what a child draws and how they explain it distinguishes a functional model from a decorative picture. A making-and-talking task with raised challenges elicits independent construction and adaptation that recognition or match items cannot.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-2-ETS1-2 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-2].
DfE KS1 Design & Technology requires pupils to generate, develop, model and communicate their ideas through talking, drawing, templates and mock-ups.
learnerActions: Take the problem: birds keep eating from the feeder, but so do the squirrels. Design a feeder birds can use but squirrels can't reach the food in.
On paper or with simple materials, sketch or build a quick model of your idea.
Point to the specific shape or structural feature that stops the squirrels (e.g. a narrow perch, a dome, or a baffle) and explain how that feature does the job.
Relate your model back to the real feeder and the real squirrels.
Raise the challenge: a squirrel can jump and hang upside down — does your shape still work? Change it and re-explain if needed.
activities.intendedInsight: A good model foregrounds the working feature and can be justified by how its shape solves the problem, and it adapts when the challenge gets harder — the model shows how a design works, not just what it looks like.

activities.title: Match the shape to its job (check of understanding)
feedback: For a correct match, prompt the reason: 'Right — why does that shape win for this job?'
For an incorrect match, point back to the function: 'What does this part need to DO? Which shape helps with that?'
activities.rationale: Image-based matching, choosing, and sorting items give a quick check of the form–function link and surface whether a child can justify a shape choice. This is an assessment/check scaffold: it does not have the child generate or refine their own model, so pair it with a making activity, which is the skill being built.
learnerActions: Look at pairs of shapes and the jobs they might do, and match each shape to the function it serves.
Given a problem, choose which of several shapes would best solve it (e.g. which roof would keep rain out).
Sort shapes into 'good for this job' and 'poor for this job' for a stated purpose, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise which shapes suit which functions and give a shape-based reason for the match.

activities.title: Inventor coach: talk through your design
feedback: If the child restates the goal, redirect: 'That's what you want it to do — now, what SHAPE makes it happen?'
Reflect good reasoning back: 'So the wide base stops it tipping — you explained the shape AND the job.'
activities.rationale: A coaching conversation can draw out and rehearse the explanation and form–function reasoning the standard asks for. It is a support scaffold, not the lead: the modelling itself is a making/drawing act, so the conversation should react to a model the child has actually produced.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Design & Technology requires pupils to generate, develop, model and communicate their ideas through talking, drawing, templates and mock-ups.
learnerActions: Share a design you have already drawn or built with an 'inventor' partner (adult or in-role character).
Answer prompts: 'How does that shape help it work?' and 'Which part solves the problem?'
Explain each chosen feature and refine your words until the form–function reason is clear.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the form–function reasoning into words sharpens it and prepares you to communicate how your design works to others.

constraints: Anchor every model to a given problem so it is a purposeful solution, not a decorative drawing.
Make the form–function link explicit: for each feature ask 'how does that shape help it work?'.
Use real objects whose shape obviously serves a function (boat hull, umbrella, spoon) as worked examples before children design their own.
Treat the sketch or model as a thinking-and-communication tool — something to show others how the design works and to improve, not just a drawing.
Encourage labelling/annotation of features with their purpose to build explanatory vocabulary.
Allow iteration: let children change a shape, re-test, and re-explain so the model develops as their idea does.

Match/choose/sort items and the real-object gallery are checks or priming scaffolds — they do not elicit a child's own constructed model, which is the core skill; always pair them with a make-and-explain task.
A coaching conversation supports but cannot replace the making/drawing act; have it react to a model the child has actually produced.

A 3D builder can suit problems where three-dimensional form is the point (e.g. a stackable/stable structure), but at 5–8 it adds spatial-manipulation load; the key shape lessons at this age (stable base, sloped roof, pointed front) read clearly in 2D or on paper, so treat 3D as an optional enhancement, not the default.

Watch for misconceptions: treating the model as a picture to make pretty; not connecting it to the problem; being unable to say WHY a shape helps; thinking any shape will do; believing a model must look exactly like the finished object; seeing the first sketch as final rather than something to test and improve.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched and are listed as verified:false in the original row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims are cited to support general teaching principles (develop a model illustrating how shape aids function; model/communicate ideas through drawing and mock-ups); they do not establish the efficacy of any specific activity described here.

The original 'ideal/strong/possible' catalog rankings and claims that recognition/quiz/conversation formats 'can't' or 'trails' have been softened into scoped scaffold limits; relative-efficacy wording was not propagated as fact.

Physics responses described (water pooling/running off, a tower wobbling on a narrow base) are qualitatively reasonable for these age-appropriate examples but depend on specific setup; they are illustrative feedback mechanisms, not guaranteed outcomes of any particular implementation.

The original's explicit design-cycle positioning (define/ask → MODEL possible solution → test → compare; 'developing possible solutions' stage) is reflected only implicitly in the activities; a facilitator may wish to name this cycle stage when framing the task.

Independent re-review confirms the two previously flagged items are resolved: the 'thinking-and-communication tool' best practice is present as a constraint, and the Inventor coach activity now cites only the DfE 'talking/communicate' claim. The 'Shape detectives' gallery retains the NGSS citation on the form–function concept it teaches; reviewers should note the claim's model-development emphasis is only indirectly relevant to a read/prime activity.

probeDeeper: Show me exactly where a squirrel would try to get in — what about your design stops it there?
Why did you make that part that shape rather than round/flat/wider?
A real squirrel can jump and hang upside down — does your shape still work against that? What would you change?
assess.correctAnswer: The child produces a sketch or model whose SHAPE or structure does functional work — e.g. a narrow perch or a dome/baffle that a squirrel can't get past — and explains how that specific feature solves the problem, relating the model back to the real feeder and the squirrels.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws a decorative, detailed picture (colours, patterns, a happy bird) rather than a model showing how the shape solves the problem.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refocus on function: 'Which part actually stops the squirrel? Draw just that big.' Value the working feature over decoration.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Effort goes into appearance; no feature is identifiable as the squirrel-stopping mechanism.

errorPatterns.pattern: Model doesn't connect to the problem — the child can't say how any part of the shape keeps squirrels out.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what would a squirrel try, and what about your shape stops it?' Build the form–function link one feature at a time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked how the shape helps, gives no shape-based reason or restates the goal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Includes the goal by wishful labelling ('no squirrels here') instead of a physical feature that achieves it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Turn each wish into a mechanism: 'What SHAPE makes that happen?' Replace the label with a feature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels state the outcome but no structure in the drawing brings it about.

responseLevels.gap: Produces a decorative picture or a model with no functional feature; can't relate shape to the problem.
responseLevels.full: Produces a model whose shape does the work, explains how that specific feature solves the problem, and relates it back to the real situation — adapting it when the challenge is raised.
responseLevels.partial: Includes a plausible working feature but explains the form–function link thinly, or the model is part decoration part function without a clear mechanism.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's the problem: birds keep eating from the feeder, but so do the squirrels. Design a bird feeder that birds can use but squirrels can't reach the food in. Make a sketch or build a quick model of your idea, and show me how the shape of your design keeps the squirrels out. (Give paper/materials, set the problem, and watch what the child draws or builds and how they explain it.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching what gets drawn distinguishes a functional model from a decorative picture: a child who understands foregrounds the working feature and can point to how its shape does the job; a child who doesn't draws a pretty, detailed feeder and can't say which part stops squirrels. The link between form and function only shows in what they emphasise and explain.

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 this is the capstone of using structure: reading algebraic form (3(n+5) = 3n+15) via the distributive property, treating a shape hierarchy as a deduction engine (all rectangles are parallelograms, so parallelogram properties transfer), and moving fluently across 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5% and ratio structures to solve proportions efficiently. The child should see a complex expression as a single object composed of parts — CCSS MP7's own example is seeing x²+9x+14 as (x+2)(x+7) via 14=2×7 and 9=2+7, and reading 5−3(x−y)² as '5 minus a non-negative amount'. The teaching aim is deliberate structural reading before manipulation, backed by the area model for distribution.
bestPractices: Ground 3(n+5) = 3n+15 in an area rectangle n+5 wide and 3 tall, split into 3n and 15, so distribution over BOTH terms is seen not memorised
Use the shape hierarchy as a reasoning tool: 'this is a rectangle, therefore it is a parallelogram, therefore…' to deduce unknown properties without measuring
Keep FDP and ratio equivalences fluent (1/8=0.125=12.5%; 3:5 as 3/8 and 5/8 of the whole) so the child picks the form that makes the comparison trivial
Prompt 'what is this expression made of? can you see it as one object?' to build structural reading before symbolic manipulation
keyRepresentations: Area / grid model for the distributive law with a letter (n+5 by 3)
Shape hierarchy tree (quadrilateral → parallelogram → rectangle/rhombus → square)
FDP equivalence bar and ratio/double number line
Algebra tiles for expressions as composed objects
commonMisconceptions: Distributes over the first term only: 3(n+5) = 3n+5 (multiplier not applied to the second term)
Treats the letter as an object or label ('n is a name') rather than a number, or conjoins 3n+5 into 8n
Denies category links in the hierarchy (a rectangle is 'not' a parallelogram), blocking property transfer
Sticks to one FDP/ratio form and converts laboriously instead of choosing the efficient equivalent

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, the aim is deliberate structural reading before manipulation: seeing a complex expression as a single object made of parts, grounding the distributive law 3(n+5)=3n+15 in an area model, using the 2-D shape hierarchy as a deduction engine (all rectangles are parallelograms, so parallelogram properties transfer), and moving fluently among fraction/decimal/percentage and ratio forms (1/8=0.125=12.5%) to make comparisons trivial. The activities span a hands-on area-model build, a shape-hierarchy reasoning task, flexible FDP/ratio comparison, and a diagnostic probe requiring justification.

activities.title: Build the distributive law with a lettered area rectangle
feedback: If the learner writes 3n+5: point to the empty 3×5 region of the rectangle that their answer ignores, and ask what area it represents.
If they accept 3n+5 as plausible, have them substitute n=2: 3n+5 gives 11 but 3×(2+5) gives 21, so the forms disagree.

To probe generality, ask whether it still holds for a fraction such as n=1/2; another matching value is consistent with the rule but does not prove it, while the area split (3 lots of n plus 3 lots of 5 for any width n) shows why it holds for every n.
If correct, ask them to describe the rectangle in words: '3 lots of (n+5) is 3 lots of n plus 3 lots of 5.'
activities.rationale: An area model that the learner partitions makes distribution over both terms visible and lets the classic 3n+5 error produce a concrete missing block, supporting structural reading backed by a representation that reveals structure.
sourceClaims: Older students using structure see an expression as composed of parts and as a single object, e.g. x²+9x+14 via 14=2×7 and 9=2+7, and read 5−3(x−y)² as 5 minus a non-negative amount
Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure, including reading expressions as descriptions of relationships, and use representations that reveal structure
learnerActions: Draw or display a rectangle that is 3 tall and (n+5) wide.
Split the width into an n-part and a 5-part, making two strips: a 3-by-n strip and a 3-by-5 strip.
Label the strips 3n and 15 (because 3×5=15) and write the whole area as 3(n+5)=3n+15.
Deliberately try the tempting wrong answer 3n+5 by multiplying only the n-strip, then look for what area is left unaccounted for.
Identify the missing 3×5 block as the reason 3n+5 is wrong, and state why the 3 must act on BOTH terms.
Check with a number: let n=2, so 3×(2+5)=21, 3n+15=21, but 3n+5=11.
activities.intendedInsight: Distribution multiplies every term inside the bracket, not just the first; the area of the whole rectangle equals the sum of the two strips, so 3(n+5)=3n+15 is built, not memorised.

activities.title: Use the shape hierarchy as a deduction engine
feedback: If the learner denies a link ('a rectangle is not a parallelogram'), place the rectangle inside the parallelogram set and ask which part of the parallelogram definition it fails — it fails none.
If they can state a link but not use it, prompt: 'opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel; is a rectangle a parallelogram? so what about its opposite sides?'
Reward chained reasoning: 'square → rectangle → parallelogram' means all parallelogram AND rectangle properties apply to the square.
activities.rationale: Treating the hierarchy as a reasoning tool turns classification into deduction, letting learners transfer properties and justify facts structurally instead of measuring; the hierarchy diagram is a representation that reveals this structure.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure, including reading expressions as descriptions of relationships, and use representations that reveal structure
learnerActions: Draw or arrange a hierarchy: quadrilateral → parallelogram → rectangle/rhombus → square.
Place a rectangle inside the parallelogram set and state 'this is a rectangle, therefore it is a parallelogram.'
List the parallelogram properties the rectangle must inherit (e.g. opposite sides parallel and equal) WITHOUT measuring.
Extend the chain: a square is a rectangle and a rectangle is a parallelogram — say what that lets you conclude about a square's sides and angles.
Use an inherited property to deduce a missing angle or side fact in a given rectangle.
activities.intendedInsight: Category membership lets properties transfer down the hierarchy, so you can deduce facts by reasoning about what a shape IS rather than by measuring each case.

activities.title: Choose the efficient fraction-decimal-percentage or ratio form
feedback: If the learner converts laboriously in one fixed direction, ask which single conversion would have made the comparison immediate.
For 1/8 vs 12% of the same amount: converting 1/8 to 12.5% allows a direct percentage comparison showing 12.5% > 12%, so 1/8 is the larger.
If a ratio is treated as two separate unrelated numbers, prompt them to find the whole (3+5=8) so each part becomes a fraction of the whole (3/8 and 5/8).
activities.rationale: Flexible FDP and ratio equivalence lets learners pick the representation that makes a comparison trivial, reinforcing structural choice over rote conversion; equivalence representations reveal the shared quantity.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure, including reading expressions as descriptions of relationships, and use representations that reveal structure
learnerActions: Record the equivalences 1/8=0.125=12.5% and explain how each is obtained from the others.
Given a comparison such as 'which is larger, 1/8 or 12% of the same amount?', decide which form (1/8, 0.125, or 12.5%) makes the comparison easiest and say why.
Rewrite a ratio such as 3:5 as fractions of the whole (3/8 and 5/8) and use that to solve a proportion.
Solve a short proportion problem by first choosing the most convenient form, then justify the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: The same quantity has several equivalent forms; fluently switching to the form that makes a comparison or calculation trivial is itself a structural skill.

activities.title: Diagnose and justify: is 3(n+5)=3n+5?
feedback: Full reasoning: rejects 3n+5, gives 3n+15 justified by the area split AND a numerical check, and reads the expression as a composed object unprompted.
Partial: corrects to 3n+15 when prompted but justifies only by a remembered rule — push for an area picture or a substitution check.

Gap: accepts 3n+5, or conjoins 3n+5 into 8n — return to the area rectangle to expose the missing 3×5, then substitute a value to show the forms disagree (at n=2, 3n+5 gives 11, 3n+15 gives 21, and 8n gives 16).
If the learner treats n as a label ('n stands for an apple'), substitute several values to show n is a number that varies, and that 3n and 5 are unlike terms that cannot be combined.
activities.rationale: An open probe requiring both a corrected answer and a justification (picture plus substitution) discriminates structural understanding from a rote rule and surfaces the specific distribute-over-first-term and conjoining errors.
sourceClaims: Older students using structure see an expression as composed of parts and as a single object, e.g. x²+9x+14 via 14=2×7 and 9=2+7, and read 5−3(x−y)² as 5 minus a non-negative amount
learnerActions: Consider: 'A friend writes 3 × (n + 5) = 3n + 5. Is that right? If not, what should it be?'
Decide whether the statement is correct and give the corrected form if not.
Convince the friend using a picture (the area rectangle splitting into 3n and 15) AND an example (substitute a value for n).
Substitute n=2 to check: 3×7=21 matches 3n+15=21, not 3n+5=11.
Test with a fraction such as n=1/2 to see that 3(n+5)=3n+15 also holds there, then use the area picture to explain why it holds for every n, since examples alone cannot prove a general rule.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct thinker sees the 3 must act on both terms and can justify 3(n+5)=3n+15 in general with the area model; substitution is decisive for rejecting 3n+5, because one counterexample is enough to disprove it, and in fact 3n+5 and 3n+15 differ by 10 for every value of n.

constraints: A multiple-choice or true/false check using the 3(n+5)=3n+5 wrong-answer option and hierarchy items can surface and check classification errors, but a correct selection can mask shaky reasoning; always pair it with a 'why' justification step, since recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own construction or explanation.

A tap-to-reveal poster or pre-built annotated split is a reference scaffold only: it does not let the learner produce the wrong 3n+5 split and see the missing block, so it should supplement, not replace, learner-constructed partitioning.

Dialogue alone provides no written symbols or diagram for the learner to partition; structural reading of expressions is better supported when the symbols and a structure-revealing representation (such as the area model) are visible to act on — an affordance observation, not a claim that dialogue can never contribute.

The optional interactive version (a lettered area-model splitter where dragging a divider cleaves the rectangle into a labelled 3n strip and a 3×5 strip, plus a linked hierarchy tree that highlights inherited properties on selection) is one proposed way that may make the mechanism concrete (efficacy untested), not a required medium; paper rectangles and a drawn hierarchy can achieve the same reasoning.

Any physical rectangles or cut shapes used are representations of the ideal mathematical region or figure, not the figure itself; the reasoning concerns the mathematical shape represented, and physical thickness is not a criterion in this 2-D work.
Keep n explicitly as a number that varies, not as an object or label, so unlike terms (3n and 5) are not conjoined.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources (CCSS MP7; EEF KS2-3 maths) support the general principle of reading expressions structurally and using structure-revealing representations; they do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any specific activity or medium. Their attachment to the shape-hierarchy and FDP/ratio activities is general-principle support only (via 'recognise and use mathematical structure' and 'use representations that reveal structure'), not activity-specific or topic-specific evidence.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3×(2+5)=21; 3n+15 at n=2 = 6+15=21 (match); 3n+5 at n=2 = 6+5=11; 8n at n=2 = 16 (both correct disagreements); 3×5=15; 1/8=0.125=12.5% (so 1/8 > 12%); 3:5 gives parts 3/8 and 5/8 of a whole (sum 8). All consistent as used.

The original's claim that '3D adds load, not insight' for this topic has been reduced to a scoped observation: 2-D area and hierarchy representations are the natural fit and a flat area model suffices; this is not asserted as a universal law about 3-D representations.
The fraction comparison 1/8 vs 12% is scoped to 'of the same amount'; as numbers these remain directly comparable, and no denominator 'rule-flipping' language is used.

probeDeeper: Ask 'check your answer by letting n = 2 — does 3(n+5) equal 3n+15 or 3n+5?' to see whether the child uses substitution as a structural check
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'does 3(n+5) = 3n+15 still hold if n is a fraction, like 1/2? test it' to probe whether the distributive structure is general, not number-specific
Ask 'a square is a rectangle and a rectangle is a parallelogram — what does that let you say about a square's sides without measuring?' to test chained property inheritance
Ask 'to compare 1/8 and 12% of the same amount, which form makes it easiest — 1/8, 0.125 or 12.5%? why?' to probe flexible FDP structure
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting 3n+5 and giving 3n+15 with a structural justification: the 3 multiplies BOTH the n and the 5 (area rectangle 3 by n+5 splits into 3n and 15), and/or a numerical check (n=2: 3×7=21, and 3n+15=21 while 3n+5=11).

errorPatterns.pattern: Distributes the multiplier over the first term only: 3(n+5) = 3n+5, leaving the 5 un-multiplied
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the area rectangle so the un-multiplied 3×5 block is visible; confirm with a numerical substitution that 3n+5 gives the wrong total
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses 3n+5, or writes it themselves, and cannot see the missing 3×5

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the letter as an object/label or conjoins terms (3n+5 collapsed to 8n), because n is not held as a number
errorPatterns.nextMove: Substitute several values for n to show 3n+5 and 8n disagree; name n as a number that varies, and 3n and 5 as unlike terms
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child combines unlike terms or talks about n as a thing ('n stands for an apple') rather than a quantity

errorPatterns.pattern: Denies a hierarchy link (a rectangle is 'not' a parallelogram), blocking property transfer used to deduce angle/side facts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the hierarchy tree to place the rectangle inside the parallelogram set; reason that it inherits parallel opposite sides
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'is a rectangle a parallelogram? so are its opposite sides parallel?' the child refuses the category link

responseLevels.gap: Accepts 3(n+5)=3n+5 or conjoins terms, denies hierarchy links, and converts FDP forms rigidly; no structural reading of the expression
responseLevels.full: Rejects 3n+5, gives 3n+15 justified by area AND a numerical check, chains hierarchy properties to deduce unknowns, and picks efficient FDP/ratio forms — reading each expression as a composed object unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Corrects to 3n+15 or states a hierarchy/FDP fact when prompted, but justifies by a remembered rule rather than the area model or a substitution check, and doesn't transfer

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A friend writes 3 × (n + 5) = 3n + 5. Is that right? If not, what should it be, and how would you convince your friend using a picture or an example?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning correctly sees the 3 must act on both terms and can prove it by area or by substituting a number; a child reasoning incorrectly accepts 3n+5 (distributes over the first term only) or cannot justify beyond a rule. Substituting a value is decisive — 3n+5 and 3n+15 disagree for every n, so a correct thinker's check exposes the error while a rote one has no check.

sources.claim: Older students using structure see an expression as composed of parts and as a single object, e.g. x²+9x+14 via 14=2×7 and 9=2+7, and read 5−3(x−y)² as 5 minus a non-negative amount

pedagogy.summary: These word problems apply multiplication of a fraction by a whole number in context — 5 people each eating 3/8 of a pizza, four 2/3-metre ribbon pieces. The core idea is a/b × n as n copies of a/b (repeated addition of a unit-fraction multiple), and the practical twist is interpreting an improper-fraction product back in context: 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8 pizzas eaten, but you must BUY 2 whole pizzas. Teach it as repeated groups on a bar or number line, estimate between whole numbers (6 × 3/4 lies between 4 and 5), convert the improper result to a mixed number, and round or interpret according to the situation.
bestPractices: Model as repeated equal groups — n copies of a/b — accumulating on a bar or number line so the product is built, not just computed
Multiply only the numerator by the whole number (n × a/b = na/b); keep the denominator as the unchanged unit
Estimate between which whole numbers the product lies before computing (6 × 3/4 is between 4 and 5)
Convert the improper product to a mixed number and INTERPRET it in context (round pizzas needed up to a whole)
Distinguish 'how much is eaten' (exact mixed number) from 'how many must be bought' (rounded up)
keyRepresentations: Number line with repeated fraction jumps of a/b
Repeated-groups bar (n copies of the fraction) accumulating past wholes
Improper → mixed conversion of the product
Context interpretation card (eaten vs needed)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies the denominator too (4 × 2/3 → 8/12), scaling the unit as well as the count
Adds the whole number to the fraction instead of multiplying (3/8 + 5)
Leaves the answer as an improper fraction with no contextual meaning, or fails to round 'pizzas needed' up
Chooses the wrong operation because the repeated-groups structure is not read

learn.summary: Learners solve word problems that multiply a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) by treating the product as n copies of the unit-fraction multiple, accumulating them on a bar or number line, converting the improper result to a mixed number, and interpreting that result in context — distinguishing exactly how much is used (e.g. 1 7/8 pizzas eaten) from how many whole units must be bought (2 pizzas). Core examples: 5 people each eating 3/8 of a pizza; four ribbon pieces of 2/3 metre; estimating that 6 × 3/4 lies between 4 and 5.

activities.title: Build the product by stacking repeated fraction groups
feedback: If the denominator changed (e.g. 4 × 2/3 written as 8/12), return to the groups: 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 — only the number of thirds grows, each piece is still a third.
If the whole number was added instead (3/8 + 5), redraw the five groups of 3/8 and name it aloud as 'five lots of 3/8' before writing ×.
If the answer was left improper, prompt: how many whole bars and how much extra does 15/8 make?
activities.rationale: Modelling multiplication as accumulating repeated groups on a visual model builds na/b concretely and confronts the documented error of scaling the denominator; keeping the denominator fixed shows the unit is unchanged.
sourceClaims: Understanding a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiplying a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) is built with visual models of repeated groups; multiplying the denominator as well is a documented error to confront
Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual fraction models and equations (e.g. n × a/b), and interpret the resulting product
learnerActions: Take a catering problem: 5 friends, each eats 3/8 of a pizza — work out the total eaten by building copies, not by jumping to a rule.
Stack five copies of a 3/8 bar (or draw five jumps of 3/8 on a number line) and track the running total: 3/8, 6/8, 9/8, 12/8, 15/8, noting when the total crosses a whole.
Record the result as the improper fraction 15/8 and convert it to the mixed number 1 7/8.
State in words: the top number (count of eighths) grows while the denominator stays eighths — the unit does not change.
Repeat the build for 4 × 2/3 (thirds accumulating to 8/3 = 2 2/3) to generalise.
If a live builder is available, set the fraction and the count and watch copies stack with a running total snapping the whole-number boundaries; otherwise draw each jump by hand.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number is repeatedly adding that fraction: n copies of a/b accumulate to na/b, so only the numerator (count of unit fractions) grows while the denominator stays the fixed unit.

activities.title: Interpret the result: eaten versus bought
feedback: If 15/8 or 1 7/8 is given as the number to buy, ask: 'You can't buy 7/8 of a pizza — how many whole ones cover 1 7/8?' The multiplication is correct; only the interpretation is missing.
If rounding is applied where it isn't needed (ribbon length), point out that 2 2/3 metres is a valid measurement — rounding depends on whether the unit can be partial.
Reinforce estimating first: if 6 × 3/4 was expected to be a whole number, note that 18/4 = 4 1/2 lies between 4 and 5, as the estimate predicts, so the product is not a whole number.
activities.rationale: Interpreting the improper product in context — distinguishing the exact amount from the whole quantity a situation demands — is the real purpose of the word problem; estimating between whole numbers provides a reasonableness check.
sourceClaims: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual fraction models and equations (e.g. n × a/b), and interpret the resulting product
learnerActions: Using the computed total 1 7/8 pizzas eaten, decide how many whole pizzas must be ordered, given you cannot buy part of a pizza.
Explain why 1 7/8 rounds UP to 2 here, and why the question 'how much is eaten' keeps the exact 1 7/8.
Answer a contrast pair: 'How much pizza is eaten?' (1 7/8, exact) and 'How many whole pizzas must be bought?' (2, rounded up).
For the ribbon problem, state 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 metres and decide whether rounding is needed (it is not — a length can be a mixed number).
Before computing another problem, estimate between which two whole numbers the product lies, e.g. 6 × 3/4 is between 4 and 5.
activities.intendedInsight: An improper-fraction product must be read back into the situation: the exact mixed number answers 'how much', but 'how many whole units are needed' may require rounding up — and some quantities (like length) sensibly stay as mixed numbers.

activities.title: Check and consolidate with targeted questions
feedback: A product with a changed denominator (8/12), often then 'simplified' to 2/3, reveals the denominator-scaling error — reteach via repeated groups.
A correct computation but a fractional buy-quantity shows a missing interpretation step, not a broken method.
An answer near 5 3/8 or an addition of whole and fraction signals the wrong operation was chosen — redraw the groups and name them before writing ×.
activities.rationale: A short set of discriminating items separates computational slips, the denominator misconception, and interpretation gaps, and checks transfer to a new context. Recognition items check reasoning but do not by themselves show independent construction, so pair them with an end-to-end solve.
sourceClaims: Understanding a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiplying a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) is built with visual models of repeated groups; multiplying the denominator as well is a documented error to confront
learnerActions: Answer: 4 × 2/3 = ? Choose and justify from 8/12, 8/3, 2 2/3, explaining why 8/12 is wrong (denominator scaled) and showing that 8/3 and 2 2/3 are the same value.
Fill in the blank: n × a/b = __/b, stating the rule in your own words.
Estimate on a scale 'between which two whole numbers is 6 × 3/4?' and place it.
Solve a fresh word problem (e.g. a new fraction × whole context) end to end: build, compute na/b, convert, and interpret whether to round.
Explain in a sentence what a party host should order for a group, separating 'eaten' from 'bought'.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent learners compute na/b (numerator only), convert to a mixed number, interpret in context, estimate between whole numbers, and transfer the method to a new word problem.

constraints: Enforce or emphasise numerator-only scaling: when multiplying, the denominator (unit) stays fixed; a builder that makes multiplying the denominator impossible is a scaffold, but learners must also be able to state and apply the rule without the tool.

Recognition/multiple-choice items (e.g. choosing 8/3 over 8/12) check whether the learner can judge answers but do not on their own demonstrate independent construction; include at least one full build-and-interpret task.
A tap-to-reveal static worked pair illustrates the accumulation and interpretation but cannot let the learner vary the count — use it as an example, not as the main practice where varying n matters.
Rounding up applies to quantities that must be whole (pizzas to buy); it is not universal — lengths and similar measures can remain mixed numbers. Always tie rounding to the situation.
A conversational/role-play framing (party-planning host) can pose the 'eaten vs bought' question well, but the accumulation itself benefits from a visual surface (bar or number line).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic audit (independently re-checked): 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8; 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3; 6 × 3/4 = 18/4 = 4 1/2, which lies between 4 and 5. The original candidate draft had written '18/4 = 4 2/3' in the interpret activity's estimation feedback; this is incorrect and now reads 4 1/2 at every occurrence.

The source row rated a 3D/physical representation as a 'poor fit' with the claim that '3D adds nothing' for planar repeated groups; this categorical modality claim is not an established pedagogical law and has been dropped. A 3D or physical representation is simply a different, non-required experience, not evidence that one medium is superior.

CCSS source is marked verified:false in the row; no new verification was performed. The IES/WWC source is marked verified:true in the row — this reflects legacy metadata, not a re-check during this rewrite.

probeDeeper: In (a), 15/8 pizzas are eaten — can you buy 15/8 of a pizza? How many whole ones do you need?
Between which two whole numbers does 6 × 3/4 lie, without computing exactly?
Show 4 × 2/3 as jumps on a number line — how many thirds altogether?
Estimate (b) — more or less than 2 metres? more or less than 3?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8 pizzas eaten; you must buy 2 whole pizzas. (b) 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 metres.

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the denominator as well: 4 × 2/3 → 8/12 (scales the unit along with the count)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to repeated groups — four lots of 2/3 is 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 — on a number line so only the count of thirds grows; the third stays the unit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Product has a changed denominator (8/12 rather than 8/3); often then 'simplified' to 2/3

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the answer as an improper fraction with no contextual meaning, or fails to round 'pizzas needed' up: reports 15/8 or 1 7/8 as the number to buy
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — 'you can't buy part of a pizza; how many whole ones cover 1 7/8?' — the multiplication is sound, only the interpretation is missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computation correct but the buy-quantity is given as a fraction/mixed number rather than 2 whole pizzas

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds instead of multiplies, or chooses the wrong operation: 3/8 + 5, because the repeated-groups structure is not read
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the groups first — 5 people each with 3/8 — and name it as 5 lots of 3/8 before writing ×
errorPatterns.revealedBy: An addition of the whole and the fraction, or an answer near 5 3/8; no repeated-groups working

responseLevels.gap: Multiplies the denominator, or adds instead of multiplies; no repeated-groups model.
responseLevels.full: Multiplies correctly (numerator only), converts to a mixed number, interprets in context (rounds pizzas needed up to 2), estimates between whole numbers, and transfers to a new fraction × whole word problem.
responseLevels.partial: Computes na/b correctly (15/8, 8/3) but cannot convert/interpret the improper result in context — leaves it improper or fails to round the buy-quantity up.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these, showing your working: (a) Each person eats 3/8 of a pizza and there are 5 people — how much pizza is eaten in total, and how many whole pizzas must be bought? (b) A ribbon is cut into pieces each 2/3 of a metre long — how long are 4 pieces altogether?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the method catches the two faults a bare answer hides: whether the denominator was wrongly scaled (4 × 2/3 → 8/12 instead of 8/3) and whether the improper product was interpreted in context. Part (a) is engineered to separate 'how much is eaten' (1 7/8, exact) from 'how many to buy' (2, rounded up) — a child who reports 1 7/8 pizzas to buy has computed correctly but not interpreted. A child who multiplies the denominator, or adds instead, reveals a broken model of a/b × n.
