pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–11 years

- **Topic:** Drawing Particle Diagrams

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter' — Particle model):** The differences in arrangements, in motion and in closeness of particles explaining changes of state, shape and density; atoms and molecules as particles. (Bridged down from KS2 states work; formal particle model is KS3.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-4 / 5-PS1-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-4]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-1]. Examples of models include drawing and diagrams.

- **Operational details:** This is a REPRESENTATIONAL node — the child learns to DRAW and READ the canonical dot diagram: solids (particles close, in a regular pattern, vibrating in place), liquids (close, irregular, sliding past each other), gases (far apart, fast, random). The diagram is a tool for reasoning: from it the child explains fixed shape (solids), flow (liquids), and compressibility (gas gaps). Two conventions must be taught precisely: (1) the PARTICLES themselves do not change size, colour or state — only their spacing, pattern and motion change; (2) the space between gas particles is EMPTY (nothing there), not air. Introduce arrangement first (a static snapshot), then motion (arrows / animation). Have pupils sketch the before/after of a state change (e.g. melting) and annotate what changed.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional). The child draws correct arrangement AND indicates motion for each state, and uses the diagram to explain at least one observable property (shape, flow, or compressibility) — without attributing macroscopic properties to individual particles.
bestPractices: Teach arrangement (a snapshot) before motion, then add movement with arrows or animation so both are represented.
Anchor every diagram to an observable property it explains (fixed shape, flow, compressibility) so drawing is reasoning, not decoration.
Insist particles keep the same size/identity across states — only spacing, pattern and motion change.
Establish that the gaps between gas particles are empty, not filled with air or 'nothing visible'.
Have pupils draw before/after a state change and annotate what changed, linking to heating/cooling.
keyRepresentations: The canonical solid/liquid/gas dot diagram (arrangement + spacing)
Motion arrows or animation showing vibrate-in-place vs slide vs fly-free
A before/after pair for a state change (e.g. melting) with annotation
Same-particle overlay proving the particles are identical across states
commonMisconceptions: Particles themselves expand, melt, change colour or change state (attributing macroscopic properties to particles).
The space between particles is filled with air/gas rather than being empty.
Gas particles sit only at the bottom of a container.
Particle size or number changes between states, rather than only spacing and motion.
Solids' particles are completely still (they actually vibrate in place).

learn.summary: Learners aged 7–11 learn to draw and read the canonical particle (dot) diagrams for solids (particles close, in a regular pattern, vibrating in place), liquids (close, irregularly arranged, sliding past each other), and gases (far apart, moving fast in random directions). The diagram is a reasoning tool: from it learners explain fixed shape, flow, and compressibility. Two conventions must be taught precisely — (1) the particles themselves do not change size, colour, number or state across states; only spacing, pattern and motion change; and (2) the space between gas particles is empty, not filled with air. Teach a static arrangement snapshot first, then add motion. Learners sketch before/after a state change (e.g. melting) and annotate what changed, linking to heating and cooling.

activities.title: Particle diagram lab: place, play, and test
feedback: If particles overlap, prompt the learner to redraw them as separate dots that do not overlap; if a gas clumps at the bottom of the container, prompt: gas particles fill the whole space and don't pile up — spread them out randomly throughout the box.
If the gas gaps are shaded or filled, ask 'what IS the gas?' — the particles ARE the gas (if the gas is air, the particles are the air); between them is empty space. Remove the fill.
If dots change size between states, remind: same object, same particles — only spacing and arrangement change. Redraw keeping every dot identical in size across all three states.

After the squash test, ask the learner to say, in their own words, why the gas compressed much more than the solid or liquid (its particles have empty gaps to close, while the others are already close-packed).
activities.rationale: An interactive model where arrangement is set, motion is played, and consequences (holding shape, flowing, compressing) are observed turns a static drawing convention into reasoning. A same-particle counter and a compression test make conservation and compressibility concrete. These are concrete, optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter/Particle model': differences in arrangement, motion and closeness of particles explain changes of state, shape and density; atoms and molecules as particles
NGSS MS-PS1-4: develop a model (incl drawings/diagrams) predicting changes in particle motion, temperature and state; 5-PS1-1 matter is particles too small to see
learnerActions: Choose a state and place particles accordingly: a solid in neat regular rows, a liquid close together but disordered, a gas spread far apart.

Add motion to the arrangement — show solid particles vibrating in place without leaving their spots, liquid particles sliding and tumbling over each other, and gas particles scattering and bouncing off the walls.

Run a 'squash the container' test and observe compression qualitatively: the gas visibly compresses as its empty gaps get smaller, while the solid and liquid show very little change (they are hard to compress, not perfectly incompressible).
Watch a running count of particles stay the same across every state, and keep every dot the same size when switching states, to show number and size are conserved.

Model melting: take the solid and show its particles loosening out of the regular pattern into a disordered arrangement and speeding up — staying close together (still touching, not moving far apart; only a small spacing change) and remaining the same particles — then annotate what changed.
activities.intendedInsight: A particle diagram becomes a working model only when it both shows arrangement and moves: from it a learner can explain why solids keep shape, liquids flow, and gases can be squashed, and why heating to melt rearranges and speeds up particles without changing the particles themselves.

activities.title: Canonical reference and hand-drawing on paper
feedback: Check hand-drawn work for the three tells: same-size dots throughout, empty gas gaps, and motion marks on every state (solids vibrate, liquids slide, gases fly).
If a learner can label a given diagram but hesitates to draw one, prompt them to generate a fresh liquid diagram from scratch rather than copy.
A reference is a memory anchor; being static it cannot show motion or let the learner test compressibility — pair it with drawing and a dynamic model to cover those.
activities.rationale: A labelled reference with 'what this explains' notes is a convention guide and memory anchor, and connecting each diagram to the property it explains instantiates the curriculum point that arrangement/motion/closeness explain state, shape and density. Hand-drawing on paper supports independent production rather than recognition. The static reference's limit (no motion, no compressibility test) is stated so it is used as a companion, not a substitute.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter/Particle model': differences in arrangement, motion and closeness of particles explain changes of state, shape and density; atoms and molecules as particles
learnerActions: Study a reference of the three canonical diagrams, each labelled with its arrangement, spacing and motion.
For each diagram, read the accompanying 'what this explains' note (fixed shape, flow, or compressibility) and connect the picture to the property.
Draw all three diagrams by hand on paper, keeping dots the same size and leaving gas gaps empty, then label arrangement and motion for each.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall and hand-production of the canonical conventions anchors the representation so it can be used without a prompt; a reference supports memory but the learner must still produce the diagrams independently.

activities.title: Read it and draw it: two-way check
feedback: If liquid particles are drawn far apart like a gas: liquids barely compress and don't spread out to fill a whole jar the way a gas does, so particles must still be touching — just disordered. Redraw touching-but-random.
If dots change size for different states: only spacing and arrangement change; keep every dot identical in size.
If gas gaps are filled: the particles ARE the gas; between them is nothing (empty space).
If motion is missing or only on one state: add motion to all three — solids vibrate in place, liquids slide, gases fly; none are truly still.

On the melting question, confirm: the dots stay the same size and number, while the regular pattern becomes disordered and the particles speed up, with only a small change in spacing — they do not fly far apart (that would be becoming a gas).
activities.rationale: Assessing both reading and generating discriminates genuine understanding: a learner who labels a textbook picture but draws liquid particles far apart, resizes dots, or fills gas gaps reveals the representation isn't yet carrying meaning. Probing prompts surface the two priority conventions (conserved particles, empty gaps).
sourceClaims: Students commonly attribute macroscopic properties to particles and imagine air/matter between particles; particles keep identity while spacing/motion change
learnerActions: Point to which of two given diagrams (dots spread far apart vs dots packed in a regular grid) is the gas and which is the solid, and explain the decision by spacing and arrangement.
On a blank box, draw the particles for a liquid — close together and touching but irregularly arranged — and add marks showing them sliding and flowing past each other.

Answer probing questions: In your liquid drawing, are the particles touching or apart, and how does that explain why water is very hard to squash? What's in the space between gas particles, and how do you know? When your solid melts, which parts of the picture change and which stay the same — do the dots themselves (their size and number) change, or is it the arrangement and motion that change while spacing changes only a little?
Critique a flawed example — 'someone drew big dots for gas and small dots for ice' — and say what you'd tell them.
activities.intendedInsight: Translating both ways — reading a given diagram AND generating a new one — catches errors a single direction hides, confirming the representation carries the meaning rather than being memorised.

constraints: The canonical curriculum representation is the 2D dot diagram; a 3D particle box can convey real spatial packing but adds interpretation load, so use it only as an optional extension, not the core drawing target.

Dialogue or in-role discussion alone does not let a learner produce or manipulate the diagram; the representational skill requires drawing/placing and reading. Discussion can still support reasoning around the diagram.
A static reference supports memory and convention but cannot show motion or let the learner test compressibility; pair it with hand-drawing and a dynamic model.
Recognition or labelling of a provided diagram does not demonstrate independent construction; always include a generate-from-blank task.
Teach arrangement (a snapshot) before motion, then add movement, so both aspects are represented.
Two conventions must be enforced: particles keep the same size, identity and number across states (only spacing, pattern and motion change); and the space between gas particles is empty, not air.
Anchor every diagram to an observable property it explains (fixed shape, flow, compressibility) so drawing is reasoning, not decoration.
Solids' particles vibrate in place — they are not completely still; gas particles fill the whole container and do not sit only at the bottom.

Melting (solid→liquid) keeps particles close/touching while changing a regular pattern to a disordered one and speeding them up, with only a small spacing change; do not depict particles moving far apart on melting (that depicts becoming a gas).
Keep the compression comparison qualitative: the gas visibly compresses while solids and liquids change very little; do not state solids/liquids are perfectly incompressible.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The pedagogy note references 'energy changes involved' during a state change (one evidence statement); for ages 7–11 this is kept qualitative (heating speeds up and rearranges particles). Depth of energy treatment should be reviewed against the intended standard tier.

The source claim about learners attributing macroscopic properties to particles and imagining matter between particles is marked unverified in the row; treat the misconception framing as research-informed, not confirmed, and do not assert efficacy of any specific remedy.

The compression claim is kept qualitative: the gas visibly compresses while solids/liquids change little; avoid implying solids/liquids are perfectly incompressible, as the effect depends on scale/representation.

The original melting probe framed the change as 'the dots, the spacing, or both?'; because the particles (dots) do not change on melting, this was reworded so no learner-facing text implies the dots change or that particles spread far apart — only arrangement and motion change, with a small spacing change for most substances.

probeDeeper: In your liquid drawing, are the particles touching or apart? How does that explain why you can't squash water?
What's in the space between the gas particles — and how do you know?
If I heated your solid until it melted, what changes in the picture — the dots, the spacing, or both?
Someone drew big dots for gas and small dots for ice. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the widely-spaced dots as gas and the packed regular grid as solid, justified by SPACING and ARRANGEMENT. Then draws a liquid as particles still close together (touching) but irregularly arranged, with movement marks showing them sliding/flowing past each other — not a neat grid (solid) and not far apart (gas). Same-size dots throughout; nothing drawn in the gaps.

errorPatterns.pattern: draws the particles themselves changing size — bigger for gas, smaller for solid ('they spread out AND get bigger')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Same object, same particles — only the SPACING and arrangement change. Have them redraw keeping every dot identical in size across all three states.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: gas dots drawn larger than solid dots; conflates particle size with spacing

errorPatterns.pattern: fills the gaps between gas particles with something ('there's air in between')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what IS the gas?' — the particles ARE the air; between them is nothing (empty space). Erase the fill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: shades or dots the space between particles in the gas box

errorPatterns.pattern: draws liquid particles spaced far apart like a gas, not close like a solid
errorPatterns.nextMove: Liquids barely compress and don't shrink to fill a jar — so particles must still be touching, just disordered. Redraw touching-but-random.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: liquid box looks like the gas box, just fewer dots

errorPatterns.pattern: draws a solid's particles as perfectly still but forgets gas/liquid particles move (or vice versa)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add motion to all three: solids VIBRATE in place, liquids slide, gases fly — none are truly still. Annotate each with its motion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: no movement marks at all, or movement only on one state; solid dots shown with no vibration

responseLevels.gap: Mislabels the diagrams or can't justify by spacing; drawing shows size-changing dots, filled gaps, or liquid-as-gas.
responseLevels.full: Reads any state diagram by spacing+arrangement AND generates a correct liquid (close, disordered, sliding) with same-size dots, empty gaps, and state-appropriate motion — and uses the picture to explain a property (e.g. incompressibility) or a state change.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and draws arrangement/spacing correctly for the three states but omits or muddles movement, or can label a given diagram yet hesitates when generating one — the representation is read, not yet fluently produced.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a particle diagram of a gas (a few dots spread far apart in a box) and one of a solid (dots packed in a regular grid). First: 'Point to the gas and the solid — how did you decide?' Then hand them a blank box and say: 'Now YOU draw the particles for a liquid, and add little marks to show how they're moving.' Watch both the reading and the drawing.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Translating BOTH ways — reading a given diagram and generating a new one — catches errors a single direction hides. A child who can label a textbook picture but draws liquid particles far apart, or shrinks/grows the dots for state, or fills the gas gaps with 'air', reveals the representation isn't yet carrying the meaning.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–11 years

- **Topic:** Comparing Possible Solutions

- **Standards — UK (DfE Design & Technology KS2, Evaluate):** pupils "evaluate their ideas and products against their own design criteria and consider the views of others to improve their work," building on generating and communicating a range of ideas.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-5-ETS1-2):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-2, 4-ESS3-2, MS-ETS1-2]."

- **Operational details:** Given a defined problem (criteria + constraints already set), the child generates AT LEAST THREE distinct candidate solutions, then compares them systematically against the same criteria and constraints rather than picking a favourite on impulse. The core skill is holding one shared yardstick across options: rating each solution on each criterion, checking each against each constraint, and then SELECTING the most promising one WITH REASONING that refers back to the evidence — not 'I like it' but 'B meets the leak and budget criteria that A fails.' Teach that comparison needs the same criteria applied to every option, and that the best solution is often a trade-off, not a winner on every row.
bestPractices: Require genuinely MULTIPLE ideas (≥3) before any judging — use a quick divergent phase so children don't anchor on their first idea.
Compare all options on the SAME criteria: a shared matrix (solutions × criteria) forces apples-to-apples rather than each idea judged on its own terms.
Separate criteria (rate how well) from constraints (pass/fail must-meet): a solution that breaks a constraint is out regardless of how well it scores elsewhere.
Demand reasoning tied to the matrix: the child must justify the pick by pointing at the rows, naming the trade-off accepted.
Normalise trade-offs — show a case where no option wins every row, so 'most promising overall' becomes the honest goal, not perfection.
keyRepresentations: Decision/comparison matrix: solutions as rows, criteria as columns, a rating in each cell, with a separate constraint pass/fail gate.
Constraint gate: a red flag that eliminates any solution breaching a materials/time/cost limit before scoring.
Side-by-side solution cards, each carrying its ratings, for at-a-glance comparison.
A 'because…' reasoning slot that must reference specific matrix cells to justify the selection.
commonMisconceptions: Picking the first or best-liked idea instead of comparing several against the criteria.
Judging each solution on different, self-chosen strengths rather than one shared set of criteria.
Ignoring constraints — choosing a solution that scores well but breaks the budget or materials limit.
Believing the best solution must win on every criterion, rather than being the best overall trade-off.
Selecting without reasoning, or with reasoning ('it looks cool') unconnected to the criteria and evidence.

learn.summary: Children aged 8–11 learn to compare multiple possible design solutions against one shared set of criteria and constraints, then select the most promising with reasoning that points at the evidence. The core skill is holding a single yardstick across at least three distinct options: rating each on each criterion, gating out any that break a must-meet constraint, and accepting that the best choice is often a trade-off rather than a winner on every row. Activities span building a working comparison matrix, defending a choice in dialogue, reading a worked matrix, and judging pre-filled comparisons — each targeting a different part of generate-compare-select.

activities.title: Solution Showdown: build and reason across your own comparison matrix
feedback: If the learner enters one design plus minor variants, ask for three genuinely different approaches (for example, different materials, structures or ways of reducing heat transfer) before any judging; praise divergence first, evaluation second.
If a chosen solution breaches a material, size, or cost limit, flag it at the constraint gate and have the child re-check each candidate pass/fail before comparing on performance.

If the justification never mentions the stated criteria, point back to the grid: 'Which keeps the ice coldest? Which fits? Which is under budget?' and require the 'because…' to tag the specific cells.

OPTIONAL interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: a live tally that re-highlights the current 'most promising' as ratings change; a red flag that drops out a constraint-breaker the instant a limit is flipped; dragging the winning card into a 'because…' slot that must reference cells. These are illustrative, not required.
activities.rationale: Systematic comparison is a procedure the child must enact, so building and reasoning across a matrix of their own options exercises generating, comparing on shared criteria, constraint-gating, and justifying — the full target skill rather than recognition of someone else's comparison.
sourceClaims: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-2, 4-ESS3-2, MS-ETS1-2].
KS2 pupils generate, develop and communicate a range of ideas and evaluate their ideas and products against their own design criteria, considering the views of others to improve their work.
learnerActions: Start from a defined brief whose criteria and constraints are already set (e.g. a lunchbox insulator that keeps an ice cube frozen from morning to lunch, fits the box, uses only allowed materials, and stays under budget).
Invent at least three genuinely different candidate solutions and lay them out as side-by-side cards before judging any of them.
Rate each solution on every criterion by filling the cells of a shared solutions×criteria grid.
Apply a constraint gate: mark each solution pass/fail on each must-meet limit (materials, size, time, cost); any solution that breaks a constraint is eliminated regardless of its ratings.
Select the most promising solution and justify it by pointing at specific grid cells — e.g. 'B keeps the ice frozen longer and stays under budget where A fails' — naming the trade-off accepted.
Work through at least one case engineered so no option wins every row, so 'most promising overall' becomes the honest goal.
activities.intendedInsight: A defensible choice emerges from one yardstick applied to every option; a constraint is a gate that eliminates, not a preference to weigh, and the best solution is usually an explicit trade-off you can point to.

activities.title: Defend your choice to a design mentor
feedback: Keep redirecting any preference- or looks-based answer back to a named criterion until the child reasons across all three options.

Treat an answer to a changed-condition question (budget, time) that explains how the changed criterion or constraint would or would not change the ranking as a sign the child is reasoning from criteria; confidence alone is not evidence, because a child can confidently defend a favourite.
activities.rationale: Spoken, responsive questioning rehearses the justification habit and can surface fixation or preference-based picks. It reinforces reasoning-from-criteria but does not by itself provide the structured matrix, so it complements rather than replaces the building activity.
sourceClaims: KS2 pupils generate, develop and communicate a range of ideas and evaluate their ideas and products against their own design criteria, considering the views of others to improve their work.
learnerActions: Present three candidate solutions and an initial pick to a mentor (teacher, peer, or in-role character) who will not accept 'I like it' or 'it looks cool'.
Answer pressing questions that force reasoning across all three ideas: 'Compared to your other two ideas, why this one?' and 'Which criterion does each idea win or lose on?'

Respond to follow-ups that test the robustness of the choice: 'Which of the other two came closest, and what ruled it out?', 'If the budget doubled, would you still choose this?', 'If it had to stay frozen until home time, would your choice change?'
activities.intendedInsight: A choice is only justified when it is argued against the alternatives on the shared criteria and constraints; impulse picks collapse under 'which criterion does it win on?'

activities.title: Read a worked comparison matrix
feedback: Prompt the child to predict a cell's rating before revealing it, then check their reasoning against the annotation.
After revealing the winner, ask the child which row the winner loses on, to make the trade-off explicit.
activities.rationale: A pre-authored worked example gives clear exposition of what a thorough comparison and an honest trade-off look like. It demonstrates the structure but does not make the child generate options or apply the yardstick themselves, so it is best used as a model before independent building.
learnerActions: Study an annotated decision matrix comparing several solutions across the same criteria.
Reveal, cell by cell, why each solution rates as it does on each criterion.
Reveal the reasoning behind the chosen winner, including where the trade-off lies and which rows it loses.
activities.intendedInsight: A good comparison applies the same criteria to every option and names the trade-off behind the winner; this is what a defensible selection looks like before you build your own.

activities.title: Judge pre-filled comparisons
feedback: If a learner selects a constraint-breaker, point out that a failed must-meet gate eliminates an option regardless of how well it scores on other rows.
If a justification cites preference rather than rows, require it to name the specific criteria the chosen solution wins and the trade-off it accepts.
activities.rationale: Reading a pre-filled matrix and drawing the conclusion can assess the evaluative judgement. Note that it hands the child a completed matrix rather than having them build and reason across their own, so it checks the comparison and selection judgement but does not elicit the generation and construction parts of the skill.
sourceClaims: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-2, 4-ESS3-2, MS-ETS1-2].
learnerActions: Given a completed solutions×criteria matrix, choose the most promising solution and state why in terms of the rows.
Sort candidate options into 'meets constraints' and 'eliminated' categories.
Rank the solutions that remain after setting aside any that fail a must-meet constraint by overall fit against the criteria.
Complete a 'chosen because…' justification that references specific rows of the matrix.
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing the right conclusion from a comparison means reading across shared criteria, gating constraint-breakers first, and tying the choice to named rows.

constraints: Require at least three genuinely distinct solutions before any judging; a quick divergent phase helps children avoid anchoring on their first idea (design fixation).
Compare all options on the SAME criteria — a shared matrix forces apples-to-apples rather than each idea judged on its own strengths.
Separate criteria (rate how well) from constraints (pass/fail must-meet): a solution that breaks a constraint is eliminated regardless of how well it scores elsewhere.
Demand reasoning tied to the matrix: the child justifies the pick by pointing at rows and naming the trade-off accepted, not 'I like it'.
Normalise trade-offs by including a case where no option wins every row, so 'most promising overall' becomes the goal rather than perfection.

The read-a-worked-matrix and judge-pre-filled activities are scaffolds for the evaluative judgement; they demonstrate or assess comparison but do not make the child generate options or apply one yardstick to their own ideas, which is the target skill.
Dialogue practice reinforces justification but does not supply the structured matrix or constraint-gating; use it alongside, not instead of, a building activity.
The misconception that the best solution must win on every criterion should be directly addressed by the rigged no-clear-winner case, so the child experiences an honest trade-off.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources (NGSS 3-5-ETS1-2 and DfE D&T KS2) were not re-fetched and both carry verified:false in the source row. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source framed a 2D interactive matrix as 'ideal' and a 3D environment as 'poor' on catalog-fit grounds; these rankings have been converted into complementary activities with stated affordances/limits rather than universal claims about which medium can teach the skill. No 'adds nothing' or 'only this teaches' claim is asserted; the 3D entry's narrow point (it adds manipulation the comparison task does not need) is noted as a limit, not a law.

The diagnostic lunchbox-insulator example assumes 'traps the most air so it insulates best' — generally true for still air, but real insulation performance depends on materials and setup; treat it as a plausible illustrative claim, not a guaranteed outcome, and it is not stated in any learner-facing activity.

The NGSS 'generate and compare' claim cited for 'Judge pre-filled comparisons' supports only the comparison/selection half of the principle; that activity does not exercise generation, so the claim is partial, topic-adjacent support rather than full coverage.

The original generic 'B meets the leak and budget criteria that A fails' example has been adapted to the lunchbox brief's actual criteria so the worked example stays internally coherent; the underlying contrast (evidence-based reasoning vs preference) is preserved.
The source links a constraint-gate reteach to prerequisite mt_Z5-fSCOBep; internal IDs have been removed from learner-facing guidance as instructed.

probeDeeper: You picked this one — which of the other two came closest, and what made you rule it out?
If the budget were doubled, would you still choose the same design? Why?
Suppose it had to keep the ice frozen until home time, not just lunch — would your choice change?
assess.correctAnswer: The child generates three genuinely different solutions, weighs each explicitly against the stated criteria (keeps ice frozen, fits the box) and constraints (allowed materials, budget), and selects one with reasons that refer back to those criteria and constraints — e.g. 'this one traps the most air so it insulates best and still fits, and it's under budget'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fixates on the first idea and elaborates it instead of generating real alternatives (design fixation) — 'I'll just make this one better'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Require three visibly different starting shapes before any judging; praise divergence first, evaluation second.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces one design plus minor variants of it, not three distinct approaches; resists sketching a genuinely different option.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares on personal preference or looks rather than against the stated criteria and constraints ('I like this one, it's cooler').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point back to the criteria card: 'Which keeps the ice coldest? Which fits? Which is under budget?' Make the comparison run through each criterion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justification never mentions keeping the ice frozen, fitting the box, materials, or budget.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the constraints — selects a design that won't fit, uses banned materials, or busts the budget.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child check each candidate against the constraints as a pass/fail gate before comparing on performance; reconnect to how the problem was defined.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chosen design violates a material, size, or cost limit and the child doesn't notice.

responseLevels.gap: Offers one idea (or near-copies of it); chooses on preference; disregards criteria or constraints.
responseLevels.full: Generates three distinct solutions, evaluates each against every criterion and constraint, and selects one with reasoning that ties the choice back to how well it meets the defined problem — and can defend it against the runner-up.
responseLevels.partial: Generates two or three options but compares them loosely — checks some criteria, or names constraints without systematically applying them, so the choice is only partly justified.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is the problem: design a lunchbox insulator that keeps an ice cube frozen from morning until lunch. It must fit inside this lunchbox, use only the materials on the table, and cost no more than the budget on the card. Come up with three different possible designs, then decide which one you'd build — talk me through why as you go. (Set the task, provide the materials/criteria/constraint card, and watch what the child does; do not explain how to compare.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching, not asking, reveals whether the child truly compares: a child who understands generates several options and holds them against the criteria, while a child who doesn't fixates on the first idea and defends it, or picks on looks. You can only see the comparison behaviour — which options were considered and rejected and why — by observing the process, not by asking 'how do you compare designs?'

pedagogy.summary: Four-quadrant coordinates extend first-quadrant plotting by carrying each axis through zero into the negatives. The key move is reading a position as an ordered pair — the FIRST coordinate on the x-axis (horizontal), the SECOND on the y-axis (vertical) — and coordinating each sign with a direction. It is best taught by building the plane as two perpendicular number lines the child can already order, teaching the axis-order convention structurally rather than by a first-quadrant rhyme, and working in all four quadrants together rather than bolting negatives on afterwards.
bestPractices: Build the plane as a horizontal and a vertical number line crossing at the origin, so negative coordinates simply inherit the ordering the child already knows from the number line.

Teach the convention structurally: the first coordinate is read on the x-axis, the second on the y-axis; rehearse against the origin (0,0). Treat 'along the corridor, up the stairs' as a first-quadrant crutch ONLY — it breaks down for negatives (to plot (4,-5) you go along then DOWN the stairs), so prioritise 'x-axis first' once negatives appear.
Use points in all four quadrants from the start; have children name the quadrant from the sign pair (+,+), (-,+), (-,-), (+,-) rather than memorising quadrant numbers.
Work both directions — plot from given coordinates AND read coordinates off a plotted point — including negative and fractional values, so fluency is not one-way.

Surface the reversal error deliberately with a compare-correct-and-incorrect task (one child says a point is (8,6), another says (6,8) — who is right and why?), and state the scale of each axis before reading or plotting, especially when grid lines represent 2, 5 or 10.
keyRepresentations: Two perpendicular number lines forming the Cartesian plane, origin labelled
'x-axis first, then y-axis' read against the origin (the 'corridor/stairs' rhyme holds only in the first quadrant)
Sign-by-quadrant grid: (+,+) | (-,+) | (-,-) | (+,-)
commonMisconceptions: Reverses the ordered pair, plotting/reading (y, x) — takes the vertical value first (the single most common coordinate error).
Sign/direction error: counts the wrong way for a negative value, landing a point in the wrong quadrant.
Misreads the scale: assumes each grid line is one unit when it is 2, 5 or 10, or reads two differently-scaled axes as if identical.
Over-relies on the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic and is stranded when a coordinate is negative (goes 'up the stairs' for a negative y).

learn.summary: Learners plot and read positions in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane using positive and negative x- and y-values. The core idea: a position is an ordered pair whose FIRST coordinate is read along the horizontal x-axis and whose SECOND is read along the vertical y-axis, with each sign tied to a direction. Build the plane as two perpendicular number lines crossing at the origin so negatives inherit the ordering the child already knows, teach the axis-order convention structurally (not via a first-quadrant rhyme), and work across all four quadrants together rather than adding negatives afterwards.

activities.title: Plot and read on a four-quadrant grid
feedback: If a point lands in the wrong quadrant, mirrored across the diagonal — for example aiming for (-3, 2) but landing where (2, -3) belongs — the pair has been reversed: re-read the first number along the horizontal x-axis, then the second up or down the vertical y-axis.

If the horizontal step is right but a negative y was counted upward (or a negative x the wrong way), rebuild the axis as a number line through zero, count the negative on that line first, then transfer the direction onto the grid.

If a read-back value comes out as half (or a fraction) of the true value, the scale was ignored: ask 'what is one grid line worth on this axis?' and count in those units — a point 3 lines right and 2 lines up on axes rising in 2s is (6, 4), not (3, 2).

When comparing (-3, 2) with (2, -3), if the learner expected a near-identical point, draw attention to the different quadrant as evidence that the order of the numbers matters, because each sign is read on the axis its position assigns.
activities.rationale: Placing a point and seeing where it lands makes the horizontal-then-vertical sequence and the sign-to-direction link concrete, and deliberately contrasting a pair with its reversal targets the most common coordinate error directly. A live grid with on-target feedback, a read-back mode, and a scale control (lines worth 1, 2, 5) makes each sub-skill visible; these interaction examples are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms — equivalent work can be done on squared paper.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants'.

Misreading the axis scale (e.g. failing to notice the axis goes up in 2s/5s/10s rather than 1s, or that two axes use different scales) is a documented student difficulty when reading coordinates and graphs.

The most common coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair / reading the axes in the wrong order (one pupil says a point is (8,6), another (6,8)); the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic works only in the first quadrant and breaks down for negatives (e.g. plotting (4,-5) requires going along then DOWN), so pupils should be taught explicitly that the first coordinate is read on the x-axis and the second on the y-axis, and the reversal is best remediated with a compare-correct-vs-incorrect reasoning task.
learnerActions: Given a target coordinate such as (-3, 2), place a point by first moving horizontally along the x-axis to -3, then vertically along the y-axis to 2, and check whether it lands on target.

Immediately after plotting (-3, 2), plot (2, -3) and compare where the two points land: note that swapping the order of the two numbers (each keeping its own sign) sends the point to a visibly different quadrant.
Switch to reading: a point is shown already marked on the grid, and the learner states its coordinates as (x, y) with correct signs.
Repeat with on-axis points such as (0, 2) and with negative and fractional values so plotting and reading are both rehearsed.
State what one grid line is worth before each plot or read, practising with grids where each line represents 1, then 2, then 5.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of the two numbers and the sign of each carry independent meaning: (-3, 2) and (2, -3) are different points in different quadrants, and the interval each grid line represents must be checked before counting.

activities.title: Name the quadrant from the signs
feedback: If a point is placed in a quadrant whose signs don't match (e.g. a (-,-) point put where (+,-) belongs), check each sign against its axis direction separately.
For (0, 2), reinforce that one coordinate being zero means the point lies exactly on an axis — here the y-axis, 2 above the origin — so it belongs to no quadrant.
activities.rationale: Naming quadrants from the sign pair reinforces the sign-to-direction link structurally and avoids rote memorisation of quadrant numbering, while still realising the curriculum expectation to work across all four quadrants. A reference layout that reveals each quadrant's sign pair and labels the axes ('x first, horizontal'; 'y second, vertical') can support this as a reference, though it does not by itself rehearse plotting or reading.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants'.
learnerActions: For a given point, state its quadrant by its sign pair: (+,+), (-,+), (-,-), (+,-), rather than recalling an abstract quadrant number.
Rehearse the convention against the origin (0,0): confirm that the first coordinate is read on the horizontal axis and the second on the vertical.
Classify on-axis points such as (0, 2): explain why a point with a zero coordinate sits on an axis and is not inside any quadrant.
activities.intendedInsight: The combination of signs locates which region of the plane a point lies in, and a zero coordinate places a point on an axis rather than inside a quadrant.

activities.title: Compare correct and incorrect readings
feedback: If the learner picks the reversed reading, trace each coordinate back to its axis: the first number is the horizontal position, the second the vertical.
If the learner still relies on 'up the stairs' for a negative y, show that a negative second coordinate means moving DOWN, and restate the axis-first convention that covers every case.
For the prediction, confirm A(3,-2) lands in the fourth quadrant (3 right, 2 down) while A(-2,3) lands in the second (2 left, 3 up) — a different point, reflected across the line y=x.
activities.rationale: A compare-correct-and-incorrect reasoning task is a documented way to remediate the reversal error, and explicitly flagging the corridor/stairs rhyme as first-quadrant-only prevents learners being stranded by negatives.
sourceClaims: The most common coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair / reading the axes in the wrong order (one pupil says a point is (8,6), another (6,8)); the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic works only in the first quadrant and breaks down for negatives (e.g. plotting (4,-5) requires going along then DOWN), so pupils should be taught explicitly that the first coordinate is read on the x-axis and the second on the y-axis, and the reversal is best remediated with a compare-correct-vs-incorrect reasoning task.
learnerActions: Consider a dispute about a point plotted 8 units right of the origin and 6 units up: one person says it is (8, 6), another says (6, 8). Decide who is right and explain why, pointing to which number belongs on which axis.

Explain, using a case like plotting (4, -5), why 'along the corridor, up the stairs' is unreliable for negatives — here you go along then DOWN — and why 'read the first coordinate on the x-axis' always holds.
Predict where A(3, -2) and A(-2, 3) each land and justify whether they are the same point or different.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning about why a reading is right or wrong fixes the ordered-pair convention more durably than a first-quadrant mnemonic, which fails once the y-coordinate is negative.

activities.title: Accuracy check across all four quadrants
feedback: Expected placements: A in the fourth quadrant (3 right, 2 down); B in the second (4 left, 1 up); C in the third (2 left, 3 down); D on the y-axis, 2 above the origin.
For the sign-change question, B(-4,1) to B(-4,-1) moves straight down by 2 units, keeping the same horizontal position (4 left of the origin).

If A and B land mirrored across the diagonal, the pair was reversed; if a negative lands in an adjacent quadrant, a sign direction was miscounted; if a read-back is a fraction of the true value, the scale was read as units.
activities.rationale: Procedural accuracy across both directions, including negative and on-axis values and non-unit scales, confirms the convention has transferred. Draw-a-path plotting and short read-back responses can score accuracy well, but such checking tasks confirm the skill rather than build the underlying sequence.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants'.

Misreading the axis scale (e.g. failing to notice the axis goes up in 2s/5s/10s rather than 1s, or that two axes use different scales) is a documented student difficulty when reading coordinates and graphs.
learnerActions: Plot and label a set of points spanning every quadrant plus an on-axis case, e.g. A(3, -2), B(-4, 1), C(-2, -3), D(0, 2).
Read back the coordinates of points already marked on the grid, including on a non-unit scale (axes rising in 2s).
Describe how a point moves when a coordinate changes sign, e.g. B from (-4, 1) to (-4, -1): which direction and how far.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means plotting from coordinates AND reading coordinates from a plotted point reliably, including negative, on-axis, and non-unit-scale cases (fractional values are practised in the first activity).

constraints: Work in all four quadrants from the start rather than adding negatives after first-quadrant practice.

Treat 'along the corridor, up the stairs' as a first-quadrant crutch only; once negatives appear, prioritise 'first coordinate on the x-axis, second on the y-axis', because the rhyme breaks for a negative y (plotting (4,-5) means along then DOWN).
Always state the scale of each axis before reading or plotting, especially where grid lines represent 2, 5 or 10, or where the two axes use different scales.
Rehearse both directions — plot from given coordinates and read coordinates off a plotted point — so fluency is not one-way.

A static labelled plane or reference card can help name quadrants and locate the origin but does not rehearse the act of plotting or reading, where the procedure lives; use it as a reference alongside active plotting.
Recognition-only or read-back-only responses confirm accuracy but do not by themselves build the plotting sequence; pair them with active placement.
Squared paper and drawn axes are a fully adequate substitute for any on-screen grid; the interactive examples are illustrative, not required.
A third spatial dimension is unnecessary for this planar ordered-pair concept and risks adding load without clarifying the two-axis sign-direction link.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the diagnostic cases: A(3,-2) is 3 right, 2 down (fourth quadrant); reversed to (-2,3) it is 2 left, 3 up (second quadrant), i.e. mirrored across the line y=x — matching the stated reversal error. B(-4,1) to (-4,-1) is a downward move of 2 units with unchanged horizontal position. A point 3 lines right and 2 lines up on axes rising in 2s is (6,4), confirming the halved read-back pattern. Activity 1 feedback now uses only the activity's own (-3,2)/(2,-3) pair to avoid switching example pairs mid-feedback.

The legacy reteach note phrased the fix as 'x is the corridor, count that first, then y up or down the stairs'; this rewrite keeps the corridor/stairs phrasing only as an explicitly first-quadrant crutch and leads with the axis-first convention, to avoid reintroducing the mnemonic's failure for negatives.

A non-preferred alternative (an in-role dialogue) was judged in the source as unable to rehearse the physical placement of points; this is retained only as the narrow objective point that dialogue does not itself exercise the plotting action, not as a universal claim that dialogue cannot teach coordinate reasoning.

The KS3 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants' claim is a curriculum requirement used to ground the all-quadrant scope of activities 1, 2 and 4; no source directly addresses the specific principle of naming quadrants from sign pairs, so that pedagogical choice is carried from the original pedagogy notes rather than from a cited source.

probeDeeper: You plotted A at (3, -2). Where would A(-2, 3) go — the same place or a different one? Show me.
Point D is (0, 2). What is special about where it sits, and why isn't it inside a quadrant?
If I changed B from (-4, 1) to (-4, -1), which way would it move, and how far?
assess.correctAnswer: A sits in the fourth quadrant (3 right, 2 down); B in the second (4 left, 1 up); C in the third (2 left, 3 down); D on the y-axis, 2 above the origin. The read-back point is named as (x, y) with correct signs and read against the '2s' scale (e.g. a point 3 lines right and 2 lines up is (6, 4)).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the ordered pair, plotting (y, x): counts the vertical value first, so A(3,-2) lands where (-2,3) belongs — second quadrant instead of fourth
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the convention against the origin — 'x is the corridor, count that first, then y up or down the stairs' — using the horizontal number line the child already orders.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watch the order of counting: A and B land in the wrong quadrants, mirrored across the diagonal from where they belong.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sign/direction error for negatives: right-count is correct but counts up instead of down for a negative y (or left/right wrong for negative x), landing the point in the wrong side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the axes as two number lines through zero and count the negative on the line first, then transfer that direction onto the grid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: B(-4,1) or C(-2,-3) lands in an adjacent quadrant; the negative is counted in the positive direction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the scale: on the read-back, states (3, 2) for a point that is 3 and 2 grid-lines along axes that go up in 2s (true value (6, 4)) — treats each line as one unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Before reading, ask 'what is one grid line worth on this axis?' Scaffold the count in the correct units; the concept is intact, only the scale was overlooked.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Read-back value is exactly half (or a fraction) of the true value; child ignores the axis interval.

responseLevels.gap: Plots points into wrong quadrants, reverses pairs, or cannot read a marked point back; treats negatives inconsistently and ignores scale.
responseLevels.full: Plots and reads all four points accurately including the on-axis and negative cases, self-checks order and sign, and correctly reads back a point on a non-unit scale — transferring the ordered-pair convention to a new point.
responseLevels.partial: Plots positive and first-quadrant points correctly and reads simple points, but slips on sign/direction for negatives or reads a non-unit scale as units — can place the parts but does not yet coordinate sign with direction reliably across all four quadrants.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a coordinate grid showing all four quadrants, with each square worth one unit. Plot and label these four points: A(3, -2), B(-4, 1), C(-2, -3), D(0, 2). When you have finished, I will point to a fifth point already marked on the grid (drawn on axes that go up in 2s) and you tell me its coordinates.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the ordered-pair convention and the sign-to-direction link places every point in the correct quadrant on the first attempt. A child who reverses the pair sends A and B into wrong quadrants in a way a correct plot never produces; D(0,2) separates those who treat 0 as a genuine coordinate sitting on the axis from those who drift off it; and the read-back on a non-unit scale exposes anyone assuming one line equals one unit.

sources.claim: The most common coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair / reading the axes in the wrong order (one pupil says a point is (8,6), another (6,8)); the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic works only in the first quadrant and breaks down for negatives (e.g. plotting (4,-5) requires going along then DOWN), so pupils should be taught explicitly that the first coordinate is read on the x-axis and the second on the y-axis, and the reversal is best remediated with a compare-correct-vs-incorrect reasoning task.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–7 years

- **Topic:** Observation vs Interpretation

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to observe closely and to use their observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions. The distinction lives inside this statement: an observation is what you notice; an 'idea to suggest an answer' is your interpretation of it — and separating the two is the seed of evidence-based reasoning.

- **Standards — US (NGSS Nature of Science / SEP 4 Analyzing and Interpreting Data, grades K–2):** Scientific knowledge is based on empirical evidence; students use observations to describe patterns and distinguish what was observed from an explanation of why. Telling 'what I saw' from 'what I think it means' is a foundational Nature-of-Science understanding.

- **Operational details:** The child learns to split a single moment into two things: the OBSERVATION ('the ice got smaller / turned to water') — what you could see, measure, or record, that everyone would agree on — and the INTERPRETATION ('the ice melted because the room was warm') — your idea about why, which could be wrong or have alternatives. They practise labelling statements as one or the other, catching interpretation words ('because', 'so', 'it wanted to'), and rewriting a mixed statement to say only what was actually observed. The point is not that interpretation is bad — it's that keeping it separate from the data is what lets you later test it, revise it, or consider another explanation.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). This is the cognitive keystone of the whole nature-of-science strand: only once observation and interpretation are held apart can a child change their mind with evidence, seek another explanation, or judge evidence strength. Success = given a statement, reliably sorts it as observation or interpretation, and can strip a mixed statement back to what was actually observed.
bestPractices: Use a consistent two-word frame — 'I SAW…' vs 'I THINK…' — so children have language to separate data from idea every time.
Teach the tell-tale interpretation words ('because', 'so', 'wanted to', 'must have') as flags that an idea has crept in.
Practise on vivid shared events (melting ice, a wilting plant, a rolling ball) so both the observation and the competing interpretations are concrete.
Show that one observation can have several interpretations, so the idea is clearly separable from the fact.
Affirm interpretation as valuable — the goal is to LABEL it, not avoid it — so children don't think 'thinking why' is wrong.
Have children rewrite mixed statements to pure observations, making the separation an active move, not just a judgement.
keyRepresentations: The 'I saw / I think' two-column frame
Observation card (agreed fact) vs interpretation card (an idea about why)
Highlighted give-away words: because, so, wanted to, must have
One-observation-many-interpretations fan (same fact, several possible 'why's)
A short event clip paired with its observation and a candidate interpretation
commonMisconceptions: Reporting an interpretation as if it were an observation ('the plant was thirsty' rather than 'the plant drooped').
Thinking interpretation is 'wrong' or unscientific, rather than a separate, useful layer.
Believing there is only one possible interpretation of an observation.
Missing the interpretation smuggled in by a 'because' clause.
Assuming that because an interpretation feels obvious it must be the observation itself.
Treating a feeling attributed to an object ('the ice was sad') as an observation.

learn.summary: Helps 6–7 year-olds separate an OBSERVATION (what you could see, measure, or record, that everyone would agree on) from an INTERPRETATION (your idea about why, which could be wrong or have alternatives). Core moves: label statements as observation or interpretation, catch tell-tale 'why' words ('because', 'so', 'wanted to', 'must have'), and rewrite a mixed statement back to only what was actually observed — while treating interpretation as valuable, not wrong. Holding data and explanation apart is intended as the foundation for later evidence-based reasoning, letting a learner change their mind with evidence or consider another explanation.

activities.title: Two Buckets: sort what I saw from what I think
feedback: If a learner drops 'It melted because the sun was warm' into WHAT I SAW, highlight the word 'because': 'That's a great IDEA about why — but did you SEE the sun make it melt, or are you thinking it?'
For 'the ice got smaller' in WHAT I SAW: confirm — everyone watching would agree they saw this.
If a learner calls 'the ice was sad' an observation, ask whether sadness is something you can see, or a feeling you are giving the ice.
Affirm interpretations: 'Thinking about why is useful science — we just want to label it as an idea, not call it something we saw.'
activities.rationale: Turning the discrimination into an active sort-and-justify task with immediate, word-level feedback is intended to make separating data from idea an active habit rather than a told rule; using a vivid shared event keeps both the observation and competing interpretations concrete. 'Because/so/wanted to' are taught as common flags that an idea may have crept in, but they are clues, not a complete test: some interpretations have no flag word (e.g. 'The sun dried up the puddle', 'The ice was sad'), so the main check is always 'could I actually see this?'. Efficacy for this age is not established and the task is a proposal.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires pupils to observe closely and to use their observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions — embedding the distinction between an observation and an interpretation of it.
NGSS Nature of Science holds that scientific knowledge is based on empirical evidence and distinguishes observation/data from interpretation; SEP 4 K–2 uses observations to describe patterns.
learnerActions: Watch or recall a vivid shared event, e.g. an ice cube in a sunny window slowly turning to a puddle.
Take statement cards one at a time and place each into a WHAT I SAW bin or a WHAT I THINK bin. Examples to sort: 'The ice got smaller', 'The ice was sad', 'It melted because the sun was warm'.
When sorting 'It melted because the sun was warm', notice the word 'because' — ask yourself: did I SEE the sun make it melt, or am I thinking that?
Say aloud why each 'saw' card is something everyone looking would agree on.

Discuss how the same observation ('the puddle got smaller') could have more than one explanation (the sun dried it, or the water soaked into the ground) — both of which are ideas about why, not things seen.
activities.intendedInsight: The puddle shrinking is something everyone would agree on; the 'because…' is a story I added, and my story might be wrong — so keeping it separate from what I saw is what lets me later test or change it.

activities.title: Snip the 'because' tail: rewrite to a pure observation
feedback: When only the observation remains, confirm it 'glows' as pure observation: everyone could agree on it.
If a learner leaves 'because the sun was warm' attached, point out that this is the why-idea, not something seen.
For 'the sun dried up the puddle', prompt: turn it into something you could actually observe — e.g. 'the puddle got smaller'.
activities.rationale: Having children rewrite mixed statements makes the separation an active construction, not just a recognition judgement, and directly addresses the misconception of smuggling an interpretation in via a 'because' clause. It is a proposed activity, not a validated one.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires pupils to observe closely and to use their observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions — embedding the distinction between an observation and an interpretation of it.
learnerActions: Take a mixed sentence such as 'The ice melted because the sun was warm' or 'The sun dried up the puddle'.
Cross out or remove the interpretation part so only what was actually observed remains (e.g. 'The ice melted' / 'The puddle got smaller').
Read the trimmed sentence back and check that everyone watching would agree it is what happened.
Then, separately, state your interpretation starting with 'I think…' so both layers are named and kept apart.
activities.intendedInsight: Stripping a statement back to the observation is an active move that shows which part was the evidence and which part was my explanation added on top.

activities.title: Science-buddy dialogue: 'What did you SEE? What do you THINK it means?'
feedback: Praise the child for catching their own interpretation and relabelling it.
If the child gives a cause as a 'saw' answer, ask again: 'Did you see that happen, or did you see something and guess why?'
When a child offers a second explanation, affirm that this shows the idea is separate from the fact.
An adult may need to scaffold the wording: at 6–7 many children cannot yet articulate the saw/think split unaided, so model the two sentence starters if they stall.
activities.rationale: A responsive dialogue can probe a child's own specific wording and gently separate data from idea, anchored to a shared picture, complementing the sorting activity by working on the child's spontaneous language. Its limitation at 6–7 is that it leans on more adult-level language and lacks the crisp, structured sorting feedback of the Two Buckets task, so it best supports rather than replaces the active sort.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires pupils to observe closely and to use their observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions — embedding the distinction between an observation and an interpretation of it.
learnerActions: Look at a shared picture or scene (melting snowman, wilting plant, rolling ball).
Answer two separate questions in turn: first 'What did you actually SEE?', then 'What do you THINK that means?'
Notice and name any time an idea slips into the 'saw' answer, and move it to the 'think' answer.
Offer a second possible explanation for the same thing you saw.
activities.intendedInsight: A single moment splits into two things — the seen fact and my idea about why — and one observation can support more than one 'why'.

activities.title: Lift-the-flap scene: observation first, idea underneath
feedback: Reinforce the order: the observation is agreed by all; the flap shows one possible idea about why.
Note that this models the pattern but does not judge the learner's own sorting — pair it with the Two Buckets or dialogue activity so the child practises on their own statements.
activities.rationale: A pre-authored worked example cleanly models the two-layer structure. As a reference/teaching exhibit it shows the pattern; because it is fixed it cannot respond to the child's own wording, so it works best alongside an active sorting task.
learnerActions: Explore a single scene (melting snowman, wilting plant) by tapping or looking at marked spots.
At each spot, first read the 'Observation: …' (what can be seen), then lift a flap to reveal 'and what might that mean?' with a candidate interpretation.
Say back, in your own words, which part was the observation and which was the idea about why.
activities.intendedInsight: Every noticed fact can have an interpretation layered on top; seeing the two-layer structure modelled is intended to make the pattern memorable.

activities.title: Check: observation or interpretation?
feedback: For a correctly flagged mixed statement, confirm the give-away word that signalled the hidden idea if there is one (e.g. 'because'); if there is no such word (e.g. 'The sun dried up the puddle'), confirm the part that claims a cause or feeling nobody actually saw.
For an error, return to the 'could I actually see this?' test rather than giving the answer outright.
activities.rationale: A short categorisation check confirms the discrimination and the 'I observed…/I think…' frames ask for some production. It is primarily a recognition check and does not by itself coach the rewrite move or respond to a child's own spontaneous wording, so use it after the active activities.
learnerActions: Given short vivid statements, label each as an observation or an interpretation. Include tempting mixed statements as the hard cases.
Complete sentence frames: 'I observed …' with a pure observation, and 'I think …' with the matching interpretation.
Explain for one item how you can tell which is which.
activities.intendedInsight: I can reliably tell a seen fact from an idea about why, including in tricky mixed wording.

constraints: Interpretation is not 'bad' or unscientific — the goal is to LABEL it, not avoid it. Keep affirming that thinking about why is valuable so children don't conclude that explaining is wrong.

The lift-the-flap scene and the categorisation check are recognition/reference formats: they model or test the distinction but do not themselves elicit the child rewriting their own mixed statements. Pair them with the active sort-and-rewrite tasks.
Use a consistent two-word frame ('I SAW…' vs 'I THINK…') so children always have language to separate data from idea.

Show that one observation can have several interpretations (e.g. the puddle shrank because the sun dried it OR because it soaked into the ground) so the idea is clearly separable from the fact — and note both of those are ideas about why, not observations.

Optional interaction examples (sliding statement cards into labelled bins, word-level highlighting of 'because/so/wanted to', a trim/snip tool that turns a pure observation green, lift-the-flap hotspots, audio for low reading load) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory — any medium that supports active sorting, rewriting and responsive discussion can serve.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that a 3D or spatial representation 'adds nothing' to this language/inference skill was dropped as catalog-ranking boilerplate; absence of a strong spatial affordance here does not establish a universal law, so no non-preferred medium is asserted to be useless.
The source for the NGSS Nature of Science / SEP 4 claim is marked unverified in the original row; treat its wording as legacy and confirm before relying on it.
The puddle 'soaked into the ground' alternative is itself an interpretation (not directly observed) and should be presented as another possible idea, not as a fact.
Efficacy wording was softened to intended/may across activity rationales because none of the proposed interactions has fresh effectiveness evidence.

The causal card wording was harmonised to 'the sun was warm' throughout activity 1 (the original row carried both 'room is warm' and 'sun was warm' variants) so the sort, the follow-up bullet and the feedback refer to one coherent card consistent with the sunny-window scene.

probeDeeper: Which of these could you check just by looking? Which is a guess about why?
What if the puddle soaked into the ground instead of the sun drying it? Which statements would still be true?
Turn 'the sun dried the puddle' into something you could actually observe.
Why is it useful to keep what we saw separate from why we think it happened?
assess.correctAnswer: 'The puddle got smaller' and 'the puddle was shrinking' are observations — things you could actually see. 'The sun dried up the puddle' is an interpretation — a guess about the cause you can't see directly (you see the puddle shrink, not the sun doing it). A strong response separates what was seen from the explanation of why, and notes that the interpretation could be wrong even when the observation is right — maybe the water soaked into the ground.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats interpretation as observation: says 'the sun dried it up' is something you saw.
errorPatterns.nextMove: 'Did you SEE the sun do it, or did you see the puddle get smaller and then guess why?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Classifies a causal claim as a direct observation.

errorPatterns.pattern: Can't hold both as separable: thinks if the puddle shrank, then 'the sun did it' must also be a fact.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the observation stays true even if the cause guess is wrong — it could have soaked into the ground instead.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Fuses the observation and its explanation into one certain thing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dismisses observation as 'just looking': thinks only the why-explanation counts as real science.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Observation is the evidence the explanation has to fit — both matter, and the explanation is only as good as the observations behind it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Undervalues the plain observation in favour of the explanation.

responseLevels.gap: Treats a causal explanation as something observed; can't separate what was seen from why it happened.
responseLevels.full: Reliably distinguishes observation ('what I could see') from interpretation ('my guess about why'), recognises the interpretation is separable and could be wrong even when the observation is true, and can recast an interpretation as a checkable observation.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts the clear observation from the clear interpretation, but wavers on borderline wording, or doesn't see that the interpretation could be wrong while the observation holds.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at three things a child wrote after watching a puddle outside: 'The puddle got smaller.' 'The sun dried up the puddle.' 'The puddle was shrinking.' Which of these are things you could actually SEE happening, and which is a guess about WHY? How can you tell the difference?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps the distinction sorts the statements by 'could I actually see this?' and recognises the causal claim as a separable guess. One who doesn't treats the plausible cause as just another thing observed, because the explanation feels obviously true. The tell is whether they can say the interpretation might be wrong while the observation stays true.
