pedagogy.summary: At 7-8 precision consolidates into consistent conventions: always specifying units in measurement answers ('35 cm', not '35'), using fraction vocabulary precisely (numerator, denominator, equivalent), and writing equations with correct notation (£/p, >, <, =, and fraction symbols). The teaching emphasis is that a written mathematical statement must be readable by anyone without guesswork — '£3.5' is ambiguous where '£3.50' is not, and calling the top number 'the denominator' confuses a listener. Precision here is about shared, agreed conventions that carry meaning, in line with CCSS MP6's call to communicate precisely and use clear definitions.
bestPractices: Require the unit as part of every measurement answer and money to be written to two decimal places (£3.50), because a bare or truncated number can be misread (CCSS: specify units, appropriate precision)
Attach each fraction term to its role — numerator counts the parts we have (top), denominator names how many make the whole (bottom) — and use 'equivalent' only for fractions of equal value
Have children proofread statements for a reader: 'could someone misunderstand this?' — turning precision into an act of communication
Read notation aloud in words (>, <, =, ¾) so the symbol and its meaning stay linked (CCSS: state the meaning of symbols)
Model correct money and fraction notation consistently and correct drift promptly, so conventions become automatic
keyRepresentations: Measurement answers written with units (35 cm, 2 kg, 500 ml)
Money notation to two decimal places (£3.50)
Fraction written with numerator and denominator labelled
Comparison and equation notation (>, <, =)
Fraction bars / number line linking symbol to quantity
commonMisconceptions: Omits or is inconsistent with units — writes '35' for 35 cm (CCSS)
Writes money imprecisely — '£3.5' for £3.50, or mixes symbols as '£3.50p'
Swaps or avoids fraction vocabulary — calls the top number the denominator, or says 'the bottom number' rather than denominator
Uses 'equivalent' loosely for any related fractions rather than only equal-value ones

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, the objective is communicating with mathematical precision: always specifying units in measurement answers ('35 cm', not '35'), using fraction vocabulary accurately (numerator for the top that counts the parts, denominator for the bottom that names how many make the whole, 'equivalent' only for equal-value fractions), and writing notation correctly (money in pounds with £ and two decimal places, e.g. £3.50, or in pence with p, e.g. 350p, but not both symbols; >, <, =, fraction symbols). The core insight is that a written mathematical statement should be readable by anyone without guesswork: '£3.5' invites misreading where '£3.50' does not, and the equals sign must mean 'is the same as' so that false statements like 7+5=12+3 are rejected. Precision here is treated as an act of communication grounded in shared, agreed conventions.

activities.title: Maths proofreader's bench: fix the almost-right statements
feedback: For '£3.5', point out that amounts in pounds are written to two decimal places: without the trailing convention a reader could take '£3.5' to mean three pounds and five pence (£3.05) rather than three pounds fifty, so writing '£3.50' makes the amount unambiguous. (Note that in strict decimal £3.5 equals £3.50; the point is that dropping the convention invites a reader's misreading, not that £3.5 literally equals £3.05.)

If a length is written as '35', ask '35 of what? Could someone read this as 35 metres?' and have the unit added so the meaning is fixed (contrast 35 cm, 35 m and 35 mm to show how the unit changes the meaning).
When the fraction sentence is corrected, link each word to the bar: the numerator (top) counts the parts we have; the denominator (bottom) names how many make the whole.

For '7 + 5 = 12 + 3', work out each side (left is 12, right is 15); because the two sides are not the same value the statement is false, and the equals sign always means the two sides are equal in value.
activities.rationale: Showing a reader act on imprecise notation makes the cost of ambiguity concrete and turns correction into communication rather than rule-following; the equals-sign item targets a documented tendency to read '=' operationally and accept false statements. The misreading of '£3.5' is used as an illustrative communication device about convention, not as a claim that £3.5 equals £3.05 or about any specific real till.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, express answers with a degree of precision appropriate to the context, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and use clear definitions and vocabulary to communicate precisely

The equal sign must be used consistently to mean 'is the same as'; children who read it operationally accept false statements like 7+5=12+3 — evidence that notation must carry an agreed, precise meaning
learnerActions: Work through a set of statements that are almost right and repair each one: '£3.5' (a price), '35' (a length), 'the top number is the denominator', and '7 + 5 = 12 + 3'.

Submit each statement first as it is written — the sloppy version — to a reader that acts only on what is written and may misread nonstandard notation, then submit the repaired version and compare what the reader does with each. For example, when the two-decimal-place convention is dropped, a reader could misread '£3.5' as three pounds and five pence (£3.05) and short-change the customer; writing '£3.50' removes that ambiguity.

Repair the price to '£3.50', add 'cm' to the 35, and rewrite the fraction sentence as 'the top number is the numerator', checking it against a fraction bar where the numerator counts the shaded parts.
Decide whether '7 + 5 = 12 + 3' is true, and state why the equals sign means 'is the same as' rather than 'here comes the answer'.
Proofread each finished statement by asking 'could someone misunderstand this?'
activities.intendedInsight: A written mathematical statement should be readable by anyone without guesswork; a dropped unit, a missing decimal place, or a swapped term can change the meaning a reader takes from it, so following shared conventions is an act of communication, not a nitpick.

activities.title: Dialogue with a literal reader
feedback: If the character shows a possible misreading of the money, prompt: 'You wrote £3.5 — amounts in pounds are written to two decimal places, so write £3.50, and use £ or p, not both,' which makes the amount unambiguous.

If the child says 'the bottom number' or swaps the terms, ask them to attach each word to its role against a fraction bar — numerator counts the parts (top), denominator names how many make the whole (bottom) — before continuing.
Reinforce correct statements by having the character act correctly, confirming the notation was unambiguous.
activities.rationale: A responsive in-role listener can produce the repair through back-and-forth and may surface the child's reasoning about why the convention matters; this supports the precision objective and complements, rather than replaces, written practice.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, express answers with a degree of precision appropriate to the context, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and use clear definitions and vocabulary to communicate precisely
learnerActions: Give notation to a character (a shopkeeper or robot) who acts only on what is written and may misread nonstandard notation: writing '£3.5' lets the character show how it could be misread as three pounds five pence (£3.05), even though £3.5 strictly equals £3.50, and writing '35' with no unit leaves the character unable to tell whether cm, m or mm is meant, so it cannot act correctly.
Correct the notation in response to what the character does: fix £3.5 to £3.50, add the missing unit, and name the numerator and denominator correctly when asked for fraction words.
Explain to the character why the corrected version removes the confusion.
activities.intendedInsight: Precision repairs can come from seeing a listener try to act on exactly what was written or said; the child supplies the convention that prevents the misreading and says why it matters.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and write-it-correctly screener
feedback: Confirm correct rewrites; for a missed item, show the precise form and name the convention (units as part of the answer, pounds to two decimal places and only one of £ or p, numerator/denominator by role).
Where a child only recognises but does not rewrite, follow up with an open task that asks them to construct the corrected statement and say why it matters.
activities.rationale: Spot-the-error items efficiently screen for which conventions need work, but they target recognition and rewriting; they do not on their own elicit the child's full reasoning about why a convention carries meaning, so pair them with the bench or dialogue for that.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, express answers with a degree of precision appropriate to the context, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and use clear definitions and vocabulary to communicate precisely
learnerActions: Work through short items that present units, money, and fraction-vocabulary slips (e.g. '35' for a length, '£3.5', '£3.50p', 'the top number is the denominator') and either flag the error or rewrite the statement correctly.
For each flagged item, write the corrected version.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and rewriting common notation slips builds fluency and shows which conventions are not yet automatic.

constraints: Precision tasks should have the child produce or repair notation (write/say the corrected statement), not merely recognise a correct label; a static labelled example or reference card can support but cannot accept the child's input to host the production/repair practice.
Recognition-only or spot-the-error items screen for slips efficiently but do not by themselves elicit the child's reasoning about why a convention matters — use open prompts for that.

Keep fraction vocabulary tied to roles: numerator counts the parts we have (top); denominator names how many make the whole (bottom); 'equivalent' applies only to fractions of equal value, not to any related fractions.
Money in pounds is written with £ and two decimal places, and money in pence is written with p and no decimal point (e.g. '£3.50' or '350p'); never use both symbols ('£3.50', not '£3.5' or '£3.50p').
A fraction bar or number line that links the symbol to the quantity helps keep the term attached to its meaning; this is a representation choice, not a required mechanism.

In strict decimal '£3.5' equals '£3.50'; the till/character device illustrates how dropping the two-decimal-place convention invites a reader's MISREADING (e.g. as £3.05), and must not be stated as £3.5 literally equalling £3.05.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Mathematically '£3.5' = '£3.50'; the original's 'till reads £3.5 as £3.05' was reframed in all learner-facing text as a possible human misreading when the convention is dropped, so the guidance does not teach a false decimal equivalence.

The legacy row rated a static labelled example and 3D as 'poor' with claims like '3D adds nothing' and that a static example 'cannot host the practice'; these are catalog-fit judgements. Retained only the genuine, narrowly scoped limit (a static display cannot accept input, so recognition does not elicit independent construction) and softened the rest.

The MP6 claim supports the precision objective the dialogue and screener activities teach but does not independently evidence that any one medium outperforms another; medium efficacy is left as proposed/may.
reteachPrerequisiteId and quiz-step/screener-feeding-the-bench vocabulary were internal routing details and were not carried into learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: You wrote 35 — 35 of what? Could I think you meant 35 metres?
Is '£3.5' the same as '£3.50'? What might someone think '£3.5' means?
In ¾, which is the numerator and which the denominator — and what does each one tell you?
Why does it matter that we all use 'denominator' to mean the same thing?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child correcting '£3.5' to '£3.50' (money to two decimal places / pounds and pence) and correcting 'the top number is the denominator' to numerator (the top counts the parts; the bottom, the denominator, names how many make the whole), and for saying why the conventions matter (£3.5 could be misread; the wrong word confuses the listener). Surfaced for discussion, not scored.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits or is inconsistent with units — writes '35' for a length that is 35 cm
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist the unit is part of the answer; contrast 35 cm with 35 m and 35 mm so the unit visibly changes the meaning. Reteach calculating with standard units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives bare numbers for measurements and is untroubled by '35 what?'

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes money imprecisely — '£3.5' for £3.50, or '£3.50p' mixing the symbols
errorPatterns.nextMove: Money is written to two decimal places, and £ OR p not both; show how £3.5 could be read as £3.05. Reteach in place — a convention, not a gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces £3.5 or £3.50p and does not see how a reader could misinterpret it

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps or avoids fraction vocabulary — names the top number the denominator, or says 'the bottom number' instead of denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Attach each term to its role against a fraction bar — numerator counts the parts (top), denominator names the size of the whole (bottom). Reteach fraction notation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Mislabels numerator/denominator or avoids the terms altogether

responseLevels.gap: Gives bare numbers, writes money loosely (£3.5), and mislabels or avoids fraction vocabulary, without noticing a reader could misunderstand.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, specifies units and correct money notation, uses fraction vocabulary precisely, writes equations with correct symbols, and can explain why shared, exact conventions are needed to be understood.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, adds units, corrects to £3.50, and can name numerator and denominator, but does not apply the conventions consistently or spontaneously.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child wrote the price as '£3.5', and said 'in three-quarters, the top number is the denominator.' Are these written and said correctly? Fix anything that isn't quite right, and tell me why it matters.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child attending to precision spots BOTH the money-notation slip and the swapped fraction term and can say what goes wrong; a child who is loose reads straight past them. Both are almost-right on the surface, so only genuine attention to convention — not arithmetic — separates the children.

sources.claim: Proficient students specify units of measure, express answers with a degree of precision appropriate to the context, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and use clear definitions and vocabulary to communicate precisely
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice — MP6 Attend to precision

sources.claim: The equal sign must be used consistently to mean 'is the same as'; children who read it operationally accept false statements like 7+5=12+3 — evidence that notation must carry an agreed, precise meaning
sources.source: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter (1999), Children's Understanding of Equality

pedagogy.summary: The inverse-size relationship: cutting a whole into MORE equal shares makes each share SMALLER. A quarter of a pizza is smaller than a half of the same pizza, and an eighth smaller still. This directly confronts the whole-number bias by which children read a bigger denominator as a bigger amount ('4 > 2 so a quarter is bigger'). It rests on comparing unit fractions of the SAME whole, and is the seed of later fraction comparison (1/3 > 1/4).
bestPractices: Compare unit fractions of IDENTICAL wholes (same pizza, same bar) so the only thing changing is the number of shares
Use predict-then-check: ask which piece is bigger before cutting, then overlay to test (surfaces the whole-number-bias reason)
Increase the number of sharers and have children watch each share shrink (IES: link to names, 1/3 of it > 1/4 of it)
Name the pattern explicitly: more equal shares of the same whole = smaller pieces
Stress that the comparison only holds when the wholes are the same size
keyRepresentations: Two identical circles/bars, one halved and one quartered, pieces overlaid
A share-counter with a slider for number of shares, one piece highlighted shrinking
A fraction wall (1 whole, halves, quarters, eighths) aligned to the same length
commonMisconceptions: Larger denominator = larger fraction / whole-number bias ('a quarter is bigger than a half because 4 is more than 2'; 1/8 > 1/3) - documented in IES
Comparing fractions of DIFFERENT-sized wholes without noticing the whole matters
Confusing the number of pieces with the amount in one piece ('4 pieces is more than 2 pieces')

learn.summary: Help 6-7 year olds grasp the inverse-size relationship: cutting the SAME whole into more equal shares makes each share smaller. A quarter of a pizza is a smaller amount than a half of the same pizza, and an eighth smaller still. This directly confronts the whole-number bias by which children read a bigger denominator as a bigger amount ('4 > 2 so a quarter is bigger'). When comparing the actual amounts, the comparison relies on the wholes being identical, and it seeds later unit-fraction comparison (1/3 > 1/4).

activities.title: Predict-then-check with two identical pizzas
feedback: If the child predicts the quarter is bigger 'because 4 is more than 2', let the overlay settle it: the half visibly covers the quarter and more, so the bigger denominator did NOT make the bigger piece.
If the child says the 4-piece pizza has 'more' because it has more pieces, refocus on one single slice versus one single slice, not the count of pieces.
When they state the pattern themselves after watching the shrink, confirm it and restate: sharing one whole among more people gives each person less.
Keep attention on the amount of pizza each piece represents; the paper is just a model of the flat region being shared.
activities.rationale: Predicting before overlaying surfaces the whole-number-bias reasoning out loud, then the physical overlay of identical wholes contradicts it, so the correction is something the child sees happen rather than a rule they are told. Keeping the wholes identical means the number of shares is the only variable.
sourceClaims: As the number of people sharing a whole increases, each share decreases; teachers link this to fraction names (1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 of it)
Children commonly view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. they think 1/8 > 1/3) - the whole-number bias
Year 2 pupils compare and understand the size of fractions such as halves and quarters
learnerActions: Give the child two identical paper 'pizzas' of exactly the same size (the paper stands in for the flat region being shared - what matters is the amount each piece represents, not the paper itself).
Before cutting, ask them to predict: if one pizza is cut into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4 equal pieces, whose single piece will be bigger, and why? Record the stated reason.
Cut both pizzas and lay one half on top of one quarter so the child can see the half blankets the quarter with room to spare.
Then cut (or imagine cutting) the same-size whole into 8, then more, and have the child watch a single piece keep getting smaller.
Name the pattern out loud together: 'more equal shares of the same whole means smaller pieces.'
activities.intendedInsight: A single share gets smaller as the same whole is split among more sharers, so a half of a pizza is a bigger amount than a quarter of the same pizza even though 4 is more than 2.

activities.title: Live share-slider: watch one piece shrink
feedback: If the child expects the piece to grow as shares increase, let them watch the highlighted slice shrink and ask them to revise their prediction.
Prompt them to connect the moving slider to the earlier paper activity: more equal shares of the same whole, smaller piece, every time.
activities.rationale: A live, adjustable number of shares with one highlighted piece lets the child generate the shrink and overlay to test a prediction, which a fixed diagram cannot be manipulated to do. An interactive model is offered as one concrete way to make the mechanism visible; it is not the only route and complements the physical paper work.
sourceClaims: As the number of people sharing a whole increases, each share decreases; teachers link this to fraction names (1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 of it)
Children commonly view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. they think 1/8 > 1/3) - the whole-number bias
learnerActions: Show two identical circular pizzas side by side, each with a control that sets the number of equal shares.
Have the child set one pizza to 2 shares and the other to 4, highlight one piece on each, then drag the highlighted pieces together to overlay them.
Ask the child to describe what happens to the overlapped pieces: the half covers the quarter with space left over.
Have the child push the share control higher (8, 10, 12) on one pizza and describe how a single highlighted piece keeps shrinking.
activities.intendedInsight: As the number of equal shares rises, one share visibly shrinks, making the inverse relationship between number of shares and size of each share concrete.

activities.title: Order and compare unit fractions of the same whole
feedback: If a child orders by the denominator digit (treating 1/8 as biggest), return to overlay or the shrinking slice to re-anchor the size order.

If a child says a quarter is 'always' a smaller amount than a half regardless of the cakes, contrast a quarter of a large cake with a half of a small one to show the two wholes must be equal for that amount comparison to hold.
Reward reasoning that names that the wholes must be the same AND that more shares means each piece is smaller.
activities.rationale: Ordering and choosing between unit fractions of the same whole consolidates the pattern and lets you check whether the child reasons from piece size or reverts to the digit. The explicit 'different-sized wholes' question guards against over-generalising the amount comparison, and the 'biggest number on the bottom' prompt confronts the whole-number bias by name.
sourceClaims: As the number of people sharing a whole increases, each share decreases; teachers link this to fraction names (1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 of it)
Year 2 pupils compare and understand the size of fractions such as halves and quarters
learnerActions: Show pictures of 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and 1/8 of the SAME cake and ask the child to order them largest to smallest.
Ask the child to explain why the order goes that way in terms of sharing.
Ask the child directly: 'Why doesn't the biggest number on the bottom mean the biggest piece?'
Pose a comparison question such as: 'Who has more, someone with a half of a cake or someone with a quarter of the same cake?' and ask for the reason.
Ask the trap question: 'Could a quarter ever be a bigger amount than a half? What would have to be true about the two cakes?'
activities.intendedInsight: Unit fractions of the same whole can be ordered by size (1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > 1/8); when comparing the actual amounts in the pieces, the comparison relies on the wholes being the same size.

activities.title: Aligned fraction wall as a reference
feedback: If the child cannot see the comparison, draw attention to one tile per row rather than the whole row.
Note that this wall shows the sizes but does not let them generate the shrink themselves; pair it with the paper or slider activity for the 'why'.
activities.rationale: A static aligned wall is a useful reference for the size order of halves, quarters and eighths, but it shows the result rather than letting the child produce the shrink or test their own prediction, so it works best as a support alongside the hands-on comparisons.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils compare and understand the size of fractions such as halves and quarters
learnerActions: Show a fraction wall with rows for 1 whole, halves, quarters and eighths, all aligned to the same total length.
Have the child point to and compare a single tile in each row against the whole and against each other.
Ask them to find which single tile is biggest and which is smallest, and to say why.
activities.intendedInsight: A single piece gets shorter as the whole is divided into more equal parts, shown against a common length.

constraints: When comparing the actual amount in a piece, use IDENTICAL wholes (same pizza, same bar) so the only thing changing is the number of shares. This is a requirement for comparing represented portions; it is NOT a claim that fractions as numbers are incomparable (as numbers, 1/2 is always greater than 1/4).

Stress that 'a quarter is a smaller amount than a half' is guaranteed only when the two physical wholes are the same size; with different-sized wholes it can go either way, for example a quarter of a large whole can be a larger amount than a half of a small whole.

The aligned fraction wall and other fixed diagrams show the size order but do not let the child generate the shrink or test a prediction; use them as supports, not as the main mechanism for confronting the misconception.

Ordering/multiple-choice tasks can check whether the child selects the right size order, but selection alone does not show the child constructing the reasoning, so pair selection tasks with 'explain why' prompts.
Keep the focus on the amount in ONE single piece, not the number of pieces, when confronting the 'more pieces = more to eat' confusion.
Paper pizzas and cards are physical stand-ins for the ideal flat regions being shared; compare the amounts they represent rather than any property of the paper itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source rated a 3D manipulation as adding 'nothing' and plain conversation as 'poor' because the misconception 'yields to physical comparison, not to talk'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established facts; they have been softened. Physical comparison is well suited here, but talk and discussion can still support reasoning, and this rewrite does not assert any format is universally useless or uniquely necessary.

The claim that an interactive slider is uniquely able to teach the inverse relationship was softened: a fixed diagram cannot be manipulated, but can still support learning; the slider is presented as one concrete option.
The 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > 1/8 size ordering, the overlay demonstration, and the whole-number-bias description are internally consistent and arithmetically sound.

The common-whole requirement is scoped to comparing the represented amounts; as numbers, fractions remain comparable (1/2 > 1/4 always), which is a nuance beyond the explicit scope of the cited sources for this age.

assess.poeTask: Give the child two identical paper 'pizzas'. BEFORE cutting, ask them to predict: if one is cut into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4, whose single piece will be bigger, and WHY - record the reason. Then cut both and lay one half on top of one quarter. Observe the half covers the quarter and more. The pre-cut REASON is the diagnostic part: a '4 is bigger than 2' justification reveals whole-number bias, which the overlay then contradicts.
probeDeeper: If Bea cut hers into 8 pieces instead, would her piece be bigger or smaller than a quarter?
Could a quarter ever be bigger than a half? What would have to be true about the two pizzas?
Order these for size: a half, a third, and a quarter of the same cake.
Why doesn't the biggest number on the bottom mean the biggest piece?
assess.correctAnswer: Ali has more - a half is bigger than a quarter of the same pizza. Cutting the same whole into more equal pieces makes each piece smaller, because one whole is being shared among more parts. (Tier 2: the more sharers, the less each one gets.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Larger denominator means larger fraction - 'a quarter is bigger because 4 is more than 2' (whole-number bias)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Predict-then-overlay two identical wholes (see poeTask); name the pattern 'more shares = smaller piece'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Bea - a quarter is bigger because 4 is more than 2
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Bea and justifies with the size of the denominator digit

errorPatterns.pattern: More pieces means more to eat - confuses the NUMBER of pieces with the AMOUNT in one piece
errorPatterns.nextMove: Focus on the size of a single piece; overlay one slice on one slice.
errorPatterns.distractor: Bea - she cut hers into more pieces, so she has more
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Bea 'because she has 4 pieces and Ali only has 2', even though each eats one piece

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores that the wholes must be the same size to compare
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast 1/4 of a large pizza with 1/2 of a small one; the whole must be equal for the rule to hold.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Later claims 'a quarter is always smaller than a half' regardless, or cannot see why 'same size pizza' was stated

responseLevels.gap: Picks the larger-denominator fraction as bigger and reasons from the digits ('4>2').
responseLevels.full: States that more equal shares of the same whole means smaller shares, orders 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 and explains why, recognises the wholes must be identical, and transfers to 1/8.
responseLevels.partial: Orders unit fractions of the same whole correctly when shown a picture, but reverts to 'bigger number = bigger' without the model, or overlooks that the wholes must be the same size.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two children each have a whole pizza, exactly the same size. Ali cuts hers into 2 equal pieces and takes one piece. Bea cuts hers into 4 equal pieces and takes one piece. Ask: 'Who has more pizza to eat - and how do you know?' Then ask: 'Why does cutting the same pizza into MORE pieces make each piece smaller?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-bias child reasons '4 is more than 2, so Bea's quarter is bigger' and gives the wrong answer with a confident, articulable wrong reason - exactly the tell we want. A child who understands sharing picks Ali and explains that more pieces from the same whole means smaller pieces. Identical pizzas remove the 'it depends on the pizza' escape, so the denominator size is the only thing in play.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Local weather patterns

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Year 1, Seasonal changes / Working scientifically):** pupils "observe and describe weather associated with the seasons," and might work scientifically by "making tables and charts about the weather."

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-ESS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1].

- **Operational details:** The learning here is PROCEDURAL — children gather their own weather observations and look for patterns, rather than being told facts. Set up a simple, repeated daily routine: each day, observe and record the weather with picture symbols (sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, snowy) and simple measures a 5-year-old can take (is it warm or cold? did it rain?). Keep records on a class chart or pictograph over days and weeks, then read the chart together to describe patterns — 'we had more rainy days than sunny days this week', 'it is colder in the mornings'. The key skills are consistent observation, recording with agreed symbols, and describing (not explaining) what the collected data shows over time. This builds directly on knowing the four seasons and feeds later graph-based seasonal-weather work.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational-procedural, KS1). The child records daily weather with symbols over time and describes simple patterns from the class chart, without needing numerical measurement or causal explanation.
bestPractices: Make it a repeated daily routine so a pattern emerges from many observations over time, not a one-off.
Use agreed picture symbols (sun, cloud, rain, wind, snow) so young children can record consistently without writing.
Keep records visible on a class chart/pictograph and regularly READ it together to describe patterns.
Keep the goal descriptive — what the data shows — not explanatory (no causes of weather yet).
Link the weather record back to the current season so observation and seasonal knowledge reinforce each other.
keyRepresentations: A daily weather chart / calendar filled with picture symbols.
A weekly pictograph or bar of weather types (count of sunny vs rainy days).
Standard weather symbols (sun, cloud, rain, wind, snow).
A warm/cold marker or simple temperature cue.
A 'read the chart' prompt comparing column heights.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a single day's weather represents the whole season or that 'today = always'.
Confusing weather (what it's doing now) with season, or expecting weather to be identical every day.
Reading a pictograph by counting the wrong thing (e.g. the shortest column) or ignoring that each symbol stands for one day.
Believing weather is fully predictable, or conversely totally random with no patterns.
Recording what they wish the weather was rather than what they observe.

learn.summary: For 5–6 year-olds learning local weather patterns, the core skill is procedural: children gather their own daily weather observations with agreed picture symbols, record them over days and weeks on a visible chart or pictograph, then READ the accumulated record together to describe simple patterns (e.g. 'more rainy days than sunny days this week') and make a simple, tentative prediction grounded in that record. The goal is descriptive, not explanatory — no causes of weather yet. The main activity is an ongoing record-and-read routine; vocabulary priming and reading a pre-made pictograph are useful scaffolds with stated limits.

activities.title: Daily weather station: record over time, then read your own chart
feedback: If the chart has gaps or the categories change day to day, prompt: use the same simple symbols, recorded at the same time each day, so a pattern can appear.
When reading, ask simple pattern questions aloud ('which column is tallest?' 'more rainy or sunny days?') and let the child answer by comparing column heights.
If a child records what they wish the weather was instead of what they see, ask them to look outside again and record what is actually happening now.
If a child predicts tomorrow from a wish ('sunny because I want to play out'), ask what the weather has actually been doing and what is likely next based on the recorded pattern.
If a child expects the weather to be identical every day within a season, note that days still differ within a season — that is exactly why we record over time and look for patterns.
Remind that each symbol stands for one day, so the taller column shows the weather that happened on more days; if unsure, count the day-symbols within each column together.
For pre-readers, read prompts and symbol names aloud so the reading step does not depend on text.
For safety, point children to shadows on the ground and the general daylight to tell it is sunny, and remind them never to look straight at the sun.
activities.rationale: The standard is a repeated observe–record–read-the-pattern procedure that also feeds a simple prediction, so the activity should enact it: logging each day, watching a pictograph build, reading the accumulated pattern, and predicting tentatively from it. A physical class weather chart is the essential hands-on form; a screen weather-station may model the same routine and let children replay a whole week quickly, but it complements rather than replaces the real daily observation.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils observe and describe weather associated with the seasons and may make tables and charts about the weather.
Students [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1].
learnerActions: Each day, look outside and choose today's weather symbol(s) from an agreed set: sun, cloud, rain, wind, snow. To tell if it is sunny, look at shadows on the ground (sharp shadows mean sunshine) and the overall daylight — never look directly at the sun.
Add a simple warm/cold marker (is it warm or cold today?).
Place that day's entry onto a growing weekly chart or pictograph so a column builds up for each weather type.
At the end of the week, step back and READ the chart: which column is tallest? Say the pattern aloud — e.g. 'this week was more rainy than sunny.'

Use the pattern to make a simple prediction about tomorrow, and say what on the chart makes you think so (e.g. 'it's been rainy most days, so maybe rainy again') — keeping it a guess, not a certainty.
Keep the routine going into a new week and compare: did the pattern change?
Link the record to the current season so weather observation and seasonal knowledge reinforce each other.
activities.intendedInsight: A pattern emerges from many observations collected over time; children can describe what their own data shows, and base a simple prediction on it, rather than being told a fact.

activities.title: Weather-symbol vocabulary primer
feedback: If a symbol is mismatched, replay the name and point to the matching picture.
Encourage saying the weather word aloud while pointing to the symbol.
activities.rationale: Agreed picture symbols let young children record without writing. A vocabulary primer builds this shared code first; it is a preparatory scaffold that teaches the names, but on its own it does not elicit the record-over-time-and-find-a-pattern skill that is the heart of the standard.
learnerActions: Explore an illustrated sky scene and tap or point to each weather type.
Hear and say its name (sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, snowy) and see its matching symbol.
Match each weather symbol to its spoken name before starting the weather diary.
activities.intendedInsight: Children learn the shared vocabulary and symbols for weather types so they can record consistently later.

activities.title: Read a finished weather pictograph
feedback: If the child picks the shortest column, remind them 'most days' means the taller column.
If they ignore that each symbol is one day, count the symbols in a column together.
If the child reads the wrong column, point at and compare the two columns side by side.
activities.rationale: Reading a pre-made pictograph is a checkable sub-skill and a useful support, but a fixed set of questions on a finished chart does not include the ongoing daily recording that defines the skill. Use it to practise chart-reading, not as a substitute for collecting data over time.
learnerActions: Look at a simple pre-made weather pictograph of a week.
Answer aloud: which column is tallest? Were there more rainy or sunny days?
Match weather symbols to their names.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a completed pictograph means checking what each symbol stands for (in this chart, one symbol = one day), then comparing column heights, which works when the symbols are the same size and evenly spaced, or counting the symbols in each column.

constraints: Keep the goal descriptive — what the data shows — not explanatory; causes of weather are not introduced at this age.
The real daily classroom weather chart with genuine outdoor observation is essential; a screen weather-station may model the routine but does not replace observing the actual weather each day.
A vocabulary poster teaches weather-word names only; it does not enact recording over time or finding a pattern.
Reading a pre-made pictograph practises chart-reading but omits the ongoing daily recording that defines the procedural skill — use it as a scaffold, not the main activity.
Record what is actually observed, not what the child wishes the weather to be, and base predictions on the record rather than a wish, keeping predictions tentative.
For safety, children should judge sunshine from shadows on the ground and general daylight and must never look directly at the sun.
Numerical measurement and causal explanation are not required at this checkpoint (concrete/observational-procedural, KS1).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted '3D adds nothing' and that 'dialogue cannot substitute' — these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws. They have been reframed: spatial/3D framing is simply not needed for a charting task, and open dialogue demands language beyond age 5 as a practical limit, not an absolute impossibility.
The NGSS K-ESS2-1 source is marked verified:false in the row; the UK DfE source is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is not upgraded here.

The row's description mentions 'recording temperature, rainfall' numerically, while the checkpoint states no numerical measurement is needed at this age; activities use warm/cold and simple categories consistent with the checkpoint, treating precise measurement as beyond this tier.
Simple prediction is retained because it is required by the objective and assessment, but is framed as a tentative guess from the recent record rather than a reliable forecast.

probeDeeper: Looking at your chart, what has the weather been like most days this week?
What do you think tomorrow will be like, and what on your chart makes you think so?
Why do we write it down each day instead of just remembering?
assess.correctAnswer: Records each day's conditions consistently with clear symbols or words, keeps it going over time, spots a simple pattern (e.g. 'it's been rainy all week,' 'colder in the mornings') and makes a sensible prediction grounded in the recent record.

errorPatterns.pattern: Records inconsistently or only once, so no pattern can appear
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the same simple categories, recorded at the same time each day.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: gaps in the chart; categories change day to day

errorPatterns.pattern: Predicts from a wish, not the record ('sunny because I want to play out')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask: 'what has the weather been doing, and what is likely next?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: prediction ignores the recorded pattern

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The weather is the same every day in a season' — doesn't expect day-to-day variation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Within a season days still differ — that's why we record and look for patterns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: assumes the season fixes each day exactly, so recording seems pointless

responseLevels.gap: Can't record consistently; has no usable chart; prediction unrelated to observations.
responseLevels.full: Observes and records systematically over time, identifies a simple pattern from the record, and makes a sensible prediction grounded in it — and could keep the routine going.
responseLevels.partial: Records daily but inconsistently, or reads the chart but predicts without using the pattern.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Over a week or two, ask the child to observe the weather each day and record it on a simple chart (sunny/cloudy/rainy, warm/cold, windy). Then ask them to point out any pattern and predict tomorrow. Watch how they observe, record consistently, and read their own chart — don't ask them to define 'weather.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching reveals whether the child observes and records systematically day to day and reads their own data, versus recording once, inconsistently, or predicting from a wish rather than the chart.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11; compare historical polar exploration with modern polar science — the Heroic Age (1897–1922) relied on ships, dogs and raw human endurance with many deaths, while today's polar scientists use GPS, satellites, icebreakers, heated research stations and aircraft; modern work centres on measuring climate change, and today's polar science includes diverse international teams and women scientists such as glaciologist Liz Thomas and marine biologist Sylvia Earle.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 History (changes within/beyond living memory; significant people) and Science working-scientifically (how methods and technology change what we can know).
• Standards—US: NGSS science-and-engineering practices and Nature-of-Science (advances in technology extend investigation); ELA compare-accounts.
• Operational details: a THEN-vs-NOW comparison across purpose, technology, danger, and who takes part. Then = reach places first, survive; tools = sextant, dogs, wooden ships, furs; huge risk. Now = understand the system (especially climate); tools = GPS/satellites, icebreakers, ice-core drills, heated stations, aircraft; risk much reduced; teams international and diverse, including prominent women scientists. The throughline: better tools change the QUESTIONS science can ask — from 'can we get there?' to 'what is happening to the ice, and why?'.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (9) name one old and one new piece of polar technology; Tier B (10) explain how a modern tool changed what explorers/scientists can do; Tier C (11) explain how the PURPOSE of polar expeditions shifted from reaching/surviving to understanding climate, and note that teams are now diverse and international.
bestPractices: Compare across clear dimensions (purpose, tools, danger, people) rather than just old-vs-new gadgets
Show how new tools change the QUESTIONS — from getting there to measuring and understanding the system
Feature diverse, contemporary scientists (e.g. Liz Thomas, Sylvia Earle) to update the image of who does polar science
Use paired then/now images so the contrast is immediate and concrete
Link to the Heroic-Age explorers topic so pupils see continuity and change, not two disconnected eras
keyRepresentations: Then/now toggle: sextant/dogs/wooden ship ↔ GPS/icebreaker/heated station
Purpose-shift arrow: 'reach the Pole & survive' → 'measure & understand the climate'
Modern-scientist profile cards (glaciologist, marine biologist) with what they study and how
Timeline from the Heroic Age (1897–1922) to present-day research stations
commonMisconceptions: Polar exploration ended with the Heroic Age — it continues as high-tech international science
Modern polar work is just easier sightseeing — it is demanding scientific research, especially on climate
Explorers were all men — today's diverse teams include leading women scientists
New technology only makes old goals safer — it also changes what questions science can ask
The point was always science — the Heroic Age was largely about reaching places first and surviving

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, compare Heroic-Age polar exploration (c.1897–1922: wooden ships, dog sleds, man-hauling, sextants, furs, and high fatality) with modern polar science (GPS, satellites, icebreakers, ice-core drills, heated research stations, aircraft, and diverse international teams). The core insight is that better tools change not just how safely people work but the QUESTIONS science can ask — shifting from 'can we reach the Pole and survive?' to 'what is happening to the ice and climate, and why?'. Learners compare across clear dimensions (purpose, technology, danger, who takes part), name specific technologies and how each enables survival or new measurement, identify a modern scientist to update the image of who does polar science, and transfer the idea to a new case.

activities.title: Then vs Now: a four-dimension comparison
feedback: If a learner writes 'same thing, just with better gear', prompt: the main GOAL changed — Heroic-Age expeditions did some science, but their headline aim was often to be first and survive, while today's work is centred on research questions. Point to the purpose row and ask what each team was mainly trying to find out.
If a learner says modern polar work is 'easy sightseeing', note it is demanding scientific research, especially measuring climate change in harsh conditions.
If a learner lists tools but cannot link them to survival or measurement, ask: 'What exactly does a heated station / GPS / ice-core drill let a scientist do that furs and a sextant could not?'
Affirm answers that name BOTH a tool change and a question change, e.g. 'satellites let scientists measure ice across the whole continent, so they can ask how fast it is melting.'
activities.rationale: Comparing across stated dimensions (purpose, tools, danger, people) rather than just old-vs-new gadgets makes continuity-and-change visible and matches KS2 History and working-scientifically aims about how methods change what we can know.
sourceClaims: KS2 History examines change over time and significant people; working-scientifically considers how technology changes investigation
Advances in technology and instrumentation extend the questions science can investigate (Nature of Science)

The Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration (c.1897–1922) relied on ships, dogs and human endurance; modern polar science uses GPS, satellites, icebreakers, ice-core drilling and heated stations, with diverse international teams including women scientists such as glaciologist Liz Thomas and marine biologist Sylvia Earle
learnerActions: Study paired images or descriptions of a 1911 polar expedition and a present-day research station.
Fill in a four-row comparison table across: PURPOSE, TECHNOLOGY, DANGER, and WHO TAKES PART.
For PURPOSE, write the 1911 goal (e.g. 'reach the Pole first and survive — national glory') beside the modern goal (e.g. 'measure the ice and understand the climate').
For TECHNOLOGY, list then-tools (sextant, dog teams, wooden ship, furs) beside now-tools (GPS/satellites, icebreaker, ice-core drill, heated station, aircraft).
For DANGER, note the high fatality of the Heroic Age versus greatly reduced risk today, and say which modern tool most reduces a given risk.
For WHO TAKES PART, contrast small, mostly nationally organised all-male parties with today's diverse international teams including women scientists.
Write one sentence answering: 'What changed most — the tools or the question?'
activities.intendedInsight: Polar exploration did not end with the Heroic Age; it continued and changed. Better tools both reduce danger AND change the questions science can ask — from reaching a place to understanding a system.

activities.title: The purpose-shift arrow and the new question
feedback: If a learner says 'new technology only makes old goals safer', point out that ice cores and satellites let scientists investigate new questions about climate that could not be answered before.
If a learner cannot form a new question, offer the glaciologist example: a core of ice holds a record of past climate going back many thousands of years — ask what that lets us find out.
Praise responses that connect a specific tool to a specific new question.

For the transfer task, reward answers that link a specific lost tool to a specific lost capability (e.g. 'without GPS, navigation and locating safe routes would get much harder and more dangerous again'), rather than a vague 'everything would be worse'.
activities.rationale: Showing how new tools change the QUESTIONS, not just the equipment, directly targets the Nature-of-Science idea that instrumentation extends what science can investigate; the transfer task checks that learners understand the dependence of modern questions on modern tools.
sourceClaims: Advances in technology and instrumentation extend the questions science can investigate (Nature of Science)

The Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration (c.1897–1922) relied on ships, dogs and human endurance; modern polar science uses GPS, satellites, icebreakers, ice-core drilling and heated stations, with diverse international teams including women scientists such as glaciologist Liz Thomas and marine biologist Sylvia Earle
learnerActions: Draw an arrow from 'reach the Pole & survive' to 'measure & understand the climate'.
Pick one modern tool (e.g. an ice-core drill or satellite) and write the NEW question it lets scientists ask that a Heroic-Age explorer could not.
Explain in two or three sentences how the purpose of polar expeditions shifted, and why the technology made that shift possible.
Answer the lift-the-flap prompt: 'What changed most — the tools or the question?' and justify your choice.

Transfer task: imagine modern scientists suddenly lost GPS and satellites. Explain how much of today's polar work would become more like the Heroic Age again, which jobs would be hardest or most dangerous, and which would still be possible.
activities.intendedInsight: Technology does more than make old goals safer; it opens new goals. An ice-core drill makes it possible to read many thousands of years of past climate — a question nobody could investigate with a sextant and dog sled. Because today's science depends on these tools, removing them would bring back many Heroic-Age difficulties.

activities.title: Interview a modern polar scientist
feedback: If a learner assumes 'explorers were all men' or all from one country, introduce the glaciologist and marine-biologist profiles and note teams today are international and diverse.
If a learner cannot name a modern scientist, revisit a profile card before moving on.
Reward answers that contrast the scientist's research mission with an explorer's race-to-be-first goal.
activities.rationale: Featuring contemporary, diverse scientists updates the image of who does polar science and makes the purpose-shift concrete through a real role.
sourceClaims: The Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration (c.1897–1922) relied on ships, dogs and human endurance; modern polar science uses GPS, satellites, icebreakers, ice-core drilling and heated stations, with diverse international teams including women scientists such as glaciologist Liz Thomas and marine biologist Sylvia Earle
learnerActions: Read or role-play a short profile/interview with a modern scientist — e.g. a glaciologist who reads climate records from ice cores, or a marine biologist studying the Southern Ocean.
Write or speak three questions you would ask about what that scientist studies and how.
Compare that scientist's stated mission with a Heroic-Age explorer's goal, writing one sentence on how they differ.
Name at least one modern polar scientist and say what field that scientist works in.
activities.intendedInsight: Today's polar teams are international and diverse and include leading women scientists; the work is science-driven, which is a sharp contrast to the small national, all-male parties of the Heroic Age.

activities.title: Kit out the expedition: then and now
feedback: If a learner explains Heroic-Age deaths as 'weakness' or Amundsen's success as 'luck', redirect to the planning and technology differences (dogs and preparation vs man-hauling).
If a learner sorts correctly but gives no 'what it lets you do' reason, prompt for the function of each tool.
The sorting step checks recognition of era and tool function but does not by itself elicit explanation; have learners then give a spoken or written reason so they go beyond matching to reasoning.
activities.rationale: A structured sort plus justification links specific technology to survival and method, countering the luck/weakness misconception while still demanding explanation.
sourceClaims: The Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration (c.1897–1922) relied on ships, dogs and human endurance; modern polar science uses GPS, satellites, icebreakers, ice-core drilling and heated stations, with diverse international teams including women scientists such as glaciologist Liz Thomas and marine biologist Sylvia Earle
learnerActions: Given a mixed set of items (sextant, GPS unit, dog harness, ice-core drill, fur parka, satellite phone, wooden ship, icebreaker), sort each into THEN or NOW.
For each NOW item, state one thing it lets a scientist do or survive that the matching THEN item could not.
Explain why Amundsen's careful planning and use of dogs is a method/planning difference, not just luck, compared with Scott's man-hauling — using the equipment as evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Differences between eras come from technology, methods and planning, not from early explorers being weak or modern ones being merely lucky.

constraints: Build the comparison with the then/now contrast FIRST (paired images and structured dimensions); use matching or sorting tasks afterwards to check it, since matching alone recognises eras rather than eliciting explanation of the purpose-shift.

A paired/tappable then-now image and optional interactions (a slider between 1911 and today, tapping ship/navigation/shelter/goal to reveal detail, drill-down scientist profile cards, a lift-the-flap 'tools or question?' prompt) are helpful ways to make the contrast immediate and concrete; they are suggested affordances, not required mechanisms, and a static paired image can still support the comparison.
Require learners to produce explanations (written or spoken) linking each named technology to survival or to a new question — not merely to recognise or name tools.

Keep the climate-science framing accurate: modern polar work is demanding research, not sightseeing. Avoid implying the Heroic Age was mainly about science: many expeditions (e.g. Scott's Terra Nova, Mawson's) did real scientific work, but headline goals such as reaching places first, national prestige and survival dominated.
Distinguish causal claims carefully: differences between eras stem from technology, methods and planning, so do not let learners settle on 'luck' or 'weakness' as explanations.

Do not assert a specific ice-core time-span (e.g. '800,000 years') as fact until verified; use qualified phrasing such as 'many thousands of years', treating this as a conservative placeholder rather than the true limit.

The interview activity foregrounds women scientists as the source emphasises, but the generic naming step accepts any correctly named modern polar scientist regardless of gender; keep pronoun usage consistent and non-presupposing in the generic steps.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all three sources are marked verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that ice cores record '800,000 years' of climate appears in the legacy recommendation but is not stated in the sources; activities deliberately use the softer, source-consistent phrasing 'many thousands of years'. This is a conservative under-claim, not the verified upper limit — confirm the fuller figure against a current source before presenting any larger number as fact.

Specific attributions (glaciologist Liz Thomas; marine biologist Sylvia Earle) come from the source claim but were not independently re-verified in this rewrite; confirm names, fields and any biographical details before publishing.

The Amundsen-vs-Scott planning/technology contrast is a reasonable historical framing, but keep it evidence-based and avoid overstating; present it as 'methods and planning differed' rather than a definitive single cause of the outcomes.

Two originally distinct non-preferred alternatives (a match-the-tool quiz and a kit-out-the-expedition 2d game) were consolidated into a single sorting-plus-justification activity; they are functionally equivalent here, but the distinction is recorded so it is not silently lost.
Legacy confidence was recorded as 'high'; this rewrite does not independently confirm that rating.

probeDeeper: Name two pieces of modern technology and say exactly how each keeps a polar scientist alive that an early explorer didn't have.
If you could talk to a scientist at a research station today, what would they say they're trying to find out — and would Scott have understood that goal?
Was Amundsen just lucky to survive when Scott didn't? What's your evidence?
What if modern scientists suddenly lost GPS and satellites — how much would polar work go back to being like the Heroic Age?
assess.correctAnswer: The PURPOSE changed: the Heroic Age (roughly 1897–1922) was about being first and national glory — reaching the pole itself — whereas modern polar work is about SCIENCE (studying climate, ice, biology). Technology changed survival too: GPS and satellites for navigation and communication, icebreaker ships and aircraft for supply, and heated research stations for shelter mean scientists no longer rely on dogs, man-hauling and sheer endurance, so far fewer people die. Today's teams are also diverse and international (e.g. glaciologist Liz Thomas, marine biologist Sylvia Earle) rather than small national parties of men.

errorPatterns.pattern: polar exploration is still about being first and planting flags — 'they still race to the pole today'
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast conquest-for-glory with research stations studying climate; the goal changed
errorPatterns.distractor: People still go to Antarctica mainly to be the first to reach places
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes modern work as more races or firsts rather than science

errorPatterns.pattern: the past explorers were just weak or foolish, or Amundsen only won by luck — misses the planning/technology/method differences
errorPatterns.nextMove: compare Amundsen's dogs and careful planning with Scott's man-hauling, and old vs modern technology
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains the deaths by weakness or the success by luck

errorPatterns.pattern: polar explorers and scientists are all men, or all from one country — misses diverse international teams
errorPatterns.nextMove: introduce Liz Thomas and Sylvia Earle; modern teams are international and diverse
errorPatterns.revealedBy: can't name a modern scientist or assumes all-male single-nation teams

responseLevels.gap: Thinks modern polar trips are still about being first, or that early explorers just died from weakness; can't name modern tech or a scientist.
responseLevels.full: Explains the shift from conquest/glory to international science, names at least two technologies and how each enables survival, names a modern (diverse) scientist, and transfers to a new case (e.g. losing GPS).
responseLevels.partial: Lists old methods (dogs, sledges) and some modern tech, but treats it as 'same thing, better kit' — doesn't connect the purpose shift (glory->science) or link specific tech to survival.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A hundred years ago, explorers like Amundsen and Scott raced to reach the South Pole with dogs and man-hauled sledges, and some died trying. Today scientists live and work in Antarctica too. What's the biggest difference in WHY people go there now compared to then, and what lets them survive when the early explorers couldn't? Tell me, and then tell me WHY those things make the difference.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'it's the same, just with better gear' misses that the PURPOSE shifted from conquest to science, and may not connect specific technologies to survival; the concept child names both the why-shift and at least two enabling technologies and can name a modern scientist. The reason-tier forces the causal links tech->survival and purpose->conquest-vs-knowledge.
