Checked arithmetic: 45 + 30 = 75, 82 − 40 = 42, 45 + 3 = 48 are all correct as stated across the source fields.

The source listed 48 as the correct answer for 45 + 3 (not for 45 + 30); this is consistent, and 48 is used only as the correct answer to the add-ones contrast item and as a named misconception for 45 + 30, never as a valid alternative answer to 45 + 30.

Two CCSS/NCETM source claims are marked verified:false in the original; comparative, necessity or efficacy claims should not be inferred from them. The CCSS claim was removed from the fluency activity's sourceClaims because it supports topic coverage, not the efficacy of speeded practice.

The DfE claim retained in the first activity provides curriculum/method-level support (concrete, pictorial, mental methods are expected for this skill); it is not evidence that the manipulative is more effective than any other medium.

The original rated 3D interactive as 'poor' because it 'adds nothing' — this comparative/necessity framing was not retained as a universal law; adding tens is a one-dimensional place-value move and alternative media may still illustrate it.
Additional source representations (empty number line, Gattegno chart, arrow cards) are retained as optional representations rather than required mechanisms.

probeDeeper: Which digit changed in 45 + 30, and why only that one?
How is 45 + 30 different from 45 + 3?
Predict the answer to 82 − 40 before you work it out — what will the ones digit be?
Show me 45 + 30 on the hundred square — which way do you move?
assess.correctAnswer: 75 (tens change, ones stay 5); 42 (tens change, ones stay 2); 48 (ones change — this one adds ONES, not tens). Watch that the child keeps the ones digit fixed when adding/subtracting tens and correctly switches to changing the ones on the last item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the added tens as ones — 45 + 30 handled as 45 + 3, giving 48.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Base-ten blocks: 30 is three ten-sticks, not three ones; add them to the tens while the ones pile is untouched.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 48 for 45 + 30; adds to the ones place.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the ones digit as well as the tens when adding/subtracting tens.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Highlight the invariant ones digit; use the hundred square vertical move where the ones column stays constant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ones digit differs from the start number after adding tens (e.g. 45 + 30 → 70 or 78).

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the number of tens jumps (adds 20 or 40 instead of 30).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the ten-jumps aloud with the blocks or hundred square; track with fingers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tens digit off by one ten (65 or 85 for 45 + 30).

responseLevels.gap: Adds tens to the ones place or changes both digits arbitrarily; cannot keep the ones fixed.
responseLevels.full: Adds/subtracts multiples of ten in one step, keeps the ones digit fixed with justification, and correctly switches procedure when ones are added instead.
responseLevels.partial: Gets add/subtract-tens right by repeated +10 steps but is unsure why the ones stay fixed, or confuses it with adding ones.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out mentally and tell me which digit changed each time: 45 + 30; 82 − 40; 45 + 3.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two items add/subtract tens (ones must stay fixed) and the third adds ones (ones must change) — a deliberate contrast. A child who confuses the two procedures, or who alters the ones when adding tens, is exposed: 45 + 30 → 48 or an altered ones digit is the tell. Asking 'which digit changed?' makes the place-value reasoning visible.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** How Diffusion Works

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Cells & organisation):** "the role of diffusion in the movement of materials in and between cells."

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No standalone MS diffusion performance expectation; diffusion is the mechanism underlying MS-LS1-3 (body subsystems) and gas-exchange/transport ideas — taught as supporting DCI content in most US schemes rather than as its own PE. (US/UK divergence: the UK names diffusion explicitly at KS3; NGSS folds it into systems PEs.)

- **Operational details:** Children define diffusion using particle theory as the NET movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, until evenly spread. They apply it to real cellular contexts — oxygen diffusing from alveoli into blood and carbon dioxide the other way; glucose diffusing from blood into respiring cells — and identify the factors that change the RATE: steeper concentration gradient, larger surface area, and shorter diffusion distance (thinner membrane). The key move is from 'smell spreads across a room' to a quantitative, directional model of particles crossing a selectively permeable membrane.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B→C. Builds on the cell membrane as a boundary; underpins gas exchange, respiration substrate supply and (later) osmosis/active transport. A child is secure when they can predict the DIRECTION of net movement from a stated concentration difference and name a factor that would speed it up and why.
bestPractices: Start from a familiar macroscopic example (a smell or food colouring spreading) then zoom to the particle model, so the invisible mechanism is grounded in something observed.

Stress that particles move randomly in BOTH directions and that 'net' movement is a statistical result of there being more particles on one side — this pre-empts the 'particles are pushed' and 'diffusion stops' misconceptions.
Teach the three rate factors by controlled variation (change one, hold the rest) so children build a genuine cause–effect model rather than a memorised list.
Immediately apply diffusion to real cell contexts (alveoli, respiring cells) so it is seen as the mechanism the body relies on, not an isolated idea.
Introduce dynamic equilibrium explicitly: at equal concentrations particles keep moving but there is no net change.
keyRepresentations: Particle-model before/after diagram showing spreading from high to low concentration
Two-chamber-with-membrane schematic and concentration bars for each side
Alveolus–capillary diagram with arrows for O₂ in and CO₂ out
Rate-factor comparison panels (steeper gradient / larger surface area / shorter distance = faster)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking diffusion stops once concentrations are equal because particles stop moving — in fact motion continues; only NET movement is zero (dynamic equilibrium).
Believing particles are actively 'pushed' or 'want' to spread out, rather than moving randomly with a statistical net drift down the gradient.
Confusing diffusion (of any particle down its own gradient) with osmosis (net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane).
Thinking diffusion needs energy from the cell (it is passive) — confusing it with active transport.
Assuming diffusion only happens in gases, not in liquids/solutions.

learn.summary: Teach diffusion (ages 12–13) as the NET movement of particles from higher to lower concentration, arising from random motion in both directions, continuing to a dynamic equilibrium with no energy input. Ground the invisible mechanism in an observed macroscopic spreading (including a still cold vs still hot beaker comparison), build a directional particle model, derive the three rate factors (steeper gradient, larger surface area, shorter diffusion distance) by controlled variation, and apply it to real cell contexts (O₂/CO₂ at alveoli, glucose into respiring cells). A live particle simulation is the preferred vehicle because net flow emerging from random motion is a dynamic process; static diagrams, a 3D alveolar scene, and a checking quiz are retained as distinct supports with stated limits.

activities.title: Observed spreading then the particle picture
feedback: If a learner says the dye must be pushed or stirred to spread, show the still-water beaker spreading on its own and establish that particles are always moving randomly without any push.
If a learner says the particles 'want' to fill the empty space, replace the intention with random motion: the outward net drift is just a statistical result of starting crowded, not a goal.

If a learner is unsure about the hot vs cold result, connect faster spreading in hot water to faster random particle motion (more energetic jiggling), and mention that currents in warm water can also add to the spreading in a real beaker; note this temperature effect on diffusion is about particle speed and is distinct from the three curriculum rate factors.
Reinforce: once the colour looks even, the particles have NOT stopped — random motion continues, but there is no longer any net direction.
activities.rationale: Starting from a familiar observed example before zooming to the particle model grounds the invisible mechanism in something seen, and pre-empting the 'needs a push' and teleology misconceptions early sets up a correct random-motion basis.
learnerActions: Drop a spot of food colouring (or a tea bag) into a beaker of still COLD water and, separately, into a beaker of still HOT water; watch both for several minutes without stirring and compare how far the colour spreads. Diffusion alone takes a long time to spread colour evenly through a whole beaker (possibly hours or longer), so check back later instead of waiting for it to finish in one lesson.
State predictions first: will the dye spread at all without stirring, in which beaker will it spread faster, and why?
Draw a before/after particle picture: particles crowded on one side at the start, evenly spread at the end.
Describe in words why the colour spreads on its own, using the idea of particles moving by themselves.
activities.intendedInsight: Diffusion happens on its own with no stirring or energy input because particles are already in constant random motion; the net spreading is driven by there being more particles in one region to begin with. Particles move faster when warmer, so diffusion is faster in hot water; this fits the idea that the motion belongs to the particles themselves and is not an external push. In a real beaker, faster spreading in hot water can also be partly due to convection currents, so the demo supports the particle model but does not isolate diffusion on its own.

activities.title: Two-chamber particle simulation: net flow from random motion
feedback: If a learner expects all particles to march to the empty side, slow the view to show particles also crossing back; the net flow is the imbalance between two random streams.
If a learner says movement stops when the bars are equal, point to the still-jiggling particles: only net movement is zero.
If a learner invokes a force pushing particles down the gradient, remove the idea of a force: random motion plus starting imbalance is sufficient.
activities.rationale: A live particle simulation lets the learner set up a gradient and watch emergent net movement, making the statistical, directional nature of diffusion and the dynamic-equilibrium idea observable and manipulable in a way a static picture cannot show. Optional live concentration bars and slow-motion crossing make the random-two-way-but-net-one-way mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is that diffusion stops at equilibrium because particles stop moving; in fact particle motion continues but net movement becomes zero (dynamic equilibrium).
learnerActions: Load many particles onto one side of a two-chamber box divided by a membrane, leaving the other side empty, then start the motion.
Watch each particle jitter randomly while a concentration bar for each chamber ticks toward equal.
Slow the simulation and track individual particles crossing the membrane in BOTH directions.
State what produces the one-way NET flow even though individual motion is two-directional.
Continue until the bars are equal, and describe what the particles are doing at that point.
activities.intendedInsight: Individual particles cross the membrane randomly in both directions; the NET flow runs one way only because there are simply more particles on the crowded side. At equilibrium the two-way traffic balances, so net movement is zero while motion continues (dynamic equilibrium) — nothing is pushed and nothing stops.

activities.title: Deriving the three rate factors by controlled variation
feedback: If a learner changes several settings at once, reset and vary only one so the cause of the rate change is unambiguous.
If a learner recalls the factors but cannot say why, link each back to the particle picture (more crowding = bigger imbalance; more area/shorter path = more crossings per unit time).
Check reasoning on a fresh comparison, e.g. a very wide glass means the dye reaches the far side more slowly — that is the diffusion-distance factor.
activities.rationale: Controlled variation (change one, hold the rest) builds a cause–effect model rather than a memorised list, and a live rate readout lets the learner connect each manipulation to its effect.
sourceClaims: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration; rate increases with a steeper concentration gradient, larger surface area and shorter diffusion distance.
learnerActions: From a baseline simulation run, steepen the concentration gradient (add more particles to one side) and read whether the rate meter rises, holding the other settings fixed.
Separately, enlarge the membrane surface area only, and note the effect on rate.
Separately, thin the diffusion distance (thinner membrane) only, and note the effect on rate.
Record each result and state the three factors that speed diffusion up, each with a reason.
Order or compare two scenarios and predict which diffuses faster.
activities.intendedInsight: Diffusion rate increases with a steeper concentration gradient, a larger surface area, and a shorter diffusion distance; changing one factor at a time shows each as a genuine cause, not a memorised list.

activities.title: Apply the model to gas exchange and glucose supply
feedback: If a learner reverses a direction at the alveoli, return to the stated concentrations and re-derive net movement high → low; this links to the membrane-as-boundary prerequisite.
If a learner treats gas exchange as a separate rule, show it is the same gradient-driven diffusion seen in the simulation.
Praise reasoning that ties a named surface feature back to one of the three rate factors.
activities.rationale: Immediately applying diffusion to real cell contexts frames it as the mechanism the body relies on rather than an isolated idea, and anchoring direction high → low addresses the direction-reversal misconception.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Biology requires teaching 'the role of diffusion in the movement of materials in and between cells'.
Diffusion is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration; rate increases with a steeper concentration gradient, larger surface area and shorter diffusion distance.
learnerActions: Using a 'cell mode' overlay or an alveolus–capillary diagram, mark which way oxygen diffuses (air/alveolus → blood) and which way carbon dioxide diffuses (blood → air).
Justify each direction from the stated concentration difference (high → low).
Explain how a respiring cell obtains glucose from the blood by diffusion.
Name one feature of the gas-exchange surface that speeds diffusion (large surface area, thin membrane, maintained gradient) and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: The same particle model explains how the body moves materials: net movement is always from high to low concentration, so O₂ enters blood, CO₂ leaves, and glucose moves from blood into respiring cells, with real surfaces built to maximise rate.

activities.title: Predict-and-check quiz on direction and rate
feedback: For a wrong direction, re-anchor net movement high → low and re-check the alveolar concentrations.
For a rate error, return to the single-variable simulation runs that established that factor.
Treat a correct choice with a wrong or missing reason as not yet secure; the reason is what shows understanding.
activities.rationale: Predicting direction, ordering rate factors, and labelling alveolar gas exchange are clean checkable items, best used after the model is built rather than as the primary teaching. This sort/quiz can check classification and prediction with reasons but does not itself elicit independent construction of the mechanism.
sourceClaims: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration; rate increases with a steeper concentration gradient, larger surface area and shorter diffusion distance.
learnerActions: Answer: which way does O₂ diffuse at the alveolus, and which way does CO₂ go?
Use a slider to predict the relative rate of diffusion as the concentration gradient steepens.
Sort factors into 'speeds up' / 'slows down' categories (e.g. steeper gradient, larger surface area, shorter distance vs the opposites).
For each answer, give the reason, not just the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can reliably predict the direction of net movement and relate rate to the three factors, with reasons, after the simulation has built the underlying model.

constraints: Define diffusion as the NET movement of particles from higher to lower concentration down a gradient until evenly spread; always stress motion is random and two-directional, so net drift is a statistical result, not a push or a goal.

State explicitly that diffusion is passive (no cell energy/stirring required); distinguish it from active transport, and distinguish diffusion of any particle from osmosis (net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane).
Make clear diffusion occurs in liquids/solutions as well as gases, countering the 'gases only' assumption.
Introduce dynamic equilibrium explicitly: at equal concentrations particles keep moving but net change is zero — do not say particles stop.

Temperature increases particle speed and so the observed spreading rate; use it as evidence of intrinsic random motion, but keep it distinct from the three named curriculum rate factors (gradient, surface area, distance).

The static before/after diagram with tappable labels can define terms and show direction but cannot show emergent net movement or let learners vary rate factors; use it only as a support, not the main teach.
The quiz/sort checks prediction, classification and reasoning, not independent construction of the model; use it after the mechanism is built.

A 3D alveolus–capillary scene adds spatial realism for gas exchange context only; the diffusion mechanism and rate reasoning are handled fully in the 2D particle model. Treat idealised on-screen particles/membranes as a model, not a literal depiction of molecules.

An in-role 'interview the particle' dialogue was judged a poor fit here: diffusion is a mechanism to manipulate and observe. This is a scoped suitability judgement, not a universal claim that dialogue cannot teach.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three sources (BBC Bitesize; BEST/STEM Learning) are marked verified:false in the row; the DfE curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is not upgraded here.

The original 'fit' language included strong comparative claims ('nothing static can convey', '3D adds nothing', dialogue 'adds little'). These have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances/limits; comparative efficacy is not established by the source claims provided.

Self-audit of science content: diffusion directions (O₂ air→blood, CO₂ blood→air, glucose blood→cell), rate factors, passive nature, and dynamic-equilibrium framing are internally consistent and match the particle model; no arithmetic or force/motion errors were present to correct. The reteach link to the membrane-boundary prerequisite (noted in the source) is carried as provided but not asserted as verified efficacy.

assess.poeTask: Drop a drop of food colouring (or a tea bag) into a beaker of still cold water and, separately, into a beaker of hot water, stirring neither. Before observing, ask the child to predict whether the dye will spread at all without stirring, in which beaker it spreads faster, and WHY. The reason is diagnostic: predicting it won't spread without stirring holds the diffusion-needs-a-push misconception; predicting it spreads by itself, faster when hot because the particles move faster, shows the random-motion idea.
probeDeeper: At the alveoli, which way does oxygen diffuse and which way does carbon dioxide go? Why those directions?
Would the dye spread faster in hot or cold water? Why?
If the glass were enormous, would the dye reach the far side faster or slower? Which factor is that?
Do the particles actually stop when the colour looks even, or is something still happening?
assess.correctAnswer: The dye particles move randomly in all directions; because they start crowded together (high concentration) there is a net movement outward to where there are fewer of them (low concentration) until they are evenly spread. It doesn't really stop — the random movement continues, but once evenly spread there is no NET movement in any direction (equilibrium). No stirring or energy input is needed.

errorPatterns.pattern: particles need a push, energy or stirring to spread (diffusion seen as active)
errorPatterns.nextMove: establish that particles are always moving randomly by themselves; diffusion is passive, needing no energy or stirring
errorPatterns.revealedBy: the reason says something must push or pump the dye

errorPatterns.pattern: particles 'want' to spread out or deliberately move to empty space (teleology)
errorPatterns.nextMove: replace intention with random motion; the net direction is a statistical result of crowding, not a goal
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes intention to the particles

errorPatterns.pattern: the particles stop moving completely once equilibrium is reached
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify the particles keep moving randomly; only the NET movement is zero (dynamic equilibrium)
errorPatterns.distractor: The particles stop moving once the colour is even
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the particles stop once the colour is even

errorPatterns.pattern: diffusion can run from low to high concentration / direction confusion
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor net movement high → low; check oxygen (air → blood) and carbon dioxide (blood → air) at the alveoli
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the probe reverses the direction of net movement at the alveoli

responseLevels.gap: Says the dye needs stirring or pushing, or that particles want to spread; cannot define diffusion by particle motion.
responseLevels.full: Explains diffusion as random particle motion producing net movement down a concentration gradient to a dynamic equilibrium, needing no energy, and applies it to O2/CO2 at the alveoli and glucose into cells, relating rate to gradient, surface area and distance.
responseLevels.partial: Defines diffusion as movement from high to low concentration and names a factor, but as separate facts — cannot explain the random-motion basis, net-versus-total movement at equilibrium, or apply the direction correctly at the alveoli.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You drop a spot of coloured dye into a glass of still water and don't stir it. Over time the colour spreads until the whole glass is evenly coloured. Why does the dye spread out on its own — and why does it stop spreading once the colour is even?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks particles 'want' to fill space, or that something must push them, or that movement stops at equilibrium, answers differently from one who invokes random motion plus net movement down a gradient to a dynamic equilibrium. The reason tier is essential.

pedagogy.summary: Writing algebraic equations means translating a situation — a 'think of a number' process or a comparison — into symbols, with letters standing for the NUMBER of things (not the things themselves) and an equals sign expressing genuine equality. The two documented traps are the reversal error (mapping words left-to-right onto symbols, so '4 times as many cats as dogs' becomes 4c=d instead of c=4d) and treating letters as object-labels. Both are defeated by anchoring translation to quantities and always testing the finished equation with real numbers.
bestPractices: Model the quantity, not the word order: before writing, ask 'if there were 3 dogs, how many cats?' and build the equation to fit the numbers.
Insist letters stand for the NUMBER of things ('c = the number of cats'), never the object ('c = cats') — the label reading drives reversal.
Build process ('think of a number...') equations step-by-step with a function machine, so operations and their order are captured faithfully.
Always check the finished equation by substituting a value — 4c=d with d=3 predicts three-quarters of a dog, exposing the reversal.
Read the equation back in words and compare it to the original statement (Clement's self-check).
keyRepresentations: Bar model (a cats-bar made of 4 copies of the dogs-bar)
Function machine for 'think of a number' processes
Table of values to test a candidate equation
Two-way word↔symbol translation cards
commonMisconceptions: Reversal error via word-order matching: '4 times as many cats as dogs' → 4c=d, mapping words directly to symbols instead of modelling the relationship.
Letter-as-object/label (static comparison): treats c as 'cats' and reads 4c=d as 'four cats for each dog', with '=' meaning correspondence not equality.
Writes an expression with no equals sign when an equation is required.
Mis-orders operations in a process translation ('double it and add 5' written wrongly), ignoring order of operations.

learn.summary: Writing algebraic equations means translating a situation — a 'think of a number' process or a comparison — into symbols, where each letter stands for the NUMBER of things (not the thing itself) and the equals sign expresses genuine equality. Two documented traps recur: the reversal error (mapping words left-to-right onto symbols, so '4 times as many cats as dogs' becomes 4c=d instead of c=4d) and reading letters as object-labels. Anchor every translation to quantities, and always test the finished equation by substituting real numbers.

activities.title: Bar-model translator with a numerical reality check
feedback: If the learner writes 4c = d: substitute d = 3. The equation then claims c = 0.75 — three-quarters of a cat, and fewer cats than dogs, though the picture shows 12 cats. Ask 'can there be three-quarters of a cat? Should there be more cats or more dogs? What does that tell you about the equation?'
If c = 4d survives the substitution (d = 2 gives c = 8, matching the picture), confirm: the equation agrees with real counts.
Read the finished equation aloud in words and compare it to the original story: does 'the number of cats is four lots of the number of dogs' match?

For the process mode, if operations are misread or mis-ordered (e.g. n² + 5, which squares instead of doubling, or 2(n + 5), which adds before doubling), rebuild one step at a time and name each operation in turn.
activities.rationale: The reversal error is defeated when a wrong equation is tested against real quantities; building the situation with a bar first, then checking with numbers, makes the collision visible. An interactive slider that recolours the picture and recomputes the count as the learner sets the number of dogs is one way to make the check concrete, but the same cycle works on paper with a table of values.
sourceClaims: The reversal error is the dominant mistake in translating comparison statements to equations: Clement, Lochhead & Monk (1981) found 37% of engineering freshmen wrote 6S=P instead of S=6P, and ~68% of the incorrect responses were reversals; it stems from word-order matching (direct left-to-right mapping) or a static-comparison/letter-as-label reading, not carelessness.
learnerActions: Read a comparison statement such as '4 times as many cats as dogs'.
Before writing anything, answer 'if there were 3 dogs, how many cats?' (12) and build the picture: a cats-bar made of 4 copies of the dogs-bar.
Write the equation that fits the picture: c = 4d (equivalently 4d = c), where c = the number of cats and d = the number of dogs.
Test it: set d = 2, check that the equation gives c = 8, and confirm the picture agrees.

Deliberately try the reversed equation 4c = d, set d = 3, and see that it demands c = 0.75 — three-quarters of a cat, not the 12 cats the picture shows, and fewer cats than dogs. Notice that d = 4 gives c = 1, a whole number but still fewer cats than dogs, so compare with the picture rather than only checking for a whole number. Explain why this shows word-order matching is wrong.
In a second mode, turn a 'think of a number' process into an equation step by step, e.g. 'think of a number, double it, add 5, get 17' → 2n + 5 = 17.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading words straight into symbols left-to-right is NOT the same as modelling the relationship; testing an equation against counts built from the situation (3 dogs → 12 cats) reveals a reversed equation, which predicts fewer cats than dogs and sometimes even a non-whole count such as three-quarters of a cat.

activities.title: Function machine for process equations
feedback: If the learner writes operations in reading order regardless of the process, step through the machine box by box and rebuild the expression.
After solving, substitute the value back through the machine to confirm it produces the stated result.
activities.rationale: Building process equations step-by-step with a function machine captures operations and their order faithfully, addressing the mis-ordering misconception; connecting to order of operations supports correct notation.
learnerActions: Take a 'think of a number' process, e.g. 'think of a number, treble it, subtract 4, and you get 20'.
Feed the unknown through a function machine one operation at a time: n → ×3 → −4 → 20.
Write the equation capturing the operations in order: 3n − 4 = 20.
Find the value of n that works (n = 8), and check by substituting it back (3×8 − 4 = 20).
Contrast with a mis-ordered attempt and explain why operation order matters.
activities.intendedInsight: A process translates faithfully only when each operation and its order are captured in turn; the letter is an unknown number flowing through the machine.

activities.title: Match stories to equations, including reversal traps
feedback: When a reversal distractor is rejected, confirm with the counterexample: 4c = d with d = 3 would give three-quarters of a cat instead of 12 cats, which is fewer cats than dogs, the opposite of the story.
When a match is made, require the number check so the choice is defended, not guessed.
activities.rationale: A scored matching and fill-in-the-blank check targets the exact errors (reversal, mis-ordering) efficiently, but recognition alone does not require the learner to construct and defend an equation from scratch.
sourceClaims: The reversal error is the dominant mistake in translating comparison statements to equations: Clement, Lochhead & Monk (1981) found 37% of engineering freshmen wrote 6S=P instead of S=6P, and ~68% of the incorrect responses were reversals; it stems from word-order matching (direct left-to-right mapping) or a static-comparison/letter-as-label reading, not carelessness.
learnerActions: Connect comparison statements to the correct equation, with reversal distractors present (e.g. 4c = d offered alongside c = 4d for '4 times as many cats as dogs').
Fill in the blanks of a process equation, e.g. 'think of a number, treble it, subtract 4, get 20' → __n − __ = __.
For any match you make, justify it by substituting a value — and for any distractor you rejected, say which number exposes it.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising correct translations and spotting reversal distractors sharpens the distinction between word-order matching and modelling; justification by substitution turns recognition into reasoning.

activities.title: Puzzle-setter dialogue: write, read back, and defend
feedback: If the read-back does not match the story — e.g. 4c = d read faithfully as 'four lots of the number of cats equals the number of dogs' (four dogs for every cat), whereas the story 'four times as many cats as dogs' means four cats for every dog — that mismatch signals a reversal; test it with a value.
If a letter is described as the object ('c = cats'), restate it as 'the number of cats' and substitute a value to show the letter behaves like a number.
activities.rationale: Posing situations and probing 'read it back — does it match?' rehearses the self-check and surfaces reasoning; the numerical-collision insight is made sharper when paired with an actual substitution rather than discussion alone.
learnerActions: A puzzle-setter poses a situation (process or comparison) and asks you to write an equation for it.
Read your equation back in words and judge whether it matches the original statement (Clement's read-back self-check).
When challenged ('someone wrote 4c = d for 4 times as many cats as dogs — are they right?'), argue your case using specific numbers.
State plainly what each letter stands for, e.g. 'c is the number of cats', and confirm the equals sign means equality.
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken justification and reading the equation back out loud can catch reversal and letter-as-label errors that a silent write-down may hide.

activities.title: Annotate a worked translation
feedback: After the annotation, require the learner to translate a new statement and substitute a value — the example is a model, not a substitute for constructing and testing an equation.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example does not itself run the try-and-test cycle that corrects reversal, but it can make one correct translation explicit; it is a scaffold toward independent construction, not a replacement for it.
learnerActions: Examine a finished translation such as 2n + 5 = 17.
Reveal which words of the original statement each symbol came from (n ← 'a number', ×2 ← 'double it', +5 ← 'add 5', =17 ← 'to get 17').
Then write your own equation for a fresh statement and run the number check yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the word-to-symbol mapping of a correct example clarifies what faithful translation looks like, before attempting the full try-and-test cycle independently.

constraints: Letters must stand for the NUMBER of things ('c = the number of cats'), never the object ('c = cats'); the object-label reading drives the reversal error.

Always close translation with a numerical test: substitute a value and check the equation gives the count you predicted from the situation (e.g. 3 dogs → 12 cats). A non-whole count of objects is a warning sign, but a whole answer alone does not prove the equation is right (4c = d with d = 4 gives c = 1).
An equation requires an equals sign expressing equality; an expression alone is not an equation and the equals sign does not mean correspondence.

Matching and fill-in-the-blank checks are recognition tasks: they assess and rehearse but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and defend an equation independently — pair them with construction.
A fixed annotated example is a scaffold; it does not itself run the try-and-test cycle, so follow it with learner-generated translations that are tested with numbers.
For comparison statements, build the quantities (e.g. 'if 3 dogs, then 12 cats') before writing the equation, rather than mapping words left-to-right.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The MacGregor & Stacey (1993) source is marked unverified in the row (>50% reversals among 9th graders on 'y is eight times z'); treat its figures cautiously and verify before citing.

Self-audit of the reversed-equation counterexample: for 4c = d with d = 3, the equation gives c = 3/4, i.e. three-quarters of a cat (a valid fraction but not a whole count of animals). The original text said '4c=d with d=3 predicts three-quarters of a dog' in one place and 'half a dog' in another — these conflate which animal is fractional and are inconsistent. The correct reading is that c (cats) becomes fractional; activities state three-quarters of a cat for d = 3. The 'half a dog' phrasing (from d = 2 in the recommendation) is dropped as inconsistent.

Self-audit of process arithmetic: 'double it, add 5, get 17' → 2n + 5 = 17 gives n = 6; 'treble it, subtract 4, get 20' → 3n − 4 = 20 gives n = 8; '4 times as many cats as dogs' with 3 dogs gives 12 cats — all consistent.
The claim that a 3D/spatial environment 'adds nothing' to symbolic translation was removed as a non-established universal; it is simply not developed here because the learning target is symbolic.

The DfE curriculum claim was removed from activity-level sourceClaims because it supports the objective/topic and curriculum necessity, not the specific teaching principles (numerical reality check; function-machine ordering). It remains part of the row's evidence base for the objective overall.

probeDeeper: If there are 3 dogs, how many cats — and does your equation give that when d = 3? (a numerical counterexample to the reversal)
Read your equation out loud in words. Does it match the story exactly? (Clement's read-back check)
In 2n + 5 = 17, can n be any number, or is it one particular number? How would you find it?
Someone wrote 4c = d for '4 times as many cats as dogs.' Are they right? Convince me using numbers. (counterexample confronting the reversal head-on)
assess.correctAnswer: Interpret: n is the number I first thought of; doubling it and adding 5 gives 17 (so n = 6). Translate: c = 4d (equivalently 4d = c) — there are four times as many cats, so the number of cats is four lots of the number of dogs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal error by word-order matching — writes 4c = d for '4 times as many cats as dogs', mapping the words straight onto symbols left-to-right.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor to quantities: 'if there are 3 dogs, how many cats?' (12). Does 4c = d give that? Build a small table of values BEFORE writing the equation, then read the equation aloud to check it matches.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 'four times as many cats as dogs' the child writes 4c = d, and reads it back as 'four cats for every dog'; the equation fails a numerical test.

errorPatterns.pattern: Letter-as-object / static comparison — treats c as 'cats' and the equals sign as correspondence, not the NUMBER of cats and equality.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Restate every letter as 'the number of ___'; substitute a value to show the letter behaves like a number, not a name.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Interprets 2n+5=17 as involving a thing called n rather than an unknown number; in translation uses letters as units/labels ('c cats').

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-orders operations when translating a process — 'double it and add 5' written with the operations in the wrong order or notation reversed.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the expression one step at a time with a function machine, capturing each operation in turn; connect to order of operations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes something like n2+5, or applies the operations in reading order regardless of the process described.

responseLevels.gap: Maps words directly to symbols (4c=d) or treats letters as object-labels; the equation does not survive a numerical check, and interpreting a given equation is vague or thing-based.
responseLevels.full: Translates both process and comparison statements so they survive a numerical check, interprets a given equation back into a matching story, treats letters as numbers of things, and self-corrects by substituting values or reading the equation back.
responseLevels.partial: Translates simple one-operation and process statements correctly and interprets a given equation's operations, but reverses or mis-models comparison ('times as many') statements, or is inconsistent about whether the letter is a number.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two parts. First (interpret): show the child 2n + 5 = 17 and ask 'in words, what is this saying, and what does n stand for?' Then (translate): 'Now write an equation for this — At the shelter there are 4 times as many cats as dogs. Use c for the number of cats and d for the number of dogs.' Listen and watch what they write; offer no options.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The translate direction separates the reasoners: a child who models quantities writes c = 4d and can justify it with numbers; a child using word-order matching writes 4c = d ('4 times cats as dogs', straight off the sentence) and reads it back as 'four cats per dog'. The interpret direction exposes letter-as-label — saying n is the tag 'number' rather than a particular unknown number to be found.

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils should express missing number problems algebraically and use simple formulae (algebra introduced as a language for solving problems).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 6 Algebra)

sources.claim: The reversal error persists into school-age translation even with helpful phrasing (e.g. >50% reversals among 9th graders on 'y is eight times z').

pedagogy.summary: Partitioning a shape into equal parts means parts of equal AREA — the same amount of the whole — not parts of the same SHAPE. A square can be split into 4 equal parts as four strips, four small squares, or four triangles, and each is 1/4 because the areas are equal. The denominator counts how many equal-area pieces the whole is cut into, and each piece is 1/b of the whole. Equal shares of the same whole need not look alike.
bestPractices: Define equal parts as equal AREA, and show several correct partitions of one shape that look different but cover the same amount
Contrast valid equal-area partitions with tempting invalid ones (four pieces of different sizes) so 'four pieces' does not automatically mean 'quarters'
Use overlay/rearrangement or a squared grid to check that differently-shaped parts really have equal area
When reading a pre-partitioned shape, count the equal REGIONS (not the cut lines) and check they are equal before writing 1/b
Connect to the unit-fraction meaning: each equal-area part is 1/b of the whole
keyRepresentations: A square partitioned several ways into 4 (strips, quadrants, both diagonals)
Squared/grid paper to measure and compare areas
Overlay or cut-and-rearrange to prove two differently-shaped parts are equal
Area-model rectangle labelled in unit fractions
commonMisconceptions: Believes equal parts must be the same SHAPE (rejects a valid differently-shaped 1/4)
Counts pieces without checking equal area — calls any shape cut into 4 pieces 'quarters', even unequal ones
Writes the unit fraction from the number of cut lines rather than the number of regions
Thinks only the 'standard' partition (e.g. four small squares) is correct

learn.summary: Equal parts of a shape means parts of equal AREA — the same amount of the whole — not parts of the same SHAPE. A square can be split into four equal parts as strips, as quadrants, or as four triangles (both diagonals), and each is 1/4 because the areas are equal. The denominator counts how many equal-area regions the whole is cut into, and each region is 1/b of the whole. Learners should partition shapes several ways, check equal area by cutting and rearranging or by counting grid squares, contrast valid partitions with unequal 'four-piece' traps, and read a pre-partitioned shape by counting equal regions rather than cut lines.

activities.title: Quarter a square two different ways
feedback: If the learner makes only look-alike splits, prompt: 'Can you quarter it a way that does NOT make four identical pieces?' Offer the both-diagonals triangle split.
When four triangles and four strips both read 1/4, highlight: 'These look nothing alike, yet each is one quarter — because each covers the same AREA.'

If a learner rejects the triangle-quarter, verify equal area: cut the triangle into pieces and reassemble them to fill a strip, or count grid squares, putting the half squares cut by the diagonal together, to show the triangle and the strip cover the same number of squares (for example, 4 each on a 4-by-4 grid). A bare overlay of the two different shapes does not by itself prove equal area.
activities.rationale: Producing and comparing genuinely different equal-area partitions targets the belief that equal parts must be congruent, and grounds the unit fraction in area. An interactive version where the learner draws cut lines and each region's area is reported as a fraction of the whole would make 'equal area, any shape' directly checkable; a challenge mode asking for TWO valid ways reinforces that the standard partition is not the only correct one.
sourceClaims: CCSS 2.G.A.3 requires students to 'recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.'

CCSS 3.G.A.2 requires partitioning shapes into parts with EQUAL AREAS and expressing the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole (e.g. partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area and describe each part as 1/4 of the shape's area) — grounding 'equal parts = equal area'.

NCETM lists as a common error 'children thinking that equal means they must look identical'. It teaches that a square's four parts can each have the same area (1/4 of the whole) yet be non-congruent (not look identical), and recommends starting with congruent partitions then deliberately varying examples (including non-straight cut lines, different ways to quarter a square) to expose the misconception.
A unit fraction 1/b is one part of a whole partitioned into b equal parts; the area model represents fractions as equal-area regions of a shape.
learnerActions: Take a square and cut (or draw cut lines) to make 4 equal parts.
Now make 4 equal parts a DIFFERENT way — e.g. four vertical strips, then four quadrants, then four triangles using both diagonals.

For each attempt, check that every part covers the same amount: cut and rearrange the parts to see if they match, or draw the square on grid paper and count the squares (putting half squares together) in each part.
Label each part 1/4 and state in words why it is one quarter.
Compare a set of four triangles with a set of four strips: confirm both read 1/4 even though they look nothing alike.
activities.intendedInsight: Parts that look completely different can each be 1/4 as long as their AREAS are equal and together they cover the whole.

activities.title: Spot the trap: four pieces vs four equal parts
feedback: If the learner calls a shape with four unequal pieces 'quarters', compare the areas on a grid: 'These pieces are different sizes, so they can't each be one quarter.'
Reinforce: 'A quarter means one of four EQUAL parts — same amount each — not just one of four pieces.'
activities.rationale: Contrasting valid equal-area partitions with tempting unequal ones breaks the 'four pieces = quarters' shortcut and forces an area check before naming the fraction. A sorting task with distractors built from congruence-required and count-the-pieces errors makes the judgement explicit and checkable, though it rehearses the decision rather than eliciting the learner's own partitioning.
sourceClaims: CCSS 3.G.A.2 requires partitioning shapes into parts with EQUAL AREAS and expressing the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole (e.g. partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area and describe each part as 1/4 of the shape's area) — grounding 'equal parts = equal area'.
A unit fraction 1/b is one part of a whole partitioned into b equal parts; the area model represents fractions as equal-area regions of a shape.
learnerActions: Look at a square cut into four pieces of clearly different sizes. Decide: is each piece a quarter? Explain.
Check by comparing the areas — on squared/grid paper, or by cutting and rearranging the pieces to see if they match.
State whether 'four pieces' is the same as 'four equal parts', and why.
Sort several partitioned shapes into 'shows quarters' and 'does not': include an equal-area-but-different-shape example (YES) and a four-unequal-pieces example (NO).
activities.intendedInsight: Counting four pieces is not enough — a quarter must be one of four EQUAL-area parts. Unequal pieces are not quarters even though there are four of them.

activities.title: Read a pre-partitioned shape: count regions, not lines
feedback: If the learner writes 1/3 for a shape with three parallel cut lines and four regions, say: 'Count the PARTS, not the lines — three cuts make four parts, so each is 1/4.'
If the learner names a fraction without checking the regions are equal, prompt: 'Are all these regions the same amount? Check before you write the fraction.'
activities.rationale: Reading pre-partitioned shapes is a distinct skill from making partitions, and the off-by-one cut-line error and the skip-the-equality-check error are common. Requiring both an equality check and region-counting addresses both errors.
sourceClaims: A unit fraction 1/b is one part of a whole partitioned into b equal parts; the area model represents fractions as equal-area regions of a shape.
learnerActions: Given a shape already cut into equal parts, first check the regions really are equal in area.
Count the number of equal REGIONS (the parts), not the number of cut lines.
Write the unit fraction for one part, e.g. 1/5 for one of five equal regions.
Check your reasoning on a case with three parallel cut lines: three cuts make four parts, so each is 1/4 — not 1/3.
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator is the number of equal regions the whole is cut into, so you count the parts, not the cuts; and the regions must be equal in area before you name the fraction.

activities.title: Prove two different shapes are equal area
feedback: To show a triangle-quarter and a strip-quarter are the same amount, cut one into pieces and reassemble them to fill the other, or check they cover the same number of grid squares, putting the half squares cut by the diagonal together; then name it: 'Same amount, different shape — both are one quarter.' A bare overlay of two different shapes does not by itself prove equal area.
If the learner cannot justify beyond appearance, steer toward an area check: 'Cut it up and fit the pieces into the other shape, or count grid squares, to see if the amounts match.'
If using paper or card cutouts, note they are approximations of the ideal flat figure: their slight thickness is not part of the area being compared — only the flat region matters.
activities.rationale: Giving learners a concrete method to verify equal area turns the abstract claim 'equal parts = equal area' into something they can test, and supports the deeper justification tier where understanding shows rather than rote production of two partitions.
sourceClaims: NCETM lists as a common error 'children thinking that equal means they must look identical'. It teaches that a square's four parts can each have the same area (1/4 of the whole) yet be non-congruent (not look identical), and recommends starting with congruent partitions then deliberately varying examples (including non-straight cut lines, different ways to quarter a square) to expose the misconception.
CCSS 2.G.A.3 requires students to 'recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.'
learnerActions: Pick a differently-shaped candidate quarter (a triangle, an L-shape, a strip) and a square.
Use cut-and-rearrange to test whether the candidate covers the same area as a known quarter, or place both on squared/grid paper and count squares, putting any half squares together.
Decide whether the candidate really is 1/4 and justify by area.
Try the diagnostic: show two DIFFERENT ways to split a square into 4 equal parts, label each part, and explain how you know each is 1/4 even when the parts are different shapes.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal area can be verified by cutting pieces and reassembling them to fill the other shape, or by measuring on a grid — so you can confirm a differently-shaped part is genuinely 1/4.

constraints: Define equal parts as equal AREA throughout; the shape of a part may differ as long as it covers the same amount of the whole.

Start with congruent (look-alike) partitions, then deliberately vary examples — including non-straight cut lines and multiple ways to quarter a square — to expose the 'must look identical' misconception.
Require an equal-area check (cut and reassemble to fill, or count grid squares) before naming any fraction; do not let 'four pieces' or a count of cut lines determine the denominator.
A bare overlay of two differently-shaped parts does not prove equal area; use cutting-and-reassembling or grid-square counting to demonstrate it.

A static gallery of partitioned shapes with tap-to-reveal areas can illustrate the idea and serve as a reference, but it does not let the learner partition a shape or test their own cuts; use it as a scaffold, not as the main activity.

A sort or multiple-choice judgement (shows quarters vs not, 'is the triangle a quarter?') can rehearse and check the decision but does not itself elicit the learner constructing their own partitions; pair it with hands-on partitioning.
This is a 2D area idea; introducing a third dimension is unlikely to help and may distract from equal-area partitioning of a flat shape.

When using paper/card cutouts to cut, reassemble and compare, treat them as approximations of the ideal flat regions — their thickness is not part of the area being compared; state this to the learner in the activity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated conversation and 3D as 'poor' and asserted a third dimension 'confuses rather than clarifies' and that insight comes 'not from in-role dialogue'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established efficacy claims; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints.

The off-by-one cut-line example is sound for parallel straight cuts: three parallel cuts producing four equal regions gives 1/4, not 1/3. No arithmetic or geometric errors were found in the source examples; the equal-area-by-decomposition reasoning is valid for the flat-figure idealisation.

Verification of equal area between a triangle-quarter and a strip-quarter requires cutting one into pieces and reassembling (or grid-square counting); a single uncut piece will not coincide with a differently-shaped piece. Feedback wording was corrected accordingly.

The legacy 'area meter refuses to call them quarters' framing is an optional interactive feedback example (live area reporting, flagging unequal pieces); it is preserved as an optional mechanism, not a required one, and its learner-testing status is unknown.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a square split into 4 parts of clearly different SHAPES but equal AREA (e.g. one large right-triangle and several strips that together equal it). Before any measuring, ask: 'Are these four parts equal? Is each one a quarter?' Have them predict and say why. A child judging by appearance predicts 'no, they're different sizes'. Then check by overlaying/rearranging on a grid — the areas match — refuting the shape-based prediction and revealing that equal parts are about area, not looks.
probeDeeper: I've split this square into a big triangle and some strips — is the triangle a quarter? How could we check the areas are equal?
Here is a shape already cut into 5 equal parts — what fraction is one part, and how do you know it is 1/5?
If I cut a square into 4 pieces but they are different sizes, is each one 1/4? Why not?
Can two quarters of the same square look completely different and still both be 1/4?
assess.correctAnswer: Two distinct equal-area partitions (e.g. four vertical strips, and four triangles by both diagonals), each part labelled 1/4. Each part is 1/4 because the four parts have EQUAL AREA and together make the whole — the shape of a part can differ as long as it covers the same amount.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes equal parts must be the same shape — 'those aren't quarters because they don't look the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay or rearrange a triangle-quarter and a strip-quarter to show they cover the same area; equal parts means equal amount, not identical shape.
errorPatterns.distractor: The parts must all be the same shape, or they aren't quarters
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can produce only congruent-looking splits; rejects a valid differently-shaped 1/4 (e.g. a triangle) as 'not a quarter'

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts pieces without checking equal area — 'four pieces, so each is a quarter', even when the pieces are different sizes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the areas on a grid; unequal pieces are not quarters. A quarter must be one of four EQUAL-area parts.
errorPatterns.distractor: Any shape split into 4 pieces shows quarters, even if the pieces are different sizes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels an unequally-cut shape as quarters; counts regions but never compares their areas

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes the unit fraction from the number of cut LINES rather than the number of regions (off by one)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the equal REGIONS, not the lines: three cuts make four parts, so each is 1/4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a pre-partitioned shape, counts the cuts (e.g. 3 lines) and writes 1/3 for what are actually 4 regions

responseLevels.gap: Insists equal parts must be identical in shape, or labels unequal pieces as fractions by counting them; cannot produce a second valid partition.
responseLevels.full: Produces two genuinely different equal-area partitions, labels each 1/4, justifies by equal area covering the whole regardless of shape, reads a pre-partitioned shape by counting equal regions, and rejects unequal partitions.
responseLevels.partial: Produces equal-area partitions and labels 1/b, but only congruent-looking ones, or cannot articulate that equal AREA (not shape) is what matters, or is unsure about a differently-shaped quarter.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a square. Show me two DIFFERENT ways to split it into 4 equal parts, and label each part. Then tell me: how do you know each part really is 1/4, even when the parts are different shapes?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Tier 1 (produce two partitions) can be done by rote. Tier 2 — justifying that differently-shaped parts are still 1/4 because their AREAS are equal — is where understanding shows. A child judging by appearance offers only look-alike splits, rejects a valid triangle-quarter, or accepts four unequal pieces as quarters by counting them. A secure child produces genuinely different partitions and appeals to equal area.

pedagogy.summary: Comparing decimals with the SAME number of decimal places uses exactly the same process as comparing whole numbers: work from the highest place value down, and decide at the first place where the digits differ. Because the numbers are the same length, there is no ragged-length trap, so this is the foundational easy case — the whole-number strategy and correct place-value reasoning happen to agree. The genuine misconceptions (longer-is-larger, shorter-is-larger) only surface with unequal-length decimals and belong to the next topic.
bestPractices: Compare the highest place value first (whole number, then tenths, then hundredths) and stop at the first place where they differ — for 3.72 vs 3.27 the wholes tie, so tenths (7 vs 2) decides
Align the decimal points vertically so equal places line up in columns
Read every digit by its place-value name ('4 tenths 5 hundredths'), never as a bare digit string
Use a number line and a length model (linear blocks, LAB) rather than area/volume blocks, because length shows relative size directly
Flag that reading the decimal part as a whole number ('72 beats 27') happens to work here but will fail on ragged decimals like 0.4 vs 0.15 — build the place-value habit now
keyRepresentations: Number line marked in hundredths (0–1, and 3–4 for the 3.72/3.27 pair)
Place-value columns aligned on the decimal point
LAB / linear arithmetic (length) blocks
10×10 hundredths grid for area backup
commonMisconceptions: Reads the decimal part as a whole number ('72 > 27') — lands the right answer here but is a fragile, non-place-value strategy
Compares from the right (last digit first) as if column-adding
Ignores or misreads the whole-number part when it is present

learn.summary: Comparing decimals that have the SAME number of decimal places (up to two) uses the same process as comparing whole numbers: work from the highest place value down and decide at the first place where digits differ. Because the numbers are equal length here, there is no ragged-length trap — correct place-value reasoning and an (incorrect) read-it-as-a-whole-number strategy happen to agree, so this is the foundational easy case. The genuine longer-is-larger / shorter-is-larger misconceptions only surface with unequal-length decimals (a later topic). The teaching aim is to build the place-value habit now, before it is tested by ragged decimals.

activities.title: Order decimals on a number line and a length bar
feedback: If a child reads '72 beats 27', accept the right answer but push the reasoning: rebuild each number as tenths and hundredths on the line and ask what the 7 and the 2 are actually worth.
If a child compares from the right (last digit first), use the number line to show the biggest place decides size; practise reading left-to-right and naming the highest place first.
Reinforce correct reasoning by having them re-voice it: '3.72 and 3.27 — the wholes are equal at 3, so the tenths decide, and 7 tenths is more than 2 tenths.'

Probe transfer: 'Would "fifteen beats four" still work for 0.4 vs 0.15? Why or why not?' to flag that the whole-number trick breaks on ragged decimals (here 0.4 > 0.15, so the 'fifteen beats four' trick fails).
activities.rationale: Ordering is a spatial act; placing cards on a line and seeing the winner settle furthest right, backed by a length-bar view, is intended to turn 'compare the highest place first' into something felt. A length model may show relative size more directly than an area or volume model, but the cited source does not establish this comparative efficacy — treat it as a design preference. The 3.72/3.27 pair adds the check that learners establish equal wholes before moving to tenths.
sourceClaims: Comparing decimals uses the same highest-place-value-first process as whole numbers; comparisons between EQUAL-LENGTH decimals are a weak diagnostic because a correct place-value strategy and an (incorrect) treat-as-whole-number strategy produce the same answer — the longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger misconceptions require ragged-length decimals to reveal.
learnerActions: Take three cards — 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 — and place each on a number line ticked every 0.1 with minor ticks every 0.01, smallest to largest.
Say aloud why 0.54 lands furthest right and 0.39 nearest the start, naming the tenths: 'five tenths beats four tenths beats three tenths'.
View each number also as a growing length bar so the relative sizes are visually clear (0.54 is the longest bar).
Then place 3.72 and 3.27 on a 3–4 number line, first checking the whole-number parts tie at 3, then deciding on the tenths (7 vs 2).
State the order and justify by comparing the highest differing place first.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimal size can be read as position on a line: ordering is decided by the highest place at which the digits differ, read left to right, not by the raw digit string or the rightmost digit.

activities.title: Align place-value columns and read every digit by its name
feedback: If a learner says 0.60 is bigger than 0.6 'because it has more digits', align the columns and read the hundredths place: 0 hundredths adds nothing, so 0.60 = 0.6.
If they name digits as bare numbers ('sixty'), re-prompt for the place-value name ('six tenths').
Praise stopping at the first differing column rather than reading all the way to the end.
activities.rationale: Column alignment and place-value naming build the durable strategy that will survive ragged-length decimals later, where reading the decimal part as a whole number fails.
sourceClaims: Comparing decimals uses the same highest-place-value-first process as whole numbers; comparisons between EQUAL-LENGTH decimals are a weak diagnostic because a correct place-value strategy and an (incorrect) treat-as-whole-number strategy produce the same answer — the longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger misconceptions require ragged-length decimals to reveal.
learnerActions: Write a pair such as 3.72 and 3.27 one above the other with the decimal points aligned vertically so equal places line up in columns.
Read each digit by its place-value name — 'three ones, seven tenths, two hundredths' — never as a bare digit string.
Scan from the highest place downward and circle the first column where the digits differ; declare that column the decider.
Compare 0.6 and 0.60: first write 0.6 as 0.60 by appending a trailing zero so both have two decimal places, then read the places (6 tenths and 0 hundredths in each) to show they are equal in value.
activities.intendedInsight: Aligning on the decimal point and naming each digit by its place makes the comparison a place-value decision, and shows a trailing zero can be appended (0.6 = 0.60) to equalize length without changing the value.

activities.title: Pairwise comparison and placement practice (scorable check)
feedback: Correct order: 0.39 < 0.45 < 0.54 (decided on the tenths: 3, 4, 5).
Correct comparison: 3.72 > 3.27 (wholes tie at 3, so tenths 7 > 2 decide).
A right answer with 'seventy-two beats twenty-seven' reasoning is fragile — follow up with the number-line rebuild and a ragged pair (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.15) to make place value explicit.
activities.rationale: Ordering and pairwise comparison map cleanly onto scorable items and give quick practice, but they confirm the answer more than the method. Because equal-length pairs are a weak diagnostic, pair every scored item with a request for the reasoning. Keep all items equal length to stay within this topic.
sourceClaims: Comparing decimals uses the same highest-place-value-first process as whole numbers; comparisons between EQUAL-LENGTH decimals are a weak diagnostic because a correct place-value strategy and an (incorrect) treat-as-whole-number strategy produce the same answer — the longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger misconceptions require ragged-length decimals to reveal.
learnerActions: Order 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 from smallest to largest.
Choose which is larger: 3.72 or 3.27, and give the reason.
Place a given two-decimal-place value at the right spot on a 0–1 line.
For each item, say which digit you looked at first and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal-length comparisons can be done quickly and correctly by comparing the highest differing place, and the reasoning (not just the answer) should be stated.

constraints: Keep all practised and scored comparisons the same length (up to two decimal places) within this topic; teaching the ordering of unequal-length / ragged decimals, which reveal longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger, belongs to the next topic. Two exceptions are allowed: appending a trailing zero to show equivalence (writing 0.6 as 0.60 so 0.6 = 0.60) as an equal-value demonstration, and a single brief, unscored verbal transfer probe (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.15) used only to show that the read-it-as-a-whole-number trick breaks.

Equal-length comparisons are a weak diagnostic on their own: a correct place-value strategy and a read-it-as-a-whole-number strategy give the same answer, so always elicit the reasoning, not just the ordering.
A static number line with tap-to-reveal place values is useful as a reference card, but ordering should remain an active decision the child makes, not a result they read off.

Prefer a number line and a length (linear) model for showing relative size; a 10×10 hundredths grid can serve as an area backup. Depth/volume models are not needed for this one-dimensional size idea (a design preference, not a proven ranking of media).
Watch for the specific error of comparing from the right (last digit first) as if column-adding, and for ignoring or misreading a present whole-number part.
Optional interaction examples (drag-and-snap cards, a colour-the-winner cue, a growing length bar, slider placement, tap-to-reveal place values) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the single source was not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source supports that equal-length decimal comparisons are a weak diagnostic (place-value and whole-number strategies agree); it does not establish comparative efficacy of number-line vs other media, so claims that a length model 'shows relative size more directly' are presented as a design preference, not proven necessity.

The non-preferred 'static image / reference card' option is retained as a scaffold note and the 'conversation' option as an omission; the original rated the conversation format poor ('no persona or open inquiry'), which is a fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law.

Trailing-zero equivalence (0.6 = 0.60) appears in the assessment probes and response levels, so it is included here as a reading/naming equivalence check within scope, framed as appending a trailing zero to equalize length rather than as ragged ordering.

probeDeeper: Which digit did you look at first, and why that one?
In 3.72, what is the 7 worth? And what is the 2 worth in 3.27?
What about 0.6 and 0.60 — are those the same size or different? How do you know?
If I gave you 0.4 and 0.15, would 'fifteen beats four' still work? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.39 < 0.45 < 0.54 (decided on the tenths: 3, 4, 5), and 3.72 > 3.27 (wholes tie at 3, so the tenths 7 > 2 decide). Justifies by comparing the highest place first.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the decimal part as a whole number: 'point-seventy-two is bigger than point-twenty-seven because 72 beats 27'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Accept the answer but push the reasoning: rebuild each number as tenths and hundredths on the number line, then show a ragged pair (0.4 vs 0.15) where the whole-number trick fails — make the place-value habit explicit now.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies by the digit string rather than place value; says 'seventy-two' not 'seven tenths'; lands the right answer here but for the wrong reason

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares from the right, starting at the last digit as if adding in columns
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the number line, show that the biggest place decides size; practise reading left-to-right and naming the highest place first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to the hundredths digit first, or hesitates about which end to start from; mis-orders when the whole-number part carries the decision

responseLevels.gap: Orders by the raw digit string or from the right and cannot justify by place value; mis-orders when the whole part matters.
responseLevels.full: Compares the highest differing place first, articulates 0.54 = 5 tenths > 0.45 = 4 tenths, places numbers correctly on a line, recognises 0.6 = 0.60, and transfers cleanly to a new equal-length set.
responseLevels.partial: Gets equal-length comparisons right and can say 'more tenths wins', but relies on the numbers being the same length and cannot yet explain place value or handle a trailing-zero case like 0.6 vs 0.60.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child these cards: 0.45, 0.54, 0.39. Say: 'Put these in order, smallest to largest, and tell me how you decided.' Then hand them 3.72 and 3.27 and ask which is larger. Watch which digit they look at first and listen to the reason — do not prompt a method.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because all three cards are the same length, a correct place-value strategy and a treat-it-as-a-whole-number strategy give the SAME order (per Steinle & Stacey, equal-length pairs are a weak diagnostic on their own). So this task is not trying to catch longer-is-larger — that lives in the ragged-decimal topic (mt_933BohS9BH). What it discriminates is HOW the child reasons: a secure child names tenths and compares from the highest place; a fragile child says 'seventy-two beats twenty-seven' or starts from the right — a right answer reached by a method that will break the moment lengths differ. The 3.72/3.27 pair adds the check that they establish the wholes are equal before moving to the tenths.
