pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Sunlight warms things up

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** no KS1 'energy' content (energy enters at KS3), so no direct UK statutory match; the honest UK home is KS1 'Working scientifically' (observing closely, performing simple tests, gathering and recording data) and the Year-1 'Seasonal changes' unit (observe weather/day-length across seasons).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NATIONAL (NGSS): K-PS3-1 (verbatim) '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-1]'; clarification examples — sand, soil, rocks, water; assessment boundary — temperature limited to RELATIVE measures (warmer/cooler). NGSS-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Children make firsthand observations that sunlight WARMS Earth's surface: ground, water, rocks and objects in the sun feel warmer than the same things in the shade. Strictly RELATIVE and sensory (warmer/cooler by touch, or a simple thermometer) — NO degrees, no mechanism, no light-vs-heat theory; the win is the observed cause: sun on a surface → it warms up. This observation feeds 'Building shade from the sun' (reduce that warming) and, much later, Sun-driven weather.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 5-6, pre-readers).
bestPractices: Lead with firsthand sensory observation: have children touch surfaces in sun vs shade — sunny tarmac vs shaded grass, a sunny windowsill vs a shaded one — and say which feels warmer; the felt contrast IS the evidence.
Hold the comparison fair without naming it: same object/surface, two spots (one sunny, one shaded), at the same time — so 'the sun' is the only difference.
Move from touch to a simple relative thermometer or colour-change strip to confirm warmer/cooler, but keep it relative — the assessment boundary excludes degrees at this age.
Use a leave-and-revisit investigation: put two identical cups of water (or rocks) in sun and shade, predict, then check later — building the sun-as-source-of-warmth idea over time.
Name the source plainly in talk: 'the Sun warms it up; in the shade the sun can't reach, so it stays cooler' — framing shade as blocking the sun, not as a maker of cold.
keyRepresentations: Paired sun/shade comparison of the SAME object (sunny rock vs shaded rock) — the canonical observation.
Touch/feel as the primary instrument, backed by a simple relative thermometer or a colour-changing temperature strip.
A sun-as-source picture: rays reaching the ground/water/objects and warming them.
Across-the-day anchor: cool ground in the morning → warm by midday → cooler again in shade/evening.
commonMisconceptions: 'Shade makes things cold' — rather than shade simply blocking the sun so the area doesn't get warmed; the cool is the absence of warming, not a cold source.
Thinking everything in the sun is equally warm — dark/heavier things warm more (a real effect, kept as enrichment, not the core claim).
Conflating the sun's LIGHT and its WARMTH, or believing only light (not warmth) reaches us — here the focus is the warming effect.
'Things stay warm by themselves' — not noticing that without the sun (shade, night) surfaces cool down again.
Believing sunlight can't warm water or see-through things — water and clear objects in the sun warm too.

learn.summary: For ages 5-6: children observe that sunlight warms Earth's surfaces — ground, water, rocks and objects in the sun feel warmer than the same things in the shade. Learning is strictly relative and sensory (warmer/cooler by touch or a simple relative thermometer or colour strip), with no degrees, no mechanism and no light-vs-heat theory. The core win is the observed cause: sun reaching a surface warms it; shade is cooler because it blocks the sun's warmth, not because it sends out cold. Firsthand outdoor observation is the heart of this objective; screen activities rehearse the cause and prediction and should accompany, not replace, real touching and leaving-and-revisiting.

activities.title: Touch the sun, touch the shade (firsthand outdoor observation)
feedback: If the child says the shade 'makes it cold', feel both spots together, then move the shaded object into the sun and wait: it warms up, showing there is no cold source — only more or less of the sun's warmth.

If a child thinks the Sun only warms things in summer and 'isn't hot' on a cold or winter day, compare a sunny spot with a shady spot of the same surface on a cold day using touch or a relative thermometer — a surface that has been in the sun for a while usually feels warmer, even if the difference is small.
Affirm the felt contrast as the evidence: 'the sunny one felt warmer, and that warmth came from the Sun.'
activities.rationale: The standard's practice is literally to make firsthand observations, and the concept is a felt one — warm sun-baked surfaces against cool shaded ones. Holding object and time constant isolates the sun as the only difference. Framing shade as blocking the sun (not making cold), and showing the cold-day sun still warms, targets the common misconceptions directly.
sourceClaims: K-PS3-1 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-1]'); clarification examples sand/soil/rocks/water; assessment boundary limits temperature to relative measures (warmer/cooler).
Young children commonly think shade 'makes cold' rather than blocking the sun's warming, and conflate the sun's light with its warmth.
learnerActions: Go outside and touch the same kind of surface in two spots — e.g. sunny tarmac vs shaded tarmac, sunny grass vs shaded grass, or a sunny windowsill vs a shaded one — and say which feels warmer.
Keep the comparison fair: same object or surface, two spots (one sunny, one shaded), checked at the same time, so the sun is the only difference.
After touching, confirm warmer/cooler with a simple relative thermometer or colour-changing temperature strip if available — staying relative, never reading out degrees.
Say in plain words what was felt: 'the Sun warms it up; in the shade the sun can't reach it, so it stays cooler.'
activities.intendedInsight: Sunlight reaching a surface warms it; a shaded spot is cooler because the sun's warmth is blocked, not because shade makes cold.

activities.title: Leave and revisit: two cups in sun and shade
feedback: If a child says the shady cup will get colder because the shade makes cold, that signals the 'shade makes cold' idea — revisit by feeling both and moving the shady cup into the sun, then checking again later to find it has warmed.
If a child expects the sunny cup to feel the same straight away as after a long wait, point to the leave-and-revisit checks: after sitting in the sun for a while, it got warmer than it was at first.
Praise prediction-then-check: 'you said the sunny one would be warmer, and we checked — that's how scientists find out.'
activities.rationale: A leave-and-revisit investigation builds the sun-as-source idea over time and makes prediction a diagnostic moment: the stated reason distinguishes 'sun warms' from 'shade makes cold', and the repeated check surfaces the 'warmth doesn't build up' misconception.
sourceClaims: K-PS3-1 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-1]'); clarification examples sand/soil/rocks/water; assessment boundary limits temperature to relative measures (warmer/cooler).
learnerActions: Put two identical cups of water filled from the same jug (or two matching rocks), so they start out equally warm, outside — one in full sun, one in shade.
Before leaving them, predict which will be warmer later and say why.
Return after a while and compare with hands or a relative thermometer; talk about what changed and whether the prediction held.
Optionally revisit the same sunny spot after a short time and again a little later to notice warmth can build up the longer it sits in the sun.
activities.intendedInsight: The sun is the source of the extra warmth that builds up over time; the shaded item stays cooler than the sunny one because the sun's warmth does not reach it.

activities.title: Sunny-day sandbox (on-screen cause-and-prediction rehearsal)
feedback: All prompts picture-and-audio for pre-readers; use warmer/cooler faces or words, never degrees.

When a prediction matches the meter, confirm the rule: 'the sun reached it, so it got warmer.' When the cloud covers the sun, name it: 'the sun is blocked, so it stops warming and starts to cool' — and remember that on screen this happens fast, while a real warm surface would cool more slowly.
Treat the sandbox as a rehearsal of the cause, then take the idea outdoors where the warmth can actually be felt.
activities.rationale: A draggable sandbox with a live warm/cool meter, colour glow, and a movable cloud/umbrella lets a 5-6-year-old act out the causal rule and do predict-then-check. It is proposed as a useful on-screen rehearsal of the cause, but it is a simplified model and cannot deliver the felt warmth that is central to the objective, so it should accompany real outdoor observation, not substitute for it.
learnerActions: Drag an object (a rock, a cup of water, a metal slide, sand) between a sunny patch and a shaded patch on screen.
Watch a simple warm/cool meter and a colour or glow cue respond live as the object moves into the sun or into the shade.

Slide a cloud or umbrella over the sun and watch the modelled scene cool — noting this is a simplified model that cools quickly, whereas a real warm surface would cool gradually once the sun is blocked.
Before moving an object, predict out loud whether it will get warmer or cooler, then move it and check.
activities.intendedInsight: You control the warmth by controlling whether the sun reaches the object — sun on it = warmer, blocked = cooler — and you can predict the result before acting.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal sunny scene (reference observation)
feedback: Keep language relative (warm/cool) and tie every reveal back to whether the sun reaches that object.
Use as a companion for naming and reinforcing, alongside firsthand touching.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal scene delivers the sun-as-source naming cleanly for pre-readers with picture+audio. It names and reinforces the idea but does not host the predict-then-check action or real observation, so it works as a reference companion rather than the main investigation.
learnerActions: In a single sunny outdoor scene, tap the rock, the puddle, the slide or the shaded bench.
Hear which is 'warm — the sun is shining on it' or 'cool — it's in the shade' with picture-and-audio.
Tap a flap on the sun that says 'I warm things up.'
activities.intendedInsight: Objects the sun shines on are warmer; objects in shade are cooler because the sun is blocked.

activities.title: Which feels warmer? (sorting check)
feedback: This checks a conclusion more than it builds the observation, so pair it with firsthand work; at this age it leans on adult or audio support.
A sort can check that a child classifies sun/shade correctly, but it does not itself elicit the felt observation or an explanation — follow it with real touching.
If a child says water or clear objects can't be warmed by the sun, revisit with a real cup of water left in the sun — it warms too.
activities.rationale: A picture+audio categorisation can confirm whether the idea has landed and surface misconceptions (e.g. that sunlight can't warm water or transparent things), but it tests classification rather than building the firsthand observation at the centre of the standard.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly think shade 'makes cold' rather than blocking the sun's warming, and conflate the sun's light with its warmth.
learnerActions: Sort pictured objects into 'in the sun = warmer' vs 'in the shade = cooler' using picture-and-audio.
Answer a 'which feels warmer?' picture choice using relative language only.
Try tricky cases: a clear cup of water or a see-through object in the sun also warms up.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can apply the sun-warms / shade-cooler rule to new objects, including water and clear things.

constraints: Keep all temperature talk RELATIVE (warmer/cooler by touch, simple thermometer, or colour strip): no degrees, no mechanism, no light-vs-heat theory at age 5-6 — this matches the assessment boundary.

Firsthand sensory observation is the objective itself; on-screen sandbox, tap-to-reveal, and sorting activities are scaffolds that rehearse the cause or check the conclusion and must not replace real outdoor touching and leaving-and-revisiting.
Frame shade as blocking the sun's warmth, not as a maker of cold; avoid any language implying cold is a substance that is sent out.
Hold comparisons fair: same object/surface, two spots, same time, so the sun is the only difference.

The tap-to-reveal scene reinforces and names the idea but does not support predict-then-check; the sorting check tests classification and leans on adult/audio support rather than building the observation.

Enrichment only (not the core claim): dark-coloured surfaces, and some materials (e.g. a metal slide vs a patch of grass), can feel warmer in the sun than lighter ones — keep this as an optional extension, not a requirement. Do NOT teach that 'heavier things warm more'.
If observing shade or a cover, look at the cool patch and the shadow it casts on the ground — never ask a child to look at the Sun through a cover or hold material up toward the Sun.

The sandbox is a simplified model; blocking the sun cools the modelled scene quickly, whereas a real warm surface cools gradually once the sun is blocked — do not present the model's instant cooling as a real-world prediction.
UK note: there is no KS1 statutory 'energy' content in England; the honest home is KS1 Working Scientifically and the Year-1 Seasonal changes unit. The specific standard anchor is US NGSS K-PS3-1.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source legacy framing that 'no digital artefact can deliver that bodily sensation' and that 3D 'adds no conceptual gain' was softened: the screen sandbox is scoped as a complement to firsthand observation with a stated affordance/limit, not as proof that screens cannot teach or that 3D is universally worthless.

The source claim about children's misconceptions (IOP Spark) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the 'shade makes cold' and light-vs-warmth conflation framing as plausible but not independently confirmed here.

The assessment errorPattern 'Sun only warms in summer / isn't hot in winter' carries reteachPrerequisiteId mt_go5i87u2b9; it is reinstated as feedback in the firsthand activity with a cold-day comparison, and reteach should route to that prerequisite micro-topic if the child denies winter warming.

The original row's enrichment wording 'dark/heavier things warm more' was corrected: greater mass warms more slowly (more thermal mass); the reliable effect is colour/material, so the guidance teaches darker/material differences and drops 'heavier'. Confirm any comparison with an adult-supervised check if used.

The sandbox sourceClaims were set to [] because K-PS3-1 concerns firsthand observation, which the simulation explicitly cannot deliver; it is not a direct source for a screen-based method. The same applies to the tap-to-reveal reference scene.
The assessment row's diagnostic (two-cup predict-then-measure, reasoning tier) was preserved as the leave-and-revisit activity's prediction step; assessment fields themselves were not modified.

assess.poeTask: Put two identical cups of water (or two thermometers) out on a sunny day — one in full sun, one in shade. FIRST ask the child which will be warmer after ten minutes AND why. The reason is the diagnostic part: a 'shade makes cold' child predicts the shady one gets actively colder, while a 'sun warms' child predicts the sunny one rises and the shady one barely changes. Then measure and compare.
probeDeeper: If we move the shady bench out into the sunshine and wait, what will happen to how it feels — and why?
At night there's no sun at all. Is that because something is making cold, or because the sun's warmth has gone away?
Which will get warmer left in the sun: a metal slide or a patch of grass? How could we find out?
Where's the best place to leave a cup of water to warm it up, and where to keep it cool? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: The shady bench is cooler because the tree blocks the sun's light and warmth from reaching it — the sun isn't warming it up. The shade doesn't make cold or send out coldness; 'cooler' just means less of the sun's warming got there.

errorPatterns.pattern: The shade (or the cold) actively makes things cold, as if cold were a substance that comes out ('the shade sends cold onto the bench').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Feel both benches, then move the shady one into the sun and watch it warm; there is no 'cold source', only more or less of the sun's warmth.
errorPatterns.distractor: The shade makes cold and sends it onto the bench.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says shade produces or sends cold rather than blocking warmth.

errorPatterns.pattern: The Sun only warms things in summer / the Sun isn't hot in winter ('no warming from winter sun').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a sunny spot with a shady spot on a cold day using a thermometer — the sunny surface is still warmer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that the sun warms surfaces on a cold or winter day.

errorPatterns.pattern: Everything in the sun is the same warmth and warmth doesn't build up over time ('it's just warm or not').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Measure the same sunny spot after 5 minutes and after 15 minutes and compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Doesn't expect a surface to get warmer the longer it sits in the sun.

responseLevels.gap: Says the shade or the cold makes or sends cold; treats cold as a thing rather than as less warmth.
responseLevels.full: Explains that the sun warms surfaces and shade is cooler because it blocks that warmth (no cold source), and predicts a new case — moving an object into or out of the sun, or which surface warms more.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the sunny spot is warmer and the shady one cooler, but explains it as the shade 'making it cold' rather than blocking the sun's warmth.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a sunny day the bench in the sun feels warm but the bench under the tree feels cooler. A friend says 'the shade makes it cold.' Do you agree — what is really making the shady bench cooler?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'cold is a thing' says the shade actively makes or sends cold — different from one who says the shade simply blocks the sun's warmth. The reason tier separates 'shade makes cold' from 'shade blocks the sun's heat'.

pedagogy.summary: At age 10-11 children make a LINE PLOT of measurement data in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and then OPERATE on that data with fractions — totalling measurements, finding differences, and redistributing a total equally among the data points. Two ideas carry the teaching. First, a line plot is not a bar graph: its horizontal axis is a genuine MEASUREMENT SCALE (a number line), so every position on it exists whether or not a measurement falls there ('64 inches is not a category like spiders'), and gaps between observed values must be shown. Second, the signature problem — 'if the total were shared equally, how much would each have?' — is an informal, hands-on route to the MEAN (fair share), and to solve it children total the fractions (often re-labelling the scale in a common unit such as eighths to get like denominators) and then divide by the count. So the topic fuses data display with fraction arithmetic, and the equal-redistribution task quietly previews averaging.
bestPractices: Draw the horizontal axis as a proper measurement scale (a number line marked in the fractional unit), and include every position — mark unobserved values too, because unlike categories, measurement values have gaps that must be shown
Distinguish the line plot from a bar graph explicitly: the axis is a measurement scale you could read off a ruler, not a set of separate categories
Re-label the scale in a common fractional unit (e.g. eighths) so that totalling and comparing measurements produces like denominators
Treat 'redistribute the total equally' as a fair-share problem — pour everything together, then share among the data points — making the link to the mean concrete before it is named
Keep the fraction arithmetic (adding unlike denominators, dividing by the count) reliable, since the data questions depend on it
Attend to precision when measuring and recording to the nearest 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8, and place each mark carefully at its scale position
keyRepresentations: A number-line measurement scale marked in eighths, with an X (or dot) stacked above each measured value — the line plot itself
The same measurements re-expressed over a common denominator (eighths) for totalling
A 'pour together then share equally' image for the equal-redistribution (fair-share/mean) task
A ruler marked in halves/quarters/eighths, showing where the scale of the plot comes from
commonMisconceptions: Treating a line plot like a bar graph — showing only the values that occur, side by side as categories, with no continuous scale and no gaps for unobserved values
Adding the measurement fractions by combining numerators and denominators instead of finding a common denominator
Not seeing 'redistribute equally' as total ÷ count (the fair share / mean) — giving a middle value or leaving the data unchanged
Placing marks imprecisely on the scale, or mis-reading the fractional interval (e.g. an eighth for a quarter)

learn.summary: Learners aged 10-11 make a line plot of measurement data in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8), then operate on that data with fractions: totalling measurements, finding differences, and redistributing a total equally among the data points. Two ideas carry the teaching. First, a line plot is not a bar graph: its horizontal axis is a genuine measurement scale (a number line), so every position on it exists whether or not a measurement falls there, and gaps between observed values must be shown. Second, the signature problem — 'if the total were shared equally, how much would each have?' — is an informal, hands-on route to the mean (fair share): learners total the fractions (often re-labelling the scale in a common unit such as eighths to get like denominators) and then divide by the count. The topic fuses data display with fraction arithmetic, and the equal-redistribution task (using identical containers so equal volume reads cleanly) previews averaging before it is named.

activities.title: Place-and-share: build the plot, then pour the total
feedback: If a mark lands on the wrong fractional interval (e.g. at 3/8 when the value is 1/2 = 4/8), point to a labelled position and count the eighths across to re-place it; the plot's structure is fine, only the placement slipped.
If observed values are drawn as adjacent bars with no empty positions between them, show a ruler: every eighth exists on the scale, so unobserved positions must stay visible as gaps.
If fractions are added by combining numerators and denominators (e.g. 1/2 + 3/4 = 4/6), re-label both in eighths first (4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8) and check the sum against the scale.

If the fair share is answered with an unchanged amount, or by picking a middle or most common value without working, pour everything together to get the total, then share it among all the containers: equally means total ÷ count. (For 3/4, 1/2, 1/4, 1/2 the middle value happens to equal the fair share of 1/2, so ask to see the total-and-divide working rather than judging by the answer alone.)
activities.rationale: Placing marks on a real fractional scale and physically pouring-then-sharing is proposed to make the fill-the-gaps and fair-share ideas concrete and operable, rehearsing both the display skill and the fraction arithmetic the data questions depend on. An optional interactive version may let the learner drag each X onto the scale, auto-re-label amounts in eighths when totalling, and animate the pour-and-share so each container settles at the shared amount; these are illustrative mechanisms, not requirements — paper, a ruler and real identical beakers achieve the same work and may be preferable for measuring precision.
sourceClaims: A line plot displays measurement data on a number-line diagram whose scale corresponds to the measuring tool; unlike categorical data on a bar graph, measurement values have gaps that must be shown ('64 inches is not a category like spiders'), and a value not present is still written in its proper position on the scale

Standard 5.MD.2: make a line plot in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use fraction operations to solve problems, e.g. given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find how much each would hold if the total were redistributed equally — which Grade 6 students later see as the MEAN of the data set; solving such problems may require re-labelling the scale in eighths to produce like denominators
Adding fractions with unlike denominators requires replacing them with equivalent fractions over a common denominator (a well-documented error is adding numerators and denominators directly)
learnerActions: Measure (or use given) several lengths to the nearest 1/8 and place a mark (an X or dot) above each value on a horizontal scale marked in eighths.
Keep every eighth-position on the scale visible, including positions where no measurement falls, so the gaps are shown (for example, if nothing lands on 4 5/8, that spot stays on the number line).
Say aloud why an unobserved value still has a place on the scale: it is a measurement value on a ruler-like scale, not a separate category.

For a fair-share task, start with four identical (same-size) containers holding 3/4, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/2 cup. Combine all the liquid into one larger container that can hold at least 2 cups, and write the sum, re-labelling each amount in eighths: 6/8 + 4/8 + 2/8 + 4/8 = 16/8 = 2 cups.
Pour the combined 2 cups equally back into the four identical containers and record how much each now holds; connect the result (1/2 cup each) to total ÷ count = 2 ÷ 4.
Total the two shortest measurements and find a difference between two values, re-expressing over a common denominator first.
activities.intendedInsight: A line plot's axis is a continuous measurement scale with gaps for unobserved values, not a row of categories; and 'share the total equally' means total ÷ count — the fair share, which previews the mean made physical.

activities.title: Check the operations on a given plot
feedback: For an answer that adds tops and bottoms (e.g. 1/2 + 3/4 giving 4/6), re-express both in eighths and recompute; 4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8.
For a fair-share answer that is the most common amount or an unchanged value, re-total all amounts and divide by the number of containers.
If a difference is found without first making like denominators, re-express both values in eighths before subtracting, then check the result against the scale.
activities.rationale: A scorable check of totals, differences and the equal-share item verifies the fraction operations and the fair-share interpretation. This is a focused check on given data; it does not by itself require the learner to construct a plot from raw measurements, so pair it with the construction activity. As a design choice for this check, keep data sets small with clean fraction sums so the arithmetic stays reliable and the reasoning stays visible.
sourceClaims: Standard 5.MD.2: make a line plot in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use fraction operations to solve problems, e.g. given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find how much each would hold if the total were redistributed equally — which Grade 6 students later see as the MEAN of the data set; solving such problems may require re-labelling the scale in eighths to produce like denominators
Adding fractions with unlike denominators requires replacing them with equivalent fractions over a common denominator (a well-documented error is adding numerators and denominators directly)
learnerActions: From a provided small line plot, write the total of the two shortest measurements, showing the common-denominator step.
Answer a fair-share question such as 'If all the liquid were shared equally between identical containers, how much would each hold?' by totalling then dividing by the count.
Compare two values to find a difference, re-expressing over eighths first.
Watch for and avoid two traps: adding numerators and denominators together, and reporting a middle value instead of total ÷ count.
activities.intendedInsight: Totals, differences and fair shares read off a line plot all depend on correct like-denominator fraction arithmetic and on reading 'equally' as total ÷ count.

activities.title: Explain and stretch the fair-share idea
feedback: If the learner says the empty spot should be removed, return to the ruler image: a measurement value is not a category, so its position exists regardless of whether data falls there.

If adding the zero container does not change the learner's answer, recompute total ÷ count with the new count (2 cups ÷ 5 = 2/5 cup each): the fair share is sensitive to how many are sharing, even when the added amount is zero.
If the fruit bar chart and the line plot are treated as the same, point out that fruit names are categories with no scale, while lengths sit on a measurement number line.
activities.rationale: Explanation and counterexample probes surface whether understanding is robust and transfer the fair-share reasoning to a new case, including sensitivity to the count. Verbal explanation complements, but does not replace, the hands-on construction and computation; explaining a procedure is not the same as performing it.
sourceClaims: A line plot displays measurement data on a number-line diagram whose scale corresponds to the measuring tool; unlike categorical data on a bar graph, measurement values have gaps that must be shown ('64 inches is not a category like spiders'), and a value not present is still written in its proper position on the scale

Standard 5.MD.2: make a line plot in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use fraction operations to solve problems, e.g. given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find how much each would hold if the total were redistributed equally — which Grade 6 students later see as the MEAN of the data set; solving such problems may require re-labelling the scale in eighths to produce like denominators
Adding fractions with unlike denominators requires replacing them with equivalent fractions over a common denominator (a well-documented error is adding numerators and denominators directly)
learnerActions: Answer: 'You didn't measure any item at 4 5/8 — should that spot still be on your scale? Why?' to put the measurement-scale-vs-category distinction into words.
Explain why you changed both fractions into eighths before adding them.
Tackle a counterexample: 'If one more identical container with 0 cups joined the sharing, how much would each get now?' and state why the answer changes.
Contrast this line plot with a bar chart of favourite fruits and say what makes the axes different.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why unobserved positions remain on the scale, why common denominators are needed, and how the fair share responds to the count (including a zero) consolidates both the display and the averaging ideas.

constraints: Reliable fraction arithmetic (adding unlike denominators, dividing by a count) is a prerequisite the data questions depend on; shore it up if it is shaky.

The horizontal axis must be drawn as a proper measurement scale (an evenly spaced number line marked in the fractional unit) with every position present, including unobserved values shown as gaps — not a set of separate bar-graph categories.

A static annotated line plot can display the scale and label totals and fair shares as a reference or worked example, but it does not let the learner place data, show gaps, or carry out the pour-and-share, so it is a support rather than the main task.

An interactive drag/pour tool is one way to make the mechanism concrete; paper plots, a real ruler, and physical identical beakers accomplish the same learning and may be preferable for precision in measuring and recording. A 2D scene suffices for this measurement scale and its data.
A recognition-only or multiple-choice check can verify answers but does not by itself elicit construction of a plot from raw measurements; combine it with a construction task.
Role-play or in-character dialogue does not confirm that the learner can accurately place marks or perform the fraction arithmetic, so it is not a substitute for a do-and-calculate task.

Attend to precision: measure and record to the nearest 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 and place each mark carefully at its scale position; distinguish a placement slip (scaffold) from a conceptual bar-graph error (reteach).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3/4 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/2 = 6/8 + 4/8 + 2/8 + 4/8 = 16/8 = 2 cups; shared among 4 gives 1/2 cup each (2 ÷ 4); adding a zero container gives 2 ÷ 5 = 2/5 cup each. The source example 4 3/8 + 4 1/2 = 8 7/8 inches also checks out (3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8), with 4 3/8 and 4 1/2 being the two shortest of the source pencil set. 1/2 + 3/4 = 4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8. These were checked during this review but not independently re-verified against the original sources.
'Identical beakers' was restored from the source so that equal redistribution reads as equal volume per container; the arithmetic is unchanged.

The original artefact-fit note that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it has been removed and reframed only as 'a 2D scene suffices here' within constraints, without asserting 3D is useless in general.
The original 'a static image cannot teach this / only a live tool can' framing was softened: a fixed diagram still teaches as a reference even though it cannot be manipulated.

The reteach-prerequisite links in the source assessment (unlike-denominator and line-plot prerequisites) are retained as pedagogical intent but internal prerequisite identifiers were removed as non-portable.
The efficacy of hands-on construction over other media is stated as proposed/intended, not as a verified empirical result.

probeDeeper: 'You didn't measure any pencil at 4⅝ — should that spot still be on your scale? Why?' — probes the measurement-scale (fill-the-gaps) idea versus categories
'Why did you change both fractions into eighths before adding them?' — forces the common-denominator reason into words
Counterexample: 'If one more beaker with 0 cups joined the sharing, how much would each get now?' — tests that the fair share is total ÷ count and is sensitive to the count and to a zero
'How is this line plot different from a bar chart of favourite fruits?' — checks the measurement-vs-categorical distinction on a fresh case
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: for (1) draws a number-line scale marked in eighths and stacks a mark above each measured value, leaving the positions with no data visible as gaps (not a row of bars); for (2) adds the two fractions using a common denominator (e.g. 4⅜ + 4½ = 8⅞ inches); for (3) totals ¾+½+¼+½ = 2 cups and divides by 4 to get ½ cup each (fair share). A genuine measurement scale with gaps shown, like-denominator addition, and reading 'share equally' as total ÷ count are the marks of mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Line-plot-as-bar-graph: treats the distinct measurement values as categories — shows only the values that occur, side by side, with no continuous scale and no gaps for unobserved values
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the line-plot prerequisite: the axis is a measurement scale like a ruler — every eighth-position exists and must be shown, even where no pencil falls, because a measurement value is not a category
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child draws the observed lengths as separate adjacent bars/columns with no evenly-spaced number-line scale, omitting the empty positions between values

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds fractions by combining numerators and denominators instead of finding a common denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the unlike-denominators prerequisite: re-label all the measurements in a common unit (eighths) before adding, and check the result against the scale
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) or (3) the child writes something like ½ + ¾ = 2/6 (or 2/4), adding tops and bottoms rather than re-expressing over eighths first

errorPatterns.pattern: Redistribute-not-as-fair-share: does not read 'share the total equally' as total ÷ count — gives a middle value, one of the amounts, or leaves the data unchanged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by pouring together and sharing out: combine all the liquid (the total), then share it among the four beakers; 'equally' means total ÷ count — the fair share
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child reports ½ because it is the most common amount, or picks a beaker's value, rather than totalling to 2 cups and dividing by 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Placement/interval slip: places a mark at the wrong fractional interval or miscounts eighths, though the plot's form is right
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: have the child re-read the scale mark and count the eighths from a labelled point; the understanding of the plot is intact, only the placement slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The line plot is structurally correct but a mark sits at ⅜ where the value is ½, or an eighth is read as a quarter

responseLevels.gap: Builds a bar-graph-like display (observed values as adjacent categories, no measurement scale or gaps); adds the fractions by combining numerators and denominators; treats 'share equally' as choosing a value
responseLevels.full: Constructs a proper line plot on a fractional measurement scale with gaps shown, totals and differences measurements using common denominators, solves the equal-redistribution problem as total ÷ count (the fair share), and transfers the same reasoning to a fresh measurement set
responseLevels.partial: Constructs a correct line plot on a measurement scale and reads it, and adds fractions with like denominators, but stumbles when denominators differ or does not connect 'redistribute equally' to total ÷ count — displays and reads the data but cannot fully operate on it

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a set of measurements to the nearest 1/8 (e.g. eight pencils: 4½, 4¾, 4½, 5, 4⅜, 4¾, 4½, 5 inches) and set these tasks, WATCHING how they work. (1) 'Make a line plot to show these lengths.' (2) 'What is the combined length of the two shortest pencils?' (3) 'Four beakers hold ¾, ½, ¼ and ½ of a cup. If all the liquid were shared equally between the four beakers, how much would each hold?' (Set the task and WATCH — do not tell them to use a common denominator or hint that sharing equally is total ÷ count.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (1) exposes whether the child treats the axis as a measurement scale (gaps present, evenly spaced) or as bar-graph categories (only observed values, side by side). Task (3) cannot be solved by reading the plot — it requires totalling unlike fractions and dividing by the count, so it separates a child who can operate on the data from one who can only display it, and previews the mean. The two together distinguish display-only competence from full fraction-operation competence.

sources.claim: A line plot displays measurement data on a number-line diagram whose scale corresponds to the measuring tool; unlike categorical data on a bar graph, measurement values have gaps that must be shown ('64 inches is not a category like spiders'), and a value not present is still written in its proper position on the scale
sources.source: Common Core Standards Writing Team, Progression on Measurement and Data (measurement part), 20 June 2011 draft

sources.claim: Standard 5.MD.2: make a line plot in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use fraction operations to solve problems, e.g. given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find how much each would hold if the total were redistributed equally — which Grade 6 students later see as the MEAN of the data set; solving such problems may require re-labelling the scale in eighths to produce like denominators
sources.source: Common Core Standards Writing Team, Progression on Measurement and Data; and CCSS 5.MD.B.2

sources.claim: Adding fractions with unlike denominators requires replacing them with equivalent fractions over a common denominator (a well-documented error is adding numerators and denominators directly)
sources.source: Common Core Standards Writing Team, Progression on Measurement and Data (note on producing like denominators for line-plot problems)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9, Cloud Types — identify cumulus (fluffy, fair-weather, low), stratus (flat grey layers, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (thin high wisps of ice) and know clouds form when water vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets.
• Standards — UK (DfE): supports KS1/KS2 weather observation and Y1 Seasonal changes (observe and describe weather); cloud identification is an observational science skill rather than a discrete statutory objective.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 3-ESS2-1 (describe typical weather) and K-ESS2-1 (observe/describe weather over time) as an observation-and-prediction skill. State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach as a field-guide (name + look + altitude + weather it signals) PLUS the shared formation mechanism (vapour cools and condenses on tiny particles); use real sky photos/observation over the school week; connect cloud type to a simple forecast (cirrus → change coming; towering cumulus → showers).
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — name and describe the three types from images; Tier B — explain clouds as condensed liquid droplets (not vapour) and predict weather from cloud type; Tier C — relate cloud height/type to air rising and cooling.
bestPractices: Use real sky photographs and regular outdoor observation — build a class cloud log over a week
Teach altitude as a defining feature (cirrus high and icy, cumulus/stratus lower) so height is part of identification
Explicitly state clouds are made of tiny LIQUID (or ice) droplets, not invisible vapour — confront the commonest cloud misconception head-on
Link each cloud type to a simple, testable weather prediction to give identification a purpose
If demonstrating cloud-in-a-jar, first show smoke dissipating alone so children don't mistake the smoke for the cloud
keyRepresentations: Altitude-layered sky diagram placing cirrus high, cumulus/stratus lower
Photo field-guide cards pairing each cloud with its name and typical weather
A cooling-air panel showing vapour condensing onto particles into droplets
A simple cloud → forecast lookup (fluffy = fair; grey layer = drizzle; high wisps = change coming)
commonMisconceptions: Clouds are made of water vapour or gas — visible clouds are tiny LIQUID (or ice) droplets; vapour is invisible
Steam is water vapour — it is condensed liquid droplets too
In a cloud-in-a-jar demo, the smoke IS the cloud — the smoke provides particles for droplets to condense on
Clouds are solid/fluffy things you could stand on, rather than suspended droplets
All clouds mean rain — many (cumulus, cirrus) are fair-weather or high-and-dry

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, learners identify the three main cloud types — cumulus (fluffy, fair-weather, low), stratus (flat grey overcast layers that can bring drizzle) and cirrus (thin high icy wisps) — and learn that clouds form when water vapour cools and condenses into tiny liquid droplets (or, very high up where it is freezing, tiny ice crystals). Identification works best from real sky photos paired with altitude, and each type links to a simple, checkable weather prediction. The commonest misconception to confront directly is that a visible cloud is water vapour or gas; in fact vapour is invisible and the visible cloud is tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals.

activities.title: Altitude-layered sky field guide
feedback: If a learner sorts by shape alone, point to the height differences: cirrus high and icy, cumulus and stratus lower, so altitude is part of the identification.
If a learner says the cloud is vapour or gas, show the condensation close-up: vapour is invisible; what we see is tiny liquid droplets (or ice crystals) that formed when the air cooled.
When a forecast is revealed, prompt the learner to say why that cloud signals that weather, not just to read the label; treat the forecast as likely, then checked against the real sky.
activities.rationale: Identification by appearance and altitude is fundamentally a visual task, so a layered sky image where height is read at a glance makes the organising idea concrete. Linking each type to a forecast gives recognition a purpose, and a drill-down into condensation addresses the core misconception by showing it rather than only stating it.
sourceClaims: Cumulus (fair-weather, low), stratus (layered, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (high, icy) are the canonical primary cloud types linked to simple weather prediction.

A persistent misconception is that visible clouds and steam are water vapour, when in fact they are tiny liquid (or ice) droplets; vapour is invisible. In cloud-in-a-jar demos children may mistake the smoke for the cloud.
learnerActions: Study one rich sky scene showing cirrus streaking high, cumulus billowing low, and a flat grey stratus sheet, and notice how the three types sit at different heights.

For each cloud, record its name, what it looks like, roughly how high it sits, and the weather it signals (cirrus: thin icy wisps, very high, a change may be coming; cumulus: fluffy, low, usually fair weather; stratus: flat grey layer, overcast, often bringing drizzle).
Reveal a 'What weather?' forecast for each cloud, then whenever you spot that cloud type in the real sky over the coming days, check whether the predicted weather follows.
Zoom into one cloud to see a model of invisible water vapour cooling and condensing onto tiny particles to form droplets, and state in your own words what the cloud is actually made of.
activities.intendedInsight: Clouds are not random blobs but a named, layered system you can read by look and height; and a visible cloud is made of tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals, not invisible vapour.

activities.title: Sort real sky photographs
feedback: If a learner mixes up stratus and cirrus, contrast a solid low grey sheet with thin high streaks and ask which sits higher.
If a learner expects rain from every cloud, point out that cumulus and cirrus are often fair-weather or high-and-dry; only some clouds (such as tall piled-up cumulus) signal showers soon.
activities.rationale: Practising with authentic images beyond idealised diagrams supports transfer to the real sky, and sorting with feedback turns passive recognition into active discrimination. The grouping-by-weather step also involves describing typical weather from observed data.
sourceClaims: Cumulus (fair-weather, low), stratus (layered, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (high, icy) are the canonical primary cloud types linked to simple weather prediction.
NGSS 3-ESS2-1 frames describing typical weather conditions from observed data at grade 3.
learnerActions: Collect or view a set of real sky photographs and sort each one into cumulus, stratus or cirrus.
For each photo, name one feature that decided your choice (fluffy and piled, flat grey layer, or thin high wisps).
Group the sorted photos by the weather each type tends to bring and explain the pattern.
activities.intendedInsight: Real skies are messier than diagrams; applying the look-and-height features to genuine photos builds reliable recognition and connects type to likely weather.

activities.title: Cool-the-air cloud formation
feedback: If a learner thinks the cloud appears because vapour became visible, stress that vapour stays invisible and it is the new liquid droplets we can see.
If a learner imagines the cloud as a solid fluffy thing you could stand on, clarify that a cloud is countless tiny droplets suspended in the air, not a solid surface.

If demonstrating a cloud in a jar, first show smoke dissipating on its own so the learner does not mistake the smoke for the cloud — the particles only give the water vapour something to condense on to form droplets.
activities.rationale: A dynamic cooling demonstration makes the formation mechanism observable and ties the abstract word 'condense' to a visible change, directly targeting the vapour-versus-droplet misconception and the idea that a cloud is a solid object.
sourceClaims: A persistent misconception is that visible clouds and steam are water vapour, when in fact they are tiny liquid (or ice) droplets; vapour is invisible. In cloud-in-a-jar demos children may mistake the smoke for the cloud.
learnerActions: Use a control that cools a pocket of air and watch invisible water vapour condense into a visible cloud of droplets as the temperature drops.
Describe the sequence: warm air holds invisible vapour, cooling makes the vapour condense onto tiny particles, and the gathered droplets become the cloud you can see.
Relate this to everyday examples such as breath fogging on a cold day or steam cooling above a kettle — both are condensed droplets, not vapour.
activities.intendedInsight: A cloud forms when cooling turns invisible water vapour into tiny liquid droplets that together become visible; the visible part is always liquid or ice, never the gas itself.

activities.title: Build a class cloud log
feedback: If a prediction fails, treat it as data: ask what else the sky showed and whether more than one cloud type was present.
Encourage noting altitude cues (very high wisps versus low fluffy heaps) to strengthen each day's identification.
activities.rationale: Regular outdoor observation over a week turns the field guide into a lived skill and connects naming to real weather outcomes, matching how weather observation is taught.
sourceClaims: NGSS 3-ESS2-1 frames describing typical weather conditions from observed data at grade 3.
Cumulus (fair-weather, low), stratus (layered, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (high, icy) are the canonical primary cloud types linked to simple weather prediction.
learnerActions: Observe and photograph (or sketch) the sky at a set time across a week and name the cloud type each day.
Beside each entry, note the weather that followed and compare it with what that cloud type predicts.
At the end of the week, review which predictions held and discuss why a cloud type signals the weather it does.
activities.intendedInsight: Cloud identification is an observational skill: watching real skies over time links cloud type to weather and shows prediction can be tested.

activities.title: Check recognition and prediction
feedback: If a learner picks the high wisps as the rain sky, revisit that tall piled-up cumulus often signals showers soon, while high cirrus may signal a change later rather than immediate rain.
If a learner answers that a cloud is made of vapour, gas, smoke or cotton wool, correct it: a cloud is tiny liquid water droplets (sometimes ice crystals) formed when vapour cools and condenses.
activities.rationale: Matching and short questions give a clean check of identification and prediction, and including the ice discriminator and a 'what is it made of' item surfaces the key misconception.
sourceClaims: Cumulus (fair-weather, low), stratus (layered, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (high, icy) are the canonical primary cloud types linked to simple weather prediction.

A persistent misconception is that visible clouds and steam are water vapour, when in fact they are tiny liquid (or ice) droplets; vapour is invisible. In cloud-in-a-jar demos children may mistake the smoke for the cloud.
learnerActions: Match each cloud image to its name (cumulus, stratus, cirrus).
Answer: which cloud is made mostly of ice crystals? (cirrus), and which sky — tall dark piled-up clouds or thin high wisps — is more likely to bring rain soon?
Explain in a sentence what a cloud is actually made of.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can name types from images, pick out the ice-cloud discriminator, and read cloud shape as a rain signal while stating the condensation model.

activities.title: Ask a weather watcher
feedback: Prompt the learner to connect the answer to a visible feature (height, shape, colour) so the reasoning stays grounded in observation.
If the conversation drifts to 'all clouds bring rain', redirect to naming a fair-weather cloud and its signal.
activities.rationale: Explanatory dialogue supports learners who reason by discussing, and it reinforces prediction; it works best alongside visual identification rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Cumulus (fair-weather, low), stratus (layered, overcast/drizzle) and cirrus (high, icy) are the canonical primary cloud types linked to simple weather prediction.
learnerActions: Pose questions to a knowledgeable adult or imagined meteorologist, such as 'What does that cloud mean?' or 'Why do those two clouds bring different weather?'
Explain back, in your own words, the reasoning behind one answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through what a cloud signals deepens understanding of the type-to-weather link and invites reasoning, though the recognition itself still rests on seeing the clouds.

constraints: Identification is primarily a visual, height-based skill, so visual tasks should carry the core learning; discussion-only activities reinforce reasoning but do not by themselves replace seeing the clouds.

State explicitly that a visible cloud is tiny liquid droplets (or tiny ice crystals), not invisible water vapour, and not a solid thing you could stand on; this is the commonest misconception and must be confronted directly.

Not every cloud means rain — cumulus and cirrus are often fair-weather or high-and-dry; only relate specific types (e.g. tall piled-up cumulus) to imminent showers, and treat predictions as likely rather than certain.
Treat altitude as a defining identification feature (cirrus high and icy; cumulus and stratus lower), not just an extra fact.
A single sky image or diagram is a scaffold: pair it with real sky photos and outdoor observation so recognition transfers to genuine, variable skies.

In a cloud-in-a-jar demonstration, show smoke dissipating alone first so the smoke is not mistaken for the cloud; the particles only provide surfaces for water vapour to condense on, forming droplets.
A reveal-the-answer forecast should add new information a learner can check against the real sky, not merely restate the cloud's name.
Matching and short-question checks confirm recognition and prediction but do not by themselves require the learner to construct an explanation of cloud formation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were not re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three source claims (the misconception source and the Met Office/NOAA classification claim) are marked unverified in the original row; treat the cloud-type and misconception details as provisional pending source verification.

The original materials sometimes framed a static layered image as uniquely suited ('plays exactly to a static image's strength') and judged 3D as adding 'novelty more than insight' and a conversation as unable to deliver recognition 'as directly as a picture'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy findings; they are softened here to scoped suggestions. A fixed image cannot be manipulated but can still teach, and 3D or dialogue can support learning without being necessary.
Rain-signal guidance is simplified for ages 7–9: cloud appearance indicates likely rather than certain weather, so predictions should be treated as testable rather than definitive.

Ordinary cumulus is usually a fair-weather cloud, whereas tall, piled-up (towering) cumulus signals showers; the field guide labels cumulus 'usually fair weather' and the check specifies the tall form, so the two activities stay consistent for this age group.

The NGSS claim is attached to the photo-sorting and cloud-log activities only because their weather-grouping/observation steps involve describing weather from observed data; the discrimination/transfer rationale is otherwise supported by the cloud-type claim.

probeDeeper: Why can you see a cloud but not the water vapour rising off a wet playground?
The tall dark cloud and the thin wispy cloud are both 'clouds' — why do they bring such different weather?
When a cloud forms, what is happening to the water and where did it come from?
assess.correctAnswer: A cloud is made of tiny water droplets (and sometimes ice crystals) formed when water vapour cools and condenses. The tall, dark, piled-up cloud is far more likely to bring rain soon than the thin, high, wispy streaks.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Clouds are made of smoke / cotton wool / fog stuff'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link kettle-steam and breath-on-cold-glass to droplets condensing from vapour.
errorPatterns.distractor: A cloud is fluffy cotton-like stuff, not water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names a non-water substance

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Any cloud means rain is coming / all clouds are the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort cloud photos by the weather each type brings.
errorPatterns.distractor: Any cloud in the sky means it will rain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot tell rain clouds from fair-weather clouds

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A cloud is the water vapour itself — that's why we can see it'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stress vapour is invisible; the visible cloud is liquid droplets.
errorPatterns.distractor: A cloud is the water vapour, which is why we can see it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the visible cloud is vapour

responseLevels.gap: Describes clouds as smoke/cotton/gas; treats every cloud as the same.
responseLevels.full: Explains clouds as condensed water droplets and reads cloud type (tall/dark vs high/wispy) as a signal of likely weather, transferring to a new sky.
responseLevels.partial: Knows clouds are water droplets but cannot link cloud type to the weather it signals, or still confuses the visible cloud with invisible vapour.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: One day you see thick, tall clouds with dark bottoms piling up like cauliflowers. Another day, thin wispy streaks sit high in the sky. What is a cloud actually made of, and which sky is more likely to bring rain soon?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks clouds are smoke, gas or cotton-wool cannot connect a cloud to condensed water or read its shape as a rain signal; only the condensation model plus shape-reading answers both tiers.
