pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9; the race to the South Pole in detail — Norway's Roald Amundsen and Britain's Robert Falcon Scott both set out in 1911; Amundsen arrived first on 14 December using dog sleds and careful planning; Scott arrived 34 days later using man-hauled sledges and died with his team on the return; plus Shackleton's 1914 Endurance expedition, ship crushed by ice, and his extraordinary open-boat rescue voyage to South Georgia.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 History (a significant turning point / study of an aspect beyond 1066; significant individuals) linked with polar-science context; geography of Antarctica.
• Standards—US: primarily historical/ELA (analysing accounts, cause and effect, point of view); connects to engineering trade-offs in survival planning.
• Operational details: go beyond 'who won' to WHY — Amundsen's dogs, skiing skill, fewer men, well-placed supply depots and single clear goal versus Scott's ponies/man-hauling, mixed science-and-race aims, and thinner margins. Treat it as decisions-with-consequences and human character (courage, leadership, endurance). Shackleton reframes 'success': he never crossed Antarctica yet saved all 27 men. Handle Scott's death with age-appropriate gravity.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (7) say who reached the South Pole first and one reason (dogs/planning); Tier B (8) give one difference between Amundsen's and Scott's methods that affected the outcome; Tier C (9) explain why Shackleton is celebrated despite failing his goal, and how choices shaped each expedition's fate.
bestPractices: Move from 'who won' to 'why' — compare the decisions (dogs vs man-hauling, depots, number of men, single vs mixed goals) that drove the outcomes
Use primary voices (diary extracts, photographs) so children meet the explorers as real people making hard choices
Frame Shackleton to separate 'reaching a goal' from 'leading well' — a powerful lesson in what success can mean
Handle Scott's death honestly but sensitively, focusing on courage and the fine margins of survival
Draw out cause and effect: small planning differences compounded into life-and-death results
keyRepresentations: Parallel route map of Amundsen and Scott with dates and depots marked
Decision-comparison table (transport, food, men, goals) beside the outcome
Endurance photo-timeline: trapped → crushed → camp on ice → boat voyage to South Georgia
Explorer portrait cards with each person's methods, character, and fate
commonMisconceptions: Amundsen won simply by luck — his dogs, skiing, depots and focused planning were decisive choices
Scott failed because he was weak — fine margins, method choices and brutal conditions, not cowardice, doomed his return
Shackleton reached the Pole — he never did; his fame is for saving every man after disaster
Man-hauling sledges was just as good as using dogs — it exhausted Scott's team and cost precious time and strength
These are legends/stories — they are documented real expeditions with diaries and photographs

learn.summary: History/ELA topic for ages 7–9: the 1911 race to the South Pole (Amundsen vs Scott) and Shackleton's 1914 Endurance expedition. The learning goal moves beyond 'who won' to WHY — comparing decisions (dog sleds vs man-hauling, supply depots, number of men, single vs mixed goals) and their life-and-death consequences, meeting the explorers as real people making hard choices, and reframing 'success' through Shackleton, who never reached his goal yet brought every man home. Scott's death should be handled with age-appropriate honesty and gravity.

activities.title: In the explorer's own voice: asking 'why'
feedback: If a learner says the result was simply luck, ask them to name one decision Amundsen made that Scott did not, and say how it helped.
If a learner calls Scott weak or a coward, reframe: his team showed great courage; the difference was method and margins, not bravery — judge the decisions, not the person's worth.
Affirm when a learner connects a specific choice (dogs, depots, specialism) to a specific effect on speed, energy or safety.
Prompt reflection on Shackleton: he never reached the Pole and lost his ship, yet brought every man of the Endurance crew home — what does that say about what 'success' can mean?
activities.rationale: The human heart of this topic is motive, decision and character. A role-play dialogue is one proposed approach that may let children interrogate reasoning directly and reason about cause-and-effect through the explorers' explanations. Other media (maps, timelines, primary sources) also convey the sequence and comparison; no single medium is required.
learnerActions: Take on the role of a questioner interviewing each explorer, in turn, about the choices they made.
Ask Amundsen why he brought dogs and laid so many supply depots, and listen for his reasoning about margins, speed and safety.
Ask a member of Scott's party what man-hauling a sledge for hundreds of miles did to the team's strength and time.
Ask Shackleton how he decided to leave most of his men on Elephant Island and sail a small lifeboat roughly 800 miles across stormy sea to South Georgia.
Push back with a challenge such as 'Why not turn around?' and consider the in-character reply.
After each exchange, write or say one sentence naming the decision and the consequence it produced.
activities.intendedInsight: The outcomes of the expeditions were shaped by choices and character, not just luck; leading well (Shackleton bringing every man of the Endurance crew home) can be a form of greatness distinct from reaching a goal.

activities.title: Plan your own expedition: decisions with consequences
feedback: If a plan runs out of supplies, trace back to depot placement or over-ambitious goals rather than blaming weather alone.
Highlight that dogs were fast and, on Amundsen's plan, some could be used as food, while man-hauling exhausted the team and cost time and strength.
Note that weather genuinely played a part, but ask the learner to separate the factors they controlled from the ones they did not.
activities.rationale: Modelling choices and running their consequences is a proposed approach that may make the cause-and-effect of planning more concrete, supporting the shift from 'who won' to 'why'. It is intended as a complement to the dialogue, not a replacement for meeting the explorers as people; efficacy relative to other media is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Choose transport (dog sleds vs ponies/man-hauling), where to place supply depots, and how many people to take.
State your single clear goal or a mixed goal (race plus science) and predict how that choice affects the journey.
Run or narrate the journey step by step and observe how each choice affects speed, energy reserves and safety margin.
Compare your outcome to Amundsen's and Scott's real decisions and explain the match or mismatch.
activities.intendedInsight: Small planning differences can compound into life-and-death results; well-placed depots, suitable transport and a focused goal create a real margin of safety.

activities.title: Parallel maps, timelines and primary voices
feedback: If a learner says Scott's polar party used dog sleds to reach the Pole, attributes death to Amundsen, or gives the crushed ship to the wrong person, re-sort the facts by explorer (Scott did take some dogs, but his final Pole party man-hauled).
Use the side-by-side table to show how differing decisions shaped speed, energy and safety margins.
Invite the learner to point to a diary extract or photo that changed how they saw an explorer.
activities.rationale: Maps, comparison tables and photo-timelines can convey the events and the comparison and ground the topic in primary evidence. They support sequencing and recall; a sort can check classification but does not itself elicit the empathy or causal explanation that are the topic's core, so pair them with discussion.
learnerActions: Trace a parallel route map of Amundsen and Scott with dates and depots marked, comparing their paths and timing.
Build a decision-comparison table (transport, food, number of men, goals) placed beside each expedition's outcome.
Follow an Endurance photo-timeline: ship trapped → crushed → camp on the ice → lifeboats to Elephant Island → open-boat voyage to South Georgia → crew rescued.
Read short diary extracts and study photographs so the explorers appear as real people, then discuss what each voice reveals.
Sort explorer facts correctly: Amundsen (first, dogs, survived); Scott (second, man-hauling, died returning); Shackleton (1914, Endurance crushed, crew saved).
activities.intendedInsight: These were documented real expeditions, recorded in diaries and photographs; laying choices and outcomes side by side reveals the causal links, and the three explorers must not be muddled.

activities.title: Checkpoint: contrast decisions, not luck
feedback: Gap response (blames luck or Scott's weakness, thinks the teams did the same thing): line up the choices side by side — transport, depots, experience — and show how each shaped speed, energy and safety.
Partial response (names one difference but leans on luck/character elsewhere, or muddles expeditions): build on the difference named, then add a second and re-sort the explorers.
Full response: affirm the contrast of several decisions plus the acknowledgement that weather mattered but was not the whole story.
activities.rationale: Asking whether the decisions differed is intended to push analysis beyond 'bad luck' and to discriminate between recall and genuine causal understanding. Recall tasks assess facts but do not by themselves elicit the empathy and causal reasoning that are the topic's core, so pair them with explanation.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt: a student says 'Scott just had worse luck with the weather — the two teams did basically the same thing.' Did they do the same thing, or did their decisions differ in ways that mattered?
Name at least one decision Amundsen made that Scott did not, and explain how it helped.
Explain why man-hauling sledges could leave a team more worn down than using dogs.
Explain why Shackleton's expedition is still remembered as a triumph despite never reaching the Pole and losing his ship.

Tier A (age 7): say who reached the South Pole first and give one reason (dogs/planning). Tier B (age 8): give one difference between the methods that affected the outcome. Tier C (age 9): explain why Shackleton is celebrated despite failing his goal, and how choices shaped each fate.
activities.intendedInsight: A full answer contrasts multiple specific decisions (dogs, depots, polar specialism vs man-hauling and thin margins) as the real edge, acknowledges weather as a factor but not the whole story, and keeps the three expeditions straight.

constraints: Handle Scott's death honestly but with age-appropriate gravity, focusing on courage and the fine margins of survival rather than failure or blame.

Address common misconceptions explicitly: Amundsen's success rested on decisive choices (dogs, skiing, depots, focused planning), not luck; Scott was not weak or cowardly — method and margins, plus brutal conditions, doomed his return; Shackleton never reached the Pole; man-hauling was not as effective as dogs and exhausted Scott's team; and these are documented real expeditions, not legends.

Sequencing and sorting/matching tasks can check classification and recall but do not on their own elicit the empathy and causal reasoning that are the central value of the topic; use them alongside explanation and discussion.

Role-play and simulation are proposed approaches with distinct observable affordances (interrogating reasoning; feeling consequences); maps, timelines and primary sources also teach the events and comparison. No single medium is required or proven superior by the sources.

Keep the '14 December 1911' and '34 days later' dates (from the cited sources) and the ~800-mile open-boat voyage figure (from the original guidance text, not the source claims); present them as historical facts and note they are unverified here.

probeDeeper: Name one decision Amundsen made that Scott didn't, and say how it helped.
Why might man-hauling sledges leave a team more worn down than using dogs?
'Bad luck' and 'poor planning' can both be true. Which do you think mattered more here, and why?
Shackleton didn't even reach the Pole and lost his ship. Why is his expedition still remembered as a triumph?
assess.correctAnswer: They did NOT do the same thing — key decisions differed and mattered. Amundsen relied on dog sleds (fast, and dogs could be used for food), laid well-stocked supply depots, and specialised in polar travel; Scott depended heavily on man-hauling (exhausting) and troubled ponies/motor sledges, with thinner margins for supplies. So Amundsen's planning and transport choices gave him a real edge in speed and safety, while Scott's team was worn down and caught with too little in reserve. Bad weather played a part, but the outcome wasn't just luck. (Shackleton's later Endurance expedition, ship crushed by ice, is remembered for bringing every man home alive.)

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Scott just had bad luck / Amundsen got lucky' — outcome attributed to chance, not choices.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up the choices side by side (transport, depots, experience); show how they shaped speed, energy and safety margins.
errorPatterns.distractor: The teams did basically the same thing — Scott just had worse luck with the weather.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the result by weather/luck alone; names no differing decisions.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Scott was simply weak / not brave enough' — blames character, ignoring fine margins and hard choices.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe: Scott's team showed great courage; the difference was method and margins, not bravery. Judge decisions, not worth.
errorPatterns.distractor: Scott failed because he just wasn't brave or tough enough.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses Scott as a failure or coward rather than analysing decisions and conditions.

errorPatterns.pattern: Muddles the three expeditions/outcomes — mixes Amundsen, Scott and Shackleton.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort the facts: Amundsen (first, dogs, survived); Scott (second, man-hauling, died returning); Shackleton (1914, Endurance crushed, all saved).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes dogs to Scott, death to Amundsen, or the crushed ship to the wrong person.

responseLevels.gap: Explains the outcome as luck or Scott's weakness; thinks the teams did the same thing.
responseLevels.full: Contrasts multiple decisions (dogs, depots, specialism vs man-hauling, thin margins) as the real edge, acknowledges weather as a factor not the whole story, and correctly separates Amundsen, Scott and Shackleton.
responseLevels.partial: Names one difference (e.g. dogs vs man-hauling) but leans on luck/character for the rest, or muddles the expeditions.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In 1911 Amundsen and Scott both raced for the South Pole. Amundsen arrived first on 14 December using dog sleds and pre-placed supply depots; Scott arrived 34 days later after man-hauling his sledges, and died with his team on the way back. A student says 'Scott just had worse luck with the weather — the two teams did basically the same thing.' Did they do the same thing, or did their DECISIONS differ in ways that mattered? Explain what gave Amundsen the edge.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student crediting pure luck says the teams did the same thing; a student with the concept contrasts specific decisions (dogs + depots + specialism vs man-hauling + thin margins) as the cause. Asking whether their decisions differed forces analysis beyond 'bad luck'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 (10–90) using place value and properties (7×30 = 7×3 tens = 21 tens = 210).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3–Y4 use place value and known facts to multiply mentally; underpins Y4 short multiplication and estimation.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.NBT.3 — 'multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 (e.g. 9×80, 5×60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.'
• Operational details — the reasoning, not the trick, is the objective: 7×30 = 7×(3×10) = (7×3)×10 = 21×10 = 210 (associativity + place value). The '×10 shifts digits one place left' understanding must replace the dangerous 'just add a zero' rule (which breaks for decimals later). Use place-value counters/columns and the known fact 7×3=21 scaled by ten. This is the engine of estimation (234×5 ≈ 200×5) and a stepping-stone to × multiples of 100/1000 and to long multiplication.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): 3×40 via 3×4 tens with counters. Tier B (age 8–9): any 1-digit × multiple of 10 mentally, explaining via the known fact and place value. Tier C (age 9): explain why the product gains a zero in terms of ten-times-larger, and use the skill to estimate a larger product.
bestPractices: Reason from the known fact scaled by ten: 7×30 = (7×3) tens = 21 tens = 210, using associativity and place value explicitly.
Teach 'ten times larger → digits shift one place left', NOT 'add a zero', so the idea survives the move to decimals.
Use place-value counters and columns so 21 tens visibly becomes 210 (regrouping ten tens into a hundred).
Connect immediately to estimation — rounding a factor to a multiple of ten to bound a larger product.
Extend the same reasoning to multiples of 100/1000 once secure, keeping the place-value story constant.
keyRepresentations: Place-value counters / columns — 21 tens regrouped to 210
Known-fact-×-ten chain (7×3=21 → 7×30=210)
Gattegno/place-value chart — the leftward digit shift for ×10
Number line in tens — skip counting by 30
commonMisconceptions: Over-relying on 'add a zero' as a rule without understanding, which later misfires with decimals (0.7×30).
Multiplying the wrong part (7×30 as 21 rather than 210) — losing the place-value scaling.
Adding an extra or too few zeros through miscounting places.
Not connecting 7×30 to the known fact 7×3, so it's computed from scratch.
Confusing multiplying by a multiple of ten with adding tens.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 (10–90) by reasoning from a known fact scaled by ten — 7×30 = 7×(3×10) = (7×3)×10 = 21 tens = 210 — using place value and the associative property. The objective is the reasoning, not the 'add a zero' trick: learners should understand multiplying by 10 as making a number ten times larger so its digits shift one place left, which is why 210 ends in a zero (the ones place empties). This understanding survives the later move to decimals, where 'add a zero' fails (0.7×10 = 7, not 0.70), and powers estimation (234×5 ≈ 200×5) and multiplication by multiples of 100/1000.

activities.title: Scaling a known fact by ten with place-value counters
feedback: If a learner writes 7×30 = 21, point back to the rods: 'You took three tens seven times, not three ones. Count the tens — 21 tens is 210.'
If a learner gives 210 but only explains 'you add a zero', ask them to show it with the rods: 'Where did that zero come from? Watch the ones column empty when everything grows ten times bigger.'
If a learner miscounts zeros (e.g. 2100), have them regroup the tens carefully onto the place-value chart and reread each column.
Affirm reasoning that names the known fact: 'Yes — knowing 7×3 = 21 let you get 7×30 without starting over.'
activities.rationale: Place-value counters and regrouping make '21 tens = 210' a visible exchange rather than a memorised rule, and tie the standard's required place-value/property strategy directly to the known single-digit fact.
sourceClaims: 3.NBT.3 requires multiplying one-digit numbers by multiples of 10 (10–90) using place-value and property strategies.
Y3–Y4 pupils use place value and known facts to multiply mentally, underpinning short multiplication and estimation.
learnerActions: Build the known fact 7×3 as an array of 21 single counters (or draw them).
Replace each single counter with a rod of ten, stating aloud 'now there are 21 tens'.
Regroup the 21 tens: exchange ten tens for one hundred, repeat, ending with 2 hundreds and 1 ten.
Record the result on a place-value chart (hundreds | tens | ones) and read it as 210.
Say the full reasoning chain: '7×3 = 21, so 7×30 = 21 tens = 210, because 30 is 3 tens.'
Repeat for 5×60 (5×6 = 30, so 5×60 = 30 tens = 300) and 3×40 (3×4 = 12, so 3×40 = 12 tens = 120), each time naming the known single-digit fact first.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by a multiple of 10 is multiplying by the single-digit fact and then by ten; the extra zero in the product is the result of every digit shifting one place left as the amount becomes ten times larger, not a zero 'stuck on the end'.

activities.title: Why 'add a zero' is not the real rule
feedback: If a learner says 0.7×10 = 0.70, show the shift on the chart: 'Sliding left makes 7, not 0.70. The zero rule breaks here — but the shift still works.'
If a learner adds too many or too few zeros for the 7×300 extension, count the place shifts together: '×100 means shifting two columns left.'
Encourage precise language: 'ten times larger' and 'shifts one place left' rather than 'add a zero'.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting the whole-number case with a decimal case targets the misconception that 'add a zero' is the underlying rule, replacing it with the place-value shift that generalises.
sourceClaims: Teach multiplying by ten as a place-value shift (ten times larger) rather than 'adding a zero', which fails for decimals.
learnerActions: On a place-value chart, place 7 in the ones column, then slide it one column left to make 70; describe what happened to the digit.
Do the same with 21: slide it one column left so the ones place becomes empty and a 0 fills it, giving 210.
Now try 0.7×10 on the same chart: slide 0.7 one column left to get 7 — notice no zero was added.
State in your own words why '×10 shifts digits one place left' is safer than 'add a zero'.
(Optional extension, once the tens pattern feels secure) Predict and check 7×300 using the same idea: 7×3 = 21, shifted two places = 2100.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by ten always shifts digits one place to the left; for whole numbers this shows up as a trailing zero, but the shift — not the zero itself — is the real rule, which is why it still works for decimals.

activities.title: Using tens facts to estimate
feedback: If a learner rounds the wrong way or forgets to scale, revisit the known-fact chain: '6×4 = 24, so 6×40 = 240.'
If a learner treats the estimate as exact, prompt: 'Is 6×43 more or less than 6×40? By about how much?'
Praise clear connections between the rounded factor and the place-value reasoning.
activities.rationale: Multiplying by multiples of ten is a useful tool for estimation (the standard itself only names place-value and property-based strategies for products in the range 10–90); applying it keeps the place-value story in a purposeful context.
sourceClaims: Y3–Y4 pupils use place value and known facts to multiply mentally, underpinning short multiplication and estimation.
learnerActions: Estimate 6×43 by rounding 43 to 40 and computing 6×40 = 240 (6×4 = 24, so 6×40 = 24 tens = 240), explaining the reasoning.

(Optional extension, once the tens case is secure) Estimate 234×5 by rounding 234 to 200 and computing 200×5 = 1000 (2×5 = 10, so 200×5 = 10 hundreds = 1000), using the same known-fact-then-scale reasoning.
Compare each estimate to the exact answer (6×43 = 258; 234×5 = 1170) and say whether the estimate is high or low and roughly by how much.
Make up one estimation of your own using a multiple of ten and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by a multiple of ten (and, by the same reasoning, a multiple of a hundred) lets you quickly bound or approximate a larger product, which checks whether an exact answer is reasonable.

activities.title: Spot and explain the error
feedback: For '7×30 = 21': 'The 30 is three tens, so the answer must be 21 tens = 210 — ten times bigger than 21.'
For '8×40 = 32': 'That's just 8×4. Scale by ten: 32 tens = 320.'
Confirm the correct ones (5×60 = 300 and 9×80 = 720) and ask the learner to articulate the reasoning, not just the verdict.
activities.rationale: Identifying and repairing errors consolidates the reasoning and surfaces whether a learner can justify answers rather than apply a rote appendage; this is a consolidation/check activity that tests fluency rather than a substitute for building the scaling intuition with counters.
learnerActions: Decide whether each worked example is correct: 7×30 = 21; 5×60 = 300; 8×40 = 32; 9×80 = 720.
For any that are wrong, say exactly what went wrong (e.g. multiplied the tens as ones, or dropped/added a zero).
Rewrite each incorrect one with the full reasoning chain to make it correct.
Explain in words why 5×60 = 300 ends in a zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Common slips — multiplying the tens digit as ones, or miscounting zeros — can be caught by checking against the known-fact-times-ten chain.

constraints: The learning objective is the reasoning (known fact × ten via associativity and place value), not a memorised 'add a zero' step; any activity must require the learner to explain where the zero comes from.
Teach 'ten times larger → digits shift one place left' explicitly, because 'add a zero' misfires for decimals (0.7×10 = 7).
Secure the underlying single-digit fact (e.g. 7×3) first; if it is shaky, the whole derivation is unreliable.

Recognition/multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank checks test fluency but do not by themselves build the scaling intuition; use them for consolidation alongside construction with counters and spoken reasoning.
Physical base-ten equipment and a drawn or on-screen place-value chart are both suitable; manipulatives make the regrouping of ten tens into a hundred concrete.
Extend the identical place-value story to multiples of 100/1000 only once the tens case is secure; the 7×300 step is presented as an optional extension for this reason.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 7×3=21 so 7×30=210; 5×6=30 so 5×60=300; 3×4=12 so 3×40=120; 6×4=24 so 6×40=240; 8×4=32 so 8×40=320; 9×8=72 so 9×80=720; 7×3=21 so 7×300=2100; 6×43=258; 234×5=1170; 2×5=10 so 200×5=1000 — all check out. The 'spot the error' items 7×30=21 and 8×40=32 are intentionally incorrect for learners to catch, with corrected values (210, 320) supplied in feedback.
Decimal check: 0.7×10=7 (not 0.70); the shift-left framing is correct and the 'add a zero' rule correctly fails here.
Source note: the CCSS 3.NBT.3 and NCETM claims are marked unverified (verified:false) in the original row; retained as cited without upgrading their evidence status.

Original source row legacy vocabulary describing specific interactive formats (e.g. a 'scaler' widget, tap-to-reveal, lift-the-flap) has been generalised into medium-independent learner actions while preserving the live-regrouping mechanism as an optional illustration.

The decimal example (0.7×10), the 200×5 estimation step and the 7×300 extension may exceed the typical age-band comfort zone; all are retained from the original design but flagged as needing teacher judgement/support.

probeDeeper: What does 7 × 30 have to do with 7 × 3?
Why does the answer end in a zero — where does that zero come from?
How could 6 × 40 help you estimate 6 × 43?
If you know 7 × 3 = 21, what is 7 × 300?
assess.correctAnswer: 210 and 240. The teacher watches for the child reasoning '7 × 3 tens = 21 tens = 210' — using the single-digit fact and scaling by ten — rather than a disconnected zero-adding rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: multiplies the tens digit as ones — 7×30 treated as 7×3 = 21, forgetting the ten (answer 21)
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason 7 × 3 TENS = 21 tens = 210; use base-ten equipment to show three tens taken seven times.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer is ten times too small; child computes 7×3 and stops

errorPatterns.pattern: 'adds a zero' as a rote rule with no meaning — works here but cannot say why, and will misapply it to decimals later
errorPatterns.nextMove: tie the zero to 'ten times bigger': multiplying by 30 is multiplying by 3 then by 10, and ×10 shifts digits one place, showing up as a zero for whole numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gets 210 but explains only 'you add a zero'; cannot connect to 7×3

errorPatterns.pattern: not fluent in the underlying single-digit fact, so the whole derivation is shaky
errorPatterns.nextMove: shore up the single-digit fact before layering the tens reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child hesitates or errs on 7×3 itself

responseLevels.gap: multiplies the tens digit as ones (answer ten times too small), or has no reasoning at all.
responseLevels.full: reasons via the known fact scaled by ten ('7 × 3 tens = 21 tens'), explains the zero as the result of ×10, and uses the skill to estimate larger products.
responseLevels.partial: gets the right answer via 'add a zero' but cannot connect it to the single-digit fact or explain why the zero appears.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to work out 7 × 30 and 6 × 40 in their head, saying how they did it. Watch whether they use the known fact (7×3) and reason about tens, or whether they just 'add a zero' without understanding — then probe by asking what 7 × 30 has to do with 7 × 3.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Multiplying by a multiple of ten is the first place the 'add a zero' shortcut appears; watching HOW the child reasons (does the zero come from 'ten times', or is it a rote appendage?) reveals whether place-value understanding underpins the shortcut — essential because the same rule misfires later on decimals.

pedagogy.summary: At 9-11 the star life cycle is a story with a BRANCH decided by one variable — mass. All stars are born in clouds of gas and dust (nebulae/molecular clouds) that gravity pulls together until the core gets hot and dense enough to FUSE hydrogen into helium; this fusion is what makes a star shine, for millions to billions of years (the long, stable 'main sequence' — where our Sun is now). When the core's hydrogen runs low the star swells and then dies — and HOW it dies depends on how massive it was: lower-mass, Sun-like stars gently puff off their outer layers and leave a small, cooling core called a WHITE DWARF, while very massive stars end in a colossal SUPERNOVA explosion. The two big ideas are (1) the born→shine→die sequence powered by hydrogen fusion, and (2) mass decides the ending.
bestPractices: Tell it as a life story with named stages — nebula → (protostar) → main-sequence star fusing hydrogen → swelling giant → white dwarf OR supernova — so the sequence has a clear shape the child can retell.

Make MASS the pivot and teach the branch explicitly: same beginning for all stars, but massive stars live fast and die in a supernova, while smaller stars live long and fade to a white dwarf — 'how big it is decides how it ends'.
Anchor 'why stars shine' in fusion at an age-appropriate level: the core squeezes hydrogen together to make helium and releases energy — no need for equations, but name fusion as the engine.

Use real imagery (nebulae like Orion, a supernova remnant, the Sun as a main-sequence star) to keep the abstract timescales tangible and awe-driven; connect to prior learning that the Sun is an ordinary main-sequence star.

Handle the enormous timescales carefully: stars live millions-to-billions of years, so we never watch one star change — we see many stars at different stages, like photographing a forest to infer a tree's life.
keyRepresentations: Life-cycle flow with a branch: nebula → main-sequence star → [low mass → giant → white dwarf] / [high mass → supergiant → supernova]
A MASS dial/scale that sends the same starting star down the small-star or big-star path
Nebula ('star nursery') image where gravity clumps gas into a new star
Side-by-side endings: gentle planetary-nebula + white dwarf vs violent supernova
The Sun marked as 'here, now' on the main sequence, roughly halfway through its life
commonMisconceptions: Thinking all stars end the same way — not realising a star's MASS decides whether it becomes a white dwarf or explodes as a supernova.
Believing stars are 'on fire'/burning like a bonfire, rather than shining by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium.
Thinking we can watch a single star go through its life — missing that the stages take millions/billions of years and we infer the cycle from many stars at different stages.
Assuming bigger stars live longer (they actually burn out far faster) — confusing size with lifespan.
Thinking a star's death is a total disappearance, not realising it leaves a remnant (white dwarf, or after a supernova a dense core) and scatters material that seeds new stars.
Confusing a nebula (gas-and-dust cloud where stars form) with a galaxy (a vast collection of stars).

learn.summary: Teach the star life cycle (ages 9-11) as a story with one branch point decided by MASS: all stars are born in clouds of gas and dust (nebulae) that gravity pulls together until the core is hot and dense enough to fuse hydrogen into helium — which is what makes a star shine for millions to billions of years on the stable main sequence. When core hydrogen runs low the star swells and dies, and HOW it dies depends on mass: lower-mass Sun-like stars swell to a giant, puff off their outer layers and leave a cooling white dwarf, while very massive stars swell to a supergiant and end in a supernova. Two big ideas: the born→shine→die sequence powered by fusion, and mass deciding the ending (including the surprising twist that bigger stars live SHORTER lives). A mass-controlled interactive may be a particularly direct way for a learner to discover mass→fate; a labelled branching diagram, awe imagery, and a sequencing check are valuable alternatives serving different purposes.

activities.title: Set the mass, watch the fate
feedback: If a learner expects the big star to last longest, point to the two lifespan counters: the massive star's ran out first — more fuel but burned far faster and hotter, lasting only a few million years versus billions for a small star.

If a learner thinks the Sun will explode, replay the low-mass/Sun path: it swells into a giant, then sheds a ring and leaves a white dwarf — no supernova; supernovae are reserved for much more massive stars.

If a learner calls the shining 'fire', note the star shines by fusion (joining hydrogen into helium in the core), not by burning like a bonfire; ordinary burning could never release enough energy to keep a star shining for millions or billions of years.
Reinforce the click-moment: 'Same birth — the mass you set decided the ending.'
activities.rationale: The concept is a process with a single-variable branch, so letting the learner set mass and watch the fate follow is intended to turn 'mass decides fate' from a told fact into a discovered one; the lifespan readout directly confronts the 'bigger lives longer' misconception.
sourceClaims: Stars form in large clouds of gas and dust (molecular clouds/nebulae) that collapse under gravity into protostars; main-sequence stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores, which releases energy that balances gravity; the Sun is a main-sequence star about midway through its life.

The details of a star's death depend strongly on its MASS: lower-mass, Sun-like stars shed their outer layers as a planetary nebula and leave a white dwarf, while massive stars end in a supernova (leaving a dense remnant); more massive stars burn their fuel far faster and live much shorter lives.
learnerActions: Start with a glowing cloud of gas and dust (a nebula) on screen and a single MASS dial/slider as the control.

Set the mass LOW and press play: watch the cloud collapse, a star ignite (hydrogen fusing into helium), shine steadily for a very long time, then swell into a giant and gently puff off a glowing ring, leaving a tiny white ember (white dwarf).
Rewind, crank the mass dial HIGH, and press play again: watch the star blaze through its life startlingly fast, swell into a supergiant, and end in a blinding supernova.
Read a lifespan counter each run so the 'live fast, die young' contrast is concrete — the massive star's counter runs out far sooner.
Try a 'Sun' preset that drops a marker on the main sequence 'here, now', roughly halfway along the gentle low-mass path.
Say in your own words what stayed the same across both runs and what changed.
activities.intendedInsight: It is the SAME kind of birth for every star; how massive the star is decides how it dies — and the biggest stars die youngest, not oldest.

activities.title: Walk the branching life-cycle diagram
feedback: If a learner stumbles on the order, have them re-tap the stages from nebula to ending before retelling.
If a learner forgets the branch, point back to the labelled fork: small star → giant → white dwarf, massive star → supergiant → supernova.
Confirm the Sun sits on the gentle low-mass path heading to white dwarf, not supernova.
activities.rationale: A labelled branching diagram with tap-to-reveal facts reliably teaches the sequence and the two endings and supports retelling; it depicts the branch clearly even though it does not let the learner set the mass and watch the fate follow, so it complements rather than replaces the interactive.
sourceClaims: The details of a star's death depend strongly on its MASS: lower-mass, Sun-like stars shed their outer layers as a planetary nebula and leave a white dwarf, while massive stars end in a supernova (leaving a dense remnant); more massive stars burn their fuel far faster and live much shorter lives.
learnerActions: Follow a labelled life-cycle flow with the fork at the main-sequence stage: nebula → main-sequence star, then branching to [low mass → giant → white dwarf] OR [high mass → supergiant → supernova].
Tap each stage to reveal what is happening there (gravity clumps gas; the core fuses hydrogen into helium; the star swells; the ending).
Use the clearly labelled fork marked 'small star' vs 'massive star' to state which ending each path leads to and why.
Open the flap on the Sun to read 'a main-sequence star, about halfway through its life'.
Retell the whole sequence from memory, naming each stage including the giant or supergiant step.
activities.intendedInsight: The life cycle has a clear, retellable shape with named stages, and the ending forks on whether the star is small (giant → white dwarf) or massive (supergiant → supernova).

activities.title: Awe imagery of birth and death
feedback: If a learner expects to watch a single star age, remind them each stage lasts millions to billions of years; astronomers piece the cycle together from many stars at different stages.
If a learner confuses a nebula with a galaxy, clarify: a nebula is a cloud of gas and dust where stars form; a galaxy is a vast collection of stars.
Link the Sun image to prior learning that it is an ordinary main-sequence star.
activities.rationale: Spectacular imagery builds engagement and anchors the enormous timescales, and the 'many stars at different stages' framing addresses the misconception that we observe one star's whole life; this supports wonder and timescale understanding rather than the causal mass→fate move.
sourceClaims: Stars form in large clouds of gas and dust (molecular clouds/nebulae) that collapse under gravity into protostars; main-sequence stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores, which releases energy that balances gravity; the Sun is a main-sequence star about midway through its life.
learnerActions: View real imagery of a star nursery nebula (e.g. the Orion Nebula), the Sun as an ordinary main-sequence star, and a supernova remnant.
Optionally take a fly-through of a nebula or a supernova set-piece as a wonder moment.
Match each image to its place on the life-cycle story you learned.
Discuss why we never watch one star change: stages take millions to billions of years, so we see many stars at different stages — like photographing a forest to infer one tree's life.
activities.intendedInsight: The abstract timescales become tangible and awe-inspiring through real images, and we infer the cycle from many stars caught at different stages rather than watching one.

activities.title: Check the sequence and the branch
feedback: If a learner orders the stages wrongly, replay the diagram walkthrough and retry.
If a learner picks 'size/brightness' over mass, restate that mass is the property that decides both lifespan and ending.
If a learner says the massive star lasts longer, explain it burns its larger fuel supply far faster and hotter, so it lasts only a few million years while the Sun shines for billions.
activities.rationale: A short sequencing-and-matching check verifies the stage order and the mass branch after teaching; it confirms recall but does not itself build the causal 'mass decides fate' intuition, so it belongs after the interactive or diagram work.
sourceClaims: The details of a star's death depend strongly on its MASS: lower-mass, Sun-like stars shed their outer layers as a planetary nebula and leave a white dwarf, while massive stars end in a supernova (leaving a dense remnant); more massive stars burn their fuel far faster and live much shorter lives.
learnerActions: Put the life stages in order with the branch intact: nebula → main-sequence star → then either (low mass) giant → white dwarf, or (high mass) supergiant → supernova.
Answer: 'What single property decides whether a star becomes a white dwarf or a supernova?' (its mass).
Match each mass (small / massive) to its ending (white dwarf / supernova).
Answer the surprise puzzle: which lasts longer, a huge massive star or a small one like the Sun — and why?
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can recall and apply the stage order and its branch, name mass as the deciding property, and recognise that massive stars live shortest.

constraints: Keep fusion age-appropriate: name it as the core squeezing hydrogen together to make helium and releasing energy; no equations required.
Emphasise that mass decides BOTH how a star lives (lifespan) and how it dies — and surface the counter-intuitive twist that more massive stars burn out far faster, so they live shorter lives.

The Sun will NOT supernova: it becomes a red giant then sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf; reserve supernovae for much more massive stars (which swell to supergiants first).
Keep the two swollen stages distinct: low-mass stars become giants before the white dwarf; massive stars become supergiants before the supernova.
Address the timescale honestly: stars live millions to billions of years, so we never watch one star change — we infer the cycle from many stars at different stages.
Distinguish a nebula (gas-and-dust cloud where stars form) from a galaxy (a vast collection of stars).
Note that a star's death leaves a remnant (white dwarf, or a dense core after a supernova) and scatters material that seeds new stars — death is not total disappearance.
The sequencing/matching check confirms recall of the order and branch but does not by itself build the causal mass→fate intuition; use it after hands-on or diagram work.
The awe-imagery and fly-through serve wonder and timescale understanding; they are not required to grasp mass→fate and should not replace the branching model.

The mass dial, lifespan counter, play/rewind controls, Sun preset, tap-to-reveal stages and labelled fork are illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory; any medium that lets a learner vary mass and see the resulting ending and lifespan serves the same purpose.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims are cited as directly supporting the teaching principles (fusion as the shining mechanism; mass deciding death type and lifespan). Citation does not establish that any specific activity here was empirically tested or that one medium is superior to another.

The legacy row asserted '3D adds awe without being needed' and that a quiz/conversation 'can't build the causal intuition' as near-universal claims; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. Internal fit rankings and artefact-type labels were removed and not treated as pedagogical laws.

Editor note: the summary previously called the interactive 'the richest way' to discover mass→fate; this unqualified superiority claim was softened to 'may be a particularly direct way', consistent with the untested-proposal framing.

Verified-resolved: the earlier branch error (both mass paths routed through a single 'giant', with 'supergiant' only tacked onto the massive path) is corrected so the fork sits at the main sequence with distinct giant (low-mass) and supergiant (high-mass) stages, matching the original key representation across summary, diagram, check and constraints.

Self-audit of science content otherwise found the born→shine→die sequence, fusion of hydrogen to helium, mass-dependent endings, the Sun's white-dwarf fate, and the massive-stars-die-young twist consistent across the pedagogy, assessment and source fields.

probeDeeper: Which lasts longer — a huge massive star or a small one like the Sun — and why is that surprising?
What will actually happen to the Sun at the end of its life, if not a supernova?
What is going on inside a star to make it shine, if it isn't ordinary fire?
What single property of a star decides how it will live and how it will die?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the Sun is too small to explode as a supernova. At the end of its life it will swell into a red giant, then gently shed its outer layers and shrink into a white dwarf; only much more massive stars end in supernovae. And the puzzle's answer is surprising: the biggest, most massive stars actually live the SHORTEST lives, not the longest. Even though they hold more fuel, they burn it enormously faster and more furiously, so they last only a few million years, while a small star like the Sun sips its fuel and shines for billions of years. A star's MASS decides both how it lives and how it dies.

errorPatterns.pattern: the biggest stars live the longest because they have the most fuel
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain massive stars burn their fuel far faster and hotter, so they last only a few million years, while small stars like the Sun last billions.
errorPatterns.distractor: The most massive stars live the longest, because they have the most fuel to burn.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child reasons more fuel means a longer life

errorPatterns.pattern: our Sun will end its life by exploding as a supernova
errorPatterns.nextMove: Only much more massive stars supernova; the Sun will become a red giant and then a white dwarf — no explosion.
errorPatterns.distractor: When it dies, our Sun will explode in a giant supernova.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child predicts a supernova for the Sun

errorPatterns.pattern: stars are balls of fire, burning like a bonfire
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stars shine by nuclear FUSION — joining hydrogen into helium in the core — not by ordinary burning; there's no fire and no oxygen out there.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child describes a star as on fire or combusting like burning wood

responseLevels.gap: Thinks big stars live longest and/or the Sun will supernova; may believe stars burn like fire.
responseLevels.full: Explains mass decides fate and lifespan — massive stars burn fast and die young in supernovae, small stars like the Sun last billions of years and end as white dwarfs — and that stars shine by fusion, not burning.
responseLevels.partial: Describes the stages (nebula → fusion → death) and knows massive stars supernova, but holds the more-fuel-longer-life idea or is unsure of the Sun's fate.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Our Sun is a fairly small-to-medium star. When it reaches the end of its life, will it explode in a giant supernova like the biggest stars do? And here's a puzzle: do the biggest, most massive stars live the LONGEST, because they have the most fuel? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two intuitive-but-wrong ideas are tested at once: that the Sun will supernova, and that more fuel means a longer life. A child who understands stellar life cycles says the Sun becomes a white dwarf (no supernova) and that massive stars die fastest because they burn fuel far faster. The 'why' tier surfaces the mass-decides-fate-and-lifespan idea.

sources.claim: Stars form in large clouds of gas and dust (molecular clouds/nebulae) that collapse under gravity into protostars; main-sequence stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores, which releases energy that balances gravity; the Sun is a main-sequence star about midway through its life.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11; Antarctica is governed by the Antarctic Treaty (signed 1959, in force 1961), which sets the continent aside for peaceful purposes and science, bans military activity and mining, and now has over 50 signatory countries; international research stations study climate, astronomy, biology and geology — making Antarctica the closest thing on Earth to a continent run for science rather than politics.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 Geography (locational knowledge; how places are used and governed) and Citizenship links (rules, cooperation, shared resources).
• Standards—US: NGSS science-and-society connections (ESS3 human activity; engineering constraints of remote stations) plus civics standards on international cooperation.
• Operational details: two ideas — (1) the Treaty as an unusual act of international COOPERATION (no country owns Antarctica; no armies, weapons testing or mining; open science and inspection), and (2) what the science actually is (ice cores and climate, dark-sky astronomy, penguin and krill biology, meteorites and geology). Emphasise WHY a whole continent kept for peace and science is remarkable and fragile. Keep the values discussable without turning it into abstract politics.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (9) state that no country owns Antarctica and it is kept for peaceful science; Tier B (10) name two things the Treaty bans (military use, mining) and one kind of science done there; Tier C (11) explain why an internationally shared, science-first continent is valuable and why keeping it that way is difficult.
bestPractices: Frame the Treaty as a rare, deliberate choice — nations agreeing NOT to claim, arm or mine a continent — so its significance stands out
Ground the abstract governance in concrete station life and real science (ice cores, telescopes, penguin studies) so it isn't dry politics
Use the ban list (no military, no weapons testing, no mining, open inspection) as memorable anchors
Discuss why cooperation is fragile as resources and access grow more tempting, without heavy politics
Connect to pupils' experience of shared rules that protect a common space (a shared playground/library)
keyRepresentations: Research-station cutaway showing labs for climate, astronomy and biology
Treaty timeline and 'what it bans / what it allows' summary card
Map of Antarctica dotted with international stations from many nations
'Who owns Antarctica?' answer graphic: no one — held in trust for peace and science
commonMisconceptions: A country owns Antarctica (or the country nearest it) — no nation owns it; claims are set aside under the Treaty
People can mine or drill Antarctica for resources — mining is banned under the Treaty
Anyone can do anything there — activities are restricted to peaceful, scientific ones and are open to inspection
The stations are permanent towns — they are research bases staffed by rotating scientists, not settled cities
The Treaty is guaranteed forever — it depends on continued cooperation and could face pressure as resources tempt nations

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: learners come to understand that no country's ownership of Antarctica is recognised (seven countries have claims, but the Treaty froze them), that the Antarctic Treaty (signed 1959, in force 1961, now 50+ parties) reserves the continent for peaceful, scientific use and bans military activity, that its 1991 Environmental Protocol (in force 1998) adds a ban on mining, and that real science there includes ice-core climate study, dark-sky astronomy, penguin/krill biology and meteorite geology — making it the closest thing on Earth to a continent run for science rather than politics. The guidance pairs a labelled research-station exploration (intended to carry the core facts in a vivid setting) with role-play/debate (intended to develop why cooperation matters and is fragile), plus optional recall checks and a system mini-game, each with stated purposes and limits. All activities are untested proposals, not validated interventions, and no source verifies the effectiveness of any chosen medium.

activities.title: Explore an Antarctic research base: who owns it and what is studied
feedback: If a learner says a particular country owns the land under its station or flag: the Treaty froze all territorial claims — building a base and flying a flag does not create ownership; decisions are made jointly by the signatory nations.

If a learner says mining would be fine if done carefully: distinguish sampling for knowledge (e.g. ice cores) from extraction for profit — the Treaty and its Environmental Protocol ban mineral resource exploitation.
If a learner thinks the stations are permanent towns: these are research bases staffed by rotating scientists, not settled cities.
If a learner lists the rules but can't say who decides: the rules exist because 50+ nations agreed to share the continent, so the agreement — not any single country — decides.
activities.rationale: Interactive exploration where examining each lab reveals its science and the flag-map reveals 'no owner, peaceful use only' is intended to deliver the facts within a vivid setting at a 9–11 grain, grounding abstract governance in concrete station life so it is not dry politics. This medium match is a design intent only; its effectiveness is untested and no source verifies it.
learnerActions: Explore a cutaway of an Antarctic research base, examining each facility in turn.
At the ice-core lab, note how scientists read ancient climate from air trapped in old ice.
At the rooftop telescope, note why the dark, dry, still polar sky suits astronomy.
At the biology hut, note penguin and krill studies; at the meteorite store, note rocks from space found on the ice.

Open a flag-map showing the research stations run by about 30 nations (more than 50 countries have joined the Treaty) and answer 'Who owns Antarctica?' before revealing the answer: no one's ownership is recognised — seven countries have claims, but the 1959 Treaty froze them and keeps the continent for peaceful science with no armies, and a later 1991 agreement (the Environmental Protocol) bans mining.
Consider a follow-up prompt: 'Could that change?' and note the pressure as resources grow tempting.
State in your own words two things the Treaty bans and one kind of science done in Antarctica.
activities.intendedInsight: No country's ownership of Antarctica is recognised; the Antarctic Treaty and its later Environmental Protocol reserve the whole continent for peaceful science and ban military activity and mining — an unusual, deliberate act of cooperation that is valuable and fragile.

activities.title: In role: talk to a station scientist and debate the mining ban
feedback: If a learner frames it as one country deciding: remind them all signatory nations agreed together; no single nation can override the shared rules.
If a learner says it's lawless because no one lives there: contrast 'empty of residents' with 'governed by agreement' — 50+ nations signed binding rules even though no one permanently settles.
Reward reasoning that connects the banned activities (military, mining) to nations choosing to share rather than claim.
activities.rationale: Talking in role and debating is intended to make the cooperation and its fragility discussable and to develop the 'why it matters' reasoning, while the baseline facts are better carried by the labelled visual. This is a proposed strong extension; the efficacy of the role-play is untested and no source verifies it.
learnerActions: Take the role of a visitor speaking with an Antarctic station scientist about daily life on the ice and why no country owns the continent.
Ask why over 50 countries would agree to set aside arguments about who owns land and not to mine there — and what they gain instead (shared, open science).
Debate the question: should the ban on mining ever change? Argue both why keeping it protects a shared space and why pressure to change it grows as resources become tempting.

Respond to a challenge case: a new country wants to join — explain that it must accept the same Treaty rules (no new territorial claims, no military, open inspection), and that most members have also signed the Environmental Protocol, which bans mining.
activities.intendedInsight: The Treaty is a shared agreement among nations, not a list handed down by one authority; cooperation over a common space is valuable and can be fragile when resources tempt nations.

activities.title: Check and apply: what the Treaty bans and why
feedback: Target answer: No — the Antarctic Treaty (1959, in force 1961), now joined by 50+ countries, sets Antarctica aside for peaceful, scientific purposes only and bans military activity, and its 1991 Environmental Protocol bans mining; neither the company nor the army is allowed.

A strong answer explains the agreement froze ownership claims and transfers the principle to new cases (a new member must accept the same rules); a partial answer lists banned activities without connecting them to nations agreeing to share.
If a learner says the first or strongest country may mine: the Treaty set aside all territorial claims — there is no 'first-comer owns it'.
On the Arctic probe: treat it as open discussion — the Arctic is not governed by an equivalent single treaty, so there is no fixed answer expected.
activities.rationale: Recall-and-match checks confirm the baseline facts efficiently; the open diagnostic and probe questions are designed to discriminate learners who hold the 'shared agreement' concept from those who think the continent is owned or up for grabs. Recall-only items confirm facts but do not on their own build the sense of why the arrangement matters.
learnerActions: Answer the diagnostic case: a mining company has found valuable metals under Antarctic ice and wants to dig; an army wants to build a base. Are they allowed? Say yes or no, then explain WHICH rule decides.
Recall and match: name two things the Treaty bans and match areas of science (climate, astronomy, biology, geology) to what each studies.

Answer probing extensions: Does building a station and flying a flag mean a country owns that land? What stops the Treaty from being 'just words on paper'? Is the Arctic protected the same way, and why might the North differ from the South?
activities.intendedInsight: Antarctica is governed by a shared agreement that bans military use and mining and reserves it for cooperative science — the reason 'no' is given is that all signatory nations agreed, not that any one country is in charge.

activities.title: Optional: run a research station (engagement extension)
feedback: If a learner chooses a banned action (mining for profit, a military base): flag that the rules permit only peaceful science and that activities are open to inspection.
Connect the experience back to the main idea: the station operates under rules all nations agreed to.
activities.rationale: A system-style mini-game may add engagement and reinforce the 'peaceful science only, open to inspection' constraints, but the topic is fundamentally knowledge-and-values rather than a system to operate, so this is an optional supplement rather than the core. Any engagement benefit is a proposal, not an established finding.
learnerActions: Play a short 'run a research station' or 'allocate the science' activity: decide which projects to support (ice cores, telescope time, biology surveys, meteorite collection) and keep operations peaceful and within the rules.
After playing, state which activities the rules allowed and which were off-limits, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Antarctic activity is restricted to peaceful, scientific purposes and is open to inspection — operating a station means working within shared constraints, not doing whatever one wants.

constraints: Keep the values discussable as shared rules protecting a common space (like a shared playground or library); avoid turning it into abstract or partisan politics.
Recall-and-match checks confirm facts but do not by themselves elicit the reasoning about why a shared, science-first continent matters — pair them with the open diagnostic and discussion.

The labelled station exploration is a scaffold for the setting and facts; developing the reasoning about cooperation's value and fragility needs the role-play/debate or open prompts, not exploration alone.
Describe stations accurately as rotating research bases, not permanent settled towns.
The mini-game is an engagement extension; do not treat operating a simulated station as the core learning objective.
Present the Treaty's continuation as dependent on ongoing cooperation, not guaranteed forever.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both sources are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no human review or empirical effectiveness is claimed.

Historical/legal facts (Treaty signed 1959, in force 1961, 50+ parties, mining banned via the Environmental Protocol) should be confirmed against an authoritative current source before publication; figures such as party counts change over time.
The Arctic-comparison probe is open-ended; the Arctic is not governed by an equivalent single treaty, so treat it as a discussion prompt rather than expecting a fixed factual answer.

All activity sourceClaims were set to [] because the available sources support only the topic/content and curriculum fit, not the untested medium/method principles asserted in each rationale (interactive delivery, role-play reasoning, assessment discrimination). This avoids topic-level over-attribution.

Observations that recall checks alone do not build the reasoning, and that this topic does not need 3D, are scoped to this topic and medium, not established comparative efficacy findings; the categorical '3D adds nothing' phrasing from the source was dropped.

probeDeeper: Why would over 50 countries agree to give up the chance to own land and mine there — what do they get instead?
A country builds a research station and flies its flag on it. Does that mean it now owns that piece of Antarctica? How do you know?
What if a country secretly started mining anyway — what stops the treaty from just being words on paper?
Is the Arctic protected the same way? Why might the North be different from the South?
assess.correctAnswer: No. The Antarctic Treaty (signed 1959, in force since 1961), signed by over 50 countries, sets Antarctica aside for peaceful, scientific purposes only — it bans military activity and mining. So neither the mining company nor the army is allowed; the treaty reserves the whole continent for cooperative science, not national ownership or resource extraction.

errorPatterns.pattern: someone owns Antarctica — the country that discovered it or planted a flag can do what it likes ('Britain/America owns that part so they can mine it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: show the treaty froze all territorial claims; no country owns Antarctica and decisions are made together
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — whichever country claimed that area first is allowed to mine it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says a particular country can decide, or divides the continent up like colonies

errorPatterns.pattern: it's empty and lawless so it's up for grabs — 'no one lives there so anyone can take what they want'
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast empty-of-residents with governed-by-agreement; 50+ nations signed binding rules
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — nobody lives there so there's nothing stopping them
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reasons that because it's uninhabited there are no rules

errorPatterns.pattern: mining is fine if it's careful, or scientists dig things up too — confuses permitted research (ice cores) with banned commercial mining
errorPatterns.nextMove: distinguish sampling for knowledge from extraction for profit; the treaty and its Protocol ban mineral resource exploitation
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says mining is ok if done cleanly, or can't distinguish science drilling from mining

responseLevels.gap: Says a country owns Antarctica or can mine/build if strong or first; treats it like any other land to be claimed.
responseLevels.full: Explains the treaty as a shared agreement among many nations that reserves the whole continent for peaceful science, froze ownership claims and bans military use and mining; transfers the principle to a new case (a new country joining must accept the same rules).
responseLevels.partial: Knows mining and armies are banned and that it's 'for science', but states it as a list of rules without connecting them to nations AGREEING to share it — can't say who decides or why.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A mining company says it has found valuable metals under Antarctic ice and wants to dig them up, and an army wants to build a base there. Are they allowed to? Tell me yes or no, and then tell me WHY — what rule decides it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks Antarctica is owned or up-for-grabs will say the country that got there first, or the strongest, can mine or build; a child holding the treaty concept says no because ALL signatory nations agreed to keep it for peace and science. The reason-tier separates 'someone owns it' from 'it is governed by a shared agreement'.

sources.claim: KS2 pupils study how places are used and governed and develop citizenship ideas of rules and cooperation over shared spaces
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum, Geography KS2 and Citizenship guidance
