pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — How Fossils Form (ages 7–9): explain the basic sequence of fossilisation — an organism dies and is QUICKLY BURIED in sediment; over a very long time minerals seep in and replace the remains while the sediment hardens to rock, preserving the shape — and understand that fossilisation is RARE.
• Standards — UK (DfE): direct anchor — Y3 'Rocks' (recognise that fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock); uses correct vocabulary (sediment, minerals, rock).
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports grade-3 3-LS4-1 (fossils as evidence of past life) and the MS-ESS/MS-LS fossil-record strand; the process explains why the fossil record is patchy.
• Operational details — Teach as an ordered CAUSAL sequence with conditions, not just a list: (1) death; (2) RAPID burial in sediment (mud/sand) — the critical step, because exposed remains rot or are scavenged; (3) soft parts decay, hard parts (bone/shell/teeth) remain; (4) over millions of years, groundwater minerals permeate/replace the remains (permineralisation) and sediment compacts into rock; (5) uplift and erosion later expose it. Emphasise WHY it's rare (most organisms never get buried fast enough) so children understand the fossil record is incomplete — a key later idea. Keep timescales as 'millions of years' with relative framing.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7): orders the basic steps (dies → buried → turns to rock over a long time). Tier B (~8): explains why quick burial matters (otherwise it rots/is eaten) and uses sediment/minerals/rock correctly. Tier C (~9): explains that minerals replace the remains over millions of years and that fossilisation is rare, so most living things leave no fossil.
bestPractices: Teach it as a conditional CAUSAL chain (each step enables the next), foregrounding rapid burial as the make-or-break step.
Make rarity explicit — have children reason that most animals rot or are eaten, so only a tiny fraction fossilise; this seeds 'the fossil record is incomplete'.
Distinguish soft parts (usually lost) from hard parts (bone, teeth, shell) that typically fossilise, explaining why we mostly find skeletons.
Insist on correct vocabulary (sediment, minerals, rock, buried) used in context, per Y3 'Rocks'.
Use a compare-conditions approach (buried fast vs left exposed) so the necessity of burial is discovered, not asserted.
keyRepresentations: A staged cross-section: dead animal on a riverbed → layers of sediment pile on → minerals replace bone → rock with fossil → erosion exposes it.
A timeline slider showing 'millions of years' compressing the mineralisation step.
A 'fossil or lost?' branching diagram: buried quickly → fossil; left exposed → rots/scavenged → no fossil.
Soft-parts-vs-hard-parts labelling on an organism.
commonMisconceptions: 'Fossils are the original bone, unchanged' — minerals usually replace the remains; a fossil is rock in the shape of the original.
'Any dead animal becomes a fossil' — fossilisation is rare; most decay or are eaten before burial.
'Fossils form quickly' — mineral replacement and rock formation take (typically) millions of years.
'Soft parts fossilise as easily as bones' — usually only hard parts (bone, teeth, shell) survive; soft tissue rarely preserves.
'Fossils form on the surface where the animal died' — burial in sediment (often water-laid) is essential; surface remains are lost.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach fossilisation as an ordered CAUSAL chain with conditions: (1) an organism dies; (2) it is RAPIDLY BURIED in sediment (mud/sand) — the make-or-break step, because exposed remains rot or are scavenged; (3) soft parts decay while hard parts (bone, teeth, shell) remain; (4) over millions of years minerals carried by groundwater seep into the hard remains, filling tiny spaces and often gradually replacing the original material, while the sediment compacts and hardens into rock, preserving the shape; (5) later uplift and erosion expose it. Burial is necessary but does not guarantee a fossil. Make RARITY explicit so children reason that most living things leave no fossil, seeding the big idea that the fossil record is an incomplete, lucky sample. Use correct vocabulary (sediment, minerals, rock, buried) in context. The strongest proposed activity is intended to let children choose settings, with quick burial decided by setting-dependent chance, and run time forward so that rarity may become an observed outcome rather than a stated fact; staged diagrams and ordering/check tasks support the sequence and vocabulary.

activities.title: Play fate for a dead animal: vary conditions and run time forward
feedback: If a learner's quickly buried animal becomes a fossil, confirm: quick burial protected the hard parts from rotting and scavengers long enough for minerals to soak in and gradually replace them, and for the sediment to harden into rock. If a buried animal still leaves no fossil, explain that burial is needed but does not guarantee a fossil.
If a learner leaves the body exposed and gets 'no fossil', confirm: in the open it rotted or was eaten before it could be buried, so nothing was preserved.

When the tally shows only a few fossils from 20 animals, prompt: 'Why did so few become fossils?' Expected reasoning: most were never buried quickly enough, and even some buried ones did not last. If a tally is higher, compare settings and discuss that most animals die where quick burial is unlikely.

If a learner expects the bone to stay unchanged, point out the colour-shift step: minerals gradually fill and often replace the remains, so the fossil is usually mostly rock in the shape of the original bone, not the unchanged original bone.
activities.rationale: The key lesson — why fossilisation so rarely succeeds — is intended to be made concrete by running the process and comparing conditions (buried fast vs left exposed). Burial is decided by setting-dependent chance rather than chosen directly, so the necessity of burial may be reasoned out rather than asserted, and rarity may appear as an observed outcome. This is a proposed format, not a separately validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Fossilisation typically requires rapid burial in sediment before decay/scavenging; over long periods minerals permeate and replace hard remains (permineralisation) as sediment lithifies to rock; soft tissues rarely preserve, so fossilisation is rare and the record is incomplete.
learnerActions: For each of about 20 animals, choose where the body falls (e.g. muddy river delta, dry plain, open ground); the model then decides by chance whether sediment covers it quickly or it is left exposed. The odds depend on the setting: quick burial is more likely in a muddy delta and unlikely on dry open ground.
Advance a time dial forward through 'millions of years' and watch what happens for each choice.

For buried-quickly cases, observe the sequence: soft parts fade, hard parts (bone/teeth/shell) remain, minerals seep in and the bone colour-shifts to 'stone', sediment layers compact and harden into rock, then uplift and erosion reveal the fossil. Notice that some buried cases still end with no fossil (for example, the bone dissolves or the rock is later worn away), and some fossils are never exposed.
For left-exposed cases, observe scavengers and decay strip the body to nothing — 'no fossil'.
Keep a running tally of how many of the 20 animals became fossils, then state in your own words why fossils are rare.
Label each stage with the correct words: sediment, minerals, rock, buried.
activities.intendedInsight: Fossilisation is a conditional sequence in which rapid burial before decay is the crux. Burial is needed but not a guarantee, and because most animals are never buried fast enough, only a tiny lucky fraction fossilise, so the fossil record is incomplete.

activities.title: Compare buried vs exposed: the 'fossil or lost?' branch
feedback: If the learner predicts both become fossils, contrast the two paths: only the buried one is protected from rotting and scavengers.
Reinforce that 'exposed' usually ends in 'no fossil', which is why most animals leave none.
activities.rationale: A direct compare-conditions task is intended to foreground rapid burial as the make-or-break step and may let the necessity of burial be discovered through contrast rather than assertion.
sourceClaims: Fossilisation typically requires rapid burial in sediment before decay/scavenging; over long periods minerals permeate and replace hard remains (permineralisation) as sediment lithifies to rock; soft tissues rarely preserve, so fossilisation is rare and the record is incomplete.
learnerActions: Look at two identical animals that die in the same place; one is buried quickly by sediment, the other is left on the surface.
Predict what will happen to each after a very long time, and say why.
Trace a branching diagram: buried quickly → hard parts remain → minerals replace them → rock → fossil; left exposed → rots/scavenged → no fossil.
Explain in one sentence why quick burial is the step that makes the difference.
activities.intendedInsight: Burial before decay is the pivotal condition that determines whether anything is preserved at all.

activities.title: Read the staged cross-section and label soft vs hard parts
feedback: If a learner labels soft parts as fossilising, explain that soft tissue usually decays, so bone, teeth and shell are what normally remain.
Check that each stage is retold in the correct order and that the vocabulary is used in context.
activities.rationale: A labelled staged diagram is intended to teach the ordered sequence and the soft-vs-hard distinction cleanly; note it shows one fixed successful path, so it cannot by itself let a learner test failure conditions — pair it with a conditions-varying task that may help make rarity observable.
sourceClaims: Fossilisation typically requires rapid burial in sediment before decay/scavenging; over long periods minerals permeate and replace hard remains (permineralisation) as sediment lithifies to rock; soft tissues rarely preserve, so fossilisation is rare and the record is incomplete.
learnerActions: Study a staged cross-section: dead animal on a riverbed → layers of sediment pile on → minerals replace the bone → rock holding a fossil → erosion exposes it.
Reveal each stage's caption in order and retell the sequence aloud using the words sediment, minerals, and rock.
On a picture of an organism, label which parts are soft (usually lost) and which are hard — bone, teeth, shell — and typically survive.
Explain why we mostly find skeletons rather than whole animals.
activities.intendedInsight: The ordered sequence of fossilisation, and why hard parts are usually what we find because soft tissue rarely preserves.

activities.title: Order the stages and explain why burial matters (check)
feedback: Full response: explains the sequence AND that rapid burial before decay is the crux, that minerals replace the remains over millions of years, and that this is why fossils are rare — transferring to the garden-bone or open-ground counterexample.
Partial response: lists steps (dies, buried, turns to rock) but cannot explain why quick burial matters or why fossils are rare — recites a sequence without the mechanism; prompt for the 'why'.

Gap/misconception — 'any dead animal becomes a fossil, bones just slowly turn into fossils': contrast the millions of animals that have died with the few fossils found, and make burial-before-decay the pivotal step using the rotting-in-the-open image.

Misconception — 'the real bones are still there, just very old and hard': introduce mineral replacement — over millions of years, minerals from groundwater soak in and the original material is often gradually swapped for rock minerals, so the fossil is usually stone in the shape of the bone rather than the unchanged bone.
Misconception — timescale collapse ('fossils form in a few years'): anchor the millions-of-years timescale with the sediment-turning-to-rock step; a buried bone next year is still just a buried bone.

Follow-up probes: 'Why don't we find fossils of most animals that ever lived?'; 'If you buried a chicken bone in your garden, would it be a fossil next year? Why not?' (treat as a relative, condition-dependent teaching device, not an absolute); 'What does the word sediment actually mean?'; 'Where do the minerals come from?'
activities.rationale: An ordering plus short-answer check is intended to confirm the process and may surface specific misconceptions; it verifies rather than builds the process intuition, so use it after the hands-on and diagram tasks.
learnerActions: Put the stages in the correct order: dies → buried in sediment → minerals replace the remains → sediment hardens to rock → erosion exposes it.
Answer: why don't most animals that die become fossils?
Answer: what happens to the original hard parts over millions of years?

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: 'A dinosaur dies out in the open on dry ground and its body just lies there. Millions of years pass. Will there be a fossil of it? Say yes or no — and explain what has to happen for a fossil to form.'
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate and check the sequence, the role of rapid burial, mineral replacement, and the rarity of fossils.

constraints: Keep timescales as 'millions of years' with relative framing appropriate to ages 7–9; a buried bone 'next year' is not a fossil.
Teach as an ordered causal chain where each step enables the next, foregrounding rapid burial as the make-or-break step; do not present fossilisation as a mere list.
Make rarity explicit and have children reason it out (most animals rot or are eaten before burial) rather than simply being told.
Distinguish soft parts (usually lost) from hard parts (bone, teeth, shell) that typically preserve; explain why we mostly find skeletons.
Insist on correct vocabulary — sediment, minerals, rock, buried — used in context, consistent with Y3 'Rocks'.
Clarify that a fossil is usually rock in the shape of the original remains after mineral replacement, not the unchanged original bone.

The staged cross-section is a scaffold that shows one fixed successful path; it cannot by itself let a learner test failure conditions, so it does not on its own convey rarity — pair it with a conditions-varying task.
An ordering/short-answer check confirms and assesses understanding; a learner can sequence correctly without grasping the mechanism, so probe the 'why' of burial and rarity.

The optional elements described (setting choice, time dial, colour-shift to stone, fossil tally, tap-to-reveal captions, buried/exposed flap) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms or specific products.
Water-laid sediment is common and useful as an example, but do not overstate conditions beyond 'burial in sediment before decay' as the general requirement.
State efficacy of any proposed activity format with proposed/may/intended wording; the formats here are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the single source is marked verified:false and was not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row ranked a 2D interactive 'ideal' and rated a 3D dig as adding 'cost without deepening' and dialogue as 'poor'. These are catalog fit preferences, not evidence of comparative efficacy or necessity; they are reframed here as scaffolds with stated limits and should not be read as universal pedagogical laws. A diagram or ordering/check task may teach or check the sequence and vocabulary but does not by itself let a learner vary the burial conditions and observe rarity as an outcome.

The garden-bone counterexample in the assessment assumes ordinary garden soil/short timescale; it is a reasonable teaching device for 'not a fossil next year', but exact burial outcomes depend on conditions — keep it as a relative, not absolute, claim.
One source citation underlies several activities; a citation supporting the general principle does not establish that any specific activity format was tested or is superior to another medium.
'Permineralisation' is used loosely in the source to mean minerals permeating and replacing remains; the age-appropriate simplification is retained, but strictly the two processes differ.

probeDeeper: Why don't we find fossils of most of the animals that have ever lived?
If you buried a chicken bone in your garden, would it be a fossil next year? Why not?
In your explanation, what does the word 'sediment' actually mean?
Where do the minerals come from that end up making the fossil?
assess.correctAnswer: Probably not. To become a fossil the body must be buried quickly in sediment before it rots or is eaten; then over millions of years minerals seep in and replace the remains while the sediment hardens into rock, keeping the shape. Left in the open it would decompose, so fossilisation is rare — most animals leave no fossil at all.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fossilisation is automatic and common: 'when animals die their bones just slowly turn into fossils over time.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the millions of animals that have died with the few fossils found; make burial-before-decay the pivotal step, using a rotting-in-the-open counter-image.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — when animals die their bones slowly turn into fossils.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'yes' with no mention of burial, sediment, or the rarity of fossils.

errorPatterns.pattern: A fossil is the actual original bone that simply got old and hard — no mineral replacement.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce mineral replacement: the original material is gradually swapped for rock minerals so the fossil is stone in the shape of the bone.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the real bones are still there, just very old and hard.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'yes, the real bones are still there, just very old,' with no idea that minerals replace the remains.

errorPatterns.pattern: Timescale collapse: fossils form in a few years.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the millions-of-years timescale with the sediment-turning-to-rock step; a buried bone next year is still just a buried bone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts fossilisation but says it happens quickly, e.g. within a lifetime or a few years.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks any dead animal becomes a fossil; makes no mention of burial or the vast timescale, and treats fossils as the leftover original bones.
responseLevels.full: Explains the sequence AND that rapid burial before decay is the crux, that minerals replace the remains over millions of years, and that this is why fossils are rare — transferring the reasoning to the garden-bone counterexample.
responseLevels.partial: Lists steps — dies, gets buried, turns to rock — but cannot explain why quick burial matters or why fossilisation is rare; recites a sequence without the mechanism.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A dinosaur dies out in the open on dry ground and its body just lies there. Millions of years pass. Will there be a fossil of it? Say yes or no — and explain what has to happen for a fossil to form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks any dead animal automatically becomes a fossil answers 'yes, the bones will slowly turn into a fossil' and never mentions burial. A child who understands the process names quick burial-before-decay as the crux and recognises that lying exposed means no fossil.

sources.claim: Fossilisation typically requires rapid burial in sediment before decay/scavenging; over long periods minerals permeate and replace hard remains (permineralisation) as sediment lithifies to rock; soft tissues rarely preserve, so fossilisation is rare and the record is incomplete.
sources.source: Natural History Museum (UK) — How do fossils form? education pages; UK DfE Y3 'Rocks'

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Global Wind Patterns for ages 11–13 — the planet-scale engine that organises wind into bands: three circulation cells per hemisphere, the surface trade winds/westerlies/polar easterlies they produce, the Coriolis deflection that bends them, and the high-altitude jet streams.
• Standards — UK: KS3 geography 'weather and climate' / 'atmospheric circulation' and links to KS3 science 'Energy' (uneven heating drives convection). Foundational for GCSE geography global atmospheric circulation and climate zones.
• Standards — US: NGSS MS-ESS2-6 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-6, MS-PS1-5]). DCI ESS2.C, ESS2.D.
• Operational details: build from the child's known idea that warm air rises (local convection) to the GLOBAL case — intense heating at the equator drives rising air that would flow in one giant loop except the planet's rotation breaks it into three cells (Hadley, Ferrel, polar); introduce Coriolis as APPARENT deflection due to rotation (right in N hemisphere, left in S), not a real sideways force; connect cells→surface wind belts→why deserts sit at ~30° and rainforests at the equator; add the jet stream and its waviness/Arctic-amplification as an extension.
• Checkpoint: [Tier B] child can explain that the equator gets more direct sunlight, warm air rises there and sinks near 30°, creating predictable wind belts, and that Earth's spin bends the winds; [Tier C] child can name the three cells, predict wind direction with Coriolis, and link cell descending/ascending branches to desert and rainforest locations.
bestPractices: Start from what they own — warm air rises, cool air sinks (convection they've felt over a radiator) — then scale it to the planet: the equator is heated most, so a giant convection loop wants to form; show why one loop breaks into three cells once rotation is added.

Teach Coriolis as an APPARENT deflection arising from observing motion on a rotating sphere, not a push. The classic demo: draw a straight line 'poleward' on a spinning disc/globe and watch it curve; winds deflect right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern.

Link the cells causally to what children can check on a map: rising air at the equator → clouds and rainforest; descending dry air at ~30° → the world's great deserts (Sahara, Australian); this makes the abstract circulation predict real geography.

Name the surface belts as the OUTPUT of the cells: trade winds (equatorward, easterly), mid-latitude westerlies, polar easterlies — and connect the westerlies to why weather in the UK/US generally moves west-to-east.

Extend to the jet streams as fast high-altitude rivers of air at cell boundaries; for older/able pupils introduce Rossby-wave waviness and the debated link between a warming Arctic and a wavier, more stuck jet stream — flagged as active science, not settled fact.
keyRepresentations: The three-cell cross-section: a hemisphere in profile showing Hadley (0–30°), Ferrel (30–60°) and polar (60–90°) cells with rising/sinking arrows and the surface wind belts beneath.
Rotating-globe/spinning-disc Coriolis demo: a straight-intended path curving into an arc, showing right-deflection (N) and left-deflection (S).
Global wind-belt map: trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies drawn as arrows over the real continents, aligned with equatorial rainforests and 30° deserts.
Jet-stream ribbon on a polar-view globe, shown both as a tidy circle and as a wavy meandering path.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the Coriolis effect is a real sideways force pushing the air, rather than an apparent deflection from viewing motion on a spinning planet (and the myth that it determines which way sinks/toilets drain — far too small at that scale).
Believing air simply flows in one straight loop from equator to pole; missing that rotation splits it into three cells per hemisphere.
Assuming winds are named for where they blow TO; in fact winds are named for the direction they come FROM (a 'westerly' blows from the west).
Thinking the equator is hottest because it is closer to the Sun, rather than because sunlight strikes it more directly (higher angle, energy concentrated over less area).
Treating deserts as random hot places rather than the predictable result of descending dry air in the subtropical high-pressure belts at ~30°.

learn.summary: Global wind patterns for ages 11–13: how uneven solar heating plus Earth's rotation together produce the three circulation cells per hemisphere (Hadley 0–30°, Ferrel 30–60°, polar 60–90°), the surface wind belts they generate (trade winds, mid-latitude westerlies, polar easterlies), the apparent Coriolis deflection (rightward in the Northern Hemisphere, leftward in the Southern), and the high-altitude jet stream that steers weather systems along it. Core target is NGSS MS-ESS2-6 'develop and use a model': build the pattern from two drivers (heating contrast and spin) rather than only labelling a finished diagram, and connect descending dry air at ~30° to the world's great deserts and rising equatorial air to rainforests, with jet-stream waviness/Arctic amplification as a debated extension linked to prolonged extreme weather.

activities.title: Build the planet's circulation from two dials: heating and spin
feedback: If the learner expects one loop from equator to pole: increase the spin dial and watch the loop fragment into three cells — rotation is what breaks the simple picture.

If the learner thinks a parcel curves because something pushes it sideways: note that the parcel travels nearly straight while the ground rotates beneath it; the curved trace is how that looks from our spinning frame.
When the map is overlaid, prompt: where does the descending dry branch land? Connecting ~30° sinking air to real deserts shows the deserts are predictable, not random.
If the learner confuses which way winds bend: compare a Northern-Hemisphere launch (curves right) with a Southern-Hemisphere launch (curves left).

On the jet-stream extension: prompt how a wavier, more 'stuck' jet stream could let a heatwave or cold snap persist much longer by holding a weather pattern in place — and flag the Arctic-amplification link as debated, active science rather than settled fact.
activities.rationale: The objective is to develop and use a model of how unequal heating and rotation cause circulation patterns; manipulating the two drivers and seeing the belts emerge targets that performance expectation directly, and building from the familiar 'warm air rises' convection the learner already owns scaffolds the global case. Sliders, the parcel-launch tool, and the map overlay are optional concrete mechanisms that make the causal relationship manipulable rather than merely labelled.
sourceClaims: Unequal heating of Earth's surface and the planet's rotation together produce large-scale [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-6] — the target of a develop-and-use-a-model performance expectation.

Global circulation is organised into three cells per hemisphere (Hadley 0–30°, Ferrel 30–60°, polar 60–90°), producing surface trade winds, mid-latitude westerlies and polar easterlies; subtropical descending air at ~30° creates the major desert belts.
learnerActions: Starting with the planet's spin set to zero, increase the equator-to-pole heating contrast and observe a single giant convection loop per hemisphere form: warm air rising at the equator, drifting poleward aloft, sinking, and returning along the surface.

Now increase the spin dial up to Earth's rotation rate and observe the single loop break into three side-by-side cells per hemisphere, arranged by latitude, with surface wind belts drawn beneath (trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies).
Use a 'launch a parcel' tool to fire a puff of air poleward and watch its path curve — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern.
Slide a real world map underneath and check where the circulation's branches land: rising equatorial air over the rainforests, descending ~30° air over the Sahara and Australian deserts.

As an extension, toggle a jet-stream ribbon at a cell boundary and observe how this fast high-altitude river of air steers weather systems along its path; then explore a 'wavier jet' slider and reason about what a more meandering, 'stuck' jet might do to the weather beneath it.
activities.intendedInsight: Large-scale wind bands are the emergent OUTPUT of two interacting drivers — uneven heating by latitude and the planet's rotation. The single convection loop you expect splits into three cells once spin is added, and the bending of the winds is an apparent deflection that only appears once the planet turns beneath the moving air, not a sideways push.

activities.title: Spin a globe and launch parcels across it (spatial Coriolis)
feedback: If the learner predicts a straight trace, or a curve 'because a force bends it': point out that no sideways push is applied — the disc or globe rotates beneath the straight-moving pen, so the trace curves.
If the learner cannot say why the hemispheres differ: have them view the spin from above each pole and notice the rotation appears opposite, which flips the apparent deflection.
activities.rationale: Coriolis is a spatial, frame-dependent phenomenon; a spinnable globe or turntable offers a different, hands-on experience of the same idea the 2D lab shows, and either can support the intuition. This is a complementary route to the spatial understanding, not a claim that 3D is required.
sourceClaims: The Coriolis effect is an apparent deflection of moving air (to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern) arising from Earth's rotation, not a real applied force; it is negligible at small scales such as draining sinks.
learnerActions: On a spinnable 3D globe, launch a 'straight' path from the equator toward a pole and watch the trace curve relative to the rotating surface: in both hemispheres, a parcel moving toward the pole arcs eastward. On a physical turntable/lazy-Susan, which stands for one hemisphere seen from above its pole, draw a straight line with a pen across the spinning disc and watch the trace curve.
Compare launches in the Northern Hemisphere (path curves right) and the Southern Hemisphere (path curves left), and say why the two differ.
Peel back or tilt to view the three cells as latitude bands girdling the planet, and view the jet stream as a meandering ribbon from a polar vantage.
activities.intendedInsight: Circulation wraps a rotating sphere; seeing a straight-intended path curve on a surface you can spin makes the apparent (frame-dependent) nature of Coriolis concrete, and the opposite deflection in each hemisphere follows from the direction of rotation seen from each pole.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, sequence, predict, and locate
feedback: If a learner names a wind for where it blows TO: remind them winds are named for the direction they come FROM — a 'westerly' blows from the west.
If a learner says the equator is hottest because it is nearer the Sun: refocus on the angle of incidence — direct rays concentrate energy over a smaller area.
If a learner treats deserts as randomly placed hot spots: trace them to descending dry air in the subtropical high-pressure belts at ~30°.
If a learner cannot say why UK/US weather tends to arrive from the west: link it to the prevailing mid-latitude westerlies, which blow from west to east.
activities.rationale: Recognition and recall tasks are well suited to consolidating specific discriminations and are best used after the model has been explored, since recognition-format responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the model.
learnerActions: Match each cell to its latitude band (Hadley 0–30°, Ferrel 30–60°, polar 60–90°) and each surface belt to its wind direction (trade winds easterly/equatorward, mid-latitude westerlies, polar easterlies).
Sequence the causal chain: equator heated most → air rises → drifts poleward → sinks near 30° → returns as surface wind belt.
Given a poleward-launched parcel, draw or select its correctly curved path in each hemisphere (right in N, left in S).
Categorise named regions as wet-equatorial (rising air) or dry-subtropical (descending air at ~30°), e.g. placing the Sahara and Australian deserts under descending air.
Explain in your own words why the equator is hottest — sunlight strikes it more directly, concentrating energy over less area — rather than because it is closer to the Sun.
Connect the mid-latitude westerlies to everyday experience: because they blow from the west, weather systems in the UK and US generally move from west to east.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure the discriminations after exploring the model: naming cells and belts, predicting deflection direction, locating deserts/rainforests from the circulation, and linking the westerlies to west-to-east weather turn the model into reliable, transferable knowledge.

activities.title: Ask the meteorologist: untangle Coriolis and wind-naming
feedback: If the learner invokes a sideways force: steer back to the rotating-frame account — the air moves nearly straight while the ground turns beneath it.

If the learner cites the plughole myth: note that at that scale the basin's shape and any leftover swirl in the water decide the spin direction; Coriolis matters only over large distances and long times.

If the learner says winds blow straight from high pressure to low pressure: the pressure difference starts the flow, but for large-scale winds rotation then curves it, so they do not travel in a straight line from high to low pressure. Near the equator and in small local winds such as sea breezes, this curving is weak.
activities.rationale: Responsive dialogue is a useful supporting probe for persistent verbal misconceptions, complementing the model work; it targets explanation and misconception repair rather than the emergent spatial system itself.
learnerActions: Pose and discuss whether the Coriolis effect is a real push on the air, and explain in your own words what actually makes a north-bound wind veer right in the Northern Hemisphere.
Ask why 'a westerly' is named for where the wind comes from, and check the drain/toilet-spin claim against the fact that Coriolis is negligible at small scales.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the explanation aloud and responding to follow-up questions can expose and help repair the Coriolis-as-force and winds-named-from misconceptions that a diagram may leave hidden.

constraints: Build from the learner's existing 'warm air rises, cool air sinks' convection idea before scaling to the global case; the single-loop-then-three-cells progression matters for understanding WHY rotation changes the picture.
Teach Coriolis as an apparent (frame-dependent) deflection, not a real sideways force, and explicitly correct the plughole/toilet-drain myth as too small a scale for Coriolis to dominate.
Winds are named for the direction they come FROM, not where they blow to.

A static labelled cross-section or wind-belt map is a useful summary/reference but does not let the learner generate the pattern from its two drivers; use it alongside, not instead of, the manipulable model.

A turntable or an on-screen globe are physical or modelled approximations; name the screen model as a model, and treat the pen-on-disc demo as an analogy for the atmosphere's frame-dependent deflection, not an exact replica.
Recognition and matching tasks consolidate discriminations but do not by themselves require the learner to independently construct or explain the model; pair them with explanation tasks.
Treat the Arctic-amplification / wavier-jet-stream link as active, debated science flagged as an extension, not as settled fact.

Climate connections (deserts at ~30°, equatorial rainforests, westerlies steering UK/US weather west-to-east) describe the dominant large-scale pattern; local geography and other factors also shape real regional climates.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all four sources carry verified:false in the row and were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated or tested interventions.

Source claims support the underlying science principles (NGSS target, three-cell structure, Coriolis as apparent deflection) but do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular activity format or medium; sourceClaims on the consolidation and conversation activities were set to [] because no source supports their pedagogical rationales.

The original row asserted that a static image 'can label but not let the child generate' the causal relationship and that 3D 'adds real depth the 2D cross-section can't'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances (static image as reference/summary; globe as a complementary spatial route).

The jet-stream waviness / Arctic-amplification link was flagged in the source as debated active science; retained only as an extension, now including the objective's link to prolonged extreme weather and the jet's steering role, with the 'debated' caveat preserved.

The pen-on-turntable demo is an analogy (a horizontally moving pen on a flat disc) rather than a full physical model of poleward atmospheric motion — kept as a demonstration of the frame-dependent effect, not an exact atmospheric replica.

assess.poeTask: Set a turntable (or lazy-Susan) spinning and hold a pen still, moving it in a straight line across the spinning disc. Before doing it, ask the student to PREDICT what line the pen leaves ON the disc, and WHY. The reason — the disc rotates beneath the straight-moving pen so the trace curves even though no force acts sideways on the pen — is the diagnostic part; a student who predicts a straight line, or who predicts a curve 'because a force bends it,' reveals the Coriolis-as-force misconception.
probeDeeper: On a merry-go-round you roll a ball straight across and it seems to curve. How is that the same as the wind's deflection?
The Coriolis deflection is rightward in the Northern Hemisphere. What happens in the Southern Hemisphere, and why the difference?
How could a wavier jet stream make a heatwave or cold snap last much longer?
assess.correctAnswer: There's no real sideways force pushing the air. The air moves nearly straight, but the Earth rotates beneath it; from our rotating frame the path appears deflected — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. It's an apparent deflection due to Earth's rotation, not a force acting on the air. Combined with unequal heating by latitude, this shapes the three-cell circulation and the prevailing winds.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The Coriolis force physically pushes the moving air sideways'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Spin a globe/turntable and draw a 'straight' line — the trace curves with no push applied.
errorPatterns.distractor: A real sideways force pushes the wind and makes it curve.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names a real sideways force acting on the air

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Winds blow in a straight line directly from high pressure to low pressure'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The pressure gradient starts the flow; rotation then curves it (qualitative geostrophic balance).
errorPatterns.distractor: Winds go straight from high pressure to low pressure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: ignores rotation and deflection entirely

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The Coriolis effect decides which way water spins down a plughole or toilet'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Too small a scale — basin shape dominates; Coriolis matters only over large distances.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cites the drain myth as evidence

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Global winds are just local breezes scaled up, nothing to do with latitude cells'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link unequal heating by latitude to the Hadley/Ferrel/polar cells.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: no three-cell structure; can't tie winds to latitude

responseLevels.gap: Treats Coriolis as a real push, or has winds going straight from high to low pressure.
responseLevels.full: Explains Coriolis as an apparent deflection from Earth's rotation (not a force), links unequal heating and rotation to the three-cell circulation, prevailing winds and jet stream, and reasons about jet-stream waviness prolonging extreme weather.
responseLevels.partial: Knows winds curve and names the cells or prevailing winds but explains the curving as a force, or can't connect unequal heating → three-cell circulation → surface winds.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Winds don't travel in straight lines from the equator to the poles — they curve. A student says 'that's because the Coriolis force pushes the moving air sideways.' Is the Coriolis effect a real push on the air, and what actually makes a north-bound wind in the Northern Hemisphere veer to the right?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who treats Coriolis as a physical force gives a different account from one who explains it as an apparent deflection that arises because the ground rotates under the moving air.

sources.claim: Unequal heating of Earth's surface and the planet's rotation together produce large-scale [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-6] — the target of a develop-and-use-a-model performance expectation.

sources.claim: Global circulation is organised into three cells per hemisphere (Hadley 0–30°, Ferrel 30–60°, polar 60–90°), producing surface trade winds, mid-latitude westerlies and polar easterlies; subtropical descending air at ~30° creates the major desert belts.

sources.claim: The Coriolis effect is an apparent deflection of moving air (to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern) arising from Earth's rotation, not a real applied force; it is negligible at small scales such as draining sinks.

sources.claim: KS3 geography requires understanding of weather and climate including atmospheric circulation, and KS3 science covers energy transfer by convection driven by uneven heating.

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 this is the capstone of repeated reasoning: abstracting an algebraic rule from a run of cases and VERIFYING it. The child builds the interior-angle-sum rule (n−2)×180° from triangle/quadrilateral/pentagon, writes the nth-term rule of a linear sequence to predict any term, and generalises structural facts — always testing the generalisation on a specific case. CCSS MP8's own high examples live here: abstracting slope into (y−2)/(x−1)=3, and spotting the cancelling pattern in (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1)… to reach a general formula. Teaching should organise cases in a table so the regularity is visible, press for the general rule in symbols, and demand a verifying case — the difference between a conjecture and a checked generalisation.
bestPractices: Tabulate a family of cases (polygon sides vs angle sum; position vs term) so the constant step and the offset are visible before the rule is written
Move from 'what's the pattern?' to 'write the rule for the nth/any case' in words then symbols
Always verify a stated generalisation on a fresh specific case (test (n−2)×180 on a hexagon) before trusting it
Decompose the geometric case (split a polygon into n−2 triangles) so the rule is explained, not just fitted
keyRepresentations: Polygon triangulation (an n-gon splits into n−2 triangles)
Position-vs-term tables and the nth-term expression
Linear-sequence graphs/number lines showing constant difference and offset
Algebra tiles / area models for operation-property generalisations
commonMisconceptions: Uses a term-to-term rule and cannot produce an nth-term rule for a far term
Assumes direct proportion — e.g. angle sum is n×180° or the 20th term is 20×(first term) — ignoring the −2 offset / start value
States a generalisation but never verifies it on a specific case, so errors go uncaught
Fits a rule to the given cases that fails to generalise (a pattern that works for 3, 4, 5 sides but wasn't reasoned from structure)

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, this is the capstone of 'look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning': abstract a general algebraic rule from a run of specific cases AND verify it on a fresh case. Learners build the interior-angle-sum rule (n−2)×180° from triangle/quadrilateral/pentagon, write the nth-term rule of a linear sequence to predict any term, and generalise structural facts about operations — each time testing the generalisation on a specific case. The core discrimination is twofold: (a) capturing the −2 offset / start value instead of assuming direct proportion (n×180°, or 20th term = 20×first term), and (b) treating verification on a new case as a reflex, not an afterthought. Teaching should tabulate the cases so the constant step and offset are visible, press for the rule in words then symbols, decompose the geometric case so the rule is explained rather than curve-fitted, and always demand a verifying case.

activities.title: Polygon angle-sum explorer: build, tabulate, abstract, verify
feedback: If the learner writes n×180° (e.g. 6×180 = 1080° for a hexagon), triangulate the hexagon together and count: there are 4 triangles, not 6. Test the n×180 rule against the known pentagon (it gives 900°, not 540°) and watch it fail — a convex n-gon triangulated from one vertex always yields exactly n−2 triangles, so the sum is (n−2) lots of 180°, not n.

If the learner states a rule and stops, do not confirm it; ask 'does it give the pentagon's 540°? Now test the hexagon, which you held back and did not use to build the rule.' Make the verifying case a required step every time.
If the learner reaches (n−2)×180° with the triangle reasoning and checks the hexagon at 720°, affirm both the structural justification AND the check as the target — the formula alone is not enough.
activities.rationale: Tabulating a family of cases makes the constant step (+180°) and the offset (−2) visible before the rule is written; decomposing the polygon into n−2 triangles explains the rule structurally so it generalises instead of merely fitting 3,4,5 sides; demanding a fresh verifying case separates a conjecture from a checked generalisation.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Start with a triangle (angle sum 180°). Add one side at a time to make a quadrilateral, then a pentagon (convex shapes); for each, split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex. Keep the hexagon back as a fresh test case.
Record in a running table: number of sides, number of triangles, and angle sum. Notice the sum climbs by a steady +180° each time while the triangle count stays at (sides − 2).

Explain WHY: in a convex polygon, from one vertex you can reach the n−3 non-adjacent vertices by diagonals, so an n-sided polygon splits into exactly n−2 triangles, and its angle sum is (n−2) lots of 180° — reason the rule from the structure, don't just fit it to the numbers.
Write the general rule in words ('two fewer than the number of sides, times 180°') then in symbols: (n−2)×180°.

Verify on a case you did not build the rule from: test a hexagon — (6−2)×180° = 720° — and check it matches the measured/added angles. Then stretch it: a decagon (10 sides, 1440°) and a 100-gon — does it still make sense?
activities.intendedInsight: The angle sum is (n−2)×180° BECAUSE the polygon decomposes into n−2 triangles — a rule explained by structure, and confirmed by testing a new polygon rather than trusted on faith.

activities.title: nth-term rule tester for a linear sequence
feedback: If the learner extends the sequence step by step instead of writing a rule, tabulate position against term and ask for the 100th term — continuing by hand becomes impractical, motivating the nth-term rule.

If the learner writes 20 × (first term) for the 20th term, test that rule against a known term (does term = position × first term give the 2nd term correctly? 2×5 = 10, but the 2nd term is 9) and see it fail; locate the missing offset.

If the learner writes 4n + 1, checks it against the listed terms and then confirms it on a fresh term such as the 5th (21), affirm that testing a case not used to build the rule is how you move from a conjecture to a checked generalisation.
activities.rationale: Position-vs-term tables reveal the difference and offset; requiring prediction of a far term forces a genuine nth-term rule rather than term-to-term iteration; checking the rule against a listed term builds verification into the habit and exposes the direct-proportion misconception.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Take a linear sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and tabulate position (1, 2, 3, 4) against term so the constant difference (+4) and the start value are visible.
Move from the term-to-term rule ('add 4') to a position-to-term rule: difference × n + offset. For 5, 9, 13, 17 this is 4n + 1.
Predict a far term you cannot easily count to — the 20th term (81) and the 100th term (401) — using the rule, not step-by-step continuation.

Verify: first check your rule reproduces every listed term (e.g. the 4th term should give 4×4+1 = 17), then test a fresh case not used to build it — extend the sequence by one step to get the 5th term (21) and check that 4×5+1 = 21. If a conjectured rule breaks any term, it is wrong — fix it.
Explain why direct proportion fails here: the 20th term is NOT 20 × the first term, because the sequence does not pass through zero at position zero (the rule 4n+1 gives 1 at n=0, not 0).
activities.intendedInsight: A general nth-term rule lets you jump to any term directly, and the offset (start value) matters — direct proportion from the first term is a classic error that verification against a known term catches.

activities.title: Generalise a structural fact and find the case that disproves a false rule
feedback: If a learner cannot say what the −2 corresponds to, return to the triangulation of a convex polygon: from one vertex you can draw diagonals only to the n−3 non-adjacent vertices, which splits the polygon into exactly n−2 triangles (a hexagon gives 4). Each side not touching the chosen vertex is the base of one triangle; the 2 sides that meet at the chosen vertex do not get a triangle of their own, which is where the −2 comes from.
If a learner accepts a false rule, ask them to find one polygon (or one sequence term) where it breaks; a single counterexample is enough to reject it.
Affirm a response that states the rule, grounds it in structure, and can name a disproving case for a false alternative.
activities.rationale: Reasoning about why a relationship holds (not just that it fits cases) is what makes a generalisation reliable; practising counterexample selection trains the verification habit the assessment targets. Algebra tiles/area models are offered as optional representations that may make the structure visible for simpler products.
sourceClaims: MP8's advanced examples: abstracting slope into an equation from repeated checks, and noticing the cancelling regularity across (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1)… to reach a general formula — generalising from repeated reasoning
Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Generalise an operation property with a reason, e.g. 'any whole number m divided by a non-zero whole number n can be written as the fraction m/n, so dividing by n gives a denominator of n (before any simplifying)' — state it, then justify why it holds, not just that it works on examples.

Explore the cancelling regularity in products like (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1), … and describe the general pattern that emerges; an area model or algebra tiles may help visualise the simpler binomial product (x−1)(x+1), but are harder to apply to the cubic case, so treat them as an optional aid rather than a required method.

Practise verification-by-counterexample: given a false claim such as 'a polygon's angle sum is n×180°', name the specific polygon that shows it is wrong and state what it gives versus the true value (e.g. pentagon: rule gives 900°, truth is 540°).
Answer the discriminating prompt: 'Why n−2 and not n — what does the −2 correspond to in the shape?'
activities.intendedInsight: Generalising means stating a rule, justifying why it holds from structure, and being able to produce the single case that would disprove a false version — all three are part of mathematical reasoning.

constraints: Verification is not optional: every stated generalisation must be tested on a fresh specific case before it is trusted. Do not let a learner stop at a rule, and do not simply confirm a rule for them — ask for the verifying case.
Guard against the direct-proportion misconception explicitly: n×180° for angle sums and 20×(first term) for the 20th term are the key errors to surface and refute, not avoid.

The rule must be reasoned from structure (a convex n-gon triangulated from one vertex is n−2 triangles), not merely curve-fitted to 3, 4, 5 sides; a pattern that happens to fit the given cases but wasn't reasoned may not generalise.

A static triangulation diagram or a pre-filled table is a useful reference for showing the decomposition, but by itself it does not let the learner conjecture a rule and test it on a new case — pair any static display with an actual conjecture-and-check task.

An interactive explorer or a well-designed quiz (deriving the rule, finding a far term, and selecting the case that disproves a false rule) can each be used during teaching, not only for assessment; choose by what the learner needs to do, not by assuming one medium alone can teach generalisation.

3D representation is unlikely to be needed here because polygon angle sums, linear sequences and operation properties are flat/symbolic; it may add handling load rather than insight for this specific content. This is a scoped judgement about this topic, not a universal or verified claim about 3D.
Area models/algebra tiles are an optional representation whose fit is strongest for simple binomial products; do not present them as a verified or required method for the cubic cancelling pattern.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the legacy 'verified' flags were not independently re-checked.

Self-audit of the examples used: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon (6−2)×180° = 720°, decagon (10−2)×180° = 1440° — all consistent with (n−2)×180°. The n×180 distractor gives pentagon 900° and hexagon 1080°, correctly shown as wrong. Sequence 5,9,13,17 has rule 4n+1: 4th term 4×4+1 = 17 ✓, 20th term 81, 100th term 401 — consistent.

The legacy 'possible'/'poor' fit entries carried universal-sounding claims (a tap-to-reveal 'cannot' let the child conjecture; 'open talk gives nothing to test'; '3D adds load, not insight'). These have been softened to scoped, qualified observations with stated affordances/limits in the constraints; catalog fit rankings and quiz-step vocabulary were removed.

The operation-property example was tightened to 'any whole number m divided by n can be written as the fraction m/n'; the exact source wording ('dividing by n always gives a denominator of n') was looser and reviewers may wish to confirm the intended statement.

The original source listed an algebra-tile/area-model representation for operation-property generalisations and for the (x−1)(x+1)… cancelling pattern; the applicability of area models to the polynomial-factoring (cubic) example is plausible but not established by the cited sources and is now scoped as optional and reviewable.

probeDeeper: Ask 'why n−2 and not n — what does the −2 correspond to in the shape?' to test whether the rule is reasoned from structure or curve-fitted

Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'a classmate says the angle sum is n×180° — which polygon would show that's wrong, and what does it give versus the true value?' to probe verification by counterexample
Ask 'use your rule to find the angle sum of a decagon (10 sides), then a 100-gon — does it still make sense?' to test generality and reasonableness
Ask 'write the rule for the nth term of 5, 9, 13, 17… and prove it gives the 4th term correctly' to link generalisation with verification
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for (n−2)×180° reached by reasoning (each extra side adds 180° / an n-gon is n−2 triangles), and a verification on the hexagon giving (6−2)×180 = 720°. The reasoned rule AND the check are the target, not the formula alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes direct proportion — writes the angle sum as n×180° (or the 20th term as 20×the first term), ignoring the −2 offset / start value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Triangulate the polygon to show it is n−2 triangles, not n; test the n×180 rule against the known pentagon and see it fail
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives 6×180 = 1080° for a hexagon, or scales the first term by the position

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses a term-to-term rule and cannot produce a general nth-term rule for a far term
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tabulate position against term so the position-to-term relationship (difference×n + offset) is visible; ask for the 100th term
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For the linked sequence task the child extends step-by-step rather than writing an nth-term rule

errorPatterns.pattern: States a generalisation but never verifies it on a specific case, so a wrong rule goes uncaught
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT simply confirm the rule; require a verifying case every time ('does it give the pentagon's 540°?') so checking becomes automatic
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a rule and stops; when asked to test the hexagon, hasn't thought to

responseLevels.gap: Spots '+180°' or 'add 4' but writes no general rule, or uses n×180 / direct proportion, and does not verify
responseLevels.full: Abstracts (n−2)×180° (and nth-term rules) with a structural justification and verifies on a new case, catching direct-proportion errors — generalising AND checking unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Produces a general rule when prompted (often needing the table) but omits the offset reasoning or does not test it on a fresh case

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A triangle's angles add to 180°, a quadrilateral's to 360°, a pentagon's to 540°. What is the rule for the angle sum of a polygon with n sides? How did you get it — and test your rule on a hexagon.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Spotting '+180° each time' is easy; the discriminating parts are (a) capturing the −2 offset in a general rule rather than n×180, and (b) verifying on a new case. A child reasoning correctly explains the n−2 triangles and checks the hexagon; a child reasoning incorrectly writes n×180 (direct proportion) or states a rule without testing it.

sources.claim: MP8's advanced examples: abstracting slope into an equation from repeated checks, and noticing the cancelling regularity across (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1)… to reach a general formula — generalising from repeated reasoning

sources.claim: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Find 10 more/less and 100 more/less than any number to 1000, mentally, by recognising WHICH digit changes: +10 changes the tens, +100 changes the hundreds, and the other digits stay — except when a boundary forces a carry/exchange (e.g. 190 + 10 = 200).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): mental methods and place value to 1000 (find 10/100 more or less).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.8 'mentally add 10 or 100 to, and mentally subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100-900'.
• Operational details — Extend the two-digit '10 more' vertical-move idea to a place-value chart / Gattegno chart where +10 steps the tens digit and +100 steps the hundreds digit while others hold. Explicitly teach the boundary cases where a column 'fills up' and rolls over (190+10, 950+100). Demand the explanation of which digit changes and why.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): finds 10/100 more/less with no boundary crossing, using a chart. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): does it mentally for any number to 1000 and names the changing digit. Tier C (age 8, extending): handles roll-over boundaries (190+10, 890+100) and explains the exchange.
bestPractices: Extend the two-digit pattern: +10 steps the tens digit, +100 steps the hundreds digit, others unchanged — make the 'which digit?' question explicit.
Use a Gattegno / place-value chart so the child selects a new tens- or hundreds-row and physically sees one digit change.
Teach boundary roll-overs deliberately (190+10=200, 950+100=1050 later) as the interesting cases, not exceptions to memorise.
Contrast +10 vs +100 side by side so the child tracks different columns.
Insist on the reasoning ('the hundreds digit goes up by one, tens and ones stay') to keep it place-value based, not counting.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (change one row = change one digit)
H|T|O place-value counters (add/remove one 10 or one 100)
0-1000 number line with ±10 and ±100 hops
100-square generalisation / number grid
Base-ten flats/rods for the concrete +100 / +10 move
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding 100 but stepping the tens).
Failing at boundaries — 190 + 10 giving '1100' or '190' unchanged instead of 200.
Counting on in ones instead of jumping the place.
Confusing 10 more with 100 more.
Assuming only one digit ever changes, so mishandling the carry when a column rolls over.

learn.summary: For ages 7-8: find 10 more/less and 100 more/less than any number up to 1000, mentally, by reasoning about which digit changes. +10 steps the tens digit, +100 steps the hundreds digit, and the other digits stay the same \u2014 except at a boundary where a column 'fills up' and rolls over (e.g. 190 + 10 = 200, where the tens roll 9\u21920 and carry into the hundreds). Learners should name which digit changes and explain why, keeping the method place-value based rather than counting in ones.

activities.title: Digit stepper: watch one column respond
feedback: If the wrong column is predicted: name explicitly which column '10 more' and '100 more' act on, add the matching base-ten piece (one ten or one hundred), and watch only that column move.
If a learner counts on in ones to reach the answer, prompt: 'Can you jump straight to the column that changes instead of counting?'
Reinforce correct reasoning by restating it: 'The hundreds digit goes up by one; tens and ones stay.'
activities.rationale: Making the 'which digit?' question explicit and showing exactly one column respond to one operation builds place-value reasoning rather than rote counting. An interactive chart where the affected digit highlights and ticks while others are locked can make the mechanism concrete; a number-line view showing \u00b110/\u00b1100 hops is an optional alternative representation. These interaction examples illustrate the mechanism and are not required mechanisms \u2014 base-ten counters or a paper chart reach the same insight.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils develop mental place-value methods to 1000, including finding 10 or 100 more or less.
learnerActions: Start with a three-digit number shown in an H|T|O place-value chart (e.g. 638).
Predict which digit will change before pressing +100, then press it and check: only the hundreds digit ticks up (638\u2192738) while tens and ones stay fixed.
Repeat with +10, -10, -100 on several numbers, each time saying aloud which column changes and which stay the same.
Contrast +10 and +100 side by side on the same starting number to track that they act on different columns.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding/subtracting 10 acts on the tens column and adding/subtracting 100 acts on the hundreds column; when no column rolls over (as with 638), the other digits hold still. This is a place-value jump, not counting on in ones. Boundary cases such as 190 + 10 come in the next activity.

activities.title: Boundary roll-overs: when a column fills up
feedback: If a learner writes a malformed number (190+10 = '1100' or '190' unchanged; 10 more than 695 = '6,105'): don't reteach the whole idea \u2014 rehearse the single roll on a number line or base-ten mat, e.g. 305\u2192295 (a ten taken by exchanging one hundred for ten tens), 695\u2192705 (9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens make a new hundred, hundreds 6\u21927, ones stay 5).
If a learner assumes only one digit ever changes: show them the carry/borrow so they see a second column move when a column overflows.
Confirm correct regrouping: '950 + 100 fills the hundreds, so it rolls into a new thousands column: 1050.'
activities.rationale: Boundary roll-overs are the key teaching case and are best met deliberately rather than treated as exceptions. Seeing or physically working a cascade \u2014 the tens rolling 9\u21920 while a carry moves leftward, or exchanging base-ten pieces \u2014 makes the carry/borrow visible. Base-ten counters and a 0-1000 number line give concrete and linear views of the same jump.
sourceClaims: Boundary roll-overs (e.g. 190+10) are the key teaching case and should be made explicit rather than treated as exceptions.
learnerActions: Start at 190 and find 10 more. Watch (or work out on a base-ten mat/number line) the tens roll 9\u21920 and a ten carry up to make one more hundred, so 190 becomes 200.
Find 10 less than 305: the tens are 0, so a hundred must be exchanged for ten tens before removing one \u2014 305, 295.
Find 10 more than 695: the tens fill up (9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens), which rolls over to make a new hundred, so the hundreds go 6\u21927 and the ones stay 5 \u2014 695 becomes 705.
Find 100 more than 950 and decide whether the answer is still a three-digit number (it becomes 1050, which rolls into a new thousands column).

For each, say which digits moved and why, e.g. for 190 + 10: 'the tens filled up, so they rolled to 0 and added one to the hundreds'; for 305 - 10: 'there were no tens, so I exchanged a hundred for ten tens and took one away'; for 950 + 100: 'the hundreds filled up, so they rolled to 0 and made one thousand.'
activities.intendedInsight: The rule 'only one digit changes' has a meaningful exception: when a column reaches its limit (a 9 going up, or a 0 going down), it rolls over and carries/borrows into the next column. These boundary cases are the interesting core of the skill, not exceptions to memorise.

activities.title: Fluency practice with boundary items
feedback: For plain-case errors adjusting the wrong place (100 more than 456 \u2192 466): re-name which column the operation acts on and redo with the matching base-ten piece (the answer is 556).
For boundary errors: rehearse just the single roll, not the whole concept.

Use probing questions to check reasoning, e.g. '10 less than 305 \u2014 what happens to the tens and the hundreds?', 'Which digit changes when you find 100 more? Does any other digit move?', '100 more than 950 \u2014 is the answer still a three-digit number?'
activities.rationale: Scored practice can consolidate a fluency skill after understanding is built, and deliberately mixing boundary items checks that learners handle regrouping rather than mechanically bumping one digit. Practice items assess and reinforce; they should follow, not replace, the conceptual work above.
learnerActions: Answer quick fill-in items: '100 more than 638 = __', '10 less than 305 = __', '100 more than 950 = __'.
Answer 'which digit changes?' when finding 100 more (or 10 less) for a given number.
Mix plain cases (456 + 100) with boundary cases (190 + 10, 695 + 10, 305 - 10) so the two are not predictable.
Optionally use a slider on a 0-1000 line to land on answers and self-check.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the place-value reasoning is understood, the skill can become quick mental recall, applied reliably even when a boundary forces a regroup.

constraints: Fill-in and multiple-choice practice consolidates and checks fluency but should follow conceptual work with a chart, counters, or number line; recognition-only responses do not by themselves build the place-value reasoning or the explanation of which digit changes.

A static annotated chart can serve as a reference for which digit +10/+100 changes, but learners need to carry out the transformation (physically, with counters, or interactively) to experience the roll-over; treat a fixed image as a reference scaffold, not the whole lesson.
Always require learners to explain which digit changes and why, so the method stays place-value based rather than counting on in ones.

Interactive highlights, locked digits, animated carries, number-line toggles, timed rounds, and sliders are optional illustrations of the mechanism; the same insight can be reached with base-ten counters, a Gattegno/place-value chart, or a paper number line.

Tier the work: emerging learners find 10/100 more/less with no boundary crossing using a chart; secure learners do it mentally for any number to 1000 and name the changing digit; extending learners handle genuine roll-over boundaries (190+10, 950+100) and explain the exchange.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, the CCSS 2.NBT.8 claim and the NCETM boundary-roll-over claim are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat citation strength accordingly.

The source's parentTitle and standards describe numbers up to 1000, but 950 + 100 = 1050 crosses into the thousands; this is used intentionally as an extending example, framed as 'does the answer stay three digits?' rather than contradicting the 'to 1000' scope.

The original Tier C checkpoint listed '890+100' as a roll-over boundary, but 890+100=990 does not cross any boundary (hundreds 8\u21929, no overflow). This non-rolling example was corrected out of the learner-facing guidance; a genuine tens roll-over in that region would be e.g. 890+10=900.

The original assessment feedback contained a garbled phrase for 695\u2192705 ('ten ones... a ten makes the next hundred'); it was corrected in both the learner action and feedback to describe a tens roll-over (9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens \u2192 new hundred, hundreds 6\u21927, ones stay 5), with the regrouping intent preserved.
CCSS 2.NBT.8 is a Grade 2 US standard while the UK Year 3 placement is ages 7-8; the age framing (7-8) was retained from the row but the cross-standard age mapping is approximate.
Standards citations establish the skill/objective but do not themselves evidence the efficacy or necessity of any particular medium; efficacy wording is kept as proposed/optional.

probeDeeper: 10 less than 305 — what happens to the tens and the hundreds?
Which digit changes when you find 100 more? Does any other digit move?
100 more than 950 — is the answer still a three-digit number?
assess.correctAnswer: 556; 295; 705; 1,050 — changing only the right digit unless a boundary forces a regroup, and regrouping correctly across it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adjusts the wrong place — adds 100 to the tens digit, or adds 10 to the hundreds
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name which column '10 more' and '100 more' act on; add the matching base-ten piece and watch only that column (until it overflows).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 100 more than 456 comes out as 466 or 1,456; 10 more changes the hundreds.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to regroup across a boundary: 10 less than 305 → 315 or 300; 10 more than 695 → 6,105 or 605
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole idea — rehearse the single roll on a number line or base-ten mat: 305, 295 (a ten borrowed from the hundred) and 695, 705 (ten ones... a ten makes the next hundred).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The boundary cases give a malformed number or don't roll into the next place.

responseLevels.gap: Adjusts the wrong place or cannot cross a boundary.
responseLevels.full: Finds 10/100 more or less for any number to 1000, adjusting the correct place and regrouping across boundaries, and names which digit changes.
responseLevels.partial: Handles plain cases (456 + 100) but stumbles when a zero/nine forces a regroup.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask quickly and watch the method: '100 more than 456? ... 10 less than 305? ... 10 more than 695? ... 100 more than 950?' The last three cross a boundary — watch what happens to the neighbouring digits.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 456 checks the plain case (one digit changes); 305 (10 less) and 695 (10 more) force a roll across a zero/nine into the next place; 950 + 100 crosses into thousands. Watching reveals whether the child adjusts the right place and handles the carry/borrow, versus mechanically bumping one digit.

sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 3 Number & place value / mental methods)

sources.claim: Mentally add/subtract 10 or 100 to/from a number 100-900 (2.NBT.8).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Number & Operations in Base Ten, Grade 2

sources.claim: Boundary roll-overs (e.g. 190+10) are the key teaching case and should be made explicit rather than treated as exceptions.
