pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 the reasoning practice reaches its primary-school ceiling: formal, multi-step arguments and their sharpest tool, the counter-example. A child chains angle facts to PROVE a given angle must be 60° (not measure it), finds and explains an error in a peer's fraction division, and — the signature move — disproves a false conjecture such as 'multiplying always makes bigger' with a single case (×1/2 makes smaller). This is where the empirical→deductive asymmetry Hoyles & Küchemann document becomes explicit content: one counter-example kills a universal claim, while no number of confirming examples establishes it. SMP3's critique half is now central — arguments span fractions, ratio, algebra and geometry, and a competent Y6 reasoner locates a flawed step, explains why it fails, and offers a correct alternative. Teaching aims at the felt logic of implication: 'if… then…', the difference between a claim and its converse, and why a counter-example is decisive.
bestPractices: Make the counter-example a taught tool: give false 'always/sometimes/never' conjectures ('multiplying makes bigger', 'the more sides, the bigger the angles') and reward the single case that breaks them, per Hoyles & Küchemann's finding that a counter-example reveals WHY a claim is false

Require proof by chained fact, not measurement: to show an angle is 60°, insist on a logical progression of angle facts ('angles on a line sum to 180°, and these two are 60° and 60°, therefore…'), reserving measuring for checking

Use peer critique across arenas — a flawed fraction division ('invert the first fraction'), a mis-added ratio, a misaligned calculation — and demand 'which step, why, and what's the correct method' (SMP3 explain-the-flaw plus alternative)
Draw the claim/converse distinction with concrete cases so 'if it's a square then it has four right angles' is not confused with its converse
Keep pressing convince→justify: a confident explanation that has gaps is convincing; a correct, complete because/therefore chain is justifying — name which one the child has produced
keyRepresentations: A single well-chosen counter-example as a disproof object (e.g. 6 × 1/2 = 3 against 'multiplying makes bigger')
Chained angle-fact diagrams (angles on a line / in a triangle / vertically opposite) building to a proved value
Scaling picture of multiplication (× less than 1 shrinks, × 1 keeps, × more than 1 grows) to reason about product size without computing
A because/therefore proof frame linking givens through steps to conclusion
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplication always makes bigger / division always makes smaller' — the whole-number generalisation that fails for factors below 1
Confirming a conjecture with examples and calling it proved (empirical proof scheme)
Confusing a statement with its converse ('if square then 4 right angles' ⇒ 'if 4 right angles then square')
Inverting the wrong fraction in division, or 'dividing straight across', and critiquing only by the odd-looking answer rather than the faulty step
Believing a proved geometric result holds only for the specific diagram drawn

learn.summary: For 10-11 year-olds, this builds formal, multi-step mathematical argument and its critique half: constructing proofs by chaining facts (not measuring), finding and explaining errors in a peer's working, and the signature move of disproving a false 'always' conjecture with a single counter-example. Learners meet the proof asymmetry — one honest counter-example kills a universal claim, while confirming examples cannot establish it unless every possible case is checked (impossible for claims about all numbers) — and the logic of implication, including the claim/converse distinction. Activities span fractions, ratio, algebra and geometry, with a live adversarial dialogue as the primary vehicle and a manipulable conjecture/proof workspace, static critique cards, and a recognition warm-up as complementary alternatives serving different purposes.

activities.title: The confident conjecture champion (adversarial dialogue)
feedback: Revoice and extend the learner's chain rather than scoring it; when they offer only confirming examples, press 'so is it proved, or could there still be a breaker?'
If they name a counter-example, ask them to say exactly why that one case is enough to sink the whole 'always' rule.

When they repair the champion's fraction-division flip, ask them to state which step was wrong and what the correct step is (inverting the divisor, not the first fraction), not just that the answer looked odd.
Separate convincing from justifying: if an explanation sounds confident but has gaps, name it as convincing; if it is a complete because/therefore chain, name it as justifying.
activities.rationale: Defending a proof against a skeptic and disproving a confident false claim are naturally real-time exchanges; a responsive adversary can press on the learner's specific gaps and adapt to a patched claim or a converse in a way a fixed artefact cannot — an affordance of responsiveness, not a claim that only dialogue can teach this logic (the workspace activity also makes the if/therefore structure tangible). This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures; use counterexamples; distinguish correct logic from flawed and explain the flaw; older students can compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments.

A general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false; empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the shift to understanding logical implication (and the claim/converse distinction) is slow and fragile, so one counter-example being decisive is a hard-won idea.

Primary proof types include proof by counter-example; specific confirming examples do not constitute a watertight proof, and recognising this is a key step on the describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder.
learnerActions: Face an in-role character who asserts a universal claim with total confidence: 'Multiplying ALWAYS makes a number bigger — I've tried 3×4, 5×6, 10×10, works every time. So it's proved, right?'
Decide whether piling up more agreeing examples settles it, or whether you must HUNT for a case that breaks the claim.
Produce and state a decisive counter-example, e.g. '6 times a half is three — that's smaller, so it's not always,' and explain why that single case is enough.

When the champion patches the claim ('okay, multiplying always makes bigger OR the same') test the patch again: × 1/2 still shrinks it (so it breaks the patch), while × 1 only reaches the 'same' boundary the patch now allows.

When the champion defends a flawed fraction division ('just flip the FIRST fraction') locate the faulty step, say why it fails, and give the correct method (invert the divisor — the second fraction — then multiply).
Answer the champion's probes: 'Is that a proof or just examples?' and 'Does the opposite — the converse — also hold?'
activities.intendedInsight: A universal claim is destroyed by one honest counter-example, while confirming cases cannot prove it unless every possible case is checked (impossible for claims about all numbers); constructing arguments and critiquing flawed ones are the same reasoning practice, and a claim is not the same as its converse.

activities.title: Conjecture-testing and proof-building workspace
feedback: Report whether the chosen counter-example truly breaks the claim as scoped (for 'multiplying makes bigger': is the product actually not bigger, either smaller as with × 1/2 or equal as with × 1?), not merely whether a value was placed.
Report whether the proof chain is complete — every step justified from givens to conclusion — rather than answer-matching the final angle.
On the fraction-division panel, confirm whether the tapped step is the genuinely faulty one (inverting the first fraction instead of the divisor) and whether the selected method is correct.
activities.rationale: A manipulable workspace makes the decisive-single-case logic and the if/therefore structure tangible: dragging a value to watch a claim collapse and snapping facts into a chain externalise the reasoning. The live recolouring/collapse and drag interactions are illustrative mechanisms, not required tooling. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: A general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false; empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the shift to understanding logical implication (and the claim/converse distinction) is slow and fragile, so one counter-example being decisive is a hard-won idea.

SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures; use counterexamples; distinguish correct logic from flawed and explain the flaw; older students can compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments.
learnerActions: Sort 'always / sometimes / never' claims and use a counter-example finder: drag values and watch a claim collapse when, say, × 1/2 makes the product shrink. Use claims whose truth value is determinate — e.g. 'multiplying makes bigger' (an 'always' claim broken by a factor below 1 such as × 1/2). If including 'the more sides a shape has, the bigger its angles', state inside the task which angle is meant (e.g. each interior angle): for regular polygons each interior angle does grow with the number of sides, but it fails for irregular shapes, so it sorts as 'sometimes' — do not present it as a straightforwardly false 'always' claim.

Build an angle-fact proof chain: snap facts ('angles on a line sum to 180°', 'angles in a triangle sum to 180°', 'vertically opposite angles are equal') into an if/therefore track to reach a proved angle such as 60°, reserving measuring only to check — and only when the chosen givens genuinely force that value.
Critique a peer's fraction division: tap the mis-inverted step and select the correct method, then state in your own words why the flawed step fails.
activities.intendedInsight: Chaining established facts yields a proved value that holds generally, not just for the drawn diagram; a well-chosen single case breaks an 'always' claim; and locating a faulty step is more productive than rejecting an answer for looking odd.

activities.title: Annotated sound-vs-flawed proofs and conjecture cards
feedback: Prompt talk around each revealed card: 'Does this one case prove the rule, or just this instance?'

Draw the claim/converse contrast with a concrete pair, e.g. 'if it's a square then it has four right angles' versus 'if it has four right angles then it's a square' — the second is false because a non-square rectangle also has four right angles.
activities.rationale: Static annotated examples and reveal cards are a scaffold that can launch discussion and model what a flaw and a counter-example look like. They cannot respond to a learner's own implication errors or elicit a learner-constructed proof or hunted counter-example, so they support rather than replace the dialogue and workspace activities.
sourceClaims: Primary proof types include proof by counter-example; specific confirming examples do not constitute a watertight proof, and recognising this is a key step on the describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder.

SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures; use counterexamples; distinguish correct logic from flawed and explain the flaw; older students can compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments.
learnerActions: Compare an annotated correct fraction division with a flawed one side by side, and discuss where and why the flawed one goes wrong (it inverts the first fraction rather than the divisor).
Work through a set of true/false conjecture cards; tap a card to reveal either a counter-example that breaks it or a short proof sketch that supports it.
Use these as a springboard for talk: say aloud whether each revealed case is a proof or just an example, and whether the converse of a true claim also holds.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a flawed step laid out beside a correct one, and cards that reveal breakers or sketches, can seed critique vocabulary and prime the claim/converse distinction before learners construct their own arguments.

activities.title: Pick-the-breaker warm-up
feedback: Confirm whether the chosen case genuinely makes the product NOT bigger than the starting number: either smaller (e.g. a positive starting number times a factor below 1, or times 0) or equal (e.g. × 1). Then ask the learner to articulate the reason.
Do not treat a correct selection as evidence that the learner can construct a proof chain or explain a flaw independently.
activities.rationale: A recognition task can quickly surface whether a learner can spot a counter-example and serve as a warm-up, but it rewards fast selection over constructed reasoning and so must not stand in for the productive core. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Primary proof types include proof by counter-example; specific confirming examples do not constitute a watertight proof, and recognising this is a key step on the describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder.
learnerActions: From several candidate cases, pick the one that disproves a stated 'always' claim (e.g. which case breaks 'multiplying makes bigger'?).
After choosing, say aloud why that case is decisive and why the other candidates do not break the claim.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising which case is a counter-example is a useful entry step, but choosing from options does not itself elicit a constructed proof or a flaw explained in one's own words.

constraints: Insist on proof by chained fact, not measurement: measuring is only for checking a value, never for establishing that an angle MUST be a given size.
A proved geometric result holds generally, not only for the specific diagram drawn — make this generality explicit so learners do not think the proof applies only to one picture.

Reward finding the single breaker over listing confirming cases; explicitly name the asymmetry (one counter-example disproves an 'always'; no number of confirming cases proves it unless every possible case has been checked, which is impossible for claims about all numbers).
Keep the claim/converse distinction concrete: 'if square then four right angles' is not the same as 'if four right angles then square' (a non-square rectangle breaks the converse).

Recognition and selection tasks (pick-the-breaker, tap-the-step) are scaffolds; they do not elicit a learner-constructed proof chain or a flaw explained in the learner's own words, so do not treat a correct selection or score as evidence of the full reasoning practice.

If a learner endorses 'multiplication always makes bigger', treat it as a genuine false belief: reteach multiplication as scaling (for a positive starting number: × less than 1 shrinks, × 1 keeps, × more than 1 grows) with a picture, not only the argument skill.

When a learner suspects a rule is false but cannot yet find the counter-example, prompt the search ('what if a number were less than 1? try a half') without handing over the answer — the deductive instinct is forming.

The flawed fraction-division cue is 'invert/flip the first fraction'; it must always be presented as the error to find and critique, never as a method to follow — the correct method inverts the divisor (second fraction) then multiplies.

Any conjecture used in a sort must have a determinate truth value as stated; if a claim's truth depends on scope (e.g. 'more sides, bigger angles' depends on angle type and regular vs irregular), state that scope inside the activity so the sort is fair.
Static annotated examples and reveal cards cannot respond to a learner's own implication errors; pair them with dialogue or discussion.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and all activities are research-informed proposals rather than validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked examples: 6 × 1/2 = 3 is correct and is a valid counter-example to 'multiplying always makes bigger'; 8 × 0 = 0 is also valid. For the strict claim 'makes bigger', × 1 is also a breaker (6 × 1 = 6 is not bigger). The angle proof target of 60° is used illustratively and depends on the specific givens in a diagram — ensure the chained facts actually force 60° before presenting it to learners.

Comparative necessity over other media is NOT established by the sources provided; the original's 'only live dialogue teaches this' framing has been reduced to the narrow affordance of real-time responsiveness to the learner's gaps.

The patched claim 'multiplying always makes bigger OR the same' remains false for 0 < factor < 1 (× 1/2 shrinks), so × 1/2 is still a valid breaker; × 1 only reaches the 'same' boundary the patch allows and no longer breaks the patched claim. Keep the two tests distinct when guiding learners.

The flawed fraction-division cue 'flip/invert the first fraction' is a deliberate error to be critiqued (the divisor, i.e. the second fraction, is the one inverted); ensure it is always framed as the error to find, never as a method to follow.

The conjecture 'the more sides a shape has, the bigger its angles' is now scoped in-activity as a 'sometimes' claim: each interior angle of a regular polygon does grow with sides (triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°...), but it fails for irregular shapes and for exterior angles. The original pedagogy's treatment of it as flatly false is imprecise; specify the intended angle type before using it.

probeDeeper: 'How many examples where it works would it take to PROVE the rule always holds? And how many where it fails to prove it doesn't?'
'You found 6 × 1/2 = 3. Say exactly why that one case is enough to sink the whole rule.'
'The classmate now says "okay, but multiplying always makes it bigger OR the same". Is that fixed, or can you still break it? Try × a half again — and try × 1.'
'Is "multiplying makes bigger" the same claim as "if the answer is bigger then you multiplied"? Give me a case that separates them.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child producing a counter-example with a factor less than 1 (e.g. 6 × 1/2 = 3, or 8 × 0 = 0) AND recognising that ONE such case is enough to disprove the 'always' claim, rather than adding more confirming examples or hedging.

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplication-makes-bigger generalisation: endorses the rule because every whole-number case tried confirms it — the classic over-extension of whole-number multiplication to all numbers.
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a genuine false belief about multiplication — confront with scaling: 'what is 6 lots of a half?' Reteach multiplication as scaling (× less than 1 shrinks) using a picture, not just the argument skill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child agrees the rule is true, or tests only whole numbers and confirms it; when nudged, cannot see why a fraction would behave differently.

errorPatterns.pattern: Empirical proof scheme: responds to 'prove it's wrong' by trying MORE examples, or judges the rule 'usually/mostly true', not grasping that one counter-example is decisive and confirming cases never prove an 'always'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the asymmetry explicitly: 'How many YES examples would prove an ALWAYS? How many NO examples to disprove it?' Elicit that one counter-example is enough; celebrate finding the breaker over listing confirmers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child piles up examples on either side, or says 'it's right most of the time' — treats proof as accumulation of cases rather than a single decisive breaker.

errorPatterns.pattern: Suspects the rule is false and rejects the example-piling, but cannot yet find or articulate the counter-example — the deductive instinct is present but the productive step lags.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT read as not-knowing. Prompt the search without giving the answer: 'you think there's a case — what if one of the numbers were less than 1? Try a half.' Let the child produce and state the breaker; the logic of implication is already forming.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'I don't think it's always true' or 'there might be a case where it's not' but stalls when asked to produce one; may hover near fractions without landing 6×1/2.

responseLevels.gap: Endorses the rule, or tries only whole numbers and confirms it, or says 'mostly true'; does not produce a counter-example.
responseLevels.full: Produces a factor-below-1 counter-example (6 × 1/2 = 3, or ×0) AND states that a single such case disproves the 'always' claim while no number of confirming cases could prove it — then applies the same counter-example strategy unprompted to a repaired or new conjecture (e.g. the converse or the '≥' patch).
responseLevels.partial: Suspects or states the rule is false, or even offers a fractional case, but cannot explain why one counter-example is DECISIVE — may still want more cases to be sure, or gets the verdict without the sufficiency reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate is sure of this rule: 'When you multiply two numbers, the answer is always bigger than both of them — I've tried loads and it always works.' Are they right? Talk me through how you'd decide, and if you think the rule is wrong, show me the most convincing way to prove it's wrong.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands proof-by-counter-example knows that a single case with a factor below 1 settles it decisively, and reaches for one; a child in the empirical scheme keeps testing whole numbers, confirms the rule, or says 'mostly true' — never grasping that one breaker overturns 'always'. The prompt is hard to answer right for the wrong reason: guessing 'wrong' isn't enough; the discriminating act is generating the decisive case AND stating that one is sufficient. It's hard to answer wrong for the right reason because a correct reasoner cannot help but see the ×1/2 case once looking for a breaker.

sources.claim: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures; use counterexamples; distinguish correct logic from flawed and explain the flaw; older students can compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments.
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP3

sources.claim: A general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false; empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the shift to understanding logical implication (and the claim/converse distinction) is slow and fragile, so one counter-example being decisive is a hard-won idea.
sources.source: Hoyles & Küchemann (2002), Students' Understandings of Logical Implication, Educational Studies in Mathematics 51(3)

sources.claim: Primary proof types include proof by counter-example; specific confirming examples do not constitute a watertight proof, and recognising this is a key step on the describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder.
sources.source: NRICH, 'Reasoning: The Journey From Novice to Expert' (Cambridge)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 9–11 — identify ways humans harm the ocean (plastic pollution, overfishing, oil spills, acidification from CO2) and understand that MOST ocean pollution comes from land-based activities, not just ships.
• Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2): Y6 'recognise the impact of… human activity on environments' and Y4 changing-environments strand; links to citizenship/geography.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 5-ESS3-1 (human activities affect Earth's resources/environment) and MS-ESS3-3/MS-LS2-4 (human impact and ecosystem disruption) — human effects on the ocean system.
• Operational details: two ideas — (1) NAME the main harms and how each hurts animals (plastic entangles/is eaten; overfishing removes species and collapses webs; oil coats/poisons; CO2 acidifies water); (2) the counter-intuitive KEY FACT that ~80% of marine pollution originates on LAND (runoff, litter, sewage, farm chemicals via rivers), not mainly from ships. Emphasise the invisible pathway from inland activity → rivers/runoff → sea. Build on ecosystem/food-web systems thinking so harms are traced as cascades.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~9): names ≥3 harms; Tier B (~10): explains one harm's effect on a marine animal and states most pollution comes from land; Tier C (~11): traces a land activity through runoff to a cascading effect in the ocean food web.
bestPractices: Correct the 'pollution comes from ships/at the sea' image head-on with the ~80%-from-land fact and the runoff pathway (inland → river → sea).
Make each harm concrete via its effect on a specific animal (turtle eating a plastic bag it mistakes for a jellyfish; seabird stomach full of plastic; otter coated in oil).
Trace harms as system cascades (overfishing one species → web disruption) using the ecosystem/food-web understanding already built.
Distinguish point-source (a single spill — dramatic but rarer) from nonpoint-source runoff (diffuse, cumulative, the bigger problem) so students grasp why land runoff dominates.
Keep it evidence-based and avoid guilt/doom framing; pair with the protecting-the-ocean topic so problems have solutions.
keyRepresentations: A land-to-sea pathway map: inland runoff/rivers carrying pollutants to the ocean
Harm–animal cards (plastic→turtle, oil→otter, overfishing→collapsed web, CO2→acidified water)
A point-source vs nonpoint-source comparison
A food-web overlay showing a harm cascading through trophic levels
commonMisconceptions: 'Most ocean pollution comes from ships/dumping at sea' — the core misconception; ~80% is land-based via runoff.
'Pollution only affects the spot where it enters' — not seeing it spread and cascade through the web (e.g. via currents, bioaccumulation).
'Overfishing just means fewer of one fish' — missing the knock-on collapse of the wider ecosystem.
'Plastic goes away / breaks down quickly' — not knowing it persists and fragments into microplastics eaten by animals.
'If I live far from the sea, my actions don't affect the ocean' — ignoring the inland-runoff pathway.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: identify the main ways humans harm the ocean (plastic pollution, overfishing, oil spills, and acidification from CO2), and grasp the counter-intuitive key fact that roughly 80% of marine pollution originates on land — carried by runoff, litter, sewage and farm chemicals down rivers and drains to the sea — not mainly from ships. Learners name each harm and how it affects a specific marine animal, trace the invisible inland→river→sea pathway, and follow a harm as it cascades through the food web. Builds on prior ecosystem/food-web systems thinking.

activities.title: Live a day on land, then watch it reach the sea
feedback: When runoff carries a pollutant to sea, highlight that none of this happened at the sea itself — it began inland.
When the tally reaches roughly 80/20, note that about four-fifths of marine pollution comes from land, not ships (an approximate global estimate).
When overfishing is triggered, show the knock-on effect on other species, not just fewer of one fish.
If the learner expects ships to dominate, point to the growing land share and the river/drain pathway they just watched.
activities.rationale: The load-bearing idea is a source→pathway→consequence system; letting the child trigger inland actions and watch pollutants ride rivers to the sea and ripple through marine life is intended to make the invisible land–sea link that the '80% from land' fact names concrete. A live source tally (land vs ship) and a food-web overlay are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required mechanics.
sourceClaims: About 80% of pollution to the marine environment comes from the land (NOAA; the global figure is attributed by NOAA to a UN estimate), largely via nonpoint-source runoff rather than from ships.

The largest source of ocean pollution is nonpoint-source pollution carried by runoff from many diffuse inland sources (farms, vehicles, septic systems), contrasted with rarer point-source events like oil/chemical spills.

Marine debris (including plastic) comes overwhelmingly from people, with the majority originating on land and entering the ocean via littering, poor waste management and stormwater; plastic persists and is ingested by marine animals.
learnerActions: Look at a scene split between an inland town-and-farm on top and the ocean below.
Perform ordinary land actions: spread fertiliser on a field, drop a bottle by the kerb, flush the drains.
Trigger the rain and watch each pollutant wash into a stream, down a river, and out to sea.
Observe the consequences: the fertiliser feeds an algal bloom, and the bottle drifts out to sea and slowly breaks into fragments that a seabird or fish swallows, mistaking them for food.
Overfish a fish stock and watch the loss ripple visibly through a food-web overlay to other species.
Read a running source tally that shows land vs ship contributions, with land arriving at roughly four-fifths of the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Most ocean POLLUTION (about four-fifths) starts on LAND, often far from any ship, and travels via drains, runoff and rivers to the sea. Ocean harms, including pollution and overfishing (which happens at sea from fishing boats), can then cascade through the marine food web rather than staying at one spot.

activities.title: Harm–animal cards: naming harms through their victims
feedback: If only visible litter and spills are named, prompt that an invisible gas (CO2) dissolving into seawater also counts as pollution because it makes water more acidic and attacks shells and coral.
If the learner thinks plastic breaks down and disappears, note that it persists and fragments into microplastics that animals eat.
Confirm correct harm→animal matches with the specific mechanism (e.g. the turtle mistook the bag for a jellyfish).
activities.rationale: Making each harm concrete via a specific animal supports the evidence goal of naming at least three harms and describing how plastic or overfishing harms marine animals, and surfaces the misconceptions that plastic vanishes and that gases cannot be pollutants. A matching/sort can check classification but does not by itself elicit the learner's own explanation, so a state-it-yourself step is included.
sourceClaims: Marine debris (including plastic) comes overwhelmingly from people, with the majority originating on land and entering the ocean via littering, poor waste management and stormwater; plastic persists and is ingested by marine animals.
learnerActions: Match each harm to a specific animal and effect: plastic bag → turtle that eats it mistaking it for a jellyfish; plastic fragments → seabird with a stomach full of plastic; oil spill → otter with coated fur; overfishing → fewer fish left for seals and seabirds that eat them, disrupting the food web; CO2 → more acidic water that makes it harder for shellfish and coral to build and keep their shells and skeletons.
Name at least three distinct ways humans harm the ocean.
For one harm, state out loud or in writing exactly how it hurts a named animal.
activities.intendedInsight: Each ocean harm has a concrete, nameable effect on real animals; plastic persists and fragments into microplastics, and CO2 is an invisible gas that still pollutes the water.

activities.title: One bottle, many victims: tracing a cascade
feedback: If the learner says banning ships would clean the ocean, point out that around 80% starts on land via litter, runoff, sewage and chemicals, so most of the problem would remain.
If the learner says plastic only harms the one turtle that swallows it, follow microplastics or a toxin up the web to show one input reaching many victims.
Distinguish a single dramatic oil spill (point source, rarer) from diffuse everyday runoff (nonpoint source, the larger cumulative problem).
activities.rationale: This targets the discriminating idea that a child anchored on the 'ships and oil spills' image names only sea-based sources, while a child with the concept names a land pathway and a spreading mechanism. Contrasting point-source and nonpoint-source helps explain why land runoff dominates.
sourceClaims: The largest source of ocean pollution is nonpoint-source pollution carried by runoff from many diffuse inland sources (farms, vehicles, septic systems), contrasted with rarer point-source events like oil/chemical spills.
About 80% of pollution to the marine environment comes from the land (NOAA; the global figure is attributed by NOAA to a UN estimate), largely via nonpoint-source runoff rather than from ships.
learnerActions: Trace a plastic bottle dropped on a city street hundreds of miles from the coast to the sea, naming the route (drain → river → sea).
Follow a toxin or microplastic from plankton up through fish to predators, noting that one input can reach many animals that never touched the plastic directly.
Explain whether banning all ships would mostly stop ocean pollution, and why or why not.
Explain how carbon dioxide, a gas in the air, can count as ocean pollution.
activities.intendedInsight: Pollution does not stay where it enters: it spreads through currents and bioaccumulation up the food web, and because the bulk comes from land, stopping ship leaks alone would leave most of the problem untouched.

activities.title: Talking it through with a marine biologist or a sea turtle
feedback: Probe the learner's reasoning rather than simply confirming: ask them to say how the bottle actually travels or how the collapse spreads.
Pair the problem with solutions so the framing is empowering rather than guilt- or doom-laden.
Redirect to the land-to-sea mechanism if the dialogue drifts to ships as the main cause.
activities.rationale: Open dialogue may engage empathy and reasoning about responsibility and agency, complementing the modelled mechanism. Offered as a complement; the source row did not establish that dialogue teaches the empirical cascade better than a worked model.
learnerActions: Ask a marine-biologist character 'how does MY town's rubbish reach the sea?' and respond to their follow-up questions about the runoff pathway.
Discuss why overfishing hurts more than just one fish, explaining the web disruption in your own words.
Hear a turtle character recount mistaking a plastic bag for a jellyfish, and discuss what could be done differently.
activities.intendedInsight: Ocean harm has a values and agency dimension — who is responsible, whether distant inland behaviour matters, and what we can do — alongside the factual mechanism.

activities.title: Check: pollution sources, main cause, and a traced cascade
feedback: For the source item, reinforce that about four-fifths is land-based via runoff, litter, sewage and chemicals.
For the scenario, confirm the full chain (land activity → river/drain → sea → effect on an animal → spread through the web).
Recognition items check whether the idea is held; they do not by themselves show the learner can independently construct and explain the pathway, so pair with the explain/trace tasks above.
activities.rationale: Questions naming harms, a 'where does most pollution come from?' item, and a scenario tracing land activity to a marine effect map onto all three evidence goals. Recognition alone does not elicit production, so an open traced-chain task is included.
learnerActions: Name three ways humans harm the ocean.
Answer where most ocean pollution comes from — land or ships — and give the approximate share.
Work a scenario that traces a specific land activity through runoff to a cascading effect in the ocean food web.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can demonstrate naming harms, identifying the land-based majority source, and tracing a land activity to a cascading marine effect.

constraints: Correct the 'pollution comes from ships / at the sea' image directly using the ~80%-from-land fact and the inland→river→sea runoff pathway.
Keep framing evidence-based and avoid guilt or doom; pair problems with solutions (e.g. a protecting-the-ocean follow-up).

Distinguish point sources (a single identifiable source such as an oil spill or a sewage or factory pipe; a big spill is dramatic but rarer) from nonpoint-source runoff (diffuse and cumulative, often the larger problem). Note that land-based pollution includes both kinds.

A static pathway map or card set can present sources and effects clearly and cheaply; it is a valid exposition tool but does not itself let the child trigger a source and watch the cascade unfold, so pair it with an interactive or traced task for the systems insight. This is a scoped affordance, not a claim that only an interactive can teach the concept.

Recognition/multiple-choice items assess whether the concept is held but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the pathway explanation; include tasks where learners state or write the chain themselves.
The ~80% figure is an approximate global estimate (NOAA attributes it to a UN estimate); present it as 'about four-fifths', not an exact measured constant.
Build on prior ecosystem and food-web understanding so harms can be traced as cascades.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified here. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles/facts rather than proving any activity was tested.
The source row rated a 3D artefact as adding 'cost without deepening' the reasoning; this has been reframed as a narrowly scoped preference rather than a categorical claim that 3D adds nothing.
The original marked conversation and static image as not able to let the child trigger/watch the cascade; preserved as scoped affordance limits, not as 'only an interactive can teach this'.

The ~80% land-based figure is attributed by NOAA to a UN estimate; keep it as approximate. No arithmetic or force/motion content exists in this row to correct; the science (land-based majority, CO2 acidification, microplastic persistence, overfishing cascade) is consistent with the cited sources.

probeDeeper: A plastic bottle dropped on a city street hundreds of miles from the coast ends up in the sea. How does it get there?
If we banned all ships tomorrow, would ocean pollution mostly stop? Why or why not?
How can carbon dioxide — a gas in the air — count as ocean pollution?
One turtle swallows a plastic bag. Name one way that harm could reach animals that never touched any plastic.
assess.correctAnswer: No — most ocean pollution comes from LAND, not from ships. Around 80% of it starts on land: plastic litter, farm and sewage run-off, and chemicals wash down rivers and drains and out to sea, plus carbon dioxide from burning fuels dissolves into the water and makes it more acidic. Dramatic oil spills are real but are a small share of the total. So stopping ship leaks alone would leave most of the problem untouched, because the bulk pours off the land.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Ocean pollution mostly comes from ships and oil spills at sea' — the memorable disaster image stands in for the main cause.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the ~80%-from-land figure and trace a plastic bottle from a street drain down a river to the sea; ships are the exception, not the rule.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — ships and oil spills are the main source, so stopping leaks would make the ocean basically clean.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names only ships, tankers and oil spills; leaves out rivers, drains, litter and run-off from land.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Pollution only hurts the animal that eats/meets it' — no sense of it spreading through the food web.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Follow microplastics or a toxin from plankton up through fish to predators; one input, many victims.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says plastic only harms the one turtle that swallows it; doesn't mention it moving up the web or breaking into microplastics.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Acidification is just rubbish/chemicals in the water' — doesn't see invisible CO2 gas as a pollutant.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain CO2 from burning fuels dissolving to form acid that lowers pH and attacks shells and coral — pollution you can't see.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists only visible litter and spills; surprised that a gas dissolving in seawater counts as harm.

responseLevels.gap: Names only ships/oil spills; believes the ocean would be clean if sea-based leaks stopped.
responseLevels.full: States most pollution is land-based (~80%), traces a land-to-sea pathway, and explains a specific harm mechanism (plastic through the food web, or CO2 → acidification) — transferring to judge whether a given action would fix much.
responseLevels.partial: Names several harms (plastic, overfishing, spills, acidification) but still frames pollution as sea-based, or can't say most of it comes from land.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child says 'the ocean gets polluted mostly by ships and oil spills out at sea — so if we stopped ships leaking, the ocean would be basically clean'. Do you agree that ships are the main source? Where does most ocean pollution actually come from, and how does it get there?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child anchored on the vivid 'ships and oil spills' image names only sea-based sources and thinks the problem would be solved by fixing ships; a child with the concept says most pollution is land-based and can name a land pathway (rivers/drains/run-off) or the CO2-acidification route. The 'would the ocean be clean?' clause forces them to reveal whether they know where the bulk comes from.

sources.claim: About 80% of pollution to the marine environment comes from the land (NOAA; the global figure is attributed by NOAA to a UN estimate), largely via nonpoint-source runoff rather than from ships.

sources.claim: The largest source of ocean pollution is nonpoint-source pollution carried by runoff from many diffuse inland sources (farms, vehicles, septic systems), contrasted with rarer point-source events like oil/chemical spills.
sources.source: NOAA National Ocean Service — Pollution tutorial: nonpoint source (page fetched and confirmed)

sources.claim: Marine debris (including plastic) comes overwhelmingly from people, with the majority originating on land and entering the ocean via littering, poor waste management and stormwater; plastic persists and is ingested by marine animals.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Common Plants & Trees

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 Plants):** "identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees." Naming real plants from observation, and sorting trees into deciduous (loses leaves) vs evergreen (keeps leaves), is statutory in England.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no direct naming PE; nearest anchor 1-LS1-1 / DCI LS1.A):** NGSS does not require naming particular plants; it frames plants by their external parts (roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits) and their functions. The US connection here is recognising plants as organisms with parts, not the UK naming/deciduous–evergreen task.

- **Operational details:** This is primarily a NAMING-from-observation topic, best rooted in direct, first-hand encounters with real plants — a nature walk, the school grounds, a planted pot — rather than pictures alone, because the objective is that children recognise and name plants they actually meet. Build a shared vocabulary of five-plus common local plants (daisy, dandelion, buttercup, rose, oak, holly...) and repeatedly name them in context. Introduce deciduous vs evergreen through the single observable test: does this tree drop all its leaves in autumn/winter, or stay green? Reinforce across seasons if possible (the same tree, bare then leafy). Keep 'plant' inclusive of trees — children often don't count a tree as a plant.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–6, KS1 Y1). Children can name at least five common plants from real specimens/pictures, match names to plants, and sort trees into deciduous and evergreen with examples. Appropriate: local, familiar species; the leaf-drop test. NOT appropriate yet: classification keys, Latin names, flower-part reproduction. Watch the 'a tree is not a plant' and 'evergreens never lose any leaves' misconceptions.
bestPractices: Root naming in first-hand observation of real, local plants (nature walk, school grounds, a grown pot) rather than pictures alone, since the objective is recognising plants children actually meet.
Build and rehearse a shared vocabulary of five-plus common local species, naming them repeatedly in context.
Teach deciduous vs evergreen through one observable test — does it drop all its leaves in autumn/winter or stay green — ideally by revisiting the same tree across seasons.
Explicitly include trees within the category 'plant' to counter the common belief that trees are not plants.
Use real specimens and picture cards together, and matching/sorting activities with self-checking feedback.
keyRepresentations: A named local-plant gallery (daisy, dandelion, buttercup, rose, oak, holly) tied to real specimens.
Two sorting bins: deciduous (loses leaves) vs evergreen (keeps leaves), with tree examples.
Same-tree seasonal pair images (summer leafy / winter bare or still-green) to make the leaf-drop test visible.
Name–to–picture matching cards for common plants.
commonMisconceptions: 'A tree is not a plant' — children exclude large woody plants from the category 'plant'.
'Evergreen means it never loses a single leaf' — rather than keeping foliage year-round while shedding gradually.
Calling any small green plant 'grass' or 'weed' instead of using specific names.
Thinking deciduous trees are 'dead' in winter because they have no leaves.

learn.summary: For 5–6 year-olds learning to name common local plants and sort trees as deciduous (drops all its leaves in autumn/winter) or evergreen (stays leafy year-round, shedding only gradually). Learning is rooted in first-hand observation of real, local plants, supported by an illustrated tap-to-reveal scene that binds each plant to its name and one recognition cue, a season slider that makes the leaf-drop test visible on the same tree, and matching/sorting follow-up checks. Key misconceptions to pre-empt: a tree is not a plant, evergreens never shed any leaf, and a bare winter tree is dead.

activities.title: Nature walk: find, name and rehearse real local plants
feedback: If a child calls any small green plant 'grass' or 'weed', offer the specific name and have them repeat it in context.
If a child excludes a tree from 'plants', point out its roots, stem/trunk and leaves and confirm a tree is a plant too.
Praise naming tied to a feature ('yes — holly, because the leaves are shiny and spiky all year').
activities.rationale: The statutory objective is naming from first-hand observation, so direct encounters with real, local species build recognition rather than only testing it. Explicitly placing trees inside 'plant' counters a documented misconception.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees'.
Children frequently do not classify trees as plants, and hold that 'evergreen' means a tree never loses any leaves — common primary botany misconceptions to pre-empt.
learnerActions: Go outside to the school grounds, a park, a nature walk, or a planted pot and look closely at real plants.
Find and name at least five common local plants (for example daisy, dandelion, buttercup, rose, oak, holly), saying each name aloud as you find it.
Point to a recognition feature as you name each one — for example the dandelion's jagged leaves and clock seedhead, the holly's shiny spiky leaves.
Deliberately include a big tree (such as an oak) and say 'a tree IS a plant' to confirm trees belong in the plant group.

Over the seasons, especially from autumn into winter, return to the same tree to see whether it keeps its green leaves or goes bare (some young oaks and beech hedges hold dry brown leaves until spring, but they are still deciduous).
activities.intendedInsight: Plants (including trees) are organisms you can recognise and name from how they really look, and the names belong to plants you actually meet.

activities.title: Tap-to-explore seasonal park scene (indoor anchor)
feedback: When a tree is flipped bare, confirm 'deciduous — it drops all its leaves, then grows new ones in spring'.
When the evergreen stays green, confirm 'evergreen — it keeps leaves all year, though it does drop a few at a time'.
If a child says the bare tree is dead, show that new leaves grow back in the spring state.
activities.rationale: A pre-authored word–image mapping ties each plant to its name and distinguishing look, and showing the same tree in two seasonal states makes the single observable test (does it go bare?) visible. The scene also directly works against two documented misconceptions: tapping the oak among the plants confirms a tree is a plant, and the 'drops a few at a time' feedback counters the belief that an evergreen never loses any leaf. This indoor scene is a proposed scaffold to name and rehearse what the child then finds for real outdoors; it supplements rather than replaces the walk.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees'.
Children frequently do not classify trees as plants, and hold that 'evergreen' means a tree never loses any leaves — common primary botany misconceptions to pre-empt.
learnerActions: Tap each plant in an illustrated park scene to see/hear its name plus one recognition cue (tap the dandelion to highlight its jagged leaves and clock seedhead; tap the daisy, buttercup, rose).
Tap a big oak included among the plants to confirm that a tree is a plant.

For each tree, open a lift-the-flap or slide a year-slider that swings the SAME tree from summer to winter: flip the oak and watch it go bare ('deciduous: drops its leaves'); flip the holly beside it and watch it stay glossy green ('evergreen: keeps its leaves').
Say whether each tree is deciduous or evergreen based on what you just saw happen.
activities.intendedInsight: The deciduous/evergreen rule is something you observe — a deciduous tree goes completely bare and regrows, an evergreen stays green all year (shedding only gradually) — not just a definition to memorise.

activities.title: Sort trees into two bins with a year that runs forward
feedback: If a sort is wrong, run the year forward so the leaf-drop (or not) is visible, then let the child re-sort.
If a child judges by how a tree looks on one day, remind them the rule is about the whole year, not a single snapshot.
activities.rationale: Sorting makes the defining leaf-drop test observable through a season control, while matching rehearses name recognition. The year-slider that drops and regrows leaves is the key interaction that makes the rule visible.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees'.
learnerActions: Use two labelled bins: deciduous (loses leaves) and evergreen (keeps leaves).
Drag each tree into a bin, then run a season slider forward ('run the year forward') to check: a deciduous tree strips all its leaves while an evergreen stays green.
Pair this with a name-the-plant drag-match: drag each plant name onto the matching picture or real specimen.
Explain how you could tell which group a tree belongs to by watching it across a whole year.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciduous vs evergreen is decided across the whole year (does the tree go completely bare?), and each plant has a name you can match to its appearance.

activities.title: Check: match names and sort trees (follow-up assessment)
feedback: Full understanding: explains a deciduous tree drops all its leaves seasonally and regrows them (bare ≠ dead), an evergreen keeps leaves year-round, and transfers the rule to a new example such as a larch (a conifer that drops all its needles, so deciduous).
Partial: knows 'deciduous loses its leaves' as a fact but still leans on present appearance or thinks a bare tree has died — revisit the same-tree seasonal pair.
Gap: names trees only by how they look right now and calls a bare deciduous tree 'dead' — reteach with the four-season picture strip and the dormant-not-dead check.
activities.rationale: Matching and categorization assess the naming and sorting objectives directly. Because they check recognition rather than build it from observation, they belong after the observational and interactive work, as follow-up; recognition alone does not elicit the spoken naming or reasoning the objective also expects.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees'.
learnerActions: Match five named plants to their pictures or real specimens.
Sort six trees into deciduous and evergreen, giving an example of each.
Answer the diagnostic: 'The oak is bare with no leaves in winter; the holly has green leaves all year. Which is deciduous — and how could you tell just by watching it across a whole year?'
activities.intendedInsight: A secure learner reasons from leaf loss over the year (the oak goes bare then regrows), not from how a tree looks on one day.

activities.title: Dormant-not-dead twig investigation (predict–observe–explain)
feedback: If a child predicts nothing will happen because the stick is dead, keep the twigs visible as the buds swell and open, then revisit the prediction; if a twig does not open, use the scratch test and a spring photo instead.
Confront the 'bare = dead' idea directly with a spring photo of the same tree in full leaf.
Clarify for evergreens: they do shed leaves, a few at a time and continuously replaced, so the tree is never completely bare — show fallen holly or pine leaves beneath an evergreen.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain task is proposed to surface and challenge the 'bare tree is dead' misconception by letting children watch buds leaf out; observing real bud-burst may make the dormant-not-dead idea more concrete than a verbal statement, though its relative effectiveness is not established here.
learnerActions: In late winter, with permission, have an adult cut a few bare twigs from a deciduous tree (for example horse chestnut with sticky buds) and stand them in water on a windowsill.
Predict what the bare 'dead-looking stick' will do over the next few weeks, and say WHY.
Watch over the next two to four weeks as the buds usually swell and begin to open into small leaves (some twigs may not open).
Discuss: is a bare winter tree alive or dead, and how could you check (scratch a twig to show green underneath, point to waiting buds)?
activities.intendedInsight: A bare deciduous tree in winter is dormant, not dead — it still holds buds and will leaf again in spring.

constraints: Appropriate content: local, familiar species and the single leaf-drop test. NOT appropriate yet: classification keys, Latin names, and flower-part reproduction.
Keep 'plant' inclusive of trees throughout, since children often exclude large woody plants from the category.

The illustrated scene and sorting bins are indoor scaffolds that name and rehearse; they supplement but do not replace the first-hand outdoor observation the naming-from-observation objective requires.
Matching and sorting checks confirm recognition but do not by themselves build it from observation, nor elicit spoken naming; use them as follow-up, not as the main teaching.
Teach that evergreens DO shed leaves gradually (never going bare), rather than that they never lose a single leaf.

NGSS has no plant-naming performance expectation; its nearest anchor (1-LS1-1 / LS1.A) frames plants by external parts and functions, which is a different objective from the UK naming/deciduous–evergreen task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The in-role conversation and manipulable 3D tree were judged poor fit in the source; omitted as activities rather than reproduced as categorical 'medium adds nothing' claims, since no distinct learning purpose was given.

The larch example (a conifer that drops all its needles) is used as a 'tricky case' for deciduous reasoning; keep it as an extension for learners who have secured the basic rule, not as an early example.

The 'bare winter tree is dead' misconception targeted by the twig investigation is drawn from the assessment error patterns in the original row, not from a cited sources[].claim; its activity sourceClaims are therefore [].
The twig investigation's efficacy relative to verbal correction is an untested proposal; efficacy wording is kept qualified.

assess.poeTask: In late winter, cut a few bare twigs from a deciduous tree (e.g. horse chestnut with sticky buds) and stand them in water on the windowsill. Ask each child to predict what the 'dead-looking stick' will do over two weeks and WHY. A child holding 'bare = dead' predicts nothing will happen; watching the buds burst and leaf out forces the dormant-not-dead idea.
probeDeeper: What will happen to the oak's leaves and branches in spring?
If I showed you both trees in July, when both are covered in leaves, how else could you work out which is deciduous?
Is the bare oak in winter alive or dead — how could you check?
A larch is a conifer with needles, but it drops every needle in winter — would you call it deciduous or evergreen, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: The oak is deciduous because it drops all its leaves in autumn and grows new ones in spring; the holly is evergreen because it keeps leaves all year. The way to tell is to watch across the seasons for whether the tree goes completely bare.

errorPatterns.pattern: A bare tree in winter is dead ('the oak's got no leaves, it must have died')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish dormant from dead: scratch the twig to show green underneath, point to buds already waiting; it will leaf again in spring. Confront directly with a spring photo of the same tree.
errorPatterns.distractor: The oak is dead, not deciduous, because it has no leaves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the leafless winter oak 'dead' rather than deciduous, and is surprised it could grow leaves again

errorPatterns.pattern: Evergreens never drop a single leaf ('holly leaves stay on forever')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Evergreens do shed leaves — a few at a time, replaced continuously — so the tree is never bare. Show fallen holly/pine leaves under an evergreen.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists evergreen leaves never fall, so cannot explain how the tree replaces old leaves

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges the group by what the tree looks like right now, not across the year ('it has leaves today so it's evergreen')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Deciduous vs evergreen is about the whole year, not one day. Use a four-season picture strip of each tree.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In summer, when both trees are leafy, cannot tell them apart; relies on the present snapshot

responseLevels.gap: Names trees only from how they look at the moment; calls a bare deciduous tree 'dead'; cannot use the idea of losing leaves across the year.
responseLevels.full: Explains that a deciduous tree drops all its leaves seasonally and regrows them (bare ≠ dead), an evergreen keeps leaves year-round, and transfers the rule to a new example such as the larch.
responseLevels.partial: Knows 'deciduous loses its leaves' as a fact but still leans on the tree's present appearance, or thinks a bare tree has died, and cannot handle a tricky case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two trees. The oak is bare with no leaves in winter; the holly has green leaves all year round. Which one is deciduous — and how could you tell, just by watching it across a whole year?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the concept reasons from leaf loss over the year (the oak goes bare then regrows). A child who lacks it judges from the tree's state right now ("the oak has no leaves so it's dead / it's not a real tree") or picks an irrelevant cue like size, and cannot say what to watch for over time.

sources.claim: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common wild and garden plants, including deciduous and evergreen trees'.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study (KS1)

sources.claim: NGSS 1-LS1-1 / DCI LS1.A frames plants by their external parts (roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits) and functions rather than by naming particular species; NGSS has no plant-naming performance expectation.
sources.source: NGSS (Next Generation Science Standards), nextgenscience.org

sources.claim: Children frequently do not classify trees as plants, and hold that 'evergreen' means a tree never loses any leaves — common primary botany misconceptions to pre-empt.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–7; What Is Wind? (CONCEPTUAL, 0.06): wind is moving air; it can be a gentle breeze or a strong gale; wind can move things — leaves, kites, flags — and even push people.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 weather observation (Y1 'Seasonal changes' — describing windy weather). The cause of wind (uneven heating) is deferred to 7-9 'What Causes Wind'. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS): K-ESS2-1 (VERIFIED verbatim) names wind among weather conditions (DCI ESS2.D). Keep it to 'wind is moving air' + strength, observed by its EFFECTS — mechanism is later.
• Operational details — The core idea is that wind is AIR that is MOVING — invisible itself, known by what it does (things move, flags flap, you feel it push). The second idea is strength as a spectrum: breeze → gale. At this age, do NOT explain what makes wind blow (uneven heating/rising air is the 7-9 topic this feeds); keep to observing and describing. Confront the intuitive gap that 'air is nothing' — wind proves air is real 'stuff' that can push. Prerequisite: none; feeds What Causes Wind (7-9) and Using Weather Instruments (anemometer/wind vane). Evidence: define wind as moving air; distinguish breeze vs strong wind; give examples of what wind moves.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/observational): the child defines wind as moving air, tells a gentle breeze from a strong wind, and gives examples of things wind can move or push — recognising wind by its effects, with no requirement to explain what causes it.
bestPractices: Make wind's invisibility concrete: we can't see air, but we see and feel what it DOES (leaves swirl, flag snaps, hair blows, it pushes you) — wind is evidence that air is real 'stuff'.
Build strength as a spectrum (breeze → wind → gale) with matching effects (leaves flutter → branches sway → hard to walk), rather than just 'windy/not windy'.
Use first-hand experience — blow on a hand, wave a fan, take a windy-day walk, fly a streamer — before any screen, so the concept is embodied.
Keep cause OUT at this age: resist 'wind is made by trees waving' (reversed cause) or 'the sky/clouds make wind'; the uneven-heating explanation is the 7-9 topic.
Link to safety and daily life gently (strong wind can knock things over, makes kites fly) without tipping into the separate storm-safety content.
Distinguish wind (moving air outdoors) from a fan/breath (moving air we make) — same idea, different source.
keyRepresentations: A wind-strength slider from breeze to gale with a scene that responds (leaves → branches → whole tree), an informal Beaufort-style scale for young children.
Wind socks / flags / streamers whose angle shows wind strength and direction — the classic 'see the invisible' device.
Effect cards: things wind moves (kite, leaves, flag, hat, washing) vs things it can't easily move (heavy rock).
A hand feeling a fan/blow — embodied 'air is real and can push'.
commonMisconceptions: 'Wind is made by trees waving' (or fans/clouds) — reversed cause: the moving air makes the trees wave, not the other way round.
'Air is nothing / empty' — wind demonstrates air is real matter that can push objects and be felt.
'Wind blows because the weather is angry / on purpose' — animistic framing; keep it to observation, defer real cause.
'Windy always means cold' — wind can be warm or cold; strength and temperature are separate.
'You can see the wind' — we see its EFFECTS and things it carries, not the moving air itself.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, build the idea that wind is moving air — invisible itself, but known by what it does (leaves swirl, flags snap, hair blows, it pushes you) — and that wind has a strength spectrum from gentle breeze to strong gale. Confront the intuition that 'air is nothing' by showing air is real stuff that can push. Keep the CAUSE of wind (uneven heating/rising air) out at this age; that is a later 7–9 topic. Ground learning in first-hand experience (blowing, fanning, a windy-day walk) before any screen model.

activities.title: Make your own wind
feedback: If a learner thinks air is 'nothing', have them blow on their hand: 'You just felt the air push — so air is real stuff, even though we can't see it.'
If a learner thinks wind must come from one place like the sky, show it can be made from any direction by fanning: 'Wind is air moving from place to place, not pouring out of one spot.'
Distinguish gently: 'A fan and your breath are moving air YOU make; outdoor wind is moving air outdoors — same idea, different source.'
activities.rationale: First-hand, embodied experience of moving air makes 'air is real and can push' concrete before any screen model and directly addresses the 'air is nothing' and 'wind comes from one fixed source' misconceptions. Leading with this hands-on work matches the stated pedagogy of first-hand experience before any on-screen model.
sourceClaims: Common young-learner ideas: 'air is nothing', 'you can see the wind', and reversed cause ('trees waving make the wind'); teaching should establish air as real matter known by wind's effects.
learnerActions: Blow on the back of your own hand and feel the push.
Wave a hand or a fan at your face and feel the moving air.
Wave a streamer or strip of paper and watch it flutter in the air you move.
Talk about where outdoor wind is the same idea (moving air) but comes from outside rather than from you.
Indoors with the windows shut, work out how you could still make a little wind yourself (blow, fan, wave) — showing wind is just air moving, not something from a single fixed source.
activities.intendedInsight: Air is real stuff you can feel, and wind is simply air that is moving. You can make moving air yourself with your breath or a fan — the same idea as outdoor wind, just a different source.

activities.title: Crank the wind from breeze to gale
feedback: When a learner says 'but I can't see any wind', affirm it: 'Right — we never see the air. We see what it DOES: the leaves move, the flag snaps, the hat rolls away.'
If a learner expects everything to move equally, point to the rock: 'A gentle breeze moves a leaf but not a heavy rock. How strong did you have to make it before the branches moved?'
Connect to their body: 'When you crank it to a gale the character leans in to walk — have you ever felt the wind push you like that?'
activities.rationale: Used after the first-hand experience, a responsive scene the child controls lets them vary strength and watch what each level can and cannot move, building both 'wind is moving air (seen through effects)' and the breeze–gale spectrum together. The draggable 'can it move this?' test and the leaning windsock are concrete ways to make the invisible readable. This is one effective model, not the only way, and it supports rather than replaces feeling real wind.
sourceClaims: Common young-learner ideas: 'air is nothing', 'you can see the wind', and reversed cause ('trees waving make the wind'); teaching should establish air as real matter known by wind's effects.
learnerActions: Use a wind-strength control (e.g. a slider or dial) that goes from gentle breeze up to strong gale, coupled to an outdoor scene that responds live.
Nudge the strength up a little and watch a few leaves stir and a flag ripple — name this a breeze.
Push the strength higher and watch branches sway, a kite lift and pull on its string, and hair stream sideways.
Push to the top and watch the whole tree bend, a hat tumble off and roll away, and a character lean hard into the gust to keep walking — name this a gale.
Drag objects into the scene and test 'can the wind move this?' — compare a leaf (blows away) with a heavy rock (stays put).
Read a windsock or flag whose angle leans further as the strength increases, showing the invisible wind's strength and direction.
activities.intendedInsight: Wind is moving air: you never see the air itself, only what it does. By changing the strength yourself in the model, you see wind as moving air of varying strength — a spectrum from breeze to gale — recognised by its effects, and you can link this to how real wind has felt on your body.

activities.title: Which way does the cause go? (trees and wind)
feedback: Correct answer: 'It's the other way round. Wind is moving air. The moving air pushes the branches, which is why they wave — the trees aren't making the wind. We can't see the air itself, but we can see what it does.'
If a learner names the moving object as the cause, flip it: show a still day (nothing waves), then a fan making a still branch wave — the air moves the object, not the other way round.
Keep the real cause of wind aside: 'We're not working out what makes the wind blow today — just that the wind moves the trees, not the trees making the wind.'
activities.rationale: Reversed causality ('trees waving make the wind') is a documented young-learner misconception; directly contrasting a windless scene with a fan moving a still object makes the direction of cause visible without introducing the deferred uneven-heating mechanism.
sourceClaims: Common young-learner ideas: 'air is nothing', 'you can see the wind', and reversed cause ('trees waving make the wind'); teaching should establish air as real matter known by wind's effects.
learnerActions: Look at or imagine a windy day with tree branches waving about.
Consider a claim: 'The trees are making the wind by waving.' Decide whether it is right and explain why.
Compare a windless day where nothing waves with a fan (moving air) making a still branch wave — notice the moving air moves the branch.
State in your own words what wind actually is and what is really happening with the trees.
activities.intendedInsight: Wind is moving air, and the moving air pushes the branches, which is why they wave — the trees do not make the wind. Cause goes from moving air to moving object, not the reverse.

activities.title: Sort and order by what wind does
feedback: For sorting, link back to the scene: 'A leaf blows away in a breeze, but it takes a much stronger wind to move heavier things like a hat or branches — and a big heavy rock barely moves at all.'
If ordering is muddled, anchor on effects: 'Fluttering leaves is gentler than a bending tree.'
If a learner says you can SEE the wind, correct: 'We see what the wind does and the things it carries — not the moving air itself.'
activities.rationale: A sort/order/question check confirms the observational targets (define wind, breeze vs gale, examples of what wind moves). This sort and ordering can check classification and recall but does not itself build the felt breeze-to-gale spectrum; use it after hands-on and model experience.
learnerActions: Sort objects into 'the wind can move this easily' (kite, leaves, flag, hat, washing) versus 'the wind can't easily move this' (heavy rock).
Put effects in order from gentle to strong: leaves flutter → branches sway → hard to walk / tree bends.
Answer 'what is wind?' and explain how you know it's windy if you can't see the wind.
Tell a gentle breeze apart from a strong gale and give an example of each.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking that wind is moving air known by its effects, that some things move in wind and heavy things resist, and that strength runs along a spectrum from breeze to gale.

activities.title: How do you know it's windy? (talking it through)
feedback: Prompt for a second clue if a learner gives only one: 'That's one way — the flag is flapping. What else tells you it's windy?'
Praise effect-based answers: 'Yes — you feel it push and you see things move; both tell you the air is moving.'
activities.rationale: A brief eliciting conversation can draw out effects-based reasoning and give the learner practice producing an explanation, though a 5–7 observational concept does not require extended open dialogue.
learnerActions: Answer a prompt such as 'How do you KNOW it's windy if you can't see the wind? Give me two ways.'
Describe the difference between a gentle breeze and a strong gale in your own words.
Work out, with windows shut indoors, how you could make a little wind yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating that we detect wind only by its effects, and that strength varies, strengthens the observe-by-effects reasoning.

constraints: Keep the CAUSE of wind (uneven heating / rising air) out at this age — it is the later 7–9 'What Causes Wind' topic. Confine work to observing and describing.
Resist reversed cause ('wind is made by trees/fans/clouds waving') and animistic framing ('the weather is angry'); the moving air makes things move, not the reverse.
Build strength as a spectrum (breeze → wind → gale with matching effects) rather than a simple windy/not-windy split.
Clarify that windy does not always mean cold — wind can be warm or cold; strength and temperature are separate.

Lead with first-hand experience (blowing, fanning, a windy-day walk, flying a streamer) before any screen model; the responsive on-screen scene is a model of real wind, not a substitute for feeling it.
Sorting/quiz tasks check recognition and recall but do not themselves build the felt breeze-to-gale spectrum; use them after hands-on and model work, not instead of it.
Link to safety/daily life only gently (strong wind can knock things over, lifts kites) without drifting into separate storm-safety content.
Distinguish wind (moving air outdoors) from a fan or breath (moving air we make) — same idea, different source.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Activities were reordered on review so the embodied 'Make your own wind' precedes the on-screen responsive scene, resolving a contradiction with the summary and constraint that first-hand experience come before any screen model.

Two of the three sources are marked verified:false in the row (DfE KS1 detail and the misconception-research claim); the NGSS K-ESS2-1 claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

The NGSS K-ESS2-1 claim establishes wind as a named weather condition (topic-level support) but does not directly support the specific teaching approach of any single activity, so it was not attached as an activity sourceClaim.

Interactive examples (wind-strength slider/dial, draggable objects, windsock angle, 'blow' button) are retained as optional ways to make the concept concrete, not as mandatory mechanisms; a tap-to-reveal windy scene is an acceptable lighter alternative for recap.

The non-preferred 3D option was rated 'poor' in the row with the note that observing wind by effects 'has no 3D requirement' — retained only as the catalog's narrow judgement for this concept, not as a universal claim that 3D adds nothing to learning.

No arithmetic or force-direction claims required correction here; the main conceptual safeguards are keeping the deferred cause-of-wind mechanism out and preserving the correct direction of cause (moving air moves objects).

probeDeeper: If we can't see the wind, how do we know it's there? Give me two ways.
What's the difference between a gentle breeze and a strong gale?
Indoors with the windows shut, could you make a little wind yourself? How?
assess.correctAnswer: No — it's the other way round. Wind is moving air. The moving air pushes the branches, which is why they wave; the trees aren't making the wind. We can't see the air itself, but we can see what it does.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversed causality — 'trees (or waves, or leaves) make the wind by moving'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Flip the cause: show a windless day where nothing waves, then a fan (moving air) making a still branch wave — the air moves the object.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the trees make the wind by waving their branches.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the moving object as the cause of the wind rather than its effect

errorPatterns.pattern: Wind isn't air — 'it's a special thing on its own'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make air tangible: fan the child's face, wave a hand, blow — that felt push is moving air, which is all wind is.
errorPatterns.distractor: Wind isn't air — it's a special thing on its own.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that wind is simply air that is moving

errorPatterns.pattern: Wind issues from a fixed source — 'it comes out of the sky'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show wind can come from any direction and that we make it by moving air ourselves, so it isn't from a single source.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Locates wind as pouring from one place rather than air moving from place to place

responseLevels.gap: Says the trees (or waves) make the wind; treats wind as not-air or as coming from a source.
responseLevels.full: States wind is moving air that pushes the branches (not the reverse), knows we detect it by what it moves, distinguishes breeze from gale, and can make wind by moving air.
responseLevels.partial: Says wind is moving air but hesitates on the direction of cause, or can't connect that we detect it only by its effects.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a windy day, the branches of a tree are waving about. A child says, 'The trees are making the wind by waving.' Is that right? What is the wind actually, and what's really happening with the trees?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands wind as moving air says the air moves the branches. A child with the reversed-causality idea says the trees make the wind — a documented young misconception — giving the opposite direction of cause.

sources.claim: K-ESS2-1 names wind among weather conditions; DCI ESS2.D: [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1] at a particular time/place.
sources.source: NGSS K-ESS2-1 (Earth's Systems)

sources.claim: DfE KS1 Year 1 weather observation includes describing windy weather; the cause of wind (uneven heating/rising air) is developed later, not at KS1.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum, KS1 Science (from prior-session fetch; not re-fetched this session)

sources.claim: Common young-learner ideas: 'air is nothing', 'you can see the wind', and reversed cause ('trees waving make the wind'); teaching should establish air as real matter known by wind's effects.
