pedagogy.summary: At 9-10, repeated reasoning is used to build general METHODS and predict beyond the drawn cases: seeing that ×25 can be done as ×100 then ÷4 and explaining why, building 35% from 10% (÷10) and 5% (half of 10%) as a reusable percentage toolkit, and describing a sequence's general rule to predict the 20th term without listing all twenty. The pivotal MP8 shift here is from a term-to-term (recursive) view to a position-to-term (functional) rule that lets you jump straight to any term. Teaching should force the 'jump' — ask for the 20th or 100th term — so the recursive habit becomes insufficient and a general rule is needed.
bestPractices: Derive percentage facts from 10% (÷10) and build others by halving/scaling, naming it as a general method for any percentage
Ask for a FAR term (20th, 100th) so listing becomes impractical and a position-to-term rule is needed
Justify equivalent methods (×25 = ×100 ÷4) by why they work, not as isolated tricks
Have the child state the general rule and verify it against a known term before trusting it
keyRepresentations: Percentage bar / double number line (100% → 10% → 5% → 35%)
Sequence tables pairing position (n) with term to expose the position-to-term rule
Equivalent-fraction and factor models for ×25 = ×100 ÷4
Ratio tables for scaling methods
commonMisconceptions: Predicts the 20th term by extending term-by-term (or drawing all terms) instead of a position-to-term rule
Uses only a term-to-term rule ('add 4') and cannot jump to a far term efficiently
Treats each percentage as a separate conversion rather than building from 10% and 5%
States a general rule from a few cases without verifying it on a known term

learn.summary: Help 9-10 year-olds shift from term-to-term (recursive) reasoning to position-to-term (functional) rules so they can jump straight to any term, and build a reusable percentage toolkit from 10% and 5%. The core move is forcing the 'jump' — asking for a far term (20th, 100th) so listing becomes impractical and a general rule is needed — then insisting the rule be verified against a known term. Equivalent calculation methods (×25 = ×100 then ÷4) should be justified by why they work, not memorised as tricks.

activities.title: Sequence machine: force the jump to a far term
feedback: If the child writes 21, 25, 29… or says 'just keep adding 4', note that this term-to-term habit works but won't reach the 100th term efficiently — tabulate position against term so the relationship (4×position + 1) is visible, then ask for the 100th term.

If the child scales a known term by the position ratio (e.g. says the 20th term = 4×the 5th term), test that shortcut against a known term: does 4×(the 1st term) give the 4th term correctly? (4×5 = 20, but the 4th term is 17.) Use the position table to show that scaling multiplies the constant start-offset too, so the result is too big.
If the child announces a rule but won't check it, ask 'does your rule give the 3rd term correctly? check it' so verification becomes a habit rather than an afterthought.
activities.rationale: Asking for a far term rather than the next one is what forces the distinction between recursive and functional thinking; a position table reveals the structure (difference × position + offset) and makes the general method efficient. An optional interactive form — a position slider that tempts listing alongside a 'rule' box that leaps straight to the chosen term and checks against the listed value — can make the contrast concrete, but the learning works on paper with a table too.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
Pupils should recognise and use structure to find efficient general methods and choose efficient strategies; representations should reveal the relationship
learnerActions: Look at a sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and notice the constant difference of 4.
Try to reach the 20th term by extending term-by-term and feel how slow and error-prone this gets.
Make a table pairing position (n) with term so the relationship becomes visible.
State a position-to-term rule (e.g. term = 4×position + 1) and use it to jump straight to the 20th term (81).
Check the rule against a known early term (does it give the 3rd term correctly?) before trusting it.
Then be asked for the 100th term, where listing is clearly impractical, so the general rule proves its worth.
activities.intendedInsight: A position-to-term rule lets you reach any term in one step, which counting-on cannot do efficiently; a rule is only trustworthy once checked against a known term.

activities.title: Build a percentage toolkit from 10% and 5%
feedback: If the child treats each percentage as a separate calculation, prompt them to start from 10% (÷10) and 5% (half of 10%) and ask which combination of those parts makes the target.
If the child assembles 35% correctly, ask whether the same approach gives 65% so they generalise the method rather than memorising one case.
An optional 'builder' where 10% and 5% tiles snap together to make 35% can make the part-whole structure tangible, but a drawn percentage bar or a ratio table serves the same purpose.
activities.rationale: Deriving unknown facts from known facts and naming the reusable method embodies the repeated-reasoning target; a percentage bar, double number line or ratio table reveals the part-whole and scaling relationship.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
Pupils should recognise and use structure to find efficient general methods and choose efficient strategies; representations should reveal the relationship
learnerActions: Find 10% of an amount by dividing by 10.
Find 5% by halving the 10% value.
Assemble 35% of an amount by combining three 10% parts and one 5% part (e.g. 35% of £80 = 24 + 4 = 28).
Explain that this is a general method: name which parts you'd combine to make a different percentage such as 65%.
Use a percentage bar or double number line (100% → 10% → 5% → 35%) to see how the parts make up the whole.
Use a ratio table to scale the 10% and 5% parts to a different total amount, showing the method generalises across amounts, not just one figure.
activities.intendedInsight: Any multiple of 5% can be built by combining derived facts (10% and 5%) rather than treated as a separate one-off conversion. Other percentages, such as 37%, need further derived facts like 1%. This gives a reusable method that scales to any amount.

activities.title: Justify an equivalent calculation method
feedback: If the child only states the shortcut, ask them to explain why ×100 then ÷4 equals ×25, using 25 = 100 ÷ 4.
If the child's explanation holds, ask them to check it against a direct calculation to confirm reasonableness.
activities.rationale: Justifying equivalent methods rather than memorising them is central to MP8 and to choosing efficient, structurally-grounded strategies.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
Pupils should recognise and use structure to find efficient general methods and choose efficient strategies; representations should reveal the relationship
learnerActions: Work out why multiplying any number by 25 can be done by multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4.
Use a factor/equivalent-fraction model (25 = 100 ÷ 4) to explain the equivalence, not just assert it.
Try the method on a worked example and check the result matches the direct multiplication.
Explain in words why the two routes must give the same answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent methods and shortcuts are reliable because of structure (25 = 100 ÷ 4), not because they are isolated tricks; understanding why lets you judge when a shortcut applies.

activities.title: Probe and discuss the generality of a rule
feedback: Listen for a position-to-term rule (term = 4×position + 1, so the 20th is 81) reached by linking the constant difference 4 to the position, plus a check against a known term — using the rule to jump rather than counting on is the target.

If the child uses a proportional shortcut (scaling a known term by the position ratio), have them test it on an early known term so the mishandled start-offset is exposed — e.g. 4×(the 5th term) gives 4×21 = 84, whereas the true 20th term is 81. The gap of 3 appears because scaling multiplies the +1 offset by 4 as well (4×1 = 4 instead of 1), so the answer is 3 too big.
There is no single scored answer here; the goal is reasoning that is general and self-checked.
activities.rationale: Open probing distinguishes genuine functional understanding from recursive habits and surfaces the proportional-reasoning trap of treating the sequence as proportional, which wrongly scales the constant offset. These prompts also require learners to construct and justify, not merely recognise.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
learnerActions: Answer 'how would you find the 100th term — does your method still work?' to test whether a rule is genuinely general.
Evaluate a classmate's claim: 'the 20th term is 4×(the 5th term) — is that right? check it on the 2nd term' and explain the flaw.
Explain how to build 35% of £80 from 10% and 5%, and whether the same method gives 65%.
Explain why ×25 equals ×100 then ÷4.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a rule is not enough; its generality must be tested against far cases and known terms, and proportional shortcuts that wrongly scale the constant offset along with the term fail these checks.

constraints: A static percentage bar or sequence table can display the relationship but cannot force the far-term jump or test a learner's stated rule; use it as a reference scaffold, not as the task that elicits independent generalisation.

Recognition-only formats (picking the correct method or the 20th term from options) can test the general method, but should be paired with a 'why/how' step so they elicit justification rather than guessing; on their own they do not require the learner to construct and verify a rule.
Include a term-by-term distractor (one that gives only the next term) when testing sequences, to catch recursive-only thinking.
Verification against a known term should be required, not optional: a rule stated from a few cases is not yet trusted.

Percentages and linear sequences are numeric relationships; manipulable numbers, tables, ratio tables or bars support the work. 3D representation is not needed here, though this is a judgement about this content, not a universal claim.

Open discussion without a concrete referent gives the learner nothing to manipulate or test; pair any discussion with an actual sequence, number or percentage to reason about (as the probing activity does).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked examples: sequence 5, 9, 13, 17 has first term 5 and common difference 4, giving term = 4n + 1; the 20th term is 4×20 + 1 = 81 (consistent with the source). 35% of £80 = (10% = 8)×3 + (5% = 4) = 24 + 4 = 28; the source's part-structure is correct. ×25 = ×100 ÷ 4 is valid since 25 = 100 ÷ 4. No arithmetic errors found in migrated examples.

The original 'force the jump / only this teaches why the rule beats counting on' framing is retained as a pedagogical rationale but softened: a static table, ratio table or paper task can also teach the position-to-term rule; the interactive contrast is one effective way, not the only way.
The claim that '3D adds no structure' was reframed as a scoped judgement about this numeric content rather than a universal law.

The proportional-shortcut misconception (20th term = 4×5th term = 4×21 = 84, rather than the correct 81) ignores the start-offset; retained as an error to probe and critique, never offered as a valid method or answer.

Ask 'to find 35% of £80, how do you build it from 10% and 5%? would the same method give 65%?' to test the general percentage method
Ask 'why does multiplying by 25 equal multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4?' to surface justification of an equivalent method

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses only a term-to-term rule ('add 4') and extends term-by-term, unable to jump to the 20th efficiently

errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child starts writing 21, 25, 29… or says 'keep adding 4' with no position rule

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a position rule but uses a proportional shortcut wrongly (e.g. 20th = 4×(5th term)), ignoring the constant offset
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test their shortcut against a known term (does it give the 4th term correctly?); expose the offset with the position table
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child scales a known term by the position ratio rather than using term = difference×position + start-offset

responseLevels.gap: Extends term-by-term, cannot reach a far term without listing, and treats each percentage as a separate conversion
responseLevels.full: Derives a position-to-term rule and jumps to the 20th/100th term, verifies it on a known term, and builds any percentage from 10%/5% — stating and checking general methods unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Finds a far term or builds a percentage when prompted, but relies on term-to-term steps or an unverified rule and doesn't justify the general method

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A sequence starts 5, 9, 13, 17, … What is the 20th term? Don't write out all twenty — tell me the general rule you'd use and how you found it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Counting on 'add 4' sixteen more times can also reach 81, but shows a recursive, not general, grasp. A child with repeated-reasoning insight builds a position-to-term rule and jumps; a child without it extends term-by-term or cannot handle '20th' without listing. Asking for the 20th (not the 5th) is what forces the distinction.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Real Dinosaurs vs Fiction (ages 5–7): tell real dinosaurs apart from creatures often confused with them — pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (sea reptiles) were NOT dinosaurs — and understand that movie/cartoon dinosaurs are not always accurate.
• Standards — UK (DfE): supports 'working scientifically' (identify, classify, and use simple criteria) and the critical-thinking seed of distinguishing evidence from fiction; no KS1 statutory dino content but strong media-literacy value.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports K–2 observation/patterns and the science-practice of using defined criteria to classify; nearest content anchor is later fossil/evidence work.
• Operational details — Two distinctions: (1) DINOSAUR vs NOT-A-DINOSAUR by a simple rule kids can apply — dinosaurs were land animals whose legs go straight DOWN under the body; pterosaurs flew (wings), plesiosaurs swam (flippers, long neck in water), so they are cousins, not dinosaurs. (Also flag the sail-backed Dimetrodon as a common not-a-dinosaur.) (2) REAL vs MOVIE — films exaggerate (roaring, wrong sizes, missing feathers, humans + dinos together) so a screen dinosaur isn't always what the real animal was like. Keep the rule concrete and forgiving; the aim is 'ask: is this really a dinosaur?', not exhaustive taxonomy.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~5): says a flying pterosaur or swimming plesiosaur is not a dinosaur. Tier B (~6): applies the 'legs under the body / lived on land' idea to sort one or two creatures. Tier C (~7): sorts several creatures into dinosaur / not-a-dinosaur and gives one way a movie dinosaur can be wrong.
bestPractices: Give a single child-usable rule ('a dinosaur is a land animal with legs straight underneath') rather than formal taxonomy, then apply it to clear cases.
Use the strongest confusions as teaching cases: pterosaur (flies), plesiosaur (swims), Dimetrodon (sail) — name why each is NOT a dinosaur.
Frame flyers/swimmers as 'cousins that lived at the same time' so children don't think they're being told these animals aren't real or important.
Introduce simple media literacy: compare a movie dinosaur to the best current science (feathers, size, no upright 'zombie' hands) so 'the film isn't always right'.
Keep it playful and non-punitive — near-misses are learning moments about the rule, not wrong answers to feel bad about.
keyRepresentations: A two-bin sorter: DINOSAUR vs NOT-A-DINOSAUR, with the rule shown on each drop.
Side-by-side leg posture diagram: dinosaur legs under body vs sprawling/flippered/winged.
'Movie vs real' compare pairs (feathered vs scaly, correct vs exaggerated size).
Labelled 'cousins' gallery: pterosaur (air), plesiosaur (sea), dinosaur (land).
commonMisconceptions: 'Pterodactyls/pterosaurs are flying dinosaurs' — they are flying reptiles, not dinosaurs.
'Plesiosaurs (and other big sea reptiles) are dinosaurs' — they are marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.
'Dimetrodon (the sail-back) is a dinosaur' — it lived before dinosaurs and is not one.
'Movie dinosaurs show exactly what they looked like' — films exaggerate size, sounds, and often omit feathers.
'If it's big, extinct, and scaly, it's a dinosaur' — being extinct or reptile-like doesn't make an animal a dinosaur.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, help children apply one child-usable rule to tell real dinosaurs apart from commonly confused prehistoric creatures (flying pterosaurs, swimming plesiosaurs, sail-backed Dimetrodon), and to recognise that movie/cartoon dinosaurs are not always accurate. The rule to teach: a dinosaur was a land animal whose legs went straight DOWN underneath its body; flyers and swimmers are 'cousins' that lived at the same time, not dinosaurs. A second strand builds early media literacy: compare a screen dinosaur to current science (feathers, size, sounds, and whether humans appear alongside it) to see that confident-looking pictures aren't always right, and that some details (exact sound and colour) simply aren't known from bones. Keep it playful and non-punitive — near-misses are chances to re-apply the rule.

activities.title: Dinosaur Club bouncer: sort with a clue lens
feedback: When a pterosaur is placed in NOT-A-DINOSAUR: 'Right — wings mean it flew. It's a flying reptile, a cousin that lived at the same time, not a dinosaur.'
When a plesiosaur is placed in NOT-A-DINOSAUR: 'Yes — flippers and a long neck for swimming. A sea reptile, a cousin, not a dinosaur.'

When Dimetrodon is placed in NOT-A-DINOSAUR: 'Good spot — look at its legs: they sprawl out to the sides instead of going straight down. It lived before the dinosaurs and isn't one, even though a few real dinosaurs had sails too.'

When a pterosaur is placed in DINOSAUR (near-miss): 'Close! It looks fierce, but check the clue lens — wings, so it flew. That makes it a flying-reptile cousin, not a dinosaur. Want to try the rule again?'
When T. rex/Triceratops is placed in DINOSAUR: 'Yes — see the legs going straight down under the body, and it lived on land. That's a dinosaur.'
activities.rationale: Sorting ambiguous cases with immediate, reason-giving feedback lets the misconception (pterosaur = dinosaur) surface through the child's own choice and then be corrected, which suits a rule-application target. A drag-into-bins interaction with a feature-highlighting 'clue lens' makes the deciding criterion concrete; these are suggested interaction examples, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (marine reptiles) are not dinosaurs but contemporaneous reptile groups; Dimetrodon is a pre-dinosaur synapsid, not a dinosaur. Dinosaurs are defined partly by an upright limb posture (legs beneath the body).
learnerActions: Act as a 'bouncer' at the Dinosaur Club where only real dinosaurs get in; creatures line up one at a time: T. rex, Triceratops, a leathery-winged pterosaur, a long-necked flippered plesiosaur, and a sail-backed Dimetrodon.
For each creature, decide DINOSAUR or NOT-A-DINOSAUR and place it in that bin.
Use a 'clue lens' that highlights the deciding feature — legs straight down under the body (dinosaur), or leathery wings, flippers, or legs sprawling out to the sides (not a dinosaur).
Say or tap the reason out loud, e.g. 'wings — a flying reptile, a cousin, not a dinosaur.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being scary, scaly, big, or extinct does NOT make an animal a dinosaur — there is a simple rule (land animal, legs straight underneath) that you can apply yourself to decide.

activities.title: Movie vs real: spot what the film got wrong or guessed
feedback: On spotting missing feathers: 'Good — many dinosaurs, especially smaller ones, had feathers, so when the science version of this animal has them a bare scaly film version is wrong.'
On spotting the wrong size: 'Yes — films often make them far bigger or smaller than the real animal.'
On spotting humans with dinosaurs: 'Right — people and the dinosaurs never lived at the same time, so that part is a clear mistake.'
On questioning the roar: 'Right to wonder — we have bones, not recordings, so nobody knows the exact sound; the roar is a guess, not a fact.'
On questioning skin colour: 'Yes — bones don't tell us exact colour, so the film is guessing there, even if it looks sure.'

If the child treats the film as exactly right: 'It looks real, but remember we only have bones. Which parts are the film guessing about, and which are plain wrong? Try the feathers, the size, the people, the sound, and the colour.'
activities.rationale: Comparing a familiar media depiction against current science builds early critical thinking about evidence versus artistic guess. Separating definite errors (feathers for a feathered species, size, humans coexisting) from unknown details shown as certain (sound, colour) keeps the point honest. A side-by-side compare (or a flap that reveals the science version) makes the differences tappable and concrete; this is a suggested format, not mandatory technology.
sourceClaims: Popular film depictions of dinosaurs are frequently inaccurate (exaggerated size/sounds, missing feathers, humans coexisting), so media portrayals should be checked against current science.
learnerActions: Look at an exaggerated screen/cartoon dinosaur beside a 'best-science' version of the same animal.

Point to the things the film clearly got wrong: the wrong size, humans shown living alongside the dinosaur, and — where the best-science version of this animal has feathers — a bare scaly skin that leaves those feathers out.
Then point to the things the film shows as if certain but that we can't actually know from bones — the exact loud roar and the exact skin colour.
Name one difference out loud, e.g. 'the real one may have had feathers', 'people never lived with giant dinosaurs like this one', or 'we don't actually know the sound it made.'
activities.intendedInsight: A confident-looking picture on a screen isn't always what the science says: films exaggerate size, often leave out feathers, and sometimes show people with dinosaurs who never actually lived together, while some details (exact colour, exact sound) simply aren't known from bones, so showing them as certain is a guess dressed up as fact.

activities.title: Land / air / sea cousins gallery (scaffold)
feedback: On tapping the pterosaur: 'A flying reptile — a cousin of dinosaurs, but not one.'
On tapping the dinosaur: 'Lived on land with legs straight underneath — that's a dinosaur.'
On tapping the plesiosaur: 'A sea reptile with flippers — a cousin, not a dinosaur.'
activities.rationale: A tappable labelled gallery introduces the categories and the 'cousins lived at the same time' framing clearly, which reassures children these animals are still real and important. Treat it as a scaffold: it presents categories rather than having the child test borderline cases or hunt movie errors, so pair it with the sorting and movie-comparison activities where the discrimination is actually practised.
sourceClaims: Pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (marine reptiles) are not dinosaurs but contemporaneous reptile groups; Dimetrodon is a pre-dinosaur synapsid, not a dinosaur. Dinosaurs are defined partly by an upright limb posture (legs beneath the body).
learnerActions: Explore a labelled scene with three cousins: a dinosaur on land, a pterosaur in the air, a plesiosaur in the sea.
Tap each creature to reveal 'dinosaur / not a dinosaur — because…' with the deciding feature named.
Open a flap that contrasts a movie dinosaur with a real one.
activities.intendedInsight: Dinosaurs, flying reptiles, and sea reptiles are different groups that lived at the same time; flyers and swimmers are important, real cousins — not dinosaurs, and not 'fake'.

activities.title: Ask the palaeontologist (alternative)
feedback: On asking about a pterodactyl: 'Good question — it flew, so it's a flying reptile. A cousin of dinosaurs, but not one.'
On asking about the movie roar: 'We only have bones, so no one knows the real sound — the film is guessing.'
activities.rationale: A dialogue with an expert character suits the myth-busting theme and can rehearse the reasoning, but for 5–7 a hands-on sorter gives a different kind of practice at applying the rule, so this is offered as an alternative rather than the main route. Listening and responsive questioning here give practice at hearing and restating reasons, which differs from the practice sorting gives; this is a narrow affordance, not a claim that dialogue is required or superior.
sourceClaims: Pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (marine reptiles) are not dinosaurs but contemporaneous reptile groups; Dimetrodon is a pre-dinosaur synapsid, not a dinosaur. Dinosaurs are defined partly by an upright limb posture (legs beneath the body).
Popular film depictions of dinosaurs are frequently inaccurate (exaggerated size/sounds, missing feathers, humans coexisting), so media portrayals should be checked against current science.
learnerActions: Pose 'is this a dinosaur?' questions to a palaeontologist character — e.g. 'Is a pterodactyl a dinosaur?' or 'Is the movie right about the roar?'
Listen to the gentle correction and then restate the rule in your own words.
Try a follow-up: give the character one creature and predict what they'll say before they answer.
activities.intendedInsight: An expert uses the same simple rule you can use — flyers and swimmers are cousins, not dinosaurs — and separates known bone evidence from guesses about sound and colour.

activities.title: Quick check: which is NOT a dinosaur? (light assessment)
feedback: On correctly naming the non-dinosaur: 'Yes — and the reason matters: leathery wings, flippers, or sprawling legs instead of a land animal with legs straight underneath.'
On naming a movie error: 'Good — feathers, size, or showing people alongside dinosaurs are things films get wrong, and sounds and colour are things films guess at.'
If a reason is missing: 'You picked the right one — now tell me the clue that gave it away.'
activities.rationale: Short categorization and selected-response items can confirm whether the rule and the media-accuracy idea have landed. These response formats check understanding rather than elicit the child's own sorting reasoning, so use them after the sorting and comparison activities, not instead of them.
learnerActions: Sort a small set of creatures into dinosaur / not-a-dinosaur.
Answer 'which of these is NOT a dinosaur?' and give the reason.
Answer 'name one thing a movie might get wrong about a dinosaur.'
activities.intendedInsight: You can state that pterosaurs flew but were not dinosaurs, that plesiosaurs swam but were not dinosaurs, and name at least one way a movie dinosaur differs from the real animal.

constraints: Teach one forgiving, child-usable rule ('a dinosaur is a land animal with legs straight underneath'), not formal taxonomy; the aim is 'ask: is this really a dinosaur?', not exhaustive classification. The rule is meant for the prehistoric animals in these activities: birds are scientifically living dinosaurs, so do not present the rule as true of every animal.
Frame flyers and swimmers as real, important 'cousins that lived at the same time' so children don't think they're being told these animals aren't real.
Keep it playful and non-punitive: near-misses are moments to re-apply the rule, not wrong answers to feel bad about.
The labelled cousins gallery is a scaffold that presents categories; it does not have the child test borderline cases or hunt movie errors, so pair it with sorting and movie-comparison tasks.
Recognition and selected-response checks confirm understanding but do not elicit the child's own sorting reasoning; use them as light assessment after the constructive tasks.

Be careful about certainty: bones do not reveal exact colour or sound, so present roars/skin colour in films as guesses shown as if certain, while missing feathers (for a feathered species), wrong size, and humans shown alongside dinosaurs are genuine errors — keep the honest point that sound and colour are unknown.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched and both carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Both sources are marked verified:false in the original row; the claims (upright limb posture defining dinosaurs; Dimetrodon as a pre-dinosaur synapsid; common film inaccuracies including humans coexisting) are widely accepted in palaeontology education but should be confirmed against the cited museum pages before relying on specifics.

Simplification caution: 'legs straight down under the body' is a correct but simplified cue for this age group; it is a teaching heuristic rather than the full technical definition of Dinosauria (birds, for example, are feathered flying dinosaurs), and edge cases exist beyond the scope of ages 5–7.

Framed the 'movie roar/skin colour' points as unknown-from-evidence (guesses shown as certain) rather than definitively wrong, to avoid over-claiming; the original correctAnswer already supports this. Missing feathers (for a feathered species), wrong size, and humans-with-dinosaurs remain genuine errors.
The original row rated 3D as 'poor' because the distinction is rule-based; this rewrite omits that comparative modality claim as a catalog preference rather than an established pedagogical law.

probeDeeper: What made an animal a dinosaur, if flying and swimming reptiles don't count?
Name one thing a movie might get wrong about a dinosaur.
Could scientists really know the exact roar a dinosaur made? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The book is wrong: pterosaurs (flying) and plesiosaurs (swimming) lived at the same time as dinosaurs but were NOT dinosaurs — dinosaurs were a particular family of mostly land animals. And movies aren't always accurate: we don't actually know the sounds dinosaurs made or their exact skin and colour, and many had feathers — so a roaring, scaly movie dinosaur may not match the real animal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Any big prehistoric reptile is a dinosaur — flying and swimming ones included.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the boundary: pterosaurs and plesiosaurs are relatives that lived alongside dinosaurs but aren't dinosaurs; dinosaurs were land animals of a specific group.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, the book is right — flying and swimming reptiles are dinosaurs too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts pterosaurs and plesiosaurs as dinosaurs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Movies show exactly what dinosaurs were really like.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate evidence from artistic guess: we have bones, not recordings or skin colour; discuss what films add or get wrong.
errorPatterns.distractor: The movie is exactly right — that's how they really looked and sounded.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the film's sounds, skin and colour as certain fact.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dinosaurs were all scaly with no feathers.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce feathered-dinosaur evidence; many did have feathers, especially the smaller theropods.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists no dinosaurs had feathers.

responseLevels.gap: Calls any prehistoric reptile a dinosaur, and treats movie depictions as exact truth.
responseLevels.full: Separates dinosaurs from other prehistoric reptiles AND recognises film depictions are partly guesswork (sound, colour, feathers), giving a concrete example.
responseLevels.partial: Knows pterosaurs/plesiosaurs weren't dinosaurs OR that movies can be inaccurate, but not both.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A picture book shows a flying reptile (a pterosaur like Pteranodon) and a long-necked sea reptile (a plesiosaur) and calls them both 'dinosaurs'. Is the book right? And in a movie, the dinosaurs roar loudly and have dry scaly skin — is that definitely how the real ones were? Explain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who lumps all prehistoric reptiles together calls the pterosaur and plesiosaur dinosaurs; a child who treats films as fact says the movie is exactly right. Only a child who both draws the dinosaur boundary AND knows depictions involve guesswork answers both halves.

sources.claim: Pterosaurs (flying reptiles) and plesiosaurs (marine reptiles) are not dinosaurs but contemporaneous reptile groups; Dimetrodon is a pre-dinosaur synapsid, not a dinosaur. Dinosaurs are defined partly by an upright limb posture (legs beneath the body).
sources.source: Natural History Museum (UK) / Smithsonian — 'What is a dinosaur?' education pages

sources.claim: Popular film depictions of dinosaurs are frequently inaccurate (exaggerated size/sounds, missing feathers, humans coexisting), so media portrayals should be checked against current science.
sources.source: Natural History Museum (UK) — dinosaur myths & media accuracy articles

pedagogy.summary: At KS3 (age 11-13) accurate drawing and measuring with ruler and protractor is extended in two directions: constructing a triangle from a given specification (e.g. two sides and the included angle, SAS) to the nearest degree and millimetre, and interpreting scale drawings to extract real measurements. The construction half carries forward the protractor hazards of Y6 — chiefly reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor and misplacing vertex/baseline — now under a tighter accuracy demand. The scale-drawing half introduces a distinct and heavily-documented conceptual hazard: children reason ADDITIVELY about scale (adding a constant) instead of MULTIPLICATIVELY (multiplying by a scale factor), and drop or muddle units when converting between drawing and reality. Effective teaching keeps the placement/estimate-first routine for construction, and for scale makes the multiplicative structure explicit — 'each 1 cm on the drawing stands for so many metres, so I multiply' — with pictorial models, precise language about dimensions, and reasonableness checks.
bestPractices: Keep the estimate-first protractor routine (is the angle bigger or smaller than a right angle? then choose the scale that agrees) and centre-on-vertex / zero-on-line placement, now to nearest-degree accuracy

Sequence SAS-style construction: rule one side from the ruler's zero, set the included angle at its endpoint, measure the second side, rule the third to close; treat a non-closing triangle as a signal of accumulated error
Teach scale as a MULTIPLIER: write 'real = drawn × scale factor' (and drawn = real ÷ factor), draw children's attention explicitly to the multiplicative and away from the additive relationship
Keep units explicit and precise — say 'each 1 cm represents 2 m' and carry the units through the conversion; avoid the vague word 'size', which conflates length with area
Use pictorial/scale-plan models, which research shows reduce the tendency toward additive strategy, and demand a reasonableness check on the real length
keyRepresentations: Protractor with the estimate-first rule to disambiguate the two scales (to nearest degree)
Base-then-included-angle-then-side SAS construction sequence
Scale statement 'real = drawn × scale factor' with a worked ratio (e.g. 1 cm : 2 m)
Scale plan / map with a stated scale for measuring and converting real lengths
Double number line or ratio table linking drawn cm to real m (to make the multiplier visible)
commonMisconceptions: Reasons additively about scale — adds a constant difference rather than multiplying by the scale factor — the classic additive-strategy error, most common in the ratio/proportion literature
Drops or muddles units in a scale conversion, or treats 'size' loosely (confusing length scale with area scale)
Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, measuring/drawing the supplement of the intended angle
Misplaces the protractor centre or zero-line, so measured angles are consistently a few degrees out
Accepts a nearly-closing constructed triangle as accurate rather than as evidence of accumulated placement/measurement error

learn.summary: KS3 (age 11-13) learners extend accurate ruler-and-protractor work in two directions: constructing a triangle from a specification (e.g. two sides and the included angle, SAS) to the nearest degree and millimetre, and interpreting scale drawings to extract real measurements. Construction carries forward the protractor hazards of earlier years — reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor (drawing the supplement) and misplacing vertex/baseline — now under a tighter accuracy demand. Scale drawing introduces a well-documented conceptual hazard: reasoning ADDITIVELY about scale (adding a constant) instead of MULTIPLICATIVELY (multiplying by a scale factor), and dropping or muddling units when converting. Effective teaching keeps the estimate-first placement routine for construction, and for scale makes the multiplicative structure explicit — 'each 1 cm on the drawing stands for so many metres, so I multiply' — with pictorial models, precise language about dimensions, and reasonableness checks.

activities.title: SAS construction with the estimate-first protractor routine
feedback: If your measured third side or remaining angles differ noticeably from about 6.7 cm, 47° and 78°, do not accept them as 'close enough'. This is evidence of accumulated error: recheck the protractor centre on the vertex, the zero-line along the side, and which scale you read
If you set 125° where 55° was asked, you read the wrong scale and drew the supplement; re-estimate 'bigger or smaller than a square corner?' and pick the scale that agrees

If the sides or angle drift from 6 cm / 8 cm / 55°, rehearse the base-then-included-angle-then-side sequence on another figure. Use the self-check of measuring the third side and the remaining angles against their expected values
activities.rationale: On a dual-scale protractor, pupils struggle with which scale to read and with vertex/baseline placement. Estimate-first strategies reduce these errors. Comparing the measured third side and remaining angles with expected values reveals accumulated inaccuracy; closure alone is not a check, because an SAS triangle always closes when the endpoints are joined. An interactive canvas can make this routine concrete: the protractor shows both scale numbers with a 'bigger/smaller than a square corner?' lock, the ruler measures from zero, and a tick confirms that the measured third side and angles are within tolerance. The same routine works with a physical ruler, protractor and paper.
sourceClaims: On a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with which scale to read (drawing the supplement) and with vertex/baseline placement; estimate-first strategies and numberless/single-scale protractors reduce these errors.
learnerActions: Construct a triangle from two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm with an included angle of 55° between them: rule the first side from the ruler's zero, place the protractor with its centre on the endpoint vertex and zero-line along the side, set the 55° angle, measure and mark the second side, then rule the third side to close the triangle

Before reading the protractor, estimate first: 'Is 55° bigger or smaller than a right angle (a square corner)?' Smaller, so choose the scale that gives a value under 90°, not the 125° on the other scale

Because you finish by joining the two free endpoints, an SAS triangle always closes, so closing does not show it is accurate. Instead, measure the third side and the other two angles and compare them with the expected values. For 6 cm, 8 cm and 55°, the third side should be about 6.7 cm and the other angles about 47° and 78°, and all three angles add up to 180°. A clear mismatch signals placement or measurement error: recheck the vertex placement, the zero-line and the scale you chose
Aim for accuracy to about the nearest degree and nearest millimetre
activities.intendedInsight: Accurate construction depends on a disciplined sequence (base → included angle → side → join the endpoints) and on choosing the right scale on a dual-scale protractor by first estimating against a right angle. Joining the endpoints always closes an SAS triangle, so accuracy is checked by comparing the measured third side (about 6.7 cm) and remaining angles (about 47° and 78°) with the expected values, not by whether the triangle closes.

activities.title: Scale conversion as a multiplier, not an addition
feedback: If you added a constant (e.g. treated '1 cm represents 2 m' as '+2'), compare 4.5 + 2 = 6.5 with 4.5 × 2 = 9: the scale says every 1 cm is 2 m, so you multiply
If you dropped the units and just wrote '9', restate it as 9 m and carry 'm per cm' through the working so the result has the right units
Avoid the vague word 'size': say which dimension (side-length) you mean, since length scale and area scale are different
Check against reality for the actual object and scale given: does the converted length make sense for what the plan depicts?
activities.rationale: The additive strategy — computing a difference and applying it rather than a common multiplier — is the most commonly reported erroneous strategy in the ratio/proportion literature, geometric-figure problems are the most vulnerable, and pictorial models reduce it. Scale factor is a multiplier and teaching should draw attention to the multiplicative relationship and away from the additive one, refer precisely to 'dimensions (side-length)', and avoid the imprecise word 'size'. A live converter bar and a scale slider that shows the real length multiply while the drawn length stays put can make the multiplicative structure felt, but a ratio table, double number line, or physical scale map serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: The additive strategy — computing the difference between terms and applying it, rather than a common multiplier — is the most commonly reported erroneous strategy in the ratio/proportion literature; geometric-figure problems are the most vulnerable to additive errors, non-integer scale factors most strongly trigger it, and pictorial models reduce it. Builds on Hart/CSMS (1981/1985).

Scale factor is a multiplier: teaching should 'ensure children's attention is drawn to the multiplicative relationship between side-lengths and not to the additive relationship'; shapes are similar only when every dimension is scaled by the SAME factor (adding a constant to each dimension does not produce a similar shape); refer precisely to 'dimensions (side-length)' and avoid the imprecise word 'size', which can be confused with area.
learnerActions: On a printed or on-screen scale plan labelled 'Scale: 1 cm represents 2 m', measure a wall to the nearest millimetre (e.g. read 4.5 cm)

Convert to the real length by multiplying: write 'real = drawn × scale', so 4.5 cm × 2 m per cm = 9 m, carrying the units through the whole conversion. Equivalently, with the unitless scale factor of 1:200, 4.5 cm × 200 = 900 cm = 9 m
State the scale in words: 'each 1 cm on the drawing is 2 m in real life, so I multiply'
Use a double number line or ratio table linking drawn cm to real m to keep the multiplier visible
Check the real length is reasonable for the object (e.g. a 9 m wall in a room)

Explore what happens when the scale changes, as a thought experiment about the scale factor: imagine the same drawn length read at a different scale — if 1 cm represented 5 m (a 1:500 scale) instead of 2 m (a 1:200 scale), the real length multiplies, so the same 4.5 cm would stand for 22.5 m while the drawn length on the plan stays the same. Apply the reasonableness check to whatever object and scale are actually given — at 1:500 the plan would depict a correspondingly larger space
activities.intendedInsight: Scale is a multiplicative relationship: real length = drawn length × scale factor (and drawn = real ÷ factor). Changing the scale factor multiplies the real length while the drawing is unchanged; adding a constant does not model scale.

activities.title: Feeling the scale factor by zooming from plan to real room
feedback: If the expansion feels surprising, it is because scale multiplies: each small step on the plan stands for a much larger real distance
Always come back to the numeric conversion — the zoom builds intuition, but the answer still comes from drawn × scale factor with units
activities.rationale: The spatial 'zoom from plan to real room' is an optional enrichment that can make a scale factor feel concrete; the core conversion remains numeric and planar, so this supports rather than replaces the measuring-and-multiplying work. Offered as an alternative with a different (intuition-building) purpose, not as the main vehicle. Its intuition-building efficacy is untested.
learnerActions: Starting from a floor-plan with a stated scale (e.g. 1 cm represents 2 m), zoom from the plan into a representation of the actual-size room to experience how a small drawn length corresponds to a large real one
Connect the visual expansion back to the number: a 4.5 cm wall on the plan becomes a 9 m wall in reality at 1 cm : 2 m
Return to the plan and do the measuring and conversion numerically
activities.intendedInsight: A scale factor can be made viscerally real by seeing a drawn length expand to its actual size, reinforcing that the real object is the drawing multiplied by the factor.

activities.title: Check scale reasoning and protractor scale choice (recognition practice)
feedback: If you picked the additive option (6.5 m), recall that each 1 cm represents 2 m, so the relationship multiplies: 4.5 × 2 = 9 m
If you picked the answer with no units, remember the real length is in metres (9 m)
For the scale item, estimate the angle against a right angle first, then pick the agreeing scale
activities.rationale: Fixed-response items can test scale conversions and scale-choice decisions with targeted distractors. This is recognition practice and consolidation; on its own it does not elicit or assess a learner's actual construction accuracy or their independent assembly of the conversion, which require doing and explaining.
sourceClaims: The additive strategy — computing the difference between terms and applying it, rather than a common multiplier — is the most commonly reported erroneous strategy in the ratio/proportion literature; geometric-figure problems are the most vulnerable to additive errors, non-integer scale factors most strongly trigger it, and pictorial models reduce it. Builds on Hart/CSMS (1981/1985).

On a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with which scale to read (drawing the supplement) and with vertex/baseline placement; estimate-first strategies and numberless/single-scale protractors reduce these errors.
learnerActions: Answer a conversion item such as: a wall measures 4.5 cm on a plan at 1 cm : 2 m — what is the real length? Choose from options that include an additive distractor (6.5 m from adding) and a units-dropped distractor ('9' with no units) alongside the correct 9 m
Answer a 'which scale reads this angle?' item: given an angle estimated smaller than a right angle, decide which of the two protractor scales to read
Explain in words why you multiply rather than add, and why the units matter
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising additive and units-dropped distractors and choosing the correct protractor scale reinforces the multiplicative structure and the estimate-first habit; recognising the right answer among options is not the same as independently constructing or converting, so this consolidates rather than replaces the full task.

constraints: Construction accuracy is a doing skill within the KS3 curriculum: it is built by actually ruling sides, placing a protractor, and measuring. A static diagram or tap-to-reveal picture can serve as a reference for the scale statement and protractor routine but does not itself elicit placement accuracy or the learner performing the multiplicative conversion.

Recognition-only items (choosing among options, naming the right scale) do not elicit independent construction of the triangle or independent assembly and explanation of the scale conversion; use them to consolidate, and assess the full skill through a performance task.
A zoom-from-plan-to-real-room experience is optional enrichment for intuition; the core conversion is numeric and should still be carried out and explained with units.
Keep units explicit throughout a conversion; avoid the vague word 'size', which conflates length with area — length scale and area scale differ.

Interactive affordances (ghosted dual-scale numbers, a 'bigger/smaller than a square corner?' lock, a live converter bar, a scale slider from 1:200 to 1:500, a green tick when the constructed triangle's measured third side and angles are within tolerance) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete. They are helpful options, not required, and the same learning is achievable with a physical ruler, protractor, paper, scale maps, ratio tables and double number lines.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a static image and conversation as 'poor' and a 2D interactive as 'ideal' / the only way to 'defeat' the two hazards. These are catalog fit preferences; the exact sources support the teaching principles (estimate-first routine, multiplicative scale, pictorial models) but do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any one medium. Medium-specific necessity claims have been softened to scoped proposals.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit: 4.5 cm × 2 m/cm = 9 m is correct. The 22.5 m figure is also correct — 1:500 denotes 1 cm : 5 m, so 4.5 cm × 5 m/cm = 22.5 m, consistent with 1:200 denoting 1 cm : 2 m. It is presented in activity 2 as a scale-factor thought experiment (same drawn length, different scale) illustrating that the real length multiplies while the drawn length is unchanged, not as a graded item or a claim about a specific room's wall. 55° is less than a right angle and its supplement is 180 − 55 = 125°, matching the dual-scale hazard. The additive distractor 4.5 + 2 = 6.5 m is one plausible incorrect-strategy illustration.

The KS3 statutory source claim was removed from the activity sourceClaims arrays because it states the curriculum objective/topic rather than the specific teaching principle in each rationale; the objective itself is preserved in the activity content. Legacy reteach prerequisite IDs and quiz-step vocabulary were removed per rewrite rules, with the underlying reteach moves preserved as feedback.

probeDeeper: Your drawing shows 4.5 cm here — how do you turn that into a real length? Why multiply and not add?
If the scale were 1 cm to 5 m instead, would this wall be longer or shorter in real life? By how much?
Before you read the protractor — is 55° bigger or smaller than a right angle? So which of the two numbers is it?
How do you know your triangle is accurate — what would you check?
assess.correctAnswer: Constructs the SAS triangle accurately (side ruled from the ruler's zero, 55° set with centre-on-vertex and the correct protractor scale, second side measured, third side ruled to close) to about ±2° / ±2 mm; measures the wall on the plan to the nearest millimetre and converts by multiplying by the scale factor (drawn length × 2 m per cm), keeping units, and explains 'each 1 cm on the drawing is 2 m in real life, so I multiply.'

errorPatterns.pattern: Reasons additively about scale — adds a constant difference instead of multiplying by the scale factor when converting between drawing and reality
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the multiplier explicit — 'real = drawn × scale factor' on a ratio table / double number line; draw attention to the multiplicative relationship and away from the additive one; use pictorial models, which reduce additive responses
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a 4.5 cm wall at 1 cm:2 m gives an answer got by adding (e.g. treats the '2' as +2, or scales dimensions inconsistently), rather than 4.5 × 2 = 9 m; on 'similar shape' checks accepts adding the same amount to each side as an enlargement

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, drawing or measuring the supplement of the intended angle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinstate the estimate-first rule ('bigger or smaller than a square corner?') then pick the agreeing scale; rehearse on a single-scale/numberless protractor until scale choice is automatic
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sets 125° where 55° was asked (or reports an angle as its supplement), so the SAS triangle is wrong or fails to close

errorPatterns.pattern: Constructs by eye rather than to the given spec, so the triangle does not close or the sides/angle are off — a lapse of the drawing skill under the tighter accuracy demand
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach from scratch: rehearse the base-then-included-angle-then-side sequence and the 'does it close?' self-check on a couple of figures
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The triangle nearly-but-not-quite closes, or sides/angle drift from 6 cm / 8 cm / 55°, despite the child knowing the routine

responseLevels.gap: Cannot construct to the given spec and converts scale by adding or with no units; reads whichever protractor scale.
responseLevels.full: Constructs the SAS triangle accurately to the nearest degree/millimetre, measures precisely, and converts drawing↔real by the multiplicative scale factor with units, explaining the scale and checking the real length is reasonable — and transfers correctly to a different scale.
responseLevels.partial: Constructs the triangle and can measure on the plan, but converts scale inconsistently — adds instead of multiplies, or drops units — or slips on the protractor scale; has the component moves (measure, multiply) without reliably assembling and explaining the conversion (lists parts without the relational whole).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler, a protractor, and a printed scale drawing of a room or map labelled 'Scale: 1 cm represents 2 m'. Say: 'First, draw a triangle accurately with two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm and an angle of 55° between them. Then, on this plan, measure this wall and tell me its real length, and explain the scale you used.' Watch the construction and how they convert — do not talk them through it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The constructed triangle and the stated real length together reveal the reasoning: a child who thinks multiplicatively converts by × scale-factor with units intact; a child who thinks additively adds a constant or muddles units, and a dual-scale slip yields the supplementary angle and a triangle that will not close. Right answers are hard to reach by an additive route — the numbers diverge.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Magnetic Poles

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** England DfE KS2 Year 3 'Forces and magnets' — 'describe magnets as having 2 poles; predict whether 2 magnets will attract or repel each other, depending on which poles are facing';

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NGSS 3-PS2-3 (cause-and-effect: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-3]).

- **Operational details:** Best practice builds the rule from repeated predict-then-test trials with two labelled magnets, using precise pole language.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 7-9). The goal is a predictive RULE grounded in observation — every magnet has two poles (north-seeking/south-seeking); like poles repel, opposite poles attract; predict the outcome of bringing two magnets together from how their poles face. NO field model or explanation of WHY yet (that is KS3).
bestPractices: Build the rule empirically: child orients two labelled bar magnets, predicts attract or repel, then tests — across enough trials the pattern 'like repel, opposite attract' emerges as their own discovery.

Use precise, consistent pole language — 'north-seeking' and 'south-seeking' (a freely-moving magnet's north-seeking pole points north) — then progress to 'north pole'/'south pole' as understanding consolidates (IOP Spark progression).
Colour-code and label the poles (e.g. N red / S blue) so orientation is unambiguous while children are still learning the rule.

Confront the repulsion case explicitly and often — children adopt repulsion of like poles much more slowly than attraction of opposites, so give plentiful like-pole trials and the felt 'invisible push'.
Show magnets of different shapes (bar, ring, button, horseshoe) so pupils learn poles are a property of every magnet, not 'the two ends of a bar'.
keyRepresentations: Two colour-coded bar magnets (N/S labelled) brought together in the four orientations: N-N, S-S (repel) and N-S, S-N (attract)
A predict-then-test record table: orientation drawn → prediction → observed outcome
The 'like repel, opposite attract' rule stated as a short, memorable line
A freely-suspended/floating magnet swinging to point north (anchors the 'north-seeking' name)
commonMisconceptions: Children are slow to adopt the idea of poles and only gradually come to see magnetic effects as attraction of unlike poles and repulsion of like poles (IOP Spark) — repulsion is grasped later than attraction.
Reversing the rule (thinking like poles attract) — hence the need for many disconfirming like-pole trials.
Thinking poles are always 'the two ends' — not true for ring/button magnets; poles are a property of every magnet whatever its shape.
Thinking any two magnets always just 'stick' — ignoring that orientation determines attract vs repel.
Assuming a bigger magnet is automatically the stronger one (carried over from the materials topic).

learn.summary: For children aged 7-9, build the rule 'like poles repel, opposite poles attract' from repeated predict-then-test trials with two labelled magnets. The target is a predictive rule grounded in observation: every magnet has two poles (north-seeking/south-seeking); predict whether two magnets attract or repel from how their poles face. No field model or explanation of why yet. Repulsion of like poles is grasped more slowly than attraction of opposites, so give plentiful like-pole trials. Poles are a property of every magnet, whatever its shape.

activities.title: Predict-then-test with two labelled magnets
feedback: When two like poles (e.g. two north ends) face, you feel them resist and push apart, and the push gets stronger the closer you bring them. That is repulsion, and it surprises many people because we often assume magnets always stick.
When opposite poles face (north and south), they snap together — attraction.
If you flip one magnet and the outcome changes from repel to attract with the same pair, that shows the pole orientation decides the result, not the push or the particular magnets.
If you predicted they would always stick, try the like-pole case again and pay attention to the felt push — magnets do not always attract.
activities.rationale: The learning objective is a predictive rule about orientation. Letting the child set the orientation and immediately feel/see the consequence (snap or spring-apart), then flip one pole to reverse the outcome, makes the cause unmistakable and matches the predict-then-test loop the curriculum asks for.
sourceClaims: Year 3 statutory: describe magnets as having 2 poles, and predict whether 2 magnets will attract or repel depending on which poles are facing.
3-PS2-3 cause-and-effect example: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-3] (objects not in contact).
learnerActions: Take two bar magnets with poles colour-coded and labelled (e.g. north red, south blue).
Set an orientation by bringing two ends toward each other; before pushing, say aloud your prediction: will they attract or repel?
Slowly push them together and observe/feel what happens: do they snap together, or meet an invisible springy resistance that pushes them apart unless you force them?
Work through all four orientations: N-N, S-S, N-S, S-N. Record each in a table: draw the orientation, write your prediction, write what actually happened.
On one pair that repels (e.g. N-N), flip just ONE magnet and push again — notice the outcome reverses.
After enough trials, state the pattern you discovered in your own short rule.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether two magnets attract or repel depends on which poles face each other: like poles push apart, opposite poles pull together. Because flipping one magnet reverses the outcome with the SAME pair, the result depends on which poles face each other, not on which particular magnets you use.

activities.title: Confront the repulsion case head-on
feedback: Feeling the push with your own hands, or watching the ends spring apart, is direct evidence that 'magnets always attract' is incomplete.
If you can predict repulsion before you push for like poles, you have grasped the harder half of the rule.
activities.rationale: Research reviews note children adopt repulsion of like poles more slowly than attraction of opposites, so plentiful disconfirming like-pole trials, and observing/feeling the push, are needed.
sourceClaims: Students are slow to adopt the idea of magnetic poles and only gradually come to see magnetic effects in terms of attraction of unlike poles and repulsion of like poles.
learnerActions: Spend extra trials on like-pole orientations (N-N and S-S), slowly pushing and feeling the resistance.
Describe the sensation: an invisible springy wall that slides and bounces and pushes the ends apart unless you force them together.
Predict the like-pole outcome ahead of each push, then test, until you reliably expect repulsion.
activities.intendedInsight: Two magnets can push each other away. Repulsion is just as real as attraction and happens specifically when like poles face.

activities.title: Poles on magnets of every shape
feedback: If you thought a ring or horseshoe magnet has no poles, locating them with filings or another magnet shows otherwise, and testing with a labelled magnet tells you which pole is north and which is south.
Finding that the attract/repel behaviour still depends on which pole you present confirms the rule holds for any shape.
activities.rationale: Addresses the misconception that poles are always at the ends; using differently shaped magnets shows poles are a general property.
sourceClaims: Use full pole names (north-seeking/south-seeking) to consolidate understanding, progressing to north/south pole; address the misconceptions that all magnets look the same and that poles are always at the ends, via differently shaped magnets.
learnerActions: Examine magnets of different shapes: bar, ring, button, horseshoe.

For a horseshoe or ring magnet, find where the poles are using iron filings (they cluster at the poles but cannot tell you which is north and which is south), then test with a labelled magnet to name each pole: the part that repels the labelled north pole is a north pole. Ring and button magnets often have their poles on the flat faces rather than at the ends.
State where the north and south poles are on each magnet — not just on the two ends of a bar.
activities.intendedInsight: Every magnet has a north and a south pole whatever its shape; poles are a property of the whole magnet, not simply 'the two ends of a bar'.

activities.title: Name the poles: the north-seeking anchor
feedback: If the freely-turning magnet (on a thread or on its float) always settles pointing the same way, that is the north-seeking pole revealing itself.
Using consistent names for the poles makes your attract/repel predictions clearer.
activities.rationale: Precise, consistent pole language supports the rule; naming can serve as a vocabulary/reference layer alongside the hands-on trials.
sourceClaims: Use full pole names (north-seeking/south-seeking) to consolidate understanding, progressing to north/south pole; address the misconceptions that all magnets look the same and that poles are always at the ends, via differently shaped magnets.
learnerActions: Let a single magnet turn freely: suspend it on a thread, or rest it on a small float (e.g. a cork or foam disc) on water, and watch it swing until it settles.
Keeping it away from other magnets and steel objects, notice which end points roughly north; name that end the 'north-seeking' pole and the other the 'south-seeking' pole.
Use this precise language ('north-seeking'/'south-seeking', progressing to 'north pole'/'south pole') when describing your predict-then-test trials.
activities.intendedInsight: A freely-moving magnet's north-seeking pole points north, which is where the name comes from. Consistent pole language keeps orientation unambiguous.

activities.title: Retrieval practice: predict the outcome
feedback: Correct: like poles (N-N, S-S) repel; opposite poles (N-S, S-N) attract.
If a question flips one magnet, the outcome switches — check your answer reflects that the orientation changed.
Make sure like-pole items are answered as 'repel', since children often learn that case more slowly.
activities.rationale: Prediction, matching and categorising orientations give a precise, direct test of the rule and strong retrieval practice. This checks and consolidates the rule rather than discovering it, so it works best after the hands-on trials. A sorting/matching task can check classification of orientations but does not itself elicit the felt repulsion or an explanation.
sourceClaims: Year 3 statutory: describe magnets as having 2 poles, and predict whether 2 magnets will attract or repel depending on which poles are facing.
learnerActions: Given a diagram of two magnets in a stated orientation (e.g. 'north facing north'), decide: attract or repel?
Match orientation diagrams to their outcomes.
Sort a set of orientations into two groups: those that attract and those that repel.
Answer transfer items: 'If a magnet is flipped, what changes?' and 'Where are the poles on this horseshoe?'
activities.intendedInsight: The rule can be applied reliably to new orientations, including the slower-learned like-pole (repel) cases and flipped magnets.

constraints: Keep to Tier A (concrete/observational): the goal is a predictive rule from observation. Do not introduce a magnetic field model or an explanation of WHY poles attract/repel — that is later (KS3) material.
Colour-code and label the poles (e.g. N red / S blue) while the rule is still being learned, so orientation is unambiguous.
Give plentiful like-pole trials: repulsion of like poles is learned later than attraction, so do not under-represent it.
Retrieval-practice items check and consolidate the rule but do not let the child discover it or feel the repulsion; use them after hands-on predict-then-test work, not instead of it.

A naming/reference layer (tappable labels, lift-the-flap answers) supports vocabulary but states the rule rather than letting orientation be manipulated; pair it with manipulation rather than relying on it alone.
Watch for the carried-over idea that a bigger magnet is automatically stronger — size is not the subject of this rule.
Use classroom-grade magnets with normal supervision; avoid strong rare-earth magnets that can pinch or shatter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a 3D-interactive artefact 'poor', asserting depth/viewpoint 'add nothing' and that a static image 'cannot' give live recompute. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped. A static representation can still teach the rule by presenting labelled orientations, and a 3D model would simply offer a different experience. The affordance worth keeping is that live re-evaluation as a magnet rotates can make the orientation-to-outcome link vivid — offered as a helpful option, not a necessity.
The source also rated an in-role 'conversation' format poor; this is a fit judgement, not evidence that dialogue cannot support the topic, so it is not asserted as a universal limit.

One source (Oak National Academy) is marked verified:false in the row; its claims about pole-naming progression and shape-based misconceptions are used as pedagogical guidance, not as established efficacy.

Physical bar/ring/horseshoe magnets are safe for this age with normal supervision; strong rare-earth magnets can pinch or shatter — this practical caution was not in the source and is flagged for review, not asserted as sourced.

The claim that feeling/seeing repulsion is the decisive evidence reflects a preferred scaffold (hands-on predict-then-test); it is not asserted that touch is uniquely required, and seeing the ends spring apart serves the same observable purpose.

The free-turning magnet demonstration was corrected: a magnet sinks if placed directly on water, so the activity now specifies suspending it on a thread or resting it on a cork/foam float. This practical detail is a standard classroom method, not a sourced specification.

assess.poeTask: Hand the child two bar magnets with poles marked. Ask them to predict what happens as two same-coloured ends approach, and WHY, before pushing them together — then repeat with opposite ends. Feeling like poles REPEL is the surprise that breaks 'magnets always attract'; the pre-push reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Now I flip ONE magnet so a red end faces a blue end. What happens now, and why is it different?
Can two magnets ever PUSH each other away? When?
Where are the poles on this horseshoe magnet — does it even have them?
assess.correctAnswer: They push apart / you feel them resist — they repel. Two like poles (north and north) repel each other; only opposite poles (north and south) attract. So facing two norths together makes them push away.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'They'll snap together — magnets always attract each other.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give plentiful like-pole trials so the child FEELS the repulsion; label the poles and state the rule.
errorPatterns.distractor: They'll pull together and stick — magnets always attract.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts attraction regardless of which poles face each other.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A magnet only has poles if it's a straight bar with two ends — a ring or horseshoe magnet doesn't have them.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that every magnet has a north and a south pole whatever its shape; locate them with iron filings or another magnet.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't locate poles on a horseshoe or ring magnet.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Whether they attract or repel is random, or about how hard you push them.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the poles and show that flipping ONE magnet reliably switches attract to repel and back.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Doesn't attribute the outcome to the pole orientation.

responseLevels.gap: Predicts the magnets always attract/stick whatever the ends; treats repulsion as impossible or as something random.
responseLevels.full: Predicts attraction or repulsion from the pole orientation, explains it by like/opposite poles, transfers correctly when a magnet is flipped, and recognises every magnet has two poles whatever its shape.
responseLevels.partial: States 'like poles repel, opposite poles attract' and may predict the like-pole case, but recites the rule without linking the outcome to WHICH poles face — e.g. can't predict reliably after a magnet is flipped, or thinks only bar ends have poles.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I have two bar magnets. I turn them so their two RED (north) ends face each other and slowly push them together. What will happen as they get close — and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Children learn 'magnets attract' long before they accept that two magnets can PUSH APART. A child who only holds 'magnets stick together' predicts they snap together whatever the ends. A child with the pole rule predicts repulsion for like poles and, in tier 2, refers to the two SAME poles — not just 'magnets attract'. Facing like poles is the case that separates the rule from the everyday 'magnets stick' idea.
