pedagogy.summary: The digestive system is best taught at 7–9 as a JOURNEY food takes through a single long tube, with a distinct job happening at each stop: mouth (teeth break food up, saliva starts to soften/digest it), oesophagus (a squeezing tube pushing food down to the stomach), stomach (churns food with acid into a mush), small intestine (the long coiled tube where digested nutrients pass into the blood), large intestine (removes water from what's left, forming waste). The two ideas children must take away are the ORDER of the organs and the KEY function at each — especially that the small intestine is where nutrients are absorbed into the blood (linking to circulation) and the large intestine handles water and waste. Physicalise the surprising facts: the intestines are metres long, coiled up; the stomach is a stretchy bag, not where 'poo is made'. Trace the journey repeatedly, mapping it onto the child's own torso, so the sequence becomes a story rather than a labelled diagram.
bestPractices: Trace one mouthful's whole journey in order, out loud and repeatedly (mouth→oesophagus→stomach→small intestine→large intestine), naming the ONE main job at each stop — sequence-with-function is the objective.
Make length and coiling concrete: unroll a ~7-metre length of string/rope for the intestines, or show them coiled into the belly, to correct 'the tummy is one small bag'.

Use safe hands-on models for the mechanical steps — mash a cracker with water in a bag (stomach churning), squeeze food along a tights-leg (peristalsis) — so digestion is seen as physical breakdown plus chemical help, not magic.
Emphasise absorption as the PURPOSE: at the small intestine, the useful nutrients pass into the blood to be delivered around the body (an explicit hook to the circulation topic).
Separate 'breaking food down' from 'absorbing nutrients' from 'removing waste', mapping each to its organ, so children don't collapse the whole system into 'the stomach digests everything'.
keyRepresentations: A single continuous tube from mouth to end, folded/coiled, traced as the food's path (not scattered organ labels)
Journey map of one mouthful with a one-line job at each stop
Length model — unrolled string/rope showing how long the intestines really are
Stomach-as-stretchy-bag churning food with acid into mush (a sealed bag demo)
Small-intestine-to-blood zoom: nutrients crossing the gut wall into blood vessels
commonMisconceptions: 'The stomach digests everything / is where it all happens' — missing that most nutrient absorption is in the small intestine.
'Food goes to the stomach and waste comes straight out' — skipping the long intestines and the absorption and water-removal steps.
'There are two tubes — one for food, one for wee' — confusing the digestive tract with the urinary system; digestion is one continuous food tube.
'The stomach is where poo is made' — waste is formed in the large intestine after nutrients and water are removed.
'Digestion means food dissolving into nothing' — missing that useful nutrients are absorbed into the blood and the rest becomes waste.
'The intestines are short' — not appreciating they are several metres long, coiled up inside the belly.
'Gravity moves food down' — not knowing muscles squeeze food along (you can swallow upside down).

learn.summary: Teach the digestive system to 7–9s as the journey one mouthful takes through a single long tube, with a distinct job at each stop: mouth (teeth break food up, saliva starts to soften it), oesophagus (a squeezing tube pushing food down), stomach (churns food with acid into mush), small intestine (the long coiled tube where nutrients cross into the blood), and large intestine (removes water from the leftovers, forming waste). The two things children must take away are the ORDER of the organs and the KEY job at each — especially that nutrients are absorbed into the blood at the small intestine (a hook to circulation) and that waste and water are handled by the large intestine. Make the surprising facts physical: the intestines are metres long, coiled up; the stomach is a stretchy bag, not where 'poo is made'; muscles — not gravity — push food along.

activities.title: Follow your food: tracing one mouthful through the tube
feedback: If a learner stops at the stomach as the destination, continue the journey past it and ask where nutrients actually cross into the blood and where water is removed.

If a learner describes a straight in-and-out pipe with nothing crossing into the body, focus on the small-intestine wall as a crossing point: nutrients pass through it into the blood; only the leftovers continue as waste.
If a learner says gravity moves the food down, point out you can swallow while upside down because muscles squeeze the food along.
Reinforce by asking: 'If nutrients never crossed into the blood, could the apple ever help your leg move? Why not?'
activities.rationale: Digestion is a sequential process with a distinct job at each stage, so following a mouthful through the tube in order makes the order-plus-function understanding explicit: the food is seen to move and transform (chop, squeeze, churn, absorb, remove water) across the sequence, which a static labelled diagram shows only as fixed labels and does not animate. A replay/retell step lets the child narrate the sequence themselves.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils should describe the simple functions of the basic parts of the digestive system in humans.

The digestive system is a continuous tract (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine); most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine and water is reabsorbed in the large intestine.
learnerActions: Trace the path of one mouthful out loud and in order — mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine — naming the ONE main job at each stop.
Map the journey onto your own torso with your hands as you narrate, so the sequence becomes a remembered story rather than a labelled diagram.

At the small intestine, describe the moment of insight: the useful nutrients pass THROUGH the gut wall INTO the blood, which carries them around the body (for example to the leg muscles); only the leftovers travel on.
At the large intestine, describe water being drawn back out and the remainder forming waste.
Replay the journey yourself, narrating the order and each job without prompts, to check it holds together.
activities.intendedInsight: Digestion is not food 'vanishing in the stomach' — it is an ordered sequence that extracts nutrients into the blood at a specific place (the small intestine), while the large intestine deals with water and waste.

activities.title: How long are the intestines really?
feedback: If a learner thinks the intestines are short, lay the full length out so the scale is unmistakable before coiling it back up.
Connect back to the journey: most of this length is the small intestine, the long coiled part where nutrients have time to cross into the blood; the shorter, wider large intestine then removes water.
activities.rationale: Making length and coiling concrete with a physical model corrects the common underestimate of gut size and supports why the small intestine is where absorption happens. The ~7-metre figure is a vivid teaching approximation, not a precise anatomical measurement.
learnerActions: Unroll roughly a 7-metre length of string or rope to represent the intestines, then coil it into a small space to show how they pack into the belly.
Compare this length against your own height and against the small 'tummy' many children imagine.
Explain in your own words why 'the tummy is one small bag' is wrong — the gut is a very long, coiled tube.
activities.intendedInsight: The intestines are several metres long and coiled up inside the belly, not short — this corrects the idea that digestion happens in one small bag.

activities.title: Hands-on models of the mechanical steps
feedback: If a learner says food 'dissolves into nothing', point to the mash left in the bag: it is broken down, and the useful part is later absorbed while the rest becomes waste.
If a learner credits gravity for moving food, relate the tights-squeeze model to swallowing upside down.
activities.rationale: Safe hands-on models make the mechanical steps tangible, while the chemical help (saliva, acid, digestive juices) is named rather than modelled, and they separate 'breaking food down' from 'absorbing nutrients' from 'removing waste', so children don't collapse the whole system into 'the stomach digests everything'. These bag and tights models are approximations of the real soft, acidic, muscular organs; the water in the bag is not acid.
learnerActions: Mash a cracker with a little water inside a sealed bag to model how the stomach churns food with acid into a mush.
Push a small soft object along inside a length of tights/stocking to model how muscles squeeze food along the tube (peristalsis).

Say that both models show physical breaking-down and moving (churning, squeezing), then name the chemical help in the real body that the models do not show (saliva, stomach acid and other digestive juices), so digestion is understood as both, not as magic.
activities.intendedInsight: Digestion involves physical breakdown and movement driven by teeth and muscle action, plus chemical help from saliva, stomach acid and digestive juices — food is actively worked on, not simply dissolved into nothing.

activities.title: Explain-the-journey diagnostic: apple to leg muscle
feedback: Full understanding: nutrients are absorbed through the small-intestine wall into the blood, which carries them to the muscles, and the large intestine is distinguished as removing water and forming waste.
Partial: lists the organs in order and says food is 'broken down' but can't explain absorption — prompt specifically for where nutrients pass into the blood.
Gap: describes a straight-through pipe (mouth to toilet) with nothing crossing into the body, or names only the stomach — return to the small-intestine wall as the crossing point.
Probe further: 'Is the large intestine absorbing nutrients too, or doing a different job?' and 'If nutrients never crossed into the blood, could the apple help your leg move?'
activities.rationale: Asking how the useful part of the apple reaches the leg is exactly where the absorption idea shows or fails to show: a 'straight-through pipe' model cannot explain it, while an absorption model can. This transfers the journey to a new food rather than testing recall of a fixed diagram.
sourceClaims: The digestive system is a continuous tract (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine); most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine and water is reabsorbed in the large intestine.
learnerActions: Answer: 'After you eat an apple, some of it ends up helping your leg muscles work, and some comes out later as waste. How does a bit of the apple get all the way from inside your tummy to your leg? Talk me through the journey and explain how the useful part gets there.'
Point to WHERE the useful part leaves the gut and enters the blood.
Say whether the large intestine absorbs nutrients too, or does a different job, and name that job.
activities.intendedInsight: Only a learner who grasps absorption into the blood can bridge gut to muscle; stating where nutrients cross and distinguishing the large intestine's water-and-waste job shows real understanding.

activities.title: One shared food tube, not two pipes
feedback: If a learner describes food and liquid taking different internal routes, clarify the single shared tract: water is absorbed through the intestine walls along the way, with the large intestine drawing the remaining water out of the leftovers.
If a learner names the stomach as where waste is made, trace onward to the large intestine where the leftovers form waste.
activities.rationale: Naming the single continuous tract and the correct site of waste formation targets persistent confusions (two tubes; stomach as waste-maker) that otherwise distort the whole model.
sourceClaims: The digestive system is a continuous tract (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine); most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine and water is reabsorbed in the large intestine.
learnerActions: Explain that the digestive tract is ONE continuous food tube from mouth to the end — not a separate pipe for food and another for drink.

Say that water travels along the same tube as food and is absorbed through the intestine walls (much of it in the small intestine, with the large intestine drawing back the remaining water from the leftovers), rather than imagining it carried by a second internal pipe.
Correct the idea that 'the stomach is where poo is made' by naming the large intestine as where waste is formed, after nutrients and water have been removed.
activities.intendedInsight: Digestion happens in one continuous tract; waste is formed in the large intestine, not the stomach, and there is no second internal food/drink pipe.

constraints: National curriculum (Y4) expectation: pupils describe the simple functions of the basic parts of the digestive system in humans; keep functions at this simple level.
The two learning objectives are the ORDER of the organs and the KEY job at each stop — especially absorption into the blood at the small intestine and water/waste at the large intestine.

A labelled torso map that reveals each organ's job and its coiled length is a useful companion reference, but on its own it shows fixed labels rather than the food MOVING and being transformed — treat it as a scaffold alongside tracing the journey, not a substitute for it.

Ordering organs and matching organ-to-job are good consolidation checks after the journey is understood; choosing or arranging given options confirms recognition and does not by itself elicit the learner's own explanation of absorption.

A physical model of belly packing (showing how the long intestines coil inside) can help with length/spatial intuition; the causal sequence and jobs can be conveyed without it, so use it for the coiling/length point rather than as the main teaching medium.
Paper/card or string models are approximations of the real soft, coiled organs — distinguish the model from the real body when using them.

This mechanism is better traced than debated: an open interview/persona format does not fit a process to follow step by step (it may still support other goals, but not this sequence-with-function objective).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One cited source (Britannica digestive-system overview) is marked verified:false in the row; the specific absorption/water-reabsorption claim rests on it, so treat that detail as informed but not independently re-checked here.
The curriculum source (DfE) is marked verified:true in the row but has not been re-fetched in this rewrite.

The ~7-metre string length for the intestines is a commonly used teaching approximation; exact length varies by source and whether small and large intestine are combined — present it as an approximate, vivid comparison rather than a precise figure.
Simplification note for this age band: saliva 'starts to digest/soften' food is a correct simple framing; avoid over-claiming chemical detail beyond the Y4 level.

sourceClaims were removed from the length and hands-on-model activities because the available source claims support the topic (functions, continuous tract, absorption sites) but not those activities' specific teaching principles (physical length modelling; bag/tights mechanical models). Set to [] rather than citing a claim that only matches the topic.

The original pedagogy's 'two tubes' misconception (food vs. wee/urinary system) and the assessment's version (food vs. drink) differ; the activity follows the assessment framing (water absorbed in the large intestine). The fuller correction also distinguishes the digestive tract from the separate urinary system. Both framings exist in the original row.

probeDeeper: Where exactly does the useful part of the apple leave the gut and get into the blood?
Is the large intestine absorbing nutrients too, or is it doing a different job? What job?
If nutrients never crossed into the blood, could the apple ever help your leg move? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: As the apple moves through the gut it is broken down; in the small intestine the useful nutrients pass THROUGH the gut wall INTO the blood, and the blood carries them around the body to places like the leg muscles. The leftover waste carries on into the large intestine, where water is removed, and leaves as faeces. The key idea is that nutrients cross out of the gut into the blood — food doesn't just run through one tube and come straight out.

errorPatterns.pattern: Food just travels through one tube and whatever isn't used comes straight out the other end — nothing crosses into the body.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Focus on the small intestine wall as a crossing point: nutrients pass through it into the blood; only the leftovers continue as waste.
errorPatterns.distractor: It can't — the apple stays in the tube and only comes out as waste; nothing reaches the leg.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a straight in-and-out pipe; when pushed, says the apple can't reach the leg.

errorPatterns.pattern: Digestion happens only in the stomach / the stomach is where food ends up and stays.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Continue the journey past the stomach; name where absorption (small intestine) and water removal (large intestine) actually happen.
errorPatterns.distractor: It goes to the stomach, and the stomach sends the goodness straight to the leg.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the stomach as the destination; omits the intestines or their jobs.

errorPatterns.pattern: There are two separate tubes inside — one for food and one for drink.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify one shared digestive tract; water is absorbed mainly in the large intestine, not carried by a second pipe.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes food and liquid taking different internal routes.

responseLevels.gap: Describes a straight-through pipe (mouth to toilet) with nothing crossing into the body, or names only the stomach.
responseLevels.full: Explains that nutrients are absorbed through the small-intestine wall into the blood, which carries them to the muscles, and distinguishes the large intestine's water-and-waste job — a coherent journey that transfers to a new food.
responseLevels.partial: Lists the organs in order and says food is 'broken down', but can't explain absorption — doesn't say nutrients pass into the blood, so can't link the apple to the leg.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: After you eat an apple, some of it ends up helping your leg muscles work, and some of it comes out later as waste. How does a bit of the apple get all the way from inside your tummy to your leg? Talk me through the journey and explain how the useful part gets there.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the 'straight-through pipe' model can't explain how any part of the apple reaches the leg — they say it can't, or that the stomach sends it. Only a child who grasps absorption into the blood can bridge gut to muscle. The tier-two 'how does the useful part get there' is exactly where the absorption idea shows or fails to show.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Species Distribution & Change — how environmental change (climate change, habitat loss, pollution) shifts where species live, including range shifts, local extinction, and invasive species

- **Standards — UK (DfE Key Stage 3, Biology — Relationships in an ecosystem):** how organisms affect, and are affected by, their environment, including the accumulation of toxic materials; the interdependence of organisms; and how environmental changes may affect the distribution of species.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS2-4):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-4] — here, their distribution.

- **Operational details:** This is the KS3 extension of the KS2 'environments change and endanger living things' idea, now made spatial and mechanistic. Build three linked ideas. (1) RANGE SHIFT: as conditions change (warming especially), the band of suitable habitat moves, so species track it — poleward and uphill — with real documented cases (e.g. UK butterflies and birds shifting north, alpine species climbing until they run out of mountain). (2) LOCAL EXTINCTION: where a species cannot move or the suitable zone vanishes (a mountaintop, a fragmented habitat with no corridor), the population dies out in that place even if it survives elsewhere. (3) INVASIVE SPECIES: change can open a door — warming, disturbance or human transport lets a non-native species establish and outcompete residents that evolved under the old conditions. The connective tissue is DIFFERENTIAL VULNERABILITY: specialists, poor dispersers, cold/high-altitude endemics and species with no northward escape are most at risk; generalists and good dispersers cope. Insist on evidence and mechanism, not just labels — pupils should argue WHY a given species shifts, disappears locally, or invades.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/quantitative-relational). Pupils can now reason about a moving zone of suitability, interacting drivers, and asymmetric outcomes across species, and support claims with data. Success = two mechanisms of distribution change described, a real climate-driven range-shift example, a correct account of invasive species and how change enables them, and an explanation of why some species are more vulnerable than others.
bestPractices: Teach distribution change as a MOVING band of suitable conditions that species track, not as animals 'choosing' to migrate — the habitat moves, the species follows or fails.
Use real, documented range-shift data (UK butterflies/birds moving north, montane species moving upslope) so claims rest on empirical evidence per the standard.
Make the 'nowhere left to go' case vivid — mountaintop and poleward-edge species that run out of suitable habitat — to explain local extinction mechanistically.
Frame invasive species as change OPENING A DOOR (warming, disturbance, human transport) plus release from the competitors/predators that held them in check at home.
Foreground differential vulnerability: have pupils predict which of two species copes and justify it from traits (specialist vs generalist, disperser vs sessile).
Require argument-from-evidence: pupils state a claim about a species and back it with the mechanism and data, not just a label.
keyRepresentations: Range maps showing a species' distribution shifting north / upslope over decades
A 'moving band of suitable climate' diagram with species tracking it (and one trapped against a coast or summit)
Before/after invasion food-web showing a non-native outcompeting residents
A vulnerability comparison: specialist vs generalist, good vs poor disperser
Real case cards (e.g. comma butterfly, Cetti's warbler, ptarmigan, signal crayfish / grey squirrel)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking individual animals consciously decide to migrate to a better climate, rather than populations shifting as suitable habitat moves and unsuited individuals fail.
Believing a species that shifts its range is 'fine' — missing that trailing edges suffer local extinction and mountaintop/polar species can run out of room.
Assuming all species can simply move — ignoring dispersal limits, habitat fragmentation with no corridors, and rooted or slow species.
Thinking 'invasive' just means 'non-native' — missing that the harm comes from outcompeting or preying on residents lacking co-evolved defences.
Believing warming is universally bad or universally good for wildlife, rather than creating winners (generalists moving in) and losers (specialists squeezed out).
Treating climate change, habitat loss and pollution as separate unrelated threats rather than compounding drivers of distribution change.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13: how environmental change (climate change, habitat loss, pollution) shifts where species live, covering three linked mechanisms — range shift, local extinction, and invasive species — unified by differential vulnerability. The core insight is that distribution change is a MOVING band of suitable conditions that populations track (most often poleward and uphill under warming), not animals consciously choosing to migrate; a species that depends on tracking the band persists only if it can follow AND has somewhere suitable left to go. Learners should argue from mechanism and real data, not just apply labels, and explain why specialists, poor dispersers, and montane/polar endemics are most at risk while generalists usually cope better.

activities.title: Warming the living map: watch suitable habitat move
feedback: If a learner says the species 'adapted its body to the heat and stayed put', distinguish an individual adapting within its lifetime from a range shifting: it is about WHERE conditions let the population breed over generations, not individuals remodelling to tolerate heat.

If a learner says the butterflies 'felt the heat and decided to fly north', replace intention with survival: populations persist and breed where conditions became newly suitable; the range moves as a result, with no decision involved.

If a learner treats warming as pure gain ('it now lives across the whole country'), ask what happens in the far south if warming continues until it exceeds the species' tolerance — a sustained shift can mean losing the trailing edge, not only gaining a leading edge.

If a learner says a species that shifts is simply 'fine', point to the trailing edge and the summit/coast cases: shifting can still mean local loss, and a species with nowhere left to go can be lost entirely.
activities.rationale: Making the moving band of suitability visible and letting learners predict then compare outcomes targets the core misconceptions (conscious migration, adapt-in-place, pure expansion) directly, and grounds the reasoning in the mechanism rather than a label. A dynamic or multi-frame view makes the contraction and local-extinction moment legible in a way a single static map does not; printed sequential frames are a workable low-tech substitute.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should learn how organisms are affected by their environment and how environmental changes may affect the distribution of species, within relationships in an ecosystem.

Many species are shifting their ranges poleward and to higher elevations as climate warms, with trailing-edge populations declining and range-restricted montane/polar species most at risk of local extinction.
learnerActions: Work with a map where a coloured band of 'suitable climate' can be shifted north and upslope as temperature rises (e.g. a slider, successive overlays, or a sequence of printed map frames for 1970, today, and a warmer future).

Predict for each of several species where its range will go as the band moves: a generalist butterfly, a heather-moor or alpine specialist pinned near a summit, and a coastal species pinned against the sea.

Advance the warming and observe what happens to each range: the generalist's range glides north and persists; the mountaintop specialist creeps upslope until the mountain ends and its range contracts to a point and disappears from that site — a local extinction if the species still persists on other mountains or further north, but a total loss if it is a montane endemic with no cooler refuge anywhere; the coastal species is trapped with no room to shift.
State in writing, for each species, WHY it coped, shifted, or was lost, naming the trait (generalist vs specialist, good vs poor disperser, 'nowhere to go').
Repeat for the trailing (southern) edge: explain what happens to the population in the far south as it keeps warming and that area becomes too hot.
activities.intendedInsight: Distribution change is a band of suitability on the move; populations persist only where conditions let them breed. A full range shift means a trailing edge is lost as a leading edge is gained (though early on, or where the warm limit lies elsewhere, a range may simply expand for a time), and a species with nowhere suitable to follow to (summit, coast, fragmented habitat with no corridor) dies out at that site — a local extinction if it survives elsewhere, but a total loss for an endemic with no refuge anywhere.

activities.title: Introduce an invader: the same change opens a door
feedback: If a learner equates 'invasive' with 'non-native', redirect to the harm mechanism: the damage comes from outcompeting, eating or spreading disease to residents that often never evolved defences against it.
If a learner says warming is simply good or simply bad for wildlife, point to the paired outcomes: generalists moving in win, squeezed-out specialists lose.
If a learner treats climate change, habitat loss and pollution as unrelated, show how they compound — disturbance plus warming together open more doors than either alone.

If a learner calls enemy release itself a 'change in the new habitat', clarify that enemy release concerns the species' native range; the door-opening changes (warming, disturbance) act in the newly colonised area, human transport is the way the species arrives, and these factors are separate.
activities.rationale: A before/after comparison ties invasion to the same moving-conditions mechanism rather than a separate memorised fact, and forces a mechanistic definition of 'invasive' that addresses the common non-native confusion while keeping the door-opening change distinct from the enemy-release factor.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should learn how organisms are affected by their environment and how environmental changes may affect the distribution of species, within relationships in an ecosystem.
learnerActions: On the same map (or a before/after food-web diagram), introduce a non-native species into disturbed or newly warmed ground and observe its range expanding while residents' ranges shrink.

Write what 'invasive' means precisely — not merely 'non-native', but a non-native species that spreads and harms residents, for example by outcompeting them, preying on them, or spreading disease to them, often because they lack co-evolved defences.

Explain how the invasion is enabled: human transport delivering the species (a way in, not a habitat change), plus environmental change in the NEW area such as warming making new ground suitable or disturbance opening space — and, as a separate factor, add that the invader may also thrive because it has escaped the competitors, predators or diseases that held it in check in its native range.
Connect back to the range-shift activity: articulate how the same change that evicts one species opens the door for another.
activities.intendedInsight: Invasive harm comes from effects such as outcompeting, preying on or spreading disease to residents that are often co-evolutionarily naive; human transport delivers the species, environmental change in the new area (warming, disturbance) can enable establishment, and escape from the enemies of its native range is an additional, distinct factor that can help it thrive. Change produces winners and losers, not a uniform good or bad outcome.

activities.title: Argue from evidence: justify each species' fate
feedback: A full answer explains the range shift as suitable conditions moving and the population tracking them over generations (north gained, and the south at risk of loss if it becomes too hot), and extends the reasoning to invasive spread and to why specialists are more vulnerable.

A partial answer says warming made the north livable but frames it as individual movement/choice or pure expansion; prompt for what becomes unsuitable at the trailing edge and link to vulnerability traits.
A gap answer says the butterflies adapted in place or chose to migrate; reteach the distinction between individuals adapting and a range shifting, and between gaining and losing range edges.
activities.rationale: The NGSS performance expectation is argument from empirical evidence; requiring a claim backed by data and mechanism, and contrasting winners with losers, exercises exactly that practice and reveals whether understanding is mechanistic or label-deep.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-LS2-4: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-4].

Many species are shifting their ranges poleward and to higher elevations as climate warms, with trailing-edge populations declining and range-restricted montane/polar species most at risk of local extinction.
learnerActions: Work from real, documented case cards (e.g. comma butterfly and Cetti's warbler moving north; ptarmigan and other montane species running out of upslope room; signal crayfish or grey squirrel as invaders), each paired with range maps or data for an earlier decade versus today.
For a chosen species, state a claim about what has happened to its distribution and support it with BOTH the data shown and the mechanism and traits, not a label alone.
Answer challenge questions such as: why did the ptarmigan disappear here but the comma thrive? Why is a specialist more vulnerable to climate change than a near-ubiquitous generalist?
Optionally run this as a role-play debrief: one learner acts as a field ecologist posing the challenge questions and offering case data while others justify each species' fate.
Attempt the diagnostic prompt: 'As the climate warms, a butterfly that used to live only in the south is now found much further north. Explain what has made the butterfly's range move north.'
activities.intendedInsight: Claims about distribution change must be backed by mechanism and empirical data; differential vulnerability (specialist vs generalist, disperser vs sessile, cold/high-altitude endemic with no escape) predicts which species cope and which are squeezed out.

activities.title: Winners and losers: sort species and sequence the change
feedback: If a sort is correct but unjustified, require the trait-based reason — the categorisation only shows understanding when the mechanism is named.
If the sequence places local extinction before the habitat band moves, re-anchor on cause: conditions shift first, then the trailing edge becomes unsuitable, then the population is lost.

Use these sorting and sequencing tasks as a check on recall and classification; follow them with a construction or explanation task, since recognition alone does not show a learner can independently build the argument from evidence.
activities.rationale: Classification and sequencing consolidate vocabulary and the causal chain and give a quick check, but they test recognition; they are paired with the production tasks above so that independent construction of the evidence-based argument is still required.
learnerActions: Categorise species as likely winners or losers under warming, and justify each sort from traits (specialist vs generalist, good vs poor disperser, mountaintop/coastal vs those with room to move north).

Put the stages of a trailing-edge local extinction in order: warming → suitable band shifts north → southern/trailing edge becomes unsuitable → local population declines → local extinction at that edge.
Decide what makes a non-native species invasive versus merely non-native, and give the reason.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can classify species by vulnerability with justification and can order the causal sequence from warming to trailing-edge local extinction, consolidating the mechanisms from the earlier activities.

constraints: Teach distribution change as a moving band of suitable conditions that species track, not as animals consciously 'choosing' to migrate — the habitat moves and the population follows or fails over generations.
Use real, documented range-shift data (e.g. UK butterflies/birds moving north, montane species moving upslope) so claims rest on empirical evidence as the standards require.
Insist on mechanism and data, not labels: learners should argue WHY a species shifts, disappears locally, or invades.

Distinguish local extinction (species dies out at one site but survives elsewhere) from total loss (a montane/polar endemic with nowhere cooler left to go can be lost entirely); do not frame every 'nowhere to go' case as survival elsewhere.

Static range maps and case cards efficiently present documented examples and vocabulary but do not themselves show the dynamic tracking and contraction of ranges; pair them with a dynamic or multi-frame view, or with explicit before/after comparison, when the moving-band insight is the goal.

Sorting, sequencing and multiple-choice tasks check recognition and classification; they do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an evidence-based argument, so include at least one task where learners write or speak their own explanation.

A 3D terrain view could make upslope retreat and 'nowhere left to go' spatially vivid, but a 2D map with elevation shading is sufficient; 3D is optional and adds complexity rather than a decisive gain.

Distinguish 'invasive' from 'non-native': the harm comes from effects such as outcompeting or preying on residents, spreading disease to them (e.g. squirrelpox from grey squirrels, crayfish plague from signal crayfish), or altering their habitat, often against residents lacking co-evolved defences. Arrival usually comes through human transport, and environmental change in the new area (warming, disturbance) can help establishment; escape from the enemies of its native range is a separate additional factor, not itself a change in the new habitat.

Treat climate change, habitat loss and pollution as compounding drivers of distribution change, not isolated threats, and avoid framing warming as universally good or universally bad — it creates winners and losers.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested or effective.
The original flagged two of three sources (NGSS MS-LS2-4 and IPCC AR6) as verified:false; treat the range-shift and vulnerability claims and the NGSS wording as unverified pending source check.

The original 'ideal' recommendation asserted a coded 2D simulation is 'exactly the mechanism to be felt' and implied static images 'can't convey' the dynamic insight. Softened: a dynamic or multi-frame view aids the moving-band insight, but printed sequential map frames and before/after comparisons are workable alternatives; no comparative efficacy over other media is established by the source material.

The quiz/3D framings ('a linear quiz can't exercise evidence-based argument', '3D adds nothing decisive') were retained only as scoped affordance/limit notes rather than universal laws: sorting tasks do check recognition, and 3D is optional, but neither claim is a proven pedagogical necessity.

The diagnostic prompt and error patterns (adapt-in-place/Lamarckian, teleological migration, expansion-not-shift) were migrated into feedback; their mapping to 'gap/partial/full' response levels is from the source assessment and was not independently re-validated.

In the invasive-species activity, enemy release is kept separate from the door-opening environmental changes to avoid implying that escape from native enemies is itself a form of environmental change in the newly colonised area.

The mountaintop/summit case is used to illustrate local extinction but was clarified so that a truly range-restricted montane or polar endemic running out of all cooler refuge can face total (global) loss, matching the original's 'run out of room entirely' point.

probeDeeper: You said new northern areas became suitable — what happens to the butterflies in the far south as it keeps warming?
What makes a specialist butterfly more vulnerable to climate change than a pigeon that lives almost everywhere?
An invasive plant arrives and spreads fast in the new warmer conditions — what does 'invasive' mean, and why does the changing climate help it?
assess.correctAnswer: As temperatures rise, northern areas that were once too cold have become warm enough for the butterfly to survive and breed, so the population spreads and persists there; meanwhile the far south may become too hot. Over generations the range shifts north — the suitable conditions moved, and the population tracked them. It isn't individuals deciding to migrate or changing their bodies.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adapt-in-place — 'the butterflies changed their bodies to cope with the heat and stayed put'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish an individual adapting from a range shifting: it's about WHERE conditions let the population breed, not individuals remodelling to tolerate heat.
errorPatterns.distractor: The butterflies adapted their bodies to the warmer weather, so they didn't need to move.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the change as individuals altering themselves within their lifetime rather than the range shifting

errorPatterns.pattern: Teleological migration — 'the butterflies felt the heat and decided to fly north to find cooler places'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Replace intention with survival: butterflies that happened to be further north survived and bred where it was newly suitable; the range moves as a result, without any decision.
errorPatterns.distractor: The butterflies felt the heat and chose to fly north to find cooler places.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes the shift to conscious, goal-directed choice by individual butterflies

errorPatterns.pattern: Expansion not shift — 'the warmth just let it spread everywhere, so now it lives across the whole country'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what happens in the far south as it keeps warming; establish that a shift means losing one edge as another is gained.
errorPatterns.distractor: The warm weather simply let the butterfly spread everywhere, so it now lives across the whole country.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats warming as pure gain of range, missing that the southern edge becomes unsuitable

responseLevels.gap: Says the butterflies adapted in place or chose to migrate; treats warming as simply good or bad for the species with no shift of range.
responseLevels.full: Explains the range shift as suitable conditions moving and the population tracking them over generations (north gained, south lost), and applies the reasoning to invasive spread and to why specialists are more vulnerable.
responseLevels.partial: Says warming made the north livable so the butterfly is found there, but frames it as individual movement/choice or as pure expansion; does not connect to which areas become unsuitable, or to invasive species and vulnerability.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: As the climate warms, a butterfly that used to live only in the south of the country is now found much further north than before. Explain what has happened to make the butterfly's range move north.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands distribution change explains it as suitable conditions shifting and the population persisting where it can breed. A child holding a Lamarckian or teleological idea says the butterflies adapted in place or chose to fly to cooler spots — different answers that ignore the north-gained/south-lost shift the correct reasoner describes.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Energy stores and transfers

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** , KS3 Physics 'Energy' — 'Energy changes and transfers' and 'Changes in systems': 'energy as a quantity that can be quantified and calculated; the total energy has the same value before and after a change'; compare the starting and final conditions of a system, describing increases and decreases 'in the amounts of energy associated with movements, temperatures, changes in positions in a field, in elastic distortions and in chemical compositions'; and the explicit instruction to 'use physical processes and mechanisms, rather than energy, to explain the intermediate steps' — the IOP start/end-stores approach in statutory form. (Verified by fetch of gov.uk KS3 science.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** , middle school MS-PS3: MS-PS3-2 (model how changing [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS3-2] their stored/potential energy; DCI PS3.A 'a system of objects may contain stored (potential) energy depending on relative positions') and MS-PS3-5 (argue that when an object's kinetic energy changes, energy is transferred to or from it). CCC Energy and Matter: 'the transfer of energy can be tracked as energy flows through a designed or natural system.' Assessment boundaries exclude energy calculations at MS. (Verified by fetch of nextgenscience.org MS.Energy.)

- **Operational details:** The child moves from everyday energy WORDS to a disciplined MODEL: a small set of quantifiable energy STORES, connected by a small set of transfer PATHWAYS. It is qualitative tracing (name the stores at the start and end of a process, name the pathway between them), with quantification just beginning — full joule calculations and efficiency come later (Tier C). This is the conceptual hinge of the whole Energy domain: conservation, dissipation, heat transfer, efficiency and resources all hang off it.

The modern IOP/SPT framework (now embedded in the English KS3 curriculum) is deliberate and should be taught precisely: STORES are snapshots you could quantify — kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic/electrostatic. PATHWAYS are processes (named with '-ing') by which energy is shifted — mechanical working, electrical working, heating by particles, heating by radiation. Crucially, electric current, light and sound are PATHWAYS, not stores: there is no 'electrical store' and no 'light energy store'. The two big teaching moves: (1) focus on the START and END stores of ONE process at a time — do NOT build long energy chains; the DfE KS3 curriculum itself says to 'use physical processes and mechanisms, rather than energy, to explain the intermediate steps'. (2) Keep store (a thing you can quantify at an instant) and pathway (a process happening over time) categorically distinct — the '-ing' naming makes pathways sound like the processes they are.

Best taught with start→end energy 'bar charts' (how full is each store before and after?), one process at a time, naming the pathway, and beginning to attach actual quantities so energy reads as a calculable bookkeeping quantity rather than a vague essence.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional / early-formal, ≈11–12, KS3).
bestPractices: Use start→end energy 'bar charts': show how full each store is BEFORE and AFTER one process, so the model is read as which store empties and which fills.

Study ONE process at a time and focus on the start and end stores — do not build long energy chains; the DfE KS3 curriculum itself says to use physical mechanisms, not energy, for the intermediate steps.

Keep STORE and PATHWAY categorically distinct: stores (kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic) are quantifiable snapshots; pathways (mechanical working, electrical working, heating by particles, heating by radiation) are processes over time — the '-ing' naming signals this.
Explicitly teach that electric current, light and sound are PATHWAYS, not stores — there is no 'electrical energy store' or 'light energy store' (the highest-value correction at KS3).
Begin attaching actual quantities (joules) early so energy reads as a calculable bookkeeping quantity rather than a vague essence — even before full efficiency calculations.
Name the pathway for each transfer explicitly (a torch: chemical store → by electrical working then heating by radiation → thermal store of the surroundings).
keyRepresentations: Start→end energy bar charts (one bar per store, fill level = how much energy)
A labelled store-and-pathway diagram: the set of quantifiable stores, the four pathways as arrows
A STORE-vs-PATHWAY sorting layout (chemical/kinetic/thermal = stores; electrical/light/sound = pathways)
Worked single-process snapshots (falling ball: gravitational → kinetic; kettle: chemical/electrical working → thermal)
commonMisconceptions: Treating 'electrical energy', 'light energy' or 'sound energy' as STORES rather than pathways/processes — the central KS3 error the stores-and-pathways model is designed to fix.
Building long energy chains and 'renaming' energy at every intermediate step instead of focusing on the start and end stores.
Confusing a store (quantifiable at an instant) with a pathway (a process over time) — e.g. calling 'heating' a store, or 'thermal' a process.
Thinking energy is a tangible substance/fluid that physically flows, rather than an abstract quantity tracked between stores.
Believing only moving things have energy, missing stored (potential) energy in raised, stretched, chemical or thermal stores.
Calling the thermal store 'heat' — heat is a process (heating), not the way energy is stored.

learn.summary: For 11–12 year-olds (KS3 / NGSS MS), replace everyday energy WORDS with a disciplined MODEL: a small set of quantifiable energy STORES (kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic/electrostatic) connected by a small set of transfer PATHWAYS (mechanical working, electrical working, heating by particles, heating by radiation). The core teaching moves are: (1) trace ONE process at a time from its start stores to its end stores — do not build long chains, naming the pathway(s) between; and (2) keep STORE (a quantity at an instant) categorically distinct from PATHWAY (a process over time), with the '-ing' naming signalling processes. The highest-value KS3 correction is that electric current, light and sound are PATHWAYS, not stores. Start→end 'bar charts' (how full is each store before and after?) make the model concrete; attaching joules early previews energy as a bookkeeping quantity.

activities.title: Energy tracker: predict and trace the start and end stores of one process
feedback: If a learner says the energy is 'used up and gone' (e.g. 'the battery's energy is gone'), prompt them to name where it ENDS UP — usually the thermal store of the surroundings; it is relocated, not destroyed.
If they can't name the END store, ask: when the torch runs in a sealed box, where does the light/warmth go? It is absorbed and warms things (thermal store).

If they confuse a store with the object or a force ('gravity is the energy', 'the moving is the energy'), clarify that a store is a labelled account of energy in the system — the gravitational store depends on height and mass; gravity the force is not the store.
Reinforce correct traces: naming the start store, end store and the pathway(s) for one process is exactly the target skill.
activities.rationale: The IOP/SPT stores-and-pathways model, embedded in the KS3 curriculum, asks learners to compare start and final conditions and use physical mechanisms rather than energy for intermediate steps. Predict-then-trace on one process embodies the 'focus on start/end, don't chain' rule, and bar charts make store levels readable.
sourceClaims: IOP/SPT 'stores and pathways': a small set of quantifiable stores (kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic/electrostatic) and four pathways (mechanical working, electrical working, heating by particles, heating by radiation); electric current, light and sound are pathways NOT stores; focus on start/end stores of one process and don't build long energy chains.

DfE KS3 Physics 'Energy' requires: 'energy as a quantity that can be quantified and calculated; the total energy has the same value before and after a change'; comparing start and final conditions across movements, temperatures, positions in a field, elastic distortions and chemical compositions; and 'using physical processes and mechanisms, rather than energy, to explain the intermediate steps'.

NGSS MS-PS3-2 (stored/potential energy depends on relative positions of interacting objects) and MS-PS3-5 (when kinetic energy changes, energy is transferred to/from the object); CCC: energy transfer can be tracked as it flows through a system; MS assessment boundaries exclude energy calculations.
learnerActions: Pick a familiar process one at a time: a falling ball, a torch switched on, a kettle heating, a bow firing an arrow, a car braking.
Before running it, PREDICT which store empties and which fills, and name the pathway (or pathways) between them (e.g. mechanical working; electrical working; heating by radiation).
Represent the start and end as energy bar charts: one bar per store, with fill level showing how much energy is in each at the START snapshot and at the END snapshot.
Check your prediction against the recomputed end snapshot and name where the energy ends up (often the thermal store of the surroundings).

Worked single-process examples to study: falling ball (gravitational store → kinetic store, by mechanical working); electric kettle (energy transferred by electrical working from the mains supply into the thermal store of the water and kettle — one unchained process; the store that empties is outside the kettle, e.g. at the power station, so the bar chart shows energy coming in rather than a kettle store emptying); torch (chemical store of the battery → [electrical working, then heating by radiation] → thermal store of the surroundings).
activities.intendedInsight: Energy can be tracked as a quantity that moves between a small set of stores along named pathways; focusing on just the start and end stores of a single process makes conservation and relocation visible without renaming energy at every intermediate step.

activities.title: Sort it: STORE or PATHWAY?
feedback: If a learner drops light/electrical/sound into the STORE bin, point out these describe transfer between stores, not storage — ask where that energy actually ends up (a store such as thermal).
If they call 'heating' a store or 'thermal' a process, re-anchor: heating is the process (pathway); the thermal store is where energy sits — do not call the thermal store 'heat'.
Confirm correct sorts by having them justify one store and one pathway in their own words.
activities.rationale: The model has crisp, checkable discriminations that suit sorting and matching tasks. This consolidates the store/pathway boundary that underlies the whole Energy domain. A sort can teach and check this classification, but it does not by itself have the learner build and trace a process, so it complements the tracing activity.
sourceClaims: IOP/SPT 'stores and pathways': a small set of quantifiable stores (kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic/electrostatic) and four pathways (mechanical working, electrical working, heating by particles, heating by radiation); electric current, light and sound are pathways NOT stores; focus on start/end stores of one process and don't build long energy chains.
learnerActions: Sort cards into two bins — STORES (kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic/electrostatic) and PATHWAYS (mechanical working, electrical working, heating by particles, heating by radiation).
Place the tricky cards: electric current, light and sound — these go in the PATHWAY bin, because they describe how energy is carried, not where it sits.

For each of the four named pathway cards, explain that its 'working/heating' naming marks it as a process happening over time (electric current, light and sound lack this ending but still describe transfers: electrical working, radiation and mechanical working by vibrations); for each store card, explain it is something you could quantify at an instant.
Catch and correct the distractor claim: 'The torch stores electrical energy and light energy, which are two of the energy stores.' State why that is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Stores (quantifiable snapshots) and pathways (processes over time) are different categories; 'electrical', 'light' and 'sound' name transfers, not storage — the central KS3 error the model fixes.

activities.title: Store-and-pathway reference anchor
feedback: When a learner is unsure, direct them back to which column a term sits in and why (quantifiable snapshot vs process over time).
Prompt them to generate their own example for each store to check understanding beyond recognition.
activities.rationale: A static labelled reference anchors vocabulary and the two-category distinction. It supports rather than replaces the active tracing: it cannot recompute or enforce the distinction through the learner's own actions, so pair it with construction tasks.
sourceClaims: IOP/SPT 'stores and pathways': a small set of quantifiable stores (kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic/electrostatic) and four pathways (mechanical working, electrical working, heating by particles, heating by radiation); electric current, light and sound are pathways NOT stores; focus on start/end stores of one process and don't build long energy chains.
learnerActions: Study a labelled reference: each store with one real-world example (e.g. raised object = gravitational; stretched bow = elastic; hot water = thermal; battery = chemical) and the note that each store is something you could quantify.
Study the four pathways listed as arrows/processes, each marked as 'a process, over time'.
Examine a fixed worked example laid out side by side: torch — chemical store → [electrical working + heating by radiation] → thermal store of the surroundings.
Use the two-category layout (stores on one side, pathways on the other) to self-check before and during the tracing task.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the two categories side by side, with examples, pre-empts the store/pathway confusion and gives a glossary learners can return to while tracing.

activities.title: Optional numbers mode: energy as a bookkeeping quantity
feedback: If totals don't reconcile, prompt the learner to find the store they have missed (often the thermal store of the surroundings).
Reassure that full joule calculations and efficiency come later; here the goal is to see the total balance, not to compute efficiency.
activities.rationale: Attaching quantities early previews conservation and makes energy concrete. Keep this optional and qualitative-leaning: formal energy-equation and efficiency calculations go beyond core MS/KS3 expectations, so this is a conservation preview, not a calculation requirement.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Physics 'Energy' requires: 'energy as a quantity that can be quantified and calculated; the total energy has the same value before and after a change'; comparing start and final conditions across movements, temperatures, positions in a field, elastic distortions and chemical compositions; and 'using physical processes and mechanisms, rather than energy, to explain the intermediate steps'.

NGSS MS-PS3-2 (stored/potential energy depends on relative positions of interacting objects) and MS-PS3-5 (when kinetic energy changes, energy is transferred to/from the object); CCC: energy transfer can be tracked as it flows through a system; MS assessment boundaries exclude energy calculations.
learnerActions: Re-run a traced process whose stores are all included (e.g. falling ball, car braking) with joule values attached to each store bar; for a mains device such as a kettle, record the joules supplied by electrical working from outside as an input, rather than expecting a store inside the kettle to empty.
Check that the total across all stores is accounted for before and after the process — what leaves one store appears in another.

State in words that, when every store involved (including the surroundings and any energy supplied from outside) is counted, the total energy has the same value before and after the change, even though it has moved between stores and often ended in the thermal store of the surroundings.
activities.intendedInsight: Energy reads as a calculable, conserved bookkeeping quantity rather than a vague essence; the total is conserved while stores fill and empty.

constraints: Trace ONE process at a time, focusing on start and end stores; do not build long energy chains — the KS3 curriculum directs using physical mechanisms, not energy, for intermediate steps.

Keep STORE and PATHWAY categorically distinct. Valid stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic/electrostatic. Valid pathways: mechanical working, electrical working, heating by particles, heating by radiation. Electric current, light and sound are pathways, never stores.
Do not call the thermal store 'heat'; heating is the process. Do not call a pathway a store or a store a process.

When choosing worked examples, pick ones whose start store and pathway(s) are clear within one process (e.g. falling ball from its gravitational store by mechanical working; torch from its chemical store, by electrical working then heating by radiation). For an electric kettle, treat it as electrical working from the mains supply filling the thermal store of the water and kettle rather than chaining back to a chemical/fuel source, and say explicitly that the store that empties lies outside this process.

Keep joule/numbers work qualitative and conservation-focused; efficiency and formal energy-equation calculations belong to a later checkpoint and go beyond core MS/KS3 expectations (KS3 does include simple everyday energy comparisons such as food kJ values and domestic fuel costs).

Sorting and matching tasks check whether a learner can discriminate categories; they do not by themselves demonstrate that the learner can build and trace a process, so pair recognition tasks with construction/tracing.
The static reference anchor supports vocabulary but cannot enforce or recompute the distinction through learner action; use it alongside active tracing, not in place of it.

An interactive bench that refuses to let 'electrical/light/sound' be placed as stores is one way to surface the boundary; such enforcement is a proposed scaffold, not a proven requirement, and the distinction can also be taught via sorting, discussion and worked traces.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'description' and 'evidence' fields list the field-position store as 'electromagnetic', while the pedagogy and IOP source use 'magnetic/electrostatic'. The guidance uses magnetic/electrostatic consistently; reviewer should confirm preferred terminology for this age group.

The original row is internally inconsistent on store count (the diagnostic correctAnswer/responseLevels say six stores, omitting magnetic/electrostatic as not relevant to the torch; pedagogy says seven). The guidance uses seven consistently; reviewer may wish to confirm the expected count.

The torch worked example uses two pathways in sequence (electrical working then heating by radiation). This is the canonical IOP example and is preserved, but reviewers should confirm it does not read as the long chaining the 'one process' rule warns against; the start store (chemical) and end store (thermal surroundings) remain the focus.

The original diagnostic 'correctAnswer' states the torch energy ends 'mostly in the thermal store of the surroundings (the light is absorbed and warms things)'. This is a reasonable qualitative account for the torch; a sound store is not relevant here. Retained as framed.
Original source claims were marked verified:true in the row, but sources have not been re-fetched for this rewrite; do not treat the retained claims as re-verified.

The legacy row framed an interactive that 'enforces' the store/pathway boundary and claimed this is 'better than any static or verbal medium' and 'directly fixing the central KS3 misconception'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources; softened to a scoped scaffold proposal, with sorting, reference and discussion preserved as alternatives.

probeDeeper: Trace a falling ball: which store empties, which fills, and what's the pathway?
You called light a store. If I put the torch in a sealed box, where does the light energy end up — is it still 'light', or has it become something else?
Name a store that depends on an object's HEIGHT, and one that depends on its TEMPERATURE.
In a wind-up toy: name the store at the start, the store while it moves, and the pathway between them.
assess.correctAnswer: It starts in the chemical store (battery) and ends mostly in the thermal store of the surroundings (the light is absorbed and warms things). The pathways are electrical working (battery to bulb) then radiation and heating. 'Electrical', 'light' and 'sound' are PATHWAYS — ways energy is carried between stores — not stores it sits in; only kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical and nuclear are stores.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats every named 'energy' as a store, so 'electrical energy', 'light energy' and 'sound energy' are stores things sit in ('the wire is full of electrical energy').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort cards into STORES (kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear) and PATHWAYS (mechanical, electrical, heating, radiation); light/electrical/sound describe transfer, not storage.
errorPatterns.distractor: The torch stores electrical energy and light energy, which are two of the energy stores.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names pathways (electrical, light, sound) as stores when tracing the torch.

errorPatterns.pattern: Energy is a fuel or substance that gets used up and disappears, rather than ending in another store ('the battery's energy is gone').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Always name where the energy ENDS UP (usually the thermal store of the surroundings); it's relocated, not destroyed.
errorPatterns.distractor: The chemical energy is used up and gone once the battery runs down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't name the END store; says the energy is consumed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the store with the object or with a force ('gravity is the energy', 'the moving is the energy').
errorPatterns.nextMove: A STORE is a labelled account of energy in the system (the gravitational store depends on height and mass); gravity the force is not the store.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names a force or an object where a store belongs.

responseLevels.gap: Lists 'electrical/light/sound energy' as stores; treats energy as a used-up fuel; can't separate store from pathway.
responseLevels.full: Separates the six stores from the transfer pathways, identifies start and end stores (usually the thermal surroundings) and the pathway between, and traces energy through a multi-step system without inventing stores.
responseLevels.partial: Names several genuine stores and identifies start/end in a simple case, but conflates a pathway (electrical, light, heating) with a store, or can't trace a multi-step system.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A battery-powered torch is switched on and shines. Name the energy STORE it starts in and the store it ends up in, and name the PATHWAY that carries the energy between them. Someone writes 'chemical energy turns into light energy and electrical energy.' What's wrong with calling light and electrical 'stores'?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who lists 'electrical/light/sound energy' as stores (the old types model) differs from one who separates the six stores from the transfer pathways. The reason tier separates 'energy comes in named types' from 'stores hold it, pathways move it'.
