pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Efficiency, Sankey diagrams, and work done

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** this is KS4 (GCSE) content (late-KS3 lead-in). KS4 Physics 'Energy' (statutory, verified): 'calculating energy efficiency for any energy transfers' and 'conservation of energy in a closed system, dissipation'; KS4 Forces (statutory): 'calculating work done as force x distance'. KS3 carries only the qualitative precursors ('total energy has the same value before and after a change'; 'simple machines… product of force and displacement unchanged'). Sankey diagrams are the standard GCSE representation though not named in statute.

- **Standards — US NATIONAL (NGSS):** efficiency/quantitative energy modelling is HS, not MS — HS-PS3-1 (computational model of energy in a system) and HS-PS3-3 (design a device that works within constraints, accounting for efficiency); MS has no efficiency PE. Builds on 'Energy can't be created or destroyed'; needs percentage skills.

- **Operational details:** A PROCEDURAL topic spanning three linked calculations/representations: efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy (as a ratio/percentage), constructing and interpreting Sankey diagrams (arrow WIDTH proportional to energy, total in = total out), and work done = force × distance (joules). This is genuinely quantitative — percentages, proportional drawing, and a formula — and rests on conservation/dissipation (no real device is 100% efficient; the 'wasted' energy is dissipated, usually to the thermal store of the surroundings, NOT destroyed).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/quantitative, age 12-13).
bestPractices: Anchor efficiency in conservation FIRST: total input = useful output + wasted (dissipated) energy, so efficiency is the fraction that ends up useful; this makes >100% impossible and explains why the 'wasted' arrow must exist.

Build Sankey diagrams from the conservation constraint: the input arrow's width must equal the sum of the output arrows' widths — draw to scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 J) so the proportionality is real, not decorative, and the widths visibly balance.

Teach 'useful vs wasted' as CONTEXT-dependent, not intrinsic: a lamp's thermal output is wasted, a heater's thermal output is useful — the same transfer is useful or wasted depending on the device's purpose.

Define work done operationally and confront the everyday meaning: W = Fd is energy transferred when a force moves through a distance IN ITS DIRECTION; holding a heavy bag still (no movement) does NO work in physics, even though it feels effortful.
Separate the trio of confusable quantities — work/energy (J), force (N), and (next topic) power (W) — with units and worked examples, since students blur them.
keyRepresentations: A to-scale Sankey diagram (input arrow splitting into a useful branch and a wasted/dissipated branch; widths summing to the input).
The efficiency bar/ratio: useful output as a fraction of total input, shown as a percentage.
The conservation ledger: input = useful + wasted, with the wasted share labelled 'dissipated to surroundings (thermal)'.
A work-done diagram: a force arrow moving an object through a distance, W = F × d with units (N × m = J).
commonMisconceptions: 'Wasted energy is lost/destroyed' — it is dissipated (spread out, usually to the thermal store of the surroundings), still conserved; the Sankey's wasted arrow accounts for it.
Drawing Sankey arrows not to scale, or with output widths that don't sum to the input — breaking conservation in the representation.
Believing a device can be >100% efficient, or that a more efficient device 'creates' or 'saves' energy rather than wasting less of it.
Thinking 'useful' vs 'wasted' is a fixed property of an energy type rather than depending on the device's purpose.
Work-done errors: counting work when there is no movement (holding still), using the wrong (perpendicular) distance, or conflating work, force and power.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13 (GCSE lead-in / NGSS HS placement), this procedural topic covers three linked quantitative skills: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (as a ratio/percentage), constructing and interpreting to-scale Sankey diagrams, and work done = force × distance (joules). All three rest on conservation of energy and dissipation: no real device is 100% efficient, and 'wasted' energy is dissipated (usually to the thermal store of the surroundings), not destroyed. The core activity is a build-and-calculate bench where learners set an input, drag the useful/wasted split, see arrows redraw to scale and an efficiency readout update, plus a work-done tool linking force and distance to W = Fd. Reading-a-Sankey reference, calculation practice, and predict-then-check problems support this.

activities.title: Sankey-and-efficiency bench: build energy transfers to scale
feedback: If a learner tries to exceed 100%: the useful output can never be larger than the total input — the wasted branch can shrink toward zero, but total out cannot exceed total in.
If branch widths don't sum to the input: set a scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 J), measure each arrow, and check useful + wasted adds back to the input — energy is conserved.
If arrows are drawn the same width for different values (e.g. 60 J and 40 J): the width must be proportional to the energy, so the 60 J arrow should be wider than the 40 J one.
If a learner says wasted energy is lost: ask where the 40 J actually goes — it spreads out to the thermal store of the surroundings and is still accounted for on the diagram.
activities.rationale: Building the Sankey from the conservation constraint, with widths that must sum to the input and an efficiency cap at 100%, confronts the 'wasted = destroyed' and non-proportional-arrow misconceptions directly and makes the quantitative relationships concrete. The live recompute and drag-the-split interactions are optional means of making the proportionality and ceiling tangible.
sourceClaims: Students treat 'wasted' energy as destroyed rather than dissipated, draw non-proportional Sankey arrows that break conservation, and count work done when there is no movement.
learnerActions: Set a device's input energy (e.g. 100 J into a motor).
Drag the split between the useful output branch and the wasted (dissipated) branch; watch the arrow widths redraw to scale in real time.
Read the live efficiency meter showing useful ÷ total as a percentage.
Try to drag the useful arrow wider than the input — notice it cannot exceed the input, and efficiency cannot pass 100%.
Observe the wasted branch labelled 'dissipated to surroundings (thermal)' peeling off rather than vanishing.
Check that the useful and wasted branch widths sum back to the input width every time.
Work predict-then-check problems: predict the efficiency and arrow widths, then set the split and compare.
activities.intendedInsight: Efficiency is the fraction of input energy that ends up useful; input = useful + wasted, so efficiency can never exceed 100% and 'wasted' energy is dissipated, not destroyed. Drawing arrow widths in proportion makes conservation visible rather than decorative.

activities.title: Work done = force × distance: make W = Fd a felt quantity
feedback: If a learner claims work is done while holding something still: no distance moved means W = F × 0 = 0 J of work done on the load; the physics definition requires movement in the force's direction. Your muscles still transfer energy inside your body (it ends up dissipated thermally), which is why holding feels tiring, but that energy is not work done on the load.
If the wrong (perpendicular) distance is used: match the distance to the direction the force acts in.
If units are dropped: force in newtons × distance in metres gives work in joules (N·m = J).
activities.rationale: Defining work operationally and explicitly confronting the everyday meaning ('holding a heavy bag does no work') addresses a documented error of counting work with no movement, and keeps work/energy (J) distinct from force (N).
sourceClaims: Students treat 'wasted' energy as destroyed rather than dissipated, draw non-proportional Sankey arrows that break conservation, and count work done when there is no movement.
learnerActions: Push an object (e.g. a crate) with a force arrow through a distance; watch W = F × d accumulate with units (N × m = J).
Adjust force and distance (e.g. sliders) and observe how W changes.
Compute a worked case: W = 20 N × 2 m = 40 J, stating units.
Test the 'holding still' case: keep the load stationary and see that zero distance gives zero work, even though holding feels effortful.
Check that the distance used is the distance moved in the direction of the force, not a perpendicular distance.
activities.intendedInsight: Work done is energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance in the force's direction; no movement means no work in physics, which contrasts with the everyday sense of 'effort'.

activities.title: Useful vs wasted depends on the device's purpose
feedback: If a learner treats thermal energy as always wasted: ask what the device is for — a heater's thermal output is exactly its useful job.
If a learner treats 'useful' as intrinsic to the energy type: the classification follows the device's purpose, so compare the lamp and the heater to see the same transfer switch roles.
activities.rationale: Treating useful/wasted as context-dependent addresses the misconception that these labels are intrinsic to an energy type; the lamp-vs-heater contrast is a specific, well-chosen example.
learnerActions: Compare two devices: a lamp (whose thermal output is wasted) and a heater (whose thermal output is useful).
For each, label the same type of transfer as useful or wasted according to what the device is for.
State the device's purpose and then decide which output branch of its Sankey is 'useful'.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Useful' and 'wasted' are not fixed properties of an energy type — the same thermal output can be useful or wasted depending on what the device is meant to do.

activities.title: Read and interpret a given Sankey diagram
feedback: If a learner picks a diagram where outputs don't sum to the input: that breaks conservation — the branches must add back to the input.
If a branch is mislabelled: relate the branch to the device's purpose to decide useful vs wasted.
activities.rationale: Reading practice builds the interpretation evidence (identifying useful/wasted branches, checking balance) and serves as a reference scaffold. On its own, reading a fixed diagram does not give construct-and-calculate practice, so it supplements rather than replaces the building activity.
sourceClaims: Students treat 'wasted' energy as destroyed rather than dissipated, draw non-proportional Sankey arrows that break conservation, and count work done when there is no movement.
learnerActions: Examine a labelled Sankey diagram (e.g. tap branches to reveal energy values and useful/wasted labels).
Identify which branch is the useful output and which is wasted/dissipated.
Explain why the input arrow's width equals the sum of the output arrows' widths.
Spot the error: given several Sankey diagrams, pick the one that conserves energy and say what is wrong with the others (e.g. outputs that don't sum to the input).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a Sankey means recognising that arrow width represents energy amount, that each branch is useful or wasted, and that total in must equal total out.

activities.title: Consolidate with calculation practice
feedback: If efficiency comes out over 100%: efficiency is useful ÷ total, and since useful output can never exceed total input the result cannot exceed 100% — an over-100% result usually means the ratio has been inverted (total placed on top), so check the values and put useful ÷ total.
If W = Fd is applied with the wrong distance or with no movement: recheck that the distance is moved in the force's direction and is non-zero.
activities.rationale: Mixed calculation and spot-the-error items assess the procedural outcomes efficiently. These recognition/calculation items check fluency but do not by themselves require learners to construct a scaled diagram from scratch.
sourceClaims: KS4 Physics 'Energy' statutory: 'calculating energy efficiency for any energy transfers'; 'conservation of energy in a closed system, dissipation'. KS4 Forces statutory: 'calculating work done as force x distance'. KS3 carries qualitative precursors only.
learnerActions: Calculate efficiency as a percentage from given input and useful output values, placing useful energy over total input.
Solve W = Fd problems for given force and distance, stating units.
Given a Sankey diagram, identify the useful and wasted branches.
Decide 'which Sankey conserves energy?' from a set, justifying the choice by checking the outputs sum to the input.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency with the efficiency ratio and the work formula, and the ability to spot a conservation error in a Sankey, demonstrate the procedural outcomes.

constraints: Learners need prior fluency with percentages and proportional reasoning before this topic.

Quantitative efficiency/Sankey/work content is GCSE/KS4 (England) and HS-level in NGSS (HS-PS3-1, HS-PS3-3); KS3 and NGSS MS carry mainly qualitative precursors (e.g. energy is conserved; in an ideal, frictionless simple machine the product of force and displacement is unchanged, while real machines transfer less useful work out than is put in). Treat as a late-KS3 lead-in only with that caveat.
Keep work/energy (joules), force (newtons), and power (watts, a later topic) distinct with units and worked examples, since learners blur them.
Reading a fixed/tappable Sankey is a reference scaffold: it supports interpretation but does not provide the construct-and-calculate practice that is the main objective.
Recognition and calculation-answer items assess fluency but do not require learners to independently construct a to-scale Sankey diagram; include at least one build-from-scratch task.
When drawing Sankey diagrams, require a stated scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 J) so proportionality is real and branch widths can be checked to sum to the input.
Always label the wasted branch as dissipated (usually to the thermal store of the surroundings), not destroyed, to keep conservation explicit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated 3D and conversation formats as 'poor' with claims that '3D adds nothing' and 'dialogue doesn't build them'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been dropped; the planar build-and-calculate task is proposed on its clear fit to proportional drawing and calculation, not on a universal law that other media cannot teach it. Spoken explanation (e.g. 'talk me through it') is used in the original diagnostic and is retained as a useful teaching move.

Corrected a feedback error that had labelled the useful output as 'the larger number'; useful output can never exceed total input, so efficiency ≤ 100% comes from useful being the smaller (or equal) quantity, not from any denominator rule. Also softened the over-100% feedback so inversion is given as the usual (not sole) cause.

The 100% energy-efficiency ceiling and the 'cannot drag past the input' behaviour are certain consequences of conservation of energy for any energy transfer; they are offered as optional interaction examples, not mandatory interface mechanisms. (A heat-pump COP >1 is a different ratio and not a counterexample.)

Two sources (NGSS placement and IOP Spark misconceptions) are marked verified:false in the row; the DfE statutory source is verified:true. Confidence should reflect that the misconception and HS-placement claims are unverified.
Arithmetic checked: efficiency 60/100 = 60%; W = 20 N × 2 m = 40 J; input 100 J = 60 J useful + 40 J wasted. All consistent.

probeDeeper: Your Sankey — do the wasted and useful arrows add back up to the input? What law says they must?
Could a machine ever be more than 100% efficient? What would that violate?
You held the load still for a minute — how much work did you do on it by the formula, and does that match your intuition?
Where does the 40 J of wasted energy actually GO, and how would you show that on the diagram?
assess.correctAnswer: Efficiency = useful/total × 100 = 60/100 = 60%. Sankey: one 100 J input arrow splitting into a 60 J useful arrow (straight on) and a 40 J wasted arrow (branching down, usually to thermal), widths in proportion and summing to the input. Work done = F × d = 20 N × 2 m = 40 J. Throughout, input energy equals useful plus wasted (energy conserved).

errorPatterns.pattern: Calculates efficiency as total/useful or the wrong ratio, giving over 100% ('120% efficient').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Efficiency is USEFUL out over TOTAL in; it can never exceed 100% because you can't get more useful energy out than you put in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watching the calculation — puts the larger number on top or divides the wrong way.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws Sankey arrows that aren't proportional, or whose branches don't sum back to the input ('60 and 40 drawn the same width').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Set a scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 J), measure each arrow to it, and check the branches add back to the input — energy is conserved.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Arrow widths ignore the numbers, or the input doesn't equal the sum of the outputs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses W = Fd with a distance not in the direction of the force, or computes work when nothing moves ('holding it still does work').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Work needs movement in the force's direction; no distance moved = no work done on the load; check the distance matches the force.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Plugs in the wrong distance, or claims work is done with zero movement.

responseLevels.gap: Gets efficiency the wrong way up (over 100%), draws non-proportional or unbalanced Sankey arrows, or misuses W=Fd.
responseLevels.full: Computes efficiency as useful/total, draws a scaled Sankey whose branches conserve the input, and applies W=Fd with the correct distance — explaining wasted energy as dissipated, not destroyed.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates efficiency and work correctly for the given numbers but draws the Sankey loosely (not to scale, or not quite balancing), or can't say where wasted energy goes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are the figures for a motor: 100 J of electrical energy in, 60 J transferred usefully to lifting. Calculate its efficiency, draw a Sankey diagram to scale for this motor, then use W = Fd to find the work done lifting a 20 N load through 2 m. Talk me through it as you go. [Watch: efficiency = useful/total; wasted 40 J shown branching; arrows proportional and summing to the input; W = 20×2 = 40 J with units.]
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the calculation and the drawing separates a child who applies useful/total, conserves energy in the Sankey (arrows proportional and summing) and uses W=Fd with the right distance, from one who gets efficiency over 100%, draws non-proportional arrows that don't balance, or misuses the work formula.

pedagogy.summary: This is an observational topic for ages 5–7: noticing that there is MORE daylight in summer and LESS in winter, and relating that pattern to the seasons and to changes in weather and nature. It is kept to relative comparisons (longer/shorter days), not counted hours, and deliberately NOT the axial-tilt cause, which is a much later topic. It is taught through year-long observation and simple recording tied to the child's lived experience — dark when I wake in winter, still light at bedtime in summer.
bestPractices: Anchor in the child's lived experience across the year ('it's dark when we get up in winter; still light at bedtime in summer'), then formalise it as a relative pattern.
Record simply over time — compare winter vs summer sunrise/sunset with pictures or clock faces — staying with relative 'more/less', not counting hours (matching the NGSS assessment boundary).
Link the amount of daylight to seasonal weather and nature changes (colder, darker winter; warmer, lighter summer) as correlated patterns.
Do NOT teach the tilt cause here — keep it observational; the mechanism and the distance misconception are handled in a later age-appropriate topic.
Use the four-seasons cycle framing so children see the pattern repeats every year.
Avoid seeding the 'closer to the Sun in summer' idea — keep explanations to observed daylight length, not distance.
keyRepresentations: Winter vs summer daylight bars — a short bar against a long one — showing relative length.
A four-seasons wheel pairing day-length with weather and nature cues.
Paired clock faces: dark-at-wake and dark-at-tea in winter vs light in summer.
A year timeline marking the shortest (winter) and longest (summer) days.
commonMisconceptions: It is colder in winter because Earth is further from the Sun and warmer in summer because it is closer (the classic distance misconception — avoid seeding it here, correct it fully later).
Summer is hot only because the Sun is bigger or closer, not because days are longer.
The amount of daylight is the same all year, or day and night are always equal in length.
Seasons and shorter winter days are caused simply by clouds or 'it just gets cold'.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: observe and describe that there is MORE daylight in summer and LESS in winter, tying this relative pattern to the seasons and to changes in weather and nature. Stay with relative 'longer/shorter days' comparisons, not counted hours, and deliberately do NOT teach the axial-tilt cause (a later topic). Anchor in the child's lived experience across the year and keep explanations to observed daylight length, not distance from the Sun.

activities.title: A year in a slider: watch the daylight grow and shrink
feedback: If the child reads the bar as 'the Sun goes away' in winter: point out that where we live the Sun still comes up every day in winter — it is just up for a shorter time; compare the short winter day-bar with the long summer day-bar.
If the child says days are the same all year: slide slowly and have them watch the bar clearly change length, and connect it to 'dark when I wake in winter, still light at bedtime in summer.'
Reinforce when the child slides toward summer and names the growing daylight: 'Yes — more daylight in summer, less in winter.'
activities.rationale: The concept is a pattern across the year, so a draggable year with a growing/shrinking daylight bar is intended to let the child perceive the relative change and its repetition, fitting the relative-comparison boundary without counting hours. The interactive example (month handle, stretching bar, paired clock) is intended to make the relative daylight pattern visible — no cause or mechanism is shown, since the axial-tilt explanation is deferred to a later topic. It is one possible option, not the only way to teach this, and its effectiveness here is untested.
sourceClaims: NGSS 1-ESS1-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-2]' — emphasis is on relative comparisons of daylight amount (e.g. winter vs spring/fall); [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-2] hours.
learnerActions: Drag a month handle across a year and watch a daylight bar stretch toward summer and shrink toward winter while the same garden scene shifts from a dark, short winter's day to a long, bright summer evening.

Watch a little clock show it's still dark at wake-up in winter but light at bedtime in summer, with no numbers — relative length only. (December is winter and June is summer north of the equator; it is the other way round in the Southern Hemisphere.)
Say out loud what you notice as you slide from winter toward summer: 'more daylight in summer, less daylight in winter.'
Keep sliding forward past December into the next year, and watch the bar grow and shrink again, to see that the pattern repeats every year.
activities.intendedInsight: There is more daylight in summer and less in winter, and this is a smooth, repeating yearly pattern. In most places away from the equator you can see it from your own window.

activities.title: Winter morning vs summer evening: two scenes side by side
feedback: If the child gives warmth as the reason ('because summer is hotter'): separate 'how long it stays light' from 'how warm it is' — they travel together, but this question is about how long it stays light, not heat.
Affirm time-of-day observations: 'light at bedtime in summer' and 'dark by teatime in winter' are exactly the kind of noticing we want.
activities.rationale: A paired winter/summer contrast is intended to present the relative difference in daylight in a form pitched for 5–7. It is a scaffold, not a validated intervention, and a static pair does not show the gradual year-long cycle, so it supports rather than replaces year-long observation.
sourceClaims: NGSS 1-ESS1-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-2]' — emphasis is on relative comparisons of daylight amount (e.g. winter vs spring/fall); [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-2] hours.
learnerActions: Look at a two-panel scene: a dark winter morning and a light summer evening.
Tap each panel to reveal a daylight bar and a clock face — short/dark for winter, long/light for summer.
Describe the contrast in your own words: 'In winter it's dark when I get up; in summer it's still light at bedtime.'
activities.intendedInsight: Summer has more daylight and winter has less. You can see a clue to this in the scenes: it is still dark on a winter morning, but still light on a summer evening. To make a fair comparison, look at the same time of day in each season.

activities.title: Record the change yourself over real weeks
feedback: If the child insists days are the same length: scaffold the observation rather than reteach — keep tracking when it gets dark for a few more weeks so they see the change for themselves (near midsummer or midwinter the change is small, so it may take longer to notice).

Help the child keep daylight-length and temperature as two separate things that travel together, by charting sunset time and a weather/temperature cue side by side — these move together across seasons but neither is presented as the cause of the other.
activities.rationale: Simple recording over real time ties the pattern to the child's lived experience and lets them discover the change first-hand, matching the relative-comparison (not counted-hours) boundary. Linking day length to weather and nature treats them as correlated patterns, not cause.
sourceClaims: NGSS 1-ESS1-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-2]' — emphasis is on relative comparisons of daylight amount (e.g. winter vs spring/fall); [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-2] hours.
DfE Year 1 statutory science requires pupils to observe changes across the four seasons and describe the weather associated with each, including how day length varies.
learnerActions: Mark on a simple chart roughly when it gets dark (soon after sunset) over several weeks, using pictures or a clock face rather than numbers. The change is easiest to see in autumn or spring.
Notice whether the dark-time is getting earlier or later and say which way it is moving.
Pair the daylight amount with seasonal cues — colder and darker in winter, warmer and lighter in summer — as patterns that go together.
Place the shortest (winter) and longest (summer) days on a year timeline or four-seasons wheel.
activities.intendedInsight: The amount of daylight really does change across the year, and it goes together with seasonal changes in weather and nature; the pattern repeats every year.

activities.title: Check and sort: season to more-or-less daylight
feedback: If the child only parrots 'more in summer' without a reason, prompt for the second tier: 'How do you know? What have you noticed about winter and summer evenings?'
If the reason given is heat, gently redirect to light-time: 'That's about how warm it is — what about how long it stays light?'
activities.rationale: A sorting/sequencing/selected-response check lets the child apply the relative pattern and, paired with a 'how do you know' prompt, helps separate genuine observation from a memorised phrase. Recognition and sorting can check classification of seasons by daylight amount, but they do not by themselves elicit the child's own spoken observation, so pair them with a justification prompt.
learnerActions: Sort summer into 'more daylight' and winter into 'less daylight,' then place spring and autumn in between.
Put the four seasons in order so you can see the cycle repeat.
Answer: when are the days longest, and when are they shortest?
Explain how you know using something you have noticed about summer evenings and winter evenings.
activities.intendedInsight: You can reliably tell which seasons have more or less daylight and back it up with an observation, not just a memorised answer.

constraints: Keep to relative comparisons — 'more/less' or 'longer/shorter' daylight — not counted hours, matching the NGSS assessment boundary for this age.
Do NOT teach the axial-tilt cause here; this topic is observational. The mechanism and the distance misconception are handled in a later, age-appropriate topic.
Avoid seeding the 'closer to the Sun in summer' distance idea; keep explanations to observed daylight length.
Keep daylight-length distinct from temperature: they travel together across seasons, but warmth is not the cause of day length, and day length is not presented as the cause of warmth at this level.
The two-panel static contrast is a scaffold for the relative difference; it does not show the gradual, repeating year-long cycle, so combine it with year-long observation or a year-scrubber.
Recognition/sorting checks confirm the relative pattern but do not elicit the child's independent spoken observation; always pair them with a 'how do you know' justification prompt.
If any observation of daylight or the Sun is used, inspect light/shadow on the ground or the clock time it gets dark — never ask a child to look toward or stare at the Sun.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions; efficacy is untested.

The correctAnswer field in the source assessment says 'fewer hours in winter,' which drifts toward counting hours; the stated topic boundary is relative comparison only. Corrected activities deliberately keep to relative 'more/less' language to stay within the assessment boundary.

Two of three sources (DfE National Curriculum and Beyond Penguins misconceptions) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat the day-length/seasonal-change and misconception-avoidance claims as unverified here.

The source's design note calling a 3D/axial-tilt treatment a poor fit here is a scope decision for this age (mechanism deferred), not a universal claim that 3D adds nothing; retained only as a scope limit.

The source's 'open dialogue adds nothing' note is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; omitted as a universal claim. Spoken justification is still used within activities as a teaching/assessment prompt.

probeDeeper: Think about going to bed in summer — is it dark outside yet? What about in winter?
Is the Sun still in the sky in winter, or does it go away? How do you know?
My friend says the days are the same length all year. What could you show her to check?
assess.correctAnswer: More daylight in summer, fewer hours in winter — justified from lived observation, e.g. 'in summer it's still light when I go to bed; in winter it's dark by teatime.'

errorPatterns.pattern: 'summer has more daylight because it's hotter' — treats warmth as the cause of day length
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate 'how long it stays light' from 'how warm it is' — chart sunset time and temperature side by side; they travel together but the question is about hours of light, not heat.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because summer is hotter than winter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: gives heat/weather as the reason for how long it is light

errorPatterns.pattern: 'it's dark in winter because the Sun goes away / stops shining' — the Sun is thought absent in winter
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Sun is still there every single day — it is just up for a shorter time; compare a short winter day-bar with a long summer day-bar.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because the Sun goes away in winter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says there is less daylight because the Sun isn't there or has gone somewhere

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the days are the same length all year' — the pattern has simply not been noticed yet
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the observation rather than reteach: track sunset time over a few weeks and mark it, so the child sees the change for themselves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says daylight is the same in summer and winter

responseLevels.gap: Says daylight is the same all year, or gives temperature as the reason for how long it is light.
responseLevels.full: States more daylight in summer / less in winter AND justifies it from observation of lived day-length (light at bedtime in summer, dark early in winter), keeping daylight-length distinct from temperature; transfers to comparing two named months.
responseLevels.partial: Knows summer has more daylight than winter but justifies it by warmth/weather rather than a light-time observation, or cannot compare sunrise/sunset.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In summer, do we get more hours of daylight or fewer than in winter? … Now tell me how you know — what have you noticed about summer evenings and winter evenings?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child parroting 'summer has more daylight' without having observed it either fails the second tier or gives a temperature reason ('because summer is hot'). A child who has genuinely noticed gives a time-of-day observation. The reason tier separates a daylight-length idea from a heat idea — two children can both answer 'more in summer' for opposite reasons.

pedagogy.summary: KS3 transformations pull translation, rotation and reflection into one family unified by the idea that all three are RIGID motions producing a CONGRUENT image (same lengths and angles), differing only in what they do to position, orientation and 'sense' (handedness). Best taught by making each transformation's defining data explicit — a translation needs a vector, a reflection needs a mirror line, a rotation needs a centre, an angle and a direction — and by using 'sense' (whether the shape is flipped) as the single test that separates a reflection from a rotation. Extend beyond the horizontal/vertical mirrors of KS2 to diagonal mirror lines (y=x, y=−x) so pupils stop treating reflection as 'the same shape moved straight across'.
bestPractices: Insist every transformation is described by its full data set: translation = column vector; reflection = equation of the mirror line; rotation = centre + angle + direction (clockwise/anticlockwise). An under-described rotation is not yet a rotation
Use SENSE (handedness — whether the shape is flipped over) as the diagnostic that distinguishes reflection (sense reverses) from rotation and translation (sense preserved)
Teach the mirror line as the PERPENDICULAR BISECTOR of every segment joining a point to its image — this generalises to diagonal mirrors and replaces vague 'straight across' language
Include diagonal mirror lines (y=x, y=−x) and centres of rotation away from the shape early, so pupils don't overfit to horizontal/vertical mirrors and vertex-centres
Make congruence explicit: after every transformation check that lengths and angles are unchanged, naming the image congruent to the object
Find a centre of rotation by joining object points to their images and intersecting the perpendicular bisectors — turning 'describe the rotation' into a construction
keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid showing object and image shapes
Tracing paper / transparent overlay for testing rotation (pin the centre and turn) and for checking congruence
Mirror line drawn as the perpendicular bisector of each point→image segment
A 'sense' / handedness marker — an L-shaped or scalene shape whose flip is visible at a glance
Column-vector notation for translations
commonMisconceptions: Reflecting in a diagonal mirror but keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane (overuse of H/V mirrors)
Confusing rotation and reflection because sense is never checked
Describing a rotation without its centre or direction, or assuming clockwise
Swapping x and y when reading or writing image coordinates (reversal) carried into the image
Thinking a rigid transformation can change the size of the shape

learn.summary: KS3 pupils learn to identify, describe and perform the three rigid plane transformations — translation, reflection and rotation — treating them as one family that produces a CONGRUENT image (same lengths and angles) and differs only in effect on position, orientation and 'sense' (handedness). The core teaching moves: insist every transformation be fully specified by its defining data (translation = column vector; reflection = equation of mirror line; rotation = centre + angle + direction), use sense (whether the shape is flipped) as the test separating reflection from rotation, treat the mirror line as the perpendicular bisector of each point→image segment, and extend beyond horizontal/vertical mirrors to diagonal mirrors (y=x, y=−x) and off-shape rotation centres. A clearly-handed scalene shape (an 'F' or a flag) on a four-quadrant grid makes a flipped vs unflipped image visible at a glance.

activities.title: Reflect, then try to copy it with a rotation
feedback: If the reflected image is a slide or an axis-aligned flip rather than the true reflection in y=x (coordinates not swapped), reteach the mirror line as the perpendicular bisector of each point→image segment: fold tracing paper along y=x to check, and contrast y=x with y=−x so horizontal/vertical is not treated as the only case.

If the shape's handedness is reversed yet the pupil still calls it a rotation (or vice versa), use the tracing-paper test: trace the shape and turn the tracing — a rotation can be laid exactly on top, a reflection cannot without flipping the paper over.
If the pupil claims the rotation reproduces the reflection, point to the sense marker: the rotated 'F' is not mirror-imaged, so the shapes do not match.
activities.rationale: A handed shape makes a wrong sense visible at a glance, and directly juxtaposing a reflection with an attempted rotation of the same object targets the misconception that rotation and reflection are interchangeable 'moves to over there'. Building the perpendicular-bisector guides for each vertex generalises reflection beyond H/V mirrors.
sourceClaims: Sense reverses ONLY under reflection (the test separating rotation from reflection); a rotation needs three pieces — centre, size and direction; reflecting in a diagonal mirror must not leave the image 'in the same vertical or horizontal plane' (a named misconception from overuse of H/V mirrors); the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image segment; rigid transformations preserve congruence
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant coordinate grid, take a scalene, obviously-handed shape (an 'F' or a flag) and reflect it in the line y=x, recording the image coordinates of each vertex (e.g. (1,4) maps to (4,1) — for y=x, swap the coordinates).

For each vertex not lying on the mirror line, draw the segment from the point to its image and check it meets the mirror line at a right angle, crossing at the midpoint — confirming the mirror is the perpendicular bisector of every such point→image segment (a vertex on y=x maps to itself, so it has no segment).
Note whether the shape's handedness has changed: for the reflection the 'F' should appear mirror-imaged.

Now try to land the ORIGINAL shape on top of your reflected image using a ROTATION instead: pin a centre, choose 90° clockwise, and compare. Observe that the rotated shape keeps its handedness and so cannot coincide with the flipped reflection.
State in your own words why reflection and rotation give different results here: one reverses sense (handedness), the other preserves it.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection reverses sense while rotation and translation preserve it; this handedness test is what distinguishes a reflection from a rotation even when the image lands in a similar place. Reflecting in y=x swaps the x and y coordinates (reflection in y=−x swaps and negates them: (x,y)→(−y,−x)), not merely slides the shape across.

activities.title: Fully describe a rotation — centre, angle and direction
feedback: If the description omits the centre or the direction (e.g. 'I rotated it 90°'), require all three pieces every time; show two 90° rotations about different centres landing differently so the centre is felt as essential.
If the pupil assumes clockwise by default, prompt them to state the direction explicitly, since anticlockwise would give a different image.
If finding the centre is difficult, remind them that the centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of every point→image segment, so intersecting two such bisectors locates it.
activities.rationale: Turning 'describe the rotation' into a construction (intersecting perpendicular bisectors) and contrasting two different centres both make the defining data concrete rather than nominal, addressing the common under-specification of rotations.
sourceClaims: Sense reverses ONLY under reflection (the test separating rotation from reflection); a rotation needs three pieces — centre, size and direction; reflecting in a diagonal mirror must not leave the image 'in the same vertical or horizontal plane' (a named misconception from overuse of H/V mirrors); the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image segment; rigid transformations preserve congruence
learnerActions: Rotate the original shape 90° clockwise about the point (0,0) and describe exactly what you did, naming the centre, the angle AND the direction (clockwise/anticlockwise).
Check that your description is complete enough for someone else to reproduce the image uniquely: 'a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin'.
Carry out two 90° rotations of the same shape about two different centres and compare where the image lands, to feel why the centre is essential and not optional.
Given only an object and its image, reconstruct the centre of rotation by joining two or more object points to their images and intersecting the perpendicular bisectors of those segments.
activities.intendedInsight: A rotation is not fully described — and cannot be uniquely reproduced — without its centre, angle and direction (direction can only be left out for a 180° turn, where both directions give the same image). The centre genuinely changes where the image lands, and can be found by construction.

activities.title: Translate and prove congruence
feedback: If image coordinates come out as the correct point with the pair reversed (e.g. recording (4,1) as (1,4)), separate this coordinate-recording slip from the transformation itself (which may be correct) and reteach x before y when recording every coordinate.

If the pupil asserts congruence without evidence, press: 'Are the object and image exactly the same size and shape? How could you PROVE it, not just look?' — expecting a tracing-paper overlay or a measurement of corresponding sides and angles.
If the pupil thinks a rigid transformation can change the shape's size, revisit that translation, reflection and rotation leave all lengths and angles unchanged by definition.
activities.rationale: Explicitly checking lengths and angles after a transformation names the image congruent to the object and counters the misconception that a rigid motion can resize a shape; keeping coordinate reversal separate avoids mislabelling a correct transformation as wrong.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should identify, describe and perform reflections, rotations and translations, and understand that the image is congruent to the object under these transformations
Pupils commonly put the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate (reversal), giving incorrectly placed positions
learnerActions: Translate the original shape by the column vector with top entry 4 and bottom entry −3, i.e. 4 right, 3 down (shift every vertex +4 in x and −3 in y), writing the image coordinates.
State whether the lengths and angles have changed, and explain how you know: because the transformation is rigid, the image is congruent to the object.
Prove congruence rather than assume it — trace the object on tracing paper and lay it over the image, or measure corresponding sides and angles, confirming they match.
Record every coordinate as x before y ('along the corridor then up the stairs') to avoid reversing the pair.
activities.intendedInsight: All three transformations are rigid motions: they preserve length and angle, so the image is always congruent to the object. Congruence should be checked, not taken on trust. Coordinates are written x before y.

activities.title: Identify and describe the transformation from object and image
feedback: If a flipped image is labelled a rotation, return to the tracing-paper test — a traced copy of a reflected image cannot lie on the original without flipping the paper over.
If a rotation description lacks a centre, or lacks a direction for any angle other than 180°, it cannot be uniquely reproduced; require them before the answer counts.
Reinforce that matching the transformation needs more than 'it ended up over there' — the sense and the full data must agree.
activities.rationale: An identify-and-describe task with a sense-based distractor (a reflection mislabelled as a rotation) directly rehearses the diagnostic distinction the topic hinges on, and complements the 'perform' activities. Recognition-and-description tasks assess classification and completeness of data, but should accompany, not replace, actual performance.
sourceClaims: Sense reverses ONLY under reflection (the test separating rotation from reflection); a rotation needs three pieces — centre, size and direction; reflecting in a diagonal mirror must not leave the image 'in the same vertical or horizontal plane' (a named misconception from overuse of H/V mirrors); the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image segment; rigid transformations preserve congruence
learnerActions: Given an object A and an image B, name which single transformation maps A to B and describe it with its full data set (vector, or mirror line, or centre+angle+direction).
Use sense first: decide whether the shape has been flipped. If flipped, it is a reflection; if not, it is a rotation or translation.
Guard against a tempting wrong answer: an image in the 'right place' but with reversed handedness is a reflection, NOT a rotation, even if a rotation seems to put it roughly there.

Pair several object→image cases with the correct transformation, and for any rotation make sure you have supplied the centre, the angle and (unless the angle is 180°) the direction before accepting the description as complete.
activities.intendedInsight: Describing a transformation is the reverse task of performing one: checking sense immediately narrows the family, and a rotation's description is incomplete until the centre, the angle and (except for 180°) the direction are given.

activities.title: Pre-teach the vocabulary with a labelled diagram
feedback: If terms are confused, re-link each word to the diagram feature it names before attempting a performance task.
Make clear this diagram fixes vocabulary; it does not substitute for performing a transformation and testing sense and congruence yourself.
activities.rationale: A static labelled diagram with reveal prompts can efficiently establish terminology as a pre-teach. It is a scaffold: it does not let the learner perform a transformation or test sense and congruence, which is the core skill, so it should precede rather than replace the performance activities.
sourceClaims: Sense reverses ONLY under reflection (the test separating rotation from reflection); a rotation needs three pieces — centre, size and direction; reflecting in a diagonal mirror must not leave the image 'in the same vertical or horizontal plane' (a named misconception from overuse of H/V mirrors); the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image segment; rigid transformations preserve congruence
learnerActions: On a labelled diagram of an object and its image, point to the mirror line and name it: 'the perpendicular bisector of each point-to-image line'.
Point to the image and name its relationship to the object: 'congruent to the object — same lengths and angles'.
Match each transformation to the data that defines it: translation→vector; reflection→mirror line; rotation→centre, angle and direction.
Use this only to fix terms, then move on to actually performing and checking a transformation.
activities.intendedInsight: The precise vocabulary — perpendicular bisector, congruent, centre/angle/direction, vector, sense — underpins describing transformations accurately before performing them.

constraints: Every transformation must be described by its full data: translation = column vector; reflection = equation of the mirror line; rotation = centre + angle + direction. The one exception is a 180° rotation, where clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, so the direction may be left out. An under-described rotation should not be accepted as complete.

Include diagonal mirror lines (y=x, y=−x) and rotation centres away from the shape early, so pupils do not overfit to horizontal/vertical mirrors and vertex-centres. Note that the coordinate shortcut differs: y=x swaps coordinates while y=−x swaps and negates them ((x,y)→(−y,−x)), so each diagonal should be derived rather than assumed from a single rule.
Use a scalene, clearly-handed shape (an 'F' or a flag) so that a reversed sense is visible at a glance; a symmetric shape would hide the flip.

Keep the work on the 2D coordinate grid used by the assessment. A 3D handling could dramatise chirality (a left hand cannot be rotated into a right hand) but adds a dimension the assessment does not use and complicates coordinate reading; reserve it for a later chirality extension rather than the core task.

The labelled-diagram and recognition/matching tasks are scaffolds for vocabulary and classification: recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent construction of performing and checking a transformation, so include actual performance (drawing images, setting mirror/centre/direction, measuring congruence).
Treat coordinate reversal (y before x) as a separate recording slip from the transformation itself; a transformation can be correct while the recorded coordinates are reversed.
Congruence should be checked (tracing-paper overlay or measuring corresponding sides and angles), not assumed; emphasise that rigid transformations cannot change size.

Interactive features such as live sense badges, springing perpendicular-bisector guides, a ghost overlay confirming congruence, pinning a rotation centre, and refusing to run a rotation until a centre and direction are set are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they illustrate the learning, they are not mandatory for teaching it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the stated teaching principles, not the efficacy of any specific activity.

Self-audit of the worked example: reflecting (1,4) in y=x gives (4,1) by swapping coordinates — correct. The reflection in y=x reverses sense; a 90° clockwise rotation about the origin (which maps (x,y)→(y,−x)) preserves sense, so it cannot reproduce the reflected image — the contrast in Activity 1 is geometrically sound.

Activity 1's intended insight scopes the 'swap the coordinates' rule to y=x; reflection in y=−x maps (x,y)→(−y,−x), i.e. swaps AND negates. Constraint 2 flags that each diagonal be derived separately rather than from one rule.

Self-audit of the rotation claim: a rotation determines the image uniquely only with centre, angle AND direction; two different centres give different images, and the centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of each point→image segment — consistent and retained. (The NCETM source phrases the three pieces as 'centre, size and direction'; here 'angle' is used in place of 'size' to avoid implying a change of scale.)

The legacy source for the KS3 national-curriculum claim was marked verified:false in the row; the congruence/identify-describe-perform principle it supports should be treated as unverified pending a source check.

The original row asserted that 3D 'adds nothing' and that conversation/dialogue has no value for this spatial procedure; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements (3D is a dimension the assessment does not use; discussion alone does not substitute for performing and checking a transformation) rather than universal medium-superiority claims.
Corrected Activity 4's intended insight from 'the inverse of performing one' to 'the reverse task of performing one' to avoid conflation with the inverse (undoing) transformation.

probeDeeper: After the rotation, ask 'if I'd picked a different centre, would the shape land in the same place? Show me' — a counterexample that forces the centre to matter
'Which of your three transformations flipped the shape over, and how can you tell?' — pushing sense into a stated reason
'Are the object and image exactly the same size and shape? How could you PROVE it, not just look?' — pressing for a congruence check with tracing paper
'Could you get from the object to your reflected image by a rotation instead? Why not?' — a counterexample linking sense to the choice of transformation
assess.correctAnswer: For (a) the image is the mirror across y=x with each point's coordinates swapped (e.g. (1,4)→(4,1)) and the shape's sense reversed. For (b) they pin (0,0), turn 90° clockwise, and describe it as 'a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin' — the shape's sense is unchanged. For (c) they shift every point 4 right and 3 down, and say lengths and angles are unchanged because the transformation is rigid — the image is congruent to the object, confirmable with tracing paper.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflects in the diagonal mirror but leaves the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane — treats reflection as 'the same shape moved straight across' ('it just slides over the line')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the mirror line as the perpendicular bisector of every point-to-image segment; fold tracing paper along y=x to check; contrast y=x with y=−x and non-standard mirrors so H/V is not the only case
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a) the image is a translation or an axis-aligned flip rather than the true reflection in y=x; the point coordinates are not swapped

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses rotation with reflection because sense is never checked — produces a flipped shape and calls it a rotation, or vice versa ('it ended up over there, so it's a turn')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce SENSE as the test: trace the shape and turn the tracing — a rotation can be laid exactly on top, a reflection cannot without flipping the paper over
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (b) the shape's handedness is reversed (a reflection) yet described as a rotation; a traced copy will not lay on top without flipping

errorPatterns.pattern: Under-specifies the rotation — omits the centre or the direction, or assumes clockwise ('I rotated it 90°', with no centre or sense given)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Require all three pieces every time — centre, angle, direction; show two 90° rotations about different centres landing differently so the centre is felt as essential
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (b) the description lacks a centre and/or clockwise-anticlockwise, so the image cannot be uniquely reproduced; a different centre would give a different result

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps x and y when reading or writing image coordinates (reversal carried into the image)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach 'along the corridor then up the stairs', x before y, when recording every coordinate; separate the coordinate-recording slip from the transformation, which may be correct
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Image coordinates are the correct point with the pair reversed, e.g. records (4,1) as (1,4), independent of the transformation itself

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably perform the transformations — reflects a diagonal mirror as a slide, or produces images with the wrong sense or in the wrong place, and cannot state the data that defines each transformation
responseLevels.full: Performs reflection (including diagonal mirrors), rotation (with centre, angle and direction) and translation accurately, uses sense to distinguish reflection from rotation, and justifies that the image is congruent by checking lengths and angles — transferring to a new mirror line or centre unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Performs and names the transformations on standard cases but stumbles on the diagonal mirror, omits a centre or direction for the rotation, or checks nothing about congruence — can list the transformations but not reason about sense and invariants, or cannot transfer to a non-standard mirror or centre

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a scalene, clearly-handed shape (an 'F' or a flag) drawn on a four-quadrant grid, with tracing paper available. Ask them to: (a) reflect it in the line y = x and write the image coordinates; (b) rotate the ORIGINAL shape 90° clockwise about the point (0,0) and describe what they did; (c) translate the original by the vector '4 right, 3 down', then tell you whether the lengths and angles have changed and how they know. Watch whether they reverse the shape's sense for the reflection but NOT the rotation, whether they specify a centre and a direction for the rotation, and whether they CHECK congruence rather than assuming it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the family reverses sense for the reflection and keeps it for the rotation, and supplies a centre AND direction unprompted. A child with a partial idea reveals it precisely: a diagonal mirror exposes those who only know 'straight across', an unflipped reflection or a centre-less rotation exposes the sense/data gaps, and asking HOW they know congruence holds separates checking from assuming. The handed shape makes a wrong sense visible at a glance.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Building an energy-converting device

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** no general KS2 'energy' topic, so no direct UK science statutory match; the design-make-evaluate element lives in UK Design & Technology, and the science reasoning is anchored on KS2 'Working scientifically' (and Y6 Electricity for the electrical examples).

- **Standards — US NATIONAL (NGSS):** 4-PS3-4 (verbatim) '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4]' (an engineering PE, asterisked); clarification gives examples (electric circuit → motion/light/sound; passive solar heater → heat) and constraints (materials, cost, time); assessment boundary limits devices to converting motion↔electric energy or using stored energy to cause motion/light/sound. NGSS-anchored. Builds on 'How energy travels' (transfer by sound/light/heat/electric current).

- **Operational details:** An ENGINEERING-DESIGN topic: children design, build, TEST and REFINE a simple device that converts energy from one carrier/store to another (e.g. a battery-and-buzzer that turns stored chemical energy into sound, a torch that makes light, a solar heater that turns sunlight into warmth, a windmill that turns moving air into motion). The science is qualitative — name the input and output — and the heart of the task is the design→test→improve cycle, NOT efficiency calculations or formulas. Honest framing per the modern model: every device TRANSFERS energy from a starting store to a useful output (it does not make energy from nothing); NGSS itself notes 'produce energy' really means converting stored energy into a useful form.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/procedural, age 9-10).
bestPractices: Make it a genuine design cycle, not a craft: define the goal and constraints (materials/time), build a first version, TEST it against the goal, then identify one improvement and rebuild — the refine step is the learning, so plan time for at least one iteration.

Anchor each device in a clear input→output energy story the child can state: 'stored chemical energy in the battery → sound from the buzzer' / 'sunlight → warmth in the dark cup' — naming the start store and the useful output.

Use the everyday 'form' words as the on-ramp but keep the honest message that the device TRANSFERS energy from a starting store (battery, wound elastic, sunlight, moving air) — it never creates energy — so children don't build a 'free energy' mental model.
Test with a measurable-enough goal (does the buzzer sound? how far does the car go? how warm did the water get?) so 'what works well / what to improve' is evidence-based, not opinion.
Surface that not all the input becomes the useful output — some spreads to the surroundings (the motor gets warm, some light is wasted) — named simply, with efficiency/Sankey deferred to KS3/HS.
keyRepresentations: An input→device→output energy-flow strip for the chosen device (e.g. battery [chemical] → motor → wheels [motion]).
A design-loop diagram: design → build → test → refine → (test again), making iteration explicit.
A test-and-improve record: goal, what happened, one change to try next.

Concrete buildables: battery+buzzer (sound), battery+bulb (light), battery+motor car (motion), wound-elastic or rubber-band racer (elastic→motion), black-cup passive solar heater (light→heat), simple windmill (moving air→motion).
commonMisconceptions: 'The device makes/produces energy' from nothing — it converts a starting store (battery, sunlight, wound spring); name the input every time to break the free-energy idea.
'Energy changes form' taken literally as a substance morphing — reframe as energy TRANSFERRED from one store/carrier to another, so KS3 store-and-pathway teaching isn't undermined.
Expecting 100% of the input to become the useful output — some always spreads to the surroundings (warmth, wasted light/sound); kept qualitative here.
Treating the FIRST build as the finished answer — missing that test-and-refine (iteration) is the point of the task.
Confusing 'it works' with 'it meets the goal/constraints' — a device can run but still fail the brief (too slow, uses too much, wrong output).

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, children apply scientific ideas to design, build, [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4] a starting source into a useful output (e.g. battery+buzzer for sound, battery+bulb for light, battery+motor car for motion, wound-elastic racer, black-cup passive solar heater, simple windmill). The science stays qualitative — name the input (e.g. a battery, wound elastic, sunlight or moving air) and the useful output — and the heart of the task is the design→test→refine cycle under real constraints (materials, time), not efficiency formulas. The honest framing is that a device TRANSFERS energy from a starting store or carrier to a useful output (some always spreads to the surroundings); it never creates energy. A hands-on build kit is the authentic home for this objective; a screen design-bench is a companion for rehearsing the energy-flow reasoning and the iteration loop, and a cutaway reference or matching/sequence task supports naming and consolidation.

activities.title: Design, build and refine a real energy-converting device
feedback: If a learner describes the device as 'making' movement or light, ask what went IN to make that happen and trace the chain back to the source (chemical energy in the battery, elastic energy you wound in, sunlight falling on the cup) — nothing is created.

If a learner names only the output ('it buzzes', 'it lights up'), prompt 'where did the energy for that come from?' to draw out the full input→output chain, and have them point to the part where the energy is transferred to the output.
If a learner swaps parts at random when it underperforms, ask what exactly is going wrong first, then change one thing and re-test — model fair, targeted iteration.
Ask: could the device run forever without the battery, or without re-winding it? Use the 'no' to reinforce that the energy comes from a finite starting store or an ongoing supply like sunlight.
Prompt: is any energy going somewhere you didn't intend, like heat or sound? Not all the input becomes the useful output.
activities.rationale: 4-PS3-4 is an engineering-design performance expectation requiring children to design, test, and refine a real device under constraints of materials, cost and time; the deepest learning at this age is the hands-on iteration (the motor too weak, the elastic that snaps, the cup that warms only in sun). Naming the energy source every time and refusing a device with no source counter the common 'device makes energy' idea.
sourceClaims: 4-PS3-4 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4]'); clarification examples (electric circuit→motion/light/sound; passive solar heater→heat) and constraints (materials, cost, time); DCI PS3.D "'[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4]"; assessment boundary limits devices to motion↔electric or stored-energy→motion/light/sound.
Children commonly think a device 'makes' energy and that all input becomes useful output; the honest model is energy transferred from a starting store with some spreading to the surroundings.
learnerActions: Take a design brief with a measurable-enough goal, e.g. 'make the buggy cross this line', 'warm the water in the cup', or 'make the buzzer sound'.

Choose an energy source and a matching converter from real kit: a battery with a motor, bulb or buzzer; a wound elastic band turning an axle and wheels; sunlight on a black cup (or foil reflector); or moving air turning windmill blades; plus parts (wheels, card, black cup, foil).
Build a first version, then TEST it against the goal and record what actually happened (did it cross the line? how far? how warm?).
State the energy story out loud: name where the energy starts and the useful output, e.g. 'stored chemical energy in the battery → the motor turns → the wheels move'.
Identify ONE specific weakness from the test evidence, change just that one thing (fresher/bigger source, lighter load), and re-test to see if it improved.

Point to the part where the energy is transferred to the useful output (e.g. the motor, where the electric current makes it spin), and name any energy that spread to the surroundings (e.g. the motor got warm, or some light or sound was wasted).
activities.intendedInsight: A device moves energy from a starting source to a useful output — it never makes energy from nothing — and the first build is meant to be improved: targeted test-and-refine, not random tinkering, is the point of the task.

activities.title: On-screen design-bench to rehearse the energy flow and the refine loop
feedback: When the first run stops short, prompt the learner to name the observed weakness before changing anything, then change one variable and re-test.
Use the refused 'no source' run to ask aloud 'where would the energy come from?' and connect back to real starting sources.
When the energy-flow strip shows a 'to surroundings' leak, point out that not all the input becomes the useful output.
activities.rationale: A live-state design sandbox may make the design→test→refine loop and the input→output energy flow visible and lets a learner change one thing and re-test, which is intended to support the reasoning half of the engineering task. It is proposed as a companion to, not a replacement for, the physical build; its effectiveness relative to the real kit is untested.
sourceClaims: 4-PS3-4 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4]'); clarification examples (electric circuit→motion/light/sound; passive solar heater→heat) and constraints (materials, cost, time); DCI PS3.D "'[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4]"; assessment boundary limits devices to motion↔electric or stored-energy→motion/light/sound.
Children commonly think a device 'makes' energy and that all input becomes useful output; the honest model is energy transferred from a starting store with some spreading to the surroundings.
learnerActions: Pick an energy source from a palette (battery, wound elastic, or a sunbeam) and snap it to a converter and load that can use it (e.g. battery to motor, bulb or buzzer; wound elastic to an axle and wheels; sunbeam to a black cup of water); a pairing that cannot work, such as a sunbeam straight to a motor with no solar cell, should not run.
Take a goal card (e.g. 'make the car cross the line' / 'warm the water') and run the test.
Watch the input→output energy-flow strip light up (e.g. battery [chemical] → motor → wheels [motion]) and note the small 'to surroundings' leak as the motor warms.
When the buggy crawls halfway and stops, use a refine panel to change ONE thing — swap to a bigger source or a lighter load — and re-test, with each attempt logged so the iteration is visible.
Try building a device with NO energy source and see the bench refuse to run ('where is the energy coming from?').
activities.intendedInsight: The device only ever moves energy from a starting source to a useful output, the first try is meant to be improved, and a device with no energy source cannot do anything — there is no free energy.

activities.title: Cutaway reference: name the input→output story of real devices
feedback: If a learner gives only the output, prompt them to add the starting source and the converter step so the full chain is spoken.
Ask which part is the energy source and which is the useful output for each device.
activities.rationale: A cutaway reference is a support for the naming half of the topic and for consolidation; by itself it does not elicit the design, test or refine actions that are the core of the engineering objective, so it should be used alongside building, not instead of it.
learnerActions: Explore a tappable cutaway of real devices (torch, buzzer car, solar heater).
For each, read out its energy story, e.g. tap a torch → 'chemical (battery) → electrical → light'.
Compare devices and say which starting source and which useful output each uses.
activities.intendedInsight: Every device has a nameable energy story: a starting source feeding through a converter to a useful output.

activities.title: Consolidation: match devices to conversions and order the design loop
feedback: For a matching error, prompt the learner to say the energy story aloud and re-check the starting source.
If the loop is mis-ordered, ask what you must do before you can refine something (build and test it first).
activities.rationale: A matching-and-sequencing task can check understanding of conversions and the design-loop order, but it assesses recognition and ordering and does not itself elicit the independent build-test-refine construction the objective requires.
learnerActions: Match each device to its input→output conversion (device → conversion).
Put the steps of the design loop in order: design → build → test → refine.
Answer 'where does the energy come from?' style questions, choosing the starting source.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that devices convert from a named source, and that engineering follows a repeating design→build→test→refine loop.

constraints: Keep the science qualitative at this age: name the input (starting store or carrier) and the useful output; defer efficiency calculations, Sankey diagrams and formulas to later stages.

Make it a genuine design cycle, not a craft project: define goal and constraints, build, test against the goal, identify one improvement, and rebuild — plan time for at least one iteration, since the refine step is the learning.
Test against a measurable-enough goal (does the buzzer sound? how far did the car go? how warm did the water get?) so 'what works / what to improve' is evidence-based, not opinion.
Always name where the energy starts so children do not build a 'free energy' mental model; a device transfers energy, it does not create it.
Reframe 'energy changes form' as energy transferred from one store or carrier to another, so later store-and-pathway teaching is not undermined.
Surface simply that not all the input becomes the useful output — some spreads to the surroundings (warmth, wasted light/sound) — kept qualitative.

The screen design-bench, cutaway reference and matching/sequence tasks are companions for reasoning and consolidation; the explicit engineering objective (NGSS 4-PS3-4) needs a real build kit (cells, motors, buzzers, bulbs, wheels, elastic, black cups/foil) with a design brief and a test-and-refine sheet. Recognition and ordering tasks do not elicit independent construction.
Distinguish 'it works' from 'it meets the goal/constraints': a device can run but still fail the brief (too slow, uses too much, wrong output).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Standards framing: NGSS 4-PS3-4 is cited as verified in the source; the IOP Spark 'stores and pathways / energy dissipates' claim was marked verified:false in the original record and is retained but flagged, not treated as confirmed evidence. The UK framing (no general KS2 energy topic; design-make-evaluate in D&T; reasoning in Working Scientifically; electrical examples in Y6 Electricity) is retained as stated but not independently checked here.

The row's input list treats sunlight and moving air as 'stores'. In the stores-and-pathways model the kinetic energy of moving air is itself a store, while radiation (sunlight) is a pathway/carrier. Learner-facing text uses the generic 'starting store or carrier' and lists the four example inputs without bucketing moving air as a carrier, while preserving the age-appropriate simplification.

The original labelled a hands-on 3D build as adding 'handling cost without conceptual gain', which conflicts with the stated catalog gap that the standard requires a real built-and-refined device. Resolved: the physical build is the authentic objective; the digital bench and reference/matching tasks are proposed companions of untested relative effectiveness.

Catalog-ranking language ('ideal/possible/poor fit', '3D adds nothing', 'not recommended' for dialogue) and internal IDs (including the reteach-prerequisite pointer mt_X_aDUBh-HF) were removed; the misconception reteach step is retained conceptually in feedback, and objective affordance/limit statements are kept without treating any medium as universally superior.

probeDeeper: What form of energy goes into your device, and what form comes out? Is any energy going somewhere you didn't intend, like heat or sound?
When it didn't work as well as you wanted, how did you decide what to change?
Could your device run forever without the battery, or without you winding it up again? Why not?
Point to the exact part of your device where one form of energy becomes another.
assess.correctAnswer: The child builds a working device (e.g. battery → motor spinning a card fan: chemical → electrical → kinetic; or a plucked elastic band across a box: kinetic → sound), tests it, identifies a specific weakness, makes one purposeful change that improves it, and correctly names the energy conversion at each stage — including energy that ends up as unwanted heat or sound.

errorPatterns.pattern: Device 'makes' energy: describes the device as creating movement/light out of nothing, omitting the input store (the battery, the winding, the push).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what went IN to make the output happen; trace the chain back to the store (chemical energy in the battery, elastic energy you put in) — nothing is created.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The spoken conversion account has an output form but no input source — energy appears from the device itself.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names only the output, not the conversion: says 'it makes light' or 'it buzzes' but not that electrical energy is being converted into light/sound.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: prompt 'what turned into that?' to draw out the full chain; have them point to where the conversion happens.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When explaining, gives the end result without the input→output chain, though the child does know energy comes in forms.

errorPatterns.pattern: Untargeted trial and error: when the device underperforms, changes parts at random rather than the part that isn't working.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what exactly is going wrong before changing anything, then change one thing and re-test — model fair, targeted iteration.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: During the improve step, swaps or adjusts components with no link to the observed weakness.

responseLevels.gap: Assembles parts without a working conversion, or cannot say what turns into what; talks as if the device makes energy.
responseLevels.full: Designs and builds a working converter, names the energy conversion at each stage (including unintended heat or sound), tests it, and makes a purposeful change aimed at the identified weakness — coordinating design, energy analysis, and iteration, and transferring the reasoning to a different conversion.
responseLevels.partial: Builds something that works and names the final form ('it lights up'), and tinkers when it fails, but cannot state the full conversion chain (input → output) or target improvements at the actual weak point.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Using these materials — a small motor, a battery and wires, card, elastic bands, a buzzer and a bulb — design and build a device that turns one form of energy into another (for example electrical energy into movement, or movement into sound). Build it, test whether it works, then change one thing to make it work better. As you go, tell me what form of energy is turning into what. I'll watch rather than help.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the build separates a child who understands energy conversion — names the input and output forms, and targets the improvement at the actual weak point — from one who assembles by trial and error and can only name the final form. The quality of the iteration and the spoken conversion chain reveal the understanding; a verbal description of a procedure would not.
