pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–12 years

- **Topic:** Drawing Force Diagrams

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics — Forces):** Using force arrows in diagrams, adding forces in 1 dimension, balanced and unbalanced forces (the formal arrow representation; informal force arrows are introduced earlier across KS2 forces).

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no discrete elementary PE; relates to 3-PS2-1 / MS-PS2-2):** Balanced and unbalanced forces are assessed at 3-PS2-1 and force-sum reasoning at MS-PS2-2; the formal free-body diagram convention is introduced at HS-PS2.

- **Operational details:** This is a REPRESENTATIONAL skill spanning ages 7-12: representing forces as labelled arrows on an object, where the arrow's LENGTH shows the force's size and its DIRECTION shows which way the force acts. Pupils show multiple forces on one object, read the diagram to decide whether forces are BALANCED (equal arrows in opposite directions, no resultant, no change in motion) or UNBALANCED (unequal arrows, a resultant that speeds up, slows, or turns the object), and draw the resultant as a single arrow. The disciplined habit to instil is the free-body / 'replacement principle': pick ONE object and draw only the forces acting ON it, with arrow tails attached to the object (not floating in mid-air) and each arrow labelled by force type. For younger pupils it is a relative diagram, not a precise scale drawing.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal).
bestPractices: Draw ONE body at a time: start from a situation with NO arrows, then add only the forces acting on the chosen object (the replacement principle), repeating per object if several interact.
Attach every arrow's tail to the object and label it by force type — explicitly avoid 'arrows hanging in mid-air' and ambiguity about which object a force acts on.
Use the physical 'cardboard arrows' manipulative (IOP, 5-11) to build diagrams before drawing them on paper.
Use arrow LENGTH for relative magnitude (longer = bigger); treat it as a diagram, not a strict scale drawing, for younger learners — prioritise correct direction and attachment.

Teach explicitly that BALANCED forces does not mean 'no forces' and does not necessarily mean 'stationary' — it can mean moving at constant speed; confront this with a coasting/constant-velocity case drawn with equal opposing arrows.
Always link the diagram to a prediction of motion ('what will the object do?') so the arrows mean something physical.
keyRepresentations: The labelled force arrow (length = magnitude, direction = way it acts)
IOP 'cardboard arrows' physical manipulative for building diagrams
Single-object free-body diagram (other objects 'replaced' by arrows on the chosen body)
Opposing-arrow pair: equal (balanced) vs unequal (unbalanced)
The resultant arrow (single arrow summarising the net force)
commonMisconceptions: Drawing arrows 'hanging in mid-air', detached from the object, or unclear which object a force acts on (so it's impossible to tell push-of-A-on-B from B-on-A).
Motion implies a force: drawing a forward force arrow on anything that is moving, even at constant velocity (impetus).
Confusing the direction of velocity with the direction of the net force (Viennot's juggler task — persists after instruction).
Believing balanced forces must mean the object is stationary (not realising constant-velocity motion also has balanced forces).
Ignoring arrow length (all arrows drawn the same), or over-demanding an exact scale that obscures the physics for young learners.
Reading the diagram as a literal picture of the scene rather than as a representation of vector forces.

learn.summary: Learners aged 7-12 build and interpret force diagrams: forces shown as labelled arrows on one chosen object, where arrow LENGTH shows relative size and DIRECTION shows which way the force acts. They use diagrams to decide whether forces are balanced (equal, opposite arrows, no resultant) or unbalanced (unequal arrows, a resultant), draw a single resultant arrow, and link the diagram to a prediction of motion. The core habit to instil is the free-body / replacement principle: pick ONE object and draw only the forces acting ON it, with arrow tails attached to the body (not floating in mid-air) and each arrow labelled by force type. Key conceptual targets include that balanced forces do not mean 'no forces' and do not necessarily mean 'stationary' (constant-velocity coasting also has balanced forces), that a resultant force determines how an object's motion CHANGES (its acceleration) relative to how it is already moving, and that motion does not require a forward force.

activities.title: Arrow editor: forces that drive the crate
feedback: If arrows are equal and opposite, state that forces are balanced: no resultant, so no change in motion — the crate either stays at rest or keeps moving at the same steady speed it already had.

If one arrow is longer, name the resultant's direction, then describe the change relative to the crate's current motion: it speeds up if already moving that way, slows if moving the opposite way, or turns if the resultant is sideways.
If an arrow floats away from the crate, prompt: every arrow's tail starts ON the crate and shows a force acting ON it — one body at a time.

On the coasting challenge, state the friction model first. Assume negligible horizontal friction: the gliding crate needs NO horizontal arrows at all (only the vertical weight-down and support-up pair, which balance), and it keeps gliding at steady speed with zero net force. If a learner adds a forward push, do not reject it just because the crate is moving — ask what balances it: with no friction nothing does, so the crate would speed up. (If the model instead has appreciable friction, a forward push exactly balanced by backward friction keeps constant speed; the net force is still zero.) Either way, no NET forward force is required to keep moving.
activities.rationale: Editing arrows and observing the resulting motion makes balanced-vs-unbalanced a felt cause and gives a concrete way to confront the impetus misconception that moving things need a forward force. Live coupling between arrow and motion lets the learner test how changing an arrow changes the motion (an affordance of the interactive, not a claim that static images cannot teach the concept).
sourceClaims: 'Motion implies force' is the most-reported force misconception (K-12 and college); students conflate the direction of velocity with the direction of net force (Viennot's juggler task), a confusion pervasive even after instruction.

A free-body diagram is a diagram of ONE object with other objects replaced by forces on it (replacement principle); a common flaw is arrows 'hanging in mid-air' making it unclear which object a force acts on; arrow length encodes relative magnitude but it is a diagram, not a scaled drawing; teach one body at a time starting from a no-arrows situation.
learnerActions: Start from a crate with NO arrows drawn on it.

Add force arrows to the crate; set each arrow's length and direction (for example by dragging a handle at the arrow's tip), with every arrow's tail locked to the crate — only forces acting ON the crate are allowed.
Make two opposing arrows equal in length and predict, then check, what the crate does; then make one arrow longer and predict/check again, stating the crate's current motion each time.
Read or draw the resultant as a single arrow summarising the net force.

Attempt the 'coasting' challenge: a crate is already sliding to the right on a surface with negligible horizontal friction — decide what arrows (if any) it needs to keep gliding at steady speed, then test it.
Label each arrow by force type (e.g. push, friction, weight, support).
activities.intendedInsight: The arrows cause the CHANGE in motion (the acceleration): equal opposing arrows give no change (an object stays still if it was still, or keeps gliding at constant speed if it was already moving), while unequal arrows give a resultant whose direction determines how the motion changes — a box already moving the resultant's way speeds up, a box moving the opposite way first slows. A still-moving crate kept at steady speed with no net forward force overturns 'motion needs a forward force'.

activities.title: Cardboard arrows: build the diagram by hand first
feedback: Check each arrow's tail touches the object — a piece lying away from the object has no clear owner.
If both pieces are the same length when the forces differ, ask which force should be bigger and swap in a longer piece.
When two objects interact, confirm the learner has drawn only the forces on the single chosen object, not forces that object exerts on others.
activities.rationale: A hands-on manipulative supports younger learners in identifying the forces acting on each object before the drawing convention is formalised; this is offered as a bridge to paper diagrams, not as the only route to the skill.
sourceClaims: Many students cannot correctly identify the forces acting on each object when two or more objects interact, so they struggle to construct accurate free-body diagrams; the recommended primary manipulative is 'cardboard arrows' (5-11) to build up force diagrams, plus a 'describing interactions' framework.

A free-body diagram is a diagram of ONE object with other objects replaced by forces on it (replacement principle); a common flaw is arrows 'hanging in mid-air' making it unclear which object a force acts on; arrow length encodes relative magnitude but it is a diagram, not a scaled drawing; teach one body at a time starting from a no-arrows situation.
learnerActions: Use physical 'cardboard arrows' (cut to different lengths) laid onto a picture or model of one object to build up its force diagram before drawing on paper.
Place each arrow so its tail sits on the object and point it the way the force acts; pick a longer piece for a bigger force.
For a pair of interacting objects, build the diagram for ONE object at a time, replacing the other object with the force arrow it exerts.
Describe out loud which object each arrow acts on and name the force type.
activities.intendedInsight: A force diagram is a representation of one chosen object with the forces acting ON it; building it physically makes the replacement principle and arrow attachment concrete before committing to pencil.

activities.title: Interpret and construct: the resting book and the pushed box
feedback: Box: the arrows are opposite and the push is longer, so forces are unbalanced with a resultant to the right — and because the box is already moving right, it speeds up.
Resting book: draw two arrows ON the book — weight DOWN and the table's support force UP — equal in length (balanced), both starting on the book, so it stays still.
If nothing is drawn on the book: a still book has weight down and the table pushing up, equal and opposite — balanced does not mean absent.
If only the weight is drawn: the table also pushes up on the book; without it the book would not stay still.
Equal push and friction → balanced → no change in motion, so the box keeps moving right at the steady speed it already had.

Friction longer than push → resultant to the left → the rightward-moving box slows down and comes to a stop. It does NOT reverse: sliding (kinetic) friction only opposes the box's current rightward slip, so it cannot by itself drive the box backward. Once the box stops, reassess the forces: kinetic friction no longer acts, but the rightward push is still present and is now balanced by static friction, so the box stays at rest rather than reversing or re-accelerating. Reversal would need a sustained non-friction force pushing left.
activities.rationale: Mixing interpretation (read direction and length) with construction (translate a situation into arrows attached to and acting on one object) surfaces the specific misconceptions — floating arrows, 'still = no forces', and ignoring length as magnitude — and requires the learner to produce a diagram, not only recognise one.
sourceClaims: A free-body diagram is a diagram of ONE object with other objects replaced by forces on it (replacement principle); a common flaw is arrows 'hanging in mid-air' making it unclear which object a force acts on; arrow length encodes relative magnitude but it is a diagram, not a scaled drawing; teach one body at a time starting from a no-arrows situation.
learnerActions: Look at a force diagram of a box being pushed to the right across the floor (already moving right): a long arrow right labelled 'push' and a shorter arrow left labelled 'friction'. State what the lengths and directions tell you about what the box is doing.
Identify the resultant's direction and justify it from the arrow lengths.
Draw the force arrows for a book resting still on a table, attaching each arrow to the book and labelling it.
Redraw the box with push and friction EQUAL and say what the box is now doing.
Answer: if the friction arrow became longer than the push, what would happen to the box that is moving right?
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a diagram: the longer opposing arrow sets the resultant's direction → unbalanced → the motion changes that way relative to how the box is already moving. Constructing a diagram: even a still object has forces — weight down AND the table's support (normal) force up, equal and opposite (balanced), both starting on the book — so 'still' is drawn with balanced arrows, not a blank.

activities.title: Spot the error / match the motion (quick checks)
feedback: Reject 'must be stationary' when the object is already moving: balanced forces mean no change in motion, which includes constant-speed gliding.
For a mid-air arrow, reattach its tail to the object and confirm which object the force acts on.

When identifying the resultant, confirm it points in the direction of the net force and is drawn as a single arrow. For two opposite arrows, that is the way of the longer arrow. For several arrows along one line, add up the arrows pointing each way and compare the totals; the longest single arrow does not always win. Then state how the resultant changes the object's motion relative to how it is already moving.
activities.rationale: Short targeted items check and reinforce the conventions and can expose the named misconceptions; recognition-style items check interpretation and should be paired with at least one construction (draw/sketch) item, since selecting an answer does not itself elicit independent diagram construction.
learnerActions: Error-finding: given a diagram, spot the arrow that does not start on the object ('spot the mid-air arrow') and redraw it correctly.
Choose from outcomes for 'balanced or unbalanced — what happens next?', including a 'must be stationary' option to be rejected when the object is already moving.
Match each diagram to its motion description.
Identify the resultant for a given pair or set of arrows.
Sketch the arrows onto a pictured object for a described situation, stating the object's current motion.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent learners consistently attach arrows to the object, read length as magnitude and direction as the way the force acts, and know balanced forces can accompany steady motion, not only rest.

constraints: For learners aged 7-12 treat the diagram as a relative diagram, not a strict scale drawing: prioritise correct direction and attachment, with longer = bigger, rather than exact scaling that can obscure the physics.
Always enforce the replacement principle: one chosen object, only the forces acting ON it, every arrow's tail attached to the body, each arrow labelled by force type.

A static annotated gallery (tap an arrow for its meaning, tap for the balanced/unbalanced verdict and outcome) is useful reading and recap practice but does not let the learner test how changing an arrow changes the motion; use it as a companion, not the primary construction task.
A multiple-choice/recognition item assesses interpretation but does not by itself elicit independent construction of a diagram; include at least one draw/sketch task.

When describing changes in motion, state the object's current motion: a resultant (unbalanced) force determines ACCELERATION — it changes motion (speeds up, slows, or turns) RELATIVE to how the object is already moving, not the instantaneous direction of travel. Balanced forces mean no change in motion, which may be rest OR constant-velocity gliding.

In the coasting case, declare the friction model explicitly. With negligible horizontal friction a gliding object needs no horizontal arrows (only the balanced vertical weight/support pair); with appreciable friction a forward push balanced by backward friction keeps constant speed. Do not reject a learner's forward push merely because the object is moving — ask what balances friction in the stated model.

Kinetic (sliding) friction opposes an object's current slip: it can slow a sliding box to rest but cannot keep acting in one direction to reverse it. When a sliding object stops, reassess the forces — kinetic friction no longer applies, but static friction may balance a continuing applied push so the object stays at rest. Only a sustained non-friction applied force can reverse the direction of travel.
Physical cardboard arrows and a screen-based arrow editor offer different experiences; the manipulative is a bridge for younger learners and neither is presented as universally necessary.

Force diagrams use a deliberately planar 2D convention; a flat representation matches the skill being taught. (This is a fit note, not a claim that 3D rendering can never support any related learning.)
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, the IOP/cardboard-arrows claim is marked verified in the source row; the free-body/replacement-principle claim and the 'motion implies force'/Viennot claim are marked unverified. Do not treat legacy confidence as fresh verification.

The original 'ideal' entry asserted the live editor 'directly defeats' the impetus misconception and that 'live state is essential'. These comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources; softened here to a stated affordance (live coupling lets the learner test arrow→motion) without a necessity claim.

The original 'poor' ratings for 3D and conversation included universal-sounding claims ('rendering in 3D undermines the very representation', dialogue 'offers no efficient route'). These are not established by the sources and have been reduced to narrowly scoped fit notes.

Audit of the worked example: for a box already moving right with push (right, long) and friction (left, short), resultant is to the right and the box speeds up — consistent. For the resting book, weight down and support up, equal and opposite, balanced — consistent. The 'friction longer than push' case is corrected so the rightward-moving box decelerates to a stop and does NOT reverse: kinetic friction only opposes the current rightward slip. Once stopped, kinetic friction ceases but the still-present rightward push is balanced by static friction, so the box remains at rest; reversal would require a sustained non-friction force to the left.

The coasting challenge declares its friction model (default negligible horizontal friction, with the appreciable-friction alternative noted) so that a learner's forward push is questioned against what balances friction rather than rejected for the object being in motion.

probeDeeper: In the box diagram, which way is the resultant force, and how did the arrow lengths tell you?
For your resting book — which object is each arrow acting ON? Point to where each arrow starts.
Draw the arrows for the same box when the push and friction are EQUAL. What is the box doing now?
If I made the friction arrow longer than the push, what would happen to the box?
assess.correctAnswer: The two arrows are opposite (push right, friction left) and the push arrow is LONGER, so the forces are unbalanced with a resultant to the right — the box speeds up / moves right. For the resting book: two arrows ON the book — weight pointing DOWN and the table's support (normal) force pointing UP — equal in length (balanced), both starting on the book, so it stays still.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A still object has no forces, so I'll draw no arrows.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A still book has weight down AND the table pushing up, equal and opposite; balanced does not mean absent.
errorPatterns.distractor: Nothing is happening to the book, so there are no forces to draw.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws nothing on the resting book, or only the weight arrow.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Arrows can float anywhere near the object.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Every arrow starts ON the object and shows a force acting ON it — one body at a time (the replacement principle).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws arrows not starting on the object, or is unclear which object each force acts on.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The arrow's length doesn't mean anything — you read the force from the label, not the size.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Length = relative magnitude; a longer arrow is a bigger force, and it tells you the direction of the resultant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws both arrows the same length regardless of size, or can't say which force is bigger from the diagram.

responseLevels.gap: Leaves arrows floating or draws none on a still object; reads no meaning from arrow length or direction.
responseLevels.full: Interprets arrow direction as the way a force acts and length as its relative size (concluding balanced/unbalanced and the resultant), and translates a situation into a correct diagram — arrows attached to and acting ON one object, with a still object shown as balanced forces.
responseLevels.partial: Draws labelled arrows with correct directions and reads a single diagram, but slips on one convention — arrows not clearly on the object, 'still = no forces', or ignoring length as magnitude — interpreting OR drawing, but not both cleanly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at this force diagram of a box being pushed across the floor: a long arrow points right labelled 'push', and a shorter arrow points left labelled 'friction'. What do the lengths and directions of the two arrows tell you about what the box is doing? Then draw the force arrows for a book resting still on a table.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting: does the child read arrow LENGTH as magnitude and DIRECTION as the way the force acts, concluding motion from the longer arrow? Translating (draw the resting book): the tells are whether arrows are ATTACHED to the object (not floating), act ON the book (not forces the book exerts elsewhere), and that a still book still has forces drawn (balanced, not blank). Floating arrows, only a downward arrow, or 'still = no forces' reveal the representational gap.

sources.claim: Many students cannot correctly identify the forces acting on each object when two or more objects interact, so they struggle to construct accurate free-body diagrams; the recommended primary manipulative is 'cardboard arrows' (5-11) to build up force diagrams, plus a 'describing interactions' framework.
sources.source: IOP Spark (Institute of Physics) — 'Many students are unable to identify correctly the forces acting on each object...'

sources.claim: A free-body diagram is a diagram of ONE object with other objects replaced by forces on it (replacement principle); a common flaw is arrows 'hanging in mid-air' making it unclear which object a force acts on; arrow length encodes relative magnitude but it is a diagram, not a scaled drawing; teach one body at a time starting from a no-arrows situation.
sources.source: physicsteacher.blog ('Fear of Forces? Keep Calm and Draw Free Body Diagrams'); The Physics Classroom (free-body diagram conventions); arXiv physics/0512158 (replacement principle)

sources.claim: 'Motion implies force' is the most-reported force misconception (K-12 and college); students conflate the direction of velocity with the direction of net force (Viennot's juggler task), a confusion pervasive even after instruction.
sources.source: Student Misconceptions about Force and Acceleration review; arXiv 1603.06024 (Clement, Viennot, FCI)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Organ Systems Vocabulary (LANGUAGE)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 'Animals, including humans', vocabulary underpinning Y3–Y6):** the technical terms cut across the statutory content — skeletal/muscular (Y3), digestive and 'digestion'/nutrient (Y4), and circulatory 'identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system... heart, blood vessels and blood' (Y6). This LANGUAGE topic consolidates the correct vocabulary used across those years.

- **Standards — US (supporting NGSS 4-LS1-1 / MS-LS1-3):** the systems vocabulary supports structure-function reasoning (4-LS1-1) and the middle-school treatment of the body as interacting subsystems (MS-LS1-3); NGSS has no standalone vocabulary PE.

- **Operational details:** This is a LANGUAGE/naming topic: children must USE technical terms precisely — organ, organ system, and the named systems (circulatory, digestive, respiratory, skeletal, muscular) — plus component terms (nutrient, oxygen, carbon dioxide, blood vessel, artery, vein, capillary, enzyme) and describe each system's function using them. The pedagogy is vocabulary instruction: pair each term with a canonical image and a one-line function; distinguish easily-confused pairs (artery vs vein, organ vs organ system); and require the words in the child's own spoken/written descriptions (e.g. explaining artery vs vein correctly). It is not new conceptual content but the precise labelling of concepts met across KS2.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B. Recognising and matching terms to systems is Tier A; USING the vocabulary accurately in written explanation and correctly distinguishing confusable pairs (artery/vein, organ/system) is the transitional target.
bestPractices: Pair every term with a canonical image AND a one-line function so the word is anchored to both a picture and a meaning, not memorised in isolation.
Target confusable pairs explicitly (artery vs vein by DIRECTION; organ vs organ system as part vs team) since these are the predictable error points.
Require PRODUCTIVE use — children writing or saying descriptions with the correct terms — not just recognising them, because a LANGUAGE objective is about using the words.
Group component terms under the system they belong to (artery/vein/capillary under circulatory; enzyme under digestive) so vocabulary is organised, not a flat list.
Revisit terms across the KS2 topics they came from (Y3 skeletal/muscular, Y4 digestive, Y6 circulatory) so vocabulary is consolidated in context.
Use consistent, correct definitions and avoid loose synonyms (e.g. 'tube' for blood vessel) that blur the technical meaning.
keyRepresentations: A layered labelled body with one togglable layer per organ system
Term→image→function cards for each vocabulary item
A confusable-pairs contrast (artery/vein; organ/organ system)
A component-term map grouping words under their system
Sentence frames requiring the target term in a description
commonMisconceptions: Confusing artery and vein (thinking arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood, or muddling direction) rather than defining them by flow relative to the heart.
Using 'organ' and 'organ system' interchangeably, missing that a system is several organs working together.
Treating 'digestion', 'nutrient' and 'enzyme' as vague synonyms rather than distinct terms with precise meanings.
Thinking a technical term and an everyday word mean the same (e.g. 'vessel', 'tissue') and using loose synonyms.
Assigning a component term to the wrong system (e.g. placing 'enzyme' under circulatory) through weak organisation of vocabulary.

learn.summary: Vocabulary/naming guidance for 9–11 year-olds on the major human organ systems. The teaching objective is PRODUCTIVE, precise use of technical terms (organ, organ system, circulatory, digestive, respiratory, skeletal, muscular, plus component terms nutrient, oxygen, carbon dioxide, blood vessel, artery, vein, capillary, enzyme), each anchored to a canonical image and a one-line function, with explicit work on predictably confused pairs (artery vs vein by direction; organ vs organ system as part vs team). Labelled-figure and matching activities build and check term→structure→function links; productive speaking/writing moves learners from recognition to independent use. This mostly consolidates vocabulary met across KS2 (Y3 nutrition and skeletal/muscular, Y4 digestive, Y6 circulatory); some terms such as enzyme and respiratory system go beyond KS2 statutory content and need a simple introduction.

activities.title: Labelled body 'vocabulary map': one system at a time
feedback: If the learner names an organ correctly but gives a vague function ('the breathing thing'), supply and model the precise sentence, then ask them to repeat it with the technical term.
If a component term is placed under the wrong system (e.g. 'enzyme' under circulatory), re-show it as a callout on its owning system and ask which system digests food.
Confirm correct use by asking the learner to restate the function sentence in their own words while keeping the exact term.
activities.rationale: Pairing every term with a canonical image and a one-line function anchors the word to both a picture and a meaning rather than memorising it in isolation; grouping component terms under the system or systems they belong to or link keeps vocabulary organised. Toggling one system at a time (an optional interaction example) makes the term→structure mapping concrete without clutter.
sourceClaims: Explicit vocabulary instruction — pairing each technical term with a representation and requiring its use in student explanation — is an effective practice for science academic language.
learnerActions: Reveal one organ system at a time (circulatory, digestive, respiratory, skeletal, or muscular) on a labelled body figure, so only the organs of that system are highlighted while the others are hidden.

Tap or point to any highlighted part to surface its exact name and a single precise one-line function sentence using the target term, e.g. 'the artery is a blood vessel that carries blood AWAY from the heart'.

Read the component terms where they appear as callouts: capillary (with artery and vein) on the circulatory system and enzyme on the digestive system, while nutrient, oxygen and carbon dioxide appear as callouts linking the systems they connect (e.g. oxygen on both the respiratory and circulatory systems), so each word is tied to the system or systems it belongs to.
Say aloud, for two systems, the name of each organ and what it does, using the exact technical term each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Each technical term names a specific structure or substance with a specific function or role. Some component terms belong to one system (arteries, veins and capillaries to the circulatory system; enzyme, in the sense of digestive enzymes, to the digestive system), while others (oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrient) link more than one system.

activities.title: Pin down the confusable pairs
feedback: If the learner reverses the vessels ('veins carry blood away from the heart'), correct it directly and anchor with the mnemonic 'A for Artery, Away from the heart', then have them use both words correctly in several sentences until secure.

If the learner defines artery by oxygen content alone, note that the defining difference is direction relative to the heart (arteries usually carry oxygen-rich blood and are under higher pressure, but the pulmonary artery is an exception because it carries oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs), and return to the direction rule.
If the learner calls the heart a 'system' or the circulatory system an 'organ', restate: the heart is one organ; the circulatory system is the heart and blood vessels working together.
activities.rationale: Targeting confusable pairs explicitly addresses the predictable error points; learners also write sentences using the terms. Defining artery/vein by direction (rather than oxygen content) avoids the common misconception that arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood.
sourceClaims: Explicit vocabulary instruction — pairing each technical term with a representation and requiring its use in student explanation — is an effective practice for science academic language.
learnerActions: Place 'artery' and 'vein' side by side and state the main difference that distinguishes them: an artery carries blood AWAY from the heart; a vein carries blood back TO the heart.
Compare 'organ' and 'organ system' side by side and state that an organ (e.g. the heart) is one part, while an organ system is several organs working together.
Write or say one sentence for each pair that makes the contrast explicit (e.g. 'An artery carries blood away from the heart, but a vein carries blood back to it.').
activities.intendedInsight: Artery and vein differ by the DIRECTION of flow relative to the heart (not simply 'oxygen-rich vs not'); an organ is a single part and an organ system is a team of organs.

activities.title: Match, sort and complete to practise the terms
feedback: On the fill-in sentence 'The ___ carries blood away from the heart', the correct answer is 'artery'; if 'vein' is given, re-anchor with 'A for Artery, Away'.

On a mis-sort of a single-system term (e.g. enzyme under circulatory), ask which system breaks down food; in this topic, enzyme (the digestive enzymes that break down food) belongs with the digestive system.

For oxygen and carbon dioxide (exchanged in the respiratory system but carried by the circulatory system) and nutrient (absorbed via the digestive system and carried by the circulatory system), accept either linked system and discuss the connection rather than marking it wrong.

Note that these matching/sorting items check recognition and placement; they do not by themselves show the learner can produce the terms in their own connected explanation — pair them with the speaking/writing task.
activities.rationale: Active matching and sorting with feedback organises vocabulary and checks confusable pairs; matching each term to its representation and function is a recognition/placement task, useful for practice and assessment but not a substitute for productive use. Cross-system terms are handled by naming links, not forcing a single box.
sourceClaims: Explicit vocabulary instruction — pairing each technical term with a representation and requiring its use in student explanation — is an effective practice for science academic language.
learnerActions: Match each term to the correct organ/system and to its one-line function.

Sort the terms that have a single owning system in this topic under that system — artery, vein and capillary under circulatory; enzyme (here meaning digestive enzymes that break down food) under digestive. For terms that span systems (oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrient), name the systems they link rather than forcing one box.
Complete short sentences that require the exact term, e.g. 'The ___ carries blood away from the heart.'
Choose the correct term in a contrast item on artery vs vein and justify the choice by direction of flow.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can select and place the precise term rather than a loose everyday synonym, and recognises that some terms link more than one system.

activities.title: Explain a running scenario in your own words
feedback: Full command looks like: the respiratory system takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide (breathing gets faster and deeper, so more air moves in and out of the lungs); the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels) pumps blood faster, with the heart doing the pumping, to carry that oxygen to the muscles; arteries carry blood away from the heart while veins carry it back.
If the learner says the respiratory system pumps blood, or the circulatory system breathes, pair each system again with its organs and its job and rehearse both in the running scenario.

If the learner reaches for everyday paraphrases ('the blood system', 'the breathing thing'), do not treat it as an error: supply and model the precise term each time the everyday phrase appears, until it is adopted.

Probe further: 'Name two organs in the circulatory system and what each does'; 'Is the heart an organ or an organ system — what's the difference?'; 'Use artery and vein in one sentence that makes the difference clear.'
activities.rationale: A LANGUAGE objective is about using the words, so productive spoken/written description in a live scenario (plus the artery/vein contrast) shows genuine command rather than recitation. An in-role dialogue is one optional way to prompt productive use and in-context correction; it is not the only way and its effectiveness here is not separately tested.
sourceClaims: Explicit vocabulary instruction — pairing each technical term with a representation and requiring its use in student explanation — is an effective practice for science academic language.
learnerActions: Describe what happens in your body when you run for the bus, using these words as you go: respiratory system, circulatory system, artery, oxygen.
Say what each system is doing and how the two systems work together (breathing rate and heart rate both rise).
State how an artery differs from a vein, using the direction of blood flow relative to the heart.
Optionally, explain a body system to a listener who asks follow-up questions, so misused terms can be corrected in context (e.g. if 'vein' and 'artery' are swapped).
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can USE the vocabulary spontaneously and correctly in connected explanation, not merely recognise it — the real target of a language objective.

constraints: This is mainly vocabulary/naming consolidation: most terms label concepts met across KS2 (Y3 nutrition and skeletal/muscular, Y4 digestive, Y6 circulatory), but some terms (e.g. enzyme, respiratory system, capillary) go beyond the KS2 statutory content and need a brief, simple introduction.

Matching, sorting and fill-in tasks check recognition and placement; they do not demonstrate independent productive use — always follow them with a speaking or writing task in which the learner constructs explanations with the terms.

A labelled 2D figure conveys the term→structure mapping adequately at this age; spatial 3D manipulation is not required for naming the systems. This is a scope note for this naming objective, not a claim that 3D models have no value for anatomy generally.
Define artery and vein by direction of flow relative to the heart, not by oxygen content alone: arteries are usually oxygen-rich but the pulmonary artery is an exception.

Some component terms (oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrient) legitimately relate to more than one system; sorting tasks should assign single-system terms only (artery/vein/capillary → circulatory; enzyme → digestive, in this topic's sense of digestive enzymes that break down food, since enzymes are also found throughout the body) and accept reasonable multi-system placement for the rest.

Use consistent, correct definitions and avoid loose synonyms (e.g. 'tube' for blood vessel) that blur technical meaning; model the precise term when an everyday phrase appears rather than marking it wrong.
Distinguish an organ (a single part, e.g. the heart) from an organ system (several organs working together).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'correct answer' described arteries as carrying blood 'usually oxygen-rich, under high pressure'. This is generally true but the pulmonary artery is an exception; the defining property is direction of flow. Activities define artery/vein by direction to prevent reinforcing the 'arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood' misconception flagged in the source.

One supporting source (vocabulary instruction practice) was marked unverified in the original; its claim is retained only to support the general principle of explicit vocabulary teaching, not any efficacy claim about these specific activities.

The DfE KS2 claim was kept out of Activity 1's sourceClaims because that activity's rationale concerns image+function pairing, not KS2 consolidation; the consolidation context is retained in the summary and constraints.

The sort activity originally listed oxygen and carbon dioxide alongside unambiguous single-system terms; because these gases (and nutrients) span the respiratory/circulatory and digestive/circulatory systems, the activity and feedback were adjusted to accept reasonable multi-system placement rather than a single correct box.

probeDeeper: You used 'circulatory system' — name two organs that belong to it and say what each does.
Is the heart an organ or an organ system? What's the difference?
When you run, why do your breathing AND your heart rate both go up — how do the two systems work together?
Use 'artery' and 'vein' in one sentence that makes the difference between them clear.
assess.correctAnswer: The child uses each term correctly: the respiratory system takes in oxygen (the lungs breathe faster); the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels) pumps blood faster to carry that oxygen to the muscles; arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart (usually oxygen-rich, under high pressure) while veins carry blood back TO the heart. Each term appears in a meaningful, correct sentence.

errorPatterns.pattern: swaps 'artery' and 'vein' ('veins carry blood away from the heart')
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor with 'A for Artery, Away from the heart'; use in several sentences until it is secure
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reverses the direction each vessel carries blood

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses the respiratory and circulatory systems (gives one the other's job)
errorPatterns.nextMove: pair each system with its organs and its job, and rehearse them in the running scenario
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the respiratory system pumps blood, or the circulatory system breathes

errorPatterns.pattern: uses 'organ' and 'organ system' interchangeably
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify an organ (the heart) is one part; an organ system is organs working together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls the heart a 'system', or the circulatory system an 'organ'

errorPatterns.pattern: reaches for everyday paraphrases instead of the technical term ('the blood system', 'the breathing thing')
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not treat as an error; supply and model the precise term each time the everyday phrase appears, until it is adopted
errorPatterns.revealedBy: uses vague everyday phrases rather than the precise vocabulary

responseLevels.gap: Swaps artery and vein, or muddles which system does what; the terms function only as labels.
responseLevels.full: Uses respiratory/circulatory, artery/vein, organ/organ system and oxygen accurately and spontaneously in the running scenario, correctly naming organs and their functions and contrasting arteries with veins.
responseLevels.partial: Uses some system names correctly but confuses artery with vein, or organ with organ system — applying the vocabulary inconsistently across the scenario.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Describe what happens in your body when you run for the bus, using these words as you go: respiratory system, circulatory system, artery, oxygen. Say what each system is doing, and how blood in an artery is different from blood in a vein.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the words as labels swaps artery and vein, or muddles which system does what. Correct USE in a live scenario, plus the artery/vein contrast, shows genuine command rather than recitation.

sources.claim: The technical vocabulary consolidates DfE KS2 content taught across years: skeletal/muscular (Y3), digestive/nutrient (Y4), and the Y6 circulatory statement naming heart, blood vessels and blood.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS1–2)

pedagogy.summary: Year-1 children make the leap from comparing lengths to quantifying them: laying identical units (cubes, paper clips) end to end and counting them, then beginning to read a centimetre ruler. The concept underneath the procedure is that a measurement is a count of equal-sized length-units tiling the object with no gaps or overlaps, always recorded as a number WITH a unit.
bestPractices: Begin with non-standard units (interlocking cubes, paper clips) laid end to end; count and record the result before any ruler is introduced.
Insist the units are identical in size — deliberately contrast a row measured with mixed-size units so children see why equal units matter.
Make iteration self-checking: units abut with no gaps and no overlaps; have children build their own paper ruler by marking off one repeated unit, tying the ruler back to iteration.
Always attach a unit to the number ('8 cubes', '12 cm') and ask 'what are you counting?' so the number stays tied to length, not to how many objects.
Introduce the centimetre ruler as a tool that simply counts the same iterated units, with the start of the object aligned to the beginning of the ruler.
keyRepresentations: Interlocking / unit cubes laid end to end along an object
Paper-clip chains as a non-standard unit
A child-made paper ruler with a single unit marked off repeatedly
Centimetre ruler
A recording strip: '____ cubes' / '____ cm'
commonMisconceptions: Leaves gaps between units or overlaps them, treating measuring as 'placing things along' rather than covering the length.
Uses mixed-size units yet counts them as one total.
Counts the number of discrete objects (cardinality) rather than the length covered — e.g. a row of 6 short matches is called 'longer' than an equal row of 5 longer matches.
Begins counting the ruler at the numeral '1' instead of the zero/start.

learn.summary: Year-1 children move from comparing lengths to quantifying them: laying identical units (cubes, paper clips) end to end, counting them with no gaps or overlaps, and then beginning to read a centimetre ruler. The core concept is that a measurement is a count of equal-sized length-units tiling the object completely, always recorded as a number WITH a unit.

activities.title: Tile the length with identical cubes
feedback: If there is a gap between cubes, run a finger along the uncovered stretch and ask: is that length being counted? Close the gap and re-count.
If two cubes overlap, point out that the same stretch is being counted twice; separate them so they just abut.
When the row is clean and gap-free, confirm the count and always restate it with the unit: 'about 8 cubes long.'

In a digital version the running counter can redden or refuse to total a gappy or overlapping row, and only count a cleanly tiled row — so the no-gaps/no-overlaps rule is felt, not just told. This live recompute is one optional way to make the rule self-checking.
activities.rationale: Year-1 children often slide units without abutting them exactly and are not concerned about accuracy, so self-checking iteration (abutting units, finger-check, or a recompute that only counts a clean row) targets the actual procedural leap of covering the length rather than merely placing units along it.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.

In the Length Unit Relater and Repeater level children iterate a single unit and understand the need for equal-length units; children often are not concerned about accuracy when iterating (sliding a unit without abutting it exactly), so the best activities are self-checking.
learnerActions: Place a pencil or book in front of you and a tub of same-size cubes beside it.
Lay cube after cube along the pencil, end to end, from one end of the pencil.
Nudge the cubes so each one touches the next with no gaps and no overlaps.
Count the cubes and say the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes'.
Run a finger along the pencil to check no uncovered stretch is left between cubes.
activities.intendedInsight: A length-count only means the length when identical units cover the object completely, with no gaps and no overlaps.

activities.title: Why the units must all be the same size
feedback: If the child counts mixed sizes as one total, pause on the '3 large and 4 small' challenge: are these 7 of the same thing? Establish that the units must all match before the count means anything.
After re-measuring with one size, confirm the total and connect it back to the clean, equal-unit row.
Ask 'would bigger units give you more or fewer?' to check they expect a larger unit to give a smaller count.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting equal versus mixed units exposes the equal-unit rule directly; this addresses the documented misconception of counting mixed-size units as a single total.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.

In the Length Unit Relater and Repeater level children iterate a single unit and understand the need for equal-length units; children often are not concerned about accuracy when iterating (sliding a unit without abutting it exactly), so the best activities are self-checking.
learnerActions: Measure the book again, but this time use a bin that has a few oversized blocks mixed in with the small cubes.
Report the total and check whether it makes sense.
Try the challenge: '3 large blocks and 4 small blocks laid in a row — is the book 7 blocks long?' Explain your answer.
Re-measure the book using only one size of unit and compare.
activities.intendedInsight: A measurement is only meaningful when every unit is the same size; mixing sizes makes the count nonsense.

activities.title: Length is extent, not how many pieces
feedback: If the child says the 6-match row is longer because it has more pieces, lay the two rows side by side aligned at one end so they can see whether the extents match.
When asked 'what are you counting?', steer from 'the matches' toward 'the length' — the number of pieces alone does not tell you the length unless the pieces are the same size.
If the child lines the rows up and finds they reach the same point, confirm they are the same length and ask how aligning at one end let them tell.
activities.rationale: Children often judge length by cardinality, calling a row of more, smaller items 'longer'. The two rows are set up to be the same total length (an off-stage setup condition the child is not told); direct side-by-side comparison re-anchors length as extent independent of the number of pieces.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.
learnerActions: Look at two rows of matches: one row made of 6 short matches and one row made of 5 longer matches.
Decide which row is longer, or whether they are the same length, and say what you are counting.
Lay the two rows directly side by side, aligned at one end, to check your answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Length is how far something extends, not how many pieces make up the row; more pieces does not mean longer.

activities.title: Build a paper ruler and read a centimetre ruler
feedback: If the child lines the object up with '1', show that the stretch from 0 to '1' is already one unit, so reading the numeral at the far end gives one centimetre too many; realign to 0 and re-read.
If they read off the last numeral the object touches without aligning the start, go back to the paper ruler to re-connect numerals to counted units.
Confirm the recorded result always carries its unit ('15 cm'), not a bare number.
In a digital version a virtual ruler can be required to align at 0 before it reads out, linking the tiled units to the tool. This is one optional way to make the zero-start concrete.
activities.rationale: Building a paper ruler from a single repeated unit ties the ruler back to iteration, and keeps ruler work light at this age. Starting at '1' or reading the last numeral touched are common Year-1 errors the zero-alignment work addresses.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils measure and begin to record lengths and heights using non-standard and then standard units, and begin to use a ruler.

Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.
learnerActions: Take a strip of paper and mark off one chosen unit over and over, end to end, to make your own ruler.
Use your paper ruler to measure a short object, counting the units.
Now take a centimetre ruler and line its start (the 0) up with one end of the object, not the '1' mark.
Read off how many centimetres long the object is and record it as a number with its unit, e.g. '15 cm'.
activities.intendedInsight: A ruler is just a tool that counts the same iterated units; you start from zero because the numerals name the units of space already covered.

activities.title: Spot-the-gap and how-many checks
feedback: For a 'spot the gappy row' choice, name exactly what is wrong with each rejected row — a gap, an overlap, or mixed-size units.
For a how-many answer that is off by one, check where the count started: for a cube row, the first cube is counted as 1; for a ruler picture, the object should start at the 0 mark.
Use these as checks after hands-on practice, not instead of it.
activities.rationale: Recognition items and sliders can check the idea and a spot-the-gap step is discriminating, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the hand-action of building a clean row; keep these as post-practice checks.
learnerActions: Look at several pictured rows and pick which one has been measured correctly (no gaps, no overlaps, equal units).
For a tidy row of cubes, say or set a slider to how many cubes long it is.
For a ruler picture, say how many centimetres long the object is.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise a correctly measured row and read a count, but recognising one does not by itself build the skill of producing a clean row yourself.

constraints: Begin with non-standard units (interlocking cubes, paper clips) laid end to end; count and record before any ruler is introduced.
Always attach a unit to the number ('8 cubes', '12 cm') and ask 'what are you counting?' so the number stays tied to length, not to how many objects.
Keep ruler work light at this age; a child-made paper ruler tying the ruler back to a single repeated unit is the bridge to the centimetre ruler.

Recognition/selection items (spot-the-gap, how-many sliders) check understanding but do not by themselves build the hand-action of iterating and fixing a gappy row; use them as post-practice checks, not the main activity.

A static tap-to-reveal of a cube-row or ruler ('each cube = one length-unit', '0 starts here') can clarify the meaning of the marks as a reference, but a fixed image cannot be re-tiled by the child; pair it with hands-on or interactive iteration.

Physical cubes and an on-screen model offer different experiences; neither is claimed as the only way to learn iteration. Prefer whichever lets the child iterate units and get honest feedback on gaps, overlaps and mixed sizes.
When probing cardinality-vs-length, present or compare rows by aligning the objects side by side at one end; reteaching may require returning to direct length comparison as a prerequisite.

The matches example only demonstrates cardinality-vs-length if the two rows are genuinely the same total length; set the rows to be physically equal but do NOT tell the child they are equal, so the comparison stays open and is discovered by aligning them.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated 3D as 'poor' because length is one-dimensional, and dialogue/conversation as 'poor' for a procedural skill. These catalog fit-rankings are not retained as universal pedagogical laws; the relevant objective limit (recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction) is kept, but claims that a static image or a conversation 'cannot teach' are softened or dropped.
The UK National Curriculum source is marked verified:false in the row; treat the Year-1 ruler claim accordingly.

Self-audit of the matches example: a row of 6 shorter matches and a row of 5 longer matches must be set to the same total length to illustrate cardinality-vs-length. This equality is a setup condition kept off-stage; the child-facing prompt no longer states the rows are equal (that would give away the answer) and instead offers 'same length' as one allowed answer the child can reach by aligning the rows.

Self-audit of ruler logic: aligning the object end with 0 (not '1') is correct — the space before the '1' mark is already one unit — so reading from '1' loses a unit; this correction is retained in the activity.

Corrected the cardinality activity on independent review: the prior feedback 'end to end' (which joins rows lengthwise) was already changed to side-by-side alignment, and the learner-facing setup that revealed the rows as 'the same total length' has now been removed so the probe is neither leading nor self-answering; the equality remains only as an off-stage setup condition in the constraints and rationale.

probeDeeper: You said 8 — 8 what? Point to one of them.
If I measured this same book with these bigger blocks instead, would I get more than 8 or fewer than 8? Why?
Watch — I'll lay them like this (place with a gap). Is that measuring properly? What's wrong with it?
Can you start the ruler somewhere other than the end and still get the right length?
assess.correctAnswer: The child lays identical units end to end from one end of the book with no gaps or overlaps, counts the length-units (not the objects at random), states and records the count WITH a unit ('about 12 cubes' / '15 cm'), and — when they reach for the ruler — aligns its start (0) with the end of the book rather than the '1' mark.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gaps or overlaps: lays units with spaces between them or overlapping, as if measuring is 'putting things along' the object rather than covering its whole length with no holes.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place: have them run a finger along the object to feel the uncovered length between cubes; use abutting, self-checking units and re-count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cubes placed with visible gaps or overlapping; the child still counts them and offers a number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixed-size units counted as equal: combines cubes and larger blocks and reports one total, not noticing the units differ.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pose the '3 large blocks and 4 small blocks — is it 7 blocks long?' challenge; establish that measuring units must all be the same size, then re-measure with one size.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A row of different-sized objects counted as a single number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts discrete objects, not length (cardinality): judges length by how many pieces there are, so a row of more, smaller units is called 'longer' than an equal-length row of fewer, larger units.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the matches-experiment discussion and to direct length comparison so length is re-anchored as extent independent of the number of pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shown two equal-length rows, the child says the one with more items is longer; answers 'what are you counting?' with 'the cubes' not 'the length'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ruler read from '1': treats the numerals as signals for where to start counting, so lines the book up with the '1' mark or reports the last numeral touched.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that 0 is the start and that a numeral names the units of space already covered; keep ruler work light at this age and build a paper ruler by iterating a single unit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Object aligned to the '1' on the ruler, or the final numeral crossed read off as the length; answer off by one.

responseLevels.gap: Lays units with gaps/overlaps or mixes sizes, or gives a bare number with no unit, or judges length by how many pieces there are regardless of the actual extent.
responseLevels.full: Lays identical units with no gaps or overlaps from one end, counts the length-units, records the number with its unit, aligns the ruler's zero, and can say a bigger unit would give a smaller count.
responseLevels.partial: Lays equal units end to end and counts them, but the procedure is fragile: e.g. iterates cubes cleanly yet starts the ruler at '1', or omits the unit unless prompted — succeeds in the practised case but does not transfer to the ruler.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out a book, a tub of same-size cubes with a few larger blocks mixed in, and a centimetre ruler. Say: 'Measure how long this book is and tell me the number.' Do not tell them how. Watch how they lay the units, whether they mix sizes, and where they start the ruler; then ask them to write the result down.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the concept produces a clean, gap-free row of equal units and a number-with-unit, and starts the ruler at zero. A child who lacks it reveals precisely which sub-idea is missing in the way they lay and read — gaps/overlaps, mixed units, counting objects, or starting at 1 — none of which a child with the full concept does. The performance is watched, never asked about.
