pedagogy.summary: Thousandths continue the tenfold nesting one place further: split a hundredth into ten and each piece is a thousandth, so 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000, and the places march ones → tenths → hundredths → thousandths, each a tenth of the one before. The coordinating facts are 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, and 1000 thousandths = 1 whole. In notation, 25 thousandths is 25/1000 = 0.025, where the leading placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place. The recurring obstacle is again whole-number bias — believing a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth 'because 1000 > 100' — and the placeholder error 25/1000 → 0.25. Build thousandths by repeated ÷10 subdivision and by zooming in on the number line between two hundredths.
bestPractices: Derive thousandths by subdividing a hundredth into ten, making 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000 an action the child performs, so the recursive tenfold structure is felt rather than told.
Coordinate two levels of nesting explicitly: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth AND 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, so children compose the ×10 steps instead of applying a single one.
Zoom the number line: locate 0.345 by zooming between 0.34 and 0.35 and splitting into ten, so a thousandth is seen as a tenth of the gap between hundredths.
Drill the placeholder in notation: 25/1000 = 0.025 (two leading places filled), contrasting 25/100 = 0.25 and 25/10 = 2.5, so place governs the number of zeros.
Confront whole-number bias directly — compare 0.05 and 0.005, or one hundredth against one thousandth — so 'more parts, smaller each' overturns 'bigger denominator, bigger part'.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart: ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths
Number line with zoom between two hundredths, split into ten thousandths
Recursive subdivision model (whole → tenth → hundredth → thousandth, ten-for-one each step)
Comparison pair 0.05 vs 0.005 to break whole-number bias
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias: a thousandth taken as bigger than a hundredth or tenth 'because 1000 > 100'.
Placeholder error: writing 25 thousandths as 0.25 (or 0.0025), not 0.025.
Miscoordinating the nesting: saying 10 thousandths = 1 tenth (one ×10 step) instead of 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Treating the digits after the point as a whole number, so 0.025 is read as 'twenty-five' and mis-sized.
Thinking the number line 'runs out' at hundredths, so not subdividing further to place a thousandth.

learn.summary: Thousandths continue the tenfold nesting one place further: split a hundredth into ten and each piece is a thousandth, so 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000, and the places march ones → tenths → hundredths → thousandths, each a tenth of the one before. The coordinating facts are 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, and 1000 thousandths = 1 whole. In notation, 25 thousandths = 25/1000 = 0.025, where the leading placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place. The recurring obstacles are whole-number bias (believing a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth 'because 1000 > 100') and the placeholder error (writing 25/1000 as 0.25). Build thousandths by repeated ÷10 subdivision and by zooming in on the number line between two hundredths.

activities.title: Zoom the number line to place 0.345
feedback: If a learner says the line stops at hundredths, prompt: 'The gap between 0.34 and 0.35 can itself be cut into ten — what is each new piece called?'
If they place 0.345 at the wrong mark, have them count the ten equal steps aloud and check that 0.345 sits on the fifth mark (5 thousandths past 0.34).
If a learner thinks a thousandth is the smallest piece possible, invite them to split it into ten again and name the ten-thousandth, reinforcing that the ÷10 subdivision can always continue.
Confirm success when they can name each step as one thousandth and justify the position of 0.345 by counting thousandths.
activities.rationale: Locating a thousandth by zooming between two hundredths and subdividing into ten makes the recursive tenfold structure an action the child performs, rather than a rule stated to them. If a live number line is used, dragging a zoom control and watching the gap split into ten labelled steps makes the mechanism concrete; a drawn paper number line zoomed and re-divided on a fresh strip serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Start with a number line showing just 0.34 and 0.35, with nothing marked between them, and predict aloud roughly where 0.345 should go.
Zoom into the gap between 0.34 and 0.35 and divide it into ten equal steps; name what each single step is worth (one thousandth, a tenth of the gap between two hundredths).
Count the steps and place 0.345 exactly on the fifth mark (the midpoint of the gap), then state why: it is 5 thousandths past 0.34.
Repeat the zoom-and-split for another thousandth, e.g. place 0.347, so the subdivision becomes a repeatable action, not a one-off.
Extend the action one level further: split a single thousandth into ten equal parts and name each tinier piece a ten-thousandth, illustrating that the ÷10 subdivision can always be repeated again.
activities.intendedInsight: A thousandth is a tenth of the gap between two hundredths; the number line never 'runs out' — you can always subdivide one more time by ten to locate a finer value (a tenth of a thousandth is a ten-thousandth).

activities.title: Split a hundredth and compare sizes to break whole-number bias
feedback: If the learner predicts the thousandth is bigger 'because 1000 beats 100', do not just correct — have them physically lay one thousandth against one hundredth so the size difference is visible, then restate the rule 'more parts means each is smaller'.
For 0.05 vs 0.005, if they pick 0.005, point to the split: 0.005 is 5 thousandths while 0.05 is 50 thousandths (ten times larger); have them count how many thousandths are in each.
Confirm success when the learner states that a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth and can explain why the larger number 1000 does not make the part larger.
activities.rationale: Directly predicting, then confronting the prediction with a visible length comparison, targets whole-number bias in the moment the child commits to a wrong reason. Showing one thousandth beside one hundredth makes 'more parts, smaller each' concrete; a live splitter that recolours or relabels each new piece, or a paper strip cut into ten, both make the subdivision tangible. A paper strip cut into ten has slight thickness, so treat it as a model of the ideal zero-thickness partition, not identical to it.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
learnerActions: Before comparing, predict which is bigger, one hundredth or one thousandth, and say WHY in words.
Take one hundredth and split it into ten equal parts; identify each part as one thousandth.
Lay a single thousandth beside a whole hundredth and describe what you see — the thousandth is tiny next to the hundredth.
Reconcile this with your prediction: even though 1000 is a bigger number than 100, a thousandth is a smaller amount because it comes from cutting into more, smaller parts.
Compare 0.05 and 0.005 directly and state which is bigger and why, when both use the digit 5.
activities.intendedInsight: More, smaller parts means each part is smaller: a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100, overturning 'bigger denominator, bigger part'.

activities.title: Write thousandths and justify the placeholder zero
feedback: If the learner writes 0.25 for 25 thousandths, return to the chart: thousandths is the third place after the point, so 25 must occupy hundredths and thousandths, leaving tenths empty and needing a 0.
If they write 0.0025, check column by column: the 5 should sit in thousandths (third place), not further right.
Confirm success when they both write 0.025 correctly and explain, using the chart, why the zero after the point is needed and why 25/100 and 25/1000 differ.
activities.rationale: Writing thousandths within an explicit place-value chart and contrasting 25/10, 25/100, 25/1000 makes the placeholder error visible and correctable by reasoning about place rather than digit-copying. A running chart that updates as the learner fills each column, or a hand-drawn chart, both make the empty tenths cell explicit.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Using a place-value chart with columns ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths, write 25 thousandths: place the 2 in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.
Fill the empty tenths column with a 0 and write the decimal 0.025, then explain that the zero holds the empty tenths place.
Contrast the set 25/10 = 2.5, 25/100 = 0.25, 25/1000 = 0.025, and describe how the place of the value decides where the digits land and how many leading places are filled.
Write a second example, e.g. 35 thousandths = 35/1000 = 0.035, and say why there is one placeholder zero straight after the decimal point (in the tenths place).
activities.intendedInsight: The place a value occupies, not just the digits, fixes the written decimal; the placeholder zero in 0.025 holds the empty tenths position so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.

activities.title: Compose two tenfold steps: 10 and 100 thousandths
feedback: If the learner says 10 thousandths = 1 tenth, build it in stages: 'How many thousandths in a hundredth? And how many hundredths in a tenth? So how many thousandths in a tenth?'
Have them count on a subdivided line through both levels to see the two steps accumulate to 100.
Confirm success when they answer 100 thousandths per tenth and can name both tenfold steps that compose it.
activities.rationale: Explicitly coordinating two levels of nesting addresses the miscoordination error (saying 10 rather than 100 thousandths per tenth) by having the child compose the steps instead of applying one. Counting through the levels on a subdivided line or stacking the facts on a chart both make the two steps visible.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: State and show that 10 thousandths make 1 hundredth (one ÷10 subdivision).
Then show that 10 hundredths make 1 tenth, so composing the two steps gives 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Continue the chain to 1000 thousandths = 1 whole, naming each tenfold step.
Answer the trap question 'How many thousandths are in one tenth?' and justify 100 (two tenfold steps), explaining why 10 is wrong (it skips a step).
activities.intendedInsight: Getting from thousandths to tenths is two tenfold steps, not one: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth and 100 thousandths = 1 tenth; the nesting composes rather than applying a single ×10.

activities.title: Check and diagnose with targeted questions
feedback: For the comparison item, if the learner selects 0.005 citing 1000 > 100, route back to the split-and-compare activity to re-establish 'more parts, smaller each'.
For 25/1000, if they omit the placeholder zero, return to the place-value chart activity.
Treat the 'why' answers as diagnostic: a learner who answers correctly but cannot explain the two-step nesting or the placeholder still needs the composing and notation activities.
activities.rationale: These checkable items with distractors (the 1000 > 100 comparison, the missing placeholder) surface whole-number bias and placeholder errors diagnostically. Checks assess outcomes rather than build the nesting insight, so they complement, not replace, the subdivision and zoom activities.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
learnerActions: Complete 25/1000 = 0.0__ and justify where the 2 and 5 sit and why the zero is there.
Complete '100 thousandths = __ tenth' and explain the two-step reasoning.
Decide which is bigger, 0.05 or 0.005, and give a reason that does not rely on 'more digits means bigger'.
Place 0.345 between 0.34 and 0.35 by stating how many equal steps are in the gap and which step 0.345 is.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct answers plus a stated reason distinguish genuine grasp of the recursive tenth-of-a-tenth-of-a-tenth structure from a memorised conversion or digit-copying.

constraints: Target age roughly 9–10 (Year 5): recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents.
Build thousandths by subdivision and zooming as actions the child performs, so the recursive tenfold structure is felt, not merely asserted.

A reference chart or diagram with tappable nesting facts and a notation flap can communicate the structure as a reference, but on its own it does not let the child perform the subdivision or the zoom; use it as a reference scaffold alongside, not instead of, hands-on subdivision.

Checkable question formats with distractors assess outcomes and can diagnose errors (whole-number bias, placeholder) but do not by themselves elicit the construction of the nesting; use them to check and route, not as the sole means of teaching the insight.
Always use placeholder cases (25/1000 = 0.025) and comparison cases (0.05 vs 0.005) because faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items.
Address whole-number bias directly by making 'more, smaller parts means each is smaller' visible, rather than by rule assertion.
Treat any physical paper split as a model of the ideal zero-thickness partition: real card has slight thickness and only approximates the mathematical subdivision.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The second listed source (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified:false in the source row; it is cited only for the Year 5 scope/content statement, not for comparative efficacy.

Self-audit of arithmetic and place value: 25/1000 = 0.025 (2 in hundredths, 5 in thousandths, 0 placeholder in tenths); 25/100 = 0.25; 25/10 = 2.5; 35/1000 = 0.035 — all consistent. The ten-for-one chain 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, 1000 thousandths = 1 whole is internally consistent. Dividing 0.34–0.35 into ten equal steps puts 0.345 on the fifth mark, i.e. the midpoint and 5 thousandths past 0.34; 0.05 = 50 thousandths and 0.005 = 5 thousandths — consistent.

The original 'conversation' and '3D' fit entries asserted a character/depth 'adds nothing'; these universal-dismissal claims were dropped rather than propagated, since the source ratings do not establish such necessity/impossibility claims. No source establishes that the 2D interactive is superior to any other medium; the medium preference is a pedagogical proposal only.

The source probeDeeper and responseLevels.full extend the ÷10 action to ten-thousandths; this was restored as an action and feedback in the zoom activity so the 'never runs out' claim is enacted, not merely asserted.

Physical paper cut into ten parts is an approximation with thickness; it represents the ideal zero-thickness partition and should be treated as a model of it, not identical to it (noted in the relevant activity, not only here).

assess.poeTask: Before comparing, ask the child to PREDICT which is bigger, one hundredth or one thousandth, and to say WHY. The reason is diagnostic: predicting the thousandth is bigger 'because 1000 beats 100' reveals the whole-number bias. Then split one hundredth into ten and lay a single thousandth beside a hundredth — the thousandth is plainly tiny. Have the child reconcile this with their prediction.
probeDeeper: You wrote 25 thousandths as 0.025. Where does the 2 sit, and where does the 5 sit — and why the zero right after the point?
Which is bigger, 0.05 or 0.005 — and why, when the digits are both 5?
If I split one thousandth into ten equal parts again, what would each tiny piece be called?
Show me where 0.345 goes between 0.34 and 0.35 — how many equal steps are in that gap, and which one is 0.345?
assess.correctAnswer: 10 thousandths in one hundredth; 100 thousandths in one tenth. 25 thousandths = 25/1000 = 0.025; the placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths (each place a tenth of the one before).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias: 'a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth because 1000 is bigger than 100'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay one thousandth against one hundredth so the thousandth is visibly tiny; re-establish 'more, smaller parts means each is smaller'. Reteach the tenfold place structure from tenths/hundredths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a comparison probe (0.05 vs 0.005, or 'which is bigger, a hundredth or a thousandth') picks the thousandth; treats a larger denominator as a larger part.

errorPatterns.pattern: Placeholder error: writes 25 thousandths as 0.25 (or 0.0025) rather than 0.025.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the place-value chart — thousandths is the third place, so 25 occupies hundredths and thousandths with a zero in tenths; contrast 25/100 = 0.25 with 25/1000 = 0.025. Reteach place-fixes-the-value.
errorPatterns.distractor: 25 thousandths is written 0.25.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 0.25 for 25/1000; does not fill the tenths place with a zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscoordinates the nesting: says there are 10 thousandths in a tenth (one ×10 step) instead of 100 (two steps).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build it in stages — 10 thousandths make a hundredth, and 10 hundredths make a tenth, so 100 thousandths make a tenth; count on the subdivided line. Reteach composing tenfold steps.
errorPatterns.distractor: There are 10 thousandths in one tenth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers '10' for thousandths in a tenth; applies a single tenfold step instead of composing two.

responseLevels.gap: Believes a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth, writes 25/1000 as 0.25, or gives 10 thousandths per tenth. No coordinated nesting.
responseLevels.full: Coordinates the nesting (10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 = 1 tenth, 1000 = 1 whole), writes 25/1000 = 0.025 with the placeholder and justifies it, holds that a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100, places 0.345 by zooming between hundredths, and extends the ÷10 action to ten-thousandths.
responseLevels.partial: Can write 0.025 and recite that 1000 thousandths make a whole, but cannot explain the two-step nesting (100 thousandths = 1 tenth) or why the placeholder is needed — lists facts without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: How many thousandths are in one hundredth, and how many thousandths are in one tenth? Then write 25 thousandths as a fraction and as a decimal, and tell me why it is written that way.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 'How many thousandths in a tenth' checks whether the child composes two ×10 steps (100) or applies just one (10). Writing 25/1000 exposes the placeholder — a digit-copier writes 0.25. The tier-2 'why' separates a memorised conversion from grasp of the recursive tenth-of-a-tenth-of-a-tenth structure and of a thousandth being smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100.

pedagogy.summary: This is deductive reasoning from a rectangle's defining properties: because a rectangle has four right angles and two pairs of equal opposite sides, a child can DEDUCE unknown facts — a missing angle must be 90°, an opposite side equals the given one, and a missing side follows from the perimeter (P = 2(l+w)) or the area (A = l×w). The work is reasoning, not measuring: the diagram is usually not drawn to scale, so lengths and angles must come from the stated properties and given numbers, not from the picture. The dominant obstacle is confusing area and perimeter (and their inverse operations); a second is reading unknown lengths off the not-to-scale drawing; a third is forgetting that opposite sides are equal, so a single given side already fixes its opposite.
bestPractices: Reason from the definition: all four angles are 90° and opposite sides are equal, so a given side determines its opposite — mark the equal sides and squared corners on the diagram before calculating
Keep perimeter and area distinct: perimeter is the distance round (P = 2(l+w), cm), area is the space inside (A = l×w, cm²); read which one the problem gives before choosing the inverse step
Work the inverse deliberately: from a perimeter, halve to get l+w then subtract the known side; from an area, divide by the known side — model each as 'undoing' the formula
Treat the diagram as NOT to scale — use the marked and given information, never a ruler on the picture (a side that looks longer may be the equal one)
Attach correct units throughout (cm for length, cm² for area) and sense-check the answer against the rectangle
keyRepresentations: The rectangle with opposite sides tick-marked equal and all four corners squared (90°), given values labelled and the unknown as a box
P = 2(l+w) and A = l×w overlaid on the shape, with 'undo' arrows for the inverse step
A bar / part-whole model for perimeter showing l+w as half the perimeter
Deliberately not-to-scale rectangles where the marks and numbers override the look
commonMisconceptions: Confuses area and perimeter, or their formulae/units — e.g. divides by a side when the problem gave the perimeter, or halves the area (Machaba: taught together, learned instrumentally)
Short-cuts the perimeter inverse — subtracts the known side straight from the whole perimeter instead of from half of it
Reads unknown lengths or angles off the not-to-scale diagram instead of deducing them from the properties and givens
Forgets that opposite sides are equal, so treats all four sides as unknown even after one is given, or doubts that the fourth angle is 90°

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils (age 9-10) learn to DEDUCE missing lengths and angles of a rectangle from its defining properties (four right angles; two pairs of equal opposite sides) and the given numbers, rather than measuring the diagram. Core work: find a missing side from a given side and the perimeter (P = 2(l+w): halve, then subtract) or from a given side and the area (A = l×w: divide); state that the fourth angle must be 90°; attach correct units (cm, cm²). The deliberately not-to-scale drawing forces reliance on numbers and properties. The dominant obstacle is confusing area with perimeter (and their inverse operations); others are reading lengths/angles off an inaccurate picture, short-cutting the perimeter inverse (subtracting from the whole perimeter instead of from half), and forgetting that one given side already fixes its opposite.

activities.title: Deduce the missing side: perimeter then area, from a not-to-scale rectangle
feedback: If the child types the missing perimeter side correctly, an optional boundary-trace can run a pen round all four sides and click shut at exactly 28, confirming the sides total the perimeter; for the area task, an optional interior-tiling can fill the inside exactly with a 6-by-8 region — these visual confirmations are supportive, not required to validate the reasoning.

If the child writes 28 - 8 = 20, point out that 28 is the whole way round (two lengths plus two widths); undo P = 2(l+w) by halving to 14 first, then subtract the known 8 — a bar or part-whole model showing l+w as half the perimeter makes the halving step visible.

If the child divides 28 by 8 (applying the area method to a perimeter), or halves 48 (applying the perimeter method to an area), ask which quantity the problem gave — distance round or space inside — before choosing the step.
If the child measures or eyeballs the picture, remind them the drawing is not to scale: a side that looks longer may be the equal one; trust the marked and given numbers.
If the child leaves two sides unknown, point back to the tick marks — one given side already fixes its opposite because opposite sides are equal.
If the child says the fourth angle 'looks like' 90°, press that it must be 90° because every rectangle angle is a right angle.
activities.rationale: Deducing missing lengths and angles from rectangle properties is the stated Year 5 objective, and the common error of measuring an inaccurate diagram is addressed by making the figure not-to-scale so facts, not the picture, must be used. Pairing perimeter and area tasks targets the well-documented area/perimeter confusion by forcing a deliberate choice of inverse operation.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory content: pupils use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles

Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae A = l×b and P = 2(l+b) are taught at about the same time and learned instrumentally, without conceptual grounding; they over-generalise the rectangle area formula to other figures

A common error is trying to MEASURE a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'when the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure ... we need to use [the] facts to calculate' — i.e. deduce from given information rather than read lengths/angles off the picture
learnerActions: Work with a rectangle labelled '8 cm' on one side and 'perimeter = 28 cm', drawn deliberately almost square so measuring is useless; one side is a blank box.
Before calculating, mark the equal opposite sides (tick marks) and the four squared (90°) corners so the given 8 cm is seen on its opposite side too.
Reason the perimeter case aloud or in writing: two sides are 8; the four sides total 28; half the perimeter is 14; 14 - 8 = 6, so the missing side is 6 cm.
Switch to an area task: '48 cm², one side 8 cm' — divide 48 ÷ 8 = 6 to find the missing side, and note the inside is filled by a 6-by-8 region.
State the size of the fourth angle (90°) and justify it from the definition, not the picture.
Attach units throughout: cm for sides, cm² for area.
Transfer to a fresh rectangle with different numbers, choosing halve-then-subtract for perimeter and divide for area.
activities.intendedInsight: Missing facts about a rectangle are deduced from its properties and the given numbers, not read off the drawing; 'going round' (perimeter: halve, then subtract) and 'filling in' (area: divide) are different inverse operations that must be chosen by what the problem gives.

activities.title: Short-answer deductions with targeted wrong-answer options
feedback: For an answer of 28 - 8 = 20: the subtraction was from the whole perimeter; halve to 14 first, then subtract 8.

For an answer found by halving the area: halving 48 cm² only gives 24 cm², which is half the area, not a side. Halving is the first step for undoing a perimeter, not an area. To undo A = l×w, divide by the known side: 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm.
If a length is labelled cm² (or an area cm), re-link the unit to the quantity: lengths are cm, areas cm².
If the child picks the misleading pictured proportion, restate that the figure is not to scale.
activities.rationale: Fixed items can score the deductions cleanly and present carefully chosen wrong-answer options (halved-area; subtract-from-whole-perimeter) that reveal the specific misconceptions. This format checks recognition and single-answer production but does not let the child watch the boundary close as the inverse lands, so it complements rather than replaces the constructive task.
sourceClaims: Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae A = l×b and P = 2(l+b) are taught at about the same time and learned instrumentally, without conceptual grounding; they over-generalise the rectangle area formula to other figures
learnerActions: Given one side and the perimeter, construct the other side (e.g. side 8 cm, perimeter 28 cm → fill in 6 cm) and show the halve-then-subtract working.
Given the area and one side, find the other side (e.g. 48 cm², one side 8 cm → 6 cm) and show the division.
Answer a units item: decide whether a given answer should be in cm or cm².
Face a not-to-scale figure whose proportions mislead, and justify the answer from the numbers rather than the look.
When choosing among options, reject the halved-area answer and the subtract-from-whole-perimeter answer (28 - 8 = 20) and explain why each is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The child can reliably select and carry out the correct inverse operation and attach the correct unit, resisting the area/perimeter confusion and the not-to-scale picture.

activities.title: Rectangle properties reference card
feedback: If asked whether a rectangle can have only three right angles, reason that the angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360°, so three right angles force the fourth to be 90° too — it cannot have exactly three.
When comparing a square and a rectangle, note both have four right angles and opposite sides equal; a square additionally has all four sides equal.
activities.rationale: A properties reference supports recall of the definitions that underpin the deduction and seeds NCETM reasoning discussion. It is a static reference: the child does not perform the deduction here, so it is a scaffold beside active practice, not the skill itself.
sourceClaims: Year 5 objective on the properties of rectangles; suggested probes include 'tell me some facts about rectangles', 'is it possible for a rectangle to have only three right angles?', and 'what is the same and what is different about a square and a rectangle?' — reasoning from properties (opposite sides equal, four right angles); the area of a right-angled triangle can be seen as half its enclosing rectangle
learnerActions: Consult a labelled rectangle: each corner reveals '90°', each side reveals 'equals its opposite', and the formulae P = 2(l+w) and A = l×w reveal their undo steps.
Use it alongside practice to recall the defining properties before calculating.

Answer NCETM-style reasoning probes: 'Tell me some facts about rectangles'; 'Is it possible for a rectangle to have only three right angles?'; 'What is the same and what is different about a square and a rectangle?'
activities.intendedInsight: A rectangle's defining properties — two pairs of equal opposite sides and four right angles — are the authority for deduction, and holding them in mind prevents treating sides or the fourth angle as unknown.

constraints: The task is reasoning and calculation with feedback, not measuring: diagrams should be marked as not to scale so lengths and angles come from stated properties and given numbers.
Keep perimeter and area (and their inverse operations and units) explicitly distinct; present both side by side so the child must choose the correct step rather than apply one method by default.
The reference/tap-to-reveal card is a recall scaffold only — it does not require the child to perform a deduction, so it should sit alongside active practice, not replace it.

Fixed-item practice (single-answer construction and multiple-choice) checks recognition and single-answer production and can present diagnostic wrong-answer options, but it does not let the child construct and visually confirm the inverse step; use it to complement constructive practice.
Boundary-trace and interior-tiling animations are optional confirmations of a correct answer, not the mechanism the child must use to reason.

Keep the work planar: length, area and perimeter of a rectangle are two-dimensional; adding a third dimension risks drifting toward surface area and volume, which is a different objective at this stage.
The perimeter inverse is halve-then-subtract (28 → 14 → 14 - 8 = 6); do not subtract the known side from the whole perimeter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The National Curriculum source (Year 5 'use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles') is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its support as unconfirmed.

Legacy claims that open dialogue and 3D are 'poor' fits were framed as near-universal in the source. Retained only as narrowly scoped affordance notes: open dialogue suits reasoning probes but not step-by-step compute-and-deduce practice with feedback, and a third dimension can mislead toward volume for a planar objective. No comparative efficacy is asserted.

Arithmetic self-audit: perimeter 28 cm with one side 8 cm → half is 14, 14 - 8 = 6 cm (correct); area 48 cm² ÷ 8 = 6 cm (correct); the value 28 - 8 = 20 is deliberately wrong and must appear only as a flagged misconception, never as a valid answer.

The NCETM claim also mentions 'the area of a right-angled triangle can be seen as half its enclosing rectangle'; this is beyond the current missing-side objective and was not built into an activity to avoid scope creep.

probeDeeper: This problem gives the PERIMETER — why do you halve it before subtracting? What would 28 - 8 give you, and is that a side?
The picture looks almost square, but the numbers say one side is 8 cm and the perimeter 28 cm — which do you trust, and why?
You found one side is 6 cm — what are the other three sides, and how do you know without measuring?
The second rectangle gives an AREA — why do you divide here, but halve-and-subtract for the first one?
assess.correctAnswer: First rectangle: reasons that opposite sides are equal, so half the perimeter is 14 cm and the missing side = 14 - 8 = 6 cm; states that all angles, including the fourth, are 90°. Second rectangle: missing side = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm. Uses the given numbers and rectangle properties (not the drawing), with correct units (cm and cm²).

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses area and perimeter, or their inverse operations — e.g. divides when the problem gave the perimeter, or halves the area to find a side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two ideas: perimeter is the distance round (halve to l+w, then subtract), area is the space inside (divide by the side); read which is given before choosing the step (Machaba: the two are taught together and confused when learned instrumentally).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies the area method to the perimeter task or vice-versa (divides 28 by 8, or halves 48), or labels a length in cm²

errorPatterns.pattern: Short-cuts the perimeter inverse — subtracts the known side straight from the whole perimeter (28 - 8 = 20) instead of from half of it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model P = 2(l+w) as two lengths plus two widths; undo by halving to get l+w, then subtract the known side — a bar model showing the half-perimeter helps.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 28 - 8 = 20 (or similar) rather than halving to 14 first

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the missing length or angle off the not-to-scale drawing instead of deducing it — measures or eyeballs the picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: State that the diagram is not to scale — the numbers and the rectangle's properties are the authority; use the marks, not the picture (Third Space: when a diagram is not drawn accurately you cannot measure, you must use the facts).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports a length close to what the wrong-proportioned picture shows, or reaches for a ruler; says the fourth angle 'looks like' 90° rather than knowing it must be

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets opposite sides are equal — treats the given side as fixing only itself, so tries to solve with all sides unknown, or is unsure that the fourth angle is 90°
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground the defining properties — a rectangle has two pairs of equal opposite sides and four right angles; mark the equal sides and squared corners before calculating.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Does not use '8 also appears on the opposite side'; leaves two sides unknown, or hesitates over the fourth angle

responseLevels.gap: Applies the wrong operation (divides the perimeter, halves the area, or subtracts from the whole perimeter), or reads the length off the not-to-scale picture; cannot reliably state that the fourth angle is 90°.
responseLevels.full: Deduces each missing side from the rectangle's properties and the given numbers — halving the perimeter then subtracting, and dividing for the area — states that the fourth angle is 90° from the definition, ignores the not-to-scale drawing, attaches correct units, and transfers to a new rectangle problem.
responseLevels.partial: Handles one type — say the area division — but slips on the perimeter inverse (subtracts from 28 rather than 14), or gets the numbers but muddles the units, or needs prompting to use opposite-sides-equal; manages the routine case but not both reliably.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a rectangle drawn deliberately NOT to scale (make it look almost square), with one side labelled 8 cm, the perimeter labelled 28 cm, and one side left blank — plus a second rectangle with area 48 cm² and one side 8 cm. Say: 'Find the missing side of each, and tell me the size of the fourth angle. Show your working.' Say nothing about method; watch how they get the missing sides and whether they measure the picture or reason from the numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The perimeter and area problems sit side by side so the child must pick the right inverse, and the not-to-scale drawing means measuring the picture gives a wrong answer — exposing the child who reads lengths off the diagram. A child reasoning from properties halves the perimeter before subtracting and divides for the area; a child confusing the two divides the perimeter or subtracts from the whole 28; a child trusting the picture reports the wrong measured length. Watching the working — not asking 'what is the difference between area and perimeter?' — shows which.

sources.claim: Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae A = l×b and P = 2(l+b) are taught at about the same time and learned instrumentally, without conceptual grounding; they over-generalise the rectangle area formula to other figures
sources.source: Machaba, F.M. (2016), 'The concepts of area and perimeter: Insights and misconceptions of Grade 10 learners', Pythagoras (peer-reviewed; ERIC full text)

sources.claim: Year 5 objective on the properties of rectangles; suggested probes include 'tell me some facts about rectangles', 'is it possible for a rectangle to have only three right angles?', and 'what is the same and what is different about a square and a rectangle?' — reasoning from properties (opposite sides equal, four right angles); the area of a right-angled triangle can be seen as half its enclosing rectangle

sources.claim: A common error is trying to MEASURE a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'when the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure ... we need to use [the] facts to calculate' — i.e. deduce from given information rather than read lengths/angles off the picture
sources.source: Third Space Learning — GCSE Maths, Angles (Common misconceptions)

pedagogy.summary: Expanding two binomials applies the distributive law twice: every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second, so (x + 3)(x − 2) produces FOUR products (x², −2x, +3x, −6) that collect to x² + x − 6. It is best seen as a generalisation of the grid method for multiplying two-digit numbers — (x + 2)(x + 3) mirrors 12 × 13 as (10 + 2)(10 + 3). The grid / area model makes all four products visible and is preferred over opaque tricks (FOIL, smiley face) that hide the distributive structure. Squaring a bracket means multiplying it by itself, so (a + 3)² = (a + 3)(a + 3), not a² + 9. Directed-number fluency is essential for handling the signs.
bestPractices: Use the grid / area model so each of the four products occupies its own cell — nothing can be forgotten — and connect it to numerical grid multiplication (12 × 13, 24 × 36)
Say explicitly 'the product of two binomials has FOUR terms before collecting', so a missing middle term is noticed
Treat (a + 3)² as (a + 3)(a + 3), never squaring each term separately
Insist on directed-number care for negative terms (+3 × −2 = −6); reject the false 'keep the same sign in the middle' rule
Write all four products first, then collect the like middle terms — collecting is the final step, not optional
Check an expansion by substituting a number, and link back to factorising as the inverse ('if the product is this, what were the two brackets?')
Avoid teaching FOIL as a rule divorced from the distributive law
keyRepresentations: 2×2 multiplication grid / area model (four cells, one per product)
Algebra tiles arranged as a rectangle
The numerical grid analogue, e.g. (10 + 2)(10 + 3) for 12 × 13
Substitution check (put x = 1 into both forms)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies only the first terms and the last terms, MISSING the two middle cross-products, e.g. (x + 3)(x − 2) → x² − 6
Squares each term of a squared bracket: (a + 3)² → a² + 9 (or (a + b)² → a² + b²), forgetting the 2ab middle term
Sign errors with negative terms — applies a false 'same sign in the middle' rule, or drops the minus on a cross-product
Miscollects or mis-multiplies the middle/constant terms (e.g. 3b + 4b handled wrongly, or 3 × 4 written as 7)
Leaves the answer uncollected as x² + 3x − 2x − 6 instead of simplifying to x² + x − 6

learn.summary: Expanding two binomials applies the distributive law twice: every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second, so (x + 3)(x − 2) produces FOUR products (x², −2x, +3x, −6) that collect to x² + x − 6. It generalises the grid method for multiplying two-digit numbers — (x + 2)(x + 3) mirrors 12 × 13 as (10 + 2)(10 + 3). The grid/area model keeps all four products visible, which helps against the two most common errors: dropping the middle cross-products (writing x² − 6) and squaring each term of (a + 3)² to get a² + 9 instead of a² + 6a + 9. Directed-number care is essential for the signs; collecting like terms is a required final step.

activities.title: Build the expansion on a 2×2 grid
feedback: If a learner jumps to 'x² − 6', point to the grid: two cells (−2x and +3x) are still empty. Every term must multiply every term — ask them to fill those two cells and then collect.
If the answer is left as x² + 3x − 2x − 6, say that is correct but not finished: collecting the two middle like-terms (−2x + 3x = +x) is the required final step, giving x² + x − 6.
If a cross-product carries the wrong sign, have them multiply the signed terms out loud: +3 × −2 = −6. There is no 'keep the same sign in the middle' shortcut.
activities.rationale: Expanding a product of two binomials is a generalisation of the grid method; the grid/area model makes all four products visible so the missing-middle error becomes noticeable. Algebra tiles arranged as a rectangle are an equivalent concrete model for the same four products. An optional interactive grid may make this felt — e.g. cells auto-filling with the signed product, a '4 of 4 products' counter, negatives rendered in a distinct colour, and attempting the shortcut 'x² − 6' leaving two middle cells visibly empty — though paper grid work serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Expanding a product of two binomials is a generalisation of the grid method for multiplication; the product of two binomials has four terms before simplifying, and the area/grid model makes all four visible. Example 3 targets the error of mishandling the middle terms ('Ahmed thinks (b+3)(b+4) = b²+3b+4b+7'); Example 4 targets squaring a binomial ('Carol thinks (a+3)² = a²+9'); a false procedure of 'putting the same sign in the middle' and difficulties with negative terms are explicitly flagged, requiring directed-number fluency. Expanding and factorising are inverse processes.
KS3 pupils should simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions to maintain equivalence by expanding products of 2 or more binomials (and collecting like terms).
learnerActions: Draw a 2×2 grid. Write the terms of the first bracket down the left of the rows (e.g. x and +3) and the terms of the second across the top of the columns (e.g. x and −2).
Fill each of the four cells with the product of its row term and its column term, writing the sign explicitly: x², −2x, +3x, −6. Keep a running tally of how many of the four cells you have completed.
Identify the two middle like-terms (−2x and +3x) and collect them (−2x + 3x = +x) to write the simplified answer x² + x − 6.
Connect it to numbers: set out 12 × 13 as (10 + 2)(10 + 3) on the same grid and check the four cells add to 156 (100 + 30 + 20 + 6).
activities.intendedInsight: A product of two binomials has FOUR products before collecting; the grid gives every product its own cell so none is forgotten, and it is the same idea as grid multiplication of two-digit numbers.

activities.title: Square a bracket without squaring each term
feedback: If a learner writes a² + 9, ask them to rewrite the square as (a + 3)(a + 3) and grid it — the two identical middle cells give 6a that the shortcut throws away.
Use the a = 2 check as the deciding evidence: 25 ≠ 13, so the term-by-term square cannot be right.
Generalise gently: (a + b)² has a middle 2ab term for the same reason — two identical cross-cells.
activities.rationale: Squaring each term is a documented misconception (Carol thinks (a+3)² = a²+9); rewriting as a repeated product and substitution make the missing 2ab term concrete. A 'square it' preset in an interactive grid showing two identical middle cells can make this vivid, but the substitution check works on paper equally well.
sourceClaims: Expanding a product of two binomials is a generalisation of the grid method for multiplication; the product of two binomials has four terms before simplifying, and the area/grid model makes all four visible. Example 3 targets the error of mishandling the middle terms ('Ahmed thinks (b+3)(b+4) = b²+3b+4b+7'); Example 4 targets squaring a binomial ('Carol thinks (a+3)² = a²+9'); a false procedure of 'putting the same sign in the middle' and difficulties with negative terms are explicitly flagged, requiring directed-number fluency. Expanding and factorising are inverse processes.
learnerActions: Rewrite (a + 3)² as (a + 3)(a + 3) before doing anything else.
Grid it: the four cells give a², +3a, +3a, +9. Notice the two identical middle cells.
Collect the middle terms (3a + 3a = 6a) to get a² + 6a + 9.
Check numerically with a = 2: (a + 3)² = 5² = 25, while a² + 9 = 13. They disagree, so a² + 9 is wrong; a² + 6a + 9 = 4 + 12 + 9 = 25 matches.
activities.intendedInsight: Squaring a bracket means multiplying it by itself, which still produces a middle term; (a + 3)² = a² + 6a + 9, not a² + 9, and substitution confirms which form is correct.

activities.title: Link expanding to factorising and check by substitution
feedback: If substitution values disagree, the expansion has an error — most often a dropped or mis-signed middle term; return to the grid.
If a learner says (p + 4)(p − 4) 'has no middle term', clarify that it has two middle terms (+4p and −4p) that sum to zero — different from forgetting them.
activities.rationale: The curriculum links expanding to collecting like terms and treats expanding/factorising as inverse processes; a substitution check gives learners an independent way to verify their own work. An optional 'expand ↔ factorise' toggle that re-tiles the rectangle into the two brackets can make the inverse relationship concrete.
sourceClaims: Expanding a product of two binomials is a generalisation of the grid method for multiplication; the product of two binomials has four terms before simplifying, and the area/grid model makes all four visible. Example 3 targets the error of mishandling the middle terms ('Ahmed thinks (b+3)(b+4) = b²+3b+4b+7'); Example 4 targets squaring a binomial ('Carol thinks (a+3)² = a²+9'); a false procedure of 'putting the same sign in the middle' and difficulties with negative terms are explicitly flagged, requiring directed-number fluency. Expanding and factorising are inverse processes.
KS3 pupils should simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions to maintain equivalence by expanding products of 2 or more binomials (and collecting like terms).
learnerActions: After expanding (x + 3)(x − 2) = x² + x − 6, substitute x = 1 into both forms and confirm they match (4 × (−1) = −4; 1 + 1 − 6 = −4).
Run it backwards: given x² + x − 6, ask 'what two brackets multiply to give this?' and recover (x + 3)(x − 2).
Try a difference-of-squares case (p + 4)(p − 4): expand to p² − 16 and notice the middle terms (+4p and −4p) cancel.
activities.intendedInsight: Expanding and factorising are inverse processes; a substitution check catches errors, and some expansions (like (p+4)(p−4)) have middle terms that cancel rather than being absent.

activities.title: Fluency check with signed and squared brackets
feedback: For (x − 2)(x + 5): the constant is −2 × +5 = −10, and the middle is −2x + 5x = +3x. A wrong middle sign may come from the false 'same sign' rule or another sign slip, so have the learner multiply each signed term out loud.
For the (a + 3)² question: choosing a² + 9 is the term-by-term squaring error; the correct form a² + 6a + 9 includes the 2ab middle term.
If a learner can select the right answer but cannot construct one independently, return them to the grid-building activity — recognition alone does not show they can expand unaided.
activities.rationale: A selection-based fluency check using the wrong answers x²−6 and a²+9 checks expansion fluency efficiently, but recognising a correct answer does not by itself demonstrate independent construction of the expansion; use it after the building activities, not instead of them.
learnerActions: Expand and simplify (x − 2)(x + 5), showing the sign of each of the four products and the collected answer (x² + 3x − 10).
Choose the correct expansion of (a + 3)² from several options, one of which is the common wrong answer a² + 9, and explain why that answer is wrong.
Fill in the missing middle terms of a partly-completed grid for a given bracket pair, then collect.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means producing all four correctly-signed products and collecting them, and recognising the signature wrong answers (x² − 6 for a missing middle, a² + 9 for term-by-term squaring).

constraints: Collecting like terms is a required final step, not optional: x² + 3x − 2x − 6 is unfinished and must be simplified to x² + x − 6.
Directed-number fluency is a prerequisite for the signs; reject the false 'keep the same sign in the middle' rule and multiply signed terms explicitly (+3 × −2 = −6).
Always treat (a + 3)² as (a + 3)(a + 3); never square each term separately.

FOIL and similar mnemonics can give correct answers but hide the distributive structure and do not generalise to longer products; if used, tie them explicitly to 'every term × every term' via the grid.

A static filled grid or a selection-based check can present and check expansions but cannot, on its own, surface a learner's own missing-middle or sign error — pair them with tasks where the learner constructs the four products.
A static worked grid is a reference and a selection-based check is a check; neither elicits independent construction, so use them alongside build-it-yourself practice.
The 2×2 area/grid model is planar; representing it in three dimensions would suggest volume and obscure the four-product structure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic, all correct as checked): (x + 3)(x − 2) = x² − 2x + 3x − 6 = x² + x − 6; (a + 3)² = a² + 6a + 9, with a=2 giving 25 vs a²+9=13; (x − 2)(x + 5) = x² + 5x − 2x − 10 = x² + 3x − 10; (p + 4)(p − 4) = p² − 16; 12 × 13 = 156 and (10+2)(10+3)=100+30+20+6=156; substitution x=1 into (x+3)(x−2) gives 4×(−1)=−4 and 1+1−6=−4.

The source Example 3 ('Ahmed thinks (b+3)(b+4) = b²+3b+4b+7') illustrates a mis-collection where the constant 3×4=12 is wrongly written as 7; this is preserved as a misconception type, never reproduced as a correct worked line in any learner question.

The original guidance asserted an interactive builder uniquely makes errors 'FELT'; this has been softened to an optional interaction example, since comparative necessity over paper grid or algebra-tile methods is not established by the sources.
The original keyRepresentation 'algebra tiles arranged as a rectangle' was reinstated as an optional concrete model equivalent to the paper grid.

Original diagnostic/assessment fields (diagnosticPrompt, probeDeeper, errorPatterns, responseLevels) are unchanged in the source row; their content is reflected here as feedback and checks where appropriate.

probeDeeper: Before you simplify (x + 3)(x − 2), how many products should there be? Point to each one on a grid.
Is (a + 3)² the same as a² + 9? Work out (a + 3)² with a = 2 and check against a² + 9.
In (x − 2)(x + 5), what sign does the number term take, and why?
You wrote x² + 3x − 2x − 6. Is that finished — what is the tidy answer?
assess.correctAnswer: (x + 3)(x − 2) = x² + x − 6 (from the four products x², −2x, +3x, −6, collecting −2x + 3x = +x). (a + 3)² = a² + 6a + 9 (because it means (a + 3)(a + 3); the middle terms 3a + 3a give 6a).

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies only the first terms and the last terms, missing the two middle cross-products — (x + 3)(x − 2) → x² − 6
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the grid: a product of two binomials has FOUR cells — show the two empty middle cells (−2x and +3x); every term must multiply every term
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer has no x term; only two of the four products are present

errorPatterns.pattern: Squares each term of a squared bracket: (a + 3)² → a² + 9, forgetting the 2ab middle term
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rewrite (a + 3)² as (a + 3)(a + 3) and grid it — the two identical middle cells give 3a + 3a = 6a; verify with a = 2 (25, not 13)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A squared bracket produces only two terms with no middle term

errorPatterns.pattern: Sign error with a negative term — uses a false 'keep the same sign in the middle' rule or drops the minus on a cross-product
errorPatterns.nextMove: Multiply the signed terms explicitly (+3 × −2 = −6); there is no shortcut rule for the middle sign — shore up directed-number fluency
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A cross-product or the constant carries the wrong sign (e.g. +6 instead of −6, or wrong middle sign)

errorPatterns.pattern: Gets all four products but leaves them uncollected (x² + 3x − 2x − 6) or miscollects the middle like-terms
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the final step, do not reteach expanding: collect the two middle like-terms (−2x + 3x = +x); simplifying is a required last step
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Four terms remain, or the middle coefficient is wrong after collecting

responseLevels.gap: Cannot systematically multiply the brackets; produces two products (x² − 6) or squares term-by-term (a² + 9); sign and collection errors throughout.
responseLevels.full: Expands via all four products (grid or distributive law), handles the signs of negative terms correctly, treats (a + 3)² as (a + 3)(a + 3) giving a² + 6a + 9, collects the middle like-terms, and checks by substitution — transferring to cases like (p + 4)(p − 4) = p² − 16.
responseLevels.partial: Gets all four products for simple positive brackets, but drops or mis-signs a middle term when a negative is present, or writes a² + 9 for a squared bracket — has the multiply-out steps but not the secure 'every term × every term, then collect' structure, and cannot transfer to squaring.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Expand and simplify these two, showing all your working. First: (x + 3)(x − 2). Then: (a + 3)². Say nothing about which method to use — just work them out.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who applies the distributive law fully writes all four products and collects them; a child using a shortcut multiplies only the firsts and lasts (x² − 6) or squares term-by-term (a² + 9), and mishandles the −2x sign. The (a + 3)² item is decisive — a² + 9 is the signature of 'square each term', while a² + 6a + 9 shows the middle term is understood. The negative in (x − 2) exposes sign errors that two positive brackets would hide.

Example 3 targets the error of mishandling the middle terms ('Ahmed thinks (b+3)(b+4) = b²+3b+4b+7'); Example 4 targets squaring a binomial ('Carol thinks (a+3)² = a²+9'); a false procedure of 'putting the same sign in the middle' and difficulties with negative terms are explicitly flagged, requiring directed-number fluency. Expanding and factorising are inverse processes.
