pedagogy.summary: This is a history-of-science topic with a nature-of-science payload: ideas about what's at the centre CHANGED as evidence accumulated. Ancient astronomers (Ptolemy) held a GEOCENTRIC model — Earth fixed at the centre with Sun, Moon and planets circling it — which matched everyday appearances (the Sun 'rises' and 'sets'). Copernicus revived and developed the HELIOCENTRIC model — the Sun at the centre, Earth and planets orbiting it. Galileo, using the newly invented telescope (c.1610), gathered evidence that fitted the Sun-centred picture — above all four moons circling JUPITER (proof that not everything orbits Earth), and the phases of Venus. The two teaching goals are (1) contrast the two models and (2) show that science advances by testing ideas against EVIDENCE — models are held, challenged, and revised, not simply believed.
bestPractices: Frame it as a story of competing MODELS tested against evidence, not a list of names: start from why geocentrism was reasonable (the sky really does appear to go around us), then show what new evidence forced a rethink.

Make Galileo's telescope evidence the pivot and keep it concrete: Jupiter's four moons visibly orbit Jupiter, not Earth — so 'everything orbits Earth' cannot be right; Venus showing a full set of phases fits a Sun-centred system.
Teach the nature-of-science lesson explicitly: scientists changed their minds because of evidence; a long-held, authority-backed idea can be overturned — this models how science actually works.

Attach names to roles, lightly: Ptolemy = the influential geocentric model; Copernicus = proposed Sun-centred; Galileo = telescope evidence supporting it — but keep the ideas, not the trivia, central.

Acknowledge the human/social dimension at an age-appropriate level: the new idea met resistance (it clashed with common sense and authority), which is part of why changing ideas is hard — without turning it into a caricature.
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side model diagrams: Earth-centred (Ptolemy) vs Sun-centred (Copernicus), with the same objects arranged differently
Galileo's-telescope view of Jupiter with four moons lined up beside it, shifting night to night
Phases of Venus as evidence: the pattern Venus shows fits a Sun-centred orbit
A simple timeline: ancient geocentric → Copernicus (1500s) → Galileo's telescope evidence (c.1610)
An 'apparent vs actual' contrast: the sky LOOKS like it circles us, but the evidence shows Earth moves
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the geocentric model was just 'stupid' — not appreciating it matched the everyday appearance of the sky and was carefully worked out, which is why it lasted so long.
Believing Copernicus or Galileo 'proved' heliocentrism single-handedly and instantly, rather than it being a gradual accumulation of evidence and acceptance over time.
Thinking Galileo INVENTED the telescope or the heliocentric idea, rather than improving the telescope and providing evidence for Copernicus's model.
Assuming scientific ideas are fixed facts handed down, missing the core lesson that models change when new evidence appears.
Confusing 'the Sun appears to move across the sky' (an appearance caused by Earth's spin) with the Sun actually orbiting Earth.
Believing everyone accepted the new model at once, ignoring the real resistance from common sense and authority.

learn.summary: History-of-science topic for ages 9-11: ideas about what sits at the centre of the solar system changed as evidence accumulated. Learners contrast the geocentric model (Earth fixed at the centre, Ptolemy) with the heliocentric model (Sun at the centre, proposed by Copernicus), and examine Galileo's telescope evidence from c.1610 — four moons circling Jupiter and the phases of Venus — that supported the Sun-centred picture. Two teaching goals: (1) contrast the two models, and (2) show that science advances by testing ideas against evidence, so models are held, challenged and revised rather than simply believed. Start from why geocentrism was reasonable (the sky really does appear to go around us), keep Galileo's telescope evidence as the pivot, and make the nature-of-science lesson explicit.

activities.title: Two sky-machines, side by side: which model fits the evidence?
feedback: If a learner says 'everything orbits Earth,' point them back to Jupiter's four moons shuffling beside the planet night after night: those are clearly going around Jupiter, not Earth.
If a learner thinks the ancients were foolish, note that before the telescope the Earth-centred model fitted what anyone could see very well — the Sun and stars really do appear to cross the sky.
If a learner treats the change as mere opinion, trace the specific evidence (Jupiter's moons, Venus's phases) that the old model could not account for.
Make clear the phases of Venus and the moons' positions build up over many nights; the model compresses weeks of real observation into a sequence so the pattern can be seen.
activities.rationale: The topic's core is comparing two models and seeing which the evidence fits; a manipulable side-by-side comparison lets learners discover 'ideas changed because of evidence' rather than be told it. A toggle between arrangements, a telescope tool that advances night to night, and a 'which model does this fit?' assignment make the mechanism concrete. These interaction examples are illustrative, not mandatory; the same comparison can be built with paper diagrams and a sequence of dated Jupiter sketches.
sourceClaims: The geocentric (Earth-centred, Ptolemaic) model gave way to the heliocentric (Sun-centred) model proposed by Copernicus, and Galileo's telescopic discovery of Jupiter's four large moons (1610) and the phases of Venus provided evidence supporting a Sun-centred system.
A core nature-of-science aim of this topic is that scientific models change in response to evidence rather than being fixed — a widely emphasised teaching goal in national science curricula.
learnerActions: Study two diagrams of the same sky objects arranged differently: one Earth-centred (Ptolemy, geocentric), one Sun-centred (Copernicus, heliocentric).
Use a 'Galileo's telescope, 1610' view aimed at Jupiter and advance night by night; watch four tiny points of light shuffle back and forth, always strung out beside Jupiter.
State in your own words what those four moons show: they orbit Jupiter, so it cannot be true that everything circles the Earth.
Assign that observation to each model and judge which one accounts for it — the Sun-centred arrangement works, the strict 'everything orbits Earth' claim breaks.
Advance the view to Venus over successive observations and watch it cycle through a full set of phases; decide which model this clue best fits.
Say which model the evidence supports and why a long-held idea gave way.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientists' minds began to change, over many years, because new evidence (Jupiter's moons and Venus's phases) could not be explained by Ptolemy's Earth-centred model, in which everything circles Earth; models are tested against observation, not merely believed.

activities.title: Interview Galileo (and Copernicus): why change your mind?
feedback: If a learner thinks Galileo invented the telescope or the Sun-centred idea, clarify: Copernicus proposed the Sun-centred model; Galileo improved the telescope and gathered evidence supporting it.
If a learner expects instant acceptance, highlight Galileo's account of resistance — the new idea took time and argument to be accepted.
activities.rationale: The topic is anchored in named people, so an in-role dialogue fits the human story and the nature-of-science theme (why change your mind, why did people resist). A character can recount the evidence but cannot let a learner watch it unfold, so this complements rather than replaces the model comparison. A spoken or written in-role exchange (live or scripted) serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: The geocentric (Earth-centred, Ptolemaic) model gave way to the heliocentric (Sun-centred) model proposed by Copernicus, and Galileo's telescopic discovery of Jupiter's four large moons (1610) and the phases of Venus provided evidence supporting a Sun-centred system.
A core nature-of-science aim of this topic is that scientific models change in response to evidence rather than being fixed — a widely emphasised teaching goal in national science curricula.
learnerActions: Talk in role to Galileo on the night of 1610 he first sees Jupiter's moons: ask 'what did you see?', 'how do you know they orbit Jupiter?', and 'why don't people believe you?'
Optionally interview Copernicus on why he moved the Sun to the centre.
Capture, in your own words, the evidence Galileo gives and the resistance he met.
Explain why changing a long-held, authority-backed idea was hard — it clashed with common sense and with accepted authority.
activities.intendedInsight: The shift to a Sun-centred model was a human story: it rested on evidence and met real resistance, showing how science advances through argument over evidence.

activities.title: Then-and-now: labelled models, timeline and the Jupiter observation
feedback: If a learner swaps roles, restate: Copernicus proposed the model; Galileo found the evidence for it.
If a learner treats the switch as instantaneous, point to the timeline gap between Copernicus (1500s) and Galileo's evidence (c.1610).
activities.rationale: A labelled then-vs-now pair with a tap-to-reveal timeline and the Jupiter observation presents the models, names and evidence clearly. It presents evidence but does not let learners test which model each observation supports, so it supports the comparison activity rather than replacing it. Reveal/flap interactions are illustrative; folded paper cards or a drawn timeline work equally.
sourceClaims: The geocentric (Earth-centred, Ptolemaic) model gave way to the heliocentric (Sun-centred) model proposed by Copernicus, and Galileo's telescopic discovery of Jupiter's four large moons (1610) and the phases of Venus provided evidence supporting a Sun-centred system.
learnerActions: Reveal the label on each model: geocentric diagram → 'Earth at centre, Ptolemy'; heliocentric diagram → 'Sun at centre, Copernicus'.
Reveal the Jupiter observation → four orbiting moons and the point 'so not everything orbits Earth'.
Order a simple timeline: ancient geocentric → Copernicus (1500s) → Galileo's telescope evidence (c.1610).
Attach each name to its role: Ptolemy = influential geocentric model; Copernicus = proposed Sun-centred; Galileo = telescope evidence supporting it.
activities.intendedInsight: The labelled pair, timeline and reveals are intended to help learners attach the models, the names and the key evidence to one another and see the chronological development of the ideas.

activities.title: Check and explain: who proposed what, and what the evidence showed
feedback: A 'they were just silly' answer signals the misconception: send the learner to observe that the Sun really does appear to move over a still-feeling Earth, so the old model matched what anyone could see.
If a learner names the models but cannot say why geocentrism was reasonable or what evidence changed minds, revisit the Jupiter and Venus observations.
If a learner says the earlier scientists had 'failed,' reframe: being replaced by better-supported ideas is how science works, not a sign of failure.
activities.rationale: Matching and sequencing check recall of the story efficiently, and the 'why' prompt pushes beyond recall into explanation — a child with the 'they were just silly' view cannot say why geocentrism was reasonable, while a child who understands explains that it fitted the observations and that new telescope evidence drove the change. Recognition and sequencing tasks check recall but do not by themselves elicit the independent explanation, so pair them with the 'why' prompt.
sourceClaims: A core nature-of-science aim of this topic is that scientific models change in response to evidence rather than being fixed — a widely emphasised teaching goal in national science curricula.
learnerActions: Match each person to their model or contribution (Ptolemy, Copernicus, Galileo).
Answer 'what did Jupiter's moons show?' and explain the reasoning, not just pick the fact.
Sequence the timeline of ideas from ancient geocentrism to Galileo's evidence.
Respond to the prompt: 'Were the ancients simply foolish, or did the Earth-centred idea make sense from what they could see? What evidence helped change people's minds? Tell me WHY.'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can both recall the roles/evidence and articulate why geocentrism was reasonable and how evidence drove the change — distinguishing reciting names from grasping evidence-driven model change.

activities.title: Optional: view each model in space with a 3D orrery
feedback: Bring learners back to the evidence: the spatial view is a picture of the model, but what the argument rests on is observations such as Jupiter's moons and Venus's phases.
If a learner thinks the 3D view itself proves which model is correct, clarify that the evidence, not the clearer or prettier diagram, decides.
activities.rationale: A 3D orrery can let learners view each model in space and may add spatial clarity for some. The deciding evidence and the model contrast are already conveyed in 2D, so this is an optional enrichment with a spatial affordance, not a necessity for the argument.
learnerActions: Switch a 3D orrery between the Earth-centred and Sun-centred arrangements and view each from different angles.
Relate the spatial layout back to the deciding evidence you already examined (Jupiter's moons orbiting Jupiter, Venus's phases).
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing each model as a spatial arrangement can reinforce the contrast between the two layouts for some learners.

constraints: Keep names attached to roles lightly: the ideas and evidence are central, not the biographical trivia.
Start from why geocentrism was reasonable (the sky appears to circle a still-feeling Earth) before showing what forced a rethink; do not present the ancients as foolish.

Recognition, matching and sequencing tasks check recall of the story but do not by themselves elicit independent explanation of evidence-driven model change; pair them with a 'why' explanation prompt.
The in-role conversation and reveal/timeline diagrams can present evidence but cannot let a learner test which model each observation supports; use the model-comparison activity for that.
Acknowledge the human/social dimension at an age-appropriate level — the new idea met real resistance from common sense and authority — without turning it into a caricature.

Interaction examples (toggles, telescope night-by-night advance, drag-to-assign, reveal flaps, 3D orrery) are illustrative of the learning mechanism and are optional, not mandatory; paper diagrams, dated Jupiter sketches and spoken role-play can achieve the same goals.
Distinguish the apparent motion of the Sun across the sky (caused by Earth's spin) from the Sun actually orbiting Earth; the appearance is real but does not by itself establish geocentrism.
Make clear that the Venus phase cycle and the moons' night-to-night shifts build up over weeks or months in the real sky; any simulation or sketch sequence compresses that time.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both source claims are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Both sourced claims are historical/pedagogical generalities (standard history of astronomy; nature-of-science curriculum aims) and support teaching principles rather than the efficacy of any specific activity format.

The legacy row asserted '3D adds spatial polish without being necessary' and framed the quiz as testing recall 'rather than building model-based reasoning'; these comparative/necessity claims have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, as catalogue ratings do not establish comparative efficacy.

Minor historical nuance not to overstate: Galileo observed the four large (Galilean) moons of Jupiter; later many more Jovian moons were found. The 'four moons' framing is correct for Galileo's 1610 observation and is retained as such. Galileo improved the telescope but did not invent it.

Venus's phases are strong evidence against the pure Ptolemaic model but are also consistent with some intermediate (e.g. Tychonic) geocentric arrangements; for this age range the simplified 'fits a Sun-centred system' framing is pedagogically appropriate but is a simplification, noted here for reviewer awareness.

probeDeeper: If you stand still and watch the sky all day, does it LOOK like you're moving or the Sun is — and how does that help explain the old belief?
What did Galileo see through his telescope that the Earth-centred model couldn't explain?
Does a scientific idea being replaced mean the earlier scientists had failed?
Who proposed the Sun-centred model, and who later found evidence for it?
assess.correctAnswer: They weren't foolish. The Earth-centred (geocentric) idea, set out by Ptolemy, fitted everyday experience really well: we don't feel the Earth moving, and the Sun, Moon and stars all APPEAR to cross the sky each day as if going around us. Copernicus proposed the Sun-centred (heliocentric) model, but what changed people's minds was new EVIDENCE: when Galileo turned his telescope to the sky he saw things the old model couldn't explain — four moons orbiting Jupiter (so not everything orbits Earth) and the changing phases of Venus. The story shows scientific ideas change when new evidence arrives, not because earlier people were stupid.

errorPatterns.pattern: people back then were just stupid — it was obvious the Earth goes round the Sun
errorPatterns.nextMove: Go outside and note the Sun really does APPEAR to move over a still-feeling Earth — the old model matched exactly what anyone could see without a telescope.
errorPatterns.distractor: The ancient people believed the Earth was at the centre simply because they weren't clever enough to see the truth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child dismisses the ancients rather than seeing geocentrism as a reasonable reading of the evidence

errorPatterns.pattern: Copernicus or Galileo just decided it, or proved it instantly, with no evidence
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the actual evidence — Jupiter's four moons and the phases of Venus — that the Earth-centred model could not account for.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun-centred idea was accepted straight away, just because Copernicus said so.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats the switch as opinion or a single announcement rather than an evidence battle

errorPatterns.pattern: Galileo invented the Sun-centred model, or Copernicus built the first telescope (roles swapped)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Copernicus PROPOSED the Sun-centred model; Galileo later found telescope EVIDENCE supporting it — keep the two roles distinct.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child mixes up who proposed the model and who found the evidence

responseLevels.gap: Says the ancients were foolish and/or muddles who did what; treats the change as mere opinion.
responseLevels.full: Explains geocentrism fitted the apparent motion of the sky, that Copernicus proposed and Galileo's telescope evidence (Jupiter's moons, Venus's phases) drove the shift, and draws the lesson that evidence changes scientific models.
responseLevels.partial: Names the geocentric and heliocentric models and Copernicus/Galileo, but can't explain why geocentrism was reasonable or what evidence changed minds.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: For a very long time, intelligent people were certain the Sun and planets all went around a still Earth. Were they simply being foolish, or did it make sense from what they could see? And what finally convinced people that the Earth goes round the Sun instead? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the 'they were just silly' view cannot say why geocentrism was reasonable. A child who understands the nature of science explains that geocentrism fitted the observations and that the telescope's NEW evidence drove the change. The 'why' tier separates reciting the names Copernicus/Galileo from grasping evidence-driven model change.

sources.claim: The geocentric (Earth-centred, Ptolemaic) model gave way to the heliocentric (Sun-centred) model proposed by Copernicus, and Galileo's telescopic discovery of Jupiter's four large moons (1610) and the phases of Venus provided evidence supporting a Sun-centred system.
sources.source: Standard history of astronomy (Ptolemy / Copernicus / Galileo); NASA & ESA educational history materials

sources.claim: A core nature-of-science aim of this topic is that scientific models change in response to evidence rather than being fixed — a widely emphasised teaching goal in national science curricula.
sources.source: Nature-of-science pedagogy (e.g. NGSS 'Science is a Human Endeavour' / DfE working-scientifically aims)

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, with teacher prompting, the child moves from merely showing a method to EXPLAINING and beginning to JUSTIFY it — using drawings, number sentences, or words to say not just what they did but why the answer is right, including confirming it by an alternative method and spotting an error in a worked example. On the NRICH ladder this spans explaining and convincing. The characteristic gap here is between convincing and justifying: a child at this stage is often confident ('I reckon it's right') with an argument that does not yet hang together as a complete because-chain. Teaching supplies the logical connectives and sentence stems that turn a confident assertion into a reasoned justification, uses alternative-method agreement as a form of justification, and treats error-finding as reasoning practice.
bestPractices: Prompt 'why does that work?' and 'how do you know it's right?' — not just 'what did you do?'
Teach logical connectives and sentence stems ('because', 'so', 'therefore', 'this can't be right because…') to move confident asserting toward complete justification
Use an alternative method that gives the same result as a justification ('the other way also gives 13, so it makes sense')
Use worked examples containing errors and ask children to find and EXPLAIN the mistake
Keep concrete/visual support (drawings, number sentences) as the backbone of the explanation
Distinguish, for yourself and the child, confident-but-incomplete (convincing) from a correct complete chain (justifying), and push gently toward the latter
keyRepresentations: Drawings and number sentences as the medium of explanation
Alternative-method check (two routes to the same answer)
Sentence stems with connectives (because / so / therefore)
True-or-false equation judgements
The explain → convince → justify steps of the NRICH ladder
commonMisconceptions: Confident assertion ('I reckon it's right') offered as justification, with an incomplete or incoherent chain (convincing mistaken for justifying)
Describing the method but stopping short of saying WHY it gives the right answer unless heavily prompted
Spotting that a worked example is wrong but being unable to explain the flaw
Treating 'justify' as 'do the sum again' rather than giving a reason

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, with adult prompting, children move from showing a method to EXPLAINING and beginning to JUSTIFY it — using drawings, number sentences, or words to say not just what they did but WHY the answer is right. The characteristic gap is between convincing (confident but with an incomplete chain, 'I reckon it's right') and justifying (a correct, complete because-chain). Teaching supplies logical connectives and sentence stems, uses alternative-method agreement as a form of justification, and treats finding and explaining errors in worked examples as reasoning practice.

activities.title: The 'convince me' partner
feedback: When the child only asserts confidently: 'You've convinced me you're sure — now tell me WHY, starting with because…'
When they narrate steps but no reason: 'You made ten first — but why does making ten give the right answer?'
When an alternative method agrees: 'The other way also gives 13, so it makes sense — two routes, same answer.'
When they spot a flawed example only by the odd-looking answer: 'What should have happened at this step? Is each side really the same?'
When they produce a complete chain: name it back so they hear their reasoning hold together.
activities.rationale: Explaining and justifying with prompting is naturally a guided dialogue: a responsive partner can ask 'why does that work?', supply because/so stems, accept an alternative method as evidence, and fold error-critique into the same conversation. Reasoning and its communication develop separately and both benefit from explicit support such as sentence stems and modelling.
sourceClaims: Proficient students justify their conclusions and communicate them, and can distinguish correct reasoning from flawed reasoning and explain what the flaw is; all students can decide whether others' arguments make sense.

Convincing (confident, possibly inaccurate, incomplete chain) is a distinct rung below justifying (a correct, complete chain using because/therefore/so); reasoning and its communication develop separately and both need explicit support (sentence stems, modelling).
learnerActions: Pose the child a within-20 calculation (e.g. 8 + 5) and ask them to explain HOW they worked it out.
Then ask 'why does that work?' and 'how do you know it's right?' — not just 'what did you do?'.
When the child stalls or only asserts ('I just know', 'I reckon it's right'), hand over a sentence stem: 'Start with because…' and prompt for the missing link.
Have the child upgrade a confident hunch into a chain, e.g. 'because 5 is 2 and 3, and 8 and 2 make 10, so 10 and 3 more is 13'.
Ask the child to show the same calculation a different way and check whether it also gives the answer ('the other way also gives 13 — what does that tell us?').
Present a worked example containing a slip (e.g. a number bond that doesn't actually make ten) and ask 'Is this right? How can you tell?' — pushing for WHICH step is wrong and WHY.
activities.intendedInsight: A confident answer is not the same as a justification; a reason that works can be built by linking steps with 'because' and 'so', and an alternative method that agrees is supporting evidence that backs up the reason, though it does not replace explaining why.

activities.title: Build an explanation you can test
feedback: If the chain skips a link: 'Something's missing between here and here — what goes in between, starting with because?'
If the second method disagrees: 'Two routes gave different answers — one of them has a slip; let's find it.'
On a correctly identified and explained error: confirm the step AND the reason, not just the flag.
If the child flags an error without a reason: 'You're right it's wrong — now which step, and what should have happened?'
activities.rationale: Arranging steps and connective words (because/so/therefore) and running an alternative-method or error check can make justification a concrete thing the child constructs and tests, rather than a phrase to recite; the explicit support of sentence stems and modelling is what the research emphasises. Draggable step cards, connective tiles, an 'check it another way' tool and a tap-the-wrong-step error mode are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required.
sourceClaims: Convincing (confident, possibly inaccurate, incomplete chain) is a distinct rung below justifying (a correct, complete chain using because/therefore/so); reasoning and its communication develop separately and both need explicit support (sentence stems, modelling).
learnerActions: Give the child step cards (number sentences / method steps) and connective tiles ('because', 'so', 'therefore') to arrange into an argument chain for why a calculation is right.
Have the child read the assembled chain aloud to check it actually hangs together and establishes the claim.
Check the answer a second way (an alternative method) and compare — do the two routes agree?
In an error-spotting task, give a worked example and have the child point to the wrong step AND say why it is wrong.
Keep drawings and number sentences as the backbone of the explanation throughout.
activities.intendedInsight: Justification is something you assemble and test, not just a confident feeling: steps linked with connectives form a chain; a second method checks whether the answer agrees, and checking each step tests whether the chain really holds.

activities.title: Model a complete because-chain (scaffold)
feedback: After modelling: 'Now you say it for a new sum — start each step with because…'
If the child only copies the words: ask them to explain why one of the steps is needed.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal justified example models a complete because-chain and gives a reference point, but it is a scaffold: while only viewing, the child does not construct their own argument, so it must lead into independent construction.
learnerActions: Show a justified worked example where each step is paired with its 'because' reason, e.g. reveal one step at a time so the child sees what a full chain looks like.
After viewing, ask the child to re-tell the chain in their own words, then produce one for a fresh calculation themselves.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked justification shows the TARGET: every step has a reason, and the reasons connect to establish the answer.

activities.title: Critique items: real reason or just saying it's right? (complement)
feedback: After a choice, ask the child to say WHY the chosen reason is the proper one, so selection leads back to constructing their own explanation.
On the counterexample: 'The answer is right — but does the reasoning always work?'
activities.rationale: Selected-response critique items can probe whether a child recognises flaws and distinguishes reasons from assertions, but a recognition/selected-response format cannot assess a child BUILDING their own justification, so it complements rather than replaces the dialogue and construction activities. No comparative efficacy of this format over others is claimed.
sourceClaims: Proficient students justify their conclusions and communicate them, and can distinguish correct reasoning from flawed reasoning and explain what the flaw is; all students can decide whether others' arguments make sense.
learnerActions: Present short 'find the error' items where the child selects the faulty step in a worked example, then says why it is faulty.
Present 'which is a proper reason vs just saying it's right?' items where the child picks the genuine justification over a confident restatement.
Use an open discussion counterexample (child must explain, not just pick): 'Someone got the right answer with a method that only works because these numbers are small — is their reasoning good?'
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the difference between a reason and a confident assertion, and between good reasoning and a lucky right answer, may help a child see what a proper justification needs; recognising a good reason does not by itself produce one, so these items complement — not replace — the construction tasks.

constraints: Target the gap between convincing and justifying: confident-but-vague is a normal developmental rung, NOT wrong reasoning — hand over connectives and ask for the missing link rather than marking it wrong.
Do not accept 'do the sum again' or 'because it's right' as justification; the target is a reason WHY the method gives the right answer.
Keep concrete/visual support (drawings, number sentences) as the backbone of explanation at this age.
Modelled/tap-to-reveal justified examples are scaffolds: the child sees a chain but does not build one, so always follow with independent construction.

Selected-response critique items assess recognition of flaws and reasons, not the child's own construction of a justification; use them to complement, not replace, dialogue and building tasks. Recognising a good reason does not by itself elicit producing one.
Error-finding should require naming the faulty step AND why it is faulty, anchored on the meaning of equality (is each side really the same?), not just flagging that the answer looks off.
Alternative-method agreement is used here as a form of justification ('two routes, same answer') — frame it as supporting the reason, not as a substitute for explaining why the method works.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that 'explaining arithmetic reasoning is not spatial' (used to dismiss a 3D format) is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; it has been omitted rather than asserted as universal.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 8 + 5 = 13 via make-ten (8 + 2 = 10, then 10 + 3 = 13) is correct and preserved. The flawed-worked-example task deliberately contains an error for the child to find — ensure any wrong step shown is clearly labelled as the item to critique, not presented as a correct model.

The source claims support the general principles (justifying vs convincing; distinguishing correct from flawed reasoning) but do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any specific format (dialogue, step-card builder, critique items, etc.); efficacy wording is kept qualified (proposed/may/intended).

Independent review confirms activity 4's intended insight and rationale are consistent with the limit that recognition does not elicit production; the embedded counterexample is now explicitly an open explain-why probe, not a scored selection.

probeDeeper: 'Why does making ten first give the right answer — start with because…' (pushes assertion into a reason)
'Show it a different way — does that also give 13? What does that tell us?' (alternative method as justification)
'This worked example is wrong — which step, and why?' (explain a flaw, not just flag it)
Counterexample: 'Someone got the right answer using a method that only works because these numbers are small — is their reasoning good?' (reasoning vs a lucky answer)
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who explains the method AND gives a reason it works ('because 8 and 2 make 10, then 3 more is 13'), uses an alternative method as confirmation, and, shown the flawed example, says it is wrong and points to WHY. A complete because-chain and the ability to explain an error are the targets, not the arithmetic.

errorPatterns.pattern: Convincing mistaken for justifying — confident assertion ('I reckon it's right', 'definitely') with an incomplete or incoherent chain of reasoning.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not treat confident-but-vague as wrong reasoning; hand over connectives ('because… so…') and ask for the missing link. This is a normal rung below justifying and firms up with modelling.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child is sure and fluent but the argument skips steps or does not actually establish the claim; confidence outruns the logic.

errorPatterns.pattern: Describes the method but stops short of WHY it works, unless heavily prompted.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'why does making ten work?' and use the alternative-method check ('the other way also gives 13 — what does that tell us?') to surface a reason.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child narrates 'I made ten first' but, asked why that gives the right answer, restates the steps rather than giving a reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Spots that a worked example is wrong but cannot explain the flaw.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the step and ask 'what should have happened here?'; anchor on the meaning of equality (is each side really the same?) and model naming the flaw.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says 'that's wrong' because the answer looks off, but cannot identify the faulty step or say why it is faulty.

responseLevels.gap: Restates the answer or 'because it's right'; no reason; can flag the flawed example only by the wrong answer, if at all.
responseLevels.full: Gives a complete because/so chain for why the method works, uses an alternative method as genuine confirmation, explains precisely why the worked example is wrong, and does so with only light prompting.
responseLevels.partial: Explains the method and, prompted, is confident it is right and may check another way — but the justification is asserted rather than reasoned (convincing), and the error is spotted without a clear why.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Pose a calculation such as 8 + 5. Ask: 'Explain how you'd work it out — and why is your answer right? Can you show it a different way to check?' Then show a worked example with an error (e.g. a bond that doesn't make ten) and ask: 'Is this right? How do you know?' Discuss the reasoning; do not mark a number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who justifies produces a connected because/so chain and can say why the error is an error. A child who only convinces asserts confidently ('I reckon it's right') with gaps, and on the flawed example can say 'it's wrong' (answer mismatch) but not name the faulty step. The presence of a complete reasoned chain, and of an explained flaw, is the discriminator.

sources.claim: Proficient students justify their conclusions and communicate them, and can distinguish correct reasoning from flawed reasoning and explain what the flaw is; all students can decide whether others' arguments make sense.

pedagogy.summary: Recognising and naming 2-D shapes is the entry point to geometry, but the real target is recognition by DEFINING FEATURES (a triangle is a closed figure with three straight sides) rather than by matching a single remembered picture. Young children form each shape category around a visual PROTOTYPE — an equilateral, horizontal-based triangle; a long, brick-like rectangle — and judge new figures by how much they resemble it. So they reliably name prototypes but reject perfectly valid non-prototypical shapes (long-thin, right, obtuse, or point-down triangles; a tilted square they call a 'diamond'). It is taught well by presenting many VARIED examples (different sizes, orientations, proportions, colours) alongside carefully chosen NON-examples, naming them precisely, and asking the child to say WHY.
bestPractices: Present many varied examples of each shape — different sizes, orientations, colours and proportions (fat, thin, tilted) — shown together, so identity is built from features rather than one prototype.
Pair examples with NON-examples ('is it or not? — and how do you know?'), e.g. an unclosed figure or one with a curved side, so the child has to name the defining feature.
Include non-prototypical and rotated cases from the start (a tilted square, a long-thin scalene triangle, a triangle pointing down), because these are exactly the ones children wrongly reject.
Name shapes precisely and model the reasoning ('this is a triangle — three straight sides, all joined up'), while accepting informal language ('pointy', 'fat triangle') as a bridge to correct terms.
Have children sort and pick out ALL of one shape from a mixed set and justify the borderline cases — the sorting surfaces the prototype and orientation errors for the teacher.
keyRepresentations: A set of varied exemplars of one shape (many sizes/orientations/proportions) displayed together
Example / non-example pairs ('is it or not?')
Feature cues: 'closed', 'straight sides', counting the sides and corners
Shape sort / shape hunt (find all the triangles in the room)
commonMisconceptions: Judges a shape only against a visual prototype: accepts the equilateral, horizontal-based triangle but rejects long-thin, right, obtuse, or point-down triangles (non-prototypical TYPES are hardest — about half of children miss isosceles and right triangles).
Treats ORIENTATION as if it defines the shape: a square rotated 45° is called a 'diamond' not a square; a triangle without a horizontal base is rejected.
Names by overall resemblance to an object (a 'roof', a 'mountain') rather than by counting straight sides and corners.
Uses 'diamond' for a rotated square, rhombus or kite — there is no 2-D shape called a diamond.

learn.summary: Help 4–6-year-olds recognise and name common 2-D shapes (circle, triangle, rectangle, square) by their DEFINING FEATURES — a triangle is a closed figure with three straight sides — rather than by matching a single remembered 'prototype' picture. Young children build each category around a prototype (an equilateral, horizontal-based triangle; a long, brick-like rectangle) and wrongly reject valid non-prototypical cases (long-thin, right, obtuse or point-down triangles) and mis-name a tilted square as a 'diamond'. Teach with many VARIED examples (sizes, orientations, proportions, colours) shown together, carefully chosen NON-examples, precise naming, and asking the child to say WHY each figure is or isn't the shape.

activities.title: Catch every triangle (varied-case shape hunt)
feedback: When a correct triangle is chosen, confirm the feature: 'Yes — three straight sides, all joined up, so it's a triangle.'

Optional interaction (not required): a correct tap glows green; the caught triangles then slide together and gently morph between one another — huge, tiny, tipped over — while the label 'triangle' stays, making the shared family visible. If used, keep the label fixed so it reads as 'all the same family', not 'one shape turning into another'.
If a curved-sided or unclosed near-miss is chosen, point out the specific feature: 'This side is curved / these lines don't meet, so it isn't a triangle.'
If a long-thin or point-down triangle is skipped, count its three straight sides together and confirm it counts just like the tidy one.
activities.rationale: Recognition by feature is learned by DECIDING across many varied cases and getting feedback tied to the defining property; including non-prototypical and rotated cases from the start targets exactly the figures children wrongly reject, and near-miss non-examples force attention to straightness and closure.
sourceClaims: Young children identify a prototypical (equilateral, horizontal-based) triangle at very high rates (93-96%) but non-prototypical TRIANGLES are much harder: identifying triangle TYPES was hardest (about 48.5% missed the isosceles and 51.2% the right triangle; only ~30.5% got all three), followed by ORIENTATION (rotated triangles), and children rely on 'imposed attributes' such as a horizontal base being treated as if it defined the shape; the recommended remedy is exposing children to typical AND atypical examples plus non-examples in varied sizes, types and orientations.

Children perceive/discriminate shapes and can learn names early, but naming is superficial; the real goal is analysing shapes by defining properties (a triangle must have three sides and be closed) that are invariant over changes in size, orientation and colour, achieved by exposing children to non-prototypical examples and teaching the properties explicitly rather than labels alone.

NCETM lists as common early errors that children think only regular triangles are triangles and only brick-like rectangles are rectangles (shapes defined by their image, not properties) and that squares are only squares when the bottom is horizontal (defined by orientation); it recommends ensuring children see a range of examples of triangles and rectangles in different orientations, sizes, colours and materials.
learnerActions: Look at a field of many shapes that mixes tidy triangles with long-thin, tilted and point-down triangles, plus near-miss non-examples such as a figure with one curved side and three lines that do not quite close.
Tap/pick out every triangle you can find, including the ones that look unusual.
After choosing, say for one of the unusual ones WHY it is a triangle (e.g. 'three straight sides, all joined up').
Say why a near-miss is NOT a triangle (its side is curved, or it isn't closed).
activities.intendedInsight: Sameness of a shape lives in its features — three straight sides and a closed figure — not in its size, proportions, or which way it points. A long, thin, upside-down triangle belongs to the same family as the tidy one.

activities.title: Is it or not? — and how do you know?
feedback: Accept informal language ('pointy', 'fat triangle') as a bridge, then restate precisely: 'Yes — pointy because it has corners where straight sides meet.'
If a child names by resemblance ('it's a roof/mountain'), shift attention to counting straight sides and checking closure by tracing each side with a finger.
Model the reasoning yourself on one case: 'This is a triangle — three straight sides, all joined up.'
When a borderline case is justified correctly, name the feature the child used so it becomes reusable.
activities.rationale: The explicit decide-and-explain routine (drawing shapes and asking children whether each is or is not the shape, and why, using defining properties and correct names) is a recognised early-geometry activity; sorting and picking all of one shape surfaces prototype and orientation errors for the teacher.
sourceClaims: In the Clements & Sarama learning-trajectories approach the early 2-D level is 'Shape Recognizer — Circles, Squares, and Triangles', and a recommended activity is 'Is it or not?' where a teacher draws shapes and children decide whether each is or is not (e.g.) a circle and EXPLAIN why, using defining properties (straight sides, corners) and correct names.

Children perceive/discriminate shapes and can learn names early, but naming is superficial; the real goal is analysing shapes by defining properties (a triangle must have three sides and be closed) that are invariant over changes in size, orientation and colour, achieved by exposing children to non-prototypical examples and teaching the properties explicitly rather than labels alone.
learnerActions: For each figure the teacher shows or draws, decide: is this a triangle (or circle, rectangle, square) — yes or no?

Say out loud which feature makes you sure: count the straight sides, check it is closed, and point to each corner (for rectangles and squares, also check the corners are square corners, and for a square that all four sides are the same length).
Work through deliberately tricky cases: an unclosed figure, a figure with a curved side, a tilted square, and a triangle with no horizontal base.

Sort a mixed set of cut-out shapes into groups and justify the borderline cases. (The cut-outs are thin cards that stand in for the flat shapes we mean — look at the outline, its sides and corners, not the card's thickness.)
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding and explaining — not just naming the obvious prototype — is what reveals and repairs prototype and orientation thinking. The reason ('three straight sides, closed') matters as much as the answer.

activities.title: Turn the same shape (orientation does not change identity)
feedback: If the child calls the tilted square a 'diamond', rotate it back and forth and ask them to count sides and corners each time: 'Same four equal straight sides, four square corners — still a square, just turned.'
Confirm correct reasoning: 'You said the sides didn't change when it turned — that's exactly right.'
Optional: rotate the SAME physical cut-out rather than swapping pictures, so the child sees the one object simply turning.
Reinforce that a triangle does not need a horizontal base to be a triangle.
activities.rationale: Treating orientation as defining ('imposed attributes' such as a horizontal base, or naming a rotated square a 'diamond') is a documented error; rotating a single invariant object directly addresses it by showing the defining features are unchanged.
sourceClaims: NCETM lists as common early errors that children think only regular triangles are triangles and only brick-like rectangles are rectangles (shapes defined by their image, not properties) and that squares are only squares when the bottom is horizontal (defined by orientation); it recommends ensuring children see a range of examples of triangles and rectangles in different orientations, sizes, colours and materials.

Young children identify a prototypical (equilateral, horizontal-based) triangle at very high rates (93-96%) but non-prototypical TRIANGLES are much harder: identifying triangle TYPES was hardest (about 48.5% missed the isosceles and 51.2% the right triangle; only ~30.5% got all three), followed by ORIENTATION (rotated triangles), and children rely on 'imposed attributes' such as a horizontal base being treated as if it defined the shape; the recommended remedy is exposing children to typical AND atypical examples plus non-examples in varied sizes, types and orientations.
learnerActions: Hold one cut-out square and slowly rotate it: at each turn answer 'Is it still a square now? And now?' (The card is a thin stand-in for the flat square — watch its outline, not its thickness.)
Check that the number of straight sides and corners does not change as the shape turns.
Rotate a triangle until its point is at the bottom and confirm it is still a triangle.
Notice that a square turned 45° is still a square. 'Diamond' is an everyday word, not the mathematical name for this shape, so we call it a square.
activities.intendedInsight: Turning a shape does not change what it is; identity is invariant over orientation because the sides and corners stay the same. 'Diamond' is an everyday word, not the mathematical shape name — a rotated square is still a square.

activities.title: Sort-and-justify check (tricky cases)
feedback: Reward the reason, not just the sort: 'Correct — and you knew because it had three straight sides, closed.'
If a tilted square is excluded as a 'diamond', return to rotating the cut-out, counting sides/corners and checking the four sides are equal and the corners are square corners.
Keep illustrations unambiguous — straightness and closure must be visually clear, as drawn shapes can be evocative rather than exact.
If a curvy near-miss is placed with the triangles because it 'looks pointy', retrace its curved side together.
activities.rationale: An include/exclude sort with tricky wrong options built from prototype and orientation errors can surface the exact misconception; because it works as an assessment-style check, keep the defining features unambiguous in any artwork and follow correct answers with a 'why' (sorting alone shows the choice, not whether the child reasoned from features).
sourceClaims: Young children identify a prototypical (equilateral, horizontal-based) triangle at very high rates (93-96%) but non-prototypical TRIANGLES are much harder: identifying triangle TYPES was hardest (about 48.5% missed the isosceles and 51.2% the right triangle; only ~30.5% got all three), followed by ORIENTATION (rotated triangles), and children rely on 'imposed attributes' such as a horizontal base being treated as if it defined the shape; the recommended remedy is exposing children to typical AND atypical examples plus non-examples in varied sizes, types and orientations.

In the Clements & Sarama learning-trajectories approach the early 2-D level is 'Shape Recognizer — Circles, Squares, and Triangles', and a recommended activity is 'Is it or not?' where a teacher draws shapes and children decide whether each is or is not (e.g.) a circle and EXPLAIN why, using defining properties (straight sides, corners) and correct names.
learnerActions: Drag or place figures into 'triangle' and 'not a triangle' groups, where the 'triangle' group must include long-thin and point-down positives and the 'not' group includes a curved-sided near-miss.
Answer 'Which of these are still squares?' when one option is a tilted (correct) square.
For each tricky choice, give the feature-based reason.
Transfer: find another triangle that looks very different from the first but is still a triangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A child who reasons from features will accept non-prototypical positives AND reject near-miss non-examples for the right reason; the 'how do you know' part distinguishes feature reasoning from prototype or object reasoning.

constraints: The learning target is deciding-and-justifying on new, varied cases; a static display showing one shape in many guises (e.g. a wall-card where tapping a fat/thin/tilted/upside-down triangle reveals 'three straight sides — still a triangle') is a useful reference and scaffold but does not rehearse the act of deciding on fresh figures.
Recognition-only responses (tapping or sorting without a stated reason) do not show whether the child reasons from features; always pair the choice with 'how do you know?'
Include non-prototypical and rotated cases from the start — these are exactly the figures children wrongly reject, so leaving them until 'later' hides the misconception.
Accept informal language ('pointy', 'fat triangle') as a bridge but model and expect precise terms ('three straight sides', 'closed', 'corners').
Keep any drawn or on-screen figures clear enough that straightness and closure are unambiguous; illustrations are evocative, not exact.

Paper/card cut-outs have slight thickness and can be held and turned; they are thin models of the flat (ideal, zero-thickness) shape. Use them as approximations and ask the child about the shape REPRESENTED by the outline (its sides and corners), not about the physical card.
'Diamond' should not be used as a 2-D shape name for a rotated square, rhombus or kite; name the actual shape.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source statistics (e.g. ~48.5% missed isosceles, ~51.2% missed right triangles, 93–96% prototype identification) are carried from the cited row claim and have not been re-checked against the original study.

The original row asserted a conversation format 'cannot rehearse the visual decide-and-justify act' and that a third dimension 'adds load and misleads' — these are catalog fit judgements, not established necessity claims, and have been softened to scope: a spoken decide-and-explain routine is in fact used here (the 'Is it or not?' activity is partly verbal), and 2-D focus is chosen because the target shapes are planar, not because other media teach nothing.
The claim that a static image 'cannot teach' the target has been reframed as a scaffold limitation (it does not rehearse deciding on new cases) rather than an absolute.

The original characterised recognition for this age as purely 'perceptual sorting'; that absolute was not propagated. A sort may check or surface classification but does not itself elicit the child's spoken reasoning, which is why every choice is paired with 'how do you know?'.

No arithmetic, force/motion, or physics-modelling content appears in this topic. The only idealisation point is that paper/card cut-outs have slight thickness and model the flat ideal shape; this is stated in the two handling activities and in constraints, and child-facing prompts ask about the shape represented by the outline, never whether the card can be picked up.

probeDeeper: If I turn this triangle upside down, is it still a triangle? How do you know?
Here is a shape with three sides but one of them is bent — is it a triangle? Why not? (counterexample forcing 'straight')
How many straight sides does a triangle have? Point to each one and check it's joined up.
Find me another triangle that looks really different from this one but is still a triangle. (transfer)
assess.correctAnswer: Picks every triangle regardless of size, proportion or orientation (including the long-thin and point-down ones), leaves out the circle, the tilted square and the curved-sided near-miss, and justifies by the defining feature — 'it has three straight sides and it's closed' — not by how it looks or which way it points.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only the 'proper' equilateral, point-up triangle counts as a triangle; long-thin, right, obtuse or point-down ones are rejected ('that's too thin/pointy the wrong way to be a triangle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show many varied triangles together and count the three straight sides on each; run 'is it or not?' with the child saying which feature makes each one a triangle.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is not a triangle — it is too long and thin.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks only the tidy horizontal-based triangle from the set and leaves the long-thin and point-down triangles behind; research finds about half of children miss isosceles and right triangles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats orientation as defining ('imposed attribute'): a tilted square is a 'diamond', a triangle 'must' sit on a flat/horizontal base
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the SAME cut-out slowly — 'is it still a square now? and now?' — so the child sees the sides and corners do not change when it turns.
errorPatterns.distractor: That one is a diamond, not a square.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the tilted square (calls it a diamond) or the point-down triangle; reasons from which way it points rather than its sides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names by resemblance to a familiar object rather than by features, so a non-triangle that 'looks pointy' is wrongly accepted or a valid triangle that doesn't match the object is rejected
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shift attention from the whole look to counting straight sides and checking the figure is closed; trace each side with a finger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies 'it's a triangle because it looks like a roof/mountain' and then mis-sorts the curved-sided near-miss into the triangle pile.

responseLevels.gap: Names only the prototypical shape; rejects tilted, long-thin or point-down triangles, or calls a tilted square a diamond; justifies by looks or orientation, and may accept a curved-sided near-miss.
responseLevels.full: Identifies each shape across size, proportion and orientation including non-prototypical cases, rejects near-miss non-examples, and justifies by the defining feature ('three straight sides, closed') — transferring the reasoning to a new, unfamiliar example.
responseLevels.partial: Names varied shapes correctly in familiar orientations and can count sides, but still slips on a strongly non-prototypical or rotated case, OR picks correctly yet cannot say why (gives the label without the defining feature).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out a mixed set of cut-out shapes including a tidy triangle, a long thin triangle, a triangle turned so its point is at the bottom, a tilted square, a circle, and a near-miss with one curved side. Say: 'Show me all the triangles.' Then point to the point-down triangle and to the curved-sided near-miss in turn and ask: 'How do you know this one is / isn't a triangle?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who recognises by defining features picks the long-thin and point-down triangles AND rejects the curved-sided near-miss for the right reason; a prototype-bound child picks only the tidy triangle, rejects the others, and may accept the curvy one because it is 'pointy'. The 'how do you know' tier is decisive: 'three straight sides, closed' versus 'it looks like a triangle' or 'it points the right way'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2), META. Use place-value understanding AND known number facts together to solve problems: knowing 34 = 30 + 4 and a bond like 3+2=5 lets you reason 34 + 20 = 54, or work backwards ('add 10 to my number and I get 45'). This is the application layer that turns tens-and-ones knowledge into a problem-solving tool.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'use place value and number facts to solve problems'; recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.4/5/6 and 2.NBT.5–9 — add/subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value and properties of operations; mentally find 10 more/less.
• Operational details — Keep it strategy-based, not algorithm-based at this stage: partition (34 = 30 + 4), operate on the parts, recombine. Model missing-number and 'I think of a number' problems that demand working backwards. Emphasise that a known fact (3+2) plus place value (these are TENS) generates a new fact (30+20). Use concrete/pictorial support and expect children to explain WHICH fact and WHICH partition they used.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): use 34 = 30 + 4 to add a multiple of ten (34 + 20) with blocks. Tier B (age 6-7): solve a one-step missing-number problem ('__ + 10 = 45') by reasoning about the tens. Tier C (age 7): solve a two-step or unfamiliar-context problem, choosing a partition and a known fact, and explain the reasoning.
bestPractices: Teach partition–operate–recombine explicitly: split into tens and ones, act on the relevant part, put it back together — making the place-value structure the engine of the strategy.
Connect a known bond to its place-value scaling out loud: 'I know 3 + 2 = 5, and these are tens, so 30 + 20 = 50' — so number facts and place value are used together, not in isolation.
Use missing-number and 'think of a number' problems to force flexible, backwards reasoning rather than one-directional calculation.
Insist on explanation/justification ('which fact did you use? how did you split it?') so the META goal — choosing and applying structure — is assessed, not just the answer.
Support with concrete/pictorial models (blocks, part-whole diagrams, number lines) while the strategy forms, then fade them as reasoning becomes secure.
keyRepresentations: Part-whole (cherry) diagram splitting a number into tens and ones
Base-ten blocks for partition–operate–recombine
Empty/marked number line for jumps of tens and ones
Bar model for missing-number and comparison problems
Fact-family / derived-fact chains (3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54)
commonMisconceptions: Reaching for a counting-in-ones or column method instead of using place-value structure, because the number-fact link was never made.
Applying a known bond but forgetting the unit — saying 30 + 20 = 5 (using 3+2 but dropping the tens).
Unable to work backwards — treating 'think of a number' problems as if they can only be solved forwards.
Partitioning incorrectly under a problem's wording (mis-splitting 34 as 3 + 4 rather than 30 + 4).
Focusing on getting an answer without checking it fits the problem, so an unreasonable result goes unquestioned.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y2), help children use place-value structure together with known number facts to solve problems — e.g. knowing 34 = 30 + 4 and 3 + 2 = 5 to reason that 34 + 20 = 54, and to work backwards on 'I think of a number' problems. The core strategy is partition–operate–recombine: split a number into tens and ones, act on the relevant part, then put it back together, saying aloud which fact and which partition were used. Keep it strategy-based (not column algorithm) at this stage, support with concrete and pictorial models, and insist on explanation so the META goal — choosing and justifying structure — is what develops.

activities.title: Problem playground: partition, operate, recombine
feedback: If the child counts all 54 from one, prompt 'what do you already know that's close?' and show the shortcut (30 + 20) beside the count rather than reteaching the bonds.

If the child refuses to attempt because 'we haven't done this one', think aloud how a known fact generates a new one, name derivation as real mathematics, and invite them to build the next step themselves.
If they say 30 + 20 = 5, point back to the blocks: these are tens, so the answer is 50, not 5 — the unit must be kept.
If they split 34 as 3 + 4, re-anchor on the part-whole diagram: the 3 stands for 30 (three tens).
For the work-backwards mode, if they treat it as only solvable forwards, invite them to test a value and check whether '+10' lands on 45, adjusting up or down.
activities.rationale: Making partition–operate–recombine visible and generative lets the place-value structure act as the engine of the strategy; auto-generating fresh problems supports transfer, and a work-backwards mode forces flexible reasoning. Linked fact-chains and live recombination (e.g. a fact ribbon lighting up, number-line testing) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils use place value and number facts to solve problems, and derive/use addition and subtraction facts to 100.
Partition–operate–recombine and deriving new facts from known bonds are core mastery strategies for using place value in calculation.
learnerActions: Take a problem such as 34 + 20 and split 34 into a 30-part and a 4-part (using base-ten blocks, a part-whole 'cherry' diagram, or drawing).
Add the 20 onto the tens part only, saying aloud 'I know 3 + 2 = 5, and these are tens, so 30 + 20 = 50'.
Recombine the parts: 50 + 4 = 54, and state the full chain 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54.
Try a 'mystery number' / work-backwards problem such as '__ + 10 = 45': cover or guess the start number and test candidate values on a number line until the equation holds.
Repeat with fresh problems (e.g. 34 + 30, 56 + 20) so the strategy — not one answer — is what transfers.
activities.intendedInsight: A number bond you already own (like 3 + 2) can do the heavy lifting on tens, so an unfamiliar calculation can be derived by partitioning and recruiting a known fact rather than counted out from one.

activities.title: Socratic coaching: which fact and which split?
feedback: If the child reverts to counting, nudge toward place value: 'what known fact is hiding in here?'
If they cannot say why splitting 34 into 30 and 4 is legitimate, revisit the part-whole model to show the whole is unchanged.
Affirm reasoning that names both the partition and the fact, even if the final arithmetic needs a small correction.
activities.rationale: Because this is a META skill about choosing and justifying, dialogue that asks the child to state and defend a method can develop the reasoning and respond to the child's chosen approach. This is offered as one effective format alongside hands-on work, not as the only way to teach justification.
sourceClaims: Partition–operate–recombine and deriving new facts from known bonds are core mastery strategies for using place value in calculation.
learnerActions: Face a posed problem (e.g. 34 + 20 or a two-step unfamiliar-context problem) and explain the method you would choose before calculating.

Answer probes: 'What did you already know that you leaned on?', 'How could you use what you already know to solve this?', 'Which fact helped, and why?', 'Is it allowed to split 34 into 30 and 4 — why doesn't that change the answer?'
Compare cases: 'Could you solve 34 + 30 the same way? What changes?' and 'Would this splitting trick help for 34 + 9, or would you do something different there?'
Justify out loud which partition and which known bond you used.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing and justifying a strategy — recognising that partitioning preserves the total and that known facts can be scaled by place value — is the real mathematical work, beyond getting a single answer.

activities.title: Consolidation problems, including missing-number and trap items
feedback: For a dropped-unit choice (30 + 20 = 5), reconnect to blocks: twenty added to thirty is five tens, i.e. 50.
If a missing-number item is only attempted forwards, encourage testing values or using the bar model to work backwards from the whole (45) and the known part (10) to reach 35.
Ask the child to check the answer fits the problem's wording so an unreasonable result is questioned.
activities.rationale: Problem sets consolidate application and let specific misconceptions (dropping the unit, forwards-only thinking) be surfaced by targeted items, with a bar model making the missing-part structure visible. This format presents problems rather than coaching the forming strategy, so it suits practice after the strategy has been modelled.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils use place value and number facts to solve problems, and derive/use addition and subtraction facts to 100.
learnerActions: Solve missing-number and 'think of a number' problems (e.g. '__ + 10 = 45', 'I think of a number, add 10, and get 45 — what was my number?'), using a bar model to show the known part, the unknown part, and the whole.
Decide which partition would help a given problem before solving it.
Spot and reject the trap answer where the unit is dropped (e.g. recognise that 30 + 20 is 50, not 5).
Explain, for each item, which fact and which partition were used.
activities.intendedInsight: Place value and known facts can be applied across varied problem types, and keeping track of the unit (tens vs ones) is essential.

activities.title: Worked-example reference anchor
feedback: If a child treats the anchor as the only problem they can do, hand them a fresh problem and ask them to apply the same three steps — naming that deriving a new result is itself mathematics.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example is a useful reference for the structure of the strategy. Because problem-solving is generative, a single static example should be paired with new problems the child generates or attempts; it anchors rather than replaces practice.
learnerActions: Study one fully worked derived-fact chain (partition–operate–recombine on a single problem), revealing each step: split, operate on the relevant part, recombine.
Retell the steps in your own words before tackling a new problem of your own.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear model of the full chain (e.g. 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54) gives a template children can imitate on new problems.

constraints: Keep the work strategy-based (partition–operate–recombine), not column-algorithm based, at this stage.
Always name the unit: a known bond like 3 + 2 scales to 30 + 20 = 50 only because these are tens; dropping the unit (saying 5) is the error to catch.
Partition correctly: 34 = 30 + 4, not 3 + 4 — the leading digit stands for tens.

Recognition/selection-only items (choosing which partition, spotting a trap answer) assess application but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or spoken justification; pair them with building, writing, or explaining.
Support with concrete/pictorial models (blocks, part-whole diagrams, number lines, bar models) while the strategy forms, then fade them as reasoning becomes secure.
Insist on justification ('which fact? how did you split it?') so the META goal is assessed, not just the final answer.
A single static worked example cannot pose or respond to new problems; use it as an anchor alongside generative practice.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a 3D format 'poor' claiming '3D adds nothing' and said a static image 'cannot pose or respond to new problems'; these catalog-style comparative claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal laws.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 34 + 20 = 54 and 30 + 20 = 50 are correct; the derived chain 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54 is consistent. Fresh examples check out: 34 + 30 = 64 and 56 + 20 = 76. The '30 + 20 = 5' statement appears only as a labelled misconception/distractor, never as a valid answer. The missing-number example '__ + 10 = 45' correctly resolves to 35.
The bar model (an original key representation for missing-number problems) is present in the consolidation/missing-number activity's learner actions, so the preservation claim is now accurate.
Both assessment error patterns are now reflected in feedback (the refusal/myth in the hands-on and anchor activities; defaulting to counting in the hands-on and Socratic activities).
Two source claims (CCSS-M and NCETM) are marked verified:false in the row; retained verbatim only where they directly support a rationale, with no upgrade of their evidence status.

probeDeeper: What did you already know that you leaned on?
Could you solve 34 + 30 the same way? What changes?
Is it allowed to split 34 into 30 and 4? Why doesn't that change the answer?
Would this splitting trick help for 34 + 9 too, or would you do something different there?
assess.correctAnswer: Not scored. A rich response reasons that you can split 34 into 30 and 4, use a fact you know (30 + 20 = 50), then recombine (50 + 4 = 54) — and can say why breaking a number up and leaning on known facts is a legitimate move.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes each calculation must be taught or memorised as its own item: 'I can't do it, we haven't done that one'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Think aloud how a known fact generates a new one; name derivation as real mathematics and invite the child to try building the next one themselves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child refuses to attempt an untaught combination or waits to be shown the method.

errorPatterns.pattern: Defaults to counting everything from one even when a known bond would shortcut the work
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the bonds — prompt 'what do you already know that's close?' so the known fact gets recruited; make the shortcut visible next to the count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child has the bonds but counts all 54 rather than recruiting 30 + 20.

responseLevels.gap: Insists the sum must be counted out or taught first; does not recruit any known fact.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously reasons that unfamiliar calculations can be derived by partitioning and leaning on known facts, and explains why partitioning preserves the total.
responseLevels.partial: Uses a known fact when prompted but treats it as a one-off, not as a general way to reach untaught answers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Here's 34 + 20. Suppose you'd never been shown this exact one before. Is there something you already know that could help you work it out without counting it all? Talk me through how you'd decide.' Surface the thinking for discussion — don't grade it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe reveals the child's belief about where answers come from: whether calculations must be individually taught/memorised, or can be DERIVED from facts already held. That epistemic stance — not the single answer — is what is being surfaced.
