pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Deep-Ocean Exploration Technology (ages 13–14): the engineering that lets humans reach the deep sea — crewed submersibles, ROVs, AUVs and sonar mapping — and why, despite this, most of the seafloor remains unmapped at high resolution.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS3 physics — pressure in fluids increases with depth, and forces/pressure on submerged objects; KS3 working scientifically / applications of science; links to KS3 waves (sonar, sound in water).
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-PS2/MS-ETS1 engineering-design framing (defining problems and evaluating solutions under constraints); MS-ESS2 (mapping Earth's systems); use of technology to extend human observation — the pressure physics is the core science constraint.
• Operational details — Anchor everything in the physics of the environment: pressure rises ~1 atm per 10 m, so the deep sea means crushing pressure, near-freezing cold, total darkness and no radio (water blocks EM, so comms/positioning use sound/sonar). Contrast the tool classes: crewed submersibles (Alvin; Deepsea Challenger to Challenger Deep) put people there at great cost; ROVs (tethered, piloted from a ship) and AUVs (untethered robots) extend reach cheaply; multibeam sonar maps the seafloor from the surface. Explain the coverage paradox — roughly a quarter of the seafloor is now mapped at modern high resolution while under ~0.001% of the deep seafloor has been seen with human/camera eyes — and why the deep sea is in some ways harder to access than the Moon. Close on ocean-worlds astrobiology (Europa/Enceladus) reusing the same tech ideas.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete, ~12): names tools (sub, robot, sonar) and knows the deep sea is dark, cold and high-pressure. Tier B (transitional, ~13): explains why pressure and no-radio drive the design (thick hulls, tethered/sonar comms) and distinguishes mapping from seeing. Tier C (formal, ~13–14): reasons quantitatively about pressure with depth, evaluates the trade-offs of crewed vs ROV vs AUV vs sonar, and explains why so little is mapped/seen despite the technology.
bestPractices: Start from the ENVIRONMENT's physics (pressure, cold, dark, no radio) and let the hardware follow as solutions to those constraints — an engineering-design framing, not a parade of gadgets.
Make the pressure gradient quantitative (~1 atm per 10 m) so students can compute why a 4,000 m dive needs a pressure sphere, connecting to KS3 fluid-pressure physics.
Sharply distinguish 'mapped' (sonar, broad, coarse) from 'seen/observed' (cameras/eyes, tiny footprint) — the single most clarifying distinction for the coverage paradox.
Compare tool classes on explicit trade-offs (cost, depth, endurance, data, risk to humans) rather than ranking one as 'best'.

Use the honest, current 'harder than reaching the Moon in some ways' comparison, and correct the outdated 'we know less about the ocean than the Moon' myth into a precise statement about mapping resolution and direct observation.
Bridge to astrobiology (Europa/Enceladus subsurface oceans) so students see the same engineering ideas reused beyond Earth.
keyRepresentations: Depth–pressure column (~1 atm per 10 m) with each vehicle placed at its operating depth.
Submersible/ROV cutaway: pressure sphere, thrusters, manipulator arm, lights, tether/sonar.
'Mapped vs seen' coverage graphic — a broad coarse sonar swath vs a pinprick camera footprint.
Tool-comparison table: crewed sub / ROV / AUV / sonar across cost, reach, endurance, data.
Timeline of milestone dives (Trieste, Alvin, Deepsea Challenger) against depth.
commonMisconceptions: 'We've explored most of the ocean' — only ~a quarter is mapped at high resolution and far less than 1% (<0.001% of deep seafloor) has been directly observed.
'Mapping the seafloor means we've seen it' — sonar gives shape/depth, not imagery; 'mapped' and 'seen' are very different coverage.
'Radio works underwater like it does in air' — seawater blocks radio/EM, so deep vehicles rely on sound (sonar/acoustic comms) and tethers.
'Submarines can just go to the bottom of any trench' — pressure at full-ocean depth is over 1,000 atm; only specially engineered craft survive it.
'We know less about the ocean than the Moon' (as a blanket fact) — an outdated slogan; the accurate claim is about high-resolution mapping and direct observation, not knowledge in general.

learn.summary: Students (ages 13–14) learn the engineering of deep-ocean exploration as a set of trade-offs forced by a harsh, quantifiable environment: pressure rising ~1 atm per 10 m, near-freezing cold, total darkness, and the fact that seawater strongly absorbs radio waves, so radio works only over very short distances (sound/sonar and tethers are used instead; visible light also fades within tens of metres, which is why craft carry their own lights). They distinguish 'mapped' (broad, coarse sonar) from 'seen/observed' (tiny camera footprint), compare tool classes (crewed submersibles such as Alvin and Deepsea Challenger, ROVs, AUVs, and multibeam sonar) on cost/depth/endurance/data/risk, and reason about why roughly a quarter of the seafloor is mapped at high resolution while only about 0.001% or less of the deep seafloor has been directly observed. A mission-planning simulation is the central activity; a labelled cutaway, an in-role pilot conversation, an ROV-piloting spatial task, and a consolidation quiz support and extend it.

activities.title: Mission control: descend, survive the pressure, and cover the seafloor
feedback: When a thin hull implodes: 'Pressure rose about 1 atm every 10 m — divide your depth in metres by 10 to estimate how many atmospheres the hull faced (for example, about 400 atm at 4,000 m). Full-ocean-depth trenches exceed 1,000 atm, which is why only specially engineered craft (like Deepsea Challenger reaching Challenger Deep) survive them. A thicker pressure sphere survives, but it is heavier and costlier, which is exactly why deep dives are expensive.'

When radio fails: 'Salty seawater strongly absorbs radio waves, so radio reaches only a very short distance underwater. Deep vehicles communicate and navigate using sound (sonar/acoustic links) or a physical tether instead.'

At the coverage moment: 'Sonar maps shape and depth over a wide area but does not give camera-style photos or video; cameras see a tiny patch. That is why the mapped area grows while the directly seen area barely moves.'

On tool choice: 'There is no single best tool — a crewed sub puts people there at high cost and risk, ROVs are tethered and piloted from a ship, AUVs roam untethered, and surface sonar maps broadly but coarsely.'
activities.rationale: Letting students feel the pressure gradient, the comms failure, and the mapped-versus-seen gap through their own decisions is intended to build trade-off intuition that viewing a static list of components alone does not itself elicit, and grounds the engineering-design framing in the environment's physics. The coverage figures are approximate estimates, and the simulation's depth–pressure scale is an idealised model.
sourceClaims: As of recent seafloor-mapping efforts, roughly a quarter (~25%, ~28.7% reported by Seabed 2030) of the global ocean floor has been mapped with modern high-resolution sonar, while under ~0.001% of the deep seafloor has been directly observed by humans or cameras.

Water pressure increases by about one atmosphere (~1 bar) for every 10 metres of depth, so deep-sea vehicles must withstand crushing pressure; radio/EM waves do not travel well through seawater, so acoustic (sonar) methods are used for communication, positioning and mapping.

Crewed submersibles (e.g. Alvin) and remotely/autonomously operated vehicles (ROVs, AUVs) are the primary means of reaching and observing the deep ocean, each trading cost, depth reach, endurance and data return.
learnerActions: Choose a vehicle (crewed submersible, ROV, AUV, or surface multibeam sonar) with the goal of exploring the deep seafloor under a cost/time budget.

Send a craft down while watching a live depth/pressure gauge rise about +1 atm every 10 m and a hull-stress indicator climb; if a thin hull is sent too deep it implodes, so re-spec a thicker pressure sphere and note the resulting rise in weight and cost.
When radio communication drops out underwater, switch the comms panel to sonar/acoustic links or a physical tether.

Switch to a coverage map: spend a dive and watch a crewed sub or ROV light only a pinprick footprint of the seafloor grid, then turn on the ship's multibeam sonar and watch it paint broad but coarse swaths.

Race budget and time and observe the 'mapped' area creep toward about a quarter of the seafloor while the directly 'seen' area stays an almost invisible sliver (roughly 0.001% or less of the deep seafloor).
Compare tools in a picker/table showing cost, depth reach, endurance, and data return.
activities.intendedInsight: Each vehicle earns its place by trading cost, reach, endurance, data and risk; crushing pressure forces heavy pressure spheres and expensive dives; radio fails underwater so sound and tethers are needed; and 'mapped' and 'seen' are very different, which is why so much of the deep sea is mapped coarsely yet almost none is directly observed.

activities.title: Labelled cutaway and depth–pressure column
feedback: 'The pressure sphere resists crushing pressure; thrusters and the manipulator arm let the craft move and work; lights and cameras overcome total darkness; the tether or sonar carries data because radio cannot.'
'At 4,000 m the pressure is roughly 400 atmospheres (~1 atm per 10 m). That is why the crew compartment must be a thick sphere.'
'Mapped means shape and depth over a wide swath; seen means imagery of a tiny patch — very different kinds of coverage.'
activities.rationale: A labelled cutaway and depth column teach the hardware taxonomy and the pressure gradient cleanly; the limitation is that fixed states show the components but not the decision-making where the core trade-off learning lives, so this works best as support to the simulation.
sourceClaims: Water pressure increases by about one atmosphere (~1 bar) for every 10 metres of depth, so deep-sea vehicles must withstand crushing pressure; radio/EM waves do not travel well through seawater, so acoustic (sonar) methods are used for communication, positioning and mapping.

Crewed submersibles (e.g. Alvin) and remotely/autonomously operated vehicles (ROVs, AUVs) are the primary means of reaching and observing the deep ocean, each trading cost, depth reach, endurance and data return.
learnerActions: Examine a submersible/ROV cutaway and identify the pressure sphere, thrusters, manipulator arm, lights, and tether/sonar, noting the function of each.

Read a depth column that marks the operating depths of Alvin, ROVs, AUVs and multibeam sonar against a pressure scale (~1 atm per 10 m), alongside milestone dives such as Trieste and Deepsea Challenger (to Challenger Deep).
Compare a 'mapped' panel (broad, coarse sonar swath) against a 'seen' panel (pinprick camera footprint).
Compute the approximate pressure a craft faces at a stated depth, e.g. ~400 atm at 4,000 m, using ~1 atm per 10 m.
activities.intendedInsight: The hardware components are solutions to specific environmental constraints, each tool class works at a characteristic depth range, and mapping coverage is far broader than direct observation coverage.

activities.title: Interview a deep-sea pilot or ocean engineer
feedback: 'A good answer explains why radio is replaced by sonar and tethers and why the pressure sphere is so heavy, not just that the deep sea is scary.'

'The honest Moon comparison is that the deep sea can be harder to reach and observe in some ways — it is hidden under kilometres of water, while the Moon is airless and visible from afar. Avoid the blanket slogan that we know less about the ocean than the Moon.'
activities.rationale: A persona can convey the lived reality and judgement calls and field the Moon-comparison and ocean-worlds questions as a rich companion once the mechanics are grasped; a conversation can elicit reasoning but should follow, not replace, the quantitative work. Efficacy of this medium is a proposal, not demonstrated by the listed sources.
learnerActions: Interview an in-role Alvin pilot or ROV engineer about what a dive feels like — the pressure, the darkness, the cold, and how communication works.
Ask why crewed dives happen at all given the cost and risk, and how the team decides where to look.
Raise the 'harder than reaching the Moon in some ways' comparison and the idea of reusing this technology on ocean worlds like Europa and Enceladus, and press for reasons.
activities.intendedInsight: Deep-sea exploration involves real human judgement and lived constraints; the Moon comparison is about high-resolution mapping and direct observation, not knowledge in general; and the same engineering ideas are proposed for reuse in astrobiology missions beyond Earth.

activities.title: Pilot an ROV through a dark trench (spatial task)
feedback: 'With only a narrow light cone, you see a sliver of the scene at once — this is why direct camera observation covers so little of the seafloor.'
'The tether both carries data (since radio fails) and limits where you can go.'
activities.rationale: Piloting conveys the spatial difficulty and darkness, but the load-bearing ideas (pressure trade-offs and mapped-versus-seen coverage) are better carried by the instrumented simulation, so this is a strong-but-secondary enrichment rather than the main vehicle.
learnerActions: Fly an ROV through a dark canyon or wreck with only a limited cone of light, managing a tether as you go.
Notice how little of the surroundings you can see at any moment and how the tether constrains movement.
activities.intendedInsight: The deep sea is genuinely three-dimensional and dark; direct observation covers only a tiny footprint at a time, which reinforces why 'seen' coverage stays so small.

activities.title: Consolidate the physics and tool taxonomy
feedback: 'Pressure at 4,000 m ≈ 400 atm (~1 atm per 10 m).'
'Radio fails over useful distances because salty seawater strongly absorbs radio waves; sound (sonar/acoustic links) and tethers are used instead.'
'Sonar data counts as mapped; camera imagery counts as seen.'
activities.rationale: Matching, sequencing and slider tasks consolidate knowledge and check understanding of the physics and taxonomy; because these elicit recognition and recall rather than independent construction, they verify rather than build the trade-off intuition.
sourceClaims: Water pressure increases by about one atmosphere (~1 bar) for every 10 metres of depth, so deep-sea vehicles must withstand crushing pressure; radio/EM waves do not travel well through seawater, so acoustic (sonar) methods are used for communication, positioning and mapping.

Crewed submersibles (e.g. Alvin) and remotely/autonomously operated vehicles (ROVs, AUVs) are the primary means of reaching and observing the deep ocean, each trading cost, depth reach, endurance and data return.
learnerActions: Use a slider to read the pressure at a given depth (e.g. 4,000 m) and check it against ~1 atm per 10 m.
Match each tool (Alvin-type crewed sub, ROV, AUV, multibeam sonar) to its role and typical depth.
Sequence the steps of a dive and categorise example coverage as 'mapped' or 'seen'.
Answer why radio fails underwater and what is used instead.
activities.intendedInsight: Students can recall and apply the pressure relationship, the tool taxonomy, the comms physics, and the mapped-versus-seen distinction.

constraints: Frame hardware as solutions to the environment's physics (pressure, cold, darkness, no radio), not as a parade of gadgets.
Keep the pressure gradient quantitative (~1 atm per 10 m) so students can compute why a 4,000 m dive needs a pressure sphere, linking to KS3 fluid-pressure physics.
Sharply distinguish 'mapped' (broad, coarse sonar) from 'seen/observed' (tiny camera footprint); this is the key distinction for the coverage paradox.
Compare tool classes on explicit trade-offs (cost, depth, endurance, data, risk to humans) rather than crowning one as best.
Correct the outdated 'we know less about the ocean than the Moon' slogan into a precise statement about high-resolution mapping and direct observation, not knowledge in general.
The labelled cutaway and depth column show fixed states and teach the hardware and gradient, but do not by themselves build the trade-off decision-making.
The quiz and matching/slider tasks are recognition-and-recall checks; they verify understanding and do not elicit independent construction of the trade-off reasoning.
The ROV-piloting spatial task enriches the sense of darkness and scale but should supplement, not replace, the quantitative coverage and pressure work.
Treat any idealised depth–pressure scale or on-screen depth column as a model of the represented situation, not the situation itself.
Satellite-derived seafloor maps are coarse gravity-based pictures, not high-resolution sonar; do not present satellites as having already mapped the seafloor in detail.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources carry verified:false in the source row (the pressure/sound fact and the submersible/ROV/AUV technology claim); only the ~25% mapped / <0.001% observed coverage claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

The source states ~25% mapped with a parenthetical '~28.7% reported by Seabed 2030'; activities use the rounded 'about a quarter' consistent with the source. The <0.001% figure refers specifically to the deep seafloor directly observed by humans/cameras.

Pressure estimate ~400 atm at 4,000 m follows from ~1 atm per 10 m; this approximation ignores small variations in water density and does not add the ~1 atm of surface atmosphere, which is acceptable at this age but noted for transparency. Full-ocean-depth trenches exceed ~1,000 atm (e.g. Challenger Deep).

The assessment's 'mapped more of Mars than we've seen of our own deep ocean' style comparison is pedagogically useful but should be scoped to mapping resolution/direct observation; avoid asserting a blanket 'harder than the Moon' as established fact beyond the cited coverage comparison.

Astrobiology extension (Europa/Enceladus) is a topic bridge from the pedagogy notes and is not supported by the listed sources; present it as context, not a sourced claim, and use proposed/intended wording for the technology reuse.

Milestone examples (Trieste; Deepsea Challenger to Challenger Deep) and the >1,000 atm full-ocean-depth point are retained from the original representation/misconception set; the interview activity's sourceClaims are [] because no listed claim supports the conversation-medium rationale.

The pressure and submersible sourceClaims attached to the simulation, cutaway and consolidation activities are borderline: they support the taught/checked content rather than any claim about medium efficacy, and each rationale explicitly describes teaching or consolidating that content.

probeDeeper: The Moon is 380,000 km away yet more of it is mapped in detail than the seabed a few km down. Give two physical reasons the near thing is harder.
Why can't we just radio-control a vehicle on the deep seafloor the way we drive a Mars rover — what do we use instead?
If satellites can photograph the whole land surface, why can't they map the whole seafloor the same way?
A submersible must survive pressure hundreds of times greater than at the surface. What does that force designers to do, and what's the trade-off?
assess.correctAnswer: It's not lack of effort — the deep ocean is genuinely one of the hardest places to explore. The obstacles are physical: crushing pressure (hundreds of times surface pressure, needing extremely strong crewed submersibles like Alvin/Deepsea Challenger or uncrewed ROVs), total darkness (must carry powerful lights and cameras), intense cold, and the fact that radio waves DON'T travel through seawater — so communication and positioning rely on acoustics (sonar), and deep vehicles are often tethered or use acoustic links, not radio. Mapping is slow because high-resolution maps need ships criss-crossing with sonar (satellites only give a coarse picture through water), which is why only ~25% is mapped at high resolution. So a 'strong sub and a radio' fails at the first hurdle: the radio won't work and the pressure/darkness/scale still have to be engineered around — the same reasons the deep sea can be harder to reach than the Moon's surface.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It's just lack of effort — closer means easier' — equates proximity with accessibility.
errorPatterns.nextMove: List the physical barriers that distance doesn't capture — pressure, darkness, cold, comms — and note the Moon is airless/visible from afar while the deep sea is hidden under kilometres of water.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — nobody's bothered; a strong submarine and a radio would let us explore it quickly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says we could easily explore it if we tried; treats the Moon comparison as absurd rather than instructive.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Radio works underwater like it does in air' — unaware seawater blocks radio waves.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain that seawater rapidly absorbs radio waves, so the deep relies on SOUND (sonar, acoustic modems) and physical tethers; sound is also how the floor is mapped.
errorPatterns.distractor: A normal radio would keep us in contact with the sub the whole way down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Proposes radio for deep communication/control; surprised that sonar/acoustics or tethers are needed instead.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'We've basically mapped the seafloor from satellites already' — overrates satellite mapping through water.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish coarse satellite-derived gravity maps from true high-res sonar mapping done ship-by-ship — slow, costly, and far from complete.
errorPatterns.distractor: Satellites have already mapped the whole seafloor in detail from space.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes global high-res seafloor maps already exist; surprised only ~25% is mapped at high resolution.

responseLevels.gap: Blames lack of effort; assumes radio works underwater and/or that the seafloor is already fully mapped.
responseLevels.full: Explains the physical barriers (pressure, darkness, cold, radio not penetrating water), matches each to its technology (submersibles/ROVs, lights/cameras, sonar/acoustic comms), explains why high-res mapping is slow and incomplete, and uses this to justify why the deep sea can be harder to reach than the Moon.
responseLevels.partial: Names some obstacles (pressure, darkness) or some tools (subs, ROVs, sonar) but as loose facts — doesn't match technologies to the specific problems they solve, or explain why mapping is only ~25% complete.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Only about a quarter of the ocean floor has been mapped in high resolution, and reaching the deep sea needs special submersibles and ROVs — even though it's on our own planet and far closer than the Moon. A student says 'that's just because nobody's bothered to go — if we wanted to, a strong submarine and a radio would sort it out quickly'. Is it mainly a lack of effort, and would a tough sub plus a radio really do it? Explain the real obstacles and how the technology gets around them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who thinks proximity means ease blames lack of effort and proposes radio; a student with the concept names the physical barriers (pressure, darkness, cold, radio not penetrating water) and matches technologies to them (sonar/acoustics, ROVs, submersibles), and explains why mapping is slow. The 'would a radio do it' clause specifically catches the widespread belief that radio works underwater.

pedagogy.summary: Compound units measure one quantity PER another — speed (distance per time), density (mass per volume), unit price (cost per gram/item), flow rate. Fluency means (1) computing the rate by dividing the right way round, (2) using the rate to scale up or down and to compare (best-buy, faster-of-two), and (3) converting units correctly, including two-stage conversions like km/h ↔ m/s. The recurring procedural trap is average speed: it is TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, NOT the mean of two speeds. Teaching should build the rate from a double number line or ratio table so 'per one' is visible, and treat the formula triangle with caution because it lets pupils get answers without proportional understanding.
bestPractices: Derive every compound measure as a UNIT RATE first ('how much for exactly one?') using a double number line or ratio table, before any formula.
For best-buy comparisons, insist on a common basis — cost per 100 g for both products — rather than comparing raw price to raw size.
Teach average speed as total distance ÷ total time by working a two-leg journey where the naive mean-of-the-two-speeds answer is demonstrably wrong.
Do km/h↔m/s as a deliberate two-step chain (×1000 m per km, ÷3600 s per hour) with units tracked through each step, not a memorised single factor.
Prefer double number lines / ratio tables over the formula 'magic triangle', which can block proportional reasoning by reducing it to symbol-shuffling (NCETM).
keyRepresentations: Double number line pairing the two quantities (e.g. km against hours, cost against grams)
Ratio table for scaling a rate up and down and for unit conversion
Unit-rate label ('£ per 100 g', 'm per s') as the object of comparison
Distance–time context for average speed (total over total)
commonMisconceptions: Averaging two speeds directly (60 and 40 → '50') instead of using total distance ÷ total time.
Dividing the wrong way round when forming a rate (time ÷ distance for speed, or cost basis inverted).
Comparing unit prices on different bases (price of the big pack vs unit price of the small) and concluding the cheaper total is the better value.
Botching km/h↔m/s by using a single wrong factor (e.g. ×60 or ÷60) instead of the ×1000÷3600 chain.
Treating the formula triangle as the concept — getting a number without knowing whether it should be bigger or smaller.

learn.summary: Compound units measure one quantity PER another: speed (distance per time), density (mass per volume), unit price (cost per gram/item), flow rate. Fluency means (1) computing the rate by dividing the right way round, (2) using the rate to scale up/down and to compare (best-buy, faster-of-two), and (3) converting units correctly, including two-stage chains like km/h↔m/s. The recurring trap is average speed: it is TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, not the mean of two speeds. Build every rate as a visible 'per one' using a double number line or ratio table before any formula, and treat the formula triangle cautiously because it can reduce proportional reasoning to symbol-shuffling. The activities below span an interactive rate workshop, a paper performance task, a short check, and a consolidation reference card, each with a distinct purpose.

activities.title: Rate workshop: best-buy, two-leg journey, and km/h↔m/s converter
feedback: If the pupil writes (60+40)÷2 = 50, show the two leg times (1 h vs 1.5 h) and ask which speed the cyclist spent more time at; more time at 40 pulls the average below 50. Rebuild on a double number line, total over total.

If a division is done the wrong way round (e.g. 40÷60 instead of 60÷40 for the time of a 60 km leg at 40 km/h, or size÷price for a unit price), anchor 'per one': 40 km/h means 40 km in ONE hour, so 60 km takes 60÷40 = 1.5 h. Track units so km ÷ km/h leaves hours. For a unit price, cost goes on top so the result is £ per g (or per item), not g per £.
If the converter uses a single ×60 or ÷60, redo the chain as two labelled steps with units cancelling, and apply the magnitude check (36 km/h ≈ 10 m/s).
If best-buy is decided on total price or pack size, require both products as cost per 100 g (or per item) first; only same-basis figures are comparable.
When the prediction '50' differs from the computed 48, name the gap as the insight: equal distances covered at unequal speeds cannot be averaged by taking the mean of the speeds.
activities.rationale: Compound measures are procedural and comparative, so the learner should perform the rate calculation and get immediate feedback on best-buy, faster-of-two, and unit conversion, with a double number line that recomputes as they scale. Deriving the unit rate first and comparing on a common basis follows guidance to secure the meaning of 'per' and reason multiplicatively via the unit rate. A recomputing double number line, drag-onto-shared-line, a plotted distance-time graph, and on-screen unit cancelling are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
sourceClaims: KS3 Ratio, proportion and rates of change requires pupils to 'use compound units such as speed, unit pricing and density to solve problems' and to 'change freely between related standard units'; KS4 adds 'convert between related compound units (speed, rates of pay, prices, density, pressure) in numerical and algebraic contexts'.

NCETM treats compound measures (speed = distance÷time, density = mass÷volume) as multiplicative comparisons and names as a common misconception that 'compound measures are different from other forms of proportional relationship' when they follow the same multiplicative rules; it stresses securing the meaning of 'per', recommends double number lines and ratio tables, and raises formula triangles as a practice to scrutinise for whether they promote understanding.
Reasoning about rate multiplicatively via unit rate (per one) rather than additively underpins best-buy and speed comparisons.
learnerActions: Best-buy station: compare two shelf tags (e.g. 400 g for £1.80 vs 250 g for £1.20). Put both onto a shared 'cost per 100 g' line and state which is cheaper.
Two-leg journey station: assemble a journey of 60 km at 60 km/h then 60 km at 40 km/h, and — before doing any arithmetic — predict the average speed for the whole journey.

Now compute it: write down the time each leg takes (60÷60 = 1 h and 60÷40 = 1.5 h), then total distance (120 km) and total time (2.5 h), then average speed (120 ÷ 2.5 = 48 km/h). Compare this with your prediction and explain the gap.
Converter station: turn a km/h figure into m/s as two visible steps — ×1000 (km→m), then ÷3600 (per hour→per second) — tracking units so they cancel on screen.
Sanity-check magnitude: 36 km/h should come out as about 10 m/s — a fast cycling/sprinting pace, well above a walk — not 0.6 or 600.
activities.intendedInsight: A rate is 'how much for exactly one', computed by dividing the right way round; average speed is total distance ÷ total time (not the mean of speeds) because more time spent at the slower speed pulls the average down; conversions are a tracked chain, not a single memorised factor; and fair comparisons need a common per-unit basis.

activities.title: Average-speed performance task: work the journey on paper
feedback: Correct answer: 48 km/h. First leg 60÷60 = 1 h; second leg 60÷40 = 1.5 h; total 120 km over 2.5 h gives 120÷2.5 = 48 km/h.
If the answer is 50 from (60+40)÷2, have them find each leg's time first and ask which speed was ridden longer; more time at 40 drags the average below 50.

For the equal-times variant (1 h at 60 then 1 h at 40): total 100 km over 2 h = 50 km/h — here the mean IS correct because equal times are spent at each speed. Use this as a contrasting counterexample, not the general rule.

Full response: produces 48 via leg times → total÷total, forms rates the right way round, converts km/h↔m/s as a correct two-step chain with sensible magnitude, compares best-buys on a common per-unit basis, and transfers to an unfamiliar rate.
Partial response: computes total÷total correctly but slips on a related procedure (inverts a division or botches the conversion) — method not yet secure across compound units.
activities.rationale: Asking the pupil to work the journey on paper discriminates between those computing average speed as total distance ÷ total time and those averaging the speeds, because the equal-distance, unequal-speed setup makes 48 and the naive 50 genuinely different numbers. The equal-times counterexample is mathematically precise: the mean equals the true average speed only when equal times are spent at each speed.
sourceClaims: Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, which equals the arithmetic mean of the two speeds ONLY when equal TIMES are spent at each; for equal DISTANCES the average is the harmonic mean 2uv/(u+v). The page proves the harmonic mean is ≤ the arithmetic mean (difference factorises to (u−v)²/[2(u+v)]), so averaging the two speeds overestimates the true average speed on equal-distance legs — the exact 48-vs-50 trap in this record.
learnerActions: Work out: a cyclist rides 60 km at a steady 60 km/h, then another 60 km at a steady 40 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey, showing every step on paper.
Find each leg's time first (60÷60 = 1 h; 60÷40 = 1.5 h), then total distance (120 km), total time (2.5 h), and average speed (120 ÷ 2.5 = 48 km/h).
Answer probes: which leg took more time, so should the average be nearer 60 or nearer 40 — does 50 fit? Then redo with equal TIMES (1 h at 60, 1 h at 40) and explain why the average is 50 this time.
Convert your 48 km/h into metres per second, talking through each step and the units.

Compare two products (e.g. 400 g for £1.80 vs 250 g for £1.20): put both on a cost-per-100 g basis (45p vs 48p), say which is the better buy, and explain what would go wrong if you just compared their prices.
activities.intendedInsight: Watching the pupil compute (rather than recite a rule) reveals whether they use total÷total or average the speeds; because equal distances are covered at unequal speeds, the correct 48 cannot be reached by the mean method, so the method is visible in the number produced. The equal-TIMES counterexample shows the mean is correct only when equal times are spent at each speed.

activities.title: Short check on rates, best-buy and conversion
feedback: If the mean-of-speeds option is chosen, route back to computing leg times and total÷total.
If the 'bigger pack is automatically cheaper' option is chosen, require both products on a common per-100 g basis before deciding.
For a wrong conversion, prompt the two-step ×1000 then ÷3600 chain and the magnitude check.

Use this check to confirm or challenge mastery; it records which answer was produced but does not by itself show the pupil can construct the full method independently — pair it with the paper performance task.
activities.rationale: Rate computation, best-buy choice, and conversion are cleanly checkable in short formats, and the characteristic errors make strong tempting wrong options. A recognition/short-answer format is efficient for surfacing specific slips but does not elicit the independent step-by-step construction that the performance task requires; it is a complement, not a replacement.
learnerActions: Work out and type the cost per 100 g for a product given its price and weight.
Choose the better buy between two differently sized packs where the smaller pack is actually cheaper per unit, so that 'the bigger pack must be cheaper per unit' is a tempting but wrong option.
Choose the average speed of a two-leg equal-distance journey, with the mean-of-the-two-speeds value (e.g. 50) offered as the key trap.
Give a km/h→m/s conversion as a typed value, then check its magnitude.
activities.intendedInsight: The mean-of-speeds error and wrong-way-round division make sharp, diagnostic wrong options, so a quick check can surface whether these specific slips persist after teaching.

activities.title: Consolidation reference card: 'per one' facts and the average-speed warning
feedback: Use the card to remind yourself what 'per one' means for each measure, then go and perform an actual calculation to check you can apply it.
Treat the revealed 'total distance ÷ total time' statement as a prompt to redo a worked journey, not as the whole lesson.
activities.rationale: A static labelled double number line or reference card with tap-to-reveal facts consolidates the idea and keeps the key warning visible. It cannot let the learner perform and check a calculation, which is the heart of this procedural topic, so it functions as a consolidation aid alongside the workshop and performance task rather than as the main teaching activity.
sourceClaims: NCETM treats compound measures (speed = distance÷time, density = mass÷volume) as multiplicative comparisons and names as a common misconception that 'compound measures are different from other forms of proportional relationship' when they follow the same multiplicative rules; it stresses securing the meaning of 'per', recommends double number lines and ratio tables, and raises formula triangles as a practice to scrutinise for whether they promote understanding.
learnerActions: Tap a shelf tag to reveal its unit price (e.g. cost per 100 g) and restate it in words: 'this much for one hundred grams'.
Tap 'average speed' to reveal 'total distance ÷ total time, NOT the average of the two speeds'.
Tap density, speed, and unit-price entries to reveal the 'per one' meaning behind each formula before using it in a calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: A labelled double number line and tap-to-reveal 'per one' facts consolidate the meaning of each compound unit and keep the average-speed warning salient.

constraints: Derive every compound measure as a unit rate first ('how much for exactly one?') using a double number line or ratio table before introducing any formula.
For best-buy, insist on a common basis (cost per 100 g, or per item for both products) rather than comparing raw price to raw size.

Teach average speed as total distance ÷ total time by working a two-leg journey where the naive mean-of-speeds answer is demonstrably wrong; include the equal-TIMES counterexample where the mean IS correct, so pupils learn the precise condition rather than a blanket 'never average speeds'.
Do km/h↔m/s as a deliberate two-step chain (×1000 m per km, ÷3600 s per hour) with units tracked, not a single memorised factor; include a magnitude sanity check (e.g. 36 km/h ≈ 10 m/s).
Prefer double number lines / ratio tables over the formula 'magic triangle', which can reduce proportional reasoning to symbol-shuffling; use the triangle only with care if at all.
The reference card is a consolidation scaffold: it holds facts but does not let the learner perform or check a calculation, so it must not be the sole activity for this procedural skill.

The short check records which answer was produced and surfaces specific slips, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the full method; pair it with the paper performance task.
Density and unit price follow the same multiplicative 'per one' structure as speed; comparisons and conversions should be modelled on that shared structure rather than treated as separate rules.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles, not the tested effectiveness of these specific activities.

Self-audit (arithmetic): 60÷60 = 1 h; 60÷40 = 1.5 h; total 120 km over 2.5 h = 48 km/h — confirmed. Equal-times variant: 100 km over 2 h = 50 km/h — confirmed; the arithmetic mean is exact only for equal times, matching the harmonic-mean argument in the sources. Conversion: 36 km/h = 36000 m / 3600 s = 10 m/s — confirmed.

Self-audit note on framing: the equal-distance case gives the harmonic mean 2uv/(u+v) = 2·60·40/100 = 48, consistent with the computed answer; the activities state the correct method (total÷total) and present the mean only as the trap, so no erroneous instruction is taught.

The original row described 10 m/s as 'walking-fast'; this is inaccurate (10 m/s ≈ 36 km/h, a fast cycling/sprinting pace), so the activity now describes it as a fast cycling/sprinting pace while keeping the numeric magnitude check.

The original row contained non-preferred-format rationales asserting '3D adds nothing' and that an in-role dialogue 'cannot exercise' the required doing-and-checking. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened or dropped; the short check and reference-card activities are retained with scoped affordances and stated limits rather than universal exclusions.

The original 'formula triangle blocks proportional reasoning' claim is retained as a cautious preference (prefer number lines/tables; use the triangle with care), consistent with the practitioner source scrutinising rather than universally banning it.

probeDeeper: Which leg did the cyclist spend more time on — the fast one or the slow one? So should the average be nearer 60 or nearer 40? Does 50 fit that?

Redo it with the two legs the same TIME instead of the same distance (1 hour at 60, then 1 hour at 40). Now what is the average speed — and why is it 50 this time? (counterexample: equal times DO give the mean.)
Show me how you'd turn 48 km/h into metres per second — talk me through each step and what the units are.
For the best buy, how did you make the two products comparable? What would go wrong if you just compared their prices?
assess.correctAnswer: 48 km/h. First leg takes 60÷60 = 1 hour; second leg takes 60÷40 = 1.5 hours. Total distance = 120 km, total time = 2.5 hours, so average speed = 120÷2.5 = 48 km/h.

errorPatterns.pattern: Averages the two speeds directly — (60+40)÷2 = 50 km/h — instead of total distance ÷ total time
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them find the TIME for each leg first (1 h and 1.5 h). Ask 'which speed did the cyclist spend more time at?' — more time at 40 pulls the average below 50. Rebuild on a double number line, total over total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes (60+40)÷2 or otherwise combines the speeds without ever computing the two times; answer is 50

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides the wrong way round when forming a rate (time÷distance for speed, or inverts a unit price)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor 'per one': speed is 'km for ONE hour', so distance goes on top. Track units through the division so km/h falls out, not h/km.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 60÷60 correctly by luck but on a leg like 60 km at 40 km/h writes 40÷60, or forms cost-per-pound as size÷price

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the km/h↔m/s conversion, using a single wrong factor (×60 or ÷60) instead of the ×1000 then ÷3600 chain
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the chain as two labelled steps with units cancelling: km→m (×1000), then per hour → per second (÷3600). Check magnitude: 36 km/h should be a walking-fast 10 m/s, not 0.6 or 600.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up conversion, multiplies or divides by 60 once, or forgets one of the two steps, giving an answer out by a factor of 60 or 1000

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares best-buys on different bases — assumes the bigger pack or the lower total price is automatically better value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist both are expressed as cost per 100 g (or per item) before deciding; only same-basis figures are comparable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a best-buy task picks the cheaper total or the bigger pack without reducing both to a common per-unit basis

responseLevels.gap: Answers 50 by averaging the speeds; does not compute the leg times or total÷total, and cannot correctly form or convert a rate.
responseLevels.full: Produces 48 km/h via leg times → total distance ÷ total time, forms rates the right way round, converts km/h↔m/s as a correct two-step chain with sensible magnitude, and compares best-buys on a common per-unit basis — and can transfer to an unfamiliar rate.
responseLevels.partial: Computes total distance ÷ total time correctly for the average-speed task, but slips on a related procedure (inverts a division, or botches the km/h↔m/s chain), showing the method is not yet secure across compound units.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a journey to work out. A cyclist rides 60 km at a steady 60 km/h, then rides another 60 km at a steady 40 km/h. Find the cyclist's average speed for the whole journey. Work it out on paper — show your steps.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the pupil work (not asking them to explain the rule) separates those who compute average speed as total distance ÷ total time from those who average the two speeds to get 50. Because equal DISTANCES are covered at unequal speeds, the correct answer (48) differs from the naive mean (50) — a pupil cannot land on 48 by the mean method, so the procedure is visible in the number they produce.

sources.claim: KS3 Ratio, proportion and rates of change requires pupils to 'use compound units such as speed, unit pricing and density to solve problems' and to 'change freely between related standard units'; KS4 adds 'convert between related compound units (speed, rates of pay, prices, density, pressure) in numerical and algebraic contexts'.
sources.source: DfE, National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study, KS3/KS4 Ratio, proportion and rates of change (statutory; Crown copyright)

sources.claim: Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, which equals the arithmetic mean of the two speeds ONLY when equal TIMES are spent at each; for equal DISTANCES the average is the harmonic mean 2uv/(u+v). The page proves the harmonic mean is ≤ the arithmetic mean (difference factorises to (u−v)²/[2(u+v)]), so averaging the two speeds overestimates the true average speed on equal-distance legs — the exact 48-vs-50 trap in this record.
sources.source: University of Cambridge, Underground Mathematics — 'Average speed: Averages'

sources.claim: The speed–distance–time formula triangle is procedural, gimmicky and error-prone (students misread which pair to multiply, or put the wrong quantity on top — e.g. carrying 'd on top' from speed to density), and it hides the underlying y=mx proportional structure; Foster argues speed is better understood as the constant of proportionality (d = st), building multiplicative reasoning rather than symbol-shuffling.
sources.source: Foster, C. (2021), 'On hating formula triangles', Mathematics in School (peer-reviewed practitioner journal)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11; know the main CONSERVATION approaches — protected areas/national parks, reforestation & rewilding, sustainable certification (Rainforest Alliance, FSC), recognition of INDIGENOUS LAND RIGHTS as the single most effective protection, and international payment schemes like REDD+ that pay countries to keep forests standing.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (sustainability, resource management, human impact) and Science Y6 (human impact, positive/negative); leads to KS3 'Earth and atmosphere' and citizenship.
• Standards — US: NGSS 5-ESS3-1 and MS-ESS3-3/-4 (monitoring and minimising human impact; managing resources sustainably).
• Operational details — present conservation as a TOOLKIT of complementary tools, each with a mechanism and a trade-off, not a single fix: protected areas (a legal fence, but need enforcement); reforestation (replant, but slow and not equal to primary forest); certification labels (FSC/Rainforest Alliance let consumers reward sustainable producers); indigenous land rights (evidence shows indigenous-managed forests have the LOWEST deforestation — stress this as the standout); REDD+ (rich nations pay tropical nations to leave forests standing, valuing a living tree over a felled one). Emphasise that solutions combine and that demand-side (consumer) and supply-side (policy) both matter.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (9): name three approaches. Tier B (10): explain why protecting indigenous territories is one of the most effective methods. Tier C (11): describe what an FSC/Rainforest Alliance label means and how a consumer choice feeds back to the forest.
bestPractices: Present conservation as a TOOLKIT of complementary approaches, not a single silver-bullet fix.
Give each approach a mechanism AND a trade-off/limit so pupils reason rather than list.
Foreground the evidence-backed standout: indigenous-managed forests have the lowest deforestation.
Show the real FSC and Rainforest Alliance labels so pupils recognise and can act on them as consumers.
Connect demand-side (consumer choices) and supply-side (policy, payments) as both mattering.
keyRepresentations: A five-tool panel: protected areas, reforestation, certification, indigenous land rights, REDD+.
The recognisable FSC tick and Rainforest Alliance frog logos.
A map contrasting deforestation inside vs outside indigenous territories.
A REDD+ 'pay to keep it standing' flow (money → country → forest preserved).
commonMisconceptions: 'One solution will fix it' — effective conservation combines several approaches.
'Replanting fully replaces cleared forest' — young reforestation is not equal to ancient primary forest's biodiversity.
'Protected on a map means safe' — protection needs enforcement to be real.
'Indigenous peoples harm the forest' — evidence shows their territories are among the best-protected.
'Nothing an ordinary shopper does matters' — choosing certified products rewards sustainable producers.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, learners meet rainforest conservation as a TOOLKIT of complementary approaches — protected areas/national parks, reforestation and rewilding, sustainable certification (FSC, Rainforest Alliance), recognition of indigenous land rights, and international payment schemes like REDD+ — each with a mechanism, a real example, and a trade-off. The central insight is that there is no single magic fix: solutions combine, demand-side (consumer) and supply-side (policy) both matter, and the evidence-backed standout is that indigenous-managed forests show among the lowest deforestation rates.

activities.title: The five-tool forest guide
feedback: If a learner says one method alone is enough (e.g. 'just make it a national park'), ask which driver that measure actually stops and which pressures — logging, cattle, soy, palm, mining — keep going; map each driver to the measure that addresses it.
If a learner thinks a line on a map means the forest is safe, ask who stops someone clearing it once it is 'protected' — draw out that protection needs enforcement to be real.

If a learner says replanting fully undoes clearing, contrast a centuries-old primary forest with a young replanted stand: decades to regrow, and some biodiversity never returns, so preventing loss beats replacing it.

If a learner says a shopper can do nothing, point to the certification labels: choosing FSC or Rainforest Alliance products rewards sustainable producers, connecting a consumer choice back to the forest.

If a learner treats indigenous residents as a threat, show the map evidence that indigenous-managed territories are among the best-protected forests, and reframe them as partners in protection rather than people to exclude.
activities.rationale: The objective is breadth: knowing five distinct approaches, each with mechanism, example and trade-off. Pairing every tool with a limit pushes learners to reason rather than list, and the recognisable real labels let them act as consumers. Foregrounding the indigenous-land-rights evidence corrects a common misconception and reflects the reported evidence standout, stated cautiously as 'among the most effective'.
sourceClaims: Recognition of indigenous land rights is among the most effective forms of forest protection: indigenous-managed territories show significantly lower deforestation rates

Certification schemes (FSC, Rainforest Alliance) and international mechanisms like REDD+ (results-based payments to keep forests standing) are established conservation approaches alongside protected areas and reforestation
learnerActions: Work through five conservation approaches one at a time — protected areas/national parks, reforestation/rewilding, certification labels, indigenous land rights, and REDD+ payments — using a labelled picture of one forest shown 'guarded' in five different ways (a ranger's gate, fresh saplings, two product labels, a map of an indigenous territory, a payment flow).
For EACH approach, write or say three things: (a) how it works (the mechanism), (b) one real example, and (c) one trade-off or limit.
For protected areas, note the mechanism 'a legal boundary that restricts or forbids clearing' and the limit 'a boundary on a map only holds if someone enforces it on the ground'.

For reforestation, note 'replanting cleared land helps' and the limit 'a young replanted plot is not the same as ancient primary forest — it takes decades to rebuild the carbon and biodiversity, and some is never fully recovered'.

For certification, examine the real Rainforest Alliance frog logo and the FSC tick; explain that buying labelled products rewards producers who farm or log sustainably, and the limit that a label is a strong signal but not an absolute guarantee.

For indigenous land rights, study a map contrasting deforestation inside versus outside indigenous territories and state why securing the rights of people already caring for the forest is one of the most effective protections.

For REDD+, trace the money-to-forest flow (richer nations and other funders pay tropical nations when they reduce forest loss) and explain that this gives a standing forest a money value, so keeping it can compete with the money made from clearing it. Note the limit: the payment is not always bigger than what cattle, soy, palm oil or logging would earn.
activities.intendedInsight: Saving rainforests is a set of tools working together, not one silver bullet; each tool works in a different way, tackles different pressures or repairs different damage, and carries its own trade-off, and respecting the people who have long protected the forest is one of the most effective measures.

activities.title: Spend the forest-protection budget
feedback: If a learner pours everything into one tool, name the pressures that measure does not address and ask what still threatens the forest.
If a learner can allocate but not justify, prompt them to attach each tool to a specific driver (logging, cattle, soy, palm, mining) before confirming the split.
Remind learners that the budget figures are a reasoning aid, not real-world quantities, so the lesson is the complementary-tools logic rather than exact numbers.
activities.rationale: Actively allocating scarce resources makes the complementary-tools principle concrete and consequential rather than a stated fact. This is a toolkit demonstration focused on knowing the approaches; a full stakeholder trade-off and competing-interests debate is a separate, more advanced objective (see constraints). The efficacy of any specific funding mix is not quantified by the sources, so the activity is framed as qualitative reasoning.
learnerActions: Given a limited pot of money and the five approaches, decide how to split the funds and reason about how much forest each allocation MIGHT protect and at what rough cost — treat any forest-saved and cost figures as an illustrative model for reasoning about complementarity, not a validated prediction.
Justify the split: say which driver of deforestation each funded tool tackles and why spreading across several tools plausibly protects more than pouring everything into one.
Try an extreme allocation (all funds into a single tool) and explain what pressures would still get through, reinforcing that tools are complementary.
activities.intendedInsight: Because deforestation has many drivers at once, a mix of complementary measures usually protects more forest than any single measure funded alone.

activities.title: Defend a conservation plan
feedback: A full response explains that different drivers need different measures acting together, argues that securing indigenous land rights is among the most effective, and transfers the reasoning to a new case (such as balancing a poor community's income against protection) rather than reciting a list.
A partial response lists several real measures but treats them as a menu of separate fixes; prompt the learner to say which driver each one answers and why they must combine.

A gap response equates conservation with a fence ('keep people out') or names one measure ('plant more trees') with no sense of competing pressures; reteach that people can be part of a working forest system and that deforestation has many drivers.

Model answer to anchor feedback: No — excluding the people who already live there is not the most effective protection; indigenous-managed lands are among the best-protected forests. The strongest approach combines securing indigenous land rights, protected areas that still allow residents to stay, reforestation of cleared land, certification that rewards sustainable production, and finance like REDD+ that pays to keep forests standing, because no single fence addresses pressures coming from many directions at once.
activities.rationale: The 'why' tier distinguishes a memorised list from genuine understanding that no one method covers every driver. The fence scenario is diagnostic: it surfaces whether a learner treats humans as a threat to exclude or as partners in a living forest system, which is the key misconception this objective targets.
sourceClaims: Recognition of indigenous land rights is among the most effective forms of forest protection: indigenous-managed territories show significantly lower deforestation rates
learnerActions: Respond to the scenario: a country wants to protect a rainforest and someone suggests the surest way is to fence it off completely and keep ALL people out, including the indigenous communities who already live there. Decide whether that is the most effective plan and explain WHY, saying what you would do instead.
Match each approach to how it works (approach → mechanism) and answer which approach the evidence points to as among the most effective, and what a certification label actually means for the forest.

Tackle probing questions: why a forest cared for by its long-term inhabitants may be better protected than one guarded from afar; what 'Rainforest Alliance certified' cocoa is supposed to change and why it is not a complete guarantee; how a plan could protect the forest AND support poor families who earn money from cleared land; and which single measure you would drop LAST, with your reason.
activities.intendedInsight: Effective conservation combines measures matched to different drivers; excluding the people who already live there is not the most effective protection, because indigenous-managed lands are among the best-protected forests and the pressures on a forest come from many directions at once.

constraints: Present conservation as a toolkit of complementary approaches, never a single silver-bullet fix; always pair each approach with both a mechanism and a trade-off so learners reason rather than list.

Use the real, recognisable FSC tick and Rainforest Alliance frog logos so learners can identify and act on them as consumers; describe certification as a strong signal that rewards sustainable producers, not an absolute guarantee.

State the indigenous-land-rights evidence as 'among the most effective / among the best-protected' (matching the cited FAO-FILAC 'significantly lower' wording), not as a proven 'single most effective' or 'lowest of all'.

A matching or multiple-choice task can assess recognition of approaches and labels but does not by itself build the comparative, reasoned overview; use it alongside the explanation and defence tasks where learners construct and justify a plan.

The budget-allocation activity is a toolkit demonstration using illustrative, non-sourced figures; the fuller stakeholder trade-off with competing voices (e.g. a park ranger versus an indigenous leader versus a company) is a more advanced 'futures/decisions' objective and should be deferred rather than fully built here.
A tap-to-reveal picture panel is a presentation scaffold; ensure learners still produce their own mechanism/example/trade-off statements and a justified plan, not just tap and read.
Any labelled picture or map is a representation of the real situation; distinguish the illustrated 'forest guarded five ways' from the actual landscapes and policies it stands for.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the listed sources were NOT re-fetched, and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated or empirically tested interventions.

All three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row; treat the indigenous-land-rights efficacy claim and the REDD+/certification descriptions as reported but unconfirmed, and avoid presenting them as established fact beyond what the cited reports state.

The claim that indigenous-managed forests have 'the lowest' deforestation is softened in learner-facing text to 'among the lowest / among the best-protected', matching the cautious wording of the FAO-FILAC source claim ('significantly lower'), since 'single most effective' and 'LOWEST of all' are stronger than the exact claim supports.

Certification efficacy and the 'not a complete guarantee' caveat are retained; do not overstate that buying labelled products definitely protects a specific forest, as the sources establish these as established approaches, not quantified outcomes.

The budget-allocation activity uses invented, illustrative figures for forest protected and cost; no source quantifies these outcomes, so its sourceClaims is [] and it is framed as qualitative reasoning about complementarity.
The DfE KS2 source supports only curriculum/age placement, not any pedagogical-efficacy principle, so it was removed from activity sourceClaims and is retained as context only.

probeDeeper: Why might a forest looked after by the people who have always lived there be better protected than one guarded by a distant government?
A chocolate company says its cocoa is 'Rainforest Alliance certified'. What is that supposed to change, and why might it not be a complete guarantee?
What if the country is poor and the cleared land earns money for families — how would your plan keep the forest AND support those families?
Which single measure would you drop last if you could only keep one, and why that one?
assess.correctAnswer: No. Excluding the people who already live there is not the most effective protection — indigenous-managed lands are among the best-protected forests in the world. The strongest conservation combines several approaches: recognising and securing indigenous land rights, protected areas that still allow the people who live there to stay, reforestation of cleared land, certification schemes (Rainforest Alliance, FSC) that reward sustainable production, and finance like REDD+ that pays to keep forests standing. No single fence solves it because the pressures come from many directions at once.

errorPatterns.pattern: conservation means removing all people and locking the forest away ('the only way to save it is to keep everyone out')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the evidence that indigenous-managed territories have lower deforestation than many official parks; reframe protection as securing the rights of people already caring for the forest.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the safest way to protect a rainforest is to fence it off and keep everyone out, including the people who live there.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child endorses the fence plan and treats indigenous residents as a threat to be excluded rather than partners in protection

errorPatterns.pattern: one method alone is enough ('just make it a national park and it's saved')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Map each driver of deforestation to the measure that addresses it; show why parks, land rights, certification and finance have to work together.
errorPatterns.distractor: Making it a national park is enough on its own to stop the forest being lost.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child names a single measure and treats the problem as solved, ignoring that logging, cattle, soy, palm and mining pressures continue

errorPatterns.pattern: replanting instantly undoes the damage ('we can cut it now and just replant later, so it's fine')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a centuries-old primary forest with a young replanted stand — decades to regrow the carbon and biodiversity, and some is never recovered; prevention beats cure.
errorPatterns.distractor: It doesn't matter much if we clear it, because replanting brings the whole forest straight back.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats reforestation as a full, immediate reversal and so sees no urgency in protecting standing forest

responseLevels.gap: Equates conservation with a fence — 'keep people out' — or offers a single measure ('plant more trees') with no sense of competing pressures.
responseLevels.full: Explains that different drivers need different measures acting together, argues that securing indigenous land rights is among the most effective, and transfers the reasoning to a new case (e.g. balancing a poor community's income against protection) rather than reciting a list.
responseLevels.partial: Lists several real measures (protected areas, replanting, certification, land rights) but treats them as a menu of separate fixes and cannot say which driver each one answers or why they must combine.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A country wants to protect a rainforest. Someone suggests the surest way is to fence it off completely and keep ALL people out — including the indigenous communities who already live there. Is that the most effective plan? Tell me what you'd do instead, and WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks conservation = 'remove humans and lock it away' gives the fence answer confidently. A child who understands that people are part of a working forest system and that deforestation has many drivers rejects the fence and names the LIVING communities as part of the solution. The 'why' tier separates a memorised list of methods from understanding that no one method covers all the drivers.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11; compare Arctic and Antarctic ecosystems — the Arctic has BOTH terrestrial (tundra) and marine ecosystems, supporting large land mammals and indigenous human communities; the Antarctic is almost entirely MARINE, with virtually no land plants or land mammals; both have short, intense food chains anchored by phytoplankton and krill, and both are hit hard by climate change and human activity.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (ecosystems; food chains) and Geography (biomes); KS3 Biology (interdependence; ecosystems).
• Standards—US: NGSS 5-LS2-1 (matter/energy in ecosystems) and MS-LS2-1/-3 (resource availability; energy/matter flow in ecosystems).
• Operational details: the organising contrast is land-plus-sea (Arctic) vs almost-all-sea (Antarctic), which follows from the earlier ocean-vs-continent structure and drives who lives where (land mammals and people in the Arctic; life crowded into the sea and coasts in the Antarctic). Then the shared pattern: both run short, productive food chains built on phytoplankton and krill, and both are disproportionately vulnerable. Compare and contrast systematically rather than listing animals.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (9) state that the Arctic has land AND sea life while Antarctica's life is mostly in the sea; Tier B (10) explain why the Arctic supports land mammals and people but Antarctica largely doesn't; Tier C (11) compare both ecosystems on structure, food-chain base, and shared vulnerability to change.

Use a systematic compare/contrast frame (land vs marine, producers, top predators, humans, threats) rather than animal lists
Highlight the SHARED base — phytoplankton and krill — so pupils see a common pattern beneath the differences
Bring in humans as part of the Arctic ecosystem (indigenous communities) but not the Antarctic
Connect both systems' vulnerability to the climate and conservation topics for coherence across the domain

Shared food-chain base card: phytoplankton → krill/zooplankton feeding both systems
Compare/contrast table (land life, marine life, humans, producers, threats)
