learn.summary: Pupils aged 9–11 compare Arctic and Antarctic ecosystems systematically rather than listing animals. The organising idea is a structural contrast with a cause: the Arctic is a largely frozen ocean ringed by land joined to other continents, so it has BOTH tundra (land) and marine ecosystems, supporting land mammals (caribou, Arctic foxes, musk oxen), sea-ice hunters such as polar bears, and indigenous human communities; Antarctica is a high continent almost entirely covered by ice, extremely cold, and isolated by the Southern Ocean, so its land is nearly bare of plants and has no land mammals, and life crowds into the surrounding sea. Beneath the difference lies a shared base — phytoplankton feeding krill/zooplankton — on which both short, productive food chains depend. Both regions are disproportionately affected by climate change (they are warming fast and losing sea ice that many animals rely on) and by human activity such as fishing; in this teaching model, the short chains help show why harm to the base spreads upward. Build, sort, and reason activities are proposed to make the compare/contrast active; a dialogue or categorise check are offered as companions.

activities.title: Build both poles side by side
feedback: If a learner fills the Antarctic land with mammals, show the land staying bare and ask two questions: how would a land animal reach an isolated continent across the vast Southern Ocean, and what could it eat on land that is almost all ice and extremely cold?
If a learner treats the two poles as identical, point to the Arctic's filled land panel beside Antarctica's empty one and ask what difference in geography caused that.

When the stressor collapses a chain, prompt: which tiny organism was every bigger animal depending on, and why does losing it hit everything above? Present this as illustrating sensitivity in this short-chain model, not a precise prediction of real population numbers.
activities.rationale: The learning objective is a structured, causal comparison of two systems. Actively building each system — and discovering the Antarctic land cannot easily be populated — is intended to make the land-vs-almost-all-sea contrast something the learner produces and reasons about rather than only reads, and tracing the shared base plus applying a stressor is meant to link structure to vulnerability. This is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: The Arctic has both tundra (terrestrial) and marine ecosystems with land mammals and human communities, while Antarctica is almost entirely marine with negligible land flora/fauna; both rest on phytoplankton/krill and are highly climate-sensitive
learnerActions: On an Arctic panel, stock a tundra with mosses, caribou and foxes, add a human community, AND stock the surrounding sea with seals, fish and whales — notice land and ocean both fill up.

Switch to an Antarctic panel: try to stock the land and find it stays almost empty (a few mosses, no land mammals, no permanent human community) while penguins, seals and whales pile into the surrounding sea.
At the base of both panels, trace a shared conveyor showing phytoplankton feeding krill/zooplankton that feed everything above.
Drag a 'warming' or 'fishing' stressor across both systems and watch each short food chain wobble.
State in one sentence the single structural difference that explains why the Arctic has land AND sea life while Antarctica's life is mostly in the sea.
activities.intendedInsight: One structural difference — ocean-ringed-by-land (Arctic) versus an isolated, ice-covered continent ringed by ocean (Antarctic) — shapes who can reach and survive where, yet both ecosystems rest on the same phytoplankton/krill-zooplankton base, and in this model their short food chains show how harm to that base spreads to everything above.

activities.title: Compare-and-contrast table
feedback: If the learner lists only animals, redirect to the factor rows — e.g. 'who are the producers?' and 'which humans are part of this system?'
If the learner omits humans from the Arctic, note that indigenous communities are integral to the Arctic ecosystem but not the Antarctic.
Confirm the shared producer row: both systems are built on phytoplankton eaten by krill/zooplankton.
activities.rationale: Paired, tappable diagrams with a compare/contrast table give structure to the comparison and surface both the differences and the shared base; this is a strong support, though it presents the systems rather than having the learner construct them. Any live manipulation is optional — the same table can be done on paper.
sourceClaims: Students analyse matter and energy flow and resource availability in ecosystems

The Arctic has both tundra (terrestrial) and marine ecosystems with land mammals and human communities, while Antarctica is almost entirely marine with negligible land flora/fauna; both rest on phytoplankton/krill and are highly climate-sensitive
learnerActions: Fill in a side-by-side table with rows for land life, marine life, humans, producers, and threats for the Arctic and the Antarctic.
For each row, tap the paired ecosystem diagrams (Arctic tundra+sea vs Antarctic sea-dominated) to check what belongs where.
Mark the row that is most clearly the SAME for both poles (producers: phytoplankton, eaten by krill/zooplankton) and write why that shared base matters.
activities.intendedInsight: A systematic multi-factor frame (land, sea, humans, producers, threats) reveals both the differences and the common engine beneath them, avoiding a mere animal list.

activities.title: Sort to the correct pole and explain why
feedback: If a learner places penguins in the Arctic, note that wild penguins live almost entirely in the Southern Hemisphere and polar bears only in the far north; they do not share a habitat in the wild.
If a learner assumes losing one species wouldn't matter, trace phytoplankton → krill → everything and show that, in this short-chain model, removing krill collapses much of the web.

For the grazing question, point to the isolated, ice-covered continent: almost all the land is under thick ice and extremely cold, so very few plants can grow, and land animals would also have had to cross the Southern Ocean to get there — so large grazers are absent.
activities.rationale: Categorise-and-justify tasks make a solid companion check and surface misconceptions (bears and penguins together; penguins at the North Pole; long robust chains); they assess and reinforce classification rather than build the full systematic comparison.
learnerActions: Sort cards (polar bear, caribou, penguin, indigenous community, moss, krill, whale, phytoplankton) to Arctic, Antarctic, or both.
For any card placed in only one pole, give the reason — e.g. 'wild penguins live almost entirely in the Southern Hemisphere; polar bears live only in the far north; they never meet in the wild'.

Answer a reasoning probe: 'Reindeer graze on Arctic land but no large animals graze on the Antarctic mainland — why?' and 'If krill numbers crashed, what happens to whales, penguins and seals, and why?'
activities.intendedInsight: Correct categorisation plus a stated reason shows the learner links geography to what can live where and recognises the shared, fragile krill base. A sort checks classification but does not by itself elicit the full explanation, so the stated-reason step is needed to reach the reasoning.

activities.title: Talk it through: why are the two poles so different?
feedback: If the learner says the poles are interchangeable, contrast the Arctic (ocean with surrounding land) with the Antarctic (isolated, ice-covered continent with surrounding ocean): geography decides who can reach each place and how cold and icy the land is.
Push for the shared base: good answers name phytoplankton → krill and explain that, in this model, the short chain is productive but fragile.
activities.rationale: A guided dialogue can surface differences and reasoning and may support transfer. It is offered as a companion because a multi-factor comparison may be easier to make concrete by building and sorting; open discussion alone can still teach the explanation. The efficacy of either medium here is untested.
learnerActions: Respond to the prompt: 'Polar bears live in the Arctic hunting seals on the sea ice; penguins live in the Antarctic. Why do you never find them living together, and why do big Antarctic animals almost all feed from the SEA rather than the land? Tell me, then tell me WHY the two poles are so different for animals.'
Extend to a transfer case: 'What if a land bridge connected Antarctica to South America — could land animals walk there, and would the ice and cold still stop most of them from living there?'
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the geographic cause (ocean ringed by land vs continent ringed by ocean → what can reach and live there → sea-based food webs) is intended to consolidate the explanation and to probe transfer.

constraints: Frame the comparison causally: anchor the ecosystem difference in the ocean-vs-continent structure so it is explained, not just described.
Use a systematic compare/contrast frame (land vs marine, producers, top predators, humans, threats) rather than animal lists.
Always surface the SHARED base — phytoplankton eaten by krill and other zooplankton (in the Arctic, tiny copepods are especially important) — so the common pattern beneath the differences is visible.
Include humans (indigenous communities) as part of the Arctic ecosystem but not the Antarctic.

The sort/categorise and dialogue tasks function as checks and consolidation; on their own they assess or discuss rather than have the learner construct the systematic comparison. Pair them with a comparison-building task (the build panels OR the compare/contrast table, which can be done on paper) rather than relying on them alone.

Live manipulation (stocking panels, dragging a stressor, tappable diagrams) is an optional way to make the mechanism concrete; the same comparison can be done with paper panels, cut-out cards, and a drawn table.
3D representation is not required: the comparison here is relational and structural, so a flat side-by-side layout carries the content; this is a scoping note, not a claim that 3D could never help.
Treat the short-chain fragility and 'krill crash collapses the web' point as a model-level explanation, not an absolute; real polar food webs have more structure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all three listed sources carry verified:false. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source lists polar bears as reaching the Arctic because it is an ocean ringed by continents; keep this framing accurate — bears live on Arctic land and sea ice, whereas Antarctica's isolation by the Southern Ocean explains the near-absence of land mammals. The 'ocean vs continent' causal claim rests on an unverified source.

The claim that polar food chains are uniformly short and that losing krill collapses the whole web is a useful teaching simplification; real polar food webs have more structure. Treat the short-chain fragility point as a model-level explanation rather than an absolute, and avoid implying every link loss is catastrophic beyond the krill example. This qualifier is carried into the learner-facing feedback, not only this note.
Climate/fishing vulnerability outcomes depend on specifics; present the stressor activity as illustrating sensitivity, not as a precise prediction of real population changes.

Efficacy language in rationales was softened: no source establishes that building/sorting is superior to a table or dialogue, so comparative and 'active building works' claims are presented as proposed/intended.

probeDeeper: What one tiny animal are both polar food webs built on, and why does that make them fragile?
Reindeer graze on Arctic land but there's nothing like that grazing on the Antarctic mainland. Why the difference?
If krill numbers crashed, what would happen to whales, penguins and seals — and why?
What if a land bridge connected Antarctica to South America — how might its animals change?
assess.correctAnswer: The Arctic is a frozen OCEAN surrounded by continents, so land animals (polar bears, foxes, reindeer) can reach it and it has land-and-sea food webs; Antarctica is a continent isolated by the vast Southern Ocean, so almost nothing can cross to live on the land — its large animals (penguins, seals, whales) all feed from the sea. Both food webs rest on tiny phytoplankton eaten by krill, so the chains are short, which makes them productive but vulnerable: losing one link (like krill) hits everything above it.

pedagogy.summary: Placing fractions on a number line is the move from 'fraction = part of a shape' to 'fraction = a number with a magnitude', locatable, orderable and equivalence-checkable. The load-bearing idea is that a fraction 1/b is made by splitting ONE unit (the distance between two whole numbers) into b equal SEGMENTS — needing b−1 marks between them — and the point at the a-th mark is a/b. Teach with the unit held visible so children stop treating the whole line as the unit and stop placing 3/4 'between 3 and 4'.
bestPractices: Start from pre-segmented 0-to-1 lines, then minimally-labelled lines with landmarks (0, 1/2, 1, 1½, 2), then unmarked lines to force interval thinking (IES Rec 2)
Teach fourths as four equal SEGMENTS between 0 and 1 made by THREE marks; generalise 1/n needs n−1 marks
Use contrasting cases to kill 'between 3 and 4': locate 3 and 4 on a 0-to-4 line, then 3/4 within 0-1, and discuss why each sits there
Reason with landmarks and distance ('is 1/12 closer to 1/4 or to 0?') so magnitude, not counting, drives placement
Use dual labelling (fifths above the line, tenths below) to show equivalent fractions land on the same point
keyRepresentations: 0-to-1 number line partitioned into equal segments (the core model)
Minimally-labelled landmark line (0, 1/2, 1)
Dual-labelled line (two fractional-unit sequences) for equivalence
Fraction strip laid alongside the line to link area-model and length-model
commonMisconceptions: Treats the number line like a ruler — counts tick marks (or draws 4 marks for fourths) instead of equal segments (IES Roadblock 2.1)
Places 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers (IES Roadblock 2.2)
Treats the whole line as the unit — e.g. locates 3/4 three-quarters of the way across a 0-to-5 line
Sees a fraction only as part of a shape, not as a single number that has a place on a line
Larger-denominator-is-larger — places 1/8 further from 0 than 1/3

learn.summary: Help 7-8 year olds move from 'fraction = part of a shape' to 'fraction = a number with a place on the line'. The load-bearing idea: a fraction 1/b is made by splitting ONE unit (the distance between two whole numbers) into b equal SEGMENTS, which needs b−1 marks between them, and a/b is the point at the end of the a-th equal segment counted from 0 (for a less than b, this is the a-th interior mark). Keep the unit visible so children stop treating the whole line as the unit and stop placing 3/4 'between 3 and 4'. Core model is a 0-to-1 line partitioned into equal segments; progress to landmark lines and then unmarked lines to force interval thinking, and use dual labelling to show equivalence as the same point.

activities.title: Three marks make fourths: partition and place on an interactive line
feedback: If the child draws or expects four interior marks for fourths, point out four interior marks make FIVE parts; count the equal segments together and confirm three marks give four parts.
If the bead is read as 4/4 or 4/5, recount the equal segments from 0 and name the end of the third segment as 3/4.
If 3/4 is placed between 3 and 4 on the longer line, locate 3 and 4 first, then ask 'is 3/4 bigger or smaller than 1?' and relocate it within the first unit.
When 1/2 lands on 5/10, name it: 'same point, two names — that's what equivalent means.'
activities.rationale: Partitioning a unit into equal segments and reading the end of the a-th segment directly targets the ruler-counting error (Roadblock 2.1) and the 'between 3 and 4' error (Roadblock 2.2); dual-labelled lines show equivalent fractions occupying the same point. Live controls (cut-into-parts dial, draggable bead that reports its fraction, length toggle, tenths track) make the segment-counting mechanism and the fixed unit concrete, but are optional ways to realise the task and the same learning can be done on paper.
sourceClaims: Recommendation 2 (Moderate Evidence): use number lines to teach fractions as numbers. Dividing a number line into 1/n units needs n-1 marks between two whole numbers; students err by drawing 4 marks for fourths or treating the whole line as the unit (Roadblock 2.1), and by placing 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction's numbers as separate whole numbers (Roadblock 2.2).

Students often view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), diagnosable by having them label hatch marks on a 0-to-1 number line; equivalent fractions can be shown to occupy the same point using dual-labelled lines.
learnerActions: On a 0-to-1 line, set a 'cut this unit into ___ parts' control to 4 and watch exactly THREE marks drop in, splitting the line into four equal segments.
Say aloud how many marks made four parts (three, not four), and colour each of the four segments, counting SEGMENTS rather than marks.
Drop a bead on the third mark; if the line reports a fraction, check it announces '3/4' and explain why that point is 3/4.

Extend the line from 0-to-1 to 0-to-4, keeping each whole-number unit the same length (or redraw it that way), and notice the 3/4 bead stays three-quarters of the way from 0 to the first '1', nowhere near the '3'.
On a second track below, lined up with the same 0 and 1 and labelled in tenths, slide a 1/2 bead until it lands exactly on 5/10, and state that the two labels name the same point.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction 1/b comes from cutting one unit into b equal segments (needing b−1 interior marks), and a/b is the point at the end of the a-th segment. The unit stays 'one whole' even when the line gets longer, so 3/4 lives between 0 and 1, not between 3 and 4. Equivalent fractions are the same point under different labels.

activities.title: Place and reason on paper lines: pre-marked, landmark, then unmarked
feedback: If a child drifts toward whole-number placement on the longer or unmarked line, return to naming the unit (0 to 1) and ask how many equal parts the denominator calls for.
For 'is 1/12 closer to 1/4 or 0?', prompt: twelfths are small, so compare how far 1/12 sits from 0 against how far it sits from 1/4, rather than which number looks bigger.
If an unmarked line is partitioned unequally, fold or measure to check the segments are the same length before placing the point.
activities.rationale: Fading from pre-segmented to landmark to unmarked lines forces interval thinking and shifts the child from counting to magnitude reasoning (IES Rec 2). Contrasting 3 and 4 with 3/4 on the same 0-to-4 line directly confronts the separate-whole-numbers error. Landmark distance questions support ordering fractions and address larger-denominator-is-larger.
sourceClaims: Recommendation 2 (Moderate Evidence): use number lines to teach fractions as numbers. Dividing a number line into 1/n units needs n-1 marks between two whole numbers; students err by drawing 4 marks for fourths or treating the whole line as the unit (Roadblock 2.1), and by placing 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction's numbers as separate whole numbers (Roadblock 2.2).
learnerActions: On a 0-to-1 line already divided into four equal segments (fourths), place 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 by counting equal segments from 0.

On a minimally-labelled line showing only 0, 1/2, 1, 1½ and 2, place a concrete fraction such as 1¾ using landmarks — reasoning that it sits just below 2 (between 1½ and 2) — rather than counting every mark.
On an UNMARKED 0-to-1 line, decide how many segments you need, make the b−1 marks yourself, then place the fraction.
Answer landmark-reasoning questions such as 'Is 1/12 closer to 1/4 or to 0?' and 'Is 3/4 closer to 0 or to 1?', explaining using distance.
On a 0-to-4 line, place both 3 and 4, then separately place 3/4, and say in your own words why 3/4 does not go between 3 and 4.
activities.intendedInsight: Placement is driven by magnitude and distance from landmarks, not by counting ticks. Children who can partition an unmarked line themselves have internalised that the unit is divided into equal segments, and they keep fractions within the correct whole-number interval.

activities.title: Bridge from the shape model and compare unit fractions
feedback: If the child says a line 'isn't a shape so you can't do fractions on it', use the strip-along-the-line bridge until the shaded part and the point coincide, then name the point.
If 1/8 is placed further from 0 than 1/3, compare one eighth-segment with one third-segment of the same unit: more parts, shorter parts, so 1/8 sits nearer 0.
If a reference point is misnamed, recount the equal segments from 0 and describe the point as 'the end of the a-th of b equal parts'.
activities.rationale: Linking the area model to the length model addresses children who see fractions only as parts of shapes and refuse or randomise line placement. Comparing segment lengths of the same unit partitioned differently reteaches 'more parts means smaller' before ordering, targeting the larger-denominator-is-larger misconception. A labelled reference line supports reading, but being fixed it cannot by itself make the child confront miscounting — pair it with the partitioning task.
sourceClaims: Students often view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), diagnosable by having them label hatch marks on a 0-to-1 number line; equivalent fractions can be shown to occupy the same point using dual-labelled lines.
learnerActions: Shade 3/4 of a fraction strip exactly as long as the 0-to-1 unit, starting the shading at one end, then lay that end at 0 along the line so the shaded part reaches a point; name that point as the number 3/4.
Partition one unit into thirds, then partition an identical unit into eighths, and compare the lengths of a single segment in each.
Place 1/3 and 1/8 on the same 0-to-1 line and decide which is further from 0, explaining using segment length.
State in your own words whether a fraction such as 3/4 is 'a number' or 'just a piece of a shape', and point to where it lives on the line.
Reference check: label 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1 on a line and explain for each point which segment's end it marks.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction names one number and has a single location on the line; the area (shape) model and the length (line) model agree. More equal parts of the same unit means each part is smaller, so 1/8 is closer to 0 than 1/3 — the denominator counts how many parts split ONE whole.

constraints: Hold the unit (the 0-to-1 distance) visible and fixed so children do not treat the whole line as the unit; test transfer on a 0-to-4 or unmarked line, not only on a pre-segmented 0-to-1 line.
Teach fourths as four equal SEGMENTS made by THREE interior marks; generalise that 1/n needs n−1 interior marks. Insist on counting segments, not tick marks.

A fixed labelled reference line can teach and be used while teaching, but on its own it does not require the child to construct segments or re-place a point on a longer line; combine reference-reading with active partitioning and placement.

Fraction strips and paper cutouts have real slight thickness and only approximate the ideal flat model; use them to bridge area and length, and treat any on-screen line as a model of the idealised (zero-thickness) number line.

When comparing unit fractions such as 1/8 and 1/3, keep the SAME whole and compare how one segment's length changes as the denominator changes; describe this as 'more parts means smaller parts', never as a denominator rule that 'flips'.

Placing and comparing points is a construct-and-check task: recognition-only or matching responses can check placement but do not by themselves elicit the child independently partitioning a unit and justifying a location. Include at least one task where the child makes the marks and states the reasoning.

Live controls (cut-into-parts dial, snapping/announcing bead, length toggle, tenths track) are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required equipment; the same learning can be done on paper with careful partitioning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed the two headline errors are 'refuted on contact' and 'die on sight' with a dynamic line, and that a static image 'can't let the child confront miscounting', a dialogue 'can't substitute', and 3D 'adds nothing'. These are catalog-fit assertions, not established efficacy claims; softened here to scoped affordances/limits. Comparative medium superiority is not asserted by the cited Moderate-Evidence source.
Geometry self-audit: a fraction's point on the number line is the END of the a-th equal segment, and b−1 interior marks produce b equal segments; four interior marks would produce five segments.

Landmark question audit: 1/12 ≈ 0.083 and 1/4 = 0.25, so 1/12 is closer to 0 than to 1/4; and 1/8 = 0.125 is closer to 0 than 1/3 ≈ 0.333. These are kept as reasoning prompts for the child to work out, not pre-stated answers. The added example 1¾ = 1.75 sits between 1½ and 2, just below 2.

The Year 3 'count up and down in tenths' curriculum claim was removed from the paper-lines activity (which contains no tenths) to avoid citing a source that supports only the topic context rather than that activity's teaching principle.
Edit this pass: the second activity's landmark-placement action was made concrete (place 1¾ using the 1½/2 landmarks) so it models landmark reasoning rather than leaving the fraction unspecified.

probeDeeper: Is 3/4 closer to 0 or closer to 1? How do you know?
Point to where 1/8 would go and where 1/3 would go. Which is further from 0, and why?
Someone put 3/4 in the space between the 3 and the 4 on this line. What would you tell them?
Is a fraction like 3/4 a number, or just a piece of a shape? Where does that show up on the line?
assess.correctAnswer: The dot is at 3/4, because 0-to-1 is divided into four equal parts (segments) and the dot sits at the end of the third part. On the 0-to-4 line, 3/4 goes three-quarters of the way from 0 towards 1 (just below 1, NOT between 3 and 4) and 1/2 goes halfway between 0 and 1; each is a single number between 0 and 1 because its denominator splits ONE unit.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Show fourths as four equal SEGMENTS made by THREE marks between 0 and 1; have the child colour each segment and count segments, not marks (IES Roadblock 2.1)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads the 3/4 point as 4/4 or 4/5, counts the 0 mark as one, or when drawing puts four interior marks to make fourths

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number placement — treats the numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers and puts 3/4 between the 3 and the 4 on the 0-to-4 line
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrasting cases: locate 3 and 4, then 3/4 as a number between 0 and 1; reteach fraction as a single quantity of one whole before returning to the line (IES Roadblock 2.2)

errorPatterns.nextMove: Bridge the area model to length: lay a fraction strip along the 0-1 line so the shaded part reaches the same point; name the point as the number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses the task, treats the line as decoration, or places the fraction with no relation to the unit

errorPatterns.pattern: Larger-denominator-is-larger — places 1/8 further from 0 than 1/3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Partition the same unit into thirds then eighths and compare segment lengths; reteach more-parts-means-smaller before ordering on the line
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to place unit fractions, puts the one with the bigger denominator further to the right

responseLevels.gap: Counts tick marks, draws four marks for fourths, places 3/4 between 3 and 4, or says a line can't show fractions — treats the two numbers separately.
responseLevels.full: Interprets the marked point as 3/4 by segments, produces 3/4 and 1/2 on a fresh 0-to-4 line both within 0-1 and reasoned by landmarks, and explains a fraction is a single number whose denominator partitions one unit — transferring to locate or compare a new fraction.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and places 3/4 and 1/2 on a pre-marked 0-to-1 line by counting equal segments, but on a 0-to-4 or unmarked line loses the unit (miscounts or drifts toward whole-number placement) and cannot yet say a fraction is one number located relative to landmarks.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First, look at this number line from 0 to 1. There are three marks spaced equally between 0 and 1, and I have put a dot on the third mark. What number is at the dot, and how do you know? Now here is a fresh line labelled from 0 to 4. Put 3/4 on it, and put 1/2 on it, and tell me why each one goes where you put it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting the marked point separates ruler-counting (reads it as 4/4 or miscounts marks) from interval thinking (end of the third equal segment). The 0-to-4 placement is the decisive translate move: a child who treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers puts 3/4 between 3 and 4, which a part-of-a-shape understanding alone cannot avoid, whereas seeing a fraction as one number keeps it inside the first unit.

sources.claim: Recommendation 2 (Moderate Evidence): use number lines to teach fractions as numbers. Dividing a number line into 1/n units needs n-1 marks between two whole numbers; students err by drawing 4 marks for fourths or treating the whole line as the unit (Roadblock 2.1), and by placing 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction's numbers as separate whole numbers (Roadblock 2.2).
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide 'Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for Kindergarten Through 8th Grade' (Siegler et al. 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)

sources.claim: Students often view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), diagnosable by having them label hatch marks on a 0-to-1 number line; equivalent fractions can be shown to occupy the same point using dual-labelled lines.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide 'Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K-8' (Siegler et al. 2010), Recommendations 2 and 5

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils count up and down in tenths and recognise, find and write fractions of a set; the number line is used to represent fractions as numbers.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS2, Year 3 fractions)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 9–11 — the ocean is Earth's climate engine: it absorbs a large share of the Sun's heat and atmospheric CO2, drives the water cycle through evaporation, and its currents distribute warmth around the planet, shaping weather in distant places.
• Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2): Y4 states of matter/water cycle (evaporation & condensation) and KS2 geography (climate zones); builds toward KS3 Earth's systems.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 5-ESS2-1 (interactions of geosphere/hydrosphere/atmosphere) and MS-ESS2-6 (ocean currents and atmosphere influence regional climates) — the ocean–atmosphere coupling.
• Operational details: three coupled roles — (1) HEAT & CARBON SINK: water stores huge amounts of heat and dissolves CO2, buffering the atmosphere; (2) WATER CYCLE: evaporation from the warm ocean feeds clouds, rain and weather; (3) HEAT DISTRIBUTION: currents (e.g. the Gulf Stream) carry tropical warmth poleward, so the ocean makes some distant coasts far milder than their latitude. The big idea is coupling and TELECONNECTION — the ocean links places that seem unrelated. Keep quantitative detail (>90% heat, ~25% CO2, thermohaline) for KS3.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~9): states the ocean stores heat and CO2 and feeds the water cycle; Tier B (~10): explains evaporation's role and that currents move warmth; Tier C (~11): explains how a current warms a distant coast (a place milder than its latitude because of ocean heat transport).
bestPractices: Frame the ocean as a giant heat store: use the everyday fact that water heats and cools slowly (a coastal town has milder swings than inland) to make the buffering role tangible.
Trace the water-cycle link explicitly: Sun warms ocean → evaporation → clouds → rain/weather — the ocean is the water cycle's main reservoir and engine.
Use a real teleconnection (the Gulf Stream keeping NW Europe milder than same-latitude Canada) so 'currents move heat to distant places' is concrete, not abstract.
Distinguish the three roles clearly (heat/carbon sink, water-cycle driver, heat distributor) then show they operate together as one climate system.
Connect to prior currents work (7–9) and to climate-change basics — the ocean's buffering is why it matters when it warms or acidifies.
keyRepresentations: A coupled ocean–atmosphere diagram: sunlight in, heat stored, evaporation up, currents carrying warmth
A global surface-current map (warm/cold) showing heat carried from tropics to poles
A same-latitude comparison (Gulf-Stream-warmed coast vs a colder one) illustrating teleconnection
A heat-capacity demo visual: land heats/cools fast, ocean slow
commonMisconceptions: 'The atmosphere alone controls climate' — underestimating the ocean's dominant role as heat/carbon store and distributor.
'The ocean is just where weather happens, not a cause of it' — missing that ocean heat and evaporation DRIVE weather.
'Currents only affect the water' — not linking currents to air temperature and climate on distant land.
Confusing weather (today) with climate (long-term pattern) when describing the ocean's influence.
'Places at the same latitude have the same climate' — ignoring ocean heat transport (why NW Europe is mild).

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: the ocean is Earth's climate engine with three coupled roles — (1) a heat and carbon sink that stores a large share of the Sun's heat and dissolves CO2, buffering the atmosphere; (2) a water-cycle driver, where evaporation from the warm ocean feeds clouds, rain and weather; and (3) a heat distributor, where currents (e.g. the Gulf Stream) carry tropical warmth poleward so some coasts are far milder than is typical for their latitude. The big idea is coupling and teleconnection — the ocean links places that seem unrelated. Learners should move from naming separate ocean facts to explaining how a current warms a distant coast and how the three roles operate together as one system. The ocean is a major cause of such mild distant coasts, alongside latitude and prevailing winds, not the only cause. Quantitative detail (>90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases, ~25% of human CO2 emissions, thermohaline terms) is held back for later (KS3).

activities.title: Drive the climate engine: warm the Sun, run the water cycle, reroute a current
feedback: If a learner expects only the water near the current to change, point out the coast's land/air temperature readout and ask: how did the moving water reach the air and land there? (The current carries heat like a conveyor; the sea warms the air above it.)
If a learner says warming the Sun makes the whole Earth hotter immediately, highlight how much heat the ocean takes up first — it stores and buffers heat rather than instantly heating the air.
If a learner treats the three controls as unrelated, ask them to run all three and describe how heat storage, evaporation, and current transport are parts of one connected system.

If a learner concludes the current is the sole reason the coast is mild, acknowledge it is the driver this model spotlights and a major real cause, then note that latitude and prevailing winds also play a part.
activities.rationale: Manipulating a world model with a Sun-intensity control, an evaporation loop, and draggable currents lets coupling and teleconnection be observed through cause and effect rather than only described, and a live current-rerouting action makes the distant-coast consequence concrete. This is one proposed interactive scaffold; the same reasoning can be reached with maps and explanation (see alternatives). The sources support the ocean-science content taught here, not the effectiveness of this medium, and the model's readouts are designed behaviour rather than measured data.
sourceClaims: The ocean absorbs a large share of the Sun's heat and atmospheric carbon dioxide and, through evaporation and currents, drives weather and distributes heat around the planet — acting as Earth's climate regulator.
Ocean surface currents such as the Gulf Stream transport warm tropical water poleward, keeping regions like north-west Europe milder than other locations at the same latitude.
learnerActions: Turn up the tropical Sun in an ocean–atmosphere model and watch the ocean absorb heat and send up plumes of evaporation that build into clouds and rain-belts — the water cycle running visibly.
Trace one warm current (the Gulf Stream) from the tropics toward north-west Europe and read that coast's temperature.

Drag the warm current away from the coast and observe the distant coast's temperature readout drop: it gets colder, but in this model not all the way to the value typical of same-latitude eastern Canada, because the current explains only part of the difference. (The model deliberately spotlights the ocean's heat transport; in reality prevailing winds, blowing off the ocean onto Europe but off a cold continent onto eastern Canada, also contribute, so the ocean is a major — not the only — cause.)
State in your own words why that coast is mild even though it is far from the tropics, and what changed when the current was cut.
activities.intendedInsight: A coast thousands of miles from the tropics can be mild partly because the ocean ferries heat to it; cutting the current chills a place you never touched directly — this is teleconnection and coupling, seen by driving the system. The ocean is a major cause of the mild climate, alongside latitude and winds.

activities.title: Trace the three roles on a coupled ocean–atmosphere diagram
feedback: If a learner names only one role, prompt them to find the other two pathways on the diagram and describe each.
If a learner says the two same-latitude coasts should have the same climate, draw attention to the warm current reaching one of them, while noting latitude and winds also matter.
Reinforce that these roles operate together: the heat the ocean stores is also the heat its currents move and the energy that drives evaporation.
activities.rationale: A tappable or traceable diagram presents the three roles clearly and supports exposition. As a fixed representation it shows the pathways but does not let the learner perturb the Sun or reroute a current, so pair it with manipulation or discussion to build the causal, coupled picture. This is an affordance difference, not evidence that either medium teaches better. The sources support the content shown, not the medium's efficacy.
sourceClaims: The ocean absorbs a large share of the Sun's heat and atmospheric carbon dioxide and, through evaporation and currents, drives weather and distributes heat around the planet — acting as Earth's climate regulator.
Ocean surface currents such as the Gulf Stream transport warm tropical water poleward, keeping regions like north-west Europe milder than other locations at the same latitude.
learnerActions: Study a labelled ocean–atmosphere scene and tap or point to each of the three roles in turn: heat/carbon sink, evaporation (water cycle), and warm current.
For the current, follow its path from the tropics to a distant coast and explain what it carries.
For evaporation, follow the pathway Sun → warm ocean → evaporation → clouds → rain/weather.
Use a same-latitude comparison panel (a Gulf-Stream-warmed coast vs a colder coast at the same latitude) to explain why latitude alone does not set climate.
activities.intendedInsight: The ocean plays three distinct but connected roles, and the same-latitude comparison shows that ocean heat transport, not just latitude, shapes a region's climate.

activities.title: Heat-store comparison: coastal vs inland (water heats and cools slowly)
feedback: If a learner expects the coast and inland town to be identical, link back to the ocean's large heat store that releases warmth slowly.
If a learner says the ocean 'heats the planet up like a radiator', clarify that storing heat and CO2 actually slows how fast the air warms — it buffers rather than simply adds heat.

If you run the physical demo, remember the exact temperatures depend on the materials, quantities and setup; treat the readings as approximate evidence of the general pattern (water changes temperature more slowly than land), not as fixed values.
activities.rationale: Grounding the buffering role in the everyday fact that water changes temperature slowly makes an abstract 'heat sink' tangible and connects to the coastal-vs-inland misconception check in the assessment. If a physical demo is used, outcomes depend on the materials, quantities and setup, so treat measured results as approximate rather than fixed.
sourceClaims: The ocean absorbs a large share of the Sun's heat and atmospheric carbon dioxide and, through evaporation and currents, drives weather and distributes heat around the planet — acting as Earth's climate regulator.
learnerActions: Consider or investigate how water and land differ in how fast they heat and cool (e.g. compare a container of water with dry sand/soil warmed and then cooled, or reason from a given comparison).
Compare a coastal town and an inland town at the same latitude and predict which has milder winters and cooler summers.
Explain, using the idea that the ocean stores heat, why the coast's temperature swings less than inland.
activities.intendedInsight: Because water heats and cools slowly and holds a large amount of heat, the ocean buffers temperature — coastal places have milder swings than inland places at the same latitude.

activities.title: Ask a climate scientist: why is Britain milder than eastern Canada at the same latitude?
feedback: If the learner accepts 'the ocean just sits there', have the scientist contrast coastal and inland climates and name what the sea is doing.
If the learner stops at one mechanism, ask the scientist follow-up questions until two mechanisms and their 'how' are stated.
If the learner treats the current as the only cause, have the scientist confirm it is a major driver while noting latitude and prevailing winds also contribute.
activities.rationale: A dialogue may supplement the other activities by letting learners voice and refine their explanations and handle the teleconnection question directly. On its own it does not let learners perturb the system, so it works best alongside the model or diagram. The source supports the Gulf Stream content, not the dialogue's effectiveness.
sourceClaims: Ocean surface currents such as the Gulf Stream transport warm tropical water poleward, keeping regions like north-west Europe milder than other locations at the same latitude.
learnerActions: Pose questions to (or role-play a dialogue with) a climate scientist about the ocean's three climate roles.
Ask specifically why north-west Europe is milder than many places at the same latitude (such as eastern Canada), and press for how the mechanism works.
Summarise the answer in your own words, naming at least two active ocean roles and how each works.
activities.intendedInsight: The ocean actively stores heat and carbon, drives the water cycle, and redistributes warmth; a distant mild coast is explained largely by heat the ocean carries and releases to the air, alongside latitude and prevailing winds, not by latitude alone.

activities.title: Check your reasoning: the ocean's three roles
feedback: For the warming item, correct 'the ocean heats the whole Earth' to 'absorbing heat and CO2 slows how fast the air warms' with a sink/store analogy.
For the current scenario, if the learner credits latitude only, point to the warm current delivering heat — while noting the ocean is a major, not sole, cause alongside latitude and winds.
Watch for weather/climate confusion: weather is today's conditions, climate is the long-term pattern the ocean helps shape over time.
activities.rationale: Selected-response items can efficiently check each of the three roles and surface specific misconceptions. Recognition items alone do not elicit independent construction of the explanation, so include at least one constructed written or spoken explanation.
sourceClaims: The ocean absorbs a large share of the Sun's heat and atmospheric carbon dioxide and, through evaporation and currents, drives weather and distributes heat around the planet — acting as Earth's climate regulator.
Ocean surface currents such as the Gulf Stream transport warm tropical water poleward, keeping regions like north-west Europe milder than other locations at the same latitude.
learnerActions: Answer questions on how the ocean absorbs heat and CO2 and what that does to atmospheric warming.
Answer questions on evaporation's role in the water cycle.
Work a scenario explaining why a Gulf-Stream coast is mild compared with a same-latitude coast, choosing and justifying the answer.
Where possible, write or say a short explanation rather than only selecting an option, so you construct the mechanism yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can apply all three evidence goals: heat/carbon absorption slowing atmospheric warming, evaporation driving weather, and currents warming distant coasts (a major cause of a mild coast, alongside latitude and winds).

constraints: Hold quantitative detail (>90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases, ~25% of human CO2 emissions, thermohaline circulation terms) for later study (KS3); at this level keep to qualitative roles.

Checkpoint progression: Tier A (~9) states the ocean stores heat and CO2 and feeds the water cycle; Tier B (~10) explains evaporation's role and that currents move warmth; Tier C (~11) explains how a current warms a distant coast (a place milder than its latitude because of ocean heat transport).
Avoid the error that 'absorbing heat' means the ocean heats the whole planet: absorbing heat and CO2 buffers/slows atmospheric warming, and the store is not limitless.
Present the ocean as a major cause of a mild distant coast, not the sole cause: latitude and prevailing winds also contribute. Avoid 'only the ocean' phrasing in learner-facing text.
Distinguish weather (today) from climate (long-term pattern) when describing the ocean's influence.

A tappable/labelled diagram is a fixed representation: it shows pathways but cannot be perturbed, so pair it with manipulation or discussion for causal reasoning. Do not claim a static or 3D representation 'cannot teach' or 'adds nothing' — these are affordance differences, not proven efficacy gaps.
Recognition-only items check knowledge of the roles but do not elicit independent construction; include at least one constructed explanation.
Physical heat-capacity demos depend on materials, quantities and setup; state in the activity itself that measured temperatures are approximate, not fixed outcomes.
Connect to prior currents work (ages 7–9) and to climate-change basics — the ocean's buffering is why warming and acidification matter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both sources carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed the interactive 2D model teaches coupling in a way a static image 'can't' and that a 3D globe 'adds nothing'; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to affordance/limit statements. A static diagram still teaches the pathways; a 3D globe offers a different view at added cost.

The original recommendation said a distant coast is mild 'ONLY because the ocean ferries heat to it' — latitude, prevailing winds and other factors also contribute; the Gulf Stream example is retained but phrased, in both the activity actions, insight and feedback, as the ocean being a major, not sole, cause. The exact relative magnitude of ocean, latitude and wind contributions is beyond the cited sources.
The interactive model's temperature readouts are designed-artefact behaviour illustrating the mechanism, not measured empirical data.

Source claims support that the ocean regulates climate and that the Gulf Stream keeps NW Europe milder than same-latitude locations, but do not establish comparative efficacy of any teaching medium or that any activity has been tested.

probeDeeper: Two towns sit at the same latitude, one by the sea and one far inland. Which has milder winters, and what is the ocean doing to cause that?
You said the ocean absorbs CO2 and heat — does that make the air warmer or cooler than it would be without the ocean? Why?
If the ocean's currents suddenly stopped moving, would climates in distant places change? Which way?
Where does the water in clouds and rain mostly come from, and what does that have to do with the sea?
assess.correctAnswer: The ocean is not passive — it is Earth's climate engine. It soaks up a huge share of the Sun's heat and a lot of the carbon dioxide from the air, which slows warming; water evaporating from it feeds clouds and rain (the water cycle); and its currents carry warmth from the tropics toward colder places, so a current can make a distant coast far milder than it would otherwise be. So the ocean stores heat and carbon and moves warmth around the planet — it actively shapes weather and climate.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The ocean is a passive puddle; only the Sun/atmosphere drive climate' — no active ocean role.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a coastal town with an inland one at the same latitude; ask why the coast is milder — introduce the sea storing and moving heat.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the ocean just sits there; the Sun and the wind do all the work of making weather and climate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains climate with Sun and air alone; can't name anything the ocean does.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The ocean warms the whole planet up' — hears 'absorbs heat' as making Earth hotter rather than buffering/storing it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a sink analogy: the ocean soaks up heat and CO2, keeping the air cooler than it would be — but the store isn't limitless.
errorPatterns.distractor: The ocean heats the planet — it soaks up the Sun's warmth and then makes the whole Earth hotter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the sea heats the Earth like a radiator; misses that absorbing heat and CO2 actually slows atmospheric warming.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Currents are just for animals/boats, not for heat' — doesn't connect moving water to moving warmth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace a warm current (e.g. the Gulf Stream) from the tropics to a mild northern coast; the water carries heat like a conveyor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Knows currents exist but doesn't link them to distant climates; surprised a current could warm another continent.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the ocean as a passive container; credits climate to the Sun/air alone.
responseLevels.full: Explains at least two active mechanisms — heat/CO2 absorption slowing warming, evaporation feeding the water cycle, currents redistributing warmth — with how each works, and applies them to a new case (coastal vs inland climate, or a stalled current).
responseLevels.partial: Names one or two ocean roles (absorbs heat, has currents) as separate facts but can't explain the mechanism or connect them into 'climate engine'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child says 'the ocean is just a big puddle sitting there — it's the Sun and the air that make the weather and the climate, the sea doesn't really do anything'. Do you agree the ocean is just a passive puddle? If it does more than that, tell me two things the ocean actually DOES to the climate, and how.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who sees the sea as a passive container credits only the Sun and air and can name nothing the ocean does; a child with the concept names active roles — absorbing heat/CO2, driving evaporation, redistributing warmth via currents — and can say how. Requiring TWO mechanisms 'and how' blocks a lucky one-word guess.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Shapes of land and water (landforms & water bodies)

- **Standards — UK (KS1/KS2 Geography — use basic geographical vocabulary for physical features; use maps and simple models):** Children name and describe landforms (mountain, valley, hill, plain, cliff) and water bodies (river, lake, ocean, pond) and represent an area's features on a simple map/model.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-ESS2-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-2].

- **Operational details:** Two joined goals: (1) a vocabulary of physical features — mountain, valley, hill, plain, cliff; river, lake, ocean, pond — each pinned to its defining shape (a valley is a low dip between higher land; a plain is flat and wide); and (2) the modelling skill of representing those features for a real area on a map or relief model, understanding that a map is a bird's-eye stand-in for the real place. Use photographs to build the words, then a map or a built model (sand tray, salt-dough relief, blue for water) so children translate 3D land into a 2D/scaled representation. Emphasise that models leave out detail but keep the shapes and positions that matter.
bestPractices: Pin each landform/water word to its defining SHAPE using photographs before mapping (valley = dip between highlands, plain = wide and flat).
Move from real place → model: build a sand tray or salt-dough relief, or draw a map, so children translate 3D land into a scaled representation.
Make the map's conventions explicit — bird's-eye view, blue = water, and that a model keeps shapes/positions but drops detail.
Contrast confusable pairs (hill vs mountain; lake vs pond; river vs lake) by their defining features.
Have children model THEIR local area or a story's setting so the representation maps to something real to them.
keyRepresentations: Photo cards of landforms and water bodies matched to their names.
A simple map (bird's-eye) with blue water and shaded relief.
A physical relief model (sand tray, salt dough) of an area.
A landform–description matching set (mountain ↔ 'very high, steep land').
commonMisconceptions: 'A map shows what you see standing there' — not grasping the bird's-eye/top-down view.
'Hill and mountain are the same' (or lake and pond) — not distinguishing by size/height.
'Rivers and lakes are the same because both are water' — missing that a river flows and a lake is still.
'The blue on a map is the sky' — not reading blue as water.
'A model is a toy, not a representation' — not seeing the model as standing for a real place.

learn.summary: For 7–8 year-olds learning the shapes of land and water: pin each landform and water-body word to its defining shape using photographs, then have children build or draw a simple model/map of a real area so they translate 3D land into a scaled, bird's-eye representation. The culminating goal (NGSS 2-ESS2-2 / KS1-2 Geography) is developing a model that keeps key features and their positions while deliberately dropping detail. A vocabulary scene, matching/sorting checks, and 3D terrain sculpting are complementary approaches with different purposes.

activities.title: Build a map of an area from land and water features
feedback: If the river is drawn running uphill or away from lower water, ask: which way does water flow? Trace from the high mountains down to the lowest water body.
When a learner matches the top-down map to the side-on relief, confirm that the blue squiggle on the flat map is the same river seen from above.
If a child worries the model is 'wrong' because it is small or missing trees, affirm that a good model keeps the important features and their arrangement and drops the rest on purpose.
activities.rationale: The standard asks learners to develop a model of land and water in an area, so active composition plus linking top-down to side-on views turns passive naming into representation and shows how features relate. An optional interactive builder that nudges a river toward the lowest water, and a toggle between bird's-eye and relief views, make this mechanism concrete; a physical sand/salt-dough build serves the same goal hands-on. Efficacy of any specific builder is untested and proposed only.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-ESS2-2: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-2].
KS1/KS2 geography: use basic geographical vocabulary for key physical features and use maps and simple models to represent places.
learnerActions: Compose an area by placing landform pieces (a mountain range along one edge, hills, a valley between higher land, a flat wide plain, a cliff) and water pieces (a lake in a hollow, a river, an ocean at an edge).
Draw or lay down a river so it runs downhill from the mountains, through the valley, into the lake and on towards the sea.
Label each feature in place as it is added.

Switch or compare between the bird's-eye (top-down) map and a side-on relief view of the same area, so the flat blue line you drew for the river becomes a river threading the valley in the relief model.
As a hands-on complement, build a salt-dough or sand-tray relief of your own local area (blue for water) and then draw its bird's-eye map.
activities.intendedInsight: A map is the same land seen from directly above; features connect sensibly (water flows downhill, so a modelled river runs toward lower water), and a model keeps the shapes and positions that matter while leaving out detail.

activities.title: Name and compare landforms and water bodies from photographs
feedback: For 'river vs lake', prompt: does the water flow along a long channel, or mostly stay in one hollow? A river flows along from higher to lower land; a lake's water mostly stays in one place, even if it has small waves.
For 'hill vs mountain', compare height and steepness with clear side-by-side examples.

In a photograph, if a child mixes up blue water with the sky, use position and shape to tell them apart: a water body sits low in the land (a hollow, valley or at the coast), while the sky is above the horizon. (The separate convention that blue means water on a map is covered in the map-reading activity.)
activities.rationale: Pinning vocabulary to defining shapes with real photographs builds the naming half of the goal and pre-empts confusable-pair misconceptions. This activity supports vocabulary strongly; recognition on its own does not elicit the build-a-model skill the standard foregrounds, so pair it with a construction task.
sourceClaims: KS1/KS2 geography: use basic geographical vocabulary for key physical features and use maps and simple models to represent places.
learnerActions: Explore a rich landscape scene (or photo cards) containing a mountain, valley, hill, plain, cliff, river, lake, ocean and pond.
Reveal each feature's name and its defining shape (valley = a low dip between higher land; a plain = flat and wide).

Answer shape-comparison prompts that contrast confusable pairs: 'mountain or hill?' (height/size), 'lake or pond?' (size), 'river or lake?' (a river flows along a long channel; a lake's water mostly stays in one hollow, though it may have waves and streams flowing in or out).
activities.intendedInsight: Each landform and water-body word is tied to a defining shape or behaviour, not just a label, so similar features can be told apart.

activities.title: Sort and match features; read a simple map
feedback: If a learner calls the blue area on the map 'sky', remind them that on a map blue stands for water and the view is looking straight down from above.
If land/water sorting slips, revisit the defining feature of each item.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorising and single map-reading questions give a clean check of naming and classification. This checks recognition and classification; it does not by itself require the learner to construct a model, so pair it with a build/draw task.
learnerActions: Match photographs to landform/water names (e.g. mountain ↔ 'very high, steep land').
Categorise features as land or water.
Read a simple bird's-eye map and answer: 'what is the blue area on this map?'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can classify features and begin reading map conventions (bird's-eye view, blue = water).

activities.title: Sculpt 3D terrain and flip to its map (extension)
feedback: After sculpting, ask the child to look straight down at their terrain and compare what they see to the flat map.
Check that raised land and hollows on the model correspond to the right places on the map.
Note that a physical clay/sand relief has real thickness and only approximates the land, whereas the flat map is its top-down representation; neither is the real place.
activities.rationale: Hands-on or 3D terrain work is genuinely spatial and may strengthen the link between 3D land and a 2D map. For this age the core targets are met in 2D, so treat 3D as a rich extension that offers a different experience rather than a required mechanism; its added benefit over 2D is not established here.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-ESS2-2: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-2].
learnerActions: Raise a mountain, carve a valley, and flood a lake in a manipulable 3D terrain (physical modelling clay/sand, or a screen model).
Then view or draw the same terrain's flat bird's-eye map to connect the 3D shape to its top-down representation.
activities.intendedInsight: The same piece of land can be experienced as a 3D shape and as a 2D map; the map records the shapes and positions seen from above.

constraints: Cover at least four landforms (mountain, valley, plain, hill, cliff) and at least three water bodies (river, lake, ocean, pond).
Make map conventions explicit: bird's-eye/top-down view, blue = water, and that a model keeps shapes and positions but drops detail on purpose.
Anchor at least one modelling task to something real to the child (their local area or a story's setting).

Matching, sorting and single-answer map questions assess recognition and classification; they do not on their own require the learner to construct a model, so pair them with a build/draw task to meet the standard.
A tappable naming scene builds vocabulary but does not by itself elicit the build-a-model skill; use it alongside a construction activity.

Treat 3D terrain sculpting as an optional extension, not a requirement; a physical cutout or relief has real thickness and approximates the land, while a flat map is the top-down representation of it.
Present the river rule as the age-appropriate heuristic 'water flows downhill' (so a modelled river runs toward lower water), not as an invariant of all real drainage.

The 'river runs downhill to the lowest water body' rule is a sound simplification for this age: water flowing downhill under gravity is physically correct, but the claim that a river always reaches the lowest water body on the map is a modelling heuristic, not an invariant of all real drainage; present it as 'water flows downhill'.

probeDeeper: If your model doesn't show every house and tree, does that make it useless? Why or why not?
How is a mountain different from a hill on your model?
Someone new to the area uses your map. What should it help them do?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes, it can still be a good model. A model or map represents where things are and their shapes — not every detail — and it doesn't have to be full size. Its job is to show the arrangement of land (hills, valleys, plains) and water (rivers, lakes) so you can understand the area or find your way around it.
