pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** What Living Things Need

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y2 Animals including humans & Y2 Plants):** "find out about and describe the basic needs of animals, including humans, for survival (water, food and air)" and "find out and describe how plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy." The two need-lists are deliberately DIFFERENT and children compare them.

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-LS1-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-LS1-1]." DCI LS1.C: all animals need food and get it from plants or other animals; plants need water and light. The emphasis is on OBSERVING PATTERNS across many organisms, not memorising a list.

- **Operational details:** Teach need as something that has CONSEQUENCES when withheld — the concept only becomes real when the child sees what happens if a need is missing. Run the classic split-plant investigation (one plant with water/light, one deprived) and observe over days; the wilting plant is the evidence that anchors 'need'. For animals, build on the child's own experience (hunger, thirst, needing air) and extend it to other animals. Crucially, contrast the two lists: animals need FOOD (they cannot make their own), plants need LIGHT (they make their own food) — this seeds the later idea that animals depend on plants. Keep 'air' concrete (we breathe; a candle/animal needs air) without going into gas exchange.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can list animal needs (water, food, air, shelter/warmth) and plant needs (water, light, air, suitable temperature) and predict a consequence of a missing need ("no water → the plant wilts"). Appropriate here: observing and describing over days. NOT appropriate: mechanism (photosynthesis, respiration as gas exchange) — that is KS2/KS3. Watch for the over-generalisation that plants 'eat' soil food like animals.
bestPractices: Define 'need' through consequence: run a controlled deprivation (one watered/lit plant vs one deprived) and observe over days so children see that a missing need causes a visible change.
Explicitly contrast the animal list (needs food it cannot make) with the plant list (needs light and makes its own food) to seed the animals-depend-on-plants idea.
Build animal needs from the child's own body experience (hunger, thirst, breathing) then generalise the pattern to other animals, per the NGSS observe-patterns emphasis.
Keep 'air' and 'warmth' concrete and observational; avoid mechanism (photosynthesis, gas exchange) which belongs to later key stages.
Change one variable at a time in any investigation so the cause of a change is unambiguous to young children.
keyRepresentations: Split-plant fair test: identical plants, one given water/light, one deprived, observed over a week.
Two parallel 'need charts' side by side — animal needs vs plant needs — to make the contrast visible.
A care/keep-alive scenario (windowsill or terrarium) where each need is a supply the child provides.
Need → consequence pairing cards ('no water → wilts', 'no food → weak', 'no light → pale').
commonMisconceptions: 'Plants get their food from the soil' — treating soil/water as food and missing that plants make food from light.
Assuming plants and animals need the SAME things (e.g. that plants need to be 'fed' food, or that animals photosynthesise).
Thinking a need is optional or cosmetic rather than survival-critical, because consequences are slow and unseen.
Confusing 'want' with 'need' (a pet 'needs' a toy) — not distinguishing survival needs from comforts.

learn.summary: For 5–7 year olds learning what living things need to survive. The core idea is that a 'need' is defined by what happens when it is withheld: observing a visible consequence (a wilting plant) anchors the concept. Children build animal needs from their own body experience (hunger, thirst, breathing), then compare the animal list (needs food it cannot make) with the plant list (needs light and makes its own food), seeding the later idea that animals depend on plants. Keep air and warmth concrete and observational; avoid mechanism (photosynthesis, gas exchange) which belongs to later key stages.

activities.title: Side-by-side windowsill care bench
feedback: If a learner gives only water and expects the plant to thrive in the dark, point to the pale, leggy growth: water alone is not enough; the plant also needs light.
If a learner tries to give the plant a food bowl, note that a plant in the light grows without one because it makes its own food using light — only the animal needs feeding.
When a learner restores a missing need and the plant recovers, name it: 'You found the need — without light it went pale; back in the light, its new leaves turn green and it grows stronger.'
Reinforce that changing one thing at a time (e.g. only the light) shows clearly what caused the change.
activities.rationale: Defining 'need' through a controlled deprivation is intended to make the abstract concept concrete and survival-critical for young children, and running plant and animal cases in parallel makes the contrast between the two need-lists visible, seeding the animals-depend-on-plants idea. Standards emphasise observing patterns of what organisms need rather than memorising a list.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y2 requires pupils to describe the basic needs of animals, including humans, for survival (water, food and air), and separately that plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy.

NGSS K-LS1-1 asks children to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-LS1-1] need to survive; DCI LS1.C states all animals need food (obtained from plants or other animals) and plants need water and light.
learnerActions: Set up (or run a model of) two living things to care for: a bean plant in a pot and a small animal such as a hamster in a hutch.

Choose what to provide to each from a shared set of supplies: a watering can, a lamp for light, air, warmth, and a food bowl. With a real hamster, always give it everything it needs; only leave needs out in the model.
Give the plant water but leave it in the dark, and watch over time (days, or time-compressed in a model) to see it stay alive but grow pale and leggy.
Notice that the plant has NO food bowl and still grows, while the animal must be fed — then explain why the two lists differ.
Rescue a wilting or pale plant by restoring the one missing need, and describe what changed.
activities.intendedInsight: A need is proven by its consequence: withhold it and the living thing visibly suffers. Plants and animals need different things — plants need light and make their own food, animals cannot make food and must be fed.

activities.title: Classroom split-plant fair test over a week
feedback: A prediction that the dark plant 'will be fine because it has water' reveals the water-is-enough view; use the observed pale, weak growth to show light is also essential.
A prediction that it goes pale and weak 'because it also needs light' shows an understanding of multiple needs — affirm and extend to air and suitable temperature.
Emphasise the fairness of the test: both plants had the same water, soil and temperature, so a clear difference is most likely due to the one thing we changed — light.
activities.rationale: A real, slow investigation lets children witness that a missing need causes a visible change over time, and the one-variable design helps make the cause clear for young learners. The prediction-and-reason step is diagnostic of whether a child holds a single-need or multiple-need view.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-LS1-1 asks children to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-LS1-1] need to survive; DCI LS1.C states all animals need food (obtained from plants or other animals) and plants need water and light.
learnerActions: Plant two identical seedlings and give both equal water.
Place one in a bright spot and cover the other with a lightproof box (or put it in a dark cupboard) in the same room, keeping water, pot, soil and temperature as similar as possible.
Before the week passes, predict whether the dark seedling will grow as healthily (green and sturdy) as the light one, and say WHY. Remember a plant in the dark may grow taller but pale and floppy.
Observe both plants over several days and record what changes.
Compare the result to the prediction and state which need was missing from the weaker plant.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing only one variable (light) while keeping water, temperature and everything else as similar as possible shows that light is a genuine need for healthy growth: water alone is not enough.

activities.title: Name the needs and what uses them
feedback: If a learner names only a healthy state, prompt: 'What if this one were missing — what would you see?'
If a learner lists animal needs for the plant (e.g. a food bowl), revisit that the plant makes its own food from light and does not eat.
Confirm correct need–part pairings and have the learner say the matching consequence.
activities.rationale: Naming the needs cleanly and tying each to a body part or behaviour supports the standards' need-lists; pairing each with its consequence keeps the concept causal rather than a memorised list. This is a naming/recall-supporting activity: a reveal scene can name each need and show a prepared picture of the missing-need state, but it does not let the child dynamically cause and observe the deprivation, so it works best alongside the deprivation investigations that build the causal insight.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y2 requires pupils to describe the basic needs of animals, including humans, for survival (water, food and air), and separately that plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy.
learnerActions: Look at a plant and an animal and name each basic need aloud: for the plant — water, light, air, suitable temperature; for the animal — water, food, air, shelter/warmth.
Pair each need with the part or behaviour that uses it, e.g. roots take up water, leaves use light, the animal's mouth takes in food.
For each need, say what the living thing would look like if that need were missing (e.g. 'no water → wilts', 'no light → pale', 'no food → weak').
activities.intendedInsight: Each need is linked to a part or behaviour of the organism and to a specific consequence if it is missing.

activities.title: Sort and match: plant needs, animal needs, both
feedback: If a learner places a food bowl under 'plant needs', revisit that soil and water are not the plant's food — the plant makes food from light; soil gives water and support.
If a learner says 'plants get their food from the soil', explain that at this age we establish plants need light to grow and make their own food.
Confirm correct sorts by having the learner say which needs are shared and which differ.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and matching check whether a child has internalised the comparison between the two lists, and the chosen common misconception directly surfaces the soil-as-food error. This activity checks recall of the lists rather than building the causal insight on its own, so pair it with the investigations.
sourceClaims: Children commonly hold that plants get their food from the soil like animals eat, rather than making their own food from light — a persistent teleological/animal-analogy misconception to address when contrasting plant and animal needs.
learnerActions: Sort need cards into three groups: 'plant needs', 'animal needs', and 'both'.
Match each 'need' card to a 'consequence of lacking it' card (e.g. no water → wilts; no food → weak; no light → pale).
Consider the common wrong idea that 'plants get their food from the soil' and explain why it is incorrect.
Optionally use a 'how much water' slider to show that too little or too much is a problem.
activities.intendedInsight: The two need-lists overlap (water, air, suitable temperature/warmth) but differ in key ways (plants need light and make their own food; animals need food they cannot make).

activities.title: Talk in-role with a thirsty plant or hungry pet
feedback: If a learner offers a plant food, use the character to redirect: 'I don't eat food — I make mine from light; what I need is...'
Praise correct inferences and ask the learner to name the consequence that would follow if the need stayed unmet.
For the goldfish, confirm that it needs to be in water to breathe and stay alive, so out of water it is missing what it needs; for the worm, confirm that even underground it still needs air.

If a learner says a plant needs to sleep, gently separate the survival needs shared by plants and animals (water, air, suitable conditions — plus light for plants and food for animals) from behaviours like sleeping that not every living thing does.
activities.rationale: In-role dialogue can motivate care-reasoning and elicit children's ideas, which may surface misconceptions. Dialogue describes consequences rather than letting the child observe them, so it complements the deprivation investigations rather than replacing them.
learnerActions: Take part in a conversation where a plant or animal gives graded hints about how it feels (e.g. 'my leaves are drooping...', 'I feel hungry...').
Infer which need is missing from the hints and say what to provide.
Explain, for a plant, why you would NOT offer it food, and for an animal why you would.
Extend the pattern to other animals: say what a goldfish would be missing if it were taken out of the water, and point out that a worm in the soil still needs air.
Talk about whether sleeping is a need that all living things share — note that an animal such as the hamster sleeps but a plant does not, so sleeping is not a universal survival need.
activities.intendedInsight: Caring reasoning — matching a described symptom to the missing need — reinforces that each need has a felt consequence, that the same pattern holds across different animals, and that plant and animal needs differ, with some human/animal behaviours (like sleeping) not being universal needs.

constraints: Keep content at the concrete/observational level for ages 5–7: children list animal needs (water, food, air, shelter/warmth) and plant needs (water, light, air, suitable temperature) and predict a consequence of a missing need.
Do not teach mechanism (photosynthesis, respiration as gas exchange) — that belongs to later key stages. Keep 'air' and 'warmth' concrete (we breathe; a candle or animal needs air).
Address the over-generalisation that plants 'eat' soil food like animals: at this age establish that soil gives water and support, and plants make their own food from light.
Distinguish survival needs from wants/comforts (a pet 'needs' a toy) and from human/animal-specific behaviours (a plant does not need to sleep or have a house).
Change only one variable at a time in any investigation so the cause of a change is unambiguous.
Sort/match and reveal-the-state scenes check recall of the lists; they do not on their own build the causal insight that comes from observing deprivation, so use them alongside an investigation.
A time-compressed care model is a scaffold that compresses the real waiting period; pair it with a real classroom investigation over a week so children see the genuine timescale and evidence.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Legacy source flags: the DfE KS1 claim was marked verified; the NGSS K-LS1-1 claim and the Rueschhoff plant-misconceptions claim were marked not verified. Treat the latter two as unconfirmed.

The legacy row asserted that a live care-sim delivers cause-and-effect 'exactly what a static picture cannot deliver' and that a 3D environment 'adds nothing'. These are catalog-preference claims, not established efficacy findings, and have been removed/softened. A fixed image can still teach the need-lists; a 3D view simply offers a different experience without being necessary or useless for this spatially-independent concept.
The time-compressed model is pedagogically useful but it is a representation, not real growth; retained as a scaffold with the real week-long investigation preserved alongside.

Conceptual audit: a plant watered but kept dark growing pale/leggy while surviving for a while is biologically reasonable for a seedling living on stored reserves; kept qualitative ('pale, weak, eventually dies') rather than asserting an exact timeline.

The DfE wording names plant needs as water, light and a suitable temperature and does not mention air; air is retained as a plant need because it is biologically correct and the original row treats 'plants don't need air' as a misconception to correct. The child-facing plant list therefore includes a need beyond those named in the cited DfE claim.

Concrete probe examples from the source assessment (goldfish out of water, worm in soil, and sleeping as a human/animal-specific behaviour) were restored into the conversation activity and constraints so they are not lost.

assess.poeTask: Grow two identical seedlings with equal water — one on a bright windowsill, one shut in a dark cupboard — for a week. Before the week passes, ask the child to predict whether the dark one will grow as well as the light one, and WHY. The reason is diagnostic: predicting it grows fine 'because it has water' holds the water-is-enough view; predicting it goes pale and weak because it also needs light shows an understanding of multiple needs.
probeDeeper: What would happen to a goldfish if we took it out of the water? Which need is missing?
Does a plant need air? What about a worm in the soil?
A plant needs light, but you need to sleep — is sleeping a need that all living things share?
If we forgot to feed a hamster, which of its needs are we not meeting?
assess.correctAnswer: It won't grow well — it's missing light. Plants need light (as well as water, air and a suitable temperature); without light the plant goes pale, weak and eventually dies, because water alone isn't enough. Living things suffer if any one of their basic needs is missing.

errorPatterns.pattern: plants only really need water (light and air not essential)
errorPatterns.nextMove: list all a plant's needs — water, light, air, suitable temperature — and show light is essential using a dark-grown seedling
errorPatterns.distractor: It will be fine — as long as a plant has water it will grow
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the watered plant will be fine in the dark

errorPatterns.pattern: plants get their food from the soil / plants 'eat' soil
errorPatterns.nextMove: at this age, establish that plants need light to grow and make food; soil gives water and support, it isn't 'food'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the probe says soil is the plant's food and light isn't needed

errorPatterns.pattern: plants don't need air (only animals do)
errorPatterns.nextMove: include air among plant needs, alongside animals'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: omits air from a plant's needs

errorPatterns.pattern: living things need the same things humans do (a plant needs to sleep, or needs a house)
errorPatterns.nextMove: distinguish universal needs (water, air, food/light, suitable conditions) from human-specific wants
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes human wants to plants

responseLevels.gap: Says the plant will be fine with just water, or lists no needs; cannot say what happens when a need is missing.
responseLevels.full: Names the basic needs of both plants (water, light, air, suitable temperature) and animals (water, food, air, shelter), predicts what happens when one is missing, and distinguishes shared needs from human wants.
responseLevels.partial: Lists some needs for plants or animals, but as a memorised list — cannot predict the consequence of a specific missing need, or applies animal needs to plants inconsistently.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A plant is watered every day but kept in a dark cupboard with the door shut. It's getting plenty of water — so will it grow well, or is it missing something it needs? Explain what will happen and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks water is the main thing a plant needs says it'll be fine; a child who knows plants also need light predicts it fails and names the missing need. The reason tier surfaces which needs the child actually holds.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 — describe a simple ocean food chain: tiny plants (phytoplankton) → small animals → bigger fish → top predators like sharks, showing all ocean life depends on others for food.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS1): Y2 'describe how animals obtain their food from plants and other animals, using the idea of a simple food chain, and identify and name different sources of food' — this is the ocean instance of the KS1 food-chain objective.
• Standards — US (NGSS): builds toward 5-PS3-1 / 5-LS2-1 (matter and energy movement) but at K–2 the accessible anchor is 'animals get food from plants and other animals' — who-eats-whom sequencing.
• Operational details: teach the ARROW as 'is eaten by' (energy/food flows in the arrow's direction) — the single most important convention and the classic error source. Start the chain with tiny plants (phytoplankton) so children grasp that the ocean, like land, is powered by plants they can barely see. Keep to a clear 3–4 link chain (phytoplankton → small fish/krill → big fish → shark).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete, ~5–6): orders pictures big-eats-small and says 'the shark eats the fish'; Tier B (~6–7): builds a ≥3-link chain and states it starts with tiny plants; Tier C (~7): reads the arrow correctly as 'is eaten by' and explains each animal depends on the one before it.
bestPractices: Define the arrow explicitly as 'is eaten by' and rehearse reading chains aloud in the arrow direction — pre-empt the near-universal 'arrow points to who eats' reversal.
Always begin the chain with a producer (phytoplankton/algae): make visible that even the ocean's food starts with tiny plants using sunlight.
Use physical/manipulable cards the child arranges into order, then link with arrows — building beats being shown a finished chain.
Probe dependence with 'what if?' removal ('if the tiny plants vanished, what happens to the small fish? the shark?') to establish the chain-of-dependence idea (seeds later food-web work).
Use real, recognisable ocean species (phytoplankton, krill/small fish, mackerel, shark) rather than abstract 'small/medium/big'.
keyRepresentations: A left-to-right ocean food chain with clearly labelled 'is eaten by' arrows
Drag-and-arrange picture cards (phytoplankton, small fish, big fish, shark) that snap into a chain
A nested 'who's inside who' cutaway showing energy passing up the chain
A sun → phytoplankton starter icon making the energy source explicit
commonMisconceptions: Arrow reversal: reading the arrow as 'eats' rather than 'is eaten by' — the dominant error in food-chain teaching.
'Ocean food chains start with a big animal' — missing that they start with tiny plants/plankton because those aren't obvious.
'Big/scary animals are the most important' — not seeing that predators depend on everything below them.
Believing the sea has no plants ('there's nothing green down there') so children can't locate the producer.
Thinking each animal eats only one thing / the chain is the whole story (the web extension corrects this later).

learn.summary: Help children aged 5–7 describe a simple ocean food chain: tiny plants (phytoplankton) → small animals (krill/small fish) → bigger fish → top predator (shark). The two core goals are (1) understanding that this ocean food chain STARTS with tiny plants that make their own food from sunlight, and (2) reading the arrow correctly as 'is eaten by' so food/energy flows up the chain toward the eater. A central proposed activity is to have children build a chain from cards, then remove a link to notice that every animal depends on the one below it.

activities.title: Build-and-break the ocean food chain
feedback: If a child puts the shark first because it is biggest/strongest, ask 'what does the shark's dinner eat, and what does THAT eat?' — keep going down until you reach the tiny plant that makes its own food. That base is where the chain starts.

If a child reads or draws the arrow as 'eats' (pointing from predator to prey), re-state the arrow as 'is eaten by' / 'gives its energy to': it points TOWARD the eater. Trace energy flowing UP the chain, not the mouth pointing down.

If a child asks what feeds the phytoplankton, explain that phytoplankton make their own food using sunlight (like plants on land), so they do not need to eat any other living thing — they are the true start of the chain.
When a link is removed and the child notices the animals above lose their food, name it: 'every animal depends on the one below it.'
activities.rationale: This activity instantiates the KS1 objective of describing a simple food chain and centres the phytoplankton producer base that everything else depends on. Constructing and then disrupting the chain lets children build the sequence themselves and reason about dependence, rather than being shown a finished chain, and it rehearses the two common error sources (start-point and arrow direction). Using real, recognisable species keeps it concrete for this age. Efficacy of this specific task is proposed, not empirically validated.
sourceClaims: UK KS1 Y2 science requires pupils to describe how animals obtain food from plants and other animals using the idea of a simple food chain, and to identify and name different sources of food.
Phytoplankton are microscopic marine algae that form the base of the ocean food web, using sunlight to produce food (photosynthesis) — nearly all ocean life ultimately depends on them.
learnerActions: Take a set of picture cards — phytoplankton (tiny sea plants), krill or small fish, a bigger fish (e.g. mackerel), and a shark — and arrange them into who-eats-whom order along a lane.
Place the tiny plants first and say aloud why the chain starts there ('the plants make their own food from sunlight').

Draw or place an arrow between each pair and read the chain aloud in the arrow direction, saying 'is eaten by' at each arrow (phytoplankton is eaten by the small fish, which is eaten by the big fish, which is eaten by the shark).
Remove one card (for example the small fish) and talk through what happens to the animals that depended on it — which ones no longer have food?
activities.intendedInsight: This ocean food chain begins with tiny plants that make their own food from sunlight, and each animal depends on the one before it; the arrow means 'is eaten by' and shows food/energy travelling up toward the eater.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal predator and prey
feedback: If a child names only what an animal eats, prompt 'and what eats IT?' to surface its two-way position in the chain (except the shark, which nothing in this chain eats; and the phytoplankton, which makes its own food and eats nothing).
Reinforce that the arrow reads 'is eaten by' every time, in the same direction.
activities.rationale: A labelled reveal clearly presents the sequence and arrow meaning and is a lower-effort companion to construction. It shows the chain rather than letting the child build it or experience a link being removed, so it works best alongside the build activity. It does not by itself elicit the dependence reasoning.
learnerActions: Look at a pre-drawn ocean food chain with labelled 'is eaten by' arrows.
Tap each animal to reveal what it eats and what eats it, then say the relationship aloud ('the mackerel eats the small fish and is eaten by the shark').
Point along the chain and say which way the food/energy travels.
activities.intendedInsight: The producer (phytoplankton) makes its own food and has nothing below it; each animal above the base has prey below it, and every animal except the top predator also has a predator above it. The arrow consistently points to the eater.

activities.title: Order the chain and explain the arrow
feedback: If the order is wrong, return to building a chain from cards and tracing down to the plant base.
If the arrow is read as 'eats', re-rehearse 'is eaten by' pointing toward the eater.
activities.rationale: A sequencing task plus a direct question on arrow meaning is a tight check of the two core evidence goals. This format confirms the ordered answer and the stated meaning but does not by itself elicit the dependence reasoning that removing a link produces.
learnerActions: Put the pictures in order: phytoplankton → small fish → big fish → shark.
Answer: what does this ocean food chain start with?
Answer: what does the arrow between two animals mean, and which way does it point?
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the child can both sequence the chain producer-first and state that the arrow means 'is eaten by', pointing to the eater.

activities.title: What-if dependence talk (optional companion)
feedback: If a child says the shark is most important because it is biggest, trace the dependence downward until the plant base is reached.
Keep the conversation anchored to the child's own built or drawn chain so the reasoning stays concrete.
activities.rationale: Removal 'what-if?' questions can establish the chain-of-dependence idea and pre-empt the 'big/scary = most important' misconception. Dialogue is a useful curiosity and reasoning supplement; it supports but does not replace having the child construct the ordered chain.
learnerActions: With a built chain in front of them, discuss: 'If there were no phytoplankton at all, what would happen to the little animals, then the fish, then the shark?'
Discuss 'Which is more important to the whole chain — the shark or the tiny plants? Why?'

If a marine expert or knowledgeable adult is available, ask curiosity questions like 'what does a shark eat, and what does that eat?' and be nudged to keep tracing down until they name the plant at the bottom.
activities.intendedInsight: Removing the producer collapses everything above it, so the tiny plants — not the biggest animal — underpin the whole chain; this seeds later food-web work.

constraints: Keep to a clear 3–4 link chain (phytoplankton → small fish/krill → big fish → shark); avoid longer chains at this age.

Always begin the chain with a producer (phytoplankton/algae) and make the sunlight→plant energy source explicit, so children can locate the producer despite there being 'nothing obviously green' in the sea.
Define the arrow explicitly as 'is eaten by' and rehearse reading chains aloud in the arrow direction to pre-empt the common 'arrow points to who eats' reversal.
Use real, recognisable ocean species rather than abstract 'small/medium/big'.

Recognition/ordering and tap-to-reveal formats confirm the sequence and stated arrow meaning but do not on their own elicit the dependence reasoning; pair them with construction and removal to meet that goal.
The chain simplifies reality (each animal shown eating only one thing); flag that real feeding relationships form a web, to be developed later.
Card or screen pieces are concrete stand-ins for living organisms; the represented organisms, not the pieces, are what depend on each other.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched, and both carry verified:false in the source row.
All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions; no empirical efficacy for these specific tasks is claimed.

The original source asserted fixed comparative value for live build/break ('that live recompute is precisely what makes dependence FELT') and that '3D adds nothing'. These format-superiority claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits; the underlying observation that a food chain is a relational rather than spatial structure is retained.

The non-preferred conversation and ordering/check approaches were retained as distinct activities because they serve different purposes (curiosity/reasoning and confirmation) rather than being dropped.

The original diagnostic prompt presents a deliberately wrong chain (shark first, plants last) for the child to critique; this is an assessment design detail, preserved as such and never turned into a learner-facing model of a correct chain.
One source-row reteach prerequisite id is internal routing metadata and was not carried into learner-facing guidance.

Both retained sourceClaims support activity[0] because that activity directly instantiates the describe-a-food-chain objective and teaches the phytoplankton producer base; neither source attests to the efficacy of the build-and-break method itself.

probeDeeper: 'You put the tiny plants first. Where do THEY get their food from — does something feed them?'
'Point along your chain — which way does the food/energy travel, up to the shark or down to the plant?'
'If there were no phytoplankton at all, what would happen to the little animals, and then the fish, and then the shark?' (dependence counterexample)
'Which is more important to the whole chain — the shark or the tiny plants? Why?'
assess.correctAnswer: It's the wrong way round. The chain should START with the tiny sea plants (phytoplankton), because they make their own food from sunlight and everything else depends on them. Then small animals eat the phytoplankton, bigger fish eat the small animals, and the shark (a top predator) comes LAST. The arrows point from the food to the eater (phytoplankton → small animal → fish → shark) and mean 'is eaten by' — they show which way the food/energy goes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Starts the chain with the biggest/strongest animal because it seems most important ('the shark is the boss, so it goes first')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what does the shark's dinner eat, and what does THAT eat?' — keep going down until you reach the tiny plant that makes its own food. That base is where the chain starts.
errorPatterns.distractor: The shark comes first because it's the biggest and strongest
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts the top predator first; treats the plant as least important / last

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the arrows — draws them from the eater to its food ('shark → fish' meaning shark eats fish)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-define the arrow as 'is eaten by' / 'gives its energy to' — it points TOWARD the eater. Trace energy flowing UP the chain, not the mouth pointing down.
errorPatterns.distractor: The arrows point from each animal to the food it eats
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says the arrow means 'eats', pointing from predator to prey

errorPatterns.pattern: Puts a tiny plant first but thinks something must feed it too — doesn't grasp that plants make their own food
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain phytoplankton make their own food from sunlight (like plants on land) — nothing has to feed them, so they are the true start of the chain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asks what feeds the phytoplankton; looks for an earlier animal before it

responseLevels.gap: Starts with the biggest predator and/or reverses the arrows; sees the plant as unimportant.
responseLevels.full: Starts the chain with phytoplankton (which make their own food), orders small→big to the top predator, states the arrow means 'is eaten by' pointing to the eater, AND reasons about dependence (removing the base collapses the chain) — not a memorised order.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the order roughly right (plants first) OR the arrow meaning, but not both — e.g. starts with phytoplankton yet still points arrows the wrong way, or can't say plants make their own food.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is an ocean food chain someone made: they put the SHARK first because it's the biggest and strongest, then a fish, then tiny sea plants (phytoplankton) last. Is that the right way round? Tell me what should come FIRST in the chain and why, and what the arrows between them mean.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands food chains starts with the producer (tiny plants) and can say the arrow points to the eater. A child who thinks 'most important = first' starts with the biggest/strongest predator, and often reverses the arrows (predator eats prey, so points at prey). The two tiers catch both the start-point error and the arrow-direction error — each a documented, distinct mistake.

sources.claim: Phytoplankton are microscopic marine algae that form the base of the ocean food web, using sunlight to produce food (photosynthesis) — nearly all ocean life ultimately depends on them.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; apply the commutative, associative and distributive properties as STRATEGIES to multiply and divide (not as formal named laws to memorise).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity', 'multiply … three numbers' (associativity), and use the distributive law within written/mental methods; Y3 begins distributive partitioning.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.5 — 'Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide' (commutative: 6×4=4×6; associative: 2×(3×5) via (2×3)×5; distributive: 8×5+8×2 = 8×7). Note CCSS says pupils need not know the property names.
• Operational details — the point is flexible, efficient calculation: commutativity halves facts to learn and lets you reorder; associativity lets you regroup three factors into an easy pair (2×3×5 → 6×5 or 2×15); distributivity is the big one — split a hard fact/large factor into friendly parts (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) and it is the conceptual seed of the area model and ALL formal written multiplication. Show each property in the array/area model where it is visibly true, then use it to make calculation easier. Division is NOT commutative or associative — make that explicit.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): use commutativity (know 4×6 → 6×4) and split a fact distributively with support (7×6 = 5×6 + 2×6). Tier B (age 8–9): use all three to simplify a calculation and justify with an array. Tier C (age 9): choose the most efficient property for a given calculation and explain why division isn't commutative.
bestPractices: Prove each property visually first — rotate an array for commutativity, regroup counters for associativity, split an array for distributivity — then use it to make a calculation easier, so properties are tools not vocabulary.

Lead with the distributive property as the highest-value strategy: it turns unknown facts into known ones (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) and is the direct bridge to the area model and formal written multiplication.
Use the area model as the shared home of all three properties so the later written algorithm is 'properties made compact', not a new trick.
Explicitly contrast × (commutative/associative) with ÷ (neither) using counterexamples so children don't overgeneralise.
Prioritise strategy CHOICE — give calculations where different properties are most efficient and discuss which to pick.
keyRepresentations: Rotatable array — commutativity (same array, two orientations, same total)
Split area model — distributivity (8×7 as 8×5 + 8×2 two sub-rectangles)
Regroupable groups-of-groups — associativity (2×3×5 rebracketed)
Bar model / number sentence chains showing the equivalent forms
commonMisconceptions: Overgeneralising commutativity/associativity to division (32÷8 = 8×32; (24÷4)÷2 = 24÷(4÷2)).
Applying the distributive split incorrectly — e.g. 8×7 = 8×5 + 2 (forgetting to multiply the second part) or splitting the wrong factor.
Treating the properties as names to memorise rather than strategies to use, so they aren't deployed in calculation.
Not seeing that the area model IS the distributive law, so written multiplication later feels disconnected.
Thinking reordering changes the answer, or conversely that any reordering is always allowed.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, teach the commutative, associative and distributive properties as calculation STRATEGIES (not named laws to memorise) that leave a total invariant. Prove each property visibly in an array/area model first, then use it to make a hard calculation easy. Centre the distributive split (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as the highest-value strategy and the direct bridge to the area model and formal written multiplication. Explicitly contrast × (commutative/associative) with ÷ and − (neither), and prioritise strategy choice — which property is most efficient for a given calculation.

activities.title: Property playground: rotate, split, regroup on one array
feedback: If a learner writes 8×7 = 8×5 + 2 = 42, draw 8 rows of 7, cut into 8 rows of 5 and 8 rows of 2, and ask how many squares are in the second block: it is 8×2 = 16, not 2, so 40 + 16 = 56. Make the split visible before returning to symbols.

If a learner distrusts regrouping and recomputes (2×3)×4 and 2×(3×4) separately each time, build both with cubes (e.g. 4 lots of a 2-by-3 group, which is 6 taken 4 times, versus 2 lots of 12, where 12 is 3×4), count once each (24 both times), and name associativity as 'regrouping a multiplication never changes the total'.

If a learner says order 'doesn't matter' for division or subtraction (e.g. 8−7 = 7−8), show quick counterexamples such as 10−3 = 7 while 3−10 cannot be done with whole numbers (it goes below zero on a number line), and 12÷3 = 4 while 3÷12 is less than 1, so the property stays bound to × and + specifically.
Prompt justification: 'You said 8×5 + 8×2 — why is that the same as 8×7 and not more or less?' and 'Could you use 8×5 to help work out 8×9? Show me the split.'
activities.rationale: For multiplication, these properties are transformations that leave the total invariant, so letting a learner rotate, split and regroup while a live total holds is intended to help them discover each property rather than be told it, and immediately use it to simplify a calculation. A visible split-array is the area model, which embodies the distributive property and bridges to written multiplication. A division mode in which swapping the numbers changes the answer directly addresses the common overgeneralisation of commutativity to division. Dragging, live recolouring and the equal-total display are concrete examples of how the mechanism is made felt, not required implementations.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity, multiply three numbers, and use distributive partitioning within methods.
3.OA.5 requires applying commutative, associative and distributive properties as strategies to multiply and divide; pupils need not know the property names.
The area model embodies the distributive law and bridges to formal written multiplication; properties should be shown in arrays before being used as calculation strategies.
learnerActions: On an array/area canvas, meet an 'ugly' fact like 8×7. Drag a divider through the 7 to carve the array into 8×5 and 8×2; watch the two sub-rectangles light up as 40 and 16 and combine to 56.
Rotate the same array 90° and confirm the total does not change (8×7 = 7×8) — commutativity as 'same array, two orientations, same total'.
For three factors (2×3×5), toggle or drag the bracket between (2×3)×5 and 2×(3×5), and confirm the total holds — associativity as regrouping into an easier pair (6×5 or 2×15).

Switch to a division mode: swap the two numbers in a ÷ calculation (e.g. 32÷8 = 4 becomes 8÷32, which is less than 1) and see that the answer changes, then say in your own words why division is not commutative (32÷8 is not 8÷32).
Choose your own split for a new ugly fact (e.g. 8×9 = 8×5 + 8×4) and check the partial products add to the whole (40 + 32 = 72).
activities.intendedInsight: In multiplication, reordering, regrouping and splitting change how a calculation is written without changing its total; a hard multiplication fact can be cut into two friendly facts and reassembled. This 'cut-the-hard-one-into-two-easy-ones' move is the distributive property, and it is the same move that formal written multiplication later makes compact. Division and subtraction are not commutative or associative, so swapping or regrouping their numbers can change the answer.

activities.title: Split-area anchor for the distributive fact
feedback: If the learner cannot explain the invariance, point to the shared height (8) across both parts and the widths adding to 7 (5 + 2), so no squares are added or lost.
Connect the picture back to symbols: the whole rectangle's area is the sum of the two parts' areas.
activities.rationale: A fixed, pre-split area diagram is a clean anchor for the distributive idea and the area-model bridge. Because it cannot be moved to vary the split, it shows one case rather than invariance across many, so it supports rather than replaces manipulable exploration; use it as a static anchor or consolidation after the playground.
sourceClaims: The area model embodies the distributive law and bridges to formal written multiplication; properties should be shown in arrays before being used as calculation strategies.
learnerActions: Study an area rectangle for 8×7 that is pre-split into 8×5 and 8×2.
Reveal the labels: left part '8×5 = 40', right part '8×2 = 16', whole '= 56'.
Answer the prompt 'Why does splitting the 7 into 5 and 2 not change the total?' before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: The distributive split keeps the whole fixed because the two sub-rectangles together are exactly the original rectangle; 8×7 and 8×5 + 8×2 name the same quantity.

activities.title: Consolidate and sort: valid forms and the division trap
feedback: For the fill-in, if the learner writes anything other than 2, return to the array: the second part must be 8 rows of 2, i.e. 8×2.
If the learner picks a division distractor for 6×4, remind them commutativity is about reordering the SAME operation, and test the division claim with small numbers (e.g. 6÷4 ≠ 4÷6).
When sorting, have the learner give a counterexample for each 'not true for ÷' statement (e.g. 32÷8 = 4 but 8÷32 is less than 1; (24÷4)÷2 = 3 but 24÷(4÷2) = 12).
activities.rationale: Completing a split, selecting the correct equivalent form and sorting always-true versus division statements target the overgeneralisation misconception. These checks assess and consolidate property USE; they do not by themselves build the invariance intuition, so pair them with the manipulable or anchor activities.
learnerActions: Complete a distributive split: 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×□.
Choose which expression equals 6×4, with 4×6 correct and 6÷4 and 4÷6 offered as tempting wrong choices.
Sort statements into 'always true' versus 'not true for division', e.g. is 32÷8 = 8÷32? Is (24÷4)÷2 = 24÷(4÷2)?
activities.intendedInsight: Property use can be checked and the overgeneralisation to division can be caught: reordering and regrouping hold for × but not for ÷.

activities.title: The lazy mathematician: justify the easiest strategy
feedback: Push for reasons, not just answers: 'Is there an easier way to work that out, and how do you know it gives the same total?'
If the learner accepts an invalid division or subtraction reorder, ask them to test it with a concrete counterexample.
activities.rationale: A Socratic 'is there an easier way?' dialogue prompts strategy choice and verbal justification, which supports deployment of the properties. Discussion complements rather than substitutes for seeing the properties as visual transformations, so use it alongside the array work.
learnerActions: Talk with a 'lazy mathematician' character who always wants the easiest split or reorder for a given calculation.
When the character proposes a move (e.g. regroup 2×3×5 to 6×5, or split 7×6 into 5×6 + 2×6), explain why it gives the same answer.
Decide together which property is most efficient for different calculations and say why.
Catch the character out when it tries to 'reorder' a division or subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the most efficient property and justifying it out loud is part of fluent calculation; not every operation permits reordering.

constraints: Teach these as strategies for efficient calculation, not as formal named laws to memorise; CCSS-M notes pupils need not know the property names.
Make explicit that division is NOT commutative or associative, and that subtraction is not either; use counterexamples so learners do not overgeneralise.
Guard against the additive-split error (8×7 = 8×5 + 2): both parts must be multiplied by the shared factor (8×5 + 8×2).

The static split-area anchor and the sort/fill tasks check and consolidate property use, but a fixed diagram cannot vary the split or regrouping across many cases; manipulable exploration across varied cases can let learners meet the invariance across many instances, so pair the static anchor and check tasks with it.
Recognition and fill-in tasks assess property use; they do not themselves elicit the learner independently choosing and justifying a strategy, which the dialogue and open splits target.
Three-factor associativity can suggest a cuboid, but that belongs to volume; keep properties-as-strategies work in planar arrays/area to avoid added manipulation cost and off-topic meaning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels a 3D treatment as adding 'no invariance insight'; this rewrite keeps the planar focus as a scoped design choice (arrays/area are where these properties are most directly visible) rather than a universal claim that 3D cannot teach anything here.

Arithmetic checked: 8×7 = 56; 8×5 = 40, 8×2 = 16, 40+16 = 56; 8×9 = 72 via 8×5 + 8×4 = 40 + 32; 2×3×5 = 30 via 6×5 or 2×15; 6×4 = 24 = 4×6; (24÷4)÷2 = 3 but 24÷(4÷2) = 12; 32÷8 = 4 but 8÷32 < 1. The additive-split error 8×5 + 2 = 42 appears only as a misconception to correct, never as a valid alternative.
The source mentions 'double 8×3.5' in passing for 8×7; this involves a non-integer partial and is not appropriate for this age group, so it is omitted from learner-facing actions.
The assessment's responseLevels, diagnosticPrompt and probe questions were not altered by this rewrite; they inform but are not restated as separate guidance fields.

Efficacy wording in constraint 4 was softened from 'is what lets learners feel the invariance' to a qualified affordance, since no source establishes manipulation as the necessary mechanism for building the invariance intuition.

probeDeeper: You said 8×5 + 8×2. Why is that the same as 8×7 and not more or less?
What if it had been 8 × 9 — could you use 8 × 5 to help? Show me the split.
Does this trick also work for 8 − 7? Why or why not?
Someone says 6 × 7 = 6×5 + 2. What went wrong in their thinking?
assess.correctAnswer: 8 × 7 = 56. A child reasoning correctly splits the 7: 8 × 7 is 8 × 5 plus 8 × 2, so 40 + 16 = 56 — because seven groups of eight is the same as five groups of eight and two more groups of eight (distributive property). Any valid split (8×7 = 8×6+8, or double 8×3.5 is not expected here) counts if the REASON is about decomposing one factor into parts that are added.

errorPatterns.pattern: treats distributive split additively on both parts: '8×7 = 8×5 + 2 = 42' — adds the leftover 2 instead of 8×2
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw the array: 8 rows of 7, cut it into 8 rows of 5 and 8 rows of 2; ask how many squares are in the second block — it is 8×2=16, not 2. Make the split visible before returning to symbols.
errorPatterns.distractor: 8 × 7 = 42 (I did 8×5 then added 2)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gets 42 and, when probed, says 'I had 8×5 then added the 2 more'

errorPatterns.pattern: believes changing the grouping changes the answer — does not trust that (2×3)×4 = 2×(3×4); recomputes each time as if they could differ
errorPatterns.nextMove: build both groupings with cubes (2 stacks of 3, taken 4 times vs 2 stacks of 12) and count once each; name associativity as 'regrouping never changes the total'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked if reordering/regrouping factors is 'allowed', child hedges or checks by full recomputation rather than asserting it must be equal

errorPatterns.pattern: over-generalises commutativity/associativity to subtraction or division: 'if 8×7=7×8 then 8−7=7−8'
errorPatterns.nextMove: confront with a quick counterexample (10−3 vs 3−10 using a number line) so the property is bound to × and + specifically, not to all operations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child asserts order 'doesn't matter' for a subtraction or division example

responseLevels.gap: gives 56 only by recomputing or recall, or gets 42 via the additive-split error; cannot explain why decomposing a factor is valid.
responseLevels.full: decomposes a factor and adds the partial products, justifies it as breaking the groups into parts that recombine to the whole (distributive), and transfers the strategy to a new fact (e.g. 8×9 via 8×5+8×4); correctly refuses to apply it to subtraction.
responseLevels.partial: correctly derives 56 from 8×5 and 8×2 for this case but treats it as a one-off trick — cannot generalise the split to a new factor or name why it must work.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I know that 8 × 5 = 40. Without working out 8 × 7 the long way, can you use what you already know to figure it out? Tell me what you did and why it works.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who merely memorises facts can state 56 but cannot justify deriving it and will say 'I just know it' or recompute from scratch. A child who holds the property explains WHY 8×5+8×2 must equal 8×7 — the split of the factor, not luck. The reason-tier separates fact-recall from structural understanding, and the classic distributive error (adding to the wrong factor, or 8×7 = 8×5+2) surfaces here.

sources.claim: Y4 pupils recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity, multiply three numbers, and use distributive partitioning within methods.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Year 4 Number — multiplication and division

sources.claim: 3.OA.5 requires applying commutative, associative and distributive properties as strategies to multiply and divide; pupils need not know the property names.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 3, Operations & Algebraic Thinking (3.OA.B.5)

sources.claim: The area model embodies the distributive law and bridges to formal written multiplication; properties should be shown in arrays before being used as calculation strategies.
sources.source: NCETM primary multiplication guidance & IES/WWC area-model recommendations

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9 (REPRESENTATIONAL). Identify, represent and estimate numbers to 10,000 across MULTIPLE representations — place-value counters, base-ten, expanded form, numeral, and crucially position on a 0-10,000 number line — and move between them. Estimation on the line makes four-digit magnitude concrete.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.2 read/write/compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms; number-line reasoning about magnitude.
• Operational details — Teach representations as interchangeable views of one number, with the number line as the magnitude spine: locate/estimate a four-digit number on 0-10,000 using benchmark landmarks (halfway = 5000, quarters, thousands). Move both ways: given a numeral, place it; given a point, name it. Connect estimation to rounding and to reasoning about 'about how big'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): places a four-digit number roughly on a landmarked 0-10,000 line. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): translates among numeral/expanded/counters and estimates position using benchmarks. Tier C (age 9, extending): estimates on a sparsely-marked line and justifies using nearest landmarks.
bestPractices: Use the 0-10,000 number line as the magnitude spine, with benchmark landmarks (5000 halfway, thousands, 2500/7500) to anchor estimation.
Treat numeral / expanded form / counters / number-line point as interchangeable views and translate in all directions.
Practise both directions on the line: place a given number, and name a marked point.
Progress from densely-marked to sparsely-marked lines so estimation relies on proportional reasoning, not counting ticks.
Link estimation to rounding ('4,367 is about 4,000') and to sense-checking calculations.
keyRepresentations: 0-10,000 number line with benchmark landmarks (the magnitude spine)
Place-value counters and Th|H|T|O chart
Expanded form and numeral (with comma)
Base-ten thousand/hundred/ten/one pieces
Bar/strip model for proportional estimation on the line
commonMisconceptions: Placing numbers by leading digit only (putting 4,900 and 4,100 at the same spot).
Treating the number line as evenly-spaced counting rather than proportional magnitude.
Ignoring landmarks and guessing position.
Confusing representations (reading expanded form as separate numbers).
Mis-scaling: putting 5,000 not at the halfway point of 0-10,000.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, teach four-digit numbers (to 10,000) as one quantity seen through interchangeable views — numeral, expanded form, place-value counters/base-ten, and a point on a 0-10,000 number line — and have learners translate in every direction. The number line acts as the magnitude spine: estimate and place numbers using benchmark landmarks (halfway = 5,000, quarters at 2,500/7,500, thousands), so four-digit magnitude becomes a felt distance rather than a string of digits. A bar/strip model can support proportional reasoning about position. Link estimation to rounding and sense-checking.

activities.title: Linked-representations estimator on a 0-10,000 line
feedback: If the marker is placed by leading digit only (6,300 near a '6' tick on a miscounted scale), reveal the true position lit against the 5,000 halfway and 7,500 three-quarter landmarks so the learner sees 6,300 sits a little past 6,000, past halfway but not yet three-quarters, about midway between 5,000 and 7,500.

When a learner bunches numbers at one end or spaces them evenly regardless of value, build the landmarks together — locate 5,000 first, then 2,500 — and let them self-adjust rather than marking it wrong; proportional sense is still forming at this age.
When one view disagrees with another, translate back and forth explicitly: point to a digit and ask what term it contributes to the expanded form, and where that moves the marker.
activities.rationale: Estimation and multi-representation can be made concrete by acting — moving a marker and seeing proportional feedback, or changing one view and watching the others recompute. Linked, recompute-on-action panels (numeral, expanded, counters, line marker), a bar/strip model, and a fading-ticks estimation game are optional ways to make the mechanism visible; the essential element is the learner acting on the line and reasoning from benchmarks, which is achievable on paper too.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
Read, write and compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (4.NBT.2); number-line reasoning supports magnitude.
The number line as a proportional magnitude model, with benchmark landmarks, is central to estimation and to number sense.
learnerActions: Work with four synced views of one number: numeral, expanded form, place-value counters (Th|H|T|O), and a draggable marker on a 0-10,000 number line.
Change any one view (e.g. add/remove counters) and watch the others, including the marker's position on the line, update to match.
Play an estimation round: a target such as 6,300 appears; drag the marker to where you think it sits, then compare with the revealed true position and your error.

Use landmark hints — find 5,000 (halfway) first, then 2,500 and 7,500 — and decide where the number falls: ask yourself 'is 6,300 past halfway? is it yet past three-quarters?' and justify your answer before checking.
Optionally use a bar/strip model alongside the line to reason about proportion (e.g. shade roughly 6,300 out of a 10,000 strip) and relate the shaded length to where the marker should sit.
As you improve, work on lines where tick marks are removed so placement must come from proportional reasoning, not counting ticks.
Say aloud what you found first on the line and why the number lands where it does (e.g. '6,300 is past the middle but not yet at three-quarters, about halfway between 5,000 and 7,500').
activities.intendedInsight: The same number can be expressed as a numeral, expanded form, and counters, and these all correspond to one proportional position on the number line; magnitude is a distance anchored by landmarks, not the leading digit alone.

activities.title: Three-view translation with a placeholder zero
feedback: If a learner drops the empty hundreds column or misplaces digits (342, 3,42, or 30,042), return to the columns and show that removing the zero slides the 3 down into the hundreds place (342), while an extra zero pushes it up into the ten-thousands place (30,042); either way its value changes. The zero holds the hundreds place open.

If the expanded form or line placement contradicts the numeral just written (e.g. writing 3,000 + 400 + 2 for 3,042), translate explicitly: point to the 0 in 3,042 and ask what term it contributes (none — that is why there is no hundreds term).

Probe with: 'Why is there no "+ something hundred" in the expanded form?', 'If I take the zero out and write 342, what happened to the 3?', and 'How did you decide where on the line to put it — what did you find first?'
activities.rationale: A number with an internal zero forces learners to reveal whether they treat position as value. Requiring three representations (numeral, line, expanded) from one source exposes whether the views are genuinely linked or memorised separately.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
Read, write and compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (4.NBT.2); number-line reasoning supports magnitude.
learnerActions: Read place-value counters such as 3 thousands, 0 hundreds, 4 tens, 2 ones and write the numeral (3,042).
Write the same number in expanded form (3,000 + 40 + 2) and explain why there is no hundreds term.
Show roughly where 3,042 sits on a 0-10,000 line — a little above the 3,000 mark, just under a third of the way along.
Translate in the reverse directions too: given a marked point, name the number; given expanded form, build the counters.
Explore what changes if a column changes: e.g. 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones gives 3,402 — and discuss how moving the counts between columns shifts the number's value and its line position.
activities.intendedInsight: Position determines value: the zero in the hundreds column is a placeholder that must be kept, and the numeral, expanded form, and line position must all agree because they describe one number.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal reference poster (scaffold)
feedback: Use the highlighted links to confirm or correct your own translation; for estimation, you still need to place the marker yourself to build proportional judgement.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal reference clarifies the links between the different representations of one number and is a useful reference. As an observable affordance, it shows correspondences rather than requiring the learner to estimate or construct, so independent line placement still needs separate learner action.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
learnerActions: Study one number shown simultaneously as numeral, expanded form, counters, and a point on the line.
Tap a representation to highlight the matching parts in the others and the matching line position.
Use it as a reference check after attempting a translation yourself, not as a substitute for acting on the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the correspondences across representations highlighted together reinforces that they are views of one quantity.

activities.title: Quick-check items for placement and matching
feedback: For 'which point is 4,900?', if 4,900 and 4,100 are placed at the same spot (leading-digit error), re-anchor on the nearest thousand and halfway landmarks to separate them.
Use mismatches between a chosen match and the line position to prompt a re-check in both directions.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and slider items efficiently sample matching and placement across many numbers. As an observable limit, selection-based items confirm fluency but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and reasoning that the translation and estimator activities require.
sourceClaims: Read, write and compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (4.NBT.2); number-line reasoning supports magnitude.
learnerActions: Place a given number (e.g. 6,300) on a 0-10,000 line using a slider.
Match a numeral to its expanded form and to a counter/base-ten depiction.
Choose which marked point on the line is 4,900 (distinguished from 4,100).
Supply a missing representation given one of the others.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent movement between representations and benchmark-based placement can be demonstrated across short, varied prompts.

constraints: Treat numeral, expanded form, counters/base-ten, and the number-line point as interchangeable views of one number and practise translating in all directions, not just one way.

Use the 0-10,000 line as the magnitude spine with benchmark landmarks (5,000 halfway, 2,500/7,500 quarters, thousands); progress from densely-marked to sparsely-marked lines so estimation relies on proportional reasoning rather than counting ticks.
Link estimation to rounding ('4,367 is about 4,000') and to sense-checking calculations.

The tap-to-reveal poster and selection/slider quick-checks are scaffolds and samples: they show or test correspondences but do not require the learner to construct or estimate independently; include construction and line-placement tasks for that.

Address common errors directly: placing by leading digit only, treating the line as even counting rather than proportional magnitude, ignoring landmarks, reading expanded form as separate numbers, and mis-scaling (5,000 not at the halfway point).

For the developmental error of bunching/even spacing, do not mark it wrong or drill in isolation — co-build landmarks and let the learner self-adjust, as proportional sense is still forming at ages 8-9.

Linked live-recompute panels, draggable markers, fading tick marks, landmark hints, and a bar/strip model for proportional estimation are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory tools; the learning goal is learner action and benchmark reasoning on the line, achievable on paper too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source list marks the DfE National Curriculum claim as verified; the CCSS-M 4.NBT.2 and NCETM number-line claims are listed as not verified in the original row — treat their support as unconfirmed.

sourceClaims on the scaffold (poster) and quick-check activities support the representational/number-line CONTENT being shown or sampled; they do not evidence the affordance LIMITATIONS stated in those rationales, which are objective/pedagogical observations (recognition/selection does not itself elicit independent construction), not sourced findings.

The original rated open dialogue and 3D as 'poor' with rationales like 'open dialogue can't capture line placement' and 'magnitude on a line is planar'. These are reframed as narrow affordance notes (selection/discussion does not by itself elicit independent line placement) rather than universal claims that such media cannot teach; no catalog ranking is asserted as a pedagogical law.

Arithmetic/representation self-audit: 3 thousands, 0 hundreds, 4 tens, 2 ones = 3,042 = 3,000 + 40 + 2, placed just above the 3,000 mark (3,042/10,000 ≈ 0.304, a little under a third) — consistent. The variant 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones = 3,402. 6,300/10,000 = 0.63 — past halfway, not yet three-quarters.
The bar/strip model (an original keyRepresentation omitted from the prior candidate) has been restored as an optional proportional-estimation representation.
Error-pattern examples (342, 3,42, 30,042, and 3,000 + 400 + 2) are retained as diagnostic signs of dropping/concatenating the placeholder or detaching representations, not as correct answers.

probeDeeper: Why is there no '+ something hundred' in the expanded form?
If I take the zero out and write 342, what happened to the 3?
How did you decide where on the line to put it — what did you find first?
What if the counters were 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones — how does the number change?
assess.correctAnswer: 3,042 — placed just under a third of the way along the line (a little above the 3,000 mark) — expanded as 3,000 + 40 + 2.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the empty hundreds column or concatenates the counts — writes 342, or writes 3,42 / 30042, because the zero 'has nothing so it doesn't count'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the columns: show that removing the zero slides the 3 out of the thousands place and changes its value; the zero holds the hundreds place open.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Numeral has the wrong number of digits or a missing placeholder; child cannot say why a zero is needed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bunches numbers at one end of the number line or spaces them evenly regardless of value — places 3,042 near the middle or crams small-thousands together.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark it wrong or drill placement in isolation; build the line's landmarks together (find 5,000 first, then 2,500) and let the child self-adjust — the sense of proportional position is still forming.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Number-line placement ignores relative magnitude (e.g. 3,042 put at the halfway mark).

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the three representations as unrelated tasks — can write the numeral but the expanded form or line does not match it (e.g. writes 3,000+400+2).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Translate back and forth explicitly: point to the 0 in 3,042 and ask what term it contributes to the expanded form (none — that is why there is no hundreds term).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expanded form or line contradicts the numeral the child just wrote; no cross-checking.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a correct numeral from the counters; loses the placeholder or the digit order.
responseLevels.full: Produces all three consistently, uses the zero as a placeholder deliberately, places on the line by proportional reasoning, and can translate from any one representation to the others.
responseLevels.partial: Writes 3,042 correctly but one representation is detached — expanded form or line placement does not agree with the numeral, or cannot translate back.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are place-value counters: 3 in the thousands column, none in the hundreds, 4 in the tens, 2 in the ones. Write this as a number. Then show me roughly where it sits on a 0-to-10,000 number line, and write it in expanded form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The empty hundreds column forces the child to reveal whether they treat position as value: a child who understands place value writes 3,042 and holds the zero as a placeholder, while a child who reads columns as a running total writes 342 or 3,42 or 30,042. Requiring three representations (numeral, line, expanded) exposes whether they are linked or memorised separately.
