pedagogy.summary: By Y6 children should reach van Hiele level 3 (informal deduction): not just that a square is a special rectangle, but a full quadrilateral hierarchy where attributes flow downward — anything true of a parallelogram is automatically true of a rhombus, rectangle and square, because each is a special parallelogram. The two load-bearing ideas are (a) attribute inheritance (a subcategory has every property of its parents plus extra) and (b) the ASYMMETRY of class inclusion: all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares. Persistent obstacles are exclusive/oblong-prototype thinking carried up from KS2, and treating 'all A are B' as if it were symmetric ('so all B are A'). Teaching succeeds when children build and defend the hierarchy from properties rather than from appearance.
bestPractices: Make attribute inheritance explicit: a rhombus is a parallelogram with all sides equal, a rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles, a square is both — so a square inherits every parallelogram property (opposite sides parallel, diagonals bisect each other) automatically
Draw the hierarchy as a family tree / nested sets and have children justify each subset link ('why is every rectangle a parallelogram?') from properties
Confront the asymmetry directly with the two statements 'all squares are rectangles' vs 'all rectangles are squares' and demand the reason for which is true
Use everyday class-inclusion analogies (every spaniel is a dog and an animal, but not every dog is a spaniel) to make the one-directional logic intuitive
Ask for defining vs shared properties: what do ALL parallelograms share, and what EXTRA property makes each special case — forcing the necessary/sufficient distinction
keyRepresentations: Quadrilateral hierarchy diagram (family tree) with quadrilateral ⊃ parallelogram ⊃ {rhombus, rectangle} ⊃ square
Nested Venn sets showing rhombus and rectangle overlapping, with square in the intersection
Property table: rows = shapes, columns = properties (opposite sides parallel, all sides equal, right angles, equal diagonals) showing how ticks accumulate down the hierarchy
A parallelogram with adjustable angles and side lengths that becomes a rhombus, rectangle, or square as constraints are added
commonMisconceptions: Treating 'all squares are rectangles' as symmetric — concluding 'so all rectangles are squares' (or that both are equally true/false)
Reversing the subset direction — thinking a rectangle is a special square rather than a square a special rectangle
Exclusive/oblong prototype persisting from KS2: a 'real' rectangle must be longer than it is wide, so a square is not a rectangle at all
Not applying inheritance: agreeing a rhombus is a parallelogram in words, but not granting that it therefore has all parallelogram properties (e.g. opposite sides parallel, diagonals bisecting)

learn.summary: Year 6 learners (ages 10-11) build the quadrilateral hierarchy from properties rather than appearance, grasping two load-bearing ideas: attribute inheritance (a subcategory has every property of its parents plus an extra constraint) and the asymmetry of class inclusion (all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares). The target understanding is the van Hiele informal-deduction level (level 3 when levels are numbered from 1, level 2 when numbered from 0): learners justify and defend subset links from properties, overcoming the exclusive/oblong prototype formed in earlier school years and the tendency to treat 'all A are B' as symmetric.

activities.title: Build the shape by adding properties
feedback: If a learner builds a square but denies it is a parallelogram, point back to the property table: it has opposite sides parallel, so it meets the parallelogram definition.

If a learner expects removing 'right angles' from a rectangle to leave it a rectangle, show that the 'rectangle' label depends on that very property — removing it moves the shape up to plain parallelogram.

When a learner sees the reverse challenge is impossible, name the insight: 'all rectangles are parallelograms but not all parallelograms are rectangles' (just as all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares) is something you bumped into, not a rule to memorise.
activities.rationale: Adding and removing defining properties and watching a shape's position in the hierarchy change makes attribute inheritance and the one-directional asymmetry concrete and reasoned rather than memorised. A live constraint model with linked hierarchy diagram, nested Venn sets and a ticking property table is an optional way to make the mechanism visible; the same reasoning can be done with paper cut-outs and a drawn family tree.
sourceClaims: Attributes of a category belong to all its subcategories (5.G.3); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties (5.G.4)
At van Hiele level 3 (informal deduction) students can explain why all squares are rectangles; the levels progress from visual to descriptive to relational reasoning
A square is a subclass of rectangle; children must learn class inclusion and often resist inclusive membership
learnerActions: Start with a general 'floppy' quadrilateral and switch on one property at a time: make opposite sides parallel, add right angles, make all sides equal.

Watch how the shape changes and where it belongs: making opposite sides parallel turns it into a parallelogram; adding right angles makes it a rectangle; instead making all sides equal makes it a rhombus; doing both makes it a square.

After each change, record in a property table which properties the shape now has (opposite sides parallel, all sides equal, right angles, equal diagonals), noticing that these ticks accumulate as you go down each branch of the family tree.

Attempt the reverse challenge: try to make a rectangle that is NOT a parallelogram, and explain why you cannot — four right angles force each pair of opposite sides to be parallel (two sides that are both perpendicular to the same side are parallel), so every rectangle automatically meets the parallelogram definition.
Place the finished square, rhombus and rectangle onto a family-tree (hierarchy) diagram and into nested Venn sets, saying why the square sits inside BOTH the rhombus and rectangle regions.
activities.intendedInsight: A square inherits every property of the parallelogram, rhombus and rectangle because it is a special case of each; adding an extra constraint moves a shape DOWN the hierarchy, and the inheritance runs one way only — removing the extra property moves back up, but you cannot have a rectangle that is not also a parallelogram.

activities.title: Defend the asymmetry: which statement is true?
feedback: If a learner picks statement (2), use nested sets: the square set sits INSIDE the rectangle set, so square→rectangle always holds but rectangle→square does not.

If a learner rejects statement (1) because 'a rectangle must be longer than it is wide', show rectangles ranging from very long to square and test each against the definition (right angles, parallel opposite sides) rather than its typical look.
If a learner treats both statements as equally true or false, return to the spaniel/dog/animal analogy to feel the direction of the inclusion.
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the two statements and demanding a property-based reason surfaces whether the learner treats inclusion as symmetric, reverses the direction, or holds the oblong prototype — each error leads to a distinct, identifiable answer, so this both teaches and discriminates reasoning.
sourceClaims: 'All squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares'; guiding questions 'Is a square a special rectangle? Is a rectangle a special parallelogram? Is a rhombus a special kite?'
Children impose non-defining attributes and reason from prototypes, causing them to reject inclusive relationships between quadrilaterals
A square is a subclass of rectangle; children must learn class inclusion and often resist inclusive membership
learnerActions: Consider two statements: (1) all squares are rectangles, (2) all rectangles are squares. Decide which is true and which is false.

Justify the choice from properties: a square has every property a rectangle needs (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) PLUS all four sides equal, so every square qualifies as a rectangle; a rectangle only becomes a square when it also has equal sides, which most do not.
Test the everyday analogy: every spaniel is a dog and every dog is an animal, but not every animal is a dog — explain how this one-directional logic matches squares and rectangles.
Attempt counterexamples: draw a rectangle that is NOT a square, a parallelogram that is NOT a rectangle, and try to draw a square that is NOT a rectangle (explaining why the last is impossible).
activities.intendedInsight: Class inclusion is one-directional: 'all A are B' does not mean 'all B are A'. The subset asymmetry follows from the extra defining property, not from which shape is more familiar.

activities.title: Shared versus extra properties across the parallelogram family
feedback: If a learner agrees in words that a rhombus is a parallelogram but lists its properties in isolation, build the property table so the shared parallelogram properties are seen carrying down to every special case.
If a learner cannot name the EXTRA property for a rhombus or rectangle, prompt: 'What does this shape have that a general parallelogram need not have?'
Praise reasoning that distinguishes a property ALL members share from the extra property that makes a case special.
activities.rationale: A property table makes inheritance visible and forces the necessary/sufficient distinction, addressing the misconception where learners grant category membership in name but withhold the inherited properties. A tap-to-reveal hierarchy with properties highlighted in parent nodes is one optional consolidation reference once the idea is understood.
sourceClaims: Attributes of a category belong to all its subcategories (5.G.3); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties (5.G.4)
A square is a subclass of rectangle; children must learn class inclusion and often resist inclusive membership
learnerActions: List the properties that ALL parallelograms share (opposite sides parallel and equal, diagonals bisect each other).

For each special case, state the extra property that defines it compared with a general parallelogram: a rhombus adds all sides equal, a rectangle adds right angles, and a square adds both (or just one extra property compared with a rhombus or a rectangle).
Fill a property table (rows = shapes, columns = properties) and confirm that each subcategory keeps every shared parallelogram property and adds its extra constraint.
Transfer the reasoning to a new or less familiar shape: given its properties, say where it belongs in the hierarchy and why, and which properties it inherits.
Justify a subset link in words, e.g. 'why is every rectangle a parallelogram?', using shared properties rather than appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: Every special parallelogram inherits all the shared parallelogram properties and adds extra defining constraints (one for a rhombus or a rectangle; two for a square, which is one more than a rhombus or a rectangle); this separates necessary/shared properties from the extra property or properties that name each shape.

activities.title: Convince the shape sceptic
feedback: If the learner argues from appearance ('it just looks like one'), the sceptic should ask which defining properties are met.
If the learner accepts the reverse ('every rhombus is a square'), ask for a rhombus that is not a square as a counterexample.
Reward justifications that cite shared and extra properties explicitly.
activities.rationale: Dialogue that demands property-based justification can surface reasoning and press the asymmetry, and can complement structural work done with diagrams and manipulatives.
sourceClaims: At van Hiele level 3 (informal deduction) students can explain why all squares are rectangles; the levels progress from visual to descriptive to relational reasoning
learnerActions: Respond to a sceptic who accepts a hierarchy claim only when it is justified from properties: 'Convince me a square belongs inside the rhombus family.'
Answer the follow-up pressure: 'Then is every rhombus a square?' — explaining why the reverse does not hold.
State, for each claim, which properties make it true and which extra property the reverse would require.
Use a counterexample when the sceptic over-generalises (e.g. produce a rhombus that is not a square).
activities.intendedInsight: Being made to articulate and defend each subset link, and to expose the reverse as false, consolidates property-based justification over appearance-based classification.

activities.title: Classify and check the hierarchy
feedback: If a shape is misplaced, ask which defining property is missing or extra for the region chosen.
For the true/false item, if the reversal is chosen, revisit the nested sets showing the square set inside the rectangle set.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, matching and a well-built true/false item check that reasoning is secure and are well suited to confirming the hierarchy and asymmetry. Recognition and correct placement alone do not require the learner to construct the inheritance, so use these alongside or after construction and reasoning work.
sourceClaims: Attributes of a category belong to all its subcategories (5.G.3); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties (5.G.4)
learnerActions: Drag or place a set of quadrilaterals into nested regions of a hierarchy, putting the square in the intersection of the rhombus and rectangle sets.
Match each shape (parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square) to its extra defining property.
Answer a true/false question on the asymmetry — 'Which is true: all squares are rectangles, or all rectangles are squares?' — and spot the reversal as a wrong option.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall and correct placement confirm the hierarchy is stable, including the asymmetry and each shape's extra defining property.

constraints: Build and defend the hierarchy from properties, not from appearance; the oblong/prototype view ('a rectangle must be longer than it is wide') must be directly confronted, not reinforced.

Classification, matching and true/false items check that the hierarchy is secure but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the inheritance insight; use them to confirm understanding alongside or after construction and reasoning work.

A tap-to-reveal hierarchy/property table is a useful reference once the idea is understood, but it does not let the learner add or remove constraints to feel a shape descend the hierarchy; pair it with construction activities.
Dialogue with a sceptic supports property-based justification; the structural subset relationships can be seen clearly in a diagram, nested sets or manipulative, so pair dialogue with those.

Optional interactive features (live constraint handles, animated descent down the tree, updating nested Venn sets, a ticking property table, tap-to-reveal nodes) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; paper cut-outs and a drawn family tree can serve the same reasoning (a paper cut-out has slight thickness and only approximates the ideal flat quadrilateral it represents).
Keep class-inclusion attention one-directional: contrast 'all squares are rectangles' with 'all rectangles are squares' as genuinely different claims, not as a reversible rule.

Use 'equal diagonals' (true of rectangles and squares, not of general parallelograms or rhombuses) as the distinguishing property-table column so ticks genuinely accumulate; keep 'diagonals bisect each other' as a shared parallelogram property, not as an accumulating column.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a 2D constraint sandbox as 'ideal' and dismissed a third spatial dimension as 'adds nothing'; this comparative/necessity claim is a catalog preference not established by the cited sources, so it has been softened to an optional affordance rather than a universal law.

The original claimed a scored linear quiz 'tests the reasoning rather than building the inheritance insight' and that dialogue 'supports rather than delivers'; these have been reframed as narrow affordances/design cautions, not proven efficacy or medium-superiority claims.
The National Curriculum (Year 6 Geometry) source is marked verified:false in the row; treat that citation with caution.

If using physical cut-outs to model quadrilaterals, note that paper has slight thickness and only approximates an ideal plane figure; discuss the represented flat shape, not whether the card can be handled.

The property-table column was changed from 'diagonals bisect each other' (a shared parallelogram property that does not accumulate) to 'equal diagonals' (parallelogram ✗, rhombus ✗, rectangle ✓, square ✓) so the accumulation observation stays coherent; the bisecting property is retained as a shared parallelogram property.

probeDeeper: 'What do ALL parallelograms have in common? What extra property makes a rhombus special? A rectangle?' (tests inheritance and the necessary/sufficient distinction)
'A spaniel is a dog and every dog is an animal — is every animal a dog? How is that like squares and rectangles?' (class-inclusion analogy pushing the one-directional logic)
'You said a square is a rectangle — is a square also a rhombus? Is it a parallelogram? Why?' (transfer down two branches of the hierarchy)

'Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square, and a parallelogram that is NOT a rectangle? Could you ever draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?' (counterexamples; the last is impossible — the asymmetry made concrete)
assess.correctAnswer: Statement (1) is true, statement (2) is false. A square has every property a rectangle needs (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) plus the extra property that all four sides are equal, so every square qualifies as a rectangle. A rectangle only becomes a square when it gains that extra property of equal sides, which most rectangles do not have — so not every rectangle is a square.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the subset direction — picks 'all rectangles are squares' as the true one (treats the more familiar/larger category as the special case)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use nested-set and property-table work to show which set contains which: the square set sits INSIDE the rectangle set, so going square→rectangle always holds but rectangle→square does not. Revisit classifying by parallel/perpendicular-line properties.
errorPatterns.distractor: Statement (2) is the true one — all rectangles are squares
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses statement (2) and, on the reason tier, argues that a rectangle 'is a kind of square' or that the two claims are interchangeable

errorPatterns.pattern: Oblong-prototype exclusion persisting from KS2 — 'a square isn't a rectangle at all because a rectangle has to be longer than it is wide', so (1) is judged false
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate defining properties from typical appearance; show rectangles ranging from very long to square and test each against the definition. Reground in property-based classification.
errorPatterns.distractor: Neither is true — a square is not a rectangle
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects statement (1) and, on the reason tier, defines a rectangle by its unequal-sides look rather than its right angles and parallel opposite sides

errorPatterns.pattern: Inheritance not applied — agrees a rhombus/rectangle is a parallelogram in name, but does not grant that it therefore has all parallelogram properties, and describes rhombus/rectangle as unrelated to the parallelogram family
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the property table so shared parallelogram properties (opposite sides parallel and equal, diagonals bisect) are seen to carry down to every special case, with each subcategory adding exactly one extra constraint.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Under the parallelogram probe, lists a rhombus's or rectangle's properties in isolation and cannot say what EXTRA property each adds to a shared parallelogram base

responseLevels.gap: Picks the wrong statement or says both are equally true/false; or rejects 'all squares are rectangles' on appearance. Cannot use defining properties to reason about inclusion.
responseLevels.full: Picks statement (1) and explains the asymmetry from properties — a square has all a rectangle's properties plus equal sides, so every square is a rectangle but only equal-sided rectangles are squares; places quadrilaterals correctly in a hierarchy, states the properties all parallelograms share, and explains rhombus and rectangle as parallelograms each adding one extra property, transferring the reasoning to a new shape.
responseLevels.partial: Picks statement (1) and can say a square is a special rectangle, but lists shared/defining properties without using them to explain the asymmetry, and cannot apply inheritance to the parallelogram family (does not identify what extra property makes a rhombus or rectangle special, or transfer to a new case).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell the child: 'Here are two statements — (1) all squares are rectangles, and (2) all rectangles are squares. One is true and one is false.' Ask: 'Which one is true? And how do you know — what makes it true and the other one false?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands one-directional class inclusion picks statement (1) and explains the asymmetry via the extra property. A child treating inclusion as symmetric, or reversing the direction, picks (2) or says both are true/false. A child still holding the oblong prototype rejects (1) outright ('a square isn't a rectangle'). Each faulty reasoning route lands on a different, identifiable answer, and the reason tier separates a memorised 'square is a special rectangle' from genuine grasp of WHY the reverse fails.

sources.claim: Attributes of a category belong to all its subcategories (5.G.3); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties (5.G.4)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Earth's four systems interacting (geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere)

- **Standards — UK (KS2 Science working scientifically — use and develop models; report relationships):** Children model how Earth's land, water, air and living things are connected and how a change in one affects the others.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-ESS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS2-1].

- **Operational details:** This is a systems-thinking / modelling node that ties the whole domain together (high centrality). Children first NAME the four spheres — geosphere (rock/land), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air), biosphere (living things) — then, crucially, trace INTERACTIONS between them with concrete examples (a river/hydrosphere carving a canyon/geosphere; plants/biosphere releasing water vapour to the atmosphere; wind/atmosphere shaping dunes/geosphere). The load-bearing skill is causal modelling: change one sphere and follow the ripple to others. Use a labelled model (diagram or built system) and push children to predict knock-on effects rather than list definitions. Keep examples local and observable before global.
bestPractices: Establish the four sphere names with clear examples before tracing interactions — naming precedes modelling.
Centre the lesson on INTERACTIONS with concrete cause-and-effect examples (river erodes rock; plants transpire into air), not four separate definitions.
Use a model children can perturb: change one sphere and predict/trace the effect on the others (systems ripple).
Start with local, observable interactions before scaling to global ones (volcanoes affecting climate).
Have children build/annotate their own model with labelled arrows showing the direction of each interaction.
keyRepresentations: A four-sphere Venn/overlap or node-and-arrow diagram with labelled interactions.
Example event cards (rainstorm, volcanic eruption, forest growth) traced across spheres.
A cause-and-effect ripple map: 'change X in one sphere → effects in others'.
Photographs annotated to tag which spheres are interacting in a scene.
commonMisconceptions: 'The four spheres are separate places' — not seeing them as constantly overlapping and exchanging matter/energy.
'Only living things count as an Earth system' — forgetting rock, water, and air are systems too.
'Interactions go one way' — missing that spheres affect each other reciprocally.
'The biosphere doesn't change the land or air' — underestimating living things' geological/atmospheric role.
'A change in one system stays contained' — not anticipating knock-on effects across systems.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year-olds modelling how Earth's four systems — geosphere (rock/land), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air), biosphere (living things) — interact. The load-bearing skill is causal modelling: name the four spheres with concrete examples, then trace how a change in one ripples reciprocally through the others. Start with local, observable interactions before global ones, and push beyond listing definitions to predicting knock-on effects.

activities.title: Living Earth-systems board: change one thing, trace the ripple
feedback: If you listed the systems without connecting them, scaffold forward: 'and then what does the ash do to the air? and to the plants?' — don't restart from the names.
If you traced only one step, push one more: after ash reaches the air, what happens to the plants below, and which system is that?
If every arrow points one way, add a return path — e.g. plants (biosphere) release water vapour back into the atmosphere — to show interactions are reciprocal.

Check your terrarium: where did the water droplets on the lid come from, and which systems did the water pass through to get there? Remember the sealed jar is a simplified model of Earth's systems, not the whole Earth.
activities.rationale: A perturbable node-and-arrow model lets a child enact 'change one system, show the effect on others', which is the modelling objective; predicting before releasing turns it into causal reasoning rather than definition recall. The sealed terrarium gives an observable physical case of matter cycling between systems. The causal steps are plausible pathways whose magnitude depends on scale and conditions, not fixed quantitative outcomes.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-ESS2-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS2-1].
The four Earth systems (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere) continually exchange matter and energy; a change in one causes effects in others.
learnerActions: Set up four labelled nodes — geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere — and draw directed arrows between them to show which systems can affect which.
Drop an event onto one node and, BEFORE releasing it, write down your prediction of how it will ripple to the other spheres.

Trace a volcano on the geosphere: ash and gases pump into the atmosphere → can block some sunlight and change weather → can affect rain and water (hydrosphere) → can stress plants and animals (biosphere).
Trace deforestation on the biosphere: less transpiration can dry the atmosphere, while bare soil lets water (hydrosphere) strip and erode the land (geosphere).
Take on a 'change just ONE thing' challenge: label each arrow in your chain with what is being exchanged (matter or energy) and in which direction.
Build a physical terrarium (soil, water, air, and plants sealed in a jar) as a hands-on complement, and observe over days how the water cycles between the systems.
activities.intendedInsight: The four spheres are not separate places but one connected system that continually exchanges matter and energy; a single change can cascade reciprocally through all of them.

activities.title: Tag the interaction in a real scene
feedback: If you only tagged interactions involving animals or plants, find a river-erodes-rock or wind-shapes-dune example to show physical systems act too.
If you named one sphere, ask which SECOND sphere it is exchanging with — every interaction needs at least two.
Name what is exchanged (water, sediment, gas, energy), not just the two spheres.
activities.rationale: Tagging real scenes builds naming and recognition of interactions and is intended to give a chance to surface and discuss the 'only living things cause change' and 'spheres are separate places' misconceptions. This recognition work supports but does not replace perturbing a model.
sourceClaims: The four Earth systems (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere) continually exchange matter and energy; a change in one causes effects in others.
learnerActions: Study a rich landscape photo or scene and point to places where two systems meet — a river meeting rock, a tree meeting the air, waves meeting a beach.
For each spot, name the two spheres involved and state what is being exchanged, e.g. 'hydrosphere ↔ geosphere: the river carves the valley.'
Use lift-the-flap or cover-and-reveal: predict 'which two spheres?' before checking.
Find at least one physical–physical interaction (water eroding rock, wind shaping dunes) and one involving living things (plants transpiring, roots breaking rock).
activities.intendedInsight: Interactions between spheres are visible in ordinary scenes, and both physical systems and living systems actively cause change — not just living things.

activities.title: Sort, match, and sequence the systems
feedback: If you can order the chain but not say why each step follows, talk through the mechanism: what does the ash actually DO to the air?
If a sort is wrong, ask: is this made of rock, water, air, or is it alive? Some items (soil, a muddy river) touch more than one system — discuss which.
Matching shows reasoning only when you can state the exchange; naming the spheres without the link is incomplete.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, matching, and sequencing cleanly check both naming and interaction reasoning. These response formats verify understanding but, being selection-based, do not on their own elicit the independent model-building the standard calls for, so pair them with the board activity.
learnerActions: Categorise items and objects into geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere.
Match each event card (rainstorm, volcanic eruption, forest growth, drought) to at least two spheres it links, and notice that many events link more than two.
Sequence the steps of a cause-and-effect ripple chain into the correct order (e.g. eruption → ash in air → less sunlight reaching the ground → locally and temporarily cooler / stressed plants).
Explain aloud why each step causes the next, not just that it comes next.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming the spheres and ordering a causal chain are different skills; a correct sequence must be justified by cause, not memorised order.

activities.title: 'And then what?' — reasoning out a ripple with a questioner
feedback: If you stop after one link, the questioner extends it: 'the river is muddier now — what does that do to the plants and animals in it?'
If you only name systems, you've shown you can list them; connecting a change from one into another is what shows you understand interaction.
Reward chains that loop back (a change returning to where it started) — that captures reciprocity.
activities.rationale: A Socratic questioner can elicit and extend a child's causal chain and surface whether they treat spheres as sealed boxes. It is strong for drawing out reasoning but does not itself produce the built/labelled model the standard asks children to make, so pair it with the modelling activity.
learnerActions: Pick an event (cutting down a forest, a long drought, a volcanic eruption) and explain its first effect on another sphere.
Respond to repeated 'and then what?' prompts, extending the causal chain one sphere at a time until you reach the biosphere or loop back to the start.
State, for a drought, one way it reaches living things AND one way it reaches the land.
Discuss the idea 'if a change in one system never touched the others, could we still call them connected?' and explain why scientists say they interact.
activities.intendedInsight: Tracing a change several steps across spheres, out loud, reveals whether you grasp interaction (relational) rather than merely naming systems.

constraints: Establish the four sphere names with clear examples before tracing interactions — naming precedes modelling.
Centre the work on INTERACTIONS with concrete cause-and-effect examples, not four separate definitions.
Start with local, observable interactions before scaling to global ones (e.g. volcanoes affecting climate).

Recognition tasks (scene-tagging, sorting, matching, sequencing) support naming and interaction reasoning but do not elicit independent construction of a model; include a build/annotate step where the child makes their own labelled arrows.
A questioner/persona can elicit reasoning but does not itself produce the labelled model the standard asks children to build — use it alongside, not instead of, the modelling activity.
A layer-toggle 3D globe can motivate by showing spatial overlap, but the target learning is causal interaction; keep the causal model in a form the child can perturb and annotate.
The terrarium is an approximation of Earth's systems; name what each component represents and acknowledge a sealed jar is a simplified model, not the whole Earth.

Present the ripple pathways (ash dimming sunlight and locally cooling water; deforestation drying the air; bare soil increasing erosion) as plausible qualitative effects whose size and duration depend on scale and conditions, not guaranteed quantitative outcomes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Listed sources[].claim are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Original row confidence was 'high'; this has not been independently re-established here.

Causal claims in the ripple examples (ash dims sunlight and cools nearby water; deforestation dries the atmosphere; bare soil increases erosion) are broadly consistent with Earth-systems science but are qualitative illustrations whose magnitude depends on scale and conditions.
The volcano-cools-hydrosphere step is a real but regional/temporary effect; the activity and constraints qualify it so it does not imply every eruption measurably cools all the oceans.

Activity 3 (sort/match/sequence) carries no sourceClaims because its distinctive teaching point — that selection formats check but do not build a model — is not directly supported by either source claim.

probeDeeper: Trace it one more step: after the ash is in the air, what happens to the plants below? Which system is that?
Give me an example where water changes the land — which two systems interact there?
If a change in one system never touched the others, could we still call them 'connected'? Why do scientists say they interact?
A drought means less water. Name one way that reaches living things and one way it reaches the land.
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree. The four Earth systems are connected, so a change in one spreads to the others. The eruption (geosphere) sends ash and gas into the atmosphere, which can block sunlight and change weather, affect rain and water (hydrosphere), and harm or change plants and animals (biosphere).

errorPatterns.pattern: The Earth systems are separate and don't affect each other ('rock is rock, air is air')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it — trace one concrete pathway (ash → atmosphere → less sunlight → plants) step by step.
errorPatterns.distractor: I agree — the eruption only changes the rock; the other systems are separate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees the eruption stays within the geosphere.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names the spheres but gives an interaction only as a list, not a cause→effect link ('there's air and water and rocks and animals')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — 'and then what does the ash do to the air? and to the plants?'; don't reteach the names.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists the systems without connecting them; can't complete the pathway from one to another.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only living things (biosphere) cause change; the physical systems are just passive backdrops
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give a physical→physical example — a river eroding rock, rain filling a lake — to show physical systems act too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Credits only animals/plants with causing change, not air, water, or rock.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the systems as separate; says the eruption only affects the rock.
responseLevels.full: Traces at least one cause→effect pathway across systems (geosphere → atmosphere → biosphere/hydrosphere) and transfers to a new case (water eroding land, a drought reaching life) — explaining interaction, not just naming.
responseLevels.partial: Names the four spheres and asserts they're connected but can only list them, not trace a change from one into another.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A volcano erupts — that's the geosphere. A friend says it only changes the rock; it can't affect the air, the water, or living things because those are separate systems. Do you agree? Explain, tracing how the eruption reaches at least one other Earth system.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can name the four spheres yet still treat them as sealed boxes. Requiring them to TRACE a change from one sphere into another catches whether they grasp interaction (relational) versus mere naming (multistructural) — the heart of the modelling objective.

sources.claim: NGSS 5-ESS2-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS2-1].
sources.source: NGSS, 5-ESS2 Earth's Systems

sources.claim: The four Earth systems (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere) continually exchange matter and energy; a change in one causes effects in others.
sources.source: NASA / UCAR Center for Science Education — Earth's Spheres and Systems

pedagogy.summary: This KS3-level topic upgrades 'white blood cells fight germs' into a two-arm immune system. The INNATE arm is fast and non-specific: barriers (skin, mucus) and general responses (inflammation, phagocytes engulfing invaders) that act immediately against anything. The ADAPTIVE arm is slower but SPECIFIC and MEMORY-FORMING: B cells make antibodies shaped to fit a particular pathogen's antigens (lock-and-key), and T cells destroy the body's own infected cells. The pivotal idea is IMMUNOLOGICAL MEMORY — after a first infection, memory B and T cells persist, so a second exposure triggers a far faster, stronger response and you don't fall ill. This is exactly why VACCINES work: a harmless version presents the antigen, the adaptive system responds and forms memory, so the real pathogen is defeated pre-emptively. Add the GUT MICROBIOME — trillions of resident microbes that help train and regulate immune function — as a modern, important nuance (not all microbes are enemies). The teaching crux is the timing story: WHY the first response is slow (the matching B cell is rare and must be found and multiplied) and the second is fast (memory). Keep molecular detail qualitative; this is enrichment relative to DfE KS3 (immunity is GCSE in England) so anchor on immunology/public-health sources under the blended alignment.
bestPractices: Contrast the two arms on the axes that matter: innate = fast + general + no memory; adaptive = slow-first + specific + memory — a clean two-column comparison students can reason with.

Tell the TIMING story explicitly: the first response is slow because the one matching B cell is rare and must be found and cloned; the second is fast because memory cells are already waiting — this is the conceptual heart and the vaccine rationale.
Use the lock-and-key model for antibody–antigen specificity (each B cell makes just one antibody shape; only the matching one works), and give T cells the distinct job of killing infected body cells.
Derive vaccines from memory, not as a separate fact: a safe antigen → adaptive response → memory → pre-emptive protection; use a primary-vs-secondary response curve.

Include the gut microbiome as a regulator/trainer of immunity to counter 'all microbes are harmful', and flag the curriculum status (enrichment/GCSE-level, blended anchor) while keeping molecular depth qualitative.
keyRepresentations: Two-arm comparison table: innate (fast, non-specific, no memory) vs adaptive (specific, memory)
Antibody–antigen lock-and-key: B cells each making one antibody shape; only the fit works
Primary vs secondary response curve (slow small first response; fast large second response)
B cell (antibodies) vs T cell (kills infected cells) division of labour
Gut microbiome as a community of trillions of microbes that trains/regulates immunity
commonMisconceptions: 'Immunity is one single system' — missing the innate (fast/general) vs adaptive (specific/memory) division.
'The immune response is instant against everything' — missing that the FIRST specific response is slow (days) because the matching cell is rare.
'Antibodies kill germs directly like a poison' — they mainly bind/mark antigens (lock-and-key), flagging pathogens for destruction; T cells kill infected cells.
'Vaccines work by a different mechanism than natural infection' — they use the SAME adaptive-memory process, just triggered safely.
'You make memory to a pathogen instantly on first contact' — memory forms AFTER the first response; it speeds up later encounters.
'All microbes are harmful' — the gut microbiome is largely beneficial and helps regulate immunity.
'Natural infection is always better than vaccination' — both build memory, but infection carries the disease's risks.

learn.summary: KS3-level enrichment (immunity is GCSE in England) upgrading 'white blood cells fight germs' into a two-arm immune system. INNATE = fast, non-specific, no memory (barriers like skin and mucus; inflammation; phagocytes engulfing invaders). ADAPTIVE = slower-first but SPECIFIC and MEMORY-FORMING (B cells make antibodies shaped to fit a pathogen's antigens via lock-and-key; T cells kill the body's own infected cells). The conceptual heart is the TIMING story and immunological memory: the first specific response is slow because the few B cells with a matching antibody shape are rare and must be found, activated and cloned; memory B and T cells are made during this response and persist after the infection clears, so a second exposure to the SAME pathogen is far faster and stronger and you usually don't fall ill. Vaccines exploit exactly this: a harmless antigen triggers the adaptive response and memory without the first illness. The gut microbiome (trillions of resident microbes that help train and regulate immunity) is included to counter 'all microbes are enemies'. Keep molecular detail qualitative.

activities.title: Run an infection, then re-run it: watch memory form
feedback: If a learner expects an instant specific response: point to how long the first run takes while the rare matching B cells are located and cloned — specificity has a time cost the first time.

If a learner thinks the second response uses a different mechanism than the vaccine: show that both the 'vaccinate' run and the natural first infection produce the same kind of memory cells, so re-exposure gives a similar fast secondary curve (how strong and how long-lasting the protection is can differ between vaccines and infections).
If a learner treats the microbiome as harmful: highlight that these resident microbes are tuning, not attacking, the system.

If a learner says antibodies 'poison' the germ: show antibodies binding to antigens by shape, which can block or clump the pathogens and mark them so phagocytes destroy them, while T cells separately kill the body's own infected cells.
activities.rationale: The concept is fundamentally about timing and specificity across a dynamic response, which a live, learner-driven simulation can make concrete: the primary/secondary curve emerges from the learner's own actions rather than being asserted. A live recolouring of the response curve, draggable 'vaccinate' control, and a toggleable microbiome layer make the mechanism concrete; these are optional illustrative controls, not required.
sourceClaims: The adaptive immune system recognises pathogens by antigens (surface proteins/sugars); each antibody-producing white blood cell (B cell) makes one antibody shape and only the matching one works (lock-and-key); the first response is slow because the right cells are rare and must multiply, and afterwards memory cells remain so a second exposure is defeated fast — which is how vaccines protect.

Immunity has two arms — innate (fast, non-specific: barriers, inflammation, phagocytes) and adaptive (specific, memory-forming: B cells make antibodies, T cells kill infected cells) — and the gut microbiome, a community of trillions of microbes, significantly influences immune function.
learnerActions: Start an infection and observe the innate defenders (phagocytes, inflammation, barriers) respond instantly and generally, but in this simulated infection fail to finish the pathogen alone (innate defences do clear many minor infections by themselves).

Watch the adaptive search: the system hunts through a large library of B cells for the rare few whose antibody shape fits this pathogen's antigen (lock-and-key), finds them, and clones them into a production line while T cells destroy infected body cells. Note how many days this takes.
Watch a response curve plot the slow, small first (primary) response as the infection is slowly cleared.

Re-release the SAME pathogen and observe the much faster, much larger second (secondary) response (it still takes a few days, but far fewer than the first time); watch the curve draw the large, fast peak.
Use a 'vaccinate' option that introduces a harmless antigen, then re-release the real pathogen, and compare the protection to the natural first infection.
Toggle a microbiome layer to see resident microbes tuning/regulating the response.
activities.intendedInsight: The first specific response is slow because matching B cells are rare and must be found and multiplied; the second is fast because memory cells are already waiting. A vaccine buys that fast second-response protection WITHOUT suffering the first illness, using the same adaptive-memory process.

activities.title: Ask the immunologist: boosters, infection vs vaccination, and friendly microbes
feedback: If a learner says natural infection is simply better: acknowledge both build memory, then surface the risks of the actual disease that vaccination avoids.
If a learner expects one vaccine to protect against everything: use the flu-vaccine-vs-cold case to re-establish specificity.
If a learner cannot say why boosters exist: connect to how protection can wane over time and how re-exposure or a further dose re-strengthens the specific memory response.
activities.rationale: Discussion-based evidence evaluation suits the topic's many authentic questions and myth-correction needs; a responsive dialogue can probe and extend reasoning. This complements rather than replaces the simulation, which is better suited to making the timing dynamics felt.
sourceClaims: The adaptive immune system recognises pathogens by antigens (surface proteins/sugars); each antibody-producing white blood cell (B cell) makes one antibody shape and only the matching one works (lock-and-key); the first response is slow because the right cells are rare and must multiply, and afterwards memory cells remain so a second exposure is defeated fast — which is how vaccines protect.
learnerActions: Pose genuine public-health questions to an immunologist persona, e.g. 'Why do I need a booster?', 'Is catching the illness naturally better than a vaccine?', 'Are all germs bad?'
Explain your current reasoning and let the persona probe it Socratically and correct myths.
Weigh evidence for vaccination vs natural infection, noting that both build memory but infection carries the disease's own risks.
activities.intendedInsight: Immunological memory and specificity explain real public-health decisions; natural infection and vaccination use the same memory mechanism, but only vaccination avoids the disease's risks.

activities.title: Consolidate: sort, sequence and read the response curve
feedback: If a learner labels barriers as adaptive: remind that innate defences are always present and work with no prior exposure to a specific pathogen.
If a learner orders memory before clearance: memory cells are made during the first response and remain after the pathogen is cleared; they are not there before first contact.
If a learner cannot explain the flu-vs-cold case: re-anchor on antigen specificity — memory fits one antigen only.
activities.rationale: A categorise/sequence/graph-interpret task is a solid consolidation that checks whether learners can reason with the two-arm contrast and the timing story after the simulation. It combines selection/sequencing with brief 'explain why' prompts, so it checks structured reasoning and some targeted explanation, but it gives limited room for extended explanation in the learner's own words — pair it with the immunologist dialogue for fuller production.
sourceClaims: Immunity has two arms — innate (fast, non-specific: barriers, inflammation, phagocytes) and adaptive (specific, memory-forming: B cells make antibodies, T cells kill infected cells) — and the gut microbiome, a community of trillions of microbes, significantly influences immune function.
learnerActions: Categorise features as innate vs adaptive (e.g. skin/mucus barriers, inflammation, phagocytes → innate; B-cell antibodies, T-cell killing, memory → adaptive).
Put the adaptive response steps in order: antigen recognised → matching B cell found → cloned/multiplied → antibodies produced → pathogen cleared → memory cells remain.
Match each cell to its role: B cells = make antibodies; T cells = kill infected body cells.
Interpret a primary-vs-secondary response graph: identify which curve is slow/small (first) and which is fast/large (second) and explain why.
State why a flu vaccine gives no protection against a cold virus.
activities.intendedInsight: The two arms, the division of labour between B and T cells, and the primary/secondary timing can be reasoned about explicitly and transferred to the specificity of vaccine protection.

activities.title: Reference poster: the two arms at a glance
feedback: If a learner uses the poster alone and expects to grasp the timing: note that the curve shows the outcome (slow, small first response vs fast, large second), but the dynamic search-and-clone PROCESS behind that outcome is best seen unfolding step by step in the simulation.
Check that learners can restate each arm's three properties (speed, specificity, memory) rather than just locate labels.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference supports recall of structure and vocabulary, and its response curve can display the primary-vs-secondary outcome. As a fixed diagram, though, it cannot be manipulated to show the search-and-clone process over time, so it works best as a companion reference alongside the simulation rather than the primary teaching artefact.
sourceClaims: Immunity has two arms — innate (fast, non-specific: barriers, inflammation, phagocytes) and adaptive (specific, memory-forming: B cells make antibodies, T cells kill infected cells) — and the gut microbiome, a community of trillions of microbes, significantly influences immune function.
learnerActions: Explore a labelled two-arm immunity reference: innate (fast, non-specific, no memory) vs adaptive (specific, memory) in a two-column comparison.
Lift flaps to reveal cell types and their jobs (B cells → antibodies; T cells → kill infected cells) and a primary-vs-secondary response curve.
Use it as a lookup aid while doing the simulation or consolidation tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: A clean two-column contrast on the axes that matter (speed, specificity, memory) gives learners a stable reference structure to reason with.

constraints: This topic is enrichment relative to DfE KS3 (immunity is GCSE-level in England); anchor on immunology/public-health sources and keep molecular detail qualitative.

Teach vaccines as derived from immunological memory (safe antigen → adaptive response → memory → pre-emptive protection), not as a disconnected fact; and state that vaccination and natural infection use the SAME memory mechanism, differing in that infection carries the disease's risks.

The reference poster is a scaffold: its static response curve can show the primary-vs-secondary outcome, but a fixed diagram cannot be manipulated to show the search-and-clone process over time; use the simulation for that dynamic timing story.

The consolidation task is mainly selection/sequencing with some brief explanation prompts; it does not fully elicit extended independent explanation, so pair it with the immunologist dialogue or a written/spoken explanation for sustained production.
Present the gut microbiome as largely beneficial/regulatory to counter 'all microbes are harmful', without overstating specific mechanisms beyond 'trains and regulates immune function'.
Keep the lock-and-key model qualitative: each B cell makes one antibody shape and only the matching one works; antibodies mainly bind/mark antigens rather than poisoning pathogens directly.

Optional interactive controls (live response curve, 'vaccinate' button, microbiome toggle, draggable/lift-the-flap elements) are illustrative examples of the learning mechanism, not mandatory features.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles rather than proving any activity was tested.

One source (British Society for Immunology — Bitesized Immunology, innate/adaptive/T cells/microbiome) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claims (two-arm structure and microbiome influence) as unconfirmed pending fresh verification.

The legacy row asserted comparative/necessity claims ('only a live simulation can make felt', 'static art can't convey', '3D adds no conceptual value'). These are not established by the sources; they were softened to narrowly scoped affordances/limits. The simulation is a strong fit for timing dynamics but is not asserted to be the sole way to teach the concept.
The reteach link mt_4JpMXUIxeD (for the 'vaccine gives you the disease' myth) is referenced in the assessment field but not expanded here; routing is a platform concern outside this rewrite.

The newborn probe in the assessment (strong innate, little adaptive at birth) is a useful discriminator but simplifies maternal/passive immunity; if used, keep it qualitative and avoid implying newborns have no antibody protection at all.

probeDeeper: You've had a flu vaccine but you still catch a cold. Why doesn't the flu vaccine protect you against the cold virus?
Why do some vaccines need a booster dose months or years later?
A newborn baby's innate defences work from day one, but it has almost no adaptive immunity yet. What does that tell you about the difference between the two kinds?
What's your evidence that memory cells actually stay in the body, rather than the body just happening to make antibodies faster the second time?
assess.correctAnswer: After the first exposure, antigen-specific memory B and T cells stay in the body. On re-exposure they recognise that same antigen and multiply and make antibodies far faster and in greater quantity, clearing the pathogen before symptoms appear. This memory is why a vaccine — a safe first exposure — protects you, and why the protection is specific to that one pathogen.

errorPatterns.pattern: immunity is a general strength boost — 'after you've been ill your body just gets tougher so germs can't get in'
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast with catching a different virus they've never met — they still get ill — to force the idea that protection is specific, then introduce antigen-specific memory cells
errorPatterns.distractor: Your body is generally stronger now, so all germs find it harder to get in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains the faster second response as generic toughness or a stronger body, and cannot say the protection is specific to that one virus

errorPatterns.pattern: the vaccine gives you the disease — 'the injection has the real illness in it so it makes you a bit ill on purpose'
errorPatterns.nextMove: distinguish a weakened/inactivated antigen or fragment that triggers memory-cell formation without causing the disease
errorPatterns.distractor: The vaccine puts a small dose of the real disease in you so your body practises fighting it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says a vaccine works by giving a mild version of the actual illness, or fears the vaccine itself is the disease

errorPatterns.pattern: no memory — 'each time a germ gets in, the white blood cells start from scratch and fight it the same way'
errorPatterns.nextMove: introduce memory B and T cells that persist after the first exposure and pre-arm the response
errorPatterns.distractor: Nothing is different — the white blood cells fight it exactly the same way as the first time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies any lasting change; describes the second fight as identical to the first

errorPatterns.pattern: antibodies are external medicine — 'antibodies are like the medicine the doctor gives to kill the germs'
errorPatterns.nextMove: locate antibody production in B cells and show antibodies binding specific antigens; separate this from medicines
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats antibodies as a drug taken into the body rather than proteins the body's own B cells make

errorPatterns.pattern: innate and adaptive are the same — 'all the body's defences are the specific germ-recognising kind'
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast always-present, non-specific barriers (innate) with the slower learned, specific, memory-forming response (adaptive)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot identify skin, mucus and inflammation as immediate non-specific defences that work with no prior exposure

responseLevels.gap: Treats immunity as a single generic strength; cannot distinguish innate from adaptive or explain why protection is specific to one pathogen.
responseLevels.full: Explains that first exposure leaves antigen-specific memory B/T cells; on re-exposure they recognise that antigen and respond faster and stronger; transfers this to explain vaccine protection and its specificity (flu vaccine ≠ cold protection).
responseLevels.partial: Lists innate, adaptive, B cells, antibodies and memory cells as separate facts, but cannot say how they act together — e.g. cannot explain why the second exposure is faster, or why a flu vaccine gives no protection against a cold.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The first time you catch chickenpox you're ill for a week. If the very same virus enters your body years later, you usually don't get ill at all. Your body hasn't 'remembered' feeling ill — so what is actually different inside your body the second time, and why does that make the response so much faster?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks immunity is a generic 'stronger body' cannot explain why protection is specific to the same virus, nor name a mechanism for the faster second response. A child with the real idea names specific memory cells that recognise that antigen and respond faster and stronger — a distinction a vague 'gets tougher' answer cannot fake.

sources.claim: The adaptive immune system recognises pathogens by antigens (surface proteins/sugars); each antibody-producing white blood cell (B cell) makes one antibody shape and only the matching one works (lock-and-key); the first response is slow because the right cells are rare and must multiply, and afterwards memory cells remain so a second exposure is defeated fast — which is how vaccines protect.
sources.source: Oxford Vaccine Group — Vaccine Knowledge Project: How do vaccines work?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; multiply and divide whole numbers AND decimals by 10, 100 and 1000, understanding the digit shift.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'multiply and divide whole numbers and those involving decimals by 10, 100 and 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.2 — 'explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and … in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10'; 5.NBT.1 place-value ten-times relationship.
• Operational details — the essential understanding is that ×/÷ by a power of ten SHIFTS every digit left/right across the place-value columns — the digits move, the decimal point stays put (or equivalently the point moves relative to the digits). This must replace the false 'add a zero / move the decimal point' rule, which breaks for decimals (3.45×100 is 345, not 3.4500). Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart where digits physically slide. ×1000 = three places left; ÷1000 = three places right, introducing tenths/hundredths/thousandths. This underpins metric conversions and powers-of-ten notation.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): × and ÷ whole numbers by 10/100 with digit-shift language. Tier B (age 9–10): 3.45×100, 72÷1000 correctly, explaining the shift. Tier C (age 10): explain why 'add a zero' fails for decimals and connect to metric conversion.
bestPractices: Teach as a digit SHIFT across place-value columns (digits move left for ×, right for ÷), not 'add a zero' or 'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
Use a place-value/Gattegno chart where digits physically slide the correct number of places, with the decimal point fixed.
Introduce tenths/hundredths/thousandths through ÷10/100/1000 so the columns to the right of the point are meaningful.
Link the number of places to the power of ten (×1000 → 3 places) and later to exponent notation.
Connect to metric conversions (m↔cm↔mm, kg↔g) as an authentic application.
keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart with sliding digits (point fixed)
Arrow/shift diagram showing 1/2/3 places for 10/100/1000
Decimal place-value columns (tenths, hundredths, thousandths)
Metric conversion tables as an application
commonMisconceptions: 'Add a zero' rule misapplied to decimals (3.45×100 wrongly written as 3.4500).
'Move the decimal point' causing confusion about direction or number of places.
Shifting the wrong number of places for the power of ten.
Forgetting to fill empty places with zeros as placeholders when needed (e.g. 72÷1000 = 0.072).
Thinking dividing always makes the digits smaller in value without understanding the place shift.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000 by understanding that each digit SHIFTS across the place-value columns — digits move left for multiplying and right for dividing, while the decimal point stays fixed. This replaces the fragile 'add a zero' rule, which breaks for decimals (3.45×100 is 345, not 3.4500), and the memorised 'move the point' rule, which gives the same numerical result but hides why the value changes and is easily misapplied (for example where to put the point in a whole number, or forgetting placeholder zeros). The skill underpins metric conversions and powers-of-ten notation.

activities.title: Sliding digits on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner appends zeros to a decimal (3.45×100 → 3.4500): on the chart, multiplying by 100 makes every digit worth 100× more, so each digit moves two columns left — the '3' becomes 3 hundreds. The point does not move; the digits do. The correct answer is 345.

If 72÷1000 comes out as 720 or 7.2: dividing makes each digit worth a thousandth as much, so the digits move exactly three columns to the RIGHT. 720 has moved them left (the wrong direction), and 7.2 has moved them only one place right instead of three.
If 72÷1000 is written as 0.72 (too few decimal places): count every column each digit crosses and drop a zero into each empty one so 72 lands correctly as 0.072.

If the place count is off by one under speed: this may be a counting slip rather than a misunderstanding. Recount the zeros in 10/100/1000, match them to the places shifted, and check whether the error comes back on similar items.
activities.rationale: The target concept is itself a digit shift across place-value columns, so watching digits slide while the point stays fixed makes the mechanism visible and exposes why the memorised 'add a zero' rule fails for decimals. Labelling the columns tenths/hundredths/thousandths gives meaning to the places opened up by division.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.2 requires explaining patterns in zeros and decimal-point placement when ×÷ by powers of ten; 5.NBT.1 the ten-times place-value relationship.
Teach ×÷ by powers of ten as a place-value digit shift, not 'add a zero'/'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with labelled columns from hundreds down to thousandths (… H  T  O • t  h  th) and a fixed decimal point.
Place 3.45 in the columns, then multiply by 100: slide every digit TWO columns to the LEFT so the 3, 4 and 5 become 345. Note that nothing was appended — the digits moved.
Now test the tempting 'just add two zeros' shortcut on 3.45 and compare: it gives 3.4500, which is wrong. Discuss why the shortcut fails for decimals.
Divide 72 by 1000: slide every digit THREE columns to the RIGHT, and fill each empty column it crosses with a placeholder zero, giving 0.072 (including the leading 0).
Compute 6 × 10 by sliding one place left (giving 60), and connect the number of places shifted to the number of zeros in 10/100/1000 (×1000 → 3 places).
Optionally switch the chart to a metric mode so the same kind of shift is reread as a conversion: metres → centimetres is ×100 (two places left) and centimetres → millimetres is ×10 (one place left).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten changes what each digit is worth, so the digits shift the matching number of place-value columns; the decimal point does not move, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.

activities.title: Reference chart with reveal-able shift arrows
feedback: If the direction is reversed: multiplying moves digits LEFT (larger value), dividing moves them RIGHT (smaller value).
If the count is wrong: match the number of places to the number of zeros in the power of ten.
activities.rationale: A static annotated chart is a clean, reusable reference that consolidates the direction-and-count rule, though it cannot itself let a learner slide digits through many cases — pair it with active manipulation for the shift intuition.
sourceClaims: Teach ×÷ by powers of ten as a place-value digit shift, not 'add a zero'/'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
learnerActions: Study a place-value chart annotated with arrows that show the shift for ×10 (one place), ×100 (two places) and ×1000 (three places), and the reverse for division.
Answer the prompt 'why isn't 3.45 × 100 = 3.4500?' and check your reasoning against a revealed explanation.
State in your own words how many places each power of ten shifts the digits and in which direction.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference links each power of ten to a fixed number of places and direction, reinforcing that the direction and count — not zero-appending — determine the result.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and fill-in consolidation
feedback: For the 3.45×100 choice: 3.4500 keeps the point fixed and tacks on zeros, leaving the value unchanged — wrong. Sliding each digit two places left gives 345.
For 72÷1000: a missing placeholder zero gives 0.72; count the crossed columns to reach 0.072.
An off-by-one place error may be a counting slip, so recount and see whether it happens again; a wrong direction signals the digit-shift idea needs revisiting.
activities.rationale: Checkable items that deliberately include the decimal trap and placeholder cases let a learner apply and test whether the shift understanding transfers; such items consolidate, check and diagnose but do not themselves provide the digit-sliding manipulation, so use them after active manipulation.
learnerActions: Complete 72 ÷ 1000 = ___ , writing all placeholder zeros.
Choose the correct value of 3.45 × 100 from options including the trap value 3.4500, and explain why the trap is wrong.
Find and fix the mistake in a worked example where a digit has been shifted the wrong number of places.
Explain, for one of your answers, how the value of each digit changed.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidation surfaces the specific decimal trap (3.4500) and the placeholder-zero requirement (0.072), confirming whether digit-shift reasoning is secure rather than a fragile trick.

activities.title: Testing the 'just add a zero' claim out loud
feedback: If the learner defends 'add a zero': ask what each digit is now worth — in 345 the 3 is 3 hundreds, so the digits moved, they were not padded.
If they are unsure how to express it: 'multiplying by 100 makes every digit worth 100 times more, so each slides two columns left.'
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue can draw out and challenge the misconception by prompting the learner to test it; it works best alongside a chart where the shift can be seen, since discussion alone does not let the learner manipulate the digits.
sourceClaims: Teach ×÷ by powers of ten as a place-value digit shift, not 'add a zero'/'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who insists you can always 'just add a zero' to multiply by ten.
Test the claim on a whole number (6 × 10 = 60) where it seems to work, then on a decimal (3.45 × 100) where it produces 3.4500.
Argue, using place value, why the claim is unsafe and what actually happens to the digits.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why 'add a zero' works for whole numbers but fails for decimals turns a half-learned rule into reasoned understanding of the digit shift.

constraints: Teach the operation as a digit shift across place-value columns (left for ×, right for ÷), not as 'add a zero' or 'move the decimal point': 'add a zero' gives wrong answers for decimals, and 'move the decimal point', although it gives the same numerical result, hides the change in place value and is easily misapplied to whole numbers and placeholder zeros.
Always fill empty columns crossed by a shift with placeholder zeros, including leading zeros (e.g. 72 ÷ 1000 = 0.072).
Introduce tenths/hundredths/thousandths through dividing by 10/100/1000 so the columns to the right of the point are meaningful before relying on them.
Link the number of places shifted to the number of zeros in the power of ten (×1000 → 3 places) and, later, to exponent notation.

Reference charts and multiple-choice / fill-in items consolidate, check and diagnose whether digit-shift reasoning transfers, but do not themselves provide the sliding manipulation; pair them with active manipulation rather than treating them as sufficient alone.

A manipulable sliding chart, a static annotated chart, a dialogue, and consolidation items each serve a different observable purpose; none is inherently sufficient alone, and no claim is established here that only one medium can teach this.

Arithmetic checked: 3.45×100=345, 72÷1000=0.072, 6×10=60. The original assessment 'correctAnswer' listed '345; 0.072; 60'; the '60' corresponds to the 6×10 diagnostic item and is correct, so it is retained — it is not an erroneous alternative.

The DfE claim attests only curriculum topic coverage, so it is not carried as support for a digit-shift teaching rationale. No comparative-efficacy or medium-superiority claims are asserted beyond what the sources support.

The original row rated a 3D treatment as 'poor'/'adds no insight'; this catalog rating is kept only as a narrow note rather than carried as a universal claim, since a catalog rating does not establish that 3D can teach nothing here.

probeDeeper: When you multiplied 3.45 by 100, did the decimal point move or did the digits move? Which is it really?
Why does 72 ÷ 1000 need those zeros after the point?
Explain what multiplying by 10 does to the value of each digit.
Someone got 3.4500 for 3.45 × 100. What did they do wrong?
assess.correctAnswer: 345; 0.072; 60. The teacher watches for the child moving each digit the correct number of places (two places left for ×100, three places right for ÷1000) with the decimal point staying put and zeros filling empty places — not a memorised 'add two zeros' trick that breaks on decimals.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'add zeros' rule — for 3.45 × 100 appends zeros to give 3.4500 instead of 345
errorPatterns.nextMove: use the place-value chart: multiplying by 100 makes every digit worth 100× more, so each digit SHIFTS two columns left; the '3' becomes 3 hundreds. The point does not move — the digits do.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer keeps the decimal point in place and tacks on zeros; magnitude unchanged

errorPatterns.pattern: 'move the decimal point' with the wrong direction or count — moves it right for division, or by the wrong number of places
errorPatterns.nextMove: reframe as digits shifting: dividing by 1000 makes each digit worth a thousandth as much, so digits move three columns RIGHT; fill empty places with zeros, including leading 0.0…
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 72 ÷ 1000 comes out as 720 or 7.2 rather than 0.072

errorPatterns.pattern: forgets to insert zeros as placeholders — 72 ÷ 1000 written as 0.72 (only shifts what's visible)
errorPatterns.nextMove: count the columns crossed and insert a zero in each empty one so 72 lands in the correct places (0.072).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: too few decimal places; digits shifted but empty columns not filled

errorPatterns.pattern: shifts correctly but miscounts places by one under speed
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child recount the number of zeros in 10/100/1000 and match to places shifted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer off by a factor of ten; self-corrects when recounting columns

responseLevels.gap: relies on 'add zeros', gives 3.4500, or moves the point the wrong way/amount; no place-value reasoning.
responseLevels.full: shifts digits the correct number of places in both directions for whole and decimal numbers, fills placeholders, keeps the point fixed, and explains each digit's changed value.
responseLevels.partial: handles whole-number cases by shifting but slips on decimals or forgets placeholder zeros in division.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to work these while you watch, using a place-value chart if they wish: 3.45 × 100, 72 ÷ 1000, and 6 × 10. Watch whether they SHIFT the digits across the place-value columns or whether they just 'add/remove zeros' or 'move the decimal point' as a rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'add a zero' rule works for whole numbers but fails on 3.45 × 100 (gives 3.4500, wrong) — so watching a decimal case exposes whether the child understands digit-shift or has memorised a fragile trick. 72 ÷ 1000 forces filling in leading zeros (0.072), catching those who only shuffle visible digits.
