pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Muscles Work in Pairs

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Skeletal & muscular systems):** "the function of muscles and examples of antagonistic muscles" (within biomechanics — the interaction between skeleton and muscles).

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS1-3):** the muscular system as an interacting subsystem; antagonistic-pair detail is UK-led.

- **Operational details:** Children explain that a muscle can only PULL (contract), never push, so movement in two directions needs an ANTAGONISTIC PAIR — one muscle contracts to move a bone one way while its partner relaxes, and vice versa to move it back. The canonical example is the biceps (contracts to bend/flex the elbow) and triceps (contracts to straighten/extend it); when one contracts the other relaxes. They give a second example (e.g. hamstring/quadriceps at the knee). The move that matters is the 'pull-only' insight — because muscles cannot push, the body needs opposing pairs to reverse a movement.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B→C. Builds on joints/tendons (how muscles attach and move bones); a natural endpoint of the musculoskeletal strand. A child is secure when they can explain why muscles work in pairs, state what the biceps and triceps each do when bending and straightening the arm, and give a second antagonistic pair.
bestPractices: Lead with the 'muscles only pull' principle — the whole need for pairs follows from it.
Use the biceps/triceps as the worked example, tracking BOTH muscles' states through bending and straightening.
Have pupils feel their own arm muscles contract/relax to make it embodied.
Generalise with a second pair (quadriceps/hamstrings) so 'antagonistic pair' is a rule, not one fact.
Tie back to tendons/joints — the pulling force reaches bone via tendons across a joint.
keyRepresentations: Biceps/triceps arm diagram in bent and straight positions
Contracted-vs-relaxed state labels for each muscle
Antagonistic-pair schematic (one pulls one way, the partner pulls back)
Second example (knee: quadriceps/hamstrings)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking muscles can push as well as pull.
Believing only one muscle (the biceps) works to both bend and straighten the arm.
Thinking both muscles of a pair contract at the same time.
Assuming a relaxed muscle actively pushes the bone back (it is pulled back by its antagonist).
Not recognising other antagonistic pairs beyond biceps/triceps.

learn.summary: Help 11–13 year-olds understand that muscles can only PULL (contract), never push, which is exactly why the body needs antagonistic pairs: one muscle contracts to move a bone one way while its partner relaxes, then the partner contracts to move it back. Use the biceps/triceps at the elbow as the worked example, tracking BOTH muscles' states through bending and straightening, then generalise to a second pair such as quadriceps/hamstrings at the knee. The decisive insight is that 'muscles work in pairs' is a direct consequence of pull-only action, not an arbitrary fact to memorise.

activities.title: Bend and straighten a controllable arm
feedback: When you can only use the biceps and the arm won't straighten: 'A muscle can pull but never push — so the biceps alone can only bend the arm. To straighten it you need the triceps to pull the other way.'
If a learner expects the relaxed muscle to do nothing: 'The relaxing muscle lengthens so the joint can move, and it is poised to pull the bone back next — both muscles are essential.'
On the knee example: 'Correct — the quadriceps contracts to straighten the knee while the hamstring relaxes, and the hamstring contracts to bend it. Same antagonistic rule as the arm.'
activities.rationale: Antagonistic action is a dynamic, reciprocal mechanism; a model the learner bends and straightens while watching the muscles swap between contracted and relaxed makes the pairing concrete and causal. Handing the learner only one muscle and asking them to reverse the movement engineers the 'muscles only pull' insight by letting them experience why one muscle is not enough. A dynamic model is one effective way to show reciprocal motion; a static diagram can still present the individual states.
sourceClaims: Muscles can only pull (contract), not push, so they work in antagonistic pairs; the biceps contracts to bend the elbow while the triceps relaxes, and the triceps contracts to straighten it while the biceps relaxes.
learnerActions: Drag the forearm up and down (or use a flex/extend control) on a model elbow and watch what happens to the biceps and triceps.
Observe that as the forearm rises, the biceps shortens and bulges (contracted) while the triceps lengthens (relaxed); as the model actively straightens the arm, the two swap.
Read the colour-coding that marks each muscle as contracted or relaxed so the reciprocal swap is unmistakable.
Try to straighten the arm when given control of ONLY the biceps — discover you cannot, because a muscle can pull but not push.
Call in the triceps to pull the arm straight, then explain in your own words why two opposing muscles are needed.
Repeat with a second joint (the knee, with quadriceps and hamstrings) and state which muscle contracts for each movement.
activities.intendedInsight: Because a muscle can only pull (contract), a single muscle cannot reverse a movement; the body needs an antagonistic pair where one contracts while the partner relaxes, and the roles swap to move the bone back. This rule generalises beyond the biceps/triceps.

activities.title: Feel your own muscles take turns (predict, then test)
feedback: If a learner predicts the biceps will push the arm straight: feeling the triceps harden and the biceps soften shows the biceps did not push; the triceps pulled the arm straight.
When asked what the biceps is doing as the triceps straightens the arm: 'It is relaxing and lengthening so the joint can move.'

If a learner says both muscles tighten together to straighten the arm: 'To move the joint, one muscle in the pair contracts while the other relaxes; if both pulled hard against each other, the joint would be held stiff rather than move — that is how we hold a joint steady, not how we move it.'
activities.rationale: Predicting before testing surfaces the 'muscles push' misconception, and feeling the reciprocal change makes the pull-only pairing tangible and personally verifiable. This embodied step complements a visual model.
sourceClaims: Muscles can only pull (contract), not push, so they work in antagonistic pairs; the biceps contracts to bend the elbow while the triceps relaxes, and the triceps contracts to straighten it while the biceps relaxes.
learnerActions: Rest one hand across your biceps and triceps while your arm is bent.
Predict first: which muscle will tighten as you slowly straighten your arm, and why?

Slowly straighten the arm against resistance (for example, press your palm down firmly on a table, or straighten your arm while it is raised above your head so the forearm lifts against gravity) and feel which muscle hardens (contracts) and which softens (relaxes). If you just let your forearm drop downwards, gravity does much of the work and the biceps may stay firm as it controls the fall, so use resistance for a clear test.
Compare what you felt with your prediction and explain any surprise.
Answer: when the triceps contracts to straighten your arm, what is the biceps doing at that moment?
Answer: what would happen at the elbow if both muscles contracted hard at the same time?
activities.intendedInsight: Making the biceps/triceps swap embodied — predicting then feeling the triceps harden while the biceps softens as the arm is straightened against resistance — confronts the belief that a muscle 'pushes' the arm straight and shows that, to produce movement, one muscle in the pair contracts while the other relaxes.

activities.title: Name the states and transfer the rule
feedback: Bending the arm: biceps contracts, triceps relaxes. Straightening the arm: triceps contracts, biceps relaxes.
'A muscle can only pull. It cannot push — that is precisely why movement in two directions needs an opposing pair.'
A correct second pair, e.g. 'The quadriceps contracts to straighten the knee; the hamstring contracts to bend it.'
activities.rationale: Stating which muscle contracts/relaxes in each position and identifying a second antagonistic pair are clean checks that distinguish a learner who grasps the pull-only cause from one who still thinks a single muscle pushes and pulls. A recognition or naming task can check understanding but does not by itself elicit the embodied discovery of why a pair is needed.
sourceClaims: Muscles can only pull (contract), not push, so they work in antagonistic pairs; the biceps contracts to bend the elbow while the triceps relaxes, and the triceps contracts to straighten it while the biceps relaxes.
learnerActions: State which muscle contracts and which relaxes when the arm is bent, and again when it is straightened.
Decide whether a muscle can push as well as pull, and justify the answer.
Name a second antagonistic pair in the body (for example quadriceps/hamstrings at the knee) and say which movement each muscle produces.
Explain in one or two sentences why pull-only muscles force the body to use muscles in pairs.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the naming/state layer (which muscle is contracted/relaxed in each position) and confirm the learner can transfer the antagonistic-pair rule to a new joint and articulate the underlying cause.

constraints: Lead with the 'muscles only pull' principle — the whole need for pairs follows from it; do not present 'muscles work in pairs' as an arbitrary fact to memorise.
Track BOTH muscles' states (contracted and relaxed) through bending and straightening, not just the one doing the work.
Address the misconception that a relaxed muscle does nothing: it lengthens to allow movement and is poised to pull the bone back next.

Address the misconception that both muscles of a pair contract together to produce a movement: if both pulled hard against each other the joint would be held stiff rather than move (the body does this on purpose to hold a joint steady); to produce movement, one contracts while the other relaxes.
Tie the pulling force back to tendons and joints — the muscle's pull reaches the bone via a tendon across the joint (prerequisite knowledge).

A two-state (bent vs straight) model or diagram can label which muscle is contracted/relaxed, but a static presentation does not animate the reciprocal motion; use it as a naming/state scaffold alongside a dynamic demonstration or the learner's own arm.
A naming or multiple-choice check verifies the state labels but does not by itself produce the 'why a pair is needed' discovery; pair it with manipulation or embodied feeling.
A 3D model can add spatial realism to the muscle bulge/relax shape change, but the antagonistic concept is fully expressible in 2D or with the learner's own arm; 3D is optional, not required.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One cited source (BBC Bitesize KS3) is marked unverified in the row; the pull-only/antagonistic-pair claim it supports is also standard curriculum content, but its evidence status should be checked on review.

The DfE KS3 Biology source supports the curriculum requirement to teach the function of muscles and antagonistic pairs rather than any specific activity's teaching method, so it is not attached to an activity's sourceClaims; it remains a valid row source documenting the standard.

The original 'live arm makes it felt in a way a static diagram cannot' framing was softened: a dynamic model is one effective way to convey reciprocal motion, and a static image's limit is only that it cannot animate the swap, not that it cannot teach the states.

Optional interaction examples (dragging the forearm, flex/extend control, colour-coded contracted/relaxed states, a lift-the-flap 'Can a muscle push?' prompt, a tappable two-state arm, an optional 3D view) are retained as ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory mechanisms or as evidence of medium superiority.

assess.poeTask: Ask each child to slowly straighten a bent arm while a hand rests on the biceps and triceps. Have them PREDICT first which muscle will tighten and why. Predicting the biceps 'pushes' it straight, then feeling the triceps harden while the biceps softens, forces the antagonistic-pair idea.
probeDeeper: When the triceps contracts to straighten your arm, what is the biceps doing at that moment?
What would happen at the elbow if both muscles contracted hard at the same time?
Muscles can only pull — so how does that force the body to use muscles in pairs?
Name another antagonistic pair in the body and say which movement each one produces.
assess.correctAnswer: Muscles can only pull (contract), never push. So the biceps can pull the arm into a bend but cannot push it straight; a second muscle, the triceps, must pull it back the other way. As one contracts, its partner relaxes — an antagonistic pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: A muscle can push as well as pull ('the biceps pushes it back straight')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish pull-only action first; then the need for an opposing muscle follows. Feel the biceps and triceps take turns.
errorPatterns.distractor: The biceps just pushes the arm straight again by itself.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says one muscle both bends and straightens the joint by pushing

errorPatterns.pattern: Both muscles contract at the same time to move the joint
errorPatterns.nextMove: In an antagonistic pair one contracts while the other relaxes; if both contracted the joint would lock. Have them feel one soften as the other hardens.
errorPatterns.distractor: Both muscles tighten at the same time to straighten the arm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the biceps and triceps both tighten together to straighten the arm

errorPatterns.pattern: The relaxing muscle is doing nothing / is switched off and irrelevant
errorPatterns.nextMove: The relaxing muscle lengthens so the joint can move, and it is poised to pull the bone back next — both are essential.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the relaxed muscle as unimportant, as if only the contracting one matters

responseLevels.gap: Thinks a single muscle pushes and pulls; cannot explain why two are needed.
responseLevels.full: Explains muscles pull only, so antagonistic pairs are required — one contracts while the other relaxes — and transfers the idea to another pair such as hamstrings/quadriceps.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the biceps/triceps take turns but still says a muscle can push, or that both contract together, or ignores the relaxing partner.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You bend your arm by contracting your biceps. To straighten it again, the triceps contracts and pulls. Why do you need two separate muscles here — why can't the biceps just push the arm straight again by itself?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps antagonistic action explains that pull-only muscles are exactly why a pair is needed. A child who thinks a muscle can push, or that both muscles contract together, sees no reason for two and can't explain the relaxing partner.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Using a Microscope (PROCEDURAL)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 'Cells and organisation'):** the practical skill embedded in "how to observe, interpret and record cell structure using a light microscope"; also draws on KS3 working-scientifically expectations for apparatus and measurement.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** the SEP 'Planning and Carrying Out Investigations' underlying MS-LS1-1 ('conduct an investigation... that living things are made of cells'); microscope technique is the investigative tool.

- **Operational details:** This is a PROCEDURAL/skills topic: the correct, safe sequence for using a light microscope — set up and carry safely; prepare a wet-mount slide (specimen, water drop, lower the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles); start on the LOWEST power; focus with the COARSE knob first while watching from the side, then the FINE knob down the eyepiece; centre and increase magnification; and calculate magnification (total = eyepiece × objective; or magnification = image size ÷ actual size). Finish with an accurate labelled drawing at a stated scale. The skill is a fixed ordered procedure with specific safety and error-avoidance rules, learned by repeated hands-on practice.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (procedural fluency). Success is reliably obtaining a clear, correctly-focused image of a well-made slide and recording it accurately; the common failure points (air bubbles, focusing coarse on high power and cracking the slide, over-staining) are where the procedure must be drilled.
bestPractices: Teach it as an explicit ordered procedure (carry safely → wet mount → lowest power → coarse then fine focus → increase magnification → record) and have pupils rehearse the whole sequence, not isolated tips.
Drill the two highest-value error-avoidance rules: lower the coverslip at an angle (no air bubbles) and coarse-focus only on low power watching from the side (don't crack the slide).
Integrate the numeracy — total magnification = eyepiece × objective; magnification = image ÷ actual size — as part of the procedure, not a separate maths lesson.
Require an accurate labelled biological drawing with a scale as the recorded outcome.
Give repeated low-stakes practice so the procedure becomes fluent and automatic before it matters for content.
Pair with the concept topic 'Cells Under the Microscope' so technique is learned in the service of seeing real cells.
keyRepresentations: A labelled light microscope (eyepiece, objectives, stage, coarse/fine focus, light source)
A step-by-step wet-mount preparation sequence
A focusing sequence (blurred → sharp) showing coarse-then-fine on low power
A magnification calculation (eyepiece × objective; image ÷ actual size)
A labelled biological drawing with a scale bar as the recorded output
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the coverslip flat and then reading the resulting air bubble as a cell.
Using the coarse focus on high power and driving the objective into (and cracking) the slide.
Starting on the highest magnification rather than the lowest to locate the specimen first.
Thinking magnification is just the objective value, forgetting to multiply by the eyepiece.
Shading or 'artistic' drawings instead of clear labelled line drawings with a scale.

learn.summary: Procedural skills topic for ages 11–12: using a light microscope correctly and safely. Learners rehearse the full ordered sequence (carry safely → prepare a wet mount → start on lowest power → coarse-then-fine focus → centre and increase magnification → record an accurate labelled drawing at a stated scale) and calculate total magnification. The priority is building fluent, safe procedure through repeated practice, with explicit attention to the common failure points (air bubbles, coarse-focusing on high power, over-staining when a stain is used, drawing from memory). A simulator can front-load the procedure and let learners safely meet error consequences; real bench practice is where the motor skill is consolidated.

activities.title: Rehearse the whole microscope procedure (simulated or stepped build)
feedback: If the coverslip is dropped flat and a bubble appears: because the coverslip was dropped flat, air was trapped — that dark circle is an air bubble, not a cell. Lower the coverslip at an angle so the water spreads without trapping air.

If coarse focus is used on high power: this is where the objective can drive into and crack the slide — coarse-focus only on the lowest power, watching from the side; on higher powers use fine focus only.
If the learner starts on high power and finds nothing: start low to find and centre the specimen, then increase magnification.
If total magnification is reported as only the objective (or only the eyepiece): with a ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective the total is 10 × 40 = 400×, not 40×.

If the drawing is idealised or shaded: a biological drawing records observation, not memory — draw exactly what is in view (artefacts and folds included) as a clean labelled line drawing with a scale.
activities.rationale: The topic is procedural: an ordered sequence with decision points and failure modes is best learned by performing the whole sequence repeatedly, not by isolated tips. Rehearsing the full procedure and meeting its consequences is intended to build fluency and embed the error-avoidance rules.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Biology 'Cells and organisation' requires observing, interpreting and recording cell structure using a light microscope; KS3 working-scientifically expects correct use of apparatus and measurement/calculation (including magnification).

Correct light-microscope procedure: prepare a wet mount lowering the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles; focus with the coarse then fine adjustment starting on low power; total magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens.
learnerActions: Carry and set up the microscope safely, then prepare a wet mount in order: place the specimen (e.g. onion skin), add a drop of water (or iodine stain where used), and lower the coverslip at an angle.

Observe the consequence of coverslip technique: dropping it flat is likely to trap air bubbles that could later be mistaken for cells; lowering it at an angle lets the water spread and push air out, so bubbles are much less likely.
Rack to the LOWEST power objective first to locate and centre the specimen.

With the lowest-power objective in place, bring the objective and slide close together using the COARSE adjustment while watching from the side (to avoid driving the lens into the slide); then look down the eyepiece and focus by increasing the gap between them (objective up or stage down, depending on the microscope), switching to the FINE adjustment to sharpen.
Centre the specimen, then step up magnification.
Calculate total magnification = eyepiece × objective, and where image and actual sizes are given, magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
Produce a clear labelled line drawing with a stated scale, recording only what is actually seen.
activities.intendedInsight: Using a microscope is a fixed, safe, ordered procedure; each step avoids a specific error (bubbles, cracked slides, lost specimens, inaccurate records), and the two numeracy rules are part of the procedure.

activities.title: Safe focusing drill: watch from the side, move the lens away
feedback: If the learner closes the gap between objective and slide while looking through the eyepiece: only bring them together while watching from the side, then focus by widening the gap (objective up or stage down).
If the learner tries coarse focus on high power: coarse focus is for low power only; switch to fine focus once magnified.
activities.rationale: This isolates the single highest-risk motor error (racking down onto the slide) so learners build the safe habit before it matters with real specimens. Presented as a focused drill within the overall procedure, not a replacement for it.
sourceClaims: Correct light-microscope procedure: prepare a wet mount lowering the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles; focus with the coarse then fine adjustment starting on low power; total magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens.
learnerActions: With the lowest-power objective in place, bring the objective and slide close together (lower the objective or raise the stage, depending on the microscope) while watching from the side (not through the eyepiece).
Then look down the eyepiece and focus by increasing the gap between objective and slide (objective up or stage down, depending on the microscope) using the coarse adjustment on low power.
Switch to the fine adjustment to sharpen the image.
Explain why coarse focus is used only on the lowest power.
activities.intendedInsight: Focusing safely means bringing the lens close while watching from the side, then focusing by moving away from the slide — this prevents cracking the slide and damaging the objective.

activities.title: Labelled microscope reference and 'why' flaps
feedback: For the coverslip-angle flap: lowering at an angle lets the water spread without trapping an air bubble that would obscure or mimic a cell.
For the focus flap: coarse focus moves the objective a long way; on high power this can drive it into the slide, so coarse is used on low power only.
activities.rationale: A labelled reference and ordered step cards give a clean map of the apparatus and sequence and present the reasons behind the two key rules. On its own this does not have the learner perform the ordered actions or meet the failure modes, so it works best alongside hands-on or simulated practice.
sourceClaims: Correct light-microscope procedure: prepare a wet mount lowering the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles; focus with the coarse then fine adjustment starting on low power; total magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens.
learnerActions: Match each labelled part of the microscope (eyepiece, objectives, stage, coarse/fine focus knobs, light source) to its job.
Order the step cards for the full procedure from carrying the microscope to recording the drawing.
Reveal explanations for the two key rules: why lower the coverslip at an angle, and why coarse-focus only on low power.
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing the parts, their functions, and the reasons behind the key rules supports correct independent use of the procedure.

activities.title: Check the procedure and the numeracy
feedback: For magnification: multiply both lenses; ×10 eyepiece × ×40 objective = 400×, not 40×.
For order: locate and centre on low power before increasing magnification.

For bubble vs cell: an air bubble is often rounder with a thick, dark rim, can shift or merge when the slide is nudged, and tends to lie above the cell layer; confirm against the actual view rather than relying on the outline alone.
activities.rationale: Ordering, multiple-choice and fill-in tasks efficiently check recall of the sequence and the numeracy, and can check reasoning about artefacts. These checks confirm understanding but do not build the motor procedure, so they complement rather than replace practice.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Biology 'Cells and organisation' requires observing, interpreting and recording cell structure using a light microscope; KS3 working-scientifically expects correct use of apparatus and measurement/calculation (including magnification).
learnerActions: Put the steps of using a microscope in the correct order.
Answer which knob is used on which power and why.
Calculate total magnification by combining eyepiece × objective (e.g. ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective = 400×).
Decide whether a described circular feature is a cell or an air bubble and justify the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state the correct order, the safe focusing rule, and the magnification calculation, and can give reasons to distinguish an artefact from a real structure.

activities.title: Perform and record at the real bench
feedback: If the learner draws the textbook cell rather than the view: record observation, not memory — include artefacts and folds as seen.
If the slide has bubbles or the image won't focus safely: revisit coverslip angle and the side-watching coarse-focus habit before retrying.
If an iodine stain is used and detail is lost in a dark wash: too much stain obscures structure — use a small amount, and if needed remake the mount.
If magnification is reported from one lens only: multiply eyepiece × objective.
activities.rationale: The checkpoint is procedural fluency demonstrated on real apparatus; a simulator or diagram can prepare and rehearse, but the skill is ultimately performed and consolidated at the bench. Repeated low-stakes practice is intended to make the procedure automatic.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Biology 'Cells and organisation' requires observing, interpreting and recording cell structure using a light microscope; KS3 working-scientifically expects correct use of apparatus and measurement/calculation (including magnification).
learnerActions: Prepare a real wet mount of a biological specimen (e.g. onion skin, using a drop of water or iodine stain as directed) and obtain a clear, bubble-free, correctly focused image.
Talk through each step while focusing, then increase magnification once the specimen is centred.
Make an accurate labelled line drawing with a scale, recording exactly what is seen.
State the total magnification used and, where sizes are given, work out magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
activities.intendedInsight: Reliably obtaining and honestly recording a clear image of a well-made slide is the real target of the skill; fluency comes from doing it, not just describing it.

constraints: Success means reliably obtaining a clear, correctly focused image of a well-made slide and recording it accurately; the common failure points (air bubbles from a flat coverslip, coarse-focusing on high power and cracking the slide, over-staining when a stain is used, drawing from memory) are where practice must concentrate.
Teach as one explicit ordered procedure rehearsed as a whole, not as isolated tips.
Integrate the numeracy (total = eyepiece × objective; magnification = image ÷ actual size) within the procedure rather than as a separate maths lesson.
Require a clear labelled line drawing with a stated scale as the recorded outcome — not shaded or 'artistic' drawings.

A static labelled diagram or step cards support the order and reasons but do not have the learner perform the ordered actions or meet the failure modes; use them as a reference scaffold alongside practice.
Ordering/multiple-choice/calculation tasks check recall and numeracy but do not build the motor procedure.

A simulator can let learners safely meet error consequences and build fluency before bench time, but it is a scaffold: consolidate the physical skill with real hands-on practice. Pair with a cells concept topic so technique is learned in the service of seeing real cells.
An optional 3D handling model can add realism to manipulating the microscope and coverslip, but is not required for the core decision points.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The BBC Bitesize source (procedure and magnification formula) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat the specific procedural details as unconfirmed pending review.

The legacy entry asserted a simulator builds fluency 'a video or picture can't' and that the cracked-slide consequence teaches 'far more memorably than a warning ever could.' These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped proposals; the simulator is framed as a scaffold that complements real practice.

The legacy 'conversation poor fit' claimed a motor procedure 'can't be learned through open dialogue'; this universal was dropped, while talk-through during focusing is retained as a useful element of the performance task.
Original evidence descriptor lists 'course focus' (typo for coarse focus); corrected to 'coarse focus' throughout the activities.

The focus step in activity 1 was tightened to the correct safe sequence (bring the lens close while watching from the side, then focus by moving it up and away), matching the dedicated focusing drill, so it cannot be read as achieving focus while looking from the side.

Over-staining is listed as a failure point in the original pedagogy; it only applies when a stain (e.g. iodine for onion) is used, so it has been anchored to the optional staining step rather than left unexplained. Confirm whether the specific practical uses a stain.

The air-bubble vs cell distinction is a general observational heuristic (thick dark rim, rounder, shifts/merges, lies above the cell layer); confirm against the specimens and optics in use, as appearance can vary with focus and lighting.

probeDeeper: Why do you start on the lowest power rather than the highest?
When you turn the coarse focus, which way should the lens move relative to the slide, and why watch from the side?
You're using a ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective — what's the total magnification?
Is that dark circle a cell or an air bubble — how can you tell?
assess.correctAnswer: The student makes a bubble-free wet mount, starts on the lowest-power objective, uses coarse focus while watching from the side to avoid driving the lens into the slide, then fine focus, centres the specimen before increasing magnification, draws only what is actually seen with a scale, and calculates total magnification as eyepiece × objective.

errorPatterns.pattern: Focuses by lowering the objective toward the slide while looking through the eyepiece
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lower the lens while watching from the side, then focus by moving it UP and away from the slide. Model it once, then let them redo.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Drives the objective down onto the slide, risking cracking it, and can't find focus

errorPatterns.pattern: Start on the highest power to see the most detail
errorPatterns.nextMove: Always start on the lowest objective to find and centre the specimen, then step up the magnification.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Begins on the high-power objective and cannot locate anything in the field

errorPatterns.pattern: Total magnification is just the objective number (or just the eyepiece)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective; work through the multiplication with the actual lenses in use.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports 40× when using a ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective, instead of 400×

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws the textbook cell rather than what's actually in view
errorPatterns.nextMove: A biological drawing records observation, not memory; draw exactly what is seen, artefacts and all. Scaffold, don't reteach the concept.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces an idealised diagram (or omits bubbles/folds) that doesn't match the slide

responseLevels.gap: Cannot set up or focus safely, starts on high power, and can't calculate magnification.
responseLevels.full: Prepares a clean wet mount, focuses safely from low power upward, draws exactly what is observed with a scale, and calculates total magnification as eyepiece × objective.
responseLevels.partial: Gets an image but focuses unsafely, mounts with bubbles, or reports magnification from only one lens.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a light microscope, a slide of onion cells and the kit to make a wet mount. Prepare the slide, find the cells, and make a labelled drawing. Talk me through what you're doing as you focus — then work out the total magnification you're using.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: You watch the technique, not a recalled definition. A skilled student starts low, focuses by raising the lens away from the slide while watching from the side, mounts without bubbles, draws honestly, and multiplies eyepiece by objective. Errors show as racking down onto the slide, starting on high power, mislabelling bubbles, or reporting only one lens's magnification.

pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, attending to precision means using mathematical words carefully — 'more than / fewer than / the same as' for comparing, shape names with 'sides' and 'corners', and positional words (above, below, next to) — and beginning to refine vague everyday language into words that pin down the meaning. The EEF Early Years guidance frames this as a staged informal→formal journey: start from a child's own words ('pointy', 'big') and help them rephrase precisely ('has points', 'taller'). A key move is exposing children to a WIDE VARIETY of examples of each shape so they do not form a narrow, prototype-bound concept (only a 'point-up' triangle counts).
bestPractices: Seize everyday moments to reinforce precise vocabulary — who is 'first', who has 'more than', where the teddy is 'behind' — rather than teaching words in isolation (EEF)
Help children refine ambiguous everyday words: when a child says 'big', ask 'taller, or more?' so they choose the word that carries the meaning (EEF's big→tall example)
Move informal→formal: accept 'pointy'/'curved' first, then introduce formal shape names gradually and reinforce them in routine (EEF)
Expose children to varied examples and non-examples of each shape (many kinds of triangle, tilted squares) to prevent an over-generalised, prototype-only concept (EEF)
Pair each word with the action or feature it names — run a finger along a SIDE, point to a CORNER — so the vocabulary is grounded, not recited
keyRepresentations: Comparison language with matched groups (more than / fewer than / same as)
A varied shape gallery (many triangles, rotated squares) with sides and corners traced
Positional-language scenes (objects above/below/behind/next to)
Real objects and manipulatives named in play
commonMisconceptions: Uses ambiguous everyday words where a precise one exists — 'big' for tall or for 'more', 'by' for a specific position (EEF)
Recognises only prototype shapes — rejects a long or upside-down triangle as 'not a triangle', calls a tilted square a 'diamond' (EEF: needs varied exposure)
Uses 'sides' and 'corners' interchangeably, or counts corners when asked for sides
Thinks a shape's name depends on how it is turned or how big it is, rather than its properties

learn.summary: For children aged 5-6, attending to precision means using mathematical words carefully: comparison words ('more than / fewer than / the same as'), shape vocabulary ('sides', 'corners', shape names), and positional words (above, below, behind, next to). A key proposed teaching move is to make vague language have a visible consequence so the child can discover the value of a precise word — a research-informed approach rather than a uniquely required method — following an informal→formal journey that starts from the child's own words ('pointy', 'big') and helps them rephrase ('has points', 'taller'). Children also need exposure to a WIDE VARIETY of examples of each shape so they do not form a narrow, prototype-bound concept.

activities.title: Tell the literal robot where teddy goes
feedback: When the child says 'by the box' and the robot puts teddy near the box but not where the child meant (e.g. behind it instead of on top), the mismatch itself is the feedback — prompt: 'Did the robot put teddy where you wanted? How could you say it so teddy lands exactly there?'
If the child says 'bigger' and is handed the taller-but-fewer tower, ask 'Do you mean taller, or more blocks?' and have the CHILD choose the precise word rather than supplying it.
When the child uses a precise word and the robot succeeds first time, name the success: 'On top of told the robot exactly where — it worked straight away.'
activities.rationale: Precision of communication becomes meaningful when vagueness has an immediate, repeatable consequence the child can see and repair. A responsive surface (or in-role character) lets the child produce and refine language rather than merely recognise it, following EEF's informal→formal refinement (big→tall). This is a proposed design, not a validated or uniquely-best format.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
Mathematically proficient students communicate precisely, use clear definitions, and in the elementary grades give carefully formulated explanations to each other
learnerActions: Direct a friendly robot (or puppet/character) to place teddy somewhere, e.g. say 'put teddy by the box'.

Watch the robot do EXACTLY what the words say — 'by the box' only means near the box, so the robot might put teddy behind it, in front of it, or beside it — so the ambiguity can produce a result that is not where the child meant.
Refine the instruction to a precise positional word ('on top of the box', 'behind the box') and check the robot now gets it right.
Repeat with a comparison round: ask for 'the tower with MORE blocks' rather than 'the bigger tower', to distinguish taller from more.
Say, in the child's own words, why the exact word helped the robot understand.
activities.intendedInsight: A vague everyday word (like 'by' or 'big') often fails to pin down the meaning; choosing a precise word (on top of / behind; taller / more) lets a listener do exactly what you intend.

activities.title: A character who takes your words literally
feedback: When the character deliberately misunderstands, prompt the child to explain which precise word they meant.
Praise the moment the child spontaneously refines: 'You changed by to behind so I knew exactly where.'
activities.rationale: An in-role character who misunderstands can generate precise-language repair through unscripted, responsive dialogue, giving the child spoken production practice. Short turns suit the age. This is a proposed format; the sources do not establish it as superior to other media.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
learnerActions: Talk with a playful character (puppet or robot friend) who cheerfully misunderstands vague instructions, e.g. 'You said BY the box, so I put teddy BEHIND it — right?'
Answer the character's clarifying questions to pin down the position, comparison, or shape word you meant.
Keep each exchange short, and restate the instruction precisely until the character gets it right.
activities.intendedInsight: Being asked 'did you mean this or that?' makes a child notice an ambiguity and reach for the word that removes it — the repair IS the practice.

activities.title: The varied shape gallery (sides, corners and non-prototypes)
feedback: If the child rejects a long or upside-down triangle, show more varied examples and non-examples and return focus to the defining property: a closed shape with three straight sides.
If the child calls a tilted square a 'diamond', count the four equal sides and four square (right-angle) corners together and confirm it is still a square however it is turned.
If the child swaps 'sides' and 'corners', re-pair each word with its action (run a finger along a side, point to a corner) in play rather than marking it wrong — it resolves with exposure.
activities.rationale: Varied examples and non-examples counter the prototype-only concept. A tap-to-reveal gallery can label and prime the vocabulary; on its own it primes recognition and does not require the child to produce or refine language, so pair it with the directing/dialogue activities.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
learnerActions: Explore a gallery of many triangles and quadrilaterals shown in varied orientations and sizes — long thin triangles, upside-down triangles, tilted squares.
Trace a finger along each SIDE and point to each CORNER as they are named, then reveal the shape's name.

Decide whether a tilted square is still a square (it has four equal sides and four square corners, however it is turned) and whether a long or upside-down triangle is still a triangle (it is a closed shape with three straight sides).
Sort a tilted square into the 'square' group by its properties rather than by how it looks or how it is turned.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's name depends on its properties (its straight sides and its corners), not on its size or orientation; 'side' and 'corner' name different features.

activities.title: Place the object in a spatial scene
feedback: If the placement does not match the word used, ask which word would describe where teddy actually is.
Confirm when the chosen word and the placement agree: 'Behind — and that's just where you put it.'
activities.rationale: Positional vocabulary is genuinely spatial, so placing an object in a scene (a simple room or picture) exercises that strand concretely. This supports only the positional strand; the comparison and shape-name strands are not spatial, so this activity is a companion rather than the main vehicle.
sourceClaims: Practitioners should reinforce precise vocabulary (first, more than, fewer) and help children refine ambiguous everyday words (e.g. 'big' → 'tall'); move from informal to formal language; and expose children to a wide variety of shapes (not just prototypes like equilateral triangles) to prevent a narrow shape concept
learnerActions: Place teddy in a scene above, below, behind, or next to another object, choosing the positional word that matches where you want it.
Describe aloud where you put teddy using the precise positional word.
Swap roles: a partner states a position and you place teddy to match, then check it agrees.
activities.intendedInsight: Positional language describes genuine spatial relationships; the right word lets another person find the object exactly.

constraints: Seize everyday moments to reinforce precise vocabulary — who is 'first', who has 'more than', where the teddy is 'behind' — rather than teaching words in isolation.

Build informal→formal: accept the child's own words ('pointy', 'curved', 'big') first, then introduce and reinforce formal words gradually; have the CHILD choose the precise word rather than simply supplying it.
Pair each word with the action or feature it names (run a finger along a side, point to a corner) so vocabulary is grounded, not recited.
Treat interchangeable use of 'sides' and 'corners' as a developmental stage that resolves with exposure, not an error to drill or mark wrong.

A picture-word matching or tap-to-reveal task can check or prime recognition but does not by itself elicit the child producing or refining language; use it as a warm-up alongside the directing/dialogue activities, not as the sole vehicle.
The spatial-scene activity supports only the positional strand; it does not exercise comparison or shape-name vocabulary.

Diagnostic prompts deliberately use an ambiguous word (e.g. 'by') so the vagueness is detectable; a precise word like 'behind' would not reveal whether the child attends to precision. Responses are surfaced for discussion, not marked right or wrong.

When naming a square, use the properties that define it (four equal sides and four square corners), so a non-square rhombus is not accepted as a square; the teaching point is that turning a shape does not change its identity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The legacy entry asserted that precision 'is best taught' by a live surface with a literal robot and framed alternatives as unable to make the child produce or refine language. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources; they have been softened to scoped proposals noting each format's affordance and limit, including in the summary.

Both cited sources (CCSS MP6 and EEF Early Maths) are general-practice guidance, not evaluations of the proposed robot game, puppet dialogue, or gallery; no comparative efficacy among these formats is established.

The original row defined a tilted square as a square by 'four equal sides' alone; this under-specifies a square (a rhombus also has four equal sides). Corrected in the learner action, feedback and constraints to include four square corners while keeping the age-appropriate focus on orientation invariance.

probeDeeper: If I said 'the cup is by the sink', show me two different places the cup could be.
Is this one [a long thin triangle] a triangle? How do you know?
Point to a side, and now a corner — which is which?
Sam says his tower is 'big'. What could you ask him so you know exactly what he means?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child noticing that 'by' is vague (teddy could be on top, behind, beside, inside) and reaching for a precise positional word, and ideally saying why it matters (so the listener isn't confused). This is surfaced for discussion, not marked right or wrong.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses an ambiguous everyday word where a precise one exists — 'big' for tall or for 'more', 'by' for a definite position — and does not notice the ambiguity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model refining in the moment ('do you mean taller, or more blocks?') and have the CHILD choose the precise word; build informal→formal, don't just supply the answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Repeats 'by'/'big' contentedly and cannot say what else it might mean when shown alternatives

errorPatterns.pattern: Recognises only prototype shapes — rejects a long or upside-down triangle as 'not a triangle', or calls a tilted square a 'diamond'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a wide variety of examples and non-examples and focus on defining properties (three straight sides) rather than the look or orientation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the triangle counterexample the child denies it is a triangle, or renames a rotated square

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'sides' and 'corners' interchangeably while the vocabulary is still forming
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill definitions or treat it as an error to mark wrong; keep pairing each word with the action (trace a side, point to a corner) in play — it resolves with exposure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts corners when asked for sides, or swaps the words, but self-corrects with modelling

responseLevels.gap: Uses vague everyday words and does not notice the ambiguity; names only prototype shapes; conflates sides and corners.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, chooses precise comparison, shape and positional words, notices when a word is ambiguous and refines it, recognises varied (non-prototype) examples by their properties, and can say why saying it exactly helps the listener.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, offers a more precise word (taller, on top of) and names common shapes, but does not spontaneously refine vague language or accept non-prototype examples.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I'm going to tell you where teddy is: 'teddy is by the box.' Does that tell you EXACTLY where to find teddy, or could teddy be in lots of different places? Show me. How would you say it so I know exactly where teddy is?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who uses words loosely just repeats 'by' and is satisfied; a child attending to precision notices the ambiguity and refines it, showing awareness that a word must pin down the meaning. The prompt deliberately uses an ambiguous everyday word so the vagueness is detectable — a precise word like 'behind' would not separate the children.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (in 4.378 the 7 represents 7 hundredths).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 recognise place value of digits in numbers with up to 3 decimal places; Y6 applies this to determine each digit's value.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.1 and 5.NBT.A.3a — understanding the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, with each place one tenth the place to its left.
• Operational details: For each digit, state its value as digit × place-unit (7 in 4.378 = 7 × 1/100 = 7 hundredths). Reinforce the ten-times-smaller relationship between adjacent decimal places. Reverse the task — given digit values, reconstruct the number — to prove flexible understanding and to surface placeholder-zero handling (4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'In 2.635 what is the value of the 3?' Tier B: 'Explain the relationship between adjacent decimal places.' Tier C: 'Write the number with 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths.'
bestPractices: Require each digit's value as digit × place-unit ('7 hundredths', '7 × 1/100'), not just its place name
Explicitly state and re-derive that each place is one tenth of the place to its left (the ÷10 chain through decimals)
Run the task in reverse — give digit values, reconstruct the numeral — to force placeholder-zero handling (0 tenths → 4.073)
Contrast identical digits in different places within one number (the two 3s' values differ) to separate face value from place value
Use a decimal place-value chart so each column's unit is explicit as the child reads a digit
keyRepresentations: Decimal place-value chart Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths with unit labels 1, 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000
Digit-value cards: '7 → 7 hundredths → 0.07'
Thousandths grid showing each place as ten of the next-smaller
Reverse-build slots (digit-into-place) with a live numeral readout
commonMisconceptions: Naming the place but giving the wrong value (the 7 is 'in the hundredths' but stated as '7' or '0.7')
Reading the decimal part as one whole number (378) rather than digit-by-place values
Confusing tenths and hundredths (off-by-one place), especially with a leading zero
Dropping placeholder zeros when reconstructing (writing 4.73 for 4 ones/0 tenths/7 hundredths/3 thousandths)
Believing adjacent places differ additively rather than by a factor of ten

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (e.g. in 4.378 the 7 represents 7 hundredths, 7 × 1/100 = 0.07). Learners state each digit's value as digit × place-unit, re-derive that each decimal place is one tenth of the place to its left, and reconstruct a numeral from given digit-values to surface placeholder-zero handling (4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073). A key discrimination is that 3 tenths is worth more than 7 hundredths even though 7 is the larger digit.

activities.title: Reveal each digit's value (digit × place-unit)
feedback: If a learner gives just the digit or just the place name ('7' or 'hundredths'), ask them to finish the sentence '7 × 1/100 = ___' so the value is named, not only the place.
If they say the 7 is worth 7, rebuild the chart and read 4.378 aloud as '4 ones, 3 tenths, 7 hundredths, 8 thousandths', anchoring each digit to its fraction.
If they miscount by one column (calling the 7 tenths or thousandths), count columns aloud left-to-right from the point — tenths, hundredths, thousandths — landing deliberately on the 7.
Confirm the two 3s in 2.335 differ because one sits in the tenths column, worth ten times the adjacent hundredths column — separating face value from place value.
activities.rationale: Requiring value as digit × place-unit (not just the place name) and contrasting identical digits in adjacent columns directly targets the common error of naming the place but stating the wrong value, and separates face value from place value. An optional interactive form — tapping a digit to bloom its value with the column highlighted and ÷10/×10 arrows to neighbours — can make the ten-times relationship concrete, but a labelled chart with spoken/written values teaches the same idea.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places.
5.NBT.A.1/A.3a: understand the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, each place one tenth of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Write or display a number to three decimal places, e.g. 4.378, above a place-value chart with columns labelled Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths and units 1, 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000.
For each digit, say and write its value as digit × place-unit: the 7 is 7 × 1/100 = 7 hundredths = 0.07; the 8 is 8 × 1/1000 = 8 thousandths = 0.008.
State explicitly how adjacent places relate: the hundredths place is one tenth of the tenths place (÷10 moving right, ×10 moving left).

Within a single number containing two identical digits in adjacent decimal columns, e.g. 2.335 (2 ones, 3 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths), compare the two 3s and explain why their values differ (3 tenths = 0.3 versus 3 hundredths = 0.03) even though the digit is the same.
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's worth is its face value times the unit of the column it sits in; adjacent decimal places differ by a factor of ten, not by addition, so the same digit can mean very different amounts.

activities.title: Reverse build: reconstruct the numeral from given values (placeholder zeros)
feedback: If a learner writes 4.73, point out that the 7 has slid from the hundredths column into the tenths column (and the 3 from thousandths into hundredths) — ask which column each digit now occupies and whether that matches the given values.

If they omit the zero, have them read both numbers aloud — 4.73 as '4 and 73 hundredths' and the correct 4.073 as '4 and 7 hundredths 3 thousandths' (73 thousandths) — to hear that these are different numbers.
Confirm success when they keep the 0 to hold the tenths column and can say why the zero is not optional.
activities.rationale: Running the task in reverse forces explicit placeholder-zero handling, which the forward 'name the value' task can hide. This addresses the documented error of dropping placeholder zeros when reconstructing. A drag-and-assemble interface with a live numeral readout is one effective way to make the empty column visible, but the same learning occurs by writing digits into chart cells on paper.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places.
5.NBT.A.1/A.3a: understand the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, each place one tenth of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Given a set of digit-values — 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths — place each into its column on a place-value chart and read off the numeral.
Write the resulting number: 4.073.
Deliberately try leaving the empty tenths column blank and read what you get: 4.73. Compare 4.073 with 4.73 and explain why they are different numbers.
Repeat with another set that includes a zero in a middle place (e.g. 3 ones, 0 tenths, 0 hundredths, 5 thousandths = 3.005) and justify each zero's job.
activities.intendedInsight: A placeholder zero is worth 0 itself, but it does real work by holding a column open; omitting a zero that comes before other digits shifts every later digit into the wrong place and produces a different number. Reconstruction proves flexible, two-way understanding of place value.

activities.title: Which is worth more — the smaller digit or the larger?
feedback: If a learner ranks 7 hundredths above 3 tenths, place 0.3 and 0.07 on a 0–1 line so the sizes of the chunks are visible.
If they say the 7 is worth more because it comes later (further right), re-anchor each digit to its fractional unit and compare the units, not the positions.
Confirm when they justify 3 tenths > 7 hundredths by comparing place-units rather than digits.
activities.rationale: This comparison is the discriminating task: it exposes 'bigger-digit-is-bigger-value' and 'later-is-larger' misconceptions and demands reasoning from place-units. A spoken, responsive discussion lets a mentor probe why the values differ; a 0–1 number line gives a concrete size check.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1/A.3a: understand the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, each place one tenth of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Compare the value of the 3 and the 7 in 4.378: state the 3 is 3 tenths (0.3) and the 7 is 7 hundredths (0.07).
Decide which is worth more and justify it — the 3, because tenths are ten times bigger chunks than hundredths, so 3 tenths outweighs 7 hundredths even though 7 is the larger digit.
Mark 0.3 and 0.07 on a 0–1 number line to see that 3 tenths is a bigger portion than 7 hundredths.
Discuss: when 4.378 becomes 4.387, whose value changed — the 7's or the 8's? Explain using the columns: both changed, since the 7 and 8 swapped between the hundredths and thousandths places.
activities.intendedInsight: Place, not face value, determines worth in a decimal: reasoning about the column must override the surface impression that the bigger digit is worth more or that a digit further right is larger.

constraints: Learners must state each digit's value as digit × place-unit (e.g. '7 hundredths', '7 × 1/100 = 0.07'), not only name the place.
Include the reverse reconstruction task; naming values forward alone can hide the placeholder-zero error, so reconstruction from values is needed to prove two-way understanding.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. 'value of the 3 in 2.635', 'reconstruct 4 ones/0 tenths/7 hundredths/3 thousandths = ___') can consolidate and check understanding but do not themselves build the place-unit link; pair them with construction and explanation.

A fixed labelled diagram with revealed per-digit values is a strong reference for the reveal step but cannot host the reverse-build that tests placeholder zeros, so it is a partial scaffold for this objective.

Optional interactive affordances (tap-to-reveal, drag value tiles into columns, live numeral readout, ÷10/×10 arrows) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; equivalent learning is possible with a paper chart and spoken reasoning.

When contrasting identical digits, use a number where the repeated digit appears in genuinely different places and state the correct factor between those places (adjacent columns = ten times; non-adjacent columns differ by a larger power of ten).
Checkpoint tiers: age-10 'In 2.635 what is the value of the 3?'; explain 'the relationship between adjacent decimal places'; write 'the number with 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum) was marked verified in the original row and one (CCSS-M) was marked unverified; verification status was not re-checked here.

The original candidate's identical-digits example 3.303 contained three 3s (not two) and had a 'ten times' feedback that was false for its non-adjacent columns; it was replaced with 2.335, which has exactly two 3s in adjacent columns (tenths and hundredths) so the ten-times relationship holds.

In this independent review, activity 2's zero-dropping feedback was corrected: both read-aloud phrases previously named 4.073, so the intended contrast failed; the feedback now reads 4.73 as '73 hundredths' versus 4.073 as '7 hundredths 3 thousandths'.

Original diagnostic/answer text uses 4.378 with digits 3 tenths, 7 hundredths, 8 thousandths; one checkpoint/compare example uses 2.635 (6 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths). These are internally consistent and preserved as distinct examples.

The original 'possible'/'poor' fit framing (conversation and 3D) was converted to pedagogical notes: dialogue is retained as a genuine teaching option for the comparison task rather than dismissed; no universal 'static image cannot teach' or '3D adds nothing' claim is asserted.

probeDeeper: Which is worth more, the 3 or the 7 — and why isn't it just 'the bigger digit'?
What is the value of the 8 in 4.378, and how does it relate to the 7?
Write me a number with 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths and 3 thousandths.
If I change 4.378 to 4.387, whose value changed — the 7's or the 8's?
assess.correctAnswer: The 7 represents 7 hundredths (0.07); the 3 represents 3 tenths (0.3). The 7's place is worth ten times less than the 3's place, so the 3 is worth more even though 7 is the larger digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the decimal part as a whole number — 'the 7 is worth 7', treating .378 like three hundred seventy-eight.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the places with a decimal place-value chart; read 4.378 as '4 ones, 3 tenths, 7 hundredths, 8 thousandths', anchoring each column to a fraction.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 7 is worth 7.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Values are stated as bare digits with no fractional place named.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the place by one — calls the 7 'tenths' or 'thousandths' instead of hundredths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count columns aloud left-to-right from the point (tenths, hundredths, thousandths), landing deliberately on the 7; do not just supply the name.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 7 is 7 thousandths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct idea of fractional places but the label is off by one column.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer/later-is-larger — thinks the 7 is worth more than the 3 because it comes further right.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare 0.3 and 0.07 on a 0–1 line; show tenths are bigger chunks than hundredths so 3 tenths outweighs 7 hundredths.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 7 is worth more than the 3 because it comes later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks 7 hundredths above 3 tenths.

responseLevels.gap: Reads decimal digits as whole numbers or cannot name fractional places.
responseLevels.full: Names each digit's fractional value, states the ten-times relationship between adjacent places, and correctly judges 3 tenths > 7 hundredths with justification.
responseLevels.partial: Names 7 hundredths correctly but defaults to 'bigger digit = bigger value' when comparing with the 3, or is off by one place under pressure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the number 4.378, what is the value of the 7? And how does that compare with the value of the 3?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads decimal place value names 7 hundredths and sees the 3 is worth more despite being the smaller digit — the reasoning must override the surface 'bigger digit'. A child reading the decimal as a whole number, or miscounting places, or applying longer-is-larger gives a different answer and a revealing reason.
