pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Series vs parallel circuits

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** KS3 'Current electricity' — statutory wording 'electric current... in circuits, series and parallel circuits, currents add where branches meet and current as flow of charge' and 'potential difference, measured in volts, battery and bulb ratings' (verified by fetch); the series/parallel contrast and the 'currents add where branches meet' rule are explicitly KS3. NOTE the KS2→KS3 progression: KS2 Year 6 is SERIES only, and parallel is first met here.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** no middle-school PE covers series/parallel DC-circuit analysis, so this is UK-ANCHORED (state honestly).

- **Operational details:** At KS2 the child built SERIES circuits only; this topic introduces the PARALLEL configuration and the contrasting rules for current and voltage in each, plus why the choice matters in practice (household wiring). The rules to secure: in SERIES the current is the same everywhere and the voltages across components ADD UP to the supply; in PARALLEL each branch gets the FULL supply voltage and the branch currents ADD where they meet. The deepest, most counter-intuitive idea — worth foregrounding — is that adding a parallel branch LOWERS the total resistance and RAISES the total current (more routes for charge), the opposite of adding components in series. Teaching is most effective as a structured contrast: build the same components two ways, place meters at several points, predict-then-test, and tie each rule to a practical consequence (parallel keeps every device at full brightness and independently switchable; one failing does not kill the rest).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational / quantitative, ~12–13).
bestPractices: Teach by structured CONTRAST, not two separate topics: build the same two bulbs in series and in parallel side by side, so each rule is learned against its opposite.

Tie every rule to a meter reading at several points: SERIES — ammeters everywhere read the same, voltmeters across components add to the supply; PARALLEL — voltmeters across each branch read the full supply, ammeters in the branches add to the main current (the KS3 'currents add where branches meet').

Foreground the counter-intuitive resistance result: adding a parallel branch gives charge MORE routes, so total resistance DROPS and total current RISES — directly opposite to adding a series component. Predict before testing to surface the wrong intuition.

Anchor 'why parallel for homes' in observable consequences: each device gets the full mains voltage (so full brightness/power), each can be switched independently, and one failing leaves the others working — contrast old series fairy-lights (one blows, all go out) with parallel wiring.

Use predict-then-test relentlessly: 'add a second bulb in series — what happens to the brightness of the first?' (both dim, current drops); 'add a second bulb in parallel — what happens to the first?' (unchanged, still full brightness; total current rises).

Keep the rules causal, not just memorised: series bulbs share the supply voltage (so each gets less → dimmer); parallel bulbs each get the whole supply (so each stays bright), and the cell delivers more total current.

Guard against the resurfacing current-used-up error in series — in a series loop the current is reduced but still the SAME at every point; the bulbs are equally bright, not brighter nearest the battery.
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side series vs parallel diagrams of the SAME components, with ammeters and voltmeters placed at multiple points and their readings shown.
A junction close-up where branch currents ADD where they meet (the KS3 phrase made visual).
Brightness comparison — two bulbs in series (both dimmer than one) vs two in parallel (each as bright as one), with the supply voltage shared vs full.
Household/parallel wiring schematic — appliances each across the full supply, independently switched, with the 'unscrew one, the rest stay on' consequence.
A total-resistance dial — adding series components pushes resistance up and current down; adding parallel branches pulls total resistance down and current up.
commonMisconceptions: Mixing up which quantity is shared vs added — e.g. thinking voltage is the same everywhere in series, or that current splits but voltage adds in parallel; the rules are crossed between the two configurations.
Believing current splits EQUALLY at a parallel junction regardless of the branches — it divides according to resistance, with more current through the lower-resistance branch.
Thinking adding a parallel branch reduces the total current — it INCREASES it (lower total resistance, more routes for charge).
Expecting parallel bulbs to be dimmer than a single bulb — each branch gets the full supply voltage, so each is as bright as a lone bulb (unlike series, where they share and dim).
The current-used-up error resurfacing in series — thinking the bulb nearest the battery is brighter; in series the current is the same everywhere and identical bulbs are equally bright.
Assuming more components always means more total resistance — true in series, FALSE in parallel, where adding branches LOWERS the total resistance.
Thinking household circuits are series — they are parallel, so each appliance gets full voltage and works independently.

learn.summary: Teach series vs parallel circuits (ages 12–13) by structured CONTRAST of the SAME two bulbs built both ways, tying each rule to meter readings at several points and to a practical consequence. Secure: in series the current is the same everywhere and component voltages add to the supply; in parallel each branch gets the full supply voltage and branch currents add where they meet. Foreground the counter-intuitive result that adding a parallel branch LOWERS total resistance and RAISES total current — the opposite of adding a series component. Use predict-then-test relentlessly (add/remove a bulb, watch brightness and meters) and anchor 'why homes are wired in parallel' in observable consequences. A recomputing circuit simulation (or a hands-on physical build) is the central activity; a comparison quiz, an annotated diagram-pair reference, and an electrician design dialogue are complementary. This is a UK KS3-anchored topic (parallel first met here after KS2 series-only); no middle-school NGSS PE covers series/parallel DC-circuit analysis.

activities.title: Build it both ways: series and parallel on the same two bulbs
feedback: If a learner predicts the series bulb nearest the battery is brighter: place ammeters before and after it — the readings agree, so current is not 'used up'; identical bulbs carry the same current and share the supply voltage equally, so they are equally dim.

If a learner predicts a parallel bulb dims when you add another branch: each branch gets the FULL supply voltage, so the first is unchanged; it is the current that adds, not the voltage that splits (for an ideal cell).
If a learner predicts both parallel bulbs go out when one is removed: trace each branch — every parallel branch is its own complete loop to the cell, so breaking one leaves the other intact.

If a learner expects adding a parallel branch to reduce total current: more routes mean lower total resistance and therefore MORE total current; contrast with series where adding a component raises resistance and lowers current.
activities.rationale: Series-vs-parallel is a comparison of live behaviours — brightness, meter readings, and add/remove consequences — that a recomputing simulation can display and the learner can probe. Building both from the same components and predicting before testing surfaces and overturns the crossed-rules and resistance misconceptions. A live-recomputing model and multi-point meters are the mechanism that makes each rule visible; a static diagram can state the rules but not show the readings or consequences change. Hands-on physical circuits with real bulbs, cells and meters achieve the same contrast.
sourceClaims: Crossed series/parallel rules, the belief that adding a parallel branch reduces current, expecting parallel bulbs to be dimmer, and the resurfacing current-used-up error are documented difficulties best tackled by structured contrast, multi-point meter readings, and predict-then-test with add/remove consequences.
learnerActions: Start with one bulb lit from a cell; note its brightness as a baseline.
Add a SECOND bulb IN SERIES; before testing, predict what happens to the first bulb's brightness, then observe (both dim together) and watch the ammeter reading fall.
Reconfigure the same two bulbs into PARALLEL; predict first, then observe the first bulb stays at full brightness (ideal cell) while the main-line current rises.
Place an ammeter at several points: in series confirm all readings are equal; in parallel confirm the branch currents add to the main-line current where branches meet.
Place a voltmeter across components: in series confirm the component voltages add to the supply; in parallel confirm each branch reads the full supply voltage.
Do the unscrew/remove test: remove one bulb in series (whole circuit goes dark) and in parallel (the other stays lit); trace the loop for the remaining parallel bulb to see it is still complete.
If a total-resistance readout is available, compare it as you add a series component (resistance up, current down) vs a parallel branch (resistance down, current up).
Try a household mode wiring appliances across the full supply in parallel, switching each independently.
activities.intendedInsight: Series and parallel obey crossed rules: series shares the voltage (bulbs dimmer, current same everywhere, one break kills all) while parallel gives each branch the full voltage on its own loop (full brightness with an ideal cell, currents add, independent switching). Adding a parallel branch opens more routes for charge, so total resistance drops and total current rises. Houses are wired in parallel because each device gets the full supply voltage and can be switched, or can fail, independently.

activities.title: Sort and predict: series vs parallel rules
feedback: For a mis-sort crossing the rules: re-pair each quantity with its configuration — in series the current is the same everywhere and the supply voltage is shared, so component voltages add to the supply; in parallel each branch gets the full supply voltage and branch currents add where they meet.
For 'adding a parallel branch reduces total current': it increases it, because total resistance drops with more routes.
For 'parallel bulbs are dimmer': each branch sees the full supply, so each is as bright as a lone bulb (ideal cell).
activities.rationale: Stating what is shared vs added, predicting brightness, and choosing a configuration for a purpose are well-defined checks that target the crossed-rules and resistance misconceptions. The sort can check whether rules are stated and matched, but it does not by itself elicit reasoning through live brightness and meter changes, so it is best used after hands-on or simulated building.
sourceClaims: Crossed series/parallel rules, the belief that adding a parallel branch reduces current, expecting parallel bulbs to be dimmer, and the resurfacing current-used-up error are documented difficulties best tackled by structured contrast, multi-point meter readings, and predict-then-test with add/remove consequences.
learnerActions: Sort statements into SERIES vs PARALLEL columns: 'current same everywhere', 'voltages across components add to the supply', 'each branch gets the full supply voltage', 'branch currents add where they meet'.
Predict the brightness of the first bulb when a second bulb is added in series, then when added in parallel.
Answer 'why is household wiring parallel?' and justify by a consequence (full voltage to each device, independent switching, one failing leaves others working).
Predict what happens to the total current when a parallel branch is added.
Rank circuits by total resistance as series components are added vs as parallel branches are added.
activities.intendedInsight: The rules and their practical consequences can be stated precisely and matched to the correct configuration, consolidating the contrast learned by building.

activities.title: Reference diagram pair: the rules at a glance
feedback: If a learner reads the parallel diagram as 'voltage splits': re-read the branch voltmeter labels — each branch shows the full supply.

If a learner thinks series bulbs differ in brightness because of their position: the equal ammeter readings along the loop show the current is the same everywhere, so identical bulbs are equally bright.
activities.rationale: A static annotated pair can present the rules and the household case as a reference summary. It states rather than demonstrates: it cannot show brightness changing or meters updating, so it works best beside the simulation or physical build, not instead of it.
learnerActions: Study a labelled pair of diagrams of the SAME components in series and in parallel, with meters placed at multiple points.
On the series diagram, note 'current same everywhere / component voltages add to supply'; on the parallel diagram, note 'each branch full supply voltage / branch currents add at the junction'.
Reveal the 'unscrew one' outcome for each: series goes dark, parallel keeps the rest lit.
Use the junction close-up to see branch currents adding where they meet.
activities.intendedInsight: A compact reference ties the crossed rules and the household-wiring case to clear diagrams, supporting recall after the active work.

activities.title: Electrician's design problem: series or parallel?
feedback: If a learner picks series for the house 'to save wire': point to the consequence — shared voltage means dimmer devices and one failure breaks the whole loop.
If a learner cannot justify parallel: prompt them to trace what happens to each other device when one branch is removed.
activities.rationale: A Socratic design dialogue can probe the practical choice and the misconceptions and press for consequence-based reasoning. The underlying rules are felt most strongly through manipulation and meter readings, so this works best as a debrief around the building activity rather than the sole route to the rules.
learnerActions: Take on real design problems with an electrician persona: how to wire old-style fairy lights vs a house lighting circuit.

Argue, for each case, whether series or parallel is appropriate and give the consequence-based reason (does one failing kill the rest? does each device get full voltage? can each be switched independently?).
Explain why a house is NOT wired in series by describing what would go wrong if one lamp failed.
Contrast old series fairy-lights (one blows, all go out) with parallel wiring.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing a configuration for a real purpose forces the learner to reason from the rules to consequences, reinforcing why parallel is standard for independent, full-brightness, fault-tolerant devices.

constraints: UK KS3-anchored: parallel is first met here after KS2 Year 6 series-only work; no middle-school NGSS performance expectation covers series/parallel DC-circuit analysis — state this honestly.

Keep brightness/full-voltage claims in the context of an ideal (negligible internal resistance) cell; with a real cell, adding parallel branches draws more current and can slightly reduce terminal voltage. Treat 'each parallel bulb stays at full brightness' as the ideal-cell idealisation, not a universal law.
Current divides between parallel branches according to resistance, NOT equally regardless of the branches — more current flows through the lower-resistance branch.
Guard against the current-used-up error: in a series loop the current is reduced overall but the SAME at every point, so identical bulbs are equally bright, not brighter near the battery.
The recognition/sorting quiz checks whether rules can be stated and matched; it does not by itself show the learner can reason through live brightness and meter changes — pair it with building.

The reference diagram pair and the dialogue state or discuss the rules; they do not let the learner observe readings and consequences change, so they are scaffolds/consolidation, not substitutes for building a working or simulated circuit.

Live-recomputing simulation, drag-in meters, live recolouring of brightness, a total-resistance readout and a household mode are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — offer them where available, but do not treat any one interaction as mandatory. Hands-on physical circuits with real bulbs, cells, ammeters and voltmeters achieve the same contrast.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source IOP claim (crossed rules, parallel-reduces-current belief, dimmer-parallel belief, current-used-up error) is marked verified:false in the row; the two DfE/NGSS curriculum claims are marked verified:true. Evidence strength is carried over unchanged, not upgraded.

The row repeatedly asserts parallel bulbs stay at 'full brightness'; this holds for an ideal cell. With a real cell, internal resistance means more total current can lower terminal voltage slightly. The activities keep the ideal-cell idealisation and this caveat is flagged in constraints; do not teach 'always exactly full brightness' as a universal law.

The original artefact-fit entries for a static image, dialogue and 3D included strong comparative/necessity phrasing ('only a recomputing sim can show', '3D adds nothing', 'weakly conveyed by talk'). These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances and limits.

The KS3 curriculum claim was kept out of the per-activity sourceClaims of the building and electrician activities because it supports only the topic/content status, not those activities' medium/pedagogical rationales; the curriculum anchoring is preserved in the summary and constraints.

The IOP claim is retained on the sort/predict activity only because that activity includes predict-then-test of add/remove consequences named in the claim; it must not be read as evidence that the sort alone is sufficient to overturn the misconceptions.

The 'total-resistance DOWN, current UP when adding a parallel branch' result is physically correct for added resistive branches across a fixed supply and is retained as an outcome to predict-then-test, not merely asserted.
The 3D-interactive option was dropped from activities as redundant (a 2D schematic or physical build already conveys the topology); this is a catalog-ranking omission, not a pedagogical law.

assess.poeTask: With two identical bulbs in a parallel circuit, both lit, ask the child to predict what happens to the SECOND bulb when you unscrew the first, AND why. The 'all connected, so all go off' child predicts it goes dark; the independent-loops child predicts it stays lit. Then unscrew one to reveal.
probeDeeper: Put an ammeter before and after the first bulb in the series circuit. What will the two readings be, and what does that prove about 'using up' current?
Why does your house use parallel wiring rather than series — what would go wrong with series if one light failed?
Counterexample: in the parallel circuit you unscrew one bulb. Trace the loop for the OTHER bulb — is it still complete?
In series the voltages across the two bulbs add up to the battery voltage; in parallel each bulb has the full battery voltage. How does that explain the brightness difference?
assess.correctAnswer: In series the two bulbs share the battery's voltage, so each is dimmer than a single bulb; and because it's one loop, unscrewing either one breaks the loop and BOTH go out. In parallel each bulb gets the full battery voltage across its own branch, so each is as bright as a single bulb and the branches are independent — unscrew one and the other stays lit. That full voltage and independence is why household wiring is parallel.

errorPatterns.pattern: In series the first bulb is brighter because it gets the current first and 'uses some up' before the second ('the electricity runs down along the loop').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Current is the same everywhere in a series loop (ammeters agree); the bulbs are equally dim because they SHARE the voltage, not because current is consumed.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bulb nearer the battery is brighter because it gets the current first and uses some up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts unequal brightness in series, with the nearer bulb brighter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Unscrewing one bulb in parallel makes the other go out too, because they're on the same battery ('they're all connected, so all go off').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Each parallel branch is its own complete loop to the cell; breaking one leaves the other loop intact — trace both loops.
errorPatterns.distractor: If you unscrew one parallel bulb, the other goes out too, because they share the battery.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts both parallel bulbs die when one is removed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adding bulbs in parallel splits the voltage so each parallel bulb is dimmer, just like series ('more bulbs, less each, always').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Parallel branches each get the FULL supply voltage; it's the current that adds, not the voltage that splits — each bulb is at full brightness (ideal cell).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts parallel bulbs are dimmer than a single bulb.

responseLevels.gap: Uses a current-consumption or equal-sharing story — predicts unequal series brightness, or that removing one parallel bulb kills the other.
responseLevels.full: Explains series bulbs share voltage (equally dim, both die if one breaks) and parallel bulbs each get full voltage on independent loops (full brightness, independent), and connects this to why homes use parallel wiring.
responseLevels.partial: States the series/parallel rules and knows household wiring is parallel, but can't apply them to the brightness comparison or the unscrew-one case, or reverts to 'current used up'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You have two identical bulbs. In circuit A they're in series; in circuit B they're in parallel, both on the same battery. Compare how bright the bulbs are in A versus B, and explain what happens to EACH bulb if you unscrew one of the two.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks current is 'used up' or 'shared equally regardless' predicts unequal series brightness or that removing one parallel bulb changes the other; the rules-based child predicts equally-dim series bulbs (both die together) and full-brightness independent parallel bulbs. The reason tier separates a consumption/sharing story from a voltage-distribution story.

sources.claim: KS3 'Current electricity' statutory content covers series and parallel circuits, 'currents add where branches meet', current as flow of charge, and potential difference in volts; series and parallel are explicitly contrasted at KS3 (with parallel first introduced here, after KS2 Year 6 series-only).

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Reading and drawing circuit diagrams

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England, KS2 Year 6 Electricity, statutory):** 'use recognised symbols when representing a simple circuit in a diagram'; non-statutory note confirms recognised symbols are introduced at Year 6 (Year 4 draws circuits pictorially).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** US NATIONAL (NGSS): no direct grade-4/5 circuit-diagram performance expectation (UK-anchored).

- **Operational details:** Children read and draw simple circuit diagrams using standard symbols (cell, bulb/lamp, switch, buzzer, wire), judge from a diagram whether a circuit is complete or broken (switch open/closed → will the bulb light?), and match a diagram to the physical circuit it represents. The core representational idea: a circuit diagram is a SCHEMATIC CONVENTION — a map of what connects to what — NOT a literal picture of the layout; wires are drawn as straight lines. NOTE: in England recognised symbols are formally introduced in Year 6 (Year 4 uses pictorial drawings), so this sits at that transition. This representational skill underpins 'Drawing circuits with proper symbols' and reading circuit diagrams for the KS3 current/voltage work.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/representational, age 9-10).
bestPractices: Introduce each symbol as a name-tag for a real component the child has handled — map the physical bulb to its symbol — so the notation labels known objects, not abstractions.

Teach the schematic convention explicitly: wires are STRAIGHT lines, the diagram shows CONNECTIONS not physical positions, and it is read as a loop — contrast a tidy schematic with a messy 'picture' of the real wires.
Work both directions and matching: build a circuit then draw it; read a diagram and build it; and match a photo of a physical circuit to the correct diagram from a set (the Y6 evidence task).
Use the diagram to PREDICT behaviour: from the drawn switch (open/closed) decide whether the loop is complete and the bulb lights — tying the representation back to the complete-loop rule.
Distinguish the cell and battery symbols early (one long + one short line = a cell; repeated pairs = a battery; the long thin line is the positive end) to head off the commonest symbol slip.
keyRepresentations: A symbol key: cell, battery, bulb/lamp (cross-in-circle), switch (open and closed), buzzer, wire — each beside its real photo.
Photo↔diagram matching pairs (a physical circuit and its schematic).
A straight-line schematic contrasted with a curvy 'picture' of the same circuit to teach the convention.
Complete vs broken diagrams (switch open vs closed) for 'will it light?' reading.
commonMisconceptions: Diagram-as-picture: drawing curvy wires or arranging symbols to mimic the physical layout instead of a straight-line schematic of the connections (the same iconic-representation trap as graph-as-picture).
Cell vs battery symbol confusion — calling one cell 'a battery' or drawing the wrong number of line-pairs.
Ignoring which line is positive (the long thin line) / orientation of the cell symbol.
Reading a gap or an open switch in a diagram as 'still works' — not connecting open/broken in the diagram to the bulb not lighting.
Treating the diagram as exact scale/position — thinking the component drawn nearest the cell is special, rather than only the connections mattering.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, learners read and draw simple circuit diagrams using standard symbols (cell, battery, bulb/lamp, switch open/closed, buzzer, wire). The central representational idea is that a circuit diagram is a schematic convention — a map of what connects to what, drawn with straight wires — not a literal picture of the physical layout. Learners work in both directions (build then draw; read then build), match photographs of real circuits to the correct diagram, and use the drawn switch state to predict whether the loop is complete and the bulb lights. This connects the notation back to the complete-loop rule and heads off common symbol and reading slips.

activities.title: Build a circuit, then draw its diagram
feedback: If the learner draws little pictures (a battery drawing, a light-bulb picture) instead of symbols, pair each real component with its agreed symbol on a key card, then redraw using only symbols.
If the drawn parts are strung along an open line or end in a dead-end, trace the path aloud — it must return to the other terminal of the cell; close the loop.
When the second drawing (symbols moved, connections kept) is accepted as the same circuit, name the insight: position is free, connections are fixed.
activities.rationale: The standard requires using recognised symbols to represent a simple circuit, and producing a drawing (not just recognising symbols) exposes learners who cannot translate to a working loop. Building both directions ties the notation to a real, handled circuit.
sourceClaims: Y6 Electricity statutory requirement: 'use recognised symbols when representing a simple circuit in a diagram'; recognised symbols are introduced at Year 6 (Year 4 draws pictorially).
learnerActions: Build or examine a simple physical circuit with a cell, a switch and a bulb joined by wires.

Draw a circuit diagram of it using only standard symbols: cell (one long thin line + one short thicker line, long line = positive terminal), bulb/lamp (cross-in-circle), switch (drawn open as a gap/lever or closed, matching the real switch), a buzzer symbol only if the circuit includes a buzzer, and wires as straight lines.
Trace the drawn loop with a finger to check it returns to the other terminal of the cell — close any open or dead-end path.
Redraw the same circuit a second time placing the symbols in different positions on the page but keeping the same connections, then confirm it represents the same circuit.
activities.intendedInsight: A circuit diagram records connections, not physical positions or appearance: where you put a symbol on the page does not matter, only what it joins to. The drawing must form a single closed loop back to the cell.

activities.title: Straight-line schematic vs curvy picture
feedback: If the learner keeps wires curved to 'look like' the real wires, point out that the schematic is a map of connections, not a photo of the layout — straighten the wires without changing what joins to what.
If the learner thinks the component drawn nearest the cell is special, have them redraw with that component moved further away but still connected — the circuit behaves identically.
activities.rationale: Treating a schematic as a literal picture is a recurring representational error akin to graph-as-picture confusion; directly contrasting the two forms targets that convention.
sourceClaims: Treating a schematic as a literal picture (drawing wires to mimic physical layout) is a recurring representational error, of a kind with iconic graph-as-picture confusion.
learnerActions: Look at a 'picture-style' drawing of a circuit where the wires are drawn curvy to mimic the real tangle of leads.
Redraw the same circuit as a tidy schematic: straight-line wires and standard symbols.
Check that both represent the same circuit by tracing each loop and confirming the same components are connected in the same order.
State in your own words why both 'work' even though they look different.
activities.intendedInsight: A tidy straight-line schematic and a messy curvy picture of the same connections describe the same circuit; the schematic convention (straight wires, standard symbols) makes the connections easy to read without implying anything about physical shape or layout.

activities.title: Read the switch and predict: will the bulb light?
feedback: If the learner reads an open (gap) switch as closed ('the line's there, so it's on'), line up the open-switch symbol beside a real open switch and the closed one beside a closed switch; a gap means a broken loop means no light.
If the learner says a diagram with a break will still light, have them trace the loop and find where it fails to return to the cell.
activities.rationale: Using the diagram to predict behaviour ties the representation back to the physical complete-loop rule and surfaces learners who misread switch state. This is one of the stated evidence outcomes for the topic, though the complete-loop rule itself is not quoted in the cited sources.
learnerActions: Examine a diagram and identify each symbol and what it stands for.
Decide whether the switch is drawn open (a gap/lever breaking the line) or closed, and say how you can tell.
Predict whether the bulb lights, giving the reason: the bulb lights only if the loop is complete, which requires the switch to be closed.
Redraw the switch in its other state and re-predict.
Given a diagram with a break in the loop just after the bulb, predict whether it lights, then redraw it so it does.
activities.intendedInsight: An open switch or any gap in the drawn loop means a broken loop, so the bulb does not light; reading the diagram's switch state connects the notation directly to the complete-loop rule.

activities.title: Match the photo to the diagram
feedback: If a learner cannot justify the rejection of distractors, have them trace the loop in each diagram and compare, component by component, with the photo.
Confirm success when the learner names the ruling-out detail, not just the correct match.
activities.rationale: Matching a photograph of a physical circuit to the correct diagram is a stated Year 6 evidence outcome and assesses the reading/translation skill. A tappable key and linked photo/diagram panels make the reference layer concrete, but these are optional supports, not required mechanisms. The matching outcome is not the content of the quoted statutory claim, so no source is cited for the principle.
learnerActions: Look at a photograph of a real physical circuit.
Choose, from a set of candidate diagrams, the one that matches it.
Say which specific detail rules out each of the other options (e.g. a missing connection, wrong switch state, an extra component).

Where available, use a tappable symbol key (tap a symbol to see its name, a photo of the real component, and what it does) and a side-by-side photo/diagram view with linked parts as a reference while deciding.
activities.intendedInsight: Translating fluently between a physical circuit, a photograph and a schematic depends on matching connections rather than surface appearance; justifying the rejected options forces attention to the connections that distinguish circuits.

activities.title: Cell vs battery, and which line is positive
feedback: If the learner calls one cell 'a battery' or draws the wrong number of pairs, show the one-pair cell beside the repeated-pairs battery and have them count.
If orientation/positive end is ignored, have them label the long thin line as positive on each of their own drawings.
activities.rationale: Cell-vs-battery confusion and ignoring which line is positive are identified common misconceptions; a dedicated discrimination and spot-the-error task targets them. No cited source.claim directly states this discrimination principle, so no source is attributed.
learnerActions: Study the cell symbol (one long thin line and one short line) and the battery symbol (repeated line-pairs).
Identify which line is the positive terminal (the long thin line).
Draw a single cell, then draw a battery of two cells, labelling the positive end.
Spot the error: given a few diagrams, find the one that draws the wrong number of line-pairs or mislabels/omits the positive end, and correct it.
activities.intendedInsight: A single cell and a multi-cell battery have distinct symbols, and the long thin line marks the positive terminal; getting this right avoids a common symbol slip.

constraints: Learners must produce their own diagrams (draw and construct), not only recognise or select symbols; recognition-only tasks do not themselves elicit independent construction of a working loop.

A tappable symbol key and linked photo/diagram panels are useful reference and matching supports, but they cannot host the learner's own drawing; pair them with an activity that requires constructing a diagram.

An interactive editor that lights the on-canvas bulb only when the loop is complete and the switch closed is a strong optional way to give immediate feedback and reveal that symbol position is free while connections are fixed; it is a proposal, not a required medium. Pairing with a real build-then-draw activity is a natural complement.

Keep diagrams flat: the whole point is that spatial position does not matter, only connections. A 3D treatment is not recommended because it works against this idea; this is a scope judgement for this topic, not a universal claim about 3D.
This sits at the England transition where recognised symbols are formally introduced in Year 6 (Year 4 uses pictorial drawings); learners may arrive expecting to draw pictures.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's one IOP Spark source on schematic-as-picture error is marked verified:false in the source data; the comparison to graph-as-picture confusion should be treated as an illustrative analogy, not established efficacy.

The legacy entry asserted that dialogue 'adds little' and that 3D 'works against' the concept; these are scoped design judgements, not established comparative efficacy. A conversation can still support teaching the convention, and the 3D note is retained only as a topic-scope preference.

SourceClaims on the predict-lighting, photo-matching, and cell-vs-battery activities were set to [] because the quoted statutory claim directly supports representing a circuit with symbols, not the complete-loop prediction, matching, or cell/battery-discrimination principles; those remain research-informed outcomes without a directly supporting source.claim.

Self-audit: the complete-loop reasoning (open switch or any gap = broken loop = bulb off; closed complete loop = bulb on) and the cell-symbol convention (long thin line = positive, one pair = cell, repeated pairs = battery) are internally consistent with the source and retained as taught.

probeDeeper: Point to the switch symbol — is it open or closed, and how can you tell? Now draw the OTHER state.
Here's a photo of a real circuit and three diagrams. Which diagram matches, and which detail rules the others out?
In your drawing, trace the loop with your finger — does it come back to the cell?
Counterexample: I draw the bulb symbol with a break in the loop just after it. Will it light? Redraw it so it does.
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the symbols correctly (long/short parallel lines = cell terminals, circle-with-cross = bulb, gap or lever = switch), states whether the switch is open (gap) or closed, and predicts the bulb lights only if the loop is complete and the switch closed. Then draws a correct single-loop diagram: cell, closed-switch symbol and bulb joined by straight lines into a closed loop.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws little pictures — a battery drawing, a light-bulb picture — instead of the standard symbols ('I'll just draw what it looks like').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match each real component to its agreed symbol on a key card, then redraw using only symbols.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The production step yields pictorial drawings, not symbols.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the switch symbol — reads an open (gap) switch as closed, so predicts the bulb lights when it wouldn't ('the line's there, so it's on').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up the open-switch symbol beside a real open switch and the closed one beside a closed switch; a gap = broken loop = no light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gets the open/closed reading and the lighting prediction wrong.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws components strung along an open line or a dead-end rather than a closed loop ('a row of parts').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the drawn path — it must return to the other terminal; close the loop.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn diagram doesn't form a complete loop back to the cell.

responseLevels.gap: Draws pictorial components or open/dead-end arrangements, or misreads the open/closed switch.
responseLevels.full: Reads each symbol and the switch state to predict lighting, and produces a correct closed-loop diagram in standard symbols, translating fluently between physical circuit, photo and diagram.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and draws standard symbols but makes a translation slip — misreads switch state, the drawn loop isn't quite closed, or can't match photo to diagram confidently.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a circuit diagram. First, tell me what each symbol stands for and what this circuit would do — in particular, is the switch open or closed, and will the bulb light? Then draw me the diagram for a circuit with a cell, a closed switch and a bulb in a single loop.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking the child to READ (what does this symbol mean?) and then PRODUCE (now draw one) exposes those who recognise symbols passively but can't translate to a working loop, who draw pictures instead of symbols, or who misread the open/closed switch.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years (KS1)

- **Topic:** The Heart & Blood — the heart is a muscle that pumps blood around the body through tubes (blood vessels); you can feel your heartbeat at your chest and pulse points

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1, Animals including humans):** at KS1 the statutory content is the basic needs of animals including humans for survival (water, food and air) and the importance of exercise; the heart-as-pump is TOPICAL/enrichment framing at this age (the circulatory system is formalised at Y6: 'identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system, and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood'). Honest note: there is no KS1 statutory 'heart pumps blood' line — treat this as an age-appropriate first encounter that seeds Y6.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** nearest is K-LS1-1 (what animals need to survive); the circulatory system as an interacting subsystem lands formally at MS-LS1-3. So at age 5–7 this is enrichment on both sides, not a graded standard.

- **Operational details:** Keep it embodied and concrete — the whole point at KS1 is that the heart is REAL, inside YOU, and working right now. Three ideas: (1) the heart is a MUSCLE that squeezes (pumps) over and over, never stopping; (2) it pushes BLOOD through tubes called blood vessels that reach every part of the body — fingertips, toes, everywhere; (3) you can FEEL the pump as a heartbeat (hand on chest) or a pulse (fingers on wrist/neck), and it speeds up when you run or jump. Anchor every abstract claim in a felt experience: make a fist to show its size, squeeze a soft ball to 'be' the pump, find your own pulse, then run on the spot and feel it race. Correct the cartoon heart early — the real heart is a fist-sized muscle slightly left of centre, not the ❤ symbol. Avoid the blue-blood trap: blood is always red (bright red when full of oxygen, darker red when not) — veins only LOOK blue through the skin.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, embodied). Success = locate own heartbeat/pulse by touch, say the heart pumps blood continuously, and describe blood vessels as tubes carrying blood to every part of the body. Depth stops at 'pump + tubes + you can feel it' — chambers and the double loop are Y6, not now.
bestPractices: Anchor every claim in an embodied action — make a fist for size, squeeze a ball to be the pump, find a pulse, run and feel it race — so the heart is felt, not just told.
Correct the cartoon-heart image explicitly: the real heart is a fist-sized muscle roughly centre-left of the chest, not the ❤ shape.
Head off the blue-blood misconception from the start — blood is red; veins only look blue through skin.
Link heartbeat speed to activity (rest vs running) to make the pump's job — delivering to working muscles — intuitive without formal detail.
Use the tube/network image (vessels reach everywhere) rather than any chamber detail; keep the depth at KS1 level and let Y6 add structure.
Use simple, consistent language: 'pump', 'squeeze', 'blood vessels are tubes' — avoid arteries/veins/capillaries naming at this age.
keyRepresentations: A fist held up to show the heart's real size and location (centre-left of chest)
A soft squeeze-ball as a stand-in pump the child works with their hand
Pulse points (wrist, neck) the child presses to feel the beat
A simple body outline with tubes (vessels) branching to hands, feet and head
A rest-vs-running heartbeat comparison (slow thump → fast thump)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the heart is shaped like the ❤ symbol, rather than a fist-sized muscle.
Believing the heart is on the far left edge of the chest rather than roughly centre-left.
Thinking blood is blue inside the body and turns red only in air — blood is always red.
Believing the heart only 'beats' with emotions (love/fright), not that it pumps blood every second of life.
Thinking blood just sits still in the body or only appears when you are cut, rather than constantly circulating.
Confusing the heartbeat with breathing, or thinking the heart and lungs are the same thing.

learn.summary: KS1 (ages 5-7) first encounter with the heart and blood: the heart is a fist-sized muscle, roughly centre-left of the chest, that pumps (squeezes) blood continuously through tubes called blood vessels to every part of the body, and you can feel this pumping as a heartbeat (hand on chest) or pulse (fingers on wrist/neck), which speeds up with activity. Keep depth at 'pump + tubes + you can feel it'; chambers and the double circulation are later content (the circulatory system is introduced from Year 6, and the detailed structure of the heart is often taught later still). This is enrichment, not a graded KS1/early-elementary standard. Activities are embodied and concrete, anchoring every abstract claim in a felt experience, and explicitly correct the valentine-shape, far-left-placement, blue-blood, 'heart only beats with emotions/only beats when you move', 'blood only where you are cut', and heart-is-the-same-as-lungs misconceptions.

activities.title: Be the heart: pump blood around the body
feedback: If a child says the heart stops or rests when sitting still: have them feel the pulse while sitting completely still to prove it is beating now - it speeds up when you run but never stops.
If a child thinks blood only appears where you are cut: trace the tubes reaching the hands and feet and point out blood is travelling everywhere all the time.
Reinforce that blood is always red - bright red when carrying lots of oxygen, darker red when carrying less; it only looks blue through the skin.
Praise locating the pulse by touch and saying 'the pump I feel is my heart moving blood around me'.
activities.rationale: At KS1 the single felt idea - the heart is a real muscle inside you, pumping blood continuously - is intended to be built mainly by doing and feeling, with telling in a supporting role. Pairing a driveable pump with the child's own synced pulse can tie the invisible internal process to a felt, controllable cause and effect. An optional on-screen 'be the heart' model (each tap squeezes out a pulse of red blood, a wrist dot throbs in time, a 'go for a run' button makes the body call for more blood so the child pumps faster) can make 'the heart never stops' and 'it races when you run' concrete; a squeeze-ball offers the same mechanism tactilely.
sourceClaims: The heart is a muscular pump about the size of a fist, located slightly left of centre in the chest; a pulse felt at the wrist/neck reflects each heartbeat, and heart rate rises with physical activity.
learnerActions: Make a fist and hold it to the centre-left of your chest to show how big your real heart is and where it sits.
Squeeze a soft ball (or tap/press a beating heart on screen) over and over, never stopping, to 'be' the pump.
Watch or imagine each squeeze pushing a pulse of red blood out along the tubes (blood vessels) to the hands, toes, and head, then looping back for the next squeeze.
Place two fingers on your own wrist or neck and find the beat; notice it throbs in time with each pump.
Pretend to go for a run (run on the spot), then feel your pulse again and notice it is faster - the working muscles are asking for more blood, so the heart pumps faster.
activities.intendedInsight: The heart is a never-stopping muscle that squeezes blood through tubes to every part of the body right now; the beat you feel at your wrist is that pump working, and it speeds up when you are active.

activities.title: Find it, name it, bust the myths: a body you can explore
feedback: If a child picks the valentine symbol as the real heart: explain the symbol is just a picture people use; the real heart is a lumpy fist-sized muscle that squeezes blood.
If a child places the heart at the far-left edge: correct gently to roughly centre-left of the chest.
If a child says blood turns red only in air: blood is always red - bright red when carrying lots of oxygen, darker red when carrying less; it only looks blue through the skin.
Confirm correct pulse-point finds and correct vessel tracing to hands and feet.
activities.rationale: Locating the heart and pulse and busting the shape and colour myths directly target documented KS1 misconceptions and build the vocabulary (pump, squeeze, blood vessels are tubes) without introducing arteries/veins/capillaries or chambers. A tap-to-reveal body illustration with a 'not this heart-symbol' myth-buster flap and a lift-the-flap 'is blood blue? -> always red!' is an optional way to make the reveals concrete; this is a scaffold for locating and naming and does not by itself convey the continuous pumping motion.
sourceClaims: The heart is a muscular pump about the size of a fist, located slightly left of centre in the chest; a pulse felt at the wrist/neck reflects each heartbeat, and heart rate rises with physical activity.
learnerActions: On a body outline (or your own body), point to where the real heart is - centre-left of the chest, about the size of your fist.
Compare the real fist-sized heart muscle with the valentine heart symbol and say which one is the real organ and what the real one does.
Find the pulse points at the wrist and neck by pressing gently with two fingers (on one side of the neck only).
Trace the tubes (blood vessels) branching out to the hands, feet and head to show blood reaches everywhere.
Answer 'is blood blue?' and give the correct answer: blood is always red; veins only look blue through the skin.
activities.intendedInsight: The heart is a fist-sized muscle (not the valentine shape) sitting centre-left; blood is always red and travels through tubes to every part of the body, and you can find your pulse where those tubes run near the skin.

activities.title: Ask the heart: why do you pound when I run?
feedback: Prompt the child to connect the faster beat to the running, not just to name it.
If the child says the heart stops when resting, return to feeling the pulse while sitting still.
Celebrate explanations that use 'pump', 'squeeze' and 'blood vessels are tubes'.
activities.rationale: A short spoken, responsive exchange after the hands-on model lets the child articulate and may consolidate what they discovered by doing. Its narrow affordance is eliciting explanation in the child's own words; it is intended to follow, not replace, the feeling and doing that the embodied activities are designed to build at this age.
learnerActions: Talk with a friendly cartoon heart or school nurse: first find your own pulse, then say what you feel.
Jump or run on the spot, feel your pulse again, and describe out loud what changed.
Explain back, in your own words, why the heart beats faster when you run (the muscles are working harder and need more blood).
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the felt experience into your own words - the pump speeds up when your body works harder - can consolidate that the heart responds to what your body is doing.

activities.title: Quick checks: real heart, pulse points, always pumping
feedback: For the two-cuts question, confirm both bleed because blood vessels carry blood to every part of the body - blood is everywhere, not only where you are cut.
Reinforce 'the heart keeps pumping even when you sleep' as true - it never stops.
Use any wrong answer as a cue to return to feeling the pulse or tracing the vessels, not just to mark it wrong.
activities.rationale: Picture-based recognition and simple true/false items verify the core facts at an age-appropriate level, and the two-cuts prompt pushes the child to state the 'blood is everywhere' idea rather than assume it. These recognition items check what a child can identify; they do not require the child to independently construct or demonstrate the pumping action, so pair them with the hands-on activities rather than relying on them alone.
learnerActions: Choose the real heart from two pictures (fist-sized muscle vs the valentine symbol).
Tap or point to where you can feel a pulse.
Answer true/false: 'the heart keeps pumping even when you are asleep.'
Answer: if you got a tiny cut on your finger and on your toe, would both bleed? Why?
activities.intendedInsight: Checking the basics confirms the child can recognise the real heart, knows where to feel a pulse, and can state that the heart pumps blood everywhere, all the time.

constraints: Keep depth at 'pump + tubes + you can feel it': do not introduce heart chambers, the double circulation, or arteries/veins/capillaries naming at KS1 - these belong to later study (the circulatory system is introduced from Year 6, and the detailed structure of the heart is often taught later still).

This topic is enrichment, not statutory/graded at this age: UK KS1 statutory content is the basic needs of animals (water, food, air) and the importance of exercise, with the circulatory system formalised at Year 6; the nearest US standard is K-LS1-1 (what animals need to survive), with the circulatory system as an interacting subsystem treated at MS-LS1-3.
Use simple, consistent language: 'pump', 'squeeze', 'blood vessels are tubes'.

Keep blood-colour language accurate: blood is always red, bright red when carrying lots of oxygen and darker red when carrying less; do not say blood is 'full of air' or that it turns red only in air.

Explicitly correct the valentine-shape, far-left-placement, blue-blood, 'heart only beats with emotions', and 'blood only where you are cut' misconceptions, and distinguish the heartbeat from breathing (heart and lungs are not the same thing).

Anchor every abstract claim in a felt action (fist for size, squeeze-ball or screen pump, finding a pulse, running and feeling it race); do not rely on telling alone, though telling in a supporting role is valuable.
Recognition-only check items verify identification and do not elicit independent construction of the pumping idea; use them alongside the embodied activities, not as a replacement.

The tap-to-reveal body and the dialogue are scaffolds for locating/naming and for consolidating; they do not by themselves build the felt understanding of continuous pumping. This does not mean telling or dialogue cannot contribute to learning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source notes honestly that there is no KS1 statutory 'heart pumps blood' line and treats this as an age-appropriate first encounter seeding Year 6; two of the three sources (NGSS and BHF) are marked verified:false in the row.

The original row framed the driveable 2D model as uniquely able to convey continuous pumping and rated a 3D model 'poor' as adding nothing; these are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy/necessity claims. They have been softened to scoped proposals - a squeeze-ball or screen pump each make the mechanism concrete in different ways - without asserting one medium is necessary or that other media cannot teach the idea.

Candidate phrasing 'blood full of air' was corrected to 'carrying oxygen' to avoid reinforcing an air-in-blood confusion; 'blood is always red' is retained as an accurate KS1 simplification, with richer arterial/venous oxygenation detail intentionally omitted as beyond-age.
Near-categorical modality phrasing in the pump and dialogue rationales was scoped with 'intended to/can/may' wording; efficacy of these specific activities is untested.

Independent re-audit confirmed the prior blood-colour and modality corrections are present at every learner-facing occurrence, and additionally scoped one remaining efficacy claim ('ties' -> 'can tie') in the first activity's rationale.

probeDeeper: Put two fingers on your neck or wrist and stay very still — can you feel a beating? What is that?
If your heart stopped beating for a while, why would that be dangerous — what does the blood do for your body?
Can you find any part of your body that has NO blood in it at all? Where?
assess.correctAnswer: The heart is beating and blood is moving all the time, even sitting still — it beats faster when you run but never stops. Both the finger and the toe bleed because blood travels through tubes (blood vessels) to every part of the body, so blood is everywhere, not only in one spot and not only when you exercise.

errorPatterns.pattern: The heart only beats and blood only moves when you run or move about.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Feel the pulse while sitting still to prove it beats now; explain it speeds up with exercise but never stops.
errorPatterns.distractor: It only beats when you run — when you sit still it stops.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the heart rests or stops when sitting still.

errorPatterns.pattern: Blood is only in the place where you get cut / not spread all through the body.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the two-cuts evidence: both bleed because vessels carry blood everywhere; trace vessels reaching hands and feet.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only the finger would bleed, because that's where the blood is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects only the finger to bleed; treats blood as localised.

errorPatterns.pattern: The heart is for feelings or love (the valentine shape) rather than a pump for blood.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the everyday 'heart' symbol from the organ; the real heart is a muscle that pumps blood.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the heart's job as holding feelings, not pumping blood.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the heart beats only during exercise, or that blood is only where you bleed / appears only when cut.
responseLevels.full: States the heart beats and blood flows all the time (faster when active) AND that blood travels through vessels to every part of the body, using the two-cuts evidence to justify it.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the heart pumps blood but is unsure it happens continuously, or that blood reaches every part — holds one idea but not both.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Right now, sitting still, is your heart beating and is your blood moving — or does that only happen when you run around? And if you got a tiny cut on your finger AND on your toe, why would BOTH bleed? What does that tell you about where your blood is?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the heart rests when still, or that blood sits in one place, gives the wrong answer to at least one half. Only a child who holds 'always pumping' AND 'blood everywhere' answers both, and the two-cuts evidence in tier two forces the 'blood is everywhere' idea to be stated, not assumed.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 4–6 (UK Reception–Y1, US K–Grade 2, formalised Grade 3). Division as equal SHARING (partitive: share 12 among 3 → how many each?) and equal GROUPING (quotitive: how many groups of 3 in 12?) — the domain's most central concept (centrality 0.43, highest in Maths).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'solve one-step problems involving multiplication and division, by calculating the answer using concrete objects, pictorial representations and arrays with the support of the teacher'; non-statutory 'through grouping and sharing small quantities, pupils begin to understand … division'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): concept seeded in K–Grade 2; formalised at 3.OA.2 'interpret whole-number quotients — e.g. 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 are partitioned into 8 equal shares, OR as the number of shares when partitioned into groups of 8'.
• Operational details: teach BOTH structures explicitly — sharing (deal out one-to-each) meets children's fairness intuition first; grouping (make groups of a fixed size) links division to repeated subtraction and to the multiplication tables/inverse. Same equation, two different pictures. Keep quantities small, concrete, and initially remainder-free.
• Checkpoint: model and distinguish the two meanings. Tier A (4–5): fairly share a small set one-to-each and say how many each got. Tier B (5–6): solve both a sharing and a grouping story for the same numbers with counters. Tier C (6): explain that 12÷3 can mean '3 equal shares' OR 'groups of 3', and that both give 4.
bestPractices: Teach BOTH division structures deliberately, not just sharing: sharing (partitive — 'share 12 among 3 plates, how many each?') and grouping (quotitive — 'how many groups of 3 can I make from 12?'). Children default to sharing; grouping must be taught because it is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to reading a times-table fact as a division.
Start fully concrete with a 'one for you, one for me' dealing action for sharing, and a 'scoop groups of n' action for grouping, before any symbol — the physical act carries the meaning.
Show the SAME numbers under both stories so children see one division fact (12÷3=4) can be pictured two ways — this prevents them treating sharing and grouping as unrelated.
Link division to multiplication as its inverse from the start using the array/equal groups (3 groups of 4 is 12, so 12 shared into 3 is 4) — builds the fact-family idea early.
Use fair-sharing language to connect to early fractions (sharing 1 cake among 2 = a half), and keep first examples exact (no remainder) so the core idea is secure before remainders complicate it.
keyRepresentations: Equal-sharing model — dealing counters one-at-a-time into plates/hoops (partitive)
Equal-grouping model — scooping a set into groups of a fixed size (quotitive)
Arrays and equal groups linking division to its inverse multiplication
Bar model (whole split into equal parts) and number line (equal jumps back for grouping/repeated subtraction)
commonMisconceptions: Believing division only means sharing-out (partitive), so a 'how many groups of 3?' problem is not recognised as division at all.
Treating sharing and grouping as different operations rather than two meanings of the same ÷ — not seeing they give the same answer.
Thinking division is commutative: that 12÷3 and 3÷12 are the same (they are not).
Confusing which number is shared and which is the number of groups/size of group (dividend vs divisor) when moving to symbols.
Assuming every sharing must come out exactly and being thrown by leftovers, or sharing unequally and still calling it 'fair'.

learn.summary: For ages 4–6 (roughly UK Reception–Y1, US Pre-K–Grade 1; division with symbols is formalised later, e.g. US Grade 3), build division from two concrete meanings on the same quantity: equal SHARING (partitive: share 12 among 3 plates → how many each?) and equal GROUPING (quotitive: how many groups of 3 fit in 12?). Children default to sharing, so grouping must be taught deliberately — it is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to reading a times-table fact as a division. Keep quantities small, concrete, and initially remainder-free, and show the same numbers under both stories so children see one division fact (12÷3=4) pictured two ways.

activities.title: Share-and-group the same pile
feedback: If a learner makes groups of 3 when asked to share among 3 plates, act out both situations separately side by side — 'share between 3 plates' (3 shares) versus 'make groups of 3' — and name the difference out loud.
If shares come out unequal, model round-robin dealing ('one for you, one for you'), then count both piles and compare, so 'fair' is pinned to 'equal'.
When a total does not divide evenly, simply name 'there's one left over, it won't share fairly' and move on — do not treat the leftover as an error to reteach; remainders come later.
Reinforce the link to multiplication: '3 groups of 4 make 12, so 12 shared into 3 gives 4' — the actions are inverses.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects division to be met through both grouping and sharing of small quantities using concrete objects, pictorial representations and arrays, and standards describe interpreting a quotient as either the number in each share or the number of equal groups. Enacting both structures on one quantity makes the two meanings concrete and comparable.
sourceClaims: Y1: solve one-step problems involving multiplication and division using concrete objects, pictorial representations and arrays; through grouping and sharing small quantities pupils begin to understand division.
3.OA.2 interpret whole-number quotients as the number in each share (partitive) OR the number of equal groups (quotitive) — the two structures of division.
Division should be taught through both sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) structures; grouping links division to repeated subtraction and to multiplication facts.
learnerActions: Take 12 counters and 3 plates (or hoops). Deal counters out one at a time — 'one for this plate, one for this plate, one for this plate' — until the pile is gone, then count how many each plate got (4).
On the SAME 12 counters, now scoop them into groups of 3, setting each group aside until none remain, then count how many groups you made (4).
Say the matching division sentence for both actions: 12÷3=4. Notice the same answer arrived from two completely different actions — sharing among 3, and making groups of 3.
Try a total that will not share evenly (e.g. 13 counters among 3 plates): deal fairly until you cannot give everyone one more (4 each), and name the leftover (1 left over).

Optional with an interactive counters tool: toggle between a SHARE mode (choose number of plates, tap 'deal', watch counters distribute one at a time) and a GROUP mode (choose a group size, lasso groups); flip modes on the identical pile to see the same equation form on screen.
activities.intendedInsight: Division has two meanings — equal shares and equal groups — and the same numbers can be pictured both ways, giving the same answer; this is the twin meaning children most often miss.

activities.title: Fair-share check with teddies
feedback: Correct full answer for the 2-teddy share: '6 each — it's fair because both teddies have the same number with none left over; I gave them out one at a time until they were gone.'
If a learner offers unequal piles and is untroubled by the difference, model one-for-you dealing, then count and compare both piles so equality becomes the test of fairness.
If a learner shares equally but never checks the piles match, prompt them to count both and confirm they are the same before calling it fair.
With an odd total (e.g. 13 between 2), name the leftover plainly rather than reteaching; noticing 'one left over, won't share evenly' is the goal, not resolving the remainder.
activities.rationale: A 'share fairly and justify' prompt discriminates children who use equality as the governing idea (deal one-to-one, verify equal shares) from those who split unevenly or call it fair without checking. Asking 'how do you know it's fair' surfaces whether 'equal' rather than 'everyone got some' is the constraint. The share-among-3 and groups-of-3 follow-ups revisit 12÷3 under both meanings.
learnerActions: Share 12 counters fairly between 2 teddies so each gets the same. Say how many each teddy gets (6) and explain how you know it is fair.
Count each teddy's pile and compare — are they the same, with none left over?
Describe your method: 'I gave them out one at a time to each teddy until they were gone.'
Now share the same 12 counters among 3 teddies and say how many each gets (4); then answer the matching grouping question: how many groups of 3 can you make from 12? (4) — both are 12÷3.
Try 13 counters: can you still share them fairly between the 2 teddies? What happens? (6 each with 1 left over — it won't share evenly).
activities.intendedInsight: Fairness here means everyone gets an equal amount. When the total shares evenly there are none left over, and when it does not (e.g. 13 between 2), the leftover is simply named. A child shows understanding by checking the groups match, not just by giving everyone 'some'.

activities.title: Sort the stories: sharing or grouping?
feedback: If a learner does not recognise a 'how many groups of 3?' problem as division, act it out with counters alongside a sharing version and name both as division.
If a learner thinks 12÷3 and 3÷12 are the same, show with counters that sharing 12 among 3 differs from sharing 3 among 12 — division is not commutative.
This sorting and matching can check whether the child holds both meanings; it checks classification rather than eliciting the physical dealing/scooping, so use it after hands-on sharing and grouping.
activities.rationale: Categorising stories and matching a division sentence to both picture types can verify that a learner holds both meanings and does not treat sharing and grouping as unrelated operations. It checks classification and is best used after concrete work; it does not itself elicit the physical handling that builds the concept.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.2 interpret whole-number quotients as the number in each share (partitive) OR the number of equal groups (quotitive) — the two structures of division.
Division should be taught through both sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) structures; grouping links division to repeated subtraction and to multiplication facts.
learnerActions: Read or hear short word problems and sort each into 'sharing' (share a total among a number of people/plates) or 'grouping' (make groups of a fixed size).
Match a division sentence like 12÷3=4 to BOTH a shared picture (3 plates with 4 each) and a grouped picture (4 groups of 3).
Fill in the answer to simple remainder-free division sentences, using counters to check.
activities.intendedInsight: Both wordings — 'share among 3' and 'how many groups of 3' — are division, and a single division fact matches both a sharing picture and a grouping picture.

activities.title: Correct the unfair sharer
feedback: If a learner accepts the unequal shares, hand them the counters and have them redeal one-to-one, then count each friend's share.
Use fair-sharing language to connect to early fractions — sharing 1 cake between 2 is a half — keeping first examples exact with no remainder.
A talking partner cannot move the counters for the child, so make sure the child physically redistributes the quantity rather than only talking about it.
activities.rationale: A fair-share dilemma can prompt reasoning about equality, but a talking character cannot let the child manipulate the quantity, so dialogue works best paired with hands-on dealing. Fair-sharing language also seeds early fraction ideas.
learnerActions: A puppet or story character shares a set unfairly on purpose (gives one friend 'a lot'). Fix it so every friend gets an equal share.
Explain to the character why the new sharing is fair and the old one was not.
Pose and solve a fair-share dilemma aloud: 'We have 12 sweets and 4 friends — what's fair?' (3 each).
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through fairness reinforces that equal shares are the rule, while actually moving the counters is what lets the child make and check the equal shares.

constraints: Keep totals small, concrete, and initially remainder-free so the core idea is secure before leftovers complicate it.

Teach BOTH structures deliberately: sharing meets the fairness intuition first, but grouping must be explicitly taught because children default to sharing and grouping is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to multiplication facts.
Treat leftovers gently at this age: name 'there's one left over' and move on; do not reteach remainders as a misunderstanding — remainder work comes later.
Start fully concrete (dealing and scooping actions) before introducing symbols; the physical act carries the meaning.
Sorting/matching and fill-in-the-answer tasks can check classification but do not themselves elicit the physical dealing/scooping — use them after hands-on sharing and grouping, not instead of it.
A talking character or puppet cannot let the child manipulate quantity, so keep dialogue as a supplement to concrete dealing.

Watch for the dividend/divisor confusion as symbols appear: be clear which number is the total being shared and which is the number of groups or the size of each group; division is not commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source claims for 3.OA.2 and NCETM are marked unverified in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified. Confidence levels were not independently re-checked.

The optional interactive counters tool (share/group mode toggle, tap-to-deal, lasso grouping, live recompute, highlighted leftover) is offered as one way to make the mechanism concrete, not as a required medium; equivalent learning can occur with physical counters and plates.

The original research rated a 3D environment as adding no conceptual gain and a static picture as unable to deliver the 'same answer, two pictures' moment; these are presented as scoped design preferences, not evidence of necessity. A fixed picture can still introduce vocabulary even if it cannot be re-manipulated.

Activity 2 (diagnostic fair-share) and Activity 4 (puppet dialogue / fair-sharing dilemma) have empty sourceClaims: the available source claims support the division topic and concrete sharing/grouping method, but no cited claim directly backs activity 2's diagnostic-discrimination principle or activity 4's dialogue-supplement and early-fraction rationale (the fraction connection comes from pedagogy best-practice notes, not a source claim).

probeDeeper: Count each teddy's pile — are they the same?
Now share the same 12 between 3 teddies — how many each?
How many groups of 3 can you make from 12?
What if you had 13 counters — could you still share them fairly?
assess.correctAnswer: 6 each — it's fair because both teddies have the same number with none left over. I gave them out one at a time to each teddy until they were gone.

errorPatterns.pattern: shares unequally — makes two piles that aren't equal or hands 'a lot' to one teddy; equality isn't yet the constraint
errorPatterns.nextMove: model round-robin dealing ('one for you, one for you'), then count both piles and compare so 'fair' is pinned to 'equal'
errorPatterns.distractor: One teddy gets more because that pile looks big.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: offers unequal piles as the answer and is untroubled by the difference

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses sharing-between with grouping-into — asked to share between 2 teddies, instead makes groups of 2
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out the two situations separately — 'share between 2 teddies' (2 groups) versus 'make groups of 2' — and name the difference
errorPatterns.revealedBy: builds sets of 2 rather than 2 equal shares

errorPatterns.pattern: mishandles a leftover — with a number that won't share evenly, quietly gives one teddy extra
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat as a misunderstanding to reteach — remainder understanding comes later; simply name 'there's one left over, it won't share fairly' and move on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: with an odd total, produces unequal piles without noticing the remainder

responseLevels.gap: Splits into unequal piles or stops before all are shared; equality is not the governing idea.
responseLevels.full: Deals out one-to-one into equal groups, verifies the shares are equal with none left over, and handles both sharing-between and grouping-into forms.
responseLevels.partial: Shares equally by dealing but doesn't check the groups match, or handles sharing-between but not the 'how many groups of' form.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 12 counters. Share them out fairly between these 2 teddies so each teddy gets the same. How many does each teddy get — and how do you know it's fair?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands equal sharing deals out one-to-one and checks the two groups are equal, justifying fairness by equal amounts. A child without it splits unevenly (a big pile and a small one), stops before all are shared, or calls it fair without checking. The 'how do you know it's fair' tier surfaces whether 'equal' is the governing idea rather than just 'everyone got some'.
