pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: use written division where the answer has up to two decimal places — divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers (e.g. 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69), and continue division past the decimal point.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.7 — divide decimals to hundredths using place-value strategies, models, and relating to a written method; 6.NS.3 fluency with decimal division.
• Operational details — the key move is continuing short/long division past the decimal point, carrying the remainder to the next place: 14.76 ÷ 4 proceeds 14÷4 = 3 r2, bring down 7 (as 27 tenths), 27÷4 = 6 r3, bring down 6 (36 hundredths), 36÷4 = 9 → 3.69, keeping the point aligned. Where a whole number doesn't divide exactly, annex zeros after the point (18.6 → 18.60) to continue. Context problems (sharing £18.60 among 5) motivate decimal quotients and connect to money/measures.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): compute 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69 keeping the point aligned. Tier B (10–11): explain how to continue past the decimal point / annex a zero when a place won't divide. Tier C (11): solve a context problem needing decimal division (share £18.60 among 5) and interpret the answer as money.
bestPractices: Teach the decimal point in the quotient as ALIGNED with the point in the dividend — place it first, then divide place by place — so the point's position is structural, not an afterthought.

Show that continuing past the point is the SAME process as whole-number division: the remainder is regrouped into the next-smaller place (tenths, then hundredths), which children already know from long division of whole numbers (mt_WsM4EmdOLe).
Use annexing zeros deliberately: when there is a remainder at the last given place, adding a zero (13 ÷ 4 → 13.00 ÷ 4 = 3.25) lets division continue — grounded in equivalence, not a trick.
Anchor in context and estimation: sharing money/measures makes decimal quotients meaningful, and an estimate (14.76÷4 ≈ 15÷4 ≈ 3.7) sanity-checks the point placement.
Connect to ×÷ by powers of ten and place value (mt_wPgpMJ0-PA): dividing regroups a unit into ten of the next-smaller unit, exactly the place-value structure underpinning the method.
keyRepresentations: Short/long division layout (bus stop) with the quotient's decimal point drawn directly above the dividend's point before dividing.
Place-value regrouping picture: a leftover one 'exchanged' into ten tenths, a leftover tenth into ten hundredths, mirroring the carry.
Money/measure context model (£18.60 shared into 5 equal parts) that names the tenths and hundredths as 10p and 1p.
Annexing-zeros illustration: 13 = 13.00 shown as equivalent, enabling the division to continue to 3.25.
commonMisconceptions: Misplacing or omitting the decimal point in the quotient (getting 369 or 36.9 for 14.76÷4).
Stopping at a remainder instead of continuing past the point or annexing a zero (13÷4 = 3 r1 left unfinished rather than 3.25).
Treating the tenths/hundredths digits as separate whole-number divisions without carrying the remainder down.
Writing the remainder as a whole number when the context calls for a decimal (money answer given as '3 remainder 2').
Losing place-value alignment so digits drift into the wrong column.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers using written division, continuing past the decimal point. The central insight is that the quotient's decimal point sits directly above the dividend's point (structural, not guessed), and that continuing past the point is the SAME regrouping used in whole-number division — each leftover is exchanged into ten of the next-smaller place. Worked anchor: 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69; and annexing zeros (13 → 13.00 ÷ 4 = 3.25) lets division continue when a remainder is left after the dividend's last digit (a place where the divisor doesn't fit instead gets a 0 in the quotient). Context problems (sharing £18.60 among 5 = £3.72) motivate decimal quotients and connect to money and measures.

activities.title: Step-by-step divider: walk 14.76 ÷ 4
feedback: If the answer comes out as 369 or 36.9, the point was misplaced — line the quotient's point directly above the dividend's point and check the magnitude: 14.76 ÷ 4 is about 15 ÷ 4 ≈ 3.7, so 3.69 is sensible.
If a leftover is dropped instead of exchanged, show the counters: 2 leftover ones become 20 tenths and join the next column before dividing again.
Verify the result by multiplying back: 3.69 × 4 = 14.76.
activities.rationale: Decimal division is a step-by-step regrouping procedure whose critical insight is point alignment; animating each remainder being exchanged into ten of the next-smaller unit and locking the quotient point above the dividend point makes both the process and its place-value structure felt. Optional supports — counters that visibly exchange one unit into ten of the next, and an estimate strip that flags a mis-placed point — make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Aligning the quotient's decimal point with the dividend's and regrouping remainders into the next-smaller place makes decimal division continuous with whole-number division.
Y6 pupils use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places.
Pupils divide decimals to hundredths using place-value strategies and models, relating the strategy to a written method and explaining the reasoning.
learnerActions: Before finding any digit, place the quotient's decimal point directly above the point in 14.76 — establish that its position is fixed by the dividend, not guessed.
Work left to right: 14 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 2. Show the leftover 2 ones being EXCHANGED into 20 tenths, which join the 7 tenths to make 27 tenths.
Continue: 27 tenths ÷ 4 = 6 remainder 3. Exchange the leftover 3 tenths into 30 hundredths, joining the 6 hundredths to make 36 hundredths.
Finish: 36 hundredths ÷ 4 = 9, giving 3.69 with the point aligned.
Narrate at each step: continuing 'past the decimal point' is the same regrouping already used for whole numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: The decimal point in the quotient is aligned structurally with the dividend's point, and dividing past the point is the familiar regrouping of a leftover into ten of the next-smaller place.

activities.title: Annex a zero to continue the division
feedback: If the child stops at '3 r1', remind them the leftover can be shared further: extend the dividend with a zero and keep dividing past the point.
If a decimal place is skipped when the divisor doesn't fit, insist that every brought-down decimal digit yields a quotient digit — write a 0 in the quotient for that place rather than omitting it.
Check 3.25 × 4 = 13 to confirm.
activities.rationale: Annexing zeros deliberately — grounded in equivalence rather than as a memorised rule — resolves the common error of stopping at a whole-number remainder, and reinforces that the written method continues place by place.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places.
Aligning the quotient's decimal point with the dividend's and regrouping remainders into the next-smaller place makes decimal division continuous with whole-number division.
learnerActions: Try 13 ÷ 4 and reach 3 remainder 1; notice the division is not finished.
Rewrite 13 as 13.00 (an equivalent value) and place the quotient point above it.
Continue dividing: carry the remainder 1 as 10 tenths, 10 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 2, carry 2 as 20 hundredths, 20 ÷ 4 = 5, giving 3.25.
Conclude that there was no real remainder — just more decimal places to find.
Repeat with 18.6 ÷ 5: annex a zero (18.60), continue to 3.72.
activities.intendedInsight: Annexing zeros after the decimal point is grounded in equivalence (13 = 13.00), not a trick; it lets division continue until it terminates or reaches the required number of places.

activities.title: Money and measures context: £18.60 shared among 5
feedback: If the answer is given as '3 remainder 3', ask what happens to the leftover money — it is shared further into 10p and 1p coins, so the division continues.
Estimate first: £18.60 ÷ 5 is about £20 ÷ 5 = £4, so £3.72 is sensible; an answer like £37.2 or £0.372 should be questioned by sense.
Confirm by multiplying back: £3.72 × 5 = £18.60.
activities.rationale: Context and estimation anchor decimal quotients and make the point placement checkable by sense; naming tenths and hundredths as 10p and 1p coins connects the abstract regrouping to money.
sourceClaims: Pupils divide decimals to hundredths using place-value strategies and models, relating the strategy to a written method and explaining the reasoning.
Y6 pupils use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places.
learnerActions: Set up £18.60 ÷ 5 as a written division, aligning the quotient point above the point in 18.60.

Divide: 18 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 3; exchange 3 leftover pounds into tenths (as 10p coins) with the 6 to make 36 tenths; 36 ÷ 5 = 7 remainder 1; exchange into hundredths (1p coins) with the 0 to make 10 hundredths; 10 ÷ 5 = 2, giving £3.72.
Name the tenths as 10p coins and the hundredths as 1p coins so the regrouping is meaningful.
Interpret the answer as money: each person gets £3.72.
Check with multiplication: £3.72 × 5 = £18.60.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimal quotients are meaningful in context: sharing money or measures requires continuing past the point, and the answer must be interpreted (e.g. as pounds and pence), not left as a whole-number remainder.

activities.title: Place-the-point and finish-the-division practice
feedback: For the point-placement choice, reason from magnitude: 14.76 ÷ 4 ≈ 3.7, so 3.69 is right and 369 or 36.9 are off by powers of ten.
If the ordering omits annexing a zero where a remainder persists, point back to the equivalence 13 = 13.00.
These checks test the result; still ask the child to carry out an unaided written division to show the regrouping is understood, not guessed.
activities.rationale: Recognition and ordering items give efficient practice and expose the signature point-placement error, but they check results more than they build the regrouping procedure, so they supplement rather than replace independent written working.
learnerActions: Fill in the missing quotient digits for a partly-worked 14.76 ÷ 4.
Decide where the decimal point belongs, choosing between answers like 369, 36.9 and 3.69, and justify the choice by magnitude.
Put a set of division steps in order, including the step of annexing a zero to continue.
Match each quotient to the context problem it answers (e.g. a money-sharing problem).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising a correct point placement and ordering the steps consolidates the procedure; estimation justifies the choice rather than guesswork.

activities.title: Talk it through: the leftover money problem
feedback: If the child says 'there's a remainder and we stop', prompt: can the £2 be shared as coins? Lead them to tenths (10p) and hundredths (1p).
Follow the discussion with written working so the verbal idea is grounded in the actual procedure.
activities.rationale: A spoken prompt about a leftover can probe whether the child sees that division continues past the point, but the procedural walk is better carried out through written working and manipulation, so this is a lead-in, not the main teaching.
learnerActions: Consider a scenario: money is shared equally but there is £2 left over — what now?
Explain aloud how to divide the leftover further into smaller coins (tenths and hundredths).
State where the decimal point goes in the answer and why.
Then carry out the full written division to confirm the spoken reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating what to do with a leftover surfaces the idea of continuing past the decimal point before formalising it in symbols.

constraints: The learning objective is carrying out written division past the decimal point: learners must produce the quotient digit by digit with correct point alignment, not merely recognise a correct answer.
Recognition and ordering tasks check results and expose point-placement errors, but they do not elicit independent construction of the regrouping procedure; pair them with unaided written division.
Tap-to-reveal worked examples are a reference model only — they do not let the child drive the division or annex zeros themselves, so follow them with learner-driven working.
Annexing zeros must be justified by equivalence (13 = 13.00), not presented as a memorised trick.

Prerequisite links: regrouping a unit into ten of the next-smaller place draws on long division of whole numbers and on ×÷ by powers of ten / place value; reteach these if the point drifts or leftovers are dropped.
Every brought-down decimal place must yield a quotient digit, including a 0 when the divisor does not fit that place, to avoid losing place value.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (CCSS-M 5.NBT.7/6.NS.3 and the NCETM decimal-division guidance) were marked unverified in the source row; treat the point-alignment/regrouping principle as guidance, not established comparative efficacy.

The source row claimed 3D 'adds nothing' for symbolic column procedures; this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been dropped rather than asserted. A non-spatial symbolic procedure simply has limited need for a spatial model here.

Optional interaction examples (exchanging counters, annex-a-zero control, money skin naming coins, estimate strip) are retained as concrete illustrations of the mechanism, not as mandatory implementations.

The Y6 written-division curriculum claim is the governing method standard and is cited on the construction activities (1–3) whose core action is carrying out written division to two decimal places; it is omitted from the recognition/ordering practice activity, whose recognition-supplements-construction rationale it does not support.

Independent editorial re-review conducted afresh: all quotients, remainders, exchanges, money interpretations, estimates and multiply-back checks confirmed consistent; no categorical medium-superiority claims, internal IDs, or quiz-step vocabulary remain in learner-facing text; no new unresolved learner-facing errors found.

probeDeeper: Where does the decimal point go in your answer, and how did you decide?
When you had a remainder, what did you do to keep going past the decimal point?
Estimate 14.76 ÷ 4 — is 3.69 sensible?
How could you check £18.60 ÷ 5 = £3.72 using multiplication?
assess.correctAnswer: 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69. £18.60 ÷ 5 = £3.72. The teacher watches for the decimal point in the answer placed directly above the point in the dividend, and for the child continuing the division into the decimal places (bringing down the tenths/hundredths, or annexing zeros) rather than stopping at a whole-number remainder.

errorPatterns.pattern: misplaces or ignores the decimal point in the quotient — divides the digits as if whole, giving 369 or 36.9
errorPatterns.nextMove: line the quotient's decimal point directly above the dividend's; reason about magnitude (14.76÷4 is about 3.7, so 3.69 not 369).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer off by a power of ten; point not aligned above the dividend's point

errorPatterns.pattern: stops at a whole-number remainder instead of continuing into decimals — e.g. 18.60÷5 as '3 r3' rather than 3.72
errorPatterns.nextMove: show that the leftover can be shared further: bring down the tenths and hundredths (or annex zeros) and keep dividing past the point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child leaves a remainder where a decimal quotient is expected; does not bring down/annex to the hundredths

errorPatterns.pattern: loses place value of a digit after the point — forgets a zero in the quotient when the divisor doesn't go into a decimal place
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist every brought-down decimal digit yields a quotient digit — write a 0 in the quotient when the divisor doesn't fit that place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quotient missing a decimal place (e.g. 3.9 instead of 3.09-type errors)

errorPatterns.pattern: correct method, arithmetic slip; caught by estimation
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child estimate and check with multiplication (3.69×4 = 14.76?).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one step wrong; estimate (15÷4 ≈ 3.75) flags it

responseLevels.gap: misplaces the decimal point or stops at a whole-number remainder; answer off by a power of ten.
responseLevels.full: divides accurately into the decimal places with the point correctly aligned, continues past a remainder by annexing zeros, and checks the result by estimation/multiplication.
responseLevels.partial: places the point correctly on straightforward cases but stops early on a remainder, or drops a decimal-place zero.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 14.76 ÷ 4 using a written method while you watch, and then to share £18.60 equally among 5 people. Watch how they handle the decimal point in the quotient and whether they continue dividing past the point (adding zeros) when there is a remainder.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The signature errors are dropping/misplacing the decimal point in the quotient and stopping at a whole-number remainder instead of continuing past the point. Watching the process exposes both; a correct final answer alone can't show whether the point placement was understood or lucky.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** What Plants Need to Thrive (comparing requirements)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y3 'Plants'):** 'explore the requirements of plants for life and growth (air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow) and how they vary from plant to plant.' Two demands: the FULL set of five requirements (adding air, nutrients-from-soil and room to the Y2 water/light/warmth), and that requirements VARY between plants.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-LS2-1 / K-LS1-1):** the US anchors plant needs at '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1]' (2-LS2-1); the fuller five-factor list and the 'varies plant to plant' comparison is a UK-specific KS2 elaboration.

- **Operational details:** This extends the Y2 'water, light, warmth' to the Y3 FIVE: air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow. Two of these are newly non-obvious to children — AIR (plants need it too, not just animals) and ROOM/space (crowded plants compete and grow poorly) — so give them deliberate attention. The distinctive Y3 move is COMPARISON: different plants need different AMOUNTS (a cactus thrives on little water; a fern needs lots and shade), so 'requirements vary from plant to plant' — this pre-empts a one-size-fits-all rule and connects to habitat/adaptation. Teach through comparative fair tests (vary one factor, including crowding and nutrients, across plant types) and through matching plants to the conditions they prefer. Note carefully: 'nutrients from soil' are minerals for health, NOT the plant's food/mass source — keep that door open for the later 'plants make their own food / mass from air & water' idea; don't let 'nutrients from soil' harden into 'plants eat soil'.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B. The child lists the five requirements (including the easily-missed air and room), predicts the effect of removing/limiting one, and — the Y3 discriminator — explains that different plants need different amounts (e.g. cactus vs fern water needs), matching a plant to suitable conditions.
bestPractices: Explicitly add and dwell on the two non-obvious requirements — AIR (plants need it as well as animals) and ROOM to grow (overcrowding starves plants of light/water/space) — which children routinely omit.
Centre the Y3 upgrade on COMPARISON: different plants need different amounts (cactus vs fern), so requirements vary — use matching/sorting of plants to preferred conditions.
Run comparative fair tests that include the new variables (crowding, nutrient-poor vs rich) not just water/light, changing one factor at a time.
Frame 'nutrients from soil' as minerals for HEALTH, not as the plant's food or mass — avoid cementing 'plants eat soil' (bridge to the air/water idea later).
Link 'requirements vary' to habitat — a plant thrives where its needs are met — seeding adaptation without over-reaching.
keyRepresentations: A five-icon requirements set (air, light, water, nutrients, room) as condition labels.
A plant–conditions matching board (cactus → dry/bright; fern → damp/shady) showing needs vary.
A crowding comparison: seedlings sown dense vs spaced, showing competition for room.
A comparative fair-test layout varying one factor across two plant types.
commonMisconceptions: Omitting air and room to grow — listing only water and light as plant needs.
Assuming all plants need identical conditions/amounts (watering a cactus like a fern).
Believing plants 'eat' soil / that soil nutrients are the plant's food and the source of its mass (should be minerals-for-health only at this stage).
Thinking more of any requirement is always better (over-watering, no limit to fertiliser).
Not recognising that overcrowding harms plants (seeing 'more plants together' as fine).
Treating light as optional if the plant is watered (carryover from the Y2 misconception).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8, extend the earlier 'water, light, warmth' idea to the full set of five plant requirements — air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow — with deliberate attention to the two children routinely omit: AIR (plants need it too, not just animals) and ROOM/space (crowded plants compete and grow poorly). The distinctive Year-3 move is COMPARISON: different plants need different AMOUNTS of the same requirements (a cactus thrives on little water; a fern needs lots and shade), so 'requirements vary from plant to plant'. Teach through comparative fair tests (vary one factor, including crowding and nutrients, across plant types) and by matching plants to the conditions they prefer, linking this to habitat/adaptation. Keep 'nutrients from soil' as minerals for health, not the plant's food or source of mass, so the later 'plants make their own food from air and water' idea stays open.

activities.title: Plant compare-lab: same care, different outcomes
feedback: If a learner predicts both plants thrive with lots of water, show the over-watered cactus yellowing/rotting: the right AMOUNT matters and it differs by plant — more isn't always better.
If a learner says all plants need identical amounts, compare a desert home to a forest floor: the plants are suited to different conditions, so their needs differ in amount.

If a learner lists only water and light, crowd seedlings in one pot so they visibly compete for space, light, water and nutrients and tend to grow weaker or smaller — room to grow and nutrients are needs too; and prompt that plants also need air.
activities.rationale: The Year-3 heart is comparison, and two new factors (air, room) are easier to grasp when their effects are seen. An interactive compare-lab gives deterministic, time-lapsed outcomes a child can produce quickly, so 'different plants need different amounts' becomes a result they generate rather than a rule they are told; a live cactus and fern ground the comparison in real plants. Real-plant results should be framed as expected tendencies, since living-plant outcomes are not guaranteed. The crowding comparison makes the easily-missed 'room to grow' requirement concrete.

learnerActions: Use an interactive compare-lab (a simulated side-by-side setup) to grow a cactus and a fern together, with dials for water, light, nutrients and how tightly each is planted, plus an air toggle, so you can adjust conditions and time-lapse growth; pair this with a real cactus and fern on the windowsill to ground the comparison in living plants you tend.
Set each plant's conditions and compare how each responds to the same settings.

Predict before observing, and say why: what will happen to each plant if you turn BOTH plants' water up high? Keep a second cactus and fern on low water to compare against. Then watch what happens — in the compare-lab the high-water fern flourishes while the high-water cactus yellows and rots, unlike the low-water cactus (with real plants, treat this as the expected tendency over a fortnight, not a guaranteed result).
State in your own words why the SAME generous watering helps one plant and harms the other.

Crowd several seedlings of the same kind tightly together and compare them with well-spaced seedlings given the same water and light, watching how the crowded ones compete for space, light, water and nutrients and tend to grow weaker, thinner or smaller (real seedlings may instead grow tall and spindly).
Use the air toggle and consider air as a requirement too: plants need air as well as animals.
activities.intendedInsight: Different plants need different AMOUNTS of the same requirements because they are suited to different homes — so 'more is always better' is false, and 'room to grow' and air are real needs alongside water and light.

activities.title: Match each plant to the conditions it likes
feedback: If a learner gives every plant the same water amount, revisit the compare-lab outcome: the cactus suffered with the fern's amount of water.

If a learner cannot connect thick, waxy leaves to low water needs, link back to the desert home where little water is available: thick, fleshy leaves can store water and a waxy coating helps stop water escaping, so these features often (though not always) suggest a plant that needs little water.
Reward answers that both name the five requirements AND tie differing amounts to the plant's habitat, in the learner's own words.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorising, and choosing a suitable amount check the five requirements and the varies-plant-to-plant idea, and connect 'requirements vary' to habitat without over-reaching. These tasks confirm and consolidate the comparative understanding; recognition/matching alone checks rather than builds it and does not by itself elicit a learner's own explanation, so pair them with observation and ask for the 'why'.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory: 'explore the requirements of plants for life and growth (air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow) and how they vary from plant to plant'.
learnerActions: Match plants to their preferred conditions (e.g. cactus → dry/bright; fern → damp/shady), explaining each choice.
Name the five requirements — air, light, water, nutrients, and room — naming especially the ones people forget (air and room).
Decide how much water suits THIS plant: pick a suitable amount for a cactus versus a fern, rather than one amount for all plants.
Given a plant with thick, waxy leaves, infer what you would guess about how much water it needs, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: A plant thrives where its needs are met; reading a plant's features helps you predict the conditions it prefers, which shows that requirements vary from plant to plant.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: water both plants generously
feedback: A full response says the cactus struggles with lots of water (its roots rot; it is adapted to little), the fern is fine with plenty, AND generalises that needs vary in amount because plants suit different homes.
A partial response names variation and most of the five requirements but cannot explain WHY the cactus suffers or tie variation to habitat — prompt them to connect the plant to its home.

If a learner predicts both thrive, treat it as the 'more is always better' misconception and show the over-watered cactus outcome (an expected tendency with living plants, deterministic in the compare-lab).
activities.rationale: Over-watering both plants is the discriminator: only a child who knows a desert plant's needs predicts the cactus suffers. The pre-observation prediction separates genuine understanding of varying needs from the 'more is better' or 'all plants are the same' models.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory: 'explore the requirements of plants for life and growth (air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow) and how they vary from plant to plant'.

learnerActions: Before observing, predict which of a cactus and a fern will thrive and which will struggle when BOTH are watered equally and generously for a fortnight — and say WHY.
Observe over the fortnight and record what actually happens to each plant.
Explain the result: why the same generous watering hurts a cactus but suits a fern.
Answer probe questions: What happens if you plant twenty seeds crammed in one tiny pot — which need runs short? Which of the five things do people most often forget?
activities.intendedInsight: The pre-observation reasoning is the key part: a child who understands that needs vary by plant predicts the cactus suffers from over-watering, while a 'more water is better' model wrongly predicts both thrive.

constraints: 'Nutrients from soil' means minerals for health, NOT the plant's food or the source of its mass; avoid letting this harden into 'plants eat soil', so the later 'plants make their own food from air and water' idea stays open.
More of a requirement is not always better: over-watering and excess fertiliser can harm, and the right amount differs by plant.

A static comparison poster (tap the cactus → 'little water, lots of light'; tap the fern → 'lots of water, shade'; tap the 'room' and 'air' icons) names the new factors and is a useful reference, but it does not let the child run the comparisons; use it to support, not replace, observation.

Matching, multiple-choice and slider tasks primarily check and consolidate understanding and may not by themselves build the comparative understanding or elicit a learner's own explanation; pair them with growth observation and ask for the 'why'.
Link 'requirements vary' to habitat (a plant thrives where its needs are met) to seed adaptation, without over-claiming more than the evidence supports at this stage.
Recognition and matching responses do not by themselves elicit independent explanation; ask learners to construct the 'why' in their own words.

Real-plant demonstrations (e.g. over-watering a cactus) are expected tendencies dependent on plant health, timing and conditions, not guaranteed results; the simulated compare-lab outcome is deterministic by design.

One source (OU OpenLearn §2.3) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim about children omitting air/room and misreading soil nutrients as unconfirmed.

The original artefact notes asserted that dialogue 'would displace the comparison' and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established facts, and have been dropped. Practical caution: real over-watering/rotting demonstrations take time and depend on actual plant health and watering amounts; outcomes with living plants are expected tendencies, not guaranteed, and should be framed that way to learners.

The Y2-carryover misconception 'light is optional if the plant is watered' from the source pedagogy is not explicitly tackled in an activity; it is only implicitly covered by naming light among the five requirements. Consider adding an explicit check if desired.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: water a cactus and a fern equally and generously for a fortnight. Ask the child to predict which thrives and which struggles, and WHY, before observing. A 'more water is better' model predicts both thrive. The cactus suffers/rots. The pre-observation reasoning about differing needs is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Why would too much water hurt a cactus but not a fern?
Name the five things plants need to thrive — which ones do people forget?
What happens if you plant twenty seeds crammed in one tiny pot? Which need runs short?
If you found a plant with thick waxy leaves, what would you guess about how much water it needs?
assess.correctAnswer: The CACTUS struggles with lots of water — it's adapted to little water and its roots rot if over-watered; the fern is fine with plenty. Different plants need different AMOUNTS of the same requirements (air, light, water, nutrients, space) because they're suited to different homes. Full marks say the cactus suffers from too much water AND generalise that needs vary between plants.

errorPatterns.pattern: more water/light is always better for any plant
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a waterlogged cactus rotting — the right AMOUNT matters, and it differs by plant. More isn't always better.
errorPatterns.distractor: Both will thrive, because more water is always good for plants.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts both plants thrive with lots of water, or that the cactus loves extra water

errorPatterns.pattern: all plants need exactly the same things in the same amounts

errorPatterns.distractor: They need the same amount, because all plants are the same really.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Crowd seedlings in one pot — they compete and stay small; space and nutrients are needs too.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks more water/light is always better, or all plants need identical amounts; lists only water and light.
responseLevels.full: Predicts the over-watered cactus struggles, explains needs vary in amount because plants are suited to different habitats, names all five requirements (air, light, water, nutrients, space), and reads a plant's features to infer its needs.
responseLevels.partial: Says needs can vary and names most of the five requirements, but can't explain WHY the cactus suffers or ties variation to habitat — the list without the matched-to-home reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A cactus from the desert and a leafy fern from the forest floor are grown side by side, and I water BOTH of them a lot every single day. One thrives and one struggles. Which struggles — and the important part, why do two plants not need the same amount of the same things?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who understands needs vary by plant (matched to habitat) from one who thinks 'more is always better' or 'all plants need the same'. Over-watering both is the discriminator — only a child who knows a desert plant's needs predicts the cactus suffers.

pedagogy.summary: These real-world problems multiply fractions AND mixed numbers in context — scaling a recipe (2 1/3 cups × 1 1/2 batches), with estimation used to judge reasonableness. The signature difficulty is mixed-number multiplication: pupils who multiply the whole parts and the fraction parts separately and add (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 + 1/6) omit the cross terms and get a badly wrong answer. The fix is to convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying (7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2) or to use an area model that shows ALL four partial products. Reasonableness via scaling (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 ≈ 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5) is the check that catches the incomplete-distribution error.
bestPractices: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying (2 1/3 = 7/3), avoiding incomplete distribution
Or use an area model for mixed × mixed that lays out ALL four partial products so none is dropped
Estimate by scaling before computing (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups) and check the exact answer against it
Use the scaling meaning — more than one batch means MORE than 2 1/3 cups — to sense-check direction
Draw a fraction/area model of the context so the computation is grounded, not rote
keyRepresentations: Area model of mixed × mixed with four partial-product regions
Improper-fraction rewrite of both mixed numbers
Recipe/scaling bar showing the ingredient stretched by the batch factor
Estimation with rounded decimals or whole numbers
commonMisconceptions: Incomplete distribution: multiplies whole × whole and fraction × fraction, omitting the cross terms (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 1/6)
Multiplies without converting mixed to improper, mishandling the parts
Leaves the denominator unchanged / seeks a common denominator (importing add/subtract habits into ×)
Skips the reasonableness check, so an implausible product goes unnoticed

learn.summary: Pupils (ages 10–11) solve real-world problems multiplying fractions and mixed numbers, e.g. scaling a recipe of 2 1/3 cups by 1 1/2 batches. The signature error is incomplete distribution: multiplying whole×whole and fraction×fraction separately and adding (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 + 1/6 = 2 1/6), which drops the two cross-term contributions. Fixes are converting both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying (7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2) or using an area model that shows ALL four partial products; a scaling estimate (≈2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5) catches the error.

activities.title: Recipe scaler with a four-region area model
feedback: If the learner answers 2 1/6, point to the rectangle: the 2×1/2 and 1/3×1 strips — the biggest contributions after the main block — were left out. Ask them to add those regions in.
If a common-denominator step appears, note that this is a multiplication: both denominators multiply (3×2=6) and no common denominator is needed; contrast with how addition of fractions works.

If an out-of-range answer is accepted without doubt, ask: 'More than one batch means more or less than 2 1/3 cups?' — since 1 1/2 batches is more than one, the answer must exceed 2 1/3, so 2 1/6 is impossible.
Confirm success when the area total, the improper-fraction result, and the estimate all agree on about 3 1/2 cups.
activities.rationale: The incomplete-distribution error is literally a missing piece of an area, so an area model that displays and sums all four partial products is intended to make the omission visible and to tie the recipe context to the computation. An optional interactive version can light up or flash the two cross-term regions as uncounted when the shortcut is attempted, with a parallel improper-fraction panel and an estimate slider rounding to 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 — these are illustrative mechanisms, not required ones.
sourceClaims: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers using visual fraction models or equations, converting mixed numbers to improper fractions (or using the area model) to compute completely

The misconception that multiplication always makes numbers bigger, and the need to check reasonableness (e.g. multiplying by a factor less than 1 gives a smaller product), must be confronted; real/personalised contexts and visual models improve fraction multiplication problem-solving
learnerActions: Take a recipe needing 2 1/3 cups of flour and a goal of 1 1/2 batches, and first estimate by scaling (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups) before doing any exact computation.
Draw or build a rectangle 2 1/3 wide and 1 1/2 tall to represent the product.
Tile the rectangle into its four regions: the 2×1 block, the 2×1/2 strip, the 1/3×1 strip, and the 1/3×1/2 corner; label each region's value (2, 1, 1/3, 1/6) and add them to get 3 1/2 cups.
Alongside, rewrite both mixed numbers as improper fractions and compute 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2, checking it matches the area total.
Check the exact answer (3 1/2 cups) against your earlier scaling estimate of about 3.5 cups.
activities.intendedInsight: Mixed × mixed produces four partial products; the shortcut of only multiplying wholes and fractions omits the two large cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1), so the answer 2 1/6 is far too small. Converting to improper fractions or counting all four regions gives the complete product, and a scaling estimate confirms direction and magnitude.

activities.title: Spot the forgotten pieces (static area diagram)
feedback: If the learner picks the small 1/3×1/2 corner as the 'forgotten' piece, point out the two long strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1) are the usually-dropped and far larger contributions.
Confirm when they name both cross-term strips and show the running total reaching 3 1/2.
activities.rationale: A static annotated diagram supports reading complete distribution and naming the typically omitted terms. It is a scaffold for interpretation; it does not by itself let the learner build a new product or catch their own omission while working, so it should precede or accompany independent construction rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers using visual fraction models or equations, converting mixed numbers to improper fractions (or using the area model) to compute completely
learnerActions: Study a labelled area diagram of 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 split into four regions.
Reveal each region's partial product in turn and keep a running total to 3 1/2 cups.
Answer: 'Which two pieces do people most often forget?' and explain why leaving them out gives 2 1/6.
activities.intendedInsight: Complete distribution means all four regions are counted; the commonly forgotten pieces are the two cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1), which together are large enough that omitting them wrecks the answer.

activities.title: Chef scaling challenge (reasonableness in role)
feedback: If the learner assumes any multiplication increases the amount, use the 1/2-batch case: half a batch needs less than 2 1/3 cups, so the product is smaller.
Prompt them to state the direction before arithmetic so an out-of-range answer stands out.
activities.rationale: A spoken/role scenario is well suited to rehearsing the direction-of-scaling and reasonableness judgement and to confronting the 'multiplication makes bigger' misconception, including a less-than-one factor. The precise four-region computation still benefits from a visual surface, so pair this with the area or improper-fraction work rather than relying on discussion alone.
sourceClaims: The misconception that multiplication always makes numbers bigger, and the need to check reasonableness (e.g. multiplying by a factor less than 1 gives a smaller product), must be confronted; real/personalised contexts and visual models improve fraction multiplication problem-solving
learnerActions: Work with a chef scenario that scales recipes up and down.
Before computing, answer 'more or less than 2 1/3 cups?' for a given batch factor and justify it.
Also tackle a shrinking case, e.g. making 1/2 a batch, and predict whether the flour needed is more or less than 2 1/3 cups.
Then compute the exact amount and check it against your prediction.
activities.intendedInsight: Scaling by more than one gives more than the original amount; scaling by a factor less than one gives less — so multiplication does not always make a number bigger. The reasonableness prediction is a check that catches implausible products.

activities.title: Targeted practice: convert, distribute, estimate
feedback: If 2 1/6 is chosen, revisit the two omitted cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1) and add them back in.
If 3 is chosen, point out it ignores or rounds away part of the fractional contributions; the full four-region total is 3 1/2, not 3.
If the conversion is wrong, remind them 2 1/3 = (2×3+1)/3 = 7/3.
Confirm when the learner selects 3 1/2, justifies it, and their estimate (≈3.5) supports it.
activities.rationale: Short-answer and matching items can probe whether conversion and complete distribution happened and whether an estimate was used, using the error patterns as sharp distractors. Such recognition-and-fill items assess and rehearse components but do not by themselves elicit the independent building of the area reasoning, so use them alongside the construction activities.
learnerActions: After first estimating the product by rounding (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5), choose the correct value of 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 from 2 1/6, 3, and 3 1/2, and explain why the others are wrong.
Fill in the improper-fraction conversions: 2 1/3 = 7/3 and 1 1/2 = 3/2.
Match each of the four area regions to its partial product.
Estimate the product by rounding before carrying out the exact calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: The distractor 2 1/6 is exactly the incomplete-distribution result; 3 is a plausible wrong answer whose likely origin (rounding 2 1/3 down to 2, or dropping part of the fractional contribution) is not pinned down by the source, so it is used only as an explicitly-wrong option. Recognising why each is wrong reinforces complete distribution and the reasonableness check.

constraints: Target age 10–11; procedural real-world fraction and mixed-number multiplication.
Convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying, OR lay out all four partial products in an area model; do not multiply whole×whole and fraction×fraction and add.
This is multiplication: both denominators multiply and no common denominator is required — do not import addition/subtraction habits.

Require a scaling estimate before computing and check the exact answer against it; include at least one less-than-one (shrinking) factor so learners meet a case where the product is smaller than the original.

The static diagram and the recognition/matching items are scaffolds or checks: they support interpretation but do not by themselves require the learner to construct a new product or catch their own live omission.
The area model is a 2D representation of the product (cups × batches), not a physical area: cups of flour are actually a volume measure, but a 3D volume model is unnecessary and could mislead here.
Interactive touches (flashing uncounted regions, estimate slider, tappable regions) are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory.
The '3' option is an explicitly-wrong distractor only; do not present it or 2 1/6 as a valid answer, and do not assert a certified origin for the '3' error beyond plausible rounding/omission.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic: 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 = 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2. The four partial products are 2×1=2, 2×1/2=1, 1/3×1=1/3, 1/3×1/2=1/6, summing to 2+1+1/3+1/6 = 3 3/6 = 3 1/2 — consistent. The incomplete-distribution result 2 + 1/6 = 2 1/6 is the stated misconception and is used only as an explicitly-wrong distractor, never as a valid answer.

The distractor '3' from the original quiz is retained as a plausible wrong option; its likely origin (rounding or dropping a term) is not specified in the source, so its exact diagnostic meaning is uncertain and is not asserted as fact.
One source (Common Core 5.NF.6) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its citation as a standards reference, not as evidence of empirical effectiveness.

The source claim that visual models and real contexts 'improve' fraction multiplication problem-solving describes general research findings and does not establish that any specific activity here was tested or is superior to alternatives.
Efficacy language in activity rationales was kept to intended/illustrative wording, as none of these proposed activities has been empirically validated.

probeDeeper: Estimate first — roughly how many cups? Does your exact answer match?
If you made only 1/2 a batch instead of 1 1/2, would you need more or less than 2 1/3 cups — why?
Draw the recipe as a rectangle — how many pieces are there, and did you count all of them?
Turn both mixed numbers into improper fractions — does multiplying them give the same answer as your method?
assess.correctAnswer: Estimate: about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups (a bit more than one batch's 2 1/3). Exact: 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 = 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2 cups.

errorPatterns.pattern: Incomplete distribution: multiplies the whole parts and the fraction parts only — 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → (2×1) + (1/3×1/2) = 2 1/6 — omitting the two cross terms
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay out the area with all four regions (or convert both to improper fractions) so the two large cross-term strips are counted; check against the scaling estimate
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 2 1/6 (or similar too-small value); working shows only two products, no conversion to improper fractions

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies without converting mixed to improper, or leaves a denominator unchanged / seeks a common denominator (importing add-subtract habits into multiplication)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert to improper fractions first (7/3 × 3/2) and recall that multiplication multiplies both denominators and needs no common denominator; contrast with addition
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A common-denominator step appears in a multiplication, or the mixed numbers are multiplied part-wise with a kept denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Skips the reasonableness check — no estimate, so an implausible product (2 1/6, or a value below one batch) is accepted
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the scaling estimate — 'more than one batch, so more than 2 1/3 cups' — and require it before computing; the check, not the arithmetic, is what's missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No estimate offered; an out-of-range answer reported without doubt

responseLevels.gap: Incomplete distribution (2 1/6) or leaves a denominator unchanged; no estimate and no sense that the answer is wrong.
responseLevels.full: Estimates by scaling, computes 3 1/2 via improper fractions or a complete area model, checks the exact answer against the estimate, and transfers to a new real-world product including a shrinking-factor (less-than-one) case.
responseLevels.partial: Converts to improper fractions and computes 3 1/2 but purely by rule — no estimate or reasonableness check — or estimates sensibly yet distributes incompletely in the exact working.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve this, showing your working and giving a rough estimate first: a recipe needs 2 1/3 cups of flour, and you want to make 1 1/2 batches — how much flour do you need?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Mixed × mixed is the exact place the incomplete-distribution error bites: a child who converts to improper fractions (or lays out all four partial products) gets 3 1/2; a child who multiplies whole×whole and fraction×fraction and adds gets 2 1/6 — and the estimate (≈3.5) instantly flags 2 1/6 as impossible. Requiring an estimate first plus the full working reveals both whether the distribution was complete and whether the answer was sense-checked, neither visible from a bare number.

sources.claim: The misconception that multiplication always makes numbers bigger, and the need to check reasonableness (e.g. multiplying by a factor less than 1 gives a smaller product), must be confronted; real/personalised contexts and visual models improve fraction multiplication problem-solving
sources.source: IES / What Works Clearinghouse — Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K–8 (Siegler et al. 2010), Recommendation 3

sources.claim: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers using visual fraction models or equations, converting mixed numbers to improper fractions (or using the area model) to compute completely
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics — 5.NF.6

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Evolution vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y6 'Evolution and inheritance'):** supplies the language for the three Y6 statements — 'living things have changed over time… fossils', 'offspring vary and are not identical', 'adapted to suit their environment… adaptation may lead to evolution'. Terms: adaptation, evolution, natural selection, extinct/extinction, fossil record, species, common ancestor, variation, and (lightly) mutation.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-LS4-1/2/3):** the mechanism words (variation, survival advantage, natural selection) and fossil-record ideas are spread across grade-3 LS4; NGSS avoids the word 'evolution' at that grade, so 'evolution/natural selection' as named terms are the UK Y6 framing.

- **Operational details:** A LANGUAGE node with a twist — besides binding each term to a clear example, the child must ASSEMBLE several terms into the natural-selection MECHANISM in the right order: variation exists → a selection pressure in the environment → better-suited individuals survive and reproduce more → over many generations the population changes (evolution). So two jobs: (1) term↔meaning anchoring (adaptation = feature that aids survival; species = one kind that interbreeds; common ancestor = shared origin of two species; extinct = none left anywhere; fossil record = the evidence-trail in rock; variation = differences within a species; mutation = a new change in inherited information); (2) correct SEQUENCING of the mechanism. Two precise distinctions matter: extinct vs endangered (gone forever vs at-risk-but-surviving), and adaptation (the feature/outcome) vs natural selection (the process that produces it). Keep 'mutation' light (a source of new variation, no molecular detail). Build on the Batch-4 mechanism the child has already felt in the selection sim — now they NAME its parts.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C. The child uses each term correctly in context, sequences the natural-selection mechanism using variation/selection pressure/survival/reproduction/over-generations in order, and draws the extinct-vs-endangered and adaptation-vs-natural-selection distinctions correctly.
bestPractices: Anchor every term to a concrete example and USE it (adaptation → point to a specific feature; extinct → name a specific lost species) rather than reciting definitions.

Treat the mechanism words as an ordered CHAIN to assemble — variation → selection pressure → differential survival & reproduction → change over generations — so 'natural selection' is a sequence, not a single word.
Drill two high-value distinctions explicitly: extinct vs endangered, and adaptation (outcome/feature) vs natural selection (process).
Build on the already-felt selection simulation from the prior topic — now attach the correct labels to parts the child has seen work.
Keep 'mutation' light: a new change in inherited information that adds fresh variation; avoid molecular/DNA mechanism at KS2.
Guard against 'evolution has a goal / strives for better' and Lamarckian phrasing when the child uses the new words.
keyRepresentations: A glossary gallery: each term pinned to an image/example (adaptation on a camel; extinct on a dodo; fossil record as rock strata).
An ordered mechanism strip the child assembles: variation → selection pressure → survive & reproduce → over generations → evolution.
An extinct-vs-endangered contrast pair; an adaptation-vs-natural-selection (feature vs process) contrast.
A common-ancestor branch diagram showing two species sharing an origin.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing extinct and endangered (using 'extinct' for at-risk species that still survive).
Conflating adaptation (a feature/outcome) with natural selection (the process that produces it), or using 'evolution' and 'adaptation' interchangeably.
Using the mechanism words out of order or dropping steps (e.g. 'natural selection' without variation or a selection pressure).
Teleology — 'evolution tries to make animals better / has a goal' embedded in how the words are used.
Lamarckian phrasing sneaking back in ('the species adapted itself because it needed to').
Treating 'mutation' as always harmful or as a conscious change, rather than a random source of new variation.
Thinking 'common ancestor' means one species descended directly from a living one (e.g. 'humans came from monkeys').

learn.summary: Evolution vocabulary for ages 10–11: binding ~9 terms (adaptation, evolution, natural selection, extinct/extinction, fossil record, species, common ancestor, variation, and lightly mutation) to concrete examples, AND assembling the mechanism words into the natural-selection sequence in the correct order. Two distinctions are high-value: extinct vs endangered, and adaptation (the feature/outcome) vs natural selection (the process). Learners first fix each word's meaning against a vivid example, then order the words into the story of natural selection; usage is exercised in live narrative, not just recognition.

activities.title: Evolution glossary gallery: term pinned to an example
feedback: If the learner calls a rare-but-surviving group 'extinct', contrast extinct (none left anywhere) with endangered (few left, at risk) and give a real example of each.
If 'common ancestor' is read as one living species coming directly from another, show the branch point: both species descend from a shared earlier origin; neither came from the other.
If the learner only recognises a term but cannot use it, ask them to put it in a new sentence about a different animal.
activities.rationale: A language node's core job is anchoring terms to vivid examples and nailing the extinct-vs-endangered and adaptation-vs-process distinctions. Pinning each word to an image with a myth-busting contrast, and showing the word used in a sentence, binds meaning and usage together. A tap-to-reveal gallery and lift-the-flap contrast are offered as concrete mechanisms for this; a fixed labelled diagram or paper glossary cards could serve the same end.
sourceClaims: Learners commonly confuse extinct with endangered, conflate adaptation with natural selection, and carry teleological/Lamarckian phrasing into their use of evolution terms.
learnerActions: Explore a rich scene where each key term lives on something concrete the learner can point to and reveal: a camel reveals 'adaptation — a feature that helps it survive here'; a dodo reveals 'extinct — none left anywhere'; layered rock reveals 'fossil record — the trail of evidence in the rocks'; a point where two branches meet reveals 'common ancestor — the shared origin'.
Read each term used in a real sentence at the moment of reveal, so meaning and usage arrive together rather than as a recited definition.
Use a lift-the-flap / contrast pair that sets the extinct dodo directly beside a tiger labelled 'endangered — still here, but at risk', and say aloud why each word fits its creature.
At the common-ancestor branch point, explain why it does NOT mean one living species descended directly from another (e.g. heading off 'humans came from monkeys').
After exploring, say each term in a fresh sentence of the learner's own to confirm usage, not just recognition.
activities.intendedInsight: Each technical term names something specific and concrete; the exact line between extinct (gone forever) and endangered (few left, still surviving) and between adaptation (the feature an organism has) and the across-generations process that produces it matters.

activities.title: Assemble the natural-selection mechanism in order
feedback: If the learner sequences reproduction or selection before variation, insist on the order: variation must exist first, then a selection pressure acts, then survivors reproduce.

If 'adaptation' is used for the whole process ('the moths did an adaptation to survive'), fix adaptation = the helpful feature and natural selection = the process that spreads it; rehearse both in one narrative.
If 'evolution' and 'natural selection' are used as identical synonyms, distinguish evolution (the change over time, the outcome) from natural selection (the mechanism that drives it).

If teleological phrasing appears ('evolution tries to make animals better / has a goal') or Lamarckian phrasing ('the species adapted itself because it needed to'), restate: variation arises first and the environment simply favours some variants — there is no goal or striving.
activities.rationale: The second job of this node is correct sequencing of the mechanism — a build-and-check task that can flag wrong orders with a nudge. Labelling an already-seen selection process lets learners attach names to parts they have watched work. A drag-into-chain sequencer is one concrete mechanism; movable paper cards or a spoken retelling of the moth story in order serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Learners commonly confuse extinct with endangered, conflate adaptation with natural selection, and carry teleological/Lamarckian phrasing into their use of evolution terms.
learnerActions: Build the mechanism as an ordered chain, placing the steps in the correct sequence: inherited variation exists within the population → a selection pressure acts in the environment → better-suited individuals survive and reproduce more, passing on their helpful features → over many generations the population changes (evolution).
If a step is placed out of order (e.g. selection or reproduction before any variation exists), fix it and say why variation must come first.
Ideally label the stages of a selection animation or story the learner has already seen work — dropping the right term onto each stage — so the words attach to a process they have already observed.
State in the learner's own words what 'variation', 'selection pressure', and 'reproduction' each contribute to the chain.
Say where 'mutation' fits: a new change in inherited information that can add fresh variation — kept light, with no molecular/DNA detail.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Natural selection' is not a single label but an ordered chain: variation must already exist before a selection pressure can act on it, and the population change (evolution) emerges over many generations. Evolution is the outcome/change over time; natural selection is the mechanism that drives it.

activities.title: Tell the moth story using the words in sequence (use-in-context)
feedback: Target (full command) looks like: there was inherited variation (pale and dark moths); dark colour was an adaptation suiting the sooty trees; birds ate the more visible pale moths (a selection pressure), so more dark moths survived and passed on their colour through reproduction (natural selection); over many generations the population became mostly dark (evolution). The pale form becoming rare is not extinction, because pale and dark moths are the same species. A species is extinct when none are left anywhere (e.g. the dodo), and endangered when it still survives but is at high risk of dying out (e.g. the tiger).

Partial command: several terms used correctly but not in a coherent sequence, or adaptation blurred with natural selection, or evolution with natural selection — ask the learner to re-order and re-tell.
Gap: terms used as loose labels, out of order, or extinct confused with endangered — return to the gallery contrast pair and the ordered chain before retelling.

A single organism can possess adaptations (features), but it does not EVOLVE within its lifetime, and it does not adapt in the heritable, across-generations sense — evolution and the process of adaptation apply to the population over generations; redirect if the learner attaches an individual's lifetime change to these process words.
activities.rationale: Assessing by use-in-context with a live narrative and probing questions discriminates learners who hold the words as labels (using them out of order or interchangeably) from those with genuine command. Dialogue that asks the learner to explain natural selection in their own words and challenges misuse ('you said it adapted because it needed to — is that right?') catches teleological and Lamarckian slips.
sourceClaims: Learners commonly confuse extinct with endangered, conflate adaptation with natural selection, and carry teleological/Lamarckian phrasing into their use of evolution terms.
learnerActions: Tell the story of how a population of moths in a sooty, polluted city came to be mostly dark-coloured, using these words in a sensible order as you go: variation, adaptation, natural selection, reproduction.

Explain why 'extinct' would NOT be the right word if pale moths became very rare in the city: pale and dark moths are colour forms of the same species, and extinction means a whole species (every member, everywhere) has died out. Then say how 'extinct' differs from 'endangered', using real species as examples.

Answer probing follow-ups in your own words: what exactly was the selection pressure in the moth story? Could a single moth 'evolve' in its lifetime, or does that word apply to the population over generations — and which word goes with which? Give a real animal that is extinct and one that is endangered, saying why each word fits. Where does 'mutation' fit as a source of new variation?
activities.intendedInsight: Genuine command shows in sequenced USE within a live narrative — using each term precisely and in order, and cleanly distinguishing extinct from endangered with examples — not in reciting isolated definitions.

constraints: Keep 'mutation' light at this level: a random new change in inherited information that can add fresh variation; avoid molecular/DNA mechanism and avoid framing mutations as always harmful or as conscious changes.
Guard against teleology ('evolution tries to make animals better / has a goal') and Lamarckian phrasing ('the species adapted itself because it needed to') whenever the learner uses the new words.

Matching, ordering and multiple-choice formats (e.g. term↔example matching, sequence the steps, 'extinct or endangered?') can be used to practise and check these terms, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit the independent, sequenced USE in a live narrative that demonstrates command; include a produce-and-explain task.
A fixed glossary image or diagram anchors term↔example meaning but cannot show a process unfolding; pair it with an ordering/retelling task so learners also sequence the mechanism.

Curricula frame these terms differently: the England KS2 Year 6 'Evolution and inheritance' unit names evolution and adaptation explicitly, while US NGSS spreads related ideas (inherited traits, fossils, survival in environments, natural selection and adaptation) across grade bands with differing emphasis. Align terminology to the learner's curriculum context.

Evolution, and the across-generations process of adaptation, apply to populations over generations, not to a single organism changing within its lifetime; an individual can nonetheless possess adaptations (features). Keep this distinction explicit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the two UK/NGSS curriculum claims as verified and the OU OpenLearn misconceptions claim as unverified (verified:false); treat the specific misconception list as plausible but not independently re-checked here.

The original recommendation's framing that a static gallery 'anchors more cleanly' than alternatives and that 3D 'adds nothing' are catalog fit preferences, not established comparative efficacy; retained only as narrowly scoped suggestions with stated affordances/limits.

Internal wording note: the source's 'full' response level lists the order as 'variation → adaptation → selection pressure → reproduction' while the mechanism chain elsewhere orders selection pressure before differential survival/reproduction. The build task (activity 2) uses variation → selection pressure → survive & reproduce → over generations; the moth retelling (activity 3) preserves the original narrative order, where naming the favourable trait (adaptation) before describing the pressure is still coherent.

The NGSS curriculum-framing claim was removed from the sequencing activity's sourceClaims because it supports a terminology convention, not the sequencing teaching principle; it remains reflected in the constraints.

The DfE curriculum-supply claim was removed from the glossary activity's sourceClaims because it establishes which terms the curriculum requires (topic/necessity) rather than supporting the term-anchoring teaching principle; the DfE curriculum point remains reflected in the constraints.

probeDeeper: You used 'natural selection' — say in your own words what the selection pressure was in the moth story.
Could a single moth 'adapt' or 'evolve' in its lifetime, or does the word apply to the population? Which word goes with which?
Give me a real animal that is extinct and one that is endangered, and say why each word fits.
Where does 'mutation' fit into your story — what would it be the source of?
assess.correctAnswer: The child uses the terms in a correct sequence: there was variation (pale and dark moths); dark colour was an adaptation suiting the sooty trees; birds ate the more visible pale moths (a selection pressure), so dark moths survived and passed on their colour through reproduction (natural selection); if every last pale moth died out they would be extinct, whereas endangered means very few remain but some still survive.

errorPatterns.pattern: uses 'adaptation' for the whole process instead of for the feature ('the moths did an adaptation to survive')
errorPatterns.nextMove: fix 'adaptation' = the feature and 'natural selection' = the process that spreads it; rehearse both in one narrative
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 'adaptation' names the mechanism rather than the helpful trait, and natural selection is skipped

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses 'extinct' with 'endangered' ('the pale moths are extinct because there aren't many left')
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast extinct (none left anywhere) with endangered (few left, at risk); give real examples of each
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls a rare-but-surviving group extinct

errorPatterns.pattern: sequences the terms wrongly — reproduction or selection before variation
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist on the order: variation must exist first, then a selection pressure acts, then survivors reproduce
errorPatterns.revealedBy: tells the story with selection acting before any variation exists

errorPatterns.pattern: uses 'evolution' and 'natural selection' as identical synonyms
errorPatterns.nextMove: distinguish evolution (the change over time, the outcome) from natural selection (the mechanism that drives it)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: swaps the two as if interchangeable

responseLevels.gap: Uses the terms as loose labels, out of order, or confuses extinct with endangered.
responseLevels.full: Narrates natural selection with variation → adaptation → selection pressure → reproduction in the correct order, uses each term precisely, and cleanly distinguishes extinct from endangered with examples.
responseLevels.partial: Uses several terms correctly but not in a coherent sequence, or blurs adaptation with natural selection, or evolution with natural selection — vocabulary applied inconsistently.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell the story of how a population of moths in a sooty, polluted city came to be mostly dark-coloured, using these words in a sensible order as you go: variation, adaptation, natural selection, reproduction. Then tell me what 'extinct' would mean for the pale moths, and how that's different from 'endangered'.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the words as labels uses them out of order or interchangeably — calling the whole process 'adaptation', or 'extinct' for merely rare. Correct sequenced USE in a live narrative, plus the extinct/endangered distinction, shows genuine command.
