pedagogy.summary: Children operate transformations as rules on coordinates: translating a shape changes every vertex by adding/subtracting the horizontal and vertical moves (right +x, left −x, up +y, down −y), while reflecting in an axis changes the sign of exactly ONE coordinate — reflection in the x-axis sends (x, y) to (x, −y), reflection in the y-axis sends (x, y) to (−x, y). The conceptual anchor is that the axis you reflect IN is the mirror, points move PERPENDICULAR to it, and so the coordinate measuring distance from that mirror flips sign while the other is unchanged. Fluency means predicting image coordinates from the rule and explaining why each rule takes the form it does.
bestPractices: Derive the sign rules from the geometry, not memorised swaps: reflecting in the x-axis flips the shape VERTICALLY, so the vertical (y) coordinate changes sign and x stays; reflecting in the y-axis flips it HORIZONTALLY, so x changes sign and y stays.
Tie the rule to equal distance: the image is the same distance from the axis as the original, on the opposite side — (x, y) and (x, −y) are both |y| from the x-axis (Oak National Academy).

Explicitly separate the two axis rules with worked pairs — e.g. (−4, 1) reflects to (4, 1) in the y-axis but to (−4, −1) in the x-axis — so pupils feel which single coordinate changes each time (Oak).

Confront reflection-as-translation head-on with examples and non-examples: a slid shape keeps its orientation, a reflected shape is reversed; use real mirrors as a scaffold, then move to reasoning with coordinates (Oak).
For translation, treat each direction as a signed change to the matching coordinate — '2 down' subtracts 2 from y — and have pupils PREDICT image coordinates before plotting.
Avoid 'straight across/down' language; say points move perpendicular to the mirror line, so the correct coordinate change is understood rather than transposed (NCETM KS3 6.3).
keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid with the x- and y-axes as mirror lines
Coordinate mapping notation: translation (x, y) → (x+a, y+b); reflection in x-axis (x, y) → (x, −y); in y-axis (x, y) → (−x, y)
Real mirror / Mira placed on an axis to check the image, as a scaffold
Paired worked example showing the same vertex reflected in each axis to contrast which coordinate changes
commonMisconceptions: Reflecting in the x-axis but changing the sign of the WRONG coordinate (negating x instead of y), effectively reflecting in the other axis.
Reflecting by sliding/translating the shape rather than reflecting it, so the image is not reversed.
Getting the translation sign wrong — adding when the move is left or down instead of subtracting.
Reversing the coordinate pair (writing the y-value before the x-value) when stating image vertices.

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils learn to translate shapes on a four-quadrant coordinate grid (adding/subtracting signed amounts to matching coordinates) and to reflect shapes in the x- or y-axis by negating exactly one coordinate. The goal is to DERIVE the sign rules from geometry — points move perpendicular to the mirror axis, so the coordinate measuring distance from that axis flips sign while the other stays — rather than memorise a swap. Core errors: changing the wrong coordinate (reflecting in the wrong axis), sliding instead of reflecting (no reversal), wrong translation signs for left/down moves, and reversing the ordered pair.

activities.title: Predict, then reflect: watch the single coordinate flip
feedback: If a predicted point lands in the wrong quadrant, diagonally opposite the true image (e.g. (4, 1) in the first quadrant instead of (−4, −1) in the third for an x-axis reflection), you likely negated the wrong coordinate — ask which direction the shape actually moves and which coordinate measures distance from that axis.
If the image keeps facing the same way (not mirrored), you slid/translated instead of reflecting; rebuild one vertex at an equal perpendicular distance on the opposite side so the reversal appears.
Check the image and original are the same distance from the axis and the same size and shape — e.g. (x, y) and (x, −y) are both |y| from the x-axis.
activities.rationale: Acting on a shape and watching the coordinate table update makes the single-coordinate sign change visible, and predicting first surfaces the wrong-coordinate and slide-not-reflect misconceptions as a visibly misplaced point. Contrasting the SAME vertex reflected in each axis separates the two rules by reasoning rather than memorised swap. A live table, ghost original, and predict-mode are optional supports that make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: The most common mistake pupils make when reflecting is to flip/translate the shape rather than reflect it; the reflection and original should be the same distance from the axis and the same size and shape, and real mirrors help pupils notice the direction the reflection faces.

Reflecting a vertex at (−4,1) in the y-axis gives (4,1) (only x changes sign) while reflecting it in the x-axis gives (−4,−1) (only y changes sign); reflecting in both axes gives (4,−1). Distractor answers that change the wrong coordinate correspond to the classic 'wrong coordinate / wrong axis' error.

Reflection should be taught via the perpendicular structure — every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line — avoiding 'straight across/down' language, so the correct coordinate change is derived rather than memorised; examples should span all quadrants and the axes.
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant grid, start with a triangle plotted in the second quadrant and its vertices labelled with coordinates.
Before anything moves, choose 'reflect in the x-axis' and write down what you predict each vertex will become.
Run the reflection: watch each vertex move perpendicular to the x-axis (vertically, to the opposite side) while, in a coordinate table, only the y-value changes sign and x stays the same.
If a real mirror or Mira is available, stand it on the x-axis to check the image faces the opposite way and sits the same distance from the axis.
Now, starting from the SAME triangle, reflect in the y-axis instead and predict again: this time the shape flips sideways (perpendicular to the y-axis) and only x changes sign.
Compare the two results on the same vertex, e.g. (−4, 1) → (−4, −1) in the x-axis but (−4, 1) → (4, 1) in the y-axis.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflecting in the x-axis flips the shape vertically, so the y-coordinate (vertical distance from the x-axis) negates and x is unchanged; reflecting in the y-axis flips it horizontally, so x negates and y is unchanged. The axis you reflect IN is the mirror and points move perpendicular to it.

activities.title: Translate by signed changes — predict before plotting
feedback: If a '2 down' move made the y-value increase, you added instead of subtracted — down and left reduce the coordinate; re-predict then check one vertex on the grid.
If the whole shape moved but didn't reverse, that is correct for a translation — a translation never produces a mirror image.
Check each vertex against the grid before trusting the rule.
activities.rationale: Predicting signed coordinate changes before plotting targets the add-when-it-should-subtract error and distinguishes a slide (orientation preserved) from a reflection (orientation reversed).
learnerActions: Take a triangle on the grid and a translation instruction such as '3 squares right and 2 squares down'.
Treat each direction as a signed change to the matching coordinate: right adds to x, left subtracts from x, up adds to y, down subtracts from y. So '3 right, 2 down' gives (x, y) → (x+3, y−2).
Predict the new coordinates of every vertex BEFORE plotting, then plot and check against the grid.
Say back how the whole shape kept its orientation (a slide does not reverse the shape).
activities.intendedInsight: Translation adds or subtracts a signed amount to the matching coordinate and preserves orientation; left and down are negative changes, not additions.

activities.title: Contrast slide versus reflect, and keep the pair in order
feedback: If you reported a vertex as (y, x) though the plotted point looks right, re-anchor 'x before y, along then up/down' and recheck.
If an on-axis point moved, remember a point on the mirror is already on it, so its distance from the axis is zero and it does not move.
Use examples and non-examples (and a real mirror on the axis) to confirm the reflection faces the other way.
activities.rationale: Pairing reflection against translation on the same shape elicits the reversal/equidistance idea versus a straight slide, and explicit (x, y) ordering guards against the common pair-reversal interference error. The on-axis fixed-point case is a useful boundary check.
sourceClaims: The most common mistake pupils make when reflecting is to flip/translate the shape rather than reflect it; the reflection and original should be the same distance from the axis and the same size and shape, and real mirrors help pupils notice the direction the reflection faces.
A recurring coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair (stating the second value before the first); guard against it with 'x before y / along then up'.
learnerActions: Reflect a triangle in the x-axis and separately translate the same triangle 'down' by a fixed amount; place the two results side by side.
Describe how they differ: the reflected image is reversed and equidistant on the opposite side of the axis; the translated image faces the same way and simply slid.
Find a vertex that sits ON the mirror axis, e.g. (0, 4) on the y-axis, and reflect in that axis: note it stays fixed.
When listing every image vertex, write x before y ('along then up/down') and check one plotted point matches the pair you wrote.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection reverses sense and is equidistant across the mirror; translation preserves sense. Points on the mirror axis map to themselves. Ordered pairs are always (x, y).

activities.title: Diagnose with paired axis items (assessment)
feedback: Choosing (4, 1) for an x-axis reflection means you changed x instead of y — you effectively reflected in the y-axis; re-anchor to the vertical flip.
Choosing (−1, −4) means you swapped the coordinate order of the correct image (−4, −1); apply 'x before y'.
A correct choice or plot with no 'why' is not yet secure — ask for the perpendicular/equidistance reason.
activities.rationale: Multiple-choice items whose distractors ARE the misconceptions diagnose cleanly, and the draw-and-list step adds some image construction. However, selecting among options does not by itself build the felt derivation of why one coordinate changes, so pair this assessment with the predict-and-construct activities above.
sourceClaims: Reflecting a vertex at (−4,1) in the y-axis gives (4,1) (only x changes sign) while reflecting it in the x-axis gives (−4,−1) (only y changes sign); reflecting in both axes gives (4,−1). Distractor answers that change the wrong coordinate correspond to the classic 'wrong coordinate / wrong axis' error.
learnerActions: Answer items such as '(−4, 1) reflected in the x-axis = ?' where the correct answer is (−4, −1), the wrong-coordinate answer (4, 1) and the reversed-pair answer (−1, −4) are offered as options.
Complete fill-in-the-blank image coordinates after a stated translation.
Plot a reflection by drawing the image, then list its vertices.
Explain in words why only one coordinate changed for each reflection.
activities.intendedInsight: Picking the correct image while rejecting wrong-axis and reversed-pair distractors, plotting the image correctly, and explaining why only one coordinate changes together show the rule is reasoned rather than guessed.

constraints: Reflection and translation here are 2-D coordinate operations on the plane; a third dimension (z-values, planes of reflection) is not needed and distracts from the (x, y) sign rules.

Avoid 'straight across / straight down' as a generic rule; say points move perpendicular to the mirror axis so the correct coordinate change is understood rather than transposed (for the x-axis this motion happens to be vertical, for the y-axis horizontal).

Recognition/multiple-choice items diagnose and check but do not themselves elicit independent construction of an image or an explanation; use them alongside tasks where the child predicts, plots and justifies.
A real mirror or Mira is a helpful scaffold for noticing reversal and equidistance, but pupils should progress to reasoning directly with coordinates.

A static annotated grid can label a vertex's image and its coordinate change on tap, but it cannot let the child predict and test their own image, which is where the sign confusion lives — treat it as a supporting illustration, not the main task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked coordinates: (−4, 1) reflected in x-axis → (−4, −1); reflected in y-axis → (4, 1); in both → (4, −1); these are internally consistent across pedagogy, assess and sources. '3 right, 2 down' maps (x, y) → (x+3, y−2) — consistent with the diagnostic.
Reversed-pair distractor: the order-swap of the correct image (−4, −1) is (−1, −4); an earlier draft listed (1, −4), which is not a reversed pair and was fixed in activity 4.

Activity 4 contains both recognition (multiple-choice) and production (draw-and-list) steps; its stated limitation is scoped to the multiple-choice selection only, not to the whole activity, to avoid implying the activity never elicits construction.
The 'reflect in the x-axis flips vertically so y changes' reasoning is sound geometrically; retained as derivation, not as an unverified claim of comparative teaching efficacy.

The UK National Curriculum source is verified:false in the row and only establishes the curriculum expectation that Year 6 pupils translate and reflect shapes; it does not support the teaching principle in activity 2, so activity 2's sourceClaims is [].

On-axis fixed-point case ((0,4) reflected in the y-axis stays fixed) was present only in the assessment probes; added as a boundary check in an activity because it is mathematically correct and pedagogically useful.

probeDeeper: 'You reflected in the x-axis and the y-coordinates changed sign. Why that coordinate and not the x?' (listen for vertical flip / perpendicular-to-the-axis reasoning, not a recited rule).
Counterexample: 'Now reflect the SAME triangle in the y-axis instead. What changes this time?' (tests that the child does not apply the x-axis rule to both).
'Reflecting in the x-axis moves the triangle downward, and translating 2 down also moves it downward. How are the two results different?' (elicits reversal/equidistance versus a straight slide).
'One vertex sits at (0, 4), on the y-axis. Where does it go when you reflect in the y-axis?' (points on the mirror axis stay fixed).
assess.correctAnswer: For the translation, each vertex gains 3 on x and loses 2 on y (right +x, down −y). For the reflection in the x-axis, each vertex keeps its x and negates its y — (x, y) → (x, −y) — so the image sits the same distance below the axis as the original is above, reversed in sense. The child explains that translating adds/subtracts to the coordinates while reflecting in the x-axis changes the sign of the y-coordinate only (and reflecting in the y-axis would change x only), because points move perpendicular to the mirror axis.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflects in the x-axis but changes the sign of the wrong coordinate — negates x instead of y — effectively reflecting in the other axis
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor to the geometry: reflecting in the x-axis flips the shape vertically, so the vertical (y) coordinate changes; move each vertex perpendicular to the axis and read off (x, −y). Contrast with a y-axis reflection on the same shape.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives (−x, y) for an x-axis reflection (e.g. maps (−4,1) to (4,1) instead of (−4,−1)); the image appears on the wrong side/quadrant; the child recites 'x-axis so change x'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflects by sliding/translating the shape across the axis rather than reflecting it, so the image is not reversed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use examples and non-examples and a real mirror on the axis to show the reflection faces the other way; rebuild one vertex by equal perpendicular distance so the reversal emerges.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The image keeps its orientation (not a mirror image) and/or is not equidistant from the axis; the child moves the whole shape as a block.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gets the translation sign wrong — adds instead of subtracts for a left or down move (treats every move as increasing the coordinate)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rehearse each direction as a signed change on a signed axis — down subtracts from y, left subtracts from x; predict the coordinate before plotting and check against the grid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For '2 down' the y-value increases (or for 'left' the x increases); the translated image goes the wrong way on one axis.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the coordinate pair, stating the y-value before the x-value, when listing image vertices
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'x before y, along then up/down'; check one image vertex together against the grid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports an image vertex as (y, x) though the plotted point is right; e.g. writes (−1,−4) for a point at (−4,−1).

responseLevels.gap: Changes the wrong coordinate when reflecting (or reflects by sliding), and/or gets translation signs wrong; cannot say why a coordinate changes.
responseLevels.full: Translates with correct signed changes, reflects in either axis by negating the correct single coordinate with an equal-distance/perpendicular justification, keeps on-axis points fixed, states image coordinates as (x, y), and explains the add/subtract (translation) versus sign-change (reflection) rules — transferring correctly between the two axes.
responseLevels.partial: Reflects in the x-axis and translates by rule in familiar cases but cannot justify why the y-coordinate (not x) changes, slips on the y-axis reflection or on a 'down/left' translation sign, or reverses a pair. Executes the steps but cannot connect the sign change to the perpendicular flip or transfer to the other axis.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a four-quadrant grid with a small triangle plotted in the second quadrant (vertices labelled with their coordinates). Say: 'First, translate this triangle 3 squares right and 2 squares down, and write the new coordinates of each vertex. Then, starting from the original, reflect it in the x-axis and list the reflected vertices. Finally, tell me how the coordinates changed in each case, and why.' Set the task and WATCH which coordinate the child changes and whether the reflected image is reversed — do not state the rules.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reflecting in the x-axis, a child who grasps the perpendicular structure negates y and keeps x, landing the image in the correct quadrant; a child who has memorised a swap negates x instead — effectively reflecting in the WRONG axis — and the image lands in a visibly different place. A child who translates instead of reflecting produces an un-reversed image. Watching which single coordinate changes, and whether sense reverses, separates true understanding from rule-transposition; the 'why' further exposes memorisation.

sources.claim: The most common mistake pupils make when reflecting is to flip/translate the shape rather than reflect it; the reflection and original should be the same distance from the axis and the same size and shape, and real mirrors help pupils notice the direction the reflection faces.
sources.source: Oak National Academy (KS2 Year 6): 'Reflect simple shapes in the axes on a full coordinate grid'

sources.claim: Reflecting a vertex at (−4,1) in the y-axis gives (4,1) (only x changes sign) while reflecting it in the x-axis gives (−4,−1) (only y changes sign); reflecting in both axes gives (4,−1). Distractor answers that change the wrong coordinate correspond to the classic 'wrong coordinate / wrong axis' error.
sources.source: Oak National Academy (KS2 Year 6) exit-quiz items

sources.claim: Reflection should be taught via the perpendicular structure — every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line — avoiding 'straight across/down' language, so the correct coordinate change is derived rather than memorised; examples should span all quadrants and the axes.
sources.source: NCETM KS3 Mastery PD 6.3 'Transforming shapes'

sources.claim: A recurring coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair (stating the second value before the first); guard against it with 'x before y / along then up'.
sources.source: NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives'

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils should draw and translate simple shapes on the coordinate plane and reflect them in the axes.
sources.source: UK National Curriculum, Mathematics KS2 (Year 6 geometry: position and direction)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Wave Properties & Types

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 'Waves' + KS4 'Wave motion'):** KS3 statutory: "waves on water as undulations which travel through water with transverse motion; these waves can be reflected, and add or cancel – superposition"; "frequencies of sound waves, measured in hertz (Hz)"; "sound produced by vibrations of objects… sound waves are longitudinal"; "sound needs a medium to travel, the speed of sound in air, in water, in solids." The FORMAL properties framework — "amplitude, wavelength, frequency, relating velocity to frequency and wavelength" and "transverse and longitudinal waves" — is DfE KS4 'Wave motion'. NOTE: at 11–12 the qualitative observations (transverse water, longitudinal sound, frequency in Hz) are statutory KS3, but the amplitude/wavelength terminology, the transverse↔longitudinal general classification, and the v = fλ equation are KS4 — so the full framework here is an early KS3→KS4 bridge.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS4-1, with HS-PS4-1):** MS-PS4-1 — "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS4-1]" (amplitude/wavelength model). The velocity–frequency–wavelength relation v = fλ is HS-PS4-1 ("mathematical representations… relationships among the frequency, wavelength, and speed of waves"). Transverse vs longitudinal is not a distinct NGSS PE at this level.

- **Operational details:** Describe ANY wave by four quantities — AMPLITUDE (maximum displacement from rest; height of a crest / depth of a trough; more amplitude = more energy), WAVELENGTH (distance of one full cycle, crest to crest), FREQUENCY (cycles passing a point per second, in Hz), and WAVE SPEED. Two TYPES: TRANSVERSE (oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel — water ripples, light, all EM) vs LONGITUDINAL (oscillation parallel to travel — compressions and rarefactions; sound). BOTH transfer ENERGY without net transport of matter. The wave equation v = fλ links them: for a fixed speed, frequency and wavelength are INVERSELY related (raise frequency → wavelength shrinks). Amplitude is INDEPENDENT of frequency, wavelength and speed — it sets energy, not timing, and does NOT change wave speed (speed is set by the medium). CAUTION on the oscilloscope/graph: a sound (longitudinal) wave drawn as a wavy trace is a displacement-vs-TIME graph — the spacing between peaks is the PERIOD, not the wavelength, and the picture is not the shape of the wave in space.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal), reaching C on the v = fλ calculation. Success = label a wave diagram (amplitude, wavelength, crest, trough), distinguish transverse from longitudinal with an example of each, use v = fλ to find the third quantity given two, and reason that raising frequency at fixed speed shrinks wavelength. Watch for amplitude-proportional-to-frequency/speed, treating the two wave types as unrelated, 'radio waves are sound/longitudinal', and reading the horizontal axis of a sound trace as distance/wavelength rather than time/period.
bestPractices: Diagnose FIRST (IOP): use a diagnostic question to surface whether pupils believe amplitude scales with frequency or speed BEFORE teaching — this is the central relational misconception and instruction should target it directly.

Establish amplitude and frequency as INDEPENDENT with a live model: vary one while holding the other — raising amplitude only makes peaks taller, raising frequency only packs peaks closer (IOP signal-generator + oscilloscope, or the slink-o-scope analogue).

Separate the two wave TYPES with matched mechanical models: a slinky shaken side-to-side (transverse) vs pushed along its length (longitudinal compressions), so perpendicular-vs-parallel motion is seen — and stress that BOTH transfer energy without moving matter along.

Confront the oscilloscope trap explicitly (IOP, verified): a sound wave is longitudinal, but its oscilloscope trace LOOKS transverse because the horizontal axis is TIME — peak spacing is the PERIOD, not wavelength; introduce the 'slink-o-scope' mechanical analogue BEFORE the real oscilloscope.

Derive v = fλ empirically before using it as a formula: ripple-tank measurements show f × λ ≈ the measured speed, and that changing amplitude does NOT change speed — so the equation is discovered, not asserted (IOP).

Teach the inverse f–λ relationship with a 'what stays constant?' prompt: name that wave speed is fixed by the medium while f and λ trade off — pupils routinely forget which quantity is held constant when applying v = fλ.

Anchor the abstract terms to concrete waves pupils have already met (water ripples, sound, light) and connect back to the earlier amplitude→loudness and frequency→pitch experience, so the framework UNIFIES prior sound/light topics rather than starting cold.

Attack cross-domain type confusion head-on: state that radio and light are TRANSVERSE (EM) while sound is LONGITUDINAL — because the types are taught in separate lessons (sound, then light) and never connected, pupils merge them ('radio waves are sound').
keyRepresentations: Labelled transverse wave diagram: crest, trough, amplitude (rest → crest), wavelength (crest → crest) — the canonical picture pupils must be able to annotate.
Longitudinal wave as compressions and rarefactions along a slinky/spring, with wavelength measured compression-to-compression.
Matched slinky demonstrations: side-to-side shake (transverse) vs push-pull along the length (longitudinal) — the same medium, two geometries.
The oscilloscope / slink-o-scope displacement-vs-TIME trace, with the horizontal axis labelled TIME and peak-spacing labelled PERIOD (not wavelength) — the anti-misconception representation.
The v = fλ relationship annotated 'speed fixed by the medium; f and λ trade off inversely'.
A ripple tank as the empirical setup for measuring f, λ and speed — and for showing that amplitude does not change the speed.
commonMisconceptions: Amplitude is proportional to (or convertible with) frequency and/or wave speed — the central relational error (IOP); amplitude is actually independent and sets ENERGY, not timing.
Bringing amplitude into a speed calculation, or believing a bigger-amplitude wave travels faster — speed depends on the medium, not amplitude.
Thinking the wave SOURCE sets the wave speed (faster oscillation → faster wave) rather than the medium determining speed.
Treating transverse and longitudinal waves as entirely unrelated with no shared properties — both transfer energy without net movement of the medium.
'Radio waves are sound' — misidentifying an EM (transverse) wave as a longitudinal sound wave, a cross-domain confusion from disconnected lessons.
Reading a sound wave's oscilloscope trace as a picture of the wave in space — treating the horizontal (TIME) axis as distance and peak spacing as wavelength rather than period.
Forgetting what is held constant in v = fλ — associating the equation blindly without tracking that speed is fixed while f and λ trade off inversely.
Confusing wavelength with amplitude on a diagram — e.g. measuring the height as a wavelength, the width as amplitude, or mislabelling crest-to-trough as one wavelength.

learn.summary: Learners describe any wave with four quantities — amplitude, wavelength, frequency and wave speed — distinguish transverse from longitudinal waves with examples of each, and use v = fλ. The central aim is for learners to SEE and REASON that amplitude is independent (it sets energy, not timing or speed), that wave speed is fixed by the medium, and that at fixed speed frequency and wavelength trade off inversely. A recurring trap is reading a sound wave's displacement-vs-time trace as a picture of the wave in space (peak spacing is the period, not the wavelength). A live/manipulable wave model is proposed as the lead activity; labelling diagrams, calculation and a physical rope/slinky demonstration support and assess it.

activities.title: Wave bench: vary one property, watch the others
feedback: If a learner expects a bigger-amplitude wave to travel faster: point them to the pinned speed readout, which does not move when amplitude changes — speed is set by the medium, not by amplitude.

If a learner expects faster shaking (higher frequency) to speed the wave up: have them watch the speed readout stay fixed while the wavelength collapses — frequency sets the packing, the medium sets the speed.
If a learner reads the oscilloscope peak spacing as a wavelength: relabel the horizontal axis as TIME and confirm that spacing is the period; switch to space view to see the actual wavelength.

If a learner treats the two wave types as unrelated: compare them side by side — in both, particles oscillate about fixed positions and energy is carried along the direction of travel; what differs is whether the oscillation is perpendicular (transverse) or parallel (longitudinal) to that direction. Do not claim the two types must travel at the same speed in a given medium.
activities.rationale: These properties are a set of independently manipulable quantities plus a type distinction; varying one while holding others fixed lets the covariation and independence be observed directly rather than asserted. Separating amplitude and frequency responds to the documented tendency to treat amplitude as proportional to frequency/speed, and the space-view/oscilloscope-view contrast targets the time-axis trap.
sourceClaims: Many students think amplitude — like wavelength — is proportional to frequency and speed; remedy with ripple-tank measurement showing f × λ ≈ the measured velocity and that amplitude does not influence frequency or speed.

Sound is longitudinal but its oscilloscope trace LOOKS transverse because the horizontal axis is TIME (peak spacing = the period, not wavelength); teach the slink-o-scope mechanical analogue before a real oscilloscope; raising amplitude makes peaks bigger while raising frequency makes them closer; 14–16s find longitudinal motion hard and everyday language compounds the confusion.
learnerActions: Use a wave model (e.g. a wave on a string with independent amplitude and frequency sliders, ideally with wavelength and speed shown live) — PhET 'Waves Intro' / 'Wave on a String' are similar models, though in them wavelength and speed may need to be measured with the on-screen ruler/tape measure and timer rather than read from a live readout.
Raise frequency and observe that the wavelength visibly shrinks while the amplitude bar and the speed readout stay put; state in your own words what this shows.
Raise amplitude alone and observe that only the peak height grows — speed and wavelength do not change.

Use a model that can show both wave types (or two side-by-side models) to compare a transverse wave (oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel, seen as a side-to-side ripple) with a longitudinal wave (oscillation parallel to the direction of travel, seen as travelling compressions/rarefactions); note that in both, the particles oscillate about fixed positions and energy is transferred without the medium travelling along with the wave.
Switch between a 'space view' and an 'oscilloscope (displacement-vs-time) view' and label on the time view that peak-to-peak spacing is the PERIOD, not the wavelength.
activities.intendedInsight: Amplitude is independent of frequency, wavelength and speed; at a fixed wave speed (set by the medium) frequency and wavelength trade off inversely — this is the physical heart of v = fλ. Transverse and longitudinal waves are two different types of wave that both transfer energy without transferring matter, differing in whether the oscillation is perpendicular or parallel to the direction of travel; an oscilloscope trace of sound is a time graph, not a spatial picture.

activities.title: Rope/slinky demonstration: shake faster, measure what changes
feedback: Target reasoning to listen for: 'closer together, because the rope's speed can't change.' Reasoning like 'faster, because I'm shaking faster' reveals the frequency-drives-speed misconception — demonstrate the leading edge advancing at the same rate however fast you shake.

Useful check prompts: 'What decides how fast a wave moves along THIS rope — something you do at the end, or something about the rope itself?' and 'Sound in air travels at about 340 m/s whether the note is high or low — does that fit your rule about frequency and speed?'
If a learner brings amplitude into a question that only changed frequency, point separately to height (amplitude) versus crest-to-crest spacing (wavelength) on a diagram.
activities.rationale: Holding the medium constant makes speed fixed, so the intuitive 'shake faster → wave goes faster' rule is directly tested and can be seen to fail; requiring a reason surfaces whether the learner treats v = fλ as a real relationship with v pinned by the medium. The tighter-rope variation shows that changing the medium is what changes speed.
sourceClaims: Persistent post-instruction misconceptions: the wave source is thought to set frequency/period/wavelength and even wave speed (faster oscillation → faster wave); these survive extensive textbook practice.
learnerActions: On a long slinky or rope under fixed tension, shake the end to send a train of waves, then shake it TWICE as fast.
Before the second run, predict with a reason whether the waves will (a) travel faster, (b) get closer together, or (c) both.
Watch the leading edge advance at the same rate while the crests bunch up; compare with your prediction.
Shake the slinky (or rope) side-to-side to make a transverse wave, then, using the slinky, push–pull along its length to make longitudinal compressions and rarefactions, naming which is which.
Optionally, keep the shake rate the same but pull the rope TIGHTER and describe which of speed, frequency and wavelength changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Wave speed on a given rope is set by the rope itself (tension and mass), not by how you shake it; doubling the frequency therefore halves the wavelength, with speed unchanged. Tightening the rope changes the medium and so can change the speed.

activities.title: Label, classify and calculate
feedback: For 'frequency doubles at fixed speed': the wavelength HALVES; an 'unchanged' or 'doubles' answer means the learner is not holding speed constant — restate that v is fixed, so λ = v/f must fall.
For the oscilloscope item: the correct answer is the PERIOD, because the horizontal axis is time; choosing 'wavelength' treats the time graph as a spatial picture.
For 'radio waves are sound': note that radio and light are transverse electromagnetic waves while sound is longitudinal — the types are often taught in separate lessons and wrongly merged.
If height and width are swapped on the diagram: re-anchor amplitude as vertical displacement from rest and wavelength as one full horizontal cycle.

Note on the sort: at this level water surface ripples are classified as transverse (the KS3 'transverse motion' convention); their real surface motion is more complex, which is a refinement for later study, not a reason to reclassify them here.
activities.rationale: These tasks match the stated evidence of mastery and can probe the amplitude-independence, held-constant and oscilloscope-axis misconceptions with targeted options. Recognition and plug-in items assess and consolidate but do not by themselves build the covariation feel, so they support the manipulable model rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: US national anchor: a mathematical model of waves relating amplitude to energy (MS); the frequency–wavelength–speed relation v = fλ at high school.

Sound is longitudinal but its oscilloscope trace LOOKS transverse because the horizontal axis is TIME (peak spacing = the period, not wavelength); teach the slink-o-scope mechanical analogue before a real oscilloscope; raising amplitude makes peaks bigger while raising frequency makes them closer; 14–16s find longitudinal motion hard and everyday language compounds the confusion.
learnerActions: Label a wave diagram: amplitude (rest level to crest), wavelength (crest to crest), crest and trough — taking care not to mislabel the height as a wavelength or crest-to-trough as one wavelength.
Sort example waves — water ripples, sound, light, radio — into transverse or longitudinal, and give a reason for each.
Use v = fλ to find the missing quantity given the other two, working the calculation in both directions.
Answer: 'If frequency doubles while wave speed stays constant, what happens to the wavelength?' and justify the answer using which quantity is held constant.
Answer: 'Peak-to-peak spacing on a sound wave's oscilloscope trace is the …?' choosing between period and wavelength, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can annotate the canonical diagram correctly, classify wave types across domains (radio and light are transverse EM; sound is longitudinal), and apply v = fλ while tracking that speed is held fixed so frequency and wavelength trade off.

activities.title: Measure the wave equation (empirical option)
feedback: If f × λ does not match the measured speed well, discuss measurement uncertainty rather than concluding the relationship is false; look at whether timing or wavelength readings are the larger source of error.

If a learner expects larger-amplitude waves to be faster, compare the measured speeds at different (small) amplitudes — they should be close within measurement error for the same medium, depth and frequency.
activities.rationale: Deriving the equation from measurement grounds it as a real relationship and directly confronts the amplitude-affects-speed misconception; it also provides the empirical backing for the 'speed fixed by the medium' idea used elsewhere.
sourceClaims: Many students think amplitude — like wavelength — is proportional to frequency and speed; remedy with ripple-tank measurement showing f × λ ≈ the measured velocity and that amplitude does not influence frequency or speed.
learnerActions: In a ripple tank (or equivalent setup), measure frequency and wavelength for several waves and compute f × λ.
Compare f × λ with an independently measured wave speed and note how closely they agree.
Change the amplitude of the waves and check whether the measured speed changes.
Write a one-sentence conclusion about the relationship f × λ represents and about whether amplitude affects speed.
activities.intendedInsight: v = fλ can be discovered from measurement rather than taken on faith, and for small amplitudes changing the amplitude does not noticeably change the wave speed — speed depends on the medium and setup (e.g. water depth).

constraints: Begin by diagnosing whether learners believe amplitude scales with frequency or speed before teaching, since this is the central relational misconception to target.

Recognition and plug-in questions (labelling choices, sorting, 'what happens to wavelength' items) assess and consolidate understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction or the felt covariation that manipulating a live model or rope provides; use them alongside, not instead of, the manipulable/physical activities.

A static labelled diagram or tap-to-reveal image is a useful reference and a clean way to present the anti-misconception labels, but it cannot let learners vary a property and watch the others respond; treat it as a companion to the manipulable model.

An oscilloscope/displacement-vs-time view must be clearly labelled as a time graph; its peak spacing is the period, not the wavelength, and it is not the shape of the wave in space. Introducing a mechanical analogue (e.g. slink-o-scope) before a real oscilloscope is advised by the source.

A physical rope/slinky and a screen model offer different experiences; the rope shows the medium pinning the speed tangibly, while the screen model isolates one variable at a time. Neither is claimed to be uniquely necessary.
When describing the rope demonstration, keep the tension/medium fixed while varying frequency so speed is genuinely constant; only the tighter-rope variation changes the medium and hence the speed.

The full framework (amplitude/wavelength terminology, transverse↔longitudinal classification, v = fλ) bridges KS3 qualitative observations into KS4; v = fλ calculation is the most advanced element and may be a stretch for 11–12-year-olds.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles, not the efficacy of any specific activity here.

Several source rows carry verified:false (the IOP Spark amplitude-misconception review, the 2022 PhysRevPER mechanical-waves study, and the NGSS MS-PS4-1 page). Treat the associated claims as informative but unconfirmed in this rewrite.

Self-audit on v = fλ: with speed fixed, doubling frequency halves wavelength (λ = v/f). This is consistent across the diagnostic, correct answer and activity feedback. The 340 m/s speed-of-sound check (independent of pitch) is a sound approximation and is used consistently.

Audit note on medium vs source: wave speed is set by the medium/tension, not by how fast the source oscillates. The original fields are consistent with this; the tighter-rope case correctly implies speed can change because the medium changed.

The original claimed 3D rendering 'adds nothing' for the abstract diagram and equation; this comparative/universal framing is softened — 3D handling of a spring or water surface may make longitudinal compressions or transverse ripples more tangible, without asserting it is unnecessary or that 2D is universally sufficient.

The original asserted a conversation 'cannot deliver' the property relationships; this is removed as an unestablished universal. A dialogue persona can motivate and prompt reasoning, though it does not by itself verify labelling or calculation.

The KS3 standards claim was removed from the rope-demonstration activity's sourceClaims because it is a curriculum-placement/topic citation and does not support that activity's rationale (medium fixing speed). The standards context is retained in the preservation audit.

Water surface ripples are retained as transverse per the DfE KS3 convention; an explicit learner-facing note in the sort activity flags that their real surface motion is a later refinement, so the convention is not presented as an absolute truth.

assess.poeTask: On a long slinky or rope under fixed tension, shake the end slowly to send a train of waves, then shake it TWICE as fast. Before the second run each child predicts, with a reason, whether the waves will (a) travel faster, (b) get closer together, or (c) both. The reason is the diagnostic: 'closer together, because the rope's speed can't change' is the target; 'faster, because I'm shaking faster' exposes frequency-drives-speed. Then watch the leading edge advance at the same rate while the crests bunch up.
probeDeeper: What actually decides how fast a wave moves along THIS rope — something you do at the end, or something about the rope itself?
If instead you kept shaking at the same rate but pulled the rope TIGHTER, which of speed, frequency and wavelength would change?
Sound in air travels at about 340 m/s whether it's a high note or a low note. Use that fact to check your rule about frequency and speed.
Point to the amplitude on this wave diagram, then the wavelength — if I only changed the amplitude, would the wavelength change too?
assess.correctAnswer: The wavelength HALVES and the speed stays the SAME. Wave speed on a given rope is fixed by the rope itself (its tension and mass), not by how you shake it. Since v = fλ and v is unchanged, doubling the frequency must halve the wavelength.

errorPatterns.pattern: Frequency controls wave speed — 'if I shake it faster the wave travels faster down the rope'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demo on a real rope/slinky at fixed tension: the leading edge advances at the same rate however fast you shake. Establish 'the MEDIUM sets the speed; the source sets the frequency; wavelength is whatever v = fλ leaves'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Wave B travels faster along the rope, and its wavelength stays the same.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers that B is faster and often that its wavelength is unchanged; treats speed as an output of how hard/fast you drive the source.

errorPatterns.pattern: Amplitude and frequency are conflated — 'a bigger/faster wave' is one thing, so louder or taller waves also travel faster or have longer wavelengths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the three independent knobs explicitly on a diagram: amplitude (height), wavelength (crest-to-crest), frequency (crests per second) — change one at a time in a simulation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Brings amplitude into a question that only changed frequency, e.g. says B is 'bigger' or reasons about how high the wave is.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses v = fλ as blind plug-in without knowing which quantity is fixed — changes frequency AND holds wavelength, letting speed float to whatever the numbers give.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor each variable to its physical cause before any calculation: 'on this rope, what is allowed to change and what isn't?' Then use the equation to find the forced variable.
errorPatterns.distractor: Wave B's speed doubles because frequency doubled and the wavelength is fixed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Manipulates the formula but keeps wavelength fixed by default, concluding speed doubles; cannot say what physically pins one variable.

responseLevels.gap: Says the faster-shaken wave travels faster (and/or brings in amplitude); treats speed as driven by the source.
responseLevels.full: States wavelength halves and speed is unchanged AND explains speed is set by the medium (so v = fλ forces λ down), transferring correctly to the tighter-rope case and to the fixed-speed-of-sound check.
responseLevels.partial: Knows wavelength decreases when frequency rises and can quote v = fλ, but cannot articulate that the MEDIUM fixes the speed — so wavers on a new case (tightening the rope, a different medium) or lets speed change when only frequency did.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two waves travel along the SAME stretched rope. Wave B is made by shaking the end twice as fast as wave A — so B has double the frequency. What happens to wave B's WAVELENGTH compared with A's, and what happens to its SPEED along the rope? Explain why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Same medium is held constant, so speed cannot change — yet the intuitive rule 'shake faster → the wave goes faster' predicts a speed increase. A child who treats v = fλ as a real relationship (with v set by the medium) says wavelength halves, speed constant; a child who thinks frequency drives speed says the wave speeds up and wavelength is unchanged. Tier 2 forces the reason, so the right answer can't be reached by 'faster shaking feels faster'.

sources.claim: Sound is longitudinal but its oscilloscope trace LOOKS transverse because the horizontal axis is TIME (peak spacing = the period, not wavelength); teach the slink-o-scope mechanical analogue before a real oscilloscope; raising amplitude makes peaks bigger while raising frequency makes them closer; 14–16s find longitudinal motion hard and everyday language compounds the confusion.
sources.source: Institute of Physics — 'Teaching sound waves', Classroom Physics (Mar 2020), incl. the Slink-o-scope activity

sources.claim: Many students think amplitude — like wavelength — is proportional to frequency and speed; remedy with ripple-tank measurement showing f × λ ≈ the measured velocity and that amplitude does not influence frequency or speed.
sources.source: Institute of Physics — IOP Spark misconception review, 'amplitude proportional to frequency and speed'

sources.claim: KS3 'Waves' statutory content: transverse water waves and superposition; frequencies of sound in hertz; sound waves are longitudinal; speed of sound in air/water/solids. Amplitude, wavelength, 'relating velocity to frequency and wavelength', and 'transverse and longitudinal waves' are KS4 'Wave motion'.
sources.source: DfE — National curriculum in England: science programmes of study (KS3 'Waves' + KS4 'Wave motion')

sources.claim: Persistent post-instruction misconceptions: the wave source is thought to set frequency/period/wavelength and even wave speed (faster oscillation → faster wave); these survive extensive textbook practice.
sources.source: 'Difficulties in understanding mechanical waves: remediated by problem-based instruction' (2022), Physical Review Physics Education Research 18, 010140

sources.claim: US national anchor: a mathematical model of waves relating amplitude to energy (MS); the frequency–wavelength–speed relation v = fλ at high school.
sources.source: NGSS — MS-PS4-1 (with HS-PS4-1), Waves and their Applications

pedagogy.summary: The capstone add/subtract problem-solving node: multi-step problems in real contexts with numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals, where the child decides which operations AND which method — mental, written, or calculator — to use for each step, and justifies the choice. Beyond the multi-step reasoning inherited from earlier years, the distinctive demands are (1) choosing the calculator wisely (for genuinely awkward large/decimal computation, not for steps doable mentally) and (2) checking calculator/written output for reasonableness with an estimate, because a single keying or place-value slip is now worth millions.
bestPractices: Model the whole problem (bar model) and plan every step before computing
Choose method per step by the numbers: mental for round/near steps, written for structured ones, calculator for awkward large/decimal arithmetic - and say why
ALWAYS estimate the expected result so a calculator keying error (missed digit, misplaced point) is caught
Track intermediate quantities and re-read the actual question so the final step is not dropped
Interpret the answer back in context (units, sense, magnitude)
keyRepresentations: Multi-bar / running-total model
Step-and-method planner (step | operation | method | why)
Estimate strip for the reasonableness check
Real contexts: populations, money, distances, measures (decimals)
commonMisconceptions: Offers an intermediate quantity as the final answer, or drops a step
Word-spots operations rather than modelling the situation
Over-relies on the calculator (keys in steps doable mentally) or refuses it for genuinely awkward computation
Trusts the calculator display without an estimate, so a keying/place-value error goes unnoticed
Loses track of the decimal point or a period (thousands/millions) in large or decimal numbers

learn.summary: Year 6 capstone for add/subtract multi-step problem solving in real contexts with numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals. The distinctive demands beyond multi-step reasoning are: choosing a method per step (mental, written, or calculator) and justifying it, and checking any calculator/written output against an estimate so a keying or place-value slip (now worth millions) is caught. Learners must model the whole situation, track intermediate quantities, and answer the actual question rather than report a running total.

activities.title: Charity accounts mission planner
feedback: If a learner keys 345,000 where about 3,450,000 was expected, prompt: 'that's ten times too small - check the place value: have you missed a zero or put the decimal point in the wrong place?'
If the final answer equals an intermediate (e.g. the post-March figure), prompt: 're-read the question; which steps are still marked on your bar? Is the April-costs step included?'
If a learner keys in +2,000,000 on a calculator, ask: 'could you do this one in your head?' - discuss method fit without reteaching the arithmetic.
If a learner hand-grinds the awkward 675,450.75 subtraction unnecessarily, ask whether a calculator would suit that step and why.
activities.rationale: The national curriculum requires pupils to solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why, and to use estimation to check answers and judge an appropriate degree of accuracy. Making method choice and a reasonableness gate the core loop targets exactly this content. An optional interactive version can hold the estimate and flash a magnitude warning when the entered result is an order of magnitude off, and can feed each result into a visible running bar; these are illustrative mechanisms, not requirements - the same loop works on paper with a planner grid and an estimate strip.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to 'solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why' and to 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'; Year 6 place value covers reading and ordering numbers up to 10,000,000 (verbatim statutory wording).
Estimation is essential for judging the reasonableness of calculator/written output; sensible calculator use is a taught competence.
learnerActions: Read a real multi-step problem, e.g. 'A charity had 3,450,000 pounds. In March it spent 1,280,000 pounds and received donations of 2,000,000 pounds. In April its costs were 675,450.75 pounds. How much does it have at the end of April?'
Before computing, model the whole problem with a running-total bar and mark every event as a signed change on the bar.

Build a running estimate first: estimate each step's expected result as well as the final total (about 3.45m - 1.28m + 2m - 0.68m is roughly 3.5m, with intermediate ballparks of about 2.17m then 4.17m along the way).
For each step, choose mental, written, or calculator, carry out the computation, and write one sentence saying WHY that method fits those numbers.
After any calculator or written step, compare that result's order of magnitude against your estimate for that same quantity before accepting it.
Re-read the original question and give the end-of-April balance (3,494,549.25 pounds), interpreted back in context, not an intermediate total.
activities.intendedInsight: A calculator does not free you from thinking: the estimate is what tells you whether to trust the display, and the final answer must answer the question asked, not report a running total.

activities.title: Defend your plan and tool choices
feedback: If justification is vague ('it just seemed right'), press for the specific feature of the numbers that makes the chosen method fit.
If the learner cannot say the expected ballpark, send them back to build the estimate before defending the tool choice.
activities.rationale: The topic explicitly requires justifying which operations and methods to use and why; an in-role defence dialogue exercises that judgement directly. A spoken, responsive defence can surface reasoning that a written answer alone may not reveal.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to 'solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why' and to 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'; Year 6 place value covers reading and ordering numbers up to 10,000,000 (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: After solving a multi-step problem, explain the plan aloud to a partner or character who challenges it.
Answer probing challenges: 'Why calculator there but mental here? Roughly what should this step come to? Does that final answer make sense in the context?'

Justify each method choice by reference to the specific numbers (for example, round or near-round steps often suit mental methods, structured ones written methods, and awkward large or decimal ones a calculator - but the choice is a reasoned judgement, not a fixed rule).
State the ballpark estimate and say how it would have exposed a mis-keyed result about ten times too small or too large, such as 349,454.93 or 34,945,492.50.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify which operations and methods you used - and what the answer should roughly be - is part of competent problem solving, not an optional extra.

activities.title: Sequence, method, and spot the impossible answer
feedback: If an impossible answer is accepted (e.g. one order of magnitude off), prompt the learner to compare it digit-by-place against the estimate.
If the wrong final step is chosen, ask whether the selected figure is an intermediate or the balance the question requests.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, method selection, and identifying an unreasonable result are useful checks of understanding. This format mainly assesses recognition and ordering; it does not require the learner to independently construct the plan and computation, so pair it with the planner activity for production.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to 'solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why' and to 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'; Year 6 place value covers reading and ordering numbers up to 10,000,000 (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Put the steps of a given multi-step problem into the correct order.
For each step, select the best method (mental / written / calculator) and give a reason.
Given an estimate for a step, identify which of several candidate calculator answers is impossible because it is the wrong order of magnitude.
Flag any answer that reports a running total instead of answering the actual question.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking an answer against an estimate lets you reject results that are impossible by magnitude, and the correct final answer is the one that matches the question asked.

activities.title: Walk through an annotated worked example
feedback: Prompt learners to explain in their own words why each annotated method was chosen before moving on, so the walkthrough does not become passive reading.
activities.rationale: A worked example displays the structure of a good solution, the bar-model representation, and the role of the estimate. As a scaffold it does not by itself require the learner to generate their own plan or method choices, so it should precede or support independent problem solving rather than replace it; comparing it to the learner's own attempt can, however, prompt reflection on method choice.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to use visual representations (Recommendation 3, rated STRONG evidence) improves problem solving; the guide frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, 'not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'.
learnerActions: Study a complete multi-step worked example; reveal, for each step, the operation used, the method chosen, and the reasonableness check applied.
Identify where the estimate was built and how it confirmed (or would have caught an error in) each computed result.
Compare the annotated plan to your own attempt and note any step you dropped or any method you would change.
activities.intendedInsight: A well-structured solution makes its operation, method choice, and reasonableness check explicit at every step.

constraints: Numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals (e.g. pounds-and-pence) must appear so the magnitude stakes of a keying/place-value slip are real.
Problems must be modelled from the situation, not solved by word-spotting operations from keywords.
The estimate should be built before or alongside computing, not after, and as a running/per-quantity estimate so it can actually gate each calculator/written result.

Recognition and ordering tasks assess understanding but do not elicit independent construction of the plan and computation; include at least one task where the learner builds and justifies the whole solution.

The worked-example walkthrough is a scaffold: it displays structure but does not by itself require the learner to generate their own plan and method choices; pair it with a task where the learner constructs and justifies the whole solution.
Interactive magnitude-warning gates, running bars, and live checks are optional illustrative mechanisms; the same learning works on paper with a planner grid and estimate strip.
Method fit is a reasoned choice about the numbers, not a fixed rule; do not teach 'always use a calculator' or 'never use a calculator'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit of the source example: 3,450,000 - 1,280,000 = 2,170,000; + 2,000,000 = 4,170,000; - 675,450 = 3,494,550. This matches the stated correct answer 3,494,550 and the ~3.5m estimate. The distractors 349,455 (ten times too small) and 34,945,500 (ten times too large) are correctly characterised as order-of-magnitude errors.
The source claim on estimation and sensible calculator use (Sowder 1992; NCTM) is marked verified:false in the row; treat it as supporting guidance, not established efficacy evidence.

The IES/WWC visual-representations claim is rated STRONG for visual representations and reasoning-about-structure generally; it does not independently establish the efficacy of the worked-example walkthrough format, which is proposed as a scaffold.

The original catalog rationale implied non-interactive formats 'cannot' let the child plan or make method choices; this has been softened to scope-limited statements about what each format exercises, without asserting universal necessity of the interactive format.

probeDeeper: Roughly how much should be left at the end - before you calculate exactly?
Which step did you use the calculator for, and why not that one?
Is the question asking for the balance after March, or at the end of April?
If your calculator showed 349,455, would you believe it - how would you know it was wrong?
assess.correctAnswer: Plans the steps: 3,450,000 - 1,280,000 + 2,000,000 - 675,450 = 3,494,550. Chooses methods per step (the +2,000,000 mental; the 675,450 subtraction written or calculator), estimates (about 3.45m - 1.28m + 2m - 0.68m is roughly 3.5m) and checks the final figure against it. Answers the end-of-April balance, not an intermediate, and reads it back in context.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives a running total (e.g. the post-March figure) as the final answer, or drops the April-costs step
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-read the question; mark all steps on the bar so the last subtraction is not dropped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Final answer equals an intermediate; a step is missing from the working

errorPatterns.pattern: Word-spots operations or applies them in the wrong order rather than modelling the situation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Narrate the story in sequence; each event maps to one signed change on the bar.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds a cost or subtracts a donation; steps out of order

errorPatterns.pattern: Trusts the calculator display without an estimate, so a keying or place-value slip (missed digit, misplaced point) goes unnoticed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the estimate FIRST; teach the display is only trustworthy if it matches the ballpark.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts an answer an order of magnitude off (e.g. 349,455 or 34,945,500) without pause

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-relies on the calculator for steps doable mentally, or grinds by hand an awkward computation a calculator suits - no reasoned method choice
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss method fit step by step; scaffold 'could you do this one in your head?' Do not reteach the arithmetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Keys in +2,000,000, or laboriously hand-computes the pence figure, without justifying

responseLevels.gap: Grabs numbers and operations by keywords; drops steps or reports an intermediate; trusts any result without checking.
responseLevels.full: Models the problem, sequences all steps, chooses and justifies a method per step, estimates and checks the result for reasonableness, and answers the actual question in context; transfers to a differently-structured large-number/decimal problem.
responseLevels.partial: Completes the chain and can use a calculator, but with no reasoned method choice, or stops at a running total, or does not estimate to check; lists steps without modelling.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Read this aloud and watch the child plan, choose methods, and check: 'A charity had 3,450,000 pounds. In March it spent 1,280,000 pounds and received donations of 2,000,000 pounds. In April its costs were 675,450 pounds. How much does it have at the end of April?' Ask which steps, in what order, which method for each and why, and whether the final figure is sensible.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The four steps, mixed magnitudes and a decimal-scale pence figure catch the child who drops a step, offers a running total as the answer, or word-spots operations. Requiring an estimate exposes whether the child would notice an unreasonable (e.g. calculator-mis-keyed) result, and the per-step method choice separates thoughtful tool use from blanket calculator reliance.
