pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2). Add and subtract within 20 using STRATEGIES — making ten (8+6 = 8+2+4 = 14), decomposing to bridge ten (13−4 = 13−3−1 = 9), and using known facts. A high-centrality strategy hub (0.17): bridging through ten is the reasoning that later powers column carrying/borrowing.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1/Y2): represent/use bonds and related facts within 20; Y2 derive and use related facts; bridging-ten strategies are core KS1 mental methods.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.6 add/subtract within 20 using 'making ten… decomposing a number leading to a ten… and relationship between addition and subtraction'; 2.OA.2.
• Operational details — Teach making-ten explicitly on the ten-frame/rekenrek: to add 8+6, fill the first frame to 10 by moving 2 from the 6, leaving 4, so 10+4. For subtraction across ten, decompose to reach ten first (13−4 → 13−3 to 10, then −1). Emphasise ten as a friendly landmark. This is about REASONING to a fact, bridging the gap between counting and full recall (within-20).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): use a ten-frame to make ten when adding a bridging fact (8+6). Tier B (age 6-7): explain a making-ten or decompose-to-ten step for a within-20 fact. Tier C (age 7): choose flexibly between making-ten, near-doubles and known facts, and derive subtractions from additions.
bestPractices: Teach making-ten physically on two ten-frames/a rekenrek: children MOVE counters to complete the first ten, seeing why 8+6 becomes 10+4.
For subtraction bridging ten, model decomposing to land on ten first (13−4 = 13−3−1), so ten is the landmark in both directions.
Frame ten as a 'friendly number' and connect making-ten to the bonds-to-10 facts children already know.
Encourage strategy flexibility — near-doubles, known facts and making-ten — and discuss which is efficient for a given calculation.
Use the empty number line to record bridging jumps (+2 to 10, then +4), linking strategy to a spatial model that scales to larger numbers.
keyRepresentations: Two ten-frames showing one filled to 10 and the extra spilling into the second
Rekenrek for shifting beads to make ten
Empty number line with a jump to 10 then beyond
Part-whole model decomposing the second addend (6 = 2 + 4)
Bead string of 20 partitioned at the ten
commonMisconceptions: Counting on/back in ones across ten instead of using ten as a landmark (slow and error-prone at the boundary).
Splitting the wrong addend or splitting it wrongly when making ten (e.g. taking 4 not 2 from the 6 to fill an 8).
For subtraction, decomposing incorrectly across ten (13−4 done as 13−4 in ones with a boundary error).
Not connecting making-ten to known bonds to 10, so the strategy feels arbitrary.
Applying making-ten rigidly even when a known fact or near-double would be quicker.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2): add and subtract within 20 using strategies — making ten (8+6 = 8+2+4 = 14), decomposing to bridge ten (13−4 = 13−3−1 = 9), and deriving from known facts. The core insight is treating ten as a friendly landmark reached in both directions; this bridging reasoning later underpins column carrying and borrowing. The focus is the method, not just a correct answer, since counting all by ones can reach 14 without showing the intended understanding.

activities.title: Make ten by moving counters on a double ten-frame
feedback: If the leftover is wrong (answer 12 or 16), count exactly how many counters spill past ten and rehearse partitioning the second addend: 6 = 2 + 4, so only 2 cross to the 8.
If a child takes the wrong amount (e.g. 4 from the 6 to fill an 8), ask: how many empty cells does the first frame have? Move exactly that many.
Connect the move to bonds they know: 8 needs 2 to make 10, which is the pair 8+2 they already recognise.
If a child counts on in ones across ten, model the make-ten move on two frames so ten becomes the landmark rather than a boundary counted through.
activities.rationale: Physically completing the first ten and watching the second addend split lets children perform and see the partition-and-recombine, linking the strategy to bonds-to-10 they already know. The number line records the bridging jump in a spatial model that scales to larger numbers.
sourceClaims: Y1/Y2 pupils use and derive number facts within 20; bridging-through-ten mental strategies are core KS1 methods.
1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20 using making ten, decomposing a number leading to a ten, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
Making-ten and decompose-to-ten strategies, taught on ten-frames/rekenreks with the empty number line, build bridging reasoning that underpins later column methods.
learnerActions: Set out 8 counters in the first ten-frame (two cells empty) and 6 in the second to add 8 + 6.
Move 2 counters from the 6 across to fill the first frame to 10, and notice the 6 has broken into 2 and 4.
Read the result as 10 + 4 = 14, and say aloud which part you moved and why.
Record the same move on an empty number line as a jump of +2 to reach 10, then +4 to reach 14.
Repeat with other bridging facts (e.g. 7+5, 9+6), each time completing the first ten first.
activities.intendedInsight: Making ten is a MOVE: reorganising an awkward fact around the friendly ten (8+6 becomes 10+4) shows WHY the strategy works, not just that it gives 14.

activities.title: Bridge down to ten for subtraction
feedback: A common error is subtracting to ten and then ADDING the remainder (13 − 3 = 10, then +1 → 11). Both parts must be subtracted: after reaching 10, take the remaining 1 away, not add it, so 13 − 4 = 9.
If a child answers 11, track the 4 explicitly as 3-then-1 BOTH removed, using number-line jumps backward to and past ten.
If a child subtracts in ones and makes a boundary slip, slow down at ten and say the two jumps separately.
activities.rationale: Modelling subtraction as decompose-to-ten makes ten the landmark in both directions and prevents the frequent boundary error of losing track of how much is left to subtract.
sourceClaims: Y1/Y2 pupils use and derive number facts within 20; bridging-through-ten mental strategies are core KS1 methods.
1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20 using making ten, decomposing a number leading to a ten, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
learnerActions: To work out 13 − 4, start at 13 and first subtract enough to land on 10: 13 − 3 = 10.
Then subtract the rest: the 4 was split into 3 and 1, so take the remaining 1, giving 10 − 1 = 9.
Show both jumps back on a number line — back to 10, then one more past it.
Check you have subtracted the whole amount (3 + 1 = 4), not just part of it.
Try more subtractions that cross ten (12−5, 15−7), each time stepping onto ten first.
activities.intendedInsight: Ten is a landmark in BOTH directions: decomposing the number being subtracted so you land on ten first keeps the calculation accurate across the boundary.

activities.title: Explain and compare strategies aloud
feedback: If a child applies make-ten rigidly where a known fact or near-double is quicker, acknowledge their method then ask whether another way would be faster here.
If the strategy feels arbitrary, link it back to bonds to 10 the child already knows so making ten feels purposeful.
Praise a correct method even when the arithmetic needs a nudge, and separately correct the number slip.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning may elicit and refine a child's bridging method and probe flexibility, and relating additions to subtractions reflects the 1.OA.6 emphasis on the relationship between the two operations.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20 using making ten, decomposing a number leading to a ten, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
learnerActions: Talk through how you worked out 8 + 6, step by step: which number did you split, and what did that make?
Answer probing questions: 'Why did you take 2 across to the 8 — what does that make?' and 'For 13 − 4, why break the 4 into 3 and 1?'
Offer a second method for 8 + 6 (e.g. treat it as a near-double: move 1 from the 8 to the 6 to make the double 7 + 7 = 14, or use 6 + 6 + 2, or a known fact) and say which felt quicker.
Use a known addition fact to derive a subtraction: if 8 + 4 = 12, explain how that gives 12 − 8 = 4.
Describe how a ten-frame shows what is happening in your method.
activities.intendedInsight: Because this is a reasoning strategy, explaining and comparing methods builds flexibility — children learn to choose making-ten, a near-double or a known fact according to the calculation, and to see addition and subtraction as related.

activities.title: Fill the bridging step
feedback: This checks the recorded steps; it does not by itself build the reorganisation insight, so pair it with hands-on making-ten first.
If the blank is wrong, return to moving counters to see exactly how the second number splits.
activities.rationale: Fill-in-the-step items can assess whether a child can carry out and articulate the intermediate bridging step, as a complement to hands-on construction rather than a replacement for it.
learnerActions: Complete the make-ten decomposition: 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + ___ , then give the total.
Complete a subtraction decomposition: 13 − 4 = 13 − 3 − ___ , then give the answer.
Say which number got split and why that amount was chosen.
activities.intendedInsight: Recording the intermediate bridging step makes the strategy's structure explicit and checkable.

constraints: Assess the METHOD, not just the answer: a correct 14 reached by counting all by ones does not demonstrate making-ten. Watch how the child reaches the answer.
Reaching ten first requires splitting the correct number: for 8 + 6 only 2 (not 4) crosses to the 8, matching the first frame's two empty cells.
In subtraction bridging, both parts of the decomposed amount must be SUBTRACTED (13 − 3 then − 1 = 9); subtracting to ten and then adding the remainder gives the wrong answer 11.
Fill-in-the-step and recognition tasks check recorded steps but do not elicit the hands-on reorganisation; use them after children have performed the move with counters.
A static worked example of a bridging split anchors the strategy but does not let a child perform the move on varied facts; treat it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.
Counters, paper ten-frames, bead strings and number lines are all suitable concrete media; an on-screen draggable version is one option, not a requirement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

For 8+6, a near-double route uses 7+7=14 (adjusting from the double of 7); if offering near-doubles to a child, state the double explicitly so the adjustment is clear. 'Near-double' is used loosely here for a balancing step and is not established as superior to making-ten by the cited sources.

The legacy entry asserted a static image 'can only show the finished regrouping' and that '3D adds nothing'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scope-limited notes about what each medium affords.
Two CCSS/NCETM sources are marked unverified in the source row; treat their claims as cited standards, not as evidence that any specific activity above was tested.

The dialogue activity's sourceClaims were trimmed to the CCSS 1.OA.6 claim, which supports the relating-addition-to-subtraction principle; the NCETM ten-frame/number-line claim is retained only on the ten-frame activity it directly describes.

probeDeeper: Why did you take 2 across to the 8 — what does that make?
For 13 − 4, why break the 4 into 3 and 1?
Is there another way you could work out 8 + 6?
How does a ten-frame show what is happening?
assess.correctAnswer: 8 + 6 = 14 via make-ten (8 + 2 = 10, then + 4 → 14); 13 − 4 = 9 via decomposing to ten (13 − 3 = 10, then − 1 → 9). Any valid bridging strategy is fine — the point is a strategy, not counting all.

errorPatterns.pattern: Partitions the wrong amount when bridging — e.g. 8 + 6: takes 2 to make ten but then adds 6 again, or miscombines 8 + 2 + 4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a ten-frame to see exactly how many spill past ten; rehearse partitioning the second addend (6 = 2 + 4).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Make-ten attempted but the leftover is wrong (answer 12 or 16).

errorPatterns.pattern: No bridging — counts on or all by ones; the make-ten strategy is absent.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model make-ten explicitly with two ten-frames; here counting-all is not the target, so make the strategy the focus.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Fingers and no use of a ten landmark.

errorPatterns.pattern: Decomposes subtraction the wrong way — 13 − 4 as 13 − 3 = 10 then + 1 → 11, losing track of how much is left to subtract.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track the 4 as 3-then-1 both subtracted, using number-line jumps back to and past ten.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 13 − 4 answered 11.

responseLevels.gap: Counts all by ones or misbridges so the answer is wrong; no reliable strategy.
responseLevels.full: Applies make-ten and decomposing-through-ten fluently to both addition and subtraction within 20, and explains the steps.
responseLevels.partial: Uses make-ten / decomposition on addition but not subtraction, or needs support to partition correctly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show me how you work out 8 + 6 — talk me through your steps. Now do 13 − 4 and tell me how.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This topic is about the STRATEGY, so watch the method, not just the answer. Making-ten / decomposing-through-ten shows the intended understanding; a correct answer reached by counting all by ones does not demonstrate it. The subtraction reveals whether decomposition is tracked correctly.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y2→Y3, US Grade 2). Counting within 1,000, including skip-counting by 5s, 10s and 100s and understanding what changes as you cross into the hundreds.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in tens from any number' and use of <, >, =; Y3 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100' and 'find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number', with fluent order and place value to 1,000.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; 2.NBT.8 'mentally add/subtract 10 or 100 to a given number 100–900'.
• Operational details: the leap from within-100 to within-1000 is a PLACE-VALUE leap, not just a longer chant — +10 rolls the tens digit, +100 rolls the hundreds digit, and the child must see WHICH digit changes. Skip from non-round starts (e.g. 5s from 315, 100s from 240). The reliable stall is crossing hundred boundaries (190→200, 995→1000) where a digit carries.
• Checkpoint: skip-count aloud and predict the crossing. Tier A (7): count on in 10s and 100s from a round number within 1000 with a hundred-square/number-line prop. Tier B (7–8): skip-count by 5s/10s/100s from any start and state 10-more/100-more without counting. Tier C (8): cross 190→200 and 970→1000 explaining which digit rolls and why.
bestPractices: Frame within-1000 counting as PLACE VALUE in motion: use base-ten materials (hundreds flats, tens rods, unit cubes) so +10 physically adds a rod and +100 adds a flat — the child sees the digit that changes rather than reciting.

Make crossing a hundred boundary the explicit teaching event: pause at 190, ask 'what comes next in 10s?', and show the ten tens rods trading for one hundred flat so the roll from 190→200 is felt, not mysterious.
Skip-count from non-round and 'ragged' starts (5s from 315, 10s from 268, 100s from 240) so the pattern is a rule about which digit moves, not a memorised round-number chant.

Sync three representations of the same skip count — hundred/thousand grid highlights, equal jumps on a number line, and equal groups of counters — so 100s counting is seen as repeated equal groups (the multiplication/place-value bridge).
Separate '10 more' from 'count on ten by ones': ask for 10-more and 100-more instantly and check the child is rolling a digit, not counting 1,2,3… to prove the place-value idea has landed.
keyRepresentations: Scalable number line marked to 1,000 with equal jumps (jumps of 10 and of 100) to show constant step size and boundary crossings
Thousand grid / linked hundred squares where each skip count lights a column or diagonal, exposing the 5s, 10s and 100s patterns
Base-ten blocks (unit cubes, tens rods, hundreds flats) with regrouping — ten rods trade for one flat at the hundred boundary
Place-value columns (H T U) with digit-rollers so a step by 10 or 100 visibly advances one column and carries into the next
commonMisconceptions: Hundred-boundary stall — reaching 190 the child says '191, 192…' or '100-ten', not knowing 200 comes next; the decade/hundred bridge is the classic breakdown point.
'+10 means add a zero' / '+100 means add two zeros' — over-generalised from round numbers, so 268+10 becomes 2680 or 26810.
Treating the count as a longer rote chant and losing track of which digit changes, so skip-counting from a non-round start collapses.
Confusing tens and hundreds steps (counting 240, 250, 260 when asked to skip in 100s) because the difference between which column moves is not yet secure.
Losing the ones digit when skip-counting by 10s or 100s from a ragged start (315→320 instead of 325) because the child re-rounds to a decade.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2→Y3, US Grade 2), skip-counting within 1,000 by 5s, 10s and 100s is a place-value event, not a longer chant: the learner must see WHICH digit rolls when adding 5, 10 or 100, and why a carry happens when crossing a hundred (190→200) or thousand (995→1000) boundary. Core activities drive a live place-value counter from round and ragged starts, with static reference and checking tasks as supports. Non-round starts (5s from 315, 100s from 150/240, 10s from 268) are emphasised so the learner holds the other digits fixed rather than re-rounding to a decade.

activities.title: Place-value skip-count playground (drive the carry)
feedback: If the learner predicts '2680' for 268+10 (the 'add a zero' error), pause the counter and show only the tens column advancing 6→7 to give 278; name that +10 moves one column, it does not append a digit.
If a ragged start collapses to a decade when counting on in 10s (315→320 instead of the correct 325), highlight the fixed ones digit (5) and replay the jump so the learner sees the ones stay put.
At the boundary, if the learner hesitates, show the ten tens-rods snapping into one hundred-flat so the carry is seen rather than recited.

When a '10 more' answer is produced instantly and correctly, confirm by rolling the tens digit (plus the regrouped next digit if a boundary is crossed), reinforcing that this is a place-value move, not counting on by ones.
activities.rationale: The classic stall is at hundred/thousand boundaries and from non-round starts; a learner-driven counter that synchronises grid, number line and place-value columns lets the child predict then see the exact digit that rolls, targeting the 'add a zero' and re-rounding misconceptions directly.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s. 2.NBT.8: mentally add 10 or 100 to, and subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100–900.
Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Set a start number — round (e.g. 240) or ragged (e.g. 315, 268) — and choose a step of +5, +10 or +100.
Before tapping, predict aloud the next number and say which digit you think will change.

Tap the step and watch three linked views move together: a thousand grid lights the landed number, a number line draws one equal jump, and place-value columns (H-T-U, with a Th column that appears when you reach 1000) roll the digit or digits that change.
Stop deliberately at 190 and predict 'what comes next in 10s?', then tap +10 and watch ten tens-rods trade for one hundred-flat while the hundreds digit rolls 1→2 and the tens resets to 0.
Repeat the boundary move by counting in 5s up to 995→1000 and describe, in your own words, which columns carried.

Switch to a '10 more / 100 more instantly' challenge: state the answer without counting on by ones, then tap to check which digit rolled (just one digit unless the step crosses a hundred or thousand boundary, e.g. 195 → 205).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding 10 rolls the tens digit and adding 100 rolls the hundreds digit; if no boundary is crossed, the other digits stay the same. When a hundred/thousand boundary is crossed (e.g. 190 → 200), the next place up also changes because of regrouping (ten of one place trading for one of the next), not a mysterious jump.

activities.title: Hands-on regrouping with base-ten materials
feedback: If the learner counts 150, 250, 350 but drops the 50 to say 100, 200, 300, point to the five tens rods still sitting on the mat and ask what should have stayed the same.
If the learner recites a number but adds the wrong piece, map the spoken digit to the matching column of blocks before continuing.
activities.rationale: Base-ten materials make +10/+100 a concrete regrouping action, so the child can see which digit changes rather than reciting a longer chant; this grounds the live on-screen counter.
sourceClaims: Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Build a start number with hundreds flats, tens rods and unit cubes (e.g. 190 as one flat and nine rods).
To add 10, physically add one tens rod; to add 100, add one hundreds flat — and say which digit changed.
At 190, add the tenth rod, then trade ten rods for one hundreds flat to make 200, and say 'the tens rolled to 0 and the hundreds went up by one'.
Skip-count by 100s from 150 using flats, keeping the five tens and nothing in the ones fixed, to reach 250, 350 … 950.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding 10 or 100 physically adds a rod or a flat, and crossing a boundary is the concrete act of trading ten rods for one flat — making the digit that changes something the learner can handle and see, not just recite.

activities.title: Annotated thousand-square and place-value reference
feedback: If the learner names the wrong column for a step, point back to the lit pattern and the H-T-U labels so the step size maps to a single column.
Use the boundary flap as a reminder that the join between 190 and 200 is a trade, to be practised live with the counter or blocks.
activities.rationale: A static annotated reference is a strong support for recognising patterns and naming columns, but recognition alone does not enact the carry or recompute from a ragged start, so it accompanies rather than replaces the manipulable counter.
learnerActions: Study a thousand grid / linked hundred squares where a 10s count lights one column, a 5s count lights two columns, and a 100s count lights the same position in each hundred square, and name the pattern you see.
Tap a highlighted 100s column to reveal the note 'each step adds one hundred — the hundreds digit changes', and name the H, T, U columns.
Open the flap at the 190→200 join to read how ten tens trade for one hundred.
activities.intendedInsight: The 5s/10s/100s patterns fall in predictable places (columns for 5s and 10s, the same position in each hundred square for 100s), and naming the place-value columns helps the learner say which digit each step advances.

activities.title: Checking and diagnostic skip-count tasks
feedback: Expected: 150, 250 … 950; 480, 485 … 520 crossing 500 correctly; 1000, 990, 980 …; and 620, 720, 820, 920, 1020 crossing the thousand boundary cleanly. (985, __, 1005 fills to 995.)
'10 more than 268' = 278; if a learner offers 2680, that is the 'add a zero' error — show the tens digit rolling 6→7 instead. ('100 more than 613' = 713.)
If the learner snaps 100s-from-150 to 100, 200, 300, name the dropped 50 and re-run keeping tens and ones fixed.

If an error appears precisely at 495→500 or at 1000 while mid-run counting is fine, treat it as a boundary-bridge gap: rehearse just 490, 495, 500, 505 and 980, 990, 1000, 1010 on a number line, naming the regrouping — do not re-drill the whole sequence.
If backward counting breaks only at boundaries, practise short backward runs across each boundary as its own skill; do not assume backward fluency arrives with forward.
activities.rationale: Boundary-crossing and ragged-start items probe the key misconceptions crisply and separate secure three-digit place value from a learner who snaps to pure multiples or re-rounds; placed after the constructive activities they primarily verify the insight, while their feedback can reteach when an error appears.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s. 2.NBT.8: mentally add 10 or 100 to, and subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100–900.
Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Order a set of 100s cards from 240 and fill blanks in sequences that cross a boundary, e.g. 985, __, 1005.
Answer '100 more than 613' and '10 more than 268', writing the single digit that changed.
Count on in 100s from 150 up to 950; count in 5s from 480 up to 520; count back in 10s from 1000; count on in 100s from 620 and say what happens when the count passes 1000 (920 → 1020).
Explain for each: which digit changed and which stayed the same.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means changing only the relevant place and crossing hundred and thousand boundaries cleanly, from non-round starts and in both directions.

activities.title: Count-with-me partner rehearsal (spoken practice)
feedback: If the learner supplies a wrong boundary number, pause and return to a number line or blocks to show the regrouping before resuming the count.
Reward a correct boundary supply by having the learner name the digit that changed.
activities.rationale: Spoken turn-taking rehearses the sequence orally and prompts boundary crossings; it adds oral practice alongside the visual/place-value work rather than replacing the manipulable or concrete activities.
learnerActions: Take turns skip-counting aloud with a counting buddy, alternating each number in a 10s or 100s run.
When the buddy hesitates at 190 in a 10s run, supply the next number (200) and say which digits rolled.
Say each number clearly and, at boundaries, state what carried before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Rehearsing the count aloud, especially at the deliberate hesitation at a boundary, builds oral fluency and the habit of naming the carry.

constraints: The annotated thousand-square and place-value reference is a scaffold: it shows patterns and names columns but does not itself enact the carry or recompute from a ragged start, so pair it with a manipulable counter or base-ten materials.

Checking/diagnostic tasks are primarily for verifying the pattern and catching misconceptions; their feedback can also prompt reteaching, but they are best placed after the constructive activities rather than being the sole means of building the place-value insight.
Spoken partner practice rehearses the sequence orally but does not by itself make the digit-rolling visible; keep it alongside visual/concrete work.

Base-ten cutouts and rods are physical approximations of the ideal place-value idea: use the trade of ten rods for one flat to represent regrouping, and connect the concrete piece to the spoken digit and the written column.
Practise backward counting across boundaries as its own skill rather than assuming it transfers automatically from forward fluency.
When crossing a boundary during a ragged-start count, keep the ones/tens that should stay fixed in view so the learner does not re-round to a decade.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claims a talking character 'adds little the manipulative doesn't do better' and that a 3D scene 'adds spatial overhead with no conceptual payoff'; these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources, so the conversation activity is retained as optional spoken practice and the 3D option is omitted rather than asserting it has no value.

The legacy 'strong' quiz note says it 'verifies rather than builds' the insight; this has been scoped to a placement limit (checking tasks follow constructive work; their feedback can still reteach), not retained as a universal claim that such tasks cannot teach.
One source (CCSS-M 2.NBT) is marked verified:false and the NCETM claim is unverified; confidence should not be upgraded on that basis.

Diagnostic answer sequences and expected errors (150→250…950; 480→520 crossing 500; 620→1020 crossing 1000; blank 995 in 985,__,1005; 2680 as the add-a-zero error; 268+10=278; 613+100=713) were checked for arithmetic consistency and carried through to learner-facing feedback.

The original misconception example '315→320 instead of 325' is only an error when counting on in 10s (315+10=325); 315→320 is correct under a +5 step, so the step is named explicitly in the feedback to avoid ambiguity.

probeDeeper: What digit changes when you count in 100s from 150? What stays the same?
What comes after 995 in 5s?
Count back in 100s from 1000.
What's 100 more than 940?
assess.correctAnswer: 150, 250, …, 950; 480, 485, …, 520 (crossing 500 correctly); 1000, 990, 980…; and 620, 720, 820, 920, 1020 — changing only the relevant place and crossing the thousand boundary cleanly.

errorPatterns.pattern: snaps to pure multiples — counting in 100s from 150 drops the 50 and gives 100, 200, 300
errorPatterns.nextMove: use a place-value chart or bead string so only the hundreds digit ticks while the 50 stays fixed; name what stays and what changes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: loses the tens/ones and recites round hundreds

errorPatterns.pattern: hundred/thousand boundary break — 5s or 10s stall or err when crossing 500 or 1000 (e.g. 495→'400', or can't pass 1000)
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT re-drill the whole sequence — rehearse just the bridges (490, 495, 500, 505; 980, 990, 1000, 1010) on a number line, naming the regrouping
errorPatterns.revealedBy: an error precisely at the boundary while mid-run counting is fine

errorPatterns.pattern: backward collapse over boundaries — counts back in 10s fine until a hundred or the thousand, then errs
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT expect backward to arrive with forward — practise short backward runs across each boundary on a number line as its own skill
errorPatterns.revealedBy: backward errors that appear only at boundaries

responseLevels.gap: Reverts to pure multiples (100, 200…) instead of keeping the other digits; breaks down at hundred/thousand boundaries.
responseLevels.full: Counts within 1000 by 5s/10s/100s forwards and backwards from any start, changing only the relevant place and crossing hundred and thousand boundaries cleanly.
responseLevels.partial: Skip-counts within 1000 from standard starts but falters counting from a non-multiple, or when crossing 500/1000, or backwards.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count on in 100s starting from 150: 150, 250, 350… up to 950. Now count in 5s from 480 up to 520. Then count backwards in 10s from 1000 for a bit. Last, count on by 100s from 620 — what happens at 1000? (Watch counting in 100s from a non-multiple, crossing 500 in 5s, and crossing 1000.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Counting in 100s from 150 (a non-multiple of 100) tests holding tens and ones constant while moving hundreds; the 5s run 480→520 tests crossing a hundred boundary; going through 1000 tests the thousand boundary. A child with three-digit place value handles all; a weaker child snaps 100s-from-150 to 100, 200, 300, mis-crosses 495→500, or stalls at 1000.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — What Ocean Animals Need (ages 5–7): ocean animals need food, shelter, and the right conditions (water, oxygen, suitable temperature) to survive — just like land animals — and different parts of the ocean provide for different animals' needs.
• Standards — UK (DfE): directly supports KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' — most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals; and Y1 basic needs of animals for survival.
• Standards — US (NGSS): K-ESS3-1 (relationships between the needs of organisms and the places they live); 2-LS4-1 (diversity of life in different habitats).
• Operational details: establish the shared list of needs — food, shelter/safety, and the right conditions — and that these are the SAME kinds of needs a familiar land animal has, met in ocean-specific ways (a clownfish shelters in an anemone; a crab hides in rocks; a fish feeds on smaller creatures; animals need the right water temperature and oxygen dissolved in water). Emphasise that DIFFERENT parts of the ocean suit different animals (warm shallow reef vs cold open sea), a first taste of habitat-matching.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~5–6): name what an ocean animal needs (food, a safe place, water it can live in). B (transitional, ~6–7): give an example of how one ocean animal gets food or shelter. C (early formal, ~7): compare an ocean animal's needs to a land animal's and say that different ocean places suit different animals.
bestPractices: Bridge from the familiar: start with what a pet or garden animal needs, then show an ocean animal needs the SAME things met in watery ways — making needs a universal idea.
Make each need concrete with a real animal (clownfish + anemone for shelter; a fish eating smaller creatures for food) rather than listing abstract nouns.
Introduce habitat-matching gently — a warm-reef animal wouldn't do well in the freezing deep — to seed the 'suited to its habitat' idea.
Include 'right conditions' physically: animals need oxygen (they breathe in water) and the right temperature, correcting the idea that only food matters.
keyRepresentations: A needs checklist (food / shelter / right conditions) shown for a land animal beside an ocean animal.
An animal-meets-need pairing: clownfish–anemone (shelter), fish–smaller prey (food), animal–right water (conditions).
A 'which ocean home suits me?' matching of animals to reef / open sea / seabed.
A shelter close-up showing an animal safe in its hiding place.
commonMisconceptions: 'Ocean animals only need water' — they also need food, shelter, and the right conditions, like all animals.
'Fish don't breathe / don't need oxygen' — they take oxygen from the water through gills.
'Any ocean animal can live anywhere in the ocean' — different parts suit different animals (warm reef vs cold deep).
'Ocean animals' needs are completely different from land animals'' — the needs are the same kinds, just met in the water.
'Shelter isn't important underwater' — many animals need hiding places from predators and rough water.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, help children discover that ocean animals need the same basic things as land animals — food, shelter/safety, and the right conditions (oxygen, which fish take from the water through gills while whales, dolphins and sea turtles come up to breathe air, and a suitable temperature) — met in watery ways, and that different parts of the ocean suit different animals. The row's preferred (proposed) approach lets children actively meet an animal's needs and watch a thriving cue respond, with a side-by-side comparison to a familiar land animal and a habitat-matching moment intended to make 'the right conditions' felt rather than recited. This reflects the row's design preference, not an evidenced ranking of media; the sources are unverified.

activities.title: Care for an ocean animal: meet its needs and watch it thrive
feedback: When each need is met, a thriving cue brightens so the child can see cause and effect: 'The clownfish is safe now that it's tucked in the anemone.'
If a warm-reef animal is placed in the very cold deep sea, it falters in the pretend scene: 'This home is too cold for this fish — where could it thrive instead?' then recovers when moved back.
On the comparison panel: 'A rabbit needs food, a safe burrow, and air to breathe — your ocean animal needs the same kinds of things, just found in the water.'
activities.rationale: Needs are intended to become concrete and causal when a child provides them and sees an animal respond, rather than reciting an abstract list. The habitat-matching moment is meant to make 'the right conditions' a felt need and to seed the habitat-suited idea. Bridging to a familiar land animal frames needs as a universal pattern. The thriving cue and drag-to-place are optional live-response mechanisms that make the learning concrete; they are not a required product feature, and their effectiveness is untested.
sourceClaims: Most living things live in habitats to which they are suited, and habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals.
There are relationships between the needs of different organisms and the places they live.
Ocean animals need food, shelter, and suitable conditions (including oxygen taken from water and appropriate temperature), and different ocean regions suit different animals.
learnerActions: Choose a sea creature (e.g. a clownfish or a crab) to look after.
Give it food, offer a hiding place (tuck the clownfish into an anemone, the crab under a rock), and set the water conditions.
Watch a simple thriving/happiness cue brighten as each need is met.
Try a pretend habitat-matching step in the scene: drop a warm-reef fish into the very cold deep sea, watch it flag, then move it back to its warm home and see it perk up.
Compare the ocean animal's needs with a familiar pet or garden animal using a side-by-side needs list (food / shelter / right conditions).
activities.intendedInsight: Ocean animals need the same kinds of things as all animals — food, shelter or other ways to stay safe, and the right conditions — but met in the water; and different parts of the ocean suit different animals because conditions differ.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal reef scene: who is meeting which need?
feedback: On a correct tap: 'Yes — the clownfish hides in the anemone, that's its shelter from predators.'
If a child says an animal needs only water: 'It also needs food and a safe place — can you find where it eats or hides?'
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal scene pairs each abstract need with a concrete animal example, supporting the example-driven content. It is a useful introduction or recap; because the child reveals rather than provides, it does not itself elicit the act of meeting needs, so it works best alongside the care activity.
sourceClaims: Ocean animals need food, shelter, and suitable conditions (including oxygen taken from water and appropriate temperature), and different ocean regions suit different animals.
learnerActions: Explore a reef/sea scene and tap each animal to reveal which need it is meeting (tap the clownfish → 'shelter in the anemone'; tap a feeding fish → 'food from smaller creatures').
Point to an animal that is getting food, one getting shelter, and one in water that suits it.
Say in your own words what each animal needs and how it gets it.
activities.intendedInsight: Each basic need is met by a real animal doing a real thing — shelter, food, and the right conditions are all visible in the scene.

activities.title: Which ocean home suits me? Animal-to-habitat matching
feedback: On a correct match: 'The clownfish belongs on the warm reef with its anemone — that's where it thrives.'
On a mismatch: 'The deep sea is very cold and dark — would a warm-reef fish be comfortable there? Where else could it go?'
activities.rationale: Matching animals to zones makes habitat-suitability explicit and checks whether a child treats the ocean as uniform. It can verify classification and reasoning; for this age the deeper understanding may be better supported by enacting the care activity, so use matching as a complement or check, not the sole activity.
sourceClaims: Most living things live in habitats to which they are suited, and habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals.
There are relationships between the needs of different organisms and the places they live.
learnerActions: Look at several ocean zones (warm shallow reef, open sea, seabed, cold dark deep sea) and a set of animals.
Match each animal to the ocean home where its needs are met.
Explain why a warm-reef animal would not do well in the very cold, dark deep sea.
activities.intendedInsight: Different parts of the ocean provide for different animals; an animal must be in a place where its needs (right temperature, shelter, food) are met.

activities.title: Does the sea just hand it over? Talk it through
feedback: If a child says ocean animals need nothing: 'What does a crab eat? Where does it hide from predators? The sea doesn't hand it over — the animal has to find these.'
If a child denies fish need oxygen: 'Fish take in oxygen from the water through their gills — they do need to breathe, just in a different way.'
When a child maps needs onto a rabbit: 'Yes — food, a safe place, and air to breathe: the same kinds of needs, met in the water.'
activities.rationale: A short spoken discussion can surface and challenge the 'sea provides everything' and 'fish don't breathe' misconceptions through questioning and comparison. At this age such talk supports, but does not by itself provide-and-observe, so it complements rather than replaces the enacted care activity.
sourceClaims: Ocean animals need food, shelter, and suitable conditions (including oxygen taken from water and appropriate temperature), and different ocean regions suit different animals.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt: 'A child says ocean animals don't need anything — the sea gives them everything. Do you agree?'
Name what an ocean animal actually needs to survive.
Pick one animal (e.g. a crab) and say where it gets its food and where it hides — naming one thing it must find for itself.
Compare: does a rabbit need the same kinds of things as a fish? Which does the fish get differently?
activities.intendedInsight: Ocean animals must find and meet their needs; the sea does not automatically provide everything, and their needs match a land animal's, just met in the water (including oxygen, which fish take in through gills).

constraints: Target age is 5–7; keep needs concrete with real animals (clownfish + anemone for shelter, a fish eating smaller creatures for food) rather than listing abstract nouns.
Address 'the right conditions' physically: animals need oxygen (fish breathe it from water through gills) and a suitable temperature — not only food.
Bridge from the familiar: start with what a pet or garden animal needs, then show the ocean animal needs the SAME kinds of things met in watery ways.

A tap-to-reveal scene and a matching task check recognition/classification but do not by themselves elicit the act of providing for an animal; use them alongside the enacted care activity. This is an observable affordance limit, not proof one medium teaches and another cannot.
The thriving cue, drag-to-place, and zone-matching are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete — they are not mandatory and not product-specific.

Common misconceptions to watch: 'ocean animals only need water'; 'fish don't need oxygen'; 'any animal can live anywhere in the ocean'; 'ocean animals' needs are completely different from land animals''; 'shelter isn't important underwater'.
reviewNotes: Independent re-review: the comparative medium claims flagged previously were verified as softened to proposed/may wording in the summary and in activities[0] and activities[2] rationales; no unqualified medium-superiority claim remains, and no new factual, causal, or internal-contradiction errors were found.

No source establishes that one medium outperforms another; efficacy of the enactment, tap-to-reveal, matching, and talk activities remains untested and is stated as proposed.

probeDeeper: 'You said it needs food. WHERE does an ocean animal get its food and its shelter — does the sea just hand it over?'
'A rabbit needs food, a burrow, and air. Does a fish need those same kinds of things? Which does it get differently?' (land-animal comparison)
'Could a warm-water clownfish live in the freezing deep sea? Why not?' (right-conditions counterexample)
'Name one thing a crab needs that it has to find for itself.'
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree — ocean animals need the SAME basic things as land animals: food to eat, a safe place/shelter, and the right conditions (oxygen in the water, the right temperature). The sea doesn't magically hand them everything; they have to find food and shelter, and different parts of the ocean suit different animals. So an ocean animal's needs are much LIKE a rabbit's — just met in the water.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the sea automatically provides everything, so ocean animals have no needs of their own
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pick one animal (a clownfish) and ask: what does it eat? where does it hide from predators? Make each need concrete — the sea doesn't hand it over, the animal must meet it.
errorPatterns.distractor: Ocean animals don't need anything — the sea gives them everything
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says ocean animals need nothing; can't name food/shelter/conditions

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks ocean animals don't need oxygen/air because they live underwater ('only land animals need to breathe')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain fish take in oxygen from the water through gills — they DO need oxygen, just get it differently. All animals need oxygen; the ocean supplies it dissolved in water.
errorPatterns.distractor: Ocean animals don't need to breathe because they live in water
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: denies fish need oxygen; thinks breathing is a land-only need

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks every part of the ocean is the same, so any animal could live anywhere in it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a warm shallow reef with the cold deep sea — different animals live in each because conditions differ. Needs must be MET by the right place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't say different areas suit different animals; misses 'the right conditions'

responseLevels.gap: Says ocean animals need nothing, or that only land animals have needs / need to breathe.
responseLevels.full: Lists food, shelter and the right conditions (including oxygen), explains the animal must find/meet these (the sea doesn't just provide them), AND maps the needs onto a land animal — seeing the shared pattern of what living things need.
responseLevels.partial: Names one or two needs (food, shelter) but treats them as separate facts — can't connect to a land animal's needs, or misses that the animal must MEET its needs and that different places suit different animals.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child says: 'Ocean animals don't really need anything — the sea just gives them everything, so they're not like land animals that need food and a home.' Do you agree? Tell me what an ocean animal actually needs to survive, and whether that's like or unlike a land animal such as a rabbit.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands needs lists food/shelter/conditions AND maps them onto a land animal. A child with the 'sea provides everything' idea says ocean animals need nothing, or can't say they need oxygen/food, treating water life as effortless. The second tier (compare to a rabbit) exposes whether they see the shared pattern of living-thing needs or think sea life is a special case.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7–9; understand that rainforest indigenous peoples hold deep ecological knowledge built over thousands of years — plants as medicine/food/materials, sustainable shifting cultivation, and animal/forest understanding modern science is only starting to appreciate.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (human geography: land use, resources; how people relate to environment) and KS2 Science 'Living things and their habitats' (interdependence); citizenship/respect-for-diversity strand.
• Standards — US: NGSS 3-5-ESS3 (human impacts and sustainable practice) and social-studies strands on indigenous knowledge systems and stewardship.
• Operational details — make the knowledge CONCRETE and expert: specific ethnobotany (a bark used to lower fever, a vine used as a fish-stunning agent, curare/quinine-style examples framed age-appropriately), and shifting cultivation explained as a CYCLE — clear a small plot, farm a few years, move on and let the forest regrow — contrasted with permanent clear-cutting that exhausts the thin soil. Stress two-way respect: indigenous knowledge and modern science can work TOGETHER. Keep present tense; these are living experts.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (7): give two examples of indigenous forest knowledge. Tier B (8): explain what shifting cultivation is and why it harms the forest less than permanent clearing. Tier C (9): describe how indigenous knowledge and modern science can combine to protect rainforests.
bestPractices: Present indigenous peoples as living EXPERTS with sophisticated, tested knowledge — not folklore or luck.
Teach shifting cultivation as a regenerative CYCLE (clear small → farm → move → regrow) explicitly contrasted with permanent clear-cutting on thin soil.
Ground ethnobotany in concrete, verifiable examples (medicinal plants that entered modern medicine) to show the knowledge's real value.
Frame the relationship as two-way: indigenous knowledge and Western science complement each other, not one 'correcting' the other.
Use correct people-names and present tense; avoid romanticising ('noble savage') or dismissing ('primitive') framings.
keyRepresentations: A shifting-cultivation cycle diagram (plot cleared → cropped → fallow → forest regrown) vs a permanent-clearance strip that stays bare.
An ethnobotany 'forest pharmacy' — plants paired with their traditional uses (medicine, food, poison, building).
A two-columns-meet image: traditional knowledge + lab science converging on a shared goal.
A map of forest peoples and the biodiverse territories they steward.
commonMisconceptions: 'Indigenous knowledge is just superstition/stories' — it is detailed, empirical and often centuries ahead of documented science.
'All farming destroys rainforest' — small-scale shifting cultivation can be sustainable; scale and permanence are the problem.
'These peoples lived long ago' — they are contemporary communities managing forests today.
'Modern science knows best' — much rainforest medicine and ecology was first known to indigenous peoples.
'Shifting cultivation = slash-and-burn destruction' — conflating small rotational plots with large permanent burning for cattle/soy.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, build respect-centred understanding that rainforest indigenous peoples are living experts whose deep ecological knowledge — plants as medicine/food/materials, and shifting cultivation that is sustainable when plots are small and rested long enough — has been built and tested over thousands of years, and that modern science continues to learn from it. Make knowledge concrete with specific ethnobotany examples and treat shifting cultivation as a regenerative cycle contrasted with permanent clearance of nutrient-poor rainforest soil.

activities.title: Forest pharmacy: plants and their tested uses
feedback: If a learner calls the knowledge 'just stories' or 'luck', point to the concrete examples, the fish-stunning vine and the fever bark, where modern chemists studied the same plants and confirmed the effect.
If a learner speaks in the past tense ('they used to know'), correct gently to present tense: these are living communities who hold and use this knowledge today.

Reinforce correct answers by naming the two-way link: for these documented plants (the fish-stunning vine and the fever bark) the forest people knew the use first and modern chemists later studied and confirmed it, and more broadly science continues to learn from this knowledge.
activities.rationale: Concrete, verifiable ethnobotany (documented plant uses, such as a fish-stunning vine and a fever bark) counters the 'superstition' misconception and shows the knowledge's real value. An optional tap-to-reveal panel — tap a plant to reveal its use, then a flap adds the beat that scientists later studied the same plant — makes the reveal concrete; this is one way to present it, not a required mechanism. The broader 'science is only now catching up' framing is from the source row and is unverified, so it is qualified rather than stated to learners as certainty.
sourceClaims: Indigenous peoples practise shifting (rotational) cultivation that, at small scale, allows forest regrowth and is less damaging than permanent clearance, and hold extensive ethnobotanical/medicinal plant knowledge
learnerActions: Examine a scene showing several rainforest plants, each paired with a traditional use: a slender vine used to stun fish for easy catching, a bark used to ease fever, a fruit tree providing both food and building wood.

For each plant, state its traditional use in your own words. For the fish-stunning vine and the fever bark, read the added note that chemists later studied the very same plant or a substance from it (the vine's fish-stunning substance and the bark's fever medicine); the fruit tree simply shows food and building wood.
Explain aloud why 'the people of the forest knew this first' shows real expertise rather than luck or guesswork.
Give at least two examples of indigenous forest knowledge from memory.
activities.intendedInsight: Indigenous ecological knowledge is detailed, empirical expertise — and for several documented plants, modern science later studied and confirmed the same effect — not folklore or stories.

activities.title: The shifting-cultivation cycle vs permanent clearance
feedback: If a learner says 'any cutting of trees destroys the forest', contrast scale and permanence: a small plot left to regrow for long enough is a sustainable cycle, unlike large permanent clearing for cattle ranches or soy and palm-oil plantations.
If a learner conflates small rotational plots with large-scale slash-and-burn, separate the two explicitly: the problem is clearing huge areas permanently, not farming a small plot and moving on.
Confirm full answers that name all three ideas: small plot, left to regrow, soil restores.
activities.rationale: Teaching shifting cultivation as a clear cycle (clear small -> farm -> move -> regrow) explicitly contrasted with permanent clear-cutting on nutrient-poor soil addresses the 'all farming destroys rainforest' and 'shifting cultivation = slash-and-burn' misconceptions. An animated-on-tap cycle beside a static bare strip can make the regrowth logic concrete; this is an optional presentation choice.
sourceClaims: Indigenous peoples practise shifting (rotational) cultivation that, at small scale, allows forest regrowth and is less damaging than permanent clearance, and hold extensive ethnobotanical/medicinal plant knowledge
learnerActions: Follow a small clearing through its full cycle: a small plot is opened, cropped for a few years, then left to rest while the forest slowly closes back over it.

Beside it, observe a permanently cleared strip, shown in this illustration as bare and cracked, that never regrows into forest and becomes degraded because the nutrient-poor soil is used up and never rested.
Explain in your own words what shifting cultivation is and why it harms the forest less than permanent clearing (the plot is small, is left to regrow, and the soil restores).
Answer the probe: if a shifting-cultivation patch were never left to regrow, would it still be sustainable? Explain why not.
activities.intendedInsight: Small-scale, rotational clearing left to regrow for long enough is a sustainable cycle; it is large scale, permanence, or rest periods too short for recovery — not any tree-cutting at all — that destroy rainforest.

activities.title: Operate the cycle: a shifting-cultivation simulation
feedback: If a learner expects any small plot to be fine regardless of rotation, show that never leaving it to rest also exhausts the soil.
If a learner expects all clearing to collapse, show that a small, rested plot recovers.
Prompt the learner to connect the simulation result back to why real indigenous practice keeps plots small and rotational.
activities.rationale: An interactive model that links plot size/permanence to soil fertility and regrowth may let the sustainability logic be actively discovered rather than told; this is a proposed, untested design. It covers the farming-cycle half of the topic; the ethnobotany half remains reference knowledge better met by the forest-pharmacy activity.
sourceClaims: Indigenous peoples practise shifting (rotational) cultivation that, at small scale, allows forest regrowth and is less damaging than permanent clearance, and hold extensive ethnobotanical/medicinal plant knowledge
learnerActions: Choose a plot size and how many years before moving on, then watch soil fertility and forest regrowth respond.
Try a small plot farmed for only a few years before moving on and left to rest for a long time, and observe that in the model the soil restores and forest regrows.
Try a large, permanent plot and observe that fertility collapses and the land stays bare.
State the rule you discovered: small + rotational sustains, large + permanent collapses.
activities.intendedInsight: The sustainability of shifting cultivation can be felt as a system: outcomes depend on plot size and whether the land is left to regrow.

activities.title: Learning from the expert: a respectful apprentice dialogue
feedback: If the learner frames the expert as 'primitive' or from 'long ago', redirect: these are living experts with sophisticated, tested knowledge.
If the learner suggests science should 'correct' the knowledge, reframe as two-way: traditional knowledge and science complement each other toward a shared goal.
Affirm follow-up questions that show genuine curiosity and respectful listening.
activities.rationale: In-role dialogue with a respectfully portrayed knowledge-holder may humanise the expertise and let a 7–9 follow curiosity; efficacy is untested. Any such portrayal carries authenticity/representation responsibility and should be co-designed with community voices, positioning the child as apprentice and the character as expert; the most concrete factual knowledge may be more reliably delivered through curated reference material, though efficacy of either medium is untested here. An optional map of forest peoples and a 'knowledge meets science' convergence image situate them as present-day communities, aligning with reporting that indigenous ecological knowledge is increasingly recognised alongside science.
sourceClaims: Indigenous-managed forests show lower deforestation and higher biodiversity; indigenous ecological knowledge increasingly recognised alongside science in conservation
learnerActions: Take the role of a respectful learner asking a knowledge-holder questions such as 'How do you farm without exhausting the soil?' and 'Which plant would you use for a fever?'
Listen to the expert's spoken answers and ask a follow-up question driven by your own curiosity.
Afterwards, retell two things the expert taught you, using present tense.
Describe how this knowledge and modern science could work together to protect the forest.

Optionally, look at a map of forest peoples and the biodiverse territories they steward, and at an image showing traditional knowledge and lab science converging on a shared goal, to see that these are contemporary communities whose expertise works alongside science today.
activities.intendedInsight: Indigenous peoples are contemporary experts; a learner can follow curiosity to understand their expertise and how it complements modern science.

constraints: Present indigenous peoples as living experts with sophisticated, tested knowledge — never as folklore, luck, or 'primitive'; and never romanticised as 'noble savage'.
Use correct people-names and present tense throughout; these are contemporary communities managing forests today.
Frame the relationship between indigenous knowledge and Western science as two-way complementarity, not one 'correcting' the other.
Keep ethnobotany examples concrete and age-appropriate (e.g. a bark for fever, a vine that stuns fish); frame curare/quinine-style examples carefully for 7–9.

Any voiced or dramatised portrayal of a living people carries representation responsibility and should be co-designed with community voices; it is a scaffold for engagement, not a substitute for accurate curated knowledge.

A scored quiz can check concept recall (define the cycle; give two knowledge examples) but risks trivialising a respect-centred topic; keep it a light companion and keep questions about concepts, not cultural 'trivia'. Recognition-only responses do not elicit the learner's own explanation of why the cycle is sustainable.
The simulation covers only the farming-cycle half of the topic; it does not operate the ethnobotany knowledge, which remains reference material.
The 'science is only now catching up' framing is unverified source row framing; present only the specific documented medicinal examples as confirmed, and keep the broader claim qualified.
Do not assert that any one medium teaches this topic better; the sources do not establish comparative efficacy. Describe medium choices as design judgements, not proven requirements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both listed sources are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Both cited claims are marked unverified in the source row; treat 'modern science is only now catching up' and 'indigenous-managed forests show lower deforestation' as framing to be checked against the cited organisations, not as established facts delivered to learners as certainties.

The original recommendation leaned on a single preferred tap-to-reveal image; the simulation and dialogue alternatives were preserved here because they serve distinct pedagogical purposes (felt system-logic; humanised expertise).

Avoid asserting comparative efficacy or necessity of any one medium; the sources do not establish which artefact best teaches this topic. The dialogue rationale's curated-reference comparison is a qualified design judgement, not an evidenced claim.

Activity 3's source claim is the shifting-cultivation claim rather than the WWF deforestation/biodiversity claim, because the former directly supports the simulation's soil-fertility/regrowth mechanism; this was an editorial sourceClaim decision, not fresh source verification.

The 'map of forest peoples and the biodiverse territories they steward' and the 'traditional knowledge + lab science converging' representations from the original row were restored as optional elements in the dialogue activity.

probeDeeper: Why does leaving the patch to regrow make shifting cultivation different from clearing land for cattle?
Give one example of forest knowledge that scientists have learned from indigenous peoples.
How could indigenous knowledge and modern science work together to protect the forest?
What if a shifting-cultivation patch were never left to regrow — would it still be sustainable?
assess.correctAnswer: No — it isn't the same. In shifting cultivation the patch is small and is left to regrow, so the forest recovers and the soil restores; it's a sustainable cycle developed over thousands of years. Destructive deforestation clears huge areas permanently (for cattle, soy, palm, logging) and never lets them grow back. Indigenous ecological knowledge — which plants heal, how to farm without exhausting the forest — is real expertise that modern science is still learning from.

errorPatterns.pattern: all forest clearing is the same destruction — 'they cut trees, so they're destroying it too'
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast scale and permanence; a small plot left to regrow is a sustainable cycle
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, it's the same — any cutting of trees destroys the forest
errorPatterns.revealedBy: equates small regrowing plots with permanent large-scale clearing

errorPatterns.pattern: indigenous knowledge is just folklore, not real knowledge — 'they don't really know science'
errorPatterns.nextMove: give concrete examples (medicinal plants, forest ecology) that scientists now study and confirm
errorPatterns.revealedBy: dismisses their knowledge as stories or luck

errorPatterns.pattern: indigenous peoples are of the past — 'they used to farm like that long ago'
errorPatterns.nextMove: present tense; these are living communities practising this knowledge now
errorPatterns.revealedBy: speaks only in the past tense

responseLevels.gap: Says shifting cultivation is the same as destructive deforestation, or dismisses indigenous knowledge.
responseLevels.full: Explains shifting cultivation as small, cyclic and regrowing (sustainable) versus large permanent clearing, gives examples of indigenous ecological knowledge as real expertise, and describes it working with modern science.
responseLevels.partial: Senses a difference or gives one example of indigenous knowledge, but can't explain the scale/regrowth distinction or why it's sustainable.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Indigenous farmers clear a small patch of forest, grow food on it for a few years, then move on and let the forest grow back — this is called shifting cultivation. Is that the same as the deforestation that destroys the rainforest? Tell me yes or no, and then tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who lumps all forest clearing together says shifting cultivation is 'just deforestation'; the concept child distinguishes small+regrowing+cyclic from large+permanent, and values indigenous knowledge as expertise. The reason-tier forces the regrowth/scale distinction.
