pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Measuring Earthquake Strength — scientists use a seismometer to detect and record ground shaking; earthquakes release energy that travels outward as waves; and a magnitude scale gives a number for an earthquake's strength.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement):** In England this is KS2 **Geography** enrichment (earthquakes), not KS2 science. Wave/energy formalism and measurement are DfE **KS3** (physics waves; Geography hazards). Frame as 'how do we measure something we can't see?'.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No dedicated elementary PE; earthquakes as measured hazards connect to **4-ESS3-2** (monitoring/reducing impacts) and the wave/energy detail to **MS-PS4** and **MS-ESS**. Reading a magnitude number is a data-interpretation (SEP) skill. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisites 'Why Earthquakes Happen' and 'Ring of Fire'. Three linked ideas: a seismometer works because a heavy mass stays still (inertia) while the ground and frame move under it, tracing a record; the earthquake's energy spreads OUT as waves that shake the seismometer; and magnitude summarises strength as a single number — with the crucial subtlety that each step up the scale is a BIG jump (roughly ten times the shaking amplitude, far more energy), so a magnitude 6 is not just '20% more' than a 5. Keep the log idea intuitive, not computational.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (early-formal; instrument model + a non-linear scale). Children grasp 'a machine records shaking' but often read magnitude as a linear ruler and confuse the CAUSE's strength with the shaking FELT at a place. Success = explain what a seismometer records, describe energy travelling as waves, and read a magnitude number as strength (bigger number = much stronger).
bestPractices: Make the seismometer's principle concrete via inertia: a suspended heavy mass with a pen stays still while the ground/paper moves under it, drawing the wiggly trace — model it physically (a weight on a spring over a moving strip).
Show the record (seismogram) as the DATA: bigger wiggles = stronger shaking; teach children to read amplitude qualitatively.
Confront the linear-scale misconception gently: each whole number up the magnitude scale means roughly ten times the shaking and much more energy — use a visual step-jump, not arithmetic.
Separate magnitude (the earthquake's size at the source, one number) from intensity (how strongly it's felt at a given place, which varies with distance) — a common conflation.
Link to prior topics: the waves are the energy released when rocks snapped (Why Earthquakes Happen), spreading out from the source and fading with distance.
keyRepresentations: Suspended-mass seismometer model (inertia: mass stays still, ground moves, pen traces)
Seismogram trace — amplitude of wiggles as a read-out of shaking strength
A magnitude 'staircase' where each step is a ~10× jump in shaking (non-linear)
Ripples spreading and shrinking from the source — waves fading with distance
commonMisconceptions: The magnitude scale is linear (a 6 is only a bit more than a 5) — in fact each step is ~10× the shaking amplitude and far more energy.
A seismometer 'feels' the quake like a person (it works by a heavy mass staying still by inertia while the frame/ground moves).
Magnitude and how strongly you FEEL it are the same (magnitude is the source size; felt intensity depends on distance and ground).
Earthquake energy travels in straight lines to one place (it spreads outward as waves in all directions, fading with distance).
Bigger wiggles on the trace always mean a bigger earthquake regardless of distance (distance matters; scientists account for it).

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, build understanding of how scientists measure earthquakes: a seismometer records ground shaking using a heavy mass that stays nearly still by inertia while the frame and paper move under it; earthquake energy spreads outward as waves that fade with distance; and a magnitude scale gives one number for an earthquake's strength, where each whole step up is a BIG jump: the recorded waves are roughly ten times bigger when compared at the same distance (not a linear notch), and much more energy is released. Keep the log idea intuitive, never computational. Core activity: a shakeable seismometer model with a live trace, a magnitude dial that visibly multiplies the wiggles, and a distance control that separates magnitude (the quake's true size) from how strongly a place feels it. Reference diagrams, quiz-based consolidation, and an optional 3D view are preserved as distinct supports.

activities.title: Shake a seismometer and read the trace
feedback: If a learner thinks the machine senses or feels the shaking: point out the mass barely moves — it is the frame and paper that move under it, and that difference is what draws the line.
If they read any wiggle as 'an earthquake' regardless of size: compare a gentle and a hard shake and have them rank the traces by wiggle size.
Reinforce: bigger wiggles (bigger amplitude) = stronger shaking at that spot.
activities.rationale: Enacting the inertia principle and watching the live trace respond makes concrete why a still mass records motion, directly confronting the 'the machine feels it' misconception. A physical weight-on-a-spring over a moving strip is a welcome concrete realisation; a screen model offers a live amplitude read-out.
sourceClaims: A seismometer records ground motion using a suspended mass that remains nearly still by inertia while the frame moves with the ground; earthquake energy travels outward as seismic waves.
learnerActions: Shake a model ground (physically with a weight hanging on a spring over a moving paper strip, or with an on-screen shake control) with quick, sharp shakes and watch the suspended heavy mass lag behind and stay nearly still while the frame and paper move under it (in a homemade model it may still swing or bob a little, and slow shakes can carry it along).
Watch the attached pen draw a live wiggly trace (a seismogram) and say in your own words why a mass that stays still can record motion: the GROUND and paper move, not the mass — that is inertia.
Shake harder and gentler and describe how the size (amplitude) of the wiggles changes: bigger wiggles mean stronger shaking.
Point to the parts and label them: the heavy mass (stays nearly still), the frame (moves with the ground), the pen, and the paper record.
activities.intendedInsight: A seismometer does not 'feel' a quake like a person; it works because a heavy suspended mass stays nearly still by inertia while everything else moves under it, tracing a record whose wiggle size shows how strong the shaking is.

activities.title: The magnitude staircase: each step is a big jump
feedback: If a learner expects a small change from 5 to 6: replay the step and have them compare the before/after wiggle heights side by side.
If they try to do arithmetic (e.g. '20% more'): steer back to the visual — count how many times taller the new wiggles are, not the difference in numbers.
Confirm: one step up on the scale is a BIG jump, with waves roughly ten times bigger on the trace at the same distance.
activities.rationale: Manipulating the dial and seeing the trace and energy meter leap gives a visceral, non-computational sense of the logarithmic scale, gently confronting the linear-ruler misconception. The energy meter and amplitude leap are optional illustrative mechanisms that make the jump vivid.
sourceClaims: The moment magnitude scale is logarithmic: each whole-number step corresponds to ~10× greater shaking amplitude and roughly 32× more energy release.
learnerActions: Before changing anything, predict: 'How much bigger is the shaking from a magnitude 6 than a magnitude 5 — a little, or a lot?'

Keeping the seismometer at the same distance, turn a magnitude dial from 5 up to 6 (or use a visual step-staircase) and watch the trace amplitude leap roughly ten times bigger, with a released-energy meter jumping far more.
Step up again (6 to 7) and describe the pattern in words: each whole number means waves about ten times bigger on the trace (at the same distance), not 'one more'.
State the correction to a friend who says 'a 7 is just one more than a 6': no — measured at the same distance, a 7 makes waves about ten times bigger than a 6, and releases far more energy.
activities.intendedInsight: The magnitude scale is not like ordinary counting: each whole-number step means roughly ten times greater recorded wave amplitude when compared at the same distance (and much more energy released), so a magnitude 7 is vastly stronger than a 6.

activities.title: Same quake, different places: magnitude vs felt intensity
feedback: If a learner says magnitude is bigger near the epicentre and smaller far away: separate the two ideas — the magnitude number stays the same; it is the shaking you FEEL that fades with distance.
If they assume a bigger magnitude always means more damage: note that damage also depends on distance, depth, ground type and how buildings are built — not magnitude alone.
Reinforce: one earthquake = one magnitude everywhere; the felt intensity varies from place to place.
activities.rationale: Varying distance while magnitude stays fixed makes the magnitude-vs-intensity distinction tangible and links to the prior 'Why Earthquakes Happen' idea of energy released by snapping rocks. Reading smaller wiggles farther away also guards against 'bigger wiggles always mean a bigger quake'.
sourceClaims: A seismometer records ground motion using a suspended mass that remains nearly still by inertia while the frame moves with the ground; earthquake energy travels outward as seismic waves.
learnerActions: With one fixed earthquake set, drag a distance control (or move a marker) to place a seismometer nearer and farther from the source, and watch the trace get smaller with distance.
Explain why people nearby feel the quake strongly while people far away barely notice it: the waves spread outward and fade with distance.
Answer: does moving farther away change the earthquake's MAGNITUDE, or only how strongly you FEEL it? (It changes only the felt intensity; magnitude is one fixed number for the quake.)
Connect to what you already know: the waves are the energy released when rocks snapped, spreading out in all directions from the source and shrinking as they go.
activities.intendedInsight: Magnitude is a single fixed number describing the earthquake's size at its source (from the energy released), while felt intensity depends on distance (and ground and buildings) and fades the farther away you are.

activities.title: Reference: label the seismometer and the seismogram
feedback: If a part is mislabelled: re-reveal its role (e.g. the mass stays still; the frame moves).
If a learner reads magnitude off a trace as if it were linear: direct them to the ~10× reveal.
activities.rationale: A labelled diagram and annotated seismogram are strong reference material that explain the parts clearly, but a static reference cannot enact the live trace or the step-jump; use it alongside the manipulable model, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: A seismometer records ground motion using a suspended mass that remains nearly still by inertia while the frame moves with the ground; earthquake energy travels outward as seismic waves.
learnerActions: Study a labelled seismometer cutaway and tap or point to each part: the suspended mass (reveal 'stays still — inertia'), the frame, the pen, the paper.
Examine an annotated seismogram and mark where the wiggles are biggest (largest amplitude = strongest shaking).
Open a 'Is a 6 just a bit more than a 5?' flap or note and read the ~10× reveal in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming the parts of a seismometer and reading amplitude on a seismogram gives a clear reference model that supports, but does not replace, the hands-on trace-building.

activities.title: Check and consolidate
feedback: Full response: explains each step means about ten times bigger waves (compared at the same distance) AND that magnitude is one fixed number while felt intensity fades with distance.
Partial: gets one idea (e.g. the 7 is much bigger) but still confuses magnitude with felt intensity, or vice versa — reteach the missing half.
Gap: treats magnitude as linear and thinks it changes with location — return to the staircase and distance activities.
activities.rationale: The two-part diagnostic is discriminating because it targets two independent traps at once (linear scale, and magnitude-vs-intensity); a learner holding either misconception gets one part wrong. These tasks consolidate and assess rather than first reveal the concepts.
sourceClaims: The moment magnitude scale is logarithmic: each whole-number step corresponds to ~10× greater shaking amplitude and roughly 32× more energy release.
learnerActions: Order a set of seismograms from smallest to largest amplitude (weakest to strongest shaking).
Answer: 'How much bigger is the shaking from a magnitude 6 than a magnitude 5?' and justify with the step-jump idea.

Respond to the two-part prompt: 'A friend says a magnitude 7 is just a little bit (about one) stronger than a 6 — is that right? And does the same earthquake have the same magnitude whether you are on top of it or far away? Explain.'
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who has grasped the ideas can read traces by amplitude, state that each step is about ten times stronger, and separate the fixed magnitude from the distance-dependent felt intensity.

constraints: Keep the logarithmic idea intuitive and visual (step-jumps, leaping wiggles), not arithmetic — these learners should feel 'much bigger', not compute 10× or 32×.
Prerequisites: 'Why Earthquakes Happen' and 'Ring of Fire'. The waves are the energy released when rocks snapped.

Standards placement is mixed: in England this is KS2 Geography enrichment, with wave/energy formalism and measurement being KS3; in the US it connects to NGSS 4-ESS3-2 (monitoring/reducing hazards) with wave/energy detail at middle school (MS-PS4 / MS-ESS). Reading a magnitude number is a data-interpretation skill. Do not teach the formal wave/energy equations at this age.

A labelled diagram or seismogram is a reference scaffold: it explains parts and lets learners read amplitude, but it cannot enact the live trace or the step-jump; pair it with a manipulable or physical model for the dynamic insight.
Recognition/ordering and multiple-choice tasks consolidate and assess but do not by themselves elicit independent explanation; also ask learners to explain in their own words.
The energy meter, magnitude dial, distance slider and tap-to-reveal flaps are optional illustrative mechanisms to make the mechanism concrete — not mandatory, and not product-specific requirements.
Optional extension: a 3D seismometer the child can shake and view from any angle may show the mass-and-frame motion in space, but the principle reads clearly in 2D — this is polish, not required.
Avoid implying bigger wiggles always mean a bigger earthquake regardless of distance: distance (and depth, ground, building quality) matter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row (USGS seismometer/inertia claim and the USGS logarithmic-scale claim); the ~10×-amplitude and ~32×-energy figures are presented as claims carried from the source, not independently re-checked here.

The source states the moment magnitude scale is logarithmic with ~32× more energy per step; the learner-facing material deliberately keeps only the intuitive '~10× shaking, much more energy' framing to avoid computation at this age — the 32× figure is retained in a consolidation sourceClaim but not taught as arithmetic.

The original row's artefact-fit notes asserted that a static image 'can't enact' the insight and a quiz 'tests rather than reveals'; these have been softened to scope-limited affordance statements rather than universal claims that only one medium can teach.
The physical weight-on-a-spring model and card/paper strip are approximations of an idealised seismometer; treat them as models of the real instrument.

probeDeeper: About how much bigger is the shaking in a magnitude 7 than a magnitude 6 — a bit, or a lot?
If one earthquake happens, why might people nearby feel it strongly but people far away barely notice?
Does moving further from an earthquake change its magnitude, or just how much you feel it?
What does a seismometer actually record, and how does that give a magnitude?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the scale isn't like ordinary counting. Each step up is about TEN times bigger shaking (and much more energy), so a magnitude 7 is vastly stronger than a 6, not 'one more'. And magnitude is a single number for the earthquake itself (from the energy released where the rocks broke) — it doesn't change with where you stand. What changes with distance is how strongly you FEEL it (the intensity), which fades the further away you are.

errorPatterns.pattern: The magnitude scale is like normal counting — a 7 is just one more than a 6
errorPatterns.nextMove: Each step is about 10x the shaking; show the jump in wiggle size on a seismogram.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — a 7 is just a little bit (about one) stronger than a 6.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the steps as equal / linear.

errorPatterns.pattern: The same earthquake has different magnitudes depending on where you are
errorPatterns.nextMove: Magnitude is one fixed number for the quake; it's the felt INTENSITY that fades with distance.
errorPatterns.distractor: The magnitude is bigger if you're near it and smaller if you're far away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the magnitude is bigger near the epicentre and smaller far away.

errorPatterns.pattern: A bigger magnitude number always means more damage, no matter what
errorPatterns.nextMove: Damage also depends on distance, depth and how buildings are built — not magnitude alone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ignores depth, distance, ground and building quality.

responseLevels.gap: Treats magnitude as linear and thinks it changes with location.
responseLevels.full: Explains each magnitude step is about ten times bigger shaking, and that magnitude is a single fixed number for the quake (from energy released) while the felt intensity fades with distance — read from a seismometer.
responseLevels.partial: Gets one idea (e.g. that a 7 is much bigger) but still confuses magnitude with felt intensity, or vice versa.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A magnitude 7 earthquake and a magnitude 6 earthquake — a friend says 'the 7 is just a little bit stronger, about one more'. Is that right? And does the same earthquake have the same magnitude whether you're right on top of it or far away? Explain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two independent traps: treating the scale as linear, and confusing the fixed magnitude with felt intensity. Asking both forces the ~10x-per-step idea AND the magnitude-vs-intensity split; a child holding either misconception gets one part wrong.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Read and write Roman numerals to 100 (I, V, X, L, C and combinations, incl. subtractive pairs like IV, IX, XL) and convert to/from Hindu-Arabic. The deeper aim: appreciate BY CONTRAST that our system has place value and a zero, which Roman numerals lack — illuminating why place value is powerful.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): not a CCSS-M topic; taught in some US curricula as enrichment/history of number.
• Operational details — Teach the symbol values and the additive rule (XVII = 10+5+1+1), then the subtractive rule (IV = 5−1, IX, XL, XC) as the tricky exception. Convert both directions. Crucially, run the CONTRAST explicitly: try 'writing' large or zero quantities in Roman and feel the absence of place value and a placeholder — making our base-ten system's efficiency vivid.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): reads/writes additive numerals (XVII, LX). Tier B (age 8-9, secure): handles subtractive pairs (XLIV = 44) both directions. Tier C (age 9, extending): explains why Roman has no zero/place value and why that makes calculation harder.
bestPractices: Teach symbol values, then the additive rule, then subtractive pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC) as the key exception.
Practise conversion in both directions with real artefacts (clocks, dates, chapter numbers).
Run the explicit contrast: attempt a large number or 'zero' in Roman to FEEL the missing place value and placeholder.
Use the contrast to deepen appreciation of base-ten (position carries value; zero holds a place).
Watch the subtractive-notation errors (IIII vs IV, or invalid forms like IL).
keyRepresentations: Roman symbol→value reference (I,V,X,L,C)
Additive decomposition (XVII = 10+5+1+1) vs subtractive (IX = 10−1)
Side-by-side Roman | Hindu-Arabic conversion chart
Real artefacts: clock faces, monument dates, book chapters
Place-value chart as the contrast (what Roman lacks)
commonMisconceptions: Pure additive thinking, writing 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII instead of IV/IX.
Inventing invalid subtractive forms (IL for 49 instead of XLIX).
Misordering symbols or ignoring the subtractive-position rule.
Thinking Roman numerals have a zero or place value.
Reading a subtractive pair additively (IX as 11).

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: read and write Roman numerals to 100 (I, V, X, L, C and their combinations, including subtractive pairs like IV, IX, XL, XC) and convert both ways to Hindu-Arabic numbers. The deeper aim is to appreciate BY CONTRAST that our base-ten system carries value by position and uses zero as a placeholder, which Roman numerals lack — making vivid why place value is powerful. Teach symbol values, then the additive rule (XVII = 10+5+1+1), then the subtractive rule (IV = 5-1) as the tricky exception, and run the contrast explicitly by trying to write numbers that need many repeated symbols, a very large number, and zero in Roman.

activities.title: Build-a-numeral bench with a contrast challenge
feedback: If IIII or VIIII is built, show the standard subtractive fix (IV = 5-1, IX = 10-1) and explain that a smaller symbol placed before a larger one in one of the allowed pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC) means subtract.
If an invalid form like IL is built for 49, show the valid XLIX and explain which subtractive pairs are allowed (IV, IX, XL, XC).

During the contrast challenge, place the Roman form beside the tidy base-ten numeral and name the real limits: unwieldy strings of repeated symbols (long for 88, far longer for a number like 3,000 within the taught set, with conventional large-number symbols like M lying beyond the taught set), and genuinely no symbol at all to put where our zero sits.
activities.rationale: Building and converting numerals by action with immediate correction surfaces the subtractive exception at the moment of error, and staging the 'write a long numeral / write zero' challenge lets the learner feel the absence of place value and a placeholder rather than just be told about it. A live value display and invalid-form flagging make the additive-versus-subtractive mechanism concrete; these are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
Contrasting Roman numerals with base-ten deepens appreciation of place value and the placeholder role of zero.
learnerActions: Place or drag symbol tiles (I, V, X, L, C) into a row and read the value aloud as you build, e.g. XVII = 10+5+1+1 = 17.
When you write 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII, notice it is flagged and rewrite it the valid subtractive way (IV = 5-1, IX = 10-1).
Convert both directions: given 44, build XLIV; given XLIV, read it as 40 + 4.

Take the contrast challenge: write 88 (LXXXVIII) and notice how many repeated symbols it needs; then try a very large number like 3,000 and see how unwieldy it becomes — within the taught symbols you would need a huge string of C's, and the usual Roman form MMM uses M, a symbol beyond those you are taught; then try to write zero and find there is NO symbol at all — each shown beside the compact base-ten numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Roman numerals combine fixed symbol values by adding (and sometimes subtracting the smaller-before-larger pair); because they have no place value and no zero placeholder, numbers with many repeats become unwieldy, very large numbers become enormous strings or need symbols beyond the basic set, and zero cannot be written at all — which is exactly why position-carries-value and a placeholder zero are powerful inventions.

activities.title: Talk to a Roman accountant about why the system changed
feedback: If the learner thinks the Roman system just needs a zero symbol added, point out that position must also carry value for zero to do its placeholder job.
Prompt the learner to connect the accountant's difficulty adding large numbers to the missing place value, not just unfamiliar symbols.
activities.rationale: A responsive dialogue may suit the history-of-number objective because the 'why did the system change?' story invites questioning and discussion; recognition tasks alone do not require the learner to articulate the reason. This is a proposed affordance rather than established superiority over other media, and it complements the building activity by foregrounding the reason behind the contrast.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
Contrasting Roman numerals with base-ten deepens appreciation of place value and the placeholder role of zero.
learnerActions: In role, interview a Roman merchant or scholar about how they wrote numbers and did sums.
Ask them to add two large numbers using only Roman numerals and notice where it gets hard.
Probe: why was there no way to write zero, and why did the world later adopt place value and zero?
Summarise in your own words what base-ten gives us that Roman numerals do not.
activities.intendedInsight: The history-of-number aim — that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value — can become meaningful through an unscripted 'why is this so hard?' exchange that carries the contrast the curriculum emphasises.

activities.title: Consolidate conversion with real artefacts and validity checks
feedback: If XLIV is read additively as 66, show that a smaller symbol before a larger one in an allowed pair (IV, IX, XL, XC) means subtract: XL = 50-10 = 40, IV = 5-1 = 4, so XLIV = 44.

If the learner says the first symbol 'is in the tens place', contrast directly: in 44 position sets value, but in XLIV each symbol keeps its own value and we add or subtract — Roman has no place value and no zero.
Reinforce the standard subtractive forms (IV, IX, XL, XC), reject invalid ones like IL, and treat IIII as a non-standard clock-face variant rather than the standard way to write 4.
activities.rationale: Conversion in both directions, validity-of-form checks and real artefacts anchor the skill in genuine contexts. Recognition and matching tasks are useful for consolidation and checking but do not by themselves require the learner to construct a full explanation, so pair them with the spoken 'how do the two 4s differ?' prompt.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
learnerActions: Read Roman numerals on real artefacts — clock faces, monument or building dates, book chapter numbers — and write their Hindu-Arabic values (note that many clocks show 4 as IIII, a traditional variant; the standard written form is IV).
Write given numbers (e.g. 44, 49, 88) in Roman numerals, choosing valid subtractive forms.
Decide which of several forms is valid for a number like 49 (XLIX, not IL) and explain why.
Explain aloud how the two 4s in 44 differ (40 and 4 by position) and why XLIV instead uses subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion and recognising valid versus invalid forms consolidate the reading/writing skill, while explaining the two 4s in 44 reinforces the place-value contrast.

activities.title: Reference chart and annotated clock face
feedback: When a learner uncovers a numeral's make-up, confirm whether it is additive (VII = 5+1+1) or subtractive (IX = 10-1).
Use the adjacent place-value chart to point out there is no column or symbol in Roman that behaves like our zero placeholder.
activities.rationale: A fixed chart or annotated image is a valuable reference and can teach symbol values, though it cannot itself be manipulated to compute values or stage the contrast — so it supports rather than replaces the building and dialogue activities.
learnerActions: Keep a symbol-to-value reference to hand (I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100).
Tap or point to each clock numeral to reveal its value and whether it is built additively or subtractively.
Use a side-by-side Roman | Hindu-Arabic chart to check your conversions, and a place-value chart alongside to see what Roman lacks.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference supports recall of symbol values and makes the additive/subtractive make-up of familiar numerals (like clock numbers) explicit.

constraints: The deeper objective is conceptual appreciation of place value and zero by contrast, not just symbol decoding; the contrast must be run explicitly (try to write a long numeral, a very large number, and zero in Roman).

Recognition and matching tasks consolidate and check the skill but do not by themselves elicit an independent spoken or written explanation of why our system differs; include a construct-an-explanation prompt.
A static chart or annotated image teaches symbol values and make-up but cannot be manipulated to compute values live or stage the balloon/zero contrast; treat it as a reference scaffold.

Valid subtractive forms are IV, IX, XL, XC; when writing, treat IIII and VIIII as non-standard (use IV and IX), noting that IIII is a traditional variant still seen on many clock faces, and reject invalid forms such as IL (for 49, use XLIX).
Roman numerals genuinely have no zero symbol and no positional place value — present this as the real system contrast, not as a claim about any particular teaching medium being uniquely necessary.

This topic teaches symbols I to C only; large numbers (e.g. 3,000) should be used to show how numerals become unwieldy within the taught set and that conventional large-number symbols such as M lie beyond those taught — not presented as part of the required symbol set, and not framed as literally 'running out' of symbols.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and logic: XVII = 10+5+1+1 = 17 (correct); XL = 50-10 = 40 and IV = 5-1 = 4, so XLIV = 44 (correct); LXXXVIII = 88 (correct); XLIX = 49 is the valid form, IL is invalid. The legacy additive misreading 'XLIV = 66' is retained only as an error pattern to correct, never as a valid answer.

The row's contrast example '3,000' is conventionally MMM (uses M, outside the taught I–C range); within the taught set it would require roughly thirty C's, i.e. an unwieldy ballooning string. It is therefore treated as a ballooning/beyond-taught illustration, NOT as a case of 'running out of symbols'. The only genuine 'no symbol at all' case is zero.

Two cited sources (CCSS-M absence note and NCETM place-value PD) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is not upgraded here.
Comparative-efficacy wording about dialogue versus recognition has been softened to proposed/may phrasing; the source row does not establish superiority of any medium.

probeDeeper: In 44, how is the first 4 different from the second 4?
Does the Roman system have a symbol for zero? Why does our system need one?
Read XLIV and split it into its chunks.
assess.correctAnswer: XLIV = 44 (XL = 40 by subtraction, IV = 4 by subtraction). It differs because Roman numerals combine symbols by value with no place value and no zero, whereas in 44 the two 4s mean different amounts (40 and 4) because of their POSITION, and we use 0 to hold empty places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads Roman numerals additively, ignoring subtractive order: XLIV = 10 + 50 + 1 + 5 = 66
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show smaller-before-larger means subtract: XL = 50 − 10 = 40, IV = 5 − 1 = 4. Re-read XLIV as 40 + 4.
errorPatterns.distractor: XLIV = 66.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child sums all symbols regardless of a smaller-before-larger pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: Imports place value into Roman numerals — thinks a symbol's position gives it a tens/ones value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast directly: in 44 position sets value; in XLIV each symbol keeps its own value and we add/subtract. Roman has no zero and no place value.
errorPatterns.distractor: In XLIV the symbols get tens/ones values from their position, just like 44.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the first symbol 'is in the tens place' or that our 44 and XLIV work the same way.

responseLevels.gap: Reads Roman numerals additively (XLIV = 66) or claims they work like place value.
responseLevels.full: Reads/writes Roman numerals to 100 with subtraction and explains that Roman lacks place value and zero, unlike our positional system.
responseLevels.partial: Converts simple Roman numerals but cannot articulate why our place-value system (with zero) differs.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Read XLIV for me. Now tell me: how is the Roman way of writing forty-four different from the way we write 44? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Contrasting XLIV with 44 forces the child to articulate what place value actually does. A child who understands names position (the two 4s differ) and the role of zero; a child who doesn't either reads Roman additively (66) or wrongly imports place value into the Roman symbols. The reason tier exposes the systems contrast.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Dissolving & Solutions

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y5 Properties & changes of materials):** Pupils should be taught to know that some materials will dissolve in liquid to form a solution, and describe how to recover a substance from a solution.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-PS1-2 / 5-PS1-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-2] (e.g. dissolving), the total weight of matter is conserved; develop a model [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-1].

- **Operational details:** The load-bearing idea is CONSERVATION: when a soluble solid dissolves it does NOT disappear — it breaks into pieces far too small to see and spreads evenly through the liquid to form a clear solution, and it can be RECOVERED by evaporating the liquid. Teach with the whole-system move: mass the sealed jar of water + sugar BEFORE and AFTER dissolving — the reading is unchanged, proving the sugar is still there. Then evaporate a little salt solution to reveal the solid returning. Distinguish dissolve from melt, and soluble from insoluble (sand does not dissolve — it can be filtered). Introduce saturation lightly (a limit to how much dissolves). Keep the explanation at 'tiny pieces too small to see' — formal particle theory is KS3.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal, quantitative). The child predicts and confirms that mass is conserved when a solid dissolves, explains that the dissolved solid is still present, and describes evaporation as the way to recover it.
bestPractices: Use the whole-system mass check: weigh water + solid before and after dissolving so the unchanged reading proves the solid is still present.
Recover the solid by evaporation so the child sees dissolving is reversible and the matter was never lost.
Contrast soluble vs insoluble with a control (sand) that is separated by filtering, not dissolving.
Explain dissolving as the solid breaking into pieces too small to see and spreading evenly, without invoking formal particle theory (KS3).
Introduce saturation lightly with a 'keep adding until it stops dissolving' path.
keyRepresentations: A dissolve tank on a balance showing an unchanged reading before/after
A zoom-in showing the solid splitting into too-small-to-see bits spreading through the liquid
An evaporate step recovering the crystals
An insoluble control (sand) filtered out, and a saturation limit
commonMisconceptions: A dissolved solid has disappeared or been destroyed (Piagetian intuition).
Dissolving and melting are the same process.
The mass of the solution is less than water + solid because 'the sugar is gone'.
Anything can dissolve if you stir enough (missing insolubility and saturation).
The solid cannot be got back once dissolved (missing recovery by evaporation).

learn.summary: Teach conservation of mass during dissolving for ages 9–10: a soluble solid that dissolves does not disappear but breaks into pieces too small to see and spreads evenly through the liquid to form a clear solution, and can be recovered by evaporation. The load-bearing move is weighing the whole system (water + solid) in a sealed/covered container and comparing the reading before and after the solid dissolves to show it is unchanged, then evaporating a solution to recover the solid. Distinguish dissolving from melting, soluble from insoluble (sand can be filtered), and introduce saturation lightly. Keep the explanation at 'tiny pieces too small to see'; formal particle theory is later (KS3).

activities.title: Dissolve, weigh, recover bench
feedback: If a learner predicts the reading will drop as the sugar dissolves, draw attention to the unchanged balance in the sealed jar: the weight did not leave, so the solid cannot have disappeared.

If a learner says the solid is 'gone' or 'turned into water', run the evaporation step together so the solid reappears — show, don't just assert. (Use the salt solution for heated evaporation. Heating a sugar solution strongly tends to make syrup or caramel, so to get sugar crystals back, leave the solution to evaporate slowly at room temperature.)
If a learner expects sand to dissolve like sugar, contrast the two: sand stays visible and is filtered out, showing dissolving depends on the substances.
When extra sugar stops dissolving and settles, name this as saturation — a limit to how much the liquid can hold.
Keep the container covered or sealed: the conservation claim is that the reading is the same before and after dissolving, which an open jar can confound by losing water to evaporation over time.
activities.rationale: The curriculum asks children to support conservation with measurement (NGSS 5-PS1-2 measures quantities to evidence that total weight is conserved); a measured, observed before/after reading on a sealed whole system plus recovery by evaporation can target the intuition that dissolving destroys matter. Recording the reading with the solid present but undissolved, then again once dissolved, isolates the conservation point rather than merely showing that adding solid raises the reading. Contrasting a soluble solid with an insoluble control and a saturation limit builds the distinctions the standards require.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5: some materials dissolve in liquid to form a solution; pupils describe how to recover a substance from a solution
NGSS 5-PS1-2: measure and graph quantities to show total weight of matter is conserved regardless of change (incl dissolving); 5-PS1-1 matter is particles too small to see
Children hold a Piagetian 'the sugar disappears/is destroyed' view; measuring mass before and after and evaporating to recover the solid targets it; 'think about the whole system'
learnerActions: Place a jar of water on a balance, add a measured spoon of sugar, and cover or seal the jar so no matter can escape or enter during the experiment.
Record this starting reading while the sugar is still visible and has not yet dissolved.
Predict whether the reading will go up, down, or stay the same as the sugar dissolves, and state WHY, before stirring.
Stir and watch the grains break into finer and finer specks that spread out until the water looks clear.

Read the balance again and compare with the starting reading: in a sealed jar it should be the same, apart from tiny flickers within the balance's precision. The dissolved sugar's weight is still there, so the sugar cannot have disappeared.
Place a shallow salt solution under a heat/evaporation step, let the water steam away, and watch the salt crystals reappear.
Try a sand control: stir it in and observe that it stays visible and settles, then separate it by filtering rather than dissolving.
Follow a 'keep adding sugar' path until extra sugar settles undissolved, to meet a saturation limit.
activities.intendedInsight: When a soluble solid dissolves it is still present — spread through the liquid as bits too small to see — because the sealed system weighs the same before and after it dissolves; and it can be recovered by evaporating the liquid. Some solids (sand) do not dissolve in water and can be filtered, and there is a limit to how much will dissolve (saturation).

activities.title: Zoom-in: where did the sugar go?
feedback: If a learner says the clear liquid is 'just water', revisit the zoom-in showing the bits spread throughout, and the recovery step that returns the solid.
Reinforce the vocabulary: solid + liquid → solution; evaporation returns the solid.
activities.rationale: A revealable diagram communicates the dissolving-and-recovery sequence and vocabulary and the 'still here' idea, serving as a companion to measured work. It makes the invisible dispersion visible, but on its own it asserts rather than demonstrates conservation, so it supports rather than replaces the weigh-it-yourself experience.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5: some materials dissolve in liquid to form a solution; pupils describe how to recover a substance from a solution
learnerActions: Reveal a magnified view of a dissolving grain splitting into ever-smaller specks that spread through the liquid.
Trace the sequence dissolving → solution → evaporate → recovered solid, lifting a 'the sugar is still here' flap at the solution stage.
State in your own words why the clear solution still contains the solid.
activities.intendedInsight: A dissolved solid becomes clear not because it vanished but because it has broken into pieces too small to see and spread evenly; the sequence can be reversed to recover the solid.

activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain and check your reasoning
feedback: A prediction that the reading will fall as the salt dissolves signals the 'dissolving destroys matter' misconception; use evaporation and the before/after balance to show mass is conserved.

If a learner explains the vanishing as melting, clarify the distinction: dissolving is a solid mixing into a liquid (a second substance is needed), while melting is one substance turning from solid to liquid when it is heated; then rebuild the conservation idea.
If a learner predicts sand or flour will dissolve like salt, contrast soluble and insoluble and note the saturation limit — dissolving depends on the substances and there is a limit.
Keep the two weight claims distinct: 'heavier than plain water' comes from adding the salt, whereas 'unchanged just before versus just after dissolving' is what shows the matter was conserved.
'Still there' with no way to check is memorised, not understood: push for at least one recovery or test method.
activities.rationale: The 'how do you know' tier separates a child who holds matter conservation (offers taste/weigh/evaporate) from one who thinks dissolving destroys the solid. Requiring prediction-with-reason before observation surfaces the diagnostic reasoning; requiring a recovery method guards against rote recall. A predict-and-question format like this can be used while teaching, not only to assess; on its own, recognition responses do not elicit independent construction of the conservation argument.
sourceClaims: Children hold a Piagetian 'the sugar disappears/is destroyed' view; measuring mass before and after and evaporating to recover the solid targets it; 'think about the whole system'
NGSS 5-PS1-2: measure and graph quantities to show total weight of matter is conserved regardless of change (incl dissolving); 5-PS1-1 matter is particles too small to see
learnerActions: Weigh a glass of plain water and record the reading. Add a spoon of salt without stirring, cover the glass if possible, and record the reading again while the salt is still visible. Before stirring, predict whether the balance will read more, less, or the same as this second reading once the salt has dissolved, and say why.
Stir until the salt is invisible, read the balance, and compare it with both earlier readings (plain water, and water with undissolved salt) and with your prediction.

Note the two distinct comparisons: the salty water weighs MORE than the plain water you started with (because you added salt), while the reading is UNCHANGED from just before to just after the salt dissolves (the conservation point).

Answer probing questions: If all the water dried up, what would be left, and does that show the salt was there all along? Would salty water weigh more, less, or the same as the plain water you started with, and why? If it had been sand instead of salt, would stirring make it disappear — what's different? Is salty water one substance or a mixture of two, and how would you argue it?

Give the most important part: how you KNOW the salt is still there — weight, evaporating it to find it left behind, or taste (only if the teacher says so, using clean food-safe cups, never science equipment).
activities.intendedInsight: A full understanding says the solid is still there AND offers converging evidence — weight, taste, and recoverability by evaporation — not just a memorised 'still there'. It also transfers: sand won't dissolve, and solutions can saturate.

constraints: Keep the explanation at 'pieces too small to see' spreading evenly; do not introduce formal particle theory, which belongs to later study (KS3).

A revealable diagram or flap communicates sequence and vocabulary but cannot let the learner watch the balance hold steady or drive recovery; use it as a companion, not a substitute, for measured work.

A fixed quiz (slider for 'what will the balance read?', MCQs on soluble/insoluble and recovery) can check understanding but does not provide the weigh-it-yourself experience; recognition responses do not elicit independent construction of the conservation argument.

Weigh the whole system in a sealed/covered container so evaporation during the experiment does not confound the before/after mass comparison; record the reading with the solid present but undissolved, then again once dissolved.
Distinguish the represented idea from the setup: evaporation recovers the solid but requires appropriate heat safety for a classroom evaporating-dish activity.

Insolubility and saturation outcomes depend on the specific materials and amounts used; frame sand as a chosen insoluble control and 'extra sugar settles' as the observed saturation limit for that setup, not a universal rule for all solids.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The ACS Inquiry in Action source supporting the Piagetian misconception and whole-system framing is marked unverified in the source row; treat the misconception-targeting and 'whole system' claims as legacy, not independently confirmed here.

The source POE describes weighing an open glass of water and adding salt, with the glass+water+salt expected to read 'heavier by the salt's weight'. Over a longer dissolving period an open container can lose mass to evaporation; prefer a sealed/covered system for the strict conservation demonstration, and keep 'heavier than plain water' (true: you added salt) distinct from 'unchanged before vs after dissolving' (the conservation point). Both framings appear in the source and are kept distinct.

The preferred bench takes the starting reading with the solid present but undissolved (whole-system move), rather than a water-only baseline followed by adding solid, which would show mass addition instead of conservation during dissolving.

The activity-1 rationale was softened from the original 'conservation is a claim the child must weigh to believe / impossible in static media' to a scoped, curriculum-grounded statement; comparative necessity of the measured medium is not established by the available sources.

Claims in the original that conservation is 'impossible in static media', that 3D 'adds nothing', and that discussion/chat 'cannot teach' conservation have been softened to scoped affordances and objective limits.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: weigh a glass of water on a balance, note the reading, then ask the child to predict what the balance shows AFTER a spoon of salt is stirred in until invisible — and crucially WHY. A child who thinks dissolving destroys matter predicts the same or a lower reading. Stir, watch it vanish, read the balance (heavier by the salt's weight). The pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I let all the water dry up, what would I find in the glass — and does that tell you the salt was there all along?
Would the glass-of-salty-water weigh more, less, or the same as the plain water I started with? Why?
What if it had been sand instead of salt — would stirring make it disappear? What's different?
Is the salty water one substance or a mixture of two? How would you argue it?
assess.correctAnswer: The salt is still there, dissolved — spread through the water as pieces too small to see, making a solution. You know because you could taste it (salty), weigh it (glass+water+salt weighs the same as before, more than plain water), or let the water evaporate and find the salt left behind.

errorPatterns.pattern: the dissolved solid has been destroyed ('it turned into water' / 'it's gone')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Evaporate the solution together so the salt reappears; weigh before and after to show mass is conserved. This is the Piagetian conservation gap — show, don't just assert.
errorPatterns.distractor: The salt disappeared — it turned into water, so it's gone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: tier one answer 'it's gone' or tier two offering no recovery method

errorPatterns.pattern: dissolving is a kind of melting ('the water melted the salt')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the vocabulary distinction (dissolve needs the liquid; melt needs only heat) before rebuilding the conservation idea.
errorPatterns.distractor: The water melted the salt into liquid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains the vanishing as melting rather than dispersing into the liquid

errorPatterns.pattern: everything dissolves if you stir long enough (no notion of solubility limit or insoluble solids)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast salt (dissolves) with sand (doesn't) and a saturated solution (no more will dissolve) — dissolving depends on the substances, and there is a limit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts sand or flour will dissolve just like salt

responseLevels.gap: Says the salt is gone/destroyed, or 'still there' with no way to check; may call it melting.
responseLevels.full: Salt is still there as a solution; justifies with conservation reasoning (weight unchanged, recoverable by evaporation, still tastable) AND transfers to a new case — predicts sand won't dissolve and a solution can saturate.
responseLevels.partial: Says the salt is still there and names one recovery idea, but treats it as a rote fact — can't connect taste, weight, and evaporation as converging evidence, or over-generalises that everything dissolves.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I stir a spoon of salt into a glass of water and keep stirring until I can't see any salt at all. Is the salt still in the glass or has it gone? Then tell me the most important part: how do you KNOW — what could you do to check?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two 'how do you know' separates a child who believes matter is conserved (offers taste/weigh/evaporate as recovery) from one who thinks dissolving destroys the solid. Both tiers must agree: 'still there' PLUS a recovery method. 'Still there' with no way to check is memorised, not understood.

pedagogy.summary: The right angle is the benchmark angle of Y3: a quarter turn, the corner of a square, marked with a small square. Children learn to identify it with a right-angle checker (folded paper / L-shape) and to classify other angles relative to it — less open or more open. The turn facet is quantitative: two right angles make a half turn, four make a complete turn (360°). The pedagogical goal is that the right angle becomes a reusable UNIT of comparison whose identity is independent of orientation and of arm length.
bestPractices: Make the checker: fold paper (or a circle) twice to build a right-angle tester and have children place it into real corners to test — a concrete, self-checking tool (NCETM 'Monster Right Angle Measurer').
Build right angles from turns: a quarter turn is one right angle, two quarter turns make a half turn (a straight line), four bring you back to the start; link to the four compass points.
Classify by comparison before naming: is this corner more open or less open than my checker? — establishing the less-than / greater-than idea informally ahead of the words acute/obtuse.
Vary orientation on purpose — rotate and mirror right angles off the upright — so 'right angle' is not tied to a standard L.
Connect the two facets: a quarter turn LEAVES a right angle between the start arm and the finish arm.
keyRepresentations: The right-angle checker / folded-paper tester, and the small-square right-angle mark
The clock face and compass rose showing quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns
Body turns and a hinge / geo-strip opened exactly to a right angle
The four right-angled corners of squares and rectangles
commonMisconceptions: A right angle must be 'upright' like a standard L; a rotated or mirrored one is not recognised as a right angle (orientation dependence)
A right angle drawn with long arms is 'bigger' or 'more than' one with short arms (the arm-length misconception carried over)
Any sharp-looking corner is a right angle — labelling corners by rough appearance rather than testing against the checker
Miscounting right angles in a turn — e.g. two right angles make a full turn, or a half turn returns you to the start

learn.summary: Year 3 children learn the right angle as a reusable benchmark unit: a quarter turn, the corner of a square, marked with a small square. They build and use a right-angle checker (folded paper / L-shape) to test real corners, classify other angles as less open or more open than a right angle, and compose turns from right angles (two make a half turn, four a complete turn / 360°). Key goal: the right angle's identity is independent of orientation and arm length.

activities.title: Make and use a right-angle checker
feedback: If the checker sits flush, it is a right angle — stamp the small square; a rectangular window corner should fit exactly.
If the corner is more open than a right angle, the checker's arm cannot reach the corner's other side and leaves a gap between them.

If the corner is less open than a right angle, the checker's arm overhangs past the corner's side — a pizza slice tip is usually less open than a right angle when the pizza is cut into more than four equal slices, but test it to check.
For the tilted right angle, turn the checker to match its orientation: it still fits exactly, so it is still a right angle — being 'on its side' does not change it.
For the long-armed corner, place the checker on both the long-armed and a short-armed right angle: both fit, so arm length does not make a corner 'bigger'.
(Adult note: the more-open case is an obtuse angle and the less-open case an acute angle; keep the child's language to 'more open' / 'less open' at this stage.)
activities.rationale: A concrete, self-checking tester lets children test rather than eyeball corners, intended to counter the 'sharp-looking = right angle' habit. Seeding tilted and long-armed right angles aims at the orientation-dependence and arm-length misconceptions; framing angle as opening (fit of the checker) rather than side length addresses the whole-object/side-length misconception, which the cited source notes is countered by framing angle as turn/opening.
sourceClaims: Recommended teaching reinforces that an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines (one for the start, one for the finish); children make and use a right-angle tester (a 'Monster Right Angle Measurer') to find right angles in shapes and objects, and make right-angled turns between the four compass points.

Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties including the length of the sides (a same-size angle drawn with longer sides is judged bigger), a misconception robust from preschool through elementary years; it stems from a whole-object assumption and is countered by framing angle as the measure of turn/opening.
learnerActions: Fold a piece of paper (or a paper circle) in half and in half again to make a right-angle tester with a crisp square corner.
Place the checker into real corners around the room and on shapes — a window frame, a book corner, a slice of pizza, an open pair of scissors.
For each corner, decide: does the checker fit flush (a right angle), or is the corner less open / more open than the checker?
Mark each confirmed right angle with a small square symbol.
Deliberately test corners that are tilted off-upright and corners drawn with very long arms, turning the checker to match each corner before reading the fit.
activities.intendedInsight: A right angle is one reusable unit of comparison; a corner is a right angle only if it fits the checker exactly, regardless of how it is turned or how long its arms are.

activities.title: Build turns from right angles
feedback: If you predicted two turns to get home, notice that after two quarter turns in the same direction from your stated starting direction you are facing backwards — it takes four quarter turns in the same direction to return home.
After each quarter turn, confirm one right angle has been added; two make a half turn / straight line, four make 360°.
If you lose count, mark each quarter position on the floor or compass rose so the right angles stack visibly.
activities.rationale: Physically composing turns, with a prediction stated first against a named starting direction, surfaces the common miscount (that two right angles make a full turn, or that a half turn returns you to the start). Connecting the quarter turn to the static square corner joins the two facets of the concept.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should identify right angles, recognise that 2 right angles make a half-turn, 3 make three-quarters of a turn and 4 a complete turn, and identify whether angles are greater than or less than a right angle.

Recommended teaching reinforces that an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines (one for the start, one for the finish); children make and use a right-angle tester (a 'Monster Right Angle Measurer') to find right angles in shapes and objects, and make right-angled turns between the four compass points.
learnerActions: Stand facing a chosen landmark (e.g. the window). Predict: how many quarter turns will bring you back to facing exactly the way you started? Say why before turning.
Make the turns one quarter at a time, always turning the same way (e.g. all clockwise), counting one right angle each time and noticing which way you face after each.
Pause after two quarter turns: notice you are facing backwards (a half turn / straight line), not home.
Link to the four compass points and a clock face: a quarter turn is one right angle, two a half turn, three a three-quarter turn, four a full turn (360°).
With a hinge or two geo-strips, open exactly to a right angle and connect: a quarter turn leaves a right angle between the start arm and the finish arm.
activities.intendedInsight: Turns are composed of right angles: two right angles make a half turn (facing back), three make a three-quarter turn, and four make a complete turn (360°) back to the start.

activities.title: Sort and classify mixed angles
feedback: You should select the tilted and long-armed right angles as well as the upright one — all three fit the checker exactly.
Leave out the just-less and just-more angles: the checker will not sit flush on them.
Justify by fit / quarter turn / square corner, not by which way the angle points or how long its arms are.
If you missed the tilted right angle, turn the checker to match its orientation and re-test.
activities.rationale: A mixed set including a tilted and a long-armed right angle lets the task discriminate a child who tests against the benchmark from one who recognises only an upright L or judges by arm length. Asking for the reason exposes whether 'right angle' means a quarter-turn / square-corner benchmark or merely a familiar picture.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should identify right angles, recognise that 2 right angles make a half-turn, 3 make three-quarters of a turn and 4 a complete turn, and identify whether angles are greater than or less than a right angle.

Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties including the length of the sides (a same-size angle drawn with longer sides is judged bigger), a misconception robust from preschool through elementary years; it stems from a whole-object assumption and is countered by framing angle as the measure of turn/opening.
learnerActions: Look at a set of about five angles laid out in mixed orientations: a true right angle tilted off-upright, a true right angle with very long arms, one angle just less open than a right angle, one just more open, and one obvious upright right angle.
Point to every right angle you can find, testing each with your checker rather than judging by appearance.
Sort the remaining angles into 'less open than a right angle' and 'more open than a right angle'.
Pick one angle you called a right angle and explain how you know — 'it fits my checker / it's a quarter turn / it makes a square corner'.
Order a few angles from least open to most open.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying angles relative to the right-angle benchmark (less / equal / greater) establishes the less-than and greater-than idea informally, ahead of the words acute and obtuse, and relies on testing not appearance.

constraints: The right-angle concept is planar; turning in space or testing real 3D object corners can add interest but is not required to establish the benchmark idea.

Classification/counting questions (right / less / greater, order by openness, count right angles in a turn) can reliably assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the hands-on testing of fitting a checker or the physical composing of turns — pair any such assessment with hands-on testing and turning.

A static picture that reveals 'right angle / not' when corners are tapped can support recognition and the small-square notation, but does not let a child test corners or compose turns; treat it as a partial scaffold for one facet only.
Deliberately include rotated/mirrored and long-armed right angles in any task so the benchmark is not tied to a standard upright L or to arm length.
When children predict turns, have them state the result relative to a stated starting direction (e.g. 'facing the window') so the count of right angles is unambiguous.
Keep child-facing language to 'less open' / 'more open' than a right angle at this stage; introduce acute/obtuse only as later vocabulary, not within these Year 3 prompts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Removed the formal terms acute/obtuse from child-facing feedback to stay consistent with the stated goal of establishing less-open/more-open informally ahead of those words; retained them only as an adult note.

An optional on-screen version could use a draggable checker that glows green and stamps a small square on an exact fit (showing 'less open' / 'more open' otherwise) and a turn dial that adds quarter turns while a counter shows right angles (2 = facing back, 4 = home / 360°). These are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.

The source claimed 3D 'adds cost without deepening' and that an in-role dialogue 'cannot deliver' the felt fit of a checker; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited evidence and have been softened to scoped notes about affordances.

The source framed a quiz as assessing but 'not building checker intuition' — retained only as an objective limit that recognition/selection tasks do not themselves elicit hands-on testing; a selected-response format can still be used during teaching.
Efficacy phrasing in activity rationales was kept as 'intended/aims to' because these are unvalidated proposals; only the side-length-as-opening framing is directly supported by sources[2].claim.

assess.poeTask: Ask the child to PREDICT how many right-angle (quarter) turns it takes to end up facing exactly the way they started, and to say WHY, before doing it. Then have them make the turns one quarter at a time, counting a right angle each time and noticing where they face after two. A child who predicts two must confront landing facing backwards after two turns; the stated reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: This corner is tilted over on its side. Is it still a right angle? How could you check?
If you stand facing me and make two quarter turns, which way are you facing now, and how many right angles was that?
I drew this right angle with really long arms and this one with short arms. Is the long one a bigger angle? Why?
How is a right angle different from this one that's just a little bit more open than your checker?
assess.correctAnswer: Selects the true right angles regardless of orientation or arm length (including the tilted one and the long-armed one), leaves out the just-less and just-more ones, and justifies by 'it's a quarter turn / it fits my right-angle checker / it makes a square corner' rather than by how it looks or which way it points.

errorPatterns.pattern: A right angle must point up like an L; a tilted or mirrored one is not a right angle ('that one's on its side, so it's different')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the checker itself onto the tilted corner so it still fits exactly — show the right angle is preserved under rotation; have the child re-test each corner with the checker turned to match.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Misses the tilted right angle and selects only upright ones

errorPatterns.pattern: The right angle with long arms is bigger / 'more than' a right angle ('its lines are longer so the corner is bigger')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place the checker on the long-armed and the short-armed right angles in turn — both fit exactly; return to opening-not-length with the hinge.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the long-armed right angle as too big, or ranks it as more open than the checker

errorPatterns.pattern: Any sharp-looking corner is a right angle ('that looks about square to me')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the checker — place it and read 'more open' or 'less open'; build the habit of testing rather than eyeballing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Selects the just-less and just-more angles as right angles without testing them

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts right angles in a turn — two right angles make a full turn, or a half turn brings you back to the start
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically make the turns, one right angle per quarter, marking each: two land you facing backwards (a half turn / straight line), four bring you home.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to count right angles in a turn, says two make a full turn, or cannot say four make 360°

responseLevels.gap: Recognises only the upright L as a right angle, or labels corners as right angles by appearance without testing; miscounts right angles in a turn.
responseLevels.full: Uses the right angle as an orientation- and length-independent benchmark: tests any corner against it, classifies less/greater confidently, and explains a turn as built from right angles (two make a half turn, four a full turn / 360°), transferring to new corners and turns (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Identifies upright right angles, uses the checker on standard cases, and can recall that four right angles make a full turn, but treats these as separate skills — fails on the tilted or long-armed right angle, or cannot connect the quarter turn to the static square corner (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out about five angles in mixed orientations: a true right angle tilted off-upright, a true right angle drawn with very long arms, one angle just less open than a right angle, one just more open, and one obvious right angle. Ask: 'Point to every right angle you can find.' Then: 'Pick one you chose and tell me how you know it's a right angle.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Including a tilted right angle and a long-armed right angle separates a child who tests against the quarter-turn/checker benchmark from one who recognises only an upright L or judges by arm length. The tier-2 reason exposes whether 'right angle' means a quarter-turn / square-corner benchmark or merely a familiar picture.
