pedagogy.summary: Distinguishing flat (2-D) from solid (3-D) shapes is a foundational classification that young children find genuinely hard because everyday language mislabels solids with flat names (a ball called 'a circle', a box 'a square'). It is best taught by handling real objects — holding, turning and feeling whether a shape takes up space — rather than by pictures, and by giving the child a physical test ('can you draw it but not pick it up? then it's flat') alongside precise vocabulary (circle/sphere, square/cube). Instruction, not maturation, moves children from judging a shape by its overall look to reasoning about dimensionality (van Hiele).
bestPractices: Use real solids and flat cut-outs the child can hold and turn, not drawings — the felt three-dimensionality is what teaches the distinction.
Acknowledge the child's observation, then press for precision: 'Yes, the ball is round like a circle, but it is round every way and you can hold it — that is a sphere.'
Offer a child-friendly discriminator: a flat shape lies on the paper (length and width only); a solid takes up space and can be held and turned (length, width and height).
Sort mixed sets into 'flat' and 'solid', including less familiar solids (cone) and non-prototypical exemplars, and go on 'shape hunts' for solids in the room.
Teach the twin pairs explicitly — circle/sphere, square/cube, triangle/pyramid — so the flat and solid names are not confused.
keyRepresentations: Real objects to handle: ball, cube/box, tin, cone beside paper circle, square, triangle
Twin-pair cards: circle–sphere, square–cube, triangle–pyramid
The 'draw it vs hold it' test
Flat/solid sorting hoops or bins
commonMisconceptions: Applies a flat (2-D) name to a solid object — calls a ball 'a circle', a cube 'a square', a cone 'a triangle' (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023; Nurnberger-Haag).
Sorts by overall appearance as a whole rather than by dimensionality — groups the round ball with the round circle because both 'look round' (van Hiele visual level).
Confuses a drawing of a solid with the solid itself — treats a cube drawn on paper as 'solid' because of its name.

learn.summary: Young children (ages 5–6) distinguish flat (2-D) from solid (3-D) shapes. This is genuinely hard because everyday language mislabels solids with flat names (a ball called 'a circle', a box 'a square'). A central, curriculum-supported approach is handling real objects — holding, turning and feeling whether a shape takes up space in every direction — supported by a dimensional discriminator ('is it round or thick in every direction, or is it thin and essentially flat like the shape drawn on a card?') and the explicit twin-pair vocabulary (circle/sphere, square/cube, and loosely triangle/pyramid, since a pyramid has triangle faces). A paper cut-out can itself be picked up and has a slight thickness, so 'can you pick it up?' is not the reliable test; treat the card as a stand-in for an ideal flat shape. Instruction and experience, not age alone, help move children from judging a shape by its overall look to reasoning about dimensionality.

activities.title: Hold-and-turn sort with real solids and flat cut-outs
feedback: When the child calls a solid by a flat name ('the ball is a circle'), acknowledge then press for precision: 'Yes, the ball is round like a circle — but it is round every way and takes up space all around, so it is a sphere.'

If the child groups round things together regardless of flat/solid, prompt the dimensional test: 'Is it round or thick in every direction, or is it thin and flat like the shape on a card?' Sort by that, not by how round it looks.
Reinforce correct sorts by naming the twin pair: 'Yes — the thin flat one is a circle, the one that is round in every direction is a sphere.'
activities.rationale: Handling real solids beside flat cut-outs lets the child feel three-dimensionality, which is the property being taught; sorting mixed and non-prototypical sets and naming twin pairs targets the specific confusions documented for this age. The test is framed around taking up space in every direction rather than holdability, because a paper cut-out can also be held.
sourceClaims: Shown a real cube, young children named it 'square'; in the pretest 12 of the children named the square and cube both 'square' and 12 named the triangle and pyramid both 'triangle'; the cone name was unknown — children preferred the 2-D shape names their teacher had taught. The circle/sphere pair was easiest (75%). Building the solids from flat paper (pop-up) let children touch and count faces, sides and vertices and raised naming accuracy.

At the van Hiele visual level, shapes are judged by their appearance and viewed as a whole, not by distinguishing parts or properties ('it's a square because it looks like one'); deliberate instruction, not maturation alone, is needed to move children to property-based (descriptive) thinking.
Kindergarten geometry requires children to identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, 'flat') or three-dimensional ('solid').
learnerActions: Gather a mixed set the child can handle: a ball, a cube-shaped box, a pyramid, a tin, a cone, beside a paper circle, square and triangle. The paper shapes can also be picked up and have a tiny thickness, so treat each as a stand-in for the ideal flat shape it represents.
Pick up and turn each object over in your hand. Ask: is it round or thick in every direction so it takes up space (solid), or is it thin and essentially flat like the shape drawn on a card (flat)?
Sort the set into two hoops or bins labelled 'flat' and 'solid'.
Include a cone and other less familiar or non-prototypical solids, not only balls and boxes.
Go on a 'shape hunt' around the room to find more solids (a tin, a ball, a box) and say why each takes up space in every direction.
Name the twin pairs aloud as you sort: circle/sphere, square/cube, and triangle/pyramid (a pyramid has triangle faces, though its base may be a square).
activities.intendedInsight: A flat shape has length and width but (ideally) no thickness, and a paper card stands in for it; a solid takes up space in every direction (length, width and height). 'Round like a circle' is not the same as flat — a ball is round every way and takes up space all around, so it is a sphere, not a circle. (For the adult: because a paper cut-out can also be held and turned and has a slight thickness, 'can you pick it up?' is not the real test — ask whether the shape takes up space in every direction.)

activities.title: Build a solid from flat paper (pop-up)
feedback: If the child keeps the flat name after building, point out that it now takes up space in every direction: 'This stands up and takes up space in every direction now — it is a cube, not just a square.'
Encourage counting faces to ground the solid/flat difference in something the child can touch.
activities.rationale: Constructing the solid from flat paper makes the flat-to-solid transition concrete and lets the child touch and count faces, grounding the solid name in properties the child can feel.
sourceClaims: Shown a real cube, young children named it 'square'; in the pretest 12 of the children named the square and cube both 'square' and 12 named the triangle and pyramid both 'triangle'; the cone name was unknown — children preferred the 2-D shape names their teacher had taught. The circle/sphere pair was easiest (75%). Building the solids from flat paper (pop-up) let children touch and count faces, sides and vertices and raised naming accuracy.
learnerActions: Start with a flat paper net (an unfolded pattern of joined flat shapes) and fold/assemble it into a solid (e.g. a pop-up cube or pyramid).
As the solid takes shape, touch and count its faces, edges and corners (vertices).

Compare the finished solid, which now takes up space in every direction, with the flat sheet you started from. Name the solid and the flat shapes of its faces: a cube has square faces, and a pyramid has triangle faces (a square pyramid also has a square base). The unfolded sheet (the net) is several joined shapes, not one square or triangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid takes up space in every direction and has faces you can feel and count, whereas the flat paper it came from only lies in a plane — the same name family splits into a flat word and a solid word.

activities.title: Spin-to-compare on screen (scaffold alongside handling)
feedback: If the child still calls the spun ball a circle, pair it with the physical hold: 'The one that vanished edge-on is flat; the one that stays round in every direction is a sphere.'
Note that the on-screen ball is itself a picture on a flat screen — the rotating model stands in for the real object, so pair it with a real hold-and-turn.
activities.rationale: Rotating a model shows depth from every side and a flat shape vanishing edge-on, a useful visual analogue; it is proposed as a scaffold paired with handling, not a replacement, because a flat screen does not provide the physical, tactile handling of a real object.
learnerActions: On screen, spin a circle and a ball. Watch the circle thin to a line and vanish when turned edge-on, while the ball stays round from every side.
Say why: the ideal circle has no thickness, so it disappears edge-on; the ball is round every way and never flattens — it cannot be a circle, it is a sphere.
Immediately repeat with a real paper circle and a real ball in your hand, turning each to feel that the ball is round in every direction while the card is thin.
activities.intendedInsight: An ideal flat shape has no thickness and disappears edge-on; a solid takes up space from every direction. Rotating a model shows this effect, while handling a real object additionally lets the child feel the three-dimensionality directly, so the two are paired. (A real paper circle is a thin card standing in for the zero-thickness ideal.)

constraints: Handling is central here because it lets the child feel that a ball has depth every way while a cut-out is thin. Screen activities (spin-to-compare, drag-to-sort, tap-to-reveal label cards) are offered alongside handling real objects.

A drag-to-sort flat/solid game can give feedback, but every picture on a flat screen is itself flat — this risks reinforcing appearance-based sorting, so on its own it does not elicit physical handling of real objects.
A sort or multiple-choice check can verify or practise the classification but does not itself elicit physical handling or an explanation; use it as a post-check alongside handling real objects.
Conversation alone does not let a child physically handle a shape or see it take up space; use it to prompt the child to justify a sort rather than as the sole medium.
Everyday mislabelling (ball='circle', box='square') is the main obstacle; always acknowledge the child's accurate observation ('yes, round like a circle') before correcting to the solid name.

A paper cut-out is only an approximation of an ideal flat (zero-thickness) shape: it can be picked up and has a slight thickness. So the reliable discriminator is whether the shape takes up space in every direction, not whether it can be physically held — ask the child about the mathematical shape the thin card represents.

Distinguish the drawn solid from the real one: a cube drawn on a page is flat on that page even though its name is 'cube'; contrast the drawing (whose corners you cannot grasp) with a real cube that takes up space in every direction. When naming an example a cube, use a cube-shaped object, since a generic box need not be a cube.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source framed the 3-D interactive as the 'recommended' artefact while also stating the true lesson is physical handling; this rewrite demotes the screen rotation to an explicit scaffold paired with real objects and foregrounds the hands-on sort and pop-up build, without claiming either medium is the sole means of learning.

Original catalog text included claims that a flat screen 'cannot show' the property and that talk 'cannot convey' dimensionality. These are retained only as narrowly scoped affordances in constraints, not as universal laws; a screen model and conversation can still support learning as scaffolds.

The original row's discriminator ('can you draw it but not pick it up? then it's flat' / 'a solid can be held and turned') is an idealisation error: a paper cut-out can also be held and turned and has a slight thickness. The guidance now tests whether a shape takes up space in every direction and treats the paper card as an approximation of the ideal flat shape; this correction is applied in the activities and constraints, not only here.

probeDeeper: Can you pick the circle up off the paper and turn it over in your hand? What about the ball?
The ball looks round like a circle — so why do we call it solid and the circle flat?
Here is a cone. Is it flat or solid? How can you tell?
Draw a circle on the paper, then find something in the room that is solid and round like a ball.
assess.correctAnswer: Puts the paper circle and square with the flat shapes and the ball and cube with the solids; explains that the ball is solid because it is round in every direction and you can hold and turn it and it takes up space, whereas the circle just lies flat on the paper — so the ball is a sphere, not a circle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies a flat (2-D) name to a solid object — shown a real ball or cube, calls it 'a circle' or 'a square' and sorts it with the flat shapes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand the child the object to hold and turn: 'a circle is flat on the paper; the ball is round every way and you can pick it up — that is a sphere'; teach the twin-pair names
errorPatterns.distractor: The ball is round, so it is a circle — it goes with the flat shapes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the solid with a 2-D word and places it in the flat group

errorPatterns.pattern: Sorts by overall appearance as a whole rather than by dimensionality — groups round things together regardless of whether they are flat or solid
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give the physical test — can you hold it and turn it over, or does it only lie on the paper? — and sort by that, not by look
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts the ball with the circle 'because they both look round'

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses a drawing of a solid with a real solid — judges by the name, so a cube drawn on paper is called 'solid' or a real object 'flat' inconsistently
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the drawn cube (flat on the page, you cannot grasp its corners) with the real cube you can hold and turn
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls a picture of a cube 'solid' but cannot say the drawing itself is flat on the page

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by the name or overall look — calls the ball a 'circle' and groups it with the flat shapes because it is round.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by dimensionality — flat shapes lie on the paper, solids take up space and can be held and turned — justifies the ball as solid despite looking round, and extends the rule to unfamiliar solids.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts the familiar cases (paper circle flat, ball solid) correctly but by rote naming; cannot say what makes one flat and the other solid, and slips on less familiar solids such as a cone.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a ball, a paper circle, a cube (box) and a paper square. Sort them into 'flat' shapes and 'solid' shapes. Then tell me: why isn't the ball flat, even though it looks round like the circle?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps dimensionality classes the ball as solid despite it 'looking round like a circle'; a child at the naming/visual level calls the ball a 'circle' and puts it with the flat shapes because both look round. The reason tier ('why isn't the ball flat?') separates 'it is round every way and you can hold it' from silence or 'because it is a circle'.

sources.claim: Shown a real cube, young children named it 'square'; in the pretest 12 of the children named the square and cube both 'square' and 12 named the triangle and pyramid both 'triangle'; the cone name was unknown — children preferred the 2-D shape names their teacher had taught. The circle/sphere pair was easiest (75%). Building the solids from flat paper (pop-up) let children touch and count faces, sides and vertices and raised naming accuracy.
sources.source: Mohamed & Kandeel (2023), 'Playful Learning: Teaching the Properties of Geometric Shapes through Pop-up Mechanisms for Kindergarten', IJEMST 11(1):179-197 (ERIC EJ1357339)

sources.claim: At the van Hiele visual level, shapes are judged by their appearance and viewed as a whole, not by distinguishing parts or properties ('it's a square because it looks like one'); deliberate instruction, not maturation alone, is needed to move children to property-based (descriptive) thinking.
sources.source: Way (2011), 'The Development of Spatial and Geometric Thinking: The Importance of Instruction', NRICH, University of Cambridge

sources.claim: Kindergarten geometry requires children to identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, 'flat') or three-dimensional ('solid').
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, K.G.A.3

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to describe 3-D solids by three distinct properties — faces, edges and vertices — and to count each for common solids (canonically: a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices). The two teaching challenges are (1) keeping the three properties distinct (a face is a flat 2-D surface, an edge is the straight line where two faces meet, a vertex is the point where edges meet) rather than blurring them under everyday words like 'side' and 'corner', and (2) counting reliably including the hidden features on the far side. It is best taught by handling real solids and counting each property by touch in a fixed order, marking features as they are counted, and being explicit about how curved solids are described.
bestPractices: Count by touch in a fixed order — colour or number each face, trace each edge, dot each vertex — so the three properties stay distinct and nothing is double-counted or missed.
Hand children the real solid to turn while looking at pictures of it, so hidden faces, edges and vertices are included in the count rather than only the visible ones.
Define each term against the object: a face is a flat surface (itself a 2-D shape), an edge is the straight line where two faces meet, a vertex is the corner where edges meet.

Be explicit about curved solids: a curved surface is described as a 'curved surface', not a face, and the curved boundary is not an edge — and note that schemes differ, so state the convention being used.
Connect faces to 2-D shapes and (later) to nets, where each face appears as a separate flat shape, reinforcing the face count.
keyRepresentations: Handleable solids (cube, cuboid, pyramid, sphere, cylinder, cone) counted by touch
Colour-a-face / trace-an-edge / dot-a-vertex marking system while counting
Nets that fold up into the solid, showing each face as a separate 2-D shape
A cube-vs-cylinder pair to contrast flat faces with a curved surface
commonMisconceptions: Blurs faces, edges and vertices under everyday words, calling edges 'sides' and vertices 'corners' so the three properties run together when counting.
Counts only the faces/edges/vertices that are visible, missing the hidden ones on the far side (gives a cube 3 faces, 9 edges or 4 corners).
Counts a curved surface as a 'face' and the curved boundary line as an 'edge' (e.g. says a cylinder has 3 faces).
Treats the whole solid as if it were the 2-D shape of a face, not distinguishing the flat face from the 3-D object.

learn.summary: Children aged 6-7 learn to describe common 3-D solids by three distinct properties — faces (flat surfaces, each itself a 2-D shape), edges (the straight line where two faces meet) and vertices (the corner where edges meet) — and to count each reliably for solids such as a cube (6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices). The two core challenges are keeping the three properties distinct rather than blurring them under everyday words like 'side' and 'corner', and counting the hidden features on the far side rather than only those visible. A well-supported route for this age is handling real solids (including while looking at a flat picture of the same solid), counting each property by touch in a fixed order with a marking system, and being explicit about how curved solids are described.

activities.title: Count a real cube by touch in a fixed order
feedback: If a child calls an edge a 'side' or a vertex a 'corner' and runs the properties together, pause and name each property against the object as they touch it: 'This flat part is a face; this straight line where two faces meet is an edge; this point where edges meet is a vertex.'
If the recount from a different starting face gives a different total, the marking slipped — re-mark systematically so each feature is counted exactly once.
If a child reaches only 3 faces or 9 edges, prompt: 'Turn the cube over — are there features round the back you haven't marked yet?'
activities.rationale: Faces, edges and vertices are spatial properties; counting by touch in a fixed order with a marking system keeps the three distinct and ensures hidden features are included. Handling the real solid while naming each property is a recommended approach for this age.
sourceClaims: A curved surface is NOT a face and the curved line where a curved surface meets a flat face is NOT an edge; each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling solids while viewing images supports counting faces, edges and vertices. Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
KS1/early-years practice: attend to 3-D properties (edges, faces, vertices), handle real objects, and count by physically tracking features; each face relates to a 2-D shape.
learnerActions: Hold a real cube and turn it in your hands.
Count the faces first: colour or number each flat surface as you touch it, saying 'face' each time, until every face is marked. Record the total.
Then trace each edge with a finger, marking each traced edge (e.g. a gold line or sticker), saying 'edge' each time, until all are traced. Record the total.
Then dot each vertex (corner) with a sticker, saying 'vertex' each time. Record the total.
Recount starting from a different face to check your totals stay the same (6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices).
activities.intendedInsight: A face, an edge and a vertex are three different things; counting each property separately in a fixed order, and marking features as you go, keeps them distinct and makes sure nothing hidden is missed or double-counted.

activities.title: Predict then count the hidden features
feedback: A child who predicts around 9 edges (the most you can see at once, when three faces are showing) is reasoning only about the visible faces — celebrate noticing the gap when the far-side edges bring the total to 12. (The '9' is a rough illustrative expectation, not a measured value; from one view you see at most 3 faces, 9 edges and 7 vertices.)

If a child reads all the information straight from the flat picture, prompt them to turn the real solid to check for features the picture hides; the point is linking the 2-D view to the full 3-D object.
If a friend's claim is used ('a cube has 3 faces because they can only see 3'), ask the child to explain, turning the cube, why that friend missed some.
Reinforce that recounting from a different face should reach the same total once hidden features are included.
activities.rationale: Under-counting arises specifically from representing only the visible side of a 3-D figure and difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure; a predict-then-count routine that pairs a flat picture with the real solid and forces attention to the hidden back is intended to target this error.
sourceClaims: Students represent only the visible side of a 3-D figure and under-count features that are not directly visible, reflecting difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure — grounds the hidden-feature under-count when counting faces/edges/vertices.
learnerActions: Before counting, look at a cube and predict out loud how many edges it has altogether, saying your number first.
Look at a flat picture or drawing of the cube next to the real cube, and point out which edges, faces and corners in the picture are hidden from view.
Now trace and mark every edge on the real cube together, turning it so the far side comes into view and you find the hidden features from the picture.
Compare your prediction with the counted total of 12, and talk about the edges 'round the back' you could not see at first.
Repeat the routine for vertices and faces: each time, predict the visible-only number aloud first, then turn the real solid to reach the full totals (8 vertices, 6 faces).
activities.intendedInsight: A solid has features on its hidden far side that a flat picture does not show directly; a count based only on what you can see is too small, so you must turn the real object to catch every feature.

activities.title: Flat face versus curved surface
feedback: If a child says a cylinder has 3 faces, have them feel the round wall and ask whether it is flat like a face — then introduce 'curved surface' for it.
State explicitly which convention you are using, because schemes differ in how they describe curved solids; tell the child the rule you are following so they are not confused by other wording.
Reinforce by linking each flat face to the 2-D shape it matches (the circular faces of the cylinder, the square faces of the cube).
activities.rationale: The curved-surface distinction is an explicit curriculum convention that must be taught directly and stated, since schemes differ; feeling flat versus curved on real solids makes the distinction concrete.
sourceClaims: A curved surface is NOT a face and the curved line where a curved surface meets a flat face is NOT an edge; each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling solids while viewing images supports counting faces, edges and vertices. Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
learnerActions: Hold a cylinder and run a hand over the round wall and over the flat ends.
Count the flat faces — the two circles on a cylinder — and mark them.
Decide whether the round wall is a face: feel that it is not flat, and name it a 'curved surface' rather than a face.
Check the circle-to-curve boundary: is it a straight line where two flat faces meet? Under the convention we are using, if not, it is not counted as an edge (some schemes call it a curved edge).
Say the full description: a cylinder has two flat (circular) faces and one curved surface.
Then repeat with a cone and note it has one flat circular face, one curved surface, and a single pointed apex; say whether your scheme calls the apex a vertex, since no edges meet there.
Compare the solids directly with the cube to contrast flat faces with a curved surface.
activities.intendedInsight: Under the convention used here, a face is a flat surface and an edge is a straight line where two flat faces meet; the round part of a cylinder or cone is described as a curved surface, not a face, and its curved boundary is not counted as an edge, while a cone has a pointed apex that many schemes call a vertex even though no edges meet there.

activities.title: Faces as 2-D shapes and nets
feedback: For a flat-faced solid, if the number of shapes in the net does not match the touch-count of faces, recount both and find the discrepancy together; for curved solids, expect one extra piece that forms the curved surface.
Emphasise that the whole solid is not the same as one of its flat faces — the solid is a 3-D object, each face is a flat 2-D shape.

Note for the adult: a paper or card net has a slight real thickness and is a physical model of the ideal flat faces, which mathematically have no thickness. Ask the child about the flat 2-D shape the card represents (a square, a circle), not whether the card itself can be held or how thick it is.
activities.rationale: Connecting faces to 2-D shapes and to nets, where each face appears as a separate flat shape, reinforces the face count and addresses treating the whole solid as if it were a 2-D shape; the card is an approximation of the ideal flat face and this is made explicit in the activity.
sourceClaims: A curved surface is NOT a face and the curved line where a curved surface meets a flat face is NOT an edge; each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling solids while viewing images supports counting faces, edges and vertices. Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
learnerActions: For a solid you have counted (e.g. a cube), name the 2-D shape of each face (a square).
Unfold a net that folds up into the solid, laying out each face as a separate flat shape.

For a solid with only flat faces (e.g. a cube), count the flat shapes in the net and check the number matches the face count you found by touch; for a cylinder or cone, notice that one piece of the net becomes the curved surface, not a face.
Fold the net back into the solid to see each flat shape become a face.
Talk about the shape each face represents — a square, a circle — rather than about the card itself.
activities.intendedInsight: Each face of a 3-D solid is a 2-D shape; seeing the faces laid out flat in a net, each as its own shape, reinforces the face count and links 3-D solids to 2-D shapes.

activities.title: Check and explain the counts
feedback: Recall questions check the totals but do not by themselves build the counting strategy — if a count is wrong, return to handling and marking the real solid rather than just stating the right number.
A child who can give numbers but cannot say how a face differs from an edge may be reciting; probe the distinction and reteach by touch if needed.
activities.rationale: Direct questions and matching can check recall of counts but do not by themselves build the counting strategy or the face/edge/vertex distinction; they are best used as an end-check alongside asking the child to articulate the difference. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested design.
learnerActions: Answer direct questions such as 'How many edges does a cube have?' and match a solid to its face count.
Explain in your own words what makes a face different from an edge, and an edge different from a vertex.
Respond to a friend's wrong claim (e.g. 'a cube has 3 faces because I can only see 3') by explaining and demonstrating the correct count.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state the counts and articulate the difference between the three properties shows the properties are genuinely held apart, not just recited.

constraints: Tap-to-reveal or labelled-model activities that show a feature's name and definition on tap can teach vocabulary, but they display the answer rather than requiring the child to build the count or feel the flat-versus-curved distinction; use them to introduce terms, not to replace counting.

A flat-screen tally that colours each tapped face/edge/vertex can build the keep-them-distinct skill, but a flat screen makes it harder to reveal hidden features on the far side — a main source of miscounting; pair it with a solid the child can turn.

A rotatable on-screen 3-D model lets a child turn the solid to catch hidden features and can toggle to a cylinder for the curved-surface convention; it is one good way to surface the hidden-feature error, but real solids in the hand should confirm what the screen shows, and the on-screen model should be understood as a model of the solid, not the solid itself.
Scored recall questions check whether a child remembers counts; they do not on their own build the counting strategy or the property distinction, so use them as an end-check.
Always state explicitly which convention you are using for describing curved solids, because schemes differ.

Paper nets and card cutouts have a slight real thickness and are approximations of the ideal flat faces, which have no thickness; use them to represent faces but keep attention on the flat 2-D shape represented rather than on picking up or handling the card as a definition of the shape.
Recognising or recalling counts is not the same as producing a reliable count by handling and tracking features; expect production, not only recognition.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The cited study on under-counting hidden features (Sudirman et al., 2023) used a junior-high sample and documents the general obstacle, not the 6-7 age group specifically; treat its applicability to this age as indicative, not established.

The legacy source material asserted in places that no flat medium can target these challenges and that a 3-D interactive is uniquely necessary; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been softened to scoped affordances and limits.
The 'typically predicts around 9' figure for visible cube edges, and the 'stall at 3 or 4', are illustrative expectations, not measured results; use them as rough guides only.
The hypothetical friend's claim of '4 faces' is a child-level undercount used only as a wrong claim to refute; the correct cube total is 6 faces.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a cube. 'Predict how many edges this cube has altogether. Say your number before we trace them.' A child who counts only what they see typically predicts around 9 (the visible edges). Then trace and mark every edge together, turning the cube. The gap between the predicted number and the counted 12 — and their reaction to the edges 'round the back' — is the diagnostic: it exposes whether they reasoned about the whole solid or only its visible face.
probeDeeper: Here is a cylinder. How many flat faces does it have? Is the round curved part a face? How can you tell?
You counted the corners you can see. Turn the cube over — did you miss any? How many are there altogether?
Show me an edge. Now show me a vertex. What is the difference between them?
A friend says a cube has 4 faces because they can only see 4. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. A face is a flat surface (itself a 2-D shape — here a square); an edge is the straight line where two faces meet; a vertex/corner is the point where edges meet. The child counts systematically — turning the cube and tracking the hidden features — rather than counting only what faces them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Blurs the three properties, using 'side' or 'corner' loosely so face, edge and vertex run together when counting.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count by touch in a fixed order — colour each face, trace each edge, dot each vertex — naming the property each time, so the three stay distinct.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot say what makes a face different from an edge, calls edges 'sides', and gives inconsistent counts when asked to recount.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts only the visible faces/edges/vertices and misses the hidden ones — gives a cube 3 faces or 4 corners.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand them the solid to turn, marking each feature as it is counted (sticker on vertices, line on edges) so hidden ones are included; recount from a different face to confirm the total is stable.
errorPatterns.distractor: A cube has 3 faces and 4 corners.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States fewer than 6 faces / 8 vertices / 12 edges; on questioning, admits counting only what faced them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts a curved surface as a 'face' and the curved boundary line as an 'edge' — e.g. says a cylinder has 3 faces.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Feel the solids: a face is FLAT and an edge is a straight line where two flat faces meet; adopt 'curved surface' language for the round part, and state the scheme's convention explicitly since schemes differ.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a cylinder or cone, counts the curved surface as a face or calls the circle-to-curve boundary an edge.

responseLevels.gap: Blurs faces, edges and vertices (calls edges 'sides', cannot distinguish them) or counts only the visible features, giving inconsistent counts.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes face (flat 2-D surface), edge (line where two faces meet) and vertex (corner where edges meet), counts all three correctly including hidden features by tracking systematically, and transfers the distinction to a new solid — e.g. correctly says a cylinder has two flat faces and a curved surface (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Counts the faces, edges and vertices of a cube correctly when handling it and can define each, but lists the three counts without coordinating them, miscounts hidden features on a less familiar solid, or wrongly counts a curved surface as a face (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a real cube. Ask: 'Count the faces, then the edges, then the corners (vertices). Now tell me — what makes a face different from an edge?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three counts together with the face-vs-edge distinction separate a child who genuinely holds the three properties apart from one who blurs them (calling edges 'sides', miscounting because the properties run together) or who counts only the visible half. Reaching 12 edges in particular requires tracking hidden edges, so it is hard to fluke by looking; the second tier exposes whether the child can articulate the difference or is just reciting numbers.

Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 11–12 (KS3) — thermohaline circulation (the global conveyor belt) driven by temperature and salinity differences that make dense water sink; the AMOC transfers tropical heat toward Europe; oceans absorb >90% of excess heat and ~25–31% of human CO2; what happens to NW European climate if circulation weakens.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS3): chemistry/physics of density; geography 'how human and physical processes interact'; builds on the 9–11 ocean-as-climate-engine topic.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-ESS2-6 (ocean currents and regional climate) and MS-ESS3-5 (factors causing climate change) — density-driven circulation and the ocean's heat/carbon uptake.
• Operational details: the mechanism is DENSITY — cold and/or salty water is denser and SINKS, driving a global overturning loop that carries heat. AMOC = the Atlantic limb that warms NW Europe. Two headline sinks: the ocean has taken up >90% of the extra heat and ~25–31% of anthropogenic CO2, buffering the atmosphere (at the cost of warming and acidifying the sea). The tipping-point exploration: freshwater from melting ice reduces salinity/density, weakening the sink and potentially slowing AMOC → a paradoxically COLDER NW Europe in a warming world. Emphasise density as the driver and the counter-intuitive regional cooling.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~11, concrete): states cold/salty water sinks and currents carry heat; Tier B (transitional): explains the conveyor belt and that oceans absorb most excess heat + much CO2; Tier C (formal, ~12): reasons how added freshwater could weaken AMOC and cool NW Europe, linking density → sinking → heat transport.
bestPractices: Ground the whole system in DENSITY: demonstrate/show that colder and saltier water sinks below warmer/fresher water — the single mechanism behind the conveyor.
Build the conveyor stepwise (sinking in the North Atlantic → deep return flow → upwelling → warm surface return) rather than presenting the finished global loop.
Quantify the sinks with the verified figures (>90% of excess heat; ~25–31% of CO2) and unpack the trade-off: buffering the atmosphere WHILE warming and acidifying the ocean.
Explore the tipping point with a predict-then-check: add meltwater → fresher, less dense surface → weaker sinking → slower AMOC → counter-intuitive NW European cooling.
Confront the paradox explicitly — global warming could make one region colder — to deepen systems thinking and dispel 'warming = everywhere hotter'.
keyRepresentations: A density diagram: cold/salty water sinking beneath warm/fresh water
The global conveyor-belt map (sinking regions, deep return, upwelling, warm surface flow)
The AMOC limb with a NW Europe temperature readout
Sink bars: >90% of excess heat and ~25–31% of CO2 taken up by the ocean
commonMisconceptions: 'Currents are driven only by wind' — missing the density (temperature+salinity) driver of deep circulation.
'Warmer water sinks' or salinity is irrelevant — reversing the density logic (cold/salty sinks).
'Global warming means everywhere gets hotter' — not seeing that a weakened AMOC could cool NW Europe.
'The ocean's heat/CO2 uptake is harmless/free' — ignoring that it drives ocean warming and acidification.
Thinking the conveyor is fast/local rather than a slow, global loop taking centuries.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: thermohaline circulation (the global conveyor belt) is driven by DENSITY — cooling raises water's density and added salt raises it further, so cold, salty water becomes dense and sinks, especially in the North Atlantic, drawing warm tropical water north (the AMOC) and helping keep NW Europe mild (westerly winds blowing off the warm Atlantic also contribute). Oceans absorb more than 90% of excess heat and roughly 25–31% of human CO2, buffering the atmosphere while warming and acidifying the sea. The key counter-intuitive insight: freshwater from melting ice lowers surface salinity and density, which can weaken the sinking and slow the AMOC, potentially cooling NW Europe even as the globe warms. Teaching should build the mechanism density → sinking → heat transport, then explore the tipping point with predict-then-check. Note that in the salinity comparison temperature is held fixed: at the same temperature, salty water is denser than fresh.

activities.title: Chill, salt, and watch it plunge: the density demo
feedback: If a learner predicts 'it'll just mix' or 'cold water floats', surface the density gap: note that the demo shows the parcel plunging and flowing along the bottom, then ask what was different about it (it was both colder and saltier than the tank water).

If a learner explains the sinking by cold alone, add the salt explicitly: at the same temperature, salty water is denser than fresh. Contrast two equally-cold parcels — the saltier one sinks while the fresher one is less dense and stays above it — which is why fresh Arctic meltwater floats on the cold, salty ocean rather than sinking.
Reinforce that near the poles, surface water cools and, as sea ice forms, salt is left behind in the remaining water, making it cold, salty and dense enough to sink.
activities.rationale: A reason-before-observing (predict–observe–explain) density-current demo makes the driving mechanism concrete and diagnoses the 'cold alone' and 'it just mixes' misconceptions. Because the single pour would also sink from cold alone, the salty-vs-fresh comparison is made at a fixed temperature to isolate the salinity effect cleanly.
sourceClaims: Thermohaline circulation (the global conveyor belt) is driven by temperature- and salinity-controlled density differences that cause cold, salty water to sink; the AMOC transports warm water toward the North Atlantic/Europe, and freshening can weaken it.
learnerActions: Before pouring anything, PREDICT in writing what a small cup of chilled, salted, dyed water will do when poured gently into a clear tank of room-temperature water: mix evenly, float, or sink and spread along the bottom — and state your reason first.
Pour the chilled salty dyed water in gently and OBSERVE whether it plunges and flows along the floor as a density current.
EXPLAIN which property (or combination) made it sink, and describe how this models polar surface water starting the deep conveyor.
Compare two surface parcels that are at the SAME (cold) temperature: one salty, one fresh meltwater. Predict and reason which one sinks relative to the other and why that matters for the conveyor.
activities.intendedInsight: Water sinks when it is dense enough. Cooling water increases its density, and adding salt increases it further, so the densest surface water is both cold and salty. Holding temperature fixed, fresh water is less dense than salty water, so cold-and-salty water sinks beneath cold-but-fresh water — which is why fresh meltwater rides on top of the cold, salty ocean surface. This sinking is the pump that starts the deep ocean conveyor.

activities.title: Build the conveyor one step at a time
feedback: If a learner says wind pushes the whole circulation round, separate the two systems: wind moves the surface, but the deep loop is powered by dense water sinking — point back to the density-current demo.
If the loop is described as fast or local, emphasise it is a slow, global circulation taking centuries to complete.

For the wind-stops-for-a-day prediction: the deep overturning would not stop, because it is driven mainly by density differences and is a slow, centuries-long loop that one day cannot halt, though surface currents would start to change; use this to keep the two systems distinct (in the long run, winds also help the overturning, e.g. by driving upwelling).
Confirm the link: more/stronger sinking pulls more warm surface water north, which is one important reason NW Europe stays mild.
activities.rationale: Constructing the loop stepwise, rather than presenting a finished global diagram, helps learners trace causation and keeps the density driver distinct from wind-driven surface currents.
sourceClaims: Thermohaline circulation (the global conveyor belt) is driven by temperature- and salinity-controlled density differences that cause cold, salty water to sink; the AMOC transports warm water toward the North Atlantic/Europe, and freshening can weaken it.
learnerActions: Starting from the North Atlantic sinking you demonstrated, sequence the stages of the loop: dense water sinks → deep return flow south → upwelling → warm surface flow returns north.
On a global conveyor map, locate the sinking regions, the deep return limb, upwelling zones, and the warm surface return, and label the AMOC limb that carries heat toward NW Europe.

Explain in your own words why NW Europe is milder than its latitude would suggest, tying it to the warm surface water pulled north by the sinking (one important reason; westerly winds blowing in over the warm Atlantic also help).

Distinguish what wind drives (surface currents) from what powers the deep overturning (density differences): predict whether the deep conveyor would stop if the wind stopped for a day, and say what would and wouldn't change.
activities.intendedInsight: The conveyor is a slow, global overturning loop whose deep limb is powered by dense water sinking (not by wind), and this loop delivers tropical heat to NW Europe.

activities.title: The ocean's hidden sinks: heat and carbon
feedback: If a learner treats the uptake as harmless, point to acidification and ocean warming as the cost of the buffering.

If a learner expects all added heat to show up as air temperature, explain that over 90% of it has gone into the ocean, which is why air warming is slower than the total energy imbalance would suggest.
activities.rationale: Quantifying the sinks with verified figures and unpacking the trade-off counters the misconception that the ocean's uptake is cost-free.
sourceClaims: The ocean has absorbed more than 90% (NOAA cites ~91%) of the excess heat trapped in the Earth system by human-caused greenhouse warming.
The ocean absorbs roughly 25% (some NOAA/Science sources ~31%) of human CO2 emissions, buffering the atmosphere while acidifying seawater.
learnerActions: Record the two headline figures: the ocean has absorbed more than 90% (NOAA ~91%) of the extra heat humans have added, and roughly 25–31% of human CO2 emissions.
Explain where most of that extra heat has gone and why we don't feel all of it in the air.
State the trade-off: the ocean buffers the atmosphere, but at the cost of warming and acidifying the seawater.
Discuss why calling this uptake 'free' or 'harmless' is misleading.
activities.intendedInsight: The ocean is a vast buffer that soaks up most of the excess heat and much of the CO2, which slows atmospheric change but drives ocean warming and acidification.

activities.title: The meltwater paradox: could Europe get colder?
feedback: If a learner insists NW Europe must warm because the globe is warming, walk through the mechanism step by step: freshening lowers density, weakens sinking, and reduces the warm water delivered north.

If a learner treats a slowed conveyor as impossible, connect back to the reasoning: at the same temperature fresh water is less dense than salty water, so flooding the surface with fresh meltwater makes it less dense and reluctant to sink — the same effect at ocean scale.

Reinforce that the regional cooling is counter-intuitive but follows directly from density → sinking → heat transport, and is described as a potential weakening/slowing, not a guaranteed instantaneous shutdown.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check exploration of the freshening→weakening→cooling chain makes the tipping point felt and directly confronts the 'warming = everywhere hotter' misconception; a dynamic model lets learners manipulate drivers, while a diagram or demo can also carry the causal chain.
sourceClaims: Thermohaline circulation (the global conveyor belt) is driven by temperature- and salinity-controlled density differences that cause cold, salty water to sink; the AMOC transports warm water toward the North Atlantic/Europe, and freshening can weaken it.
learnerActions: PREDICT first: if a warming Arctic floods the North Atlantic with fresh meltwater, what happens to the surface water's salinity, its density, and the rate of sinking? Give your reasoning.
Trace the chain: meltwater → fresher surface → less dense → weaker sinking → slower AMOC → less warm water pulled north → regional cooling.
Explain the paradox explicitly: how could a warming world leave NW Europe colder?

Explore via a controllable model or diagram where you vary polar temperature, salinity, and meltwater input and watch the sinking rate, conveyor speed, and a NW Europe temperature readout respond (e.g. pour in meltwater and see the surface freshen, the sinking stall, and the readout fall).
activities.intendedInsight: Because the whole system hangs on dense water sinking, adding freshwater can weaken the heat delivery and cool a specific region even while the planet warms overall — global warming does not mean everywhere gets hotter.

constraints: Emphasise that density is the driver of the DEEP conveyor; wind drives surface currents. Keep these two systems distinct.

Density increases with cooling and increases further with added salt, so the densest sinking water is both cold and salty. At the same temperature, salty water is denser than fresh, so cold-salty sinks beneath cold-fresh; 'floating' of fresh meltwater is relative to the colder, saltier water below, not relative to warm water. Do not let learners settle for 'cold alone', and keep the salinity comparison at a fixed temperature.

The physical density-current demo (chilled, salted, dyed water in a tank) is an analogue/model of polar sinking, not the ocean itself; name it as a model when drawing conclusions. In the room-temperature tank the demonstrated parcel is both cold and salty, so the pour alone does not isolate salinity — use the fixed-temperature salty-vs-fresh comparison to make that point.
Use the verified ranges as stated: >90% (NOAA ~91%) of excess heat and ~25–31% of CO2. Do not present a single precise figure as the only correct value.

A static conveyor map or flap diagram can clearly present structure and the sink figures, but cannot by itself run the freshening→weakening→cooling chain; pair exposition with a predict-then-check exploration for the tipping point.

Multiple-choice items (density driver, conveyor sequence, sink percentages, meltwater→AMOC→NW Europe scenario) are suitable as companion assessment; recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit the learner's independent explanation of the mechanism.
A 3D globe can enrich the spatial picture of surface vs deep limbs; the causal reasoning can also be carried by a 2D cross-section plus map. Treat 3D as spatial enrichment, not a requirement.
Stress that the conveyor is a slow, global loop (centuries), not a fast or local flow, and describe AMOC weakening as a potential slowing rather than a guaranteed sudden shutdown.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the NOAA thermohaline-circulation claim as verified:false (unverified at capture); the two sink-figure claims are marked verified:true. Treat the density/AMOC mechanism claim as not independently re-checked here.
The CO2 uptake is stated as 'roughly 25%' in the topic description but '~25–31%' in the detailed pedagogy and sources; the broader range is retained to avoid overstating precision.

Density clarification: cooling or salting each raise density, so cold fresh water is denser than warm water and a cold-fresh parcel poured into a room-temperature tank would sink. Meltwater 'floats' only relative to the colder, saltier water it sits on. The demo as described pours cold-SALTY dyed water; the salty-vs-fresh contrast should be made at a fixed temperature, and this is maintained across the intended insights, feedback and constraints.

The single room-temperature demo does not by itself prove salinity is essential, because cold-fresh water would also sink in a warm tank; salinity's role is established by the fixed-temperature thought comparison. The intendedInsight was adjusted to say cooling raises density and salt raises it further, rather than implying both are strictly required.

The original listed a 2D interactive simulation as the preferred format; that preference reflects a catalog ranking, not established comparative efficacy. The underlying objectives (manipulate drivers, observe the loop and regional readout, predict-then-check the tipping point) are preserved and can be met by a physical demo, a dynamic model, or guided diagram work.

Original non-preferred formats (interactive image/flap map, companion multiple-choice assessment, 3D globe, oceanographer conversation) are preserved as scaffolds/companions in constraints and activities rather than discarded.

assess.poeTask: In a clear tank of room-temperature water, ask the student to PREDICT (and give their reason first) what a small cup of chilled, salted, dyed water will do when poured in gently: mix evenly, float, or sink and spread along the bottom? They pour and OBSERVE it plunge and flow along the floor as a density current. Then EXPLAIN: which property made it sink, and how this models polar water starting the deep conveyor. The reason-before-observing is the diagnostic — a 'it'll just mix' or 'cold floats' prediction reveals the density gap.
probeDeeper: Two parcels of surface water are equally cold; one is salty, one is fresh meltwater. Which sinks, and why does that matter for the conveyor?
If wind stopped entirely for a day, would the deep conveyor stop too? What would and wouldn't change?
Greenland ice melts and floods the North Atlantic with fresh water. Walk me through what that does to the sinking — and to Britain's winters.
The ocean has absorbed over 90% of the extra heat humans have added. Where has most of that heat gone — and why don't we feel all of it in the air?
assess.correctAnswer: The deep conveyor (thermohaline circulation) is driven by DENSITY, not wind: water becomes denser — and sinks — when it gets both cold AND salty. Near the poles, surface water cools and, as sea ice forms, leaves its salt behind in the remaining water, making it cold and salty and therefore dense enough to sink to the deep ocean; this sinking pulls warm surface water (e.g. via the AMOC / Gulf Stream) north to replace it, which is why NW Europe is milder than its latitude suggests. Wind drives SURFACE currents, but the deep overturning is powered by temperature and salinity differences. If the sinking weakened (e.g. lots of fresh meltwater lowering the salinity/density), that heat delivery could slow and NW Europe could actually get COLDER even in a warming world.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Ocean currents are all driven by wind' — applies the surface-current rule to the deep conveyor.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two systems: wind moves the surface; the deep loop is powered by dense water sinking. Show a density-current demo.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — wind pushes the surface water along, and that drags the whole conveyor round.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says wind pushes the whole circulation; can't name density or sinking as the deep driver.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Water sinks just because it's cold' — has the temperature half but misses salinity's role in density.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the salt: cold AND salty = dense. Contrast cold-but-fresh meltwater (which floats) with cold-salty water (which sinks).
errorPatterns.distractor: It sinks only because it's cold — saltiness has nothing to do with it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains sinking by cold alone; surprised that saltiness (from sea-ice formation/evaporation) is essential.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A warming world just warms everywhere, so Europe gets hotter' — can't see how warming could cool a region via a weakened AMOC.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the mechanism: meltwater freshens the North Atlantic → less sinking → less warm water pulled north → regional cooling despite global warming.
errorPatterns.distractor: Impossible — if the planet is warming, Europe can only get warmer, not colder.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists NW Europe must warm; treats a slowed conveyor as impossible or irrelevant.

responseLevels.gap: Attributes the deep conveyor to wind and/or 'cold alone'; expects uniform warming everywhere.
responseLevels.full: Explains deep overturning as density-driven (cold + salty → sinks), distinguishes it from wind-driven surface currents, links it to NW European mildness, and reasons that freshening could slow the AMOC and cool the region even as the globe warms.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the conveyor moves heat and that dense water sinks, but lists these — can't tie sinking to combined cold+salt density, or reason about a weakened AMOC cooling a region.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The 'global ocean conveyor belt' carries warm surface water north across the Atlantic, and somewhere near the poles that water sinks and returns south in the deep. A student says 'the water sinks up there simply because it's cold, and the whole thing is driven by the wind pushing the surface along'. Is wind the engine of the DEEP conveyor, and what actually makes the water sink? Explain what sinks and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student with the naive model credits wind and says 'cold alone' makes it sink, and predicts a warming world simply warms everywhere; a student with the concept names density from combined cold+salt as the driver, separates deep overturning from wind-driven surface currents, and can reason that a weakened AMOC could cool NW Europe. The 'what sinks and why' clause blocks a hand-wavy 'the current goes round' answer.
