pedagogy.summary: Composing 2-D shapes — combining triangles, squares, trapezoids and half-/quarter-circles into composite shapes and finding new shapes within them — develops through Clements & Sarama's trajectory from unsystematic Piece Assembly, through trial-and-error Picture Making, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION and substituting equivalent pieces. It is taught best with outline (puzzle) tasks engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, prompting children to choose pieces by side length and angle rather than general appearance, and asking them to decompose a composite and name the simpler shapes that make it up.
bestPractices: Use outline puzzles engineered to require the next level of thinking (e.g. remove one internal guide line to push from Piece Assembler to Picture Maker).
Nudge from trial and error to anticipation: 'Can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
Have children choose pieces by attributes — matching side lengths and angles — and use turns and flips intentionally.
Ask children to decompose the composite ('what smaller shapes make this up?') and to find new shapes within it (two triangles make a square; two half-circles make a circle).
Pitch tasks one level beyond the child's current level and fade support — this out-performed jumping straight to the target level (Clements et al. 2019, effect size .55).
keyRepresentations: Pattern blocks and tangram pieces
Outline puzzle cards of increasing difficulty
Two triangles composing a square or larger triangle; half-circles composing a circle
Angle-and-side-length matching between a gap and a piece
commonMisconceptions: Assembles by trial and error with no advance plan and does not anticipate the new shape (an expected early trajectory level, not a fault).
Chooses pieces by general shape only, not by matching angles and side lengths, so pieces do not fit the gap.
Sees the composite as one whole and cannot decompose it into the simpler shapes it is made from.

learn.summary: Children compose 2-D shapes — combining triangles, squares, trapezoids, and half-/quarter-circles into composite shapes and finding new shapes within them. The goal is to move along Clements & Sarama's trajectory: from unsystematic trial-and-error assembly (Piece Assembler), through trial-and-error picture making, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION — choosing a piece because its angle and side length will fit, using turns and flips intentionally, and decomposing a composite back into the simpler shapes that make it up. The core teaching medium is manipulating flat pieces into outline (puzzle) tasks engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, with immediate fit/misfit feedback.

activities.title: Fill the outline with the right pieces
feedback: If the child places pieces at random until one fits and cannot say in advance which will fit: this is an expected early trajectory level, not an error — do NOT mark it wrong. Offer a puzzle just one step ahead (for example, remove a single internal guide line) and ask 'Can you see what will fit before you place it?'
If the child grabs a triangle of the wrong size or angle that won't fit: say 'This gap has a slanted edge — which piece has an edge that matches it?' and compare edges and corners before placing.
When a piece snaps into place because its angle and side matched, name it: 'You picked that because its edge was the same length as the gap.'
activities.rationale: Outline puzzles engineered to require the next level of thinking, with pieces chosen by angle and side length and intentional rotation/reflection, are the tasks through which this trajectory was researched. Pitching one level beyond the child's current level and fading support is the recommended progression.
sourceClaims: Shape composition progresses from the Piece Assembler and Picture Maker levels (building by unsystematic trial and error, choosing pieces by general shape or side length) to the Shape Composer level (composing with anticipation, choosing pieces by angle as well as side length and using rotations and reflections intentionally); outline puzzles are engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, and instruction one trajectory level ahead out-performed skipping to the target level (effect size .55).
learnerActions: Give the child flat shape pieces (for example, pattern blocks, tangram pieces, or cut-out triangles, squares, rectangles, trapezoids, half-circles and quarter-circles) and an outline puzzle card that those pieces can cover exactly. Standard pattern blocks and tangrams do not include half-circles or quarter-circles, and tangrams have no trapezoid, so add cut-out pieces for any shapes the set lacks.
As they work, ask them to say which shape they are using and why.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Will this piece fit this gap? How do you know?' — encouraging a prediction from the gap's edges and corners.
When a piece doesn't fit, have them compare the gap's edge length and corner angle to the piece, then choose one that matches.
Let them use turns and flips to make a piece fit, naming what they did ('I flipped it so the slanted edge lines up').
activities.intendedInsight: A piece can be chosen in advance by matching its side length and angle to the gap, rather than by trying pieces at random until one happens to fit.

activities.title: Same pieces, different shapes
feedback: If the child treats each arrangement as unrelated, overlay or re-join the same two right-angled triangles in front of them to show the square and the larger triangle come from the same pieces.
Praise the moment they predict a new shape before building it: that is composing with anticipation.
activities.rationale: Composing new shapes from the same component pieces, using rotation and reflection intentionally, is explicitly required by the trajectory and the grade-1 standard. The square/larger-triangle example only holds for congruent right-isosceles triangles, so pieces are chosen accordingly.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 geometry requires pupils to compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles and quarter-circles) to create a composite shape, and to compose new shapes from the composite shape.

Shape composition progresses from the Piece Assembler and Picture Maker levels (building by unsystematic trial and error, choosing pieces by general shape or side length) to the Shape Composer level (composing with anticipation, choosing pieces by angle as well as side length and using rotations and reflections intentionally); outline puzzles are engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, and instruction one trajectory level ahead out-performed skipping to the target level (effect size .55).
learnerActions: Using two congruent right-isosceles (tangram-style) triangles, have the child join them along their long (hypotenuse) edges to form a square. Then have them rejoin the same two triangles along one of the shorter equal edges, mirrored so the two right-angle corners sit side by side, to form a larger triangle instead. Joining them along a shorter edge with one triangle turned the other way makes a parallelogram, which is another new shape worth naming. (Note for the adult: two equilateral pattern-block triangles would instead make a rhombus, not a square, so choose right-isosceles triangles for this square example.)
Have them put two half-circles together to form a circle, and explore what else the pieces can make.
Ask: 'You made a square from two triangles — can you make a different shape with those same two pieces?'
activities.intendedInsight: The same pieces can compose different shapes depending on how they are turned and joined — composing is a deliberate, reversible act.

activities.title: Find the shapes hiding inside
feedback: If the child names only the whole composite and cannot show its parts, lift and overlay the pieces to reveal the two right-angled triangles inside the square, then hunt together for 'shapes hidden within shapes'.
Confirm when they both name a part and show where it sits in the whole.
activities.rationale: Decomposing the composite and naming its component shapes is a listed objective in the row's own evidence and directly addresses the misconception that a composite is one undifferentiated whole. Neither cited source claim directly attests to decomposition, so no source claim is attached here.
learnerActions: Show the child a completed composite shape and ask 'Which smaller shapes are hiding inside this?'
Have them lift and separate the pieces to reveal, for example, that the square is made of two right-angled (right-isosceles) triangles or the circle of two half-circles.
Ask them to name each component shape as they take the composite apart, then rebuild it.
activities.intendedInsight: A composite shape is built from — and can be pulled apart into — simpler named shapes; seeing the whole does not mean you can only see the whole.

activities.title: Reference and post-check (supporting activities)
feedback: If a child can match or name parts but still fits pieces by trial and error, return to the hands-on outline puzzles — matching checks recognition, not the composing action.
Use the spoken prediction to surface anticipation, then have the child actually place the piece to confirm.
activities.rationale: A static decomposition display supports naming parts but does not exercise the act of fitting pieces; a matching/sequence check can verify which pieces make a shape but not the composing action; a spoken prediction can prompt anticipation but the manipulative act carries the learning. These supports are useful alongside, not instead of, hands-on composition.
learnerActions: As a reference, show a composite alongside a reveal of its decomposition ('this is made of two triangles') to support naming the parts.
As a post-check after hands-on building, have the child match composites to the component pieces that make them, or sequence which pieces make a given shape.
Use a short spoken prediction before a build: 'Which piece will fit here, and why?'
activities.intendedInsight: Naming and matching parts consolidates vocabulary and checks understanding, but the composing skill itself is built through the hands-on fitting activities above.

constraints: The core skill is a manipulative, spatial act: children must physically (or on-screen) fit, turn, and flip pieces into outlines. Recognition-only tasks (matching a composite to its parts, naming shapes) check understanding but do not elicit the independent act of composing.
A static composite with a tap/reveal of its decomposition is a reference and naming aid; it cannot exercise choosing and fitting pieces.
This is a planar concept; it needs a flat working surface (physical blocks or a 2-D screen). A 3-D rendering is not needed and can distract from the flat composition being learned.
Spoken prediction ('which piece will fit?') is valuable for eliciting anticipation but should accompany actual placement, not replace it.
Trial-and-error assembly with no advance plan is an expected early trajectory LEVEL, not a fault to be marked wrong; respond by offering a puzzle one step ahead and fading support.

Engineer puzzles to require the next level of thinking (e.g. remove one internal guide line at a time) and pitch one level beyond the child's current level; the cited study reports this out-performed jumping straight to the target level (effect size .55).
For the 'two triangles make a square' example, use congruent right-isosceles (tangram-style) triangles; two equilateral pattern-block triangles form a rhombus, not a square.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims support the learning-trajectory principle and the grade-1 composition standard; they do not establish that these specific activity designs were tested, nor do they establish comparative efficacy of any particular medium.

Decomposition ('find the shapes hiding inside') is drawn from the row's objective, evidence and misconception list; neither sources[].claim directly attests to decomposition, so the decomposition activity carries no source claim.

The legacy row asserted that 3-D 'adds nothing and can mislead' and that dialogue 'cannot carry' composing. These have been softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements (planar concept needs a flat surface; spoken prediction supports but does not replace placement), since the cited sources do not establish such necessity or medium superiority.

The original row's keyRepresentations/evidence stated 'two triangles compose a square' without specifying triangle type; standard equilateral pattern-block triangles cannot make a square (they make a rhombus), so the corrected activity specifies congruent right-isosceles (tangram) triangles for that example.

Overlaying/separating pattern-block pieces assumes idealised flat shapes; physical blocks have slight thickness, which is acceptable as an approximation of the planar shapes represented and need not be treated as an error.

probeDeeper: Before you place that piece — will it fit this gap? How do you know?
You made a square from two triangles — can you make a different shape with those same two triangles?
Which smaller shapes are hiding inside this composite?
This gap has a slanted edge — which piece has an edge that matches it?
assess.correctAnswer: Selects pieces by their attributes and places them to fill the outline exactly, choosing pieces with anticipation rather than only trial and error; combines two triangles into a square (and, e.g., two half-circles into a circle); and decomposes and renames the composite by its component shapes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assembles by trial and error with no advance plan and does not anticipate the composite shape being made
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark this 'wrong' — it is an expected level; offer a puzzle one step ahead (remove just one internal guide line) and prompt 'can you see what will fit before you place it?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places pieces at random until one fits and cannot say in advance which piece will fit the gap

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses pieces by general shape only, not by matching angles and side lengths, so the piece does not fill the gap
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the gap's edges and corners to the piece before placing — match by side length and angle
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Grabs a triangle of the wrong size or angle that will not fit the space

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees the composite as one undifferentiated whole and cannot find the simpler shapes within it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lift and overlay the pieces to show the square is two triangles; hunt for shapes hidden within shapes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the whole composite but cannot show the two triangles inside the square

responseLevels.gap: Places pieces by trial and error with no plan and cannot decompose the composite into simpler shapes.
responseLevels.full: Selects pieces by side length and angle with anticipation, fills the outline efficiently, and decomposes and recomposes the composite (two triangles make a square; two half-circles make a circle), naming the parts.
responseLevels.partial: Fills the outline, often by trial and error, and names some pieces, but does not choose by matching angles and sides or reliably find new shapes within the composite.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are pattern-block pieces — triangles, squares, trapezoids and some half-circles and quarter-circles. Cover this outline puzzle exactly using the pieces, and as you work tell me which shapes you are using. Then show me two triangles making a square, and tell me one other shape you could make from the pieces.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the build separates the Shape Composer, who picks a piece knowing from its sides and angles that it will fit, from the Piece Assembler, who tries pieces at random until one happens to fit. Asking the child to make a square from two triangles and to name another composable shape exposes whether they see composites as built from — and decomposable into — simpler shapes.

sources.claim: Shape composition progresses from the Piece Assembler and Picture Maker levels (building by unsystematic trial and error, choosing pieces by general shape or side length) to the Shape Composer level (composing with anticipation, choosing pieces by angle as well as side length and using rotations and reflections intentionally); outline puzzles are engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, and instruction one trajectory level ahead out-performed skipping to the target level (effect size .55).
sources.source: Clements, Sarama, Baroody, Joswick & Wolfe (2019), 'Evaluating the Efficacy of a Learning Trajectory for Early Shape Composition', American Educational Research Journal 56(6) (ERIC ED594902)

sources.claim: Grade 1 geometry requires pupils to compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles and quarter-circles) to create a composite shape, and to compose new shapes from the composite shape.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 1.G.A.2

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Aerobic Respiration

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Cellular respiration):** statutory — "aerobic and anaerobic respiration in living organisms, including the breakdown of organic molecules to enable all the other chemical processes necessary for life; a word summary for aerobic respiration".

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** MS-LS1-7 — "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS1-7]"; secondary DCI PS3.D (verbatim): "Cellular respiration in plants and animals involve chemical reactions with oxygen that release stored energy. In these processes, complex molecules containing carbon react with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and other materials." Strong UK/US alignment.

- **Operational details:** Two ideas carry the topic. (1) Aerobic respiration RELEASES energy from glucose using oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water — word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released). It happens in EVERY living cell, specifically in the mitochondria, all the time — not just during exercise. (2) The single most important distinction: respiration is NOT breathing. Breathing (ventilation) is the muscular movement of air in and out of the lungs; respiration is the chemical release of energy inside cells. Breathing and heart rate rise during exercise precisely to supply more oxygen and glucose to — and remove more CO2 from — respiring muscle cells. Note 'energy released' rather than 'energy made' (energy is not created). Keep the mitochondria link concrete (ties back to the cell-parts topic) and keep the equation as a word summary, not a balanced symbol equation, at KS3.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal / quantitative-adjacent). The child writes and explains the word equation, states respiration occurs in mitochondria in all cells, explains WHY exercise raises breathing/heart rate (oxygen and glucose supply, CO2 removal), and clearly separates respiration from breathing. Not yet expected: ATP, balanced symbol equation, or the biochemical stages.
bestPractices: Attack the respiration≠breathing confusion head-on and early — it is the defining misconception and everything else depends on separating the cellular chemistry from lung ventilation.
Insist respiration happens in EVERY cell ALL the time (in mitochondria), not only during exercise — exercise just increases the rate.
Teach the word equation as a story of transfer: glucose + oxygen go in, energy is RELEASED (not made), CO2 and water come out; check pupils say 'released', not 'created'.
Use the exercise link as the motivating phenomenon — measure pulse/breathing before and after activity and explain it as the body ramping up supply to respiring cells.
Anchor the location to the mitochondria the pupils met in the cell-parts topic, closing the loop between structure and function.
keyRepresentations: The word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released)
A cell/mitochondrion 'engine' taking in glucose and oxygen and releasing energy plus CO2 and water
A supply-chain diagram: lungs→blood→cells (oxygen and glucose IN) and the reverse for CO2, distinguishing breathing from respiration
Before/after-exercise pulse and breathing-rate data linked to increased demand
commonMisconceptions: Believing respiration IS breathing — conflating cellular energy release with lung ventilation.
Thinking respiration only happens during exercise or only in the lungs — it occurs constantly in every cell's mitochondria.
Saying respiration 'makes' or 'creates' energy — energy is released/transferred from glucose, not created.
Thinking plants don't respire (only photosynthesise) — all living cells, including plant cells, respire all the time.
Assuming the purpose of breathing faster is to 'get rid of tiredness' rather than to supply more oxygen and remove more CO2 for respiration.

learn.summary: Aerobic respiration for ages 12–13: respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen, mainly in the mitochondria of living plant and animal cells, ALL the time (not only during exercise), producing carbon dioxide and water — word summary: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released). The defining goal is to separate respiration (the chemical release of energy inside cells) from breathing/ventilation (the muscular movement of air in and out of the lungs), and to explain why breathing and heart rate rise during exercise: faster breathing brings in more oxygen and removes more CO2, and a faster heart rate delivers more oxygen and glucose to, and carries more CO2 away from, respiring muscle cells. Keep it as a word summary, not a balanced symbol equation; do not yet require ATP or biochemical stages. Activities below include a driveable supply model, a consolidation and recognition check, a tap-to-reveal supply-chain image, a Socratic exchange, and a predict–observe–explain investigation with germinating vs boiled peas.

activities.title: Power a runner from the inside: driveable cell-and-body model
feedback: If the learner only speeds breathing but ignores the cell, point to the labelled boundary: pumping the lungs faster is breathing — where is the energy actually released?
If the energy gauge drops, prompt: supply has fallen behind the mitochondria's demand — what two inputs do the cells need more of?
When the figure stands still, highlight that the mitochondria are still consuming glucose and oxygen: respiration has not switched off.
Confirm the word equation only once the outputs (CO2 and water) and the released energy are correctly traced from the flows; check the learner says energy is 'released', not 'made' or 'created'.
activities.rationale: NGSS MS-LS1-7 asks for a model of how matter and energy move through an organism; a two-level driveable model is proposed to make the 'every cell, all the time' point and the respiration≠breathing boundary visible and manipulable, grounding the word summary in a process the learner has driven. The ramp-up-with-demand mechanism (sliders, energy gauge, visible flows) is an optional interaction example, not a required product, and its comparative efficacy is untested.
sourceClaims: NGSS PS3.D (secondary DCI for MS-LS1-7): 'Cellular respiration in plants and animals involve chemical reactions with oxygen that release stored energy. In these processes, complex molecules containing carbon react with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and other materials.'
learnerActions: Set an on-screen figure to rest or sprint and watch the zoomed-in muscle cell and its mitochondria below.
On 'sprint', raise breathing rate and heart rate (via sliders/controls) to keep oxygen and glucose flowing down the supply chain to the mitochondria.
Watch the mitochondrion 'engine' consume glucose and oxygen and release energy (shown as the legs doing work), plus CO2 and water as outputs.
Deliberately let supply fall behind demand and observe the energy gauge sag and the runner flag; then restore supply.

Read the labelled boundary that stays on screen: 'breathing = air in/out of lungs; respiration = this reaction in the cell', and note the reaction keeps running even when the figure just stands still.
Assemble the word equation from the glucose and oxygen flowing in and the CO2 and water flowing out.
activities.intendedInsight: Breathing (moving air at the lungs) and respiration (energy released by a reaction in the mitochondria) are different processes; respiration runs in every cell all the time, and exercise raises its rate so breathing/heart rate must rise to supply oxygen and glucose and remove CO2.

activities.title: Consolidate and check the key facts and misconception
feedback: For a 'breathing vs respiration' item, confirm by reference to location and mechanism: air movement at the lungs = breathing; energy-releasing reaction in the cell = respiration.
If a learner picks 'energy created', restate: respiration releases stored chemical energy from glucose; energy is not created from nothing.
If a learner says only animals respire, note that plant cells respire too — plants both photosynthesise (in cells with chloroplasts) AND respire (in all their living cells).
activities.rationale: These facts are crisply assessable, so a short recognition/recall set consolidates and checks the core knowledge and the central misconception. This format mainly confirms recall and recognition and does not by itself elicit the dynamic supply reasoning; pair it with a construction or investigation task.
learnerActions: Complete a fill-in-the-blank of the word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released).
Decide for several short scenarios whether each describes breathing or respiration, and justify the choice.
Answer items on 'energy is released, not created' and 'all living cells respire, including plant cells'.
activities.intendedInsight: The word equation, the location (mitochondria), and the respiration-vs-breathing distinction are crisp, checkable facts the learner can state independently.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal supply chain: lungs → blood → cell → mitochondrion
feedback: When the learner contrasts the two flaps, confirm the mechanism: the lungs move air; the mitochondrion runs the energy-releasing reaction.

If the learner expects the chain to change with activity, note that this static image shows the players and relationships but does not animate the ramp-up with demand — use the driveable model for that.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal image clearly presents the components, the supply relationship and the equation, and the lift-the-flap contrast makes the key distinction concrete. Its stated limit is that a static layout does not show the dynamic ramp-up with increasing demand.
learnerActions: Tap each stage of a lungs-to-cell chain to reveal what is happening there.
Lift the flap on the lungs vs the mitochondrion to contrast 'breathing happens here' with 'respiration happens here'.
Reveal the word equation at the cell, tracing oxygen and glucose IN and CO2 and water out.
activities.intendedInsight: The players (lungs, blood, cell, mitochondrion) and the equation can be laid out explicitly, and the lungs-vs-mitochondrion contrast directly addresses the breathing/respiration confusion.

activities.title: Socratic exchange with an exercise physiologist
feedback: If the learner says breathing provides the energy, redirect: breathing moves air — where is the energy-releasing reaction, and what do the muscle cells need more of?

Accept the answer once the learner locates energy release in the cell/mitochondria and frames faster breathing as bringing in more oxygen and removing CO2, and faster heart rate as delivering oxygen and glucose to the cells in the blood.
activities.rationale: A guided dialogue can prompt the learner to state and repair the misconception in their own words. It does not display the matter/energy flows, so pair it with the model or supply-chain image when the visible mechanism matters.
learnerActions: Respond in role to an exercise physiologist asking 'Why are you panting after a sprint? Where does the energy actually come from?'
When tempted to say 'breathing gives energy', answer the follow-up: where does the reaction actually happen, and what is breathing for?

Reach the conclusion that extra breathing brings in more oxygen and removes more CO2, while a faster heart rate carries oxygen and glucose to respiring cells (and CO2 away), where the energy is released.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the reasoning out loud surfaces and corrects the breathing/respiration muddle through the learner's own explanation.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: germinating vs boiled peas
feedback: A prediction of 'no change' because nothing is exercising or breathing signals the exercise/breathing misconception — revisit that respiration is continuous and cellular.
If the learner is surprised the living peas warm, connect the warming to energy released by respiration in the peas' living cells.

Probe extensions: Does a potato in a dark cupboard respire, and how could you tell? Does a plant respire? If a person held their breath for a while, do their cells stop respiring immediately, or is something else going on?
activities.rationale: This predict-then-observe design makes the pre-observation reason diagnostic: the learner's stated 'why' reveals whether they think respiration needs exercise or breathing, and any warming of the living peas compared with the control provides evidence that respiration is continuous in living cells. Boiled (dead), disinfected peas act as the control, so warming from microbes or from the setup itself can be ruled out.
learnerActions: Set up two vacuum flasks, each with a temperature probe and loosely plugged with cotton wool so air can get in: one with living germinating peas, one with peas that were boiled (dead) then cooled. Rinse both batches in dilute disinfectant first so microbes on the peas cannot respire and warm either flask.
BEFORE observing, predict which flask (if either) will warm up over a day, and explain WHY.
Over the day, record the temperatures and compare them with the prediction.

Explain the result: if the living peas warm while the boiled peas do not, that is evidence that respiration releases energy (some of it as heat) even in still organisms that do not breathe; relate this to 'every living cell, all the time'.
activities.intendedInsight: Respiration releases energy continuously in living cells, independent of breathing or exercise — a resting organism with no lungs or ventilation (germinating peas) is expected to warm because its cells respire, while the disinfected boiled-pea control should not.

constraints: Keep the equation as a word summary (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy released), not a balanced symbol equation, at this level.
Do not yet require ATP, the balanced symbol equation, or the biochemical stages.
Always use 'energy released'/'transferred', never 'energy made' or 'created' — energy is not created.
Anchor the location to the mitochondria met in the earlier cell-parts topic, linking structure to function.

The recognition/recall check mainly confirms facts and the misconception; it does not by itself elicit independent construction of the supply reasoning — pair it with the model, dialogue, or investigation.
The static supply-chain image shows players and relationships but does not animate the ramp-up with demand; use the driveable model when the dynamic mechanism matters.
The Socratic dialogue surfaces and repairs reasoning but does not display the matter/energy flows.

In the pea investigation, use proper safety when boiling. Plug the vacuum flasks loosely with cotton wool rather than sealing them airtight, so the living peas keep getting oxygen. Rinse both batches of peas in dilute disinfectant so microbes do not respire and warm the dead control. The boiled peas are the dead control and must be cooled before going into the flask.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a 3D interactive as 'poor' because the concept is chemical/supply rather than spatial. This is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, so it is omitted rather than asserted as '3D adds nothing'; a 2D model is proposed on the stated affordance that it makes the flows and boundary manipulable.

The source's claim that the driveable model is the only way to make the distinction 'felt' is a design preference, not established comparative efficacy; multiple activities (image, dialogue, investigation) are retained as genuine alternatives.
One error-pattern entry referenced a reteach prerequisite id (mt_V9SQS9gLFw) for the respiration=breathing misconception; this is an internal catalog link, dropped from learner-facing guidance.

The pea investigation assumes measurable warming over a day in sealed vacuum flasks; actual temperature rise depends on pea mass, germination vigour and insulation, so treat observed magnitudes as condition-dependent rather than guaranteed.

Activity 1 cites the NGSS PS3.D claim, which supports the respiration chemistry the model represents (oxygen in, CO2/water out, stored energy released) but not the comparative efficacy of a driveable model; the modelling design remains an unvalidated proposal and the medium claim is not evidenced by any source.

assess.poeTask: Set up two sealed vacuum flasks each with a temperature probe: one holding living germinating peas, one holding peas that have been boiled (dead) then cooled. Before revealing anything, ask the child to predict which flask (if either) will warm up over a day, and WHY. The pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part: a child who thinks respiration needs exercise or breathing predicts no change; a child with the cellular idea predicts the living peas warm up because respiration releases energy even in still, non-breathing organisms.
probeDeeper: You said she breathes faster when she runs — what is that extra breathing actually FOR; what do the muscle cells need more of?
Does a potato left in a dark cupboard respire? How could you tell?
If she held her breath for a while, do her cells stop respiring immediately, or is something else going on?
Where exactly in the cell does aerobic respiration take place, and why does that location matter?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — respiration happens in every living cell all the time, releasing energy from glucose using oxygen (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water) to keep the body working even at rest; it is not the same as breathing and does not switch off when she stops exercising.

errorPatterns.pattern: respiration is the same as breathing ('respiring just means taking breaths in and out')
errorPatterns.nextMove: separate the words explicitly: breathing = the physical movement of air; respiration = the chemical release of energy inside every cell; show a leaf cell respires though it has no lungs
errorPatterns.revealedBy: in the reason tier justifies 'yes' with 'because she's still breathing', or uses the two words interchangeably

errorPatterns.pattern: respiration only happens during exercise ('you only respire when you run, that's why you puff')
errorPatterns.nextMove: point out the heart still beats and the brain still works at rest, all needing energy from respiration; exercise raises the RATE, it does not switch respiration on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answers 'no' on the grounds that she is resting

errorPatterns.pattern: only animals respire; plants photosynthesise instead of respiring
errorPatterns.nextMove: establish respiration is universal to living cells, plant and animal; plants both photosynthesise AND respire
errorPatterns.revealedBy: surfaces on the probe when asked whether a plant respires

errorPatterns.pattern: respiration 'makes' or 'creates' energy
errorPatterns.nextMove: reframe as releasing stored chemical energy from glucose, not creating energy from nothing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says respiration produces/creates energy rather than releasing it from glucose

responseLevels.gap: Equates respiration with breathing, or says respiration only happens during exercise; cannot write the word equation.
responseLevels.full: Explains respiration as continuous energy release in every cell's mitochondria, distinct from breathing, and relates raised breathing/heart rate during exercise to greater oxygen and glucose demand — transferring the idea to a resting body or a plant.
responseLevels.partial: Writes glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water and knows it releases energy, but lists these as separate facts — cannot connect why breathing and heart rate rise during exercise to the cells' increased oxygen/glucose demand, or cannot state that respiration is continuous and cellular.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A footballer sits completely still on the bench, not moving at all. Are the cells in her body still respiring right now? Say yes or no — and tell me how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who confuses respiration with breathing, or thinks respiration only happens during exercise, answers 'no, she's resting' or 'only when she runs'; a child holding the cellular idea says yes and separates the constant cellular process from the raised breathing rate that exercise demands. The reason tier is essential because both types could guess 'yes'.

sources.claim: DfE KS3 Biology statutory content requires 'aerobic and anaerobic respiration in living organisms, including the breakdown of organic molecules to enable all the other chemical processes necessary for life; a word summary for aerobic respiration'.
sources.source: DfE National curriculum in England: science programmes of study — Key stage 3 Biology (Cellular respiration)

sources.claim: NGSS PS3.D (secondary DCI for MS-LS1-7): 'Cellular respiration in plants and animals involve chemical reactions with oxygen that release stored energy. In these processes, complex molecules containing carbon react with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and other materials.'

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-6 (Y1). Add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, INCLUDING zero (14+5=19, 17−3=14, and the +0/−0 case). The procedural application of within-20 bonds; also where the identity role of zero is established.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including 0'; non-statutory: pupils 'realise the effect of adding or subtracting 0'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.5/6 relate counting to addition/subtraction and add/subtract within 20; the additive identity (n+0=n) is an early property.
• Operational details — Use bonds and within-20 strategies to calculate, not counting-all. Give the +0/−0 case explicit attention because young children often assume every operation must change the number — model with objects that adding or taking nothing leaves the quantity unchanged. Keep to the 0-20 range including the teen boundary (crossing ten), reinforcing making-ten. Record with number sentences.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): add/subtract within 20 using bonds or a fast strategy for non-bridging cases (14+5). Tier B (age 5-6): handle bridging cases (8+7) and correctly compute +0/−0. Tier C (age 6): calculate fluently within 20 and explain why adding/subtracting 0 leaves the number unchanged.
bestPractices: Calculate using known bonds and making-ten rather than counting all, so this procedural work reinforces the fact base.
Give +0 and −0 explicit, concrete treatment (adding/taking nothing) to establish zero as the additive identity and dispel 'every operation changes the number'.
Attend to the teen boundary: bridging-ten cases (8+7, 15−7) need the making-ten strategy, not ones-counting.
Record calculations as number sentences and connect to the child's representations to keep meaning attached.
Vary which quantity is unknown lightly to connect with missing-number work.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames / rekenrek for within-20 sums and bridging
Empty number line for jumps (including a 0 jump that stays put)
Part-whole model linking the calculation to bonds
Objects demonstrating 'add nothing / take nothing' for the zero case
Number track 0-20
commonMisconceptions: Assuming +0 or −0 must change the number (giving 5+0=6 or 5−0=4).
Counting all/counting on in ones across the ten boundary instead of making ten.
Errors at the teen boundary (miscounting when crossing 10).
Ignoring the operation and just combining the two numbers seen.
Reversing subtraction to keep the larger number first without noticing the meaning changes.

learn.summary: For ages 5-6 (UK Y1), learners add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers within 20, including the +0/−0 case, using known number bonds and making-ten rather than counting all. Core aims: fluent within-20 calculation, correct bridging across ten (e.g. 8+7), and understanding that adding or subtracting zero leaves a quantity unchanged. Activities centre on acting out calculations with ten-frames and number lines, with a concrete treatment of the zero case to dispel the belief that every operation must change the number.

activities.title: Drive a ten-frame and number-line calculator
feedback: If the learner counts all from one, prompt: hold the first number in mind and count on only the second (hold 14, count on 5 more).
For a bridging case, ask how many more are needed to fill the frame to ten, then how many are left over (8 needs 2 more to make ten, leaving 5, so 15).
If the answer is off by one on the number line, have them name the first jump aloud and check they didn't count the starting number itself as a jump (17 − 3: start at 17, jump back 3 to 14).
activities.rationale: Acting out a calculation on a ten-frame and number line keeps the procedure tied to meaning and reinforces the making-ten strategy at the teen boundary, where ones-counting is error-prone. A live, re-drivable calculation where counters move and a number sentence forms makes the strategy visible; a fixed worked example cannot be re-driven with new numbers.
sourceClaims: Explicit concrete treatment of the +0/−0 case dispels the common belief that every operation must change the number; bridging-ten cases need making-ten not ones-counting.
learnerActions: Build the first number on a double ten-frame (two ten-frames, since one frame holds only 10) (e.g. place eight counters on the first frame for 8+7).

Add or subtract the second number by moving counters, and for bridging cases split the second number to fill the frame to ten first (slide two counters over to complete ten, leaving five, to reach 15).
Show the same calculation as a jump on a 0-20 number line.
Write the matching number sentence alongside the action (e.g. 8 + 7 = 15).
Repeat with a non-bridging case (14 + 5) and a take-away (17 − 3).
activities.intendedInsight: Within-20 sums and differences can be found by using bonds and making ten, not by counting all in ones; bridging reorganises the quantity around ten.

activities.title: Add nothing, take nothing: the zero case
feedback: If the learner changes the number (e.g. 12 + 0 = 13), act out physically putting zero more counters on, then recount to show the quantity is the same.
Ask directly: when you added nothing, did any counter move? So what is the answer?
Reinforce the contrast: taking 3 away changes the number, taking 0 away does not.
activities.rationale: Young children often assume every operation must change the number, producing errors like 5+0=6 or 5−0=4. Concretely acting out 'add nothing / take nothing' and seeing the quantity unchanged targets this directly and establishes zero's identity role. A side-by-side contrast with a non-zero operation sharpens the point.
sourceClaims: Explicit concrete treatment of the +0/−0 case dispels the common belief that every operation must change the number; bridging-ten cases need making-ten not ones-counting.
1.OA.5/6: relate counting to add/subtract and add/subtract within 20; the additive identity n + 0 = n is a foundational property.
Y1 pupils add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including 0, and realise the effect of adding or subtracting 0.
learnerActions: Build a number on a double ten-frame (e.g. 12: one full frame and 2 on the second frame).
Choose 'add 0' and watch that no counters move and the number stays 12.
Choose 'subtract 0' from another number (e.g. 16) and confirm it stays 16.
Show the same on the number line as a jump of length zero that stays on the spot.
Say or write why the number did not change: adding or taking nothing leaves the quantity exactly as it was.
Contrast with a nearby case that does change (17 − 3 vs 17 − 0).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting 0 leaves a number unchanged (n + 0 = n, n − 0 = n); not every operation changes the quantity.

activities.title: Spoken probe: what happens if we add zero?
feedback: If the explanation is 'it just stays', press for why: because no amount was added or taken away.
Accept correct reasoning expressed in the child's own words; follow a wrong prediction by acting it out with objects.
activities.rationale: A short dialogue may surface the identity idea and let the child articulate reasoning, which the top checkpoint tier expects. Discussion complements, but is not itself calculation practice; the hands-on activities remain the vehicle for building and rehearsing the procedure. Efficacy of the dialogue as a standalone is proposed, not evidenced.
learnerActions: Discuss: 'What happens to 12 when you add nothing to it?'
Explain in your own words how 17 − 3 is different from 17 − 0.
Predict and justify the answer to a new zero case before checking it with objects.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state why adding or subtracting zero leaves a number unchanged shows understanding beyond getting the answer.

activities.title: Mixed within-20 practice set
feedback: For an answer like 14 + 5 = 64, show that the 5 ones are added to the 4 ones, not to the ten; make place value visible with tens-and-ones.
For a changed zero answer, re-act adding/taking nothing.
For an off-by-one slip with a sound method, scaffold the count aloud rather than reteaching the strategy.
activities.rationale: Varied practice is needed to build procedural fluency and to probe specific errors (the zero misconception, adding to the wrong part, crossing-ten slips). Including missing-number items lightly connects to later algebraic work. A practice set drills the procedure but relies on the making-ten strategy having been built elsewhere (for example, in the hands-on calculator activity); it does not by itself teach that strategy.
sourceClaims: Explicit concrete treatment of the +0/−0 case dispels the common belief that every operation must change the number; bridging-ten cases need making-ten not ones-counting.
learnerActions: Work a varied set spanning non-bridging sums (14 + 5), bridging sums (8 + 7), take-aways (17 − 3, 15 − 7), and several +0/−0 items (12 + 0, 16 − 0).
Occasionally solve a missing-number item (e.g. 14 + ? = 19) to vary which quantity is unknown.
Jot a number line or ten-frame when helpful.

For non-bridging items, say which digit changed and which stayed the same (14 + 5 → the ones change, 4 + 5 = 9 → 19); notice that in bridging items like 8 + 7 the tens change too, and in ±0 items no digit changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency comes from applying bonds and making-ten across the full 0-20 range, including the zero cases and the teen boundary.

constraints: Keep calculations within the 0-20 range, including the teen boundary (crossing ten).
Use bonds and making-ten rather than counting all; the procedural work should reinforce the fact base.
Give +0 and −0 explicit, concrete attention — it is where zero's identity role is established and a common misconception lives.
Record calculations as number sentences and connect them to the child's own representations to keep meaning attached.
A fixed worked example can anchor the ideas but cannot supply the varied, re-drivable practice the procedure needs; use it as an anchor, not the main vehicle.

A practice set drills and assesses the procedure but does not by itself build the making-ten strategy; discussion surfaces reasoning but is not calculation practice. The hands-on calculation is the proposed primary vehicle for building the strategy here, with efficacy stated as proposed rather than proven.

Tiered expectations: at age 5, non-bridging cases via a fast strategy; age 5-6, bridging cases and correct +0/−0; age 6, fluent within-20 calculation with an explanation of why ±0 leaves the number unchanged.

Distinguish subtraction meaning when ordering: 17 − 3 is not the same as 3 − 17; do not reorder subtraction to keep the larger number first without noting the meaning changes (and 3 − 17 lies outside the Y1 within-20 range).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (CCSS-M 1.OA.5/6 and the NCETM mastery claim); treat citations accordingly and do not infer tested efficacy.

Self-audit of worked examples: 14 + 5 = 19, 17 − 3 = 14, 8 + 7 = 15, 15 − 7 = 8, 12 + 0 = 12, 16 − 0 = 16, and 14 + ? = 19 → 5 — all checked correct. The diagnostic answer string in the source (19, 14, 12, 16) is consistent.
The source states 14 + 5 'stays within the decade' with 'no crossing of ten'; 14 + 5 = 19 is within the teens with no bridge, so this is correct as stated.

The error-pattern example '14 + 5 given as 64 (added to the tens)' is retained only as a feedback/diagnostic target with corrected framing (ones add to ones); no wrong instruction is presented to the learner.

sourceClaims were trimmed where a cited claim supported only the topic/scope rather than the activity's teaching principle: the DfE scope claim was removed from the ten-frame calculator and mixed-practice activities, and the spoken-probe activity carries no sourceClaims because no source directly supports dialogue efficacy. The DfE claim is retained on the zero-case activity because it explicitly includes 'realise the effect of adding or subtracting 0'.

Medium-superiority language was softened: the practice set's reliance on prior strategy-building is scoped to 'elsewhere' rather than asserting hands-on is the only route, and 'Neither replaces hands-on calculation' was reworded to a proposed primary vehicle, consistent with the untested efficacy of the specific interaction.
The 3D/spatial 'skip' framing was dropped as a catalog judgement rather than an established pedagogical law; within-20 calculation is simply better served by the ten-frame/number-line medium here.

probeDeeper: For 14 + 5, which digit changes and which stays the same? Why?
What happens to 12 when you add nothing to it?
How is 17 − 3 different from 17 − 0?
Show me on the number line how you got 19.
assess.correctAnswer: 19, 14, 12, 16 — the first two stay within the decade (add/subtract to the ones), and adding or subtracting 0 leaves the number unchanged.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds/subtracts to the wrong part, or counts all from one instead of counting on from 14.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use tens-and-ones or a number line — hold 14, count on 5, adding ones to the ones; make the place value visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 14 + 5 given as e.g. 64 (added to the tens) or laboriously counted from one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks ± 0 must change the number — 12 + 0 = 13 (or 120), 16 − 0 = 15.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act out adding nothing / taking nothing away to establish that zero leaves the quantity unchanged.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child alters the number when adding or subtracting zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Method right but counting-on/back slips by one (off-by-one).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold count-back, naming the first jump aloud; the strategy is sound, so do not reteach it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 17 − 3 given as 15 (counted the starting number as the first jump).

responseLevels.gap: Adds to the wrong part, counts all from one, or changes the number when adding/subtracting zero.
responseLevels.full: Adds/subtracts ones within the teens by place value, counting on/back efficiently, and treats ± 0 as leaving the number unchanged.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates within the decade correctly but slowly by counting, or is unsure about the zero cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out (you can jot or use a number line): 14 + 5? … 17 − 3? … 12 + 0? … 16 − 0?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These stay within the teens with no crossing of ten, so a child who understands place value adds the ones to the ones digit (14 + 5 → 4 + 5 = 9 → 19). Watch for adding to the wrong part or counting all from one; the ± 0 items catch the belief that an operation must change the number.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 — know that whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish: they breathe air, are warm-blooded, and feed their babies milk, even though they live in the ocean.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS1): Y1 'identify and name a variety of common animals… that are… mammals, fish…' and 'describe and compare the structure of a variety of common animals (… including pets)'; classifying by shared features is the KS1 hook.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 1-LS1-2 / 2-LS4-1 reasoning about animal groups and features; the mammal-defining traits (air-breathing, warm-blooded, milk) are the criteria.
• Operational details: this is a CLASSIFY-BY-FEATURE topic whose whole point is defeating a misconception ('lives in water = fish'). Teach the mammal criteria as a checklist the child applies (breathes air at the surface / feeds babies milk / warm-blooded / (usually) has some hair) and contrast directly with a fish (breathes water through gills, lays eggs, cold-blooded, scales). The single most memorable evidence is the blowhole breath and the calf drinking milk.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~5–6): states a whale/dolphin is a mammal and gives one reason (comes up to breathe); Tier B (~6–7): gives ≥2 mammal reasons and names one contrast with a fish; Tier C (~7): applies the criteria to a new animal (e.g. is a shark a fish or mammal? why?) — reasoning from features, not appearance.
bestPractices: Confront the misconception head-on: start by asking 'is a dolphin a fish?' and let the surprising answer drive the lesson (predict–then–check).
Give a concrete feature CHECKLIST the child applies rather than a label to memorise — breathes air / feeds milk / warm-blooded — so the reasoning transfers to new animals.
Contrast side-by-side with a real fish (gills vs blowhole, eggs vs milk, scales vs smooth skin) so the categories are defined by criteria, not habitat.
Use vivid, verifiable anchors: a whale surfacing to breathe through its blowhole; a calf nursing underwater — these are the memorable proofs.
Connect to what the child already knows: they are a mammal too (they breathe air and drank milk as a baby) — the dolphin is 'like us', not 'like a fish'.
keyRepresentations: A two-column compare chart: MAMMAL (breathes air, milk, warm-blooded) vs FISH (gills, eggs, cold-blooded)
A tick-the-features checklist card the child runs against a mystery animal
A cutaway of a dolphin surfacing to breathe through its blowhole
An image of a whale/dolphin calf nursing to anchor 'feeds babies milk'
commonMisconceptions: 'It lives in water and swims, so it's a fish' — the core habitat-equals-category error this topic exists to fix.
'It has fins, so it's a fish' — classifying by superficial body shape rather than defining features.
'Mammals can't live in water / can't hold their breath that long' — not knowing whales surface to breathe air.
'A shark is a mammal because it's big/smart' — over-applying the new category; sharks are fish (gills, no milk).
Thinking 'warm-blooded' means the animal feels warm to touch, rather than regulating its own body temperature.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish, because they breathe air at the surface, are warm-blooded, and feed their babies milk — even though they live in the ocean. The teaching target is classification BY FEATURE, deliberately confronting the 'lives in water = fish' misconception. The lead activity has the child run a mammal feature-checklist against several sea animals and sort them; supporting activities provide a side-by-side mammal/fish contrast, an assessment sort, and an optional in-role dialogue spark.

activities.title: Sort the sea animals by feature, not by where they live
feedback: If the child drops the dolphin into FISH, gently block it: 'It lives in water… but look at your checklist — does it breathe air? does it feed its baby milk?' and let them re-drop it into MAMMAL.
When the dolphin is placed correctly, a 'looks like a fish but breathes air!' reveal confirms the insight.

If the child calls the shark a mammal because it is big or lives in the sea, point back to its clues: it breathes with gills and does not feed its babies milk, so it is a fish — the feature test, not size, decides.
If a child reads 'warm-blooded' as 'feels warm to touch', clarify that it means the animal keeps its own body warm even in cold water.
Praise reasoning that names a feature ('milk', 'comes up to breathe') rather than just the right box.
activities.rationale: Classification is itself an act of applying criteria, so having the child recompute the category from ticked features — and feel the correction when the 'lives in water' shortcut fails — is intended to target the misconception and may build reasoning intended to transfer to new animals. Including a true fish (shark) is intended to block over-applying the new mammal category.
sourceClaims: Whales and dolphins are marine mammals: they breathe air through lungs, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and nurse them with milk — distinguishing them from fish.
UK KS1 Y1 science requires pupils to identify and name a variety of common animals including mammals and fish, and to describe and compare their structure.
learnerActions: Meet a line-up of sea animals — dolphin, whale, seal, shark, cod, clownfish — each shown with tappable feature clues (surfaces to breathe / has gills / calf nursing / lays eggs / keeps its body warm even in cold water).

For each animal, tick the features you find and use a simple checklist to decide: does it come up to breathe air? does it feed its baby milk? does its body stay warm even in cold water? does it have gills?
Drop each animal into the MAMMAL box or the FISH box based on the ticked features, not on the fact that it swims in the sea.

Try the dolphin: tap its blowhole to see it surface and breathe air, and tap the nursing calf — then deliberately leave the shark (it breathes with gills and does not feed its babies milk) in the FISH box to avoid over-generalising.
State out loud: 'A dolphin is a mammal, and two reasons are ___ and ___.'
activities.intendedInsight: The rule that decides mammal vs fish is the animal's defining FEATURES (breathes air, feeds milk, warm-blooded) — not its habitat or body shape. The same test applies to a brand-new animal.

activities.title: Side-by-side: dolphin vs fish, reveal the matching features
feedback: When a flap is lifted, name the trait and its contrasting counterpart so the pair is explicit.
If the child expects the dolphin to have gills, show the blowhole flap: it must surface to breathe and cannot breathe underwater.
If the child thinks 'warm-blooded' means warm to touch, explain it means keeping its body warm even in cold water, unlike a cold-blooded fish.
activities.rationale: A crisp, cheap exposition that presents the contrast clearly. This activity shows the answer rather than having the child do the classifying, so it works best as a lead-in or companion to the sorting task; recognition of a shown contrast does not by itself require the child to classify independently.
sourceClaims: Whales and dolphins are marine mammals: they breathe air through lungs, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and nurse them with milk — distinguishing them from fish.
learnerActions: Look at a split scene: a dolphin (with blowhole and nursing calf, and that stays warm in cold water) beside a real fish (with gills, eggs, scales).
Tap each hotspot to lift a flap — tap the blowhole → 'breathes air'; tap the calf → 'drinks milk'; tap the gills → 'breathes using water through gills'; tap the eggs → 'lays eggs'.
Say which trait on the dolphin matches which trait on the fish, pairing each mammal feature with its fish counterpart.
activities.intendedInsight: Mammals and fish differ by traits that can be compared one-to-one (blowhole vs gills, milk vs eggs for most fish, keeps-warm vs cold-blooded for most fish), so the categories are set by features, not by where the animal lives.

activities.title: Check and extend: sort, say why, and test a new animal
feedback: If a child answers 'fish' for the dolphin because of fins or swimming, re-run the three mammal tests — breathes air, feeds milk, keeps its body warm — which it passes.
If a child answers 'mammal' for the shark, point to its gills and the fact that it does not feed its babies milk: those features make it a fish.
activities.rationale: A recognition-and-sort check confirms both evidence goals and the transfer step. Recognition responses can confirm understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction that the hands-on sorting and spoken justification provide, so pair it with those.
sourceClaims: UK KS1 Y1 science requires pupils to identify and name a variety of common animals including mammals and fish, and to describe and compare their structure.
learnerActions: Sort a fresh set of animals into mammal vs fish.
Answer 'Why is a dolphin a mammal?' choosing the feature-based reason (breathes air / feeds milk) over a habitat reason.
Tackle a transfer question: 'Is a shark a mammal?' and give the reason from its features (breathes with gills, does not feed its babies milk → fish).
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can independently justify the category with defining features and apply the test to an animal they were not taught directly.

activities.title: Optional spark: ask the dolphin why it keeps surfacing
feedback: Follow the dolphin's answer by connecting it to the child: 'You breathe air too, and you drank milk as a baby — so a dolphin is like you.'
Steer the conversation back to the feature test so the spark leads into sorting or justification.
activities.rationale: A charming, personal hook that may surface the air-breathing evidence and link the animal to the child's own experience. It is a motivational spark, not the main classification mechanism; reliable feature-based sorting is intended to be trained by the hands-on activity, not by the spark alone.
sourceClaims: Whales and dolphins are marine mammals: they breathe air through lungs, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and nurse them with milk — distinguishing them from fish.
learnerActions: Talk in role to a friendly dolphin (or a marine biologist) and ask 'Why do you keep coming up to the top of the water?'
Hear the dolphin explain: 'I have to breathe air like you — that's why I'm not a fish,' and ask a follow-up about how its baby feeds.
activities.intendedInsight: The air-breathing proof becomes memorable and personal — the dolphin is 'like us', not like a fish.

constraints: The core objective is classification by defining feature; do not let activities reward the 'lives in water = fish' or 'has fins = fish' shortcuts.

Teach the mammal criteria as a checklist the child applies (breathes air at the surface / feeds babies milk / warm-blooded / usually some hair), contrasted with a typical fish (breathes using gills, usually lays eggs, usually cold-blooded, usually has scales); gills are the most reliable fish clue, since some fish such as many sharks give birth to live young.
Always include a true fish such as a shark so the child does not over-apply the new mammal category to any large or clever sea animal.
Clarify 'warm-blooded' means the animal keeps its own body temperature steady (stays warm even in cold water), not that it feels warm to touch; do not present a 'warm to touch' clue.
The side-by-side reveal activity and the recognition quiz show or test the answer; they support but do not replace the child's own act of sorting and spoken justification that builds transfer.

Connect to the child's own mammal traits (breathing air, having drunk milk as a baby) to make the category concrete, without implying mammals cannot live in water — whales are sea mammals, bats are flying mammals.
The dialogue activity is an optional spark; it should not be the sole mechanism for training reliable classification at this age.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources are marked verified:false in the row and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed a sorting interaction is uniquely able to 'dismantle the misconception' and rated 3D as adding 'nothing' and dialogue/quiz as merely showing or checking the answer. These comparative-efficacy and necessity claims are not established by the available sources; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (e.g. recognition confirms but does not elicit independent construction).

Minor factual care: the checklist's 'usually has some hair' holds for mammals generally but adult whales/dolphins have very little or no hair — presented as a general mammal cue, not a strong whale/dolphin feature, to avoid confusing young learners.
'Breathes water through gills' is a simplification for this age band (fish actually extract dissolved oxygen from water); retained to match the row's age-level wording.

Warm-bloodedness is hard to represent observably for ages 5–7; the 'stays warm even in cold water' clue approximates temperature regulation and deliberately avoids a 'warm to touch' cue, which the row flags as a misconception. Air-breathing and milk-feeding remain the two strongest, most verifiable anchors.

probeDeeper: 'Why does a dolphin have to keep coming up to the top of the water — what would happen if it couldn't?'
'A shark also lives in the sea and has fins. Is a shark a fish or a mammal — and how is it different from a dolphin?' (near-miss counterexample: shark IS a fish)
'How does a baby dolphin feed — and what does that tell you about what kind of animal it is?'
'Does living in the water decide whether an animal is a fish? Give me your reason.'
assess.correctAnswer: It's not right — a dolphin (and a whale) is a MAMMAL, not a fish, even though it lives in the sea. You can tell because it breathes AIR: it has to come up to the surface to breathe and cannot breathe underwater. It is also warm-blooded, and it feeds its babies milk. Living in water and having fins does not make an animal a fish.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks anything that lives in the sea, swims, and has fins is a fish
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate 'where it lives' from 'what it is'. List mammal tests — breathes air, milk, warm-blooded — and apply them to the dolphin. It passes all three, so it's a mammal despite the fins.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it lives in the sea and has fins, so it's a fish
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the dolphin a fish; justifies by fins/swimming/living in water

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks whales and dolphins breathe underwater through gills like fish
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a whale/dolphin surfacing and spouting through its blowhole — it MUST come up for air and would drown if held under. Contrast with a fish's gills.
errorPatterns.distractor: It breathes underwater with gills, like a fish
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says it breathes underwater; doesn't know it surfaces for air

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a mammal must live on land, so a sea creature can't be a mammal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give the rule: a mammal is defined by breathing air, warm blood and milk — NOT by where it lives. Whales are sea mammals; bats are flying mammals. Home doesn't decide the group.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts the milk/air facts but still refuses 'mammal' because it lives in water

responseLevels.gap: Calls the dolphin a fish because it lives in water / has fins; no mammal reasoning.
responseLevels.full: States dolphin/whale is a mammal and justifies with air-breathing (surfaces, no gills), milk-feeding and warm blood, AND explains that habitat doesn't determine the group — distinguishing it correctly from a shark (a true fish).
responseLevels.partial: Says 'mammal' but can give only one weak reason, or knows it breathes air yet still hesitates because it lives in the sea — the label without the full 'how you can tell'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A dolphin lives in the sea, swims fast, and has fins and a smooth tail. A child says: 'So a dolphin must be a fish.' Is that right? Tell me what a dolphin really is, and how you can tell.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the concept says 'mammal' and gives an air-breathing / milk reason. A child holding the very common 'lives in water + fins = fish' rule says fish and justifies it by the swimming/fins. The second tier ('how can you tell?') is decisive: the mammal answer rests on breathing air and feeding milk, which a child reasoning only from habitat cannot supply.
