pedagogy.summary: Converting tenths to hundredths applies the equivalent-fraction principle (×10/×10) so that tenths and hundredths share a common denominator and can be added. It rests on place value: one tenth IS ten hundredths, so 3/10 is 30 hundredths, and 3/10 + 4/100 becomes 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100. The whole point is that you cannot combine the two until they are the same-sized pieces.
bestPractices: Anchor every conversion on a 10×10 hundredths grid: one full column of ten small squares is one tenth, making '1 tenth = 10 hundredths' visible rather than a rule
Convert BEFORE combining — shade the tenths as whole columns, then the extra hundredths as single squares, then count all the small squares
Connect to place-value columns (tenths | hundredths) and to money/metric (£0.30 = 30p, 3/10 m = 30 cm) so the ×10 relationship is felt in familiar units
Insist the answer is read back in hundredths and, when ready, as a decimal (34/100 = 0.34) to bridge to decimal notation
Contrast a correct conversion with the '7/110' error out loud so children can articulate why you never add the denominators
keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundredths grid (column = tenth, square = hundredth)
Place-value chart with tenths and hundredths columns
Number line 0–1 marked in hundredths
Base-ten flat/rod (rod = tenth of the flat, small cube = hundredth)
commonMisconceptions: Adds across both denominators: 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110 (adds tops and bottoms)
Treats 3/10 as 3 hundredths, shading three single squares, and reports 7/100
Thinks the denominators can be added because 'they are close', ignoring that the pieces are different sizes

learn.summary: Converting tenths to hundredths rests on place value and the equivalent-fraction principle (×10/×10): one tenth is ten hundredths, so 3/10 = 30/100, and 3/10 + 4/100 becomes 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100. Learners cannot combine tenths and hundredths until the pieces are the same size, so the conversion must happen before adding. A 10×10 hundredths grid (each column = one tenth = ten small squares) makes this relationship concrete; a base-ten flat/rod model, place-value columns, number lines, money (£0.30 = 30p) and metric (3/10 m = 30 cm) anchor it in familiar units, and the decimal form (34/100 = 0.34) bridges to decimal notation.

activities.title: Build 3/10 + 4/100 on a hundredths grid
feedback: If three columns are shaded, confirm: 'One column is ten small squares, so three columns is thirty hundredths — 3/10 = 30/100.'

If only three single squares are shaded for 3/10, lay a tenth-column (strip of ten) beside one single square and ask how many small squares fit in the column; rebuild the column-of-ten before returning to the sum.
When the total is reported, prompt the learner to read it back in hundredths (34/100) and, when ready, as the decimal 0.34.
activities.rationale: The concept is a transformation that becomes undeniable when seen: shading three tenths and watching them occupy thirty small squares makes '1 tenth = 10 hundredths' concrete rather than a memorised rule. An optional live tally that counts '30 hundredths' as the columns land, and shows 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100 with the decimal 0.34, can make the recomputation visible; letting the learner first shade three lone squares turns the common error into a self-correcting moment. A base-ten flat/rod set offers the same ×10 structure in a different medium, and a static labelled grid (tap a column to reveal 'this column = 10 hundredths') works as a reference companion, though a fixed picture is not manipulable and so does not let the learner carry out the conversion themselves.
sourceClaims: Creating a common denominator via the equivalent-fraction principle (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) is the foundation for adding fractions with unlike denominators, and adding numerators AND denominators is a documented, high-frequency error.
learnerActions: Take a blank 10×10 hundredths grid where each full column of ten small squares represents one tenth.
Shade 3/10 by filling three whole columns, then count the small squares covered to confirm it is 30 hundredths.
Add 4/100 by shading four more single squares.
Count all the shaded small squares and report the total as hundredths (34/100), then, when ready, write it as a decimal (0.34).
Deliberately try shading just three lone single squares for 3/10 first, notice that this is only 3/100, then correct it to three full columns.

Optionally model the same amounts with base-ten blocks, where the flat is one whole, a rod is one tenth, and a small cube is one hundredth, to see the same ×10 relationship in a different manipulative.
activities.intendedInsight: Three tenths covers the same shaded area as thirty hundredths, so tenths must be converted to hundredths before they can be added to hundredths.

activities.title: Explain why 5/10 = 50/100 and challenge the 7/110 error
feedback: If the learner says 5/10 = 5/100, ask them to count the squares in five full columns on the grid to see it is 50.
If they write 7/110, return to the grid: one column is ten squares, so 3/10 covers thirty squares; you can only add once the pieces are the same size — rebuild 3/10 = 30/100 first.
Confirm correct reasoning: 'A tenth is ten hundredths, so you scale both the top and bottom by ten — the amount does not change, only the size of the pieces.'
activities.rationale: Articulating why the add-across-both-denominators error is wrong, and distinguishing which addends already share a denominator, strengthens the equivalence rather than the mechanical count. Checkable prompts (rewrite 7/10 = 70/100; choose between 34/100, 7/110 and 7/100 where the last two are distractors to reject; sort by whether conversion is needed) surface the add-across error directly. Response-selection formats like these can be used during teaching to prompt reasoning, though on their own they check recognition rather than eliciting independent construction.
sourceClaims: Creating a common denominator via the equivalent-fraction principle (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) is the foundation for adding fractions with unlike denominators, and adding numerators AND denominators is a documented, high-frequency error.
learnerActions: On a hundredths grid, show 5/10 and explain why it covers 50 small squares, not 5.
Rewrite 7/10 as an equivalent fraction over 100 (70/100).
Respond to a classmate who claims 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110: explain out loud why you never add the denominators, using the idea that the pieces are different sizes until converted.
When offered answer choices such as 34/100, 7/110 and 7/100, pick 34/100 and say explicitly why each of the other two is wrong.
Sort several sums into 'already hundredths' versus 'convert a tenth first' before solving them.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent tenths-to-hundredths conversions come from multiplying numerator and denominator by ten; denominators are never added because they name the size of the pieces, which must match before combining.

activities.title: Connect to place value, money and metric, then to decimals
feedback: If a learner cannot yet convert on paper without the grid, that is partial mastery — return to the grid to re-anchor '1 tenth = 10 hundredths', then retry on paper.

If the method is sound but the square count slips (e.g. 33 or 35), scaffold the count ('ten, twenty, thirty… thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three, thirty-four') rather than reteaching the concept — the idea is held, the count slipped.
Confirm the money/metric link: '30p out of 100p is 30 hundredths of a pound, just like 30/100.'
activities.rationale: Anchoring the conversion in money, metric units and the place-value chart lets the ×10 relationship be felt in familiar quantities, and reading answers back as decimals builds the bridge to decimal notation. Transfer to a new pair without the grid distinguishes fluent understanding from grid-dependent success.
learnerActions: Place tenths and hundredths into a place-value chart with labelled tenths and hundredths columns and read the conversion from the columns.
Match each fraction to a familiar unit: 3/10 = £0.30 = 30p, and 3/10 m = 30 cm, noting the ×10 relationship.
Mark 0.34 on a 0–1 number line divided into hundredths and relate it to 34/100.
Write a converted answer such as 34/100 as the decimal 0.34 and say why they are the same quantity.
Transfer to a fresh pair, e.g. 6/10 + 7/100 (= 67/100), aiming to convert without needing the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: The tenth-to-hundredth ×10 relationship is the same structure seen in place value, money and metric measures, and it bridges directly to decimal notation.

constraints: Convert before combining: shade tenths as whole columns, then extra hundredths as single squares, then count all the small squares — do not add until the pieces are the same size.
Never add denominators; 3/10 + 4/100 is not 7/110, and 3/10 is not 3/100. These are the two priority errors to surface and correct, not merely caveat.
A static labelled grid or tap-to-reveal image is a reference scaffold: it can show 7/10 = 70/100 but is not manipulable, so it supports rather than replaces active grid or base-ten work.

Paper or card grid cutouts have slight thickness and can be handled; a drawn or on-screen grid is a flat model of the same quantity — in every case the question is about the fractional amount represented, not the physical object.
Response-selection and sorting tasks can prompt reasoning during teaching but, used alone, check recognition rather than eliciting independent construction of the conversion.

An optional live-tally/snap-counting grid makes the recomputation visible but is one way to realise the activity, not a required mechanism; the same learning works with a drawn grid, base-ten blocks, or spoken counting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The single cited source supports the equivalent-fraction/common-denominator principle and the add-across error as high-frequency; it does not establish the comparative efficacy of the grid, the base-ten model, the live tally, or any specific response format.

An earlier version asserted that spatial depth 'adds nothing' and that dialogue 'adds no value'. These are unsupported categorical claims, not pedagogical laws, and have been softened to affordance statements; the flat grid is well-suited to this planar, quantitative concept but is not proven uniquely necessary.
The earlier claim that a static image 'cannot let the child do the conversion' is retained only as an objective scaffold limit (a fixed image is not manipulable), not as a claim that it cannot teach.
The base-ten flat/rod representation from the original was restored as an optional alternative manipulative; its comparative effectiveness is not independently established.

Arithmetic self-audit: 3/10 = 30/100; 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100 = 0.34; 7/10 = 70/100; 5/10 = 50/100; 6/10 + 7/100 = 67/100 — all consistent. The erroneous values 7/110 and 7/100 appear only as misconceptions to be corrected or as distractors to reject, never as valid answers in learner-facing tasks.

probeDeeper: How many small squares are in one whole column? So how many hundredths is 3/10?
If a friend told you 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110, what would you say to them?
What about 5/10 — how many hundredths is that? Show me on the grid why it is 50 and not 5.
Could you write your answer of 34/100 as a decimal as well?
assess.correctAnswer: Shades three full columns for 3/10 (recognising that is 30 small squares / 30 hundredths), adds four single squares for 4/100, and reports 34/100 (may also say 0.34).

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across both denominators: 'three tenths plus four hundredths is seven over a hundred-and-ten' — combines numerators and denominators as if they were whole numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the grid and count: one column is ten squares, so 3/10 covers thirty squares. You can only add once the pieces are the same size. Rebuild the equivalence 3/10 = 30/100 before re-adding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7/110 (or 7/100) without converting; on the grid, shades correctly but then ignores the shading and just adds the written numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 3/10 as three hundredths — shades three single squares for 3/10 and reports 7/100
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay a tenth-strip beside a single hundredth-square and ask how many small squares fit in the strip; rebuild the column-of-ten before returning to the sum.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shades three tiny squares (not three columns) for 3/10; treats a tenth and a hundredth as the same-sized piece

errorPatterns.pattern: Converts correctly but miscounts the squares when tallying (loses track counting in tens then ones)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the count ('ten, twenty, thirty… thirty-one, two, three, four'); do not reteach the concept — the idea is held, the count slipped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Method is sound — three columns plus four squares — but the reported total is off by a small amount (e.g. says 33 or 35)

responseLevels.gap: Adds numerators and/or denominators directly (7/110 or 7/100), or shades three lone squares for 3/10 — no conversion happens and tenths and hundredths are treated as the same size.
responseLevels.full: Converts 3/10 → 30/100 fluently, combines to 34/100, explains that a tenth is ten hundredths, writes 0.34, and transfers to a fresh pair such as 6/10 + 7/100 without needing the grid.
responseLevels.partial: Converts 3/10 to 30/100 when working on the grid and reaches 34/100, but cannot yet do it fluently on paper without the grid, or lists the steps without being able to say why one column is ten hundredths.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a blank 10×10 hundredths grid in front of the child. Say: 'Show me 3/10 on this grid, then show me 4/100 as well, and tell me how much you have altogether written as hundredths.' Then watch — say nothing about how to do it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands turns the tenths into hundredths physically — three columns become thirty squares — before combining, so the answer is 34/100. A child who does not either shades three lone squares for 3/10 (reporting 7/100) or writes 7/110 by adding tops and bottoms. The grid forces the tenth-as-ten-hundredths relationship into the open, so the error is visible in what they shade, not just what they write.

sources.claim: Creating a common denominator via the equivalent-fraction principle (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) is the foundation for adding fractions with unlike denominators, and adding numerators AND denominators is a documented, high-frequency error.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for Kindergarten Through 8th Grade

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–14 years

- **Topic:** The Rock Cycle

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Earth and atmosphere):** pupils are taught "the rock cycle and [curriculum wording omitted; reference ON-SCI-2022-G4-E2.1]," building on KS2 rock properties and linking to plate tectonics.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-ESS2-1 / MS-ESS2-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-1, MS-ESS2-4, MS-LS2-3] driven by energy from the Sun and Earth's interior, and construct explanations [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-2].

- **Operational details:** Teach the rock cycle as a CYCLE with no fixed start, driven by two energy sources: the Sun (weathering, erosion, transport, deposition at the surface) and Earth's internal heat (melting, uplift, metamorphism). Fix how each rock class forms: igneous from cooled magma/lava (granite — slow, deep, large crystals; basalt — fast, surface, small crystals); sedimentary from weathered fragments compacted and cemented in layers, often with fossils (limestone, sandstone); metamorphic from existing rock changed by heat and pressure without melting (limestone → marble, mudstone → slate). The key move is TRACING a pathway: any rock can become any other — e.g. granite weathers to sediment → sandstone → buried and heated to metamorphic → melted to magma → igneous again. Anchor geological time: these changes take thousands to millions of years, far beyond a human lifetime, which is why we rarely see them happen.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal). The child describes how each rock type forms with an example, traces a valid multi-step path through the cycle, and explains that transformations occur over geological time driven by surface and internal processes.
bestPractices: Teach it as a genuine cycle with no start or end — emphasise that any rock type can transform into any other given the right conditions, rather than a fixed one-way sequence.
Tie each rock class to its forming process and a concrete example (granite/basalt from cooling magma, limestone/sandstone from compacted sediment, marble/slate from heat and pressure).
Have pupils TRACE multi-step pathways through the cycle, since tracing a valid route is the key assessed skill.
Make geological time explicit and felt (thousands to millions of years) so pupils understand why the cycle is rarely observed directly.
Link the two engines — the Sun (surface weathering/erosion/deposition) and Earth's internal heat (melting, metamorphism, uplift) — to connect with plate tectonics.
keyRepresentations: The rock-cycle wheel/diagram with igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic nodes and process arrows.
Rock-texture cues: interlocking crystals (igneous), layers/fossils (sedimentary), banding (metamorphic).
A crust cross-section showing burial, heat/pressure at depth, and magma rising and cooling.
Example rocks per class (granite, basalt, limestone, sandstone, marble, slate).
A geological-time scale contrasting rock-cycle steps with a human lifetime.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the rock cycle has a fixed start and runs one way, rather than being a cycle any rock can enter and leave.
Believing metamorphic rock forms by melting, when it forms by heat and pressure WITHOUT melting (melting gives igneous).
Assuming rocks form quickly, missing the geological timescales involved.
Confusing weathering (breakdown in place) with erosion (transport of the fragments).
Thinking each rock type is permanent, rather than able to transform into the others over time.

learn.summary: Learners aged 12–14 study the rock cycle as a set of linked processes rather than a fixed one-way sequence, learning that any rock type can transform into any other given the right conditions, over geological time. Core activities centre on transforming a rock and tracing a valid multi-step pathway through the cycle (e.g. granite → sand → sandstone → a metamorphic rock such as quartzite → magma → new igneous rock), tying each rock class to a forming process and concrete example, distinguishing metamorphism (heat + pressure, no melting) from igneous melting, linking surface steps to the Sun's energy and deep steps to Earth's internal heat, and making deep time felt. Supporting work includes classification/matching/sequencing and a reference diagram with texture cues; handling real rock samples is a valuable hands-on complement.

activities.title: Transform and trace a rock through the cycle
feedback: When a learner melts a rock and then cools it, confirm the result is igneous — and point out that melting followed by cooling makes igneous rock, not metamorphic rock.

When a learner applies heat and pressure to limestone and gets marble, highlight that the rock recrystallised WITHOUT melting — that is what makes it metamorphic; the same heat-and-pressure-without-melting step turns sandstone into quartzite and mudstone into slate.
If a learner only ever follows one fixed order, prompt them to find a shortcut, e.g. a metamorphic rock melting straight back to magma, to show the cycle is not a one-way conveyor.

When the learner uses 'weather and erode', note these surface processes are driven by energy from the Sun, while 'heat and squeeze' and 'melt' rely on Earth's internal heat — the two engines that keep the cycle turning.
When the time counter reaches millions of years, connect this to why a nearby cliff looks unchanged across a human lifetime: we see a snapshot, not the process.
activities.rationale: Tracing a valid pathway is the key assessed skill, and the insight that any rock can become any other is best supported by letting learners apply processes and watch the transformation and the loop close. An interactive representation with a live texture redraw and a running geological-time counter makes both the pathway logic and deep time concrete, and sorting steps by energy source links the cycle to the Sun and Earth's internal heat. These interaction examples (process buttons, renaming, texture redraw, time counter, pathway challenge) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism visible, not mandatory features, and this is a proposed activity rather than a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught the rock cycle and [curriculum wording omitted; reference ON-SCI-2022-G4-E2.1].
Students [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-1, MS-ESS2-4, MS-LS2-3] driven by energy from the Sun and Earth's interior.
learnerActions: Start with a chunk of granite and choose a process to apply to it: 'weather and erode', 'bury and compact', 'heat and squeeze', 'melt', or 'cool'.

Watch the sample transform as each process is applied — granite crumbles to sand, sand becomes layered sandstone, sandstone recrystallises under heat and pressure into a metamorphic rock such as quartzite (note that limestone would instead give marble and mudstone would give slate), melting gives magma, and cooling gives new igneous rock — with the rock renamed and its texture redrawn at each step (interlocking crystals for igneous rock, layers for sandstone, and tightly interlocking recrystallised grains for quartzite, which is usually not banded).
Trace your own chosen path through the loop and record the sequence of rocks and processes you passed through.

Attempt a 'get me from granite to marble' challenge: find and record a valid route (routing through a limestone/carbonate parent to reach marble), and check whether your route is one of several possible paths.
Note the elapsed time counter that ticks up, typically by thousands to millions of years for most steps (lava cooling at the surface can be much quicker), and compare that to a human lifetime.

Sort the processes you used by their energy source: surface steps (weathering, erosion, transport, deposition) driven by the Sun, versus deep steps (melting, metamorphism, uplift) driven by Earth's internal heat.
activities.intendedInsight: The rock cycle has no fixed start or end: material can route between igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic forms depending on conditions, and these transformations happen over geological time far beyond a human lifetime, which is why we rarely see them occur. The cycle is kept turning by two energy engines — the Sun powering surface weathering, erosion and deposition, and Earth's internal heat powering melting, metamorphism and uplift.

activities.title: Classify, match and sequence rock-cycle knowledge
feedback: If a learner places marble as sedimentary, note that marble is limestone changed by heat and pressure, so it is metamorphic.
If a learner selects 'melting' as the way to make metamorphic rock, correct it: melting and cooling makes igneous rock; metamorphism is heat and pressure without melting.
Reinforce that granite's large crystals come from slow cooling deep underground, while basalt's small crystals come from fast cooling at the surface.
activities.rationale: Classification, matching and sequencing target the assessable sub-skills of identifying rock types, their formation and ordering a valid path. These recognition tasks build and check vocabulary and categories but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and test their own pathway, so they complement rather than replace the transform-and-trace work.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught the rock cycle and [curriculum wording omitted; reference ON-SCI-2022-G4-E2.1].
learnerActions: Sort granite, basalt, limestone, sandstone, marble and slate into the three classes: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic.

Match each rock example to its formation process (cooled magma/lava; sediment — rock fragments, shells or minerals settling out of water — compacted and cemented; existing rock changed by heat and pressure without melting).
Order the steps of a granite-to-new-igneous-rock journey into a valid sequence.
Answer: which process makes metamorphic rock? (heat + pressure, without melting).
For granite and basalt, decide which cooled slowly at depth (large crystals) and which cooled fast at the surface (small crystals).
activities.intendedInsight: Each rock class is tied to a specific forming process and concrete example, and a valid cycle path is an ordered sequence of those processes.

activities.title: Explore a rock-cycle diagram and rock textures
feedback: When a learner identifies banding, prompt them to link it to heat and pressure acting on an existing rock.
If a learner sees layers or a fossil, connect this to sediment being deposited and compacted over time.
When handling samples, encourage learners to state which class and forming process each specimen shows and why.
activities.rationale: A reference diagram with texture photos and a crust cross-section is a strong vocabulary and spatial anchor, and real samples give a tactile experience of the texture cues. These are supports for the core transform-and-trace skill: a fixed diagram shows the map but does not by itself let a learner build and test their own route, so it is used alongside the interactive and hands-on work.
learnerActions: Tap each rock type and each arrow on a rock-cycle wheel to reveal the process it represents, an example rock, and a photo of its texture.

Compare texture cues across classes: interlocking crystals, large or too small to see (igneous); layers, rounded grains or fossils (sedimentary); banding or foliation in some metamorphic rocks (e.g. gneiss), thin splitting sheets in slate, and a sugary mass of interlocking crystals in marble or quartzite. Note that marble and quartzite also have interlocking crystals, so use more than one cue.
Use a crust cross-section view to see where burial, heat and pressure at depth, and rising/cooling magma occur, and how crystal size relates to cooling depth.
Where possible, handle real rock samples (granite, basalt, limestone, sandstone, marble, slate) and match each to its class using the texture cues.
activities.intendedInsight: Rocks carry visible evidence of how they formed, and a diagram plus real samples anchors the vocabulary, processes and spatial setting (depth of burial, cooling) of the cycle.

constraints: Teach the rock cycle as a genuine cycle with no fixed start or end: any rock type can transform into any other given the right conditions.

Metamorphic rock forms from existing rock changed by heat AND pressure WITHOUT melting (e.g. limestone → marble, mudstone → slate, sandstone → quartzite); melting followed by cooling produces igneous rock. Keep these two contrasted and keep the metamorphic pairings accurate.
Link the cycle's two energy engines: the Sun drives surface weathering, erosion, transport and deposition, while Earth's internal heat drives melting, metamorphism and uplift.

Make geological time explicit: most rock-cycle changes take thousands to millions of years (although some steps, such as lava cooling at the surface, can happen in days to years), which is why we mostly observe snapshots rather than the process.
Distinguish weathering (breakdown of rock in place) from erosion (transport of the fragments).

Classification, matching, sequencing and multiple-choice tasks check recognition and vocabulary but do not elicit independent construction of a pathway; include a transform-and-trace or written route-tracing task for that.

A fixed diagram and photos are a useful reference and can teach texture cues and vocabulary, but they do not let a learner trace and test their own pathway; treat them as a complement, not a substitute.
Real rock samples give tactile experience of textures; interactive and physical media offer different experiences and both are valuable — neither is presented as universally necessary.
Full attainment requires describing a specific route BETWEEN rock types AND invoking the vast timescale; naming the three types alone is not sufficient.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists NGSS MS-ESS2-1 as not verified (verified:false) and the DfE KS3 claim as verified:true; original row confidence is marked 'high'. No new verification has been performed here.

The original design notes paired the metamorphic step for sandstone with 'slate/marble', which is geologically inaccurate (slate forms from mudstone, marble from limestone, quartzite from sandstone). This was corrected to quartzite in learner-facing text; the original simplification is recorded here and in the audit's uncertain list, not presented as a valid learner option.

The 'granite to marble' challenge follows the source pedagogy's 'any rock can become any other' framing. Reaching marble specifically requires routing through a limestone/carbonate parent over geological time, because granite-derived silica sediment yields sandstone/quartzite; the learner action now makes this routing explicit so the challenge stays geologically coherent.

The two energy engines (Sun driving surface processes; Earth's internal heat driving melting/metamorphism/uplift) were present in the source pedagogy and cited via the NGSS claim but were not taught in the earlier candidate; they have been added to activity[0], a constraint and the audit.

The original marked a 3D crust cross-section as 'possible' and open conversation as 'poor fit' for the transform-and-trace skill; these were catalog fit rankings, not established efficacy claims. The spatial cross-section content has been retained as a supporting exploration, and a geological-time 'geologist chat' is noted as optional light enrichment of the deep-time strand rather than discarded.

Claims in the source that 'static reveals cannot let the child trace their own pathway' and that 2D delivers the learning 'as well or better than 3D at lower cost' are catalog preferences, not verified comparative efficacy; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

Self-audit: formation facts (granite = slow/deep/large crystals; basalt = fast/surface/small crystals; metamorphism = heat + pressure without melting; melting + cooling = igneous) are internally consistent across pedagogy and assessment fields and were preserved. No arithmetic or force/motion content present.

probeDeeper: Trace a single grain of sand from a mountain to a sedimentary rock and then to a metamorphic one — what happens at each step?
Marble comes from limestone by heat and pressure. Was it melted? How is that different from how granite forms?
If rocks really change, why has the cliff near my house looked the same my whole life?
Could a metamorphic rock become igneous without first becoming sedimentary? How?
assess.correctAnswer: Not true — over GEOLOGICAL time (millions of years) rock is continually recycled. Granite could be weathered into grains, the grains compacted into sedimentary rock, then heated and squeezed into metamorphic rock, or melted to magma and cooled into new igneous rock. We never watch it because the processes are unimaginably slow compared with a human life. Full marks describe a route BETWEEN types AND invoke the vast timescale.

errorPatterns.pattern: rocks are permanent and unchanging ('a rock is always the same rock')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce deep time and the cycle: weathering, sedimentation, heat/pressure and melting continually remake rock. Trace one grain through several forms.
errorPatterns.distractor: True — granite stays granite forever; rocks never change into other kinds.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies any rock can become another type; treats rock as fixed

errorPatterns.pattern: the rock cycle is a fixed one-way sequence (igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic, always in that order)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the cycle has many pathways and shortcuts — any type can become any other; it isn't a fixed conveyor. Trace several different routes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only in one fixed order — igneous first, then sedimentary, then metamorphic, never skipping.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: recites a single loop and can't describe shortcuts (e.g. metamorphic melting straight back to magma)

errorPatterns.pattern: metamorphic rock forms by melting (confused with igneous formation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Metamorphism changes rock by heat AND pressure WITHOUT fully melting (limestone→marble); melting then cooling makes IGNEOUS rock. Contrast the two directly.
errorPatterns.distractor: By melting the rock completely and letting it cool again.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says heat MELTS rock to make metamorphic rock, not distinguishing it from igneous

errorPatterns.pattern: geological processes are fast, on a human timescale ('it happens in a few years')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build deep-time intuition (mountains rise/erode over millions of years); that's why we see snapshots, not the process. Use timeline analogies.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: expects rock change to be observable quickly; no sense of millions of years

responseLevels.gap: Treats rocks as permanent; no notion of transformation or deep time; confuses metamorphism with melting.
responseLevels.full: Describes rock as continually recycled over geological time, traces specific routes between types (including shortcuts), distinguishes metamorphism from melting, and explains that the vast timescale is why we observe snapshots rather than the process.
responseLevels.partial: Names the three rock types and how each forms, but presents the cycle as a fixed one-way order or can't invoke geological time to explain why change is unseen — the parts without the dynamic, deep-time whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A student says 'rocks are permanent — a granite boulder is just always granite, it can't turn into any other kind of rock.' Is that true over a very long time? Then the important part: explain how a piece of one rock type could end up as a completely different type, and why we never see it happen.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who holds a dynamic, cyclic model over deep time from one who sees rocks as fixed and permanent (because change is never observed). Requiring a specific transformation route AND the timescale explanation is the discriminator — naming the three types isn't enough.

pedagogy.summary: A fraction a/b is understood as a copies of a unit fraction 1/b, where 1/b is the quantity made by one part when the whole is cut into b EQUAL parts. Teach the unit fraction first as an amount (a specific length/area), then build a/b by iterating (counting) that unit: 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. The pivotal idea is that the denominator names how many equal parts the whole is split into — and therefore the SIZE of each part — while the numerator counts how many of those parts we take. Hold the whole fixed and insist the parts be equal.
bestPractices: Introduce the unit fraction 1/b as a quantity (a definite amount/length), naming it, before non-unit fractions a/b (IES Rec 1 equal-sharing progression).
Build a/b by iterating the unit fraction — 'three-quarters is three one-quarters' — counting unit fractions the way you count objects.
Keep the whole fixed and require parts equal in AREA; accept differently-shaped pieces if they are treated as equal-area.
Vary the whole (bar, circle, length, set) and vary b so children see that the denominator controls the size of each part.
Guard against mechanical part-counting: ask 'how big is ONE part?' not only 'how many are shaded?' (IES caution that strips/circles can mislead if counted without meaning).
Link the area model, the length/number-line jump, and the set model for the same fraction so a/b is not tied to one picture.
keyRepresentations: Area model — a bar or circle partitioned into b equal parts, a shaded
Fraction strips of a single unit size
Length / number-line jump of size 1/b iterated a times
Set model — a of every b·k objects
Cuisenaire rods where a rod is chosen as the whole
commonMisconceptions: Equal-parts ignored — any b pieces are called bths regardless of size (IES Roadblock 1.2)
Counting shaded parts mechanically without grasping that numerator and denominator together name one quantity (IES caution)
Reading the denominator as a group SIZE ('thirds = groups of three') rather than the number of equal parts
Whole-number bias — a bigger denominator means a bigger part or a bigger value
Non-unit fraction taken as a unit fraction — for 3/4 shading just one part
Calling every fractional part 'a half'

learn.summary: Teach a/b as a copies of the unit fraction 1/b, where 1/b is the definite amount made by ONE part when a whole is cut into b EQUAL parts. Build the unit fraction first as a quantity, then iterate it (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4). The pivotal insight is that the denominator names how many equal parts the whole is split into — and so, for a given whole, fixes the SIZE of each part — while the numerator counts how many such parts are taken. Within any comparison keep the whole fixed and insist parts be equal (equal area in area models, equal length on lengths/number lines, equal number in sets); vary b on a fixed whole so part-size visibly depends on the denominator, and vary the kind of whole across separate tasks so the idea is not tied to one picture.

activities.title: Cut it fair, then count the unit
feedback: If a learner shades without equalising the parts, ask: 'Are these parts the same size? If not, is one really one-sixth?' Have them re-cut until the parts are equal before naming any as 1/6.
If a learner says 2/6 and 2/4 are 'the same, both are 2', ask 'How big is ONE part in each bar?' and have them overlay a sixth on a fourth to see the sixth is thinner.
If a learner says 2/6 is more 'because 6 is bigger than 4', return to the overlay of one sixth on one fourth; once they see the sixth is the smaller piece, re-ask the comparison.
Reinforce correct reasoning by having them restate: 'the bottom number says how many equal parts, so it sets how big each part is.'
activities.rationale: Introducing the unit fraction as an amount and iterating it to build a/b follows the equal-sharing-before-notation progression and directly confronts whole-number bias and equal-parts errors. Requiring learners to check and re-cut until the parts are equal before labelling any as a fraction, and letting them iterate and overlay the unit themselves, is proposed to make equal-parts and unit-size felt rather than told. The side-by-side 2/6 vs 2/4 comparison with overlay targets the specific misconception that matching numerators mean equal amounts.
sourceClaims: A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.
learnerActions: Take one whole bar (a chocolate bar works well) and cut it into equal parts, e.g. 6, checking that the parts are genuinely equal in area before accepting them.
Shade ONE part and name it as a quantity: 'this is one-sixth, 1/6'.
Build 2/6, then 3/6, by copying that single 1/6 piece and counting as you go, saying 'two one-sixths, three one-sixths' and writing the label each time.
Reset the sixths bar to show 2/6, then set an identical bar beside it, cut into 4 equal parts, and shade 2 parts on it (so you have 2/6 next to 2/4).
Slide the two shaded regions over one another to compare how much chocolate each shows, and state which is more and why.
activities.intendedInsight: a/b is a copies of an equal part whose size is fixed by the denominator; shading the same NUMBER of parts does not give the same amount, because sixths are smaller than fourths of the same whole (so 2/6 < 2/4).

activities.title: How big is ONE part? (vary the whole and the denominator)
feedback: If a learner counts shaded pieces mechanically, redirect with 'how big is one part?' before accepting the answer.
If a learner thinks 1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4, have them cut the SAME whole into 4 then into 8 and compare one piece of each.
Accept differently-shaped pieces as equal if the learner can show they are equal in area; praise reasoning that focuses on amount rather than appearance.
activities.rationale: Linking area, length/number-line, set and Cuisenaire-rod models for one fraction prevents the concept being tied to a single representation, and varying b while holding the whole fixed makes the denominator-controls-size idea visible. Asking 'how big is one part?' guards against mechanical part-counting.
sourceClaims: A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.
learnerActions: Build the SAME fraction across different wholes — a bar, a circle, a fraction strip, a length/number line, a set of objects (e.g. 2 of every 6), and Cuisenaire rods with one chosen rod as the whole.
On a number line, make the fraction by repeating a jump of size 1/b, a times, instead of shading an area.
Re-cut one bar into 8 equal parts and name one part (1/8); compare its size to one quarter of that same bar and state which is bigger and why.
Draw a given fraction, e.g. 2/6, of the SAME whole a DIFFERENT way — differently shaped parts but the same amount.
For each model, answer not just 'how many are shaded?' but 'how big is ONE part?'
activities.intendedInsight: The same fraction names the same relationship to its whole (and the same number) whatever picture is used, but the amount it shows depends on the size of the whole; for any given whole the denominator controls how many equal parts it is cut into (regardless of that whole's shape), and more equal parts of the SAME whole means each part is smaller (1/8 < 1/4).

activities.title: Predict, then check: comparing same-numerator fractions
feedback: If the stated reason is 'the same, both are 2', after the overlay ask them to explain why 2/4 covers more despite both counting two parts.
If the reason is '6 is more so sixths-bar is more', use the overlay of one sixth on one fourth, then have them re-state the rule about part size.

For the small-bar/big-bar trap, clarify that comparing the ACTUAL amounts of chocolate requires equal wholes, while as numbers 3/4 is still greater than 1/2; praise learners who notice the wholes differ.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check routine with a reason stated before observing surfaces whole-number and part-counting reasoning diagnostically, and the physical overlay refutes both 'they're the same' and 'more parts means more'. The whole-size caveat protects against over-generalising when comparing physical amounts, without denying that fractions as numbers are comparable.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.

A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
learnerActions: Before cutting, look at two identical bars. Predict and give a REASON: if 2 parts are shaded on a bar cut into 4, and 2 parts on an identical bar cut into 6, which shows more chocolate — or the same? State the reason out loud BEFORE observing.
Then cut both bars and slide the shaded regions over each other to check.
Revise or confirm your prediction, explaining what the comparison showed.
Build 3/4 from single pieces and say how many quarters and how big each one is.
Tackle the trap question: could 3/4 of a small bar be LESS chocolate than 1/2 of a big bar? State what must be true about the wholes to compare the amounts fairly.
activities.intendedInsight: With the whole held fixed, more equal parts means each part is smaller, so 2/4 > 2/6 and 3/4 > 3/6 even though the counts match; comparing the AMOUNTS shown by two models is only fair when the wholes are the same size, though the fractions themselves, as numbers, remain comparable (3/4 > 1/2 always).

activities.title: Identify, match and construct across models (consolidation)
feedback: For the unequal-pieces item, if a learner accepts it as quarters, overlay or measure the pieces to show they are not equal, so cannot be quarters.
A sort into equal-parts vs not can check classification, but it does not by itself show the learner can build and justify a fraction — follow matching with a construct-and-explain step.
Use evocative illustrations for recognition, but return to a measured/equal-area model whenever size is in question.
activities.rationale: Retrieval, matching and categorisation consolidate the concept once it is built, and the explicit equal-parts-vs-not sort targets the equal-parts misconception by checking classification. This supports, rather than replaces, hands-on partitioning and iterating.
sourceClaims: A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.
learnerActions: Identify the fraction shaded in a given model, e.g. one shaded part of a shape in 5 equal parts named as 1/5.
Match a written fraction a/b to the model that shows it.
Sort models into 'equal parts' vs 'not equal parts', and judge whether a bar cut into 4 UNEQUAL pieces with one shaded really shows a quarter.
Construct a requested fraction yourself — draw it, or choose/colour the right number of equal parts.
Explain in words what the denominator and numerator each tell you for one chosen example.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure, flexible recognition and construction of a/b across representations, with equal parts as the non-negotiable criterion.

constraints: Always hold the whole fixed and require parts to be equal when naming fractions: equal in AREA for area models, equal in length for length/number-line models, equal in number for set models; differently-shaped pieces of an area model are acceptable only if they are genuinely equal in area.
Introduce the unit fraction 1/b as a named quantity before non-unit fractions a/b.

When comparing the AMOUNTS two models show by counting shaded parts, this is only valid when the wholes are the same size; state this explicitly, especially in trap questions mixing a small and a large whole. Note that fractions as numbers remain comparable regardless (3/4 > 1/2).

A static reference such as a fraction wall can label parts ('one of six equal parts = 1/6') but does not let the learner enforce equal parts or iterate the unit themselves; treat it as a reference layer alongside active partitioning, not a substitute for it.

Recognition-only tasks (identify/match) and sorts confirm classification/fluency but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or justification; pair them with a construct-and-explain step.

Keep the work in the plane (area/length/set); a third spatial dimension is not needed for this planar concept and can obscure equal-area partitioning. This is a scoped limitation here, not a universal claim about 3D media.
Guard against mechanical part-counting: routinely ask 'how big is ONE part?', not only 'how many are shaded?'
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source assessment's worked comparison is sound: with the whole fixed, 3/6 < 3/4 and 2/6 < 2/4 because more equal parts makes each part smaller. These were preserved as the target reasoning.

The whole-size 'fair comparison' caveat applies to comparing physical amounts across different-sized wholes; the fractions themselves as numbers remain comparable (3/4 > 1/2). This scoping was added to avoid implying fractions are not comparable, and Activity 2's part-size claim was tightened to a FIXED whole to match it.
Cuisenaire rods and fraction strips from the source key representations were restored in Activity 2, which an earlier draft had dropped.
The England National Curriculum Year 3 placement claim is marked verified:false in the source; treat the age mapping (ages 8–9 / Year 3) as unconfirmed.

Source claims about equal-sharing progression and documented misconceptions support the general teaching principles cited; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity or interactive format proposed here.

The original research rated non-interactive and 3D/dialogue formats as poor fit with strong wording (e.g. 'adds nothing', 'where the learning happens'); these were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints rather than treated as universal pedagogical laws.

assess.poeTask: Before cutting, show two identical bars. Ask the child to PREDICT and give a REASON: if I shade 2 parts of a bar cut into 4, and 2 parts of an identical bar cut into 6, which shows more chocolate — or the same? The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part. Then cut and slide the two shaded regions over each other: 2/4 covers more than 2/6, refuting both 'the same, both are 2' and '6 is more'.
probeDeeper: Build 3/4 for me from single pieces — how many quarters, and how big is each one?
If I cut the same bar into 8 equal parts instead of 4, what is one part called, and is it bigger or smaller than one quarter?
Could 3/4 of this small bar be less chocolate than 1/2 of that big bar? What has to be true about the wholes for us to compare fairly?
Draw 2/6 a different way — a different shape, but the same amount.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/4. The 4 (denominator) tells how many EQUAL parts the whole is cut into, so each part is 1/4; the 3 (numerator) counts how many of those parts we take, i.e. 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. The second bar shows 3/6, which is LESS than 3/4: both have 3 shaded parts, but each sixth is smaller than each fourth because the same whole is cut into more pieces.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — 'the second one is more because it has sixths and 6 is bigger than 4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to identical wholes; overlay one sixth on one fourth so the child sees the sixth is the smaller piece; only then re-ask the comparison
errorPatterns.distractor: 3/6 is more — it's in sixths and 6 is more than 4
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 3/6 > 3/4, pointing to the larger denominator as the larger amount

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts shaded parts and ignores their size — 'they're the same, both have 3 pieces shaded'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'how big is ONE part in each bar?'; overlay a sixth on a fourth; establish that same count of different-sized parts is not the same amount
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same — both have 3 pieces shaded
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says equal because the numerators match, without attending to part size

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal-parts ignored — describes the denominator as 'cut into 4 pieces' with no requirement they be equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a bar cut into 4 UNEQUAL pieces with one shaded and ask if that shaded piece is a quarter; establish equal-area as the criterion
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When explaining what the 4 means, omits 'equal'; would accept a 4-unequal-piece bar as showing quarters

responseLevels.gap: Reads numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers; counts shaded pieces; says 3/6 equals or beats 3/4; cannot say how big one part is.
responseLevels.full: Names 3/4 as three copies of 1/4, explains the denominator sets the equal-part SIZE while the numerator counts them, and concludes 3/6 < 3/4 because sixths are smaller than fourths of the same whole; transfers by redrawing 2/6 a different way.
responseLevels.partial: Names 3/4 correctly and says '4 parts, 3 shaded', but handles the comparison by counting or whole-number reasoning, or can name the parts without explaining that each 1/b's size depends on b — listing the parts without relating part-size to the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a bar cut into 4 equal parts with 3 shaded. Ask: 'What fraction is shaded? In your own words, what does the 4 tell us and what does the 3 tell us?' Then show an identical bar cut into 6 equal parts with 3 shaded and ask: 'Is this more chocolate, less, or the same as the first — and why?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands a/b as a copies of a unit whose size is set by b will say 3/6 < 3/4 and justify by part size; a child using whole-number or part-counting reasoning will call them equal ('both have 3') or say 3/6 is more ('6 is bigger'). It is hard to answer 'less, because sixths are smaller' for the wrong reason, and hard to answer 'equal/more' if you truly grasp unit-part size.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Biodiversity & Keystone Species (ages 9–11): biodiversity is the variety of species in an ecosystem; it underpins ecosystem health and resilience, and some KEYSTONE species have an outsized effect — removing one can trigger a cascade of change (a trophic cascade) affecting many others.
• Standards — UK (DfE): enriches Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (interdependence, food chains) and Y6; introduces ecosystem stability and the disproportionate role of certain species.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS2-2 (interactions among organisms), MS-LS2-4 (disruptions affect populations), MS-LS2-5 (evaluate solutions for maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem services); builds on 3-LS4-3.
• Operational details: define biodiversity as variety of species (and why variety brings stability/resilience and ecosystem services — pollination, clean water, food). Define keystone species: one whose impact is far larger than its abundance. Use the canonical cases — Yellowstone wolves (their loss let elk overgraze; their return regrew vegetation and even shifted rivers), sea otters (control urchins that would destroy kelp forests), bees (pollination). Teach the trophic cascade: adding/removing one species ripples through the food web. Emphasise that not all species have equal impact.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~9): define biodiversity and say why variety is good for an ecosystem. B (transitional, ~10): define a keystone species and give 2 examples. C (formal, ~11): trace a trophic cascade from removing/adding a keystone species through the food web.
bestPractices: Distinguish 'lots of individuals' from 'lots of DIFFERENT species' — biodiversity is about variety, not sheer numbers — early and explicitly.

Teach keystone impact with the Yellowstone wolf cascade traced step-by-step (wolves → fewer/warier elk → regrown willows → beavers/birds return → stabilised riverbanks) so the ripple is followed, not just stated.
Use remove-a-species thought experiments across a food web so pupils predict cascades and see that some removals matter far more than others.
Link biodiversity to resilience with a simple argument: a varied web has backups, so losing one link is less catastrophic than in a simple web — connecting to ecosystem services humans rely on.
keyRepresentations: A food-web diagram where a node can be removed and the knock-on effects highlighted (cascade).
The Yellowstone wolf cascade as a labelled chain of consequences.
A biodiversity comparison: a species-rich web vs a species-poor one, showing which is more resilient.
A keystone-species callout showing small abundance but large arrows of influence.
commonMisconceptions: 'Biodiversity just means lots of animals' — it means a variety of different species, not a large number of individuals.
'Every species matters equally / removing one animal barely changes anything' — keystone species have disproportionate effects and their loss can cascade.
'The biggest or most numerous animal is always the most important' — keystone species can be small or few (sea otters, bees).
'Ecosystems bounce back easily from any loss' — losing a keystone species can permanently reshape an ecosystem.
'A trophic cascade only goes one step' — effects ripple through multiple levels of the food web (and even to physical features like rivers).

learn.summary: Teaches biodiversity (the variety of different species in an ecosystem) and keystone species (those whose impact far exceeds their abundance or size) to ages 9\u201311. Core goal: learners trace trophic cascades through a food web, distinguish variety from sheer numbers, and connect biodiversity to resilience and ecosystem services. A proposed core approach has learners perturb a food web (remove/restore a species) and follow the ripple across levels; supporting activities include a prediction-based case study of the Yellowstone wolves, ordering/matching to catch key misconceptions, and discussion of why a small species can hold a whole system together. These are research-informed proposals, not validated or required interaction designs.

activities.title: Perturb a food web: remove a species and follow the ripple
feedback: If a learner predicts only 'more elk', point back to what elk eat and who depends on those plants: follow the arrows one more step, and then another.

If a learner expects every removal to cause the same damage, have them compare the wolf removal with the minor-species removal side by side and describe the difference in the number of knock-on effects.
When the restoration partially recovers the system, ask what changed and why \u2014 reinforce that the chain runs both when a species is lost and when it returns.

If a learner assumes the system simply returns to normal after wolves come back, ask which parts recovered and which did not, and how long it took \u2014 counter the idea that an ecosystem bounces back easily from any loss.
activities.rationale: A trophic cascade is systems reasoning: being able to change one node and trace consequences across levels makes 'keystone' a traceable chain rather than a definition to memorise. A manipulable web (with live population indicators and restore/compare controls) is one way to make the mechanism concrete; these interaction examples are optional ways to realise the goal, not required features, and the specific design is a proposal rather than a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: A keystone species has an effect on its ecosystem disproportionate to its abundance; removing one can cause a trophic cascade (e.g. sea otters and kelp forests; Yellowstone wolves).
Interactions among organisms, disruptions affecting populations, and evaluating solutions to maintain biodiversity and ecosystem services.
learnerActions: Start from a connected food web (e.g. Yellowstone: wolves, elk, willow/aspen, beavers, songbirds, riverbanks) with a visible population indicator for each species.
Predict in writing what will happen to elk, to willow and aspen, and to beavers/birds if the wolves are removed \u2014 before changing anything.

Remove the wolves and observe the chain: the elk that wolves had kept in check increase, willows get grazed to almost nothing, beavers and songbirds that depended on the willows decline, and riverbanks become less stable as bank vegetation is lost.

Restore the wolves and watch the system partially knit back together \u2014 fewer/warier elk, willows regrow, beavers return, banks steady \u2014 noting that recovery can be partial and slow, and some changes may not fully reverse.
Repeat removing a minor, weakly connected species and compare how small the ripple is.
Write one sentence explaining what made the wolves' removal cause a far bigger cascade than removing the minor species.
activities.intendedInsight: Some species are keystones: their impact on the whole system is disproportionate to their size or numbers, because of the strong role they play (for example, controlling a plant-eater that would otherwise overgraze). Removing one keystone ripples through multiple levels of the food web and can even reshape physical features like rivers. Recovery after restoring a keystone can be incomplete or slow \u2014 ecosystems do not always bounce back easily from a keystone loss.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: the Yellowstone wolves
feedback: If the prediction stops at 'more elk', ask: what do the extra elk eat, and who else needs those plants?
If a learner is surprised rivers changed, trace the link: fewer plants on banks \u2192 more erosion; recovered plants \u2192 steadier banks.
Affirm reasoning that follows a chain, even if some steps differ from the documented case; the goal is multi-step causal thinking.
activities.rationale: A prediction that is then violated by evidence is a strong way to surface the 'one animal barely matters' misconception and make the cascade memorable. This case is widely taught in keystone-species ecology, although scientists still debate how strong the Yellowstone cascade is.
sourceClaims: A keystone species has an effect on its ecosystem disproportionate to its abundance; removing one can cause a trophic cascade (e.g. sea otters and kelp forests; Yellowstone wolves).
learnerActions: Read/hear the case: wolves were removed from Yellowstone for decades, then reintroduced.
Before any reveal, predict with reasons what happened to the elk, to the willow and aspen, and to the rivers.

Compare predictions with what scientists have reported: elk heavily browsed willow and aspen while wolves were gone; after wolves returned (alongside other changes such as elk hunting, more bears and cougars, and drought), willow and aspen recovered in some places, beaver colonies increased (helped by beavers released near the park), and some stream banks may be steadier \u2014 though recovery is patchy and scientists still debate how much was caused by wolves.
Discuss why a one-step prediction like 'more elk' misses the far-reaching effects.
activities.intendedInsight: Effects of losing or restoring a keystone species ripple through many levels, surprising a naive 'one-step' prediction. Interdependence means a single change can reshape an ecosystem.

activities.title: Biodiversity vs. abundance, and why variety means resilience
feedback: If a learner calls the million-fish pond high-biodiversity, highlight that it is one species: variety, not headcount, is the measure.
If a learner can't explain resilience, point to the 'backups' idea: more different species means more ways to keep functions going when one link is lost.
Ask for a concrete service (a bee pollinating crops) rather than a general 'nature is good'.
activities.rationale: Directly targets the 'biodiversity = lots of animals' misconception and links variety to resilience and ecosystem services, which the standards emphasise. Comparing webs makes the abstract stability claim observable; the biodiversity\u2013stability link is stated as an association, not an absolute guarantee.
sourceClaims: Greater biodiversity is associated with greater ecosystem stability, resilience, and the delivery of ecosystem services such as pollination.
Interactions among organisms, disruptions affecting populations, and evaluating solutions to maintain biodiversity and ecosystem services.
learnerActions: Compare two ponds/fields: one with a million individuals of a single species, one with many different species. Decide which has higher biodiversity and justify it.
Compare a species-rich food web with a species-poor one. In each, remove one link and describe what happens.

Explain why the rich web often copes better with a loss (other species can fill similar roles \u2014 'backups'), while the sparse web is more likely to collapse \u2014 though even a rich web can change greatly if the lost species is a keystone with no backup.
Name at least two ecosystem services that biodiversity supports (e.g. pollination, clean water, food).
activities.intendedInsight: Biodiversity is the variety of different species, not the number of individuals. Greater variety is associated with greater stability and resilience and underpins services people rely on.

activities.title: Order the cascade and match keystones to their roles
feedback: If a learner names the biggest or fiercest animal as the keystone, redirect to impact relative to role \u2014 sea otters are relatively few yet shape the whole kelp forest, and bees are tiny yet their pollination supports many plants.

If 'remove the predator = prey thrive', show the overgrazing (elk heavily browsing willows without wolves; urchins turning kelp forests into bare 'urchin barrens' without otters) that harms the whole system including the prey's own food.
If the cascade order skips a step, ask what each species eats or provides so the missing link is restored.
activities.rationale: Ordering, matching and short-answer checks catch the key misconceptions (biggest = keystone; removing a species barely matters; predator removal is purely good; biodiversity = many animals). These checks test understanding but do not themselves let a learner manipulate the web, so pair them with the hands-on web activity rather than using them instead of it.
sourceClaims: A keystone species has an effect on its ecosystem disproportionate to its abundance; removing one can cause a trophic cascade (e.g. sea otters and kelp forests; Yellowstone wolves).
learnerActions: Put the steps of a cascade in order, e.g. sea otters \u2192 urchins \u2192 kelp \u2192 many kelp-forest species (otters removed \u2192 urchins explode \u2192 kelp grazed down \u2192 dependent species decline).

Match keystone species to the role that makes them keystones: sea otters (control urchins that would destroy kelp forests), wolves (limit and move elk, which can help vegetation recover in places), bees (pollination).
Answer: a pond with a million fish all of one kind \u2014 is that high biodiversity? Explain.
Answer: is removing a predator always good for the animals it used to eat? Explain using overgrazing/overpopulation.
activities.intendedInsight: Keystone status comes from a species' role in the web, not from its size or numbers; cascades run through several linked steps; removing a predator can harm the whole system via overpopulation.

activities.title: Discussion: how can something small hold a whole ecosystem together?
feedback: If the explanation defaults to size, ask what the otter does that nothing else does there.
Encourage extending reasoning to a fresh scenario to test transfer, not just recall.
activities.rationale: A guided discussion is an engaging entry point and lets learners articulate reasoning, though tracing a cascade is best done by also manipulating or ordering a web. Offered as a complementary hook, not a replacement for the systems work; the discussion can elicit explanation but does not by itself exercise the web-perturbation reasoning.
learnerActions: Discuss the hook question: 'Why did bringing back one predator change a whole park?' or 'The sea otter isn't big \u2014 how can it be a keystone for the whole kelp forest?'
Explain in your own words that a keystone's importance is about its role and connections, not its size.
Give a new example or scenario and predict what losing that species might cause.
activities.intendedInsight: Importance in an ecosystem is about role and connectedness, not size or numbers \u2014 a felt answer to a counterintuitive question.

constraints: Introduce early and explicitly that biodiversity means variety of different species, not sheer number of individuals.

Trace the commonly described Yellowstone cascade step by step (wolves \u2192 fewer/warier elk \u2192 regrown willows \u2192 beavers/birds return \u2192 stabilised riverbanks) so the ripple is followed, not just stated, while noting that scientists still debate how strong each link is and that other factors (hunting, bears, cougars, drought, beaver reintroductions) also played a part.

Keystone must be defined by disproportionate impact relative to abundance/size, using examples that are not the biggest or fiercest (e.g. sea otters, which are relatively few; bees, which are small though numerous and are often called keystone pollinators) \u2014 not by being the biggest or fiercest animal.
Removing a predator is not automatically good for its prey: show overpopulation/overgrazing collapse that can harm the whole system, including the prey's own food supply.
Ordering, matching and short-answer checks assess understanding but do not let learners perturb a web and watch it respond; use them alongside, not instead of, manipulable or predict-and-check work.

A static web diagram can label keystone nodes but cannot show a cascade recomputing; if only a fixed image is available, pair it with explicit step-by-step tracing or a predict-then-reveal case rather than treating the image as sufficient on its own.
Make clear that recovery after restoring a keystone can be partial and slow and may not fully reverse \u2014 counter the idea that ecosystems bounce back easily from any loss.

Checkpoints: (A, ~9) define biodiversity and say why variety is good; (B, ~10) define a keystone species and give two examples; (C, ~11) trace a trophic cascade from removing/adding a keystone through the food web.
Cascades ripple through multiple levels (and even physical features like rivers), not just one step \u2014 require more than a single-step prediction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Listed sourceClaims are exact copies that support the stated teaching principle but do not show any activity here was empirically tested \u2014 activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original flagged 3D as adding 'no conceptual value' and framed a quiz as unable to teach; these were softened to scoped affordance statements (systems/network reasoning is not primarily spatial; fixed-response checks assess but do not elicit web manipulation) rather than universal laws.
The claim that a static image 'can't' teach the cascade was reframed: a fixed diagram can still support learning if paired with explicit tracing; only the dynamic recompute affordance is lost.

Biodiversity\u2013stability/resilience and ecosystem-service claims are context-dependent generalisations in ecology; presented as 'associated with', not absolute guarantees, matching the source wording.

The DfE interdependence/food-chains claim was dropped from the Yellowstone predict-then-check activity's sourceClaims because it supports the topic/curriculum placement rather than the predict-then-check principle in that rationale.
Standards citations (DfE Y4/Y6; NGSS MS-LS2-2/4/5) are marked unverified in the source and were not re-checked here.

assess.poeTask: Present the Yellowstone case: wolves were removed. Ask students to predict, with reasons, what happens to the elk, to the willow and aspen, and to the rivers BEFORE revealing. Then show the documented cascade — elk overbrowsing, vegetation and beavers recovering after wolves returned, and even riverbanks stabilising. Most predict only 'more elk', so the far-reaching cascade violates the naive prediction.
probeDeeper: The sea otter isn't big. How can such an animal be a 'keystone' for the whole kelp forest?
A pond with a million fish all of one kind — is that high biodiversity? Why or why not?
Wolves were removed from Yellowstone. Predict what happened to the deer, the plants, and even the rivers.
Is removing a predator always good for the animals it used to eat?
assess.correctAnswer: Removing the otters sets off a chain reaction (a trophic cascade). Otters eat sea urchins; with the otters gone, urchin numbers explode and the urchins graze the kelp forest down until it disappears. That kelp forest was home and food for many other species, so they decline too. The sea otter is a keystone species — not because it's big, but because its role holds the whole ecosystem together — so losing it changes far more than one species.

errorPatterns.pattern: Removing one species — especially a small one — won't affect the others much
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the cascade step by step (otter→urchins→kelp→fish); show species are linked through food webs.
errorPatterns.distractor: Removing the otters won't change much, because they're not the biggest animal there.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts little change from losing the otter; can't trace knock-on effects.

errorPatterns.pattern: The keystone species is the biggest or fiercest animal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define keystone by outsized impact relative to its abundance or size — bees, otters, beavers — not by being biggest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the largest animal as the keystone; surprised that a bee or otter qualifies.

errorPatterns.pattern: Removing predators is good because the prey animals get to thrive
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show overpopulation and overgrazing collapse (deer without wolves, urchins without otters) harming the whole system.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sees loss of a predator as purely beneficial for the prey.

errorPatterns.pattern: Biodiversity just means lots of animals
errorPatterns.nextMove: Biodiversity is the VARIETY of species, not sheer numbers — a field of a single species is low-diversity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates a big population of one species with high biodiversity.

responseLevels.gap: Sees an ecosystem as independent animals; predicts little effect from losing one species, thinks the keystone is just the biggest animal, and equates biodiversity with sheer numbers.
responseLevels.full: Defines biodiversity as the variety of species, explains why it matters (stability, resilience, ecosystem services), defines keystone by disproportionate role (with examples like otters or bees), and traces a trophic cascade in a new scenario — recognising that impact isn't about an animal's size.
responseLevels.partial: Defines biodiversity and keystone species and recalls an example, but can't trace a full cascade in a new case, or explains keystone impact by size rather than role — knowing the terms without applying interdependence.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In some seas, hunters removed nearly all the sea otters. Sea otters aren't the biggest animal there, so a student predicts 'removing them won't change much.' What actually happens to the kelp forest when the otters are gone — and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who sees an ecosystem as independent animals predicts little change from losing a 'small' species. A child who understands interdependence and the keystone role traces the cascade (otter→urchin→kelp→many species) and explains that impact isn't about size. Tracing the chain is the discriminator.
