pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 by deciding which multiple it is CLOSER to on the number line (4,367 → 4,370 / 4,400 / 4,000), using the midpoint as the tipping point and the convention 'halfway rounds up'.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.3 'use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place'.
• Operational details — Teach rounding as a nearness decision on the number line FIRST: mark the two bounding multiples, find the midpoint, and see which side the number sits. Only then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule, justified by the midpoint. Emphasise that the target place determines the bounding multiples, and handle the halfway convention and cascade cases (e.g. 4,970 to nearest 100). Link to estimation.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): rounds to the nearest 10 using a number line. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): rounds to 10/100/1000 and explains via nearer multiple / midpoint. Tier C (age 9, extending): handles halfway and cascade cases and uses rounding to estimate calculations.
bestPractices: Teach rounding as a nearness decision on the number line before any digit rule — the line gives the meaning.
Always mark the two bounding multiples and the midpoint; the midpoint is the tipping point.
Derive the 'look at the next digit' rule FROM the midpoint so it is understood, not memorised.
Make explicit that the target place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 100 → bound by hundreds).
Teach the halfway-rounds-up convention and cascade cases (4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100) deliberately; link to estimating calculations.
keyRepresentations: Number line with the two bounding multiples and midpoint (the canonical model)
Place-value chart to identify the rounding digit and the decider digit
'Rounding hill'/rollercoaster midpoint image
0-10,000 line for rounding to 1000
Estimation contexts (sensible approximations)
commonMisconceptions: Rounding by the wrong digit or to the wrong place (ignoring which place is the target).
Always rounding down (truncating) or always up.
Chained/successive rounding (rounding the ones then tens then…) instead of one decision.
Mishandling the halfway case or the cascade (4,970 to nearest 100 → 4,900 not 5,000).
Treating rounding as a rule with no sense of 'nearer to', so unable to check reasonableness.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: round whole numbers to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 by treating rounding as a nearness decision on a number line FIRST — mark the two bounding multiples, find the midpoint, and see which side the number sits — then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule as a shortcut justified by the midpoint. Core worked example: 4,367 rounds to 4,370 (nearest 10), 4,400 (nearest 100), 4,000 (nearest 1000). Deliberately teach the halfway convention (half rounds up) and cascade/carry cases (4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100). Includes a number-line manipulation activity, a consolidation assessment with targeted traps, and a static reference image as a scaffold.

activities.title: Number-line rounding bench: snap to the nearer multiple
feedback: If a learner rounds 4,367 to 4,300, drag the marker and point to the midpoint 4,350: 4,367 is past it, so it is nearer 4,400.

If a learner uses the wrong digit for nearest 100 (inspecting the 7, which is the ones digit, or the 3, the hundreds digit itself, instead of the 6, the tens digit that decides), name the decider digit — one place to the right of the rounding place — mark it, and look only at that.
If a learner keeps trailing digits (4,367 → 4,467, or keeps the 67), show on the line that the rounded value must be a multiple of 100, so everything after the hundreds becomes zero.
For the cascade 4,970 → 5,000, walk the single carry rather than reteaching everything: 4,970 is 49 hundreds and 70, so 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000; rehearse near the boundary.
activities.rationale: Grounding rounding in number-line nearness and the midpoint before formalising the digit rule builds understanding and helps avoid rote truncation errors; dragging across the midpoint makes the decision rule concrete and visible. The place selector and cascade animation are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism tangible, not mandatory implementation.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
Rounding should be grounded in number-line nearness and the midpoint before the digit rule is formalised, to avoid rote truncation errors.
learnerActions: Place or drag the target number (e.g. 4,367) as a marker on a number line between its two bounding multiples — 4,300 and 4,400 when rounding to the nearest 100 — with the midpoint 4,350 clearly flagged.
See that 4,367 sits PAST the midpoint, so it is nearer to 4,400; watch the marker snap to 4,400 (an arc or snap animation makes the 'nearer multiple' choice visible rather than recited).

Drag the marker back and forth across the midpoint and watch the rounded result flip at 4,350: whole numbers below 4,350 (e.g. 4,349) round down to 4,300, while 4,350 itself and anything above round up to 4,400. This shows that the midpoint is the tipping point, and that the half-rounds-up convention decides the exact-halfway case.
Use a target-place selector (10/100/1000) that rescales the line and changes the bounding multiples, so you feel how the target place chooses which multiples bound the number.
Work a cascade case: round 4,970 to the nearest 100 and watch the roll up to 5,000 — the hundreds carry over (49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000).
After the line meaning is built, name the 'decider' digit — the one immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to — and connect it to which side of the midpoint you are on.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding means choosing the nearer multiple of the target place; the midpoint is the tipping point, and the 'look at the next digit' rule is just a quick way of telling whether the number is below halfway (decider 0-4, round down) or at or past halfway (decider 5-9, round up, with exactly halfway going up by the agreed convention).

activities.title: Consolidation across places with targeted traps
feedback: For a halfway case like 2,650 to the nearest 100, if the learner always rounds down (2,600), state the agreed convention (half rounds up, so 2,650 → 2,700) and mark the midpoint on the line so they see 2,650 is exactly halfway and the rule decides.
For 1,970 to the nearest 100, the carried answer is 2,000; if they produce 1,900 or a malformed value, walk the single carry: 1,970 is 19 hundreds and 70, so 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000.
If a rounded answer is not a clean multiple of the target place, return to the number line to show the rounded value must land exactly on a multiple.
activities.rationale: After the line meaning is built, varied practice across places with specific traps consolidates the procedure and surfaces the remaining failure mechanisms (wrong decider digit, halfway habit, carry past 9). A recognition/fill format is useful for consolidation and checking; note it does not by itself elicit independent construction of the number-line justification, which the first activity provides.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
learnerActions: Round given numbers to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000 (e.g. round 4,367 to each place) via fill-in or multiple choice.
First select the target place, then round, so the two steps stay distinct.
Tackle deliberately chosen trap cases: the halfway case 2,650 to the nearest 100 (which rounds up to 2,700), and the cascade case 1,970 to the nearest 100 (which carries to 2,000).
Match numbers to their rounded values across places.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding can be applied reliably across different target places, including the halfway (5) and nine-cascade cases, once the nearness meaning is secure.

activities.title: Rounding-hill reference image (scaffold)
feedback: If a learner cannot say why a number rounds a certain way, point to the midpoint on the hill and ask which side the number is on.
Prompt the learner to then carry out the nearness decision themselves on a live number line, not just read it off the poster.
activities.rationale: A static image or 'roll to nearer multiple' tap is a helpful reference and reminder, but the nearness decision is best made by the learner acting on a line; treat this as a scaffold that supports, rather than replaces, active rounding.
sourceClaims: Rounding should be grounded in number-line nearness and the midpoint before the digit rule is formalised, to avoid rote truncation errors.
learnerActions: Use a static rounding-hill / number-line poster showing the two bounding multiples and the marked midpoint as a reference while rounding.
Optionally tap a number on the hill to watch it roll to the nearer multiple, with the midpoint marked, as a reminder of the nearness decision.
activities.intendedInsight: A visual 'hill' with a marked midpoint reminds learners that rounding goes to the nearer multiple and that the midpoint decides direction.

constraints: Teach rounding as a number-line nearness decision FIRST; only then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule, justified by the midpoint, so it is understood rather than memorised.
Always mark the two bounding multiples and the midpoint; the target place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 100 → bound by hundreds).

Deliberately teach the halfway-rounds-up convention and cascade/carry cases (e.g. 4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100); state the convention explicitly since 'half rounds up' is a chosen convention, not a mathematical necessity.
The rounded value must be a multiple of the target place: all digits after the rounding place become zero.
Avoid chained/successive rounding (rounding ones, then tens, then hundreds); rounding to a target place is a single decision from the original number.

The static hill/poster is a reference scaffold; its limit is that it shows rather than requires the learner's own nearness decision. A fill/multiple-choice format consolidates and checks but does not by itself require the learner to construct the number-line justification.
When assessing, watch the working (which digit decides and what happens to trailing digits), not only the final number, to reveal which rule the child is running.

The decider digit for a target place is the digit one place to the RIGHT of it (for 4,367 to nearest 100 the decider is the tens digit 6, not the hundreds digit 3, the ones digit 7, or the thousands digit 4).
Carry arithmetic must match the actual number: 4,970 → 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000; 1,970 → 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The candidate originally miscomputed the 4,970 cascade carry as '19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000' (reasoning that belongs to 1,970). Corrected to 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000 at every learner-facing occurrence.

The source's wrong-decider-digit misconception listed 'the 7 or the 4' for 4,367 to the nearest hundred; the 4 is the thousands digit and contradicts the pattern's own description (hundreds digit itself or ones digit). Corrected to the 7 (ones) or the 3 (hundreds digit itself), with 6 (tens) as the correct decider.

The source assessment includes a double-rounding probe (4,347): rounding to the nearest ten gives 4,350, then to the nearest hundred (half-up) gives 4,400, whereas rounding straight to the nearest hundred gives 4,300 — these differ. Any demonstration must make clear the straight-to-hundred answer (4,300) is correct and chained rounding is the error being exposed.

The source correctAnswer '4,400; 2,000; 2,700' maps to the diagnosticPrompt cases (4,367 / 1,970 / 2,650 to nearest hundred), not the probeDeeper prompts (e.g. 2,999 to nearest ten is 3,000); these probe numbers were not reconstructable and were not propagated into learner-facing material. Reviewers should confirm intended probe numbers and answers.

The original row's '3D adds nothing' / 'open dialogue adds little' fit judgements were catalog preferences and are not propagated as universal claims. A number line is naturally planar, but this does not establish that other media cannot support rounding.

Two of three sources are marked unverified in the source row; comparative efficacy or necessity of the number-line-first approach is not independently established here beyond the cited claim about grounding rounding in nearness.

probeDeeper: Round 2,999 to the nearest ten — what happens to the other digits?
Show me on a number line why 4,367 rounds to 4,400 and not 4,300.
Round 4,347 to the nearest ten, then round THAT to the nearest hundred. Now round 4,347 straight to the nearest hundred — do you get the same? (double-rounding)
assess.correctAnswer: 4,400; 2,000; 2,700 — deciding by the digit one place to the right of the hundreds, then replacing all digits after the hundreds place with zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Decides using the wrong digit — the hundreds digit itself, or the final (ones) digit — instead of the digit one place to the right of the rounding place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the 'decider' digit: the one immediately to the right of the place you're rounding to. Mark it, then look only at that. Reground with place-value columns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 4,367 to the nearest hundred the child inspects the 7 or the 4, not the 6.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the target digit but leaves the trailing digits unchanged (4,367 → 4,467, or keeps the 67)
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a number line, show the rounded value must be a multiple of 100 — so everything after the hundreds becomes zero.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The rounded answer still carries the original tens/ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Always rounds a 5 down (or always up) regardless of convention: 2,650 → 2,600
errorPatterns.nextMove: State the class convention (half rounds up) and mark the midpoint on a number line so they see 2,650 is exactly halfway and the rule decides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Halfway case is resolved by a fixed 'down' habit rather than the agreed rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to carry when rounding up past a 9: 1,970 → 1,900 or 1,1000 instead of 2,000
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole procedure — walk the single carry: 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000. Rehearse on a number line near the boundary.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The nine-cascade case gives a malformed or non-carried answer.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the wrong decider digit or leaves trailing digits in place; rounded value is not a clean multiple.
responseLevels.full: Rounds to nearest 10/100/1000 accurately including the 5 and 9-cascade cases, zeroes trailing digits, and justifies by nearer multiple on a number line.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds clear cases correctly but mishandles the halfway 5, the carry past 9, or which place to look at.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 4,367 to the nearest hundred. Now round 1,970 to the nearest hundred. Now round 2,650 to the nearest hundred.' Ask them to show it on a number line for at least one. Watch which digit they use to decide and what they do to the digits after it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three cases are chosen to trip specific mechanisms: 4,367 checks whether trailing digits are zeroed; 1,970 forces a carry past 9 into the thousands; 2,650 is the halfway (5) case. Watching the working — not the final number alone — reveals which rule the child is running.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Will the bulb light up?

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS2 Year 4 Electricity, statutory):** 'identify whether or not a lamp will light in a simple series circuit, based on whether or not the lamp is part of a complete loop with a battery.'

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** National (NGSS): no direct grade-3/4 performance expectation; nearest strand 4-PS3-2 is foreshadowed only. UK-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Children predict and check whether a lamp will light, on the basis of whether the circuit forms a complete, unbroken loop. The reasoning is qualitative and visual (is the path closed? is anything broken or loose?), not about current magnitude. This is the conceptual pivot of Year-4 electricity: the COMPLETE LOOP rule, applied as a predict-then-test judgement and as fault-finding when a build doesn't work.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 8-9).
bestPractices: Use predict-then-test relentlessly: show a circuit, ask 'will it light?', have children commit, then close the circuit to check — the gap between prediction and result is where the loop rule is learned.
Build a bank of near-identical circuits differing by ONE feature (a gap, a clip on insulation, a flat cell, a bulb not in its holder, an extra bulb) so children isolate what breaks the loop.
Teach finger-tracing the loop as the diagnostic move: follow the path from one terminal back to the other; if you can't get all the way round, it won't light.
Frame failures as fault-finding, not mistakes: 'it didn't light — where is the break?' turns every dark bulb into a diagnosis task.
Keep it qualitative — lights / doesn't light — and resist 'brighter/dimmer' reasoning, which belongs to later years; the standard is binary.
keyRepresentations: Matched pairs of circuit diagrams — one complete, one with a single break — for 'will it light?' judgements.
The finger-trace loop overlay used as a fault-finding tool.
A close-up gallery of common breaks: gap in a wire, crocodile clip on plastic, bulb loose in holder, reversed/flat cell.
A green-loop / red-break visual code showing the path either closing or stopping at the fault.
commonMisconceptions: Current-used-up / attenuation: thinking the bulb 'uses up' the electricity so the return wire is unnecessary — leads to accepting an incomplete loop.
Unipolar model: one connection to the bulb should be enough to light it.
Believing a bulb merely touching the battery will light without a full path through both its contacts.
Thinking a visible, tidy-looking circuit must work — not checking that every join actually conducts (clip on bare metal, bulb seated).
Assuming more cells or more wire guarantees lighting regardless of whether the loop is complete.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year olds judging whether a lamp lights in a simple series circuit: the core rule is that a bulb lights only when it sits in a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal of a working cell, through the bulb (both its contacts) and back to the other terminal, with any switch closed. Learners commit to a prediction (lights / won't light), then test, then trace the loop to locate any break. The reasoning is qualitative (is the path closed?), never about current magnitude or brightness. Activities move from live predict-test-repair work to scored sorting of circuit pictures to annotated fault-finding references, with explicit attention to the unipolar, 'used-up current', and 'touching is enough' misconceptions.

activities.title: Will it light? Predict, test, then trace the break
feedback: On a wrong 'will light' call, show the traced path stopping at the break so the learner sees precisely where the loop fails, then name the fault (e.g. 'the clip is on the plastic, not the metal').
When a repair succeeds, confirm that closing the one break completed the loop end-to-end, so the bulb now lights.
If the learner judges by distance from the battery, point out that the same single loop feeds the bulb wherever it sits, so distance does not decide lighting.
activities.rationale: Predict-then-test makes the gap between expectation and result the place where the loop rule is learned; single-variable variation lets the learner attribute the result to one cause; repairing and re-testing turns a dark bulb into a diagnosis task rather than a failure. A live model can show the stopping point of the path, but a finger-trace on paper or on real apparatus achieves the same diagnostic move.
sourceClaims: Current-used-up/attenuation and unipolar models lead children to accept incomplete loops; predict-then-test and tracing the complete loop are effective remedies.
Year 4 statutory requirement: identify whether or not a lamp will light based on whether it is part of a complete loop with a battery.
learnerActions: Look at a circuit and commit out loud (or on paper) to 'will light' or 'won't light' BEFORE anything is powered.
Power the circuit (close the switch, or run a screen model) and compare the result to your prediction.
When a prediction is wrong, trace the loop: follow the path with a finger (or watch a moving dot/marker) from one battery terminal all the way round — note exactly where it stops.
In a repair step, fix the fault you found (close the gap, reseat a loose bulb, move a clip off the plastic coating, or re-route a wire to the correct terminal) and re-test.

Work through a sequence of near-identical circuits where each one differs from the last by a single feature (a gap, a clip on insulation, a flat cell, a bulb not seated in its holder, an extra bulb added into the same loop — use bulbs and a cell matched so that both bulbs visibly light).
activities.intendedInsight: A bulb lights when it is part of a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal of a WORKING cell, through the bulb (both its contacts), and back to the other terminal (switch closed). Any single break in the path stops the whole loop; separately, a flat (discharged) cell leaves the loop complete but cannot drive enough current to light the bulb, so that bulb also stays dark. Isolating one variable at a time reveals that, with a working cell strong enough for the bulbs used, loop completeness decides every case in this sequence.

activities.title: Sort the circuits: lights vs won't light
feedback: For each sorted circuit, confirm or correct the placement and name the deciding feature (the completed loop, the exact break, or the flat cell).
If a single-wire or same-terminal picture is placed in 'lights', prompt the learner to trace for a RETURN path to the other terminal before deciding.
activities.rationale: A scored sorting bank cleanly matches the binary standard and can check that the rule generalises across many pictures. Its limit is that the learner cannot repair-and-retest, so it assesses whether the rule is applied but does not itself build the predict-test reflex; pair it with the live predict-test-repair work above. Keep illustrations visually unambiguous rather than relying on fine wiring detail.
sourceClaims: Year 4 statutory requirement: identify whether or not a lamp will light based on whether it is part of a complete loop with a battery.
learnerActions: Given a set of clear, unambiguous circuit pictures, decide for each whether the bulb lights and place it in a 'lights' or 'won't light' group.
For each 'won't light' picture, name the fault (gap in a wire, clip on insulation, loose bulb, open switch, both wires on the same terminal, or a flat cell).
Justify at least one judgement by describing the full loop you traced (or the point where the trace stopped).
activities.intendedInsight: The judgement is binary — lights or does not — and depends on whether an unbroken loop exists with a working cell. Naming the specific fault for each non-working circuit reinforces that a path break can sit anywhere in the loop, while a flat cell fails for a different reason (no working energy source).

activities.title: Fault-finding reference: where is the fault, and why does the bulb stay dark?
feedback: When a fault is revealed, confirm the explanation links it to the cause (a broken path, or a dead cell) rather than just 'it's wrong'.
If a learner assumes a neat circuit must work, highlight an example where a clip sits on insulation or a bulb is unseated so the join does not conduct.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal annotated reference supports the language of fault-finding and the 'check that every join actually conducts' habit. On its own it does not deliver the predict→test cycle, so it works best as a companion to hands-on or live-model practice.
learnerActions: On a single annotated circuit, reveal each marked fault in turn (gap in a wire, crocodile clip on plastic, bulb loose in its holder, flat cell).

For each revealed fault, state in your own words why it stops the bulb lighting — a break means no complete path, while a flat cell means the loop is complete but the cell cannot drive enough current to light the bulb.

Build a checklist of what to check, in order, when a real circuit won't light (e.g. is every join on bare metal? is the bulb seated? is the switch closed? is the cell flat? is there a return path to the other terminal?).
activities.intendedInsight: Fault-finding vocabulary: a tidy-looking circuit can still fail if any single join does not conduct, or if the cell is flat. Learners build a systematic diagnostic routine rather than guessing.

activities.title: Counterexample probe: both wires on the same terminal
feedback: If the learner predicts the same-terminal circuit lights, trace with them from a terminal and show the path never reaches the other terminal — no return, no loop.
When the re-route lights the bulb, confirm that moving one wire created the missing return path and completed the loop.
activities.rationale: This targets the unipolar and 'touching = works' misconceptions directly by forcing a prediction on a circuit that looks connected but has no return path. The reveal-then-repair structure shows the exact feature that decides the outcome.
sourceClaims: Current-used-up/attenuation and unipolar models lead children to accept incomplete loops; predict-then-test and tracing the complete loop are effective remedies.
learnerActions: Examine a circuit where both wires from the bulb go to the SAME battery terminal, so it looks fully connected.
Predict whether the bulb lights and give a reason.
Test (or reveal the result): it stays dark. Then re-route one wire to the OTHER terminal and observe it light.
Explain, by tracing, why the same-terminal version has no return path and so no complete loop.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Connected to the battery' is not the same as 'forms an unbroken loop back to the other terminal'. A bulb needs a full path through BOTH its contacts; one connection, or both wires on one terminal, will not light it.

constraints: Keep the standard binary: judge lights / doesn't light only. Do not introduce brighter/dimmer reasoning, which belongs to later study.

The rule is qualitative and topological (is the path closed?), not about current magnitude. Correct the idea that current is 'used up' along the way: in a single series loop the current is the same all around and is not consumed, so lighting does not depend on distance from the cell.
A complete loop must pass through BOTH contacts of the bulb and return to the other battery terminal; one connection, or both wires on the same terminal, does not light the bulb.

A break anywhere in the path (gap, open switch, clip on insulation, unseated bulb) breaks the whole loop and the bulb stays dark; a tidy-looking circuit can still fail if any join does not conduct. A flat (discharged) cell is a DIFFERENT kind of fault: the loop can be complete but the cell can no longer drive enough current to light the bulb, so distinguish 'no complete path' from 'no working energy source'. Note: a merely reversed but healthy cell still lights a non-polar (filament) bulb in a simple single-cell loop, so do not present reversed polarity as a won't-light fault — only a flat cell reliably prevents lighting.

Sorting or multiple-choice picture tasks check whether the learner can apply the rule but do not let them repair-and-retest; they assess application rather than build the predict-test reflex, so pair them with hands-on or live-model practice.
An annotated static circuit supports fault-finding vocabulary but does not provide the predict→test cycle; use it as a companion, not a replacement.
A screen model of a circuit is a representation of real apparatus; where possible connect it to real bulbs, cells, wires and clips so learners meet real conducting joins.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The IOP Spark misconceptions source is recorded as unverified in the source row; claims that predict-then-test and loop-tracing are 'effective remedies' should be treated as informed practice, not established comparative efficacy.

The original research asserted that a live/2D interactive builds the rule 'faster than any static medium' and that other formats 'can't' teach the predict-test cycle; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to affordance-and-limit statements.

Battery polarity: the source listed 'reversed/flat cell' together as a single fault, but a reversed healthy cell still allows a non-polar lamp to light in a simple single-cell loop. Learner-facing activities and the constraint name only a FLAT (discharged) cell as the fault; review before ever presenting a reversed healthy cell as a 'won't light' case.

Flat cell framing: a flat cell leaves the loop topologically complete but unpowered, so it is not strictly a 'break' in the loop. The intended insight, sort-fault list and constraint have been corrected to distinguish a path break from a dead energy source; the pure 'complete loop → light' rule is now qualified to a working cell.
The source row's reteach pointer for the 'used-up current' misconception is null; a prerequisite reteach step may need to be identified during review.

assess.poeTask: Lay out a circuit where both wires from the bulb go to the SAME battery terminal, so it looks fully connected. Ask the child to predict — will the bulb light? Why? The complete-loop child says no (there's no return path); the 'touching' child says yes. Then reveal it stays dark, and re-route one wire to the other terminal to light it.
probeDeeper: Trace this circuit with your finger from one end of the battery. Does the path get all the way back to the other end?
This circuit has an open switch. The bulb is still wired to the battery — why doesn't it light?
Counterexample: both wires go to the SAME battery terminal. It looks connected — will it light? Why not?
If you found a real circuit that wouldn't light, what would you check first, second, third?
assess.correctAnswer: The bulb lights only when there's a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb, back to the other terminal, with the switch closed. Any gap — a break, an open switch, or both wires on the same terminal (no return path) — means no complete loop, so the bulb stays off. You tell by tracing the loop with your finger.

errorPatterns.pattern: It lights as long as a wire reaches the bulb from the battery — one path is enough ('electricity goes to the bulb') — the unipolar model.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace for a RETURN path to the other terminal; no loop, no light.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the wire carries electricity from the battery to the bulb, so it lights.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts that the same-terminal or single-wire picture will light.

errorPatterns.pattern: Current gets 'used up' on the way, so a bulb closer to the battery lights but a far one doesn't ('the electricity runs low').
errorPatterns.nextMove: The current is the same all around a series loop and isn't consumed — trace that the same loop feeds any bulb in it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges lighting by distance from the cell rather than by loop completeness.

errorPatterns.pattern: A gap or open switch doesn't matter as long as the bulb still touches a wire ('it's still connected').
errorPatterns.nextMove: A gap anywhere breaks the whole loop — the entire path must be unbroken; demonstrate by opening and closing the switch.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the bulb is still joined to the battery by a wire, so the gap doesn't stop it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the circuit with an open switch or a small gap will still light.

responseLevels.gap: Predicts lighting from a single connection or 'touching the battery'; ignores whether the loop returns to the other terminal or whether a gap breaks it.
responseLevels.full: Judges every case by tracing an unbroken loop from terminal to terminal through the bulb (switch closed), rejects any circuit lacking a return path, and locates the fault in a non-working one.
responseLevels.partial: Knows a complete loop is needed and spots an obvious break, but is caught out by a same-terminal circuit, an open switch, or 'used-up current' reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are four circuit pictures: one complete loop, one with a gap in a wire, one where both wires from the bulb go to the SAME battery terminal, and one with an open switch. For each, will the bulb light? How can you tell just by looking, without building it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the unipolar or 'touching = works' model says a single-wire or same-terminal circuit lights; the complete-loop child rejects any circuit without a full return path. The reason tier separates 'it's connected to the battery' from 'it forms an unbroken loop back to the other terminal'.

sources.claim: Year 4 statutory requirement: identify whether or not a lamp will light based on whether it is part of a complete loop with a battery.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, KS2 Year 4 Electricity

sources.claim: Current-used-up/attenuation and unipolar models lead children to accept incomplete loops; predict-then-test and tracing the complete loop are effective remedies.
sources.source: IOP Spark / SPT — electric circuits misconceptions

pedagogy.summary: Collecting like terms means combining terms that share the SAME letter AND the same power, keeping each term's sign, and leaving unlike terms uncombined. The deep obstacle is not the procedure but 'acceptance of lack of closure' (Collis): children see 3a + 2b as an instruction to be finished rather than an answer in its own right, so they force it closed — conjoining to 5ab, or reaching for a single number. Teach it as sorting a mixed pile into groups, using quantities ('the number of a's') rather than objects, and make explicit that a fully-simplified expression can be several terms.
bestPractices: Treat collecting as sorting: group a-terms, b-terms and constants separately; only terms in the same group combine.
Insist on same letter AND same power — 3a and 2a² are NOT like terms; contrast a (length) with a² (area).
Keep each term's sign attached to it: in 4a − b + 2a, the − belongs to the b; collect signed coefficients.
Directly confront lack of closure: rehearse that 3a + 2b IS the answer and cannot be made shorter — an expression is an object, not an unfinished sum.
Prefer 'number of apples' over 'a = apple': the object/fruit-salad analogy breeds the letter-as-object error and licenses conjoining (a+b='ab').
keyRepresentations: Algebra tiles (an x-tile, a y-tile, a unit tile — only identical tiles stack)
Sorting groups / columns by term type
Area square for a² vs a bar for a (why powers differ)
Signed-coefficient bar model
commonMisconceptions: Conjoins unlike terms to 'close' the expression: 3a + 2b → 5ab or one number, because an open sum feels unfinished (lack of closure, Collis).
Combines terms with the same letter but different powers: 3a + 2a² → 5a² or 5a³.
Loses or mishandles a sign when collecting: treats −b as +b, or 5a − 3a as 8a.
Drops the variable when combining: 3a + 5a → 8 instead of 8a.
Letter-as-object thinking (a = apple) that makes a + b feel like it should be 'ab'.

learn.summary: Collecting like terms means combining only terms that share the SAME letter AND the same power, keeping each term's sign, and leaving unlike terms uncombined. The deep obstacle is 'acceptance of lack of closure' (Collis): learners treat 3a + 2b as an instruction to be finished rather than as an answer in its own right, so they force it closed by conjoining to 5ab or reaching for a single number. Teach collecting as sorting a mixed pile into groups, talk in quantities ('the number of a's') rather than objects, and make explicit that a fully-simplified expression can be several terms.

activities.title: The sort that refuses to merge (algebra-tile bench)
feedback: If a learner forces an a-tile onto a b-tile, point to the refusal: different tiles cannot pool, so 3a + 2b stays as two terms.
When three tidy stacks remain, confirm explicitly: '3a + 2b + 5 is finished — it does not need to become one number or one term.'
In negative mode, if a red tile is ignored, show the cancellation: one anti-b removes one b, so 3b − b = 2b, not 4b.
activities.rationale: Tiles that physically refuse to combine give a concrete counter to the closure urge, and sorting mirrors the 'group a-terms, b-terms and constants' structure of the procedure. A manipulative lets learners rehearse the comparison directly; this is a proposed design, not evidence that tiles outperform other media.
sourceClaims: Children are reluctant to 'accept lack of closure' (Collis): asked what e+f+g is when e+f=8, only ~41% of Year 9 gave 8+g in 1976 and there was no improvement 30 years later; interviews show '8g' feels like a finished answer while '8+g' feels like an unfinished sum to be worked out — the drive that produces conjoining.
learnerActions: Start with a jumbled heap of a-tiles, b-tiles and unit-tiles mixed together.
Drag identical tiles together so they stack and label themselves (three a-tiles become '3a', two b-tiles become '2b', five unit-tiles become '5').
Deliberately try to press an a-tile onto a b-tile — notice it will not fuse and springs apart; you cannot build an 'ab' tile this way.
State the finished result as three separate stacks: 3a, 2b, 5, and say aloud that this is fully simplified.
Switch on a negative-coefficient mode where red 'anti-tiles' cancel matching tiles, e.g. show how 3b − b leaves 2b.
activities.intendedInsight: Unlike terms genuinely cannot be merged, and the leftover collection of separate terms IS the complete answer — an expression is an object, not an unfinished sum.

activities.title: Sort and complete the expression
feedback: If 'a' and '2b' land in the same bin, remind: same letter AND same power required to share a group.
If 5ab is chosen, respond that a-terms and b-terms are different piles and cannot pool — the answer keeps both.
If the − is dropped from 2b, re-attach the sign to its term before combining.
activities.rationale: A categorisation and completion check surfaces conjoining and sign errors through learners' own responses. This response format can both assess and, used while teaching, rehearse the sort; recognising a correct form does not by itself show a learner can independently construct a simplified expression, so learner-produced simplifications are also required.
learnerActions: Drag each term of 4a − 2b + 3 + a into the correct bin: 'a-terms', 'b-terms', or 'numbers' (the − stays attached to the 2b).
Complete the simplification: 4a − 2b + 3 + a = ____ (answer: 5a − 2b + 3).
Choose the correct simplified form from options that include the closure-driven trap '5ab' and a sign-error option — and give a one-line reason for rejecting 5ab.
activities.intendedInsight: Correctly sorted, signed terms simplify to several terms; conjoining to a single term or number is wrong, and each sign travels with its own term.

activities.title: Name the parts of a term
feedback: If a learner groups a with a², contrast the bar (length a) with the square (area a²): visibly different objects that do not combine.
Prefer 'the number of a's' over 'a = apple'; the object analogy encourages a + b feeling like it should be 'ab'.
activities.rationale: A labelled, tappable reference builds term vocabulary and the length-vs-area contrast for powers. It is a glossary scaffold: because the example is fixed it cannot be rearranged by the learner, so it does not elicit independent sorting — pair it with the construction activities.
sourceClaims: Letter-as-object interpretations of algebraic letters (a = apple), which license conjoining unlike terms, are a long-documented CSMS-tradition difficulty among secondary students.
learnerActions: Given a pre-sorted expression such as 3a + 2b + 5, tap each term to reveal its type (a-term, b-term, constant) and its signed coefficient.
Say in words what each term counts: 'the number of a's is 3', 'the number of b's is 2', '5 is a constant on its own'.
Explain why 2a and a² are different terms: a can stand for a length (a bar) and a² for an area (a square), so they are different objects and 3a + 2a² cannot be collected.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary of terms, coefficients and powers, and why same-letter-different-power terms (a vs a²) are unlike and cannot pool.

activities.title: Confront lack of closure in words
feedback: If a learner insists on one number, affirm that 6a + 2b + 5 is itself the answer — there is nothing further to do.

If 7ab is accepted, talk in quantities: the number of a's (4) and the number of b's (3) stay in different groups. Substituting a = 2, b = 5 gives 23 for 4a + 3b but 70 for 7ab, so they are not equivalent.
If the − is attached to the wrong term, re-read 4a − b + 2a as 'take away one b', so the b-total is −b and the result is 6a − b.
activities.rationale: Explicit discussion targets the closure belief head-on and rehearses sign handling, which a silent sort may leave implicit. Discussion is one route to articulating the reasoning and complements the manipulative; it is not claimed here to be more effective than other media.
sourceClaims: Children are reluctant to 'accept lack of closure' (Collis): asked what e+f+g is when e+f=8, only ~41% of Year 9 gave 8+g in 1976 and there was no improvement 30 years later; interviews show '8g' feels like a finished answer while '8+g' feels like an unfinished sum to be worked out — the drive that produces conjoining.
learnerActions: Decide whether 6a + 2b + 5 is finished or whether there should be a single number at the end, and explain how you know.

Answer: is 4a + 3b equivalent to 7ab, meaning equal for every value of a and b? Test a = 2, b = 5 (23 vs 70) and explain why they are not equivalent, even though a few special values (such as a = b = 1) happen to give equal numbers.
Use quantity language to test conjoining: say 'the number of a's is 4 and the number of b's is 3', then explain why these two counts stay separate instead of becoming 7 of a new thing called 'ab'.
Track a sign: in 4a − b + 2a, say where the minus sign belongs and simplify (answer: 6a − b).
activities.intendedInsight: A multi-term expression can be the complete answer; conjoining unlike terms is never valid, and each sign belongs to its own term.

constraints: Insist on same letter AND same power: 3a and 2a² are not like terms; contrast a (length) with a² (area).
Keep each term's sign attached before combining: in 4a − b + 2a the − belongs to the b; collect signed coefficients.
Prefer 'the number of a's' over 'a = apple'; the object/fruit-salad analogy breeds letter-as-object thinking and licenses conjoining (a + b = 'ab').
Make explicit that a fully-simplified expression can be several terms — an expression is an object, not an unfinished instruction.

The tap-to-reveal labelled expression is a vocabulary scaffold: its fixed example cannot be rearranged by the learner, so it does not elicit independent sorting or construction. Pair it with tasks where learners build and sort.

The categorisation/selection check uses recognition and selection; recognising a correct form does not guarantee a learner can independently construct a simplified expression, so also require learner-produced simplifications.
Algebra tiles and discussion offer different experiences (manipulation vs articulation); neither is claimed here to be the only way to fix the closure misconception.
Watch written working rather than only final answers: a merged single term, a wrong sign, or a dropped variable each show as a distinct final line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row asserted the tile 'directly defeats the closure urge', that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing', and that a static image 'cannot stage' the merge experience. These are catalog-style comparative/necessity claims not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances and limits.

The Küchemann/Hart CSMS claim is marked verified:false in the source and should be checked before relying on it; the two DfE and Hodgen et al. claims are marked verified:true in the legacy data but were not re-verified in this rewrite.

The source row's own error examples '5a − 3a as 8a' and '3a + 5a → 8' are listed as misconceptions to detect, not as correct arithmetic; correct values are 5a − 3a = 2a and 3a + 5a = 8a. These appear only in diagnostic/feedback framing, never as valid learner answers.

The KS3 DfE claim is a topic/curriculum statement and does not directly support any activity's teaching-principle rationale, so it is not attached as sourceClaims to the tile or sort activities; the scored-sort activity likewise has sourceClaims set to [].

probeDeeper: Is 6a + 2b + 5 finished, or should there be a single number at the end? How do you know? (probes lack of closure head-on)
Could 4a + 3b ever be written as 7ab? If so, when — if never, why not? (counterexample confronting conjoining)
What is the difference between 2a and a² — and can you collect 3a + 2a²? (powers)
When you dealt with − b, where did the minus sign go, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 6a + 2b + 5. (4a + 2a = 6a; 3b − b = 2b; the 5 is a constant on its own; nothing else combines.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Conjoins unlike terms to force closure — '3a + 2b must make 5ab' or 'there has to be a proper answer' — because an open expression feels unfinished (documented: only ~41% of Year 9 accept e+f+g = 8+g; 'ab feels finished, a+b feels like an unfinished sum').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a quantities context (4 apples + 3 bananas is not '7 abananas') and tiles that refuse to merge; establish explicitly that 6a + 2b + 5 IS the answer — an expression can be an object, not an instruction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Merges a-terms and b-terms into a single term (5ab), or insists on reducing to one number; says the expression 'isn't finished' until it is one item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Combines same-letter, different-power terms — treats 3a and 2a² as like, giving 5a² or 5a³.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Like terms need the SAME letter AND the same power; contrast a (a bar) with a² (a square) so they are visibly different objects that cannot pool.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds coefficients of a and a² together; groups a with a² when sorting.

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses a sign when collecting — reads −b as +b, or mishandles a negative coefficient, e.g. 3b − b → 4b.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach collecting — attach each sign to its own term first (the − belongs to the b), then combine signed coefficients; rehearse directed-number addition in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The sign attached to a term is dropped or flipped in the working; b-total comes out too large.

responseLevels.gap: Merges unlike terms into one term or a single number, or cannot begin; treats the expression as a sum to be 'worked out' to one answer.
responseLevels.full: Collects a-terms, b-terms and constants separately with correct signs, leaves the answer as several terms without unease (accepts lack of closure), rejects 3a+2b=5ab with a reason, and transfers to unfamiliar variables and powers.
responseLevels.partial: Collects like terms correctly when coefficients are positive and single-variable, but slips on the negative term, on the lone constant, or on same-letter-different-power — combines the parts it recognises but not reliably, and may still be uneasy leaving several terms.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child this card and say 'simplify this as far as you can, showing your working': 4a + 3b + 2a − b + 5. Say nothing about method. Watch whether they keep a-terms, b-terms and the constant separate, how they treat the −b, and whether they try to force everything into a single term.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the teacher watches the written working rather than asking, each error shows as a different final line: a child driven to close writes one merged term (e.g. 15ab, or a single number); a child who mishandles the sign gets 4b instead of 2b; a child who drops variables gets a bare number; a sound child leaves three separate terms with correct signs and shows no unease that the answer 'isn't one number'.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions by collecting like terms.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–8 years

- **Topic:** Comparing Design Solutions

- **Standards — US (NGSS K–2-ETS1-3, Engineering Design):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-3]. This is the data-and-evidence engineering-design performance expectation at the K–2 band, drawing on SEP 4 (Analyzing and Interpreting Data).

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Design & Technology — Evaluate; Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to evaluate their ideas and products against design criteria, and (in science) to perform simple tests and use observations to answer questions. Testing two solutions and using the results to judge which works better combines the D&T 'evaluate' skill with the science 'gather and use data' skill.

- **Operational details:** The child tests TWO designs that tackle the same problem (two paper-bridge shapes; two boat hulls; two shade structures), gathers simple performance data on each (how much weight held, how far it went, how cool it stayed), and then COMPARES the results to name each design's strengths and weaknesses — finally using the data as evidence to recommend which works better and to suggest an improvement. The key move beyond a single test is evidence-based comparison: the recommendation must rest on what the numbers/observations showed, not on which design the child liked or made. This begins to fuse the doing (testing), the recording (data), and the arguing (evidence-based judgement) strands.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete, early evidence-use). This is the first time data is used to judge between competing designs — the root of design comparison and evidence-based evaluation. Success = tests two designs for the same problem, records how each performed, and uses that evidence to say which is better and why, naming a strength and a weakness of each.
bestPractices: Test both designs the SAME way (same load, same drop) so the comparison is fair and the data is meaningful.
Record each design's performance simply (a number, tally or mark) so the comparison rests on evidence, not memory or preference.
Draw out strengths AND weaknesses of each design, so children see trade-offs rather than a single 'winner'.
Insist the recommendation cite the data ('the arch held more bricks') rather than 'I like it / I made it'.
Follow the comparison with a 'how could we improve it?' step, seeding iteration.
Use problems where each design wins on a different measure, so comparison becomes multi-dimensional.
keyRepresentations: Two designs tested the same way on a shared problem
Side-by-side results chart (Design A vs Design B)
Strength/weakness tags on each design
Evidence-based recommendation ('better because the data showed…')
An improvement note for the chosen design
commonMisconceptions: Recommending the design you liked or built rather than the one the data supports.
Testing the two designs differently, making the comparison unfair.
Seeing only a 'winner' and missing that each design has strengths and weaknesses.
Judging on appearance rather than measured performance.
Not recording results, so the comparison rests on memory or feeling.
Thinking the better design needs no improvement.

learn.summary: For ages 5–8, teach evidence-based comparison of two engineering designs that solve the same problem: test both the SAME way, record each one's performance, then recommend the better-performing design by citing the recorded data (not preference or looks), name a strength AND weakness of each, and suggest one improvement. The central move beyond a single test is that the recommendation must rest on what the numbers/observations showed. The same test–record–compare loop works with other same-problem contexts (two bridge shapes, two boat hulls, two shade structures). The strongest version has children generate the head-to-head data through their own fair tests; pre-authored scenes, dialogue, and scored questions can support interpretation and vocabulary but do not let the child produce the comparison themselves.

activities.title: Best Design Wins: testing two bridges with a shared load
feedback: If a winner is named before both are tested, withhold the verdict: 'What did the bricks actually show for each one?' Anchor the decision to the results, not the look.
If nothing is written down, prompt recording each trial as it happens so the comparison is a matter of reading the record, not recalling it.
If the two designs were handled differently (different gap, dropping vs placing weights, unequal time), ask the child to state what was kept the same, then re-run so only the design differs.
If only a single 'winner' is seen, prompt: 'this one held more — but which was quicker to build? which used less material?' so the other design can earn a strength too.

If the shade context is used, keep conditions fair (same spot, same exposure time) and judge the result by the shadow or transmitted light patch on the ground over equal elapsed time — never by looking at the sun through a cover; shade reduces warming over time rather than cooling a hot spot instantly.
activities.rationale: The objective is a test–record–compare loop the child runs themselves, so the evidence-over-preference lesson is felt through their own data rather than read off a finished chart. A live scoreboard that fills as each test runs can make the data visibly come from the child's actions; these are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: NGSS K–2-ETS1-3 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-3].

DfE KS1 Design & Technology requires pupils to evaluate their ideas and products against design criteria; KS1 science Working Scientifically requires performing simple tests and using observations to answer questions.
learnerActions: Set up two designs for the same problem — e.g. a flat bridge and an arched bridge made from the same material and spanning the same gap (or, as alternatives, two boat hulls floated the same way, or two shade structures compared by how much light gets through — judged by the cast shadow or transmitted light patch on the ground — and/or by how cool the shaded spot stays, checked with a thermometer or hand touch over the same time; never by looking toward the sun or holding material up to the eyes).
State out loud what you will keep the same for both (same gap, same way of adding weight, same exposure time) before you start, so the test is fair.
Add weights (toy bricks or marbles) to the first design one at a time, and record the number it held before it sagged or dropped (e.g. flat bridge held 8).
Test the second design exactly the same way and record its number (e.g. arch held 12).
Fill both numbers into a side-by-side comparison chart (Design A row vs Design B row).
Recommend which design performed better and point to the recorded numbers as your reason.
Say one way you would improve the weaker design, linked to why it underperformed.
activities.intendedInsight: The recorded data — not your favourite or the one you built — shows which design performed better on the measure you tested, and you can point to the numbers to prove it.

activities.title: Trade-offs: when each design wins on a different measure
feedback: If the child only tracks one measure, add the second measure and ask which design wins on each.
If they insist one design is best at everything, point to the record showing the other's strength.
If the recommendation ignores purpose, ask 'better for what — holding weight, or being quick to build?'
activities.rationale: Comparison becomes multi-dimensional when each design wins on a different measure, moving children past a single-winner view toward naming strengths and weaknesses on both sides.
sourceClaims: NGSS K–2-ETS1-3 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-3].
learnerActions: Choose a problem where each design can win on a different measure — e.g. one bridge holds more weight but the other is quicker to build or uses less paper.
Test and record each design on BOTH measures (e.g. weight held, and time or material used).
Tag each design with a strength and a weakness based on the records.
Explain why there is no single 'best' — each design has trade-offs — and recommend one for a stated purpose, citing which measure mattered most.
activities.intendedInsight: Real designs have trade-offs: one design can be strong on one measure and weak on another, so the recommendation depends on which measure matters for the problem.

activities.title: Read the results chart and defend the pick (interpretation practice)
feedback: If a 'liked it more' option is chosen, ask what the table actually shows before deciding.
If a design is called the winner on appearance, redirect to the measured numbers in the table.
When a correct pick is made, prompt the child to name a weakness of the chosen design too, so trade-offs stay visible.
activities.rationale: Interpreting a given results table and distinguishing evidence from preference builds the vocabulary and reasoning of comparison; offering a tempting option for the design the learner liked more probes the evidence-over-preference idea directly. This is recognition/interpretation practice and does not have the child run the tests or build the comparison.
sourceClaims: NGSS K–2-ETS1-3 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-3].
learnerActions: Look at a small side-by-side results table for two designs tested on the same problem.
Decide which design the data supports as better for the stated problem.
Reject a 'liked it more' or 'looks stronger' reason and give the data-based reason instead.
Match each design to its strength and its weakness from the table; sort listed features into strengths vs weaknesses.
activities.intendedInsight: An evidence-based recommendation reads the recorded results and names strengths and weaknesses, rather than relying on appearance or preference.

activities.title: Justify-it dialogue: pressing for evidence and a weakness
feedback: If the justification is 'I like it' or 'I made it', press: 'what in the results shows that?'
If only strengths are given, ask for a weakness of the chosen design.
If the child can't say how to retest an improvement, prompt: 'how would we test whether your change actually helped?'
activities.rationale: Spoken justification reinforces evidence-based judgement and surfaces trade-offs through responsive questioning. It depends on the child having already run and seen the two tests, so dialogue supports rather than leads the comparison.
learnerActions: After running the two tests, answer a prompt like 'the data shows A held more — so which do you recommend, and what's a weakness of A?'
Point to the specific result that supports the recommendation.
Name a weakness of the design you chose, not just its strength.
Answer a follow-up on how you'd check your improvement actually helped.
activities.intendedInsight: A good recommendation can be defended by pointing to evidence and still acknowledges the chosen design's weaknesses.

constraints: Both designs must be tested the SAME way (same kind of weights, same gap, same way of adding weight, same exposure time where time matters) so the comparison is fair and the data is meaningful.
Record each design's performance simply — a number, tally or mark — so the comparison rests on evidence, not memory or preference.
Draw out strengths AND weaknesses of each design so children see trade-offs, not just a single winner.
The recommendation must cite the data (e.g. 'the arch held more bricks'), not 'I like it' or 'I made it'.
Follow the comparison with a 'how could we improve it?' step to seed iteration.

Interpretation/recognition tasks (reading a given table, matching, sorting features) check the judgement but do not elicit the child running the two tests and building the comparison, which is the core objective; use them as supports, not substitutes.
A pre-authored tap-to-reveal comparison scene can teach the vocabulary but does not have the child generate the head-to-head data from their own testing.
Dialogue prompts are designed to follow the child having run and seen both tests; use them alongside, not instead of, the hands-on comparison.
Keep the better-design message honest: the recommended design can still be improved — avoid implying the winner needs no change.

If a shade structure is used as the problem, observe safely: inspect the cast shadow or the transmitted light patch on the ground (or measure how cool a spot stays) over equal elapsed time; never ask a child to look at the sun through a cover or hold material up toward the sun. Shade reduces warming under fair conditions rather than cooling a hot spot instantly, and mesh may partially reduce warming depending on weave — compare actual outcomes, do not predetermine a winner.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources carry verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Physical results depend on build quality and materials (e.g. an arch is not guaranteed to outperform a flat bridge); the 8-vs-12 brick figures are illustrative examples, not expected outcomes. Treat observed numbers from the child's own test as the evidence, whatever they are.

Shade comparisons reduce solar warming under fair conditions; outcomes should be compared with equal elapsed time and conditions, observing the shadow/transmitted patch on the ground rather than looking toward the sun. Mesh or thin covers may partially reduce warming depending on weave and setup; do not assume mesh fails or an opaque cover instantly cools.

The legacy row claimed 3D 'adds navigation cost without sharpening' the idea and that scored quizzes 'can't' carry the core; these are reframed as scoped affordance/limit notes — a 3D physical test or a quiz can still contribute, they just do not replace child-run fair testing.
The 'test again tomorrow — same result?' probe is a good reliability idea but may exceed some 5-year-olds; keep it optional/extension.
Alternative concrete problem contexts (two boat hulls, two shade structures) from the original are retained as substitutes for the bridge scenario.

probeDeeper: Your record shows one held more marbles — what was it about that design that made it stronger?
You changed one thing to improve the weaker bridge — how would we test whether your change actually helped?
If we tested them again tomorrow, do you think we'd get the same result? How could we be more sure?
assess.correctAnswer: The child tests both bridges under the same conditions, records each one's performance (e.g. marbles held before collapse), compares the recorded results to name each design's strength and weakness, and recommends the better design by pointing to the data — then suggests an improvement tied to why the weaker one failed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by appearance or preference rather than by how each performed in the test ('the blue one looks stronger, it wins').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Withhold the verdict until both are tested; ask 'what did the marbles actually show?' Anchor the decision to the results, not the look.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Announces a winner based on looks or a favourite, sometimes before finishing the tests.

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't record results — relies on memory, so the comparison can't be justified with data.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on recording each trial as it happens; then the comparison is a matter of reading the record, not recalling it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tests both but writes nothing down; when asked which was better, guesses or misremembers the counts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Tests the two designs under different conditions (different gap, dropping marbles vs placing them), so the comparison isn't fair.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child state what they kept the same for both before testing; re-run so only the design differs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Handles each bridge differently; the two tests aren't comparable.

responseLevels.gap: Picks a winner by looks or preference; tests unequally or not at all; no record of results.
responseLevels.full: Tests both fairly, records each one's performance, recommends the better design by citing the data, and suggests an improvement linked to why the other underperformed.
responseLevels.partial: Tests both and records something, but the comparison is loose — tests aren't quite fair, or the recommendation isn't clearly tied to the recorded data.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two paper bridges that were built to solve the same problem: hold as many marbles as possible across this gap. Test both, keep a record of how each one does, and then tell me which design is better and why — and one thing you'd change to improve it. (Provide the two bridges, marbles, and a way to record; watch how the child tests and what they base the verdict on.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Only watching shows whether the verdict rests on evidence: a child who understands tests both the same way, writes the numbers down, and cites them; a child who doesn't judges by appearance, tests them differently, or relies on memory. Asking 'how do you compare designs?' wouldn't reveal that they actually declared a winner before testing.
