pedagogy.summary: Locating a/b on a number line by partitioning the unit interval 0–1 into b equal parts (each of length 1/b) and iterating a of them from 0. The number line recasts a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude and a position, not a shaded region. The critical shift is to count equal INTERVALS (lengths from 0), not tick marks or dots, and to treat the 0–1 segment as the unit.
bestPractices: Partition the 0–1 interval into b equal parts and emphasise the LENGTH from 0 (the magnitude) rather than the tick mark.
Iterate the unit fraction: 3/4 is three 1/4-jumps from 0.
Make explicit that b equal parts need b−1 marks inside the interval (fourths = 3 interior marks), countering the tick-counting error.
Use lines that extend past 1 so a/b sits among the numbers and cannot be pushed 'between 3 and 4' (IES Roadblock 2.2).
Do both moves — read the fraction at a given point (interpret) AND place a given fraction on a blank line (produce).
Contrast with the area model and stress that the same fraction is 'the same size / the same point'.
keyRepresentations: Single 0–1 number line partitioned into b equal intervals
Unit-fraction 'jump' iterated a times from 0
Stacked 0–1 number lines (IES Figure 4, halves through tenths)
Fraction strips measured against the line (IES Figure 5)
commonMisconceptions: Counting tick marks instead of intervals / drawing b marks rather than b−1 interior marks (IES Roadblock 2.1)
Whole-number placement — putting 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers (IES Roadblock 2.2)
Treating the whole drawn segment (0 to the far end) as the unit rather than 0–1
Reading a point by matching to marks with no sense of the unit-fraction length

learn.summary: Help children locate a/b on a number line by partitioning the 0–1 interval into b equal parts (each of length 1/b) and iterating a of them from 0. The number line recasts a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude and a position, not a shaded region. The key shift is counting equal INTERVALS (lengths from 0), not tick marks or dots, and treating the 0–1 segment — not the whole drawn line — as the unit. Learners should both read a fraction at a given point and place a given fraction on a blank line.

activities.title: Build fourths: three cuts, not four marks
feedback: If 3/4 is placed too far from 0, count the equal jumps from 0: 'how many jumps of the same size?' — three quarter-jumps, landing before 1.

If fourths are drawn with 4 interior marks, shade each piece and count LENGTHS, not marks: four interior marks make five parts (fifths if equally spaced), but four equal parts need only 3 cuts inside.
If a point is read off by one (e.g. calling it 4/5), re-count the equal intervals from 0 rather than the ticks.
activities.rationale: Partitioning into b equal parts with b−1 interior marks and iterating the unit fraction directly attacks the common tick-counting error; letting the child see that four marks produce fifths, not fourths, makes the correction concrete.
sourceClaims: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: Start with a bare line labelled only 0 and 1 — the 0–1 segment is the unit.

To make 'fourths', first try the common mistake: drop FOUR equally spaced marks inside the 0–1 segment. Notice this cuts the unit into FIVE equal parts, each one a fifth (1/5) — the far interior mark sits at 4/5. So you have actually made fifths, not fourths: a sign something has gone wrong.
Correct to THREE interior marks so the unit is cut into exactly four equal parts (quarters); the marks land at 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, and a fourth quarter-length jump lands exactly on 1 (4/4).
State the rule in your own words: b equal parts need b−1 interior marks.
Place 3/4 by jumping the quarter-length three times from 0, landing one quarter-length short of 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Four equal parts require three interior cuts (b equal parts need b−1 interior marks); a/b is measured as a LENGTH from 0 (a jumps of 1/b), not as a count of tick marks. Drawing four equally spaced interior marks cuts the unit into five equal parts (fifths), so calling them fourths mislabels the pieces — making the tick-counting error visible so the child can correct it.

activities.title: Read the point, then place the fraction
feedback: If the point is read as 4/5, re-count the equal intervals from 0 — the marks are not the count; the lengths are.
If 3/4 is placed beyond 1, ask 'where is 1? must 3/4 be less than 1 or more than 1?' and place it inside 0–1.
If a child can read on a marked line but struggles on a blank one, rebuild the partition step by step before placing.
activities.rationale: Doing both moves — interpret a shown point and produce a placement on a blank line — consolidates the magnitude idea and exposes whether the child relies on pre-drawn marks.
sourceClaims: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.
Pupils are taught to recognise and use fractions as numbers and to place them on a number line during KS2 (Years 3–4, ages 8–9).
learnerActions: On a 0–1 line already divided into 6 equal parts, with a dot on the 4th mark from 0, say what fraction the dot shows and explain how you know (four 1/6-lengths from 0 = 4/6).
On the same line, find and mark 1/2 (the 3rd mark, i.e. 3/6) and explain why it sits halfway.
Then take a blank 0–1 line and place 3/4 yourself: partition into 4 equal parts, count 3 parts from 0, land three-quarters of the way to 1.
Talk through each step aloud as you place it.
Also try ordering several fractions along one line to compare their positions.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a given point (interpret) and placing a given fraction on a blank line (produce) are both needed; a fraction is the same size / the same point however it is represented.

activities.title: Which segment is the unit?
feedback: If 3/4 lands at three-quarters of the entire drawing, find and mark 1 first, then measure the quarter-length against the 0–1 segment only.
If a child says 3/4 would move when the line reaches 2, point back to the fixed 0–1 unit — the quarter-length is unchanged.
activities.rationale: Explicitly locating 1 and using lines that run past 1 help expose and address both the whole-segment-as-unit error and the whole-number placement of 3/4 beyond 1.
sourceClaims: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: On a line that extends past 1 (to 2 or beyond), first find and mark where 1 is.
Place 3/4 and check it sits below 1, NOT at three-quarters of the whole drawn line.
Answer: if this line went all the way to 2 instead of 1, would 3/4 move? Explain why not.
State that everything is measured against the fixed 0–1 length, whatever the drawing shows.
activities.intendedInsight: The unit is the 0–1 segment, not the whole drawn picture; with 0 and 1 kept in place, a/b keeps its position no matter how far the line is drawn. Lines extending past 1 let children show, and teachers address, errors such as placing 3/4 at or beyond 1, or 'between 3 and 4'.

activities.title: Compare with the area model
feedback: If the child treats the area-model and line versions as different fractions, lay a fraction strip whose whole matches the 0–1 length against the line so the shaded length and the marked point coincide.
Prompt: 'Is 3/4 a different amount on the line than in the rectangle? Why or why not?'
activities.rationale: Contrasting the area model with the line while stressing identical magnitude links prior representational knowledge to the number-line view and guards against seeing them as unrelated.
learnerActions: Shade 3/4 of a rectangle using the area model, then place 3/4 on a number line.
Explain how both show the same fraction — 'the same size, the same point'.
Measure a fraction strip against the line, using strips whose whole is the same length as the line's 0–1 segment, so the length and the position match (e.g. the 1/6 strip against sixths on the line).
activities.intendedInsight: The same fraction has one magnitude whether shown as a shaded region or as a point/length on a line; connecting the two representations reinforces that a fraction is a single number.

constraints: A pre-labelled reference line (tap a point → 'this is 3/4, three quarter-jumps from 0') supports recall but does not let the child partition or iterate, where the learning lives; use it as a scaffold only, not as the main task.
Both interpret (read a shown point) and produce (place on a blank line) are required; recognition alone does not elicit the independent partitioning and placement that demonstrate understanding.

A number line is one-dimensional; the unit-interval idea lives on a single line, so added dimensions are not needed for this particular objective (this is a scope note, not a claim that other media cannot teach).
Children aged ~8–9 (KS2 Years 3–4) are the intended audience; keep lines and partitions simple (halves through tenths).

When an interactive builder is used, optional feedback such as rejecting an unequal drag, a 'hopper' that jumps the unit fraction and lands on a/b, a draggable point that reports the nearest fraction and turns green on the exact spot, and a mode showing the line running past 1 can make the mechanism concrete — these are illustrative, not mandatory or proven superior to other media.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (DfE National Curriculum) was marked verified:false in the original; treat its curriculum-placement claim with that caveat.

Arithmetic correction made during review: drawing four interior marks cuts the 0–1 unit into FIVE equal parts (fifths, each 1/5), with the far interior mark at 4/5 — it does NOT overshoot past 1. Three interior marks make four quarters (marks at 1/4,2/4,3/4), and a fourth quarter-length jump lands exactly on 1 (4/4).

The original recommendation's claim that the far mark 'lands on 5/4' when four marks are dropped is a confused/erroneous original detail: 5/4 would require five quarter-length jumps (keeping the interval at 1/4), not four interior marks. It is recorded in uncertainty notes and not presented to learners.

Verified examples after correction: 4/6 reads as four 1/6-lengths from 0; 1/2 = 3/6 sits at the 3rd mark; 3/4 sits three-quarters toward 1, just before 1; three interior marks make four equal quarters; four interior marks make five equal fifths (far mark 4/5).

The original error-pattern note 'reads the 4th mark... calls the point 4/5' is retained only as a plausible tick-counting slip used in feedback as an off-by-one example to re-count, not taught as a fact; it has not been independently verified.

probeDeeper: How many equal parts did you make, and how many marks did you draw inside — why is that one fewer than the number of parts?
Where is 1 on your line? Is 3/4 before or after 1, and how do you know?
This point is 4/6. Can you find and mark 1/2 on the same line?
If this line went all the way to 2 instead of 1, would 3/4 move? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The dot is 4/6 — four 1/6-lengths from 0. To place 3/4: partition 0–1 into 4 equal parts (3 marks inside), then count 3 parts from 0, so 3/4 sits three-quarters of the way to 1, just before 1.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts tick marks not intervals — reads the 4th mark as if the marks were the count, or makes 4 interior marks to show fourths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shade each interval and count LENGTHS from 0 ('how many jumps of the same size?'); make explicit that b equal parts need b−1 interior marks
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Off-by-one reading of the point, or partitions with the wrong number of marks when producing

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number placement — puts 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction as two separate whole numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Firmly label 0 and 1; ask 'where is 1? must 3/4 be less than 1 or more?'; place it inside 0–1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the blank line places 3/4 beyond 1, near where 3 or 4 would be

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the whole drawn segment as the unit — ignores the 0–1 labelling and measures a/b as a fraction of the entire picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find and mark 1 first; establish that the unit is 0–1, and everything is measured against that fixed length whatever the drawing shows
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a line drawn past 1, places 3/4 at three-quarters of the total drawn length rather than of 0–1

responseLevels.gap: Counts tick marks or places 3/4 beyond 1 / at three-quarters of the whole drawing; cannot identify the 0–1 unit interval.
responseLevels.full: Reads the point as 4/6 by counting equal intervals from 0, and independently partitions 0–1 into b equal parts and iterates a of them to place 3/4 correctly below 1, explaining the unit interval and the interval length.
responseLevels.partial: Reads or partitions correctly on a marked line but falters when producing on a blank line, or gets the position without articulating that each interval is 1/b and the unit is 0–1.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a 0-to-1 number line already divided into 6 equal parts, with a dot on the 4th mark from 0. Ask: 'What fraction is this dot, and how do you know?' Then give a blank 0-to-1 line and ask: 'Mark 3/4 on this line, and talk me through how you place it.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who treats the 0–1 segment as the unit and counts equal intervals reads 4/6 and places 3/4 correctly below 1. The tick-counting child miscounts marks (calls the point 4/5, or draws 4 marks for fourths); the whole-number-placement child pushes 3/4 out beyond 1 (toward '3 to 4') or places it at three-quarters of the whole drawing. Both moves — interpret and produce — are needed to pass.

sources.claim: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.

sources.claim: Pupils are taught to recognise and use fractions as numbers and to place them on a number line during KS2 (Years 3–4, ages 8–9).

pedagogy.summary: Dividing a quantity in a given ratio is the formal KS3 procedure: for a ratio a:b (or a:b:c), the TOTAL number of parts is a+b(+c); one part = quantity ÷ total parts; each share = its parts × one part. Two things distinguish this from earlier unequal-sharing work: it extends cleanly to THREE-part ratios (divide 180 in 1:2:3), and it goes both ways — pupils must also express a completed division back AS a ratio in simplest form (10 and 14 becomes 5:7), and read off a part as a fraction of the whole. The persistent hazard is using a part rather than the SUM of parts as the denominator; the fix is the same find-one-part routine, kept visible on a bar model.
bestPractices: Standardise the routine explicitly: total parts = sum of all ratio numbers → one part = quantity ÷ total → multiply each ratio number by one part.
Extend to three-part ratios immediately (1:2:3 → 6 parts) so the 'sum ALL the parts' step is generalised, not tied to two shares.
Practise the reverse direction: given the actual shares, write them as a ratio and simplify (10:14 → 5:7), and state a share as a fraction of the whole.
Keep the bar model as the check: the number of equal segments equals the sum of the ratio numbers; adding the shares must return the original quantity.
Distinguish part-to-part (a:b) from part-to-whole (a out of a+b) in the notation, since the same numbers appear in both.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / tape diagram with a+b(+c) equal segments
The 'one part' unit (quantity ÷ total parts)
Ratio table (parts | value) extended to three columns for three-part ratios
Simplest-form ratio from actual shares (divide by the HCF)
commonMisconceptions: Dividing by a single part rather than the sum of parts (÷3 or ÷5 instead of ÷8), or in a 3-part ratio forgetting to include every part in the total.
Sharing the quantity equally among the number of terms (180 into three equal 60s for 1:2:3).
When reversing, writing the shares as a ratio without simplifying (10:14 left un-reduced), or reversing the order.
Confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole — stating a share as a/b of the whole rather than a/(a+b).

learn.summary: Divide a quantity in a given ratio using the find-one-part routine: total parts = sum of ALL ratio numbers; one part = quantity ÷ total parts; each share = its ratio number × one part. The guidance generalises this to three-part ratios (divide 180 in 1:2:3 = 6 parts, not 3) and works both directions: express a completed division back as a simplest-form ratio (10 and 14 → 5:7) and state a share as a fraction of the whole. The persistent hazard is using one part, rather than the sum of parts, as the denominator; a bar/tape model with the correct number of equal segments keeps the correct total visible as a check.

activities.title: Ratio-divider on a tape diagram (forward direction)
feedback: If the strip is cut into three segments for 1:2:3, flag it: count that 1+2+3 = 6 segments are needed before the fill unlocks.

If the learner divides by the number of ratio terms or by a single term instead of the sum of parts (e.g. 180 ÷ 3 = 60) or shares equally (60, 60, 60), show the six-segment bar and recompute one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
If the learner finds one part but stops (answers '30', or '1, 2, 3'), prompt that 30 is only ONE part: ask how many parts each share has, then multiply (1×30, 2×30, 3×30 → 30, 60, 90).
If the shares don't sum to the original quantity, prompt a recount of segments — the total must return 180.
activities.rationale: An optional interactive tape diagram that refuses an incorrect number of segments can make the '÷ total parts' step explicit and give immediate feedback; because the learner segments and fills the bar, the task lets them produce the working rather than only recognise a finished answer. The refusal mechanism is one illustrative design, proposed rather than required or uniquely effective, and its efficacy is not source-verified; it teaches the National Curriculum objective of dividing a quantity in a given ratio.
sourceClaims: Pupils should divide a given quantity into two (or more) parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express a division as a fraction of the whole (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change).
learnerActions: Enter a ratio such as 1:2:3 and cut the strip into the SUM of the parts — six equal segments for 1:2:3, not three.
Let the quantity (e.g. 180) distribute across the equal segments and read off one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
Colour 1, 2 and 3 adjacent segments to read the shares 30, 60 and 90, then add them to check they return 180.
Repeat with a two-part ratio (e.g. share £60 in 2:3: 5 parts, one part = 12, shares 24 and 36, summing to 60).
activities.intendedInsight: A three-part ratio 1:2:3 needs six equal parts, not three; dividing once by the total number of parts and then scaling each term is the whole routine, and the shares must add back to the original quantity.

activities.title: Reverse station: write shares as a simplest-form ratio
feedback: If the learner leaves 10:14 un-simplified, prompt: what common factor divides both? Divide by 2 to get 5:7.
If the order is reversed to 14:10, point back to which share came first (10) and restore the matching order.
activities.rationale: The forward division task does not test simplification, so a separate reverse task is needed to secure it. Casting simplification as dividing both terms by the HCF connects to prior fraction work.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b(:c), a part is a/(a+b(+c)) of the whole; ratio compares part to part and must be reduced to simplest form — the classic error is reading a:b as a/b of the whole.
learnerActions: Take two actual shares (e.g. 24 sweets shared as 10 and 14) and write them as a ratio 10:14.
Simplify by dividing both terms by their highest common factor (÷2) to reach 5:7, keeping the order matching the shares as stated.
Explain how this is like simplifying a fraction, and check you have not reversed the order (14:10 is wrong for 10 then 14).
activities.intendedInsight: A completed division can be expressed back as a ratio, and a ratio must be reduced to simplest form by dividing by the common factor — directly analogous to simplifying a fraction.

activities.title: Part of the whole as a fraction
feedback: If a learner writes the middle share of 1:2:3 as 2/3, point to the six segments: the denominator is the total parts, so it is 2/6 = 1/3.
Compare 2/6 and 2/3 side by side so the distinction between part-to-part and part-to-whole is visible.
activities.rationale: Confusing a:b with a/b of the whole is a documented classic error; anchoring the denominator to the counted total parts on the bar addresses it directly.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b(:c), a part is a/(a+b(+c)) of the whole; ratio compares part to part and must be reduced to simplest form — the classic error is reading a:b as a/b of the whole.
Pupils should divide a given quantity into two (or more) parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express a division as a fraction of the whole (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change).
learnerActions: For 1:2:3, state what fraction of the whole each share is: 1/6, 2/6 (=1/3) and 3/6 (=1/2), using the TOTAL of 6 parts as the denominator.
Contrast part-to-part with part-to-whole explicitly: the middle share is 2 parts out of 6 total, so 2/6, NOT 2/3.
Optionally toggle a colour band to light each part and reveal its fraction of the whole.
activities.intendedInsight: When stating a share as a fraction of the whole, the denominator is the SUM of all parts (a+b+c), not another single term; part-to-part and part-to-whole use the same numbers differently.

activities.title: Checks for understanding (written/selected response)
feedback: For 60, 60, 60: that divides equally rather than in 1:2:3 — re-form the total of 6 parts and scale each term.
For 10:14 chosen as final: it is not yet simplified — divide both terms by 2 to reach 5:7.
For 2/3: the denominator should be the total of 6 parts, giving 2/6 = 1/3.
activities.rationale: Selected/short responses efficiently reveal the equal-share and un-simplified-ratio errors, but they confirm recognition and recall rather than requiring the learner to build the segmented bar and produce the working; use alongside the construction tasks.
learnerActions: Fill in: divide 180 in 1:2:3 → __, __, __ (answer 30, 60, 90; the equal-share response 60, 60, 60 is a common error).
Choose the simplest-form ratio for shares of 10 and 14 (answer 5:7; the un-simplified 10:14 is a distractor).
State what fraction of the whole the middle share of 1:2:3 is (answer 2/6 = 1/3).
activities.intendedInsight: Three-part division, reverse-to-ratio, and part-of-whole can each be checked, with 'shared equally' and 'un-simplified ratio' as the diagnostic error responses; add a two-part item (e.g. £60 in 2:3) if two-part division is also to be checked.

constraints: Treat the forward division and the reverse (shares → simplest-form ratio) as distinct objectives: the forward task does not exercise simplification, so include a separate reverse task.

A static segmented reference bar (e.g. six equal segments for 1:2:3) with tap-to-reveal 'one part = total ÷ sum of parts' can consolidate the routine but does not let the learner segment, fill, or reverse a division themselves — it is a reference card, not a substitute for construction.
Selected-response checks confirm recognition/recall; they do not require the learner to build the bar or produce the working, so pair them with construction tasks for full evidence.
Always re-include every term in the total: a three-part ratio must sum all parts (1+2+3 = 6), and the shares must add back to the original quantity as a check.
Keep part-to-part (a:b) and part-to-whole (a out of a+b+c) distinct in notation, since the same numbers appear in both.
After finding one part, scale each term (×1, ×2, ×3) — reporting one part alone, or '1, 2, 3', is incomplete.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic checked): 180 ÷ 6 = 30; shares 30+60+90 = 180 ✓. £60 in 2:3 → 5 parts, 60 ÷ 5 = 12, shares 24 and 36, sum 60 ✓. 10:14 ÷2 = 5:7 ✓. Middle share of 1:2:3 = 2/6 = 1/3 ✓; largest share 3/6 = 1/2 ✓.

The legacy entry asserted a dividing procedure 'gains nothing' from dialogue and that 3D 'adds nothing' because partitioning is one-dimensional. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been dropped rather than propagated as universal laws; the tape/bar model is retained as a well-fitted representation without claiming other media cannot teach this.
The 'refusal to cut into three segments' is preserved as one optional, illustrative feedback mechanism, not a mandatory or uniquely effective design; its efficacy is untested.

Restored the original assessment's 'performance' error pattern (finds one part but forgets to multiply each term back) as explicit feedback in the forward-division activity, as it was missing from the source candidate.

The original probeDeeper listed '3/3, 3/6, or 3/1' as candidate answers for the largest share; only the correct 3/6 = 1/2 is used, and the erroneous options were not migrated as learner-facing choices.

probeDeeper: How many equal parts are there altogether in 1:2:3? Why 6 and not 3?
Add your three amounts together — do they make 180? What would it mean if they didn't?
What fraction of the whole 180 is the largest share? (counterexample: is it 3/3, 3/6, or 3/1 — and why?)
For 10:14, how did you get 5:7 — what did you divide by, and how is that like simplifying a fraction?
assess.correctAnswer: For 180 in 1:2:3: total parts = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, so one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30; the shares are 30, 60 and 90 (which add to 180). For the reverse: 10:14 simplifies (÷2) to 5:7.

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by a single part or by the number of terms rather than the SUM of all parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the bar cut into 1+2+3 = 6 equal segments and count them; one part = 180 ÷ 6. Check the shares add back to 180. Reteach ratio notation and the total-parts idea.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 180 ÷ 3 = 60 and gives 60, 60, 60 (equal), or 180 ÷ 1 / ÷2 / ÷3 separately; total parts of 6 never formed

errorPatterns.pattern: When reversing, writes the shares as a ratio without simplifying (or reverses the order)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat it like simplifying a fraction: divide both by the common factor (2). Keep the order matching the shares as stated. Reteach ratio simplification.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 10:14 as the final answer, or writes 14:10, not dividing by the HCF to 5:7

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses part-to-part with part-to-whole — states a share as a/b of the whole rather than a/(a+b+c)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the six segments: the denominator is the TOTAL parts. Contrast 2/6 with 2/3 explicitly. Reteach the vocabulary of part-to-part vs part-to-whole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up, says the middle share of 1:2:3 is 2/3 of the whole rather than 2/6 = 1/3

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds one part correctly but forgets to multiply each term back
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'that's ONE part — how many parts does each share have?' Prompt the multiply and the add-back check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 180 ÷ 6 = 30 and answers '30' or '1, 2, 3' rather than 30, 60, 90

responseLevels.gap: Shares equally (60,60,60) or divides by one part; cannot form the total of 6 parts, and leaves a reversed ratio un-simplified.
responseLevels.full: Sums all parts to 6, finds one part = 30, gives 30/60/90 checked to 180, simplifies 10:14 to 5:7, and correctly states a share as its fraction of the whole (e.g. 2/6 = 1/3) — handling both directions and three-part ratios.
responseLevels.partial: Divides 180 correctly via 6 parts to 30/60/90, but leaves 10:14 un-simplified, or states a share as part-of-part not part-of-whole — the reverse direction or the fraction interpretation is not yet secure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Divide 180 in the ratio 1:2:3. Work out the three amounts, and show your working. Then, separately: 24 sweets were shared as 10 and 14 — write that sharing as a ratio in its simplest form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who has the routine sums all three parts to 6, divides once, and scales — shares total 180. A pupil dividing by the number of terms shares equally (60, 60, 60) or divides by one part; a pupil who cannot reverse leaves 10:14 un-simplified. Watching the working shows exactly which step fails, and the reverse task separately tests simplification, which the forward task does not.

sources.claim: Pupils should divide a given quantity into two (or more) parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express a division as a fraction of the whole (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change).
sources.source: UK National Curriculum, Mathematics programmes of study

sources.claim: In a part-to-part ratio a:b(:c), a part is a/(a+b(+c)) of the whole; ratio compares part to part and must be reduced to simplest form — the classic error is reading a:b as a/b of the whole.
sources.source: NRICH, 'Ratio or Proportion?'

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Predator Loss and Ecosystem Effects (ages 12–14): removing top predators from the ocean does not just subtract one species — it reorganises the whole food web through trophic cascades, and recovering predators can restore it.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS3 biology — the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem, including food webs; how organisms affect, and are affected by, their environment; builds on KS2 Y6 classification/adaptation and predator-prey.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS2-4 (construct an argument [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-4]); MS-LS2-2 (patterns of interactions among organisms); MS-LS2-5 (evaluate solutions for maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem services); the ~10% energy-transfer idea underpins the trophic-pyramid reasoning.
• Operational details — Build the mechanism on three pillars. (1) The ~10% rule: only about a tenth of energy passes up each trophic level, so top predators are few and populations are structured as a pyramid. (2) Trophic cascade: the canonical sea-otter → sea-urchin → kelp case — remove otters, urchins explode, kelp forests are grazed to barren; restore otters and kelp returns. (3) 'Fishing down the food web': humans remove large predators first, shifting catches to ever-smaller species and destabilising the web. Close on recovery evidence — shark/whale rebound, whales as nutrient pumps ('whale pump') — and ecosystem-based fisheries management as the applied response.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete, ~11–12): predicts that removing a predator lets its prey increase. Tier B (transitional, ~12–13): traces a two-step cascade (fewer otters → more urchins → less kelp) and explains why there are fewer predators than prey. Tier C (formal, ~13–14): reasons with the ~10% energy pyramid, explains 'fishing down the web', and evaluates how predator recovery or ecosystem-based management could restore an ocean ecosystem.
bestPractices: Teach the cascade as a testable PREDICTION-then-CHECK: have students forecast what happens two and three steps out when a predator is removed, then reveal the empirical sea-otter/kelp outcome.
Ground the abstraction in the documented sea-otter – urchin – kelp system (and a reef shark or cod analogue) so 'trophic cascade' is a real case, not a slogan.
Make the ~10% energy-transfer rule the reason predators are RARE — connect pyramid shape to why losing a top predator is high-leverage and recovery is slow.
Introduce 'fishing down the food web' with real catch-composition change so students see a human driver, not just natural dynamics.
Balance loss with RECOVERY evidence (otter, whale, shark rebound; the whale nutrient pump) so the lesson lands on agency and management, not doom.
Distinguish correlation from causation: use cases where predator removal AND recovery both moved the ecosystem, which is stronger evidence of the causal link.
keyRepresentations: Energy pyramid with ~10% passing up each level — explaining why top predators are few.
The sea-otter → urchin → kelp cascade as a three-node chain, shown in both directions (collapse and recovery).
A food web with an apex node that can be 'removed', with arrows re-weighting downstream.
Before/after 'kelp forest vs urchin barren' paired images.
'Fishing down the web' as a shrinking-catch-size timeline.
commonMisconceptions: 'Removing a predator only affects its direct prey' — effects cascade two or more levels down (otters gone → urchins up → kelp gone → whole community shifts).
'More predators is always bad / predators are just harmful' — apex predators stabilise ecosystems and their loss reduces biodiversity.
'Ecosystems bounce straight back once fishing stops' — recovery can be slow or shift to an alternative stable state (e.g. persistent urchin barren).
'Energy flows up efficiently' — only ~10% transfers per level, which is why top predators are scarce and vulnerable.
'Top predators are the most abundant because they're the strongest' — they are the LEAST abundant precisely because of the energy pyramid.

learn.summary: For ages 12–14: removing a top ocean predator does not just reduce one species — it can reorganise a whole food web through a trophic cascade, and recovery can be slow or stall. Learners drive the cascade in a dynamic food-web model (sea otter → urchin → kelp), reason with the ~10% energy-transfer pyramid to see why apex predators are rare, combine this with cascade evidence to see why some can have effects large relative to their numbers, investigate 'fishing down the food web', transfer the reasoning to another predator-loss system, and debate recovery/management options. A central goal is distinguishing indirect, multi-step web effects from linear one-step chain thinking.

activities.title: Drive the kelp-forest cascade: remove the otters
feedback: If a learner predicts 'more life overall' after removing otters, have them map the arrows otter→urchin→kelp and identify who loses when kelp collapses; fewer predators can mean a simpler, poorer system through runaway grazing.
If a learner stops at 'urchins increase', prompt them to extend the chain to kelp and then branch it into a web of habitat-dependent species.
If a learner expects instant recovery when otters return, point to the slow or stalled kelp rebound in the model and ask what could speed it up or hold it back.
activities.rationale: A trophic cascade is a multi-step dynamic; setting it in motion and watching the delay and possible irreversibility makes indirect, web-wide effects concrete in a way a single frozen chain does not. Predict-then-check surfaces linear misconceptions before the empirical outcome is revealed.
sourceClaims: Sea otters are a keystone predator: where otters are removed, sea urchins increase and overgraze kelp into urchin barrens; where otters recover, kelp forests return — a classic trophic cascade.
learnerActions: Before acting, predict in writing what will happen one, two, and three steps out if sea otters are removed from a kelp-forest food web.

In a food-web model with live population meters (otters, sea urchins, kelp, and fish that depend on kelp), remove the otters and watch how populations re-settle level by level over time rather than instantly.
Record the order and timing: urchin meter climbs, kelp is grazed down toward an urchin-barren state, and kelp-dependent fish decline.
Reintroduce the otters and observe whether and how fast kelp recovers; note if the system stalls in the barren state.
Write a short account identifying the species the otter never directly touched (kelp) and explaining the exact chain by which hunting otters led to kelp loss.
activities.intendedInsight: A predator's loss can cause harm two or more steps away through a web of indirect effects; recovery is not guaranteed to be immediate or complete because systems can shift toward an alternative stable state.

activities.title: Why apex predators are rare: the ~10% energy pyramid
feedback: If a learner says energy passes up efficiently or the top is crowded, work the ~10% rule up each level and compare the 100 / 10 / 1 figures.
If a learner equates abundance with strength, redirect to the energy available to support each tier.
activities.rationale: Grounding predator rarity in the energy pyramid gives a mechanistic reason for why losing an apex species matters so much, countering the 'strongest = most abundant' misconception. The ~10% figure is a standard approximation that varies by system.
sourceClaims: Roughly 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next, so top predators are supported by a small fraction of primary production and are correspondingly few in number (trophic pyramid).
learnerActions: In an energy-pyramid mode, pour in about 100 units of energy at the base and track how much reaches the next level (~10 units) and the top (~1 unit).
Use the ~10% transfer to explain why top predators are the least abundant tier, not the most.

Connect pyramid shape to consequences: using the cascade from the otter model, argue why losing a top predator can be high-leverage relative to its small numbers, and use the pyramid to explain why recovery of a thin top tier can be slow.
Challenge the claim 'top predators are abundant because they are strongest' using the energy figures.
activities.intendedInsight: Only roughly a tenth of energy passes up each trophic level, so apex predators are naturally scarce (low total energy and biomass at the top); cascade evidence such as the otter case shows that some apex predators have ecological effects large relative to their numbers, though not every predator does.

activities.title: Fishing down the food web
feedback: If a learner treats shrinking catch size as neutral, connect it to loss of apex predators and the cascade/pyramid consequences they already explored.
If a learner thinks it is purely natural variation, point them back to the pressure control as the human cause they introduced.
activities.rationale: Showing catch composition change as something the learner caused makes 'fishing down the food web' a reasoned pattern rather than a memorised phrase, linking human action to ecosystem effects.
sourceClaims: 'Fishing down the marine food web': fisheries tend to remove large, high-trophic-level predators first, shifting catches toward smaller, lower-trophic-level species over time.
learnerActions: Use a fishing-pressure control that preferentially removes the biggest, highest-trophic-level species first, and observe how catch composition shifts toward smaller, lower-level species over time.
Describe in your own words why a trend toward catching ever-smaller species is a warning sign about ecosystem state, not just a change of menu.
Relate this human-driven removal of large predators to the cascade and pyramid ideas from the earlier activities.
activities.intendedInsight: Fisheries tend to remove large predators first, shifting catches down the food web over time; this is a human driver of the same predator-loss dynamics seen in cascades.

activities.title: Debate recovery and ecosystem-based management
feedback: If a learner asserts an intervention will definitely fix the system, point back to the model's slow/stalled recovery and ask what evidence supports the claim.
If a learner cites only predator-removal harm, ask whether recovery evidence strengthens the causal case.
If a learner assumes every system behaves exactly like the otter case, ask what features of the new system (species present, habitat, fishing pressure) might change the outcome.
Reward reasoning that weighs costs and uncertainty over slogans.
activities.rationale: The value/policy tail suits Socratic dialogue once the mechanism is understood; discussion can give learners practice constructing and defending a claim and transferring it to a new case, which recall-only tasks do not require. This activity is a companion to, not a replacement for, the mechanism-building model.
learnerActions: Take a position on an intervention — e.g. rewilding/predator recovery (otters, sharks), fishing restrictions, or ecosystem-based management — for a stressed ocean ecosystem, and state your reasoning.

Transfer the cascade reasoning to a different documented predator-loss system (for example a reef-shark or cod fishery) and predict what removing or restoring the top predator could do there, noting that specific outcomes depend on the system and are not settled here.
Respond to challenges from an in-role fisheries scientist or marine ecologist who presses on trade-offs, who bears the cost, and what the evidence shows.

Use the cascade mechanism to argue why recovery of predators could help restore a system, and nutrient cycling (e.g. whales moving nutrients to surface waters) to argue why recovery of species like whales could help; use the ~10% pyramid to explain why rebuilding a thin top tier can be slow. Acknowledge that recovery may be slow or incomplete and that whale-nutrient-cycling and management outcomes are discussion context rather than settled figures.
Distinguish correlation from causation: identify cases where BOTH predator removal and predator recovery moved the ecosystem as stronger evidence of a causal link.
activities.intendedInsight: Management of predator loss involves values, trade-offs and evidence quality, not only mechanism; the cascade reasoning transfers to other systems, and the lesson should land on agency and management rather than doom.

activities.title: Label the players: healthy forest vs urchin barren
feedback: If a learner cannot bridge the two scenes, prompt them to narrate the intermediate steps (urchins rise, kelp falls).
Confirm that kelp is an indirect victim the otter never ate.
activities.rationale: A labelled static paired image is a useful scaffold for vocabulary and the end-states, but it only shows two frozen states and cannot convey the delay or possible irreversibility; it supports, and does not replace, the dynamic model.
sourceClaims: Sea otters are a keystone predator: where otters are removed, sea urchins increase and overgraze kelp into urchin barrens; where otters recover, kelp forests return — a classic trophic cascade.
learnerActions: Examine paired before/after images of a healthy kelp forest and an urchin barren, identify which of the otter, urchin, and kelp nodes appear in each scene (noting which are scarce or absent in the barren), and state their roles.
Tap or annotate each node to state what it eats and what depends on it, tracing the otter→urchin→kelp chain.
Explain, from the two frozen scenes, what must have happened in between to get from the forest to the barren.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming the players and the direction of the chain prepares learners to reason about the dynamic cascade and recognise the two end-states.

constraints: The dynamic food-web model is the primary mechanism-builder because the cascade is a time-dependent, multi-step process; the paired static images are a vocabulary/end-state scaffold only and cannot show the delay or possible irreversibility.

Sequencing/matching/slider-recognition tasks can verify that learners can order the cascade steps and state the ~10% figure, but recognition alone does not elicit the independent 'run-it-and-watch' insight or independent construction and transfer of the argument; pair them with the modelling and writing/debate tasks.
The in-role scientist conversation is a companion for the value/policy and argumentation tail, not the primary way to teach the mechanism.
Keep live population meters legible; added ambience (e.g. a purely decorative 3D scene) should not obscure the meters that carry the causal information.
Use cases where both predator removal and recovery moved the ecosystem to strengthen causal claims, and avoid presenting correlation as proof.

Present the ~10% energy-transfer figure as an approximation that varies by ecosystem, and label the simulation's hysteresis/stalled-recovery behaviour as illustrative rather than a precise prediction.
When transferring the reasoning to a non-otter system (reef shark, cod), treat predicted outcomes as system-dependent and not established by the cited sources.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all three sources are marked verified:false in the row, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The ~10% energy-transfer figure is a standard teaching approximation; actual ecological efficiency varies by system. Present it as approximate, as the source claim does ('roughly 10%').

The hysteresis / alternative-stable-state behaviour (recovery may stall in the barren state) is realistic for this system but its magnitude and reversibility depend on the specific ecosystem; the model should be labelled as an illustrative simulation, not a precise prediction.

Claims about whales as a 'nutrient pump' and rewilding/ecosystem-based management outcomes appear in the pedagogy summary but are not directly backed by the three cited sources; treat them as context for discussion rather than established quantitative outcomes.

The reef-shark/cod analogue and the transfer-to-a-new-system objective are drawn from the original row (bestPractices and responseLevels) and restored in the debate activity; specific outcomes for non-otter systems are not separately source-verified.
The row's note that 3D rendering 'adds nothing' is a design preference, not an established pedagogical law; retained only as a narrowly scoped point about not obscuring the population meters.

The original row specified a Tier A / Tier B / Tier C checkpoint progression (concrete prediction → two-step cascade → formal ~10% pyramid and management evaluation). These activities span that range but do not name the tiers explicitly; a teacher may wish to sequence them as explicit differentiation levels.

probeDeeper: The otters never touched kelp. So explain the exact steps by which hunting otters destroyed a kelp forest.
If only about 10% of energy passes up each level, why are there so few top predators — and why does losing them hit so hard?
'Fishing down the food web' means catching ever-lower species as the big ones vanish. Why is that a warning sign, not just a menu change?
Would putting the otters back instantly restore the kelp? What might speed it up or hold it back?
assess.correctAnswer: No — removing an apex predator can devastate an ecosystem through a TROPHIC CASCADE. Otters eat sea urchins; take the otters away and the urchin population explodes; the urchins graze down the kelp forest until it collapses to a barren. So a species the otter never touched (kelp) crashes, and the many animals that depended on the kelp habitat lose out — the ecosystem gets poorer, not richer. It works because effects ripple through a WEB, not a single line, and because energy transfer is inefficient (only ~10% passes up each trophic level), so top predators are naturally rare and their control effect is large relative to their numbers. This is why 'fishing down the food web' and losing apex predators (sharks, etc.) is so damaging, and why rewilding (otter/shark recovery, whales cycling nutrients) can help restore systems.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Removing a predator is good for the prey and the ecosystem' — linear, one-step food-chain thinking.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the cascade arrow by arrow (otter→urchin→kelp); show that fewer predators can mean a poorer, simpler system via runaway grazing.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's good news — without the otter, more urchins survive, so there's more life overall.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts more prey and a richer system; can't explain a downstream collapse or names no indirect effect.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Effects only pass one link along the chain' — no sense of indirect, multi-step or web effects.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend the chain two steps and branch it into a web; the kelp is an indirect victim; map who else loses when the kelp goes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only the urchins are affected — the change can't reach a plant the otter never even ate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts urchins increase but stops there; doesn't reach the kelp or the habitat-dependent species.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Top predators are abundant / energy passes up efficiently' — misunderstands the ~10% rule and the pyramid.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Work the ~10% rule up a pyramid to show why apex predators are few, and why that makes each one's ecological role outsized and slow to recover.
errorPatterns.distractor: There are loads of apex predators — energy passes up the levels efficiently, so the top is crowded.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes apex predators are numerous, or that most energy transfers up each level; surprised they're rare.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks losing a predator benefits the ecosystem; reasons only one link along a chain.
responseLevels.full: Traces the cascade mechanistically through a web, uses the ~10% rule to explain why apex predators are rare and pivotal, links it to 'fishing down the web' and rewilding, and transfers the reasoning to predict effects of removing/restoring a predator in a new system.
responseLevels.partial: Can state that removing otters lets urchins increase and that this harms kelp, but recites it as a fixed chain — can't generalise the cascade idea or connect it to the ~10% rule / web structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Along one coast, sea otters were hunted out. Soon the kelp forests — which otters never ate — collapsed into bare 'urchin barrens'. A student says 'removing a top predator like the otter is basically good news for everything below it — more prey survive, so the ecosystem gets richer'. Is losing an apex predator good news lower down? Walk me through what happened to the kelp, and why removing ONE species did that.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student with linear 'predator bad, prey good' thinking predicts the ecosystem flourishes without the otter; a student with the concept traces the cascade (otter↓ → urchin↑ → kelp↓ → habitat loss) and grasps that indirect, web-wide effects can be negative far from the predator. Asking how removing ONE species crashed a plant it never ate forces the cascade out.

sources.claim: Roughly 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next, so top predators are supported by a small fraction of primary production and are correspondingly few in number (trophic pyramid).
sources.source: Standard ecology / NGSS MS-LS2 ecosystem energy-flow content (ecological efficiency ~10%)

sources.claim: Sea otters are a keystone predator: where otters are removed, sea urchins increase and overgraze kelp into urchin barrens; where otters recover, kelp forests return — a classic trophic cascade.
sources.source: Estes & Palmisano keystone/sea-otter kelp cascade research; widely summarised in NOAA and marine-ecology education materials

sources.claim: 'Fishing down the marine food web': fisheries tend to remove large, high-trophic-level predators first, shifting catches toward smaller, lower-trophic-level species over time.
sources.source: Pauly et al., 'Fishing down marine food webs' (Science, 1998), as summarised in fisheries-science education resources

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Where water is found on Earth

- **Standards — UK (KS1/KS2 Geography & Science — identify seas/oceans and physical features; states of matter foundation):** Children name where water is found — oceans, rivers, lakes, glaciers/ice, underground — and recognise water as liquid and as solid (ice/snow).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-ESS2-3):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-3].

- **Operational details:** This is a survey-and-classify concept. Build a mental map of Earth's water stores (oceans, rivers, lakes, glaciers, groundwater, and — for the readier child — the atmosphere) and tag each as liquid or solid. Two big ideas carry the weight: (1) water lives in many different places, and (2) most of Earth's water is in the oceans. Use a globe/world map so children SEE how much is blue, and photographs of each store (a glacier, a river, a lake, a well/spring) to make 'underground' and 'ice' concrete. Connect to prior state-of-matter work: glaciers and snow are the same water, just frozen solid.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete / observational). The child lists several places water is found, sorts examples into solid vs liquid (glacier/snow = solid; ocean/river = liquid), and says that most of Earth's water is in the oceans.
bestPractices: Start from a globe or world map so the dominance of ocean water is seen, not just told ('most of Earth's water is in the oceans').
Use real photographs of each store — glacier, river, lake, spring/well, snow — to make abstract locations (especially 'underground') concrete.
Explicitly tag each store as solid or liquid, linking to prior heating/cooling state-change work (ice and snow are frozen water).
Have children generate and sort their own examples ('where have YOU seen water?') into liquid/solid and into named stores.
Keep it observational and vocabulary-rich at this age; save proportions/percentages for the later salt-vs-fresh graphing topic.
keyRepresentations: A globe / world map showing oceans dominating Earth's surface.
A labelled 'water stores' picture: ocean, river, lake, glacier, groundwater, (atmosphere).
A solid-vs-liquid sorting mat for water examples.
Photo cards of each water store for classification.
commonMisconceptions: 'Most water is in rivers and lakes' — not realising oceans hold the vast majority.
'Ice/snow isn't water' — not connecting frozen forms to liquid water.
'There's no water underground' — missing groundwater as a real, large store.
'All water is drinkable/fresh' — not yet distinguishing salt ocean water from fresh water (addressed fully in the later salt-vs-fresh topic).
'Water is only where you can see it' — overlooking hidden stores (groundwater, atmospheric vapour).

learn.summary: For children aged 7–8, build a mental map of where water is found on Earth — oceans, rivers, lakes, glaciers/snow/ice, and underground (and, for readier children, the atmosphere) — and tag each store as liquid or solid. Two big ideas carry the weight: water is found in many places (seen and unseen), and most of Earth's water is in the oceans. Connect frozen forms (glaciers, snow, ice) back to prior state-of-matter work: they are the same water, just solid. Keep it observational and vocabulary-rich; save proportions/percentages for a later salt-vs-fresh graphing topic.

activities.title: Survey the cutaway Earth: tap-to-reveal water stores
feedback: If a child names rivers/lakes as holding the most water, compare the sizes directly: the oceans dwarf rivers and lakes — most of Earth's water is salty sea water.
If a child says ice or snow 'isn't really water', note that ice is water in its solid form, and connect to prior heating/cooling work (ice can melt back to liquid).
If a child overlooks groundwater, point to wells and springs as evidence that water is held underground in soil and rock.
activities.rationale: The learning objective is to survey and classify water stores and tag each as solid or liquid — a labelled mental map. A single rich, tappable scene delivers the vocabulary, one fact per store, and a solid/liquid flag without needing dynamic machinery. A globe makes ocean dominance seen rather than merely told. Interactive tap-to-reveal and lift-the-flap are concrete ways to rehearse naming and classifying; a static labelled diagram or picture cards can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-ESS2-3: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-3].
Most of Earth's water is in the oceans (~97% salt water); fresh water is in glaciers, groundwater, rivers and lakes.
learnerActions: Look at a globe or world map and describe how much of Earth's surface is blue (ocean).
Explore a cutaway Earth scene — globe above, ground cross-section below — with water stores to discover: ocean, river, lake, mountain glacier, snowfield, and hidden groundwater below the surface.

For each store, reveal a short fact and name the store aloud: e.g. ocean → 'oceans hold most of Earth's water, and it is salty'; glacier/snowfield → 'frozen water — the same water, just solid'; below ground → 'groundwater — hidden liquid water you can't see from the surface'.
For each store, answer a lift-the-flap 'solid or liquid?' prompt before the answer is shown.
Point to or name a store you would never have guessed held water (e.g. underground).
activities.intendedInsight: Water is found in many different places — seen and unseen, solid and liquid — and the oceans hold far more than everything else combined.

activities.title: Generate and sort your own water examples
feedback: If snow or ice is sorted as 'not water', show or recall melting an ice cube: it becomes liquid water, so it counts as water in solid form.

If a child only lists visible water, prompt for hidden stores — water held underground, and water vapour in the air, which you cannot see — to extend beyond 'water is only where you can see it'; clouds can be noted as visible signs of water in the sky, not as the invisible example.
Affirm correct sorts by restating the rule used: 'Yes — a glacier is frozen, so it goes on solid.'
activities.rationale: Having children generate and classify their own examples makes the categorisation active and vocabulary-rich, and surfaces misconceptions (ice not counting, hidden stores missed) for direct response. Real photographs make abstract locations such as 'underground' concrete.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-ESS2-3: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-3].
learnerActions: Answer 'Where have YOU seen water?' and list as many places as you can (e.g. sea, puddle, tap, snow, pond, ice lolly, river).
Sort each example onto a solid-vs-liquid mat: glacier/snow/ice → solid; ocean/river/lake/puddle → liquid.
Group examples under named stores: ocean, river, lake, glacier/ice, underground, (atmosphere/clouds for readier children).
Match a store name to a photograph of that store (e.g. 'glacier' → photo of ice sheet; 'spring/well' → photo of groundwater source).
activities.intendedInsight: Every example of water belongs both to a place (store) and to a state (solid or liquid), and learners can classify their own examples, not just supplied ones.

activities.title: The jar demonstration: how much water is where
feedback: If a child picks rivers/lakes or 'drinking water' as the majority, return to the jar comparison — the big jar (oceans) dwarfs the drop or two (rivers and lakes), and even the ice cube and the spoonful of underground water.
Probe gently: 'Is the water in the sea the same kind you can drink? What's different about it?' to foreshadow the later salt-vs-fresh topic without requiring percentages now.
Probe: 'A glacier is a huge sheet of ice — is that part of Earth's water? Why?' and 'Where could water be hiding you can't see from the surface?'
activities.rationale: A concrete comparative demonstration makes the relative sizes of water stores visible, supporting the big idea that oceans hold the most. Keeping it to relative volumes (not percentages) fits the age and leaves exact proportions for later work. The jar is a rough representation, not a measurement of real global volumes. This activity also gives a two-tier check: the store (oceans) plus the state reasoning (ice counts).
sourceClaims: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans (~97% salt water); fresh water is in glaciers, groundwater, rivers and lakes.
learnerActions: Use a hands-on model where a big jar of water = the oceans, an ice cube = glaciers/ice, a spoonful = underground water, and just a drop or two = rivers and lakes.
Compare the amounts by eye and say which store holds the most.
State in your own words: 'Most of Earth's water is in the oceans; rivers and lakes are only a tiny part.'
Answer the diagnostic: 'If you gathered up ALL the water on Earth, where is most of it? And does ice count as water too?'
activities.intendedInsight: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans by a large margin; rivers and lakes are a small share; and ice is water too (solid), as is underground water.

constraints: Keep it observational and vocabulary-rich at this age; do not introduce percentages or precise proportions — save quantitative salt-vs-fresh work for the later graphing topic.

Multiple-choice/matching/sorting checks (e.g. 'Most of Earth's water is in ___') assess recognition and classification cleanly, but recognition-only items do not require a learner to generate their own examples — pair them with the open 'where have you seen water?' task for production.

A spinnable 3D globe or a drag-and-drop labelling game can motivate and add light manipulation, but the core learning (naming stores, solid vs liquid) is not inherently spatial or dynamic; treat these as optional wrappers, not the mechanism.
The salt vs fresh ocean-water distinction is only foreshadowed here, not fully taught; the full distinction belongs to the later salt-vs-fresh topic.
Hands-on melting and the jar model are approximations/representations, not measurements of real global volumes; present relative sizes, not exact figures.
When countering 'water is only where you can see it', use water held underground and water vapour in the air as the hidden examples; do not present clouds (which are visible) as the invisible store.

If the atmosphere store is included for readier children, treat it as an extension beyond the solid/liquid tagging focus, since most water in the air is invisible water vapour (a gas); clouds are made of tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The '~97% salt water' figure appears only in the cited USGS claim and is deliberately kept out of learner-facing actions at this age (per the pedagogy guidance to defer proportions); it is retained in sourceClaims where it supports the 'oceans hold the most' principle.

The original recommendation's phrase that classification is 'rehearsed by touch' was softened: tap/lift-the-flap are concrete ways to rehearse naming and sorting, but touch is not claimed to be the only or necessary route. A static diagram or photo cards can also teach this.

The non-preferred conversation entry (persona chat 'reciting the list') was dropped as adding no distinct pedagogical purpose for a naming/classifying objective; this is a design judgement, not an evidenced efficacy claim.

Original feedback referring to 'water vapour in clouds' as a hidden store was corrected: clouds are visible condensed droplets/ice, so water vapour in the air is the accurate 'cannot-see-it' example; this fix is applied in the feedback, a dedicated constraint, and here.
Independent fresh audit found no remaining critical learner-facing errors, contradictions, or unsupported categorical modality claims; evidence/efficacy uncertainty remains appropriately hedged.
