pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Measuring accurately

- **Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to make systematic and careful observations and, where appropriate, take accurate measurements using standard units, using a range of equipment, including thermometers and data loggers. This sits alongside setting up simple practical enquiries and comparative and fair tests.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, grades 3–5):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1, 2-PS1-1, 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 3-PS2-2, 4-ESS2-1, 4-PS3-2, 5-PS1-3, 5-PS1-4]; use appropriate tools and units. The grade-3–5 shift is from guided observation to independently taking accurate measurements in standard units with the correct instrument.

- **Operational details:** The child selects and correctly uses at least several measuring instruments — ruler (cm/mm), thermometer (°C), measuring jug/cylinder (ml), balance/scales (g) — and reads each in standard units with reasonable accuracy. Correct technique is explicit: aligning the zero of the ruler with the object's end, reading a scale at eye level to avoid parallax, reading the liquid level at the bottom of the meniscus, and letting a thermometer settle. 'Systematic' means following a planned method consistently — measuring the same way each time, in the same conditions — so results are comparable. Accuracy here means reading to the resolution of the instrument and recording the number WITH its unit.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete, moving toward procedural rigour). This is where qualitative observation becomes quantitative data. Success = independently chooses the right instrument for a quantity, uses correct reading technique (zeroing, eye level, meniscus), records the value with its standard unit, and follows the same method across a set of measurements — the measurement foundation for the age-9+ precision/repeat-reading topic and for presenting data in tables and graphs.
bestPractices: Teach reading technique explicitly and physically: zeroing the ruler, reading at eye level to avoid parallax, reading the bottom of the meniscus, letting the thermometer settle — name each as a rule with a reason.
Insist every recorded value carries its standard unit; treat a bare number as an incomplete measurement.
Practise instrument selection: give the quantity and let children choose from several tools, discussing why a finer-scale instrument suits a small quantity.
Define 'systematic' concretely — same method, same conditions, same reading technique each time — so measurements are comparable across a set.
Use repeated hands-on measuring of real objects with immediate check against a known/agreed value, so children calibrate their own accuracy.
Connect measuring to a purpose (a fair test or a table to fill), so accuracy is felt as necessary, not busywork.
keyRepresentations: The core instruments and their units: ruler (cm/mm), thermometer (°C), measuring cylinder/jug (ml), balance (g)
Meniscus diagram — reading the liquid level at the bottom of the curve at eye level
Parallax illustration — how viewing angle changes an apparent reading
Zeroing the ruler — aligning the object's end with 0, not the ruler's edge
A results table where each column heading names the quantity and its unit
commonMisconceptions: Recording a number with no unit, or mixing units within a set of measurements.
Reading a ruler from its physical edge instead of the zero mark.
Reading a scale from an angle (parallax error) instead of at eye level.
Reading the top of the meniscus or the liquid's edge rather than the bottom of the curve.
Believing any instrument will do — not matching the instrument's resolution to the quantity (using a litre jug for a few millilitres).
Reading a thermometer before it has settled, or moving it out of the substance while reading.

learn.summary: For ages 7-9, this topic builds accurate measurement as a practical, perceptual-motor skill: selecting the right instrument for a quantity, using correct reading technique (zeroing a ruler, reading at eye level to avoid parallax, reading the bottom of the meniscus, letting a thermometer settle), and recording every value WITH its standard unit (cm/mm, °C, ml, g). 'Systematic' means following the same method and conditions across a set of measurements so results are comparable. Hands-on work giving children real or simulated instruments to USE, with immediate feedback on the act of reading plus practice choosing the right tool, is proposed as the strongest fit for this perceptual-motor skill. Recognition-style checks (which unit? which instrument?) assess scale-reading and unit choice but do not coach live technique as it happens. Concrete reference cards and spatial (eye-lowering) work are useful supports for specific sub-skills such as parallax.

activities.title: Measuring stations: use each tool correctly
feedback: If a ruler reading starts from the end or the '1' mark: line the object up with the 0 mark; the gap before 0 is not part of the length.
If a liquid or thermometer is read from an angle, or the top of the meniscus is read: bring your eye level with the scale and read the bottom of the meniscus for liquids.

If a value is recorded without a unit, or with the wrong unit: every measurement needs a suitable standard unit — for these stations, length→cm or mm, mass→g, volume→ml, temperature→°C (larger amounts may use m, kg or l).
If the thermometer is read before settling or lifted out while reading: wait for the reading to stop drifting and keep the bulb in the substance.
activities.rationale: Accurate measurement is a visual-manual skill that shows in the doing, not the telling; practising on real instruments with immediate comparison (e.g. the same liquid read from different angles) is proposed to help children feel why technique determines the number. This supports the curriculum requirement to take accurate measurements in standard units using a range of equipment; the comparative efficacy of the hands-on method itself is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to make systematic and careful observations and, where appropriate, take accurate measurements using standard units and a range of equipment including thermometers and data loggers.
NGSS SEP 3 (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations) grades 3–5 has students make observations and measurements to produce data that serve as the basis for evidence, using appropriate tools.
learnerActions: Set up stations with real instruments: a ruler (cm/mm), a thermometer (°C), a measuring jug or cylinder (ml), and a balance/scales (g).
At the ruler station, measure a pencil: deliberately line its end up with the '1 cm' mark and read, then re-align its end with 0 and read again; notice the length you record changes.
At the measuring-cylinder station, read the water level from above, at eye level, and from below; compare the three numbers, then read the BOTTOM of the meniscus at eye level as the correct value.
At the thermometer station, place it in a cup of warm (not hot) or cold water and watch the reading change; wait until it settles before recording, and keep the bulb in the substance while reading.
At the balance station, zero (tare) the scales before placing an object, then read the mass.
Record every value WITH its unit in a results table whose column headings name the quantity and its unit; treat a bare number as incomplete.
activities.intendedInsight: The liquid, length, or temperature did not change — how you look at and use the scale changes the number you record. Correct technique and the right instrument are what make a measurement accurate.

activities.title: Grab the right tool: instrument selection
feedback: If any instrument is treated as equally good: compare the graduations — a jug's marks are too coarse to read a few millilitres accurately, so a measuring cylinder is better.
If selection is correct, prompt the reason: which quantity, which tool, and why that resolution?
activities.rationale: Choosing the instrument is a distinct decision from reading it; giving the quantity and letting children choose, then compare, makes instrument resolution concrete rather than merely told. This is proposed as a research-informed approach and connects to the requirement to use appropriate tools.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 3 (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations) grades 3–5 has students make observations and measurements to produce data that serve as the basis for evidence, using appropriate tools.
learnerActions: Given a quantity to measure (e.g. '5 ml of water', 'the length of a seed', 'the mass of a feather'), choose from several available instruments before measuring.
Try measuring 5 ml in a large litre jug, then in a small measuring cylinder; compare how easy each is to read.
Explain why a finer-scale instrument suits a small quantity and match each quantity to the best-resolution tool.
activities.intendedInsight: A measurement is only as good as the tool behind it: matching an instrument's resolution (how fine its graduations are) to the quantity makes an accurate reading possible.

activities.title: Measure for a purpose, systematically
feedback: If methods vary between measurements: keep the same instrument, reading technique, and conditions so the numbers are comparable.
If a reading is far from an agreed value: re-check technique (zeroing, eye level, meniscus) and measure again the same way.
activities.rationale: Embedding measurement in a purpose and a repeated method teaches the 'systematic' requirement concretely and is intended to make accuracy feel necessary rather than busywork. This is the foundation for later precision/repeat-reading work and for presenting data in tables.
sourceClaims: DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to make systematic and careful observations and, where appropriate, take accurate measurements using standard units and a range of equipment including thermometers and data loggers.
NGSS SEP 3 (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations) grades 3–5 has students make observations and measurements to produce data that serve as the basis for evidence, using appropriate tools.
learnerActions: Connect measuring to a real goal — filling a results table for a fair test or comparing several objects.
Agree a method before starting (same instrument, same technique, same conditions each time) and follow it consistently across the whole set.
Where possible, check a reading against a known or agreed value and discuss any difference, then re-measure using the same method.
Read each instrument to its resolution (e.g. to the nearest mm on a ruler) and record the number with its unit.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Systematic' means doing it the same careful way each time so measurements in a set can be compared; accuracy matters because the data will be used.

activities.title: Technique reference cards and scale-reading checks
feedback: If a check is failed, return to the relevant station and perform the reading physically to see why the technique matters.
If a bare number is chosen as acceptable, restate that an incomplete measurement is missing its unit.
activities.rationale: A static card can show the correct reading and name each rule, and a recognition check can verify scale-reading and unit choice; these consolidate and check but do not coach the live act of aligning, settling, or reading a meniscus, so they work best beside hands-on practice.
learnerActions: Keep a set of 'how to read each instrument' cards with technique callouts: 'line up the zero', 'read at eye level', 'read the bottom of the meniscus', 'let the thermometer settle'.
Use short recognition checks alongside the hands-on work: pick the correct unit for a quantity, match quantities to instruments, and read a value off a realistic scale illustration.
Include discrimination items such as a reading taken from the wrong angle (parallax error) and a bare-number-versus-with-unit choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Reference cards consolidate the named rules-with-reasons, and short checks confirm a child can read scales and choose units — a useful complement to, not a substitute for, measuring with real tools.

constraints: Every recorded value must carry its standard unit; a bare number counts as an incomplete measurement.
Teach each technique as a named rule WITH its reason (zeroing, eye level/parallax, meniscus, settling), not just as a step.

Recognition-only checks (which unit? which instrument? read this fixed scale) assess scale-reading and unit choice but do not elicit or coach the independent, physical act of reading an instrument; pair them with hands-on measuring.

Technique reference cards are a static primer: they can show the correct reading and name each rule but do not respond to a child's own reading technique; use them alongside, not instead of, measuring.

A screen simulation with a viewpoint control can make the parallax/eye-level lesson vivid, but it is a model of a physical skill; real instruments give the actual perceptual-motor experience. Neither is presented here as the only way to learn.
Match instrument resolution to the quantity (do not use a litre jug to read a few millilitres); discuss why.
This is Tier A–B: the move from qualitative observation to quantitative data, and the foundation for later precision/repeat-reading and data presentation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a 2D interactive 'measuring lab' as 'ideal' and asserted a worksheet cannot give live feedback and a conversation 'cannot' let a child read an instrument with feedback. These are catalog-fit preferences, not established efficacy or necessity claims; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (simulation can make parallax vivid; recognition checks assess scale-reading), with the underlying skill best practised on real instruments where feasible.
The legacy 3D entry judged extra navigation cost usually outweighs benefit except for the parallax/eye-level focus; retained as a narrowly scoped point, not a universal ruling.

The two cited sources support the curriculum requirements (standard units, range of equipment, appropriate tools, measurements as evidence) but do NOT establish the comparative effectiveness of any particular artefact format or the hands-on technique method; sourceClaims are attached only to activities whose rationale rests on those requirements, and Activity 2 is pointed to the NGSS 'appropriate tools' claim as the one most directly supporting instrument selection.

probeDeeper: Where on the ruler does the pencil need to start? Why not at the end?
Where should your eye be when you read the thermometer?
What unit goes with each measurement, and why?
If you read the jug from above, looking down at it, would you get the same number? What could go wrong?
assess.correctAnswer: The child uses each instrument correctly — measures the pencil from the ruler's zero (not the end), reads the thermometer and jug at eye level, reads the meniscus at the bottom, zeroes and reads the scales — and states each measurement with the correct standard unit (cm, °C, ml, g), following a consistent, careful method.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ruler zero-error: measures from the end of the ruler or from the '1' mark instead of 0.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line the object up with the 0 mark; the gap before 0 isn't part of the length.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watching where the child lines up the pencil against the ruler.

errorPatterns.pattern: Parallax / not reading at eye level: reads the thermometer or jug from an angle, or reads the top of the meniscus.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bring the eye level with the scale; read the bottom of the meniscus for liquids.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Head position and the value read differ from an eye-level reading.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits or muddles units: says '15' not '15 cm', or gives ml for a mass.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Every measurement needs its standard unit; match the unit to the quantity (length→cm, mass→g, volume→ml, temperature→°C).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The stated measurement lacks a unit or uses the wrong one for the quantity.

responseLevels.gap: Misreads scales (ruler not zeroed, reads at an angle) or gives numbers without correct units.
responseLevels.full: Uses each instrument correctly (zeroed ruler, eye-level readings, meniscus at the bottom, zeroed scales), reports every measurement with the right standard unit, and follows a consistent careful method.
responseLevels.partial: Uses the instruments and gives units, but makes an occasional reading error or needs reminding about eye level or the zero mark.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are a ruler, a thermometer, a measuring jug of water, and some scales. Measure: the length of this pencil, the temperature of the water, how much water is in the jug, and the mass of this stone. Do each one and tell me the measurement with its unit. I'll watch how you read each scale.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching reveals the classic reading errors — starting the ruler at the end or at '1', reading a scale at an angle (parallax), reading the top of the meniscus, forgetting units — that a child could hide if merely asked 'how do you use a ruler?'. Correct technique shows in the doing, not the telling.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 (Year 1 → Year 2). SKIP COUNTING in 2s, 5s and 10s — the first move beyond counting by ones into counting equal GROUPS. The gateway to multiplication (equal groups / repeated addition), even numbers, telling time (5s) and place value (10s).
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: 'counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop their recognition of patterns in the number system (for example, odd and even numbers).'
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.1 'count … by tens'; Grade 2 extends — 2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s.' Skip counting underpins the multiplication foundations of 2.OA.3–4 and Grade 3 OA.
• Operational details: Teach as counting equal GROUPS, not a new chant — each 'step' is one more group of 2/5/10 (link to repeated addition, the multiplication seed). Use the HUNDRED SQUARE (shade 5s → two columns; 10s → one column; 2s → even columns) and the NUMBER LINE (equal jumps landing on multiples) so the pattern is seen. Count from different starting multiples, not only 0. Anchor 2s↔even, 5s↔clock/tallies/fingers, 10s↔place value.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5–6) counts in 10s to 100 and 2s to 20 from 0. Tier B (6) counts in 5s to 50 and links 2s to even numbers. Tier C (6–7) counts in 2s/5s/10s from a non-zero multiple and explains each step adds a group ('5s go up by five each time = one more group of five').
bestPractices: Teach each skip count as adding one equal GROUP (repeated addition), not a disconnected chant — this is the multiplication seed.
Shade multiples on a hundred square so the visual pattern (columns/diagonals) makes the sequence predictable rather than memorised.
Use a number line with equal-sized jumps landing on multiples — the jump size IS the step, making 'counting in 5s' concrete.
Count from different starting multiples and in both directions so it is flexible, not a fixed rote song.
Anchor to real contexts: 2s (pairs, even numbers), 5s (fingers, tally marks, clock minutes), 10s (tens, money).
keyRepresentations: Hundred square with multiples shaded (pattern by column/diagonal).
Number line with equal jumps (the jump = the step size).
Equal groups / arrays of 2, 5, 10 (the bridge to multiplication).
Fingers (5s/10s), tally marks (5s), coins (5s/10s).
commonMisconceptions: Reciting the multiples as a chant with no sense that each step is +one group — so it doesn't transfer to multiplication.
Thinking the multiples are the ONLY numbers that 'exist', or that skip counting removes the in-between numbers (7 isn't 'skipped away').
Only able to start from 0 — can't skip-count from a different multiple or backwards.
Confusing 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', or losing the pattern at decade boundaries (5s: '…45, 50, 55').

learn.summary: Skip counting in 2s, 5s and 10s for ages 5–7, taught as counting equal GROUPS (one more group of 2/5/10 each step) rather than a memorised chant — the bridge to multiplication, repeated addition, even numbers, clock minutes and place value. Core representations are the hundred square (on a standard 10-wide square, shaded multiples of 2, 5 and 10 form straight column patterns) and the number line (equal-sized jumps landing on multiples). Learners should count from different starting multiples and in both directions, not only forward from 0.

activities.title: One hop, one group: linking jumps, counters and the hundred square
feedback: If a learner recites fluently from 0 but can't say what comes after 40 in 10s, bring them back to one jump: 'each hop adds ten — show me the next group.'
When the shaded 10s form a single straight column and the 5s two columns, prompt: 'what do you notice about where they are?' so the pattern, not memory, drives the next number.

If a learner sub-counts the in-between numbers under their breath, that is a normal developing step — let the equal jump and the shaded pattern gradually make it feel like one move; do not mark it wrong.
If starting at 30 they restart from 0, say 'start here and keep hopping' and practise entering mid-sequence from several multiples.
activities.rationale: Showing the jump, the stacked group of counters and the shaded hundred-square cells together makes 'counting in fives' concrete as repeated equal groups rather than a chant, and counting from varied multiples and in both directions keeps it flexible. Linked, simultaneously-moving views (number line + counters + hundred square) are offered as one way to make the group structure visible; the panels moving together is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; skip counting underpins multiplication foundations (equal groups / repeated addition).
Skip counting is taught as counting equal groups (the multiplication bridge) using the hundred square and number line to make patterns visible.
learnerActions: Pick which step size you are counting in: 2, 5 or 10.
Take one step forward on a number line, making an equal-sized jump (a jump of 5 for 5s) that lands on the next multiple.
For each jump, add a GROUP of that many counters into a new stack/tower, so you see the jump as 'one more group of five'.
Shade or light up the cells you land on (5, 10, 15 …) on a hundred square as you go.
Say aloud what each step adds: 'each hop adds five — one more group of five.'
Try starting from a non-zero multiple (e.g. start at 30 and count on in 10s: 30, 40, 50 …).
Try counting in the other direction too (e.g. count back in 10s from 50: 50, 40, 30 …).
activities.intendedInsight: Each step of skip counting adds (or, going back, removes) one equal group, so the next multiple can be predicted from the pattern and from 'one more group' instead of recited — this is the seed of multiplication and repeated addition.

activities.title: Spotting the pattern on a multiples chart
feedback: If a learner says the multiples are the 'only numbers that exist' or that in-between numbers are 'skipped away', point to the chart: 7 is still there, we are just landing on every second/fifth/tenth number.
At a decade boundary, if they lose the pattern (…45, 50, 55), have them trace the column to confirm the next landing cell.
activities.rationale: A pre-marked multiples chart is a genuinely useful reference whose pattern is visible even when static; it supports recognising multiples and crossing decade boundaries. It shows the pattern but does not itself require the learner to generate each step, so pair it with tasks where the learner constructs and explains steps.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
learnerActions: Look at a hundred square or multiples chart with the 2s, 5s or 10s already marked.
Tap or point to a multiple to reveal it and the group it stands for (e.g. 15 = three groups of five).
Describe the visual pattern: 10s make one straight column, 5s make two columns, 2s shade the even columns.
Use the chart as a reference to answer 'what comes next in 5s after 45?' across a decade boundary.
activities.intendedInsight: The multiples sit in a predictable visual pattern, so you can find the next one by reading the pattern rather than restarting the chant — and the pattern survives decade boundaries like 45, 50, 55.

activities.title: Anchoring 2s, 5s and 10s to real things
feedback: If a learner confuses 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', re-ground in pairs: each new pair adds two to the total.
Use fingers and tally marks to re-establish the fives if the 5s pattern slips.
activities.rationale: Anchoring each step size to familiar contexts gives meaning to the groups and supports transfer to even numbers, telling time and place value.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
learnerActions: Count pairs of objects in 2s and connect to even numbers (2, 4, 6 …).
Count hands/fingers and tally marks in 5s (5, 10, 15 …) and clock minutes in 5s.
Count groups of ten — tens blocks or 10p coins — in 10s and link to place value (how many tens).
Say how each context shows 'one more group': one more pair, one more hand of five, one more ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Skip counting describes real repeated groups — pairs, fives and tens — so 2s↔even, 5s↔clock/tallies/fingers, 10s↔place value make the counts meaningful and memorable.

activities.title: Fluency practice: fill, continue, match
feedback: A 'next multiple' or 'fill the gap' task checks fluency but, on its own, may let a learner answer by recognition; follow up with 'how did you know?' to check for group reasoning.
In the oral partner game, use the caught slip to prompt 'how did you know that was wrong?' rather than just correcting.
activities.rationale: These tasks give targeted fluency practice and the array-matching links sequences back to equal groups. Fill/continue tasks check recall and recognition but do not by themselves show the learner is reasoning from groups, so pair them with the construction and explanation tasks. The oral call-and-response gives fluency and listening practice but lacks a seen pattern, so it complements rather than replaces the visual work.
learnerActions: Fill in a missing multiple in a sequence (…, 10, __, 20 in 5s).
Say what comes next in 2s/5s/10s from a given number, including across a decade boundary.
Put a set of multiples in order.
Match a skip-count (e.g. 5, 10, 15) to an array or picture of equal groups.
Do an oral count-in-5s with a partner as call-and-response, and catch a deliberate slip in the other person's count.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated varied practice — including continuing from non-zero starts and matching counts to equal-group arrays — builds fluency while keeping the count tied to groups.

constraints: Teach skip counting as adding one equal group each step (repeated addition), not as a disconnected chant — this is the multiplication seed.
Count from different starting multiples (not only 0) and in both directions, so the skill is flexible rather than a fixed rote song.

A pre-marked multiples chart and fill/continue practice items are references and recognition checks; they show or test the pattern but do not require the learner to independently construct each step, so pair them with tasks where the learner generates and explains steps.

Reverting to counting the in-between numbers by ones, and difficulty starting from a non-zero multiple, are developmental stages that improve with practice — do not mark them as errors; scaffold with equal jumps and hundred-square patterns.
Do not imply that only the multiples 'exist' or that in-between numbers are removed; the full number sequence is still present, we just land on every 2nd/5th/10th number.
Watch decade boundaries in 5s (…45, 50, 55) where the pattern is easily lost.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the CCSS 2.NBT.2 and NCETM claims as verified:false; only the DfE Year 1 claim is marked verified. Treat the standards-alignment and 'taught as equal groups' statements as unverified; they are retained only where they directly support the equal-groups principle.

The legacy note that a third dimension 'adds nothing' to a grid/line pattern was removed as a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; a planar hundred square and number line are well-suited here, which is sufficient without the universal claim.

The legacy framing of one interactive as 'the killer move' / 'the insight clicks' was softened: the linked number-line/counters/hundred-square views are presented as one effective way to make equal groups visible, not as uniquely necessary.

The oral call-and-response and static chart are described by narrow affordances (fluency/listening practice; visible but non-generative reference); no categorical 'only this teaches' or 'cannot teach' claim is asserted.
Catalog/product vocabulary ('quiz', artefact-fit rankings) was removed from learner-facing text; where mentioned in these notes it only documents the removal.

probeDeeper: What comes after 16 when counting in 2s?
Count in 10s but start at 30.
Look at the 5s you tapped — what do you notice about where they are?
How is counting in 2s like counting groups of 2?
assess.correctAnswer: Recites 2s, 5s, 10s accurately to the stated limits; the hundred-square taps fall in a straight column (10s) and a regular pattern (5s, 2s); continues 30, 40, 50… when started at 30 — treating skip counting as counting equal groups, not a fixed jingle.

errorPatterns.pattern: skip-counting-as-chant — recites the sequence as a memorised rhyme but can't say what comes after a given multiple without restarting, and can't map it to the numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: link each step to a group — a jump of 2 on the number line, a column of 10 on the square — saying 'each hop adds two' so the sequence carries meaning
errorPatterns.revealedBy: fluent from 0 yet stuck on 'what's after 40 in 10s?' or unable to point the sequence out on the hundred square

errorPatterns.pattern: reverts to counting by ones — gets the next multiple by counting the ones in between under their breath rather than stepping by the group size
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat as an error — the group-step speeds up with practice; use number-line equal jumps and hundred-square patterns to make the step feel like one move
errorPatterns.revealedBy: pauses and sub-counts between multiples

errorPatterns.pattern: can't start from a non-zero multiple — counts in 10s only from 0; asked to start at 30, restarts at 0 or 10
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT correct as a mistake — practise 'start here and keep hopping' from various multiples on a number line; entering mid-sequence develops with exposure
errorPatterns.revealedBy: restarts rather than continuing from 30

responseLevels.gap: Cannot sustain a skip-count sequence, or produces it only as a memorised chant with no link to the numbers on a track or square.
responseLevels.full: Skip-counts 2s, 5s, 10s to the limits, continues from any multiple, and connects each step to adding an equal group (jumps on a number line, patterns on a hundred square).
responseLevels.partial: Recites 2s/5s/10s from 0 fluently but reverts to counting by ones for the next multiple, or can't start from a non-zero multiple — the equal-group structure isn't yet seen.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count out loud in 2s from 0 up to 20. Now count in 10s up to 100. Now count in 5s up to 50, and this time point to each number as you say it on this hundred square. Then start at 30 and count on in 10s. (Watch fluency, whether the taps land in the right pattern, and whether they can start from a non-zero multiple.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reciting from 0 is the baseline; the pointing-on-the-square and start-at-30 tasks reveal whether the child sees skip counting as adding equal groups or is just chanting. A chant-only child can say '5,10,15,20' but can't point to them correctly, can't start from 30, or drops back to counting by ones to get the next number.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Why Earthquakes Happen — rocks underground are pushed until they suddenly move or break along a fault, releasing energy that travels out as shaking; the underground CAUSE is distinct from the surface EFFECT.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement):** In England, earthquakes are taught in KS2 **Geography** (physical geography: volcanoes and earthquakes), not KS2 science. The underlying mechanism (plate tectonics, forces in rock) is DfE **KS3** (Geography, and science 'structure of the Earth'). So this causal model runs ahead of the KS2 science sequence — frame via Geography.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No elementary PE names earthquake mechanism directly; earthquakes appear as a mapped feature in **4-ESS2-2** ('patterns of Earth's features'; clarification includes earthquakes) and as a rapid Earth event in **2-ESS1-1**. The stress-release/plate-boundary mechanism is developed at **MS-ESS2-2/3**. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Builds on 'What Is an Earthquake' (5–7, shaking can be strong/weak). The one new idea is CAUSE: stuck rocks under growing push suddenly slip or snap, and the released energy is what shakes the ground. Keep it pre-plate-tectonics (rocks move/break underground); the plate-boundary explanation is the next topic. Separate cause (underground) from effect (surface shaking, felt damage).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A/B boundary (concrete cause→effect, early mechanism). Children can grasp 'stuck then suddenly slips → shaking' with a physical model but tend to picture the ground simply 'opening up'. Success = state that earthquakes are caused by rock suddenly moving/breaking underground and that the shaking is released energy spreading out from that spot.
bestPractices: Make the cause a build-then-release story: push slowly, resistance grows, then a SUDDEN slip — the suddenness is why shaking is violent even though plates creep slowly.
Use a hands-on stick-slip analogy (push two rough blocks/bricks past each other until they jerk; snap a dry stick/spaghetti) so the release is felt, then map it to rock underground.
Explicitly separate the underground cause from the surface effect: draw the slip at depth (the focus) and the shaking spreading up and out to where people feel it.
Correct the 'ground opens and swallows people' image directly and reassuringly — the ground shakes and can crack, but the main hazard is shaking, and most earthquakes are small.
Introduce 'energy travels out as shaking (waves)' informally as ripples spreading from the slip point, seeding the later idea of seismic waves without formal wave vocabulary.
keyRepresentations: Two rough blocks pushed until they suddenly jerk (stick-slip friction model) — the canonical analogy for fault movement
Snapping a bent stick or dry spaghetti to model slow bending then sudden break + release
Cross-section showing the underground slip (focus) with shaking rippling up to the surface
Ripples spreading on water / a shaken tabletop as an image of energy travelling outward from one spot
commonMisconceptions: Earthquakes happen because the ground simply 'opens up' and swallows things (the cause is rock slipping/breaking; large open chasms are rare).
The shaking starts everywhere at once (energy spreads OUT from the slip point, arriving and fading with distance).
Rocks move smoothly and slowly, so shaking should be gentle (rocks stick then release suddenly — the sudden slip causes strong shaking).
Earthquakes are caused by the weather, or by volcanoes only (most are caused by rock movement underground along faults).
The cause and the shaking are the same thing (the underground slip is the cause; the felt shaking is its effect).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach that earthquakes are caused by rocks underground being pushed until they suddenly slip or break along a crack (a fault), releasing energy that spreads outward as shaking. The central insight is the slow build-up then SUDDEN release, and the separation of the underground CAUSE from the surface EFFECT (felt shaking and cracks). Keep it pre-plate-tectonics: rocks move/break underground. A hands-on or simulated stick-slip model makes the build-then-snap tangible; a labelled cross-section supports the cause/effect distinction; targeted questioning and myth-busting address the 'ground swallows people' and 'earthquake weather' ideas.

activities.title: Feel the stick-then-slip: a build-up-then-release model
feedback: If the child predicts a steady, smooth glide, draw attention to what actually happened: it stayed stuck, then jerked. Ask what had to build up before it moved.
If they say the band or rock 'just moves', point to the moment of delay-then-jolt and name it: stuck (stress building), then sudden slip.

Reinforce: the suddenness of the slip is why the ground shakes, and in big earthquakes the shaking can be strong, even though the push was slow — real rock faults can build up strain slowly then release all at once.
activities.rationale: A build-then-release model lets children feel the delay-then-jolt — a time sequence that a still picture cannot show — seeding the mechanism that stuck rock slips suddenly. Predicting before pulling surfaces whether a child assumes motion is always smooth.
sourceClaims: Earthquakes are caused by a sudden slip of rock along a fault (elastic rebound / stick-slip), releasing energy as seismic waves.
learnerActions: Loop an elastic band around a small block or brick sitting on rough sandpaper. Before pulling, PREDICT: as the far end of the band is pulled slowly and steadily, will the block slide smoothly and evenly, or do something else — and WHY?

Pull the band slowly and watch: usually the block stays STUCK while the band stretches (tension builds), then suddenly JERKS forward — stick, then slip. Repeat several times and notice whether it happens the same way each time.
As an alternative release model, slowly bend a dry stick or piece of dry spaghetti and feel the slow bend end in a sudden snap.
Map the model to the ground: the stuck block is like rocks underground being pushed; the sudden jerk is the slip that causes an earthquake.

Optionally work a simulated side-view fault rig: slowly crank a push on two rough rock blocks, watch a stress meter climb while the blocks stay stuck, then see them snap and ripples race up to houses that wobble harder near the slip and gently far away; reset and repeat.
activities.intendedInsight: Force can build up while nothing visibly moves, then release all at once; this sudden slip of underground rock is why the ground shakes, sometimes strongly, even though the pushing is slow and invisible.

activities.title: Cross-section: where the cause is and how shaking spreads
feedback: If a child treats the surface shaking as the cause, point back to the slip point at depth and ask what happened there first.
If they think shaking starts everywhere at once, trace the arrows outward from the slip point and note it arrives and fades with distance.
Confirm when they can point to the underground slip as cause and the surface shaking as effect.
activities.rationale: A labelled cross-section makes the spatial separation of underground cause and surface effect explicit and gives a place to represent energy spreading outward. It supports the distinction but cannot by itself deliver the build-then-snap dynamic, so pair it with a release model.
learnerActions: Study (or draw) a side-view cutaway of the ground showing two rough rock blocks meeting along a fault line, the slip point deep underground, and arrows of shaking rising up to houses on the surface.
Tap or point to reveal/label: the fault, the underground slip point (the cause), and the shaking spreading up and outward to the surface (the effect).
Mark where the shaking would be strongest (near the slip) and where it would be gentler (far away).
Say in your own words which part is the CAUSE (underground slip) and which is the EFFECT (surface shaking and cracks).
activities.intendedInsight: The underground slip is the cause; the felt surface shaking is its effect, and the energy spreads out from one spot rather than starting everywhere at once.

activities.title: Myth-buster: does the ground swallow people?
feedback: If the child says the ground opening is what causes the shaking, clarify that rocks slipping past each other cause it; cracking is a possible effect, not the cause.
If they blame hot or still weather, confront it directly and reassuringly: no weather causes earthquakes; they come from underground rock movement.
Reassure that most earthquakes are small and the main danger is shaking, correcting frightening cartoon images.
activities.rationale: These are named, common misconceptions at this age; addressing them directly and reassuringly separates cause from effect and removes a frightening but inaccurate image.
sourceClaims: The common fear that the ground opens and swallows people is a misconception; ground shaking is the primary hazard.
learnerActions: Consider the question 'Does the ground open up and swallow people in an earthquake?' and predict the answer.
Reveal/discuss the answer: no — the ground shakes and can crack, but the main hazard is the shaking; huge open chasms are rare, and most earthquakes are small.
Discuss a second myth: 'Can a hot, still, sunny day cause an earthquake?' Explain why not — earthquakes come from rock moving underground, not from weather.
State what actually causes an earthquake in your own words, rejecting the 'ground opens up' and 'earthquake weather' explanations.
activities.intendedInsight: Earthquakes are caused by rock slipping/breaking underground along faults, not by the ground opening to swallow things and not by the weather; shaking (not swallowing) is the primary hazard.

activities.title: Explain and check the cause→effect chain
feedback: Gap response (blames weather or says 'the ground just shakes'): reteach with the stick-slip model — stress builds on a fault, snaps, energy travels up; cause below, effect above.
Partial response (knows something underground moves but can't separate cause from effect, or mixes in opening/weather ideas): ask specifically WHERE the cause is and WHAT travels to the surface.
Full response: confirm they distinguished the underground cause from the surface shaking and described energy spreading outward.
activities.rationale: Asking WHERE and WHAT caused the shaking discriminates 'something underground suddenly moved' from surface-only or weather explanations, requiring the child to construct the causal chain — the stick-slip mechanism — rather than only recognise it.
sourceClaims: Earthquakes are caused by a sudden slip of rock along a fault (elastic rebound / stick-slip), releasing energy as seismic waves.
learnerActions: Answer: 'When you feel an earthquake, the ground at the surface shakes. But what actually happened to CAUSE it, and where — at the surface, or somewhere else?'
Put the stages in order: rocks pushed → stuck → sudden slip → shaking spreads to the surface.

Answer probing questions: Is the cause at the surface where we stand, or deeper down? What travels through the ground from the underground movement to make things shake? How does the underground slip reach us up at the surface?

Give a full explanation that rocks underground suddenly move/break along a fault, releasing energy that travels as waves to shake the surface, clearly naming the underground cause and the surface effect.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can state that earthquakes are caused by rock suddenly moving/breaking underground and that the shaking is released energy spreading out from that spot to the surface.

constraints: Keep this pre-plate-tectonics: describe rocks moving/breaking underground along a fault, not plate boundaries — the plate-boundary explanation is the next topic.
Builds on prior understanding that shaking can be strong or weak; the one new idea here is the CAUSE (stuck rocks under growing push suddenly slip or snap, releasing energy that shakes the ground).
Introduce 'energy travels out as shaking (waves)' informally — ripples spreading from the slip point — without formal seismic-wave vocabulary.
Keep the surface cracking/damage framed as an effect, and address the swallowing image reassuringly; most earthquakes are small.

A multiple-choice or sequencing check (e.g. 'What actually causes an earthquake?' with a 'ground opens up' distractor) can confirm the cause→effect chain but only verifies recognition; it does not by itself elicit the child independently constructing or feeling the mechanism.
A static cross-section supports the cause/effect distinction but cannot show the build-then-snap time sequence; pair it with a physical or simulated release model.

Standards placement: in England earthquakes sit in KS2 Geography (physical geography), with the mechanism a later KS3 topic; in NGSS the mechanism is developed at middle school, so this causal model runs ahead of elementary science — frame accordingly.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two USGS-attributed claims (stick-slip/elastic rebound causing seismic waves; the swallowing myth) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat them as unverified pending review. They are cited as sourceClaims only where they directly describe the mechanism being taught or assessed, but their verification status is unconfirmed.

The NGSS 4-ESS2-2 claim supports only standards placement (topic), not the cross-section teaching principle, so learn.activities[1].sourceClaims is [] rather than citing it — independently re-verified in this review.

The legacy entry asserted 'no static image can convey' the concept and '3D adds cost without new insight'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by catalog ratings; softened here to narrow affordance/limit statements (a still picture cannot show a time sequence; 3D is an optional extension), not universal medium-superiority claims.
A simulated 'stress meter' and buildings wobbling by distance are retained as optional feedback examples illustrating the mechanism, not as mandatory or tested mechanisms.

assess.poeTask: Loop an elastic band around a small block or brick sitting on rough sandpaper. Ask the child to PREDICT what the block will do as you slowly and steadily pull the far end of the band — will it slide smoothly and evenly, or something else, and WHY? A child who assumes motion is smooth predicts a steady glide; what actually happens is the block STAYS STUCK while the band stretches (stress builds), then suddenly JERKS forward — stick, then slip. Pull it to check. The prediction and reason given before pulling reveal whether they grasp that force can build up while nothing moves and then release suddenly — exactly how stress builds on a fault and releases as an earthquake.
probeDeeper: The rocks underground were stuck, then suddenly slipped. How does that reach us up at the surface?
Is the CAUSE of the earthquake at the surface where we stand, or deeper down?
Could a hot sunny day cause an earthquake? Why or why not?
What travels through the ground from the underground movement to make things shake?
assess.correctAnswer: The shaking is caused by rocks deep UNDERGROUND suddenly moving or breaking along a crack (a fault). That sudden movement releases energy that travels outward as waves and shakes the ground at the surface. So the cause is underground; the shaking we feel is the surface effect.

errorPatterns.pattern: Earthquakes are caused by the weather ('earthquake weather' — hot, still days)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it — earthquakes come from rock movement underground, not weather; no weather causes them.
errorPatterns.distractor: Hot, still weather causes earthquakes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes the quake to weather, temperature, or the air.

errorPatterns.pattern: The shaking just happens at the surface — nothing underground (no cause/effect separation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a stick-slip model — stress builds on a fault, snaps, waves travel up; cause below, effect above.
errorPatterns.distractor: The ground just shakes on its own at the surface.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes only surface shaking; can't point to an underground cause.

errorPatterns.pattern: The ground shakes because it opens up / cracks apart (confuses cause with the swallowing myth)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rocks slipping past each other cause it; the ground doesn't open to swallow people.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the ground opening is what causes the shaking.

responseLevels.gap: Attributes earthquakes to weather or 'the ground just shaking'; no underground cause.
responseLevels.full: Explains rocks underground suddenly move/break along a fault, releasing energy that travels as waves to shake the surface — clearly distinguishing the underground cause from the surface effect.
responseLevels.partial: Knows something underground moves but can't clearly separate the underground cause from the surface shaking, or mixes in the opening/weather ideas.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: When you feel an earthquake, the ground at the surface shakes. But what actually happened to CAUSE it, and where did that happen — at the surface, or somewhere else?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can say 'the ground shakes' (the effect) without knowing the underground cause, or blame the weather. Asking WHERE and WHAT caused it separates 'something underground suddenly moved' from surface-only or weather explanations.

pedagogy.summary: For 5–7s this topic pairs each of the five senses with its body part and with what it DETECTS: sight/eyes detect light, hearing/ears detect sound, touch/skin detects pressure and temperature, taste/tongue detects flavours, smell/nose detects smells. It is best taught experientially — children USE each sense on real objects (a feely bag, listening games, tasting, smelling jars) and name the sense, the organ and what it picked up. The step beyond naming is the idea that each sense detects a different KIND of information about the world, and that senses often work together (taste and smell especially). Keep it hands-on and everyday; the objective is confident matching of sense–organ–stimulus plus real examples, not anatomy of the eye or ear (those come later). This also feeds the brain topic: senses are how the brain finds out about the world.
bestPractices: Lead with direct experience: feely bags, sound-guessing, smell jars, taste tests, spotting things — children use the sense, then name it, its organ and what it detected.
Make the sense–organ–stimulus triple explicit for each (eyes–light, ears–sound, skin–pressure/temperature, tongue–flavour, nose–smell), the core matching objective.
Show senses working TOGETHER — e.g. hold your nose while tasting and flavour fades — so children see the senses as a team informing the brain.
Anchor to safety and daily life (smelling smoke, feeling something too hot) so each sense has a purpose, not just a label.
Keep detail age-appropriate — no receptor or wave physics; 'ears detect sounds', 'eyes detect light' is enough at this stage.
keyRepresentations: Five sense–organ–stimulus cards (eye/light, ear/sound, skin/pressure & temperature, tongue/flavour, nose/smell)
Hands-on stations: feely bag, sound jars, smell pots, taste trays, spot-it pictures
A child-figure with the five sense organs highlighted
'Senses team up' demo (nose-hold changes taste)
Everyday-use examples matched to each sense
commonMisconceptions: 'We have exactly five senses and that's all' — fine as an age-appropriate model, but balance and body-position senses exist too (keep as a light aside).
'Taste comes only from the tongue' — missing that smell contributes much of flavour.
'Skin only feels touch' — missing that it also detects temperature and pain.
'You hear/see with your brain-eyes' — confusing the organ that detects with the brain that interprets; the organ detects, the brain makes sense of it.
'The tongue has zones for each taste' — the old 'tongue map' myth; tastes are detected all over the tongue.
'Senses work separately' — not seeing that they combine to build one picture of the world.

learn.summary: For children aged 5–7, teach the five senses as a sense–organ–stimulus triple: eyes detect light, ears detect sound, skin detects pressure and temperature, tongue detects flavours, nose detects smells. Lead with direct experience at hands-on stations, then have children name the sense, the body part, and what it picked up. Beyond naming, build the idea that each sense detects a different KIND of information and that senses often work together (especially taste and smell for flavour). Keep it everyday and age-appropriate — no eye/ear anatomy or wave physics yet. This also lays groundwork for the idea that all senses report to the brain.

activities.title: Sense stations: use it, then name it
feedback: If a child names the organ but not what it detects, prompt: 'Your eyes — but what do eyes pick up?' (light) and 'Your ears pick up…?' (sound).
If a child leaves out touch/skin, hand them the feely-bag object: 'What is your skin telling you — can you name two things, like bumpy, cold, or wet?'
Confirm correct triples by repeating them back: 'Yes — nose, smell, you smelled the flowers.'
activities.rationale: Direct experience before labelling suits this age and anchors the sense–organ–stimulus matching objective, which is the core target. The curriculum asks pupils to say which body part is associated with each sense.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should identify, name, draw and label the basic parts of the human body and say which part of the body is associated with each sense.
learnerActions: Visit hands-on stations and USE each sense before naming it: a feely bag (reach in and feel without looking), sound jars or a listening game, smell pots, a taste tray, and spot-it pictures.
After each station, say three things aloud: the sense used, the body part (organ) that detected it, and WHAT it picked up — e.g. 'touch, my skin, it felt bumpy and cold'.
Match five cards that pair each sense to its organ and to an everyday example: eyes catch a rainbow, ears catch a barking dog, skin feels warm sand, tongue tastes lemon, nose smells baking.
activities.intendedInsight: Each sense uses a particular body part to detect a different kind of information about the world.

activities.title: Senses team up: the nose-hold taste test
feedback: If a child predicts the tongue alone will manage and is surprised, name it: 'The flavour faded because smell helps taste — they team up.'

If a child says taste and smell are the same sense, separate them: the nose detects smells (odours in the air), the tongue detects tastes like sweet, sour, salty and bitter; together they make the full flavour of food, but they are different senses.
Link to daily life: 'That's why an orange tastes boring when you have a very blocked-up nose with a cold.'
activities.rationale: A predict-then-test contrast with a surprising result targets the misconception that taste comes only from the tongue and shows taste and smell working as a team. An optional 'hold your nose' toggle that dims the on-screen taste is one way to represent the same idea when real food is not available; it supplements the real tasting rather than standing in for it.
learnerActions: Before tasting, predict: 'If I pinch my nose shut, will I still tell these two flavours apart?' Say why you think so.
Taste two foods with the same texture but different flavours (e.g. two jellybean flavours, or finely grated apple and pear) with the nose pinched, then again with the nose open, and compare.
Say what changed and which two senses were working together.
activities.intendedInsight: Taste and smell cooperate: much of flavour comes from smell, so for flavour the tongue does not do the job by itself — these two senses combine to build the taste you recognise. (This is about flavour specifically; other senses can still work on their own.)

activities.title: Tongue-map myth buster
feedback: If a child expects a specific zone, invite them to test the same flavour on another part: 'Can you still taste it here?'
Affirm the corrected idea and tie it back: 'Taste buds all around your tongue can pick up every kind of taste — there are no special zones. Taste is one of our five senses.'
activities.rationale: Actively testing the myth replaces a wrong belief with a checked observation rather than just asserting the correction. A lift-the-flap representation is an optional way to reveal this when direct tasting is impractical.
sourceClaims: The classic 'tongue map' (separate zones for each taste) is a myth; different tastes are detectable across the whole tongue.
learnerActions: Taste a strong flavour (e.g. something sour or salty) touched to different parts of the tongue, such as the tip and each side.
Notice whether you can taste the same flavour in each place you tried, not just in one 'zone'.
State the myth and the correction in your own words: 'There are no separate zones for each taste.'
activities.intendedInsight: The old 'tongue map' (separate zones for each taste) is a myth: taste buds on the tip, sides and back of the tongue can each pick up all the basic tastes. The middle has fewer taste buds, so tastes can feel weaker there.

activities.title: Which sense would help? Reasoning game
feedback: Full answer to the orange task: smell (nose picks up the odour), taste (tongue detects sweet and sour tastes), and touch (skin/fingers feel the bumpy peel and the wet, juicy inside) can identify it; hearing wouldn't help much; sight fails because eyes need light and are covered.
If a child lists only eyes, ears, nose, tongue and omits skin, add touch as a full sense: the skin detects pressure, texture, and temperature — feel the peel to show it.
If a child names organs but not what each detects, pair each: eyes–light, ears–sound, nose–smell, tongue–taste, skin–touch/temperature.

Optional deeper probe: 'If the room were pitch dark and you were blindfolded, would smell still work — and why doesn't smell need light the way sight does?' (Smell picks up odours in the air, so it doesn't rely on light.)
activities.rationale: Applying the triples to a novel situation checks understanding beyond recall and surfaces gaps (omitting touch, merging taste and smell). Dragging a stimulus to its sense turns naming into active play; the 'how do you know it's raining' prompt folds in the optional guessing-game conversation as a reasoning hook.
learnerActions: Blindfolded, hold a slice of orange and work out which senses could still tell you it's an orange, and what each one would be picking up.
Explain why your EYES can't help right now (they need light and are covered).
Try a drag-and-match: move stimuli (a bell, a flower, an ice cube) to the sense that detects each, and answer 'how do you know it's raining without looking?'
activities.intendedInsight: Different senses detect different information, so you can pick the right sense for a situation and explain when one (like sight) can't help.

constraints: Keep detail age-appropriate: 'eyes detect light', 'ears detect sounds' is enough — no receptor biology or wave physics at this stage; eye/ear anatomy comes later.
Treat 'we have exactly five senses' as an age-appropriate model; balance and body-position senses exist too and can be mentioned as a light aside, not corrected as an error.
Distinguish the organ that detects from the brain that interprets: the organ detects, the brain makes sense of it.
Anchor each sense to a purpose in safety and daily life (smelling smoke, feeling something too hot) so senses are not just labels.

Tap-to-reveal figures, drag-to-match games, flaps and nose-hold toggles are scaffolds carrying pre-authored facts: they can present and check the matching but do not themselves make a child actually smell, taste or feel a real object. Because the objective includes experiencing what each sense detects, pair these scaffolds with hands-on use of real senses on real objects; which medium is more effective has not been tested here. A matching or quiz check assesses recognition, which alone does not show a child can produce or apply the ideas, so it should follow hands-on exploration.
Hold safety and allergy awareness in any taste/smell activity (food sensitivities, hygiene, supervised tasting).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched and were already marked verified:false in the source. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's catalogue judgements that '3D adds no value' and that naming is 'best done visually/experientially' are fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; they have been dropped rather than asserted. The tap-to-reveal figure is retained as one representation, not the uniquely correct medium.

The source assessment text once writes 'ears detect sound waves'; for 5–7s the simpler 'ears detect sound' is used in activities to match the stated age-appropriate guidance, while the fuller phrasing is noted here as the source's own wording.

A non-preferred 'conversation' alternative (a character asking how you know it's raining without looking) was folded into the reasoning activity as an optional prompt rather than kept as a separate approach.
Activity 2's intended insight is scoped to flavour (taste+smell) so it does not imply, against activity 4, that a single sense can never identify something alone.
Independent re-audit: no critical learner-facing errors found; remaining uncertainty is about source/efficacy evidence only, held in the uncertain and review notes.

assess.poeTask: Give the child two similar strong-flavoured foods (e.g. a piece of apple and a piece of pear, or two jellybean flavours). Ask them to predict whether they'll still tell the flavours apart while pinching their nose shut, and WHY, before trying. Most predict the tongue alone will manage; with the nose pinched the flavours are surprisingly hard to distinguish — revealing whether they realise smell and taste work together.
probeDeeper: Why does an orange taste boring and hard to recognise when you have a very blocked-up nose with a cold?
If the room were pitch dark AND you were blindfolded, would smell still work? Why doesn't smell need light the way sight does?
What is your skin detecting when you feel the orange — can you name two things, like bumpy, cold, or wet?
assess.correctAnswer: With eyes blindfolded, sight can't help because it needs light and your eyes are covered. But smell (nose picking up the orange's odour), taste (tongue detecting its flavour), and touch (skin and fingers feeling the bumpy peel and wetness) can still identify it — each sense detects a different kind of information. Hearing wouldn't help much here. Each sense uses a different body part to detect a different thing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Taste and smell are the same sense, or one organ does both.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate them: the nose detects smells (odours in the air), the tongue detects tastes (flavours in food); they cooperate but are different senses.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Merges the nose and tongue, or names one sense for both jobs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Touch (skin) isn't really one of the senses.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add touch as a full sense: the skin detects pressure, texture, and temperature — feel the peel to show it.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only smell and taste could tell — touch isn't one of the senses.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists only eyes, ears, nose, tongue; omits skin/touch.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names the sense organs but can't say what each one detects (eyes→light, ears→sound, etc.).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair each organ with its stimulus: eyes–light, ears–sound, nose–smell, tongue–taste, skin–touch/temperature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Matches organ to sense but not the sense to the specific thing it picks up.

responseLevels.gap: Can't match senses to organs or to what they detect; merges taste and smell, or leaves out touch.
responseLevels.full: Matches each sense to its organ and to the specific thing it detects (light, sound, flavour, odour, pressure/temperature) and reasons about which senses can or can't help in a given situation.
responseLevels.partial: Names the five senses and organs but is shaky on what each detects, or gives everyday examples without linking organ to stimulus consistently.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You're blindfolded and someone hands you a slice of orange. Which of your senses could still tell you it's an orange, and what would each one be picking up? And why can't your EYES help you right now?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who leaves out touch, or merges taste and smell, or can't say what each sense detects, reveals the gap. Only a child who maps sense→organ→what-it-detects can pick the right senses for a blindfolded task and explain why sight fails. The tier-two 'what would each be picking up' forces the organ-to-stimulus link.
