pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Types of Rock — the three main kinds: igneous (lava/magma cools and hardens), sedimentary (layers of material pressed together), and metamorphic (heat and pressure change existing rock); fossils are found in sedimentary rock.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement — note the mismatch):** DfE Y3 **Rocks** (statutory) is: "compare and group together different kinds of rocks on the basis of their appearance and simple physical properties"; "describe in simple terms how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock"; "recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter." Crucially, the NAMES igneous/sedimentary/metamorphic and the rock cycle are NOT KS2 statutory — 'sedimentary rock' appears only in the non-statutory notes (fossils context), and the three rock types + rock cycle are formally DfE **KS3 Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere**. So this topic teaches KS3 vocabulary using a KS2-appropriate hands-on approach; treat naming as enrichment atop the statutory 'compare/group + fossils' work.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No elementary PE names the three rock types; rock/soil formation and change connect to **4-ESS1-1** and **4-ESS2** (evidence of change; weathering/erosion). Rock formation processes are developed at **MS-ESS2**. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisites 'Earth Is Made of Rock' and 'What Is a Volcano' (igneous links to cooled lava). Two facets: (1) classify real rocks by appearance/properties (statutory KS2 skill — grains vs crystals, layers, fossils), and (2) the big idea that rock TYPE encodes how it FORMED. Land the load-bearing link: fossils are found in sedimentary rock BECAUSE it forms gently in layers — things can be trapped and preserved — whereas igneous rock forms from melt that would destroy them.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A/B (classify by observable properties; begin process→product reasoning). Children can sort by look/feel and match a type to its formation with support, but tend to treat 'rock' as one undifferentiated material and to think all rocks contain fossils. Success = name the three types, state igneous forms from cooled lava/magma, and explain fossils are in sedimentary rock because it forms in layers.
bestPractices: Ground naming in hands-on classification first (hand lens: grains vs crystals, visible layers, fossils) — the statutory KS2 skill — then attach the type name to what was observed.
Teach each type by its FORMATION STORY, not just a label: igneous = melt cooled and hardened; sedimentary = layers of bits pressed together; metamorphic = existing rock changed by heat and pressure.
Make the fossils–sedimentary link causal, not a coincidence: gentle layering can trap and preserve remains; melting (igneous) and intense heat/pressure (metamorphic) would destroy them.
Use real specimens (granite, sandstone/chalk, marble/slate) and building stones/gravestones so classification is evidential and local (links to Geography).
Address the 'rock = human-made too' misconception (Oak National Academy): brick, tarmac and concrete are manufactured, not natural rock — sort natural vs made.
keyRepresentations: A 'rock factory' with three formation processes: cooling melt → igneous; pressing layers → sedimentary (with a trapped shell); heat+squeeze → metamorphic
Real rock specimens examined with a hand lens (crystals vs grains vs layers vs fossils)
Sedimentary layers building up with a shell caught between them → revealed as a fossil
Natural-vs-manufactured sort (granite/sandstone vs brick/tarmac/concrete)
commonMisconceptions: All rock is basically the same material (there are distinct types formed by distinct processes).
All rocks contain fossils / fossils can be in any rock (fossils are found in sedimentary rock because it forms in gentle layers).
Brick, concrete and tarmac are kinds of rock (they are human-made materials, not natural rock).
Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic are just names to memorise (each name IS its formation story).
Rocks never change from one type to another (they can, very slowly — the rock cycle, taught next at 9–11).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: learn the three main rock types — igneous (melt cools and hardens), sedimentary (layers of material pressed together), metamorphic (existing rock changed by heat and pressure) — and that fossils are found mainly in sedimentary rock BECAUSE it forms gently in layers that can trap and preserve remains, whereas melting destroys remains and intense heat/pressure usually destroys or badly squashes them. Ground the naming in hands-on classification of real specimens first (grains vs crystals vs layers vs bands vs fossils), then attach each name as shorthand for its formation story. Note the standards context: classifying rocks and describing fossil formation is the statutory KS2 skill, while the three type-names and rock cycle are formally KS3 vocabulary taught here as enrichment atop that hands-on work.

activities.title: Run the rock factory: make each type and test what survives
feedback: If the shell burns away in the lava and is crushed/smeared in the heat-press but survives in the layers, that is exactly why fossils are found in sedimentary rock — not by coincidence but because of how each rock forms.
If you expected a fossil in the igneous rock: igneous forms from hot melt that would destroy a once-living thing; only the gentle layering step keeps a shell intact.
Tie the name back to what you did: 'sedimentary' = layers that settled and were pressed; 'igneous' = melt that cooled; 'metamorphic' = rock changed by heat and pressure.
activities.rationale: Doing each formation process and testing shell survival turns 'fossils are found in sedimentary rock' from a fact to memorise into a conclusion the learner reaches, and makes the causal link (gentle layering preserves; heat destroys) concrete.
sourceClaims: Igneous rock forms from cooled magma/lava; sedimentary from compacted layers of sediment (fossil-bearing); metamorphic from heat and pressure altering existing rock.
learnerActions: At a 'melt' step, cool a glowing lava/magma pool and watch crystals lock together, forming igneous rock.

At a 'layers' step, drop layers of sand and mud with a small shell tucked between them, press them down to make sedimentary rock, then split it open to reveal the shell as a fossil. (In real rock, hardening the layers and turning a shell into a fossil takes a very long time.)

At a 'heat and squeeze' step, take an existing rock and increase heat and pressure until it changes, for example its minerals lining up in bands, forming metamorphic rock (many, though not all, metamorphic rocks show bands).
Try to preserve a shell in each process: drop it into the lava, put it through the heat-and-press, and set it among gentle layers — observe which process preserves it and which destroy it.
State in your own words why fossils are found mainly in sedimentary rock: why melting in igneous rock destroys them, and why heat and pressure in metamorphic rock usually destroy or squash them.
activities.intendedInsight: A rock's type is its formation story, and fossils are found mainly in sedimentary rock because gentle layering can trap and preserve remains, while melting (igneous) destroys them and intense heat/pressure (metamorphic) usually destroys or distorts them.

activities.title: Hand-lens classification of real specimens
feedback: If you grouped a specimen by a single feature, check a second property with the lens — grains (which may rub off) or visible layers/fossils point toward sedimentary, interlocking crystals of mixed colours toward igneous, and bands or thin splitting sheets toward many metamorphic rocks. Remember marble is metamorphic yet crystalline and usually has no bands, so tell it apart from igneous rock by its mostly single-coloured crystals, its softness, and its fizzing in vinegar.
Name the type only after describing what you saw, so the label stays tied to the evidence.
Using real building stones or gravestones shows these rock types are all around you, not just in a classroom.
activities.rationale: Hands-on classification by observable properties is the statutory KS2 skill and gives an evidential foundation before type-names are attached.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 'Rocks' statutory objectives: compare/group rocks by appearance and simple physical properties; describe how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock; recognise soils are made from rocks and organic matter. The named three rock types + rock cycle are KS3 Chemistry, not KS2.
learnerActions: Examine real rock specimens such as granite, sandstone or chalk, and marble or slate with a hand lens.
Look for distinguishing clues: interlocking crystals, loose grains, visible layers, embedded fossils, or bands/stripes (foliation).

Sort the specimens into igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic based on what you observe, then say which clue led to each decision. (Note crystals can appear in both igneous rock such as granite and some metamorphic rock such as marble. Marble usually has no bands, so compare the crystals instead: granite has mixed colours, marble is mostly one pale colour. With an adult, you can also check whether it fizzes in vinegar.)
Where possible, link to local examples such as building stones or gravestones.
activities.intendedInsight: Rocks can be compared and grouped by their appearance and simple physical properties, and the observable texture (crystals, grains, layers, bands, fossils) is evidence of how the rock formed.

activities.title: Natural rock or made by people?
feedback: If you called brick a rock: brick, concrete and tarmac are made by people, while rocks form through natural processes like cooling, layering, or heat and pressure.
A good test is to ask: did this form in nature, or did someone manufacture it?
activities.rationale: Directly targets the common belief that manufactured materials are kinds of rock, keeping the natural/made distinction explicit.
sourceClaims: A common Y3 misconception is that manufactured materials (brick, tarmac, concrete) are rock; teaching should distinguish natural rock from human-made materials.
learnerActions: Look at a mixed set including natural rocks (granite, sandstone) and manufactured materials (brick, tarmac, concrete).
Sort each item into 'natural rock' or 'made by people'.
Give a reason for each sort, focusing on whether the material formed by a natural process or was manufactured.
activities.intendedInsight: Brick, concrete and tarmac are human-made materials, not natural rock, even though they can look rock-like.

activities.title: Explore examples and consolidate naming
feedback: For the fossil question, a full answer names sedimentary AND gives the reason (gentle layers trap and preserve remains).
If a match is wrong, revisit the formation story: melt → igneous, pressed layers → sedimentary, heat and pressure → metamorphic.
These grouping and matching tasks check what you already understand; they work best after doing the formation processes rather than instead of them.
activities.rationale: Reading formation facts and grouping/matching consolidates naming and classification, but checks rather than generates the causal insight, so it follows the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: Igneous rock forms from cooled magma/lava; sedimentary from compacted layers of sediment (fossil-bearing); metamorphic from heat and pressure altering existing rock.
learnerActions: Explore examples of the three rock types; for each, find out how it formed and where it is found.

Look closely at the distinguishing texture of each: crystals (igneous), layers with a fossil (sedimentary), bands or thin splitting sheets in many metamorphic rocks such as gneiss or slate (though marble has crystals and usually no bands).
Answer the question: 'Which rock holds fossils, and why?'
Consolidate by grouping specimen images by type, matching each type to its formation process, and answering: 'In which rock would you find a fossil, and why?'
activities.intendedInsight: The three names are shorthand for distinct formation processes, and fossils are found mainly in sedimentary rock because of its gentle layered formation.

constraints: Grouping, matching and short-answer consolidation checks and assesses understanding but does not, on its own, elicit the learner's independent construction of the causal fossils-in-sedimentary reasoning; use it after the hands-on formation work.

A view-only presentation conveys the naming and classification half well but presents the causal fossils link as a stated fact; learners benefit from also running or observing the formation contrast to reach it themselves.

Rotating/zooming 3D specimens can aid close observation of texture, but rock-type learning does not hinge on 3D spatial reasoning; a 2D view with hand-lens zoom is sufficient, so treat 3D as an optional enhancement.

Keep the formation mechanisms distinct: igneous = cooled melt, sedimentary = pressed layers, metamorphic = existing rock changed by heat and pressure (often, but not always, showing bands; marble usually has none). Do not let the layering idea bleed into igneous.

Crystalline texture is not unique to igneous rock (some metamorphic rock such as marble is crystalline). Banding helps identify some metamorphic rocks (e.g. gneiss), but marble usually has no bands, so separate it from igneous rock such as granite using other clues: marble's crystals are mostly one pale colour, it is softer (a steel nail can scratch it), and it fizzes in vinegar (adult-led), whereas granite has crystals of mixed colours and does not fizz.

The three type-names and the rock cycle are enrichment (formally KS3) layered on top of the statutory KS2 skills of classifying rocks and describing fossil formation; prerequisites include understanding that Earth is made of rock and what a volcano is (igneous links to cooled lava).

The rock cycle (one type changing into another over long timescales) is formally taught later, at KS3 (ages 11–14); here, note only that rocks can change very slowly, without developing the full cycle.

Simulated melting/pressure stations model what would happen to a fossil; use them as representations of real geological processes, not as literal claims that every fossil in every real setting is always destroyed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources (Oak National Academy misconception guidance; USGS/BGS rock-type claim) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE standards claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

The source states intense heat/pressure (metamorphic) and melting (igneous) destroy fossils; real geology is more nuanced (some fossils can partially survive mild metamorphism). The 'usually destroys' framing in the assessment answer is a reasonable simplification for ages 7–9; keep it as a strong general rule rather than an absolute law.
The standards note flags a KS2/KS3 placement mismatch (three type-names are formally KS3); preserved as context so teaching treats naming as enrichment atop statutory work.

Crystalline texture overlaps igneous and some metamorphic rock (e.g. marble); the hand-lens clues add banding to keep the metamorphic category identifiable, an age-appropriate simplification not independently source-verified.
Product/UI mechanic vocabulary (gallery, lift-the-flap, tap/zoom/drill-down) and quiz-step labels were reworded into descriptive learner actions in the final guidance.

probeDeeper: How does sedimentary rock form, step by step — and why does that let a fossil survive?
What would happen to a fish's body if it were caught in hot lava that then cooled into igneous rock?
Is a brick a rock? Why or why not?
Name the three rock types and give one way each is different.
assess.correctAnswer: Sedimentary rock. It forms gently, as layers of sediment settle and press together over time, so a buried animal or plant can be preserved as a fossil inside the layers. Igneous rock forms from hot melted rock (lava/magma cooling), which would destroy a fossil; metamorphic rock is changed by great heat and pressure, which also usually destroys fossils.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fossils can be found equally in any type of rock
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link formation to survival — heat and melting destroy fossils; only gentle layered sedimentary rock preserves them.
errorPatterns.distractor: It doesn't matter — fossils are found in all three types equally.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks igneous/metamorphic, or says it doesn't matter which type.

errorPatterns.pattern: Igneous rock forms from squashed layers / all rocks form by layers pressing (muddles formation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Igneous = cooled lava/magma; sedimentary = pressed layers — keep the mechanisms distinct.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's igneous — because igneous rock forms from layers pressing together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says igneous forms from pressed layers rather than cooled melt.

errorPatterns.pattern: Manufactured materials like brick, concrete or tarmac are types of rock
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rocks are natural; brick, concrete and tarmac are made by people.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Classifies man-made materials as natural rock.

responseLevels.gap: Can't name the types, or thinks fossils occur in any rock; may call brick a rock.
responseLevels.full: Identifies sedimentary and explains its gentle layered formation preserves fossils whereas igneous (cooled melt) and metamorphic (heat/pressure) destroy them — and distinguishes natural rock from manufactured materials.
responseLevels.partial: Names the three types and says fossils are in sedimentary but can't explain why (the gentle-layering vs heat contrast).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A fossil of a fish is found inside a rock. Which of the three rock types — igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic — is it most likely to be in, and WHY does that type keep fossils safe while the others usually don't?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can recite the three names yet not connect how each type FORMS to whether a fossil survives. Asking why sedimentary keeps fossils forces the gentle-layering mechanism contrasted with heat destroying them — separating memorised names from understanding formation.

sources.claim: DfE Y3 'Rocks' statutory objectives: compare/group rocks by appearance and simple physical properties; describe how fossils are formed when things that have lived are trapped within rock; recognise soils are made from rocks and organic matter. The named three rock types + rock cycle are KS3 Chemistry, not KS2.
sources.source: DfE — National curriculum in England: science programmes of study (gov.uk)

sources.claim: A common Y3 misconception is that manufactured materials (brick, tarmac, concrete) are rock; teaching should distinguish natural rock from human-made materials.
sources.source: Oak National Academy — KS2 'Rocks and soils' unit guidance

sources.claim: Igneous rock forms from cooled magma/lava; sedimentary from compacted layers of sediment (fossil-bearing); metamorphic from heat and pressure altering existing rock.

pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, 'showing your working' is the first rung of mathematical argument: the child shows and tells HOW an answer was found — with objects, a drawing, or spoken words — and begins to respond to 'how do you know?' by pointing to what they did rather than just restating the answer. On the NRICH novice-to-expert ladder this is the describing (and beginning-to-explain) stage. The crucial teaching insight is that at this age a child's REASONING typically runs ahead of their ability to COMMUNICATE it: a child who says little may nonetheless have reasoned soundly. So teaching separates the two — building the habit of demonstrating a method concretely, and, separately, scaffolding the language to narrate it — and treats listening to a peer and agreeing/disagreeing as the seed of critiquing reasoning.
bestPractices: Ask 'how do you know?' and 'show me' routinely, accepting objects, pointing, and drawings as valid ways to show working
Separate reasoning from its communication — judge whether a quiet child needs help thinking or help putting it into words, and support each differently
Model narrating a method aloud ('first I… then I…') and provide simple spoken stems
Use concrete referents (counters, ten frames, drawings) as the medium of explanation, as elementary arguments legitimately rest on objects and actions
Have children listen to a peer's method and say whether they agree, beginning to evaluate reasoning rather than just answers
Value the demonstration itself; do not treat limited vocabulary as limited mathematics
keyRepresentations: Concrete objects / counters moved to enact and show a method
Ten frame and part-part-whole drawing
Number sentence alongside the objects
Spoken sentence stems ('first… then… so…')
The describe → explain step of the NRICH reasoning ladder
commonMisconceptions: Restating the answer ('because it's 8') when asked 'how do you know?' instead of showing the method
A quiet or brief response mistaken for weak reasoning, when it is really communication that lags
Judging a peer's work only by whether the answer matches, not by whether the method makes sense
Believing 'showing your working' means writing the sum again rather than revealing the thinking

learn.summary: For 5-6 year olds, 'showing your working' means demonstrating and narrating HOW an answer was found — with objects, drawings, or spoken words — and beginning to answer 'how do you know?' by pointing to what was done rather than restating the answer. A key teaching insight is that at this age reasoning can often run ahead of the ability to communicate it: a quiet child may have reasoned soundly. Teaching therefore separates two threads — building the habit of demonstrating a method concretely, and separately scaffolding the language to narrate it — and treats listening to a peer and agreeing/disagreeing as the first seed of evaluating reasoning, not just answers.

activities.title: The curious listener who wants to know HOW
feedback: When the child shows and narrates a method, reflect it back as a short story so they hear their own doing turned into an explanation.
Accept spoken, pointed, tapped, or dragged responses, and never penalise sparse words — value the demonstration itself.
If the child only restates '8' or 'because it's right', prompt 'show me with your counters' and 'point to where the 3 went'.
When presenting a muddled-but-correct route, help the child attend to the steps rather than accept it just because the answer matched; make clear the muddled route is not the model to copy.
activities.rationale: Showing and telling how you worked something out is inherently dialogic. A character that keeps asking 'how do you know? show me!' and genuinely listens — accepting objects and pointing — rehearses the describe/explain habit and gives the child a reason to narrate a method aloud, which is where communication of reasoning is built. A deliberately wrong-but-plausible worked route plants the first seed of judging reasoning rather than answers. These are research-informed design proposals, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents (objects, drawings, diagrams, actions), and students at all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask questions to improve them.

Reasoning develops along a describe → explain → convince → justify → prove spectrum; the reasoning itself and the communication of it are distinct and often develop at different rates, with young children's reasoning frequently ahead of their ability to communicate it.
learnerActions: Solve a within-10 problem such as 5 and 3 using counters (physical objects or on-screen draggable counters).
When asked 'how did you get 8? show me!', move or point to the counters to re-enact the method — for example, 'I put 5, then counted on 3 more'.
Hear the method echoed back as a little story ('first you put 5, then you counted on 3 more, so you got 8') and notice that explaining = showing the doing, not repeating the answer.
Watch the listener solve a problem its own way — sometimes by a muddled or wrong route — and answer 'do you agree with how I did it? how can you tell?'
activities.intendedInsight: 'How do you know?' is answered by demonstrating the method, not by restating the answer; and a method can be judged by whether its steps make sense, not only by whether the final number is right.

activities.title: Show-how workspace with a compare-two-methods panel
feedback: Prompt the child to narrate alongside the replay so the demonstration and its words are built together.
On the compare panel, ask the child to point to the specific step they agree or disagree with rather than give a yes/no.
Treat a correct answer reached by an odd route as a chance to notice the method, not to approve it automatically.
activities.rationale: A workspace where the child moves counters or ten-frames to show a method and then narrates it makes the demonstration concrete and repeatable; a simple 'do you agree?' comparison introduces evaluating reasoning. Draggable counters, a replay of the steps, and a side-by-side compare panel are illustrative interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms, and are not validated here.
sourceClaims: Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents (objects, drawings, diagrams, actions), and students at all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask questions to improve them.
learnerActions: Move counters or fill a ten frame to solve an addition or subtraction, then use a 'show how you did it' replay to retrace the steps.
Narrate the recaptured steps aloud using stems such as 'first… then… so…'.
View a peer's or character's method beside your own and decide 'do you agree?', then 'show why' by pointing to a step that does or does not make sense.
activities.intendedInsight: A method can be made concrete, repeatable, and comparable; evaluating reasoning means looking at the steps, not only matching the final answer.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal a worked method (modelling scaffold)
feedback: Use the revealed stages as a model, then quickly move the child to demonstrating their own method so they do not only watch.
Name each revealed step in 'first… then… so…' form so the language of narration is modelled.
activities.rationale: Revealing a worked method's steps one at a time can model what showing your working looks like, but the child watches rather than demonstrates their own thinking, so it should lead into own-method demonstration. Recognition of a modelled method does not by itself elicit the child producing and narrating one. This is a modelling scaffold whose effectiveness is untested by the cited sources, not a substitute for the child producing and narrating a method.
learnerActions: Tap each stage of an already-solved problem to reveal 'what I did and why' at that step.
Afterwards, re-solve a fresh problem and show your own steps with objects or a drawing, narrating as you go.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the stages of a worked method named out loud shows what 'showing your working' can look like before producing one's own.

constraints: The target is demonstrating AND beginning to evaluate a method — not producing a single scored answer. An answer-only, scored format can record only the final result and cannot capture showing or telling a method, and it tends to reward the answer-restating this topic must move beyond; if used at all, treat it as a check of the final result, not of the reasoning.
A tap-to-reveal worked example is a modelling scaffold: the child watches rather than demonstrates, so it must be followed by the child producing and narrating their own method.

Separate reasoning from its communication: when a child is quiet or brief, judge whether they need help thinking or help putting it into words, and support that thread. Do not treat limited vocabulary as limited mathematics, and do not drill vocabulary in isolation.
Elementary arguments legitimately rest on objects, pointing, and drawings; accept these as valid ways to show working rather than requiring written sums or rich sentences.
At this age, full critique of a peer's reasoning is only emerging; expect the child to begin attending to steps (e.g. 'can you show what I did?') rather than deliver a complete evaluation.

Showing arithmetic working here does not need elaborate 3D spatial environments: simple concrete arrangements such as counters and ten frames are useful for showing a method, but complex spatial/3D manipulation is not needed for this objective, though it may serve other topics.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified in this independent review, and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit of every summary, insight, action, feedback, constraint and note found no new critical learner-facing errors or unsupported categorical claims; the previously flagged activities[2].sourceClaims=[] correction is confirmed already applied.

The included diagnostic routine (solve 5+3 with counters, ask 'how do you know? show me', then model an alternative or deliberately slipped method and ask 'do you agree?') is arithmetically sound: 5+3=8. No numeric errors were found in the source examples.

A deliberately 'wrong way' demonstration by the character should remain clearly a muddled route to test the child's attention to steps; ensure any wrong demonstration is not left as the child's takeaway model of correct method.

The tap-to-reveal activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because neither cited claim directly supports the efficacy of a watch-first modelling scaffold; the claims concern reasoning development generally, not evidence that this interaction helps.

The original source framed an answer-only scored format and a 3D/spatial format as 'poor fit'; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal 'cannot teach' claims.

probeDeeper: 'Show me with the counters how you got 8.' (turns 'how do you know?' into a demonstration)
'Can you tell me the first thing you did, and the next thing?' (scaffolds narrating the method)
'I'll do it my way — watch. Do you agree with how I did it?' (evaluating a method, not an answer)
Counterexample: solve it by a muddled route that still lands on 8 — does the child notice the method was odd, or accept it because the answer is right?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who responds to 'how do you know?' by SHOWING the method (moving or pointing to counters, or drawing) and telling it in some form ('I had 5, then 3 more'), and who, watching your method, judges it by whether the actions make sense rather than only whether the answer matches. Demonstrating the method and beginning to evaluate a method are the targets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reasoning runs ahead of communication — the child clearly used a sound method but 'just tells the answer' or cannot yet put the how into words.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT conclude the child cannot reason, and do not drill vocabulary in isolation. Ask them to SHOW with counters and narrate alongside; decide whether it is the reasoning or the communication that needs developing, and support that one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'how do you know?', the child gives the correct answer and a shrug or a single word, yet can correctly re-do the problem when watched — the thinking is there, the language is not.

errorPatterns.pattern: Restates the answer when asked 'how do you know?' ('because it's 8') instead of showing the method.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the move explicitly: 'show me with your counters', 'point to where the 3 went'; model narrating a method so the child hears what 'how' sounds like.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child repeats the result rather than demonstrating; the show-and-tell habit is not yet triggered by the prompt.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges a peer's (or teacher's) method only by whether the answer matches, not by whether the steps make sense.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not expect full critique yet; ask 'can you show what I did?' so the child attends to the steps, and use agree/disagree talk with clear listening turns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shown a method that reaches the right answer by a muddled route, the child agrees simply because the answer is right; evaluating the reasoning itself is only emerging.

responseLevels.gap: Gives only the answer or 'because it's right'; cannot show the method even with objects; judges others solely by the answer.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously demonstrates the method with objects/drawing and narrates it in some form, and when watching another method attends to whether the steps make sense — the seed of critiquing reasoning — not just the answer.
responseLevels.partial: Shows and describes WHAT they did with objects or a drawing (the describing step), but not yet WHY, and needs prompting; begins to look at a peer's steps only when asked.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child counters and a problem like 5 + 3. Once they have 8, ask: 'How do you know it's 8? Show me and tell me how you worked it out.' Then solve it yourself a different way (or with a deliberate slip), and ask: 'Do you agree with how I did it? How can you tell?' Treat it as a conversation about their thinking, not a marked answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child developing this practice turns 'how do you know?' into a demonstration — they re-enact the doing. A child at answer-only restates '8' or 'because it's right' and, when judging your method, checks only the final number. Because a young child's words may lag their thinking, the tell is whether they can SHOW the method (with objects) even when they cannot fully narrate it — not the richness of their vocabulary.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Drawing conclusions from evidence — causal relationships & trust

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils are taught to use "reporting and presenting findings from enquiries, including conclusions, causal relationships and explanations of and degree of trust in results, in oral and written forms such as displays and other presentations" (verbatim). Two step-ups from lower KS2: explaining CAUSAL relationships, and judging DEGREE OF TRUST in results.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 6 Constructing Explanations + SEP 4 Analyzing Data, grades 3–5):** SEP 6 requires constructing explanations that specify a causal account supported by evidence; SEP 4 requires analysing data to make sense of phenomena and considering the limitations of data (measurement error, sample size) in interpretation. Degree of trust maps onto evaluating the quality and quantity of evidence behind a claim.

- **Operational details:** Builds on recording complex data (prerequisite mt_rDjtmDogJr) and prediction-driven testing (mt_5PgQB0QkWi); draws on the 'understanding why' habit (mt_Y6P9y1Rz-u). The distinctive skills are: (1) stating a CAUSAL relationship ('X caused Y because…') grounded in evidence, not mere correlation — seeding the correlation-vs-causation distinction taught elsewhere; and (2) articulating a DEGREE OF TRUST by reasoning about sample size, repeat readings, anomalies and possible errors ('we can be fairly confident because we repeated it three times and the readings were close, but the sample was small'). Feeds forward to evaluating others' evidence and to KS3 error analysis (dependents mt_AstzvYDU2m, mt_3jmBpEepYX).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). A learner who can present findings with appropriate scientific vocabulary, state an evidence-supported causal relationship, and discuss how much to trust the results by reference to sample size, repeats and possible errors has met the bar. Formal systematic-vs-random error analysis is the KS3 tier (mt_3jmBpEepYX).
bestPractices: Teach 'degree of trust' as a spectrum, not a yes/no: pupils qualify their confidence ('fairly confident because…, but less sure about…') by explicitly citing repeats, closeness of readings, sample size and anomalies.
Require the causal claim to carry a mechanism or evidence link ('the darker leaf grew less BECAUSE it got less light, shown by…'), distinguishing a genuine causal explanation from a bare correlation.
Use anomalous results deliberately: give pupils a dataset with an outlier and have them decide how it affects trust and whether to repeat — building the evaluative habit.
Connect trust to the design choices from the experimental-design spine (sample size, repeat readings) so pupils see reliability as something built in during planning, not judged only at the end.
Model honest uncertainty as good science — a well-reasoned 'we can't be fully sure because…' is stronger than false certainty.
keyRepresentations: A 'degree of trust' scale annotated with the reasons (repeats, sample size, spread, anomalies)
A causal statement frame: 'X caused Y because ___ (evidence/mechanism)'
A results table with an anomaly flagged and its effect on trust discussed
A confidence-reasoning card (what makes us more / less sure)
A repeats-and-spread visual (close readings = higher trust; scattered = lower)
commonMisconceptions: Stating a causal relationship from correlation alone ('they happened together, so one caused the other') without evidence of mechanism or a controlled comparison.
Treating results as simply 'right' or 'wrong' rather than as more or less trustworthy depending on how they were obtained.
Ignoring anomalies or silently deleting them instead of reasoning about their effect on the conclusion.
Equating a single tidy result with high trust, not recognising that repeats and sample size underpin reliability.
Presenting a conclusion with false certainty, treating any acknowledgement of uncertainty as a weakness rather than good scientific practice.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, learners report findings and defend a causal conclusion from evidence while calibrating how much to trust it — citing sample size, repeat readings, spread of readings, anomalies, control of variables, and possible errors. 'Degree of trust' is treated as a spectrum, not a right/wrong verdict, and a genuine causal claim ('X caused Y because…') is distinguished from mere correlation ('they happened together'). Activities combine a proposed interactive data-and-trust bench, a skeptical questioning dialogue, and ranking/categorising tasks, so learners construct calibrated claims both out loud and in writing and practise evaluating evidence quality.

activities.title: Data-and-trust bench: watch confidence respond to the evidence
feedback: If a conclusion is asserted with no qualification: prompt 'How many plants did you test at each dose? Would more change how much you trust the pattern?'
If the sample is tiny or a single run: 'With so few data points it is hard to tell whether the pattern is real or just chance — how might more plants and repeats change your confidence?'
If a cause is claimed without ruling out confounds: 'Could light, water or soil also explain the taller plants? Only a controlled comparison lets you attribute the effect to fertiliser.'
When repeated readings cluster closely: affirm that close, repeated readings support higher trust; when they scatter widely, support lower trust.
If an anomaly is silently deleted: 'Reasoning about the odd reading — repeat or investigate — is stronger than quietly dropping it.'
activities.rationale: Degree of trust depends on design choices (repeats, sample size, control) and responds to them, so a live model where confidence visibly rises and falls as the learner varies the evidence is intended to make reliability concrete rather than a memorised phrase. A causal-claim checker is intended to surface the correlation-vs-causation distinction by asking what else differed. The trust-meter and causal-claim checker are optional, unvalidated interaction examples that may make the mechanism visible; they are not required mechanisms. The cited standards support teaching causal reporting and degree of trust, not the efficacy of these proposed interactions.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires reporting and presenting findings including conclusions, causal relationships and explanations of and degree of trust in results, in oral and written forms.
learnerActions: Study a provided dataset (e.g. plant growth at different fertiliser doses) and write a conclusion as a causal claim using the frame 'X caused Y because ___ (evidence/mechanism)'.

Explore how trust changes: add repeat readings and observe whether the readings cluster closely or scatter; shrink the sample to only two plants; reveal a hidden outlier/anomaly. Remember that adding repeats reveals whether readings are close — close, repeated readings support higher trust, scattered ones support lower trust; adding repeats does not by itself force the readings together.
After each change, state whether your confidence should rise or fall and why, before consulting the optional 'trust meter' scaffold (a proposed, unvalidated aid) to compare your reasoning.
When an outlier appears, decide: repeat the measurement, investigate the odd reading, or keep it — and justify the choice.
Feed a causal claim into the optional causal-claim checker (e.g. type 'the fertiliser caused more growth') and answer its prompt about whether anything else differed between the groups.
activities.intendedInsight: How much we can trust a conclusion is earned by how the evidence was gathered — a larger sample and repeat readings that turn out to cluster closely justify higher confidence, while small samples, widely scattered repeats and unexplained anomalies justify caution. A real causal claim requires ruling out other explanations, not just two things occurring together.

activities.title: Defend it to a skeptical scientist (oral report and confidence)
feedback: If the learner claims certainty: ask 'What would make you less sure here?' to model honest uncertainty as good practice.
If a confound is unaddressed: 'What else differed between the plants besides fertiliser? How would you know it was the fertiliser?'
If confidence is vague: ask them to name the specific reasons — repeats, closeness of readings, sample size, anomalies — behind their level of confidence.
Affirm responses that distinguish 'the data show a pattern' from 'fertiliser causes taller growth.'
activities.rationale: The standard names oral as well as written reporting, and trust reasoning is naturally elicited by challenge-and-justify dialogue. Spoken rehearsal of calibrated confidence and causal justification exercises the reporting and trust strands. This complements, and does not replace, written presentation of findings.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires reporting and presenting findings including conclusions, causal relationships and explanations of and degree of trust in results, in oral and written forms.
learnerActions: Present your findings aloud, stating the causal conclusion in appropriate scientific vocabulary.
Respond to a skeptical questioner who presses: 'You say the fertiliser caused it — could something else explain that?' and 'How confident are you, given only three plants?'
Qualify your confidence out loud on a spectrum: 'We can be fairly confident because we repeated it three times and the readings were close, but the sample was small.'
Answer follow-ups that probe whether other variables were controlled and whether any measurements might be off.
activities.intendedInsight: Presenting findings and discussing degree of trust is a dialogic skill: a well-reasoned 'we can't be fully sure because…' is stronger science than false certainty, and a causal claim must survive the question 'what else could explain it?'

activities.title: Rank and sort: which evidence deserves more trust?
feedback: For a trust ranking, require the reason, not just the choice — 'trust more because it was repeated and the readings were close.'
If a correlation is mislabelled causal: 'What evidence of a mechanism or a controlled comparison supports calling this a cause?'
If an anomaly is ignored: 'How does that odd reading change how confident you can be?'
activities.rationale: Judging which conclusion is best supported, ranking by trustworthiness, and separating causal from correlational claims are evaluative skills that extend the learner from making their own claims toward evaluating others' evidence. Selection/sorting tasks assess recognition and comparison; they do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of a written or spoken causal argument that the first two activities require.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 6 (constructing causal explanations from evidence) and SEP 4 (analysing data and considering its limitations) at grades 3-5 underpin causal reporting and judging degree of trust.
learnerActions: Compare two or more results and choose which should be trusted more, giving the reason (e.g. more repeats, larger sample, readings that cluster closely).
Order several datasets from most to least reliable and justify the ordering.

Sort statements into 'causal' vs 'correlational' categories (e.g. 'the plants given more light grew taller because they could photosynthesise more' vs 'the taller plants also happened to be near the window').
Examine a results table with a flagged anomaly and state how it affects the trust in the conclusion.
activities.intendedInsight: Reliability can be compared and reasoned about: evidence quality (sample size, repeats, spread, control, anomalies) determines how much weight a conclusion deserves, and a causal claim says more than a correlational observation, so it needs more support (a controlled comparison and a plausible mechanism) before it can be trusted.

constraints: Degree of trust must be taught as a spectrum ('fairly confident because…, but less sure about…'), not a right/wrong verdict.

A causal claim must carry a mechanism or evidence link ('the plant kept in the dark grew less BECAUSE it got less light, shown by…'), distinguishing it from a bare correlation; learners must consider what else could explain the result, because a plausible mechanism alone does not rule out other explanations.
Anomalies should be reasoned about (repeat or investigate), never silently deleted.
Connect trust to design choices (sample size, repeat readings, control of variables) so reliability is seen as built in during planning, not judged only at the end.
Model honest uncertainty as good science; false certainty is the weaker response.

Adding repeat readings reveals whether readings cluster or scatter; it does not by itself force individual readings together, so trust is judged from whether repeats are close, not from the mere act of repeating.
Builds on recording complex data and prediction-driven testing; formal systematic-vs-random error analysis is a later (KS3) tier and is not required here.

Ranking/sorting tasks assess recognition and comparison; they do not elicit independent construction of a causal argument, so pair them with tasks that require the learner to state and defend their own calibrated claim.

Static reference scales (e.g. a 'degree of trust' scale annotated with reasons) are useful aids but cannot let the learner vary the evidence and see confidence respond; use them alongside, not instead of, construction tasks.
The trust-meter and causal-claim checker are optional, proposed scaffolds whose efficacy is untested; they are not required for the activity to work.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels a trust-meter interactive as 'ideal' and a static image as 'poor' on the grounds that 'a static image can't let the child vary the evidence.' This is a catalog fit preference; it is retained only as a narrowly scoped observation about manipulability (static scales cannot be varied), not as a claim that a static image cannot teach the concept.
The source's claim that a 3D/spatial artefact 'adds nothing' ('Not spatial') is a catalog ranking and has been omitted rather than asserted as a pedagogical law.
Worked examples (plants, fertiliser doses, light/leaf growth) are illustrative; conclusions about growth depend on actual controlled conditions and are not asserted as established outcomes.
The NGSS SEP source is marked verified:false in the row; treat that citation's status accordingly — it is cited to name the standard, not as evidence of effectiveness.

Statistically, adding repeat readings does not force individual readings to converge; it reveals whether they cluster. Feedback and actions are phrased so learners judge trust from whether repeats are close, avoiding the implication that more repeats mechanically shrink the spread.
Activity 1's sourceClaims support teaching the causal-plus-trust skill named in the standard; they are not evidence that the proposed interactive scaffold is effective, which remains untested.

probeDeeper: How many plants did you test at each dose? Would more change how much you trust the pattern?
Could anything other than fertiliser have made those plants taller? How would you know?
If two plants had grown taller just by chance and the rest were the same, would your conclusion still hold? How do repeats help?
What's the difference between saying 'the data show a pattern' and 'fertiliser causes taller growth'?
assess.correctAnswer: A strong response states the causal conclusion but qualifies the degree of trust: whether the pattern is consistent, whether there were enough plants (sample size) and repeat readings, whether other variables (light, water, soil) were controlled so it was the fertiliser and not something else, and whether any measurements might be off. Confidence grows with a clear, repeated pattern from a controlled test and a decent sample, and stays cautious when data are few or noisy — distinguishing 'the data show a pattern' from 'I'm certain fertiliser caused it'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Result treated as certain proof: 'the plants were taller, so more fertiliser definitely causes taller growth — done.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce degree of trust: how many plants? were readings repeated? were other causes ruled out?
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The conclusion is asserted with no qualification of confidence.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores sample size / single run: draws a confident conclusion from one plant per dose.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss how few data points make a pattern unreliable; more plants and repeats raise trust.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No attention to how many data points or repeats support the pattern.

errorPatterns.pattern: Causal claim without ruling out confounds: asserts fertiliser as the cause without checking other variables were held constant.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link trust to whether the test was fair — only a controlled test lets you attribute the effect to fertiliser.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The causal claim ignores alternative explanations for the taller plants.

responseLevels.gap: Asserts the causal conclusion as certain, with no attention to sample size, repeats, control, or error.
responseLevels.full: Draws the causal conclusion but calibrates trust to the evidence — weighing sample size, repeat readings, whether variables were controlled, and possible errors — and distinguishes an observed pattern from a proven cause.
responseLevels.partial: States a causal conclusion and mentions one trust factor (e.g. 'we should repeat it'), but doesn't coordinate sample size, control of variables, and possible error into an overall judgement of confidence.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You investigated whether plants grow taller with more fertiliser and found taller plants at higher doses. You want to conclude 'more fertiliser causes taller growth.' How confident should you be in that causal conclusion, and what would you need to consider — about your data and your method — before trusting it? Talk it through.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The discriminator is whether the child calibrates trust to the quality of the evidence rather than treating any result as proof. A child with the idea raises sample size, repeats, control of variables, and possible error; one without simply asserts the causal claim with full confidence because the numbers 'went up'.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Seasonal changes — representing weather data

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Working scientifically / Y2–Y3 data handling):** pupils gather, record, classify and present data in a variety of ways (tables, charts, pictograms and bar charts) to help answer questions — here, about typical weather in a season.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-ESS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]. Clarification: data such as average temperature, precipitation and wind direction. Assessment boundary: graphical displays limited to pictographs and bar graphs; does not include climate change.

- **Operational details:** This is a PROCEDURAL, data-representation topic that builds on younger seasonal observation. Give pupils real or realistic seasonal weather data (daily temperatures, rainfall totals, wind direction over a month) and have them ORGANISE it into a table and then a pictograph or bar graph, and READ it to state what weather is TYPICAL for that season ('most autumn days were between 10 and 15°C'; 'summer had far more dry days than winter'). Emphasise the idea of 'typical'/most-common as distinct from any single day, and comparing seasons using the graphs. Keep graphs to pictographs and bar graphs and keep the focus on THIS-place, THIS-season patterns — climate change is explicitly out of scope at this level.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete data handling, upper KS2). The child builds a table and a bar/pictograph from seasonal weather data and reads it to describe the typical conditions of a season, comparing seasons, without inferential statistics or climate-trend reasoning.
bestPractices: Move from raw readings → table → graph so pupils experience organising data, not just reading a finished chart.
Stress 'typical'/most-common for a season as distinct from any single day's weather.
Use the graphs to COMPARE seasons, which makes patterns visible and purposeful.
Keep displays to pictographs and bar graphs and ensure each icon/interval is correctly counted (a common slip).
Keep scope to this place and season; explicitly exclude climate change / long-term trends at this level.
keyRepresentations: A data table of daily seasonal readings (temperature, precipitation, wind).
A bar graph of weather conditions or temperature bands.
A pictograph where one icon represents a fixed count of days.
Side-by-side seasonal graphs for comparison.
A wind-direction tally/rose (simple).
commonMisconceptions: Treating one unusual day as representative of the whole season instead of the typical pattern.
Miscounting pictograph icons (ignoring that one symbol may stand for several days).
Confusing the tallest bar with the answer to every question, regardless of what is asked.
Thinking 'typical' means the single highest or lowest value rather than the most common.
Mixing weather (short-term) with climate/long-term trends, which are out of scope here.

learn.summary: For children aged 8–9, this procedural Earth-science topic teaches pupils to organise seasonal weather data (daily temperature, precipitation, cloud cover and wind direction over a month) into a table, build a pictograph or bar graph from it, and read the display to describe what weather is TYPICAL of a season — comparing seasons as evidence. The emphasis is on experiencing the full raw-readings → table → graph → interpretation procedure, on 'typical/most-common' as distinct from any single day, and on keeping displays to pictographs and bar graphs. Climate change and long-term trends are explicitly out of scope at this level.

activities.title: Weather-data studio: sort, table, graph, describe
feedback: If the learner's axis has uneven steps (e.g. labelling gridlines only with the data values instead of using a fixed interval), revisit equal-interval scaled bar charts and the idea that each gridline step is the same amount — reteach the graphing, not the seasons.
If the learner describes the season from prior knowledge ('summer's hot, everyone knows that'), ask 'show me on your chart' and redirect them to read their own display.
If the learner reads a single extreme day as typical ('it was −6°C one day, so winter is −6°C'), model looking at the most-common range across the whole month rather than one unusual reading.

If a pictograph total is wrong, point out that the key defines how many days one icon represents, so the same key must be applied to every icon when adding up — whether one icon stands for one day or several.

If asked whether three days would give the same confidence as a month, prompt the learner to see that a short run of days could miss the typical pattern, so more readings support a firmer description.
Confirm success when the table is organised, the chart is correctly scaled and labelled, and the typical pattern and seasonal comparison are stated from the display while dismissing a single outlier.
activities.rationale: The target skill is procedural — to organise and represent data and then read it — so the learner should enact the whole sort → table → graph → interpret sequence rather than only read a finished chart. An interactive builder where the graph updates as cards are placed and a prompt asks for the most-common band and a two-season comparison makes the organising work and the 'typical' insight concrete. A live-updating graph, draggable cards, and a built-in icon-count check are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Students represent data in tables and graphical displays (pictographs and bar graphs) [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]; climate change is excluded.
KS2 pupils gather, record, classify and present data in a variety of ways (tables, pictograms, bar charts) to help answer questions.
learnerActions: Start with a month of daily weather cards, each showing a temperature, a rain-or-dry mark, cloud cover and a wind arrow, presented mixed together.
Sort the cards and organise the readings into a data table (temperature, precipitation/cloud cover, wind).

Build a bar graph or pictograph from the table — for a pictograph, first fix what one icon stands for (e.g. one icon = one day, or several days per icon) and then apply that key consistently to every icon when counting totals; for a bar graph, use a uniform equal-interval scale and label the axes.

Read the finished graph to state the typical/most-common condition for the season (e.g. 'most winter days were between 3 and 7°C', or 'this summer had more dry days than this winter' if the graphs show that).
Place two seasons' graphs, drawn with the same scale and the same temperature bands, side by side and compare them, saying how the shapes differ and which season is which.
Point to the specific part of your graph that shows one season is warmer than the other, using the display itself as the evidence.
Decide whether one unusually cold day changes which season the data represents, and explain why the typical pattern across the whole month still identifies the season.
Consider how confident the description would be with only a few days of data versus a full month, and explain why more readings make the typical pattern clearer.
Discuss how the display would look different if rainfall rather than temperature had been measured (e.g. counts of rainy versus dry days), to see that the chosen variable shapes the chart.
Check that the display, not memory of 'summer is hot', is used as the evidence for every statement.
activities.intendedInsight: The shape of an organised graph answers a question the scattered raw cards cannot: the tallest bar or bars, showing the temperature band or bands with the most days, make it obvious what is typical of a season, and placing two graphs drawn on the same scale side by side makes seasonal comparison much easier. 'Typical' means the most-common pattern across the whole month, not a single unusual day, and more days of data make that pattern clearer.

activities.title: Read and compare seasonal weather graphs
feedback: If the learner always picks the tallest bar regardless of the question, re-read the question aloud and ask what it is actually asking for.
If a pictograph is misread, remind them that the key defines how many days one symbol represents and must be applied to every icon.
If 'typical' is read as the single highest or lowest value, redirect to the most-common band.
activities.rationale: Reading displays is squarely assessable with selection-and-matching tasks and matches the standard's read-the-display aim. This recognition-style practice complements, but does not replace, the build-it-yourself studio: selecting answers rehearses and checks reading but does not elicit the learner's own construction of a table and graph from raw data.
sourceClaims: Students represent data in tables and graphical displays (pictographs and bar graphs) [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]; climate change is excluded.
learnerActions: Read a given seasonal bar graph or pictograph and answer what temperature or condition was most typical.
Match each season to its bar graph from a set.
Order a set of seasonal graphs by rainfall, from least to most.
Answer varied questions about the same graph (not only 'which bar is tallest?') so the question asked determines which bar to read.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluently reading pictographs and bar graphs — identifying the most-common condition, matching displays to seasons, and comparing across seasons — is a core part of the standard's goal of using displays to describe typical seasonal weather.

activities.title: Annotated graph walkthrough: the parts of a chart
feedback: If the learner skips the key, highlight it and ask how many days one icon represents.
If axis intervals are overlooked, point to two gridlines and ask what the gap between them is worth.
activities.rationale: An annotated example clarifies chart anatomy and vocabulary. This is a scaffold: it explains the parts of a display but does not itself have the learner build a graph from data, which is the target procedural skill, so it should precede or support the studio task rather than stand in for it.
learnerActions: Explore an annotated bar graph or pictograph, revealing what the axes, bars/icons and key each mean.
Name what one icon stands for in the pictograph's key and how to use it to count a total.
Identify where the scale intervals and labels are, before building a graph of your own.
activities.intendedInsight: A bar chart/pictograph has named parts — axes, scaled intervals, bars or icons, and a key — and understanding each part is a step towards building and reading displays accurately.

constraints: Keep displays to pictographs and bar graphs, per the standard's assessment boundary; do not introduce other chart types at this level.
Keep scope to this-place, this-season patterns; climate change and long-term climate trends are explicitly out of scope and should not be introduced.
Emphasise 'typical'/most-common across the whole month as distinct from any single day's weather; avoid treating one unusual day, or the single highest/lowest value, as representative.
Ensure the pictograph key is fixed first and applied consistently to every icon, and that bar intervals are uniformly scaled — miscounting icons and uneven axis spacing are common slips to watch for.
Do not require inferential statistics or climate-trend reasoning; this is concrete data handling (ages 8–9, lower KS2/Year 4, Tier A–B).
Recognition/selection tasks assess and rehearse reading displays but do not by themselves elicit the learner's independent construction of a table and graph from raw data.
Annotated-example and read-only activities are scaffolds for vocabulary and reading; they do not substitute for building a display from raw data.
A real class weather log is a natural, welcome hands-on data source and complement to any on-screen builder.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels a 2D interactive studio as the ideal format and rates 3D and dialogue formats as 'poor' with claims such as '3D adds no value' and 'dialogue cannot deliver the sort-and-graph task'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been reframed as a scope/affordance note (the task is not spatial and is hands-on procedural) rather than universal claims, and the recognition quiz is kept as a complementary practice, not discarded.

The source states 'static reveals cannot let the child build a graph from data'; retained as the narrower, genuine point that an annotated example does not itself require construction, not as a claim that static images cannot teach.

Self-audit of the worked example: a tall cluster of bars at 3–7°C supporting 'most winter days were cold' is internally consistent; the arithmetic-free interpretive claims (most-common band, more dry days) are reasonable as data-reading, not as climate claims. No numeric errors found in the source to correct.

Data variables differ slightly across the source fields (NGSS clarification: temperature, precipitation, wind direction; objective evidence: temperature, precipitation, cloud cover). Both sets are treated as in-scope seasonal measures; none is asserted as the sole correct set.

probeDeeper: Point to the part of your chart that shows this is the warmer season.
One day here was very cold. Does that change which season this is? Why?
If I gave you just three days instead of a month, could you still tell the season as confidently?
How would your chart look different if you had measured rainfall instead of temperature?
assess.correctAnswer: The child sorts the cards by season, organises them into a table, produces a correctly-scaled and labelled bar chart, and reads it to describe the typical conditions — e.g. 'this season is warmer, most bars are higher; the other has more rainy days' — using the display as the evidence.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uneven scale on the axis — spaces bars by their value rather than a fixed interval ('each bar just goes where its number is')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the graphing — revisit equal-interval scaled bar charts; don't reteach seasons.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Bar heights not on a uniform scale; gridline intervals unequal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Describes the season from prior knowledge, not from the data in front of them ('summer's hot, everyone knows that')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'show me on your chart' — redirect to reading their own display; don't reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers about the season without pointing to the table or chart.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a single extreme day as 'typical' rather than the overall pattern ('it was 3°C one day, so winter is 3°C')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model looking at the most-common range across the whole month rather than one bar.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks an outlier value as the season's typical condition.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot organise the mixed data, or produces a chart with no usable scale or labels.
responseLevels.full: Correctly organises the data into a table, makes a properly scaled and labelled chart, and reads the typical pattern from it — comparing seasons using the data as evidence and dismissing a single outlier.
responseLevels.partial: Builds a table and a chart but with scaling or labelling errors, or reads the season correctly only from memory rather than from the display.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a month of daily weather cards (temperature and rain) for two different seasons, mixed together. Sort them, put each season's data into a table, make a bar chart of the temperatures, then tell me which season is which and how your chart shows it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who can talk about seasons from memory will still produce an unscaled or mislabelled chart, or describe the season without looking at their data. Watching the build separates 'knows the seasons' from 'can represent and read seasonal data' — the actual procedural claim.
