pedagogy.summary: A mixed number (2¾) and an improper fraction (11/4) name the SAME quantity in two forms; converting between them rests on 'how many wholes fit', because b/b = 1 whole. So 11/4 = 8/4 + 3/4 = 2 wholes and 3/4 = 2¾; reversing, 3⅖ = 3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5. It is grounded in iterating unit fractions past the whole (counting quarters past 4/4) and in recognising that b copies of 1/b rebuild one whole.
bestPractices: Build from unit-fraction iteration on a number line or bar — count quarters past 4/4 = 1 whole — so the child SEES wholes forming inside an improper fraction
Make 'b bths = 1 whole' explicit, so 11/4 groups into wholes and 3 wholes = 15 fifths is understood, not memorised
Teach mixed→improper as 'each whole is b bths' (3 wholes × 5 = 15 fifths, add the 2) rather than a bare '× then add' trick; keep the denominator unchanged
Always verify by converting back (17/5 → 3⅖) so the two forms are seen as equal
Treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers, not mistakes to be 'fixed'
keyRepresentations: Number line with unit-fraction jumps continuing past 1 whole
Fraction bars/tiles where b pieces fuse into one whole tile
Area circles showing 11/4 as two full circles plus three quarters
Improper fraction and mixed number marked at the SAME point
commonMisconceptions: Mixed→improper adds the whole to the numerator: 3⅖ → (3+2)/5 = 5/5
Multiplies but forgets to add the numerator (15/5), or concatenates the digits (32/5)
Improper→mixed miscounts the wholes (e.g. 11/4 → 3¾)
Believes an improper fraction is 'not allowed' and must always be written as a mixed number
Changes the denominator during conversion

learn.summary: A mixed number (2¾) and an improper fraction (11/4) name the same quantity in two forms. Converting between them rests on 'how many wholes fit', because b copies of 1/b rebuild one whole (b/b = 1). So 11/4 = 8/4 + 3/4 = 2 wholes and 3/4 = 2¾; reversing, 3⅖ = 3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5. Ground the work in iterating unit fractions past the whole (counting quarters past 4/4) rather than a bare rule, and treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers.

activities.title: Stamp quarters past the whole and watch wholes form
feedback: If a learner writes 3⅖ = 5/5, rebuild the 3 wholes as fifths on the bar: one whole is 5 fifths (not 1), so 3 wholes = 15 fifths, then add the 2 → 17/5.
If a learner writes 15/5, praise the ×b step (three wholes make fifteen fifths) and prompt the missing step: 'now add the two more fifths'.
If a learner writes 32/5, point out that gluing the 3 and 2 together ignores what the digits count; ask how many fifths are in 3 wholes.
If a learner reads 11/4 as 3¾ or subtracts 11 − 4, group the eleven quarters into fours on the bar: two complete groups of four (2 wholes) with three quarters left.

As an alternative representation, show 11/4 as area circles: two fully shaded circles plus three quarters of a third circle give the same 2¾ — another way to see the wholes already sitting inside the improper fraction.
Always close by converting back (17/5 → 3⅖, or 2¾ → 11/4) to confirm the two forms are equal.
activities.rationale: Building from unit-fraction iteration lets the child SEE wholes forming inside an improper fraction, so conversion is understood as regrouping rather than a half-remembered digit trick. Making 'b bths = 1 whole' explicit is intended to target the add-to-numerator error by showing a whole becoming b pieces rather than one.
sourceClaims: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
learnerActions: On a number line marked in quarters, add one quarter at a time, counting aloud: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.
At the 4th quarter, group the four quarters into one whole unit; do the same again at the 8th quarter.
Keep going to the 11th quarter and read off what you have: two whole units with three quarters sitting past them, so 11/4 = 2¾.
Now work the other way for 3⅖: break each of the 3 wholes into fifths (one whole = 5 fifths, so 3 wholes = 15 fifths), then add the 2 extra fifths to get 17/5.
Keep the denominator unchanged throughout, and say the running total in both forms as you go.
activities.intendedInsight: The improper form and the mixed form mark the SAME point: every b copies of 1/b fuse into one whole, and each whole breaks back into b pieces. This is why you multiply 3 × 5 (each whole is 5 fifths) and then add the 2, not add the whole to the numerator.

activities.title: Convert both directions and verify by reversing
feedback: Answers: 11/4 = 2¾ (8/4 = 2 wholes, 3/4 left over); 3⅖ = 17/5 (3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths), denominator unchanged.
If a learner insists 7/4 must become 1¾ to be 'allowed', confirm 7/4 and 1¾ are the same size and that a top-heavy fraction is a legitimate number sitting past 1.
If a learner changes the denominator during conversion, stop and ask what size the pieces are — the piece size (the denominator) does not change, only how they are grouped.
Probe with: 'How many quarters make one whole? So how many quarters are in 2 wholes?' and 'For 3⅖, why work out 3 × 5 before adding the 2 — what does the 15 count?'
activities.rationale: Bidirectional conversion with a built-in reverse-check makes the equality of the two forms explicit (grounded in b copies of 1/b rebuilding a whole) and surfaces the distinct add-to-numerator (5/5), forgot-to-add (15/5), and concatenate (32/5) errors as visibly different wrong answers to diagnose.
sourceClaims: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
learnerActions: Convert 11/4 to a mixed number and 3⅖ to an improper fraction, showing your working for each.
For the improper→mixed task, state how many wholes you found and how many pieces are left over.
For the mixed→improper task, say out loud what the first product counts (e.g. '15 counts the fifths in 3 wholes') before adding the leftover pieces.
Check each answer by converting it back to the other form and confirming you return to where you started.
Also write 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 as both an improper fraction and a whole number (2).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion with a reverse-check confirms the forms are equal and that improper fractions such as 7/4 or 17/5 are valid answers, not mistakes to be 'fixed'.

activities.title: Reveal the wholes hidden inside an improper fraction (support)
feedback: If the learner marks the wrong number of groups, re-count: four quarters per whole, so eleven quarters give two full groups with three left.

This labelled picture is a reference aid; follow it up by actually performing the grouping and the reverse (breaking wholes back into pieces) so the conversion is practised as a reversible action, not only recognised.
activities.rationale: A labelled static bar helps a learner who needs to first SEE the wholes inside 11/4 before enacting the regrouping; it is a stepping stone toward independent conversion. The source supports the underlying content (whole groups sit inside an improper fraction); the scaffold itself is an unvalidated design choice.
sourceClaims: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
learnerActions: Look at a bar showing 11/4 drawn as individual quarters.
Circle or mark off the complete groups of four quarters, naming each group as one whole.
Read what is left after grouping and write the mixed number: 2 wholes + 3 quarters = 2¾.
activities.intendedInsight: An improper fraction already contains whole groups; finding them is a matter of grouping b pieces at a time, with the leftover pieces naming the fraction part.

constraints: Keep the denominator unchanged during conversion — only the grouping of equal-sized pieces changes.
Teach mixed→improper as 'each whole is b bths' (3 wholes × 5 = 15 fifths, then add 2), not as a bare '× then add' trick, so the first product is understood as counting pieces.
Treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers, not errors that must always be rewritten as mixed numbers.

The labelled static-bar activity is a scaffold: it can show and name the wholes inside an improper fraction but does not require the learner to enact the reversible grouping, so pair it with hands-on or line-based conversion.

Multiple-choice or fill-in tasks using the distractors 5/5, 15/5 and 32/5 can surface misconceptions, but watching the learner's working (grouping pieces vs. manipulating digits) is what discriminates understanding from a half-remembered rule; a recognition-only response does not by itself show independent construction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Depth/3D and open-dialogue formats were noted in the source as weak fits for this quantitative, procedural topic; this was retained as a design observation only and not asserted as a universal pedagogical law.

Worked arithmetic was independently checked: 11/4 = 8/4 + 3/4 = 2¾; 3⅖ = 15 fifths + 2 fifths = 17/5; 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 = 2. The distractors 5/5, 15/5, 32/5 are deliberately WRONG answers for diagnosis and must never be presented as correct.
The audible 'click'/'snap' fusing effect from the original recommendation is an optional interaction detail; it is offered as an example of making the grouping concrete, not as a required mechanism.

The area-circle model (two full circles plus three quarters for 11/4) is reinstated from the original key representations as an alternative to the number line/bar; efficacy of any one representation over another is not independently measured here.

The IES/WWC source directly supports the mathematical basis of conversion (b copies of 1/b rebuild one whole; improper fractions as legitimate numbers), not the comparative effectiveness of the specific scaffolds proposed; scaffold choices remain unvalidated.

probeDeeper: How many quarters make one whole? So how many quarters are in 2 whole ones?
For 3⅖, why do we work out 3 × 5 before adding the 2 — what does the 15 count?
Is 7/4 a proper answer, or must it be written as a mixed number? Are 7/4 and 1¾ the same size?
Check your 17/5 by turning it back into a mixed number — what do you get?
assess.correctAnswer: 11/4 = 2¾ (8/4 = 2 wholes, 3/4 left over); 3⅖ = 17/5 (3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5), denominator unchanged.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixed→improper adds the whole number to the numerator: 3⅖ → (3 + 2)/5 = 5/5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild 3 wholes as fifths on the bar: one whole is 5 fifths, not 1, so 3 wholes = 15 fifths. Then add the 2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 5/5 (or 5 over 5) for 3⅖; adds 3 + 2

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the whole by the denominator but forgets to add the numerator (15/5), or concatenates the digits (32/5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two steps ('three wholes make fifteen fifths… now add the two more fifths'); the method is nearly there — do not reteach the concept.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 15/5 (dropped the +2) or 32/5 (glued 3 and 2); the × b step is present but the +a step is missing or mis-executed

errorPatterns.pattern: Improper→mixed miscounts the wholes: 11/4 → 3¾, or subtracts (11 − 4) to get the numerator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Group the eleven quarters into fours on the bar: two complete groups (2 wholes) with three quarters left.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports the wrong number of wholes, or manipulates 11 and 4 by subtracting rather than grouping into fours

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes an improper fraction is 'not allowed' — calls 11/4 a mistake or insists everything must be written as a mixed number
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iterate unit fractions past the whole on a number line to show 11/4 is a real, legitimate number that simply sits past 1.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a top-heavy fraction is wrong, or refuses to accept 17/5 as a valid answer

responseLevels.gap: Adds the whole to the numerator or miscounts the wholes; treats improper fractions as invalid; changes the denominator.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions fluently, explains each step from b/b = 1 whole, verifies by converting back, and accepts improper fractions as legitimate numbers; transfers to a new pair.
responseLevels.partial: Converts one direction reliably but stumbles on the other, or reaches the answer by a rule without being able to explain the × b step as 'each whole is b bths'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Convert 11/4 into a mixed number, and convert 3⅖ into an improper fraction. Show me how you work each one out.' Watch the method for each — do not tell them a rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the working shows whether the child groups b bths into wholes (understanding) or manipulates digits by a half-remembered rule. 3⅖ is the hinge for mixed→improper: adding the whole to the numerator gives 5/5, multiplying but forgetting to add gives 15/5, concatenating gives 32/5 — three visibly different wrong answers — while a secure child gets 17/5 and can say why (3 wholes = 15 fifths). The 11/4 direction checks whether they count the wholes correctly.

sources.claim: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction (Recommendation 1, unit-fraction iteration and fractions on the number line)

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, problem solving grows from single-step sense-making into planning a pathway through a two-step or more complex problem: the child, with teacher guidance, identifies what is known and what must be found, decides which information is relevant, chooses and sequences operations, and checks the answer for reasonableness. Two documented habits work against this. First, keyword/number-grabbing: choosing an operation from a cue word or simply using every number present, ignoring which information is relevant. Second, the compulsion to calculate: rushing to an answer without an estimate or sense-check. The most effective supports are teacher-modelled self-questioning (strong evidence) and teaching children to build visual representations — strip/bar diagrams — that map the relevant quantities and reveal the sequence of steps (strong evidence).
bestPractices: Model self-questioning aloud and give a short prompt list: 'What do I know? What must I find? What shall I do first?' (WWC Rec 2, strong evidence)
Teach children to build their OWN visual representation (bar/strip diagram) that maps knowns to the unknown — building it beats being handed one (WWC Rec 3, strong evidence)
Use the representation to keep the WHOLE multi-step situation visible so the child does not stop after step one
Include problems with an irrelevant number so 'identify relevant information' is actually exercised, not assumed
Estimate first to set a reasonableness benchmark, then compute, then ask 'does this make sense?' and check by a different method
Encourage strategy-switching: if the first approach stalls, represent it a different way rather than abandoning — name this as normal
keyRepresentations: Bar / strip diagram mapping known parts to the unknown
Part-part-whole and comparison ('more than') structures
Number line for two-step jumps
Numberless staged reveal to build relationships before numbers appear
A prompt list / four-move frame: understand → plan → solve → check
commonMisconceptions: Answering only the first step of a two-step problem (treating multi-step as single-step)
Using every number in the problem, including an irrelevant one, because 'they must all be needed'
Choosing the operation from a cue word rather than the problem's structure
Computing an answer and stopping, with no estimate or reasonableness check (compulsion to calculate)

learn.summary: For 6-7 year olds, help children plan a pathway through two-step and more complex word problems: identify what is known and what must be found, decide which information is relevant (setting aside any red-herring number), choose and sequence operations, estimate first, and check the answer for reasonableness. Two documented habits work against this: keyword/number-grabbing (choosing an operation from a cue word or using every number present) and the compulsion to calculate (rushing to an answer with no estimate or sense-check). The strongest supports in the sources are teacher-modelled self-questioning and children building their OWN visual representations (strip/bar diagrams, or a number line for two-step jumps) that map relevant quantities and reveal the sequence of steps. Several activities below address the same objective through different media (a build-your-own workspace, a planning dialogue, a worked-example companion, and a reasonableness-judgement item); keep more than one because they exercise construction, talk, and recognition respectively.

activities.title: Build-your-own 'plan-it' workspace with a red herring and an estimate-first step
feedback: When the computed answer strays far from the estimate, flag it with a reasonableness gauge and invite a re-check by a different method rather than supplying the answer.
If the child incorporates the irrelevant number, prompt: 'Which numbers do you actually need here, and which one can you ignore? Why?'

On a genuinely two-step problem (e.g. two successive departures), if the child gives the intermediate result (16) as the final answer, keep both parts of the representation visible and ask 'Have we answered what it asked?'
activities.rationale: Building and using one's own visual representation that maps problem quantities, and modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine, are both reported as strong-evidence levers; estimating and checking by a different method and planning before jumping in are part of proficient problem solving. An estimate slider, draggable bar-model or number-line canvas, staged reveal, and a reasonableness gauge are concrete examples of these mechanisms, not mandatory implementations.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to build and use their own visual representations (e.g. strip/schematic diagrams) that map problem quantities has strong evidence of improving problem solving; modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine also has strong evidence.

The 'compulsion to calculate' — rushing to compute rather than reasoning about knowns and unknowns — undermines problem solving; teachers should push back by focusing on relationships before computing and using numberless word problems.

Proficient solvers analyse givens, constraints and goals, plan a solution pathway rather than jumping in, monitor and change course if necessary, and check answers with a different method asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Meet a problem revealed a piece at a time: first the story, then the question, then the numbers (a staged, numberless-to-numbered reveal).
Build your OWN representation by dragging parts onto a canvas to map the known parts to the unknown — a bar/strip diagram, or a number line to show the jumps — rather than using a pre-made diagram.

Identify and physically set aside the irrelevant number. For example, in 'There are 24 children and 3 teachers; 8 children go home. How many children are left?' the 3 teachers are not needed (this one is a single step, 24 − 8 = 16, chosen to practise spotting a red herring).

Practise the sequencing on a genuinely two-step version, e.g. '8 children go home in the morning and 6 more go home at lunch; how many are left?' — here finding 16 is only step one (24 − 8), and 10 is the answer (16 − 6).
Before computing, set an estimate ('about how big will the answer be?') to create a reasonableness benchmark.

Compute, then compare the answer to your own estimate; when the answer lands far from the estimate, re-check — did you stop after step one, use the spare number, or (in problems where order matters) do the steps in the wrong order?
Return to the still-visible model to complete or fix the second step.
activities.intendedInsight: Planning, relevance-sorting, and self-checking become things the child does and watches on a live representation, rather than rules they are told. Keeping the whole situation visible helps the child notice when they have stopped after step one on multi-step problems, and comparing to a self-made estimate can make an unreasonable answer stand out.

activities.title: Planning dialogue with a 'detective partner' that models self-questioning
feedback: The partner helps plan a pathway without giving the steps away, and explicitly asks which information is a red herring.
If the child stalls, the partner suggests representing the problem a different way and names strategy-switching as normal, not failure.
Always prompt an estimate before computing and a 'does this make sense?' check at the end.
activities.rationale: Modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine has strong evidence, and proficient solvers plan a pathway, monitor, and check with a different method; a conversational partner can rehearse exactly this talk. Dialogue is one route to the routine; it does not replace the child building their own representation.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to build and use their own visual representations (e.g. strip/schematic diagrams) that map problem quantities has strong evidence of improving problem solving; modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine also has strong evidence.

Proficient solvers analyse givens, constraints and goals, plan a solution pathway rather than jumping in, monitor and change course if necessary, and check answers with a different method asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Work with an in-role partner who models self-questioning aloud and asks you to answer: 'What do I know? What must I find? What shall I do first? Does that make sense?'
Say which information is needed and which is a red herring, and justify your plan aloud before computing.
Before computing, estimate ('about how big should the answer be?'), then close every problem by sense-checking the result against that estimate.
When your first approach stalls, try 'let's show it another way' — represent the problem differently (for example, swap a bar model for a number line) rather than abandoning it.
activities.intendedInsight: Rehearsing the monitoring routine in talk — planning the pathway, naming relevant versus irrelevant information, and sense-checking — builds the habit of reasoning about structure before numbers.

activities.title: Worked-example companion: reveal a good solver's self-questions and why a number was ignored
feedback: Each revealed phase names the self-question and the reason, not just the arithmetic step.
Follow with a problem the child plans themselves so the worked example is a model, not the whole task.
activities.rationale: A worked example can make the self-questioning and relevance-sorting frame visible. This is a scaffold: because the child watches rather than plans, it must be paired with the child doing their own planning and representation to build the skill; recognition of a good solver's moves does not by itself elicit the child's own production.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to build and use their own visual representations (e.g. strip/schematic diagrams) that map problem quantities has strong evidence of improving problem solving; modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine also has strong evidence.
learnerActions: Work through a tap-to-reveal worked two-step problem, uncovering each phase: understand → plan → solve → check.
At each phase, reveal the self-question a good solver asks and why the irrelevant number was ignored.
After viewing, retell the plan in your own words and then try a fresh problem where YOU do the planning and relevance-sorting.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the plan-then-check frame and the reasoning for discarding a spare number makes the usually-invisible monitoring moves explicit before the child performs them independently.

activities.title: 'Which answer is unreasonable, and why?' judgement item
feedback: Credit the reasoning ('smaller than the start because some left'), not just the verdict.
If the child cannot say why, prompt an estimate first: 'About how big should it be?'
activities.rationale: A reasonableness-judgement item targets the 'does this make sense?' check. A recognition/judgement format can be used during teaching to surface reasoning, but on its own it does not elicit the child's independent planning or construction of a representation, so use it sparingly and avoid a battery of two-step sums.
sourceClaims: Proficient solvers analyse givens, constraints and goals, plan a solution pathway rather than jumping in, monitor and change course if necessary, and check answers with a different method asking 'Does this make sense?'.

The 'compulsion to calculate' — rushing to compute rather than reasoning about knowns and unknowns — undermines problem solving; teachers should push back by focusing on relationships before computing and using numberless word problems.
learnerActions: Read a 'take away' story and an offered answer that is larger than the starting amount.
Decide whether the answer is reasonable, and explain WHY using the situation (e.g. 'fewer than 24 should be left because some children went home').
Where possible, state roughly how big the answer should be before judging it.
activities.intendedInsight: Judging reasonableness against the situation — not re-computing — rehearses the estimate-and-sense-check habit and can surface the compulsion-to-calculate pattern.

activities.title: Replace keyword cues with problem-structure reasoning
feedback: If the child picks an operation from a word, ask them to retell the situation and build the strip diagram first.
Discuss explicitly why a cue word pointed the wrong way in the trap problem.
activities.rationale: The keyword strategy ties a word to an operation without understanding the text and is unreliable because keywords are not exclusive to one operation; teaching problem structure (schema) is the recommended replacement.
sourceClaims: The keyword strategy ties a word to an operation without understanding the text and should be replaced by teaching problem structure (schema); it is unreliable because keywords are not exclusive to one operation.

Teaching students to build and use their own visual representations (e.g. strip/schematic diagrams) that map problem quantities has strong evidence of improving problem solving; modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine also has strong evidence.
learnerActions: Retell a word problem in your own words before touching any numbers.
Decide the operation from the problem's structure (part-part-whole, comparison/'more than', two-step change), not from a cue word.
Map the relevant quantities onto a part-part-whole or comparison bar so the structure, not a keyword, drives the plan.
Test a trap problem where a 'more than' phrase does not mean 'add', to see that keywords are unreliable.
activities.intendedInsight: Keywords are not tied to one operation; reasoning from the problem's structure (schema) is more reliable than grabbing an operation from a cue word.

constraints: This is guided problem solving: at 6-7 the teacher scaffolds by modelling self-questioning and keeping the whole situation visible; holding both steps of a two-step problem in mind is still emerging.
Include at least one irrelevant number so 'identify relevant information' is actually exercised, not assumed.

When illustrating multi-step work and stop-after-step-one, use a genuinely two-step problem (two operations); a single-operation problem with a distractor exercises relevance-sorting but not step sequencing.
Build-your-own representations are the target; being handed a pre-made diagram or watching a worked example are scaffolds and must be followed by the child planning and building independently.
Avoid teaching keyword rules; reason from problem structure instead.

Scoring final answers rewards fast computing and does not assess planning, relevance-sorting, or reasonableness reasoning. A reasonableness-judgement item can be used during teaching, but a battery of two-step sums should be avoided and recognition-only items do not elicit independent construction of a plan or representation.
When a child solves only the first step, do not simply supply step two or drill two-step sums; keep both parts represented and ask 'have we answered what it asked?'
When a child computes with no check, make an estimate the opening move and 'does this make sense?' the closing move, and check by a different method.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row's canonical example ('24 children, 3 teachers, 8 go home → 16 left') is labelled a two-step problem but is a single operation (24 − 8) with a distractor. It is retained to practise relevance-sorting, and a genuinely two-step variant (two successive departures, 24 − 8 − 6 = 10) was added so the stop-after-step-one feedback is coherent.

Worked arithmetic check: 24 − 8 = 16; in the two-step variant 16 − 6 = 10; both results are less than 24, consistent with 'some went home'. The original framing 'a bit less than 24' is a loose estimate; the essential reasonableness check is 'fewer than 24'.

The carpenter counterexample (4 planks, each 1 metre, how many half-metre pieces) correctly yields 8 pieces (4 metres ÷ 0.5 m); it is intended to test situation reasoning versus number-combining, so keep it as a discussion probe, not a scored item.

Worked-example and reasonableness-judgement items were reframed from the legacy 'quiz/interactive-image can only assess' phrasing to narrow objective limits: a recognition or judgement format can support teaching but does not on its own elicit independent planning; no comparative-efficacy claim is asserted beyond the cited sources.

The legacy '3-D adds nothing / no pedagogical return' claim was dropped as catalog boilerplate rather than migrated as a universal law; planning a pathway is simply not a spatial task, so a 3-D manipulative is not indicated here, but no universal necessity claim is made.

The number line for two-step jumps was reinstated as an explicit alternative representation in the workspace and dialogue activities, since it is a distinct keyRepresentation and objective evidence point in the original row.
The WWC strong-evidence claims are drawn from a Grades 4-8 guide; applying them to 6-7 year olds is a research-informed extension not directly evidenced for this age band.

probeDeeper: 'Which numbers do you actually need here, and which one can you ignore? Why?' (forces relevance reasoning)
'You found 16 after one step — have we answered the whole question yet?' (surfaces the stop-after-step-one signature)
'About how big should the answer be, before you work it out exactly?' (estimate as a reasonableness benchmark)
Counterexample: 'A carpenter has 4 planks. Each is a metre long. How many half-metre pieces can she cut?' — does the child reason about the situation, or just combine the numbers?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who identifies the relevant numbers (24 and 8) and sets aside the 3 teachers as not needed, plans a pathway (start with 24, take away 8), estimates it will be 'a bit less than 24', gets 16, and checks it makes sense (fewer than 24 because some went home). The planning, relevance-sorting and reasonableness talk are the targets, not the subtraction itself.

errorPatterns.pattern: Solves only the first step of a two-step problem — stops once one operation is done, treating the multi-step problem as single-step.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT simply supply step two or drill two-step sums. Keep the whole situation represented (a bar model showing both parts) so the unfinished second step stays visible; ask 'have we answered what it asked?' It consolidates with guided exposure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a two-step problem the child produces the intermediate result as the final answer and is satisfied; holding both steps in mind is still emerging at this age.

errorPatterns.pattern: Number-grabbing / keyword: uses every number given (including an irrelevant one) or picks an operation from a cue word, rather than reasoning about which information is relevant.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child retell the situation and build their own strip diagram, mapping only the relevant quantities; discuss why the spare number is not needed. Avoid keyword rules.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child incorporates the 3 teachers into the calculation, or chooses add/subtract from a word, ignoring the situation's structure.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compulsion to calculate: computes and stops with no estimate or reasonableness check, accepting an answer even when it is clearly too big or too small.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make estimate-first routine ('about how big?') and 'does this make sense?' the closing move; check by a different method. Help the child notice the feeling of an answer not adding up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives an answer larger than the starting amount for a 'take away' story and is untroubled; offers no estimate.

responseLevels.gap: Uses all numbers or a cue word; computes with no estimate; answers only the first step or accepts an unreasonable answer without noticing.
responseLevels.full: Plans the pathway explicitly, sets aside the irrelevant number with a reason, estimates the answer's size, completes both steps, and uses the estimate/situation to confirm reasonableness — then transfers the same routine to a new problem unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Can list the plan and, when prompted, identify the relevant numbers or estimate — but does the steps in sequence without connecting them: does not spontaneously use the estimate to catch an error or notice an unfinished second step unless asked.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a two-step problem within 100 that contains one irrelevant number, e.g. 'There are 24 children and 3 teachers. 8 children go home. How many children are left?' Before any answer ask: 'How do you decide what to do first? Which numbers do you actually need? Show me your plan.' Then: 'About how big should the answer be — and once you have it, how would you know it makes sense?' Discuss the thinking; do not mark the number right or wrong.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A guided planner reasons about STRUCTURE before numbers: they say what must be found, ignore the irrelevant 3, and can justify roughly how big the answer should be. A child running on keyword/number-grabbing uses all three numbers (or picks an operation from a word) and computes with no estimate; a child who treats multi-step as single-step answers only the first sub-step. The tells are in relevance-sorting and the reasonableness benchmark, not the arithmetic.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 13–14 years

- **Topic:** Predicting Inherited Traits — how alleles are inherited in sexual reproduction, using Punnett squares to predict offspring probabilities, including dominant and recessive alleles

- **Standards — UK (DfE Key Stage 3, Biology — Inheritance, chromosomes, DNA and genes):** heredity as the process by which genetic information is transmitted from one generation to the next. (Formal Punnett-square/allele work is developed at GCSE/KS4; at KS3 this is an introductory bridge — so NGSS MS-LS3 is the primary anchor.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS3-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS3-1, MS-LS3-2] — grounding the probabilistic inheritance of alleles.

- **Operational details:** This is the most PROCEDURAL node in the spine: pupils must both understand the biology and execute the Punnett-square method reliably. Build the vocabulary scaffold first and keep the layers distinct: GENE (a unit of heredity) → ALLELE (a version of that gene) → GENOTYPE (the allele pair an individual carries, e.g. Bb) → PHENOTYPE (the observable characteristic that genotype produces). Teach dominant (expressed whenever present, one copy is enough) vs recessive (only expressed when both alleles are recessive) with a concrete trait. Then the procedure: identify each parent's genotype, split into single-allele gametes down the side and top of the 2×2 grid, fill the four cells by combination, and read off genotype and phenotype RATIOS as probabilities (e.g. Bb × Bb → 3:1 dominant:recessive phenotype; 1:2:1 genotype). The load-bearing conceptual points: (a) offspring get ONE allele from each parent at random — this is why sexual reproduction generates variation; (b) the square gives PROBABILITIES over many offspring, not a guarantee for any one; (c) a recessive allele can be carried unseen and reappear. Anchor with a real human dominant/recessive example handled sensitively.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/procedural-quantitative). Pupils execute a multi-step algorithm and interpret ratios as probabilities — genuinely abstract-symbolic work. Success = allele/dominant/recessive defined, a correct monohybrid Punnett square with ratio calculated, genotype vs phenotype distinguished, and a named human example.
bestPractices: Build the vocabulary ladder explicitly — gene → allele → genotype → phenotype — before running any cross, since confusion here derails the whole procedure.
Model the Punnett method as a fixed algorithm (parent genotypes → gametes on the headers → fill cells → read ratio) and have pupils narrate each step.
Interpret outputs as PROBABILITIES over many offspring, explicitly warning that a 3:1 ratio does not guarantee outcomes in a small family.
Use the carrier idea to explain why a recessive trait can skip a generation and reappear — a common source of family-genetics puzzlement.
Choose real human dominant/recessive examples carefully and handle sensitively, avoiding stigmatising conditions.
Connect back to why sexual reproduction generates variation: each offspring draws one allele at random from each parent.
keyRepresentations: The 2×2 Punnett square with gamete headers and four combination cells
The gene→allele→genotype→phenotype ladder
Colour-coded genotype→phenotype key (e.g. BB and Bb both brown; bb blue)
A carrier diagram showing a hidden recessive allele passed on and resurfacing
A large-sample tally showing the 3:1 phenotype ratio emerging as probability
commonMisconceptions: Confusing genotype (the alleles carried) with phenotype (the trait expressed) — e.g. thinking Bb looks different from BB.
Reading the ratio as a guarantee ('3:1 means exactly 3 of every 4 children'), rather than a probability over many offspring.
Thinking a dominant allele is 'stronger', 'better', or more common in a population, rather than simply expressed when present.
Believing a recessive trait must appear every generation, missing that it can be carried unseen by heterozygotes.
Assuming each child's outcome depends on the siblings' outcomes, rather than each being an independent draw.
Mixing up which alleles are gametes — putting genotypes rather than single alleles on the square's headers.

learn.summary: Learners aged 13–14 learn to predict inherited traits: defining allele, dominant and recessive; building a monohybrid Punnett square; distinguishing genotype from phenotype; and interpreting the resulting ratios as probabilities over many offspring, not guarantees for any one child. The vocabulary ladder (gene → allele → genotype → phenotype) is built first, then the procedure, anchored to a sensitively handled human example and connected to why sexual reproduction generates variation.

activities.title: Build the vocabulary ladder, then run a cross
feedback: If a learner puts a whole genotype (Bb) on a header, point out that each parent contributes only ONE allele per offspring, so headers carry single alleles; the pair reappears only inside the cell.
If a learner says Bb looks different from BB, revisit the colour key: both express the dominant brown phenotype, so genotype and phenotype are not the same thing.
If a learner calls the dominant allele 'stronger' or 'more common', clarify that dominance only describes which version is expressed when both are present — rare alleles can be dominant.
activities.rationale: Confusion in the gene→allele→genotype→phenotype vocabulary derails the whole procedure, so it is built explicitly first; modelling the cross as a narrated fixed algorithm supports reliable execution. Punnett squares are an endorsed model for gene transmission at this level.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-LS3-2 (exact wording): '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS3-1, MS-LS3-2].' Its clarification statement explicitly endorses 'Punnett squares, diagrams, and simulations' as models for gene transmission, and DCI LS3.B states each parent contributes half of the genes acquired at random by the offspring — directly authorising Punnett-square modelling at this level.
A monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes (Bb × Bb) yields a 3:1 dominant:recessive phenotype ratio and a 1:2:1 genotype ratio, interpreted as probabilities over many offspring.
learnerActions: Lay out the four terms as a ladder before touching a grid: gene (a unit of heredity) → allele (a version of that gene, e.g. B or b) → genotype (the allele pair carried, e.g. Bb) → phenotype (the observable trait, e.g. brown eyes).
State a dominant/recessive rule for a chosen trait: a dominant allele is expressed whenever present (one copy is enough); a recessive allele is expressed only when both alleles are recessive.

For a cross such as Bb × Bb, write each parent's genotype, then split each into single-allele gametes placed on the top and the side headers of a 2×2 grid — headers hold single alleles, never full genotypes.
Fill the four cells by combining the header alleles: BB, Bb, Bb, bb.

Read off the genotype ratio (1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb) and the phenotype ratio (3 dominant : 1 recessive), and colour or label each cell by its expressed trait so genotype→phenotype is visible (BB and Bb both brown; bb blue). Treat eye colour here as a simplified single-gene teaching model — real human eye colour is polygenic — so use it to show the mechanic, not as a literal complete account.
activities.intendedInsight: The Punnett square is a fixed procedure: identify parent genotypes, place single-allele gametes on the headers, fill cells by combination, and read genotype and phenotype ratios. Genotype (alleles carried) and phenotype (trait shown) are distinct — Bb and BB share a phenotype but differ in genotype.

activities.title: Ratios as probabilities: sample many offspring
feedback: If a learner says the fourth child is 'due' to be affected to balance a 3:1 ratio, reframe: the ratio is an expected proportion over many births, and a fresh pair of alleles (one from each parent) is drawn at random each pregnancy — the fourth child still has a 3-in-4 chance of being unaffected.

If a learner expects exactly 5 affected out of 20 children (treating the 1-in-4 as a guaranteed count), stress that expected proportions — about 5 affected and 15 unaffected — are not fixed quotas; real small samples scatter around the expectation.

If a learner thinks a recessive trait must appear every generation, use a carrier diagram: two heterozygotes can each carry an unseen recessive allele that resurfaces only when both are passed to the same child.
activities.rationale: The ratio-as-certainty/gambler's-fallacy error and the 'recessive disappears' error are high-frequency; sampling many offspring makes the probabilistic meaning and independence concrete rather than asserted. Interpreting outputs as probabilities over many offspring is the load-bearing conceptual point.
sourceClaims: A monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes (Bb × Bb) yields a 3:1 dominant:recessive phenotype ratio and a 1:2:1 genotype ratio, interpreted as probabilities over many offspring.

NGSS MS-LS3-2 (exact wording): '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS3-1, MS-LS3-2].' Its clarification statement explicitly endorses 'Punnett squares, diagrams, and simulations' as models for gene transmission, and DCI LS3.B states each parent contributes half of the genes acquired at random by the offspring — directly authorising Punnett-square modelling at this level.
learnerActions: After computing the 3:1 phenotype ratio for Bb × Bb, predict what a family of just four children might actually look like.

Simulate or tally many offspring (for example 100 crosses), recording each outcome by independently drawing one allele from each parent at random, and watch the phenotype tally settle near 3 brown : 1 blue.

Also run several small samples of four offspring and check whether any produce no recessive-phenotype child at all. This is quite likely: each family of four has about a 32% chance, since (3/4)^4 ≈ 0.32, even though the long-run proportion is 1 in 4.

Explain, for two carriers (Bb × Bb) who already have three unaffected children and expect a fourth, why the fourth child still has a 1-in-4 chance of being affected — each pregnancy is an independent draw with no memory of earlier children.
activities.intendedInsight: A Punnett square predicts expected PROPORTIONS over many offspring, not a guaranteed quota for a small family. Each offspring is an independent event, so earlier children do not change the next child's probability. This also shows why drawing one allele at random from each parent generates variation in sexual reproduction.

activities.title: Carriers and a real human example
feedback: If a learner says a healthy parent cannot carry a condition, point to the carrier's genotype (Bb): the recessive allele is present and passed on, not lost, even though the phenotype looks unaffected.
If a conversation drifts into stigmatising language about a condition, redirect to neutral, accurate description of inheritance and probability.

If a learner treats the counsellor dialogue as the whole method, remind them the dialogue can explain meaning while building and reading the Punnett square is what generates the prediction — the conversation supplements, it does not replace, the procedure.
activities.rationale: The carrier idea resolves a common family-genetics puzzle and directly targets the genotype=phenotype misconception; a human anchor is required by the objective and must be handled sensitively. A spoken/role-play discussion may support the probability nuance but narrates rather than trains the square-building procedure, so it supplements rather than replaces it.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should learn heredity as the process by which genetic information is transmitted from one generation to the next (formal allele/Punnett work develops at GCSE).
learnerActions: Use a carrier diagram to trace a hidden recessive allele: two brown-eyed parents (both Bb) who produce a blue-eyed (bb) child because each passed on their hidden b. (Treat eye colour here as a simplified single-gene teaching model — real human eye colour is polygenic — so use it to illustrate carriers, not as a literal complete account.)
Explain in words how a recessive trait can skip a generation and reappear, and why a healthy-looking parent can still carry a condition's allele.
Name a human characteristic controlled by dominant/recessive alleles, chosen and discussed sensitively, and state the genotype(s) that would and would not show the trait.
Optionally, discuss with a role-play genetic counsellor what 'a 1-in-4 chance' means for a family — to rehearse the probability nuance in plain language.
activities.intendedInsight: A recessive allele can be carried unseen by a heterozygote and reappear in a later generation; carrier status is about genotype, not visible phenotype. Real examples ground the abstract procedure in heredity that runs in families.

activities.title: Check and apply the procedure
feedback: Illustrations can be playful, but every genotype, cell and ratio must be arithmetically exact — check the four cells before reading a ratio.

If a learner produces a procedure without meaning (builds the square and states 1-in-4 but says the four children must 'even out'), send them back to the many-offspring sampling to recover the independence idea.
Reward transfer: a correct ratio on a new cross with a probability interpretation shows the method is understood as a probability tool, not a rote grid.
activities.rationale: Construction, ratio reading, genotype↔phenotype matching and probability estimation map directly onto the stated evidence and let misconceptions surface for reteaching. Recognition-style checks assess the procedure and vocabulary but do not by themselves require independent construction, so include tasks where the learner builds and transfers a cross.
learnerActions: Complete partially-filled Punnett cells for a given cross and verify the four genotypes.
Read a completed square to state the phenotype ratio (e.g. identify 3:1) and justify it from the cells.
Match each genotype to its phenotype using the dominance rule (BB→brown, Bb→brown, bb→blue), remembering eye colour is used as a simplified single-gene model.
Estimate the probability that two carriers (Bb × Bb) have a child showing the recessive phenotype, and justify the 1-in-4 figure.
Transfer the method to a new, unseen cross and interpret its ratio as a probability.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent learners can both execute the square correctly AND interpret its ratios as probabilities, distinguishing genotype from phenotype and separating dominance from frequency across novel crosses.

constraints: Build the gene→allele→genotype→phenotype vocabulary before running any cross; confusion here derails the procedure.
Headers of the 2×2 grid carry single-allele gametes, not whole genotypes — this is a frequent error to pre-empt.

Always interpret the 3:1 (and 1:2:1) outputs as expected proportions over many offspring; never present them as a guaranteed quota for a small family, and stress each birth is an independent event (e.g. 20 children gives ~5 affected / 15 unaffected expected, not an exact count).

Choose human dominant/recessive examples carefully and handle sensitively, avoiding stigmatising conditions; where eye colour is used, flag it at first use as a simplified single-gene model since real eye colour is polygenic.

Recognition and fill-in tasks assess the procedure and vocabulary; include at least one task where the learner independently builds and transfers a cross, since recognition alone does not elicit independent construction.
A role-play counsellor conversation may support probability meaning but narrates rather than trains the procedure; keep it supplementary to actual square-building.

Live/simulated many-offspring sampling (e.g. a 'run 100 crosses' control, auto-populating gamete headers, live ratio tallies, colour-by-phenotype panels, carrier-reveal) are optional interaction examples that may make the probability mechanism concrete; they are helpful but not mandatory, and no medium is established as uniquely able to teach this.
At KS3 this is an introductory bridge; formal allele/Punnett work is developed at GCSE/KS4, so pitch depth accordingly.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One cited source (Khan Academy monohybrid 3:1 / 1:2:1 claim) was marked unverified in the source row; the 3:1 phenotype and 1:2:1 genotype ratios are standard Mendelian results and are used here, but the citation's verification status is unconfirmed.

The original material at times implied an interactive builder is uniquely able to teach the probabilistic insight and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been reframed as optional interaction examples rather than requirements.
Arithmetic for the 20-children case: at a 1-in-4 chance the expected affected count is ~5 (and ~15 unaffected); any claim of ~15 affected would be an inversion and is not used.

Brown/blue eye colour is retained as the single-gene illustration (matching the original colour key) but real human eye colour is polygenic; it is flagged in-activity from first use as a simplified teaching model rather than silently reproduced as an exact monohybrid trait.

Activity 4's assessment-design rationale (recognition does not elicit independent construction) is not directly supported by any cited source claim, so its sourceClaims is left empty rather than over-attributed to the ratio citation.

Self-audit: Bb × Bb genotypes BB, Bb, Bb, bb give genotype ratio 1:2:1 and phenotype ratio 3:1; the carrier scenario's 1-in-4 affected per independent birth is internally consistent, and no 'due to be affected' reasoning is presented as valid in any activity.

probeDeeper: If they went on to have twenty children, what would you expect, and would it be exactly fifteen healthy and five affected?
Both parents look perfectly healthy — how can their child have a condition neither parent shows?
Does 'dominant' mean the allele is more common in the population? How could you check?
assess.correctAnswer: No. Each child is an independent event: for every pregnancy the chance is 1 in 4, regardless of the earlier children. The 1-in-4 is the expected proportion over many offspring, not a quota that has to be filled. The fourth child still has a 3-in-4 chance of being unaffected.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ratio as certainty / gambler's fallacy — '3:1 must come out exactly, so the next one is due'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe the ratio as expected proportion over many, and stress independence: the alleles combine afresh each pregnancy with no memory of previous children.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the ratio is 3:1, so after three healthy children the fourth must have the condition.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the fourth child must be affected to make the ratio balance

errorPatterns.pattern: Dominant means stronger or more common
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate dominance from frequency and strength: dominance is only about which version is expressed when both are present; rare alleles can be dominant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains dominance as the allele being physically stronger or more frequent in the population, rather than as the allele whose phenotype shows in a heterozygote

errorPatterns.pattern: Genotype = phenotype / recessive allele disappears when masked
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the two: a carrier's genotype (Bb) includes the recessive allele even though the phenotype looks unaffected; the allele is passed on, not lost.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a healthy-looking parent can't be carrying the condition, or uses genotype and phenotype interchangeably

responseLevels.gap: Says the fourth child is 'due' to be affected; treats the ratio as a fixed quota or conflates genotype with phenotype.
responseLevels.full: Treats each offspring as independent with a constant 1-in-4 expectation, explains the ratio as an expected proportion over many, distinguishes genotype from phenotype (carriers), separates dominance from allele frequency, and transfers to a new cross.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly builds the Punnett square and states 1-in-4, but still implies the outcome must even out over four, or can't explain genotype vs phenotype or why dominance isn't strength; has the procedure without the probability meaning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two parents who each carry one allele for a recessive condition (both Bb) already have three healthy children and are expecting a fourth. A student says: 'The Punnett square shows a 1-in-4 chance, and they've already had three healthy ones, so this fourth child is bound to have the condition.' Is that right? Explain what the 1-in-4 actually means.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands probability treats each birth as independent and rejects the 'due for it' reasoning. A child with the common ratio-as-certainty (gambler's fallacy) idea says the fourth child must be affected — opposite answers, and the misconception is high-frequency, so the wrong reasoner reliably takes the distractor.

sources.claim: NGSS MS-LS3-2 (exact wording): '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS3-1, MS-LS3-2].' Its clarification statement explicitly endorses 'Punnett squares, diagrams, and simulations' as models for gene transmission, and DCI LS3.B states each parent contributes half of the genes acquired at random by the offspring — directly authorising Punnett-square modelling at this level.
sources.source: NGSS / Next Generation Science Standards, [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS3-1, MS-LS3-2]

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should learn heredity as the process by which genetic information is transmitted from one generation to the next (formal allele/Punnett work develops at GCSE).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (Key Stage 3, Biology — Inheritance, chromosomes, DNA and genes)

sources.claim: A monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes (Bb × Bb) yields a 3:1 dominant:recessive phenotype ratio and a 1:2:1 genotype ratio, interpreted as probabilities over many offspring.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7; key facts about polar bears — they live only in the Arctic (not the Antarctic), have thick white fur and a layer of fat (blubber) to keep warm, are excellent swimmers, and hunt seals by waiting at holes in the sea ice.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 Y1 'Animals, including humans' (identify/describe animals; carnivores) and Y2 'Living things and their habitats' (how habitats provide for animals).
• Standards—US: NGSS 1-LS1-1 (external parts help animals survive); K-ESS3-1 (organisms and environment); 2-LS4-1.
• Operational details: anchor a few sticky true facts — Arctic ONLY (never with penguins), two ways to stay warm (thick fur + blubber), a strong swimmer, and a patient ice-hole hunter of seals. Two lovely truths to include gently: the fur looks white but isn't truly white (it scatters light), and the skin underneath is black to soak up warmth. Keep the sea-ice link so children start to sense why bears need the ice to hunt.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) say polar bears live in the cold Arctic, not with penguins; Tier B (6) name one way a polar bear stays warm (thick fur or fatty blubber); Tier C (7) explain that polar bears wait by holes in the sea ice to catch seals.
bestPractices: Fix the Arctic-only fact firmly to break the near-universal polar-bear-with-penguins image
Give TWO warmth mechanisms (fur AND blubber) so 'staying warm' is concrete, not a single vague idea
Use the memorable truths that the fur only looks white and the skin is black to hold warmth — surprising and sticky
Link hunting to the sea ice (waiting at breathing holes) to plant the idea that the bear depends on the ice
Keep to 3–4 vivid facts with real images rather than an exhaustive profile
keyRepresentations: Labelled polar-bear picture: thick fur, blubber layer, big paws for swimming/walking on ice
Cutaway showing white-looking fur over black skin
Ice-hole hunting scene: bear waiting patiently by a hole for a seal to surface
Warmth-layers diagram (fur outside, fat inside) like coats over a jumper
commonMisconceptions: Polar bears and penguins live together — polar bears are Arctic (north) only; penguins are in the south
Polar bears are white all the way through — the fur only looks white and the skin beneath is black
They stay warm with fur alone — they also have a thick layer of fat (blubber)
Polar bears can't swim — they are strong swimmers who cross open water
They catch seals by chasing them — they mostly wait patiently at holes in the sea ice

learn.summary: Help 5–7 year-olds hold a few vivid, accurate polar-bear facts: polar bears live only in the Arctic (the far North, never with Antarctic penguins); they stay warm with BOTH thick fur AND a layer of fat (blubber) that trap the bear's own warmth rather than making heat; their fur only looks white while the skin beneath is black; they are strong swimmers; and they hunt seals by waiting patiently at breathing holes in the sea ice. A picture-first, explore-and-reveal approach suits this age, with a behaviour mini-scene and a true/false check as supports.

activities.title: Explore a labelled polar bear on the sea ice
feedback: When a child says the skin is white, reveal the black skin: the fur only looks white (it scatters/reflects light), while the skin beneath is black and is thought to help soak up a little of the Sun's warmth — though the main warmth comes from the fur and blubber.
When a child names only one way to stay warm, point to both layers — fur on the outside and fat inside, like a coat over a jumper.

If a child places the bear near penguins, point to the top of the globe: polar bears live only in the Arctic in the far North; wild penguins live in the southern half of the world, many near Antarctica at the bottom of the globe.
Reinforce that fur and blubber trap the bear's own warmth and keep the cold out — they do not make heat.
activities.rationale: For this age a small set of vivid facts is better met by a picture-first explore-and-reveal than by an exhaustive profile; revealing the black skin and blubber cutaway makes the surprising, sticky truths concrete, and the lift-the-flap directly confronts the common polar-bear-with-penguins image. The accuracy of the revealed facts is grounded in the biology source; the source does not establish that this medium teaches better than another.
sourceClaims: Polar bears live only in the Arctic, insulate with dense fur over black skin plus a blubber layer, swim strongly, and hunt seals at breathing holes in the sea ice
learnerActions: Look at a labelled picture of a polar bear standing on Arctic sea ice, and point to or tap each part to reveal one fact.
Reveal the coat: 'thick fur traps the bear's own warmth, like a thick coat.'

Open a cutaway of the fur to find TWO things underneath — a layer of fat (blubber) and, surprisingly, black skin. The main way the bear stays warm is the fur plus the blubber working together; alongside that, the dark skin is thought to help soak up a little warmth from the Sun, and the fur only looks white.
Reveal the big paws to see the bear swimming strongly across open water.
Reveal a dark hole in the ice to watch the bear wait patiently beside it until a seal's nose appears.
Lift a flap answering 'Would a polar bear ever meet a penguin?' — the bear maps firmly to the far North, wild penguins to the southern half of the world, so in the wild the answer is never.
activities.intendedInsight: A polar bear is built for the Arctic: it keeps warm mainly with thick fur on top of black skin, with a layer of blubber underneath the skin, swims strongly, and depends on the sea ice to hunt seals — and in the wild it never shares a home with penguins.

activities.title: Act out the patient ice-hole hunt and the warm layers
feedback: If the child makes the bear chase the seal, replay the waiting: in this ice-hole hunt the bear stays still by the breathing hole until the seal comes up for air.
If the child leaves out a layer, prompt for the missing one — both fur and blubber are needed.
If a child says blubber is 'hot' or makes heat, correct gently: the fat traps the bear's own warmth, it is not a heater.
activities.rationale: Acting out a behaviour and physically assembling the warm layers lets young children rehearse a process that a static fact can only state; it is offered as a hands-on support alongside the main picture work, not a replacement for the factual illustration. The source grounds the facts, not the comparative effectiveness of the activity.
sourceClaims: Polar bears live only in the Arctic, insulate with dense fur over black skin plus a blubber layer, swim strongly, and hunt seals at breathing holes in the sea ice
learnerActions: Play the bear waiting silently and still beside a hole in the ice until a seal surfaces — notice the bear mostly waits rather than chases.
Build the warm layers by placing or dragging 'fur' on the outside and 'fat (blubber)' on the inside of a bear outline, like putting a coat over a jumper.
Say aloud what each layer does: it keeps the bear's warmth in and the cold out.
activities.intendedInsight: Staying warm comes from two trapping layers working together, and a key way polar bears hunt seals is by waiting patiently at breathing holes in the ice rather than chasing — both make the bear's dependence on the sea ice felt.

activities.title: Fix the friend's facts: diagnostic check
feedback: Full response: polar bears live only in the Arctic (never with penguins); the skin is black under the white-looking fur; and they stay warm with both thick fur and a fat layer that trap warmth. Add that they swim strongly and wait at ice holes to catch seals.

Partial response (knows Arctic and one warmth feature, or treats fat as 'hot'): re-anchor insulation — fur and blubber keep heat in and cold out, they do not make heat — and prompt for the second warmth feature.

Gap response (places bears at both poles and/or says skin colour keeps them warm): re-anchor the Arctic-only fact at the top of the globe, then separate the colour story from the insulation story — reveal the black skin and the two trapping layers.
activities.rationale: Asking a child to fix a friend's mixed-up statement separates surface repetition ('both poles', 'white skin') from conceptual understanding (Arctic-only, insulation by fur plus blubber); asking 'how does it actually keep warm' pushes past a colour story to a trapping-layers story. The correct answer is grounded in the biology source.
sourceClaims: Polar bears live only in the Arctic, insulate with dense fur over black skin plus a blubber layer, swim strongly, and hunt seals at breathing holes in the sea ice
learnerActions: Listen to a friend's claim: 'Polar bears live at both the North and the South Pole, and their fur is white because their skin is white underneath — that's what keeps them warm.'
Say what you would fix in what the friend said.
Explain how a polar bear ACTUALLY keeps warm.
activities.intendedInsight: A secure understanding restricts polar bears to the Arctic, corrects the skin to black (fur only looks white), and names fur PLUS blubber as insulation that traps warmth — not skin colour.

constraints: Keep to 3–4 vivid, accurate facts with real images rather than an exhaustive species profile for this age.

True/false and matching checks (Arctic not Antarctic; match the layer to its job) can confirm recall but do not by themselves build the conceptual picture — use them after the facts have been explored.
An open-ended chatty-bear dialogue is engaging but risks drifting from the few concrete facts for 5–7 year-olds; if used, steer it tightly to the target facts.
State insulation carefully: fur and blubber trap the bear's own warmth and keep the cold out; they do not generate heat. Avoid implying blubber is 'hot'.
The black-skin-soaks-up-warmth point should be given gently as an interesting truth, not overstated — the main warmth mechanism is the fur-plus-blubber insulation.
Picture cutaways and acted-out scenes are simplified representations of a real animal; keep the sea-ice link so children sense why the bear needs the ice to hunt.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the listed sourceClaims were marked verified:false in the original row.

Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions; no claim of tested effectiveness is made, and no source attests that any proposed activity or medium teaches better than another.

The source states the fur 'is not truly white' and 'scatters light'; this is a widely repeated simplification. It is described simply as the fur 'only looks white' and, where a mechanism is mentioned, as 'scatters/reflects light', without asserting detailed optics as fact for this age band — consistent with the activity feedback.

The 'black skin soaks up the Sun's warmth' claim is popular but its real contribution to a polar bear's heat balance is debated; it is retained as a gentle interesting fact and kept secondary to fur/blubber insulation in both the activity text and the constraints.

Two standards source claims (DfE KS1 and NGSS) from the original row were not attached to any activity's sourceClaims because the activity rationales are about picture-first/diagnostic pedagogy rather than curriculum alignment; the facts themselves remain curriculum-relevant and the claims remain in the original row.

Independent re-audit: content checked for scientific accuracy, insulation framing, the penguin misconception, and absence of unsupported categorical modality claims; found internally consistent with the minor in-activity clarifications applied above.

probeDeeper: Which pole does a polar bear live at — and could it ever meet a penguin?
A polar bear takes off into freezing water to swim. What two things stop it from freezing?
If blubber made its own heat, the bear would never feel cold at all — so what is the blubber really doing?
The fur looks white. What colour is the skin hiding underneath, and why might dark skin help?
assess.correctAnswer: Two fixes: polar bears live ONLY in the Arctic (the North), never near the penguins in the Antarctic; and their skin is actually BLACK, not white — the fur only looks white. They keep warm with two things: a thick coat of fur AND a thick layer of fat called blubber under the skin. They are also strong swimmers and hunt seals by waiting at breathing holes in the ice.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Polar bears live at the South Pole too / near penguins' — opposite-poles confusion.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor: polar bears = Arctic (North) only. Point to the top of the globe.
errorPatterns.distractor: Polar bears live at both poles, so they share the ice with penguins.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places polar bears in the Antarctic or says they meet penguins.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Blubber/fur makes its own heat / is hot' — thinks fat and fur are warm rather than insulating.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insulation idea: fur and blubber are like a thick coat — they trap the bear's own warmth and keep the cold out; they don't make heat.
errorPatterns.distractor: The blubber is hot, like a little heater inside the bear.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the blubber 'is hot' or 'makes heat'; doesn't say it keeps heat IN / stops the cold getting through.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The bear's skin is white like its fur' — surface-colour assumption.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reveal the black skin (helps soak up warmth from the Sun); the fur only looks white because it reflects light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the skin is white; surprised it's black under the fur.

responseLevels.gap: Places bears at both poles and/or thinks skin colour keeps them warm.
responseLevels.full: Restricts polar bears to the Arctic, names fur AND blubber as insulation (trapping the bear's warmth, not making heat), and adds hunting seals at ice holes / black skin under white-looking fur.
responseLevels.partial: Knows bears are Arctic and names fur or blubber, but treats the fat as 'hot' or leaves out one of the two warmth features.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a polar bear on the sea ice. A friend says 'polar bears live at both the North and the South Pole, and their fur is white because their skin is white underneath — that's what keeps them warm.' What would you fix in what your friend said, and how does a polar bear ACTUALLY keep warm?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child repeating surface facts says 'both poles' and 'white skin'; a child with the concept restricts them to the Arctic and names fur PLUS blubber as the warmth mechanism (not skin colour). Asking 'how does it actually keep warm' separates a colour story from an insulation story.
