pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — What Is the Ocean? (ages 5–7): the ocean is a huge body of SALT water that covers most of Earth's surface (about 71% — more sea than land) and is home to an enormous number of living things.
• Standards — UK (DfE): supports KS1 Y1/Y2 'Animals, including humans' and 'Living things and their habitats' (habitats provide for living things), and links to geography KS1 (name/locate seas and oceans); an early awareness-and-wonder foundation.
• Standards — US (NGSS): K-ESS3-1 relevance (organisms and the places they live); 2-LS4-1 (there are many kinds of living things in different places) — the ocean as the largest such place.
• Operational details: establish three concrete ideas — (1) the ocean is SALTY, unlike the fresh water children drink, swim in at a pool, or see in rivers/lakes; (2) there is MORE ocean than land on Earth (a blue planet); (3) it is FULL of life, more than anywhere else. Use a globe/world map so 'covers most of Earth' is seen, and a taste-memory hook (seawater is salty, you can't drink it). Keep quantities qualitative ('most', 'huge') at this age.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~5–6): say the ocean is huge, salty water with lots of animals in it. B (transitional, ~6–7): state there is more ocean than land on Earth and that ocean water is salty, unlike river/lake water. C (early formal, ~7): explain the ocean covers most of Earth's surface and is home to more living things than land.
bestPractices: Use a globe or blue-marble image so 'covers most of Earth' is a seen fact (more blue than green), not a told one.
Anchor 'salty' to sensory memory — seawater tastes salty and can't be drunk — and contrast with the fresh water of taps, rivers and lakes so salt vs fresh is concrete.
Lead with wonder and variety (the ocean is stuffed with living things) to motivate the whole domain, not just facts about water.
Distinguish 'sea/ocean' from other water children know (puddles, pools, ponds, rivers) by size and saltiness.
keyRepresentations: A globe/world map with ocean vs land clearly contrasted (blue dominating green).
A salt-vs-fresh water pairing (sea beside a river/tap) with a 'don't drink me' salt cue.
A cutaway 'peek beneath the surface' teeming with varied sea life.
A simple size comparison: how much of Earth is ocean vs land.
commonMisconceptions: 'There's more land than sea' — the ocean covers most of Earth (about 71%).
'Ocean water is like the water we drink' — it is salty and unsafe to drink, unlike fresh river/lake/tap water.
'The sea is just a big puddle / empty water' — it is vast, deep, and full of more life than land.
'Seas and oceans are totally separate pools' — the ocean is really one connected body of water around the world.
'Only fish live in the ocean' — mammals, invertebrates, plants/algae and countless others live there too.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, build awareness and wonder that the ocean is a huge body of salty water covering most of Earth's surface and home to an enormous variety of living things. Core moves: let children SEE on a globe/world map that there is more blue (ocean) than green (land); anchor 'salty' to sensory memory and contrast with the fresh water of taps, rivers and lakes; and reveal the teeming life beneath the surface. Keep quantities qualitative ('most', 'huge') at this age.

activities.title: Meet the ocean: globe reveal, salt flap, and dive-in
feedback: When the child notices more blue than green: 'You spotted it yourself — Earth has more sea than land. That's why it's sometimes called the blue planet.'

On the salt flap: 'Sea water is salty, so we can't drink it even when we're thirsty. River and tap water are fresh, not salty. Tap water has been cleaned so it is safe to drink, but river water needs cleaning before anyone drinks it.'
When the underwater scene opens: 'Look how many different animals live here! So many kinds of creatures live in the ocean — big ones, tiny ones, and all sorts of shapes.'
activities.rationale: A seen fact (blue dominating green on a map) lands the 'covers most of Earth' idea as something the child noticed rather than was told. A sensory salt anchor and a fresh-water contrast make salt vs fresh concrete. Leading with the variety of sea life motivates the whole domain at an awareness level appropriate for 5–7.
sourceClaims: The ocean covers more than 70 percent (about 71%) of Earth's surface and holds about 97% of Earth's water.
Ocean (salt) water differs from the fresh water of rivers, lakes and taps and is not safe to drink.
Living things live in habitats that provide for their needs; there are many kinds of living things in different places — the ocean being the largest.
learnerActions: Look at a globe or world map and point to the blue parts (water) and the land parts (often green or brown — check the map's colours); say out loud which there is more of.
Lift a flap or reveal panel on the water to meet the question 'Why can't you drink it?' and hear the salt fact, with a river or tap pictured alongside for contrast.

'Dive in' beneath the waves (turn a page, open an underwater scene, or tap a drill-down panel) to discover a world packed with creatures of many shapes and sizes — whales, fish, crabs, jellyfish, seahorses.
activities.intendedInsight: Our planet's surface is mostly ocean; ocean water is salty (unlike the fresh water we drink); and the ocean is home to a huge variety of living things.

activities.title: Paint the globe / sort the water (hands-on scaffold)
feedback: After painting: 'Which colour covered the most? Blue — so there is more ocean than land.'
After sorting: 'The sea went in the salty group; the rivers, lakes and taps in our pictures are fresh water. Most lakes are fresh, though a few special lakes are salty.'
activities.rationale: A simple manipulable lets children feel the proportion and the salt/fresh split. At this age the concept is awareness-level, so this is an optional reinforcing activity rather than a required live model.
sourceClaims: The ocean covers more than 70 percent (about 71%) of Earth's surface and holds about 97% of Earth's water.
Ocean (salt) water differs from the fresh water of rivers, lakes and taps and is not safe to drink.
learnerActions: Paint or place blue tiles over the water parts of a world outline and green over the land, then look at how much more blue there is.
Sort pictures or labels of water sources into two groups: salty (the sea/ocean) and fresh (river, lake, tap).
activities.intendedInsight: 'Most of Earth is ocean' and 'salty vs fresh' become felt through doing, not just seen.

activities.title: Talk it through: how is the ocean different from a lake?
feedback: Correct response: 'Ocean water is salty, while river and most lake water is fresh — the salt is why you can't drink sea water. And the ocean covers more of Earth than land does — most of the planet's surface.'
If the child says there's more land: show a globe and estimate blue vs green — most of it is blue; let the map overrule the land-dweller's hunch.
If the child says ocean water is fresh like a river: recall a seaside taste memory (salty, stings a cut) versus tap/river water, and name fresh vs salt. (No tasting of unknown water in class.)
If the child describes the ocean only as 'the beach we went to': zoom out on a globe — the ocean is one enormous connected body of salt water around most of the planet, not just one beach.
activities.rationale: Short spoken discussion surfaces the three common misconceptions (more land than ocean; ocean water is fresh; 'ocean' means one local beach) and lets responsive feedback address each. The two independent facts (salty; covers-more) separate genuine understanding from everyday guessing.
sourceClaims: The ocean covers more than 70 percent (about 71%) of Earth's surface and holds about 97% of Earth's water.
Ocean (salt) water differs from the fresh water of rivers, lakes and taps and is not safe to drink.
learnerActions: Respond to: 'A lake is big too. Name one thing that makes the OCEAN different from a big lake.' (Looking for salt and/or vast scale.)
Decide and explain: 'Is there just one ocean or lots of separate ones — what do you think?' then look at a globe to see the water is really one connected body wrapping the planet.

Answer the challenge: 'Someone says the ocean is just a really big lake, the water is the same as a river, and there's more land than ocean. Are they right? Tell me one way ocean water is different, and whether land or ocean covers more of Earth.'
activities.intendedInsight: The ocean is distinguished from familiar water (puddles, pools, ponds, rivers, lakes) by its saltiness and its vast, connected scale — and both facts can be held at once.

constraints: Keep quantities qualitative at this age ('most', 'huge'); do not require children to work with the precise 71% or 97% figures.
Safety: never have children taste unknown or sea water in class; rely on remembered seaside taste and pictured comparisons.

A couple of picture recognition questions (which is salty? more sea or land?) can check recall but do not by themselves elicit the child's own explanation; use them as a light check, not the main activity.

Painting the globe and sorting water sources are reinforcing scaffolds; the central aim is that the child notices and can state both facts and picture the ocean's life, not just complete a sorting task.
Address the connectedness idea (the ocean is really one body of water around the world) as part of 'what the ocean is', since children often picture separate pools.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original artefact notes claimed '3D adds no conceptual payoff' and that a scored quiz 'can't build the wonder'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been removed from learner-facing text and reframed as narrow scope limits (a quiz is a light recall check; a rotatable globe is an optional dramatisation).

One source (NGSS/DfE habitats claim) is marked verified:false in the row; the 'ocean is the largest such place' framing — and the derived 'more living things than on land' message — is attributed but not independently verified here. The original's stronger 'more than anywhere else on Earth' superlative has been narrowed to 'more than on land' in learner-facing text.

The original diagnostic feedback said 'about two-thirds' while NOAA cites about 71% (which exceeds two-thirds). Learner-facing feedback now uses the qualitative 'most'; the two-thirds/71% imprecision is recorded here only, not presented to children.
The 'only fish live in the ocean' misconception from the source is addressed implicitly via the varied-creatures reveal rather than named explicitly; could be made explicit if desired.

probeDeeper: 'Why can't you drink sea water when you're thirsty, but you can drink water from a tap?'
'Look at the globe — point to more blue or more green? So which is there more of, ocean or land?'
'A lake is big too. Name one thing that makes the OCEAN different from a big lake.' (salt + scale counterexample)
'Is there just one ocean or lots of separate ones — what do you think?'
assess.correctAnswer: They're not right on either count. Ocean water is SALTY, while river and lake water is fresh (not salty) — that's why you can't drink sea water. And the ocean covers MORE of the Earth than land does (about two-thirds / most of the planet's surface is ocean).

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks there is more land than ocean on Earth ('we live on land, there's loads of it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a globe or world map and spin/estimate blue vs green — most of it is blue. Name it: about two-thirds ocean. Let the map overrule the land-dweller's intuition.
errorPatterns.distractor: There's more land than ocean on Earth
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says land covers more; surprised the ocean is the majority of the surface

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks ocean water is the same fresh water as a river or lake ('water is just water')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a taste memory (seaside — salty, stings a cut) with tap/river water. Name fresh vs salt; that's the key difference. (No tasting of unknown water in class.)
errorPatterns.distractor: The ocean is fresh water, the same as a river
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the ocean is salty, or says you could drink sea water like river water

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks 'the ocean' is one particular place they've visited (a beach) rather than a huge body of water covering most of Earth
errorPatterns.nextMove: Zoom out on a globe: the ocean is one enormous connected body of salt water wrapping most of the planet, not just one beach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the ocean only as 'the beach we went to'; no sense of its vast global scale

responseLevels.gap: Says there's more land than ocean, or that ocean water is fresh like a river; treats 'ocean' as just a local beach.
responseLevels.full: States the ocean is salt water (unlike fresh rivers/lakes) AND that it covers more of Earth than land, and can picture it as one huge body of water home to countless living things — connecting the facts rather than reciting one.
responseLevels.partial: Gets one fact (salty OR covers-more) but not both, or states them as memorised words without conviction — e.g. says 'salty' but thinks land covers more.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Someone says: 'The ocean is just a really big lake — the water is the same as the water in a river, and there's more land on Earth than ocean anyway.' Are they right? Tell me one way ocean water is different from river water, and whether land or ocean covers more of the Earth.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who knows what the ocean is says salt water (not fresh) AND that ocean covers more than land. A child guessing from everyday experience — we live on land, maps show lots of countries — says there's more land, or that 'water is just water' with no salt/fresh distinction. The two tiers separate the two independent facts; getting both right can't easily happen by luck.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Food Chains & Energy Transfer

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Year 4 'Animals, including humans'):** 'construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey.'

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-LS2-1 / 5-PS3-1):** 5-LS2-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS2-1]'; 5-PS3-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS3-1]... was once energy from the sun.'

- **Operational details:** Children move from a single chain to constructing and INTERPRETING varied chains, naming producer, predator and prey, and tracing that the energy in every consumer traces back through the producer to the SUN. They interpret consequences — predicting what happens along the chain if one organism is removed — which is the first step toward web thinking. Same-organism-different-role (a rabbit is prey to a fox but a consumer of grass) is a key idea.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (relational, multi-link reasoning). Success = constructing a 4-organism chain with producer/predator/prey labelled, explaining that the energy came from the sun via the plant, and predicting a knock-on effect of removing one organism — not treating each link in isolation.
bestPractices: Have children CONSTRUCT and INTERPRET chains (both directions) with real data, not just copy a given one.
Trace energy back to the sun explicitly — the producer captures sunlight; consumers inherit that energy.
Use the remove-an-organism prediction to introduce knock-on effects (bridge to food webs).
Stress role-relativity: the same animal is predator to one, prey to another.
Distinguish predator/prey (a feeding relationship) from producer/consumer (an energy role).
keyRepresentations: A four-link chain labelled producer / prey / predator.
An energy-to-sun trace (sun → plant → herbivore → carnivore).
A 'remove this organism' prediction prompt showing knock-on effects.
Role tags showing one organism as both predator and prey.
commonMisconceptions: Arrows drawn from eater to eaten (reversing energy flow).
Thinking removing a predator only helps its prey, missing further knock-on effects down/up the chain.
Believing energy is created by animals rather than inherited from food tracing back to the sun.
Treating 'predator' and 'producer' as the same kind of label.
Assuming a food chain shows a fixed pecking order rather than energy flow.

learn.summary: Help 8–9-year-olds construct AND interpret food chains of four or more organisms, labelling producer, prey and predator, tracing the energy in every consumer back through the producer to the sun, and predicting the knock-on effects of removing one organism. The central insight is that a food chain is an energy flow that ripples when broken, not a fixed pecking order, and that one organism can hold two roles at once (e.g. a rabbit is prey to a fox yet a consumer of grass).

activities.title: Build-and-test chain bench with a removal shock
feedback: If a learner draws arrows from eater to eaten, re-establish that the arrow shows energy passing TO the eater: the sun's energy enters at the plant and moves up the chain.
If a learner says removing a predator only helps its prey, prompt them past the first step — what happens to what the prey eats, and (if anything eats the predator) to that organism above it?

If a learner says an animal is 'either predator or prey', show an animal (e.g. a frog) that eats another animal (so it is a predator) and is eaten by another (so it is prey); the labels describe relationships, not permanent identities. An animal that eats only plants, like a rabbit, is a consumer but not a predator.
If a learner says an animal makes its own energy, trace the food backward until it reaches a plant capturing sunlight — the energy was inherited, not created.
activities.rationale: Pairing construction with a predict-then-observe removal makes both the chain's structure and its knock-on consequences concrete, supporting the interpret-consequences objective that is the first step toward web thinking. The live energy pulse from a sun source and the role toggle are optional interaction examples that make the energy-trace and role-relativity ideas visible; they are ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 4 'Animals, including humans': 'construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey.'
NGSS 5-PS3-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS3-1], [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS3-1].' 5-LS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS2-1].'
learnerActions: Assemble a four-organism chain from pieces plus arrows, e.g. grass → rabbit → fox, extending to a fourth organism; draw the arrows in the direction energy travels (toward the eater).
Tap or label each organism with its role — producer, prey, or predator — and justify each label aloud or in writing.

Trace energy from a glowing sun source: show the sun's energy entering at the plant (producer) and pulsing along the arrows to each consumer; state in words where each animal's energy ultimately came from.

Run a removal test: pull the rabbit out of grass → rabbit → fox and predict first, then observe the model — in this single-chain model the fox loses its food supply and the grass, no longer grazed by rabbits, tends to increase (real foxes might switch to other prey).
Use a role toggle to show the same rabbit tagged as prey (to the fox) AND consumer (of grass); explain why both tags are correct at once.
activities.intendedInsight: A food chain is a flow of energy originating from the sun; breaking one link ripples up and down the chain, and predator/prey are roles in a relationship rather than fixed identities.

activities.title: Two-direction removal reasoning: the frog's two jobs
feedback: If a learner says 'they're all connected, so everything goes down together', separate the frog's two jobs: as a predator it held slugs down (remove it → slugs rise); as prey it fed herons (remove it → herons fall).
If a learner refuses to call the frog a predator ('it's small / it's prey') and so mis-predicts the slug effect, show it eating slugs; predator/prey are roles, not sizes or fixed identities.
Correct answer to reinforce: slugs increase because their predator the frog is gone; herons decrease because they lost the frogs they feed on.

For the second-order step, expect lettuce to decline: more slugs graze more lettuce, so the level two below the frog falls. For the transfer case, expect frogs to increase: removing the herons removes the frog's predator.
If a learner traces the heron's energy backward from heron to lettuce, affirm it: energy enters at the lettuce from the sun and passes up the chain to the heron — never created by the animals.
activities.rationale: A diagnostic that asks for opposite-direction predictions discriminates children who track the two roles of an organism from those using linear or 'all-connected' thinking who move every population the same way. Following a second-order effect and transferring to a new removal case checks relational, multi-link reasoning rather than isolated links. Population-direction claims are treated as single-chain reasoning, not an exact ecological law.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 4 'Animals, including humans': 'construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey.'
learnerActions: Study the chain lettuce → slug → frog → heron.
Predict: if a disease killed all the frogs, what happens to the number of slugs, and separately to the number of herons? Give a reason for each.
Explain that the frog is BOTH predator (it eats slugs) and prey (herons eat it), and use that to justify why slugs go UP while herons go DOWN.
Follow a second-order effect: once slugs increase, what then happens to the lettuce?
Trace where the heron's energy originally came from — follow the chain back to the lettuce capturing sunlight — confirming the energy was inherited, ultimately from the sun.
Transfer the method to a new case: if instead all the herons died, what would happen to the frogs?
activities.intendedInsight: In this single chain, removing an organism tends to move the level below it UP (its predator is gone) and the level above it DOWN (its prey is gone); direction depends on which side of the removed organism you are on.

activities.title: Labelled chain reference and ecologist prediction talk
feedback: If a learner treats 'predator' and 'producer' as the same kind of label, point out one describes who eats whom while the other describes who first captures the sun's energy.
Push past a single prediction: ask the learner to name a second organism affected and say why, pointing to the relevant link.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference and an ecologist persona support recognition of roles and rehearsal of justified predictions. These support, but do not by themselves run, the removal-consequence that carries the interpretation objective, so they work best alongside an activity where the learner constructs a chain and tests a removal.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 4 'Animals, including humans': 'construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey.'
learnerActions: Explore a labelled chain where each organism reveals its role and 'where its energy came from', with a sun element revealing the ultimate source — use this as a reference to check your own labels.
With an ecologist prompt ('what if we removed the foxes?'), predict the knock-on effects and justify each prediction by pointing to the chain.
Define producer, predator and prey in your own words, giving an example of each; distinguish predator/prey (a feeding relationship) from producer/consumer (an energy role).
activities.intendedInsight: Roles and energy source can be read off a chain, and predictions must be justified by the chain's structure; feeding-relationship labels and energy-role labels are different kinds of label.

constraints: Have children construct and interpret chains themselves with real data, not just copy a given chain; interpretation means naming roles AND predicting consequences.
Trace energy explicitly back to the sun: the producer captures sunlight and consumers inherit that energy; do not let 'animals make their own energy' stand.
Arrows must point in the direction energy flows — toward the eater; watch for reversed (eater-to-eaten) arrows.
Stress role-relativity (the same animal is predator to one organism, prey to another) and distinguish predator/prey from producer/consumer.

A labelled reference image or tap-to-reveal panel supports recognition of roles but does not by itself elicit the removal prediction or independent construction; use it as a scaffold alongside a build-and-predict task.

Quiz, sequence, categorization and multiple-choice formats can assess construction and interpretation and are also usable during teaching, but recognition-only responses do not on their own show that a learner can independently construct a chain or reason through a removal.

Include at least one 'nothing changes' distractor cautiously: the intended learning is that removals do ripple, so use such distractors to surface, then correct, 'all-connected' or no-effect thinking, with a debrief.
Treat the 'below up / above down' pattern as single-chain reasoning for this age, not as an exact ecological law; real webs with shared predators and time lags can differ.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a 3D scene as adding 'cost without insight' for relational energy flow; this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law. It is reframed as a scoped note that a 3D spatial scene offers little extra for a relational energy-flow idea here, without claiming 3D never helps.

The source states a reference image 'can't run the removal consequence'. This is retained as a scaffold limit (a fixed reference does not itself run a removal), not as a claim that static images cannot teach interpretation.

Population-direction claims (slugs up, herons down after frog removal; lettuce down; frogs up after heron removal) are simplified single-chain idealisations; real ecosystems have webs and time lags. Presented as chain-reasoning for this age, not as empirical ecological prediction.

Attribution of the DfE claim to the removal-reasoning rationale (activity 2) is partial: the standard covers 'interpret' and identifying predators/prey but does not itself warrant the knock-on prediction method; retained because the activity does identify predator/prey roles, flagged for reviewer awareness.
The original keyRepresentations phrase 'four-link chain' is ambiguous; 'four-organism chain' is used throughout to match the checkpoint and evidence.

probeDeeper: Is the frog a predator, prey, or both? Explain how.
Once the slugs increase, what then happens to the lettuce?
Where did the energy stored in the heron originally come from?
If instead all the herons died, what would happen to the frogs?
assess.correctAnswer: Slugs would increase — their predator (the frog) is gone, so fewer are eaten. Herons would decrease — they have lost the frogs they feed on. Because the frog is both the slug's predator and the heron's prey, removing it pushes the level below UP and the level above DOWN.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'They're all connected, so if the frogs die everything goes down' — no notion of predator-release; every population falls together.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the frog's two jobs: as a predator it held slugs down (remove it → slugs rise); as prey it fed herons (remove it → herons fall). Direction depends on which side of the frog you're on.
errorPatterns.distractor: Both the slugs and the herons would decrease, because they are all connected in the chain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts both slugs and herons decrease.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'An animal is either a predator or prey' — fixed labels, so the frog can't be both.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the frog eats slugs (predator) AND is eaten by herons (prey); predator/prey are roles in a relationship, not permanent identities.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to call the frog a predator ('it's small / it's prey'), so mis-predicts the slug effect.

errorPatterns.pattern: Energy/arrow direction reversed — thinks food or energy flows from predator down to prey.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish the arrow as energy passing to the eater; the sun's energy enters at the lettuce and moves up the chain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When tracing energy, points it from heron back toward lettuce.

responseLevels.gap: Moves all populations the same way or cannot trace any effect.
responseLevels.full: Predicts slugs up and herons down with reasons, recognises the frog as both predator and prey, and follows a second-order effect (the lettuce), transferring to the heron-removal case.
responseLevels.partial: Predicts one correct effect (e.g. herons decline) but not the opposite move of the slugs, or names organisms without linking cause to effect.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the chain: lettuce → slug → frog → heron. Ask: 'If a disease killed all the frogs, what would happen to the number of slugs, and what would happen to the number of herons? Explain your reason for each.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with only linear or 'all-connected' thinking moves both populations the same way (both down, or both up). A child who tracks the two roles of the frog moves them in OPPOSITE directions and can say why — prey released, predator starved.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–8 years

- **Topic:** Changing Your Mind with Evidence

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1–Lower KS2 Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to use observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions, and to use results to draw simple conclusions and suggest improvements. Being willing to let a result overturn your prediction is the disposition that makes 'using results to draw conclusions' honest rather than confirmatory.

- **Standards — US (NGSS Nature of Science, grades K–2/3–5):** Scientific knowledge is based on empirical evidence and is open to revision in light of new evidence; scientists' explanations are revised when evidence does not support them. Treating a surprising, prediction-breaking result as valuable is a core Nature-of-Science understanding.

- **Operational details:** The child makes a genuine prediction, tests it, and — when the result contradicts the prediction — updates their belief instead of ignoring, denying, or 'fudging' the result. The key affective move is reframing a surprise: a result that breaks your prediction is not a failure or an embarrassment but the most INFORMATIVE outcome, because it tells you the world is not as you thought. Children practise saying 'I predicted X, but I observed Y, so I've changed my mind' — and resisting the strong pull of confirmation bias (remembering/valuing only results that fit). This rests on the prior observation-vs-interpretation split: you revise the interpretation, the data stands.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete, early disposition). This is the emotional-cognitive core of empiricism: evidence outranks prior belief. Success = when a result contradicts a prediction, the child acknowledges the mismatch, updates their idea rather than defending it, and can articulate why the surprising result was the useful one.
bestPractices: Have children COMMIT a prediction in writing/visibly before testing, so the later mismatch is honest and undeniable.
Explicitly celebrate surprising, prediction-breaking results as the most interesting — build a classroom norm that 'I was wrong, and here's what I learned' is high status.
Model belief revision aloud: 'I thought the big one would sink faster — it didn't — so I need a new idea'.
Name confirmation bias in kid terms: the pull to notice only the results that agree with you, and how to resist it.
Separate the data from the ego — lean on observation-vs-interpretation so it's the IDEA that changes, not the child that 'failed'.
Use predict–observe–explain cycles with genuinely counter-intuitive outcomes so revision is regularly required, not rare.
keyRepresentations: Predict → Observe → (surprise?) → Update cycle
A committed-prediction card set beside the actual-result card for direct comparison
'I predicted … but I observed … so I changed my mind' sentence frame
A 'surprise = treasure' badge that rewards prediction-breaking results
Confirmation-bias 'magnet' image — the pull to keep only results that agree
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a wrong prediction means you failed, rather than that you learned something.
Ignoring, dismissing, or re-reading a result so it seems to fit the original prediction (confirmation bias).
Believing scientists are people who are always right, rather than people who update when wrong.
Changing the RECORDED data to match the prediction instead of changing the idea.
Treating a confirming result as more valuable than a surprising one.
Feeling that admitting 'I changed my mind' is weakness rather than good science.

learn.summary: For ages 6–8, teach the disposition of changing your mind when evidence contradicts your prediction: a prediction-breaking surprise is a highly informative result, not a failure. Learners commit a prediction visibly before testing, confront a genuine mismatch, and explicitly update their idea (not the recorded data), while resisting confirmation bias. Builds on separating observation from interpretation.

activities.title: Predict-o-Tron: lock it in, then watch
feedback: On a surprise, mark it positively: 'Surprise! You just found out something the world didn't tell you before — that's worth keeping.' Avoid a buzzer, red cross, or any 'wrong' framing.

If the learner tries to re-read the result so it fits the old prediction, return to the raw observation and look again together, scoped to the actual challenge — for the ramp, 'Did one ball reach the bottom first, or did they arrive together?'; for a float test, 'Is it above or below the water?' — then change the idea, not the data.
Reward the explicit update action and the spoken sentence frame, so revision itself is what earns recognition.
activities.rationale: Committing a prediction before seeing the outcome makes the later mismatch honest and undeniable, and a live predict-then-reveal sequence can enforce commit-before-see and make updating an explicit, rewarded action — something a one-way presentation that simply tells the learner the answer does not require them to do. Counter-intuitive outcomes make revision regularly required rather than rare.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1–Lower KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to use observations and results to draw simple conclusions and suggest improvements — which depends on letting results, not prior belief, decide.
NGSS Nature of Science holds that scientific knowledge is open to revision in light of new evidence and that explanations are revised when evidence does not support them.
Young children can engage in evidence-based belief revision and hypothesis testing, and benefit from treating surprising results as informative.
learnerActions: Face a genuinely counter-intuitive challenge, choosing one setup for this run — e.g. two solid balls (not hollow), one big and heavy, one small and light, released at the same moment from the top of identical ramps (which reaches the bottom first?), OR two objects placed in water (which sinks and which floats?).
Commit your prediction visibly and in a way you cannot quietly retract — say or write 'I predicted the big one', and pin that choice where it stays visible.
Run the test and watch the actual outcome within the setup you chose (e.g. the two solid balls arrive at about the same time, give or take a small difference; or an object floats/sinks unexpectedly).

When the result breaks your prediction, perform an explicit 'update my idea' move within the setup you ran: for the ramp, drag your idea-token from 'the big one is faster' to a new bin you name yourself; for the float test, drag it from 'the big one sinks' to a new idea you name — change the idea, not the data.
Say the sentence frame aloud: 'I predicted X, but I observed Y, so I've changed my mind.'
Collect the surprise as a 'treasure' — keep a shelf/collection of prediction-breaking results you learned from across several challenges.
activities.intendedInsight: The mismatch between what I guessed and what happened is not me failing — it is me learning. A surprising result taught me more than a confirming 'I was right' would have.

activities.title: Spot the confirmation-bias move
feedback: If the learner discards a surprising trial as a fluke, repeat the observation together to check whether it happens again, then ask 'if it keeps happening, what does that tell us about our idea?'
Praise honestly recording and counting the results that broke the prediction.
activities.rationale: Naming confirmation bias in child terms and requiring that disagreeing results be recorded and counted makes the habit of weighing all evidence concrete, supporting honest conclusion-drawing rather than confirmatory reading.
sourceClaims: Young children can engage in evidence-based belief revision and hypothesis testing, and benefit from treating surprising results as informative.
learnerActions: Across several trials, keep a tally of every result — including the ones that disagreed with your prediction, not just the ones that agreed.
Notice when you only remembered or valued the trials that fit your guess, and name that pull (the 'magnet' that makes you keep only agreeing results).
Decide what the full set of results — including the surprising ones — says about your idea.
activities.intendedInsight: There is a strong pull to notice only results that agree with you; a good scientist counts the disagreeing results too and lets the whole evidence decide.

activities.title: Talk it through: 'I was wrong, and that's great'
feedback: Celebrate the child's 'I changed my mind' warmly; never shame a wrong prediction.
If the child reacts with disappointment ('I got it wrong, I'm bad at this'), reframe the surprise as the best moment — it taught something new.
activities.rationale: Responsive dialogue can surface and address a child's actual reluctance to let go of a belief and model revision warmly; it complements, rather than replaces, the commit-then-be-surprised experience because it does not make the child commit and feel their own prediction broken.
learnerActions: Talk with an adult or in-role character who asks: 'What did you predict? What happened? So what will you do with your idea now?'
Hear the adult/character share their OWN belief-change story ('I thought the big one would sink — but it floated — so I need a new idea').
Describe aloud how you feel about being surprised and practise treating it as curiosity, not shutdown.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing your mind in light of evidence is normal, high-status science — not weakness or embarrassment.

activities.title: Story of a surprise (primer)
feedback: After the story, connect it forward: 'Now it's your turn to make a prediction and see if the world surprises you.'
activities.rationale: A worked example of a surprising, mind-changing result can model the disposition and vocabulary as a primer. It introduces the stance but does not itself make the child commit a prediction and feel it broken, so it works best before a hands-on predict-reveal activity.
learnerActions: Explore a short scene or story of a scientist's 'I thought … but I found …' moment, including a famous 'oops that changed science'.
Pick out the vocabulary: prediction, observation, surprise, changed my mind.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientists are people who update when the evidence surprises them, not people who are always right.

activities.title: What should the scientist do? (short reasoning probe)
feedback: Full response: treats the surprise as valuable evidence, is willing to change the idea or re-test to confirm, and says why a surprise is worth more than a confirmation.
Partial response: accepts the idea was wrong but frames it as personal failure or doesn't see the surprise as informative — reframe the surprise as useful and separate the idea from the self.

Gap response: protects the prediction by explaining the surprise away ('I did it wrong', 'the marble is broken') or reinterpreting it — repeat the observation together and hold interpretation separate from what is seen.
activities.rationale: Short scenarios can probe whether the learner reasons toward updating a belief and can identify confirmation bias. A scored scenario checks understanding of what to do with a surprise; it does not create the personal, committed prediction whose overturning builds the habit, so use it alongside hands-on prediction tasks.
sourceClaims: Young children can engage in evidence-based belief revision and hypothesis testing, and benefit from treating surprising results as informative.
learnerActions: Read a short scenario: a result did not match the prediction — what should the scientist do?
Choose and justify a response, and spot the confirmation-bias move in a scenario where someone kept only the agreeing results.

Answer probes: 'If you tried it three more times and the big one floated every time, would you keep your first idea or change it? Why?' and 'Which is more useful to a scientist — a result that surprises you or one you already expected? Why?' and 'If you really wanted your prediction to be right, would that change what the marble actually did?'
activities.intendedInsight: Strong reasoning treats a surprising result as real information to learn from (change the idea, or re-test to be sure), not a mistake to hide or explain away; wanting a prediction to be true does not change what actually happened.

constraints: Requires the prior skill of separating observation from interpretation: the data stands, the interpretation is what gets revised.
Challenges must be genuinely counter-intuitive so that revision is actually required; a prediction the child would always get right does not exercise the disposition.
The learner must commit the prediction visibly/in writing BEFORE testing, or the later mismatch is not honest and undeniable.
Never reframe a changed recorded value as acceptable: change the idea, not the recorded data.
Each prediction, result, update and feedback prompt must stay within one stated setup (the ramp OR the float test); do not mix a ramp prediction with a 'above or below the water' observation.

Story/example and reasoning-probe tasks are primers and checks — they model or assess the disposition but do not make the child commit a prediction and feel it broken, which is where the habit forms; pair them with hands-on prediction tasks.
Reasoning-probe items (recognising what a scientist should do) check understanding and do not by themselves elicit the independent act of committing and then revising a personal belief.

A screen 'predict-o-tron' simulation and a real physical investigation offer different experiences; the mechanic described (locking a prediction, explicit update, treasure badge) is one concrete way to stage commit–surprise–update and is not the only way to teach this disposition.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source physics for the ramp example needs care: two balls of different mass released from rest down identical frictionless ramps (or two uniform solid balls rolling without slipping) arrive together because acceleration is independent of mass (and of radius) — correct as a counter-intuitive demonstration. However, real ramps have friction and rolling inertia (moment of inertia depends on mass distribution, not simply size/weight), so a classroom demo can differ; verify the specific objects behave as intended before presenting 'they arrive together' as guaranteed.

The sink/float examples rely on density/buoyancy, not weight alone, so heavier does not mean it sinks first; note that two real glass marbles both sink, so the objects used must be chosen deliberately to produce the intended counter-intuitive result, and this should be checked in the real setup.

Two source claims (NGSS Appendix H; PMC developmental research) were marked verified:false in the source row; treat their evidential strength as unconfirmed. The DfE claim was marked verified:true in the row but has not been re-checked here. The source claims attached to activities support the disposition being taught, not the comparative efficacy of any medium.

The original 'a static telling cannot' enforce commit-before-see was rescoped: static or spoken formats can still teach this disposition; the interactive's claimed advantage is limited to requiring the learner to commit before an undeniable mismatch and rewarding an explicit update, not established comparative efficacy.
The original '3D adds nothing / 3D adds cost without deepening' claim was not carried as a universal law; omitted as a catalog ranking rather than an objective limit.
reteachPrerequisiteId references from the assessment error patterns are retained conceptually as 'separate observation from interpretation' prerequisites, but internal IDs were removed.

probeDeeper: If you tried it three more times and the big one floated every time, would you keep your first idea or change it? Why?
Which is more useful to a scientist — a result that surprises you or one you already expected? Why?
Suppose you really wanted your prediction to be right. Would that change what the marble actually did?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning treats the surprising result as real information to learn from, not a mistake to hide or explain away: the child says they should change their idea (or test again to be sure) because the evidence didn't match the prediction, and shows that a surprising result is valuable — it tells you something you didn't know. The key is willingness to update the belief in light of the evidence rather than defend the original prediction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Discounts the surprising result as a mistake or a fluke to protect the prediction ('I must have done it wrong', 'the marble is broken').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Repeat the observation together so it can't be dismissed; then ask 'if it keeps happening, what does that tell us about our idea?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the anomaly away instead of treating it as data; keeps the original belief.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a surprise as a failure to feel bad about, rather than as useful information ('I got it wrong, I'm bad at this').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe surprises as the best moments in science — they teach you something new; celebrate the unexpected result.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reacts to the mismatch with disappointment or shutdown, not curiosity.

errorPatterns.pattern: Refuses to give up the prediction and reinterprets the observation to fit it ('it only LOOKS like it's floating').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the raw observation — is it above or below the water? — and hold the interpretation separate from what is seen.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Bends the observation to preserve the belief.

responseLevels.gap: Protects the prediction — explains the surprise away as a mistake or a broken marble, or reinterprets it; keeps the original belief.
responseLevels.full: Treats the surprising result as valuable evidence, is willing to change the idea (or re-test to confirm), and can say why a surprise is worth more than a confirmation — connecting the emotional stance to the epistemic point.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts the result and says the idea was wrong, but frames it as a personal failure or doesn't see the surprise as informative — updates reluctantly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You were sure the big marble would sink and the small one would float. You try it — but the big one floats and the small one sinks. That's the opposite of what you thought! What should you do now, and how do you feel about being surprised?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who protects prior belief says 'I must have done it wrong' or 'the marble is cheating', discounting the anomaly. A child who updates says the result means the idea was wrong and should change. Because the natural pull is to preserve the prediction, choosing to revise is a genuine signal of the habit under test.

pedagogy.summary: The coordinate system is built from two perpendicular NUMBER LINES — the x-axis (horizontal) and the y-axis (vertical) — crossing at the origin (0,0). An ordered pair (x, y) names ONE unique point by two distances from the origin: the first number is how far ALONG the x-axis (horizontal), the second how far UP the y-axis (vertical). The order is a convention that carries meaning, so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points. The dominant error is reversal — reading or writing the pair in the wrong order (y before x, 'up before across'); a second is treating the axes as blank space rather than number lines, so the child counts squares instead of reading the numbered lines and/or loses the origin as the (0,0) anchor.
bestPractices: Build the axes as two number lines the child already knows, laid perpendicular and meeting at 0 (the origin); a point's coordinates are just readings on those two number lines
Fix the order with a memorable rule — 'x is a-cross, then up', 'along the corridor, then up the stairs', x before y — and always read horizontal first
Contrast (2,4) with (4,2) explicitly so the child sees that changing the order changes the point
Read from the numbered LINES, not by counting squares, and anchor every reading at the origin (0,0)
Name and point to the x-axis, y-axis and origin repeatedly so the vocabulary is secure
keyRepresentations: Two perpendicular number lines meeting at the origin, each labelled; the point reached by reading along then up
The 'corridor then stairs' / 'a-cross then up' journey traced from the origin to the point
(2,4) and (4,2) plotted together to show the order matters
A grid with numbered lines (not just squares) to read off directly
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — gives/reads the pair as (y, x): up before across (NCETM: 'putting the y-coordinate before the x')
Treats order as arbitrary — thinks (2,4) and (4,2) are the same point
Counts squares/gaps from the edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin (off-by-one)
Loses the origin as the (0,0) start, or thinks the axes are just the borders of the grid rather than number lines

learn.summary: Teach the coordinate pair as an ORDERED address read off two perpendicular number lines (x-axis horizontal, y-axis vertical) that meet at the origin (0,0). The first number is distance ALONG the x-axis, the second is distance UP the y-axis, so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points. Target the two dominant errors: reversal (writing/reading y before x) and counting squares from a grid edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin. Core activities use a plotting/journey task where swapping the same two numbers lands on different points; alternatives include a labelled reference grid and a navigator-talk task that each serve a narrower purpose.

activities.title: Along then up: the swapped-pair journey
feedback: If both markers landed in the same place, check whether you moved along the x-axis FIRST for both — the first number is always the across move.
Use 'x is a-cross, then up' or 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' to fix the order.

Read the numbered LINES, not the squares: start at 0 (the origin) and find the line by READING its printed label — the line labelled 4 is the one printed with a 4 — rather than counting squares or gaps from the edge.
If you reversed a pair, re-trace from the origin saying the first number aloud as the across move.
activities.rationale: Plotting both reversed pairs and seeing them land on different points is intended to target the reversal error and the 'order is arbitrary' misconception; starting every journey from the origin and reading numbered lines targets the count-squares/off-by-one error. Fixing the order with a stated mnemonic is a commonly used remedy.
sourceClaims: A coordinate system uses two perpendicular number lines (axes) meeting at the origin; an ordered pair locates a point by distances travelled from the origin along each axis in the given order, with the first number relating to the first axis

Common coordinate error = 'putting the y-coordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position' from a lack of knowledge of the order or names of the axes; also counting squares rather than numbered lines; remedies = 'x is a-cross', 'along the corridor then up the stairs'
learnerActions: On a numbered coordinate grid (first quadrant), first point to and name the x-axis, the y-axis and the origin. Then start at the origin (0,0) and plot (4,2): move 4 ALONG the x-axis first, then 2 UP, tracing the corridor-then-stairs path and marking the point where the lines cross.
Now plot (2,4) from the origin the same way (2 along, then 4 up) and mark that point too.
Compare: describe out loud where each marker landed and why the two points are in different places on the grid even though they use the same two numbers.
Write a sentence: 'The order matters because ___.'
Check your work: point to and name the x-axis, the y-axis and the origin again, and confirm that both journeys started at the origin (0,0).
activities.intendedInsight: The pair is an ordered address, not just two numbers: swapping the order sends you to a different place, and every reading starts from the origin and is read off the numbered lines.

activities.title: Read it back: name the pair for a given point
feedback: Correct order: horizontal (x) reading first, then vertical (y).
The origin is (0,0) because it is where both number lines read zero — the start of every journey, not the first square.
For 'same or different', (2,4) and (4,2) are DIFFERENT points because the across and up amounts are swapped.
activities.rationale: Producing the pair for a shown point (rather than only recognising it) checks the convention in the reverse direction and is intended to surface reversal and origin-naming errors; making reversal and origin-naming the discriminating cases keeps the items focused on the core convention.
sourceClaims: Common coordinate error = 'putting the y-coordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position' from a lack of knowledge of the order or names of the axes; also counting squares rather than numbered lines; remedies = 'x is a-cross', 'along the corridor then up the stairs'
learnerActions: Look at a point shown on a numbered grid and state its coordinate pair, saying the across reading first then the up reading.
For a point such as the one at 3 across and 5 up, write (3,5) and complete: '(3,5) means 3 along the ___-axis and 5 up the ___-axis.'
Decide for a 'same or different' pair such as (2,4) and (4,2) and justify your choice.
Point to the origin and state its coordinates, explaining why it is (0,0).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a point back into an ordered pair uses the same across-then-up convention and the origin as the zero start; naming the axes and origin secures the vocabulary.

activities.title: Labelled grid reference (scaffold)
feedback: Match each label to the move: first number = along the x-axis, second = up the y-axis.
Confirm the origin reading is (0,0) before reading any other point.
activities.rationale: A labelled reference can secure vocabulary and the reading convention, best used after active plotting. Because it is fixed, it supports consolidation but does not by itself let the learner vary the order and see the point change; it is a useful reference, not a replacement for active plotting.
learnerActions: Study a labelled grid where tapping or pointing to the origin reveals '(0,0), where the axes cross' and a point reveals 'along 3, up 5'.
Use it as a reference to check your own readings after plotting.
Name the x-axis, y-axis and origin from the labels.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly labelled grid consolidates the vocabulary (x-axis, y-axis, origin) and the along-then-up reading as a reference.

activities.title: Navigator talk: give the pair before I move (alternative)
feedback: If the navigator does not reach your target, check that your first number is the across amount.
Say the order aloud: 'across first, then up.'
activities.rationale: A talk-based task may surface the reversal misconception through explanation and self-correction; it complements, rather than replaces, plotting on the grid where the effect of the order is seen directly.
sourceClaims: Common coordinate error = 'putting the y-coordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position' from a lack of knowledge of the order or names of the axes; also counting squares rather than numbered lines; remedies = 'x is a-cross', 'along the corridor then up the stairs'
learnerActions: Direct a navigator to a target point you have been shown by giving its coordinate pair, saying the across move first; the navigator moves exactly as told (first number across, second number up), so check whether it reaches the target.
When the navigator asks 'across or up first?', answer and explain before it moves.
Re-state a pair correctly if the navigator queries the order.
activities.intendedInsight: Because the navigator always moves the first number across and the second number up, a reversed pair sends it to a different point than the target, which is intended to make the reversal error audible and visible and to prompt self-correction.

constraints: This microtopic is a first-quadrant, 2-D coordinate idea; a third axis is a much later topic and would distract from the ordered-pair convention here.

Recognition/matching items (which point is (3,5)?) check the convention but do not require the learner to construct the pair or watch the order change the point; pair them with plotting or spoken production.

A labelled reference grid is a consolidation scaffold: it is fixed, so the learner cannot themselves vary the order on it — use it after active work; this is a limitation of that one reference, not a claim that fixed images cannot teach.
Always read from the numbered lines and anchor at the origin (0,0); counting squares/gaps from a grid edge invites off-by-one errors.
If a learner cannot name x-axis/y-axis/origin at all, reteach that prerequisite (naming the axes and establishing the origin as (0,0)) before coordinate reading.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One cited source (National Curriculum in England mathematics programmes of study) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the Year 5/Year 6 placement detail as unconfirmed.

The original 'read-mode' interactive, the animated along-then-up trail, the side-by-side (2,4)/(4,2) comparison toggle, and tap-to-reveal labels are preserved as optional interaction/feedback examples, not mandatory mechanisms.

The source's framing that a static reference 'cannot test the order for themselves' is retained only as a scoped limitation (it is fixed), not as a claim that fixed images cannot teach the convention.

Independent re-review confirmed the two previously flagged items (feedback line-labelling risk and navigator-insight efficacy overclaim) are resolved; no learner-facing contradictions or unsupported categorical claims remain.

probeDeeper: Point to the origin. What are its coordinates, and why (0,0)?
In (2,4), what does the 2 tell you to do, and what does the 4 tell you?
If I gave you (4,2) instead, would the point be in the same place? Show me.
Which axis is the x-axis — and does the first number go with it or the second?
assess.correctAnswer: A is (2,4) and B is (4,2) — they are DIFFERENT points. In each pair the first number is the distance ALONG the x-axis (horizontal) from the origin and the second is the distance UP the y-axis (vertical); because the order is swapped, A is 2 across and 4 up while B is 4 across and 2 up, so they land in different places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal — reads/writes the pair as (y,x): up before across
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix the order with 'x is a-cross, then up' / 'along the corridor then up the stairs'; always read horizontal first (NCETM). Reteach in place — the order convention is the core of this topic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives A as (4,2), or reads B as (2,4); on the reason tier says the first number is 'how far up'

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats order as arbitrary — thinks (2,4) and (4,2) name the same point
errorPatterns.nextMove: Plot both together so the child sees two different squares; stress that the pair is an ordered address, not a set of two numbers.
errorPatterns.distractor: A and B are the same point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says A and B are the same, or that 'it doesn't matter which way round the numbers go'

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts squares/gaps from the edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin (off-by-one)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the numbered LINES and anchor at the origin (0,0) — the origin is the zero start, not the first square.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads A as one out (e.g. (3,5) or (1,3)) by counting squares rather than lines, or by starting the count at 1 instead of 0

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses the origin / treats the axes as borders — starts counting from a grid corner rather than (0,0), or cannot name x-axis/y-axis/origin
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the origin as (0,0) where the two number lines cross; name and point to the x-axis, y-axis and origin before reading any point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts from the top-left or a grid corner; cannot point to the origin or name the axes

responseLevels.gap: Reverses the pair, or says (2,4) and (4,2) are the same point; counts squares from a grid corner; cannot name the axes or the origin.
responseLevels.full: Reads (2,4) and (4,2) as different points, explains the first number as distance along the x-axis and the second as up the y-axis from the origin, names the x-axis/y-axis/origin, and reads from the numbered lines anchored at (0,0).
responseLevels.partial: Reads a point correctly in a standard case and names the axes, but reverses under pressure, reads by counting squares (off-by-one), or is shaky on why the origin is (0,0) — has the procedure without the ordered-address concept.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a coordinate grid, mark point A at (2,4). Ask: 'What are the coordinates of A?' Then plot a second point B at (4,2) and ask: 'And what about B? Are A and B the same point or different — and how do you know? What does each number in the pair tell you?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A and B are reversals of each other, so a child who reads the order correctly gives (2,4) and (4,2) and calls them different, explaining across-then-up; a child who reverses gives A as (4,2); a child who thinks order is arbitrary says A and B are the same point. Each faulty route lands on a distinct, identifiable answer, and the reason tier ('what does each number tell you?') separates a correct-by-luck reading from real understanding.

pedagogy.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting ones to a three-digit number rests on one insight: only the ones digit changes, UNLESS the calculation bridges a ten (then the tens digit changes too, and possibly the hundreds). Children apply their secure within-20 bonds at the end of a larger number, keeping the hundreds and tens as an untouched 'anchor'. It is taught with place-value apparatus and a number line so the local change is visible against the stable larger part.
bestPractices: Anchor the hundreds/tens and operate only on the ones — 345+7 keeps '34_' fixed and works 5+7
Reuse within-20 make-ten bonds for the bridging cases (345+7 = 345+5+2 = 350+2)
Contrast a non-bridging case (345+3) with a bridging case (345+7) so the child notices when more than the ones digit changes
Use a marked number line / hundred-square segment to show the small jump near a decade
Ask the child to predict which digits will change before calculating (DfE evidence: explain that only the ones digit changes unless bridging)
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart / Gattegno chart (only the ones row moves; bridging cascades)
Number line segment around the nearest ten
Base-ten blocks (add/remove ones, exchange at the ten)
Bead string near a decade
Partitioning jotting (345 = 340 + 5)
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding the ones to the tens or hundreds digit)
Failing to bridge: 345+7 given as 342 or 3412 (keeps 2, drops the extra ten) instead of 352
Smaller-from-larger on the ones when subtracting bridges down (462−5 given as 463: does 5−2)
Believing 'only the ones digit ever changes', so bridging cases are mishandled

learn.summary: Year 3 pupils mentally add or subtract ones to a three-digit number. The core insight: only the ones digit changes UNLESS the calculation bridges a ten, in which case the tens digit (and possibly the hundreds) also changes. Children anchor the hundreds and tens as a stable 'larger part' and operate only on the ones, reusing secure within-20 make-ten bonds for the bridging cases. Contrasting a non-bridging case directly with a bridging case is what refines the rough rule 'only the ones change' into the accurate 'only the ones change unless we cross a ten'.

activities.title: Anchor the larger part, spin only the ones
feedback: If the child changes the wrong digit (e.g. gives 345+3 as 375, adding to the tens): re-anchor with the chart — the 3 is three ones, so it joins the ones. Name the value of each digit before adding.
Reinforce by asking which column the added amount belongs to, every time, until anchoring is automatic.
activities.rationale: Anchoring the larger part and operating only on the ones makes the local nature of the change explicit; naming place value directly counters the wrong-digit error. A coded or physical chart where only the ones row moves makes this concrete, while base-ten blocks, a bead string or a partitioning jotting (345 = 340 + 5) show the same stable-anchor idea in other media.
learnerActions: Show 345 on a place-value chart (e.g. a Gattegno chart) with the hundreds, tens and ones rows visible.
Work 345 + 3: change only the ones from 5 to 8, keeping '34_' fixed, and say aloud which digits stayed the same and which changed.
Name the value of each digit before adding (the 3 you add is three ones, so it joins the ones), to guard against adding to the wrong column.
Predict, before calculating, which digits will change.
activities.intendedInsight: A change to the ones stays local: the hundreds and tens act as an untouched anchor, so for a non-bridging case only the ones digit moves.

activities.title: Bridge a ten with make-ten bonds
feedback: If the child fails to bridge (e.g. 345+7 given as 342, keeping the 2 and dropping the extra ten, or strings digits as 3412): rebuild with make-ten on the number line — 345 to 350, then +2 — and connect it to the within-20 bond they already know.
Highlight that keeping the tens digit at 4 cannot be right because the answer passed 350.
activities.rationale: Bridging reuses within-ten make-ten bonds, and multiple representations (number line, hundred-square, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy. Showing the ones filling to the decade then the remainder makes visible why the tens digit moves. The cascading chart and number-line toggle are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required apparatus.
sourceClaims: Bridging a ten reuses within-ten 'make ten' bonds; multiple representations (number line, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy.
learnerActions: Work 345 + 7 on a marked number line (or a hundred-square segment near the decade): jump +5 to land on 350, then +2 more to reach 352.
Connect this to the within-20 bond already known: split 7 into 5 + 2, so 345 + 7 = 345 + 5 + 2.
Notice the moment the tens digit changes (4 becomes 5 as you cross 350) — this is the exception to 'only the ones change'.
Optionally watch a place-value chart where the ones roll past 9 and cascade a carry of +1 into the tens, with a number-line toggle showing the same jump onto 350 then stepping to 352.
activities.intendedInsight: When a calculation crosses a ten, the ones 'fill up' to the next decade and the tens digit also changes; make-ten bonds the child already knows handle the split.

activities.title: Contrast non-bridging and bridging side by side
feedback: If the child insists only the ones can ever change, point to the bridging case where the tens visibly moved past a decade, and ask them to re-predict.
Praise correct predictions that name the crossing of a ten as the reason the tens digit changes.
activities.rationale: Contrasting a non-bridging case with a bridging case isolates exactly when more than the ones digit changes, which is the heart of this skill. Prediction-before-calculation surfaces the misconception for discussion. Rapid mixed items can rehearse and check the skill but mainly confirm rather than build the insight.
learnerActions: Place 345 + 3 and 345 + 7 next to each other and predict, for each, which digits will change before calculating.
Calculate both, then state which digits actually changed and why they differed.
Articulate the refined rule: 'only the ones change, unless we cross a ten'.
Try a mixed set of items sorted by whether they bridge, predicting each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Directly comparing a case where only the ones change with one that bridges turns the rough rule into the accurate rule and exposes the 'only the ones ever change' overgeneralisation.

activities.title: Bridge downwards when subtracting
feedback: If the child does 'five take two is three' and gives 463 (subtracting the smaller from the larger within the column): show on the number line that 462 − 5 must move down past 460 — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more. Sanity-check that subtracting makes the number smaller.
Reinforce the direction check as the first move on any subtraction that bridges.
activities.rationale: The smaller-from-larger error can produce an answer larger than the start, as with 462 − 5 → 463, though not always (464 − 7 → 463). A number-line model travelling down past the decade corrects it. A direction check, plus a check that the tens digit dropped, catches it. Answers across the set: 345+3 = 348 (only ones change), 345+7 = 352 (bridges up, tens change), 462−5 = 457 (bridges down, tens change).
sourceClaims: Bridging a ten reuses within-ten 'make ten' bonds; multiple representations (number line, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy.
learnerActions: Work 462 − 5 on a number line (or hundred-square segment near the decade), moving DOWN: take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more to land on 457.
Check direction first: subtracting should make the answer smaller than 462, so an answer above 462 is wrong.
State which digits changed (the tens digit drops from 6 to 5) and why.
Thinking aloud, do 345 + 3, 345 + 7 and 462 − 5 in turn, saying which digits change after each.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting across a decade moves the number down past the ten, so the tens digit drops. A direction check catches the smaller-from-larger error when it gives an answer above the start (462 − 5 → 463), but it cannot catch every case. Checking that the tens digit dropped, because the answer passed below 460, makes the check complete.

constraints: The target is mental calculation: apparatus (place-value/Gattegno chart, number line, hundred-square segment, base-ten blocks, bead string, partitioning jottings) are scaffolds to make the local-versus-bridging change visible, to be faded as the child calculates reliably in their head.

Multiple-choice or rapid mixed items (e.g. 345+7 with a 342 distractor) chiefly check whether the child bridges and catch the 'only ones change' overgeneralisation; they do not by themselves build the bridging insight, which needs the child to construct and explain the steps.
A static tap-to-reveal chart can show which digit changes but does not let the child follow the carry cascade; pair it with a number line or manipulation if the bridging mechanism is the goal.
Prerequisites: secure within-20 make-ten bonds and confident place-value naming of hundreds/tens/ones digits; reteach these if the wrong-digit or no-bridge errors persist.
Partial mastery looks like handling the non-bridging case and bridging only with a number line or apparatus, not yet reliably in the head, and possibly missing direction on subtraction.

The source row's worked subtraction note contained a garbled fragment ('462−52 wait — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more = 457'); the intended method is take 2 to reach 460 then 3 more to 457. The corrected steps are used in the activity; the original garble is recorded here only.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 345+3=348, 345+7=352, 462−5=457 all confirmed. The distractors named (342, 3412, 463, 467) are explicitly error patterns, not valid answers.

probeDeeper: For 345 + 3, which digits changed and which stayed the same? Why?
For 345 + 7, why did the tens digit change when it didn't for 345 + 3?
Is your answer to 462 − 5 bigger or smaller than 462? Should it be?
What would 345 + 7 be if it were 345 + 70 instead — which digit changes then?
assess.correctAnswer: 348, 352, 457. 345+3 changes only the ones (348). 345+7 bridges: ones fill to 350 then +2 = 352 (tens digit also changes). 462−5 bridges down: 462−52 wait — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more = 457 (tens digit changes).

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the wrong digit — adds the ones amount to the tens or hundreds ('345 + 3 is 375')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor with the place-value chart: the 3 is three ones, so it joins the ones. Name the value of each digit before adding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The altered digit is not the ones; the child adds to the wrong column

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to bridge — '345 + 7: five and seven is twelve, so 342' (keeps the 2, drops the extra ten) or 3412
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild with make-ten on the number line (345+5 to 350, then +2); connect to the within-20 bond they already know.

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger when subtracting bridges down — '462 − 5: five take two is three, so 463'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the number line that 462−5 must move DOWN past 460; take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more. Sanity-check direction: subtracting makes it smaller.

responseLevels.gap: Changes the wrong digit, or gives 342/3412 and 463; believes only the ones digit ever changes.

responseLevels.partial: Handles the non-bridging case and can bridge with a number line or apparatus, but not yet reliably in his head; may miss the direction on subtraction.

The contrast between the non-bridging and bridging items isolates the misconception.
