pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 6–7 (Year 2). COUNTING IN TENS FROM ANY NUMBER (not just multiples of 10) — e.g. 7, 17, 27, 37… A place-value insight: adding/subtracting 10 changes only the TENS digit; the ones digit stays the same. The foundation for mental +10/−10 and column place value.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 2 'count … in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; Year 3 'find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.5 'Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count'; extends to 2.NBT.8. Directly parallel to the UK statement.
• Operational details: Teach on the HUNDRED SQUARE as a VERTICAL move — straight DOWN a column = +10, straight UP = −10 — so the child SEES the tens digit tick while the ones digit is fixed; contrast with counting in ones (a horizontal move). Use base-ten blocks (add a ten-rod; ones untouched) for the concrete why. Say the rule aloud: 'the ones stay the same'. Practise forwards and backwards from non-multiples (83, 73, 63…).
• Checkpoint: Tier A counts in 10s from a non-multiple forward (4, 14, 24…). Tier B counts in 10s forward and backward from any two-digit number and states that the tens digit changes. Tier C explains WHY only the tens digit changes (one more ten, ones unchanged) and does it mentally.
bestPractices: Teach it as a VERTICAL move on the hundred square (down = +10, up = −10) so the tens-digit change and the fixed ones-digit are seen.
Use base-ten blocks: add one ten-rod while the ones pile is untouched — the concrete 'why' behind the digit rule.
Say the rule aloud — 'the ones stay the same, the tens go up by one' — and test it from many non-multiple starts.
Practise backward (−10) from any number; connect to mental 10-more / 10-less.
keyRepresentations: Hundred square (vertical move = ±10; ones digit fixed down a column).
Base-ten blocks / Dienes (add or remove a ten-rod).
Place-value chart (tens column changes, ones column unchanged).
Number line with 10-jumps from a non-round start.
commonMisconceptions: Changing the ones digit too (e.g. 27 → 38) — not isolating the +10 to the tens.
Only able to add 10 to multiples of 10 (can't start from 7 or 23).
Treating +10 as 'just add a 0' — which fails for non-round numbers (27 ≠ 270).
Losing the column on the hundred square (drifting sideways instead of straight down).

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (Year 2): counting in tens from ANY number, not just multiples of ten (e.g. 7, 17, 27, 37…). The core place-value insight is that adding or subtracting 10 keeps the ones digit the same while the tens digit changes by one — and at a hundred boundary such as 96 → 106 the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears (backwards, 106 → 96, they roll from 0 to 9), while the ones digit still does not move. This is the foundation for mental +10/−10 and later column place value. It is best made visible as a vertical move on a hundred square (on a standard square numbered from 1 at the top, straight down = +10 and straight up = −10; check the direction on squares numbered from the bottom), with concrete support from base-ten blocks (add/remove a ten-rod, ones untouched). Practise forwards and backwards from non-multiples and say the rule aloud.

activities.title: Down a column, ones frozen — the +10/−10 move on the hundred square
feedback: If a learner recites decade names (7 → 10, 20, 30) and drops the 7: on the hundred square move straight DOWN the column from 7 to show 7, 17, 27 keep the ones digit; name aloud what stays (the 7) and what changes (the tens).

If the ones digit drifts (7, 17, 28, 38): do NOT reteach counting — highlight that the ones column stays the same, using place-value arrow cards or adding one ten-rod each time so the +10-only structure is felt.

If a learner stalls at the hundred boundary (fine to 97, then stuck or says 100, 110): extend the square past 100 and rehearse just the 97 → 107 → 117 bridge, pointing out the ones digit (7) still stays while the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears. Saying 100 means the ones digit has changed, so revisit what stays the same and give more practice crossing 100.

If a learner says +10 means 'add a 0' (27 → 270): compare 27+10 on the grid with the actual answer 37. Show that adding a 0 multiplies by ten, so it never gives +10, even for round numbers (20 with a 0 added is 200, but 20+10 = 30).
activities.rationale: A vertical hop on the hundred square keeps all numbers in a column sharing the same ones digit, so the fixed ones and ticking tens are seen directly. An optional linked panel updating the numeral — ones digit staying lit while the tens change — and a synchronised base-ten rod can make the mechanism concrete, though a printed hundred square with a counter supports the same move.
sourceClaims: Counting in tens from any number is a place-value move best shown as a vertical move on the hundred square (tens change, ones fixed).
learnerActions: Start on a non-multiple, e.g. 27, on a hundred square.
Make a +10 move by dropping straight DOWN one row: 27 → 37 → 47 → 57, saying each number aloud.
Each step of this 27 → 57 run, point to the ones digit (the 7) and say 'the ones stay the same'; point to the tens digit and say 'the tens go up by one' (true while you stay inside a hundred).
Reverse it: make −10 moves by going straight UP one row: 83 → 73 → 63 → 53, saying what stays (the ones) and what changes (the tens).
Watch for drifting sideways — keep the move strictly vertical so you stay in the same ones-digit column.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting ten never touches the ones digit; it is the same single downward (or upward) step on the hundred square whatever number you start from. '+10' is not 'add a zero' — it is 'one row down'.

activities.title: Concrete why: add a ten-rod with base-ten blocks
feedback: If a learner changes the ones to make +10, point out the ones pile should not have been touched and rebuild it.
Connect the blocks back to the digits: the number of ten-rods is the tens digit, the ones pile is the ones digit.
activities.rationale: Manipulating ten-rods gives a physical cause for the digit rule, complementing the grid picture with hands-on structure.
learnerActions: Build a two-digit number with base-ten blocks, e.g. 23 as two ten-rods and three ones.
To add 10, bring in ONE more ten-rod and leave the ones pile untouched; read the new number (33).
To subtract 10, take one ten-rod away and leave the ones pile untouched; read the new number.
Say the rule as you go: 'one more ten, the ones don't change'.
Link each action to its numeral and, if available, to the hundred-square move.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically, +10 is just one extra ten-rod; the ones stay as they are. This is the concrete reason the ones digit never changes.

activities.title: Say-it and spot-the-slip practice
feedback: If a learner finds 10 more only by counting on in ones, encourage the direct 'one row down' move instead.
When a learner spots the wrong digit, ask them to correct it and state the rule.
Recognising a wrong sequence is a check; it does not by itself show the learner can produce a correct one, so also ask the learner to generate their own sequences aloud.
activities.rationale: Mixed forward/backward retrieval and error-spotting consolidate the rule and surface misconceptions. This reinforces, rather than replaces, the grid and blocks work where the insight is first seen.
learnerActions: Answer quick questions: 'What is 10 more than 47?' and 'What is 10 less than 47?'
Fill in a tens sequence from a non-multiple, e.g. 4, 14, __, __, 44.
Look at a wrong sequence (e.g. 7, 17, 28, 38) and say which digit changed that shouldn't have.
Count aloud forwards from a non-multiple and backwards from a two-digit number, stating each step is +10 or −10.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent +10/−10 from any starting number, with the ability to notice when the ones digit has wrongly moved.

activities.title: Explain the pattern out loud
feedback: Accept explanations like 'you add one more ten, so the ones don't move'.
For ten more than 96, let the learner use the extended grid to see 96 → 106: point out that the ones digit (6) still does not move, while the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears.
activities.rationale: Explaining the structure distinguishes a child who understands tens-and-ones from one who is reciting a memorised sequence.
learnerActions: Count in tens from a non-multiple, then answer: 'What stays the same each time, and what changes?'
Answer in your own words why the ones digit stays the same each time and what happens to the tens.
Try harder prompts: ten less than 43 (33); ten more than 96 (106, crossing 100).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate that each step adds or removes one ten — so the ones digit always stays the same while the tens digit changes by one, rolling over into a new hundred at a boundary like 96 → 106 where the ones (6) still does not move — shows place-value reasoning rather than just the chant.

constraints: Always practise from NON-multiples (7, 23, 83…), not just 10, 20, 30 — multiples can be done by chanting decade names without the place-value insight.
Include backward (−10) as well as forward counting; backward from a two-digit number additionally tests subtraction of ten.

State the robust invariant to children: the ones digit always stays the same. The tens digit normally goes up (or down) by one, but at a hundred boundary it rolls over: forwards (96 → 106) it goes from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears; backwards (106 → 96) it goes from 0 to 9 and the hundred goes. The ones digit is unchanged either way.
A hundred-square counter or screen model shows the move but is a representation; pair it with base-ten blocks for the concrete 'why' when a learner only mimics the grid.
Error-spotting and 'which digit is wrong' tasks check recognition; also require the learner to produce sequences and explanations independently.
Do not teach '+10 means add a 0' — adding a 0 multiplies by ten, so it never gives +10 (27+10 = 37, not 270; 20+10 = 30, not 200).
Keep the move strictly vertical on the hundred square; drifting sideways reverts to counting in ones.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original flagged a 3D representation as 'adding nothing'; this universal comparative claim has been dropped. A planar hundred square is well suited here, but no comparative-efficacy claim against other media is asserted.

The original rated an oral back-and-forth as only 'possible' because the ones-fixed insight is 'best seen on the grid'. Spoken practice is retained as useful consolidation; the categorical claim that the grid is uniquely able to teach the insight is softened to a scoped affordance (the grid makes the fixed ones/ticking tens visible).

The original summary and probe phrase the rule as '+10/−10 changes only the tens digit'. This holds within a hundred but not across a hundred boundary (96+10=106: the ones digit 6 is unchanged, but the tens roll 9→0 and a new hundred appears). Learner-facing text foregrounds the always-true invariant — the ones digit stays fixed — while describing the tens roll-over; the original simplification is noted here only.

The 'number line with 10-jumps from a non-round start' listed in the source representations is not implemented as a dedicated activity; it is compatible but was not carried into the learner-facing tasks.

Arithmetic checked: 27+10=37,47,57; 83−10=73,63,53; 23+10=33; 96+10=106; 97+10=107, 107+10=117; 43−10=33; 4,14,24,34,44 is consistent. Decade-snapping error (7→10,20,30) and ones-drift (7,17,28,38) are preserved as learner errors to diagnose, not as instructions to follow.

probeDeeper: What stays the same each time, and what changes?
Count back in tens from 83 — what's ten less than 43?
What's ten more than 96?
Why does only the tens digit change?
assess.correctAnswer: 7, 17, 27, 37, …, 97, 107… and 83, 73, 63, …, 13, 3 — keeping the ones digit fixed and changing only the tens digit by one each step.

errorPatterns.pattern: snaps to multiples of ten — asked to count in tens from 7, produces 10, 20, 30, ignoring the ones digit and reciting the decade names instead
errorPatterns.nextMove: on a hundred square move straight DOWN the column from 7 to show 7, 17, 27 keep the ones digit; name aloud what stays (the 7) and what changes (the tens)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: drops the 7 and recites 10, 20, 30…

errorPatterns.pattern: ones digit drifts — changes the ones as well ('7, 17, 28, 38'), not holding the +10-only rule
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT reteach counting — highlight that the ones column stays the same, using place-value arrow cards or adding one ten-rod (Dienes) each time so the +10-only structure is felt
errorPatterns.revealedBy: the ones digit wanders across steps

errorPatterns.pattern: hundred-boundary break — fine to 97 then stalls or says '100, 110' wrongly, or can't pass 100
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat as a place-value failure — extend the hundred square past 100 and rehearse just the 97, 107, 117 bridge; it comes with exposure
errorPatterns.revealedBy: breakdown specifically at 97→107

responseLevels.gap: Reverts to reciting multiples of ten (10, 20, 30) instead of keeping the ones digit; cannot count in tens from a non-multiple.
responseLevels.full: Counts forwards and backwards in tens from any number, holding the ones digit fixed and changing only the tens, and articulates that each step is +10/−10.
responseLevels.partial: Counts on in tens from a non-multiple but the ones digit occasionally drifts, or breaks at a hundred boundary, or cannot go backwards.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Start at 7 and count on in tens: 7, 17, 27… keep going as far as you can. Now start at 83 and count backwards in tens. (Watch whether only the tens digit changes while the ones stays fixed, and whether they cross the hundred boundary cleanly.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Counting in tens from a NON-multiple (7, not 10) can't be done by chanting the decade names — the child must hold the ones digit constant and move only the tens. A child with tens-and-ones place value keeps the 7 and marches the tens; a child without it drifts to multiples of ten (7, 10, 20…), lets the ones digit wander, or breaks at the hundred boundary. Backward from 83 additionally tests −10.

pedagogy.summary: This KS3-level topic bundles three related ideas and is best taught in that order. (1) NEURON SIGNALLING: a neuron carries an electrical impulse along its axon; at the synapse (the tiny gap to the next neuron) chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) cross and start a new impulse in the next cell — so the brain runs on electro-chemical signals passed cell to cell, and a myelin sheath speeds the impulse. (2) BRAIN ORGANISATION: the cerebral cortex has four lobes with broad roles (frontal – planning/decisions/movement; parietal – touch/space; temporal – hearing/memory; occipital – vision), plus deeper structures (limbic system) for emotion. (3) NEUROPLASTICITY: repeatedly used neural pathways get stronger and faster — this IS the biological basis of learning and practice ('cells that fire together wire together'), a genuinely motivating idea for students about their own effort. Tie it off with optical illusions as EVIDENCE that the brain actively CONSTRUCTS what we perceive rather than passively recording it — the same signals can be interpreted into a picture that isn't 'really there'. Keep mechanisms qualitative and avoid ion-channel/action-potential biochemistry (that's GCSE+); the aim is a coherent electro-chemical, plastic, constructive picture of the brain.
bestPractices: Teach signalling with the electrical-along-axon then chemical-across-synapse two-step, using a relay/'pass it on' analogy; introduce myelin as insulation that speeds the impulse — keep it qualitative, not biochemical.

Map the lobes by FUNCTION with memorable hooks (occipital-at-the-back = vision; frontal = planning/decisions), and place emotion with the limbic system, so structure is learned via what each part does.

Make neuroplasticity personal and motivating: repeated practice physically strengthens pathways ('what you practise, you get better at, because the wiring changes') — a direct, evidence-based message about their own learning.
Use optical illusions as EVIDENCE, not entertainment: have students experience an illusion, then reason that if the brain can be 'tricked', it must be constructing perception, not just recording it.
Flag the curriculum status honestly (this is enrichment beyond core KS3; the sensory-receptor→brain→memory idea is the anchored standard) and keep depth qualitative and misconception-aware.
keyRepresentations: Two-step signalling model: electrical impulse along the axon → neurotransmitter across the synapse → new impulse in the next neuron
Myelin-as-insulation speeding the impulse (a relay analogy)
Four-lobe cortex map colour-coded by function (frontal/parietal/temporal/occipital) + limbic system for emotion
Neuroplasticity as a pathway that thickens/strengthens with repeated use ('fire together, wire together')
Optical illusions as evidence the brain CONSTRUCTS perception (same input, brain-made interpretation)
commonMisconceptions: 'Nerve signals are purely electrical, like a wire' — missing the chemical step across the synapse (it's electro-chemical).
'We only use 10% of our brain' — a myth; the whole brain is active with different regions specialised.
'The brain stops changing after childhood / you can't get better at things' — contradicted by neuroplasticity across life.
'Left-brained vs right-brained personalities' — a pop-myth; functions are distributed and networked, not split by personality.
'Perception is a faithful recording of reality' — illusions show the brain actively constructs and infers.
'Neurons physically touch and pass signal by contact' — there is a synaptic gap bridged by chemical messengers.
'Memories/skills live in one spot' — rather than in strengthened, distributed pathways.

learn.summary: KS3 enrichment on the brain, taught as three connected ideas in order: (1) neuron signalling as an electro-chemical relay — an electrical impulse runs along the axon, then a neurotransmitter crosses the synaptic gap and can trigger a new impulse in the next neuron, with myelin acting as insulation that speeds the impulse; (2) brain organisation — four cortical lobes mapped by function (frontal: planning/decisions/movement; parietal: touch/space; temporal: hearing/memory; occipital: vision) plus the limbic system, which plays a key role in emotion; (3) neuroplasticity — repeatedly used pathways strengthen and can speed up, which is the biological basis of learning and practice. Cap with optical illusions used as evidence that the brain actively constructs perception rather than passively recording it. Keep all mechanisms qualitative; avoid ion-channel/action-potential biochemistry (GCSE+). This is enrichment beyond the anchored standard, the sensory-receptor → brain → memory idea (NGSS MS-LS1-8, a US middle-school standard used here as the reference point for this KS3-age content).

activities.title: Build and run a neuron relay (signalling + myelin)
feedback: If a learner describes one continuous electrical wire with no gap, highlight the synaptic gap: at the chemical synapses modelled here, neurons do not touch; a neurotransmitter bridges the gap and can begin a fresh impulse in the next cell.
If a learner treats the whole signal as purely electrical, name the two steps explicitly — electrical along the axon, chemical across the synapse — so 'electro-chemical' is grounded.
When myelin is added and the impulse speeds up, link it to insulation speeding transmission (kept qualitative, not biochemical).
activities.rationale: Signalling is a dynamic two-step process; acting it out or watching it run makes the electrical-then-chemical sequence concrete and directly targets the 'purely electrical wire' and 'neurons touch' misconceptions. A live interactive build (fire impulse, release neurotransmitter, speed with myelin) is one effective medium; a labelled neuron diagram with a lift-the-flap synapse reveal, or an in-role explanation, can carry the same two-step without animation.
sourceClaims: Neurons transmit information by electrical impulses that travel along the axon; a layered myelin sheath accelerates the transmission of these electrical signals; dendrites receive messages from other neurons at synapses, the contact points where one neuron communicates with another.
learnerActions: Fire an impulse and trace it along the axon of one neuron to the synapse.
At the synaptic gap, describe/show how a chemical messenger (neurotransmitter) crosses the gap and can start a NEW impulse in the next neuron.
Add a myelin sheath and compare the impulse speed with and without it.
State in your own words why the signal is 'electro-chemical' rather than one continuous electrical wire.
activities.intendedInsight: The brain's signal is not one continuous wire but a chain of cells passing an electro-chemical baton: electrical along the axon, chemical across the synapse. Myelin acts as insulation that speeds the impulse.

activities.title: Practice mode: observe neuroplasticity
feedback: If a learner says the adult brain is fixed and practice cannot change it, introduce neuroplasticity: strengthened, faster pathways across life are the physical substance of learning.
If a learner locates a skill or memory in one single spot, reframe it as strengthened, distributed pathways rather than one storage location.
Tie the observed strengthening back to their own effort: what you practise, you get better at, because the wiring changes.
activities.rationale: The motivational, evidence-based message that effort rewires the brain is powerful when learners see or reason through the pathway strengthening with repetition rather than being told. A repeat-and-strengthen interactive makes the change observable; a reflective dialogue with a neuroscientist persona using the learner's own experiences is an alternative route to the same insight (it discusses rather than demonstrates the change).
sourceClaims: Neuroplasticity: repeated use strengthens neural connections, which is the biological basis of learning; the cerebral cortex is organised into frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes with distinct broad functions.
learnerActions: Fire the SAME pathway repeatedly in the model and observe what happens to it over many repetitions (in the model it is drawn as strengthening/thickening with a shrinking delay — a simplified picture of stronger connections and, over longer periods, faster signalling).
Connect this to a personal example: name a skill you have got better at with practice and describe what you think changed in your brain.
State the rule in your own words: repeated use strengthens and can speed up a pathway, and that physical change is the biological basis of learning.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeatedly used neural pathways get stronger and faster — 'cells that fire together wire together.' Practice physically changes the brain's wiring, so getting better at something is a real biological change driven by your own effort, not just a claim you are told.

activities.title: Map the lobes by function
feedback: If a learner cites the 10% myth, retire it: imaging shows widespread activity; different regions are active for different tasks, none are 90% unused.

If a learner invokes left-brain/right-brain personalities, clarify that although some functions lean more to one side (e.g. language is mostly left-sided in most people), the two halves work together in networks and people are not 'left-brained' or 'right-brained' in personality.
Reinforce learning structure through function — name the lobe by what it does.
activities.rationale: Learning structure via function with memorable hooks supports recall and directly addresses the brain-capacity and left/right myths. A tappable lobe map that reveals each function makes the structure-to-function link explicit; a static labelled map or an optional 3D brain fly-around can orient where lobes sit, though the core signalling/plasticity/perception ideas are not spatial.
sourceClaims: Neuroplasticity: repeated use strengthens neural connections, which is the biological basis of learning; the cerebral cortex is organised into frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes with distinct broad functions.
learnerActions: On a four-lobe cortex map, reveal and state one broad function for each lobe: frontal (planning/decisions/movement), parietal (touch/space), temporal (hearing/memory), occipital (vision).
Place the limbic system as the deeper structure for emotion.
Use memorable hooks to anchor placement (e.g. occipital-at-the-back = vision).
Explain why 'we only use 10% of our brain' and 'left-brained vs right-brained personalities' are both false.
activities.intendedInsight: The cortex is organised into lobes with broad specialised roles, with emotion handled by the limbic system; the whole brain is active with distributed, networked functions — not 90% unused and not split into personality halves.

activities.title: Optical illusions as evidence the brain constructs perception
feedback: If a learner blames faulty eyes or 'a trick of the paper,' reframe: the lines really are equal on the paper and form equal-length images in the eye; the difference comes from how the visual system interprets them, which is why the illusion survives measuring.
If a learner treats seeing as a passive camera recording, use the surviving illusion as strong evidence for active construction.
Push the deeper follow-up — what does this reveal about seeing? — so the learner commits to passive-recording vs active-construction rather than dodging with 'it's just a trick.'
activities.rationale: Using the illusion as evidence (predict, commit to a reason, measure, then confront persistence) forces the passive-vs-constructive commitment and directly targets the 'perception is a faithful recording' misconception. Interactive illusions with a 'why did your brain do that?' reveal make the reasoning explicit; static illusion plates with a reveal, or a Socratic discussion, can serve the same evidential role.
learnerActions: Look at the Muller-Lyer illusion (two lines of equal length, one with inward arrowheads, one with outward). Predict which line is longer and commit to WHY before measuring.
Measure the lines and note that they are identical — and that the illusion persists even after you know the truth.
Explain what the persistence reveals: the brain builds the percept automatically, below conscious control.
Name one more everyday case where your brain fills in or changes what is really there.
activities.intendedInsight: Perception is not a faithful recording of reality. The brain actively constructs what we see using rules and past experience; in an illusion those rules are fooled, so we 'see' a length that isn't there and keep seeing it because the construction is automatic.

constraints: This is enrichment beyond the anchored standard, the sensory-receptor → brain → memory idea (NGSS MS-LS1-8, a US middle-school standard, not an English KS3 programme-of-study statement). Flag the curriculum status honestly to learners.
Keep all mechanisms qualitative. Avoid ion-channel and action-potential biochemistry — that is GCSE+ and out of scope here.

Recognition-only responses (sequencing the signalling steps, matching lobe→function, choosing the correct myth-buster) can check recall of the signalling steps and lobe functions, but recognition alone does not elicit the dynamic/plastic/constructive explanation; pair them with tasks that ask learners to produce that reasoning.

An interactive simulation lets plasticity be observed through repetition and signalling be animated; a static diagram or dialogue cannot animate these but can still teach the two-step relay and the plasticity rule. Treat the live manipulables (fire impulse, release neurotransmitter, add myelin to speed it, repeat pathway to strengthen it, interactive illusion reveal) as helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as the only way to learn.
A 3D brain only orients where lobes sit; the core ideas (signalling, plasticity, constructed perception) are not spatial, so 3D is optional orientation rather than the lesson.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research. Sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified; all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three sources, only the BrainFacts neuron claim is marked verified in the row; the NGSS anchor claim and the Queensland Brain Institute neuroplasticity/lobe claim are marked unverified. Do not treat the plasticity or lobe-function activities as empirically validated.

The row asserts a live 2D build 'serves all three better than any static or spatial form' and that plasticity 'can't be FELT' without the sim; these are catalog-fit preferences, not established comparative efficacy. Softened to affordance/limit statements. Multiple media can teach these ideas.
'Cells that fire together wire together' is a useful qualitative slogan; keep it qualitative and do not overstate it as a precise mechanistic law at this level.
The Muller-Lyer illusion is a well-known example; the claim that it persists after measuring is a standard observation but was not re-verified in this rewrite.

assess.poeTask: Show the Müller-Lyer illusion (two equal lines, one with inward arrowheads, one with outward). Ask the child to predict which line is longer and commit to WHY before measuring. They confidently predict one is longer; measuring shows the lines are identical — and the illusion persists even after measuring. Their pre-measurement reason and their reaction to the persistence reveal whether they hold a passive-recording or active-construction model of perception.
probeDeeper: When you practise a skill until it becomes automatic, what is physically happening to the pathways in your brain?
A signal travels along a neuron electrically, but between two neurons there's a tiny gap. How does the message get across the gap?
If perception were a perfect recording, illusions couldn't exist. Can you name another everyday case where your brain fills in or changes what's really there?
assess.correctAnswer: The brain doesn't passively record what the eyes send like a camera — it actively constructs what you see, using rules and past experience to interpret the signals. In an illusion those rules are fooled, so you 'see' a length that isn't there, and it persists even when you know the truth because the construction happens automatically, below conscious control. It shows perception is built by the brain, not a faithful recording of reality.

errorPatterns.pattern: The brain records and replays reality like a camera or video — seeing is passive.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe perception as active construction; the illusion persists because the brain builds the percept automatically, even against what you know.
errorPatterns.distractor: Your eyes must be faulty — the brain just shows exactly what the eyes record.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Blames faulty eyes or a trick of the paper; can't explain why the illusion persists after measuring.

errorPatterns.pattern: You only use 10% of your brain.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Retire the myth with evidence (imaging shows widespread activity); different regions are active for different tasks, not 90% unused.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cites the 10% claim when discussing brain capacity or learning.

errorPatterns.pattern: Signals pass directly from neuron to neuron like touching wires — no gap or chemical step.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce the synapse: electrical impulse along the axon, then a chemical (neurotransmitter) crosses the tiny gap to start a new impulse in the next neuron.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes one continuous electrical wire with no synapse or neurotransmitter.

errorPatterns.pattern: The adult brain is fixed — learning and practice don't physically change it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce neuroplasticity: repeated pathways strengthen and speed up — that physical change IS learning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that practice changes brain structure; treats the brain as unchanging hardware.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the brain as a passive recorder (blames the eyes for illusions), repeats the 10% myth, or describes neurons as continuous wires.
responseLevels.full: Explains perception as active construction (why the illusion survives knowing the truth), describes synaptic transmission across the gap, and links repeated pathways (plasticity) to learning — an integrated model that transfers to a new illusion or skill.
responseLevels.partial: Says the brain 'interprets' signals and can name lobes or the synapse as separate facts, but doesn't connect construction, synaptic transmission, and plasticity into an account of why the illusion persists.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In an optical illusion, two lines are exactly the same length but you SEE one as longer — and you keep seeing it that way even after you've measured them and know they're equal. If your eyes are working fine, why does your brain show you something that isn't true? What does that reveal about how seeing actually works?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the 'brain as camera' model blames the eyes or the paper and can't explain why the illusion survives measuring. Only a child with an active-construction model can. The tier-two 'what does this reveal about seeing' forces the passive-vs-constructive commitment that a simple 'it's a trick' dodges.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Reading Ancient Climate Records for ages 12–14 — HOW we know Earth's climate before thermometers: proxy evidence (ice cores, tree rings, ocean sediments, corals, pollen) that lets scientists reconstruct temperature and CO2 back hundreds of thousands of years, and how these records test and validate climate models.
• Standards — UK: KS3 science 'working scientifically' (evidence, data, drawing conclusions from indirect measurement) and geography 'climate change over time'; underpins GCSE understanding of the evidence base for climate change.
• Standards — US: NGSS MS-ESS2-3-adjacent and HS-ESS2-4 / MS-ESS3-5 (evidence of factors causing temperature change over time); strongly a NATURE-OF-SCIENCE topic — how indirect proxies yield reliable knowledge. DCI ESS2.D, ESS3.D.
• Operational details: the pedagogical crux is INFERENCE FROM INDIRECT EVIDENCE — a tree ring is not a thermometer, yet a wide ring records a good growing year; teach each proxy as a signal-with-a-mechanism (why does this thing record climate?) and stress cross-validation (independent proxies agreeing gives confidence); use the 800,000-year ice-core CO2/temperature record as the anchor and connect to how models are validated by reproducing past climate; frame IPCC consensus as the product of many converging lines, not one graph.
• Checkpoint: [Tier B] child can explain that we read past climate from natural recorders like tree rings and ice bubbles, not direct measurement, and give the mechanism for at least two proxies; [Tier C] child can explain cross-validation across independent proxies, why trapped air bubbles give past CO2 directly, and how palaeoclimate data tests climate models.
bestPractices: Lead with the epistemic puzzle: 'thermometers only go back ~150 years — so how can anyone claim to know the temperature 100,000 years ago?' This makes proxies a satisfying answer to a real question rather than a list to memorise.

Teach each proxy as a MECHANISM, not a fact: ice cores trap actual ancient air bubbles (direct CO2) and their isotope ratios encode temperature; tree rings record annual growth (wide=good year); ocean-sediment shells and corals lock in isotopic/chemical climate signals; pollen layers record which plants (hence climate) dominated. Understanding WHY each records climate is the learning.

Emphasise cross-validation: independent proxies (ice, trees, sediment, coral) that were laid down by completely different processes yet agree on the same past temperature curve — that convergence is what makes the reconstruction trustworthy. This directly counters 'it's just one scientist's graph'.

Anchor on the ~800,000-year ice-core record from Antarctica showing CO2 and temperature marching together through ice ages and warm periods, and that today's CO2 is far above anything in that entire record — a powerful, concrete data story.

Connect proxies to model validation and consensus: climate models are tested by whether they can reproduce known past climates from proxy data; the IPCC synthesises many independent lines of evidence — present the nature-of-science honestly (uncertainty ranges, error bars, how confidence is built).
keyRepresentations: An ice core with visible annual layers and trapped air bubbles, callouts showing 'ancient air = direct CO2' and 'isotopes = temperature'.
A tree-ring cross-section with wide and narrow rings mapped onto good and poor growing years.
The overlaid proxy curves: ice-core, tree-ring, sediment and coral temperature reconstructions plotted together to show independent records agreeing (a 'many lines, one story' graph).
The 800,000-year CO2–temperature sawtooth from Antarctic ice cores, with a sharp modern CO2 spike shooting off the top of the historic range.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking there is no way to know pre-thermometer climate, so claims about the ancient past are guesswork; missing that proxies provide physically-grounded measurement.
Believing a proxy like a tree ring IS a direct temperature reading, rather than a signal that must be calibrated and interpreted (and affected by other factors like rainfall).
Assuming the whole case rests on a single graph or study, rather than many independent proxies converging — the source of 'it's just one hockey stick' dismissals.
Confusing ice-core air bubbles (which are literally trapped ancient atmosphere, giving CO2 directly) with the isotope signal (which gives temperature indirectly).

Thinking climate has never changed naturally before (proxies show it has, dramatically) OR the opposite — that because it changed naturally, today's rapid human-driven change is nothing unusual; the proxy record shows the current rate and CO2 level are exceptional.

learn.summary: For ages 12–14: how scientists reconstruct Earth's climate before thermometers using proxy evidence (ice cores, tree rings, ocean sediments, corals, pollen). The core learning goal is inference from indirect evidence — teaching each proxy as a signal-with-a-mechanism (WHY it records climate), stressing cross-validation when independent proxies agree, anchoring on the ~800,000-year ice-core CO2/temperature record, and connecting proxy data to how climate models are validated and how the IPCC synthesises many lines of evidence. Ice cores also preserve volcanic ash/sulfate marker layers that help date and align the record. The recommended lead activity has learners actively reconstruct a past climate curve and feel the payoff of independent records converging; a scientist-interview dialogue supports the epistemic 'how do we really know?' questions; a field-guide reveal and a consolidation check support naming and verifying.

activities.title: Palaeoclimate detective: reconstruct a past climate curve
feedback: When a bubble is read, make explicit: 'You are measuring real ancient air here, not calculating it from a model — this is why ice-core CO2 counts as a direct measurement, even though it still has small measurement and dating uncertainties.'
Contrast the two readings from the same core: the bubble gives CO2 directly, while the isotope ratio gives temperature indirectly and must be interpreted.
When a volcanic marker layer is found, note that a dated eruption layer acts as a fixed time anchor that helps align this core with other records.

When the second and third proxy curves settle close to the first, prompt: 'Different natural processes, different places — yet the same story. That convergence is what makes the reconstruction evidence rather than one person's graph.'
If a single ring looks ambiguous, note that tree-ring width can also be affected by other factors such as rainfall, so proxies are calibrated and interpreted, not read like a thermometer.
When the model hindcast matches the reconstructed curve, prompt: 'A model that reproduces an ice age it was never shown has passed a real test before we trust it going forward.'

When the modern CO2 value shoots off the top, prompt reflection: the fact that climate changed naturally in the past does not make today's rate and CO2 level ordinary — the record shows they are exceptional.
activities.rationale: The target skill is active inference from indirect evidence: measuring signals, reading mechanisms, and assembling and cross-checking a reconstruction. Carrying out the reconstruction rather than only viewing it is intended to let the learner experience cross-validation as a felt payoff, which aligns with the nature-of-science objective. The ~800,000-year record, volcanic-marker dating and model-validation step are anchored to the described evidence base.
sourceClaims: Antarctic ice cores provide a continuous record of atmospheric CO2 and temperature spanning about 800,000 years, showing CO2 and temperature co-varying across glacial cycles, with modern CO2 far exceeding any level in that record.

Ice cores contain trapped bubbles of ancient air giving a direct sample of past atmospheric composition, while oxygen/hydrogen isotope ratios in the ice record past temperature; independent proxies (tree rings, ocean sediments, corals, pollen) are cross-validated against each other to reconstruct past climate.

The IPCC assessment reports synthesise multiple independent lines of palaeoclimate and instrumental evidence, and climate models are validated in part by their ability to reproduce past (proxy-reconstructed) climates.
KS3 science 'working scientifically' requires interpreting data and drawing conclusions, including from indirect measurement, and geography addresses how and why climate has changed over time.
learnerActions: Open with the epistemic puzzle on screen: 'Widespread thermometer records only go back about 170 years — so how could anyone know it was colder 20,000 years ago?'

Drag up an Antarctic ice core layer by layer: count the visible annual layers near the top, where yearly snow layers can still be told apart, to establish that deeper ice is older; deeper down the layers thin and blur, so spot a volcanic ash/sulfate marker layer as a dated reference horizon that helps pin the timeline, alongside other dating methods.

Extract/'pop' a trapped air bubble and read a direct CO2 readout (e.g. 'this is real trapped air from roughly 12,000 years ago — CO2 about 250–260 ppm'), noting this is a direct measurement of a sample of the ancient atmosphere, not a model calculation, though it still has small measurement and dating uncertainties.
Read the ice isotope ratios to obtain a past temperature value and place that point on an empty temperature graph.

Cut a tree section, measure wide and narrow ring widths (wide = good growing year), and, using a calibration against recent thermometer records from a site where temperature limits growth, plot a second, independent temperature line for the recent part of the record that tree rings cover (thousands of years, not tens of thousands).

Add a coral and an ocean-sediment sample as further independent proxies, plotting each curve on the same graph over the time span it actually covers (a coral usually records centuries; ocean sediments can reach back well beyond 20,000 years).
Watch a 'confidence' indicator respond as each independent proxy curve lands close to the others — the convergence of records made by different natural processes is the key moment.

In a final mode, overlay the reconstructed curve against a climate-model hindcast (does the model reproduce the past it was never shown?), then extend the CO2 curve forward and see today's value rise far above the entire 800,000-year range.
activities.intendedInsight: Past climate is read from physical recorders laid down at the time, not measured by instruments at the time; trapped air gives CO2 as a direct sample while isotopes give temperature indirectly; and the trustworthiness of a reconstruction comes from independent proxies converging and from models reproducing the known past — not from a single graph.

activities.title: Interview the ice-core scientist (epistemic dialogue)
feedback: Reward questions that probe mechanism ('why does that record climate?') and corroboration ('do other proxies agree?') over simple appeals to authority.
If the learner accepts 'because the scientist says so', redirect them to ask what evidence and cross-checks support the claim.
Model honest nature-of-science talk: name uncertainty ranges and error bars as a strength of the method, not a weakness.
activities.rationale: This nature-of-science/consensus topic suits an in-role expert who can address epistemic and 'is it just one graph?' questions through Socratic dialogue. It is offered as a companion to the reconstruction lab, which is intended to build the mechanism-and-reconstruction core through active doing; the dialogue supports the epistemic dimension and is not a replacement for hands-on reconstruction.
sourceClaims: The IPCC assessment reports synthesise multiple independent lines of palaeoclimate and instrumental evidence, and climate models are validated in part by their ability to reproduce past (proxy-reconstructed) climates.
learnerActions: Take on a questioner role and interview an in-role palaeoclimatologist / IPCC scientist.
Ask directly: 'How can you possibly know the climate 100,000 years ago?' and 'Isn't this just one scientist's graph?'
Ask how trapped bubbles capture ancient air, why isotopes are trusted for temperature, how volcanic marker layers help date cores, and how other factors (e.g. rainfall on tree rings) are handled.
Ask how climate models are tested against the past, and how the IPCC builds a consensus from thousands of independent studies.
Push back with sceptic lines and evaluate whether the scientist's answers appeal to mechanism, independent corroboration and stated uncertainty.
activities.intendedInsight: Indirect evidence can yield reliable, uncertainty-bounded knowledge; scientific confidence is built from converging independent lines and honest error ranges, not from a single authority or graph.

activities.title: Proxy field guide: tap each recorder to see how it stores climate
feedback: When the ice-core callout is opened, reinforce the bubble-vs-isotope distinction explicitly and that volcanic layers date the record rather than record temperature.
After revealing several proxies, prompt the learner to say in their own words why each stores a climate (or timing) signal before moving on.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal diagram names each proxy and its mechanism clearly, which supports vocabulary and the signal-with-a-mechanism framing. It is a scaffold: it does not itself have the learner perform the reconstruction or cross-validation, so it works best as a companion to the detective lab.
sourceClaims: Ice cores contain trapped bubbles of ancient air giving a direct sample of past atmospheric composition, while oxygen/hydrogen isotope ratios in the ice record past temperature; independent proxies (tree rings, ocean sediments, corals, pollen) are cross-validated against each other to reconstruct past climate.
learnerActions: Tap each proxy in a diagram — ice core, tree-ring cross-section, ocean-sediment core, coral, pollen layer — to reveal what it records and the mechanism.

For the ice core, read callouts distinguishing 'trapped ancient air = direct CO2' from 'isotope ratios = temperature', and note that volcanic ash/sulfate marker layers act as dated reference horizons for timing the record.
For the tree ring, map wide and narrow rings onto good and poor growing years.
For sediment/coral/pollen, note the isotopic/chemical signal or dominant-plant signal each locks in.
activities.intendedInsight: Each proxy records climate through a specific physical mechanism; knowing WHY a thing records climate is what makes it evidence rather than a label to memorise.

activities.title: Consolidation check: proxies, sequencing and cross-validation
feedback: For sequencing, confirm the reasoning (undisturbed deeper material was laid down earlier, and a dated volcanic layer fixes a known time point), not just the order.
For the bubble-vs-isotope item, restate that one is a direct sample and the other an interpreted signal.
For the cross-validation item, reinforce that agreement among independently formed records is what builds confidence.

For the calibrated ring-width slider, make clear the temperature comes from an established calibration relationship between ring width and climate, not from reading the ring as a direct thermometer, and that width is also affected by other factors such as rainfall.
activities.rationale: A check-style set reinforces matching, sequencing and interpretation after the detective lab builds the model. As a recognition/short-response check it verifies understanding but does not by itself elicit the independent reconstruction the lab provides.
sourceClaims: Ice cores contain trapped bubbles of ancient air giving a direct sample of past atmospheric composition, while oxygen/hydrogen isotope ratios in the ice record past temperature; independent proxies (tree rings, ocean sediments, corals, pollen) are cross-validated against each other to reconstruct past climate.
learnerActions: Match each proxy to what it records and how (e.g. ice bubble → direct CO2; ice isotopes → temperature; volcanic ash layer → dated time marker; tree ring → annual growth/temperature; sediment & coral → isotopic/chemical signal; pollen → dominant plants/climate).
Order layers/rings by age (e.g. deeper ice = older; outer tree rings = younger).
Answer multiple-choice items on why independent proxies agreeing matters, and on the distinction that bubbles give CO2 directly while isotopes give temperature indirectly.
Use a slider to read a temperature off a calibrated ring width.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate proxy→mechanism matching, age-sequencing, and the cross-validation logic after the reconstruction has built the underlying model.

constraints: The field-guide tap-to-reveal diagram is a naming/mechanism scaffold; on its own it does not have the learner perform the reconstruction or experience cross-validation, so pair it with the active reconstruction task rather than using it alone to teach the core skill.

The consolidation set is a check that verifies recognition and short responses; it does not elicit the independent construction of a reconstructed curve and should follow, not replace, the detective lab.
Teach tree-ring and other proxies as calibrated, interpreted signals, not as direct thermometers — ring width can be affected by other factors such as rainfall, and proxies must be calibrated.

Keep the bubble-vs-isotope distinction precise: trapped air is a direct sample of past CO2, while isotope ratios give temperature indirectly; do not let learners conclude ice-core CO2 is computed by a model.
Treat volcanic ash/sulfate marker layers as dating/alignment reference horizons, not as a temperature or CO2 proxy.
Present the nature of science honestly: include uncertainty ranges and error bars as part of how confidence is built, not as a flaw.

Address both misuse directions of natural change: proxies show climate has changed dramatically before, but the current rate and CO2 level are exceptional — do not let 'it always changed naturally' stand as a dismissal.
A 3D core-handling environment adds little to the core skill, which is reading 2D signals and comparing curves; if used at all it is a minor flourish, not a necessity.

probeDeeper: If only tree rings showed warming, would that be convincing? Why does agreement between ice cores, corals and sediments matter more?
How can trapped bubbles of air be a more direct record than isotope ratios?
What does it tell us if a climate model can correctly reproduce a past ice age it was never shown?
assess.correctAnswer: We read proxies — physical records laid down at the time. Ice cores trap actual ancient air in bubbles (so CO₂ is measured directly, not inferred) and their isotope ratios record temperature; tree rings, ocean sediment and coral layers, and pollen give independent proxy records. Because multiple independent proxies agree, and climate models reproduce the known past record, it is evidence, not guesswork. The IPCC then synthesises thousands of such studies into consensus assessments.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You can't know past climate without being there — it's guesswork'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Proxies are physical records laid down at the time; trapped air is a direct sample of the past atmosphere.
errorPatterns.distractor: Nobody measured it back then, so it can only be a guess.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: dismisses proxy data as speculation

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Ice-core CO₂ is worked out by a model, not measured'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bubbles hold actual ancient air; the gas is extracted and measured directly.
errorPatterns.distractor: The CO₂ figures are calculated by a computer, not taken from real old air.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: thinks CO₂ is inferred rather than sampled

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The climate has always changed naturally, so today's change must be natural too'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Proxies show today's RATE and its CO₂ driver differ sharply from past natural cycles.
errorPatterns.distractor: The records show climate always changed by itself, so humans aren't the cause now.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: uses past natural change to dismiss the human cause

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A climate model is just an opinion / can't be trusted because it's a prediction'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Models are validated by reproducing the known palaeoclimate record before being trusted forward.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats models as unfalsifiable guesses

responseLevels.gap: Treats past climate as unknowable guesswork; can't name a proxy.
responseLevels.full: Explains proxy mechanisms, distinguishes a direct sample (trapped air) from an inferred proxy (isotopes), argues that independent corroboration and model validation against the palaeorecord turn proxies into evidence, and rebuts the 'always changed naturally' misuse.
responseLevels.partial: Names one or more proxies (ice cores, tree rings) but can't explain the mechanism (trapped air vs isotopes), or can't say why independent agreement and model validation make it evidence.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A sceptic says, 'Scientists can't really know what the climate was like 100,000 years ago — nobody was there measuring it, so it's just guesswork.' How can we know past temperatures and CO₂ levels that far back, and what makes ice-core evidence more than guessing?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who thinks the past is unknowable/guessed answers differently from one who can name a proxy mechanism (trapped air, isotopes, annual layers) and cite independent corroboration as what turns a proxy into evidence.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Animal Homes, ages 5–7 — animals make or find many different kinds of home (nest, burrow, hive, web, shell, den, lodge) and these shelters protect the animal and its babies. Second-most-central young topic (0.134), building directly on 'Animals Everywhere'.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' — how habitats provide for the basic needs of animals (shelter); links to the curriculum 'Habitats & Basic Needs' topic.
• Standards — US: NGSS K-ESS3-1 (needs of organisms and the places they live) and 1-LS1-1 (animals use external parts / behaviours to help them survive and meet their needs — building, digging, spinning a home).
• Operational details: teach the distinction MAKE vs FIND (a bird builds a nest and a beaver builds a lodge, but a hermit crab FINDS an empty shell); connect every home to its JOB — shelter from weather/predators and a safe place for young; match common animals to their homes; use a cutaway view so children see the animal (and babies) INSIDE, which anchors 'a home keeps them safe' rather than 'a home is just where it sits'.
• Checkpoint: [Tier A] names ≥4 home types (nest, burrow, hive, web, shell, den, lodge), explains that homes give shelter and keep babies safe, and correctly matches common animals to their homes.
bestPractices: Tie every home to its PURPOSE (shelter from cold/rain, hiding from predators, a safe nursery for young) so 'home' means protection, not just a location — a cutaway showing the animal and its babies tucked inside makes this concrete.

Draw the MAKE-vs-FIND contrast explicitly: some animals build their home (nest, web, hive, lodge, burrow) and some find or borrow one (hermit crab in a shell, animals sheltering in a hollow log) — this adds a satisfying sorting dimension for 5–7.
Use matching as the core activity (animal ↔ home) because the KS1 evidence is 'matches common animals to their homes'; give immediate feedback so a wrong match is a gentle, correctable surprise.
Cover a spread of home types across land, water and air to reinforce the just-learned 'animals everywhere' idea (underground burrow, treetop nest, underwater lodge, garden web).
Keep human houses as a relatable bridge but distinguish them — animals build with what nature provides (mud, twigs, wax, silk), no shops or tools.
keyRepresentations: Cutaway home illustrations (a burrow underground, a nest in a tree, a hive's cells, a lodge in water) showing the animal and its young sheltered inside.
An animal↔home matching board (bird→nest, rabbit→burrow, bee→hive, spider→web, hermit crab→shell, fox→den, beaver→lodge).
A MAKE / FIND sort (built homes vs found/borrowed homes).
Home→material pairings (nest = twigs & grass, hive = wax, web = silk, lodge = sticks & mud) to show animals build from nature.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking every animal builds its own home — missing that some FIND or borrow one (the hermit crab uses a cast-off shell; some animals shelter in existing holes).
Believing a home is just 'where the animal sits/lives', not grasping its job as protection and a safe place for babies.
Assuming animals build like people do (with tools or bought materials) rather than from natural materials (mud, twigs, wax, silk).
Over-generalising one home type ('all animals live in nests') to every animal.
Confusing a whole HABITAT (the woodland, the pond) with the animal's specific HOME (its nest, its burrow) within that habitat.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7 (Animal Homes): children learn that animals MAKE or FIND many kinds of home (nest, burrow, hive, web, shell, den, lodge), that each home has a JOB — shelter from weather and predators and a safe place for young — and can match common animals to their homes. The central activity is an active animal↔home match where a correct match reveals the animal and its babies sheltered inside, plus a BUILT-vs-FOUND sort. Supporting scaffolds (tap-to-reveal cutaway scenes and a short recognition check) and a hands-on 'gather natural materials' step are included to make 'home = protection' concrete and to distinguish the specific home from the wider habitat.

activities.title: Take each animal home (match and peek inside)
feedback: On a correct match: open a cutaway revealing the animal sheltered inside, with its young where that home is used for raising them, plus a short cue such as 'keeps them warm' or 'keeps them hidden'.
On a wrong match: a gentle nudge — the animal politely won't fit there — prompting a rethink rather than marking it simply 'wrong'.
Prompt the child to name the home's job after each match ('What does this home do for the animal?').
activities.rationale: Active matching with immediate, correctable feedback targets the stated KS1 evidence ('matches common animals to their homes'), and revealing sheltered young on a correct match makes the protection purpose something the child causes and sees rather than only reads.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of animals, including shelter.
Animals use external parts and behaviours (building, digging, spinning) to help them survive and meet their needs, including shelter for themselves and their young.

Young children commonly assume all animals build nests or that a home is merely a location rather than protective shelter; contrasting built vs found homes and showing young sheltered inside addresses this.
learnerActions: Look at a scene with several places — a tree, a grassy bank, a pond, a garden corner and a seashore rock pool — and a row of animals waiting to go home.

Match each animal to its home: bird→nest (in the tree), rabbit→burrow (in the grassy bank), bee→hive (in a hollow in the tree), spider→web (in the garden corner), hermit crab→shell (in the seashore rock pool), fox→den (in the bank), beaver→lodge (in the pond).

On a correct match, look inside the opened/cutaway home to see how it protects the animal (eggs warm in the nest, kits deep in the burrow, cubs in the den, bee grubs in the wax cells). Not every home holds babies: the hermit crab's shell protects its soft body, and a spider's web mainly catches food, with eggs kept in a silk egg sac.
Say out loud what the home is for — e.g. 'it keeps them warm', 'it hides them from danger'.
When a match is wrong, notice the animal won't fit and try a different home.
activities.intendedInsight: A home is not just where an animal sits — it is shelter that protects the animal, and many homes also keep babies safe; different animals have different homes.

activities.title: Built or found? (a sorting surprise)
feedback: Confirm a correct sort and name the reason ('the bird made this', 'the crab found this one, it didn't build the shell').
For a mis-sort, revisit how that home comes to be (who made it) before re-sorting.
activities.rationale: An explicit MAKE-vs-FIND contrast directly addresses the common misconceptions that every animal builds its own home and that people make animals' homes, while adding a satisfying sorting dimension suited to this age.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly assume all animals build nests or that a home is merely a location rather than protective shelter; contrasting built vs found homes and showing young sheltered inside addresses this.
Animals use external parts and behaviours (building, digging, spinning) to help them survive and meet their needs, including shelter for themselves and their young.
learnerActions: Sort the homes into two groups: ones the animal BUILT (nest, web, hive — bees build the wax comb, often inside a hollow they found — lodge, burrow) and ones it FOUND or borrowed (the hermit crab's empty shell; an animal sheltering in a hollow log).
Explain for one or two examples how it was made or found — a bird gathers twigs and grass; a hermit crab backs into an empty shell left behind by a sea snail.
Talk about the surprise that not every animal makes its own home.
activities.intendedInsight: Some animals build their home and some find or borrow one — so 'animals have homes' does not mean 'every animal builds a nest'.

activities.title: Explore the habitat scene (tap to peek inside)
feedback: Each tap reveals the home and a brief purpose cue; invite the child to name the home type before or after revealing it.
activities.rationale: A calm tap-to-reveal scene reliably introduces several home types and the 'safe inside' idea across land, water and high places, reinforcing the just-learned 'animals everywhere' idea. It is a scaffold for exposure; it does not require the child to commit to a match, so pair it with an active matching task.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of animals, including shelter.
learnerActions: Explore a habitat picture spanning land, water and high places (underground burrow, treetop nest, beaver lodge in a pond with an underwater entrance and a dry room above the water, garden web).
Tap a place — the tree, the ground, the pond — to open a cutaway of the home with the animal and its young inside.
Read or hear a one-line 'what it's for' and point to where the babies are kept safe.
activities.intendedInsight: Animals live in homes all around us — underground, up in trees and bushes, and in and beside water — and each cutaway shows the animal sheltered inside.

activities.title: Build like an animal does (natural materials)
feedback: Praise correct home→material pairings; if a child names a shop-bought material, point back to what the animal could actually find in nature.
activities.rationale: Pairing each home with its natural material confronts the pedagogy-identified misconception that animals build like people do with tools or purchased materials, and a hands-on gathering step makes the idea tangible. This materials-vs-shops point is a research-informed proposal drawn from the pedagogy guidance rather than a verified source claim.
learnerActions: Gather pretend or real natural materials to make a simple home — twigs and grass for a nest, sticks and mud for a lodge.
Name the material for each home: nest = twigs & grass, hive = wax, web = silk, lodge = sticks & mud.
Notice that animals build from what nature provides — no shops, no bought tools.
activities.intendedInsight: Animals build with natural materials they find, not with tools or materials bought from shops the way people do.

activities.title: Home vs whole place, and who makes it (talk check)
feedback: Target answer: the nest is for shelter and protection — a safe place to lay eggs and keep chicks warm and hidden from predators and weather; the bird builds it from twigs, grass and moss, and people do not make it.

If the child describes the bird sleeping there all year with rooms/furniture, note that many nests are mainly for eggs and chicks and adults often don't 'live' there once the young fledge; focus on protection of the young.
If the child says a person builds or gives the nest, revisit a bird gathering material and building it itself.
If the child names the forest or garden as the home, distinguish the specific shelter (nest) from the wider place.
activities.rationale: Asking FUNCTION and MAKER together separates a child who pictures a nest as a little human house from one who understands a home as protection the animal makes or finds, and it surfaces the habitat-vs-home confusion.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly assume all animals build nests or that a home is merely a location rather than protective shelter; contrasting built vs found homes and showing young sheltered inside addresses this.
learnerActions: Answer: 'A bird's nest and your house are both called homes. What is a nest FOR — what does it do for the bird? And who makes a bird's nest?'

Answer follow-ups: Why do many birds build a nest when they lay eggs? Does a bird stay in its nest all day and night the way you stay in your house? Where is a rabbit's home — up a tree or under the ground, and why? Did the hermit crab build its shell or find it?
Point to the specific home (the nest) versus the wider place the animal lives in (the forest, the garden).
activities.intendedInsight: A home is the specific shelter that protects the animal and its young, which the animal builds or finds itself — different from the whole habitat it lives in.

constraints: Checkpoint (Tier A): the child names ≥4 home types (from nest, burrow, hive, web, shell, den, lodge), explains that homes give shelter and keep babies safe, and correctly matches common animals to their homes.
Tie every home to its purpose (shelter from cold/rain, hiding from predators, a safe nursery) so 'home' means protection, not merely a location.
Cover a spread of home types across land, water and high places (trees, bushes), including homes of flying animals, to reinforce that animals live everywhere.
Keep human houses only as a relatable bridge, and distinguish them: animals build from natural materials (mud, twigs, wax, silk), not shop-bought materials or tools.

A tap-to-reveal scene can teach and check recognition of home types, but recognition alone does not require the child to independently commit to and self-correct a match; include an active matching task for that production.
A peek-inside 3D den can serve as a novelty reward, but spatial navigation is not the learning goal here; the goal is matching and purpose.

Open in-role dialogue is a weaker fit for this factual matching content with 5–7s and can drift; prefer the matching/sorting tasks, using the focused spoken questions above as a check. This is a suitability judgement for this topic, not a claim that dialogue cannot teach.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
All three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their support as unconfirmed.
The natural-materials-vs-shops point in the 'Build like an animal does' activity derives from pedagogy.commonMisconceptions, not from a source claim, so its sourceClaims is []; keep it as a proposal.

The original source rated conversation 'poor' and asserted 3D 'adds nothing' / dialogue 'adds little'; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened to narrowly scoped suitability notes with stated limits.
The claim that a static/tap-reveal scene does not elicit active match-and-check is treated as a narrow recognition-vs-production affordance, not a claim that such scenes cannot teach.

Treating 'web' and 'shell' as protective homes for young is an age-appropriate simplification inherited from the original; it is not biologically precise (webs are chiefly prey traps; spiders guard eggs in egg sacs) and should be refined if later accuracy is needed.

probeDeeper: Why do birds need a nest when they lay their eggs?
Does a bird stay in its nest all day and night the way you stay in your house?
Where is a rabbit's home — up a tree or under the ground? Why there?
A hermit crab uses an empty shell as its home — did it build that shell, or find it?
assess.correctAnswer: The nest is for shelter and protection — a safe place to lay eggs and keep the chicks warm and hidden from predators and weather. The bird itself builds the nest, gathering twigs, grass and moss; people do not make it for the bird.

errorPatterns.pattern: A nest is a human-style house — the bird lives there all the time with its things, like we live in our house.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Many nests are only for eggs and chicks; adult birds often don't 'live' in them once the young fledge. Focus on protection of eggs and babies.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the bird sleeping there every night year-round, or gives it rooms/furniture; treats it as a residence rather than a shelter for raising young.

errorPatterns.pattern: People make animals' homes for them.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Watch a bird gathering material and building; the animal makes or finds its own home (hermit crab finds a shell, rabbit digs a burrow).
errorPatterns.distractor: A person builds the nest for the bird.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a person builds the nest, or that the bird was 'given' its home.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the home with the whole habitat — 'the bird's home is the forest'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the specific shelter (the nest) from the wider place the animal lives in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the wider place (forest, garden) rather than the specific shelter.

responseLevels.gap: Treats a nest as a human-style house or thinks people make it; no sense of shelter/protection.
responseLevels.full: Explains the home shelters and protects the animal and its young, and that the animal builds or finds it itself, giving an example (nest, burrow, shell).
responseLevels.partial: Names several homes and matches animals to them, but explains 'home' as just 'where it lives' without the protection function, or is unsure who makes it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A bird's nest and your house are both called 'homes'. What is a nest FOR — what does it do for the bird? And who makes a bird's nest?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking the FUNCTION and the MAKER together separates a child who pictures a nest as a little human house (where the bird 'lives', furnished, built by people) from one who understands a home as protection the animal makes or finds itself. The 'who makes it' tier catches the very common 'people build it' idea.
