pedagogy.summary: Universal gravitation reframes gravity from 'the force that makes things fall down on Earth' to a universal attractive force acting between ALL objects with mass, everywhere — the same force that pulls an apple down also holds the Moon to Earth and the planets to the Sun. Two ideas do the heavy lifting at KS3. First, orbits: an orbiting body is not 'balancing' or 'free of gravity' — it is continuously falling toward the central body, but moving sideways fast enough that it keeps missing, so its path curves into a closed loop (Newton's cannonball). Second, weight vs field strength: weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), mass is invariant but g differs between planets, so the same astronaut weighs less on the Moon though their mass is unchanged. The most damaging misconception — 'there is no gravity in space' — must be tackled head-on: astronauts float not because gravity is absent (it is nearly as strong in orbit) but because they and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall together. Newton's thought experiment (cannon on a mountain, faster and faster) is the canonical bridge from projectile to orbit.
bestPractices: Teach the orbit as 'falling sideways' using Newton's cannonball: fire a projectile faster and faster from a mountaintop until it falls all the way around — making orbit continuous with everyday falling rather than a separate phenomenon
Confront 'no gravity in space' directly: contrast the near-full strength of Earth's gravity at the ISS with the free-fall explanation for weightlessness (everything falling together)
Separate mass from weight relentlessly with weight = mass × g: compare a fixed mass's weight on Earth, Moon, and Jupiter to show g — not mass — is what changes
Stress universality: the SAME attractive force operates between an apple and Earth, Earth and Moon, Sun and planets — scaling with mass — so gravity is not special to Earth's surface
Use predict-then-observe with orbital speed: let students see that too slow spirals in, too fast escapes, and a 'just right' sideways speed gives a stable orbit
keyRepresentations: Newton's cannonball diagram/simulation (projectile speed increasing until the path closes into an orbit)
Free-body 'falling sideways' vector picture: velocity tangent to the orbit, gravity pointing to the central body, path curving
weight = mass × g comparison table across planets/Moon (same mass, different weight)
Two-mass attraction diagram showing the force acts on BOTH bodies (Sun–planet, Earth–Moon)
Free-fall / weightlessness illustration (astronaut and station falling together)
commonMisconceptions: There is no gravity in space / astronauts float because there is no gravity (they are in free fall; gravity in orbit is nearly as strong as at the surface)
Gravity only acts downward on Earth, or only large/special objects like planets have gravity (all masses attract all masses)
Mass and weight are the same thing / your mass changes on the Moon (mass is constant; only weight, = mass × g, changes)
Orbiting objects are 'balancing' gravity with an outward force, or gravity switches off in orbit (orbit is continuous free fall; the only force is inward gravity)
Gravity requires air / there is no gravity without an atmosphere
Heavier objects fall faster (in free fall, acceleration due to gravity is the same regardless of mass)

learn.summary: Reframe gravity from 'the force that makes things fall on Earth' to a universal attractive force acting between all masses everywhere — the same force pulling an apple down holds the Moon to Earth and planets to the Sun. Two strands do the KS3 heavy lifting: (1) orbits as 'falling sideways' (Newton's cannonball) — an orbiting body is continuously falling toward the central body but moving sideways fast enough to keep missing, so its path curves into a closed loop; and (2) weight vs field strength, weight = mass × g, where mass is invariant but g differs between planets. Tackle 'there is no gravity in space' head-on: astronauts float not because gravity is absent (in a low orbit like the International Space Station's it is still about 90% as strong as at the surface) but because they and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall together.

activities.title: Newton's cannonball: tune launch speed until it orbits
feedback: If a learner expects the orbiting ball to need an outward or balancing force, point out the only force shown is gravity pointing inward; the net force is not zero — it constantly changes the direction of motion.
If they think a faster ball should fly straight off immediately, show that gravity still curves its path — only beyond escape speed does it leave for good.
If they say the orbiting ball is 'weightless' or 'free of gravity', highlight that gravity is fully acting the whole time; that is exactly what bends the path.
activities.rationale: Orbit-as-falling-sideways is a dynamic cause–effect best discovered by tuning one variable and watching the trajectory respond, making the counterintuitive 'orbit is continuous falling' concrete. Newton's cannonball is the canonical bridge from projectile to orbit. A live simulation that holds the gravity state and recomputes the path each frame lets the learner find the critical speed themselves; predict-then-observe strengthens the reasoning. Offered as a proposed interaction, not an empirically validated one.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS1-2 asks students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS1-2, MS-LS1-2]; gravity holds the solar system and galaxies together and controls orbital motions (Kepler's laws are outside the boundary).

KS3 physics requires: gravity force and weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), with g on Earth about 10 N/kg and different on other planets and stars; and that gravity forces hold the Earth–Moon and Earth–Sun systems (qualitative treatment).
learnerActions: Set a launch speed for a cannonball fired horizontally from the top of a tall mountain and predict where it will land before firing.
Fire at a gentle speed and watch it arc out and hit the ground a short distance away.
Nudge the speed higher repeatedly, observing the ball land further each time and the curve of its fall starting to echo the curve of the planet.
Find the critical speed at which the ball falls all the way around without reaching the ground and loops back — a stable orbit.
Push faster still to stretch the circle into an ellipse, then faster again until the ball escapes entirely.
In your own words, state what the ball is actually doing when it orbits (it is only falling — it is just going sideways fast enough to keep missing the Earth).
activities.intendedInsight: An orbit is continuous free fall: in this idealised model (no air resistance), the only force is gravity pulling inward, curving otherwise-straight sideways motion into a closed loop. Too slow and the ball arcs down and hits the ground; from the circular-orbit speed up to just below escape speed it orbits (a circle at first, then longer ellipses as speed rises); at or above escape speed it leaves for good. Orbit is continuous with everyday falling, not a separate phenomenon.

activities.title: Same mass, different weight: weight = mass × g across worlds
feedback: If a learner says the Moon astronaut has less mass, correct that mass is the same everywhere — only weight changes because g is smaller on the Moon.
If they confuse which quantity is in newtons, note weight is a force (N) found by multiplying mass (kg) by g (N/kg).

Check the arithmetic: a 40 kg mass weighs about 400 N on Earth (40 × 10); on the Moon, where g is about 1.6 N/kg, it weighs only about 64 N (40 × 1.6); on a hypothetical world with g half of Earth's it would weigh about 200 N. The half-g world is an illustrative example, not the Moon.
activities.rationale: Separating mass from weight relentlessly with weight = mass × g, comparing one fixed mass across Earth, Moon and Jupiter, targets the mass–weight conflation directly and shows g, not matter, is what changes. A live recolour/readout where the mass number stays fixed while the weight readout changes makes the distinction vivid.
sourceClaims: KS3 physics requires: gravity force and weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), with g on Earth about 10 N/kg and different on other planets and stars; and that gravity forces hold the Earth–Moon and Earth–Sun systems (qualitative treatment).
learnerActions: Stand a fixed mass on a scale and read its weight on Earth.
Switch the planet selector to the Moon, then Jupiter, each time reading the new weight while noting the mass number never changes.

Using weight = mass × g (with g ≈ 10 N/kg on Earth), calculate the weight of a 40 kg mass on Earth; then work out its weight on the Moon using the Moon's g ≈ 1.6 N/kg, and compare with a hypothetical world of half Earth's g.
State explicitly what changed (weight, because g changed) and what stayed the same (mass, the amount of matter).
activities.intendedInsight: Mass (amount of matter) is invariant; weight = mass × g changes because gravitational field strength g differs between planets. The same astronaut weighs less on the Moon though their mass is unchanged.

activities.title: Free fall explains floating: drop the whole station
feedback: If a learner says 'there is no gravity in space', show the gravity indicator still on and recall that at the ISS gravity is roughly 90% of surface strength.
If they say gravity and speed 'cancel to zero force', point out the net force is not zero — the unbalanced inward gravity is what curves the path; zero net force would give a straight line.
Reinforce: everything in the station falls at the same rate together, so nothing feels its weight pressing down.
activities.rationale: 'No gravity in space' is the most damaging, documented misconception; contrasting near-full gravity in orbit with the free-fall explanation for weightlessness confronts it head-on. Seeing the station and astronaut fall together, with gravity shown as still acting, is intended to supply conviction a verbal claim may not.
sourceClaims: 'There is no gravity in space' and 'astronauts float because there is no gravity' are documented, persistent misconceptions; weightlessness in orbit is due to continuous free fall, not the absence of gravity.
learnerActions: Toggle the cannon-and-station into free fall and watch the astronaut inside floating.
Note that the gravity indicator shows gravity fully on the whole time — nothing has switched off.
Explain why the astronaut floats: they and the station are falling together, so there is nothing to press them against a floor.
Predict what path the station would follow if gravity really were zero (a straight line off into space, not a circle).
activities.intendedInsight: Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall together, not because gravity is absent — in a low orbit like the ISS's, gravity is about 90% as strong as at the surface. Gravity provides the centripetal (inward) force; remove it and the station would fly off in a straight line.

activities.title: Talk it through with an astronaut in orbit (Socratic dialogue)
feedback: If the learner insists gravity is absent, the character asks what path they would follow with no force at all — a straight line, not an orbit.
If they reach free fall, the character confirms gravity is supplying the inward pull that keeps the path curving.
activities.rationale: An in-role dialogue may help surface and challenge a child's reasoning Socratically about a verbal, sticky misconception. Offered as a complement to the simulation rather than a replacement; conviction about the geometry is also well supported by seeing the free-fall/orbit trajectory, so pair this with hands-on tuning. Dialogue is one proposed route, not a proven superior medium.
sourceClaims: 'There is no gravity in space' and 'astronauts float because there is no gravity' are documented, persistent misconceptions; weightlessness in orbit is due to continuous free fall, not the absence of gravity.
learnerActions: Pose the question to an in-role astronaut character: 'Is there gravity up here? Why do you float if gravity is still pulling you?'
Offer your own explanation and have the character probe it with follow-up questions.
Revise your reasoning toward: gravity is present and strong, and floating is because everything is in free fall together.
activities.intendedInsight: The 'no gravity in space' belief is verbal and sticky; articulating and defending reasoning aloud can help surface and challenge it. The goal is to replace 'gravity is absent' with 'we are falling around the Earth'.

activities.title: Universality: the same force everywhere
feedback: If a learner says 'only planets or big things have gravity', explain gravity acts between all masses; it is simply too weak to notice between small objects.
If they think gravity needs air, note gravity acts in the vacuum of space — it does not depend on an atmosphere.
If they think only one body is pulled, show the force diagram acting equally on both bodies.
activities.rationale: Stressing universality — the same force between apple–Earth, Earth–Moon, Sun–planet, scaling with mass — counters the belief that gravity is special to Earth's surface or to large/special objects, and that gravity requires air. A diagram showing the mutual pull on both bodies makes the symmetry concrete. The MS-ESS1-2 claim supports the cosmic-scale (Sun–planet/solar-system) aspect; the everyday-object and no-atmosphere points are standard physics not directly cited by a source.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS1-2 asks students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS1-2, MS-LS1-2]; gravity holds the solar system and galaxies together and controls orbital motions (Kepler's laws are outside the boundary).
learnerActions: Examine a two-mass attraction diagram showing the force acting on BOTH bodies (apple–Earth, Earth–Moon, Sun–planet).
State the common rule: every mass attracts every other mass; the pull is stronger for bigger masses and weaker the farther apart they are.
Explain why we do not notice the pull between two everyday objects (it is real but far too weak to feel), and why planets' pull is obvious (huge mass).
Decide whether gravity could act in a vacuum with no air, and justify the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Gravity is universal: the same attractive force operates between an apple and Earth, Earth and Moon, Sun and planets; it is stronger for larger masses and weaker at greater distances. It is not special to Earth's surface, does not require an atmosphere, and acts equally on both bodies in a pair.

activities.title: Check and consolidate: weight calculations and the orbit diagnostic
feedback: A learner saying 'there is no gravity up there' holds the dominant misconception; reteach that gravity at the ISS is ~90% of surface strength and floating is free fall together.
A learner saying 'gravity and speed cancel to zero force' misreads free fall; the net force is the unbalanced inward gravity constantly changing direction of motion.
A learner saying their mass changes on the Moon has the mass–weight conflation; mass is fixed, weight = mass × g changes with g.

A full response explains orbit as continuous free fall with gravity as the centripetal force, affirms gravity is universal, distinguishes fixed mass from g-dependent weight, and transfers to a different planet or orbit.
activities.rationale: An assessment tests weight = mass × g, universality, and the 'why do astronauts float?' misconception, checking rather than building intuition, so it is placed after the simulation. The two-tier design is discriminating because the first tier (does gravity exist up there) is silent — the reasoning tier separates the misconception from the mechanism; asking what KEEPS the station in orbit forces the causal account. Recognition-only items check answers but do not elicit the learner's own explanation, so the open prompt is retained.
sourceClaims: KS3 physics requires: gravity force and weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), with g on Earth about 10 N/kg and different on other planets and stars; and that gravity forces hold the Earth–Moon and Earth–Sun systems (qualitative treatment).
learnerActions: Complete weight = mass × g calculations for a fixed mass on different planets (give the missing weight for Earth, Moon and Jupiter).
Answer the diagnostic: 'Astronauts on the Space Station float as if weightless. Does that mean there is no gravity up there? Explain what is really keeping the station in orbit.'

Give the two-part answer: there IS gravity (roughly 90% of surface strength at the Station), and floating is because the station and astronauts are in continuous free fall, with gravity supplying the inward (centripetal) force that curves their motion into an orbit.
Answer the probe: 'If gravity in orbit were really zero, what path would the Station follow — a circle or a straight line?' and justify (a straight line, because no force means no curving).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidation: apply weight = mass × g numerically and articulate orbit as continuous free fall with gravity providing the centripetal force. Both 'no gravity' and 'gravity provides the orbit' predict floating, so the reasoning must be stated to distinguish them.

constraints: KS3 treatment is qualitative for orbital systems; Kepler's laws are outside the boundary. Use g ≈ 10 N/kg on Earth.
Address the 'no gravity in space' misconception explicitly — do not let a demonstration imply gravity switches off; always show gravity as still acting during free fall.

Make clear the net force on an orbiting body is not zero: there is no outward or balancing force. Gravity is the single unbalanced inward force; 'balanced forces in orbit' is itself a misconception to correct, not a model to teach.

When comparing weights across worlds, keep named bodies and their actual field strengths consistent (Earth g ≈ 10 N/kg, Moon g ≈ 1.6 N/kg); label any 'half-g' or round-number world as a hypothetical example so it is not confused with the Moon or Jupiter.

A static annotated cannonball figure or weight-vs-mass table is useful as a consolidation reference but does not let the learner tune orbital speed and watch the path respond; the manipulation is what builds the intuition, so treat static labelling as a scaffold, not the main activity.
Recognition-only quiz items check calculations and distractor-selection but do not elicit the learner's own causal explanation; include the open two-tier prompt so the reasoning is stated.

A 3D view can convey orbital planes and the Sun–planet–moon hierarchy but adds navigation cost; the core 'falling sideways' insight is a planar trajectory that reads clearly in 2D. Use 3D only when exploring how multiple orbits sit in space; this is a scope note, not a claim that 3D adds nothing.

Optional interaction examples (speed slider, planet selector with live weight readout, free-fall toggle, lift-the-flap 'why doesn't it fall down?' cards, in-role astronaut dialogue) are illustrative of the learning mechanism, not mandatory mechanisms or evidence of medium superiority.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original bestPractices described too-slow launches as spiralling in; for a dragless Newton's cannonball this is imprecise — a below-orbital projectile follows a suborbital ellipse and crashes into the ground. Corrected to 'arcs down and crashes into the ground' in the activity.

Independent review added the Moon's actual g ≈ 1.6 N/kg (~64 N for 40 kg) to the weight activity so the named Moon and the worked 'half-g = 200 N' example cannot be conflated; the half-g world is now explicitly labelled hypothetical.

Source row states gravity at the ISS is 'roughly 90%' (and elsewhere 'nearly as strong as') surface strength; this is approximate and altitude-dependent — retained as stated but flagged as an estimate.

The claim that weightlessness is due to free fall rather than absence of gravity is marked verified:false in the source (NASA/IOP-SPARK misconception guidance); treated as well-established physics but note the specific citation is unverified in the row.

No source[].claim directly supports the universality facets that gravity acts between everyday objects (too weak to notice) or in a vacuum with no air, nor the Moon's specific g value; MS-ESS1-2 supports only the cosmic-scale aspect. These are standard physics, not source-verified.

Legacy confidence was 'high'; not independently re-validated here. Comparative-efficacy framing in the original (that only a live simulator delivers conviction, that 3D 'adds nothing', that a quiz only assesses) has been softened to narrowly scoped affordances/limits, as catalog ratings do not establish necessity.
Self-audit of arithmetic: a 40 kg mass weighs ~400 N on Earth at g≈10 N/kg; ~64 N on the Moon at g≈1.6 N/kg; ~200 N on a hypothetical half-g world. These figures are correct as written.

probeDeeper: If gravity in orbit were really zero, what path would the Station follow — a circle or a straight line off into space? Why?
Newton imagined firing a cannonball faster and faster from a mountain until it never lands. What is it actually doing then?
Your mass is 40 kg here. On the Moon, does your mass change, your weight, or both? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: There IS gravity in orbit — at the Station's height it's roughly 90% as strong as at the surface. The astronauts float because they and the station are in continuous FREE FALL: gravity keeps pulling them toward Earth, curving their straight-line motion into an orbit — they are 'falling around' the Earth. Gravity provides the centripetal force; with no gravity they would fly off in a straight line, not orbit.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'there's no gravity in space — that's why astronauts float' (the dominant space-gravity misconception)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Gravity at the ISS is ~90% of surface strength; they float because they're in free fall, falling around the Earth together with the station.
errorPatterns.distractor: There is no gravity in space, so they float.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'an orbiting object floats because the forces are balanced / it has escaped Earth's pull' (misreads free fall as zero net force)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The net force is NOT zero — gravity is the unbalanced centripetal force constantly changing the direction of motion (Newton's cannonball).
errorPatterns.distractor: The station floats because Earth's gravity and its speed cancel out to zero force.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the station floats because gravity and its speed cancel to zero force

errorPatterns.pattern: 'gravity only acts between huge bodies — not between everyday objects' (gravity treated as non-universal)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Gravity is universal — every mass attracts every other; it's simply far too weak to notice between small objects.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies gravity acts between all masses; 'only planets have gravity'

errorPatterns.pattern: 'on a planet with weaker gravity your MASS is less — you'd have less matter' (mass–weight conflation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mass (amount of matter) is fixed everywhere; weight = mass × g is what changes with gravitational field strength.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says mass changes when g changes

responseLevels.gap: Says there is no gravity in space; treats orbit as floating free of any force, or thinks mass changes with gravity.
responseLevels.full: Explains orbit as continuous free fall with gravity supplying the centripetal force that curves otherwise-straight motion, affirms gravity is universal (all masses attract), and distinguishes fixed mass from g-dependent weight across planets; transfers to a different orbit or planet.
responseLevels.partial: Knows gravity acts in orbit but describes floating as 'balanced forces' rather than free fall, or can't say why gravity curves the path into an orbit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Astronauts on the Space Station float around as if weightless. Does that mean there is no gravity up there? … Explain what is really keeping the station in orbit.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 'No gravity in space' and 'gravity provides the orbit' both predict floating astronauts, so tier one is silent — the reasoning tier separates them. A child saying 'there's no gravity up there' holds the dominant misconception; one explaining free fall / gravity curving the path has the mechanism. Asking what KEEPS it in orbit forces the causal account: no force means a straight line, not a circle.

pedagogy.summary: This lower-KS2 topic makes the skeleton specific: children name and locate at least six major bones/groups — skull, spine (vertebrae), ribcage, pelvis, femur (thigh), humerus (upper arm) — and articulate the skeleton's three jobs (support, protection, movement). It also widens the lens: not all animals have an INTERNAL skeleton like ours — some have shells or an EXOSKELETON (insects, crabs), and some (worms) have no bony skeleton at all — so 'skeleton' means the structure that supports and protects, which can sit inside or out. Teach the naming on the child's OWN body (find your femur, feel your spine's vertebrae) and by labelling a skeleton diagram, then attach each bone to a job (femur supports your weight; skull protects the brain; humerus moves your arm with muscles). The scientific names are new vocabulary worth using precisely, paired with the everyday name. Keep function tied to specific bones, and use the animal comparison to generalise the idea of a skeleton.
bestPractices: Name bones on the child's own body AND on a diagram — locate your femur, feel the vertebrae down your spine — so names attach to felt locations, not just labels.
Pair each scientific name with its everyday name and its JOB (femur = thigh bone, supports your weight; humerus = upper-arm bone, moves the arm), so vocabulary and function are learned together.
Teach the three jobs as a lens applied to specific bones (which bones support? which protect? which move?), rather than as three abstract words.
Use the internal-vs-external comparison (insects/crabs have exoskeletons; snails have shells; worms have neither) to generalise 'skeleton' beyond human bones.
Reinforce with active labelling/sorting and precise vocabulary use; keep to major bones (not every bone) at this age.
keyRepresentations: Labelled human skeleton with the six target bones (skull, spine, ribcage, pelvis, femur, humerus)
Scientific-name / everyday-name / job triples for each bone
The three-jobs lens mapped onto specific bones (support/protect/move)
Internal skeleton vs exoskeleton vs shell comparison across animals
The child's own body as a locating map (find and feel each bone)
commonMisconceptions: 'All animals have bones inside like us' — missing exoskeletons (insects/crabs) and animals with no bony skeleton (worms).
'The spine is one single bone' — it's a column of many vertebrae, which is why it bends.
'Scientific bone names are interchangeable/decorative' — femur and humerus name specific bones, not any big/arm bone.
'The ribcage is solid armour' — it's a cage of curved bones that also moves for breathing.
'Bigger animals have more bones' — no simple size–count relationship; focus on structure and function.
'The skeleton only helps movement' — forgetting support and protection as equally important jobs.

learn.summary: Lower-KS2 learners name and locate at least six major bones/groups on their own body and on a diagram — skull, spine (vertebrae), ribcage, pelvis, femur (thigh bone), humerus (upper-arm bone) — pairing each scientific name with its everyday name and its job. They tie the skeleton's three jobs (support, protection, movement) to specific bones, then widen the idea of 'skeleton' using an internal-vs-external animal comparison: vertebrates have internal skeletons (usually bone; sharks' are cartilage), arthropods (insects, crabs) have exoskeletons, snails have shells, and worms have no bony or hard skeleton at all.

activities.title: Find it on you, then label it
feedback: If a learner feels only one hard ridge down the back, guide them to feel the bumps one after another: the spine is a column of many vertebrae, which is why it can bend.
If a learner uses a scientific name loosely (e.g. calls any large bone a femur), point back to the felt location: the femur is the single long bone between hip and knee.
Confirm success when the learner locates all six on their body and matches each to the correct spot and name on the diagram.
activities.rationale: Naming on the child's own body and on a diagram attaches new vocabulary to felt locations; the national curriculum expects pupils to identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement, and locating and naming the major bones builds on that requirement.
sourceClaims: Y3 pupils should identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement.
learnerActions: On your own body, locate and feel each target bone: run a finger down your spine to feel the separate vertebrae, press your ribcage, find the femur (thigh bone), the humerus (upper arm), the pelvis (hips) and the skull.
On a labelled human skeleton diagram, place or write the name for each of the six bones/groups: skull, spine (vertebrae), ribcage, pelvis, femur, humerus.
For each bone, say aloud the scientific name AND the everyday name together (e.g. 'femur — thigh bone'; 'humerus — upper-arm bone').

(Optional) If using an interactive skeleton, tap each bone to reveal its scientific name, everyday name and job — this is a convenience, not the thing that teaches the names; the felt location on your own body is the anchor.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific bone names attach to real, felt locations on your own body, not just to labels on a picture; femur and humerus name specific bones, not any big or arm bone.

activities.title: Match each bone to its job
feedback: If a learner names only support, prompt: 'What protects your brain? What lets your arm move?' to surface protection and movement.
If a learner thinks the ribcage is solid armour, note it is a cage of curved bones that also moves as you breathe.
Confirm success when the learner gives all three jobs with at least one specific bone example each.
activities.rationale: Teaching the three jobs as a lens on specific bones (rather than three abstract words) ties function to anatomy; the curriculum frames the skeleton as being for support, protection and movement.
sourceClaims: Y3 pupils should identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement.
learnerActions: Match or write the job of each bone: which bones SUPPORT (hold the body up and give it shape), which PROTECT organs, and which enable MOVEMENT with muscles.
Give a worked example for each job: femur supports your weight; skull protects the brain; ribcage protects the heart and lungs; humerus moves your arm when muscles pull on it.
Notice that some bones do more than one job, and name all three jobs rather than only 'holding you up'.

(Optional) If using an interactive skeleton, a 'three jobs' filter can recolour bones to show at a glance which ones SUPPORT, which PROTECT and which MOVE — treat this as a sorting aid, then still state the job in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: The skeleton has three important jobs — support, protection AND movement — and each can be tied to specific bones with examples.

activities.title: Do all animals have bones inside?
feedback: If a learner says the crab has bones inside and the shell is just extra armour, correct it: the hard outer casing IS the skeleton (an exoskeleton), doing the support and protection jobs from the outside.
If a learner says a shell or exoskeleton does nothing a skeleton does, match the jobs across designs: it supports and protects just like your bones, only from outside.

Extend thinking: ask what problem a worm faces with no bony skeleton at all, or why a crab has to shed its exoskeleton and grow a new one as it gets bigger (whereas a snail's shell grows along with the snail).
activities.rationale: The internal-vs-external comparison generalises the idea of a skeleton beyond human bones and directly addresses the 'all animals have bones inside' misconception.
sourceClaims: Animals have different skeleton types — vertebrates have an internal bony skeleton (endoskeleton), arthropods (insects, crabs) have an external exoskeleton, and some animals have hydrostatic or no bony skeleton.
learnerActions: Compare animals by how their body is held up and protected: a beetle or crab has a hard OUTER casing (an exoskeleton); a snail has a shell; a worm has no bony skeleton inside or out.
Sort several animals into groups: internal skeleton, exoskeleton, shell, or no hard skeleton.

Explain what is the SAME and what is DIFFERENT between a crab's exoskeleton and your skeleton (same jobs — support, protection and movement with muscles attached; different design — outside versus inside).

(Optional) A lift-the-flap 'do all animals have a skeleton like mine?' reveal — e.g. a beetle wearing its skeleton on the outside and a snail's shell — can prompt the comparison, but any side-by-side comparison serves the same goal.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Skeleton' means the structure that supports and protects a body, which can sit inside or outside; not all animals have internal bones like ours.

activities.title: Build-and-name self-check
feedback: For a mislabelled bone, send the learner back to feel the location on their own body before retrying.
For a mis-sorted animal, ask where its support and protection come from — inside or outside.

This is recognition/placement practice: a correct match shows the learner can pick the right label, but does not by itself show they can explain why, so also have the learner explain a choice in their own words.
activities.rationale: Active labelling and sorting with instant self-check turn naming into practice and can double as consolidation; keep to major bones (not every bone) at this age.
learnerActions: Assemble or label a skeleton by dragging/writing each bone name onto the correct bone, then check against the correct placement.
Match each bone to its job (support / protect / move).
Categorise a set of animals by skeleton type (internal / exoskeleton / shell / no hard skeleton) and check your sorting.
activities.intendedInsight: Active labelling and sorting can consolidate precise naming and the internal/external distinction, and can reveal any remaining gaps.

constraints: Keep to the six major bones/groups (skull, spine/vertebrae, ribcage, pelvis, femur, humerus) at this age — do not require every bone in the body.
Always pair the scientific name with the everyday name so vocabulary and meaning are learned together.

Tap-to-reveal, drag-the-label and sorting formats are recognition/placement practice; they can teach and check naming and classification but do not by themselves elicit an explanation, so also ask learners to explain a bone's job or the inside/outside difference in their own words.
A rotatable 3D skeleton can help locate bones in the round (e.g. pelvis position, spine curvature) but is optional — naming and function are fully served by a 2D diagram and the child's own body.
Treat the diagram and any screen model as representations; the felt locations on the learner's own body are the anchor for the vocabulary.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row marked a conversation/dialogue format as 'poor' for this naming task; that is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, so it is omitted rather than asserted as a universal limit on dialogue teaching.
The exoskeleton source claim (Britannica) is marked verified:false in the row; the internal/external comparison rests on it and has not been re-checked here.

The source claim notes some animals have hydrostatic skeletons (e.g. worms); activities simplify this to 'no bony skeleton', which is age-appropriate but is an approximation, not independently re-verified.

Original text framed a 'moment of insight' as tied to a specific flap interaction; this has been reframed as a learning goal reachable by any comparison activity, with the flap/recolour/tap interactions retained only as optional examples, not mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: Which of your bones protects your brain? Which protect your heart and lungs?
A worm has no skeleton inside OR outside. What problem does that create for a worm that you don't have?
Why might an animal with its skeleton on the OUTSIDE have to shed it and grow a new one as it gets bigger?
assess.correctAnswer: A crab and beetle don't have bones inside — they have a hard outer casing called an exoskeleton that supports and protects them from the outside; your skeleton does similar jobs but is on the INSIDE. The three jobs of your skeleton are support (holding your body up and giving it shape), protection (the skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs), and movement (bones work with muscles). Same jobs, different design — inside versus outside.

errorPatterns.pattern: All animals have bones inside like us — a crab has bones inside its shell.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce the exoskeleton as a hard OUTER casing that replaces internal bones; the shell IS the skeleton, on the outside.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the crab has bones inside, and its shell is just extra armour on top.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the crab or insect has an internal skeleton under its shell.

errorPatterns.pattern: The skeleton's only job is to hold you up (misses protection and movement).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the other two jobs with examples — skull/ribs protecting organs, bones plus muscles for movement.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names only support; omits protecting organs and enabling movement.

errorPatterns.pattern: A shell or exoskeleton isn't a skeleton at all and does nothing a skeleton does.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match the jobs across designs: the exoskeleton supports and protects just like your bones, only from outside.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the exoskeleton supports or protects the animal.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks all animals have internal bones, or names only 'holding you up' as the skeleton's job.
responseLevels.full: Names and locates major bones, gives all three functions with examples, and contrasts internal skeletons with exoskeletons — reasoning about an animal with neither.
responseLevels.partial: Names bones and some functions, but can't cleanly give all three jobs, or is unsure about internal versus external skeletons.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A crab and a beetle are hard on the OUTSIDE, but you are soft on the outside and hard on the inside. Do they have bones like you, just in a different place? What is the same and what is different about how their bodies are held up — and what are the THREE jobs your own skeleton does?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who assumes all animals have internal bones, or who names only 'holding you up', reveals the gap. Only a child who contrasts internal and external skeletons AND gives all three functions answers fully. The tier-two 'same and different' forces the internal/external distinction rather than a rote bone list.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 7–9 — ocean food webs: multiple interconnected food chains where energy flows from phytoplankton (producers) through zooplankton, small fish and large predators, and removing one species affects the whole web.
• Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2): Y4 'construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey' — the web extends this to interconnected chains.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 5-LS2-1 (model movement of matter among producers, consumers, decomposers and the environment); 3-LS4-4 (effects when the environment changes) — the interdependence and disturbance ideas.
• Operational details: the leap from chain to WEB is that most animals eat, and are eaten by, MORE THAN ONE thing — so the diagram branches. Introduce producer/consumer vocabulary and (lightly) that energy flows upward and thins at each level. The signature reasoning move is DISTURBANCE: remove or crash one species and trace the knock-on effects along multiple paths (a cascade). Keep the arrow = 'is eaten by' / 'energy flows to' convention rigorous.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7–8): distinguishes a web (branching) from a single chain; Tier B (~8–9): traces ≥2 energy paths through a web; Tier C (~9): predicts and explains knock-on effects of removing one species along more than one path.
bestPractices: Build the web up FROM chains the child already knows: overlay two or three ocean chains that share species and let the branching structure emerge — don't present a finished tangle.
Make interdependence testable by disturbance: 'remove the small fish — now what?' and trace effects along every connected arrow (this is the web's whole payoff over a chain).
Keep arrow semantics explicit and consistent ('energy flows to / is eaten by') to prevent reversal in the more complex diagram.
Introduce producer/consumer roles and that many animals occupy multiple links (eat several prey, eaten by several predators) — the defining property of a web.
Use a real, coherent ocean web (phytoplankton–zooplankton–small fish–squid–seals–sharks) rather than mixing incompatible species.
keyRepresentations: A branching ocean web with multiple arrows in/out of key species
Overlaid transparent food chains that combine into one web (build-up view)
A disturbance/removal overlay that greys out everything a lost species fed or fed on
Producer/consumer role tags and an upward energy-flow indicator
commonMisconceptions: 'A web is just a longer chain' — missing that the defining feature is multiple, branching feeding links.
Arrow reversal — reading arrows as 'eats' rather than 'energy flows to / is eaten by', more error-prone in a dense web.
'Removing a predator only helps' — not anticipating cascades (prey booms, overgrazes, other species crash).
'Only the directly-connected animal is affected' — not tracing effects along multiple/indirect paths.
'Top predators are most important; tiny plankton don't matter' — undervaluing producers at the web's base.

learn.summary: Ocean food webs for ages 7–9: multiple interconnected food chains where energy flows from phytoplankton (producers) through zooplankton, small fish, squid, seals and sharks. The core moves are seeing that most animals eat and are eaten by MORE THAN ONE thing (so a chain becomes a branching web), tracing energy along multiple paths, and reasoning about disturbance — removing one species and following the likely knock-on effects (a cascade) along several paths, both up to predators and down to prey. Outcomes are kept qualitative ('may increase/decline') rather than guaranteed.

activities.title: Overlay chains to build a branching web, then pull one thread
feedback: If arrows get reversed in the denser diagram, re-read each as 'energy flows TO the eater' and re-point it; reversal is a common error in a crowded web.
If the child says only the removed species is affected, prompt: who ate it? (they lose that food) and what did it eat? (that may increase) — follow two or three links so the ripple becomes visible.
If the child treats removal as simply 'good' for the prey, balance the ledger: the prey may increase, but predators lose food and that spreads too — effects go in BOTH directions.
If the child reasons as one straight chain, point to a predator with several prey and ask what its backup food is: losing one prey still hurts, but the branching links share the impact.
activities.rationale: The topic's signature reasoning is interconnection and cascading disturbance. Building the web up from familiar chains (rather than presenting a finished tangle) lets the branching structure emerge, and running removals makes interdependence testable and traceable along multiple paths.
sourceClaims: UK Lower KS2 Y4 science requires pupils to construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey.
NGSS 5-LS2-1 asks students to model the movement of matter among producers, consumers, decomposers and the environment, capturing interdependence in a food web.
In marine food webs most species have multiple feeding links, and removing or depleting one species (e.g. through overfishing) can trigger cascading changes across the web.
learnerActions: Start with two or three ocean food chains the child already knows (e.g. phytoplankton→zooplankton→small fish→squid→seals→sharks) and find the species they share.

Draw or drag 'energy flows to / is eaten by' arrows to join the chains where they share a species, so a single line becomes a branching WEB — notice that many animals now feed on, or are fed on by, more than one other species (though not every one: in this web sharks are not eaten by anything shown, and zooplankton eat only phytoplankton).
Check each arrow points from the eaten to the eater (energy flows to the eater); fix any reversed arrows.

Remove or crash one species (e.g. overfish the small fish) and trace the likely effects out loud along every connected arrow: predators that ate it (squid and seals) lose that food source and may decline; prey it used to eat (zooplankton) may increase; follow the ripple to indirectly connected species too (e.g. sharks that ate the squid and seals), which may also be affected.
Run two or three different removals and compare how far and in which directions each cascade may spread.
activities.intendedInsight: A food web is many food chains linked together: because most animals have multiple feeding links, removing one species can spread change along many paths at once, unlike a single straight chain where each animal has at most one link above and one below.

activities.title: Read a web: tap a species to see all its links
feedback: If the child names only one predator or one prey, point back to the diagram and ask them to trace every arrow touching that species.
If plankton are dismissed as unimportant, note that producers at the base support everything above them.
This reading view shows first-order (directly connected) effects only; to see how change may spread further, trace the links yourself along successive arrows.
activities.rationale: A pre-drawn web with highlightable links can convey branching structure at low cost and supports the 'distinguish web from chain' and 'trace a path' goals. It is a scaffold for reading structure; a static view shows first-order effects and does not by itself play out a multi-step cascade, so pair it with hands-on tracing or removal reasoning.
sourceClaims: In marine food webs most species have multiple feeding links, and removing or depleting one species (e.g. through overfishing) can trigger cascading changes across the web.
learnerActions: On a pre-drawn ocean web, select a species and identify every arrow in and out of it — list all its predators and all its prey.
Count how many feeding links the species has to show it is part of a branching web, not a single chain.
For one species, state the first-order effects if it vanished (which neighbours directly lose food or lose a predator).
Tag each species as producer or consumer and note that energy flows upward from the plankton base and thins at each level as it rises (kept light at this age).
activities.intendedInsight: A web's defining feature is that species have multiple feeding links; you can read branching structure directly even before reasoning about cascades.

activities.title: Check understanding: web vs chain, trace a path, predict a removal
feedback: For web-vs-chain, correct answers cite multiple branching links, not merely the length of the diagram.
For a removal, a full response names predators that may decline AND prey that may increase, plus at least one further knock-on — not a single one-directional effect.
If the child stops at the first link, prompt them to follow the ripple one more step.
activities.rationale: Prediction, path-tracing and structural discrimination items check the three stated evidence goals. Recognition/selection items assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction that building and running a web provides.
learnerActions: Decide whether a given diagram is a web or a single chain and justify using the branching links.
Select and trace at least two different energy paths from the plankton base up to a top predator.
Given a removal scenario (e.g. almost all of one kind of small fish is fished out), predict the likely knock-on effects along more than one path and explain them.
activities.intendedInsight: Understanding is shown by distinguishing a branching web from a chain, tracing multiple energy paths, and predicting the likely cascading effects of a removal in both directions.

activities.title: Debate a fishing decision as a marine ecologist (supplementary)
feedback: If the child traces only one direction, ask them to also follow the opposite direction (e.g. after predators, consider the prey below).
If they treat a many-prey predator the same as a single-prey one, draw out that alternative food softens the loss.
activities.rationale: Discussion exercises cascade reasoning and makes thinking audible. Tracing multiple paths precisely may be clearer when the child manipulates or draws a web, so use dialogue to supplement, not replace, the hands-on building and removal work; its relative effectiveness is not established by the sources.
sourceClaims: In marine food webs most species have multiple feeding links, and removing or depleting one species (e.g. through overfishing) can trigger cascading changes across the web.
learnerActions: Take on an ecologist role responding to 'what happens if we fish out the sardines (small fish)?'
Predict the cascade out loud, naming animals that lose food, animals whose prey may increase, and any indirectly affected species.

Answer probing follow-ups: 'the small fish ate zooplankton — with the small fish gone, what happens to the zooplankton and why?'; 'why does damage spread further in a web than in a single chain?'; 'would a predator with three prey be hit as hard as one that ate only the lost prey?'
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating a predicted cascade in words rehearses multi-path reasoning and can surface whether the child can contrast web with chain.

constraints: Keep arrow semantics explicit and consistent ('energy flows to / is eaten by'): arrow reversal is more error-prone in a dense web.
Build the web up from chains the child already knows rather than presenting a finished tangle, so the branching structure is understood, not just copied.

Use a real, coherent ocean web (phytoplankton, zooplankton, small fish, squid, seals, sharks) rather than mixing incompatible species; do not introduce species outside this set (e.g. seabirds) unless the whole web is redefined to include them.
Treat producer/consumer roles and upward, thinning energy flow lightly at this age; the core target is branching interconnection and disturbance reasoning.
A static reading view (tap-to-highlight links) is a scaffold: it conveys structure and first-order effects but does not play out a multi-step cascade on its own.
Recognition/selection items assess understanding but do not elicit independent construction of a web or a traced cascade.

Keep removal outcomes qualitative ('may increase/decline') and cover both directions (predators losing food and possibly declining AND prey possibly increasing) plus at least one further knock-on, not a single guaranteed happy outcome.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all three sources remain marked verified:false and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted an interactive canvas is 'the definitive way to teach' and that 3D 'adds nothing' and a static image 'can't' teach the cascade. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits: a relational food web is not spatial, so a 3D build adds cost without aiding the interconnection insight; a static view shows first-order effects; hands-on building supports multi-path tracing but its relative effectiveness is untested.

The original assessment correctAnswer named 'seabirds' and 'bigger fish' as predators of the small fish, which are not in the stated coherent species set (squid, seals, sharks); the rewrite aligns predators to the stated set for internal coherence and reframes the original seabird probe. Flagged rather than silently adopting the wider species list.

Population-dynamics outcomes of a removal (prey increasing, predators declining) are simplified for ages 7–9; real cascades depend on many ecological factors. Predictions are kept qualitative and framed as 'may increase/decline' rather than guaranteed outcomes.

probeDeeper: 'You said the seabirds lose food. What happens next to THEM, and to anything that depends on them?'
'The small fish ate tiny zooplankton. With the small fish gone, what happens to the zooplankton — and why?' (downward path)
'A single food chain vs this web — why does damage spread further in a web?'
'If a predator had three different prey and one disappeared, would it be hit as hard as a predator that ate ONLY that prey? Why?'
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree — removing the small fish ripples through the whole web. Animals that ate the small fish (bigger fish, seabirds, seals) lose food and decline; the creatures the small fish used to eat (zooplankton) may increase; and predators higher up are affected too. A food WEB is many food chains linked together — most animals eat, and are eaten by, several others — so a change in one place spreads along many paths, unlike a single straight chain where each animal has just one link above and below.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks removing one species affects only that species (or only the one animal that eats it directly)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace out loud in both directions: who eats the small fish? (they lose food) and what did the small fish eat? (it may boom). Follow two or three links so the ripple becomes visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: It only affects the small fish — nothing else changes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says nothing else changes, or names just one knock-on; effect stops at the first link

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks each animal eats only ONE food (reasons as a single chain, not a web)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw two chains that share a species and show they connect into a web — a predator with several prey has a backup; losing one food still hurts but the links branch.
errorPatterns.distractor: Each animal eats only one thing, so it's just one chain
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: describes one straight chain; can't see alternative feeding paths or branching

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes removing a species is simply 'good' for whatever it ate, with no wider downside
errorPatterns.nextMove: Balance the ledger: yes the prey may increase, but predators lose food and that spreads too. Removal has effects in BOTH directions, not one happy outcome.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Focuses only on the prey booming; ignores predators starving and further knock-ons

responseLevels.gap: Says removing the small fish affects only that species; reasons as one isolated link.
responseLevels.full: Traces effects along multiple paths — predators declining AND prey increasing, plus further knock-ons — and explains a food web as interconnected chains where change spreads along many links, unlike a single chain.
responseLevels.partial: Traces one knock-on effect and knows a web has many chains, but follows only a single direction (just predators, or just prey) and can't fully contrast web with chain.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In an ocean food web, fishing boats catch almost all of one kind of small fish that many animals rely on. A child says: 'That only matters for those small fish — nothing else is really affected.' Do you agree? Trace what happens to the OTHER animals in the web, and tell me how a food web is different from a single food chain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands webs traces effects along MULTIPLE paths (both up to predators and down to prey) and contrasts web with chain. A child who thinks in single chains says only the small fish (or only its direct predator) matters. The second tier (web vs chain) exposes whether they see the branching interconnection — the whole reason removal spreads.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4): the insect body plan — three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs attached to the THORAX, antennae on the head, most have wings, and an exoskeleton (hard outer shell) instead of internal bones.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (grouping by observable features; classification). Builds the shared body plan that the 'is it an insect?' and classification-key topics depend on.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 1-LS1-1 (external parts) extended; supports 3-LS4 diversity/classification reasoning.
• Operational details — the load-bearing facts are the count (6 legs, 3 parts) and WHERE they attach (legs on the thorax). Use real specimens/large photos and get children to label and count. Introduce exoskeleton by contrast with our internal skeleton (armour on the outside). This is the definitional backbone for later sorting — precision matters.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): labels head, thorax, abdomen on an insect diagram. Tier B (age 8): states 'six legs, attached to the thorax' and that insects have an exoskeleton not bones. Tier C (age 9): uses the body plan as a rule to justify whether a creature is an insect ('6 legs and 3 parts, so yes').
bestPractices: Make the count and location load-bearing: 'six legs, all attached to the thorax' — children must know WHERE, not just how many.
Use real specimens or large clear photos and have children label and count for themselves.
Introduce exoskeleton by direct contrast with our internal skeleton (armour on the outside vs bones inside).
Treat the body plan as the definitional rule they will apply later to sort insects from non-insects — insist on precision now.
Address 'most have wings' carefully — wings are common but not the defining feature; the six legs and three parts are.
keyRepresentations: A large labelled insect diagram/photo (head, thorax, abdomen; legs on thorax; antennae).
An exoskeleton-vs-endoskeleton comparison (beetle armour vs human x-ray).
A leg-count highlight (count to six along the thorax).
A 'build a valid insect' assembly tray.
commonMisconceptions: 'Spiders are insects' — spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts; the six-legs/three-parts rule excludes them.
'Insects have bones' — they have an exoskeleton, not an internal skeleton.
'Legs come from all over the body' — all six attach to the thorax specifically.
'All insects have wings / anything with wings is an insect' — wings are common but not defining.
'Any small crawly thing is an insect' — the term is precise, not a synonym for 'bug' or 'minibeast'.

learn.summary: For ages 7-9 (Lower KS2 / Grades 2-4): the insect body plan. Adult insects have three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen), exactly six legs that all attach to the thorax, usually one pair of antennae on the head, and a hard outer exoskeleton instead of internal bones. Most adult insects also have wings. The load-bearing facts are the count (six legs, three parts) and the location (legs attach to the thorax). This becomes the main rule children use to recognise an adult insect (young stages such as caterpillars or maggots can look different).

activities.title: Label and count on a real insect
feedback: If a learner traces a leg to the abdomen or head, invite them to follow it again on the real specimen/photo: every leg meets the body at the middle segment.
If they count other than six, have them count aloud touching each leg once; confirm six (if a real specimen is damaged and missing a leg, point out where it would have been).
Reinforce the thorax as 'the part the legs and wings come from' so location is attached to the name, not just memorised.
activities.rationale: Using a real specimen or large photo and having children label and count for themselves makes the count and location load-bearing rather than a recited list. A fixed labelled diagram can present the plan clearly; counting and tracing on an actual specimen adds the learner's own verification. A real specimen may vary (damaged legs, folded wings), so treat the labelled plan as the ideal rule.
sourceClaims: Insects are defined by three tagmata (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs attached to the thorax, typically one pair of antennae, and an exoskeleton.
learnerActions: Look closely at a real specimen or a large, clear photo of a beetle or bee.
Point to and label the three body parts: head (front), thorax (middle), abdomen (back).
Count the legs one by one, 1 through 6, and trace each leg back to where it joins the body.
State out loud: 'Six legs, and they all attach to the thorax — the middle part.'
Find and name the antennae on the head; point to where the wings attach (the thorax).
activities.intendedInsight: An insect has three body parts and exactly six legs, and all six legs (and the wings) attach to the thorax specifically — not the head or abdomen.

activities.title: Bones inside or shell outside?
feedback: If a learner says the insect has bones inside, contrast directly: feel your own arm bone inside, then handle/examine the beetle's hard outer shell. The support is on the outside.
If they treat 'skeleton' as always internal, name exoskeleton = 'outside skeleton' and point to where it is.
Prompt: 'Why does the beetle need that hard outer shell?' to check they grasp external support, not just repeat the word.
activities.rationale: Introducing exoskeleton by direct contrast with our internal skeleton targets the common misconception that insects have bones inside, and the 'why does it need that?' probe checks whether the learner grasps that support can be external rather than importing the human body plan.
sourceClaims: Insects are defined by three tagmata (head, thorax, abdomen), six legs attached to the thorax, typically one pair of antennae, and an exoskeleton.
learnerActions: Feel an arm or leg and notice the hard bone is on the INSIDE of the body.
Look at a beetle shell or a shed exoskeleton (or a close-up photo) and notice the hard part is on the OUTSIDE.
Compare a human x-ray picture (skeleton inside) with the beetle's armour (skeleton outside).
Say in your own words: 'An exoskeleton is a skeleton on the outside — a hard shell that holds the insect's shape and protects it.'
Answer: if an insect has no bones inside, what holds its shape? (Its exoskeleton.)
activities.intendedInsight: Support and protection can come from a hard covering on the OUTSIDE (exoskeleton), not only from bones on the inside; insects use an exoskeleton instead of an internal skeleton.

activities.title: Build a valid insect / apply the rule
feedback: If a learner attaches legs to the abdomen or adds an extra pair, point out which rule is broken and have them move the legs to the thorax / remove the extra pair.

If they count only two body parts (merging head+thorax or thorax+abdomen), use a three-segment or three-bead model — front (head), middle (thorax, where legs join), back (abdomen) — and count three each time.
Praise correct justification that names BOTH the count and the location.
activities.rationale: An assembly or rule-checking task gives active reinforcement and asks the learner to construct, not just recognise, the plan, and then transfer it to classify. The spider counterexample addresses the 'spiders are insects' misconception by contrasting 8 legs / 2 parts.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 requires pupils to explore and use classification to group living things by observable features, for which the insect body plan is the definitional basis.
learnerActions: Assemble a model insect from parts: one head, one thorax, one abdomen, joined front-to-back.
Attach exactly six legs — all to the thorax (middle part).
Check your build against the rule: three parts, six legs, legs on the thorax.
Test whether other creatures fit the rule: a spider has 8 legs and 2 body parts, with legs coming off the front part — is it built the same way? (No — not an insect.)
Explain your decision: 'It has six legs and three parts, legs on the thorax, so it is an insect' — or why something is not.
activities.intendedInsight: The body plan works as a recognition rule: an adult insect has three parts and six legs attached to the thorax, so a creature that breaks the rule, like a spider with 8 legs and 2 body parts, is not an insect.

constraints: Precision matters: insist on both the count (six legs, three parts) AND the location (legs attach to the thorax), not just how many.

Handle 'most have wings' carefully — wings are common but NOT the defining feature. The six legs and three parts (with legs on the thorax) are the key features used at this level to recognise an adult insect.
Keep the term 'insect' precise — it is not a synonym for 'bug' or 'minibeast'. Any small crawly thing is not automatically an insect.

Labelling, leg-count, and fill-the-blank questions assess the definitional facts but only check recognition/recall; they do not by themselves require the learner to construct the plan or justify a classification. Pair them with a build or explanation task.
A labelled picture or model shows a fixed, idealised plan; real specimens vary (damaged legs, folded wings). Use the ideal plan as the rule and note that real specimens may be imperfect.

Tap-to-reveal regions (e.g. select a segment to highlight it and show captions, count legs by selecting each) are optional ways to make the plan concrete; they are not required, and spoken explanation plus the 'why?' probe remain valuable.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Both source claims are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original material notes 'typically/one pair of antennae' and 'most have wings'; retained as typical, not universal, to avoid overstating. Some insect groups differ, but at this age the shared plan is taught as the rule.

The original listed an open-dialogue format as a poor fit for fixed vocabulary; this is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, so it has been dropped rather than asserted as a universal limit. Spoken explanation and the 'why?' probe are still valuable during teaching.

A prerequisite reteach link (internal identifier) referenced for the leg-attachment misconception is preserved conceptually but the internal identifier is omitted; a reviewer should confirm the intended prerequisite topic.

probeDeeper: 'You said six legs. Where exactly do they all join — the head, the middle, or the back?'
'A spider has its legs coming off the front part and has eight of them. Is a spider built the same way as this beetle, or differently?' (arachnid counterexample)
'If an insect has no bones inside, what stops it from being squishy — what holds its shape?'
'Point to where the wings would attach. Head, thorax, or abdomen?'
assess.correctAnswer: The beetle has three body parts: head (at the front, with the antennae), thorax (the middle), and abdomen (the back). It has exactly six legs, and they all attach to the thorax (the middle part), never to the head or abdomen. A beetle has no bones inside — it has an exoskeleton, a hard outer shell on the outside, which protects and supports its body.

errorPatterns.pattern: Attaches legs to the abdomen or spreads them along the whole body, rather than all six to the thorax
errorPatterns.nextMove: Look at a real beetle or a large clear photo and trace each leg back to where it joins — all to the middle. Name the thorax as 'the part the legs and wings come from'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The legs are spread out all along the body
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws or points to legs coming off the back/abdomen; can't identify the thorax as the leg-bearing segment

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the insect has a skeleton/bones inside like a human — imports the human body plan onto the insect
errorPatterns.nextMove: Handle a shed exoskeleton or beetle shell — show the hard support is on the OUTSIDE. Contrast with feeling their own arm bone inside. Name exoskeleton = 'outside skeleton'.
errorPatterns.distractor: It has bones inside, like we do
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says the beetle has bones inside, or doesn't know what holds it up; treats 'skeleton' as always internal

errorPatterns.pattern: Merges head and thorax (or thorax and abdomen) into one — counts only two body parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a three-bead or three-segment model and match to the beetle: front (head), middle (thorax, where legs join), back (abdomen). Count three every time.
errorPatterns.distractor: An insect has two body parts — a head and a body
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names only 'head and body'; cannot separate thorax from abdomen

responseLevels.gap: Miscounts legs, attaches them to the wrong part, or says the insect has bones inside; body parts not separable.
responseLevels.full: Labels all three parts, attaches all six legs to the thorax, explains the exoskeleton is a hard OUTER covering that supports the body, AND transfers the plan — e.g. contrasts a spider's 8 legs / 2 parts as built differently.
responseLevels.partial: Names head/thorax/abdomen and says six legs, but as a memorised list — can't reliably attach the legs to the thorax specifically, or can't explain the exoskeleton as external support.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a picture of a beetle. Point to its head, its thorax, and its abdomen, and tell me how many legs it has and where they attach. Then tell me: does a beetle have bones inside like we do, or something else — and why does it need that?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the body plan attaches all six legs to the THORAX and names the exoskeleton as an outer covering. A child with a fuzzy picture spreads legs along the whole body, miscounts, or says the beetle has bones/a skeleton inside like a person — the second-tier 'why does it need that?' exposes whether they grasp that support can be external, or whether they are just importing the human body plan onto the insect.
