pedagogy.summary: Angle sum rules are the first place children use angle facts to REASON rather than measure: because a full turn is 360° and a straight line is a half turn (180°), the angles that fill a point must total 360° and the angles on a straight line must total 180°, and vertically opposite angles are equal. The load-bearing idea underneath is ADDITIVITY — an angle decomposed into parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts (CCSS 4.MD.7). Taught well, the child sees a straight line or a point as a fixed 'whole' (180° / 360°) that the parts share out, so a missing part can be found by subtraction without a protractor. The conceptual jump is from 'measure each angle' to 'the whole is fixed, so the parts are constrained'.
bestPractices: Ground the two totals in turn: a straight line is a half turn (180°), a full point is a whole turn (360°) — connect directly to the degrees-as-fraction-of-a-turn idea rather than presenting 180/360 as arbitrary.
Build additivity concretely: decompose an angle into two parts, measure each and the whole, and show the parts sum to the whole; then reverse it to FIND a missing part by subtraction.
Use the fixed-whole framing explicitly — 'these angles share out 180° (or 360°); if one takes 110° the rest must be 70°' — so children reason instead of reaching for the protractor.
Contrast the two rules deliberately (line = 180° vs point = 360°) so they are not confused; anchor 270° as three right angles and 360° as four.
Derive vertically opposite = equal from the straight-line rule (both share the same partner angle to make 180°), rather than asserting it as a separate fact to memorise.
keyRepresentations: Straight line as a half turn = 180°; full point as a whole turn = 360°
The fixed 'whole' shared out among parts (bar-like partition of 180° or 360°)
Right angle as the 90° quarter unit: two make a straight line, four make a point, three make 270°
Decompose-and-recombine diagram showing angle measure is additive
Vertically opposite pair derived from two straight-line sums
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the two totals — uses 360° for angles on a straight line or 180° for angles at a point.
Angle measure treated as non-additive / not conserved — insists on measuring every angle separately and does not believe a missing angle is determined by the others.
Does not recognise a straight line as an angle of 180° (a straight/half-turn angle 'doesn't look like an angle'), so cannot apply the rule.
Thinks vertically opposite angles are supplementary (add to 180°) rather than equal, confusing them with the adjacent straight-line pair.
Assumes the parts must be equal (splits 180° as 90° + 90° by default) regardless of the given angle.

learn.summary: Teach children that a straight line is a half turn (180°) and a full point is a whole turn (360°), so the angles filling each are parts that share out a fixed whole. The load-bearing idea is additivity: an angle split into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts. Once the whole is seen as fixed, a missing part is found by subtraction without a protractor, and vertically opposite angles can be derived as equal rather than memorised. The conceptual jump is from 'measure each angle' to 'the whole is fixed, so the parts are constrained.'

activities.title: The shared-whole angle bench
feedback: If a learner expects the total to change as they drag, pause and point to the banner: the parts trade size but their sum stays locked — that is exactly why one part fixes the other.
When a learner first says 'the other one must be 70° without measuring', confirm this is the key move: 70° is simply 180° − 110°.

In the crossing-lines view, if a learner expects the opposite angles to add to 180°, show the two measures staying equal as the lines turn — the pair that always adds to 180° is the adjacent pair on the straight line; the opposite pair adds to 180° only when the lines are perpendicular (90° each).
activities.rationale: Letting one angle grow as the other shrinks while the sum stays visibly locked makes the invariant-sum relationship concrete and lets the child predict a hidden part rather than be told the rule. A live, draggable model makes the constrained sum observable; a static picture can state the totals but cannot show them staying constant as the parts change.
sourceClaims: Angle measure is additive: when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the whole's measure is the sum of the parts' measures; solve addition/subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram (4.MD.7). The whole turn is 360° and degrees are a fraction of that turn (4.MD.5).

The Progressions develop angle additivity from decomposing angles and relate benchmark degrees to fractions of a turn (right angle = quarter turn = 90°, straight = half turn = 180°, full = 360°), the basis for angle-sum reasoning at a point and on a line.
learnerActions: Watch a ray that pivots on a straight line, with two angle wedges filling it; each wedge shows its degrees and a banner reads the running total, e.g. '110° + 70° = 180°'.
Drag the pivoting ray and notice that one wedge swells while the other yields, but the total never moves off 180°.
Say aloud the moment you realise you no longer need to measure the second angle: it is whatever is left of 180°.
Switch to a point version where three or four wedges share 360°, and drag to see the total stay locked at 360°.
Open a crossing-lines view: drag the lines and watch the vertically opposite pair stay equal as everything turns.
activities.intendedInsight: The whole (180° on a line, 360° at a point) is fixed, so the parts are constrained; a missing part is whatever is left of the whole, and vertically opposite angles are equal because each pair shares the same partner angle to make 180°.

activities.title: Hide and predict the missing angle
feedback: If a learner says 'you can't tell without measuring', decompose and recombine first: measure two parts and the whole to show the parts sum to the whole, then reverse it to find the missing part by subtraction.
If a learner answers 90° by assuming an equal split, show the ray redrawn so the angles are visibly unequal yet still total 180° — the equal case is just one of many.
If a learner subtracts from 360° on a straight-line diagram, place a line diagram and a point diagram side by side and re-derive from turn: a line is a half turn (180°), a point a whole turn (360°).
activities.rationale: Predicting before revealing forces reasoning from the fixed whole rather than measurement, and directly confronts the non-additive, equal-split, and wrong-whole errors by making the correct subtraction explicit.
sourceClaims: Angle measure is additive: when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the whole's measure is the sum of the parts' measures; solve addition/subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram (4.MD.7). The whole turn is 360° and degrees are a fraction of that turn (4.MD.5).
UK national curriculum Year 5 expects pupils to know angles at a point total 360°, angles on a straight line total 180°, and to identify 270° as three right angles / other multiples of 90°.
learnerActions: On a straight-line diagram with one angle given (e.g. 110°), state the other angle before any reveal and say why it must be that size.
Explain the reason in words: 'the two angles sit on a straight line, which is a half turn of 180°, so together they make 180° and 180 − 110 = 70.'
Repeat for a point where three or four angles share 360°, finding the missing one by subtracting the others from 360°.
Try a case where the ray is clearly not up the middle, so the two parts are visibly unequal yet still total 180°.
activities.intendedInsight: A missing angle is determined by the others through subtraction from the fixed whole; the parts need not be equal.

activities.title: Contrast the line and the point, anchor on right angles
feedback: If a learner confuses the two totals, re-anchor on turn: a straight line is half of a full turn, so 180° is half of 360°.
If a learner marks vertically opposite angles as adding to 180°, revisit the crossing-lines model: the pair sharing a straight line adds to 180°, the opposite pair is equal.
Praise correctly identifying 270° as three right angles and connect it to 360° as four right angles.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting line and point prevents the two rules being muddled, and anchoring on the right-angle unit grounds 180°, 270°, and 360° in a shared quarter-turn benchmark rather than arbitrary numbers. Recognition and sorting tasks give scorable practice; they consolidate application but do not by themselves build the fixed-whole intuition that the live, draggable model provides.
sourceClaims: UK national curriculum Year 5 expects pupils to know angles at a point total 360°, angles on a straight line total 180°, and to identify 270° as three right angles / other multiples of 90°.

The Progressions develop angle additivity from decomposing angles and relate benchmark degrees to fractions of a turn (right angle = quarter turn = 90°, straight = half turn = 180°, full = 360°), the basis for angle-sum reasoning at a point and on a line.
learnerActions: Sort a set of diagrams by which whole applies: 180° for angles on a straight line, 360° for angles at a point.
Tap a straight-line diagram to reveal '180° = half turn' and a point to reveal '360° = whole turn'.
Build the benchmarks: two right angles make a straight line (180°), four make a point (360°), and three make 270°.
Answer practice items that find a missing angle on a line and at a point, including an item that checks whether vertically opposite angles are equal (not that they add to 180°).
activities.intendedInsight: The two totals come from half-turn versus whole-turn; 270° is three right angles; vertically opposite angles are always equal, but they add to 180° only in the special case where the lines are perpendicular (both 90°), whereas adjacent angles on a straight line always add to 180°.

constraints: Ground both totals in turn (straight line = half turn = 180°, point = whole turn = 360°) rather than presenting the numbers as arbitrary facts to memorise.
Derive vertically opposite = equal from two straight-line sums sharing a partner angle, rather than asserting it as a separate memorised fact.

Recognition, sorting, and fill-in items consolidate applying the rules but do not elicit the independent reasoning that predicting a hidden part before revealing it requires; use them as practice, not as the sole check of understanding.
A static diagram can reveal and label the totals but cannot show the sum staying constant as the parts change, so the reasoning move stays told rather than discovered with it alone.
Always include cases where the two parts are unequal, so children do not infer that angles on a line must be 90° each.
Angles at a point and on a line are planar; a three-dimensional setting is not needed and can distract from the fixed-whole idea.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The cited standards and curriculum documents support angle additivity, benchmark turns, and the Year 5 angle facts; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific interactive design, so claims of one medium being uniquely able to teach this have been softened to scoped affordances.

The core subtraction (180 − 110 = 70) and benchmark facts (two right angles = 180°, three = 270°, four = 360°) were checked and are correct. The original row's wrong-whole distractor printed '290°' while labelling it 360 − 110; this is an original error, since 360 − 110 = 250°. Neither the inconsistent 290° nor the corrected 250° is reproduced in any learner-facing item here; the wrong-whole pattern is taught abstractly as 'subtracting from 360° instead of 180°.'

assess.poeTask: Draw a straight line with a point on it and one ray up, making two angles; mark one as 110°. Ask the child to PREDICT the other angle and — before any measuring — say WHY it must be that size. Then measure both and add them. The reason given before measuring is the diagnostic part: a child who predicts 70° 'because it looks about right' but cannot say the two must total 180° (a straight line = half turn) reveals the additive straight-line rule is not yet there, even if the number happens to be close.
probeDeeper: 'If I'd told you the first angle was 30° instead of 110°, what's the other one? How did you get it so quickly?' — a rule-holder answers instantly by subtraction; a measurer stalls.
'Now there are THREE angles sitting on the straight line, not two. What do all three add up to?' — tests that additivity generalises beyond two parts.
Counterexample: 'A friend says these two angles must be equal, 90° each. Is that always true? Show me a case where it isn't.' — confronts the equal-split assumption.
'Angles at a point make 360° but on a straight line only 180° — why the difference?' — surfaces the half-turn vs whole-turn reasoning.
assess.correctAnswer: 70°, because the two angles sit on a straight line, which is a half turn of 180°, so together they must make 180° and 180 − 110 = 70. (The reason — a straight line is 180° and the parts share it — is the part that matters.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong whole — subtracts from 360° instead of 180° because the two rules (line = 180°, point = 360°) are confused.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two configurations side by side and re-derive from turn: a straight line is a HALF turn (180°), a full point a WHOLE turn (360°); sort diagrams by which whole applies.
errorPatterns.distractor: 290°, because the angles around the point add up to 360°
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 290°, or explains 'angles round a point make 360°' for a straight-line diagram; may give 180° for angles at a point on other items.

errorPatterns.pattern: Angle measure treated as non-additive — does not believe the second angle is determined by the first, so insists it must be measured.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Decompose-and-recombine: measure two parts and the whole to show the parts sum to the whole, then reverse to FIND a missing part by subtraction; frame the straight line as a fixed 180° shared out.
errorPatterns.distractor: You can't tell — you'd have to measure the other angle
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches for a protractor, or says 'you can't know without measuring'; cannot compute the missing angle even though 110° is given.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes an equal split — halves the whole regardless of the given angle, answering 90°.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that the ray is not up the middle; drag/redraw it so the two angles are visibly unequal yet still total 180°; the equal case is just one of many.
errorPatterns.distractor: 90°, because the line is split into two equal angles
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 90° and justifies with 'they're the same' or 'it's split in the middle', ignoring the 110°.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find the missing angle without measuring, or uses the wrong whole; treats each angle as independent and gives no valid reason.
responseLevels.full: Gets 70° and justifies it by the straight line being a half turn (180°) whose parts are additive; distinguishes it cleanly from the 360° point rule, transfers to three-part sums and angles at a point, and derives vertically opposite angles as equal rather than supplementary.
responseLevels.partial: States and uses the fact ('they add to 180°') to get 70°, but cannot explain WHY 180° (does not connect it to a straight line being a half turn) and does not transfer to a point, to three-angle sums, or to vertically opposite equality — lists the rules without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a straight line with a point on it and one ray going up, making two angles. Mark one angle as 110° and leave the other blank. Ask: 'What is the other angle?' — and then, whatever they say: 'How do you know it has to be that, without measuring it?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has only pattern-matched a number can sometimes land on 70°, but the second tier forces the reason: only a child who holds the straight-line-is-180°-and-additive idea can say WHY. A child using the wrong whole says 290° (360−110); a child who doesn't believe the sum is fixed says 'you can't tell without measuring'; a child assuming equal split says 90°. Each wrong route reveals a distinct, documented misunderstanding, and a right answer for the wrong reason is caught by the second tier.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–7 years

- **Topic:** Animal Life Stages

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y2 Animals including humans):** "notice that animals, including humans, have offspring which grow into adults." Non-statutory guidance: focus on questions that help pupils RECOGNISE growth (they should not be expected to understand how reproduction occurs), with example sequences egg→chick→chicken; egg→caterpillar→pupa→butterfly; spawn→tadpole→frog; lamb→sheep; and human baby→toddler→child→teenager→adult.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-LS1-1, nearest anchor):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS1-1]." The KS1 version is the simpler offspring→adult growth idea; the full birth–growth–reproduction–death cycle is the later Life Cycles topic.

- **Operational details:** Teach it as SEQUENCING young-to-adult: match babies to their parents (kitten→cat, chick→hen, lamb→sheep) and order the growth stages. Anchor firmly in the child's own human sequence (baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult) which they can feel and see in family photos, then generalise to other animals. Keep the focus on GROWTH and CHANGE, not the mechanics of reproduction (explicitly out of scope at KS1). Introduce that some young look like miniature adults (kitten, lamb) while others look completely different (caterpillar→butterfly, tadpole→frog) — this contrast is the hook and seeds metamorphosis and full life-cycles later.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈6–7, KS1 Y2). Children can describe human life stages, match young animals to their adults, and explain that offspring grow and change into adults. Appropriate: observing and ordering growth. NOT appropriate yet: reproduction mechanism, gestation detail, complete vs incomplete metamorphosis terminology. Watch the 'babies are just small adults' over-generalisation and the belief that a caterpillar and its butterfly are different, unrelated animals.
bestPractices: Teach by matching young to adults (kitten→cat, chick→hen, lamb→sheep) and ordering the growth stages, not by verbal definition.
Anchor in the child's own human life stages (baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult), ideally with family photos, then generalise to other animals.
Keep the focus on growth and change; explicitly leave the mechanics of reproduction out of scope at KS1 per DfE guidance.
Contrast animals whose young resemble the adult (kitten, lamb) with those whose young look completely different (caterpillar, tadpole) to preview metamorphosis.
Use first-hand observation where possible (classroom caterpillars, tadpoles) so change is witnessed over time.
keyRepresentations: Young-to-adult matching pairs (kitten–cat, chick–hen, lamb–sheep).
Ordered life-stage strips (baby→toddler→child→teenager→adult; spawn→tadpole→frog).
Family photo timelines for the human sequence.
Side-by-side 'looks the same' vs 'looks different' growth comparisons.
commonMisconceptions: 'Babies are just tiny versions of adults' — not expecting change beyond size.
Believing a caterpillar and its butterfly (or tadpole and frog) are different, unrelated animals.
Thinking all animals lay eggs, or that all give live birth.
Assuming animals reach adult size almost immediately rather than growing over stages.

learn.summary: For 6–7 year-olds: recognise that animals, including humans, have offspring that grow and change into adults. Core skills are matching young to their adults (kitten→cat, chick→hen, lamb→sheep) and ordering growth stages (baby→toddler→child→teenager→adult; spawn→tadpole→frog). Anchor in the child's own human sequence, then generalise. Contrast young that resemble the adult (kitten, lamb) with young that look completely different (caterpillar→butterfly, tadpole→frog) to confront the belief that young and adult forms are separate animals. Reproduction mechanics are out of scope at KS1.

activities.title: Growing-up matching and ordering bench
feedback: On a correct pairing or sequence, optionally play a short grow-up animation so the change is visible rather than only labelled.

For the frog ordering, an optional sped-up transformation animation (a tadpole sprouting legs, losing its tail and becoming a frog) makes 'same animal changing' concrete; explain that in real life this takes weeks.

If the child treats a very-different-looking young (such as the tadpole, or a caterpillar if included) and its adult as unrelated, prompt: 'This odd-looking baby and this adult are the SAME animal growing up — watch it change.'
Place the kitten→cat strip beside the frog strip so the two patterns of growth (looks the same / looks different) are felt side by side.
activities.rationale: The objective is matching young-to-adult and ordering growth stages, so direct manipulation turns sequencing into an action rather than a caption. Including one looks-the-same and one looks-different animal surfaces the key contrast that seeds later metamorphosis learning.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2 statutory content requires pupils to 'notice that animals, including humans, have offspring which grow into adults'; guidance focuses on recognising growth (not how reproduction occurs) with examples egg→chick→chicken, egg→caterpillar→pupa→butterfly, spawn→tadpole→frog, lamb→sheep, and baby→toddler→child→teenager→adult.
learnerActions: Pair each baby animal to its grown-up: drag the kitten to the cat, the lamb to the sheep, the chick to the hen.
Order a set of growth stages into the correct young-to-adult sequence; a misordered card returns to the start so the child tries again.
Order the frog sequence: spawn, tadpole, tadpole-with-legs, frog, in order.
Order the human sequence: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult.
Say aloud which looks-the-same animal (kitten→cat) and which looks-different animal (spawn→frog) you placed, and state that each is one animal growing up.
activities.intendedInsight: Offspring grow into adults of the same kind; some young resemble their parent and some change form completely, but it is one creature changing as it grows, not two separate animals.

activities.title: Anchor in the child's own human life stages
feedback: Confirm that the child's own photos show the same person at different ages, reinforcing one-individual-over-time; point out that pictures of older relatives show later stages in a different person's life.
Draw the link explicitly: 'Just as you grew from a baby, the kitten grew into the cat.'
activities.rationale: Anchoring firmly in the child's own human sequence, which they can see and feel in their own photos, gives a concrete basis before generalising to animals whose growth they cannot personally recall. The human sequence (baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult) is given as an example in the DfE's non-statutory guidance for this content.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2 statutory content requires pupils to 'notice that animals, including humans, have offspring which grow into adults'; guidance focuses on recognising growth (not how reproduction occurs) with examples egg→chick→chicken, egg→caterpillar→pupa→butterfly, spawn→tadpole→frog, lamb→sheep, and baby→toddler→child→teenager→adult.
learnerActions: Order your own human life stages: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult.

Bring photos of yourself at different ages (where available) and place them along the baby→child part of the timeline; for the teenager and adult stages, use pictures of older people and say that these show later stages, not you.
Describe what changes between stages (size, what you can do) while keeping it the same person growing up.
activities.intendedInsight: Children experience growth in their own lives; the human sequence is a felt, familiar anchor from which the same young-to-adult idea generalises to other animals.

activities.title: Reveal-the-stages growing-up strip
feedback: Each reveal names the stage and states what changed (e.g. the tadpole grew legs and lost its tail).
Use this to introduce vocabulary; follow with an ordering task where the child, not the strip, arranges the sequence.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal strip can introduce stage vocabulary and young/adult pairs. Note this presents a pre-ordered sequence, so it is a scaffold for introducing the sequence rather than a check of the child's own independent ordering.
learnerActions: Tap each stage along a labelled life-stage strip to reveal its name.
Lift a flap between stages to see what changed from one stage to the next.
Do this for an animal whose young looks like the adult and one whose young looks different.
activities.intendedInsight: Each growth stage has a name and visible changes, and the young/adult pairs can be learned cleanly before ordering is practised independently.

activities.title: In-role animal tells its growing-up story
feedback: Prompt the child to state which stage comes next in the animal's story.
Confirm the narrator is a single animal throughout, reinforcing continuity across forms.
activities.rationale: An in-role narration can make change vivid and personal and suits a single animal's story. For matching and ordering many animals, direct manipulation may be more efficient for this age, so narration is proposed as a complement rather than the main ordering practice; this is a design judgement, not a proven superiority.
learnerActions: Listen to an animal narrate its own change ('when I hatched I was a tiny tadpole with a tail and no legs...').
Name or order the stages the animal describes as it talks.
Explain back that the narrator is one creature at different points in its life.
activities.intendedInsight: Hearing change described from the animal's own point of view can make the same-animal-growing idea vivid and personal.

activities.title: Rear and observe real growth over time
feedback: If a child predicts a bigger caterpillar, a bigger tadpole, or nothing, revisit once the change has been observed: the same creature they cared for became the butterfly (or the frog).

Where possible, follow one reared individual through the stages you can observe (classroom kits often begin at the caterpillar stage: caterpillar→chrysalis→butterfly, or spawn→tadpole→tadpole-with-legs→frog) so the continuity of one creature is clear; if an individual does not survive, explain this and follow another.
activities.rationale: First-hand observation lets change be witnessed over time, which may help confront the 'different, unrelated animals' misconception with a tended individual the child has followed. This observation-method claim is a research-informed proposal not directly supported by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Rear classroom caterpillars or tadpoles and observe them over days and weeks.
Before the next big change — a butterfly emerging from its chrysalis, or a tadpole growing legs and losing its tail — predict what will come next and say WHY.
After the change, compare your prediction to what actually happened and describe the change you witnessed.
activities.intendedInsight: Watching the reared creature change — a butterfly emerging from the very chrysalis the class has tended, or a tadpole becoming a frog — gives first-hand evidence that the odd-looking young and the adult are the same animal changing form.

constraints: Keep the focus on growth and change; the mechanics of reproduction are explicitly out of scope at KS1 per DfE guidance.
Do not introduce complete vs incomplete metamorphosis terminology, gestation detail, or the full birth–growth–reproduction–death cycle at this stage — that is the later Life Cycles topic.
Watch for the 'babies are just small adults' over-generalisation: deliberately include young that look very different from their adult.
Watch for the belief that a caterpillar and its butterfly (or tadpole and frog) are different, unrelated animals.

Watch for the belief that all animals lay eggs, or that all animals give live birth; different kinds reproduce in different ways (reproduction mechanics stay out of scope, but do not let this misconception go unchallenged).
Watch for the assumption that animals reach adult size almost immediately; growth happens gradually over stages.
Offspring become adults of the SAME kind; counter the idea that an animal grows into a different species (e.g. chick into duck).
The tap-to-reveal strip presents a pre-ordered sequence, so it introduces vocabulary but does not check the child's independent ordering; pair it with an ordering task.

Real rearing takes weeks and depends on conditions; a caterpillar forms a chrysalis before becoming a butterfly while a tadpole changes without a chrysalis — plan observation over time and do not expect change on demand.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Optional animations (live frog transformation, grow-up clips) are illustrative interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms.

The source marks the DfE claim as verified:true and the NGSS 3-LS1-1 claim as verified:false; the NGSS standard is the later, fuller life-cycle (birth, growth, reproduction, death) that KS1 builds toward and is beyond this topic's scope.

The claim that a 3D environment 'adds nothing' over a 2D bench is a design preference, not an established pedagogical law; retained only as a note that life stages are a temporal sequence well served by ordering and matching.

Comparative efficacy claims between media (manipulation vs dialogue, interactive bench vs alternatives) are design judgements not established by the cited sources and are stated with may/proposed wording.

assess.poeTask: Rear caterpillars in the classroom. Before the chrysalis opens, ask each child to predict what will come out and WHY. A child holding 'they're different animals' or 'babies look like parents' predicts a bigger caterpillar or nothing; watching a butterfly emerge from the same chrysalis they have tended forces the same-animal-changing idea.
probeDeeper: When the caterpillar is inside the chrysalis, is it alive — what is happening in there?
A baby human and a baby kitten both grow up — what stays the same about them from baby to adult?
A tadpole has a tail and no legs, but a frog has legs and no tail — how can they be the same animal?
If you found a tiny animal, how could you find out which grown-up it will become?
assess.correctAnswer: The kitten grows into the cat and the caterpillar grows into the butterfly. They are the same animal at different life stages — it is one creature changing as it grows (metamorphosis), not two separate animals.

errorPatterns.pattern: The caterpillar and the butterfly are two different animals ('the caterpillar just disappears and a butterfly turns up')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Follow one reared individual through egg→caterpillar→chrysalis→butterfly so the child sees it is the same creature changing form.
errorPatterns.distractor: They are two different animals that live in the same place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the caterpillar is one animal and the butterfly another that happens to be nearby

errorPatterns.pattern: Babies always look like tiny versions of their parents ('a baby frog must be a mini frog')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort young/adult pairs into 'looks like its parent' (kitten, chick) and 'looks very different' (caterpillar, tadpole); both are still offspring growing up.
errorPatterns.distractor: The caterpillar can't be the butterfly's baby because it doesn't look like a butterfly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists young must resemble the adult, so rejects caterpillar→butterfly or tadpole→frog

errorPatterns.pattern: Young grow up into a bigger, different kind of animal ('a chick could grow into a duck')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Offspring become adults of the SAME kind; match each baby to its own adult with real examples.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Suggests an animal could change into a different species as it grows

responseLevels.gap: Treats young and adult forms as separate animals, or insists all babies look like small adults; cannot say a kitten becomes the cat.
responseLevels.full: Explains that offspring grow into adults of the same kind, that some young look like the parent and some change form completely, and applies this to a new metamorphosis case.
responseLevels.partial: Matches look-alike pairs (kitten→cat) but cannot accept a very different-looking young (caterpillar→butterfly) as the same animal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are four photos: a kitten and a cat, and a caterpillar and a butterfly. Which grown-up does the kitten turn into, and which does the caterpillar turn into? And how do you know the caterpillar and the butterfly are really the same kind of animal?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the concept treats the caterpillar and butterfly as one individual passing through stages. A child without it either says they are two different animals, or expects every baby to be a miniature version of its parent and so denies the caterpillar could become the butterfly.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** How Shadows Form

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 3 Science, Light):** recognise that shadows are formed when the light from a light source is blocked by an opaque object; find patterns in the way that the size of shadows change.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No dedicated elementary shadow performance expectation. The Framework develops shadows under 1-PS4-3 — the PS4.B core idea states that opaque materials '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-3]' — with the boundary that 'light travels from place to place' is built through experiences with sources, mirrors and shadows but the speed of light is not discussed.

- **Operational details:** The decisive obstacle is the deeply documented belief that a shadow is a REFLECTION or copy of the object — a dark image that belongs to and mimics the thing (Feher & Rice; IOP). Teach toward the correct idea that a shadow is the ABSENCE of light, where an opaque object blocks light from reaching a surface, and use cognitive conflict rather than telling: move the object closer to the lamp and the shadow GROWS though the object hasn't changed (a reflection/copy wouldn't resize); show the shadow always falls on the side AWAY from the light. Run the distance pattern as a measured fair test against a blank wall in a dark room (torch, ruler/tape measure) — closer to the source means a bigger shadow because the object blocks a wider spread of straight-travelling light. Use sentence stems ('the closer the object to the light, the bigger the shadow') and predict-then-measure.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). At 7–8 success is explaining a shadow as an opaque object blocking light (not a reflection) and describing/predicting the distance–size pattern from measurements. The threshold is dislodging the 'shadow is a dark copy that lives on the object' intuition. The full straight-line ray account (why the shadow shape matches the outline) is formalised later in 'Light Travels in Straight Lines'.
bestPractices: Confront the 'shadow is a reflection/copy of the object' misconception head-on with cognitive conflict — e.g. resize the shadow by moving the object while the object itself stays the same, which a copy/reflection could not do.
Teach the correct core idea explicitly: a shadow is the absence of light where an opaque object blocks light from reaching a surface.
Run the distance–size pattern as a measured fair test in a darkened room against a blank wall (torch, ruler/tape measure), controlling which distance is varied.
Use sentence stems for the pattern ('the closer the object is to the light source, the bigger the shadow') and predict-then-measure cycles.
Surface prior ideas first with a diagnostic (e.g. BEST 'A penguin's shadow' / 'Making a shadow') and expect resistance — conceptual change needs repeated experiences, not a single telling.
Reinforce that the shadow falls on the side away from the light and that the darkest shadows come from opaque objects (linking back to transparent/translucent/opaque).
keyRepresentations: Torch–object–wall line-up in a darkened room, shadow cast on a blank wall
Measured shadow with a ruler/tape measure and a results table of object-distance vs shadow-size
Straight light lines grazing the object's edges to a screen (outline match)
Predict-then-measure recording sheet with pattern sentence stems
commonMisconceptions: A shadow is a reflection or a dark image/copy of the object (so its shape must always match exactly, like a 'dark reflection').
A shadow is a thing or object in its own right — it exists in the dark, just unseen, and is revealed by light.
A shadow belongs to / comes from within the object and simply follows it around.
Shadow size depends only on the size of the object, not on the object's distance from the light.
Shadows only occur outdoors or only in the daytime.
The object 'absorbs' the light and that is the shadow, rather than the shadow being the unlit region beyond the object.

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds learning how shadows form: a shadow is the region where an opaque object blocks light from reaching a surface (the absence of light), NOT a reflection or dark copy of the object. The key teaching move is cognitive conflict — resize the shadow by moving the object toward or away from the light while the object itself stays the same size, something a reflection or copy could not do. Learners also run a measured fair test of the distance–size pattern (for a torch close by, closer to the light source = bigger shadow) and observe that the shadow always falls on the side away from the light. Observe the shadow where it falls on the wall rather than looking at the light itself. The full straight-line ray account of why the shadow matches the outline is formalised later.

activities.title: Resize the shadow: a shadow is blocked light, not a copy
feedback: If the learner says the shadow shows the object's face or colours: contrast it with a mirror, which DOES show the object's detail and colour; a shadow is only the region where light was blocked, so it can only be a plain, featureless outline.

If the learner treats the shadow as a dark thing that belongs to the object wherever it goes: ask what happens with no light at all — no light source means no shadow, because the shadow is an absence of light on a surface, not an object the thing carries.

If the learner is surprised the shadow resizes: point back to the object staying the same size throughout — only its distance to the light changed, so the shadow's change cannot be a property of the object itself.
activities.rationale: The deeply documented obstacle is the belief that a shadow is a reflection or dark copy of the object. Conceptual change here needs cognitive conflict and repeated hands-on experience rather than telling; resizing the shadow while the object is unchanged directly contradicts the 'copy' intuition. Dragging the light, object, and screen and watching the shadow respond live makes the blocked-light mechanism a felt result.
sourceClaims: Documented misconception that shadows are a reflection of an object and pupils therefore expect the shadow shape always to match the object — some describe it as 'a dark reflection'; grounded in Wenham & Guesne (1984), Feher & Rice (1988), Primary SPACE Project (1990), Ramadas & Driver (1989); BEST diagnostics 'A penguin's shadow' and 'Making a shadow' surface it.

Children commonly view shadows as entities that mimic the object (Feher & Rice: ~75% predicted a shadow would be circular regardless of object shape; a 'trigger model' where light merely reveals a shadow that is a property of the object); a shadow is correctly the relative absence of light, not a reflection; conceptual change needs cognitive conflict and repeated hands-on experience.
learnerActions: Set up a light source, an opaque shape (e.g. a star or toy), and a wall or screen in a darkened space so a clear shadow is cast on the wall.

Slide the object toward the light and watch the shadow on the wall grow larger; slide it back toward the wall and watch the shadow shrink — noting the whole time that the object itself has NOT changed size.

State out loud: the object stayed the same size, but the shadow grew and shrank as the object moved between the light and the wall, so the shadow is not a fixed dark copy of the object — it is the part of the wall the object is keeping the light off.

Keeping the object and wall in place, move the light from one side of the object (e.g. left) across to the other side (right) and watch the shadow on the wall move the opposite way (the shadow always falls on the side of the object away from the light).
Swap the opaque shape for a translucent one and observe the shadow go pale, linking back to transparent/translucent/opaque materials.
activities.intendedInsight: A shadow is the absence of light where an opaque object blocks light from reaching a surface; it is not a reflection, dark copy, or an object the thing carries around. Its size changes as the object moves between the light and the wall while the object itself stays the same size, which fits blocked light rather than a fixed copy of the object.

activities.title: Measured fair test: the distance–size pattern
feedback: If the learner predicts the shadow shrinks as the object moves toward the light (inverted pattern): demonstrate the enlarging shadow and explain that nearer the source the object blocks a wider cone of the spreading light, so the shadow grows.
If the learner thinks shadow size depends only on the object's size: point out the object was identical in every trial, yet the shadow size changed — so distance must matter.
If the test is not fair (e.g. the torch or wall also moved): reset so only the object's distance changes, so the measured pattern can be trusted.
activities.rationale: The statutory objective requires finding patterns in how shadow size changes, run as a controlled fair test. Predict-then-measure cycles and sentence stems help learners articulate and bank the distance–size pattern, and controlling which variable changes supports valid reasoning about the cause.
sourceClaims: Year 3 statutory light: recognise that shadows are formed when light from a light source is blocked by an opaque object, and find patterns in the way the size of shadows change; NGSS develops shadows under 1-PS4-3 with no separate elementary shadow PE.
learnerActions: In a darkened room, use a torch, an opaque object, and a blank wall, with a ruler or tape measure to measure the shadow on the wall.
Decide which single thing to vary — the object's distance from the torch — and keep the torch and wall fixed so it is a fair test.
Before each trial, predict whether the shadow will be bigger or smaller, then measure the shadow and record object-distance against shadow-size in a results table.
Complete a pattern sentence stem from the results, e.g. 'the closer the object is to the light source, the bigger the shadow'.
Explain why: with the small nearby torch, closer to the source the object blocks a wider spread of the straight-travelling light, so the shadow grows.
activities.intendedInsight: Shadow size depends on the object's distance from the light source, not only on the size of the object; with a small nearby source (a torch), moving the object toward the light makes the shadow larger because it blocks a wider cone of spreading light.

activities.title: Predict-explain-test: outline or copy?
feedback: If the learner expects the shadow to show the toy's front, face, or colours (copy/reflection): a shadow is where light is BLOCKED, so it can only be a dark outline; contrast directly with a mirror, which does show the toy's detail and colour.

If the learner says the shadow is a dark thing that belongs to the toy wherever it goes: no light source means no shadow — the shadow is an absence of light on a surface, not an object the toy carries around.

For full understanding, look for: the shadow is the featureless outline where the opaque object blocked light, AND moving the object toward the lamp enlarges the shadow, AND the clear-glass object would not cast the same dark shadow because light passes through it.
activities.rationale: Asking whether the shadow shows detail or only an outline, and WHY, discriminates 'shadow = dark copy' from 'shadow = absence of light where the object blocked it', because the blocking mechanism can only produce a featureless outline. The clear-glass and no-light probes test transfer of the underlying mechanism.
sourceClaims: Documented misconception that shadows are a reflection of an object and pupils therefore expect the shadow shape always to match the object — some describe it as 'a dark reflection'; grounded in Wenham & Guesne (1984), Feher & Rice (1988), Primary SPACE Project (1990), Ramadas & Driver (1989); BEST diagnostics 'A penguin's shadow' and 'Making a shadow' surface it.
learnerActions: Look at a toy standing in front of a lamp casting a shadow on the wall. Predict whether the shadow will show the toy's FRONT — its face and colours — or only its outline shape, and say why BEFORE testing.
Also predict whether the shadow gets bigger or smaller when the toy slides toward the lamp, and say why.
Test both predictions and explain what you see.
Consider the counterexample: if the toy were made of clear glass instead, would it cast the same dark shadow? Explain your reasoning.
Consider: could there be a shadow with no light at all in the room? What does a shadow actually need to exist?
activities.intendedInsight: The shadow can only be a featureless dark outline, because it is the region where the opaque object blocked light from reaching the wall — it cannot be a picture (face/colours) of the object. A clear/transparent object lets light through, so it does not cast a dark shadow like an opaque one; without a light source there is no shadow at all.

activities.title: Diagnose prior ideas and check understanding
feedback: Treat a persistent 'copy/reflection' answer as expected resistance, not failure: return to the resize-the-shadow and mirror-contrast experiences rather than simply re-stating the correct answer.
If the learner gives the right answer but weak reasoning, press on WHY the shadow is only an outline, since the reasoning is what reveals real understanding.

A recognition question ('is a shadow a reflection?') can check whether a learner selects the right classification, but it does not by itself show they can explain the blocking mechanism — follow it with a 'why' or a predict-and-explain step.
activities.rationale: Surfacing prior ideas first and expecting resistance reflects that misconception change needs repeated cognitive conflict. Checks that require predicting and explaining (not just recognising) reveal whether the blocking mechanism is understood rather than memorised.
sourceClaims: Children commonly view shadows as entities that mimic the object (Feher & Rice: ~75% predicted a shadow would be circular regardless of object shape; a 'trigger model' where light merely reveals a shadow that is a property of the object); a shadow is correctly the relative absence of light, not a reflection; conceptual change needs cognitive conflict and repeated hands-on experience.
learnerActions: At the start, surface prior ideas with a diagnostic prompt (e.g. BEST 'A penguin's shadow' / 'Making a shadow'): does a shadow show the object's front and colours, or just its outline, and why?
Answer a short check: is a shadow a reflection of the object? (expect resistance and probe the reasoning, not just the answer).
Given a lamp and object at stated positions, predict the relative size of the shadow and explain the reasoning.
Describe what happens to the shadow as the object moves from near the wall to near the lamp, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state that a shadow is blocked light (not a reflection) and can predict and justify the distance–size pattern — and recognise that conceptual change may need several experiences, not a single telling.

constraints: Target understanding at a concrete/observational level: success is explaining a shadow as an opaque object blocking light (not a reflection) and describing/predicting the distance–size pattern from measurements. The full straight-line ray account of why the shadow shape matches the outline is formalised later in 'Light Travels in Straight Lines'.
The distance–size fair test must control variables: vary only the object's distance from the light source while keeping the light and wall fixed, otherwise the measured pattern cannot be trusted.
The 'closer = bigger shadow' pattern is stated for the small, nearby torch used here; it holds for this set-up and is the appropriate statutory conclusion for 7–8.
Observe the shadow where it falls on the wall or screen; do not look directly at the lamp or towards it through the object — the safe observation is the cast shadow itself.

A draggable on-screen lamp–object–wall scene is a model of a real light–object–wall set-up; where feasible, pair or confirm it with a real torch, object, wall and tape measure so the pattern is grounded in physical measurement.

Recognition/selection checks (e.g. 'is a shadow a reflection?' choices, slider predictions, sequencing) can check whether a learner classifies correctly but do not by themselves produce the resize-it-yourself cognitive conflict or elicit an explanation; use them alongside, not instead of, the hands-on resizing.

A labelled tap-to-reveal diagram can name the parts and assert 'blocked light' but a fixed picture cannot be resized by the learner; use it as a support, not as the experience intended to overturn the reflection idea.
Expect resistance: conceptual change here typically needs repeated experiences rather than a single demonstration or telling.
Keep the translucent/opaque comparison tied to material: a pale shadow from a translucent object vs a dark shadow from an opaque object depends on the material letting some light through.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One cited source (Science Learning Hub NZ, including the Feher & Rice ~75% figure) is marked verified:false in the source row; it appears only in non-learner-facing sourceClaims. Treat the specific statistic and 'trigger model' framing with caution pending verification.

The legacy row asserted that a static image 'cannot' overturn the reflection idea and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources, so they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints (a fixed picture cannot be resized by the learner; a 2D view reads the core claim clearly while a real 3D scene better shows Sun-angle/length effects).

The legacy row stated no persona dialogue can carry shadow geometry; this universal claim is not supported by the sources and has been omitted rather than asserted — the hands-on resizing and measuring is retained as the primary mechanism without a blanket claim about dialogue.

Physics note: the distance–size pattern assumes a small/nearby (torch-like) source so that moving the object toward the source enlarges the shadow; with a very large or very distant source the relationship weakens. For 7–8 year olds using a torch this is appropriate as stated and is signalled in the fair-test activity and constraints.

Teaching simplification: the clear-glass counterexample treats a transparent object as casting no dark shadow. This matches the transparent/translucent/opaque curriculum and is sound for 7–8; real glass casts a faint shadow via edges and refraction, which is not needed at this level.

assess.poeTask: Predict what the shadow of this toy on the wall will look like — will you see its face and colours, or just an outline? Then predict whether the shadow gets bigger or smaller when you slide the toy toward the lamp. Say why for each before we try, then we test it and you explain.
probeDeeper: Move the toy closer to the lamp — does the shadow get bigger, smaller, or stay the same? Why?
If the toy were made of clear glass instead, would it cast the same shadow? Why not?
Could there be a shadow with no light at all in the room? What does a shadow actually need to exist?
assess.correctAnswer: Only the outline shape — a dark silhouette, with no face and no colours. The shadow is the region where the opaque toy has blocked light from reaching the wall, so it can only be the shape of the block, not a picture of the toy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shadow as a reflection/copy: 'the shadow shows the toy's front, its face and colours, like a copy'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A shadow is where light is BLOCKED, so it can only be a dark outline; contrast it directly with a mirror, which DOES show the toy's detail and colour.
errorPatterns.distractor: It shows the toy's front, with its face and colours, like a copy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects colour or facial detail in the shadow; says the shadow 'looks like' the toy rather than being a plain outline

errorPatterns.pattern: Shadow as an object attached to the toy: 'the shadow is a dark thing that belongs to the toy wherever it goes'
errorPatterns.nextMove: No light source, no shadow — the shadow is an absence of light on a surface, not an object the toy carries around.
errorPatterns.distractor: The shadow is a dark thing that belongs to the toy wherever it goes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about the shadow as a thing the toy 'has' regardless of any light source

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverted size pattern: 'moving the toy nearer the lamp makes the shadow SMALLER'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate the enlarging shadow — nearer the source, the object blocks a wider cone of the spreading light, so the shadow grows.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the shadow shrinks as the toy moves toward the light source

responseLevels.gap: Expects the shadow to show the toy's front/colours (copy or reflection), or treats the shadow as an object stuck to the toy.
responseLevels.full: Explains the shadow is the featureless outline where the opaque object blocked the light, AND predicts and explains that moving the object toward the lamp enlarges the shadow — transferring to the clear-glass counterexample.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the shadow is a dark outline made by blocking light, but cannot predict or explain the size pattern (bigger when nearer the lamp), or muddles it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A toy stands in front of a lamp and casts a shadow on the wall. Does the shadow show the toy's FRONT — its face and its colours — or only its outline shape? Explain why the shadow looks the way it does.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks a shadow is a reflection or a dark copy expects to see the toy's front and colours in it. Asking whether the shadow shows detail or just an outline, and WHY, separates 'shadow = dark copy' from 'shadow = the absence of light where the object blocked it'. The blocking mechanism can only produce a featureless outline, so the reasoning gives it away.
