pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Sound Fading with Distance

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 4 Sound):** Pupils should recognise that sounds get fainter as the distance from the sound source increases.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no direct elementary PE):** There is no elementary NGSS performance expectation for sound attenuating with distance. The nearest conceptual anchor is 4-PS4-1 ("[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-1]"), since fading is the amplitude at the ear falling as the vibration spreads; the quantitative spreading/attenuation idea sits at MS-PS4 and above. This topic is therefore UK-anchored, stated honestly.

- **Operational details:** Children establish the pattern that a sound gets quieter the further you are from its source, and — crucially — the RIGHT reason for it: the sound vibrations spread out in all directions from the source, so the further away you are, the smaller the share of that spreading vibration your ear catches. Best taught as a measured fair-test investigation: fix one source (a buzzer, a ticking timer, a speaker at constant volume) and measure loudness with a sound-level app at marked, increasing distances, then record and graph the falling pattern. Frame the cause as SPREADING, not slowing and not 'running out': contrast a torch beam (only some of a circle of children see it) with a sound all of them hear, to show sound spreads in every direction. Explicitly head off the speed misconception — how FAST sound travels depends only on the material, never on distance or loudness. Connect back to the prerequisite that loudness = size of vibration: spread-thin vibrations arrive smaller at a distant ear.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can predict and confirm by measurement that loudness falls with distance, and can explain it as the vibrations spreading out in all directions (so a distant ear catches less) rather than the sound slowing down or simply stopping. Mastery is the correct spreading explanation for an observed, graphed pattern — not a quantitative inverse-square relationship (Tier C, teacher background).
bestPractices: Run it as a measured fair test: one fixed source, a sound-level app, loudness read at marked increasing distances, then recorded and graphed so the falling pattern is the child's own data.
Frame the cause as vibrations SPREADING OUT in all directions (so a distant ear catches a smaller share) — not the sound slowing down, and not simply 'running out'.
Explicitly refute the speed misconception: how fast sound travels depends only on the material it travels through, never on distance or loudness.
Use the torch-beam-vs-all-around-source contrast (only some of a circle see the beam, but all hear the sound) to show sound spreads in every direction, underpinning why it fades.
Have children draw, then revisit and improve, a diagram of how the sound travels from the source — surfacing and correcting the 'one-direction' and 'sound-as-object' ideas.
Tie back to the prerequisite loudness = size of vibration: because the vibration is spread thin far away, it arrives smaller at the ear and sounds quieter.
keyRepresentations: Concentric rings / ripples expanding and thinning from a central source (top-down) — the spreading model made visible.
Sound-level (decibel) app readings taken at marked distances — the measured, objective pattern.
A distance-versus-loudness line graph that falls with distance.
Torch beam versus all-around sound source — contrasting one-directional light with sound spreading in every direction.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking sound gets fainter because it SLOWS DOWN with distance — in fact speed depends only on the medium, not on distance or loudness.
Thinking sound travels only towards the listener (one direction, like a torch beam) rather than spreading out in all directions.
'Sound just dies away / runs out' as a vague catch-all, instead of the same energy being spread over an ever-larger area.
Treating sound as an object/blob that travels and shrinks, rather than a spreading vibration — a process.
Confusing fainter-with-distance with being blocked or muffled by a material (a different cause entirely).

learn.summary: For 8–9 year-olds (UK Year 4 Sound): sounds get fainter as distance from the source increases, and the correct reason is that vibrations spread out in all directions, so a distant ear catches a smaller share of the same spreading vibration. Key goals: establish the distance→loudness pattern through measurement, pin the cause as SPREADING (not slowing, not 'running out', not a shrinking object), and explicitly refute the misconception that sound slows with distance (speed is set by the medium and its conditions, not by distance). Mastery is the correct spreading explanation for an observed, graphed pattern — not a quantitative inverse-square law (teacher background only).

activities.title: Measured fair test: loudness versus distance
feedback: If the graph shows loudness rising with distance, check that the source volume stayed constant, that distances were measured from the same source point, that the device was held the same way each time, and that echoes from walls or background noise did not affect a reading. Repeat the readings to check.

If the child expects loudness to snap to zero past a certain line, point out that the readings fall gradually and stay above the room's background level. Sound thins gradually; it does not stop at an edge.
Praise naming the controlled variable (constant source volume) as what makes this a fair test.
activities.rationale: A measured, graphed investigation makes the distance→loudness pattern the child's own evidence and matches the UK objective that pupils recognise sounds get fainter with distance.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should recognise that sounds get fainter as the distance from the sound source increases.
learnerActions: Fix one constant sound source (a buzzer, a ticking timer, or a speaker at a steady volume) in one place.
Mark increasing distances from the source on the floor (for example 1 m, 2 m, 4 m, 8 m).
Use a sound-level (decibel) app to read the loudness at each marked distance, keeping the source volume unchanged.
Record each reading and plot a distance-versus-loudness line graph.

Describe the pattern in your own words: as distance goes up, loudness generally goes down. Check whether your graph falls gradually rather than dropping to zero at a line. Small bumps can come from echoes or background noise.
activities.intendedInsight: Loudness falls as distance from a fixed source increases, and the falling pattern is the child's own measured data.

activities.title: Explore the spreading cause with a top-down ripple model
feedback: If a child predicts the meter will snap to zero at some distance, show the smooth fall and connect it to their measured graph.
If a child says the distant sound is slower, point to the constant speed readout: speed does not change with distance.
When the 'why?' overlay is used, prompt the child to say the share of the ring is smaller far away, not that the sound got used up.
activities.rationale: Letting distance and loudness co-vary while the child causes the change makes the spreading explanation observable rather than merely told; the constant speed readout directly confronts the slowing misconception. A live model is proposed here as one effective way to make co-variation visible, not as the only method; efficacy is untested.
sourceClaims: Sound vibrations spread out in all directions from the source; the loudness reaching a detector depends on the size of the source's vibration, the distance from the source (because the vibrations spread out in all directions), and the medium. Pupils commonly misattribute the fading to a change in the SPEED of sound — but speed depends only on the material the sound travels through, not on distance or loudness.

Sound is best modelled with a source–medium–detector frame; as vibrations travel away from the source they spread and the sounds we hear become quieter. Children readily say sound 'dies away' but need a more precise idea; some treat sound as an object that travels rather than a process.
learnerActions: Watch a source at the centre of a top-down room pulse and send concentric rings (ripples) expanding outward in ALL directions and visibly thinning as they grow.
Drag an ear/detector around the room and watch a loudness meter read high near the source and fall smoothly as you pull the ear away.
Turn on a 'why?' overlay that highlights the ever-smaller slice of each expanding ring the distant ear actually catches.
Check a separate 'speed' readout that stays constant wherever the ear is placed, and say what that tells you about how fast sound travels.
Take a predict-then-place challenge: before dragging, say where the ear should go for the meter to show about half its close-up reading, then test your prediction.
activities.intendedInsight: The SAME vibration is shared over a bigger and bigger circle as it spreads, so any one ear far away catches less — that is why it is fainter, while the speed stays the same.

activities.title: Torch beam versus all-around sound
feedback: If a child says sound 'aims' at the listener, use the opposite-sides test: both friends hear it, so the sound went both ways (and all ways) at once.
Reinforce that 'everyone hears it' is evidence of spreading in all directions, not of the sound choosing a direction.
activities.rationale: The torch-vs-source contrast surfaces and corrects the 'sound travels one way' misconception by direct comparison.
sourceClaims: Children may think sound travels only to the listener (one direction, like a torch beam); in fact vibrations spread out in all directions — a contrast used to explain why sound fades with distance.
learnerActions: Shine a torch beam across a circle of classmates and notice that the beam mainly lights up the few in its path.
Make a sound (clap, drum, buzzer) from the same centre spot and notice everyone in the circle hears it, whichever direction they stand.
Stand with a friend the same distance from a drum but on opposite sides; both listen and compare whether you both hear it.
Explain what the difference shows: a torch is designed to send its light mostly one way, but sound from a clap or drum spreads out in every direction from its source.
activities.intendedInsight: Sound spreads in all directions (concentric), unlike a one-directional torch beam; this is why a listener anywhere around the source hears it, and why the share thins with distance.

activities.title: Draw, test, and improve your sound-travel diagram
feedback: If a drawing shows the sound as a shrinking object/blob, point out it is a process: the same vibration spread over a larger area, not a thing getting smaller.
If only a single arrow to the listener is drawn, ask how a friend on the opposite side still hears it, then add rings in all directions.
activities.rationale: Tying back to the prerequisite that loudness depends on the size of the vibration helps children explain the far ear hearing a smaller, spread-thin vibration; revisiting a diagram makes the conceptual change explicit.
sourceClaims: Sound is best modelled with a source–medium–detector frame; as vibrations travel away from the source they spread and the sounds we hear become quieter. Children readily say sound 'dies away' but need a more precise idea; some treat sound as an object that travels rather than a process.
learnerActions: Draw how you think the sound travels from the source to a listener.
After the investigation and the spreading model, revisit your diagram and change anything that now looks wrong.
Add concentric rings expanding and thinning from the source if your first drawing showed a single arrow or a shrinking blob.
Write one sentence saying why the far ear hears less: the vibration is spread thin over a bigger area, so a smaller share reaches it.
activities.intendedInsight: Capturing and then revising an initial drawing surfaces 'one-direction' and 'sound-as-object' ideas and replaces them with a spreading-process picture.

activities.title: Check and sort: what changes loudness versus speed
feedback: If 'the sound slows down' is chosen, remind that speed is set by the material, not distance; a faint far sound and a loud near sound travel at the same speed.
If 'the sound runs out' is chosen, restate it is the same vibration spread over a bigger area, not a supply being exhausted.
activities.rationale: Ordering, estimating and a targeted multiple choice with the core misconception as an option confirm the pattern and the target reason. These checks can verify classification and the chosen reason but do not by themselves let a child discover the spreading cause, so pair them with the investigation and model.
sourceClaims: Sound vibrations spread out in all directions from the source; the loudness reaching a detector depends on the size of the source's vibration, the distance from the source (because the vibrations spread out in all directions), and the medium. Pupils commonly misattribute the fading to a change in the SPEED of sound — but speed depends only on the material the sound travels through, not on distance or loudness.
learnerActions: Estimate how loud the buzzer is at a given distance (for example 8 m) compared with up close.
Put four distances in order from quietest to loudest.
Answer 'why is it fainter far away?' by choosing 'the vibrations spread out' rather than 'the sound slows down' or 'the sound runs out'.
Sort scenarios into 'changes loudness' versus 'changes speed' — noticing that moving further away changes loudness, while the medium sets the speed.
activities.intendedInsight: The pattern and its correct cause can be confirmed, keeping 'quieter' distinct from 'slower' and from 'used up'.

activities.title: Diagnostic: is the drummer's sound slowing down?
feedback: Full response: fainter because the vibrations spread out in all directions, so a far ear catches only a small share, AND the speed is unchanged (set by the air).

Partial response (knows the pattern but blames slowing/weakening): the near and far beats travel at the same speed — the far one is only fainter, not slowed. Over a classroom distance any delay is negligible, so what changed is the loudness, not the speed.

On the timing probe: a far beat may reach the ear a fraction later because it has further to travel, but it travels at the same speed — so the change the child should name is loudness, not speed. (At stadium distances the delay becomes noticeable, still without any change in speed.)
Gap response (blames slowing or running out, or one-direction beaming): revisit the opposite-sides test and the ripple model showing all-directional spreading.
activities.rationale: Offering the speed explanation as bait discriminates children who hold the spreading concept from those who conflate 'quieter' with 'slower'; the timing probe keeps the focus on constant speed while allowing that extra distance adds a small, real travel delay.
sourceClaims: Sound vibrations spread out in all directions from the source; the loudness reaching a detector depends on the size of the source's vibration, the distance from the source (because the vibrations spread out in all directions), and the medium. Pupils commonly misattribute the fading to a change in the SPEED of sound — but speed depends only on the material the sound travels through, not on distance or loudness.
learnerActions: Read the scenario: a drummer plays a steady beat; you walk far away and the drum sounds much fainter. A friend says 'that's because the sound is slowing down as it travels to you.'
Decide whether the friend is right and explain what is really making it fainter.

Answer probe questions: if you and a friend stand the same distance but on opposite sides of the drum, do you both hear it, and what does that show? Does the faint far beat reach you much later than a near one, and what does that tell you about the speed of the sound? Why can a whole stadium hear one loudspeaker but it is quieter at the back?
activities.intendedInsight: A full explanation rejects slowing (speed is set by the medium) and attributes fading to vibrations spreading in all directions so a distant ear catches a smaller share — and transfers to the stadium and opposite-sides cases.

constraints: Target mastery is the correct spreading explanation for an observed, graphed pattern — NOT a quantitative inverse-square relationship, which is teacher background for this age.
Frame the cause as vibrations spreading over an ever-larger area, not the sound slowing, 'running out', or being a shrinking object.
Keep speed and loudness distinct: how fast sound travels depends on the medium and its conditions (such as air temperature), not on distance or loudness.
Distinguish fainter-with-distance from being blocked or muffled by a material — those are different causes.

A sound does take slightly longer to reach a far listener (from the extra distance, not from slowing); keep the lesson point as constant speed, treat the delay as negligible at the short classroom distances used here, and do not mark 'arrives a little later but at the same speed' as wrong.
Check-and-sort tasks confirm the pattern and chosen reason but do not by themselves let a child discover the spreading cause; use them alongside the measured investigation and the ripple model.
A static concentric-rings diagram can label and name the spreading model but cannot let distance and loudness co-vary; treat it as a reference companion, not the core experience.

Sound genuinely spreads spherically; a 3D expanding-sphere model is the most truthful picture but adds navigation cost without clear benefit at this tier — the top-down 2D rings capture the pattern and explanation. 3D is an optional extension, not a requirement.

The live-model details (expanding ripples, draggable ear, falling meter, constant speed readout, predict-then-place, 'why?' overlay) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms or a specific product.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four sources were marked verified:false in the legacy row (IOPSpark 'A sequence to develop ideas about hearing'; Oak National Academy 'How vibrations travel'). Treat claims drawn from them as unverified.

The US NGSS note in the source states there is no direct elementary performance expectation for sound attenuating with distance; this topic is UK-anchored. 4-PS4-1 is only a loose conceptual anchor, not a direct standard match.

The timing probe is pitched at constant speed; strictly, a far sound arrives after a small propagation delay (from distance, not slowing). The probe wording and feedback now accept 'a little later but same speed' and reserve 'normal time' as a classroom-distance approximation rather than a literal truth.

Self-audit: no arithmetic or force/motion claims required correction. The key physics claim (speed set by the medium, fading from spreading) is internally consistent across the activities and sources.

The legacy 'conversation' artefact was rated poor fit with the reasoning that an in-role character 'cannot deliver the observe–measure–explain experience'; this is a catalog preference, not an established law. Dialogue is not included as a core activity because this objective needs measurement and a drawn/spoken explanation, but a brief spoken prediction before testing remains acceptable.

assess.poeTask: Predict: if we clap loudly and three of you stand the same distance away but in different directions (in front, to the side, behind), will all three hear it, or only the one it's 'aimed' at? Say why first, then we try it and you explain.
probeDeeper: If you and a friend stand the same distance from the drum but on opposite sides, do you BOTH hear it? What does that tell you about which way the sound went?
Does the faint, far-away beat reach you noticeably LATER, or at the normal time? What does that say about its speed?
Why can a whole stadium hear one loudspeaker, but it's quieter at the back?
assess.correctAnswer: No. The sound does not slow down — its speed depends on the material it travels through (the air), not on distance. It gets fainter because the vibrations spread out in all directions as they travel, so by the time they reach a far-away ear, that ear catches only a small share of them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fading equals slowing: 'the sound slows down as it travels, so it gets fainter'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Speed depends only on the medium, never on distance or loudness — a faint far sound and a loud near sound travel at the same speed. Hold speed constant while loudness drops.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the sound slows down as it travels, so it gets fainter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes the fading to a drop in speed

errorPatterns.pattern: Sound beams one way like a torch: 'it goes in a straight line to you and just weakens along that line'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sound spreads in ALL directions (concentric); a listener anywhere around catches a share, and that share thins with distance.
errorPatterns.distractor: The sound beams straight at you and just weakens on the way.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says or draws the sound going in one direction toward the listener

errorPatterns.pattern: Sound as an object that shrinks: 'the sound gets smaller or uses itself up, like a shrinking thing'
errorPatterns.nextMove: It's a spreading process, not a shrinking object — the same vibration spreads over a bigger and bigger area, so each part is weaker.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about the sound shrinking or being used up as if it were an object

responseLevels.gap: Blames the fading on the sound slowing down or running out, or thinks sound beams one way to the listener.
responseLevels.full: Explains fainter = vibrations spread out in all directions so a distant ear catches a smaller share, AND holds that the speed is unchanged (set by the medium), transferring to the stadium and opposite-sides cases.
responseLevels.partial: Knows sound gets fainter with distance and can describe the pattern, but attributes it to slowing/weakening rather than to vibrations spreading out and being shared.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A drummer plays a steady beat. You walk far away and the drum sounds much fainter. Your friend says 'that's because the sound is slowing down as it travels to you.' Is your friend right? Explain what is really making it fainter.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The intuitive story is that a fading sound is 'running down' or slowing. The prompt offers the speed explanation as bait; a child with the concept rejects it (speed is fixed by the medium) and instead invokes the vibrations spreading out and being shared. Distinguishing 'quieter' from 'slower' is the whole game.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to read and use the £ and p symbols and to combine coins to make a stated amount. The language work is: saying and writing amounts correctly ('fifty pence' = 50p; 'one pound fifty'), reading prices, and — the key notation rule — NOT writing £ and p together (£1.50p is wrong; write 150p, or £1 and 50p, or £1.50). At Year 2 pounds and pence are recorded separately, and the same amount has more than one correct written form (150p is the same money as £1 and 50p). Taught by using money language in real shop / price contexts and listening for correct USE.
bestPractices: Use £ and p in real contexts — price tags, shopping role-play — and listen for correct use
Read amounts aloud both ways (150p / one pound fifty) and match them to written prices
Teach the notation rule explicitly: never write £ and p together (not £1.50p)
Combine coins to hit a target amount, saying the running total by value
Record pounds and pence separately at Year 2
keyRepresentations: Price tags and till displays showing £ and p
Real coins combined to make a target amount
A 'say it / write it' pairing (150p to £1 and 50p)
A part-whole model of an amount split into coins
commonMisconceptions: Writes £ and p together (£1.50p, £50p)
Muddles the two symbols or which side the symbol goes
Reads 150p and £1 and 50p as different amounts (misses the equivalence)
When combining coins, counts the number of coins rather than their value toward the total

learn.summary: Year 2 children recognise and use the £ and p symbols, read and say amounts of money two ways (150p and 'one pound and fifty pence'), and combine coins to make a stated target amount by tracking value. The central notation rule is that £ and p are never written together: '£1.50p' is wrong — write 150p, or £1 and 50p, or £1.50. At Year 2 pounds and pence are recorded separately and the same amount has more than one correct written form (150p is the same money as £1 and 50p). Taught through real shop/price contexts, listening for correct use rather than asking for symbol definitions.

activities.title: Build a price with coins and record it correctly
feedback: If a child writes '£1.50p' or '£50p', stop at the point of writing: 'We never write the pound sign and the p together.' Then help them rewrite the amount they actually meant: for one pound and fifty pence write £1.50, 150p or £1 and 50p; for fifty pence write 50p.

If a child says 'I've got three coins, so that's enough' regardless of value, re-count the VALUE onto the total as each coin lands ('50... 70... 75') and ask whether the total — not the count — matches the price.

If a child treats 150p and '£1 and 50p' as different amounts, lay the two forms beside the same coins and count their value: 100p makes one pound, and 50p more makes 150p, which is one pound and fifty pence.
activities.rationale: The National Curriculum requires Year 2 pupils to use the £ and p symbols and combine amounts to make a particular value; building to a target with coins while recording makes the notation rule live at the point of writing. An optional interactive version — dragging coins into a till where the display writes the running total in correct notation, rejects '£1.50p', and offers a 'say it two ways' toggle flipping 150p to '£1 and 50p' — may make the feedback immediate; this is one proposed way to realise the task, not a requirement.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'recognise and use symbols for pounds (£) and pence (p); combine amounts to make a particular value'.

NCETM guidance states the writing convention explicitly: 'It is important that children do not write the £ and p together: 100p, £1.00, but not £1.00p', and that pupils 'read and say amounts of money confidently and use the symbols £ and p accurately, recording pounds and pence separately'.
learnerActions: Look at a price tag (e.g. 75p, or £1 and 50p) and choose real or on-screen coins to make exactly that amount
Say the running total by VALUE as each coin is added — e.g. '50... 70... 75' — not by the number of coins
Write the amount down in a correct form, then write it a second way if possible (150p / £1 and 50p)
Check your written amount against the rule: never put £ and p together
activities.intendedInsight: An amount of money can be built from coins by adding their values to a target, and the same amount has more than one correct written form, but £ and p are never written together.

activities.title: Shop role-play: pay, read tags and spot a wrong price
feedback: If the child reads '£1.50p' happily without noticing a problem, prompt: 'Someone wrote the pound sign AND the p — can we do that? How should it be written instead?'
If the child pays with the wrong value, re-say the price and count the value of the coins handed over together.
Praise reading an amount both ways (150p and 'one pound and fifty pence') as a sign of understanding equivalence.
activities.rationale: Because the objective is USING money language in authentic context, a spoken shop exchange elicits real use — reading tags, paying, and judging notation — rather than defining symbols in the abstract. A conversational character naming prices and asking the child to pay and read is one proposed format; a sort or matching item alone would check recognition but would not elicit this spoken use.
sourceClaims: NCETM guidance states the writing convention explicitly: 'It is important that children do not write the £ and p together: 100p, £1.00, but not £1.00p', and that pupils 'read and say amounts of money confidently and use the symbols £ and p accurately, recording pounds and pence separately'.
Year 2 pupils should 'recognise and use symbols for pounds (£) and pence (p); combine amounts to make a particular value'.
learnerActions: Take part in a shop/market-stall exchange where a shopkeeper names a price ('one pound and fifty pence') and asks you to make and hand over that amount in coins
Read a price tag aloud (e.g. read '150p' and offer an equivalent spoken form)
Judge a price written as '£1.50p': say whether it looks right and explain what is wrong with it
activities.intendedInsight: Money language is used in context — reading, saying and paying amounts — and a confident user flags '£1.50p' as wrongly written because £ and p should not appear together.

activities.title: Match and write amounts; catch the notation error
feedback: For a matching error, place the same coins beside both forms so the equivalence is visible.
For an accepted '£1.50p', state the rule and ask for a correct rewrite (£1.50 / 150p / £1 and 50p).
For a combine-to-target error, recount by value, not by number of coins.
activities.rationale: Short written and matching items let the child practise producing correct notation and identifying the £/p error. These recognition and short-answer items check and rehearse the rule; they do not by themselves demonstrate confident use in a real context, so pair them with the building and role-play activities above.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'recognise and use symbols for pounds (£) and pence (p); combine amounts to make a particular value'.

NCETM guidance states the writing convention explicitly: 'It is important that children do not write the £ and p together: 100p, £1.00, but not £1.00p', and that pupils 'read and say amounts of money confidently and use the symbols £ and p accurately, recording pounds and pence separately'.
learnerActions: Write a given price (e.g. hear '75p' spoken, write the amount) using correct notation
Match a spoken or written form to its equivalent: draw a line from '150p' to '£1 and 50p'
Combine coins to reach a stated total such as 75p (e.g. 50p + 20p + 5p)
Decide whether '£1.50p' is written correctly and, if not, rewrite it
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising correct notation and equivalent forms, and selecting coins that sum to a target, consolidate the rule that £ and p are recorded separately.

constraints: At Year 2 the central rule is recording pounds and pence separately and never writing £ and p together. The objective and the verified NCETM convention accept forms such as £1.50 and £1.00 (but not £1.50p); accept £1.50 as correct. The White Rose scheme (verified:false in the row) suggests Year 2 avoids decimal notation and uses 'and' (£5 and 30p); treat that stricter 'no decimal' guidance as unverified and do NOT use it to reject £1.50.
Keep any pence component below 100p when writing the split form (£1 and 50p, not £1 and 150p); this does not forbid the all-pence form 150p, which is a valid written form throughout.
The same amount has more than one correct written form (150p = £1 and 50p = £1.50); accept any correct form and treat them as equal money.
Assess by listening for correct USE in context — avoid asking the child to define a symbol in the abstract, as stated in the source's assessment approach.
A static price-tag poster or tap-to-reveal image can label £ and p but does not let the child build amounts or use the symbols in context; treat it as a labelling scaffold, not the main task.
Recognition/matching items check and rehearse the convention but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or real-context use; combine them with building and speaking tasks.
Interactive feedback examples (till display writing the running total, rejecting '£1.50p', 'say it two ways' toggle) are optional proposed illustrations of the mechanism, not required technology.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original catalog claimed a 3D/spatial format 'adds nothing' and that a static image 'can't' teach use in context. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established findings; softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements. A static image can still teach labelling.

The White Rose Education scheme is marked verified:false in the row; its Year-2 'record pounds and pence separately, pence below 100p, use "and" not decimal' guidance is unverified and conflicts with the objective's listed correct form £1.50, so it is not applied as a hard constraint against £1.50.
The example 150p = £1 and 50p was checked for arithmetic consistency: 150 pence = £1 (100p) + 50p — correct. 75p = 50p + 20p + 5p is correct. '£1.50p' is correctly flagged as invalid notation.

probeDeeper: 'You read 150p — is that the same as £1 and 50p, or different? Show me with the coins.'
'Someone wrote £1.50p — what is wrong with that?'
'As you add each coin, what is the total now?' (value not count)
'Is 5p the same as £5? How would you write five pounds?' (the symbol and its place matter)
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the price correctly and offers an equivalent form (150p is £1 and 50p); combines coins to make 75p while tracking the value (not the count); recognises '£1.50p' as wrongly written because £ and p should not appear together.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes or accepts £ and p together (£1.50p, £50p)
errorPatterns.nextMove: State and rehearse the rule in context — pounds and pence are recorded separately (150p, or £1 and 50p, or £1.50), never £ and p together; correct it at the point of writing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes £1.50p, or reads it as fine when asked if it looks right

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads 150p and '£1 and 50p' as different amounts — doesn't hold the equivalence
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair the two forms with the same coins in front of the child; count 150 pennies as one pound and fifty pence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 150p and £1 and 50p are not the same money

errorPatterns.pattern: When combining coins, tracks the NUMBER of coins rather than their value toward the target
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the VALUE onto the total each time a coin is added ('50... 70... 75'), not the number of coins.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'I've got three coins, so that's enough' regardless of the coins' values

responseLevels.gap: Muddles £ and p, writes them together, or treats 150p and £1 and 50p as different; counts coins by number.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes amounts in correct £/p notation (never £ and p together), holds the 150p to £1 and 50p equivalence, and combines coins to a target by tracking value.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes simple amounts and combines coins for easy totals, but slips on the £/p equivalence or writes £ and p together under pressure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a shopping context, listen for correct USE (never ask the child to define a symbol): (1) Show a price written '150p': 'Read this price to me', then 'Can you write it another way?' (2) 'I want to buy something that costs 75p — use these coins to make 75p and tell me the total as you go.' (3) Show '£1.50p' written down: 'Does this look right to you? Read it.' Listen for correct reading, the £/p equivalence, and whether they flag £ and p written together.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The '£1.50p — does this look right?' item is the hinge: a child who has the notation convention flags it, while one who hasn't reads it happily. Making 75p while stating the running total catches counting coins by number rather than value.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), REPRESENTATIONAL. Represent addition and subtraction using objects, drawings, and mental images — the bridge between the concepts (combining / taking away) and their symbolic notation. Children externalise a calculation so they can reason about and communicate it.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): solve problems 'using concrete objects and pictorial representations'; the concrete–pictorial–abstract progression is the backbone of KS1 additive work.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.1 'represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings…, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations'.
• Operational details — Deliberately cycle the SAME calculation through multiple representations — real objects → drawing → finger/mental image → spoken → number sentence — and ask the child to connect them ('show me where the 2 is in your drawing'). The aim is fluency in MOVING between representations, and progressively internalising them as mental images so counting-all can give way to more efficient strategies.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): use cubes/counters to show a given addition or subtraction. Tier B (age 5): draw a picture that matches a spoken add/subtract situation. Tier C (age 5-6): represent the same problem two ways (e.g. objects AND a drawing) and explain how they show the same calculation.
bestPractices: Cycle ONE calculation through several representations and explicitly link them ('point to the 3 in the cubes, now in your drawing') — the skill is the mapping between representations, not any single one.
Move along concrete → pictorial → mental image → symbolic, encouraging children to eventually 'see it in their head' so representations become efficient mental tools rather than crutches.
Use consistent structured models (ten-frames, part-whole, fingers) so representations accumulate meaning rather than being ad hoc each time.
Have children narrate their representation aloud ('I drew 5 and crossed out 2') to tie drawing to action to language.
Value the child's own drawings/jottings while nudging toward clearer, more mathematical ones (dots/marks over detailed pictures) to keep focus on quantity.
keyRepresentations: Counters/cubes and fingers (concrete)
Ten-frames and five-frames as structured object layouts
Part-part-whole ('cherry') diagram
Children's own drawings/jottings (dots, marks, crossing-out for removal)
Mental images and the spoken number sentence as the bridge to symbols
commonMisconceptions: Treating each representation as a separate, unrelated task and not seeing that the objects, drawing and number sentence all show the SAME calculation.
Drawing elaborate pictures that obscure quantity (detailed apples instead of countable dots), losing the mathematical point.
Staying dependent on concrete objects and not progressing toward drawings/mental images, so efficiency never develops.
Mis-mapping between representations — e.g. drawing the total when the story described only one part.
Using a drawing as decoration after getting an answer another way, rather than as a tool to find or explain the answer.

learn.summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), help children represent addition and subtraction using objects, drawings, fingers, mental images, spoken language, and number sentences — and, crucially, move fluidly between these so they see that they all show the SAME calculation. Deliberately cycle one calculation through multiple representations and link them explicitly ('show me where the 2 is in your drawing'), progressing from concrete toward mental imagery so efficient strategies can replace counting-all.

activities.title: Linked windows onto one calculation
feedback: When the linked panes update together, say: 'The two counters, the two dots, and the 2 in your sentence all show the same two — they match.'
If the child predicts the hidden drawing correctly, affirm: 'You pictured it in your head before you saw it — that's carrying the maths in your mind.'
If the child can't find the matching two in another pane, prompt: 'You tapped the 2 — point to where the two counters are, and the two dots.'
activities.rationale: This topic is about fluidly moving between representations. A live linked canvas where acting in one pane updates the others, with a tap-to-highlight tool that glows the same quantity across all panes, makes the 'these all show the same thing' insight visible and manipulable. The hide-a-pane challenge pushes toward mental imagery, the developmental goal. The linked updating and highlight are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory; a fixed worked example with tappable cross-links can anchor the same idea.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve addition and subtraction problems using concrete objects and pictorial representations (concrete-pictorial-abstract progression).
K.OA.1: represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, acting out, verbal explanations, expressions or equations.
Explicitly linking multiple representations of the same calculation and progressing toward mental imagery supports additive reasoning.
learnerActions: Place counters onto a mat to show a given sum such as 3 + 2.
Watch linked representations update together: a ten-frame fills, a dot-drawing sketches itself, and the number sentence 3 + 2 = 5 assembles alongside the counters.
Tap the '2' in the number sentence and see exactly two counters, two dots, and two ten-frame cells light up at once across every pane.
Try a 'cover a window' challenge: predict what the drawing will look like before it is revealed, then check.
activities.intendedInsight: The objects, drawing, ten-frame and number sentence are not separate exercises — they are the same quantity shown different ways; and I can begin to carry the picture in my head.

activities.title: Show it with cubes, then with a drawing
feedback: If the child draws elaborate apples, gently redirect: 'Try quick dots so we can count them fast — the number is what matters.'
When drawing and cubes match, say: 'You showed 3 + 2 with cubes AND with dots — both tell the same story.'
If the child narrates the action while drawing, affirm the link between drawing, action, and words.
activities.rationale: Having children produce their own representations and map between them (the two-ways-and-explain checkpoint) builds the generative skill, not just recognition. Narrating aloud ties drawing to action to language; nudging toward dots over detailed pictures keeps focus on quantity.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve addition and subtraction problems using concrete objects and pictorial representations (concrete-pictorial-abstract progression).
Explicitly linking multiple representations of the same calculation and progressing toward mental imagery supports additive reasoning.
learnerActions: Use cubes or counters to show a spoken addition, e.g. build 3 and 2 pushed together to make 5.
Draw a picture (dots or marks) that matches the same calculation.
Narrate aloud what you did, e.g. 'I drew 3 dots and 2 more dots, and that makes 5.'
Point to the '3' and the '2' in the cubes, then point to them in your drawing.
activities.intendedInsight: I can represent the same calculation two different ways and show how they correspond, using quick countable marks rather than detailed pictures.

activities.title: Enact subtraction as taking away
feedback: If the child builds a pile of 5 and a pile of 1 for 5 − 1, re-link the minus to the action: 'Start with 5, now take 1 away — how many are left?'
If the structure is right but the count slips (e.g. says 5 − 1 = 3), scaffold a careful one-to-one recount; the subtraction idea is intact, so don't reteach it.
When removal is enacted correctly, affirm: 'You started with five and took one away — that's what the minus means here.'
activities.rationale: A common error is treating any two numbers as 'put together', building 5 and 1 as separate piles for 5 − 1. Enacting the removal and attaching the number sentence links the minus symbol to the take-away action. Translating BOTH ways — reading a model as a sentence and enacting a sentence with objects — is what demonstrates a secure representation-operation link.
sourceClaims: K.OA.1: represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, acting out, verbal explanations, expressions or equations.
Explicitly linking multiple representations of the same calculation and progressing toward mental imagery supports additive reasoning.
learnerActions: Start with 5 cubes and show 5 − 1 by actually removing one cube, leaving four.
Say the number sentence aloud: '5 take away 1 leaves 4, so 5 − 1 = 4.'
Explain which cube you took away and how many are left.
Contrast this with 4 + 1: show how combining to make 5 is different from taking away to leave 4.
activities.intendedInsight: One way subtraction works is taking away: starting with an amount and removing part of it. That is different from putting two groups together.

activities.title: Match and talk about representations (supporting activities)
feedback: After a correct match, ask the child to point to the matching part in each ('where is the 2 in both?') so matching becomes connecting.
For 'another way', if the child restates the same drawing, prompt a different format: 'Could you show it on a ten-frame instead?'
activities.rationale: Matching (drawing ↔ number sentence) checks that a child recognises correspondence and can sit within broader early-number practice, but a scored linear matching task does not by itself develop the generative move-between-representations skill and is developmentally light at 4-6; use it as support, not the main vehicle. 'Show me another way' dialogue can prompt re-representation, but the drawing/object work is the manual/visual part, so pair the talk with a drawing or object tool rather than relying on talk alone.
learnerActions: Match a drawing to the number sentence that shows the same calculation.
Respond to the prompt 'Show me another way to draw that' and produce a second representation.
Use structured models consistently — ten-frames, five-frames, or a part-part-whole ('cherry') diagram — so representations accumulate meaning.
activities.intendedInsight: The same calculation can be recognised across formats, and structured models give it a consistent, reusable shape.

constraints: The core skill is MAPPING between representations, not mastering any single one — always link them explicitly ('point to the 3 in the cubes, now in your drawing').

Matching or recognition-style tasks assess recognition of correspondence but do not elicit the independent construction of a child's own representations; keep them as a supporting check, not the main activity.

Dialogue prompts ('show me another way') work best alongside a drawing or object tool, since much of the re-representation work here is manual/visual; talk can still prompt and explain re-representation.
Tap-to-highlight, live-updating linked panes, and the hide-a-pane challenge are optional illustrative mechanisms to make the correspondence concrete — not mandatory features.
Value children's own jottings while nudging toward quick countable marks (dots) over elaborate pictures, so quantity stays in focus.
Aim to progress concrete → pictorial → mental image → symbolic so representations become efficient mental tools rather than permanent crutches; do not leave children dependent on objects.

Paper/cubes and an on-screen canvas offer different experiences; neither is required, and a fixed worked example can still anchor the parallel-representations idea even though it cannot be manipulated.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The row claimed the linked live canvas shows the insight 'in a way no static medium can' and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits.

Arithmetic in examples was checked: 3 + 2 = 5, 5 − 1 = 4, 4 + 1 = 5 are correct. The row's own distractor '3 + 2 = 6' (and the analogous '5 − 1 = 3') are deliberate error examples for the miscount pattern and appear only in a feedback/diagnostic context, never presented as correct.
Two source claims (CCSS K.OA.1 and the NCETM/Bruner CPA claim) are marked verified:false in the row; treat their evidential strength as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: Point to the part of the cubes that is the '3', and the part that is the '2'.
Now show me the same thing with a drawing instead of cubes.
For 5 − 1, which cube did you take away, and how many are left?
Could you show 4 + 1 with the cubes so it makes 5 too?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the cubes as 3 + 2 = 5 (combining); then models 5 − 1 by starting with five cubes and taking one away, leaving four, and can say 5 − 1 = 4.

errorPatterns.pattern: For 5 − 1 builds two groups (5 and 1) and combines them — treats any two numbers as 'put together', not enacting removal.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-link the minus symbol to the take-away action on the cubes; narrate 'start with 5, take 1 away, how many left'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child makes a pile of 5 and a pile of 1 for 5 − 1 rather than removing one from five.

errorPatterns.pattern: Represents only the numbers, not the operation — lays out 3 and 2 but cannot say the model means 3 + 2 = 5.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the joining action and attach the sentence; move deliberately between story → cubes → number sentence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child describes the cubes as '3 and 2' with no combining or total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Correct representation but miscounts when reading it off (says 3 + 2 = 6).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a one-to-one recount; the representation concept is intact, so do not reteach it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Structure is right, but the count of the combined cubes slips.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot translate a model into a sentence, or builds an addition when asked to show a subtraction.
responseLevels.full: Moves fluently both ways — interprets a concrete model as a sentence and enacts a sentence with objects — including distinguishing take-away from combining.
responseLevels.partial: Translates in one direction only (reads a model OR builds from a sentence), or needs support to connect the operation to the action.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 3 cubes and 2 more cubes pushed together (show them). What number sentence does this show? Now YOU show me 5 − 1 using the cubes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Translating BOTH ways is the test: interpreting a given concrete model into a symbolic sentence, then enacting a symbolic sentence with objects. A child who can only go one way, or who builds '5' and '1' as two separate piles for 5 − 1 (treating − as +), reveals a shaky link between representation and operation.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Waves & How They Move

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum — KS3 Physics, bridged):** England introduces the formal wave model — amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and transverse vs longitudinal waves — at Key Stage 3 (Physics: 'Waves'), not in KS2. At age 9–10 this record is an early bridge to that KS3 content, building the amplitude/wavelength vocabulary and the energy-transfer idea on concrete media before the quantitative treatment (v = fλ) at KS3/KS4.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 4-PS4-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-1]." (Clarification limits this to standard, repeating waves; the assessment boundary excludes interference, electromagnetic waves, non-periodic/non-uniform waves, and any quantitative model.) This is the anchoring standard for the topic.

- **Operational details:** Children build a first MODEL of a wave: amplitude = the height/size of the wave (bigger amplitude carries more energy, so it moves objects more), and wavelength = the distance from one peak to the next. Develop it on concrete media — a slinky, a rope, water in a tray/ripple tank — observing and describing before naming the quantities on a drawn transverse waveform (crest, trough, amplitude, wavelength). The threshold idea to secure is that a wave transfers ENERGY, not matter: a cork or bead floating on water bobs up and down in place while the wave travels on through it; a ribbon tied to a slinky oscillates but does not travel along the coil. Use the domino / Mexican-wave analogy for energy passed neighbour-to-neighbour, and demonstrate that waves DO work — a bigger-amplitude wave pushes a floating object more — which ties directly back to the volume–amplitude prerequisite from sound.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). The child can label amplitude and wavelength on a wave, model wave patterns on a slinky/rope/water and describe them, relate larger amplitude to more energy (moves objects more), and — the key threshold — explain that the medium bobs in place while only energy travels through it. Mastery is a qualitative, correctly-modelled wave with the energy-not-matter idea held; the wave equation and transverse/longitudinal formalism are deferred (Tier C, KS3).
bestPractices: Develop the model on concrete media first — slinky, rope, water tray/ripple tank — observing and describing wave patterns before naming the quantities.

Introduce amplitude = height/size of the wave (linked to energy: bigger amplitude moves objects more) and wavelength = distance between successive peaks, anchored on a drawn transverse waveform (crest, trough).

Directly confront the energy-not-matter misconception with a floating cork/bead (bobs in place) or a ribbon on a slinky (oscillates but doesn't travel along) — the observable evidence that matter is left behind.
Use the falling-dominoes and stadium 'Mexican wave' analogies for energy passed neighbour-to-neighbour while each particle stays roughly in place.
Demonstrate that waves do WORK — a bigger-amplitude wave pushes a floating object more — connecting amplitude–energy back to the sound volume–vibration-size prerequisite.
Have children label crest, trough, amplitude and wavelength on their own diagrams, and distinguish amplitude (how tall) from wavelength (how long) explicitly.
keyRepresentations: Slinky or rope pulse — a coil oscillates but does not travel the length of the spring (energy transmitted, not mass).
Water ripple tank with a floating cork/buoy that bobs up and down in place as waves pass.
Labelled transverse waveform — crest, trough, amplitude as height, wavelength as peak-to-peak distance.
Falling-dominoes / stadium Mexican-wave analogy for neighbour-to-neighbour energy transfer.
commonMisconceptions: Believing waves carry MATTER along with them (the water or cork travels to the shore) rather than the medium bobbing in place while only energy travels through — the central wave misconception.
Confusing amplitude with wavelength (mixing up 'how tall' with 'how long').
Thinking a bigger (higher-amplitude) wave automatically travels faster — wave speed depends on the medium, not the amplitude.
Reading a drawn sine curve as the literal path an object or a sound takes (sound is actually longitudinal).
Treating 'energy' as a substance/stuff that flows along, reinforced if 'energy travels' is taught carelessly.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, build a first qualitative model of waves: amplitude (the height/size of a wave from the middle line to a peak) and wavelength (the distance from one peak to the next), plus the threshold idea that a wave transfers energy, not matter. Develop the model on concrete media (slinky, rope, water in a tray or ripple tank) by observing and describing before naming the quantities on a drawn transverse waveform. The central misconception to confront is that waves carry matter along; for a standard repeating wave a floating cork or duck bobs roughly in place while only the wave pattern (energy) travels through. Keep the treatment qualitative: the wave equation (v = fλ) and the transverse/longitudinal formalism are deferred to later study. Amplitude links energy to a visible effect (bigger-amplitude waves push floating objects more), connecting back to the sound idea that louder means a bigger vibration; wave speed, by contrast, is set by the medium, not the amplitude.

activities.title: Does the cork ride the wave? (water-tray investigation)
feedback: If the learner predicted the cork rides to the far end: watch again closely — the cork bobs up and down and ends up near where it started, even though wave after wave passes under it. What crossed the tray was the wave pattern (energy), not the water itself.

If the learner says the water travelled across: a single bit of water moves round in a small loop (up and down and a little back and forth) and stays roughly in place; the pattern moves across, the water does not travel with it.
Reinforce correct observation: the cork stayed roughly put and bobbed — so the wave carries energy, not matter, across the tray.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain task on real water directly surfaces and tests the central wave misconception (matter travels with the wave). Watching the cork stay put while waves pass provides observable evidence that it is energy, not matter, that crosses. (In a small tray a very large disturbance can produce some visible drift; keep disturbances modest so the bob-in-place behaviour is clear.)
sourceClaims: Classical waves transfer energy without transporting matter through the medium: waves in a pond do not carry water molecules along; the wave's energy travels through the water leaving the molecules in place, like a bug bobbing on ripples. Mechanical waves pass energy molecule to molecule like falling dominoes. Wavelength is the distance between crests.

A common misconception is that matter travels with a wave; in fact particles move back and forth (perpendicular to the wave's travel) and take part by bumping into one another and passing on energy, so the average particle position does not change. Useful teaching analogies: a bobbing buoy and the stadium 'Mexican wave'.
learnerActions: Float a cork or bottle-top on one end of a tray of water.
Before making any waves, predict in writing or speech: will the cork travel to the far end with the waves, or do something else — and why?
Make waves from one end and watch the cork carefully as several waves pass under it.
Describe what actually crossed the tray: did the water (and cork) travel across, or did the cork stay roughly in place and bob up and down?
Repeat with a bigger disturbance and note whether the cork is now carried across or just bobs more strongly in roughly the same place.
activities.intendedInsight: A wave transfers energy through a medium without carrying the matter along: the cork bobs up and down roughly in place while the wave pattern sweeps on through it.

activities.title: Pass it along: slinky, rope, and the stadium wave
feedback: If the learner thinks the ribbon travels along the coil: it returns to roughly its own spot — only the pulse travels the length, showing matter stays put while the wave (energy) moves.

If the learner predicts the big pulse arrives first: on the same slinky the big and small pulses reach the far end at about the same time; amplitude carries more energy, not more speed. Wave speed is set by the medium, not the size of the wave.

For the stadium/domino analogy: no single person travels round the stadium and no single domino moves along the row — each only moves and nudges its neighbour, so what travels round is the wave (energy), not the people or dominoes.
activities.rationale: The slinky/rope makes energy-not-matter directly observable and lets a same-speed comparison confront the 'bigger wave travels faster' misconception. The domino and Mexican-wave analogies make neighbour-to-neighbour energy transfer concrete.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is that matter travels with a wave; in fact particles move back and forth (perpendicular to the wave's travel) and take part by bumping into one another and passing on energy, so the average particle position does not change. Useful teaching analogies: a bobbing buoy and the stadium 'Mexican wave'.

Classical waves transfer energy without transporting matter through the medium: waves in a pond do not carry water molecules along; the wave's energy travels through the water leaving the molecules in place, like a bug bobbing on ripples. Mechanical waves pass energy molecule to molecule like falling dominoes. Wavelength is the distance between crests.
learnerActions: Lay a slinky or long rope on the floor and send a single pulse from one end to the other; watch the far end react.
Tie a ribbon or marker near the middle of the coil and watch what the ribbon does as the pulse passes it.
Describe what the ribbon does (oscillates and returns to roughly its own spot) versus what the pulse does (travels the length).
Send a big pulse and a small pulse and compare how fast each reaches the far end.
Act out or describe a stadium 'Mexican wave' or a line of falling dominoes, then say which individuals actually travel round/along and which only pass the motion to their neighbour.
activities.intendedInsight: Energy is passed neighbour-to-neighbour while each part of the medium stays roughly in place; for ordinary-sized pulses, the size of a pulse makes little or no difference to how fast it travels along a given medium.

activities.title: Label the wave: amplitude vs wavelength
feedback: If amplitude is marked as the peak-to-peak distance: that distance is the wavelength; amplitude is the height from the middle line up to a peak.
If wavelength is marked as the height: that height is the amplitude; wavelength is measured from one peak across to the next peak.
When both are labelled correctly and the two 'change one at a time' drawings differ as expected, confirm: the learner has separated how tall a wave is from how long it is.
activities.rationale: Explicitly labelling on the learner's own diagram and drawing waves that vary one quantity at a time targets the amplitude/wavelength confusion directly and builds the vocabulary the later formal model depends on.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-PS4-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-1]; clarification limits to standard repeating waves and the boundary excludes interference, EM waves, non-periodic waves and quantitative models.

Classical waves transfer energy without transporting matter through the medium: waves in a pond do not carry water molecules along; the wave's energy travels through the water leaving the molecules in place, like a bug bobbing on ripples. Mechanical waves pass energy molecule to molecule like falling dominoes. Wavelength is the distance between crests.
learnerActions: Draw (or be given) a transverse waveform and mark the crest (highest point) and trough (lowest point).
Mark amplitude as the height from the middle line to a peak, and label it 'how big / how much energy'.
Mark wavelength as the distance from one peak to the next peak, and label it 'how long'.
State in your own words the difference between amplitude (how tall) and wavelength (how long).
Draw a second wave with the same wavelength but larger amplitude, and a third with the same amplitude but longer wavelength, to show the two quantities change independently.
activities.intendedInsight: Amplitude and wavelength are two separate, independent features of a wave: amplitude is the height (linked to energy), wavelength is the peak-to-peak distance.

activities.title: Bigger wave, bigger push: amplitude and energy
feedback: If the learner attributes the bigger push to higher speed: recall the slinky — big and small pulses travelled at the same speed. The bigger push comes from more energy (larger amplitude), not greater speed.
Reinforce the sound link: just as a louder note is a bigger vibration, a bigger water wave is a bigger disturbance carrying more energy.
Confirm correct reasoning: bigger amplitude = more energy = bigger effect on the floating object, with speed set by the medium.
activities.rationale: Demonstrating that waves do work ties the amplitude–energy idea to a visible effect and reconnects to the sound volume–vibration-size prerequisite, while the same-speed result guards against conflating amplitude with speed.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-PS4-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-1]; clarification limits to standard repeating waves and the boundary excludes interference, EM waves, non-periodic waves and quantitative models.
learnerActions: Float a small object (toy boat, bottle-top) on a water tray and make a small-amplitude wave, noting how much the object is pushed or bobs.
Make a bigger-amplitude wave (same medium) and compare how much the object is pushed or bobs now.
State the relationship: a bigger-amplitude wave carries more energy and moves the object more.
Connect to sound: louder sound comes from a bigger vibration (bigger amplitude), just as a bigger water wave is a bigger disturbance carrying more energy.
Decide and explain whether a bigger wave moves the object more because it travels faster or because it carries more energy — and justify using the slinky same-speed result.
activities.intendedInsight: Larger amplitude means more energy, which does more work on objects (a bigger push), but it does not make the wave travel faster.

activities.title: Optional: side-on wave model with amplitude and wavelength controls
feedback: If the learner expects the cork to ride to the far side: the model shows it bobbing in place and left behind — the pattern travels, the cork does not.
When amplitude is raised and the push grows but the crossing time does not shorten, confirm: amplitude sets energy/push, not speed.
If amplitude and wavelength are confused on the labels, point to which control changed height versus peak spacing.
activities.rationale: A manipulable side-on model makes the two independent quantities and the energy-not-matter behaviour visible together; live labels and linked recolouring of crest/trough and a pushed boat make the mechanism concrete. This is offered as an optional complement to the hands-on media, not a replacement for real investigation; its smooth surface and marked particle are an idealised model of a real wave.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-PS4-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-1]; clarification limits to standard repeating waves and the boundary excludes interference, EM waves, non-periodic waves and quantitative models.

A common misconception is that matter travels with a wave; in fact particles move back and forth (perpendicular to the wave's travel) and take part by bumping into one another and passing on energy, so the average particle position does not change. Useful teaching analogies: a bobbing buoy and the stadium 'Mexican wave'.
learnerActions: Use a side-on model of a rope or water wave with two separate controls: one that raises the amplitude (a taller wave) and one that stretches the wavelength (peaks further apart), with the terms shown live on the crest and trough as they change.
Predict where a floating cork on the surface will end up, then send a wave across and watch: the cork bobs straight up and down and is left near its starting point while the pattern sweeps through.
Increase the amplitude and observe the same cork bob higher and a floating boat rock and bob more strongly, while both still stay near their starting points — bigger wave, more energy, bigger effect.
Compare a tall wave and a short wave sent across and note whether changing amplitude changed how fast the wave crossed.
activities.intendedInsight: Amplitude and wavelength can be varied independently, and a wave carries energy (which can push objects) without carrying the floating object along with it.

activities.title: Check and consolidate the wave model
feedback: If the learner says the duck is carried to the far bank: revisit the cork/slinky evidence — for a standard repeating wave the medium bobs in place while energy crosses.

If waves are ordered by wavelength instead of amplitude when ranking energy: for these same-wavelength waves, the difference in energy comes from amplitude (height), so compare heights, not peak spacing.
If the learner reads the curve as the route the water follows: the curve is a graph of displacement; a marked particle actually moves up and down (or back and forth), not along the wavy line.
Confirm a full response: duck bobs in place, energy crosses, amplitude is distinguished from wavelength, and amplitude does not set speed.
activities.rationale: A focused set of recognition and short-explanation checks consolidates the model and re-tests each misconception; recognition-style items confirm vocabulary but do not by themselves elicit the independent, hands-on observation that overturns the matter-travels misconception, so they should follow the investigations rather than replace them.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-PS4-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-1]; clarification limits to standard repeating waves and the boundary excludes interference, EM waves, non-periodic waves and quantitative models.

A common misconception is that matter travels with a wave; in fact particles move back and forth (perpendicular to the wave's travel) and take part by bumping into one another and passing on energy, so the average particle position does not change. Useful teaching analogies: a bobbing buoy and the stadium 'Mexican wave'.
learnerActions: Label amplitude, wavelength, crest and trough on a given waveform.
Answer: as a standard, repeating wave crosses a pond toward the far bank, does a floating duck get carried to the bank, or bob in place? Justify the answer.
Order several drawn waves that have the same wavelength (in the same medium) by the energy they carry, using their amplitudes.
Explain, using a marked particle, why the drawn wavy curve is NOT the path the water or duck physically travels.
Write one or two sentences summarising what a wave carries across (energy) versus what stays behind (the matter/medium).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the vocabulary (amplitude, wavelength, crest, trough), the energy-from-amplitude ordering, and the energy-not-matter threshold idea, including why a drawn sine curve is a displacement graph rather than a travel path.

constraints: Keep the treatment qualitative at this age: the wave equation (v = fλ) and the transverse/longitudinal formalism are deferred to later study (KS3/KS4).
Scope to standard, repeating waves; exclude interference, electromagnetic waves, non-periodic/non-uniform waves and any quantitative model (per the NGSS 4-PS4-1 assessment boundary).
The central threshold to secure is energy-not-matter: ensure learners observe the medium bobbing in place, not merely hear it stated.
Distinguish the drawn sine curve (a displacement graph) from the actual motion of a particle (up and down, or back and forth); do not let learners treat the curve as a travel path.
Amplitude is linked to energy and to how much a wave moves objects, not to wave speed; wave speed is set by the medium. Any example comparing wave sizes should keep speed constant.
Recognition/labelling checks confirm vocabulary but do not elicit the independent hands-on observation; use them after, not instead of, concrete investigation on slinky/rope/water.
A side-on screen model is an idealised representation; use it alongside, not in place of, real media, and treat its smooth surface and marked particle as a model of the real wave.
A paper waveform diagram represents an ideal wave shape; keep learners aware it is a graph, not a photograph of moving water.
Tie amplitude–energy explicitly back to the sound prerequisite (louder = bigger vibration) so the two topics reinforce one another.

The bob-in-place answer applies to the idealised standard repeating wave; frame learner prompts around a pond/tray crossing rather than a breaking shoreline, where wind and surf can drift objects inshore (outside this objective's scope).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row marked two citations (Science Learning Hub; DfE National Curriculum) as verified:false; confidence in those claims should be treated accordingly and re-checked before relying on them. Activity 1's energy-not-matter principle is independently supported by the verified:true NASA claim.

Self-audit: the original 'bigger wave travels faster' is a listed misconception and is correctly treated as wrong in the activities (wave speed depends on the medium, not amplitude); the big/small pulse same-speed comparison is used to confront it.

Self-audit on energy language: 'energy/the wave pattern travels' is used, but the row warns that treating energy as a flowing substance can reinforce a misconception. Activities frame energy as what is transferred/passed neighbour-to-neighbour while matter stays in place, rather than a stuff that physically flows along.

The claim that water-wave particles trace small circular orbits is accurate for deep-water surface waves but is beyond this Tier-B objective and is intentionally not taught; mentioned only as a note on why a 3D view was considered.

The original strongly asserted a coded interactive is 'ideal' and that a quiz 'only assesses' / a static image 'cannot show' the dynamic behaviour; these comparative-efficacy claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped affordances and limits.

The consolidation 'shore/beach' wording was reframed to a pond/far-bank crossing: at a real breaking shoreline, wind and surf can genuinely carry a floating object inshore, which conflicts with the idealised bob-in-place answer and is outside the standard-repeating-wave scope.
Activity 1's sourceClaims were trimmed to drop the NGSS 4-PS4-1 claim, which supports the general model/topic but not the specific energy-not-matter principle that activity teaches.

Independent re-audit confirmation: physics claims, initial conditions and amplitude/speed/energy logic were re-checked occurrence-by-occurrence and found consistent; no new learner-facing errors identified. Whether a classroom water tray reliably shows a clean amplitude-dependent push without visible drift remains setup-dependent and unverified.

assess.poeTask: Float a cork or bottle-top on a tray of water and make waves from one end. Predict: will the cork travel to the far end with the waves, or do something else? Say why first, then make the waves and explain what actually crossed the tray.
probeDeeper: On a slinky you send a big pulse and a small pulse together — which reaches the far end first, or do they arrive together? What does that tell you about speed and size?
When a Mexican wave goes round a stadium, does any single person travel round the stadium? So what actually moves round?
You said this wave is bigger — does that mean it carries more energy, or moves faster, or both?
assess.correctAnswer: The duck bobs up and down mostly in place as each wave passes under it — it is NOT carried along to the far bank. The wave transfers ENERGY across the pond; the water (and the duck) stay roughly where they are, just moving up and down.

errorPatterns.pattern: Matter travels with the wave: 'the duck rides the wave to the far bank' — the water moves bodily across
errorPatterns.nextMove: Float a cork and watch it bob in PLACE while the wave passes through; the wave moves, the water doesn't travel with it — energy is what crosses.
errorPatterns.distractor: The duck is carried across to the far bank by the waves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the duck is carried along in the direction the wave travels

errorPatterns.pattern: Amplitude and wavelength confused: mixes up the height of the wave with the distance between peaks
errorPatterns.nextMove: Amplitude = height from the middle to a peak (how big/energetic); wavelength = distance from one peak to the next; label both on a marked diagram.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels amplitude as the peak-to-peak distance, or wavelength as the height

errorPatterns.pattern: Bigger wave = faster: 'a taller wave must travel across faster'
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a slinky, a big pulse and a small pulse travel at the SAME speed (set by the medium); amplitude carries more energy, not more speed.
errorPatterns.distractor: A bigger (taller) wave travels across faster than a small one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a bigger-amplitude wave moves across the pond faster than a small one

errorPatterns.pattern: Sine curve as a literal path: reads the drawn wave shape as the route a particle physically follows
errorPatterns.nextMove: The curve is a graph of displacement; a marked particle actually moves straight up and down (or back and forth), not along the curve.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the water or duck moves ALONG the wavy line drawn on paper

responseLevels.gap: Says the duck/water is carried along in the direction of travel (matter travels with the wave), or reads the wave curve as a physical path.
responseLevels.full: Explains the duck bobs in place while ENERGY is transferred across, distinguishes amplitude (height/energy) from wavelength (peak spacing), holds that amplitude doesn't set speed, and transfers to the Mexican-wave and slinky cases.
responseLevels.partial: Knows waves have amplitude and wavelength and that bigger waves carry more energy, but still thinks the medium (duck/water) travels along with the wave, or confuses amplitude with wavelength.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A duck floats on a pond. Waves travel across the pond from left to right and pass under the duck. Does the duck get carried along to the right-hand bank by the waves, or does it do something else? Explain what the waves actually carry across the pond.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Everyone has 'seen' waves carry things to shore, so the intuitive answer is the duck rides along. Asking what actually crosses the pond forces the energy-not-matter distinction. A child with the threshold idea says the duck bobs in place while the wave carries energy; the misconception child has the duck transported. This is the single central wave misconception at every age.

sources.claim: Classical waves transfer energy without transporting matter through the medium: waves in a pond do not carry water molecules along; the wave's energy travels through the water leaving the molecules in place, like a bug bobbing on ripples. Mechanical waves pass energy molecule to molecule like falling dominoes. Wavelength is the distance between crests.

sources.claim: A common misconception is that matter travels with a wave; in fact particles move back and forth (perpendicular to the wave's travel) and take part by bumping into one another and passing on energy, so the average particle position does not change. Useful teaching analogies: a bobbing buoy and the stadium 'Mexican wave'.

sources.claim: England introduces the formal wave model — amplitude, wavelength, frequency, transverse and longitudinal waves — at Key Stage 3 (Physics), not KS2; the wave equation v = fλ follows at KS3/KS4.
