pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Heating & Cooling Changes

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'States of matter'):** Pupils should be taught to "observe that some materials change state when they are heated or cooled, and measure or research the temperature at which this happens in degrees Celsius (°C)." Non-statutory guidance: "note the changes to water when it is heated or cooled"; research melting/condensing temperatures (e.g. when iron melts, when oxygen condenses); explore the effect of temperature on chocolate, butter, cream. Note: teachers should AVOID materials where heating causes chemical change (baking, burning).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-4):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]." Clarification: reversible examples include water and butter at different temperatures. DCI PS1.B: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]." SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence.

- **Operational details:** Establish the two reversible state changes for water — melting (solid→liquid) and freezing (liquid→solid) — plus boiling/evaporation, and tie each to a MEASURED temperature: water freezes/melts at 0°C and boils at 100°C. Have children read a thermometer in °C and record the temperature at which a change happens, so the abstract change is pinned to a number. Use gentle everyday examples (chocolate, butter, ice) and explicitly keep to physical, reversible changes, avoiding burning/cooking. Confront the melting–dissolving confusion head-on (ice melting is heat-driven state change; sugar dissolving is a different process). The particle-level 'why' (heating gives particles more energy to move) is a light bridge to KS3, not the KS2 core, which is observe-and-measure.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (observational→early-quantitative). The child can describe melting and freezing with everyday examples, state that water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C, read a thermometer in °C to record where a change occurs, and keep melting distinct from dissolving.
bestPractices: Pin every state change to a MEASURED temperature in °C (water: 0°C freeze/melt, 100°C boil), so children read and record, not just watch.
Teach melting and freezing as the same reversible boundary crossed in opposite directions (0°C for water).
Explicitly separate melting from dissolving — a classic conflation — with side-by-side examples (ice melting vs sugar dissolving).
Keep to physical, reversible changes and avoid heating that burns or cooks (chemical change), per DfE guidance.
Use thermometer-reading practice as a genuine measurement skill, discussing units and scale.
Reference researched melting/boiling points of other materials (iron melts very hot; oxygen condenses very cold) to show every material has its own change temperatures.
keyRepresentations: A thermometer scale in °C with 0°C (ice/water) and 100°C (boiling) marked
A melt↔freeze reversible-boundary diagram for water
A heating timeline: ice → water → steam with the temperatures of change
Side-by-side 'melting vs dissolving' contrast cards
A materials-and-their-change-temperatures table (water, chocolate, iron, oxygen)
commonMisconceptions: Confusing melting with dissolving (thinking ice in a drink 'dissolves', or that melting needs a liquid to melt into).
Believing melting/boiling temperatures are vague or variable for a given substance, rather than fixed (water always 0°C / 100°C at normal pressure).
Thinking 'cold' is a substance that flows into things, rather than cooling being the removal of heat energy.
Assuming heating always makes new materials (over-generalising to chemical change) instead of many heating/cooling changes being reversible state changes.
Thinking a material must 'soften' gradually with no particular temperature, missing the idea of a specific melting point.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: observe that some materials change state when heated or cooled, and pin each change to a MEASURED temperature in °C (pure water melts/freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C at normal atmospheric pressure). Core skill is observe-and-measure: read a thermometer and record the temperature where a change happens. Some mixtures, such as chocolate, soften and melt over a range of temperatures rather than at one sharp point. Keep melting distinct from dissolving, keep to physical reversible changes (avoid burning/cooking), and show that melting and freezing are the same boundary crossed in opposite directions. Particle-level 'why' is a light bridge, not the core.

activities.title: Heat-and-cool bench: watch the change track the temperature
feedback: If the child expects the change at any warm temperature, draw attention to the marker landing at the same °C every run.

Point out that the reading pauses at the change temperature while the change happens (0°C during melting, 100°C during boiling) and only climbs again once the change is complete — the same sticking behaviour the real melting-ice task shows.

If the child calls melting 'dissolving', use the side-by-side panel: melting needs only heat and one substance; dissolving needs a second substance (a liquid the solid spreads into) and does not need heating, although warming can make it happen faster.
When reversing the dial re-freezes the water, confirm it is the SAME water, only the state changed — the change runs both ways.
activities.rationale: Live coupling of a readable number to a visible change makes the fixed-temperature idea concrete and lets the learner read-and-record rather than only watch; showing the reading hold at the change temperature keeps it coherent with the real-thermometer task. Reversibility and the melting-vs-dissolving contrast are built into the same model. A real thermometer and ice-water is the natural hands-on partner. (Proposed design; efficacy untested.)
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'States of matter' statutory: 'observe that some materials change state when they are heated or cooled, and measure or research the temperature at which this happens in degrees Celsius (°C)'; avoid heating causing chemical change.
NGSS 2-PS1-4 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]'; DCI PS1.B '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]... sometimes reversible, sometimes not.'
Elementary misconceptions include melting/dissolving confusion, treating 'cold' as a substance, and not grasping fixed change temperatures; conceptual change needs hands-on, repeated observation.
learnerActions: Drag a heat dial under a beaker of ice and watch a thermometer climb in °C.

Notice the ice stays solid as the temperature rises, and observe that it begins to melt at 0°C, with a marker snapping onto the scale at that reading; the reading holds at 0°C while there is still ice melting.
Keep heating: once all the ice has melted the water warms to 100°C, where the reading holds while the water boils, with a marker at 100°C.
Reverse the dial to cool: watch steam recondense and the water refreeze at 0°C, showing the change runs both ways.
Use a side panel to run melting ice next to dissolving sugar and describe how the two processes differ.
Swap the material (chocolate, iron, oxygen) to discover each has its own change temperature or range (chocolate softens and melts gradually over a range of temperatures, not at one sharp point).
activities.intendedInsight: For water, melting, freezing and boiling do not happen vaguely 'when it gets warm': they happen at specific, readable temperatures (0°C and 100°C at normal atmospheric pressure) that are the same every time. The reading pauses at that temperature while the change is happening, and melting/freezing are the same boundary crossed in opposite directions. (Evaporation is different: it can happen slowly at temperatures below boiling.)

activities.title: Real thermometer in melting ice: predict the sticking point
feedback: A prediction of a steady climb signals the child hasn't grasped that energy first goes into changing state — use the observed sticking at 0°C to address this.

The 0°C plateau only shows while there is still unmelted ice in the beaker; use ordinary water ice as a melting ice-and-water mixture (never dry ice, which is frozen carbon dioxide, not water). Ice straight from the freezer may first read below 0°C and climb to 0°C, then hold there while it melts.
If the child says the melt-water is a new liquid, refreeze it to recover the ice and note the mass is unchanged (in a covered container, so none evaporates): same material, only the state changed.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain task with a real thermometer makes the fixed melting point and the energy-goes-to-state idea observable, and the diagnostic prediction exposes misconceptions before teaching.
sourceClaims: Elementary misconceptions include melting/dissolving confusion, treating 'cold' as a substance, and not grasping fixed change temperatures; conceptual change needs hands-on, repeated observation.
learnerActions: Put a thermometer into a beaker of crushed melting ice (a genuine ice-and-water mixture), stir gently and let it warm slowly (for example in a warm room or with gentle warming), reading the temperature aloud.
Before starting, predict what the thermometer does WHILE the ice is still melting, and say why.
Observe whether the reading climbs steadily or sticks, and record the temperature where it holds.
Afterwards, refreeze the melt-water and check it is the same water (e.g. mass stays the same if the container is covered so no water evaporates).
activities.intendedInsight: While a melting ice-and-water mixture still has ice in it the temperature holds at about 0°C (the energy first goes into changing state), then climbs once all the ice has melted; the melt-water is the same material as the ice.

activities.title: Melting is not dissolving — and freezing is heat leaving
feedback: If the child uses 'dissolve' for ice becoming water in a warm room, contrast: dissolving needs a second substance the solid spreads into; melting does not.
If the child says the freezer 'puts cold in', reframe: heating ADDS energy (melt, boil), cooling REMOVES it (freeze); 'cold' is just less heat, not a thing that moves in.
If melted chocolate is called a new material, note it hardens back to the same chocolate when cooled — a reversible change of state.
activities.rationale: These are the classic KS2 conflations (melting/dissolving, change-of-state/new-material, cold-as-substance); confronting them head-on with side-by-side contrasts supports conceptual change.
sourceClaims: Elementary misconceptions include melting/dissolving confusion, treating 'cold' as a substance, and not grasping fixed change temperatures; conceptual change needs hands-on, repeated observation.
learnerActions: Compare ice melting in a warm room with sugar dissolving in water, and say what is different about each.
State which process needs heat and which needs a second substance.
Explain what happens when water freezes: does cold go IN, or does heat come OUT?
Decide whether melted chocolate is a new material or the same chocolate.
activities.intendedInsight: Melting is a heat-driven change of state of ONE substance; dissolving spreads a solid into a second liquid and does not need heating (though warming can speed it up). Freezing is heat energy leaving, not 'cold' moving in; a melted material is still the same material.

activities.title: Every material has its own change temperatures
feedback: If the child treats water's melting and boiling points as vague or variable, point to the fixed values (pure water always 0°C/100°C at normal atmospheric pressure), while noting that some mixtures such as chocolate do soften over a range.
When reading the scale, discuss the units (°C) and the spacing between marks so reading is accurate.
Iron, oxygen and boiling water are read/research examples only, not materials to handle at those temperatures.
activities.rationale: Referencing researched change temperatures of other materials generalises the fixed-temperature idea and gives genuine thermometer-reading practice, consistent with the measure-or-research standard.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'States of matter' statutory: 'observe that some materials change state when they are heated or cooled, and measure or research the temperature at which this happens in degrees Celsius (°C)'; avoid heating causing chemical change.
learnerActions: Read a table of materials and their change temperatures (water, chocolate, iron, oxygen).
Note that iron melts very hot and oxygen condenses very cold, while water melts at 0°C and boils at 100°C.
Place 0°C and 100°C correctly on a thermometer scale and read other values off it.
Match each state change (melting, freezing, boiling) to its temperature for water.
activities.intendedInsight: Each material has its own change temperatures. For pure substances like water these are specific readable values (at normal atmospheric pressure); some mixtures, like chocolate, melt over a range instead. Thermometer-reading is a real measurement skill.

activities.title: Check and consolidate: place the temperatures, tell the changes apart
feedback: Confirm matches against the fixed values for water and address any 'steady softening with no particular temperature' thinking about water by pointing to the specific °C (some mixtures like chocolate or butter really do soften gradually).
For the melting/dissolving item, restate the one-substance vs two-substance distinction if needed.
activities.rationale: Recall, matching and sequencing checks consolidate and assess the knowledge; this format reinforces recall rather than letting the learner watch the change track the temperature, so it works best after the bench and hands-on tasks.
learnerActions: Place 0°C and 100°C on a thermometer scale.
Match each state change for water to its temperature (melt/freeze → 0°C, boil → 100°C).
Answer a question distinguishing melting from dissolving.
Sequence a heating timeline: ice → water → steam, with the temperature at each change point.
Explain whether melted ice is the same water, and give the reason.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can state the fixed temperatures, keep melting distinct from dissolving, and explain change of state as the same material at a readable temperature.

constraints: Keep to physical, reversible changes; avoid heating that burns or cooks (chemical change), per DfE guidance.
The KS2 core is observe-and-measure; the particle-level 'why' (heating gives particles more energy to move) is a light bridge to KS3, not the main objective.

A recall/matching/sequencing check reinforces and assesses knowledge but does not let the learner see the change occur at the temperature; pair it with the interactive bench and real hands-on measurement.

A tap-to-reveal annotated timeline consolidates and labels change points but does not drive the temperature to show the change happening at it; treat it as a static scaffold that can still teach the change points.
Fixed change temperatures (water 0°C/100°C) assume normal atmospheric pressure; state this assumption.

The material examples (chocolate, iron, oxygen) illustrate that change temperatures vary; iron/oxygen/boiling values are read/research examples, not precise figures to memorise or materials to handle at those temperatures.
A real thermometer, ice and gentle warming is the natural partner to any on-screen model; the on-screen version is a model of the real measurement.

The 0°C plateau demonstration requires a genuine melting ice-and-water mixture; without remaining ice the reading will not hold at 0°C, and the on-screen bench should mirror this holding behaviour for coherence.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no medium-superiority or hands-on-necessity efficacy has been established.

Legacy claims that 'live coupling is what a static medium cannot show' and that 3D 'adds no conceptual value' are catalog-fit judgements, not efficacy findings; softened to scoped affordances/limits. A static image or timeline can still teach the change points.

The phrase 'energy first goes into changing state, not raising temperature' (latent heat) is correct for a melting substance held at its melting point; the ice beaker must be a genuine melting ice-and-water mixture for the 0°C plateau to appear, as stated in the activities and constraints.

The bench activity was adjusted so the thermometer reading holds at the change temperature during melting/boiling, matching the real-thermometer plateau task; without this the two scenarios would conflict.

Molten iron, condensed oxygen and boiling water are not suitable for literal classroom handling; treat extreme-temperature materials as read/research examples, consistent with the standard's 'measure OR research' wording.
The assess field frames the particle explanation ('particles move more') within the 'correct answer'; retained as a light bridge only, not as the KS2 mastery criterion.

The NGSS reversibility claim is attached to the bench activity, whose model explicitly demonstrates reversal (re-freeze/recondense); it is not used on the fixed-temperature table activity, which it would not directly support.

assess.poeTask: Put a thermometer into a beaker of crushed melting ice and warm it gently, reading the temperature aloud. Ask the child to PREDICT what the thermometer does WHILE the ice is still melting, and WHY, before you start. Most predict it climbs steadily. It STICKS at 0°C until all the ice has melted, then climbs. The prediction's reason is diagnostic — a child who expects a steady climb hasn't grasped that the energy first goes into changing state, not raising temperature.
probeDeeper: If I melt the ice then refreeze it, is it the same water? How do you know?
Is melting the same as dissolving? What's different about them?
Chocolate melts too — is melted chocolate a new material, or the same chocolate?
When water freezes, does cold go INTO it, or does heat come OUT of it?
assess.correctAnswer: It's the same water — melting is a change of STATE (solid to liquid), not a change into a new material; cooling reverses it back to ice. Ice melts at 0°C and water boils at 100°C. Heating adds energy so the particles move more and the solid becomes liquid.

errorPatterns.pattern: Melting = dissolving — 'the ice dissolved into water'; the two processes are treated as the same.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast: melting needs only heat and involves one substance changing state; dissolving needs a SECOND substance (a liquid the solid spreads into) and no heating is required.
errorPatterns.distractor: The ice dissolved into water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses 'dissolve' for ice becoming water in a warm room; can't say how melting and dissolving differ.

errorPatterns.pattern: Change of state = new material — melted ice is thought to be a different liquid from the ice it came from.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Freeze the melt-water again to recover the ice, and note the mass is unchanged — same material throughout, only the state changed.
errorPatterns.distractor: When ice melts it turns into a completely new liquid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that the melt-water is the same water as the ice.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Cold moves in' — freezing explained as coldness entering the water rather than heat energy leaving it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe as energy: heating ADDS energy (melt, boil), cooling REMOVES it (freeze); 'cold' is just less heat, not a thing that moves in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the freezer 'puts cold into' the water; treats cold as a substance.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks melting makes a new substance or is the same as dissolving; has no fixed temperatures for the changes.
responseLevels.full: Explains melting, freezing and boiling as reversible changes of state of the SAME material at fixed temperatures, driven by adding or removing heat energy, and distinguishes melting from dissolving.
responseLevels.partial: Knows melting/freezing and the 0°C/100°C values, but is shaky on whether the material stays the same, or confuses melting with dissolving.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Two children argue about melting ice. One says when ice melts it turns INTO a new liquid; the other says it's still exactly the same water, just changed state. Who is right, and why?' Then: 'At what temperature does ice melt, and what temperature does water boil?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'new liquid vs same water' choice separates a change-of-state understanding from a substance-change belief; the temperature question checks the specific mastery criterion. A child who thinks melted ice is a new liquid, or who confuses melting with dissolving, is exposed by the tier-2 reasoning.

sources.claim: Elementary misconceptions include melting/dissolving confusion, treating 'cold' as a substance, and not grasping fixed change temperatures; conceptual change needs hands-on, repeated observation.

pedagogy.summary: Comparing and ordering fractions — including those greater than 1 — uses common denominators (always reliable), benchmarks (1/2, 1), or 'distance from a landmark'. For a set clustered just below 1, such as 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12, the elegant method is complement-to-1: the gaps to a whole are 1/4, 1/6, 1/8, 1/12, so the smallest gap is the largest fraction (11/12 largest, 3/4 smallest). For fractions above 1, compare via common denominators (7/5 = 21/15 vs 4/3 = 20/15) or convert to mixed numbers and place on a number line.
bestPractices: Choose a strategy that fits the numbers: common denominators always work; benchmark to 1/2 or 1; complement-to-1 for sets clustered near a whole
Recognise a fraction greater than 1 sits past 1 on the number line, and convert improper↔mixed to place and order it
Justify the ordering (why one is bigger), not just rank the symbols
Use a common denominator to make numerators directly comparable, rather than comparing tops and bottoms separately
Simplify or find common multiples to reach a shared denominator efficiently
keyRepresentations: Number line spanning past 1 (place 7/5, 4/3 and mixed numbers)
Common-denominator fraction strips
Benchmark markers at 1/2 and 1
Complement-to-1 gap diagram for near-whole sets
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias: bigger numerator and/or denominator means a bigger fraction (may land the right order for the wrong reason)
Compares numerators and denominators separately ('7 > 4 and 5 > 3 so 7/5 > 4/3')
Same-numerator lock reversed — with equal numerators, picks the bigger denominator as bigger (2/5 > 2/3)
Treats a fraction greater than 1 as if it were less than 1, or places it wrongly on the line
Compares without finding a common denominator

learn.summary: Help learners (age 10–11) compare and order fractions, including fractions greater than 1, by reasoning about value rather than digit size. Core strategies: common denominators (always reliable), benchmarking to 1/2 and 1, and complement-to-1 for sets clustered just below a whole (e.g. 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12, where the gaps to 1 are 3/4 → 1/4, 7/8 → 1/8, 5/6 → 1/6, 11/12 → 1/12, so the smallest gap means the largest fraction). For fractions above 1, convert to a common denominator (7/5 = 21/15 vs 4/3 = 20/15) or to mixed numbers and place on a number line. Throughout, the discriminating goal is a justified ordering, since whole-number bias can produce a correct rank for the wrong reason on favourable sets.

activities.title: Place and order fractions on a number line, measuring each gap to 1
feedback: If a learner ranks by digit size, note that this particular set happens to come out right by digits — press them to justify by value or gaps to 1, then try 2/3 vs 2/5 where digits mislead.

For 2/3 vs 2/5: both count two pieces, but fifths are smaller pieces than thirds, so two thirds exceed two fifths and 2/3 > 2/5 — a larger denominator makes each piece smaller, not the fraction larger.
If 7/5 is placed between 0 and 1, point back to the line: 7/5 is five fifths (one whole) plus two more fifths, so it must sit past 1 at 1 2/5.
Confirm 7/5 > 4/3 by the common denominator: over fifteenths, 21/15 > 20/15, so the single numerator comparison settles it.
activities.rationale: A number line makes relative size and 'distance to a landmark' visible, which can target the whole-number-bias error that treats numerator and denominator as independent, and supports correct placement of fractions greater than 1. Common denominators are presented as the always-reliable fallback.
sourceClaims: Fractions are compared by value using equivalent fractions/common denominators or benchmarks; the dominant error is whole-number bias (judging by numerator/denominator digit size and comparing numerators and denominators separately), which reflects treating the two parts as independent whole numbers rather than one quantity.
learnerActions: Place the set 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12 onto a number line running from 0 past 2.
For each fraction, mark or measure the distance from the fraction to the '1' mark (its gap to a whole): 3/4 → 1/4, 7/8 → 1/8, 5/6 → 1/6, 11/12 → 1/12.
State the order smallest to largest (3/4 < 5/6 < 7/8 < 11/12) and explain the link: the BIGGEST gap to 1 means the SMALLEST fraction, so 3/4 is smallest and 11/12 (hugging 1) is largest.
Place 7/5 and 4/3 on the same line and notice both land PAST 1; convert each to a mixed number (7/5 = 1 2/5) to confirm position.
Rewrite 7/5 and 4/3 over a common denominator (21/15 vs 20/15) and compare the numerators to decide which is larger.
Compare the counter-pair 2/3 and 2/5: which is larger, and why does the same number of larger-denominator pieces come to less?
activities.intendedInsight: Fraction size is one quantity located on the number line, not two independent whole numbers. For a near-whole set the fraction closest to 1 is largest; fractions greater than 1 sit past 1; and a common denominator turns any comparison into a single numerator comparison.

activities.title: Justify the ordering, not just the rank
feedback: Reward an explanation tied to value, size of pieces, or distance to a landmark over one tied to digit size.
For 5/6 vs 7/9, show the common denominator (45/54 vs 42/54), so 5/6 > 7/9 even though both of its digits are smaller — exactly the case the separate-comparison method gets wrong.
Encourage efficiency: for a set clustered near a whole, complement-to-1 is quicker than finding a full common denominator, but the common denominator always works.
activities.rationale: Because whole-number bias can yield a correct rank for the wrong reason on favourable sets, eliciting justification is how understanding is distinguished from a lucky rank; a pair where digit size and value diverge forces the reasoning. Offering multiple strategies supports flexible, number-sensitive choice.
sourceClaims: Fractions are compared by value using equivalent fractions/common denominators or benchmarks; the dominant error is whole-number bias (judging by numerator/denominator digit size and comparing numerators and denominators separately), which reflects treating the two parts as independent whole numbers rather than one quantity.
learnerActions: Order a fresh near-whole set (e.g. 2/3, 5/6, 9/10, 7/8) using the complement-to-1 method, writing each gap to 1 and explaining your reasoning.

Then tackle a pair where digit size and value DISAGREE — for example 5/6 vs 7/9, where '7 > 5 and 9 > 6' wrongly suggests 7/9 is larger — and settle it by writing both over a common denominator and comparing the deciding numerators.
Explain in words why comparing numerators and denominators separately is not a valid method, using the pair above as the case where it breaks down.
State for each answer the strategy you chose (common denominator, benchmark, or complement-to-1) and why it fitted those numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct ranking is not the same as a correct method; the justification is what shows genuine understanding, and the chosen strategy should fit the numbers.

activities.title: Short comparison and placement checks
feedback: For 7/5 vs 4/3, a response of 'equal' or '4/3 because 4 and 3 are bigger' signals whole-number bias; revisit the common denominator 21/15 vs 20/15.
For 2/3 vs 2/5, choosing 2/5 is the bigger-denominator distractor; return to same-numerator reasoning about piece size.
Pair any quick check with a request to explain the choice, since selecting the right answer does not by itself show the learner can construct the reasoning.
activities.rationale: Brief targeted checks can surface specific misconceptions through purpose-built distractors. They assess application but, on their own, do not elicit independent construction of a justification, so they should accompany the explanation work above.
sourceClaims: Fractions are compared by value using equivalent fractions/common denominators or benchmarks; the dominant error is whole-number bias (judging by numerator/denominator digit size and comparing numerators and denominators separately), which reflects treating the two parts as independent whole numbers rather than one quantity.
learnerActions: Order 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12 smallest to largest.
Decide which is larger, 7/5 or 4/3, and show the common-denominator working.
Decide which is larger, 2/3 or 2/5, and explain the role of the denominator.
Place 7/5 on a 0–2 number line.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can apply comparison strategies quickly and avoid common distractors (choosing 'equal', choosing 4/3 'because 4 and 3 are bigger', or choosing 2/5 because its denominator is larger).

activities.title: Reference fraction wall (support tool)
feedback: Treat the wall as a check or reference, not as the reasoning itself — after confirming, ask the learner to restate which is larger and why in terms of value.
activities.rationale: A prepared length reference supports comparison and can reinforce the magnitude idea. As a fixed scaffold it does not require the learner to place a new set or measure gaps themselves, so it should support, not replace, the active ordering and justification tasks.
learnerActions: Use a fraction wall extended past 1 to reveal which of two bars is longer and by how much.
Use it to check an ordering you have already reasoned out, or to settle a disputed pair.
activities.intendedInsight: A length model reinforces that fractions represent magnitudes that can be directly compared, including beyond one whole.

constraints: Target age is roughly 10–11; the content assumes prior work on equivalent fractions and common denominators.
Recognition/selection checks (choosing which is larger, placing a given fraction) assess application but do not by themselves elicit an independent justification; pair them with explanation tasks.
A pre-built fraction wall is a reference/support: it does not require the learner to order a new set or measure gaps to a landmark independently, so it should not be the only activity.
Complement-to-1 is efficient specifically for sets clustered just below a whole; present common denominators as the always-reliable general method so learners do not over-apply the shortcut.
Keep the goal on justified value comparison: a correct rank produced by digit-size reasoning should not count as mastery, so include at least one set where digit size and value diverge.
Explain same-numerator comparisons by piece size (more same-size pieces is more; a larger denominator makes each piece smaller) rather than any claim that a denominator rule 'reverses' or 'flips'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Critical-editor pass performed without new source verification: arithmetic and logic checked — complement-to-1 gaps for 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12 are 1/4, 1/8, 1/6, 1/12; ordered smallest-to-largest 3/4 < 5/6 < 7/8 < 11/12 (gaps 1/4 > 1/6 > 1/8 > 1/12); 7/5 = 21/15 > 20/15 = 4/3; 7/5 = 1 2/5 sits past 1; 2/3 > 2/5; 5/6 vs 7/9 = 45/54 vs 42/54 so 5/6 > 7/9. No arithmetic errors found.

The original row's fresh practice set (2/3, 5/6, 9/10, 7/8) is a case where digit size coincidentally matches value; a divergent pair (5/6 vs 7/9) is included in Activity 2 so the justification requirement genuinely bites.
The summary's gap list was relabelled per fraction (3/4 → 1/4, etc.) to match the activity text, since the unlabelled set-order list could be misread as already size-ordered.

The source material's claims that the number line is the single 'best'/'killer' way to see the insight, that depth/3D 'adds nothing', and that in-role dialogue cannot teach this are catalog-fit judgements not established by the cited WWC evidence; they have been softened to affordance-based framing (number line may make magnitude visible) rather than stated as universal pedagogical laws.
reteachPrerequisiteId values and the diagnostic/assessment design remain in the original row's assess field and were not altered; only learning guidance was rewritten.

probeDeeper: Which of 2/3 and 2/5 is bigger? Explain why the one with the bigger denominator is the smaller fraction.
How far is each of 3/4, 7/8, 5/6 and 11/12 from one whole? What does that tell you about which is biggest?
Is 7/5 bigger or smaller than 1? Where does it sit on a number line?
You said 7/5 > 4/3 — show me using a common denominator.
assess.correctAnswer: Smallest to largest: 3/4 < 5/6 < 7/8 < 11/12 (gaps to 1 are 1/4 > 1/6 > 1/8 > 1/12, so 3/4 is furthest below 1 and 11/12 closest). 7/5 > 4/3 (common denominator /15: 21/15 > 20/15).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — 'bigger numbers make a bigger fraction', ranking by digit size ('11/12 is biggest because 11 and 12 are the biggest numbers')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a common denominator or same-size-pieces reasoning: more parts of the same size is more, but bigger denominators make smaller pieces. Order by value, not digits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies the order by the size of the digits rather than the value; gets 2/3 vs 2/5 wrong (picks 2/5) when probed

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares numerators and denominators separately — '7 > 4 and 5 > 3, so 7/5 > 4/3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rewrite both over a common denominator (21/15 vs 20/15) so a single numerator comparison decides it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats top and bottom as two independent comparisons; the method fails on pairs where the two comparisons disagree

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot handle fractions greater than 1 — treats 7/5 as if less than 1, or cannot reach a common denominator to compare
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 7/5 sits past 1 on the number line (7/5 = 1 2/5); find a common denominator via the LCM of 5 and 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 7/5 between 0 and 1, or leaves the pair uncompared for want of a common denominator

responseLevels.gap: Ranks by digit size (whole-number bias) and cannot justify; cannot find common denominators; treats fractions greater than 1 as less than 1.
responseLevels.full: Orders using common denominators or complement-to-1 with justification, compares fractions greater than 1 correctly (7/5 > 4/3 via /15), places improper and mixed numbers on a number line, and handles the 2/3-vs-2/5 counter-case; transfers to a new set.
responseLevels.partial: Orders correctly using common denominators for some pairs but relies on surface cues for others, or gets the near-1 set right without a secure method (cannot explain complement-to-1), or hesitates with fractions greater than 1.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Order 3/4, 7/8, 5/6 and 11/12 from smallest to largest, and tell me how you decided. Then compare 7/5 and 4/3 — which is larger?' Watch the strategy and listen to the justification.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands uses common denominators or complement-to-1 and can justify each step. A child running whole-number bias may still rank THIS set correctly, because bigger digits happen to align with bigger value here — so the justification, not the ranking, is what discriminates. The follow-up 2/3-vs-2/5 probe (bigger denominator, smaller fraction) catches the biased child, and 7/5 vs 4/3 checks they compare fractions above 1 by size rather than by 'which has bigger numbers'.

sources.claim: Fractions are compared by value using equivalent fractions/common denominators or benchmarks; the dominant error is whole-number bias (judging by numerator/denominator digit size and comparing numerators and denominators separately), which reflects treating the two parts as independent whole numbers rather than one quantity.

pedagogy.summary: This is the procedural workhorse of percentages: finding a percentage of an amount (15% of 360) and using percentages to COMPARE quantities. At this age the reliable, meaning-preserving method is to build any percentage from friendly known facts — 10% (divide by 10), 5% (half of 10%), 1% (divide by 100) — and combine them (15% = 10% + 5%), which keeps the calculation grounded in 'parts per hundred' rather than a memorised rule. The second, subtler skill is comparison: a percentage is always relative to its base, so comparing two percentages of DIFFERENT amounts requires calculating the actual amounts, not just comparing the percentages. Teaching should anchor percentages to a 100-grid or bar, drill the 10%/5%/1% building blocks, and force explicit attention to 'percent of WHAT' whenever comparing.
bestPractices: Build percentages from benchmark facts: 10% (÷10), 1% (÷100), 5% (half of 10%), 25% (÷4), 50% (÷2), then combine (15% = 10% + 5%; 35% = 25% + 10%).
Anchor to a 100-square or a bar split into ten 10% chunks so 'parts per hundred' stays visible and 10% of 360 = 36 is seen, not just computed.

Make 'percent of what?' explicit in every comparison problem: a bigger percentage of a smaller amount can be less than a smaller percentage of a bigger amount — always compute the actual amounts to compare.
Connect the three forms fluently — 15% = 15/100 = 0.15 — and check the decimal is placed correctly (15% = 0.15, not 1.5), since misplacing it is a common source of tenfold errors.
Use bar models for percentage-of-amount: the whole bar is 100%, partition and shade to read off the required percentage.
Progress from friendly percentages (multiples of 5) to any percentage, and to a single-multiplier method (×0.15) once the benchmark method is secure.
keyRepresentations: 100-square (each cell = 1%) and a bar split into ten 10% chunks
Benchmark fact ladder: 10%, 5%, 1%, 25%, 50% and how to combine them
Percentage bar model (whole = 100%, shade the required part)
The equivalence triple 15% = 15/100 = 0.15
Two labelled bars of different totals for comparison (percent of WHICH base)
commonMisconceptions: Compares two percentages while ignoring their different bases (assumes 30% off always saves more than 25% off, whatever the prices)
Misplaces the decimal when converting: treats 15% as 1.5 (or 6% as 0.6), giving a tenfold error
Cannot assemble a percentage from benchmarks, or takes 5% as 10% ÷ 5 instead of 10% ÷ 2
Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount rather than a proportion of the given whole

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils learn to find a percentage of an amount (e.g. 15% of 360) by building from benchmark facts — 10% (÷10), 5% (half of 10%), 1% (÷100) — and combining them (15% = 10% + 5%), keeping the calculation grounded in 'parts per hundred'. The subtler skill is comparison: because a percentage is always relative to its base, comparing two percentages of DIFFERENT amounts requires computing the actual amounts, not just comparing the percentages. Anchoring to a 100-grid or bar, drilling the benchmark building blocks, and forcing explicit attention to 'percent of WHAT' when comparing are the core moves.

activities.title: Build a percentage from benchmark chunks
feedback: If 10% of 360 is given as 3.6 or 360, return to 'parts per hundred': 10% means one of ten equal chunks, i.e. ÷10, so 10% of 360 = 36. Rebuild the triple 10% = 10/100 = 0.1.
If 5% is computed as 360÷5 = 72, point out that dividing the whole by 5 gives a fifth, which is 20%, not 5%. 5% is HALF of 10%, so 5% of 360 = 36 ÷ 2 = 18.
If the pupil cannot combine, show that 15% = 10% + 5%, so £36 + £18 = £54.

A running total shown as chunks snap together is one way to let the pupil watch £36 + £18 = £54 build up rather than only computing it (an optional illustration of the mechanism, not a required tool).
activities.rationale: Building percentages from benchmarks keeps the meaning (proportion of a hundred) in view and is treated here as the reliable, meaning-preserving method at this age; the equivalence triple and decimal-placement work directly target the documented percent-to-decimal conversion errors. An interactive bar with a live running total is a proposed way to make the build-and-combine action concrete; efficacy of the specific interaction is not established by the sources, which also note that benchmark-then-combine can be inefficient relative to a single multiplier.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures, such as 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison.

Documented common student errors include converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (e.g. treating 6% as 0.6) and using inefficient benchmark-then-combine methods; the underlying idea is percentage as a proportion, and translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty.
learnerActions: Treat a bar as the whole amount (e.g. £360 = 100%) and partition it into ten equal 10% chunks.
Find 15% of £360 by taking one 10% chunk (£36) and half of another (5% = £18), then combining them to read £54.
Say aloud how each benchmark is found: 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100, 5% = half of 10%, 25% = ÷4, 50% = ÷2, and combine (e.g. 35% = 25% + 10%).
Record the matching equivalence each time: 15% = 15/100 = 0.15, and check the decimal point is in the right place (0.15, not 1.5).
Progress from friendly multiples of 5 to any percentage, and later to a single multiplier (×0.15) once the benchmark method is secure.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a percentage of an amount is assembling friendly known pieces, not recalling an opaque rule; 'parts per hundred' stays visible on the bar.

activities.title: Compare mode: percent of WHICH base?
feedback: If the pupil picks the 30% deal with no calculation, ask 'percent of WHAT?' and have them compute both actual savings on the two labelled bars.
If they compute one base and assume it applies to both, draw attention to the different bar totals and have them compute the second separately.
Two bars of different totals shown side by side, with each discount slice drawn to scale, can let the pupil SEE the 25%-of-£80 slice (£20) come out taller than the 30%-of-£60 slice (£18).
activities.rationale: The comparison is deliberately rigged so the smaller percentage gives the larger saving, which directly addresses the base-ignoring misconception; the underlying principle is that a percentage is a proportion of its own base. Drawing both slices to scale on different-height bars is a proposed way to make the relationship visible; its comparative efficacy over other formats is not established.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures, such as 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison.

Documented common student errors include converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (e.g. treating 6% as 0.6) and using inefficient benchmark-then-combine methods; the underlying idea is percentage as a proportion, and translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty.
learnerActions: Look at two bars of different totals side by side, e.g. an £80 coat at 25% off and a £60 jacket at 30% off.
First predict which deal saves more, then compute both actual savings: 25% of £80 = £20 and 30% of £60 = £18.
State the result: the COAT saves more (£20 > £18) even though its percentage is smaller, because the two percentages are taken of different prices.
Test the base explicitly: if the jacket had cost £100 instead of £60, recompute — 30% of £100 = £30 would now win — to show that the base matters.
Finish by writing a one-sentence explanation of why a smaller percentage can give a larger amount.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage is relative to its own base; to compare two percentages of different amounts you must compute the actual amounts, not compare the percentages.

activities.title: Scored practice set with a base-ignoring distractor
feedback: Mark the 'bigger-percentage-wins' choice as a base error and prompt recomputation of both actual amounts.
If an answer is out by a factor of ten (e.g. 15% of 360 given as 5.4 or 540), flag the decimal/place-value slip and rebuild 15% = 0.15.
If the build-up blanks are inconsistent (10% right but 15% wrong), show 15% = 10% + 5%.
activities.rationale: A scored set can check percentage-of-amount and comparison cleanly, and a base-ignoring option is diagnostic; it consolidates and diagnoses rather than being the main place the comparison concept is constructed. Recognition-style items can check whether an answer is correctly classified but do not by themselves elicit the independent build-and-combine construction.
sourceClaims: Documented common student errors include converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (e.g. treating 6% as 0.6) and using inefficient benchmark-then-combine methods; the underlying idea is percentage as a proportion, and translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in build-ups: 10% of 360 = ☐, 5% of 360 = ☐, so 15% of 360 = ☐.
Answer a multiple-choice comparison of two discounts on differently-priced items, where one option is the 'bigger percentage must win' answer.
Use a slider to estimate a percentage on a 0-to-amount scale as a proportional sanity check before computing exactly.
Convert between forms in short items: write 15% as a fraction and a decimal and check decimal placement.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency with benchmark build-up and correct decimal conversion, plus recognising when a percentage-only comparison is wrong.

activities.title: 100-grid reference and shop-context discussion
feedback: If the pupil answers the shopkeeper by percentage alone, challenge with the rigged case where the smaller percentage wins and ask them to compute both actual amounts.

For '15% is 54 — roughly what fraction of 360 is that, and does that seem about right?', prompt a proportional check: 54 lies between a tenth of 360 (36) and a fifth (72), not 540 or 5.4. It is one and a half times 36 because 15% is one and a half times 10%.
activities.rationale: A static grid can anchor one worked percentage as a reference, and a conversational shop context can surface the base question and check reasoning; a conversation of this kind may prompt justification but does not itself drill computation, so repeated practice across cases is still needed for fluency.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures, such as 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison.
learnerActions: On a 100-square where the whole grid is 360 and each cell = 1% (worth 3.6), reveal 10 cells (10% = 36), then a further 5 cells (5% = 18), then read 15 cells (15% = 54), as a benchmark reference.
Discuss a shopkeeper's competing deals on differently-priced items: 'which saves more?', and justify by computing actual amounts rather than comparing percentages.
Answer probing questions: 'How did you get 10% of 360 — and how do you know it isn't 3.6?'; 'Give me a quick way to find 5%, and 1%, of any amount.'
activities.intendedInsight: The 100-grid keeps 'parts per hundred' concrete, and talking through a real comparison forces 'percent of what?' into the reasoning.

constraints: 5% is HALF of 10% (÷2). It is not the amount ÷ 5, which gives 20%, and it is not 10% ÷ 5, which gives 2%. These are common slips to pre-empt.
Always make 'percent of what?' explicit in comparison problems — a bigger percentage of a smaller amount can be less than a smaller percentage of a bigger amount, so compute the actual amounts.
Check decimal placement: 15% = 0.15, not 1.5; misplacement gives tenfold errors.
The static 100-grid is a benchmark reference, not the main practice: fluency and comparison require the pupil to compute across multiple cases, not just view one worked example.

The scored set consolidates and diagnoses; recognition-style items can check whether an answer is right but do not by themselves elicit the independent build-and-combine construction, so they supplement rather than replace the bar work.

Bar/grid models are representations of proportion; keep the numeric meaning (parts per hundred) explicit so pupils do not treat the picture as the whole method. Percentages and fractions are comparable as numbers (e.g. 0.15 < 0.30) irrespective of any base; it is the actual amounts they produce that depend on the base, so when comparing represented portions use a common whole.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the interactive mechanisms are optional illustrations of the learning mechanism, not mandatory tools or product features.

Self-audit of the worked numbers: 10% of 360 = 36, 5% = 18, 15% = 54 (correct). 25% of £80 = £20; 30% of £60 = £18, so the coat saves more (£20 > £18) — the comparison is correctly rigged. 30% of £100 = £30 (correct for the counterexample). No arithmetic errors found.

Tension in source claim 2: it describes 'benchmark-then-combine' as an inefficient method and a documented difficulty, whereas the pedagogy recommends it as the reliable Year 6 method. The claim is retained because it also supports percentage-as-proportion and decimal-conversion errors; it is NOT treated as evidence that benchmark-then-combine is efficient or best. Progression to a single multiplier (×0.15) once benchmarks are secure is kept to acknowledge the efficiency point.

Comparative efficacy of the interactive bar over static grid or quiz formats is not asserted; sources establish the curriculum objective and document misconceptions but do not establish necessity or superiority of any medium.

probeDeeper: 'How did you get 10% of 360 — and how do you know it isn't 3.6?' — checks the place-value meaning of 10%.
'You said 15% is 54 — roughly what fraction of 360 is that, and does that seem about right?' — checks a proportional sanity check (15% ≈ a bit more than a tenth).

Counterexample: 'If the jacket had been £100 instead of £60, would your answer change?' — a child who understands base recomputes (30% of £100 = £30 now wins); a percentage-only reasoner does not see why it would matter.
'Give me a quick way to find 5%, and 1%, of any amount' — surfaces whether the benchmark toolkit is fluent.
assess.correctAnswer: 15% of 360 = 54 (10% is 36, 5% is 18, total 54). Coat saving = 25% of £80 = £20; jacket saving = 30% of £60 = £18; so the COAT saves more (£20 > £18) even though its percentage is smaller, because the amounts are percentages of different prices.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares the percentages and ignores the different bases: 'the jacket, because 30% is more than 25%' — without working out the actual savings
errorPatterns.nextMove: Force 'percent of WHAT?' — compute both actual amounts on two labelled bars of different heights; show the smaller percentage taking the bigger slice. Reinforce percentage as relative to its own base.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child picks the bigger percentage as the bigger saving with no calculation, or calculates one base and assumes it applies to both

errorPatterns.pattern: Misplaces the decimal / mis-converts the percentage: takes 10% of 360 as 3.6 or 360, or treats 15% as 1.5, giving a tenfold error
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the 100-grid / 'parts per hundred': 10% means ÷10 (one whole chunk of the ten), 1% means ÷100; check 15% = 0.15 not 1.5. Rebuild the equivalence triple.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The percentage-of-amount answer is out by a factor of ten (e.g. 15% of 360 given as 5.4 or 540)

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot assemble the percentage from benchmarks, or takes 5% as 10% ÷ 5 instead of half of 10%
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach percentages — scaffold the benchmark relationships: 5% is HALF of 10%; 15% = 10% + 5%. A lapse in assembling, not a conceptual gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child finds 10% correctly but computes 5% as 360÷5 = 72, or cannot combine 10% and 5% into 15%

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find a percentage of an amount reliably (tenfold errors, faulty benchmarks) and compares discounts by percentage alone, ignoring the base.
responseLevels.full: Fluently builds any percentage of an amount from benchmarks (or a single multiplier), places decimals correctly, and when comparing always computes the actual amounts relative to each base, explaining why a smaller percentage can give a larger amount.
responseLevels.partial: Finds friendly percentages of an amount via 10%/5% build-up for the practised case, but the method is fragile (place-value slips, awkward percentages) or still compares percentages without consistently computing both bases when they differ.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two things, do them however you like and I'll watch. First, find 15% of 360. Second, two shops: a coat that normally costs £80 has 25% off, and a jacket that normally costs £60 has 30% off — work out which sale saves you more money.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The comparison is rigged so the SMALLER percentage (25%) gives the LARGER saving (£20 vs £18): a child who understands that a percentage is relative to its base computes both actual amounts and picks the coat; a child who treats the percentage as the whole story picks the jacket (30% > 25%) without computing. And 15% of 360 exposes the build-up method and the decimal placement — whether 10% is read as 36 (correct) or 3.6/360 (place-value slip). Watching, not asking, surfaces both.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–8 years

- **Topic:** Local Plants & Animals

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'):** 'identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including microhabitats' (e.g. under a log, in a pond).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-LS4-1):** '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1].'

- **Operational details:** Children go beyond generic habitats to identify and NAME the specific plants and animals living in a real, local place, and explore microhabitats — the very small habitats within a bigger one (under a stone, in leaf litter, in a pond). They link each creature to the microhabitat's conditions ('under a stone is damp and dark, woodlice like that'). This is first-hand, observational fieldwork: look closely, identify, name, and describe where and why.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, observational identification). Success = naming at least three plants and animals from a specific local habitat, explaining what a microhabitat is with an example, and describing a microhabitat's conditions and which creature suits it — grounded in observation rather than recall of exotic species.
bestPractices: Prioritise first-hand fieldwork — look closely at real local organisms — over recall of exotic species from books.
Use simple picture keys/spotter sheets so children identify and NAME what they find, building precise vocabulary.
Explore microhabitats by searching (lift logs, turn stones, dip ponds) and link each find to the conditions there.
Tally and compare what lives in different microhabitats to surface diversity ('more under the damp log than on the dry path').
Model respectful observation — look, record, and return creatures — as part of the practice.
keyRepresentations: A local-habitat scene with searchable microhabitats (log, pond, long grass, stone).
Picture-key / spotter sheet for naming common local organisms.
A microhabitat 'conditions' tag set (damp, dark, wet, sunny) attached to each find.
A tally/species list comparing organisms across microhabitats.
commonMisconceptions: Naming only exotic animals (lions, tigers) rather than the organisms actually present locally.
Not recognising a microhabitat as a habitat — thinking 'under a log' is too small to count.
Assuming the same creatures live everywhere, missing that conditions sort them into different microhabitats.
Overlooking plants and tiny invertebrates as part of the habitat's life.
Thinking a creature is 'lost' rather than suited when found in a damp/dark place.

learn.summary: For 6–8 year-olds learning to identify and name local plants and animals, including microhabitats (under a log, in a pond, in leaf litter). The core work is first-hand observational fieldwork: search real tiny places, identify and name what lives there using a simple picture key, and link each creature to the microhabitat's conditions (damp/dark suits woodlice). The central insight is that different tiny places shelter different, suited creatures — grounded in observation, not recall of exotic species. A searchable scene can scaffold the nested-scale idea, but because the curriculum prioritises first-hand fieldwork it supplements rather than replaces a real minibeast hunt.

activities.title: Real minibeast hunt: search, name, and record conditions
feedback: If a child names only exotic animals (lions, tigers), redirect: 'Those live far away — let's name the creatures we can actually see right here.'
If a child says 'under a log is too small to be a habitat', point out the log is a small habitat inside the whole garden habitat — small places count.
If a child links a creature to a condition ('woodlice are here because it's damp and dark'), confirm and extend: 'What would happen to a woodlouse out on the hot, dry wall?'
If a child treats a creature found in a damp/dark place as 'lost' or in the wrong place, explain it is not lost but suited: the damp, dark conditions are exactly what it needs.
If a child overlooks plants or tiny invertebrates, prompt them to add the plants and the smallest creatures to the species list too.
activities.rationale: The standards require children to identify and NAME specific local organisms and explain microhabitats from first-hand observation, not recall, and to compare the diversity of life across habitats. Searching, naming with a key, tagging conditions, and tallying what lives where directly build the precise vocabulary and the conditions-sort-creatures idea.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2: 'identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including microhabitats.'
NGSS 2-LS4-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1].'
learnerActions: Go outdoors to a local habitat (garden, school grounds, park) and gently search several microhabitats: lift a log, turn a stone, dip a net in a pond, part the long grass, sift leaf litter.
For each find, use a simple picture key / spotter sheet to identify and say the creature's NAME aloud (woodlouse, centipede, pond skater, tadpole, grasshopper, worm).
Attach a conditions tag to each microhabitat: damp, dark, wet, sunny, dry — and say it ('under the log is damp and dark').
Keep a tally/species list of what lives where, then compare: which microhabitat had the most living things?
Model respectful practice throughout: look closely, record, and return every creature and replace each log/stone where it was found.
activities.intendedInsight: Different tiny places (microhabitats) within one habitat have different conditions, and creatures are usually found where the conditions suit them; a microhabitat is a small habitat inside a larger one.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: where will more minibeasts live?
feedback: If a child predicts the sunny open ground and is surprised by the teeming damp underside, use that surprise: 'The damp dark place had more — why might that be?'

If a child says 'the woodlice could live on the wall too, they just haven't crawled there yet', address it directly: a woodlouse needs damp to breathe and loses water quickly, so if it stayed on a hot, dry wall in the daytime it could dry out and die. It is not simply absent by chance — the conditions mostly keep it in damp places like under the log (woodlice may come out at night or in wet weather, when it is damp).
If a child describes the log as damp and dark but cannot say why that helps woodlice, bridge with 'What happens to a woodlouse left in the hot sun?' to connect condition to consequence.
activities.rationale: Stating a prediction and reason before observing exposes whether a child reasons from conditions or from a 'creatures are everywhere' misconception, and the violated prediction makes the conditions→suitability link memorable.
learnerActions: Before looking, predict: 'Will I find more minibeasts under this damp log, or on this sunny open patch / brick wall?' and state WHY.
Lift the log (or paving slab) and check the sunny patch; observe what is actually there.

Compare the prediction with what you actually found and explain it: for example, if you found woodlice or worms under the damp log but not on the sunny wall, why might that be? If your results were different, talk about what might explain that.
Transfer the reasoning to a new place: name two creatures that live in the pond water (such as tadpoles or pond skaters) that you would not expect to find under a dry log, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: Creatures are not scattered at random; they are mostly found where the conditions (damp/dark vs hot/dry) suit what their bodies can tolerate — a woodlouse left in the hot sun soon dries out.

activities.title: 'Microhabitat' means a small place, not a small animal
feedback: If a child says a microhabitat is 'where small/tiny animals live', correct it: it means a small habitat within a bigger one — and even a larger creature can use a small microhabitat.
Confirm good explanations that name the bigger habitat the microhabitat sits inside.
activities.rationale: A common error is reading 'micro' as describing animal size. Naming the larger habitat and pointing to a surprisingly large resident of a small place corrects this conservatively.
learnerActions: Point to the log and say what bigger habitat it is part of (the whole garden/wood).
Explain in your own words that a microhabitat is a small habitat INSIDE a larger one.
Find a creature that is bigger than you'd expect in a tiny place (e.g. a centipede under a small log) to show 'micro' is about the place, not the animal's size.
Give an example of a microhabitat and describe its conditions.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Micro' refers to the small scale of the place, not the size of the animals that live there; a small habitat still counts as a habitat.

activities.title: Searchable habitat scene (scaffold for the nested-scale idea)
feedback: When a search reveals woodlice and a centipede in the damp dark but grasshoppers in the sunny grass, prompt: 'Why are different creatures hiding in different places?'
For matching/identification, confirm correct organism→microhabitat pairings and, for errors, ask what the conditions are like where that creature belongs.
activities.rationale: A searchable scene with name and conditions tags mirrors the searching action of fieldwork and offers immediate feedback, and the child names organisms found in habitats including microhabitats; matching and picture-identification let a child practise naming and suitability. These support the concept but present a fixed set of creatures and do not elicit the handling and independent searching of real fieldwork, so the scaffold's efficacy relative to fieldwork is not claimed.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2: 'identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including microhabitats.'
learnerActions: In a local-habitat scene, search by tapping to lift a log, dip a net in the pond, or part the long grass; each search reveals the creatures that live there.
Read the name label and conditions tag (damp, dark, wet, sunny) that pops up for each find, and say the name aloud.
Watch a species list / tally build as you search, then compare which microhabitat held the most creatures.
Use matching and picture-identification activities ('which lives under a damp log?') to check naming and link each organism to the microhabitat whose conditions suit it.
activities.intendedInsight: Reveal-on-search gives immediate naming feedback and shows that different tiny places hide different suited creatures; it rehearses the nested-scale idea when outdoor fieldwork is not available.

constraints: First-hand observation of real local organisms is the curriculum priority; a searchable scene and picture-matching are scaffolds that present a fixed cast and cannot substitute for a real minibeast hunt.

Success means naming at least three real plants and animals from a specific LOCAL habitat, explaining what a microhabitat is with an example, and describing a microhabitat's conditions and which creature suits it — not reciting exotic species.

Matching and picture-identification check naming and suitability but assess recognition; recognition alone does not elicit the independent searching, identifying and recording that the standard requires.
Model respectful practice: look, record, and return every creature and replace logs/stones — this is part of the learning, not an afterthought.

A conversational 'nature guide' can respond to a child's descriptions and rehearse describing conditions; a picture key and visuals show the organism itself, which description-only dialogue cannot, so they may give clearer identification support.
A 3D explorable scene may add immersion, but naming creatures and linking them to conditions is not spatial reasoning, so the added navigation is not required for this objective.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels one microhabitat example as a 'brick/sunny wall' with 'sun-loving insects'; a butterfly resting is plausible but a child's local wall may show few insects. Kept the damp-log vs dry-wall contrast because the conditions logic (woodlice need damp, dry out in sun) is sound; actual outdoor finds will vary with site and weather, so treat predicted species as examples not guarantees.

The original 'correctAnswer' states woodlice 'dry out and die in the sun'; this is biologically reasonable (woodlice are crustaceans that lose water quickly and rely on moisture to breathe) and is retained in the feedback as the conditions rationale, phrased for young learners without asserting any fixed timescale.
One NGSS source is flagged verified:false in the row; the comparative-diversity claim is retained as a standard reference only, not as evidence of activity efficacy.

The claim that a picture key gives clearer identification support than open dialogue is retained only as an affordance (visuals show the organism itself); relative efficacy between the two media was not tested.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain, outdoors: before lifting a damp log (or a paving slab) and checking a sunny open patch, the child predicts WHERE they will find more minibeasts and states WHY. Many predict the open sunny ground; observing the damp, dark underside teeming with woodlice/worms while the sunny patch is bare violates that, and the pre-stated reason exposes whether they were reasoning from conditions or from 'creatures are everywhere'.
probeDeeper: Does 'microhabitat' describe the size of the place or the size of the animal? Which log-creature is bigger than you'd expect?
Why would a woodlouse be in trouble on the hot, dry wall?
Name two creatures you'd find in a pond but never under a dry log.
The log is a microhabitat — what bigger habitat is it part of?
assess.correctAnswer: Under the log it is damp and dark, which woodlice need — they dry out and die in the sun. The sunny wall is hot and dry, which suits sun-loving insects but not woodlice. Different microhabitats have different conditions, and each creature is found where the conditions suit it.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'They could live on the wall too, they just haven't gone there' — thinks creatures are distributed at random and could be found anywhere.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to habitats-provide-needs (prerequisite), then make it local: what does damp/dark give a woodlouse that hot/dry cannot? Predict where each creature is BEFORE looking.
errorPatterns.distractor: The woodlice could live on the sunny wall too — they just haven't crawled there yet.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the woodlice could live on the sunny wall as well; gives no condition-based reason for their absence.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Microhabitat means the home of tiny animals' — reads 'micro' as being about the size of the creature, not the small scale of the place.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the log as a small habitat WITHIN the whole garden habitat; contrast a big creature that could still use a small microhabitat.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked what 'microhabitat' means, says 'where small/tiny animals live' rather than 'a small habitat inside a bigger one'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not connect the physical condition to the creature's need — notices damp/dark but cannot say why it matters to a woodlouse.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: prompt 'what happens to a woodlouse in the hot sun?' to bridge condition→consequence; the classification idea is already there.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the log as damp and dark but, asked why that helps woodlice, cannot link it to drying out.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks any creature could be anywhere; cannot say why woodlice avoid the wall, and misreads 'microhabitat' as tiny animals.
responseLevels.full: Explains the match by linking specific conditions (damp/dark vs hot/dry) to what each creature can tolerate, uses 'microhabitat' as a small place within a larger habitat, and transfers the reasoning to a new microhabitat such as a pond.
responseLevels.partial: Says woodlice belong under the log and notes it is damp/dark, but does not connect the condition to the creature's need, or blurs microhabitat with 'small animals'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell the child: 'Under a damp log I found woodlice and worms. On a sunny brick wall nearby I found none of them — but I did see a butterfly.' Ask: 'Why do the woodlice live under the log and not on the sunny wall? What is it like in each place?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who believes creatures can be anywhere ('they just haven't crawled over yet') cannot explain the woodlice's absence from the wall. A child who grasps that a microhabitat has particular conditions names damp/dark versus hot/dry and links each to what the creature can tolerate.
