pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11; understand rainforests as BIODIVERSITY HOTSPOTS — ~6% of Earth's land surface holding over half of all known plant and animal species — and why that concentration makes them irreplaceable and a conservation priority.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (biomes, distribution of natural resources) and Science Y4 classification / Y6 living things; leads to KS3 Biology 'interdependence and biodiversity'.
• Standards — US: NGSS 3-LS4-3/-4 and MS-LS2-4/-5 (biodiversity, ecosystem services, and maintaining biodiversity).
• Operational details — the concept lives in a DISPROPORTION: a tiny slice of land, a giant slice of life. Teach it as a proportion contrast — 6% land vs >50% of known species — using a strong visual (two bars, or two pie slices). Ground it in a vivid concrete: a single hectare of Amazon can hold more tree species than all of Europe/North America combined. Be precise on caveats appropriate for the top tier: it's TROPICAL rainforests, and KNOWN/documented species (many are still undiscovered); credible figures range from 'more than half' up to WWF's '80% of documented species'. Land the 'so what': such concentration means clearing a small area destroys an outsized share of life → priority for protection.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (9): state ~6% land holds over half of all species. Tier B (10): explain why that concentration makes rainforests a conservation priority. Tier C (11): cite a concrete example (one hectare > all Europe's tree species) and add the 'tropical/known-species' caveat.
bestPractices: Teach the concept as a DISPROPORTION — tiny land share vs huge species share — with a direct side-by-side visual.
Ground the abstract percentage in a vivid concrete (one hectare holds more tree species than all of Europe).
State the caveats honestly at the top tier: tropical rainforests specifically, and KNOWN species (many undiscovered).
Land the 'so what': high concentration means clearing a small area destroys an outsized share of life → conservation priority.
Use up-to-date, authoritative figures (WWF, National Geographic) rather than advocacy aggregators.
keyRepresentations: Two proportion bars/pies: land ~6% vs known species >50%.
A one-hectare Amazon plot vs all-of-Europe tree-species comparison.
A gallery of example species (toucan, jaguar, dart frog) plus 'many still undiscovered'.
A 'shrink the sliver → lose a big chunk of species' cause-effect visual.
commonMisconceptions: 'Rainforests cover most of the Earth' — they cover only about 6% of land.
'Half the species means half of a small number' — it means over half of ALL known life on Earth.
'We know all the species already' — many, especially insects, remain undiscovered; figures are for KNOWN species.
'All rainforests (including temperate) hold this biodiversity' — the claim is specifically about tropical rainforests.
'Losing a small area is no big deal' — because life is so concentrated, small losses destroy an outsized share of species.

learn.summary: Learners (ages 9–11) build the concept that tropical rainforests are biodiversity hotspots: they cover only about 6% of Earth's land yet hold over half of all KNOWN plant and animal species. The central insight is a disproportion — a tiny slice of land, a giant slice of life — and its consequence: because so many species are packed into so little land, clearing tropical rainforest destroys habitat for far more species per area than most other land, and can permanently wipe out species found nowhere else, making protection a priority. Learners also distinguish biodiversity (variety of different species) from mere abundance (many animals of one kind).

activities.title: The mismatch made visible: 6% of land, over half of life
feedback: If a learner says rainforests must cover most of the Earth, point back to the thin sliver: tropical rainforests are only about 6% of land, yet still hold over half of known species.

If a learner reasons 'it's only 6%, so losing it isn't a big deal', have them re-run the shadow demo: contrast the 6% of land with the >50% of known species that live there and depend on that habitat.
If a learner thinks 'over half the species' means half of a small number, clarify it means over half of ALL known plant and animal life on Earth.
Reinforce that the example species shown are just a handful; captions note many more remain undiscovered, so the real variety is even greater.
activities.rationale: The concept lives in a proportion contrast, so a direct side-by-side visual of land share vs species share makes the disproportion concrete; grounding the abstract percentage in a vivid example (hundreds of tree species in a single hectare, sometimes compared to the tree variety of whole northern European regions) and a shadow demo showing how many species depend on the small sliver is intended to land the conservation consequence.
sourceClaims: Tropical forests cover just 6% of the planet's land surface but are some of the richest, most biodiverse places on Earth, home to a very large share of the world's species (WWF states 80% of documented species; other authorities state 'more than half of known species')
Rainforests cover roughly 2–6% of Earth's surface yet more than half of the world's known plant and animal species live in them; a single hectare can hold hundreds of tree species
learnerActions: Study a side-by-side pair of proportion bars (or two pie slices): one bar shows all of Earth's land with only a thin sliver (~6%, about a sixteenth) marked as tropical rainforest; the second bar shows all known living species with more than half marked as living in tropical rainforests.
Describe in your own words the mismatch you see between the land share and the species share.

Explore a drill-down (tap or reveal) that zooms the sliver to a single hectare of Amazon, with a caption presenting the often-cited illustration that it can hold more kinds of tree than all of northern Europe (authoritative sources confirm hundreds of tree species per hectare), and reveals example species — toucan, jaguar, poison dart frog — plus a note that many more species (especially insects) are still undiscovered.

Drag a shadow across the small green land sliver and watch the rainforest part of the species bar light up, showing how many known species depend on that small area; then explain why harming even part of it puts the homes of many species at risk (this is a model of concentration, not an exact count of species lost).
activities.intendedInsight: A tiny patch of the planet carries a staggering share of its known life; because life is so concentrated, clearing tropical rainforest destroys habitat for far more species per area than most other land, and can wipe out species found nowhere else — which is why protecting them matters so much.

activities.title: Estimate then reveal: predict the species share
feedback: If a learner guesses a small share, highlight the gap between their guess and the >50% reality, and tie it back to the 6%-of-land contrast.
Whatever the guess, confirm the two anchor figures explicitly: ~6% of land, over half of known species.
activities.rationale: An estimate-then-reveal interaction is intended to make the surprise active and can double as a check of understanding, while the core insight still rests on the proportion contrast that the cited figures support.
sourceClaims: Rainforests cover roughly 2–6% of Earth's surface yet more than half of the world's known plant and animal species live in them; a single hectare can hold hundreds of tree species
learnerActions: Before seeing the answer, predict what share of the world's known species live in tropical rainforests — for example by setting a slider or writing a percentage.
Reveal the actual figure (over half, i.e. >50%) shown against the fact that tropical rainforests are only about 6% of land, and compare it with your guess.
Say whether the real figure was higher or lower than you expected, and explain what surprised you.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners may underestimate how concentrated rainforest biodiversity is; committing to a prediction first is intended to make the true disproportion more memorable and surprising, though this prediction effect is a design hypothesis rather than a verified outcome.

activities.title: What 'biodiversity' really means, and why loss is irreversible
feedback: If a learner says biodiversity just means lots of animals, define it as the variety of different KINDS of species: 10,000 identical animals is low biodiversity, many different kinds is high.
If a learner says lost species exist elsewhere too, explain that many are endemic — found only in that forest — so losing the forest loses them entirely.

A full response links ~6% of land to >50% of known species, defines biodiversity as variety, and justifies the conservation priority; a partial response knows rainforests are rich but can't yet articulate the disproportion or the variety definition.
activities.rationale: The target concept pairs the disproportion with a correct definition of biodiversity as variety and the idea of endemism, so prompts that force learners to reason about both are intended to surface the common misconceptions directly; the disproportion element is supported by the cited WWF figures, while the biodiversity definition and endemism are inherited from the row's assessment rather than from a cited source.
sourceClaims: Tropical forests cover just 6% of the planet's land surface but are some of the richest, most biodiverse places on Earth, home to a very large share of the world's species (WWF states 80% of documented species; other authorities state 'more than half of known species')
learnerActions: Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'Rainforests cover only about 6% of Earth's land. If they're such a small slice of the planet, why do scientists say protecting them matters so much for life on Earth? Tell me why, and then tell me what biodiversity actually means here.'
Decide whether 10,000 animals that are all the same species would count as high biodiversity, and justify your answer.
Explain why we can't simply recreate a cleared rainforest's species somewhere else.
Write a short justification linking the 6%-of-land to the >50%-of-species figure and using it to argue for conservation priority.
activities.intendedInsight: Biodiversity means the VARIETY of different species, not just the number of animals; many tropical rainforest species are endemic (found nowhere else), so clearing their only habitat can wipe those species out entirely — this is why protection is a priority.

constraints: Be precise on caveats at the top tier: the claim is about TROPICAL rainforests specifically (not temperate rainforests), and about KNOWN/documented species — many, especially insects, remain undiscovered, so figures describe documented life.

Authoritative figures vary: credible sources range from 'more than half of known species' up to WWF's '80% of documented species'. Present a range rather than a single hard number, and cite authoritative sources (WWF, National Geographic) rather than advocacy aggregators.
Land-area figures also vary by source (National Geographic gives roughly 2–6%); use 'about 6%' as a teachable anchor while acknowledging the range.

A prediction slider or multiple-choice item can check that learners recall the two percentages and the conservation reasoning, but recognition/estimation alone does not show a learner can independently articulate the disproportion or define biodiversity — use an open written or spoken justification for that.

The shadow/shrink demo is a vivid representation of 'small area, outsized species loss'; keep it as an illustration of concentration, not a literal claim that species loss is exactly proportional to area cleared.

Tap-to-reveal species galleries and drill-downs are optional illustrative mechanisms; the core learning is the proportion contrast and its conservation consequence, which can also be shown with static paired bars or pie slices.

The 'one hectare holds more tree species than all of northern Europe' comparison is an original row claim not directly stated by the cited sources (National Geographic says only 'hundreds of tree species per hectare'); it is presented as a qualified illustration and the exact comparison and wording should be verified against an authoritative source before publishing.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source row marks the National Geographic and DfE claims as verified:false and the WWF claim as verified:true; the two biodiversity percentage figures (>50% vs WWF's 80%) and the land-area figures (~6% vs 2–6%) come from different authorities and are not identical, so the activities present ranges rather than asserting one exact number.

The estimate-then-reveal 'prediction makes it more memorable' rationale and the 'learners underestimate' claim are design hypotheses; no cited source establishes this effect, so they are stated with proposed/intended wording. The claim attached to Activity 2 supports only the revealed proportion content, not the prediction mechanism.

The legacy row rated 3D and conversation formats as 'poor' with claims like '3D adds nothing' and 'no essential persona'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have not been carried forward as universal claims. A proportion-contrast visual is a good fit here, but this does not prove other media cannot teach the concept.

The 'one hectare holds more tree species than all of Europe/northern Europe' example appears with slightly different wording across the row (Europe, Europe/North America combined, northern Europe) and National Geographic's claim says only 'hundreds of tree species per hectare'; the comparison is retained as a qualified vivid illustration but exact phrasing should be checked against the cited source before publishing.

Endemism and the biodiversity-as-variety definition are inherited from the row's assessment content and are not directly backed by a cited source; treat as topic-standard framing pending source confirmation.

probeDeeper: Rainforests are 6% of land but hold over half of known species — what does that comparison tell you?
What does the word 'biodiversity' mean in your own words?
Why can't we just recreate a rainforest's species somewhere else if it's cleared?
Would 10,000 animals that are all the same species count as high biodiversity? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Because that tiny 6% of land holds more than half of all the world's known plant and animal species — an astonishing concentration of DIFFERENT kinds of life (a single hectare can hold more tree species than all of northern Europe). Biodiversity means the VARIETY of different species, not just the number of animals. Losing that small area would wipe out a huge share of the planet's species, many found nowhere else — which is why it's a top conservation priority.

The reason-tier forces the disproportion-plus-variety reasoning.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Use counting on and counting back as strategies for addition and subtraction (8 + 3 by counting on 9,10,11; 12 − 3 by counting back 11,10,9). Ages 6–7, the bridge from counting-all to more efficient calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including zero' and count on/back; underpins Y2 mental strategies.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.5 'Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g. by counting on 2 to add 2)'; a stepping stone toward 1.OA.6 strategies.
• Operational details: teach counting ON from the larger number (start at 8, not 1) as more efficient than counting-all, and counting BACK for subtraction, tracking the number of steps. Best supported on a number line/track so the steps are visible and the child doesn't count the start as a step. This is a transitional strategy — valued, then increasingly replaced by known facts and derived facts.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds 8 + 3 by counting on from 8. Tier B (age 7) — counts back accurately for 12 − 3 and starts count-on from the larger addend for 2 + 9. Tier C (age 7+) — explains counting on as adding and chooses count-on vs count-back sensibly.
bestPractices: Teach counting ON from the larger addend, not counting all from one, as the efficiency step.
Use a number line or number track so jumps are visible and the start number isn't miscounted as a step.
Track the number of steps with fingers or marks to prevent off-by-one errors.
Model counting back for subtraction and connect it to 'one less each time'.
Treat counting on/back as a transitional strategy — celebrate it, then nudge toward known and derived facts for efficiency.
keyRepresentations: Number line / number track with hops
Fingers used to keep track of the count of steps
Hundred square for later extension
Bead string showing jumps
'Start big, count on' prompt card
commonMisconceptions: Counting all from one instead of counting on from a number (a normal earlier stage).
Counting the starting number as the first step (8 + 3 → 8,9,10 = 10), an off-by-one error.
Counting on from the first-written number rather than the larger one, making more steps than needed.
Counting in the wrong direction for subtraction.
Over-relying on counting for facts that should become instant recall.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7, teach counting on for addition and counting back for subtraction as the efficiency step beyond counting-all. The core skills: start from the larger number (e.g. begin at 8 for 8+3), say the NEXT number as the first count ('9'), and track the number of steps so the start isn't miscounted. Best anchored on a visible number line/track where hops are seen and counted, then gradually replaced by known and derived facts. Target sums: 8+3=11 (count on), 12−3=9 (count back), 2+9 (start from the larger addend, 9).

activities.title: Hop along the number line: count on and count back
feedback: If a child counts the start number as the first step (8+3 → '8,9,10' = 10), point out that 8 is where you START, and the first hop lands on 9 — count the landings, not the starting spot.
If a child starts at 1 and counts everything, gently cover the first group, say '8', and count on from there; this earlier stage matures with number sense, so model rather than drill.
For subtraction going the wrong way, link counting back to 'one less each time' and track the backward hops with fingers.
If a child always starts from the first-written number (2 for 2+9), ask which number gives fewer hops and why starting at 9 is quicker.
activities.rationale: Counting on/back is literally movement along a number line, so a track where hops are visible and counted is intended to make the strategy and the off-by-one error observable, so the child can self-correct. A live track that counts each landing (and does not count the start as a step) is intended to target the classic '8,9,10'=10 slip. Starting-number highlighting, count-on/count-back modes, and a 'start from the bigger number' prompt for commutative pairs are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete. Efficacy of this interaction is a proposal, not a tested result.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers to 20 including zero, using counting strategies.
1.OA.5 relates counting to addition and subtraction, e.g. counting on 2 to add 2.
Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: On a number line or number track, set the start at the larger number (8 for 8+3) and make three hops forward, saying the number you LAND on each time: '9, 10, 11' — not '8'.
Keep track of how many hops you have made using fingers or marks, so you take exactly three.
Switch to count-back mode for 12−3: start at 12 and hop backward three times, saying '11, 10, 9'.
For 2+9, decide which number to start from and explain why you start at 9, not 2.
Narrate out loud where you start and how many steps you take.
If it helps, show the same forward hops on a bead string; a hundred square can be used later to extend counting on and back to larger numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Starting AT the larger number and taking just a few hops lands on the same answer as counting everything from one, but is faster; the first count is the next number along from the start (9 for 8+3; 11 when counting back from 12 for 12−3), not the start number.

activities.title: Spaced practice: draw the hops and choose the start
feedback: Watch for an off-by-one answer (10 for 8+3): the result is 11 — recount the landings, not the start.
If the chosen start for 2+9 is 2, note that starting at 9 means only two hops instead of nine.
For 6+2, start at 6 and count on '7, 8' — two hops lands on 8.
activities.rationale: Fixed items give good spaced consolidation but cannot correct the count as it happens, so they work best after the live hopping activity rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: Draw the jumps on a number line for 8+3 and for 12−3, labelling each landing number.
Answer: 'Which number should you start counting from for 2+9?' and justify the choice.
Fill in results for several count-on and count-back sums (for example 6+2), checking you did not count the start as a step.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated, varied practice consolidates counting on from the larger addend and counting back accurately, reinforcing where the count begins.

activities.title: Talk it through: why start at the bigger number?
feedback: If the explanation defends counting all from one, model covering the first group and counting on, and ask which took fewer counts.
Praise explanations that connect counting on to adding and counting back to 'one less each time'.
activities.rationale: Spoken reasoning reveals the underlying strategy and lets a tutor probe the counting-all habit; it complements, rather than replaces, watched practice where the procedure is performed and tracked.
sourceClaims: Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: Work out a sum and narrate where you start and how many steps you take.
Answer questions like 'Why did you start at 8 and not at 1?' and 'Which is quicker for 8+3 — counting everything or counting on? Why?'.
Explain in your own words how counting on is a way of adding.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why you start from the larger number and that counting on is adding surfaces (and helps move past) a counting-all habit.

constraints: Counting on/back is a transitional strategy: celebrate it, then nudge toward known and derived facts so it isn't over-relied on for instant-recall facts.

Counting-all from one is a normal earlier developmental stage; model counting on but do not drill it as an error — children typically move beyond it as number sense grows with experience and modelling.
A static worked number line can anchor what counting on looks like but gives no practice tracking one's own steps, where the errors occur; use it as an anchor, not the main practice.
Recognition/multiple-choice items can check the choice of start number but do not elicit the child independently performing and tracking the count; pair them with doing and narrating.
Watching HOW the child counts is central: the overt count reveals strategy and off-by-one errors that the final answer alone can hide.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source row flagged the US CCSS 1.OA.5 claim and the Cognitively Guided Instruction claim as verified:false; treat their cited support as unconfirmed even though they are topically relevant.

The original rated a 3D treatment 'poor' asserting '3D adds nothing'; this universal claim is not established by the row and has been dropped. A number line is naturally one-dimensional, which is a sufficient rationale without claiming 3D is universally useless.
Arithmetic checked: 8+3=11, 12−3=9, 2+9=11, 6+2=8; the off-by-one distractor (10 for 8+3) is correctly flagged as an error, not a valid answer.

probeDeeper: Why did you start counting at 8 and not at 1?
Show me on the number line how you got 12 − 3.
Which is quicker for 8 + 3 — counting everything, or counting on? Why?
For 2 + 9, which number would you start from, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 11; 9; 8. Watch for the child counting ON from the larger number (starting at 8, saying '9, 10, 11'), counting BACK for the subtraction, and NOT counting the start number as a step.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts all from one rather than counting on from a number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill or correct as an error — this stage self-resolves with number sense; gently model covering the first set, saying '8', and counting on, and let it mature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 8 + 3, starts at 1 and counts out all eight then all three.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the starting number as the first step (8 + 3 → '8, 9, 10' = 10).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Start the count on the NEXT number; use a number line and fingers so the start isn't a step. Not a concept reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 10; observed saying the start number as step one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back unreliably or in the wrong direction for subtraction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model back-counting on a number line and link to 'one less each time'; track steps with fingers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 12 − 3 counts up, or miscounts the backward steps.

responseLevels.gap: Counts all from one, or cannot track the count reliably; frequent errors.
responseLevels.full: Counts on from the larger addend and counts back accurately, tracking the number of steps, and explains counting on as a way of adding.
responseLevels.partial: Counts on/back but with off-by-one slips, or always starts from the first-written number rather than the larger.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out and show me how you count each one: 8 + 3; 12 − 3; 6 + 2.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW the child counts is the whole test: a counting-all child starts at 1 and counts every item; a counting-on child starts at 8. An off-by-one child audibly counts the start number as step one and lands on 10. The overt count reveals the strategy and the classic error in a way the answer alone cannot.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–7; Temperature & Thermometers (CONCEPTUAL, 0.08): temperature is how hot or cold something is; a thermometer measures it; use hot/warm/cool/cold to describe how the air feels on different days.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 weather observation (Y1 'Seasonal changes' — describing warmer/colder seasons); measuring temperature in °C with a thermometer is developed at KS2. At 5-7, relative warm/cool language + recognising the tool. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS, ANCHOR): K-ESS2-1 (VERIFIED verbatim) names temperature among weather conditions; its assessment boundary limits quantitative observation [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]' — so relative hot/warm/cool/cold is exactly the target, not precise °C. DCI ESS2.D lists temperature as part of weather.
• Operational details — Two ideas: (1) temperature = how hot/cold, a felt property we can order (hot > warm > cool > cold); (2) a thermometer is the TOOL that measures it, and its reading goes UP when warmer, DOWN when cooler. Keep it relative/qualitative per the K-ESS2-1 boundary — the child reads 'higher = warmer' not exact degrees. Connect felt experience (a warm sunny day vs a cold frosty day) to the thermometer moving. Prerequisite: none; feeds Using Weather Instruments (7-9, reading °C) and Dressing for the Weather. Evidence: explain temperature is how hot/cold; identify a thermometer as the measuring tool; use hot/warm/cool/cold appropriately.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/observational): the child explains temperature as how hot or cold something is, identifies a thermometer as the tool that measures it, and orders/uses hot–warm–cool–cold correctly for different days — relative and felt, not exact degrees.
bestPractices: Ground temperature in FELT experience first (hold something warm vs cool; a sunny vs shady spot) before introducing the instrument — the word names a sensation the child already knows.
Introduce the thermometer as a tool whose reading rises when warmer and falls when cooler; keep it relative (higher/lower) not precise °C, matching the K-ESS2-1 'warmer/cooler' boundary.
Practise ordering hot–warm–cool–cold as a scale (e.g. bath, room, fridge, freezer) so temperature is understood as a continuum, not two boxes.

Surface the classic hot/cold conflation: what FEELS cold (metal) isn't necessarily colder than what feels warm (wood) at the same temperature — at 5-7 keep this light but avoid reinforcing 'metal is always colder'.
Tie readings to weather routine: check whether today is warmer or cooler than yesterday, connecting the instrument to lived weather.
Avoid number precision and negative numbers at this age; 'warmer/cooler/about the same' is the right grain.
keyRepresentations: A large thermometer whose coloured column rises and falls, with a hot–warm–cool–cold band beside it (no fine °C scale needed).
An ordering strip: freezer → fridge → room → warm bath, placing everyday things on a hot–cold scale.
Paired 'today' scenes (sunny beach vs frosty morning) with the thermometer reading higher/lower for each.
Felt-experience cards (ice cube, warm drink, cool shade, hot sand) matched to temperature words.
commonMisconceptions: 'Hot and cold are opposite THINGS' rather than points on one temperature scale — build the continuum (warm and cool are in between).
'What feels colder IS colder' — metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature; sensation is an unreliable exact measure (that's why we use a thermometer).
'The thermometer makes/adds heat' or controls temperature — it only measures and reports it.
'Higher number = the thermometer is bigger/fuller of liquid, not hotter' — tie the rising column explicitly to warmer.
'Temperature and weather are the same thing' — temperature is one PART of the weather, alongside rain, wind, cloud.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach temperature as how hot or cold something is, that a thermometer is the tool that measures it, and the use of hot/warm/cool/cold to describe how the air feels on different days. Keep observation relative and qualitative (warmer/cooler/about the same), not exact °C. This is a design choice that stays within the K-ESS2-1 assessment boundary, which limits quantitative observations [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]. Ground the word in felt experience first, then connect that sensation to a thermometer's reading rising when warmer and falling when cooler, and build hot–warm–cool–cold as one continuous scale rather than two opposite boxes.

activities.title: Warm it up, cool it down: watch the thermometer respond
feedback: When the column climbs as the scene warms: 'The day got warmer, and the thermometer climbed up to warm — the thermometer tells us how hot it is.'
When the child orders ice, cool drink and cocoa: 'The ice is coldest and the cocoa warmest — warm and cool sit in between, all on one scale from cold to hot.'
If a child treats the thermometer as decoration: 'Watch the coloured column — it isn't just a picture, it moves to show how hot or cold it is.'
For today-vs-yesterday: 'The column is lower today, so today is cooler than yesterday.'
activities.rationale: A live cause→reading coupling lets a child see a felt change (warming/cooling) produce a moving reading, building both target ideas together: temperature is orderable, and the thermometer reports it. Keeping it to higher/lower rather than exact degrees stays within the K-ESS2-1 boundary ([curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]) and matches the KS1 qualitative grain.
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1 names temperature among weather conditions; assessment boundary limits quantitative observation [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]'; DCI ESS2.D lists temperature as part of weather.
DfE KS1 weather observation describes warmer/colder conditions qualitatively; measuring temperature in °C with a thermometer is developed at KS2.
learnerActions: Start from a plain scene with a large friendly thermometer beside it whose coloured column can rise and fall against a hot–warm–cool–cold band (no fine °C scale).
Warm the scene (e.g. drag the sun high into the sky, brighten the day) and watch the thermometer's column climb up onto 'warm', then 'hot'.
Cool the scene (slide the sun behind a cloud, or move the character and the thermometer into the shade) and watch the column sink lower, toward 'cool'.
Drop everyday things onto a shelf — an ice cube, a mug of cocoa, a cool drink — and touch the thermometer to each one to see it read lower or higher for each.
Line those things up coldest to hottest, and compare 'today vs yesterday' as higher or lower on the same thermometer.
Say in words whether each change made it warmer or cooler, and how the thermometer showed it.
activities.intendedInsight: Temperature is how hot or cold something is, it can be ordered along one scale from cold to hot, and a thermometer is a tool that reports it — the reading moves up when warmer and down when cooler, so 'higher means warmer.'

activities.title: Feel first, then name it
feedback: 'Warm and cool sit in between hot and cold — that's why we can line things up from coldest to hottest.'
If a child uses only 'hot' and 'cold': 'Is it exactly hot, or more like warm? There are steps in between.'
For the freezer-to-bath strip: 'Nice ordering — the freezer is coldest and the warm bath hottest, with steps in between.'
activities.rationale: Grounding temperature in felt experience before the instrument lets the instrument name something the child already senses, and ordering everyday things builds the continuum that counters the hot/cold 'two opposite things' misconception.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 weather observation describes warmer/colder conditions qualitatively; measuring temperature in °C with a thermometer is developed at KS2.
Classic temperature misconceptions: hot and cold treated as distinct kinds rather than a single scale, and 'what feels colder is colder' (thermal-conductivity sensation confusion).
learnerActions: Hold or look at things that are clearly warm, cool or cold (a warm drink, an ice cube, a sunny spot, cool shade) and say how each feels.
Match felt-experience cards — ice cube, warm drink, cool shade, hot sand — to the words hot, warm, cool, cold.
Order familiar places as a scale: freezer → fridge → room → warm bath, from coldest to hottest.
Decide for the air outside today whether it feels hot, warm, cool, or cold.
activities.intendedInsight: The word 'temperature' names a sensation children already know, and warm and cool are the in-between points between hot and cold — it is a continuum, not two boxes.

activities.title: Label the thermometer and compare two days
feedback: 'Right — the beach scene reads higher because it's warmer than the frosty morning.'
If a child says the thermometer makes it hot: 'The thermometer only measures and reports the temperature — it doesn't add any heat.'
If a child reads 'fuller' as 'bigger not hotter': 'No liquid gets added — the same liquid spreads up the tube when it gets warmer, so a higher column means warmer.'
activities.rationale: A clean, labelled reference consolidates the tool's parts and the relative 'higher = warmer' rule and counters the 'thermometer adds heat' and 'fuller not hotter' misconceptions. This is a static scaffold: because a key idea is that the reading MOVES with temperature, pair it with the dynamic warming/cooling activity so the rule is seen in action, not only shown statically. (The cited claim supports the relative 'higher = warmer' element; the parts-labelling and adds-heat/fuller points are standard pedagogy rather than source-specific.)
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1 names temperature among weather conditions; assessment boundary limits quantitative observation [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]'; DCI ESS2.D lists temperature as part of weather.
learnerActions: Explore a labelled thermometer: tap or point to the bulb, the coloured column, and the scale to learn the parts.
Open a 'higher = warmer' flap or prompt that explains which way the reading moves when it gets warmer.
Look at paired scenes — a sunny beach and a frosty morning — and say which thermometer reads higher and why.
Describe in your own words what the thermometer does: it measures and reports how hot or cold it is; it does not make heat.
activities.intendedInsight: A thermometer has parts (bulb, column, scale), it reports temperature rather than creating it, and a higher reading means warmer.

activities.title: Coldest-to-hottest ordering check
feedback: Correct ordering: 'That's the whole scale from coldest to hottest — the in-between things take the in-between places.'
If two items are swapped: 'Which of these two would feel warmer? Put the warmer one higher.'
Slider: 'Good — warmer than the fridge means above it on the scale, but you don't need an exact number.'
activities.rationale: Ordering, matching and relative-slider tasks can check the evidence targets and the continuum idea. This is a confirmation check: it verifies the scale idea but does not by itself build the cause→reading coupling, so use it after the dynamic activity.
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1 names temperature among weather conditions; assessment boundary limits quantitative observation [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]'; DCI ESS2.D lists temperature as part of weather.
learnerActions: Order a set of everyday things from coldest to hottest.
Match an object to the right temperature word (ice → cold, warm drink → warm, and so on).
Use a relative-position slider to set the thermometer 'warmer than the fridge' or 'cooler than a warm bath' without using exact degrees.
activities.intendedInsight: Temperature items can be placed in order along one scale, and relative language (warmer than / cooler than) describes positions on that scale.

activities.title: Warmer or cooler than yesterday? Talk it through
feedback: 'Warmer than yesterday — and you noticed the thermometer is higher today. Nice link.'
If the child only says 'hot': 'Compared with yesterday, is it warmer, cooler, or about the same?'
activities.rationale: A short spoken comparison can elicit comparative language and tie readings to the weather routine. This is an optional extension; a measurement concept at this age does not require open dialogue, so keep the prompt focused on warmer/cooler reasoning.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 weather observation describes warmer/colder conditions qualitatively; measuring temperature in °C with a thermometer is developed at KS2.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Is it warmer or cooler than yesterday, and how do you know?'
Give the comparison in words and the reason (how it feels, or what the thermometer shows).
Connect the thermometer reading to the daily weather routine — check today against yesterday.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparative temperature language (warmer/cooler/about the same) describes how one day differs from another, tying the instrument to lived weather.

activities.title: Same room, same temperature: feel versus measurement
feedback: When both read the same: 'They match — both sat in the same room, so both are at room temperature. The metal only FEELS colder.'

If a child predicted the metal is really colder: 'It feels colder because it pulls heat from your hand quickly — let's look at the thermometer: if both read about the same, they really are the same temperature.'
Fridge follow-up: 'Now the metal really is colder — because of where it has been, not because it's metal. Temperature depends on surroundings.'
Keep the conductivity point light at this age: name that metal feels colder without insisting 'metal is always colder.'
activities.rationale: Stating a prediction and reason before measuring, then confronting it with equal readings, targets the well-documented 'what feels colder is colder' and 'metal is always cold' misconceptions and reinforces why we trust a thermometer over touch.
sourceClaims: Classic temperature misconceptions: hot and cold treated as distinct kinds rather than a single scale, and 'what feels colder is colder' (thermal-conductivity sensation confusion).
learnerActions: Leave a metal object and a wooden or plastic object side by side in the same room for at least an hour, away from sunlight, heaters and draughts.
Feel both, then predict what a thermometer will read on each — and say your reason BEFORE measuring.

With an adult, measure both by holding the same contact thermometer probe firmly against each object until the reading stops changing (do not use an infrared thermometer on shiny metal, which can read wrongly low), then compare the readings with your prediction.
Discuss: 'If both sat in the same room all morning, could they really be different temperatures?' and 'Which do you trust more to tell you the temperature — your hand or the thermometer?'
Try the follow-up: put the metal object in the fridge and leave the wooden one out, then measure both and say what changed.
activities.intendedInsight: How something feels is not a reliable measure of its temperature: things that have sat together in the same room for long enough, away from sun and heaters, end up at about the same temperature even if the metal feels colder, because metal draws heat from your hand faster. A thermometer measures the object or air, not your sensation.

constraints: Keep observation relative and qualitative at this age — warmer/cooler/about the same, not exact °C and no negative numbers. Reading real degrees belongs to a later (7–9) weather-instruments topic.
Ground temperature in felt experience before introducing the instrument; the thermometer names a sensation the child already knows.
Build hot–warm–cool–cold as one continuous scale, not two opposite boxes.
Distinguish temperature from weather as a whole: temperature is one part of the weather, alongside rain, wind and cloud.
Handle the feel-versus-temperature point gently: acknowledge that metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature, but do not reinforce 'metal is always colder.'
The ordering/matching/slider check confirms the scale idea but does not build the cause→reading coupling; use it after the dynamic warming/cooling activity.
The labelled-thermometer reference is a static scaffold; because the core idea is that the reading moves with temperature, pair it with the dynamic activity rather than relying on it alone.
The warmer/cooler conversation is an optional extension, not a required step for a 5–7 measurement concept.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the 2D interactive as 'ideal' and claims a static image 'can't convey' the live coupling and that '3D adds nothing'; these are catalog fit rankings, not established efficacy or necessity claims. They have been softened to scoped affordances (a dynamic model makes the moving reading visible; a labelled image is a useful static reference).

Two of three sources (DfE KS1 and AAAS Project 2061 misconception research) are marked not verified/not re-fetched this session; treat the KS1 °C-at-KS2 claim and the misconception descriptions as legacy, unverified.

Conductivity note: 'metal draws heat from your hand faster, so it feels colder' mirrors the source's own assessment nextMove and is used here in qualified, qualitative child-facing feedback kept light for 5–7 — it is optional emphasis, not a required teaching point, and whether to surface conductivity at all at this age remains a judgement the source flags ('keep this light').

Activity 3 ('Label the thermometer') cites K-ESS2-1 for its relative 'higher = warmer' element; the parts-labelling and the 'thermometer adds heat'/'fuller not hotter' misconception content is standard pedagogy not directly backed by a cited source string, and no source claim was invented to cover it.

assess.poeTask: Leave a metal object and a wooden or plastic object in the same room for an hour. Ask children to feel both and predict what a thermometer will read on each, giving their reason first — most predict the metal is colder. Measuring both at the same room temperature confronts the feels-cold-equals-is-cold idea. The reason stated before measuring is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If both spoons sat in the same warm room all day, could they really be at different temperatures? Why or why not?
Which do you trust more to tell you the temperature — your hand or a thermometer? Why?
If we put the metal spoon in the fridge and leave the wooden one out, then measure both — what changes?
assess.correctAnswer: The thermometer would read the SAME temperature for both, because they have been in the same room all morning — both are at room temperature. The metal only FEELS colder to your hand; how something feels isn't a reliable way to know its temperature, which is why we use a thermometer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Touch is the true temperature — 'the metal is colder because it feels colder'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast feel with measurement: leave both in the same room, measure, find them equal; the metal just draws heat from your hand faster so it feels colder.
errorPatterns.distractor: The metal spoon really is a colder temperature, because it feels colder.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the thermometer will confirm the metal is at a lower temperature

errorPatterns.pattern: The thermometer reports how you feel — not the object's temperature
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify what the tool does: a thermometer measures the object/air, not your sensation; that's why it's more reliable than touch.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects the thermometer to agree with the hand rather than with the room

errorPatterns.pattern: Temperature is a fixed property of the material — 'metal is always cold'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the same metal warms up on a radiator and cools in a fridge — its temperature depends on surroundings, not on being metal.
errorPatterns.distractor: Metal is always cold no matter where it is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says metal is cold everywhere, no matter where it has been

responseLevels.gap: Says the metal is genuinely colder because it feels colder; treats touch as the true measure.
responseLevels.full: Predicts equal readings because both sat in the same room, explains the metal only feels colder, states the thermometer (not touch) gives the reliable temperature, and transfers to the fridge case.
responseLevels.partial: Senses the thermometer matters but is unsure the readings match, or still says 'metal is just colder' while half-trusting the tool.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have both been sitting on the same table in the same room all morning. Sam touches them and says the metal one is colder, so it must be at a colder temperature. If we put a thermometer on each, what would it read, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who separates how-it-feels from measured temperature predicts equal readings. A child who trusts touch says the metal really is at a lower temperature — the well-documented feels-cold-equals-is-cold tell.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Accurate Measurement

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to take measurements using a range of scientific equipment, with increasing accuracy and precision, taking repeat readings when appropriate. They also record data with increasing complexity and use test results to make predictions.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, grades 3–5):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1, 2-PS1-1, 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 3-PS2-2, 4-ESS2-1, 4-PS3-2, 5-PS1-3, 5-PS1-4], and plan [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4] IS CONSIDERED. The idea that repeating a measurement and considering multiple trials strengthens the evidence is explicit at this band.

- **Operational details:** The child takes at least three repeat readings of the same quantity, recognises that repeats improve reliability (the results should cluster if the method is sound), and combines them — typically by identifying and discarding an anomalous result (one that clearly doesn't fit the pattern) before calculating a mean of the remaining values. 'Increasing precision' means choosing finer-resolution equipment and reading it carefully; 'reliability' means results you can trust because they are reproducible. Crucially the child learns that an outlier signals a possible mistake in that reading, not a fact about the world, and that averaging several close readings gives a better estimate than any single one.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional). This is the bridge from 'take a reading' to 'produce trustworthy data': repeats, spotting anomalies, and averaging. Success = independently takes three or more readings, identifies an anomalous result and excludes it with a reason, calculates the mean of the rest, and can explain why repeating improved reliability — the direct foundation for the KS3 precision-vs-accuracy topic.
bestPractices: Have children take three or more repeats of the SAME measurement and physically see whether the results cluster, so reliability is observed, not just defined.
Teach anomaly-spotting as 'a reading that clearly doesn't fit the pattern' and treat it as a signal of a possible mistake, not a fact to keep.
Calculate the mean AFTER excluding a clear anomaly, and discuss why the outlier would otherwise distort the average.
Contrast a single reading with the mean of repeats to show the mean is a better, steadier estimate.
Distinguish 'more repeats → more reliable' from 'finer instrument → more precise' — two different routes to better data.
Tie repeats to fair testing: reliable data is what lets you trust a comparison between conditions.
keyRepresentations: A results table with columns for repeat 1, 2, 3 and a mean
Dot-plot / number line showing repeats clustering with an anomaly flung wide
The mean as the balance point of the clustered readings (anomaly excluded)
Single-reading estimate (wobbly) vs mean-of-three (steady) comparison
Instrument-resolution ladder — finer graduations giving greater precision
commonMisconceptions: Thinking one reading is enough, or that repeating gives 'the same answer so why bother'.
Keeping an obvious anomaly in the data and averaging it in, dragging the mean off.
Confusing reliability (reproducible repeats) with accuracy (closeness to the true value).
Believing an anomalous result is an interesting fact about the world rather than a likely mistake in that reading.
Thinking a mean is 'more accurate' simply because it has more decimal places.
Treating precision (fine instrument) and reliability (repeats) as the same thing.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, this topic teaches reliable measurement: take at least three repeat readings of the same quantity, recognise that trustworthy results cluster, spot an anomalous reading (one that clearly doesn't fit the pattern) and exclude or re-take it, then calculate the mean of the remaining consistent readings. Learners should feel why repeating and averaging turn a jittery single reading into a value you can trust, and should keep reliability (reproducible repeats) distinct from accuracy (closeness to true value) and from precision (finer instrument resolution / careful reading). The worked scenario uses stopwatch timing, but the same repeat-and-average procedure applies across equipment such as thermometers, scales and measuring cylinders. The central hands-on activity is a repeatable measurement whose results scatter onto a number line; supporting activities assess mean calculation and anomaly-spotting numerically, and provide a vocabulary reference.

activities.title: Repeat-Reading Bench: tame the scatter
feedback: If the mean is dragged upward (e.g. from about 2.09 s to about 2.17 s), check whether the anomalous reading (2.41 s) was folded in; identify the reading that doesn't fit and exclude or re-take it before averaging.
If only one reading is taken, point out that a single reading can be off — take at least three and compare them.
If repeats are taken but one is just picked rather than combined, prompt: combine the consistent readings into a mean to get the best single value.
Reinforce when the learner excludes with a stated reason and reports the mean of the rest (about 2.09 s, i.e. roughly 2.1 s, in this marble example).
activities.rationale: A live, repeatable measurement where results scatter onto a number line and the mean recomputes from the learner's own exclusion choices lets 'repeats improve reliability' be experienced rather than asserted. Comparing a wobbling single reading against a steady mean across re-runs makes the reliability intuition concrete. The 'average-with-the-anomaly' trap directly exposes how outliers distort a mean. A live dot-plot, exclusion control and recomputing mean are offered as an illustrative mechanism, not a required technology — the same lesson works with physical stopwatch timings recorded by hand onto a drawn number line, and with other measuring equipment.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to take measurements using a range of scientific equipment with increasing accuracy and precision, taking repeat readings when appropriate.

NGSS SEP 3 (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations) grades 3–5 requires [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4] is considered, and making measurements to produce data as the basis for evidence.
learnerActions: Run the SAME measurement several times — for example, time how long a marble or toy car takes to roll down a fixed ramp, pressing go and recording each stopwatch reading (e.g. 2.11 s, 2.06 s, 2.41 s, 2.09 s).
Plot each result as a dot on a number line and observe whether the readings cluster or one flies wide.
Identify which reading is anomalous and justify it ('far from the cluster'); exclude or re-take it before combining.
Calculate the mean of the remaining consistent readings.

Compare 'report just my first reading' with 'report the mean of three' across several full re-runs, and see which reported value usually jumps around more and which tends to stay steadier (averaging reduces random wobble on average, but it is not guaranteed in every single re-run).
Deliberately average WITH the anomaly left in, and observe the mean being dragged off, then remove it and recompute.
Note that the same take-repeats, spot-the-anomaly, average-the-rest method applies to other equipment too — e.g. repeated thermometer, scale or measuring-cylinder readings.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeating a measurement and averaging the consistent readings gives a value you can trust, because a single reading can be off and an anomaly left in distorts the mean. Reliability is something you can see emerge from your own repeats, not just a definition.

activities.title: Does the anomaly matter? Mean with and without
feedback: The mean of all five readings (including 3.8) is about 2.44 s; the mean of the four consistent readings (2.1, 2.0, 2.2, 2.1) is exactly 2.1 s — show this gap so the distorting effect is seen numerically.
If the learner thinks the anomaly is a real result to keep, clarify it most likely reflects a slip in taking that reading (e.g. a late stop).
activities.rationale: A data-manipulation task with a clear outlier rigorously tests anomaly-spotting and mean calculation and lets the distorting effect of the outlier be seen numerically. This checks the arithmetic skill but does not by itself give the run-to-run experience of a single reading wobbling while a mean steadies, so it complements rather than replaces the bench activity.
learnerActions: Given a data set containing one clear outlier (e.g. 2.1 s, 2.0 s, 2.2 s, 3.8 s, 2.1 s), identify which reading is anomalous.
Calculate the mean WITH the anomaly included and again WITHOUT it.
Compare the two results and state how much the outlier shifted the answer.
Answer why taking repeats helps and explain what an anomalous reading signals.
activities.intendedInsight: An outlier distorts a mean in a measurable way, so excluding a reading that doesn't fit gives a more trustworthy best value. An anomaly signals a possible mistake in that reading, not a fact about the world.

activities.title: What makes data reliable — a reference
feedback: If reliability and accuracy are conflated, note that tightly clustered repeats can still all be off the true value; reliability is about reproducibility, accuracy about closeness to truth.
If a mean is thought 'more accurate' just for having more decimal places, clarify that extra decimals do not by themselves mean closer to the true value.
If precision and reliability are treated as the same, note that a finer instrument sharpens a single reading while repeats guard against a one-off slip.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated example cannot be re-run by the learner to generate their own scatter, so it works best as a reference for vocabulary alongside a hands-on activity rather than as the primary means of building the reliability intuition. It remains a useful consolidation and a place to separate reliability, accuracy and precision across a range of equipment.
learnerActions: Study an annotated number line showing several readings clustering with one anomaly flung wide.
Reveal explanations for 'these cluster — reliable', 'this one is anomalous — exclude it', and 'the mean sits here among the clustered readings'.
Restate in your own words the difference between reliability (reproducible repeats), accuracy (closeness to the true value) and precision (finer instrument resolution / careful reading).

Relate the precision idea to an instrument-resolution ladder — finer graduations on a thermometer, scale, cylinder or stopwatch allow a more precise reading, a different route to better data from taking more repeats.
activities.intendedInsight: Builds and consolidates the vocabulary of reliable measurement: cluster, anomaly, mean, reliability, accuracy, precision — and keeps these distinct, including that repeats and finer instruments are two different routes to better data.

constraints: Reliability should be observed, not just defined: have learners take three or more repeats of the SAME measurement and see whether results cluster.
Calculate the mean AFTER excluding or re-taking a clear anomaly; discuss how including the outlier would otherwise distort the average.

Keep three ideas distinct: reliability (reproducible repeats), accuracy (closeness to true value), and precision (as used at this level: finer instrument resolution / careful reading; later science courses also use 'precision' for how closely repeated readings agree). 'More repeats -> more reliable' and 'finer instrument -> more precise' are different routes to better data.
An anomalous reading usually signals a mistake or a change in conditions during that reading (e.g. a late stop or a bumped ramp), so check or re-take it rather than treating it as the true value.
A mean is not 'more accurate' merely because it has more decimal places.

Keep each activity's numbers internally consistent: the marble/ramp set (2.11, 2.06, 2.41, 2.09 s) has anomaly 2.41 s; the diagnostic set (2.1, 2.0, 2.2, 3.8, 2.1 s) has anomaly 3.8 s — do not mix figures across the two.

The objective spans a range of scientific equipment (scales, thermometers, measuring cylinders, stopwatches); use the stopwatch timing as the worked example but make clear the repeat/anomaly/mean procedure transfers to other instruments.

The mean-with-and-without quiz and the annotated reference test or explain the ideas but do not reproduce the run-to-run wobble of a single reading versus a steadying mean; use them to support, not replace, a hands-on repeatable measurement.

Recognition or single-answer questions do not by themselves show that a learner independently takes and uses repeats; a watched performance task (take readings, spot the anomaly, report a best value) is needed to confirm the procedure.
Live dot-plots, exclusion toggles and recomputing means are illustrative supports; the same learning is achievable with physical measurement and hand-drawn number lines.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked examples: for the diagnostic set 2.1, 2.0, 2.2, 3.8, 2.1 the mean of the four consistent readings is exactly 2.1 s and the mean of all five including 3.8 is 2.44 s (the original variously says 'about 2.4 s'). For the marble set 2.11, 2.06, 2.41, 2.09 the mean of the three consistent readings is about 2.09 s and including the 2.41 anomaly is about 2.17 s. These figures were kept to their own activity's data set so no mismatched value reaches learners.
The candidate had earlier imported the 3.8 s / 2.4 s figures into the marble activity's feedback; confirmed corrected to use the 2.41 s anomaly and its actual distortion (2.09 s -> 2.17 s).

The original narrowed delivery to stopwatch timing; the broader equipment range and instrument-resolution ladder from the source have been restored to a constraint and the reference activity so the full objective is represented.

The original's claims that '3D adds nothing' and that a dialogue 'can't' build this intuition were catalog fit judgements, not universal laws; the reliability lesson centres on the spread of numbers rather than spatial structure, which is why a number-line/data representation is emphasised, but this does not establish comparative efficacy of formats.

The row frames precision as finer instrument resolution and reliability as reproducibility of repeats; in standard metrology precision also covers the spread of repeats. This simplification is the row's own and is retained unchanged, not corrected into learner questions.
Source claims cited support the curriculum requirements (repeat readings, number of trials, measurement as evidence) but do not establish the efficacy or necessity of any particular activity format.

probeDeeper: Which of the previous group's readings doesn't fit? What should you do with it?
Why take several readings instead of just one?
How did you work out your final value? Which readings did you use?
If you included the 3.8 s in your average, what would happen to your answer — and would that be more or less accurate?
assess.correctAnswer: The child takes at least three careful repeat readings (consistent start/stop), spots the 3.8 s as an anomalous result that doesn't fit the pattern, excludes it (or re-takes it) rather than including it, and gives a best value as the mean of the consistent readings (about 2.1 s). They can say repeats are taken because a single reading might be off, and the mean of close repeats is more reliable.

errorPatterns.pattern: Averages in the anomaly: includes 3.8 s in the mean, dragging the answer to about 2.4 s.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Identify the reading that doesn't fit the pattern; exclude or re-take it before averaging.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The final calculation folds in the outlier.

errorPatterns.pattern: Single reading, no repeats: takes one reading and calls it the answer.
errorPatterns.nextMove: One reading can be off; take at least three and compare them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No repeat readings are taken.

errorPatterns.pattern: Repeats taken but not used: records three readings but just picks one, or doesn't combine them into a mean.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Combine the consistent readings into a mean to get the best single value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No mean of the consistent readings is calculated.

responseLevels.gap: Takes a single reading, or averages the anomaly in without noticing it doesn't fit.
responseLevels.full: Takes careful repeat readings, identifies the anomalous result and excludes or re-takes it, and reports a best value as the mean of the consistent readings — explaining that repeats and anomaly-handling improve reliability.
responseLevels.partial: Takes repeats and computes a mean, but includes the anomaly or needs prompting to spot and handle it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Time how long this toy car takes to roll down the ramp, using the stopwatch. Take several readings, then give me your best single value for the time. Here are readings a previous group got: 2.1 s, 2.0 s, 2.2 s, 3.8 s, 2.1 s — use those too. Show me how you take your readings and how you decide on your final answer. I'll watch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching reveals whether the child genuinely takes and USES repeats and identifies the anomaly — versus taking one reading, or averaging the 3.8 s outlier in, which drags the mean upward. Handling the anomaly correctly (exclude, don't average blindly) is the discriminator.
