pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Speed & Distance-Time Graphs

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics — Motion):** Speed and the quantitative relationship between average speed, distance and time (speed = distance ÷ time); the representation of a journey on a distance–time graph and the gradient of a straight segment as speed.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS SEP — Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking):** Use mathematical representations to describe and predict an object's motion (speed as distance ÷ time); supports MS-PS2 Motion and Stability and CCSS-Math 6.RP/7.RP ratios and proportional relationships.

- **Operational details:** This topic is the quantitative heart of motion: calculating average speed with speed = distance ÷ time, attaching correct units (m/s, km/h), and tying that number to the gradient of a distance-time graph. The most effective sequencing, per Oak National Academy, builds from distance = speed × time FIRST ('metres per second means metres travelled each second'), because the multiplicative form is more intuitive than the division form. The deeper goal is proportional reasoning — understanding speed as the rate that links distance and time — so representations that expose the proportional structure (double number lines, ratio tables) are preferred over rote use of the 'formula triangle', which research shows can block more productive reasoning. Average speed must be taught as TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time (including any stationary periods), not the mean of the separate speeds.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Calculating average speed rests on emerging proportional reasoning: pupils build from distance = speed × time, attach units (m/s), and connect the value to a graph's gradient. The key threshold at 11–12 is defining average speed as TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time — including stationary periods — rather than averaging the separate speeds, and reasoning proportionally (double number lines, ratio tables) instead of leaning on the formula triangle as a substitute for understanding.
bestPractices: Teach distance = speed × time before speed = distance ÷ time; anchor on 'm/s = the number of metres travelled each second' (Oak National Academy).

Use double number lines and ratio tables (NCETM) to make the proportional relationship visible — e.g. scaling distance and time together to predict how far in a new time — rather than relying solely on the formula triangle, which can short-circuit reasoning.
Define average speed explicitly as total distance ÷ total time, including stopped periods; give journeys with stops so the 'mean of the speeds' error is confronted.
Connect the calculation to the graph: average speed of a straight segment IS its gradient; have pupils compute it both ways and reconcile.
Use precise language — qualify 'constant'/'steady' with a value ('a constant speed of 4 m/s') and always state units; keep distance distinct from displacement.
Use predict-then-calculate tasks (estimate the speed, then compute) and real contexts (cyclists, cars) to keep the abstraction grounded.
keyRepresentations: Double number line linking distance and time (NCETM) — the central proportional model
Ratio table for distance:time, scaled by a functional multiplier
Distance-time graph with gradient = average speed
The speed-distance-time 'formula triangle' (a memory aid, used with caution, not as a substitute for reasoning)
Unit unpacking: m/s as 'metres each second', km/h, mph
commonMisconceptions: Calculating average speed as the mean of the individual speeds rather than total distance ÷ total time (Third Space Learning).
Forgetting to include stationary periods in the total time when finding average speed.
Reading a value off the vertical axis and calling it the speed instead of finding the gradient.
Treating the formula triangle as the whole concept — procedural recall that blocks proportional reasoning (Susac et al., Phys. Rev. PER).
Language slips: 'constant speed' read as 'always moving', 'steady speed' as 'not too fast'; conflating distance with displacement (Oak National Academy).

learn.summary: For ages 11–12, teach average speed as a proportional rate linking distance and time, built up from distance = speed × time ('m/s means metres travelled each second') before introducing speed = distance ÷ time. The central threshold is that average speed = TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, including any stationary periods — not the mean of the separate speeds (the mean is only correct when equal time is spent at each speed). Use double number lines and ratio tables to expose the proportional structure and support prediction, connect the calculation to the gradient of a distance-time graph (a single leg's speed is its segment gradient; the whole-journey average is the start-to-end chord gradient), and confront the 'mean of the speeds' and 'ignore the stop' errors directly. A journey-building activity with live, synchronised feedback is the richest approach; a quiz consolidates the procedure; a worked-example reference card scaffolds a single case.

activities.title: Build a journey and watch the average speed update
feedback: If a learner expects the average of 8 m/s and 4 m/s to be 6 m/s (which is correct here only because the two legs last equal times), show that after inserting a 20-second stop the average-speed readout drops below 6, because the stopped seconds are added to the total time while the distance does not grow.
When prediction and calculation disagree, point back to the running denominator: 'the cart is sitting still, but the total time keeps climbing — what does that do to distance ÷ time?'

If the learner reads a speed off the vertical axis, redirect them to compute the gradient (distance change ÷ time change) of a straight segment to get that leg's speed; for the whole-journey average, compare with the gradient of the line joining the start and end points rather than a single leg's gradient.
Reinforce correct units: the readout is in metres per second because you divided metres by seconds.
activities.rationale: Live, synchronised feedback (an animating cart, a drawing distance-time graph, and a running total-distance-over-total-time calculator) is intended to let learners feel speed as a trade-off between distance and time and work out the 'include the stops' rule rather than memorise it. The double number line keeps the proportional structure visible and supports prediction, which cited research associates with deeper understanding than formula-triangle recall. The animation, graph, double-number-line widget and challenge mode are suggested ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features; their effectiveness is untested here.
sourceClaims: Pupils find speed easier built from distance = speed × time first; 'm/s is the number of metres travelled each second'; 'constant'/'steady' speed language must be qualified with a value.
Double number lines and ratio tables make the proportional structure of compound measures (speed) visible and support prediction; a functional multiplier shows deep understanding.

Reliance on formulas can block more productive reasoning strategies; slope-height and iconic confusions are common; average speed is often mis-computed as the mean of speeds or by ignoring stationary periods.
learnerActions: Assemble a trip from segments, choosing a speed for each leg; for the core demonstration use two legs of EQUAL DURATION (e.g. a leg at 8 m/s then an equal-time leg at 4 m/s), and insert optional STOP blocks of a chosen duration.
Before inserting a 20-second stop between the two equal-duration legs, predict the average speed over the whole trip and write down your reasoning.
Insert the stop and observe how the average-speed readout changes; note whether it rose, fell, or stayed the same, and explain why.
Use a double-number-line widget beside the journey to predict: 'keeping this leg's speed, how far would you travel in 10 seconds?' by scaling distance and time together.
Attempt a challenge: adjust the journey to hit a target average speed when one stop is forced into the trip.

State the speed of a single leg with its units and check it against the gradient of that leg's straight segment on the distance-time graph; then note that the whole-journey average speed matches the gradient of the straight line joining the journey's start and end points (the chord), not any single intermediate segment.
activities.intendedInsight: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, and stopped seconds still count in the denominator. With two equal-time legs the mean of the two speeds (here 6 m/s) is genuinely correct; but inserting a stop adds time without adding distance, so the average drops below it — showing that total time, including stops, is what matters. Speed is a proportional rate you can scale to predict new distances and times.

activities.title: Consolidate the calculation and graph reading
feedback: For the multi-leg item, confirm that the 'mean of the speeds' option is a distractor and reinforce total distance ÷ total time.
If a learner picks a steeper-looking segment that is actually less steep, prompt them to read off the actual distance and time changes rather than judging by eye.
Flag any answer where metres and seconds are mismatched with the stated unit.
activities.rationale: A checking activity makes the procedure crisply assessable across step types and is well suited as a follow-up that consolidates the calculation. Note that it mainly drills the procedure; it does less to build the proportional intuition than the journey-building activity, so use it after that work rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: Reliance on formulas can block more productive reasoning strategies; slope-height and iconic confusions are common; average speed is often mis-computed as the mean of speeds or by ignoring stationary periods.
learnerActions: Fill in the missing quantity for distance = speed × time and for speed = distance ÷ time rearrangements, attaching correct units each time.
Read the speed of a straight distance-time graph segment by computing its gradient (distance change ÷ time change).
For a multi-leg journey that includes a stop, choose the correct average speed from options that include the 'mean of the speeds' answer, and justify the choice.
Order several graph sections from slowest to fastest by comparing their gradients.
activities.intendedInsight: The speed = distance ÷ time procedure can be applied reliably with correct units, average speed over a whole journey is not the mean of the leg speeds, and the gradient of a straight distance-time segment gives that leg's speed.

activities.title: Walk through a worked example as a reference card
feedback: If the learner forgets units, the card re-shows that dividing metres by seconds gives m/s.
If they divide in the wrong order, the card re-shows distance on top and time underneath.
activities.rationale: A step-revealing reference card scaffolds one worked case and reinforces units. It is a recap aid: because the quantities are fixed it cannot let the learner vary distance and time and feel the rate, so it under-serves the proportional core and should supplement, not replace, the hands-on journey work.
sourceClaims: Pupils find speed easier built from distance = speed × time first; 'm/s is the number of metres travelled each second'; 'constant'/'steady' speed language must be qualified with a value.
learnerActions: Step through one worked journey: reveal the total distance, reveal the total time, then reveal the division and the resulting speed with its units.
Note the unit reminder at each step (metres ÷ seconds = metres per second).
Use the card as a recap aid when stuck on a later calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: A single average-speed calculation follows a fixed, checkable sequence: identify total distance, identify total time, divide, and attach units.

activities.title: Measure and reconcile average speed in a real run
feedback: If learners predict the midpoint of the two speeds, highlight that the slow leg takes more seconds, so it carries more weight in the total time.
Connect the measured result back to the rule: total distance ÷ total time, with both legs' actual measured times summed.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-measure task in a real context grounds the abstraction and directly confronts the 'mean of the speeds' error using the learner's own measured times. It targets the same key misconception as the journey-builder through physical investigation. Because the legs are equal in distance (not time), the midpoint over-estimates the true average — a useful contrast with the equal-time case.
sourceClaims: Reliance on formulas can block more productive reasoning strategies; slope-height and iconic confusions are common; average speed is often mis-computed as the mean of speeds or by ignoring stationary periods.
learnerActions: Mark two equal 10 m stretches. Have one person jog the first and walk the second while others time each leg.
Before calculating, predict the average speed over the whole 20 m and say WHY.
Calculate average speed from the measured times as total distance ÷ total time, and compare it with your prediction.

Work out each leg's speed from its measured time (10 m ÷ that leg's time), find the midpoint of those two speeds, and discuss why the whole-run average (20 m ÷ total time) is lower than that midpoint whenever the jogging leg was faster than the walking leg.
activities.intendedInsight: Over two equal-distance legs, more time is spent on the slower (walking) leg, so the true average speed is pulled below the simple midpoint of the two speeds — the average is weighted by time spent, not by distance.

constraints: Teach distance = speed × time before speed = distance ÷ time, anchored on 'm/s = metres travelled each second'.
Define average speed explicitly as total distance ÷ total time, including stopped periods; always give at least one journey with a stop so the 'mean of the speeds' error is confronted.

The mean of the two leg speeds equals the true average when equal time is spent at each speed; for equal-distance legs at different speeds the true (time-weighted) average is lower than the mean. State the leg configuration whenever a specific average value is claimed.

Connect calculation to graphs precisely: a single leg's speed equals the gradient of its straight segment, while the whole-journey average speed equals the gradient of the straight line joining the journey's start and end points — not any single intermediate segment.
Use double number lines and ratio tables to make the proportional relationship visible; treat the formula triangle only as a cautious memory aid, never as a substitute for proportional reasoning.
Use precise language: qualify 'constant'/'steady' speed with a value (e.g. 'a constant speed of 4 m/s'), always state units, and keep distance distinct from displacement.

The step-revealing reference card and the quiz are scaffolds/consolidation: they drill or display a fixed procedure and do not let learners vary quantities to feel the rate, so they should supplement, not replace, hands-on proportional work.

Suggested interactive features (animating cart, live-drawing graph, running denominator readout, double-number-line widget, draggable segments, challenge mode) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required components, and their efficacy is untested.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source-field arithmetic check: the diagnostic answer of ~2.86 m/s is correct for two EQUAL-DISTANCE 100 m legs at 5 m/s and 2 m/s (times 20 s and 50 s; 200 m ÷ 70 s ≈ 2.857 m/s). However, the assessment's poeTask describes two 10 m stretches (20 m total) while the correctAnswer narrative uses 100 m legs (200 m total). The numeric method is sound, but the distances are inconsistent between fields — resolve the scenario distances before using with learners. The measure-and-reconcile activity uses the 10 m/20 m poeTask framing and leaves exact numbers to be computed from measured times.

Coherence fix applied to activity 1: the '8 and 4 m/s average 6, then drops after a stop' demonstration is only valid for equal-time legs, so the activity specifies equal-duration legs; otherwise the pre-stop average is already below 6 and the narrative would be inconsistent.

Gradient fix applied to activity 1: an earlier draft told learners to check the whole-journey average speed against 'the matching straight segment'. Because a single segment's gradient is only that leg's speed, the actions and feedback now distinguish a single leg (segment gradient) from the whole-journey average (start-to-end chord gradient).
The car example (60 km, stop for 1 hour, 60 km in 1 hour) gives 120 km ÷ 3 h = 40 km/h; verify this is presented consistently if used.

Several sources are marked unverified in the original row (NCETM representations; Susac et al./Third Space Learning); confidence was legacy-'high' but is not independently re-established here. The claim that formula-triangle reliance 'blocks' reasoning reflects cited research tendencies, not a universal law; present it as a caution.

The original ruled out 3D and conversation formats as adding nothing / not advancing the content; these are treated as scope-limited notes (those media do not themselves illuminate the numeric/proportional structure or require an in-role dimension) rather than universal claims, and were not carried as learner-facing restrictions.

assess.poeTask: Mark two equal 10 m stretches. Have a student jog the first and walk the second while others time each leg. Ask the class to predict the average speed over the whole 20 m, and WHY, before calculating from the measured times. Predicting the midpoint of the two speeds is the diagnostic tell; the measured total-distance-over-total-time result coming out lower (more time spent walking) is the payoff.
probeDeeper: If the runner had spent EQUAL TIME (not equal distance) at 5 and 2 m/s, would 3.5 be right then? Why?
A car drives 60 km in 1 hour, stops for 1 hour, then drives 60 km in another hour. What's its average speed over the whole trip?
Which section of a distance-time graph shows the fastest speed, and how do you get a number from it?
What units should your average speed be in, and how do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: No, 3.5 m/s is wrong. Average speed = TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, not the mean of the two speeds. The first 100 m takes 100/5 = 20 s; the second takes 100/2 = 50 s. Total 200 m in 70 s gives an average of about 2.86 m/s. It's below 3.5 because the runner spends MORE time going slowly.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Average speed is just the mean of the speeds — halfway between them.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define average speed = total distance ÷ total time; compute the two times to show the result is weighted by time spent, not distance.
errorPatterns.distractor: 3.5 m/s — halfway between 5 and 2 m/s.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives (5+2)/2 = 3.5 with no reference to the times.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'When there's a stop, only count the time spent moving.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Total time includes stops; a stop lowers the average speed over the whole trip.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a journey with a stop, divides distance by the moving-time only.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Speed is distance times time.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build speed = distance ÷ time from a double number line / ratio table rather than a magic triangle; check units (m/s = metres per second).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Multiplies instead of dividing, or mis-rearranges the formula triangle.

responseLevels.gap: Averages the two speeds (3.5), or divides distance by moving-time only; may multiply distance by time.
responseLevels.full: Computes average speed as total distance ÷ total time (including stopped time), explains why time spent at each speed weights the result (so the answer is below the midpoint), and reads/represents it on a distance-time graph, with correct units.
responseLevels.partial: Knows speed = distance ÷ time and can find a single-section speed, but for a two-part journey still averages the speeds or forgets to use TOTAL time — applies the formula per section without combining correctly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A runner covers the first 100 m at 5 m/s, then walks the next 100 m at 2 m/s. A friend says 'the average speed is 3.5 m/s — halfway between 5 and 2'. Is that right? What is the average speed, and how should you work it out?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The signature error is averaging the two speeds (mean of 5 and 2). A student who understands says average speed = total distance ÷ total time, gets about 2.86, and explains that more time is spent at the slower speed so the average is pulled down. A student with the misconception gives 3.5 and can't say why the time spent at each speed matters. Tier 2 (how you work it out) is decisive.

sources.claim: Pupils find speed easier built from distance = speed × time first; 'm/s is the number of metres travelled each second'; 'constant'/'steady' speed language must be qualified with a value.
sources.source: Oak National Academy — KS3 Science, Calculating speed

sources.claim: Double number lines and ratio tables make the proportional structure of compound measures (speed) visible and support prediction; a functional multiplier shows deep understanding.
sources.source: NCETM — KS3 representations: double number lines and ratio tables

sources.claim: Reliance on formulas can block more productive reasoning strategies; slope-height and iconic confusions are common; average speed is often mis-computed as the mean of speeds or by ignoring stationary periods.
sources.source: Susac et al., 'Student reasoning about graphs in different contexts', Phys. Rev. Phys. Educ. Res. 12, 010106; Third Space Learning topic guide

pedagogy.summary: This Year 5 topic explains day and night by Earth's rotation on its axis (one turn per 24 hours): your side facing the Sun is day, facing away is night, and the Sun only APPEARS to move across the sky because we are turning. The dominant challenge is the deep geocentric, 'moving-Sun' intuition built from everyday experience (Baxter's documented progression of ideas) and the frequent confusion of spin (rotation) with orbit (revolution). It is best taught by eliciting ideas first, then having children manipulate a globe and single light source — or act out the rotation themselves — while connecting the model back to real sunrise/sunset observations.
bestPractices: Elicit initial ideas first with a diagnostic probe ('what causes day and night?') to surface the 'Sun goes behind hills/clouds/behind the Earth' wrong tracks before teaching.

Use a globe and one strong light in a darkened room, with the CHILD rotating the globe (or acting as the spinning Earth) — manipulating beats watching a demo; mark 'your' location and watch it turn into and out of the light.
Explicitly distinguish rotation (spin on the axis, once a day → day and night) from revolution (orbit the Sun, once a year), because children routinely conflate them.
Reframe the apparent motion: the Sun seems to cross the sky because WE rotate; flag that 'sunrise/sunset' language reinforces the moving-Sun idea.
Sequence from a simple illumination model to the full picture and keep connecting the model to observations children make outdoors (shadows, the Sun's position).
Directly confront the 'blocking' explanations (night = Sun hidden behind hills or clouds) and the geocentric 'Sun orbits the Earth once a day'.
keyRepresentations: A globe plus a single lamp 'Sun': a marked location rotates into day and out into night.
Child-as-Earth enactment: spin to face and turn away from a lamp Sun; add walking the orbit to contrast spin with orbit.
A day/night terminator diagram — a half-lit sphere, your side vs the far side.
A spin-vs-orbit comparison: once a day vs once a year.
commonMisconceptions: Night happens because the Sun goes behind hills/mountains or behind clouds (a 'blocking' explanation).
The Sun orbits/moves around a stationary Earth once a day (the geocentric model).
The Earth orbits the Sun once a DAY to make day and night (misusing the real annual orbit).
Confusing rotation (spin) with revolution (orbit) — 'the Earth spins around the Sun in a year'.
The Sun really moves across the sky, rather than the Earth turning beneath it.
Night is caused by the Moon covering the Sun, or by Earth moving away from the Sun.

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils explain day and night by Earth's ~24-hour rotation on its axis: the half facing the Sun has day, the half facing away has night, and the Sun only APPEARS to cross the sky because we are turning beneath it. The deep obstacle is the geocentric 'moving-Sun' intuition built from everyday sunrise/sunset experience (documented by Baxter as a progression of ideas), plus routine confusion of spin (rotation, once a day) with orbit (revolution, once a year). Elicit ideas first, then have children manipulate a globe with a single light — or act as the spinning Earth themselves — and keep linking the space-view model back to their own outdoor observations of the Sun and shadows.

activities.title: Spin the Earth beside a fixed Sun — and watch the Sun 'rise'
feedback: If a learner says the Sun is travelling, pause the spin: the lamp has not moved at all — only the globe turned. The apparent motion of the Sun is the learner's own motion.

If a learner explains night as the Sun going behind hills or clouds, point to the whole half of the globe in shadow: night is the entire far side facing away from the Sun, not something passing in front of it.
Prompt them to connect back outdoors: 'When you saw the Sun low in the morning and high at midday, what was really turning?'
activities.rationale: The documented difficulty is coordinating two viewpoints — the space view of a rotating lit globe and the ground view of the Sun crossing the sky. Learner-driven manipulation (child turns the globe, or acts as Earth) rather than watching a demonstration is the recommended approach, and coupling the space view to a ground view is intended to link the perspectives that children struggle to reconcile.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 statutory 'Earth and space' requires pupils to use the idea of the Earth's rotation to explain day and night and the apparent movement of the sun across the sky.

Everyday experience of the Sun rising and setting leads children to a geocentric 'moving-Sun' model; teachers should distinguish spin from orbit and have students manipulate a globe-and-flashlight model themselves rather than watch a demonstration; 'sunrise/sunset' language reinforces the misconception.
learnerActions: In a darkened room, set up one strong lamp as a fixed Sun and a globe with your own location clearly marked with a sticker.

Slowly rotate the globe yourself (don't just watch someone else) from west to east (anticlockwise when seen from above the North Pole), and track your marked spot as it sweeps from the dark side into the light and back out again.

If using a screen model: drag to spin the Earth west to east next to the fixed Sun, with a 'you-are-here' pin that sweeps from the dark side into daylight, while a coupled ground-level view below shows the Sun rise in the east, climb to its highest point around midday, then sink and set in the west, in step with your spin.
Say out loud, at the moment the Sun appears to rise in the ground view, what is actually moving — the Sun, or you?
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun did not move — YOU did. Turning the Earth is what makes the Sun appear to cross the sky, and night is simply your side facing away from the Sun, not the Sun hiding behind hills or clouds.

activities.title: Be the Earth: spin versus orbit
feedback: If a learner says 'the Earth spins around the Sun in a year', separate the two words: spinning is turning on the spot (the day); going around the Sun is the loop (the year).

If a learner claims the Earth orbits the Sun once a day to cause night, remind them that the real orbit takes about 365 days while day and night repeat about every 24 hours; have them keep spinning slowly as they walk the lap to show that many day-night turns happen during one orbit (about 365 in reality).

If a learner thinks a non-spinning Earth would still give normal day and night, point out that the daily cycle comes from the spin: with no spin, your spot would face the Sun for roughly half the year and away for the other half, so there would be no normal 24-hour day and night — only one extremely slow change across the whole year.
activities.rationale: Children routinely conflate rotation and revolution, and the recurring astronomy error is attributing day/night to a daily orbit. Acting out spin-on-the-spot versus a slow walked lap makes the distinction kinetic and memorable, and the 'stopped spinning but still orbiting' probe isolates the spin as the cause of the daily cycle.
sourceClaims: Everyday experience of the Sun rising and setting leads children to a geocentric 'moving-Sun' model; teachers should distinguish spin from orbit and have students manipulate a globe-and-flashlight model themselves rather than watch a demonstration; 'sunrise/sunset' language reinforces the misconception.
learnerActions: Stand and spin slowly on the spot facing a lamp Sun: notice your front (day) and your back (night) — one full turn is one day and night, about 24 hours.
Now, keeping facing the same direction in the room, walk a slow large loop around the lamp: this is the orbit, which takes a whole year (about 365 days).
Describe in your own words: which motion causes day and night, and which causes the year?

Try the wrong version deliberately — 'the Earth goes right round the Sun each day' — and explain why that is not what makes daytime and night-time: the real trip round the Sun takes about a year, but day and night repeat about every 24 hours.
Now imagine the Earth stopped spinning but still travelled its yearly loop round the Sun: decide whether you would still get the normal daily day and night, and explain why or why not.
activities.intendedInsight: Spinning on the axis once a day makes the daily day-and-night cycle; orbiting the Sun once a year makes the year. These are two different motions and must not be conflated — the daily cycle depends on the spin, not on the orbit.

activities.title: Elicit and confront: what causes night?
feedback: A learner can state 'day and night' correctly yet still give a wrong cause when asked why — press on the 'why' every time.
If the geocentric 'Sun travels round the Earth' answer appears, return to the fixed lamp: it did not move.
If the Earth-orbits-the-Sun-daily answer appears, return to the walked lap, which stands for the real orbit taking about a year, while day and night repeat about every 24 hours with each spin.
activities.rationale: Eliciting initial ideas with a diagnostic probe surfaces the wrong tracks before teaching, and asking for the cause separately from the surface statement separates a correct first answer from the documented underlying misconceptions. This activity is diagnostic and consolidating; recognition/selection tasks can check which misconception persists but do not by themselves build the causal-spatial model.
sourceClaims: Baxter (1989) documented a developmental progression of day/night ideas — Sun goes behind hills; clouds cover the Sun; Moon covers the Sun; Sun goes behind the Earth once a day; Earth goes around the Sun once a day; Earth spins on its axis once a day — children advancing through these with age.

Everyday experience of the Sun rising and setting leads children to a geocentric 'moving-Sun' model; teachers should distinguish spin from orbit and have students manipulate a globe-and-flashlight model themselves rather than watch a demonstration; 'sunrise/sunset' language reinforces the misconception.
learnerActions: Before any teaching, answer the probe 'What causes day and night?' in your own words and sketch what you think.
Compare your idea with the common wrong tracks: the Sun goes behind hills or clouds; the Moon covers the Sun; the Sun travels round the Earth once a day; the Earth loops the Sun once a day.
After the globe and enactment work, revisit your first answer and mark what you would now change.
Explain why, right now, it can be daytime where you are but night-time on the far side of the world — and why the Sun looks like it moves across the sky during the day.

Answer in two steps — first what happens (day/night), then WHY — choosing from the real spin explanation and the documented alternatives (Sun behind hills; Sun orbiting Earth daily; Earth orbiting Sun daily; Moon/clouds covering the Sun).
Categorise statements as 'spin (once a day)' or 'orbit (once a year)', and put a marked location in order through day → night.
activities.intendedInsight: Surfacing your own starting idea and naming the specific wrong tracks makes it possible to notice exactly which one you held and to replace it with the rotation explanation.

constraints: Learners should physically manipulate the globe or act as the Earth themselves; source guidance (NSTA) recommends this over passively watching a demonstration, which is likely a weaker way to challenge the entrenched moving-Sun intuition (comparative efficacy is not independently established here).

A static half-lit terminator diagram (tap to reveal day side / night side) is useful as a reference but cannot run the rotation or couple the space-view with the ground-view, so treat it as a support, not the main teaching.

A 3D rotatable lit Earth that zooms to the surface is vivid and genuinely spatial, but the essential perspective-coupling (space view + ground view) can also be achieved in 2D; choose based on available tools, not on an assumption that 3D is required.

Multiple-choice and categorisation tasks can check whether the misconception persists but do not by themselves elicit the independent, hands-on reasoning that builds the model; use them alongside manipulation, not instead of it.

A discussion-only (conversation) format may talk through the idea or help elicit/check a learner's thinking, but it does not itself elicit the hands-on manipulation this spatial model depends on, and there is no strong in-role persona for the day/night mechanism at this age; treat it as a weaker fit for building the model.
Flag that 'sunrise' and 'sunset' language itself reinforces the moving-Sun idea; name this explicitly when it comes up.
Keep connecting the space-view model to real outdoor observations children make (the Sun's changing position, shadows) rather than leaving the model abstract.

A physical globe and lamp are approximations: a real globe has a tilted axis and the lamp is close, so use them to show the facing/away-from mechanism, not to make precise claims about angles or distance.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (Baxter via Beyond Penguins; NSTA/IOPSpark) were marked verified:false in the source row; treat the Baxter progression and the manipulation-over-demonstration guidance as plausible but not independently re-checked here.

The source row asserted the 2D coupled model 'targets the exact misconceptions', that a static image 'will not dislodge' the intuition, and that 3D 'adds nothing essential'; these are design judgements from catalogue ratings, not established comparative efficacy, and have been softened into affordance/limit statements.
The reteach-prerequisite links (rotation/revolution and orbit prerequisites) from the assessment were not carried into learner-facing actions; they are a routing concern for the assessment layer.

The 'stopped spinning but still orbiting' answer is simplified for Year 5: strictly, an orbiting non-spinning Earth would still see the Sun's direction change once per year, so there is a very slow annual light/dark change rather than literally no change — but no normal daily cycle. Keep the emphasis on the daily cycle depending on the spin. Note too that walking a loop while keeping the same body orientation is itself the non-spinning case, which is why it is used to isolate the orbit from the daily cycle.

probeDeeper: If the Earth stopped spinning but kept travelling round the Sun, would we still get day and night? Why?
You said the Sun looks like it moves — what's actually moving? Show me with a globe and a lamp.
My friend says day and night happen because the Earth goes right round the Sun each day. What's wrong with that?
assess.correctAnswer: The Earth spins (rotates) on its axis once about every 24 hours; the half facing the Sun has day, the half facing away has night. The Sun only APPEARS to move across the sky because we are turning — the Sun is not travelling round us.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Sun travels round the Earth once a day — that's why it rises and sets' (geocentric, from sunrise/sunset language)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix a lamp as the Sun and spin the child or a globe; the moving horizon makes the fixed Sun appear to travel — the child feels the apparent motion is theirs.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun travels all the way around the Earth once a day.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes day/night to the Sun's own motion around the Earth

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Earth goes right round the Sun once a day' (rotation↔revolution conflation — the recurring astronomy error)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate SPIN (once/24h → day and night) from ORBIT (once/365 days → the year) kinetically — spin on the spot vs walk a slow lap.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Earth travels all the way around the Sun once each day.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the Earth's orbit round the Sun causes day and night

errorPatterns.pattern: 'at night the Moon or clouds cover up the Sun' (blocking model — an early Baxter stage)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Night is the whole half of the Earth facing away from the Sun, not something passing in front of it; show the terminator on a globe.
errorPatterns.distractor: At night the Moon moves in front of and covers the Sun.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: invokes the Moon or clouds hiding the Sun to explain night

responseLevels.gap: Attributes day/night to the Sun moving round the Earth, the Moon/clouds covering the Sun, or the Earth orbiting the Sun daily.
responseLevels.full: Explains day/night by the Earth's ~24-hour rotation (facing the Sun = day, away = night), attributes the Sun's apparent motion to our own spin, and cleanly distinguishes the daily spin from the yearly orbit; transfers to 'why is it night on the far side right now?'
responseLevels.partial: Says 'the Earth spins' but cannot coordinate facing/away-from the Sun, or still mixes rotation with revolution when pressed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Right now it's daytime here and night-time on the far side of the world. What is the Earth doing to turn our day into night? … And why does the Sun look like it moves across the sky during the day?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reason tier separates 'the Earth spins' (correct) from the documented alternatives: the Sun going round the Earth, the Earth orbiting the Sun once a day, or the Moon/clouds covering the Sun. A child can say 'day and night' correctly at tier one yet reveal any of these causes at tier two.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Levers, Pulleys & Gears

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 5 Forces):** Recognise that some mechanisms including levers, pulleys and gears allow a smaller force to have a greater effect (verbatim this topic); it ties forward to KS3 moments / mechanical advantage.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no direct simple-machines PE at this grade band):** NGSS has no direct simple-machines performance expectation at the elementary band; the topic is UK-curriculum anchored and links forward to NGSS forces/energy and engineering-design ideas (e.g. MS-PS3, MS-ETS1) later.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A→B boundary (concrete/observational moving toward early-formal, age 9-10). The goal is the QUALITATIVE big idea — levers, pulleys and gears let a smaller force have a greater effect, with a lever's effort depending on where the pivot sits — grounded in measuring real effort, NOT the quantitative moment = force × distance (reserve for KS3, topic mt_vuNjYx3qOy).
bestPractices: Anchor in measurement: use force meters, a stiff ruler/rod, masses and a pivot so children MEASURE that the effort needed to lift a fixed load drops as the effort is applied further from (and the pivot is moved closer to) the load.
Name the three lever parts in child-friendly terms — load (object being lifted), effort (force you apply), pivot/fulcrum (fixed point it turns on) — teaching 'pivot' and 'fulcrum' together.
Teach honestly that a machine does not create force from nothing — it trades force for distance: less effort means moving the effort end a greater distance (keeps the big idea from becoming 'magic').

Cover all three mechanisms and what each changes: lever (reduce effort by pivot position), pulley (change the direction of the force, and adding wheels reduces effort), gears (change size and/or direction of force; small gear turns fast with less force, large gear slow with more).
Classify and connect to everyday objects — seesaw, crowbar, scissors, wheelbarrow, bottle opener, tweezers, the elbow joint — so the abstraction is grounded in things children know.
Use predict-then-measure: predict where to put the pivot for least effort, then test and read the force meter, so the relationship is evidenced not asserted.
keyRepresentations: A lever (ruler) on a movable pivot with a mass as load and a force meter reading the effort — slide the pivot, watch the effort change
Seesaw as the relatable first-class lever model (effort/load/pivot)
A pulley with a string and hanging load; add a wheel to see effort fall and/or direction change
Two meshed gears of different sizes (small fast/low force vs large slow/high force)
Everyday-object cards labelled with effort/load/pivot for classification
commonMisconceptions: 'All levers work the same way' (Oak) — children miss that pivot position and effort-vs-load placement change how much effort is needed.
Thinking a machine creates extra force from nothing — missing the force-for-distance trade-off.
'Gears only exist in bicycles and cars' (Oak) — not recognising gears more widely.
'All pulleys have the wheel fixed to a ceiling' (Oak) — over-narrow image of a pulley.
Confusing which part is the effort and which is the load, especially in second/third-class arrangements (wheelbarrow, tweezers).

learn.summary: For ages 9–10 (UK Year 5 Forces), teach the qualitative big idea that levers, pulleys and gears let a smaller force have a greater effect — and that this is not free, but a trade: you apply a smaller force but must move the effort end a greater distance. Anchor in real measurement (force meters, a rigid ruler/rod, masses, a movable pivot) using predict-then-measure, supported where helpful by an on-screen workbench that recomputes effort live as the pivot moves. Name load, effort and pivot/fulcrum, cover all three mechanisms and what each changes, and connect to everyday objects to challenge 'all levers work the same' and over-narrow images of pulleys and gears. Reserve quantitative moment = force × distance for later (KS3).

activities.title: Measure the effort drop on a real lever (predict-then-measure)
feedback: If a child predicts 'it makes no difference where the pivot is', have them measure both positions: the force-meter reading visibly changes, so pivot and effort position matter.

If a child says the lever 'lifts for free' or 'makes you stronger', ask what their end of the bar had to do — show the effort end moves much further than the load rises, so the smaller force is paid for by the greater distance moved; nothing is free.
Confirm correct reasoning: 'A smaller force lifts the load because the pivot is close to the load and the effort is far from it, and the cost is that your end moves a longer way.'
activities.rationale: Grounding the cause-effect relationship in real measurement with predict-then-measure lets the relationship be evidenced rather than asserted, and directly probes the 'all levers work the same' and 'lifts for free' misconceptions. Reading a real (noisy) force meter and feeling the effort drop is a sensory/measurement anchor central at this age.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: recognise that some mechanisms including levers, pulleys and gears allow a smaller force to have a greater effect; non-statutory guidance suggests exploring their effects on movement and designing products using them.

A lever allows a smaller force to have a greater effect; load = object lifted, effort = force applied, pivot/fulcrum = fixed turning point; effort needed depends on where the pivot sits; gears change size/direction of force (small gear fast/less force, large gear slow/more force); misconception 'all levers work the same way'; equipment = force meters, rulers/rods, masses.

A lever (and any simple machine) trades force for distance — more force gives less distance and vice versa; positioning the fulcrum close to a heavy load lets a small effort lift it; build-and-test with a ruler and pencil pivot to observe how fulcrum position changes effort.
learnerActions: Set up a stiff ruler or rod across a movable pivot (e.g. a pencil or small log), with a fixed mass as the load near one end.
Before testing, predict: as you move the pivot toward the load (and apply the effort further from the pivot), will the effort needed go up or down — and why? Write or say your prediction.
Hook a force meter at the effort end (or push and feel the effort) and read the effort needed to lift the fixed load with the pivot in its first position.
Slide the pivot closer to the load, repeat the measurement, and record how the force-meter reading changes.
Notice and describe what your hand/the effort end has to do: how far it moves compared with how far the load rises.
activities.intendedInsight: As the pivot moves closer to the load, so that the effort is applied further from the pivot than the load is, the effort needed to lift a fixed load drops. A smaller force has a greater effect, but the effort end travels a longer distance. You apply a smaller force at the cost of moving further. The lever does not create energy: the bigger force on the load is paid for by your end moving further.

activities.title: On-screen mechanism workbench: drag the pivot and watch effort change
feedback: If the child expects the effort to stay the same when dragging the pivot, pause on the falling needle and ask them to relate it to where the pivot now sits.
If the child treats the longer arc as unimportant, link it explicitly: the meter shows less force, the arc shows more distance — that is the trade.

For pulley mode, prompt: did adding the wheel change how hard you pull, the direction you pull, or both? Remind them a fixed overhead wheel only changes direction, while a movable wheel lowers the effort.
For gear mode, prompt: the small gear turns fast with less turning force; the large gear turns slowly with more turning force — which did you drive and which did it turn?
activities.rationale: A relationship between pivot position and effort suits an interactive that recomputes a force-meter live and renders the force-for-distance trade as a longer arc. This is proposed as a strong digital model that makes the mechanism legible in a 2D cross-section; it should accompany, not replace, real measurement.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: recognise that some mechanisms including levers, pulleys and gears allow a smaller force to have a greater effect; non-statutory guidance suggests exploring their effects on movement and designing products using them.

A lever allows a smaller force to have a greater effect; load = object lifted, effort = force applied, pivot/fulcrum = fixed turning point; effort needed depends on where the pivot sits; gears change size/direction of force (small gear fast/less force, large gear slow/more force); misconception 'all levers work the same way'; equipment = force meters, rulers/rods, masses.
learnerActions: On a lever workbench, try to lift a heavy crate; read the force-meter with the pivot in the middle — the reading is high because, with equal distances either side of the pivot, the push needed is about the same as the load's weight (it needs a big push).
Predict what will happen to the effort, then drag the pivot toward the crate and watch the effort reading fall as the same load lifts under a gentler push.
Observe the ghosted 'effort arc' showing the effort end sweeping through a longer path — name the bargain: less force, more distance.

Switch to pulley mode: thread an extra movable (supporting) wheel to build toward a block-and-tackle and watch the effort reading fall; note that a single fixed wheel would only change the direction you pull, while a movable wheel reduces the effort.
Switch to gear mode: mesh a small driver gear into a large gear and describe what happens to force and to speed/direction.
activities.intendedInsight: The live recompute of the effort meter as the pivot/pulley/gears change makes 'a smaller force has a greater effect' something the child drives and sees, including the force-for-distance trade shown as a longer effort arc. A fixed pulley changes direction; a movable pulley reduces effort.

activities.title: Name the parts and classify everyday machines
feedback: If a child swaps effort and load on a wheelbarrow or tweezers, have them identify what is being lifted (load) versus where they apply force (effort), then find the fixed pivot.
If a child says gears are only in bikes and cars, show an egg-whisk or clock; if they think a pulley only hangs from a ceiling, show a movable pulley that reduces effort.

Reinforce: on a lever like the ruler or seesaw, where the pivot is between the load and the effort and you push at the far end, moving the pivot toward the load reduces the effort needed. This matches what the measurement and workbench showed. Remember that some levers, like tweezers, need more effort instead.
activities.rationale: Classifying and labelling gives targeted consolidation and directly probes the 'all levers work the same' and over-narrow pulley/gear images; this task can check and reinforce classification and vocabulary but does not itself produce the measured relationship or the felt effort drop, so it best follows hands-on measurement.
sourceClaims: A lever allows a smaller force to have a greater effect; load = object lifted, effort = force applied, pivot/fulcrum = fixed turning point; effort needed depends on where the pivot sits; gears change size/direction of force (small gear fast/less force, large gear slow/more force); misconception 'all levers work the same way'; equipment = force meters, rulers/rods, masses.
learnerActions: On a lever diagram, label the load (object being lifted), the effort (force you apply) and the pivot/fulcrum (fixed point it turns on) — learn 'pivot' and 'fulcrum' as the same thing.
Sort everyday objects into lever, pulley or gear: seesaw, crowbar, scissors, wheelbarrow, bottle opener, tweezers, the elbow joint, egg-whisk, flagpole pulley.
For each lever example, mark where the effort, load and pivot are — including trickier arrangements like the wheelbarrow and tweezers.

Match each mechanism to what it changes: a lever reduces the effort when the effort is further from the pivot than the load is (e.g. crowbar, bottle opener, wheelbarrow), but some levers, such as tweezers and the elbow, need a larger effort in exchange for a bigger, faster or more precise movement at the load; a pulley changes direction and (with an extra movable wheel) reduces effort; gears change the size and/or direction of the turning force and the speed of turning.
Answer prediction prompts such as: 'Move the pivot toward the load — does the effort go up or down?'
activities.intendedInsight: Grounding the abstraction in familiar objects, and correctly locating effort/load/pivot even in awkward arrangements, consolidates the vocabulary and challenges over-narrow images (gears only in bikes/cars; pulleys only fixed overhead).

activities.title: Build-and-test extension: gear trains and a block-and-tackle
feedback: If a gear train won't turn, check the cogs mesh; link the small-fast/large-slow behaviour back to what they saw in gear mode.
If adding a movable pulley doesn't seem to help, count the supporting ropes and relate more ropes to lower effort but a greater length of rope to pull.
activities.rationale: Mechanisms are physical, and a hands-on build sandbox is offered as a richer extension where 3D assembly and space matter; the core effort-versus-pivot relationship is already captured in a 2D cross-section, so this enriches rather than replaces the core teaching.
sourceClaims: A lever allows a smaller force to have a greater effect; load = object lifted, effort = force applied, pivot/fulcrum = fixed turning point; effort needed depends on where the pivot sits; gears change size/direction of force (small gear fast/less force, large gear slow/more force); misconception 'all levers work the same way'; equipment = force meters, rulers/rods, masses.
learnerActions: Assemble a simple gear train with different-sized cogs and turn the driver; observe which gear turns faster and which turns with more force.
Rig a real pulley with a string and hanging load, then add a movable wheel to build a simple block-and-tackle; feel the effort change and note any change in pull direction.
Describe how the physical assembly (spacing, meshing, number of supporting ropes) affects what the mechanism does.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically assembling mechanisms adds tangibility and an engineering feel, letting children see how real spacing and meshing produce the force/direction/speed changes modelled elsewhere.

constraints: Keep to the qualitative big idea at this age; reserve the quantitative moment = force × distance (and formal mechanical advantage) for KS3.

Always include the force-for-distance trade so the big idea does not become 'magic': a machine does not create force from nothing — applying a smaller force means moving the effort end a greater distance.

Labelling, sorting and prediction prompts (the classify/label activity) can check and reinforce vocabulary and classification but do not themselves produce the measured relationship or elicit the felt effort drop.

The on-screen workbench models the relationship; a real kit with force meters, rulers/rods, masses and a movable pivot should accompany it so children feel the effort reduction and read a real (noisy) measurement.

Teach 'pivot' and 'fulcrum' as the same fixed turning point; cover all three mechanisms (lever, pulley, gears) and what each changes — and distinguish a fixed pulley (changes direction only) from a movable pulley (reduces effort), and gears beyond bikes/cars.
A static reference image can name parts and show examples but cannot, on its own, display effort falling as the pivot moves; use it as a companion, not the primary teacher of the causal idea.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's claim that 'a static picture can only assert' the relationship and that a sim is what makes it 'felt' overstates comparative necessity; softened here to scoped affordances and limits. No source establishes comparative efficacy of interactive vs static media.

The 'conversation' artefact was rated a poor fit with the claim that dialogue cannot advance this concept; that universal claim is not supported by the sources and has been omitted rather than propagated.
One source (TeachEngineering — 'Levers That Lift') is marked verified:false in the row; its force-for-distance and fulcrum-position claims are curriculum-consistent but carry lower verification.

Physics check: pushing further from the pivot lets a small effort move a big load; moving the pivot toward the load reduces effort; the smaller applied force is paid for by the effort end moving a greater distance. A single fixed pulley changes direction only, while a movable pulley reduces effort — this distinction is preserved. Small-gear-fast/low-force and large-gear-slow/high-force are retained as stated in the sources.

Activity 1's predict step was realigned so the learner predicts the effect of the variable actually measured (pivot position/effort placement), matching the source's 'predict where to put the pivot' design and the subsequent measurement.

Any specific magnitude of the force-meter drop (and the earlier 'needle halves' detail for one added pulley wheel) is an in-sim illustration, not a guaranteed real-world outcome; wording now says effort 'falls' rather than a fixed ratio.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a ruler-lever on a pencil pivot and a heavy object. Ask them to predict whether it's easier to lift by pushing near the object or far from the pivot, and WHY, before trying both. Predicting 'it makes no difference' or 'it lifts for free' reveals the everyday view; feeling the far push lift it easily — while their hand travels much further — makes the force-distance trade concrete.
probeDeeper: If you move the log (pivot) closer to the rock, is it easier or harder to lift? Why?
Name the load, the effort and the pivot on your bar.
A single pulley on a flagpole — does it make the flag lighter to pull, or just change the direction you pull?
You lifted the rock easily, but what did your end of the bar have to do that the rock didn't?
assess.correctAnswer: It's a lever: the log is the pivot (fulcrum), the rock is the load, the child's push is the effort. Pushing far from the pivot lets a small effort move a big load — a smaller force has a greater effect. It isn't free: the child's end moves a LONGER way (and pushes down further) than the rock rises — the machine trades distance for force, it doesn't create energy.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The machine gives you the extra force for free — you get more out than you put in.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the effort end travels much further than the load rises — force is multiplied, distance is traded; nothing is free.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the lever gives you the lifting force for nothing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies any cost and can't say what is traded.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All levers work the same way — the pivot position doesn't matter.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Move the log closer to and further from the rock and feel the effort change; effort depends on where the pivot is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Thinks moving the fulcrum makes no difference to the effort needed.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Gears and pulleys are only in bikes and cars, and a pulley always hangs from a ceiling.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show varied examples (egg-whisk gears, a flagpole pulley, a movable pulley); a pulley can change the direction of a force and, if movable, reduce the effort.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't recognise gears/pulleys in other machines, or assumes only a fixed overhead pulley.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the machine makes you stronger / lifts for free, or that all levers and pulleys are the same and the pivot doesn't matter.
responseLevels.full: Explains that these mechanisms let a smaller force have a greater effect by applying it further from the pivot (or via extra pulley ropes / different gear sizes), names load/effort/pivot, and recognises the force-for-distance trade — transferring to varied real machines.
responseLevels.partial: Knows a lever/pulley/gear can make a job easier and can name some parts, but explains it as 'gives more force' without the distance trade, or over-generalises one example — stating the effect without the 'nothing for free' idea.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child can't lift a heavy rock by hand, but by pushing down on the far end of a long strong bar resting on a small log, they lift it easily. How does the bar let them lift something they couldn't lift on their own — and are they getting the lift for free?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands says the lever lets a small force do a big job because the effort is applied far from the pivot, AND recognises the trade (their end moves further). A child with the everyday view thinks the bar 'makes them stronger' or gives the lift 'for free', with no sense of the distance trade, or thinks it only works because the bar is special. Tier 2 ('for free?') is the discriminator.

sources.claim: A lever (and any simple machine) trades force for distance — more force gives less distance and vice versa; positioning the fulcrum close to a heavy load lets a small effort lift it; build-and-test with a ruler and pencil pivot to observe how fulcrum position changes effort.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; multiply up to 4-digit × 1-digit AND 2-digit × 2-digit using formal long multiplication, illustrated with the area model.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'multiply numbers up to 4 digits by a one- or two-digit number using a formal written method, including long multiplication for two-digit numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.5 — 'fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm'; 4.NBT.5 covers up to 4-digit × 1-digit with area/place-value strategies.
• Operational details — the new challenge over Y4 short multiplication is the TWO-DIGIT multiplier: 34×27 requires multiplying by both the ones (7) and the tens (20), then adding partial products. The area model (45×23 as four sub-rectangles 40×20, 40×3, 5×20, 5×3) is the conceptual scaffold that shows WHY there are two rows of partial products and why the second row is shifted (it's ×20, not ×2). The classic error — forgetting the placeholder zero on the second partial product — is precisely a lost-place-value error the area model prevents. Estimate first (34×27≈30×30=900) to bound the answer.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): 4-digit × 1-digit (2347×6) securely. Tier B (age 9–10): 2-digit × 2-digit long multiplication (34×27) with correct partial-product placement. Tier C (age 10): draw the matching area model and explain why the second partial product is shifted / carries a zero.
bestPractices: Anchor long multiplication in the area model: 2-digit×2-digit as four sub-rectangles, so the two partial-product rows and the shift are seen as ×ones and ×tens.
Make the placeholder zero meaningful — the second row is ×20 (tens), not ×2 — rather than a rule to 'put a zero down'.
Estimate first by rounding both factors to bound the answer and catch magnitude errors.
Progress grid method → expanded partial products → compact long multiplication, keeping the area link visible.
Check with the inverse or by comparing to the estimate; watch carrying across multiple columns.
keyRepresentations: Area/grid model with four sub-rectangles (the home of the partial products)
Expanded partial-products layout bridging grid to compact form
Compact long-multiplication layout with the placeholder zero
Estimation (rounding both factors) to bound the product
commonMisconceptions: Omitting the placeholder zero on the second partial product (treating ×20 as ×2).
Multiplying only by the ones digit of the two-digit multiplier and forgetting the tens.
Carrying errors across several columns, or adding carries into the wrong place.
Misaligning partial products when adding them.
Not connecting the algorithm to the area model, so errors can't be self-diagnosed.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning formal long multiplication (up to 4-digit × 1-digit and 2-digit × 2-digit), anchor the written algorithm in the area model so the two partial-product rows and the placeholder zero become meaningful place-value facts rather than memorised rules. The central objective: the child sees that the second partial-product row is '×20 (tens)', not '×2', and that the four sub-rectangles of an area model sum to the same total as the two added partial products. Estimation by rounding both factors bounds the answer and catches magnitude slips.

activities.title: Bridge the area model to the written method (34 × 27)
feedback: If the second partial product comes out as 68 instead of 680: you multiplied by 2 instead of 20. Look at the 34×20 region of your grid — it is twenty rows worth 680, not 68. Write the zero first to reserve the ones place, saying 'we are multiplying by twenty'.

If you only computed 34 × 7 and stopped: every part of 27 (both the 20 and the 7) must multiply every part of 34. Check your grid has all four regions — a missing region means a missing partial product.
If you wrote 34×2 + 34×7: you split 27 into digits 2 and 7 without place value. The tens digit is worth 20, so draw the ×20 regions explicitly.
If 238 + 680 doesn't total 918, recheck your column alignment and any carries — your estimate of ~900 tells you the answer should be near there.
activities.rationale: Coupling a partitioned area model to the columnar layout makes the place value of each partial product (and the meaning of the placeholder zero) visible, so a lost place value can be self-diagnosed. A live split-screen where partitioning tiles fill the long-multiplication frame, with tiles sliding together to show 600+210+80+28 = 918 matching the two added partials, is one concrete way to make this mechanism visible; a running estimate panel can flag magnitude slips.
sourceClaims: The area model should scaffold long multiplication, making partial products and the placeholder zero (× tens) meaningful.
learnerActions: Estimate first by rounding both factors: 34 × 27 ≈ 30 × 30 = 900, and keep this estimate in view as you work.
Draw an area model for 34 × 27 and partition it into four labelled sub-rectangles: 30×20, 30×7, 4×20, 4×7.
Alongside, set up the long-multiplication layout and compute the first partial product 34 × 7 = 238 (which is the 30×7 and 4×7 tiles: 210 + 28).
Compute the second partial product 34 × 20 = 680, writing a 0 in the ones place FIRST because this whole row is ×20, i.e. tens (this is the 30×20 and 4×20 tiles: 600 + 80).
Add the two partial products: 238 + 680 = 918, and confirm it matches the sum of all four area tiles (600 + 210 + 80 + 28 = 918).
Check the result against your estimate of 900 — are they close?
activities.intendedInsight: The second partial-product row is shifted and carries a placeholder zero because it is ×20 (tens), not ×2; the four area sub-rectangles are exactly the same quantities as the two written partial products broken apart, so the algorithm and the area model are two views of the same calculation.

activities.title: Secure 4-digit × 1-digit short multiplication (2,347 × 6)
feedback: If a carry is added into the wrong column, recheck each step and compare with your estimate. Note that rounding 2,347 DOWN (to 2,000 or 2,300) gives an underestimate, so the true answer should sit a little above those figures — 14,082 (just over 13,800) is reasonable.
If any column is skipped, remember every digit of 2,347 must be multiplied by 6.
activities.rationale: This activity enacts the Y5 curriculum requirement to multiply a number up to four digits by a one-digit number using a formal written method; it also secures the carrying and place-value fluency that two-digit long multiplication builds on, forming a sensible progression before the two-row layout.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils multiply numbers up to 4 digits by a one- or two-digit number using a formal written method, including long multiplication for two-digit numbers.
learnerActions: Estimate first: 2,347 × 6 ≈ 2,000 × 6 = 12,000 (or 2,300 × 6 = 13,800 for a tighter bound).
Compute 2,347 × 6 in formal written layout, carrying across each column: 7×6=42 (write 2 carry 4), 4×6=24 plus 4 = 28 (write 8 carry 2), 3×6=18 plus 2 = 20 (write 0 carry 2), 2×6=12 plus 2 = 14.
Read off the answer 14,082 and check it against your estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying a multi-digit number by a single digit requires multiplying every digit and correctly handling carries across several columns; estimation bounds the magnitude.

activities.title: Map each written partial product to its area region (45 × 23)
feedback: If a region is missing or a partial product doesn't account for the full value of a digit, redraw the grid so every part of 23 (20 and 3) multiplies every part of 45 (40 and 5).
If the ×20 partial product lacks its placeholder zero, link it to the 800 + 100 = 900 tens regions: the row lives in the tens.
If the two totals (region sum and partial-product sum) disagree, recheck each region's arithmetic against the matching partial.
activities.rationale: Explicitly connecting the four area regions to the two partial products is the discriminating task that separates understanding from rote execution, and it directly targets the common error of omitting partial products.
sourceClaims: The area model should scaffold long multiplication, making partial products and the placeholder zero (× tens) meaningful.
learnerActions: Draw an area model for 45 × 23 with four regions: 40×20, 40×3, 5×20, 5×3.
Add all four regions to get the product: 800 + 120 + 100 + 15 = 1,035.
Now compute 45 × 23 by long multiplication and point to which area regions make up each partial product: 45×3 = 135 (= 120 + 15) and 45×20 = 900 (= 800 + 100).
Confirm the two partial products 135 + 900 = 1,035 equal the sum of the four area regions.
activities.intendedInsight: Each written partial product is a sum of two area sub-rectangles, so a child who can map regions to partials understands WHY there are two rows rather than following steps by rote.

activities.title: Consolidation: spot-the-error and estimate checks
feedback: For the spot-the-error item: the second row is ×20, so it must occupy the tens — the 0 marks the empty ones place, meaning '×20 not ×2'.
For the estimate item: rounding 48 to 50 and 52 to 50 gives 2,500, close to the true product 2,496, so it is a good magnitude check.
activities.rationale: Procedural consolidation with error-spotting and estimation tests and reinforces the procedure efficiently. This recognition/fill-in format checks the procedure rather than independently eliciting construction of the area link, so it is best used after the construction activities, not in place of them.
learnerActions: Examine a worked 34 × 27 in which the placeholder zero is missing from the second partial product; identify the error and explain why the zero belongs there.
Fill in a missing second partial product in a given long-multiplication layout.
Choose or state the best estimate for 48 × 52 by rounding both factors (≈ 50 × 50 = 2,500).
activities.intendedInsight: The missing placeholder zero and estimation are the quickest self-checks for magnitude; recognising the error reinforces the place-value reasoning behind the shifted row.

constraints: Recognition and fill-in/spot-the-error tasks consolidate the procedure but do not elicit the child independently constructing an area model and mapping it to the written method; use them after, not instead of, the bridging construction work.

Annotated static worked examples (area model above, written method below, tap to reveal each partial product's region) are useful reference scaffolds, but a fixed example cannot give feedback on a child's own fresh calculation or their own placeholder-zero error — pair them with tasks the child computes.

Spoken dialogue alone lacks a shared visible written layout, so it cannot display aligned columns or reliably catch column-placement errors in this spatial, multi-step procedure; keep a written/drawn layout at the centre rather than relying on talk alone (this is a layout-affordance limit, not a claim that dialogue can never support the procedure).

The area model is a conceptual scaffold for place value; the goal is eventual fluent compact long multiplication with the area link available for self-diagnosis, not permanent dependence on drawing grids.
Treat carrying/alignment slips as performance errors (re-estimate and recheck the flagged column) rather than reteaching the whole method.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit (all confirmed correct): 34×7=238, 34×20=680, 238+680=918; area tiles 600+210+80+28=918; 2,347×6=14,082; 45×23 regions 800+120+100+15=1,035 and partials 135+900=1,035; 48×52=2,496 with estimate 50×50=2,500. The source's correctAnswer states the 45×23 region sum as 1,035 — matches.

The source's 3D-interactive dismissal ('3D adds cost without insight') was removed as a catalog-fit judgement rather than an established pedagogical law; the planar area model is simply the natural representation for this place-value procedure, stated without claiming 3D could teach nothing.
CCSS 5.NBT.5/4.NBT.5 and the NCETM/IES area-model guidance are marked verified:false in the row; they are retained as cited but their evidence strength is not independently confirmed here.

The original prerequisite reteach IDs (mt_18fK9sQdIz, mt_AQo4u7O4sM) are catalog-internal and have been dropped from learner-facing guidance; the underlying reteach moves are preserved in the feedback.

For 2,347 × 6 both rounding choices (2,000 and 2,300) are underestimates, so the true answer exceeds them; feedback states this explicitly so the estimate is not mistaken for a bracket that must contain the answer.

The Y5 curriculum claim attached to the 2,347×6 activity directly supports the content requirement the activity enacts; the progression/sequencing point stated in that rationale is an editorial judgement the claim does not itself assert.

probeDeeper: Why did you write a zero before the second row of the multiplication?
In your grid, which region equals 40 × 20, and how much is it?
Estimate 34 × 27 roughly — is 918 reasonable?
How does adding the four grid regions match adding your two partial products?
assess.correctAnswer: 34 × 27 = 918 (34×7 = 238, 34×20 = 680, sum 918). 2,347 × 6 = 14,082. Area model for 45×23 has four regions 40×20=800, 40×3=120, 5×20=100, 5×3=15, sum 1035. The teacher watches for the placeholder zero when multiplying by the tens digit, correct partial products, and the child mapping each grid region to a partial product.

errorPatterns.pattern: omits the placeholder zero — multiplies by the tens digit as if it were ones (34×2 recorded as 68, not 680)
errorPatterns.nextMove: connect to the area model: the 34×20 region is twenty rows, worth 680, not 68; write the zero first to reserve the ones place, saying 'we are multiplying by twenty'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: second partial product is ten times too small; final total far too low

errorPatterns.pattern: treats 34×27 as 34×2 + 34×7 (adds tens and ones digits without place value), or only multiplies by one digit
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw all four regions of the grid so every part of 27 (20 and 7) multiplies every part of 34; nothing may be left out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: partial products do not account for the full value of each digit; area model has missing regions

errorPatterns.pattern: carrying error within a partial product or misaligned column addition
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach the method; have the child estimate first and recheck the flagged column.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one partial product or the final addition wrong; often caught by estimate (34×27 ≈ 30×30 = 900)

responseLevels.gap: omits the placeholder zero, multiplies by only one digit, or cannot link the method to the area model.
responseLevels.full: executes long multiplication with correct placeholders and partial products, maps each partial to an area region, and checks against an estimate.
responseLevels.partial: completes 4-digit × 1-digit correctly but slips on the 2-digit × 2-digit placeholder, or draws the grid without connecting regions to partial products.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 34 × 27 by long multiplication while you watch, and separately to compute 2,347 × 6. Then ask them to draw an area (grid) model for 45 × 23 and point to where each partial product sits. Watch the placeholder zero on the tens row and whether the partial products match the area regions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Long multiplication's signature failure is the missing placeholder zero on the second partial product (multiplying by 2 tens but recording as 2 ones). Connecting the written partials to the four area regions distinguishes a child who understands WHY there are partial products from one following steps by rote.
