pedagogy.summary: This Y6 topic consolidates three configurations of angle facts at their sharpest: angles at a point (sum 360°), angles on a straight line (sum 180°), and — the new element — vertically opposite angles (EQUAL). The pedagogical crux is getting children to hold TWO relationships apart on the same intersecting-lines diagram: the OPPOSITE pair is equal, while each ADJACENT pair (on a straight line) is supplementary (sums to 180°). Confusing which pair does which is the characteristic error. The NCETM's recommended route is a dynamic one — two hinged sticks crossing at a point — so children SEE that as one angle grows its vertically opposite partner grows with it and stays equal, while the neighbour shrinks to keep the straight line at 180°. The signature task is 'given one angle, what else do you know?', reasoning out and JUSTIFYING every other angle from the two rules.
bestPractices: Surface both relationships side by side on one crossing-lines diagram: 'opposite = equal' AND 'adjacent (on a straight line) = supplementary', so children see they are different claims, not the same one (NCETM).

Use a hinged two-sticks / dynamic-geometry model: as one angle opens, its vertically opposite partner opens equally and the adjacent angle closes — the equality is seen to be invariant, not memorised.
Teach with 'given one angle, find and justify the others': mark one angle (e.g. 43°) at an intersection and have the child deduce and NAME the rule for each remaining angle.
Insist on reasoned language — 'this angle is 130° BECAUSE vertically opposite angles are equal' / '…because angles on a straight line sum to 180°' — not shape mnemonics.
Vary orientation: present tilted intersections (neither line horizontal) so 'vertically opposite' is understood as sharing the vertex, not as up-and-down.
Derive vertically-opposite-equal from the straight-line rule (both angles are 180° minus the shared neighbour) rather than adding it as a separate fact to memorise.
keyRepresentations: Two straight lines crossing at a point, forming two pairs of equal opposite angles and two straight lines of supplementary angles
Hinged two-sticks / dynamic model where opposite angles stay equal as the crossing angle changes
'Given one angle, find the rest' diagram (e.g. 43° marked, three unknowns)
Angles-at-a-point (360°) and angles-on-a-line (180°) diagrams as the two 'wholes'
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the two relationships — applies the straight-line 180° rule to the opposite pair, giving the vertically opposite angle as 180° minus the known angle instead of equal to it.
Over-generalises 'opposite angles are equal' to conclude all four angles at the intersection are equal, ignoring the supplementary straight-line pairs.
Attaches 'vertically opposite' to up–down orientation, so fails to recognise the opposite pair when the lines are tilted, or mislabels which angles are opposite.
Carries over the wrong whole — uses 180° for angles at a point (or 360° on a straight line).

learn.summary: Year 6 geometry consolidating three angle configurations: angles at a point (sum 360°), angles on a straight line (sum 180°), and the new element — vertically opposite angles (equal). The pedagogical crux is holding TWO relationships apart on one intersecting-lines diagram: the opposite pair is EQUAL, while each adjacent pair (on a straight line) is SUPPLEMENTARY (sums to 180°). The signature task is 'given one angle, find and justify every other angle', naming the rule used each time. Deriving 'opposite = equal' from the straight-line rule (both angles equal 180° minus the shared neighbour) is preferred to memorising it as a separate fact. Orientation should be varied — tilted intersections — so 'vertically opposite' is understood as two angles opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not as up-and-down.

activities.title: Crossing-lines reasoner: watch the opposite pair stay equal
feedback: If a learner expected the angle opposite 130° to be '180 − 130 = 50°', highlight that this value belongs to the ADJACENT angle (on the straight line); the OPPOSITE angle tracks at 130°. Show both on the diagram at once.
If a learner thinks all four angles are equal, draw attention to one straight line and its two angles summing to 180°: a = a and b = b, but a ≠ b unless the lines are perpendicular.

If a learner loses the opposite pair once the figure is tilted, clarify that 'vertically opposite' means opposite each other across the shared vertex (vertex, not up-and-down), with no arm in common, and rotate the same intersection through several orientations while tracking the pair.
activities.rationale: NCETM recommends a hinged two-sticks / dynamic model so children SEE that as one angle increases its vertically opposite partner increases equally while the neighbour closes to hold the straight line at 180°; manipulating the crossing angle makes the invariance observable rather than asserted. OPTIONAL interactive features that make this concrete: draggable crossing lines, all four angles labelled with live-updating values, the opposite pair highlighted as it stays equal, and each straight line showing its two angles summing to 180°.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
learnerActions: Work with two straight lines crossing at a point, with all four angles labelled.

Rotate one line and observe how all four angle values change together: each pair of vertically opposite angles grows and shrinks TOGETHER and stays equal, while each adjacent angle changes so that the two angles on each straight line always sum to 180°.
Set the crossing angle to several values and each time read off the opposite pair, confirming it matches the given angle exactly (not 180° minus it).

Deliberately predict what the angle opposite a 130° angle will be; set the crossing angle to 130° and check the opposite angle reads exactly 130° rather than 50°, then rotate and check the opposite angle keeps matching the changing angle.

Repeat with the whole figure tilted so neither line is horizontal or vertical, confirming the opposite pair is still identified as the two angles opposite each other across the vertex, sharing no arm.
activities.intendedInsight: As an intersection turns, vertically opposite angles stay equal while each adjacent pair stays supplementary — these are two different claims about the same diagram, and 'vertically opposite' means opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not pointing up-and-down.

activities.title: Given one angle, find and justify the rest
feedback: If a learner gives the angle opposite 130° as 50° or justifies it with 'angles on a straight line', the rules have been swapped: the opposite pair is equal; only the adjacent pair is supplementary.
If a learner subtracts from 180° at a point, re-anchor the whole: a full turn around a point is 360°. Check: 360 − (150 + 90) = 120°, not 180 − (150 + 90).
If values are given without justification, ask 'which rule tells you that?' before accepting the answer — a correct number reasoned from the rule is the goal, not a lucky guess.
activities.rationale: NCETM's signature task 'given one angle, find and justify the others' forces deployment of BOTH relationships and makes any confusion immediately visible. Requiring the named rule for each angle distinguishes reasoning from guessing. Common Core notes angle measure is additive: unknown angles at a point and on a straight line are found by adding/subtracting known angles. Tilting the figure prevents up-and-down intuition standing in for reasoning.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
Angle measure is additive; unknown angles at a point (360°) and on a straight line (180°) are found by adding/subtracting the known angles (4.MD.7).
learnerActions: On a tilted intersection with one angle marked (e.g. 43°), work out each of the other three angles.

For EACH angle, state both the value AND the rule that justifies it — e.g. 'this angle is 43° BECAUSE vertically opposite angles are equal' or 'this angle is 137° BECAUSE angles on a straight line sum to 180°'.
Repeat with a different given angle (e.g. 130°, giving an opposite angle of 130° and adjacent angles of 50° each).
Switch to an angles-at-a-point diagram: given two angles (e.g. 150° and 90°) find the unknown as 360 − (150 + 90) = 120°, naming the 360° whole.
Write down every equation you can for an intersection diagram, surfacing both the equal pairs and the two 180° straight lines.
activities.intendedInsight: Every unknown angle at an intersection or point can be deduced and JUSTIFIED from a named rule, and the correct 'whole' must be chosen — 360° at a point, 180° on a straight line.

activities.title: Sort angle pairs: equal or supplementary
feedback: A choice of '180 − known' for a vertically opposite angle reveals the straight-line rule wrongly applied to the opposite pair; mark it and show the opposite pair is equal.
If the derivation is unclear, walk through it: angle A and its opposite each sit with the same neighbour B on a straight line, so A = 180 − B and the opposite = 180 − B, hence they are equal.
Errors on tilted items signal orientation-dependence; return to rotating a single intersection and tracking the pair.
activities.rationale: Classification and fill-in practice with a deliberate '180 − known' distractor targets the characteristic error directly and checks the two relationships are held apart. This supports and assesses the reasoning but, on its own, presents fixed diagrams the learner cannot manipulate, so pair it with a dynamic model to let the equality be observed changing. Deriving the equality rather than memorising it is an NCETM best practice.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
learnerActions: Look at a crossing-lines diagram with the four angles labelled and sort each pair of angles into 'vertically opposite — equal' or 'adjacent (straight line) — supplementary'.
Answer which rule applies to a specifically named pair, choosing between 'equal' and 'sums to 180°'.
Fill in the value of each unknown angle, resisting the tempting '180 − known' value when the angle is actually the opposite (equal) one.
Try a tilted-intersection item where orientation cannot be used to guess, and a point-diagram item that uses the 360° whole.
Explain WHY vertically opposite angles are equal: both equal 180° minus their shared straight-line neighbour, so they equal each other.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying each pair by its relationship — and deriving 'opposite = equal' from the straight-line rule — cements that the two claims are distinct and reasoned, not interchangeable.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal angle relationships (vocabulary scaffold)
feedback: Confirm correct naming; where a learner swaps the rules, re-show the straight-line pair and the opposite pair side by side.
Encourage stating the rule before revealing, so the reveal confirms reasoning rather than supplying it.
activities.rationale: A static reveal can introduce the vocabulary and the paired structure and can be used during teaching, but it shows fixed values and cannot let the learner watch the opposite pair stay equal as the angle changes, so the invariance is told rather than observed. Use it to seed language, then move to a manipulable model and to reasoning tasks.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
learnerActions: On a static crossing-lines diagram, tap an angle to reveal its vertically opposite partner (equal) and its two straight-line (adjacent) partners (each supplementary to it).
Use a 'given 130°, what are the other three?' reveal: predict each value and its rule, then lift the flap to check (opposite 130°, adjacent 50° each).
Name each revealed pair aloud with its rule before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeds the vocabulary — 'vertically opposite' vs 'adjacent/straight-line' — and the paired structure of an intersection.

constraints: Learners must JUSTIFY each angle with its named rule, not just state values; a correct number without reasoning does not demonstrate understanding.
Both relationships must appear on the SAME intersecting-lines diagram so children see they are different claims: opposite = equal, adjacent = supplementary.
Vary orientation with tilted intersections so 'vertically opposite' is understood as two angles opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not up-and-down.
Keep the two 'wholes' distinct: 360° at a point, 180° on a straight line.
Prefer deriving 'vertically opposite angles are equal' from the straight-line rule over memorising it as a separate fact.
The static tap-to-reveal image is a vocabulary scaffold only: it shows fixed values and cannot display the equality holding as the angle changes.

Fill-in and sorting practice can score reasoning and target the characteristic error, but on their own present non-manipulable diagrams; pair them with a dynamic model so the invariance can be observed.

Vertically opposite angles are always equal; an adjacent angle equals the given one only in the special perpendicular (90°) case, where all four angles become 90° — do not let learners generalise all four angles to be equal otherwise.
OPTIONAL interactive features (draggable lines, live angle readouts, highlighting, tilt) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory requirements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed a 3D environment 'adds no conceptual value' and that a character/dialogue 'cannot' teach the distinction. These are categorical catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped rather than propagated; a conversation could still support reasoning talk, and a 2D dynamic model is proposed on its stated affordance (manipulable, live-updating) without claiming other media are incapable.

The legacy recommendation's strong framing ('it must be manipulated to be felt', opposite pair 'locked equal') was softened: manipulation makes the invariance observable but is one effective route, not the only possible one.

Self-audit arithmetic checks all passed: angle opposite 130° = 130°; adjacent = 180 − 130 = 50°; at a point 360 − (150 + 90) = 120°; opposite 43° = 43°, adjacent = 137°. The error value '50°' for the opposite angle is retained only as a labelled misconception/distractor, never as a correct answer.

Confirmed the special-case caveat: the two adjacent angles equal the given one only when the lines are perpendicular (all four become 90°); the diagnostic counterexample about 90° crossings was preserved in substance within constraints and feedback.

The DfE curriculum claim was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims because it is a general topic/necessity requirement and does not support that activity's specific dynamic-model teaching principle; it remains part of the source record but is not cited as supporting a teaching principle in any activity.

Activity 4's NCETM sourceClaim is retained because the activity's learning target is distinguishing the equal pair from the supplementary pair, which the claim directly supports; the static-medium limitation is stated as an affordance observation, not as a source-backed efficacy claim.

probeDeeper: 'You said this angle is 130° — which rule tells you that, and which rule tells you the one next to it?' — checks the two relationships are held apart, not blurred.

Counterexample: 'If I told you these lines crossed at exactly 90°, would the opposite angle still equal the given one? Would the neighbours?' — probes that equal-opposite always holds while supplementary-opposite is only the perpendicular special case.
'I've turned the whole diagram on its side. Which angles are vertically opposite now?' — tests that opposite-ness survives rotation (not orientation-bound).
'Write down every equation you can for this diagram' — surfaces whether the child sees both the equal pairs and the 180° straight lines (NCETM 'what else do you know?').
assess.correctAnswer: At the intersection: the angle vertically opposite the 130° is 130° (vertically opposite angles are equal); the two adjacent angles are each 50° (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, 180−130). At the point: unknown = 360 − (150+90) = 120°. Justifies each with the correct named rule and is not misled by the tilt.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the two relationships — applies the straight-line rule to the opposite pair, giving the vertically opposite angle as 180 − 130 = 50° instead of 130°.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put both relationships on the same diagram with the hinged model: show the opposite pair staying EQUAL as it turns while each straight line holds at 180°; name which pair is which explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States the angle opposite 130° as 50°, or justifies it with 'angles on a straight line' when the two angles are actually the opposite pair; may get the genuinely adjacent angle right, showing the rules are swapped.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises 'opposite angles are equal' — declares all four angles at the intersection equal (all 130°), ignoring the supplementary straight-line pairs.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw attention to each straight line and its two angles summing to 180°; show that a=a and b=b but a≠b unless the lines are perpendicular.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels every angle 130°; no angle is given as 50°; cannot say why the neighbours differ.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ties 'vertically opposite' to up–down orientation — on the tilted diagram fails to identify the opposite pair, or insists the term needs a vertical line.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify 'vertical' means sharing the vertex, not up–down; rotate the same intersection through several orientations so the opposite pair is tracked as the figure turns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot pick out the vertically opposite pair once the figure is tilted, or points to an adjacent pair as 'opposite'; comments about the lines not being upright.

errorPatterns.pattern: Carries over the wrong whole at a point — subtracts the known angles from 180° instead of 360°.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor the whole to the configuration — a full point is a whole turn 360° — before computing; no reteaching of vertically-opposite needed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the point diagram gives 180 − (150+90) or an answer 180° short of 120°; the intersection work may be correct.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find the other angles reliably: guesses, uses no named rule, or cannot identify the opposite pair; wrong whole at a point.
responseLevels.full: Finds all angles at an intersection using BOTH relationships correctly, justifies each with the named rule, is unfazed by tilt, keeps the point (360°) and line (180°) wholes distinct, and can explain WHY vertically opposite angles are equal (via the shared straight-line neighbour).
responseLevels.partial: Finds the vertically opposite angle equal in a simple upright cross and can state 'they add to 180°' for a straight line, but blurs the two on a tilted diagram (opposite comes out as 180−given, or all four equal), or gives values without justifying them — lists angles without relating the equal and supplementary structures.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Draw two straight lines crossing at a point, TILTED so neither line is horizontal or vertical, and mark just one of the four angles as 130°. Say: 'Find the other three angles, and tell me how you know each one.' Then show a second diagram — angles round a point marked 150°, 90° and an unknown — and ask for the unknown. Watch which rule they use for each angle and whether tilt throws them; do not prompt.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: One given angle forces the child to deploy BOTH relationships — equal for the opposite, supplementary for the adjacent — so confusing them is immediately visible (the opposite comes out as 50°, or all four as 130°). The deliberate tilt separates a child who understands 'vertically opposite = shares the vertex' from one who relies on up–down orientation. The second diagram checks the point (360°) rule is not swapped with 180°. Requiring the justification distinguishes a correct answer reasoned from the rule from a lucky guess.

sources.claim: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
sources.source: NCETM, Mastery Professional Development — 6.1 Geometrical Properties (Key Stage 3), Crown Copyright 2019

sources.claim: Upper Key Stage 2 (Year 6) pupils should recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles.
sources.source: UK Department for Education, Mathematics programmes of study: Key Stages 1 and 2 (Year 6 geometry — properties of shapes)

sources.claim: Angle measure is additive; unknown angles at a point (360°) and on a straight line (180°) are found by adding/subtracting the known angles (4.MD.7).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 4 Measurement & Data

pedagogy.summary: Positional language names WHERE things are relative to a landmark — on, under, behind, in front of, next to, above, below — plus the frame-dependent left and right. Children perceive these relations early and describe them with vague words ('over there', with a point); the teaching job is to attach precise words to the concepts and to model them in everyday talk. Positions are relative and abstract (whether something is 'behind' depends on the landmark and the viewer's side), so the deepest difficulties are holding two relations at once (dual relations) and left/right, which depend on the direction the child faces and are not mastered until early elementary school.
bestPractices: Model correct language in reply to vague answers: when a child says 'over there' and points, recast it — 'yes, on the shelf next to the coat closet'.
Name the landmark explicitly as object + landmark + relation ('the ball is behind the sofa') so position is heard as a relation, not a property of the object.
Embed the words in daily routines and directional games — table-setting ('cups next to the plates, juice in the middle'), hopscotch, board games with forward/back.
Build left and right on the body first (a sticker on the right hand, shaking hands) before applying them to objects; be patient and don't treat early errors as failure.
Have the child both FOLLOW and GIVE instructions ('put the cube behind the box') so the vocabulary becomes a productive tool, not just receptive.
keyRepresentations: Object–landmark–relation triples acted out with real toys and objects
The child's own body, with a right-hand sticker, for left and right
Everyday scenes — a set table, a shelf, a bedroom — and simple picture scenes to describe
Barrier games: the child describes a hidden layout precisely enough for a partner to reproduce it
commonMisconceptions: Uses vague deictic language ('over there', 'this one') with a gesture instead of a positional word
Judges left/right from the child's own current facing and cannot adjust it for an object or person facing the other way
Cannot hold two relations at once — a thing that is above one object and below another is described with only one relation (egocentrism / dual relations)
Treats a position as belonging to the object ('the front') rather than as a relation to a named landmark and a viewpoint

learn.summary: Positional language names WHERE things are relative to a landmark (on, under, behind, in front of, next to, above, below, left, right). Left/right, and behind/in front of when the landmark has no front of its own (e.g. a plain box), depend on viewpoint. Young children (4-6) perceive these relations early but describe them vaguely ('over there', with a point); the teaching job is to attach precise words to the concepts and model them in everyday talk as object + landmark + relation ('the ball is behind the sofa'). The deepest difficulties are holding two relations at once (dual relations) and left/right. Left/right for objects and for people facing you depends on viewpoint and is typically not mastered until early elementary school. Because this is a language-in-context topic, the core goal is productive AND receptive use: the child should both FOLLOW and GIVE positional instructions, not merely recognise words.

activities.title: Place the object: follow spoken positional instructions
feedback: When the relation is correct, confirm concretely: 'yes — the teddy is behind the box.'

When the object is placed in the wrong relation (e.g. beside instead of behind), show where the correct relation is from the child's own viewpoint (for a plain box, 'behind' is the side away from the child) — for example gently outline or point to the 'behind' location, then let the child try again.
Optional interactive version: a correct drop settles with a happy chime; a wrong drop highlights/outlines the target relation so 'behind' is shown, not just told.
activities.rationale: Children locate things early but must learn both the positional words and the concepts they refer to; pairing each word with a named landmark (object–landmark–relation) and acting it out is intended to make position heard as a relation rather than a property of the object.
sourceClaims: Young children locate things but use vague, informal language and must learn both the positional words and the concepts they refer to; adults should model correct language and use landmarks (object–landmark–relation). Left and right are notoriously difficult and frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces), typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early failure should not be over-corrected. Holding dual relations at once (a thing above one object and below another) is hard because young children are egocentric. Everyday routines and directional games (table-setting, hopscotch, board games) build the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken instruction naming an object, a landmark, and a relation, e.g. 'put the teddy behind the box'.
Move the named object into the correct relation to the landmark (for example drag it in a bedroom scene, or place a real toy with a real box and cup).
Try a short series that varies the relation: 'put the cup next to the teddy', 'put the pencil under the book'.
activities.intendedInsight: A positional word is an instruction that tells you exactly where to put something relative to a named landmark.

activities.title: Your turn to tell me: give the instruction (barrier / role-flip)
feedback: When the child names a relation and landmark the partner can act on, celebrate that the word worked: 'you said behind the box, so I put it right there.'
If the child falls back on 'there' with a gesture, recast into a usable instruction ('do you mean next to the cup?') and invite them to try the word themselves.

Optional interactive version: the child taps a relation word ('behind' / 'in front of' / 'next to'), a cartoon friend places its object to match, and the two scenes snap together when the word was right.
activities.rationale: Because the objective is both words and concepts, asking the child to produce (not just recognise) an instruction is intended to turn the vocabulary into a usable tool and to show whether the child has both the words and the concepts: a precise relation plus landmark is hard to produce by chance, so giving instructions is proposed as a way to distinguish genuine use from receptive familiarity. This production-discrimination logic is an unvalidated design proposal, not a source-established finding.
sourceClaims: Young children locate things but use vague, informal language and must learn both the positional words and the concepts they refer to; adults should model correct language and use landmarks (object–landmark–relation). Left and right are notoriously difficult and frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces), typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early failure should not be over-corrected. Holding dual relations at once (a thing above one object and below another) is hard because young children are egocentric. Everyday routines and directional games (table-setting, hopscotch, board games) build the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Place or choose where a toy goes, then TELL a partner (adult, another child, or a cartoon friend) where it is using a precise positional word and a named landmark, e.g. 'behind the box'.
Have the partner act only on what the child says, so the child sees whether the word carried the meaning.
Play a barrier game: the child describes a hidden layout precisely enough for the partner to reproduce it without seeing it.
activities.intendedInsight: A position word is a tool that carries meaning to someone else — when I say the right relation and landmark, my partner can act correctly without seeing or pointing.

activities.title: In-role conversation: answering 'where is it?'
feedback: Recast vague deictic answers into the precise form instead of marking them wrong: 'yes — next to the cup.'
Affirm when the child supplies a relation and landmark unprompted.
activities.rationale: As a language-use topic, an in-role dialogue is intended to elicit productive spoken use and to model precise words in context (the source supports adults modelling correct language); its narrow observable limit is that it does not provide the concrete manipulate-and-see feedback of a placing game, so it complements rather than replaces that activity. Its comparative efficacy is untested.
sourceClaims: Young children locate things but use vague, informal language and must learn both the positional words and the concepts they refer to; adults should model correct language and use landmarks (object–landmark–relation). Left and right are notoriously difficult and frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces), typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early failure should not be over-corrected. Holding dual relations at once (a thing above one object and below another) is hard because young children are egocentric. Everyday routines and directional games (table-setting, hopscotch, board games) build the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Respond in role when a character asks 'where's the teddy?', answering with a positional word and landmark rather than a point.
Let the character act on the answer so the child hears whether it was clear.
Have the character gently model precise words by recasting vague answers ('over there' → 'yes, on the shelf next to the coat closet').
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday talk is where positional words become natural: naming the relation and landmark lets someone find or place a thing without seeing where you point.

activities.title: Build left and right on the body first
feedback: Reinforce correct own-body left/right with the sticker anchor.
When the child reverses left/right for a facing partner or a turned object, do not drill it as failure — acknowledge it is tricky, keep exposure, and expect later maturation.
activities.rationale: Left and right are frame-dependent and notoriously difficult, typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early errors should not be over-corrected (as the source notes). Building them on the body first with a right-hand sticker is a recommended scaffold for anchoring the terms before applying them to objects; this specific method comes from the row's best-practice synthesis rather than being prescribed by the source.
sourceClaims: Young children locate things but use vague, informal language and must learn both the positional words and the concepts they refer to; adults should model correct language and use landmarks (object–landmark–relation). Left and right are notoriously difficult and frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces), typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early failure should not be over-corrected. Holding dual relations at once (a thing above one object and below another) is hard because young children are egocentric. Everyday routines and directional games (table-setting, hopscotch, board games) build the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Put a sticker on the right hand and use it as an anchor for 'left' and 'right'.
Play own-body directional games — shaking hands with the right hand, raising the left foot.
Later, try applying left/right to objects, with the adult expecting errors and not over-correcting.
activities.intendedInsight: Left and right start from my own body; applying them to objects and to people facing me is harder and comes later.

activities.title: Embed positional words in daily routines and games
feedback: Keep supplying positional language in routines and recast vague answers; expect precise words to firm up gradually rather than immediately.
Notice and name when the child uses a relation + landmark during a real routine.

When a target sits between two landmarks, accept the one relation the child gives and add the second in a recast ('yes, on top of the red block — and it's also under the shelf') rather than forcing both at once.
activities.rationale: Everyday routines and directional games build the vocabulary in meaningful context and give repeated authentic practice across varied scenes, as the source notes.
sourceClaims: Young children locate things but use vague, informal language and must learn both the positional words and the concepts they refer to; adults should model correct language and use landmarks (object–landmark–relation). Left and right are notoriously difficult and frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces), typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early failure should not be over-corrected. Holding dual relations at once (a thing above one object and below another) is hard because young children are egocentric. Everyday routines and directional games (table-setting, hopscotch, board games) build the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Set the table following and giving position talk: 'cups next to the plates, juice in the middle'.
Play directional games — hopscotch (forward/back) and board games with forward/back moves.
Describe everyday scenes — a set table, a shelf, a bedroom — naming object, landmark, and relation.
activities.intendedInsight: Positional words belong in everyday talk, not just lessons; using them in routines firms up the vocabulary over time.

constraints: The core objective is productive AND receptive USE: the child must both follow and give instructions. Recognition-only tasks (matching or categorising position words to pictures) can check recognition but do not by themselves elicit independent production, so they cannot alone demonstrate mastery of this language-in-context topic — use them, if at all, only as a recognition check.

Tapping a static picture scene to reveal position words is useful for exposure, but on its own it does not let the child produce instructions or receive manipulate-and-see feedback; treat it as a scaffold, not the full objective. This is a scope limit, not a claim that static images cannot teach.

Do not mark vague deictic language ('over there', 'this one' with a point) as an error for 4-6 year olds: informal language normally precedes precise words. Recast and keep supplying positional language, expecting it to firm up over time.

Do not drill left/right for facing partners/turned objects as failure, and do not force two relations (above AND below) at once: both are developmentally hard and typically not mastered until early elementary school. Accept one relation and add the second in a recast.

A rotatable 3D scene could make frame-dependence (how behind/in front and left/right flip as you move around) felt, but that perspective-taking is the hard part not expected at 4-6 and exceeds the core naming goal; it is an optional enrichment, not required.

Always pair a position word with a named landmark. Move the object to new places to show that position is a relation to the landmark, not a fixed feature of the object. As light, optional enrichment, moving the viewer around a landmark with no front of its own (e.g. a plain box) can show that 'behind' depends on where you stand. For landmarks with their own front (a sofa, a person), 'behind' usually means the landmark's own back.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The single cited source (DREME Network / Stanford) supports the general principles (model language, use object–landmark–relation, left/right and dual relations are developmentally late, use routines/games). It does not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity format (placing game vs. dialogue vs. 3D scene); legacy catalog claims such as 'a static image cannot teach' or '3D exceeds the goal' have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

The production-discriminates-mastery logic (activity 2) and the efficacy of the dialogue format (activity 3) come from the original row's own assessment analysis and remain untested proposals; efficacy wording has been qualified accordingly.
The body-first-with-sticker scaffold for left/right (activity 4) is from the row's best-practice synthesis; the source supports only the late-mastery and patience principle, not this specific method.
Receptive-only formats are limited only in the narrow, observable sense that recognition does not itself elicit production — this is not a claim about which medium is superior.

probeDeeper: You told me the teddy is 'there' — if I close my eyes, can you tell me a word so I know exactly where it is without pointing?
You said it's on your left. If I come and sit on the other side of the table, is it still on my left?
The pencil is on top of the book. Is anything above the pencil too?
Put the cube 'behind' the box — now if you turn the box around, is the cube still behind it?
assess.correctAnswer: Follows each positional instruction by placing the object in the correct relation, and, when giving the instruction, uses a precise positional word (behind / next to / on top of / under) together with a named landmark, so the teacher can act on it unambiguously — not a vague 'there' with a point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Says 'over there' or 'this one' with a point instead of a position word ('put it... there!')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark this as an error — vague informal language normally precedes precise words; recast it ('yes, next to the cup') and keep supplying positional language in routines, expecting it to firm up over time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When GIVING an instruction, gestures or says 'there' rather than naming a relation

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses left/right fixed to their own body, so it is wrong for an object or a person facing the other way ('it's on the left' — but only from where I'm sitting)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill this as a failure — left/right is frame-dependent and typically not mastered until early elementary school; reinforce own-body left/right (sticker) and keep exposure, expecting later maturation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives or follows left/right correctly for self but reverses it for a facing partner or a turned object

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot say a thing is above one object and below another at the same time ('it's on top' — ignoring what is above it)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT push both relations at once — accept the one they give and add the second in your recast ('yes, on top of the red block — and it's also under the shelf'), letting the coordination develop.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When a target sits between two landmarks, describes only one relation

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a position word as a fixed feature of the object rather than a relation to a landmark ('the front', with no reference to what it is in front of)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Always pair the word with a named landmark and physically move the viewer or the object to show that 'behind' changes with viewpoint.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names a position with no landmark, or insists 'behind' is a fixed side of the object regardless of the viewer

responseLevels.gap: Relies on gesture and 'there / this one'; follows only the most familiar single instruction; cannot produce a usable positional instruction.
responseLevels.full: Uses precise positional words productively and receptively across new scenes, names the landmark, and begins to coordinate two relations and adjust for viewpoint (relational) — with a full grasp of left/right for others expected only later.
responseLevels.partial: Follows and produces common single relations (on / under / behind / next to) with a named landmark in simple familiar setups, but breaks down on left/right for a facing partner, on dual relations, or in an unfamiliar scene — handling one relation at a time without coordinating them (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set up a real or pictured scene with a box, a toy and a cup. Give a short series of doing-instructions and one telling task, and watch/listen for USE: 'Put the teddy behind the box. ... Now put the cup next to the teddy. ... Now YOU tell me where to put the pencil, so I can do exactly what you say.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has both the words and the concepts follows correctly AND produces a usable instruction that names a relation and a landmark. A child with only receptive familiarity may follow simple cases but, when asked to give an instruction, falls back on 'there' with a gesture or names the object with no relation — revealing the word is not yet a tool. Requiring production is the discriminator: a precise relation cannot be produced by luck.

Left and right are notoriously difficult and frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces), typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early failure should not be over-corrected. Holding dual relations at once (a thing above one object and below another) is hard because young children are egocentric. Everyday routines and directional games (table-setting, hopscotch, board games) build the vocabulary.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Fair testing

- **Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils are taught to use the following practical scientific methods, processes and skills — "setting up simple practical enquiries, comparative and fair tests" and "making systematic and careful observations and, where appropriate, taking accurate measurements using standard units". Fair/comparative testing is one of the five named enquiry types (observing over time; pattern seeking; identifying/classifying/grouping; comparative and fair testing; researching secondary sources) — it should be named honestly, not defaulted to.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 3 Planning & Carrying Out Investigations):** the K–2 progression is "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-2, 1-PS4-1, 1-PS4-3, 2-LS2-1, 2-LS4-1, 2-PS1-1, K-PS2-1, K-PS3-1]"; the 3–5 progression sharpens this to "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4]." This topic (ages 7–9) sits on that K–2→ 3–5 boundary: fair tests are introduced and the control-one-variable idea is made explicit.

- **Operational details:** Builds on the KS1 root of performing simple tests (prerequisite mt_Wa44s-f8Ws). The core move is the three-variable analysis of any comparative test: the variable you CHANGE (independent), the variable you MEASURE (dependent), and the variables you KEEP THE SAME (controls) — taught at this age in child language ('change one thing, measure one thing, keep everything else the same'). A test is 'fair' precisely because only one thing changed, so any difference in the result can be attributed to that one change. Feeds forward to controlling variables and independent enquiry planning (dependents mt_ArVBEpMAPk, mt_7VrR1GzhrN).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). A learner who can explain what makes a test fair (one variable changes, the rest stay the same), identify the change/measure/keep-same variables in a given test, and set up a simple comparative or fair test with support has met the bar. Formal independent/dependent variable vocabulary and full independent planning are later tiers (mt_ArVBEpMAPk, mt_Ae56umVlTT).
bestPractices: Teach the three-variable frame in child language on a concrete example first — 'change one thing (the ramp surface), measure one thing (how far the car rolls), keep everything else the same (same car, same height, same push)' — before ever using the words independent/dependent/control.

Make UNFAIRNESS the teaching engine: show a rigged test where two things were changed at once (rougher surface AND steeper ramp) so pupils feel that you genuinely cannot tell which change caused the result — this builds the necessity of controlling variables far better than being told the rule.

Name the enquiry type honestly and don't over-default to fair testing — the AKSIS research shows fair tests dominate over half of primary practicals at the expense of pattern-seeking, observing over time, classifying and research; help pupils recognise WHEN a fair test is the right tool versus another enquiry type.
Use predict-then-test: pupils commit to a prediction before running the comparative test, so the result is something to check against an idea, not just an activity.
Keep the number of variables tiny and the apparatus familiar (ramps, plants, materials, dissolving) so cognitive load is on the fair-test reasoning, not on unfamiliar equipment.
keyRepresentations: The change / measure / keep-the-same three-column planner (the age-appropriate precursor to independent / dependent / control)
A side-by-side comparative set-up (e.g. two ramps, two cups, two plants) where exactly one condition differs
A 'spot the unfair test' contrast pair — one where two things changed, one where only one changed
A simple results table with the changed variable in one column and the measured outcome in the next
A predict → test → compare loop card
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a 'fair test' means being nice/taking turns (the everyday meaning of 'fair') rather than a controlled comparison where only one variable changes.
Changing more than one variable at a time and still believing the result is trustworthy — not seeing that you then can't attribute the effect to any single cause.
Believing every scientific question needs a fair test — over-applying it to questions better answered by observing over time, pattern-seeking or research (the AKSIS over-default).
Confusing the variable you change with the variable you measure (mixing up the input and the outcome).
Forgetting the 'keep the same' variables entirely — controlling only the obvious ones and leaving hidden variables uncontrolled.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach fair/comparative testing through the child-language three-variable frame — change one thing, measure one thing, keep everything else the same — anchored in concrete apparatus (ramps and cars, paper planes, plants, dissolving). Build the necessity of controlling variables by letting an unfair test (two things changed at once) become genuinely uninterpretable, so pupils feel why isolation matters rather than only being told. Complement design practice with recognition tasks (spot-the-unfair-test, sort factors into change/measure/keep-same) and justification dialogue, and honestly name when a fair test is the right enquiry type versus observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying, or research.

activities.title: Design the ramp race: isolate one variable
feedback: If two variables differ between the runs, respond: 'Two things changed — we can't tell which one caused the difference. Which of your two set-ups differs in more than one way?' Have the child rebuild so only one variable changes.

When exactly one variable differs and the rest match, confirm: 'Only the surface changed — that's what makes it fair. Run it again: if the difference in distance keeps showing up, we can put it down to the surface.'
If the child muddles the input and outcome ('I'll measure the surface'), sort the factors into the three-column frame before running.
activities.rationale: Fair testing is a design skill: the child actively chooses what to change, measure, and hold constant and then sees the consequence. Letting an unfair comparison fail to yield an interpretable answer makes the one-variable rule felt. An interactive bench that greys out the result when two variables change (with 'Hmm — two things changed, so we can't tell which caused this') is one concrete way to deliver the insight, not the only medium; the same reasoning can be run with real ramps, a car and a tape measure. NGSS's 3–5 emphasis on controlling variables and considering the number of trials matches the intended insight here.
sourceClaims: DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to be taught to set up simple practical enquiries, comparative and fair tests, as one of the named enquiry types.
NGSS SEP 3 progresses from K-2 'simple investigations based on fair tests' to 3-5 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4]'.
learnerActions: Set up two ramps and a toy car. For each ramp choose values for the conditions: surface (smooth/rough), height, and starting push.
Choose what to measure — e.g. how far the car rolls.
First deliberately make ramp B BOTH rougher AND steeper than ramp A, run both, and try to say which change caused the difference in distance.
Notice you cannot attribute the result to one cause; then rebuild so only ONE condition (e.g. the surface) differs and everything else is identical, and run it again.
Run each set-up more than once and check the result is consistent before concluding.
As you configure, fill in a 'change / measure / keep-the-same' tray recording which variable you changed, which you measured, and which you held constant.
activities.intendedInsight: A test is fair because only one thing changed, so a difference in the result that shows up again when you repeat the runs can be put down to that single change; when two things change at once the result cannot tell you which cause produced it.

activities.title: Paper-plane fair test: build it and throw it
feedback: If the big-wing plane is made from thicker card or paper too, or thrown harder: 'Your two planes differ in more than one way, so a difference in distance can't be pinned on the wings. Rebuild so only the wings change.'
If throws drift (different spots or throwers) without the child noticing: 'Name each thing that must stay the same and why it would otherwise affect how far the plane flies.'
If the plan muddles roles ('I'll change the distance'): sort into change / measure / keep-the-same before starting.
activities.rationale: This activity is exactly the DfE requirement to set up and carry out a comparative/fair test. Genuine set-up — not recitation — reveals real understanding: a child can recite 'change one thing' yet build a confounded test (this production-vs-recitation and predict-then-test framing is pedagogy, not a specific source finding). Predict-then-test makes the result something to check against an idea, and familiar apparatus keeps cognitive load on the fair-test reasoning.
sourceClaims: DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to be taught to set up simple practical enquiries, comparative and fair tests, as one of the named enquiry types.
learnerActions: Question: do paper aeroplanes fly further with bigger wings? Using paper and a tape measure, set up a fair test to answer it.
Before throwing, state what you will change (wing size), what you will measure (how far each plane flies), and what you will keep the same (same paper, same throwing spot, same thrower, same effort).
Make a prediction, then throw both planes a couple of times, holding the one-variable rule as you go.
Record each throw's distance in a simple two-column results table (changed variable | measured distance).
Compare the results against your prediction and say which variable was changed, which measured, and which kept the same.
activities.intendedInsight: Setting up and carrying out a real comparative test requires deliberately holding hidden conditions constant; what you DON'T hold the same (different paper, a harder throw for one plane, a different thrower) is what breaks fairness.

activities.title: Spot the unfair test and sort the variables
feedback: For a wrong 'fair' judgement, point to the second changed variable: 'Two things differ here, so you couldn't tell which caused the result.'
If a question is forced into a fair test when it suits observing over time (e.g. 'how does the plant change over weeks?'), name the better-fitting enquiry type and why.
Confirm correct role sorting by linking each column to the reasoning: the kept-the-same column is what lets us link the result to the one thing we changed (and repeating the test helps check it).
activities.rationale: These recognition and matching tasks assess the evidence statements reliably but mainly check recognition; they consolidate rather than build the design intuition, so they should pair with the hands-on set-up tasks rather than replace them. Honest naming of enquiry type counters the tendency to over-apply fair testing.
sourceClaims: Primary practicals over-default to fair testing (over half) at the expense of other enquiry types such as pattern-seeking and observing over time.
learnerActions: Look at a contrast pair of set-ups: one where two things changed and one where only one changed. Decide which is fair and explain why.
For a given test, sort its factors into three columns: what is changed, what is measured, what is kept the same.
Match investigation questions to the right enquiry type — fair test, observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying/grouping, or researching — and say why a fair test is or isn't the best tool.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising fairness and correctly assigning variable roles reinforces the frame; not every question needs a fair test — some are better answered by observing over time, pattern-seeking, or research.

activities.title: Justify your plan with a science partner
feedback: If the child can't say why a condition matters, ask how that condition would otherwise affect the measured outcome.
If a hidden variable is uncontrolled, prompt: 'Is there anything else different between your two set-ups that we haven't talked about?'
activities.rationale: Socratic dialogue probes justification and surfaces hidden variables, useful after a hands-on test; a conversation alone cannot run the test or show the uninterpretable result, so it supplements the design work rather than replacing it.
learnerActions: Explain your planned test aloud to a partner or in-role scientist.

Answer probing questions: Why keep the ramp height (or throwing spot) the same? What is the one thing you're changing, and what are you measuring? Name two things you're keeping the same and why they matter.
Hunt for hidden uncontrolled variables you may have missed and adjust your plan.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify WHY each condition is held constant — not just list them — shows the reasoning behind fairness and surfaces hidden variables.

constraints: This topic sits on the K–2 → 3–5 boundary: fair tests are introduced and the control-one-variable idea made explicit. Teach the three-variable frame in child language first; formal independent/dependent/control vocabulary and full independent planning are later stages.

Builds on the prerequisite of performing simple tests (KS1). The checkpoint is met when a learner can explain what makes a test fair, identify the change/measure/keep-same variables in a given test, and set up a simple comparative/fair test with support.

Recognition and matching tasks (spot-the-unfair-test, sorting factors) can teach and check classification but do not by themselves elicit the independent design of a controlled comparison; include genuine set-up tasks.

A labelled static set-up with tap-to-reveal can serve as a reference aid naming the parts of a fair test, but a fixed picture cannot recompute, so it cannot deliver the 'two things changed' consequence on its own; use it to support, not as the main teach.
Keep the number of variables small and apparatus familiar so cognitive load stays on fair-test reasoning, not unfamiliar equipment.
Don't over-default to fair testing: help pupils recognise when another enquiry type (observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying, research) fits the question better.
Watch out for the everyday meaning of 'fair' (being nice / taking turns); clarify the scientific meaning of a controlled comparison where only one variable changes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels its interactive-bench rationale with 'no static medium can do' and '3D adds nothing' style comparative-necessity claims; these are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped proposals (an interactive bench is one concrete route to the insight, equivalent to real apparatus). The grey-out panel and settable-condition examples are preserved as optional interaction mechanisms, not mandatory ones.

The production-vs-recitation and predict-then-test justifications in the paper-plane activity are pedagogy; the attached DfE claim supports only the curricular content (setting up comparative/fair tests), not those specific efficacy claims.
The AKSIS over-default claim is marked verified:false in the source; it is retained as supporting the 'name the enquiry type honestly' principle, but its evidence strength is unconfirmed.

The ramp and paper-plane apparatus is used only illustratively: changing more than one condition confounds a distance comparison. No specific distances and no directional force/motion outcomes are asserted, so no force/motion idealisation claim is made; keep it that way if the activity is extended.

Feedback was softened from 'the difference must be down to the surface' to 'can be put down to the surface' and a repeat-trial check was added, so a single run is not treated as conclusive — consistent with the cited NGSS number-of-trials element.

probeDeeper: What is the one thing you're changing? What are you measuring?
Name two things you're keeping the same, and why they matter.
If you used thick card for the big-wing plane and thin paper for the small one, would that be fair? How would you know what caused the difference?
Is this a fair test, or would watching something over time fit this question better?
assess.correctAnswer: The child changes only the wing size, measures how far each plane flies, and keeps everything else the same — same paper, same throwing spot, same thrower, same effort. They set it up and throw while holding the one-variable rule, and can name which variable is changed, which measured, and which kept the same.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confounded test: changes more than one variable — makes the big-wing plane from thicker paper too, or throws it harder — so any difference can't be pinned on the wings.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'which of your two planes is different in more than one way?' Rebuild so only the wings change.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The set-up: two planes differ in more than one way, or the throw differs between them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Variable-role confusion: muddles what to change with what to measure — 'I'll change the distance' or 'I'll measure the wings'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort into a three-column frame — what I change / what I measure / what I keep the same — before starting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child's declared plan assigns the wrong role to a variable.

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't hold conditions constant: throws from different spots, or lets different people throw, without seeing the problem.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name each thing that must stay the same and why it would otherwise affect the distance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: During the throws, the keep-the-same conditions drift and the child doesn't flag it.

responseLevels.gap: Sets up a test where several things differ, or muddles which variable to change and which to measure.
responseLevels.full: Sets up a genuinely fair test — one variable changed, one measured, the rest deliberately kept the same — and can say why controlling the others makes the result trustworthy.
responseLevels.partial: Changes one variable and measures an outcome, but forgets to hold some conditions constant, or needs prompting to name the keep-the-same variables.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: We want to find out whether paper aeroplanes fly further with bigger wings. Here's paper and a tape measure. Set up a fair test to answer it — as you get it ready, show me what you'll change, what you'll measure, and what you'll keep the same. Then do a couple of throws. I'll watch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching reveals whether the child genuinely isolates one variable — the give-away is what they DON'T hold constant (different paper, a harder throw for the big-wing plane, different throwers). A child can recite 'change one thing' yet build an unfair test; the set-up, not the recitation, shows real understanding.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5-7 (KS1/Grades K-2): minibeasts in simple food chains — who eats whom (leaf → caterpillar → bird), that minibeasts are both eaters and eaten, and that the arrow means 'is eaten by' / energy flows this way.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' — describe how animals obtain their food from plants and other animals, using the idea of a simple food chain, and identify and name different sources of food. Working-scientifically: identifying and classifying.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports K-LS1-1 (what animals need to survive/food) and 2-LS4-1 (diversity of life); food-web depth comes later (5-LS2-1).
• Operational details — start with a plant as the food source (producer, though the word isn't needed yet). The ARROW is the load-bearing convention: it points from the food to the eater (leaf → caterpillar means the caterpillar eats the leaf). Minibeasts sit in the middle — a caterpillar eats leaves AND is eaten by a bird. Keep chains short (3-4 links) and real (garden creatures).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): says what one minibeast eats and one thing that eats it. Tier B (age 6): builds a correct 3-link chain and reads the arrows aloud. Tier C (age 7): explains the arrow direction ('the arrow shows who eats who — it points to the eater') and places a minibeast as both eater and eaten.
bestPractices: Teach the arrow convention explicitly and repeatedly — it points from food to feeder and shows energy passing along; misreading it is the classic error.
Always start the chain with a plant/leaf as the food source so children see where the energy enters.
Highlight minibeasts as MIDDLE links — both eater and eaten — to break the idea that a creature is only ever predator or only ever prey.
Use real, local garden chains children can picture (leaf → caterpillar → blue tit) rather than abstract examples.
Keep chains short (3-4 links) at this age; food WEBS and producer/consumer vocabulary come later.
keyRepresentations: A left-to-right food-chain diagram with clear directional arrows (leaf → caterpillar → bird).
Drag-to-order organism cards that snap into a chain.
A 'both arrows' highlight on the middle creature showing it is eaten AND eats.
Read-aloud sentence frames ('the caterpillar is eaten by the bird').
commonMisconceptions: Arrow-direction reversal — children read 'bird → caterpillar' as 'the bird is eaten by the caterpillar'; the arrow points to the eater.
'A creature is either a hunter or food' — not grasping that a minibeast can be both (eats plants, eaten by birds).
'Chains start with an animal' — missing that the plant is the starting food source.
'Big animals always eat small ones / the last animal is the strongest' — size and 'winner' confusions.
Treating the chain as who-is-friends-with-whom rather than who-eats-whom.

learn.summary: Teaches 5-7 year olds simple garden food chains: who eats whom (leaf → caterpillar → bird), that minibeasts are both eaters and eaten, and that the arrow means 'is eaten by' / energy flows toward the eater. Core activity is constructing a short chain and reading the arrows aloud; a quiz and a tap-to-reveal scene are companions; role-play is an alternative for surfacing the middle-of-chain idea. The eater is identified by its role in the chain, not by being the bigger animal.

activities.title: Build and read a garden food chain
feedback: If a child tries to link the leaf directly to the blue tit (leaf → blue tit, with no caterpillar between): ask 'in our chain, who eats the leaf?' and prompt them to find the caterpillar, which the blue tit then eats.
When the order is correct, confirm the arrow snaps into place and energy passes along leaf → caterpillar → bird.
When the caterpillar is tapped, highlight both sides so the child sees it is eaten AND eats.
If the chain is read with the arrow backwards, re-read it as 'is eaten by / energy flows to' and point to the animal that gets the meal, whatever its size.
activities.rationale: A food chain is an ordered relationship, and this activity proposes building it as a way to make who-eats-whom and arrow direction concrete rather than only viewing a finished diagram. Live feedback on wrong versus right order and an explicit 'both sides' highlight are intended to surface the reasoning. Live recolouring, snapping arrows and an energy pulse are optional interaction examples that may make the mechanism visible, not required features.
sourceClaims: The food-chain arrow convention (points from food to feeder, showing energy flow) is a known source of confusion best taught explicitly.
learnerActions: Start with a shuffled set of garden organism cards — leaf, caterpillar, blue tit — and arrange them into the correct order to show who eats what.
Place the caterpillar next to the leaf and draw or confirm an arrow from leaf to caterpillar (leaf → caterpillar).
Add the bird after the caterpillar and draw the arrow caterpillar → bird.
Tap or point to the caterpillar in the middle and say both things about it: 'I eat the leaf' AND 'the bird eats me'.
Read the finished chain aloud using the arrow convention: 'the leaf is eaten by the caterpillar, the caterpillar is eaten by the bird'.

Try the deliberate wrong move of linking the leaf directly to the blue tit (leaf → blue tit, skipping the caterpillar) to see why it does not fit this chain: in this chain the caterpillar eats the leaf and the blue tit eats the caterpillar.
Optionally remove one link and say what happens to the chain.
activities.intendedInsight: The arrow points from the food to the eater (it means 'is eaten by' and shows energy passing along), and a minibeast in the middle is both an eater and something that is eaten.

activities.title: Order, match and choose the arrow direction (companion checks)
feedback: For arrow-direction choices, confirm the arrow points toward the eater (caterpillar → bird means the bird eats the caterpillar).
For a reversed answer, re-read the arrow as 'is eaten by' and point to the animal that gets the meal, whatever its size.
activities.rationale: Ordering, matching and a direction question check the idea directly and cheaply. These are recognition-style checks: they assess and reinforce but do not by themselves require the child to construct and explain the chain, so they work best after the build-and-read activity.
sourceClaims: The food-chain arrow convention (points from food to feeder, showing energy flow) is a known source of confusion best taught explicitly.
learnerActions: Put the three organism cards (leaf, caterpillar, bird) in the correct sequence.
Match each eater to its food (bird ↔ caterpillar, caterpillar ↔ leaf).
Choose which way the arrow points between the caterpillar and the bird, and say what it means.
activities.intendedInsight: Who-eats-whom order and arrow direction can be stated reliably and transferred to a new chain.

activities.title: Interview a caterpillar (role-play alternative)
feedback: If the child says the caterpillar is only food, prompt them to name what the caterpillar itself eats.

If the child says big animals always eat small ones, offer a real counterexample: a small caterpillar eats a much bigger leaf, and a garden spider can catch an insect bigger than itself. (The ladybird is bigger than the aphids it eats, so it shows a tiny hunter, not a smaller eater.)
activities.rationale: Spoken role-play surfaces the eater-and-eaten relationship through responsive questioning and gives a distinct experience from card-building. It is offered as an alternative route into the same idea, not a replacement for constructing and reading a chain.
learnerActions: Pretend to be a caterpillar and answer two questions aloud: 'What do I eat?' and 'Who eats me?'
Say the sentence 'I eat the leaf and the bird eats me' to capture the middle-of-chain idea.
Swap roles and interview a ladybird to find out it hunts aphids.
activities.intendedInsight: A minibeast sits in the middle of a chain — it both eats and is eaten — and even a tiny creature can be a hunter.

activities.title: Read the arrow in a labelled garden scene (scaffold)
feedback: Confirm that the arrow always points to the animal that gets the meal, whatever its size.
Prompt the child to then build the same chain themselves so they move from recognising to constructing.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal scene can show a chain and name the arrow convention, which supports children who are not yet ready to build from scratch. Because the chain is already ordered for them, it functions as a scaffold; the intended deeper engagement is proposed to come from constructing and reasoning about order, so following it with the build-and-read task is recommended.
learnerActions: Look at a garden picture with a pre-drawn chain leaf → caterpillar → bird.
Tap or lift the 'what does the arrow mean?' label and read the explanation aloud.
Point along the chain in the direction the energy travels.
activities.intendedInsight: The arrow between two organisms means 'is eaten by' and shows energy moving to the eater.

constraints: Start every chain with a plant/leaf as the food source so children see where the energy enters, even though the word 'producer' is not needed yet.
Teach the arrow convention explicitly and repeatedly: it points from food to feeder and shows energy passing along; misreading it is the classic error.
Keep chains short (3-4 links) and use real, local garden creatures children can picture; food webs and producer/consumer vocabulary come later.
Highlight minibeasts as middle links — both eater and eaten — to break the idea that a creature is only ever a predator or only ever prey.
Identify the eater by its role in the chain, never by being the bigger animal; the eater can be smaller than or the same size as its food.

Ordering, matching and multiple-choice checks are recognition-style: they confirm and reinforce but do not require the child to independently construct or explain a chain. Use them after construction.
The tap-to-reveal garden scene is a scaffold with the chain pre-ordered; it supports but does not substitute for the child building and reading a chain.

Correct the size misconception directly: the eater is not always the bigger one. For example, a small caterpillar eats a much bigger leaf, and a garden spider can catch an insect bigger than itself in its web. A ladybird hunting aphids shows that a tiny minibeast can be a hunter, but it is not a size counterexample, because ladybirds are bigger than aphids.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all sources[].verified flags were false in the row and have not been re-checked. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original labelled the 3D-interactive option 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing'. This has been dropped as an unsupported universal claim rather than migrated as a pedagogical law; a food chain is an ordered relationship, so a spatial 3D scene is simply a weaker fit here, not inherently without value.
The original framed the tap-to-reveal scene as something a 'static reveal can't provide' learning for. Softened to a scaffold-with-a-stated-limit rather than asserting it cannot teach.

Efficacy wording was softened in the build and scaffold rationales: the claim that constructing a chain is 'best' or produces 'deeper learning' than viewing one is a plausible design rationale but is not source-verified, so it is stated as proposed/intended.
'Energy flows this way' is used at a child-appropriate level; at ages 5-7 this is an intuitive gloss on the arrow convention rather than a formal energy-transfer concept.

Candidate feedback originally directed children to 'point to the bigger animal that gets the meal' and mislabelled the deliberate wrong move as placing the leaf before the bird; both were corrected because they reinforced the size misconception and contradicted the correct leaf → caterpillar → bird ordering.

probeDeeper: The bird eats the caterpillar — so which way should the arrow point?
Name something the caterpillar eats AND something that eats the caterpillar.
Can a tiny ladybird be a hunter? What does it hunt?
assess.correctAnswer: The arrow points from the caterpillar TO the bird, meaning the caterpillar is eaten BY the bird (the food and energy pass to the bird). And yes — the caterpillar itself eats leaves. Minibeasts both eat (plants or smaller creatures) and are eaten by bigger animals.

errorPatterns.pattern: The arrow points to what the animal eats — so 'caterpillar → bird' means the caterpillar eats the bird.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-read the arrow as 'is eaten by' / 'energy flows to' — it points toward the animal that gets the meal.
errorPatterns.distractor: The arrow means the caterpillar eats the bird.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reverses the arrow, making the smaller animal the eater of the bigger.

errorPatterns.pattern: Minibeasts only get eaten — they don't eat anything themselves.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the caterpillar eating leaves — minibeasts are both eaters and eaten, links in the chain.
errorPatterns.distractor: Caterpillars are just food for birds; they don't eat anything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the caterpillar purely as food, never as a feeder.

errorPatterns.pattern: Big animals always eat small ones, so a tiny minibeast could never be a hunter.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give a counterexample — a ladybird hunting aphids — to break the size rule.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies a small creature (e.g. a ladybird) can prey on anything.

responseLevels.gap: Reads the arrow backwards or thinks minibeasts only ever get eaten.
responseLevels.full: Reads the arrow as 'eaten by / energy to,' places a minibeast as both eater and eaten, and transfers the idea to a new food chain.
responseLevels.partial: Gets who-eats-whom right but treats the chain as a one-way list, not grasping that the arrow shows energy flowing to the eater or that a minibeast both eats and is eaten.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the food chain leaf → caterpillar → bird, what does the arrow between the caterpillar and the bird mean — who eats whom? And does the caterpillar eat anything itself?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads the arrow backwards says the caterpillar eats the bird. A child who understands reads the arrow as 'is eaten by / energy goes to,' and knows a minibeast both eats and is eaten.
