pedagogy.summary: Solving a linear equation means finding the value of the unknown that makes the two sides genuinely equal, by doing the SAME operation to both sides until the unknown is isolated. The relational meaning of the equals sign is the foundation: each written line must be a true equality, not a running commentary strung together with '='. The persistent errors — treating subtraction as commutative, refusing negative solutions, mishandling the unknown on both sides, and operating on one side only — are addressed with a balance model, inverse operations, and a substitution check.
bestPractices: Teach 'do the same to both sides' with a balance model so operations that keep the scale level are felt as legal and one-sided moves as illegal.
Insist on ONE valid equality per line — forbid run-on chains like 5−x=6=x=−1; each line must itself be true.
Isolate the unknown with inverse operations; for the unknown on both sides, gather it on one side by subtracting the smaller term from both.
Always check by substituting the solution back into the ORIGINAL equation.
Handle negatives explicitly (number line / zero-pairs) rather than assuming the answer must be positive; discuss whether an equation has one, none, or infinitely many solutions.
keyRepresentations: Balance scale (unknown-boxes and unit-weights; same action on both pans)
Algebra tiles with zero-pairs for negatives and unknown-on-both-sides
Inverse-operation / function-machine unwinding
Number line for negative solutions
Substitution-back check
commonMisconceptions: Treats subtraction as commutative: 5−x=6 solved as x−5=6 giving x=11.
Considers positive numbers only, so rejects or never reaches a negative solution.
Run-on / operational equals sign: writes 5−x=6=x=−1 or 3x−5=2x=x=5, using '=' to mean 'and then'.
Mishandles the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x): stops at 'unlike terms' or subtracts incorrectly.
Performs an operation on one side only, unbalancing the equation.
Thinks every equation has exactly one solution (misses none/infinitely-many).

learn.summary: Solving a linear equation means finding the value of the unknown that makes both sides genuinely equal, by doing the SAME operation to both sides until the unknown is isolated. The relational meaning of '=' is the foundation: each written line must itself be a true equality, not a running commentary strung together with '='. Target the persistent errors — treating subtraction as commutative, refusing negative solutions, mishandling the unknown on both sides, and operating on one side only — with a balance model, inverse operations, explicit handling of negatives, and a substitution check back into the original equation.

activities.title: Balance-scale solver: keep both pans level
feedback: If a one-sided action is attempted: the scale tips because the two sides are no longer equal; redo the same action on both pans.

When isolating 8x − 6 = 2x: after removing 2 x-boxes from each side you have 6x − 6 = 0; adding 6 to both sides gives 6x = 6; dividing both sides by 6 gives x = 1. Substitute back: 8(1) − 6 = 2 and 2(1) = 2 — equal, so x = 1 checks.
For 5 − x = 6: using zero-pairs gives −x = 1, so x = −1. Substitute back: 5 − (−1) = 6 — correct; note 5 − x is NOT the same as x − 5.
activities.rationale: 'Do the same to both sides' is a physical intuition made legal-feeling by a balance the learner must keep level; illegal one-sided moves visibly tip it, so the rule is enforced by the model. Dragging actions onto both pans, live tipping, and zero-pair anti-weights are offered as concrete ways to make the balancing mechanism visible; they are examples, not the only possible setup, and are proposed rather than validated as superior to other media.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
Children frequently read the equals sign operationally ('work out the answer') rather than relationally (the two sides are equal), which underlies run-on chains and difficulty balancing equations.
learnerActions: Represent an equation as two pans: unknown-boxes (x) and unit-weights, using 'anti-weights' (zero-pairs) for any negative amount. Set up 8x − 6 = 2x with the −6 shown as six anti-weights on that pan.

Choose an action (add or remove the same number of units, using zero-pairs where a pan has none to remove; remove an x-box; halve everything) and apply it to BOTH pans at once; watch the scale stay level.
Try a one-sided action on purpose and observe that the scale tips — that move is not allowed because it breaks the equality.

Solve 8x − 6 = 2x: remove 2 x-boxes from each pan to reach 6x − 6 = 0, then add 6 units to each pan (cancelling the six anti-weights) to reach 6x = 6, then divide both pans into 6 equal groups (÷6) to reach x = 1.

Use an anti-x-box for −x, plus unit zero-pairs, to model 5 − x = 6: remove 5 units from both pans to reach −x = 1, then swap every item on both pans for its opposite (multiply both sides by −1) to reach x = −1, so the negative solution is something you build and see rather than distrust.
Write down each balanced state as its own line — one true equality per line.
activities.intendedInsight: The only way to keep the scale level while stripping it down to a single x is to mirror every move on both sides — that mirroring IS the solving method, and a negative result is a legitimate, visible outcome.

activities.title: One true equality per line: fix the run-on equals sign
feedback: In 5 − x = 6 = x = −1, the middle '6 = x' is false (6 does not equal −1); the valid working is 5 − x = 6 → −x = 1 → x = −1, one true equality per line.

For 3x − 5 = 2x: subtract 2x from both sides to get x − 5 = 0, then add 5 to both sides to get x = 5. Check: 3(5) − 5 = 10 and 2(5) = 10 — equal, so x = 5. (Note the first item here, 5 − x = 6, has solution x = −1; the two tasks are different equations.)
activities.rationale: The operational (left-to-right 'compute') reading of '=' underlies run-on chains; reading written maths aloud and reformatting into vertical true equalities confronts that reading directly.
sourceClaims: Children frequently read the equals sign operationally ('work out the answer') rather than relationally (the two sides are equal), which underlies run-on chains and difficulty balancing equations.

Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
learnerActions: Read aloud, left to right, the chain 5 − x = 6 = x = −1. Decide whether each '=' states a genuine equality (does 6 really equal x?).
Rewrite the working as a vertical chain where every single line is itself true: 5 − x = 6, then −x = 1, then x = −1.
Do the same for 3x − 5 = 2x: rewrite the run-on 3x − 5 = 2x = x = 5 as separate true lines, subtracting 2x from both sides first (3x − 5 = 2x → x − 5 = 0 → x = 5), and check by substitution.
Spot the invalid line: given a worked solution containing a run-on chain, identify which '=' is false and correct it.
activities.intendedInsight: '=' means the two sides have equal value, not 'and then'. Every line of correct working must be a standalone true statement.

activities.title: Solve, then check by substitution; classify how many solutions
feedback: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 expands to 2x + 6 = 2x + 6, true for every x, so infinitely many solutions — an identity, not a single answer.
If substitution does not make both sides equal, the solution is wrong; retrace which line first stopped being a true equality.
activities.rationale: Substitution into the original equation makes correctness self-verifiable and pushes past guess-and-check; the identity 2(x+3)=2x+6 is a concrete counterexample to 'every equation has one solution'.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
KS3 pupils should use algebraic methods to solve linear equations in one variable, including all forms that require rearrangement.
learnerActions: Solve a set of equations by inverse operations, writing one true equality per line: start with 5 − x = 6 and 8x − 6 = 2x, then extend to equations with brackets and fractional/negative coefficients.
For each solution, substitute it back into the ORIGINAL equation and confirm both sides are equal.
Solve 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 and decide what happens: after expanding the bracket, both sides are identical (2x + 6 = 2x + 6), so every value of x works — infinitely many solutions.
Construct or examine an equation that simplifies to a false statement (e.g. a contradiction) and recognise it has no solution.
Sort equations into 'one solution', 'no solution', 'infinitely many solutions'.
activities.intendedInsight: A solved equation must survive a substitution check in the original; and not every equation has exactly one solution — some have none and some have infinitely many.

activities.title: Sequenced steps and worked-solution annotation (supporting practice)
feedback: 3x + 5 = 20: subtract 5 from both sides (3x = 15), then divide both sides by 3 (x = 5); check 3(5) + 5 = 20. ✓
If a line in the annotated solution alters only one side, it is invalid — the equality no longer holds; the matching move must act on both sides.
A static worked solution can display one correct balanced chain, but it does not itself let the learner perform the balancing; pair it with the balance-scale activity where the construction happens.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and fill-in-the-line tasks make the stepwise structure explicit and can surface run-on-equals and one-sided errors through forced choices; annotation of a fixed solution can display a model chain and support recognition/consolidation, but recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own production of the balancing moves.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
learnerActions: Order the correct solving steps for 3x + 5 = 20 from a scrambled set, stating what is done to both sides at each step.
Fill in each missing line of the working for 8x − 6 = 2x, keeping one true equality per line.
For a step in progress, state what operation should be applied to both sides next.
Examine an annotated worked solution and, line by line, name the inverse operation applied to both sides; then flag any invalid line (e.g. a run-on chain like 5 − x = 6 = x = −1).
activities.intendedInsight: Solving is a reproducible sequence of 'same operation to both sides' moves, and being able to name each inverse operation and reject invalid lines consolidates the procedure.

constraints: Each written line must be a single true equality; forbid run-on chains like 5 − x = 6 = x = −1 or 3x − 5 = 2x = x = 5 where the '=' means 'and then'.
Every operation must be applied to BOTH sides; operating on one side only unbalances the equation and makes the line false.
Handle negatives explicitly (number line or zero-pairs) rather than assuming the answer must be positive; 5 − x is not the same as x − 5.
On a balance model, represent any negative amount (e.g. the −6 in 8x − 6) with anti-weights (zero-pairs) so the pans and the written equality stay consistent.
For the unknown on both sides, gather it on one side by subtracting the same term from both sides (e.g. subtract 2x from 8x − 6 = 2x to reach 6x − 6 = 0).
Always check by substituting the solution back into the ORIGINAL equation.
Discuss that an equation may have one solution, no solution, or infinitely many (e.g. the identity 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6).

A fixed/annotated worked solution and ordering/fill-in tasks support recognition and consolidation but do not elicit the learner's own balancing; they complement, rather than replace, hands-on solving where the learner performs each move.
Prerequisite support for negative-number reasoning and collecting like terms may be needed before equations with negative/fractional coefficients or the unknown on both sides.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the balance-scale approach as uniquely able to 'force' discovery and claims 3D 'adds nothing' and that a static image 'cannot' fix the misconceptions. These are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to a scoped proposal (balance model as a vivid way to make the rule visible) and the static worked solution retained as a consolidation/recognition support rather than dismissed.
The Kieran (1981) source is marked verified:false in the row; treat its support for the relational-equals principle as unconfirmed here.

Independent self-audit of worked examples: 5 − x = 6 → x = −1 (check 5 − (−1) = 6); 8x − 6 = 2x → x = 1 (check 8 − 6 = 2 = 2); 3x − 5 = 2x → x = 5 (check 10 = 10); 3x + 5 = 20 → x = 5 (check 20 = 20); 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 is an identity. The incorrect misconception outputs (x = 11 for 5 − x = 6; the run-on chains) are presented only as errors to confront, never as valid answers.

Balance-scale walkthrough is coherent: after removing 2 x-boxes the state is 6x − 6 = 0, the −6 is modelled with anti-weights so adding 6 units to both pans cancels them to 6x = 6, then ÷6 gives x = 1. Activity 0 feedback was made explicit about the ÷6 step to match the learnerActions and the 'show every line' emphasis.

The diagnostic items 5 − x = 6 and 8x − 6 = 2x are reused across activities as teaching items; they are kept as distinct equations with distinct solutions (−1 and 1) to avoid confusion when both appear in one task.

probeDeeper: Check your answer to (a) by putting it back into 5 − x = 6 — does it work?
In (b), how do you know x = 1 is the ONLY solution and not just A solution? (pushes past guess-and-check)
You wrote 5−x=6=x=−1 — read that out loud left to right. Is 6 really equal to x? (confronts the run-on equals sign)
Here is 2(x+3) = 2x + 6 — solve it. What happens, and what does that tell you about how many solutions it has? (counterexample: an identity / infinitely many solutions)

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats subtraction as commutative / rejects negatives — solves 5−x=6 as if it were x−5=6 to get x=11, or insists 'you can't take x from 5 to make 6' and stops.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Substitute x=11 to show 5−11=−6≠6; rewrite as −x=1 and use a number line to reach x=−1; establish that 5−x is not x−5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes x=11, or abandons the problem as impossible; does not consider a negative solution.

errorPatterns.pattern: Run-on / operational equals sign — writes 5−x=6=x=−1 or 3x−5=2x=x=5, using '=' to mean 'and then' rather than 'is equal to'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: One equation per line; read the written maths aloud left-to-right — 'does 6 really equal x?'; rewrite as a vertical chain of true equalities.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A single strung-together line whose equalities are not actually true when read left to right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the unknown on both sides — for 8x−6=2x either stops at 'these aren't like terms' or subtracts wrongly (e.g. treats 8x−6 as 2x).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the balance model to remove 2x from each side, reaching 6x−6=0; then isolate x; check by substitution.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Does not subtract 2x from both sides; leaves the unknown on both sides or mis-collects.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operates on one side only — changes one side without doing the same to the other, unbalancing the equation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Balance-scale model — every operation must act on both pans or the scale tips; redo the step on both sides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A line where one side has been altered (a term added/removed) but the other has not, yet an '=' is kept.

responseLevels.gap: Treats subtraction or sides as swappable (x=11), operates on one side only, or strings steps together with '=' incorrectly; no valid balancing and answers fail a substitution check.
responseLevels.full: Solves equations with the unknown on both sides, negative/fractional coefficients and brackets by doing the same to both sides, writes one valid equality per line, checks by substituting into the original, and can classify an equation as having one, none, or infinitely many solutions.
responseLevels.partial: Solves one- and two-step equations with positive whole-number solutions by inverse operations, but breaks down with negatives, fractional coefficients, brackets, or the unknown on both sides, and may not check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child this card and say 'solve these, showing every line of your working': (a) 5 − x = 6 and (b) 8x − 6 = 2x. Say nothing about method. Watch how they deal with the subtraction and the negative in (a), and how they gather the unknown from both sides in (b), and whether each line is a genuine equality.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items expose different faults on paper without a single question being asked: 5−x=6 catches treating subtraction as commutative (x=11) and refusing negatives; 8x−6=2x catches failure to gather the unknown from both sides and the run-on equals-sign chain. A child who is secure keeps the scale balanced, reaches x=−1 and x=1, and writes one true equality per line.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11. The K-Pg (Cretaceous–Paleogene) mass extinction ~66 Mya that ended the non-avian dinosaurs — taught as a DETECTIVE CASE built from converging physical evidence, not a told story.
• Standards — UK (DfE): no direct statutory KS2 dinosaur content; anchor to Y3 Rocks (fossils form when things living in rock are trapped) and Y6 Evolution & inheritance (fossils tell us about the past), plus 'asking scientific questions and using evidence to answer them' from the KS2 working-scientifically strand. Leads to KS3 Earth's history.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-1 (fossils as evidence of past organisms/environments) is the anchor; extends to MS-ESS1-4 (geologic time) and the nature-of-science idea that scientific knowledge is based on empirical evidence.
• Operational details: build the argument in layers — (1) the worldwide clay layer rich in IRIDIUM, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids; (2) shocked quartz + tektites (melt droplets) that need enormous pressure; (3) a buried ~180 km crater at Chicxulub, Yucatán, same age as the layer; (4) drilling INTO the crater (2016) found the same iridium signature inside it, tying crater to global layer. Then the mechanism: dust/soot/sulfate aerosols blocked sunlight → impact winter → photosynthesis crashed → food chains collapsed.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (concrete, ~9): point to the special worldwide clay layer and say what it is made of and where it came from. Tier B (transitional, ~10): name two independent clues (iridium AND the crater) and explain why one clue alone is weaker than two. Tier C (formal, ~11): explain the causal CHAIN from impact → blocked sunlight → collapsed food chains, and note that a rival idea (Deccan Traps volcanism) exists — evidence, not authority, decides.
bestPractices: Frame it as evidence-to-conclusion detective work: present the clues (iridium, shocked quartz, crater) and let children infer the cause, rather than announcing 'an asteroid did it' first.
Emphasise CONVERGING independent lines of evidence — the strength is that chemistry, geology and the crater's age all point the same way; one clue alone would be weak.

Teach the mechanism as a causal chain (impact → dust/soot → sunlight blocked → plants die → herbivores → carnivores), so extinction is understood as ecosystem collapse, not direct killing by the blast.

Explicitly model nature-of-science: a rival hypothesis (Deccan Traps volcanism) still has supporters, and the impact case strengthened over decades as new evidence arrived — science is provisional and evidence-led.
Anchor deep time — 'birds are the dinosaurs that survived' — to avoid the total-annihilation misconception.
keyRepresentations: The K-Pg boundary rock column: dinosaur bones below, thin grey iridium clay layer, none above.
An iridium-vs-depth graph with a sharp spike at the boundary.
A world map with boundary sites all showing the same layer, converging on Chicxulub.
A food-web/energy-pyramid diagram going dark as sunlight is removed.
A before/after Cretaceous scene (thriving) vs impact-winter (dim, cold).
commonMisconceptions: 'The asteroid killed the dinosaurs on impact' — most died from the global aftermath (impact winter, food-chain collapse), not the blast itself.
'All dinosaurs died' — avian dinosaurs (birds) survived; dinosaurs are not entirely extinct.
'Dinosaurs and early humans overlapped' — ~66 My separate the extinction from humans.
'One clue proved it' — the case rests on multiple independent evidence lines, not a single discovery.
'Science has closed the book' — a genuine minority hypothesis (Deccan volcanism) persists; debate continues.

learn.summary: Teach the K-Pg mass extinction (~66 Mya, ending the non-avian dinosaurs) for ages 9-11 as evidence-to-conclusion detective work rather than a told story. Learners assemble converging independent clues (a worldwide iridium-rich clay layer, shocked quartz and tektites, the buried ~180 km Chicxulub crater, and iridium found inside the crater by drilling) and then reason through the causal chain: impact -> dust/soot/sulfate aerosols block sunlight -> impact winter -> photosynthesis crashes -> plants die -> herbivores starve -> carnivores starve -> ecosystem collapse. Core nature-of-science goals: the strength of a case comes from multiple independent lines agreeing; a genuine rival hypothesis (Deccan Traps volcanism) persists and evidence, not authority, decides; and birds are surviving dinosaurs, so extinction was near-total, not total.

activities.title: Assemble the case file: what killed the dinosaurs?
feedback: If a learner says one discovery 'proved' it, point back to the case file: ask them to name a second independent clue and say what the case would look like with only one.
If a learner treats the crater and the clay layer as unrelated, direct them to the drill-core result — the same iridium signature inside the crater is what connects the two.
Affirm correct reasoning that iridium's rarity in the crust plus its abundance in asteroids is what makes a worldwide iridium layer surprising and meaningful.
If a learner cannot say why iridium is a clue, prompt: where is iridium common, and where is it rare?
activities.rationale: The target understanding is the reasoning move of gathering independent evidence and tying a local cause (crater) to a global effect (worldwide layer). Having learners collect and compare clues, rather than being told the answer first, makes that reasoning the thing they practise. An interactive map/assay format (measurement that spikes at the layer, a core-drill that reveals iridium inside the crater, a visual link joining crater to layer) can make the converging-evidence idea concrete; these interaction examples are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required features.
sourceClaims: The Chicxulub crater (~180 km wide, Yucatán) was formed by an asteroid impact ~66 Mya at the end of the Cretaceous; the impact and resulting climate change caused a mass extinction that wiped out ~75–80% of species including the (non-avian) dinosaurs.

The asteroid hypothesis originated with Luis Alvarez's team finding unusually high iridium at the K–Pg boundary; iridium is rare in the crust (siderophile, sank to the core) but abundant in asteroids, and similar iridium spikes were found at the boundary worldwide.

Drilling into the crater (IODP-ICDP Expedition 364) found the iridium anomaly WITHIN the peak-ring sequence, conclusively tying Chicxulub to the global iridium layer and K-Pg boundary sections worldwide; lead author Steven Goderis: 'The circle is now finally complete.'

Impact evidence includes a global iridium-rich clay layer, shocked quartz and tektites; expedition found dust, sulfate aerosols and soot driving global cooling and reduced photosynthesis as extinction drivers; a rival Deccan Traps volcanism hypothesis (Gerta Keller) persists.
learnerActions: Open a 'case file' and visit several boundary sites on a world map (e.g. Italy, Denmark, New Zealand, and a land site such as Hell Creek in Montana, USA); at each, examine the rock column and find the thin clay band at the boundary. At land sites like Hell Creek, non-avian dinosaur fossils are found below the band and none above it; at old sea-floor sites like Italy and Denmark, many kinds of tiny sea fossils found below the band disappear above it.

Run an iridium measurement at each site and record where the reading spikes — notice the spike lands at the clay layer at each site you visit, and that similar spikes have been found at the boundary at many sites around the world.

State in your own words why iridium at this layer points to space: iridium is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids, so a worldwide layer of it suggests material that fell from the sky everywhere at once.

Examine two more independent clues from a large impact: shocked quartz, which forms under the intense shock pressure of an impact, and tektites, which are droplets of rock melted and flung out by the impact's heat and energy — both are products of one large impact rather than both being pressure-formed.
Reveal the buried ~180 km Chicxulub crater in the Yucatan on a geophysics view, and check that its age matches the clay layer.
Drill a core into the crater and find the same iridium signature inside it; draw or describe the link that ties the crater to the global layer.
Write down which clues are independent and explain why two or more clues that agree make a stronger case than any single clue alone.
activities.intendedInsight: A scientific conclusion is built from converging independent evidence: chemistry (iridium), geology (shocked quartz, tektites, crater), and matching ages all point the same way, and drilling into the crater closed the link between the local crater and the global layer.

activities.title: Run the aftermath: trace the causal chain
feedback: If a learner says the asteroid burned or crushed all the dinosaurs, separate the local impact from the global aftermath: ask how a strike in Mexico could reach animals on the other side of the world, and lead them to the blocked-sunlight/food-chain route.
If a learner reverses the order (carnivores first), prompt: where does the food chain get its energy, and which group depends on plants most directly?
If a learner says every dinosaur died, note that non-avian dinosaurs died out but birds — living dinosaurs — survived.
Affirm answers that name the global 'impact winter' and food-chain collapse as the mechanism reaching the whole planet, supported by the worldwide iridium layer and the crater.
activities.rationale: A common misconception is that the impact killed dinosaurs directly; the discriminating idea is the indirect, global mechanism of blocked sunlight and food-chain collapse. Letting learners manipulate the sunlight and watch trophic levels fail in sequence makes causation something they trace rather than recite. The sunlight slider and sequential dimming are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Impact evidence includes a global iridium-rich clay layer, shocked quartz and tektites; expedition found dust, sulfate aerosols and soot driving global cooling and reduced photosynthesis as extinction drivers; a rival Deccan Traps volcanism hypothesis (Gerta Keller) persists.

The Chicxulub crater (~180 km wide, Yucatán) was formed by an asteroid impact ~66 Mya at the end of the Cretaceous; the impact and resulting climate change caused a mass extinction that wiped out ~75–80% of species including the (non-avian) dinosaurs.
learnerActions: Starting from a thriving Cretaceous scene, release the dust and soot from the impact and reduce incoming sunlight (for example, by lowering a sunlight slider) to model an 'impact winter'.
Observe and describe, in order, what happens as sunlight drops: plants dim and die, then plant-eaters (herbivores) starve, then meat-eaters (carnivores) that fed on them starve.
Explain in your own words why plant-eaters are affected before meat-eaters, using the idea that energy enters a food chain through plants/photosynthesis.
Write the full causal chain as a sequence: impact -> dust/soot/aerosols -> sunlight blocked -> photosynthesis crashes -> plants die -> herbivores die -> carnivores die -> ecosystem collapse.
State clearly that worldwide extinction came from these after-effects, not from the blast crushing or burning dinosaurs everywhere, and note that the impact itself mainly devastated the local area.
Add a note that birds are surviving dinosaurs, so the extinction was near-total, not total.
activities.intendedInsight: Mass extinction was caused by ecosystem collapse — blocked sunlight shutting down the food supply across the whole planet — rather than by the impact directly killing animals far from the crater; and survival of birds means dinosaurs are not entirely extinct.

activities.title: Weigh the rival hypothesis
feedback: If a learner thinks 'science has closed the book', note that a genuine minority hypothesis (Deccan volcanism) persists and that the impact case itself strengthened over time as evidence accumulated.

If a learner dismisses the rival outright, ask what the volcanism idea can explain (huge Deccan eruptions happened around the same time and could change the climate) and what evidence would help decide how much each cause mattered.
Affirm reasoning that cites specific converging evidence rather than appealing to who said it.
activities.rationale: Modelling nature-of-science explicitly — rival hypotheses, provisional knowledge, evidence over authority — is an anchor standard for this topic and guards against the misconception that the debate is settled or that one discovery decided it. A short discussion or interview with a researcher (e.g. asking why the iridium finding was surprising) can extend this, though the core work is weighing evidence.
sourceClaims: Impact evidence includes a global iridium-rich clay layer, shocked quartz and tektites; expedition found dust, sulfate aerosols and soot driving global cooling and reduced photosynthesis as extinction drivers; a rival Deccan Traps volcanism hypothesis (Gerta Keller) persists.

The asteroid hypothesis originated with Luis Alvarez's team finding unusually high iridium at the K–Pg boundary; iridium is rare in the crust (siderophile, sank to the core) but abundant in asteroids, and similar iridium spikes were found at the boundary worldwide.
learnerActions: Compare two explanations for the extinction: the asteroid impact and Deccan Traps volcanism, considering what each can explain and whether both might have played a part.
List which pieces of evidence (worldwide iridium layer, shocked quartz, matching-age crater, iridium inside the crater) fit the impact explanation.
Discuss or write why the impact case grew stronger over decades as new evidence arrived, and why a minority of scientists still support the volcanism idea.

Conclude with a statement about how scientists decide between rival ideas — by how much evidence each explains, not by authority — and that scientific conclusions can be revised as evidence accumulates.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific knowledge is based on empirical evidence and is provisional: competing hypotheses are judged by how well they explain the evidence, and a genuine rival idea can still have supporters while the main case strengthens.

activities.title: Check your understanding of the case
feedback: A strong answer names the global impact winter and food-chain collapse reaching the whole planet, cites the iridium layer and Chicxulub crater, and notes that birds survived.
A partial answer names the asteroid, crater, or iridium layer but explains deaths by the direct blast and cannot describe the worldwide food-chain collapse — redirect to the aftermath activity.
A gap answer pictures the asteroid crushing or burning the dinosaurs with no global mechanism — reteach by separating the local impact from the global after-effects.
On the 'biggest extinction' probe: note that earlier extinctions (End-Permian) killed a far greater share of species; K-Pg is famous, not the largest.
activities.rationale: Recall and sorting tasks are useful companion checks that surface the specific misconceptions this topic targets. Such checks confirm whether learners can reproduce the argument; they do not, on their own, require learners to construct the argument, so they work best alongside the assembling and aftermath activities rather than replacing them.
learnerActions: Put the causal chain in the correct order: impact -> dust cloud -> less sunlight -> photosynthesis crashes -> plants die -> herbivores die -> carnivores die -> ecosystem collapse.

Sort clues into 'impact evidence' (e.g. worldwide iridium layer, shocked quartz, matching-age Chicxulub crater, iridium inside the crater) and items that are NOT impact evidence (e.g. an ordinary dinosaur fossil from older rock, a present-day volcanic rock, a river-worn pebble).
Answer why iridium is a clue (it is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids).

Answer the diagnostic question: 'An asteroid hit near Mexico ~66 Mya and most dinosaurs died. Did it kill them all just by crushing or burning them on impact? Explain how a strike in one place could wipe out dinosaurs all over the world.'

Respond to probes such as: since birds are living dinosaurs, is it right to say the asteroid killed ALL the dinosaurs? Why do plant-eaters die before meat-eaters? What evidence shows the effects reached the whole world? Was the K-Pg really the deadliest extinction ever?
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state the age (~66 Mya), name the Chicxulub crater, cite the worldwide iridium layer, order the food-chain-collapse mechanism, and avoid the direct-killing, total-annihilation, and 'biggest-ever' misconceptions.

constraints: Target age 9-11. Anchor to fossils-as-evidence (UK Y3 Rocks, Y6 Evolution; NGSS 3-LS4-1), geologic time (MS-ESS1-4) and the working-scientifically/nature-of-science strand; there is no direct statutory KS2 dinosaur content.
Present clues first and let learners infer the cause; avoid announcing 'an asteroid did it' before the evidence is assembled.

Address the key misconceptions directly: most dinosaurs died from the global aftermath (impact winter, food-chain collapse) not the blast; birds are surviving dinosaurs so extinction was near-total not total; non-avian dinosaurs and humans did not overlap (separated by roughly 66 million years); the case rests on multiple independent evidence lines not one discovery; and the debate is not closed (the Deccan volcanism hypothesis, as a main cause or a contributor, still has supporters).

Recall/sorting checks assess whether learners can reproduce the argument but do not by themselves require independent construction of it; pair them with the evidence-assembling and aftermath activities, and populate both sort categories with real items so the task is a genuine discrimination.

A single annotated cross-section (tap-to-reveal: clay band = iridium from space, bones below, crater inset facts) is a useful scaffold for the boundary layer, but being fixed it does not let learners assemble the multi-clue argument or trace the cascade themselves — use it as support, not as the whole lesson.

Interaction examples (iridium meter that spikes, drill-core reveal, sunlight slider, sequential dimming of trophic levels, a wire linking crater to layer) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
Keep the distinction between the local impact (blast/heat near the crater) and the global after-effects (blocked sunlight worldwide) explicit so learners do not conflate them.

Distinguish the impact clues accurately: shocked quartz records intense shock pressure, while tektites are impact-melt droplets flung out by the impact's heat/energy — do not describe both as simply 'needing pressure.'
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the stated principle without proving any specific activity was tested.

Of the four source claims, only the UT Austin drill-core claim ('circle is now finally complete') is marked verified in the row; the Britannica, Wikipedia/Alvarez, and Science Advances claims are marked verified:false. Treat extinction percentages (~75–80%), the 'conclusively tying' language, and the characterisation of the Deccan rival as reported-but-unverified at this rewrite.

The source's 'circle is now finally complete' / 'conclusively tying' phrasing is strong; the rewrite presents the drill-core as closing only the link between crater and global layer, while the 'weigh the rival' activity preserves that a minority volcanism hypothesis persists, so the topic is not treated as fully closed.

Original research contained a non-preferred claim that '3D adds nothing' / depth 'adds cost without adding insight' and that dialogue 'cannot make tactile' the learning; these universal comparative claims are not established by the evidence and have been dropped or softened — a fixed cross-section and a researcher interview are retained as legitimate scaffolds/extensions with stated limits.

The original row grouped shocked quartz and tektites as both needing 'enormous pressure.' Shocked quartz forms under shock pressure, but tektites are impact-melt droplets formed by heat/energy and ejection; the corrected activity distinguishes them. This refinement was not re-verified against a fresh source.

Self-audit of the causal/biological logic found the mechanism (blocked sunlight -> photosynthesis crash -> herbivores before carnivores -> collapse), the local-vs-global distinction, the birds-survived point, and the End-Permian being larger than K-Pg to be internally consistent and retained as stated.

The ordering check in the final activity was aligned with the full taught chain (adding photosynthesis crash and ecosystem collapse) and the 'not impact evidence' sort category was populated with distractors so the classification task is performable.

probeDeeper: Birds are alive today and they are dinosaurs — so is it right to say the asteroid killed ALL the dinosaurs?
Why would plant-eaters die first and the meat-eaters soon after?
The crater is in Mexico. What evidence shows the effects reached the whole world?
Was the K-Pg really the deadliest extinction Earth has ever seen?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the impact itself only devastated the local area. Worldwide extinction came from the after-effects: dust and soot thrown into the sky blocked sunlight for years, so plants died, plant-eaters starved, and then the meat-eaters that fed on them starved — the food chain collapsed globally. Evidence includes the worldwide iridium layer and the Chicxulub crater.

errorPatterns.pattern: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs directly by hitting or burning them everywhere.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the local impact from the global aftermath — blocked sunlight, dying plants, collapsing food chains reaching animals far from Mexico.
errorPatterns.distractor: The asteroid crushed and burned all the dinosaurs when it hit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains worldwide death by the impact's blast/heat rather than by after-effects.

errorPatterns.pattern: It killed every single dinosaur — none survived at all.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Note that the non-avian dinosaurs died out but birds — living dinosaurs — survived; extinction was near-total, not total.
errorPatterns.distractor: It killed every single dinosaur, so no dinosaurs exist today.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States that no dinosaurs of any kind lived on, overlooking that birds are surviving dinosaurs.

errorPatterns.pattern: The K-Pg was the biggest extinction the Earth has ever had.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mention that earlier extinctions (End-Permian) killed a far greater share of species; K-Pg is famous, not the biggest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims K-Pg was the deadliest ever, unaware of the larger End-Permian event.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the asteroid crushed or burned the dinosaurs directly, with no global mechanism.
responseLevels.full: Explains the impact-winter/food-chain-collapse mechanism reaching worldwide, cites the iridium layer and Chicxulub crater as evidence, and recognises birds survived.
responseLevels.partial: Knows an asteroid caused it and can name the crater or iridium layer, but explains the deaths by direct impact and cannot describe the worldwide food-chain collapse.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: About 66 million years ago an asteroid hit the Earth near Mexico and most dinosaurs died out. Did the asteroid kill all those dinosaurs just by crushing or burning them when it hit? Explain how a strike in one place could wipe out dinosaurs all over the world.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who pictures the asteroid as a giant direct killer says it flattened or burned the dinosaurs. A child who understands names the global 'impact winter' and food-chain collapse as the mechanism that reached the whole planet.

sources.claim: The Chicxulub crater (~180 km wide, Yucatán) was formed by an asteroid impact ~66 Mya at the end of the Cretaceous; the impact and resulting climate change caused a mass extinction that wiped out ~75–80% of species including the (non-avian) dinosaurs.
sources.source: Encyclopædia Britannica — Chicxulub

sources.claim: The asteroid hypothesis originated with Luis Alvarez's team finding unusually high iridium at the K–Pg boundary; iridium is rare in the crust (siderophile, sank to the core) but abundant in asteroids, and similar iridium spikes were found at the boundary worldwide.
sources.source: Wikipedia — Chicxulub crater (Alvarez hypothesis / iridium)

sources.claim: Drilling into the crater (IODP-ICDP Expedition 364) found the iridium anomaly WITHIN the peak-ring sequence, conclusively tying Chicxulub to the global iridium layer and K-Pg boundary sections worldwide; lead author Steven Goderis: 'The circle is now finally complete.'
sources.source: UT Austin (Jackson School of Geosciences) news release — asteroid dust found in crater

sources.claim: Impact evidence includes a global iridium-rich clay layer, shocked quartz and tektites; expedition found dust, sulfate aerosols and soot driving global cooling and reduced photosynthesis as extinction drivers; a rival Deccan Traps volcanism hypothesis (Gerta Keller) persists.
sources.source: Goderis et al., Science Advances (2021) abstract; Wikipedia review/dissent

pedagogy.summary: Two distinct ideas sit inside this topic and should be taught in order: (1) foods are sorted into the FOOD GROUPS of an appropriate local healthy-eating guide — in the UK the Eatwell Guide (fruit and vegetables; potatoes, bread, rice, pasta and other starchy carbohydrates; beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads), in Australia the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating (vegetables and legumes/beans; fruit; grain (cereal) foods; lean meats and poultry, fish, eggs, tofu, nuts and seeds, and legumes/beans; milk, yoghurt, cheese and/or alternatives) — while NUTRIENTS are what foods supply, taught separately, each with a job: carbohydrates for energy, proteins for growth and repair, fats for energy/warmth and storage, and vitamins, minerals and fibre (with water) for keeping the body working and protected; most foods supply several nutrients; and (2) a BALANCED diet means a variety of foods from each food group in the right AMOUNTS shown by the guide, not just having them all. Children readily learn the nutrient jobs but the balance/proportion idea is the harder, more important one — it is why 'eat lots of everything' or 'fat is bad' are wrong. Never call nutrients 'food groups', and never imagine a balanced plate as equal shares of seven nutrients: proportions belong to food groups (Eatwell: fruit/veg and starchy foods biggest, protein and dairy smaller, oils/spreads tiny, sugary/fatty treats outside and occasional). Teach with real/pictured foods the child eats, classify them with the guide, then BUILD a balanced plate so proportion is something they construct, not a rule they recite. Note that mixed dishes (pizza, sandwich) combine several food groups — a subtlety worth surfacing.
bestPractices: Teach nutrients and their jobs with familiar foods (bread supplies carbohydrate for energy; chicken supplies protein for growth and repair), noting that each food supplies several nutrients; separately, classify foods into the food groups of a local guide; then move to the harder idea of BALANCE — the right amounts from each food group.

Use a local healthy-eating guide's plate (e.g. the UK Eatwell Guide or the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating) as a 'build a plate' proportion model so balance is constructed and seen, not memorised; with Eatwell, fruit/veg and starchy foods are largest, protein and dairy smaller, oils/spreads small, treats outside and occasional.
Classify real or pictured everyday foods into the guide's food groups, and explicitly handle MIXED dishes (a sandwich, pizza) so children see a dish can combine several food groups.
Correct 'good food / bad food' thinking: no single food is banned; it's the overall balance and amount over a day or week that matters (per NHS guidance).
Avoid over-precision — no calorie counting; keep to groups, jobs and rough proportions appropriate to age, and connect diet to energy for activity and materials for growth.
keyRepresentations: Nutrient→job table with example foods (carbs=energy, protein=growth/repair, fats=energy/warmth, vitamins/minerals=protection, fibre=digestion, water=hydration), noting that each food supplies several nutrients

A local healthy-eating guide plate showing its food groups and recommended proportions (for example, the five groups of the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating); use the groupings of the selected local guide rather than assuming every guide has five groups
A 'build a balanced plate' sorting surface where portions fill each segment
Food-group sorting bins for classifying everyday foods with the guide (and a 'mixed foods' bin for pizza/sandwiches)
Over-a-day/week framing rather than every-meal-perfect
commonMisconceptions: Calling nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins) 'food groups', or imagining a balanced plate as equal shares of seven nutrients — food groups are groups of foods in a healthy-eating guide, and proportions follow those groups.
'Fat (or carbs, or sugar) is bad and should be avoided' — missing that fats/carbs are needed for energy; it's balance and amount that matter.
'A balanced diet means eating a bit of everything equally' — missing that the PROPORTIONS differ (more fruit/veg and starchy food, less oil).
'Each food supplies just one nutrient' or 'a mixed dish fits one food group' — pizza and sandwiches combine several food groups, and foods such as milk supply several nutrients.
'Vitamins/minerals give you energy' — they protect and help the body work; energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats.
'Healthy food = salad only / treats are forbidden' — rather than occasional treats fitting within an overall balance.
'You must eat perfectly at every meal' — missing that balance is judged over a day or week.
'Protein is only meat' — missing beans, pulses, eggs, dairy and fish as protein sources.

learn.summary: Teach two ideas in order for ages 7–9: (1) foods are sorted into the food groups of an appropriate local healthy-eating guide (the UK Eatwell Guide's five groups; in Australia, the five food groups of the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating), while nutrients are taught separately — what foods supply and the job each does (carbohydrates for energy; proteins for growth and repair; fats for energy, warmth and storage; vitamins, minerals and fibre, with water, for keeping the body working and protected), recognising that most foods supply several nutrients; and (2) a balanced diet means a variety of foods from each food group in the RIGHT AMOUNTS shown by the guide, not just having a bit of everything. The nutrient→job layer is easier; the proportion/balance idea is the harder, more valuable one and explains why 'eat lots of everything' and 'fat is bad' are wrong. Proportions belong to food groups, never to equal shares of nutrients (the UK Eatwell Guide, which replaced the earlier Eatwell plate in 2016: fruit/veg and starchy carbs biggest, protein and dairy smaller, oils/spreads tiny, sugary/fatty treats outside and occasional). Build balanced plates by hand rather than reciting rules, surface that mixed dishes (pizza, sandwiches) combine several food groups, and frame balance over a day or week rather than per-meal perfection. Avoid calorie counting; keep to food groups, nutrient jobs and rough proportions.

activities.title: Build a balanced plate
feedback: If the plate is all one food, ask: which food groups are missing, and which nutrient jobs (energy, growth material, protection) may now go short? Point back to the empty segments.

If portions are equal across all groups, prompt: the guide does not use equal shares — with the Eatwell Guide, fruit/veg and starchy foods are the biggest parts and oils/spreads tiny — adjust the amounts, not just which foods are present.
If a treat is placed into a main group, note that high fat/sugar foods sit outside the main groups and are eaten less often.
Praise correct reasoning that names a food's food group and the nutrients it supplies, not just that a food 'is healthy'.
activities.rationale: Constructing and adjusting proportions makes the abstract ratio of a balanced diet concrete and lets children discover, rather than memorise, that amounts differ by group. Building a plate matches the food-group proportion model of a local guide (here the Eatwell Guide) and the curriculum requirement to reason about the right types AND amount of nutrition.
sourceClaims: The Eatwell Guide divides foods into five main groups — fruit and vegetables and starchy carbohydrates (each just over a third of the plate), protein foods, dairy and alternatives, and oils/spreads (small amounts) — with high fat/salt/sugar foods outside the main groups, eaten less often; balance is judged over a day or week, not every meal.

The Australian Guide to Healthy Eating groups foods into five food groups — vegetables and legumes/beans; fruit; grain (cereal) foods, mostly wholegrain and/or high cereal fibre varieties; lean meats and poultry, fish, eggs, tofu, nuts and seeds, and legumes/beans; milk, yoghurt, cheese and/or alternatives, mostly reduced fat — and recommends a wide variety of foods from these groups every day.
Y3 pupils should identify that animals, including humans, need the right types and amount of nutrition, and that they cannot make their own food; they get nutrition from what they eat.
learnerActions: Collect real or pictured everyday foods the child actually eats, then sort each into the food groups of a local healthy-eating guide (Eatwell: fruit and vegetables; starchy carbohydrates; proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads, with treats outside the main groups — or the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating's five food groups).

Arrange foods onto a plate divided into the guide's food-group proportions (with Eatwell, fruit/veg and starchy foods fill the largest areas, protein and dairy smaller areas, oils/spreads a tiny area, and sugary/fatty treats sit off to the side as occasional).
Deliberately try an unbalanced plate — a mountain of chips only, or nothing but fruit — and describe which food groups are missing and which nutrient jobs may not be covered.

As each food is placed, say its food group and one main nutrient it supplies and what that nutrient does (e.g. bread: starchy food, supplies carbohydrate for energy; chicken: protein food, supplies protein for growth and repair), noting that most foods supply several nutrients.
Look across a whole day or week and check whether one wobbly meal is evened out by the others.
activities.intendedInsight: Balance is not 'a bit of everything equally' — it is the right amounts of each food group, with (in the Eatwell Guide) fruit/veg and starchy foods making up most of the plate and treats only occasional; and balance is judged over a day or week, not at every single meal.

activities.title: Match each nutrient to its job
feedback: If a learner says vitamins give energy or build muscle, separate the jobs: energy comes from carbohydrates, growth from protein; vitamins keep the body working and protect it, but are not fuel.
If protein is named only as meat, broaden to eggs, beans, lentils, fish and dairy — the nutrient does the job, not one specific food.
If energy is attributed only to sweets, distinguish quick sugar from the sustained energy of starchy carbohydrates.
activities.rationale: Establishing nutrient→job with familiar foods gives learners the vocabulary and functional reasoning they need before tackling proportion, and directly targets the common 'vitamins give energy' and 'protein = meat only' misconceptions. The specific nutrient functions are an age-appropriate framing not stated verbatim by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Reveal, one nutrient at a time, what each nutrient does for the body and list foods that supply it: carbohydrates = energy; protein = growth and repair; fats = energy, warmth and storage; vitamins and minerals = protection and keeping the body working; fibre = digestion; water = hydration.
For each nutrient, predict and then check what might happen if you had too much or too little of it.

Name at least five nutrients with a food that supplies each, say which food group each food belongs to, notice foods (such as milk) that supply several nutrients, and explain the job of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Each nutrient does a distinct job; vitamins and minerals protect and help the body work but do NOT supply energy — energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats.

activities.title: Sort mixed foods
feedback: If a sandwich is forced into a single group, ask what the bread, filling and spread each contribute.
Confirm when a learner explains that milk sits in one food group (dairy and alternatives) yet supplies several nutrients, such as protein, fat and calcium.
activities.rationale: Explicitly handling mixed dishes prevents the 'a dish fits one food group' misconception and makes real-world classification honest; the NHS Eatwell Guide treats pizzas, casseroles, pasta dishes and sandwiches as combinations of the food groups. Noting that single foods supply several nutrients keeps food groups and nutrients distinct.
sourceClaims: The Eatwell Guide divides the foods and drinks we consume into five main food groups (fruit and vegetables; potatoes, bread, rice, pasta and other starchy carbohydrates; beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads) and shows how much of what we eat overall should come from each; choosing a variety of foods from each group helps provide the wide range of nutrients the body needs, combination foods such as pizzas and sandwiches contain several food groups, and balance can be achieved over a day or a week.
learnerActions: Classify everyday foods into the guide's food-group bins, including a dedicated 'mixed foods' bin.
Break down mixed dishes — a pizza, a sandwich — into the food groups their ingredients come from, naming each part, and list the several nutrients a single food such as a glass of milk supplies.
Discuss why a mixed dish draws on several food groups, and why even a single food supplies several nutrients.
activities.intendedInsight: Mixed dishes combine foods from several food groups, and most foods supply several nutrients, so neither classification is one-to-one.

activities.title: Myth-busting: is this food bad for me?
feedback: If a learner says fat should be avoided completely, explain the body needs some fat for energy, warmth and storage; the issue is amount and balance, not cutting out a whole nutrient.
If a learner endorses Sam's oranges/vitamin-tablet plan, point out vitamins don't supply energy or build muscle — identify the carbohydrate source for energy and the protein source for growth.
If treats are called forbidden, reframe: occasional treats can fit within an overall balance.
Reward answers that reject 'healthy = strong' reasoning and correctly assign carbohydrates to energy and protein to growth.
activities.rationale: Discussion is well suited to confronting value-laden 'good food/bad food' thinking and the 'fat is bad' and 'vitamins give energy' misconceptions; it may complement, rather than replace, the hands-on plate building where proportion is best constructed. The Eatwell claim supports the 'no food banned / eaten less often / balance over a day or week' principle this activity rests on.
sourceClaims: The Eatwell Guide divides foods into five main groups — fruit and vegetables and starchy carbohydrates (each just over a third of the plate), protein foods, dairy and alternatives, and oils/spreads (small amounts) — with high fat/salt/sugar foods outside the main groups, eaten less often; balance is judged over a day or week, not every meal.
learnerActions: Pose 'is X bad for me?' questions and answer using nutrient jobs and overall balance rather than a 'good food / bad food' verdict.

Consider Sam's claim that fat is always bad and should be avoided completely — explain why the body still needs some fat (for energy, warmth and storage) and that it is the amount and balance that matter, not banning a whole nutrient.

Work through the swimmer example: Sam says he'll eat lots of oranges and take vitamin tablets because 'vitamins give you energy and make you strong' — decide whether to agree and explain what he should eat for energy (carbohydrates: bread, pasta, rice) and for building muscle (protein: chicken, fish, eggs, beans), and why each helps.
Reason about what might go wrong on race day if someone ate only protein and no carbohydrates, and why we still need vitamins regularly in our food even though they give no energy.
activities.intendedInsight: No single food or nutrient is simply 'bad' or 'banned' — even fats are needed for energy, warmth and storage; it is the overall balance and amount across a day or week that matters, and each nutrient must be matched to the job it actually does.

constraints: Teach nutrients and their jobs with familiar foods, classify foods separately with a local guide's food groups, then move to the harder balance/proportion idea.

Classify foods with an appropriate local healthy-eating guide's food groups (e.g. the UK Eatwell Guide or the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating); never call nutrients 'food groups', and set plate proportions by the guide's food groups, never as equal shares of seven nutrients.
Do not introduce calorie counting; keep to food groups, nutrient jobs and rough age-appropriate proportions.
Correct 'good food / bad food' thinking: no food or nutrient is banned, including fat; overall balance and amount over a day or week is what matters.
Food-group classification must explicitly include mixed dishes (pizza, sandwich), and nutrient tasks must note that one food (e.g. milk) supplies several nutrients.

Recognition/matching tasks (categorising foods, picking the balanced plate) consolidate and assess but do not by themselves require learners to construct and adjust proportions — pair them with hands-on plate building.
A tap-to-reveal or lift-the-flap plate teaches the nutrient→job layer well but does not let the learner construct and adjust proportions; treat it as a scaffold toward building a plate.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: dragging foods into segments that fill up, a balance gauge that visibly tips when a tray is overloaded, instant group-classification feedback, and a day/week view showing a single wobbly meal evening out. These are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source listed a 3D format as 'poor' with the claim '3D adds no conceptual value'; this universal comparative claim is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped rather than propagated as a pedagogical law.

The original 'ideal' rationale asserted that building proportions is something 'no static image or quiz can do'; this comparative necessity claim is not supported by the cited sources. It has been softened to a narrowly scoped affordance (construction/adjustment) plus an objective limit (recognition tasks don't elicit independent construction).

sourceClaims remain [] on the 'Match each nutrient to its job' activity: no cited claim states the nutrient→job mapping, so that content is a sound, age-appropriate proposal rather than a source-evidenced finding. The 'Sort mixed foods' activity now cites the NHS Eatwell Guide, which treats pizzas and sandwiches as combinations of food groups. The build-a-plate activity retains the curriculum claim because it references the right 'amount' of nutrition (borderline rather than clear-cut support) and now also cites the Australian food groups.

The 'fat is always bad' probe question from the original assessment had been dropped from the candidate's learner-facing activities despite being a prominent misconception; it has been restored to the myth-busting activity with matching feedback.

The diagnostic 'correctAnswer' states vitamins do not 'directly build muscle'; this is consistent with the age-appropriate framing (energy from carbohydrates/fats, growth from protein) and no error was found. Framing fats as 'warmth and storage' is simplified but acceptable for ages 7–9.

Source claims cite the Eatwell Guide and the national curriculum; they support the teaching principles of proportion and 'right types and amount of nutrition' but do not constitute evidence that any specific activity here was tested for effectiveness.

Nutrition review (October 2026): the topic previously grouped foods 'by the nutrient they mainly provide' and called nutrients food groups. Corrected throughout: foods are classified with the food groups of a local healthy-eating guide (UK Eatwell Guide; Australian Guide to Healthy Eating for Australian examples); nutrients and their functions are taught separately, and most foods supply several; plate proportions follow food groups, not equal shares of nutrients. The NHS Eatwell page was fetched and checked; the Eat for Health page could not be fetched (timeout), so its claim is verified:false. Learning aims and activities are kept.

probeDeeper: Sam says fat is always bad and should be avoided completely. Is there any reason the body needs some fat?
If Sam ate only protein and no carbohydrates at all, what might go wrong on race day?
If vitamins don't give energy, why do we still need them every day?
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree with Sam. Vitamins don't give energy or directly build muscle — they help the body work properly and protect it from illness. For energy he needs carbohydrates (bread, pasta, rice); for building and repairing muscle he needs protein (chicken, fish, eggs, beans). What matters is the JOB each nutrient does, not whether a food merely seems 'healthy'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Vitamins give you energy and build muscle ('oranges make you strong').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the jobs: energy comes from carbohydrates, growth from protein; vitamins keep the body working and protect it — useful, but not fuel. Sort foods by the job they do.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — oranges and vitamin tablets give energy and build muscle, so Sam's plan is good.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endorses Sam's plan; names vitamins as the energy or muscle source.

errorPatterns.pattern: Energy only comes from sugary or sweet foods ('eat sweets for energy').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish quick sugar from the sustained energy of starchy carbohydrates; connect to what athletes actually eat before endurance events.
errorPatterns.distractor: He should eat sweets and sugary drinks for energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Recommends sugary foods/drinks as the energy source rather than carbohydrates.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only meat builds muscle, so you can't build muscle without eating meat.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Broaden protein sources beyond meat (eggs, beans, lentils, fish, dairy); the nutrient, not the specific food, does the job.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only meat can build muscle, so Sam must eat meat.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names meat as the sole protein source; excludes eggs, fish, beans, dairy.

responseLevels.gap: Judges foods only as 'healthy' or 'unhealthy', or thinks vitamins give energy; can't match a nutrient to its job.
responseLevels.full: Matches each nutrient to its function AND reasons about a real diet — why carbohydrates fuel the race, protein builds muscle, vitamins protect without giving energy — and can say what fails if a nutrient is missing.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts foods into food groups and names nutrients with examples, and can recite carbs=energy, protein=growth, but treats them as a list — can't reason about whether a particular diet meets a specific need, or slips on vitamins.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Sam is training for a swimming race and wants stronger muscles. He says 'I'll eat lots of oranges and take vitamin tablets, because vitamins give you energy and make you strong.' Do you agree with Sam's plan? What SHOULD he eat for energy and for building muscle — and why does each food help with its job?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'healthy = strong/energy' or 'vitamins give energy' endorses Sam. A child who understands nutrient function rejects the plan and correctly assigns carbohydrates to energy and protein to growth. Because the tier-two 'why' forces the nutrient-to-job link, you can't land it by guessing that oranges are healthy.
