pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Acid Reactions & Salts

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Chemical reactions):** pupils are taught "reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen" and "neutralisation of acids by alkalis, e.g. to produce a salt plus water," and to represent chemical reactions using word equations.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-2):** analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred — the salt formed is a new substance with new properties.

- **Operational details:** Build from the pupil's existing pH/neutralisation knowledge to the idea that neutralising an acid does not make the atoms vanish — it converts them into a NEW substance, a salt, plus water (or plus hydrogen when a metal is used). Anchor the two reaction families: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen (test the gas with a lit splint, the squeaky pop); acid + alkali → salt + water (neutralisation, follow with an indicator to pH 7). Teach the naming rule that the acid decides the salt's surname: hydrochloric → chloride, sulfuric → sulfate, nitric → nitrate; the metal or the metal in the alkali gives the first name. Keep it to word equations at KS3 — symbol equations and mole calculations are KS4. Recover the salt by evaporating the solution to grow visible crystals, closing the loop that a dissolved product is still there.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). The child predicts the products of acid + metal and acid + alkali reactions and names the salt from the acid used, writing a correct word equation — without yet needing balanced symbol equations.
bestPractices: Anchor to the two canonical reaction families explicitly — acid + metal → salt + hydrogen, and acid + alkali → salt + water — and keep returning to them so pupils sort any new example into one or the other.

Make the salt-naming rule a predictable pattern the child applies, not a list to memorise: the acid fixes the ending (hydrochloric→chloride, sulfuric→sulfate, nitric→nitrate), the metal fixes the first word.
Use the hydrogen pop-test and an indicator endpoint as observable signatures that distinguish the two families in real time.
Recover the salt by evaporation so the child sees the dissolved product is a real, tangible solid — reinforcing conservation of matter across the reaction.
Stay at word-equation level; defer symbol equations, state symbols and moles to KS4 so the productive naming rule is secure first.
keyRepresentations: The two family templates: 'acid + metal → salt + hydrogen' and 'acid + alkali → salt + water'.
A word-equation builder that assembles reactants and products with the salt auto-named from the acid.
The pH/indicator scale used as a neutralisation endpoint (stops at 7).
The hydrogen squeaky-pop test as the gas signature.
Evaporating basin growing salt crystals as the recovered product.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking neutralisation makes the acid 'disappear' rather than converting it into a salt plus water.
Believing a salt means only table salt (sodium chloride), not a whole family of compounds.
Assuming every acid reaction gives off a gas — confusing acid + metal (hydrogen released) with acid + alkali (no gas, water formed).
Mixing up the salt endings, e.g. expecting sulfuric acid to give a 'sulfide' rather than a sulfate.
Thinking the dissolved salt is 'gone' once it is in solution, rather than recoverable by evaporation.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12–13 learn that reacting an acid does not make matter vanish — atoms are rearranged into NEW substances: a salt plus water when the acid is neutralised by an alkali or a metal oxide/hydroxide, or a salt plus hydrogen when a reactive metal reacts. Learners anchor the reaction families (acid + metal → salt + hydrogen, shown with reactive metals such as magnesium, zinc or iron and dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid; acid + alkali → salt + water; acid + metal oxide or metal hydroxide → salt + water), apply a predictable salt-naming rule (the acid fixes the ending: hydrochloric→chloride, sulfuric→sulfate, nitric→nitrate; the metal or metal-in-the-base gives the first word), observe family-distinguishing signatures (hydrogen squeaky-pop test; indicator reaching pH 7), and recover the dissolved salt by evaporation to crystals. Work stays at word-equation level; symbol equations, state symbols and moles are deferred. Activities are proposals; concrete bench chemistry and manipulable models are complementary ways to run the predict–observe–name loop.

activities.title: The salt maker: run reactions, name the salt, write the word equation
feedback: If a learner expects every acid reaction to give off a gas, contrast the two runs directly: a reactive metal in dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid fizzes and gives hydrogen (squeaky pop), while acid + alkali gives no gas and forms water — same acid, different partner, different products.
If a learner writes 'sulfide' for a sulfuric-acid salt, point back to the ending rule: sulfuric→sulfate, nitric→nitrate, hydrochloric→chloride.

If a learner thinks the neutral mixture holds 'nothing', have them evaporate it — the leftover crystals prove the salt was dissolved there all along; 'neutral' means acidity and alkalinity are balanced, not that matter disappeared.
Once three or four runs are done, ask the learner to predict the salt's name before any writing appears, confirming the rule is felt rather than looked up.
activities.rationale: The topic is a set of rule-governed transformations: pick reactants, run the reaction, observe products, name the salt. Letting learners choose reactants and see the fizz / pop-test / indicator endpoint makes the naming rule felt through repetition, and the evaporation step makes it tangible that the products did not vanish (the dissolved salt is recovered, although the water driven off is lost, so evaporation does not itself demonstrate mass conservation). Optional interactive affordances (dragging reactants into a flask, a splint giving a pop, an indicator sweeping colour to pH 7, an auto-assembled word equation, an evaporate-to-crystals step) make the learning mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not required.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen, and neutralisation of acids by alkalis to produce a salt plus water, using word equations.

Salt naming follows the acid: hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, sulfuric acid gives sulfates, nitric acid gives nitrates; acids react with metals to give salt + hydrogen and with alkalis to give salt + water.
learnerActions: Choose dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid and pair it with a moderately reactive metal such as magnesium, zinc or iron (not copper, which does not react, and never sodium or potassium); observe bubbles rising and test the gas at the mouth of the tube with a lit splint — a squeaky pop signals hydrogen. (Nitric acid is fine for the naming rule with alkalis and oxides, but with metals it usually gives nitrogen oxides rather than hydrogen, so it is not used for this run.)

Keep the same acid but this time use an alkali (e.g. sodium hydroxide solution) instead of the metal; with indicator already in the acid, add the alkali gradually, a little at a time — observe that there is no fizz, and watch the indicator change until it shows pH 7 (neutralisation), giving salt + water.

After each run, state the salt's full name before it is written out, deriving the surname from the acid (chloride/sulfate/nitrate) and the first word from the metal or the metal in the alkali, then write the complete word equation (e.g. magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen).

Finish by evaporating the neutral solution to drive off the water and leave visible salt crystals in the dish (for purer crystals, repeat the neutralisation with the same volumes but no indicator, because indicator left in the solution colours the salt).

Repeat with new pairings — acid/reactive metal (dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid), acid/alkali, and acid/metal oxide or hydroxide (e.g. copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water) — so the naming rule generalises across examples rather than being memorised as a list.
activities.intendedInsight: Neutralising or reacting an acid converts it into a real, recoverable salt (plus hydrogen or water) — matter is conserved and rearranged, not destroyed — and the salt's name follows predictably from the acid and the metal.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: what is left when the water evaporates?
feedback: If the learner predicts an empty dish, treat that prediction as the diagnostic: the crystals that appear show matter remained — reframe 'neutral' as balanced acidity/alkalinity, not annihilation.

Full-credit reasoning names salt + water as the products and explicitly rejects 'cancelled to nothing'; a partial answer rejects 'nothing' but cannot yet name the specific salt for a new acid/base pair.
Probe generalisation: hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide gives potassium chloride, not sodium chloride — the first name comes from the metal in the alkali used.
activities.rationale: Eliciting a pre-observation prediction about the products is the diagnostic that separates a learner who tracks conservation of matter from one who reads 'neutral' as things disappearing. The written prediction must come before the observation so the reasoning, not just the outcome, is assessed.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen, and neutralisation of acids by alkalis to produce a salt plus water, using word equations.
Students analyse and interpret data on properties of substances before and after they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Neutralise an acid with an alkali until the indicator reads pH 7.
BEFORE evaporating, write down a prediction: if all the water is driven off, what (if anything) will remain, and WHY?
Evaporate the water and compare the result with the prediction.
Write the word equation for what happened (acid + alkali → salt + water) and explain in words why 'neutral' does not mean 'empty'.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'cancelled to nothing' model predicts an empty dish; the solid salt crystals that remain disprove it. Neutralisation produces a salt plus water, and mass is conserved as atoms rearrange into new products.

activities.title: Complete and name: word-equation practice across families
feedback: For 'sulfuric acid + zinc', the correct completion is 'zinc sulfate + hydrogen'; if a learner writes 'zinc sulfide', return to the sulfuric→sulfate ending.

If a learner answers 'salt + water' for an acid + metal reaction, re-anchor the squeaky-pop test: reactive metals in dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid release hydrogen, whereas alkalis, metal oxides and metal hydroxides form water.
Treat 'salt' as a whole family of compounds (copper sulfate, potassium nitrate, …), not only edible table salt; the specific salt depends on the acid and base used.
activities.rationale: Completing equations, matching endings, choosing the gas, and naming salts for new pairs exercise the productive rule rather than mere recognition. Constructing the full equation and the salt name — not just picking from options — is what demonstrates the generalisation. A related prerequisite on acid+metal products can be revisited if hydrogen is persistently omitted.
sourceClaims: Salt naming follows the acid: hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, sulfuric acid gives sulfates, nitric acid gives nitrates; acids react with metals to give salt + hydrogen and with alkalis to give salt + water.
KS3 pupils are taught reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen, and neutralisation of acids by alkalis to produce a salt plus water, using word equations.
learnerActions: Complete partial word equations, e.g. 'sulfuric acid + zinc → zinc ____ + ____', filling both the salt surname and the gas.
Match each acid to its salt ending: hydrochloric→chloride, sulfuric→sulfate, nitric→nitrate.
Decide, for a given pairing, whether hydrogen or water is produced, and justify the choice by naming the family (acid+reactive metal vs acid+alkali or acid+metal oxide/hydroxide).
Name the salt from an unfamiliar acid/base pair (e.g. hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide → potassium chloride + water) and state why it is not sodium chloride.
State the pH at the neutralisation endpoint (7) and name the gas test for hydrogen (lit splint, squeaky pop).
activities.intendedInsight: The productive salt-naming rule and the family distinction (hydrogen vs water) can be applied to new pairings, not just recognised in familiar ones.

activities.title: Vocabulary and family contrast (introductory scaffold)
feedback: Use this to establish terms, then move to running varied pairings — a fixed picture introduces vocabulary but does not let the learner change reactants or feel the naming rule generalise, so follow it with the salt-maker and equation-completion activities.
Check understanding by asking the learner to produce (not just recognise) one word equation from each family after studying the diagram.
activities.rationale: A static labelled diagram with reveal-on-tap parts can introduce vocabulary and contrast the two families efficiently, but it is a scaffold: it cannot let the child vary reactants, observe the gas test, or construct and name salts independently, which is the heart of the topic.
learnerActions: Study a labelled picture of a neutralisation (acid + alkali → salt + water), revealing the names of the acid, the alkali, the salt crystals and the role of each part.
Contrast a side-by-side pair of the two reaction families and say, for each, whether a gas is released and what the other product is.
Connect the vocabulary to a real application: indigestion tablets neutralise stomach acid, and treating acidic soil raises its pH.
activities.intendedInsight: Names and family vocabulary (acid, alkali, salt, neutralisation, hydrogen) and the two product patterns are introduced before learners run and generalise them.

constraints: Stay at word-equation level; defer symbol equations, state symbols, balancing and mole calculations to the next stage (KS4).

The labelled-diagram activity is an introductory scaffold: it builds vocabulary but does not elicit independent construction of equations or salt names, so it must be followed by activities where learners run reactions and name salts themselves.

Keep returning to the canonical templates (acid + reactive metal → salt + hydrogen, using dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid; acid + alkali → salt + water) and include acid + metal oxide or metal hydroxide → salt + water as a required third route, because the objective covers metal oxides/hydroxides; sort each new example into one of these families.
Screen or app models of the reactions are complements to, not substitutes for, a real bench neutralisation and evaporation done in class; pair the simulated loop with hands-on practical work.

Recognition-only tasks (matching, multiple choice) check the rule but do not by themselves show the learner can independently construct a correct word equation or name a salt for a new pairing — include construction tasks.
Teach 'salt' as a general class of acid+base products; do not let examples imply every neutralisation yields edible table salt.
In the neutralisation step, the alkali (or acid) is added gradually with indicator already present to reach pH 7; the indicator only reports pH and does not itself drive the reaction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles rather than proving any activity was tested.
The original row listed two sources as not verified (NGSS MS-PS1-2 and the RSC making-salts resource); their claims are reused here as teaching principles, not as verified evidence.

Self-audit of chemistry: 'sulfuric acid + zinc → zinc sulfate + hydrogen' is correct (sulfate, not sulfide; hydrogen gas, not water). Acid+metal releases hydrogen; acid+alkali forms water; acid+metal oxide/hydroxide forms water — these product sets are distinct and were kept distinct. The salt's first name derives from the metal (or the metal in the alkali): hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide gives potassium chloride, not sodium chloride. No arithmetic or force/motion content required checking here.

Fixed a sequencing incoherence in the salt-maker neutralisation step: the alkali is now added gradually once, with the indicator already present in the acid, so the learner observes both the absence of fizz and the indicator sweep to pH 7; the indicator reports pH and does not drive the reaction.

The original 'poor fit' rationales asserting that a 3D lab 'adds nothing' and that dialogue 'cannot deliver' the loop were softened: these are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the sources. The genuine, retained limit is that recognition-only formats do not elicit independent construction and that a static diagram cannot let learners vary reactants.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: neutralise acid with alkali to pH 7, then ask the child to predict what remains if the water is evaporated away, and WHY, before doing it. A 'cancelled to nothing' model predicts an empty dish. Evaporation leaves solid salt crystals. The pre-observation reasoning about products is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I evaporate the neutral mixture, what would I find — and what does that prove about 'cancelling to nothing'?
Indigestion tablets work by neutralising stomach acid. What's being made in your stomach when they work?
Hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide — name the salt. Why isn't it sodium chloride?
How is the acid+metal reaction different in its products from acid+alkali? What test proves it?
assess.correctAnswer: No — nothing vanished. Neutralisation produces a SALT plus WATER: here sodium chloride dissolved in water (acid + alkali → salt + water). 'Neutral' means the acidity and alkalinity are balanced, not that matter disappeared — the atoms rearranged into new products (mass is conserved). Full marks name salt + water as the products and reject 'cancelled to nothing'.

errorPatterns.pattern: neutralisation makes the substances disappear / cancel to nothing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Evaporate the neutral mixture — solid salt is left behind, proving matter remained. Reframe 'neutral' as balanced, not empty; write acid + alkali → salt + water.
errorPatterns.distractor: Nothing — the acid and alkali cancelled each other out completely.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the beaker holds 'nothing' or 'just cancelled out' after neutralising

errorPatterns.pattern: 'salt' means only table salt (NaCl), not a general class of compounds
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce 'salt' as the whole family of acid+base products; the specific salt depends on the acid and base used. Table salt is just one member.
errorPatterns.distractor: It makes table salt you could eat, whatever acid and alkali you use.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: expects edible table salt from every neutralisation, or is confused when the salt is copper sulfate/potassium nitrate

errorPatterns.pattern: acid + metal gives the same products as acid + alkali (misremembers hydrogen vs water)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the three routes: acid+metal → salt + HYDROGEN; acid+alkali → salt + water; acid+metal oxide → salt + water. Use the squeaky-pop test to anchor hydrogen.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: writes 'salt + water' for acid+metal, or omits the hydrogen gas

responseLevels.gap: Says neutralisation leaves 'nothing'/cancels out; thinks 'salt' only means table salt; muddles the product sets.
responseLevels.full: Names salt + water as neutralisation products, treats 'salt' as a general class and names the specific salt from the acid/base used, distinguishes all three acid-reaction routes with their gas/water products, and grounds it in conservation of mass and a real application.
responseLevels.partial: States acid+alkali → salt + water and rejects 'nothing', but can't name the specific salt for a new acid/base pair or distinguish acid+metal (hydrogen) from acid+alkali (water) — the pattern without generalisation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I mix hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide (an alkali) in the right amounts and the mixture ends up neutral, pH 7. A student says 'so now there's nothing left — they cancelled each other out to nothing.' Is that right — what is actually in the beaker now? Then explain what neutralisation really produces.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two question distinguishes a child who tracks the products of neutralisation (a salt + water form; matter conserved) from one who reads 'neutral' as annihilation. It also probes whether 'salt' is understood as a general class (any acid+base salt) rather than only table salt.

pedagogy.summary: Composing 3-D shapes — stacking and combining solids to build new structures and composite shapes — develops through a well-charted progression from unsystematic stacking, through trial-and-error assembly, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION ('I know the cone goes on top'). It is best taught with plentiful block-building using real solids, where the teacher notices and gently nudges children toward the next level — asking them to predict which shape will fit before placing it and to describe their creation by its component solids. Matched building challenges pitched one level ahead move children forward more effectively than jumping straight to the target.
bestPractices: Give rich, open block-building with a range of solids (cubes, prisms, cylinders, cones) and let children build and knock down freely at first.
Nudge toward anticipation: 'Can you see which shape will fit on top before you place it?' — shifting from trial and error to planning.
Pitch challenges one level beyond the child's current building (e.g. from stacking identical blocks to combining a cone on a cylinder), scaffolding then fading support.
Ask the child to describe the composite by its parts — name each component solid and where it sits.
Attend to which faces sit flat: choosing a flat-faced solid for the base keeps a structure stable.
keyRepresentations: Real 3-D blocks and construction manipulatives
Target-picture cards of composites (cone-on-cylinder rocket, cube tower, house)
The stack ('on') relationship; flat-faced base vs rolling curved base
Component-labelled composite diagrams
commonMisconceptions: Adds blocks unsystematically and only recognises what it 'looks like' after building — no advance plan (a normal early trajectory level, not a fault).
Builds a composite but describes it only as one whole ('a rocket') and cannot name the component solids or their positions.
Places solids without regard to which faces are flat, so a cone or sphere used as a base makes the structure topple.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 learn to compose 3-D shapes by stacking and combining real solids (cubes, prisms, cylinders, cones, spheres) into composite structures. The target skill is a progression: from unsystematic stacking, through trial-and-error assembly, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION — knowing in advance which shape will fit ('the cone goes on top') and naming a build by its component solids and their positions. Hands-on block-building with challenges pitched one level ahead, plus prompts to predict and describe, carries children forward; because this is a procedural, construction-based goal, physical block-building is the core medium. An on-screen 3-D sandbox is an optional supplementary model that preserves stacking, balance and depth, while flat drag-and-combine and matching tasks are useful scaffolds for naming parts but do not exercise balance or anticipation.

activities.title: Build a rocket with real solids
feedback: If the child places shapes at random and names the result only afterwards, do not mark this wrong — it is an expected early level. Offer a challenge one step ahead and prompt 'can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
If the child names only the whole ('a rocket') but not the parts, take the composite apart and name each solid together, then rebuild it, naming each shape as it goes on.

If the tower topples, look together at which faces rest on the table or on the shape below: a sphere rolls because it has no flat face, a cone balanced on its point has no flat face down, and a piece placed off-centre can tip over. So choose a flat-faced solid (a cube, prism, or cylinder on a flat face) for the base, keep each piece centred, and don't stack anything on a cone's point, rather than blaming the blocks.
Reinforce correct anticipation: when the child reaches for the cone before placing it, confirm the plan aloud ('yes — the cone fits on top of the cylinder').
activities.rationale: Composing is an action: building, balancing and anticipating are exercised by actual construction with solids, not by recognising a finished picture. The documented trajectory runs from trial-and-error, post-hoc recognition to composing with anticipation and advance planning, and the curriculum asks children to compose and model shapes by building from components.
sourceClaims: Composing 3-D shapes develops through levels — Stacker and Same-Shape Stacker (using the 'on' relationship), Piece Assembler and Picture Maker (building components, arches and enclosures by unsystematic trial and error), then Shape Composer (composing with anticipation, understanding what 3-D shape a combination will produce and building systematically).

Shape composition progresses from trial-and-error, post-hoc recognition (Piece Assembler, Picture Maker) to composing with anticipation and advance planning (Shape Composer); teaching contiguous trajectory levels, scaffolded one level ahead, produced greater learning than jumping to the target level (effect size .55).
Kindergarten geometry asks children to compose simple shapes to form larger shapes and to model shapes by building from components.
learnerActions: Offer a set of real 3-D blocks: cubes, a cylinder, a cone, some prisms, and a sphere.
Ask the child to build a rocket by combining shapes so that it stands up.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Which shape will fit on top before you place it? Where will it go and why does it fit?'
After building, ask the child to point to and name each shape used and say where it sits (e.g. 'a cylinder at the bottom, a cone on top').

Try using the sphere as the base (or balancing the cone on its point) and let the child notice that it rolls or will not support more shapes, then choose a flat-faced solid — a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face — for the base.
activities.intendedInsight: A composite is made of named component solids combined on purpose; resting flat faces down keeps a structure stable, and you can plan which shape fits before placing it rather than only recognising the result afterwards.

activities.title: Challenges pitched one level ahead
feedback: If the challenge is too hard, step back one level and rebuild success before advancing again.
Praise the planning talk ('I'll put the cone on top next'), not just the finished structure.
activities.rationale: Teaching contiguous trajectory levels, scaffolded one level ahead, produced greater learning than jumping to the target level in the cited study.
sourceClaims: Shape composition progresses from trial-and-error, post-hoc recognition (Piece Assembler, Picture Maker) to composing with anticipation and advance planning (Shape Composer); teaching contiguous trajectory levels, scaffolded one level ahead, produced greater learning than jumping to the target level (effect size .55).
learnerActions: Watch how the child currently builds to judge their level (free stacking, trial-and-error assembly, or anticipating).
Set a building challenge just one step beyond that level — for example, from stacking identical cubes to combining a cone on a cylinder, or from trial-and-error assembly to predicting the next piece.
Scaffold with prompts and modelling, then gradually fade support as the child succeeds.
Repeat the same build and ask the child to say each shape as they add it.
activities.intendedInsight: Children advance most when the next task is just ahead of their current building, with support that fades, rather than jumping straight to the final target.

activities.title: On-screen 3-D building sandbox (optional)
feedback: If a build topples because of a rolling base, let the child retry with a flat-faced base and connect the failure to the face that rolled.
Use the tap-to-name feature to help a child who sees only the whole begin to decompose it into component solids.
activities.rationale: An interactive 3-D build space preserves the stacking, balance and depth that define 3-D composition, which flat 2-D drag-and-combine loses. It is offered as a supplementary medium option alongside physical blocks, not as a replacement for hands-on construction, and the cited sources do not establish that either medium is superior.
learnerActions: Drag 3-D solids into a build space and snap a cone onto a cylinder to make a rocket.
Try placing a sphere as a base; if the sandbox simulates gravity, watch whether it rolls and the tower falls, and talk about which faces must sit flat.
Before placing a piece, respond to the prompt 'which shape will fit on top?'
Tap the finished build to hear its component solids named in order ('cylinder… cone').
activities.intendedInsight: A 3-D model lets a child stack, combine and test balance, plan placements and have parts named — exercising the composing skill, including why a solid with no flat face, such as a sphere, makes a poor base.

activities.title: Match composites to their parts (naming activity)
feedback: If the child names only the whole, point to each region and name the solid, then ask them to repeat which part is the cylinder and which is the cone.
Treat this as a recognition and vocabulary scaffold; follow it with actual building so the child plans and balances, not just recognises.
activities.rationale: Matching and tap-to-name references can build and check part-naming vocabulary, but they support and check recognition rather than the act of composing with anticipation or managing balance; no cited source establishes a matching task as necessary or sufficient for the composing skill.
learnerActions: Show a picture or model of a composite (e.g. a cone-on-cylinder rocket, a cube tower, a house).
Ask the child to choose which component solids make it up and where each one sits.
Optionally use a reference image where tapping a part names it (rocket = cone + cylinder).
activities.intendedInsight: A composite can be decomposed into named component solids, each in a particular position — reinforcing part-naming vocabulary.

constraints: The core objective is composing with anticipation and describing a build by its component solids and their positions — this is a procedural curriculum goal that requires actual construction, with physical block-building as the core medium, not only recognising a finished shape.
Treat unsystematic stacking and post-hoc recognition as an expected early developmental level, not an error to drill or mark wrong; advance with one-step-ahead challenges.
Matching tasks and tap-to-name reference images support/check part-naming vocabulary (recognition) but do not themselves elicit independent construction, balancing, or advance planning.
Flat 2-D drag-and-combine can name parts but cannot convey which faces sit flat or how a tower balances; use it only as a naming scaffold.

Balance depends partly on resting flat faces down: a sphere (no flat face) rolls; a cone stands steadily base-down, but it topples if balanced on its point, rolls if laid on its side, and cannot hold a block on its apex; a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face is stable on its own, although a tower can still topple if pieces are placed off-centre or it gets too tall and narrow. Use this to explain why a flat-faced base is a good choice, not as a claim about any specific product.
A fixed labelled picture can still teach part-naming as a reference, but cannot be manipulated to practise stacking or anticipation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The cited effect size (.55) and the trajectory-level descriptions are copied from the original source claims and were not independently re-verified here.

The original marked an on-screen 3-D sandbox as 'ideal' and dialogue/2-D as poor; these catalog fit rankings have been removed. Comparative-necessity framing ('dialogue cannot substitute', 'a static picture cannot teach') has been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. The cited sources establish the developmental trajectory and one-level-ahead scaffolding, not the superiority of any particular medium.

Physical blocks and an on-screen model offer different experiences (real tactile balance vs. resettable digital trials); physical construction is the curriculum-required core medium and neither is asserted as universally necessary over the other for every learner.

The original row stated a cone used as a base topples; this was clarified because a cone can sit stably on its flat circular face. The instability is specific to a sphere (no flat face) or a cone balanced on its point / used to support further stacking on its apex.

probeDeeper: Before you place that shape — can you tell me where it will go and why it fits?
Point to each shape you used and name it — which is the cylinder, which is the cone?
Why does the tower fall when the cone is at the bottom? Which shapes make a good base?
Can you build the same rocket again, telling me each shape as you add it?
assess.correctAnswer: Selects and stacks solids with anticipation to make the intended composite (e.g. a cylinder body with a cone on top), keeps it stable by resting flat faces down, and describes the result by naming its component solids and their positions ('a cylinder at the bottom, a cone on top').

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds blocks unsystematically and recognises what the structure 'looks like' only after building — no advance plan for the composite
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill or mark this 'wrong' — it is an expected early level; offer building challenges one step ahead and prompt 'can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places shapes at random and names the result post hoc; cannot say in advance which shape will fit

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a composite but describes it only as one whole ('a rocket') and cannot name the component solids or their positions
errorPatterns.nextMove: Take the composite apart and name each solid, then rebuild it naming each shape as it goes on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the whole structure but not the cylinder/cone parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Places solids without regard to which faces are flat, so the structure will not balance — a cone or sphere used as a base makes it topple
errorPatterns.nextMove: Notice together which faces are flat and rest on the table, and choose a flat-faced solid for the base
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tower falls; the child blames the blocks rather than the choice of base

responseLevels.gap: Stacks blocks unsystematically and names only the whole ('a tower'); cannot say which solids make it up.
responseLevels.full: Selects and combines solids with anticipation to make a planned composite, keeps it stable by resting flat faces down, and describes the result by its component solids and their positions.
responseLevels.partial: Builds the intended composite, often by trial and error, and names some parts, but does not choose shapes with anticipation or explain why a shape fits or balances.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are some 3-D blocks — cubes, a cylinder, a cone, some prisms. Build me a rocket by putting shapes together so it stands up. As you build, and when you finish, tell me which shapes you used and where each one is.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the build separates the child who composes with anticipation ('I know the cone goes on top', reaching for it before placing) from the trial-and-error assembler who stacks unsystematically and recognises the result only afterwards. Asking the child to name the parts exposes whether they can decompose the composite into its component solids rather than seeing it as one undifferentiated 'rocket'.

sources.claim: Composing 3-D shapes develops through levels — Stacker and Same-Shape Stacker (using the 'on' relationship), Piece Assembler and Picture Maker (building components, arches and enclosures by unsystematic trial and error), then Shape Composer (composing with anticipation, understanding what 3-D shape a combination will produce and building systematically).

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Recognise that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place is worth TEN TIMES what the same digit is worth in the place to its right (and one-tenth of the place to its left): the 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300; 700 ÷ 70 = 10. This names the multiplicative ×10 structure that has been implicit since 'ten ones make a ten'.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): place value work where pupils recognise the value of each digit and the relationships between places (×10 between adjacent columns).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.1 'a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right'; 5.NBT.1 extends to 1/10 to the left.
• Operational details — Make explicit the multiplicative relationship between adjacent columns using a Gattegno/place-value chart: sliding a digit one column left multiplies its value by 10; one column right divides by 10. Contrast with the ADDITIVE view (partitioning) so children hold both: 3,452 is 3000+400+50+2 AND each place is ×10 the next. Use division sentences (700÷70=10) to expose the relationship.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): states the 3 in 3,000 is worth more than in 300 and by how much with support. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): explains any digit is ×10 the place to its right and computes 700÷70. Tier C (age 10, extending): quantifies 'how many times greater' across non-adjacent places (5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 5,000) and links to ×/÷ by powers of 10.
bestPractices: Use a Gattegno / place-value chart: sliding a digit left ×10s its value, right ÷10s it — make the multiplicative move physical.
Hold the additive (partition) and multiplicative (×10 between places) views together so place value is understood both ways.
Expose the relationship with division/multiplication sentences (700 ÷ 70 = 10; 30 = 3 × 10).
Compare the same digit across places ('how many times greater is the 5 in 50,000 than in 5,000?').
Bridge to multiplying/dividing by 10/100/1000 so the pattern has calculation payoff.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno place-value chart (rows scale ×10 down each column)
Place-value chart with a digit sliding between columns
Base-ten pieces showing ten-of-one-unit = one-of-next
Multiplication/division sentences (×10, ÷10) between places
Arrow-card / expanded form as the additive counterpart
commonMisconceptions: Seeing place value only additively and missing the ×10 relationship between places.
Thinking the 3 in 3,000 is '10 more' than in 300 rather than 10 times.
Confusing 'ten times' with 'add a zero' as a meaningless trick (fails for decimals later).
Miscounting the factor across non-adjacent places (×10 vs ×100).
Not connecting 700÷70=10 to the adjacent-place relationship.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: pupils recognise that in a multi-digit whole number a digit in one place is worth ten times what the same digit is worth in the place to its right (and one-tenth of the same digit in the place to its left). The 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300; 700 ÷ 70 = 10. The aim is to name the multiplicative ×10 structure between adjacent places that has been implicit since 'ten ones make a ten', and to hold it alongside the additive (partition) view. A central scaffold is a place-value / Gattegno chart where moving a digit one column left multiplies its value by 10 and one column right divides it by 10; a static or paper chart with counters can serve the same purpose.

activities.title: Slide a digit across the place-value chart
feedback: If a learner says the move 'adds a zero', agree the written numeral gains a zero (for whole numbers) but ask WHY: push for 'because its value became ten times bigger' so the idea still works for decimals later, where 'add a zero' breaks down.
If a learner says 3,000 is '10 more' than 300, build 300 with place-value counters and stack it ten times to reach 3,000, showing it is ten lots of 300, i.e. ten TIMES, not ten more.

Confirm correct answers by having the learner read both numbers aloud with place names (three hundred vs three thousand) so the VALUE, not just the digit, is heard — this also counters 'they're the same, both are 3'.
activities.rationale: Making the ×10/÷10 move physical on a chart turns an abstract multiplicative fact into an observable action and directly contrasts with the 'add a zero' trick. An interactive chart that recomputes the value live as the digit moves (e.g. a '×10' tag flashing on the leftward move) may make the relationship vivid; a static annotated chart or a paper chart with counters can serve the same purpose with the learner stating the change.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils recognise the value of each digit and the ×10 relationships between adjacent places in numbers to 1,000,000.
The multiplicative ×10 relationship between places should be taught explicitly (Gattegno chart) to avoid the 'add a zero' misconception that breaks with decimals.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns for ones, tens, hundreds, thousands (and more).
Place a single digit — say a 3 — in the hundreds column so it is worth 300.

Move that same 3 one column to the LEFT and state its new value (3,000). Say what happened to the value and by how much: it became ten TIMES as much, not 'ten more'. (For whole numbers the written numeral also gains a zero, but that is a by-product — the reason is the ×10 in value.)
Move the 3 back to the RIGHT (÷10): from 3,000, one column right returns it to 300, and a further column right makes it 30.
Write the matching sentence each time, e.g. 300 × 10 = 3,000 and 3,000 ÷ 10 = 300.
activities.intendedInsight: Shifting a digit one place left multiplies its value by 10 and one place right divides it by 10; place value is multiplicative between adjacent columns, not merely 'adding a zero'.

activities.title: How many times greater? Counting the place-shifts
feedback: If a learner answers 'ten times' for a two-shift gap (50,000 vs 500), have them slide the digit place by place and count: one shift ×10, a second shift ×10 again, so ×100 in total.

If a learner gives a subtraction answer ('45,000 more' for 50,000 vs 5,000, or '49,500 more' for 50,000 vs 500), re-voice the question as scaling: 'how many of the smaller value fit into the larger?' and build with counters.
Praise answers that name both the factor and the reason (number of shifts), not just a number.
activities.rationale: Comparing a digit across adjacent and non-adjacent places exposes the common over-application of 'ten times' to any gap, and ties the factor to counting place-shifts rather than to a memorised rule. The adjacent ×10 relationship is the defining structure of base-ten place value; the two-shift ×100 case is its direct consequence.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils recognise the value of each digit and the ×10 relationships between adjacent places in numbers to 1,000,000.
A digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (4.NBT.1); extended to 1/10 to the left (5.NBT.1).
learnerActions: Compare the same digit in two different places, e.g. the 5 in 50,000 and the 5 in 5,000.
Slide one placement of the 5 towards the other, counting the number of column hops.
State the factor: one hop = ×10, so the 5 in 50,000 is ten times the 5 in 5,000.
Repeat for a non-adjacent pair, e.g. the 5 in 50,000 compared with the 5 in 500: count the hops (two), so the factor is ×10×10 = ×100.
Say in words how many times greater, and justify by the number of place-shifts.
activities.intendedInsight: The factor between two placements of a digit equals ten raised to the number of column shifts: one shift is ×10, two shifts is ×100. Non-adjacent places are not automatically 'ten times'.

activities.title: Division and multiplication sentences as the place-value step
feedback: If a learner computes 700 ÷ 70 as something other than 10, have them see 700 as ten 70s on the chart (70 shifted one place left) before recomputing.
If a learner gets 10 but cannot explain it, ask them to point to where 70 and 700 sit and say how many columns apart they are.
Give full credit only when the sentence is linked to the place-shift, not just the correct number.
activities.rationale: Using ÷ and × sentences gives the ×10 structure calculation payoff and prevents it from being an isolated verbal fact; linking the quotient to adjacent columns anchors the abstract result in place value.
sourceClaims: The multiplicative ×10 relationship between places should be taught explicitly (Gattegno chart) to avoid the 'add a zero' misconception that breaks with decimals.
learnerActions: Complete 700 ÷ 70 = ___ and explain the answer using place names, not just the computed digits.
Explain how 700 ÷ 70 = 10 connects to 70 and 700 sitting in adjacent place-value columns (the 7 in 700 is one place to the left of the 7 in 70, so 700 is ten times as much as 70).
Write a few matched pairs showing both directions, e.g. 30 = 3 × 10 and 3 = 30 ÷ 10.
Point to or highlight the two adjacent columns involved for each sentence so the quotient of 10 is seen as a single left/right place step.
activities.intendedInsight: Division and multiplication sentences such as 700 ÷ 70 = 10 express the adjacent-place relationship itself: moving one place is ×10 or ÷10.

activities.title: Ten times or ten more? Correcting the claim
feedback: If a learner cannot say why 'ten more' fails, compute 300 + 10 = 310 and compare with 3,000, showing 'ten more' gives the wrong number.
Reinforce that the multiplicative view is what lets the ÷10 direction keep going into tenths and hundredths.
If the learner self-corrects confidently, extend by asking them to state the one-tenth (÷10) relationship: this place is one-tenth of the same digit in the place to its left.
activities.rationale: Explicitly confronting the additive-vs-multiplicative confusion, rather than only demonstrating the correct move, gives learners a chance to articulate and repair the misconception. A short Socratic exchange in which a character insists on 'ten more' and the learner corrects to 'ten times' is one way to surface this; it is a proposed scaffold, not the only effective medium.
sourceClaims: The multiplicative ×10 relationship between places should be taught explicitly (Gattegno chart) to avoid the 'add a zero' misconception that breaks with decimals.
learnerActions: Consider a claim that 'the 3 in 3,000 is ten MORE than the 3 in 300' and decide whether it is right.
Explain why it is wrong and restate it correctly as 'ten TIMES'.
Support the correction with evidence: 300 × 10 = 3,000, or ten stacks of 300 reaching 3,000, or the single left-shift on the chart.
Preview the right-hand direction: a dimmed column to the right of the ones is where tenths will later live (the ÷10 direction continues past the ones).
activities.intendedInsight: 'Ten times' (multiplicative) and 'ten more' (additive) are different; place value is multiplicative, which is why the pattern extends consistently into decimals.

constraints: Hold the additive (partition) view and the multiplicative (×10 between places) view together: 3,452 is 3,000+400+50+2 AND each place is ten times the next. Do not drop the partition view.

Avoid teaching 'add a zero' as the rule; name the underlying ×10 relationship so the idea still works when extended to decimals (÷10 into tenths). For whole numbers the written zero is a by-product, not the explanation.
A static or paper place-value chart is a valid reference and teaching tool; an interactive sliding chart may make the live recompute more vivid but is not the only way to teach this relationship.

Recognition/fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. '700 ÷ 70 = __', 'which is ten times 400?') are useful for consolidation and assessment but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and explain the place-shift reasoning; pair them with tasks that ask for the factor AND its justification.
When comparing non-adjacent places, require the number of place-shifts to be counted (one shift ×10, two shifts ×100); do not let any gap be treated as a single ×10.
Distinguish the digit's face value (3 in both 300 and 3,000) from its place value (300 vs 3,000) whenever learners say the numbers are 'the same'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source citations for CCSS-M (4.NBT.1 / 5.NBT.1) and the NCETM Primary Mastery claim are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

Arithmetic check: 300 × 10 = 3,000; 700 ÷ 70 = 10; 300 + 10 = 310 (≠ 3,000, correctly showing 'ten more' ≠ 'ten times'); 5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 5,000 = one shift = ×10 (ratio 10); 5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 500 = two shifts = ×100 (ratio 100). The additive-difference '2,700 bigger' (3,000 − 300) appears only as an error pattern to correct, never as a valid answer.

The source Tier C example '5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 5,000' is labelled a 'non-adjacent' comparison but is in fact adjacent (one shift, ×10); the activities use the correct factors and reserve the two-shift ×100 case for 50,000 vs 500.

The non-adjacent over-application error (answering 'ten times' for a two-shift gap) is a critical learner error; it is addressed directly by requiring the learner to count place-shifts, not merely flagged.
Source claims support the adjacent per-place ×10 convention; the two-shift ×100 composition in activity 2 is a mathematical derivation of that principle, not an independently cited claim.

Independent re-audit found the content mathematically sound and internally coherent across summary, insights, actions, feedback and constraints; no unsupported categorical modality claims remain and medium-efficacy wording is appropriately qualified.

probeDeeper: Now the 5 in 50,000 and the 5 in 5,000 — how many times bigger? Why?
And the 5 in 50,000 compared with the 5 in 500 — is it still ten times? (two shifts)
Complete 700 ÷ 70 = ___ and explain it using places.
assess.correctAnswer: Ten times bigger. Each place to the left is worth ten times the place to its right, and 3,000 is one place to the left of 300, so its 3 is worth ten times as much.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares the two values by subtracting instead of by a scale factor: '3,000 is 2,700 more than 300'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-voice the question as scaling: '300 fits into 3,000 how many times?' Build both with place-value counters and show 300 stacked ten times to reach 3,000.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is 2,700 bigger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives an additive difference when asked 'how many times'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Attends to the face value of the digit, not its place: 'they're the same — both are 3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast value vs digit: the digit is 3 in both, but its VALUE is 300 vs 3,000. Read each aloud with place names.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same — both are 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says there is no difference because the digit is 3 in both.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-applies 'ten times' to non-adjacent places, treating any gap as a single ×10
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the place-shifts explicitly: one shift = ×10, two shifts = ×10×10 = ×100. Have them slide the digit place by place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the follow-up (5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 500) the child still answers 'ten times' rather than 'a hundred times'.

responseLevels.gap: Gives an additive difference or says the digits are 'the same', with no scaling idea.
responseLevels.full: States each left place is ×10, and composes shifts multiplicatively (two places = ×100), justifying with place-value reasoning and inverse (÷10).
responseLevels.partial: Says 'ten times' for the adjacent pair but treats it as a rote 'one more zero' rule and calls non-adjacent pairs ten times too.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 300 and 3,000 side by side. Point to the 3 in each. Ask: 'The value of this 3 compared with that 3 — how many times bigger is one than the other? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A multiplicative place-value thinker says 'ten times' and justifies by the single left-shift; an additive thinker gives the difference ('2,700 more'); a face-value thinker says 'they're the same, both are 3'. The reason tier, plus the non-adjacent follow-ups, separates a rote 'count the extra zero' rule from genuine ×10-per-place reasoning.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Could there be another explanation?

- **Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to use results to draw simple conclusions, suggest improvements and raise further questions, and to identify differences, similarities or changes related to scientific ideas. Actively asking whether a different explanation could fit the same results is what turns a first conclusion into a considered one.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 6/7 Constructing Explanations & Engaging in Argument from Evidence, grades 3–5):** Construct and compare multiple explanations, and use evidence to evaluate which explanation an investigation best supports. Considering and weighing alternative explanations is explicit in the argument and explanation practices.

- **Operational details:** The child learns that the FIRST explanation that fits a result is not automatically the right one — usually more than one idea can account for the same observation — so a good scientist deliberately generates alternatives before committing ('the plant died — was it too little water? too much? not enough light? too cold?'). They practise proposing at least a second and third candidate explanation for a given result, and recognising that you then need MORE evidence to decide between them. This directly builds on the disposition to change your mind: rather than defending your first idea, you widen the field of possible ideas, which is also the seed of controlling variables (each alternative is a variable to isolate) and of correlation-vs-causation.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional). This is the pivot from 'an explanation' to 'the best-supported explanation among several'. Success = for a given result the child generates two or more plausible alternative explanations and recognises that further evidence is needed to decide between them, rather than locking onto the first idea.
bestPractices: Routinely ask 'what ELSE could explain this?' after any result, making a second and third explanation an expected move, not an optional one.
Reward the generation of alternatives itself (before deciding which is right), so children don't rush to lock onto the first fit.
Show that deciding between rival explanations needs MORE evidence, linking each alternative to a test that could rule it in or out.
Use everyday mysteries with several genuinely plausible causes so alternatives are real, not token.
Connect to controlling variables: each competing explanation is a variable you could isolate to test.
Model open-mindedness — 'I have a favourite idea, but let me hold it lightly until the evidence decides'.
keyRepresentations: Explanation board: one result with several candidate-explanation cards
Clue tokens that mark each explanation as supported or contradicted
'One result → many possible causes' fan diagram
A 'which test would decide?' prompt pairing rival explanations with distinguishing evidence
Narrowing funnel from many explanations to the best-supported one
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the first explanation that fits must be the correct one.
Thinking there is only ever one possible explanation for a result.
Believing a single clue settles the matter, without checking it against rival explanations.
Generating alternatives but then not seeing that more evidence is needed to choose.
Defending a favourite explanation instead of weighing it fairly against others.
Treating 'I'm not sure which yet' as failure rather than honest, in-progress science.

learn.summary: For children aged 7–9: build the habit of asking 'what ELSE could explain this?' after any result. The teaching objective is for a child to generate two or more plausible alternative explanations for the same observation and recognise that MORE evidence is needed to decide between them, rather than locking onto the first idea that fits. The central worked example is a wilted houseplant with several rival causes (too little water, too much water, no light, too cold, bugs), where incoming clues support some explanations and rule out others.

activities.title: Explanation Detective Board: one clue is rarely enough
feedback: When a learner proposes a second or third explanation, affirm the generating itself: 'Good — thinking of another explanation is exactly the scientist's move.'
When a learner locks onto the first fit, ask 'what ELSE could explain this?' and prompt them to list differences before choosing.

When one clue is treated as settling everything, show it against the rival explanations: a soggy-soil clue rules out too-little-water but still leaves too-much-water, no-light, too-cold, and bugs to weigh.
Treat 'I'm not sure which yet' as honest, in-progress science rather than failure.
When two explanations survive, ask which single further clue would tell them apart, linking to fair testing.
activities.rationale: An interactive board makes the generate-and-weigh loop concrete: because each new clue recomputes which explanations survive, the child can experience that one clue rarely settles it and that alternatives must be actively weighed. Live support/contradiction marking across several hypotheses at once is intended to make 'there might be another explanation' something the child does rather than is told. This aligns with the NGSS practice of constructing and comparing multiple explanations and using evidence to evaluate which an investigation best supports; separately, the closing 'what clue would decide?' step serves the DfE Working Scientifically element of raising further questions and suggesting improvements.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 6 and SEP 7 (grades 3–5) have students construct and compare multiple explanations and use evidence to evaluate which explanation is best supported.

DfE Lower KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to use results to draw simple conclusions, suggest improvements and raise further questions, and to identify differences, similarities or changes related to scientific ideas.
learnerActions: Look at a result on the board — a houseplant has wilted — and, instead of guessing THE reason, propose or select as many plausible 'suspects' as you can: TOO LITTLE WATER, TOO MUCH WATER, NO LIGHT, TOO COLD, BUGS.
Earn credit for each additional plausible explanation you add, so proposing a second and third idea is the scored move, not just picking one.

Reveal clues one at a time and mark how each clue affects every suspect: for 'the soil is soggy and wet', strike through TOO LITTLE WATER and brighten TOO MUCH WATER; for 'the identical plant next to it in the same dark corner is thriving', strike through NO LIGHT and also TOO COLD, because both plants share the same spot, so they get the same light and the same warmth.
Watch the field of surviving explanations narrow with each clue, and notice when a confident first guess (it looked dry, so — no water!) gets eliminated by the soggy-soil clue.
When two suspects are still standing, answer the closing prompt: 'what one clue would tell them apart?' — pairing each surviving explanation with the evidence that would distinguish it.
activities.intendedInsight: The first explanation that fits a result is not automatically the right one; usually more than one idea can account for the same observation, so you deliberately hold several open and gather more evidence to decide between them.

activities.title: Detective dialogue: 'good — what else?'
feedback: Celebrate 'I'm not sure yet' as good science when it is paired with a plan to get more evidence.
When the learner offers only agent-based causes (someone did something), draw attention to non-agent differences like light, warmth, or water.
Accept a favoured explanation as one candidate, then insist each candidate needs a test; ask what test would tell it apart from the others.
activities.rationale: Open dialogue can adaptively probe the child's specific reasoning and model open-minded weighing, pushing for alternatives and for distinguishing evidence in a way a pre-authored, fixed task cannot adapt to in the moment. This is a complement, not evidence of superiority: spoken dialogue does not display the live support/contradiction bookkeeping across several hypotheses that the board makes visible, so the two formats work together. Efficacy of this dialogue format is proposed, not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 6 and SEP 7 (grades 3–5) have students construct and compare multiple explanations and use evidence to evaluate which explanation is best supported.
learnerActions: Talk through a result with an in-role investigator who, each time you give one explanation, asks 'good — what ELSE could explain that?' and refuses to let you settle on the first idea.
For each pair of rival explanations, say what evidence would tell them apart ('what would tell us which is right?').
Practise saying 'I'm not sure yet' as a legitimate scientific position while you gather more evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Asking for another explanation, and for the evidence that would decide between explanations, is a repeatable reasoning habit you can apply to any result.

activities.title: Primer: one result, several possible causes
feedback: After the primer, prompt the learner to add explanations the scene did NOT show, moving from recognising pre-set causes to generating their own.
activities.rationale: A pre-authored reveal scene is a useful primer for the 'one result, many possible causes' idea. Its limit: because explanations are authored in advance, it cannot reward the child for generating their OWN alternatives or update as new clues arrive, so it should lead into, not replace, generative work.
learnerActions: Explore a mystery scene where tapping each hotspot reveals a different possible explanation for the same result, so you see several explanations can fit one observation.
Use this as a warm-up before the detective board, then move on to generating your own alternatives.
activities.intendedInsight: A single result can have several possible causes — more than one idea can fit what you observed.

activities.title: Check: name another explanation and the test that decides
feedback: Full response: spontaneously generates several plausible alternatives (light, water, warmth), treats them as rival candidates, and can say how you'd test one against another.
Partial response: produces one alternative when pushed, but treats explanations one at a time rather than as competing possibilities — prompt 'how would you decide between these two?'

Gap response: accepts or defends the single given explanation and generates no alternative — prompt 'what else was different between the windowsill and the cupboard?' and make listing alternatives the habit before choosing.
If every alternative involves a person or action, point to differences between the two locations that involve no person at all.
activities.rationale: Recognition and open-probe items can check whether the child resists the first fit and searches for competitors — a habit that is hard to fake because it requires generating rivals. Note a limit: fixed recognition items alone do not elicit the generative habit of actively proposing alternatives, so pair them with open 'tell me as many as you can' prompts.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 6 and SEP 7 (grades 3–5) have students construct and compare multiple explanations and use evidence to evaluate which explanation is best supported.
learnerActions: Read a short scenario: a plant on the windowsill grew tall and one in the cupboard stayed short; a friend says 'the windowsill plant grew because someone talked to it every morning.'
List as many other explanations as you can for why the windowsill plant grew taller (e.g. more light, more warmth, more water).

For a chosen pair of explanations, say how you would find out which one is really right — for example, growing two matching plants in the cupboard with the same water and warmth, talking to only one of them every morning, and comparing their growth to see whether talking alone makes a difference.

Answer recognition items such as 'which of these is ALSO a possible explanation?' and 'what evidence would help decide between these two?', framed as 'the first idea was X; what else could explain the result?'
activities.intendedInsight: Strong reasoning produces more than one plausible explanation rather than accepting the first, and treats rivals as competing candidates that must be tested against each other.

constraints: Checkpoint is Tier B (transitional): success = for a given result the child generates two or more plausible alternative explanations AND recognises that further evidence is needed to decide between them, not just naming one cause.
Reward generating alternatives before deciding which is right, so children do not rush to lock onto the first fit.
Use everyday mysteries with several genuinely plausible causes so alternatives are real, not token.
Link each competing explanation to a test that could rule it in or out, connecting to controlling variables (each alternative is a variable to isolate) and to correlation-vs-causation.
A pre-authored tap-to-reveal scene is a primer only: it cannot reward the child's own generated alternatives or update as new clues arrive.

Fixed recognition/quiz items can check whether a child picks out a valid alternative or distinguishing evidence, but on their own they do not elicit independent generation of alternatives; pair them with open generative prompts.

Spoken dialogue models weighing and probes reasoning well, but does not show the live cross-hypothesis support/contradiction tracking that the board makes visible; the two formats complement each other rather than one being universally superior.
Treat 'I'm not sure which yet' as honest in-progress science, not failure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D as 'poor' with the claim '3D adds navigation cost without conceptual benefit.' This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it has been reframed as 'weighing alternatives is a reasoning rather than a spatial task' and 3D is simply not proposed here, without asserting it adds nothing in general.

The legacy 'quiz' entry asserted a fixed quiz 'can't cultivate the generative habit'; softened to a scoped limit (recognition items alone do not elicit independent generation) consistent with objective recognition-vs-production limits.

One cited source (NGSS Appendix F) is marked verified:false in the row; the DfE source is marked verified:true but supports only the 'draw conclusions / raise further questions / identify differences' element, not the generate-multiple-explanations principle (which rests on NGSS). Evidence strength is carried over as-is and not upgraded. The two 'evidence' tags ('alternative possible worlds research', 'scientific thinking promotes critical thinking, MDPI 2025') are not structured sources[].claim entries and are not cited as sourceClaims.

The reteach prerequisite id attached to the 'defends a favoured explanation' error pattern is retained conceptually (holding candidates open vs defending one), but internal IDs are omitted from learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: Of the explanations you gave, how could we find out which one is really right?
Suppose we grew a plant in the cupboard but talked to it every morning too — what would that tell us about the talking idea?
Why might a scientist deliberately try to think of an explanation she doesn't like?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning generates more than one plausible explanation rather than accepting the first — most obviously that the windowsill plant got light (or warmth, or water) the cupboard plant didn't — and recognises that the talking explanation is only one of several possibilities that would need to be tested against each other. The mark of it is actively producing alternatives, not defending or settling on one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts the first explanation that fits and stops searching ('yes, it must be the talking').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'what else was different between the windowsill and the cupboard?'; make listing alternatives the habit before choosing one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Offers no alternative; endorses the given explanation.

errorPatterns.pattern: Defends a favoured explanation and dismisses rivals rather than holding several open ('no, it was DEFINITELY the talking').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Accept it as one candidate, then insist each candidate needs a test; ask what test would tell talking apart from light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Argues for one cause and rejects alternatives without testing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only considers explanations that involve someone doing something (an agent), overlooking non-agent causes like light or temperature.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw attention to the differences between the two locations that involve no person at all.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Every alternative involves a person or action; never names environmental factors.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts or defends the single given explanation; generates no alternative.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously generates several plausible alternatives (light, water, warmth), treats them as rival candidates, and can say how you'd test one against another — connecting alternative-generation to how you'd decide between them.
responseLevels.partial: Produces one alternative when pushed, but treats explanations one at a time rather than as competing possibilities to be tested against each other.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A plant on the windowsill grew tall and one in the cupboard stayed short. Your friend says 'the windowsill plant grew because someone talked to it every morning.' Could there be another explanation for why it grew taller? Tell me as many as you can.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child prone to theory-preservation accepts the first explanation that fits ('yes, talking made it grow') and stops. A child who can generate alternatives keeps going — light, water, warmth — and this is hard to fake, because it requires resisting the first fit and searching for competitors, the very habit under test.
