pedagogy.summary: At upper KS2 the nervous system is taught as the body's high-speed communication network in two parts: the CENTRAL nervous system (brain + spinal cord), which processes and decides, and the nerves branching to every part of the body (the peripheral side) that carry messages in and out. The signature idea is the REFLEX ARC — for danger (a pin, a hot pan) the message takes a shortcut: stimulus → sensory nerve → spinal cord → motor nerve → muscle, so you pull away BEFORE the brain has consciously 'decided'. This explains why reflexes feel automatic and instant, and it upgrades the KS1 'brain controls the body' loop by adding the spinal cord as a fast local router and by emphasising SPEED. Teach it with the child's own reflexes (knee-jerk, blink, pulling from heat) and contrast a reflex (spinal shortcut, no thinking) with a considered action (routed via the brain). Keep to CNS/PNS, the reflex arc and the idea of fast electrical-type signals — neurons and synapses come next.
bestPractices: Split the system cleanly into central (brain + spinal cord) and the nerves reaching the body, then show messages travelling IN (sensory) and OUT (motor) along them.
Teach the reflex arc as a labelled pathway (stimulus→sensory nerve→spinal cord→motor nerve→muscle) and demonstrate a real reflex (knee-jerk, blink) so 'automatic and fast' is experienced.
Contrast reflex vs considered action: a reflex routes through the spinal cord (no conscious thought, very fast); deciding to catch a ball routes up to the brain — same network, different path.
Emphasise SPEED as the reason reflexes protect us (you pull away before you feel the pain), linking to why the signals must be fast.
Build explicitly on the KS1 sense→brain→muscle loop — now with named parts and a spinal-cord shortcut — and set up neurons as what the nerves are made of.
keyRepresentations: Central-vs-peripheral map: brain + spinal cord highlighted, nerves branching to the body
Labelled reflex arc: stimulus → sensory nerve → spinal cord → motor nerve → muscle
Reflex-vs-thought comparison: spinal shortcut (fast, automatic) vs up-to-brain route (considered)
Real reflex demos (knee-jerk, blink, hand-from-heat) as evidence of speed
Nerves as fast message-wires carrying signals in and out
commonMisconceptions: 'The brain does everything / all messages go to the brain first' — missing the spinal-cord reflex shortcut that bypasses conscious thought.
'Reflexes are just fast decisions' — missing that they are automatic and don't wait for the brain to decide.
'You feel the pain and THEN pull away' — reversed; the reflex pulls you away first, the feeling arrives after.
'Nerves are the same as veins/blood vessels' — confusing the nervous network with the circulatory one; nerves carry signals, not blood.
'Signals travel like something physically running along' slowly — underestimating the near-instant speed of nerve signals.
'The spinal cord is just for holding you up' — missing its role as part of the CNS that routes reflexes and carries messages.

learn.summary: Upper KS2 learners study the nervous system as the body's fast communication network with two parts: the central nervous system (brain + spinal cord) that processes and decides, and the peripheral nerves branching to the body that carry messages IN (sensory) and OUT (motor). The signature idea is the reflex arc — for danger the message takes a spinal-cord shortcut (stimulus → sensory nerve → spinal cord → motor nerve → muscle) so the body reacts BEFORE the brain consciously feels or decides. Teaching emphasises SPEED and the shortcut, contrasts a reflex with a considered (brain-routed) action, and builds on the KS1 sense→brain→muscle loop by adding the spinal cord as a fast router.

activities.title: Race the signal: the reflex-arc pathway
feedback: If a learner routes the reflex all the way through the thinking brain, ask: 'Your hand pulled away before you felt the pain — if the message had to reach the brain and get a decision first, could it be that fast?' Then re-trace the spinal-cord shortcut.
If a learner says 'you feel the pain and THEN pull away', point out the order is reversed: the muscle moves first; the pain signal reaches the brain slightly later.
If a learner treats 'nerves are just fast' as the whole reason, probe for the bypassed-brain idea: the shortcut through the spinal cord, not only signal speed, is what saves time.
Reinforce: the pain signal DOES reach the brain — just a moment after the hand has already moved.
activities.rationale: Making the two paths and their relative timing visible (sensory-in, motor-out, spinal shortcut vs brain route) targets the core insight that the muscle fires before conscious feeling. A dynamic/animated or acted-out representation may let learners follow the sequence and timing rather than only read a static label sequence; a timing comparison can make 'faster' concrete. This is a proposed activity, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Animals receive information through their senses, process it in the brain (and spinal cord), and respond in different ways; a model can describe this sense–process–respond system.

The nervous system comprises the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nerves; a reflex arc (stimulus→sensory neuron→spinal cord→motor neuron→effector) produces rapid, involuntary responses that bypass conscious processing.
learnerActions: Trace the pathway of a danger signal: a hand touches a hot pan, a signal travels up the sensory nerve to the spinal cord, and straight back down the motor nerve to the muscle so the hand recoils.
Follow a second signal that continues up to the brain, where the 'ouch!' registers a beat LATER than the hand has already moved.
Use a toggle or comparison to contrast a reflex (spinal-cord shortcut, automatic) with a deliberate action such as deciding to wave, whose signal routes all the way up to the brain and back.
Compare the timing of the two paths using the simulation's or model's timing readout to see the reflex path is faster (a real reflex is too quick to time accurately with a hand-held stopwatch).
State in your own words why the hand moves before the pain is felt.
activities.intendedInsight: The nervous system is one network, but a danger message takes a spinal-cord shortcut that fires the muscle before the brain consciously feels or decides — which is why reflexes are automatic and fast and protect us.

activities.title: Feel your own reflexes
feedback: If a learner claims they decided to kick, point out it happened before any decision could be made — the spinal cord acted first.
Connect the felt experience back to the pathway: no decision was needed because the message looped through the spinal cord, not up to the thinking brain.
activities.rationale: Observing or experiencing one's own reflexes can give direct evidence that 'automatic and fast' is real, which may anchor the abstract pathway for the learner. No source claim directly supports this experiential-anchoring rationale, so none is cited; the activity is a proposal, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Observe or experience a safe real reflex, such as the knee-jerk when the leg is tapped gently just below the kneecap. Recall a time you pulled your hand away from something hot, but do not recreate it.
After a reflex such as the doctor's knee tap (where the leg kicks with no decision), explain what that tells you about where the message went.
Describe whether you chose to make the movement happen, and what that shows about the reflex arc.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflexes are automatic and happen without a conscious decision, giving first-hand evidence that the response does not wait for the thinking brain.

activities.title: Map and sort the nervous system
feedback: If a learner says nerves carry blood or are like veins, clarify: nerves carry fast electrical-type signals, not blood; blood vessels are a separate network.
If a learner thinks the spinal cord is just structural support, reinforce its role as part of the CNS that routes reflexes and carries messages.
For a learner who places a part in the wrong group, restate the rule: brain and spinal cord = central; nerves reaching the body = peripheral.
activities.rationale: A labelled map with sorting can consolidate the CNS/PNS vocabulary and in/out message directions, and addresses the nerves-as-blood-vessels and spinal-cord-is-just-support misconceptions. A sort/label task can check and practise classification but does not by itself elicit an extended explanation; it works as a companion reference and consolidation after the pathway work.
sourceClaims: The nervous system comprises the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nerves; a reflex arc (stimulus→sensory neuron→spinal cord→motor neuron→effector) produces rapid, involuntary responses that bypass conscious processing.
learnerActions: On a body map, identify the central nervous system (brain + spinal cord) and the peripheral nerves branching to the body.
Sort or label parts as central vs peripheral.
Identify which messages travel IN to the CNS (sensory) and which travel OUT to muscles (motor); note that a single nerve in the body often carries both kinds of message.
Distinguish nerves (which carry fast signals) from blood vessels (which carry blood) — they are different networks.
activities.intendedInsight: The nervous system splits cleanly into central and peripheral parts, with sensory nerves carrying signals in and motor nerves carrying signals out, and is distinct from the circulatory system.

activities.title: Consolidation questions
feedback: For the key question, a strong answer names the sensory→spinal cord→motor→muscle loop that bypasses the thinking brain, and notes the pain reaches the brain slightly later.
If an answer relies only on 'nerves are fast', push for the shortcut idea: the signal does not make the full trip to the brain before the muscle fires.

If a learner chooses 'your brain thinks that's hot and decides to pull back', ask how that could be faster than feeling the pain, then re-trace the spinal-cord shortcut (this option is the misconception, not the correct answer).
activities.rationale: Ordering, categorising and a focused why-question check the assessable core and surface whether the bypassed-brain idea is secure. This format checks recognition and recall and does not by itself require the learner to construct an extended explanation unprompted.
sourceClaims: The nervous system comprises the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nerves; a reflex arc (stimulus→sensory neuron→spinal cord→motor neuron→effector) produces rapid, involuntary responses that bypass conscious processing.
learnerActions: Put the reflex-arc steps in order: stimulus → sensory nerve → spinal cord → motor nerve → muscle.
Categorise given body parts as central or peripheral.
Answer why the hand moves before the pain is felt, explaining the spinal-cord-shortcut reason rather than 'you decided to move' or 'the brain thought it was hot first'.
Transfer the idea to the knee-jerk case: explain where the message went.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can independently sequence the arc, classify parts, and justify the before-you-feel-it timing by the bypassed-brain shortcut rather than by vague speed alone.

activities.title: Talk it through: why before you think?
feedback: Prompt for the full path if the learner stops at 'it's a reflex': which nerves, through what, to what?
If the learner cannot say why it is useful, link speed to protection: moving before you feel pain reduces injury.
activities.rationale: A spoken, responsive discussion lets a teacher or guide probe the exact reasoning and press for the spinal-cord route. This is an optional discussion scaffold; the timing/routing insight may be clearer when also shown dynamically.
learnerActions: Respond to the prompt: 'You touch something scalding and your hand jerks away BEFORE you feel the pain or decide to move — how can your hand pull back faster than you can think?'
Explain the path the message takes, in full.
Answer follow-ups: Do you still feel the pain afterwards, and why does it arrive a moment later? Why is it USEFUL that this happens without waiting for you to think?
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the pathway and the usefulness of the shortcut forces the bypassed-brain idea to surface rather than a vague 'nerves are fast'.

constraints: Keep content to CNS/PNS, the reflex arc, and the idea of fast electrical-type signals; neurons and synapses are the next step and are out of scope here.
Build explicitly on the KS1 sense→brain→muscle loop, now with named parts and the spinal-cord shortcut.

A static diagram can label the arc's stations but does not show the signal travelling or the reflex-vs-thought timing; if used alone, pair it with an animated, acted-out, or timed representation so the before-you-feel-it sequence is experienced. This is a scaffold limit, not a claim that one medium is universally superior.
Ordering, grouping and selection (multiple-choice) questions check recognition and recall; they do not by themselves require the learner to construct an independent spoken or written explanation.
Treat 'signals travel extremely fast' as a contributing reason but not the whole explanation — the bypassed-brain shortcut is the key idea.

The spinal-shortcut explanation here is a simplified upper-KS2 model; it omits neuron/synapse-level detail by design, and the 'separate signal to the brain' is a simplification of a single ascending sensory pathway.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no human review or empirical effectiveness is claimed.
The second source (Britannica reflex/nervous system) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed pending source review.

The original row asserted a dynamic 2D model shows timing 'in a way no static diagram can' and that '3D adds no conceptual value'. These are catalogue-fit judgements, not established comparative-efficacy findings; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements and should not be read as proven claims.

The NGSS claim cited in 'Race the signal' supports modelling a sense→process→respond system (which that activity builds) but does not itself address reflex timing or the spinal-cord shortcut; the distinctive timing principle is supported only by the Britannica claim.

Physiological simplification note: at upper KS2 the reflex is taught as a spinal-cord shortcut that fires before conscious feeling, and the 'second signal to the brain' is a simplification of a single ascending sensory pathway. This is a deliberate model; neuron/synapse/interneuron detail is intentionally deferred and should be flagged if a learner over-generalises.
The 'Feel your own reflexes' activity has no directly supporting source claim for its experiential-anchoring rationale; its sourceClaims were set to [] rather than citing a merely topical claim.

probeDeeper: Do you still feel the pain afterwards? If your hand already moved, why does the pain arrive a moment later?
Why is it USEFUL that this happens without waiting for you to think?
The doctor taps just below your knee and your leg kicks with no decision from you — what does that tell you about where the message went?
assess.correctAnswer: It's a reflex: the message from the skin travels along a sensory nerve to the spinal cord, which sends a message straight back along a motor nerve to the arm muscle to pull away — without waiting to travel up to the thinking part of the brain and back. That short-cut through the spinal cord is why it happens before you consciously feel or decide. The pain signal does reach the brain, but slightly later. Nerve signals travel extremely fast, so it feels instant.

errorPatterns.pattern: You consciously decide to move your hand — the thinking brain plans the pull-away.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast reflex with decision: the spinal cord acts first for protection; conscious feeling arrives afterwards.
errorPatterns.distractor: Your brain thinks 'that's hot!' and decides to pull your hand back.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the brain thinks 'that's hot' and then decides to move.

errorPatterns.pattern: Every signal must travel all the way to the brain and back for any action — there is no spinal-cord short-cut.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce the reflex arc through the spinal cord as a protective short-cut that skips the trip to the brain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Routes the reflex through the brain and so can't explain the speed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Nerves carry blood or are like blood vessels carrying liquid messages.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish nerves (carry fast electrical signals) from blood vessels (carry blood); they are different networks.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes nerves as tubes of blood or fluid rather than signal-carriers.

responseLevels.gap: Says you consciously decide to pull away, or routes everything through the thinking brain; may think nerves carry blood.
responseLevels.full: Explains the reflex arc (skin→sensory nerve→spinal cord→motor nerve→muscle) bypassing the thinking brain for speed, notes the pain reaches the brain slightly later, and transfers the idea to the knee-jerk case.
responseLevels.partial: Knows it's a fast reflex and names the brain and nerves, but can't explain the spinal-cord short-cut — treats 'fast signals' as the whole reason without the bypassed-brain idea.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You touch something scalding hot and your hand jerks away BEFORE you even feel the pain or decide to move. How can your hand pull back faster than you can think about it? Explain the path the message takes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who says you consciously decide to move, or routes the signal all the way through the brain, can't account for it happening before you think. Only a child who grasps the spinal-cord reflex arc can. The tier-two 'path the message takes' forces the by-passed-brain idea to surface rather than a vague 'nerves are fast'.

sources.claim: Animals receive information through their senses, process it in the brain (and spinal cord), and respond in different ways; a model can describe this sense–process–respond system.
sources.source: NGSS 4-LS1-2 (Grade 4, From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes)

sources.claim: The nervous system comprises the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nerves; a reflex arc (stimulus→sensory neuron→spinal cord→motor neuron→effector) produces rapid, involuntary responses that bypass conscious processing.
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica — reflex action / human nervous system

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** White Light & Colour

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Physics, 'Light waves'):** "colours and the different frequencies of light, white light and prisms (qualitative only); differential colour effects in absorption and diffuse reflection." This is the DIRECT statutory home for the topic — spectrum/frequency, prism dispersion of white light (qualitative), and why objects appear coloured (selective absorption + diffuse reflection) all sit at KS3.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS4-2):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS4-2]." Colour is the WAVELENGTH-SELECTIVE case of this — a red object reflects red and absorbs the rest — so MS-PS4-2 is the honest national anchor, though NGSS has NO colour-specific performance expectation; the spectrum/dispersion and subtractive-colour detail are UK-led.

- **Operational details:** White light is a MIXTURE of all visible colours (ROYGBIV; red = lowest frequency/longest wavelength → violet = highest frequency/shortest). A PRISM disperses white light because different frequencies refract by different amounts (violet bends most, red least) — dispersion RESTS ON refraction (the hard prereq); a second prism recombines the spectrum back to white, proving white = all colours together. Objects appear coloured by SELECTIVE ABSORPTION: a red apple in white light absorbs most frequencies and reflects red to the eye; white reflects all, black absorbs all. Apparent colour depends on BOTH the pigment AND the illuminating light — a red object looks red in white light but BLACK in pure blue light (no red present to reflect). Filters are colour SUBTRACTORS: a red filter transmits red and absorbs the rest (it does NOT dye all light red); a coloured object is itself a selective filter. Present 'black' as the idealised limiting case (real pigments/lights give 'very dark', not perfectly black).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). The qualitative model (absorb some, reflect the rest; light + pigment together) is age-appropriate, but SUBTRACTIVE reasoning is documented as genuinely hard even for motivated secondary students (only ~27% correctly predict a yellow object looks dark under blue light). Success = list ROYGBIV by frequency, explain prism dispersion via differential refraction, predict AND explain a red object going black under blue light, and predict the colour seen through a filter. Watch for colour-as-innate-property, light-just-brightens, and filter-as-adder thinking.
bestPractices: Use the IOP 'Wrong Track / Right Lines' refutation explicitly: name the intuition ('the dress is red and the light just brightens it up') and contrast it with the model ('white light falls, the dress absorbs most frequencies and reflects red to your eye') — a refutation-text move that outperforms simple telling.

Secure 'what IS white light' FIRST (Haagen-Schützenhöfer): pupils conceive white light as 'normal light', which blocks colour understanding — use a prism to split white light AND a second prism to RECOMBINE it, so white = all colours together is seen, not asserted.

Run predict-observe-reconcile with coloured light: pupils predict, then WATCH a red object go black under blue light (and a white object take the lamp's colour) — the observation directly refutes colour-as-innate-property.

Confront adder-vs-subtractor head-on (IOP 'Understanding colours'): ask 'does the red filter turn all the light red, or just cut out everything except the red already in white light?' — establish filter = selective SUBTRACTOR, and a coloured object = a selective filter.

Sharply separate SUBTRACTIVE pigment/filter behaviour from ADDITIVE light mixing (red + green LIGHT = yellow) — the two are opposite and routinely conflated (70%+ of students wrongly expect red+green spotlights to make brown); teach objects and filters as subtractive.

Order the spectrum by a PHYSICAL quantity (frequency/wavelength), not just 'rainbow order' — red = lowest frequency/longest wavelength through to violet = highest — tying colour to the wave property that dispersion sorts.

Present 'black under blue' as the idealised/limiting case: use saturated pigments and reasonably pure coloured light for a clean effect, and acknowledge real objects look 'very dark', not perfectly black.
Build in accessibility (NASA JPL): for colourblind pupils, label colours with numbers/legends so the assessed reasoning is the absorption model, not hue discrimination.
keyRepresentations: A prism dispersing white light into ROYGBIV (violet refracts most, red least) — paired with a SECOND prism recombining the spectrum back to white.
The visible spectrum ordered by frequency/wavelength (red → violet), labelled with the physical quantity, not just colour names.
Selective-absorption diagram: white light (all colours) strikes a red apple; most colours absorbed (greyed), red reflected to the eye.
The 'same object, different light' comparison: a red object in white light (red) vs the same object in blue light (black).
Filter-as-subtractor diagram: white light through a red filter — red transmitted, the rest absorbed — with a coloured object shown as itself a selective filter.
The IOP Wrong Track / Right Lines paired statements as a refutation representation.
commonMisconceptions: Colour is an innate, fixed property of the object (a red dress 'just is' red), independent of the light illuminating it.
The light merely 'brightens' the object's own colour, rather than the object selecting some frequencies from the light and absorbing the rest.
Colour is ADDED by the light or a filter 'dyes' all light its own colour (adder), rather than SUBTRACTED by selective absorption.
White light is 'just light' / 'normal light', not a mixture of all colours — which undermines both dispersion and colour.
Confusing additive light mixing (red + green LIGHT = yellow) with subtractive pigment/filter behaviour; e.g. expecting red + green spotlights to make brown (documented 70%+ error).
Believing a prism 'adds' or 'creates' colours, rather than separating colours already present in white light.
Predicting a red object under blue light stays red or looks blue/dark-red, instead of black (no red present to reflect).
Forgetting the whole path — perceived colour is the light REACHING THE EYE, which depends on BOTH the pigment and the illuminating light.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12, build understanding that white light is a mixture of all visible colours (ROYGBIV ordered by frequency), that a prism disperses white light because different frequencies refract by different amounts (violet bends most, red least) and a second prism recombines it, that objects appear coloured by selective absorption and reflection (so a red object looks red in white light but near-black in pure blue light), and that filters subtract rather than add colour. The pivotal learning move is predict-observe-reconcile: a learner predicts and explains an object's colour under coloured light, then watches it change, which refutes colour-as-innate-property. Subtractive reasoning is documented as genuinely hard, and additive light mixing must be kept visibly distinct from subtractive pigment/filter behaviour.

activities.title: Colour lab: drive the light, swap the objects
feedback: If a learner predicts the red apple stays red under blue light, point to the absorbed/reflected display: the blue lamp supplies no red, so there is nothing red for the surface to reflect, and the surface absorbs the blue — almost no light reaches the eye, so it looks near-black.

If a learner expects red+blue to blend to purple on the object, distinguish arriving light from returned light: under blue-only light no red arrives, so no red can come back; blending is paint/pigment thinking, not what happens to reflected light.

If a learner says the object just takes the lamp's colour, contrast it with the white shirt (which does look blue because it reflects all colours) versus the red apple (which absorbs blue) — the surface decides what it keeps and returns.

If a learner thinks the prism 'makes' the colours, use the recombination with the second prism: the colours were present all along and dispersion only separates them because each frequency refracts by a different amount.

Name the intuition explicitly ('the object just is that colour and the light brightens it') and contrast it with the model ('white light falls, the surface absorbs some frequencies and reflects the rest to your eye').
activities.rationale: The concept lives in covariation (illuminating light × pigment → perceived colour) and in refutation; a learner-driven simulation supports predict-observe-reconcile and makes absorbed-versus-reflected wavelengths visible. Securing 'what is white light' first via split-and-recombine addresses a documented prerequisite, and keeping additive and subtractive panels distinct targets a routinely conflated pair.
sourceClaims: Objects appear coloured by selective absorption/reflection; the Wrong Track ('object just has that colour, light brightens it') vs Right Lines ('white light falls, object absorbs most frequencies, reflects the rest to the eye') framing; a red dress appears black in blue light; apparent colour depends on both pigment and illuminating light.
A physically adequate concept of WHITE LIGHT is a prerequisite for understanding colour; students conceptualise white light as 'normal light', which impedes colour learning.
Filters are colour SUBTRACTORS — they transmit their own colour and absorb the rest, not dye all light their colour; a coloured object is a selective filter.

Subtractive colour reasoning is genuinely hard: only ~27% correctly predicted a yellow object looks dark under blue light, and over 70% wrongly expected red + green spotlights to make brown (correct: yellow); colour-vision mechanism was less problematic (>85% correct).
learnerActions: Before each reveal, write a prediction AND a reason for what colour an object will appear (e.g. 'red apple under a pure blue lamp').

Dial a light source from white to pure red, green, or blue and shine it on a shelf of objects (red apple, white shirt, black cloth, multicoloured toy); observe which wavelengths are absorbed and which reflect back to the eye.
Watch the red apple turn near-black under pure blue light, and the white shirt take on the lamp's colour; reconcile each observation with your prediction.
Split a white beam through a prism into ROYGBIV, then pass the spectrum through a second prism to recombine it back to white.

Compare the subtractive object/filter behaviour with a separate panel showing overlapping red, green and blue spotlights (additive mixing to yellow/cyan/magenta/white), noting the two rules give opposite results.
Pass white light through coloured filters and describe what is transmitted versus absorbed.
activities.intendedInsight: Perceived colour is light-and-pigment together, not a fixed property of the object: a surface returns only the colours the light supplies and the surface does not absorb. White light is a mixture a prism separates (not creates), and filters/pigments subtract colour while light sources add.

activities.title: Predict-observe-reconcile with a real coloured lamp
feedback: The reason is the diagnostic, not just the colour named: 'red because it's a red object' reveals colour-as-innate; 'black because there's no red light for it to reflect' shows the target model.

If a learner says the red object will take the lamp's colour (blue), use the white control: the white surface reflects all colours so it looks blue, but the red surface absorbs the blue, so it reflects almost nothing and looks near-black.
Reinforce that perceived colour is the light reaching the eye, which depends on both the pigment and the illuminating light.
Treat the near-black result as the idealised limiting case — with real pigment and real lamps the object looks 'very dark' rather than a perfect black.
activities.rationale: A physical investigation with real saturated pigment and reasonably pure coloured light stages the refutation directly and asks the learner to commit to a reasoned prediction, which exposes the misconception before the reveal.
sourceClaims: Objects appear coloured by selective absorption/reflection; the Wrong Track ('object just has that colour, light brightens it') vs Right Lines ('white light falls, object absorbs most frequencies, reflects the rest to the eye') framing; a red dress appears black in blue light; apparent colour depends on both pigment and illuminating light.
learnerActions: Under normal lighting, note that the object is a bright red; then, in a darkened space and before the coloured lamp is switched on, write down the colour you predict it will appear under a pure blue (or green) LED lamp AND your reason.
Switch on the lamp and observe how the object appears (with a saturated red pigment and a narrow-band blue or green lamp it should look very dark, close to black); compare with your prediction.
Repeat with a WHITE object for comparison and note that it takes on the lamp's colour (blue under a blue lamp, green under a green lamp).
State in your own words why the two objects behave differently.
activities.intendedInsight: A discrepant event that colour-as-innate cannot explain: the red object goes near-black because no red light is present to reflect, while the white object reflects whatever colour the lamp provides.

activities.title: Reason about colour: spectrum order, filters, and prisms
feedback: For the spectrum, order by the physical quantity (frequency/wavelength), not just 'rainbow order'.
For red+green spotlights, the answer is yellow; expecting brown conflates subtractive pigment mixing with additive light mixing.
For the red filter, it TRANSMITS red and ABSORBS the rest — it does not dye all the light red.
For the prism, dispersion separates colours already present because each frequency refracts by a different amount; it does not create colour.
Treat 'black' as the idealised limiting case — real pigments and lights give 'very dark', not perfectly black.
activities.rationale: Each learning target maps to a checkable prediction-and-explanation, giving a diagnostic and consolidation route for reasoning research shows is hard; written or selected answers consolidate but do not substitute for the covariation experience of the lab or live demo.
sourceClaims: Subtractive colour reasoning is genuinely hard: only ~27% correctly predicted a yellow object looks dark under blue light, and over 70% wrongly expected red + green spotlights to make brown (correct: yellow); colour-vision mechanism was less problematic (>85% correct).
Filters are colour SUBTRACTORS — they transmit their own colour and absorb the rest, not dye all light their colour; a coloured object is a selective filter.
learnerActions: Order the visible spectrum by increasing frequency (red = lowest frequency/longest wavelength → violet = highest frequency/shortest).
Predict and explain the colour of a red object seen under blue light, and of a white and a black object under the same light.
Match an object plus an illuminating colour to the perceived colour.

Predict what is seen when white light passes through a red filter, and explain why an opaque coloured object behaves like a selective filter, except that it selects the light it reflects rather than the light it transmits.
Predict the result of overlapping red and green spotlights and explain why it is yellow, not brown.
Explain why a prism disperses white light and why a second prism can recombine the spectrum to white.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the subtractive model and separate it from additive light mixing, tying colour order to the physical wave property that dispersion sorts.

constraints: Secure 'what is white light' before colour reasoning: use split-and-recombine with two prisms so 'white = all colours together' is seen, not asserted.
Keep subtractive pigment/filter behaviour visually and conceptually distinct from additive light mixing (red + green LIGHT = yellow); they are opposite rules and routinely conflated.
Present 'black under blue' as the idealised limiting case; use saturated pigments and reasonably pure coloured light, and acknowledge real objects look 'very dark', not perfectly black.
Dispersion rests on refraction as a prerequisite; treat the prism as separating colours already present, never creating them.

Treat qualitative reasoning as the KS3 target (UK statutory home); NGSS MS-PS4-2 is the broader wave reflect/absorb/transmit anchor and has no colour-specific performance expectation, so spectrum/dispersion/subtractive detail is UK-led.

Recognition or selection-only responses (ordering, matching, multiple choice) consolidate and diagnose but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an explanation; include prediction-with-reason and spoken/written explanation.
For accessibility, label colours with numbers or legends so the assessed reasoning is the absorption model, not hue discrimination (supports colourblind learners).

A static annotated scene is a useful reference and refutation display but cannot let a learner change the light and watch the object flip; use it as a companion to the lab or live demo, not a replacement for the predict-observe move.
A persona/role-play framing (lighting designer, artist) may motivate but does not by itself stage or verify the prediction-and-explanation that demonstrates understanding.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source lists several sources with verified:false (Haagen-Schützenhöfer 2017; IOP 'Understanding colours'; the 2024 TLS colour paper with the ~27% and ~70% figures; NASA JPL; NGSS MS-PS4-2). Quantitative claims (~27% yellow-under-blue, >70% red+green→brown, >85% colour-vision) are reproduced as reported but not independently confirmed here.

The original 'colour-as-innate kills on contact', 'a static picture cannot teach the predict-observe move', '3D adds nothing conceptually', and 'conversation cannot deliver the mechanism' framings are catalog fit judgements, not established comparative-efficacy findings; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than universal claims.

Physics self-audit: the red-object-under-blue-light-goes-near-black claim is sound for saturated pigment and reasonably pure monochromatic light; kept as an idealised limiting case ('very dark') to avoid overstating a perfect black with real materials and lamps. Dispersion described as frequency-dependent refraction (violet bends most, red least) and as separation not creation, consistent with the recombination demo.

Coherence of Activity 2: the object's red colour is established under normal light before the darkened-space prediction, since the colour cannot be observed in full darkness before the coloured lamp is on.

The KS3 statutory claim was removed from Activity 3 sourceClaims because it anchors curriculum scope rather than the activity's pedagogical rationale; the KS3 anchor remains in constraints. The original probeDeeper double-selection case (a red object viewed through a blue filter in daylight, which also appears dark) is a richer transfer example that could optionally be added to the filter task.

assess.poeTask: Show a bright red object in a blackout, then illuminate it with a pure blue (or green) LED lamp. BEFORE switching on, each child writes down the colour they predict AND their reason. The reason is the diagnostic: 'red because it's a red object' exposes colour-as-innate; 'black because there's no red light for it to reflect' shows the target model. Switch on — the object appears near-black — then have them reconcile prediction with observation. (Use a WHITE object as the control: it looks blue.)
probeDeeper: What colour would a WHITE van look under that same pure blue lamp — and why is that different from the red bus?
Under normal daylight, why does the red bus look red — what happens to the green and blue that also land on it?
A prism spreads white light into a rainbow. Where did those colours come from — did the prism make them? How could you prove your answer?
You look at the red bus through a blue filter in ordinary daylight. What do you see, and is that the same reason or a different one from the blue-lamp case?
assess.correctAnswer: It looks BLACK (very dark). A red object looks red because its surface reflects red light and absorbs the others; under pure blue light there is no red for it to reflect, and it absorbs the blue, so almost no light comes off it to our eyes — it appears black.

errorPatterns.pattern: Colour is an innate property of the object — 'the bus IS red, so it stays red whatever light you shine on it'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refute with the live demo (red object under a pure blue/green lamp goes black) — a discrepant event they cannot explain with the innate model. Rebuild colour as 'the object returns only the colours the light gives it and its surface doesn't absorb'.
errorPatterns.distractor: It still looks red, because the bus is red.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'red' and, when pushed, insists the paint is red so it can't change; ignores which colours the lamp actually provides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Colours mix additively on the object — 'red bus + blue light = purple bus' — treating illumination like mixing paint.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two ideas: pigment ABSORBS (subtractive), light sources ADD. On the object, ask 'what colours are arriving, and which does the surface send back?' — under blue-only, no red arrives, nothing red comes back.
errorPatterns.distractor: It looks purple, because red and blue mix.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'purple' or 'a bluey-red'; reasons by blending the object colour with the lamp colour.

errorPatterns.pattern: The object takes on the lamp's colour — 'blue light, so the bus looks blue' — treating the surface as a neutral screen.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a WHITE object (which does look blue under blue light because it reflects all colours) with the RED object (which absorbs blue). The surface decides what it keeps and what it returns.
errorPatterns.distractor: It looks blue, the same colour as the lamp.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'blue'; does not account for the red surface absorbing the blue.

errorPatterns.pattern: White light is a single 'pure' colourless thing that a prism STAINS or adds colour to, rather than a mixture the prism separates.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the recombination demo — a second inverted prism turns the spectrum back to white — to show the colours were there all along; dispersion is separation, not creation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In probing, says the prism 'colours' the light or 'makes' the rainbow, rather than spreading colours already present because each bends by a different amount.

responseLevels.gap: Says the bus stays red (or takes the lamp's colour, or mixes to purple) and defends it with colour-as-innate or paint-mixing reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Says black/very dark AND explains via selective reflection and absorption (surface reflects only red, which the blue lamp doesn't supply, and absorbs the blue), and transfers correctly — predicts the white van looks blue, and explains a filter or daylight case with the same mechanism.
responseLevels.partial: Gets that the appearance changes and may say 'darker' or 'black', but explains it as a rule ('no red light so it can't be red') without the reflection/absorption mechanism, and cannot reliably transfer to the white-object or filter case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A red London bus is parked in a dark garage. I switch on a lamp that gives out ONLY pure blue light — no other colours at all. What colour does the bus look now? And explain WHY it looks that colour.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks colour is a fixed property painted onto the object ('it's a red bus, so it's red') answers 'red' and cannot budge. A child who understands colour as selective reflection of the light that is PRESENT reasons that no red is available to reflect, so the object goes dark. The two models give opposite answers to the same question, and tier 2 forces the reflection/absorption mechanism, so 'red' cannot be reached by correct reasoning.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Light Travels in Straight Lines

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 6 Science, Light):** recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines; use the idea that light travels in straight lines to explain why shadows have the same shape as the objects that cast them.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No elementary performance expectation names rectilinear propagation directly. The Framework develops it implicitly — under 1-PS4-3 the boundary states 'the idea that light travels from place to place is developed through experiences with light sources, mirrors, and shadows, but no attempt is made to discuss the speed of light' — and the geometric light-path model is assessed at 4-PS4-2 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-2]'). Explicit ray/straight-line modelling is formalised later at the MS-PS4 band.

- **Operational details:** The leap here is to treat light as something that TRAVELS, along a continuous straight path, through the dark space between source and object — not merely as brightness that exists in lit places. Demonstrate rectilinear travel directly: a narrow torch beam in a darkened, slightly dusty/smoky room; the classic three-holes-in-card line-up (light reaches the eye only when the holes are collinear); a rolled tube proving you cannot see round corners. Teach ray-diagram conventions deliberately — ruler-straight lines, an arrow on every ray showing direction, rays drawn from the source. Then USE straight-line travel to explain shadows: rays graze the edges of an opaque object, so the shadow reproduces the object's outline; children try (and fail) to make light bend round the object. Keep correcting the language trap that 'a ray' is a real thin sliver of light — it is a model of the path's direction.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). At 10–11 this is a transitional abstraction: light is modelled as a continuous straight path through space (including the dark gap), represented by the ray diagram. The threshold is moving from 'light is in the bright bits' to 'light travelled there in a straight line', and then deploying that model to PREDICT and EXPLAIN (shadow shape, why holes must align). Mastery is using straight-line travel as an explanatory tool, not just stating the slogan.
bestPractices: Demonstrate rectilinear travel directly: a narrow torch beam in a darkened (slightly hazy) room; the three-holes-in-card line-up where light only reaches the eye when the holes are collinear; a rolled tube showing you cannot see round corners.
Teach ray-diagram conventions explicitly — ruler-straight lines, a direction arrow on every ray, rays drawn starting from the light source.
Use straight-line travel as an explanatory tool: show rays grazing an opaque object's edges so the shadow reproduces the outline, and have children predict shadow shape from the rays.
Set a 'try to break it' task — ask children to make light bend round a corner or wrap behind the object — so the impossibility makes 'light goes straight' a felt constraint.
Correct the language trap that a 'ray' is a real thin piece of light; frame it as a model of the path and its direction, and that light does not 'add up' from separate rays.
Anchor to the idea that light fills the dark space between source and object as it travels, not only the bright patches where it lands.
keyRepresentations: Ray diagram with ruler-straight, arrowed lines drawn from the source
Three holes in card threaded onto a straight line (often with string) so light reaches the eye only when aligned
A rolled tube held to the eye — 'you can't see round corners'
A torch beam through a slit/smoke showing the straight path
Opaque object on a screen with rays grazing its edges, casting an outline-matching shadow
commonMisconceptions: Light isn't thought of as travelling at all — it simply 'is' wherever it is bright.
Light exists only in the bright regions, not in the space in between as it journeys.
Light bends or curves around edges/corners (so why would shadows be sharp?).
A 'light ray' is a real, physical thin sliver of light rather than a model of the path's direction.
Light is 'made of rays added together'.
Light only travels in straight lines when it comes from a mirror or a laser, not in general.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: build the idea that light TRAVELS along a continuous straight path through the dark space between a source and an object — not merely that light 'is' wherever it is bright. Learners test rectilinear travel by trying to violate it (holes must align, light won't turn corners), then USE straight-line travel to explain why a shadow reproduces the object's outline. The target is deploying the straight-line model to predict and explain, not reciting the slogan. The ray is taught explicitly as a model of the path and its direction, not a physical sliver of light.

activities.title: Fire a beam, block it, and discover light won't turn corners
feedback: If a learner expects light to still get through an off-line hole, show the alignment failure directly, then connect it: a shadow keeps the object's outline because light does not bend round behind the object either.
If a learner draws only bright patches and no travelling ray, reveal the path with chalk dust or smoke in the beam — the ray IS the path light is taking, present whether or not it has yet landed.
When the 'make light bend' task fails every time, name it: light travels in straight lines, and in this setup, with no mirror or other surface to redirect it, it does not curve round the corner.
activities.rationale: Shadow and image tasks are hard because learners rarely work through what straight-line travel implies; a predict-try-observe cycle that invites learners to attempt to break the rule is intended to turn 'light goes straight' into a felt constraint rather than a stated fact.
sourceClaims: Research finds tasks on shadows and images are very difficult because students have rarely thought through what it means for light to travel in a straight line; inquiry-based, prediction-observation curricula effectively build understanding of the implications of light's linear travel for shadows and images.

Year 6 statutory light content: recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines and use this to explain why shadows have the same shape as the objects that cast them; Oak Year 6 teaches ray diagrams, the journey of light, and names the 'a ray is a thin piece of light' / 'light made of rays added together' misconceptions, recommending demonstrations and diagram practice.
learnerActions: Aim a torch across a darkened scene so the beam's straight-edged path becomes visible (use a slightly hazy/dusty or smoky room, where particles scatter some light to your eyes, or draw the beam with straight ray lines, so the travelling path shows).

Place a card with a single hole in the beam's path. Slide the hole until light passes through and reaches a small 'eye' on the far side; note it only gets through when the hole sits on the straight line between torch and eye.
Nudge the hole off that line and observe the light is blocked — it will not bend to find the gap.

Drop an opaque shape into the beam and observe the light passing straight past its edges, throwing a shadow on a screen whose outline matches the shape as seen from the torch (it may be bigger or stretched depending on distances and how the shape and screen are angled).
Try to 'make the shadow wrap round the back of the object' or 'bend the light round the corner' — and find you cannot.
activities.intendedInsight: Light travels in straight lines through the space between source and object; a shadow has the object's outline (as seen from the source) because light travels straight past the edges and does not turn corners into the space behind the object, unless something such as a mirror redirects it.

activities.title: Three holes in a line — predict, then break the alignment
feedback: Expected result: you no longer see the light. Light travels in straight lines, so it passes through all three holes only when they are lined up; it cannot bend to reach the offset middle hole.
If a learner predicts the light still gets through (light 'finds its way' or curves round), run the demo so the failure is seen, then link it to why shadows have the same outline as the object.
If a learner says 'you'd still see it because light is everywhere in the room anyway', revisit the beam-in-dust observation to separate light that has landed from light still travelling.
On the dust question: you are seeing the dust scattering the light into your eye, not light that is simply 'everywhere' — the visible beam marks the straight path the light is travelling along.
activities.rationale: Requiring a straight alignment and then deliberately breaking it, while asking WHY, is intended to force the straight-line mechanism into the open: a 'spreads everywhere / curves to find its way' intuition makes a wrong, testable prediction here.
sourceClaims: Research finds tasks on shadows and images are very difficult because students have rarely thought through what it means for light to travel in a straight line; inquiry-based, prediction-observation curricula effectively build understanding of the implications of light's linear travel for shadows and images.
learnerActions: Line up three cards, each with a small hole punched in the middle, and shine a torch so light passes through all three holes to your eye (threading string through the holes helps show the straight line).
Before moving anything, predict: if you slide the MIDDLE card sideways, will you still see the light? Say why first.
Slide the middle card off-line and check your prediction.
Explain what the result proves about how light travels.
Discuss: when you see the beam in dusty air, are you seeing the light itself or the dust it lights up?
activities.intendedInsight: Light reaches the eye only when the holes are lined up; the offset-hole result contradicts a 'light bends to find its way' model and supports the model that light travels in straight lines.

activities.title: Draw and use ray diagrams to predict a shadow
feedback: Check for the conventions: rays start at the source, are ruler-straight, and carry a direction arrow.

If a learner treats a 'ray' as a real thin sliver of light you could touch, reframe it: a ray is a representation of the direction light travels — a line with an arrow — not a physical strand, and light is not 'made of rays added together'.
If the predicted outline doesn't match, trace the edge-grazing rays together to see where they land on the screen.
activities.rationale: Explicit teaching of ray-diagram conventions, combined with predicting shadow shape before checking, is intended to move learners from stating the rule to using it as an explanatory and predictive tool.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory light content: recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines and use this to explain why shadows have the same shape as the objects that cast them; Oak Year 6 teaches ray diagrams, the journey of light, and names the 'a ray is a thin piece of light' / 'light made of rays added together' misconceptions, recommending demonstrations and diagram practice.

Research finds tasks on shadows and images are very difficult because students have rarely thought through what it means for light to travel in a straight line; inquiry-based, prediction-observation curricula effectively build understanding of the implications of light's linear travel for shadows and images.
learnerActions: Draw rays with a ruler as straight lines starting from the light source, putting a direction arrow on every ray.
Draw rays grazing the edges of an opaque object and continuing to a screen to show where the shadow falls and why its outline matches the object.
Predict the shadow's outline for a given shape BEFORE revealing or checking the actual result, then compare.
Explain in words why the shadow reproduces the object's outline, referring to the straight rays past its edges.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct source–object–screen ray diagram with ruler-straight, arrowed rays from the source both represents straight-line travel and lets you predict shadow shape.

activities.title: You can't see round corners
feedback: If a learner expects to see round the bend, have them trace the straight tube with a ruler or string to show the sightline cannot curve.
Connect back: the same straightness is why shadows have the object's outline and why the three holes must align.
activities.rationale: A quick, concrete demonstration gives a memorable everyday anchor for rectilinear travel that complements the beam and ray-diagram work.
learnerActions: Hold a rolled tube to your eye and confirm you can only see what is straight ahead through it.
Try to use the tube to see something off to one side, around a corner — and find you cannot.
Explain how this shows that light travels in straight lines from an object to your eye.
activities.intendedInsight: Because light travels in straight lines from an object to your eye, you cannot see round a corner without something like a mirror to redirect the light.

constraints: Keep correcting the language trap: a 'ray' is a model of the path's direction (a line with an arrow), not a real thin piece of light; and light is not 'made of separate rays added together'.
Emphasise that light fills and travels through the dark space between source and object as it journeys, not only the bright patches where it lands.

This is a transitional/early-formal abstraction for 10–11: mastery is using straight-line travel to predict and explain (shadow shape, hole alignment), not merely stating 'light travels in straight lines'.

Recognition-only checks (e.g. choosing 'straight' vs 'curves' from options) can assess the conclusion but do not require the learner to build the model against the 'light is just in bright places' intuition, so pair them with predict-and-explain tasks.

A labelled, non-manipulable ray diagram is a useful reference for conventions but asserts the straight path rather than letting learners test what happens at a hole or an edge; use it alongside, not instead of, the test-it tasks.

Shadow POSITION and length are genuinely spatial and a three-dimensional sun–object–ground setup can help with those; the specific claim here (shape from straight rays grazing edges) reads cleanly in a flat ray view, so a 3D model is an optional affordance for this sub-concept, not required.

Smoke/dust/haze to reveal the beam needs a suitably darkened space and sensible safety; it is one way to make the travelling path visible, not the only one. Use an ordinary torch rather than a laser or the sun: children may glance briefly through aligned holes to see a modest torch, but should never stare into an intense source and should otherwise keep observations to the beam, the holes, and the cast shadow or a screen.

NGSS note: no elementary performance expectation names rectilinear propagation directly; grade 1 work on light (1-PS4-3, which excludes the speed of light) uses materials placed in a beam and shadows, 4-PS4-2 models light reflecting from objects into the eye, and tracing light's path as straight lines is developed at the middle-school PS4 band.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources are marked verified:false in the row (Oak National Academy unit; Wosilait/Heron/Shaffer/McDermott PER citation); only the NextGenScience boundary claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

A conversation/dialogue format was judged a poor fit in the source. Reframed as a narrow affordance: narration can convey information but does not itself elicit the hands-on beam manipulation this discovery task relies on; this is a design judgment, not demonstrated evidence that dialogue cannot teach the concept. Retained as context only, not as an activity.

The source's framing that a flat ray view makes 3D 'add cost beyond what this sub-concept needs' is a design preference, not an established efficacy claim; recast as an optional affordance with a stated scope (shape vs. position/length).

The pedagogy lists the misconception 'light only travels straight when it comes from a mirror or a laser, not in general', which is not directly addressed by any activity; consider adding a prompt that general (non-mirror, non-laser) light also travels straight.

No arithmetic or force/motion errors were present to correct; the physics of rectilinear propagation and shadow formation as stated is sound for this level. The main conceptual care point is keeping 'ray' as a model, which is retained in constraints and feedback.

assess.poeTask: Predict whether you will still see the torch through all three holes after the middle card is nudged sideways. Say why first. Then slide the card and explain what the result proves about how light travels.
probeDeeper: Why does a shadow have the same outline shape as the object that casts it?
If light COULD bend round objects, what would shadows look like — could you even have a sharp shadow at all?
When you see a torch beam in dusty air, what are you actually seeing — the light itself, or the dust it lights up?
assess.correctAnswer: No — you no longer see the light. Light travels in straight lines, so it can only pass through all three holes when they are lined up straight; it cannot bend to get through the offset middle hole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Light bends round corners: 'the light curves round the edge to get where it needs to go' — the tell is 'I can see light near a corner so it must bend'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the align-the-holes demo so the failure is seen; then connect it to shadows — a shadow has the object's sharp outline precisely because light cannot bend round the object.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — light bends around inside to get through the middle hole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts light still passes the offset hole; says light 'finds its way' or bends round the card

errorPatterns.pattern: Light is only in bright patches: light exists where it lands, not travelling through the space between torch and wall (no ray in the air between)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reveal the travelling path with chalk dust or smoke in the beam — the ray IS the path light takes; it is there whether or not it has landed yet.
errorPatterns.distractor: You'd still see it, because the light is everywhere in the room anyway.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws bright spots but no travelling ray; denies light is 'in' the air between source and object

errorPatterns.pattern: Ray as a physical object: 'a ray is a thin solid piece of light you could touch'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A ray is a representation of the DIRECTION light travels, drawn as a line with an arrow — not a physical strand of light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about a ray as a thing/object rather than as the path or direction light travels

responseLevels.gap: Predicts light still passes the offset hole / says light bends round corners, or denies light travels through the space between the source and the wall.
responseLevels.full: Predicts the offset hole blocks the light AND explains it by straight-line travel; transfers the idea to shadow shape and draws a correct source-object-screen ray diagram.
responseLevels.partial: States that light travels in straight lines but cannot use it — e.g. cannot explain the offset-hole result, or why a shadow matches the object's outline.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You line up three cards, each with a small hole punched in the middle, and shine a torch so you can see the light through all three holes. Now you slide the MIDDLE card sideways a little. Will you still see the light coming through? Explain what this tells you about how light travels.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks light 'spreads everywhere' or 'curves to find its way' predicts you'd still see it through the offset hole. Requiring a straight alignment and then breaking it, while asking WHY, forces the straight-line mechanism: the offset-hole result simply cannot be explained by a light-bends-round model.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–7 (CONCEPTUAL): understand that 10 can be thought of as a single BUNDLE of ten ones — a 'ten' — and that ten ones can be exchanged for one ten and back. This unitising move (centrality 0.41) is the bedrock of the entire base-ten system.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1–Y2): recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones); non-statutory guidance on grouping in tens.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.2a '10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a ten'.
• Operational details — the child physically groups ten single cubes into one tens-rod, and reverses it (exchange one ten for ten ones), grasping that '1 ten' and '10 ones' are the SAME quantity named/organised differently. This is UNITISING: treating a group as one thing while knowing it contains ten. It follows teen composition and precedes all multi-digit place value, comparison and column arithmetic.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): group 10 single cubes into one rod and say why. Tier B (6–7): explain that 10 ones is the same as 1 ten. Tier C (7): exchange 10 ones for a single tens block (and vice versa) fluently, using it in a simple problem.
bestPractices: Make the EXCHANGE physical and two-way: swap ten loose ones for one tens-rod and back, so children feel that regrouping conserves quantity — the ten IS ten ones, just bundled.
Use materials that show the ten is made of ten (a rod visibly ten cubes long, a ten-bead bar) BEFORE pre-grouped abstract tokens, so the bundle's tenness is seen, not asserted.
Name the unit deliberately — 'one ten' — and contrast counting 'ten ones' vs counting 'one ten' for the same pile, surfacing the unitising idea.
Link to the teens (prerequisite): a teen number already has one such bundle; now generalise the bundle itself as a countable unit toward decade numbers and two-digit place value.
Foreshadow regrouping in arithmetic: this exchange is exactly the 'carry/borrow' move children will meet in column addition and subtraction.
keyRepresentations: Ten single cubes physically snapping into one tens-rod (and the reverse).
Ten-bead bar / bead string where the ten is one strung unit of ten beads.
Exchange mat: 'ones' column and 'tens' column with a swap action (10 ones ↔ 1 ten).
Ten-frame filled completely = 'one ten' label.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a tens-rod is 'one' (counting bundles as single objects), so 3 rods = 3 rather than 30 — the core unitising error.
Believing the ten and the ten ones are different amounts (not conserving quantity across the exchange).
Being unable to reverse the bundling (can make a ten from ones but not break a ten back into ones).
Treating pre-grouped tens tokens as arbitrary symbols without knowing each holds ten.
Confusing 'ten' the count word with 'a ten' the unit.

learn.summary: For children aged 6–7, build the concept that 10 ones can be bundled into a single 'ten' and exchanged back again, with the quantity conserved across the swap. This unitising move — treating a group of ten as one countable thing while knowing it still contains ten — is the foundation of base-ten place value, comparison and column arithmetic. The central activity is a two-way physical/interactive exchange with proportional materials (a rod visibly made of ten cubes) and deliberate naming of the same pile as 'ten ones' or 'one ten'. Supporting activities anchor the equivalence with a reveal, probe reasoning through dialogue, and check retention.

activities.title: Base-ten exchange: bundle and break a ten
feedback: If the child calls a rod 'one', break it apart in front of them and count the ten cubes, then rebuild it: '10 ones make 1 ten — same cubes, bundled up.'
If the child thinks the rearranged amount changed, do it reversibly — build, break, rebuild — counting each time and stressing nothing was added or taken away.
Confirm success when the child exchanges both directions without recounting and names the same pile as either 'ten ones' or 'one ten'.
activities.rationale: Unitising is a physical bundling/exchange action; performing the two-way swap with proportional material lets conservation be felt and directly confronts the 'a rod is one' error. Proportional materials where the ten is visibly ten should precede pre-grouped abstract tokens so the bundle's tenness is seen, not asserted.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils understand that 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a 'ten'.
Year 1–2 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones), grouping in tens.

Unitising — treating a bundle of ten as a single countable unit while knowing it contains ten ones — is the foundational concept of base-ten place value, best built with proportional materials and physical exchange.
learnerActions: Gather ten loose single cubes and join them into one tens-rod that is visibly ten cubes long.
Reverse the move: break (or separate) one tens-rod back into ten loose ones.
Watch or track a running count of the total cubes before and after each swap, and confirm it does not change.
Toggle/say the name for the very same pile two ways: 'ten ones' and 'one ten'.
Respond to challenges such as 'make one ten' and 'break a ten into ten ones, then give me 3 of them — how many loose ones are left?'
activities.intendedInsight: One ten and ten ones are the same quantity, named and organised two ways; bundling or unbundling changes the arrangement, not the amount, and the ten is itself a countable unit.

activities.title: Reveal the ten inside the rod
feedback: If the child guesses a number other than ten, count the revealed cubes together one by one.
Reinforce: 'The rod IS ten ones joined up.'
activities.rationale: A reveal image is a good anchor for the equivalence and counters treating pre-grouped tokens as arbitrary symbols. It is a scaffold: it shows the equivalence but does not let the child perform the exchange, so use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on bundling.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils understand that 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a 'ten'.
learnerActions: Look at a tens-rod shown beside a pile of ten single cubes.
Tap or lift to reveal the rod splitting into ten cubes, with the label 'one ten = ten ones'.
State how many ones are inside one ten.
activities.intendedInsight: A tens-rod is not an arbitrary token: it holds exactly ten ones.

activities.title: Prove it to the doubter
feedback: Accept the full explanation 'they are the same — the stick is ten ones bundled into one ten, so joining them doesn't change how many cubes there are.'
If the child only justifies by counting the loose cubes one by one, nudge toward the bundling relationship: 'What does the stick tell you without counting?'
If the child agrees the rod came from ten but still won't call them equal because 'it looks different now', rebuild and rebreak it, emphasising nothing was added or removed.
activities.rationale: Dialogue can surface and probe the unitising idea and distinguish 'equal because I counted' from 'equal because a ten IS ten ones'. Efficacy of the dialogue medium is not established by the cited sources, so it is proposed as a probe best paired with materials, so the child can act out the proof rather than only assert it.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who claims 'three rods is just three' or 'the loose pile is more than the stick'.
Explain and, if possible, demonstrate why one ten equals ten ones.

Answer probes: 'If I snap the stick back into loose cubes, how many will there be — and how did you know before I did it?', 'Can you make a ten out of these loose ones?', 'If I only had nine loose cubes, could I bundle a ten? Why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: A ten can be counted as one unit that is also ten ones; the learner can justify the equivalence rather than only count.

activities.title: Check the ten-ones equivalence
feedback: For a wrong value, return to the reveal or exchange activity and recount the ten.
Correct answer is ten ones.
activities.rationale: Matching, multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank items are useful for checking whether the equivalence has stuck. Recognition items check retention; they do not elicit the independent bundling and exchange that builds the concept, so use them after hands-on work.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils understand that 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a 'ten'.
learnerActions: Match representations of a ten (ten ones ↔ one ten).
Answer 'a tens-rod is worth how many ones?'
Complete '1 ten = __ ones'.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirm the learner reliably recognises that one ten and ten ones are the same quantity.

constraints: Use proportional materials where the ten is visibly made of ten (a rod ten cubes long, a ten-bead bar, a filled ten-frame) before introducing pre-grouped abstract tokens, so the tenness is seen not asserted.
Make the exchange genuinely two-way: bundling ten ones into a ten AND breaking a ten back into ten ones; reversing the bundle is the move needed later for borrowing in subtraction.
Name the unit deliberately as 'one ten' and contrast counting 'ten ones' versus 'one ten' for the same pile.
The reveal image and the recognition quiz are scaffolds/checks: they anchor or test the equivalence but do not let the child perform the conserving exchange that builds unitising.

Checkpoint tiers: (A, age 6) group 10 single cubes into one rod and say why; (B, 6–7) explain that 10 ones is the same as 1 ten; (C, age 7) exchange 10 ones for one tens block and back fluently and use it in a simple problem.

Watch for the core errors: counting a rod as 'one' (so 3 rods = 3), non-conservation across the swap, inability to reverse the bundling, treating pre-grouped tens tokens as arbitrary symbols without knowing each holds ten, and confusing 'ten' the count word with 'a ten' the unit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-review found no critical learner-facing errors: arithmetic (1 ten = 10 ones), conservation logic, and medium claims are coherent across all summaries, insights, actions, feedback and constraints.

Source row marked two of three citations as verified:false (the CCSS 1.NBT.2a claim and the NCETM unitising claim); only the DfE National Curriculum claim was verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

The dialogue activity ('Prove it to the doubter') carries no sourceClaim because no cited source supports spoken dialogue as the medium; its efficacy is proposed/untested and it is qualified as best paired with materials.

The legacy source asserted a static image 'can't let the child perform the exchange' and that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing'. These are catalog-fit comparisons, not established efficacy/necessity claims; they have been softened to scoped scaffold/affordance notes. A fixed reveal still teaches the equivalence even though it cannot be manipulated.
Prerequisite reteach IDs referenced in the source assessment (e.g. the internal reteach identifier) are internal identifiers and were not carried into learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: If I snap the stick back into loose cubes, how many will there be? How did you know before I did it?
Can you make a ten out of these loose ones? Show me.
If I only had nine loose cubes, could I bundle a ten? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: They are the same. The stick is ten ones bundled into one 'ten', so 1 ten = 10 ones; joining them together doesn't change how many cubes there are.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the ten-stick as a single unit worth one, so the loose cubes look like more: 'there are ten over here but the stick is just one'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Break the stick apart in front of them and count 10; rebuild it. Name it: '10 ones make 1 ten — same cubes, bundled up.' Use exchange games (10 ones ⇄ 1 ten).
errorPatterns.distractor: The loose cubes are more — the stick is only one thing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child points to the stick, calls it 'one', and says the loose pile has more.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks changing the arrangement changed the amount (non-conservation): 'the stick is different so it can't be the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do it reversibly: build the stick, break it, rebuild it, each time counting. Emphasise nothing was added or taken away.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're different amounts because the stick looks different.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child agrees the stick came from ten cubes but still won't call them equal because 'they look different now'.

responseLevels.gap: Calls the ten-stick 'one' and judges the loose pile larger, or must recount the stick every time; treats bundle and loose as different amounts.
responseLevels.full: States that 1 ten = 10 ones because the stick IS ten ones bundled, decomposes and recomposes freely, and knows the quantity is conserved without recounting.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees both are ten, but justifies only by counting the loose cubes one-by-one — does not appeal to the bundling relationship.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put ten loose cubes on the table and, next to them, one stick made of ten cubes joined together. Ask: 'Is there the same number of cubes in the loose pile as in the stick — or is one more? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has unitised sees the stick AS ten and calls them equal without recounting; a child who hasn't treats the stick as a single object ('one thing') and so judges the loose pile bigger, or has to count the stick cube-by-cube to be convinced. The reason tier separates 'equal because I counted' from 'equal because a ten IS ten ones'.
