pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Understand that the multiples of 100 (100, 200 … 900) are 'some hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones' — 300 = 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones. This isolates the hundreds column and reinforces two placeholder zeros.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100'; three-digit place value (hundreds, tens, ones).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.1b 'the numbers 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 refer to one, two, three… nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones)'.
• Operational details — Build multiples of 100 from hundred-flats only, pairing with skip-counting in 100s and placement on a 0-1000 number line. Emphasise the DOUBLE placeholder (two zeros) and connect to the analogous decade structure (300 is to hundreds what 30 is to tens). Read and write them and locate them as landmark numbers.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): builds 500 with 5 flats, says 'five hundreds'. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): reads/writes any multiple of 100 and explains the two zeros. Tier C (age 8, extending): places multiples of 100 on a 0-1000 line and links them to the tens/decade pattern.
bestPractices: Build multiples of 100 from hundred-flats alone so 'pure hundreds, no tens, no ones' is visible — both empty columns justify the two zeros.
Skip-count in 100s aloud (100, 200, 300…) while placing flats, binding count to structure.
Explicitly parallel the decade pattern: 300 is 'three hundreds' as 30 is 'three tens' — the ×10 self-similarity again.
Use the 0-1000 number line to treat multiples of 100 as landmark/benchmark numbers for later estimation and rounding.
Contrast 300 with 30 and 3, and with 303/330, to sharpen the meaning of each zero.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten hundred-flats (multiples of 100 as pure hundreds)
0-1000 number line with hundred landmarks
H|T|O place-value chart with empty tens and ones columns
Gattegno chart hundreds row (100,200…900 = 'n hundreds')
Skip-counting-in-100s track / bead string
commonMisconceptions: Treating the two zeros as meaningless or writing 300 as 3 / 30.
Reading 300 as 'three-oh-oh' or as three separate digits.
Confusing multiples of 100 with multiples of 10 (300 vs 30).
Not connecting 'three hundreds' to the parallel 'three tens' pattern.
Placing multiples of 100 wrongly on the number line by ignoring magnitude.

learn.summary: For ages 7-8: understand that multiples of 100 (100, 200 … 900) each name a count of hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones, so 300 = 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones. The focus is isolating the hundreds column, giving meaning to the two placeholder zeros, reading/writing these numbers as whole quantities, and placing them as landmarks on a 0-1000 line. Learners also connect the pattern to the familiar tens pattern (300 is to hundreds as 30 is to tens).

activities.title: Hundreds-only builder with live numeral and placeholder zeros
feedback: If a learner writes 300 as 3 or 30, rebuild it from 3 hundred-flats with nothing in tens or ones and point out that the empty columns ARE the zeros; contrast 3, 30, and 300 side by side on the chart.
If a learner reads the leading 3 as 'three' rather than 'three hundreds', name its place: '3 in the hundreds place means 3 hundreds, which is 300', and count the hundreds together.

If a learner reads 300 as 'three-oh-oh' or as three separate digits, read it as the single quantity 'three hundred', tying the 3 to the hundreds place and the two zeros to the empty tens and ones places.
When the tens-rod turns 300 into 310, highlight that the middle zero was holding that place open until something filled it.
activities.rationale: Building pure hundreds makes both empty columns concrete, so the double placeholder is felt rather than memorised; toggling a single tens-rod in and out demonstrates that the zero marks a genuine, currently-empty place. An optional synced numeral, a spoken skip-count, a Gattegno chart hundreds row, a bead string, and a number-line hop are examples of ways to bind the count to the structure, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100' and work with three-digit place value.
The numbers 100, 200…900 refer to one to nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones) — 2.NBT.1b.
learnerActions: Build 100, 200, 300 … 900 using only hundred-flats placed in the hundreds (H) column of a place-value chart, leaving the tens (T) and ones (O) columns visibly empty.
Watch or write the numeral as each flat is added (100 → 200 → 300) and note that two zeros appear because the T and O columns hold nothing.
Add a single tens-rod to the empty tens column of 300 and observe the numeral change to 310, then remove it to return to 300.
Say aloud what each digit means, e.g. '300 is 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones', and read the whole number as 'three hundred'.

Skip-count in 100s aloud while building: 100, 200, 300 …; optionally track the same count on a Gattegno chart hundreds row (100, 200 … 900 = 'n hundreds') or a skip-counting bead string as alternative representations.
activities.intendedInsight: The two zeros in a multiple of 100 are not padding: they record that the tens and ones places are empty. When something is actually placed in the tens column, the zero is replaced, which shows the zero was holding a real place.

activities.title: Landmark family wall and number-line placement
feedback: If a multiple is placed out of order or in the wrong region, count the hundreds along the line together (100, 200, 300 …) to check magnitude.
If a learner confuses 300 with 30, locate both on the same 0-1000 number line and compare how far along each sits: 30 is very close to 0, while 300 is three hundred-marks along.
A static reference wall is useful for recognition and recall, but confirm understanding of the zeros through building or explanation, not just tapping.
activities.rationale: Treating multiples of 100 as benchmarks on a 0-1000 line links symbol to magnitude and builds the landmark intuition used in estimation and rounding. A reference chart supports recall but, on its own, does not require the learner to construct or justify the place-value structure.
sourceClaims: Multiples of 100 serve as landmark numbers on the number line supporting estimation and rounding.
learnerActions: Study a family chart of the multiples of 100 (each shown as its flats, its numeral, and the words 'n hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones').
Tap or point to a chosen multiple (e.g. 400) and state how many flats it has and how many tens and ones (four hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones).
Place 300, 500, 700, and 800 on a 0-1000 number line, using the hundred marks as labelled landmarks.
Order a scrambled set of multiples of 100 from smallest to largest.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiples of 100 are evenly spaced landmark numbers on the line to 1000; their position reflects their magnitude, which later supports estimation and rounding.

activities.title: Explain and consolidate the place-value structure
feedback: If a learner says the zeros are meaningless, revisit the builder: the empty tens and ones columns are exactly what the zeros record.
If a learner says '3 hundreds' but cannot say what the zeros contribute, ask them to add a ten or a one and watch which zero changes.
For 'how many tens in 300', support reasoning that 300 is 30 tens (each hundred is 10 tens) as an extension, distinct from the fact that the tens DIGIT is 0.
activities.rationale: Explanation and matching tasks consolidate and let a teacher check whether the zeros are understood as placeholders rather than ignored. Recognition and fill-in tasks assess and reinforce after teaching but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction that the builder provides.
sourceClaims: The numbers 100, 200…900 refer to one to nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones) — 2.NBT.1b.
learnerActions: Complete statements such as '300 = 3 hundreds, __ tens, __ ones'.
Match each multiple to its flats and to its words (e.g. 500 ↔ 5 flats ↔ 'five hundreds').
Answer: 'Why isn't 300 the same as 30?' and 'How many tens are there in 300?' with a reason.
Write 300 and explain in words what the 3 tells us and what the two 0s tell us.
Contrast 300 with 30, 3, 303, and 330 to say what each zero is doing.
activities.intendedInsight: Each digit's value depends on its place; the zeros in a multiple of 100 state that the tens and ones places are empty, which is what distinguishes 300 from 30 or 3.

constraints: Learners should build or construct multiples of 100 and explain the zeros, not only recognise or tap labels; recognition-only tasks do not elicit independent construction of the place-value structure.
A static family chart or reference wall supports recall and landmark recognition but cannot show the zeros toggling; pair it with building or explanation.
Distinguish the two senses of 'tens' in 300: the tens DIGIT is 0 (nothing in the tens place), while the number 300 equals 30 tens overall. Do not conflate these when answering 'how many tens in 300'.
Be precise that 300 ≠ 30 and 300 ≠ 3: the difference is which places are filled, shown by magnitude on the number line.
Number-line placement should reflect magnitude; check spacing/order rather than treating placement as decorative.
Read a multiple of 100 as a whole quantity ('three hundred'), never digit-by-digit as 'three-oh-oh'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists the cited CCSS 2.NBT.1b claim and the NCETM landmark claim as verified:false; treat their support as unconfirmed and do not infer empirical efficacy from citation.

Self-audit: the original two-tier probe asks 'How many tens are there in 300?' while the main teaching correctly states the tens DIGIT is 0. These are different questions (tens place-value digit vs total count of tens = 30). The activity keeps both but flags the distinction to avoid teaching that '300 has 0 tens' in the counting sense.

The original rated conversation and 3D formats as 'poor' ('planar; no spatial payoff', 'open dialogue is a poor fit'). These are catalogue fit judgements, not pedagogical laws; discussion can still support explanation of the zeros, and such rankings were not propagated as universal claims.

The Gattegno chart hundreds row and bead string from the source representation inventory are reinstated as optional alternative skip-count representations, offered alongside (not in place of) the builder and number line.

probeDeeper: Place 300, 500 and 800 on a 0–1000 number line.
Why isn't 300 the same as 30?
How many tens are there in 300?
assess.correctAnswer: The 3 means 3 hundreds (300); the two 0s show 0 tens and 0 ones, holding those places empty.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the zeros as meaningless and collapses the number: '300 is the same as 3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 300 with 3 hundred-flats, no tens, no ones; the empty tens and ones ARE the zeros. Contrast 3, 30, 300 on a place-value chart.
errorPatterns.distractor: 300 is the same as 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ignores the zeros or equates 300 with 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the leading digit at face value: 'the 3 means three'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give the digit its place ('3 in the hundreds place = 3 hundreds = 300') and count the hundreds on a 0–1000 line.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 3 just means three.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the 3 stands for three rather than three hundreds.

responseLevels.gap: Reads the leading digit at face value or drops the placeholder zeros.
responseLevels.full: States 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones, explains the zeros hold the empty places, and locates multiples of 100 on a line.
responseLevels.partial: Says '3 hundreds' but is unsure what the zeros contribute.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 300. Ask: 'What is the 3 telling us, and what are the two 0s telling us? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with hundreds place value reads '3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones'; a face-value thinker says the 3 means three, and a zero-blind child collapses 300 to 3. The reason tier reveals whether the zeros are understood as placeholders.

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100' and work with three-digit place value.

pedagogy.summary: Children extend coordinate work to the full plane: plotting and reading points such as (−3,4) and (2,−5) across all four quadrants, naming which quadrant a point lies in, and describing positions where either or both coordinates are negative. The new demand is not the (across, up) convention itself — that carries over from the first quadrant — but reading a SIGNED scale on each axis: a negative x means left of the origin, a negative y means below it, and the numbers run symmetrically outward from 0 in both directions. Success rests on secure directed-number sense fused to the ordered-pair rule.
bestPractices: Anchor both axes as signed number lines meeting at the origin: rehearse pointing and chanting positive and negative values on a counting stick held horizontally (x) and vertically (y), forwards and backwards, so left/below map to negatives (NCETM).
Emphasise the symmetry about 0 — the numbers mirror outward from the origin — so children read −3 as three to the LEFT, not three to the right.
Keep the reading rule explicit and mnemonic — 'along the corridor and up (or down) the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y' — to hold off the perennial y-before-x reversal (NCETM).
Always plot the first coordinate along x from the origin THEN the second along y, treating each sign as a direction, not a decoration on the digit.
Name the four quadrants by the sign pattern of their points (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−) so 'which quadrant?' becomes a reading of the two signs, and connect this to reflections in the axes.
Use problems that force reasoning across quadrants (find the fourth vertex of a square given (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0)) rather than isolated plotting, so signs must be coordinated.
keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid with the origin and both signed axes labelled
Counting stick / number line held horizontally and vertically to model signed movement along each axis
Thermometer or below-ground scale as a familiar signed vertical axis
Sign-pattern labels for the four quadrants: (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−)
commonMisconceptions: Moving the wrong way for a negative coordinate — counting right for −3 or up for −5 — through weak grasp of order on a signed scale.
Putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, placing the point in the wrong quadrant.
Mis-ordering negatives (treating −5 as further out than −3 because 5>3), so points on a negative axis are misplaced.
Counting from '1' at the origin instead of '0', landing one square off.

learn.summary: Children extend coordinate work to all four quadrants: plotting and reading points such as (−3,4) and (2,−5), naming which quadrant a point lies in, and reasoning about positions where either or both coordinates are negative. The new demand is reading a SIGNED scale on each axis — a negative x means left of the origin, a negative y means below it, with numbers running symmetrically outward from 0 — fused to the ordered-pair (across, then up/down) rule. Live plotting with immediate feedback lets wrong-direction and reversed placements surface and be corrected; discrete practice items and labelled grids can check and clarify but elicit less of the felt signed movement.

activities.title: Plot it as a signed journey from the origin
feedback: If (−3,4) lands in the top-right (first) quadrant, the x-move went the wrong way: count the negative as LEFT from 0 and re-plot.
If the point lands as if it were (4,−3), the pair was reversed — move along x first ('along the corridor, then up or down the stairs').
Linked feedback that lights each axis's signed count as the marker travels makes the two moves and the landing quadrant visible together.
Reflecting (−3,4) in the x-axis gives (−3,−4) — the y-sign flips and the point drops to the third quadrant; check which single sign changed.
activities.rationale: Plotting on a signed grid is direct manipulation: the child performs two signed movements and can see a wrong direction or a reversed pair immediately, which is where signed-coordinate errors surface. Reading the quadrant from the sign pattern and linking sign flips to reflection connects the skill to geometry the child already knows.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants), including with negative numbers.

Recommended teaching includes mnemonics ('along the corridor and up the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y'), chanting positive and negative numbers on a counting stick held both horizontally and vertically for the two axes, and referring to the symmetry of the numbers about 0.
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant grid with a labelled origin and signed axes, plot (−3,4): move LEFT 3 along the x-axis from the origin, then UP 4 along the y-axis, treating each sign as a direction.
Name the quadrant from its sign pattern: (−,+) is the second (top-left) quadrant.
Plot (2,−5) (two right, five down) and (−4,−1) (four left, one down), naming each quadrant from its two signs.

If a live tool is available, place the marker yourself and watch it replay the two signed moves; if you counted right for the −3 and landed in the (+,+) quadrant, notice the mismatch and re-plot reading the minus as 'left'.
Where offered, use a reflect-in-axis toggle to flip (−3,4)↔(3,4)↔(3,−4) and watch a single sign change hop the point across an axis.
activities.intendedInsight: A minus sign is a DIRECTION (left of, or below, the origin), not decoration on the digit; the quadrant is read directly from the pair of signs, and flipping one sign reflects the point across an axis.

activities.title: Anchor each axis as a signed number line
feedback: If the child taps the origin while saying 'one', re-establish the origin as 0 and count moves from there; otherwise every point lands one square off.
If −5 is placed nearer the origin than −3 because 5>3, count steps out from 0 on the line: −5 is five steps out, −3 is three.
A counting stick or washing-line chanted in both directions makes the symmetry about 0 audible and visible.
activities.rationale: Secure directed-number sense underpins signed plotting; ordering negatives is genuinely hard because children treat magnitude as value, and number-line / thermometer / depth models address this by foregrounding position on the scale.
sourceClaims: Children find ordering negative integers difficult — numbers less than zero represent 'the non-existent' and the idea that 0 is greater than −1 is hard; the underlying error is treating the magnitude/digit as the value rather than the position on the scale, best addressed with number-line, washing-line, thermometer and swimming-pool (depth) models.

Recommended teaching includes mnemonics ('along the corridor and up the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y'), chanting positive and negative numbers on a counting stick held both horizontally and vertically for the two axes, and referring to the symmetry of the numbers about 0.
learnerActions: Treat the x-axis as a horizontal number line and the y-axis as a vertical one, both meeting at 0 at the origin.
Point and chant positive and negative values along a counting stick held horizontally, then vertically, forwards and backwards, so left and below map to negatives.
Use a thermometer or below-ground/depth scale as a familiar signed vertical axis.
Count the MOVES from the origin (which is 0), not the lines including it, so you do not land one square off.
Say aloud why −3 goes three to the LEFT: the numbers mirror symmetrically outward from 0.
activities.intendedInsight: Each axis is a signed number line symmetric about 0; reading position (not the bare digit) on that scale is what fixes direction and ordering.

activities.title: Reason across quadrants and name the quadrant from the signs
feedback: If a quadrant is named by memorised position rather than sign pattern, re-read the two signs: (−,−) is the third (bottom-left) quadrant.
If the child says (−3,0) is further from the origin than (−5,0), count steps from 0 along the negative axis.
For the square, use the symmetry about the origin: the vertex opposite (0,3) completes it, so the fourth vertex is (0,−3).
activities.rationale: Problems that force coordination of signs across quadrants, and distinguishing distance-from-0 from the digit, reveal whether the child reads signs as direction and can transfer to unplotted points rather than reaching a square by rote.
sourceClaims: For the Year 6 objective 'read and plot coordinates in all four quadrants', two named misconceptions are putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, and misplaced positions due to a lack of understanding of the order of negative numbers on a scale.
Year 6 pupils should describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants), including with negative numbers.
learnerActions: Without plotting, state which quadrant (−2,−7) lies in and explain how you can tell from the two signs.
Find the fourth vertex of a square given three vertices such as (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0), coordinating the signs rather than plotting in isolation.
Compare (−5,0) and (−3,0): decide which is further from the origin and justify it by position on the negative scale (five to the left versus three).
Label each quadrant by its sign pattern: (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−), and connect this to reflections in the axes.
Respond to a counterexample: 'A friend plotted (−3,4) in the top-right — what would you say?' (a negative x must go left).
activities.intendedInsight: For a point with two non-zero coordinates, quadrant membership is a reading of the two signs; a point with a zero coordinate, such as (3,0), (0,3) or (−5,0), lies on an axis and is in no quadrant. Coordinating signs across quadrants and comparing negatives by distance from the origin transfers the skill beyond single plots.

activities.title: Check and diagnose with targeted items
feedback: Picking the sign-flipped option signals a sign was read as decoration; return to reading the minus as direction.
Picking the reversed-pair option signals y-before-x; re-anchor 'x before y'.
activities.rationale: Well-designed items assess cleanly and the pattern of wrong options chosen can pinpoint the misconception, but recognition and single-step plotting elicit less independent, felt signed movement than live plotting, so they complement rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: For the Year 6 objective 'read and plot coordinates in all four quadrants', two named misconceptions are putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, and misplaced positions due to a lack of understanding of the order of negative numbers on a scale.
learnerActions: Tap/draw to plot (−3,4); choose which quadrant (2,−5) is in; fill in the coordinates of a plotted point; put −5, −3, 0, 2 in order along an axis.

For multiple-choice quadrant questions, the wrong options should encode real errors — the reversed point, the same point with one sign flipped, and the point mis-ordered on the negative scale — so a wrong answer shows which misconception is present.
activities.intendedInsight: Discrete items confirm the skill and diagnose which specific error (reversal, sign-as-decoration, or mis-ordered negatives) is present.

constraints: The (across, then up/down) ordering convention carries over from the first quadrant; the genuinely new demand is reading the SIGNED scale on each axis, so secure directed-number sense is a prerequisite.
Recognition-only practice items confirm and diagnose but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the two signed movements; pair them with actual plotting where possible.

A static labelled four-quadrant grid can reveal a point's signed path and each quadrant's sign pattern on tap, which clarifies layout, but it does not let the child plot and self-check, which is where signed errors surface — treat it as a scaffold.
Keep to the 2D plane for this objective; introducing a third axis brings octants and z-values beyond this topic and would obscure the signed 2D reading.
Reflect-in-axis toggles, axis-lighting counts, and live replay are optional feedback examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory.
Always count MOVES from the origin (0), not the grid lines including it, to avoid the one-square-off error.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The square example (vertices (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0)) has fourth vertex (0,−3) if the intended figure is a square centred on the origin (verified: right angle at (0,3), diagonal length 6); confirm the intended shape before use, as other three-point arrangements could complete different quadrilaterals.
One cited claim (National Curriculum, all-four-quadrants with negatives) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its evidential weight accordingly.

The original source framed the live-plotting tool as uniquely building fluency and a conversation/3D as unable to teach this; softened to scoped affordances/limits without asserting comparative efficacy, which the exact sources do not establish.

probeDeeper: Point at (2,−5): 'How did you know to go down rather than up for the −5?' (listen for the sign read as direction, not a rule recited).
'Which quadrant would (−2, −7) be in, without plotting it? How can you tell?' (tests reading the quadrant from the two signs alone).
Counterexample: 'A friend plotted (−3,4) up here in the top-right. What would you say to them?' (elicits that a negative x must go left, exposing the sign-as-decoration error).
'If you reflect (−3,4) in the x-axis, what are the new coordinates and which quadrant is it in now?' (links sign change to reflection across an axis).
assess.correctAnswer: The child moves along x first then y, treating each sign as a direction — (−3,4) three left and four up (second quadrant), (2,−5) two right and five down (fourth quadrant), (−4,−1) four left and one down (third quadrant) — labels each pair as (across, up), names the quadrant from the sign pattern, and reasons that (−5,0) is further from the origin than (−3,0) because −5 is further along the negative scale (five to the left versus three).

errorPatterns.pattern: Moves the wrong way for a negative coordinate — counts right for −3 or up for −5 — treating the minus as decoration rather than a direction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rehearse the axis as a signed number line with a counting stick — negatives go left/down from 0, symmetric about the origin; re-plot reading the sign as the direction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: (−3,4) lands in the first quadrant instead of the second; the child counts away from 0 in the positive direction regardless of sign.

errorPatterns.pattern: Puts the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, so the point lands in the wrong place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'along the corridor, then up/down the stairs', 'x before y'; check one point together, moving x first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: (−3,4) plotted as if (4,−3) — wrong quadrant — though the child clearly used both numbers; often surfaces as a swapped quadrant.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-orders negatives, treating −5 as nearer the origin than −3 (or vice versa) because 5>3 — magnitude read as value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a number line / thermometer through 0: count steps from the origin, showing −5 is five steps out and −3 is three; contrast distance-from-0 with the digit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says (−3,0) is further from the origin than (−5,0), or spaces negative points as if −5 sits between 0 and −3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts from '1' at the origin rather than '0', landing one square short or long
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the origin as 0; count the MOVES from the origin, not the lines including it; re-plot one point together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Every plotted point is consistently one square off along an axis; the child taps the origin as they say 'one'.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably place signed points — ignores signs or reverses the pair, so points land in the wrong quadrants — and cannot compare negatives on a scale (thinks −3 is further out than −5).
responseLevels.full: Plots points in all four quadrants by reading each sign as a direction (x then y), labels them (across, up), names each quadrant from its sign pattern, orders negatives correctly by distance from the origin, and transfers — e.g. states a point's quadrant without plotting and predicts the effect of reflecting it in an axis.
responseLevels.partial: Plots first-quadrant and single-negative points but falters when both coordinates are negative or when asked to justify — e.g. reaches the right square by rule yet cannot explain WHY −3 goes left, or names quadrants by memorised position rather than by sign pattern, and mis-orders negatives on the scale. Executes the steps but cannot connect sign to direction or transfer to an unplotted point.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a four-quadrant grid with a labelled origin and signed axes in front of the child. Say: 'Plot these three points and label each with its coordinates: (−3, 4), (2, −5), and (−4, −1). For each one, tell me which quadrant it is in. Then look at (−5, 0) and (−3, 0) — which is further from the origin, and how do you know?' Set the task and WATCH how each point is reached from the origin; do not explain the axes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Points with mixed signs give a DIFFERENT landing quadrant for a child who reads signs as directions than for one who ignores the sign, reverses the pair, or mis-orders negatives — each error sends the point to a distinct, visible wrong place. Watching the origin-to-point movement (which axis first, which direction) reveals the reasoning directly, and the (−5,0) vs (−3,0) question isolates negative-scale ordering from the plotting itself.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9-11 (Upper KS2/Grades 4-6): the many ecological roles of insects — POLLINATORS (bees, butterflies, hoverflies), DECOMPOSERS (dung beetles, fly larvae), a FOOD SOURCE (for birds, bats, fish, frogs), and PEST CONTROLLERS (ladybirds eating aphids). The thought experiment: what would happen if all insects disappeared?
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 (habitats, food chains) and Y6 ideas of interdependence; working-scientifically (reasoning about consequences in a system).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 5-LS2-1 (matter/energy movement among organisms) and 3-LS4-4 / MS-LS2 (interdependence, effects of changes to an ecosystem).
• Operational details — this is a high-centrality synthesis node: insects are not one thing in the web but MANY connected roles. The load-bearing skill is CASCADE reasoning — removing insects doesn't just lose bugs; plants unpollinated, dung/leaf litter piles up, insectivores starve, aphids explode. Build from single food chains to a web, then run the 'remove insects' thought experiment to reveal knock-on effects. Keep it evidence-based, not doom-laden (sets up the conservation topic).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): names three ecological roles of insects. Tier B (age 10): traces one knock-on effect of removing a role (no pollinators → no fruit → hungry animals). Tier C (age 11): reasons about multiple cascading effects of insect loss across pollination, decomposition, food supply and pest control.
bestPractices: Frame insects as MANY connected roles at once (pollinator, decomposer, prey, pest-controller), not a single node.
Build from familiar single food chains up to a web before running removal scenarios.
Teach cascade reasoning — trace knock-on effects several steps downstream, not just the immediate loss.
Keep it evidence-based and hopeful rather than doom-laden, setting up conservation.
Use the 'what if all insects disappeared?' thought experiment as the synthesising challenge.
keyRepresentations: An interactive food web with insect roles as central nodes.
Role cards (pollinator / decomposer / food source / pest controller) with examples.
A removal-cascade view with connected arrows and population meters.
A build-from-chain-to-web progression.
commonMisconceptions: 'Insects do just one thing in nature' — they fill several roles simultaneously.
'Losing insects would only mean fewer bugs' — it cascades to plants, vertebrates and humans.
'All insects are pests we'd be better without' — most are beneficial or neutral; few are pests.
'Decomposition happens on its own without insects' — insect decomposers are major recyclers.
'Removing a predator (ladybird) helps its prey thrive harmlessly' — pest populations can explode and damage plants.

learn.summary: For ages 9-11 (Upper KS2 / Grades 4-6), this topic builds cascade reasoning about the many ecological roles insects play: pollinators (bees, butterflies, hoverflies), decomposers (dung beetles, fly larvae), a food source (for birds, bats, fish, frogs), and pest controllers (ladybirds eating aphids). The load-bearing skill is following knock-on effects several steps downstream, not just noting the immediate loss. Progress from single familiar food chains, to a connected web, to the synthesising thought experiment: what would happen if all insects disappeared? Keep it evidence-based and hopeful, setting up conservation rather than doom.

activities.title: Build the web, then remove the insects
feedback: If a learner says 'birds would just eat something else,' trace the chain further: fewer insects → birds that depend on insects (including many that feed insects to their chicks) decline → predators of those birds are affected too → insect-pollinated plants go un-pollinated. Show the ripple spreads rather than staying contained.
If a learner names only pollination, prompt for a completely different job unrelated to flowers (decomposition, being eaten, pest control) and add it to the web with an example.

If a learner treats insects as pests we'd be better without, make a hidden service concrete: no insect pollinators → far fewer apples and strawberries; no dung beetles → dung and much dead matter would pile up and nutrient recycling would slow. (Insects are major decomposers, though fungi and bacteria also break matter down.)
activities.rationale: Building from a single chain up to a web before running a removal scenario scaffolds relational reasoning; restoring roles isolates which service each insect group provides. This mirrors interdependence standards about how changes to one part of an ecosystem affect others. This can be done on paper or on screen; an interactive simulation with a removal switch, per-role toggles, connected arrows and population meters is an optional way to make the cascade concrete, not a requirement.
sourceClaims: Matter and energy move among organisms in an ecosystem, and changes to one part affect others (5-LS2-1; MS-LS2 interdependence).
KS2 pupils study habitats, food chains and interdependence, reasoning about the effects of environmental change on living things.
Insects provide pollination, decomposition, a food base for many vertebrates, and natural pest control (e.g. ladybirds on aphids); their loss would cascade across ecosystem functions.
learnerActions: Start with one familiar food chain (e.g. plant → caterpillar → bird) and draw it with arrows showing who eats what.

Add more strands until insects sit at the centre wearing several hats: pollinator (bee), decomposer (dung beetle, fly larva), food (caterpillar for birds, bats, fish, frogs), and pest controller (ladybird keeping aphids down).

Remove all insects from the web and trace each knock-on effect out loud or in writing: insect-pollinated flowers bloom but set little or no fruit or seed, so fruit-eaters go hungry; dung and leaf litter break down more slowly and pile up; birds, bats and frogs that ate insects decline. Notice that aphids are insects too, so they would also vanish. To see the pest-control job, run a separate what-if where only the ladybirds are removed: aphids are no longer kept down, their numbers can surge, and they can damage the plants.

Then restore roles one at a time and note which job fixed which problem (returning pollinators brings back fruit on insect-pollinated plants; in the ladybird-only what-if, where aphids are still present, returning ladybirds helps bring aphids back under control).
activities.intendedInsight: Pulling out insects doesn't remove one thread — it unravels many parts of the web, because insects were doing four different jobs at once. Interdependence means a change in one part ripples across many.

activities.title: Open thought experiment with an ecologist
feedback: Probe for breadth: 'You named pollination — give me a completely different job insects do that has nothing to do with flowers.'
Probe a specific chain: 'If bees alone disappeared but other insects stayed, what exactly happens to an apple orchard, and then to the animals that eat apples?'
Probe the pest-control chain: 'Ladybirds eat aphids that damage crops. If ladybirds vanished, what happens to the aphids and then the crops?'
Probe the pest framing: 'Are ALL insects pests? Name one that helps humans and one we call a pest, and explain why the label depends on us.'
activities.rationale: Open dialogue can handle branching what-ifs and nuance (fast vs slow effects) that a fixed scenario cannot fully script, and it surfaces whether a learner follows consequences beyond the first step. A conversation partner can probe predictions responsively; this complements rather than replaces the hands-on web work. Efficacy of the medium is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Pose and explore open 'what would REALLY happen if insects vanished?' questions, predicting an outcome first before checking the reasoning.

Reason about timing: some effects would be fast (pollination failing within a season, insect-eating animals struggling to feed their young; or, if only ladybirds vanished, aphids surging) and some slow (soil nutrient cycling, effects spreading along long food chains), so predictions should distinguish quick from gradual consequences.
Defend predictions when challenged with Socratic probes and revise them when a branch doesn't hold up.
activities.intendedInsight: Cascade reasoning branches: removing insects produces many consequences on different timescales, and a good prediction follows several of them rather than stopping at the first.

activities.title: Sort, sequence and judge removal consequences
feedback: A strong response names several distinct roles and traces consequences through the web to plants, animals and humans — relational reasoning, not a memorised list.
A partial response names roles (often just pollination) but treats effects as stopping at the first step; prompt them to carry one chain two or three steps further.
If a learner agrees the world would be fine without insects, revisit the hidden services with a concrete chain they value before judging insects as pests.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorisation, sequencing and a focused multiple-choice item check that roles and simple cascades are secure; the name-then-explain check discriminates learners who can follow consequences from those who stop at a list. Recognition and matching confirm roles but do not themselves elicit independent multi-step reasoning, so pair this check with the construction and dialogue activities.
learnerActions: Match each insect to its ecological role (bee↔pollinator, dung beetle↔decomposer, caterpillar↔food source, ladybird↔pest controller).
Categorise several insects by the role(s) they fill, noting that some fill more than one.
Put a cause-and-effect chain in order (e.g. remove pollinators → insect-pollinated plants set little or no fruit → fruit-eaters go hungry).
Choose the correct single consequence of removing one role from among plausible options (a short multiple-choice check).

Answer the scenario: 'Every insect on Earth vanishes overnight. A child says that would be great — no annoying bugs and nothing important changes. Do you agree? Walk through what happens to plants, other animals, and us, and explain why.'
activities.intendedInsight: The expected answer is to disagree: losing insects breaks pollination, decomposition and food webs all at once, so consequences reach plants, vertebrates and humans. Full understanding names multiple distinct roles AND traces knock-on effects, rather than listing one role.

constraints: Target learners are 9-11 (Upper KS2 / Grades 4-6); align to UK KS2 habitats/food chains/interdependence and NGSS 5-LS2-1 and 3-LS4-4 / MS-LS2.

The central objective is cascade (knock-on) reasoning across a web, not memorising a list of roles; recognition-only sorting and matching check roles but do not elicit the independent, multi-step reasoning the topic targets, so include construction and open explanation too.
Keep it evidence-based and hopeful, not doom-laden; the topic sets up why insect conservation matters.

A tap-to-reveal annotated web can introduce each role and one linked fact, but it does not let a learner run a removal cascade themselves; treat it as an introductory scaffold, not the main reasoning task.

Address the specific misconceptions directly: insects fill several roles at once (not one); losing insects cascades beyond 'fewer bugs'; most insects are beneficial or neutral and 'pest' is a human label; insect decomposers are major recyclers (though fungi and bacteria also decompose); removing a predator like ladybirds can let prey populations explode and damage plants.
Distinguish fast from slow consequences when discussing insect loss so predictions stay realistic.

Note that insect-pollinated plants depend on pollinators; wind-pollinated plants (e.g. many grasses and trees) are affected differently, so frame pollination loss around the plants that rely on insects.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and all three source claims carry verified:false in the original row.

The original listed an interactive 2D ecosystem simulation (removal switch, per-role toggles, connected arrows, population meters, rebuild/recovery mode) as the preferred artefact. Its live-feedback mechanism is preserved as an optional way to make the cascade concrete and folded into the construction activity (paper or screen); the original claim that 'prose or a static picture cannot' convey interdependence is softened to a scoped affordance, since catalog ratings do not establish that necessity.

The original rated a 3D interactive as 'poor' because the concept is a connectivity network rather than a spatial environment; this comparative ranking is catalog-specific and has been omitted rather than asserted as a general law.

The original correctAnswer says nutrients 'wouldn't return to the soil' without insect decomposers; this overstates insects' share (fungi and bacteria also decompose) and has been softened to slowed recycling in learner-facing text, consistent with the original misconception note that insect decomposers are 'major' recyclers.

Some removal consequences carry real-world nuance (timescales, species-specific effects, partial compensation in food webs); these are presented as reasoning to explore, not settled quantitative outcomes, consistent with the source claims being general ecological reviews.

The ecology source claim was removed from the sort/sequence activity's sourceClaims because that activity's rationale states an assessment principle (recognition vs independent reasoning) that no source directly supports; the claim supports the topic content, not that teaching principle.

probeDeeper: 'You named pollination. Give me a completely DIFFERENT job insects do that has nothing to do with flowers.'
'If the bees alone disappeared but other insects stayed — what exactly would happen to an apple orchard, and then to the animals that eat apples?'
'Ladybirds eat aphids that damage crops. If ladybirds vanished, what happens to the aphids and then the crops?' (pest-control chain)
'Are ALL insects pests? Give me one that helps humans and one that we call a pest — and say why the label depends on us.'
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree — losing all insects would be a disaster, because insects do many essential jobs. Without pollinators (bees, butterflies, hoverflies) many plants couldn't make seeds/fruit, so those plants and the food we grow would collapse. Without decomposers (dung beetles, fly larvae) dead matter and dung would pile up and nutrients wouldn't return to the soil. Animals that eat insects (birds, bats, fish, frogs) would starve, and everything that eats THEM would be hit too. And pest-controllers like ladybirds keep other pests in check. So removing insects breaks pollination, decomposition, and food webs all at once.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees insects mainly as pests/nuisances — thinks losing them would be good or make little difference
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with a concrete chain the child values: no bees → no apples/strawberries; no dung beetles → dung and dead matter pile up. Make the hidden services visible before judging insects as pests.
errorPatterns.distractor: Agree — insects are just annoying pests, nothing important would change
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees the world would be fine or better without insects; can't name useful roles

errorPatterns.pattern: Names only ONE role (usually bees/pollination or 'honey') and can't identify the others
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build a role chart with an example each: pollinator (bee), decomposer (dung beetle), food (caterpillar for birds), pest controller (ladybird). Insects hold several roles at once, not just pollination.
errorPatterns.distractor: The only important insect job is bees making honey
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: mentions bees but not decomposers, food source, or pest control; stops at one job

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks effects stop at the first step — doesn't follow knock-on consequences through the food web ('birds would just eat something else')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace a chain out loud: fewer insects → insect-eating birds starve → predators of those birds affected → plants un-pollinated. Show removal ripples outward, it doesn't stay contained.
errorPatterns.distractor: If insects vanished, birds would just eat something else and nothing else would change
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sees no ripple: assumes removing insects affects only insects, or that animals simply switch food with no consequence

responseLevels.gap: Treats insects as pests that wouldn't be missed, or can't name any ecological role beyond 'they're bugs'.
responseLevels.full: Names several distinct roles (pollinator, decomposer, food source, pest controller) AND traces knock-on consequences through the web to plants, animals and humans, explaining WHY removal matters — relational, interdependence reasoning rather than a memorised list.
responseLevels.partial: Names insect roles (often just pollination) but as a list — can't trace how removing one group ripples through plants, other animals, and humans; effects stop at the first step.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Imagine every insect on Earth suddenly vanished overnight. A child says: 'That would be great — no more annoying bugs, and nothing important would really change.' Do you agree? Walk me through what would actually happen to plants, to other animals, and to us — and explain WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands ecosystem roles names MULTIPLE distinct roles (pollinator, decomposer, food source, pest controller) and traces knock-on effects through the web — relational reasoning. A child who sees insects as just pests agrees they wouldn't be missed, or names only one role (e.g. bees for honey) and stops. The second tier ('walk through plants, animals, us, and why') exposes whether they can follow consequences beyond the first step, which is the whole idea of interdependence.

sources.claim: Matter and energy move among organisms in an ecosystem, and changes to one part affect others (5-LS2-1; MS-LS2 interdependence).
sources.source: NGSS 5-LS2-1 and MS-LS2 Ecosystems

sources.claim: Insects provide pollination, decomposition, a food base for many vertebrates, and natural pest control (e.g. ladybirds on aphids); their loss would cascade across ecosystem functions.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Comparing and grouping rocks by properties

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Science, Year 3 Rocks):** Pupils compare and group together different kinds of rocks on the basis of their appearance and simple physical properties.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-1 property-classification approach applied to rocks; supports 2-ESS1 Earth materials):** Observe and describe rocks' observable properties and sort them into groups.

- **Operational details:** This is an observe-test-and-classify concept. Children examine real rocks and describe observable properties — hardness, texture (rough/smooth), colour, grain size, whether it's shiny or dull, holds together or crumbles. The core skill is choosing a property and SORTING a collection by it, then re-sorting by a different property (the same rocks group differently depending on the criterion). Emphasise evidence-based description ('this one is harder because it scratches that one') and careful observation with hand lenses. Keep it about observable physical properties, not yet rock TYPE names (igneous/sedimentary come later); grouping precedes naming.
bestPractices: Use real rock specimens and hand lenses — grouping rocks is a hands-on observation task, not a picture-only one.
Have children choose a property, sort, then RE-SORT by a different property so they see grouping depends on the chosen criterion.
Insist on evidence-based comparison (a scratch test for hardness, rubbing for texture) rather than guessing.
Build precise property vocabulary: hardness, texture, grain size, colour, lustre (shiny/dull), whether it crumbles.
Keep the focus on observable properties before rock-type names — classification by evidence comes before taxonomy.
keyRepresentations: A rock collection with hand lenses for direct observation.
A property sorting mat / Venn hoops (e.g. 'rough' vs 'smooth', 'hard' vs 'crumbly').
A comparison table: rock × property (hardness, colour, grain, texture).
A scratch-test / rub-test station for evidence gathering.
commonMisconceptions: 'Rocks can only be sorted one right way' — not seeing that different properties give different valid groupings.
'All grey rocks are the same rock' — grouping by colour alone and ignoring texture/hardness.
'Bigger rocks are harder' — confusing size with hardness.
'Shiny means precious/metal' — misreading lustre.
'You can tell a rock's properties just by looking' — skipping the test (scratch/rub) that gives evidence.

learn.summary: Children aged 7–8 learn to compare and group rocks by observable physical properties — hardness, texture (rough/smooth), colour, grain size, lustre (shiny/dull), and whether a rock crumbles. The central skill is choosing a property, sorting a collection by it, then RE-SORTING by a different property so learners discover that the same rocks group differently depending on the chosen criterion. Emphasis stays on evidence-based description ('this one is harder because it scratches that one') gathered with hands-on tests and hand lenses, and on observable properties rather than rock-type names (igneous/sedimentary come later): grouping precedes naming.

activities.title: Test, describe and sort a rock collection
feedback: If a learner sorts only by colour, ask: 'Two of these are both grey — how could you still tell them apart and put them in different groups?' Prompt a scratch or rub test.

When a learner claims a rock is harder, ask for the evidence: 'How did you test that?' Reinforce that a scratch test shows which rock scratches the other, so hardness is relative to the specimens compared (and to the tool, if a nail or coin is used). Check that the mark is a real scratch and not powder from the softer rock that rubs away.

After sorting by one property, invite the switch: 'Now sort the same rocks by hardness instead of colour — what happens to your groups?' Draw attention to the same rocks ending up in different groups.
If a learner assumes bigger rocks are harder, have them scratch-test a large soft rock against a small hard one to check directly — size and hardness are separate properties.
If a learner thinks shiny means precious or metal, note that lustre is just one observable property and ask what the scratch and texture tests show.
activities.rationale: The concept is observe-test-and-classify, so acting on real specimens — scratching, rubbing, tapping, lensing — then physically regrouping them makes the dependence of grouping on the chosen criterion visible through action. Classification by observable properties, with the same objects sortable multiple ways, is a foundational science practice named in the standards.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils compare and group together different kinds of rocks on the basis of their appearance and simple physical properties.
Classification by observable properties (hardness, texture, colour, grain) with the same objects sortable multiple ways is a foundational science-skills practice.
learnerActions: Examine a set of varied real rock specimens with a hand lens, looking closely at grain size and surface.

For each rock, carry out simple evidence-gathering tests: a scratch test for hardness (which rock scratches which), a rub test for texture (rough or smooth), a tap or gentle press to see whether it crumbles or holds together, and note colour and lustre (shiny or dull).
Record each rock's properties on a property card or a rock × property comparison table (hardness, colour, grain, texture).
Choose one property and sort the whole collection into groups (e.g. rough vs smooth, or hard vs crumbly), using sorting hoops/Venn hoops or a sorting mat.
Then re-sort the SAME rocks by a different property (e.g. switch from colour to hardness) and observe how the groups change.
State the evidence behind a comparison aloud, e.g. 'this one is harder because it scratched that one.'
activities.intendedInsight: A grouping depends on the property you choose: the same collection of rocks can fall into different groups when you sort by a different observable property, though some rocks may stay together. Describing rocks by tested evidence is more reliable than guessing by looking.

activities.title: Compare two contrasting rocks
feedback: If a learner says all rocks are the same, have them handle the varied set and feel the differences in hardness, texture and weight, and see the range of colours.
If a learner names only one property, prompt them to add another: 'You said the colour — what about how hard or rough each one is?'
Praise comparisons that cite a tested property rather than appearance alone. Keep weight and hardness distinct — a large rock can be soft and a small rock hard.
activities.rationale: Comparing a contrasting pair elicits precise property vocabulary and counters the idea that rocks are all alike; it directly targets the evidence of describing how two rocks' properties differ.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils compare and group together different kinds of rocks on the basis of their appearance and simple physical properties.
learnerActions: Take two clearly different rocks — for example one smooth, pale and crumbly, and one dark, heavy and very hard.
Describe how each differs across several properties: hardness, texture, colour, grain size and weight.
Decide and explain which group each rock would go into and why.
Answer: are all rocks basically the same, or can they be sorted into groups? Give evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Rocks differ in several observable properties at once, so a single pair can be told apart and grouped in more than one way depending on which property you focus on.

activities.title: Is it really a rock?
feedback: If a learner counts a brick as a rock, point out that bricks and concrete are made by people while rocks form naturally.
Accept reasoning that distinguishes natural from manufactured rather than relying on hardness alone.
activities.rationale: The common misconception that manufactured hard materials are rocks is worth addressing directly so classification rests on 'natural rock' rather than 'hard thing'.
learnerActions: Look at everyday manufactured items alongside rock specimens (e.g. a brick, concrete, glass).
Decide whether each is a rock and give a reason.
Discuss what makes something a natural rock versus a material made by people.
activities.intendedInsight: Rocks are natural materials; bricks, concrete and manufactured glass (such as window or bottle glass) are made by people, often from rock materials, so they are not rocks even though they can be hard.

activities.title: Build observation vocabulary with a tap-to-reveal collection (supporting scaffold)
feedback: Confirm correct matches of rock to property and discuss any mismatches by returning to the observable feature.
When ordering rocks by hardness, ask what evidence (a scratch test) would confirm the order.
activities.rationale: A reveal-and-match collection builds the observation vocabulary that the hands-on sorting relies on, and matching/ordering/categorising let classification be checked cleanly. Its limit is that the property evidence is supplied rather than tested by the learner, so it supports but does not replace doing the tests and the re-sorting.
sourceClaims: Classification by observable properties (hardness, texture, colour, grain) with the same objects sortable multiple ways is a foundational science-skills practice.
learnerActions: Tap each specimen in a rock collection to reveal a property fact-card (hardness, texture, colour) and a lens zoom on the grain.
Use a lift-the-flap prompt: 'Which group would you put this in?' and choose a group before revealing.
Practise matching a rock to a property description and sequencing rocks by hardness.
activities.intendedInsight: Precise property vocabulary (hardness, texture, grain size, colour, lustre) lets you describe and compare rocks accurately.

constraints: Rocks are physical specimens: a real box of rocks with hand lenses and a scratch-test kit is the essential hands-on complement. The specific picture-only or tap-to-reveal formats described here supply the property evidence and support vocabulary/recognition; they do not elicit the learner's own physical testing or the re-sort-by-a-new-criterion that drives the concept — the recommended simulated bench and the real specimens provide that.
Keep the focus on observable physical properties before introducing rock-type names (igneous/sedimentary); grouping by evidence comes before taxonomy.

Insist on evidence-based comparison (scratch test for hardness, rubbing for texture) rather than guessing from appearance; present hardness as relative ('which scratches which'), since outcomes depend on the specimens and tool.
Matching, ordering and categorising tasks check classification but supply the property evidence; they assess recognition rather than eliciting the learner's own testing and re-sorting.

Rotating a 3D specimen can add observational realism (seeing texture on all sides before sorting) but the core learning is property-testing and sorting logic, not spatial manipulation; treat 3D as an optional enhancement, not a requirement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row; treat the standards citations as unconfirmed.

The original framed a conversation/dialogue format as unable to substitute for hands-on observation. This has been softened: dialogue is simply not the chosen format here because the task is hands-on testing and sorting; no universal claim about dialogue's teaching ability is asserted.

The source assessment lists 'Bigger rocks are harder' as a misconception but the response-levels/diagnostic emphasise weight as a describable property — weight and hardness are distinct; keep them separate in teaching (a large rock can be soft, a small rock hard).

Scratch-test outcomes depend on the specific specimens and the tool used (e.g. a nail); real results vary by material, so present relative hardness ('which scratches which') rather than absolute claims.
A prerequisite reteach link is referenced for the 'all rocks are the same' misconception; the prerequisite linkage is not independently verified in this rewrite (internal identifier omitted).

probeDeeper: Is a brick a rock? Why or why not?
Two rocks are both grey. How could you still tell them apart and put them in different groups?
How would you test which of two rocks is harder?
assess.correctAnswer: Rocks are not all the same — they differ in observable properties, so we can group them. You can describe and sort by hardness (does it scratch easily?), texture (smooth or rough, grainy), colour, grain size and weight. Sorting by a chosen property puts similar rocks together.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All rocks are basically the same (hard and grey)'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Handle a varied set — feel hardness, texture and weight, see the range of colours.
errorPatterns.distractor: Rocks are all the same, so you can't really sort them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: sees no grounds for grouping

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Bricks, concrete and glass are rocks'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rocks are natural; bricks and concrete are made by people.
errorPatterns.distractor: A brick is a kind of rock.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: includes manufactured materials as rocks

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You can only sort rocks by colour'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce a scratch test and a texture feel as other properties.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: ignores hardness, texture and grain

responseLevels.gap: Says all rocks are the same, or that a brick is a rock; sorts only by colour.
responseLevels.full: Describes several observable properties (hardness, texture, colour, grain), sorts a collection by a chosen property, distinguishes natural rock from made materials, and compares two rocks' properties.
responseLevels.partial: Names a couple of properties and sorts, but leans on colour alone or includes manufactured materials.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two rocks: one is smooth, pale and crumbly; the other is dark, heavy and very hard. Are all rocks basically the same, or can we sort them into groups? What could you look at or test to describe and group them?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'a rock is just a rock,' or who judges only by colour, differs from one who names several observable properties and uses one to group.
