pedagogy.summary: Visible light is only a thin slice of the electromagnetic spectrum, and each band — radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma-ray — reveals different objects and processes in the universe. The big idea for ages 11-13 is that astronomers observe the SAME sky in many wavelengths to build a fuller picture, and that Earth's atmosphere BLOCKS most bands (microwave, UV, X-ray, gamma, and much infrared), which is why we put telescopes in space. Ground the abstraction with concrete pairings: microwaves show the cosmic microwave background (the Big Bang's afterglow); infrared pierces dust to reveal the earliest galaxies and forming stars (JWST); ultraviolet traces hot young stars and star formation; visible shows planets and familiar structure; X-rays and gamma-rays reveal the hottest, most violent objects — black holes, pulsars, exploding stars. Hubble (mainly visible/UV/near-IR) versus JWST (infrared) makes the 'different eyes' idea tangible.
bestPractices: Anchor everything to one idea: different wavelengths = different information about the same object, so 'seeing' in many bands is like using several senses at once
Pair each band with ONE vivid phenomenon it uniquely reveals, so the spectrum becomes a set of stories rather than a list of names
Make the atmosphere the hero of the 'why space telescopes' argument: show which bands reach the ground (radio, visible) and which are absorbed, so space observatories become a necessity, not a luxury
Use genuine multiwavelength images of the same target (e.g. a galaxy or nebula shown in visible then infrared then X-ray) to show how features appear and disappear across bands
Connect wavelength to energy and temperature: longer wavelength/cooler/gentler (radio, IR) vs shorter wavelength/hotter/more violent (UV, X-ray, gamma)
Contrast Hubble and JWST concretely — why an infrared telescope sees earlier, dustier, more redshifted galaxies than a visible one
keyRepresentations: The EM spectrum ordered strip: radio→microwave→IR→visible→UV→X-ray→gamma, annotated with wavelength/energy trend
Atmospheric-opacity ('windows') chart: a curve showing which wavelengths penetrate to the ground vs are blocked, mapped to ground- vs space-based telescopes
The SAME astronomical object imaged in multiple wavelengths, side by side
Band→phenomenon gallery: microwave/CMB, IR/early galaxies, visible/planets, UV/young stars, X-ray & gamma/black holes & pulsars
Hubble-vs-JWST comparison showing their wavelength coverage and a shared target
commonMisconceptions: 'Telescopes just magnify to see faint things' — many telescopes detect wavelengths our eyes can't see at all; it's about capturing invisible light, not only making things bigger
'Visible light is the normal/real light and the rest is exotic' — visible is just the band our eyes evolved for; every band is equally 'real' light
'We put telescopes in space to get closer to the stars' — the distance saved is negligible; it's to escape the atmosphere that blocks certain wavelengths and blurs images
'Infrared is just heat, not light' — infrared IS light (EM radiation) with a longer wavelength than visible; warm objects emit it
'All telescopes work the same way' — X-ray telescopes need grazing-incidence mirrors and there are no focusing gamma-ray telescopes; different bands need fundamentally different instruments
'Hubble and JWST see the same thing' — Hubble is mainly visible/UV while JWST is infrared, so JWST sees cooler, dustier, more distant (redshifted) objects Hubble cannot

learn.summary: Astronomers observe the same sky across the electromagnetic spectrum — radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma-ray — because each band reveals different objects and processes. The central ideas for ages 11-13: (1) different wavelengths carry different information about the same object, so observing in many bands is like using several senses at once, and many telescopes detect light our eyes cannot see rather than merely magnifying; (2) Earth's atmosphere blocks UV, X-ray, gamma-ray, much of the infrared and parts of the microwave range, while letting visible light, radio and some microwave and near-infrared through 'windows' (the CMB was first detected by a ground-based antenna, though space missions map it best), which is why many telescopes must fly in space — to escape absorption, not to get closer to the stars. Ground each band with one vivid phenomenon (microwave/CMB, IR/dust-piercing to early galaxies and forming stars, UV/hot young stars, visible/planets and familiar structure, X-ray & gamma/black holes, pulsars, violent explosions) and contrast Hubble (mainly visible/UV/near-IR) with JWST (infrared) to make the 'different eyes' idea tangible.

activities.title: Transform one object across the spectrum
feedback: If a learner says the bands just show the same scene in different colours: compare the nebula in visible (dust visible, stars hidden) versus infrared (dust transparent, newborn stars revealed) versus X-ray (only the hottest gas glows) — the actual features present differ, not just the colour.

If a learner calls non-visible images 'fake' or 'made up': all EM bands are real light carrying genuine information; false-colour is only a display choice to make invisible light visible to our eyes, the detection itself is real.

If a learner thinks a telescope's only job is to magnify faint things to look bigger: many of these images capture light our eyes cannot see at all (infrared, X-ray, radio) — the point is detecting invisible bands and the information they carry, not only enlarging the view.

If a learner can name the band but not its phenomenon: prompt with the temperature/energy link — glowing cool gas and dust often show up in radio and infrared, while the hottest, most violent processes show up in X-ray and gamma (though radio can also trace energetic jets).
activities.rationale: Pairing each band with one concrete phenomenon on a single shared object turns an abstract list of names into a set of memorable stories and directly confronts the 'same scene recoloured' and 'telescopes only magnify' misconceptions. A continuous slider makes the 'same object transforming' effect felt; a static ordered strip of real images serves the same comparison as a scaffold.
sourceClaims: Band-to-phenomenon pairings: microwave reveals the cosmic microwave background; infrared reveals earliest galaxies and dust (JWST); UV traces star formation; visible images exoplanets/structure; gamma-rays reveal pulsars, black holes and gamma-ray bursts
learnerActions: Study genuine multiwavelength images of a single rich target (e.g. a star-forming nebula or the galactic centre) ordered radio→microwave→infrared→visible→UV→X-ray→gamma.

For each band, if an interactive is available, drag a wavelength slider that cross-fades the central image to that band's real view; otherwise step through the ordered strip of real images side by side.
Observe and name what appears or disappears: dust lanes that hide stars in visible light melt away in infrared to reveal newborn stars; a knot of superheated gas blazes into view in X-ray.
Write one sentence per band stating the specific phenomenon that band uniquely reveals about THIS object.
Explain in your own words why the images differ: each wavelength reveals different physical processes at different temperatures and energies, not the same scene merely recoloured.
activities.intendedInsight: The same patch of sky looks utterly different in each band because different wavelengths reveal different phenomena — so combining bands builds a fuller picture than any single one, and much of this is about detecting light our eyes cannot see, not just magnifying it.

activities.title: Why does it have to fly? The atmosphere decides
feedback: If a learner says a tall enough or big enough mountain telescope could see X-rays: the atmosphere absorbs X-rays before they reach the ground or any mountaintop — no telescope size or mountain height recovers light that has already been absorbed; you have to get above nearly all the air (early X-ray astronomy used rockets). Contrast this with blurring of visible light, which higher altitude does help.

If a learner says space telescopes get us closer to the stars: the distance saved by orbit is negligible compared with interstellar distances; the real gain is escaping the atmosphere that blocks or blurs the light.
If a learner is puzzled that radio telescopes stay on the ground: radio waves pass through an atmospheric window, so there is no need to launch them.
activities.rationale: Making the atmosphere the 'hero' of the space-telescope argument targets two robust misconceptions (closeness and mere sharpness) by separating total blocking from blurring. Sorting real instruments by whether their band reaches the ground connects the opacity idea to observable engineering decisions.
sourceClaims: Radio and visible light reach the ground while microwave, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray are blocked by Earth's atmosphere (infrared partially blocked), which is why those observations require space telescopes
learnerActions: Read or examine an atmospheric-opacity ('windows') chart showing which wavelengths penetrate to the ground and which are absorbed.

For each band, decide and record: does this light reach the ground, or is it blocked? (Radio and visible pass through, along with some microwave and near-infrared windows; UV, X-ray, gamma, much of the infrared and parts of the microwave range are blocked.)

Sort real telescopes into 'works from the ground' (e.g. radio dish) versus 'must be in space' (e.g. an X-ray observatory, or a mid/far-infrared observatory such as JWST), justifying each placement by whether its band reaches the ground.

Answer: distinguish the atmosphere BLURRING visible light (which a higher-altitude ground telescope, or adaptive optics, can partly reduce) from the atmosphere BLOCKING whole bands entirely (which no ground telescope of any size can overcome).
State in one sentence why an X-ray telescope must be launched into space — because the atmosphere absorbs X-rays completely, so they never reach the ground, not because space is closer to the stars.
activities.intendedInsight: Earth's atmosphere absorbs certain wavelengths entirely, so telescopes for those bands must operate in space; the reason is escaping absorption, not reducing distance or only sharpening the view.

activities.title: Hubble vs JWST: two eyes, two universes
feedback: If a learner thinks the two telescopes see the same objects: point to a shared target where dust-shrouded or very distant features appear only in JWST's infrared view.

If a learner cannot explain the redshift link: light from the most distant galaxies is stretched to longer (infrared) wavelengths by the expansion of the universe, so an infrared telescope is needed to catch it.
Reinforce that infrared IS light — longer-wavelength EM radiation, emitted by warm objects — not merely 'heat' separate from light.
activities.rationale: A concrete Hubble/JWST comparison makes the 'different wavelengths, different information' idea tangible with a familiar, high-interest example, and addresses the 'infrared is just heat' and 'both telescopes see the same thing' misconceptions. The conversation variant narrates rather than shows the band comparison, so it best follows visual work.
sourceClaims: Band-to-phenomenon pairings: microwave reveals the cosmic microwave background; infrared reveals earliest galaxies and dust (JWST); UV traces star formation; visible images exoplanets/structure; gamma-rays reveal pulsars, black holes and gamma-ray bursts
learnerActions: Compare the wavelength coverage of Hubble (mainly visible and ultraviolet, with some near-infrared) and JWST (infrared).
Look at the same astronomical target as each telescope would capture it, noting what JWST reveals that Hubble cannot.
Explain why an infrared telescope can see earlier, dustier, more distant (redshifted) galaxies than a mainly visible telescope.

Write a short justification, as if advising an observing team, for choosing JWST over Hubble for imaging the first galaxies — referencing dust penetration and redshift of very distant light into the infrared.
Optionally, discuss with a peer or in a role-play 'interview a JWST scientist' why the telescope had to be flown far from Earth and kept very cold to do infrared work.
activities.intendedInsight: Hubble and JWST do not see the same thing: because they observe different bands, JWST can detect cooler, dustier and more distant objects, many of which are faint or invisible to a mainly visible telescope.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, sort, and sequence the spectrum
feedback: If a sort error appears, re-check against the atmospheric windows: radio and visible clearly reach the ground, and some microwave and near-infrared also get through; UV, X-ray, gamma, much of the infrared and parts of the microwave range are blocked.
If the sequence is scrambled, anchor to the familiar middle: visible sits between infrared (longer, cooler) and ultraviolet (shorter, hotter).

Note for teachers: matching, sorting and sequencing check recall and organisation; they consolidate but do not by themselves elicit the 'same object, different eyes' explanation, so use them after the comparison activities.
activities.rationale: Recall-and-organise tasks reinforce vocabulary, ordering and the energy/temperature trend after the conceptual work is done. The instrument-difference fact counters 'all telescopes work the same way'.
sourceClaims: X-ray telescopes require grazing-incidence mirrors and there are no focusing gamma-ray telescopes — different bands need fundamentally different instruments
learnerActions: Match each band to the phenomenon it uniquely reveals (e.g. microwave↔cosmic microwave background, X-ray↔matter around black holes, infrared↔newborn stars behind dust, radio↔cold gas clouds).
Sort telescopes into 'works from the ground' versus 'must be in space' and give the reason (which band reaches the ground).

Sequence the bands in order of wavelength (radio→microwave→infrared→visible→UV→X-ray→gamma) and describe the matching trend: shorter wavelength always means more energy per photon, and for glowing objects shorter wavelengths usually point to hotter, more violent sources while longer ones usually point to cooler ones.

Note the instrument idea: different bands need fundamentally different instruments — for example X-ray telescopes use grazing-incidence mirrors, and gamma-ray telescopes usually can't focus gamma rays with mirrors at all, so they use particle-detector methods instead.
activities.intendedInsight: The spectrum is an ordered scale linking wavelength, energy and temperature, and each band maps to distinct phenomena and often distinct instrument designs.

constraints: Use genuine multiwavelength images of the SAME target so learners see features appear and disappear across bands, not unrelated pretty pictures.
Matching, sorting and sequencing tasks assess recall and organisation; they do not elicit the independent explanation of 'same object, different eyes' and should follow, not replace, comparison work.

A static ordered strip of real images is a valid scaffold for the transformation activity; a continuous slider or cross-fade (if available) makes the 'same object transforming' effect more vivid but is not required.

Role-play conversation with a 'JWST scientist' narrates the band comparison rather than showing it; pair it with visual comparison so the explanation rests on observed differences. This is a narrow affordance, not a claim that dialogue cannot teach.

An interactive opacity marker that flips between 'reaches the ground' and 'blocked — needs a space telescope', and a Hubble-vs-JWST coverage toggle, are optional illustrative mechanisms; the underlying blocking-vs-blurring and coverage ideas can also be taught from a printed chart.

Keep clear the distinction between the atmosphere BLURRING visible light (partly reduced by higher altitude or adaptive optics, not by a larger aperture) and BLOCKING whole bands entirely (unfixable from the ground at any size) — the diagnostic hinges on this.
Treat false-colour as a display choice for making invisible light visible, not as evidence the observation is artificial.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Corrected a factual slip from the prior draft: atmospheric blurring of visible light is partly reduced by higher altitude (or adaptive optics), not by building a bigger telescope; aperture size affects light-gathering, not atmospheric seeing.

The original '3D adds no explanatory power / risks implying geometry' claim has been dropped as a catalog-fit judgement rather than an established pedagogical law; the spectral (1D wavelength) nature of the concept is retained as the reason a side-by-side or slider comparison fits well, without asserting 3D teaches nothing.

Source claims list specific band→phenomenon pairings (microwave/CMB, IR/early galaxies, UV/star formation, visible/exoplanets, gamma/pulsars and GRBs). The radio↔cold gas clouds and X-ray↔black-hole gas details are original-row content from the assessment correctAnswer, not individually among the three cited sources[].claim entries; treat them as preserved original content and confirm against the NASA source if strict sourcing is required.

Self-audit: EM ordering (radio→microwave→IR→visible→UV→X-ray→gamma) and the wavelength/energy/temperature trend are internally consistent; the atmospheric-window statement (radio and visible reach ground; microwave, UV, X-ray, gamma and much IR blocked) is consistent across summary, activities and the source claim. No arithmetic, force/motion, fraction or solid-shape content applies to this topic.

probeDeeper: What's the difference between the atmosphere BLURRING light and BLOCKING it entirely — and which one can't be fixed by a bigger ground telescope?
Name a wavelength band and one thing it reveals that visible light can't.
Why does the James Webb telescope observe mainly in infrared rather than visible light?
Radio telescopes are huge dishes ON the ground — how come they don't need to be in space?
assess.correctAnswer: An X-ray telescope must be in space because Earth's atmosphere completely BLOCKS (absorbs) X-rays, gamma rays and much infrared — they never reach the ground at all, so no ground telescope could detect them however big or high it is. Visible light and radio waves pass through 'windows' in the atmosphere, so those telescopes work from the ground. Astronomers observe across the whole electromagnetic spectrum because different wavelengths reveal different things: radio shows cold gas clouds and pulsars, infrared sees through dust to newborn stars and distant galaxies, visible shows stars like the Sun, X-rays reveal super-hot gas and matter swirling around black holes, and gamma rays flag the most violent explosions. Each band is real light carrying information the others miss.

errorPatterns.pattern: space telescopes are needed only for a sharper or closer view — a big enough ground telescope could do the same job
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish BLURRING (visible light, helped by altitude) from total BLOCKING (X-ray, gamma, much infrared absorbed entirely) — the latter can never be seen from the ground at any size.
errorPatterns.distractor: An X-ray telescope just needs to be big enough or high enough — it could work from a tall mountain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gives clarity or size as the reason, missing that the atmosphere blocks whole bands

errorPatterns.pattern: visible light is the only real way to see the universe; other wavelengths are just made-up false colour
errorPatterns.nextMove: All EM bands are real light; each carries genuine information — X-rays from black-hole gas, radio from cold clouds — that visible light simply cannot show.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only visible light shows the universe as it really is; X-ray and radio images are just made up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child dismisses non-visible bands as artificial or not real observations

errorPatterns.pattern: different wavelengths all show the same thing, just in different colours
errorPatterns.nextMove: Each wavelength reveals different PHENOMENA at different temperatures and energies — not the same scene recoloured; show a nebula in visible vs infrared vs X-ray.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats the bands as interchangeable recolourings of one scene

responseLevels.gap: Thinks space telescopes are only for a clearer or closer view and treats non-visible bands as fake.
responseLevels.full: Explains the atmosphere absorbs X-ray/gamma/much infrared entirely (so those must fly, while visible and radio have ground windows), and pairs several bands with the distinct phenomena they reveal.
responseLevels.partial: Knows some telescopes must be in space and that different bands show different things, but explains 'must be in space' as blur rather than blocking, or can't pair a band with a phenomenon.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A visible-light telescope works fine on a mountaintop here on Earth, but an X-ray telescope MUST be launched into space to work at all — and it's not just about getting a sharper view. Why can't an X-ray telescope work from the ground? And why do astronomers bother observing in X-rays, infrared and radio at all, instead of just visible light? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks space telescopes are only about a sharper or closer view cannot explain why X-ray astronomy is IMPOSSIBLE from the ground. A child who understands atmospheric opacity says certain wavelengths are absorbed entirely, so those telescopes MUST fly. The multi-band half separates 'visible is the real way to see space' from 'each wavelength reveals different physics'. The 'why' tier tests both.

pedagogy.summary: This topic is the APPLICATION layer: pupils meet real contexts and must decide which unit-fraction division is happening and set it up — partition ('3 people share 1/2 lb → how much each?', 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6) versus measurement ('how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups?', 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6). The hard part is not the computation but reading the STRUCTURE: which quantity is being split, which is the dividend, and whether the answer should grow or shrink. Teach it by modelling each story on a bar/number line before writing the equation, always sanity-checking the answer against 'more or fewer than I started with?', and by having pupils invent stories for a bare expression so the structure runs both ways.
bestPractices: Model the story before the symbols: draw the sharing or the fitting on a bar/number line, then write the matching ÷ equation — IES found personalising/real contexts improves fraction-division performance
Explicitly sort the two structures — 'sharing an amount out' (partition, gets smaller) vs 'how many portions fit' (measurement, gets bigger) — and name which each word problem is
Gate every answer with estimation: 'should there be more or fewer than 2 servings?' catches a quotient pointing the wrong way
Have pupils create a story to MATCH a given expression (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5), forcing them to own the structure, not just crank a rule
Verify with the inverse operation (6 × 1/3 = 2) so the word-problem answer is checked, not trusted
keyRepresentations: Bar model of the amount being shared (partition) or filled with portions (measurement)
Number line for 'how many 1/3s fit in 2'
Story ↔ equation ↔ picture triple laid side by side
Inverse check written under the answer
commonMisconceptions: Picks the wrong operation — multiplies, or divides in the wrong order (2 ÷ 1/3 done as 1/3 ÷ 2)
Reverses dividend and divisor — computes 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6 for '3 share 1/2 lb' instead of 1/2 ÷ 3
Expects the quotient to be smaller in a measurement problem, so distrusts '6 servings' being more than 2
Sets up the numbers but cannot tell which quantity is being split, so the model does not match the story

learn.summary: Pupils (ages 10-11) apply unit-fraction division to real contexts, deciding which structure a story has — partition ('3 people share 1/2 lb → how much each?', 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6) versus measurement ('how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups?', 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6). The core difficulty is reading the STRUCTURE — which quantity is split, which is the dividend, and whether the answer should grow or shrink — not the arithmetic. Guidance centres on modelling each story on a bar/number line before writing the equation, sanity-checking the answer against 'more or fewer than I started with?', and having pupils invent stories for bare expressions so they run the structure both ways.

activities.title: Build the model, then write the equation
feedback: If you built a sharing model for a 'how many fit' story, look: the picture cannot be made to match the words — reread which quantity is the whole and which is the portion.
When six 1/3-cup scoops fill the 2-cup bar, that is 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6 — count the portions in the picture to confirm.
Before trusting the number, ask 'should there be more or fewer than 2 servings?' A quotient pointing the wrong way signals a setup error.
activities.rationale: Modelling the situation before the symbols, with a visual model that matches the story, is the heart of this skill; both measurement and partition interpretations need pictures tied to the context.
sourceClaims: Presenting fraction-division problems in real/personalised contexts improves students' ability to solve them; the measurement ('how many fit') and partition ('share out') interpretations both need visual models that match the situation
Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions using visual fraction models and equations, and create story contexts
learnerActions: Read a word problem, e.g. 'How many 1/3-cup servings of raisins are in 2 cups?'
Decide whether the story is sharing an amount out among groups (partition) or finding how many portions fit inside an amount (measurement).
Choose and build the matching model on a bar or number line: either share one bar among N people, or fill a 2-cup bar with 1/3-cup portions and count them.
Write the matching division equation (2 ÷ 1/3 = 6) once the picture matches the words.
Lay the story, the picture, and the equation side by side so the three represent the same situation.

If a digital modeller is available, dragging the story onto a bar so the equation and answer recompute live lets pupils see a mismatched picture when they pick the wrong structure — this is one helpful interaction, not a required one.
activities.intendedInsight: The story tells you which division it is: sharing an amount out among more than one group gives each less than the whole, while asking how many sub-one-unit portions fit inside an amount gives more than you started with — and the picture either matches the words or it visibly does not.

activities.title: Sort the two structures, name the dividend, then compute
feedback: If you wrote 3 ÷ 1/2 for the chocolate story, ask: what is actually being cut up and given out? The half pound — so model that amount split into 3 before writing the equation.
If you reached for 2 × 1/3, check whether the story asks you to combine amounts or to find how many portions fit — these are different operations.
A quick estimate ('more or fewer than I started with?') catches a quotient pointing the wrong way.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating partition from measurement, naming each, and then requiring a matching model is intended to confront the wrong-operation and reversal misconceptions, rather than letting pupils crank a rule.
sourceClaims: Presenting fraction-division problems in real/personalised contexts improves students' ability to solve them; the measurement ('how many fit') and partition ('share out') interpretations both need visual models that match the situation
learnerActions: Take several word problems and classify each as 'sharing an amount out' (partition: shared among more than one group, each share is smaller than the amount) or 'how many portions fit' (measurement: when the portion is smaller than one unit, as in these problems, the count is larger than the amount).
Name, for each, which quantity is being split and which is the dividend.
For the sharing problem '3 friends share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally', identify that the half pound is what is cut up, so it is 1/2 ÷ 3, not 3 ÷ 1/2.
After classifying and naming, build the matching bar model and only then write and solve the equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming the structure and the dividend first helps prevent reversing dividend and divisor and reaching for multiplication out of habit; classifying is a start, but the setup is not complete until the model and equation match the words.

activities.title: Confront 'the answer must get smaller'
feedback: If you distrusted '6 servings' because 6 is more than 2, count the scoops in the filled bar — six 1/3-cups really do fit in 2 cups.

With 3-cup servings there would be two-thirds of one serving (2 ÷ 3 = 2/3), i.e. fewer than one whole 3-cup serving fits in 2 cups; with 1/3-cup servings there are many — the portion size decides the direction.
activities.rationale: The belief that a quotient must be smaller than the dividend interferes with measurement-division problems and is best confronted with visual counting and estimation.
sourceClaims: The misconception that a quotient must be smaller than the dividend interferes with solving measurement-division word problems and must be confronted with visual counting and estimation
learnerActions: Predict, before computing, whether 'how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups' should be more or fewer than 2.
Fit 1/3-cup portions into 2 cups on a bar or number line (or with real measuring cups) and count them: there are 6.
State in words why counting portions smaller than one unit inside a larger amount gives a count bigger than the amount.
Contrast: if servings were 3-cup servings instead of 1/3-cup, would there be more or fewer in 2 cups, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: A quotient can be larger than the dividend: when you count how many portions smaller than one unit fit inside an amount, the count exceeds the amount.

activities.title: Invent a story for a bare expression, then check it
feedback: If your story for 4 ÷ 1/5 is actually a sharing story or a 'four fifths' multiplication story, it does not match the division — revise it to 'how many 1/5-sized portions fit in 4'.
Solve your own story back: if it does not give 20, the story does not match 4 ÷ 1/5.
Writing the inverse (6 × 1/3 = 2) under your answer checks it rather than trusting it.
activities.rationale: Creating story contexts for a given expression forces ownership of the structure, and verifying with the inverse makes the answer checked rather than assumed. Being able to invent a correct story goes beyond merely recognising one among options.
sourceClaims: Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions using visual fraction models and equations, and create story contexts
learnerActions: Write your own word problem that 4 ÷ 1/5 would solve, e.g. 'How many 1/5-metre ribbons can I cut from a 4-metre roll?' (= 20).
Identify which structure your story uses (here, measurement — how many 1/5-sized portions fit in 4).
Solve your own story to confirm it really gives 20 and really matches division, not multiplication.
Check a given answer with the inverse operation, writing e.g. 6 × 1/3 = 2 under the answer to confirm 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6.
activities.intendedInsight: Running the structure backwards — building a valid story from the symbols and verifying by the inverse — shows the structure is owned, not merely recognised.

activities.title: Talk through the direction with a context character
feedback: If your prediction and your computed answer disagree, revisit which quantity is the whole — one of them is set up wrong.
Explaining why each share shrinks (sharing) or why the count grows (fitting) shows you have read the structure, not just the numbers.
activities.rationale: A role-play dialogue set in a real context can probe 'more or fewer?' reasoning and story invention; it supplements, rather than replaces, the visual modelling where pupils build and test a setup.
sourceClaims: Presenting fraction-division problems in real/personalised contexts improves students' ability to solve them; the measurement ('how many fit') and partition ('share out') interpretations both need visual models that match the situation
learnerActions: Take a kitchen or shop scenario where a character (cook, shopkeeper) poses a sharing problem and a portioning problem.
Before computing, predict aloud whether each answer will be more or fewer than the starting amount, and justify.
Explain to the character which quantity is being split and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the predicted direction and the dividend in a concrete context reinforces structure-reading and the 'more or fewer?' sanity check.

constraints: Matching stories to expressions and multiple-choice 'which calculation solves this?' check the choice only; classifying stories into 'sharing' vs 'how many fit' usefully targets the core difficulty (reading the structure, a source-endorsed move) but on its own does not elicit building the matching model and writing the equation. Pair classification with pupil-built models and pupil-written equations rather than treat selection alone as the whole learning.
Story invention must be produced by the pupil (constructing/writing a context), not selected from options, to reveal whether the measurement structure is owned.

A static worked pair of stories with reveal-the-setup flaps can illustrate the two structures but does not let a pupil attempt and test their own setup on a new story; treat it as a scaffold or reference.
When counting portions physically (measuring cups, cut ribbons), these are concrete approximations of the bar/number-line model; keep the link to the written equation explicit.

Contexts here are quantity and length sharing, which model naturally on a bar or number line; three-dimensional representations are not needed for these particular contexts (this is a scope note, not a claim that 3D could never help elsewhere).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic: 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6; 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6; 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20; 2 ÷ 3 = 2/3 (two-thirds of one 3-cup serving); inverse check 6 × 1/3 = 2 — all consistent across the source. The common reversal error 3 ÷ 1/2 (= 6) is flagged only as an error, never offered as a valid answer or option.

The Common Core 5.NF.7c source is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited only for the standard's description of using visual models and creating story contexts, not as evidence of comparative efficacy.

No source establishes that any one artefact format is uniquely able to teach this; claims about a format being superior, or that 3D 'adds nothing conceptual', are presented as scope-limited design notes rather than established pedagogical law, and the conversation/dialogue format's efficacy is not source-established.

probeDeeper: In (b), is your answer bigger or smaller than 2 — does that make sense for 'how many servings'?
In (a), which number is being shared out — the half pound or the 3 people? How do you know?
If the servings were 3-cup servings instead of 1/3-cup, would there be more or fewer of them in 2 cups — why?
Check your answer to (b) with a multiplication.
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6 lb each. (b) 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6 servings. Story for 4 ÷ 1/5: any 'how many 1/5-sized portions fit in 4' context, e.g. 'how many 1/5-metre ribbons can I cut from a 4-metre roll?' (= 20).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses dividend and divisor in the sharing problem: '3 people, half a pound' → 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6, instead of 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what is actually being cut up and given out?' — the half pound — and model that amount split into 3 on a bar before writing the equation; reteach the partition meaning
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Working shows 3 ÷ 1/2 (or answer 6 lb each); the quantity being shared is not identified as the dividend

errorPatterns.pattern: Expects the measurement answer to be smaller than the amount: distrusts or won't produce '6 servings' because 6 is more than 2 cups
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fit 1/3-cup portions into the 2 cups and count them physically; name that counting small portions gives many, so the answer exceeds the amount; reteach the how-many-fit meaning
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In (b), answers a value below 2 (e.g. 2/3), or hesitates/changes 6 because 'it can't be more than 2'

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong operation — multiplies, or cannot decide — because the story's structure (sharing vs fitting) is not read; the numbers are combined by habit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort several stories into 'sharing out' vs 'how many fit' before computing any; require a bar model that matches the words; check the invented story by solving it back
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 2 × 1/3 or 1/2 × 3; or the invented story for 4 ÷ 1/5 does not match division (e.g. a 'four fifths' multiplication story)

responseLevels.gap: Picks the wrong operation or reverses the order on one or both problems, cannot set up a matching model, and cannot invent a valid story for 4 ÷ 1/5.
responseLevels.full: Sets up and solves both with the correct operation and order, justifies each answer's direction (1/6 smaller, 6 bigger) against the context, verifies with the inverse, and invents a valid measurement story for 4 ÷ 1/5; transfers cleanly to an unfamiliar context.
responseLevels.partial: Solves the familiar sharing problem correctly but muddles the measurement one (or vice versa), or gets both numerically yet cannot judge whether the answers should grow or shrink, and writes a story that only loosely matches 4 ÷ 1/5 — lists numbers without owning the structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these two, showing your working: (a) 3 friends share half a pound of chocolate equally — how much does each get? (b) How many 1/3-cup servings of raisins are in 2 cups? Then make up your own word problem that 4 ÷ 1/5 would solve.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the SETUP separates real understanding from rule-chasing. The two problems pull in opposite directions — (a) shares an amount so the answer shrinks below 1/2; (b) counts portions so the answer grows above 2 — so a child who blindly applies one procedure gets one right and one absurd. The order of dividend and divisor in (a) exposes reversal (3 ÷ 1/2 = 6 instead of 1/6). And inventing a story for 4 ÷ 1/5 exposes whether the measurement structure is owned or only recognised — a child who writes a sharing story, or a multiplication story, reveals the gap.

sources.claim: Presenting fraction-division problems in real/personalised contexts improves students' ability to solve them; the measurement ('how many fit') and partition ('share out') interpretations both need visual models that match the situation
sources.source: IES / What Works Clearinghouse — Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K–8 (Siegler et al. 2010), Recommendation 3

sources.claim: The misconception that a quotient must be smaller than the dividend interferes with solving measurement-division word problems and must be confronted with visual counting and estimation
sources.source: IES / WWC Fractions Practice Guide — misconception step, Recommendation 3

sources.claim: Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions using visual fraction models and equations, and create story contexts
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics — 5.NF.7c

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Recording data of increasing complexity (graphs & keys)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires "recording data and results of increasing complexity using scientific diagrams and labels, classification keys, tables, scatter graphs, bar and line graphs" (verbatim). The step-up from lower KS2 is LINE and SCATTER graphs and choosing the appropriate type.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 4 Analyzing & Interpreting Data, grades 3–5 into 6–8):** the 3–5 progression covers representing data graphically to reveal patterns; the 6–8 progression adds constructing and interpreting graphical displays (including line graphs) to identify linear and nonlinear relationships. Selecting and accurately plotting the right graph type sits on this boundary.

- **Operational details:** Builds on basic tables/bar charts/keys (prerequisite mt_7IFpDVNsmt) and maths discrete/continuous graphing (mt_ChjMU2GDJa). Three moves: (1) CHOOSE the appropriate graph — bar chart for categories, LINE graph for continuous change (e.g. over time), scatter graph for relationship between two continuous variables; (2) draw it with correctly LABELLED AXES, sensible SCALES, and accurate plotting; and (3) use classification keys and scientific diagrams for complex findings. The pivotal new idea is that continuous data (a variable that changes smoothly) wants a line graph, whereas categories want bars. Feeds forward to KS3 best-fit lines/gradients and causal reporting (dependents mt_YHsUhi4Prc, mt_nyPMkeHlVJ).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). A learner who can select the correct graph type for a dataset, plot it accurately with labelled axes and an appropriate scale, and use keys/diagrams for complex findings has met the bar. Lines of best fit and gradients are the KS3 tier (mt_YHsUhi4Prc).
bestPractices: Teach graph-type SELECTION on the nature of the data: categories → bar chart; one continuous variable changing (often over time) → line graph; relationship between two continuous variables → scatter — give datasets that force the choice rather than pre-deciding.

Make axis choice a taught decision: which variable goes on x (the one you changed / independent) and y (the one you measured / dependent), plus choosing a scale that uses the grid well — a common failure point.
Confront the continuous-vs-discrete distinction directly, since drawing a line through category (discrete) data or a bar chart of continuous data is the signature upper-KS2 error.
Have pupils plot from their OWN fair-test data so the graph answers a real question and links back to the experimental-design spine.
Use accurate plotting as a habit (read the value, find the coordinate, mark precisely) and check by reading a point back off the graph.
keyRepresentations: A graph-type chooser keyed to data type (categorical / continuous-over-time / two-variable relationship)
A line graph with independent variable on x, dependent on y, labelled axes and units
A scatter graph showing a relationship between two continuous variables
A scale-choosing exercise (spread the data across the grid)
A branching classification key for complex specimens
commonMisconceptions: Drawing a line graph through discrete/categorical data (joining bars that shouldn't be joined), or a bar chart for continuous data.
Putting the wrong variable on each axis, or not distinguishing the changed (independent) from the measured (dependent) variable.
Choosing a scale that squashes the data into a corner or that isn't linear/even, distorting the pattern.
Omitting axis labels or units so the graph can't be interpreted.
Plotting inaccurately or reading points off carelessly, then trusting the resulting shape.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, learners record data of increasing complexity by choosing the right graph for the nature of the data, plotting it with labelled axes, units and an even scale on each numerical axis, and building classification keys. The pivotal idea: categorical data suits bar charts; a continuous variable tracked as another continuous variable changes (most often time) suits a line graph; and two measured continuous variables checked for a relationship suit a scatter graph. The wrong choice can bury or misrepresent the pattern; the right choice makes it easier to read. Plotting one's own fair-test data is encouraged so the graph answers a real question.

activities.title: Plot your own data: choosing type, axes and scale
feedback: If a line is drawn through categorical data (joining bars that shouldn't be joined), point out that these points aren't connected — sort the data as categories versus continuous first, then re-choose the graph type before drawing.
If the scale is spaced by the order the numbers were collected rather than by value, note that equal gaps must mean equal amounts; mark the whole axis before plotting any point.

If the scale squashes the data into a corner, suggest using fewer units per square so the data fills the grid and any pattern is easier to see; on a bar chart, keep the count axis starting at zero so the bar heights can still be compared fairly.
If axes carry numbers but no quantity name or unit, require each axis to name what was measured and its unit before the graph is 'finished'; check against the data-table headings.
Ask: why did you pick this graph type rather than a bar chart / line graph for this data? If someone else read it, would they know what each axis measures and in what units — show me where.
activities.rationale: Graph-type selection and accurate construction are the step-up skills at upper KS2 and on the NGSS 3–5 into 6–8 boundary. Forcing the choice on datasets of different natures, and making the axis and scale decisions explicit, is intended to target the signature errors (lines through discrete data, uneven scales, missing labels). Plotting one's own fair-test data ties the graph back to a real question. The cited standards establish that these graph and key skills are required at this stage; they do not by themselves establish the efficacy of this proposed design.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires recording data and results of increasing complexity using scientific diagrams and labels, classification keys, tables, scatter graphs, bar and line graphs.
NGSS SEP 4 progresses from representing data graphically to reveal patterns (3-5) to constructing and interpreting graphical displays to identify linear and nonlinear relationships (6-8).
learnerActions: Take a real dataset — ideally from your own fair test (e.g. a plant's height measured each week) — plus a categorical set (e.g. favourite-fruit counts) and a two-variable set.

Decide for each dataset whether the data is categorical, a continuous variable tracked as it changes over time (or as another continuous variable changes), or two measured continuous variables checked for a relationship.

Choose the graph type: bar chart for categories, line graph for a continuous variable tracked as it changes over time (or as another continuous variable changes), scatter graph for two measured continuous variables where you are looking for a relationship.

Put the changed/independent variable (or the categories, for a bar chart) on the x-axis and the measured/dependent variable on the y-axis; if a scatter graph compares two measured variables and neither was changed, choose one for each axis and say which. Label each axis with the quantity AND its unit where it has one.

Mark the scale on each numerical axis FIRST — equal squares for equal amounts — choosing a scale that spreads the data across the grid rather than squashing it into a corner; on a bar chart, space the categories evenly and start the count axis at zero.
Plot each point accurately (read the value, find the coordinate, mark precisely), then check by reading one point back off the graph against the data table.

Deliberately try plotting the categorical data as a line graph and notice that the joining lines suggest in-between values that don't exist, and that the line's shape changes if you reorder the categories; compare with the correct bar chart.
activities.intendedInsight: A graph isn't a decoration added at the end — the right choice of type, axes and scale is what lets the data tell its story, while the wrong one can hide the pattern or imply connections that don't exist.

activities.title: Build and test a classification key
feedback: If questions are vague or non-binary, or two organisms end at the same point, rework them: every question must be an observable yes/no that divides the remaining set.
Prompt: run this organism through your key — does every question have a clear yes or no answer? What happens if two look the same?
activities.rationale: Using classification keys and scientific diagrams for complex findings is part of the recording-complex-data standard. Testing the key against each specimen exposes non-distinguishing questions, which is where keys commonly fail.
sourceClaims: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires recording data and results of increasing complexity using scientific diagrams and labels, classification keys, tables, scatter graphs, bar and line graphs.
learnerActions: Take a small set of organisms (or specimens) to sort by observable features.
Write a sequence of yes/no questions, each about an observable feature, that splits the remaining set at every step.
Draw the key as a branching structure so each organism reaches its own endpoint.
Test the key by running every organism through it, checking that each question has a clear yes or no answer and that no two organisms end at the same point.
If two specimens look the same at a step, add a finer observable question that separates them.
activities.intendedInsight: A working key is built from clear, binary, observable distinctions that divide a set until every specimen is uniquely identified.

activities.title: Read, judge and correct graphs (checks and references)
feedback: For a value-reading task, check the answer against the plotted coordinate; if wrong, retrace reading the axis then finding the point.
For error-spotting, confirm the identified fault (missing unit, uneven interval, wrong type) and the proposed fix.
Remember: recognising the right graph or spotting an error checks understanding but does not by itself show you can construct and choose a graph independently — pair it with the plotting activity.
activities.rationale: Recognition, value-reading and error-spotting are efficient checks and make useful references, but they assess or support rather than require independent construction, so they complement the hands-on plotting task rather than replace it.
learnerActions: Given a line graph, read a specified value off the axes accurately.
Given graphs with mislabelled or unevenly-scaled axes, spot and describe the error and say how to fix it.
Decide which graph type suits a described dataset and justify the choice.
Use a tap-to-reveal reference showing when to use a bar chart vs line graph vs scatter as a support while deciding — not as a substitute for constructing your own.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to read values and diagnose scale/label errors in others' graphs reinforces what makes your own graph interpretable.

constraints: Lines of best fit and gradients belong to the later (KS3) tier and are beyond this bar; the target here is selecting the correct graph, plotting accurately with labelled axes and an even scale, and building a working key.

Builds on prior work with basic tables, bar charts and keys, and on maths discrete/continuous graphing; learners who sort data by type incorrectly may need to revisit the discrete-vs-continuous distinction first.

A static annotated exemplar or tap-to-reveal reference supports recall of when to use each graph type but does not itself require the learner to make the choice, assign axes, set a scale and plot — treat it as a scaffold alongside construction.
Recognition and error-spotting tasks check or diagnose understanding but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a graph or key.

Interactive examples (e.g. a live plotter that draws a flagged zig-zag when a line is chosen for categories, or lets a cramped scale be stretched to reveal a hidden trend) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete and add immediate feedback; squared paper, a dataset and the learner's own plotting are an equally valid route to the same independent-construction goal.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One cited source (NGSS Appendix F progression) is marked verified:false in the original row; treat the 3–5 into 6–8 boundary claim with that caveat. The DfE and NGSS claims support the standards-placement framing only, not the efficacy of any proposed activity.

The original framed a live graphing studio as teaching selection 'viscerally' with wrong-choice flagging as the core mechanism; this has been retained as an optional interaction example rather than a necessary or superior medium, since comparative efficacy is not established by the source claims.

probeDeeper: Why did you pick this graph type rather than a bar chart / line graph for this data?
If someone read your graph, would they know what each axis measures and in what units? Show me where.
Run this organism through your key — does every question have a clear yes or no answer? What happens if two look the same?
assess.correctAnswer: The child selects a graph type suited to the data (line graph for the continuous week-by-week height; bar chart for categorical counts; scatter for two continuous variables), draws axes labelled with quantities and units, uses an even, linear scale, plots accurately, and constructs a key from a sequence of yes/no questions on observable features that separates every organism.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong graph type for the data — e.g. a bar chart for continuous time data, or joins categorical bars into a line.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort data as categories versus continuous first, then map each to its graph type; re-choose before drawing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Graph form doesn't match the data type (line for categories, or bars for a continuous trend).

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses an uneven scale — spaces the axis by the order the numbers were collected rather than by value, so equal gaps mean unequal amounts.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the scale before plotting any point: equal squares equal equal amounts; mark the axis first, then plot.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Axis intervals are irregular; data points are evenly spaced regardless of their values.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits axis labels or units, so the graph doesn't say what was measured.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Require each axis to name the quantity and its unit before the graph is 'finished'; check against the data table headings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Axes carry numbers but no quantity name or unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a key from non-distinguishing or overlapping questions (vague or non-binary), so it fails to separate the organisms.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test the key by running each organism through it; every question must be an observable yes/no that divides the remaining set.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Key questions aren't clear yes/no splits on observable features, or two organisms end at the same point.

responseLevels.gap: Wrong graph type, uneven or missing scale, unlabelled axes; key questions don't reliably separate the organisms.
responseLevels.full: Chooses the appropriate graph, labels axes with units on an even scale and plots accurately, and constructs a working key of clear yes/no observable questions that identifies every organism.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the graph type right and plots reasonably but slips on scale, labels, or units; or builds a key that works for most but has a vague or overlapping question.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a set of results from an investigation [provide a dataset — e.g. a plant's height measured each week, plus a mix of organisms to sort]. Present these properly: choose the right kind of graph and draw it with labelled axes, sensible scales, and accurate points, and build a classification key that would let someone else identify each organism. (Provide squared paper and the data; watch the choices the child makes.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the construction reveals judgements a finished-graph glance would hide: whether the child CHOSE the right graph for the data type, whether the scale is even or spaced by data order, and whether the key's questions actually split the set. These process choices are exactly where increasing-complexity data recording succeeds or fails.

sources.claim: DfE Upper KS2 Working Scientifically requires recording data and results of increasing complexity using scientific diagrams and labels, classification keys, tables, scatter graphs, bar and line graphs.
sources.source: UK Department for Education — National curriculum in England: science programmes of study (Working Scientifically, upper KS2)

sources.claim: NGSS SEP 4 progresses from representing data graphically to reveal patterns (3-5) to constructing and interpreting graphical displays to identify linear and nonlinear relationships (6-8).
sources.source: NGSS Appendix F — Science and Engineering Practices, Practice 4 (Analyzing and Interpreting Data), grades 3-5 and 6-8 progressions

pedagogy.summary: Building 3-D shapes from nets is a procedural skill that consolidates the 2-D↔3-D relationship. It is best taught by having children construct a net (measure, draw, cut, fold, tape), predict which solid it makes, and verify by folding — then check that every face, edge and vertex of the built solid matches the target. Anchoring on a base face and adding faces as composites reduces trial-and-error, and diagnosing why a faulty net won't close (gaps or overlaps) turns errors into structural learning.
bestPractices: Construct-then-fold-to-verify; have the child predict the solid before folding rather than assembling by trial and error.
Start from a base face and add faces in composites; include tabs for assembly so the model closes cleanly.
Check the count: the built solid's faces, edges and vertices should match the target (a triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
Compare several valid nets for the same solid and diagnose why a non-closing net fails — is it the face-set or the arrangement?
keyRepresentations: Card or Polydron nets folded into solids
A tabbed net template that folds and tapes shut
The triangular-prism net: two congruent triangles plus three rectangles forming a band
Base-face-plus-composite layout (band of rectangles, then the two ends)
commonMisconceptions: Falls back on the familiar cube 'cross' net and cannot generate a net for a different solid.
Chooses the wrong face-set (e.g. all rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles for a prism).
Arranges the correct faces so the net cannot close; blames ragged cutting rather than the layout.

learn.summary: Building 3-D shapes from nets is a procedural skill that consolidates the 2-D to 3-D relationship. Children construct a net (measure, draw, cut, fold, tape), predict which solid it makes, then fold to verify and check that every face, edge and vertex of the built solid matches the target. Anchoring on a base face and adding faces as composites (e.g. a band of rectangles plus two triangular ends) reduces trial-and-error, and diagnosing why a faulty net won't close — gaps or overlaps — turns errors into structural learning. The worked example throughout is the triangular prism: two congruent triangles plus three rectangles, with 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices.

activities.title: Construct and fold the net of a triangular prism
feedback: Before folding, ask: which rectangle is the base, and how will each face meet its neighbours when folded? A band of three rectangles with a triangle on each end is one reliable layout to start from. Other valid layouts exist, such as one with a rectangle attached to a triangle, so test the fold rather than rejecting a net only because it has no band.

If a triangle is left flapping, or a gap remains even though the pieces were cut accurately, check two things. First, the layout: will each face meet its neighbour when folded? If not, try redrawing from the band-plus-ends composite. Second, the measurements: each triangle side should equal the width of the rectangle it joins, and all rectangles should have the same length. If the net itself is correct but only the cutting or taping is ragged, provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the layout reasoning rather than scissor control.

When counting, prompt: how many corners does each triangular end have? So how many vertices altogether? How many edges are on each triangular end, and how many edges join the two ends? Check the totals against 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.
If the child reproduces a familiar cube 'cross' net, unfold a real triangular prism to reveal its actual net and contrast the two.
activities.rationale: The procedure ends in a genuinely 3-D solid, so folding the net up and rotating the sealed shape to count faces, edges and vertices is the target skill. Successful builders anchor imaged folding to a base face and known composites; diagnosing why a net won't close moves children from judging by appearance to reasoning about structure.
sourceClaims: Successful builders use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four' wraps the cube's sides); the weakest reproduce a memorised prototype net; teacher questioning that maps net shapes/sides/points to faces/edges/vertices moves children from appearance to structure.
learnerActions: Using card, a ruler and scissors, draw the net of a triangular prism: two congruent triangles and three rectangles of equal length, each rectangle as wide as the triangle side it joins.
Before cutting, predict and say which shape will be the bottom (base) and which two shapes will cap the ends.
Cut out the net, fold along the edges and tape it shut.
Point to the finished solid and count its faces, edges and vertices (target: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
activities.intendedInsight: A valid net is more than the right set of faces — the faces must be arranged so they fold into a closed solid, and the structure of that solid (faces, edges, vertices) can be read off the built 3-D shape rather than the flat drawing.

activities.title: Drag-to-build a net and predict the fold
feedback: On folding, flag gaps, overlaps and any face left flapping so the child can see exactly where the layout fails.
Immediate close/fail feedback on the fold doubles as a check of the construction procedure.
A flat on-screen view slightly under-sells the real 3-D fold, so confirm the count on a rotatable solid or a physical model.
activities.rationale: A drag-to-build editor with a fold animation and immediate close/fail feedback exercises the construction procedure and lets children test many layouts quickly. It is offered as a supplement to physical construction, not a replacement; a flat screen view represents, rather than replaces, the 3-D fold. Efficacy relative to physical building is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Successful builders use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four' wraps the cube's sides); the weakest reproduce a memorised prototype net; teacher questioning that maps net shapes/sides/points to faces/edges/vertices moves children from appearance to structure.
learnerActions: Drag two triangles and three rectangles onto a grid to lay out a candidate net.
State which solid you predict it will make and which faces will be the base and the ends.
Fold the layout and watch how the rectangles and triangles move. Check whether every face meets its neighbour so the ends are capped and the prism closes.

If a face is left flapping or a gap or overlap appears, rearrange the faces so they meet correctly, for example by re-anchoring on a band of three rectangles with a triangle on each end, then fold again.
Rotate the sealed solid and tap round it to tally faces, edges and vertices.
activities.intendedInsight: A layout that 'looks fine' flat may still fail to close. Checking how each face will meet its neighbours when folded is what shows whether the prism seals. A band of three rectangles with triangular ends is one dependable layout, but not the only valid one.

activities.title: Compare and diagnose nets for the same solid
feedback: If the child counts wrong faces (e.g. four rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles), hand them the target prism and match each of its faces to a net shape before deciding; count faces first.

For an arrangement failure, have the child trace which edges will meet when folded and find where faces overlap or leave a gap. Rearranging into a band of three rectangles between the two triangular ends is one reliable fix, though not the only valid net.
A sorting task like this can check and build classification of nets, but it does not itself elicit independent construction of a net from scratch; use it alongside, not instead of, building.
activities.rationale: Comparing valid nets and diagnosing why a non-closing net fails separates face-set errors from arrangement errors and builds the structural scheme. Coordinating spatial visualisation with property-based reasoning is what lets children see past the 'look' of the flat drawing.
sourceClaims: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated by domain knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D representation, which is why some children build by appearance rather than structure.
learnerActions: Given several candidate nets for a triangular prism, sort them into those that will fold shut and those that will not.

For each failing net, say whether the problem is the face-set (wrong shapes, wrong number or mismatched sizes) or the arrangement (correct faces placed so that, when folded, some overlap or leave a gap).
Find two different valid nets for the same prism and explain why both work.
Reason about a near-miss: if a net has three triangles and two rectangles, could it fold into this prism, or into any closed solid at all? Explain using the faces a triangular prism needs.
activities.intendedInsight: Nets fail for two distinct reasons — the wrong set of faces, or a correct set arranged so it cannot close — and the same solid can have more than one valid net.

constraints: A static exploded or net diagram (even one tagged face-to-face, or where tapping a net face shows where it lands on the solid) is a useful planning reference but does not enact the fold-and-check procedure; use it to support planning, not as the build itself.
Matching or sequencing tasks that pair solids to nets and counts check recognition of nets and counts but do not elicit independent construction of a net; use them as a post-check.
Discussion can prompt a prediction for the child to justify, but talking does not itself elicit the physical construction and folding that is the target skill.
When cutting, folding or taping leaves ragged gaps, the fold-check becomes inconclusive — provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the reasoning rather than scissor control.
A flat 2-D interactive represents the 3-D fold and may under-sell it; confirm face/edge/vertex counts on a rotatable or physical solid.
Include assembly tabs so the model closes cleanly.

Building simple 3-D shapes, including making nets, is part of the Key Stage 2 (Year 6) national curriculum for England. Physical construction with card, ruler and scissors is the core experience in this guidance; digital editors are a supplementary option, not a replacement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the triangular prism: 2 triangular faces + 3 rectangular faces = 5 faces; 3 edges on each triangular end (6) + 3 connecting edges = 9 edges; 3 vertices on each triangular end = 6 vertices. These match the source values (5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).

The near-miss prompt (three triangles and two rectangles) is retained as a reasoning probe: that face-set does not form a triangular prism, so the expected answer is 'no'. Kept as a diagnostic question, not as a construction instruction.

The legacy row ranked a 3-D interactive as 'ideal' and a conversation as 'poor'. Comparative efficacy/necessity is not established by the cited sources, so artefacts are presented as options with stated affordances and limits rather than universal claims.

The National Curriculum claim was removed from Activity 1's sourceClaims because that activity's rationale concerns a teaching principle (imaged folding/structure) rather than the curriculum objective itself; the curriculum requirement is retained as a constraint and in the audit.

probeDeeper: Before you fold — which shape will be the bottom, and which two will be the ends?
Your model has a gap here. Is the net wrong, or the way it is arranged? Show me.
How many edges meet at that top corner? So how many vertices altogether?
If I gave you a net with three triangles and two rectangles, what solid would that build — could it be this prism?
assess.correctAnswer: Draws a net of two congruent triangles and three rectangles positioned so the rectangles form a band that wraps between the triangular ends; folds it to a closed prism with no gaps or overlaps; and, pointing to the built solid, counts 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices — self-correcting the layout if a first attempt won't close.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong faces for the solid — e.g. draws four rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles, for a triangular prism
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand the child the target prism and match each of its faces to a net shape before drawing; count faces first
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The net has too few or too many faces, or the wrong shapes, and won't wrap between the two triangular ends

errorPatterns.pattern: Places the correct faces in an arrangement that cannot fold shut — the three rectangles don't form a continuous band, so the ends never meet
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor a base rectangle, fold the band of three rectangles first, then attach the two triangular ends; re-draw from that composite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Folding leaves a gap or overlap; the child blames the cutting rather than the layout

errorPatterns.pattern: Falls back on the familiar cube 'cross' net and cannot generate a net for a different solid
errorPatterns.nextMove: Unfold a real triangular prism to reveal its actual net and contrast it with the cube net
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attempts a cross of six shapes regardless of the target prism

errorPatterns.pattern: Has the right net but cutting, folding or taping leaves gaps, so the fold-check is inconclusive
errorPatterns.nextMove: Provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the reasoning, not scissor control
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The net is correct on paper but the model is ragged and the child is unsure whether it 'worked'

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a net that closes into the target solid; reproduces a memorised cube net or an unfoldable arrangement.
responseLevels.full: Constructs a valid net by choosing the right faces and arranging them as a band-plus-ends composite, folds to a closed solid, self-corrects a faulty layout, and reads faces, edges and vertices off the 3-D structure.
responseLevels.partial: Builds the solid when given a correct net or after trial and error and counts faces, but cannot construct a valid net from scratch or explain why an arrangement fails — parts without structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is card, a ruler, and scissors. Construct the net of a triangular prism, then fold and tape it to check it makes the solid. When it is built, tell me how many faces, edges and vertices it has by pointing to them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child build separates those holding a structural scheme (base band plus two ends, faces in the right composite) from those assembling by trial and error or reproducing a memorised cube net. A wrong face-set or a net that won't close is visible immediately, and the face/edge/vertex count exposes whether the child reads the 3-D structure rather than the flat drawing.

sources.claim: Successful builders use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four' wraps the cube's sides); the weakest reproduce a memorised prototype net; teacher questioning that maps net shapes/sides/points to faces/edges/vertices moves children from appearance to structure.
sources.source: Knight & Wright (2014), 'Will this Net Work?', MERGA proceedings (ERIC ED572616)

sources.claim: Recognising, describing and building simple 3-D shapes, including making nets, is a Key Stage 2 geometry objective in the English National Curriculum.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (gov.uk)

sources.claim: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated by domain knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D representation, which is why some children build by appearance rather than structure.
sources.source: Fujita, Kondo, Kumakura, Kunimune & Jones (2020), Mathematics Education Research Journal 32(2)

pedagogy.summary: At 5-6 this is the seed of MP8: noticing that a calculation or move REPEATS and using that to count more efficiently or predict, rather than starting from scratch each time. The child sees that adding 1 always gives the next counting number, that skip-counting in 2s produces a steady odd/even rhythm, and that +10 on a hundred square always drops you straight down one row. CCSS MP8 begins here — 'notice if calculations are repeated, and look for… shortcuts' — and the teaching job is to prompt the child to expect the repeat and test it ('will it happen again?'), not to hand over the rule.
bestPractices: Use the hundred square so +10 is a physical, repeatable move (straight down a row) the child can predict before checking
Prompt prediction: 'what will happen next? will it keep happening?' so the child forms and tests an expectation rather than counting afresh
Skip-count with a visible rhythm (steps on a number track, claps) so the repeating structure is heard and seen, and highlight the odd/even alternation
Deliberately extend a pattern one more step together and confirm the rule held, building the habit of using a noticed repeat to predict
keyRepresentations: Hundred square (rows make +10 a repeated downward move)
Number track / number line for +1 and skip-count steps
Bead string or steps grouped in 2s, 5s, 10s
Ten-frames showing the steady 'one more' growth
commonMisconceptions: Counts in ones every time instead of using the repeated +10 move, treating each sum as brand new
Sees a pattern work once but does not expect it to continue, so won't use it to predict
Loses the skip-count structure partway (2, 4, 6, 8, 9) by reverting to counting in ones
Thinks 'the next number' and 'one more' are unrelated ideas rather than the same repeated +1

learn.summary: For ages 5-6, this is the seed of noticing that a calculation or move REPEATS and using that to count more efficiently or predict, rather than starting afresh each time. Children learn that adding 1 always gives the next counting number, that skip-counting in 2s from 2 lands on every second number (the even numbers, skipping the odd ones between), and that on a standard hundred square with 1 in the top row, +10 moves you straight down one row whenever there is a row below. The teaching job is to prompt the child to expect the repeat and test it ('will it happen again?'), not to hand over the rule. The most developed activity has the child predict the next repeat and then see it happen; recognition checks and highlighted references play supporting roles.

activities.title: Predict-the-jump hundred square
feedback: If the child counts ten squares each time rather than jumping straight down, don't drill the rule — keep asking them to predict the next jump before checking, until they stop recounting.

If the child gets 34 by the move but re-counts for 44 as if it might be different, ask 'will it happen again? shall we test it?' and confirm together across several jumps so they build the expectation that the pattern repeats.
When the child predicts correctly without recounting and says it works 'the same as before', confirm that the move repeats every time and invite them to put the reason in their own words.
activities.rationale: Repeated reasoning is learned by predicting the next repeat and seeing it happen; a hundred square makes +10 a physical, repeatable downward move the child can forecast then confirm. Predict-then-check is what turns 'it repeats' into an expectation rather than a memorised rule. An optional live counter that drops straight down one row, or a lit path, makes the mechanism concrete, but a paper hundred square with a movable token can serve the same purpose; the choice of medium is an optional mechanism, not established as more effective.
sourceClaims: MP8 begins with noticing repeated calculations and looking for shortcuts; upper-elementary and younger students notice repetition and use it to predict/generalise
Early maths should build understanding of the number system and counting structures using representations (e.g. number tracks, hundred squares) that make repeated patterns visible
learnerActions: Point to 24 on a hundred square.
Before moving anything, say out loud where you think 24 + 10 will land.
Move a counter straight down one row to land on 34 and check your guess.
Do it again: predict 34 + 10, then land on 44; then predict 44 + 10 and land on 54.
After a few jumps, try to say where the next +10 will land without looking closely — notice you no longer need to recount.
Try a jump from a different starting number (e.g. 'will adding ten from 57 still go straight down a row? shall we check?') to test whether the repeat always holds.
activities.intendedInsight: On this hundred square (1 in the top row), adding ten moves you straight down one row each time there is a row below, so once you notice the repeat you can predict the next result instead of counting ten squares each time.

activities.title: Skip-count rhythm track
feedback: If the child loses the structure partway (e.g. 2, 4, 6, 8, 9) by slipping back to counting in ones, re-anchor the rhythm with a beat or steps and rebuild the count. This is the skip-count structure still consolidating, not a fact error.
If the child can call the next number before reaching it, highlight that they used the repeating rhythm rather than counting every number.
Use 'is 7 in your counting-by-2s?' to check whether the child notices the odd/even structure, not just the next number.
activities.rationale: A visible, audible rhythm (steps, claps, a lit step on every 2nd count) makes the repeating structure felt, and highlights the odd/even alternation. Anticipating the next step builds the habit of using a noticed repeat to predict.
