pedagogy.summary: A terminating decimal IS a fraction with a power-of-ten denominator: 0.375 = 375/1000, which simplifies to 3/8. Converting a fraction to a decimal is division (3 ÷ 8 = 0.375) or, equivalently, scaling the denominator up to 10, 100, 1000… Whether a fraction terminates is decided entirely by the prime factors of its denominator in lowest terms: only 2 and 5 (the prime factors of ten) give a terminating decimal; any other prime factor (3, 7, 11…) produces a recurring decimal. Fractions, decimals and percentages are three notations for one value.
bestPractices: Read a decimal by its LAST place value to get the denominator (0.375 = 375 thousandths), then simplify to lowest terms
Teach fraction→decimal two ways — as division (numerator ÷ denominator) AND as scaling the denominator to a power of ten (3/8 = 375/1000 via ×125)
Make the '2s and 5s only' test explicit by contrasting terminators (1/8, 1/20, 1/40) with recurrers (1/3, 1/6, 1/7) and factorising each denominator
Treat FDP as three views of one number on a triple number line so conversion is re-notation, not new arithmetic
Show a recurring decimal actually recurring (1/3 = 0.333…) so children do not truncate it and call it exact
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns (tenths, hundredths, thousandths)
Prime-factor trees of denominators
Short division for fraction→decimal
FDP triple number line / equivalence cards
Hundredths and thousandths grids
commonMisconceptions: Reads 0.375 as 375/100 (denominator doesn't match the last place value)
Inverts the division, computing 8 ÷ 3 instead of 3 ÷ 8
Believes every fraction terminates, or truncates a recurring decimal (1/3 = 0.3) and treats it as exact
Decides whether a decimal terminates from the numerator or 'how neat it looks' rather than the denominator's prime factors

learn.summary: Terminating decimals and fractions are two notations for one value, with percentages a third. A terminating decimal is read by its LAST place value to get a power-of-ten denominator (0.375 = 375/1000), then simplified (= 3/8). Converting a fraction to a decimal is division (3 ÷ 8 = 0.375) or, equivalently, scaling the denominator up to a power of ten (3/8 = 375/1000 via ×125). The deep idea: a fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5 (the primes of ten); any other prime factor (3, 7, 11…) makes it recur. Learners should both convert fluently in both directions AND predict termination from the denominator's prime factorisation, not by dividing and guessing.

activities.title: Scale to a power of ten — does it land?
feedback: If a learner says 1/6 stops: factorise 6 = 2×3. The factor 3 is not 2 or 5, so no power of ten is a multiple of 6 and the decimal recurs (0.1666…). Show it recurring rather than truncating to 0.17.

If they truncate a recurring decimal and call it exact (1/3 = 0.3): run the division further so the 3s keep coming; 0.333… is not equal to 0.3. (Year 6 learners meet rounding recurring decimals to three decimal places — rounding is an approximation, not the exact value.)

If they decide termination from the numerator or 'how neat it looks': remind them the numerator is irrelevant once the fraction is simplified — only the lowest-terms denominator's prime factors decide.
activities.rationale: Contrasting a fraction that scales onto a power of ten against one that never does, with prime-factor readouts shown together, is intended to make the 2-and-5 rule discoverable rather than merely asserted; sorting fractions and factorising each denominator is a documented route to the rule.
sourceClaims: A fraction IN LOWEST TERMS gives a terminating decimal if and only if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5; the reason is base-10 (10 = 2x5), so the denominator terminates exactly when it divides a power of ten. Sorting fractions into terminating/recurring columns and writing each denominator as its prime factorisation makes the rule discoverable; the numerator is irrelevant and the fraction must be simplified first.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [0.375] for a simple fraction [3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents they learn about rounding to three decimal places - so recurring decimals are met and must not be treated as terminating.
learnerActions: Take 1/8 and try to turn it into tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths: find the multiplier (×125) that makes the denominator 1000, giving 125/1000 = 0.125; confirm it 'lands' exactly.
Now try 1/3 the same way: aim for 10, 100, 1000… and find that no power of ten works; carry out the division 1 ÷ 3 and watch the 3s continue (0.333…), a recurring decimal that never stops.
Write each denominator as a product of primes side by side: 8 = 2×2×2; 6 = 2×3; 3 = 3. Mark which denominators are built only from 2s and 5s.
State the rule you discover in your own words, then test it on 1/20, 1/40 (should terminate) and 1/6, 1/7 (should recur), factorising each denominator first.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator is built only from the primes 2 and/or 5 — because those are the primes of ten, so the denominator can be scaled to a power of ten. Any other prime factor forces a recurring decimal.

activities.title: Read a decimal by its last place value
feedback: If a learner writes 0.375 = 375/100: the last digit (5) sits in the thousandths place, so the denominator is 1000, not 100. Re-read several decimals aloud by their final place value before writing the fraction.

If they invert the division and compute 8 ÷ 3 for 3/8 (getting 2.66…): re-establish that a/b means a ÷ b — numerator divided by denominator — grounded in sharing 3 wholes among 8 people, which gives less than one each (0.375).
activities.rationale: Anchoring the denominator to the last place value is intended to address the most common conversion error (reading onto the wrong power of ten), and practising division-as-conversion in the reverse direction aims to reinforce fraction-as-division, a documented sticking point.
sourceClaims: Converting a fraction to a decimal is the division numerator / denominator (fraction-as-division); understanding fractions as division underpins decimal equivalence and is a documented sticking point.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [0.375] for a simple fraction [3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents they learn about rounding to three decimal places - so recurring decimals are met and must not be treated as terminating.
learnerActions: Name the place value of the LAST digit of 0.375 (thousandths), so the starting denominator is 1000: write 0.375 = 375/1000.
Simplify stepwise to lowest terms: 375/1000 = 3/8 (divide both by 125). Check the simplified fraction against the original decimal.
Repeat with other decimals (0.2 = 2/10 = 1/5; 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4; 0.35 = 35/100 = 7/20), each time naming the last place value first.
Reverse the direction: convert 3/8 to a decimal two ways — divide 3 ÷ 8, and scale 3/8 to 375/1000 — and confirm both give 0.375.
activities.intendedInsight: A terminating decimal IS a fraction with a power-of-ten denominator; reading the last place value gives that denominator, and simplifying gives lowest terms. Fraction→decimal is division (numerator ÷ denominator), equivalently scaling to a power of ten.

activities.title: Sort, match and fill the gaps (consolidation)
feedback: If a learner sorts by dividing and rounding: that only shows what happens to begin with, not whether it stops forever. Ask them to factorise the denominator in lowest terms and apply the 2-and-5 test instead.
If a chain step is wrong, point back to the place-value reading (last digit → denominator) and the simplification factor (×125 or ÷125).
activities.rationale: Matching, categorising and fill-in-and-explain tasks give repeated, checkable practice across both directions and foreground the structural (prime-factor) test over empirical division; the fill-in step asks the learner to produce values and explain each one, so this activity consolidates and partly requires articulation of the discovered rule, not its first teaching.
sourceClaims: A fraction IN LOWEST TERMS gives a terminating decimal if and only if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5; the reason is base-10 (10 = 2x5), so the denominator terminates exactly when it divides a power of ten. Sorting fractions into terminating/recurring columns and writing each denominator as its prime factorisation makes the rule discoverable; the numerator is irrelevant and the fraction must be simplified first.
learnerActions: Match terminating decimals to their simplest fractions: 0.375 ↔ 3/8, 0.2 ↔ 1/5, 0.25 ↔ 1/4.
Sort a set of fractions into two columns, 'terminates' and 'recurs', by inspecting each denominator's prime factors (not by dividing): e.g. 7/40 and 1/20 terminate; 5/12 and 1/6 recur.
Fill in the chain 0.375 = __/1000 = __/8, then explain each step (last place value → denominator, then the ÷125 simplification).

Transfer to unfamiliar fractions: predict whether 9/25, 4/15 and 6/15 terminate, justify from the prime factors of each denominator in lowest terms (6/15 = 2/5), then check by converting (9/25 = 0.36; 4/15 = 0.2666…; 6/15 = 0.4).
activities.intendedInsight: Bidirectional conversion to simplest form becomes fluent, and the terminate/recur judgement is made from the denominator's prime factors rather than by trial division.

activities.title: Predict and justify: will it stop? (optional discussion)
feedback: Accept only reasons that cite the denominator's prime factors; 'it looks neat' or 'I tried dividing' is not a structural justification.
If the learner can convert but cannot say why 1/8 stops and 1/6 does not, return to factorising the two denominators side by side.
activities.rationale: A short predict-and-justify exchange is proposed to supplement procedural practice by targeting the 'why do some fractions never stop?' reasoning; it supplements rather than replaces conversion practice, since the objective is procedural fluency. Its effect on reasoning is untested here.
learnerActions: Before converting, predict aloud whether a given fraction (e.g. 1/6, 7/40, 5/12) terminates or recurs, and say WHY from the denominator.
Justify the prediction by naming the prime factors of the denominator and relating them to the primes of ten (2 and 5).
Have a partner or adult pose the question 'How could you know without doing the whole division?' and respond with a reasoned argument, then check by converting.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the prediction and its reason is intended to reveal whether the learner reasons from structure (prime factors) or merely from procedures; articulating the reason aims to strengthen the conceptual link, though that effect is not established here.

constraints: Recurring decimals must be shown genuinely recurring (1/3 = 0.333…); do not truncate (0.3 or 0.33) and call it exact. Rounding a recurring decimal to a set number of places is an approximation introduced for Year 6, not the exact value.
The 2-and-5 rule applies only to the denominator IN LOWEST TERMS; simplify first and ignore the numerator when judging termination.

Matching is recognition-and-recall practice, a sort checks classification of denominators, and a fill-in chain asks the learner to produce values; on their own these task types do not require the learner to carry out a full conversion in both directions and articulate the reason, so pair them with at least one activity where the learner constructs and explains a full conversion and a termination prediction (as the fill-in-and-explain and predict-and-justify steps do).

A tap-to-reveal equivalence card (fraction → decimal → percentage with denominator prime factors) is a useful reference aid but cannot let a learner test the terminate/recur boundary themselves; use it alongside, not instead of, the scaling/conversion work.
Fraction-as-division must be the direction numerator ÷ denominator (3 ÷ 8), not denominator ÷ numerator.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no claim of empirical testing is made.

Legacy design described two linked on-screen panels (scale-to-power-of-ten with a prime-factor readout, and place-value decimal-to-fraction simplifier) with a 'lights up/it fits' response. These interaction examples are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory. A fixed printed chart can still teach the conversions even though it cannot be manipulated.

The legacy source framed interactive scaling as the way the rule 'clicks' and rated dialogue/3D as weaker. Those comparative fit judgements are catalog preferences, not established efficacy; the alternatives are kept here as activities with stated purposes and limits rather than as a ranking.

Editorial change: efficacy-asserting wording in the activity rationales and in activity[3]'s intendedInsight ('removes the error', 'reinforces', 'strengthening the conceptual link') was softened to intended/aims wording, since the sources identify the misconceptions/sticking points but do not establish that these specific activities fix them.

Self-audit of arithmetic and logic: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8 (÷125) is correct; 3/8 = 0.375 is correct; 1/8 = 0.125 via ×125 to 125/1000 is correct; 8 = 2³, 6 = 2×3, 3 = 3 are correct; 1/6 = 0.1666… recurs (3 is not 2 or 5) is correct; 7/40 terminates (40 = 2³×5) and 5/12 recurs (12 = 2²×3) are correct; 0.2=1/5, 0.25=1/4, 0.35=7/20 are correct; 8 ÷ 3 = 2.66… correctly identifies the inverted-division error. No arithmetic errors found in learner-facing content.

probeDeeper: What place value is the last digit of 0.375 in? So what denominator do you start with before simplifying?
For 3/8, which number do you divide by which — and why that way round?
Will 1/6 stop or go on forever? What is it about the 6 that tells you, without dividing all the way?
1/8 stops but 1/3 does not. What is different about the denominators when you break each into prime factors?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8 (dividing by 125); 3/8 = 0.375 (3 ÷ 8, or ×125 to make 375/1000). 1/6 does NOT stop — 6 = 2×3, and the factor 3 is not 2 or 5, so it recurs (0.1666…).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the decimal onto the wrong power of ten: 0.375 = 375/100
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the last digit's place (thousandths), so the denominator is 1000; then simplify. Re-read several decimals by their final place value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denominator does not match the last digit's place value; the simplified fraction is wrong or won't simplify to 3/8

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverts the division for fraction→decimal: computes 8 ÷ 3 for 3/8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish fraction-as-division: a/b means a ÷ b (numerator into denominator), grounded in sharing 3 wholes among 8.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Divides the larger number by the smaller, or gets 2.66… for 3/8

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges whether a fraction terminates from the numerator or how 'neat' it looks, or believes every fraction terminates — so claims 1/6 stops, or truncates it to 0.17 and calls it exact
errorPatterns.nextMove: Factorise the denominators side by side (8 = 2³ terminates; 6 = 2×3 recurs) and connect 2 and 5 to the primes of ten; show 1/6 genuinely recurring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 1/6 stops; decides by trying to divide and rounding rather than by the denominator's prime factors; cannot explain WHY 1/8 stops but 1/6 does not

responseLevels.gap: Mis-reads the decimal's denominator or inverts the division; believes all fractions terminate; cannot connect terminating to the denominator.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions fluently to simplest form AND predicts termination from the denominator's prime factorisation (only 2 and 5), explaining why (it can be scaled to a power of ten); transfers to a new fraction such as 7/40 (terminates) or 5/12 (recurs).
responseLevels.partial: Converts 0.375 ↔ 3/8 correctly by procedure, but decides termination empirically by dividing and rounding rather than from the denominator's prime factors, or states the 2-and-5 rule only after prompting.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Convert 0.375 to a fraction in its simplest form, and convert 3/8 to a decimal. Then tell me — will 1/6 give a decimal that stops, or one that goes on forever? How could you know without doing the whole division?' Watch how they work and listen to the reason for 1/6.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Converting 0.375 both ways is routine and does not separate understanding from memorised steps. The 1/6 question is the hinge: a child who grasps the structure inspects the denominator's prime factors (only 2 and 5 terminate) and answers WITHOUT dividing; a child who has only procedures tries to divide and rounds, guesses, or asserts that all fractions stop. Reasoning correctly and reasoning wrongly give visibly different responses here.

sources.claim: A fraction IN LOWEST TERMS gives a terminating decimal if and only if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5; the reason is base-10 (10 = 2x5), so the denominator terminates exactly when it divides a power of ten. Sorting fractions into terminating/recurring columns and writing each denominator as its prime factorisation makes the rule discoverable; the numerator is irrelevant and the fraction must be simplified first.
sources.source: NRICH (Univ. of Cambridge / Millennium Mathematics Project), 'Terminating or Not' (ages 11-14)

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [0.375] for a simple fraction [3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents they learn about rounding to three decimal places - so recurring decimals are met and must not be treated as terminating.
sources.source: DfE, National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 6

sources.claim: Converting a fraction to a decimal is the division numerator / denominator (fraction-as-division); understanding fractions as division underpins decimal equivalence and is a documented sticking point.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K-8 (Siegler et al. 2010)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Metals vs Non-Metals

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry 'The Periodic Table'):** The properties of metals and non-metals; the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements; the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity; how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the Periodic Table.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-1 / MS-PS1-2 supporting):** Use patterns in characteristic properties of substances to classify and identify materials.

- **Operational details:** Metals and non-metals are the great divide of the periodic table. Teach the cluster of PHYSICAL properties that typify metals — shiny (lustre), malleable/ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity, generally high melting points, mostly solid — versus non-metals (dull, brittle, poor conductors/insulators, lower melting points, many gases). Then the CHEMICAL signature: metals tend to form basic/alkaline oxides, non-metals form acidic oxides (the DfE 'oxides with respect to acidity' bullet); metals react by losing electrons. Tie the divide to POSITION: metals left/centre, non-metals upper right, with a staircase boundary and metalloids straddling it. Best taught by testing/sorting real property data rather than reciting lists, and by noting exceptions (mercury is a liquid metal; carbon/graphite conducts) so the pattern is a strong tendency, not an absolute rule.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child classifies elements as metal/non-metal from property evidence, links the classification to periodic-table position, and states one chemical difference (e.g. metal oxides basic vs non-metal oxides acidic).
bestPractices: Teach metal/non-metal as a CLUSTER of co-occurring properties, not a single trait.
Have pupils classify from property EVIDENCE (test/sort data) rather than memorised lists.
Add the chemical signature: metal oxides tend to be basic, non-metal oxides acidic.
Link the classification to periodic-table POSITION (metals left/centre, non-metals upper right).
Use exceptions (mercury liquid, graphite conducts, metalloids) to teach that it's a strong tendency, not an absolute.
keyRepresentations: A test-and-sort bench (conductivity, malleability, lustre, oxide pH)
A results table feeding a metal/non-metal classification
A periodic table shaded by the metal/non-metal divide with a staircase boundary
Puzzle/exception cases (mercury, graphite, metalloids)
commonMisconceptions: All metals are magnetic (only iron/nickel/cobalt are).
All metals are hard and solid (mercury is liquid; some are soft).
Any shiny material is a metal (lustre alone is not sufficient).
Non-metals never conduct (graphite does).
Metal and non-metal oxides behave the same in water (they differ in acidity).

learn.summary: Learners classify elements as metals or non-metals from a cluster of co-occurring property evidence (conductivity, malleability, lustre, oxide acidity), link that classification to periodic-table position (metals left/centre, non-metals upper right with a staircase boundary), and state a chemical difference (metal oxides tend to be basic, non-metal oxides tend to be acidic). Exceptions (liquid mercury, conducting graphite, metalloids) teach that the divide is a strong tendency, not an absolute rule. Age 11–13.

activities.title: Test-and-sort bench: metal or not?
feedback: If the learner classifies from one property alone, point to a conflicting case: a shiny plastic strip looks lustrous but won't conduct — ask them to gather the other test results before deciding.

When graphite (a non-metal) conducts, acknowledge the surprise and have them check malleability and oxide behaviour too. It is brittle and flaky rather than malleable, and its oxide (carbon dioxide) is acidic, so the full cluster still places it as a non-metal even though it has a grey sheen. Conduction alone isn't decisive.

When mercury classifies as a metal despite being liquid, confirm: state varies, but its conduction and lustre (and metallic bonding) still mark its metallic character — malleability simply can't be shown for a liquid, so it isn't the deciding test here.
After sorting, prompt: 'Where did the basic-oxide samples end up on the table, and where did the acidic-oxide ones?' to make the position–chemistry link explicit.
activities.rationale: The divide is learned by testing and sorting property data rather than reciting lists; actively generating a results table and seeing clusters fall onto table position makes the property cluster and its link to position a discovery, and the included exceptions frame the pattern as a tendency.
sourceClaims: Characteristic properties are used to classify and identify substances (NGSS PS1.A patterns)
Metal oxides are generally basic and non-metal oxides acidic; the metal/non-metal divide has metalloid/exception cases (Hg liquid, graphite conducts)
DfE KS3 Chemistry: properties of metals and non-metals; chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity; predicting patterns from the periodic table
learnerActions: Take each solid element sample and run quick tests: touch it to a circuit (does the bulb light?), tap it with a hammer (does it flatten or shatter?), and check its shine (lustrous or dull?). Then, for elements whose oxide dissolves in water, test a simulated or teacher-prepared oxide solution with universal indicator (acidic or basic?). Mercury is only simulated or shown by the teacher in a sealed sample, never hammered or burned.
Record each result in a results table, one row per element.
As evidence accumulates, place each sample onto a metal or non-metal map overlaid on the periodic table, and watch where the two clusters land.
Work through puzzle cases — liquid mercury and conducting graphite — and decide how to classify them despite one odd property.
State one chemical difference between the two classes: metal oxides tend to be basic/alkaline, non-metal oxides tend to be acidic (a strong pattern, not a guarantee for every oxide).
activities.intendedInsight: Metals and non-metals are distinguished by a CLUSTER of co-occurring properties, not one trait. The shiny, malleable, conducting, basic-oxide elements pool on the left/centre of the periodic table and the dull, brittle, insulating, acidic-oxide elements on the upper right. The staircase divide broadly matches the metal/non-metal split, with metalloids along it and hydrogen (a non-metal placed top left) as a notable exception.

activities.title: Shaded periodic table reference
feedback: If a learner reads the boundary as a hard line, point to the metalloids straddling the staircase as intermediate cases.
When predicting from position, ask them to name at least two expected properties, not one, to reinforce the cluster idea.
activities.rationale: A shaded reference and tap-to-reveal chart consolidate the position–property link and serve as a companion to active testing; as a reference tool it supports recall and prediction but does not itself let the learner generate the test evidence, so it is best paired after bench work.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: properties of metals and non-metals; chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity; predicting patterns from the periodic table
learnerActions: Study a periodic table shaded by the metal/non-metal divide, with the staircase boundary and metalloids straddling it marked.
Use a tap-to-reveal comparison chart with a metals column and a non-metals column; tap a property (e.g. malleability, conductivity, oxide acidity) to highlight which side shows it.
Given a new element's position, predict whether it is likely a metal or non-metal and which properties you'd expect.
activities.intendedInsight: Periodic-table position predicts metal/non-metal character and its associated property cluster; the boundary is a staircase with metalloids in between, so it is a graded divide rather than a hard line.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: does a magnet define a metal?
feedback: If the learner predicts all metals stick, use the observation (only iron sticks) to show magnetism is a property of a few metals, not the definition — copper, aluminium and gold also don't stick yet are metals.
If they refuse to call mercury a metal because it is liquid, note that sodium is soft and mercury liquid; state and hardness vary, while conduction, lustre and metallic bonding still unite them.
If they call the shiny plastic a metal, have them check conduction — the plastic won't conduct, the metals will; use the cluster, not one cue.

Full-credit reasoning rejects 'magnetic = metal' and 'shiny = metal' and cites conduction and malleability, correctly handling non-magnetic copper, liquid mercury and shiny plastic; a partial response lists metallic properties but cannot say which property settles a given object or link uses to properties.
activities.rationale: Counterexamples (non-magnetic copper, liquid mercury, shiny plastic) discriminate a learner using a defining property cluster from one leaning on a single misleading cue, directly targeting the common misconceptions that all metals are magnetic, all metals are hard solids, and anything shiny is a metal.
learnerActions: Lay out copper, aluminium, iron and a shiny plastic strip; the teacher presents a sealed/demonstrated sample of liquid mercury (never pupil-handled). Before testing, predict which a magnet will pick up and explain WHY.
Test with a magnet and observe: only the iron sticks (copper, aluminium and mercury do not, and the plastic is not a metal).
Explain the gap between prediction and result, then give two other tests (conductivity, malleability) that show copper IS a metal despite not being magnetic.
Decide whether the demonstrated liquid mercury is a metal, and whether a shiny sweet wrapper is really metal or just shiny plastic, saying which test settles each.

Answer: where on the periodic table would you look to predict whether an element is a metal, and why are metals chosen for saucepan bases versus electrical wires — which property does the work each time?
activities.intendedInsight: Magnetism and shine are single misleading cues; metals are identified by a coherent cluster (conductivity, malleability where state allows, lustre, mostly high melting points, left/centre periodic position). Only iron, nickel and cobalt are commonly magnetic; shiny plastic is not a metal; and liquid mercury is still a metal.

constraints: The shaded periodic table and tap-to-reveal chart are reference scaffolds: they support prediction and recall but do not let the learner generate the test evidence that produces a classification, so pair them after hands-on (or simulated) testing rather than as a substitute.

The metal/non-metal divide is a strong tendency, not an absolute rule — always include exceptions (mercury is a liquid metal; carbon/graphite conducts; metalloids straddle the boundary) so learners don't over-apply any single property.

No single property defines a metal: magnetism (only iron/nickel/cobalt commonly), shine, hardness or solidity each fail alone. Require a cluster — conduction and malleability (where state allows) are the most decisive.

Oxide acidity depends on the element and conditions, and some metal oxides are insoluble; teach 'metal oxides tend to be basic, non-metal oxides tend to be acidic' as a strong general pattern tested on soluble/pre-prepared oxides, not as a guarantee for every case.

Recognition/matching tasks (categorisation, oxide-acidity multiple choice) assess alignment but do not by themselves elicit the independent evidence-gathering of bench testing; use them to consolidate after active classification.

If run as a real lab rather than the designed interactive, the burn-and-test-oxide step and any mercury require teacher supervision and safe setup — pre-prepared/soluble oxide samples and a sealed, teacher-demonstrated mercury sample (never pupil-handled) for ages 11–13.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The recommended medium was a 2d interactive (simulated bench); if delivered physically, combustion and reactive/hot materials and the mercury counterexample are hazardous and need teacher supervision, safe setup, soluble/pre-prepared oxide samples and a sealed demonstrated mercury sample. The source did not specify safety handling; flagged for review.

The oxide-acidity test is a KS3 simplification: many metal oxides are insoluble and will not register on aqueous universal indicator, so the step is reliable only for oxides that dissolve; retained as a tendency, not a universal demonstration.
Two of three cited sources (NGSS, RSC) were marked verified:false in the source row; comparative efficacy or necessity of any one format is not established by the sources and is not asserted here.

The legacy entry rated 3D and conversation formats 'poor' and asserted a dialogue 'cannot supply the test results'; this has been softened to a narrowly scoped affordance note (reference/recognition tools don't generate the learner's own evidence) rather than a universal claim about medium superiority.

The original separated two element sets (a magnet poeTask with copper/aluminium/iron/plastic and a diagnostic prompt that showed mercury); these are merged into one coherent PoE in which mercury is a teacher demonstration, so the mercury feedback has a referent without requiring pupil handling.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: lay out copper, aluminium, iron and a shiny plastic strip. Ask the child to predict which a magnet will pick up and WHY. A 'metal = magnetic' model predicts all the metals stick. Only the iron does. The pre-observation prediction and reasoning expose whether magnetism is being used as the definition of metal.
probeDeeper: Copper isn't magnetic — give me two other tests that show it IS a metal.
Where on the periodic table would you look to predict whether an element is a metal?
Why are metals chosen for saucepan bases and electrical wires — which property is doing the work each time?
A shiny sweet wrapper: how would you decide if it's really metal or just shiny plastic?
assess.correctAnswer: The rule is wrong. Most magnets only stick to iron, nickel and cobalt — most metals (copper, gold, aluminium) aren't magnetic — and shininess alone isn't enough (shiny plastic isn't a metal; mercury is a liquid metal). Metals are better identified by a CLUSTER of properties: good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable/ductile, lustrous, mostly high melting points, and their position on the left/centre of the periodic table. Full marks reject 'magnetic = metal' and give conduction/malleability.

errorPatterns.pattern: all metals are magnetic ('if a magnet sticks, it's metal; if not, it isn't')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test copper, aluminium, gold with a magnet — none stick, all are metals. Only iron/nickel/cobalt are magnetic. Magnetism is a property of a few metals, not the definition.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — if a magnet sticks it's a metal, and metals are always magnetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: classifies copper/aluminium as non-metal because a magnet won't stick, or expects every metal to be magnetic

errorPatterns.pattern: all metals are hard solids ('metals are always solid and strong')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mercury is a liquid metal; sodium is soft enough to cut. State (and hardness) vary; conduction and metallic bonding are what unite them.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — mercury can't be a metal because metals are always hard and solid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: refuses to call mercury a metal because it's liquid, or equates 'metal' with 'hard'

errorPatterns.pattern: shiny = metal ('anything shiny is a metal')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lustre is one clue but not sufficient — test conduction: the plastic won't conduct, the metals will. Use the property cluster, not one cue.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes for shine — the shiny bag would count as metal too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls the shiny plastic bag a metal, or treats lustre as sufficient on its own

responseLevels.gap: Relies on a single cue (magnetism or shine); misclassifies copper, mercury or shiny plastic accordingly.
responseLevels.full: Identifies metals by a coherent cluster (conductivity, malleability, lustre, periodic-table position), correctly handles non-magnetic metals, liquid mercury and shiny non-metals, and matches each real-world use to the property doing the work.
responseLevels.partial: Rejects the magnet rule and lists metallic properties, but treats them as a memorised list — can't say WHICH property to use for a given object or link uses to properties.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A friend says 'you can always tell a metal because it's shiny and a magnet sticks to it.' I show you mercury (a shiny liquid metal), copper (a metal a magnet does NOT stick to), and a shiny plastic gift bag. Is your friend's rule right? Then the important part: explain what really makes something a metal.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The counterexamples (non-magnetic copper, liquid mercury, shiny plastic) split a child who identifies metals by a defining cluster (especially conductivity and malleability) from one leaning on a single misleading cue (magnetism or shine). Only the former handles all three objects correctly.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9; ice in different forms and states of matter — sea ice forms when salty ocean water freezes (salty, relatively thin); glacial ice forms from snow compacted over centuries (fresh, very thick); icebergs break off glaciers and float in the sea. Water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (vapour), and salt lowers water's freezing point.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 Y4 'States of matter' (solid/liquid/gas; freezing and melting at specific temperatures; the water cycle).
• Standards—US: NGSS 2-PS1-4 earlier; 5-PS1-1/-3 (matter and its properties); links to MS-PS1 particle model.
• Operational details: two threads — (1) states of matter and the freezing/melting change, and (2) telling apart three polar ice types by ORIGIN (frozen seawater vs compacted snow vs calved glacier). The surprising, testable fact is that salt LOWERS the freezing point, so seawater freezes below 0°C — investigate by freezing salty vs fresh water and comparing. Distinguish sea ice (from the ocean) from glacial ice/icebergs (from land snow) because it matters for fresh vs salt water and for sea level later.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (7) name the three states of water; Tier B (8) explain that salty water freezes at a lower temperature than fresh water; Tier C (9) classify sea ice, glacial ice and an iceberg by where each came from (frozen sea vs compacted snow).
bestPractices: Run a fair test: freeze salty vs fresh water and observe the salty sample needs to be colder to freeze, evidencing salt lowers the freezing point
Separate ice by ORIGIN not just appearance — sea ice (frozen ocean, salty, thin) vs glacial ice/iceberg (compacted snow, fresh, thick)
Use the particle-ish idea lightly: freezing/melting is the same water changing state, not a new substance
Connect to the water cycle so the three states link to evaporation, precipitation and meltwater
Foreshadow the sea-level idea: melting SEA ice barely changes sea level, but melting LAND ice (glaciers) adds water — a hook for later years
keyRepresentations: State-change strip: ice → (melt) → water → (evaporate) → vapour, and reverse
Salty-vs-fresh freezing comparison with a thermometer showing the lower freezing point
Three-ice classification chart by origin (sea / glacier / iceberg), salt, and thickness
Sea-ice-on-ocean vs glacier-on-land cross-section
commonMisconceptions: All ice is the same — sea ice, glacial ice and icebergs differ in origin, saltiness and thickness
Seawater freezes at 0°C like fresh water — salt lowers the freezing point, so it freezes colder
Icebergs are frozen seawater — they calve from glaciers, so they are compacted snow and fresh, not salty
Ice and water are different substances — they are the same water in different states
Melting sea ice raises sea level a lot — floating sea ice barely changes it; land ice melting is what adds water

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: ice comes in different forms and water exists in three states. Learners investigate that dissolved salt lowers water's freezing point (seawater freezes below 0°C, near about -1.8°C) and classify polar ice by ORIGIN: sea ice (frozen ocean, salty, relatively thin) vs glacial ice (snow compacted over centuries on land, fresh, very thick) vs icebergs (chunks calved from glaciers, so fresh land-born ice). Water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (vapour), and ice/water are the same substance changing state. A hands-on fair test and sorting-by-origin tasks anchor these ideas, with a later qualitative hook to how melting floating sea ice vs land ice affects sea level differently.

activities.title: Fair test: does salt change the temperature at which water freezes?
feedback: If a learner predicts both freeze at the same temperature, point to their recorded observations, for example if the salty sample was still liquid when the fresh one had frozen, or its thermometer reading was lower when ice first formed.
If a learner thinks salt warms the water, note that the salty sample actually has to reach a colder temperature before it freezes — salt is lowering the freezing point, not heating anything.
Reinforce the fair-test logic: because only the salt changed, the difference in freezing must be caused by the salt.
activities.rationale: A controlled comparison makes an invisible property (freezing-point depression) observable and lets learners reason from their own evidence rather than being told. KS2 Y4 expects observing changes of state at specific temperatures.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils compare and group materials by state (solid/liquid/gas), observe changes of state at specific temperatures, and study the water cycle
Dissolved salt depresses the freezing point of water, so seawater freezes near -1.8°C; sea ice is frozen ocean water while glacial ice and icebergs derive from compacted snow on land
learnerActions: Set up two samples: one fresh water, one salty water (e.g. with a measured spoon of salt stirred in).
Use the same amount of water, the same type of container and the same starting temperature, and place both in the same freezer/cold spot so the test is fair — only the salt differs.
Observe which freezes first, and if a thermometer is available, record the temperature at which each turns to ice.

Record what you actually observe. Fresh water normally freezes at about 0°C; salty water usually stays liquid longer and must get colder before it starts to freeze (with a lot of salt it may not freeze at all in a home freezer).
State the conclusion in your own words: salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes.
activities.intendedInsight: Dissolved salt lowers water's freezing point, so seawater must get colder than 0°C before it freezes — the two samples differ only because of the salt.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain with salt on ice
feedback: If the prediction is 'salt just warms/melts ice, so it gets warmer', contrast it with the observation that the mixture actually became colder.

If the prediction is 'nothing happens', point to the comparison: if the salted cube melted faster than the unsalted one, or its thermometer reading dropped below 0°C while plain melting ice stayed near 0°C, the salt changed something.
Praise reasoning stated before observing, since naming the expectation first makes the surprise meaningful.
activities.rationale: Eliciting a prior reason surfaces the common 'salt just melts/warms ice' intuition so the contrary observation can confront it; the road-salting link transfers the concept to a familiar context.
sourceClaims: Dissolved salt depresses the freezing point of water, so seawater freezes near -1.8°C; sea ice is frozen ocean water while glacial ice and icebergs derive from compacted snow on land
learnerActions: Before touching anything, PREDICT and give a reason: will sprinkling salt on an ice cube make it warmer, colder, or do nothing?

Sprinkle salt on one ice cube and leave a second, unsalted cube beside it for comparison, then OBSERVE: compare how quickly each melts and, if possible, read a thermometer in each (the salted mixture can drop below 0°C while plain melting ice stays near 0°C), watch for frost on the outside of a metal cup, or touch the cup only briefly to feel it getting colder.
EXPLAIN what happened: salt lowers water's freezing point, which is why the salted ice-and-water mixture can sit below 0°C and why the sea must get colder than 0°C before it freezes.
Connect to everyday life: explain why people scatter salt on icy roads and paths in winter.
activities.intendedInsight: Salt lowers the freezing point; this is the same idea behind seawater freezing below 0°C and behind salting icy roads.

activities.title: Sort the three ices by where they came from
feedback: If a learner says 'icebergs are frozen seawater', remind them icebergs calve from glaciers, so they are compacted snow and fresh.
If a learner treats all ice as identical, ask them to trace each piece back to the sea or to land snow.
Confirm correct sorting by having the learner justify each placement with its origin, not its look.
activities.rationale: Classifying by origin targets the 'all ice is the same' misconception and prepares the fresh-vs-salt distinction that matters for later sea-level reasoning.
sourceClaims: Dissolved salt depresses the freezing point of water, so seawater freezes near -1.8°C; sea ice is frozen ocean water while glacial ice and icebergs derive from compacted snow on land
learnerActions: Examine three ice examples (or labelled cards/cross-sections): frozen ocean water, compacted mountain-glacier snow, and an iceberg that snapped off a glacier.
For each, decide its ORIGIN (ocean vs land snow), whether it is salty or fresh, and whether it is thin or very thick.
Place the iceberg with the glacial/land-born group and explain why: it calved from a glacier, so it is compacted snow — fresh, not salty.
Build a short classification chart: sea ice = frozen ocean, salty, relatively thin; glacial ice = compacted snow on land, fresh, very thick; iceberg = broken-off glacier, fresh and usually thick.
State the key idea aloud: not all white ice is the same — it can come from the salty sea or from freshwater land snow.
activities.intendedInsight: Polar ice is distinguished by origin, not just appearance; this determines whether it is salty or fresh.

activities.title: The same water in three states
feedback: If a learner says ice and water are different substances, point to melting and refreezing the same sample to show it returns.
Link each state change to a familiar water-cycle event to reinforce it is one water moving between states.
activities.rationale: Addresses the 'ice and water are different substances' misconception and meets the states-of-matter and water-cycle standards.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils compare and group materials by state (solid/liquid/gas), observe changes of state at specific temperatures, and study the water cycle
Students investigate properties of matter and changes of state
learnerActions: Trace the state-change sequence: ice melts to water, water evaporates to vapour, and the reverse (vapour condenses, water freezes).
Explain that ice and liquid water are the same substance in different states, not different materials.
Connect the three states to the water cycle (evaporation, precipitation, meltwater).
Give one example of each state of water from everyday life.
activities.intendedInsight: Freezing and melting change water's state, not its identity; the same water can be solid, liquid or gas.

activities.title: Which melting ice changes the sea level? (foreshadowing)
feedback: If a learner says melting the floating sea ice will raise the sea like a glacier would, remind them the floating ice is already sitting in (displacing) the water.

Encourage connecting this back to the sorting task: ice still sitting on land (glaciers) adds water to the sea when it melts or slides into the sea; once an iceberg is already floating, its melting barely changes the level, just like sea ice.
activities.rationale: Introduces the land-ice vs sea-ice sea-level distinction at an age-appropriate, qualitative level as a hook for later climate topics, targeting the conflation misconception. No source claim directly establishes the displacement/sea-level principle, so none is cited.
learnerActions: Compare two cases: a chunk of ice already floating in the sea, and ice sitting on land (a glacier).
Predict what happens to the water level when each melts.
Reason it through: floating sea ice already displaces its own water, so melting it barely changes the level; land ice adds new water to the sea when it melts.
State why this distinction matters when thinking about how melting ice affects the ocean.
activities.intendedInsight: Melting floating sea ice barely changes sea level, whereas melting land ice adds water and raises it.

constraints: The salt-and-water freezing investigation needs an actual comparison (salty vs fresh) under fair-test conditions; a thermometer makes the freezing-point effect measurable but is ideally-available, not strictly required. Without one, learners can still observe which sample freezes first and whether the salty sample is still liquid when the fresh one has frozen. This is only an indirect sign, so keep amount, container and starting temperature the same.

Labelled cross-sections and tap-to-reveal state-change strips clearly present the categories but do not let a learner experience salty water staying liquid at 0°C; use them alongside, not instead of, the investigation.

Sorting cards and matching tasks can teach and check whether a learner classifies ice by origin, but do not by themselves build or elicit the freezing-point intuition or a spoken explanation; reserve them as a companion to the hands-on work.
The sea-level comparison is a qualitative age-appropriate hook, not a quantitative treatment; keep it to 'barely changes' vs 'adds water'.
Keep the particle idea light at this age: freezing/melting is the same water changing state.
Icebergs float because ice is less dense than liquid water — note this if the floating/density point arises, so 'floats' is not confused with 'made of frozen seawater'.
Observing the salt-on-ice mixture: for ages 7–9 the salt-ice mixture can get very cold, so keep contact brief and prefer reading a thermometer or watching frost form on a metal cup.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all source claims are marked verified:false in the original and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original listed seawater's freezing point near -1.8°C but the recommendation said 'well below zero'; -1.8°C is only slightly below 0°C. For ages 7–9 the robust takeaway is 'colder than 0°C', so activities avoid asserting a large depression and treat a home-freezer comparison as qualitative.

A simulated 'drag a temperature dial until it freezes' interaction was described in the original; it is retained as an optional way to present the fair test, not a required mechanism, and real freezing of two samples is preferred where feasible.
The claim that 3D 'adds no explanatory power' was a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; omitted rather than propagated.

Density as the reason icebergs float appears in the stated learning evidence but was underdeveloped in the recommendation; added to constraints for accuracy, not made a central activity since the focus is origin and freezing point.

The sea-level foreshadowing activity relies on a displacement principle not covered by any of the three source claims (which address states of matter, changes of state, and ice origin/freezing only); it is offered as a qualitative hook with no source cited and should be treated as unverified.

assess.poeTask: Give the child an ice cube, some salt and (ideally) a thermometer. Ask them to PREDICT, reason first, what salt sprinkled on the ice will do — make it warmer, colder, or nothing — many say 'salt melts ice, so it warms it' or 'nothing'. They add salt and OBSERVE the ice melting AND the temperature dropping below 0°C (or the mixture feeling colder / frost forming outside a metal cup). Then EXPLAIN: salt lowers water's freezing point, which is also why the salty sea must get colder than 0°C before it freezes. The pre-observation reason exposes the 'salt just melts/warms ice' intuition.
probeDeeper: Where does glacial ice come from, and why does that make it fresh, not salty?
Why do people scatter salt on icy roads and paths in winter?
If you melted a floating chunk of sea ice in a glass of water, would the level rise a lot? What about ice sitting on land?
How can the very same water be a solid, a liquid and a gas?
assess.correctAnswer: No. Sea ice forms when the ocean freezes — it's relatively thin and comes from salty water; glacial ice forms from snow compressed over centuries on land — it's fresh water and very thick, and icebergs are chunks that break off glaciers and float out to sea. And salt water does NOT freeze at the same temperature as fresh: salt LOWERS the freezing point, so seawater must get colder than 0°C before it freezes. Water can also be solid (ice), liquid (water) or gas (water vapour).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All ice is the same' — no distinction between sea ice and glacial ice.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort by origin: sea ice = frozen ocean (salty, thin); glacial ice = compressed snow on land (fresh, thick); icebergs = broken-off glacier.
errorPatterns.distractor: Ice is just ice — sea ice and glacier ice are exactly the same thing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats sea ice and glacier ice as identical; can't say where each comes from.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Salt water freezes at the same temperature as fresh (0°C)' — unaware salt lowers the freezing point.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate/explain: salt lowers the freezing point, so the sea must get colder than 0°C to freeze (why we salt icy roads).
errorPatterns.distractor: Salty seawater freezes at exactly the same temperature as fresh water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts seawater freezes at 0°C like fresh water.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Melting sea ice raises sea level the same as melting glaciers' — conflates floating sea ice with land ice.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Floating sea ice already displaces its water (level barely changes); LAND ice (glaciers) adds new water and raises the sea. This distinction returns in climate topics.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says melting the floating sea ice will raise the sea like melting a glacier would.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks all ice is the same and salt water freezes at 0°C like fresh.
responseLevels.full: Separates sea ice (salty, thin, frozen ocean) from glacial ice (fresh, thick, compressed snow) and icebergs (calved glacier), knows salt lowers the freezing point, and can reason about states of matter and the land-vs-sea-ice sea-level difference.
responseLevels.partial: Distinguishes sea from glacial ice OR knows salt lowers the freezing point, but not both, or muddles the sea-ice/land-ice sea-level effect.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: There are two kinds of ice near the poles: sea ice (frozen seawater) and glacial ice (from snow squashed down over centuries), and icebergs break off glaciers. A student says 'ice is just ice — it's all the same frozen water, and salty seawater freezes at the same temperature as fresh water.' Is all polar ice the same, and does salt water freeze at the same temperature as fresh? Explain the differences.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student with the 'ice is ice' idea can't distinguish sea from glacial ice or predict the salt effect; a student with the concept separates them by ORIGIN (sea vs compressed snow) and knows salt lowers the freezing point. Two documented misconceptions are targeted at once, so guessing right is hard.

pedagogy.summary: For 5–7s this introduces the skeleton as the hard framework INSIDE the body doing three jobs: giving the body its shape and holding it up (support), protecting soft important organs (the skull is a helmet for the brain, the ribcage a cage for the heart and lungs), and — with muscles — letting the body move. The key, often-missed idea for this age is that MUSCLES PULL on bones to move them; muscles don't push. Teach it on the child's own body: feel the hard skull, the ribs, the spine down the back; feel a muscle (the upper arm) bunch up when it works. Name just a few bones/groups (skull, ribcage, spine, leg bones) and keep muscle action to 'muscles pull bones' — the paired push/pull detail comes later. Correct the common ideas that bones are dead sticks or that we're 'like jelly' inside; the skeleton is a living, supportive, protective frame.
bestPractices: Use the child's own body as the manipulative: feel the hard skull, ribs and spine, and feel an arm muscle bunch when it lifts — so structure and function are felt, not just seen.
Teach the three jobs with vivid protection images (skull = helmet for the brain, ribcage = cage around the heart and lungs) — the most memorable hook at this age.
Establish early that MUSCLES PULL bones to move them (they can't push), setting up the antagonistic-pair idea later without over-complicating now.
Name only a few bones/groups (skull, ribcage, spine, leg bones) and locate them on the body, keeping the load age-appropriate.
Confront 'bones are dead/just sticks' and 'we're squishy with no frame' — the skeleton is a living frame that supports and shapes us.
keyRepresentations: A simple labelled skeleton showing shape/support (the frame that holds us up)
Protection images: skull-as-helmet over the brain, ribcage-as-cage around heart/lungs
The child's own body — feeling hard bones (skull, ribs, spine) and a working muscle
Muscle-pulls-bone shown as a muscle shortening to move a limb
A 'no skeleton' contrast (a floppy body) to show why we need a frame
commonMisconceptions: 'Bones are dead / just hard sticks' — they are living parts that grow and even make blood.
'Muscles push bones to move them' — muscles PULL (shorten) to move bones; they can't push.
'The skeleton is only in the arms and legs' — missing the skull, spine and ribcage.
'Without a skeleton we'd still stand up' — missing that the frame gives shape and support (we'd be floppy).
'The skull is solid all the way through' — it's a protective case around the brain.
'Bones and muscles are the same thing' — bones are the hard frame; muscles are the soft parts that pull them.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, introduce the skeleton as the hard, living framework inside the body that does three jobs: giving the body shape and holding it up (support), protecting soft important organs (skull as a helmet for the brain, ribcage as a cage for the heart and lungs), and — working with muscles — letting the body move. The often-missed key idea for this age is that muscles PULL on bones to move them; they do not push. Teach it on the child's own body: feel the hard skull, ribs and spine, and feel an upper-arm muscle bunch up when it lifts. Name only a few bones/groups (skull, ribcage, spine, leg bones). Confront the common ideas that bones are dead sticks or that we are squishy with no frame.

activities.title: Tap-to-explore skeleton: name the bones and reveal their jobs
feedback: If the child names only arm/leg bones, point them to tap the skull, spine and ribcage too so the whole frame is covered.
When a flap is opened, confirm the pairing: skull→brain, ribcage→heart and lungs.
If the child says bones are dead, reveal the living-bone flap and note that bones grow and make new blood cells inside them.
activities.rationale: Naming a few bones and the protection idea is the age-appropriate core; tap-to-reveal with protection flaps mirrors a child exploring their own body and makes structure–function concrete. Optional flaps and highlights are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Pupils should identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement (statutory at Year 3; this KS1 version is a foundational precursor).
The skeleton provides support and shape, protects internal organs (skull–brain, ribcage–heart/lungs), and works with muscles for movement; muscles produce movement by contracting (pulling) on bones.
learnerActions: Look at a simple labelled child-figure skeleton and tap the skull, ribcage, spine and leg bones one at a time; each part highlights and names itself.
Open a 'what does this protect?' flap on the skull to find it is a helmet around the brain, and on the ribcage to see it caging the heart and lungs.
Open a lift-the-flap on a bone to discover bones are alive, grow, and even make new blood cells inside them, busting 'bones are dead sticks'.
For each part, say out loud its job: 'the skull protects my brain', 'the leg bones hold me up'.
activities.intendedInsight: The hard frame inside you gives your body shape and guards the soft, important parts inside; bones are living, not dead sticks.

activities.title: Feel your own frame
feedback: If the child can't locate the spine, guide their hand down the centre of the back to feel the bumpy line.
Confirm each match: 'Yes — that hard part is your ribcage, caging your heart and lungs.'
activities.rationale: Using the child's own body as the manipulative lets structure and function be felt, not just seen, which is a strong, memorable hook at this age; pictures and flaps show structure–function but do not by themselves elicit this physical sensation.
learnerActions: Press the top and back of your head to feel the hard skull; run your fingers down the middle of your back to feel the spine; press the front of your chest to feel the ribs.
Match each hard part you feel to the same part on the picture.
Say which soft organ each hard part is guarding (skull→brain, ribs→heart and lungs).
activities.intendedInsight: The bones you can feel on your own body are the same frame shown in the picture, and they shield the soft parts inside.

activities.title: Make it move / take the skeleton away
feedback: If the child says the muscle pushes, replay the shortening and have them feel the pull in their own arm: muscles only pull.
If the child says the arm bends by itself, point out that to bend your arm yourself, a muscle must pull the bone.
When the figure flops after removing the skeleton, link it back: the frame gives shape and holds us up.
activities.rationale: A live 'make it move / take away the skeleton' interaction can show the muscle-pulls-bone and support ideas vividly; keep the detail of paired muscles pulling in opposite directions (antagonistic pairs) for later and keep the rig toy-simple for this age. The toggle and live muscle-shortening are illustrative examples of the mechanism, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: The skeleton provides support and shape, protects internal organs (skull–brain, ribcage–heart/lungs), and works with muscles for movement; muscles produce movement by contracting (pulling) on bones.
Pupils should identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement (statutory at Year 3; this KS1 version is a foundational precursor).
learnerActions: On a simple toy-like rig, tap a muscle on the figure's arm and watch it shorten and pull the limb so the arm bends.
Squeeze your own upper arm while you bend your elbow and feel the muscle get hard and pull.
Flip a 'remove skeleton' toggle and watch the figure flop, then say why a frame is needed to stand up.
Say in your own words: 'muscles pull on bones to move them.'
activities.intendedInsight: Muscles pull (shorten) on bones to move them — they don't push — and without the skeleton the body would flop with no shape or support.

activities.title: Boneless-animal reasoning check
feedback: A full answer explains support/protection (naming an organ shielded) AND that muscles pull on bones to move them, using the boneless animal to justify why we need a frame.
If the child gives only one half (shape/protection OR movement), ask the missing part directly.
If the child says muscles push, re-establish that muscles only pull (tighten and shorten).
activities.rationale: Asking a child to reason about a boneless animal and to explain what moves the arm surfaces both the support/protection role and the muscle-pulls-bone idea. This can be used during teaching as well as for checking; recognition-only matching does not itself elicit the child's own spoken explanation.
sourceClaims: Pupils should identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement (statutory at Year 3; this KS1 version is a foundational precursor).
learnerActions: Think about a jellyfish, which has no bones at all.

Say what a jellyfish can't do that you can because you have a skeleton (for example, stand up tall on land or keep its shape out of water) — remembering that a jellyfish can still swim using its muscles.
Answer the two-part question: why do you have a hard skeleton inside you, and when you bend your arm to lift a cup, what makes the arm actually move?
activities.intendedInsight: The skeleton is needed for firm shape, support and protection of soft organs, and movement comes from muscles pulling on bones.

activities.title: Optional: match and quick-check
feedback: If the match is wrong, return to the labelled figure or the child's own body to re-feel and re-name the part.
If 'push' is chosen, re-establish that muscles only pull.
activities.rationale: A short matching/labelling activity checks recall of bone names and protection pairings. Recognition-only tasks confirm recall but do not by themselves elicit the child's own explanation, so use them after the exploratory work.
learnerActions: Match each bone to the organ it protects (skull→brain, ribcage→heart and lungs).
Answer the quick question: do muscles push or pull to move bones?
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate bone names, what each protects, and that muscles pull.

constraints: Keep muscle action to 'muscles pull bones'; the detail that muscles work in pairs that pull in opposite directions (antagonistic pairs) comes later and should not be introduced now.
Name only a few bones/groups (skull, ribcage, spine, leg bones) to keep the cognitive load age-appropriate for 5–7.

A labelled picture, flaps and toggles are scaffolds and illustrative interactions that show structure–function; they do not by themselves elicit the physical sensation of feeling one's own hard bones and working muscle. Feeling one's own body is a recommended hook at this age, not a universal requirement for learning.
A matching/labelling quiz confirms recall of names and pairings but does not on its own elicit the child's own explanation; use alongside, not instead of, exploratory and explanatory tasks.
An optional 3D spin can aid orientation but is not required for naming and protection at this age; naming and protection can also be conveyed in 2D.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted that 3D 'adds nothing' and that a quiz 'assesses rather than builds understanding' as near-absolutes; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, since catalog fit ratings do not establish universal pedagogical necessity.
One listed source (Encyclopaedia Britannica) is marked verified:false in the row; its claim is retained but should be independently confirmed before relying on it as evidence.

The push-vs-pull correction is biologically sound for this age: muscles generate force by contracting (pulling); movement in the opposite direction is produced by a different muscle, which is deliberately deferred here.

activities[1] ('Feel your own frame') has sourceClaims set to [] because its rationale concerns the manipulative method's memorability, which no cited claim supports; the protection facts it practises are source-cited in activities 0 and 2.

Two original misconceptions — 'the skull is solid all the way through' and 'bones and muscles are the same thing' — are addressed only implicitly (skull as a case around the brain; distinguishing the hard frame from soft pulling muscle). Add a dedicated prompt if explicit coverage is wanted.

probeDeeper: Squeeze your upper arm while you bend your elbow — can you feel a muscle getting hard and pulling? What is it pulling on?
Which bone protects your brain, and which bones protect your heart and lungs?
A jellyfish has no bones at all. What can't a jellyfish do that you can, because you have a skeleton?
assess.correctAnswer: Without a skeleton the body would have no firm shape or support — it would flop and couldn't stand up, and the soft organs inside (like the brain and heart) would have no hard casing to protect them. The arm moves because muscles attached to the bones pull on them: when a muscle tightens it pulls the bone and bends the arm. Bones can't move themselves — muscles move them.

errorPatterns.pattern: The skeleton isn't important — bones don't do much and the body would be fine without them.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the jobs concrete: bones give shape and hold you upright, and hard bones shield soft organs; picture a body with no frame.
errorPatterns.distractor: Nothing much — you'd still stand and move the same without bones.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't state a job for the skeleton; thinks the body would work the same without it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Muscles make bones move by pushing them.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that muscles can only PULL (they tighten and shorten); feel the arm muscle pull the bone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the muscle pushes the bone to move it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bones move on their own — the arm just bends by itself with no muscle.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect movement to muscles pulling bones; nothing moves without a muscle acting on it.
errorPatterns.distractor: The arm bends by itself — nothing has to pull it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the arm bending with no mention of muscles.

responseLevels.gap: Can't say what the skeleton is for, or thinks the body would move the same without it; no muscle-pulls-bone idea.
responseLevels.full: Explains the skeleton supports and protects (naming an organ it shields) AND that muscles pull on bones to move them — reasoning about a boneless animal to justify support.
responseLevels.partial: Knows bones give shape/protection OR that muscles move the body, but not both, or thinks muscles push rather than pull.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Why do you have a hard skeleton inside you — what would happen to your body without it? And when you bend your arm to lift a cup, what makes the arm actually move?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who can't say what bones are for, or who thinks the arm bends by itself or that muscles push, reveals the gap. Only a child linking skeleton to support/protection AND muscle-pulls-bone answers both. The tier-two 'what makes the arm move' forces the muscle role to surface.
