pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Nutrients in a Healthy Diet

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Nutrition & digestion):** "the content of a healthy human diet: carbohydrates, lipids (fats and oils), proteins, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water, and why each is needed."

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No direct MS performance expectation on human dietary components; the nearest US content is 5-PS3-1 (energy in food came from the sun) and MS-LS1-7 (food rearranged to release energy / support growth). Diet composition is UK-led. (US/UK divergence.)

- **Operational details:** Children name all seven components of a healthy diet — carbohydrates, lipids (fats and oils), proteins, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water — give a food source for each, and explain its role (carbohydrates and lipids for energy; protein for growth and repair; vitamins and minerals in small amounts for specific functions; fibre for gut movement; water as the medium for reactions and transport). A key discrimination is which components provide energy (carbohydrates, lipids, and protein in emergencies) and which do not (vitamins, minerals, fibre, water). The move that matters is from 'healthy vs junk food' folk categories to a functional account: each nutrient does a specific JOB, and 'balance' means eating a variety of foods from each food group of a local healthy-eating guide (in the UK, the Eatwell Guide's five food groups) in the right proportions, not eliminating any. Keep the seven nutrients distinct from food groups: an Eatwell-style plate shows food groups, not nutrients, and each food supplies several nutrients.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B. Extends KS2 'animals need the right nutrition and cannot make their own food'; feeds energy calculations, diet-imbalance/deficiency, and digestion. A child is secure when, given a nutrient, they can state a source, its body role, and whether it supplies energy.
bestPractices: Teach each nutrient as a JOB with a food source rather than as a word, and immediately separate energy-providers from non-energy nutrients — the discrimination children most often miss.
Confront folk 'good food/bad food' categories directly: balance means the right proportions of the food groups, and no food group or nutrient is simply 'bad'.

Use the Eatwell Guide (or another local healthy-eating guide) to show that proportions apply to food groups; then trace which nutrients each food group mainly supplies, noting that most foods supply several.
Address the vitamin/mineral misconception explicitly — needed in small amounts, do specific jobs, carry no energy.
Bridge to the next topics by framing diet quantitatively (energy budget) and diagnostically (what happens if a nutrient is missing).
keyRepresentations: Eatwell Guide illustration of the five food groups and their proportions, annotated with the main nutrients each group supplies
Nutrient → source → role table, colour-coded for energy vs non-energy
Icon key distinguishing energy-providing from non-energy nutrients
Example meals annotated with which nutrients they supply
commonMisconceptions: Believing vitamins and minerals provide energy (they do not).
Thinking all fat is unhealthy and should be eliminated, rather than being a needed energy store.
Assuming protein is only for athletes/muscle-building rather than for all growth and repair.
Treating fibre and water as unimportant because they carry no energy.
Equating 'healthy diet' with eating less, rather than eating the right balance.
Treating the seven nutrients as 'food groups', or expecting a balanced plate to give each nutrient an equal share.

learn.summary: Learners (ages 11–13) name the seven components of a healthy diet — carbohydrates, lipids (fats and oils), proteins, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water — give a food source for each, and state its body role. The central discrimination is which components are the main energy providers (carbohydrates and lipids, with protein a secondary or backup energy source whose main job is growth and repair) versus which provide no or very little energy (vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre, which our own enzymes cannot digest). Activities move learners from 'healthy vs junk food' folk categories to a functional account where each nutrient does a specific job and 'balance' means the right proportions of the food groups in a local healthy-eating guide such as the Eatwell Guide, with every nutrient job filled, not eliminating any. Nutrients are kept distinct from food groups, and learners recognise that each food supplies several nutrients.

activities.title: Nutrient job cards: source, role, and energy tag
feedback: If a learner tags vitamins or minerals as an energy source: vitamins and minerals are needed only in small amounts to enable specific body reactions (e.g. vitamin C for healthy tissue, vitamin D for bones) and carry no energy; energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and lipids.

If a learner calls protein the main energy nutrient: protein is chiefly for growth and repair; the body uses it for energy mainly when carbohydrates and fats run short or when more protein is eaten than is needed for growth and repair, so it is a backup rather than a main energy source (this misconception may come partly from sports and muscle-building marketing).

If a learner says fat should be cut out completely: lipids are a concentrated energy store, provide insulation and help build cell membranes; harm comes mainly from eating too much, and from some types such as trans fats, not from fat itself.

If a learner dismisses fibre and water: fibre keeps gut contents moving and water is the medium for reactions and transport — both are essential even though neither is a significant energy source for us (water gives none, and fibre cannot be digested by our own enzymes).
activities.rationale: The KS3 curriculum requires naming the seven dietary components and why each is needed, and carbohydrates and lipids are the main energy sources, while vitamins, minerals and water provide no energy and fibre provides little or none because our own enzymes cannot digest it. Attaching a source, a role and an energy tag to each nutrient directly targets the discrimination learners most often miss. Tap-to-reveal cards, the colour key and lift-the-flap are optional interaction examples that make the energy/non-energy split visible; a non-interactive table or sorting task teaches the same content.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Biology requires teaching 'the content of a healthy human diet: carbohydrates, lipids (fats and oils), proteins, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water, and why each is needed'.

A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, each with a distinct role; carbohydrates and lipids are the main energy sources while vitamins, minerals, fibre and water do not provide energy.
learnerActions: For each of the seven nutrients — carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water — write or state one food source, the job it does in the body, and whether it provides energy.

Sort the seven nutrients into two groups: 'main energy providers' (carbohydrates, lipids; protein as a secondary or backup source whose main job is growth and repair) and 'no or very little energy' (vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre, which our own enzymes cannot digest).
Answer two myth-busting prompts explicitly: 'Do vitamins give you energy?' and 'Is all fat bad?', explaining your reasoning in a sentence each.

Optionally use an Eatwell-style plate where tapping a food reveals the nutrients it supplies (e.g. tap chicken → 'protein — building blocks for growth and repair'; tap oil → 'lipid — concentrated energy store and insulation'), with a colour/icon key tagging energy vs non-energy nutrients and a lift-the-flap reveal for the two myth questions.
activities.intendedInsight: Each nutrient has a distinct job, and only some nutrients supply energy; a healthy diet fills all seven nutrient jobs by eating foods from each food group in the guide's proportions, rather than sorting foods into 'good' and 'bad'.

activities.title: Build a balanced plate
feedback: If one food group dominates the plate: flag the imbalance and prompt the learner to adjust towards the guide's food-group proportions.
If a food group is missing: ask which nutrients that group mainly supplies and which body roles may now go short, and what food could fill the gap.
If a learner tries to give each of the seven nutrients an equal share: explain that proportions apply to food groups, and that foods supply several nutrients at once.
Reinforce that a balanced diet means the right proportions of the food groups, so no whole food group is simply 'bad' to include.
activities.rationale: A constructive 'build a balanced plate' task makes food-group proportions concrete and active rather than stated, then links them to the nutrients each group supplies, bridging toward later quantitative energy-budget work. Live food-group and nutrient feedback is an optional example that makes the balance visible; the same task works with a paper Eatwell plate and a checklist. This goes slightly beyond the naming/role core into evaluation.
sourceClaims: The Eatwell Guide divides the foods and drinks we consume into five main food groups (fruit and vegetables; potatoes, bread, rice, pasta and other starchy carbohydrates; beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other proteins; dairy and alternatives; oils and spreads) and shows how much of what we eat overall should come from each; choosing a variety of foods from each group helps provide the wide range of nutrients the body needs, combination foods such as pizzas and sandwiches contain several food groups, and balance can be achieved over a day or a week.

A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, each with a distinct role; carbohydrates and lipids are the main energy sources while vitamins, minerals, fibre and water do not provide energy.
learnerActions: Assemble a day's meals using the Eatwell Guide (or another local healthy-eating guide), aiming for its food-group proportions — fruit and vegetables and starchy carbohydrates as the largest parts, smaller amounts of proteins and dairy and alternatives, and small amounts of oils and spreads.
Check the plate against the guide's food-group segments, then list which nutrients each food supplies and confirm that all seven nutrient jobs are covered (no equal shares of nutrients are expected).
Explain in one or two sentences why your finished plate counts as 'balanced' — which food groups are present, in roughly what proportion, and how they cover the seven nutrients.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Balance' means the right proportions of the food groups, which together cover all seven nutrient jobs — not equal shares of nutrients, eliminating a food group or eating less overall.

activities.title: Food-energy investigation (supervised)
feedback: If a learner predicts a watery food will heat the water most: compare the measured rises — in a fair test with equal masses, the fatty or starchy sample usually produces a much larger rise, showing where food energy is concentrated.
If a learner concludes watery/leafy foods are therefore worthless: point out they still supply vitamins, minerals, fibre and water for non-energy jobs; low energy is not the same as low value.

Emphasise adult supervision, fire-safety and allergy checks (especially nuts) throughout the burning step; results are a comparative demonstration, not a precise calorimetry measurement, because much heat is lost to the surroundings, so compare the two rises fairly using equal food masses, the same water volume and starting temperature, and the same distance.
activities.rationale: This predict–observe–explain investigation gives learners a measured contrast between energy-dense and watery foods, confronting the misconception that all healthy food supplies energy. The probing questions extend the energy/non-energy discrimination to deficiency and the essential role of water.
sourceClaims: A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, each with a distinct role; carbohydrates and lipids are the main energy sources while vitamins, minerals, fibre and water do not provide energy.
learnerActions: Before testing, PREDICT which of two equal-mass foods will heat water more and why — e.g. a crisp (or a peanut only if no one present has a nut allergy), which is fatty/starchy, versus a grape or lettuce leaf.

Under adult supervision, burn an equal mass of each food at the same distance beneath a boiling tube holding the same volume of water at the same starting temperature, and measure the temperature rise; then repeat with the second food. Very watery foods such as grape or lettuce may barely burn, and that result itself reflects their high water content and low energy per gram.
Compare the measured temperature rises to your predictions and explain what the result shows about where dietary energy sits.

Answer the probing questions: which two of the seven components give most of your energy and which give little or none; if vitamins don't fuel you, why does eating no fruit or veg make a person ill (e.g. scurvy); is any food 'all bad' or does it depend on how much; and why can't you live without water even though it gives zero energy.
activities.intendedInsight: In a fair comparison of equal masses, energy-dense foods (fatty/starchy and low in water) usually release far more measurable heat than watery foods. This challenges the idea that all healthy foods supply lots of energy and locates most dietary energy in carbohydrates and lipids.

activities.title: Check and apply: nutrient roles and energy
feedback: If a learner accepts the 'vitamins for energy' claim: vitamins enable body processes but are not fuel; energy comes from carbohydrates and lipids — sort the foods into 'energy' vs 'other role' to see it.

If a learner is unsure where protein belongs: protein's main job is growth and repair, and it is used for energy mainly when carbohydrates and fats run short or when more is eaten than the body needs for growth and repair, so count it as a backup energy source rather than a main one.
If a learner names the seven components but still mislabels protein or vitamins as the main energy source, or dismisses fibre/water: revisit the specific role of that nutrient before moving on.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorising and responding to a realistic claim are checks that reveal whether a learner can make the energy/non-energy discrimination rather than reciting 'healthy food = energy'. The diagnostic claim mirrors common marketing messages that drive the misconception. Recognition and matching alone do not show the learner can construct the account independently.
sourceClaims: A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, each with a distinct role; carbohydrates and lipids are the main energy sources while vitamins, minerals, fibre and water do not provide energy.
learnerActions: Match each nutrient to its main job (e.g. 'which nutrient is mainly for growth and repair?' → protein).
Categorise each of the seven nutrients as 'provides energy' or 'no energy', treating protein as an energy source only in its backup role.

Respond to a real-world claim, e.g. a cereal box stating flakes are 'packed with vitamins for energy' and a friend saying vitamins give you energy to run around: explain which parts of the diet actually provide energy and what vitamins are really for.
activities.intendedInsight: A secure learner separates the main energy-providers (carbohydrates, fats) from nutrients with other jobs (vitamins, minerals, fibre, water), understands protein as a backup energy source whose main job is growth and repair, and can justify the split against a plausible everyday claim.

constraints: A learner is secure only when, given any nutrient, they can state a source, its body role, and whether it supplies energy — recognition/matching checks alone do not show they can construct this independently.

Treat the tap-to-reveal plate, colour/icon key, lift-the-flap, and live food-group and nutrient feedback as optional interaction examples, not required mechanisms; the same content can be taught with a table, a paper plate, and sorting cards.
The matching/categorise check assesses the discrimination but does not by itself build it; pair it with the job-card and plate-building tasks.
The food-burning investigation requires adult supervision and fire-safety precautions; measured temperature rises depend on setup and are a comparative demonstration, not a precise calorimetry value.

Address folk categories directly: 'balance' means the right proportions of the food groups in a local guide, protein is for all growth and repair (not only athletes), and no food is simply 'all bad' — it depends on how much.

Keep the seven nutrients distinct from food groups: classify foods with a local healthy-eating guide's food groups (e.g. the Eatwell Guide), teach nutrients and their functions separately, recognise that foods supply several nutrients, and never set plate proportions as equal shares of nutrients.
When categorising nutrients by energy, treat protein as a backup energy source (main job growth and repair) so this stays coherent with how it is framed elsewhere.

An optional 'ask-a-dietitian' conversation wrap may be offered for curiosity questions about specific foods; it is a supplement to the defined-content job-card and plate tasks, not a required or superior medium.
Diet composition here follows UK (DfE KS3) content; there is no direct US NGSS middle-school performance expectation on human dietary components, so framing may need adjustment for other curricula.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a 3D environment as adding 'nothing' and framed a static image as 'the most efficient, high-yield fit'; these categorical catalog-fit preferences have been removed. The neutral underlying observation is retained: nutrient roles are not inherently spatial, so a 3D/spatial environment offers little specific leverage here, though a fixed illustration, interactive, and physical formats each simply offer different experiences without one being universally necessary.

One source (BBC Bitesize) is marked verified:false in the row; the energy/non-energy grouping it supports is widely taught but should be confirmed against the primary curriculum source before relying on it as authoritative.

The claim that protein is used for energy 'only as a backup / in emergencies' is a standard simplification; it holds for typical diets but omits normal ongoing amino-acid turnover. Because the energy/non-energy categorisation is binary, protein is treated as a backup energy source there — flagged so the task does not appear to contradict protein's primary growth/repair role.
Food-burning temperature rises are setup-dependent and comparative only; absolute energy values are not established by this demonstration.

Nutrition review (October 2026): the plate representation and the build-a-balanced-plate activity previously showed 'seven nutrient groups' on an Eatwell-style plate and asked for proportions across nutrients. Corrected: the plate shows the Eatwell Guide's five food groups and their proportions, nutrients are traced from the foods (most foods supply several), and the activity now cites the NHS Eatwell Guide (fetched and checked). The seven-component learning aim, job cards, food-energy investigation and checks are unchanged.

assess.poeTask: Under adult supervision, burn a peanut (or a crisp) beneath a boiling tube of water and measure the temperature rise, then try the same with a grape or a lettuce leaf. Ask students to PREDICT which food heats the water most and why. The fatty/starchy food releasing far more heat challenges 'all healthy food gives energy' and shows where dietary energy really sits.
probeDeeper: Which two of the seven components give you most of your energy, and which give none at all?
If vitamins don't fuel you, why does a person who eats no fruit or veg get ill (e.g. scurvy)?
Is there any such thing as a food that's 'all bad' — or does it depend on how much you eat?
Water gives zero energy — so why can't you live without it?
assess.correctAnswer: Vitamins do not provide energy. Energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and lipids (fats), with protein used only as a backup. Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts for specific body processes (e.g. vitamin C for healthy tissue, vitamin D for bones), and fibre and water provide no energy either.

errorPatterns.pattern: Vitamins give you energy ('take your vitamins for energy')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Vitamins enable body processes but are not fuel; carbohydrates and lipids provide energy. Sort foods into 'energy' vs 'other role'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Vitamins are what give you the energy to run around.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names vitamins as an energy source rather than carbohydrates or fats

errorPatterns.pattern: Protein is the body's main energy food
errorPatterns.nextMove: Protein is chiefly for growth and repair; the body uses it for energy only when carbs and fats run short.
errorPatterns.distractor: Protein is the body's main source of energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls protein the chief energy nutrient (often from sports-drink/muscle marketing)

errorPatterns.pattern: Fat is always bad and has no useful role
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lipids are an energy store, provide insulation and build cell membranes; it is excess, not fat itself, that harms.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says fat should be cut out completely and does nothing good

errorPatterns.pattern: Fibre and water aren't really nutrients / do nothing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fibre keeps the gut contents moving; water is the medium for reactions and transport. Both are essential without providing energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Omits fibre and water, or says they are pointless because they give no energy

responseLevels.gap: Treats all food (or vitamins) as 'energy' and cannot say which nutrients fuel the body versus serve other roles.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes energy-providing nutrients (carbs, lipids) from those with specific non-energy roles (vitamins, minerals, fibre, water) and gives a food source and a function for each.
responseLevels.partial: Names the seven components and some roles but still calls vitamins or protein the main energy source, or dismisses fibre/water.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A cereal box says its flakes are 'packed with vitamins for energy', and a friend tells you vitamins are what give you the energy to run around. Is that right — which parts of your diet actually provide the energy, and if that's not what vitamins are for, what are they for?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands nutrient roles separates the energy-providers (carbs, fats) from nutrients with other jobs (vitamins, minerals, fibre, water). A child who thinks 'healthy food = energy' or that vitamins are fuel cannot make that split.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Wave Behaviour Vocabulary (refraction, absorption, reflection, scattering, amplitude, frequency, wavelength, echo, spectrum, angle of incidence, angle of reflection)

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Working Scientifically + KS2/KS3):** KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to 'read, spell and pronounce scientific vocabulary correctly.' The terms are drawn from KS2 Light (Y3/Y6: reflect) and Sound (Y4: vibration, volume, pitch) and, for the boundary/geometry terms (refraction, frequency, amplitude, wavelength, spectrum, angle of incidence, angle of reflection), from KS3 Physics 'Waves'. This record is the vocabulary spine that lets pupils APPLY those words when explaining how light and sound travel and interact with materials.

- **Standards — US (no NGSS vocabulary PE; CCSS-ELA anchor):** NGSS deliberately has no stand-alone vocabulary performance expectation — the Framework holds that terminology emerges from three-dimensional science practice, not isolated word-learning. The terms attach to the wave PEs 4-PS4-1/4-PS4-2 (elementary) and MS-PS4-2 (light/sound reflected, absorbed or transmitted through materials). The matching literacy standard is CCSS-ELA-LITERACY.L.5.6: 'acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.'

- **Operational details:** This is a LANGUAGE topic, so the goal is precise, APPLIED use of a highly confusable term set — not rote definition. Teach each word against its nearest confusable neighbour, anchored on a single discriminator: does the wave BOUNCE back into the first medium (reflection), PASS THROUGH and bend into a new medium (refraction), spray off a rough surface in many directions (scattering), or get SOAKED IN and not returned (absorption)? Pin the three wave-property words to distinct visual features of ONE wave — amplitude = height, wavelength = distance peak-to-peak, frequency = how many pass per second — varying one at a time so they don't blur. Head off the known language traps: 'bending' (refraction) means a change from one straight path to another, not a curve; reflection is NOT only mirrors and refraction is NOT only glass blocks; and angle of incidence/reflection are measured from the NORMAL (the perpendicular), never from the surface. Every term should be used immediately in an explanation (bent straw = refraction; canyon echo = reflected sound; blue sky = scattering; prism rainbow = spectrum) per the DfE read/spell/USE requirement.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal), bridging from Tier A. The concrete terms (reflection, echo, absorption) are Tier A; the boundary/geometry terms (refraction, angle of incidence/reflection, spectrum) reach into early-formal. Mastery = correctly distinguishing reflection from refraction with the right definitions, using 'refraction' to explain the bent straw, and explaining an echo as reflected sound — applied, not merely recited. The quantitative law of reflection and v = fλ are deferred (Tier C, KS3/KS4).
bestPractices: Teach each term against its nearest confusable neighbour on ONE discriminator — bounce back (reflection) vs pass-through-and-bend (refraction) vs spray off a rough surface (scattering) vs soak in (absorption); remember air is usually the first medium.

Pin the three wave-property words to distinct visual features of a single wave (amplitude = height, wavelength = peak-to-peak, frequency = number per second) and vary ONE at a time so the terms don't blur together.
Confront the language traps explicitly: 'bending' in refraction is a change from one straight path to another (not a curve); reflection is not only mirrors; refraction is not only glass blocks.
Define angle of incidence and angle of reflection from the NORMAL (the perpendicular to the surface), not from the surface itself — the classic measurement error.

Use every term immediately in an explanation of a real phenomenon (bent straw = refraction, echo = reflected sound, blue sky = scattering, prism = spectrum), matching the DfE 'read, spell and USE scientific vocabulary' requirement.
Support correct spelling with word-part cues (re-FLECT = turn/bounce back; re-FRACT = break/bend through; ab-SORB = soak in) to reduce reflection–refraction confusion.
keyRepresentations: One incoming ray meeting a boundary with branching outcomes — bounce back (reflection), pass through and bend (refraction), soak in (absorption) — plus a rough-surface many-ray version (scattering).
A single labelled wave with amplitude, wavelength and frequency each called out on its own distinct feature.
A protractor drawn on the NORMAL showing angle of incidence = angle of reflection measured from the perpendicular.
Everyday exemplar cards each pinned to one term: bent straw (refraction), canyon echo (reflection of sound), blue sky (scattering), prism rainbow (spectrum).
commonMisconceptions: Swapping reflection and refraction — treating light that crosses into a new medium (refraction) as if it bounces off it (reflection).
Believing reflection is 'only mirrors' and refraction is 'only glass blocks', rather than every surface reflecting and any change of medium refracting.
Reading 'bending' (refraction) as light travelling in a CURVE instead of a change from one straight-line path to another.
Measuring the angle of incidence/reflection from the SURFACE rather than from the normal (the perpendicular).
Blurring amplitude, wavelength and frequency into a vague single 'size' of the wave instead of three distinct measurable features.
Not recognising absorption as an option (forcing every light–surface interaction into reflect or refract), and confusing scattering with plain mirror-like reflection.
Treating an 'echo' as a mysterious separate effect rather than simply reflected sound.

learn.summary: Applied vocabulary for wave behaviour (reflection, refraction, absorption, scattering, amplitude, wavelength, frequency, echo, spectrum, angle of incidence, angle of reflection) for ages 9–11. The teaching goal is precise, applied USE of a highly confusable term set, not rote definition: each word is taught against its nearest confusable neighbour on a single discriminator, and every term is immediately used to explain a real phenomenon (bent straw = refraction, echo = reflected sound, blue sky = scattering, prism = spectrum). Core discriminator: does the wave bounce back into the first medium (reflection), pass into a new medium and change direction at the boundary when it meets it at an angle (refraction), get sent off in many directions by a rough surface or by tiny particles such as those in air (scattering), or soak in and not return (absorption)? The three wave-property words pin to distinct features of one wave — amplitude = height from the middle (rest) line to a peak, wavelength = peak-to-peak distance, frequency = how many pass per second.

activities.title: One ray, four fates: send a ray at a boundary
feedback: If a learner labels the bent straw / crossing-into-glass case 'reflection', point out the ray entered the new medium and bent — that is refraction; reflection is when it bounces back without entering.
If a learner draws refraction as a curve, show that light travels straight within each medium and only changes direction AT the surface — straight, kink, straight.

If a learner thinks reflection is 'only mirrors' or refraction is 'only glass blocks', show that most surfaces reflect some light and that light can refract whenever it crosses at an angle into a material where it travels at a different speed (water, a lens, the surface of a swimming pool).
If absorption is overlooked, point to the black card: the light is soaked in and not sent back at all — a distinct option from reflect/refract.
activities.rationale: The whole difficulty is a confusable term set that separates best when each term is pinned to a distinct, changeable referent. Sending one ray at a boundary and watching its fate change ties each word to an observable outcome; flipping the same ray between glass and mirror directly targets the reflection↔refraction swap and the 'only mirrors / only glass' trap. A static glossary can assert these distinctions but a changeable ray lets the learner see the fate switch.
sourceClaims: Documented confusable-term misconceptions: pupils restrict reflection to mirrors and refraction to glass blocks; the 'bending' language for refraction misleads pupils into imagining a curve rather than a change from one straight-line path to another; the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) applies to all surfaces, not just plane mirrors.

The core discriminator between reflection and refraction is whether light BOUNCES off the second medium (reflection) or TRAVELS THROUGH it, bending (refraction); air is often the first medium. Students commonly conflate the two, treating light crossing into a new medium as being reflected.
learnerActions: Send a single light ray at a surface at an angle (not straight along the normal) and change what the surface is: a mirror, a block of glass or water, black card, and a rough/bumpy surface.

Watch and name the main outcome each time: mirror = bounces back off the surface (reflection); glass or water = most of the light passes through and bends at the surface (refraction), though a little is also reflected; black card = most of the light is soaked in and not returned (absorption); rough surface = sprays off in many directions (scattering).

Keep the SAME incoming ray and switch the surface from glass to mirror, and describe out loud how the ray changes from refracting to reflecting — the two most-confused words are two different fates of one ray.
Trace or draw the bent ray for refraction as two straight segments with a kink at the surface, NOT a curve.
State the first medium each time (usually air) and say which medium the ray crosses into.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection, refraction, absorption and scattering are different things a wave can do when it meets a boundary; reflection (bounce back) and refraction (pass through and bend) are distinguished by whether the wave enters the new medium. Refraction is a change from one straight path to another with a kink at the boundary, not a curve.

activities.title: Measuring angles from the normal
feedback: If a learner measures from the surface, show that the standard definition uses the normal — redraw the perpendicular and measure from it.
Note that for these learners the point is correct measurement and definitions; the quantitative law of reflection (angle in = angle out as a numerical rule) and v = fλ come later.
activities.rationale: Measuring the angle from the surface instead of the normal is the classic measurement error flagged in reflection teaching; making the normal explicit and measuring from it addresses it directly. This measurement convention is a curriculum/pedagogy convention and is not restated word-for-word by any extracted source claim in this row.
learnerActions: On a reflection diagram, draw the normal — the line perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray hits.
Measure the angle of incidence between the incoming ray and the normal, and the angle of reflection between the outgoing ray and the normal (for example with a protractor aligned to the normal).
Check that the two angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface, and compare them.
State in words: the angle of incidence and angle of reflection are both measured from the normal (the perpendicular).
activities.intendedInsight: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal (the perpendicular to the surface), never from the surface itself.

activities.title: One wave, three features: amplitude, wavelength, frequency
feedback: If a learner substitutes one term for another or says 'size', point to the feature each word names (height, peak spacing, waves per second) and change the amplitude to show that height changes while spacing and frequency stay fixed; when frequency changes, show that the wavelength changes with it, but they are still different measurements.
If a learner conflates loudness and pitch, link loudness to amplitude and pitch to frequency as separate features of a sound wave.
activities.rationale: Pinning each property word to its own visual feature and varying one at a time prevents the documented blur of amplitude/wavelength/frequency into a single notion of wave size, and connects to the known sound confusion between loudness and pitch.
sourceClaims: Wavelength is the distance between crests and frequency is the number of crests that pass a given point in one second (one cycle per second = one hertz).
Loudness/volume is linked to the size (amplitude) of the vibration, and pitch to frequency (how fast it vibrates); these are distinct wave features that pupils commonly conflate.
learnerActions: Look at a single labelled wave and identify amplitude = height, wavelength = distance from one peak to the next, frequency = how many waves pass per second.

Change one control at a time (for example an amplitude control, then a frequency control) and describe which feature changed and which word names it; notice that changing the amplitude leaves the peak spacing alone, but for a wave in the same material, raising the frequency makes the peaks closer together (shorter wavelength).
Say aloud a one-line distinction for each so they don't blur into a single vague 'size': amplitude is how tall, wavelength is how far apart the peaks are, frequency is how many per second.
Connect to sound: loudness/volume links to amplitude (size of the vibration) and pitch links to frequency (how fast it vibrates).
activities.intendedInsight: Amplitude, wavelength and frequency are three distinct, separately measurable features of one wave, not interchangeable words for its overall 'size'.

activities.title: Use the word to explain the phenomenon
feedback: If a learner names the echo but treats it as a mysterious separate effect, state plainly: an echo IS reflected sound — the same bounce-off-a-surface idea as a mirror reflection.

If a learner uses 'reflection' for the bent straw or 'refraction' for the echo, re-anchor each to its example — straw/lens = passes through and bends = refraction; mirror/echo = bounces back = reflection.
If a learner can only reach vague words like 'bends' or 'bounces', prompt for the precise term and the reason (which medium, bounce or pass-through).
activities.rationale: The curriculum requires pupils to read, spell and USE scientific vocabulary, and the assessment is explicitly applied (explain the bent straw, distinguish reflection from refraction, explain an echo). Using three contrasting contexts catches term swaps that a definition-recall task would miss, especially the reflection/refraction pair and whether 'echo' is named as reflected sound. A sort can check classification but does not itself elicit the spoken/written explanation, so explanation tasks are included.
sourceClaims: KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to read, spell and pronounce scientific vocabulary correctly; the wave-behaviour terms are drawn from KS2 Light & Sound and KS3 Physics 'Waves' (reflection, refraction, absorption, frequency, wavelength, amplitude, spectrum).

CCSS-ELA-LITERACY.L.5.6: acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases — the literacy standard matching applied scientific vocabulary, since NGSS has no stand-alone vocabulary PE.
learnerActions: For each everyday scene, say which term applies and why, in a full sentence: a straw looks bent where it enters a glass of water (refraction); you shout in a tunnel and hear your voice come back (echo — reflected sound); the sky looks blue (scattering); a prism makes a rainbow (spectrum).
Explain an echo as reflected sound, linking it to the same 'bounce off a surface' idea as light reflection (like seeing yourself in a mirror).

Explain the dull red jumper in shade: it absorbs most colours and reflects/scatters red, and in shade there is less light to reflect, so it looks duller (an illustrative case that depends on the actual material and lighting).
Sort a mix of scenarios into reflect / refract / absorb / scatter and justify each choice.
Use word-part cues to spell and separate the tricky pair: re-FLECT = bounce back, re-FRACT = break/bend through, ab-SORB = soak in.
activities.intendedInsight: Each wave term earns its keep by explaining a real phenomenon; mastery is applying the right word in context, keeping reflection distinct from refraction, and recognising an echo as simply reflected sound.

constraints: This is a LANGUAGE topic: the goal is precise, applied use of a confusable term set, not rote definition — every term should be used to explain a real phenomenon.

Teach each term against its nearest confusable neighbour on ONE discriminator (bounce back vs pass-through-and-bend vs sent off in many directions by a rough surface or tiny particles vs soak in); remember air is usually the first medium.
Refraction 'bending' is a change from one straight path to another with a kink at the boundary, not a curve; draw it as straight segments with a kink.

Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal (the perpendicular), never from the surface; reflection off a mirror returns at an equal angle from the normal, not necessarily straight back along the incoming path.

Vary only one feature at a time where possible so amplitude, wavelength and frequency do not blur into a vague single 'size': amplitude can be changed on its own, but for a wave travelling in the same medium, changing the frequency also changes the wavelength (higher frequency, shorter wavelength).
The quantitative law of reflection (angle in = angle out as a numerical rule) and v = fλ are deferred to later stages (KS3/KS4); keep the focus on correct terms and measurement conventions.

A look-up reference or glossary pairing each term with its exemplar is a useful companion that can assert distinctions statically; for a confusable set, learners also benefit from seeing a ray's fate change and features vary, so a reference should support rather than replace applied discrimination (neither is a universal requirement).

Matching, sorting, multiple-choice and fill-the-blank response formats can assess the applied vocabulary and check classification, but do not by themselves build the visual discrimination or elicit an explanation; pair them with observation and spoken/written reasoning.
Recognition-only responses (choosing a label) do not elicit independent construction of an explanation; include tasks where the learner states the term AND the reason.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Several cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (DfE National Curriculum, Texas Gateway, CCSS-ELA); the IOPSpark, NASA and Explorify claims are marked verified. Citations support the stated teaching principles but do not establish that any specific activity here has been empirically tested or is comparatively more effective.

The from-the-normal measurement convention in the 'Measuring angles from the normal' activity is a curriculum/pedagogy convention; no extracted sources[].claim in this row states the surface-vs-normal measurement error directly, so that activity's sourceClaims is left empty rather than citing a topic-level claim.

The original material in places implied a static glossary 'cannot' teach confusable sets and that a changeable ray is uniquely required; this has been softened to a scoped affordance claim (changeable referents let learners observe fate/feature changes) without asserting universal necessity.

The mirror case in activity 1 was reworded from 'bounces straight back' to 'bounces back off the surface' to avoid implying retroreflection, keeping it consistent with the equal-angle-from-the-normal activity.

The 'dull red jumper in shade' explanation combines absorption/reflection of colour with reduced illumination in shade; this is reasonable at this level but depends on the actual material and lighting, so it is presented as an illustrative case, not an absolute outcome.

probeDeeper: In the bent-straw case, is the light bouncing back, or passing through and changing direction? Which word is that?
What is an echo actually made of — how is it like seeing yourself in a mirror?
The straw looks bent, but does the light travel in a curve or in straight lines with a kink at the water's surface? Which word describes it?
assess.correctAnswer: The bent straw = refraction (light changes direction and speed crossing the water-air boundary). The voice coming back = an echo, which is reflection of sound off the tunnel wall. The dull red jumper = it absorbs most colours and reflects/scatters red, and in shade there is less light to reflect. Terms are USED correctly and reflection is kept distinct from refraction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflection/refraction swapped: uses 'reflection' for the bent straw or 'refraction' for the echo
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reflection = bounces back off a surface; refraction = passes through and changes direction at a boundary; anchor each to its example (mirror/echo versus straw/lens).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies the wrong term to bending-across-a-boundary versus bouncing-back

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Bending' misread as a curve: thinks refraction makes light follow a curved path
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refraction is a change of direction AT the boundary — straight in each medium, a kink at the surface, not a curve.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the refracted ray as curving, rather than as a straight path that changes direction at the boundary

errorPatterns.pattern: Echo as a mystery, not reflected sound: names the echo but can't connect it to reflection
errorPatterns.nextMove: An echo IS reflected sound — the same 'bounce off a surface' idea as light reflection.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls it an echo but treats it as a separate phenomenon, not sound bouncing off a surface

errorPatterns.pattern: Amplitude/frequency/wavelength blurred into 'size': uses one for another or a vague 'how big'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pin each term to one feature — amplitude = height, wavelength = distance between peaks, frequency = how many per second.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Substitutes amplitude for frequency or wavelength, or uses 'size' to cover all three

responseLevels.gap: Swaps reflection and refraction, or can't reach for any correct term in context (uses only vague 'bends'/'bounces').
responseLevels.full: Applies each term accurately across the three contexts, keeps reflection distinct from refraction, names the echo as reflected sound, and pins amplitude/wavelength/frequency to distinct features.
responseLevels.partial: Uses some terms correctly but muddles the reflection/refraction pair or treats echo/absorption loosely; amplitude/frequency/wavelength blur into 'size'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three things happening: a straw looks bent where it enters a glass of water; you shout in a tunnel and hear your voice come back a moment later; and a red jumper looks dull in the shade. Tell me what's happening in each, using the right wave words — you might need reflection, refraction, absorption, scattering, echo. Explain your choices.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These terms are notoriously confused — reflection versus refraction, 'bending' misread as a curve, echo seen as mysterious rather than reflected sound. Giving three contexts and listening for which word the child reaches for catches swaps that a definition-recall task would miss, especially the reflection/refraction pair and whether 'echo' is named as reflected sound.

sources.claim: KS2 Working Scientifically requires pupils to read, spell and pronounce scientific vocabulary correctly; the wave-behaviour terms are drawn from KS2 Light & Sound and KS3 Physics 'Waves' (reflection, refraction, absorption, frequency, wavelength, amplitude, spectrum).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (Working Scientifically; KS2 Light/Sound; KS3 Physics Waves)

sources.claim: Documented confusable-term misconceptions: pupils restrict reflection to mirrors and refraction to glass blocks; the 'bending' language for refraction misleads pupils into imagining a curve rather than a change from one straight-line path to another; the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) applies to all surfaces, not just plane mirrors.
sources.source: Institute of Physics — IOPSpark, 'Reflection and refraction: teaching and learning issues'

sources.claim: The core discriminator between reflection and refraction is whether light BOUNCES off the second medium (reflection) or TRAVELS THROUGH it, bending (refraction); air is often the first medium. Students commonly conflate the two, treating light crossing into a new medium as being reflected.
sources.source: Texas Gateway (Texas Education Agency), 'Light: Reflection and Refraction'

sources.claim: Wavelength is the distance between crests and frequency is the number of crests that pass a given point in one second (one cycle per second = one hertz).
sources.source: NASA Science, 'Anatomy of an Electromagnetic Wave'

sources.claim: Loudness/volume is linked to the size (amplitude) of the vibration, and pitch to frequency (how fast it vibrates); these are distinct wave features that pupils commonly conflate.
sources.source: Explorify (Ogden Trust / STEM Learning / Primary Science Teaching Trust), 'Sound — tackle the tricky bits'

sources.claim: CCSS-ELA-LITERACY.L.5.6: acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases — the literacy standard matching applied scientific vocabulary, since NGSS has no stand-alone vocabulary PE.

pedagogy.summary: This is the representational core of transformations: reading a picture of an object and its image and saying precisely WHICH transformation maps one onto the other — and, conversely, producing the image from a described transformation. Each transformation has a defining set of marks a child must read and generate: a reflection needs a mirror line (and reverses sense); a translation needs a vector/displacement (and keeps orientation and sense); a rotation needs three things — a centre, an angle of turn, and a direction. Fluency means translating freely between the drawn image and its precise verbal description, checking congruence throughout.
bestPractices: Teach each transformation by its distinguishing evidence: reflection is the only one that reverses 'sense' (handedness); rotation changes orientation but keeps sense; translation keeps both. Have children CHECK sense to tell rotation from reflection.
Insist a rotation is described by all THREE pieces — centre of rotation, size of turn, and direction (clockwise/anticlockwise); a description missing any one is incomplete (NCETM KS3 6.3).

For reflection, draw the perpendicular lines joining each object vertex to its image and show the mirror line is their perpendicular bisector; avoid 'straight across/down' so the idea survives sloping mirror lines.
Move both ways: given an image, have the child NAME and fully describe the transformation; given a description, have the child PRODUCE the image — the two directions reinforce each other.
Use tracing paper for rotation — pin the centre, turn to the stated angle and direction — so the abstract description becomes a felt movement, and to verify congruence.

Include non-standard cases (a rotation that could be read clockwise or anticlockwise; a reflection in a sloping line) to force analysis rather than pattern-matching, and to surface the 'same-plane' and direction misconceptions.
keyRepresentations: Coordinate/squared grid showing object and image together
Mirror line with perpendicular 'joining lines' to corresponding vertices (reflection)
Centre-of-rotation marked, with an angle arc and a direction arrow (rotation)
Translation vector arrow (displacement) applied to every vertex
Tracing paper as the physical model for rotation and for congruence checks
commonMisconceptions: Calling a rotation a reflection (or vice versa) because sense/handedness is not checked.
Describing a rotation incompletely — giving the angle but omitting the centre and/or the direction.
When reflecting in a sloping mirror, keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane instead of moving each point perpendicular to the mirror.
Reversing coordinates (up before across) when labelling where the image landed.

learn.summary: Learners read a picture of a shape and its image on a squared/coordinate grid and say precisely WHICH transformation maps one onto the other, then work the other way — producing the image from a stated transformation. The defining evidence differs per transformation: reflection reverses 'sense' (handedness) and is built with a mirror line that is the perpendicular bisector of segments joining object and image points; translation keeps orientation and sense and is described by a vector/displacement applied to every vertex; rotation keeps sense but changes orientation and must be described by three things — centre, size (angle) of turn, and direction (clockwise/anticlockwise). Fluency means translating freely between the drawn image and its precise verbal description while checking congruence throughout, including non-standard cases such as sloping mirror lines and ambiguous turn directions.

activities.title: Name it: reconstruct the transformation that produced the image
feedback: If you named a reflection: ask 'does the shape read the same way round, or the mirror way round?' Only reflection reverses sense — re-decide from that check.

If you gave only the angle: a rotation needs three things — centre, size, direction. Add each and test by reproducing the image (tracing paper pinned at the centre lets you turn to the stated angle and direction and verify congruence).
If the image lands in the wrong place: check whether the centre is correct; if it turns the wrong way, check the direction.
Mark a rotation description as incomplete until centre, angle AND direction are all present.
activities.rationale: Identifying and describing a transformation is strengthened by setting the very parameters that define it and watching the image obey — binding each verbal descriptor to its visible effect. Mixing a reflection among rotations deliberately draws attention to what a rotation is not.
sourceClaims: A rotation must be described by three pieces of information — a centre of rotation, a size of turn, and a direction — and direction ambiguity (clockwise vs anticlockwise) is a documented difficulty.

Reflection is the only transformation that changes 'sense'; rotation changes orientation but maintains sense, and translation maintains congruence and orientation — so sense distinguishes rotation from reflection. Examples deliberately mix a reflection among rotations to draw attention to what a rotation is not.
learnerActions: On a grid showing a shape and its image already placed (produced by a rotation), work out which single transformation maps the first onto the second and reproduce it by setting the parameters yourself.
First try a reflection: flip the shape and compare handedness to the target — notice the 'sense' no longer matches (the target reads the same way round), so it cannot be a reflection.
Switch to rotation: choose a centre of rotation, set the angle of turn, and choose the direction (clockwise/anticlockwise) until your image lands exactly on the target.

State the full description aloud or in writing, e.g. 'rotation, 90° clockwise, about (2,1)', and check what each part controls: turning the same amount about a different centre makes the shape land somewhere else, and for a 90° turn, going the opposite direction lands it in a different place. (For a 180° turn, clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, but still state the direction to keep the description complete.)
Confirm the image is congruent to the original (e.g. by tracing or matching vertices).
activities.intendedInsight: Checking sense is what distinguishes a rotation from a reflection, and a rotation is only fully specified by centre, size AND direction together. The centre and the angle always affect where the image lands. The direction matters for 90° turns, but a 180° turn lands in the same place either way.

activities.title: Produce a reflection in a sloping mirror line
feedback: If the image sits level with the object rather than square across a sloping mirror: your joining lines are not perpendicular to the mirror. Draw the perpendicular from each vertex and step the equal distance beyond.
Avoid 'straight across' language so the idea survives sloping mirror lines.
If sense is not reversed, you have not reflected — check the handedness of the image against the original.
activities.rationale: A frequent error is keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane instead of moving each point perpendicular to the mirror; building the perpendicular-equidistant structure explicitly and testing it on a sloping line generalises the method.
sourceClaims: A common reflection misconception is keeping the image in the same vertical/horizontal plane rather than moving each point perpendicular to the mirror line; the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of segments joining object and image points.
learnerActions: Given a shape and a mirror line (including sloping or offset lines, not just horizontal/vertical), draw the reflected image.
For each vertex, draw the perpendicular from the vertex to the mirror line and step an equal distance beyond it to place the image vertex.
Check that the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each segment joining a vertex to its image, and that the sense (handedness) of the shape is reversed.
Describe what you did as 'a reflection in [this] mirror line' and confirm the image is congruent to the original.
Repeat with a sloping mirror to make sure your method does not rely on 'straight across/down'.
activities.intendedInsight: A reflection moves every point perpendicular to the mirror by an equal distance on the other side, so the mirror is the perpendicular bisector of each joining segment — this holds for sloping mirrors, not just level ones.

activities.title: Translate by a vector and label coordinates carefully
feedback: If a landed vertex is reported as (up, across): re-anchor with 'across the corridor, then up the stairs' and re-check one labelled vertex together.
If only some vertices moved the right amount, remember the same displacement applies to every vertex.
activities.rationale: Reversing the ordered pair is a recurring coordinate error; anchoring 'across then up' and checking a vertex guards against it while reinforcing that translation preserves orientation and congruence.
sourceClaims: Reversing the ordered pair (reading the second coordinate before the first) is a recurring coordinate error to guard against.

Reflection is the only transformation that changes 'sense'; rotation changes orientation but maintains sense, and translation maintains congruence and orientation — so sense distinguishes rotation from reflection. Examples deliberately mix a reflection among rotations to draw attention to what a rotation is not.
learnerActions: Translate a shape by a given displacement (e.g. 3 right and 2 up), applying the same movement to every vertex.
Describe the movement both as a vector and in left/right/up/down words.
Label the coordinates of the translated vertices, writing each as (across, up).
Check that orientation and sense are unchanged and that the image is congruent to the original.
activities.intendedInsight: A translation slides every point by the same displacement, preserving orientation, sense and size; coordinates are read across first, then up.

activities.title: Precision check: discrete items for describing transformations
feedback: Score a rotation description as correct only if centre, angle AND direction are all present.
For the rotation-vs-reflection item, point to sense: if handedness flipped it is a reflection, if sense is unchanged it is a rotation.
activities.rationale: Discrete items are useful for checking precision of description and for surfacing the rotation-vs-reflection confusion via a sense-reversed distractor; on their own they check recognition and stated description rather than independent construction of the image.
sourceClaims: A rotation must be described by three pieces of information — a centre of rotation, a size of turn, and a direction — and direction ambiguity (clockwise vs anticlockwise) is a documented difficulty.
learnerActions: Answer 'which transformation maps A to B?' where one distractor shows the same shape reflected (sense reversed) rather than rotated.
Match written descriptions to images.
Fill in the three parts of a rotation description (centre, size, direction) for a shown image.
Draw the path/image to produce a reflection in a given mirror line.
activities.intendedInsight: Describing a transformation precisely means using the correct defining marks — and a rotation description counts only when centre, angle and direction are all given.

activities.title: Annotated worked examples as a reference
feedback: Answer 'rotation or reflection?' by checking whether sense reversed, then confirm against the revealed marks.
Treat this as a reference: to build the skill, move on to naming an unlabelled image and producing images yourself.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated example cannot be manipulated by the learner, but it can make the defining marks and the sense check explicit and serve as a reference alongside generative tasks.
sourceClaims: Reflection is the only transformation that changes 'sense'; rotation changes orientation but maintains sense, and translation maintains congruence and orientation — so sense distinguishes rotation from reflection. Examples deliberately mix a reflection among rotations to draw attention to what a rotation is not.
learnerActions: Study one worked example of each transformation with its defining marks revealed: the mirror line and perpendicular joining lines for reflection; the vector arrow for translation; the centre, angle arc and direction arrow for rotation.
For each, identify whether the sense is reversed and use that to decide 'rotation or reflection?'.
Use these as a reference while attempting your own naming and producing tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each transformation has a distinct set of marks to read; sense reversal is the tell for reflection.

constraints: A complete rotation description requires all three parts — centre, size of turn, and direction; treat any missing part as incomplete.
Avoid 'straight across/down' language for reflection so methods generalise to sloping and offset mirror lines; use perpendicular-and-equidistant instead.
Label image coordinates consistently as (across, up) to guard against reversing the ordered pair.
Include non-standard cases (a turn that could be read clockwise or anticlockwise; a reflection in a sloping line) to force analysis rather than pattern-matching.
Discrete/recognition items (multiple choice, matching) check precision of stated description but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an image; pair them with producing tasks.
Tracing paper (pin the centre, turn to the stated angle and direction) is a useful physical model for rotation and for checking congruence; it is a supportive tool, not a required mechanism.

Interactive controls (mode buttons, draggable mirror line, pinnable centre with angle dial and CW/ACW toggle, live sense indicator and congruence overlay) are optional ways to make the descriptor-to-motion link concrete; the same learning can be done on paper.

These transformations are planar and are read from marks on a grid, so a third dimension is not needed to read a mirror line, vector or centre. A dialogue/persona format can discuss and prompt transformation work but does not itself present or manipulate the grid, so producing an image would still happen on the learner's own paper. These are scoping affordance notes, not claims that any medium is uniquely necessary, superior, or impossible.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims about sense/handedness, the three parts of a rotation, perpendicular-bisector reflection, and coordinate reversal are cited from NCETM materials as recorded in the source row; comparative efficacy of any specific activity format is not established by these citations.

Legacy 'fit' rankings asserting that a third dimension 'adds nothing' and that a conversation 'cannot' teach this were softened to scoped affordance notes; the source ratings do not establish universal necessity or impossibility.

The diagnostic and these activities assume a scalene/asymmetric shape so that sense and orientation changes are visible; ensure any chosen shape is asymmetric enough that reflection vs rotation genuinely differs, otherwise the sense check is not discriminating.
Note for 180° rotations specifically, clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, so the 'direction turns it the wrong way' feedback applies to turns such as 90°, not to 180°.

probeDeeper: 'How can you be sure this is a rotation and not a reflection?' (listen for sense/handedness as the deciding evidence, not orientation alone).
'If I only told you the shape was rotated 90°, could you draw exactly where it lands? What else do you need?' (elicits centre and direction as required parameters).

Counterexample: 'Your friend says the second shape is a reflection. Show me the mirror line that would do it — does one exist?' (a rotated shape has no consistent mirror line; the search exposes the error).
'Is the image congruent to the original after your reflection? How would you check?' (tracing/matching; congruence is invariant under all three transformations).
assess.correctAnswer: For the shown image: 'a rotation' named with all three descriptors — centre (the marked point), size (90°/quarter turn) and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise, matching the picture) — justified by the shape keeping its sense while changing orientation. For the produced reflection: each vertex placed perpendicular to and equidistant from the mirror, sense reversed, described as a reflection in that mirror line, and the image confirmed congruent to the original.

errorPatterns.pattern: Calls the rotation a reflection (or vice versa) without checking sense
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'does the shape read the same way round or the mirror way round?' Establish that only reflection reverses sense; re-decide from that check.
errorPatterns.distractor: A reflection in a line through the marked point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names 'reflection' for an image whose sense is unchanged, or 'rotation' for one whose handedness has flipped; cannot cite sense as the deciding evidence.

errorPatterns.pattern: Describes the rotation incompletely — gives the angle but omits the centre and/or the direction
errorPatterns.nextMove: State that a rotation needs three things — centre, size, direction; have the child add each and test by reproducing the image with tracing paper pinned at the centre.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'it's turned 90°' or 'a quarter turn' with no centre named and no clockwise/anticlockwise; treats 'rotation' as fully specified by its angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: When producing a reflection in a sloping or offset mirror, keeps the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane instead of moving each point perpendicular to the mirror
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the perpendicular from each vertex to the mirror and step the equal distance beyond; avoid 'straight across' language so it generalises to sloping mirrors.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The produced image sits level with the object rather than square across the mirror line; joining lines are not perpendicular to the mirror.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses coordinates (states the up-value before the across-value) when labelling the image
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'across the corridor, then up the stairs'; check one labelled vertex together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports a landed vertex as (up, across) though the point drawn is correct.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably name the transformation — confuses rotation and reflection, or offers only a bare word with no defining marks — and cannot produce a correct reflection (image not perpendicular/equidistant, sense not reversed).
responseLevels.full: Names each transformation from its evidence (using sense to separate rotation from reflection), describes a rotation completely (centre, size, direction), produces a reflection with each vertex perpendicular and equidistant and sense reversed, labels image coordinates as (across, up), and confirms congruence — transferring correctly to non-standard mirror lines and centres.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and names each transformation and can produce a reflection in a vertical/horizontal mirror, but treats the descriptors as a checklist rather than a structure — e.g. identifies a rotation yet omits centre or direction, or produces a reflection correctly only in standard positions while failing a sloping mirror. Lists the parts of a transformation but cannot yet explain how they jointly fix the image or transfer to a non-standard case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a squared grid with a scalene shape and its image, where the image is the shape turned a quarter-turn about a marked point (sense unchanged). Say: 'What single transformation maps the first shape onto the second? Describe it as fully as you can.' Then give a fresh copy of the original next to a mirror line and say: 'Now YOU produce the reflection of this shape in this mirror line, and describe what you did.' Read what they say about the shown transformation, then watch what they draw.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reading move forces a choice between rotation and reflection that only checking SENSE resolves — a child who reasons from sense names it correctly, one who guesses from orientation alone may call it a reflection. Requiring a FULL description exposes whether the child knows a rotation needs centre, angle and direction, not just the word. The producing move then shows whether they can generate the perpendicular-equidistant structure themselves, so reading and producing are checked separately.
