pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Mass vs Weight

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3):** This maps to the UK KS3 national curriculum ('gravity force, weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), on Earth g=10 N/kg, different on other planets and stars', placed under Space physics, qualitative only).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** In NGSS it is a threshold concept underpinning the MS-PS2 forces expectations rather than a standalone PE.

- **Operational details:** At 11-12, pupils first formalise the distinction between mass (the amount of matter, in kg, unchanged by location) and weight (the gravitational force on that matter, in N, W = m×g, g = 10 N/kg on Earth and different elsewhere).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). This is the band's first quantitative force equation; keep reasoning about other planets qualitative/proportional and define weight OPERATIONALLY (what a spring scale reads) rather than fighting the deep 'weight = heaviness' intuition head-on. Research (Bar, Brosh & Sneider 2016) shows this is a threshold concept mastered only partially by 14 (correct 'object-on-the-Moon' answers rise from ~35% at age 10 to ~77% at age 14), and that ~56% of students define weight simply as 'heavy or light' — a property idea that actually resembles mass, which is why the two conflate.
bestPractices: Define weight operationally — what a spring scale / newton meter reads — rather than trying to argue students out of the 'heaviness is a property' intuition (Stein & Galili; Bar et al.)
Teach mass and weight ALONGSIDE gravity, since the conflation is entangled with gravity misconceptions (no gravity in space; gravity needs air)
Use the transport-to-another-planet/Moon comparison as the core vehicle: weight changes on a spring scale while mass is unchanged on a balance
Contrast the two instruments explicitly — balance (mass, kg) vs spring scale/newton meter (force, N) — both show numbers but measure different things
Pin units hard (kg for mass, N for weight) and treat W = m×g as a proportional relationship (double number line / ratio reasoning for other planets), not just a 'magic triangle'
Expect only partial mastery at this age and revisit; police your own language so you don't use the words interchangeably during measuring
keyRepresentations: Same object on a balance (reads kg, unchanged) beside a spring scale/newton meter (reads N) — two readings, two quantities
Planet/Moon 'weigh-station' comparison table: mass constant, weight scaling with g
W = m × g shown as a proportional relationship with units flagged (ratio table across planets)
commonMisconceptions: Mass and weight are interchangeable words for the same property (the core error; ~56% define weight as 'heavy or light'; persists into adulthood)
Weight is a fixed property of the object that doesn't change with location — or, conversely, that mass AND weight both shrink equally on the Moon
Confusing the units — treating kg as a unit of weight/force (reinforced by grocery packaging putting grams beside force units)
A balance and a spring scale 'measure the same thing'
Entangled gravity errors: no gravity in space → no weight and no mass; gravity needs air
Carryover that 'more mass' is why heavier things fall faster

learn.summary: Help 11–12 year-olds distinguish mass (the amount of matter, in kg, unchanged by location) from weight (the gravitational force on that matter, in N, W = m×g), using the same object on two instruments — a two-pan balance compared against standard masses (kg) and a spring scale/newton meter (N) — and comparing readings across Earth, Moon and Jupiter. Define weight operationally (what a spring scale reads) rather than arguing against the 'heaviness is a property' intuition head-on, and teach alongside gravity because the two conflate. Expect only partial mastery at this age.

activities.title: Two instruments, one rock, different planets
feedback: If a learner also decreases the mass on the Moon: a balance compares amounts of matter and reads the SAME on the Moon; only the spring force-meter reads less. Mass = matter, weight = the pull.

If a learner uses kg and N interchangeably: give each quantity its own instrument — mass in kg on the balance (same everywhere), weight in N on the force-meter (changes with g) — and ask which one changed.
If a learner says the rock would weigh nothing on the Moon: the Moon HAS gravity, about a sixth of Earth's, so weight is reduced, not zero — astronauts still stand on its surface.
If a learner recites 'mass constant, weight changes' without reasons: ask them to explain it in terms of g being smaller, using the W = m×g relationship.
activities.rationale: A live divergence between a glued balance reading and a shifting spring-scale reading can make the abstract mass/weight distinction visible, and a changeable g ties the weight change to the field rather than to the object. A fixed side-by-side picture can introduce the two instruments and their units but cannot show the reading changing as g changes, so it supports rather than replaces the location-comparison activity.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory content: 'gravity force, weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), on Earth g=10 N/kg, different on other planets and stars' (Space physics, qualitative only); 'forces measured in newtons'.

Weight is most often understood as 'heaviness' (a property), ~56% of students; correct mass-constant/weight-changes answers on the Moon task rise ~35% (age 10) to ~77% (age 14); defining weight operationally (spring-scale) and teaching it with gravity improves understanding (Stein & Galili). Threshold concept underpinning many NGSS expectations.
learnerActions: Place the SAME object (e.g. a 2 kg rock) on two instruments side by side: a two-pan (equal-arm) balance that compares the rock against standard kilogram masses, and a spring scale/newton meter that reads in newtons. On Earth note the rock balances 2 kg of standard masses and the spring scale reads about 20 N. (A digital scale that shows kg actually senses force and is set up for Earth's g, so on the Moon it would read too low. Only a balance that compares against standard masses gives the same reading everywhere.)

Change the location from Earth to the Moon to Jupiter (via a planet selector, or by changing the value of g). Watch what each instrument does: the balance stays at 2 kg everywhere, while the spring scale changes — about 20 N on Earth, about 3 N on the Moon, about 50 N on Jupiter.

Write down, for each location, which reading changed and which stayed the same, and state in words why: the amount of matter (mass, kg) never changed, but the gravitational pull on it (weight, N) did.
Answer a prompt such as 'Would an astronaut float away here?' and connect your answer back to W = m×g — smaller g means smaller weight, but the same mass.
Build a short ratio/double-number-line for weight across the planets to show weight is proportional to g while mass is held fixed.
activities.intendedInsight: The kilogram reading describes the object itself (its matter); the newton reading describes the gravitational pull on it. Mass is constant with location; weight changes because g changes. W = m×g is a proportional relationship, not a magic triangle.

activities.title: Labelled instruments: which quantity, which unit
feedback: If a learner says both instruments measure the same thing: a balance compares amounts of matter; a spring scale measures the pull of gravity — same-looking numbers, different quantities.
If a learner labels weight in kg: weight is a force, measured in newtons (N); kilograms measure mass.
activities.rationale: A clean reference layer that pins units and the instrument–quantity pairing addresses the common error of treating kg as a unit of weight (reinforced by grocery packaging). Being static, it can anchor vocabulary and units but cannot itself show weight changing with g; use it to support, not replace, the location-comparison activity. A sort checks and reinforces the kg-vs-N classification but does not by itself elicit an explanation of why weight changes.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory content: 'gravity force, weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), on Earth g=10 N/kg, different on other planets and stars' (Space physics, qualitative only); 'forces measured in newtons'.
learnerActions: Examine a two-pan balance (used with standard masses) and a spring scale/newton meter side by side; for each, reveal (e.g. tap-to-reveal) the quantity it measures and its unit — two-pan balance → mass in kg; spring scale/newton meter → weight (force) in N.
State in your own words why both show numbers but measure different things.
Sort everyday examples by unit: which quantities belong in kg (amount of matter) and which in N (force).
activities.intendedInsight: A balance and a spring scale do NOT measure the same thing: one measures the amount of matter (kg), the other the gravitational force (N). Units are not interchangeable.

activities.title: Astronaut interview: weight, mass and 'no gravity in space'
feedback: If a learner says the astronaut has less mass in space: mass is the amount of matter and does not change with location; it is the weight (pull) that changes with g.
If a learner says there is no gravity on the Moon: the Moon has gravity, roughly a sixth of Earth's, so weight is reduced, not zero.

If a learner says astronauts float because there is no gravity in orbit: in low orbit gravity is still strong; they appear weightless because they are in continual free fall, and their mass is unchanged.
activities.rationale: A dialogue is well suited to surfacing the location-dependence idea and the entangled 'no gravity in space' tail, which is tightly linked to the mass/weight conflation. It is a companion to, not a substitute for, the quantitative two-instrument contrast, which it does not provide.
sourceClaims: Weight is most often understood as 'heaviness' (a property), ~56% of students; correct mass-constant/weight-changes answers on the Moon task rise ~35% (age 10) to ~77% (age 14); defining weight operationally (spring-scale) and teaching it with gravity improves understanding (Stein & Galili). Threshold concept underpinning many NGSS expectations.
learnerActions: Take part in a spoken or written exchange in the role of (or interviewing) an astronaut: 'Do you weigh less up here? What about your mass? Is there any gravity at all?'
Explain whether the astronaut's mass changes on the Moon or in deep space (far from any planet or star), and whether their weight changes, giving reasons in terms of g.

Address the 'there is no gravity in space' idea: in deep space, far from any large mass, the gravitational pull is tiny so weight is near zero while mass is unchanged; the Moon has gravity about a sixth of Earth's, so weight there is reduced, not zero.

As an optional clarification of the 'no gravity in space' tail (kept qualitative), discuss why astronauts seen 'floating' on the International Space Station are NOT in a region without gravity: gravity there is still strong, and they float because they are in continual free fall — their mass has not changed.
activities.intendedInsight: Location changes weight (the gravitational pull) only by changing g, not mass (the amount of matter). Near-zero weight in deep space is different from the apparent weightlessness of free fall in orbit, where gravity is still strong; in every case mass is unchanged and 'floating' does not mean having no mass.

activities.title: Consolidation retrieval: changes on the Moon, W = m×g, units
feedback: For the 'both decrease' choice: only weight decreases; mass is unchanged because the amount of matter is the same on the Moon.
For the 'zero weight on the Moon' choice: the Moon's gravity reduces weight to about a sixth, not to zero.
For unit confusion: mass is measured in kg, weight (a force) in N.
activities.rationale: Retrieval practice and well-chosen incorrect options consolidate the distinction and surface persistent errors. Recognition-and-recall items check and reinforce understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent explanation of why weight changes; pair with the explanation prompt and the two-instrument activity.
learnerActions: Categorise what changes and what stays the same when an object is taken to the Moon: mass (unchanged) vs weight (decreases).
Set a value for g with a slider and compute weight with a fill-in W = m × g for given masses.

Answer multiple-choice items contrasting kg (mass) and N (weight/force), where the misconception options — 'both mass and weight decrease' and 'weight is zero on the Moon' — are marked incorrect with feedback.
Explain, for one item, WHY the answer is correct in terms of g.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure retrieval of the mass/weight distinction, units, and the proportional W = m×g relationship, while exposing the 'both decrease' and unit-confusion errors.

constraints: Define weight operationally — what a spring scale / newton meter reads — rather than trying to argue students out of the 'heaviness is a property' intuition (Stein & Galili; Bar et al.).
Teach mass and weight ALONGSIDE gravity, since the conflation is entangled with gravity misconceptions (no gravity in space; gravity needs air).
Pin units hard (kg for mass, N for weight) and treat W = m×g as a proportional relationship (double number line / ratio reasoning across planets), not just a 'magic triangle'.
Keep reasoning about other planets qualitative/proportional at this age (Tier B, transitional/early-formal); this is the band's first quantitative force equation.
Police your own language so you don't use 'mass' and 'weight' interchangeably while measuring.
Expect only partial mastery at this age and plan to revisit (correct Moon-task answers reportedly rise from ~35% at age 10 to only ~77% at age 14; figures from an unverified source).
A static labelled-instrument view is a vocabulary/units scaffold; it cannot show weight changing as g changes, so it should accompany rather than replace the location comparison.
Recognition/recall items and sorts check and reinforce classification but do not elicit independent explanation of why weight changes — include an explanation step.

Distinguish near-zero weight in deep space (weak gravitational field) from apparent weightlessness in orbit (free fall in a still-strong field); do not teach that orbital 'floating' means there is no gravity, and never claim mass changes with location. Keep the orbital point qualitative and optional at this age.

Use example numbers consistently: a 2 kg rock reads ~20 N on Earth, ~3 N on the Moon, ~50 N on Jupiter (g ≈ 10, ~1.6, ~25 N/kg respectively); the diagnostic's 6 kg rock reads ~60 N on Earth and ~10 N on the Moon.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original '3D adds nothing / would only add handling cost' judgement was a catalog-fit comment; it has been dropped rather than restated as a universal claim. Tactile/physical balances and spring scales remain a legitimate hands-on route and are not precluded.
The Bar, Brosh & Sneider (2016) source is marked verified:false in the row; the ~56%, ~35%→~77% figures are reproduced as cited but have not been independently confirmed in this rewrite.

Approximate Moon/Jupiter newton values depend on the g values used (Moon ≈ 1.6 N/kg, Jupiter ≈ 25 N/kg); treat them as rounded illustrative figures, consistent with keeping other-planet reasoning qualitative/proportional.

The original framing that 'only a live recompute makes felt' the concept has been softened to an affordance (live recompute can make the divergence visible) rather than a necessity claim; comparative efficacy over other media is not established by the sources.

The astronaut activity's 'in orbit' weight-change framing was corrected: orbital apparent weightlessness is free fall in a still-strong field, physically distinct from the weak field of deep space; the original diagnostic used 'deep space', which is retained for the near-zero-weight case. The ISS free-fall point is kept qualitative/optional given the KS3 age scope.

The original pedagogy's misconception 'more mass is why heavier things fall faster' is not built into an activity here; it is tangential to the mass/weight distinction and is noted for a later revisit rather than silently dropped.

probeDeeper: Which instrument reads the SAME on Earth and the Moon — a balance or a spring scale? Why?
On Jupiter, with stronger gravity, what happens to the rock's mass and to its weight?
An astronaut floating in deep space — what is the rock's mass there? Its weight? Why?
Why do we measure mass in kilograms but weight in newtons?
assess.correctAnswer: Its mass stays the same (6 kg) — mass is the amount of matter, which doesn't depend on location. Its weight DECREASES — weight is the gravitational force on it (W = mg), and the Moon's gravitational field strength g is about a sixth of Earth's, so the rock weighs about a sixth as much. So weight changes, mass doesn't.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'On the Moon the rock has less mass too — it's lighter, so there's less of it.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Operational split: a balance (comparing amounts of matter) reads the same on the Moon; a spring force-meter reads less. Mass = matter, weight = the pull.
errorPatterns.distractor: Its mass gets smaller too, because it's lighter on the Moon.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Changes the mass along with the weight.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Weight and mass are the same thing — just different words or units.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mass in kg on a balance (same everywhere); weight in N on a force-meter (changes with g). Give each its own instrument.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses kg and N interchangeably and can't say which one changes.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'There's no gravity on the Moon, so the rock would weigh nothing.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Moon HAS gravity, about a sixth of Earth's, so weight is reduced, not zero — astronauts still stand on the surface.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the weight is zero on the Moon.

responseLevels.gap: Treats mass and weight as the same, or says the mass changes with location, or that weight is zero on the Moon.
responseLevels.full: Explains mass as the location-independent amount of matter and weight as the gravitational force W = mg, so on the Moon the mass is unchanged and the weight falls because g is smaller — transferring correctly to Jupiter (heavier) and deep space (weightless but same mass).
responseLevels.partial: States that mass is in kg and weight in N and can use W = mg, but when reasoning about the Moon still couples them (says the mass changes) or recites 'mass constant, weight changes' without explaining it's because g differs.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: An astronaut takes a 6 kg rock from Earth to the Moon. On the Moon, does the rock's MASS change, does its WEIGHT change, both, or neither — and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Mass/weight is a threshold concept — students fuse 'amount of stuff' with 'how heavy it feels'. A student who separates them says the mass is unchanged and the weight decreases because g is smaller. A fused thinker says 'it's lighter so it has less mass' (mass and weight move together) or that both are unchanged ('it's the same rock'). Tier 2 exposes whether the weight change is attributed to the field, not to the rock changing.

sources.claim: 'Many students think of mass and weight as alternative words for the same property'; you cannot resolve it by narrowing or banning the everyday words — students must learn to live with their sloppy complexity; mass relates to the 'amount of stuff' / resistance to acceleration.

Threshold concept underpinning many NGSS expectations.

pedagogy.summary: This topic is fluency with C = πd (= 2πr) and A = πr², and applying them to composite shapes with circular parts. Best taught by deriving both from the meaning of π rather than memorising two similar-looking formulae: π is the constant ratio of every circle's circumference to its diameter (a little over 3), so C = πd is almost a definition; and A = πr² comes from cutting the circle into thin wedges and rearranging them into a near-rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r. The two persistent hazards are confusing radius with diameter, and swapping the circumference and area formulae — both eased by keeping the meaning of each in view (circumference is a length, area is a covering in square units).
bestPractices: Establish π as circumference ÷ diameter — measure round several circular objects and divide by the diameter to find it is always ≈ 3.14; this makes C = πd meaningful, not arbitrary
Derive A = πr² by cutting the circle into wedges and rearranging into a near-rectangle of length πr and height r (πr × r = πr²)
Drill the radius/diameter link (d = 2r) explicitly and check which the formula needs before substituting — circumference uses d (or 2r), area uses r²
Distinguish 'squaring' from 'doubling': r² means r × r, not 2r; area grows with the square of the radius, giving square units
For composite shapes, decompose into a rectangle plus a semicircle, find each part, then add — watching which lengths are the circle's radius
Keep dimensions and units in view: circumference is a length (cm), area is a covering (cm²)
keyRepresentations: A circle with radius, diameter and circumference labelled; the d = 2r link
π as the ratio of circumference to diameter (a string round a tin measured against the diameter, ≈ 3.14)
The circle cut into wedges rearranged into a near-rectangle of length πr and height r (derivation of πr²)
A composite shape decomposed into a rectangle plus a semicircle
Unit labels distinguishing length (cm) from area (cm²)
commonMisconceptions: Confusing radius and diameter — substituting the diameter where the radius is needed (or vice versa)
Swapping the circumference and area formulae (using πr² for circumference or 2πr for area)
Forgetting to square the radius, or squaring as 'doubling' (treating r² as 2r or as the diameter)
Giving an area in linear units, or a circumference in square units
On composite shapes, using the diameter as the radius of the semicircle, or dropping a straight edge from the perimeter

learn.summary: Pupils (ages ~12–14) build fluency with C = πd (= 2πr) and A = πr² and apply them to composite shapes with circular parts. The emphasis is on deriving both formulae from the meaning of π — the constant ratio of every circle's circumference to its diameter, a little over 3 — rather than memorising two similar-looking formulae. π is almost a definition of C = πd; A = πr² follows from cutting a circle into thin wedges and rearranging them into a near-rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r. The two persistent hazards are confusing radius with diameter, and swapping the circumference and area formulae; both are eased by keeping each quantity's meaning and units in view (circumference is a length in cm, area is a covering in cm²).

activities.title: Discover π by unrolling the circumference
feedback: If your ratios differ wildly between circles, re-check your measurements — the string should wrap exactly once with no slack, and the diameter must pass through the centre and be measured where the string wraps; all circles should give roughly the same value close to 3.14, with small differences due to measurement error.
Prompt: 'Roughly how many diameters fit around the edge of a circle, and what do we call that number?'

If a learner thinks π changes with circle size, point to their own table of results showing roughly the same value (close to 3.14) for every circle, and explain that the small differences come from measurement error, not from π changing.
activities.rationale: Grounding π as a measured ratio addresses the vague-notion-of-π misconception and makes C = πd meaningful rather than memorised. An optional interactive 'roll the circle' animation — laying the circumference along a line marked in diameters — can make the ≈ 3.14 result vivid, but physical measurement of real objects achieves the same discovery.
sourceClaims: Learners confuse 'squaring' the radius with 'doubling' it (treating r² as equivalent to the diameter), reason about area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and hold vague notions of π rather than seeing it as the ratio of circumference to diameter
learnerActions: Take several circular objects (tins, lids, cups) of different sizes; wrap a string once around each and measure that length, then measure the diameter across each.

Divide each circumference by its diameter and record the result; notice the results are all close to the same value, a little over 3 (near π ≈ 3.14, allowing for small measurement errors), whatever the size of the circle.
Lay the measured circumference along a line marked off in lengths equal to that circle's own diameter, and see that it reaches to just past three diameters.
State in your own words: C = πd means the way round is 'a bit more than 3 diameters'.
activities.intendedInsight: π is the fixed ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter (≈ 3.14), so C = πd is almost a definition, not an arbitrary formula to recall.

activities.title: Build the area formula by rearranging wedges
feedback: If a learner labels the length as the full circumference, remind them each long edge of the rearranged shape is made of only half the arcs, so the length is πr, not 2πr.
Prompt: 'Which of your two results is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?'
If the height is mislabelled as the diameter, point back to the wedge: its straight side is the radius.
activities.rationale: Deriving πr² from decomposition addresses treating area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and helps keep area distinct from circumference. An optional drag-the-wedges tool that builds the πr × r rectangle can reinforce the same idea; paper cutting achieves it concretely. Note that a paper circle has slight thickness and models the ideal zero-thickness plane figure it represents — reason about the mathematical circle, not the card.
sourceClaims: Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r

Learners confuse 'squaring' the radius with 'doubling' it (treating r² as equivalent to the diameter), reason about area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and hold vague notions of π rather than seeing it as the ratio of circumference to diameter
learnerActions: Cut a paper circle into a number of thin equal wedges (sectors) and fan them out, alternating points up and down, to form a shape close to a rectangle (parallelogram).
Identify the height of the near-rectangle as the radius r, and its length as half the way round the circle — half the circumference, which is πr.
Compute the area of the near-rectangle as length × height = πr × r = πr², and connect this to the circle's area.
Explain why cutting into more, thinner wedges makes the shape look more like a true rectangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A = πr² is a product of a length (πr) and a length (r) giving square units, derived from rearranging the circle — not a lookalike string to confuse with C = πd.

activities.title: Radius-or-diameter: check before you substitute
feedback: If a learner computes π × 10² = 100π for area in the diameter-given case, flag that they used the diameter as the radius — halve it first: r = 5, A = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm².
If a learner reports area as π × 2 × 5 or π × 10, they have doubled instead of squared — r² means r × r, the area of a little square of side r.
Prompt: 'You were given the diameter — why can't you put it straight into πr²?'
Prompt: 'If the radius doubled, what happens to the circumference, and what happens to the area?' (area ×4, not ×2).
activities.rationale: Making the radius/diameter check an explicit first step and distinguishing squaring from doubling target the two most flagged hazards. An optional radius/diameter toggle that recomputes C and A, and flags a squared-vs-doubled slip, can make the check vivid; the self-check questions work on paper too.
sourceClaims: Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r

Learners confuse 'squaring' the radius with 'doubling' it (treating r² as equivalent to the diameter), reason about area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and hold vague notions of π rather than seeing it as the ratio of circumference to diameter
learnerActions: For each problem, first write 'What am I given — radius or diameter?' and 'What does this formula need?' before substituting.
Given a diameter of 10 cm, find the area: halve it to get r = 5 cm, then compute A = π × 5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² (not π × 10²).
Given a radius of 5 cm, find both the circumference C = π × 10 = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm and the area A = π × 5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm².
Investigate: if the radius doubles, what happens to the circumference and to the area? Confirm circumference doubles (×2) but area quadruples (×4).
activities.intendedInsight: Circumference uses d (or 2r) and area uses r²; you must convert a given diameter to a radius before using πr², and squaring is r × r (not doubling), so area grows with the square of the radius.

activities.title: Composite shapes: rectangle plus semicircle
feedback: If a learner uses r = 4 for the semicircle, remind them 4 cm is the diameter across the short end; the radius is 2 cm.
If a learner leaves in a straight edge where the semicircle joins (or omits the arc), re-trace the boundary: the arc takes the place of that edge.
Prompt: 'Which of your answers is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?'
Check: did you keep straight which number is the radius for each circular part?
activities.rationale: Decomposing and tracing the real boundary addresses using the diameter as the semicircle's radius and dropping/adding wrong edges in the perimeter. An optional composite-shape builder that shows each part's contribution can scaffold this; careful labelled sketching achieves the same decomposition.
sourceClaims: Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r
Pupils commonly confuse area and perimeter, which for circles surfaces as swapping circumference (a length) with area (square units)
KS3 pupils should calculate the circumference and area of circles and solve problems involving the perimeters and areas of composite shapes that include circular parts
learnerActions: Take a composite shape — e.g. a rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm with a semicircle of diameter 4 cm on one short (4 cm) end — and sketch it, labelling every given length.
Find the semicircle's radius as half its diameter (here r = 2 cm), not the full width.
For the area, add the rectangle's area to half the circle's area: 10 × 4 + ½ × π × 2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm².
For the perimeter, trace the actual boundary: include the rectangle's exposed edges plus the semicircle arc (½ × π × diameter = ½ × π × 4 = 2π), with NO straight edge where the semicircle sits.
State the units: area in cm², perimeter in cm.
activities.intendedInsight: Composite shapes are decomposed into parts whose areas are added, while the perimeter follows the true outline — the arc replaces the covered straight edge, and the semicircle's radius is half its diameter.

activities.title: Formula-choice and unit checks (retrieval practice)
feedback: If the two answers are switched (circumference in cm², area in cm), you have swapped the formulae — anchor each to what it measures: circumference from πd is a length, area from πr² is a covering.
If a method is correct but the unit is wrong, re-check the unit against what was calculated — don't re-derive, just correct the label.
If a diameter distractor is chosen in πr², note the full width was used instead of the radius — halve the diameter to the radius first.
activities.rationale: Spaced retrieval with targeted distractors (diameter-in-πr², swapped formulae, wrong units) consolidates fluency and surfaces residual misconceptions, including the radius/diameter slip. Scored recognition and matching tasks assess and rehearse choices but do not by themselves require independent derivation or transfer to a novel composite figure — pair with the construction activities above.
sourceClaims: Pupils commonly confuse area and perimeter, which for circles surfaces as swapping circumference (a length) with area (square units)

Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r
learnerActions: Match each circle to its correct circumference and area expressions, watching for distractors that use πr² for circumference or 2πr for area.
Answer a question whose tempting wrong choice uses the diameter in πr² — reject it by halving to the radius first.
For each completed calculation, label the result with its unit and justify: a distance round is cm, a covering is cm².
Given a diameter, first find the radius before applying πr².
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping the two formulae distinct and attaching correct units (cm for circumference, cm² for area) consolidates the derived understanding, while converting a given diameter to a radius before using πr² guards the most common slip.

constraints: Learners should be able to convert between radius and diameter (d = 2r) and to find the area of a rectangle before this topic; semicircle composite work also builds on perimeter/area of composite shapes.

Recognition and matching tasks (matching circles to formulae, multiple-choice with distractors) are useful for rehearsal and assessment but do not require independent derivation or application to a novel figure; they should supplement, not replace, the measurement, wedge-rearranging, and composite-construction activities.

A static labelled circle with tap-to-reveal can name radius, diameter and circumference and display both formulae, but cannot let a learner derive π, rearrange the wedges, or apply the formulae to a new shape — treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main learning activity.

Paper circles and string-and-tin measurements are physical approximations of ideal plane figures (paper and card have slight thickness); use them to approximate the mathematical circle and reason about the represented figure rather than the physical cutout.

Interactive features named here (roll-the-circle animation, drag-the-wedges tool, radius/diameter toggle, composite-shape builder, unit labels) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative, not mandatory; the same insights are reachable with physical materials and sketching.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles/misconceptions rather than proving any specific activity was tested or superior to another medium.

Worked values were independently checked: for a diameter of 10 cm, r = 5 cm, A = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² and C = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm; using the diameter wrongly gives π × 10² = 100π ≈ 314 cm². For the composite shape (10×4 rectangle, semicircle of diameter 4 ⇒ r = 2): area = 40 + ½π·2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm²; the semicircle arc = ½·π·4 = 2π. These match the source's correctAnswer.

The KS3 national-curriculum source is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited only for the composite-shape objective in the composite activity, with the verified NCTM claim supporting the radius-is-half-diameter decomposition principle. No efficacy is claimed for it, and it is a topical/curriculum requirement rather than a teaching-principle claim.

The original source claimed a 3D artefact 'adds nothing' and that unscripted dialogue does not serve this skill; these were catalog fit judgements and have been softened — circle circumference and area are planar, so 3D is not required here, and calculation practice benefits from doing-and-checking, but no universal claim of necessity or exclusion is asserted.

The source stated a static tap-to-reveal image 'cannot' let the child derive or apply; retained only as a narrowly scoped affordance limitation (it is a reference scaffold), not as a universal law about static images.

probeDeeper: 'You were given the diameter — why can't you put it straight into πr²?' — forcing the radius/diameter distinction
'Which of your answers is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?' — separating circumference from area
'If the radius doubled, what happens to the circumference, and what happens to the area?' — a counterexample exposing square-vs-linear growth (area ×4, not ×2)
'Roughly how many diameters fit around the edge of a circle, and what do we call that number?' — probing π as a ratio
assess.correctAnswer: (a) C = π×10 = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm; A = π×5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm². (b) radius = 5 cm, so A = π×5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² (NOT π×10²). (c) perimeter = the rectangle's exposed edges plus the semicircle arc (½×π×4 = 2π), with no straight edge where the semicircle sits; area = 10×4 + ½×π×2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm². π is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, a little over 3. Circumference in cm, area in cm².

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses radius and diameter — substitutes the diameter where the radius is needed ('the size across is 10, so r² is 10²')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach d = 2r and make 'which do I have, which does the formula need?' an explicit first step; halve a diameter to the radius before substituting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (b) computes π×10² = 100π instead of π×5²; uses the full width in πr²

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps the circumference and area formulae — uses πr² for circumference or 2πr (or πd) for area
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor each formula to what it measures — circumference is the distance round (a length, from πd), area is the covering (square units, from πr²); derive both so they are not two lookalike strings
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports the circumference in square units or the area as a linear multiple of the radius; the two answers are switched

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets to square the radius, or 'squares' by doubling — treats r² as 2r or as the diameter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make squaring explicit as r × r (the area of a little square), distinct from doubling; show the area is a covering that grows with r², not the diameter
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a)/(b) computes π×2×5 or π×10 for the area instead of π×5²; equates r² with the diameter

errorPatterns.pattern: On the composite shape, uses the semicircle's DIAMETER as its radius, or includes/omits the wrong edges in the perimeter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Decompose explicitly: label each part, identify the semicircle's radius (half its diameter), and trace the actual boundary for the perimeter, arc replacing the covered edge
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (c) uses r = 4 for the semicircle, or adds a straight edge where the arc replaces it (or omits the arc)

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives area in linear units or circumference in square units
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'a distance round is cm, a covering is cm²'; check the unit against what was calculated rather than reteaching
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Method correct but the unit is wrong — cm for an area or cm² for a circumference

responseLevels.gap: Cannot calculate reliably — uses the diameter in πr², swaps circumference and area, or doubles instead of squaring; units muddled
responseLevels.full: Calculates circumference and area correctly, converting diameter to radius as needed, keeps the two formulae distinct and can explain π as a ratio and A = πr² informally, handles composite shapes with circular parts, and uses correct linear/square units — transferring to a novel composite figure
responseLevels.partial: Uses the formulae correctly when handed the radius directly, but is caught by a diameter-given problem, cannot say why the formulae work or what π is, or mishandles the semicircle in a composite shape — has two formulae as strings, not a derived, distinguished pair

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a calculator and three tasks: (a) a circle with radius 5 cm — find its circumference and its area; (b) a circle given by its DIAMETER of 10 cm — find its area; (c) a composite shape: a rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm with a semicircle of diameter 4 cm on one short end — find the perimeter and the area. Also ask them to explain, roughly, what π has to do with a circle. Watch whether they use the radius (not the diameter) in πr², whether they keep circumference and area formulae apart, whether they square rather than double the radius, and whether they use square units for area.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands halves the diameter to a radius before using πr² and keeps the two formulae distinct; a child with the classic error uses the diameter in the area formula (π×10² = 314) or squares πr rather than r, giving a wildly different answer traceable to one mistake. The diameter-given circle (b) directly separates those who track radius vs diameter, and asking about π distinguishes derived understanding from formula-recall.

sources.claim: Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r
sources.source: NCTM, 'Discovering the Area Formula for Circles' (Illuminations/ARCs)

sources.claim: Learners confuse 'squaring' the radius with 'doubling' it (treating r² as equivalent to the diameter), reason about area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and hold vague notions of π rather than seeing it as the ratio of circumference to diameter
sources.source: Cox & Lo (2019), 'Measurement and Decomposition: Making Sense of the Area of a Circle', PME-NA 41 (ERIC ED606937)

sources.claim: Pupils commonly confuse area and perimeter, which for circles surfaces as swapping circumference (a length) with area (square units)
sources.source: Machaba (2016), 'The concepts of area and perimeter: insights and misconceptions', ERIC EJ1209134

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should calculate the circumference and area of circles and solve problems involving the perimeters and areas of composite shapes that include circular parts
sources.source: National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study (KS3)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Grouping Materials

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 'Everyday materials'):** Pupils should be taught to "compare and group together a variety of everyday materials on the basis of their simple physical properties." Non-statutory guidance expects pupils to "sort objects and materials into simple groups" and to explore and compare using the property vocabulary (hard/soft, shiny/dull, waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque, etc.).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." The clarification frames classifying as finding "patterns" — shared observable properties — across materials. DCI PS1.A: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." CCC: Patterns.

- **Operational details:** Move children from describing one material to comparing several and sorting them by a chosen property. Start with a single clear criterion (transparent vs opaque; waterproof vs absorbent) so groups are unambiguous, then compare two materials directly ('what is the same, what is different?'). Insist the child STATES the sorting rule and justifies each placement with a property word ('I put the window with the glass because you can see through both'). Crucially, re-sort the SAME set by a new property so children learn that grouping depends on the rule chosen, not on a fixed identity of the object. This is the first appearance of the compare-and-classify skill that recurs through states of matter, rocks and beyond.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can sort a set of materials by a chosen property, compare two materials naming a shared and a differing property, and explain a grouping decision in property words — and can re-group the same set by a different property when asked.
bestPractices: Begin with one clear either/or property (transparent vs opaque) so the sorting rule is unambiguous before introducing finer distinctions.
Require the child to name the sorting rule and justify each placement with a property word, making the reasoning explicit rather than intuitive.
Re-sort the same materials by a different property so children learn that groups depend on the chosen rule, not on a fixed property of the object — the core of the Patterns crosscutting concept.
Use direct pair comparison ('same/different') as a stepping stone from describing one material to grouping many.
Keep the sort hands-on with real materials and physical hoops/trays; concrete sorting is the KS1 route into classification.
Include ambiguous or multi-property items to prompt discussion ('could this go in either group? why?'), treating disagreement as reasoning practice.
keyRepresentations: Sorting hoops / trays labelled by a property (transparent | opaque)
A two-material compare frame: 'same' column and 'different' column
A regroupable set the child sorts, then re-sorts by a new property
A simple Carroll/Venn-style two-way mat for a later 'shiny AND hard' sort
Property-word tags the child attaches to each group to state the rule
commonMisconceptions: Believing a material has one fixed group, not realising the same set re-sorts differently when the property changes (a Patterns-concept hurdle).
Sorting by the object's identity or use (all the cups together) instead of by the stated physical property.
Grouping by irrelevant surface features (colour, size) rather than the chosen property.
Placing an item without a rule — grouping intuitively and being unable to justify it in property words.
Assuming a material can only ever be in one group, so an item that is both shiny and hard can't belong to two overlapping sorts.

learn.summary: For 5–6 year olds learning to compare and group everyday materials by simple physical properties. The core objective is that children sort a real set of materials by a stated property, justify each placement with a property word, and — crucially — re-sort the SAME set by a different property to discover that groups depend on the chosen rule, not on a fixed identity of the object. Activities centre on hands-on sorting with real materials; a drag-to-sort surface, a tap-to-reveal illustrated sort, and a short categorisation check are included as complementary supports with their limits noted.

activities.title: Sort real materials, then re-sort by a new rule
feedback: If the rule drifts mid-sort (starts by colour, slips to size or 'ones I like'), pause and have the child say their ONE rule aloud and hold it up, then re-run the sort against that fixed rule — the idea is fine, the procedure just needs anchoring.

If the child sorts by what objects are FOR ('the cup and jar go together because they hold things'), redirect to 'what is it MADE of / what is it LIKE to touch?'; if it persists, practise describing one material's properties before grouping.

If the child treats each material as having one permanent home and cannot re-sort, make the same object land in different groups in front of them — foil with the wood under 'see-through vs not see-through' (neither is see-through), foil with the fabric and sponge under 'bendy vs stiff' — so the group is seen to follow the chosen property.
Praise naming the rule and justifying placements with property words, not just getting items in the 'right' pile.
activities.rationale: Hands-on sorting of real materials and physical hoops/trays is the KS1 route into classification, and re-sorting the identical set by a new property makes the Patterns idea (groups depend on the chosen rule) enactable rather than told. Insisting the child states the rule and justifies with property words makes reasoning explicit.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y1 statutory requirement: pupils taught to 'compare and group together a variety of everyday materials on the basis of their simple physical properties'; sort into simple groups.
NGSS 2-PS1-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]'; classifying = finding patterns of shared properties; CCC Patterns; DCI PS1.A.
Documented KS1 misconceptions: sorting by object identity/use or by irrelevant surface features rather than the stated property; not realising the same set regroups under a different rule.
learnerActions: Lay out a tray of real materials: wood block, glass jar, metal key, plastic toy, sponge, foil, fabric.
Choose ONE property and say the rule out loud before touching anything (e.g. 'see-through vs not see-through').
Sort every item into two hoops or trays, saying a property word for each placement ('I put the glass jar with the clear plastic toy because you can see through both').
Now sort the SAME items again, but pick a DIFFERENT property (e.g. bendy vs stiff, or hard vs softer). Notice which items move home.

Point out an item that changed groups and say why (e.g. 'the foil was with the wood for not see-through, but with the fabric and sponge for bendy'; the glass only leaves the plastic under 'hard' if the plastic toy is soft or squashy).

If you are ready, use two overlapping hoops labelled with two different properties (e.g. 'shiny' and 'hard') and put an item that has both, such as the metal key, in the overlap; an either/or pair like see-through vs not see-through or bendy vs stiff has no true overlap.
activities.intendedInsight: A group is not a fixed fact about an object; it depends on the property you choose to look at. The same material can belong with different partners under different rules.

activities.title: Same-and-different pair comparison
feedback: If the child names a use or feeling ('I like it') instead of a property, ask 'what is it like — hard or soft? shiny or dull? see-through or not?'
Accept any defensible property as long as it is a property of the material, and check the 'same' and 'different' entries actually match the two items.
activities.rationale: Direct pair comparison ('what is the same, what is different?') is a recommended stepping stone from describing one material to grouping many, and keeps the property vocabulary active.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y1 statutory requirement: pupils taught to 'compare and group together a variety of everyday materials on the basis of their simple physical properties'; sort into simple groups.
learnerActions: Take just two materials at a time (e.g. glass jar and clear plastic toy; or wood block and metal key).
Say one property they SHARE ('both are hard' or 'you can see through both').
Say one property where they DIFFER ('the glass is see-through but the wood is not').
Record each in a 'same' column and a 'different' column, using property words.
Repeat with other pairs so comparing becomes a stepping stone into sorting a larger jumble.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing two materials by naming a shared and a differing property is the bridge from describing one material to grouping many.

activities.title: Read a finished sort and explain each placement (illustrated support)
feedback: Prompt the child to use a property word for each item, not just 'it goes there'.
Use the two arrangements to ask 'why did this one move?' so the rule-dependence is noticed, not just shown.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal illustrated sort can show a finished grouping and voice the property reasons, which reinforces vocabulary for pre-readers, and the second re-sorted arrangement targets the documented misconception that the same set cannot regroup under a new rule. Treated here as a support: it illustrates grouping but does not elicit the child's own sorting decisions, so pair it with the hands-on activity.
sourceClaims: Documented KS1 misconceptions: sorting by object identity/use or by irrelevant surface features rather than the stated property; not realising the same set regroups under a different rule.
learnerActions: Look at a completed transparent/opaque grouping of pictured materials.
Tap or point to any item to hear or say the property reason it sits where it does ('this is here because you can see through it').
Then look at the same items shown re-sorted by a new rule (e.g. waterproof vs absorbent) and notice which pictures moved.
Say which item changed group and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Each group follows a property rule, and the same items can be arranged differently under a different rule — reinforcing the vocabulary and hinting at rule-dependence.

activities.title: Drag-to-sort bench with a swappable rule (optional interactive support)
feedback: For an unambiguous either/or sort, immediate right/wrong feedback can confirm whether a placement obeys the current rule; always have the child state the rule before sorting so feedback is about the reasoning.
Ambiguous or multi-property items are not errors — route them to the 'both'/overlap zone and treat them as a discussion prompt ('could this go in either group? why?') rather than marking them wrong.
When an item moves after the rule change, draw attention to it: 'last time the metal was with the wood — why is it with the glass now?'
activities.rationale: A drag-and-sort surface with live state and a re-sort control lets a child enact the rule change and watch the same items redistribute, which a static picture cannot do. Offered as one good vehicle, not the only way: real-material sorting delivers the same core experience with tactile handling.
sourceClaims: Documented KS1 misconceptions: sorting by object identity/use or by irrelevant surface features rather than the stated property; not realising the same set regroups under a different rule.
learnerActions: Drag a jumble of pictured materials into two bins labelled 'transparent' and 'opaque' — glass and clear plastic to one side, wood and metal to the other — saying why each goes where.
Press a 'change the rule' control so the bins relabel to 'waterproof' and 'absorbent' and the items scatter, then sort the very SAME materials again.

Notice an item that genuinely changes partners — for example the metal key, which sat in the 'opaque' group with the wood but now joins the glass and plastic in the 'waterproof' group, while the wood (shown as bare, unvarnished wood, which slowly soaks up water) moves to 'absorbent'.

Use a 'both / not sure' zone for a borderline item, such as wood that soaks up water only slowly, and discuss it; for items that truly have two properties at once, use two non-opposite labels such as 'shiny' and 'hard' (for children ready to go further).
activities.intendedInsight: Switching the rule and watching the same set redistribute makes directly experienceable that groups depend on the chosen property.

activities.title: Quick categorisation and odd-one-out check
feedback: For odd-one-out, require the property reason, not just the choice.
This checks one sort at a time; follow any check with a live re-sort by a new rule to see whether the child understands rule-dependence.
activities.rationale: A categorisation step is itself a grouping task and scores cleanly; odd-one-out and compare-pair matching probe comparison. Used for assessment of applying a single rule, it does not by itself stage the re-sort realisation, so it complements rather than replaces the hands-on activity.
learnerActions: Drag or place items into two property bins to show you can apply a single rule.
Answer an 'odd one out by property' question (which one does not belong, and which property makes it the odd one?).
Match a compare-pair: given two items, say the shared property.
For pre-readers, use pictures with spoken labels.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can demonstrate they sort by a single stated property and spot shared or differing properties.

constraints: Begin with one clear either/or property (transparent vs opaque) so the sorting rule is unambiguous before introducing finer distinctions.
Always require the child to name the sorting rule aloud and justify each placement with a property word — the reasoning must be explicit, not intuitive.
The re-sort of the SAME set by a new property is the central objective; do not substitute a single sort for it.

When demonstrating that an item changes partners under a new rule, choose a pair that actually separates under that rule (e.g. foil leaves the wood and joins the fabric and sponge under 'bendy vs stiff'; metal leaves the wood and joins the glass under 'waterproof' if the wood is bare, since bare wood soaks up some water but varnished or painted wood may not). Glass leaves the plastic and joins the metal under 'hard' only if the plastic item is soft or bendy, because a rigid plastic toy is also hard. Do not claim two items separate under a rule they both satisfy (glass and clear plastic are both transparent AND both waterproof, so they stay together under either).
Include ambiguous or multi-property items to prompt discussion ('could this go in either group? why?'), treating disagreement as reasoning practice rather than as a scoring error.

Illustrated tap-to-reveal and categorisation formats can reinforce vocabulary or check a single sort, but recognition and viewing do not elicit the child's own sorting decisions or the re-grouping experience; pair them with hands-on sorting.

A screen drag-to-sort surface and physical hoops with real materials offer different affordances (immediate feedback and easy rule-swapping vs tactile handling); either can carry the core experience, so do not treat one as universally necessary.
Watch the child sort rather than only asking about it, so shifting or object-based criteria that a verbal answer would hide are caught.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources (NGSS 2-PS1-1 and the STEM Learning misconceptions page) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their claims as unconfirmed.

The original row asserted a static picture 'cannot' do the re-sort, that 3D 'adds no conceptual value', and that dialogue 'cannot deliver' the manipulation. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established facts; softened here to narrow affordance/limit statements. A fixed illustration can still teach vocabulary, and different media offer different experiences.
The original claimed re-sorting 'directly' produces the moment of insight. Retained as a strong pedagogical aim, not as a guaranteed outcome.
The worked justification example was adapted from the original 'window with the glass' to 'glass jar with the clear plastic toy' so it matches the stated material tray; meaning is unchanged.

Corrected a factual slip in the drag-to-sort example: the original recommendation claimed glass, grouped with the plastic under 'see-through', 'lands in a different place' under 'waterproof vs absorbent'. Glass and clear plastic are both waterproof and would stay together; the example was changed to the metal key moving between groups. The clean glass-separates-from-plastic contrast remains tied to the hard/soft rule.

Classifying a rigid clear plastic toy as 'softer' than glass is a relative KS1 comparison implied by the original's 'glass with metal under hard' example; phrased as a relative comparison rather than an absolute category.

probeDeeper: Could this glass jar go in the OTHER group if we picked a different rule? Which rule would move it?
Why did you put these two together — what is the same about them?
I'm going to move the foil into the other group — is that allowed under YOUR rule, or not?
If your rule is 'bendy', where does the sponge go — and how did you check whether it bends?
assess.correctAnswer: Sorts consistently by a single stated property (e.g. see-through vs not), names the rule, then re-sorts the identical set by a different property (e.g. bendy vs stiff) — showing that the groups depend on the property chosen, not on fixed identities of the materials.

errorPatterns.pattern: Criterion drifts mid-sort — starts grouping by colour, then quietly switches to size or 'ones I like', without noticing the rule changed.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: 'Say your ONE rule out loud first', write/hold it up, then re-run the sort against that fixed rule. The concept is intact; the procedure needs anchoring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The finished groups don't obey any single rule; items placed early and late follow different logics.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sorts by object type or use rather than material property — 'the cup and the jar go together because they hold things'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect to 'what is it MADE of / what is it LIKE to touch?'; if it persists, reteach the property-describing step before grouping.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Groups reflect what the objects are FOR, not a material property; property words are absent from the reasoning.

errorPatterns.pattern: Each material has one permanent group — 'glass is a see-through thing, that's where it goes' — so the child cannot re-sort the same set under a new rule.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the same object land in different groups under different rules on the table in front of them (glass with plastic under 'see-through', glass with metal under 'hard') so groups are seen to follow the chosen property.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the second sort, struggles or refuses; tries to reproduce the first grouping.

responseLevels.gap: Groups by vague, shifting or like/dislike reasons, or by what objects are used for; cannot state a rule.
responseLevels.full: Sorts by a chosen property with a clear stated rule AND re-sorts the identical set under a different property, articulating that the groups depend on the property chosen.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts consistently by one property and names the rule, but cannot re-group the SAME set by a new property — treats each material's group as fixed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out a tray of materials (wood block, glass jar, metal key, plastic toy, sponge, foil, fabric). Say: 'Sort these into two groups using ONE property you choose, and tell me your rule.' Watch them do it. Then: 'Now sort the SAME things again, but pick a DIFFERENT property this time.' Watch whether they can re-group the identical set.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The re-sort is the tell. A child who can only place each material in one 'correct' home cannot re-group the same set; a child who understands grouping-by-property applies one consistent rule, names it, and cheerfully reshuffles the SAME items under a new rule. Watching (not asking about) the sort catches shifting or object-based criteria a verbal answer would hide.

pedagogy.summary: Comparing and ordering fractions with different numerators AND denominators, using either a common denominator (rename both with equivalent fractions, then compare numerators) or benchmark reasoning (is each fraction less than, equal to, or more than 1/2 — or near 0 or 1?). Benchmarks are fast and build number sense; common denominators are general. Conclusions are justified with visual models. This is a known hard skill — on the 2004 NAEP, 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions from least to greatest.
bestPractices: Teach benchmark reasoning with 0, 1/2 and 1: decide which side of 1/2 each fraction sits on (5/8 > 1/2 because 5 is more than half of 8; 3/7 < 1/2) (IES Rec 3).
Teach the common-denominator method as renaming both fractions with equivalents, then comparing numerators.
Use minimally-labelled number lines (0, 1/2, 1) for landmark placement, and dual-labelled lines (one unit sequence above, another below) for different denominators (IES Rec 2).
Choose the strategy to fit the numbers — benchmarks when they straddle 1/2, common denominator when they are close.
Keep the same-numerator shortcut available (2/3 > 2/5).
Justify with a model and guard against whole-number bias.
keyRepresentations: Common denominator via equivalent-fraction renaming
Number line marked 0, 1/2, 1 (benchmark lane)
Dual-labelled number line for different denominators
Ratio table / times-tables for the common multiple
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone (3/8 vs 5/12 → '5 > 3 so 5/12 is bigger', or '12 > 8 so smaller') (IES)
Comparing without a common denominator (cross-adding, or comparing tops and bottoms separately)
Renaming only one fraction, or using a non-common multiple
Benchmark misapplied — e.g. judging 3/7 > 1/2

learn.summary: Learners compare and order fractions with different numerators and denominators using two complementary strategies: (1) renaming both fractions to a common denominator and comparing numerators, and (2) benchmark reasoning with 0, 1/2, and 1 (deciding which side of 1/2 each fraction sits on, or whether it is near 0 or 1). Benchmarks are quick and build number sense; common denominators are general-purpose. Conclusions are justified with visual models (partitioned bars, number lines). The core misconception to guard against is whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone. This is a known hard skill: on the 2004 NAEP, 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions from least to greatest.

activities.title: Strategy workbench: common denominator OR benchmark
feedback: If a learner compares numerators and denominators separately or cross-adds, show that only a shared denominator licenses comparing the top numbers — re-partition both bars to the same grid and compare again.

If a learner renames only one fraction or uses a denominator that is not a common multiple of both, point out both fractions must reach the SAME denominator; verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence.
If a learner misplaces a fraction relative to 1/2 (e.g. calls 3/7 more than 1/2), have them compare the numerator to half the denominator: half of 7 is 3.5, and 3 is less than 3.5, so 3/7 < 1/2.
Confirm correct reasoning by asking them to justify with the visual model, not just the final symbols.
activities.rationale: The IES/WWC guide recommends benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 as reference points and number lines (minimally-labelled for landmarks; dual-labelled for different denominators) to support comparison, and names whole-number bias as the core misconception. Offering both renaming and benchmark strategies lets learners pick the efficient method and build general competence.
sourceClaims: Comparing/ordering fractions is a key indicator of understanding and is hard (2004 NAEP: 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions least-to-greatest); benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 are recommended reference points, dual-labelled and minimally-labelled number lines support comparison of different denominators, and whole-number bias is the core misconception.
learnerActions: Take a pair such as 3/8 versus 5/12. Choose the common-denominator path: re-partition both bars (on paper or with a model) to the same fine grid — twenty-fourths — so 3/8 becomes 9/24 and 5/12 becomes 10/24, then compare the numerators 9 versus 10.

Take a pair such as 5/8 versus 3/7. Choose the benchmark path: place each on a number line marked 0, 1/2, 1. Decide which side of 1/2 each sits on (5/8 is more than 1/2 because 5 is more than half of 8; 3/7 is less than 1/2 because 3 is less than half of 7).
Switch into an ordering task: drag or write three or more fractions (e.g. 2/3, 3/5, 7/10) onto a line or into order, choosing whichever strategy fits the numbers.
State, for each comparison, which strategy you chose and why it suited those particular numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Renaming two fractions to the same denominator makes them directly comparable (the comparison collapses to comparing numerators), and the 1/2 benchmark settles many comparisons at a glance without full computation. Choosing the strategy to fit the numbers is part of the skill.

activities.title: Dual-labelled and benchmark number lines
feedback: If a learner places a fraction on the wrong side of 1/2, return to comparing the numerator with half the denominator.
If a learner is unsure whether a fraction is near 0 or near 1, check how close the numerator is to 0 or to the denominator (e.g. 1/5 is near 0, 4/5 is near 1).
If a learner struggles to compare across the two denominators, align the two labelled sequences and read off which mark lies further right.
activities.rationale: IES/WWC recommends minimally-labelled number lines for landmark placement and dual-labelled lines for comparing different denominators. A reference line aids recall and placement; note it does not by itself carry out a full ordering or re-partition, so pair it with the active strategies above.
sourceClaims: Comparing/ordering fractions is a key indicator of understanding and is hard (2004 NAEP: 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions least-to-greatest); benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 are recommended reference points, dual-labelled and minimally-labelled number lines support comparison of different denominators, and whole-number bias is the core misconception.
learnerActions: Use a number line marked only 0, 1/2, 1 and place common fractions where they belong relative to those landmarks; for each, say whether it is more than, equal to, or less than one half.
Decide whether 4/9 is more or less than a half by comparing 4 with half of 9 (4.5): 4 is less than 4.5, so 4/9 < 1/2 — no common denominator needed.
Order 1/5, 4/5, 5/9 using only benchmarks: 1/5 sits just above 0, 5/9 is just over 1/2 (5 is more than 4.5), and 4/5 is near 1, giving 1/5 < 5/9 < 4/5.
For two different denominators, use a dual-labelled line (one unit sequence of marks above the line, the other below) to see where each fraction falls and which is larger.
Explain how the landmarks 0, 1/2 and 1 let you decide a comparison without finding a common denominator.
activities.intendedInsight: A number line anchored to 0, 1/2 and 1 gives fractions a magnitude and a 'side of 1/2' (and a sense of nearness to 0 or 1), so many comparisons can be read off directly; dual labelling lets two different denominators be compared on one line.

activities.title: Check and consolidate ordering and benchmark decisions
feedback: If a learner orders by single digits ('7/10 is smallest because 10 is biggest'), rename all three to a common denominator or place them on a 0/½/1 line and compare magnitudes.
If a learner grinds a full common-denominator computation for 5/8 vs 3/7, prompt the quicker 1/2 benchmark.
Reward correct answers that also carry a model-based justification.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fill-in tasks efficiently check whether learners can apply each strategy and avoid whole-number bias, and surface whether a learner works in only one register (benchmark or common denominator). These checks confirm application but do not, on their own, elicit the independent construction that the workbench tasks require.
learnerActions: Order a set such as 2/3, 3/5, 7/10 from smallest to largest and show working (e.g. common denominator 30: 3/5 = 18/30, 2/3 = 20/30, 7/10 = 21/30, giving 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10).
Answer a quick benchmark question: 'Is 5/8 more or less than 1/2?' and justify.
Rename both fractions of a pair to a shared common denominator before comparing, and check the order you get.
Sort a set of fractions into 'less than 1/2' and 'more than 1/2'.
Keep the same-numerator shortcut in play: with equal numerators, the larger denominator gives the smaller fraction (2/3 > 2/5).
Check that a different common denominator does not change the order (e.g. using 60 instead of 30 gives the same ordering).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent comparison means ordering correctly, choosing an efficient strategy, and justifying with a model — not just getting a final symbol right. Any valid common denominator yields the same order.

constraints: Learners must reach fractions with DIFFERENT numerators and denominators; same-denominator or same-numerator pairs alone are stepping stones, not the full objective.
Both strategies should be available: benchmark reasoning when fractions straddle 1/2 or sit near 0 or 1, and common denominators when fractions are close together or benchmarks do not separate them.

A benchmark/reference number line with fractions pre-placed is a recall and placement scaffold; it does not re-partition fractions or carry out an ordering, so it must be combined with active renaming and ordering work.

Recognition-only responses (multiple choice, sorting, fill-in) check application but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a full ordering with justification; include a task where the learner produces the ordering and its reasoning.
Always require justification with a visual model and explicitly guard against whole-number bias (ordering by numerator or denominator alone).
Verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence and ensure both fractions reach the same common multiple.

Comparing a fixed numerator (as in same-numerator pairs) with a fixed denominator varies different quantities; there is no 'denominator rule that flips', so explain each comparison by magnitude rather than a sign-flip rule.

Live re-partitioning of bars to a shared grid and drag-to-order on a line are example interaction mechanisms that make the strategies concrete; they are illustrative, not required mechanisms — the same work can be done with drawn bars and written orderings.

Interpret this content for approximately ages 9–10; in the England curriculum Year 5 pupils compare and order fractions whose denominators are all multiples of the same number, and Year 6 extends this to comparing and ordering fractions more generally, including fractions greater than 1 (source marked unverified).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The IES/WWC claim is marked verified in the source row; the England National Curriculum claim is marked unverified — treat the age/year-stage framing accordingly.
Restored two benchmark-only examples (4/9 vs 1/2; ordering 1/5, 4/5, 5/9) from the original assessment so the 'near 0 or 1' landmarks are actually exercised, not merely asserted.

The consolidation activity's sourceClaims are [] because its rationale concerns recognition-task efficacy, which no source claim directly supports; the IES/WWC claim is retained only on the two activities whose rationales it does support (benchmarks, number lines, whole-number bias).

Non-preferred artefact alternatives (quiz-style checks, reference-only image line, and the noted poor fit of 3D and in-role dialogue for this planar, doing-based task) are preserved as scaffolds/limits rather than as universal pedagogical laws; a sort can check classification into </>1/2 but does not itself elicit a full justified ordering.

probeDeeper: Why does giving both fractions the same denominator let you just compare the top numbers?
Is 4/9 more or less than a half? How can you tell without a common denominator?
You used 30 as the common denominator — could a different common denominator work? Would the order change?
Order these using only benchmarks, no calculation: 1/5, 4/5, 5/9.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10 (common denominator 30: 3/5 = 18/30, 2/3 = 20/30, 7/10 = 21/30). And 5/8 > 3/7, because 5/8 is more than 1/2 (5 is more than half of 8) while 3/7 is less than 1/2 (3 is less than half of 7).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — orders by numerator or denominator alone ('7/10 is smallest because 10 is biggest')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rename all three to a common denominator, or place them on a 0/½/1 line, and compare magnitudes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders without renaming, using single digits

errorPatterns.pattern: Renames only one fraction or uses a non-common denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Both fractions must be renamed to the SAME denominator; verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts one fraction but not the other, or compares over different denominators

errorPatterns.pattern: Benchmark misapplied — 'judges 3/7 to be more than 1/2'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the numerator to half the denominator (half of 7 is 3.5, so 3/7 < 1/2)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts 3/7 on the wrong side of 1/2

responseLevels.gap: Orders by single digits (numerator or denominator); benchmark reasoning absent or wrong.
responseLevels.full: Orders correctly via common denominators (or sound benchmark reasoning) and settles 5/8 vs 3/7 with 1/2 without full computation, justifying both and selecting the efficient strategy for the numbers.
responseLevels.partial: Uses a common denominator correctly for the ordering but cannot apply the 1/2 benchmark efficiently (grinds or errs), or benchmarks but cannot carry out a general common-denominator comparison — works in only one register.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Task: order these three fractions from smallest to largest and show your working — 2/3, 3/5, 7/10. Then use the benchmark 1/2 to decide quickly which is larger: 5/8 or 3/7. I'll watch which methods you use.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who renames to a common denominator (or reasons by benchmarks) orders correctly and settles 5/8 vs 3/7 with 1/2, without full computation. A whole-number-bias child orders by numerators or denominators alone; a child lacking benchmark sense grinds a common denominator for 5/8 vs 3/7 or misjudges which side of 1/2 they fall.

sources.claim: Comparing/ordering fractions is a key indicator of understanding and is hard (2004 NAEP: 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions least-to-greatest); benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 are recommended reference points, dual-labelled and minimally-labelled number lines support comparison of different denominators, and whole-number bias is the core misconception.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K-8 (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)
