pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten → Year 1). THE SUCCESSOR PRINCIPLE — each successive counting number represents a quantity ONE LARGER than the previous (and one less going back). Turns the flat count sequence into a structure of +1 steps; the seed of the number line, counting-on and early addition/subtraction.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'given a number, identify 1 more and 1 less'; represent numbers on the number line (Y1). EYFS 'Numerical Patterns' (one more / one less within 10). Extends to 10-more/10-less (Y2–Y3).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.4c verbatim — 'Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.'
• Operational details: Link the spoken sequence to quantity change — add exactly ONE object and the count moves to the next word; on a number line/track +1 is a step right, −1 a step left. Teach 'one more' and 'one less' TOGETHER as inverse moves. Counting-on (from 5, 'one more' = 6 without restarting at 1) is the payoff and depends on cardinality. Use a staircase/tower image (each step one cube taller).
• Checkpoint: Tier A (4–5) given ≤5 objects, knows adding one makes the next number ('one more than 4 is 5'). Tier B (5–6) gives one more AND one less for numbers to 10 without recounting from 1. Tier C (6) explains one step along the number line is +1 and links it to counting-on for addition.
bestPractices: Pair the word-step with a quantity-step: add exactly one object as you say the next number, so 'the next number' MEANS 'one more thing'.
Teach one-more and one-less as inverse moves on the same model (number track hops right/left), not as two unrelated facts.
Make counting-on explicit: from a known total, say the next number WITHOUT restarting at one — this requires cardinality and bridges to addition.
Use a staircase / number track so +1 is a single visible step; contrast with a two-step jump (foreshadows skip counting).
Ask prediction questions ('if we add one more cube, what number?') before acting, then check — builds the expectation that each step is exactly one.
keyRepresentations: Number track / number line (steps of one; right = more, left = less).
Cube tower / staircase (each step one taller).
Ten-frame filled one cell at a time.
'One more / one less' arrow cards or a +1/−1 machine.
commonMisconceptions: Recounting from 1 to find 'one more' instead of counting-on (successor not yet linked to cardinality).
Knowing 'one more' but not 'one less' — the backward direction lags because the string is learned forward only.
Treating 'one more' as merely 'the next word I say' rather than a quantity one larger (fails when the count starts wrong).
Not realising every step is exactly one — thinking numbers grow by an inconsistent amount.

learn.summary: For ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten to Year 1): the successor principle — each successive counting number names a quantity exactly ONE larger than the one before, and going back one is one less. The aim is to turn the flat count sequence into a structure of +1 / −1 steps, laying the ground for the number line, counting-on and early addition/subtraction. Teach 'one more' and 'one less' together as inverse moves, link the spoken word-step to an actual quantity-step, and build towards counting-on (finding 'one more than 5' as 6 without restarting at 1).

activities.title: One more, one less in lockstep
feedback: If a learner adds one cube but names a number that skips ahead (e.g. says '10' after 6), pause and count the cubes together: adding one object moves the count to the very next word only.

If a learner can give 'one more' easily but stalls on 'one less', treat the backward direction as its own game on the same track rather than as a failure — counting back develops separately and matures with practice.
When a prediction matches the result, name the structure out loud: 'Each step added exactly one, so the number went up by one.'
If the learner struggles with a decade boundary such as 'one more than 9', slow down and step the marker one place so they see 9 then 10 is a single step.
activities.rationale: Pairing the spoken word-step with an added object makes 'the next number' mean 'one more thing', and enacting both directions on one shared model presents one-more and one-less as inverse moves rather than two unrelated facts. Prediction-then-check builds the expectation that each step is exactly one.
sourceClaims: K.CC.4c: 'Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.'
Year 1: 'given a number, identify 1 more and 1 less'; identify and represent numbers using the number line.
Counting-on and the number line as steps of one are foundational representations bridging counting to addition/subtraction (concrete–pictorial–abstract).
learnerActions: Build a tower with cubes (or fill a ten-frame one cell at a time) and say the count as you go.
Before adding, predict: 'If I add one more cube, what number will it be?' Then add exactly one cube and check that the count moves to the next word.
Add one cube and say the next number in the same beat, so that 'the next number' means 'one more thing'.
Now remove one cube and say the number that is one less, naming it as the mirror move of adding one.
On a number track, hop a marker (or a frog along lily-pads) exactly one place right for 'one more' and one place left for 'one less'.
activities.intendedInsight: Each successive counting number is a quantity exactly one larger than the previous one, and one back is exactly one smaller; +1 and −1 are a single step in opposite directions on the same track.

activities.title: Counting on from a hidden total
feedback: Correct answer to 7 + 1 is 8, because one more than 7 is the next counting number; adding one moves you one step up the count.

If the learner must open the box and recount from 1, do not force counting-on before it emerges: play 'one more' with a covered set and a number track so they repeatedly see 7→8 as a single step. It matures with practice.
If the learner names a non-successor such as 'ten' or 'lots', reteach with a visible add-one-and-count on a number track, showing 7 then 8 is exactly one step, and anchor 'one more = next number'.
activities.rationale: Hiding the set discourages recounting, so answering without opening the box calls for linking the count sequence to +1 — the heart of counting-on and the bridge from counting to addition. It can also help reveal which learners currently use the successor idea and which still rely on counting from one, though one observation is not a definitive judgement.
sourceClaims: K.CC.4c: 'Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.'
Counting-on and the number line as steps of one are foundational representations bridging counting to addition/subtraction (concrete–pictorial–abstract).
learnerActions: Count a set of objects into a box or under a cover, then agree on how many are inside (e.g. 7).
With the set hidden, drop in exactly one more and answer, without recounting, how many there are now.
Explain how you knew — 'one more than 7 is the next number, 8' — rather than reopening the box.
Try a chain: 'What's one more than 8? And one more than that?' naming each successor without restarting at 1.
Reverse it: 'If I take one back out, how many now?' to practise the predecessor the same way.
activities.intendedInsight: Once you know how many a set has (its cardinality), finding one more is just naming the next counting word — you do not need to recount from one.

activities.title: Reading the staircase and retrieval practice
feedback: Use a reference staircase to confirm answers, but remember a static picture shows the structure for reference and does not itself let the child add or remove one and feel the quantity change; use it alongside enacting the step (on objects or an interactive number track).
For a correct 'one less' answer, affirm that stepping down one place is the mirror of stepping up one.
If an answer treats numbers as growing by an inconsistent amount, return to the single-step model and count along to show each gap is exactly one.
activities.rationale: A labelled staircase and short retrieval prompts consolidate and check the +1/−1 structure after it has been enacted; contrasting a one-step with a two-step move heads off the idea that numbers grow by an inconsistent amount.
sourceClaims: K.CC.4c: 'Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.'
Year 1: 'given a number, identify 1 more and 1 less'; identify and represent numbers using the number line.
learnerActions: Study a staircase/number track labelled 1..10 and describe how each step compares to the one before.
Point to where 'one more' and 'one less' live relative to a chosen number.
Answer quick fill-in prompts: 'One more than 6 is ___', 'One less than 6 is ___', and 'What number comes next after 8?'
Contrast a single step (+1) with a two-step jump, noticing that a jump of two is not 'one more' (an early taste of skip counting).
activities.intendedInsight: The +1 structure is consistent all along the sequence: every step up is one larger and every step down is one smaller; a fixed staircase can show this structure even though you are not building it yourself.

constraints: Teach 'one more' and 'one less' together as inverse moves on the same model (steps right/left on a number track), not as two unrelated facts.
Do not force counting-on before it emerges: count-from-one dependence is developmental and matures with practice, not a deficit to drill.
Treat the predecessor ('one less') as developing separately from the successor; practise it as its own game rather than assuming backward is automatically as easy as forward.

A static staircase or labelled track supports reference and retrieval but does not itself let the child enact the add-one step or feel the quantity change; pair it with enacting the step, whether on physical objects or an interactive number track.

Fill-in and 'what comes next' prompts are useful retrieval and checking companions but assess recall of the successor; recognising an answer is not the same as enacting the quantity change, so pair them with enacting the +1/−1 step (adding or removing one, on objects or an interactive track).
Concrete objects (cubes, counters, marbles in a box) and screen/number-track models offer different experiences; either can support the step — do not present one as the only possible medium.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy source rated a third spatial dimension as adding 'nothing' and framed a fixed staircase and discussion as unable to teach the concept. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited standards; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than asserted as universal pedagogical laws.

Medium-privileging phrasing (treating physical 'building'/'objects' as the required enactment medium) has been scoped so that enactment may occur on objects or an interactive number track; the sources do not establish one medium as superior.

One diagnostic error pattern listed the distractor 'There'd be 10 now.' for 7+1; the correct answer is 8. This is retained only as an example of a non-successor error to recognise, never presented to a learner as a valid answer.
The 'counting-on mode / one-more buttons / live marker' interaction examples from the source are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as required mechanisms.
One supporting claim (NCETM counting-on guidance) was marked unverified in the source; it is cited only to support the general principle, not any claim of tested effectiveness.

probeDeeper: How many if I take ONE marble back out again?
What's one more than 9? And one more than that?
How did you know it was 8 without looking inside?
If I put in two more instead of one, how many? How do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: 8 — because one more than 7 is the next counting number, 8. Adding one moves you one step up the count.

errorPatterns.pattern: says a number for 'one more' that isn't the successor — any bigger number, or a familiar landmark like 10 — doesn't map +1 to the very next word
errorPatterns.nextMove: reteach with concrete add-one-and-count on a number track, showing 7 then 8 is exactly one step along; anchor 'one more = next number'
errorPatterns.distractor: There'd be 10 now.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answers with a non-successor such as 'ten' or 'lots'

errorPatterns.pattern: count-from-one dependence — cannot find one more without recounting the whole set from 1; treats each quantity as a fresh count, not one step along the sequence
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT force counting-on before it emerges — it matures with practice; play 'one more' with a covered set and a number track so the child sees 7→8 as a single step
errorPatterns.revealedBy: needs to see and recount all objects; cannot answer with the box closed

errorPatterns.pattern: successor known but predecessor not — gives 'one more' easily but for 'one less' counts up from the start or stalls; the sequence runs forward only
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat backward as the same skill and drill it as a deficit — it develops separately; practise counting back and 'one less' on the same number track as its own game
errorPatterns.revealedBy: fluent on 'one more', halting or erroring on 'one less than 8'

responseLevels.gap: Must see and recount the whole set to answer; cannot give one more (or one less) from a stated number.
responseLevels.full: Names one more and one less from any given number without recounting, and explains that each next number is one larger and one back is one smaller.
responseLevels.partial: Gives one more from a number reliably but recounts from the start for one less, or falters at a decade boundary (e.g. one more than 9).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: This box has 7 marbles inside — I've told you there are 7, but you can't see them. Now I drop in ONE more marble. Without counting, how many marbles are in the box now? How did you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the successor concept knows +1 lands on the very next number word and answers 8 without seeing or recounting, justifying by 'next after 7'. A child who lacks it must open the box and recount from 1 (the count sequence isn't yet linked to +1), gives a non-successor ('lots', '10'), or can do 'one more' but not 'one less' (the sequence runs forward only). Doing it hidden — no objects to recount — is the discriminator.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4): bees and pollination — how flowers and insects DEPEND on each other. A bee visits a flower for nectar, pollen sticks to its body and rubs off on the next flower; pollination lets plants make seeds and fruit. Why pollinators matter for our food.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y3 'Plants' (life cycle of flowering plants including pollination, seed formation, dispersal); links to Y6 interdependence.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 2-LS2-2 (plants depend on animals for pollination/seed dispersal) and supports 3-LS4/5-LS2 interdependence.
• Operational details — two linked ideas: the MECHANISM (nectar visit → pollen transfer flower-to-flower) and the INTERDEPENDENCE (mutual benefit: bee gets food, plant gets pollinated; without pollinators many crops fail). Make the invisible pollen transfer visible. Connect to children's food (apples, strawberries). Distinguish pollination (pollen moves between flowers) from later stages (seeds, fruit).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): describes a bee getting nectar and pollen sticking to it. Tier B (age 8): explains pollen moving from flower to flower lets plants make seeds/fruit. Tier C (age 9): explains the mutual dependence and predicts what happens to a garden/farm with no pollinators.
bestPractices: Make the invisible pollen transfer VISIBLE (grains sticking to the bee, rubbing onto the next flower) — it's the crux children miss.
Teach both the mechanism AND the mutual dependence (bee gets food, plant gets pollinated), not just one.
Anchor it to children's own food (apples, strawberries, tomatoes) so 'why pollinators matter' is concrete.
Distinguish pollination (pollen moving between flowers) from seed formation and dispersal that follow.
Use a no-pollinator contrast to make the consequence and interdependence vivid.
keyRepresentations: A bee-and-flower scene with visible pollen grains transferring between flowers.
A labelled flower (nectar, pollen, stigma) with each part's role.
A before/after 'with bees vs no bees' fruit-set comparison.
A pollinator-to-crop matching set linking to our food.
commonMisconceptions: 'Bees make/collect pollen on purpose to pollinate' — pollination is largely an accidental by-product of nectar-seeking.
'Pollen is the same as nectar / a seed' — they are different things with different roles.
'Pollination happens within one flower only' — the key idea is transfer BETWEEN flowers.
'Only bees pollinate' — butterflies, hoverflies, beetles and others pollinate too.
'Bees make honey and that's pollination' — conflating honey production with pollination.

learn.summary: For ages 7-9, teach bees and pollination as two linked ideas: the MECHANISM (a bee visits a flower for nectar, pollen sticks to its fuzzy body and rubs off onto the next flower) and the INTERDEPENDENCE (the bee gets food, the plant gets pollinated and can then make seeds and fruit; many of our foods depend on this). The crux children miss is the invisible pollen transfer BETWEEN flowers, so make it visible, distinguish pollination from the later seed/fruit stages, and anchor it to familiar foods like apples and strawberries.

activities.title: Be the bee: carry the pollen flower to flower
feedback: If a learner shows the bee taking nectar but no pollen moving, point out the grains sticking to its fuzzy body and ask what travels with the bee to the next flower.

If a learner thinks the bee's job is just to leave pollen on the same flower, stress that the bee's special role is carrying pollen to a DIFFERENT (second) flower — that transfer BETWEEN flowers is the key step in this story (some plants can also pollinate themselves, but that is not what the bee is doing here).

If a learner says the bee makes the fruit, re-trace the chain: pollen moves → flower is fertilised → flower makes seeds → fruit grows with them (around them in an apple, carrying them on the outside in a strawberry); the bee only carries the pollen, the plant makes the fruit.

If a learner says the bee brings honey/nectar TO the flower to help it, separate the two stories: nectar goes back to the hive for honey, while pollen accidentally moves BETWEEN flowers — only the pollen transfer is pollination.
When a learner explains both the transfer and the no-pollinator consequence (fewer apples/strawberries), confirm they have captured the two-way dependence, not just a memorised fact.
activities.rationale: The mechanism is a cause-and-effect process; acting it out (fly to flower, load pollen, deposit pollen, see fruit form where transfer happened in the model) makes the otherwise-invisible transfer concrete, and a 'no bees' contrast makes the interdependence and its consequence for our food vivid. A live toggle that leaves flowers unpollinated and leaves a shop shelf with far fewer apples and strawberries is an optional way to make the consequence felt.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y3 pupils explore the part flowers play in the life cycle of flowering plants, including pollination, seed formation and seed dispersal.
Plants depend on animals for pollination and seed dispersal (2-LS2-2).
A large share of leading global food crops depend, at least in part, on animal pollinators such as bees.
learnerActions: Move a bee from one flower to a second flower: at the first flower it drinks nectar and pollen grains cling to its fuzzy body; at the second flower some of that pollen rubs off onto the flower's centre (stigma).

Watch what happens next — the pollinated flower swells and ripens into a fruit (e.g. an apple or strawberry); in this model, flowers that were never visited make no fruit (in real life, unvisited flowers of these plants make little, small or misshapen fruit).
Zoom in to look closely at the pollen grains on the bee's hairs and at the stigma where they land.

Try a 'no pollinators' version: with no bee visiting, the flowers stay unvisited, and in this model none turn to fruit (real plants would make far less fruit); picture a shop shelf with far fewer apples and strawberries. Compare this with the version where bees did visit.
Say in your own words what the bee does for the flower, what the flower does for the bee, and why this matters for the food we eat.
activities.intendedInsight: For many plants, pollination happens when pollen accidentally rides from one flower to another on a food-seeking bee; this transfer is what lets the plant make seeds and fruit, so the bee and the flower (and we) depend on each other.

activities.title: Hands-on pollen transfer with a flour-dusted 'bee'
feedback: If a learner thinks the bee is deliberately helping, highlight that it came for food (nectar, and some pollen to eat) yet still left flour/pollen on the next flower — the pollination happens by accident.
If a learner stops at 'pollen moved', prompt them to say what the pollen then allows the flower to do (make seeds, then fruit).
activities.rationale: A physical investigation with flour makes the sticking-and-rubbing mechanism tangible and reinforces that pollination (the KS2 life-cycle content) is an accidental by-product of nectar-seeking. Flour is an approximation of real pollen, useful for showing transfer rather than real plant biology.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y3 pupils explore the part flowers play in the life cycle of flowering plants, including pollination, seed formation and seed dispersal.
learnerActions: Sprinkle flour (standing for pollen) on the centre of a first paper 'flower', then let a pipe-cleaner or cotton-wool 'bee' visit it so flour clings to the fuzzy 'bee'.
Touch the 'bee' to a second paper 'flower' and look at the flour (pollen) left behind.
Describe how the pollen got from the first flower to the second without the bee meaning to pollinate the flower.
Discuss which part of this is pollination (the pollen moving between flowers), and what comes after it (seeds, then fruit).
activities.intendedInsight: Pollen transfer is accidental — it sticks to and rubs off a fuzzy visitor — and it is a separate, earlier step from seed formation and fruit growth.

activities.title: Label the flower and explain why it matters
feedback: If a learner confuses pollen with nectar or with a seed, restate: nectar is the sugary food the bee drinks, pollen is the powder that transfers between flowers, and a seed forms later inside the flower after pollination.
If a learner only labels parts without roles, ask them to say what each part is for in the transfer.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal labelled scene builds vocabulary and the part-role links for pollination within the flowering-plant life cycle, and a food-link flap makes 'why pollinators matter' concrete. Reveal-style labelling supports learning but does not itself require the learner to run the transfer or consequence, so pair it with the acting-out activity.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y3 pupils explore the part flowers play in the life cycle of flowering plants, including pollination, seed formation and seed dispersal.
learnerActions: On a labelled flower-and-bee scene, identify nectar, pollen and stigma and say what each does.
Reveal a 'why it matters' note linking the flower to foods we eat (apples, strawberries, tomatoes).
In your own words, connect each part to its role in the pollination story.
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing the named parts (nectar as the bee's food, pollen as what transfers, stigma as where it lands) supports telling the full pollination-to-food story.

activities.title: Order the steps and explore pollinator variety
feedback: If a learner orders fruit before pollen transfer, point back to the idea that fruit forms after pollen reaches a flower's stigma (in this story, carried from the previous flower by the bee).

If a learner treats pollination as pollen staying within one flower, remind them that when bees pollinate, they usually carry pollen to a different flower (some plants can pollinate themselves, but bees are the movers in this story).
If a learner names only bees, note that butterflies, hoverflies and beetles also pollinate, and that a single crop may be visited by more than one kind.
If a learner says 'nothing would happen' with no pollinators, revisit the no-bees comparison showing flowers that never set fruit.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and exploring which insects visit a crop let learners rehearse the mechanism, the diversity of pollinators and the consequence. These tasks check whether learners can reconstruct the chain and recognise pollinator diversity; combine them with explanation so learners produce their own reasoning rather than only selecting answers.
sourceClaims: Plants depend on animals for pollination and seed dispersal (2-LS2-2).
A large share of leading global food crops depend, at least in part, on animal pollinators such as bees.
learnerActions: Put the pollination steps in order: bee visits flower for nectar → pollen sticks to bee → bee visits next flower → pollen rubs off → flower makes seeds → fruit grows.

Look at several pollinators (bees, butterflies, hoverflies, beetles) and work out which insects can visit a given crop, noticing that the SAME crop is often visited by more than one kind — bees are not the only ones, so there is no single exclusive partner.
Answer: what would happen to a garden or orchard if the pollinating insects vanished, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: Pollination is a sequence that leads to seeds and fruit, carried out by several kinds of insect, and losing pollinators would reduce the fruit and vegetables we grow.

activities.title: A day in the life of a bee: tell the story
feedback: If the account has the bee deliberately helping, remind them the bee is looking for food (mainly nectar, plus some pollen to eat) and pollinates the flower by accident.
If the account conflates honey-making with pollination, separate them: honey is made from nectar in the hive; pollination is the pollen moving between flowers.
activities.rationale: In-role speaking or writing turns the concept into the learner's own words and surfaces misconceptions about intent and honey. This is a production task; it complements, rather than replaces, seeing the transfer happen.
learnerActions: Take the role of a bee and tell or write a short account of visiting flowers: why you go (nectar), what sticks to you, and what you leave behind at the next flower.
Explain 'the deal' between the bee and the plant — what each one gets.
Finish by saying what would happen to the plants, and to our food, if bees like you stopped visiting.
activities.intendedInsight: Narrating the bee's visit from its own point of view consolidates both the accidental mechanism and the mutual benefit.

constraints: Teach BOTH the mechanism (flower-to-flower pollen transfer) and the mutual dependence, not just one.
Make the invisible pollen transfer visible (grains sticking to the bee, rubbing onto the next flower) — this is the crux children most often miss.

Distinguish pollination (pollen reaching a flower's stigma; with bees this usually means pollen carried BETWEEN flowers, though some plants can also pollinate within one flower) from the later seed formation and fruit growth; do not let learners treat pollen and seeds as the same thing.
Make clear the transfer is accidental — the bee is seeking nectar, not deliberately helping the plant (an age-appropriate simplification; bees do also collect some pollen as food).
Keep honey-making separate from pollination (nectar → honey in the hive vs pollen moving between flowers).

Note that bees are not the only pollinators — butterflies, hoverflies and beetles also pollinate, and a single crop may be visited by more than one kind; avoid implying exclusive one-to-one pollinator-crop pairings.
Anchor consequences to children's own food (apples, strawberries, tomatoes) so interdependence is concrete; frame 'no pollinators' as far fewer such foods rather than every food vanishing.
Flour on a model 'bee' and a paper 'flower' are approximations used to show transfer, not accurate representations of real pollen or flower anatomy.
Ordering/matching/selection tasks check reconstruction and recognition; include at least one task where the learner explains the chain in their own words so independent reasoning is elicited.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
All three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row; treat standards alignment and the crop-dependence claim as unverified.

The source notes that wind can also move pollen (pollination without an insect); the probe questions raise this as a counterexample. Activities here focus on insect pollination per the topic, but a reviewer may wish to decide how explicitly to introduce wind pollination for this age band.

An immersive 3D-meadow flythrough is an optional alternative medium where such an asset already exists; it is not claimed to be better or worse than the 2D version, which conveys the pollen-transfer cause-effect well.

The legacy source framed a static image as something that 'can't' teach interdependence and treated 3D as adding nothing; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.
Framing pollen transfer as purely accidental follows the source; bees do also actively collect pollen as food, so this is an age-appropriate simplification rather than a verified exclusive account.
The reteachPrerequisiteId references (and nulls) are catalog internals and were not carried into learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: 'The bee didn't mean to help — so how did the pollen get from one flower to the next?'
'If all the bees and pollinating insects vanished, what would happen to an apple orchard? Why?'
'Wind can carry some pollen too, with no insect at all. Is that also pollination?' (mechanism counterexample)
'Which came first for the bee — wanting to help the flower, or wanting nectar? So why does the flower still benefit?'
assess.correctAnswer: It's not right — the bee does something important for the flower even though it only came for nectar. Yellow pollen sticks to the bee's furry body, and when it flies to the next flower some pollen rubs off onto it. That is pollination, and it lets the flower make seeds and fruit. Many fruits and vegetables (apples, strawberries) need bees or other insects to pollinate them, so without pollinators we would have far less of these foods.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the bee only takes from the flower and gives nothing back ('it's just getting food')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show pollen sticking to a fuzzy bee (dust a pipe-cleaner 'bee' in flour and touch a second 'flower'). Make the accidental transfer visible — the bee carries pollen without meaning to.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the bee just takes nectar and does nothing for the flower
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the bee taking nectar but no pollen moving; sees no benefit to the plant

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses pollination with the bee making honey or bringing something TO the flower — no flower-to-flower transfer
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two stories: nectar goes back to the hive for honey; pollen accidentally moves BETWEEN flowers. Only the pollen transfer is pollination, and it's what makes seeds.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bee brings honey to the flower to help it grow
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: says the bee brings nectar/honey to the flower, or that pollination is about making honey

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the bee itself makes the fruit, or that pollen is the same as seeds — skips the step where pollen leads to seed and fruit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay out the chain: pollen moves → flower is fertilised → flower makes seeds → fruit grows around them. The bee only carries the pollen; the plant makes the fruit.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bee makes the fruit grow on the plant
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the bee makes apples, or uses 'pollen' and 'seed' interchangeably

responseLevels.gap: Says the bee just takes nectar and does nothing for the flower, or that the bee makes honey/fruit; no pollen transfer between flowers.
responseLevels.full: Explains pollen sticks to the bee and transfers to the next flower, letting it make seeds and fruit, AND reasons about the consequence — e.g. predicts fewer apples/strawberries without pollinators — showing the two-way flower–insect dependence, not a memorised fact.
responseLevels.partial: Knows bees help flowers and mentions pollen, but describes it as separate facts — can't join up pollen moving flower-to-flower → seeds/fruit → our food, or confuses pollen with seeds/honey.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A bee lands on a flower to drink its sweet nectar, then flies to another flower. Someone says: 'The bee is just getting food — it doesn't do anything for the flower.' Is that right? Tell me what the bee does for the flower without meaning to, and why that matters for the apples and strawberries we eat.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands pollination describes the accidental TRANSFER of pollen from flower to flower and links it to seeds/fruit — a two-way dependence. A child who thinks bees just take from flowers (or that bees make the fruit, or bring nectar to make honey and that's all) misses the transfer. The second tier ('why does it matter for our food?') separates 'bees are nice' from understanding the flower-insect dependence.

sources.claim: KS2 Y3 pupils explore the part flowers play in the life cycle of flowering plants, including pollination, seed formation and seed dispersal.

pedagogy.summary: The 0-to-1 probability scale formalises chance as a measured quantity: every probability is a number from 0 (impossible) through 1/2 (even chance) to 1 (certain), and can be written as a fraction, decimal, or percentage. The teaching aim is to treat probability as a magnitude on a bounded number line — placing events, converting freely between the three notations, and connecting 0.5 back to the informal 'even chance'.
bestPractices: Anchor a single 0-to-1 line marked with the landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance), 1 (certain) and use it as the home for every probability
Show the SAME point written three ways — 1/2 = 0.5 = 50% — so children see the notations as one magnitude, not three separate things
Move both directions: from a described event to a position, and from a position back to a described likelihood
Stress the bounds: nothing can be less likely than impossible (0) or more likely than certain (1), so a probability can never be negative or exceed 1
Reconnect 0.5 to 'even chance' and small values to 'unlikely', linking the numeric scale to the words learned earlier
keyRepresentations: 0-to-1 number line with 0, 1/2, 1 landmarks (impossible / even / certain)
Triple-notation labels (fraction = decimal = percentage) at each position
Event cards placed along the line
Links from likelihood words to numeric positions
commonMisconceptions: Believing a probability can be greater than 1, or giving a probability as a raw count (e.g. '6' because a die has six outcomes)
Fraction interference — thinking a larger denominator means a larger probability (1/4 > 1/2 because 4 > 2)
Comparing mixed notations by surface digits without converting (ranking 40%, 1/4, 0.3 as 40 > 4 > 0.3)
Treating 0.5 / 'even chance' as the default for any two-outcome event

learn.summary: Teach probability as a magnitude on a bounded 0-to-1 line, with landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance) and 1 (certain). The same probability can be written three ways — fraction, decimal and percentage (1/2 = 0.5 = 50%) — and children should move both directions: from a described event to a position, and from a position back to a described likelihood. Stress the bounds (never below 0 or above 1) and reconnect 0.5 to the informal 'even chance' learned earlier. Comparing mixed notations requires converting to a common form, not ranking by surface digits or by denominator size.

activities.title: One position, three notations on a draggable scale
feedback: When the three notations appear together at one point, point out: these are not three different chances but one position written three ways.
If the learner expects '2' to be placeable, note that the scale stops at 1 because nothing is more likely than certain — a probability can never be a raw count like 6.
Blocking the drag past 0 and 1 makes the bounds felt directly; name them as impossible and certain as the marker reaches each end.
activities.rationale: Showing the same point as fraction, decimal and percentage at once targets the core idea that these notations are one magnitude. Blocking movement past the endpoints makes the bounds concrete and confronts the belief that a probability can exceed 1 or be a count. The live three-way readout and snap-to-line examples are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Probability is represented on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) and expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage; the same probability can be written in each of these forms.
learnerActions: Drag a marker along a 0-to-1 line; a readout shows wherever you land simultaneously as a fraction, a decimal AND a percentage, so 2/5, 0.4 and 40% appear together at the same point.
Place the 'chance of rain 40%' event and watch the marker coincide exactly with 0.4 and 2/5 — confirm these are one position written three ways, not three different chances.
Feed a computed probability from a bag or spinner and watch it snap onto the line at its matching position.
Try to shove the marker past the 'certain' end for a 'probability of 2' and notice it refuses to move beyond 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A probability is a single magnitude on a bounded line; the fraction, decimal and percentage are three ways of writing the same position, and nothing can be less likely than impossible (0) or more likely than certain (1).

activities.title: Place, order and match mixed-notation probabilities
feedback: If a learner ranks 40% > 1/4 > 0.3 by surface digits, convert all three to decimals (0.4, 0.25, 0.3) or mark them on the line; show 1/4 = 0.25 sitting below 0.3.

If a learner treats 1/4 as largest because of the 4 in the denominator, return to meaning: one part out of four is a smaller share than one part out of two; mark quarters and halves on the same line to compare.

For a value above 1 or below 0, re-anchor the bounds: nothing is more likely than certain (1) or less likely than impossible (0). When outcomes are equally likely, probability is favourable-over-total; the favourable count can never exceed the total or be negative, so the probability is at most 1 and never below 0.
activities.rationale: Placement, ordering and matching tasks rehearse exactly the conversions and placements the topic demands. Requiring conversion to a common form targets the documented tendency to fall back on additive or surface-number comparisons. The ordering answer 1/4=0.25, 0.3, 0.4 was checked: 0.25 < 0.3 < 0.4 is correct.
sourceClaims: Quantifying and comparing probabilities requires proportional reasoning; children commonly fall back on additive or surface-number comparisons rather than converting to a common proportion, a persistent difficulty documented across the probability literature.
learnerActions: Use a slider to place 1/4 and 0.7 on the 0-to-1 line.
Order 40%, 1/4 and 0.3 from least to most likely, converting each to a common form (decimals 0.25, 0.3, 0.4) before deciding.
Match equivalent forms: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%.
Spot and reject an impossible probability, such as a value greater than 1 or below 0, explaining why it cannot be a valid probability.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing probabilities written in different notations requires converting to a common form (decimals, or positions on the line); surface digits and denominator size are not reliable guides, and every valid probability lies between 0 and 1.

activities.title: Landmark reference line with revealed equivalents
feedback: Confirm that 1/2, 0.5 and 50% all mark the even-chance midpoint, linking back to the informal word learned earlier.
Prompt the learner to supply their own event for 0 and for 1 to check they grasp impossible and certain.
activities.rationale: A fixed reference line with tap-to-reveal equivalents clearly presents the triple notation and links words to positions. As a reference it does not let the child test a mis-placement, so it supports but does not replace active placement work; this limit is recorded in constraints.
sourceClaims: Probability is represented on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) and expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage; the same probability can be written in each of these forms.
learnerActions: Tap each landmark (0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1) to reveal its fraction, decimal and percentage.
At each landmark, read an everyday event that belongs there (e.g. an impossible event at 0, a certain event at 1, an even-chance event at 1/2).
Use the revealed values as a reference while completing placement and ordering tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each landmark on the scale has a fixed fraction/decimal/percentage identity and a matching kind of everyday event, giving a stable reference for the triple notation.

activities.title: Socratic probing of the bounds
feedback: When the learner says a value cannot be placed, name the reason: nothing is more likely than certain (1) or less likely than impossible (0).

Redirect a count answer ('6 because a die has six outcomes') to favourable-over-total for a fair die's equally likely outcomes: the number of favourable outcomes can never be more than the total, so the fraction is never more than 1 (for example, 6/6 = 1 means certain).

If the learner assumes every two-outcome event is an even chance, point out that 0.5 applies only when the two outcomes are equally likely; many two-outcome events (e.g. a biased spinner) are not 1/2.
activities.rationale: A Socratic challenge surfaces the greater-than-1, count, and even-chance-default misconceptions by asking the child to justify and locate claimed values and to test a tempting generalisation. Discussion raises the ideas, but placing magnitudes may be clearer when also shown on a line, so pair this with the draggable or reference activities rather than using it alone.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'the probability is 6' or 'could a probability be 2?' by explaining what 0 and 1 mean.
Locate a claimed value like '6' or '2' on the 0-to-1 line and explain why it cannot sit there.
Describe an event at 0 (impossible) and an event at 1 (certain) in your own words.

Judge a claim like 'any event with two possible outcomes has probability 1/2' — decide whether it is always true, using an example such as a biased spinner or an event much more likely than its alternative.
activities.intendedInsight: Nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1; a raw count of outcomes is not a probability; and 0.5 is the even-chance value only when the two outcomes are equally likely, not automatically for any two-outcome event.

constraints: The 0-to-1 probability scale is a one-dimensional magnitude; a line (physical, drawn or on screen) is the appropriate representation and no additional spatial dimension is needed.
A fixed reference line shows equivalents clearly but cannot let a child test a mis-placement, so it supports rather than replaces active placement, ordering and conversion work.

Dialogue/Socratic prompts can raise the bounds, count and even-chance-default misconceptions, but should be paired with actually placing values on a line, since placing magnitudes may be clearer when shown.

Matching and recognising equivalent forms is useful practice, but is recognition-level; include tasks where the child independently places and orders values and states a reason, not only selects from options.
Mixed-notation comparison must require conversion to a common form; do not accept ordering by surface digits or by denominator size as correct reasoning.
0.5 ('even chance') is correct only when the two outcomes are equally likely; do not teach it as the default for every two-outcome event.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the ordering example: 1/4 = 0.25, 0.3, 40% = 0.4 gives least-to-most order A, B, C (0.25 < 0.3 < 0.4) — correct as stated. The listed distractors (40% > 1/4 > 0.3 by digits; 1/4 largest by denominator) are intentionally wrong patterns to diagnose and must only appear as error patterns, never as correct feedback.

The assessment's die example ('probability of rolling less than 7 on a six-sided die') is certain = 1; the count answer '6' is the targeted misconception. This is logically sound and preserved as the count/bounds-confrontation idea in the Socratic activity.

The 'even chance is the default for any two-outcome event' misconception appears only in the original pedagogy field, not among the formal assessment error patterns; it has been added as a conservative Socratic probe to preserve it. This addition is an unvalidated proposal.
Claims that one medium is clearer than another (e.g. shown vs discussed) are proposals only; efficacy is untested and such statements use 'may' wording.
Legacy source claims were marked verified in the row but have not been re-checked here; confidence should not be upgraded on that basis.

assess.poeTask: Say: 'I'm going to roll this fair six-sided die. What is the probability that I roll a number less than 7? Write it as a number and explain — and could it be more than 1?' Have the child predict AND justify before rolling. A child who thinks in counts answers '6' (six numbers are less than 7); the correct answer is 1 (certain). Roll the die several times — every roll is under 7 — to confront the count answer: the event is certain, which is 1 on the scale, and nothing can be 'more than certain'.
probeDeeper: Where does 'even chance' sit on this line, and what is it as a decimal and a percentage?
Could a probability ever be more than 1? What would that mean?
Is 1/4 the same as, bigger than, or smaller than 0.3? How can you be sure?
Point to 0 on the line — describe an event that belongs there, and one that belongs at 1.
assess.correctAnswer: Least to most likely: A (1/4 = 0.25), then B (0.3), then C (40% = 0.4). Converting all three to the same form — decimals 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, or positions on the line — shows the order; each sits between 0 and 1, with A a quarter of the way, B just above it, and C below the halfway point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares mixed notations by their surface digits without converting ('40 is biggest, then 4, then 0.3')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert all three to a common form (decimals, or positions on the line) before comparing; show 1/4 = 0.25 sitting below 0.3
errorPatterns.distractor: C (40%), then A (1/4), then B (0.3) — 40 is the biggest number, then 4, then 0.3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders by the raw numbers seen rather than their true magnitudes; may rank 1/4 above 0.3 by reading '4' as four

errorPatterns.pattern: Fraction interference — a bigger denominator is read as a bigger probability (1/4 > 1/2 because 4 > 2)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the meaning: one part out of four is a smaller share than one out of two; mark quarters and halves on the same line to compare their sizes
errorPatterns.distractor: A (1/4) is the most likely because it has the biggest bottom number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 1/4 high on the scale or calls it the most likely because of the 4 in the denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a probability can exceed 1 or gives it as a raw count (e.g. '6' for a die)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor the bounds: nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1; a probability is favourable-over-total, always at most the total, so never more than 1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places a mark beyond the 'certain' end, or states a probability greater than 1 or as a whole number of outcomes

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place probabilities on the line or convert between notations; orders by surface digits and may put marks beyond 0 or 1
responseLevels.full: Converts freely between fraction, decimal and percentage, orders mixed-notation probabilities correctly, places each between 0 and 1, and rules out values below 0 or above 1 with a reason
responseLevels.partial: Places single-notation probabilities correctly and knows the endpoints, but slips when notations are mixed — compares by raw digits or by denominator size — or is unsure a probability cannot exceed 1

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show three events with their probabilities written in different notations: Event A has probability 1/4, Event B has probability 0.3, Event C has probability 40%. Ask the child to order them from least to most likely and to place each on a 0-to-1 line. Take the order, then ask them to explain the reason (Tier 2) — how they compared numbers written in different ways.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the scale converts to a common notation and places all three between 0 and 1; a surface reasoner ranks by the visible digits (40 > 4 > 3), and a fraction-interference reasoner treats 1/4 as large because of the 4. The Tier-2 reason — did they convert to compare? — is the separator, and only converted reasoning survives.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Associative property of addition — when adding three or more numbers, they may be grouped (added) in any order without changing the total, e.g. (2+3)+5 = 2+(3+5). For ages 6–7, layered on commutativity and used as a strategy tool, not a stated law.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 pupils 'show that addition of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction of one number from another cannot'; associative grouping underpins Y2 'add numbers using... a three-digit number and ones/tens' and the Y3 formal written methods where partial sums are recombined. Named explicitly as a mental strategy in KS2 guidance.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.3 'Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract... To add 2+6+4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2+6+4 = 2+10 = 12 (Associative property of addition).' Children need not use formal terms.
• Operational details: teach as a licence to regroup for convenience — look-for-a-ten, add doubles first, add the friendly pair. Contrast with commutativity (reorder) — association is about which pair you combine FIRST. Keep the whole conserved: the three quantities are unchanged, only the sequence of combining differs.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — given 2+8+5, child chooses to add 2+8 to make 10 first and explains why that is allowed. Tier B (age 7) — regroups three addends two different ways and confirms the same total. Tier C (age 7+) — uses grouping to justify a mental strategy in a worded context and states that regrouping never changes the sum.
bestPractices: Introduce through the practical goal of making calculation easier (look for a pair that makes ten, or add a double first) rather than as an abstract named law.
Use concrete equal-status objects (counters, cubes) the child physically pushes into different pairs, so the conserved whole is seen while the grouping order varies.
Contrast explicitly with commutativity: reordering (which comes first) versus associating (which pair we combine first) — pupils confuse the two.
Have children compute the same triple by two different groupings and compare totals, making the invariance an observed result, not a told fact.
Connect forward to written column addition, where partial sums (ones, tens) are grouped and recombined, so the property is seen as load-bearing later.
keyRepresentations: Three counter groups / cube towers that can be pushed into different pairs before merging
Bracket notation over three addends, (a+b)+c vs a+(b+c), with the first-combined pair highlighted
Ten-frame showing a make-ten pair filling first, then the remainder added
Bar/part-whole model with three parts and one conserved whole bar
Empty number line where the child chooses which jump to take first
commonMisconceptions: Believing the total changes if you add in a different grouping (failing to conserve the whole).
Conflating associativity with commutativity — thinking they are the same 'any order' rule.
Over-generalising to subtraction, e.g. assuming (10−3)−2 = 10−(3−2).
Losing track of an addend when regrouping (dropping or double-counting the third number).
Thinking brackets are just decoration rather than an instruction about what to combine first.

learn.summary: Teaches the associative property of addition for ages 6–7: when adding three or more numbers, any two can be combined first without changing the total, e.g. (2+8)+5 = 2+(8+5) = 15. The point is the freedom to choose which pair to combine first, used as a practical strategy (make a ten, add a double first) rather than as a stated law. Contrast with commutativity (reordering the numbers) and avoid over-generalising to subtraction, where (10−3)−2 = 5 but 10−(3−2) = 9. Includes hands-on manipulation, a reasoning/justification layer, consolidation checks, and a static side-by-side anchor, each with its pedagogical purpose and limits noted.

activities.title: Grouping bench: choose which pair to combine first
feedback: If a learner reaches the same total both ways, name the move: 'You grouped these two first — that's allowed, and the total stayed the same.'
If a learner expects the total to change under a different grouping, have them compute both groupings of the same triple side by side and compare the equal totals; stress the amounts are unchanged.
If a learner loses or double-counts the third addend after making a ten, physically set the third object aside and bring it in last, then recount — this is a tracking slip, not a concept error.
When a make-ten pair is chosen, point out how the second step (e.g. 10+5) became easy.
activities.rationale: The concept is the freedom to decide which pair to combine first, so letting the learner physically make and compare that choice is intended to turn invariance into an observed result rather than a told fact, and to surface WHY grouping helps. Standards frame this as a strategy, not a named law.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.3 applies properties of operations as strategies, giving the associative example 2+6+4 = 2+10 = 12 and noting children need not use formal terms.
Making ten by regrouping addends is a key mental calculation strategy in early KS1/KS2.
Y2 pupils show addition can be done in any order and use this alongside grouping when adding a three-digit number and ones/tens; formal written methods recombine partial sums.
learnerActions: Set out three equal-status objects or number tiles for a triple such as 2, 8, 5 (counters, cubes, or draggable tiles).
Choose any two to combine first; merge them into a single running sum, then bring in the third.
Try the same triple a second way (e.g. combine 8+5 first) and compare the final total.
State out loud which pair you combined first and why that choice made the calculation easier.
Repeat with a triple that rewards a make-ten pair (e.g. 2+8+5, where 2+8=10 then 10+5=15) and one that rewards adding a double first (e.g. 4+4+7, where 4+4=8 then 8+7=15).
activities.intendedInsight: You may choose which pair to combine first; a smart choice (make a ten, or add a double) makes the sum easier while the total stays identical because the three amounts themselves never change.

activities.title: Why is that allowed? Justify your grouping
feedback: If the learner justifies by pointing to the unchanged amounts, name that reasoning back as 'grouping'.
If the learner cannot say why the total is the same, return to combining the same triple two ways and comparing before asking again.
Probe with 'what's your evidence the total is still the same if you group differently?' to move from a one-off trick toward a general reason.

If a learner tries the subtraction pair, confirm (10−3)−2 = 5 but 10−(3−2) = 9 — the answers differ, so subtraction cannot be regrouped the way addition can; use this only as a contrast, never as a rule to apply.
activities.rationale: Early standards ask pupils to show/apply the property and explain their strategy, so an explain/justify layer is intended to develop the reasoning the numeric answer alone does not reveal; the subtraction contrast targets the common over-generalisation.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils show addition can be done in any order and use this alongside grouping when adding a three-digit number and ones/tens; formal written methods recombine partial sums.
1.OA.3 applies properties of operations as strategies, giving the associative example 2+6+4 = 2+10 = 12 and noting children need not use formal terms.
learnerActions: Given a triple, say which two numbers you would add first.
Answer a questioner (a peer, tutor, or 'maths buddy') who asks 'Why is that allowed?' and 'Would we get the same total if we grouped the numbers differently? How do you know?'
Explain in your own words that the three amounts are unchanged, so only which pair you combine first differs.

Try a new triple such as 4+7+6 and justify which pair you would add first (here 4+6=10, then 10+7=17). Notice that 4 and 6 are not next to each other, so adding them first means changing the order as well as the grouping; the total is still 17.
Test the contrast with subtraction: work out (10−3)−2 = 5 and 10−(3−2) = 9, notice the answers differ, and conclude that the grouping freedom belongs to addition, not subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Grouping is a reasoning move you can justify: the total is conserved because the three quantities stay the same, no matter which pair you combine first — but this freedom holds for addition, not for subtraction.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, choose, and check equal totals
feedback: For the efficient-pair item, confirm the make-ten pair and show the easy second step.
For a true/false item where a number was altered, point out that the total changed because an amount changed, not because of regrouping.
activities.rationale: Closed-response items are intended to consolidate recognition of equivalent groupings after hands-on work; whether they do so is not established here. This is a check/consolidation step; it does not by itself let a learner freely explore their own alternative groupings, and recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own production of a grouping.
learnerActions: Decide which pair you would add first to make a given triple easy (e.g. for 2+8+5, which pair makes a ten?).
Match equivalent groupings, e.g. (2+8)+5 with 2+(8+5).
Judge true/false statements about whether two groupings of the same triple share a total, including an item where one number has been changed so the total genuinely differs.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising equivalent groupings and spotting the efficient first pair is intended to consolidate that regrouping preserves the total while making the calculation easier.

activities.title: Side-by-side anchor: did the total change?
feedback: Confirm that the brackets changed which pair came first but the final total stayed the same.
If a learner treats brackets as decoration, point to the highlighted first pair and the matching final totals.
activities.rationale: A fixed side-by-side display is a clear reference anchor for the bracket-reading idea. It is a scaffold: because the triples are pre-set, it cannot let the learner test their own choice of grouping, which is the heart of the property.
learnerActions: Look at two pre-set groupings of the same triple, e.g. (2+8)+5 and 2+(8+5), with brackets marking each first pair.
Reveal each intermediate sum and the shared final total (both land on 15).
Answer 'Did the total change?' and explain what the brackets tell you to combine first.
activities.intendedInsight: Brackets are an instruction about what to combine first, not decoration, and both groupings reach the same total.

constraints: Teach as a licence to regroup for convenience (look for a ten, add a double first), not as an abstract named law; children need not use the formal term 'associative'.

Distinguish associativity (which pair we combine FIRST) from commutativity (which order numbers come in); learners frequently conflate them, so address them explicitly. Note that combining two numbers that are not next to each other first (e.g. 4 and 6 in 4+7+6, or 2 and 5 in 2+8+5) uses both properties together.
Do NOT extend the grouping rule to subtraction: (10−3)−2 = 5 does not equal 10−(3−2) = 9. Use this contrast to probe, not as a rule to apply.
Keep the whole conserved: the three quantities stay the same; only which pair is combined first differs. Guard against dropping or double-counting an addend during regrouping.

Closed matching/true-false items and the fixed side-by-side anchor are consolidation and reference scaffolds; they do not let a learner freely explore alternative groupings and should follow, not replace, hands-on choice. This is an observable limit of those formats, not a claim that only manipulation can teach the concept.

The optional interactive touches (a total bar pinned at a fixed value while intermediate sums recompute, a make-ten pair glowing, tiles fusing on drag) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit arithmetic: 2+8+5=15 and 2+6+4=12 are correct in both groupings; 4+4+7=15; 4+7+6=17. The deliberately altered true/false distractor should change a number so the total genuinely differs — do not present two correct groupings as giving different totals.
Subtraction check: (10−3)−2 = 5 and 10−(3−2) = 9, so subtraction is NOT associative; this is used only as a contrast/probe in the justify activity, never taught as working.
Source note: the CCSS-M claim and the NCETM claim are marked verified:false in the row; the DfE claim is marked verified:true. Confidence should not be upgraded on that basis.

Activity 2's sourceClaims evidence associativity as a strategy and the 'show' of the property; they do not directly evidence the justify/explain pedagogy or the subtraction contrast, which rest on the pedagogy's misconception list rather than a cited claim.

The original 3D-interactive entry was judged a poor fit with the boilerplate reasoning 'a flat concept is not made 3D by rendering it in 3D'; this universal-sounding claim is not established by the source material and was dropped rather than propagated as a law.
The forward connection to column addition (recombining partial sums) is carried only in standards framing, not as its own activity; a follow-on activity could make that link explicit.

assess.poeTask: Predict whether adding (2 + 8) first or (8 + 5) first changes the answer to 2 + 8 + 5. Say your prediction and why. Then work out both ways and check — what does the result tell you about grouping?
probeDeeper: Why did you choose those two numbers to add first?
What's your evidence the total is still 15 if you group the numbers differently?
What if the numbers were 4 + 7 + 6 — which pair would you add first, and why?
Does this grouping trick work for subtraction? Try (10 − 3) − 2 and 10 − (3 − 2) and see.
assess.correctAnswer: 15. A strong answer adds 2 + 8 to make 10 first, then 10 + 5 = 15, choosing that pair because it makes a ten. The total is 15 whatever grouping is used — the three amounts don't change, only which pair is combined first.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You have to add them in the order they're written' — adds strictly left-to-right and resists regrouping to make a ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build (2+8)+5 and 2+(8+5) with cubes side by side; both reach 15. Establish that you may choose any pair to combine first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists on 2+8 then +5 only because that is the written order; will not try 8+5 or 2+... to make ten.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a different grouping changes the total.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute two groupings of the same triple side by side and compare the equal totals; stress the amounts are unchanged.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — grouping them differently would give a different total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a different answer if the numbers are grouped another way.

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses or double-counts the third addend after making a ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — physically set the third tile aside and bring it in last; check the count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Makes ten with two numbers then forgets to add the third, or adds it twice.

responseLevels.gap: Adds left-to-right only, cannot regroup, or believes a different grouping changes the total.
responseLevels.full: Explains the total is conserved under any grouping because the three amounts are unchanged, and deliberately chooses a make-ten pair to make the calculation easier.
responseLevels.partial: Can add the three and may even use make-ten, but cannot explain why any grouping gives the same total, or treats it as a one-off trick for this case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 2 + 8 + 5. Which two numbers did you add first, and why did you pick those? Would you get a different total if you added them in a different order?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child adding mechanically left-to-right can still reach 15, so the numeric answer alone doesn't discriminate. The 'which did you add first / would a different order change it' tier reveals whether the child sees grouping as a free, total-preserving choice (and spots the make-ten pair) or believes the written order is fixed / that regrouping changes the total.
