errorPatterns.revealedBy: Commits to one hypothesis and ignores evidence for the other or their interaction.

errorPatterns.pattern: If we can bring species back, extinction doesn't really matter / conservation is less urgent.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish a costly, imperfect technical possibility from protecting living species and habitats; connect to the ongoing sixth mass extinction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses de-extinction to downplay the present-day biodiversity crisis.

responseLevels.gap: Treats de-extinction as a done deal ('just clone it') and names a single cause of extinction, with no engagement with evidence quality or ethics.
responseLevels.full: Weighs overkill versus climate evidence (allowing combination), explains why degraded DNA makes true recreation infeasible, and argues both sides of de-extinction on scientific, ecological and ethical grounds while linking to the present extinction crisis.
responseLevels.partial: Summarises the overkill and climate hypotheses and knows ancient DNA is used, but can't evaluate the evidence's limits or mount substantive arguments for and against de-extinction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: We have ancient DNA from mammoths frozen in permafrost, and the mammoth went extinct only a few thousand years ago. A company says it can 'bring the mammoth back.' Should we — and could we really recreate an extinct species? Work through what the evidence and the arguments actually support.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: It separates a student who treats de-extinction as a solved 'we can clone it back' fact from one who reasons about degraded DNA, distinguishes overkill from climate evidence, and weighs competing ethical arguments explicitly.

sources.claim: Pleistocene megafauna extinctions are debated between the overkill hypothesis (human hunting, with extinctions often tracking human arrival) and the climate hypothesis (rapid end-Ice-Age warming), with much evidence pointing to a combination.
sources.source: Natural History Museum — what killed the Ice Age megafauna

sources.claim: Ancient DNA recovered from permafrost-preserved specimens reveals genetics, diet and relatedness of extinct species, but DNA degrades over time (so it is unavailable for dinosaurs); de-extinction efforts (e.g. mammoth-like Asian elephants) raise substantive feasibility and ethical questions.
sources.source: Natural History Museum / Britannica — ancient DNA and de-extinction

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2). Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of TENS and ONES: in 47, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 7 means 7 ones. This is the central node of early place value — the tens/ones column idea that every later place-value column extends.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones)'; 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.2 'understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones' with 1.NBT.2a/b/c; consolidated in 2.NBT.1.
• Operational details — Build every two-digit number CONCRETELY first (bundled tens + loose ones), then match to the written numeral and to expanded form (47 = 40 + 7). Insist the child reads the tens digit as a QUANTITY OF TENS, not the face value ('four tens', not 'four'). Contrast standard partition (47 = 40 + 7) with non-standard partition (47 = 30 + 17) once secure, because flexible partitioning underpins later column addition/subtraction.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): with base-ten blocks present, build 47 and say '4 tens and 7 ones'. Tier B (age 6-7): given 47 with no blocks, state the value of each digit (40 and 7) and write 47 = 40 + 7. Tier C (age 7): identify the tens/ones digit in any two-digit number and give a non-standard partition (47 = 30 + 17).
bestPractices: Follow the CPA sequence: bundle ten loose ones into a labelled 'ten' (concrete), draw it as a ten-rod/line (pictorial), then link to the numeral 47 and expanded form 40+7 (abstract) — never leave the digit floating free of a quantity.
Use a place-value chart with only two columns (tens | ones) and physically place bundled tens in the tens column and loose ones in the ones column so the position IS the meaning.
Read the digits by value out loud — '4 tens' and '7 ones' — and resist 'four, seven'; language that names the unit prevents the digits-are-just-two-separate-numbers error.
Introduce non-standard partitioning (47 = 30 + 17) deliberately once standard partitioning is secure, so children see the tens/ones split as flexible, not a single fixed answer.
Use 'the same number, many ways' tasks: show 47 as blocks, as 40+7, as a point on a 0-100 line, and as a bead string of 4 tens + 7 — same quantity, different representation.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (tens rods + unit cubes) — the canonical proportional model where a ten is physically ten ones
Two-column tens|ones place-value chart with bundled tens and loose ones placed in position
Expanded-form / part-whole (cherry) diagram: 47 splits into 40 and 7
Bead strings and ten-frames grouped into complete tens plus extras
Arrow/place-value cards (40 and 7) that physically overlap to build 47, making expanded form tangible
commonMisconceptions: Reading the tens digit as its face value — treating the 4 in 47 as 'four' rather than 'forty/four tens'.
Concatenation error: thinking 47 is '4 and 7' side by side (so 4+7=11 or two separate numbers) rather than 40+7.
Digit-reversal / transposition — writing or building 74 for 47 because spoken language and column order are conflated (a hangover from the teen-number naming trap).
Believing a number can only be partitioned one way (47 = 40 + 7 only), missing 47 = 30 + 17, which blocks later regrouping in subtraction.
Losing the unit when there are zero ones — thinking a decade like 40 has 'no place value in the ones' rather than 4 tens and 0 ones.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y2 / US Grade 1-2), build the understanding that the two digits of a two-digit number stand for a quantity of tens and a quantity of ones: in 47, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 7 means 7 ones. Centre the learning on concrete grouping — bundling ten loose ones into one ten — then link that quantity to the written numeral, to expanded form (47 = 40 + 7), and to flexible (non-standard) partitioning (47 = 30 + 17). Read digits by value ('four tens', 'seven ones'), never as bare faces.

activities.title: Bundling: ten ones become one ten
feedback: If the child says 'the 4 means four', have them count the single cubes inside the four bundles: there are forty, so the 4 is worth 4 tens = 40.

If the child places tens in the ones column (or vice versa), name the columns again — tens on the left, ones on the right — and compare 47 with 74 built side by side so the positions are visibly different quantities.
When partitioning as 30 + 17, confirm by re-counting the whole pile: if it is still 47, the split is valid; the quantity is conserved even though the grouping changed.
If the child thinks a decade like 40 has 'nothing' in the ones, show 40 as four tens and zero loose ones — the ones place is still there, holding none.
activities.rationale: Place value is a quantity re-seen as grouped units. Acting out the bundling (ten ones fusing into one ten) makes unitising something the child does rather than a label they repeat, which is the standard concrete-first (CPA) route and is intended to target the face-value and concatenation errors.
sourceClaims: 1.NBT.2 states the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones, with 10 as a bundle of ten ones.
Explicit CPA (concrete-pictorial-abstract) sequencing and standard/non-standard partitioning are recommended for building place-value understanding.
learnerActions: Set out a two-column mat labelled 'tens' on the left and 'ones' on the right.
Drop loose cubes one at a time into the ones column; each time you reach ten loose cubes, bundle those ten into a single labelled 'ten' (a rod) and move it to the tens column.
Build 47 by placing four bundled tens in the tens column and seven loose ones in the ones column.
Say aloud 'four tens and seven ones', then write the numeral 47 and the expanded form 47 = 40 + 7.
Break one of the four tens back into ten loose ones and re-count: show the pile is still 47 but now reads as 30 + 17.
activities.intendedInsight: The '4' in 47 is not 'four' — it is four whole bundles of ten (40). Position gives the digit its value, and the same quantity can be split in more than one way without changing how much there is.

activities.title: Many ways to show the same number
feedback: If the child marks 47 near the wrong end of the line, count up in tens (10, 20, 30, 40) then on by ones to locate it.
For 44, if the child says both 4s mean the same, point to the place of each: the left 4 sits in the tens column (40), the right 4 in the ones column (4).
If the child drops the ones place for 40, have them state it as '4 tens and 0 ones' to keep the place visible.
If the arrow cards are read as '4' and '7', separate then re-overlap them so the '40' card is seen whole underneath the '7'.
activities.rationale: Linking multiple representations of one quantity is intended to build the flexible, connected understanding named in the Y2 standard, including representing numbers on a number line, and guards against treating each representation as a separate fact.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils should recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones) and identify/represent/estimate numbers using different representations including the number line.
learnerActions: Take one number, e.g. 47, and represent it several ways: as bundled tens + loose ones, as expanded form 40 + 7, as a part-whole (cherry) diagram with 47 at the top splitting into 40 and 7, as a point marked at 47 on a 0-100 number line, as a bead string of 4 tens plus 7 beads, and by overlapping arrow/place-value cards (a '40' card with a '7' card sliding over it to read 47).
Check that every representation is the same quantity by counting back to 47 each time.
Repeat with a decade number such as 40 and with a number containing a repeated digit such as 44, explaining why the two 4s in 44 are worth different amounts (40 and 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A number is a single quantity that can be shown in many different ways; the tens/ones meaning stays the same across blocks, numerals, expanded form, the part-whole diagram, arrow cards, and the number line.

activities.title: Convince me the 4 means forty
feedback: Accept any justification that ties the digit to its place and counts the underlying ones (four tens = forty).
If the child only restates 'it's forty because it is', ask them to point to and count the actual tens to ground the claim.
Treat this as a short follow-up after concrete building, not a substitute for it — the child's reasoning can then be tied to bundles they have actually handled.
activities.rationale: A brief reasoning prompt may surface whether the child attaches the digit to its place or is reciting; it is proposed to work best as consolidation after hands-on grouping rather than as the first encounter, since the concept is grounded in manipulating quantities. Discussion alone can elicit an explanation but does not itself provide the physical grouping.
learnerActions: Respond to the challenge: 'Convince me the 4 in 47 is worth forty, not four.'
Justify using a model you built — e.g. 'because the 4 is four bundles, and each bundle is ten, so that is forty.'
Extend to a prove-it task: 'Show that the two 4s in 44 are worth different amounts.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain and defend why a digit's value comes from its place cements the idea beyond stating the rule.

activities.title: Check and sort by place value
feedback: For a swap error, rebuild 47 and 74 side by side so the different tens counts are visible.
For 4 + 7 = 11, show that the digits are not added together; the 4 counts tens and the 7 counts ones, giving 40 + 7 = 47.
For 47 = 30 + ___, confirm the missing part is 17 by regrouping one ten into ten ones.
For 47 = ___ + 7, confirm the missing part is 40 (four tens).
activities.rationale: Targeted checks that include the two headline distractors (transposition, 74, and adding the digits at face value, 11) can confirm the idea is held and probe the specific misconceptions. A check or sort can classify and verify a child's answers but does not itself elicit the physical grouping, so pair it with the building activity.
learnerActions: Complete expanded-form blanks, e.g. 47 = ___ + 7 and 47 = 30 + ___.
Choose which picture shows 4 tens and 7 ones, and match written numerals to their block pictures.
Sort or state, for a given two-digit number, which digit is the tens digit and which is the ones digit, and the value of each.
Consider tempting wrong answers — e.g. 74 (digits swapped) and 11 (adding 4 + 7) — and explain why each is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that each digit's value is fixed by its place, and conscious rejection of the swap error (74) and the digit-adding/face-value error (11, from adding 4 + 7).

constraints: Always build a two-digit number concretely first (bundled tens + loose ones), then connect it to the numeral and expanded form; never leave a digit floating free of a quantity.
Read digits by unit aloud — 'four tens', 'seven ones' — not 'four, seven'; naming the unit prevents the digits-as-two-separate-numbers error.
Introduce non-standard partitioning (47 = 30 + 17) only once standard partitioning (47 = 40 + 7) is secure.
A fixed labelled picture of 47-with-blocks is a useful reference anchor but shows one number only and does not let the child perform the bundling; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on grouping.
Recognition and fill-in-the-blank checks can confirm the idea is held and classify answers but do not on their own build the unitising insight; use them for consolidation and diagnosis.

The reasoning/convince-me prompt is proposed as a short follow-up after concrete work; grouping quantities may help young children reach this insight more reliably than discussion alone, but this comparison is not established by the provided sources.

A dynamic model where ten cubes snap into one rod (and a rod breaks back into ten) is one way to make bundling visible; physical bundles, bead strings, ten-frames, part-whole (cherry) diagrams, and overlapping arrow/place-value cards are equally valid concrete and pictorial routes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Of the cited sources, the row marks the DfE National Curriculum claim as verified and the CCSS-M (1.NBT.2) and NCETM claims as unverified; confidence levels were not upgraded here.

The original labelled the topic the 'central node' of place value and asserted that a 3D rendering 'adds nothing' and that an interactive drag model makes insight 'felt, not told'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy claims; they have been softened to scoped, proposed wording. Whether a dynamic auto-bundling model outperforms physical bundling for this age is not established by the sources provided.
The original flagged 'tens-and-ones is an inherently planar concept' to justify dropping 3D; retained only as a design preference, not a universal law.

Arrow/place-value cards (40 and 7 overlapping to build 47) and the part-whole (cherry) diagram, both present in the original key representations, had been dropped from or thinned in the candidate and are restored in the 'Many ways' activity and the concrete-routes constraint.

The assessment/check activity previously carried 1.NBT.2 as a sourceClaim; since its rationale states an assessment-design principle rather than the sourced content, the sourceClaims were set to [] (the tens/ones content remains sourced in the building activity).

probeDeeper: Build 47 with tens and ones — how many tens did you use?
Is the 4 worth more or less than the 7? Why?
If I swap the digits to 74, what changed and by how much?
assess.correctAnswer: The 4 is worth 4 tens (40); the 7 is worth 7 ones. Because in a two-digit number the left digit counts tens and the right digit counts ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the digit at face value: 'the 4 means four'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 47 with 4 tens rods and 7 ones; count the ones inside the rods (40). Say 'the 4 is in the tens place, so it's 4 tens = 40'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 means four.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the 4 stands for four ones/things rather than four tens.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses which digit is tens and which is ones (reads right-to-left)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the columns explicitly (tens on the left, ones on the right); build and compare 47 vs 74 to fix the positions.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 means four ones and the 7 means seven tens.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child calls the 7 the tens or says 47 is 'seven tens and four ones'.

responseLevels.gap: Reads both digits at face value or reverses tens and ones.
responseLevels.full: States the 4 is 4 tens (40) and the 7 is 7 ones, and can build/partition the number by place.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the tens digit but is shaky on its value (says '4' not '40').

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 47. Point to the 4, then the 7. Ask: 'What is the 4 worth, and what is the 7 worth? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with tens-and-ones place value says the 4 is worth 40; a face-value thinker says the 4 'means four'. The reason tier reveals whether they attach the digit to its place (tens) or read both digits as bare counts.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 13–14 years

- **Topic:** Writing Science Reports

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to present reasoned explanations and to report and communicate findings clearly, using SI units and standard notation, and to evaluate data and methods. The full report arc — aim, hypothesis, method, results, conclusion, evaluation — draws together the KS3 analysis, measurement and evaluation strands, and the curriculum's expectation that pupils understand how scientific claims are scrutinised.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 8 Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information, grades 6–8):** Communicate scientific information in writing (and other formats) that conveys ideas and results clearly and precisely; and understand that scientific arguments and claims are strengthened through peer review and independent replication. Communicating findings for others to scrutinise is a full-status science practice.

- **Operational details:** The student writes a structured scientific report with the conventional sections — aim, testable hypothesis, method (reproducible, in enough detail that another person could repeat it), results (tables/graphs with SI units and correct significant figures), conclusion (addressing the hypothesis with quantitative reference to the evidence), and evaluation (reliability, anomalies, systematic vs random error, improvements) — in objective, precise scientific register. Alongside the writing they learn WHY science is reported this way: peer review (other experts scrutinise the work before it is trusted) and replication (independent researchers repeating it) are the social mechanisms that make scientific knowledge reliable, which is why the method must be reproducible and the reasoning transparent.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal). This is the communicative capstone of the whole inquiry strand — it presupposes hypotheses, controlled variables, accurate measurement, graphing, conclusions and error analysis, and packages them for scrutiny. Success = produces a complete, well-structured report in appropriate register with correct units/notation, a conclusion tied quantitatively to evidence, a genuine evaluation, and can explain how peer review and replication underpin the reliability of scientific knowledge.
bestPractices: Teach the report as sections with distinct jobs (aim, hypothesis, method, results, conclusion, evaluation) using a shared exemplar and success criteria for each.
Make reproducibility the test of a good method: another person should be able to repeat it exactly from the written text — have peers try to follow each other's methods.
Require conclusions to refer QUANTITATIVELY to the evidence (cite values, a gradient, a trend), not just restate the hypothesis.
Teach objective scientific register (impersonal, precise, hedged appropriately) by contrasting it with casual or overclaiming language.
Teach peer review and replication as the reasons for the conventions — transparency and reproducibility exist so others can check the work.
Use structured critique of sample reports (spot the vague method, the overreaching conclusion) before students write their own.
keyRepresentations: The six-section report skeleton: aim → hypothesis → method → results → conclusion → evaluation
A reproducible method as a numbered, unambiguous procedure
Results section with headed SI-unit tables and correctly plotted graphs
Peer-review → revision → replication → acceptance workflow diagram
Register contrast card: objective scientific prose vs casual/overclaiming prose
commonMisconceptions: Writing the method as a past-tense story rather than a reproducible procedure.
Writing a conclusion that restates the hypothesis without citing the actual data.
Treating the evaluation as an afterthought instead of a genuine analysis of reliability and error.
Believing peer review proves a result is TRUE, rather than that it has passed expert scrutiny.
Thinking a single study settles a question, overlooking the role of independent replication.
Using casual, first-person or overclaiming language instead of objective scientific register.
Omitting units/significant figures in the results as if presentation were separate from rigour.

learn.summary: Learners aged 13–14 compose a full structured science report (aim, hypothesis, method, results, conclusion, evaluation) in objective scientific register, and come to understand WHY science is reported this way: peer review and independent replication are the social mechanisms that make scientific knowledge trustworthy. The load-bearing skill is extended scientific writing with reproducible methods and evidence-tied conclusions; the nature-of-science half is understanding that reliability comes from independent scrutiny, not authority.

activities.title: Report studio: compose the six sections with built-in checks
feedback: If the method omits what was kept constant, prompt: 'Could another person set up exactly the same test from this alone? What have you not told them to hold the same?'

If a results value appears without a unit or with inconsistent significant figures, flag it: 'A bare number isn't a measurement — add the SI unit and record values to the resolution of your instrument, keeping the precision consistent.'
If the conclusion only restates the hypothesis, prompt: 'Quote an actual value or trend from your data here — what in the evidence makes you say this?'
If the evaluation is a single line, prompt: 'Name one anomaly and classify one error as systematic or random, then give one concrete improvement.'
activities.rationale: Treating the report as sections with distinct jobs, demanding reproducible methods, requiring conclusions to cite the evidence quantitatively, and teaching objective register align with KS3 Working Scientifically and NGSS SEP 8 communication expectations. A sectioned writing surface with live structural and convention checks can scaffold these conventions as the learner writes.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Working Scientifically requires pupils to present reasoned explanations, report and communicate findings clearly using SI units and standard notation, and evaluate data and methods.

NGSS SEP 8 (Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information) grades 6–8 has students communicate scientific information clearly in writing, and treats peer review and replication as mechanisms that strengthen scientific claims.
learnerActions: Write a complete report with the conventional sections — aim, testable hypothesis, method, results, conclusion, evaluation — for an investigation you have actually run or been given full data for.
Draft the method as a numbered, unambiguous procedure that states what was kept constant (controlled variables), not as a past-tense story of what you did.
Build results tables and graphs with headed columns, SI units and correct significant figures throughout.
Write a conclusion that quotes specific values, a gradient, or a trend from your own data and states whether it supports the hypothesis — do not merely restate the hypothesis.
Write an evaluation that genuinely analyses reliability: identify anomalies, distinguish systematic from random error, and propose specific improvements.
Before finalising, check each section against stated success criteria for that section.
activities.intendedInsight: A scientific report is not a diary of what happened; each section has a distinct job, and together they present evidence and reasoning precisely enough for others to scrutinise.

activities.title: The reproducibility test: hand your method to someone else
feedback: When a replicator diverges, point to the specific sentence: 'This is where they had to guess — how would you rewrite it so there is only one interpretation?'
Reinforce success: 'They reproduced your result from the text alone — that shows your method is reproducible, a key part of what makes it trustworthy.'
activities.rationale: Making reproducibility the operational test of a good method, with peers attempting to follow each other's written procedures, is intended to teach the conventions by consequence rather than by assertion. A simulated partner that follows only the written text and stalls on ambiguity can make this mechanism concrete; efficacy here is proposed, not validated.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 8 (Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information) grades 6–8 has students communicate scientific information clearly in writing, and treats peer review and replication as mechanisms that strengthen scientific claims.
learnerActions: Give your written method — and ONLY the written text, not your verbal explanation — to a partner (or a simulated replicator) who tries to carry out the experiment following exactly what is written.
Observe where the replicator stalls, guesses, or does something different because an instruction was vague (e.g. 'heat it for a while', 'add some water').
Note every point where their result diverged from yours and check whether it can be traced to an ambiguous sentence (some differences may instead come from random variation or different equipment).
Rewrite each ambiguous step so a stranger would perform it identically, then have them try again.
activities.intendedInsight: A report must be a set of instructions precise enough for someone else to repeat and check you. Watching a reader fail to reproduce your result because of a fuzzy sentence shows why science demands reproducible methods.

activities.title: Review desk: critique a flawed report against criteria
feedback: If a learner only flags presentation (spelling, layout), redirect: 'Those are surface fixes — does the evidence actually support the conclusion? Is the method repeatable?'
If an overreaching conclusion is missed, prompt: 'Does the data cover the claim being made, or has the author gone beyond what was measured?'
activities.rationale: Structured critique of sample reports before composing one's own, and contrasting objective register with casual or overclaiming prose, are recommended teaching moves for these conventions. Comparing a strong and a flawed exemplar with section-by-section callouts can give a concrete model text to reason against.
learnerActions: Read a sample report containing deliberate flaws (a vague method, an overreaching conclusion, an unsupported claim, a missing control, missing units).
Mark each weakness and explain against explicit criteria why it fails — e.g. 'this conclusion claims more than the data shows', 'this method cannot be reproduced because…'.
Compare a gold-standard report and a flawed one section by section, articulating what makes each section strong or weak.
Suggest the specific revision each flaw requires.
activities.intendedInsight: Peer review chiefly scrutinises method, evidence, and reasoning — whether the conclusions are actually justified — rather than spelling or formatting. Learning to spot overreach and vagueness in others' work sharpens it in your own.

activities.title: Why peer review and replication make knowledge reliable
feedback: If a learner locates trust in the scientist's care, honesty, or fame, respond: 'Even careful, honest scientists make errors or hit flukes. Independent checking is precisely what catches what they cannot see themselves.'

If a learner dismisses replication as pointless repetition or treats published work as final proof, respond: 'Scientific knowledge is provisional. Replication is what upgrades a claim from tentative to trusted — and it can also overturn one.'

If a learner reduces peer review to checking spelling or formatting, respond: 'Peer review mainly scrutinises the method, evidence, and reasoning — whether the conclusions are justified — not just the presentation.'
Reinforce a full answer: 'You located reliability in independent reproducibility rather than authority, and you recognised that a result no one can reproduce should be doubted.'
activities.rationale: The nature-of-science half of this topic is well suited to dialogue in which the learner defends and critiques reports in role; an open epistemic probe targeting the authority-vs-scrutiny and non-replication distinctions is designed to discriminate genuine understanding from surface knowledge, though this efficacy is proposed rather than validated. NGSS SEP 8 treats peer review and replication as mechanisms that strengthen scientific claims.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 8 (Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information) grades 6–8 has students communicate scientific information clearly in writing, and treats peer review and replication as mechanisms that strengthen scientific claims.
learnerActions: Respond to the prompt: 'A scientist publishes a surprising result. Before other scientists accept it, the work goes through peer review, and other labs try to replicate it. Why aren't the scientist's own careful report and honest word enough — what do peer review and independent replication add? And what would it mean if no one else could reproduce the result?'

In a role-play, defend your own report to a reviewer/editor who probes: 'Is your method reproducible? Does your conclusion overreach the data? What would a replication need?' Then swap seats and review the character's flawed manuscript.

Argue through the discriminating cases: What does a reviewer check that the original scientist might have missed? If three other labs get a different result, what should happen to the claim? Does a scientist being famous and careful make replication unnecessary? Why is a result only one lab can ever produce treated with suspicion?
activities.intendedInsight: Reliability comes from independent scrutiny and reproduction by OTHER labs — not from the authority, fame, or honesty of the scientist. A result earns trust only when others independently obtain it; failure to replicate is grounds to doubt the claim. All scientific knowledge stays provisional: independent confirmation makes us more confident in a claim, but later evidence can still revise or overturn it.

activities.title: Check component knowledge of conventions and nature of science
feedback: For a mis-ordered structure, prompt: 'What must be stated before results can be interpreted?'
For a 'peer review = proofreading' choice, respond: 'Reviewers judge whether the science and reasoning hold up, not the spelling.'
For a spot-the-weakness item, confirm the specific flaw: 'Correct — this conclusion asserts a result without quoting any value from the data.'
activities.rationale: Short recognition and sequencing items efficiently check knowledge of conventions and nature-of-science facts, but by design they elicit recognition, not the independent construction of an extended report — so they support, rather than replace, the composition activities.
learnerActions: Match each piece of content to the report section it belongs in (e.g. 'what was kept constant' → method; 'the gradient of the weight–mass graph was 9.8 N/kg' → results/conclusion).
Put the sections of a report into the correct order.
Identify the purpose of peer review and of replication from short options, distinguishing scrutiny of reasoning from proofreading.
Spot the weakness in a short sample method or conclusion snippet (e.g. a conclusion that cites no data).
activities.intendedInsight: The conventions of report structure and the facts about peer review and replication can be checked quickly, but they are prerequisites for — not a substitute for — actually composing and defending a report.

constraints: The central skill is composing extended scientific prose in objective register. Section scaffolds, structural checks, and convention checks (units, significant figures, presence of a control, section order) can catch mechanical gaps but do not evaluate meaning-level qualities of the writing — whether the method is genuinely reproducible in prose, whether the evaluation reasons soundly, whether the register is appropriately objective. Those still need judgement from a teacher or a rubric-based open-response review.

A simulated replicator or role-play reviewer can model reproducibility and peer review vividly, but cannot assess the student's own extended written artefact; pair it with human or rubric-based feedback on the composed report.

Annotated exemplars (strong vs flawed reports with tappable callouts and a peer-review-to-revision-to-publication path) are valuable model texts and references, but reading a good report is not the same as composing and revising one's own — treat them as scaffolds, not the main task.
Recognition, sequencing, and spot-the-flaw items check component knowledge only; they do not elicit the independent construction or defence of an extended report.

Require conclusions to cite specific data (a value, gradient, or trend), not restate the hypothesis; require methods written as reproducible procedures that state controlled variables, not past-tense narratives; require genuine evaluations analysing reliability and error.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The two cited standards sources are marked verified:false in the source row; their claims are reproduced exactly but their accuracy has not been independently confirmed here.

The DfE KS3 source claim covers reporting, SI units/standard notation, and evaluating data/methods but does not mention peer review or replication; it has therefore been kept only where it supports reporting conventions and removed from the pure nature-of-science activity's sourceClaims.

The NGSS SEP 8 claim retained on the reproducibility-test activity supports the value of replication; whether it underwrites the specific pedagogy of teaching reproducible methods by consequence (as opposed to the underlying content) is a design inference, not source-verified efficacy.

The original recommendation asserted that genuine formative feedback on extended scientific prose is 'beyond all five artefacts' and that report writing 'has no spatial dimension; 3D offers nothing.' These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been recast as a scoped limitation (automated scaffolds do not evaluate meaning-level writing quality) and the dismissal of spatial/3D media has been dropped as unsupported boilerplate.

The misconception correction that peer review scrutinises reasoning rather than presentation is sound and has been carried into learner-facing feedback; the diagnostic probe and its discriminating cases were preserved from the assessment design.
Efficacy wording on the reproducibility-test and on the epistemic-probe discrimination was hedged because these specific interactions are unvalidated proposals.

probeDeeper: What exactly does a peer reviewer check that the original scientist might have missed?
Three other labs repeat the experiment and get a different result. What should happen to the original claim?
If the scientist is very famous and very careful, does that make replication unnecessary? Why or why not?
Why is a result that only ONE lab can ever produce treated with suspicion?
assess.correctAnswer: A strong response explains that peer review has independent experts scrutinise the method and reasoning for flaws or overclaiming before publication, and that replication by OTHER labs guards against mistakes, bias, flukes, or fraud the original team might not catch — a result earns trust only when others, independently, get it too. If no one can reproduce it, the claim is doubted (it may have been a one-off, an error, or an artefact of that lab), and the knowledge is treated as provisional until confirmed. It locates reliability in independent scrutiny, not authority.

errorPatterns.pattern: Trust from authority/honesty, not scrutiny: 'if a real scientist did it carefully and honestly, it must be true.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Even careful, honest scientists make errors or hit flukes; independent checking is precisely what catches what they can't see themselves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Locates reliability in the person rather than in independent checking.

errorPatterns.pattern: Science as fixed proven facts: 'once it's published it's proven; replication is just pointless repetition.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scientific knowledge is provisional; replication is what upgrades a claim from tentative to trusted, and can also overturn it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses replication, or treats published knowledge as final and certain.

errorPatterns.pattern: Peer review = proofreading: thinks reviewers mainly check spelling, grammar, or formatting.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Peer review scrutinises the method, evidence, and reasoning — whether the conclusions are actually justified — not the presentation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Trivialises peer review to presentation rather than scrutiny of the science.

responseLevels.gap: Locates trust in the scientist's care, honesty, or fame; sees replication as pointless or peer review as proofreading.
responseLevels.full: Explains reliability as arising from independent scrutiny (peer review of method and reasoning) and reproduction by other labs, treats failure to replicate as grounds to doubt a claim, and frames scientific knowledge as provisional until independently confirmed.
responseLevels.partial: Knows peer review and replication matter and involve checking, but can't fully explain why independent reproduction (not authority) is what confers reliability, or what non-replication implies.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A scientist publishes a surprising result. Before other scientists accept it, the work goes through peer review, and other labs try to replicate it. Why aren't the scientist's own careful report and honest word enough — what do peer review and independent replication add that makes a claim trustworthy? And what would it mean if no one else could reproduce the result?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student with the concept locates trustworthiness in independent checking and reproducibility; one without it locates it in the scientist's care, honesty, or credentials ('they're an expert, so it's true'). The failure-to-replicate probe is the discriminator: only the first view treats non-reproducibility as grounds to doubt the claim.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years (KS1)

- **Topic:** How Breathing Works — we breathe air into our lungs through the nose and mouth; lungs take in oxygen (which the body needs to live) and we breathe out carbon dioxide as waste

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1, Animals including humans):** statutory KS1 content is the basic needs for survival — water, food and AIR; the detailed respiratory system (trachea, alveoli, gas exchange) is Y5/Y6+ and KS3. So at KS1 this is the age-appropriate 'why we need air' encounter that seeds later respiratory study.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** nearest is K-LS1-1 (what animals need to survive, including air); the respiratory system as an interacting subsystem is formalised at MS-LS1-3. Enrichment on both sides at this age.

- **Operational details:** Build on what the child already does thousands of times a day but never notices. Three ideas: (1) the AIR PATH — air goes in through the nose/mouth, down the windpipe, into the two lungs in the chest; (2) the WHY — air contains oxygen, and the body needs oxygen to stay alive (that's why you can't hold your breath forever); (3) the WASTE — the body makes carbon dioxide, which we breathe OUT. Make it embodied: put hands on the ribs/chest and feel it rise and fall; take a deep breath and feel the lungs fill; breathe on a cold mirror/window to 'see' the warm, moist air you breathe out. The key conceptual correction: we breathe IN and OUT the SAME air (a mixture), not 'pure oxygen in, pure carbon dioxide out' — the lungs just TAKE SOME oxygen from the air and ADD some carbon dioxide. Also correct the location: lungs are in the chest (two of them), not the belly, and breathing is not the same as the stomach/eating. Keep the diaphragm mechanism for Y5/6 — at KS1, 'your chest gets bigger to pull air in' is enough.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, embodied). Success = trace air nose/mouth → windpipe → lungs, state that lungs take oxygen from air that the body needs, and state that we breathe out carbon dioxide as waste. Depth stops at path + oxygen-in + carbon-dioxide-out.
bestPractices: Start from the child's own body — hands on ribs to feel the chest rise and fall, a deep breath to feel the lungs fill — so breathing becomes noticed, not abstract.
Use the cold-mirror trick (breathe out onto glass to see the moist warm air) to make invisible exhaled air real and evidence the 'we breathe something out'.
Correct the 'pure oxygen in / pure carbon dioxide out' myth: we breathe the same air mixture in and out; lungs just take some oxygen and add some carbon dioxide.
Locate the two lungs correctly in the chest (not the belly) and keep breathing distinct from eating/the stomach.
Tie the WHY to a felt limit — you can't hold your breath forever because the body must keep getting oxygen — making the need visceral.
Keep the diaphragm mechanism for Y5/6; at KS1 'the chest gets bigger to pull air in' is the right grain.
keyRepresentations: Hands-on-ribs feeling the chest rise (in) and fall (out)
A simple air-path diagram: nose/mouth → windpipe → two lungs
The cold-mirror/window fogging up to show exhaled moist air
A balloon-in-chest image for lungs filling and emptying (with the limit that lungs aren't hollow balloons)
An 'air is a mixture' picture: some oxygen taken out, some carbon dioxide added
commonMisconceptions: Thinking we breathe in pure oxygen and breathe out pure carbon dioxide, rather than the same air mixture with some oxygen removed and carbon dioxide added.
Believing air/breath goes into the stomach or belly rather than the lungs in the chest.
Thinking there is one lung, or not knowing lungs are in the chest.
Confusing breathing (air in/out) with eating/drinking, or thinking the windpipe and food pipe are the same tube.
Believing you breathe out ALL the oxygen, or that exhaled air has no oxygen left in it.
Thinking breathing is optional/voluntary only, not understanding the body needs a constant oxygen supply.

learn.summary: KS1 (ages 5–7) first encounter with how breathing works: air enters through the nose/mouth, travels down the windpipe to the two lungs in the chest; the lungs take some oxygen (which the body needs to stay alive) from the air and add carbon dioxide (waste) to the breath we send back out. The core conceptual target is that the SAME air mixture goes in and out — changed, not swapped for pure gases — plus correct lung location (chest, not belly) and a felt reason we must keep breathing. Keep the diaphragm mechanism for later years; at KS1 'the chest gets bigger to pull air in' is the right grain. Activities centre on the child's own body and an animated, driveable breath model, with recognition checks kept as lighter scaffolds.

activities.title: Breathe with me: drive your own breath and watch the air change
feedback: If a learner says the out-breath is identical to the in-breath, point to the dots: some oxygen stayed in the body and carbon dioxide was added — ask why we'd keep breathing if nothing changed.
If a learner thinks all the oxygen is removed, show that oxygen dots still remain in the outgoing air — the lungs take only some.
When the hold-your-breath meter fills, connect it to the real feeling of being out of breath after running: the body can't stop needing oxygen.
activities.rationale: Breathing is an automatic, invisible process the child performs constantly but never notices; an embodied, driveable model lets them work the breath and make the oxygen-taken/carbon-dioxide-added exchange visible. The coloured-air moment targets the central KS1 misconception that we breathe pure oxygen in and pure carbon dioxide out, and the hold-your-breath meter grounds the DfE basic-need-for-air idea in a felt reason the body must keep getting oxygen. Pairing on-screen action with hands on the ribs ties the model to the real rise and fall of the chest. The oxygen-dots, carbon-dioxide-dots and hold-your-breath meter are illustrative design examples, not required mechanisms — a paper flip-sequence or acted-out breath could carry the same insight; comparative effectiveness is untested.
sourceClaims: Inhaled and exhaled air are both mixtures; the lungs take up some oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so exhaled air still contains oxygen — it is not 'pure carbon dioxide'.
DfE KS1 statutory content includes the basic needs of animals including humans for survival (water, food and AIR); detailed respiratory anatomy and gas exchange come later (Y5/Y6 and KS3).
learnerActions: Put one hand on your ribs/chest and take a slow deep breath in, then let it out, feeling the chest rise and fall.
Using an animated model, tap-and-hold to breathe IN: watch the chest widen and a stream of air carrying oxygen dots flow in through the nose/mouth, down the windpipe, and puff up the two lungs.
Release to breathe OUT and watch the air leave: notice that some oxygen dots stayed behind in the body and new carbon-dioxide dots have joined the outgoing breath.
Say in your own words what changed about the air between going in and coming out.
Watch a 'hold your breath' meter climb until the body insists on a breath, and connect this to why air must keep coming.
activities.intendedInsight: Breathing is a repeating in/out process: the SAME air goes in and out but is changed — the lungs take some oxygen (which the body needs to live) and add carbon-dioxide waste. We can't stop breathing because the body keeps needing oxygen.

activities.title: See your warm breath on cold glass
feedback: If a learner says breathing out is 'just pushing the same air', point to the fog: the out-breath is warm and moist from inside you, so it has been changed.
Reinforce that the fog is water the body added, part of how the out-breath differs from the in-breath.
activities.rationale: The cold-mirror trick makes invisible exhaled air observable and gives concrete evidence for 'we breathe something out', supporting the in-changed-out picture. It uses everyday materials and needs no screen.
sourceClaims: Inhaled and exhaled air are both mixtures; the lungs take up some oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so exhaled air still contains oxygen — it is not 'pure carbon dioxide'.
learnerActions: Take a deep breath and breathe out slowly with an open mouth ('haaa') onto a cold mirror or window.
Look at the fog that appears and feel that the breath is warm and moist.
Say what this shows: we really do breathe something out, and it is different from ordinary room air.
activities.intendedInsight: Exhaled air is real and carries moisture and warmth from inside the body — evidence that we breathe something out, not nothing, and that the out-breath differs from the in-breath.

activities.title: Trace the air path and find your lungs
feedback: If a learner says the air goes to the tummy/stomach, trace the windpipe to the lungs and note the food pipe is a separate tube; use hands on the chest to feel the lungs expand.

If a child notices their tummy moving during a big breath, acknowledge that the belly can be felt to move, but the air itself travels to the lungs in the chest — the deeper reason for the belly movement (the diaphragm) is for later years.
If a learner says there is one lung, show there are two, both in the chest.
If a learner says exhaled air has no oxygen, reveal that only some oxygen is taken out.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal chest illustration is effective for the air path and lung location and for addressing the belly-breathing and pure-gas myths. It is offered here as a scaffold: static or lift-the-flap art does not itself show the in/out cycle or the ongoing oxygen/CO2 exchange, so it supports but does not replace the driveable breath work.
sourceClaims: Inhaled and exhaled air are both mixtures; the lungs take up some oxygen and release carbon dioxide, so exhaled air still contains oxygen — it is not 'pure carbon dioxide'.
learnerActions: On a chest illustration, tap nose/mouth → windpipe → the two lungs to trace where air goes.

Put hands on your tummy and on your chest, take a big breath, and decide where the air actually goes inside you — then check that the air travels to the lungs in the chest, not into the belly or stomach.

Answer a lift-the-flap question: 'Do our lungs take ALL the oxygen out of the air?' → reveal 'No — they take just some, so the air we breathe out still has oxygen in it, and carbon dioxide has been added.'
Place the lungs correctly: a myth-buster flap shows two lungs in the chest, not one, and not in the belly.
activities.intendedInsight: Air travels nose/mouth → windpipe → two lungs in the chest; breathing is separate from the stomach/eating, and the out-breath still contains some oxygen.

activities.title: Quick checks: order the path and name the waste
feedback: For a wrong ordering, re-trace the path with the child from the nose down to the lungs.
If carbon dioxide is missed, remind that it is the waste the body adds and sends out.
For the lung-location item, confirm the lungs are in the chest, not the belly.
activities.rationale: Short recognition items can confirm the air-path and in/out facts. Recognition responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction or show the in/out cycle, so these items are a light confirmation layer, not the main embodied first encounter for this age.
learnerActions: Put the air path in order: nose → windpipe → lungs.
Choose what we breathe out as waste (carbon dioxide).
Decide true or false: 'The lungs are in the chest.'
activities.intendedInsight: Recall the air path, the location of the lungs, and that carbon dioxide is the waste we breathe out.

activities.title: Talk it through with friendly lungs
feedback: If the learner can't say why breathing can't stop, link it to the hold-your-breath feeling: the body keeps needing oxygen.
Prompt the learner to mention the warm, moist breath they saw on the glass as evidence something is breathed out.
activities.rationale: A talking-lungs dialogue can engage the child and prompt them to articulate reasoning. At 5–7 the understanding is built mainly by feeling and doing the breath, so discussion works best paired with the hands-on and mirror activities rather than on its own.
learnerActions: Respond to a friendly-lungs character that asks you to take a deep breath and breathe out slowly with an open mouth ('haaa') onto a cold mirror.
Explain to the character what you just saw and felt.
Answer the character's question: 'Why can't I stop breathing?'
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the experience into words — what was seen, felt, and why the body needs air — consolidates the idea that the body must keep getting oxygen.

constraints: KS1 depth stops at: trace air nose/mouth → windpipe → lungs; lungs take some oxygen the body needs; we breathe out carbon dioxide as waste. Do not teach trachea/alveoli detail, gas-exchange mechanism, or the diaphragm — reserve these for Y5/Y6+ and KS3.
At KS1, 'the chest gets bigger to pull air in' is the right explanation; keep the diaphragm implicit.

Core correction: we breathe the same air mixture in and out — the lungs take SOME oxygen and add some carbon dioxide; exhaled air still contains oxygen. Avoid 'pure oxygen in, pure carbon dioxide out'.

Locate the two lungs in the chest (not the belly) and keep breathing distinct from eating/the stomach; the windpipe is a separate tube from the food pipe. The air we breathe in goes to the lungs, not into the stomach/belly — though the belly may be felt to move, which is a diaphragm effect reserved for later years.
The balloon-in-chest image is an approximation only: lungs are not hollow balloons — flag this limit if the image is used.
Recognition items confirm facts but do not themselves show independent construction or the in/out cycle; use them as a secondary check, not the primary first encounter.

Oxygen dots, carbon-dioxide dots, the hold-your-breath meter, lift-the-flap reveals and the coloured-air animation are optional illustrative examples of the learning mechanism, not mandatory features; their comparative efficacy is untested.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources (NGSS and British Lung Foundation / Asthma + Lung UK) are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their claims as unconfirmed.

The source frames a 3D lung model as adding 'no conceptual gain' for KS1. Softened here: a 3D model is simply not needed for this particular path + oxygen-in + CO2-out objective at this age; no universal claim about 3D ineffectiveness is made.

The source's strong claim that the coloured-air animation 'quietly kills' or is uniquely able to defeat the misconception is softened — an animated exchange is one effective approach among several (paper sequences, acted breaths, mirror evidence); comparative necessity is not established by the available sources.

In the 'find your lungs' activity, a child's belly may visibly move during a deep breath; this is a diaphragm effect reserved for Y5/6 and does NOT mean air enters the stomach. The KS1 teaching point — air travels to the lungs in the chest, not into the belly/stomach — remains correct; the prompt asks where the air goes, and the activity feedback now acknowledges the belly movement rather than implying the belly stays completely still.

Checked air-path and physiology statements for internal consistency: exhaled air still containing some oxygen, two lungs in the chest, and 'same air changed' are consistent across pedagogy, assessment and sources; no arithmetic or force/motion content to audit here.

probeDeeper: Put one hand on your tummy and one on your chest and take a big breath — which one fills with air? Where did it really go?
If air just went in and came straight back out the same, why would we need to keep breathing all the time?
You breathe out carbon dioxide — where in your body do you think that came from?
assess.correctAnswer: The air goes down the windpipe into the lungs (not the tummy). The body wants it because the lungs take OXYGEN out of the air, and the body needs oxygen to stay alive. The air breathed out is different — it has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, which the body doesn't need — so breathing out gets rid of waste carbon dioxide.

errorPatterns.pattern: Breathed-in and breathed-out air are the same — you just push the same air back out unchanged.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that the body keeps some oxygen and adds carbon dioxide — so out-air differs; ask why we'd need to keep breathing if nothing changed.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's exactly the same air going straight back out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the out-breath is identical to the in-breath; nothing is taken from the air.

errorPatterns.pattern: Air goes into the stomach / fills your tummy.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the windpipe to the lungs (a separate tube from the one food takes); use hands on chest to feel the lungs, not the tummy, expand.
errorPatterns.distractor: The air goes down into my tummy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the tummy or stomach as where the air goes.

errorPatterns.pattern: We breathe just to move the chest / breathing isn't for getting something the body needs.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link breathing to staying alive — the lungs take oxygen the whole body needs; connect to feeling out of breath after running.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes breathing with no mention of oxygen or a bodily need for it.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks air goes to the tummy, or that in-air and out-air are identical; no sense the body takes something from the air.
responseLevels.full: Traces air to the lungs, states the body takes oxygen it needs to live, and explains the out-breath differs (less oxygen, more carbon-dioxide waste) — a coherent in-changed-out picture.
responseLevels.partial: Knows air goes to the lungs and mentions oxygen, but treats the out-breath as the same air, or can't say what changed or why the body needs it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: When you take a big breath in, where does the air actually go inside you, and why does your body want it? And is the air you breathe out exactly the same as the air you breathed in, or different — and how?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks air fills the tummy, or that in-air and out-air are the same, reveals the naive model. A child who understands says air goes to the lungs, the body takes the oxygen it needs, and the out-breath carries waste carbon dioxide. The tier-two 'same or different' forces the change to be named, which the naive 'just push the air back out' idea cannot do.

pedagogy.summary: Adding up to four two-digit numbers is where the properties of operations become a practical tool: because addition is commutative and associative, children may reorder and regroup the addends to make the work easier — hunting for pairs that make a multiple of ten, then partitioning the rest into tens and ones. The efficiency insight (look before you leap) matters as much as accuracy; the composing of several tens at once is the new demand over two-addend work.
bestPractices: Teach 'look for pairs that make ten (or a multiple of ten)' before adding — reorder using commutativity/associativity (extends adding three one-digit numbers)
Partition all addends into tens and ones, sum the tens, sum the ones, then recombine — composing as many tens/hundreds as needed
Encourage jottings to keep track when combining many ones, to prevent accumulation slips
Discuss which grouping was smartest and why, so the properties are used deliberately not accidentally
Use manipulatives/ten-frames so 'making a ten' from a pair is seen, then move to numbers
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames / bead strings (spotting pairs that make ten)
Draggable number cards (reorder addends to pair)
Part-whole / column jottings (tens together, ones together)
Number line (cumulative jumps)
Base-ten blocks (composing several tens)
commonMisconceptions: Adding strictly left-to-right and missing pairs that make ten (not using commutativity to simplify)
Losing track when combining many ones, or forgetting to compose more than one ten (ones sum to 23, only one ten carried)
Believing the addends must be added in the given order (no reordering allowed)
Miscounting during a long running total

learn.summary: Children add up to four two-digit numbers by using the commutative and associative properties as a practical tool: reorder and regroup addends to find pairs that make a multiple of ten, then partition the rest into tens and ones, sum each, and recombine. The 'look before you leap' efficiency insight matters alongside accuracy, and composing several tens at once is the new demand over two-addend work. The strongest version lets the child physically reorder addends and see pairs combine into round numbers; recognition tasks and static ringed examples are useful rehearsal and reference, but because they do not themselves require the child to reorder addends they check the strategy more than they elicit the independent habit of looking for pairs first.

activities.title: Snap the pairs that make a tidy number
feedback: If the child adds left-to-right without scanning, don't reteach addition: ask 'before you start, can you see any two that make a tidy number?' and let them re-experience the shortcut.
When two cards combine into a round number (e.g. 15 and 25 becoming 40), name it: 'those two made exactly 40, so now you only have round numbers left.'

If the child insists the numbers must stay in the written order, demonstrate with counters that the total is the same in any order, and connect it to adding three one-digit numbers where pairing to ten was allowed.

OPTIONAL: on a screen version, cards whose sum is a multiple of ten can snap into a labelled '40' or '20' block, remaining tens and ones can auto-partition and recombine to show the composed tens, and a side-by-side 'left-to-right vs paired' race can make the efficiency gain visible. These are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required features.
activities.rationale: Physically reordering and watching pairs fuse into round numbers rewards spotting the number bond and makes the commutative/associative strategy deliberate rather than accidental. Reordering to check and simplify is the curriculum route by which these properties are established at this stage.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add three one-digit numbers and, building on this, add numbers including combining several addends; adding numbers in a different order is used to check and establishes commutativity and associativity.
Choosing an efficient order of addition (identifying two addends that make ten) uses the associative and commutative laws; children need not use the formal terms at this stage.
learnerActions: Take four addends to add, e.g. 15, 8, 25, and 12, arranged as cards that can be physically moved (paper cards, counters on a tray, or draggable on-screen tiles).
Before adding anything, scan the four numbers and decide which two, placed together, would make a multiple of ten.
Pair 15 with 25 to make 40, and 8 with 12 to make 20, then add the two round numbers: 40 + 20 = 60.
Repeat with 24, 17, 6, 13 (24+6=30 and 17+13=30, giving 60) and say aloud which pair you spotted first and why.
Try one example by adding strictly left-to-right, then again by pairing first, and compare how much easier the paired route felt.
activities.intendedInsight: Because addition can be done in any order and grouping, reordering to make pairs that total a multiple of ten turns a fearsome four-number sum into an easy sum of round numbers. The properties of operations are a lever, not an abstraction.

activities.title: Partition into tens and ones, and compose the tens carefully
feedback: If the answer is off by exactly ten, the child likely composed one ten from the ones and dropped a second: have them pool all the ones again and count how many full tens they can make.
Encourage jottings to track the running total of ones so slips don't accumulate.
If the tens are right but the total drifts, slow the recombination step and check how many tens came out of the ones.
activities.rationale: Composing several tens at once is the genuinely new demand of four-addend work; pooling all ones before exchanging and making the exchange visible with base-ten targets the specific 'dropped a composed ten' error.
learnerActions: Take all four addends and split each into its tens and its ones: for 15, 8, 25, 12 the tens are 10, 0, 20, 10 (the single-digit 8 has no tens) and the ones are 5, 8, 5, 2.
Add all the tens together (10 + 0 + 20 + 10 = 40), then pool ALL the ones together before exchanging.

From the pooled ones, exchange every full ten you can: here 5 + 8 + 5 + 2 = 20, which makes two tens and no leftover ones; if the ones had totalled 23 you would make two tens (not one) and keep 3 ones.
Recombine the composed tens with the tens you already had (40 + 20 = 60) and check it matches the paired-up method.
Use base-ten blocks or ten-frames so that making more than one ten from the ones is something you can see, not just carry in your head.
activities.intendedInsight: When many ones are combined they can compose more than one ten. Pooling all the ones and exchanging every full ten before recombining is a reliable way to make sure no composed ten is lost. If a composed ten is dropped, the answer comes out ten too small, or more than ten too small if several tens are dropped.

activities.title: Explain and defend the smartest grouping
feedback: If the child can solve but can't explain, ask them to point to the pair that made a round number and say the new, simpler sum it created.
Accept informal language; the formal terms 'commutative' and 'associative' are not required at this stage.
If the child spots pairs only when prompted, praise the find and ask them to scan unprompted on the next sum to build the habit.
activities.rationale: Articulating the strategy distinguishes a child using the properties deliberately from one who adds accurately but never looks for simplifying pairs; reasoning about reordering is how the curriculum establishes commutativity and associativity.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add three one-digit numbers and, building on this, add numbers including combining several addends; adding numbers in a different order is used to check and establishes commutativity and associativity.
Choosing an efficient order of addition (identifying two addends that make ten) uses the associative and commutative laws; children need not use the formal terms at this stage.
learnerActions: After solving a four-addend sum, say which two numbers you added first and why that order made the work easier.
Answer 'you added them in a different order than they're written — does that change the answer, and how do you know?'
Given 19 + 4 + 1 + 6, decide which you would add first and justify it (19 + 1 makes 20, then + 4 + 6 reaches 30).
Pick a sum where no neat pair exists and explain what you do then (partition into tens and ones).
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the chosen grouping makes the properties a conscious, reusable strategy and shows that reordering never changes the total.

constraints: Prerequisite: pairing numbers to make ten (as in adding three one-digit numbers) and exchanging ten ones for a ten; revisit these if a child insists order is fixed or loses a composed ten.

Recognition-style tasks (matching pairs that make ten, choosing the smartest first step, filling blanks in running totals) rehearse and check the strategy and can catch left-to-right grinding, but because they do not require the child to reorder the addends themselves they do not on their own elicit the independent habit of looking for pairs first; pair them with tasks where the child reorders the addends.
A static worked example with the pairs ringed is useful reference but does not let the child try reordering; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on regrouping.
Manipulatives (ten-frames, bead strings, base-ten blocks) should make 'making a ten' and composing several tens visible before moving to numbers alone.
Keep sums engineered so tidy pairs exist when teaching the strategy, but also include a sum with no neat pair so the child learns the fallback of partitioning into tens and ones.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the listed source claims retain their original verification status (one marked verified, one not). Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original 'worked correct answer' example lists ones such as 5+8+5+2=20 for the first sum (composing two tens), consistent with the 'ones can exceed ten' point; retained as-is.

The original row asserted '3D adds nothing' and 'talk cannot supply the manipulation-and-feedback practice the strategy needs'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened: spoken discussion is used productively in the explain/defend activity, and the hands-on reordering is proposed on its affordances (physical regrouping and feedback) rather than as the only possible medium.

Comparative efficacy wording in the summary was tightened to the observable limit that recognition/static tasks do not require the child to reorder; no claim of tested superiority of any medium is made.

probeDeeper: Before adding, did any two of these numbers jump out as making a tidy total? Which?
You added them in a different order than they're written — does that change the answer? How do you know?
Your ones added up to more than ten — how many tens did you make from them?
If I gave you 19 + 4 + 1 + 6, which would you add first, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 60 and 60. Efficiently: 15+25=40 and 8+12=20 → 60; 24+6=30 and 17+13=30 → 60. Alternatively partition all into tens and ones (tens 10+20+... , ones summed and composed). Both reach 60; the strategy question is whether pairs are spotted.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds strictly left-to-right, never scanning for pairs that make ten — '15 and 8 is 23, and 25 is 48…'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach addition; prompt 'before you start, can you see any two that make a tidy number?' and let them re-experience the shortcut. Build the looking-first habit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child works in given order with no pause to look for bonds; the skill of pairing is available but not deployed

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses a composed ten when combining many ones — ones total 23 but only one ten is carried, or the running total drifts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child pool ALL the ones first and exchange as many tens as possible before recombining; use base-ten so multiple composed tens are visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens are right but the answer is off by ten; the child composed one ten from the ones and dropped the second

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the numbers must be added in the order written — resists reordering
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate with counters that the total is the same in any order; connect to adding three one-digit numbers where pairing to ten was allowed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When invited to reorder, the child says you can't, or that it would change the answer

responseLevels.gap: Adds left-to-right, drops composed tens, or insists order is fixed; answers unreliable and slow.
responseLevels.full: Scans for pairs making multiples of ten, reorders confidently using the properties, composes multiple tens correctly, and explains why the chosen grouping was efficient.
responseLevels.partial: Adds accurately by partitioning but doesn't yet look for pairs to simplify, or spots pairs only when prompted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set two calculations and watch how the child tackles each, thinking aloud: 15 + 8 + 25 + 12, then 24 + 17 + 6 + 13. Notice whether they look for pairs that make a multiple of ten before adding, and how they combine the ones.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both sums are engineered so pairs make tidy multiples of ten. A child who uses commutativity spots the pairs and finishes quickly and accurately; a child who grinds left-to-right is slower and far more likely to slip when the running total's ones exceed ten. Watching the ORDER they add in exposes whether the properties are a live tool.
