pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Heart Structure & Double Circulation

- **Standards — UK (DfE):** Builds on the statutory KS2 requirement (Year 6) to "describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood" within the circulatory system, developed at KS3 into heart structure and the double circulatory system (and completed at GCSE). (Heart chamber/valve detail is introduced at KS3 in most English schemes and is statutory content at GCSE.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS1-3):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS1-3]" (circulatory named among the subsystems). NGSS frames circulation as a subsystem interacting with the respiratory and digestive systems rather than teaching chamber anatomy explicitly.

- **Operational details:** Children label the heart (right and left atria and ventricles, valves, aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery and vein, coronary arteries) and trace the route of blood through a DOUBLE circulation: body → right side → lungs (pick up O₂, drop CO₂) → left side → body. They explain valves preventing backflow and the left ventricle's thicker wall (pumps further, to the whole body), and compare arteries (thick, elastic, high pressure), veins (valves, low pressure) and capillaries (one-cell walls for exchange). The move that matters is grasping WHY circulation is double: blood is re-pressurised by the heart between the lung loop and the body loop, so it reaches the body at high pressure after being oxygenated.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B→C. Depends on the KS2 circulatory overview and gas exchange; a high-centrality hub linking transport to respiration and gas exchange. A child is secure when they can trace a blood drop through both loops in order and explain why the two circuits and the valves are needed.
bestPractices: Teach circulation by tracing a blood drop through the whole route, so the double-loop structure is experienced as a journey, not memorised as a diagram.
Make the PURPOSE of double circulation explicit — the heart re-pressurises blood between the lung loop and the body loop — rather than just naming two circuits.
Link oxygenation state to the loop (deoxygenated on the right/to lungs; oxygenated on the left/to body) and correct the 'heart oxygenates blood' error.
Tie structure to function: thicker left ventricle wall, valves preventing backflow, and artery/vein/capillary differences all explained by their job.
Use consistent colour convention (blue deoxygenated, red oxygenated) but note it represents oxygenation, not actual blue blood.
keyRepresentations: Labelled heart diagram (chambers, valves, great vessels, coronary arteries)
Double-circulation loop diagram (body loop and lung loop meeting at the heart)
Artery / vein / capillary cross-section comparison
Colour-coded blood-route trace (deoxygenated vs oxygenated)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the heart adds oxygen to blood (the lungs do; the heart pumps).
Believing blood flows in a single loop rather than two circuits through the heart.
Thinking blue-drawn blood is literally blue rather than deoxygenated (dark red).
Confusing arteries and veins by oxygenation (the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood).
Assuming all chambers have equal muscular walls, missing why the left ventricle is thickest.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13, teach heart structure and double circulation by having learners trace a single blood drop through both the lung loop and the body loop, grasping WHY the circuit is double: the heart re-pressurises blood between the two loops so oxygenated blood reaches the body at high pressure. Core objectives: label the heart (atria, ventricles, valves, aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery and vein, coronary arteries), explain how valves prevent backflow, explain why the left ventricle wall is thickest, compare arteries/veins/capillaries, and correct the error that the heart (rather than the lungs) oxygenates blood. Crucially, arteries and veins are defined by DIRECTION of flow (away from vs toward the heart), not by oxygenation — the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

activities.title: Drive the blood: tracing one drop through two loops
feedback: If a learner routes blood from the lungs straight to the body, note that oxygenated blood returns to the LEFT side of the heart first and is re-pumped — that re-pressurising is the point of the second loop.
If a learner says the heart adds oxygen to the blood, correct: the lungs load the oxygen; the heart only pumps.
If a learner attributes pumping to the valves, clarify that valves only stop backflow — the muscular ventricle walls contract to pump.
If a learner treats the colour as literal, remind them it represents oxygenation state; deoxygenated blood is dark red, not blue.
activities.rationale: Tracing a drop makes the two-loop structure a journey with causal logic rather than a diagram to memorise, and a live pump/valve mechanism (clickable pumping, a visible valve that snaps shut on backflow, and a pressure readout on the left ventricle) makes valve function and re-pressurisation concrete. Comparing against a single-loop model surfaces the purpose of the second circuit.
sourceClaims: Humans have a double circulatory system: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; valves prevent backflow and the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to pump blood around the whole body.
learnerActions: Pump the heart and follow one blood drop all the way round, starting from the body: body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → to the lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → back to the body.

Watch (or mark, on paper) the drop's oxygenation change: it loads oxygen in the lungs (deoxygenated → oxygenated) and unloads it as body cells use it (oxygenated → deoxygenated) — note that colour represents oxygenation state, not literally blue blood.
Try to push blood backwards through a valve and observe that a valve blocks it.

Compare the two circuits with a 'single circulation' model version: route blood straight from the lungs to the body without an intermediate return to the heart, and describe what happens to its speed and pressure by the time it reaches the body.
State in one sentence WHY mammals use a double circuit, referring to the heart re-pressurising blood between the lung loop and the body loop.
activities.intendedInsight: Double circulation is a routing process: blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit, and the heart re-pressurises it between the lung loop and the body loop so it reaches the body at high pressure after being oxygenated. Valves prevent backflow; the pumping force comes from heart muscle, not valves.

activities.title: Heart anatomy: chambers, valves and vessels in three dimensions
feedback: If a learner assumes all chambers have equally muscular walls, point to the relative wall thickness and ask which chamber pushes blood furthest.
If a learner thinks blood mixes across the heart, point to the septum dividing the two sides in a healthy heart.
When labelling, if 'artery = oxygenated' is applied to the pulmonary artery, flag it for the direction-based definition activity.
activities.rationale: A three-dimensional, manipulable heart shows the spatial arrangement of chambers, valves and great vessels and the relative wall thicknesses more directly than a flat diagram; rotating, cross-sectioning and animating a beat make the anatomy inspectable. A tappable labelled diagram (e.g. tap the left ventricle to reveal 'thickest wall — pumps to the whole body', tap a valve to reveal 'stops backflow') is an efficient naming scaffold, though static diagrams do not show flow dynamics.
sourceClaims: Humans have a double circulatory system: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; valves prevent backflow and the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to pump blood around the whole body.
learnerActions: Examine and rotate a manipulable heart model (a rotatable screen model, or a real sheep/pig heart), identifying the four chambers, valve positions and the great vessels in their spatial arrangement.
Cross-section the heart to compare the thickness of the left ventricle wall against the right ventricle and the atria.
Explain why the left ventricle wall is thickest by linking it to its job: pumping blood the whole way round the body.
Locate the septum and state what it does: keeps the oxygenated (left) and deoxygenated (right) blood from mixing in a healthy heart.
Label a diagram with atria, ventricles, valves, aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein and coronary arteries.
activities.intendedInsight: Structure follows function: the four-chambered pump is spatially arranged so the two sides stay separate (septum), and the thicker left ventricle wall matches the greater pumping demand of the whole-body loop.

activities.title: Which way does water pass? Predict–observe with a valve
feedback: If the prediction and observation disagree, ask the learner to describe the valve's shape and how flow in one direction opens it while flow the other way presses it shut.
If a learner says the valve pumps or sets the heartbeat, separate the two: muscle contraction supplies the force; the valve only controls direction.
For the leaky-valve discussion: a leaky valve lets some blood flow backward (reduced efficiency), whereas a failed pump means the force to move blood is lost — both are problems, but different ones.
Remind learners that a physical specimen or water model is an approximation: it shows valve directionality but will not reproduce living pressures or flow.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain task with real water flow makes one-way valve function directly observable and confronts the 'valves pump' misconception through evidence rather than assertion.
sourceClaims: Humans have a double circulatory system: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; valves prevent backflow and the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to pump blood around the whole body.
learnerActions: Before pouring, PREDICT which direction water will pass freely through a one-way valve model (or a valve in a fresh sheep/pig heart) and which direction will be blocked, and explain why.
Pour water through the valve in each direction and OBSERVE which way flows and which way is stopped.
Reconcile prediction with observation, stating in your own words what the valve does and what it does NOT do (it does not pump).
Discuss: if a valve became leaky, what problem would that cause, and why is that different from the pump (muscle) failing?
activities.intendedInsight: Valves are passive one-way gates that prevent backflow; they are opened and closed by the pressure of blood the muscle moves, not a source of pumping themselves.

activities.title: Defining arteries and veins by direction, not oxygenation
feedback: If a learner insists the pulmonary artery must carry oxygenated blood 'because all arteries do', show the route: it goes FROM the heart TO the lungs to collect oxygen — so the blood in it has not yet been oxygenated.
If a learner is unsure how many times a cell passes through the heart, have them retrace both loops: once before the lung loop and once before the body loop.

Reinforce that the direction-based definitions work for the circulation studied here, while the oxygenation rule has a standing exception at the pulmonary vessels (and also at the umbilical vessels before birth).
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the pulmonary exception forces a correct, general definition and is the discriminating difference between surface memorisation and genuine understanding. Structure-to-function comparison of the three vessel types supports the broader transport concept.
learnerActions: State the common shortcut rule: 'arteries carry oxygenated blood, veins carry deoxygenated blood.'

Apply it to the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein, then check the actual blood each carries: the pulmonary artery carries DEOXYGENATED blood (heart to lungs); the pulmonary vein carries OXYGENATED blood (lungs to heart).
Rewrite the definition so it never fails: an artery carries blood AWAY from the heart; a vein carries blood TOWARD the heart — regardless of oxygenation.

Compare artery, vein and capillary structure and link each to its job: arteries have thick elastic walls for high pressure; veins have thinner walls and operate at low pressure, and many veins (especially in the limbs) have valves to prevent backflow; capillaries have one-cell-thick walls for exchange.
Trace a red blood cell from the vena cava all the way round until it returns, counting how many times it passes through the heart (twice per full circuit).
activities.intendedInsight: Arteries and veins are correctly defined by direction of flow, not oxygenation; the oxygenation shortcut breaks precisely at the pulmonary vessels. Vessel structure matches the pressure and function of each.

activities.title: Check your understanding: sequence, match and explain
feedback: Correct route order: body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

Diagnostic answer: the pulmonary vessels break the rule; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood; define an artery as carrying blood away from the heart and a vein as carrying it toward the heart.
If a learner orders a single loop missing the separate lung circuit, return them to the drive-the-blood trace to re-establish the two loops.
activities.rationale: Sequencing the route, matching vessels to features and explaining wall thickness are clean, high-value checks; the diagnostic prompt specifically discriminates direction-based understanding from the oxygenation shortcut. These recognition-and-short-explanation items check identification and brief reasoning and should follow, not replace, the construction and tracing activities.
sourceClaims: Humans have a double circulatory system: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; valves prevent backflow and the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to pump blood around the whole body.
learnerActions: Put the chambers and vessels in the order a blood drop passes through them on a full double circuit.
Match each vessel type (artery, vein, capillary) to its distinguishing feature.
Explain why the left ventricle wall is thicker than the other chambers' walls.

Answer the diagnostic: a student writes 'arteries always carry oxygenated blood, veins always carry deoxygenated blood' — name the one pair of vessels where this breaks down, explain why it is wrong there, and give the correct direction-based definition.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure understanding means ordering the double-loop route correctly, defining vessels by direction, explaining valves and the septum, and justifying the left ventricle's thicker wall by its workload.

constraints: A rotatable heart model and a labelled tappable diagram are naming/anatomy scaffolds: they are strong for identifying chambers, valves and vessels and for comparing wall thickness, but being static (diagram) or anatomy-focused (model) they do not themselves demonstrate the flow dynamics and re-pressurisation logic — pair them with a trace of the moving blood drop.
Colour coding (blue deoxygenated, red oxygenated) is a convention representing oxygenation state only; make explicit that deoxygenated blood is dark red, not literally blue.

Recognition and matching items check that learners can identify correct answers; they do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the double-loop explanation, so include at least one activity where learners trace and explain the route in their own words.

The 'single circulation' comparison is a teaching contrast to reveal the purpose of the second loop; present it as a model variation, not as a claim about any specific real organism's physiology without evidence.
A conversational/interview format is a poor fit for this routing-and-structure topic, which is better served by tracing and manipulating the system; it is not recommended as the main scaffold here.

When using a real sheep/pig heart or a water-and-valve model, treat the physical specimen as an approximation of the idealised pump; observed water flow demonstrates valve directionality but pressures and flow will not match living circulation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The BBC Bitesize source supporting the double-circulation and valve/wall-thickness claims is marked verified:false in the source row; the direction-based artery/vein definition and the pulmonary exception are standard curriculum content but have not been independently re-verified here, and no source claim in the row directly supports that definition (activity 4 sourceClaims left empty).

The left-ventricle re-pressurisation framing is pedagogically standard, but the 'single circulation → slow, low-pressure' contrast is a didactic model and should not be read as a measured physiological result for any particular organism.

No sources in this row establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any one medium (2D trace vs 3D model vs diagram vs physical heart); claims that only one medium can teach a given point have been kept as scoped affordances/limits.

The corrected direction-based definition of arteries/veins is placed directly in a learner activity (not merely caveated), since the row's own assessment identifies the oxygenation-only rule as the critical misconception to fix.

Activity 1's first learner action simplifies the route as '…to the lungs…' whereas activity 4 gives the full route naming the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein; this is an intentional scaffolding simplification, not an inconsistency.

assess.poeTask: Using a one-way valve model (or a valve in a fresh sheep/pig heart), ask students to PREDICT which way water will pass through and which way it will be blocked, and why. Pouring water and seeing it flow one direction but not the other makes valve function — preventing backflow — directly observable.
probeDeeper: Trace a red blood cell from the vena cava all the way round until it returns — how many times does it pass through the heart?
Why does defining an artery by 'oxygenated blood' fail at the lungs, but defining it by direction never fails?
What would happen to the blood if the wall between the two sides of the heart had a hole?
If a valve became leaky, what problem would that cause, and why isn't that the same as the pump failing?
assess.correctAnswer: The pulmonary vessels break the rule: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the heart. The correct definition is by direction — an artery carries blood away from the heart, a vein carries blood back toward it — regardless of whether the blood is oxygenated.

errorPatterns.pattern: Arteries always carry oxygenated blood, veins always deoxygenated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redefine by direction: away from the heart = artery, toward the heart = vein. The pulmonary vessels are the standing exception to the oxygenation shortcut.
errorPatterns.distractor: The pulmonary artery must carry oxygenated blood, because all arteries do.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies the oxygenation rule to the pulmonary artery/vein and gets them backwards

errorPatterns.pattern: The heart is one pump and blood does a single loop
errorPatterns.nextMove: Double circulation: the right side pumps blood to the lungs, the left side pumps it to the body — blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit.
errorPatterns.distractor: Blood travels round the whole body in one single loop, through the heart just once.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes one circuit through the heart, missing the separate loop to the lungs

errorPatterns.pattern: Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix inside the heart
errorPatterns.nextMove: The septum keeps the two sides separate; oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix in a healthy heart.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks as if all four chambers share the same blood

errorPatterns.pattern: Valves pump the blood / control the heartbeat
errorPatterns.nextMove: Valves only prevent backflow; the pumping force comes from the heart muscle contracting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes pumping to the valves rather than to muscle contraction

responseLevels.gap: Relies on the oxygenation rule, describes a single loop, and can't handle the pulmonary vessels.
responseLevels.full: Defines arteries/veins by direction (resolving the pulmonary exception), traces the double circulation, explains valves prevent backflow and the septum keeps blood unmixed.
responseLevels.partial: Labels the heart and traces flow but still gets the pulmonary artery/vein wrong, or is shaky on why there are two separate loops.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A student writes the rule: 'arteries always carry oxygenated blood, veins always carry deoxygenated blood.' There is one pair of vessels where this rule breaks down. Which vessels are they, why is the rule wrong there, and what is the correct way to define what an artery does?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who truly understands defines arteries and veins by direction of flow and can name the pulmonary exception. A child relying on the memorised oxygenation rule gets the pulmonary vessels wrong.

sources.source: DfE — National curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Key Stage 2 (Year 6, Animals including humans)

sources.claim: NGSS MS-LS1-3 names the circulatory system among the interacting body subsystems students argue about.
sources.source: NGSS — MS-LS1-3 (From Molecules to Organisms)

sources.claim: Humans have a double circulatory system: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs and the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body; valves prevent backflow and the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to pump blood around the whole body.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Newton's First & Second Laws

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3):** UK KS3 national curriculum treats this qualitatively ('forces being needed to... change speed or direction of motion (qualitative only)') and names 'Newton's First Law' only at KS4 — so the algebraic F=ma here is the upper edge of the band.

- **Standards — US (NGSS, MS-PS2-2):** NGSS MS-PS2-2 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-2]'; clarification names balanced=N1 and unbalanced/qualitative N2, frame of reference, units; 1-D, one variable, no trig).

- **Operational details:** At 12-13 pupils meet Newton's First Law (an object stays at rest or at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force) and Second Law (a resultant force changes motion; F = m×a). This is the point where formal physics collides hardest with intuition: the 'motion implies force' idea is the single most-studied misconception in physics education (FCI item AF2) and persists through instruction (~20% of students still select it post-teaching).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational/quantitative). Build both laws QUALITATIVELY first (more force, or less mass, → a bigger change in motion), then introduce F=ma as the quantification of a relationship already felt — never algebra-first. The root error is a velocity–acceleration confusion (students think zero/constant velocity needs a force), so separate those ideas explicitly and confront the intuition with low-/zero-friction cases rather than just asserting the correct rule (conceptual change needs the prior idea challenged repeatedly across contexts).
bestPractices: Confront 'motion implies force' directly with cognitive conflict — (near-)frictionless coasting, ice, space — because presenting the correct idea is not enough; challenge the intuition repeatedly across many contexts (Clement bridging/anchoring)
Build N1 and N2 qualitatively first, then introduce F=ma as quantification (NGSS MS keeps N2 qualitative; UK names the laws at KS4)
Separate velocity from acceleration explicitly — the root confusion — stressing that constant velocity (incl. rest) needs ZERO net force; only a change in motion needs a resultant force
Use the constant-velocity car: the driving force EQUALS friction (not greater) — a signature confrontation of 'moving needs a bigger forward force'
Anchor with relatable cases: seatbelts and a coasting spacecraft (N1); a heavier object needing more force for the same acceleration (N2)
Expect context-dependence (a student may accept N1 in space but deny it on Earth because of friction) and revisit; keep it 1-D, one variable at a time (NGSS boundary)
keyRepresentations: Free-body diagram → single resultant arrow that drives acceleration (builds on prior Resultant Forces work)
Motion on a (near-)frictionless track for predict-observe coasting
F = m×a as a proportional relationship (double F → double a; double m → half a) shown on a ratio table / number line, not just a formula triangle
commonMisconceptions: 'Motion implies force' — a moving object must have a force in its direction of travel (FCI AF2; ~20% persist after instruction)
Velocity–acceleration confusion: zero velocity ⇒ zero acceleration ⇒ zero force; and constant velocity must need a net force
Impetus — a moving object carries a 'motive power' that gradually runs out, then it stops
Constant-velocity car: the engine/driving force is greater than friction (it is actually equal)
'Newton's First Law can't hold on Earth because of friction and air resistance'
Force is proportional to velocity rather than to acceleration (going faster needs more force; FCI AF4)

learn.summary: For ages 12–13, teach Newton's First and Second Laws by confronting the 'motion implies force' intuition directly before quantifying it. Build both laws qualitatively first (more resultant force or less mass gives a bigger change in motion), then introduce F = m×a as the quantification of a relationship already felt — never algebra-first. The root error is velocity–acceleration confusion (learners think a moving object needs a continuing force to keep a constant velocity, and that zero resultant force must mean being at rest), so separate those ideas explicitly and challenge the intuition repeatedly with low-/zero-friction cases across many contexts.

activities.title: Coasting puck: watch friction, not a 'used-up push', stop the motion
feedback: If you predicted it slows 'because the push runs out', notice that the slowing shrinks as friction shrinks — so the real cause is friction, not a fading internal push.

With friction made negligible the puck keeps a steady velocity with no forward force at all: this is exactly what 'no resultant force' looks like for a moving object, and needing no horizontal arrows here is correct, not an error.
A zero resultant force gives rest OR constant velocity — not necessarily rest; a coasting puck has zero resultant while still moving.
activities.rationale: The 'motion implies force' idea (FCI item AF2) is rooted in velocity–acceleration confusion and persists through instruction, so conceptual change requires the intuition to be challenged repeatedly, including in (near-)frictionless cases, rather than merely asserting the correct rule. A live or physical reduction of friction lets learners see the intuition fail. An optional friction slider that can be driven to zero makes the mechanism concrete; a physical air-track glider or dry-ice puck gives the same confrontation with real apparatus.
sourceClaims: 'Motion implies force' (FCI item AF2) is a coherent, widely held cluster rooted in velocity–acceleration confusion and pre-Newtonian/impetus thinking; it persists through instruction (~20% post-test) and is context-dependent (students apply N1 in space but deny it on Earth due to friction).
learnerActions: Flick a puck across an ordinary surface and watch it glide, slow and stop; first write down what you think stopped it.
Repeat on progressively lower-friction surfaces (a smooth floor, polished ice) and, in a model with a friction control, reduce friction all the way to zero and flick again.

Observe that with zero friction the puck never stops even though nothing is pushing it forward, and there is no engine or forward force acting (the horizontal forces are negligible in this frictionless model).
State in your own words what a force is actually needed FOR here: not to keep the puck moving, but to change its motion (here, friction is what slows and stops it).
Predict before each release what will happen and why, then compare your prediction with what you see.
activities.intendedInsight: Motion does not need a continuing force to persist; a resultant force is needed only to CHANGE motion. On a real surface, stopping is caused by friction, not by a 'push running out'; with negligible friction, no horizontal force acts and the puck coasts at constant velocity (Newton's First Law).

activities.title: Force and mass dials: acceleration, not speed, tracks the force
feedback: If you expected a bigger force to just set a bigger fixed speed, look again: starting from rest, a steady resultant force keeps changing the speed — it produces a steadily growing speed, i.e. a constant acceleration.
Doubling the mass for the same force halves the acceleration — this is why a heavier object needs more force to achieve the same acceleration.
Use the ratio relationship to sense-check any F = m×a calculation before trusting the arithmetic.
activities.rationale: NGSS MS-PS2-2 keeps the Second Law qualitative and bounds it to 1-D with one variable changed at a time, so varying force and mass separately and reading acceleration as the response matches the standard; building the proportional relationship before the formula addresses the force-proportional-to-velocity error (FCI AF4). Dials or loaded trolleys are optional concrete realisations of the one-variable-at-a-time comparison.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-2].' Clarification emphasises [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-2], qualitative comparisons of forces/mass/[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS2-2] units; assessment limited to 1-D, one variable at a time, no trigonometry.
learnerActions: Use a cart with a force control and a mass control (physical trolley with varied loads, or a model with dials), starting the cart from rest each time.

Set a mass, then increase the force and watch what changes: notice that the ACCELERATION (the rate the speed changes) tracks the resultant force (the applied force, if friction is negligible), so a constant resultant force acting on the cart from rest produces a steadily increasing speed rather than one fixed speed.
Keep the force fixed and double the mass; observe the acceleration roughly halve.

Express the pattern as a proportional relationship on a ratio table or number line: double the resultant force → double the acceleration; double the mass (same resultant force) → half the acceleration.
Only after feeling the relationship, use F = m×a to calculate the missing one of force, mass or acceleration from the other two.
activities.intendedInsight: A resultant force produces acceleration (a change in velocity) proportional to the force and inversely proportional to mass; F = m×a quantifies a relationship already observed, and force is linked to acceleration, not to current speed. Starting from rest, a steady resultant force makes the speed grow steadily.

activities.title: The constant-velocity car: engine force equals friction
feedback: If you made the forward force bigger, note that a bigger forward force would give a resultant force and so acceleration — but the car's speed is steady, so the resultant must be zero.
Correct response: the resultant is zero; the driving force forwards exactly cancels the drag and friction backwards.

Saying 'the engine keeps it moving' overstates its role: by the First Law no force is needed to maintain motion when there is no resistance, so here the engine force is present only to balance the drag that would otherwise slow the car.
activities.rationale: The constant-velocity car is a signature confrontation of 'moving needs a bigger forward force'; requiring learners to say what the engine force does discriminates 'keeps it moving' (wrong) from 'cancels resistance' (right). Equal-length arrows shown live in a model make the balance visible, but a carefully drawn static diagram can also carry this point. This case uses the appreciable-friction model, in contrast to the frictionless coasting puck.
sourceClaims: For a car moving at constant velocity a common misconception is that the engine/driving force exceeds friction, when in fact the two are equal in magnitude (zero net force).
learnerActions: Consider a car cruising at a steady 70 mph on a straight road, not speeding up or slowing down.
Draw a free-body diagram: the forward driving force and the backward drag/friction. Decide how their sizes compare.
State the size of the resultant force at constant velocity and justify it.
Explain what the engine's driving force is actually doing when speed is steady.
In a model that draws the engine and friction arrows exactly equal while the car cruises, check your diagram against it; then predict how the arrows change when the car speeds up.
activities.intendedInsight: At constant velocity the driving force exactly balances drag and friction, giving a zero resultant. In this model with appreciable drag, a balancing forward push is what keeps the velocity constant; the engine force is not there to 'keep the car moving' as such but only to cancel the resistive forces, and a resultant appears only when the motion changes.

activities.title: Transfer: spacecraft, heavier loads and seatbelts
feedback: If you thought the spacecraft needs continuous thrust to keep moving, recall the frictionless puck: with no resistance, steady motion needs no force.
For the two cars starting from rest, the heavier one has a smaller acceleration for the same force, so the empty car speeds up faster.
For seatbelts, the point is that your body continues in motion when the car stops — the restraint supplies the force that changes your motion.
Accepting the law in space but denying it on Earth is a known and expected pattern; name friction as the difference and revisit the frictionless case.
activities.rationale: The misconception is context-dependent (accepted in space, denied on Earth), so explicit transfer across space, loaded masses and seatbelts, revisiting friction as the difference, supports durable conceptual change; these anchoring cases are named in the teaching objective's evidence.
sourceClaims: 'Motion implies force' (FCI item AF2) is a coherent, widely held cluster rooted in velocity–acceleration confusion and pre-Newtonian/impetus thinking; it persists through instruction (~20% post-test) and is context-dependent (students apply N1 in space but deny it on Earth due to friction).
learnerActions: A spacecraft far out in empty space switches its engines off — state what happens to its motion and why.
Explain why, with no resistance in space, no force is needed to keep a steady velocity and engines only CHANGE the motion.
Compare two cars with the same engine force, both starting from rest, one heavily loaded and one empty — predict which speeds up faster and justify with F = m×a.
Explain why seatbelts are needed using Newton's First Law (your body keeps moving at the car's speed when the car suddenly stops).
Note any case where you accepted the law in space but doubted it on Earth, and explain how friction accounts for the difference.
activities.intendedInsight: The same two laws apply across contexts; apparent exceptions on Earth are due to friction and air resistance, not a failure of the First Law. Learners connect the laws to real situations rather than reciting them.

activities.title: Retrieval and prediction checks
feedback: For a coasting object at steady speed with negligible friction, the resultant force is zero — a forward force is the tempting but wrong choice.
If a prediction treats a bigger force as a bigger fixed speed, revisit the dials activity: from rest, force sets acceleration, not a single speed.
Check each F = m×a answer against the proportional relationship, not just the arithmetic.
activities.rationale: Targeted retrieval and predict-items give practice and surface the AF2/AF4 distractors; as a companion after the exploratory work they consolidate rather than introduce the ideas. These are consolidation/assessment-style tasks and do not by themselves elicit the independent construction that the manipulation activities provide.
sourceClaims: 'Motion implies force' (FCI item AF2) is a coherent, widely held cluster rooted in velocity–acceleration confusion and pre-Newtonian/impetus thinking; it persists through instruction (~20% post-test) and is context-dependent (students apply N1 in space but deny it on Earth due to friction).
learnerActions: Complete F = m×a fill-in calculations, solving for force, mass or acceleration given the other two.
Answer 'which object has a (resultant) force on it?' items, including a puck coasting at steady speed with negligible friction (answer: no resultant force).
Predict how acceleration changes as the force or the mass changes, before revealing the outcome.
For each item, after answering, state which idea it tests (e.g. force–acceleration link, zero resultant at constant velocity).
activities.intendedInsight: Retrieval and prediction items consolidate the force–acceleration link and probe the common distractors (motion implies force; force proportional to speed) directly.

constraints: Build both laws qualitatively first; introduce F = m×a only as quantification of a felt relationship — never algebra-first.
Keep to 1-D and change one variable at a time (NGSS MS-PS2-2 boundary); no trigonometry.
Separate velocity from acceleration explicitly: constant velocity (including rest) needs ZERO resultant force; only a change in motion needs a resultant.
A zero resultant force means no acceleration (rest OR constant velocity), not necessarily rest — do not equate 'no force' with 'stationary'.
When describing a resultant force, specify the initial motion: a resultant produces acceleration (a change in velocity), which is not the same as the current direction or speed of travel.

State the friction model being used: the coasting puck's zero-friction stage uses negligible horizontal friction (so no horizontal forces are needed and this is correct, not an error), whereas its ordinary-surface stage has friction that slows it; the constant-velocity car uses appreciable drag that a balancing driving force must cancel.
Expect the 'motion implies force' idea to recur and to be context-dependent (accepted in space, denied on Earth); plan to revisit it across contexts rather than asserting the rule once.

A free-body-diagram reference and recognition/retrieval items support vocabulary and consolidation but do not, on their own, elicit independent construction or show motion persisting without a force; pair them with manipulation or prediction tasks.
Treat friction sliders, force/mass dials and equal-arrow displays as optional concrete realisations; real apparatus (air-track glider, dry-ice puck, loaded trolley) serves the same purpose.
F = m×a here is the upper edge of the UK KS3 band (the laws are named at KS4) and the quantitative tier of this topic; keep expectations age-appropriate.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original listed two sources as verified (NGSS MS-PS2-2; DfE KS3) and two as not verified (the FCI/Modified Module Analysis arXiv paper and the OpenStax constant-velocity-car claim). The ~20% post-instruction persistence figure and the context-dependence claim come from the unverified FCI source and are reported as cited, not independently confirmed.

The KS3 standards claim was removed from Activity 1's sourceClaims because that activity's rationale concerns the AF2 misconception confrontation, not the standards framing; the KS3 claim remains part of the overall standards context recorded in the summary and preservation audit.

The original artefact comparison asserted a live recompute is 'the only way' the intuition can be felt failing and that a static diagram 'cannot show motion persisting without a force'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened: manipulation/prediction is well-motivated for this misconception, but static references and physical apparatus also contribute.
The original '3D adds nothing / adds cost without conceptual gain' judgement was a catalog fit note and has been reframed only as the physics here being 1-D; no universal claim about 3D is made.

Self-audit of physics: statements have been checked so that a resultant force is tied to acceleration (change in velocity), not to current direction/speed; the F=ma dials activity names rest as the starting state for its 'steadily increasing speed' claim; balanced forces are stated to give no acceleration (rest or constant velocity), not necessarily rest; the frictionless coasting puck correctly needs no horizontal arrows; the constant-velocity car's driving force is equal to (not greater than) resistance. No arithmetic F = m×a worked examples with specific numbers were supplied in the source, so none were invented.

assess.poeTask: Give a trolley a single push along a low-friction track (or use a dry-ice puck or air-track glider). Ask students to predict what happens to its speed once your hand leaves it, and WHY, before releasing. Predicting 'it slows because the push runs out' reveals the impetus idea; seeing it glide at near-constant speed with no forward force sets up Newton's First Law.
probeDeeper: The car now speeds up. What must be true about the forces then?
A spacecraft far out in empty space switches its engines off. What happens to its motion, and why?
Two cars have the same engine force, but one is loaded heavy and one is empty — which speeds up faster? Why?
If you double the resultant force on the same object, what happens to its acceleration — and to its speed?
assess.correctAnswer: There is no resultant force — it's zero. At constant velocity the forces are balanced: the engine's driving force forwards exactly cancels the drag and friction backwards. By Newton's First Law the car would keep moving with no force at all, so the engine force isn't there to 'keep it going' — it's there only to balance the resistive forces.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It's moving forwards, so there must be a bigger force forwards keeping it going.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Work the constant-velocity case repeatedly and contrast with the frictionless/space case (First Law); confront that steady motion needs a zero resultant. Expect the idea to return.
errorPatterns.distractor: There's a resultant force forwards — that's what keeps the car moving.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a net forward force acts; can't accept balanced forces on a moving object.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'If the resultant force is zero, the object must be stationary.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: First Law: a zero resultant gives rest OR constant velocity; show a puck/glider coasting steadily.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says zero resultant means at rest, so a moving car can't have a zero resultant.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A bigger force just makes it go faster.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish force -> acceleration (change in velocity): a constant force gives steadily increasing speed, not a fixed speed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In F = ma reasoning, equates force with speed rather than with the rate of change of velocity.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'In space a spacecraft needs its engines on all the time or it will stop.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: First Law: with no resistance in space, no force is needed to keep a steady velocity; engines only CHANGE the motion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Thinks continuous thrust is needed to maintain motion in space.

responseLevels.gap: Says a moving car needs a net forward force to keep going, or that a zero resultant means stationary; treats force as producing speed.
responseLevels.full: Explains that constant velocity means a zero resultant (driving force balances drag), that a resultant produces acceleration proportional to force and inversely to mass, and transfers to space (no force needed to keep moving) and to seatbelts — connecting the laws rather than reciting them.
responseLevels.partial: States the laws and uses F = ma numerically, but reverts to 'motion needs a force' for steady motion, or recites the law statements without applying the First Law to the constant-velocity case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A car cruises down a straight motorway at a steady 70 mph, not speeding up or slowing down. Is there a resultant (overall) force on the car — and what is the engine's driving force actually doing?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The impetus / 'motion needs a force' misconception (documented to university level, FCI) predicts a net forward force whenever something moves. A student who understands the First Law says the resultant is zero at constant velocity and that the driving force only balances drag. Tier 2 forces them to say WHAT the engine force does — 'keeps it moving' (wrong) versus 'cancels the resistance' (right).

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Separating Mixtures (KS3)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry 'Pure and impure substances'):** Simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography. (Crystallisation is the evaporation-based recovery of a dissolved solid.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-2 supporting):** Use characteristic physical properties (particle size, boiling point, solubility) to separate and identify the components of mixtures.

- **Operational details:** This PROCEDURAL node extends the KS2 filter/sieve/evaporate work with two new techniques and a sharper property-to-method logic: FILTRATION separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (property: solubility/particle size); CRYSTALLISATION/EVAPORATION recovers a dissolved solid from its solution (property: solubility, solid left behind as liquid leaves); DISTILLATION separates liquids — or a solvent from a solution — by BOILING POINT (vapour boils off, is cooled in a condenser, and collected as pure liquid); CHROMATOGRAPHY separates dissolved coloured substances by how far each travels up the paper (property: relative attraction to paper vs solvent). The key skill is SELECTING the technique that exploits the relevant property difference, and for multi-component mixtures ordering a sequence. Emphasise distillation's apparatus (heat → evaporate → condense → collect) and that chromatography reveals how many substances are present (number of spots).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). Given a described mixture, the child selects the correct separation technique(s), justifies each by the property difference it exploits, and for distillation/chromatography explains what is collected/revealed.
bestPractices: Reason from the property difference to the technique (particle size→filter; solubility→crystallise; boiling point→distil; attraction to paper→chromatography).
Show distillation as a connected flow: heat→evaporate→condense→collect pure liquid.
Use chromatography to reveal how many substances a mixture contains (number of spots).
Give multi-component mixtures that require an ordered sequence of techniques.
Let a wrong technique visibly fail so method choice is justified, not guessed.
keyRepresentations: Four apparatus stations (filtration, crystallisation, distillation, chromatography)
A labelled distillation setup showing evaporate→condenser→collected distillate
A chromatogram where one spot separates into several coloured components
Property tags on each mixture linking to the right method
commonMisconceptions: Filtration can separate a dissolved solid from its solution (it passes through).
Distillation destroys or leaves the liquid behind, rather than collecting it pure after condensing.
In distillation the collected liquid is the impurity rather than the purified solvent.
Chromatography colours are added by the paper rather than separated from the mixture.
One separation step always suffices, ignoring the need for a sequence.

learn.summary: Procedural KS3 chemistry (ages 11–13) on separating mixtures: selecting and running filtration, crystallisation/evaporation, distillation and chromatography by reasoning from the relevant property difference (particle size/insolubility, solubility, boiling point, differential travel up paper). The core skill is matching technique to BOTH the exploited property AND which component is wanted, and sequencing steps for multi-component mixtures. An interactive separation lab is the primary proposal; labelled apparatus references, matching/sequencing/chromatogram tasks, and real hands-on practicals (with appropriate safety) are preserved as complements.

activities.title: Separation lab: choose, run, and check the technique
feedback: If a learner filters salty water and evaporating a few drops of the filtrate leaves salt behind: the salt is dissolved, not a suspended solid, and filter paper only holds back undissolved bits. Reconnect to dissolving, then ask which part is wanted: evaporation/crystallisation to recover the salt, or distillation to recover the water.

If a learner evaporates salty water when the WATER was wanted: ask 'which part do we want to keep?' Evaporation keeps the salt and loses the water as vapour; to keep the water you must condense it — distillation.

If a learner picks a method by memory of a past practical: prompt 'what is different about the things you're separating — dissolved? insoluble? different boiling points? different colours?' so the property drives the choice.

On the chromatogram: if the black spot splits into three colours at different heights, that shows the 'one' ink was a mixture of at least three dyes, each with a different attraction to paper versus solvent, so they travel different distances.
After a mismatched technique visibly fails, point back to the property difference that the correct method exploits rather than supplying the answer.
activities.rationale: A choose-and-operate task across the four apparatus types makes property→method reasoning and the apparatus procedures concrete, especially distillation's evaporate–condense–collect flow and chromatography's separation of a single spot into several. A visible wrong-technique failure forces property-based justification instead of guessing. The standards list these four techniques and tie them to characteristic physical properties.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
Separation techniques exploit characteristic physical properties (particle size, solubility, boiling point); characteristic properties identify substances (NGSS PS1.A)
Chromatography separates dissolved substances by differential travel and reveals the number of components; distillation collects a pure liquid via evaporation then condensation
learnerActions: Work from a mixture bank: muddy/sandy water, salty water, rock salt, a spot of black felt-tip ink.
For each mixture, first state the property difference between its components (insoluble solid? dissolved solid? liquids of different boiling point? different coloured dyes?) BEFORE choosing a method.
Choose and set up one of four stations — filtration, crystallisation/evaporation, distillation, chromatography — and run it.

At filtration: pour muddy water through filter paper. Watch a clearer filtrate drip through while insoluble mud/sand stays on the paper. Note that very fine particles can leave it slightly cloudy and that anything dissolved passes through, so the filtrate is not pure water.
At crystallisation/evaporation: heat salty water and watch white salt left behind as the water leaves.

At distillation: watch the solvent boil up, travel into the cooled condenser, turn back to liquid and drip out as pure liquid while the salt stays in the flask — trace the one flow heat→evaporate→condense→collect.

At chromatography: place an ink spot on a pencil start line near the bottom of the paper. Stand the paper in solvent kept BELOW the spot so the dye climbs the paper rather than washing straight into the solvent. Watch whether the black dot climbs and splits into separate coloured spots; many black inks do, but not all. Count the spots to give the minimum number of dyes present.

Tackle a multi-component mixture (e.g. rock salt treated as salt + insoluble rock/sand: dissolve in water, filter off the insoluble rock/sand, then recover the salt) that requires an ordered sequence of techniques.

Deliberately try a mismatched technique (e.g. filtering salty water). Show that it fails by evaporating a few drops of the filtrate: white salt is left behind, so the salt went through the paper. Then revise the choice using the property.
activities.intendedInsight: Each technique exploits a specific property difference, so the method must be selected from the mixture's properties and from which component you want to keep — not recalled from a past practical. Distillation keeps the liquid (condensed and collected pure); evaporation/crystallisation keeps the solid. Chromatography shows at least how many substances are present.

activities.title: Labelled apparatus reference with 'what it separates and why'
feedback: If the collected distillate is described as the impurity: the collected liquid is the purified solvent that boiled off and condensed; the dissolved solid stays behind in the flask.
If distillation is described as destroying or leaving the liquid behind: the liquid is recovered pure after the vapour condenses in the cooled tube.
If a learner thinks the paper adds the colours in chromatography: the colours were already in the mixture and are being separated, not created by the paper.
activities.rationale: A labelled, reveal-based reference supports the procedures and vocabulary and is a useful companion to the lab. It is a reference scaffold: it does not let the learner choose, run, and see a technique succeed or fail, so it works best alongside the active lab.
sourceClaims: Chromatography separates dissolved substances by differential travel and reveals the number of components; distillation collects a pure liquid via evaporation then condensation
learnerActions: Study a labelled diagram of each apparatus, focusing on the distillation setup: heat source, flask, vapour path, cooled condenser, and collected distillate.
For each setup, reveal a short note stating what it separates and which property it exploits.
Trace on the distillation diagram where the vapour cools and where the pure liquid is collected.
Examine a chromatography diagram showing the solvent front and spots at different heights, with the start line (and ink spot) above the solvent level.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners build an accurate mental picture of each apparatus and can name the property each technique relies on, with distillation understood as a connected evaporate-then-condense flow.

activities.title: Match, sequence, and read a chromatogram
feedback: For a match error, point back to the property difference (insoluble solid → filter; dissolved solid → crystallise/evaporate; liquids by boiling point → distil; coloured dyes → chromatography).
For a sequencing error, ask which component must be removed first and why (e.g. remove insoluble sand by filtration before recovering dissolved salt).
When reading the chromatogram, confirm that more separate spots means at least that many substances and that a higher spot was more strongly attracted to the solvent relative to the paper.
activities.rationale: Matching, sequencing, and chromatogram-reading are directly aligned check formats and are best used after the lab to consolidate. As recognition/short-response items they confirm selection and interpretation but do not by themselves require the learner to assemble and operate apparatus.
sourceClaims: Chromatography separates dissolved substances by differential travel and reveals the number of components; distillation collects a pure liquid via evaporation then condensation
learnerActions: Match each described mixture to the technique that exploits the right property difference.
Put the steps of a multi-technique separation (e.g. salt + insoluble sand in water) into a working order.

Read a given chromatogram: state how many components are present and which travelled furthest, and, where distances are provided, compute or compare Rf values (distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front).
Explain in one line why filtration removes sand from water but not dissolved salt.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners consolidate technique selection, step sequencing, and chromatogram interpretation, including that the number of spots shows the minimum number of substances.

activities.title: Real separation practicals (hands-on complement)
feedback: If the distillate still seems impure, discuss setup issues (collection timing, contamination) rather than concluding the method fails.
Compare what was expected from the property-based reasoning with what was observed.
activities.rationale: Hands-on filtration, distillation and chromatography are the ideal practical complement to any modelled version and give assembly experience that a 2D animation represents rather than reproduces. Requires appropriate safety supervision for heating and glassware, and lab products must not be tasted.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
learnerActions: Carry out a real filtration of muddy water and inspect the filtrate.

Set up a real distillation of salty water and collect the distillate. Test whether the distillate is free of salt by evaporating a few drops on a clean watch glass and checking for any white residue. Appearance can't show this, because salty water also looks clear, and salt left in the flask says nothing about the distillate. Never taste substances in the lab.
Run paper chromatography on a felt-tip ink spot, keeping the solvent level below the spot, and count the separated colours.
Where safe apparatus and supervision allow, assemble the distillation apparatus so the physical connections (flask, condenser, collection vessel) are handled directly.
activities.intendedInsight: Real practicals give direct experience of assembling apparatus, handling real materials, and observing genuine outcomes, reinforcing that method choice is justified by what actually separates.

constraints: Reason from the property difference to the technique: particle size/insolubility → filtration; solubility → crystallisation/evaporation; boiling point → distillation; relative attraction to paper vs solvent → chromatography.
Always ask which component is wanted: distillation keeps the liquid (condensed and collected pure); evaporation/crystallisation keeps the dissolved solid and loses the liquid.
Show distillation as one connected flow — heat → evaporate → condense → collect pure liquid — not as separate unlinked steps.

Use chromatography to show the minimum number of substances a mixture contains (number of separate spots in that solvent); keep the solvent level below the ink spot so the dye travels up the paper rather than washing off.
Include at least one multi-component mixture requiring an ordered sequence of techniques.
Let a wrong technique visibly fail so method choice is justified rather than guessed.
The labelled-diagram reference is a scaffold: it supports naming and procedure but does not let the learner select, run, or see a technique succeed or fail.
Match/sequence/chromatogram items are recognition/short-response consolidation and do not by themselves require independent assembly and operation of apparatus.
Real practicals involve heating and glassware and require appropriate safety supervision; substances produced or used in the lab must never be tasted.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists two of three sources as unverified (NGSS and RSC claims marked verified:false); treat the chromatography/distillation and property-mapping claims accordingly.

Independent self-audit: the distillation-vs-evaporation target distinction (keep liquid vs keep solid) is handled correctly throughout. No force/motion, fraction, geometry, or shade content is present in this chemistry node, so those specific audit rules do not apply. Two safety/accuracy corrections carried from the prior pass were verified present at every learner-facing occurrence: (a) no instruction to taste any lab product — purity is judged by appearance; (b) the chromatography solvent must sit below the ink spot so the dye separates rather than washing off (stated in the modelled lab, the real practical, and the reference diagram). No new substantive errors were found.
Rf was retained from the evidence list (spot distance ÷ solvent-front distance); confirm appropriateness for the intended tier (Tier B–C early-formal).

The original 'possible' 3D and 'poor' conversation fit judgements were catalog-fit rankings, not universal pedagogical laws; a 3D build could aid assembly understanding and dialogue can support reasoning, though neither is proposed here as a way to show whether a method actually separates a mixture.
Chemical safety for heating and distillation glassware is assumed to be managed by a supervising adult; specific apparatus and safety procedures were not specified in the source.

probeDeeper: For the salty water, you want the WATER back — why distillation and not just leaving it to evaporate?
The clear liquid that came through your filter — is it pure water or is something still in it? How do you know?
On the ink chromatogram, what does it mean if the black spot splits into three colours at different heights?
If I gave you a mixture of two liquids that boil at different temperatures, which method would you pick and why?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Muddy water → FILTRATION: mud (insoluble) stays on the paper, clear water passes through. (2) Salty water, wanting the water → (simple) DISTILLATION: boil, condense and collect the pure water; salt stays behind (evaporation/crystallisation would keep the salt and lose the water). (3) Ink → CHROMATOGRAPHY: the dyes travel up the paper at different rates and separate into spots. The critical judgements are matching technique to the property exploited AND to which component is wanted.

errorPatterns.pattern: tries to filter the salt out of salt water ('the filter paper will catch the salt')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Salt is dissolved, not a suspended solid — filter paper holds back undissolved bits only. Reconnect to dissolving; then choose distillation to recover the water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: sets up filtration for the salty water and is surprised the filtrate is still salty

errorPatterns.pattern: uses plain evaporation when the LIQUID is the target ('boil it off to get the salt out')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'which part do we want to keep?' Evaporation keeps the solid and loses the liquid; to keep the water you must condense it — distillation. Choice depends on the target.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: evaporates the salty water when the teacher asked for the water back, losing the water as vapour

errorPatterns.pattern: picks a method from memory of a past practical, not from the mixture's properties
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the techniques — prompt 'what's different about the things you're separating (dissolved? insoluble? different boiling points? different colours?)' so the property drives the choice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reaches for filtration/evaporation by default and mis-selects when the mixture is unfamiliar (e.g. ink)

responseLevels.gap: Mis-selects methods (filters dissolved salt, evaporates when liquid is wanted); can't name the property each technique exploits.
responseLevels.full: Selects and sets up the correct technique for each mixture, justifies each by the property exploited (solubility, boiling point, insolubility, differential travel) AND by which component is wanted, and interprets the chromatogram — transferring the reasoning to a novel mixture.
responseLevels.partial: Chooses the right technique for familiar cases but explains by recall, not by property; falters on the target distinction (distillation vs evaporation) or on interpreting chromatography.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out three labelled mixtures and the full kit (filter funnel + paper, distillation setup, evaporating basin, chromatography paper + solvent): (1) muddy water, (2) salty water where the teacher wants the WATER back as drinkable liquid, (3) a spot of black felt-tip ink. Say: 'For each one, choose a separation method, set it up, and tell me what you'll collect.' Watch the choices and the setups — don't name the techniques for them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The task discriminates because each mixture rewards a different property-based choice, and the salty-water case specifically tests whether the child tracks WHAT is wanted: distillation (keep the liquid) versus crystallisation/evaporation (keep the solid). Watching the setup, not asking for definitions, exposes whether the choice is property-driven or recipe-recalled.
