pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Reversible Changes

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y5 Properties & changes of materials):** Pupils should be taught to demonstrate that dissolving, mixing and changes of state are reversible changes.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-4):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4] (reversible changes are the focus here).

- **Operational details:** The organising idea is that a REVERSIBLE change alters how a material looks or its state but produces NO NEW SUBSTANCE — you can get the original material back. The canonical reversible set: changes of state (melt–freeze, evaporate–condense), dissolving (recover by evaporation), and mixing separable materials (unmix by filtering/sieving/magnet). Teach by the do-and-UNDO pairing: every reversible change is shown together with the action that reverses it, and the child confirms the SAME material is back. Contrast sharply with irreversible changes (next node) where a new substance forms and cannot be undone. Reinforce conservation — the material persists through a reversible change. Watch the intuition that melting/dissolving 'uses up' or destroys the material.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Given a change, the child predicts whether it is reversible, states the action that would reverse it, and justifies by whether the original material can be recovered (no new substance made).
bestPractices: Pair every reversible change with the action that reverses it (do-and-undo) and confirm the SAME material returns.
Group the canonical reversible set — changes of state, dissolving, and mixing separable materials — under the single test 'no new substance made'.
Contrast directly with an irreversible change so the boundary is felt, not just stated.
Reinforce conservation: the material persists through the change even when it looks gone.
Have pupils predict reversibility and name the reversing action before testing.
keyRepresentations: A do-and-undo bench with forward and reverse controls per station
Reverse-arrow pairs (melt⇄freeze, dissolve⇄evaporate, mix⇄filter)
A 'same material recovered?' confirmation indicator
A greyed-out reverse control on an irreversible teaser (burnt toast)
commonMisconceptions: Melting or dissolving destroys or uses up the material.
All changes can be undone (over-generalising reversibility to burning/cooking).
A change of state makes a new substance rather than the same substance in a new state.
Mixing is irreversible because the materials 'became one thing'.
If a material looks different after a change, it must be a different material.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year olds learning that dissolving, mixing, and changes of state are reversible (no new substance is made and the original material can be recovered). The core method is do-and-undo: perform a change, perform the action that reverses it, and confirm the SAME material has returned. Contrast this with an irreversible change (e.g. toasting bread) where a new substance forms. Emphasise conservation — the material persists even when it looks gone — and have learners judge by 'was a new substance made?' rather than by appearance or by whether heat was involved.

activities.title: The do-it, undo-it bench
feedback: When the chilled chocolate sets again, confirm: 'Same chocolate back — melting and freezing just change the state, not the substance.'
If a learner expects the salt to be gone for good, point to the recovered crystals: 'It looked gone, but it was still there dissolved — evaporating brings it back.'

At the sand station, if a learner thinks the sand and water 'became one thing', show the filter re-separating them: 'Mixing separable materials is reversible — the sand and water were never combined into a new substance, so they come apart again.'

For the toast station, state: 'The reverse control is off because toasting made a new substance — appearance changing a lot (as in dissolving) is still reversible, but a new substance forming is not.'
After the round-trips, ask the learner to state the single test that worked for all three: 'Was a new substance made?'
activities.rationale: Pairing each change with its reversal and confirming recovery lets learners experience reversibility as a felt round-trip and directly targets the intuition that melting/dissolving destroys material. The greyed-out toast reverse control provides a within-task contrast so the reversible/irreversible boundary is experienced, not just stated. The forward/reverse controls and the 'same material recovered?' indicator are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms — the same learning can come from real melt/freeze, dissolve/evaporate, and filtering activities.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5: demonstrate that dissolving, mixing and changes of state are reversible changes
Children think melting/dissolving destroys or uses up material; pairing a change with its reversal and confirming recovery targets this
learnerActions: At station 1, gently warm a chunk of chocolate (e.g. in a bowl over warm water) only until it flows, then chill it and confirm it sets back into solid chocolate. Overheated chocolate can scorch or burn, which makes new substances and cannot be undone.
At station 2, stir salt into water until it seems to disappear (it is still there, dissolved), then gently heat the dish and confirm salt crystals reappear.

At station 3, tip sand into water, pour the mixture through a filter, and confirm the sand is separated out on the filter (damp, but the same sand) while the water passes through (it may be slightly cloudy if the sand has very fine particles).

For each station, do the change and then the reversing action, and check whether the same material has been recovered before moving on (if using a screen or bench simulation, this may be a forward/reverse control and a 'same material recovered?' indicator).

At a fourth station, an adult toasts a slice of bread; try to think of any action that would turn it back into bread and notice there is none ('you can't un-toast it — a new substance was made'). In a simulation, this may appear as a greyed-out reverse control.
Before testing each station, predict whether the change is reversible and say out loud the action that would reverse it.
activities.intendedInsight: A reversible change alters how a material looks or its state but makes NO new substance, so you can get the original material back by undoing it; some changes (toasting) make a new substance and cannot be undone.

activities.title: Reverse-arrow summary chart
feedback: If a learner pairs dissolve with the wrong recovery, remind them: 'Evaporating the water leaves the solid behind.'
Reinforce that all three pairs pass the same test, so the category is organised by substance, not by appearance.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or arrow-pairing chart organises the category clearly and consolidates the vocabulary after hands-on work. It is a summary companion: on its own it does not let the learner perform the round-trip and verify recovery, so it works best after the bench or real experiments rather than instead of them.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5: demonstrate that dissolving, mixing and changes of state are reversible changes
learnerActions: Match each change to its reversing action: melt⇄freeze, dissolve⇄evaporate, mix⇄filter.
Reveal or state what gets you back to the original material for each pair.
Add the single test that unites all three pairs: 'no new substance made'.
activities.intendedInsight: The canonical reversible changes — changes of state, dissolving, and mixing separable materials — all share one test: no new substance is formed, so the original can be recovered.

activities.title: Sort and justify: reversible or not?
feedback: If a learner calls dissolving irreversible because the solution looks different, respond: 'Appearance changed, but evaporating recovers the solid, so it is reversible — judge by substance, not looks.'
If a learner calls melting irreversible because heat was used, line it up against toasting: 'Both used heat; only toasting made a new substance.'
Reward justifications that name the recovery action and the 'no new substance' test rather than just the label.
activities.rationale: The learning target here is a sorting-plus-justification judgement, so a categorise-and-match-with-reasons task is a genuinely apt format. Because recognition and matching do not by themselves require the learner to perform and observe the round-trip, pair this with the bench or real experiments so judgements rest on experienced recovery rather than guessing.
sourceClaims: DfE Y5: demonstrate that dissolving, mixing and changes of state are reversible changes
NGSS 2-PS1-4: construct an argument that some heating/cooling changes can be reversed and some cannot
learnerActions: Categorise a set of changes as reversible or irreversible.
Match each reversible change to the specific action that would reverse it.
For each judgement, state the reason: can the original material be recovered, with no new substance made?
Tackle tricky cases: is dissolving salt reversible even though the water looks completely different? Is re-set chocolate the same substance?
activities.intendedInsight: Reversibility is judged by whether a new substance was made and the original can be recovered — not by whether heat was added or whether the material looks different.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain with chocolate
feedback: If a learner predicts 'no' because heating spoils it, contrast melting ice (heated, reversible) with toasting (heated, irreversible) to move them off 'heat' and onto 'was a new substance made?'.
If a learner judges by appearance, use dissolving as the bridge: it looks totally different yet is reversible by evaporation.
Confirm a strong answer: ice↔water is reversible (same water, just a change of state); bread→toast is irreversible (a new substance forms).
activities.rationale: Eliciting the reason before observing is diagnostic because heat is present in both the melting and toasting examples, so a learner reasoning from 'heating = irreversible' gets the reason wrong even when the label is right. This separates classification by 'same substance / no new material' from classification by surface cues.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-PS1-4: construct an argument that some heating/cooling changes can be reversed and some cannot
Children think melting/dissolving destroys or uses up material; pairing a change with its reversal and confirming recovery targets this
learnerActions: Before any melting, predict: if we melt this chocolate in a bowl and then put it in the fridge, will we get chocolate back — and WHY?
State your reason out loud before observing (this reasoning is the important part).
Melt the chocolate, then let it set, and compare your prediction with what happened.

Answer probe questions: Is dissolving salt reversible even though it looks nothing like before? Would un-heating toast make it bread again, and why not? Then give your own test for 'reversible' that works no matter what the change looks like.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating the reason before observing surfaces whether a learner is reasoning from 'heating spoils it' or appearance versus the correct test of whether a new substance was made.

constraints: Use real melt/freeze, dissolve/evaporate, and filter activities as the ideal hands-on experience; screen or bench simulations are a scaffold that can preview the round-trip but should not replace acting on real materials and confirming recovery.
The summary chart and sorting/matching tasks consolidate and assess the category; on their own they do not require the learner to perform and observe recovery, so pair them with doing the changes.
Keep the focus on reversible changes as specified, but use one irreversible example (toasting) only as a contrast — do not let it become the main lesson of this node.
Heating is involved in both a reversible example (melting) and an irreversible one (toasting); never teach 'heat makes a change irreversible'. The deciding test is whether a new substance was made.
Supervise heating of chocolate, heating of salt solution, and use of the grill; these involve hot surfaces and should be adult-led or closely supervised for this age group.
Illustrative interface details (forward/reverse controls, 'same material recovered?' indicator, greyed-out reverse button) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.

Recovered material is the same substance even when its physical form differs (damp rather than dry sand, salt returning as crystals); keep learners focused on 'same substance', not identical appearance.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row rated conversation and 3D as poor fit with universal-sounding reasons ('3D adds cost without insight', dialogue 'cannot produce that evidence'). These have been reframed as scope-limited: those formats are less suited to producing recovery evidence for this specific target, not proven incapable. Comparative efficacy and necessity are not established by the source claims provided.

One source (RSC misconceptions guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; the claim about children thinking melting/dissolving destroys material is retained where it directly supports the teaching principle but is treated as unverified legacy content with no fresh verification asserted.

The original recommendation described 'dry sand' after filtering; filtered sand is actually damp. This was corrected to 'damp, same sand' so the point remains recovery of the same substance, not dryness.

Scientific note for review: salt recovered by evaporation returns as crystals that may differ in form from the original grains, and re-set chocolate may differ in texture; the substance is the same, which is the point. If learners notice such differences, clarify that reversibility concerns the substance, not the exact appearance.
The row cites NGSS 2-PS1-4, a grade-2 standard, for a 9–10 age node; retained from the original row and not treated as a learner-facing error.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: hold up a bar of chocolate. Ask the child to predict — if we melt it in a bowl and then put it in the fridge, will we get chocolate back, and WHY? A child anchored on 'heating spoils it' predicts no. Melt and re-set it. It's chocolate again (reversible). The stated reason before observing is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Dissolving salt in water — reversible or not? It looks nothing like before. How do you decide?
You melted a chocolate bar and let it set again. Same substance or new one? Reversible?
What if the toast could be un-heated back to room temperature — would that make it bread again? Why not?
Give me your own test for 'reversible' that works no matter what the change looks like.
assess.correctAnswer: Ice↔water is REVERSIBLE: melting and freezing just change the state; it's the same water, no new substance is made, so you can get the ice back by cooling. Bread→toast is IRREVERSIBLE: a new substance forms (you can't turn toast back into soft bread). The 'why' is the key: reversible changes make NO new material, so the change can run backwards.

errorPatterns.pattern: any change caused by heating is irreversible ('you heated it, so it can't go back')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up melting ice (heated, reversible) against toasting (heated, irreversible) — force the child off 'heat' and onto 'was a new substance made?'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Ice melting can't be undone because you had to heat it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls melting irreversible because heat was involved, or can't say why toast differs from melted ice when both used heat

errorPatterns.pattern: reversible means 'looks the same afterwards' rather than 'same substance, no new material'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use dissolving as the bridge: it looks totally different yet is reversible (evaporate to recover). Reversibility is about substance, not looks.
errorPatterns.distractor: Dissolving salt is irreversible because the water looks completely different now.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: judges by appearance — calls dissolving irreversible because the solution looks different, though the solid is recoverable

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by surface cue (heat added, looks different); labels may be right but reasons are wrong, or can't say why one undoes and one doesn't.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by 'same substance / no new material made', explains why heat isn't the deciding factor, and transfers the rule correctly to dissolving and melting-then-setting — reversibility judged by substance, not appearance.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly labels the two examples and says 'no new substance' for reversible, but can't yet apply it to a tricky case (dissolving, re-set chocolate) — the rule is stated, not yet transferable.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Think of ice melting into water, and water freezing back into ice. Now think of a slice of bread turning into toast under the grill. One of these can be undone to get exactly what you started with, and one can't. Which is which — and, the important part, WHY can you undo one but not the other?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason distinguishes a child who classifies by 'no new substance / same stuff in a new form' from one who classifies by surface cues like 'you added heat' or 'it looks different'. Heat is present in BOTH examples, so a child reasoning from 'heating = irreversible' gets the reason wrong even if the label is right.

pedagogy.summary: Children read and write time to the EXACT minute. The efficient procedure is NOT counting single minutes from the 12 but finding the last 5-minute interval the minute hand has passed and counting on the extra minutes (e.g. 23 past = 4x5 = 20, then +3). 'To' times add a further step: converting minutes-past into minutes-to the next hour (44 past 3 = 16 to 4, a number bond to 60). Reading the hour hand precisely also matters — near the top of the hour it sits almost on the next numeral, but the hour is the number it has LAST PASSED.
bestPractices: Teach 'find the 5-minute interval before the hand, then count on' rather than counting every minute from 12
Use a number line / number bond to 60 to convert minutes past to minutes to
Check the hour hand carefully: at 7:43 the hour hand is nearly on 8 but the hour is still 7
Match analogue and digital to the exact minute, both directions
Rehearse the multi-step 'minutes to' reading, where errors cluster
keyRepresentations: Analogue clock with a minute scale (tick marks)
Counting on from the last multiple of five
Number line for past-to-to conversion; part-whole bond to 60
Paired analogue and digital displays
commonMisconceptions: Counts individual minutes from 12 to the hand instead of counting on from the nearest 5 below (slow and error-prone)
Multi-step 'minutes to' reading breaks down (miscounts the bond to 60)
Reads the hour as the numeral the hour hand is nearest, so 7:43 becomes '8:43' (hour hand almost on 8)
Reads a digital time literally rather than converting it (says 'seven forty-three' but can't render it on analogue or as a 'to' time)

learn.summary: Children read and write time to the exact minute on analogue and digital clocks. The efficient method is not counting single minutes from the 12 but finding the last 5-minute interval the minute hand has passed and counting on (e.g. 23 past = 4×5 = 20, then +3). 'To' times add a conversion step: turning minutes-past into minutes-to the next hour using a number bond to 60 (44 past 3 = 16 to 4). The hour hand also needs care: late in the hour it moves close to the next numeral, but the hour is the number it has LAST passed (at 7:43 the hour hand is about three-quarters of the way to 8, but the hour is still 7; at 9:57 it is almost on 10, but the hour is still 9).

activities.title: Count on from the last five on a moveable clock
feedback: If the child counts every minute from the 12, prompt: 'Which five has the hand just passed?' then count on only the extra minutes from there.

If the child reads 7:43 as 8:43, say: 'The hour is the number the hour hand has LAST passed — it is still before the 8, so the hour is 7.' Slowly sweep the hour hand across the whole hour so they see it travel from just-past-7 to the 8.
For 9:57, if the child says 10, point out the hand has not yet reached the 10, so the hour is still 9 — read last-passed, not nearest.
Confirm a correct reading by restating the method: 'You found 40, then counted on 3 — that's 43, and the hour hand is still past 7, so 7:43.'
activities.rationale: Guidance documenting this error reports children count individual minutes to the hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and recommends the 4×5=20 then +3 method. A moveable clock lets the child rehearse the count-on procedure and watch the hour hand travel; a static annotated clock can still show one worked example but does not let the child try the count themselves.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Step 3, Tell the time to the minute) documents that children may count individual minutes until they reach the minute hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and that 'minutes to the hour' has several steps where errors cluster; the recommended method is 4x5=20 then +3, with a number line and part-whole bond to 60 for past-to conversion.

The hour hand is significantly harder for children to read than the minute hand, and children tend to read hour and minute separately; near the top of the hour the hour hand's position (just before the next numeral) is a documented source of error.
learnerActions: On a clock with moveable hands and a minute scale (tick marks), set the minute hand to a target such as 43 minutes.
Find the last 5-minute mark the hand has passed (40) by counting the fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40.
Count on the extra single minutes from there: 41, 42, 43 — do not count all 43 ticks one at a time from the 12.
Check the hour hand: notice it has moved about three-quarters of the way toward the next numeral, and say the hour as the number it has LAST passed.
Try another near-the-hour example: set 9:57 — the hour hand is almost on 10, but the hour is still 9 because that is the number it has last passed.
Read the whole time aloud (e.g. 'forty-three minutes past seven' / 'seven forty-three').
activities.intendedInsight: The quick, reliable way to read exact minutes is to land on the nearest 5-minute mark below the hand and count on the remaining minutes, and to read the hour as the numeral the hour hand has last passed.

activities.title: Convert 'past' to 'minutes to' with a bond to 60
feedback: If the child gives a wrong 'to' time such as '23 to 8' for 7:43, bring back the number line: 'How many more from 43 to reach 60?' (17), so it is 17 to 8.
If the child cannot convert at all, rehearse just the bond to 60 first (e.g. 43 + ? = 60) before returning to the clock; do not re-teach whole-clock reading.
Watch that the stated hour is the NEXT hour (8, not 7) when giving a 'to' time.
activities.rationale: The multi-step 'minutes to' reading is where errors cluster, and a number line / part-whole bond to 60 is the recommended scaffold for the past-to-to conversion. Isolating the conversion step from the reading step targets the specific breakdown.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Step 3, Tell the time to the minute) documents that children may count individual minutes until they reach the minute hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and that 'minutes to the hour' has several steps where errors cluster; the recommended method is 4x5=20 then +3, with a number line and part-whole bond to 60 for past-to conversion.
learnerActions: Start from an exact 'past' reading such as 43 minutes past 7.
On a number line from 0 to 60 (or a part-whole bond), find how far it is from 43 up to 60: 43 + 17 = 60.
State the 'to' time: 43 past 7 is 17 minutes to 8.
Repeat with other examples, e.g. 44 past 3 = 16 to 4; 57 past 9 = 3 to 10.
Say both forms of the same time aloud to connect them.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a 'to' time is one extra step on top of reading the 'past' time: use a number bond to 60 to find the gap to the next hour, and remember the hour named is the NEXT hour.

activities.title: Match and write analogue and digital to the exact minute, both directions
feedback: If a digital reading is copied literally but cannot be set on analogue (reads 'seven forty-three' but cannot place the hands or give the 'to' form), practise placing the minute hand at the counted-on position and sweeping the hour hand to just-past the hour.
For the hour-hand check: the answer is 7 because the hand has not yet reached 8 — read last-passed, not nearest.
For the fill-in: 44 + 16 = 60, so 44 past 3 = 16 to 4.
activities.rationale: Matching analogue to digital to the exact minute, the hour-hand question, and past-to conversion are the curriculum reading/writing/converting targets. Writing and hand-setting require the child to produce a time, not just recognise one; a recognition-only check would not show whether the child can construct the reading independently.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute'; Year 4 pupils 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks', so reading to the nearest minute is the age-8+ consolidation of this strand.
learnerActions: Read an analogue clock set to 7:43 and write it as a digital time.
Given a digital time such as 11:06, set the hands: minute hand just past the 1 (at the 6-minute tick), hour hand just past the 11.
Match several analogue faces to their digital equivalents to the exact minute.
For each, say the hour it has last passed and the minutes found by counting on.
Answer targeted checks, e.g. 'The hour hand is almost on 8 — what is the hour?' and 'Fill in: 44 minutes past 3 = ___ minutes to 4.'
activities.intendedInsight: Exact-minute times can be translated faithfully between analogue and digital in both directions, keeping the count-on method and the last-passed hour.

constraints: A static labelled clock can display one worked time but does not let the child rehearse the count-on procedure or watch the hour hand travel; use it as a worked example, not as the main practice.
Prompted oral readings (a character asking 'what time is it?') can elicit answers but do not reveal HOW the child finds the minutes; pair them with tasks where the method is visible.
Recognition/matching tasks assess and reinforce but do not by themselves require the child to construct a reading or set the hands; include writing and hand-setting for production.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: lighting the 5-minute marks in groups up to the last interval in one colour, then single count-on minutes in another colour; a toggle that rolls the reading round a 0–60 number line to show the 'to' form; an hour hand that creeps toward the next numeral so the child must read last-passed. These are illustrative, not required.
When scaffolding a child who counts single minutes, do not reteach clock reading from scratch — prompt them to the nearest five and count on.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and logic: 4×5=20 then +3 = 23 (correct); 43+17=60 so 7:43 is 17 to 8 (correct); 44+16=60 so 44 past 3 = 16 to 4 (correct); 57+3=60 so 57 past 9 = 3 to 10 (correct); for 11:06 the minute hand sits at the 6-minute tick just past the 1 (correct); for 9:57 the hour hand is nearly on 10 but the hour is still 9 (correct).
The '23 to 8' value is a documented learner ERROR, not a correct answer, and is used only as a feedback example to correct — never offered as a valid option.

The hour-hand rule ('the hour is the number the hour hand has last passed') is the key conceptual correction and is taught directly in activity 1 so the 'nearest numeral' error is fixed, not merely flagged. Independent re-check confirms the 9:57 example is present in activity 1 actions and feedback.
The source's catalog claim that '3D adds nothing' has been omitted as a comparison not established as a pedagogical fact; nothing here depends on it.

Independent review found no critical learner-facing errors; the arithmetic, hour-hand logic, and both-direction conversions are coherent from first action through final feedback. Remaining uncertainty is confined to unre-verified source evidence.

probeDeeper: 'Show me how you found 43 minutes — did you count every minute, or start from a five?'
'The hour hand is almost touching the 8 — so is the hour 7 or 8? How do you know?'
'You read 7:43 — can you say that as minutes TO the next hour?'
'Set the clock to 9:57 — where does the hour hand go, and what is the hour?' (hour hand almost on 10, still 9)
assess.correctAnswer: Finds the last 5-minute mark (40) and counts on 3 to reach 43; reads the hour as 7 (the number the hour hand has last passed); writes 7:43; sets 11:06 with the minute hand just past the 1 and the hour hand just past the 11.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts individual minutes from the 12 up to the hand instead of counting on from the last multiple of five
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach reading from scratch: prompt 'which five has the hand just passed?' then count on the extra minutes; rehearse with a clock whose fives are marked.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Taps round the dial one minute at a time; slow, and miscounts on larger minute values

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the hour as the numeral the hour hand is nearest, so 7:43 becomes 8:43
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise 'the hour is the number the hour hand has LAST PASSED'; use a moveable clock to watch the hour hand travel between two numbers across the hour.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the hour as 8 when the hour hand sits just before the 8

errorPatterns.pattern: The multi-step 'minutes to' reading breaks down — miscounts the number bond to 60
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with a number line / part-whole bond to 60 (43 + 17 = 60); rehearse the extra conversion step, don't re-teach whole-clock reading.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads 7:43 as the wrong 'to' time (e.g. '23 to 8'), or can't convert past to to at all

responseLevels.gap: Counts single minutes from the 12 and/or reads the hour by nearest numeral; can't convert to 'to' times.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes any exact-minute time both directions (analogue to digital), counting on from the nearest five, reads the hour as last-passed even near the top of the hour, and converts past to to fluently.
responseLevels.partial: Reads exact minutes for 'past' times by counting on, but slips on the hour when the hour hand is near the next numeral, or on the multi-step 'minutes to' conversion.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set exact-minute reading and writing tasks and WATCH the method: (1) Analogue clock set to 7:43 with the hour hand nearly on 8: 'Read this time to me — tell me the hour and the minutes — and show me how you work out the minutes.' (2) 'Now write it as a digital time.' (3) Give a digital 11:06: 'Set these hands on the clock.' Watch whether they count on from the last five (40, then 41-42-43) or count single minutes from the 12, and whether they keep the hour at 7 (not 8).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW the minutes are found (count-on from the nearest five vs one-by-one from the 12) separates the efficient procedure from a fragile one; the hour-hand-nearly-on-8 setup catches the child who reads the hour by nearest numeral rather than last-passed.

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils should 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute'; Year 4 pupils 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks', so reading to the nearest minute is the age-8+ consolidation of this strand.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics, Year 3 and Year 4 Measurement (statutory), gov.uk

sources.claim: White Rose Y3 Time (Step 3, Tell the time to the minute) documents that children may count individual minutes until they reach the minute hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and that 'minutes to the hour' has several steps where errors cluster; the recommended method is 4x5=20 then +3, with a number line and part-whole bond to 60 for past-to conversion.
sources.source: White Rose Education, Year 3 Summer Block 3: Time (scheme of learning), Step 3

sources.claim: The hour hand is significantly harder for children to read than the minute hand, and children tend to read hour and minute separately; near the top of the hour the hour hand's position (just before the next numeral) is a documented source of error.
sources.source: Earnest, Gonzales & Plant (2018), 'Time as a measure: elementary students positioning the hands of an analog clock', Journal of Numerical Cognition 4(1)

pedagogy.summary: Recognising that the faces of a 3-D shape are themselves 2-D shapes (a circle on a cylinder, triangles on a pyramid) is the bridge that connects the flat and solid worlds. It is best taught by taking solids apart — unfolding or 'popping up' a solid so its faces lie flat as recognisable 2-D shapes, tracing or paint-stamping a face to print its 2-D shape, and handling solids to feel which surfaces are flat faces and which are curved. The key idea to build is that a solid is BUILT FROM 2-D faces, and that a face keeps its 2-D shape whether drawn on paper or sitting on the solid.
bestPractices: Unfold or 'pop up' a solid from flat paper so children see the faces are 2-D shapes and can touch and count them (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023).
Trace round, or dip-and-stamp, a face to print its 2-D shape — the print of a tin's end is a circle.
Name the face by its 2-D shape (circle, triangle, square) distinct from the solid's name (cylinder, pyramid, cube).
Contrast flat faces (rest flat on the table) with curved surfaces (roll), so a cylinder's curved side is not mistaken for a flat face.
Link explicitly: a cube is made of six squares; a cylinder has two circular faces — every 3-D shape is made up of 2-D shapes.
keyRepresentations: Pop-up / unfoldable solids whose faces flatten into 2-D shapes
Paint-stamp or trace-around prints of each face
A cube shown as six squares; a pyramid as triangles plus a square base; a cylinder as two circles plus a curved surface
Face-count charts (faces, edges, vertices)
commonMisconceptions: Names a face by the whole solid's name — calls the flat round end of a cylinder 'a cylinder' rather than 'a circle'.
Cannot separate face from solid because the solid itself is mis-named — a cube called 'a square' has no distinct square faces to find (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023).
Sees the solid as one undifferentiated whole and does not decompose it into faces (van Hiele visual level).

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 learn that the flat faces of a 3-D solid are themselves 2-D shapes — a circle on a cylinder, triangles on a pyramid. A solid with only flat faces, such as a cube or pyramid, is built FROM those flat faces; some solids, such as a cylinder, also have a curved surface, which is not a flat face. The core teaching moves are taking solids apart (unfolding or popping up a solid so faces lie flat), tracing or paint-stamping a face to print its 2-D shape, and handling solids to feel which surfaces are flat faces and which are curved. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether drawn on paper or sitting on the solid; the whole tin is a cylinder, but each flat end is a circle.

activities.title: Take a solid apart into its flat faces
feedback: If a child names a face by the solid's name (calls a cylinder's end 'a cylinder'), trace round or stamp that face onto paper — the print is a circle; the face is the 2-D shape, the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder.
If a child calls a cube 'a square', pop up or unfold the six square faces so they see the solid is made OF squares, then help them re-name the solid.
If a child treats the solid as one undifferentiated whole, unfold it so each face lies flat and gets named, then rebuild it face by face.

Note for the teacher: a paper or card face has slight thickness and stands in for the ideal flat (zero-thickness) 2-D shape of the solid's face; ask the child what mathematical shape the flattened face represents, treating the paper as a stand-in rather than the mathematical shape itself.
activities.rationale: Physically constructing and taking apart solids lets children hold, cut, fold and touch the faces, supporting them to distinguish and name component shapes; instruction is needed to move from seeing a shape as one whole to describing and composing its parts.
sourceClaims: Building solids from flat paper (pop-up) so children hold, cut, fold and touch the faces, sides and vertices improved their ability to distinguish and name the shapes; children preferred 2-D shape names for solids until they physically constructed them, and the circle/sphere pair was the most secure.

At the van Hiele visual level shapes are viewed as a whole rather than by distinguishing their parts; instruction is needed to move children to describing shapes by their component parts and properties.
learnerActions: Handle a real solid (a tin/cylinder, a cube, a square-based pyramid) and run a finger over its surfaces.
Unfold or 'pop up' a solid made from flat paper/card so its faces lie flat, then touch and count the separated faces.

Name each flattened face by its 2-D shape (circle, triangle, square) and rebuild the solid face by face. If a paper cylinder is unrolled, its curved side flattens into a rectangle, but on the cylinder that part is the curved surface, not a flat face.
State the link aloud: 'a cube is made of six squares', 'a cylinder has two circular faces and a curved surface'.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid's flat faces are 2-D shapes; a solid with only flat faces (such as a cube or pyramid) is built from them, while a cylinder also has a curved surface. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether it is drawn on paper or sitting on the solid.

activities.title: Print the face: trace and paint-stamp
feedback: When the stamped circle appears beside the tin, confirm: 'the flat end is a circle; the whole tin is the cylinder'.
If a child tries to stamp the curved side, notice it cannot print a single flat shape — only flat faces rest flat and print cleanly.
Note for the teacher: the printed mark (and the paper it is on) has slight thickness; it represents the ideal flat 2-D shape of the solid's face, which is the shape the child names.
activities.rationale: Printing or tracing a face gives a child a 2-D artefact tied to the solid, which may reinforce that a face retains its 2-D shape off the solid as well as on it. This is a proposed activity; the cited study examined pop-up construction rather than stamping, so its efficacy here is unverified.
learnerActions: Dip the flat end of a tin in paint (or ink pad) and stamp it on paper; name the shape that appears.
Trace round a flat face of a cube or the square base of a pyramid and name the printed 2-D shape.
Set the printed 2-D shape beside the solid and say which face of the solid it came from.
activities.intendedInsight: The print of a solid's flat face is a plain 2-D shape (a tin's end prints a circle), making concrete that the face is itself a 2-D shape.

activities.title: Flat faces versus curved surfaces
feedback: If a child calls the cylinder's curved side a face, have them try to make it rest flat — it rolls, so it is a curved surface, not a flat face.
Confirm the cylinder has exactly two flat circular faces plus one curved surface.
activities.rationale: Explicitly contrasting flat faces with curved surfaces prevents miscounting the curved side of a cylinder as a flat face and sharpens the idea of a face as a flat 2-D shape. A sort can check how a child classifies surfaces but does not by itself elicit handling or an explanation, so it is paired with the resting-flat test.
learnerActions: Try to rest each surface of a cylinder flat on the table: the two ends sit flat, the curved side rolls.
Sort surfaces into 'flat faces' (rest flat) and 'curved surfaces' (roll).
Count and name the flat faces on a cube, a square-based pyramid, and the cylinder; note the cylinder's side is curved, not a flat face.
activities.intendedInsight: A flat face rests flat and has a 2-D shape; a curved surface rolls and is not a flat face — so a cylinder's curved side should not be counted as a flat face.

activities.title: Decompose every face (screen peel or physical net)
feedback: When a peeled or unfolded face matches the drawn 2-D shape, confirm they are the same shape shown in different places.
If a child forgets hidden faces, rotate the solid (or use the full net) to reveal them and count all faces before reassembling.
activities.rationale: Rotating a solid and separating each face addresses faces on all sides, including hidden ones, extending the decomposition idea beyond the faces a child can see at rest. A rotatable screen model is one optional way to show hidden faces; a physical unfoldable net works too — neither is uniquely required.
sourceClaims: At the van Hiele visual level shapes are viewed as a whole rather than by distinguishing their parts; instruction is needed to move children to describing shapes by their component parts and properties.
learnerActions: Rotate a solid, or its on-screen model, so faces on every side — including hidden ones — come into view.
On a screen model, peel each face off as a plain 2-D shape; with a physical solid, use an unfoldable net or pop-up so each face lies flat. Set each face beside a drawn version to compare.
Reassemble the solid from its faces and state how many of each 2-D shape it is made from.
activities.intendedInsight: Every flat face of a solid — not just the visible ones — is a 2-D shape, and a solid with only flat faces can be composed and decomposed from those flat shapes; a solid with a curved surface, such as a cylinder, also needs that curved part.

activities.title: Predict-then-stamp check
feedback: If a child predicts 'a cylinder' for the end's print, let the stamp reveal a circle, then discuss why the face is a circle while the whole tin is a cylinder.
A matching task confirms the outcome but not the take-apart reasoning — pair it with asking the child to explain how the solid is built from those faces.
activities.rationale: A predict-justify-observe routine makes the child's reasoning explicit before the stamp confirms or challenges it, which is more diagnostic than a match-only check.
learnerActions: Before stamping, predict and justify what shape the flat end of the tin will print.
Stamp it and compare the result with the prediction.
Match which 2-D shapes make up a given solid (e.g. two circles plus a curved surface for a cylinder) and explain the match.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a prediction and reason in advance surfaces whether a child sees the face as a 2-D shape or conflates it with the whole solid.

constraints: Use real 3-D solids and named flat faces; ensure the solid itself is correctly named, because a child who calls a cube 'a square' has no distinct square faces to find.
Use a cube-shaped object when naming a cube, and a square-based pyramid when describing triangular faces plus a square base, so the named example matches the shape.

Paper or card cutouts, printed marks, and pop-up nets have slight thickness and approximate ideal zero-thickness mathematical faces; a flattened paper face represents the 2-D shape of the solid's face. Ask children what mathematical shape it represents, not whether the paper can be picked up, and state this approximation within the activity.
A screen model where a face peels off is an idealised representation; label it as a model and pair it with handling real solids so children also feel flat versus curved surfaces.
Matching 2-D shapes to solids checks the outcome only; it does not by itself show the child understands decomposition — combine it with constructing, unfolding, or explaining.

A fixed labelled image where tapping a face reveals its 2-D shape can serve as a reference, but it does not let the child physically separate and count faces; use it as a scaffold, not the main activity.

A sort or recognition/matching task may teach or check classification but does not itself elicit the child's own explanation of how a solid is built from faces; include tasks where the child names, counts, and reassembles.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The printing/tracing activity has no sourceClaims attached because the cited pop-up study examined building solids from flat paper, not stamping or tracing; its efficacy here is unverified.

The Common Core claim frames the overall objective (analysing 2-D/3-D shapes, describing parts, composing shapes) rather than directly evidencing any single activity's teaching move; it is retained as curriculum framing, not as efficacy evidence, and so is not attached to specific activities.

The original 'conversation' entry asserted that 'talk cannot carry the visual decomposition of a solid into faces'. This is a catalog comparison, not an established law; softened to: spoken explanation is useful to elicit a child's reasoning but is best paired with handling or constructing solids, since the decomposition is primarily visual and tactile.

The original claimed a rotatable 3-D model is 'ideal' and uniquely shows hidden faces ('the spatial crux'). The affordance (revealing faces on all sides) is retained, but comparative necessity over physical unfoldable solids is not established by the sources; both are offered.
The source efficacy claim (pop-up construction improved naming) comes from one kindergarten study; this micro-topic targets ages 6–7, so transfer is plausible but not directly verified.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a solid cylinder (a tin) and a stamp pad or paint. BEFORE stamping, ask them to predict and justify what shape the flat end will print. A child who thinks the tin 'is a cylinder' may predict 'a cylinder'; a child who sees the face predicts 'a circle'. Stamp it: a circle appears. The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part — the print forces the idea that the solid's face is a 2-D circle.
probeDeeper: If I dip this flat face in paint and stamp it on the paper, what shape appears?
You called the whole tin a cylinder — but what shape is just this flat end?
How many flat faces can you find on the cube, and what shape is each one?
Is the curved side of the tin a flat face too? Can it rest flat on the table like the ends?
assess.correctAnswer: Identifies the flat round ends of the cylinder as circles and the faces of the pyramid as triangles (with a square base); explains that a face is the flat surface of the solid and is itself a 2-D shape, so the solid is built from 2-D faces — the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder, but each flat end is a circle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names a face by the whole solid's name — calls the flat round end of a cylinder 'a cylinder' rather than 'a circle'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace round or stamp the face onto paper — the print is a circle; the face is a 2-D shape, the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder
errorPatterns.distractor: It is a cylinder (naming the face with the solid's name)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked the shape of the flat face, gives the solid's name

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot separate a face from the solid because the solid itself is mis-named — a cube called 'a square' has no distinct square faces to point to
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pop up or unfold the six square faces of a cube so the child sees the solid is made of squares and re-names the solid correctly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the cube 'a square' and cannot pick out its separate square faces

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees the solid as one undifferentiated whole and does not decompose it into faces at all
errorPatterns.nextMove: Unfold the solid so each face lies flat and is named; rebuild it face by face
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the solid as a single object and cannot point out its separate faces

responseLevels.gap: Sees the solid as one whole and names its faces with the solid's name (a face of the cylinder is 'a cylinder').
responseLevels.full: Identifies each flat face by its 2-D shape and explains the solid is built from 2-D faces (a cylinder has two circular faces; a pyramid has triangular faces and a square base), distinguishing flat faces from curved surfaces.
responseLevels.partial: Points to faces and names familiar ones (the square faces of a cube) but inconsistently — misses faces on less familiar solids or denies a face is 'really' a 2-D shape.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Run your finger over this tin (a cylinder). Point to a flat face on it — what 2-D shape is that face? Now look at this pyramid: what shape are its faces? Tell me how a face can be a 2-D shape when it is part of a solid.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands names the face by its 2-D shape (a circle) as distinct from the solid (a cylinder); a child who conflates them answers with the solid's name ('it's a cylinder') or denies the flat part is 'really' a circle because it is on a solid. The reason tier — how a face can be a 2-D shape — separates those who see the solid as built from flat shapes from those who see it as one whole object.

sources.claim: Building solids from flat paper (pop-up) so children hold, cut, fold and touch the faces, sides and vertices improved their ability to distinguish and name the shapes; children preferred 2-D shape names for solids until they physically constructed them, and the circle/sphere pair was the most secure.
sources.source: Mohamed & Kandeel (2023), 'Playful Learning: Teaching the Properties of Geometric Shapes through Pop-up Mechanisms for Kindergarten', IJEMST 11(1) (ERIC EJ1357339)

sources.claim: At the van Hiele visual level shapes are viewed as a whole rather than by distinguishing their parts; instruction is needed to move children to describing shapes by their component parts and properties.
sources.source: Way (2011), 'The Development of Spatial and Geometric Thinking: The Importance of Instruction', NRICH, University of Cambridge

sources.claim: Kindergarten geometry asks children to analyse and compare 2-D and 3-D shapes and describe their parts using informal language, and to compose simple shapes to form larger shapes — framing the link between 2-D shapes and the solids built from them.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, K.G.B.4 and K.G.B.6

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Reactions That Release or Absorb Heat (Energetics)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Energetics):** pupils are taught "energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)" and "exothermic and endothermic chemical reactions (qualitative)," i.e. that some reactions give out energy to the surroundings (temperature rises) and others take energy in (temperature falls).

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-6):** undertake a design project to construct, test and modify a device that either releases or absorbs thermal energy by chemical processes — an explicit application of exothermic and endothermic reactions.

- **Operational details:** Teach energetics operationally through temperature change: an exothermic reaction transfers energy OUT, so the surroundings (and thermometer) get warmer (combustion, neutralisation, most oxidation, hand-warmers); an endothermic reaction takes energy IN, so the surroundings get colder (thermal decomposition, dissolving certain salts, the citric acid + sodium bicarbonate sherbet reaction, instant cold packs). Keep it qualitative at KS3 — measure the temperature before and after and classify by the direction of change; do NOT introduce enthalpy values, bond-energy calculations or reaction profiles with numbers (those are KS4/GCSE). The productive idea is that chemical reactions always involve an energy transfer with the surroundings, and 'feels hot' vs 'feels cold' is the everyday signature of which way energy flowed.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Given a reaction's temperature change, the child classifies it as exothermic or endothermic and states the direction of energy transfer between reaction and surroundings.
bestPractices: Define exothermic and endothermic by the DIRECTION of energy transfer with the surroundings, using the thermometer reading as the operational signature (up = out, down = in).
Have pupils measure temperature before and after and classify from their own data rather than being told which reactions are which.
Include at least one surprising endothermic example (dissolving ammonium nitrate, sherbet) so pupils don't assume all reactions release heat.
Keep it strictly qualitative at KS3 — direction of change only; defer enthalpy values, reaction profiles and bond-energy sums to KS4.
Link to everyday devices (hand-warmers, instant cold packs) so the abstract energy transfer is grounded in real products.
keyRepresentations: A thermometer / temperature–time graph rising (exothermic) or falling (endothermic).
Energy-flow arrows pointing OUT of the reaction (exo) or IN from the surroundings (endo).
Paired beakers: one warming, one cooling.
Everyday device cards: hand-warmer (exo) vs instant cold pack (endo).
A two-bin sort (exothermic / endothermic) of reactions and scenarios.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming all chemical reactions give out heat, missing that some absorb it and cool the surroundings.
Reversing the terms — thinking 'exothermic' means it gets colder because energy 'exits'.
Believing 'endothermic' reactions produce cold as a substance rather than absorbing energy from the surroundings.
Confusing the reaction system with the surroundings when deciding which way energy flowed.
Thinking heating is always needed for a reaction to occur, conflating 'needs heat to start' with 'absorbs heat overall'.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13 (UK KS3, US NGSS MS-PS1-6), teach exothermic and endothermic processes operationally through the direction of temperature change: temperature up means energy transferred OUT to the surroundings (exothermic); temperature down means energy transferred IN from the surroundings (endothermic). Keep it strictly qualitative at this level — classify from measured temperature change, do not introduce enthalpy values, bond-energy sums or numerical reaction profiles. The central activity is measuring temperature before and after several reactions (and physical changes such as dissolving) and classifying each from the pupil's own data, deliberately including a surprising endothermic case so pupils don't assume all reactions release heat. An optional NGSS design extension and everyday-example matching reinforce the idea.

activities.title: Measure, graph and classify: a temperature-change bench
feedback: If a pupil assumes every reaction warms the cup, point them back to the ammonium-nitrate run where the temperature fell — this directly challenges the 'all reactions give out heat' assumption.

If a pupil says the cup got cold because 'cold got in', recast: there is only thermal energy moving; here the process absorbed energy FROM the water, so the water has less thermal energy and reads colder. 'Cold' just means a lower temperature (less thermal energy); it is not a substance arriving.

If a pupil reverses the terms, pin the convention to the surroundings: exo = energy EXits to surroundings (they warm); endo = energy ENters the reaction from surroundings (they cool). Re-classify several runs by their temperature change.
Confirm correct reasoning: 'You classified it from the direction the temperature moved, not from what the reaction looks like — that's exactly the signature of energy transfer.'
activities.rationale: The concept is a measured change over time, so pupils classifying from their own temperature data (rather than being told which case is which) connects the term to the observed direction of energy flow. A deliberately surprising endothermic case targets the common misconception that all reactions release heat. A live thermometer, a temperature–time trace, and energy-flow arrows (OUT for exo, IN for endo) are optional representations that make the energy-transfer direction concrete; a real cup-and-thermometer practical is an equally valid form of this activity.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught exothermic and endothermic chemical reactions (qualitative) and energy changes on changes of state (qualitative).
learnerActions: Choose a reaction or dissolving process (e.g. acid + alkali neutralisation, a combustion example, dissolving ammonium nitrate, or citric acid + sodium bicarbonate) and record the starting temperature. Note that dissolving is a physical change, but it still involves an energy transfer with the surroundings.

Begin the reaction or dissolving process (e.g. pour the reactants together, or stir the salt into water; a combustion example would be run as a demonstration rather than mixed in a cup) and watch the thermometer, recording temperature over time to produce a temperature–time trace.
Decide from the direction of change whether energy flowed OUT to the surroundings (temperature rose, exothermic) or IN from the surroundings (temperature fell, endothermic).
Run at least one case you expect to warm and one that unexpectedly cools (dissolving ammonium nitrate, or the sherbet reaction), and compare.
Sort each result into an 'exothermic' or 'endothermic' bin and state the rule you discovered: temperature up = energy out; temperature down = energy in.
activities.intendedInsight: Every chemical reaction — and many physical changes such as dissolving — involves an energy transfer with its surroundings, and the thermometer reading is the everyday signature of which way energy flowed. 'Mixing chemicals' can make things colder as well as hotter, because energy can be absorbed from the surroundings.

activities.title: Design a hand-warmer or cold pack to a target temperature
feedback: If the pupil picks a warming process for a cold pack, ask which way energy must flow relative to the hand for it to feel cold, and revisit the exo/endo direction.

Reinforce measurement: if the pupil's data show that changing the amount of substance (with the same amount of water) changed the temperature reached, say: 'You adjusted the amount and the temperature changed — you're controlling the size of the energy transfer, still qualitatively at this stage.'
activities.rationale: NGSS MS-PS1-6 frames energetics as a design task: construct, test and modify a device that releases or absorbs thermal energy. This is proposed to ground the abstract energy-transfer idea in a real, buildable product and asks for construction and explanation as well as recognition; its efficacy is intended rather than independently verified here.
sourceClaims: Students undertake a design project to construct, test and modify a device that either releases or absorbs thermal energy by chemical processes.
learnerActions: Pick a goal: a device that gets warm (hand-warmer) or one that gets cold (instant cold pack).
Decide whether you need an exothermic or endothermic process to reach that goal, explaining the direction of energy transfer.
Assemble, test and measure the temperature your device reaches, then modify it to get closer to a target temperature.
Explain in terms of energy transfer with the surroundings why your device feels hot or cold.
activities.intendedInsight: Exothermic and endothermic processes are the basis of real devices; choosing the right direction of energy transfer lets you engineer a warming or cooling effect.

activities.title: Energy changes in changes of state, and conservation
feedback: If a pupil restricts energy changes to burning, show that melting absorbs energy (endothermic) and freezing releases it (exothermic), and dissolving can go either way.
If a pupil says cold flowed in, redirect to conservation: if the water cooled, the dissolving/reacting substance absorbed that energy — ask them to name where the energy went.
activities.rationale: The assessment evidence requires explaining energy changes during changes of state (melting endothermic, freezing exothermic) and tying classification to conservation of energy. This addresses the misconception that only 'burning-type' reactions involve energy changes and the 'cold is a substance' idea.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught exothermic and endothermic chemical reactions (qualitative) and energy changes on changes of state (qualitative).
learnerActions: Classify melting ice and freezing water as endothermic or exothermic, justifying each by whether energy is absorbed from or released to the surroundings.
Explain how a cold pack that cools works even though 'nothing cold' was added.
State what gained the energy when the water in a cold pack cooled, using the idea that total energy is conserved.
activities.intendedInsight: Energy changes accompany physical changes (melting, freezing, dissolving) as well as dramatic reactions, and because energy is conserved, cooling means energy was transferred from the water to the dissolving/reacting system, not that 'cold' arrived.

activities.title: Sort reactions, changes and everyday devices by energy direction
feedback: For a correct sort, prompt the pupil to state the reasoning: 'You put the cold pack with endothermic because it absorbs energy from your hand.'
For an error, return to the rule temperature up = energy out, temperature down = energy in, and have them re-check against it.

For the thermal decompositions usually met at this level (e.g. heating calcium carbonate or copper carbonate), remind pupils they are endothermic because energy must be supplied continuously: stop heating and the decomposition stops. This is different from a reaction that only needs heat to start and then keeps going by releasing energy (exothermic), such as combustion. A few decompositions are exothermic, so judge each by the direction of energy transfer during the change.
For photosynthesis, note it is endothermic because it absorbs light energy; classify it by energy taken in, not by a temperature reading.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and matching consolidate and let pupils check their classification across many cases, including the everyday examples that ground the abstract idea. A sort or match can check and reinforce classification but does not by itself elicit the measure-and-classify-from-own-data experience; it is a consolidation and checking activity, not the primary learning experience.
learnerActions: Sort given items — reactions, physical changes and scenarios (combustion, neutralisation, dissolving ammonium nitrate, sherbet, thermal decomposition, photosynthesis) — into exothermic and endothermic groups.
Match everyday products — hand-warmer, instant cold pack, campfire — to exothermic or endothermic, and say which way energy flows relative to you.
For a stated temperature change (e.g. 'the temperature fell'), state whether energy was absorbed or released, and predict whether a thermometer will end higher or lower.
activities.intendedInsight: The same classification rule applies across reactions, physical changes and real devices: match the direction of temperature change to the direction of energy transfer.

constraints: Keep strictly qualitative at this level: classify by the direction of energy transfer, usually shown by the direction of temperature change in the surroundings. For cases where no simple temperature reading applies (e.g. photosynthesis absorbing light, or a decomposition that needs continuous heating), classify by whether energy is taken in or given out. Do not introduce enthalpy values, bond-energy calculations, or numerical reaction profiles (those belong to KS4/GCSE).

Sorting, matching and multiple-choice tasks consolidate and check classification but do not by themselves elicit the measure-and-classify-from-own-data experience; use them alongside, not instead of, an experiment or temperature-trace activity.

A static tappable diagram (e.g. one warming beaker and one cooling beaker with arrows in/out) is a useful vocabulary anchor for exo/endo but a fixed reveal cannot let pupils generate and classify their own temperature data; treat it as a scaffold.
Address 'cold is a substance' language directly: there is only thermal energy moving; cooling means energy was absorbed from the surroundings, not that cold arrived.
Pin the exo/endo convention to the surroundings to prevent reversal: exo = energy exits to the surroundings (they warm); endo = energy enters the reaction from the surroundings (they cool).
Include at least one surprising endothermic example so pupils do not assume all reactions release heat.
Distinguish 'needs heat to start' from 'absorbs heat overall' — a reaction that must be heated to begin can still be exothermic.

Treat dissolving, melting and freezing as physical changes that still involve energy transfer; do not label dissolving as a chemical reaction, even though it can be classified exo/endo by the same temperature-direction rule.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NGSS MS-PS1-6 design-project source claim is marked verified:false in the original row; treat the design extension as consistent with that standard but not independently confirmed here, and read efficacy wording as proposed/intended.

The original rated 3D and open-conversation formats 'poor' with claims such as '3D adds no insight' and 'dialogue cannot substitute' for measuring. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the source evidence; they have been softened to the scoped point that the core learning depends on generating and classifying temperature data, which a tappable diagram or discussion alone does not itself provide. No universal 'only this teaches' claim is asserted.

The original (and the first-draft candidate) loosely called dissolving ammonium nitrate 'a reaction'. Dissolving is a physical change; this has been corrected in every learner-facing occurrence to 'reaction or dissolving process', consistent with the changes-of-state evidence. This is a wording correction, not new source verification.
Photosynthesis (endothermic) was named in the original evidence and had been dropped; it has been restored as an endothermic example in the sort activity.

Self-audit of science content: the state-change classifications (melting endothermic, freezing exothermic), the exo/endo direction convention, thermal decomposition as endothermic, and photosynthesis as endothermic are internally consistent and were preserved. The 'cold is a substance' correction is retained as a conceptual fix, not new verification.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: put a thermometer in water and stir in ammonium nitrate. Ask the child to predict whether the temperature rises, falls, or stays the same, and WHY, before adding it. A 'reactions give out heat' or 'nothing cold added' model predicts a rise or no change. The temperature drops sharply. The pre-observation reasoning about energy direction is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If no 'cold' entered the water, where did the water's energy GO?
A hand warmer gets hot; a cold pack gets cold. Which way is energy flowing in each, relative to your hand?
Is melting ice exothermic or endothermic — and how does that fit the cold-pack case?
Overall energy is conserved. So in the cold pack, if the water cooled, what gained that energy?
assess.correctAnswer: No cold 'gets in' — there is no such thing as cold flowing in. This is an ENDOTHERMIC change: the dissolving/reaction ABSORBS thermal energy FROM the water and surroundings, so their temperature drops. Cold is the absence of energy that has been taken away, not a substance arriving. Full marks explain the temperature fall as energy being absorbed BY the system from the surroundings.

errorPatterns.pattern: cold is a substance/thing that flows into objects to cool them ('coldness went into the water')
errorPatterns.nextMove: There is only thermal energy moving; 'cold' is where energy has been removed. Recast: the reaction absorbs energy from the water, so the water has less → colder. Confront the 'cold substance' idea directly.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — coldness from the powder moves into the water and cools it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains cooling by cold entering rather than heat energy leaving/being absorbed

errorPatterns.pattern: temperature RISE means endothermic (definitions reversed)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pin the convention to the surroundings: exo = energy EXits to surroundings, they warm; endo = energy ENters the reaction from surroundings, they cool. Re-classify several by the temperature change.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's exothermic, because a reaction always gives out energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: labels a warming reaction endothermic and a cooling one exothermic

errorPatterns.pattern: only 'burning-type' reactions involve energy changes; dissolving/state changes don't
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show melting is endothermic and freezing exothermic, and dissolving can be either — energy changes accompany physical changes too, not just dramatic reactions.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies that dissolving or melting has an energy change; restricts exo/endo to combustion

responseLevels.gap: Explains cooling by 'cold flowing in'; reverses exo/endo; thinks only burning has energy changes.
responseLevels.full: Explains temperature change purely as energy transferred to/from the surroundings (no 'cold' substance), classifies reactions and state changes as exo/endo by direction of energy flow, and ties it to conservation of energy — transferring to hand warmers, cold packs, melting and freezing.
responseLevels.partial: Labels a reaction exo/endo from its temperature change and defines the terms, but slips into 'cold as a substance' language or can't apply the idea to state changes — labels without consistent energy-transfer reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I dissolve a spoon of ammonium nitrate in water in a cup and the cup goes noticeably COLD — this is how instant cold packs work. A student says 'something cold must be getting into the water to cool it down.' Is that what's happening — and the important part, explain in terms of energy why the cup gets cold.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who reasons with energy transfer (endothermic = energy absorbed from surroundings, so they cool) from one holding the 'cold is a substance that flows in' misconception. It also tests the direction convention (exothermic releases/warms, endothermic absorbs/cools) rather than rote labels.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils are taught exothermic and endothermic chemical reactions (qualitative) and energy changes on changes of state (qualitative).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS3, Chemistry — Energetics)

sources.claim: Students undertake a design project to construct, test and modify a device that either releases or absorbs thermal energy by chemical processes.
