pedagogy.summary: At 7-9 this is a CLASSIFICATION topic: extend the child's mental map of the solar system beyond the eight planets to the smaller bodies, and pin down three commonly-confused categories. Asteroids = rocky bodies, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter. Comets = icy 'dirty snowballs' that grow a glowing tail only when they near the Sun (ice vaporises). And the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite trio, which is ONE object named by WHERE it is: a rock in space (meteoroid), a streak of light as it burns through our atmosphere (meteor / 'shooting star'), and what's left if it lands (meteorite). The load-bearing moves are (1) rocky-vs-icy for asteroid-vs-comet, and (2) location-defines-the-name for the meteor trio.
bestPractices: Teach by contrasting pairs with a clear discriminator: asteroid = ROCK, comet = ICE (+dust). Anchor comets as 'dirty snowballs' and asteroids as 'space rocks in the belt between Mars and Jupiter'.

Make the meteor trio a JOURNEY, not three separate things: same object, three names by location — meteoroid (in space) → meteor (burning streak in the atmosphere) → meteorite (landed on the ground). A single labelled arc from space to ground fixes it.

Surface the counter-intuitive comet-tail fact explicitly: a comet's tail is pushed out by sunlight and the solar wind, so it always points AWAY from the Sun — it does not trail behind the comet like a scarf. This is memorable and corrects a strong intuition.
Correct 'shooting star' language directly — a meteor is a burning space rock, not a star — tying back to the child's earlier learning that stars are Suns.
Place the new objects on the solar-system map they already know (from The Eight Planets): the belt sits between Mars and Jupiter; comets swing in from far away and loop around the Sun.
keyRepresentations: Solar-system map with the asteroid belt drawn as a ring of rubble between Mars and Jupiter
Side-by-side 'rocky asteroid vs icy comet' comparison card
Comet diagram: icy nucleus + coma + tail, with the tail pointing away from the Sun along the orbit
A single labelled journey arc: meteoroid (space) → meteor (streak in atmosphere) → meteorite (on the ground)
Size/where-they-live sorting mat (belt / near the Sun with a tail / entering our sky)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a comet's tail streams out BEHIND it like exhaust or a scarf, rather than always pointing away from the Sun.
Believing comets are burning / on fire — they are icy; the tail is vaporising ice and dust lit by sunlight, not flames.
Using meteoroid, meteor and meteorite interchangeably, not realising they are the same object named by location (space / atmosphere / ground).
Calling a meteor a 'shooting star' and thinking it really is a star.
Assuming asteroids are scattered everywhere or are tiny planets, rather than mostly rocky bodies concentrated in the belt.
Confusing asteroids and comets — not grasping rocky-vs-icy as the key difference.

learn.summary: A classification topic for ages 7-9: extend the child's map of the solar system beyond the eight planets to smaller bodies and pin down three commonly-confused categories. Asteroids are rocky bodies mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter; comets are icy 'dirty snowballs' that grow a glowing tail only when near the Sun (ice vaporises); and meteoroid→meteor→meteorite is ONE rock named by WHERE it is (a rock in space, the glowing streak of light as it burns in the atmosphere, and the landed rock). The two load-bearing moves are rocky-vs-icy (asteroid vs comet) and location-defines-the-name (meteor trio). A counter-intuitive fact to surface: a comet's tail is pushed by sunlight and the solar wind, so it always points AWAY from the Sun, not trailing behind the comet's motion.

activities.title: Explore the solar-system map: tap and reveal the small bodies
feedback: If the child merges the categories, sort them aloud: rocky asteroids (belt between Mars and Jupiter), icy comets (tails near the Sun), and the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite journey of one small rock.
When the child ties the tail to the comet's direction of travel, point to the flap: the tail points away from the Sun whichever way the comet moves.

If the child calls the streak a star, name the three stages and explain the streak is light from a tiny space rock burning up in our air, not a star, tying back to earlier learning that stars are Suns.
activities.rationale: The core objective is to identify and classify fixed categories, so a tappable illustration can present these distinctions and place the new objects on the familiar planet map to anchor them, giving at-a-glance coverage. A static scene can assert the tail rule but cannot let the child manipulate it, so pair it with the orbit activity.
sourceClaims: Comets are icy bodies ('made of ice and dust—not rock', unlike rocky asteroids) that grow a tail as they near the Sun because the ice vaporises; the ion tail always points directly away from the Sun. Most asteroids lie in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.

A meteoroid is a space rock in space; if it enters Earth's atmosphere it vaporises into a meteor (a streak of light, sometimes called a 'shooting star', but not actually a star); if it survives and lands it is a meteorite.
learnerActions: Start from a single wide solar-system scene the child already recognises: Sun, inner planets, and the asteroid belt drawn as a ring of rubble between Mars and Jupiter, plus a comet on a looping path and a meteor streaking into Earth's sky.
Tap the rubble-ring between Mars and Jupiter so it lights up and is labelled: 'asteroids — space rocks, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.'
Tap the bright comet and zoom into its icy nucleus, fuzzy coma, and streaming tail; read that a comet is an icy 'dirty snowball' that grows a tail only when it nears the Sun.
Lift a flap asking 'which way does the tail point?' and discover it points AWAY from the Sun, not behind the comet like a scarf or exhaust.

Tap the 'shooting star' streak and follow one glowing arc that splits into three labelled stages: meteoroid (a rock in space) → meteor (the glowing streak of light made as the rock burns in the sky) → meteorite (any piece of the rock that survives and lands on the ground; most burn up completely).

Lift a final flap on the 'shooting star' to reveal it is not a star at all: the bright streak is the light made when a tiny space rock burns up in our air — the rock itself is the meteoroid, and the glowing streak is the meteor.
activities.intendedInsight: Asteroids are rocky and live in the belt; comets are icy and grow a tail (which points away from the Sun) only near the Sun; and meteoroid/meteor/meteorite name the SAME rock by where it is — a rock in space (meteoroid), the streak of light it makes while burning up (meteor), and the landed rock (meteorite), so a 'shooting star' is a light-streak, not a star.

activities.title: Drag the comet round its orbit and watch the tail swing
feedback: If the child expects the tail to trail behind the motion, trace the comet round the Sun so they see the tail swing to lead the comet on the way out.
Name the cause explicitly: sunlight and the solar wind blow the gas and dust away from the Sun.
Reinforce that the tail is vaporising ice and dust lit by sunlight, not flames — a comet is icy, not on fire.
activities.rationale: The tail-direction idea is dynamic and counter-intuitive, so letting the child move the comet and see the tail re-orient can make the 'points away from the Sun' rule concrete in a way a fixed picture only states. This is offered as a helpful dynamic scaffold, not as the only way to grasp the idea.
sourceClaims: Comets are icy bodies ('made of ice and dust—not rock', unlike rocky asteroids) that grow a tail as they near the Sun because the ice vaporises; the ion tail always points directly away from the Sun. Most asteroids lie in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.
learnerActions: Drag a comet along an elliptical orbit around the Sun.
As the comet approaches the Sun, watch the tail lengthen and bloom; as it moves away again, watch it shrink.

Pay attention to the tail's direction as the comet rounds the Sun: watch it continuously re-orient to point away from the Sun, so that on the outbound leg the tail actually LEADS the comet rather than trailing it.
Predict, before dragging, which way the tail will point when the comet is heading back out, then check.
activities.intendedInsight: A comet's tail is pushed away from the Sun by sunlight and the solar wind, so it always points away from the Sun regardless of which way the comet is travelling — and it grows only when the comet is near enough for its ices to warm and stream off.

activities.title: Sort and sequence the small bodies
feedback: If sorting fails, re-anchor the discriminators: asteroid = ROCK in the belt, comet = ICE with a tail that points away from the Sun, meteor trio = one rock named by where it is.
If the child sequences the trio wrongly, walk the single arc from space to ground and re-label each stage.
If the child says the tail trails behind, revisit the orbit activity: the Sun, not the motion, sets the tail's direction.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, matching and sequencing map neatly onto this content and are well suited to checking the classifications and vocabulary after teaching. This checks and consolidates learning rather than building the initial mental map, so use it after the exploration and tail activities; sorting and matching alone do not by themselves show independent explanation, so include the 'explain why' prompt.
sourceClaims: A meteoroid is a space rock in space; if it enters Earth's atmosphere it vaporises into a meteor (a streak of light, sometimes called a 'shooting star', but not actually a star); if it survives and lands it is a meteorite.
learnerActions: Sort a set of objects into three bins: rocky asteroid (belt), icy comet (tail near the Sun), and meteor-journey.
Put the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite stages in order and label each by its location (space / atmosphere / ground).
Answer: which way does a comet's tail point, and where in the solar system do most asteroids orbit?
Explain in your own words why a comet grows a tail only when it comes close to the Sun.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall and discrimination of the three categories and the naming-by-location rule for the meteor trio, including the surprising tail direction.

constraints: Keep the two load-bearing discriminators explicit: rocky-vs-icy (asteroid vs comet) and location-defines-the-name (meteor trio).

A static tap-reveal scene can present the categories and assert the tail rule, but cannot let the child manipulate the comet; the orbit drag activity is what lets the child act on and check the 'tail points away from the Sun' behaviour.

The sort/sequence activity checks and consolidates classifications rather than building the initial mental map; treat it as consolidation or assessment after teaching, since sorting-and-matching responses do not by themselves show independent explanation.

A 3D fly-through alongside a comet or through the belt can convey scale and scatter and makes an atmospheric set-piece, but the concept is categorical not spatial, so keep it optional and not the core teach.

An in-role dialogue can rehearse or recite the category names, but does not itself provide the at-a-glance sorting or the visual tail-direction reveal; if used, pair it with the visual map rather than relying on it alone.

Name the meteor trio precisely: the meteoroid is the rock in space, the meteor is the glowing streak of light it makes while burning in the atmosphere, and the meteorite is the rock once it has landed.
Correct 'shooting star' language directly: the streak is light made when a tiny space rock burns up in our air, not a star, tying back to the child's earlier learning that stars are Suns.
Present a comet as icy, not burning: the tail is vaporising ice and dust lit by sunlight, not flames.
Keep the comet-tail rule at the age-appropriate 'always points away from the Sun'; the ion-vs-dust-tail nuance is not needed in learner text but should not be contradicted.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry included claims framed as universal (e.g. 3D 'adds spectacle without being needed', a static picture 'can only assert', a conversation 'cannot deliver' the sorting). These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits in constraints.

The outbound-leg detail — that the tail LEADS the comet when it heads away from the Sun — follows from the sourced 'tail always points away from the Sun' claim and is physically correct; it is retained as a stretch point for able learners but may be advanced for some 7-9 children.

The simplified 'single tail always points away from the Sun' is an approximation of the sourced 'ion tail' claim: the ion/gas tail points directly away, while a comet's dust tail curves and partly lags. The simplification is appropriate for ages 7-9 and is used in learner text, with the nuance recorded here only.
The meteor trio is named precisely so the meteor is the light-streak and the meteoroid the rock; this avoids conflating the object with the phenomenon in learner-facing text.
Source claims cite the teaching facts (NASA Space Place) and support the stated principles; they do not constitute evidence that these specific activities were tested for effectiveness.

probeDeeper: Where in the solar system do most asteroids orbit?
What is the SAME small rock called when it's out in space, streaking through our air, and lying on the ground?
Why does a comet only grow a tail when it comes close to the Sun?
If a comet is now heading back OUT, away from the Sun, which way does its tail point?
assess.correctAnswer: The tail does NOT simply trail behind the comet's motion. A comet's tail always points AWAY FROM THE SUN, whichever way the comet happens to be travelling, because sunlight and the solar wind push the comet's gas and dust away from the Sun. So as a comet rounds the Sun and heads back out, its tail actually goes ahead of it — still pointing away from the Sun. (A comet is an icy body that only grows a tail when it nears the Sun and its ices warm and stream off.)

errorPatterns.pattern: a comet's tail trails out behind it, like smoke behind a rocket ('it follows the direction it's moving')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that sunlight and the solar wind blow the tail away from the Sun; trace a comet round the Sun so the child sees the tail swing to LEAD the comet on the way out.
errorPatterns.distractor: The tail always streams out behind the comet, in the direction it came from.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child ties the tail direction to the comet's motion rather than to the Sun

errorPatterns.pattern: asteroids, comets and meteors are all just the same kind of thing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort them: rocky asteroids (mostly the belt between Mars and Jupiter), icy comets (tails near the Sun), and the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite journey of one small rock.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child uses the words interchangeably and cannot sort them

errorPatterns.pattern: a shooting star is a real star falling out of the sky
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain it's a tiny space rock burning up in our atmosphere, not a star; name it meteoroid in space, meteor as the streak, meteorite if it lands.
errorPatterns.distractor: A shooting star is a real star falling out of the sky.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child calls the meteor streak a star

responseLevels.gap: Merges asteroids/comets/meteors and pictures the tail trailing behind the comet's motion.
responseLevels.full: Explains the tail points away from the Sun (pushed by sunlight and solar wind), distinguishes asteroid from comet, and names the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite journey of one rock.
responseLevels.partial: Distinguishes rocky asteroids from icy comets and knows the meteor trio, but still has the tail trailing behind, or is unsure which way it points.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A comet is racing through space and grows a long glowing tail. Does the tail always trail out BEHIND the comet, in the direction it came from — like smoke behind a rocket? Or does it point some other way? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The intuitive 'tail trails behind like exhaust' picture is what almost every child brings. Only a child who knows the Sun pushes the tail says it points away from the Sun regardless of motion — and can handle the surprising outbound case where the tail leads. The 'why' tier exposes whether they think motion or the Sun sets the tail's direction.

sources.claim: Comets are icy bodies ('made of ice and dust—not rock', unlike rocky asteroids) that grow a tail as they near the Sun because the ice vaporises; the ion tail always points directly away from the Sun. Most asteroids lie in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.

sources.claim: A meteoroid is a space rock in space; if it enters Earth's atmosphere it vaporises into a meteor (a streak of light, sometimes called a 'shooting star', but not actually a star); if it survives and lands it is a meteorite.

pedagogy.summary: A translation is a slide: every point of a shape moves the same distance left/right and the same distance up/down, and nothing else changes (size, shape and orientation stay the same). This topic makes that concrete on a coordinate grid — describing the move from one position to another ('3 units right'), carrying out a two-part translation ('4 right and 2 up') and stating the new coordinates, and PREDICTING an image without plotting. The key procedural insight is that a horizontal move changes only the x-coordinate and a vertical move only the y-coordinate: right adds to x, up adds to y. Built on first-quadrant coordinates, it is the child's first taste of transformations, and its errors mirror coordinate errors — reversal (swapping the right and up amounts) and changing the wrong coordinate.
bestPractices: Separate the two components explicitly: a rightward move changes only x (add to the first number), an upward move only y (add to the second) — do the horizontal and vertical parts one at a time.
Describe moves precisely and consistently: 'units right/left and up/down', matching the along-then-up order of coordinates.
Have children PREDICT the new coordinates by adjusting x and y before plotting, then check by plotting — so the rule is used, not just the picture.
Stress translation invariance: the shape does not turn, flip, or resize — every vertex shifts by the same amounts; check two vertices moved identically.
Count moves against numbered lines from the start point, not squares, to avoid off-by-one slips.
Contrast a horizontal-only move (y unchanged) with a two-part move, so children see when a coordinate should and shouldn't change.
keyRepresentations: Coordinate grid showing a start point and its translated image with the slide arrow
Component decomposition: horizontal move (Δx) then vertical move (Δy)
Rule form: (x, y) → (x + right, y + up)
A shape and its translated copy, same size and orientation, every vertex shifted equally
Number-line counting of the move along each axis from the start position
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — swapping the right and up amounts (applying the horizontal shift to y and the vertical to x).
Changing the wrong coordinate — altering y for a move described as 'right', or changing both coordinates for a single-direction move.
Getting the direction sign wrong — moving left when 'right' is stated, or subtracting instead of adding.
Counting squares rather than numbered lines, giving an off-by-one image position.
Confusing the description of the MOVE with the destination coordinates (stating where it ends when asked how it moved, or vice versa).

learn.summary: Translation is a slide: every point of a shape moves the same amount left/right and up/down, with size, shape and orientation unchanged. On a first-quadrant coordinate grid, learners describe a move from one position to another ('3 units right'), carry out a two-part translation ('4 right and 2 up') and state new coordinates, and predict an image before plotting. The core procedural insight: a horizontal move changes only the x-coordinate (right adds to x), a vertical move only the y-coordinate (up adds to y). The main errors mirror coordinate errors — reversing the right/up amounts, changing the wrong coordinate, direction/sign slips, off-by-one line counting, and confusing the description of the move with the destination coordinates.

activities.title: Predict-then-slide on a coordinate grid
feedback: If the prediction swaps the amounts (e.g. gives (4,7) for '4 right, 2 up' from (2,3)), do the parts one at a time: right changes only the first number, up only the second — tie this back to the along-then-up order of coordinates.
If a 'right' move changed the up-number, show on the grid that a purely horizontal slide leaves the height (y) unchanged; label which number each direction affects before moving.
If the image lands one line off, recount the move as jumps from the start point: the start line is 0, and the first jump lands on the next line. Do not count the starting line as 1.
For opposite directions ('2 left, 1 down' from (5,4)), confirm left subtracts from x and down subtracts from y, landing at (3,3).
activities.rationale: Setting a move, predicting coordinates, then watching the slide turns the coordinate rule into something tested against the motion, exposing reversal and wrong-coordinate errors immediately. Live-updating coordinates, a colour-coded ('coded') grid that makes a rightward move visibly change only x, and the uniform vertex shift make the component structure (Δx separate from Δy) and translation invariance concrete. These coordinate readouts, colour-coding and the predict-then-reveal loop are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down.
Points are located by ordered pairs from the origin along the x- and y-axes in the first quadrant, so a horizontal move changes the x-coordinate and a vertical move the y-coordinate (5.G.1, 5.G.2).

A common documented coordinate misconception is reversing x and y (putting the y-coordinate before the x), and off-by-one errors from counting squares rather than the numbered grid lines — errors that carry into describing moves as changes in coordinates.
learnerActions: Set a translation such as '4 right and 2 up' on a first-quadrant grid containing a shape.
Before anything moves, predict and state (or type) the new coordinates of one named vertex — e.g. from (2,3) you should get (6,5).
Trigger the slide and watch every vertex glide by the same 4-across, 2-up while a coordinate readout ticks from the old to the new values.
Run a horizontal-only move (e.g. '3 right') and confirm the up-number (y) stays fixed while only the across-number changes.
Check two different vertices moved by identical amounts, confirming the shape did not turn, flip or resize.
Count the move in unit jumps from the start point, without counting the starting line itself as 'one'.
activities.intendedInsight: A horizontal move changes only x and a vertical move only y; the whole shape shifts uniformly without changing size or orientation, and predicting from the (x+right, y+up) rule can be checked against the actual slide.

activities.title: Describe the move between two positions
feedback: If the move is answered with '(5,3)' instead of '3 right', ask explicitly 'how did it move?' versus 'where is it now?' and have the learner give both for the same slide.
If direction is reversed (saying 'left' for a rightward shift), compare the two numbered positions and read which way along the axis the point travelled.
activities.rationale: Requiring a worded description catches children who confuse the move with the destination, a documented pattern, and reversing the move builds the idea that translations are undoable by the opposite shift. A scorable version (multiple-choice naming the move between two points, with reversed-component and 'up' distractors) can be used during teaching or for assessment, though a selection response does not elicit independent construction of the description.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down.
learnerActions: Look at two marked positions on the grid, e.g. a start at (2,3) and an image at (5,3).
State the move in words — '3 units right' — using units and direction, not the destination coordinates.
For the same slide, separately answer 'where is it now?' with the end coordinates, so the two questions are practised side by side.
Describe the reverse move that returns the image to the start (e.g. (5,3) back to (2,3) is '3 units left'), surfacing reversibility.
activities.intendedInsight: Describing a move ('how did it move?' — units and direction) is a different answer from naming the destination ('where is it now?' — coordinates); learners must hold both apart.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal before-and-after picture (scaffold)
feedback: Point out that only the across-number changed for a horizontal slide, and that both corners moved by the same amount.
Prompt the learner to say the move in words before lifting the flap, then compare.
activities.rationale: A fixed picture can present and label a completed slide, but it cannot let the learner set, carry out or predict a move, so the procedure is not exercised — use it as an introduction or revision aid, not the main practice.
learnerActions: Study a fixed picture showing a shape in its start position and its translated image with a slide arrow.
Tap the start and the image to reveal how the x- and y-coordinates changed between them.
Use a 'where does it land after 3 right?' flap to check a predicted position against the revealed answer.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked before-and-after slide shows how each coordinate changed and reinforces that the shape keeps its size and orientation.

constraints: Built on first-quadrant coordinate knowledge; learners should already read ordered pairs along-then-up before describing moves as coordinate changes.

Recognition/selection responses (multiple-choice, tap-to-reveal) can be used while teaching and for scoring, but they do not require the learner to independently construct a predicted coordinate or a worded description — keep genuine prediction and production in the sequence.

The tap-to-reveal picture is a scaffold: because the slide is fixed, the learner cannot set, carry out or predict their own move; progress to an interactive or hand-plotted grid so the rule is used, not just read.

Count moves as unit jumps from the start point: do not count the starting line as 'one'; the first jump lands on the next line. (When points sit on grid intersections, counting square widths crossed gives the same count.) This avoids off-by-one images.
Keep directions and signs explicit: right/up add, left/down subtract; state them when working opposite directions.
Translations here are planar left/right/up/down slides; a 3D setting adds complexity irrelevant to this objective rather than being inherently unteachable in other media.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic/geometry: '4 right, 2 up' from (2,3) gives (6,5); (3,1) after '2 right, 3 up' gives (5,4); '2 left, 1 down' from (5,4) gives (3,3); (2,3)→(5,3) is '3 right' and reverses as '3 left'. The worked examples are internally consistent across summary, actions and feedback.

The original listed a reversal distractor producing '(4,7) or (6,5)' for '4 right, 2 up' from (2,3) — but (6,5) is the correct answer, so it cannot also be the swapped-components distractor; the genuinely swapped result is (4,7). All learner-facing text uses (4,7) as the reversal example and (6,5) only as the correct target.

Legacy source claims were marked verified in the row but have not been re-checked here; comparative-efficacy or necessity framing from the original ('can't show the slide', 'cannot let the child predict') has been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

probeDeeper: 'When the counter moved 3 to the right, why did only the first number change?' — listen for horizontal = x, height unchanged.
Counterexample: 'If I slide the whole shape 4 right and 2 up, does it get bigger or turn at all? How do you know?' — tests translation invariance.
'Predict the landing spot after 2 left and 1 down from (5,4)' — checks the rule works for the opposite directions (subtracting).
'Describe the move that takes (5,3) back to (2,3)' — surfaces reversibility and separates move-description from position.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) '3 units to the right' (only x changes, 2→5). (2) the corner moves from (2,3) to (6,5) — x + 4, y + 2 — and the whole shape slides by the same amount, same size and orientation. (3) (5,4) — predicts by adding 2 to x and 3 to y without needing to plot.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal — swaps the horizontal and vertical amounts, applying '4 right' to the y-coordinate and '2 up' to the x.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the parts one at a time — right changes only x (first number), up only y (second) — tying the order back to along-then-up coordinates.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: After '4 right, 2 up' gives (4,7) or (6,5) with the components swapped; the image is in the wrong place along both axes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the wrong coordinate — for a move described as 'right' alters the up-number, or changes both coordinates for a single-direction move.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the grid that a purely horizontal slide leaves the height (y) unchanged; label which number each direction affects before moving.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Moving (2,3) to the right yields a change in the second number, or both numbers change when only a horizontal move was asked.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts squares not numbered lines — the image lands one line off, or the start of the count is misplaced.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the move on the numbered lines from the start position; no reteaching of translation needed — the count slipped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: New coordinates are off by one; the child counts cells crossed rather than reading line labels from the start point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the move with the destination — when asked to DESCRIBE the move, states the end coordinates instead (or vice versa).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the two questions explicitly — 'how did it move?' (units and direction) versus 'where is it now?' (coordinates); practise stating both for the same slide.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers (1) with '(5,3)' rather than '3 right'; or when asked for the new position gives the shift amounts.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot describe or carry out a translation reliably: changes the wrong coordinate, reverses components, or the shape does not slide uniformly; predictions are guesses.
responseLevels.full: Describes moves precisely, carries out horizontal-and-vertical translations by adjusting x and y correctly, states the new coordinates, predicts an image without plotting, and knows the shape's size and orientation are unchanged — the (x+right, y+up) structure is applied, not just enacted.
responseLevels.partial: Describes and carries out a single-direction move (e.g. 3 right) correctly, but a two-part translation trips reversal or a wrong-coordinate change, or the child can only find the image by plotting rather than predicting from the rule — knows the pieces but doesn't combine them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a first-quadrant grid, mark a point at (2,3). Say: (1) 'Move a counter from (2,3) to (5,3) — describe that move in words.' (2) 'Now translate this shape 4 units right and 2 units up; plot it and write the new coordinates of this corner.' (3) 'A point is at (3,1). Without plotting, tell me where it lands after moving 2 right and 3 up.' Watch how they handle each — do not prompt the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The single-direction move (1) exposes children who change both coordinates or the wrong one; the two-part move (2) exposes reversal of the right/up amounts and non-uniform sliding; the predict item (3) separates children who can only move by counting on the grid from those who apply the (x+right, y+up) rule. Requiring a worded description in (1) also catches confusing the move with the destination.

sources.claim: Year 4 pupils should describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down.
sources.source: UK Department for Education, Mathematics programmes of study: Key Stages 1 and 2 (Year 4 geometry — position and direction)

sources.claim: Points are located by ordered pairs from the origin along the x- and y-axes in the first quadrant, so a horizontal move changes the x-coordinate and a vertical move the y-coordinate (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 5 Geometry

sources.claim: A common documented coordinate misconception is reversing x and y (putting the y-coordinate before the x), and off-by-one errors from counting squares rather than the numbered grid lines — errors that carry into describing moves as changes in coordinates.
sources.source: NCETM, Misconceptions with the Key Objectives (Position, Direction, Movement and Angle)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — The Mesozoic Era (ages 7–9): place the three periods of the Mesozoic — Triassic, then Jurassic, then Cretaceous — in order, and understand that different dinosaurs lived in different periods, NOT all at the same time; vast spans of millions of years separate them.
• Standards — UK (DfE): supports 'working scientifically' and chronological/sequencing skills; forward-anchors to Y6 evolution (change over time) and KS3 Earth history.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports the fossil-record/geologic-time strand (grade-3 3-LS4-1 into MS-ESS1-4 geologic time) — organisms succeed one another through time.
• Operational details — Two goals: (1) ORDER the three periods correctly (Triassic → Jurassic → Cretaceous) and assign at least one famous dinosaur to each (e.g. early dinosaurs/Plateosaurus — Triassic; Stegosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Allosaurus — Jurassic; T. rex, Triceratops, Velociraptor — Cretaceous); (2) demolish the 'all dinosaurs coexisted' misconception. The killer hook: MORE time separates Stegosaurus (Late Jurassic, ~150 Mya) from T. rex (Late Cretaceous, ~66–69 Mya) — about 80 million years — than separates T. rex from us today (~66 million years). So Stegosaurus and T. rex never met; a Stegosaurus was more ancient to a T. rex than a T. rex is to a child. Keep numbers relative but use this comparison as the anchor.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7): puts Triassic–Jurassic–Cretaceous in order. Tier B (~8): assigns a famous dinosaur to the right period and says different dinosaurs lived at different times. Tier C (~9): explains that huge time gaps separated the periods — e.g. Stegosaurus and T. rex never coexisted (more time between them than between T. rex and us).
bestPractices: Lead with the 'not all at once' misconception and break it with the Stegosaurus–T. rex–human comparison — the single most memorable deep-time hook for this age.
Have children physically order the three periods and drop dinosaurs onto the correct one, so sequence is enacted.
Use relative deep-time language and comparisons (more time than X to now) rather than asking them to grasp raw millions.
Pair each period with one or two iconic dinosaurs so the abstract periods gain concrete inhabitants.
Reinforce that the 'Age of Dinosaurs' lasted ~150+ million years — an enormous span, not a single scene.
keyRepresentations: A left-to-right timeline: Triassic → Jurassic → Cretaceous → (extinction) → Age of Mammals → now.
Period 'homes' onto which iconic dinosaurs are dropped (Stegosaurus→Jurassic, T. rex→Cretaceous).
A gap-comparison bar: Stegosaurus→T. rex (~80 My) shown longer than T. rex→today (~66 My).
A 'they never met' crossed-out fight scene between Stegosaurus and T. rex.
commonMisconceptions: 'All dinosaurs lived at the same time' — they are spread across ~150+ million years and mostly never overlapped.
'Stegosaurus and T. rex lived together / could have fought' — ~80 million years separated them; they never met.
'Dinosaurs and the very first mammals/humans are close in time' — T. rex is far closer to us than to Stegosaurus.
'The periods are short' — each period spans tens of millions of years.
'Older period = smaller/more primitive dinosaurs only' — giants and specialists existed across all three periods.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach the three periods of the Mesozoic Era in order (Triassic → Jurassic → Cretaceous) and the key idea that different dinosaurs lived in different periods, separated by vast spans of time, rather than all coexisting. The central anchor is that more time separates Stegosaurus (Late Jurassic, ~150 Mya) from T. rex (Late Cretaceous, ~66–69 Mya) — about 80 million years — than separates T. rex from us today (~66 million years), so the two never met.

activities.title: Build the timeline and sort the dinosaurs
feedback: If a dinosaur is placed in the wrong period, show its correct period and name a well-known companion that shared it, so the period gains concrete inhabitants.

When the Stegosaurus–T. rex gap is marked, confirm it is about 80 million years: because they lived in different periods separated by that span, the two never coexisted — and note that this gap is even larger than the ~66 million years from T. rex to today.
If a learner assumes all dinosaurs could meet, lay the three periods out and show Stegosaurus and T. rex tens of millions of years apart: different dinosaurs, different eras.
If a learner accepts different periods but still imagines them short enough to overlap, make the vastness concrete with the gap comparison before accepting the answer.
activities.rationale: Physically ordering the periods and placing dinosaurs makes the sequence enacted rather than told, and a visible gap comparison targets the specific 'they all lived together' and 'close enough to meet' misconceptions. An interactive timeline where a mistaken coexistence pairing visibly springs apart may make the deep-time point memorable, though this is a design proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: The Mesozoic Era comprises the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods in that order; different dinosaurs lived in different periods across a span exceeding 150 million years.

Stegosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic (~150 million years ago) and Tyrannosaurus rex at the end of the Late Cretaceous (~66–69 million years ago), roughly 80 million years apart — a greater gap than the ~66 million years between T. rex and the present day; the two never coexisted.
learnerActions: Set up three slots left to right in order: Triassic, then Jurassic, then Cretaceous.

Sort a set of famous dinosaurs into the correct period: e.g. early dinosaurs/Plateosaurus into the Triassic; Stegosaurus, Brachiosaurus and Allosaurus into the Jurassic; T. rex, Triceratops and Velociraptor into the Cretaceous.

After placing Stegosaurus (Jurassic) and T. rex (Cretaceous), mark the distance between them on the timeline, then compare it to the distance from T. rex to a 'you, today' marker placed at the end of the line.
State in your own words whether Stegosaurus and T. rex could ever have met, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: The Age of Dinosaurs was not one crowded scene; different casts of dinosaurs lived and vanished across tens of millions of years, and the gap between two famous dinosaurs can exceed the gap between the later one and us.

activities.title: 'Who would win?' — the never-met challenge
feedback: If the learner tries to stage the fight, reveal the ~80-million-year gap and mark that it is longer than the ~66 million years from T. rex to today.
Confirm the conclusion: Stegosaurus and T. rex never met; a Stegosaurus was more ancient to a T. rex than a T. rex is to a child today.
If the learner says 'yes, they fought,' revisit which period each lived in before re-asking.
activities.rationale: Using the engaging coexistence question as the entry point lets the misconception surface and then be confronted with evidence, which may be more durable than simply stating the fact. Presented as a proposal informed by the deep-time comparison, not as proof that this format outperforms others.
sourceClaims: Stegosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic (~150 million years ago) and Tyrannosaurus rex at the end of the Late Cretaceous (~66–69 million years ago), roughly 80 million years apart — a greater gap than the ~66 million years between T. rex and the present day; the two never coexisted.
learnerActions: Pose the classic playground question: who would win in a fight — Stegosaurus or T. rex?
Before answering, locate each on the timeline and read off how far apart they lived.
Decide whether a fight was even possible, and explain the reasoning using the time gap.
Compare: was T. rex closer in time to Stegosaurus, or to you? Justify with the two gaps (~80 My vs ~66 My), kept as a comparison rather than a calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: Two famous dinosaurs people imagine fighting were separated by more time than separates the later one from the present, so staging their fight is impossible.

activities.title: Explain and probe deep time
feedback: A full response orders the periods, assigns species, and reasons that dinosaurs living tens of millions of years apart, like Stegosaurus and T. rex, never met, citing the Stegosaurus/T. rex gap.
A partial response orders the periods and assigns a dinosaur but still imagines overlap; respond by re-marking the gap magnitude.

A correct model answer: 'No. Stegosaurus lived in the Jurassic and T. rex in the Cretaceous — about 80 million years apart — so they never met; different dinosaurs lived in different periods, each spanning enormous stretches of time.'
activities.rationale: Spoken or written explanation elicits reasoning that recognition alone does not, helping distinguish a learner who grasps deep time from one who merely recalls period names. This construction task complements the manipulative timeline work; its efficacy over other formats is not established by the sources.
sourceClaims: The Mesozoic Era comprises the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods in that order; different dinosaurs lived in different periods across a span exceeding 150 million years.

Stegosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic (~150 million years ago) and Tyrannosaurus rex at the end of the Late Cretaceous (~66–69 million years ago), roughly 80 million years apart — a greater gap than the ~66 million years between T. rex and the present day; the two never coexisted.
learnerActions: Answer true/false: there is more time between Stegosaurus and T. rex than between T. rex and you — and explain how you know.
Answer: which lived longer ago, Stegosaurus or T. rex, and how can you tell from the timeline?
Answer: could a Triassic dinosaur ever have met a Cretaceous one? Explain why or why not.
Respond to the prompt: 'Stegosaurus and T. rex must have fought because they were both dinosaurs living at the same time.' Say whether this is right and explain.
Explain in a sentence or two why the 'Age of Dinosaurs' (over ~150 million years) was an enormous span, not a single scene.
activities.intendedInsight: Chronological order of the periods plus the magnitude of the gaps together explain why dinosaurs separated by tens of millions of years, such as Stegosaurus and T. rex or a Triassic and a Cretaceous dinosaur, never coexisted.

constraints: Keep large numbers relative and anchored in comparisons (e.g. 'more time than between T. rex and now') rather than asking 7–9 year olds to grasp raw millions.
Pair each period with one or two iconic dinosaurs so abstract periods gain concrete inhabitants; reinforce that the 'Age of Dinosaurs' lasted over ~150 million years.

A static timeline poster or tappable image can teach the order and the gap comparison clearly, but it does not let the child attempt the coexistence error and feel it break; use it as a presentation scaffold when an interactive build is unavailable.

Sequence, matching and single-answer checks (e.g. 'did Stegosaurus and T. rex coexist?') confirm the target but do not build the deep-time intuition on their own; use them to assess after the concept is developed, not to introduce it.
Do not imply older periods held only smaller or more primitive dinosaurs; giants and specialists existed across all three periods.
Ages 7–9 use relative not absolute dates; present the ~80 My and ~66 My figures as comparative anchors, not values children must compute with.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The second source (AMNH / Smithsonian) is marked verified in the row and supports the ~80 My vs ~66 My gap and non-coexistence; the first (NHM/Smithsonian Mesozoic pages) is marked unverified. Confidence labels were not upgraded.

The original claimed a 3D world 'adds no help' and that the interactive timeline 'detonates the misconception more powerfully than any telling' — these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped proposals noting affordances and limits.

Activity 3's rationale asserts a recognition-vs-production pedagogy benefit; this is an untested design rationale, and the copied source claims support only the dinosaur/time facts being reasoned about, not that benefit.

probeDeeper: Which lived longer ago — Stegosaurus or T. rex — and how do you know?
Is this true or false: there is more time between Stegosaurus and T. rex than between T. rex and you?
Could a Triassic dinosaur ever have met a Cretaceous one? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: No. Stegosaurus lived in the Jurassic period and T. rex in the Cretaceous period — separated by around 80 million years. They never met. Different dinosaurs lived in different periods of the Mesozoic, and those periods span enormous stretches of time.

errorPatterns.pattern: All dinosaurs lived at the same time: 'they were all around together, so they'd have met.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay the three periods on a timeline and place Stegosaurus and T. rex tens of millions of years apart; different dinosaurs, different eras.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — all dinosaurs lived together, so they would have met.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'yes' and treats every dinosaur as a contemporary of every other.

errorPatterns.pattern: Timescale compression: 'they lived in slightly different times, but close enough to still meet.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the vastness concrete — there is more time between Stegosaurus and T. rex than between T. rex and today.
errorPatterns.distractor: They lived in slightly different times, but close enough to still meet.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts different periods but imagines them as short and overlapping.

errorPatterns.pattern: Period names are arbitrary labels whose order doesn't matter.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix the chronological order and attach a familiar dinosaur to each period as an anchor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot place Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous in order or treats the sequence as unimportant.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks all dinosaurs lived together and cannot order the three periods.
responseLevels.full: Orders the periods, assigns species, AND reasons that each period spans tens of millions of years so different-period dinosaurs never coexisted — using the Stegosaurus/T. rex gap as evidence.
responseLevels.partial: Orders Triassic–Jurassic–Cretaceous and assigns a dinosaur to a period, but still imagines the periods overlapping enough for different-period dinosaurs to meet.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Someone says: 'Stegosaurus and Tyrannosaurus rex must have fought each other, because they were both dinosaurs living at the same time.' Are they right? Explain your answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who pictures all dinosaurs living together says 'yes, they'd have met.' A child who grasps the timeline explains they were separated by more time than separates T. rex from us today.

sources.claim: The Mesozoic Era comprises the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods in that order; different dinosaurs lived in different periods across a span exceeding 150 million years.
sources.source: Natural History Museum (UK) / Smithsonian — Mesozoic era education pages

sources.claim: Stegosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic (~150 million years ago) and Tyrannosaurus rex at the end of the Late Cretaceous (~66–69 million years ago), roughly 80 million years apart — a greater gap than the ~66 million years between T. rex and the present day; the two never coexisted.

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting two two-digit numbers is introduced through concrete and pictorial regrouping before any formal column method. The central idea is composing a ten when the ones exceed nine (34+27) and decomposing a ten when there are too few ones to subtract (63−28). Base-ten blocks make the exchange physical; number lines and partitioning jottings connect it to recording. This is where 'carrying' and 'borrowing' are given meaning as exchange rather than taught as digit tricks.
bestPractices: Establish the exchange principle with base-ten blocks: ten ones can be fairly swapped for one ten, and one ten for ten ones (NRICH: exchange/unitising)
Partition both numbers into tens and ones, combine like with like, then compose/decompose a ten as needed (NCETM Spine 1.15/1.16)
Use a number line for subtraction as finding a difference (count up 28→63) as an alternative to take-away
Move concrete → pictorial → jotting for the SAME calculation so the recording mirrors the action
Ask the child to explain their strategy and why 34+27 is not 511 — the recombination is where meaning is tested
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks with a place-value mat (compose/decompose a ten)
Number line (jumps for adding; count-up for difference)
Part-whole / partitioning jottings (30+20 and 4+7)
Bar model (comparison and missing-part subtraction)
Hundred square
commonMisconceptions: Failing to compose the ten: adding tens (50) and ones (11) and writing them side by side (511) or keeping 51
Smaller-from-larger subtraction: 63−28 done as 8−3 in the ones, answer 45
Counting every unit and losing the ten-structure (not treating a ten-rod as one ten)
Misaligning tens and ones when recording without a place-value mat

learn.summary: Ages 6–7 add and subtract two two-digit numbers (e.g. 34+27, 63−28) by giving meaning to 'carrying' and 'borrowing' as fair exchange: ten ones can be swapped for one ten and vice versa. Learners partition into tens and ones, combine like with like, then compose a ten when the ones exceed nine, or decompose a ten when there are too few ones to subtract. Concrete base-ten work and pictorial jottings for the SAME calculation let the recording mirror the physical action, so regrouping is felt as a swap rather than rehearsed as a digit trick.

activities.title: Exchange on a place-value mat: compose and decompose a ten
feedback: If the child writes 511 or keeps 51: have them physically swap ten of the eleven ones for one ten-rod on the mat, then re-read the result; name it — 'ten ones is the same as one ten'.
If the child does the ones of 63−28 as 8−3 and answers 45: show on the mat that 3 ones cannot give 8, so a ten must be broken open first (63 = 50+13); check by adding 45+28, which gives 73, not 63.

If the child breaks rods apart to recount everything in ones: do not stop them handling the blocks or drill exchange in isolation — treating a rod as one 'ten' is a maturing shift; each time they exchange, read both ways aloud together, 'that's ten ones AND one ten', so unitising develops.

Probe: 'You made eleven ones — can you swap some for a ten? Show me.' 'For 63−28 you needed more ones — where did the extra ones come from?' 'Would 34+25 still need an exchange? Why not?' (For 34+25 the ones are 4+5=9, below ten, so no exchange is needed.)
activities.rationale: The concept being taught is exchange, so the learner should perform the regroup, not just watch it. Partitioning into tens and ones and composing/decomposing a ten is the standard mastery progression, and pairing the concrete action with a matching jotting makes the recording mirror the exchange. Reading a ten-rod as both 'ten ones' and 'one ten' builds unitising.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add and subtract two two-digit numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mentally, and recording in columns supports place value and prepares for formal written methods.
Two two-digit numbers are added by partitioning one or both into tens and ones; subtraction partitions the subtrahend into tens and ones, decomposing a ten where the ones are insufficient.

Exchange — fairly swapping ten ones for one ten (and vice versa) — and unitising a ten as a single entity are the ideas underpinning regrouping; such resources can be used diagnostically to assess whether place value is genuinely understood.
learnerActions: Set out 34 + 27 on a place-value mat using base-ten blocks (or draggable on-screen tens and ones).

Pile the ones together to find there are eleven; because that is ten or more, perform a 'make a ten' action that swaps ten loose ones for one ten-rod moved into the tens column, leaving one loose one, then read the answer as 61 (not 511, not 51).
Set out 63 − 28; find there are not enough ones to give eight, so take a ten-rod and break it into ten loose ones, so 63 is now 50 and 13.
Hand over eight ones (13−8=5) and subtract the tens (50−20=30) to reach 35.
Record each physical step as a matching jotting: 30+20=50, 4+7=11, exchange → 61; and 63 = 50+13, 13−8=5, 50−20=30 → 35.
Say aloud why 34+27 cannot be 511 ('ten ones is the same as one ten, so the extra ten joins the tens').
activities.intendedInsight: Composing a ten (addition) and decomposing a ten (subtraction) are the same exchange run in opposite directions; 'carrying' and 'borrowing' are fair swaps between ones and tens, not separate digit tricks.

activities.title: Subtraction as finding a difference on a number line
feedback: If jumps don't land cleanly, suggest jumping first to the next multiple of ten (28 → 30) before the big jump.

If the count-up answer differs from the take-away answer, check both: revisit the ones step on the mat for a missed exchange, and re-add the jumps on the number line, since either method may hold the slip.
Ask: 'Which method did you find easier for 63 − 28, counting up or taking away? Why?'
activities.rationale: A number line presents subtraction as finding a difference (count up 28→63) as an alternative to take-away, giving a complementary model and a self-check; a bar model and hundred square are further optional representations. This is offered as an alternative representation, not a replacement for the exchange work. A number line is a pictorial method, but no cited source directly validates the count-up-as-difference principle, so no source claim is attached.
learnerActions: Place 28 and 63 on a number line.
Count up from 28 to 63 in convenient jumps (e.g. 28 → 30 is 2, 30 → 60 is 30, 60 → 63 is 3).
Total the jumps (2 + 30 + 3 = 35) and state 63 − 28 = 35.
Compare this count-up answer with the take-away/exchange answer from the mat and confirm they agree.
Optionally model the same subtraction with a bar model (whole 63, known part 28, missing part found as the difference) or on a hundred square, as further representations of the same difference.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction can be read as the difference between two numbers found by counting up, which offers a second route to the same answer and a self-check against the smaller-from-larger error.

activities.title: Annotated worked example and targeted consolidation
feedback: For a chosen '511'/'51': return to the eleven-ones-make-a-ten step and have the learner state where the extra ten goes.
For a chosen '45': have the learner break a ten in 63 to make 50+13 and redo the ones step, then check by adding.
Encourage the learner to narrate the exchange aloud each time, since the explanation is where understanding is tested.
activities.rationale: A staged annotated example can show the partition and exchange as a reference, and a set of two-digit ± two-digit items consolidates and catches the 511 and smaller-from-larger errors — but reference and recognition rehearse rather than build the exchange insight, so they follow the hands-on exchange rather than replace it. Recognising a correct answer does not by itself elicit independent production of the exchange. Asking the child to explain why 34+27 is not 511 is where the recombination meaning is tested.
sourceClaims: The 'smaller-from-larger' subtraction error is a classic systematic buggy algorithm.
Two two-digit numbers are added by partitioning one or both into tens and ones; subtraction partitions the subtrahend into tens and ones, decomposing a ten where the ones are insufficient.
learnerActions: Study a worked example of 34+27 and 63−28 where the partition and exchange step are revealed one stage at a time (e.g. reveal 4+7 becoming 'one ten and one'; reveal the tens as 30+20+10).
Explain in your own words what happened at the exchange step before moving on.
Then work a short set of two-digit ± two-digit items, including 34+27 and the decomposition of 63 into 50+13, choosing or writing the answer and giving the exchange reasoning.
When a '511', '51' or '45' answer appears, say why it is wrong rather than only marking the correct one.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly staged worked example makes the partition and exchange visible for reference, and a focused problem set surfaces whether the compose-a-ten and smaller-from-larger errors have really been overcome.

constraints: Build the skill from repeated hands-on exchange with base-ten blocks and a place-value mat before any formal column method; introduce 'carrying'/'borrowing' only as names for the exchange already performed.
Move concrete → pictorial → jotting for the SAME calculation so the recording mirrors the action; do not jump straight to abstract digit manipulation.
A static annotated worked example or tap-to-reveal reference can show the steps but does not let the child perform the regroup; use it as reference alongside, not instead of, hands-on exchange.

A set of items that includes the common wrong answers 511/51 and 45 can consolidate and expose errors, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the exchange; pair with the learner performing and recording the swap.
When describing whether an exchange is needed (e.g. 34+25 vs 34+27), check the ones sum directly — exchange is needed only when the ones reach ten or more (4+5=9 needs none; 4+7=11 does).
Treat a ten-rod being recounted as ten separate ones as a developmental stage in unitising, not an error to drill away; keep reading it both ways aloud.

The place-value mat is essentially planar (tens and ones, place value), so these activities do not propose a third dimension or spoken-only delivery as the main medium for the exchange insight; this is a design preference, not evidence that 3D or dialogue cannot teach it, and talk is still used so the child can explain their strategy.

A bar model (comparison and missing-part subtraction) and a hundred square remain available as further optional representations and should not be presented as replacements for the base-ten exchange work.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (NCETM Spine 1.15/1.16 partitioning claim; Brown & Burton 1978 / VanLehn 'Mind Bugs' 1990 on the smaller-from-larger buggy algorithm); treat their support as provisional.

Arithmetic self-check: 34+27 → 30+20=50, 4+7=11, 50+11=61 (not 511, not 51). 63−28 → 63=50+13, 13−8=5, 50−20=30, so 35; number-line count-up 28→30→60→63 gives 2+30+3=35. The smaller-from-larger error 8−3=5 yields the incorrect 45, and 45+28=73≠63. These confirm the answers used; 511/51/45 appear ONLY as named incorrect responses to diagnose, never as valid answers.

The legacy source framed digit-based side-by-side work as something hands-on exchange 'cannot fake' and spoken discussion as unable to substitute for exchange; these comparative-necessity claims are softened here to scoped affordances/limits rather than asserted as established efficacy.

No source directly supports subtraction read as a difference found by counting up on a number line; it is a pictorial method and a self-check, so the number-line activity carries no source claim rather than citing the broad DfE pictorial/mental claim as if it validated the count-up principle.

The source misconception 'misaligning tens and ones when recording without a place-value mat' is addressed implicitly by consistent use of the place-value mat and matched jottings across the first activity.

probeDeeper: You made eleven ones — can you swap some of those for a ten? Show me what you do.
For 63 − 28 you needed more ones than you had — where did the extra ones come from?
Explain to me why 34 + 27 isn't five hundred and eleven.
What if it were 34 + 25 instead of 34 + 27 — would you still need to exchange? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: 61 and 35. For 34+27: 30+20=50 and 4+7=11, exchange ten ones for a ten → 61. For 63−28: too few ones, exchange a ten for ten ones (63 as 50+13), 13−8=5 and 50−20=30 → 35.

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't compose the ten — 'thirty and twenty is fifty, four and seven is eleven, so five hundred and eleven' (or keeps 51)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child physically swap ten of the eleven ones for one ten-rod on the mat, then read the result. Name it: ten ones is the same as one ten.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child records 50 and 11 but never exchanges the eleven ones for a ten; writes 511 or 51

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger in subtraction — '63 take 28: eight take three is five', answering 45
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the mat, show 63 cannot give 8 ones from only 3, so a ten must be broken open first (63 = 50+13). Check by adding 45+28.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ones column of 63−28 is done as 8−3 with no decomposition; answer 45

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts every cube in ones and loses the ten-structure — treats a ten-rod as ten separate things to recount rather than one ten
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT stop them handling the blocks or drill exchange in isolation — treating a rod as one 'ten' is a maturing shift. Keep pairing the two readings aloud ('that's ten ones AND one ten') each time they exchange, so unitising develops.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child breaks rods apart to count all in ones, or recounts the whole set, rather than operating with rods as tens

responseLevels.gap: Gives 511/51 for the addition or 45 for the subtraction; tens and ones are handled separately with no exchange.
responseLevels.full: Composes and decomposes a ten correctly for both calculations, records the exchange in a jotting, and explains why (e.g. 'ten ones is the same as one ten').
responseLevels.partial: Exchanges correctly with the blocks in front of them but cannot yet carry it into a recording or do it mentally, or manages the addition compose but not the subtraction decompose.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child base-ten blocks and paper and set two calculations to work with the blocks and record: 34 + 27, then 63 − 28. Watch what they do at the ones in each case.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 34+27 requires composing a ten from eleven ones; a child who answers 511 or 51 has added the parts but not exchanged. 63−28 requires decomposing a ten; the smaller-from-larger child answers 45. Doing both correctly shows exchange is understood in both directions, which side-by-side digit work cannot fake.
