pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Earth Is Made of Rock

- **Standards — UK (DfE, England):** KS1 Y1 science 'Everyday materials' names **rock** as one of the everyday materials children identify and describe ('identify and name a variety of everyday materials, including wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, and rock') — a genuine hook for 'the ground is made of rock'. The broader Earth-structure content sits in KS2 Geography/science later.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No K–2 PE states 'Earth is made of rock' directly; it is foundational background for grade-2 ESS (Earth materials) and grade-4 ESS2 (the geosphere/surface processes). Treat as a conceptual foundation rather than an assessed PE at this age.

- **Operational details:** The big idea is that under the soil, grass and pavement, the Earth is solid rock — the whole planet is essentially a giant ball of rock. Two moves work at 5–7: (1) DIG DOWN — start at familiar ground (a garden, a beach) and go down through the thin layer of soil to bedrock, so children see soil is only a thin skin over rock; (2) ZOOM OUT — the stones and pebbles they hold are little pieces of that same Earth-rock. Handle real rocks and stones. Keep it to 'rock and other solid materials'; the hot interior, layers and core are the 7–9 'Earth's Layers' topic. This topic quietly underpins volcanoes (melted rock), rock types and earthquakes (rocks moving/breaking).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can state the ground is made of rock and that stones are pieces of the Earth; they are NOT yet expected to know layers or the hot interior. Confront 'the Earth is made of soil/dirt' (soil is a thin covering over rock) and 'the Earth is hollow'.
bestPractices: Handle real rocks, stones and pebbles — tie the abstract 'Earth is rock' to objects children can hold
Use a DIG-DOWN move (soil → bedrock) so children see soil is a thin skin over solid rock, correcting 'Earth is made of dirt'
Use a ZOOM-OUT move so a held pebble is understood as a small piece of the whole rocky Earth
Start from familiar local ground (playground, beach, garden) before generalising to the planet
Keep to 'rock and other solid materials'; defer layers, heat and the core to the 7–9 'Earth's Layers' topic
Bridge to Y1 materials vocabulary ('rock' as an everyday material) so the idea sits in prior science
keyRepresentations: Dig-down cross-section: grass → thin soil → solid bedrock → deep rock
A held pebble shown as a tiny piece of a big rocky Earth (zoom-out)
Real rock/stone samples to handle and compare
A simple 'Earth is a ball of rock' globe cutaway (surface-level, no internal layers yet)
commonMisconceptions: 'The Earth is made of soil/dirt' — soil is only a thin covering; solid rock lies beneath almost everywhere
'The Earth is hollow inside' — it is solid rock and other materials all the way down (interior detail comes later)
'Rocks and the ground are different things' — stones are broken-off pieces of the same Earth-rock
'Only mountains/cliffs are rock' — rock is under flat ground and under the sea too, just often hidden by soil or water
'The ground is just made of the stuff on top (grass, sand)' — those are thin surface layers over rock

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: build the idea that if you dig deep enough beneath the soil, grass and pavement (sometimes also through sand, clay or gravel), you reach rock, that the Earth is made mostly of rock and other materials, and that stones and pebbles are small pieces of the Earth's rock. Two complementary moves anchor the concept: DIG DOWN (from familiar ground through soil to bedrock) and ZOOM OUT (a held pebble is a tiny chip of the rocky planet). Keep to 'rock and other solid materials'; defer layers, heat and the core to a later 'Earth's Layers' topic for 7–9s. Confront the common beliefs that the Earth is dirt/soil all the way down, that it is hollow, and that stones are separate from the ground.

activities.title: Dig down to the rock
feedback: If a child says soil or dirt continues all the way down: soil is only a thin skin at the top — dig deeper and you reach solid rock (bedrock). Show a soil-over-rock cross-section, or a photo of a deep excavation where diggers have gone down through the soil to the hard rock below (ordinary shallow digging may stay in soil, so use a deep-enough example).
If a child says the ground beneath is rock: good — point to how thin the soil band is compared with the thick rock below, so the idea of 'thin skin over rock' is clear.
Prompt to reinforce: 'If you dug down deep, far below the soil, what hard stuff would you reach?'
activities.rationale: A concrete dig-down from familiar ground to bedrock makes the abstract 'Earth is rock' visible and directly targets the 'Earth is made of dirt' belief by showing soil as a thin surface layer. A lift-the-flap or tap-to-reveal on the soil layer makes the 'thin skin over rock' idea concrete; these are optional ways to stage the reveal, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Beneath a thin layer of soil, solid bedrock underlies the land almost everywhere; soil is a thin surface covering
learnerActions: Start from a picture or cross-section of a familiar patch of ground — a garden, playground or beach.
Work down through the layers in order: grass, then a thin band of soil, then solid bedrock, then deeper rock.
Lift or reveal the soil layer to find the message underneath: 'just a thin skin — rock is underneath'.
Say aloud what is under the soil almost everywhere (rock), and how thin the soil is compared with the rock below.
Compare a real rock or stone in hand with the rock shown deep in the cross-section.
activities.intendedInsight: Soil is a thin covering compared with the rock beneath; dig deep enough (sometimes through sand, clay or gravel as well) and you reach solid rock almost everywhere, so the Earth is not dirt all the way down.

activities.title: Hands-on dig: how thin is the soil?
feedback: If the child expects to keep finding soil the deeper they dig: pause at the hard layer and name it — that is rock (bedrock). In the real ground this rock continues far deeper than the soil; in a tray or on-screen model the hard layer stands for that deep rock.
Encourage comparing the thin soil depth with the rock beneath so the 'thin skin' idea is felt, not just told.
activities.rationale: An active dig makes the discovery the child's own and is engaging at 5–7. A depth marker contrasting thin soil with deep rock makes the relationship concrete. This is an alternative route to the same recognition goal as the dig-down reveal; either can secure the idea. Because a tray cannot hold the real deep rock, treat it as a model of the ground.
sourceClaims: Beneath a thin layer of soil, solid bedrock underlies the land almost everywhere; soil is a thin surface covering
learnerActions: Use a trowel or digging tool — a soil tray set up as a model of the ground, or an on-screen dig — to remove soil until you reach something hard.
Mark or measure how deep the soil goes before you reach the hard layer.
Describe out loud: the soil layer is thin, and in the real ground the rock keeps going far below it (in the tray or screen, the hard layer stands for that deep rock).
Handle real rock, stone and pebble samples and compare them with each other.
activities.intendedInsight: Removing the soil yourself in a model shows the idea that soil is a thin layer sitting on top of much more rock below — the tray or screen is a model of the real ground, so it represents the real depths rather than measuring them.

activities.title: Zoom out: a pebble is a piece of the Earth
feedback: If a child treats a stone as just an object lying on the ground, separate from the Earth: a stone is a small broken-off piece of the Earth's rock.
Reinforce with the question: 'Is a stone you find on the ground a piece of the Earth, or something else?'
activities.rationale: Linking a held object to the whole planet (zoom-out) turns the abstract claim into something the child can connect to a thing in their hand, addressing the belief that rocks/stones are separate from the ground. A highlighted pebble linked to the globe view makes the connection concrete; this is an optional presentation choice.
learnerActions: Hold a real pebble or stone and look at a picture of the whole Earth as a planet made mostly of rock.
Zoom out from the dug-down ground to the whole planet, seeing it as an enormous ball made mostly of rock.
Point to the pebble and state that it is a tiny piece of the Earth's rock.
Decide and explain whether a stone found on the ground is a piece of the Earth or a separate object.
activities.intendedInsight: Stones and pebbles are small pieces of the Earth's rock that have broken off and often been worn down — they are part of the Earth, not separate from it.

activities.title: Rock is everywhere, even where it's hidden
feedback: If a child thinks only mountains or cliffs are rock: rock is also under flat ground and under the sea, just hidden by soil or water.
If a child says the Earth is hollow or empty inside: it is full of rock and other materials, not empty. (Detail about the hot interior and layers comes in a later topic.)
Use the probe: 'Deep inside the Earth, is it empty or full of something? What?'
activities.rationale: Sorting can check how children classify materials and discussion surfaces where rock hides, confronting the 'only mountains are rock' and 'hollow Earth' beliefs; a sort alone checks classification but does not itself build the dig-down/zoom-out picture or elicit explanation, so pair it with talk. Keep claims to rock and other materials filling the Earth; do not introduce layers, heat or the core at this stage.
learnerActions: Sort pictures or objects into 'made of rock' and 'not made of rock'.
Discuss where rock is hidden: under flat grass, under sand at the beach, and under the sea — not only in mountains and cliffs.
Answer: 'What is under the soil almost everywhere?' (rock, not water or empty space).
Talk about what is deep inside the Earth: rock and other materials, not empty space.
activities.intendedInsight: Rock is beneath flat ground and under the sea too, often hidden by soil, sand or water; the Earth is full of rock and other materials, not hollow.

constraints: Keep to 'rock and other solid materials'; defer Earth's layers, the hot interior and the core to the later 'Earth's Layers' topic for 7–9s.
This is a Tier A concrete/observational target: children should state the ground is made of rock and that stones are pieces of the Earth; they are not expected to know layers or the hot interior.

Sorting or multiple-choice questions can check 'what is under the soil?' and 'a stone is a piece of…', but on their own they do not build the dig-down and zoom-out mental picture; use them to check, not to introduce, the idea.
Handle real rocks, stones and pebbles where possible so the abstract idea ties to objects children can hold.
Start from familiar local ground before generalising to the whole planet.
Bridge to Year 1 'Everyday materials' vocabulary, where 'rock' is one of the named everyday materials, so the idea sits on prior science.

Lift-the-flap, tap-to-reveal, drag-to-dig, depth markers and highlighted pebbles are optional ways to make the reveal concrete; they are suggestions, not required mechanisms, and a fixed cross-section picture can still teach the idea.
A rotatable 3D globe adds only mild novelty for this recognition target and is not needed; a 2D cross-section conveys 'the ground is rock' clearly.
When using the builders'/digging example, present it as digging down deep enough to reach the hard rock beneath, not as a claim that ordinary house foundations always reach bedrock.
Any tray or on-screen dig is a model of real ground: the hard layer represents bedrock that continues far deeper than any tray; make this explicit so children do not take the tray bottom literally.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both listed sources are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The assessment's correctAnswer and one diagnostic answer mention 'very hot rock and metal' and a metal interior; these go beyond the stated 5–7 scope ('rock and other solid materials', with heat/layers/core explicitly deferred). Activities here avoid teaching the hot/metal interior to stay within the age target; retained only as background for adult reference.

The original row framed the reveal-based interactive as the single best delivery and rated open dialogue and 3D as poor/unnecessary. These are presentation preferences, not established efficacy claims; this rewrite keeps the dig-down and zoom-out as the core teaching moves while treating specific interaction styles as optional.

Claim that soil overlies bedrock 'almost everywhere' is reasonable as a general Earth-science statement but is sourced to an unverified general reference, and real soil depth varies widely; treat as a plausible simplification for this age, not a verified universal.

The inherited builders'-foundations example overstates the geology: ordinary foundations are usually dug into soil/subsoil and do not reliably reach bedrock. It has been reworded to illustrate 'dig deep enough and you reach rock'; do not teach that all foundations hit bedrock.
The hands-on dig uses a tray/on-screen model; this is noted inside the activity itself, since the hard layer only represents the real, far-deeper bedrock.

probeDeeper: Is the soil in a garden as thick as the whole Earth, or just a thin layer on top?
When builders dig down to lay foundations, what hard stuff do they hit?
Is a stone you find on the ground a piece of the Earth, or something else?
Deep inside the Earth, is it empty or full of something? What?
assess.correctAnswer: Just under the thin layer of soil at the top, it's mostly solid rock. The Earth is made of rock (and deeper still, very hot rock and metal). Soil is only a thin skin at the very top — the stones we find are pieces of that same rocky Earth.

errorPatterns.pattern: It's dirt or soil all the way down
errorPatterns.nextMove: Soil is a thin skin — dig deeper and you hit solid rock (bedrock); show a soil-over-rock cross-section or a photo of digging foundations.
errorPatterns.distractor: It would be soil or dirt all the way down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the deep hole stays in soil; no rock beneath.

errorPatterns.pattern: The Earth is hollow or empty inside
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Earth is solid rock and metal all the way through, not hollow.
errorPatterns.distractor: It would be hollow and empty inside.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says there's air or an empty space inside the Earth.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rocks and stones aren't part of the Earth — they're separate things lying on it
errorPatterns.nextMove: A stone is a small broken-off piece of the same rock the Earth is made of.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that a stone is a piece of the Earth; treats it as just an object.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the Earth is dirt/soil all the way down, or hollow inside.
responseLevels.full: Explains soil is a thin top skin and beneath it the Earth is mostly solid rock, and recognises stones as pieces of that same Earth material.
responseLevels.partial: Says the ground is rock but imagines soil continuing far down, or is unsure what lies beneath the soil.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Imagine you could dig a deep, deep hole straight down — much deeper than a garden. What would you find most of the way down, and what is the Earth mostly made of underneath us?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who says 'the ground is rock' (first tier) may still imagine soil going all the way down. Asking what's DOWN THERE forces 'rock under the soil' — a child with the dirt misconception says soil or dirt continues all the way, and one with the hollow idea says it's empty inside.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Reading Food Web Diagrams

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans'):** pupils construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey — reading a web is the natural extension, tracing many overlapping chains through one diagram.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-LS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS2-1] — a food web IS that model, and reading it fluently is the entry skill.

- **Operational details:** This is a REPRESENTATIONAL topic — the concept (feeding relationships) is already known; the new learning is decoding the diagram convention. The single load-bearing rule is arrow direction: the arrow points FROM the food TO the eater, i.e. in the direction energy/matter flows. Children read a web by (a) naming producers vs consumers, (b) tracing a single chain through the tangle, (c) finding an organism that appears in several chains, and (d) predicting what happens downstream when one organism is removed. Keep webs to 6–8 organisms at this age so the arrows stay legible.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child works with a concrete, pictured web of familiar organisms and answers 'who eats whom' and 'what if' by tracing arrows — no quantities, no energy maths yet. Success = can trace any chain and correctly reason one step of removal-cascade.
bestPractices: Front-load the arrow-direction convention explicitly and check it before any web reading: the arrow points FROM the food TO the eater, the way energy flows. Most reading errors trace back to this one rule.
Start from a single chain the child can already read, then overlay a second and third that share an organism — build the web up from chains rather than presenting the full tangle cold.
Teach three read-moves in order: name the roles (producer/consumer), trace one chain end-to-end, then find a shared organism that sits in several chains.
Use 'what if we remove this?' prediction as the culminating task — it turns passive reading into causal reasoning and reveals whether the child sees the web as interconnected.
Keep webs to 6–8 familiar local organisms so arrows stay legible; complexity should come from interconnection, not from unfamiliar species.
keyRepresentations: Pictured food web (nodes = organism images, directed arrows = energy flow) — the canonical diagram to decode
Single highlighted chain traced through the web (grass → rabbit → fox) to show a web is many overlapping chains
Role colour-coding: producers one colour, consumers another, to make structure pop
Removal 'ripple': greying one node and dimming every arrow and organism downstream of it
commonMisconceptions: Drawing/reading the arrow backwards — pointing from the eater to the food (thinking the arrow means 'eats') rather than in the direction energy flows.
Believing a web is just one long chain, so removing an organism only affects the next one along, not every path it feeds.
Thinking arrows show 'who is bigger/stronger' rather than what eats what.
Assuming an organism can only be in one chain, missing that many organisms sit at the crossing point of several chains.

learn.summary: Teaching 8–9-year-olds to read and interpret food web diagrams. The concept of feeding relationships is already known; the new learning is decoding the diagram convention — above all the arrow-direction rule: the arrow points FROM the food TO the eater, in the direction energy/matter flows. Learners name producers vs consumers, trace a single chain through the tangle, find organisms shared by several chains, and predict knock-on effects of removing a species. Keep webs to 6–8 familiar local organisms so arrows stay legible; complexity should come from interconnection, not unfamiliar species.

activities.title: Lock in the arrow-direction rule first
feedback: If a learner draws bird → caterpillar or says the arrow means 'eats', re-label the arrow as 'is eaten by / energy goes to' and have them re-check that every arrowhead points toward the feeder.

If a learner describes 'who is connected to who' but cannot state a direction, they are ignoring arrowheads: reteach the directed-diagram convention (like a one-way street sign) — the arrowhead carries the meaning, not just the line.
When a learner can both read a given arrow correctly AND draw an unaided one pointing the right way, they have produced the convention, not just recognised it.
activities.rationale: This is a representational topic whose single load-bearing rule is arrow direction; most reading errors trace to it, so front-load and check it explicitly before any web reading. Drawing one unaided — and testing it by reversing a chain — catches a child who recognises but cannot produce the convention.
sourceClaims: Food-web arrow convention: the arrow points from the organism being eaten toward the organism that eats it, showing the direction of energy/matter flow; reversing it is the classic pupil misconception.
learnerActions: Look at a single arrow between two pictured organisms, e.g. grass → rabbit, and say exactly what it means: the arrow points to the eater, so energy/matter flows FROM grass TO rabbit.
Given 'a caterpillar and a bird that eats it', draw the arrow yourself, pointing the right way (caterpillar → bird).
Check every arrowhead in a small web points toward the feeder, re-reading each as 'is eaten by / energy goes to'.

Redraw a three-species chain with all its arrows reversed and decide whether it still makes sense — it does not, because energy would then appear to flow from the eater back to its food, the opposite of how feeding works.
activities.intendedInsight: The arrowhead carries the meaning: it shows the direction energy/matter travels, from food to feeder — not 'this eats that'.

activities.title: Build the web up from chains and name the roles
feedback: If a learner can trace one chain but gets lost where an animal feeds two predators, scaffold by highlighting that one animal and following every arrow leaving it; the concept is present, only the diagram-tracing needs practice — do not reteach the arrow meaning.

In a web that shows every organism's food, a producer (a plant) has food arrows only leaving it and none arriving. Use this as a quick role-check, but confirm that it is a plant, because an animal whose food is not drawn would look the same.
activities.rationale: Building from a known single chain to overlapping chains makes the mesh legible and prevents the misconception that a web is just one long chain. Role-naming is the entry read-move before tracing and prediction.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans' requires pupils to construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey.
learnerActions: Start from one chain you can already read (grass → rabbit → fox); then overlay a second and third chain that share an organism, so the web grows from chains rather than appearing as a full tangle.

Name each organism's role: producers (plants, which make their own food using sunlight) and consumers; then split the consumers into primary consumers (eat producers) and secondary consumers (eat other consumers). If decomposers (e.g. fungi, worms, bacteria) are shown, name them as feeders on dead material and waste. Notice that a producer has no food arrows arriving at it, but check that it is a plant, because an animal whose food is not drawn in the web would also have only arrows leaving it.
Trace one chain end-to-end with a finger, saying the running label aloud (grass → rabbit → fox).
activities.intendedInsight: A food web is many overlapping chains, and each organism plays a role (producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, or decomposer if shown) that you can read from the diagram.

activities.title: Find shared organisms at crossing points
feedback: If a learner assumes each organism belongs to only one chain, pick an animal that feeds two predators and trace both chains through it together.
Praise finding a node where multiple chains meet: this is the structural feature that makes a web more than a single chain.
activities.rationale: Addresses the misconception that an organism can only be in one chain; locating shared nodes is the read-move that reveals interconnection and prepares for removal-cascade reasoning.
learnerActions: Trace two different food chains that both pass through the same animal in the web.
Highlight one organism and follow every arrow that touches it to see how many chains cross there.
activities.intendedInsight: Many organisms sit at the crossing point of several chains — a web is a mesh, not a set of separate lines.

activities.title: Predict the ripple when a species is removed
feedback: If a learner says only the next organism along is affected, have them follow each arrow leaving the removed organism (these point to the animals that ate it) to reveal multiple dependents — e.g. removing rabbits can affect both the fox and the owl that fed on them.
If prediction is correct, ask them to justify it by naming the specific paths that break.
activities.rationale: 'What if we remove this?' turns passive reading into causal reasoning and reveals whether the child sees the web as interconnected — the point where reading a web becomes reasoning with a web.
learnerActions: Pick an organism (e.g. rabbits) and, following the arrows, predict whose food disappears if it is removed.
Trace along every path the removed organism fed — not just the next one along — and name each organism affected downstream.
Explain to a partner or an 'ecologist' character why removing one node can affect more than one other animal.
activities.intendedInsight: Removing one node ripples along EVERY path it fed: because a web is interconnected, one removal can affect several organisms, not just the next one in a single chain.

activities.title: Optional interactive web-reader and companion reference
feedback: Use a quick arrow-direction gate before free exploration (tap the arrow showing energy flowing from grass to rabbit) so the convention is secured first.
Include an arrow-direction distractor (an arrow drawn eater→food) as the classic misconception check when assessing reading.
activities.rationale: These interaction and feedback examples (tap-to-highlight, drag-to-trace with a running label, remove-button ripple, lift-the-flap annotations) are offered as untested options to make the learning mechanism concrete; the same moves can be done on paper by tracing chains and greying out a removed organism. The static annotated web teaches the convention crisply but does not by itself let a learner do the removal-cascade prediction, so pair it with an activity where learners predict ripples themselves.
learnerActions: On an interactive pictured web of 6–8 familiar organisms (grass, rabbit, mouse, fox, owl, beetle, hawk), tap an organism so every arrow it touches lights up, revealing the mesh of relationships.
Drag a fingertip from grass through rabbit to fox to trace a single chain, with a running 'grass → rabbit → fox' label naming it.

Press a 'remove' button on an organism and watch the arrows leaving it dim and the organisms that fed on it (e.g. fox AND owl after removing the rabbit) light up as losing one food source. They do not automatically disappear if the web shows they have other food (e.g. a fox that also eats mice).

As a pre-teach reference, use a static annotated web with lift-the-flaps: tap each arrow to reveal 'the arrow points to the eater — energy flows this way', tap each node to reveal its producer/predator/prey role.
activities.intendedInsight: Interactive highlighting, tracing, and a visible removal-ripple can make the mesh structure and the knock-on effects of removal concrete and felt.

constraints: This is Tier A (concrete/observational): work with a concrete, pictured web of familiar organisms; no quantities and no energy maths yet. Success = can trace any chain and correctly reason one step of a removal-cascade.
Keep webs to 6–8 familiar local organisms so arrows stay legible; let complexity come from interconnection, not unfamiliar species.
Front-load and check the arrow-direction convention before any web reading, since most reading errors trace to it.

A recognition-only or multiple-choice response checks reading but does not require the learner to produce the convention; include at least one task where the learner draws an arrow unaided to confirm production, not just recognition.
A static annotated web is a strong reference/pre-teach for the convention but does not by itself elicit independent removal-cascade prediction; pair it with a prediction task.
A dialogue/'explain your thinking' layer can probe reasoning but is best as a follow-up to visual tracing, since the core skill is visual-spatial diagram reading.

To identify which organisms lose a food source when one is removed, follow the arrows LEAVING the removed organism (they point to the animals that ate it); arrows arriving at it come from its own food, which may then be eaten less.
The removal-ripple shows which organisms lose a food source; at this age treat it as 'whose food disappears / is affected' rather than precise population modelling.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's arrow-direction claim is marked verified:false in the row; treat the convention statement as standard science-education guidance pending confirmation. The two standards citations (DfE Y4, NGSS 5-LS2-1) are marked verified:true.

NGSS 5-LS2-1 ('food web is that model') and DfE Y4 are topic/standards-level citations; they are not attached to individual activities whose specific teaching principle (arrow front-loading, removal-cascade prediction, interactive-media affordances) they do not directly support. sourceClaims were trimmed to [] on those activities rather than invent support.

The original row asserted a 3D rendering 'adds nothing' / is 'actively worse' and that dialogue 'cannot show the web being traced'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy claims; retained only as scoped notes that a flat graph is easier to trace without depth/occlusion and that dialogue is best as a follow-up probe. No universal necessity is claimed.

The original framed the interactive 2D reader as uniquely 'ideal' and the quiz as testing 'rather than building' intuition. These catalog rankings have been reframed as optional media and complementary roles; the underlying learner actions are preservable on paper, and efficacy of the interactive version is untested.

probeDeeper: Trace two different food chains that both pass through the same animal in this web.
If I rub out the rabbits, follow the arrows — whose food disappears?
Which organism has arrows only leaving it and none arriving? What does that tell you it is?
Redraw this three-species chain with all the arrows reversed — would it still make sense? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The arrow means 'is eaten by' — energy travels in the direction of the arrowhead, from the food to the feeder. The drawn arrow therefore goes FROM the caterpillar TO the bird (caterpillar → bird).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The arrow points to what the animal eats' — reads it as 'eats' and reverses direction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-label the arrow as 'is eaten by / energy goes to'; check every arrowhead points toward the feeder.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the arrow means 'this eats that' and draws bird → caterpillar.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores arrowheads — reads the web as unordered links and cannot state a direction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the directed-diagram convention (as with circuit diagrams): the arrowhead carries the meaning, not just the line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes 'who is connected to who' but cannot say which way energy goes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Traces along lines but cannot find species shared by two chains — misreads branching points.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: highlight one animal and follow every arrow leaving it; the concept is present, the diagram-tracing needs practice. Do not reteach the arrow meaning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Follows one chain fine but gets lost where an animal feeds two predators.

responseLevels.gap: Reads arrows as 'eats' or ignores direction entirely; cannot draw a correctly-pointed arrow.
responseLevels.full: Reads arrow direction as energy flow, produces a correctly-directed arrow on demand, and traces multiple chains through the web, identifying shared species and predicting removal effects from the diagram.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a single arrow correctly and identifies a producer/consumer, but stumbles tracing two chains through a shared species.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a food web diagram. First: 'Point to one arrow and tell me exactly what it means — which way does the food and energy travel along it?' Then: 'Now I name two animals — a caterpillar and a bird that eats it. Draw the arrow between them yourself, pointing the right way.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The interpret step catches a child who reads the arrow as 'eats' (arrowhead aimed at the food). The translate step — drawing one unaided — catches whether they can PRODUCE the convention, not just recognise it; a child right for the wrong reason draws bird → caterpillar.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Nocturnal Animals, ages 5–7 — some animals are nocturnal: active at night and sleeping by day; and nocturnal animals often have special features (big eyes like owls and tarsiers, large ears like bats and fennec foxes, sensitive whiskers) that help them find food in the dark.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS1 Y1 'Animals, including humans' (structure of common animals) and Y2 habitats — nocturnal is a behaviour/feature framing built on naming animals and their body parts.
• Standards — US: NGSS 1-LS1-1 (animals use external parts — eyes, ears — to help them survive, find food and meet needs); 1-LS3-1 background on variation.
• Operational details: teach the day/night activity swap FIRST ('when we sleep, some animals wake up') via a diurnal↔nocturnal contrast; then link each special FEATURE to its JOB in the dark (big eyes gather scarce light; big ears/whiskers/echolocation locate prey by sound/touch when seeing is hard); use a 'see the dark like an owl' perspective device so the feature's usefulness is felt; keep it observational — no evolutionary mechanism.
• Checkpoint: [Tier A] explains what 'nocturnal' means, names ≥3 nocturnal animals (owl, bat, fox, hedgehog, moth), and describes one feature that helps a nocturnal animal in the dark (big eyes, big ears, echolocation, whiskers).
bestPractices: Establish the day↔night activity contrast before the features: pair a diurnal animal (asleep at night) with a nocturnal one (awake at night) so 'nocturnal = active at night, rests by day' is grounded in a visible swap.

Tie every special feature to the PROBLEM it solves in the dark — big eyes catch more of the little light there is; big ears and whiskers and echolocation find food by sound/touch when eyes aren't enough — feature→function, not feature as decoration.

Let children experience the difficulty of the dark (a dim scene where you can barely see) and then 'switch on' the animal's feature (owl's light-gathering eyes; bat's echolocation ping) so the usefulness is FELT, not just told.
Include a small spread of nocturnal animals across groups (owl-bird, bat-mammal, moth-insect, hedgehog, fox) to avoid 'nocturnal = owls only'.
Address the sleep framing kindly — nocturnal animals aren't 'awake all the time'; they simply swap our schedule, sleeping by day.
keyRepresentations: A day/night toggle scene: by day the diurnal animals are active and nocturnal ones sleep; flip to night and the nocturnal animals wake while the others sleep.
Feature→function callouts: big eyes = gather light; big ears/whiskers = locate by sound/touch; bat echolocation = 'see' with sound.
A 'see the dark like an owl' view: a barely-visible dim scene that brightens/sharpens when the animal's night-vision feature is switched on.
A small cross-group set of nocturnal animals (owl, bat, moth, hedgehog, fox) so the category isn't just owls.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking nocturnal animals are awake all the time, rather than swapping the schedule — active at night, asleep by day.
Believing nocturnal animals can see perfectly in complete darkness / have magic night vision, rather than having features that gather scarce light or use sound and touch when light is poor.
Assuming 'nocturnal' means only owls, missing bats, moths, hedgehogs, foxes and others across animal groups.
Treating big eyes/ears/whiskers as just 'how the animal looks' rather than tools that DO a job in the dark.
Confusing nocturnal (active at night) with hibernating (sleeping through winter) — different ideas.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: nocturnal animals are active at night and sleep by day, and many have special features — big eyes (owls, tarsiers), large ears (bats, fennec foxes), sensitive whiskers, or echolocation (bats) — that help them find food in the dark. Teach the day↔night activity swap first, then link each feature to the job it does when light is scarce. Let children feel how hard it is to see in the dark before 'switching on' the feature so its usefulness is experienced, not just told. Spread examples across animal groups so the category is not just owls.

activities.title: Flip day to night: who wakes up?
feedback: If a child says the owl is asleep at night and busy in the day, replay the flip and point out the owl wakes when the scene goes dark: nocturnal = awake at night.
If a child says nocturnal animals never sleep, show that in daytime the owl and bat are resting — they simply sleep at a different time than we do.
Confirm correct answers by linking: 'When WE sleep, these animals wake up — that's what nocturnal means.'
activities.rationale: Grounding the definition in a visible swap the child controls makes 'nocturnal' a state they cause rather than a word to memorise, and directly contrasts a diurnal pattern with a nocturnal one. An optional live day/night toggle on a single scene makes the contrast concrete.
sourceClaims: Children commonly believe nocturnal animals see perfectly in total darkness or are awake all the time; teaching should link features to gathering scarce light or using sound/touch, and clarify the day/night activity swap.
learnerActions: Look at a woodland scene by day: birds flit, squirrels dart, while an owl, a bat and a hedgehog sleep tucked away.
Flip a DAY/NIGHT toggle and watch the same scene change — the daytime animals settle to sleep, and one by one the owl's eyes open, the bat unfurls, and the hedgehog snuffles out.
Say in your own words what 'nocturnal' means based on what you just changed.
Flip back and forth and point to which animals are active in each setting.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Nocturnal' means active at night and resting by day — these animals swap our schedule rather than being awake all the time.

activities.title: Feel the dark, then switch on the feature
feedback: If a child says the owl sees perfectly with no light at all, point out the scene is still dark until the eyes gather the faint moon/star light — in true blackness the owl would rely on its sharp hearing instead.
If a child names a feature but not its job ('big eyes'), ask 'but what do the big eyes DO here?' and replay the brighten effect.
Affirm when the child connects feature to function: 'Yes — the big eyes catch more of the small light, so the owl can spot its food.'
activities.rationale: Experiencing how useless ordinary sight is in the dark and then how the feature rescues it makes 'these features help find food in the dark' something felt rather than recited, and anchors each feature to the problem it solves. Optional live effects — a scene brightening when 'owl eyes' turn on, a sonar ping revealing a moth — make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Animals use external parts — such as eyes and ears — to help them survive, find food and meet their needs; variation in these parts suits different ways of living.

Children commonly believe nocturnal animals see perfectly in total darkness or are awake all the time; teaching should link features to gathering scarce light or using sound/touch, and clarify the day/night activity swap.
learnerActions: Enter an animal's point of view in a night scene that starts almost pitch black and is frustratingly hard to make out.
Switch on 'owl eyes' and watch the scene brighten to show how the owl's big eyes gather the faint light there is, so a mouse below suddenly stands out.
Or fire the bat's echolocation 'ping' and see it paint the outline of a fluttering moth out of the darkness.
Say what the feature did: what job does the big eye / the sound do for the animal in the dark?
activities.intendedInsight: Special features solve a real problem — big eyes gather the little light there is, while ears, whiskers and echolocation locate prey by sound or touch when seeing is not enough.

activities.title: More than owls: match the feature to its job
feedback: If a child thinks only owls are nocturnal, show the bat, moth, hedgehog and fox as examples across groups.
If a child treats features as just how an animal looks, re-ask what the ears or whiskers DO at night.
Confirm a correct match by restating the feature→function link, and note that not every nocturnal animal echolocates — the bat uses sound, while the owl uses light-gathering eyes and sharp hearing.
activities.rationale: A deliberate spread across bird, mammal and insect counters the 'nocturnal = owls only' idea, and feature-to-job matching keeps features framed as tools rather than decoration. A tap-to-reveal set with a one-line job per feature can make coverage reliable for this age.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils describe the structure of common animals and their body parts, the base for linking nocturnal features (eyes, ears) to function.
learnerActions: Meet a small cross-group set of nocturnal animals: owl (bird), bat (mammal), moth (insect), hedgehog, and fox.

For each animal, reveal its special feature and a one-line note on what it is for (big eyes = gather light; big ears/whiskers = locate by sound/touch; a sensitive nose or feathery antennae = find food by smell; bat echolocation = 'see' with sound).
Match each feature to the job it does in the dark.
Name three or more nocturnal animals from different animal groups.
activities.intendedInsight: Nocturnal animals come from many animal groups, not just owls, and each uses features suited to finding food in the dark.

activities.title: Wonder companion and gentle end check (optional)
feedback: For 'no light at all', guide toward: even an owl needs some faint light for its eyes; in true blackness it would hunt by hearing. Try comparing dim light with pitch dark.
For the bat question, guide toward: sound works even when there is too little light to see, so the bat's echolocation can locate a moth in the dark where eyes alone would fail.

If a child says nocturnal animals sleep all winter, separate nocturnal (every-day pattern: hunts at night, sleeps by day) from hibernating (a seasonal sleep through the cold), and note that some animals do both: hedgehogs and many bats are nocturnal and also hibernate in winter, but being nocturnal alone does not mean sleeping all winter.
Treat these as light checks and prompts for talk, not a scored gate; return to the scene for any idea that is shaky.
activities.rationale: A charming in-role companion may add wonder, and recognition-style checks and sorting can confirm the definition and the feature-to-job matches; on their own, however, they do not elicit the child explaining what a feature is FOR, so they work best after the interactive scene that lets the feature→function insight be felt.
learnerActions: Optionally, ask an in-role owl or bat 'how do you find food at night?' and listen to how it describes using its eyes or sound.
Answer a few check questions: what does nocturnal mean? match each feature to its job; sort animals into day-active vs night-active.

Discuss the probing questions: When the owl sleeps, is it day or night? If there were no moon or stars at all, could the owl still catch a mouse — and how? Why do you think a bat uses sound instead of big eyes to hunt in the dark? Are YOU nocturnal, and how do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: A child can state what nocturnal means, name several night animals across groups, and explain what one special feature is for.

constraints: Keep it observational for ages 5–7: describe that features help animals find food in the dark; do not introduce evolutionary mechanism.
Address the sleep framing kindly — nocturnal animals are not awake all the time; they swap our schedule, sleeping by day.
Distinguish nocturnal (a daily day/night pattern) from hibernating (a seasonal sleep through winter).
Correct the magic-vision idea: features gather scarce light or use sound/touch; no animal sees in truly total darkness, and in complete blackness an owl relies on hearing.

Not all nocturnal animals echolocate: many bats (like the small insect-eating bats in the scene) use sonar, while owls rely on light-gathering eyes and sharp hearing, so keep echolocation tied to the bat rather than treating it as a general nocturnal feature. Not every bat echolocates either; many fruit bats find food mainly with big eyes and smell.

Recognition-only checks (matching, sorting, multiple choice) confirm the definition and feature labels but do not by themselves elicit the child explaining what a feature is FOR; pair them with the child stating the function.

A tap-to-reveal static scene can present the animals and features but cannot animate the day↔night swap or the 'feel the dark then switch on the feature' change; those need a dynamic or enacted version.

A first-person 3D walk-through is an optional immersive flourish; the concept is conveyed well in a controllable 2D scene without extra navigation demands for this age — treat 3D as an alternative experience, not a requirement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all three listed sources carry verified:false and have NOT been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The cited sources support general principles (animals use external parts to meet needs; KS1 describes animal body parts; the stated misconceptions and day/night framing). They do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any specific interactive format.

Original research framed a scored linear quiz and tap-to-reveal image as 'missing' the key insight; these have been retained as consolidation/scaffold options with their limits scoped rather than dismissed as unable to teach.
The echolocation claim is accurate for bats; ensure children understand not all nocturnal animals echolocate (e.g., owls rely on light-gathering eyes and sharp hearing, not sonar).
The 'faint moon/star light' threshold is a simplification for this age, not a sourced measurement.

probeDeeper: When the owl is fast asleep, is it daytime or night-time?
If there were NO light at all — no moon and no stars — could the owl still catch a mouse? How?
Why do you think a bat uses sound instead of big eyes to hunt in the dark?
Are YOU nocturnal? How do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: The big eyes gather as much of the small amount of light there is at night (from the moon and stars) as they can, so the owl can see well enough in the dark to spot and catch prey. 'Nocturnal' means active at night and asleep by day. (Owls also use very sharp hearing.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Nocturnal animals can see in complete, total darkness — their eyes work with no light at all.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Big eyes collect faint light; in true blackness even an owl relies on hearing. Try seeing in dim vs pitch-dark to make the point.
errorPatterns.distractor: Its big eyes let it see even when there is no light at all.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the owl sees perfectly even with no moon or stars, as if it makes its own light.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixes up the word — thinks 'nocturnal' means sleeping at night and awake by day (like us).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort animals into 'awake at night' vs 'awake in the day'; anchor nocturnal = night-active.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the owl is asleep at night and busy in the daytime.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses being nocturnal (a daily pattern) with hibernating (a seasonal sleep).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate 'sleeps in the day, hunts at night, every day' from 'sleeps through the cold season'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says nocturnal animals sleep all through the winter.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks nocturnal animals see in total darkness, or reverses the meaning of the word.
responseLevels.full: Explains nocturnal = active at night/asleep by day, AND that features such as big eyes gather faint light (or big ears/whiskers/echolocation sense prey) to find food in the dark.
responseLevels.partial: Knows nocturnal means active at night and can name a feature (big eyes, big ears), but can't say what the feature does.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: An owl hunts at night and sleeps in the daytime. Why does it have such big eyes — what do those big eyes actually DO for it at night?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'what do the eyes DO' tier separates a child who merely names the feature ('big eyes') from one who understands its function — gathering faint light to see in the dark. It also surfaces the magic-vision idea (seeing in total blackness), which a child who understands light will reject.

sources.claim: Animals use external parts — such as eyes and ears — to help them survive, find food and meet their needs; variation in these parts suits different ways of living.
sources.source: NGSS 1-LS1-1 / 1-LS3-1 (Next Generation Science Standards)

sources.claim: KS1 pupils describe the structure of common animals and their body parts, the base for linking nocturnal features (eyes, ears) to function.
sources.source: UK Department for Education — National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, KS1 Y1 'Animals, including humans'

sources.claim: Children commonly believe nocturnal animals see perfectly in total darkness or are awake all the time; teaching should link features to gathering scarce light or using sound/touch, and clarify the day/night activity swap.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Types of Chemical Reaction

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Chemical reactions):** pupils are taught "combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions" and to represent chemical reactions using formulae and word equations, building on the idea that a chemical reaction rearranges atoms to form new substances while conserving mass.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-2):** analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred — the four types are recognised by their characteristic evidence.

- **Operational details:** Give pupils a small toolkit of four named reaction patterns so they can classify what they observe: combustion (burning a fuel in oxygen, releasing heat/light — e.g. methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water); oxidation (a substance gains oxygen — e.g. magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide, and rusting as slow oxidation); thermal decomposition (heat breaks ONE compound into simpler substances — e.g. copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide); and displacement (a more reactive element takes another's place — iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper). The key skill is sorting a reaction into the right family from its evidence: is a fuel burning? is oxygen being gained? is one substance splitting apart on heating? is one element swapping for another? Represent each with a word equation and check atoms are conserved.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Given a described or observed reaction, the child classifies it as combustion, oxidation, thermal decomposition or displacement and justifies the choice from the evidence and the word equation.
bestPractices: Give the four types as a classification toolkit and repeatedly practise sorting NEW reactions into them from evidence, rather than defining them once in isolation.

Anchor each type to a memorable observable signature — heat+light for combustion, a gained oxide for oxidation, a compound splitting on heating for thermal decomposition, a deposited metal for displacement.
Use word equations for every example and check atoms are conserved, reinforcing that reactions rearrange rather than create or destroy matter.
Surface overlap explicitly (magnesium burning is both combustion and oxidation) so pupils reason from evidence rather than assuming the categories are mutually exclusive.
Contrast thermal decomposition (one reactant → several products) with combination/oxidation (several → one) so the direction of change is clear.
keyRepresentations: A 2×2 grid of the four reaction types, each with a canonical word equation and its tell-tale evidence.
Word equations such as methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, and copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide.
The limewater test as the signature for CO2 released in thermal decomposition.
A displacement pairing (iron + copper sulfate) showing the deposited metal and colour change.
Before/after mass bars illustrating conservation of mass across each reaction type.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the four categories are mutually exclusive, when e.g. burning magnesium is both combustion and oxidation.
Confusing thermal decomposition (heat splits one substance apart) with reactions that combine substances, or thinking heating always causes decomposition.
Thinking oxidation only means rusting, missing that any gain of oxygen (including vigorous burning) is oxidation.
Believing combustion 'destroys' matter because the fuel seems to disappear, rather than forming gaseous products of equal mass.
Treating displacement as any two substances swapping, ignoring that the more reactive element must displace the less reactive one.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12–13 learn to classify chemical reactions into four families — combustion (burning a fuel in oxygen, releasing heat/light), oxidation (a substance gains oxygen, including rusting), thermal decomposition (heat breaks one compound into simpler substances), and displacement (a more reactive element takes another's place) — by reasoning from observable evidence and word equations, while checking that atoms (and therefore total mass) are conserved. The core skill is sorting NEW reactions into the right family from evidence, recognising that categories can overlap (burning magnesium is both combustion and oxidation).

activities.title: Name that reaction: sort by evidence
feedback: When magnesium burning is sorted as combustion, confirm it AND prompt: it also gains oxygen to form magnesium oxide, so it is oxidation too — the categories are not mutually exclusive.

If a reaction is sorted only by surface appearance, redirect to the defining evidence: is a fuel burning? is oxygen being gained? is ONE substance splitting on heating? is one element replacing another?
For copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide, name why it is thermal decomposition: heat breaks one compound into simpler substances (watch for the released gas and colour change).
activities.rationale: The target skill is classification from evidence, so repeated sorting of varied, novel reactions — and explicitly surfacing overlap — is intended to build evidence-based reasoning rather than rote category labels. Standards specify these four named reaction types and classifying substances by before/after evidence.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions, and to represent chemical reactions using formulae and word equations.
Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Take a shuffled set of reactions, some presented as word equations (e.g. copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide) and some as one-line observed scenes (e.g. a strip of magnesium flares white and leaves a powder; a piece of iron dipped in blue copper sulfate becomes coated with pink-brown metal).
Sort each reaction into one of four families: combustion, oxidation, thermal decomposition, displacement.
For each card, state the evidence that justifies your choice: heat and light, a gained oxide, one substance splitting apart on heating, or one element swapping for another.
Flag any reaction that seems to belong in two families and explain why (e.g. magnesium burning).
activities.intendedInsight: Each reaction family has a tell-tale observable signature, and you classify by reasoning from that evidence rather than by memorising definitions in isolation; some reactions legitimately belong to more than one family.

activities.title: Complete the word equation and check conservation
feedback: If a learner expects burning magnesium to lose mass, track the oxygen: magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide, so the solid oxide is HEAVIER because oxygen from the air was added — while total mass (metal + oxygen) is unchanged.
For a reaction where the solid appears to lose mass (e.g. wood burning), point out the lost mass has left as gases — total mass is still conserved once the escaping gases are counted.
If the atom check is skipped, prompt the learner to list the elements on each side before deciding the equation is complete.
activities.rationale: Using word equations and an atom/mass check for every example reinforces conservation of mass and counters the idea that combustion destroys matter. This connects the classification skill to the underlying representation of reactions required by the standards.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions, and to represent chemical reactions using formulae and word equations.
learnerActions: Complete word equations with missing reactants or products, e.g. methane + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water, and copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide.

After writing each equation, check that every element present before the reaction also appears after it. A word equation shows which elements are present, not how many atoms of each, so this check is consistent with atoms being neither created nor destroyed but does not prove it on its own.

Draw or compare before/after mass bars and explain that the TOTAL mass stays the same because atoms are only rearranged; then note that the solid you can actually weigh may appear to gain mass (magnesium takes in oxygen from the air) or lose mass (wood releases gases) depending on whether gas is absorbed or given off.
Match each reaction to its tell-tale sign: heat+light, gains oxygen, one substance splits into two or more simpler substances on heating, an element swapped out.
activities.intendedInsight: Reactions rearrange atoms rather than create or destroy matter, so total mass is conserved even when the weighable solid appears to change; word equations and the atom check make this explicit for every reaction type.

activities.title: Reaction bench: observe the signatures before sorting
feedback: When the carbonate is heated, point to the limewater turning cloudy as the signature that carbon dioxide was released — evidence of thermal decomposition.
For the displacement station, highlight the deposited metal and solution colour change, and connect it to the more reactive element replacing the less reactive one.

If a learner misreads heating a carbonate as melting, contrast melting (same substance, reversible) with decomposition (new substances form, here a gas is released, and often there is a colour change, e.g. green copper carbonate turning to black copper oxide).
activities.rationale: Observing each reaction's signature before abstract sorting may make the categories concrete and is intended to support evidence-based classification; this is a proposed scaffold, not a verified requirement. The limewater test and displacement colour change are concrete, optional interaction examples. Note: auto-written equations and the limewater cue are illustrative scaffolds, not the only route to the concept.
learnerActions: Visit four stations that each trigger one reaction type: light a fuel (combustion, heat and light), heat a metal in oxygen (oxidation, an oxide forms), heat a carbonate so the released gas turns limewater cloudy (thermal decomposition, CO2 detected), and dip a metal into a solution of a salt of a less reactive metal, e.g. iron into copper sulfate (displacement, a metal deposits with a colour change).
Watch each reaction auto-produce its word equation and note the observable signature.
Switch to a 'name that reaction' mode where the label is hidden and classify each reaction from its evidence alone.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing each reaction type and its signature (flame, oxide layer, gas released on heating, deposited metal) is intended to build perceptual hooks that later classification can draw on.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: weighing burning magnesium
feedback: If the learner predicts the powder weighs less, revisit: metal + oxygen -> metal oxide means oxygen is added, so the solid mass INCREASES while total mass is unchanged.
If oxidation is thought to mean only rusting, group burning, rusting, and magnesium-burning together: all are gaining oxygen, with rusting the slow case and burning the fast case.
For the wood comparison, note the escaping gases carry away the 'lost' mass — total mass is still conserved once gases are counted.
activities.rationale: The counter-intuitive solid-mass gain discriminates learners who understand combustion as combining with oxygen from those holding a 'burning destroys matter' model; the pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part. This directly supports the conservation and oxidation evidence in the objective.
sourceClaims: Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Before burning, weigh a coil of magnesium ribbon and predict whether the mass of the white powder afterwards will be more, less, or the same — and state WHY.

Heat the ribbon in a crucible with a lid, lifting the lid slightly now and then to let air in while keeping the white smoke in. Then weigh the crucible, lid and product and compare with the crucible, lid and ribbon before heating.
Compare your prediction with the result and explain what combustion/oxidation actually did to the magnesium.
Reconcile this with wood burning, which leaves only light ash: where did the wood's mass go?
activities.intendedInsight: Combustion of magnesium is oxidation: the metal combines with oxygen from the air, so the solid product gains mass. Burning does not destroy matter; where mass seems to be lost (wood, candle) it has escaped as gases, so total matter is conserved.

activities.title: Complete vs incomplete combustion
feedback: If a learner treats all burning as producing only CO2 and water, point to soot and carbon monoxide as evidence of incomplete combustion when oxygen is limited.
Reinforce that both complete and incomplete combustion are still combustion — the fuel burns in oxygen — they differ in how much oxygen is available and therefore in the products.
activities.rationale: The objective's evidence list requires distinguishing complete from incomplete combustion; contrasting the two product sets from observable clues builds that distinction, and combustion is explicitly listed in the KS3 content.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions, and to represent chemical reactions using formulae and word equations.
learnerActions: Compare complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel such as methane or candle wax (products carbon dioxide and water) with its incomplete combustion (products including carbon monoxide and soot).
Identify, from described evidence such as soot deposits or a smoky yellow flame, whether combustion was complete or incomplete.
Explain why limited oxygen leads to incomplete combustion and the formation of soot and carbon monoxide.
activities.intendedInsight: Combustion is not a single outcome: the amount of available oxygen changes the products, distinguishing clean complete combustion from sooty incomplete combustion.

constraints: Drag-to-bin sorting, multiple-choice and matching tasks can assess and rehearse classification, but a selection/recognition response does not by itself require a learner to construct an original word equation or explanation; include fill-in and explain-why tasks where independent production is the goal.

A tappable four-panel reference grid of the four reaction types is useful for vocabulary and definitions but, being a fixed reveal, does not itself give practice classifying new, unseen reactions — pair it with sorting activities.
Surface overlap explicitly: the four families are NOT mutually exclusive (burning magnesium is both combustion and oxidation); do not teach them as rigid disjoint boxes.
Distinguish thermal decomposition (one reactant -> several products on heating) from melting (same substance, reversible, no new substance) and from combination reactions (several -> one).
When discussing conservation of mass, always account for gases taken in or released: total mass is conserved even when the weighable solid appears to gain mass (magnesium) or lose mass (wood).

Any physical enactment in these activities — the reaction-bench stations AND the magnesium Predict–Observe–Explain burn — involves real flames, heating and chemicals; burning magnesium in particular emits intense bright light that must not be viewed directly, so all such tasks require appropriate supervision, eye protection and safety provision.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source labels the NGSS MS-PS1-2 claim as verified:false; treat the standards alignment to that source, and its use as support for evidence-based classification, as unconfirmed.

The original marked the 3D and conversation formats as 'poor' with reasoning such as '3D adds cost without insight' and 'open dialogue... does not deliver the sort-by-evidence practice'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened/omitted. Dialogue or spatial models are simply different, non-essential affordances here.

The original claimed 'static reveals cannot exercise the classification-from-new-evidence skill'. Reworded to the narrower, accurate point that a fixed reference grid does not itself provide new-reaction sorting practice; a fixed example can still teach.

The reaction-bench activity's claim that enacting signatures 'builds the perceptual hooks' for classification is an untested efficacy assertion; its sourceClaims were set to [] because the available source claim supports only the curriculum content, not the pedagogical ordering, and the rationale/insight were qualified as intended/proposed.

The before/after mass-bar prompt was reworded to avoid implying TOTAL mass can go up or down: total mass is conserved, while the observable solid may appear to gain mass (Mg absorbs oxygen) or lose mass (wood releases gases).

Checking atom conservation from word equations alone confirms which elements appear on each side but not numeric atom counts (that needs formulae); this reflects the original framing and is retained as an approximation.
Safety: the magnesium POE burn was previously covered by no explicit safety note; the safety constraint was broadened to include it, flagging the bright-light hazard of burning magnesium.

Self-audit of chemistry: magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide genuinely increases the solid mass (oxygen added); wood burning appears to lose mass because gaseous products escape — both consistent with conservation of total mass. Copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide is a valid thermal decomposition. No arithmetic or force/motion claims required correction.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: weigh a coil of magnesium ribbon, then burn it in a crucible and weigh the white oxide. Ask the child to predict whether the mass goes up, down, or stays the same, and WHY, before burning. A 'burning destroys matter' model predicts a decrease. The oxide is heavier (oxygen added). The pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Wood burning leaves light ash — but magnesium gains mass. Are these really both combustion? Where did the wood's mass go?
How is complete combustion (CO₂ + water) different from incomplete combustion, and why does incomplete give soot and carbon monoxide?
Why is rusting called oxidation as well as burning? What do they share?
Heating copper carbonate turns it black and gives off a gas. Melting or a reaction — how do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: The white powder weighs MORE than the ribbon. Combustion here is oxidation: the magnesium GAINS oxygen from the air, combining with it to form magnesium oxide — so the added oxygen adds mass. Burning doesn't destroy matter; it combines the fuel with oxygen. Full marks explain the mass increase by oxygen being added, not by anything being 'used up'.

errorPatterns.pattern: burning destroys matter, so products always weigh less ('it burns away')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track the oxygen: metal + oxygen → metal oxide, so mass increases. Where fumes escape (wood, candle) the lost mass leaves as gases — still conserved. Weigh magnesium before/after.
errorPatterns.distractor: Less — burning always destroys some of the material.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts the oxide weighs less than the metal; explains combustion as disappearance

errorPatterns.pattern: oxidation only means rusting ('oxidation is when iron goes rusty, nothing else')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Oxidation = gaining oxygen, of which rusting is the slow case and combustion the fast case. Group burning, rusting and magnesium-burning as oxidation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: restricts oxidation to rust; doesn't see burning or magnesium+oxygen as oxidation

errorPatterns.pattern: thermal decomposition is just melting ('heating it made it melt, not break apart')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast melting (same substance, reversible) with thermal decomposition (heat breaks ONE compound into new substances, e.g. copper carbonate → copper oxide + CO₂, colour change, gas). Use the signs of a new substance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reads heating a carbonate (which breaks into oxide + CO₂) as a physical melt rather than a reaction making new substances

responseLevels.gap: Predicts mass loss on burning; equates oxidation only with rust; reads decomposition as melting.
responseLevels.full: Explains combustion/oxidation as combining with oxygen (mass added; wood's loss leaves as gas), classifies all four reaction types from equations, distinguishes complete from incomplete combustion, and separates thermal decomposition from melting by the new-substance test.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the four reaction types and predicts the magnesium mass gain, but can't reconcile it with wood losing mass (escaping gas) or distinguish complete/incomplete combustion — recognises types without the unifying conservation reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I burn a coil of magnesium ribbon in air and it leaves a white powder (magnesium oxide). A student says 'burning always destroys stuff, so the white powder must weigh LESS than the ribbon.' Would the powder weigh less, more, or the same — and the important part, explain what combustion/oxidation actually does to the magnesium.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason distinguishes a child who understands combustion/oxidation as COMBINING WITH OXYGEN (mass added, atoms rearranged) from one who thinks burning destroys or lightens matter. The counter-intuitive mass gain is the discriminator — the 'burning = loss' model predicts the wrong direction.
