pedagogy.summary: This topic is fundamentally about SCALE and the units we invent to cope with it. Three ideas: (1) a light year is a distance — the distance light travels in one year — not a time, and it exists because kilometres are hopeless for interstellar space; (2) structure — the Sun is one ordinary star among hundreds of billions in the Milky Way, which is one galaxy among billions in the universe, so there is a nesting: solar system ⊂ galaxy ⊂ universe; (3) the staggering step-changes in distance between those levels (planets are light-minutes/hours apart, stars light-years apart, galaxies millions of light-years apart), which is why space travel needs enormous timescales and why we see distant objects as they were long ago (look-back time). The central teaching difficulty is that these magnitudes are literally unimaginable, so the work is making scale tangible through proportional reasoning, powers-of-ten zoom-outs, and relatable analogies (if the Sun-to-Earth distance were 1 step, the next star would be hundreds of kilometres away). The light-year-is-a-distance point must be taught explicitly because the word 'year' actively misleads.
bestPractices: Confront the light-year-as-time error head-on: define it as a distance (how far light goes in a year at 300,000 km/s) and practise saying 'the star is 4 light years AWAY', not 'ago'

Build scale through proportional analogies and powers-of-ten: repeatedly zoom out (Earth → solar system → nearest stars → Milky Way → galaxy groups → observable universe), each step reframing what was 'huge' as a dot
Compare distances in matched units across levels (light-minutes within the solar system, light-years to nearby stars, millions of light-years to other galaxies) so the step-changes are explicit

Connect look-back time to the finite speed of light: because light takes time to arrive, looking far out means looking back in time — we see the Sun 8 minutes ago and distant galaxies as they were millions of years ago
Locate the Sun concretely: an ordinary star part-way out in one spiral arm of the Milky Way, not at the centre and not special — countering geocentric/heliocentric-centrism
keyRepresentations: Powers-of-ten / zoom-out sequence from Earth to the observable universe (the canonical scale representation)
Light-travel-time number line: light-second (Moon), light-minutes (Sun/planets), light-years (stars), millions of light-years (galaxies)
Map of the Milky Way with the Sun's position marked in a spiral arm
Nested-scale diagram: solar system inside galaxy inside cluster inside universe
Scaled analogy models (e.g. Sun and nearest star as two grains on a map hundreds of km apart)
commonMisconceptions: A light year is a measure of time rather than of distance (the dominant misconception, driven by the word 'year')
The Sun is at the centre of the galaxy / the universe, or the Sun is special rather than a typical star
Stars in a constellation are close together / all stars are roughly the same distance away
The solar system, galaxy, and universe are the same thing or interchangeable terms (no sense of the nesting/scale hierarchy)
We see distant stars and galaxies as they are right now (ignores look-back time / finite light speed)
The gaps between galaxies are similar in scale to the gaps between planets or stars

learn.summary: Teach the scale of the universe and the vocabulary invented to cope with it: a light year is a DISTANCE (how far light travels in one year, ~9.5 trillion km, at ~300,000 km/s), not a span of time; the Sun is one ordinary star among hundreds of billions in the Milky Way, which is one galaxy among hundreds of billions or more in the observable universe, giving a nesting of solar system ⊂ galaxy ⊂ universe; and the distances step up brutally between levels (planets are light-minutes/hours apart, stars light-years apart, galaxies millions of light-years apart), which is why space travel needs enormous timescales and why we see distant objects as they were long ago (look-back time). Because the magnitudes are unimaginable, the core work is making scale tangible through proportional reasoning, powers-of-ten zoom-outs, and relatable analogies. The light-year-is-a-distance point must be taught explicitly because the word 'year' actively misleads.

activities.title: Fall backwards through the universe: a powers-of-ten zoom-out
feedback: If a learner expects the nearest star to be just beyond the solar system, point out that after all the zooming to shrink the solar system to a dot, the very next star is still light-years further — the gap between levels jumps enormously.

If a learner reads the light-year readout as a time, prompt: the panel is telling you how FAR away the object is. 'Light-years' names the distance light covers (its speed × a year), just as 'the shop is 20 minutes' walk away' names the ground your feet cover at walking speed — both are distances given via a time, not durations.

When the light-pulse mode is slow, connect it: if light itself takes years to cross, any spacecraft (far slower than light) needs vastly longer, and the light reaching your eye now left the object long ago.
activities.rationale: Scale and magnitude are the whole objective, and a continuous, learner-driven zoom lets the nesting and the step-changes in distance be experienced rather than only read; auto-switching units make 'the unit fits the scale' and 'a light year is a distance' concrete, and a look-back/light-pulse indicator ties distance to time taken by light. A 3D flythrough of the Milky Way and galaxy field is a good alternative for conveying the Sun's off-centre spiral-arm position and the three-dimensional web of galaxies, though it carries more navigation overhead and gives less direct quantitative readout than a 2D zoom. The live auto-switching unit panel and the light-pulse toggle are optional illustrative mechanisms, not required features; efficacy of any particular medium is proposed, not demonstrated by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: KS3 physics requires pupils be taught about the Sun as a star, other stars in our galaxy, other galaxies, and the light year as a unit of astronomical distance.
MS-ESS1-2's model of gravity's role includes the Milky Way galaxy and the solar system's place within it, providing the structural context for galaxies at this level.
learnerActions: Starting standing on Earth, scroll/zoom outward continuously through the levels: Earth → Moon → whole solar system → nearest stars → Milky Way → the galaxy group → the observable universe.

At each level, read the live distance panel and notice the unit it uses: the Moon tagged as roughly a light-second away, the Sun and inner planets in light-minutes, the outer planets in light-hours, the nearest star in light-years, other galaxies in millions of light-years.
Watch each thing that looked 'enormous' — the solar system, then the whole Milky Way — shrink to a dot as you reach the next level up.
Find the marker showing the Sun's position: an ordinary star partway out along one spiral arm of the Milky Way, not at the centre.
Switch on a 'watch light travel' mode that crawls a pulse of light outward, and time how slowly even light crosses a single gap between stars.
activities.intendedInsight: A light year is a DISTANCE — how far light travels in one year — made concrete by the zoom rather than only memorised; the unit panel upgrades itself to fit the scale (km → light-seconds → light-minutes/hours → light-years → millions of light-years); each level nests inside the next; and because even light is agonisingly slow across one star-gap, space travel needs enormous time and the distant light we see left long ago.

activities.title: Build the light year from speed × time
feedback: If a learner says '4 light-years means 4 years', rebuild it from speed × time: light's speed times one year is a length, just as a 'car-hour' names a distance a car covers, not a time.
If a learner gets the distance but not look-back time, layer it on: because light takes 4 years to cross that distance, what you see now set off 4 years ago — so the star could have changed since.
Reinforce correct phrasing: distances are '... away', not '... ago'; '... ago' describes when the light left.
activities.rationale: The dominant misconception is driven directly by the word 'year', so constructing the unit from speed × time and making the learner produce corrected sentences (not just recognise them) directly addresses the error and separates distance from the look-back time it also implies.
sourceClaims: Interpreting a light year as a unit of time rather than distance is a well-documented and common student misconception.
KS3 physics requires pupils be taught about the Sun as a star, other stars in our galaxy, other galaxies, and the light year as a unit of astronomical distance.
learnerActions: Work out what distance light covers in one year: start from its speed (~300,000 km per second) and multiply by the seconds in a year to reach roughly 9.5 trillion km.
Compare this to a made-up unit like a 'car-hour' (how far a car goes in an hour) to see that speed × time gives a DISTANCE, not a duration.
Rewrite the sentence 'the journey took 4 light-years' correctly, explaining why it is wrong, then say 'the star is 4 light-years AWAY' and state what that tells you.
Explain the two things '4 light-years away' tells you: the star is that far from us, AND its light took 4 years to arrive, so we see it as it was 4 years ago.
activities.intendedInsight: A light year is a distance built from speed × time; the word 'year' inside it names the time the light travelled, not a duration of the measurement. Distance and look-back time are linked because light has a finite speed.

activities.title: Scale models and matched-unit comparisons
feedback: If a learner treats interstellar and intergalactic distances as similar to solar-system ones, contrast the figures: nearest star ~4 light-years, Milky Way ~100,000 light-years across, other galaxies millions of light-years away, with the whole solar system a speck by comparison.
If a learner places the Sun at the centre, correct it: the Sun is one ordinary star partway out along a spiral arm; in the standard scientific picture the universe has no centre at all.
If units are mismatched (e.g. kilometres for a galaxy distance), ask which unit keeps the number manageable at that scale.
activities.rationale: Comparing distances in matched units across levels and using a concrete scaled analogy makes the step-changes explicit and counters both the 'space isn't that big' and the Sun-at-the-centre misconceptions, consolidating the structural nesting named by the standards. The scaled grains-on-a-map / one-step analogy is one illustrative option, not the only valid model, and is deliberately not to true scale in every dimension.
sourceClaims: KS3 physics requires pupils be taught about the Sun as a star, other stars in our galaxy, other galaxies, and the light year as a unit of astronomical distance.
MS-ESS1-2's model of gravity's role includes the Milky Way galaxy and the solar system's place within it, providing the structural context for galaxies at this level.
learnerActions: Build a proportional analogy: if the Sun-to-Earth distance were one step, work through roughly how far away the next star would be (hundreds of kilometres), feeling the jump between solar-system and interstellar scale.
Order these by distance and choose a sensible unit for each: the Moon, the Sun, the nearest star, the Andromeda galaxy — e.g. light-seconds, light-minutes, light-years, millions of light-years.
Order these by extent and state the unit for each: the solar system, the nearest star's distance, the Milky Way (~100,000 light-years across), the whole observable universe.

Mark on a Milky Way map where the Sun sits — partway out along a spiral arm, not at the centre, and note that, in the standard scientific picture, the universe has no centre at all (it is not expanding out from a central point).
activities.intendedInsight: Distances step up by huge factors between planets, stars and galaxies; matching the unit to each level makes the hierarchy explicit, and the Sun is an unremarkable star in one arm of an ordinary galaxy.

activities.title: Check and discriminate: distance, not time
feedback: Full grasp: defines a light-year as light's speed × a year, reads '4 ly away' as both distance and 4 years of look-back time, orders the scales with appropriate units, and places the Sun as an ordinary star in the Milky Way.

Partial: says a light-year is a distance but can't explain look-back time, or knows the Sun is in the Milky Way without grasping the scale jumps — return to the speed × time build or the matched-unit ordering.
Gap: treats a light-year as time or places the Sun at the centre — reteach from speed × time and the nested-scale comparison.
activities.rationale: A two-tier check whose first tier splits distance-vs-time cleanly isolates the dominant misconception, while the follow-up probes look-back time, scale ordering and the Sun's position. Selected-response and ordering items assess understanding but do not by themselves build scale intuition, so they belong after the experiential and constructive activities.
sourceClaims: Interpreting a light year as a unit of time rather than distance is a well-documented and common student misconception.
learnerActions: Answer the diagnostic: 'A star is 4 light-years away. Is a light-year a measure of distance or of time — and what does "4 light-years away" actually tell you?'
Explain: if a star is 100 light-years away, how long ago did the light we see now leave it, and could the star have changed since?
Identify and correct the error in 'the journey took 4 light-years.'
Sequence Moon / Sun / nearest star / Andromeda by distance and match each to an appropriate unit.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who answers 'distance — how far light goes in a year' and can extend to look-back time holds the concept; 'it measures time / how long ago' reveals the classic misconception. Use these after the zoom and construction work, as a check rather than first teaching.

constraints: The light-year-as-distance point must be taught explicitly; the word 'year' actively misleads, so learners should both construct the unit from speed × time and produce corrected sentences ('away', not 'ago'), not merely recognise a right answer.
Quizzes, ordering and matching items can check classification and understanding but do not by themselves build scale intuition; use them after the experiential zoom and the speed × time construction.

Static diagrams and Milky Way maps are useful references and consolidation companions for labelling levels and the Sun's position, but a fixed image cannot be driven through a continuous zoom; treat it as a scaffold alongside, not a replacement for, experienced scale.

An in-role astronomer conversation may add wonder and context but does not by itself build the quantitative scale sense that is the objective; use it as optional enrichment, not the primary scale activity.
Scaled analogy models (grains on a map, one-step-to-the-Sun) are approximations to make proportion felt; state that they are deliberately not to true scale in every dimension.
The light-pulse and auto-switching-unit panels are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; the learning goals can be met without those specific features.

Keep numerical figures as approximations (~300,000 km/s, ~9.5 trillion km, ~4 ly to the nearest star, ~100,000 ly for the Milky Way), and let learners do the speed × time estimate rather than only being told the result.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no empirical effectiveness or human review is claimed.

Two of the three cited sources are marked verified in the row (NGSS MS-ESS1-2; DfE KS3 programme of study); the light-year-misconception claim is marked unverified (verified:false) in the source row — treat it as a documented-in-literature claim pending confirmation, not established effectiveness of any particular activity.

The curriculum-source claims (KS3, MS-ESS1-2) are attached to activities to show the named content (Sun as a star, galaxies, light year as a distance, galaxy/solar-system structure) should be taught; they do NOT support the experiential/medium choices in the rationales (2D zoom, 3D, conversation), which remain untested proposals.

The original row's 3D flythrough, static diagram, quiz and conversation alternatives were framed with catalog-style 'fit' rankings and some universal claims (e.g. 'static images cannot deliver', 'a quiz only assesses', 'dialogue cannot deliver the aha'); these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than carried as laws. The conversation option's narrow affordance (may add wonder/context) is preserved as enrichment.

Self-audit: speed × time yielding a distance is correct; light-second (Moon ~1.3 light-seconds), light-minutes (Sun ~8 light-minutes), light-years (nearest star ~4.2 ly), Milky Way ~100,000 ly diameter, and galaxy separations of millions of ly are all consistent with the source and standard figures. Look-back time (we see the Sun ~8 minutes ago, a 100-ly star as it was 100 years ago) follows correctly from finite light speed. No arithmetic or physics errors were found that required removing an instruction; figures are given as approximations.

probeDeeper: If a star is 100 light-years away, how long ago did the light we see now leave it — and could that star have changed since?
Put these in order of size: solar system, galaxy, the nearest star's distance, the whole observable universe. What units would you use for each?
Someone says 'the journey took 4 light-years.' Why is that sentence wrong?
assess.correctAnswer: A light-year is a DISTANCE — how far light travels in one year (about 9.5 trillion km). '4 light-years away' means the star is that far from us, and also that its light took 4 years to reach us, so we see it as it was 4 years ago. It does not mean an amount of time.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'a light-year is an amount of time (a year, or how long ago)' (the classic light-year misconception)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build it from speed × time — light's speed times one year gives a DISTANCE (like a 'car-hour' would be a distance); then layer look-back time on top.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's a measure of time — 4 light-years means 4 years.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says a light-year measures time; reads '4 light-years' as '4 years'

errorPatterns.pattern: 'stars and galaxies are all about the same distance / space isn't really that big' (no scale hierarchy)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Nested scale — nearest star ~4 ly, the Milky Way ~100,000 ly across, other galaxies millions of ly away; the whole solar system is a speck by comparison.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats interstellar and intergalactic distances as similar to solar-system ones

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Sun is at the centre of the galaxy / the universe' (geocentrism scaled up)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Sun is one ordinary star partway out along a spiral arm of the Milky Way; the universe has no known centre.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: places the Sun at the centre of the Milky Way or the universe

responseLevels.gap: Treats a light-year as a unit of time; no sense of the distance hierarchy; may place the Sun at the centre.
responseLevels.full: Defines a light-year as a distance (light's speed × a year), reads '4 ly away' as both distance and 4 years of look-back time, orders solar-system / interstellar / intergalactic scales with appropriate units, and places the Sun as an ordinary star in the Milky Way; transfers to a new distance.
responseLevels.partial: Says a light-year is a distance but can't explain look-back time, or knows the Sun is in the Milky Way without grasping the scale jumps between star, galaxy and universe.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A star is 4 light-years away. Is a light-year a measure of distance or of time — and what does '4 light-years away' actually tell you?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The word 'year' pulls hard toward a time answer. A child who says 'it measures time / how long ago' holds the classic misconception; a child who says 'distance — how far light goes in a year' has it, and the follow-up shows whether they also grasp look-back time. Correct and incorrect reasoners split cleanly on the distance-vs-time tier.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Erosion and weathering (measuring the effects)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Science working scientifically — take measurements, gather and record data to answer questions; Rocks):** Pupils make observations and measurements providing evidence of weathering and [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS2-1].

- **Standards — US (NGSS 4-ESS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS2-1].

- **Operational details:** This is a PROCEDURAL / investigation node — the goal is the SCIENTIFIC PROCESS of gathering evidence, not just the facts. First nail the distinction: weathering = rock broken down IN PLACE (frost cracking, plant roots, abrasion); erosion = the broken material MOVED away (by water, wind, ice). Then children run fair tests measuring an effect or a RATE — e.g. how much soil a stream washes away with vs without plant cover, or how wind speed changes sand movement — controlling variables and recording measurements. The heart is: change one agent/condition, measure the effect, compare. Stream-tables and shake-jar abrasion tests are the classic vehicles. Emphasise fair testing (same rock, same time, one variable changed) and quantifying (mass lost, distance moved, particles rounded).
bestPractices: Lock down weathering (break-down in place) vs erosion (transport away) before measuring — the investigation depends on the distinction.
Run FAIR TESTS: change one agent/condition (water flow, slope, plant cover, wind speed) and measure the effect while holding others constant.
Quantify effects — mass of material lost, distance sediment travels, how rounded particles become — so evidence is measured, not just described.
Use classic vehicles: a stream-table for water erosion, a shake-jar for abrasion/weathering, ice-in-cracks for freeze-thaw.
Connect measured results back to real landscapes (why a bare slope gullies, why a planted bank holds).
keyRepresentations: A stream-table (sloped tray of soil/sand with controllable water flow).
A shake-jar abrasion test (rock chips shaken, measuring rounding/sediment produced).
A fair-test comparison table (variable changed → measured effect).
Before/after landscape photos or profiles showing change.
A freeze-thaw (water-in-crack) weathering demonstration.
commonMisconceptions: 'Weathering and erosion are the same' — conflating break-down with transport.
'Erosion is always fast/dramatic' — missing that much erosion is slow and gradual.
'Plants cause erosion' — not recognising vegetation usually PROTECTS soil (roots bind it), though roots can also weather rock.
'Harder rocks don't weather' — all rock weathers, just at different rates.
'A single trial proves it' — not valuing repeats/fair tests and measurement.
'Water only erodes, never deposits' — forgetting eroded material is dropped elsewhere.

learn.summary: Ages 9–10 Earth science: this is a PROCEDURAL investigation node whose goal is the scientific process of gathering measured evidence of weathering and erosion, not just the facts. Learners must first distinguish weathering (rock broken down into smaller pieces without being carried away — e.g. frost cracking, plant roots; abrasion, where pieces grind against each other, is often counted as weathering, although it happens while material is being moved) from erosion (the broken material moved away by water, ice, or wind), then run fair tests that change one agent/condition, measure an effect or rate, and compare. Classic vehicles are a stream-table for water erosion, a shake-jar abrasion test, and a freeze-thaw demonstration. Emphasise fair testing (same rock, same time, one variable changed) and quantifying (mass lost, distance moved, particles rounded), then connect measured results back to real landscapes.

activities.title: Stream-table fair test: does plant cover change how much soil erodes?
feedback: If a learner changes more than one thing at once (e.g. adds plants AND lowers the slope), point out the test is no longer fair: 'We can't tell which change caused the difference — hold everything else the same and change only the plant cover.'
If a learner trusts a single trial, prompt: 'Would you get the same grams if you ran it again? Repeat it and see whether the result holds.'

If a learner says plants cause erosion, show the two measured totals: the planted run usually loses less soil because roots bind it — though note roots can also help weather rock in place, which is a different process. How much less erodes depends on soil, slope and flow, so rely on the measured numbers rather than assuming a dramatic drop.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable test-bench lets learners do the fair test and read out rate change with each variable, turning 'what speeds erosion' into measured evidence rather than a described fact. Sliders, a plant-cover toggle, a grams-lost meter, and a logged comparison table are optional concrete ways to scaffold the one-variable-at-a-time discipline.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-ESS2-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS2-1].
Weathering breaks rock down in place (freeze-thaw, biological, abrasion) while erosion transports the material; vegetation cover generally reduces soil erosion.
learnerActions: Build or use a sloped tray of soil/sand with a controllable water source (a real sand/soil stream-table, or a screen bench with sliders for slope and rainfall/flow and a plant-cover toggle).
Run a baseline trial: tilt the tray, set a steady water flow, run it, and measure the soil washed into the catch tray (grams lost) and how far the sediment travelled.
Change exactly ONE variable — add a mat of plant roots — keeping slope, flow, soil, and time identical, then rerun and measure again.
Record both trials in a comparison table (variable changed → measured effect) and state which single variable differed.
Repeat the trial at least once to check whether the result holds, then compare the plant-cover and bare totals.
activities.intendedInsight: Erosion is the transport of broken material, its rate can be measured and changed, and vegetation (root binding) generally reduces soil erosion rather than causing it — a conclusion backed by numbers from a controlled comparison.

activities.title: Shake-jar abrasion + freeze-thaw: separating break-down from transport
feedback: If a learner says 'the rock eroded' for breaking in place, separate the steps: 'Did the pieces move away, or just break? Breaking where it sits is weathering.'
If a learner treats moved material as having 'disappeared', ask 'where did the washed-off bits go?' and name the settling stage as deposition.

If a learner sees no obvious rounding and concludes nothing happened, point to the fines and clouded water — abrasion is real but slow, so the worn-off sediment is the measurable evidence; and remember sugar cubes only model rock and break, round and dissolve much faster.
activities.rationale: Classifying each observation as weathering or erosion directly targets the central conflation, and running abrasion and freeze-thaw as separate demonstrations lets learners attach 'broken in place' versus 'carried away' to the right evidence.
sourceClaims: Weathering breaks rock down in place (freeze-thaw, biological, abrasion) while erosion transports the material; vegetation cover generally reduces soil erosion.
learnerActions: Shake rock chips or gravel in a jar (with some water in it if you want to see clouding) and look for the signs of abrasion — fine sediment produced, water clouding if water is present, and edges gradually dulling. Visible rounding is slow, so the fine material worn off is the clearest short-term evidence that abrasion (weathering) is happening. Sugar cubes can stand in to show the idea quickly, but they dissolve in water and break far faster than rock, so use them only to illustrate the process, not to judge real rounding or rates.
Add water, swirl, then pour the water off into another container and watch where the broken bits settle — material carried away in the water and dropped elsewhere is erosion followed by deposition.

Run a freeze-thaw demonstration: soak a porous block or fill a crack in it with water (keep it wet between cycles), then repeatedly freeze and thaw it — as the water freezes it turns to ice and expands, pushing on the crack walls. Over many cycles this can widen the crack, flake off bits or eventually split the block, though a few classroom cycles may show only small changes; nothing is carried away (weathering in place).
For each observation, state out loud whether it shows weathering or erosion and what the evidence is.
Record how rounded/dulled the particles became and roughly how much sediment/fines were produced.
activities.intendedInsight: Weathering (broken where it sits) and erosion (carried away) are distinct processes; freeze-thaw and abrasion both weather rock, and once material moves it is eventually deposited somewhere else.

activities.title: Reading real landscapes: evidence of change over time
feedback: If a learner says 'nothing happened' to the year-apart bank, use the photos to measure the small change: slow change still counts as erosion.
If a learner thinks only sudden events count, contrast a flood with gradual year-on-year wearing — both are erosion at different rates.
If a learner thinks harder rocks don't weather, note that all rock weathers, just at different rates.
activities.rationale: Connecting measured investigation results back to real landscapes and reading before/after images addresses the 'erosion is always fast' and 'hard rock doesn't weather' misconceptions, and requires learners to produce evidence of change rather than only recall definitions.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-ESS2-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS2-1].
learnerActions: Examine two photos of the same riverbank (or slope) taken about a year apart and describe what has changed.
Measure or estimate the small change (e.g. how far the bank edge retreated) and argue whether water could still be eroding it even though the change looks minor.
Classify features on a landscape image by the agent that shaped them (frost-cracked cliff, wind-carved rock, river-cut valley) and say whether each is mainly weathering or erosion.
Explain, using your measured stream-table results, why a bare slope often gullies and loses more soil while a planted bank usually holds better — and say whether your own numbers showed this.
activities.intendedInsight: Much erosion is slow and gradual, not only dramatic floods; measured change over time is still evidence, and features in real landscapes record the agents (water, ice, wind, vegetation) that acted on them.

constraints: Lock down the weathering (break-down in place) vs erosion (transport away) distinction before measuring — the whole investigation depends on it.
Fair tests require changing one agent/condition (water flow, slope, plant cover, wind speed) while holding everything else constant; otherwise the measured effect cannot be attributed to one cause.
Effects must be quantified — mass of material lost, distance sediment travels, degree of particle rounding/fines produced — so evidence is measured, not just described.

Classification/matching tasks (weathering vs erosion examples, agent ↔ effect, reading a results graph) and tap-to-reveal landscape labelling reinforce vocabulary and interpretation but do not themselves elicit the hands-on measurement and fair-testing that define this procedural node; use them as complements, not substitutes.

A virtual stream-table gives clean read-outs but is a model; a real sand/soil stream-table and shake-jar abrasion test are essential hands-on complements so learners handle genuine material with real grain, texture, and water/sediment behaviour that a model only approximates.
Sugar cubes and other models stand in for rock to show the process faster but dissolve and break unrealistically; do not treat their rates or rounding as real rock behaviour.
A 3D terrain that erodes under rain is a richer, heavier alternative that adds spatial realism but is not required; the core target is controlled measurement and the weathering/erosion distinction.
Include deposition explicitly: eroded material does not disappear, it settles elsewhere.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources are marked verified:false and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims support the standard and the weathering/erosion/vegetation principles but do not establish the comparative or empirical effectiveness of any specific activity or medium.

The legacy row at times implied a live bench is uniquely able to teach this ('a static resource can't', dialogue 'can't run the tests'); these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits. Static and recognition resources can still support classification and interpretation.

The original 'plants cause erosion' misconception handling is retained but nuanced: vegetation generally protects soil by binding it, while roots can also contribute to weathering rock — keep these two effects distinct for learners.
Deposition is central to the assessment but was only a secondary evidence point in the original learn section; it has been promoted into the activities.

The original recommendation's 'eroded total plummets' was softened to a measured, conditions-dependent reduction; the freeze-thaw mechanism was clarified (water freezes to ice and expands over repeated freeze–thaw cycles).

The shake-jar rounding observation was made realistic: visible rounding of real rock is slow over a short lesson, so the measurable short-term evidence is the fines/sediment produced; conclusions about 'rounding' remain approximate.

probeDeeper: In the jar, did the cubes get moved or just broken? Which of those is weathering?
Where did the broken pieces go once the water carried them? What do we call that?
The riverbank changed only a little in a year. Could water still be eroding it? How?
Which agent — water, ice, wind, or plant roots — could break a rock without moving it at all?
assess.correctAnswer: The child shakes the cubes and shows they break down and round in place (weathering), then shows the broken bits carried away by the water and settling elsewhere (erosion = movement, then deposition), and reads the riverbank photos as material worn away and moved over the year — keeping 'breaking in place' separate from 'being moved'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Weathering and erosion are the same thing — uses them interchangeably ('the rock eroded away' for breaking in place)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it — weathering breaks the rock where it sits, erosion carries the pieces away; demonstrate each step on its own.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels breaking-in-place as erosion, or transport as weathering; can't separate the two observations.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores deposition — the moved material just 'disappears' rather than settling somewhere else
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — 'where did the washed-off bits go?' and introduce deposition as the settling stage.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes erosion but never says where the sediment ends up.

errorPatterns.pattern: Erosion is always fast and dramatic (a flood) — slow change doesn't count ('nothing happened' to the year-apart bank)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast rapid vs slow rates; use the photos to measure the small change over a year.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Only accepts sudden events as erosion; dismisses the small year-on-year change in the photos.

responseLevels.gap: Uses weathering and erosion interchangeably; can't produce evidence of either.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes weathering (broken in place) from erosion (moved) with matched evidence, names several agents, and accounts for deposition and slow rates — reading the photos as evidence of change over time.
responseLevels.partial: Produces the observations and names the agents but blurs weathering vs erosion, or ignores where the moved material goes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two photos of the same riverbank a year apart, and a jar where you can shake sugar cubes ('rocks') in water. Show me how you'd get evidence of weathering and of erosion, and as you go, tell me which is which and what your evidence shows.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The weathering/erosion conflation is the crux: many children use the two words as synonyms. Watching whether they attach 'broken where it sits' vs 'carried away' to the right observation separates naming the agents from understanding the two distinct processes — and whether they notice deposition, which is routinely ignored.

sources.claim: NGSS 4-ESS2-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS2-1].
sources.source: NGSS, 4-ESS2 Earth's Systems

sources.claim: Weathering breaks rock down in place (freeze-thaw, biological, abrasion) while erosion transports the material; vegetation cover generally reduces soil erosion.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-7 (Y1/early Y2). Solve one-step WORD PROBLEMS involving addition and subtraction to 20, INCLUDING missing-number problems (7 = ? − 9). Extends within-10 modelling to a larger range and, importantly, to problems where the unknown is not the result.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'solve one-step problems that involve addition and subtraction… and missing number problems such as 7 = ? − 9'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.1 'use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems… with unknowns in all positions'; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
• Operational details — Continue modelling the SITUATION (act out / draw / bar model) rather than keyword-matching, now with numbers to 20 and with the unknown in the start, change or result position. Missing-number problems are the key new demand: the child must represent an unknown and reason to it, often using the inverse or a known bond. Bar/part-whole models become powerful here for making the unknown visible.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): solve result-unknown add/subtract problems to 20 by modelling. Tier B (age 6): solve change-unknown problems and simple missing-number equations with support. Tier C (age 6-7): solve start-unknown and missing-number problems (7 = ? − 9), explaining the model and using the inverse to find the unknown.
bestPractices: Keep teaching modelling of the situation (act-out, drawing, bar/part-whole) over keyword strategies, extending to numbers to 20.
Introduce the unknown in all positions (result, change, start) and use part-whole/bar models to make the unknown visible so children can reason to it.
Connect missing-number problems to the inverse relationship and to known bonds (7 = ? − 9 → ? = 16 via 7 + 9).
Have children write the equation that matches the situation, placing the unknown where it belongs (not always after =).
Progress difficulty by problem structure, not just larger numbers, and discuss why a chosen model fits the story.
keyRepresentations: Bar/tape model showing known parts and an unknown
Part-part-whole model with the unknown in any slot
Objects/drawings acted on to match the story
Empty number line for counting on to find a difference/unknown
Equations with a box/letter for the unknown in varied positions
commonMisconceptions: Keyword-matching (fails on missing-number and compare problems).
Assuming the unknown is always the result, so start- and change-unknown problems stump them.
Rejecting missing-number forms because = is read as 'answer here'.
Combining the two given numbers regardless of the structure (e.g. adding in a start-unknown problem that needs subtraction).
Not using the inverse/known bond to find the unknown, instead guessing.

learn.summary: For ages 5-7 (Y1/early Y2): solve one-step word problems involving addition and subtraction to 20, including missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9. The core objective is modelling the situation (acting out, drawing, bar/part-whole models) rather than keyword-matching, and crucially handling problems where the unknown sits in the start, change or result position — not only the answer slot. Bar/part-whole models make the unknown visible so children can reason to it using the inverse or a known bond.

activities.title: Story-to-bar-model builder
feedback: Check the structure of the model, not just the final number: does the bar place the known parts and the unknown where the story puts them?

If the pieces dragged in don't match the story — for example a given whole treated as a part, or both numbers entered as parts when one of them is actually the whole — ask them to re-read it event by event: 'What was there to begin with? What happened? What is left?'
For 7 = ? − 9, prompt: 'We start with a mystery number, take away 9, and 7 are left — so the mystery number is 9 and 7 put together, 16.'

Praise correctly reasoning to an unknown via the inverse or a known bond, and show how the model did the work: adding the parts to find a missing whole, or taking a known part from the whole to find a missing part.
activities.rationale: The skill is modelling situations with the unknown in varied positions; a build-your-own bar/part-whole model lets the child place the unknown and manipulate it so the inverse is made visible, with varied problem structures generated across a session. An interactive model can rotate the unknown position and give feedback on the structure of the model, which a fixed worked example cannot do, though a fixed example can still illustrate the method. Proposed design; efficacy not independently verified.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
1.OA.1: use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems with unknowns in all positions; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
Bar/part-whole modelling makes the unknown visible and supports reasoning (including via the inverse) across all unknown positions; keyword strategies fail on missing-number problems.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a one-step problem with numbers to 20, e.g. 'I had some sweets, ate 9, and 7 are left.'
Drag the quantities you know into a bar or part-whole frame — for this story, split a whole into a '9 eaten' part and a '7 left' part.
Mark where the unknown sits in the model (here the WHOLE — the number you started with — is the mystery).
Act on the model to find the unknown — combine the two parts to fill the whole (7 + 9 = 16), or count on along a number line.
Repeat with problems that rotate the unknown through result, change and start positions, and with pure missing-number equations like 7 = ? − 9.
Write the equation that matches your model, placing the unknown where it belongs (not always after the = sign).
activities.intendedInsight: A problem where the unknown is the START or the CHANGE, not the answer, is not impossible: the bar model shows exactly where the mystery sits. If the unknown is the whole, combining the known parts finds it. If the unknown is a part, taking the known part away from the whole (or counting on from it) finds it. Children learn to model any structure rather than hope a keyword tells them what to do.

activities.title: Hands-on modelling with counters, drawings and paper bars
feedback: If the model and story disagree, re-read the story one event at a time and adjust the counters/bar.
Reinforce that 'took away / left' does not automatically mean subtract — the structure of the story decides the operation.
Celebrate explanations that justify the operation from the situation, not from a single word.
activities.rationale: Concrete acting-out and drawing underpin the pictorial bar model and give young children a tangible way to represent an unknown before abstract equations. This supports the standards' call for concrete objects and pictorial representations.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
Bar/part-whole modelling makes the unknown visible and supports reasoning (including via the inverse) across all unknown positions; keyword strategies fail on missing-number problems.
learnerActions: Act out or draw the story with physical counters before choosing any operation.
Lay out a paper tape/bar strip and partition it into known parts and an unknown part to match the story.
Use an empty number line to count on and find a difference or an unknown.
Say aloud what you know, what you are trying to find, and why the operation you chose fits the story.
activities.intendedInsight: Modelling the situation with concrete materials — rather than matching keywords — reveals the correct operation even when the unknown is not the result.

activities.title: Coaching dialogue: 'What do we know, what are we finding?'
feedback: When a child applies an operation to the two given numbers automatically, without checking the story (e.g. trying 7 − 9 or 9 − 7 for 7 = ? − 9), redirect to the story structure with a question rather than giving the answer.
Follow the child's approach and ask for justification; adapt prompts to whether they are stuck on parsing '=' or on choosing the operation.
activities.rationale: Missing-number and start-unknown problems demand reasoning to an unknown; a Socratic dialogue may develop that reasoning by adapting to the child's approach. Dialogue complements, and does not replace, hands-on and pictorial modelling. This medium's efficacy is a proposal, not verified.
learnerActions: Respond to a coach who asks you to name what is known and what is unknown in a problem.
Justify which operation you will use and where the unknown sits, especially for start-unknown and missing-number problems.
Talk through 7 = ? − 9: identify that you need a starting number which, after removing 9, leaves 7.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning aloud about knowns and the unknown can develop the modelling and inverse reasoning needed for harder problem structures.

activities.title: Worked bar-model example with revealable steps
feedback: Prompt the learner to predict each next step before revealing it.
Ask them to point to where the unknown sits before the final number is shown.
activities.rationale: A static worked example anchors the pictorial modelling method and can be revisited; it cannot generate varied structures or let the child model their own problem, so it works best as a scaffold before or alongside the interactive builder.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
learnerActions: Study one worked problem shown with a bar model.
Reveal the solution steps one at a time and relate each step to the story.
Restate how the parts and whole map onto what the story gave and what it asked.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly worked bar model anchors the method and shows how the unknown is found from the known quantities: combining the parts when the whole is unknown, or taking a known part from the whole when a part is unknown.

activities.title: Missing-number and word-problem practice set
feedback: If a child answers 7 = ▢ − 9 as 7 − 9 or refuses, return to the bar model: whole ▢, parts 9 and 7, so ▢ = 16.

If a child subtracts on a take-away start-unknown problem (e.g. 'I had some, ate 9, 7 are left'), have them act it out to see that the start was larger than what remained. (On an add-on start-unknown problem such as 'I had some, got 5 more, now I have 12', subtracting 12 − 5 is correct.)
activities.rationale: Varied-position items probe the target directly and surface misconceptions, but practice/fill-in tasks present problems to solve and may not by themselves build the modelling process, so they belong after modelling work rather than before it.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.1: use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems with unknowns in all positions; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
learnerActions: Fill in equations with the unknown in different positions, e.g. 7 = ▢ − 9, ▢ + 5 = 12, 12 − ▢ = 8.
Answer word problems with picture support where the unknown is the result, change or start.
Mark which problems were 'find the start' problems rather than 'find what's left'.
activities.intendedInsight: Problems with the unknown in varied positions require the same modelling reasoning; recognising the structure matters more than the keyword.

constraints: Keep teaching modelling of the situation (act-out, drawing, bar/part-whole) over keyword strategies, extending the number range to 20.
Introduce the unknown in all positions (result, change, start) and use part-whole/bar models to make the unknown visible.
Connect missing-number problems to the inverse relationship and known bonds (7 = ? − 9 → ? = 16 via 7 + 9).
Have children place the unknown where it belongs in the equation, not always after the = sign.
Progress difficulty by problem STRUCTURE, not just larger numbers, and discuss why a chosen model fits the story.
Practice/fill-in items probe the target and surface misconceptions but do not by themselves build the modelling process; use them after hands-on and pictorial modelling.
A worked example is a scaffold: it anchors the method but cannot generate varied structures or let the child model their own problem.
Do not teach keyword-to-operation rules ('away/left' → subtract); these fail on start-unknown, change-unknown and missing-number problems.
Reading '=' as 'the answer goes here' causes children to reject missing-number forms; treat '=' relationally.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the diagnostic arithmetic: (1) 12 − 4 = 8 ✓; (2) start-unknown 'some cars, 5 drive away, 7 left' → start = 5 + 7 = 12 ✓; (3) 7 = ▢ − 9 → ▢ = 7 + 9 = 16 ✓. Added practice items also check out: ▢ + 5 = 12 → ▢ = 7; 12 − ▢ = 8 → ▢ = 4. These are used consistently in the activity feedback.

The source row lists two of three sources as verified:false (CCSS-M and the NCETM/IES bar-model claim). Comparative/efficacy framing from these should be treated as unverified; the rewrite scopes the 'interactive vs static', 'worked example' and 'dialogue' claims to stated affordances/limits rather than universal necessity or medium superiority.
The dialogue activity carries no sourceClaims because no listed source supports the efficacy of a Socratic dialogue medium; its benefit is stated as a proposal only.

The original rationale stated 'a static picture can't' generate varied structures and that a quiz 'presents problems rather than teaching'. These are retained only as qualified affordance/limit statements; a fixed example can still teach the method and practice items can still probe the target.
Independent re-audit confirms no learner-facing arithmetic, structural or contradiction errors; feedback remains coherent with the stated sweets example (whole = 16 from parts 9 and 7) throughout.

probeDeeper: In the cars problem, did the number of cars at the start get bigger or smaller after some drove away?
For 7 = ▢ − 9, what number do we start with so that taking 9 leaves 7?
How could counters or a bar help you see the cars problem?
Which of these was a 'find the start' problem, not a 'find what's left' problem?

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy — picks the operation from a word ('away/left' → subtract) regardless of structure, so start-unknown '5 drive away, 7 left' is computed as 7 − 5 or 5 − 7.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the situation with counters or a bar model before choosing an operation; do not teach keyword-to-operation rules.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child subtracts on the start-unknown problem (answers 2) instead of adding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the missing-number equation left-to-right as 'compute the two numbers' — 7 = ▢ − 9 answered as 7 − 9 (or 'can't do it', or 2).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat = relationally with a part-whole / bar model (whole ▢, parts 9 and 7, so ▢ = 9 + 7).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives −2, 2, or refuses, treating ▢ as 'the answer of a sum'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Correct set-up but a counting / arithmetic slip within 20.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the calculation; the modelling and operation choice are sound, so do not reteach them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Right operation and structure, answer off by one or two.

responseLevels.gap: Applies a keyword/default operation; cannot handle start-unknown or missing-number equations.
responseLevels.full: Models and solves varied structures within 20 — result-unknown, start-unknown, and missing-number equations — choosing the operation from the situation.
responseLevels.partial: Solves result-unknown problems reliably but defaults to subtracting on start-unknown, or cannot parse 7 = ▢ − 9.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these — you can use counters. (1) I have 12 sweets and eat 4 — how many are left? (2) There were some cars; 5 drive away and 7 are left — how many were there at the start? (3) Fill the box: 7 = ▢ − 9.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three problems are deliberately different STRUCTURES (result-unknown is easy; start-unknown and the missing-minuend equation are hard — CGI/Carpenter). A keyword solver does 12 − 4 fine but subtracts on 'drive away' for the start-unknown and cannot handle 7 = ▢ − 9. Watch whether the child models the situation or grabs numbers plus a keyword.
