pedagogy.summary: A linear function y = mx + c produces a straight-line graph, where m (the gradient) is the constant rate of change — the line's steepness and direction — and c is the starting value, the y-intercept. It is best taught by generating (x, y) pairs from the equation and plotting them so the straight line is DISCOVERED from a constant rate, then varying m and c independently so each parameter is bound to its visual effect. Rate contexts such as distance-time (where gradient = speed) give the numbers meaning, and the graph-as-picture and slope-height misconceptions must be confronted directly.
bestPractices: Build the line from a table of values first, so 'constant rate produces a straight line' is discovered rather than asserted.
Vary m and c independently and watch the effect: a larger m steepens the line, a negative m flips its direction, and changing c slides the whole line up or down through its intercept.
Use rate contexts (distance-time, cost-per-item) so the gradient means something real — speed, price per unit — not a bare number.
Confront graph-as-picture explicitly: a distance-time graph is a record of a relationship, not a picture of the route; a rising line is not a hill.
Contrast linear with non-linear (plot y = x^2 beside y = 2x + 1) so 'straight line' becomes a property to test, not an assumption.
keyRepresentations: Table of values → plotted points → straight line
y = mx + c with m (gradient) and c (y-intercept) annotated on the line
Distance-time graph where the gradient of the line is the speed
A family of lines pivoting (as m changes) and sliding (as c changes)
commonMisconceptions: Graph-as-picture / iconic: reads the shape of the line as a literal picture of the situation (the line goes up, so the person went up a hill).
Slope-height confusion: judges the line that is HIGHER on the graph as faster/greater, rather than the STEEPER one.
Gradient/intercept swap: reads c as the slope or m as where the line crosses the axis.
Believes every equation gives a straight line, and is surprised that y = x^2 curves.

learn.summary: A linear function y = mx + c produces a straight-line graph, where m (the gradient) is the constant rate of change — the line's steepness and direction — and c is the starting value (the y-intercept). The concept is best built by generating (x, y) pairs from the equation and plotting them so the straight line is DISCOVERED from a constant rate, then varying m and c independently so each parameter is bound to its visual effect. Rate contexts such as distance-time (gradient = speed) give the numbers meaning, and the graph-as-picture and slope-height misconceptions must be confronted directly. For ages 12-14 (KS3).

activities.title: Build the line from a table of values
feedback: If the points don't line up, check your arithmetic: each y should change by the same amount (here +2) for each step of +1 in x.
Point out that y when x = 0 is 1 — this is exactly the c value and the point where the line crosses the y-axis.
activities.rationale: Deriving the line from a value table lets 'constant rate produces a straight line' be discovered rather than asserted, and exposes the intercept concretely as the value at x = 0.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'recognise, sketch and produce graphs of linear and quadratic functions of one variable' and 'calculate and interpret gradients and intercepts of graphs of such linear equations numerically, graphically and algebraically'.
learnerActions: Take the equation y = 2x + 1 and complete a table of values for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 (giving y = -3, -1, 1, 3, 5).
Plot each (x, y) pair on axes and join them.
Observe that equal steps in x give equal steps in y, and that the points fall exactly on a straight line.
State in your own words why a constant rate of change produces a straight line.
activities.intendedInsight: A straight line is a consequence of a constant rate of change, not an assumption — 'straight' is something you can test from the numbers.

activities.title: Vary m and c independently
feedback: When a learner predicts where the line will cross the axis for a given c, confirm it lands exactly at (0, c).
If a learner thinks a negative m just makes a 'smaller' uphill line, show two points and compute the change: y decreases as x increases, so the line falls.
Emphasise that changing c never changes the steepness, and that changing m never moves the y-axis crossing (it stays at (0, c)) — this separation is the key reading.
activities.rationale: Binding each parameter to its own visual role (pivot for m, slide for c) is the central conceptual payload and directly counters the gradient/intercept swap. Live sliders with a recomputing line and a synced value table can make this relationship felt; predicting the intercept before it appears tests understanding.
learnerActions: Keep c fixed and change m: try m = 1, then m = 3, then m = -2, replotting or predicting each line.

Describe what happens as positive m gets larger (the line steepens) and as m goes negative (the line flips from climbing to falling, pivoting about the same intercept); steepness depends on the size of m ignoring its sign, so m = -2 is steeper than m = 1.
Now keep m fixed and change c: try c = 0, then c = 2, then c = -3.
Describe what happens (the whole line slides up or down and crosses the y-axis exactly at c), and predict the crossing point before plotting.
activities.intendedInsight: m controls steepness AND direction (sign), while c slides the whole line to its y-intercept — each parameter is bound to a distinct visual effect.

activities.title: Distance-time race: steepness is speed, not height
feedback: If a learner picks Maggie because her line is higher at 4 seconds, take two points on each line and compute distance-per-second together, then show Emma's steeper line draws level at 5 seconds and pulls ahead afterward — steepness, not height, is speed.

If a learner talks about hills, going uphill, or the shape of a 'track', ask: 'If someone walked in a circle around their home, what would a distance-time graph look like?' Contrast a picture of the route with a record of distance over time.
If a learner names the head-start number (the 10) as the speed, change c only (steepness untouched) and then m only (line pivots), and re-read the equation to re-attach 'speed' to the gradient.
activities.rationale: A distance-time context gives gradient real meaning (speed) and directly confronts the slope-height and graph-as-picture misconceptions in one experience, especially when two lines cross so the higher-but-slower line is visible. Choosing a comparison time before the crossing (here t = 4, where the higher-at-4-seconds runner is the slower one) forces the discrimination, and the meeting point at t = 5 makes the catch-up concrete.
sourceClaims: Students confuse 'higher on the graph' with 'faster', assuming a runner is fastest because at 5 seconds her line is above another's, and make y-intercept and slope-direction errors when producing a linear graph (e.g. drawing a positive slope where negative is needed, or an incorrect intercept such as f=30); some assume two matched graphs must share the same vertical intercept.

Students interpret distance-time graphs as pictures of the situation ('as the graph goes up and down, Tom's path is going up and down'; a straight line means a straight path; a negative slope means a detour) — the graph-as-picture / iconic misconception — and misread slope direction as speeding up/slowing down; the hill-shaped graph is a deliberate distractor (Card 2 matched to interpretation E).
learnerActions: Plot two runners' distance over time on the same axes, e.g. Emma d = 6t and Maggie d = 4t + 10.
Before computing, predict who is faster and write your reason.
At 4 seconds, note that Maggie's line is higher (26 m versus Emma's 24 m), but Emma's line is steeper.
Take two points on each line and compute distance-per-second (Emma gains 6 per second; Maggie gains 4 per second).
Identify where/whether the lines cross — here they meet at 5 seconds (both at 30 m), after which Emma pulls ahead — and say what that crossing means in the race.
In the equations, identify which number is the speed (the coefficient of t, the gradient) and which is the head start (the constant, the intercept).
activities.intendedInsight: Speed is the gradient (steepness), not the height of the line; a runner can start ahead (large c) yet be slower (small m). Emma is faster because her line is steeper, covering more distance each second, even though Maggie's line sits higher at 4 seconds — until the lines meet at 5 seconds, after which Emma pulls ahead.

activities.title: Predict-then-test: does every equation give a straight line?
feedback: If a learner predicts 'straight' because 'it's an equation with x in it, like the straight ones', the emerging parabola confronts this directly — revisit the value table and show the changing step size.
Point out the symmetry of the parabola about x = 0 and that the differences between successive y-values are themselves changing, unlike the constant difference in a linear table.
activities.rationale: A prediction stated before observing is diagnostic of the all-equations-are-linear misconception, and contrasting a curve with a line beside it makes 'straight' a testable property. Contrasting the differing step sizes grounds the distinction numerically (the constant-difference test holds for equally spaced x-values, as used in the suggested tables).
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'recognise, sketch and produce graphs of linear and quadratic functions of one variable' and 'calculate and interpret gradients and intercepts of graphs of such linear equations numerically, graphically and algebraically'.
learnerActions: Before plotting, predict: will y = x^2 give a straight line or a curve? Write your answer AND your reason first.
Build a table of values for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 (giving y = 4, 1, 0, 1, 4), plot the points, and join them.
Plot y = 2x + 1 on the same axes for comparison.
Compare how y changes: for y = 2x + 1 the step is constant (+2 each time); for y = x^2 the steps differ (-3, -1, +1, +3), so the graph curves.
State what makes an equation produce a straight line versus a curve.
activities.intendedInsight: Not every equation is linear; a straight line requires a constant rate of change. 'Straight' is a property that depends on the equation, discovered by testing, not assumed.

activities.title: Check and consolidate: match, judge, and sort
feedback: Include a 'which line is faster/steeper' item where the correct line is NOT the one highest on the graph at the compared time, so the slope-height misconception is actively tested.
For any item answered via height rather than steepness, return to taking two points and computing the change per step.
activities.rationale: Matching, comparison, and categorisation are efficient checks of the concept; a 'higher but slower' item surfaces the slope-height misconception. These checks confirm the parameter-to-feature link rather than building it, so they work best after the dynamic exploration.
sourceClaims: Students confuse 'higher on the graph' with 'faster', assuming a runner is fastest because at 5 seconds her line is above another's, and make y-intercept and slope-direction errors when producing a linear graph (e.g. drawing a positive slope where negative is needed, or an incorrect intercept such as f=30); some assume two matched graphs must share the same vertical intercept.
learnerActions: Match each equation to its graph.
Given two straight-line graphs, decide which is steeper (and in a distance-time context, which is faster), explicitly reasoning from steepness rather than height.
Sort a set of equations into 'produces a straight line' and 'produces a curve'.
For an equation like d = 6t + 10, state which number is the gradient (speed) and which is the intercept (head start).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates reading gradient and intercept from both equation and graph, and distinguishing linear from non-linear, while resisting the slope-height distractor.

constraints: Matching, multiple-choice comparison, and categorisation confirm understanding but do not themselves build the dynamic link between a parameter and its visual feature; use them after exploration, not instead of it.

A static annotated y = mx + c diagram (tap m to highlight steepness, tap c to highlight the crossing point) can summarise the gradient and intercept on one line but cannot itself show the pivot-and-slide; it works as a recap card after dynamic work, not as the first teacher of the relationship.

The slope-height and graph-as-picture misconceptions must be confronted with a case where the higher line (at the compared time) is the slower one; a single rising line can reinforce rather than break 'higher = faster'.

When using Emma d = 6t and Maggie d = 4t + 10, compare at a time before the lines cross (they meet at t = 5, both 30 m); t = 4 gives Maggie higher (26) but Emma steeper and faster, with Emma pulling ahead after t = 5.

Interactive sliders, a live-redrawing line, and a synced value table are optional ways to make the equation-to-graph relationship concrete; the same insight can be reached by hand-plotting several lines and comparing them.
Require learners to state reasons, not just answers, when judging which runner is faster — the reason is what distinguishes gradient reasoning from slope-height reasoning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original material claimed 3D rendering 'adds nothing' and that open dialogue is not a natural vehicle; these categorical modality claims have been removed. A 3D view is not the natural representation for a two-variable linear relationship, and a coaching conversation can still probe reasoning ('how do you know Emma is faster?') — such prompts are retained inside activity feedback — without claiming dialogue cannot teach the concept.

Arithmetic checked: y = 2x + 1 over x = -2..2 gives -3,-1,1,3,5 (constant +2); y = x^2 gives 4,1,0,1,4 with non-constant differences -3,-1,+1,+3. Emma d = 6t vs Maggie d = 4t + 10 are EQUAL at t = 5 (both 30 m) and cross there, so the original row's claim that 'Maggie's line is higher at 5 seconds' is false for these numbers. The race activity's comparison has been corrected to t = 4 (Maggie 26, Emma 24), with the lines meeting at t = 5 and Emma pulling ahead afterward; the steeper = faster teaching point is preserved.

At exactly t = 5 neither runner is ahead (both 30 m); Emma leads only for t > 5, so learner-facing text describes t = 5 as the meeting/catch-up point and 'pulls ahead afterward' rather than an overtake exactly at 5 seconds.
The constant-difference argument distinguishes linear from quadratic only for equally spaced x-values; this condition is built into the suggested tables.

assess.poeTask: Before plotting anything, ask the child: 'Will y = x^2 give a straight line or a curved one? Write down your answer AND your reason first.' Then have them build a table of values for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, plot the points, and join them. The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part: children who predict 'straight' because 'it is an equation with x in it, like the straight ones' reveal the all-equations-are-linear misconception, and the emerging parabola confronts it directly.
probeDeeper: At the very start (0 seconds) Maggie's line begins higher than Emma's. Does starting further ahead mean running faster? Why or why not?
Suppose Emma's race is d = 6t and Maggie's is d = 4t + 10. Which number tells you the speed, and which tells you the head start?
If the two lines crossed at some point, what would that moment mean in the race?
Would a runner who is gradually slowing down give a straight line or a curved one — and why?
assess.correctAnswer: Emma is running faster, because speed is shown by the steepness (gradient) of the line, not by how high it is: a steeper line covers more distance in each second. Maggie's line being higher at 5 seconds only means she was further ahead at that moment, not that she is faster.

errorPatterns.pattern: Slope-height confusion: 'Maggie is faster because her line is higher up the graph at 5 seconds' — reads vertical position as speed rather than steepness
errorPatterns.nextMove: Take two points on each line and compute distance-per-second together; show that the steeper line overtakes, so steepness (not height) is speed.
errorPatterns.distractor: Maggie — at 5 seconds her line is higher up the graph, so she must be the faster runner.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Maggie and justifies by how high her line sits, not by how steep it is.

errorPatterns.pattern: Graph-as-picture / iconic: reads the line as a literal picture of the route (a rising line means the runner went uphill; a steeper line means a steeper hill)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask the classic MAP prompt: 'If someone walked in a circle around their home, what would the graph look like?' Contrast a picture of the route with a record of distance over time.
errorPatterns.distractor: The steeper line just means that runner's track went up a steeper hill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about hills, going up, or the shape of the track rather than distance-over-time; may pick the 'steeper hill' reading.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gradient/intercept swap: when reading an equation like d = 6t + 10, names c (the 10) as the speed or m (the 6) as the starting distance
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bind each parameter with the slider — change c only and the steepness is untouched; change m only and the line pivots — then re-read the equation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Surfaces on the follow-up equation probe, not the runners graph: the child attaches 'speed' to the wrong number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes all equations give straight lines: expects y = x^2 to be straight and is surprised by the curve
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build a table for y = x^2 alongside y = 2x + 1 and plot both; the curvature is discovered, and 'straight' becomes a property that depends on the equation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Surfaces on the POE / follow-up, not the runners graph: predicts 'straight' for y = x^2 because 'it's an equation like the others'.

responseLevels.gap: Picks the higher line as faster, or reads the graph as a literal picture of the route; makes no link between steepness and speed.
responseLevels.full: Identifies Emma as faster because gradient = speed, distinguishes head-start (intercept) from speed (gradient), maps both onto the equation, and predicts a curve for a non-constant rate — relating the parameters and transferring to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Says the steeper line is faster, and can point to gradient and intercept when prompted, but cannot yet explain how m and c act together or map them onto the equation form (d = 6t vs d = 4t + 10) — lists the features without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two straight-line graphs showing two runners' distance from the start over time, drawn on the same axes. At 5 seconds, Maggie's line is higher than Emma's line, but Emma's line is steeper. Who is running faster — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands gradient-as-rate chooses Emma and justifies by steepness; a child holding the slope-height misconception chooses Maggie precisely BECAUSE her line is higher. The two reasoning paths give opposite first-tier answers, and the required reason (tier two) reveals whether 'faster' is being read from steepness or from height — a child cannot easily land the right answer for the wrong reason here.

sources.claim: Students confuse 'higher on the graph' with 'faster', assuming a runner is fastest because at 5 seconds her line is above another's, and make y-intercept and slope-direction errors when producing a linear graph (e.g. drawing a positive slope where negative is needed, or an incorrect intercept such as f=30); some assume two matched graphs must share the same vertical intercept.
sources.source: Mathematics Assessment Project, 'Comparing Lines and Linear Equations' (Grade 8) — Common Issues table (teacher guide, p.T-3)

sources.claim: Students interpret distance-time graphs as pictures of the situation ('as the graph goes up and down, Tom's path is going up and down'; a straight line means a straight path; a negative slope means a detour) — the graph-as-picture / iconic misconception — and misread slope direction as speeding up/slowing down; the hill-shaped graph is a deliberate distractor (Card 2 matched to interpretation E).
sources.source: Mathematics Assessment Project, 'Interpreting Distance–Time Graphs' (Grade 8) — Common Issues table (teacher guide, p.T-3)

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should 'recognise, sketch and produce graphs of linear and quadratic functions of one variable' and 'calculate and interpret gradients and intercepts of graphs of such linear equations numerically, graphically and algebraically'.
sources.source: National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study (KS3), gov.uk

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten → Year 1). ONE-TO-ONE CORRESPONDENCE — assigning exactly one number-word to each object while counting. The single most central node in the Mathematics taxonomy: the 'how-to-count' foundation every later number concept rests on.
• Standards — UK (DfE): Sits in the EYFS Mathematics programme (Development Matters: 'count objects, actions and sounds'; one-to-one correspondence). No standalone National Curriculum statement — the Year 1 statutory 'count, read and write numbers to 100' assumes accurate object counting; it is the enabling skill, not itself a line of the NC.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.4a verbatim — 'When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.' One of Gelman & Gallistel's three 'how-to-count' principles.
• Operational details: Teach TAGGING + KEEPING TRACK — the child must partition the set into 'already counted' vs 'not yet counted' (Thompson). Move/tap each object into a counted pile as it is named; one touch = one word (synchrony). Progress the arrangement: line → array/circle → scattered (hardest — no natural start or track). Start with small sets (≤5) and moveable, tangible objects.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (4–5) counts a line of ≤5 moveable objects, one touch per word, no skips/double-counts. Tier B (5–6) counts ≤10–20 in a line/array AND spots an adult's deliberate skip or double-count. Tier C (6) counts a scattered set to 20 by organising it (lining up / moving counted items) and explains how they avoided recounting.
bestPractices: Teach the 'move-it' method: physically move (or tap) each object into a counted pile so the counted/uncounted partition is visible — Thompson's core requirement for the principle.
Insist on synchrony: one point/touch = one number word; slow the count so the tag and the word land together (rushing causes the classic coordination errors).
Progress the arrangement deliberately: line → array/circle → scattered; scattered sets are the true test because the child must impose their own tracking.
Deliberately model errors (skip one; count one twice) and ask 'did I count right?' — recognising a miscount is diagnostic of the principle.
Keep sets small and objects moveable and tangible (Thompson: tangible/moveable objects help distinguish already-counted from yet-to-be-counted), then build to larger sets.
Count everyday things constantly — stairs, claps, plates (WWC: dedicate time daily and integrate counting throughout the day).
keyRepresentations: Moveable counters + a 'counted' pile / sorting tray (the partition made physical).
Five-frame and ten-frame (structured slots enforce one object per cell).
Fingers — a built-in one-to-one manipulative.
A counting track / row of boxes where each object sits in exactly one box.
Number names spoken in rhythm with points (the aural–motor pairing).
commonMisconceptions: Coordination errors: saying words faster than pointing (or vice versa) → skips or double-counts as the word and the touch drift out of sync.
No tracking strategy on scattered sets → recounting some objects and missing others (the counted/uncounted partition never forms).
Believing pointing without saying (or saying without pointing) still 'counts' — the pairing IS the principle.
Confusing one-to-one correspondence with merely reciting the number-word sequence (stable order): a child can chant '1,2,3,4,5' yet not tag objects one-to-one.

learn.summary: One-to-one correspondence for ages 4–6: assigning exactly one number word to each object while counting, which requires both tagging (one touch = one word, in synchrony) and keeping track (partitioning the set into already-counted vs not-yet-counted). The central learning mechanism is making that partition visible and manipulable — physically moving or tapping each counted object aside — and progressing arrangements from line → array/circle → scattered, where the child must impose their own tracking. Activities combine performing the count, spotting deliberate miscounts, and progressing to organising a scattered set.

activities.title: Feed the squirrel: tap-count a scattered pile
feedback: If the total comes out too high, ask: 'Did any object get two number words? Let's slide each one over as we say its number.'
When a child rushes, slow the count so each touch and each spoken word land together — one touch, one word.
If scattered counting fails, suggest lining the objects up or moving each counted one aside so you can see what is left.
Praise correct reasoning that names WHY: 'You gave each acorn exactly one number and kept the counted ones separate.'
activities.rationale: Thompson identifies the one-one principle as pairing one counting word with each item and partitioning the set into already-counted vs not-yet-counted; tangible, moveable objects help make that distinction, so physically moving counted items makes the core cognitive move visible. An optional interactive version can dim/lock already-counted objects in easy mode and allow double-taps in a challenge mode to let the error surface — this is one proposed way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required or source-proven-superior medium.
sourceClaims: The one-one principle = assigning one and only one counting word to each item; the child must partition the collection into already-counted vs not-yet-counted (tagging + keeping track); tangible, moveable objects help make this distinction.
K.CC.4a: 'When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.'
learnerActions: Count a small pile of objects (e.g. 7 acorns to feed a squirrel) by touching each one exactly once, saying one number word with each touch.
Move or tap each counted object into a 'counted' pile/basket so it is clearly separated from the not-yet-counted objects.
Deliberately rush once and double-tap an object; notice the spoken total becomes wrong (e.g. you say 'eight' even though the basket still holds only 7 acorns).
Tidy the scattered objects into a line and recount, touching each once, so it is easier to get a total you can trust.
When the line count gives the right answer, say aloud why: each object got one word and none was counted twice.
activities.intendedInsight: The rule 'one word per object, and keep track of what you've already counted' is the very difference between a wrong count and a right one; the counted/uncounted split can be made visible and must be maintained.

activities.title: Did Teddy count right? Spot the miscount
feedback: Correct answer: 'No — Teddy counted one button twice, so he said too many. Each button should get just one number word. There are 6.'
If the child accepts '7' because 'he said seven', recount together slowly, sliding each button aside with its single number word so one-word-per-object is visible.

If the child senses it is wrong but cannot locate the double-counted button, replay the count slowly and ask 'Which button did Teddy count twice?' to nudge the monitoring habit — error-monitoring of others' counts develops later, so do not treat this as a misunderstanding to reteach.
Ask probes: 'Which button did Teddy count twice?'; 'If Teddy started from the other end, how many would there be?'; 'What could Teddy do so he doesn't count a button twice?'
activities.rationale: Deliberately modelling errors and asking 'did I count right?' gives useful evidence about the principle: a child who holds the one-word-per-object pairing may reject the count because that pairing broke, while accepting the last word spoken suggests the pairing is not yet the child's rule. Results need cautious reading, because monitoring other people's counts develops later than counting accurately yourself, and recounting to get a different total is itself a legitimate way to detect the error.
sourceClaims: The one-one principle = assigning one and only one counting word to each item; the child must partition the collection into already-counted vs not-yet-counted (tagging + keeping track); tangible, moveable objects help make this distinction.
learnerActions: Watch an adult (or a 'count-with-me' character/puppet) count a set of 6 buttons, deliberately pointing to the SAME button twice (…points to one button saying 'four', points to it again saying 'five', ending on 'seven').
Decide whether the count is right and explain how you know.
Point to exactly which button got two number words.
Recount the set yourself, sliding each button aside as it gets its single number word, and give the correct total (6).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising a miscount — and locating the specific object that received two words — shows understanding that the word-to-object pairing IS the rule, not just that the last word spoken is the answer.

activities.title: Count everyday things in structured frames and in daily life
feedback: If a child skips or double-counts in a frame, point out that each cell holds exactly one object and should get exactly one word.
For daily counts, keep a steady rhythm so each action gets one number word.
When a scattered set goes wrong, invite the child to line up or move counted items — 'How can you keep track of which ones you've done?'
activities.rationale: Structured representations (five-/ten-frames, counting tracks, fingers) place one object per slot, supporting the one-object-per-word pairing, and the WWC practice guide advises dedicating daily time to maths and integrating counting throughout the day along a developmental progression. Scattered sets require the child to impose their own tracking, making them the harder test of the principle.
sourceClaims: Teaching Math to Young Children: dedicate daily time to maths, integrate counting through the day, follow a developmental progression from counting to cardinality.

The one-one principle = assigning one and only one counting word to each item; the child must partition the collection into already-counted vs not-yet-counted (tagging + keeping track); tangible, moveable objects help make this distinction.
learnerActions: Place one object per cell in a five-frame or ten-frame (or a row of boxes), so each object sits in exactly one slot, then count by touching each filled cell once.
Use fingers as a built-in one-to-one tool: raise one finger per counted object.
Count everyday things through the day — stairs as you climb, claps, plates at the table — one number word per step/clap/plate.
Progress from a line, to an array or circle, to a scattered set that you organise yourself before counting.
activities.intendedInsight: One-to-one correspondence applies everywhere and is strengthened by frequent, varied practice; structured slots and fingers support one object per number word (though a child can still skip or double-count cells), and organising a scattered set is the harder test of self-imposed tracking.

constraints: Start with small sets (≤5) of moveable, tangible objects, then build to ≤10–20 and finally scattered sets to 20.
Insist on synchrony: one point/touch = one number word; slow the count so tag and word land together, since rushing causes the classic skip/double-count coordination errors.
Progress arrangements deliberately: line → array/circle → scattered. Scattered sets are hardest because there is no natural start or track.
Distinguish one-to-one correspondence from merely reciting the number-word sequence: a child can chant '1,2,3,4,5' without tagging objects one-to-one.

A static labelled set (each object pre-tagged 1..n) can serve as a reference showing a completed correct count, but it does not let the child perform the one-tap-one-word act, so use it as a reference/scaffold alongside the child counting, not as a substitute.

A multiple-choice or matching task ('how many?' / 'did they count correctly?' / match each object to one numeral) can check recognition and verify whether a count was correct, but does not itself elicit the child's physical one-touch-one-word performance; use it as a retrieval and verification companion alongside, not instead of, the child performing the count.

Point/say coordination lag is a developmental stage, not a misunderstanding — do not drill or verbally correct; slow the pace and have the child physically move each object, which tends to self-correct with the move-it scaffold.
Error-monitoring of others' counts develops later than performing one's own count; a child may reject a wrong total yet be unable to locate the double-counted object.

This is a foundational enabling skill: the statutory Year 1 goal 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals' (National Curriculum in England) assumes accurate object counting but is not itself a line stating one-to-one correspondence.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The WWC practice guide source was marked verified:false in the row; its claim is retained but should be re-checked before relying on it.

The original 'ideal' recommendation (tap-to-count interactive) and its interaction examples (dim/lock already-counted objects, challenge-mode double-tap, tidy-up line-up) are preserved as one concrete, proposed way to make the partition visible, not asserted as the only or best medium; comparative efficacy is not source-established.

Legacy categorical claims that a static image 'cannot teach' the act, that a quiz 'assesses rather than teaches', that 3D 'adds nothing' / 'makes tracking harder', and that the learning 'is not a dialogue' were narrowed to observable affordance statements; necessity or superiority of any medium is not established by the sources provided.

Counting-logic self-check: the Teddy diagnostic has 6 buttons but reaches 'seven' because one button receives two number words (one extra word); recounting with one word per button yields 6, so the correct answer (6) and the error explanation are consistent. The acorn scenario (7 acorns, one double-tap → 8) is likewise consistent. No arithmetic errors propagate into learner-facing tasks.

K.CC.4a is cited in activity 1 because it states verbatim the one-object-to-one-number pairing the child performs there; it doubles as standards grounding rather than support for the specific 'move objects to visualise the partition' design choice, which rests on Thompson.

probeDeeper: Can you show me exactly which button Teddy counted twice?
If Teddy started counting from the other end instead, how many buttons would there be?
Count them yourself — slide each button over here as you count it.
What could Teddy do so he doesn't count a button twice?
assess.correctAnswer: No — Teddy counted one button twice, so he said too many. Each button should get just one number word. There are 6.

errorPatterns.pattern: trusts the last word said no matter how the counting went ('he said seven, so there's seven') — thinks the answer is just whatever number you end on
errorPatterns.nextMove: recount together slowly, sliding each button to one side as it gets its single number word, so one-word-per-object is visible
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, Teddy is right — there are 7.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: accepts Teddy's 7 and, when asked how, repeats 'because he said seven'

errorPatterns.pattern: child's OWN counting shows the point/say lag — fingers and words fall out of step, so a button gets two words or none
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill or verbally correct — this is a coordination stage, not a misunderstanding; simply slow the pace and have them physically move each object as they count it, and it self-corrects with the move-it scaffold
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when the child counts a fresh set, tags don't line up one-to-one (over- or under-counts)

errorPatterns.pattern: senses the count is wrong but only because recounting gave a different number — cannot point to which button was counted twice
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat this as a misunderstanding to reteach — error-monitoring of others' counts develops later; simply replay Teddy's count slowly and ask 'which button did Teddy count twice?' to nudge the monitoring habit along
errorPatterns.revealedBy: rejects 7 yet, asked how, says only 'I counted and got 6' without locating the error

responseLevels.gap: Accepts '7' because it was the last word said, or counts a set themselves with skips/double-counts and does not notice.
responseLevels.full: Identifies the specific button that received two number words, explains each object gets exactly one, and counts a fresh set accurately, touching each once.
responseLevels.partial: Says Teddy is wrong and can recount to 6, but cannot locate the double-counted button — rejects the total without seeing the broken one-word-per-object rule.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch Teddy count these 6 buttons. (Teddy points to one button, says 'four', then points to the SAME button again and says 'five', ending on 'seven'.) Teddy says there are 7 buttons. Is Teddy right? Tell me how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds one-to-one correspondence sees that the word-to-object pairing broke (one button got two words) and says the count is wrong FOR THAT REASON. A child without it either accepts '7' because that was the last word said, or says 'wrong' but can only justify by recounting to a different number — not by locating the double-tagged button. The 'how do you know' tier separates recognising the specific error from merely recounting.

sources.claim: The one-one principle = assigning one and only one counting word to each item; the child must partition the collection into already-counted vs not-yet-counted (tagging + keeping track); tangible, moveable objects help make this distinction.
sources.source: Ian Thompson, 'The Principal Counting Principles' (NCETM article, Stanford PreK-Math mirror)

sources.claim: K.CC.4a: 'When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.'
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Kindergarten Counting & Cardinality (K.CC)

sources.claim: Year 1: 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number'; 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals' — the statutory Year 1 goals that assume accurate object counting.
sources.source: DfE, National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 1, Number and place value)

sources.claim: Teaching Math to Young Children: dedicate daily time to maths, integrate counting through the day, follow a developmental progression from counting to cardinality.
sources.source: IES/What Works Clearinghouse practice guide, 'Teaching Math to Young Children' (WWC 2014-4005)

pedagogy.summary: Perimeter is the total distance around the boundary of a 2-D shape, found by measuring every side and adding the lengths (or, for a regular shape, multiplying one side by the number of sides). The concept to secure is that perimeter is a length — the once-around distance — and is distinct from area (the surface covered inside).
bestPractices: Define perimeter physically as walking all the way around the edge and back to the start.
Measure and label every side, then add — for a rectangle, remind pupils the two unmarked sides equal their opposites.
For regular shapes, connect equal sides to multiplication (side length × number of sides).
Deliberately contrast perimeter (distance around) with area (surface covered) on the same shape so the two are not confused.
Keep the length unit in the answer (cm, m).
keyRepresentations: A shape with each side measured and labelled, summed around the boundary
A finger/marker tracing the whole boundary back to the start
A regular polygon: one side labelled, perimeter = side × number of sides
A rectangle with only two adjacent sides given, the opposite two to be filled in
commonMisconceptions: Adds only the two given sides of a rectangle, forgetting the opposite two.
Confuses perimeter with area — counts the squares inside instead of the distance around.
For a regular shape, measures one side but doesn't account for all the equal sides.
Gives the perimeter as a bare number without a length unit.

learn.summary: Perimeter is the total distance once around the boundary of a 2-D shape — found by measuring every side and adding the lengths, or for a regular shape multiplying one side by the number of sides. The core idea to secure is that perimeter is a length (the once-around distance) and is distinct from area (the surface covered inside). Target age 7–8.

activities.title: Walk the boundary and build the total
feedback: If a child adds only the two given sides of a rectangle, have them first label the two opposite sides (which equal their partners), then add all four; trace the full boundary to check nothing is missed.

If a child reports the number of squares inside or an area figure, contrast the two measures on the same shape — trace the boundary for perimeter, shade the interior for area — and name which the question asks for.
If a child gives only one side of a regular polygon, establish that it has n equal sides so perimeter = side × n, and check the number of sides.
If the total is correct but the unit is missing, treat the answer as incomplete and build the habit of writing cm/m; the adding itself is sound.
activities.rationale: Tracing the boundary makes 'distance around' concrete; hiding two rectangle sides forces the learner to supply the equal opposite sides, directly targeting the most common error; a regular-shape step links equal sides to multiplication. An optional interactive version — dragging a marker so each side lights and its length clicks into a running total that will not advance past a hidden side until the opposite side is supplied, plus an area/perimeter shading toggle and a regular-polygon side×n mode — makes the once-around mechanism visible, but the same learning works with paper shapes, a ruler and labelled drawings.
sourceClaims: The perimeter of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of its sides. For rectangles and parallelograms often only two adjacent side lengths are given, and the common error is to add just those two numbers; having students first label the lengths of the other two sides is a helpful reminder. For regular polygons the perimeter is the product of one side length and the number of sides.
learnerActions: Trace a finger or marker all the way around the edge of a shape, starting and finishing at the same corner, so 'perimeter' is felt as walking once around and back to the start.
On a rectangle that shows only two adjacent side lengths, work out the two hidden opposite sides (opposite sides are equal), label them, then add all four sides.
Keep a running total as you cover each side, and only count the perimeter as complete when the whole boundary has been traced back to the start.
On a regular pentagon with one side labelled, find the perimeter as side length × 5 (or by adding five equal sides) and explain why the shortcut works.
Measure every side of a small irregular shape with a ruler and add the lengths.
Write each answer with its length unit (cm or m).
activities.intendedInsight: Perimeter is the complete once-around distance: you must account for every side (including hidden equal ones), it is a length with a unit, and for a regular shape equal sides let you multiply instead of adding one by one.

activities.title: Perimeter is not area
feedback: If the learner counts interior squares when asked for perimeter, point back to the boundary trace: perimeter follows only the edge.
If they are unsure which is asked, have them underline the word 'around' or 'covered/inside' in the question and match it to the correct action.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing area from perimeter is a distinction that must be maintained; deliberately performing both on the same shape makes the contrast explicit and discriminating.
sourceClaims: With strong, distinct concepts of perimeter and area, students differentiate the two measures; abstraction underscores the importance of distinguishing area from perimeter, a distinction that must be maintained across grades.
learnerActions: On one straight-sided shape drawn along the lines of a square grid, first trace the boundary and add the side lengths to find the perimeter, then shade the interior and count the unit squares to find the area (in square units).
State in your own words which measure is a distance around the edge and which is the surface covered inside.
Given a question, decide whether it is asking for perimeter or area before you start, and say how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Perimeter (distance around the edge, a length) and area (surface covered inside) are different measures on the very same shape and must not be swapped.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and mixed practice
feedback: For the spot-the-error item, confirm the fix is to add all four sides after supplying the equal opposite pair.
For the area distractor, confirm the learner traced the boundary rather than counting interior squares.
Flag any missing unit as an incomplete answer.
activities.rationale: Discriminating items — a two-sides-given rectangle, a side×n regular polygon, a spot-the-error on adding only two sides, and a perimeter-vs-area distractor — target the documented errors. These check and reinforce the procedure; use them alongside, not instead of, hands-on measuring and summing.
sourceClaims: The perimeter of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of its sides. For rectangles and parallelograms often only two adjacent side lengths are given, and the common error is to add just those two numbers; having students first label the lengths of the other two sides is a helpful reminder. For regular polygons the perimeter is the product of one side length and the number of sides.
learnerActions: Solve fill-the-blank items: a rectangle with only two adjacent sides given (supply the opposite two, then total), and a regular polygon with one side labelled (use side × number of sides).
Judge a worked example where another child added only the two given rectangle sides — say what went wrong and give the correct perimeter.
Answer a mixed item where one option is the area of the shape, choosing and justifying the correct perimeter.
Check every answer carries its length unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Applying perimeter across rectangle (hidden sides), regular-polygon (side×n), and perimeter-vs-area cases, and critiquing a wrong method, consolidates accurate, unit-bearing reasoning.

constraints: Keep the length unit (cm, m) in every perimeter answer; a bare number is incomplete. Area answers use square units (e.g. square centimetres or 'squares'), not length units.

A static labelled shape with the boundary highlighted can illustrate 'distance around', but it does not let the learner rehearse measuring and summing all sides — use it as a reference, not as the main practice.
Recognition-only or multiple-choice items check and reinforce the procedure but do not by themselves elicit independent measuring and summing; pair them with hands-on construction.
When using a regular-shape shortcut, first establish how many equal sides the shape has, so side × n is justified rather than guessed.
For a rectangle with only two adjacent sides given, require the learner to supply the opposite two sides before totalling; do not let them stop at the two given numbers.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D and conversation artefacts as 'poor' with claims that '3D adds nothing' and perimeter 'is not a dialogue'. These are catalog preferences, not established pedagogical laws, and have not been carried forward as universal claims; discussion (e.g. explaining where the boundary starts and ends) can usefully support this topic even if measure-and-add is the core performance.

One cited source (UK National Curriculum, Year 3 measures perimeter) is marked verified:false in the row; it is treated as unconfirmed and is not used as a sourceClaim because it supports only the topic/curriculum requirement, not a specific teaching principle.
The regular-polygon step depends on the prerequisite that the shape has n equal sides; ensure learners can identify a regular polygon before applying side×n.

probeDeeper: Show me with your finger — where does the perimeter start and where does it finish?
This rectangle only shows two side lengths — how long are the other two, and how do you know?
Is the perimeter the distance around the edge, or the space covered inside? Which did you find?
For this regular pentagon, do you need to measure all five sides, or is there a quicker way?
assess.correctAnswer: The child finds the total distance around each shape: for the rectangle, uses all four sides (supplying the two unlabelled opposite sides); for the regular pentagon, multiplies the side by 5 (or adds five equal sides); measures every side of the irregular shape and sums them; and states each perimeter with a length unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds only the two given sides of a rectangle, forgetting the opposite two.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child label the lengths of the other two sides first (opposite sides equal), then add all four; trace the full boundary to check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a rectangle with only length and width shown, gives length + width as the perimeter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses perimeter with area: counts the squares inside the shape instead of the distance around it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two on one shape — trace the boundary for perimeter, shade the interior for area; name which measure the question asks for.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports the number of interior squares, or an area figure, when asked for perimeter.

errorPatterns.pattern: For a regular shape, doesn't account for all the equal sides — measures/uses one side but doesn't multiply by the number of sides.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the shape has n equal sides, so perimeter = side × n; check the number of sides of the shape.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the single side length, or a partial sum, for the regular polygon's perimeter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the length unit: gives the perimeter as a bare number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat a perimeter without a unit as incomplete; build the habit of writing cm/m; the summing is sound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct total, no unit; supplies it only when asked.

responseLevels.gap: Adds only two sides of the rectangle, or reports an area, or uses a single side of the regular shape.
responseLevels.full: Finds the total distance around each shape — supplying unlabelled equal sides, using side×n for regular shapes — keeps it distinct from area, and states the perimeter with its length unit.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the perimeter of a fully-labelled shape by adding sides, but is caught when opposite sides must be inferred or when a regular shape invites side×n — or omits the unit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a rectangle (with only two adjacent sides labelled), a regular pentagon (one side labelled), and a small irregular shape, with a ruler. Say: 'Find the perimeter of each.' Watch whether they measure/account for every side, whether they add all sides (not just the two given), whether they confuse it with the area, and whether they keep the unit.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands perimeter accounts for every side and gives a once-around length; a child who does not adds only the two given rectangle sides, counts the squares inside (area), or uses just one side of the regular shape — each visible in the working.

sources.claim: The perimeter of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of its sides. For rectangles and parallelograms often only two adjacent side lengths are given, and the common error is to add just those two numbers; having students first label the lengths of the other two sides is a helpful reminder. For regular polygons the perimeter is the product of one side length and the number of sides.
sources.source: Common Core Progressions — K–5 Geometric Measurement (2012), Grade 3 (3.MD.8) (ISBE mirror)

sources.claim: With strong, distinct concepts of perimeter and area, students differentiate the two measures; abstraction underscores the importance of distinguishing area from perimeter, a distinction that must be maintained across grades.
sources.source: Common Core Progressions — K–5 Geometric Measurement (2012), Grade 3–4 (area vs perimeter) (ISBE mirror)

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils measure the perimeter of simple 2-D shapes.
sources.source: UK National Curriculum — Mathematics, Key Stage 2 Measurement

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–7 years

- **Topic:** Changing Shapes of Solids

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y2 'Uses of everyday materials'):** Pupils should be taught to "find out how the shapes of solid objects made from some materials can be changed by squashing, bending, twisting and stretching." Non-statutory guidance links this to identifying material uses and to Working Scientifically enquiry ('performing simple tests'; 'observing closely'; 'gathering and recording data').

- **Standards — US (NGSS, honest gap):** NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to reshaping solids by squashing/bending/twisting/stretching — it is a UK-led KS1 objective. The nearest is DCI PS1.A ('Different properties are suited to different purposes') and the K–2 investigation practice; the reshaping-and-identity idea also foreshadows 2-PS1-3 (an object's pieces can be rearranged, the matter persists).

- **Operational details:** Teach the four actions with precise, embodied definitions (squash = press/squeeze; bend = curve so not straight; twist = hold each end and turn opposite ways; stretch = pull to change shape), then run first-hand comparative tests on a deliberately varied set of materials — playdough/plasticine, sponge, elastic band, paper, a wooden stick, a stone — so children see that materials respond DIFFERENTLY. Use a predict-then-test sequence to surface ideas before handling. Crucially, keep the enquiry on the MATERIAL an object is made from (not the object), and make the identity point explicit: the shape changes but the material stays the same stuff. Include materials that keep their new shape (dough) and ones that spring back (elastic) so the contrast is unavoidable.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child can demonstrate all four actions, compare how two materials respond (clay squashes and stays; wood barely bends), and state that the material is still the same material after its shape has changed — without over-claiming that everything springs back.
bestPractices: Define each action precisely and let children embody it (turn their hands to 'twist', pull to 'stretch') before testing materials.
Use predict-then-test: children predict how each material will respond, then test by hand, so the misconception surfaces and is confronted by evidence.
Deliberately include BOTH spring-back materials (elastic band, sponge) and stay-changed materials (dough, soft wire) so 'everything is elastic' cannot survive.
Keep the enquiry framed on the MATERIAL, not the object — 'we are testing what it is made of' — reinforcing objects-vs-materials.
Make the identity point explicit: changing the shape does not change what material it is; no new material is made.
Record results in a simple table (material × does it keep its shape?) to support the classify/compare Working Scientifically skill.
keyRepresentations: A varied materials tray: playdough, sponge, elastic band, paper, wooden stick, stone, soft wire
Embodied action cards for squash / bend / twist / stretch
A predict-then-test recording grid (material down the side; springs back? stays changed? can't change?)
Side-by-side contrast of an elastic band (returns) and a lump of dough (stays)
A 'same material, new shape' before/after pair emphasising the material is unchanged
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalised elasticity — assuming ALL objects that can be squashed/bent/twisted/stretched will spring back to their original shape (the central Y2 misconception).
Believing a physical shape change cannot be undone at all — or conversely that it always can.
Thinking that changing an object's shape changes the material it is made of (it does not — no new material forms).
Testing the OBJECT rather than the material, so results are attributed to the item ('the spoon') not the substance ('metal').
Assuming a rigid material (wood, stone) simply hasn't been pushed hard enough, rather than that some materials do not change shape this way.

learn.summary: For children aged 6-7, teach how the shapes of solid objects can be changed by squashing, bending, twisting and stretching, with the key insight that materials respond DIFFERENTLY: some spring back (elastic), some keep the new shape (plastic/permanent), and some barely change this way (rigid). Keep the enquiry on the MATERIAL an object is made from, and make explicit that changing the shape does not change what the material is and makes no new material. The central misconception to confront is over-generalised elasticity (expecting everything to spring back). The strongest activity lets children apply a force first-hand and then release to witness the spring-back-vs-stay contrast; a hands-on tray of real dough, elastic and sponge is the natural companion, with a screen or picture version as a scaffold that offers a different experience.

activities.title: Materials deformation bench: apply a force, then let go
feedback: When the squeezed sponge springs back but the squeezed dough stays flat, point out the contrast directly: the same action gave different outcomes because they are made of different materials.
If a child predicts the dough will spring back, run the let-go test and let the observed result do the teaching rather than just telling them.
When a child tries to squash the wooden stick (or stone) and it barely moves, name the third case: some materials do not change shape this way when we use our hands.
Reinforce after every trial that the material is still the same — the squashed dough is still dough, the bent wire is still metal.
activities.rationale: Reshaping is a direct, hands-on investigation with a material-dependent outcome, matching the statutory 'find out how the shapes... can be changed' enquiry. Applying a force and then releasing it lets the child witness the spring-back-vs-stay distinction first-hand, which surfaces and confronts the over-generalised-elasticity misconception with evidence. Deliberately including both spring-back materials (elastic, sponge) and stay-changed materials (dough, soft wire), plus a rigid one (wood, stone), is intended to make the contrast unavoidable. A persistent 'still the same material' label keeps the identity idea in view. A screen bench can model release with live recompute; a real tray of dough, elastic and sponge supplies the genuine tactile feel — the two offer different experiences and neither is universally required.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y2 statutory requirement: 'find out how the shapes of solid objects made from some materials can be changed by squashing, bending, twisting and stretching'; non-statutory uses guidance and WS enquiry.

Central Y2 misconception = over-generalised elasticity ('all objects that can be squashed/bent/twisted/stretched will return to their previous shape'); some materials keep the new shape or cannot be changed; teach that pupils test the material, not the object.
Elastic (recoverable) vs plastic (permanent) deformation — child-accessible physics of why some materials spring back and some stay changed.
learnerActions: Choose a material from a varied set — playdough/plasticine, an elastic band, a sponge, a thick wooden stick or block, a stone, soft wire, paper.
Pick one of the four actions and apply it: press/squeeze to squash, curve it to bend, hold each end and turn opposite ways to twist, pull to stretch.
Watch the material deform as the force is applied (dough flattens, wire coils, elastic thins).
Release ('let go') and observe what happens: does it snap back to its old shape, stay in the new shape, or barely move?
Record the result for each material and the action you used in a comparison grid: springs back / stays changed / won't change this way.
Note each time that the material is still the same stuff — e.g. a tag or label 'this is still WOOD' — so the shape changed but the material did not.
activities.intendedInsight: Materials respond differently to the same action: squeeze a sponge and it springs back, squeeze dough and it stays flattened, and squeeze a thick wooden stick or a stone and it barely changes. Likewise, a stretched elastic band snaps back while twisted soft wire stays twisted. So 'everything springs back' is not true, and the result can depend on the action as well as the material. Across all of this, the material itself is unchanged.

activities.title: Embody and define the four actions
feedback: If a child only pushes/squashes regardless of the instruction, model each of the four actions once with a spare material — this is a procedural gap, so focus on the action, not on material properties.
Confirm the distinct hand movement for each: a twist needs two ends turned opposite ways, a stretch needs a pull.
activities.rationale: Defining each action precisely and letting children embody it establishes the vocabulary and motor procedure that the comparative tests depend on. Treating all four as one generic push is a common procedural gap distinct from the conceptual material-response ideas. A matching/recognition task with audio can support early readers but only checks recognition; actually performing the actions is what elicits the production skill. No row source evidences the embodiment technique itself, so none is cited here.
learnerActions: Learn each action with a precise, embodied definition: squash = press/squeeze; bend = curve so it is not straight; twist = hold each end and turn opposite ways; stretch = pull to change its shape.
Perform each action with your own hands first (turn your hands to twist, pull to stretch) before touching a material.
Match each action word to a demonstration or picture of that action.
Say the definition aloud (with audio support for pre/early readers).
activities.intendedInsight: Squashing, bending, twisting and stretching are four distinct actions, not one generic 'push'. Being able to produce each one distinctly is needed before comparing how materials respond.

activities.title: Predict, then test, and sort by how materials respond
feedback: Where a prediction was wrong (e.g. you expected the clay to spring back), treat the surprise as the learning: the same action gave a different result because the material is different.
Use the completed table to compare two materials side by side — clay squashes and stays; a thick piece of wood barely bends.

If a child says a rigid material just 'wasn't pushed hard enough', agree that a much bigger force might bend or break it, but explain that with the force our hands can give it does not change shape this way — that is what we observed.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-test sequence brings the misconception into the open before handling, so it can be confronted by evidence. Sorting and recording in a table develops the Working Scientifically classify/compare skill. Sorting and matching tasks can assess and score these ideas cleanly, but a linear recall quiz does not itself build the felt contrast — so the sort is paired with real testing.
sourceClaims: Central Y2 misconception = over-generalised elasticity ('all objects that can be squashed/bent/twisted/stretched will return to their previous shape'); some materials keep the new shape or cannot be changed; teach that pupils test the material, not the object.
Elastic (recoverable) vs plastic (permanent) deformation — child-accessible physics of why some materials spring back and some stay changed.
learnerActions: Before handling each material, predict how it will respond to a chosen action: will it spring back, stay changed, or barely change?
Test your prediction by hand and compare what happened to what you expected.

Sort the materials into three groups for the action you tested (a different action can give a different result): springs back (e.g. squeezed sponge, stretched elastic band), stays changed (e.g. squashed dough, bent soft wire), won't change this way by hand (e.g. squeezed thick wood, stone).
Build a simple table with the material down the side and columns for 'springs back?', 'stays changed?', 'won't change?'.
activities.intendedInsight: Predicting first surfaces your idea so the evidence can confirm or overturn it; recording in a table supports comparing and classifying materials by how they respond.

activities.title: Same material, new shape: show the stuff is unchanged
feedback: If a child says the squashed clay 'isn't clay any more', show it is the same clay, the same weight, and can be rolled back into a ball — only the shape changed.
Connect the weighing result to the idea: nothing was added or removed, so it is the same material with the same weight.
activities.rationale: Making the identity point explicit directly addresses the misconception that reshaping turns the stuff into a different material. Comparing before/after and checking weight gives concrete, observable evidence that the material persists through a shape change. For young learners the weight before and after a simple squash is expected to be the same because no matter is added or removed. This matter-persistence idea is not directly evidenced by the row's sources (it foreshadows later conservation-of-weight ideas such as NGSS 5-PS1-2), so none is cited.
learnerActions: Take a lump of clay, roll it into a ball, then squash it flat — look at the before and after.
Explain whether it is still clay after being squashed, and how you could show it is the same stuff (e.g. roll it back into a ball).
Weigh a ball of clay, squash it, and weigh it again; compare the two weights.
Do the same reasoning for a bent metal paperclip: is it still metal after bending?
activities.intendedInsight: Changing an object's shape does not change the material it is made of and does not make new material — squashed clay is still clay, bent metal is still metal, and the weight stays the same because nothing was added or taken away.

constraints: Keep the enquiry framed on the MATERIAL an object is made from ('we are testing what it is made of'), not on the named object, so results are attributed to the substance (metal) and not the item (the spoon).

Deliberately include BOTH spring-back materials (elastic band, sponge) and stay-changed materials (dough, soft wire), plus at least one rigid material (wood, stone), so the over-generalised-elasticity idea is challenged by evidence.

A tap-to-reveal picture or lift-the-flap can name and illustrate the four actions and show before/after, but its spring-back answers are pre-authored: it asserts the outcome rather than letting the child apply the force and witness it. Treat it as a vocabulary scaffold, not a replacement for first-hand testing.

Sorting, matching and prediction multiple-choice can assess and score these ideas but check recognition; recognition-only responses do not themselves elicit the felt contrast of applying a force and releasing it.
Pre/early readers need audio scaffolding for definitions and prompts.
A real, tactile tray (dough, elastic, sponge) and a screen model offer different experiences; the real materials supply the genuine feel of squeezing. Neither is presented as universally required.
Avoid over-claiming: do not imply everything springs back, and do not imply a physical shape change can never be undone — some can be reversed (rolling clay back), some cannot easily.
Frame rigid materials (wood, stone) as 'do not change shape this way' at this level rather than as proof they just need more force; keep claims within what a child observes by hand.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources (Oak National Academy; Kiddle Deformation) are marked unverified in the original row; the DfE National Curriculum source is marked verified. Evidence strength has not been re-checked.

The DfE source grounds the four named actions and the investigative enquiry (activity 1); it is NOT efficacy evidence for the embodiment/motor-procedure method, so the 'Embody and define' activity cites no source claim.
Activity 4's material-identity-persistence principle is not directly supported by any row source (it foreshadows NGSS 2-PS1-3); sourceClaims left empty there.

The original 3D-interactive note asserted 'genuine spatial depth adds little conceptual value' for this topic; softened here — a side view reads squashing/bending well and tactile work is a complement — without claiming 3D 'adds nothing'.

The original framed the screen bench as doing something 'a static picture cannot supply'; retained only as a narrow affordance (live recompute lets the child witness release), not as a universal law that static images cannot teach this.

The weighing check (NGSS 2-PS1 foreshadowing of matter persisting) assumes a simple reshape with no material added or removed; present it to children as 'nothing added or taken away, so the same weight'.
NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to reshaping solids by these four actions; it is a UK-led KS1 objective (nearest DCI PS1.A and the K-2 investigation practice).

probeDeeper: You bent the paperclip and it stayed; you stretched the band and it went back — why the difference?
Is the squashed clay still clay? How could you show me it's the same stuff?
Can you squash the wooden stick the way you squashed the clay? Why not?
If I weigh the ball of clay, then squash it and weigh it again, will the weight change?
assess.correctAnswer: Produces the four distinct actions; observes that some materials hold the new shape (clay squashed, paperclip bent) while others spring back (elastic band, sponge), and that some barely change (wood); states the material itself is unchanged — squashed clay is still clay, bent metal is still metal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changing the shape changes the material — 'the squashed clay isn't clay any more', bent metal 'became something else'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront on the spot: it's the same clay, same weight, and can be rolled back to a ball; only the shape changed, not the material.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: After reshaping, denies it is still the same material; treats a new shape as new stuff.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises how materials respond — expects everything to spring back (like the band), or nothing to (like the clay); doesn't separate elastic from permanent change.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run the let-go test on each and line them up: band and sponge return, clay and bent wire stay — let the contrast do the teaching.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the clay will spring back, or that the stretched band will stay stretched.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats squash/bend/twist/stretch as one generic action — just pushes on everything regardless of the instruction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model each of the four actions once with a spare material; this is a procedural gap, not a conceptual one — don't reteach material properties.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Only squashes/pushes; cannot demonstrate distinct bending, twisting and stretching.

responseLevels.gap: Applies one generic action (pushing); thinks reshaping makes a new material; cannot compare how different materials respond.
responseLevels.full: Performs all four actions, distinguishes materials that hold the shape from those that spring back, AND states the material itself is unchanged — transferring the idea to a new material.
responseLevels.partial: Performs the four actions and sees shapes change, but doesn't distinguish spring-back from permanent change, or is unsure whether the material stays the same.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out a lump of clay, a sponge, an elastic band, a wooden lolly stick and a metal paperclip. Say: 'Try to change each one's shape by squashing, bending, twisting or stretching. Which keep their new shape and which spring back? And for each — after you've changed it, is it still the SAME material?' Watch them work.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching (not asking) reveals three things a verbal answer hides: whether the child can produce all four actions distinctly, whether they distinguish spring-back (elastic) from permanent (plastic) change through the let-go test, and — the key idea — whether they think reshaping turns the stuff into a DIFFERENT material.
