pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** The Periodic Table

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry 'The Periodic Table'):** The principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; the Periodic Table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals; how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the Periodic Table; the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-1 / MS-PS1-2 supporting):** Use models and patterns in properties of substances; the periodic table organises elements by property patterns (framework PS1.A).

- **Operational details:** The big idea is ORGANISATION BY PATTERN: elements are arranged by increasing atomic number into GROUPS (columns — similar chemical behaviour) and PERIODS (rows), with metals to the left/centre and non-metals to the upper right. The table's power is PREDICTION — knowing an element's position predicts its properties and reactivity (e.g. Group 1 metals get more reactive down the group; Group 0 are unreactive). Teach Mendeleev's insight historically: he ordered by properties, left GAPS for undiscovered elements, and successfully PREDICTED their properties — the periodic law as a genuine predictive theory, not a lookup chart. Have pupils discover periodicity by arranging element cards by property and seeing the repeating pattern emerge. Emphasise position→property inference over memorising the whole table.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child locates metals/non-metals and a named group/period, uses position to predict a property or relative reactivity, and explains why Mendeleev's gaps-and-predictions made the table a scientific triumph.
bestPractices: Have pupils discover periodicity by arranging elements by property until the repeating pattern emerges, rather than presenting the finished table.
Teach position→property PREDICTION as the table's purpose, not memorisation of every element.
Tell the Mendeleev story concretely: ordering by properties, leaving gaps, predicting undiscovered elements.
Use group highlights to show trends (Group 1 more reactive down; Group 0 inert).
Distinguish groups (columns, similar chemistry) from periods (rows) explicitly.
keyRepresentations: Element cards with property tags to sort into the grid
The periodic table grid with group (column) and period (row) highlighters
A Mendeleev gap-and-predict challenge
Tap-an-element property panels
commonMisconceptions: The periodic table is an arbitrary chart to memorise rather than an ordered predictive system.
Rows (periods) share properties, confusing them with groups (columns).
The table is ordered by atomic MASS in all cases (Mendeleev's a few anomalies; modern order is atomic number).
All metals are equally reactive (missing the group/position trends).
Elements were placed by discovery date rather than by properties.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 11–12 learn the periodic table as an organisation-by-pattern system whose power is PREDICTION, not memorisation. They discover periodicity by putting element cards in order (atomic weight as Mendeleev did, or atomic number as in the modern table) and starting new rows so similar properties line up until the repeating pattern emerges, use position (group/period) to predict properties and relative reactivity, and understand Mendeleev's historical insight of leaving gaps and predicting undiscovered elements. Core distinctions: groups (columns, similar chemistry; in the main groups, the same number of outer-shell electrons, with helium the exception in Group 0) versus periods (rows), and metals (left/centre) versus non-metals (upper right, plus hydrogen).

activities.title: Become Mendeleev: sort element cards until the pattern snaps into place
feedback: When sorting locks into place, point out that the repeat the pupil just produced IS periodicity — the same pattern Mendeleev spotted.

If a prediction for the gap is close, affirm that reading the neighbours' trend is precisely how the table predicts; if far off, prompt them to re-read the column above and below the gap before revealing the real element.
When highlighting Group 1, draw attention to reactivity increasing DOWN the column; when highlighting Group 0, that these elements stay unreactive — position predicts behaviour.
If a pupil groups cards by an incidental feature (such as colour or appearance) rather than chemical property, prompt them to compare how two column-mates actually REACT.
activities.rationale: The periodic law is a discovery about pattern and prediction, intended to be grasped by re-enacting Mendeleev's move: order elements (he used atomic weight) and arrange them so similar properties line up until the repeat emerges, leave a gap, predict the missing element. Doing the sorting and committing to a prediction before the reveal is intended to make periodicity a felt insight and to foreground position→property inference over rote memorisation. Dragging, locking-on-correct-order, group/period highlighters and tap-to-reveal property panels are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; periods and groups; metals and non-metals; predicting patterns in reactions from the Periodic Table
The periodic table organises elements by patterns in properties; position predicts behaviour (NGSS PS1.A / MS-PS1-1 models and patterns)
Mendeleev left gaps and successfully predicted undiscovered elements' properties, demonstrating the periodic law's predictive power
learnerActions: Receive a shuffled set of element cards, each showing the element's atomic weight (or atomic number) and a few properties (e.g. reactivity, metal/non-metal, how it bonds).
Put the cards in order of atomic weight (or atomic number), starting a new row whenever properties begin to repeat, so that similar elements line up into columns.
Notice the moment when rows and columns align and a repeating pattern (periodicity) emerges from your own sorting rather than being handed to you.
Encounter a gap — one square that stays empty — and PREDICT the missing element's properties from its neighbours above, below, and beside it.
Commit to your prediction, then reveal the real element Mendeleev foretold and compare it against what you predicted.
Use group and period highlighters to trace Group 1 reactivity climbing down the column and Group 0 sitting inert, then tap any element to read its property panel.
activities.intendedInsight: The periodic table is a predictive law, not a chart to memorise: arranging elements so repeating property patterns fall into columns (the modern table orders by atomic number; Mendeleev ordered largely by atomic weight) means an element's POSITION lets you predict its properties and reactivity. It is this pattern-reasoning — not any particular ordering basis — that let Mendeleev leave gaps and foretell undiscovered elements.

activities.title: Tap-a-group reference table: reveal shared trends
feedback: When a group is highlighted, name the shared trait the members have in common so the highlight is tied to a reason, not just colour.
If a pupil treats a row as sharing properties, contrast it with a highlighted column to show where similar chemistry actually lies.
activities.rationale: A tappable, group-highlighting table is a useful reference and a clear shared-attribute reveal. It is offered as a companion to, not a replacement for, the sorting discovery: a fixed reference table shows the finished pattern and shared-attribute highlights well, but on its own it does not require the pupil to arrange and predict, which is what explains why the table is predictive.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; periods and groups; metals and non-metals; predicting patterns in reactions from the Periodic Table
The periodic table organises elements by patterns in properties; position predicts behaviour (NGSS PS1.A / MS-PS1-1 models and patterns)
learnerActions: Use a tappable periodic table where tapping a group highlights all its members and reveals their shared chemical trend.
Tap a group (e.g. Group 1) to see every member highlighted, then read the shared property that unites the column.
Compare tapping down a GROUP (column) against tracing across a PERIOD (row) to feel how the two directions differ.

Locate metals, non-metals and metalloids and notice they occupy a pattern (metals left/centre, non-metals upper-right, metalloids along the dividing staircase, with hydrogen a non-metal exception at top left), not scattered positions.
activities.intendedInsight: Column-mates (a group) share chemical behaviour because they share the same number of outer-shell electrons, and tapping a group makes this shared attribute visible at a glance; this serves as an ongoing reference once the arrange-and-predict discovery has established WHY the table is powerful.

activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain: Group 1 reactivity down the column
feedback: If the prediction has no stated reason, press for WHY using the group trend before observing.
A correct prediction of a fiercer sodium reaction, justified by position in Group 1, is full credit; observing confirms it.
If the pupil predicts by atom size or weight 'look' alone, redirect to the shared chemical behaviour of the group.
activities.rationale: Predict-Observe-Explain makes the predictive claim testable and exposes whether the pupil is using the pattern or treating the table as an arbitrary list. The spoken/written reason, not just the prediction, reveals understanding. Where real reactions cannot be shown safely, a clip or recorded demonstration stands in; the represented reaction, not the medium, carries the learning.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; periods and groups; metals and non-metals; predicting patterns in reactions from the Periodic Table
Mendeleev left gaps and successfully predicted undiscovered elements' properties, demonstrating the periodic law's predictive power
learnerActions: Watch a short clip or records of lithium reacting with water.
Before observing, PREDICT what sodium (the next element down Group 1) will do and state WHY, referring to the group pattern.
Observe sodium's reaction and compare it with your prediction.
Explain the result: elements lower in Group 1 react more vigorously, and say how position in the table let you predict this.
Extend: without looking it up, predict how rubidium (the element below potassium in Group 1) would react with water, and give your reason before seeing any evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading the group pattern lets you predict reactivity before observing: a pupil who sees the table as a mere list cannot predict, while one who reads the Group 1 trend predicts a more vigorous reaction further down the column — the stated reason is the diagnostic part.

activities.title: Explain the layout: why these elements share a column
feedback: Full credit links 'same group = similar properties' to the arrangement by atomic number, not just the fact on its own.

If a pupil explains column-mates by an incidental feature (similar size or weight), correct: it is ordered by atomic number so shared chemical behaviour lines up in columns — show Group 1 metals all reacting in a similar way with water, more vigorously further down.
If groups and periods are mixed up, state: columns = groups = similar chemistry; rows = periods = one shell filling across — then trace Group 1 down and Period 2 across.

If Mendeleev is credited with discovering or inventing elements, correct: he ordered KNOWN elements (largely by atomic weight) by pattern, left gaps where the pattern demanded an undiscovered element, and predicted its properties, later confirmed.
activities.rationale: Articulating why column-mates belong together distinguishes a pupil who grasps the table as a pattern of properties from one who thinks it is alphabetical, size-ordered or arbitrary. The Mendeleev gaps-and-prediction story only makes sense to the former, so requiring an explanation (not recognition) targets the core conceptual distinction and the common misconceptions directly.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; periods and groups; metals and non-metals; predicting patterns in reactions from the Periodic Table
Mendeleev left gaps and successfully predicted undiscovered elements' properties, demonstrating the periodic law's predictive power
learnerActions: Consider that lithium, sodium and potassium sit in the same COLUMN (Group 1) but are not next to each other in the element counting order.
Explain why the table puts them together in one column — what they share and why that is more useful than listing elements in order.
State explicitly the difference between going DOWN a group and going ACROSS a period.
Say why Mendeleev left empty spaces instead of filling positions in order, and why those gaps mattered.
Describe where metals and non-metals are found — in a pattern, not scattered.
activities.intendedInsight: Elements in the same group share chemical properties because they have the same number of outer-shell electrons; ordering by atomic number arranges the table so these repeating patterns line up in columns, which is what makes it predictive rather than a mere list — and why Mendeleev's gaps-and-predictions were a scientific triumph.

activities.title: Optional enrichment: interview Mendeleev
feedback: Steer the conversation back to the pattern-and-prediction reasoning if it drifts into unrelated biography.
Reinforce that the gaps were a prediction the pattern DEMANDED, later confirmed by discovery.
activities.rationale: An in-role chat can vividly convey the historical daring of leaving gaps and predicting elements. It is offered as optional enrichment: a conversation conveys the story and motivation but does not let the pupil manipulate the arrangement or verify a prediction, so it complements rather than replaces the hands-on sorting and prediction work.
sourceClaims: Mendeleev left gaps and successfully predicted undiscovered elements' properties, demonstrating the periodic law's predictive power
learnerActions: Take part in an in-role conversation interviewing Mendeleev about his table.
Ask why he trusted the pattern enough to leave gaps rather than simply placing the next-heaviest known element in every position.
Draw out how he predicted the properties of elements not yet discovered, and how confirmation later vindicated him.
activities.intendedInsight: Mendeleev's daring was spotting a property pattern and trusting it enough to predict undiscovered elements — history that dramatises why the periodic law is a genuine predictive theory, not a lookup chart.

constraints: Target the big idea 'organisation by pattern → prediction': teach position→property inference, not memorisation of every element.
Distinguish groups (columns, similar chemistry, same outer-shell electron count) from periods (rows, one shell filling across) explicitly; do not let them be treated as interchangeable.

The modern table is ordered by atomic NUMBER, not atomic mass; Mendeleev ordered largely by atomic weight and had a few anomalies. Keep these distinct when telling the history, including in any activity insight.
Credit Mendeleev with spotting the pattern, leaving gaps, and predicting undiscovered elements' properties — not with discovering or inventing the elements.

A tappable reference table and the Mendeleev conversation are companions/enrichment: they show or narrate the pattern but do not by themselves require the pupil to arrange elements and commit to a prediction, which is where the discovery of WHY the table predicts occurs. Do not assert that any one medium is the only or best way to teach this.

Recognition or tap-to-highlight responses alone do not elicit the independent explanation (linking shared group properties to atomic-number arrangement) or the independent prediction that evidence the full response level; include construction/explanation tasks.
Handle reactive-metal demonstrations safely: use a clip or recorded records of alkali-metal reactions rather than unsupervised practical work with sodium/potassium.
Reactivity increases DOWN Group 1 and Group 0 elements are unreactive; keep trend directions accurate when using highlighters or predictions.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, only the DfE KS3 programmes of study is marked verified in the source row; the NGSS and Royal Society of Chemistry claims are marked unverified. Do not treat citations as evidence that any activity here was tested or is comparatively more effective.

The original row's 3D-interactive entry was rated 'poor' with the claim that 3D 'adds no spatial meaning and obscures the row/column patterns'. This is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it is recorded here and in the audit but not asserted as universal — a 2D grid simply suits the row/column organisation that carries this concept.

The original 'static art cannot deliver the arrange-and-predict discovery' phrasing has been softened: a fixed reference table can still teach shared-attribute recognition; it simply does not itself require the pupil to arrange and predict.

Candidate activity 2's intendedInsight originally claimed tap-a-group was 'the quickest way to see group identity'; this unsupported comparative efficacy claim was removed and replaced with a narrow 'visible at a glance' affordance.

In this review, activity 1's intendedInsight was corrected: it previously implied Mendeleev ordered by atomic number. The evidence row and pedagogy state Mendeleev ordered largely by atomic weight while the modern table orders by atomic number; the insight now distinguishes the two and attributes the gap-prediction to pattern-reasoning rather than a specific ordering basis.
Activity 1's rationale previously asserted the law is 'best grasped by' re-enacting Mendeleev's move; this untested comparative efficacy claim was softened to intended/proposed wording.

The source material conflates 'ordered by atomic number' (modern) with Mendeleev's ordering 'by atomic weight'. The evidence list even states Mendeleev 'ordered elements by atomic weight'. Both are kept but clearly distinguished in constraints and activities to avoid teaching that the modern table is mass-ordered.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: show a short clip/records of lithium reacting with water, then ask the child to PREDICT what sodium (next down Group 1) will do and WHY, before observing it. A child who sees the table as a mere list can't predict; a child who reads the group pattern predicts a more vigorous version. Observing sodium's fiercer reaction tests the prediction; the stated reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If a brand-new element were discovered and it sat under potassium in Group 1, what could you predict about how it reacts — before testing it?
What's the difference between going DOWN a group and going ACROSS a period?
Why did Mendeleev leave empty spaces in his table instead of filling them in order?
Where are the metals and non-metals found on the table — scattered, or in a pattern?
assess.correctAnswer: Elements in the same group/column have SIMILAR CHEMICAL PROPERTIES (Group 1 metals all react vigorously with water, form similar compounds) because they have the same number of outer-shell electrons. The table is arranged so that ordering by atomic number makes these repeating patterns line up in columns — that's what makes it predictive, not just a list. Full marks link 'same group = similar properties' to the arrangement.

errorPatterns.pattern: the table is ordered alphabetically or by how heavy/big the atoms look
errorPatterns.nextMove: It's ordered by atomic number, arranged so repeating property patterns fall into columns. Show that Group 1 all react the same way — the point is behaviour, not size or spelling.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because they're similar sizes or weights, so they end up near each other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains column-mates by an incidental feature, not shared chemical properties

errorPatterns.pattern: groups (columns) and periods (rows) are interchangeable / mixed up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Columns = groups = similar chemistry; rows = periods = one shell filling across. Trace Group 1 down and Period 2 across to feel the difference.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because they're in the same period, and periods all behave alike.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says elements in a ROW share properties, or uses 'group' for a period

errorPatterns.pattern: Mendeleev's genius was inventing the elements or finishing the table, not predicting from gaps
errorPatterns.nextMove: He ordered known elements by pattern, left GAPS where the pattern demanded an undiscovered element, and predicted its properties — later confirmed. That's the power of the pattern.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: credits Mendeleev with discovering elements rather than spotting the pattern and predicting missing ones

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the table is alphabetical/size-ordered or arbitrary; can't say what column-mates share; mixes up groups and periods.
responseLevels.full: Explains groups share chemical properties (outer electrons), that ordering by atomic number lines the patterns into columns, distinguishes groups from periods, and uses the pattern to predict — grasping why Mendeleev's gaps mattered.
responseLevels.partial: States 'same group = similar properties' but can't connect it to the arrangement/atomic-number ordering or use it to predict an unknown element — the fact without its predictive power.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lithium, sodium and potassium all sit in the same COLUMN (Group 1) of the periodic table. They aren't next to each other in the counting order of the elements. Why does the table put them together in one column — what do they share, and why is that more useful than just listing elements in order?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason distinguishes a child who grasps the table as a PATTERN of properties (groups share behaviour; the layout predicts) from one who thinks it's an arbitrary or alphabetical/size list. Mendeleev's leaving gaps to predict undiscovered elements only makes sense to the former.

pedagogy.summary: Children read, write and convert times between 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) and 24-hour notation, and represent them on analogue clocks. The core rules: for p.m. times 1:00-11:59, ADD 12 hours (3:45 p.m. -> 15:45); for 24-hour times from 13:00 on, SUBTRACT 12 to get the p.m. time (19:30 -> 7:30 p.m.); 24-hour times always have four digits, so a single-digit hour takes a leading zero (09:45); a new day starts at midnight 00:00 (not 24:00) and noon is 12:00. The rule must be applied ONLY to the right times — a.m. times and the 12:xx noon hour are the traps.
bestPractices: Ground the +12/-12 rule in the day: a day is 24 hours starting at midnight 00:00, and the afternoon/evening hours continue counting on past 12
Pair the same time in 12-hour and 24-hour form and ask 'what is the same, what is different?'
Stress the four-digit format with a leading zero for single-digit hours (09:45)
Handle the boundary cases explicitly: midnight = 00:00, noon = 12:00, and 12:01-12:59 p.m. stay as 12:xx
Decide first whether the time is before or after noon — only p.m. times get +12
keyRepresentations: Paired 12-hour and 24-hour digital displays
Analogue clock for representing a converted time
A 12-hour to 24-hour conversion table
The 24-hour day-line (00:00 midnight -> 12:00 noon -> back to 00:00)
commonMisconceptions: Adds 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> '16:00')
Adds 12 to a.m. times too (10:17 a.m. -> '22:17')
Omits the leading zero for single-digit hours (6:38 a.m. -> '6:38')
Writes midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00
When converting FROM 24-hour, subtracts 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> '0:43 p.m.') or subtracts 10 instead of 12, or omits a.m./p.m. on the answer

learn.summary: Learners read, write and convert times between 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) and 24-hour notation and show them on analogue clocks. Core rules: for p.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59, add 12 hours (3:45 p.m. -> 15:45); for 24-hour times from 13:00 onward, subtract 12 to get the p.m. time (19:30 -> 7:30 p.m.); 24-hour times always have four digits, so a single-digit hour takes a leading zero (09:45); a new day starts at midnight 00:00 (never 24:00) and noon is 12:00. The decisive step is deciding FIRST whether a time is before or after noon — a.m. times and the 12:xx noon hour are the traps where learners wrongly apply the rule.

activities.title: Walk the 24-hour day-line and watch the two clocks agree
feedback: If a learner reads a morning time and adds 12, point to the day-line: the marker is before noon, so for the morning hours 1 a.m. to 11 a.m. the 24-hour and 12-hour hour numbers match (apart from the leading zero) — only after the noon hour do they differ by 12. (The 12:xx a.m. midnight hour is the separate boundary case, written 00:xx.)

If a learner says midnight is 24:00, ask what the clock shows one minute before and one minute after midnight; show that a standard digital clock rolls from 23:59 to 00:00, so midnight at the start of a new day is written 00:00.

When they correctly state 'from 1 p.m. the 24-hour hour is 12 more than the p.m. hour' (with the noon hour as the exception, both reading 12), reinforce by asking them to predict the next afternoon time before moving the marker.
activities.rationale: Grounding the rule in the structure of the day — a 24-hour span starting at midnight with hours counting on past noon — turns a memorised +12/-12 into a visible relationship and directly targets the +10 error and the 24:00/0:43 boundary traps. A moving marker with paired displays makes the noon crossing observable; a hand-drawn day-line with paired written times is a concrete alternative when no interactive display is available.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks'.

White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 4-5) documents the exact conversion errors: adding 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> 16:00); adding 12 to a.m. times (10:17 a.m. -> 22:17); omitting the leading zero (06:38); writing midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00; subtracting 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> 0:43 p.m.); subtracting 10 instead of 12; and omitting a.m./p.m. It teaches +12 for p.m. and grounds -12 in 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00', using paired 12/24-hour displays, analogue clocks and conversion tables.
learnerActions: Move a marker along a day-line running from midnight 00:00 through noon 12:00 and back to midnight, watching a 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) readout and a 24-hour readout change together as the marker moves.

Stop the marker just before noon and just after: just before, both displays read 11:59 (11:59 a.m. and 11:59); at noon both read 12:00 and only the 12-hour LABEL flips from a.m. to p.m. (so it shows 12:00 p.m., not 1:00). Then move on past 1 p.m. and watch the 24-hour clock tick to 13:00 while the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. — this is where the 12-of-difference first appears.
Stop at midnight and read both displays; confirm the 24-hour clock shows 00:00 (a new day starting), not 24:00, by looking at what it shows one minute before and one minute after.

For a chosen afternoon time from 1 p.m. onward, read the 12-hour value, then the 24-hour value, and state the relationship: 'from 1 p.m. the 24-hour hour is 12 more than the p.m. hour' — noting that the 12:xx noon hour is the exception, where both forms still read 12.

If a day-line is available, use its paired displays and boundary labels at 00:00 (midnight, new day) and 12:00 (noon); if not, draw the day-line on paper, mark 00:00, 12:00 and 24:00->00:00, and write both forms side by side for several times.
activities.intendedInsight: The +12 / -12 relationship is not an arbitrary rule but the afternoon and evening hours continuing to count on past 12; noon and midnight are fixed boundaries, the 12:xx noon hour still reads 12 in both forms, and the 24-hour day rolls from 23:59 straight to 00:00.

activities.title: Decide before-or-after-noon first, then convert
feedback: If a learner writes 9:45 a.m. as 21:45, stop at the first step: is this before or after noon? Morning times from 1 a.m. to 11:59 a.m. keep their hour, and a single-digit hour gains a leading zero, so 9:45 a.m. is 09:45.
If a learner writes 6 p.m. as 16:00, they added 10: count on from noon 12 -> 13 -> 14 -> 15 -> 16 -> 17 -> 18, so 6 p.m. is 18:00.
If a learner gives 12:43 as 0:43 p.m., note that 12:xx is already afternoon and stays 12:43 p.m.; only subtract 12 from 13:00 or later.
If a learner gives 19:30 as 9:30, they subtracted 10 instead of 12: 19 - 12 = 7, so it is 7:30 p.m.; if they wrote 7:30 with no label, remind them to mark a.m./p.m.
If a learner writes 6:38 instead of 06:38, remind them a 24-hour time always has four digits, so a single-digit hour takes a leading zero.
activities.rationale: A worked set covering exactly the discriminating cases (an a.m. time, the 12:xx noon hour, a midnight/noon item, and a single-digit hour) separates learners who reason 'decide before/after noon, then +/-12' from those who just +/-12 the hour. Practising the before/after-noon decision first prevents indiscriminate rule application; formatting the leading zero is rehearsed as a convention distinct from the conversion arithmetic.
sourceClaims: Children tend to treat the hour and minute of a time separately and apply whole-number reasoning to each, which is consistent with mis-applying the +12 rule to the hours alone (including to a.m. times) without reasoning about whether the time is before or after noon.

White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 4-5) documents the exact conversion errors: adding 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> 16:00); adding 12 to a.m. times (10:17 a.m. -> 22:17); omitting the leading zero (06:38); writing midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00; subtracting 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> 0:43 p.m.); subtracting 10 instead of 12; and omitting a.m./p.m. It teaches +12 for p.m. and grounds -12 in 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00', using paired 12/24-hour displays, analogue clocks and conversion tables.
learnerActions: For each time given, first state whether it is before noon (a.m.), after noon (p.m.), or a boundary (midnight/noon), BEFORE doing any arithmetic.
Convert 3:45 p.m. to 24-hour time (expected 15:45, add 12) and 9:45 a.m. to 24-hour time (expected 09:45 — add a leading zero, do NOT add 12).
Convert 19:30 to 12-hour time (expected 7:30 p.m., subtract 12) and 12:20 to 12-hour time (expected 12:20 p.m. — stays the same, do NOT subtract).
Write midnight and noon in 24-hour time (midnight = 00:00, noon = 12:00).
Write a single-digit-hour time such as 6:38 a.m. in 24-hour form and check it has exactly four digits (06:38).
Always label a.m. or p.m. when writing a 12-hour answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether to add or subtract 12 depends on deciding first if the time is before or after noon; a.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59 keep their hour (single-digit hours gain a leading zero), p.m. times from 1:00 get +12, 24-hour times from 13:00 get -12, and the 12:xx noon hour, the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour (written 00:xx) and the midnight/noon boundaries are exceptions handled by inspection, not arithmetic.

activities.title: Match and build a conversion table
feedback: If a learner matches 6 p.m. to 16:00, have them count on from 12 to find the afternoon hour; 16:00 is only 4 hours past noon, i.e. 4 p.m.
If a learner matches midnight to 24:00, remind them the new day starts at 00:00 and a standard digital clock shows 00:00 at midnight, not 24:00.

When a learner explains 'the minutes are identical and only the hour changes, by 12, from 1 p.m. onward (with the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour written 00:xx)', confirm this is the key idea linking the two forms.
If a learner cannot place a converted time on the analogue clock, link the hour and minute values back to the clock hands before continuing.
activities.rationale: Pairing times across formats and asking 'what is the same, what is different?' builds the relationship rather than isolated answers, and a forced choice against a well-chosen wrong option makes the +10 and 24:00 errors into discriminating decisions. Matching and choosing confirm whether a learner can recognise correct conversions; they do not by themselves require the learner to construct conversions unaided, so pair them with the independent-conversion activity above.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 4-5) documents the exact conversion errors: adding 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> 16:00); adding 12 to a.m. times (10:17 a.m. -> 22:17); omitting the leading zero (06:38); writing midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00; subtracting 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> 0:43 p.m.); subtracting 10 instead of 12; and omitting a.m./p.m. It teaches +12 for p.m. and grounds -12 in 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00', using paired 12/24-hour displays, analogue clocks and conversion tables.
Year 4 pupils should 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks'.
learnerActions: Match a mixed set of 12-hour times (with a.m./p.m.) to their 24-hour equivalents, including at least one morning time, one 12:xx p.m. time, and a midnight item.
Build or complete a two-column table pairing each 12-hour time with its 24-hour form, filling the missing cell in whichever direction is blank.

For a pair you matched, state in words what is the same and what is different between the two forms (same minutes; hour differs by 12 from 1 p.m. onward and in the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour, which is written 00:xx; 24-hour has four digits).

Choose correctly between a tempting wrong answer and the right one, e.g. for '6 p.m. in 24-hour time' decide between 16:00 (a +10 slip) and 18:00, and for midnight decide between 24:00 and 00:00, explaining why the wrong one is wrong.
Represent one converted time on an analogue clock to connect the notation to the clock face.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the two notations paired across many times — and articulating what stays the same (minutes) and what changes (the hour, from 1 p.m. onward, plus the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour becoming 00:xx) — consolidates the rule and exposes the specific slips (+10, adding 12 to a.m., 24:00, dropping a.m./p.m.).

activities.title: Timetable word problems that force the right decision
feedback: If a learner converts a morning timetable time by adding 12, return to the before/after-noon check before the arithmetic.
If a learner gives a 24-hour timetable time back in 12-hour form without a.m./p.m., ask which part of the day it is so the label is included.
Praise answers that state the before/after-noon decision and the reason for adding, subtracting or leaving the hour unchanged, not just the final number.
activities.rationale: Embedding conversions in timetable contexts rehearses the skill where it is actually used and keeps the decision explicit. Word problems can practise and check application but do not let a learner watch the conversion method unfold step by step, so they complement rather than replace the day-line and independent-conversion work.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks'.
learnerActions: Read short timetable or schedule problems (e.g. a train leaves at 15:45 — what time is that in the afternoon? A film starts at 9:45 a.m. — write its 24-hour time) and convert as needed to answer.
For each problem, say whether the time is before or after noon before converting, then give the answer in the format the question asks for, labelling a.m./p.m. when giving 12-hour times.
Include at least one morning time, one noon-hour (12:xx) time, and one midnight/noon reference so the morning and noon traps appear in context.
Explain your answer to a partner or in writing, justifying why you added, subtracted, or left the hour unchanged.
activities.intendedInsight: The conversion rule is applied to solve real timetable questions, and the before/after-noon check and the boundary exceptions still govern whether to add, subtract, or leave the hour alone.

constraints: Target age roughly 8-9 (Year 4); procedural measurement objective: read, write and convert between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks.

Always decide before/after noon FIRST; add 12 only to p.m. times 1:00-11:59, subtract 12 only from 24-hour times 13:00 onward. a.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59 are NOT given +12 — they keep their hour, with a leading zero only for single-digit hours (9:45 a.m. -> 09:45, but 10:15 a.m. -> 10:15); the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour is written 00:xx.

The 12:xx noon hour stays 12:xx p.m. — do not subtract 12 from it; noon is 12:00 and midnight is 00:00, never 24:00. At noon both forms read 12:00; the 24-hour ticks to 13:00 and the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. only when passing 1 p.m., so the 12-of-difference begins after the noon hour, not at noon.
24-hour times always show four digits; single-digit hours take a leading zero (09:45, 06:38).
Always label a.m./p.m. on a 12-hour answer.

Matching and multiple-choice recognition confirm a learner can identify correct conversions but do not by themselves show the learner can construct conversions unaided; pair them with activities requiring the learner to produce conversions in both directions.

A static paired-clock poster can label the two formats but cannot show the marker crossing noon or the boundary behaviour; treat a drawn or printed day-line as a static scaffold and have the learner reason through the noon/midnight transitions aloud.
An interactive day-line is one helpful representation, not the only way to teach this; a hand-drawn day-line, a conversion table, and analogue-clock work are valid concrete alternatives.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 6 p.m. = 18:00 (count on from 12: 13,14,15,16,17,18); the +10 slip gives 16:00 which is 4 p.m. — kept 16:00 only as a labelled wrong-answer distractor, never as a correct option. 3:45 p.m. = 15:45; 9:45 a.m. = 09:45; 19:30 = 7:30 p.m.; 12:20 stays 12:20 p.m.; 12:43 stays 12:43 p.m.; midnight = 00:00; noon = 12:00. All verified consistent.

Corrected the noon-crossing description inherited from the original design note/recommendation ('crossing noon ... the 24-hour ticks on to 13:00 and the 12-hour resets to 1:00'): at noon both displays read 12:00 and only the label flips to p.m.; the 24-hour reaches 13:00 and the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. one hour later. The original wording conflated the noon crossing with the 1 p.m. crossing and contradicted the lesson's own 12:xx-stays-12:xx rule.

Scoped activity[0].feedback[0] to the morning hours 1 a.m.-11 a.m. and named the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour (e.g. 12:30 a.m. = 00:30) as a separate boundary case, since the unscoped 'morning hours match' claim fails at the midnight hour. No task in these activities presents a 12:xx a.m. time; only midnight = 00:00 is exercised.

The source labels converting-notation as 'not a spatial task; 3D adds nothing'. This is a catalog-fit opinion, not an established pedagogical law; it has been omitted rather than asserted. No claim is made that any single medium is uniquely necessary.

The source framed the day-line marker as the moment the rule 'becomes something seen, not a rule to memorise' and rated it uniquely 'ideal'. This has been softened to one helpful representation among several, with a non-interactive drawn alternative provided, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy.

probeDeeper: 'Is that time in the morning or the afternoon? So do we add 12, or not?'
'You wrote 6:38 as a 24-hour time — how many digits should a 24-hour time have?'
'12:43 in 24-hour time — is that just before or just after noon? So what is the 12-hour time?'
'If midnight is 00:00, what does the clock show one minute before? Is there ever a 24:00?' (boundary counterexample)

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> '16:00')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ground the rule in the day-line — the afternoon continues 12, 13, 14... counting on from noon; count on from 12:00 rather than tacking on a half-remembered number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts a p.m. time with a +10 error (6 p.m. -> 16:00; 3 p.m. -> 13:00)

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds 12 to a.m. times as well as p.m. (10:17 a.m. -> '22:17')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Check FIRST whether the time is before or after noon; a.m. times just gain a leading zero, only p.m. times get +12.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies +12 to a morning time (6 a.m. -> 18:00)

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits the leading zero for single-digit hours (6:38 a.m. -> '6:38' not '06:38')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the 'always four digits' convention — a single-digit hour takes a zero in front (06:38); rehearse the formatting, not the conversion itself.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes a three-digit 24-hour time with no leading zero

errorPatterns.pattern: When converting FROM 24-hour, subtracts 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> '0:43 p.m.') or subtracts 10 instead of 12, or omits a.m./p.m.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Only subtract 12 from times of 13:00 or later; 12:00-12:59 are already afternoon and stay as 12:xx p.m.; always label a.m./p.m. on the 12-hour answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor on 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00'; the 24-hour day rolls from 23:59 to 00:00 and never shows 24:00.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives midnight as 24:00

responseLevels.gap: Applies +/-12 indiscriminately (to a.m. times too, or +10); no leading zero; midnight as 24:00; drops a.m./p.m.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions reliably — adds 12 only to p.m., subtracts 12 only from 13:00 onwards, uses four-digit leading zeros, labels a.m./p.m., and handles midnight (00:00) and noon (12:00).
responseLevels.partial: Converts clear p.m. and 24-hour cases correctly, but is caught by a.m. times, the 12:xx noon hour, the leading zero, or midnight/noon.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set conversions in BOTH directions and WATCH the method: (1) 'Write 3:45 p.m. as a 24-hour time', then 'Write 9:45 a.m. as a 24-hour time.' (2) 'Read 19:30 — what is that in 12-hour time?', then 'What about 12:20?' (3) 'How do you write midnight, and noon, in 24-hour time?' Watch whether they add exactly 12 to p.m. (but not a.m.), use a leading zero, subtract 12 only from 13:00 onwards, keep a.m./p.m. on the answer, and handle midnight and noon.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The a.m. item (9:45 a.m.) catches a child who adds 12 to everything; the 12:20 item catches subtracting 12 from noon-hour times; the midnight/noon item catches 24:00. A child whose rule is 'decide before or after noon, then +/-12' handles all three; a child whose rule is 'just +/-12 the hours' fails exactly these.

sources.claim: Year 4 pupils should 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks'.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics, Year 4 Measurement (statutory), gov.uk

sources.claim: White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 4-5) documents the exact conversion errors: adding 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> 16:00); adding 12 to a.m. times (10:17 a.m. -> 22:17); omitting the leading zero (06:38); writing midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00; subtracting 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> 0:43 p.m.); subtracting 10 instead of 12; and omitting a.m./p.m. It teaches +12 for p.m. and grounds -12 in 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00', using paired 12/24-hour displays, analogue clocks and conversion tables.
sources.source: White Rose Education, Year 4 Summer Block 3: Time (scheme of learning), Steps 4-5

sources.claim: Children tend to treat the hour and minute of a time separately and apply whole-number reasoning to each, which is consistent with mis-applying the +12 rule to the hours alone (including to a.m. times) without reasoning about whether the time is before or after noon.
sources.source: Earnest, Gonzales & Plant (2018), 'Time as a measure', Journal of Numerical Cognition 4(1)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3). Solving multiplication and division PROBLEMS using arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and known facts — the application layer that ties the early representations to real contexts.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'solve problems involving multiplication and division, using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods, and multiplication and division facts, including problems in contexts'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 (array totals via equal addends) building toward 3.OA.3 'use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities'.
• Operational details: the goal is to CHOOSE and use an efficient representation for a given problem — an array, repeated addition, a jump on a number line, or a recalled fact — and to recognise whether a story is multiplication or division. Push from counting-all toward using known facts.
• Checkpoint: model and solve in context. Tier A (6): solve a simple equal-groups problem with an array or repeated addition. Tier B (6–7): choose a sensible representation and solve both a grouping and a sharing story. Tier C (7): solve using a known fact rather than counting all, and explain why that's quicker.
bestPractices: Give real, contextual problems (equal groups, arrays, simple sharing) and let children choose the representation — array, repeated addition, number-line jumps, or a known fact — rather than prescribing one method.
Explicitly move children from 'count everything in ones' toward 'use a fact or a group structure', highlighting the efficiency gain so they are motivated to leave counting-all behind.
Include both multiplication and division stories (and both division structures) so problem-recognition — deciding which operation a story needs — is practised, not just computation.
Use the bar model and array to represent the structure of a word problem before calculating, so meaning drives the method.
Connect back to known 2, 5, 10 facts so problem solving rehearses and applies fluency rather than relying on re-counting.
keyRepresentations: Arrays (structure of equal-groups/array problems)
Repeated addition and number-line jumps
Bar model (representing the problem structure)
Known multiplication/division facts applied to context
commonMisconceptions: Counting every object in ones instead of using groups or a known fact — not progressing in efficiency.
Not recognising which operation a word problem needs (multiplication vs division; sharing vs grouping).
Modelling with unequal groups and still treating it as multiplication.
Grabbing the numbers and operating without representing the problem's structure first.
Muddling the roles of the numbers (number of groups vs group size) when setting up the calculation.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3): solving multiplication and division word problems by CHOOSING and using an efficient representation — an array, repeated addition, number-line jumps, or a recalled fact — and recognising whether a story calls for multiplication (combining equal groups) or division (splitting into equal parts), and within division whether it is sharing or grouping. The developmental goal is to move children from counting everything in ones toward using group structure or known facts, and to represent a problem's structure before calculating.

activities.title: Problem playground: model the story, then solve
feedback: If a child writes 5 + 2 = 7 for '5 bags of 2', act out the five groups with objects, count the total, and connect it to 2+2+2+2+2 and 5×2 so the groups-of structure is felt.

If a child shares 15 among 3 but ends with unequal piles or a miscount, model round-robin 'one for each' dealing and check at the end that the piles are equal — the sharing idea is there, the execution needs tightening.
If an array for 4 × 3 is ragged or has the wrong count, align rows and columns neatly, count rows × per-row, and connect the tidy array back to the numbers 4 and 3.
Correct answers to anchor on: 5 bags of 2 = 10 apples (2+2+2+2+2, or the fact 5×2); 15 shared among 3 = 5 each; 15 in bags of 3 = 5 bags; a 4-by-3 array totals 12.
activities.rationale: Choosing and applying a method across both multiplication and division stories (including both division structures) practises problem-recognition, not just computation, and keeps meaning ahead of calculation. Manipulable modelling lets children see whether their representation matches the story.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems involving multiplication and division using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts, including problems in contexts.
3.OA.3 use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems involving equal groups, arrays and measurement quantities.
learnerActions: Read a contextual equal-groups or sharing story (e.g. '5 bags with 2 apples in each — how many altogether?').
First decide: is this a multiplication story (combining equal groups) or a division story (splitting into equal parts — by sharing or by grouping)? State your choice before solving.
Choose how to model it: build an array, lay equal jumps on a number line, write it as repeated addition, or use a known fact.
Solve and check that your model actually matches the story (equal groups, the right group size and number of groups).

Repeat with a sharing story (e.g. 'Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children'), a grouping story (e.g. '15 sweets are put into bags of 3 — how many bags?') and an array task (e.g. 'Draw an array for 4 × 3').
activities.intendedInsight: A word problem's structure (equal groups, array, or sharing/grouping) determines which operation and representation fit; meaning should drive the method rather than grabbing the numbers and operating blindly.

activities.title: Count-all vs known fact: the efficiency race
feedback: If a child still counts every object, point out the time/effort difference they just saw and prompt: 'Which fact could land this answer straight away?'
Check that both methods reach the same total. If they agree, that agreement confirms the fact. If they differ, recount, because counting in ones can go wrong too.
Keep any demo total tied to a fact the child actually knows — e.g. if 24 is used, link it to the 2-times fact 2×12, or choose a 5- or 10-fact — so the recall step is genuinely available to them.
activities.rationale: Explicitly highlighting the efficiency gain motivates the shift from counting-all toward using facts — the developmental move this topic exists to produce. A side-by-side comparison makes the gain concrete; the demonstration shows relative speed rather than a proven intervention.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems involving multiplication and division using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts, including problems in contexts.
learnerActions: Take one problem whose total comes from a fact the child knows (e.g. 2×12 = 24, a 2-times fact) and solve it two ways: once by counting every object in ones, and once by using the recalled fact.
Watch the counting-all method work slowly up to the total while the known fact lands the answer at once.
Say why the fact is quicker, and try the next problem using a fact instead of counting all.
activities.intendedInsight: For a child who knows the fact, recalling it (or using group structure) is much quicker than counting everything in ones — this efficiency gain is the motivation to leave counting-all behind.

activities.title: Is it × or ÷? Sort and match the stories
feedback: If a story is matched to a wrong-operation sentence, return to acting out the situation to decide whether numbers are combined into equal groups or split into equal parts.
Praise reasoning that cites the story's structure ('there are equal groups, so it's multiplication') rather than guessing from the numbers.
activities.rationale: Matching stories to operations and spotting wrong-operation distractors rehearses and checks problem-recognition. This format exercises operation/method choice but does not itself elicit building a model, so pair it with hands-on modelling.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems involving multiplication and division using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts, including problems in contexts.
learnerActions: Read several everyday stories and sort each one: is it a multiplication (combining equal groups) or a division (splitting into equal parts) situation? For each division story, also say whether it is sharing (number of groups known) or grouping (group size known).
Match each story to the number sentence that fits it (e.g. an equal-groups story to 5 × 2, a sharing story to 15 ÷ 3).
For a tricky pair, explain what in the story tells you which operation to use.
Watch for distractors that combine the two numbers with the wrong operation (e.g. 5 + 2 or 15 − 3).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising which operation a word problem needs — and, within division, whether it is sharing or grouping — is a distinct skill from doing the arithmetic.

activities.title: Market-stall problems: talk through your method
feedback: If a child names a method without justifying it, ask them to point to what in the story makes that method fit.
Follow a spoken plan by actually building or jotting the model, so the reasoning is tied to a concrete representation.
activities.rationale: Prompting children to reason aloud about method choice supports problem-recognition and metacognition. Spoken reasoning elicits articulation and justification but does not itself produce a built model or the side-by-side speed comparison, so pair discussion with hands-on modelling and with the count-all vs known-fact comparison to ground the efficiency insight.
learnerActions: A character (e.g. a market-stall seller) poses an everyday equal-groups buying problem and asks 'how would you work it out?'
Say aloud which operation and representation you would use and why.
Try a follow-up that changes the numbers (e.g. 'If there were 6 bags of 2, how many apples then?') and explain how your method adapts.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate and justify a chosen strategy deepens understanding of why a representation fits a problem.

constraints: Include both multiplication and division stories, and both division structures (sharing and grouping), so problem-recognition is practised — not just computation.
Represent the problem's structure (array, bar model, or number line) before calculating, so meaning drives the method.
Connect back to known 2, 5, 10 facts so problem solving rehearses and applies fluency rather than relying on re-counting; keep any demonstrated fact within the facts the child actually knows.
Let children choose the representation rather than prescribing one method.
Matching/multiple-choice sorting rehearses and checks problem-recognition but does not by itself teach how to construct a model; pair it with hands-on modelling.

A fixed illustrated worked example (tap-to-reveal array and fact) can show one case but cannot provide the varied, decision-rich practice of choosing and applying a method; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.
These problems are modelled with flat arrays, bars and number lines; a 3D presentation is not expected to add conceptual value for this topic — a design judgement here, not a general rule.
Keep the bar model/array as a tool for the structure of the word problem, not as decoration added after the answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'race to 24' moment is retained as a motivating device; '24' is illustrative, not tied to the worked examples (which total 10, 5 each, and 12). Any concrete total used should match a fact the child actually knows (e.g. 24 = 2×12, a 2-times fact).
The second cited source (CCSS 3.OA.3) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its support as unconfirmed.

The 'efficiency race' and the framing that counting-all is slower are pedagogically motivating but not empirically established comparative efficacy; presented as a demonstration of relative speed, not a proven intervention.
Note 2.OA.4 (array totals via equal addends) was mentioned in the pedagogy as a building-block standard but is not in the row's sources[] list; it is not cited as a sourceClaim.

'Grouping' is treated as one of the two division structures (quotitive), distinct from the equal-groups structure of multiplication; the binary × vs ÷ sorts were reworded to avoid mislabelling multiplication as 'grouping'.

probeDeeper: Which of these is a sharing problem and which is a groups problem?
Could you use a times-table fact instead of drawing it all?
How does your array show 4 × 3?
If there were 6 bags of 2, how many apples then?
assess.correctAnswer: 10 apples (5 groups of 2, or 2+2+2+2+2, or the known fact 5×2); 5 each (15 shared into 3 groups); a 4-by-3 array totalling 12 — choosing a fitting representation and reaching the right total.

errorPatterns.pattern: operation confusion — for '5 bags of 2' writes 5 + 2 = 7, combining the numbers rather than making equal groups
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out the groups with objects, count the total, and connect it to 2+2+2+2+2 and 5×2 so the groups-of structure is felt
errorPatterns.revealedBy: adds or subtracts the two numbers instead of grouping

errorPatterns.pattern: shares unequally or loses track — deals 15 among 3 but ends with unequal piles or miscounts
errorPatterns.nextMove: model round-robin dealing 'one for each' and check the piles are equal at the end — the sharing idea is there, the execution needs tightening
errorPatterns.revealedBy: unequal shares or a wrong count in the sharing task

errorPatterns.pattern: array mismatched to the factors — draws 4 × 3 as a ragged or wrong-count arrangement
errorPatterns.nextMove: align the rows and columns neatly and count rows × per-row; connect the tidy array back to the numbers
errorPatterns.revealedBy: array rows/columns don't line up with 4 and 3

responseLevels.gap: Combines the two numbers with the wrong operation, or cannot represent the situation at all.
responseLevels.full: Chooses a fitting strategy for both grouping and sharing problems, represents each accurately (array / repeated addition / known fact), and reaches correct totals.
responseLevels.partial: Solves the equal-groups problem but is unreliable on sharing, or reaches answers only by drawing every object with no move toward known facts.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these, and show your working with objects, an array, or a jotting. (1) There are 5 bags with 2 apples in each — how many apples altogether? (2) Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children — how many each? (3) Draw an array to work out 4 × 3. (Watch which strategy they choose and whether it fits the problem.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The multiplication and the division sit side by side, so the task reveals whether the child selects the right structure (grouping/repeated addition versus sharing) and can represent it. A struggling child adds or subtracts the two numbers (5+2, 15−3), builds groups of the wrong size, or draws an array that doesn't match the factors. Watching the working — not the answer alone — shows whether the strategy is sound.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Animal Communication (ages 7–9): the many ways animals send messages to one another — through sound, movement/dance, light, scent, and body language — and the purposes these signals serve (attracting mates, warning of danger, finding food, defending territory).
• Standards — UK (DfE): extends KS1/KS2 animal behaviour and habitats; introduces behavioural adaptation as a communication SYSTEM (signal → receiver → response).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 1-LS1-2 relevance (young animals and adults signal to meet needs); 4-LS1-2 (animals receive information and respond); communication is animals sensing and responding to their world.
• Operational details: cover ≥4 methods with a clear example each — sound (whale song, birdsong, wolf howl, alarm calls), movement/dance (honeybee waggle dance for food direction, peacock display), light (firefly flashes, deep-sea bioluminescence), scent/chemical (ant trails, dog scent-marking, moth pheromones), and body language (dog posture, cat tail, gorilla chest-beat). For each, name its PURPOSE: mates, danger warning, food location, territory. Establish that a signal only works if another animal receives and responds to it.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~7–8): name 3 ways animals communicate with an example each. B (transitional, ~8–9): match a signal to its purpose (e.g. alarm call → warn of danger; waggle dance → show food direction). C (formal, ~9): explain that communication needs a sender AND a receiver, and give a non-sound example (scent, light, dance).
bestPractices: Cover the full sensory range deliberately — not just sound — so pupils learn animals also 'talk' with scent, light, and movement, breaking the sound-only assumption.
Pair every signal with its PURPOSE (mate, danger, food, territory) so communication is understood as goal-directed messaging, not random noise.
Make the sender-and-receiver idea concrete: a signal with no one to receive it does nothing — use the honeybee waggle dance where hive-mates read and act on the message.
Guard against over-humanising: animals communicate real information (danger, direction, readiness to mate) but not human-style conversations or words.
keyRepresentations: A signal-type gallery: one icon/example per channel (sound, dance, light, scent, body language).
A signal→purpose matching board pairing each message with its goal.
A honeybee waggle-dance diagram showing how angle/duration encode direction and distance to food.
A sender→signal→receiver→response loop diagram.
commonMisconceptions: 'Animals only communicate with sounds' — many use scent, light, movement/dance, and body posture.
'Animals talk in words / have language like ours' — they exchange specific signals, not human-style sentences.
'Communication is always to be friendly' — many signals warn, threaten, or claim territory.
'A signal works on its own' — it only matters if another animal receives and responds to it.
'Bright colours/lights and dances are just for show' — they carry real messages (mate quality, food direction, warning).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach animal communication as a goal-directed system (sender → signal → receiver → response) across at least four channels — sound, movement/dance, light, scent/chemical, and body language — each paired with a clear purpose: attracting mates, warning of danger, locating food, or defending territory. The central idea is that a signal only matters when another animal receives it and changes what it does, and that animals carry real information through many senses, not human-style words.

activities.title: Send the signal: operate a communication loop
feedback: When the receiver acts correctly, point out: the message got through because the receiver could read it AND respond.

When the receiver is confused by a mismatched channel, say: the message needs a channel the receiver can sense here — a light flash is washed out in bright daylight, and a visual display is lost in dark or murky water, which is why some deep-sea animals make their own light instead. (Whether a channel works depends on the conditions — scent, for example, works well underwater for many animals.)
In waggle-dance mode, if the bees reach the wrong flower, note that the dance's angle and duration encode direction and distance — small errors send bees to the wrong place.
activities.rationale: Communication is a send→receive→respond loop, and letting the child operate it (especially performing the waggle dance and seeing hive-mates respond) turns an abstract 'signal' into information that changes behaviour. An interactive loop lets the child act out the sender/receiver dependency, which a static reveal does not require them to do.
sourceClaims: The honeybee waggle dance encodes the direction and distance of a food source to hive-mates who then locate it.
Animals communicate via sound, movement/dance, bioluminescent light, chemical scent/pheromones, and body posture, serving purposes of mating, danger-warning, food-finding and territory defence.
Animals receive information through their senses and respond to it; young and adult animals signal to meet needs.
learnerActions: Take the role of the sender: pick an animal, choose a channel (sound, dance, light, scent, or body language), and choose a message (danger, mate, food, or territory).
Transmit the signal and watch whether the receiver reads it and acts — flee an alarm call, approach a display, follow a scent trail.
Enter a honeybee waggle-dance mode: set the dance's angle (direction) and duration (distance), then watch hive-mates fly off to the correct flower — or the wrong one when the dance is off.

Try sending a channel that does not suit the setting (a light flash in bright daylight that is washed out, or a visual body-posture display in dark, murky deep water where the receiver cannot see it) and observe the receiver fail to get the message.
activities.intendedInsight: A signal is not just a sound or a show — it is information that only works when a receiver reads it and changes its behaviour, and the channel must suit the environment and what the receiver can sense.

activities.title: Signal-channel gallery
feedback: If a child expects only sounds, highlight the silent examples: the firefly's flash and the ant's scent trail both carry messages without any sound.
Prompt the child to name the purpose for each example rather than just the channel, so a signal is tied to a job.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal gallery fits the survey-of-channels nature of the topic and deliberately includes silent channels to break the sound-only assumption. It surveys examples; pair it with the operating activity so the child also acts out the sender/receiver dependency.
sourceClaims: Animals communicate via sound, movement/dance, bioluminescent light, chemical scent/pheromones, and body posture, serving purposes of mating, danger-warning, food-finding and territory defence.
learnerActions: Explore a scene of animals and reveal each one's channel: hear a sound clip (whale song, birdsong, wolf howl, alarm call), watch a movement/dance (honeybee waggle, peacock display), see a light glow (firefly flash, deep-sea bioluminescence), see a scent puff (ant trail, dog scent-marking, moth pheromone), or read a body-language posture (dog posture, cat tail, gorilla chest-beat).
For each animal revealed, read its purpose card: mate, danger, food, or territory.
Collect at least one example from each of the five channels so the survey covers the full sensory range, not just sound.
activities.intendedInsight: Animals 'talk' through scent, light, movement, and body posture as well as sound — communication spans many senses.

activities.title: Hands-on ant-trail investigation
feedback: If the ants become confused at the wiped section, link this back to the idea that the route was marked by a chemical signal. If the ants carry on unaffected, talk about why: they may also use sight or landmarks, or some scent may still be there.
Connect this to the broader rule: scent is a real communication channel, and signals depend on the receiver being able to detect them.
activities.rationale: A real physical investigation with a prediction makes the scent-as-message idea concrete and tests whether the child treats the trail as communication or as innate knowledge.
sourceClaims: Animals communicate via sound, movement/dance, bioluminescent light, chemical scent/pheromones, and body posture, serving purposes of mating, danger-warning, food-finding and territory defence.
learnerActions: If a live ant trail to a food source is available, first predict what will happen if part of the path is wiped away.
Wipe a section of the trail with a wet cloth and watch what the ants do.
Describe what the wiping tells you about how the ants were finding their way.
activities.intendedInsight: If the ants lose their way where the trail was wiped, that suggests they were following a scent message left on the path, not simply 'knowing' the way. Wiping removes the scent, so the message is gone. (Some ants also use sight or landmarks, so the effect can vary.)

activities.title: Match signals to purposes and channels
feedback: If the child claims only noisy animals communicate, broaden the channels: show scent trails, firefly flashes, the bee waggle dance and body language, each carrying a message without sound. Make clear that 'if an animal is silent it can't send any message' is incorrect.
If the child describes signals as words or sentences, contrast an alarm call (one simple message: danger) with a spoken sentence — signals carry a few meanings, not a word-by-word language.

If the child says a bird sings 'just for fun', attach the signal to a job: birdsong mainly attracts a mate or defends territory, while other, shorter bird calls can warn of danger or tell others about food.
activities.rationale: Matching and categorisation check the range and purposes and surface the 'only sound' and 'animals use words' misconceptions. Producing a working silent example is the discriminator between equating communication with noise and understanding it as information transfer.
sourceClaims: Animals communicate via sound, movement/dance, bioluminescent light, chemical scent/pheromones, and body posture, serving purposes of mating, danger-warning, food-finding and territory defence.
learnerActions: Match each signal to its purpose (e.g. alarm call → warn of danger; waggle dance → show food direction; scent trail → lead to food; display → attract a mate).
Sort animal examples by channel (sound, dance, light, scent, body language).
Answer a short question about why a signal needs both a sender and a receiver, giving a non-sound example.
Respond to the prompt: 'Only animals that make sounds can communicate — a silent animal can't send any message. Is that right?' Name a silent channel and say what it tells the receiver.
activities.intendedInsight: Communication is any signal carrying information to a receiver; naming a working non-sound example shows you understand it is not limited to noise or words.

activities.title: Optional hook: ask a zoologist
feedback: Steer answers back toward the sender→receiver→response idea: a flash, song, trail or growl only counts as communication if another animal can read it and respond.
Use the growling-dog question to reinforce that body language is a channel carrying a real message.
activities.rationale: A role-play dialogue can feed curiosity and open the topic; the core learning is in operating real signals, so this stays a motivating hook rather than the main teaching activity.
learnerActions: Pose questions to an in-role animal behaviourist about how they decode a signal, such as how researchers worked out what whale song or the waggle dance means.

Follow up with the probe questions: who a firefly's flash is for and what it says; why a bird sings and what job the song does; how nest-mates learn where food is when many ants rely mainly on scent rather than sight or sound; and whether a growling dog is communicating.
activities.intendedInsight: Decoding real animal signals is detective work about information, mates, danger, food and territory — curiosity about the topic is grounded in how messages are read.

constraints: Cover at least four channels with a clear example each (sound, movement/dance, light, scent/chemical, body language) and deliberately include silent channels to break the sound-only assumption.
Pair every signal with its purpose (mate, danger, food, territory) so communication is understood as goal-directed messaging, not random noise.
Guard against over-humanising: animals exchange specific signals carrying real information (danger, direction, readiness to mate), not human-style conversations, words or sentences.

The gallery/reveal format surveys channels; it shows examples but does not itself require the child to operate the sender→receiver→response dependency, so use it alongside an activity where the child sends a signal and sees a receiver respond.

Matching and sorting are well suited to checking the range of channels and surfacing misconceptions; because reading or classifying examples does not itself require the child to send a signal and watch a receiver respond, pair them with an operating activity rather than relying on them for the send/receive intuition.
The ant-trail investigation depends on having a live ant trail available; offer the simulation or gallery as alternatives when it is not.
A navigable 3D hive view adds only marginal value here; the waggle-dance angle and distance are fully conveyable in 2D.

Channel-mismatch examples (a flash washed out in daylight, a visual display lost in dark water) are context-dependent illustrations of 'the channel must suit the setting and the receiver's senses'; do not teach that a whole channel universally fails — scent/chemical signals, for instance, work well underwater for many animals.

Checkpoints by developmental stage: concrete (~7–8) name 3 ways with an example each; transitional (~8–9) match a signal to its purpose; formal (~9) explain that communication needs a sender AND a receiver and give a non-sound example.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; all four sources[].claim entries were marked verified:false in the source row and have NOT been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The assessment's suggested distractor 'That's right — if an animal is silent it can't send any message' is a deliberately wrong option for diagnostic use; it must never be presented as correct in teaching. It is retained only as a misconception to rebut, not as learner-facing truth.

The original row used 'a scent trail underwater' as a channel-mismatch (failure) example; this was corrected because many aquatic animals communicate effectively via dissolved chemical/scent signals. A defensible mismatch (a visual display in dark/murky deep water, or a light flash washed out in daylight) replaces it in learner-facing text.

Comparative-necessity language in the original ('static reveals can't let the child send a signal', 'test rather than build') was reduced to scoped observable affordances; catalog fit ratings do not establish that one format alone teaches or that another only assesses.
The honeybee waggle-dance claim is cited to von Frisch research (age-simplified); it is presented at an age-appropriate level and not re-verified here.

assess.poeTask: If an ant trail is available: let ants form a trail to a food source, then wipe a section of the path with a wet cloth. Ask the child to predict what the ants will do before wiping. They become confused and lose the route — showing the trail was a scent message, not the ants simply 'knowing' the way.
probeDeeper: A firefly flashing its light — who is the message for, and what does it say?
Why does a bird sing? Is there a job the song does?
If an ant can't hear or see well, how do the others in the nest find out where the food is?
Is a dog growling communicating? What is it telling you?
assess.correctAnswer: The friend is wrong. Communicating means sending a message another animal can read, and it doesn't have to be sound. A firefly flashes patterns of light to attract a mate; ants leave a scent trail so others can follow it to food; bees dance to show the direction and distance of flowers; and many animals use body language, like a dog raising its hackles. Sound is only one channel — light, scent, movement and posture all carry messages too.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only animals that make sounds can communicate
errorPatterns.nextMove: Broaden the channels — show scent trails, firefly flashes, the bee waggle dance and body language, each carrying a message without sound.
errorPatterns.distractor: That's right — if an animal is silent it can't send any message.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that silent animals communicate; can offer only sound-based examples.

errorPatterns.pattern: Animals communicate by talking, like people using words and sentences
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast an alarm call (one simple message: danger) with a spoken sentence; signals carry a few meanings, not a word-by-word language.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes animal signals as words or sentences carrying human-like meaning.

errorPatterns.pattern: Birdsong and other signals are just for fun, not for a reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: Attach each signal to a job — attract a mate, defend territory, warn of danger, share where food is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the bird sings only because it's happy, with no survival purpose.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks communication means making sounds or 'talking like us'; gives only sound examples and denies silent animals communicate.
responseLevels.full: Describes communication as sending a message another animal can read across several channels (sound, dance, light, scent, body language), gives an animal example for each, and explains the purpose — finding mates, warning of danger, or sharing food.
responseLevels.partial: Names several communication methods and examples but treats them as a list of facts — can't reliably say what message each sends or why (mate, danger, food), or still treats sound as the only 'real' communication.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Your friend says: 'Only animals that make sounds can communicate — a silent animal can't send any message.' Is your friend right? How might a firefly or an ant that makes no sound still send a message to another animal?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who equates communication with talking or noise says silent animals can't communicate. A child who understands that communication is any signal carrying information names a non-sound channel (light, scent, dance, posture) and what it tells the receiver. Producing a working silent example is the discriminator.

sources.claim: Behavioural adaptation and animal responses to their environment extend KS1/KS2 animal-behaviour content.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS1/KS2 animals and habitats)

sources.claim: Animals receive information through their senses and respond to it; young and adult animals signal to meet needs.
sources.source: NGSS 4-LS1-2; 1-LS1-2

sources.claim: Animals communicate via sound, movement/dance, bioluminescent light, chemical scent/pheromones, and body posture, serving purposes of mating, danger-warning, food-finding and territory defence.
sources.source: Behavioural-ecology reference on animal communication

sources.claim: The honeybee waggle dance encodes the direction and distance of a food source to hive-mates who then locate it.
