pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, 'making sense of a problem' means the child learns that a word problem describes a real situation to be understood before any number is touched. The proficient young solver restates what the story is asking in their own words, represents it with objects or a drawing, works toward an answer, and then checks whether that answer makes sense in the story. The single biggest teaching risk is the opposite habit: children being conditioned to grab the numbers and 'do a sum', a compulsion to calculate that suspends real-world sense-making. Teaching therefore centres on comprehension-first routines (retell the story, act it out with counters, ask 'what are we trying to find out?') rather than on cue-words or speed.
bestPractices: Comprehension first: have the child retell the problem in their own words and say what is being asked BEFORE any calculating
Represent the situation concretely — act it out with counters, fingers, or a simple drawing so the story structure (part-part-whole) is visible
Use numberless / progressively-revealed story problems so children reason about the relationship between quantities before a number invites them to compute
Model a short self-questioning routine aloud ('What is happening? What do I need to find? Does my answer make sense?') and have the child echo it
Deliberately pose the occasional unanswerable or 'silly' story so children learn that not every set of numbers yields a sum — sense-making is required
Never teach cue-word rules ('altogether means add'): build understanding of the situation, not word-to-operation mapping
keyRepresentations: Concrete objects / counters the child physically moves to enact the story
Part-part-whole picture (two groups combining into a whole)
Simple bar or strip drawing linking the known and unknown quantities
Numberless word-problem staging (reveal the story, then the question, then the numbers last)
A four-move frame: understand → represent → solve → check
commonMisconceptions: 'I look for the special word — altogether means add, left means take away' (keyword strategy, applied before the story is even read)
'Every problem is just a sum with the numbers in it' — computes an answer even for an unanswerable or nonsensical story (suspension of sense-making / compulsion to calculate)
Restating a salient number from the story instead of the quantity actually asked for
Treating being stuck as 'I can't do it' rather than a cue to represent the story a different way

learn.summary: For 5-6 year-olds, 'making sense of a problem' means treating a word problem as a real situation to understand before touching any number. Proficient young solvers restate what the story asks in their own words, represent it with objects or a drawing, work toward an answer, then check whether it makes sense in the story. The main teaching risk is the opposite habit — grabbing the numbers and 'doing a sum' (suspension of sense-making / compulsion to calculate). The core activity is a patient spoken 'thinking partner' routine that refuses a blurted number and builds comprehension first; concrete counters, numberless/progressively-revealed staging, a worked-example reveal, and a single reasonableness check are supporting approaches with different purposes.

activities.title: The thinking partner who won't take a number yet
feedback: When the child retells the story and names what is asked before computing, affirm that move explicitly: that understanding-first step is the goal.
If the child blurts a number, the partner does not accept it yet — it asks 'what is happening?' and 'how could you show that with your counters?'
When the child catches an unanswerable story ('that doesn't make sense, you can't work that out!'), the partner delights in the catch — this is the target moment.
Always close solvable stories with 'does your answer make sense in the story?' to plant the reasonableness habit.
activities.rationale: The topic is a dialogic habit: understanding the story and explaining a pathway before computing. A partner that poses a short story, asks self-questioning prompts, and refuses a bare number models the self-questioning routine; the occasional nonsensical story directly confronts the compulsion to calculate. Spoken or tapped responses keep turns short for this age. This is a proposed design, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Modelling a self-questioning process for students to monitor and reflect on their problem solving has strong evidence of improving achievement.

Students' primary difficulty with word problems is a 'suspension of sense-making' / 'compulsion to calculate' — they apply arithmetic to the numbers regardless of whether the result makes sense; numberless word problems and focusing on relationships before computing counter this.

Mathematically proficient students explain the meaning of a problem and look for entry points, and continually ask themselves 'Does this make sense?'; younger students rely on concrete objects or pictures to conceptualise and solve a problem.
learnerActions: Listen to a tiny within-10 spoken story from a friendly partner character, e.g. 'Three frogs were on a log and two more hopped on.'
Before giving any answer, retell the story in your own words and say what is being asked ('what are we trying to find out?').
Show the story with counters/frogs or fingers ('show me with your frogs') so the part-part-whole structure is visible.
Work out an answer for a solvable story, then answer the partner's closing question: 'Does your answer make sense in the story?'
When the partner occasionally tells a deliberately silly story ('...so what colour is the pond?' or '...so how old is the cat?'), catch that it cannot be worked out and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: A word problem is a situation to understand, not just numbers to do a sum with; sense-making and a reasonableness check come before and after calculating.

activities.title: Numberless, progressively-revealed story with a part-whole workspace
feedback: The 'does this match the story?' prompt checks the child's model against the situation rather than only the final number.
If the model doesn't match the story, invite the child to re-place counters to show the two parts and the whole.
activities.rationale: Staging the reveal (picture, then question, then numbers) and giving a part-whole mat with draggable counters lets the child build a representation before a number invites computing, countering the compulsion to calculate and building the visual-representation skill. The dragging and part-whole mat are concrete interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Students' primary difficulty with word problems is a 'suspension of sense-making' / 'compulsion to calculate' — they apply arithmetic to the numbers regardless of whether the result makes sense; numberless word problems and focusing on relationships before computing counter this.

Mathematically proficient students explain the meaning of a problem and look for entry points, and continually ask themselves 'Does this make sense?'; younger students rely on concrete objects or pictures to conceptualise and solve a problem.
learnerActions: See the story picture first, then the question, with the numbers revealed last.
With a workspace of draggable counters and a part-whole mat, place objects to model the situation and the relationship between the quantities.
Only after modelling, use the number pad that appears to find the answer.
Respond to a 'does this match the story?' check that compares your model to the situation, not just the final number.
activities.intendedInsight: Children reason about the relationship between quantities before a number invites them to compute, building a visual representation of the situation.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal worked example of the four moves
feedback: Prompt the child to say which phase comes next before revealing it, so they anticipate the routine rather than only watching.
activities.rationale: A worked-example reveal makes the four-move routine explicit and models the self-questioning a solver uses. Used as a companion to the doing-centred activities: it shows the sense-making rather than requiring the child to perform it, so it supports but does not replace practising the habit.
sourceClaims: Modelling a self-questioning process for students to monitor and reflect on their problem solving has strong evidence of improving achievement.
learnerActions: Work through one story where each phase can be revealed: understand → represent → solve → check.
At each phase, see what a good solver asks themselves ('What is happening? What do I need to find? Does my answer make sense?').
Echo the self-questioning routine aloud after seeing it modelled.
activities.intendedInsight: The understand/represent/solve/check routine becomes visible as a sequence a solver actually follows.

activities.title: Single reasonableness check (which answer could not be right?)
feedback: Accept justifications grounded in the story ('she gave some away so it must be fewer'); gently redirect answers that only restate a computation.
If the child says 'more' is possible after giving away, re-enact with counters to show that, when she only gives stickers away and gets none, the number she has can only go down.
activities.rationale: A single reasonableness item keeps the focus on sense-checking rather than producing answers fast. This is deliberately restricted to reasonableness: a battery of scored sums would reward speed and reinforce the compulsion to calculate this topic must dislodge.
sourceClaims: Students' primary difficulty with word problems is a 'suspension of sense-making' / 'compulsion to calculate' — they apply arithmetic to the numbers regardless of whether the result makes sense; numberless word problems and focusing on relationships before computing counter this.
learnerActions: Given a within-10 story and a candidate answer, decide whether the answer could be right and explain why or why not.
For example: 'Maya has 6 stickers and gives some away. Could she end up with MORE than 6 stickers? How do you know?'
Explain using the situation ('fewer than 6 because she gave some away'), not by re-doing the sum.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasonableness is judged by the situation, so an answer can be ruled out before or without recomputing.

constraints: Comprehension first: have the child retell the problem in their own words and say what is being asked BEFORE any calculating.

Never teach cue-word rules ('altogether means add', 'left means take away'); build understanding of the situation, not word-to-operation mapping. Cue words misfire when the word points the wrong way — e.g. a 'more' comparison story whose answer is actually found by subtracting.
Represent the situation concretely (counters, fingers, a simple drawing, or a simple bar/strip drawing linking the known and unknown quantities) so the part-part-whole structure is visible.
Deliberately include the occasional unanswerable or 'silly' story so children learn not every set of numbers yields a sum; keep most stories genuinely solvable.
The tap-to-reveal worked example shows the routine but has the child watch rather than do it; use it as a companion, not the main practice for a habit that must be practised.

Scored, speed-oriented quizzing of multiple sums is unsuitable here: it can score the final number but not 'made sense of the story', and it reinforces the compulsion to calculate. A single reasonableness item is acceptable; a battery of sums is not.

Making sense of a word problem is a comprehension task, not a spatial one; a 3-D handling environment is not recommended for this topic because it adds handling cost without serving the comprehension-first goal. This is a scoped suitability judgement, not a claim that 3-D adds nothing in general.
When a child is stuck, scaffold by offering a representation ('let's put out the counters') and naming the move ('when it's tricky, we show it a different way'), rather than reteaching the concept.
Watch for restating a salient number from the story instead of the quantity actually asked for.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles, not these specific activities' effectiveness.

The legacy claims that a scored quiz 'cannot' teach this and that 3-D 'adds nothing' have been softened to scoped suitability notes with stated affordances/limits; the cited sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity between artefact types.

Source claims are copied exactly and attached only where they directly support the stated rationale; the WWC self-questioning evidence is for grades 4-8, while this topic targets ages 5-6, so transfer of that evidence to this age band is an assumption, not a verified finding.
The non-answerable 'silly story' device is a legitimate sense-making probe but should be used sparingly so children do not learn to distrust all stories; keep most stories genuinely solvable.

probeDeeper: 'Tell me the story again without saying any numbers — what is happening?' (checks a situation model, not word-matching)
'Show me with your counters why the answer is 4.' (pushes the assertion into a because-of-the-situation justification)
Counterexample: 'Here's another one — there are 5 red apples and 3 green apples, how old is the girl?' A sense-maker notices it can't be worked out; a number-grabber answers 8.
'Could Maya end up with MORE than 6 stickers after giving some away? How do you know?' (reasonableness by the situation)
assess.correctAnswer: There is no single scored answer — listen for a child who first makes sense of the situation: retells the story in their own words, names what is being asked (how many Maya has left), represents it (moves 6 counters and takes 2 away, or draws), gives 4, and can say why 4 makes sense (she started with 6 and lost some, so it must be fewer than 6). The disposition, not the arithmetic, is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compulsion to calculate with no real-world check: 'every problem is a sum you do with the numbers' — the child computes and stops, and will produce a number even for a story that can't be answered.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use numberless / progressively-revealed stories and occasional unanswerable ones; make 'does this make sense in real life?' a routine closing question. Confront the specific case: 'could we really know her age from the apples?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When told a nonsensical story ('5 red apples and 3 green apples — how old is the girl?'), the child confidently gives a number (usually 8) rather than saying it can't be worked out.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword operation-mapping: picks the operation from a cue word ('altogether' = add, 'gave away' = subtract) before reading or understanding the whole story.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Never use keyword posters; have the child retell the story and model it with objects so the structure, not the word, drives the choice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names an operation from one word and misfires when the word points the wrong way (e.g. a 'more' comparison story where the answer is found by subtracting).

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats being stuck as 'I can't do it' and abandons, rather than trying to represent the story another way.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach the concept: offer a representation ('let's put out the counters') and name the move — 'when it's tricky, we show it a different way'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child stops and says 'I don't get it' without attempting to act it out or draw; has the general persistence habit but doesn't yet apply it in maths.

responseLevels.gap: Jumps to a number without engaging the story; grabs the numbers and applies an operation; answers the nonsensical apples problem with a number and cannot say what is being asked.
responseLevels.full: Leads with the situation: retells the problem, represents it, and justifies the answer BY the story ('fewer than 6 because she gave some away'); spontaneously flags the unanswerable problem as making no sense, and transfers this to a new story unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Can restate the story and often gets the right number, but treats making-sense and checking as separate add-ons — recites 'understand, then check' or represents when prompted, yet does not spontaneously use the situation to justify or sense-check the answer.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Read the child a short within-10 story, e.g. 'Maya had 6 stickers. She gave 2 to her friend.' Then, before asking for any answer, ask: 'What is this story about — can you tell it back to me in your own words? What are we trying to find out? Show me how you'd work it out.' Finish with: 'How would you know if your answer makes sense?' Treat it as a discussion, not a test — you are surfacing how the child thinks about problems, not marking a number right or wrong.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who is genuinely making sense pauses on the STORY first — retells it, shows it, and can justify the answer by the situation ('fewer than 6 because she gave some away'). A child in the compulsion-to-calculate habit skips straight to a number and, tellingly, will still produce a number for a nonsensical story and cannot say why it makes sense. The gap shows in the reasoning and the sense-check, not in whether they can subtract.

sources.claim: The keyword strategy has students tie a single word to an operation without understanding the whole text; it superficially focuses on certain words rather than the problem's structure and should be replaced by schema (structure) instruction.
sources.source: Powell, Namkung & Lin (2022), An Investigation of Using Keywords to Solve Word Problems, The Elementary School Journal 122(3) (ERIC full text ED628160)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Pollination & Seed Dispersal (flowering-plant life cycle)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y3 'Plants'):** 'explore the part that flowers play in the life cycle of flowering plants, including pollination, seed formation and seed dispersal' — the flower is framed as the reproductive organ that drives a cycle; the child traces pollination → seed formation → dispersal.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-LS1-1):** '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS1-1] share a common set of stages: birth, growth, reproduction, death.' The flowering-plant cycle is a canonical model here; NGSS frames it as reproduction-within-a-life-cycle rather than naming pollination mechanisms specifically.

- **Operational details:** Two linked ideas: (1) pollination — pollen moves from flower to flower, carried by insects or wind, enabling the seed to form (keep it at 'pollen is moved so a seed can be made'; anther/stigma detail is KS3); (2) dispersal — seeds are then spread AWAY from the parent so they aren't overcrowded/shaded, by distinct mechanisms (wind/gliding, animal/sticky or eaten, water/floating, explosion). The powerful, age-right idea is STRUCTURE→FUNCTION: a seed's shape reveals HOW it travels — a sycamore's wings spin, a burr's hooks grab fur, a dandelion's parachute floats, a coconut floats on water. Teach WHY dispersal matters (a seed dropped straight down competes with its parent for light and water). Present the whole thing as a CYCLE that returns to a new plant, not a straight line.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete, with early cause/reason). The child sequences pollination → seed formation → dispersal → new plant, names ≥2 dispersal methods, and — the discriminating move — predicts a seed's dispersal method FROM its shape and gives the reason ('wings, so wind carries it far from the parent').
bestPractices: Teach dispersal as STRUCTURE→FUNCTION: examine real seeds (sycamore key, burr, dandelion clock, poppy shaker) and infer the travel method from the shape — the shape is the evidence.
Make the PURPOSE explicit — seeds spread so offspring don't compete with the parent (and each other) for light, water and space; without this, dispersal is just a list.
Keep pollination simple and mechanistic at KS2: pollen is carried (insect or wind) from flower to flower so a seed can form; reserve flower-part anatomy for KS3.
Represent the whole as a CYCLE returning to a new plant, reinforcing that this is the plant's reproduction stage of its life cycle.
Use hands-on tests — drop/spin real winged seeds, stick burrs to a woolly sock, blow dandelion seeds — so the mechanism is felt, then connect each to its shape.
keyRepresentations: A circular life-cycle diagram: flower → pollination → seed formation → dispersal → germination → new flowering plant.
A 'seed → travel method' matching set pairing seed shape (winged, hooked, parachute, floating, exploding pod) to its dispersal mode.
A bee/wind pollination illustration showing pollen moving between two flowers.
Real specimens (sycamore key, burr, dandelion clock) as the anchor representations.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing pollination with seed dispersal — treating them as the same 'spreading' step, rather than pollination (making the seed) then dispersal (moving the finished seed).
Thinking pollination is only done by bees — missing wind pollination and other carriers.
Believing seeds are dispersed so they 'find nice soil', rather than to escape competition with the parent for light/water/space.
Thinking the parent plant 'decides' or actively throws all its seeds, missing that most mechanisms are passive (wind, hitching a ride, floating).
Assuming the seed's shape is decorative/random rather than functional for how it travels.
Conflating pollen with seeds — thinking pollen itself grows into the new plant.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8, teach the flowering-plant life cycle as a repeating cycle (flower → pollination → seed formation → dispersal → germination → new plant) and anchor dispersal in a STRUCTURE→FUNCTION idea: a seed's shape reveals how it travels. Keep pollination simple and mechanistic (pollen is carried from flower to flower, by insects or wind, so a seed can form); reserve anther/stigma anatomy for older learners. Make the PURPOSE of dispersal explicit — seeds spread away so offspring don't compete with the parent for light, water and space. The discriminating skill is predicting a seed's dispersal method from its shape with a reason (e.g. 'wings, so the wind spins it far from the parent').

activities.title: Seed-launch test: match shape to travel method
feedback: When a matched seed travels well: 'Yes — the wings make it spin and fall slowly, so the wind can carry it further from the parent, where it may land somewhere with more room to grow.'
When a seed drops at the parent's feet: 'It landed right under the parent plant. Now the little seedling has to fight the big plant for light and water — that is why seeds need a way to travel.'
If a child treats the shape as random decoration: 'Try a seed with no wings or hooks in the breeze — does it go anywhere? The shape is the tool that gets the seed moving.'

If a child says seeds travel to 'find nice soil': 'Getting to new places can help, but a big reason is to get away from the crowded ground under the parent, so the new plant isn't shaded and short of water.'
activities.rationale: Dispersal is a physical, testable structure→function idea; acting on real seeds and watching the result makes the mechanism felt, then links each outcome to the seed's shape and to why distance matters. Real specimens let the child see the evidence (the shape) that supports the conclusion (the travel method).
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory: 'explore the part that flowers play in the life cycle of flowering plants, including pollination, seed formation and seed dispersal'.
Children commonly conflate pollination with seed dispersal and think seeds are spread to 'find soil' rather than to reduce competition with the parent plant.
learnerActions: Gather a set of real, differently-shaped seeds where you can — a winged sycamore key, a spiky burr, a fluffy dandelion parachute, a fruit that floats (e.g. a coconut, which is heavy but floats because of its air-filled, fibrous husk), and a poppy-style shaker pod; use pictures only to supplement, because the hands-on tests below need real specimens.
For each seed, choose how to send it off — turn up a breeze (a fan or blowing), drop it in a tray of water, or brush it past a woolly sock/fur to stand for a passing animal — and send it.

Do the hands-on tests: drop and spin the winged seed, blow the dandelion parachute, press the burr onto wool, float the fruit in water, and shake the dry poppy head to see seeds fall out of the holes at its top.
After each test, state which feature made it travel ('wings spin on the wind', 'hooks grab fur', 'parachute floats', 'air-filled husk floats on water', 'pod shakes seeds out as the stem sways').
For any seed that just drops straight down at the parent's feet, explain out loud why that is a problem for the new seedling.
activities.intendedInsight: A seed's shape is functional, not decorative: the shape predicts and explains how the seed travels, and travelling far matters because a seed dropped beside the parent competes with it for light, water and space.

activities.title: Fly the pollinator: make a seed, then close the cycle
feedback: 'The bee carried pollen from one flower to another — that is pollination. The pollen moving is what lets a seed form later; the bee itself does not build the seed.'
If a child says the bee 'makes' the seed: 'The bee is a delivery driver for pollen. After the pollen reaches the flower, the seed forms inside the plant — that is a separate step.'
If a child thinks only bees pollinate: 'Wind can carry pollen too — blow and watch it drift to the next flower.'
If pollen and seed are confused: 'Pollen is the tiny grain that gets moved; the seed is what forms afterward and grows into the new plant.'
activities.rationale: Keeping pollination at 'pollen is moved so a seed can be made' matches the age and the standard, and separating pollen transfer from seed formation directly targets the common pollination=seed-making conflation. Presenting the whole as a cycle reinforces reproduction-within-a-life-cycle.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory: 'explore the part that flowers play in the life cycle of flowering plants, including pollination, seed formation and seed dispersal'.
NGSS 3-LS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS1-1] share a common set of stages: birth, growth, reproduction, and death' — flowering-plant cycle is a canonical model.
learnerActions: Use two pictures or models of the same kind of flower and a bee token (or a cotton-bud 'bee').
Move the bee from one flower to the other, carrying 'pollen' (e.g. a dab of flour or coloured dots) between them.
Say what just happened in your own words: the pollen was MOVED from flower to flower — that is pollination — and only after that can a seed form.
Also show wind pollination by blowing pollen from one flower picture toward another, so bees are not the only carrier.

Pick a real seed to stand for the seed that would form inside a real flower over the following days or weeks, run it through the seed-launch test above, then draw the full circle: flower → pollination → seed forms → dispersal → germination → new flowering plant.
activities.intendedInsight: Pollination (moving pollen between flowers) and seed formation are different steps, and they are the reproduction stage of a repeating life cycle that returns to a new plant.

activities.title: Reference and check: cycle order, shape→method, and why disperse
feedback: For correct shape→method pairs: 'Right — the feature does the work of moving the seed.'

For 'why disperse' answers: full credit names avoiding competition with the parent (and siblings) for light, water and space; 'to reach new places' is a valid extra reason, but 'to find nice soil' alone or 'no reason' is incomplete — restate the competition reason.
If the cycle is drawn as a straight line: 'Where does it go after a new plant grows? Connect it back so it becomes a repeating cycle.'
activities.rationale: Checking sequence, the shape→method link, and the reason for dispersal maps onto the assessable core and surfaces the key misconceptions; prediction-with-reason is the discriminating move. This confirms conclusions and so works best alongside the hands-on testing, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory: 'explore the part that flowers play in the life cycle of flowering plants, including pollination, seed formation and seed dispersal'.
Children commonly conflate pollination with seed dispersal and think seeds are spread to 'find soil' rather than to reduce competition with the parent plant.
learnerActions: Order the stages of the flowering-plant life cycle into a circle that returns to a new plant.

Pair each seed shape with its dispersal method: winged → spins on wind; hooked burr → grabs animal fur; parachute → floats on wind; fruit with an air-filled husk (e.g. coconut) → floats on water; shaker pod (e.g. poppy) → shakes seeds out as the stem sways; springy pod (e.g. gorse or pea) → bursts and flings seeds out.
Answer and justify: 'Why are seeds spread far from the parent plant?' giving a competition-for-light/water/space reason, not just 'to find soil'.
For one seed of your choice, predict its dispersal method from its shape alone and state the reason before testing it.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can sequence the cycle, link seed shape to travel method, and give the survival reason for dispersal — predicting method from shape with justification.

activities.title: Bagged-flower investigation: does a flower need a pollinator?
feedback: If a child predicts both flowers make seeds equally: 'What could reach the open flower that could not reach the bagged one? The visitor that carries pollen is the difference.'
After observing: 'If the bagged flower set fewer seeds than the open one, that shows the pollinator's job of carrying pollen really matters for this plant's seeds to form.'
If a child says bright petals and scent are 'for people': 'Colour and scent are adverts for pollinators, inviting the carriers that move pollen — the flower's job is making seeds.'
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain test with a bagged and an open flower makes the pollinator's role visible and challenges the belief that flowers make seeds unaided or exist to look pretty for people. The pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part.
learnerActions: Choose a plant that needs insects to carry pollen between flowers to set seed (many flowers, such as peas and tomatoes, can pollinate themselves and would still set seed in a bag). Cover one of its flowers with a fine mesh bag so insects cannot reach it, and leave a matching nearby flower open.
Predict which flower will form seeds and explain WHY before waiting.
After time passes, compare how many seeds (or fruit) each flower set.

Explain the result: the open flower could be visited by insects carrying pollen and the bagged one could not, so if the bagged flower set fewer or no seeds, that suggests this plant needs insects to carry its pollen; if both set seed, discuss whether this plant can pollinate itself.
activities.intendedInsight: Seed formation needs pollination; in plants that rely on insects, pollen must be carried to the flower by a visitor before seeds can form.

constraints: Keep pollination at the level 'pollen is moved from flower to flower (by insects or wind) so a seed can form'; reserve anther/stigma/flower-part anatomy for older key stages.

Picture-only or matching tasks confirm that a learner recognises the shape→method link; they do not themselves provide the felt cause-and-effect of launching a real seed, so pair reference/matching work with hands-on tests of actual seeds where possible.

Matching verifies that a learner recognises the shape→method pairs; on its own it may not build the structure→function insight as fully as acting on real seeds, so combine matching with hands-on testing rather than relying on matching alone.
Sock/fur stand-ins, fans, and water trays are approximations of real wind, animals and streams; name them as stand-ins so the represented mechanism stays clear.
The bagged-flower investigation needs real flowers and time to set seed; it is a seasonal/longer task, not an instant demonstration.
Fertilisation (pollen joining the egg) is named in the assessment; for 7–8-year-olds keep it light ('the pollen joins with the egg so a seed forms') and do not demand detailed internal anatomy.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources (NGSS 3-LS1-1 and the OU OpenLearn misconceptions page) were marked verified:false in the source row; treat their claims as unconfirmed.

The original material sometimes compresses the sequence to 'pollination → seed formation', while the assessment inserts fertilisation (pollination → fertilisation → seed formation → dispersal). This is a genuine level choice, not an error: at 7–8 'pollen is moved so a seed forms' is appropriate, while the fuller chain (with fertilisation) is the full-marks version in the assessment. Activities keep the simple version for teaching and flag fertilisation lightly.

The original frames poppy dispersal as 'explosion/shaker'; the poppy is botanically a wind-shaken (censer) disperser distinct from a truly explosive/springy pod. The activities keep 'poppy-style shaker pod' and a separate 'springy pod → flings seeds' as two examples to avoid conflating the two mechanisms.

The non-preferred alternatives in the source (a 3D seed-flight simulation and a dialogue/role format) were considered: the source claimed 3D 'adds nothing needed' and that dialogue would 'replace the doing'. These are not established efficacy claims; a 3D flight view could add spatial realism (e.g. seeing a helicoptering trajectory) and discussion can support sense-making. They are retained only as optional extensions, not asserted as inferior.

sourceClaim attributions were reviewed: the OU OpenLearn claim (about conflating pollination with seed DISPERSAL and the 'find soil' idea) is kept on the two activities whose principle directly addresses that misconception (seed-launch and the reference/check 'why disperse' task) and removed from the pollinator activity, where the principle is separating pollination from seed formation.

No arithmetic or force/motion content requiring correction; geometry not applicable. The main conceptual risk (bee 'makes' the seed) is corrected directly in the activities' actions and feedback, not merely caveated.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: cover one insect-pollinated flower with a fine mesh bag (no insects can reach it) and leave a matching flower open. Ask the child to predict which forms seeds and WHY, before waiting. A child who thinks the flower makes seeds by itself predicts both do. The bagged flower sets far fewer/no seeds. The pre-observation reasoning about the pollinator's role is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: What's the difference between pollination and the seed actually forming?
Name two ways seeds get carried away, and what feature helps each (a wing? a hook? a tasty fruit?).
Why would it be bad for a plant if all its seeds landed right underneath it?
Why are many flowers brightly coloured and scented — who is that for?
assess.correctAnswer: The bee carried POLLEN from one flower to another — that's pollination; the pollen then joins with the egg (fertilisation) so seeds form; the fruit/seeds are then dispersed (wind, animals, water, or bursting). Seeds travel far so the new plants don't crowd and compete with the parent for light, water and space. Full marks put the stages in order AND give a survival reason for dispersal.

errorPatterns.pattern: pollination and fertilisation are the same event ('the bee makes the seed')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate them: pollination = pollen MOVED to another flower; fertilisation = pollen joins the egg; only then do seeds form. The bee moves pollen, it doesn't make seeds.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bee makes the seeds when it lands on the flower.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: collapses pollen transfer and seed formation into one step; credits the bee with making seeds

errorPatterns.pattern: seeds are dispersed to 'help the parent plant' or for no reason, not to avoid competition
errorPatterns.nextMove: If all seeds fell at the parent's feet they'd fight it (and each other) for light/water/space. Spreading out gives new plants room to grow.
errorPatterns.distractor: Seeds travel far just by accident — there's no reason for it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: can't give a survival reason; says seeds just drop or scatter randomly

errorPatterns.pattern: flowers exist to look pretty / smell nice for people, not for reproduction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bright petals and scent are adverts for pollinators, not for us — the flower's job is making seeds.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: no sense that the flower's colour/scent attracts pollinators for reproduction

responseLevels.gap: Merges pollination with seed-making or says the bee makes seeds; no reason for dispersal.
responseLevels.full: Sequences pollination→fertilisation→seed formation→dispersal, distinguishes pollen transfer from seed formation, names dispersal methods with matched features, and explains dispersal reduces competition with the parent — recognising flowers as reproductive, pollinator-attracting structures.
responseLevels.partial: Orders pollination→seeds→dispersal and names a dispersal method, but can't explain why dispersing far helps (competition) or still blurs pollination and fertilisation — stages without the survival logic.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A bee lands on a flower, then flies to another flower. Later that first flower makes seeds inside a fruit, and the seeds end up carried far away from the parent plant. Walk me through what the bee did and what happened next — and explain WHY it helps the plant for its seeds to travel far away rather than drop straight down.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason (why disperse far?) separates a child who understands dispersal as reducing competition/spreading the species from one who thinks seeds just 'fall off'. The sequence question also exposes the common pollination=fertilisation and 'bees make seeds' conflations.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 with answers to three decimal places, understanding that the DIGITS shift position in the place-value chart (the point moves nowhere; the digits move).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'identify the value of each digit to three decimal places and multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.2 — explain patterns in the number of zeros / placement of the decimal point when multiplying or dividing by powers of 10; extends 5.NBT.1 (a digit in one place is 1/10 of the place to its left).
• Operational details — secure the concept that ×10 shifts every digit ONE place to the LEFT (each digit becomes ten times bigger) and ÷10 shifts every digit one place to the RIGHT; ×/÷100 = two places, ×/÷1000 = three places. The decimal point is a fixed marker of the ones place; it is the digits that travel. Zeros are placeholders that appear to fill vacated places (0.0452), never 'just add a zero'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 3.456 × 100 = 345.6 correctly, describing it as digits moving two places left. Tier B (10–11): 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452, inserting placeholder zeros correctly. Tier C (11): explain WHY ×10 shifts each digit one place left in terms of each digit becoming ten times its value.
bestPractices: Teach 'digits move, the point stays' explicitly and BAN 'add a zero / move the decimal point' — the add-a-zero rule fails for decimals (3.4 × 10 is not 3.40) and mispositions the point; the movement-of-digits image generalises correctly.
Use a place-value chart (ThHTO . tenths hundredths thousandths) and physically SLIDE digit cards left/right across the columns, so the shift is enacted, not stated.
Connect ×10 and ÷10 as inverse shifts (left ↔ right) and chain them (×100 = ×10 then ×10) so the size of the shift maps to the power of ten.
Confront placeholder zeros head-on: when ÷1000 empties the ones and tenths columns, a 0 must hold each empty place (0.0452), and the leading zero before the point is written by convention.
Ground WHY in place value (5.NBT.1): a digit is worth ten times the digit one place to its right, so making a number ten times bigger moves every digit into the next-higher column.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with sliding digit cards spanning thousands to thousandths and the decimal point fixed at the ones boundary.
Left/right shift arrows annotated with the power of ten (×10 = 1 left, ×100 = 2 left, ÷1000 = 3 right).
Gattegno chart (rows of ×10 scaling) to show a digit jumping between rows as it is multiplied/divided by powers of ten.
Zoom / 'ten-times' number line to reinforce that ×10 makes the whole quantity ten times as large, not merely longer to write.
commonMisconceptions: 'Add a zero when you multiply by 10' — wrong for decimals (2.5 × 10 ≠ 2.50) and a source of place-value damage.
'Move the decimal point' — leads to moving the point the wrong way or mispositioning it; the point is fixed, the digits move.
Omitting placeholder zeros when dividing (45.2 ÷ 1000 written as 0.452 or .0452 rather than 0.0452).
Confusing the DIRECTION: multiplying making the number smaller (shifting right) or dividing making it larger.
Shifting only one digit or the wrong number of places, especially for ×/÷1000 (three places).

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 (answers up to three decimal places, with 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 as a four-decimal-place extension) by understanding that every DIGIT shifts position across the place-value chart while the decimal point stays fixed at the ones boundary. The organising principle is 'digits move, the point stays'; ×10 shifts each digit one column left (each digit becomes ten times bigger), ÷10 shifts one column right, and the number of places matches the number of zeros in the power of ten. Placeholder zeros fill vacated columns (e.g. 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452). This counters the 'just add a zero' habit, which breaks for decimals, and gives a place-value reason for 'move the point', which gets correct answers but is often learned without understanding.

activities.title: Slide the digits across a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner writes 3.456 × 100 = 3.45600, point out the value has not changed at all and the digits sit in the same columns — ask them to slide each digit two columns left instead so 3 lands in the hundreds, giving 345.6.

If 45.2 ÷ 1000 comes out as 0.452, have them count every column each digit crosses and check that each written emptied column (ones and tenths) holds a 0, giving 0.0452. If it comes out as .0452, note that the value is correct but the conventional 0 in the ones place should be written: 0.0452.
If a learner shifts the wrong way, ask whether the number should get bigger (×, shift left) or smaller (÷, shift right) and re-slide.

If the shift is in the right direction but off by one place, have them match the count to the number of zeros in the multiplier/divisor and recount; if the error repeats, check whether they are counting the decimal point or digits instead of columns.
activities.rationale: The target concept is literally a movement of digits across place-value columns, so enacting the slide (physically or on screen) with the point held fixed is intended to make 'digits move, the point stays' something the learner performs rather than recites, and dividing to a leading-zero answer forces the placeholder-zero reasoning that the 'add a zero' rule hides.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils identify the value of each digit to three decimal places and multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places.
Teaching 'digits move, the decimal point stays' avoids the 'add a zero / move the point' misconception that fails for decimals.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns from thousands down to ten-thousandths, with the decimal point marked fixed at the ones boundary (ThHTO . tenths hundredths thousandths ten-thousandths); the extra low columns are needed because 45.2 ÷ 1000 lands a digit in the ten-thousandths place.
Write 3.456 into the chart using digit cards, then multiply by 100: slide EVERY digit two columns to the LEFT in one move, keeping the point pinned in place, to land on 345.6.

Now take 45.2 and divide by 1000: slide every digit three columns to the RIGHT (the tenths digit travels into the ten-thousandths column), and write a placeholder 0 into each emptied column that is written (ones and tenths) to get 0.0452.
Say aloud for each step: 'the digits moved ___ places ___ because I multiplied/divided by ___', linking the number of places to the power of ten.
Try a target challenge: starting from 3.456, work out which single operation reaches 345.6, and which reaches 0.3456.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten moves every digit a fixed number of place-value columns while the decimal point stays put; the number of columns equals the number of zeros in the power of ten, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.

activities.title: Why ten-times moves each digit one column
feedback: If a learner treats ×10 as 'making the number longer', redirect to the quantity itself being ten times as large — 2.5 × 10 is twenty-five, not 'two point five oh'.
If they cannot say why the shift is one column, revisit that each column is ten times the one to its right, so a ten-times-bigger value lands one column left.
If they struggle to connect the power of ten to the number of places, have them break ×100 into ×10 then ×10 and count the columns.
activities.rationale: Grounding the procedure in place-value structure (each place is worth ten times the place to its right) is intended to turn a memorised rule into explained behaviour, which may support transfer to ×/÷1000 and help learners resist the 'add a zero' shortcut.
sourceClaims: Pupils explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10; a digit represents ten times the place to its right.
Teaching 'digits move, the decimal point stays' avoids the 'add a zero / move the point' misconception that fails for decimals.
learnerActions: Pick a digit in a number, e.g. the 4 in 3.456 (worth four tenths), and state its value.
Explain why, when the whole number is made ten times bigger, that digit must now be worth ten times as much (four ones) and therefore move one column to the left.
Use a scaling chart or a 'ten-times' number line to show the whole quantity becoming ten times as large, not merely gaining an extra written digit.
Chain the reasoning: ×100 is ×10 then ×10, so each digit moves one column left twice — two columns in total — and connect ÷10 as the exact inverse (one column right).
activities.intendedInsight: Because each place-value column is worth ten times the column to its right, making a number ten times bigger promotes every digit into the next-higher column; this is WHY the shift happens and why ×100 shifts two columns and ÷1000 three.

activities.title: Fluency and error checks
feedback: A missing-placeholder answer (0.452 for 45.2 ÷ 1000) should prompt counting every column and filling emptied ones — 0.0452.
An 'append zeros' answer (3.45600) should prompt re-sliding the digits two columns left.

An off-by-a-factor-of-ten answer should prompt the learner to recount places against the zeros in the operator; if it recurs, check how they are counting columns rather than assuming it is only a slip.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and fill-in tasks are efficient for checking fluency and catching recurring errors, though on their own they do not build the shift image — they complement the enacted chart work rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils identify the value of each digit to three decimal places and multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in-the-blank items such as 45.2 ÷ 1000 = ____ , writing all placeholder zeros, and 3.456 × 100 = ____ .
Answer direction questions: when dividing by a power of ten, which way do the digits move, and how many places for ÷1000?
Order a set of results by size, e.g. 2.5 × 10, 2.5 × 100, 2.5 × 1000, and explain the ordering by place-value shift.
Self-check each answer by counting the columns crossed against the number of zeros in the multiplier or divisor.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated practice with answers up to three decimal places (plus the four-decimal-place extension 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452) is intended to make the power-of-ten ↔ number-of-places mapping more automatic and to surface the common errors (missing placeholder zeros, wrong direction, miscounting by one).

activities.title: Challenge the 'add a zero' habit through dialogue
feedback: If a learner cannot explain the error, have them place both 2.5 and the proposed 2.50 in a chart and compare values — they are identical, so no multiplication has occurred.
Confirm the correct answer (25) by sliding each digit one column left.
activities.rationale: Prompting a learner to diagnose a misconception out loud may consolidate understanding; this is a supporting discussion activity that can accompany, but does not replace, enacting the digit shift on a chart.
sourceClaims: Teaching 'digits move, the decimal point stays' avoids the 'add a zero / move the point' misconception that fails for decimals.
learnerActions: Consider a claim a friend might make: '2.5 × 10 = 2.50'. Explain exactly what has gone wrong and give the correct answer with reasoning.
Explain why 3.456 × 100 is not 3.45600, referring to where each digit sits in the place-value chart.
Describe, in your own words, when 'add a zero' happens to look right (whole numbers) and why it fails for decimals.
activities.intendedInsight: The 'add a zero' rule is unreliable for decimals because it ignores place value. 'Move the point' gives correct answers, but used as a bare rule it hides why. Explaining the flaw is intended to strengthen the digits-move model.

constraints: Explicitly teach 'digits move, the point stays' and avoid 'add a zero' because it gives wrong results for decimals (3.4 × 10 is not 3.40). Do not lead with 'move the decimal point': it gives the same answers, but it hides the place-value reason, and the point is better treated as a fixed marker of the ones place.

Placeholder zeros must be confronted directly: when division empties columns, a 0 must hold each written vacated place (0.0452 has zeros in the ones — by convention — and tenths), and answers like 0.452 or .0452 should not pass unaddressed.
Match the number of places shifted to the power of ten (×/÷10 = one place, ×/÷100 = two, ×/÷1000 = three) and keep direction correct (× shifts left/bigger, ÷ shifts right/smaller).
Provide a chart with enough low columns for the task: 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 needs a ten-thousandths column, so the chart should extend beyond thousandths for the division example.
Recognition and fill-in tasks check fluency but do not by themselves build the shift image; pair them with enacted chart work.

Discussion/dialogue activities can surface and challenge misconceptions and can accompany the enacted chart work; they need not be treated as the only route, but the curriculum concept here centres on the learner performing the digit shift.

Paper or card digit cards used on a chart have slight physical thickness and are approximations of the abstract place-value idea; an on-screen chart with sliding digits is a model of the same relationship — both are legitimate ways to enact the shift.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3.456 × 100 = 345.6 (each digit two columns left), 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 (three columns right; placeholder 0 in ones by convention and in tenths, final digit in ten-thousandths), 3.456 ÷ 1000 = 0.003456, and 2.5 × 10 = 25 are correct as stated and were checked independently.

The place-value chart must extend to ten-thousandths: 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 places its final digit (2) in the ten-thousandths column, so a chart ending at thousandths (as the original representation described) cannot hold the result. Learner text now spans thousands to ten-thousandths.

The stated objective and summary say answers 'up to three decimal places', but the flagship division example 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 yields four decimal places. The arithmetic is correct; this is an original-row inconsistency flagged for review, not a learner error.

The original row's recommendation text said 'three placeholder zeros' fill the vacated ones and tenths places for 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452; that is a slip — only two written zeros are present (the ones leading zero by convention and the tenths placeholder). The learner-facing text uses the corrected 'ones and tenths' (two zeros).

The original row's optional 'drag the point instead' toggle was not carried into learner actions: moving the point and moving the digits give the same relative result only because position is relative, which can confuse learners. It is noted here for reviewers to decide whether to include such a toggle at all.
CCSS-M 5.NBT and NCETM source claims were marked unverified in the original and remain unverified here; no new verification was performed.
The reteach prerequisite links and diagnostic structure from the assessment fields were not altered and are out of scope for this rewrite.

probeDeeper: When you multiplied by 100, did the point move or did the digits move?
Why does 45.2 ÷ 1000 need those zeros after the decimal point?
Explain what multiplying by 10 does to the value of each digit.
Someone wrote 3.45600 for 3.456 × 100. What did they misunderstand?
assess.correctAnswer: 345.6; 0.0452. The teacher watches for each digit shifting two places left (×100) and three places right (÷1000), the decimal point staying fixed while digits move, and placeholder zeros inserted (the leading 0.0452).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'add zeros' / 'remove zeros' rule — 3.456 × 100 becomes 3.45600, value unchanged
errorPatterns.nextMove: place-value chart: ×100 makes each digit worth 100× more, so digits move two columns LEFT; the point doesn't move, the digits do.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer keeps the point fixed among the same digits and appends zeros; magnitude wrong

errorPatterns.pattern: 'move the decimal point' the wrong way or wrong number of places for division
errorPatterns.nextMove: reframe as digits shifting RIGHT three places for ÷1000; each digit becomes a thousandth of its value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 45.2 ÷ 1000 comes out as 45200 or 4.52 rather than 0.0452

errorPatterns.pattern: forgets placeholder zeros — 45.2 ÷ 1000 written as 0.452 (shifts only visible digits)
errorPatterns.nextMove: count every column crossed and put a zero in each empty place, giving 0.0452.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: too few decimal places; leading zeros omitted

errorPatterns.pattern: shifts correctly but miscounts by one place under speed
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; match the number of zeros in the multiplier/divisor to places shifted and recount.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer off by a factor of ten; self-corrects on recount

responseLevels.gap: relies on 'add zeros', gives 3.45600, or moves the point the wrong way/amount; no placeholders.
responseLevels.full: shifts digits the correct number of places both ways to 3 d.p., inserts all placeholder zeros, keeps the point fixed, and explains each digit's changed value.
responseLevels.partial: shifts correctly for the multiplication but drops placeholder zeros or mis-shifts on the division to 3 d.p.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to work these while you watch, using a place-value chart if they like: 3.456 × 100, then 45.2 ÷ 1000. Watch whether they SHIFT each digit the right number of places (with the point staying put) or fall back on 'add/remove zeros' and 'move the point', and whether they insert placeholder zeros.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: At 3 d.p. the 'add a zero' shortcut clearly breaks (3.456 × 100 is not 3.45600). Watching a division that produces leading zeros (45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452) exposes whether the child fills placeholders and understands digits shifting through the place-value chart rather than manipulating the point by a half-remembered rule.

sources.claim: Y6 pupils identify the value of each digit to three decimal places and multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places.
