pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Reading Dinosaur Trackways (ages 7–9): use fossil footprints (trace fossils) to INFER a dinosaur's size, speed, and behaviour — bigger prints mean a bigger animal; widely spaced prints mean running, closely spaced mean walking; parallel trackways can mean animals moving together in a group.
• Standards — UK (DfE): 'working scientifically' (gathering and interpreting data, drawing conclusions from evidence); builds on the trace-fossil category.
• Standards — US (NGSS): grade-3 3-LS4-1 (interpret fossil evidence of organisms AND behaviour); an accessible instance of using data to infer.
• Operational details — This is a PROCEDURAL inference skill: measure a feature of the tracks, then reason to a conclusion. Print SIZE → body size; STRIDE (gap between prints) relative to print size → walking vs running (longer stride = faster); several PARALLEL trackways heading the same way → possible herd/group behaviour; two converging trackways → possible predator following prey. Stress that these are INFERENCES (well-supported guesses), not certainties, and that footprints capture a MOMENT of behaviour that bones cannot. Keep the reasoning qualitative (longer gap = faster) rather than the actual speed formula (that's later).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7): says bigger footprints mean a bigger dinosaur. Tier B (~8): uses print spacing to judge walking vs running. Tier C (~9): interprets a trackway scene (e.g. parallel tracks = group; converging = chase) and notes these are evidence-based inferences.
bestPractices: Frame every reading as 'measure a clue → make an inference', explicitly labelling conclusions as well-supported guesses.
Anchor speed to STRIDE RELATIVE TO SIZE (longer gap for its size = faster), not raw gap, to avoid a size confound.
Use whole-scene trackways (parallel, converging) so behaviour — herding, chasing — becomes readable, showing traces capture moments bones can't.
Contrast body-fossil evidence (what it looked like) with trace evidence (what it was doing) to reinforce why traces matter.
Invite alternative explanations (are parallel tracks really a herd, or just a popular path?) to model tentative reasoning.
keyRepresentations: A trackway map with measurable print size and stride spacing, plus a walk/run indicator.
Side-by-side trackways: closely spaced (walking) vs widely spaced (running).
A multi-trackway scene: parallel prints (group) and two converging sets (chase).
A 'clue → conclusion' annotation layer on the footprints.
commonMisconceptions: 'Footprints show what the dinosaur looked like' — they show behaviour/movement, not anatomy.
'Wider gaps always mean a bigger dinosaur' — gap indicates speed; size is shown by print size (must separate the two).
'A trackway proves a herd/chase' — these are plausible inferences, not certainties; other explanations exist.
'The deeper/larger print means it was running' — running is inferred from long stride relative to size, not depth alone.
'Footprints and the dinosaur's bones are always found together' — tracks are usually found without the track-maker's body.

learn.summary: Children aged 7–9 learn to read fossil dinosaur trackways (trace fossils) as evidence, using a 'measure a clue → make an inference' routine: print SIZE indicates approximate body size; STRIDE (the distance from one print to the next print made by the same foot) relative to print size distinguishes walking (short stride for the print size) from running (long stride for the print size); several PARALLEL trackways in the same direction can suggest a group/herd; two CONVERGING trackways can suggest a predator following prey. Throughout, conclusions are framed as well-supported guesses, not certainties, and tracks are contrasted with body fossils to show that traces capture a moment of behaviour bones cannot. Core objective: separate the two variables — size is read from the print, speed from the spacing compared with print size — and keep reasoning qualitative (longer stride for its size = faster), not the numeric speed formula (that comes later).

activities.title: Palaeontologist's track-reading bench
feedback: If a learner calls the widely spaced prints 'the biggest dinosaur', separate the variables aloud: print size tells you approximate body size, the gap between prints compared with print size tells you speed — check each independently.

If a learner reads parallel tracks as one dinosaur pacing back and forth, have them count the distinct trackways and note they run parallel in the same direction — a pattern consistent with several animals moving together, though they could also have passed at different times.
If a learner says 'they're just marks, you can't tell anything', model one inference aloud (a short stride for the size of the print suggests walking) then hand the next track back for them to try.
If a learner judges speed from how deep or large a print is, note that running is inferred from a long stride relative to print size, not from depth alone.
Affirm tentative language: praise a learner who says a chase or herd is 'likely' and can name an alternative explanation.
activities.rationale: The skill is procedural, so learners should carry out the measure-and-reason loop themselves. Making stride adjustable against a fixed print size directly targets the common size/speed confound, and a scene with parallel and converging tracks makes herding and chasing readable while the alternative-explanation prompt models tentative reasoning.
sourceClaims: Trackways allow inferences about the track-maker: footprint size scales with body size; stride length relative to size distinguishes walking from running; parallel trackways can indicate gregarious/herd behaviour and converging tracks possible predator-prey interactions — all interpreted as evidence-based inferences.
learnerActions: Measure a single large footprint and read off an approximate, tentative body-size estimate it suggests (e.g. 'about as tall as a house'), treating that figure as a rough guide that depends on the species rather than a certainty.
Measure the stride in a trackway: the distance from one print to the next print made by the same foot.

For a fixed print size, lengthen the stride and watch a gait indicator swing from WALK toward RUN, so that speed is read from the SPACING compared with print size while size is read from the PRINT — two separate questions.

In a whole-scene mode, interpret multiple trackways: tag parallel sets as a possible herd travelling together, and two converging sets as a possible predator trailing prey, attaching your inference and how confident you are.
Respond to a 'could it be something else?' prompt by proposing an alternative explanation (e.g. parallel tracks might just be a popular path, not a herd).

Predict what the dinosaurs were doing, then watch one possible reconstruction animate them walking, running, and moving together as the tracks suggest, and compare it with your prediction, remembering the animation is an interpretation, not a recording.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading trackways is a measure-then-infer procedure: print size answers how big, stride compared with print size answers how fast, scene patterns suggest behaviour, and every conclusion is an evidence-based inference rather than a certainty.

activities.title: Annotated trackway scene: tap to reveal the reasoning
feedback: When an annotation is revealed, ask the learner to restate the clue and the conclusion in their own words before moving on.
If the reveal surprises them, revisit which measurement (print size or stride) drove that conclusion.
activities.rationale: An annotated reveal clearly conveys the clue→conclusion structure and is a useful scaffold, but because the learner cannot vary spacing or arrange the scene, it shows the procedure rather than letting them practise it — best used before or alongside the hands-on bench.
learnerActions: Study a trackway scene and, before revealing, state what each print's size and spacing suggest.
Tap individual prints to reveal size → body-size and spacing → gait annotations, checking them against your own reading.
Tap a multi-track scene to reveal the herd and chase interpretations, then say why those are plausible rather than certain.
activities.intendedInsight: The clue→conclusion links (size→body, spacing→gait, pattern→behaviour) can be made explicit and checked, reinforcing what each measurement supports.

activities.title: Check your reading: compare and interpret trackways
feedback: If a learner picks the trackway with the biggest prints as the 'running' one, point them back to stride length relative to size, not print size.
For 'what might parallel tracks mean?', accept a herd answer but prompt for at least one alternative to keep the conclusion tentative.
activities.rationale: Selected-response and slider items assess the target inferences efficiently and make a good checkpoint, but on their own they test recognition rather than building the hands-on measure-and-reason loop, so pair them with a constructive activity.
learnerActions: Given two trackways drawn to the same scale, decide which shows running and justify it from stride relative to print size.
Interpret a multi-track scene by choosing what parallel tracks might mean and what two converging sets might mean.
Use a slider to estimate 'how big was the maker?' from print size alone, keeping it separate from the speed judgement.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can demonstrate that they read size from the print and speed from the spacing, and can offer plausible behavioural interpretations as inferences.

activities.title: Explain-your-thinking with a curious expert
feedback: If the learner asserts a conclusion without evidence, ask which specific measurement supports it before accepting it.
If the learner treats a very deep print as proof of running, note that depth may reflect ground softness or weight, while running is inferred from long stride relative to size.
Reward answers that acknowledge uncertainty and name an alternative explanation.
activities.rationale: Socratic probing fits the tentative-inference theme and surfaces reasoning, especially on novel tracks (crossing, deep prints). It complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on measuring that most directly delivers the measure-and-infer skill at this age.
learnerActions: Present your reading of a trackway and answer probing questions such as 'How do you know it was running?' and 'Could parallel tracks mean something other than a herd?'

Work through novel cases aloud: if two trackways cross, reason about which dinosaur passed first; compare what very deep prints versus shallow prints in the same ground might tell you; decide whether a small dinosaur could ever leave widely spaced prints and when.
Revise a claim when you cannot justify it, distinguishing a well-supported inference from a guess.
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying each reading out loud and handling novel tracks strengthens the habit of treating conclusions as tentative, evidence-based inferences.

activities.title: Explore a 3D trackway site in situ (alternative)
feedback: If the learner judges speed from print size or depth, redirect them to stride length relative to print size.
Encourage the learner to name at least one alternative explanation before settling on a herd or chase reading.
activities.rationale: Exploring tracks in situ may add immersion and a sense of real scale. Whether the extra navigation helps or hinders the core 2D measuring reasoning is a design consideration rather than an established fact, so this is offered as an untested alternative to the flat bench, not a replacement for it.
learnerActions: Move through a preserved three-dimensional trackway and locate a continuous line of prints.
Measure a print's size and the stride between prints in place, reading an approximate, tentative body size from the print and gait from the stride relative to size.
Interpret whether nearby parallel or converging trackways might suggest a group or a chase, framing each as a possible inference and naming an alternative.
Compare how examining tracks in a 3D setting feels against reading them on a flat bench.
activities.intendedInsight: The same measure→infer reasoning (size→body, stride→gait, pattern→behaviour) applies when tracks are examined in a three-dimensional, in-situ setting.

constraints: Keep reasoning qualitative (longer stride for its size = faster); do not introduce the numeric speed formula at this age.
Anchor speed to stride RELATIVE TO print size, not raw gap, to avoid confusing size and speed.
Always frame herd, chase, and predator-prey readings as plausible inferences with possible alternatives, never as proven facts.
Treat body-size readouts (e.g. 'as tall as a house') as approximate, species-dependent estimates, not exact measurements.
Running is inferred from long stride relative to print size, not from print depth or size alone; depth can reflect ground softness or weight.

Reveal-only annotated scenes and selected-response/slider checks are scaffolds or assessments: they show or test the inference but do not let the learner vary spacing or arrange a scene, so they do not by themselves build the constructive measure-and-reason skill; this is their observable limit, not a claim that any medium is universally superior.
Tracks are usually found without the track-maker's body; use this to contrast trace evidence (what it was doing) with body-fossil evidence (what it looked like).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the single source is marked verified:false and was not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claim is attributed to Natural History Museum (UK)/USGS education resources but is unverified; treat the quantitative-sounding relationships (size↔body, stride↔gait) as qualitative teaching heuristics, not precise measurements.

A '3D trackway site' option from the legacy notes carried a categorical claim that '3D adds navigation cost without improving the inference'. That is a design preference, not an established fact, so it has been retained as a qualified alternative activity with proposed/may wording rather than deleted or asserted.

The 'about as tall as a house' body-size readout is an illustrative, approximate mapping; actual size inferences from prints depend on species and are uncertain, so such readouts are kept clearly tentative in the activity itself.

sourceClaims were narrowed to [] on the annotated-reveal, selected-response/slider, conversation, and 3D activities because their rationales concern the delivery medium (scaffold, assessment, Socratic probing, immersion), which the single source claim about trackway inferences does not directly support; the source is retained only where the rationale invokes the actual inference relationships.

probeDeeper: If two trackways cross each other, how would you work out which dinosaur passed by first?
What would very deep prints tell you compared with shallow ones in the same ground?
Could a small dinosaur ever leave prints spaced far apart? When would that happen?
assess.correctAnswer: Track A: a small dinosaur, walking (small prints, short stride). Track B: a large dinosaur, running (large prints, long stride between them). Track C: several dinosaurs travelling together as a group (parallel tracks, same direction). Print SIZE indicates body size; the GAP between prints indicates speed; PARALLEL tracks indicate a herd.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates stride with size: 'the far-apart prints mean the biggest dinosaur.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two variables explicitly — print size tells you body size, the gap between prints tells you speed; check each independently.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels Track B the biggest because the prints are spread out, ignoring the actual print size.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads parallel trackways as one busy animal rather than several: 'it's one dinosaur that walked back and forth.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the distinct trackways and note they run parallel in the same direction and spacing — a signature of animals travelling together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts Track C as a single pacing dinosaur instead of a group moving together.

errorPatterns.pattern: Denies any inference is possible: 'they're just marks, you can't tell anything.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model one inference aloud (short stride = walking) then hand the next track back for the child to try.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to reason from the prints, treating them as decoration rather than evidence.

responseLevels.gap: Reads the pictures literally with no measurement — e.g. calls the spread-out prints 'the biggest' and makes no size/speed distinction.
responseLevels.full: Coordinates print size, stride spacing and track pattern together to reconstruct size, gait and social behaviour, and reasons sensibly about a novel track such as crossing or deep prints.
responseLevels.partial: Makes single, isolated inferences (big prints mean a big dinosaur) but does not combine spacing to judge speed or read parallel tracks as a group.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three trackways drawn to the same scale. Track A: small prints spaced close together. Track B: large prints spaced far apart. Track C: several sets of prints side by side, all heading the same way. For each track, work out what it tells you about the dinosaur — how big it was, whether it was walking or running, and whether it was alone or in a group. Talk me through your reasoning as you go.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who can perform the reading measures print size and stride separately and links stride length to speed. A child who cannot guesses from the overall picture or reads body size off the spacing, conflating the two variables.

sources.claim: Trackways allow inferences about the track-maker: footprint size scales with body size; stride length relative to size distinguishes walking from running; parallel trackways can indicate gregarious/herd behaviour and converging tracks possible predator-prey interactions — all interpreted as evidence-based inferences.
sources.source: Natural History Museum (UK) / USGS — dinosaur trackway interpretation education resources

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 3). Recall and use multiplication AND division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 tables — the second fact set, exploiting the doubling chain 2→4→8.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 multiplication tables'. (By end of Y4 all tables to 12×12 memorised.)
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.7 'fluently multiply and divide within 100; by end of Grade 3 know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers'.
• Operational details: derive the 4s by doubling the 2s and the 8s by doubling the 4s (the doubling chain 2→4→8, banked from Counting & Cardinality skip counting); build 3s from counting-in-3s patterns and known facts; use commutativity and inverse to get four facts from one. Include division facts and out-of-order recall, not chanting.
• Checkpoint: recall + derive. Tier A (7): recall 3s and 4s facts in order. Tier B (7–8): recall any 3, 4 or 8 fact out of order and its division fact. Tier C (8): derive an 8s fact by doubling the matching 4s fact and explain the chain 2→4→8.
bestPractices: Build the 4s as doubles of the 2s and the 8s as doubles of the 4s — the doubling chain 2→4→8 — so the hardest of these tables (8s) is anchored to easier known facts and can be re-derived.
Learn division facts alongside multiplication as fact families and use commutativity, so one fact delivers four (4×8, 8×4, 32÷8, 32÷4).
Use the multiplication square and hundred-square patterns (3s make a diagonal stripe; 4s and 8s are doubled columns) to see the facts as a connected, patterned web rather than three isolated lists.
Rehearse out of order and in mixed problems to reach genuine recall, working toward the end-of-Y4 goal of all facts to 12×12.
Give the 8s the most rehearsal (weakest independent pattern of the three) and always tie a forgotten 8s fact back to 'double the 4s' as the repair strategy.
keyRepresentations: Multiplication square / times-table grid (patterns and commutative symmetry)
Doubling-chain number lines (2s → 4s → 8s, each jump doubling)
Arrays for each fact and its fact family
Hundred square with 3s, 4s, 8s shaded (diagonal / doubled-column patterns)
commonMisconceptions: Chanting a table but being unable to recall a fact out of order or its division fact.
Learning 4s and 8s as unrelated lists and not noticing 8s are doubled 4s — so a forgotten 8s fact can't be repaired.
Treating a×b and b×a as separate facts (not using commutativity).
Confusing adjacent tables (3s with 4s, 4s with 8s) because the steps feel similar.
Doubling errors when deriving 8s from 4s (adding instead of doubling, or doubling the wrong term).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 3): recall and use multiplication AND division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 times tables, exploiting the doubling chain 2→4→8 so the hardest table (8s) is anchored to easier facts and can be re-derived. Teach division alongside multiplication as fact families (one fact gives four), rehearse out of order, and treat a forgotten 8s fact as a chance to repair via 'double the 4s'.

activities.title: The doubling chain: 2s → 4s → 8s
feedback: If a child treats 8s as a separate list and counts from zero, ring every other multiple of 4 to reveal the 8s and make the doubling relationship explicit.
If a child adds instead of doubles, or doubles the wrong term, pause on one array and physically double it so the operation is visible.
On any 8s miss, respond not with the bare answer but with 'what's the matching 4s fact? now double it.'
activities.rationale: Anchoring the 8s to the 4s (and 4s to the 2s) via doubling gives a repair strategy that survives a forgotten fact; manipulable arrays make the doubling concrete. Linking tables on a shared grid shows them as a patterned structure rather than lists to chant.
sourceClaims: 4s are derived by doubling 2s and 8s by doubling 4s (the doubling chain); the 8s need the most rehearsal and should be anchored to the 4s.
learnerActions: Pick a 2s fact such as 3×2=6 and build it as an array (3 rows of 2).
Double the array to make 3×4=12, then double again to make 3×8=24, saying aloud 'double the 2s gives the 4s; double the 4s gives the 8s'.
Repeat the chain for several facts (e.g. 7×2=14 → 7×4=28 → 7×8=56), each time predicting the next fact before doubling.
When an 8s fact is forgotten, recover it by finding the matching 4s fact and doubling it (e.g. forgot 3×8 → find 3×4=12 → double → 24).

Shade the 3s, 4s and 8s on a hundred square (or read their rows on a multiplication square): on the hundred square, notice that the multiples of 3 make diagonal stripes, and on either grid notice that the 8s multiples are every other 4s multiple.
activities.intendedInsight: The 8s table, usually the hardest, is 'just double the 4s, which are double the 2s'. Facts are a connected, patterned web, not three isolated lists, so a forgotten fact can be rebuilt.

activities.title: One fact gives four: multiplication and division fact families
feedback: If division is noticeably slower than multiplication, return to the fact-family triangle and read every × fact together with its two ÷ facts.
If a child treats a×b and b×a as separate facts, rotate the array a quarter-turn to show it is the same quantity.
Prompt: 'What's 32÷8, and which multiplication fact helped you?'
activities.rationale: Learning division alongside multiplication as fact families and using commutativity builds genuine recall economically and closes the common gap where division trails multiplication.
sourceClaims: Y3: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 multiplication tables; by end of Y4 all tables to 12×12 memorised.
3.OA.7 fluently multiply and divide within 100 and know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers by end of Grade 3.
learnerActions: Take one fact such as 4×8=32 and write its whole family: 4×8=32, 8×4=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8.
Use a fact-family triangle (32 at top, 4 and 8 below) to read off each of the four facts, covering a corner to find the missing number.
Build the same family as an array and re-read it two ways (4 rows of 8, 8 rows of 4) to see commutativity.
Practise the division facts until they are as quick as the multiplication facts, e.g. given 24÷8, name the × fact you used (3×8=24).
activities.intendedInsight: Commutativity and the inverse relationship mean one known fact delivers four; division need not lag behind multiplication.

activities.title: Out-of-order recall and targeting the sticky facts
feedback: If errors cluster on the hard facts while easy ones are fluent, do NOT mass-drill the whole table — target those few facts with derivation and spaced retrieval.
Confusing related tables (3s with 4s, 4s with 8s): slow down and check with one array, by counting on one step, or (for 4s and 8s) by doubling or halving.
Celebrate a correct derivation as highly as a recalled fact — both show a secure, networked grasp.
activities.rationale: Out-of-order and mixed practice reaches genuine recall rather than chant-dependent sequencing; targeting hard facts with derivation and spaced retrieval is more efficient than undifferentiated drill. This supports the end-of-Y4 goal of all tables to 12×12.
sourceClaims: Y3: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 multiplication tables; by end of Y4 all tables to 12×12 memorised.
4s are derived by doubling 2s and 8s by doubling 4s (the doubling chain); the 8s need the most rehearsal and should be anchored to the 4s.
learnerActions: Answer mixed 3s/4s/8s facts in random order (both × and ÷), noting which you recalled instantly and which you had to work out.
Identify your few hardest facts (often the high ones like 4×7, 8×6, 8×7) and rehearse just those with spaced repetition rather than re-chanting the whole table.
Derive a sticky fact from partial products, e.g. 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 = 40 + 16 = 56, or 8×6 as double 4×6 (24→48).
Fill the blank in fact families and match a given fact to the correct array.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means recalling or efficiently deriving any fact out of order, with effort concentrated on the few genuinely hard facts, not mass-drilling what is already known.

constraints: The learning target is recalled facts: timed/mixed recall exercises check fluency but do not by themselves build the doubling structure — pair them with array building and the doubling chain.

A static multiplication-square or hundred-square poster is a strong reference and pattern-shower but cannot run out-of-order recall or animate the doubling; use it as a support alongside active practice.

Oral quiz-partner drill offers rehearsal and can verbally prompt the 'double the 4s' repair on an 8s miss, but talking alone does not display an array doubling in size; pair it with a visual array where you want the relationship seen.
Division facts must be rehearsed to the same security as multiplication; left implicit they tend to lag.
When using paper arrays or counters, remember they approximate the abstract fact; the point is the number relationship, not the physical objects themselves.

Interactive aids that recolour the grid, pop an array on tapping a cell, or animate an array doubling in size are helpful optional ways to make the mechanism visible — they are examples, not requirements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent final re-review performed: the prior reviewer's empty unresolved list was not trusted. Confirmed the DfE topic claim is correctly absent from the doubling-chain activity (its rationale rests on the NCETM doubling principle) and the oral quiz-partner constraint is rescoped to a narrow affordance. No fresh source verification was carried out.

The source marks the UK National Curriculum claim as verified; the CCSS 3.OA.7 claim and the NCETM doubling-chain claim are marked unverified in the source — treat their evidence strength as unconfirmed.

Out-of-order recall and spaced retrieval (activity 3) derive from the pedagogy best-practice notes; among the cited claims, the DfE claim directly supports the end-of-Y4 all-tables goal and the NCETM claim supports giving the 8s the most rehearsal, while the fact-family/commutativity principle in activity 2 is a pedagogy-note principle not directly carried by any sources[].claim.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3×8=24, 4×7=28, 8×6=48 (double 24), 3×9=27, 32÷8=4, 24÷3=8, 28÷4=7, 24÷8=3, 8×7=56 (40+16) all check out and were retained as stated. The '27' in the source correctAnswer corresponds to 3×9 from the diagnostic prompt.

The original source expressed comparative/necessity framing (e.g. that 3D 'adds no value' and that posters/quizzes/conversation can only support or test, not teach). These have been softened to scoped, observable affordances/limits rather than universal laws, since the source ratings do not establish comparative efficacy.

probeDeeper: How did you get 8 × 6?
What's 32 ÷ 8, and which × fact did you use?
Which fact is hardest for you?
assess.correctAnswer: 28, 48, 27; 4, 8, 7; and 8 × 6 is double 4 × 6 (24 → 48). Facts recalled or efficiently derived, with division as secure as multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: isolated facts, no derivation — knows some 4s but treats the 8s as a separate list, unable to use 4 × 6 to reach 8 × 6
errorPatterns.nextMove: teach doubling (8 = double 4) and ring every other multiple of 4 to reveal the 8s; make the relationship explicit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot connect 4s and 8s; laboriously counts the 8s from zero

errorPatterns.pattern: high facts are the weak spots — reliable on easy ones, slow or guessing on 4 × 7, 8 × 6, 8 × 7
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT mass-drill the whole table — target the few sticky facts with derivation (8 × 7 = 8 × 5 + 8 × 2) and spaced retrieval
errorPatterns.revealedBy: errors concentrate on the known-hard facts while easy facts are fluent

errorPatterns.pattern: division facts lag — quick on × but slow on 32 ÷ 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: use fact-family triangles linking each × fact to its two ÷ facts
errorPatterns.revealedBy: ÷ noticeably weaker than ×

responseLevels.gap: Cannot recall 3/4/8 facts and counts each from zero with errors.
responseLevels.full: Recalls 3/4/8 multiplication and division facts fluently and derives harder ones (8s from 4s, 8 × 7 from partial products).
responseLevels.partial: Recalls the easier facts but the high 7×/8× and division facts are slow or reconstructed, with little use of doubling.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Quick-fire, and tell me if you had to work any out: 4 × 7? 8 × 6? 3 × 9? Then the divisions: 32 ÷ 8? 24 ÷ 3? 28 ÷ 4? And one more — how could knowing 4 × 6 help you find 8 × 6? (Watch recall versus derivation, the harder 7×/8× facts, and whether they use doubling.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 3/4/8 tables are harder, and the 'use 4 × 6 to get 8 × 6' prompt tests whether facts are networked (doubling links 4s and 8s) or held as isolated lists. Errors clustering on the high 7×/8× facts, and weaker division, mark a fragile grasp.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5-7 (KS1/Grades K-2): the butterfly life cycle — egg → caterpillar (larva) → chrysalis (pupa) → butterfly — and the big idea that these are STAGES OF ONE CREATURE, not four different animals.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' contexts and animal life-cycle content; Y2 'Animals, including humans' (notice that animals have offspring which grow into adults — life cycles). Working-scientifically: observing changes over time.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS1-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-LS1-1] birth, growth, reproduction and death) — the KS1 version is the observational precursor.
• Operational details — the transformation is the wonder AND the tricky bit: children must grasp that the caterpillar and butterfly are the SAME individual. Best taught by observing a real class caterpillar culture over weeks (first-hand change over time). Emphasise ordered SEQUENCE and that it is a cycle (the butterfly lays eggs again). Names: larva/pupa can be introduced alongside caterpillar/chrysalis.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): names the four stages. Tier B (age 6): puts the four stages in the correct order. Tier C (age 7): explains that it is one creature changing (metamorphosis) and that the cycle repeats.
bestPractices: Observe a real class caterpillar culture over weeks so children witness the change over time first-hand — the single most effective approach.
Hammer the 'same creature' idea — track one individual through all four stages so children don't think they are four different animals.
Teach it as an ordered CYCLE that repeats (butterfly lays eggs), not a one-way line.
Introduce the technical names (larva, pupa) alongside the familiar ones (caterpillar, chrysalis) without overloading.
Use time-based media (slider, timelapse) so the slow transformation is visible in one sitting.
keyRepresentations: A circular four-stage life-cycle diagram (egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly → egg).
A timelapse/scrubbable animation of the transformation.
A single highlighted individual carried through every stage.
Stage cards for ordering.
commonMisconceptions: 'The caterpillar and butterfly are different animals' — the central misconception; they are one creature at different stages.
'The stages can happen in any order' — the sequence is fixed.
'The chrysalis is asleep/an egg' — not understanding it is the transforming pupa stage.
'It's a straight line that ends at butterfly' — missing that the cycle repeats.
'All baby animals look like small adults' — overgeneralising; metamorphosis is different from simple growth.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach the butterfly life cycle (egg → caterpillar/larva → chrysalis/pupa → butterfly) as the STAGES OF ONE CREATURE changing, not four different animals. Centre the work on (1) ordering the four stages as a repeating cycle and (2) grasping that the caterpillar and butterfly are the same individual transforming, with the chrysalis as where the body is rebuilt. First-hand observation of a real class caterpillar culture over weeks anchors change-over-time; sequence/animation and labelled-diagram activities reinforce order, vocabulary and the same-creature idea.

activities.title: Observe a real class caterpillar culture over weeks
feedback: If a learner says the caterpillar died and a new butterfly appeared, revisit the day-by-day photos of the one named individual and trace the connecting arrows as a single continuous story.
If a learner says the stages could happen in any order, lay their own dated pictures in time order to show the sequence is fixed.
activities.rationale: First-hand observation of change over time lets children witness the transformation of one creature directly, which supports the central 'same creature' idea and the ordered sequence. Following a single named individual guards against the 'four different animals' misconception.
sourceClaims: First-hand observation of a class caterpillar culture over weeks is the recommended way to teach the butterfly life cycle and the same-creature idea.
KS1 pupils learn that animals have offspring which grow into adults (life cycles) and observe changes over time; the butterfly life cycle is a standard KS1 context.
learnerActions: Keep a class caterpillar culture and look at it regularly over several weeks.
Track and name ONE individual caterpillar, recording what it looks like each day with a drawing or photo.
Draw arrows connecting your day-by-day pictures to show it is one creature's story moving through caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly (starting from the egg only if your culture began with eggs).
After the butterfly emerges, say aloud whether it is the same creature you have been watching and how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: The caterpillar and the butterfly are the SAME individual changing over time; the stages happen in a fixed order and take real time.

activities.title: Order the four stages into a repeating ring
feedback: If cards are placed in the wrong order, point to which stage comes before and after and ask what the creature would need to do to get there.
If a learner lays the cards in a straight line, ask 'what does the butterfly do next?' to reveal that eggs restart the cycle.
activities.rationale: Physically sequencing and forming a closed ring makes the ordered, cyclical structure concrete and addresses both the 'any order' and 'straight line that ends' misconceptions. Optional: a scrubbable time-slider or timelapse animation can let children watch the caterpillar grow, hang up and shed its skin to form a chrysalis, and emerge as a butterfly, with a highlight following the one individual — an example interaction, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils learn that animals have offspring which grow into adults (life cycles) and observe changes over time; the butterfly life cycle is a standard KS1 context.
learnerActions: Take four shuffled picture cards — a tiny egg, a fat caterpillar, a chrysalis, a butterfly.
Arrange them into a RING rather than a straight line, so the cycle can start again.
Place a card showing the butterfly laying eggs on a leaf to close the loop back to the egg.
Say out loud why it is a cycle that repeats and not a line that ends at the butterfly.
activities.intendedInsight: The life cycle has a fixed order AND it repeats — the butterfly lays eggs that hatch into new caterpillars, so the cycle begins again with the next generation (the butterfly itself does not turn back into an egg).

activities.title: Label the cycle and learn both names for each stage
feedback: If a learner describes the chrysalis as 'sleeping', contrast sleeping (wake up the same) with transforming (come out a different shape) using before/after images.
If a learner introduces only one name, prompt for its partner term (caterpillar↔larva, chrysalis↔pupa).
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal labelled diagram can teach vocabulary and order and introduce technical names alongside familiar ones without overload. A labelled diagram presents order and names clearly but does not itself show the transformation; pair it with observation or animation so the change is also seen.
learnerActions: Work with a circular four-stage diagram and reveal a short fact about each stage (egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly).
For each stage, match the familiar name to the technical name: caterpillar = larva, chrysalis = pupa.
Say what is happening at each stage, including that inside the chrysalis the caterpillar's body is being rebuilt (not sleeping).
activities.intendedInsight: Each stage has a name and a role; the technical terms larva and pupa name the caterpillar and chrysalis stages, and the chrysalis is where the body transforms.

activities.title: Retell or draw the transformation
feedback: If a retelling skips the chrysalis or treats it as a pause, ask what is happening to the body inside while we cannot see.

If the drawing shows the caterpillar simply 'growing wings', compare caterpillar and butterfly body parts (legs, mouth, wings) and ask 'where did the extra legs go?' to show a full rebuild, not an add-on.
activities.rationale: Producing a retelling or drawing requires the child to construct the sequence and the same-creature explanation, going beyond recognition. Comparing body parts targets the 'just grows wings' misconception. This production benefit is a research-informed proposal; no provided source directly establishes it.
learnerActions: After reading a story (e.g. The Very Hungry Caterpillar, which calls the chrysalis a 'cocoon' — real butterflies form a chrysalis, while moths spin cocoons) or watching the real change happen, retell the transformation from caterpillar to butterfly.
Draw the sequence, showing the same creature at each stage.
Answer: is the butterfly the same creature that was the caterpillar, or a new one, and how do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: Children can reconstruct the ordered transformation themselves and explain it as one creature changing.

activities.title: Compare different kinds of change (extension)
feedback: If a learner says all baby animals look like small adults, contrast the caterpillar→butterfly rebuild with the grasshopper nymph, which already looks much like a small adult and mostly gets bigger as its wings grow.
Credit answers that reason about whether the body shape is rebuilt, not just whether the animal gets larger.
activities.rationale: Transfer to counterexamples (grasshopper incomplete metamorphosis; frog) reveals whether the child understands transformation rather than a memorised list, and addresses the overgeneralisation that all young look like small adults.
sourceClaims: Students learn that organisms have diverse life cycles but all include birth, growth, reproduction and death (3-LS1-1); KS1 work is the observational precursor.
learnerActions: Consider a grasshopper, which hatches as a nymph that looks like a small grasshopper without working wings, and grows bigger by shedding its skin several times, with its wings developing gradually and no chrysalis.
Consider a tadpole that turns into a frog.
For each, say whether the change is more like the caterpillar's story (a big body rebuild) or more like simple growing bigger, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: A dramatic whole-body change (like caterpillar to butterfly, or tadpole to frog) is different from mostly growing bigger, where the young already looks much like a small adult (like a grasshopper nymph, which has no chrysalis); this distinguishes real understanding from memorised stages.

constraints: Core objective: children must grasp that the caterpillar and butterfly are the SAME individual at different stages, and that the sequence is a repeating cycle — not just name or order the four stages.

First-hand observation over weeks is time-dependent; a scrubbable animation or timelapse is a useful complement that compresses the slow change into one sitting but is not a substitute for watching a real change over time where feasible.

Picture-card ordering and labelled diagrams are scaffolds for order and vocabulary; on their own they do not show the transformation. Pair them with observation or animation so the same-creature change is actually witnessed.

Recognition/matching and multiple-choice tasks assess order, names and the same-creature idea but do not by themselves elicit independent retelling or explanation; include at least one production task (retell or draw).
Introduce technical names (larva, pupa) alongside familiar ones (caterpillar, chrysalis) without overloading young learners.

Diagnosis lives in the 'why', not the yes/no: a child may order the stages correctly yet still believe the caterpillar dies and a new butterfly is born. Always probe the reasoning behind the chrysalis stage.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims are marked verified:false in the row; cited standards (DfE KS1; NGSS 3-LS1-1) and the 'class culture is the recommended way' practice claim were not independently re-checked here.

The original artefact notes asserted that animation is 'the emotional core' and that 3D/conversation formats are less direct; these are catalog-fit opinions, not established comparative efficacy. They have been softened to optional affordances rather than claims that one medium is necessary or that others teach less.

The source's own correctAnswer describes the chrysalis as the body being 'rebuilt/reorganised'; this is biologically reasonable for this age but simplified. Kept at an age-appropriate level ('the body is rebuilt') without overclaiming cellular detail.

The grasshopper nymph and frog comparisons come from the assessment probes and are retained as an extension; they are age-appropriate counterexamples but the teacher should keep the framing simple (rebuild vs. just getting bigger).
Activity 3 (labelling and technical names) carries sourceClaims:[] because no provided source directly supports the vocabulary-teaching principle; it remains an unvalidated proposal.

Activity 4 (retell or draw) now carries sourceClaims:[]: claim 1 supports the life-cycle topic and observation but not the production-task principle (retelling/drawing beyond recognition), which remains an unvalidated proposal.

Activity 2 (order into a ring) retains claim 1 because it explicitly references 'life cycles' (the cyclical content), but this is content/topic-level support only and is not evidence that the card-ordering interaction is effective.

probeDeeper: 'When the butterfly comes out, is it the SAME creature that was the caterpillar, or a new one? How do you know?'

'A grasshopper hatches as a tiny grasshopper (a nymph) and just gets bigger — no chrysalis. Is that the same as the caterpillar's story, or different?' (a real counterexample: incomplete metamorphosis)
'What is actually happening inside the chrysalis while we can't see?'
'A tadpole turns into a frog. Is that more like the caterpillar's change, or like the grasshopper's?'
assess.correctAnswer: It is not right — the caterpillar does NOT die. It is the SAME animal changing its body. Inside the chrysalis the caterpillar's body is rebuilt (reorganised) into a butterfly. So one creature goes through stages: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly. It transforms; it is not replaced by a new animal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the caterpillar and butterfly are two separate animals — 'the caterpillar dies and the butterfly is a different creature'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Follow one named caterpillar through photos day by day into and out of the chrysalis. Emphasise it is the SAME individual the whole time — draw arrows connecting the stages as one creature's story, not four animals.
errorPatterns.distractor: They are two different animals — the caterpillar dies and a new butterfly is born
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States the caterpillar dies / disappears and a new butterfly is born; treats them as unrelated animals rather than one life cycle

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the caterpillar is just asleep/resting in the chrysalis and wakes up as a butterfly, with no real change of body
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that inside the chrysalis the body is reorganised — the caterpillar's legs, wings and shape all change. Contrast 'sleeping' (wakes up the same) with 'transforming' (comes out a different shape) using before/after images.
errorPatterns.distractor: The caterpillar is just sleeping in the chrysalis and wakes up as a butterfly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: describes the chrysalis as sleeping or hiding, not as the body being rebuilt

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the caterpillar simply 'grows wings' and stays basically the same body — misses that the whole body reorganises
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare caterpillar and butterfly body parts directly (number of legs, mouth, wings). Ask 'where did the extra legs go?' to show it is a full rebuild, not an add-on.
errorPatterns.distractor: The caterpillar just grows wings and turns into a butterfly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the caterpillar sprouts wings and keeps crawling; no sense of a rebuilt body or a chrysalis stage

responseLevels.gap: Says the caterpillar and butterfly are different animals, or that the caterpillar dies / is just sleeping; no idea of one continuous creature.
responseLevels.full: States it is the same creature transforming, explains the chrysalis as where the body is reorganised, AND transfers the idea — e.g. recognises the grasshopper nymph or frog as a different or similar kind of change, showing an understanding of transformation rather than memorised stages.
responseLevels.partial: Can list the stages (egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly) in order but describes them as separate events — cannot say it is ONE creature whose body is rebuilt in the chrysalis, or slips back to 'a new butterfly comes out'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child says: 'The caterpillar and the butterfly are two different animals — the caterpillar dies inside the chrysalis and a brand-new butterfly comes out.' Is that right? Tell me what really happens, and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands metamorphosis says the caterpillar and butterfly are ONE creature and the chrysalis is where the body is rebuilt. A child holding the common 'separate creatures' idea insists the caterpillar died and the butterfly is new — and the second-tier 'why?' exposes it, because they explain the chrysalis as a death/birth or as 'just sleeping' rather than as transformation of one continuous body. The reason, not the yes/no, is where the misconception lives.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11y; divide up to 4-digit ÷ 2-digit using formal long division, interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit whole number using the formal written method of long division, and interpret remainders as whole number remainders, fractions, or by rounding, as appropriate'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.2 — 'fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm' (Grade 6); 5.NBT.6 develops division by 2-digit divisors with models.
• Operational details — the new demand over short division is the TWO-DIGIT divisor: the child can no longer rely on recalled facts and must ESTIMATE how many times the divisor fits at each step (4752÷13: how many 13s in 47? ~3), multiply back, subtract, bring down. Building a 'menu' of helpful multiples of the divisor (13×1…×9, or chunk via 13×10=130) scaffolds the estimation. Remainder interpretation extends to expressing as a fraction (r/divisor) or decimal, or rounding by context. Chunking (partial-quotients) is a valid, more transparent bridge to the compact algorithm. Estimate first and check by multiplying back.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): long division with a small 2-digit divisor via a multiples menu, no remainder. Tier B (age 10–11): 4-digit ÷ 2-digit (4752÷13) with the remainder expressed as a fraction. Tier C (age 11): interpret the remainder three ways for three contexts and explain each long-division step.
bestPractices: Scaffold the estimate-at-each-step with a 'menu' of the divisor's multiples (or chunking/partial-quotients), since 2-digit divisors aren't in recalled facts.
Use chunking (partial quotients: subtract 13×100, 13×10…) as a transparent bridge before/beside the compact algorithm.
Interpret remainders flexibly — whole number, fraction (r/divisor), decimal, or rounded — according to context.
Estimate the quotient first (4752÷13 ≈ 4800÷12 = 400) to anchor the leading digit and catch place errors.
Always check by multiplying the quotient by the divisor and adding the remainder.
keyRepresentations: Long-division layout with the divisor's multiples menu alongside
Chunking / partial-quotients layout (repeated subtraction of multiples)
Bar model / number line for remainder interpretation
Estimation and inverse-check (quotient×divisor + remainder)
commonMisconceptions: Poor estimation of how many times the divisor fits, then repeated correction or errors.
Place-value errors in the quotient (dropping a place when the divisor doesn't fit).
Mishandling the remainder — wrong fraction denominator, or wrong rounding direction for the context.
Bring-down/subtraction slips propagating through the calculation.
Not checking with multiplication, so errors persist.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year-olds dividing up to 4-digit numbers by a 2-digit divisor with formal long division, and interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions (remainder/divisor), decimals, or by rounding to suit context. The new demand over short division is the 2-digit divisor: the child can no longer recall facts and must estimate how many times the divisor fits at each step, so a 'menu' of the divisor's multiples (and chunking/partial-quotients) scaffolds that estimation. Estimate first, multiply back, subtract, bring down, and check by inverse multiplication.

activities.title: Long-division workbench with a multiples menu (4752÷13)
feedback: If the quotient has the wrong number of digits (e.g. 35 or 3605), check that every brought-down digit produced a quotient digit — write a 0 when 13 does not fit, and align each quotient digit above the digit being divided.
If estimation stalls or uses random multipliers, jot or consult the multiples menu (13, 26, 39, 52, 65…) and read off how many fit.
If the remainder fraction is inverted (13/7) or left as a bare 'r7', name it: 7 is left out of the 13 needed for one more group, so the fraction is 7/13 — the remainder always goes over the divisor.

If one step is wrong from a subtraction/multiplication slip, don't restart the method: check your own quotient × 13 + remainder against 4752, compare with the estimate (between 13×300 = 3900 and 13×400 = 5200, so between 300 and 400), then find and fix the faulty step.
activities.rationale: A live multiples menu supports the hardest part — estimating the quotient digit for a non-table divisor — and multiply-back/subtract with immediate flagging turns error-prone estimation into guided, self-correcting practice. Standards require interpreting the remainder as whole number, fraction, or by rounding.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal long division and interpret remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate.
A multiples menu / chunking scaffolds quotient estimation for 2-digit divisors; remainders interpreted as fraction, decimal or rounded by context.
learnerActions: Set up 4752 ÷ 13 in the long-division layout.
Before dividing, build a side menu of multiples of 13 (13, 26, 39, 52, 65, 78, 91, 104, 117) to consult when estimating each quotient digit.

At each step, use the menu to decide how many 13s fit (e.g. 'how many 13s in 47?' → 3 because 39 ≤ 47 < 52), write that quotient digit above the correct column, multiply back, subtract, then bring down the next digit.

If the working number after bringing down is ever smaller than 13, write a 0 in the quotient for that place and bring down the next digit. This does not happen in 4752 ÷ 13 (the working numbers are 47, 85 and 72), so practise it on an example such as 3913 ÷ 13 = 301.
Finish with the remainder 7, then reframe it three ways: as the fraction 7/13 (remainder over divisor), as a decimal continuation (≈365.54), and rounded to suit a context.
Check the whole answer by computing 365×13 + 7 and confirming it equals 4752.
activities.intendedInsight: Long division by a 2-digit divisor is a repeating estimate–multiply–subtract–bring-down cycle; a multiples menu replaces the recalled facts you no longer have, and the same single division can yield several correct answers depending on how the remainder is interpreted.

activities.title: Chunking (partial quotients) as a transparent bridge
feedback: If the chunks don't add up to the compact quotient, check the place value of each chunk (hundreds, tens, ones) and that you kept subtracting while a value of 13 or more remained.
If chunks feel random, start with the largest hundreds multiple that still fits (13×300 = 3900 ≤ 4752, but 13×400 = 5200 is too big), then the tens multiple, then ones.
activities.rationale: Partial-quotients/chunking is a valid, more transparent bridge to the compact algorithm, exposing the place-value structure that compact long division compresses.
sourceClaims: A multiples menu / chunking scaffolds quotient estimation for 2-digit divisors; remainders interpreted as fraction, decimal or rounded by context.
learnerActions: Solve 4752 ÷ 13 by repeatedly subtracting easy multiples of 13: subtract 13×300 = 3900 (leaving 852), then 13×60 = 780 (leaving 72), then 13×5 = 65 (leaving 7), keeping a running tally of how many 13s you have removed.
Add the chunk counts (300 + 60 + 5 = 365) to get the quotient, with 7 left over.
Line up the chunking record beside the compact long-division layout and match each compact step to a bundled chunk.
activities.intendedInsight: The compact long-division digits are shorthand for subtracting bundles of the divisor (here 13×300, 13×60, 13×5, which give the hundreds, tens and ones digits of the quotient), so the algorithm is repeated subtraction organised by place value, not a magic routine.

activities.title: Interpreting the remainder for three contexts
feedback: If the rounding direction is wrong, re-read the context: 'buses needed' forces rounding up because the 7 leftover people still need a whole extra bus, whereas 'complete groups made' rounds down because the leftover 7 cannot make a full group.
If the fraction denominator is wrong, remember the remainder is written over the divisor (7/13), because 7 is left out of the 13 needed for one more.
activities.rationale: Remainder interpretation extends Y5 work to fractions/decimals and rounding by context, a core explicit requirement of the standard. A context dialogue or debate about the leftover's meaning may support the interpretation judgement.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal long division and interpret remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate.
learnerActions: Take the result 4752 ÷ 13 = 365 remainder 7 and express the remainder three ways: as the fraction 7/13, as a decimal (≈0.54, giving ≈365.54), and as a rounded whole number.

Match each interpretation to a context: e.g. sharing a divisible quantity such as 4752 g of flour equally into 13 bags (fraction/decimal), versus a context where you must round up (e.g. how many buses/containers are needed), versus one where you round down (e.g. complete full groups made).
State and justify which interpretation each context demands and why rounding up or down fits.
activities.intendedInsight: One division can give several correct answers; the context decides whether the leftover is a fraction, a decimal, or forces rounding up or down.

activities.title: Check and explain each step
feedback: If the estimate and the answer differ wildly, a quotient digit or a zero place is probably misplaced — recheck alignment.
If the inverse check fails, a subtraction or multiplication slip occurred in one step; find and fix that step rather than restarting.
activities.rationale: Estimating to anchor the leading digit and checking by inverse multiplication catch the classic quotient-placement and slip errors; voicing a step reveals genuine understanding of the algorithm.
learnerActions: Estimate the quotient before dividing (e.g. 13×300 = 3900 and 13×400 = 5200, so 4752÷13 is between 300 and 400; 4800÷13 ≈ 370 is a closer estimate, while 4800÷12 = 400 is a rougher overestimate) to anchor the leading digit.

After completing the division, voice what one specific step does — e.g. 'when I bring down the 5, what number am I now dividing by 13?' (answer: the brought-down value, here 85, since 47÷13 left 8 and the 5 comes down beside it).
Verify the full result by multiplying quotient×divisor and adding the remainder (365×13 + 7 = 4752).
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating first catches place-value errors, and multiplying back verifies the answer; being able to say what each step does distinguishes understanding from copying a routine.

constraints: Fraction, decimal, and rounded interpretations of the remainder must all be practised, not just a whole-number remainder; the context determines which is appropriate.
Chunking/partial-quotients is a legitimate method and transparent bridge, not just a crutch to discard; keep it available alongside the compact algorithm.
A multiples menu is a scaffold for estimation; the goal is for the child eventually to estimate quotient digits reliably, including writing a 0 when the divisor doesn't fit a brought-down value.

A tap-to-reveal worked example or multiple-choice item can serve as a reference or assessment, but recognition/reveal formats do not by themselves elicit the child's own estimation and self-correction cycle; include construction where the child does the dividing.
Always require an inverse check (quotient×divisor + remainder) so slips are caught rather than propagated.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit of the worked numbers: 4752 ÷ 13 = 365 remainder 7 (13×365 = 4745; 4745 + 7 = 4752), so the fraction remainder is 7/13 and the decimal ≈365.54. The original learn designNotes repeatedly cited the remainder as '12'/'12/13' and the decimal as '≈365.9'; this is arithmetically wrong and contradicts the assessment's correctAnswer (remainder 7). All activities use 7/13 throughout.
When bringing down the 5 in 4752÷13, the value being divided is 85 (47÷13 leaves 8; the 5 comes down beside it), not 105 — confirmed correct in the final activity text.
The menu of multiples of 13 up to ×9 is 13, 26, 39, 52, 65, 78, 91, 104, 117; consistent across activities.

Two sources (CCSS-M and NCETM) are marked verified:false in the row; only the DfE claim is marked verified:true. No comparative-efficacy or necessity claims are asserted beyond what the standards state.
The original 'poor' entry claimed 3D 'adds no value' for this planar place-value procedure; this is treated as a scoped fit note, not a universal pedagogical law, and is not propagated as a claim.

probeDeeper: When you 'bring down the 5', what number are you now dividing by 13?
How did you know roughly how many 13s go into 47?
Why is the remainder written as 7/13 and not 13/7?
How could you check your whole answer using multiplication?
assess.correctAnswer: 4,752 ÷ 13 = 365 remainder 7, i.e. 365 7/13. The teacher watches for a workable long-division process (estimating how many 13s, subtracting, bringing down), correct placement of quotient digits, and expressing the remainder as 7/13 (remainder over divisor).

errorPatterns.pattern: misplaces quotient digits / omits a zero in the quotient when 13 doesn't go into a brought-down value
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist that every brought-down digit produces a quotient digit — write a 0 when the divisor doesn't fit; align each quotient digit above the digit being divided.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quotient has the wrong number of digits (e.g. 35 r? or 3605) because a zero place was skipped

errorPatterns.pattern: cannot estimate how many 13s fit — no strategy for a non-table divisor, so guesses digits
errorPatterns.nextMove: jot a menu of multiples (13, 26, 39, 52, 65…) alongside; estimate each quotient digit from it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child tries random multipliers or stalls at each step

errorPatterns.pattern: expresses the remainder wrongly — as a bare 'r7', or as 13/7, or does not know remainder-over-divisor makes the fraction
errorPatterns.nextMove: name it: the leftover 7 out of the 13 needed for one more, so 7/13; the remainder is always over the DIVISOR.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: fraction inverted (13/7) or remainder left unconverted when a fraction is asked for

errorPatterns.pattern: correct algorithm, subtraction/multiplication slip mid-step; caught by estimation
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child check with multiplication (365×13 + 7 = 4752?) and estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one step wrong; estimate (4800÷13 ≈ 370) flags it

responseLevels.gap: cannot estimate quotient digits, misplaces them or omits a zero place, or cannot express the remainder correctly.
responseLevels.full: executes long division accurately with correct digit placement, expresses the remainder as a fraction (or rounds per context), explains what each step does, and checks by multiplication/estimation.
responseLevels.partial: completes the division with support but mishandles the remainder-as-fraction or a place-value zero; explains steps only mechanically.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 4,752 ÷ 13 by long division while you watch, then express the remainder as a fraction. Watch how they build multiples of 13, place each quotient digit above the correct column, and carry the remainder down. Then ask them to explain what one step (e.g. 'bring down the 5') is doing.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Long division by a two-digit divisor stresses two things at once: managing an unfamiliar divisor's multiples and correct place-value bookkeeping. Watching the process catches the classic quotient-digit-placement and 'forgot the zero' errors; asking the child to voice a step reveals whether they understand the algorithm or are copying a routine.
