pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Pollination & Pollinator Decline (food security)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 'Interactions and interdependencies' / 'Reproduction'):** the importance of plant reproduction through insect pollination in human food security; the interdependence of organisms including insect-pollinated crops.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS2-1 / MS-LS2-5 context):** analyse resource availability effects on organisms/populations; evaluate solutions for maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem services — pollination is a keystone ecosystem service.

- **Operational details:** Pupils connect a biological process (insect pollination — pollinators transfer pollen so flowers can be fertilised and set fruit/seed) to a human consequence (much of our food, and its variety, depends on animal pollinators). Key ideas: many crops (apples, almonds, oilseed rape, many fruits and vegetables) need or benefit from insect pollination; staple cereals (wheat, rice, maize) are wind-pollinated and don't; therefore pollinator decline threatens the DIVERSITY and yield of food, not calories alone. Causes of decline (habitat loss, pesticides, disease) and mitigations (wildflower margins, reduced pesticide use, hedgerows) let pupils reason about solutions. This is a specific, high-stakes case of interdependence linking ecology to society.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (relational to socio-scientific reasoning). Pupils trace pollinator → crop → food-supply and evaluate mitigations. Success = explains why losing pollinators would shrink food diversity/yield (distinguishing insect- from wind-pollinated crops) and proposes a justified mitigation.
bestPractices: Make the process–consequence link explicit: pollination → fruit/seed set → food supply, so pupils see the biology behind the food-security claim.

Distinguish insect-pollinated crops (fruits, nuts, oilseed rape) from wind-pollinated staples (wheat, rice, maize) so pupils don't over- or under-state the threat — it's diversity and yield, not all calories.
Frame decline causes (habitat loss, pesticides, disease) and mitigations (wildflower margins, hedgerows, reduced spraying) so pupils reason about solutions, not just doom.
Treat this as a case of interdependence, linking back to food webs: pollinators are a service the whole crop system depends on.
Use real examples (almond orchards' reliance on managed bees; oilseed rape) to ground the abstract dependency.
keyRepresentations: Pollinator → crop → plate dependency chain
Insect-pollinated vs wind-pollinated crop sort
Farm/landscape model coupling pollinator numbers to crop yields
A 'market shelf' that loses variety (fruit, nuts, veg) but keeps bread as pollinators fall
commonMisconceptions: Thinking pollinator decline would starve us of all food, not realising wind-pollinated staple cereals are unaffected — it's diversity and yield at stake.
Believing pollination is the same as fertilisation, or that plants set fruit without pollen transfer.
Assuming only honeybees pollinate, overlooking wild bees, hoverflies, butterflies and other pollinators.
Thinking flowers exist to look pretty rather than being adaptations to attract specific pollinators for reproduction.

learn.summary: For ages 11-12: pupils connect insect pollination (pollinators transferring pollen to the stigma so flowers can be fertilised and set fruit/seed) to human food security, learning that losing pollinators threatens the DIVERSITY and yield of food rather than all calories, because staple cereals (wheat, rice, maize) are wind-pollinated while many fruits, nuts and vegetables depend on insect pollination. Pupils reason about causes of decline (habitat loss, pesticides, disease) and mitigations (wildflower margins, hedgerows, reduced spraying), treating this as a specific, high-stakes case of interdependence. The central activity is a farm/landscape model that couples a pollinator population to crop yields; supporting activities add an in-role interview, a plate/market reveal scene, and a sorting/justification check, each with a distinct pedagogical purpose.

activities.title: Farm-and-pollinator landscape model: break and repair the dependency
feedback: If a pupil says 'all our food would disappear', point to the wheat field still yielding and ask which crops were actually affected and why.

If a pupil treats recovery as instant or automatic, note that pollinator and harvest recovery takes time and depends on the mitigation matching the cause introduced; ask them to compare outcomes over several seasons under fair conditions rather than expecting an immediate cure.
When a pupil correctly separates variety/yield loss from calorie loss and names the wheat contrast, affirm that they have traced pollinator → crop → food supply.
activities.rationale: Making the process-consequence chain (pollination → fruit/seed set → food supply) visible, and contrasting insect- with wind-pollinated crops, lets pupils reason about the socio-scientific claim instead of over- or under-stating the threat. Running decline and then recovery turns the model into reasoning about and evaluating solutions.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 requires the importance of plant reproduction through insect pollination in human food security, and the interdependence of organisms including insect-pollinated crops.

Many crops (apples, almonds, oilseed rape, many fruits and vegetables) depend on insect pollination while staple cereals (wheat, rice, maize) are wind-pollinated; pollinator decline therefore threatens food diversity and yield.
NGSS MS-LS2-5: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-5] — pollination is a key ecosystem service.
learnerActions: Tend a mixed landscape containing an apple orchard, oilseed rape, strawberry beds and a wheat field, alongside a pollinator (bee) population.

Apply a stressor — spray pesticide or clear hedgerows — and observe how the pollinator numbers fall and, crop by crop, the insect-pollinated plots set less fruit or seed so their harvests fall (sharply for apples; less for strawberries and oilseed rape, which can partly self-pollinate and benefit from, rather than wholly depend on, insects), while the wind-pollinated wheat keeps yielding.
Inspect a harvest/market-shelf readout and describe what changes: the shelf holds far fewer apples and strawberries and less rapeseed oil, but still holds bread.
State in writing whether pollinator loss threatens calories, variety, or both, using the wheat contrast as evidence.

Intervene by sowing wildflower margins, restoring hedgerows and cutting spraying, then observe over successive seasons whether pollinators and harvests recover, and explain which mitigation helped and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Pollinator decline reduces the variety in our diet and the yields of insect-pollinated crops rather than removing all calories, because insect-pollinated crops produce less (some far less) while wind-pollinated staples continue; this is a broken interdependence that can be mitigated, though recovery is gradual rather than instant.

activities.title: Interview a beekeeper, farmer or pollination ecologist
feedback: If a pupil accepts a mitigation uncritically, ask them to name a cost or limitation the persona mentioned.
Reward answers that cite a specific cause (habitat loss, pesticides, disease) when justifying a matching mitigation.
activities.rationale: An in-role dialogue can support the 'discuss consequences' and 'evaluate solutions' strand by pushing pupils to weigh trade-offs, and a real example such as almond orchards grounds the abstract dependency; it complements the model, which supplies the yield evidence the conversation can reference.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-LS2-5: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-5] — pollination is a key ecosystem service.
learnerActions: Interview an in-role beekeeper, farmer or pollination ecologist about why pollinators — wild bees and other insects as well as managed honeybee colonies — are declining or under pressure, and what it means for the harvest.
Probe a concrete real case — for example almond orchards' heavy reliance on managed honeybees, or oilseed rape — to ground the dependency in a specific farming system.
Ask which mitigations actually work and press the persona to weigh trade-offs (e.g. cost of leaving field margins uncultivated vs. benefit to yields).
Summarise the persona's reasoning and decide which proposed solution the pupil would back, justifying the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: The decline-causes-consequences-solutions strand is a socio-scientific judgement: evidence and trade-offs, not just a single 'right' fix.

activities.title: What's on your plate: reveal insect- vs wind-pollinated foods
feedback: If a pupil names only honeybees, prompt them to recall wild bees, hoverflies and butterflies as pollinators too.
If a pupil marks wheat or rice as insect-pollinated, revisit the wind-pollination distinction.
activities.rationale: A reveal scene can make the dependency vivid and quick to grasp as pre-teaching or reference. It presents the facts but does not itself run the decline-and-recovery causal story, so it should precede, not replace, the model.
sourceClaims: Many crops (apples, almonds, oilseed rape, many fruits and vegetables) depend on insect pollination while staple cereals (wheat, rice, maize) are wind-pollinated; pollinator decline therefore threatens food diversity and yield.
learnerActions: Examine a plate or market scene and, for each food, reveal whether it needs or benefits from insect pollination, is wind-pollinated, or does not depend on pollination for the part we eat (e.g. potatoes, carrots, lettuce).
For an insect-pollinated food, identify a pollinator responsible (e.g. wild bees, honeybees, hoverflies, butterflies).
Drill down into one example to see a flower being pollinated, then state in a sentence what the pollinator did.
activities.intendedInsight: Much of the variety on a plate depends on specific pollinators, while staples like bread do not — making the dependency concrete before the modelling work.

activities.title: Sort crops and justify a mitigation
feedback: For the crop sort, confirm wheat, rice and maize as wind-pollinated and apples, almonds, oilseed rape, strawberries as insect-pollinated (noting oilseed rape chiefly benefits from, rather than wholly depends on, insect pollination).
On the mitigation item, require the justification to name which decline cause the chosen mitigation addresses.
activities.rationale: A categorisation-and-justification check can verify knowledge of the crop distinction and cause→mitigation links. A sort of this kind checks classification and brief reasoning; it does not itself elicit the systems reasoning the model builds, so use it to check rather than to teach the core target.
sourceClaims: Many crops (apples, almonds, oilseed rape, many fruits and vegetables) depend on insect pollination while staple cereals (wheat, rice, maize) are wind-pollinated; pollinator decline therefore threatens food diversity and yield.
learnerActions: Sort a set of crops into insect-pollinated vs wind-pollinated.
Answer a question on the likely consequences of pollinator decline for food supply.
Match each decline cause (habitat loss, pesticides, disease) to a plausible mitigation.
Choose a 'best mitigation' for a given scenario and write a one-sentence justification linking it to the cause.
activities.intendedInsight: Pupils can retrieve the crop categories and cause→mitigation links and justify a solution choice.

constraints: Keep the insect- vs wind-pollinated distinction central: the threat is to food diversity and yield, not to all calories — the unaffected wheat/cereal contrast must be visible.

Distinguish pollination (pollen transferred to the stigma — what the pollinator does) from fertilisation (the later fusion of the pollen's male gamete and the egg cell inside the ovule — what forms the seed); do not let the two be used interchangeably.
Include a range of pollinators (wild bees, honeybees, hoverflies, butterflies), not honeybees alone.
The reveal/plate scene is a scaffold for facts and reference; it does not demonstrate the causal decline-and-recovery story and should not stand in for the modelling activity.
The sorting/justification check assesses recall and brief reasoning, not independent systems reasoning; pair it with the modelling or interview work rather than using it alone.
Treat recovery as gradual and condition-dependent: a matched mitigation reduces further decline and supports recovery over seasons under fair comparison, not an instant restoration of harvests.

Address, when it arises, the idea that hand or machine pollination could simply replace pollinators: at crop scale (billions of briefly-open flowers over vast areas) this is impractical, which is why pollinator loss is serious.

A bee's-eye 3D flight-through can engage interest in the pollination mechanism but does not supply the population/dependency reasoning that is the core target; use it only as a brief optional vignette, not as the main activity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row (the crop insect-vs-wind-pollination claim and the NGSS MS-LS2-5 claim); treat the specific crop lists and standards wording as needing confirmation against the primary documents.

The original row asserted the conversation activity 'can't show the yield collapse' and that 3D 'doesn't serve the core target' as catalog fit comparisons; these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than universal claims about what a medium can or cannot teach.

Example crop classifications (apples, almonds, oilseed rape, strawberries as insect-pollinated; wheat, rice, maize as wind-pollinated) are standard but were not independently re-verified here; oilseed rape in particular is insect-benefiting but partly self/wind pollinated. Confirm before assessment use.

probeDeeper: Walk me through the steps from a bee visiting an apple blossom to an apple forming.
Which comes first — pollination or fertilisation — and how are they different?
Name a crop that would fail without insect pollinators.
Wind pollinates wheat — so does pollinator decline matter for every crop? Which crops are safe and which aren't?
assess.correctAnswer: Not right. Bees and other insects POLLINATE many crops — they carry pollen between flowers so the plants can be fertilised and set fruit and seed. Apples, almonds and oilseed rape depend on this, so losing pollinators threatens food, not just honey. Pollination is the TRANSFER of pollen to the stigma; it is NOT fertilisation, which is the later joining of the pollen cell with the egg cell inside the ovule.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Bees only matter for honey (or just sting us) — our food would be fine without them.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace a bee from blossom to apple: no pollination, no fruit; list insect-pollinated crops to make the food link concrete.
errorPatterns.distractor: We'd only lose honey — our fruit and vegetable crops would be fine without bees.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts the claim; cannot connect bees to fruit and seed production.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates pollination with fertilisation — 'pollination is when the pollen joins the egg to make a seed.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the steps: pollination = pollen transferred to the stigma (what the bee does); fertilisation = the later fusion of cells inside the ovule (what forms the seed).
errorPatterns.distractor: Pollination is when the pollen joins with the egg cell to make a seed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses the two terms interchangeably, or defines pollination as the seed forming.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'We could just pollinate crops by hand or with machines, so bee decline doesn't matter.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront the scale: billions of flowers, briefly open, over vast areas — hand pollination is impractical at crop scale, which is why pollinator loss is serious.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses the threat because 'farmers could do it themselves'.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks bees only make honey; conflates pollination with fertilisation.
responseLevels.full: Explains pollination as pollen transfer enabling fertilisation and fruit/seed set, links pollinator decline to crop failure and food security with examples, distinguishes pollination from fertilisation, and reasons about wind- versus insect-pollinated crops.
responseLevels.partial: Knows pollinators matter for some crops and names one, but muddles pollination and fertilisation, or cannot explain the food-security link.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put this claim to the child: 'If bees disappeared we'd lose honey, but our food would be fine.' Ask: 'Is that right? Explain what bees actually do for crops like apples and almonds — and be precise about what pollination is and what it is not.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'food would be fine' claim separates a child who sees bees only as honey-makers from one who links pollination to crop yield and food security. The 'what pollination is and isn't' tier separates the pollination = fertilisation conflation from a precise account of two distinct steps.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies — especially the ×÷ relationship and derived facts — not just rote recall.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3–Y4 recall and USE ×÷ facts, and 'use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally' — fluency includes derivation and application.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.7 — 'Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g. knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) … By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.'
• Operational details — fluency = efficiency + accuracy + flexibility. Beyond recall, children deploy strategies: derive an unknown from a known (9×7 = 10×7−7 = 63; 6×8 = 5×8+8), use commutativity to reduce load, and use the inverse to get ÷ from ×. The distinguishing skill from bare table-recall is CHOOSING an efficient strategy and using facts within calculations and problems. Retrieval should be mixed, spaced, and applied, with derivation strategies made explicit and discussed.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): answer any 2/5/10 and 3/4/8 × or ÷ fact quickly. Tier B (age 8–9): answer any fact within 100 in ~3s and state its ÷ partner. Tier C (age 9): derive a not-yet-memorised fact from a known one and explain the strategy (e.g. 7×6 via 7×5+7).
bestPractices: Make derived-fact strategies explicit and named — near-tens (9s from 10s), doubling (4s from 2s, 8s from 4s), partitioning (6×8 = 5×8 + 8) — and have children compare strategies.
Interleave × and ÷ so the inverse relationship is exercised as a retrieval strategy, not just taught as a fact.
Use short, frequent, mixed, spaced retrieval and apply facts inside larger calculations and word problems so fluency transfers.
Keep timing low-stakes to protect against maths anxiety while still building speed; emphasise a correct efficient method over raw speed alone.
Diagnose which specific facts/strategies are missing and target them, rather than re-drilling everything.
keyRepresentations: Derivation chains and 'fact from a fact' diagrams (10×7−7 → 9×7; double 2→4→8)
Array/area model — justifies the partitioning strategy (6×8 = 5×8 + 1×8)
Fact-family triangle — the inverse as a fluency strategy
Multiplication square — to locate a known neighbour to derive from
commonMisconceptions: Equating fluency with speed alone, leading to guessing under time pressure instead of using a reliable strategy.
Being able to recite a table in order but unable to answer a fact out of sequence or its ÷ partner.
Not using the inverse, so division facts lag behind multiplication.
Failing to derive — stuck facts stay stuck because the child has no strategy to rebuild them.
Not transferring facts into multi-step calculations (knows 7×8 in isolation but not inside a written method).

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, build fluent multiplication and division within 100 as strategic fluency (efficiency, accuracy, and flexibility) rather than bare recall. The core skills are: deriving an unknown fact from a known one (9×7 = 10×7−7 = 63; 6×8 = 5×8+8 = 48), using the multiplication–division inverse to get division facts from multiplication (knowing 7×8=56 gives 56÷8=7), using commutativity to reduce load, and choosing an efficient strategy and applying facts inside larger calculations and word problems. Make derived-fact strategies explicit and named, interleave × and ÷, and use short, spaced, mixed retrieval, keeping timing low-stakes.

activities.title: Derive-it: rebuild hard facts from known ones
feedback: If you revert to skip-counting on a tricky fact, prompt: 'What easy fact is nearby?' Then rehearse the near-fact move (×9 via ×10 then subtract; ×6 via ×5 then add) until it is reached for first.
For a division answered by trial or counting, prompt 'what times 6 makes 54?' and link it to the matching multiplication fact family (6×9=54, so 54÷6=9).

If answers are correct but slow and effortful, treat this as developmental: do not equate slow with wrong or pile on timed pressure. Reinforce the secure strategy and use spaced retrieval over time; protect confidence.
activities.rationale: Fluency comprises efficiency, accuracy and flexibility; derived-fact strategies and the inverse are central to fluency and should be made explicit and practised until reached for first, with × and ÷ interleaved so the inverse is exercised as a retrieval strategy. An adaptive practice format may detect a stall and offer a fact-matched scaffold (an array shedding one column; an array split into 5×8+8; a one-tap flip to the solving multiplication), making strategy use a repeated felt experience. These interaction examples are illustrative of the mechanism, not required, and such adaptive benefit is proposed rather than established.
sourceClaims: Fluency comprises efficiency, accuracy and flexibility; derived-fact strategies and the inverse should be taught explicitly, with spaced interleaved retrieval.
Y3–Y4 pupils recall and use ×÷ facts and use place value, known and derived facts to calculate mentally.
3.OA.7 requires fluently multiplying and dividing within 100 using strategies such as the multiplication–division relationship.
learnerActions: Face a mixed stream of × and ÷ questions within 100.
When you stall on a fact, use a named derivation strategy rather than counting up: for 9×7, start from 10×7=70 and subtract one group of 7 to get 63; for 6×8, split into 5×8+8 = 48.
Take a round of 'derive-it' challenge facts chosen so they are best cracked by transforming a fact you already know (rather than counting up), and state the known fact you started from.
For division questions, flip to the multiplication fact family (e.g. for 54÷6 ask 'what times 6 makes 54?' → 9).
Say or write which strategy you used after each hard fact.
activities.intendedInsight: Once a few anchor facts are secure (such as ×2, ×5 and ×10), unknown facts within 100 can be reached from facts you already own, so fluency is a connected web of strategies rather than a wall of isolated things to memorise.

activities.title: Mixed ×÷ fluency check (spaced retrieval)
feedback: If you can recite a table in order but stumble on a fact out of sequence or its division partner, practise facts in random order and always pair each × fact with its ÷ partner.
Target the specific facts and strategies you marked as 'worked out' rather than re-drilling everything.
activities.rationale: A fixed, non-adaptive fact check is an authentic fluency measure and good for spaced checking; it measures fluency more than it teaches the strategies that create it, so pair it with explicit strategy work rather than treating it as the only route to fluency. Short, frequent, mixed, spaced retrieval helps fluency transfer.
sourceClaims: Fluency comprises efficiency, accuracy and flexibility; derived-fact strategies and the inverse should be taught explicitly, with spaced interleaved retrieval.
learnerActions: Answer a rapid mixed set of × and ÷ questions within 100, aiming for roughly three seconds each but keeping timing low-stakes.
Tackle a few deliberately paired items, e.g. 10×7 immediately followed by 9×7, so you can notice the derivation link.
After the set, mark which facts you 'just knew' and which you worked out, and revisit the worked-out ones in later spaced sessions.
activities.intendedInsight: Mixed, spaced retrieval measures and consolidates fluency across all facts, including the inverse division partners, not just a table recited in order.

activities.title: Multiplication square with derivation and fact-family overlays
feedback: If you rely on reading the grid rather than recalling, follow each look-up by attempting the fact unaided so the reference becomes a bridge, not a crutch.
Prompt comparison: 'Which nearby fact did you derive from, and could another neighbour work too?'
activities.rationale: A tappable square with derivation overlays and fact-family reveals is a strong strategy reference; because it shows strategies rather than drilling their fluent use, it supports but does not replace retrieval practice. Array/area and fact-family representations justify the partitioning strategy and the inverse.
learnerActions: Use a multiplication square as a reference and locate a known neighbour to a fact you are unsure of.
For a hard fact such as 9×7, trace how it is built from a neighbouring easy fact (10×7 then subtract 7 → 63).
Reveal the fact family for any cell to see its division partners (e.g. 7×8=56, 8×7=56, 56÷7=8, 56÷8=7).
After consulting it, close the reference and try to reproduce the derivation and the division partner from memory.
activities.intendedInsight: Many hard facts sit next to or near easier ones on the grid, and each product belongs to a fact family linking multiplication and division.

activities.title: Coach talk: choosing a strategy (metacognition)
feedback: Praise a clear, correct method over raw speed alone; a good strategy choice is the goal at this stage.
If no strategy is offered, model one near-fact move and have the learner apply it to a sibling fact.
activities.rationale: A short Socratic exchange may teach strategy selection and metacognition; however, conversational pacing yields relatively few rapid retrievals per session, so on its own it is not suited to building the quick, efficient retrieval that fluency also calls for (fluency being efficiency, accuracy and flexibility) — it supports but does not substitute for timed, spaced practice.
learnerActions: When a fact is tricky, answer the prompt 'What do you already know that's close?' before attempting it.
Name the strategy you will use (near-ten, doubling 2→4→8, partitioning, or inverse flip) and explain why it fits this fact.
Compare two possible strategies for the same fact and say which is more efficient here.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent calculators consciously select an efficient strategy rather than defaulting to counting; naming the choice strengthens flexibility.

constraints: Keep timing low-stakes to protect against maths anxiety while still building speed; emphasise a correct efficient method over raw speed alone, and do not equate slow-but-correct with wrong.
A fixed, non-adaptive fact check chiefly measures fluency; pair it with explicit strategy teaching rather than using it as the only route to fluency.
A reference grid or overlay shows strategies but does not drill fluent retrieval; always follow look-ups with unaided practice.

Conversation can build strategy selection and metacognition, but its slower pacing limits rapid repeated retrieval, so on its own it is not suited to building the quick retrieval that supports the efficiency side of fluency (which is efficiency, accuracy and flexibility, not speed alone).
Interleave × and ÷ so the inverse is practised as a retrieval strategy; division facts lag when only multiplication is drilled.
Apply facts inside multi-step calculations and word problems so fluency transfers beyond isolated recall.
Interaction examples (array peeling a column, splitting into 5×8+8, one-tap division flip) are illustrative of the learning mechanism and optional, not mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source row marks the CCSS-M 3.OA.7 claim and the NCETM/IES fluency claim as verified:false; only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat citations accordingly and do not upgrade their confidence.
The original '3 seconds' / 'few seconds' targets are retained as loose, low-stakes guidance consistent with the row's anxiety caution; they are age-norm heuristics, not strict thresholds.
The non-preferred 3D entry was dropped because its only content was a universal-inferiority claim ('3D adds nothing'); no qualified affordance remained to preserve.

Editor note: fluency wording was corrected so rapid retrieval is tied to the efficiency component of fluency rather than being described as what 'defines' fluency, consistent with the row's warning against equating fluency with speed alone; and catalog artefact-type vocabulary (e.g. 'quiz') was replaced with plain descriptions such as 'fixed, non-adaptive fact check'.

probeDeeper: Show me how 10 × 7 helps with 9 × 7.
What multiplication fact gives you 54 ÷ 6?
Which facts do you just know, and which do you work out?
Derive 6 × 8 from a fact you know.
assess.correctAnswer: 42, 9, 72; 9 × 7 = 10 × 7 − 7 = 70 − 7 = 63; 49 ÷ 7 = 7 because 7 × 7 = 49. Facts answered within a few seconds, with derivation and the inverse relationship used deliberately.

errorPatterns.pattern: no derived-fact strategy — when a fact isn't instantly known, counts up rather than deriving from a near fact (9 × 7 via 10 × 7 − 7)
errorPatterns.nextMove: explicitly teach near-fact strategies (×9 via ×10 then subtract; ×6 via ×5 then add) and rehearse them until they are reached for first
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reverts to skip-counting and can't produce a derivation when asked

errorPatterns.pattern: division not linked to multiplication — solves 54 ÷ 6 by trial or counting, not by recalling 6 × 9
errorPatterns.nextMove: use fact-family triangles and prompt 'what times 6 makes 54?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot state the × fact behind a ÷

errorPatterns.pattern: accurate but not yet fluent — gets everything right but well over a few seconds, still reconstructing
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT equate slow with wrong or pile on timed pressure — fluency follows from secure strategies plus spaced retrieval; protect confidence
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct but slow and effortful answers

responseLevels.gap: Cannot answer within 100 reliably; no link between × and ÷.
responseLevels.full: Answers × and ÷ within 100 in a few seconds, deploys derived-fact strategies (e.g. 9 × 7 = 10 × 7 − 7), and uses the inverse relationship for division facts.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls facts but slowly, reconstructing by counting rather than deriving from near facts; division lags.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I'll time you loosely — aim for about three seconds each. 6 × 7? 54 ÷ 6? 8 × 9? Now show me a clever way (not counting): work out 9 × 7 using 10 × 7. And 49 ÷ 7 — what multiplication tells you the answer? (Watch speed, use of derived-fact strategies, and the multiplication–division link.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This topic is about strategic fluency, not bare recall — the derive-9×7 and 'what × gives 49 ÷ 7' tasks reveal whether the child owns near-fact strategies and the inverse relationship, or falls back on rote recall and laborious counting when a fact isn't instant.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7–9; know how rainforest PLANTS are adapted — drip-tip leaves shed water to prevent rot, buttress roots brace tall trees in thin soil, epiphytes (orchids, bromeliads) perch on branches to reach light without soil, lianas climb trunks to the canopy — and use 'adaptation' to mean a survival feature.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' (how plants are suited to environment) and Y3 'Plants' (functions of roots/leaves); leads to Y6 adaptation.
• Standards — US: NGSS 3-LS4-3 and 4-LS1-1 (plant structures function for survival/growth).
• Operational details — pair each STRUCTURE → PROBLEM SOLVED: drip-tip → constant rain would rot a flat leaf, so the pointed tip drains it fast; buttress roots → thin soil can't anchor a giant, so wide flanks brace it; epiphyte → the floor is too dark, so grow up high on a branch to reach light; liana → too costly to build a thick trunk, so climb someone else's. Tie each to the LAYER problem it solves (light in the canopy, anchorage on the floor). Introduce 'adaptation' as the umbrella term.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (7): describe three plant adaptations. Tier B (8): explain the purpose of each (drip-tips shed water to stop rot). Tier C (9): use 'adaptation' correctly and explain how two adaptations solve the SAME problem of the dark, wet, thin-soiled forest differently.
bestPractices: Frame every adaptation as a STRUCTURE that solves a specific rainforest PROBLEM (too wet, too dark, too thin soil).
Contrast with a familiar plant (a daisy, an oak) to make the rainforest solution stand out.
Tie each adaptation to the LAYER where its problem is sharpest (epiphytes reaching light in the canopy; buttresses on the floor).
Introduce and repeatedly use the umbrella term 'adaptation' so it generalises beyond this list.
Use predict-then-reveal: what would happen to a flat, tip-less leaf in constant rain? before showing the drip-tip solution.
keyRepresentations: A single tree annotated with all four adaptations (drip-tip leaf, buttress root, epiphyte on a branch, liana on the trunk).
A drip-tip vs flat-leaf side-by-side showing water draining fast vs pooling.
A buttress-root cross-section spreading wide in a shallow soil layer.
Structure→problem-solved pairing cards.
commonMisconceptions: 'Epiphytes are parasites stealing food from the tree' — they only perch for a light-rich position; they make their own food.
'Buttress roots go deep' — they spread WIDE and shallow because the nutrient/anchor layer is thin.
'Drip-tips are just a leaf shape' — they serve a purpose: shedding water to prevent rot and fungal growth.
'Lianas are tree trunks' — they are climbers using other trees for support to reach light cheaply.
'Adaptation means the plant tried/chose to change' — adaptations are inherited features, not deliberate acts.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: learners come to understand rainforest plant adaptations as structures that solve specific environmental problems (too wet, too dark, too thin-soiled) — drip-tip leaves shed water to prevent rot, wide shallow buttress roots brace tall trees in thin soil, epiphytes perch high on branches to reach light without soil, and lianas climb other trunks to reach the canopy cheaply. The core activities use predict-then-reveal cause-and-effect (what fails without the adaptation, what succeeds with it), and learners repeatedly use the umbrella term 'adaptation' to mean an inherited survival feature. Supporting activities offer an annotated reference tree and matching/labelling for recall.

activities.title: Rainforest plant repair workshop: switch each adaptation on and off
feedback: If the learner only names a feature without its problem, prompt: 'What would go wrong if this plant didn't have it?' and pair the feature to the problem (drip-tip sheds water to stop rot; buttress braces a giant in thin soil).

When the learner says roots should go deep, point back to the toppling test and the thin soil: there is little good soil for roots to go deep into, so buttress roots mainly spread WIDE and shallow, making a broad base that braces the huge tree. As an extra, simpler reason, most of the goodness (nutrients) sits near the surface, where shallow roots can reach it.
If the learner calls the epiphyte a parasite, note it still makes its own food; it only borrows a bright position on the branch, it does not take food from the host.
Reinforce correct use of 'adaptation' each time: 'Yes — the drip-tip is an adaptation, a feature that helps it survive.'
activities.rationale: Framing every adaptation as a structure that solves a rainforest problem, and using predict-then-reveal on the failure case, is intended to make the structure→function link concrete for this age group; switching an adaptation ON/OFF lets the learner see success versus failure directly.
sourceClaims: Drip-tip leaves shed rainwater to reduce rot/epiphyll growth, buttress roots stabilise tall trees in shallow soils, and epiphytes grow on host trees to access light in the canopy
learnerActions: Before testing, predict: what would happen to a broad, flat, tip-less leaf sitting under constant rainforest rain?

Pour (or simulate) rain onto a flat, tip-less leaf and watch how water sits on it; then shape a pointed drip-tip and watch the water collect and run off the tip faster. (In a real rainforest, a leaf that stays wet for a long time is more likely to grow mould or rot; a short demonstration will not show rotting.) State in one sentence the problem the drip-tip solves.

Give a tall model tree ordinary narrow roots on a thin layer of soil and push it gently: it topples easily. Then unfold wide buttress flanges at its base and push again: it stays upright much better. State why wide (not deep) roots help here.

Compare an epiphyte seedling (such as an orchid) on the dark forest floor, where it gets too little light to make enough food and grows poorly, with the same kind of seedling perched high on a branch, where it reaches the light and can grow and flower. State the problem the high position solves.
Show a liana climbing an existing trunk toward the canopy instead of building its own thick trunk, and say why climbing is a cheaper route to the light.
For each test, read or write a one-line 'problem solved' caption pairing the STRUCTURE with the PROBLEM.
activities.intendedInsight: Each strange plant feature is an ANSWER to a specific rainforest problem: too wet (drip-tip), a tall tree in thin soil (buttress), too dark below (epiphyte height, liana climbing). Structure→function becomes something the learner has seen cause and effect for, not just memorised.

activities.title: One annotated rainforest tree: tap each adaptation to its purpose
feedback: If a learner states a benefit but no location, ask where in the forest that problem is worst and where the plant solves it (it is darkest near the floor, so epiphytes and lianas reach light at the top; anchorage matters at the floor).
Reinforce the umbrella word 'adaptation' for all four features so it generalises beyond this list.
activities.rationale: An annotated tree with reveal-on-tap hotspots delivers each structure→purpose pairing and serves as a reference; it states benefits rather than testing the failure case, so it is intended to complement, not replace, the workshop activity.
sourceClaims: Drip-tip leaves shed rainwater to reduce rot/epiphyll growth, buttress roots stabilise tall trees in shallow soils, and epiphytes grow on host trees to access light in the canopy
learnerActions: Explore a single hero rainforest tree with drip-tip leaves and buttress roots, plus two separate plants growing on it: an epiphyte perched on a branch and a liana climbing the trunk.
Tap or reveal each hotspot to find the problem it solves (e.g. drip-tip → constant rain would rot a flat leaf, so the point drains it fast).
Tie each adaptation to the forest LAYER that matters: darkness is the problem near the floor, so epiphytes and lianas get up to the light in the canopy; buttresses anchor the tree at the floor.
activities.intendedInsight: A single reference tree shows all four structure→purpose pairings together and anchors them to the forest layers, giving learners a clear mental map to return to.

activities.title: Contrast and consolidate: rainforest solution vs a familiar plant
feedback: If the learner says the oak also needs buttresses, revisit the thin-soil condition: buttresses solve a problem the deep-soil plant does not have.
Matching and labelling check recall; if a learner can match but not explain why, return to the 'what would go wrong without it?' question to rebuild the reasoning.
activities.rationale: Matching and labelling fit the evidence and assess cleanly but check recall rather than eliciting structure→function reasoning on their own, so they are paired here with a contrast prompt and an explanation step to keep reasoning in view.
learnerActions: Compare a rainforest plant with a familiar one (a daisy or an oak) and say what is different and why (e.g. an oak in deep British soil does not need wide buttress flanges).
Answer: would a tree still need wide buttress roots if the soil were deep and rich like a British field? Explain.
Match each adaptation to its purpose, and label a blank tree with drip-tip, buttress, epiphyte and liana in the right places.

Explain how two adaptations solve the SAME problem in different ways (e.g. epiphytes and lianas both solve 'too dark near the floor': epiphytes by perching high on branches, lianas by climbing trunks).
activities.intendedInsight: Contrasting with a familiar plant makes the rainforest solution stand out, and matching/labelling checks that the structure→purpose pairings are secured and transferable.

constraints: Keep the tiered goals: describe three adaptations (age 7), explain the purpose of each (age 8), use 'adaptation' correctly and explain how two adaptations solve the same problem differently (age 9).

Address the key misconceptions explicitly: epiphytes are not parasites (they make their own food); buttress roots spread WIDE and shallow, not deep; drip-tips serve a purpose (shedding water), they are not just a shape; lianas are climbers, not tree trunks; adaptation is an inherited feature, not a deliberate choice by the plant.
Matching and labelling activities check recall and do not by themselves elicit the structure→function reasoning; pair them with explanation prompts.
The annotated tree states benefits rather than letting the learner test the failure case; use it as a reference alongside, not instead of, the predict-then-reveal workshop.
A 3D canopy scene is optional and only worthwhile if one already exists — the concepts read fully in 2D and no genuine spatial payload requires 3D.
Model 'rain' and toppling tests are simplified demonstrations of cause and effect; treat them as illustrations of the problem each adaptation solves, not precise physical reproductions.

Present mechanical support/anchorage as the main stated reason for wide buttress roots; surface-nutrient capture may be offered as an additional simplified reason, not as the sole or equally established cause.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources are marked verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The buttress-root explanation combines TWO functions (support AND catching surface nutrients). The pedagogy/evidence text and the Kew source emphasise support/anchorage in thin soil; the assessment's correct answer also stresses nutrient capture. Mechanical support is the more widely accepted primary function; both are presented as plausible, with support foregrounded in learner feedback, rather than asserting one is the sole cause.

The claim that these mechanisms are 'better shown than discussed' and that conversation adds no value is a catalog preference, not an established fact; omitted as a universal law. Spoken discussion can still support this topic.
Liana climbing is described as 'a cheaper route to the light' — a reasonable simplification for ages 7–9, kept as interpretation rather than a precise energetic claim.

The DfE curriculum claim grounds topic/curriculum coverage (and is reflected in the tiered KS2 checkpoints) but does not directly support any activity's pedagogical rationale, so it is not attached as a sourceClaim. The Kew claim is attached where activities rest on its specific factual structure→function pairings; no tested method efficacy is implied.

probeDeeper: Why do so many rainforest leaves have a pointed 'drip-tip' at the end?
How does a liana get to the sunlight without a thick trunk of its own?
Use the word 'adaptation' in a sentence about a rainforest plant.
What if the soil were deep and rich like a British field — would the tree still need wide buttress roots?
assess.correctAnswer: Because rainforest soil is thin and the goodness (nutrients) is all near the surface, so there's nothing to anchor into deep down. Wide buttress roots spread out over the surface both to hold up the huge tree AND to catch nutrients where they actually are — in the top layer. Deep roots would reach only poor, thin soil and wouldn't support or feed the tree well.

errorPatterns.pattern: buttress roots go deep — 'a tall tree needs deep roots to hold it up'
errorPatterns.nextMove: link wide surface roots to thin soil and surface nutrients; the deep soil is poor
errorPatterns.distractor: They actually grow deep down to anchor the tall tree
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the roots go deep, or can't say why they're wide

errorPatterns.pattern: names an adaptation with no linked problem — lists drip-tips/buttress but not what they solve
errorPatterns.nextMove: pair each feature with its problem (drip-tip sheds water to stop rot; buttress = support in thin soil)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: lists adaptations without the environmental problem each fixes

errorPatterns.pattern: epiphytes need soil / can't live without it — 'a plant must be in the ground'
errorPatterns.nextMove: epiphytes perch on branches for light and take water from air and rain, no soil needed
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says epiphytes must root in soil

responseLevels.gap: Says buttress roots go deep; lists features with no purpose.
responseLevels.full: Explains buttress roots spreading wide because soil is thin and nutrients are at the surface (support plus feeding), pairs at least three adaptations with the problem each solves, and uses 'adaptation' correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Names adaptations and some purposes but can't explain buttress roots by thin soil, or treats epiphytes as needing soil.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A giant rainforest tree has huge 'buttress' roots that spread out sideways above the ground like fins. You might expect a tall tree to send roots DEEP down instead. Why do these roots spread WIDE across the surface rather than going deep? Tell me why, and then tell me what would go wrong if they grew deep instead.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who assumes 'tall tree means deep roots' can't explain buttress roots; the concept child links wide surface roots to thin soil, surface nutrients and stability. The reason-tier forces the thin-soil reason.

pedagogy.summary: Ordering and continuing patterns and sequences develops from duplicating and extending by visual matching to abstracting the UNIT OF REPEAT and identifying the smallest repeating unit — and only these last two mark genuine understanding rather than surface matching (Rittle-Johnson et al. 2013). Teaching should move children beyond 'what comes next' to seeing a pattern as made of repeating units: naming and circling the unit, recreating a pattern with different materials (abstraction, which cannot be done by visual matching), and asking for the smallest arrangement that keeps the pattern.
bestPractices: Shift the focus from 'what comes next' to structure: name and circle the unit of repeat, not just append the next item.
Use abstraction tasks — recreate the same kind of pattern with different materials or colours — which force attention to structure because visual matching won't work.
Ask for the smallest unit ('what is the smallest tower that still keeps the pattern?') to assess unit identification, the hardest and most telling skill.
Include units beyond simple AB (ABB, AAB, ABC), because children over-rely on alternation; watch for them reverting to AB.
Model 'same, same, different' language and 'start over' framing to make the repeating unit explicit.
keyRepresentations: Colour/shape cube or bead strings
The unit of repeat circled or boxed
ABB / AAB units contrasted with AB
'Same, same, different' labelling of the unit
Number sequences and skip-counting as patterns
commonMisconceptions: Extends a pattern by visually matching and appending the last item, without grasping that there is a repeating unit.
Reverts to a simple AB pattern when the model unit is longer (makes ABAB for an ABB model).
Produces a partially correct pattern — one full unit plus extra items that break the unit.

learn.summary: Patterns and sequences teaching should move children beyond 'what comes next' to seeing a pattern as made of a repeating UNIT. The telling skills are abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest repeating unit — both of which, according to Rittle-Johnson et al. (2013), cannot be done by visual matching alone and so reveal genuine structural understanding rather than surface copying. Build, extend, abstract, and isolate the unit, using units beyond simple AB (ABB, AAB, ABC) because children over-rely on alternation.

activities.title: Build, extend, and name the unit of repeat
feedback: If the child only appends the last item without a sense of the unit, label the model with 'same' and 'different' and box the repeating chunk, then rebuild from that unit before extending.
If they produce one full unit then stray cubes that break it, treat this as emerging knowledge, not simply wrong: ask 'where does the pattern start again?' and practise shorter units first.
Prompt: 'Point to the part of the pattern that repeats — where does it start again?'
activities.rationale: Economopoulos (quoted in Rittle-Johnson et al.) argues children must move from seeing a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure as repeating units in order to generalise and predict. Naming and circling the unit makes that structure explicit.
sourceClaims: To generalise and predict, children must move from looking at a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure — seeing that it is made of repeating units (Economopoulos, 1998, quoted in the study).
learnerActions: Continue a given model pattern, e.g. red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue — carry it on further with cubes, beads, or drawn shapes.
Circle or box the part that repeats and say where the pattern 'starts over'.

Name which items are the SAME and which is DIFFERENT: for red, blue, blue the two blues are the same and the red is the different cube that starts the chunk (spoken in order: different, same, same). The plain 'same, same, different' chant maps most cleanly to a two-same-then-different unit such as AAB.
activities.intendedInsight: A repeating pattern is built from a unit that repeats; the pattern is the unit, not just the next item you could add.

activities.title: Abstract the same KIND of pattern onto new materials
feedback: If the child reverts to green-yellow-green-yellow (AB) for an ABB model, lay the new pattern under the model and check unit-for-unit; count how many yellows come before the next green.
If they merely copy surface colours or cannot reproduce the structure on new materials, return to boxing the unit in the model and rebuild from that chunk.
Prompt: 'Is your green-and-yellow pattern the SAME KIND as the red-and-blue one? How can you check?'
activities.rationale: Rittle-Johnson et al. report that abstracting a pattern onto new materials is a harder skill than extending, cannot be done by visual matching, and clearly demonstrates understanding; children commonly revert to AB for longer units, so non-AB models (ABB, AAB) are important.
sourceClaims: Children can often duplicate and extend repeating patterns by visual matching without knowing there is a pattern unit that repeats; abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest unit of repeat are harder skills that cannot be done by visual matching and are the ones that clearly demonstrate understanding. Common errors include reverting to a simple AB pattern for a longer unit and producing one full unit plus extraneous items; longer units are harder to preserve.
learnerActions: Given a red-blue-blue model, use a different set (e.g. green and yellow cubes) to make 'the same KIND of pattern' — green, yellow, yellow, repeated.
Lay the new pattern directly under the model and check unit-for-unit: count how many yellows come before the next green.
Explain why your new pattern is the same kind even though the colours are different.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the 'same kind' of pattern means reproducing the STRUCTURE (one cube, then two matching cubes, then start over), not the colours — abstraction that colour matching alone cannot accomplish.

activities.title: Shrink to the smallest tower that keeps the pattern
feedback: If the child offers a longer stretch than one unit, ask them to take away cubes one whole unit at a time until only one copy of the unit is left (taking away more would break it). Then check that it still has the full arrangement: for red-blue-blue, the red that starts it and then the two matching blues; for AAB, two matching cubes then a different one; for ABC, three different cubes.
Prompt: 'If I take some cubes away, is it still the same pattern? Why?' and 'What is the smallest tower you could build that still has this pattern?'
Watch for reverting to AB on longer units; if it happens, return to the unit-for-unit check from the abstraction task.
activities.rationale: Rittle-Johnson et al. identify smallest-unit identification as the hardest and most telling patterning skill, not achievable by visual matching. Including units beyond AB counters children's over-reliance on alternation.
sourceClaims: Children can often duplicate and extend repeating patterns by visual matching without knowing there is a pattern unit that repeats; abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest unit of repeat are harder skills that cannot be done by visual matching and are the ones that clearly demonstrate understanding. Common errors include reverting to a simple AB pattern for a longer unit and producing one full unit plus extraneous items; longer units are harder to preserve.
learnerActions: From a repeating pattern, build the smallest tower that still has the same pattern (for red-blue-blue, the three-cube unit red, blue, blue).
Decide whether removing cubes keeps or breaks the pattern, and explain why.
Try the same with AAB and ABC units, not just AB.
activities.intendedInsight: The smallest arrangement that preserves the pattern IS the unit of repeat; isolating it is the clearest sign of understanding structure.

activities.title: Describe the rule and connect to number sequences
feedback: If the rule given is only 'the next one is blue', press for the whole unit and where it restarts.
If a self-made 'longer' pattern collapses to AB, prompt the unit-for-unit check before they hand it over.
Encourage children to say which items are the same and which are different (for an ABC unit, all three are different), and to use 'start over' language, to make the unit clear.
activities.rationale: The micro-topic requires describing rules and creating patterns. Using 'same/different' and 'start over' language makes the repeating unit clear. Number sequences and skip-counting can be linked as rule-based patterns, but their rule is a repeated step (e.g. add 2), not a repeating unit of items, and this difference should be pointed out.
sourceClaims: To generalise and predict, children must move from looking at a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure — seeing that it is made of repeating units (Economopoulos, 1998, quoted in the study).
learnerActions: Say aloud the rule for a given sequence of objects ('it goes red, then two blues, then starts over').

Look at number sequences and skip-counting as patterns too, but notice the difference: in skip-counting (2, 4, 6, 8, …) the numbers keep growing and do not repeat, but the step does (add 2 each time). Some parts can repeat like a unit, e.g. the last digits when counting in 5s (5, 10, 15, 20 → 5, 0, 5, 0).
Create your own pattern with a chosen unit (ABB, AAB, or ABC) and challenge someone else to find the smallest unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Saying the rule out loud and making your own patterns help children move from 'what comes next' to thinking about the repeating unit. Number sequences such as skip-counting are a different kind of pattern: the numbers grow, and what repeats is the rule or step (e.g. +2), not a unit of items.

constraints: A static pattern with the unit highlighted (e.g. tap to box the unit and reveal which items are same/different) is a useful reference, but a fixed display on its own does not let the child extend, abstract, or isolate the unit; pair it with building/doing tasks.

Sequence and fill-in-the-blank response formats can check 'what comes next' and 'circle the unit', but risk rewarding visual matching; always add an abstraction (new-materials) task and a smallest-unit task to go beyond appending.
Extending a pattern can be achieved by visual matching without understanding; use the abstraction and smallest-unit tasks to distinguish surface copying from structural understanding.
Use units beyond AB (ABB, AAB, ABC) because children over-rely on alternation and may revert to AB on longer units.
A partially correct pattern (one full unit plus stray items) is a transitional, emerging state — do not treat it as simply wrong.

The 'same, same, different' chant describes a two-same-then-different unit (AAB); for the ABB example (red, blue, blue) name the two blues as the same and the red as the different start rather than chanting the phrase in order over it.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: swapping to a new colour set for the abstraction task, a 'shrink to the smallest tower' control, laying the new pattern under the model for unit-for-unit comparison, and flagging reversions to AB. These are suggestions, not required mechanisms.

Hands-on construction is central for building and abstracting patterns; conversation can support prompting an explanation of the rule alongside that construction, without being treated as a substitute for it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D as adding nothing and conversation/static image as poor. These have been softened: patterning structure is not inherently spatial, and a fixed display or dialogue can still support reference and explanation respectively. No comparative efficacy or necessity claim is asserted beyond the specific source claim that extending can be done by visual matching while abstraction and smallest-unit identification cannot.
The claim that abstraction and smallest-unit tasks 'cannot be done by visual matching' is attributed to Rittle-Johnson et al. (2013) and retained as sourced, not generalised beyond it.

The original row applied 'same, same, different' to its red-blue-blue (ABB) example, which read in order is different-same-same. The learner-facing text now names which items are same and which is different instead of chanting the phrase over ABB, so the label and example no longer disagree; the phrase is noted as fitting an AAB unit.
Example pattern (red, blue, blue = ABB; green, yellow, yellow abstraction; three-cube smallest unit) checked for internal consistency and found coherent.

probeDeeper: Point to the part of the pattern that repeats — where does it start again?
Is your green-and-yellow pattern the SAME KIND as the red-and-blue one? How can you check?
What is the smallest tower you could build that still has this pattern?
If I take some cubes away, is it still the same pattern? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Extends the pattern preserving the red-blue-blue unit; abstracts the ABB structure into green-yellow-yellow (neither reverting to an AB alternation nor merely copying the colours); and offers the three-cube unit (green, yellow, yellow) as the smallest tower that keeps the pattern.

errorPatterns.pattern: Extends by visually matching and appending the last item, without grasping there is a repeating unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Label the model 'same, same, different' and box the repeating chunk; rebuild from that unit before extending
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Continues the given pattern acceptably but on the new-materials task cannot reproduce the structure

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverts to a simple AB pattern when the model unit is longer than two
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay the new pattern under the model and check unit-for-unit — count how many yellows come before the next green
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Makes green-yellow-green-yellow (AB) for a red-blue-blue (ABB) model

errorPatterns.pattern: Produces a partially correct pattern — one full unit followed by extra items that break the unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as simply wrong — it shows emerging knowledge; ask 'where does the pattern start again?' and practise shorter units first
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Builds one red-blue-blue unit then adds stray cubes that don't continue it (a transitional state)

responseLevels.gap: Appends items by matching the last one; on new materials reverts to AB or copies colours — no sense of a unit.
responseLevels.full: Extends, abstracts to new materials, and identifies the smallest unit of repeat for multi-element units, explaining the pattern as a repeating unit rather than 'what comes next'.
responseLevels.partial: Extends and often abstracts familiar AB patterns, but breaks down on longer units (ABB/AAB) — reverting to AB or adding extra items — and cannot isolate the smallest unit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a pattern made with coloured cubes: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue. First, carry it on for me. Now, using these different cubes (green and yellow), make the same KIND of pattern. Last, show me the smallest tower you could make that still keeps the same pattern.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Extending alone can be done by visual matching; the abstraction task (new materials) and the 'smallest unit' task cannot. A child who only appends by look reverts to AB or copies surface colours; a child who holds the unit reproduces the ABB structure and isolates the three-cube unit. The three tasks together separate visual matching from structural understanding.

Common errors include reverting to a simple AB pattern for a longer unit and producing one full unit plus extraneous items; longer units are harder to preserve.
