pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7; rainforests hold an enormous variety of plants — towering kapok and Brazil nut trees, climbing vines called lianas, colourful orchids that grow on tree branches, giant water lilies, and huge leaves that funnel rainwater.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 Y1 'Plants' (identify and name common/wild plants; parts of plants) and Y2 'Living things and their habitats'.
• Standards—US: NGSS 2-LS4-1 (diversity of life in habitats); 1-LS1-1 (external parts of plants/animals); K-ESS3-1.
• Operational details: showcase the VARIETY and the giant scale — trees taller than houses, vines that climb, flowers that grow high up on branches instead of the ground, and leaves so big they channel rain. Give each plant a hook (kapok = giant tree; liana = climbing rope; orchid = flower that lives on a branch; giant lily = big enough to sit a child; drip-leaf = funnels rain). Seed the idea that plants have clever shapes for a wet, crowded, shady world (developed fully in the 7–9 adaptations topic).
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) name two rainforest plants; Tier B (6) describe one (a giant tree, a climbing vine, a flower on a branch); Tier C (7) explain that rainforest plants come in a huge variety and have special shapes for the wet, crowded forest.
bestPractices: Emphasise scale and variety with comparisons children feel (trees taller than a house, a lily big enough to sit on)
Give each plant one vivid hook so the variety is memorable, not a blur
Introduce the surprising idea that some plants (orchids) grow high on branches, not in the ground — a hook for epiphytes later
Point out clever shapes (climbing vines, rain-funnelling leaves) to seed plant adaptations
Use real photographs to convey the lushness and unfamiliar forms
keyRepresentations: Plant gallery cards: kapok, Brazil nut tree, liana, orchid, giant water lily, drip-tip leaf
Scale comparison (giant tree vs house; giant lily vs child)
Branch close-up showing an orchid growing ON a tree, not in soil
Rain funnelling off a huge pointed leaf
commonMisconceptions: All rainforest plants are ordinary and small — many are giants or grow in surprising ways
Flowers only grow in the ground — orchids grow high up on tree branches
Vines are separate stringy things — lianas are climbing plants using trees to reach the light
Big leaves are just decoration — their shape helps shed heavy rain
Plants are the same everywhere — rainforests have an extraordinary variety of plant forms

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: rainforests hold an enormous variety of plants — towering kapok and Brazil nut trees, climbing vines called lianas, colourful orchids (many of which grow high on tree branches rather than in the ground), giant water lilies big enough to hold a small child, and huge pointed leaves that funnel rainwater off their tips. The core goal is recognising this variety and giant scale with vivid hooks, plus seeding the surprising idea that some plants grow high up and have clever shapes for a wet, crowded, shady world (adaptations are developed fully in a later 7–9 topic).

activities.title: Rainforest plant gallery: variety and giant scale
feedback: If a child thinks all rainforest plants are small and ordinary, show the scale comparison (giant tree vs house; lily vs child) and name the giants.
If a child says flowers only grow in the ground, return to the branch close-up: the orchid perches high on a tree branch, not in soil.
If a child thinks the vine is just a rope or part of the tree, point out the liana is its own plant, rooted in the ground, that climbs the tree to reach the light above the shady floor.
If a child says the big leaf is just decoration, show the rain funnelling off its pointed tip and connect shape to shedding heavy rain.
If a child assumes plants look the same everywhere, place several of the rainforest plants side by side so they feel how many different forms live in one forest.
Praise a correct name plus one described feature (e.g. 'the orchid is a flower that grows on a branch') rather than just naming.
activities.rationale: At 5–7 the objective is recognising plant variety and scale, which is well served by browsing a rich set of real images with per-plant hooks; concrete scale references and a branch close-up make the 'variety and surprising forms' idea memorable rather than a blur. An interactive gallery where tapping each plant reveals its name, scale hook, and clever form may support self-paced exploration, but a printed photo set with spoken hooks works too; the relative efficacy of these formats is not established by the source row.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils identify and name common and wild plants and describe basic plant parts, and study living things in habitats
Students observe the diversity of life in habitats
Rainforests contain enormous plant variety including emergent kapok and Brazil nut trees, climbing lianas, epiphytic orchids growing on branches, giant water lilies, and large drip-tip leaves
learnerActions: Look at real photographs of a kapok tree, Brazil nut tree, liana, orchid, giant water lily, and a drip-tip leaf.
For the kapok, compare it to a scale reference such as a child-sized figure or a house to feel 'taller than a house'.
For the liana, trace how the rope-like vine spirals up a trunk toward the light.
For the orchid, look at a branch close-up showing the flower growing ON the tree, not in soil.
For the giant water lily, see a pad big enough to hold a small child floating on water.
For the drip-tip leaf, watch or imagine a stream of rain tipping neatly off the pointed tip.
Give each plant a one-line hook and say it aloud: kapok = giant tree; liana = climbing rope; orchid = flower that lives on a branch; giant lily = big enough to sit a child; drip-leaf = funnels rain.
Name at least two rainforest plants, then describe one of them (a giant tree, a climbing vine, or a flower on a branch).
activities.intendedInsight: Rainforest plants aren't all ordinary and small — they come in an extraordinary variety, many are giants, and some grow in surprising places and shapes for a wet, crowded, shady forest.

activities.title: Why such strange shapes? A hook for clever forms
feedback: If a child can't say why a plant climbs or grows tall, connect height and climbing to reaching sunlight above the dark, shady forest floor.
If a child thinks the orchid high on a branch must be stealing from the tree, explain it only perches up high to reach light and makes its own food — it doesn't feed on the tree.
Encourage the child to link one shape to one job (pointed leaf → sheds rain; vine → climbs to light).
activities.rationale: A short physical or interactive micro-action (pouring rain off a leaf, miming a vine climbing to light) is a proposed way to make a plant behaviour felt and may plant an early, age-appropriate seed for adaptations, while the main variety-recognition goal stays with the gallery. This is an enrichment hook, not a full adaptations lesson, and its effectiveness relative to the gallery is untested.
learnerActions: Act out or pour water onto a large pointed leaf (a real leaf, or a laminated or waxed card stand-in that only approximates the real leaf — plain paper soaks up water and may not shed it) and watch it run off the tip; describe where the rain goes.
Pretend to be a liana: start low in the 'shade' and climb (with hands or a rope) up toward a 'light' at the top of the forest.
Open a lift-the-flap or answer the question 'Why such strange shapes?' and talk about the wet, crowded, shady forest.
Point to one plant and say one clever thing about its shape (a vine that climbs to reach light, a leaf that funnels rain).
activities.intendedInsight: Some rainforest plants have clever shapes and habits — climbing to reach light, funnelling off heavy rain — that help them thrive in a giant green world. This seeds the later idea of plant adaptations.

activities.title: Check and discuss: the orchid on the branch
feedback: If the child says 'yes, it takes food from the tree', gently correct: the orchid only perches for light and makes its own food; it doesn't feed on the tree.
If the child can't give a reason for growing high, link it to reaching sunlight above the dark floor.

A full answer names several plants, explains the orchid perches only to reach light and makes its own food, and links tall/climbing growth to competing for sunlight. A partial answer knows some plants and that they grow tall but still thinks the orchid feeds off the tree or can't say why it's high up.
Reward reasons, not just yes/no: the 'why' is what shows real understanding.
activities.rationale: A reason-giving prompt helps distinguish a child who holds 'epiphytes are parasites' from one who understands perching-for-light, because it asks for the light-not-theft reason rather than a yes/no guess. Matching tasks check recall of the named plants after the gallery has built recognition.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils identify and name common and wild plants and describe basic plant parts, and study living things in habitats
learnerActions: Respond to: 'An orchid grows high up on the branch of a big rainforest tree, not in the ground. Is the orchid stealing food from the tree like a thief? Say yes or no, and then say WHY it grows up there.'
Match each plant to a feature (giant tree, climbing vine, flower on a branch, rain-funnelling leaf) after browsing the gallery.

Discuss follow-ups: Where does a plant get its food — the soil, or something else? Why would it be hard for a small plant to live on the dark forest floor? What is a liana, and how does it reach the top of the forest?
activities.intendedInsight: A perching orchid isn't a thief: it grows high only to reach sunlight and makes its own food from sunlight, taking water from air and rain — not from the tree. Tall and climbing growth is about competing for light above the shady floor.

constraints: Core objective at this age is recognising plant variety and giant scale; the 'clever shapes/adaptations' material is a seed and hook, developed fully in a later 7–9 adaptations topic — don't over-teach mechanism here.
A matching or name-the-plant check confirms recall of plant names but does not by itself elicit the child's own reasoning; use the 'why does it grow up there' prompt to surface understanding.

Interactive tapping, lift-the-flaps, live rain-off-the-leaf and grow-a-vine micro-interactions are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative, not required; a photo set with spoken hooks and a paper leaf can meet the same goals.
Paper or card leaf and plant cutouts are thin approximations with slight thickness; use them to represent the real plants, not as exact models, and say so where they are used.
Keep scale comparisons concrete (taller than a house, big enough to sit a child) rather than vague 'very big'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; all sources[].claim entries remain marked verified:false in the source row and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Activity 2 ('Why such strange shapes?') carries sourceClaims:[] because no source claim directly supports its teaching principle (that a micro-action makes behaviour felt / seeds adaptations); the sources establish plant variety and curriculum coverage of the topic only.

Activity 3's retained KS1 naming claim supports only its matching-recall subtask; no source claim directly supports its core epiphyte-reasoning principle, which is retained as seed/discussion material for this age rather than a required mastery target.

The source states orchids 'make their own food from sunlight and take water from the air and rain, not from the tree.' Botanically, epiphytic orchids are non-parasitic and photosynthesise, so the core teaching point (not a parasite; perches for light) is sound; the simplified phrasing is acceptable for ages 5–7 but omits nuance (some nutrients from debris/air), which does not affect the misconception being corrected.

The assessment's probeDeeper and correctAnswer push into epiphyte/light-competition ideas that the pedagogy marks as belonging to the later 7–9 adaptations topic; retained here as discussion/seed material, not as a required mastery target for 5–7.
'Compete for sunlight' as the reason plants grow tall is a reasonable simplification; presented as a hook rather than a complete explanation.

Of the five source commonMisconceptions, four receive dedicated activity 1 feedback and the fifth ('plants are the same everywhere') is now addressed by a dedicated feedback item plus the overall variety theme.

probeDeeper: Where does a plant get its food from — the soil, or something else?
Why would it be hard for a small plant to live down on the dark forest floor?
What is a liana, and how does it reach the top of the forest?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the orchid isn't stealing from the tree. It just perches on the branch to get up high near the sunlight, because plants on the dark floor can't get enough light. It makes its own food from sunlight and takes water from the air and rain, not from the tree. Climbing up is how it reaches the light.

errorPatterns.pattern: epiphytes are parasites — 'the orchid steals food or water from the tree'
errorPatterns.nextMove: epiphytes only perch for light and make their own food; they don't feed on the tree
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it takes its food from the tree it sits on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the perching plant takes food from the tree

errorPatterns.pattern: plants grow tall for no reason — misses competing for light
errorPatterns.nextMove: link height and climbing to reaching sunlight above the shady floor
errorPatterns.revealedBy: can't say why rainforest plants grow so tall or climb

responseLevels.gap: Says perching plants steal from the tree; no sense of plants competing for light.
responseLevels.full: Names several rainforest plants, explains epiphytes perch only to reach light and make their own food (not parasites), and links tall/climbing growth to competing for sunlight.
responseLevels.partial: Knows some rainforest plants and that they grow tall, but still thinks epiphytes feed off the tree or can't say why they're high up.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: An orchid grows high up on the branch of a big rainforest tree, not in the ground. Is the orchid stealing food from the tree like a thief? Tell me yes or no, and then tell me WHY it grows up there.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding 'epiphytes are parasites' says the orchid steals food; the concept child explains it only perches for light and makes its own food. The reason-tier forces the light-not-theft reason.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–6: read and write NUMERALS 0–100 — extending secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing across the full two-digit range, leaning on the regular tens-and-ones pattern of the written system.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.1 'count to 120 ... read and write numerals'; the numeral system to 100 is embedded here and in K.CC.3.
• Operational details — once 0–20 numerals and rote counting to 100 are secure, reading/writing to 100 is mostly about the REGULAR two-digit pattern: the left digit says the tens, the right digit the ones, and decade words map to the tens digit. The persistent trouble spots are the teens/twenties boundary and the said-first-heard-first mismatch (writing 'forty-two' as 24). This is procedural fluency, not yet full place-value reasoning (that is the two-digit-composition topic).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): read two-digit numerals up to 100 on sight. Tier B (5–6): write any number 0–100 as a numeral from dictation. Tier C (6): read and write across a decade boundary (e.g. 79–80) and place/find numerals on a 0–100 grid without error.
bestPractices: Lean on the REGULAR pattern of two-digit numerals with a 100-square / Gattegno chart: the tens digit changes down the columns, the ones digit across the rows, making 0–100 a system rather than 100 things to memorise.

Directly rehearse the hear-it/write-it order for two-digit numbers where speech and writing agree in English above twenty (forty-TWO → 4 then 2) but the teens don't (thirteen) — contrast the two explicitly.
Practise decade boundaries (29→30, 79→80) which is where reading/writing and rote counting most often break down.
Keep numerals connected to quantity/position via a bead string or 0–100 number line so a two-digit numeral means 'this far along', not just two digits.
Give balanced read AND write practice (say-it → write it; show it → read it; point on the grid) to avoid one-way fluency.
keyRepresentations: 100-square and Gattegno tens-and-ones chart exposing the regular two-digit pattern.
0–100 bead string / number line linking each numeral to a position/quantity.
Place-value / arrow (Dienes) cards building 42 as 40 and 2 to reinforce which digit is which.
Decade-boundary number tracks (25–35, 75–85) for the tricky crossings.
commonMisconceptions: Transposing spoken two-digit numbers (writing 'forty-two' as 24) — confusing the ones-first teens with the tens-first pattern of the rest.
Decade-boundary errors when counting/writing (after 29 saying/writing 'twenty-ten', or 39→50).
Reading a two-digit numeral as two separate digits ('four, two' for 42) rather than as forty-two.
Miswriting the 'ty' decades (writing 70 as 17, confusing seventy/seventeen).
Omitting or misplacing 0 in decade numbers (writing 40 as 4, or 'forty' as 400).

learn.summary: For children aged 5–6 extending secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing to the full 0–100 range. The goal is procedural fluency in reading and writing two-digit numerals by exploiting the regular pattern (left digit = tens, right digit = ones), targeting the persistent trouble spots: the spoken-order transposition (writing 'forty-two' as 24), decade-boundary crossings (29→30, 79→80), and keeping the 0 in decade numbers. This is numeral fluency, not yet full place-value reasoning.

activities.title: Hear-it, build-it, place-it on a hundred square
feedback: If a learner writes 24 for 'forty-two', place both 24 and 42 on the grid and show how far apart they sit — the transposed numeral is visibly in the wrong region.

If a learner drops the zero when writing a decade number (writing 40 as 4, or 'forty' as 400), point out that the 0 holds the ones place so forty needs both digits and no extra ones; contrast 4 and 40 on the number line to show they are different sizes.
When a number is placed on the grid, an optional response is to light up the cell so a correct answer settles into the right column/row and a wrong one shows the mismatch in position.
For decade-boundary slips (saying 'twenty-ten' after 29, or 39→50), slow down and count along a bead string or number line so 29→30 is felt as one step forward.
Reinforce by linking the numeral to quantity/position on a bead string or number line so the written symbol stays tied to 'how far along'.
activities.rationale: Letting children act on the regular two-digit system — composing from tens and ones, writing from dictation, and seeing position feedback — is intended to build the pattern actively and to target the transposition, zero-omission and decade-boundary errors. Linking numerals to position/quantity keeps the symbol meaningful. Efficacy is proposed, not established.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals.
A 100-square / Gattegno chart exposes the regular tens-and-ones structure of two-digit numerals; decade boundaries and spoken-order transposition are the key difficulties.
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken two-digit number (e.g. 'sixty-eight') and write or point to its numeral.
Place the numeral in its position on a 100-square (state whether it is a 1–100 or a 0–99 layout), then check whether it lands where that number belongs.
Build a number from tens-and-ones cards: compose 42 by taking the '40' card and placing the '2' over its zero, so the tens and ones are explicitly separated.
Work across decade boundaries: continue 28, 29, __ and 78, 79, __ , writing each numeral (30 and 80).
Do both directions: say-it → write it; show it → read it aloud; point-to-it on the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: 0–100 is one regular system, not a hundred separate facts: moving down a column the tens digit goes up while the ones digit stays the same, and moving along a row the ones digit changes. On a 0–99 square each row shares one tens digit. On a 1–100 square the decade number (10, 20, … 100) ends each row, so it is the one cell in its row with a different tens digit. Either way, each numeral means 'this far along', not just two loose digits.

activities.title: Minimal-pair contrast: -teen versus -ty
feedback: If a learner writes 14 for 'forty', swaps 13/30, or confuses seventeen/seventy (writing 70 as 17), slow the word ending and contrast the pair with base-ten sticks (4 tens versus one ten and 4); firm the decade sequence by rote count.

If dictated teens come out reversed (41 for 'fourteen') while other numbers are fine, treat it as a normal transcription stage: keep modelling teens with a tens/ones frame and let exposure resolve it, rather than marking it wrong repeatedly.
activities.rationale: Minimal pairs isolate the genuine error types — auditory -teen/-ty confusion and teen transposition — so practice targets where fluency breaks rather than re-drilling secure numbers.
sourceClaims: A 100-square / Gattegno chart exposes the regular tens-and-ones structure of two-digit numerals; decade boundaries and spoken-order transposition are the key difficulties.
learnerActions: Read aloud the auditory -teen/-ty pairs: 13 and 30, 14 and 40, 17 and 70 (seventeen/seventy); then the separate reading-order/transposition pair 17 and 71 (seventeen/seventy-one).
Take dictation of 'forty' then 'fourteen'; write each and compare.
Explain or show how 40 and 14 differ, e.g. with base-ten sticks: forty is 4 tens; fourteen is one ten and 4.
Say the endings clearly: contrast the spoken ones-first teens (thir-TEEN) with the spoken tens-first rest (FORTY-two), while noting both are written tens-first (13 and 42).
activities.intendedInsight: The teens 13–19 are SAID with the ones idea first (a special '-teen' word), and eleven and twelve are irregular words. All of them, like every two-digit number, are WRITTEN tens-first (11, 12, 13, 14). Numbers from 20 up are both said and written tens-first. Seeing that teens are spoken in a different order from how they are written helps keep the two patterns apart and supports moving past writing 41 for fourteen as place value develops.

activities.title: Fluency check: read, write, place, order
feedback: A correct answer confirms fluency; a wrong one points back to the build/contrast activities — e.g. a transposition sends the learner to the tens-and-ones card build, a -teen/-ty slip to the minimal-pair contrast, a dropped zero back to placing 4 versus 40.
When a dictated 'forty-two' is written as 24, show the gap between 24 and 42 on the line rather than just marking it wrong.
activities.rationale: Two-digit numeral reading/writing is highly checkable in multiple formats; a check can consolidate and surface which specific trouble spot remains. It tests fluency rather than building the pattern insight, so it follows the active work; it does not by itself teach the pattern.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals.
learnerActions: Write the numeral for a spoken number (e.g. 'forty-two' → 42).
Read a shown numeral aloud (e.g. 68 as 'sixty-eight', not 'six, eight').
Place a numeral on a 0–100 line (e.g. position 68).
Order a short sequence across a decade boundary, e.g. fill the gaps around 29→30.
Write the number that is one more than 19 (20); write 'sixty-two' then 'twenty-six' and check they differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading and writing to 100 should be reliable in both directions and across decade crossings, with minimal pairs kept distinct and the zero kept in decade numbers.

constraints: Secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing and rote counting to 100 are prerequisites before extending to 100.

This is procedural numeral fluency, not full place-value reasoning (two-digit composition/decomposition is a separate topic); keep representations tied to quantity/position but do not assume full place-value understanding.
Writing teen numbers in spoken order (41 for 'fourteen') is a normal developmental transcription stage that matures with place value; do not drill it as a careless error or mark it wrong repeatedly.

A static tappable 100-square is a useful reference and can present a numeral and its word, but it cannot by itself rehearse the productive skills of writing from dictation or free reading; use it as a scaffold alongside writing/speaking practice.
Recognition-only (multiple-choice) responses confirm reading but do not elicit independent numeral writing; include actual writing-from-dictation for the production half of the skill.
Decade numbers keep the 0 as a ones-place holder (40, not 4 or 400); treat zero omission/misplacement as its own error alongside transposition and -teen/-ty confusion.

Teens are written tens-first (13, 14) just like all two-digit numerals; only the SPOKEN order of teens differs, so teach the spoken/written order distinction rather than implying teens are written ones-first.

Position-lighting, grid cells, card-dragging and spoken prompts are optional ways to make feedback concrete, not required mechanisms; the same work can be done on paper, with a bead string, or with spoken dictation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources (CCSS-M 1.NBT.1 and the NCETM 100-square guidance) are marked verified:false in the source row; the claims that the 100-square exposes the regular structure and that transposition/decade boundaries are the key difficulties are cited but not independently verified here.

Corrected a factual error in the -teen/-ty activity's intended insight: the candidate stated teens are 'said and written with the ones idea first'. Teens are only SPOKEN ones-first; they are written tens-first (13, 14) like every other two-digit numeral, which is precisely why writing 41 for fourteen is a mismatch error.

The legacy entries asserted 'a static picture cannot rehearse' the skill and '3D adds nothing' for flat symbols; these have been softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal claims, and the 3D dismissal was dropped as unsupported boilerplate.
The original commonMisconception on omitting/misplacing the 0 in decade numbers (40 as 4, 'forty' as 400) is reinstated in activity feedback and constraints.

The source's diagnostic prompt says to watch rather than question the child; this observation framing is retained descriptively, but comparative-efficacy claims about watching versus questioning are not asserted as established.

probeDeeper: Write the number that is one more than 19.
Read this: 40. Now this: 14. Say how you can tell them apart.
Write 'sixty-two', then 'twenty-six' — check they're different.
assess.correctAnswer: Reads all four correctly and writes 40, 14, 62, 26 — distinguishing 13 from 30 and not transposing 62/26.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the -teen and -ty sounds: writes 14 for 'forty' or reads 30 as 'thirteen'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slow the ending, contrast the pair with base-ten sticks (forty = 4 tens; fourteen = ten and 4). Firm the decade sequence in rote count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dictation of 'forty' yields 14, or reading 13/30 aloud swaps them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes teen numbers in spoken order: 41 for 'fourteen' (hears 'four' first)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill it as a careless error or mark it wrong repeatedly — it is a normal transcription stage that resolves as place value matures. Keep modelling teens with a tens/ones frame and let exposure do the work.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dictated teens come out reversed (41, 61) while decades and other two-digit numbers are fine.

responseLevels.gap: Confuses teen/decade pairs or cannot write two-digit numerals from dictation.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes all numerals 0–100 accurately from dictation and by sight, reliably distinguishing minimal pairs.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes most numerals 0–100 but slips on -teen/-ty minimal pairs or occasionally transposes teens.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch the child read and write. First: 'Read these aloud: 13, 30, 17, 71.' Then dictate for them to write: 'forty … fourteen … sixty-two … twenty-six.' Watch the minimal pairs (13/30, 14/40, 62/26) rather than asking them about the numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The contrasting minimal pairs isolate the two real errors: -teen/-ty auditory confusion (40 vs 14) and teen transposition (writing 41 for fourteen). A child who has the numeral system handles both directions; watching, not questioning, catches the slip in the act.

pedagogy.summary: Partitioning continuous shapes (circles, rectangles) into two and four EQUAL parts, naming them halves and quarters, and describing the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'. The emphasis is on equal parts and on the part-whole relationship: the equal parts together reconstitute the whole. Children meet that a shape can be partitioned validly in more than one way, provided the parts are equal.
bestPractices: Partition by folding and cutting so equality is physical; verify by overlaying parts
Show more than one correct way to halve/quarter the same shape (e.g. a rectangle split vertically or horizontally) so 'halves' is not tied to one cut
Always recompose: 'two halves make the whole', 'four quarters make the whole'
Count the resulting PARTS (regions), not the cuts
Name as you go and have children label their partitions
keyRepresentations: Circles partitioned into 2 and 4 equal sectors
Rectangles partitioned into 2 and 4 equal parts (different orientations)
Overlay/rotation to check parts are equal
Parts reassembling into the whole shape
commonMisconceptions: Accepting unequal parts as halves/quarters because the number of pieces is right
Thinking a shape can only be partitioned one 'correct' way (rejecting valid alternative cuts)
Confusing the number of CUTS with the number of PARTS
Not seeing the whole as composed of its equal parts (cannot say two halves/four quarters make the whole)

learn.summary: Children partition continuous shapes (circles, rectangles) into two and four EQUAL parts, name them halves and quarters, and describe the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'. The core ideas are equality of parts (equal in size, not necessarily the same shape), the part-whole relationship (equal parts recompose the whole), and that a shape can be partitioned validly in more than one way as long as the parts are equal.

activities.title: Cut it, check it, rebuild it
feedback: If parts don't match when overlaid, even after rotating or flipping them, they are not the same shape and size. For the strip, grid and straight-cut halves in this activity, that means they are not equal, so they are not halves/quarters even if the number of pieces looks right. (Pieces with equal area but different shapes, like the diagonal triangles below, need a different check.)
When a horizontal, vertical, or single-diagonal cut each produce two equal parts, each is a valid way to make halves: there is no single 'right' cut, only the equal-parts rule.

A rectangle can be quartered in more than one way too (four equal strips, or a 2x2 grid). Drawing BOTH diagonals also gives four triangles that each have one quarter of the AREA, but in a non-square rectangle they are different shapes and will not match when overlaid, so use strips or a 2x2 grid when you want quarters you can check by overlaying. Remember that equal parts must be the same SIZE, not necessarily the same shape.
After rebuilding, prompt: 'Two halves make what? Four quarters make what?' to rehearse the whole as composed of its equal parts.
Count the regions you ended up with, not the lines you drew: one cut through a shape makes two parts.
Real paper has slight thickness and cuts are never perfectly clean, so overlaying is a practical equality check; the cutouts stand for idealised flat shapes with zero thickness.
activities.rationale: Partitioning is a physical cutting/folding action; folding and overlaying makes equality concrete, showing several valid cuts confronts the 'only one correct way' misconception, and recomposing rehearses the part-whole relationship. Early fraction work centres on partitioning single objects into equal parts, naming them, and reconstituting the whole.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
Year 2 pupils recognise, name, and write fractions and can partition shapes; equal shares of identical wholes are emphasised
learnerActions: Take a paper circle and a paper rectangle and fold or draw a line to make two parts.
Overlay or rotate the two parts on top of each other to check they match exactly (equal).

On fresh copies of the same rectangle, make two halves a DIFFERENT way (e.g. vertically, then horizontally, then a single diagonal through opposite corners) and check equality again. For the diagonal, cut along it and turn one triangle half a turn to lay it on the other, because folding a non-square rectangle along its diagonal will not make the halves line up.
Now partition a circle and a rectangle into four equal parts (e.g. the rectangle as four equal strips or a 2x2 grid) and check all four match.
Slide or stick the parts back together to rebuild the whole, saying aloud 'two halves make the whole' and 'four quarters make the whole'.
Label each partition with 'halves' or 'quarters' and count the PARTS (regions), not the cuts.
activities.intendedInsight: Halves are two equal parts and quarters are four equal parts; the equal parts together rebuild the whole, and the same shape can be halved or quartered in more than one correct way provided the parts are equal in size.

activities.title: Halves, quarters, or neither?
feedback: A shape with two parts is only 'halves' if the two parts are equal: two unequal parts belong in 'neither'.
A rectangle cut by a single diagonal, or a circle halved by a slanted line through its centre, is still valid halves because the parts are equal.
Watch for judging by appearance of a usual cut: check equality directly by comparing part sizes.
A sorting task can check and teach how you classify partitions, but it does not itself give the experience of producing a partition; pair it with the cutting/folding activity.
activities.rationale: Categorising and matching partitions to names lets children apply the equal-parts rule and surfaces both the 'count the pieces' and 'only one correct cut' misconceptions through deliberate distractors. This is recognition practice that complements, rather than replaces, hands-on partitioning.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
learnerActions: Sort a set of partitioned shapes into three groups: 'halves', 'quarters', and 'neither'.
Include a shape split into two UNEQUAL parts (right number of pieces, wrong equality) to place in 'neither'.
Include a non-standard but valid cut (e.g. a diagonally-halved rectangle or a circle halved by a slanted line through its centre) to place in 'halves'.
For each decision, explain how you know, e.g. 'the parts are equal' or 'the parts are not the same size'.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding whether a partition shows halves or quarters depends on whether the parts are equal in size, not on the number of pieces or on a familiar orientation.

activities.title: Diagnostic: unequal pieces with the right count
feedback: Neither shape is correctly cut: in each, the parts are not equal. Halves are two equal parts (for example, a straight line through the centre of a circle or rectangle); quarters are four equal parts.
Put back together, the four parts still make the whole rectangle, but because they are not equal they are not quarters; four equal quarters would also rebuild the whole rectangle.
A circle can be halved by any line through its centre, so there is more than one correct way.
If a child says 'yes, there are two parts so they are halves', overlay or rotate the parts to test equality and contrast an equal with an unequal partition of identical shapes.
activities.rationale: Both shapes have the right number of pieces but unequal sizes, so a piece-counting child says yes while a child requiring equal parts says no; the follow-up probes whether they see the parts recompose the whole and accept more than one valid partition.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
learnerActions: Look at a circle divided by an off-centre line into two clearly unequal parts, and a rectangle divided into four parts where three are small and one is large.
Answer: 'Is the circle cut into two halves? Is the rectangle cut into four quarters? How do you know?'
Then answer: 'If you put the parts of the rectangle back together, what do they make? Is there more than one way to cut the circle into two halves?'
activities.intendedInsight: Having the right NUMBER of pieces is not enough; halves and quarters must be EQUAL parts, which together recompose the whole, and there can be more than one valid partition.

constraints: Emphasise EQUAL parts throughout; a partition with the correct number of pieces but unequal sizes is not halves/quarters. Equal means equal in size, not necessarily the same shape.

Show more than one correct way to halve the same shape (e.g. a rectangle split vertically, horizontally, or by a single diagonal through opposite corners) and more than one way to quarter it (e.g. four equal strips or a 2x2 grid). Both diagonals of a rectangle also make four triangles of equal AREA (each one quarter), but for a non-square rectangle these triangles are not congruent, so they cannot be confirmed by overlaying - prefer strips or a 2x2 grid when children verify quarters by overlay.
Always recompose the whole: 'two halves make the whole', 'four quarters make the whole'.
Count the resulting PARTS (regions), not the cuts.
A sorting/matching task checks and can teach recognition and classification; it does not by itself give children the experience of producing partitions, so pair it with hands-on cutting/folding.
A poster or display of partitioned shapes is a useful reference but does not let a child partition and test equality themselves; treat it as a scaffold, not the main activity.
Paper cutouts have slight thickness and imperfect cuts; use overlaying as a practical equality check and treat the paper as an approximation of the idealised flat (zero-thickness) shape.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source noted '3D adds nothing' for these planar shapes; dropped as a universal claim. These shapes are plane figures so a solid model is not needed here, but that is a scope point, not evidence that 3D can never help.

An interactive version could shade equal parts green and unequal parts red, accept several valid halving cuts, and provide a 'rebuild' button that slides parts back and labels 'two halves'/'four quarters'. These are optional feedback mechanisms that make the equality check and recomposition concrete; they are not required.

The source labelled a conversation format 'poor' because this is a hands-on skill; spoken discussion while cutting (naming parts, explaining equality) remains valuable and is retained within the activities, so the format is not treated as useless.
Description mixes 'quarters' and 'fourths'; both name four equal parts and are used interchangeably here.

Corrected an earlier geometry error: both diagonals of a rectangle produce four triangles of EQUAL AREA (each a quarter), not unequal parts; for a non-square rectangle they are not congruent and so cannot be verified by overlay. A single diagonal is presented as a halving method because its two triangles are congruent and overlay-checkable. This reinforces that equal fractional parts must be equal in size, not identical in shape.

probeDeeper: Put the four pieces back together - what do you get?
Is there more than one way to cut this square into two halves? Show me another.
How is this different from just cutting it into any two pieces?
If I cut the rectangle into four equal parts, what is each part called, and what do all four make?
assess.correctAnswer: No to both - the parts are not equal. Halves are two equal parts (a line through the middle); quarters are four equal parts. Put back together, the four equal quarters make the whole rectangle, and a circle can be halved by any line through its centre (more than one way).

errorPatterns.pattern: The right number of pieces means the fraction - accepts unequal parts as halves/quarters
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay/rotate the parts to test equality; contrast an equal and an unequal partition of identical shapes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes - there are two parts, so they are halves
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the unequal circle shows halves, or the unequal rectangle shows quarters

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot describe the whole as composed of its equal parts (two halves / four quarters make the whole)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically reassemble the parts into the whole; rehearse 'four quarters make one whole'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot answer what the parts make when reassembled

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a shape can be partitioned only one 'correct' way (rejects a valid alternative cut)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show several equal partitions of the same shape side by side; the rule is equal parts, not a fixed cut.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a horizontally- or diagonally-halved rectangle is 'wrong' because it isn't the usual vertical cut

responseLevels.gap: Accepts unequal parts as halves/quarters; counts pieces only.
responseLevels.full: Partitions circles and rectangles into equal halves and quarters, recognises different equal partitions are all valid, and describes the whole as composed of its equal parts.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies equal halves/quarters in the standard orientation but rejects valid alternative cuts, or cannot describe the whole as two halves / four quarters.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a circle divided by an off-centre line into two clearly unequal parts, and a rectangle divided into four parts where three are small and one is large. Ask: 'Is the circle cut into two halves? Is the rectangle cut into four quarters? How do you know?' Then ask: 'If you put the parts of the rectangle back together, what do they make - and is there more than one way to cut the circle into two halves?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both shapes have the RIGHT NUMBER of pieces but UNEQUAL sizes, so a child who counts pieces says yes while a child who requires equal parts says no. Tier 2 exposes whether they see the parts recompose the whole and accept more than one valid partition.

pedagogy.summary: Expressing one quantity as a fraction of another means writing 'a as a fraction of b' = a/b, where the quantity AFTER 'of' is the denominator (the whole) and the other is the numerator (the part). Two ideas make it conceptual rather than mechanical: (1) both quantities must be in the SAME UNIT before you form the fraction (45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours is 45/120 = 3/8, not 45/2), and (2) the result can be MORE THAN ONE when the first quantity is bigger than the second (3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2), which contradicts the young child's belief that a fraction is always less than a whole. Mastery is forming, simplifying, and INTERPRETING such a fraction in context.
bestPractices: Foreground the phrase structure: 'a as a fraction of b' → the thing after 'of' is the denominator. Rehearse identifying which quantity is the whole before writing anything.
Always convert to a common unit first; make 'same units?' a required checkpoint (45 min and 2 h → 45 min and 120 min).
Deliberately include cases where the answer exceeds 1 (e.g. 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m) so pupils accept improper-fraction results and interpret them as 'more than the whole'.
Simplify and then interpret in words — '3/8 of the two hours' — so the fraction is tied back to the situation, not left as a bare number.
Connect to ratio and percentage: a/b is the same comparison expressed as a fraction, and ×100 gives the percentage — building the ratio–fraction–percentage web.
keyRepresentations: Bar / double number line with both quantities in a common unit (45 out of 120 minutes shaded)
The sentence frame 'a as a fraction of b = a/b' with 'of' → denominator
Fraction-of-a-quantity strip that can exceed one whole (improper result)
Equivalent-fraction simplification chain (45/120 → 3/8)
commonMisconceptions: Writing the raw numbers without converting to a common unit (45/2 for 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours).
Putting the quantities the wrong way round — ignoring that the quantity after 'of' is the denominator.
Believing a fraction must be less than 1, so being unable to accept or interpret a result greater than 1 (3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2).
Forgetting to simplify, or simplifying incorrectly, leaving the comparison obscured.

learn.summary: Learners express one quantity as a fraction of another: 'a as a fraction of b' = a/b, where the quantity after 'of' is the denominator (the whole). Mastery requires (1) converting both quantities to the SAME unit before forming the fraction (45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours is 45/120 = 3/8, not 45/2), (2) accepting results greater than one whole when the first quantity is bigger (3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2), and (3) simplifying and interpreting the fraction back in context.

activities.title: The fraction-of bench: convert units, then form the fraction
feedback: If a learner writes 45/2, ask: 'Are minutes and hours the same unit?' Convert 2 hours to 120 minutes on the bar, then re-form 45/120 = 3/8.

If a learner writes 120/45 or 8/3, rehearse the sentence frame: 'a as a fraction of b' means b (after 'of') is the whole/denominator; test it on 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours, which must be 1/2, not 2.

If a learner refuses 3/2, flips it to 2/3, or says 'that can't be a fraction', return to the overflowing bar: 3 hours shaded past the 2-hour whole is 3/2 = 1½ wholes — an improper fraction meaning more than the whole amount.
If a learner stops at 45/120, prompt them to simplify and then say the answer in context ('3/8 of the two hours').
activities.rationale: Seeing both quantities on a common-unit bar grounds the part–whole comparison; a strip that overflows one whole makes an improper result visible rather than abstract, which targets the belief that a fraction must be less than 1. An optional unit toggle that withholds the fraction until units match makes the 'convert first' step explicit at the moment the error would occur. Laying both quantities on a shared scale is a concrete way to reason multiplicatively about part relative to whole.
sourceClaims: KS2/KS3 pupils should express one quantity as a fraction of another and solve problems involving relative sizes of two quantities, including where units must be made common and results simplified.
Comparing two quantities as a fraction is part of the ratio–fraction–proportion web; reasoning multiplicatively about part relative to whole underpins it.
learnerActions: Start with two quantities in different units, e.g. 45 minutes and 2 hours, and say in words which quantity is the whole (the one after 'of' — here 2 hours).
Before writing any fraction, convert both to a common unit: split the 2-hour bar into 120 minute-segments and highlight the 45.
Form the fraction from the shaded bar: 45 out of 120, then simplify the equivalent-fraction chain 45/120 → 9/24 → 3/8.

In a second round, take 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours: shade 3 hours against a 2-hour whole bar so the shading runs past the end of one whole and spills into a second bar; read the fraction as 3/2.
State what 3/2 means here in words: '3 hours is one and a half times the two hours' / 'more than the whole'.
Check yourself with an obvious case: 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours should be 1/2 — confirm your method gives it.
activities.intendedInsight: Both quantities must be in the same unit before forming a fraction, the quantity after 'of' is the denominator, and the comparison fraction can exceed one whole when the first quantity is larger.

activities.title: Form, simplify and interpret — including improper results
feedback: For 45/2: this did not convert hours to minutes; 2 h = 120 min, so the fraction is 45/120 = 3/8.
For 150/1: 1 m = 100 cm, so 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m is 150/100 = 3/2, not 150/1.
For 2/3 on the 150 cm item: the quantity after 'of' (1 m = 100 cm) is the whole/denominator, so 150 goes on top — the answer 3/2 is greater than 1.
Connect a/b to percentage: ×100 turns 3/8 into 37.5% and 3/2 into 150%, linking the fraction, ratio and percentage.
activities.rationale: Short constructed and selection items let learners rehearse forming, simplifying and interpreting the fraction and confront targeted distractors (no conversion, wrong way round, improper result). Recognition/selection confirms the rule but does not by itself require the learner to build the common-unit bar, so it complements rather than replaces the hands-on forming activity.
sourceClaims: KS2/KS3 pupils should express one quantity as a fraction of another and solve problems involving relative sizes of two quantities, including where units must be made common and results simplified.
learnerActions: Fill in the blank: '45 min as a fraction of 2 h = ___', giving the simplified fraction (3/8) and rejecting the un-converted 45/2.
Identify which quantity is the denominator in a given 'a as a fraction of b' statement and justify why.
Tackle an item whose answer exceeds 1: write 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m in simplest form (= 3/2), avoiding 2/3 (wrong way round) and 150/1 (no conversion).
After each answer, write one sentence interpreting the fraction in the original context.
activities.intendedInsight: Forming, simplifying and interpreting the fraction — including when it is greater than 1 — is a single connected skill, with the not-converting and wrong-way-round errors as the key pitfalls.

activities.title: Annotated reference bar: 'of → denominator' and 'convert units first'
feedback: If a learner still mixes up the order, point back to the tapped 'of → denominator' annotation and re-test on 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours = 1/2.
If a learner forgets conversion, re-reveal the 2 h = 120 min step on the bar.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated bar consolidates the rule and serves as a reference card. As a static scaffold it cannot make the learner perform the conversion or watch a fraction overflow one whole, so it supports but does not substitute for the interactive forming activity.
learnerActions: Study a bar showing 45 of 120 minutes shaded; tap the word 'of' to reveal that it marks the whole/denominator.
Tap the bar to reveal the common-unit conversion (2 h = 120 min) that had to happen first.
Use this card as a quick check before forming any 'fraction-of' answer.
activities.intendedInsight: The phrase 'a as a fraction of b' always puts the quantity after 'of' as the denominator, and units must be made common before the fraction is formed.

constraints: Always require a 'same units?' checkpoint before any fraction is written; converting to a common unit must precede forming the fraction.
Deliberately include cases where the answer exceeds 1 (e.g. 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2, 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m = 3/2) so learners accept and interpret improper results.
Simplify and then interpret the fraction in words tied to the situation ('3/8 of the two hours'); do not leave it as a bare number.
Selection/recognition items confirm the rule and surface distractors but do not elicit independent construction of the common-unit comparison; pair them with hands-on forming.
The static annotated bar is a reference scaffold: it cannot make the learner perform the conversion or dynamically witness a fraction exceeding one whole.
Connect to ratio and percentage (a/b as the same comparison; ×100 for percentage) to build the ratio–fraction–percentage web.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'persona dialogue' and '3D' entries were rated poor-fit; those were catalog-fit judgements for this one-dimensional comparison, not established pedagogical laws, so they are omitted rather than asserted as universal claims about the media.

The claim that only the overflowing-bar visual can dismantle the 'fractions are always <1' misconception is a catalog preference; it is presented here as a well-motivated proposal, not proven necessity.

Independent editor arithmetic/coherence check: 45/120 = 9/24 = 3/8; 150/100 = 3/2; 1 h/2 h = 1/2; 120/45 = 8/3; 3/8 = 37.5% and 3/2 = 150% all verify. 45/2 and 120/45 (=8/3) are framed only as errors, never as valid answers, and no denominator-'flip' claim is made (the unit-fraction comparison here fixes the numerator and varies the whole, so no 'flipping rule' is implied).

probeDeeper: Are 45 and 2 measured in the same unit? What do you have to do before you can compare them?
Which is the WHOLE here — the 45 minutes or the 2 hours? How does the wording tell you which goes on the bottom?
Now write 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours. Can the answer be bigger than 1? What does 3/2 mean here? (counterexample forcing an improper result.)
Check yourself: 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours — what should that be? Does your method give that?
assess.correctAnswer: 3/8. Because 2 hours = 120 minutes, 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours is 45/120, which simplifies to 3/8. (Both quantities must be in the same unit — minutes — before forming the fraction.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not convert to a common unit — writes 45/2 straight from the numbers as they appear
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'are minutes and hours the same unit?' Convert 2 hours to 120 minutes on a bar, then re-form 45/120. Make 'same units first' a fixed checkpoint.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 45/2 or 22.5, and the explanation is 'the 45 goes over the 2' with no mention of minutes vs hours

errorPatterns.pattern: Puts the quantities the wrong way round — ignores that the amount after 'of' is the denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rehearse the sentence frame: 'a as a fraction of b' → b (after 'of') is the whole/denominator. Check with an obvious case: 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours must be 1/2, not 2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 120/45 (or 8/3), treating the first-mentioned or larger quantity as the whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a fraction must be less than 1, so cannot accept or interpret a result greater than one whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the overflowing bar: 3 hours shaded past the 2-hour whole gives 3/2 = 1½ wholes. Name it an improper fraction and interpret it as 'more than the whole amount'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a case like 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours, refuses 3/2, flips it to 2/3, or says 'that can't be a fraction'

responseLevels.gap: Writes 45/2 (or flips to 120/45) without converting units or identifying the whole; treats it as a bare number-placing exercise.
responseLevels.full: Converts 2 h to 120 min, forms 45/120 with the correct quantity as denominator, simplifies to 3/8, interprets it in context, AND accepts and interprets an improper result such as 3/2 for 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours.
responseLevels.partial: Converts to a common unit and forms 45/120 but stops without simplifying, or simplifies yet cannot handle a result greater than 1, or cannot say which quantity is the whole and why.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours, as simply as you can. Then explain how you got it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands must first notice the units differ and convert 2 hours to 120 minutes; the answer 3/8 can ONLY be reached that way. A child who just writes the numbers gives 45/2 (or 22.5) and their reason reveals they never converted. The reason-tier separates 'I made the units the same first' from 'I put 45 over 2', so the two children give different answers and different explanations.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11; understand how rainforest products reach everyday life through global SUPPLY CHAINS — palm oil in snacks/soap/cosmetics, soy feeding livestock, cocoa→chocolate, rubber in tyres/gloves, timber→furniture, medicines from forest plants — and that consumer choices can drive either destruction or sustainable practice.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (trade links, economic activity, distribution of natural resources) and Science Y6 (human impact); DT 'where products come from'; leads to KS3.
• Standards — US: NGSS MS-ESS3-4 (human consumption of natural resources) and social-studies global-economics strands.
• Operational details — the core skill is TRACING a chain both ways: forest → plantation/farm → processing → shipping → factory → shelf → your home, AND the reverse (this snack → palm oil → a cleared hillside). Surface the hidden ubiquity of palm oil (in roughly half of packaged supermarket products) as the standout. Then close the FEEDBACK LOOP: because demand pulls the chain, a consumer choosing a certified/sustainable product (or less of it) sends a signal back up the chain — agency, not just guilt. Distinguish 'boycott everything' (can hurt smallholders) from 'choose sustainable', the more nuanced message.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (9): name four rainforest-linked products. Tier B (10): trace how palm oil travels from a forest region to a supermarket shelf. Tier C (11): explain how a specific consumer choice (buying certified) feeds back to reduce deforestation pressure.
bestPractices: Teach tracing BOTH directions: forest→shelf and shelf→forest, so pupils see products as the end of a chain.
Surface palm oil's hidden ubiquity (in ~half of packaged products) as the memorable hook.
Close the feedback loop: demand pulls the chain, so consumer choice can push back — frame as agency, not guilt.
Distinguish 'boycott everything' (can harm smallholders) from 'choose certified/sustainable' as the nuanced message.
Link to prior 'Everyday Foods' and 'Deforestation Drivers' so the chain connects known dots.
keyRepresentations: A supply-chain journey line: forest → farm → processing → shipping → factory → shelf → home.
A 'scan the basket' reveal showing hidden palm oil across everyday products.
Sustainable-vs-unsustainable sourcing toggle with forest-impact and farmer-income meters.
Certification labels (Rainforest Alliance frog, FSC, RSPO) on real packaging.
commonMisconceptions: 'Rainforest products are just exotic foods' — many are hidden ingredients (palm oil in soap, rubber in tyres).
'My shopping can't affect a faraway forest' — consumer demand directly pulls the supply chain.
'Boycotting everything is best' — it can devastate smallholder livelihoods; choosing certified is usually better.
'A product with a green label is automatically fine' — certification helps but varies; it's a signal, not a guarantee.
'Soy is mainly eaten by people as tofu' — most soy feeds livestock worldwide.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 9–11 learn that many everyday products are the far end of global supply chains reaching back into rainforests — palm oil hidden in snacks, soap and cosmetics; soy feeding livestock; cocoa→chocolate; rubber in tyres and gloves; timber→furniture; and medicines from forest plants. The core skill is tracing a chain BOTH directions (forest→plantation→processing→shipping→factory→shelf→home, and the reverse), surfacing palm oil's hidden ubiquity (in roughly half of packaged supermarket products per WWF), and understanding the demand feedback loop: because demand pulls the chain, consumer choices can push back. The nuanced message is 'choose certified/sustainable', not 'boycott everything', because blanket boycotts can harm smallholder farmers and remove incentives to farm sustainably.

activities.title: Build the chain from shelf to forest (and back)
feedback: If a pupil treats a product as unconnected to any forest, prompt: 'Where does the palm oil / rubber / soy in this actually begin? Build the chain one link at a time back to the land.'

If a pupil chooses to boycott everything, point to the collapsed farmer-income meter: 'A total boycott removes smallholders' income and any reward for farming well — what does choosing certified do instead?'

When the basket scan surprises them, reinforce: 'WWF estimates palm oil is in about half of packaged supermarket products — that's why reading labels matters, although in soaps and cosmetics it often appears under other chemical names.'
If a pupil assumes a green label guarantees no harm, note that certification is a signal that helps but varies — it is not an automatic guarantee.
activities.rationale: A supply chain is a trace-and-connect system with a feedback loop. Building the chain in both directions is intended to make products legible as chain endpoints, and a live sourcing toggle with impact/income meters is intended to make the demand→forest→smallholder trade-off more concrete; whether it does so better than simply stating the rule is not established — this is a design proposal, not a validated result. The meters and basket scanner are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Palm oil is found in roughly half of packaged supermarket products (foods, cosmetics, cleaning products); soy, cocoa, rubber, timber and many medicines are also major rainforest-linked commodities in global supply chains
Consumer demand drives commodity-linked deforestation, and certified sustainable sourcing can reduce pressure while supporting smallholders (boycotts can harm smallholders)
learnerActions: Start from a familiar supermarket product (e.g. a jar of chocolate spread) and build the chain link by link backwards: factory → ship → refinery → plantation → the land, until the last link reaches where the crop was grown, which may be recently cleared forest, at-risk forest or long-established farmland, depending on the source.
Then trace the SAME chain forwards from forest to home, saying each stage aloud or writing it, so the product is seen as the END of a chain, not an isolated thing.

Use a 'scan the basket' reveal: check other everyday items (biscuits, soap, shampoo) and discover how many contain palm oil or palm-derived ingredients. WWF estimates that roughly half of packaged supermarket products do, though the share in any one basket will vary.

For each product, toggle its sourcing from 'cheap/unsustainable' to 'certified' and watch, in this simplified illustrative model, a forest-impact meter fall while a smallholder-income meter holds. Then test boycotting EVERYTHING and see the model's farmer-income meter collapse too. Remember that the model shows a simplified idea, not measured real-world results.
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday shopping is the far end of a chain that reaches into the forest; demand pulls the chain, so the smarter lever is choosing the sustainable link and sending that signal back up the line — not buying nothing.

activities.title: Hidden ingredients hunt
feedback: If a pupil limits the link to obvious tropical foods, read a soap or bread label together and surface the palm oil.
If a pupil thinks soy is mainly eaten by people as tofu, clarify that most soy worldwide feeds livestock, so it is hidden behind meat and eggs.
Praise concrete label-reading evidence rather than guessing: 'You found palm oil listed — that's the kind of clue to look for.'
activities.rationale: Directly addressing the 'just exotic foods' and 'soy is tofu' misconceptions with real labels grounds the ubiquity point in evidence pupils gather themselves. The sort can check classification but does not by itself elicit the label-reading or explanation, so it is paired with gathering real evidence.
sourceClaims: Palm oil is found in roughly half of packaged supermarket products (foods, cosmetics, cleaning products); soy, cocoa, rubber, timber and many medicines are also major rainforest-linked commodities in global supply chains
learnerActions: Read real ingredient labels on everyday packaging together (biscuits, bread, soap, shampoo), and check product descriptions or material labels for items like trainers, which do not carry ingredient lists.

List the non-obvious rainforest-linked ingredients — palm oil or palm derivatives in some soaps and breads, natural rubber in some trainer soles (many use synthetic rubber), and soy animal feed behind much meat and many eggs (not shown on the label).
Sort products into 'obvious tropical treat' (chocolate, bananas, coffee) versus 'hidden ingredient' and discuss why the hidden ones are easy to miss.
Spot certification labels where they appear (Rainforest Alliance frog, FSC, RSPO) and discuss what signal they send.
activities.intendedInsight: Rainforest products are not only exotic jungle foods — many are hidden ingredients in ordinary goods, including palm oil, soy animal feed, rubber and timber.

activities.title: Sequence and match the journey (check and consolidate)
feedback: If sequencing is wrong, ask what has to happen to raw forest produce before it can reach a shelf (it must be grown, processed, shipped, manufactured).
For the certified question, if a pupil picks 'boycott', remind them a boycott removes smallholder income and the incentive to farm sustainably.
activities.rationale: Ordering and matching tasks give a clean recognition check of the chain and links. Recognition-only responses confirm recall but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction or feedback-loop reasoning built in the earlier activities, so use this to consolidate rather than to teach the systems intuition.
sourceClaims: Palm oil is found in roughly half of packaged supermarket products (foods, cosmetics, cleaning products); soy, cocoa, rubber, timber and many medicines are also major rainforest-linked commodities in global supply chains
Consumer demand drives commodity-linked deforestation, and certified sustainable sourcing can reduce pressure while supporting smallholders (boycotts can harm smallholders)
learnerActions: Order the stages of the palm-oil journey in sequence: forest → plantation → processing/refinery → shipping → factory → shelf → home.
Match everyday products to their hidden rainforest ingredient (biscuit→palm oil, tyre→rubber, chicken nugget→soy feed, furniture→timber).
Answer: how does choosing a certified product help a forest compared with buying carelessly OR boycotting everything?
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the chain order, the product→ingredient links, and the reasoning that certified sourcing is usually better than both careless buying and a blanket boycott.

activities.title: Argue the diagnostic both ways
feedback: If a pupil says distant shopping has no effect, trace one concrete product (palm oil in biscuits, or soy fed to nugget chicken) back to the land where it was grown, which in some supply chains is cleared forest, to show how demand pulls supply.
If a pupil insists boycott is ideal, explain palm oil is the highest-yielding oil crop so alternatives can need MORE land, and that certification rewards good practice a boycott cannot.
Reward answers that get BOTH halves and apply them to a fresh product, not slogans like 'rainforest products are bad'.
activities.rationale: The two-tier diagnostic discriminates between a slogan and real reasoning: a pupil must see the connection AND the boycott trade-off. Applying to a new product tests transfer rather than recall.
sourceClaims: Consumer demand drives commodity-linked deforestation, and certified sustainable sourcing can reduce pressure while supporting smallholders (boycotts can harm smallholders)
learnerActions: Respond to a friend's claim: 'My shopping in Britain can't possibly affect a rainforest thousands of miles away — and anyway, the best thing to do is boycott every single rainforest product.'
State clearly whether the friend is right on EACH of the two points, and explain WHY for each half.
Apply the reasoning to a NEW product of the pupil's choice: pick something used this morning and trace an ingredient back toward a rainforest, saying where to look on the label.
Discuss trade-offs: if everyone boycotted palm oil tomorrow, who is helped and who harmed; and is it fair to expect a family on a tight budget to pay more for certified goods?
activities.intendedInsight: Genuine supply-chain reasoning holds both halves: everyday shopping IS connected through demand, AND a blanket boycott is not the best answer because it harms smallholders and removes the reward for farming sustainably.

constraints: Teach tracing in BOTH directions (forest→shelf and shelf→forest) so products are understood as the end of a chain.
Frame consumer choice as agency, not guilt: demand pulls the chain, so choosing sustainably pushes back.
Distinguish 'boycott everything' (can harm smallholders and remove incentive to farm sustainably) from 'choose certified/sustainable' as the more nuanced message.
Present certification labels as a helpful signal that varies, not an automatic guarantee that a product is harmless.
Link to prior work on everyday foods and deforestation drivers so the chain connects known ideas.
Impact and income meters, basket scanners and sourcing toggles are illustrative interaction examples to make the feedback loop concrete; they are optional, not mandatory mechanisms.
Recognition tasks (sequencing, matching, multiple choice) consolidate and check recall but do not on their own elicit the independent construction and trade-off reasoning the objective requires.
Deep stakeholder dialogue (e.g. hearing a smallholder's voice) is a valuable extension but belongs to a later futures/stakeholder node; the focus here is tracing the chain and consumer feedback.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the three sources were not re-fetched and all carry verified:false in the original row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The 'roughly half of packaged supermarket products contain palm oil' figure is attributed to WWF in the source but was not independently verified here; present it as a sourced estimate, not an exact fact.

The 'palm oil is the highest-yielding oil crop / alternatives can need more land' point used in activity 4 feedback comes from the original reteach move and is sourced but unverified; keep it qualified.

The 'most soy worldwide feeds livestock' claim comes from the original misconception list with no attached source; it is widely accepted but was not independently verified here, so keep it as a general statement rather than a cited fact.

The original artefact note 'a 2D interactive is ideal and 3D adds nothing' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; preserved as alternatives with stated affordances/limits rather than universal claims.

The claim that a tap-to-reveal map 'can't let pupils feel the demand→forest feedback that a model makes felt' is a catalog-level comparison, not established comparative efficacy; softened to a scoped affordance note.
The KS2-geography source claim supports topic/curriculum coverage and was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims, where the rationale concerns system design rather than curriculum coverage.

probeDeeper: Pick something you used this morning and try to trace an ingredient back to a rainforest — where would you look on the label?
If everyone suddenly boycotted palm oil tomorrow, who would be helped and who might be harmed, and why?
Why might a 'certified sustainable' label be better for a forest than either buying carelessly OR boycotting completely?
What if a certified product costs more — is it fair to expect a family on a tight budget to pay extra to protect a forest?
assess.correctAnswer: Wrong on both. Ordinary shopping IS linked to rainforests: palm oil is in roughly half of packaged supermarket goods, and soy (mostly for animal feed), cocoa, coffee, natural rubber, beef and timber all come partly from cleared or at-risk forest land — consumer demand pulls the whole supply chain. But boycotting everything is not the best answer either: it can wreck the livelihoods of smallholder farmers and give them no reason to farm sustainably. The stronger choice is to buy certified sustainable products (RSPO palm oil, Rainforest Alliance, FSC), waste less, and push companies to clean up their supply chains.

errorPatterns.pattern: my shopping can't affect a distant forest ('it's on the other side of the world, nothing to do with me')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace one concrete product — palm oil in biscuits, or soy fed to the chicken in a nugget — back to cleared land; show demand pulling supply.
errorPatterns.distractor: Right — shopping in Britain is far too far away to have any effect on a rainforest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child denies any link between everyday purchases and rainforest clearance, treating the forest as too remote to be touched by demand

errorPatterns.pattern: boycotting every rainforest product is the best thing to do ('just ban palm oil / never buy any of it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain that palm oil is the highest-yielding oil crop — switching to alternatives can need MORE land — and that certified sustainable sourcing rewards good practice; boycott removes that lever.
errorPatterns.distractor: The best thing to do is boycott and never buy any rainforest product at all.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats a total boycott as the ideal action and cannot see the harm to smallholders or the loss of any incentive to farm sustainably

errorPatterns.pattern: only exotic 'jungle' foods come from rainforests ('it's just bananas, chocolate and coffee')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read ingredient labels together and list the non-obvious ones (palm oil in soap and bread, rubber in trainers, soy behind meat and eggs).
errorPatterns.distractor: Only obvious tropical treats like chocolate, bananas and coffee are linked to rainforests.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child limits the link to obviously tropical treats and overlooks hidden ingredients — palm oil, soy animal feed, rubber, timber — in everyday goods

responseLevels.gap: Insists distant shopping has no effect, or parrots 'rainforest products are bad, ban them' — no supply-chain link and no sense of trade-offs.
responseLevels.full: Explains that consumer demand pulls the supply chain so everyday goods (including hidden palm oil and soy feed) are connected, argues that certified sustainable sourcing beats a blanket boycott because a boycott harms smallholders and removes the incentive to do better, and applies this to a new product.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises SOME products come from rainforests and that individual choices matter, but treats boycott as the obvious fix, or names the link without grasping that demand drives clearance across a whole supply chain.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A friend says: 'My shopping at the supermarket in Britain can't possibly affect a rainforest thousands of miles away — and anyway, the best thing anyone can do is boycott every single rainforest product.' Are they right on either point? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks distant shopping is disconnected can't see how demand drives clearance. A child who has absorbed 'rainforest products are bad, so ban them all' misses that a blanket boycott harms the very farmers and gives no market reward for doing it right. Getting BOTH halves right — connected AND a boycott is not the answer — shows genuine supply-chain reasoning rather than a slogan.
