pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–8 years

- **Topic:** Asking scientific questions

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to ask simple questions and recognise that they can be answered in different ways. Across KS1 they experience the five enquiry types (observing over time; pattern seeking; identifying, classifying and grouping; comparative/fair testing; researching using secondary sources), which are precisely the different 'ways to answer' a question.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 1 Asking Questions and Defining Problems, grades K–2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-1, K-ESS3-2] world; ask and/or identify questions that can be answered by an investigation. Recognising that a question implies a method of answering is the entry practice here.

- **Operational details:** The child generates genuine 'how/why/what if' questions about the natural world, and — crucially — recognises that different questions call for different ways of answering: some by observing (does the snail come out in the rain?), some by a simple test (which paper towel soaks up most?), some by researching a book or asking an expert (what do owls eat?). They begin to tell an answerable/testable question from one that can't be settled by looking or trying, and to pick a sensible method for a given question. The emphasis is on curiosity made productive: turning a vague wonder into a question you could actually go and answer.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). This is the front door of inquiry — before observing, testing or researching, you need a question worth answering and a sense of how to answer it. Success = generates several genuine science questions, and for a given question chooses a sensible way to answer it (observe / test / research / ask), distinguishing questions you can investigate from those you can't.
bestPractices: Create a visible 'wonder wall' where children post questions, legitimising curiosity and giving raw material to sort and pursue.
Explicitly name the ways to answer a question — observe, test, research, ask an expert — and match example questions to each, so method-choice becomes deliberate.
Model turning a vague wonder ('why is the sky like that?') into an answerable question ('does the sky look redder in the evening than the morning?').
Distinguish questions you can investigate first-hand from those you must look up, without dismissing either.
Use the five enquiry types as a menu: for each new question ask 'which kind of enquiry would answer this?'.
Value the question itself as a scientific product — praise good questions, not just right answers.
keyRepresentations: Question 'wonder wall' of posted how/why/what-if questions
Method menu: observe / test / research / ask an expert, with an icon each
Sorting mat routing each question to its best answering method
Vague-wonder → answerable-question transformation frame
The five enquiry-type cards as a 'ways to find out' menu
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a science question always needs an experiment, when observing or researching may fit better.
Confusing a question with a guess/answer ('I think it's the heat') instead of an open question.
Believing every question can be answered by looking it up (or, conversely, by testing).
Treating only 'why' questions as scientific, overlooking 'what if' and 'how' questions.
Asking questions that can't be investigated (opinion or unanswerable) without noticing the difference.
Seeing question-asking as a sign of not knowing, rather than as the engine of science.

learn.summary: Help children aged 5–8 practise asking genuine science questions and recognising that different questions call for different ways of answering: observing, a simple fair test, researching (book/internet), or asking an expert. The core skill is generative (producing real how/why/what-if questions) plus routing (choosing a sensible method) plus discrimination (telling an investigable question from an opinion/value question that evidence can't settle). The five activities below are a question-sorting workbench that ends with the child's own questions, a task that sharpens a vague wonder into an answerable question, a sort of science-versus-opinion questions, a spoken conversation with a curious scientist, and an optional curiosity-priming scene. Each has its own role, and any sorting of pre-written cards is only a quick check that comes after the child makes up questions.

activities.title: Question Workbench: sort each wonder into how you'd answer it
feedback: If a 'look it up' question (e.g. 'what do owls eat?') is placed in TEST, nudge gently: 'Hmm, hard to test at home — could we look it up instead?' rather than marking it simply wrong.
When a routing fits, confirm the reason: 'Yes — we could watch and see, so WATCH fits.'
If every card goes to ASK SOMEONE or LOOK IT UP, prompt: 'What if no book knows about THESE snails in OUR garden? How could you find out yourself?'
Praise the child's own generated questions as a real scientific product, separately from whether the routing was right.
activities.rationale: Making method-choice an active sorting-and-justifying task (rather than being told the answer) builds the habit of pairing a question with a way to answer it. An optional on-screen version can give immediate responsive feedback (a mis-routed card wobbles back with a hint; a good fit clicks home with a tick) and use icons/audio to keep reading load low for this age; the same task also works with physical cards and four labelled bins.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires pupils to ask simple questions and recognise that they can be answered in different ways, experiencing the five named enquiry types.
NGSS SEP 1 (Asking Questions and Defining Problems) K–2 has students ask questions based on observations and identify questions that can be answered by an investigation.
learnerActions: Collect a wall of wonder-cards, e.g. 'Does the snail come out when it rains?', 'What do owls eat?', 'Which paper towel soaks up the most water?', 'Why is the sky sometimes red?'
Sort each card into one of four answering methods: WATCH (observe), TEST (try a fair test), LOOK IT UP (research a book/internet), ASK SOMEONE (an expert).
Say aloud, for each card, why that method fits — e.g. 'What do owls eat?' goes to LOOK IT UP because you can't easily watch owls at night.
Notice when the SAME curiosity could become a different kind of question depending on how you'd find out.
Generate at least three of your own wonder-cards and route them too.
activities.intendedInsight: A scientist doesn't just ask a question — they also ask 'how would I find out?'. Different questions are answered in different ways, and recognising the method is part of the question.

activities.title: Sharpen a floppy wonder into an answerable question
feedback: When the reshaped question names something to observe or compare, confirm: 'Now you can investigate this — you know exactly what to look for!'
If the question is still vague, ask: 'What exactly would you watch or measure to answer that?'
Keep valuing the original wonder — the goal is to channel curiosity, not to say the first question was bad.
activities.rationale: Transforming a vague wonder into an answerable one makes visible that answerability depends on having something concrete to observe or compare. Word-tiles (physical or on-screen) make the transformation tangible; an optional screen version can glow when the question becomes investigable.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 1 (Asking Questions and Defining Problems) K–2 has students ask questions based on observations and identify questions that can be answered by an investigation.
learnerActions: Start with a vague wonder such as 'Why is the sky like that?' or 'Why is the snail slow?'.
Use comparison words (more, than, when, which, redder) to reshape it into something you could actually check — e.g. 'Is the sky redder in the EVENING THAN the morning?'.
Explain what you would observe or compare once the question is sharpened.
Try sharpening one more wonder of your own.
activities.intendedInsight: A vague wonder becomes an investigable science question when it points to something specific you can observe or compare.

activities.title: Which questions can science settle, and which can't?
feedback: If the child labels a value question ('best minibeast') as investigable, sort a few together and name the feature: 'Could we gather evidence, or would people just disagree?'
If the child asserts a conclusion ('woodlice like damp, everyone knows'), honour the guess then ask: 'That's your prediction — now how would we FIND OUT if you're right?'
If the child can't offer any non-investigable question, give one example and ask them to explain why evidence can't settle it.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing an evidence question from an opinion/value question is the discriminating skill; producing a non-investigable question requires the very distinction under test, so it is a strong check of understanding.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 1 (Asking Questions and Defining Problems) K–2 has students ask questions based on observations and identify questions that can be answered by an investigation.
learnerActions: Sort a short mix of questions into 'we could find out' versus 'people would just disagree', e.g. 'Do woodlice go to the damp side?' versus 'Are woodlice the nicest minibeast?'.
Name the feature that decides it: evidence can settle one, but the other is a matter of opinion or taste.
Come up with your own question about an animal or object that science could NOT settle by investigating.
Discuss what you would trust if a book disagrees with what you observe (e.g. the book says woodlice like damp but the garden ones keep going to the dry side), and how you could settle it.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific questions are the ones evidence can answer; opinion and value questions can't be settled by observing or testing, no matter how hard you look.

activities.title: Wonder together with a curious scientist (spoken dialogue)
feedback: The partner stays warmly curious and never lectures, always ending by helping name how to answer the question.
If the child jumps to an answer, the partner reflects: 'That's your guess — how could we check it?'
The partner reflects back the method choice: 'Ooh — could we find that out by watching, by testing, by looking it up, or by asking someone who knows?'
activities.rationale: Question-asking is often social, and a responsive partner can model and elicit the generative skill by wondering aloud and inviting the child's own questions, helping them sharpen a wonder and name a way to answer it. At this age it needs a shared image or object to wonder about so the questions stay concrete. This is one effective route among several, not the only way to develop the skill.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 1 (Asking Questions and Defining Problems) K–2 has students ask questions based on observations and identify questions that can be answered by an investigation.
learnerActions: Look at a shared picture or real object (a puddle, a snail, a shadow) and wonder aloud about it.
Respond when the curious partner asks 'could we find that out by watching or testing, or would we need to look it up or ask someone?'.
Finish each wonder by naming HOW you would answer it (watch / test / look up / ask).
Take a turn asking the partner a question too.
activities.intendedInsight: Talking a wonder through out loud with someone can help you sharpen it and pick a way to answer it.

activities.title: Curiosity-priming scene (optional warm-up)
feedback: Use this to seed questions, then move to a task where the child's OWN questions get a response.
Point out the range of methods the scene shows — not every curiosity is answered the same way.
activities.rationale: A pre-authored scene can prime question-asking and introduce the method menu, but it cannot respond to the child's own questions, so it works as a warm-up rather than the main activity.
learnerActions: Explore a rich scene with tappable or pointable curiosities (a puddle, a snail, a shadow).
For each one, notice a model question and a suggested 'how could we find out?'.
Use what you notice to start your own questions before the workbench or conversation.
activities.intendedInsight: There are things worth wondering about everywhere, and each wonder can be paired with a way to find out.

constraints: The generative core is the child producing their own real questions; recognition-only tasks (e.g. multiple-choice 'which method answers this?' or sorting pre-written questions) can check method-matching but do not themselves elicit independent question generation, so use them only as a quick follow-up check.
A curiosity-priming scene is pre-authored and cannot respond to the child's own questions; treat it as a warm-up, not the main learning event.
Keep reading load low for ages 5–8: use icons, pictures, real objects, and audio; don't rely on reading dense text.
Honour books and experts as genuine sources — the aim is to add observing and testing as options, not to dismiss research or asking.
Both first-hand investigation and looking-up are legitimate; the point is matching method to question, not ranking methods.
Treat a child's prediction/guess as valuable, then redirect to 'how would we find out?' rather than correcting the guess.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One cited source (NGSS Appendix F) was marked verified:false in the original row; treat its citation accordingly and re-check before relying on it.

The original framed a screen-based 'Question Workbench' as giving feedback 'far better than being told' and rated a 3D environment as adding 'navigation without helping'. These comparative-efficacy claims are not established by the sources; the rewrite keeps the responsive-feedback mechanism as an optional affordance and does not assert one medium is universally superior.

The original rationale asserted question-asking is 'inherently dialogic'; this categorical claim is softened to describe dialogue as one effective, often-social route, since the sources do not establish it as necessary or best.

The example claims 'does the snail come out when it rains?' and 'woodlice like damp' are illustrative natural-world examples, not verified empirical results; present them as questions to investigate rather than established facts.

probeDeeper: You said we could watch them — what exactly would you look for that tells you they PREFER damp, not just that one happened to be there?
Suppose your book says woodlice like damp but the ones in our garden keep going to the dry side. Which do you trust, and how could you settle it?
Can you think of a question about woodlice that we could never find out the answer to, no matter how hard we looked?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning offers a way to gather evidence — set up a choice with a damp side and a dry side and watch where the woodlice go — and recognises there are several routes to an answer (observe them in the wild, do a fair test, ask an expert, read a book), choosing the one that suits the question. Crucially the child can name a question science cannot settle by investigating — a matter of opinion or value such as 'are woodlice the nicest minibeast?' — showing they grasp that scientific questions are the ones evidence can answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Every question is answered by asking a grown-up or looking in a book ('I'd ask my teacher', 'I'd look it up') — treats knowledge as coming from authority rather than from finding out.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Accept that books and experts are real sources, then push: 'What if no book knows about THESE woodlice in THIS garden? How could you find out yourself?' Model turning a wonder into a thing you do.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Every route the child names is an authority (teacher, book, internet); never proposes observing or testing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Can't tell an investigable question from an opinion or value question — treats 'are woodlice the best minibeast?' as answerable by evidence.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort a few questions together into 'we could find out' versus 'people would just disagree'; name the feature — evidence can settle one, not the other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked for a question science can't settle, offers none, or labels a value question as investigable.

errorPatterns.pattern: Jumps straight to an answer or guess instead of framing a question or a way to find out ('woodlice like damp, everyone knows').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Honour the prediction, then scaffold: 'That's your guess — now how would we FIND OUT if you're right?' Redirect from asserting to investigating; prompt the missing step rather than reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States a conclusion confidently without proposing any way to check it.

responseLevels.gap: Names only authority sources (ask, look up) or asserts an answer; cannot propose gathering evidence and cannot identify a non-investigable question.
responseLevels.full: Proposes gathering evidence, recognises several routes and picks one suited to the question, AND separates an investigable question from a value or opinion question, explaining that science answers the ones evidence can settle.
responseLevels.partial: Proposes one way to find out (usually watching) and may list others, but treats every question as investigable — does not distinguish an evidence question from an opinion question.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You wonder whether the woodlice in the garden like damp places or dry places. Talk me through it: how could you find out the answer? Is there more than one way to find out? And is there any question about woodlice you could NOT find out by investigating?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who only says 'look it up' or 'ask the teacher' treats every question as answered by authority; a child who says 'I just know they like damp' skips investigation entirely. The child who proposes gathering evidence AND can separate an investigable question from an opinion question is reasoning scientifically — and this is hard to fake, because naming a non-investigable question requires the very distinction under test.

sources.claim: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires pupils to ask simple questions and recognise that they can be answered in different ways, experiencing the five named enquiry types.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study — Key Stage 1 Working Scientifically

sources.claim: NGSS SEP 1 (Asking Questions and Defining Problems) K–2 has students ask questions based on observations and identify questions that can be answered by an investigation.
sources.source: NGSS Appendix F — Science and Engineering Practices (Practice 1, K–2 progression)

pedagogy.summary: Children compose simple shapes into larger ones — two triangles into a rectangle or a bigger triangle, pattern blocks into a hexagon, basic shapes into a picture. The deep idea is PART-WHOLE: separate pieces combine into a single new shape with its own identity. Clements & Sarama's composition learning trajectory charts the growth from a Piece Assembler (each shape a separate part, trial and error) through the Picture Maker (combines pieces but does NOT anticipate the new shape, matches side lengths not angles) to the Shape Composer (anticipates the fit — 'I know what will fit' — using angles and intentional rotation/flip). Best taught with a graded sequence of pattern-block and tangram puzzles moving from fully-outlined to open, teaching roughly one trajectory level above the child's current one.
bestPractices: Use a graded sequence of pattern-block/tangram puzzles — from fully-outlined (placement shown) to open (child must compose accurately) — as the core activity, pitched about one level above where the child is.
Before each placement ask 'what will fit here?' to grow anticipation, rather than letting the child rely only on trial and error.
When a piece won't seat, talk about the SPACE and its corners/angles — not just the side lengths — to move children off matching side length alone.
Model and encourage rotating and flipping a piece to make it fit; offer a horizontal-base version first if a rotated piece can't be 'seen'.
Name the new whole after combining ('you put two triangles together and made one rectangle') to build the part-whole idea.
keyRepresentations: Pattern blocks with outlined puzzles (e.g. a hexagon to fill) grading to open puzzles
Two identical right triangles to combine into a rectangle or a larger triangle
Tangrams for composing pictures and larger shapes
Rotate/flip actions to seat a piece by matching its corner to the gap
commonMisconceptions: Places shapes separately or by pure trial and error, not anticipating that pieces will combine into a new shape.
Matches side LENGTHS but not ANGLES, so pieces leave gaps/overlaps or a corner won't fit the space (e.g. a square's right angle in a rhombus gap).
Cannot 'see' where a piece goes when it must be rotated off a horizontal base, and doesn't turn it to fit.
Sees the result as still 'two triangles' rather than one new rectangle — misses the part-whole identity of the composite.

learn.summary: Young children (ages ~5–6) learn to compose simple shapes into larger ones — two triangles into a rectangle or a bigger triangle, pattern blocks into a hexagon, basic shapes into a picture. The deep idea is PART–WHOLE: separate pieces combine into a single new shape with its own identity. The Clements & Sarama composition trajectory describes growth from a Piece Assembler (each shape a separate part, trial and error), through a Picture Maker (combines pieces but does NOT anticipate the new shape, matches side lengths not angles), to a Shape Composer (anticipates the fit — 'I know what will fit' — using angles and intentional rotation/flip). The core vehicle is a graded sequence of pattern-block and tangram puzzles moving from fully-outlined to open, pitched about one trajectory level above the child's current one, supported by physical blocks and cut-out triangles.

activities.title: Two triangles become one rectangle
feedback: When the pair fills the outline cleanly, name the whole: 'You put two triangles together and made one rectangle — it's one shape now.'
If the child still calls the result 'two triangles', trace the outside edge of the composite together and ask 'What ONE shape is this now?'
If a triangle won't seat, invite turning or flipping it: 'Try spinning this piece, or flipping it over, so its corner matches the corner of the space.'

An optional on-screen version can let the seam between the two triangles fade and the single rectangle highlight the moment they fill the outline, making the 'two becomes one' instant visible; the insight is in the child constructing and naming the whole, not in the animation.
activities.rationale: Constructing (not just recognising) the composite and naming the new whole targets the part–whole idea directly; asking a prediction first grows the anticipation that distinguishes the Shape Composer level from the trial-and-error Picture Maker.
sourceClaims: At the Picture Maker level children put shapes together using trial and error and 'do not anticipate the creation of the new geometric shape'; they choose shapes by 'general shape' or side length and 'match side lengths (not angles)', so they get frustrated with puzzles needing different angles (e.g. a square whose right angles won't fit). Moving to Shape Composer means combining shapes with anticipation ('I know what will fit') using angles and intentional rotation/flip.
learnerActions: Take two identical right triangles (physical cut-outs and/or an on-screen pair beside a rectangle outline).
Before moving them, answer the prompt 'What ONE shape do you think these will make?'
Arrange them to fill a rectangle outline, turning one triangle (if both start facing the same way, about 180°) so the corners and edges meet with no gaps or overlaps.
Rearrange the same two triangles to make a LARGER triangle by joining matching legs; unless the triangles are isosceles right triangles, you will need to flip one over, not just turn it.
Say aloud what single shape you have made each time: 'I put two triangles together and made one rectangle.'
activities.intendedInsight: Two separate pieces combine into a single new shape with its own identity (part–whole); the same two pieces can compose into different wholes depending on how they are turned, flipped and joined.

activities.title: Fill the hexagon — graded puzzles from outlined to open
feedback: If a block leaves a gap or overlap, point to the SPACE: 'Look at the corner of this gap — does your piece's corner match it?'
When a piece seats cleanly after a deliberate choice, reflect it back: 'You looked at the corner first and knew it would fit.'
If the child relies only on trial and error, keep offering the 'what will fit here?' prompt before each placement rather than marking placements wrong.
An optional on-screen version can snap correct placements and flag gaps/overlaps, and flash a mismatched corner when a wrong-angled piece (e.g. a square's right angle) is dropped into the gap.
activities.rationale: A graded outlined-to-open sequence pitched about one level above the child's current level, with angle-focused talk about the gap, moves children off matching side length alone; multiple solutions reinforce that the whole has several valid compositions.
sourceClaims: At the Picture Maker level children put shapes together using trial and error and 'do not anticipate the creation of the new geometric shape'; they choose shapes by 'general shape' or side length and 'match side lengths (not angles)', so they get frustrated with puzzles needing different angles (e.g. a square whose right angles won't fit). Moving to Shape Composer means combining shapes with anticipation ('I know what will fit') using angles and intentional rotation/flip.
learnerActions: Fill a hexagon with pattern blocks, starting from a fully-outlined puzzle (each block's place shown) and progressing toward an open outline (only the overall hexagon shown).
Before each placement, answer 'What will fit here, and why?'
Find at least two different ways to fill the same hexagon (e.g. two trapezoids; six triangles; a trapezoid plus three triangles).
Check the finished fill for any gaps or overlaps and fix them.
activities.intendedInsight: A whole shape can be composed in more than one way, and a correct fit depends on both side length and the angle of the space being filled.

activities.title: Turning a piece to make it fit
feedback: If the child leaves a gap a rotated piece would fill but only tries it upright, say 'Try turning the piece — it's still the same shape when it's turned.'
Use the horizontal-base version as a stepping stone: 'It fit easily that way — now let's turn it until its corner matches this tilted space.'
Avoid simply showing the answer; let the child do the turning so they feel that rotation preserves the shape.
activities.rationale: Some children cannot 'see' where a piece goes when it is turned off a horizontal base; a matched horizontal-base puzzle plus hands-on turning helps them link rotation to fit while preserving shape identity.
sourceClaims: Practice-based research (Bofferding & Aqazade, 2022, cited on the level page) notes a child sometimes will not 'see' where a square block/tangram can go when it is turned off a horizontal base; comparing a similar puzzle with a horizontal-base square helps.

A common early misconception is failing to recognise a shape in a different orientation; letting children handle and rotate cut-outs helps — supports the 'rotate a piece to make it fit' move in composition.
learnerActions: Meet a gap that a square or triangle would fill only when it is rotated off its horizontal base.
First try a matched puzzle where the same piece fits with a horizontal base, then return to the rotated version.
Physically turn the cut-out piece (or rotate the on-screen piece) and watch that turning does not change what the shape is.
Seat the piece once its corner matches the corner of the gap.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape keeps its identity when rotated; turning a piece is a tool for making its corner match the space it must fill.

activities.title: Make a picture from basic shapes
feedback: Ask 'Which shapes did you put together to make this part?' to surface the part–whole structure.
When a child combines pieces into a recognisable larger shape, name it: 'Those two triangles together made a square for the window.'
activities.rationale: Open composition with tangrams extends composing beyond fixed outlines and may give children further practice applying rotation, flipping and part–whole naming in a self-directed context.
learnerActions: Use tangrams or pattern blocks to compose a picture or design (e.g. a house, a rocket, an animal) from basic shapes.
Explain which smaller shapes make up one part of the picture.
Where two pieces together form a familiar larger shape, name that larger shape.
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday pictures and designs are built by combining basic shapes, and the same basic shapes can be put together in many different ways.

constraints: This is a 2-D planar composition task; 3-D composing is a separate, later topic and depth is not used here.

A fixed quiz can check a single known combination but, being fixed, cannot provide the free rotate-and-fit composing or the graded outlined-to-open progression where most of the learning happens; use it only as an occasional spot-check, not the main activity.

On-screen snapping, seam-fade, and angle-flash cues are optional supports that make the mechanism visible; they are not required, and children should still experience physical blocks and cut-outs they can turn and glue.

Trial-and-error placement without anticipation is a normal trajectory level (Picture Maker), not an error to drill or mark wrong; respond by offering puzzles about one level up and prompting 'what will fit here?'.
Teach roughly one trajectory level above the child's current level; pitching too far ahead can cause frustration.
Recognition-only responses (e.g. tapping a correct picture) do not elicit the independent construction this objective requires.
Physical cut-outs and blocks approximate ideal flat figures; treat them as representing the mathematical 2-D shapes composed, not as objects defined by being pickable or by their slight thickness.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original labelled a static tap-to-reveal image, a 3-D environment, and an in-role conversation as 'poor' for this task. These comparative/necessity judgements reflect catalog fit ratings, not established efficacy; they are reframed as scoped suitability notes (composition needs active placement; this objective is 2-D), not universal medium-superiority laws.

Source for the core trajectory (Clements, Wilson & Sarama 2004) is marked verified:false in the row (publisher paywall; provenance confirmed via the LT platform); treat the trajectory-origin citation with that caveat.

The original claim that an on-screen seam-fade 'is the part-whole insight' is retained only as an optional visualisation cue; the insight is in the child constructing and naming the whole, not in any animation.

Physical paper/card triangles and pattern blocks have slight thickness, but the activities use them to model ideal zero-thickness plane figures; the shapes being composed are the ideal 2-D figures the pieces represent.
Claims of educational benefit from open/self-directed composition in Activity 4 are stated as proposals ('may'); their effectiveness is not source-verified.

probeDeeper: Before you place it — which piece do you think will fit in this space, and why?
You put the two triangles together — what ONE shape is it now?
This square won't sit in that gap. What is different about the corner of the gap?
Can you fill the hexagon a different way, using different blocks?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Places the two right triangles together (rotating one) to form a rectangle, and re-arranges them to form a larger triangle, recognising each result as a new single shape. (2) Fills the hexagon exactly — e.g. two trapezoids, or six triangles, or a trapezoid plus three triangles — with no gaps or overlaps, rotating pieces as needed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Places pieces by trial and error and does not anticipate the new shape — treats the two triangles as still separate, not foreseeing they will make a rectangle.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill or mark this as an error — it is a normal trajectory level; instead provide graded puzzles one level up (outlined moving toward open) and ask 'what will fit here?' before each placement to grow anticipation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tries pieces at random, shows surprise when a combination works, and cannot say in advance what a combination will make (the Picture Maker level).

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses pieces by matching side LENGTH but not ANGLE, so pieces leave gaps/overlaps or a corner won't fit the space.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Talk about the SPACE to be filled — the corners/angles of the gap — and choose a piece whose corner matches, comparing the angle of the gap to the angle of the piece.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks a piece whose side is the right length, then it won't seat because the angle is wrong; leaves a gap or forces an overlap (e.g. a square's right angle in a rhombus gap).

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot 'see' where a piece goes when it must be rotated off a horizontal base, and doesn't turn it to fit.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't just show the answer: offer a matched puzzle with a horizontal-base piece first, then rotate it; let the child physically turn the piece to feel that turning doesn't change what it is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Leaves a gap that a rotated square/triangle would fill, but only tries the piece in its upright orientation.

responseLevels.gap: Places shapes separately or by pure trial and error, leaves gaps/overlaps, matches only side length so pieces don't seat, and does not see the combination as a new shape.
responseLevels.full: Composes with anticipation ('I know what will fit'), choosing pieces by angle as well as side length and rotating/flipping them intentionally, fills the hexagon with no gaps or overlaps, and recognises the composite as a new single shape (Shape Composer level; SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Combines shapes to fill an outlined puzzle and can make a rectangle from two triangles when guided, but relies on trial and error, struggles to seat a rotated piece, or does not anticipate the fit (Picture Maker level; SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set two tasks and watch how the child works: (1) Give two identical right triangles — 'Can you put these two triangles together to make a rectangle? Now can you make a bigger triangle?' (2) Give pattern blocks and a hexagon outline — 'Fill this hexagon exactly with these blocks.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching WHETHER the child rotates a piece to make it fit, and whether they ANTICIPATE the fit or place by pure trial and error, locates them on the composition trajectory (Piece Assembler / Picture Maker vs Shape Composer). A child matching only side length leaves gaps or cannot seat a rotated piece; one who composes with anticipation seats pieces cleanly and names the new whole shape. The hexagon fill exposes gaps and overlaps directly, so it is hard to fake.

Moving to Shape Composer means combining shapes with anticipation ('I know what will fit') using angles and intentional rotation/flip.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Investigating Forces

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** UK KS3 national curriculum ('forces measured in newtons, measurements of stretch or compression as force is changed; force-extension linear relation; Hooke's Law as a special case').

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NGSS MS-PS2-2 Science-and-Engineering Practice ('Plan an investigation... identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim');

- **Operational details:** This is a working-scientifically (procedural) topic at 12-13: pupils plan and carry out force investigations — measuring force with a newton meter, investigating Hooke's Law (force vs extension), and collecting motion data to test Newton's laws. The procedural core is variable control (independent = force applied, dependent = extension, control = the spring), accurate measurement, and turning data into a force–extension graph with a line of best fit.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal-operational/quantitative). At KS3 this stops short of the spring-constant equation (F = ke) and gradient calculation — those are GCSE; the focus is the proportional relationship (straight line through the origin), the limit of proportionality where it bends, careful measurement, and the graphing skill itself.
bestPractices: Control variables explicitly: IV = force applied, DV = extension, CV = the spring; change one variable at a time (NGSS SEP; KS3 working scientifically)
Use a newton meter correctly (it reads force directly in N), or convert masses to weight via W=m×g; measure EXTENSION (the increase in length), not the total length
Add force in equal steps, let the spring settle, record carefully, and repeat on unloading; read the ruler squarely using a set square to improve accuracy (Oak)
Plot Force (y) against Extension (x), draw a line of best fit, and identify the directly proportional region (straight line through the origin) and the limit of proportionality where it bends
Hold the KS3 ceiling: do not require F = ke or spring-constant gradient (that is GCSE) — focus on the proportional relationship, graphing and measurement craft
For the Newton's-laws strand, calculate acceleration from measured force and mass and compare with the trolley's actual motion (testing F=ma); include a risk assessment for hanging masses
keyRepresentations: Clamped spring + ruler + slotted masses (or newton meter) apparatus set-up
Force–extension graph with a line of best fit through the origin and a marked limit of proportionality
Variable-control planning frame (IV/DV/CV) and a results table with load-and-unload repeat readings
commonMisconceptions: The line of best fit must pass through every data point (Oak-named graphing misconception) — antidote: have pupils invent plots with small measurement errors so the line is seen to average scatter
Measuring the spring's total length instead of its extension
Recording force in grams/kilograms rather than newtons; treating mass as if it were a force
Changing more than one variable, or not repeating readings
Assuming proportionality continues forever — ignoring the limit of proportionality
Describing the pattern as 'the length doubles per newton' rather than 'the same extension is added per newton'

learn.summary: For pupils aged 12–13, this is a working-scientifically (procedural) goal: plan and carry out force investigations — measuring force with a newton meter, investigating the force–extension relationship (Hooke's Law), and collecting motion data to test Newton's Second Law. The craft to be learned is variable control (independent = force applied, dependent = extension, control = the same spring), accurate measurement of EXTENSION (increase in length, not total length), repeating readings, and turning real, scattered data into a force–extension graph with a line of best fit. At this level, stop short of the spring-constant equation (F = ke) and gradient calculation (those are later GCSE content); focus on the proportional relationship (a straight line through the origin), the limit of proportionality where it bends, and careful measurement and graphing. The strongest learning combines a hands-on practical with real apparatus and a graph-building task that confronts the best-fit misconception as scatter appears.

activities.title: Hooke's Law practical with real apparatus
feedback: If a learner plots or records the spring's total length, prompt: extension = current length − natural length; the natural length must be measured and subtracted first.
If force is recorded in grams or kilograms, remind that those are masses; weight (a force) in newtons is W = m × g, or read force directly from the newton meter.
If only one reading is taken per load, prompt a repeat and a mean at each step so anomalies can be judged — this is a scaffold, not a reteach of the whole method.
If more than one variable changes, point back to the IV/DV/CV plan: keep the same spring and change only the force.
activities.rationale: The learning target is measurement craft with physical apparatus — handling equipment, reading instruments squarely, measuring extension, and coping with genuine scatter — which is developed through hands-on practice rather than recognition tasks alone.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-2 SEP (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, 6-8): plan an investigation individually and collaboratively and in the design identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed to gather data, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim.

KS3 statutory content: 'forces measured in newtons, measurements of stretch or compression as force is changed; force-extension linear relation; Hooke's Law as a special case'; deformation forces associated with stretching/squashing springs.

KS3 Hooke's law practical: extension is directly proportional to force (straight line through origin), measure extension not length, IV=force/DV=extension/CV=spring, draw a line of best fit (it need not pass through every point), identify the limit of proportionality; KS3 does not require F=ke or the spring-constant gradient.
learnerActions: Clamp a spring, measure and record its natural (unstretched) length first.
State the variables before starting: independent = force applied (added in equal steps), dependent = extension, control = the same spring throughout.
Add weight one equal step at a time (hang slotted masses and convert to weight using W = m × g, or read force directly in newtons from a newton meter), letting the spring settle each time.
Measure the new length at each load and read the ruler squarely — line your eye level with the mark, or use a set square against the ruler to avoid parallax error.
Calculate extension at each step: extension = current length − natural length.
Repeat each reading (and read again on unloading) and take a mean, so scatter and anomalies become visible.
Record force in newtons and extension in a results table.
activities.intendedInsight: Force is measured in newtons; extension (not total length) is the quantity that responds to force; controlling variables and repeating readings is what makes the relationship trustworthy.

activities.title: Plotting force vs extension and drawing a line of best fit
feedback: If a learner connects the points to make a kinked line, explain that real readings scatter: draw ONE best-fit straight line with points either side so anomalies stand out.
If the line does not pass through the origin and the learner doesn't notice, check whether total length was plotted instead of extension.

If a learner extrapolates the straight line indefinitely or forces a straight line through the curved high-load points, prompt them to load past the limit so they can SEE the curve and mark where proportionality ends.
Encourage the phrasing 'the same extension is added per newton' rather than 'the length doubles per newton'.
activities.rationale: The best-fit-through-every-point error and the 'proportional forever' error are the key graphing and conceptual misconceptions here; confronting real scatter and the bending line directly addresses both, while keeping the limit of proportionality distinct from the elastic limit.
sourceClaims: KS3 Hooke's law practical: extension is directly proportional to force (straight line through origin), measure extension not length, IV=force/DV=extension/CV=spring, draw a line of best fit (it need not pass through every point), identify the limit of proportionality; KS3 does not require F=ke or the spring-constant gradient.
learnerActions: Plot Force (newtons) on the y-axis against Extension on the x-axis using your recorded data.
Draw a single straight line of best fit through the scattered points — do NOT join the dots point-to-point; aim for a line with roughly equal numbers of points on each side.

Describe the pattern in words: up to the limit of proportionality, equal steps of force add the SAME extension each time (not 'the length doubles'), and with zero extension at zero force this means extension is directly proportional to force — a straight line through the origin.
Continue adding load in a second investigation (or extend the dataset) until the once-straight line starts to bend, and mark that point where proportionality ends — the limit of proportionality.

Separately, note that if the spring is loaded past its elastic limit (which for many springs is at or only a little beyond the limit of proportionality) it may be permanently stretched and no longer return to its natural length; this is a distinct idea from the limit of proportionality.
Explain why the line is drawn to average scatter rather than connecting every point.
activities.intendedInsight: A best-fit line averages real measurement scatter rather than connecting individual points; the force–extension relationship is proportional only up to a limit of proportionality, after which it bends (and, at still greater loads beyond the elastic limit, the spring may deform permanently).

activities.title: Testing Newton's Second Law with a trolley
feedback: If a learner expects perfect agreement, first check that m includes every mass being accelerated (trolley plus any hanging masses); then remind them that friction opposes the applied force, so the resultant (net) force is smaller than F and the observed acceleration is a little below the F/m prediction; measurement uncertainty adds further to the difference.

If a learner describes the force as setting the trolley's speed or current direction, remind them that the resultant force determines acceleration (change in motion), so the stated starting condition (e.g. from rest) matters when predicting how the motion changes.
activities.rationale: This strand connects measured force and mass to motion, extending the investigative method beyond springs and reinforcing variable control and quantitative reasoning.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-2 SEP (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, 6-8): plan an investigation individually and collaboratively and in the design identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed to gather data, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim.
learnerActions: Apply a measured force to a trolley of known mass (include a risk assessment for any hanging masses).
State the trolley's starting condition (e.g. starting from rest) before describing how its motion changes.

Calculate the predicted acceleration using a = F / m, where F is the applied (driving) force and m is the total mass being accelerated (the trolley plus any hanging masses that move with it), assuming friction is small.
Measure the trolley's actual acceleration (e.g. with light gates or a motion sensor/data logger) and compare it with the calculated acceleration.
Discuss sources of difference (e.g. friction opposing the applied force, measurement error) between prediction and observation.
activities.intendedInsight: A measured applied force on a known total moving mass (trolley plus any hanging masses) predicts an acceleration via a = F/m when friction is small; more precisely, it is the resultant force (applied force minus friction) that determines acceleration — a change in motion, not an instant speed or direction. Because real friction makes the resultant smaller than the applied force, the observed acceleration is usually a little below F/m, and comparing prediction with real motion tests Newton's Second Law.

activities.title: Plan and reason about the method (companion check)
feedback: If a learner chooses the dot-to-dot line, re-explain that the best-fit line averages scatter.
If a learner mislabels the variables, point back to: force is changed (IV), extension responds (DV), the spring is kept the same (CV).
activities.rationale: These recognition and sequencing tasks assess the procedural reasoning behind the investigation; they can check planning and variable identification but do not themselves elicit the physical measurement, so they complement rather than replace running the investigation.
sourceClaims: MS-PS2-2 SEP (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, 6-8): plan an investigation individually and collaboratively and in the design identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed to gather data, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim.

KS3 Hooke's law practical: extension is directly proportional to force (straight line through origin), measure extension not length, IV=force/DV=extension/CV=spring, draw a line of best fit (it need not pass through every point), identify the limit of proportionality; KS3 does not require F=ke or the spring-constant gradient.
learnerActions: Put the method steps in the correct order: plan the variables, measure natural length, add load in equal steps, measure new length, calculate extension, repeat readings, plot, draw best-fit line, identify the limit of proportionality.
Identify which quantity is the independent variable, dependent variable, and control variable for the spring investigation.
Given a graph with scattered points, select or sketch the correct line of best fit (not the dot-to-dot line).
Given a force–extension graph that curves, mark the limit of proportionality.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure procedural reasoning — correct sequencing, variable identification, best-fit choice, and recognising the limit of proportionality — underpins a trustworthy investigation.

constraints: Keep to the KS3 ceiling: do not require the spring-constant equation (F = ke) or gradient calculation; focus on the proportional relationship, the limit of proportionality, graphing, and measurement craft.

The core learning is measurement craft with physical apparatus (reading a newton meter, measuring extension squarely, repeating readings, coping with genuine scatter). A screen-based graph-building task can rehearse the variable-control and best-fit logic and can make the scatter/limit visible as load is added, but it does not substitute for handling real apparatus — pair the two.

A live graph-building task (points dropping onto a force–extension plot as load is added, and a best-fit tool that deliberately does not snap through every point) is an optional way to make the best-fit and limit-of-proportionality ideas concrete. Marking where the line bends shows the limit of proportionality; a spring left permanently deformed is a separate, heavier-load effect (past the elastic limit). This is a useful illustration, not a mandatory mechanism.

Recognition and sequencing tasks (ordering steps, identifying IV/DV/CV, selecting the best-fit line, marking the limit) assess procedural reasoning but do not let learners run the investigation or collect real data; use them alongside, not instead of, practical work.
A labelled static apparatus diagram with a 'measure extension not length' and units callout is a helpful set-up and reference, but cannot build the graph or rehearse the best-fit decision.
Include a risk assessment for hanging masses in the Newton's Second Law trolley strand.

Always state the starting condition (e.g. from rest) when describing how a trolley's motion changes, since the resultant force determines acceleration (change in motion), not the current speed or direction of travel.

In the trolley strand, be explicit that F in a = F/m is the applied (driving) force used for the prediction, while the resultant (applied force minus friction) is what actually accelerates the trolley; do not label the predicting force as the resultant while also attributing the discrepancy to friction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (Oak National Academy KS3 Hooke's law lesson) is marked verified:false in the original row; treat its specific procedural claims as unconfirmed pending a source check.

The original recommendation conflates the limit of proportionality (where the line stops being straight) with the spring 'no longer springing back' (the elastic limit, a distinct heavier-load point). The rewrite separates these in the learner-facing activity and constraints; confirm the preferred KS3 terminology against the curriculum.

Audit note on the Newton's Second Law strand: the source says to 'compare a=F/m with the trolley's actual motion.' This is sound provided the trolley's initial state is specified and F is treated as the applied force when friction is small. The rewrite clarifies that the resultant force (applied minus friction) determines acceleration, which reconciles the friction-based discrepancy; whether the source intends F as applied or net force is not stated.
Self-audit: W = m × g (mass to weight) and extension = current length − natural length are stated correctly; no arithmetic errors found in the source values used.

probeDeeper: Why did you draw the line like that instead of joining each point?
What exactly did you plot on the y-axis — the length or the extension? Why does it matter?
How many times did you measure at each load, and what did you do with the repeats?
What would happen to your graph if you kept adding heavier and heavier masses?
assess.correctAnswer: Measures the spring's natural length, adds masses one at a time, records the force (weight of the masses, or from the newton meter) and the EXTENSION (new length minus natural length) at each step, repeating readings; plots force (or mass) against extension; draws a BEST-FIT straight line through the scattered points (not dot-to-dot), showing extension proportional to force; identifies the limit of proportionality where the line starts to curve. Controls variables (same spring, measures extension not total length).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Join the dots — draw the line through every single point.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain that real readings scatter; draw ONE best-fit straight line with points either side of it, so anomalies stand out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Connects the points dot-to-dot, producing a kinked line.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Plot the total LENGTH of the spring, not the extension.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extension = current length minus natural length; measure the unstretched length first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: y-values are full lengths; the line doesn't pass through the origin and the child doesn't notice.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The spring stretches in proportion no matter how much I add.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep loading past the limit of proportionality to SEE the curve; mark where proportionality ends.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Extrapolates the straight line indefinitely, or forces a straight line through curved high-load points.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'One reading per mass is enough — I won't repeat any.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt a repeat and a mean at each load — scaffold, don't reteach the method.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Takes single readings, so scatter and anomalies can't be judged.

responseLevels.gap: Records some readings but plots total length or dot-to-dots the points, takes single readings, or doesn't keep the spring the same — the relationship can't be read reliably.
responseLevels.full: Controls variables, measures extension with repeats, plots and draws a best-fit line showing extension proportional to force, and identifies the limit of proportionality where the line curves — using the newton meter correctly and treating scatter appropriately.
responseLevels.partial: Sets up the investigation, plots force vs extension and sees a rising line, but joins the dots, can't identify the limit of proportionality, or omits repeats — collecting data without the craft that makes the relationship (and its limit) trustworthy.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a spring clamped at the top, a set of identical slotted masses, a ruler, and a newton meter. Investigate how the stretching force affects the spring's extension (Hooke's Law). Plan and carry out the investigation, record your results, plot a graph, and tell me what your graph shows about the relationship — including where, if anywhere, it stops being proportional.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch, don't ask. The load-bearing tells: (1) does the child plot EXTENSION (change in length) or mistakenly plot total length; (2) do they draw a best-fit line through real scatter, or connect every point dot-to-dot; (3) do they repeat readings and keep the spring the same; (4) do they recognise the limit of proportionality rather than forcing a straight line through curved data. Dot-to-dotting, plotting total length, or single readings show the procedure isn't secure even if numbers get recorded.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7; rainforests are home to millions of insects — leaf-cutter ants that farm fungus, giant beetles, jewel-coloured butterflies, enormous spiders, and stick insects — and insects are the most numerous animals in the rainforest.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 Y1 'Animals, including humans' (identify/name/group animals, including invertebrates) and Y2 habitats.
• Standards—US: NGSS 1-LS1-1 (external parts help survival); 2-LS4-1 (diversity of life); 1-LS1-2 (behaviours).
• Operational details: two ideas — (1) the sheer NUMBER and variety of rainforest minibeasts (insects are the most numerous animals here), and (2) a few show-stopper examples with hooks: leaf-cutter ants that carry leaf pieces to grow fungus gardens (they FARM), jewel butterflies, giant beetles, big spiders (note spiders are not insects but are minibeasts), and camouflaged stick insects. Keep the leaf-cutter 'ant farmers' as the wonder-fact. Reuse the insect/not-an-insect boundary lightly (6 legs = insect; spiders have 8).
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) say rainforests are full of insects and name one (ant/butterfly/beetle); Tier B (6) describe the leaf-cutter ants carrying leaves; Tier C (7) explain that insects are the most numerous animals in the rainforest and give an example of a special one.
bestPractices: Lead with the wonder-fact that leaf-cutter ants FARM fungus — memorable and true
Convey abundance ('most numerous animals here') with a swarming, teeming image
Give each minibeast a hook (jewel butterfly = colour, stick insect = hides, giant spider = big)
Note gently that spiders are minibeasts but not insects (8 legs vs 6), reusing the insect boundary
Use real close-up images so tiny animals become vivid and awe-inspiring
keyRepresentations: Leaf-cutter ant trail carrying leaf pieces to a fungus garden
Minibeast gallery: butterfly, beetle, spider, stick insect, ants
Camouflaged stick insect hidden on a twig (spot-it interaction)
'Most numerous' swarm visual showing insects vastly outnumbering other animals
commonMisconceptions: Big animals are the most numerous in the rainforest — insects far outnumber everything else
Leaf-cutter ants eat the leaves they carry — they use them to grow fungus, which they eat
Spiders are insects — they are minibeasts with 8 legs, not 6-legged insects
Stick insects are just twigs — they are living insects camouflaged as twigs
Rainforest insects are all dangerous — most are harmless and vital to the forest

learn.summary: For 5–7 year olds: rainforests teem with minibeasts, and insects are by far the most numerous animals there. Learners name several rainforest minibeasts, learn a memorable wonder-fact (leaf-cutter ants FARM fungus rather than eat the leaves they carry), notice camouflage (stick insects), and grasp that tiny-but-countless insects vastly outnumber big famous animals like jaguars and monkeys. A gentle insect/not-insect boundary (6 legs = insect; spiders have 8) is reused lightly. The core gallery builds recognition and abundance; a trail/spot game can make a behaviour feel concrete; recall checks follow.

activities.title: Minibeast gallery and the ant-farm wonder-fact
feedback: If a learner says the ants eat the leaves: 'Look again — the leaves go down into the garden where fungus grows. The ants eat the fungus, so they're farmers.'
If a learner calls the spider an insect: 'Count the legs — 8 means minibeast but not insect; insects have 6.'
If a learner says the stick insect is just a twig: 'It moved! It's a living insect hiding by looking like a twig.'
Reinforce each correct naming with the hook, e.g. 'Yes — the morpho butterfly, famous for its bright colour.'
activities.rationale: Concrete close-up examples with a single vivid hook each suit a 5–7 recognition goal, and a memorable true wonder-fact (ants farming) anchors one interesting behaviour. Tapping to reveal names/behaviours is one way to make the gallery interactive; a printed picture gallery or classroom minibeast cards can serve the same recognition purpose.
sourceClaims: Rainforests contain vast insect diversity and abundance; leaf-cutter ants cultivate fungus gardens from cut leaves, and insects are the most numerous animals in the forest
KS1 pupils identify, name and group animals including invertebrates and study habitats
Students observe how external parts and behaviours help animals survive and the diversity of life in habitats
learnerActions: Explore a close-up scene of the forest floor and tree trunks alive with tiny life, and point to or tap each minibeast to learn its name and a hook: jewel/morpho butterfly (colour), giant beetle (size), big spider (size), stick insect (hides), leaf-cutter ants (farmers).

Follow a line of leaf-cutter ants carrying green leaf pieces, then open a drill-down to their underground fungus garden and say in your own words: 'They don't eat the leaves — they grow food (fungus) on them, like farmers.'
Find the twig that is secretly a stick insect (it wiggles when tapped) and explain it is a living insect camouflaged as a twig, not just a stick.
Say gently why the big spider is a minibeast but NOT an insect: count 8 legs (insects have 6).
activities.intendedInsight: Rainforests hold a huge variety of minibeasts, and some do surprising things — leaf-cutter ants grow their own food on cut leaves rather than eating them.

activities.title: Which is there most of? Tiny but countless
feedback: If a learner says there are more big animals: 'Think of one ant trail — that's already more ants than all the jaguars you'd ever see. Tiny insects hugely outnumber big animals.'
If a learner says insects aren't animals: 'Insects ARE animals — a huge animal group; they just have no backbone.'
Affirm the reasoning tier: 'Yes — they're small but there are countless numbers of them.'
If a learner explores the extension: 'Because they're so small, lots of them can live in one tree, so there are far more of them than big animals that each need lots of space.'
activities.rationale: The target misconception is that big, famous animals dominate; contrasting a teeming ant trail with a rarely seen jaguar surfaces 'small but countless'. A reveal/flap is one interaction; the same comparison works with two pictures side by side or a spoken count.
sourceClaims: Rainforests contain vast insect diversity and abundance; leaf-cutter ants cultivate fungus gardens from cut leaves, and insects are the most numerous animals in the forest
learnerActions: Answer the question 'Which animals are there MOST of here — big animals like jaguars and monkeys, or tiny insects like ants and beetles?' and lift a flap / reveal to see a swarm answer: insects, by far.
Say why: you see insects everywhere in huge numbers (whole armies of ants), even though each one is tiny, while you rarely see a single jaguar.
Compare an ant trail (many, many ants) with how seldom a jaguar appears, to feel the difference in numbers.
Optional extension: talk about why tiny insects can live in so many more places than one big jaguar (they are small, so many of them fit and find food almost everywhere).
activities.intendedInsight: Insects and other minibeasts are by far the most numerous animals in the rainforest — small but countless — far outnumbering the big famous animals.

activities.title: Guide the trail / spot the hidden insect (behaviour mini-game)
feedback: If the learner drops the leaf before the garden: 'The ants take the leaf piece all the way home — it's needed to grow the fungus.'
If the learner can't find the stick insect: 'Look for a twig that's a bit too smooth or in the wrong place — its camouflage makes it hard to spot.'
activities.rationale: A guide-the-trail or spot-the-camouflage task can make a behaviour feel concrete and complements the gallery's recognition focus. This is an alternative emphasis (behaviour/survival) rather than a replacement for building variety and abundance; the same ideas can also be conveyed through pictures or spoken description.
sourceClaims: Students observe how external parts and behaviours help animals survive and the diversity of life in habitats
learnerActions: Guide the leaf-cutter ant trail to carry leaf pieces home to the fungus garden, narrating what the ants are doing.
Spot the camouflaged stick insect hidden among twigs, then say how its shape and colour help it hide.
activities.intendedInsight: Acting out a behaviour or survival trick can help it feel more concrete — carrying leaves to a farm, or finding an animal that hides by looking like its surroundings.

activities.title: Name it and sort it (recall check)
feedback: For a correct name + behaviour: confirm and restate, e.g. 'Leaf-cutter ants — they grow fungus on the leaves.'
For a leg-count sorting slip: 'Count again — 6 legs is an insect, 8 is a minibeast like a spider.'
A sort checks grouping, so follow up by asking the learner to say in their own words why insects are the most numerous — the sort alone does not elicit that explanation.
activities.rationale: A naming/sorting check confirms recognition after the gallery and game build it. Recognition and short-answer checks confirm recall but do not by themselves require learners to explain abundance; pair with the oral 'why' prompt to reach the full reasoning tier.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils identify, name and group animals including invertebrates and study habitats
learnerActions: Name a rainforest insect or minibeast and one interesting thing it does.
Sort a few minibeasts into 'insect (6 legs)' and 'not an insect (e.g. spider, 8 legs)'.
Answer: leaf-cutter ants carry bits of leaf back home — what do they use them for?
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall of at least three rainforest minibeasts, the ant-farming behaviour, and the 6-vs-8-leg boundary.

constraints: Keep the leaf-cutter 'ant farmers' fact accurate: ants carry leaves to grow fungus and eat the fungus — they do NOT eat the leaves themselves.
Use the insect/not-insect boundary lightly: 6 legs = insect; spiders have 8 and are minibeasts, not insects. Don't make it the main lesson.
A recognition/naming check confirms recall but does not elicit the abundance explanation; the full reasoning tier ('small but countless') needs the learner to say why in their own words.
The behaviour mini-game emphasises survival/behaviour; it is a complement to, not a substitute for, building variety and abundance recognition.
Most rainforest insects are harmless and important to the forest; avoid implying they are all dangerous.
Spot-the-camouflage and tap-to-reveal are example interactions, not required mechanisms; the same learning works with printed pictures, cards, or spoken comparison.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all source claims remain marked unverified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims about leaf-cutter ant farming, insect abundance, and standards alignment are attributed but listed as verified:false in the source row; treat specific figures ('millions', 'most numerous') as general, source-attributed statements rather than independently checked facts.

'Insects are the most numerous animals' is the stated objective; note that spiders and some other minibeasts are technically not insects, so the broader true claim is that insects/minibeasts far outnumber large animals — kept consistent in the abundance activity.

The third source probe question (why tiny insects can live in more places than a big jaguar) was added as an optional extension in the abundance activity to preserve it; it is a child-friendly, qualified line, not an independently verified ecological claim.

Efficacy of specific interactions (tap-to-reveal, mini-game, sort) over alternative media is not established by the sources; wording was kept qualified to describe affordances rather than assert medium superiority.

assess.correctAnswer: There are far, far more insects — insects and other minibeasts are the most numerous animals in the rainforest, way more than the big animals. You can tell because they're everywhere in huge numbers (like whole armies of leaf-cutter ants), even though each one is tiny.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a rainforest, are there more big animals like jaguars and monkeys, or more tiny insects like ants and beetles? Which is there more of, and how do you know?
