pedagogy.summary: Partitioning shapes into 2, 3 or 4 equal parts is where children learn that a fraction demands EQUAL parts — equal in AMOUNT (area), not necessarily equal in shape or appearance. The two load-bearing ideas: any-number-of-pieces is not enough (unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters), and two shares that look completely different can still be equal if they cover the same amount. Teach by cutting the same shape more than one way, and by comparing equal-area-but-different-shape pieces, so children judge shares by amount, not by look.
bestPractices: Partition the SAME shape several different ways into the same fraction (a rectangle into quarters by vertical cuts, a 2×2 grid, two diagonals) so no single picture becomes 'the' way
Deliberately show equal-AREA but different-SHAPE pieces and have children verify equality by rearranging/overlaying or counting unit squares
Contrast a correct partition with an unequal one that has the right NUMBER of pieces, forcing the equal-parts criterion open
Move beyond halving to thirds (a circle into three) where children cannot rely on repeated halving
Check equality physically — cut and re-lay pieces, or tile them onto a grid — rather than trusting appearance
keyRepresentations: Rectangle partitioned several ways into the same fraction (multiple valid cuts)
Circle partitioned into thirds (120° shares)
Equal-area different-shape pieces that rearrange onto one another
Faint unit-square grid under a shape for checking equal area
commonMisconceptions: Equal shares must look the same / be congruent — rejects equal-area different-shape pieces as 'not fair'
Any N pieces count as Nths regardless of size (ignores the equal-parts requirement)
A shape can only be partitioned into a fraction one 'proper' way
Judges share size by one dimension (length) rather than area
Thinks halving repeatedly is the only way to make parts, so thirds feel impossible

learn.summary: Children learn that a fraction requires EQUAL parts — equal in AMOUNT (area), not necessarily equal in shape or appearance. Two load-bearing ideas: having the right NUMBER of pieces is not enough (unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters), and two shares that look completely different can still be equal if they cover the same amount. Teach by partitioning the same shape several ways and by comparing equal-area-but-different-shape pieces, so children judge shares by amount, not by look. Thirds (and a circle into three) force children off repeated halving.

activities.title: Cut it, re-lay it: equal amount beats equal look
feedback: If the learner says 'the long one is more/less' by looking: have them cut and re-lay the strip onto the fat piece, so they see equal amount despite different shape.
If the learner calls any four pieces 'quarters' regardless of size: set a correct equal partition beside an unequal four-piece one and recompose/rearrange to show only equal amounts count.
If the learner insists only one 'proper' way makes quarters: show several equal-area-checked quarterings side by side and ask them to invent a new valid one.
When a second and third distinct partition each check out as equal, name this explicitly: many partitions give the same fraction.

For thirds, prompt: how do you know all three are equal? Because the three 120-degree sectors are congruent, you can overlay one onto another; otherwise compare the area each covers rather than judging by appearance.

A faint on-screen grid that tints pieces green only when every piece covers the same area is one optional way to make the equal-area check concrete; counting whole squares works only where piece edges follow the grid, and cutting and rearranging is needed to prove equality of differently shaped pieces whose edges cross grid squares.
activities.rationale: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock; instruction should establish that parts be equal in amount rather than accept any partition. Partitioning shapes into equal parts in different ways is a stated Year 2 expectation. Physically rearranging or tiling equal-area different-shape pieces, and producing several valid partitions, is intended to target the 'must look the same', 'any N pieces', and 'one right way' misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock: children must treat the parts as equal (equal amount), and instruction should establish this rather than accept any partition; the guide addresses accepting approximate drawings only if treated as equal.
Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name and write fractions of shapes and quantities and recognise equivalence, including partitioning shapes into equal parts in different ways.
learnerActions: Partition a square into four parts where the pieces look different — e.g. one long thin strip plus some oddly-shaped bits — but each covers the same amount.
Before checking, predict: is the long thin piece the same amount of the square as a fat corner piece? Say why.

Check equality physically: cut the long strip and lay it over the fat piece to see it rearranges exactly onto it. For pieces whose edges follow a faint underlying grid you can also count the unit squares each covers; for diagonal or irregular pieces use cutting and rearrangement rather than counting, since squares get split.
Decide whether all four pieces are quarters and give the reason (each is the same AMOUNT, one of four equal parts).

Now quarter the SAME shape in a completely different way (e.g. three equally spaced vertical cuts giving four equal strips, then a 2x2 grid, then two diagonals) and argue each piece is still a quarter.

Partition a circle into three equal parts (120-degree slices) and explain how you could check the three parts really are equal (overlay one onto another — they are congruent — or compare the area each covers).
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter means each part is the same amount (area) of the whole, one of four equal parts — the pieces may look different as long as each covers the same amount; and the same shape can be partitioned into the same fraction in many valid ways.

activities.title: Sort the partitions: quarters or not?
feedback: If an equal-area different-shape case is sorted into 'does not': ask how the amounts compare, and suggest rearranging/recomposing the pieces (cut and re-lay), or counting grid-aligned squares, to check before deciding — simply laying differently shaped pieces on top of each other will not make them coincide.
If an unequal four-piece case is sorted into 'shows quarters': point to the four-piece-but-unequal trap — four pieces is not enough, they must each be the same amount.
Praise reasons that mention 'same amount / same area / same number of squares' over reasons that mention how pieces look.
activities.rationale: Categorising partitions as equal vs unequal tests the equal-parts and different-shape criteria cleanly. This is a recognition/classification task: it may check and sharpen the criterion, but it does not by itself let the child construct a partition or physically prove equality, so pair it with hands-on cutting and rearranging rather than using it alone.
sourceClaims: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock: children must treat the parts as equal (equal amount), and instruction should establish this rather than accept any partition; the guide addresses accepting approximate drawings only if treated as equal.
learnerActions: Sort a set of partitioned shapes into 'shows quarters' and 'does not show quarters'.
Include cases that are equal-area but different-shape (these ARE quarters) and cases with four pieces of unequal size (these are NOT quarters).
For each 'does not' card, say what is wrong (pieces are not the same amount).
For each tricky 'is' card where pieces look different, say how you could prove they are equal (cut and rearrange/recompose, or count squares where edges follow the grid).
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a partition shows quarters depends on equal amount, not on the number of pieces or on whether the pieces look alike.

activities.title: Which is the bigger share: a third or a quarter?
feedback: If the learner thinks 'four parts means bigger because there are more': have them overlay a third onto a quarter of an identical shape, both cut the same way (e.g. strips in the same direction), to see the third covers the quarter and sticks out, so it is larger.
Tie the result back to the equal-amount idea: thirds are only thirds if all three cover the same amount, and of the same whole each must therefore be larger than one of four equal parts.

Keep the comparison to identical wholes — this is about which portion of the same shape is larger. (As abstract numbers, fractions remain comparable without a shared whole, but that is not this activity's focus.)
activities.rationale: Comparing a third with a quarter of the same whole is intended to address judging share size by appearance or by piece-count, and reinforces that thirds cannot be reached by repeated halving. Partitioning into equal parts and naming thirds/fourths is within the stated age expectations; the size-ordering of unit fractions is a research-informed extension beyond what the cited sources state directly.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name and write fractions of shapes and quantities and recognise equivalence, including partitioning shapes into equal parts in different ways.
learnerActions: Take two identical shapes; partition one into three equal parts and the other into four equal parts.
Predict which single piece is bigger: one of three equal parts, or one of four equal parts, of the same shape.

Check by overlaying one piece on the other when both wholes are cut the same way (e.g. both into strips the same direction, or both into slices from the centre of a circle) so the larger covers the smaller and sticks out; otherwise compare the area each covers.
State the reasoning: cutting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: For the same whole, one of three equal parts is bigger than one of four equal parts — cutting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.

constraints: Equal shares must be equal in AMOUNT (area); they need not be congruent or look the same.
Having the right NUMBER of pieces is not sufficient — unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters.
Move beyond halving to thirds so children cannot rely on repeated halving; a circle into three (120-degree shares) is a good non-halving case.

Compare share sizes (e.g. a third vs a quarter) only for identical wholes; this scopes the comparison to represented portions. As numbers, fractions remain comparable without a shared whole, but that is not this activity's focus.

Counting unit squares is a valid equal-area check only where piece edges follow the grid; for diagonal or irregular pieces use cutting and rearrangement, since grid squares get split. Overlay alone proves equality only for congruent pieces; for equal-area pieces of different shape, cut and recompose (or count unit squares if their edges follow the grid).

Sorting/categorisation tasks are recognition: they may check and sharpen the equal-parts criterion but do not let a child physically prove equality by rearranging, so use them alongside hands-on cutting and overlaying, not instead of it.
Physical paper/card cutouts have slight thickness and model the ideal flat figure being partitioned; the lesson is about the 2D area partition they represent, for which thickness is irrelevant.

An on-screen faint unit grid that tints pieces green when areas match is one optional way to make the equal-area check concrete, not a required mechanism — cutting and rearranging pieces works too, and is needed for differently shaped pieces whose edges do not follow the grid.
Static galleries of correct/incorrect partitions can serve as a reference but do not let the child test equality by rearranging pieces; pair them with a hands-on check.
A third spatial dimension is not needed for partitioning 2D shapes; keep the work planar unless there is a specific reason otherwise.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row framed a conversation-only approach as 'poor' and claimed talk 'can't replace' cutting/rearranging, and that a static image or 3D 'cannot' teach the equal-area judgement. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established necessity claims; they are softened here to scoped, observable affordances/limits. Discussion and static references can support this learning, even if hands-on manipulation is particularly well suited to proving equal area.
The 'green only when areas are equal' grid and draggable re-tiling pieces are preserved as an optional illustrative example, not a mandatory mechanism, and whether it was ever tested is unknown.

Geometry self-audit: three equal vertical cuts give four equal strips; a 2x2 grid gives four equal quarters; the two diagonals of a rectangle give four triangles each of area (width x height)/4, i.e. equal-area quarters (congruent only when the shape is a square); three 120-degree slices give equal thirds of a circle. No numerical errors found in the source to correct.

Activity 3's unit-fraction size ordering (a third > a quarter of the same whole) is mathematically correct but not directly stated by either cited source; the attached DfE claim supports only the partitioning-and-naming context in the rationale, so the ordering is flagged as an unvalidated extension.
Terminology note: the base shape is kept as a single 'square/shape' through Activity 1 to avoid the inherited square/rectangle switch; any rectangle works equally for the quartering demonstrations.

assess.poeTask: Show a square quartered into four equal-AREA but different-shaped pieces — one long thin strip, one fat corner piece. Ask the child to predict whether the long thin piece and the fat piece are the SAME amount of the square, and to say why before checking. A child judging by shape predicts 'the long one is more' (or 'less'). Then rearrange — cut the strip and lay it over the fat piece, or count the unit squares under each — to reveal they match. The pre-observation reason (shape-based) is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Cut this rectangle into four equal parts a completely different way from your first. How do you know the new pieces are still quarters?
Here is a circle. Cut it into three equal parts. How could you check the three parts really are equal?
If one piece is tall-and-thin and another is short-and-wide but they cover the same amount, are they equal shares? Why?
Which is a bigger share: one of three equal parts, or one of four equal parts, of the same shape? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Amir is wrong — they ARE quarters, because a quarter means each part is the same AMOUNT (area) of the whole, one of four equal parts; the pieces can look different as long as each covers the same amount. For the rectangle, shows two valid quarterings (e.g. three equal vertical cuts, and a 2×2 grid, or two diagonals) and can argue each piece is a quarter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal shares must look the same — rejects equal-area but different-shape pieces as not being quarters
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rearrange/overlay the different-shaped pieces so they tile onto one another; count unit squares under each; establish equal AMOUNT as the test
errorPatterns.distractor: They're not quarters — the pieces are different shapes, so they can't be equal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'not quarters, the pieces are different shapes', judging by appearance rather than amount

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal-parts ignored — any four pieces are called quarters regardless of their sizes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast an equal partition with an unequal one that also has four pieces; check by recomposing; only equal amounts count
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, quarters — there are four pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls an unequally-cut four-piece square 'quarters' because there are four pieces

errorPatterns.pattern: One-right-way — believes a shape can only be partitioned into a fraction a single 'proper' way
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate several valid quarterings side by side, each grid-checked for equal area; have the child invent a new one
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces only one quartering and insists other valid cuts 'aren't real quarters'

responseLevels.gap: Judges equal shares by shape (rejects equal-area different-shape pieces) or calls any four pieces quarters regardless of size.
responseLevels.full: Judges shares by equal AMOUNT not shape, produces two or more different valid partitions (including a circle into thirds), justifies equality by area/recomposition, and rejects an unequal cut with a reason.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees equal parts must be the same size and can quarter a rectangle one standard way, but cannot yet accept different-shaped equal-area pieces as equal, produce a second distinct partition, or reliably make thirds.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a paper square cut into four parts. The parts look different from each other — one is a long strip, the others are smaller shapes — but they all cover the same amount of the square. Amir says these can't be quarters, because the pieces are different shapes. Is Amir right? Say why or why not. Then show me two DIFFERENT ways to cut this rectangle into four equal parts.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who believes equal parts must be congruent judges by shape and says 'not quarters — different shapes'; correct reasoning attends to equal AREA, not look. Producing a SECOND distinct partition further separates 'one right way' thinking from a genuine grasp that many partitions give the same fraction.

pedagogy.summary: At 5-6, sorting into categories is the first act of the whole statistical process (GAISE Level A): choose an attribute, classify every object by it into non-overlapping groups, count each group, and order the groups by count to see which has most/fewest. The teaching job is to make the sorting RULE explicit and consistent (one attribute at a time), to physically arrange the sorted groups so counts can be compared, and to connect the activity to a real question ('which colour do we have most of?'). Best done with real objects the child handles — lining up or bins — so the counts are concrete before any chart appears.
bestPractices: Name the single sorting attribute out loud before sorting ('we are sorting by COLOUR') and keep it fixed, so groups don't drift into mixed criteria
Arrange sorted groups as equal-spaced lines or stacks (a proto-bar-graph) so 'most/fewest' can be read by comparing counts, not the space objects happen to fill
Sort the SAME set two different ways (by colour, then by size) so the child sees the data is fixed but the grouping is a choice
Anchor to a real question and read the result back ('so we have most red — does that answer our question?') to build early data sense
keyRepresentations: Sorting hoops / bins or trays, one per category
Objects lined up one-to-one in rows (an emerging bar graph)
A simple two- or three-row count record (category name + count)
Real class data the child helped generate (favourite colour, shape cards)
commonMisconceptions: Shifts the sorting criterion partway (starts by colour, drifts to size), producing mixed groups
Judges 'most' by the space a group takes up rather than its count (a spread-out group of big objects looks like 'more')
Miscounts a group by losing track when objects are scattered (insecure cardinality)
Thinks each object can go in more than one pile, or leaves objects unsorted

learn.summary: For 5-6 year olds, sorting into categories is an early step of the statistical process, after posing a question: choose one attribute, classify every object into non-overlapping groups, count each group, and order groups by count to find most/fewest. Make the sorting RULE explicit and fixed (one attribute at a time), physically arrange groups so counts can be compared fairly, and anchor to a real question ('which colour do we have most of?'). Work with real objects the child handles so counts are concrete before any chart appears.

activities.title: Drag-to-sort (or hands-on sort) with self-counting groups
feedback: If groups end up containing more than one colour, name the one attribute aloud again ('everything by COLOUR'), hold up a shape and ask 'what colour — so which group?', and re-sort together.

If the child names the group that fills more space as 'most', line both groups up one-to-one (one object opposite one object) and count: show that the group that spread over more space can actually have fewer — the group with objects left unmatched has more.

If the count of a scattered group is unstable, slide or set each object aside as it is counted, or line the group up first, so the last number said is how many; this is a counting lapse to steady, not a sorting error.
When re-sorting by size changes the counts, ask 'same shapes — why are the piles different now?' to surface that grouping is a choice.
activities.rationale: At GAISE Level A, sorting and counting are early steps of the statistical process (after posing a question): children represent how many times each outcome occurs and identify the most frequent. Direct handling lets the child act, see each category total grow, and read most/fewest from counts rather than appearance. An optional self-counting on-screen mat (bins with live counters rendered as stacks of equal-sized units, plus a 're-sort by size' button) can make the count-and-compare mechanism visible; physical lines with one object per equal-sized space, or stacks of same-size counters, achieve the same comparison with real objects.
sourceClaims: Sorting is the entry point of statistics: at Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable (how many times each outcome occurs) using tables and picture/bar graphs, e.g. young children line up by favourite music type and count each category; the mode is the most frequent outcome

Year 2 pupils are taught to ask and answer questions by counting the number of objects in each category and sorting the categories by quantity, and to ask and answer questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
learnerActions: Face a jumble of coloured shapes and three labelled groups/bins (physical trays or an on-screen mat).
Before starting, say aloud the single attribute: 'we are sorting by COLOUR.'
Move each shape into its matching group until every shape is placed and none is left over.

Watch or build each group as a line with one object per equal-sized space (or a stack of same-size counters standing for the objects) so groups can be compared fairly, and keep a running count of each group.
Read off which group has the most and which has the fewest by comparing the counts.
Then re-sort the SAME set a different way (by size): tip everything out, relabel the groups, and sort again, noticing the counts change.
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting means applying one consistent rule to classify every object, and 'most/fewest' is read from the counts once the groups are arranged for fair comparison. The same fixed data can also be grouped in more than one way — how you sort is a choice.

activities.title: Sort the same set two different ways
feedback: If the child treats the second sort as a 'wrong answer' to the first, remind them both sorts are correct — they just answer different questions.
If criteria drift mid-sort, pause and restate the single attribute for that round before continuing.
activities.rationale: Sorting the same set by two attributes separates the stable data from the chosen grouping rule, building early data sense and reinforcing that a single attribute must be held fixed within one sort.
learnerActions: Take one set of objects and sort it by colour; count and record each group (category name + count).
Tip the set out and sort the SAME objects by a second attribute (size: big/small); count and record again.
Compare the two records and talk about how the groups and their counts differ even though the objects are identical.
activities.intendedInsight: The data is fixed, but the grouping is a choice; different attributes give different groups and different counts.

activities.title: Answer a real question from sorted class data
feedback: If the child reports a group without tying it back to the question, re-ask the original question and have them connect the count to it.
Ask 'how do you know that group has the most — can you show me?' to check the answer rests on counting, not appearance.
activities.rationale: Anchoring to a genuine question and reading the result back builds early data sense and completes the statistical cycle from question to conclusion.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils are taught to ask and answer questions by counting the number of objects in each category and sorting the categories by quantity, and to ask and answer questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
learnerActions: Pose a real question first, e.g. 'which colour do we have most of?' or use data the child helped generate (favourite colour, shape cards).
Sort and count to answer it, then read the result back against the question: 'so we have most red — does that answer our question?'
State both the most and the fewest category by their counts (or say that groups tie when their counts are equal).
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting and counting are done for a purpose — to answer a question about real data — not as an isolated exercise.

constraints: Keep one sorting attribute fixed within a single sort; name it aloud before starting so groups don't drift into mixed criteria.

Arrange groups as lines with one object per equal-sized space (e.g. a grid mat), or as stacks of same-size counters or blocks, so 'most/fewest' is read from count, not from the space a group happens to fill — large or spread-out objects can look like 'more' while being fewer, and stacks of different-sized shapes cannot be fairly compared by height.
Every object must be classified into exactly one non-overlapping group; none left unsorted and none in two piles.
Secure cardinality supports this skill: if a child loses track counting a scattered group, that is a counting lapse to steady (slide each aside / line them up), not a sorting error to reteach.

Assess by watching the child sort and count (the doing), not by asking them to describe sorting: observe whether they hold one rule, sort exhaustively, count with cardinality, and read most/fewest from counts. Recognising an answer in a multiple-choice check is not the same as independently sorting and counting.
A tap-to-reveal of an already-sorted set with counts can serve as reference, but it does not let the child perform the sorting, which is the skill; use it only as a scaffold, not the main task.

An open conversation or a 3D handling task is not required for this flat, single-attribute classification; a multiple-choice 'which has most?' may check the read-off, but recognising the answer does not elicit independent sorting and counting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a self-counting 2D drag-to-sort mat as 'ideal' and claimed a quiz 'cannot let the child DO the sorting' and that '3D adds handling load without insight'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy claims; retained as narrowly scoped affordance/limit notes (self-counting bins make the mechanism visible; recognition-only responses don't elicit independent construction) rather than universal laws. Physical objects achieve the same learning and the source itself recommends real objects.

Activity 2 (re-sort the same set) and the 'grouping is a choice' element of activity 1's insight are best practice from the pedagogy text but are not directly supported by either source claim; activity 2's sourceClaims is therefore []. Activity 1's cited claims support its core sorting/counting/most-fewest principle, not the re-sort-is-a-choice extension. The National Curriculum 'ask and answer questions' claim is the direct support for the real-question activity.

Self-audit: the most/fewest-by-space misconception and its fix (line up one-to-one and count) are internally consistent; the re-sort-changes-counts point correctly keeps the data fixed while the grouping varies. No arithmetic, force/motion, fraction, or shade content to check. The reteachPrerequisiteId for the space-vs-count error is retained as a signal in the original row but omitted from learner-facing text as an internal catalog reference.

probeDeeper: Ask 'how did you decide where this one goes?' to check the sorting rule is conscious and consistent
Counterexample tuned to this age: hand them a counter that could fit two ideas (a big red one while sorting by colour) and watch whether they hold the colour rule
Ask 'how do you know that pile has the most — can you show me?' to see whether 'most' rests on counting or on appearance
Ask 'could we sort these a different way?' to check they grasp that grouping is a choice, not fixed
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: the child picks one attribute (colour) and sorts EVERY counter into non-overlapping groups, counts each group accurately (last-number-said = how many), and names the largest and smallest groups by their counts — ideally lining the groups up to compare.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shifts the sorting criterion partway — begins by colour then starts grouping by size or shape, ending with mixed piles
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the one attribute aloud ('everything sorted by COLOUR') and re-sort together; hold up a counter and ask 'what colour — so which pile?' to fix the single rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The finished groups contain more than one colour, or the child hesitates over where a big red counter goes

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges 'most' by the space a group occupies rather than its count — a spread-out or larger-object group looks like more even when it has fewer
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line both groups up one-to-one and count; show the shorter-but-denser line actually has more — rebuild the more/fewer comparison
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names the group that fills more table as 'most' when a tighter group actually has more counters

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses track when counting a scattered group, so category totals are wrong
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the count — slide each counter aside as it is counted, or line the group up first; this is a counting lapse, not a sorting error, so steady the count rather than reteach sorting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child double-counts or skips counters in a jumbled pile and gives an unstable total on recount

responseLevels.gap: Sorts inconsistently or leaves objects out, miscounts groups, and picks 'most' by appearance; cannot reliably answer most/fewest
responseLevels.full: Independently sorts every object by one consistent attribute, counts each group accurately, names most/fewest from the counts, and can re-sort the set a different way
responseLevels.partial: Sorts by one attribute and counts with some support, but judges most by space or needs prompting to order the groups

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a mixed pile of coloured counters. Sort them so we can see how many of each colour there are, then tell me which colour we have the most of and which the fewest. (Set the task, then WATCH — do not tell them how to sort.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the DOING is the assessment. A child who has the idea keeps one consistent rule, sorts exhaustively, counts with cardinality, and reads most/fewest from counts; a child who doesn't drifts between attributes, miscounts, or judges 'most' by how much space a group fills. You cannot see this by asking them to describe sorting — you must set the task and observe.

pedagogy.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting hundreds to a three-digit number is the simplest of the three: within 1000 only the hundreds digit changes, and the tens and ones stay fixed. Children reuse a single-digit fact (3+2 hundreds) at the scale of hundreds. It is the cleanest demonstration of place-value invariance — the local part left untouched — and is taught with a place-value chart and hundred-scaled number line. (Bridging a thousand is a later topic, so within-1000 cases do not bridge.)
bestPractices: Anchor the tens and ones; operate only on the hundreds — 345+200 keeps '_45' and works 3+2 hundreds
Reuse the known single-digit fact at the scale of hundreds (3 hundreds + 2 hundreds = 5 hundreds)
Use a place-value chart to show only the hundreds row changing
Contrast with the ones/tens topics so the child generalises 'the added amount changes its own column'
Ask the child to state which digits stay the same and why (DfE evidence)
keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart (only the hundreds row moves)
Number line marked in hundreds
Base-ten hundred-flats (add/remove flats)
Partitioning jotting (345 = 300 + 45)
Place-value counters on a H-T-O grid
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding the hundreds amount to the tens or ones)
Miscounting the hundreds (762 − 400 given as 462 vs correct 362 — a single-digit subtraction slip at the hundreds scale)
Disturbing the tens/ones when they should be untouched
Overreaching to bridge a thousand when the numbers don't require it

learn.summary: Year 3 learners mentally add and subtract hundreds to/from a three-digit number with answers below 1000, where only the hundreds digit changes and the tens and ones stay fixed. The core insight is place-value invariance: a known single-digit fact (3+2 hundreds) is reused at the scale of hundreds while the other columns are left untouched. Work with a place-value chart, a number line marked in hundreds, base-ten hundred-flats, partitioning jottings (345 = 300 + 45), and place-value counters on an H-T-O grid; contrast with +tens/+ones (using examples that need no regrouping) so children generalise that an added amount lands in its own column when that column does not go past 9. With answers below 1000 these cases never bridge a thousand.

activities.title: Freeze the tens and ones: only the hundreds move
feedback: If the learner alters the 45 in 345+200, re-anchor on the chart: 200 is two hundreds, so it joins the hundreds. Cover or grey out the tens and ones to show they cannot change, then re-read 545.
If the learner disturbs the tens/ones in subtraction, physically hold or cover the '62' of 762 and only operate on the hundreds.

If the answer to 762−400 comes out as 462, this is most likely a single-digit fact slip (the learner found 4 hundreds instead of 7−4=3 hundreds): rehearse 7−4 on its own, then reapply at the hundreds scale to get 362. The tens and ones were kept, so place value does not need reteaching.
Prompt: 'Is 762−400 bigger or smaller than 762? Should it be?' to catch direction-of-operation errors.
activities.rationale: The objective is place-value invariance, so the activity makes the stable columns visible and asks the learner to predict and name what stays fixed before checking. A manipulable or clearly staged chart lets the learner act on the hundreds while the tens and ones remain visibly still; a static reveal can show the same contrast but does not let the learner operate the pieces.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils add and subtract mentally a three-digit number and hundreds.
Place-value understanding lets a known single-digit fact be reused at the scale of hundreds, with the other columns left invariant (unitising).
learnerActions: Show 345 on a place-value chart (hundreds, tens, ones). Add 200 and watch only the hundreds change from 3 to 5, giving 545 — say aloud that the '45' tail is unchanged.
Now do 762 − 400 on the same chart: the hundreds drop from 7 to 3 while the '62' stays put, giving 362.
Before revealing each answer, point to the tens and ones and state that they will not change, then check after.
Repeat with 518 + 300, predicting the answer (818) and naming which digits stay the same.
Articulate the rule in your own words: the amount you add or take away is a number of hundreds, so it lands only in the hundreds column.
activities.intendedInsight: When the answer stays below 1000, adding or subtracting hundreds changes only the hundreds digit; the tens and ones are invariant because the added amount belongs to the hundreds column.

activities.title: Same place-value idea, one column along
feedback: If the learner moves the change to the wrong column, restate where each amount belongs (200 = hundreds, 20 = tens) and re-anchor on the chart.

If the learner thinks a different column should change when switching between +hundreds and +tens, clarify that adding tens and adding hundreds are simply different amounts, each landing in its own column — there is no rule reversing, just a different column changing.
activities.rationale: Contrasting +hundreds with +tens/+ones helps the learner generalise beyond a single case and prevents the 'change any digit' error. Juxtaposition makes the invariance principle explicit across columns.
sourceClaims: Place-value understanding lets a known single-digit fact be reused at the scale of hundreds, with the other columns left invariant (unitising).
learnerActions: Place a +hundreds example (345 + 200) beside a +tens example (345 + 20) and work both.
For each, say which single column changes and read off the two different answers (545 vs 365).
State the shared principle: when the column does not go past 9 (no regrouping), the added amount changes only its own column and leaves the others alone.
Try a mixed set, e.g. 345+200, 345+20, 345+2, naming the changing digit each time before answering.
activities.intendedInsight: The place-value rule generalises: whether you add hundreds, tens, or ones, the added amount changes only its own column as long as that column does not go past 9 (no regrouping), as in 345+200, 345+20 and 345+2.

activities.title: Explain what stays the same
feedback: Full understanding: answers quickly in the head, keeps tens and ones untouched, and explains that only the hundreds change because the added amount is a number of hundreds.

Partial: reaches answers with the chart or number line but is unsure which digits stay fixed, or makes single-digit hundreds slips — revisit the invariance naming step and rehearse the hundreds facts.
Gap: changes the tens/ones or lands the hundreds in the wrong column and cannot say what stays the same — return to the chart activity with the tens and ones covered.
activities.rationale: Articulating which digits stay fixed surfaces whether the learner understands invariance or is guessing, and separates a conceptual gap from a mere single-digit fact slip. Reasoning-focused discussion complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on chart work.
learnerActions: Work 345 + 200, 762 − 400, and 518 + 300 mentally, thinking aloud.
After each, answer: which digits changed and which stayed exactly the same, and why?
Answer the probes: How is 762−400 like 7−4, and what is different? If it were 345+20 instead of 345+200, which digit would change?
Explain in a sentence why the tens and ones do not change.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state that only the hundreds digit changes — and why — demonstrates genuine place-value understanding rather than a memorised procedure.

activities.title: Quick checks for the two common slips
feedback: A 462 answer signals a 7−4 fact slip at the hundreds scale: rehearse the single-digit fact and reapply to reach 362.
An answer where the tens/ones changed signals a wrong-column error: re-anchor on the chart and name the column the added amount belongs to.
activities.rationale: Rapid, mixed items are efficient for rehearsal and for catching the two predicted error patterns, and asking for a brief justification adds a little reasoning; even so, they do not by themselves demand the sustained construction and explanation of the chart activities, so they follow rather than replace them.
learnerActions: Answer rapid items such as 762 − 400, choosing between 362 and a tempting 462, and justify the correct choice.
Work items that mix +hundreds with +tens (e.g. 345+200 next to 345+20) and state which column moved before answering.
For any item where the tens or ones changed, go back and re-anchor on the chart.
activities.intendedInsight: Fast, mixed practice rehearses the skill and exposes wrong-digit and single-digit miscount slips.

constraints: Keep all answers below 1000 so they never bridge a thousand; bridging a thousand is a later topic and should not be introduced here.

Recognition/multiple-choice items check fluency and catch slips but do not by themselves require the learner to construct or sustain the reasoning — use them after, not instead of, the chart and explanation activities.
A static reveal can show which digit changes but does not let the learner operate the pieces; prefer a manipulable chart when the goal is for the learner to act on the hundreds.
Distinguish a single-digit hundreds-fact slip (762−400→462) from a place-value gap: the first is a fact rehearsal, not a reason to reteach place value.
Base-ten hundred-flats and place-value counters are physical approximations of the abstract place-value structure; use them as representations, not as the concept itself.
The 462 answer is an error to be diagnosed (correct is 362); never present it as a valid option.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Checked arithmetic: 345+200=545, 762−400=362, 518+300=818, 345+20=365 — all correct. The 462 answer is explicitly an error pattern (should be 362) and is only used as a labelled distractor/slip to diagnose, never presented as valid.
The '3→5' phrasing for the hundreds in 345+200 corresponds to 3 hundreds + 2 hundreds = 5 hundreds, which is correct.

An irrelevant fraction 'denominator flips' framing that had been inserted into the +hundreds vs +tens activity has been kept out; this topic has no denominators and that framing would confuse learners.

Partitioning jottings (345 = 300 + 45) and place-value counters were restored to the summary so the full set of original representations is represented; they can be used interchangeably with the chart.

Non-preferred alternatives (static reveal, spoken reasoning discussion, rapid recognition items) were retained as distinct activities with their stated pedagogical purposes rather than collapsed into the preferred chart approach.

Activities 3 and 4 have sourceClaims set to [] because no original source claim directly supports their specific pedagogical principles (articulation surfacing understanding; rapid items catching slips) beyond the general topic.

probeDeeper: For 345 + 200, which digits stayed exactly the same? Why don't they change?
How is 762 − 400 like 7 − 4? What's different?
If it were 345 + 20 instead of 345 + 200, which digit would change then?
Is your answer to 762 − 400 bigger or smaller than 762? Should it be?
assess.correctAnswer: 545, 362, 818. In each, only the hundreds digit changes: 3+2=5 hundreds (545); 7−4=3 hundreds (362); 5+3=8 hundreds (818). The tens and ones stay fixed throughout.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the wrong digit — adds the hundreds amount to the tens or ones ('345 + 200' altering the 45)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor with the chart: 200 is two hundreds, joining the hundreds; grey out the 45 to show it cannot change.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens or ones change; the hundreds addition lands in the wrong column

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the hundreds — '762 − 400 is 462' (a single-digit subtraction slip at the hundreds scale)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach place value: rehearse the single-digit hundreds fact (7−4=3) then reapply. This is a fact slip, not a place-value gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens and ones are correct but the hundreds digit is off by one; underlying 7−4 done as 7−3 or similar

responseLevels.gap: Changes the tens/ones, or lands the hundreds in the wrong column; cannot say what stays the same.
responseLevels.full: Answers all three instantly in his head, keeps the tens and ones untouched, and explains that only the hundreds digit changes because the added amount is a number of hundreds.
responseLevels.partial: Gets answers with the chart or number line but is unsure which digits stay fixed, or makes single-digit hundreds slips.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these mentally, thinking aloud: 345 + 200, then 762 − 400, then 518 + 300. After each, ask which digits changed and which stayed the same.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because within 1000 these never bridge a thousand, a fluent child answers almost instantly and can state that the tens and ones are untouched. A child without place-value invariance changes the wrong digit or disturbs the tens/ones; a single-digit slip at the hundreds scale (762−400→462) reveals shaky hundreds facts.

pedagogy.summary: Naming the parts of a circle (radius, diameter, circumference) and knowing the diameter is twice the radius is taught best by grounding each term in its DEFINING PROPERTY — the radius runs from the centre to the edge, the diameter is a line through the centre from edge to edge, the circumference is the distance all the way round — rather than by rote labels. Drawing and measuring many circles of different sizes and tabulating radius against diameter lets pupils discover the invariant d = 2r for themselves, and practising the conversion in BOTH directions guards against the pervasive radius/diameter swap.
bestPractices: Anchor each term in its defining property: a radius touches the centre; a diameter passes through the centre; the circumference is the perimeter (distance around).
Draw and measure several circles of different sizes and tabulate radius vs diameter, so pupils see d = 2r holds at every scale.
Practise conversion in both directions — diameter from radius AND radius from diameter — and monitor for confusion between the two (NCTM).
Label parts on circles in varied positions and surface the longest-chord property (the diameter is the longest line across).
Provide a vocabulary word bank (radius, diameter, circumference) and require pupils to use the terms when they reason.
keyRepresentations: A labelled circle: centre, radius, diameter, circumference
Radius vs diameter vs an off-centre chord, contrasted
A radius/diameter table across several circle sizes
String wrapped round a circle to show the circumference as a length
commonMisconceptions: Swaps radius and diameter, or substitutes a diameter where a radius is needed — the 'half/twice' error (NCTM).
Treats any line across the circle as a diameter, or draws a radius/diameter that does not reach or pass through the centre.
Applies the conversion in the wrong direction (doubles when it should halve), or thinks the radius equals the diameter.

learn.summary: Pupils (age 10–11) learn to name and identify [curriculum wording omitted; reference ON-MATH-2020-G7-E2.3] by their DEFINING PROPERTIES — the radius runs from the centre to the edge, the diameter is a straight line from edge to edge through the centre (the longest line across), and the circumference is the distance all the way around — and to apply d = 2r in both directions. The core work is drawing and measuring many circles, tabulating radius against diameter so the invariant d = 2r is discovered rather than told, and practising conversion both ways to guard against the pervasive radius/diameter swap. Several complementary media (dynamic manipulation, paper-and-string measurement, a labelled reference, and a short conversion check) each support a different part of this objective.

activities.title: Measure many circles and discover d = 2r
feedback: If a pupil's pairs don't come out close to double, check that the diameter was drawn through the centre and that both were measured along a straight line — an off-centre line is shorter and will break the pattern.
Prompt: 'Does your doubling pattern still hold for your biggest circle and your smallest circle?' to surface that the relationship is scale-independent.
If a pupil writes the names interchangeably, ask them to point to where each line starts and ends relative to the centre.
activities.rationale: Grounding each term in its defining property and tabulating radius against diameter across sizes lets pupils see d = 2r hold at every scale, which the curriculum expects pupils to know and the geometry research links to moving beyond naming toward defining properties.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to illustrate and name parts of circles, including radius, diameter and circumference, and know that the diameter is twice the radius; the non-statutory guidance expresses this as d = 2 × r.

Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Draw several circles of clearly different sizes (small, medium, large).
For each circle, mark the centre, draw a radius from the centre to the edge and a diameter from edge to edge through the centre.
Measure the radius and the diameter of each circle and record them in a two-column table (radius | diameter).
Look across the table and describe the pattern you notice between the radius and the diameter.
State the relationship in your own words and as d = 2 × r.
activities.intendedInsight: Across every size of circle, the diameter is exactly twice the radius. Pupils' own measurements will come out close to double, allowing for small measuring errors, so they can see the pattern holding for themselves rather than memorising a rule.

activities.title: Which line is longest? Predict then measure
feedback: Many pupils pick a long-looking slanted line; after measuring, point out that the through-centre line always wins, which is why the diameter is defined by the centre, not by looking long.
If a pupil labels an off-centre chord a diameter, have them check whether it passes through the marked centre.
Fold a paper circle in half (and again) to locate the centre, then confirm which drawn lines actually pass through it.
activities.rationale: Predicting before measuring makes the reasoning visible and the counterexample (an off-centre chord) directly tests the through-centre defining property rather than surface appearance, countering prototype-based reasoning.
sourceClaims: Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: On a circle with the centre marked, draw several straight lines from edge to edge — some passing through the centre and some not.
Before measuring, PREDICT which line is the longest and write down why you think so.
Measure each line and compare with your prediction.
Decide which lines pass through the centre (diameters) and which do not (other chords), and explain the difference using the word 'centre'.
activities.intendedInsight: The longest straight line across a circle is always the one through the centre — the diameter — so a line that misses the centre is a shorter chord, not a diameter. The pre-stated reason is what reveals a pupil's thinking.

activities.title: Convert both ways and reason aloud
feedback: Worked check: a radius of 4.5 cm gives a diameter of 9 cm because the diameter is twice the radius (2 × 4.5). A diameter of 10 cm gives a radius of 5 cm because the radius is half the diameter.
If a pupil gives 2.25 cm as the diameter of a 4.5 cm radius, they halved instead of doubling — return to the measured table showing the diameter is always the larger, doubled value.
Require the pupil to name which quantity is which before computing, so a radius isn't treated as a diameter.
activities.rationale: Practising conversion in both directions and requiring reasoning with correct vocabulary targets the flagged radius/diameter confusion and supports fluent, justified use of the terms.
sourceClaims: Teachers should make sure pupils identify the radius and the diameter, realise that d = 2r, be able to calculate radius from diameter and diameter from radius, and should monitor for misconceptions; difficulty using the variables C, d and r is a flagged misconception, and a word bank of circumference/diameter/radius supports the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Given a radius (e.g. 4.5 cm), work out the diameter and state how you did it.
Given a diameter (e.g. 10 cm), work out the radius and state how you did it.
For each, say in words whether you doubled or halved and why.
Use a vocabulary word bank (radius, diameter, circumference) and use the correct term in each explanation.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting diameter-from-radius and radius-from-diameter are different directions of the same relationship; knowing which to double and which to halve, with a reason, prevents the half/twice swap.

activities.title: Feel the circumference as a length
feedback: If a pupil calls a straight line across the circle 'the circumference', have them trace the edge with a finger: the circumference is the whole way round.
Compare the straightened string length with the diameter drawn straight across to reinforce that they measure different things.
activities.rationale: A tactile wrap-and-straighten activity is intended to make the circumference concrete as a go-around length, addressing the confusion between circumference and a straight measurement across. Proposed as a hands-on scaffold; its effectiveness is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Wrap a length of string once around the edge of a circle, mark where it meets, then straighten it against a ruler to measure the distance around.
Run a finger all the way around the edge and say in your own words what the circumference is.
Contrast this with a straight line drawn across the circle and explain why the circumference is not a straight line.
activities.intendedInsight: The circumference is the distance all the way around the edge — a curved length — not a straight line across the circle.

activities.title: Dynamic circle: watch d = 2r hold as the circle resizes (optional screen scaffold)
feedback: Live readout feedback: as the pupil stretches the circle, the diameter reading stays at twice the radius (the last digit may differ slightly if the display rounds), so the relationship can be observed across scales.
When a dragged line misses the centre and is refused the 'diameter' label, prompt: 'What do you need to change so it becomes a diameter?'
Pair this with the paper-and-ruler measuring so the relationship is grounded in real measurement, not only an on-screen readout.
activities.rationale: A dynamic, draggable model lets the invariant be experienced across many sizes in quick succession and can enforce the through-centre property via snapping/labelling; a static labelled reference states d = 2r but cannot show it varying. Offered as a complement to, not a replacement for, hands-on measuring; its efficacy relative to other media is not established here.
sourceClaims: Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Drag a point to make the circle bigger and smaller and watch a live readout of the radius and the diameter.
Notice whether the diameter readout always shows twice the radius as the size changes.

Drag the endpoint of a line inside the circle; observe that it is labelled 'diameter — the longest line across' only when it passes through the centre, and is refused the label when it misses the centre.
Say what stays the same (d = 2r) and what must be true for a line to be a diameter (it passes through the centre).
activities.intendedInsight: The 2× relationship is invariant across every size, and only a through-centre line earns the name 'diameter' — both the invariant and the defining property made visible together.

activities.title: Labelled circle reference (supporting scaffold)
feedback: Reveal-on-tap can confirm each term's defining property as a reference, but d = 2r is stated here, not discovered — use it alongside the measuring activity.
Varying the position of the labelled parts guards against pupils only recognising a standard horizontal diameter.
If a pupil can label a standard diagram but slips on a slanted or off-centre line, return to the defining-property test (does it pass through the centre?).
activities.rationale: A clear labelled reference with varied positions supports the vocabulary and surfaces the longest-chord property; presenting shapes in varied positions counters prototype-based recognition. This is a reference scaffold and cannot by itself build the measured discovery of the invariant.
sourceClaims: Teachers should make sure pupils identify the radius and the diameter, realise that d = 2r, be able to calculate radius from diameter and diameter from radius, and should monitor for misconceptions; difficulty using the variables C, d and r is a flagged misconception, and a word bank of circumference/diameter/radius supports the vocabulary.

Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Study a labelled circle showing centre, radius, diameter and circumference.
Reveal or read each term's defining property: radius = centre to edge; diameter = edge to edge through the centre (the longest line across); circumference = the distance all the way round.
Label parts yourself on circles drawn in varied positions and orientations, including ones where the diameter is slanted.
Match each term to its definition.
activities.intendedInsight: Each circle part is identified by its defining property and position relative to the centre, not by a fixed picture orientation.

constraints: A static labelled diagram or reveal-on-tap reference states d = 2r but does not let pupils see it vary across sizes; pair it with hands-on drawing and measuring so the invariant is genuinely discovered.

A label/match/slider conversion check can verify vocabulary and the d = 2r computation but does not by itself build the defining-property understanding; use it as a check after the measuring and reasoning activities.
Recognition-only responses (matching terms to a standard diagram) do not elicit independent construction; require pupils to draw, measure, convert both ways, and justify.
Present diameters and radii in varied positions (including slanted and non-standard) so pupils do not over-rely on a horizontal prototype.
Always insist pupils state WHY (which line passes through the centre, whether they doubled or halved); the reason is what distinguishes understanding from a lucky guess.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled a 3-D environment as 'adding nothing' for a planar concept. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it has been dropped rather than asserted. A planar concept is naturally well-served by 2-D media, but no universal 'adds nothing' claim is made here.

The source stated conversation is 'poor' for this concept. This is not a general pedagogical law; spoken justification is used throughout (predict-and-explain, reason-aloud conversion) as part of teaching, not only assessment. The medium-ranking boilerplate was removed.
The 'diameter is the longest line across (longest chord)' property is stated correctly for a circle and is used as a measurable, verifiable prediction task.

Self-audit of the worked conversions: radius 4.5 cm → diameter 9 cm (2 × 4.5) is correct; the distractor 2.25 cm correctly models halving instead of doubling; diameter 10 cm → radius 5 cm is correct. No arithmetic errors found.

The circumference string activity and the circumference-vs-straight-line confusion it targets come from the pedagogy/assessment material, not from the cited sources; its sourceClaims were set to [] and the rationale hedged accordingly, as no source establishes the method's effectiveness.
All sourceClaims were re-checked to be verbatim copies of the three original sources[].claim strings; this addresses the prior validation failure caused by a non-matching claim string.

assess.poeTask: Draw several straight lines from edge to edge across a circle, some through the marked centre and some not, and ask the pupil to PREDICT which line is longest before measuring — and to say why. Many pick a long-looking slanted chord. Then measure: the longest is always the line through the centre — the diameter. The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part; the result forces the defining property that a diameter must pass through the centre and is the longest chord.
probeDeeper: If I make the circle twice as big, is the diameter still twice the radius? Why?
This line goes across the circle but not through the centre — is it a diameter? Why not?
A circle's diameter is 10 cm — what is its radius, and how did you work it out?
Which straight line across a circle is the longest, and where must it pass?
assess.correctAnswer: The diameter is 9 cm, because the diameter is twice the radius (2 × 4.5). The centre-to-edge line is the radius and the edge-to-edge line through the centre is the diameter; a radius goes from the centre to the edge and a diameter passes through the centre, so the third line is neither (it is a chord) because it does not pass through the centre.

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps radius and diameter or applies the relationship the wrong way — the 'half/twice' error (halves when it should double)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw and measure circles and tabulate radius against diameter to see the diameter is always double the radius; practise both conversion directions
errorPatterns.distractor: 2.25 cm (halved the radius instead of doubling it)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the diameter as 2.25 cm, or labels the centre-to-edge line as the diameter

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats any line across the circle as a diameter, or a line to the edge as a radius, ignoring the centre — the defining property
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold a paper circle to find the centre; only a line through the centre is a diameter (and it is the longest line across), and a radius must start at the centre
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the off-centre chord as the diameter, or draws a 'radius' that does not reach the centre

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the circumference with a straight measurement — calls a diameter or a line across 'the circumference'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run a finger all the way round the edge — the circumference is the distance around, not a straight line across
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels a straight line as the circumference

responseLevels.gap: Uses the terms interchangeably or halves/doubles in the wrong direction; treats any line across the circle as a diameter.
responseLevels.full: States and applies d = 2r in both directions with a reason, identifies parts by their defining properties (radius from the centre, diameter through the centre, circumference around), rejects an off-centre chord as a diameter, and knows the relationship holds at any size.
responseLevels.partial: Converts one way (e.g. radius to diameter) and labels a standard diagram, but slips on the reverse conversion or on a non-standard/off-centre line — knows the names without the defining property.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A circle has a radius of 4.5 cm. What is its diameter, and how do you know? Then look at this diagram of a circle with its centre marked and three straight lines drawn on it: one from the centre to the edge, one from edge to edge passing through the centre, and one from edge to edge that does NOT pass through the centre. Which line is the radius, which is the diameter, and how can you tell?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reason tier separates a pupil who applies d = 2r with understanding from one who guesses or halves. The diagram forces the defining-property test: a pupil who thinks any line across the circle is a diameter picks the off-centre chord, whereas a pupil who knows the property rejects it because it misses the centre. Together the tiers catch both the half/twice swap and the through-centre confusion.

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils should be taught to illustrate and name parts of circles, including radius, diameter and circumference, and know that the diameter is twice the radius; the non-statutory guidance expresses this as d = 2 × r.
