pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–14 years

- **Topic:** Biodiversity & Resilience — what biodiversity means, why high biodiversity makes ecosystems more resilient, and how human activity threatens it

- **Standards — UK (DfE Key Stage 3, Biology — Relationships in an ecosystem):** the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem, including food webs; how organisms affect and are affected by their environment; and the importance of biodiversity (maintaining biodiversity and the environmental costs of human activity).

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS2-5):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-5]; (MS-LS2-4) argue from evidence that changes to an ecosystem affect populations.

- **Operational details:** Build the concept in three moves. (1) DEFINE biodiversity at three levels so it isn't just 'lots of animals': species diversity (how many different species), genetic diversity (variation within a species), and ecosystem diversity (variety of habitats) — each matters and each can be lost. (2) EXPLAIN RESILIENCE as the payoff: a species-rich food web has redundancy and alternative pathways, so when one species is knocked out others can fill the role and the system absorbs the shock; a species-poor web has no backup, so one loss can cascade and collapse. Genetic diversity gives resilience too — a varied population is more likely to contain individuals that survive a new disease or stress. This is the load-bearing insight: diversity = insurance. (3) THREATS & WHY IT MATTERS TO US: name the human drivers (habitat destruction, pollution, invasive species, climate change, overexploitation) and connect biodiversity to ecosystem services humans depend on (pollination of crops, clean water, soil fertility, disease regulation, medicines) so 'why it matters' is not only ethical but self-interested. Reason from food-web structure throughout — this topic sits directly on the pupil's prior food-web/interdependence understanding.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/systems-relational). Pupils can reason about redundancy, alternative pathways, and probabilistic buffering, and evaluate trade-offs among solutions. Success = biodiversity defined at species/genetic/ecosystem levels, a mechanistic account of why high diversity resists disruption, three human threats named, and a case that biodiversity loss harms humans, not just wildlife.
bestPractices: Define biodiversity at all three levels (species, genetic, ecosystem) from the start so pupils don't reduce it to 'number of animals'.
Teach resilience mechanistically as redundancy — alternative pathways in a food web absorb a shock; a single pathway snaps — building directly on prior food-web knowledge.
Contrast a species-rich vs species-poor web under the SAME shock so the resilience difference is a controlled comparison, not two unrelated stories.
Extend the insurance idea to the gene level: a varied population is likelier to contain survivors of a new disease — linking to variation and natural selection.
Make 'why it matters' concrete and self-interested via ecosystem services (crop pollination, clean water, medicines), not only an ethical appeal.
Have pupils evaluate and weigh competing conservation solutions, matching the NGSS design-evaluation standard rather than just listing threats.
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side high-diversity vs low-diversity food webs subjected to the same removal/shock
A three-level diagram of biodiversity: species / genetic / ecosystem
A redundancy 'safety-net' image — many strands hold when one is cut; a single strand fails
Ecosystem-services map linking biodiversity to human benefits (pollination, water, soil, medicine)
Uniform vs genetically-varied population hit by a disease, showing survivors only in the varied one
commonMisconceptions: Thinking biodiversity just means 'lots of animals', missing genetic and ecosystem levels and the variety (not just quantity) of life.
Believing every species is equally dispensable — or, conversely, that only 'important' big species matter — rather than grasping functional redundancy.
Assuming a stable-looking ecosystem is automatically resilient, not realising low diversity can look fine until a shock causes collapse.
Treating biodiversity loss as purely an ethical/animal concern, missing the human dependence on ecosystem services.
Confusing genetic diversity with species diversity, or thinking a large population is automatically genetically diverse.
Thinking one conservation solution is simply 'best', rather than weighing trade-offs among competing solutions.

learn.summary: Biodiversity and resilience for ages 12–14: define biodiversity at three levels (species, genetic, ecosystem), explain mechanistically why high diversity makes ecosystems more resilient (redundancy and alternative food-web pathways, plus genetic variation as insurance against new stresses), name human threats, and argue that biodiversity loss harms people via ecosystem services. The proposed core activity lets learners apply the SAME shock to a species-rich vs species-poor food web and observe one absorbing it while the other cascades to collapse; a role-play conservation debrief, a reveal-based contrast image, and categorisation/prediction tasks support definition, argument and assessment. High diversity raises the likelihood of absorbing a shock but does not guarantee survival (e.g. loss of a keystone species can still cause collapse). Build throughout on prior food-web/interdependence knowledge.

activities.title: Break two food webs with the same shock
feedback: If a learner expects both webs to behave the same, point them to the alternative prey in the rich web: ask what the predator in the poor web can eat instead once its only prey is gone.
If a learner thinks losing one species 'changes nothing', have them trace what fed on the removed species and what it fed on, so the knock-on becomes visible.

If a learner says the clone-like population should survive 'because they are all strong', ask what happens when the single variant they all share is exactly the one the disease targets — that is why a varied population is more likely to retain survivors.
activities.rationale: Resilience is a structural property of a food web, so a manipulable side-by-side model lets learners impose a controlled, identical shock and compare redundancy against a single pathway directly, building on prior food-web knowledge. The genetic round illustrates probabilistic buffering rather than a certain outcome. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should learn the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem including food webs, and the importance of maintaining biodiversity and the environmental costs of human activity.

Higher biodiversity increases ecosystem stability and resilience through functional redundancy and response diversity, and underpins ecosystem services such as pollination, water purification and soil fertility that humans depend on.
learnerActions: Work with two side-by-side food webs: one high-diversity web with many species and redundant links, and one low-diversity web with few species and single pathways.
Remove the SAME species (or apply the same shock such as a disease or pollutant) to BOTH webs and observe what happens in each.
In the rich web, watch a consumer switch to an alternative prey so the web wobbles and re-stabilises; in the poor web, watch the only pathway sever and a cascade of extinctions ripple outward.

Run a genetic-diversity round: set one population as uniform (clone-like) and one as genetically varied, then unleash a disease; observe survivors remaining in the varied population while the uniform population is highly vulnerable to being wiped out — and note that the real-world outcome is a matter of likelihood, not certainty.
Describe in your own words why the two webs responded differently to the identical shock.
activities.intendedInsight: High biodiversity provides redundancy — spare pathways that absorb a shock the way many strands of a net hold when one is cut, while a single strand snaps. Diversity is insurance, and the same principle extends to the gene level: variety is what makes survivors far more likely. High diversity raises the chance of absorbing a shock but does not guarantee it.

activities.title: Conservation-biologist challenge: justify and choose
feedback: If a learner dismisses a small or 'unimportant' species, return to functional redundancy: ask what jobs that species does (pollinating, feeding birds) and who covers them if it is lost.
If a learner frames biodiversity loss as purely an animal-welfare issue, prompt them to name a crop, water or medicine benefit that depends on a diverse ecosystem.
If a learner insists one solution is simply best, ask what each solution costs and what it fails to protect, so the trade-off becomes explicit.
activities.rationale: Evaluating competing solutions and arguing from evidence is the targeted reasoning; a responsive in-role challenge can draw out justification and trade-off weighing. Best used as a debrief after the food-web model so the felt insight becomes an argument. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-LS2-5: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-5].

Higher biodiversity increases ecosystem stability and resilience through functional redundancy and response diversity, and underpins ecosystem services such as pollination, water purification and soil fertility that humans depend on.
learnerActions: Take part in a role-play interview where a conservation biologist presses you to justify your reasoning: 'Why would losing one "unimportant" beetle matter?'
Respond to 'We can't save everything — how would you choose?' by weighing trade-offs between competing conservation solutions rather than naming one as simply 'best'.
Connect your argument to ecosystem services, explaining how protecting diversity protects crops, clean water and medicines people depend on.
State explicitly whether biodiversity loss matters to humans or only to wildlife, and give a concrete example.
activities.intendedInsight: Why biodiversity matters is both ethical and self-interested: diversity underpins ecosystem services humans rely on, and maintaining it means evaluating and weighing competing solutions, not picking one obvious answer.

activities.title: Reveal and compare: diverse vs degraded, and the services map
feedback: If a learner reduces biodiversity to 'lots of animals', contrast two scenes with the same number of individuals but different numbers of species, and ask which is more diverse and why.
If a learner confuses genetic with species diversity, point to variation within a single species versus the count of different species.
If a learner cannot link a service to a source, use the pinned map to trace, for example, pollination back to the insects that perform it.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal contrast presents the three-level definition and the 'why it matters to us' efficiently. Note its limit: a reveal-only image shows structure and roles but does not let learners run the shock-absorption dynamic, so pair it with the manipulable web rather than relying on it alone. A sort can teach and check classification but does not itself produce the mechanistic explanation. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Higher biodiversity increases ecosystem stability and resilience through functional redundancy and response diversity, and underpins ecosystem services such as pollination, water purification and soil fertility that humans depend on.
learnerActions: Explore a split scene showing a rich reef or meadow beside a degraded version; tap individual species to reveal their roles and how links are redundant or missing.
Use a second layer that pins ecosystem services (pollination, clean water, medicine, soil fertility) to the organisms or habitats that provide them.
Sort examples into the three levels of biodiversity: species diversity (how many different species), genetic diversity (variation within a species), and ecosystem diversity (variety of habitats).
activities.intendedInsight: Biodiversity is variety at three distinct levels, not just a headcount of animals, and the human payoff from that variety can be traced to specific services.

activities.title: Classify, predict and match (check and diagnose)
feedback: Correct answer: Field A. With many species, if the disease wipes one out, other species that do similar jobs (eating plants, feeding birds) can often take over, so the food web is more likely to keep functioning; Field B could collapse because its single species has no backup.
If a learner picks Field B 'because it has more insects in total', re-establish biodiversity as variety: ask what happens to all those insects when the one species they all are gets the disease.
If a learner says it makes no difference which field, return to food webs: trace what feeds on the lost species and what it fed on so the knock-on becomes visible.

If a learner picks Field B claiming 'fewer species means less competition and more stability', distinguish competition from resilience: variety provides backups when something is lost; a single species has none.

Probe deeper: ask for the actual mechanism (why does having other species help when one is lost?), whether loss matters to humans or only wildlife with an example, and whether high biodiversity would still guarantee survival if the disease killed a keystone species everything depended on — it would not, which is why high diversity raises the odds of recovery without guaranteeing it.
activities.rationale: Selection and matching tasks efficiently assess the definitions and threat attribution and surface nameable misconceptions, while the open 'why' prompts push beyond recognition toward explanation. Recognition-only items do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the mechanism, so pair them with the open diagnostic and probes. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should learn the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem including food webs, and the importance of maintaining biodiversity and the environmental costs of human activity.
learnerActions: Categorise worked examples into species, genetic, or ecosystem diversity.
Predict which of two webs resists collapse under a shock and state WHY, not just which one.
Match human activities (habitat destruction, pollution, invasive species, climate change, overexploitation) to the biodiversity threat each causes.

Answer the diagnostic: Two grassland fields both have plenty of grazing insects. Field A has 20 different insect species; Field B has just one species, but lots of it. A new disease arrives that kills off one insect species. In Field A it is one of the 20 species; in Field B it is the only species present. Which field's ecosystem is more likely to keep working, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can distinguish the three levels, attribute threats to human drivers, and — crucially — explain resilience by the redundancy/backup mechanism rather than by headcount.

constraints: Define biodiversity at all three levels (species, genetic, ecosystem) from the start so learners do not reduce it to 'number of animals'.
Teach resilience mechanistically as redundancy — alternative pathways absorb a shock; a single pathway snaps — building on prior food-web knowledge.
Contrast species-rich vs species-poor webs under the SAME shock so the resilience difference is a controlled comparison, not two unrelated stories.
Extend the insurance idea to the gene level: a varied population is more likely (not certain) to contain survivors of a new disease, linking to variation and natural selection.
Make 'why it matters' concrete and self-interested via ecosystem services (crop pollination, clean water, medicines), not only an ethical appeal.
Have learners evaluate and weigh competing conservation solutions, not just list threats.

Reveal-based or static contrast images show roles and structure but cannot run the shock-absorption dynamic; treat them as a scaffold for definitions and pair with the manipulable model. A sort can teach or check classification but does not itself elicit the explanation.
Recognition/matching items assess ideas but do not elicit independent construction of the redundancy mechanism; include open explanation prompts.

High biodiversity improves the likelihood of absorbing a shock but does not guarantee survival — e.g. loss of a keystone species on which others depend can still cause collapse; avoid stating diversity makes an ecosystem shock-proof.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (NGSS MS-LS2-5 and the IPBES claim) carry verified:false in the source row; the DfE KS3 claim is verified:true. Comparative efficacy or necessity of any medium is not established by these sources.

The legacy row rated a 3D rendering as adding no explanatory power and framed static images as unable to demonstrate the core dynamic; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal claims.

The diagnostic's 'correct' reasoning assumes the lost species' functions are covered by others; this holds for functional redundancy but not for a keystone species — captured in the probe prompt and a constraint so learners are not taught that diversity guarantees survival.

The genetic-diversity round is modelled as a clean contrast, but the underlying biology is probabilistic (a varied population is more likely, not certain, to retain survivors); a single simulated run shows one outcome, so learner-facing text is phrased for likelihood rather than certainty.

probeDeeper: You said the varied field copes better — what is the actual mechanism? Why does having other species help when one is lost?
Does biodiversity loss matter to humans, or only to wildlife? Give an example.
What if the disease killed a keystone species that everything else depended on — would high biodiversity still guarantee the ecosystem survives?
assess.correctAnswer: Field A. With many species, if the disease wipes one out, other species can still do its jobs — pollinating, feeding the birds — so the food web keeps functioning. Field B could collapse because its single species has no backup. High biodiversity gives an ecosystem functional redundancy, so it can absorb a loss and stay stable.

errorPatterns.pattern: Biodiversity as headcount — 'Field B is fine, it has more insects overall'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish biodiversity as variety, not amount: ask what happens to Field B's 'lots of insects' when the one species they all are gets the disease.
errorPatterns.distractor: Field B, because it has more insects in total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses by the number of individuals rather than the variety of species

errorPatterns.pattern: No knock-on effect — 'it makes no difference, losing one species changes nothing'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to food webs and interdependence: trace what feeds on the lost species and what it fed on, so the knock-on becomes visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: It makes no difference which field — losing one insect species changes nothing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats species as independent, missing that they depend on each other in the food web

errorPatterns.pattern: More species = more competition = less stable — so the single-species field is 'stronger'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish competition from resilience: variety provides backups when something is lost; a single species has none, so it is the fragile one.
errorPatterns.distractor: Field B, because fewer species means less competition and a more stable ecosystem.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Argues fewer species means less competition and therefore a more stable ecosystem

responseLevels.gap: Chooses by number of individuals or says it makes no difference; treats biodiversity as 'amount of life'.
responseLevels.full: Explains resilience through functional redundancy and multiple food-web pathways, distinguishes species/genetic/ecosystem biodiversity, links loss to consequences for humans, and applies the reasoning to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly picks the diverse field and says variety helps, but lists species without explaining the redundancy/backup mechanism or linking it to food-web interdependence; does not reach genetic/ecosystem levels or human relevance.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two grassland fields both have plenty of grazing insects. Field A has 20 different insect species; Field B has just one species, but lots of it. A new disease arrives that kills off one insect species. Which field's ecosystem is more likely to keep working, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands resilience picks the diverse field and names the redundancy/backup mechanism. A child who equates biodiversity with the amount of life picks Field B for having 'more insects', and a child holding the 'more species = more competition = less stable' idea also picks B — both give a different answer from the correct reasoner, and for a nameable wrong reason.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should learn the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem including food webs, and the importance of maintaining biodiversity and the environmental costs of human activity.

pedagogy.summary: At KS3 (ages 11-13) children move from calculating a single mean to DESCRIBING and COMPARING whole distributions: computing mean, median, mode and range, choosing which average best represents a data set, and reasoning about how an outlier affects each measure. Two ideas carry the teaching, and both are about judgement rather than calculation. First, the three averages are not interchangeable: the mean is influenced by every value (so a single outlier drags it), while the median is robust and stays representative when the data is skewed — so the CHOICE of average must fit the shape of the data. Second, an average alone does not describe a distribution: comparing two data sets requires a measure of CENTRE and a measure of SPREAD (range) together, because two sets with the same mean can differ wildly in variability. The characteristic errors are reporting the mean regardless of skew, treating the outlier as affecting all averages equally (or deleting it unthinkingly), and comparing sets on the mean alone while ignoring spread.
bestPractices: Compute all three averages on the SAME data set (especially a skewed one or one with an outlier) so children see them diverge and can discuss which best represents a typical value
Make the outlier's differential effect explicit: recompute mean and median with and without the outlier — the mean chases it, the median barely moves — so 'robust' has a concrete meaning
Teach that describing a distribution needs CENTRE and SPREAD together; compare two data sets on an average AND the range, and show two sets with equal means but different spreads
Tie the choice of average to the data's shape: median for skewed data or data with an outlier, mode for categorical / most-common questions, mean for roughly symmetric numerical data
Insist the range is a single number (highest minus lowest), a measure of spread — not the two extreme values
Draw conclusions in context ('Class A did better on average but was less consistent') so measures are used to argue, not just calculated
keyRepresentations: A data set shown on a number line with mean and median both marked, and an outlier that can be added/removed to see each measure respond
Side-by-side dot plots of two data sets with the same mean but different spreads (centre vs spread made visible)
A skewed distribution where mean, median and mode fall in visibly different places
The range shown as a labelled distance from lowest to highest value
commonMisconceptions: Reporting the mean as 'the average' regardless of skew or outliers, when the median would better represent a typical value
Thinking an outlier affects the mean and median equally, or deleting an outlier without justification, rather than seeing the mean is dragged while the median is robust
Comparing two data sets on their averages alone and ignoring the spread (a frequent error is to ignore variability entirely)
Giving the range as the two extreme values rather than their difference; or situating the mean at the centre of the range even when the data is skewed

learn.summary: KS3 learners (ages 11-13) move from calculating a single mean to describing and comparing whole distributions of one variable: computing mean, median, mode and range, judging which average best represents a data set given its shape, and reasoning about how an outlier affects each measure differently. Two judgements carry the topic: (1) the three averages are not interchangeable — the mean is pulled by every value (so an outlier drags it) while the median is robust, so the choice of average must fit the data's shape; and (2) an average alone does not describe a distribution — comparing two sets needs a measure of centre AND a measure of spread (range) together, because two sets with the same mean can differ widely in variability.

activities.title: Watch the averages diverge: move a value far out
feedback: If the learner says the median moved as much as the mean, have them recount the ordered values: the middle position stays near the cluster, whereas the sum rises by how far the value was moved, so the mean shifts by that amount divided by the number of values — a change the median does not share.

If the learner deletes the far-out value without justification, ask what real reason (e.g. a recording error versus a genuine value) would justify removing it, and show what each average does when it is kept.
If the learner reports the pulled-up mean as 'the typical score', point to the cluster and ask whether that mean sits among most of the data.
activities.rationale: Computing all three averages on a clustered set and recomputing them after one value is moved far out lets learners see the measures diverge, giving 'the mean is pulled by outliers, the median is robust' a concrete meaning rather than being a slogan. Moving an existing point (rather than adding one) keeps the count fixed so the median's stability is clearly attributable to order statistics.
sourceClaims: The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it, whereas exploratory methods based on order statistics (such as the median) are robust and not very sensitive to outliers; a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed, where the median or mode would be a better representative
learnerActions: Start with a small set of values on a stated scale (for example reaction times in whole seconds, or scores out of 40) clustered around 4-5, and compute the mean, median, mode and range by hand.
Record all four measures, then take ONE of those values and move it far out to a value the scale allows (for example 30), keeping the number of data points the same.
Recompute the mean and median with the far-out value, and compare each to its value before.
State in words which measure moved a lot and which barely moved, and explain why the mean was dragged while the median held.

If a draggable dot plot with mean, median, mode and range read out live is available, drag one point far from the cluster and watch the mean line chase it while the median stays put or moves at most to a neighbouring value in the cluster (for example, if the dragged point crosses from below the middle to above it) — this makes the differential effect visible in real time.
activities.intendedInsight: The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it a lot; the median, based on order/position, is robust and barely moves. 'Robust' becomes concrete when you see the two measures respond differently to the same far-out value.

activities.title: Same mean, different spread: why centre is not enough
feedback: If the learner concludes the sets are 'the same' from equal means, show the two ranges side by side and ask which class has students scoring far from the average.
If the learner lists the two extreme values instead of the range, ask for the single distance between them (highest − lowest).
If the learner reports only the range and forgets the centre, point out that spread without a centre also fails to describe the data.
activities.rationale: Describing and comparing distributions needs centre and spread together; comparing on an average alone is a frequent error, so building the comparison from both measures targets that gap directly.
sourceClaims: A frequent error is to ignore the spread of data; the intuitive notion of variability concerns how much values differ from each other, and different words (variation, dispersion, spread) are open to different interpretations — so describing data needs an explicit measure of spread

KS3 pupils describe, interpret and compare observed distributions of a single variable through appropriate measures of central tendency (mean, mode, median) and spread (range), including consideration of outliers
learnerActions: Take two data sets (for example two classes' test scores) that have the same mean but clearly different spreads.
Compute the mean and the range (highest minus lowest, a single number) for each set.
Decide whether 'same mean' means the classes performed identically, and justify the answer using the ranges.
Write a conclusion in context that mentions BOTH centre and spread, e.g. 'Both classes scored about the same on average, but Class A was far more consistent.'
If side-by-side dot plots with adjustable spreads at a fixed mean are available, line the two plots up and compare how wide each is while the mean stays equal.
activities.intendedInsight: An average alone does not describe a distribution. Two sets with equal means can differ widely in variability, so a fair comparison reports a measure of centre AND a measure of spread.

activities.title: Which average would you report, and why?
feedback: If the learner defaults to the mean on a skewed set, ask whether that mean sits among most of the values or is pulled toward the tail.
If the learner assumes the mean is always central, have them locate the mean and the bulk of the data on the skewed set and compare.
If the learner picks the mode where values are all distinct numerical measurements, ask whether 'most common' is meaningful here.
activities.rationale: Tying the choice of average to the data's shape confronts the fragmented notions of 'average' and the characteristic error of reporting the mean regardless of skew.
sourceClaims: Students' notions of 'average' fragment into most-frequent-value/mode, reasonable value, midpoint and algorithmic relationship — each true in some circumstances but not others — so which average is appropriate depends on the data

The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it, whereas exploratory methods based on order statistics (such as the median) are robust and not very sensitive to outliers; a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed, where the median or mode would be a better representative
learnerActions: Given a skewed data set (or one with an outlier), compute mean, median and mode and note where each falls.
Choose which average best represents a typical value and write a one-sentence justification tied to the data's shape.
For a most-common / categorical question, decide whether the mode is the right choice and say why.
Check a tempting claim such as 'the mean always sits in the middle of the range' against your skewed data and explain whether it holds.
activities.intendedInsight: The appropriate average depends on the data: the median represents a typical value better for skewed data or data with an outlier; the mode suits most-common / categorical questions; the mean suits roughly symmetric numerical data. Learners' informal notions of 'average' (most frequent, reasonable value, midpoint, algorithm) are each true only in some circumstances.

activities.title: Compute-and-justify checks
feedback: If a comparison answer mentions only averages, prompt: 'What about how spread out each set is?'
If the range is given as two values, require the single difference.
If the learner says the mean and median change equally when the outlier is removed, have them actually recompute both.
activities.rationale: Short scorable items using data sets where the averages genuinely diverge give a check that can catch report-the-mean-regardless and ignore-the-spread errors. Such items verify both procedure and judgement but do not by themselves build the underlying reasoning, which the manipulation and comparison activities develop.
learnerActions: Compute mean, median, mode and range for a given set, stating the range as one number (highest − lowest).
For a skewed set, pick which average best represents it and give the reason.
For two sets, write a conclusion that cites BOTH an average AND the range, so a centre-only comparison is marked incomplete.
For an outlier item, state which of the mean or median changes more when the outlier is removed, and by roughly how much.

Optional: a usable worked set is sleep hours 7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2 (mean 7, median 8, mode 8, range 7), where the outlier 2 pulls the mean DOWN below the cluster — note this direction is opposite to an upward-pulling outlier, and the median stays representative.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct computation plus correct judgement (choice of average, differential outlier effect, centre-and-spread comparison) are both required; getting the arithmetic right is not the same as reasoning about the distribution.

constraints: Use data sets where the three averages genuinely diverge (skewed data or a clear outlier); on near-symmetric data the point about choosing the right average is invisible.
State the measurement context/scale for any example so the outlier is a plausible value on that scale (not off-scale), and match the direction of pull (up or down) to the data.
State the range as a single number (highest − lowest), a measure of spread, not the pair of extreme values.
Always draw conclusions in context (e.g. 'better on average but less consistent') so measures are used to argue, not merely calculated.

A fixed annotated distribution can mark where mean, median and mode fall and label the range as a distance, and is useful as a reference or worked example; because its data cannot be moved, pair it with an activity where learners change the data and watch the measures respond.

Scorable compute-and-justify items can assess both procedure and judgement and can be used during teaching, but recognition/selection responses do not by themselves elicit the independent reasoning that choosing an average and comparing distributions require; include construction and explanation.

An in-role 'data analyst' who argues a naive claim ('same mean, so the classes are identical') for the learner to challenge can surface and sharpen reasoning; use it as a follow-on once learners have manipulated or computed the measures, since dialogue alone does not show the measures changing.
Removing an outlier must be justified by a reason (e.g. a recording error), not done reflexively to tidy the data.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed a live manipulable tool achieves what 'calculation alone cannot', that a static image 'cannot' teach the core idea, and that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to affordances/limits (manipulation makes the differential effect visible; a fixed image serves as reference; single-variable data is one-dimensional so an extra spatial axis is not needed here).

The outlier direction differs between the upward illustration (moving a value to 30) and the original diagnostic (sleep value 2 pulling the mean DOWN). Both are valid; facilitators should ensure the chosen direction matches the data so learners see the correct direction of pull. The concrete sleep dataset (7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2; mean 7, median 8, mode 8, range 7) from the original diagnostic is retained as an optional worked example.

Activity 1 was adjusted to MOVE an existing value far out (count fixed) rather than ADD a value, so the median's robustness is clearly due to order statistics and not to a change in the number of data points. Feedback was corrected so the mean's sensitivity is stated accurately: the sum changes by the displacement and the mean by that displacement divided by the number of values, not by the 'full size' of the value.
Source claims were retained only where they directly support an activity's teaching principle; the fourth activity cites none because no source establishes efficacy of scorable items.
Legacy confidence was 'high'; this has not been independently re-validated here.

probeDeeper: 'The mean is about 7 but one person slept only 2 hours — which number better describes a typical night, and why?' — pushes the skew/outlier → median reasoning into words
'What happens to the mean and to the median if I remove the 2? Which changes more?' — tests the differential effect directly
Counterexample: 'Both classes have a mean of 60 — does that mean they did equally well? What else would you check?' — forces spread into the comparison
'When would the MODE be the best average to report?' — probes appropriateness of measure on a fresh case
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: computes mean, median, mode and range correctly (range = highest − lowest, one number); recognises the 2 as an outlier that drags the MEAN down while the MEDIAN stays representative, and reports the median as the typical value with that reason; and when comparing the two classes uses BOTH an average AND the range/spread ('similar on average but Class A is more consistent'), not the average alone. Seeing the outlier's differential effect and comparing on centre AND spread are the marks of mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Outlier treated as affecting all averages equally, or reported mean regardless of the outlier — not seeing the mean is dragged while the median is robust
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the mean prerequisite: recompute mean and median with and without the outlier so the child sees the mean chase it while the median holds; the mean is influenced by every value, the median is not
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On tasks (1)-(2) the child reports the mean as the typical value despite the 2 pulling it below the cluster, or claims the median is affected as much as the mean, or deletes the 2 without justification

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares two data sets on the average alone, ignoring the spread — concludes two sets with similar means are 'the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront in place: show two sets with equal means but very different ranges and ask 'are these really the same?'; describing a distribution needs centre AND spread
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child bases the conclusion only on the means and does not mention the range/spread, missing that one class is far more variable

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong average for the data's shape — uses the mean for skewed data (or thinks the mean always sits in the middle of the range) rather than the more representative median/mode
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie the choice to the shape: for skewed data or data with an outlier the median represents a typical value better; for most-common/categorical questions the mode; reteach the meaning of the measures via the vocabulary prerequisite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child defaults to the mean without considering that the skew/outlier makes the median more representative, or expects the mean to be central regardless of shape

errorPatterns.pattern: Range as the extremes, not their difference: gives the range as the two end values rather than the single number highest − lowest
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the range as one number — a distance/spread from lowest to highest — by marking both ends and computing the difference; reteach the term via the vocabulary prerequisite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child states the range as '2 to 9' (or names lowest and highest) instead of 7

responseLevels.gap: Computes the measures unreliably or gives the range as two numbers; reports the mean regardless of an outlier; compares two sets on the mean alone
responseLevels.full: Computes all four measures, recognises and explains the outlier's differential pull on mean versus median, chooses the appropriate average for the data's shape, and compares two distributions on BOTH centre and spread — transferring the reasoning to a fresh pair of data sets
responseLevels.partial: Correctly computes mean, median, mode and range, but treats the mean as the average to report regardless of skew/outliers, or compares distributions using centre only — has the procedures without the judgement about which measure fits or that spread matters

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small data set with a clear outlier — e.g. hours of sleep: 7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2 — and a second pair of data sets for comparison (two classes' test scores with similar means but different spreads). Set these tasks and WATCH how they work: (1) 'Find the mean, median, mode and range of the sleep data.' (2) 'Which average best describes a typical night's sleep here? Use it.' (3) 'Compare these two classes and tell me what you can conclude.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not hint that the 2 is an outlier, nor that comparing needs spread as well as an average.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (2) forces the choice of average: a child who reports the mean regardless reveals they don't grasp that an outlier makes it unrepresentative, while a child who has the idea switches to the median and says why. Task (3) is built with similar means but different spreads, so a child comparing on the mean alone concludes 'the same' whereas a child who understands distributions cites the spread. The two separate calculation from the judgement the topic is about.

pedagogy.summary: By Y4, children move from naming shapes by look (van Hiele level 1) to reasoning about defining properties (level 2), and start the class-inclusion idea (level 3): a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) because it has every property a rectangle needs plus the extra property of four equal sides. The obstacle is prototype/partition thinking — a child sorts each shape into exactly one box and rejects a square as a rectangle because it doesn't look like the 'long' rectangle they picture. Teaching works by shifting the question from 'what does it look like?' to 'what tests must it pass?', so category membership is decided by properties, not appearance.
bestPractices: Define categories by an explicit checklist of properties (rectangle = 4 right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) and let children TEST a shape against the checklist rather than judge by eye
Use nested/overlapping Venn or set diagrams so a shape can visibly sit in two categories at once — this attacks the partition assumption that each shape belongs to exactly one box
Deliberately include non-prototypical examples: a square, a rectangle tilted 45°, a very-nearly-square rectangle, so 'rectangle' is not welded to the long-oblong prototype
Contrast examples with non-examples: ask children to draw a quadrilateral that is NOT a rectangle, rhombus, or square, forcing them to reason about which properties are absent
Insist on justification in the child's own words ('it is a rectangle because...') — knowing the shared properties is the point, not the yes/no answer
keyRepresentations: Property checklist / definition card for each category (right-angle marks, equal-side tick marks, parallel arrows)
Nested Venn diagram: quadrilaterals ⊃ rectangles ⊃ squares, with rhombuses overlapping so square sits in the intersection
A 'stretchy' square that can be pulled into an oblong rectangle or squashed to a rhombus, showing square as the special case where both hold
Set-square and ruler to physically verify right angles and equal sides
commonMisconceptions: A square is not a rectangle — they are two different, separate kinds of shape (exclusive/partition thinking)
A rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides, so a square cannot be one (oblong prototype; the unequal-sides attribute is wrongly treated as defining)
A shape can only belong to one category, so it cannot be a rectangle AND a square at the same time
A square turned 45° is a 'diamond', not a square (orientation bound to the prototype)

learn.summary: Help Year 4 children (age 8–9) move from naming quadrilaterals by appearance to deciding category membership by property tests, and begin class-inclusion reasoning: a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) because it passes every rectangle test (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) plus has the extra property of four equal sides. The core obstacle is partition/prototype thinking — a child files each shape in exactly one box and rejects a square as a rectangle because it doesn't match the 'long oblong' they picture. Teaching shifts the question from 'what does it look like?' to 'what tests must it pass?'

activities.title: Sort and stretch: does the shape pass the rectangle tests?
feedback: When a learner says a square is 'too square' to be a rectangle, walk the rectangle checklist together item by item; if it passes every test, the square belongs in the 'rectangle' ring without leaving 'square'.

If a learner thinks a rectangle must have two long and two short sides, show a run of rectangles from very long to nearly square to square, confirming each passes the same tests — length is not a defining property.

If a learner accepts the shared properties yet still won't let one shape be in two categories, offer everyday inclusion analogies (a spaniel is a dog AND an animal at once) and more nested-set practice rather than drilling the yes/no fact.
Reinforce justification: the point is naming the shared properties ('four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel'), not the bare yes/no answer.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable surface lets children test a shape against a visible checklist and watch labels attach or drop as properties change — making 'membership by property, not appearance' concrete. A stretch tool that keeps the 'rectangle' label while dropping the 'square' badge, and nested rings that show one shape in two boxes at once, directly address partition and oblong-prototype thinking. Optional interaction examples (draggable handles, a checklist that ticks green as each test passes, snapping to the deepest qualifying region) make the mechanism tangible but are not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Attributes belonging to a category also belong to all its subcategories (all rectangles have four right angles, so a square, being a rectangle, does too); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
A square is a subclass of rectangle; young children must learn class inclusion and often resist that a square can also be a rectangle
Children reject non-prototypical examples and impose non-defining attributes (e.g. a square is not accepted as a rectangle because a rectangle is expected to have unequal adjacent sides)
'A square is a special type of rectangle... all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares'; guiding questions 'Is a square a special rectangle? Is a rhombus a special kite?'
Y4 pupils should compare and classify geometric shapes, including quadrilaterals, based on their properties and sizes
learnerActions: Take a plain quadrilateral and adjust its corners until all four angles are right angles (check with a set-square); confirm whether opposite sides are equal and parallel.
Run the rectangle checklist item by item — '4 right angles? ✓ opposite sides equal and parallel? ✓' — and place the shape inside the 'rectangle' ring of a nested diagram when it passes all tests.

Now, starting from a rectangle with all four sides equal (a square), pull one pair of opposite sides longer while keeping all four right angles, so the shape stays a rectangle but is no longer a square; then shorten them, still keeping the right angles, until all four sides are equal again and watch it move into the innermost 'square' region nested inside 'rectangle', which is nested inside 'quadrilateral'.
Say out loud, in your own words, why the SAME shape can sit in two boxes at once ('it is a rectangle because... and also a square because...').
Repeat with a rhombus checklist to see the square also sits inside 'rhombus' where the rings overlap.
activities.intendedInsight: Category membership is decided by which property tests a shape passes, not by how it looks; a square passes every rectangle test, so a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) — and one shape can belong to two nested categories at once.

activities.title: Predict, test, explain with a real square
feedback: A correct answer is 'yes — a square is a rectangle: it has four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel, plus its four sides happen to be equal, so it is a special rectangle.'
If a learner judges by appearance ('it's too square-looking') and cannot state the defining properties, build the checklist together and test item by item.
For 'a square turned 45° is a diamond', confirm turning a shape does not change which property tests it passes, so it is still a square and still a rectangle.

When asked to draw a square that is NOT a rectangle, the learner should discover this is impossible: every square passes all the rectangle tests, so no such shape exists — whereas a rectangle that is not a square CAN be drawn. Noticing this one-way asymmetry is the sign of real property-based understanding.
Treat 'it can be a square OR a rectangle but not both' as a maturing class-inclusion stage, not a false fact; give more nested-set experience rather than correction drills.
activities.rationale: A predict–test–explain routine with a physical square, set-square and ruler makes the diagnostic reasoning visible and lets children verify right angles and equal sides themselves. Asking for the reason, not just the answer, discriminates property-based reasoning from a lucky 'yes' backed only by 'both have four sides'.
sourceClaims: A square is a subclass of rectangle; young children must learn class inclusion and often resist that a square can also be a rectangle
Children reject non-prototypical examples and impose non-defining attributes (e.g. a square is not accepted as a rectangle because a rectangle is expected to have unequal adjacent sides)
'A square is a special type of rectangle... all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares'; guiding questions 'Is a square a special rectangle? Is a rhombus a special kite?'
learnerActions: Before testing, predict whether a square 'counts as' a rectangle and say WHY.
Check the square against a rectangle checklist using a set-square and ruler: four right angles? opposite sides equal and parallel?
If the result differs from your prediction, explain what changed your mind.

Answer probing questions: Does it matter how long the sides are? Is a square turned to look like a diamond still a square and still a rectangle? Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square? Can you draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?
Decide whether a square is also a special rhombus, and justify.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before testing exposes prototype thinking; reconciling a 'no, too square' prediction with the square passing every rectangle test is where the concept takes hold. The asymmetry — you can draw a rectangle that is not a square, but not a square that is not a rectangle — is the tell of genuine understanding.

activities.title: Draw the exceptions and defend the claim
feedback: Accept a non-example only when the learner shows a defining property is missing for each category it must be excluded from. Some missing properties exclude only some categories: 'no right angles → not a rectangle or square' still leaves rhombus open, so also check 'the four sides are not all equal → not a rhombus or square'. One missing property can exclude all three: rectangles, rhombuses and squares all have both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so a shape without two pairs of parallel sides (e.g. a kite or trapezium) is none of them.
Accept the inclusion claim only when the learner cites the defining properties the square passes, not just that 'it looks like one' or 'both have four sides'.
If a learner cannot produce a non-prototypical rectangle, offer tilted and nearly-square examples and have them verify each against the checklist.
activities.rationale: Contrasting examples with non-examples forces attention to defining versus non-defining attributes, and justification in the child's own words is the learning target. An in-role classifier who presses 'but it doesn't look like a rectangle — why does it still count?' surfaces and names the reasoning; dialogue here supports the property inspection rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Children reject non-prototypical examples and impose non-defining attributes (e.g. a square is not accepted as a rectangle because a rectangle is expected to have unequal adjacent sides)
Y4 pupils should compare and classify geometric shapes, including quadrilaterals, based on their properties and sizes

Attributes belonging to a category also belong to all its subcategories (all rectangles have four right angles, so a square, being a rectangle, does too); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
learnerActions: Draw a quadrilateral that is NOT a rectangle, rhombus, or square, and say which defining property it is missing for EACH of those three categories.
Draw a rectangle that is not a square.
Explain to a sceptical 'shape detective' why a square still counts as a rectangle even though it doesn't look like a long oblong, citing the defining properties it passes.
Sort a mixed set of quadrilaterals (including a square, a 45°-tilted rectangle, and a nearly-square rectangle) into a nested/overlapping Venn, justifying each placement by properties.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning about which properties are ABSENT (for non-examples) and which are PRESENT (for inclusion) consolidates definition-based classification and loosens the oblong prototype.

constraints: Target concept is property-based classification and class inclusion, not shape naming; always require justification by defining properties, not a bare yes/no.

A scored sort/multiple-choice can assess whether a child accepts the inclusion (e.g. 'Is a square a rectangle?' with distractor 'No, they are different shapes') but does not by itself let the child feel a square pass the tests; use it to check, not to build, the insight.

A static tap-to-reveal Venn or hierarchy is a useful summary/reference showing where a square sits, but because nothing recomputes the child cannot TEST a shape's membership; best used after hands-on testing rather than as the primary route.

Distinguish an ideal zero-thickness plane figure from physical card/cutouts, which have slight thickness and can be held and turned; treat cutouts as approximations of the represented flat shape and ask about the mathematical shape represented, not whether the physical card can be picked up. Quadrilateral classification is a planar, 2D property idea, so a third spatial dimension is not needed here (a limit of relevance, not evidence that any one medium is superior).
Treat the one-box (class-inclusion) stage as developmental: give more nested-set and everyday-inclusion experience rather than drilling the fact.
Set-square/ruler verification and recolouring/ticking checklists are optional supports to make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (National Curriculum Year 4 Geometry) is marked verified:false in the row; treat that claim with corresponding caution.

The row frames the topic as Year 4 (age 8–9) while citing Common Core 5.G.3/5.G.4 (Grade 5) for hierarchy/subcategory attributes; this grade-band mismatch is a migration ambiguity, though the inclusion content is consistent with the stated evidence targets.

The original 'poor fit / 3D adds nothing' and 'static image can only reference, cannot teach' framings were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; catalog fit rankings and product/tool-type labels were removed. No claim of one medium's superiority is intended.
The 'diamond' probe is retained as a counterexample: turning a shape does not change which property tests it passes, so a tilted square remains both a square and a rectangle.

The 'draw a square that is not a rectangle' probe is deliberately impossible; feedback now states this explicitly so the task is used to reveal the one-way asymmetry, not left as an answerable request.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a square and ask the child to PREDICT whether it will 'count as' a rectangle — and to say WHY before testing. Then together OBSERVE: check the square against a rectangle checklist using a set-square and ruler — four right angles? opposite sides equal and parallel? It passes every test. Ask the child to EXPLAIN why the result differs from a prediction of 'no'. The stated reason before testing is the diagnostic part; a child who predicted 'no, it's too square' must now reconcile that with the square passing every rectangle test.
probeDeeper: 'You said a rectangle has four right angles and opposite sides equal — does it matter how long the sides are?' (pushes them to see length is not a defining property)
'Here is the square turned to look like a diamond — is it still a square? Is it still a rectangle?' (counterexample against orientation binding)
'Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square? Now can you draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?' (the second is impossible — the asymmetry is the tell of real understanding)
'A square has four equal sides and four right angles — is it also a special rhombus? Why?' (transfer to the second inclusion)
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — a square is a rectangle. A rectangle needs four right angles and opposite sides that are equal and parallel; a square has all of those, plus its four sides happen to be equal too, so it is a special kind of rectangle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Exclusive/partition thinking: 'a square is not a rectangle — they're two different shapes' (each shape belongs in exactly one box)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build a rectangle property checklist together and test the square against it item by item; use a nested Venn so the child sees the square can sit inside 'rectangle' without leaving 'square'. Reteach in place — this is the target concept.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a square and a rectangle are different kinds of shape
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no' and, on the reason tier, treats square and rectangle as separate named categories rather than comparing properties

errorPatterns.pattern: Oblong prototype: 'a rectangle has two long sides and two short sides, so a square can't be one' (the unequal-sides look is wrongly treated as a defining property)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate defining properties (right angles, opposite sides equal/parallel) from typical appearance; show a range of rectangles from very long to nearly square to square so the prototype loosens. Revisit shape-property work.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the reason tier gives a definition of rectangle that requires it to be longer than it is wide

errorPatterns.pattern: One-box assumption: accepts that a square and a rectangle share properties yet still won't let one shape belong to two categories at once
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill the yes/no fact. Give more nested-set experience (Venn diagrams, 'all squares are inside the rectangle ring') and everyday inclusion analogies (a spaniel is a dog and an animal at once) so the inclusion logic matures; it self-corrects with exposure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says something like 'it can be a square OR a rectangle but not both' — a class-inclusion (part–whole) reasoning stage rather than a false fact

responseLevels.gap: Says a square is not a rectangle, or judges purely by appearance ('it's too square-looking'); cannot state the properties that define a rectangle.
responseLevels.full: Says yes and argues that the square passes every defining test of a rectangle (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) and is therefore a special rectangle; extends the same reasoning to 'special rhombus', and can draw a quadrilateral that belongs to none of the subcategories.
responseLevels.partial: Says yes and can list shared features ('both have four sides / four corners') but does not use the defining properties to justify inclusion, and cannot transfer to 'square is a special rhombus' or explain why a rectangle need not be a square.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a square (and, alongside, an oblong rectangle). Ask: 'Is this square also a rectangle?' — then, whatever they answer: 'How do you know? What makes something a rectangle?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning from defining properties says yes and can name the rectangle tests the square passes. A child reasoning from appearance/prototype says no because the square doesn't look like the 'long' rectangle. The reason tier is decisive: a lucky 'yes' backed only by 'they both have four sides' is not mastery, and a confident 'no, a rectangle has to be longer than it is wide' exposes the prototype directly. Correct reasoning and prototype reasoning give genuinely different answers to 'what makes something a rectangle?'

sources.claim: Attributes belonging to a category also belong to all its subcategories (all rectangles have four right angles, so a square, being a rectangle, does too); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Geometry 5.G.3 and 5.G.4

sources.claim: A square is a subclass of rectangle; young children must learn class inclusion and often resist that a square can also be a rectangle
sources.source: Stanford DREME — 'What Children Know and Need to Learn about Shape and Space'

sources.claim: Children reject non-prototypical examples and impose non-defining attributes (e.g. a square is not accepted as a rectangle because a rectangle is expected to have unequal adjacent sides)
sources.source: Yeşildağ-Hasançebi & Halat (2016), prototype and imposed-attribute obstacles in quadrilateral classification, EJMSTE

sources.claim: 'A square is a special type of rectangle... all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares'; guiding questions 'Is a square a special rectangle? Is a rhombus a special kite?'
sources.source: NRICH — 'Completing Quadrilaterals'

sources.claim: Y4 pupils should compare and classify geometric shapes, including quadrilaterals, based on their properties and sizes
