pedagogy.summary: Children measure area by covering a figure with unit squares and counting them — in square centimetres, square metres, square inches or square feet — including irregular and L-shaped figures, and compare two shapes by their counts. The counting must be of the squares that COVER the interior with no gaps or overlaps (not the boundary), done systematically so every square is counted once, with the answer stated in square units.
bestPractices: Cover the whole interior with unit squares, no gaps or overlaps, and count the covering squares — not the squares around the edge.
Count systematically (row by row, or decompose an L-shape into rectangles) so no square is missed or double-counted.
Use real square-unit tiles (square-centimetre tiles on a book cover) before squared-paper diagrams.
Compare areas of two shapes directly by their counts.
Always state the area in square units (square cm, square m).
Keep to whole unit squares at this stage; treat part-squares informally rather than with a formula.
keyRepresentations: Square-centimetre tiles covering a book cover
L-shaped and irregular figures on squared paper
A shape decomposed into rectangles for systematic counting
A count recorded with its square unit (e.g. '18 square cm')
commonMisconceptions: Counts the squares around the boundary (perimeter) instead of the squares covering the interior.
Leaves gaps or overlaps, or counts unsystematically so squares are missed or double-counted (especially on L-shapes).
Counts every partly-covered square at the edge as a whole square, overestimating.
Gives the count as a bare number without the square unit.

learn.summary: Children measure area by covering a figure's interior with unit squares — no gaps or overlaps — and counting the covering squares systematically, stating the answer in square units (square cm, square m, square in, square ft). Work includes irregular and L-shaped figures (decomposed into rectangles), comparing two shapes by their counts, and telling the area (every covering square, including the squares along the inner edge) apart from the length of the boundary (unit lengths around the outline, i.e. perimeter) and from a count of only the border squares. Concrete tiles on a real surface precede squared-paper diagrams. Keep to whole unit squares at this stage, treating edge part-squares informally.

activities.title: Tile and count an L-shaped garden
feedback: If a child counts only the squares along the border, point out that the border squares are part of the covering but the squares further in must be counted too; shade the whole interior, border squares included, and recount every covering square. If they count unit lengths around the outline instead, explain that this is the distance around (perimeter), not the area.
If tiles leave gaps or overlap, or recounting gives a different total, cover fully with no gaps/overlaps and count row by row or by decomposing into rectangles, marking each square as it is counted.
If they lose track in the L's notch, decompose the L into two rectangles and count each separately, then add.
If they give '18' with no unit, treat the answer as incomplete and build the habit of naming the square unit — the counting itself is sound.
activities.rationale: Covering a region with no gaps or overlaps and counting the whole unit squares, including decomposing rectilinear (L-shaped) figures into rectangles, is the Grade-3 area practice described in the source progressions. Making the systematic covering the act the child performs targets the gap/overlap and edge-counting difficulties directly.
sourceClaims: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.

When iterating units children may leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering a region with no gaps; L-shaped (rectilinear) figures are decomposed into rectangles, and coordinating the covering requires spatial structuring that develops with many array activities.
learnerActions: Cover an L-shaped figure's whole interior with unit squares so there are no gaps and no overlaps, including the awkward squares inside the notch of the L.
Count the covering squares systematically — row by row, or by splitting the L into two rectangles and counting each — marking each square as you count it so none is missed or double-counted.
State the result in square units, e.g. '18 square cm' or in square metres, not just a bare number.
Repeat with a plain rectangle and then compare two shapes side by side, deciding which covers more by comparing their counts.
activities.intendedInsight: Area is the count of unit squares that cover the inside of a shape — notches and all — and is about the surface inside, not the fence or distance running around the edge.

activities.title: Tile a real surface before squared paper
feedback: If tiles overlap or leave bare patches, rearrange so they tile the surface completely and evenly before counting.
If the paper-diagram count differs from the count of physical tiles, line the two up and check that each paper square stands for exactly one tile.
activities.rationale: The progressions describe starting from covering with a two-dimensional unit; using real square-unit tiles on a concrete surface before abstract squared-paper diagrams is intended to ground the covering idea, though the cited sources do not establish the ordering's comparative efficacy.
sourceClaims: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.
learnerActions: Lay square-centimetre tiles across a small real surface such as a book cover, filling it with no gaps or overlaps; if strips narrower than a tile are left at the edges, note them informally as part-squares rather than counting them as whole tiles.
Count the tiles and say the area in square centimetres.
Then move to a squared-paper diagram of the same shape drawn at the same size (one paper square for each tile) and count the covering squares there.
activities.intendedInsight: Measuring area means physically covering a surface with equal square units and counting them; the squared-paper diagram is a picture of that same covering.

activities.title: Compare and check with quick counting questions
feedback: If a child picks the answer that comes from counting only the border squares, show that the inside squares were left out: the area includes every covering square, the border squares and the ones further in.
For part-squares at an edge, discuss them informally — do not count every touched square as a whole one, and do not apply a formula at this stage.
activities.rationale: Checking understanding with comparison and count items, including an edge-counting distractor, surfaces the boundary-counting difficulty; such questions verify understanding rather than build the systematic covering, so pair them with hands-on tiling. The part-square figure is used for discussion, not a scored count, because whole-square counting is the Grade-3 focus.
sourceClaims: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.
learnerActions: Given two shapes on squared paper, decide which covers more area by counting each one's squares.

Answer a short set of count-the-squares questions using whole-square figures — a plain rectangle and an L-shape, each with a definite count — then separately look at one shape with part-squares at the edge and discuss (rather than score) how to handle the part-squares informally.

Watch for a tempting wrong answer that comes from counting only the border squares (or the unit lengths around the outline) instead of all the squares covering the inside, and explain why it is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing areas means comparing counts of all the covering squares, edge squares included; counting only the border squares does not give the area, and the distance around the outline (perimeter) is a different thing from the area inside.

activities.title: Read a finished counted figure
feedback: Use this reference to contrast with a child's own counting — ask them to point to any square they counted that the reference did not, and discuss.
activities.rationale: A static filled figure with the count shown illustrates the target result and can prompt discussion, but it cannot rehearse the systematic gap-free counting itself, so it serves as a worked reference rather than the main practice.
learnerActions: Study a figure already filled with unit squares and its revealed count, e.g. '18 square cm'.
Retrace which squares were counted and confirm every square inside the outline, including those along the edge, is counted exactly once, and nothing outside the outline is counted.
Say back how the count and unit were obtained.
activities.intendedInsight: A completed, correctly counted figure models what a finished area measurement looks like: every interior square counted once, with the square unit named.

constraints: Count every square that covers the inside of the outline, with no gaps or overlaps — including the squares along the edge, which are part of the area. Do not count only the border squares, and do not count squares outside the outline. The distance around the outline (perimeter, measured in unit lengths) is a different kind of quantity from an area count.
Count systematically (row by row, or by decomposing an L-shape into rectangles) so each square is counted exactly once.
Always state the area in square units (square cm, square m, etc.); a bare number is an incomplete answer.

Keep to whole unit squares at this stage; treat edge part-squares informally (e.g. pairing two halves) and do NOT drill a part-square formula yet — part-square figures are for discussion, not scored counts.
Real tiles and squared-paper diagrams each support learning differently — tiles ground the physical covering, diagrams abstract it; neither is claimed as universally necessary.
A revealed static figure is a reference/scaffold: it shows the result but does not let the child practise the covering and counting, so it should not replace hands-on tiling.
A count-the-squares check verifies understanding and can catch edge-counting, but does not by itself build the systematic covering skill.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row framed the boundary-counting misconception as a total that 'matches the perimeter'. A count of boundary squares is not generally equal to the perimeter (a length); learner-facing text uses an inside-vs-around distinction without asserting a numeric match. This original imprecision was not re-verified against sources.

The source row rated a 3D scene 'poor' (risk of conflating area with volume) and a conversation 'poor'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped rather than asserted as universal claims. A spoken discussion of what was counted remains valuable (see the probe questions).

Interactive affordances from the source (tiles greying out when counted to prevent double-counting, uncovered cells flashing, a running square-unit tally, side-by-side compare mode) are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory requirements.

The source claim supports covering with a two-dimensional unit but does not directly establish the concrete-tiles-before-diagram ordering's efficacy; that ordering is retained as curriculum best practice with hedged wording.

'18 square cm' is used only as an illustrative label, not a computed answer to verify; boundary vs interior counting, no-gaps/no-overlaps covering, L-shape decomposition, and informal handling of part-squares (as discussion rather than scored counts) are internally consistent.

probeDeeper: Show me which squares you counted — the ones inside the shape, or the ones around the edge?
This L-shape — how did you make sure you counted every square once and none twice?
There are some half-squares at the edge here — what did you do with those?
You said 18 — 18 what? What is the unit for area?
assess.correctAnswer: The child covers each interior with unit squares (no gaps or overlaps) and counts them systematically — decomposing the L-shape so every square is counted once — gives the count in square units (e.g. '18 square cm'), handles edge part-squares sensibly rather than as whole units, and compares two shapes by their counts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the boundary, not the interior: counts squares around the edge (perimeter) rather than the squares covering the surface.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to what area means — the surface covered; shade the interior and count only covering squares, contrasting with the distance around.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to and counts the squares along the border; the total matches the perimeter, not the area.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gaps/overlaps or unsystematic counting: covers with gaps or overlaps, or counts without a system so squares are missed or double-counted, especially on the L-shape.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cover fully with no gaps/overlaps and count row by row or by decomposing into rectangles, marking each square as counted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tiles don't fully cover or overlap; recounting gives a different total; loses track in the L's notch.

errorPatterns.pattern: Part-squares counted as whole: counts each partly-covered edge square as a full square, overestimating the area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill a part-square formula at this stage — Grade-3 area focuses on whole unit squares; use whole-square shapes and treat part-squares informally (pair two halves) until later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Every touched square counted as one; total inflated on the irregular figure.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the square unit: gives the count as a bare number ('18') without 'square cm'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat an area answer without a square unit as incomplete; build the habit of naming the unit; the counting is sound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct count, no unit; supplies it only when asked.

responseLevels.gap: Counts the boundary/perimeter, leaves gaps or overlaps, or gives a bare number with no square unit.
responseLevels.full: Systematically counts every covering unit square once (decomposing the L-shape), handles part-squares sensibly, compares areas by their counts, and states the area in square units.
responseLevels.partial: Counts the covering squares correctly for a plain rectangle but loses systematicity on the L-shape (double-counts or misses) or mishandles part-squares — succeeds in the clean case but not the irregular one.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a few figures on squared paper — a plain rectangle, an L-shape, and one with part-squares at the edge — plus a book cover and square-centimetre tiles. Say: 'Find the area of each by counting.' Watch whether they count the covering squares or the boundary, whether they cover with no gaps/overlaps and count systematically, what they do with part-squares, and whether they state the unit.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands area counts the interior covering squares once each and names the square unit; a child who does not counts the boundary, leaves gaps/overlaps, double-counts on the L-shape, treats part-squares as whole, or drops the unit — each visible in the counting.

sources.claim: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.
sources.source: Common Core Progressions — K–5 Geometric Measurement (2012), Grade 3 (3.MD.6) (ISBE mirror)

sources.claim: When iterating units children may leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering a region with no gaps; L-shaped (rectilinear) figures are decomposed into rectangles, and coordinating the covering requires spatial structuring that develops with many array activities.
sources.source: Common Core Progressions — K–5 Geometric Measurement (2012), Grade 3 (3.MD.7d) & measurement difficulties (ISBE mirror)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; know and use the vocabulary of prime, prime factor and composite numbers; establish whether a number up to 100 is prime; recall primes up to 19.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'know and use the vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factors and composite numbers'; 'establish whether a number up to 100 is prime and recall prime numbers up to 19'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 — 'determine whether a given whole number in the range 1–100 is prime or composite.'
• Operational details — the definition is exact-and-fragile: a prime has EXACTLY two factors (1 and itself); composite has more than two; and 1 is NEITHER (only one factor) — a point pupils routinely get wrong. Build primeness ON factor-finding: a prime is a number whose only rectangle is 1×n (one factor pair). To test primality efficiently, check divisibility only by primes up to the square root (test 97: not ÷2,3,5,7 → prime). Divisibility rules (2,3,5,10) accelerate this. Recall of primes to 19 (2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19) should be memorised. Seeds prime factorisation, HCF/LCM.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): state the definition and list primes to 19. Tier B (age 9–10): determine whether a number like 51 is prime and justify (51=3×17 → composite). Tier C (age 10): explain why 1 is not prime and use square-root-bounded checking to test a number like 97.
bestPractices: Define prime as EXACTLY two factors and build it on factor-finding — a prime is a number with only the 1×n rectangle — so the definition is grounded, not memorised.
Address the '1 is prime' misconception head-on: 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
Teach efficient primality testing — check divisibility by primes up to the square root — supported by divisibility rules for 2, 3, 5.
Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square to reveal the primes and why multiples are composite.
Require justification ('51 = 3×17 so it's composite'), not just a prime/composite label; memorise primes to 19.
keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array — a prime makes only the 1×n rectangle (one factor pair)
Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square — crossing out multiples leaves the primes
Factor list / factor rainbow — counting factors to classify
Divisibility-rule checks up to the square root
commonMisconceptions: Believing 1 is prime (it has only one factor — it is neither).
Thinking all odd numbers are prime (9, 15, 21, 51 are composite) or that 2 isn't prime because it's even.
Classifying by 'feel' without checking factors/divisibility.
Checking divisibility inefficiently (testing all numbers, not just primes to the square root).
Confusing 'prime factor' with 'factor' — not every factor is prime.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning prime, prime factor and composite numbers: establish whether a number up to 100 is prime and recall the primes to 19. Primeness is grounded on factor-finding — a prime is a number whose only rectangle is 1×n (exactly two factors: 1 and itself); composite has more than two; 1 is neither because it has only one factor. Learners build this through rectangle-building, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, efficient square-root-bounded divisibility testing, and justified classification (e.g. 51 = 3×17 → composite), with checkable recall and reasoning to confirm the definition they actually hold.

activities.title: Rectangle-building: when is only 1×n possible?
feedback: If a learner calls 51 prime, prompt: try arranging the counters into 3 equal rows — do they fill? (3×17 = 51, so it is composite.)
If a learner says 1 is prime, point to the single 1×1 square: that is only one factor, and a prime needs exactly two, so 1 is neither.

When 97 forms only the 1×97 line after testing the primes up to its square root, confirm: since any larger factor would pair with a smaller one already tested, no other rectangle is possible, so its only factors are 1 and 97 and it is prime.
activities.rationale: Building primeness on factor-finding with a concrete rectangle/array model grounds the definition rather than leaving it memorised, and lets learners see directly why 1 is neither.
sourceClaims: Prime should be defined as exactly two factors (1 is neither); the Sieve of Eratosthenes and square-root-bounded divisibility testing support efficient classification.
learnerActions: Take a number and try to arrange that many counters (or squares on grid paper) into complete rectangles with more than one row and more than one column (a single line, 1×n, does not count as another rectangle).
For 51, find that a 3×17 rectangle can be built, so 51 has factors other than 1 and itself — it is composite.

For 97, try rows of 2, 3, 5 and 7 — the primes up to its square root (just under 10), since any larger factor would pair with a smaller one already tested — and find that only a single 1×97 line forms, so 97 is prime.
Try the number 1: it forms only a single 1×1 square — one factor — so it fits neither the prime nor the composite group.
Record each verdict with its factor pair as justification (e.g. '51 = 3×17, composite'; '97, only 1×97, prime').
activities.intendedInsight: A prime number can only be made into the 1×n rectangle (exactly two factors); a composite makes at least one other rectangle; and 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only a single factor.

activities.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square
feedback: If a learner expects to keep crossing out past 7 to find the primes under 100, note that once multiples of primes up to √100 = 10 are removed (2, 3, 5, 7), the survivors other than 1 are already prime.
If a learner crosses out 2 itself, remind them to circle (keep) the first number and cross out only its later multiples.
activities.rationale: The sieve reveals why multiples are composite and leaves the primes visible, connecting classification to divisibility structure.
sourceClaims: Prime should be defined as exactly two factors (1 is neither); the Sieve of Eratosthenes and square-root-bounded divisibility testing support efficient classification.
learnerActions: On a 1–100 grid, first cross out 1 (it is neither prime nor composite), then circle 2 and cross out every later multiple of 2.
Move to the next uncrossed number (3) and cross out its multiples; repeat for 5, then 7.

Notice that the numbers still standing (circled or uncrossed) are exactly the primes, and that every number crossed out as a multiple is a multiple of a smaller prime, so it is composite (1 was crossed out separately because it is neither).
Highlight the primes up to 19 (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19) for memorisation.
activities.intendedInsight: Composite numbers are exactly the multiples that get crossed out; once 1 is set aside as neither, the survivors are the primes. This also makes the primes to 19 visible for recall.

activities.title: Efficient primality testing to the square root
feedback: If a learner keeps testing divisors above the square root, explain that any factor larger than √n would pair with one smaller than √n, which would already have been found.
If a learner tests every number rather than just primes, note that a composite divisor (e.g. 4) is already covered by its prime factor (2).
activities.rationale: Square-root-bounded checking with divisibility rules gives an efficient, reasoned method for establishing primality rather than exhaustive trial.
sourceClaims: Prime should be defined as exactly two factors (1 is neither); the Sieve of Eratosthenes and square-root-bounded divisibility testing support efficient classification.
learnerActions: To test whether a whole number greater than 1 is prime, divide only by the primes 2, 3, 5, 7… up to its square root (1 is neither prime nor composite, so it is not tested this way).
Use divisibility shortcuts: even → ÷2; digit sum divisible by 3 → ÷3; ends in 0 or 5 → ÷5.
Test 97: not even, digit sum 16 (not divisible by 3), does not end in 0/5, not divisible by 7 — and since the next prime 11 has 11×11 = 121 > 97, there is no need to test further, so 97 is prime.
Test 51: digit sum 5+1 = 6, divisible by 3, so 51 = 3×17 → composite.
activities.intendedInsight: For a whole number greater than 1, you only need to check divisibility by primes up to the square root; if none divide the number, it is prime. Divisibility rules make this fast.

activities.title: Classify and justify, including the tricky cases
feedback: If a learner calls 51 prime because it is odd and unfamiliar, prompt them to check the digit sum (6) → divisible by 3 → 51 = 3×17, composite.
If a learner says 2 is not prime because it is even, point out it has exactly two factors (1 and 2), which is the definition — evenness is irrelevant.
If a learner calls 9 prime, prompt 9 = 3×3, so it has a third factor (3) beyond 1 and 9, making it composite.
If a learner confuses 'prime factor' with 'factor', note that 51's factors are 1, 3, 17, 51, but its prime factors are only 3 and 17.
activities.rationale: Direct, justified classification confronts the most common misconceptions (1 is prime, odd=prime, 2 isn't prime) and distinguishes factor from prime factor.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils know and use the vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factors and composite numbers; establish whether a number up to 100 is prime; recall primes up to 19.
4.OA.4 requires determining whether a whole number 1–100 is prime or composite.
learnerActions: Sort numbers into three groups: prime, composite, and neither — placing 1 in 'neither'.
Decide whether 51 is prime or composite and justify using a factor pair (51 = 3×17 → composite).
Explain why 2 is prime (exactly two factors) even though it is even, and why 9, 15, 21 and 51 are composite even though they are odd.
List all primes up to 19 from memory and state for each why it is prime.
activities.intendedInsight: Classification requires checking factors, not 'feel': parity does not decide primeness, 1 is neither, and every classification needs a factor justification.

activities.title: Prove it: Socratic justification challenge
feedback: If the learner says they must test all numbers up to 96, guide them to the square-root bound and to testing only primes.
If the learner struggles to say why 1 is neither, return them to the rectangle/factor count: one factor only.
Accept a correct verdict only when it comes with a factor-based justification, not just a label.
activities.rationale: A discussion/justification task surfaces the actual definition a learner holds and builds efficient-testing reasoning; it complements the concrete rectangle and sieve work.
learnerActions: Respond to the question 'How could you prove 97 is prime without checking every number below it?' by describing which divisors you need to test and why.
Explain in your own words why 1 is neither prime nor composite.
Argue whether a classmate who called 51 prime is right, and show the check that settles it.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate and defend the reasoning — which divisors to test, why 1 is neither, how to catch a false positive like 51 — shows the definition is genuinely held.

constraints: A pre-made, tap-to-reveal hundred square and definition card are useful as a reference and primes-to-19 memory aid, but do not let the learner test arbitrary numbers or run the sieve themselves; use them alongside, not instead of, hands-on building.

Multiple-choice or categorisation tasks (prime / composite / neither, 'is 51 prime?') verify recognition and recall but do not by themselves build the rectangle/sieve intuition; pair recognition with construction and justification.
Always require a factor justification ('51 = 3×17 so composite'), not just a prime/composite label.
Distinguish 'factor' from 'prime factor': not every factor is prime.
The definition is exact and fragile — a prime has exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself); 1 has only one factor and is neither; 2 is prime despite being even.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-review self-audit of arithmetic/logic: 51 = 3×17 (digit sum 6, divisible by 3) — correct. 97 is prime (not divisible by 2,3,5,7; next prime 11, 11²=121>97; √97≈9.85) — correct. 97 digit sum = 16, not divisible by 3 — correct. √100=10, so sieving multiples of primes up to 10 (2,3,5,7) suffices for numbers to 100 — correct. 9 = 3×3 has three factors; 51 has factors 1,3,17,51 with prime factors 3,17 — correct. All checked and consistent.

The legacy source characterised a static hundred square as unable to let a child test arbitrary numbers, and characterised 3D as adding 'no insight'; these catalog-fit judgements are reframed as affordance/limit notes rather than universal claims, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy, necessity, or medium superiority.

The US standard claim (4.OA.4) and the NCETM guidance claim are marked verified:false in the source row; they are retained only because they align with established curriculum conventions and the core definition, and their evidentiary weight should be treated as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: What exactly makes a number prime — how many factors must it have?
How could you test 51 for a factor other than 1 and 51?
Is 2 a prime number? Is 9? What does that say about 'odd means prime'?
List the prime numbers up to 19 — how do you know each one is prime?
assess.correctAnswer: 51 is composite, not prime, because it has factors other than 1 and itself: 51 = 3 × 17. A child reasoning correctly defines prime as having EXACTLY two factors (1 and itself) and shows 51 fails because 3 divides it.

errorPatterns.pattern: judges primeness by 'odd and not a number I recognise' — calls 51 prime because it's odd and not in the obvious tables
errorPatterns.nextMove: test 51 ÷ 3 = 17 (digit sum 6 flags divisibility by 3); primeness is about factors, not familiarity.
errorPatterns.distractor: 51 is prime because it is odd and not in the times tables I know
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child declares 51 prime citing oddness/unfamiliarity, without testing divisibility by 3

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks a prime has exactly ONE factor, or that primes are 'numbers you can't make by timesing' without pinning the two-factor definition
errorPatterns.nextMove: state precisely: exactly TWO distinct factors, 1 and itself; 1 has only one factor so is not prime.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: definition given is vague or off (‘only divisible by itself’, forgetting 1; or ‘one factor’)

errorPatterns.pattern: believes all odd numbers are prime / all primes are odd (so misses that 2 is prime, 9 and 51 are not)
errorPatterns.nextMove: counterexamples: 2 is an even prime; 9 = 3×3 is odd but composite; parity is irrelevant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child links prime to odd; would call 9 or 15 prime and 2 composite

responseLevels.gap: declares 51 prime on the strength of oddness/unfamiliarity, or cannot define prime correctly.
responseLevels.full: defines prime as exactly two factors, tests 51 and finds 3×17 so classifies it composite, handles 1 and 2 correctly, and recalls primes to 19.
responseLevels.partial: defines prime as two factors but doesn't systematically test 51 (misses the ÷3), or is shaky on 1 and 2 as special cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 51 a prime number or a composite number? Decide, and then explain how you know — what makes a number prime, and what did you check for 51?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 51 looks prime (odd, not obviously in a small table) and is a classic false-positive. A child who checks divisibility properly (digit sum 5+1 = 6, divisible by 3) catches it; one who judges by 'odd and unfamiliar = prime' declares it prime. The reason tier exposes the definition they actually hold.

sources.claim: Y5 pupils know and use the vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factors and composite numbers; establish whether a number up to 100 is prime; recall primes up to 19.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Year 5 Number — multiplication and division

sources.claim: 4.OA.4 requires determining whether a whole number 1–100 is prime or composite.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 4, Operations & Algebraic Thinking (4.OA.B.4)

sources.claim: Prime should be defined as exactly two factors (1 is neither); the Sieve of Eratosthenes and square-root-bounded divisibility testing support efficient classification.
sources.source: NCETM primes and factors guidance

pedagogy.summary: At 9-11 gravity graduates from the intuitive 'things fall down' to a directional, universal FORCE: Earth pulls every object toward its CENTRE, so 'down' is not one fixed direction in the universe but 'toward the centre of the sphere' — which is why people all around the globe are all pulled 'down' toward the middle and nobody falls off. The same pulling force reaches out to hold the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun. The load-bearing shifts are (1) down = toward Earth's centre (a local, radial direction, not absolute), and (2) gravity is a long-reach attraction that also causes orbits — not something that switches off in space.
bestPractices: Confront the 'people fall off the bottom' puzzle head-on using a globe with figures stuck all around it: each person's feet point to the centre, so every one of them experiences 'down' as toward the middle — there is no universal up/down in space.

Build the argument from evidence (the NGSS framing): unsupported objects always fall toward Earth, and they fall toward the centre wherever you are on the planet — use this pattern to argue that Earth's gravity is directed inward/down.
Extend gravity's reach explicitly to orbits: the SAME pull that drops a ball also holds the Moon to Earth and planets to the Sun — gravity acts across empty space and does not need air or contact.

Directly reframe 'no gravity in space': astronauts float because they are in continual free-fall around Earth (Earth's gravity is still strong there), not because gravity has vanished — heading off the most common upper-primary error.
Keep it qualitative and directional at this age: gravity as a pulling force with a direction (toward the centre); reserve mass-vs-weight formalism and F–m–a for KS3.
keyRepresentations: Globe cross-section with stick-figures placed all around the rim, each with a 'down' arrow pointing to the centre
Dropped-object trails on a sphere: from any starting point the object heads toward Earth's centre
Newton's-cannonball style picture: turn the pull off and the Moon flies off in a straight line; turn it on and it curves into orbit
Sun-at-centre orbit diagram with gravity arrows from each planet pointing at the Sun
Free-fall astronaut image labelled 'still lots of gravity — falling around Earth', not 'zero gravity'
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 'down' is a single absolute direction in the universe, so people on the 'other side' of the globe should fall off — not grasping that down means toward Earth's centre for everyone.
Believing there is NO gravity in space, or that astronauts float because gravity has switched off — rather than being in continual free-fall/orbit with gravity still acting.
Thinking gravity needs air (an atmosphere) to work, so it couldn't act in the vacuum of space or on the airless Moon.
Assuming gravity only acts on things that are falling or unsupported, not realising it acts on everything all the time (including things at rest and objects in orbit).
Not connecting the everyday 'falling' force with the force that holds the Moon and planets in orbit — treating them as unrelated.
Believing heavier objects are pulled much harder and so always fall noticeably faster (the Aristotelian attractor), ignoring air resistance as the real everyday difference.

learn.summary: Help 9-11 year-olds reframe gravity from the intuitive 'things fall down' to a directional, universal pulling force: Earth attracts every object toward its CENTRE, so 'down' is not a single fixed cosmic direction but 'toward the centre of the sphere' for everyone — which is why people all around the globe stay firmly on the ground and nobody falls off. The same long-reach pull holds the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun, acting across empty space with no need for air or contact. Keep it qualitative and directional at this age; reserve mass-vs-weight formalism and F=ma for later. Core misconceptions to confront: 'down' as absolute (so the far side falls off), 'no gravity in space', gravity needing air, gravity only acting on falling/unsupported things, and heavier objects always falling noticeably faster.

activities.title: Everyone's 'down' points to the centre
feedback: If a learner says the far-side person is upside-down and could fall off: place figures all the way around the globe and draw each one's 'down' arrow — every arrow points to the centre, so nobody is upside-down relative to their own ground.

Prompt: 'If you dug a tunnel straight down from Britain and from Australia, would the tunnels point the same way in space, or nearly opposite ways?' (Nearly opposite ways — Australia isn't exactly opposite Britain — yet both are 'down' because both head to the centre.)
Reinforce: a child in Australia feels their feet firmly on the ground just as you do; there is no single fixed 'down' for the whole universe.
activities.rationale: The pivotal idea is a spatial RELATIONSHIP that convinces best when the learner places people anywhere on a sphere and sees every 'down' arrow re-aim at the centre, then sees (on screen) dropped objects all fall inward. This builds the argument from a repeatable pattern rather than assertion. A physical ball/globe and a cross-section diagram both carry the argument; an interactive version lets learners test 'what if I stand here?'
sourceClaims: Grade-5 standard: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS2-1]', with the clarification that '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS2-1]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS2-1].
UK Year 5 Forces requires pupils to 'explain that unsupported objects fall towards the Earth because of the force of gravity acting between the Earth and the falling object'.
learnerActions: Using a globe (a physical ball, classroom globe, or an on-screen globe cross-section), place stick-figures all around it — top, sides, and the very bottom.
For each figure, draw or reveal a 'down' arrow from their feet and trace where it points; notice every arrow aims at the SAME place: the centre of the Earth.
Place one figure directly opposite yourself — standing 'upside-down' relative to you — and check that their 'down' still points to the middle.

On an on-screen model, use the drop-a-ball animation to release balls from several different positions and watch them all head inward toward the centre. On a physical globe, do this as a representational step instead — trace or draw each ball's path/arrow toward the model's centre — because real dropped balls fall toward the actual Earth, not toward a model globe's centre.
Answer aloud: 'If down means toward the centre, does anyone fall off? Why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: 'Down' is a local, radial direction — toward Earth's centre — not one fixed direction in the universe. Because every person's 'down' points to the centre, people all around the globe feel perfectly normal and nobody falls off, even though their 'down' points a different way in space from ours — and for someone directly opposite us, the opposite way.

activities.title: Same pull drops a ball and bends the Moon's path
feedback: If a learner says there's no gravity in space: gravity reaches out across space — it is exactly what holds the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun.
If a learner ties gravity to air: gravity acts in the airless vacuum of space too — the Moon has gravity and no air at all.
Prompt: 'What keeps the Moon circling instead of drifting off in a straight line?' (Earth's gravity continually bending its path.)
activities.rationale: Connecting the everyday falling force to orbits directly addresses the misconception that these are unrelated, and that gravity switches off in space. A predict-then-reveal 'gravity off → straight line' contrast makes the role of the force in curving the path concrete. An on/off toggle is one optional way to render this; a labelled before/after diagram also works. (The orbit extension is a pedagogy-derived link; it is kept qualitative and is not directly asserted by the cited sources.)
learnerActions: Study (or manipulate) a diagram of the Moon circling Earth with a gravity arrow pointing from the Moon toward Earth.

Predict: 'If the pull between Earth and Moon suddenly switched off, what path would the Moon take?' Then check in the simple Earth–Moon model (ignoring the Sun's pull) — with the pull off, the Moon moves off in a straight (tangent) line; with the pull on, that same pull curves its path into an orbit.
Repeat the idea with a Sun-at-centre diagram: each planet has a gravity arrow pointing at the Sun.
State in your own words how the force that drops a ball on Earth is the SAME force that keeps the Moon and planets in orbit.
Explain whether gravity needs air to work, using the airless Moon as evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Gravity is a long-reach attraction acting across empty space — no air or contact needed. The same pull that makes a ball fall is what bends the Moon's straight-line motion into an orbit around Earth, and the planets' paths around the Sun.

activities.title: Busting the 'zero gravity' myth
feedback: If a learner says gravity has switched off in space: the same pull holds the Moon in orbit; if gravity were gone, the ship and astronaut would fly off in a straight line, not circle Earth.
Reinforce that the astronaut and spacecraft fall together, so the astronaut appears to float relative to the craft.
Label the image honestly as 'still lots of gravity — falling around Earth', not 'zero gravity'.
activities.rationale: This heads off the most common upper-primary error directly and reuses the orbit reasoning from the previous activity, reinforcing that gravity acts continuously and across space. The free-fall explanation is drawn from standard physics-education guidance, though this source was not re-verified in this rewrite.
sourceClaims: Astronaut 'weightlessness' is continual free-fall (orbit) with Earth's gravity still acting, not the absence of gravity — a persistent upper-primary/secondary misconception.
learnerActions: Look at an image of an astronaut floating and discuss WHY they float.
Decide which explanation fits the evidence: (a) gravity has switched off, or (b) the astronaut and their ship are both falling around Earth together, with Earth's gravity still strongly acting.
Connect this to the orbit idea: being in orbit IS continual free-fall around Earth.
Answer: 'Is there gravity where astronauts are? How do you know?'
activities.intendedInsight: Astronauts float because they are in continual free-fall (orbit) around Earth, where Earth's gravity is still strong — not because gravity has vanished. 'Weightlessness' is free-fall, not absence of gravity.

activities.title: Check and reason: which way is 'down'?
feedback: Full understanding: explains gravity pulls toward Earth's centre so 'down' is centre-relative (opposite sides both feel normal), AND that the same pull keeps the Moon and planets in their orbits.

Partial: says gravity pulls 'down' and nobody falls off, but cannot clearly state 'down' means toward the centre, or doesn't connect gravity to orbits — revisit the arrow-drawing and orbit activities.
Gap: thinks the far side is upside-down and could fall off, or that there's no gravity in space — return to placing figures around the globe and drawing each 'down' arrow to the centre.
activities.rationale: A two-tier 'answer plus why' check discriminates between an absolute and a centre-relative notion of 'down', which recognition-only items can miss. This is a check on reasoning and should follow, not replace, the hands-on/interactive building activities.
sourceClaims: Grade-5 standard: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS2-1]', with the clarification that '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS2-1]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS2-1].
learnerActions: Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'A child in Australia is on nearly the opposite side of the round Earth from a child in Britain. Are the people in Australia hanging upside down, in danger of falling off into space? What does "down" actually mean for them? Tell me WHY.'
Decide: is there one single 'down' for the whole universe, or does 'down' depend on where you're standing?
Match each cause to its effect: Earth's pull → a ball falls toward the centre; Earth's pull → the Moon orbits; the Sun's pull → planets orbit.
Judge true or false and justify: 'There is no gravity in space.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain WHY no one falls off — because 'down' is centre-relative, not absolute — is the crux. A learner who still holds an absolute 'down' thinks the far side hangs upside-down; a learner who understands the concept says everyone's feet point 'down' toward the centre and no one falls.

constraints: Keep gravity qualitative and directional at ages 9-11: a pulling force with a direction (toward the centre). Do not introduce mass-vs-weight formalism or F=ma — reserve for later stages.

A multiple-choice/true-false check (e.g. 'which way is down for a figure on the far side?', 'no gravity in space?') can confirm the argument and surface misconceptions, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the learner's own spatial reasoning or constructed 'why'; pair any such check with the arrow-drawing and explain-why tasks.

A labelled diagram or tap-to-reveal image can show the arrangement ('their down points to the centre too'; 'Moon held by Earth's gravity') but cannot let the learner test 'what if I stand here?' or 'what if gravity switched off?'; it is a strong low-cost scaffold, while a manipulable model supports learner-driven testing of those what-ifs.

A physical ball/globe with stuck-on figures and a flat cross-section diagram serve different purposes: the physical object gives authentic 3D spatial experience, the clean cross-section makes the radial 'down' arrows easy to read. Neither is universally required; use whichever makes the centre-directed pattern clearest. Note that real dropped balls fall toward the actual Earth, so the 'all fall to the centre' pattern on a physical model must be shown by drawn/traced arrows or an on-screen animation, not by literally dropping balls.

Any on/off toggle, draggable figures, live 'down' arrows, or dropped-ball animations are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms — the same insight can be reached with a physical globe, drawn arrows, and predict-then-check discussion.

Address the Aristotelian 'heavier always falls noticeably faster' idea when it arises: in everyday life air resistance, not weight, usually explains the difference; avoid implying heavier objects are 'pulled much harder so always fall faster'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any activity was tested.

Of the three sources, only the NGSS 5-PS2-1 claim is marked verified in the source row; the UK National Curriculum Year 5 claim and the astronaut free-fall/IOP Spark misconception claim are marked unverified. Treat their wording as legacy, not independently confirmed here.

The orbit extension in activity 2 (same pull bends the Moon's path; holds planets to the Sun) is a pedagogy-derived link, not directly asserted by any of the three cited source claims; its sourceClaims is therefore [] and the content is kept qualitative.

The legacy 'conversation is poor / dialogue cannot render the conviction' and 'coded 2D model does exactly this' framings were catalog fit rankings, not established efficacy claims; softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements and not asserted as universal laws.

Minor physics care for this age: the Moon's 'straight line if gravity off' is the tangent to its orbit (Newton's cannonball reasoning); keep it qualitative. 'Free-fall' means the spacecraft and astronaut accelerate toward Earth together, so the astronaut floats relative to the craft — state this carefully to avoid implying no force acts.

Activity 1's dropped-ball step was re-scoped: a literal drop on a physical globe falls toward the real Earth, not the model's centre, so that observation is valid only on screen or as a drawn/traced representation on a physical model.

probeDeeper: If you dug a tunnel straight down from Britain and from Australia, would the two tunnels point the same way in space, or opposite ways?
What keeps the Moon circling the Earth instead of drifting off in a straight line?
Is there gravity on the Moon, where there's no air?
Is there one single 'down' for the whole universe, or does 'down' depend on where you're standing?
assess.correctAnswer: No — nobody falls off, because gravity pulls everything toward the CENTRE of the Earth, and 'down' means 'toward Earth's centre' wherever you stand. For the child in Australia, 'down' points to the centre just as it does in Britain, so their feet are firmly on the ground and everything feels perfectly normal — even though their 'down' points the opposite way in space to ours. There is no single fixed 'down' in the universe; each person's down points to Earth's centre. (That same pull, reaching across space, is what keeps the Moon orbiting Earth and the planets orbiting the Sun.)

errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — people in Australia are upside down and would fall off if gravity weren't strong enough to hold them on.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child worries the far side hangs upside-down or falls off, treating 'down' as an absolute cosmic direction

errorPatterns.pattern: there is no gravity in space ('once you leave Earth, nothing pulls')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Gravity reaches out across space — it is exactly what holds the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Gravity acts in the airless vacuum of space too — the Moon has gravity and no air at all.

responseLevels.full: Explains gravity pulls toward Earth's centre so 'down' is centre-relative (opposite sides both feel normal), and that the same pull keeps the Moon and planets in their orbits.
responseLevels.partial: Says gravity pulls 'down' and nobody falls off, but cannot clearly state that 'down' means toward the centre, or doesn't connect gravity to orbits.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child in Australia is on the exact opposite side of the round Earth from a child in Britain. Are the people in Australia hanging upside down, in danger of falling off into space? What does 'down' actually mean for them? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding an absolute 'down' (one fixed downward direction in space) believes the far side of the Earth hangs upside-down and could fall off. A child who understands gravity points toward the centre says everyone's feet are 'down' toward the centre and no one falls. The 'why' tier reveals whether 'down' is centre-relative or absolute — the crux of the concept.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Air Resistance & Friction

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 5 Forces):** Identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction, that act between moving surfaces.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no direct PE at this band; relates to 3-PS2-1):** Air resistance is not a discrete elementary NGSS performance expectation; the resistive-force idea connects to 3-PS2-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-1] an object's motion) and is formalised later under MS-PS2/HS-PS2.

- **Operational details:** At 9-10, air resistance is introduced as a frictional (resistive) force: it acts in the OPPOSITE direction to an object's motion and increases with greater surface area and greater speed. It is best taught through fair-test investigation (parachutes or paper spinners) where children change one variable — usually surface area — and measure fall time with repeat readings. The load-bearing correction is the idea that all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size and shape; this is confronted by discussion then practical test, and connected to real contexts of maximising resistance (parachutes) versus streamlining.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational).
bestPractices: Run a fair-test investigation: vary one variable (parachute/spinner surface area), measure fall time, take repeat readings and compare
Establish air resistance as a force acting OPPOSITE to motion and represent it with an arrow against the direction of travel
Use discuss-then-investigate to confront the 'all objects experience the same air resistance' misconception directly
Anchor in real contexts: parachutes maximise air resistance; streamlined shapes minimise it
Group air resistance with surface friction and water resistance as resistive forces, while distinguishing the medium
keyRepresentations: Arrow pair on a falling object: weight pulling down, air resistance pushing up (opposing motion)
Parachute-size vs fall-time data table and bar chart
Streamlined vs blunt/flat shape comparison
commonMisconceptions: All objects experience the same amount of air resistance regardless of size or shape (Oak-named misconception)
Air resistance acts in all directions, or acts downward — it is directional and acts opposite to motion
Air resistance is the same as 'wind'
Mass is irrelevant to falling — yet with air resistance present, two objects of the same shape but different mass do not fall identically
Heavier objects always fall faster (the Aristotelian carryover) — true-ish for same-shape objects in air, but it conflates air resistance with the underlying gravity story

learn.summary: For 9–10 year olds, teach air resistance as a resistive (frictional) force that acts opposite to an object's motion and grows with surface area and speed. The central corrective target is the misconception that all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape. A route well aligned with the curriculum combines a hands-on fair-test investigation using the same sheet of paper flat versus crumpled (so weight is held constant and area becomes the visible cause) with a live falling-object model, in which an upward resistance arrow grows as the object speeds up until it balances weight and the object then falls at a steady speed. Supporting retrieval (ordering by fall time, arrow-direction questions) and a static labelled force diagram serve as scaffolds, not replacements for the predict–measure experience.

activities.title: Growing resistance: drop and watch the arrows balance
feedback: If the learner expects a constant upward push, point to the arrow starting at nothing and growing as speed increases — it depends on how fast the object is moving.
When the arrows balance, name what they see: 'The forces are now balanced, so there's no more speeding up — it falls at a steady speed,' rather than saying it has stopped moving.
In fair-test mode, prompt: 'Only one thing is different between these two — so whatever changed must be causing the different fall.'
activities.rationale: A dynamic model lets children see resistance change with speed and area, which a static picture cannot animate; pairing it with single-variable comparison supports the fair-test reasoning the curriculum expects. The specific advantage of a live simulation over other media is a proposal, not source-established.
sourceClaims: Air resistance is a frictional force that acts opposite to the direction of motion; greater surface area gives more air resistance; the named misconception 'all objects experience the same amount of air resistance, regardless of size or shape' is addressed through discussion and a practical fair-test investigation.
learnerActions: Build a falling object and use a slider to change its surface area — flatten a ball into a flat sheet, or widen a parachute canopy.
Drop it down a tall chute and watch the upward air-resistance arrow grow from nothing as the object speeds up.
Keep watching until the upward arrow matches the downward weight arrow and the object stops speeding up, then falls at a steady speed.

Widen the canopy and observe the arrows balancing sooner, at a lower speed (it floats gently); streamline it and observe the upward arrow growing more slowly, so the object reaches a much higher speed before the arrows balance (it plummets).
Use a 'fair test' mode to drop two objects differing in exactly one variable (e.g. surface area) and read the cause straight off the race.
activities.intendedInsight: Air resistance is not fixed: it grows with both speed and surface area, and always pushes back against the direction of motion. When it balances weight the object stops accelerating and falls at a steady speed (it keeps moving). Two shapes of the same weight are NOT slowed the same.

activities.title: Fair-test investigation: same paper, flat vs crumpled
feedback: If the learner predicts a tie ('same paper, same weight, so same fall'), this is the diagnostic tell — run the flat vs crumpled test and a big vs small parachute with repeat readings to show resistance grows with area.
If the learner says crumpling makes the paper heavier, weigh both: they are identical, so the only change is shape/area and that must be the cause.
Confirm the correct account: 'Both weigh the same, so gravity pulls equally, but the flat sheet has a bigger surface facing the air, so more air resistance pushes up against it and slows it.'
activities.rationale: Holding weight constant while changing only shape removes the 'heavier falls faster' escape route and isolates surface area as the cause, directly confronting the named misconception through predict-then-measure.
sourceClaims: Air resistance is a frictional force that acts opposite to the direction of motion; greater surface area gives more air resistance; the named misconception 'all objects experience the same amount of air resistance, regardless of size or shape' is addressed through discussion and a practical fair-test investigation.
learnerActions: Predict first: drop a flat sheet of paper (held level, not edge-on) and the SAME sheet crumpled into a tight ball together from the same height — which lands first, and why? (Use two identical sheets, one flat and one crumpled, so both can be dropped at once.)
State the prediction and reason aloud or in writing BEFORE dropping.
Drop both and observe which lands first.
Weigh both to confirm they are identical in mass, so weight cannot explain the difference.
Repeat the drop several times and compare; extend to a big vs small parachute, taking repeat readings and recording fall times in a table.
activities.intendedInsight: Because the flat sheet and the crumpled ball are identical paper with the same weight, gravity pulls equally; the flat sheet meets MORE air because of its larger surface area facing the air, so it falls slower. At a given speed, the size of the air resistance depends on surface area and shape, not on the object's weight.

activities.title: Which way does it push? Direction and retrieval practice
feedback: If the learner places air resistance sideways or downward, restate: it acts OPPOSITE to the direction of movement, so upward on something falling; show it on the diagram.
If ordering is wrong, link each shape's area to the size of the air force pushing back on it.
Reinforce that air resistance is a force opposing motion, distinct from a gust of wind.
activities.rationale: Retrieval and direction questions consolidate the arrow direction and the area–fall-time link and surface the common 'same for all shapes' and 'acts in all directions' errors; recognition tasks reinforce but do not by themselves elicit the independent reasoning of the investigation.
sourceClaims: Air resistance is a frictional force that acts opposite to the direction of motion; greater surface area gives more air resistance; the named misconception 'all objects experience the same amount of air resistance, regardless of size or shape' is addressed through discussion and a practical fair-test investigation.
learnerActions: Order a set of parachutes/shapes by their fall time.
Answer which way air resistance pushes on a falling object — up, down, or sideways — and justify it.
Use a slider to explore how changing surface area changes fall time, predicting before each change.
Draw or complete a force diagram on a falling object showing weight down and air resistance opposing the motion (up for a falling object).
activities.intendedInsight: Air resistance acts opposite to the direction of movement — upward on a falling object — and larger area gives more resistance and a slower fall. It is not 'wind' and does not act in all directions.

activities.title: Connecting the ideas: parachutes, streamlining, water and the Moon
feedback: If the learner attributes the parachute slowdown to weight, point back to the canopy: the weight is unchanged, the area increased.
If the learner expects different fall times on the Moon, remind them air resistance needs air; with none, only gravity acts and the two papers land together.
Accept and build on valid water-resistance examples (e.g. swimming, a boat's shape), linking the size of the force to area and speed.
activities.rationale: Transfer to real contexts and the airless case checks whether the learner has generalised the resistive-force idea rather than memorised the paper result, and separates air resistance from the underlying gravity story. The water-resistance and Moon material is inherited from the row's objective and probes and is a research-informed proposal, not source-verified.
learnerActions: Explain what a parachutist changes to slow down (area, not weight) when a big canopy opens.
Contrast maximising air resistance (parachutes) with minimising it (streamlined shapes).

Give an everyday example of water resistance and explain how it, like air resistance and surface friction, opposes motion; water and air resistance act on objects moving through water or air, while surface friction acts between surfaces in contact.
Predict what the flat sheet and the crumpled ball would do if dropped where there is no air at all (e.g. the Moon) and explain why.
activities.intendedInsight: Air resistance, water resistance and surface friction are all resistive forces that oppose motion. Air and water resistance can be increased (bigger area facing the air or water) or reduced (streamlining); surface friction depends mainly on how rough the surfaces are and how hard they press together. Without air (as on the Moon) there is no air resistance, so the paper ball and the flat sheet would land together.

constraints: Fair tests must change exactly one variable at a time (e.g. surface area) and take repeat readings before comparing fall times.
Hold weight constant (same sheet flat vs crumpled) when isolating surface area, so learners cannot explain the result by weight.
Describe balanced forces carefully: at terminal velocity the object stops speeding up and falls at a steady speed — it has NOT stopped moving. Balanced forces mean no acceleration, not rest.
Air resistance acts opposite to motion (upward on a falling object), not in all directions and not simply 'downward'; it is not the same as wind.
Air resistance requires air: in the airless case (Moon) there is no air resistance, so the same-weight objects land together regardless of shape.
Static force diagrams are a useful reference but cannot animate resistance growing with speed; use them as scaffolds alongside a dynamic model or practical test.
Recognition and ordering tasks reinforce and reveal misconceptions but do not by themselves elicit the independent predict-then-measure reasoning; pair them with the investigation.

The claim that mass affects falling when air resistance is present (same-shape objects of different mass need not reach the same terminal speed) is an advanced nuance; introduce only if it does not reintroduce 'heavier falls faster' as a blanket rule, and keep it separate from the surface-area message for this age band.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The dynamic/live-model advantage over static or quiz formats is presented as a proposal; no source establishes it is necessary or superior for a given learner.

The source lists 'heavier objects always fall faster (Aristotelian carryover)' as a misconception but also notes it is 'true-ish for same-shape objects in air'. With air resistance, a heavier same-shape object can reach a higher terminal speed. To avoid reintroducing a wrong blanket rule for 9–10s, activities keep the primary message as 'surface area (and speed), not weight, changes air resistance' and treat mass effects as an optional advanced nuance.
The second source (mass affects falling with air resistance) is marked verified:false in the row; its claim is presented only as an advanced nuance and not used to drive the core activities.

Original artefact-fit text asserted the balance relationship is 'only a live sim makes felt' and that a fixed quiz/static image 'cannot' teach the dynamic balance, and that 3D 'adds nothing' / dialogue 'cannot deliver' the investigation. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the source and have been softened to scaffold/affordance statements.

The original terminal-velocity description ('object stops accelerating', 'falls at a steady speed') is physically sound and preserved; the constraint and feedback explicitly clarify the object keeps moving, to prevent a 'balanced = stopped' misreading.

Activity 4's water-resistance examples and the resistive-force grouping with the airless (Moon) case are inherited from the row's objective and probe questions, not from the cited source (which concerns air resistance only); its sourceClaims is therefore [] and the material is flagged as an unvalidated proposal.

The Moon statement is scoped to the same-weight paper scenario; in a true vacuum all objects regardless of mass fall together, but the narrower scenario-bound wording is retained to match the activity's task.

The objective's 'surface texture'/surface-friction strand is only lightly touched; emphasis follows the original row's air-resistance focus and could be extended if friction between solid surfaces is required.

assess.poeTask: Drop a flat sheet of paper and the SAME sheet crumpled into a ball, together, from the same height. Ask the child to predict which lands first and WHY before dropping. Predicting a tie ('same paper, same weight') is the diagnostic tell; the crumpled ball clearly winning — with weight held constant — pins the cause on air resistance and surface area, not weight.
probeDeeper: A parachutist opens a big parachute and slows down. What changed to give more air resistance — the weight or the area?
Which way does air resistance push on the falling paper — up, down, or sideways? Why?
Would air resistance matter if there were no air at all, like on the Moon? What would the two papers do then?
Is water resistance like air resistance? Give an example.
assess.correctAnswer: The screwed-up ball lands first. Both weigh the same, so gravity pulls equally, but the flat sheet has a much bigger surface facing the air, so it meets MORE air resistance pushing up against its fall — that slows it. Air resistance depends on surface area (and speed), not on weight; the ball has less area, so less air resistance.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'They'll land together — air pushes the same on everything, whatever the shape.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fair-test flat vs crumpled (same paper), and a big vs small parachute, with repeat readings; air resistance grows with area.
errorPatterns.distractor: They land at the same time — air resistance is the same on everything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a tie, or can't link shape to the size of the air force.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The crumpled one is heavier now — that's why it falls faster.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Weigh both — they're identical; the only change is shape/area, so air resistance must be the cause.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says screwing the paper up makes it heavier.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Air resistance pushes in all directions, or downwards too.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Air resistance acts OPPOSITE to the direction of movement — upwards on a falling object; show it on the force diagram.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws or says air resistance acting sideways or downward, not opposite the motion.

responseLevels.gap: Predicts they land together (air resistance the same on all) or says the crumpled paper is heavier; puts air resistance in the wrong direction.
responseLevels.full: Explains air/water resistance and friction as forces that oppose motion whose size grows with surface area (and speed), so the flat sheet with more area falls slower than the identical-weight ball — transferring to parachutes and to the Moon (no air -> land together).
responseLevels.partial: Knows air resistance slows things and can give examples, but explains the paper result by weight, or lists the resistive forces without linking the size of the force to surface area/speed and its opposing direction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I drop a flat sheet of paper and, at the same moment, the SAME sheet screwed into a tight ball, from the same height. Which lands first — and why, given they're made of exactly the same paper and weigh the same?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the two are the same paper and the same weight, the child can't fall back on 'the heavier one'. A child who understands air resistance attributes the difference to the flat sheet's larger area meeting more air. A child holding the Oak misconception — 'air resistance is the same on everything regardless of shape/size' — predicts a tie or says the flat one is 'lighter'. Tier 2 forces area (not weight) as the cause.

sources.source: Oak National Academy — Air resistance (KS2 lesson plan)

sources.claim: With air resistance present, mass affects falling (objects of the same shape but different mass do not reach the same terminal speed), nuancing the simple 'all objects fall at the same rate' rule.
