learnerActions: Switch to a coastal-town setting and place the pieces of a warning system: a detection buoy/sensor offshore, a warning siren, a marked evacuation route, and a high-ground or vertical-evacuation destination.
Trigger an undersea earthquake and tsunami, then run a timed evacuation and watch how quickly people reach safety.
Change one part of the system (move the route, add a siren, choose vertical evacuation) and re-run the timed evacuation to see the effect on how many reach high ground in time.

Explain in order how the system works: undersea quake detected → sea-level sensors confirm a tsunami wave (the sea may rise or first pull back) → alert reaches people → evacuate to high ground or a tall, strong building, supported by rehearsed community drills.
activities.intendedInsight: Reducing human impact is a system — detect, warn, act — not just a stronger wall; rehearsed evacuation and clear routes save time when seconds count, and a tsunami warning is distinct from feeling the earthquake itself — though near the coast, strong or long shaking is itself a natural warning to move to high ground without waiting for an official alert.

activities.title: Rotate the tower in 3D: watch it sway, topple, and decouple
feedback: If a learner cannot tell which way the tower is leaning or racking, rotate the model so the failure plane faces them before re-shaking.
If base isolation still reads as a firmer attachment, rotate to the cutaway and watch the ground slide under the lagging building.
activities.rationale: A rotatable 3D model offers a different spatial experience of sway, toppling and decoupling than a planar side-on view. The core generate-test-iterate learning is already carried by the 2D bench, so this is an optional complement that may aid spatial insight; it is not claimed to add, or to lack, conceptual value relative to the planar model, and no source establishes the value of a 3D medium.
learnerActions: Rotate a 3D model of a built tower to view it from any angle, then apply shaking and watch it sway and collapse in depth rather than only side-on.
Compare an un-braced frame racking in three dimensions with a braced or base-isolated tower that holds its shape or decouples from the ground.
View a 3D base-isolation cutaway: watch the bearings let the ground slide beneath while the building lags behind in space (inertia).
activities.intendedInsight: Toppling, centre of mass, racking and decoupling are spatial; rotating a 3D model can make the direction of sway and the ground-building decoupling easier to see than a flat side-on view.

activities.title: Anatomy of a safe building (reference primer)
feedback: If a learner thinks base isolation means the building is bolted down more firmly, point to the sliding-ground arrow: the bearings let the ground move underneath so the building is not dragged along.
If features are recalled as a checklist, ask which specific failure (toppling, racking, excessive sway) each one prevents.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal cutaway is a useful pre-build primer for the mechanisms and the correct meaning of decoupling, but it is a scaffold: because it is fixed it cannot let a learner test or fail a design, so it should hand off to the hands-on bench rather than stand alone for this design topic. Seeing the parts labelled teaches the vocabulary and mechanism but does not itself elicit the test-and-iterate practice.
sourceClaims: Earthquake-resistant structural features and their mechanisms: base isolation (decoupling), cross-bracing/shear walls (resisting racking), wide base/low centre of mass (resisting toppling), tuned mass dampers (counter-sway).
learnerActions: Before building, explore a labelled cutaway of an earthquake-resistant building and reveal, one part at a time, what the base isolators, shear walls/cross-bracing, wide base, and roof damper each do.

For each feature, state the physical failure it counters: base isolation decouples the building so the ground can move without dragging it (inertia); wide base and low centre of mass resist toppling; triangulated bracing/shear walls stop racking; a heavy roof damper counter-sways.
Study a base-isolation cutaway showing an arrow for the ground sliding while the building lags behind it.
activities.intendedInsight: Each visible feature exists to counter a specific force, and base isolation works by decoupling — the opposite of fixing the building harder to the ground.

activities.title: Talk with an engineer: what is worth the cost?
feedback: If a learner still expects a fully earthquake-proof building, have the engineer reframe the goal as protecting people and buying escape time, with damage reduced and delayed but not guaranteed to be prevented in every earthquake.
If answers stay abstract, ask the learner to tie each claim back to a specific trial from their own comparison grid.
activities.rationale: A role-play conversation can enrich the 'reduce, not eliminate' honesty and real-world trade-offs and works well as an epilogue after hands-on iteration; it complements the build-and-test work rather than replacing the generate-test-compare experience the standard requires.
sourceClaims: DCI ESS3.B: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS3-1, 4-ESS3-2] [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS3-1, 4-ESS3-2].
learnerActions: After iterating on the bench, discuss with someone in the role of a structural/earthquake engineer why tall buildings are allowed to sway, why base isolation works, and how real cities weigh cost against safety.
Pose and answer 'reduce, not eliminate' questions: what does each feature buy, and why can no realistic building be made fully hazard-proof?
Explain back which real trade-offs you would accept and why, connecting the bench's comparison grid to real decisions.
activities.intendedInsight: Real hazard engineering is a judgement about reducing impact and buying time within cost limits, not achieving invincibility.

activities.title: Consolidation checks: match mechanisms and order the chain
feedback: Treat any answer that implies a building can be made fully earthquake-proof as the target misconception to address: the aim is protecting people and buying time.
Use illustrations as evocative only; do not rely on them as exact structural renderings when assessing understanding.
activities.rationale: Matching, sequencing, selection and a trade-off control can check whether a learner recognises mechanisms and the reduce-not-eliminate principle after the hands-on work. These recognition-and-selection tasks assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent generate-test-iterate construction that defines the topic, so they belong as consolidation after building, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: DCI ESS3.B: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS3-1, 4-ESS3-2] [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS3-1, 4-ESS3-2].
Tsunami mitigation as a detect–warn–act system: detection buoys/sirens, marked evacuation routes, vertical-evacuation structures, and rehearsed community drills reduce casualties.
learnerActions: Match each structural feature to the force or failure it counters (base isolation ↔ ground motion/inertia; cross-bracing ↔ racking; wide/low base ↔ toppling; roof damper ↔ sway).
Put the evacuation steps in order: detect → warn → act (quake detected → sea-level sensors → siren/alert → evacuate to high ground).
Given a shaking scenario, choose which redesign best meets stated criteria and set a cost/safety trade-off, explaining the reasoning.
State in your own words why the goal is reduced impact rather than a hazard-proof building.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner can show they recognise the mechanisms, the system ordering, and the 'reduce not eliminate' idea.

constraints: Run this as a full engineering-design cycle — define problem, generate multiple solutions, test, compare, iterate — and do not let it collapse into building one tower.
Make failure visible and safe: learners should SEE an under-braced structure rack and topple so the need for each feature is felt, not just told.
Insist on fair testing: same shake, one change at a time, so a comparison isolates what a single feature did.
Hold the honest ceiling: engineering reduces and delays impact and buys escape time; it does not make a building or town hazard-proof. Correct any expectation of a fully earthquake-proof structure.
Base isolation DECOUPLES the building from the ground (bearings let the ground move without dragging the building); it is not the building fixed harder to the ground — correct this reversal directly.
Attach a physical mechanism to every feature so features are understood, not memorised as a checklist.
The labelled cutaway primer is a scaffold: being fixed, it cannot let a learner test or fail a design, so it should precede, not replace, the hands-on bench.
A rotatable 3D view is an optional spatial complement to the 2D bench, offering a different experience of sway and decoupling; do not claim it adds no conceptual value, nor that it is required.
Recognition/selection checks (matching, ordering, trade-off) assess understanding but do not elicit independent design construction; use them after building, not instead of it.

Prerequisites assumed: measuring earthquake strength (shaking as the load), tsunamis (the water hazard), plate boundaries (why the region is at risk), and the generate-and-compare framing for natural-disaster solutions.
Damage depends on more than magnitude — distance, ground type, building design and preparedness all shape actual impact; design targets the impact side.

Present 'flexible/base-isolated beats brute stiffness' as a strong, testable design principle rather than a universal law; the best choice is scenario-dependent on building type, soil and shaking frequency.

Optional interaction examples (shake dial, live seismogram, cost budget, accumulating comparison grid, placeable siren and route, timed evacuation, tap-to-reveal cutaway, rotatable 3D model) make mechanisms concrete but are not mandatory implementations.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Several source claims are marked unverified in the original row (3-5-ETS1 engineering progression; KS2 Design & Technology programme of study; structural-engineering feature mechanisms; NOAA/USGS tsunami guidance described as general knowledge, not fetched). Treat specific mechanism and mitigation claims as commonly accepted guidance, not freshly confirmed here.

The claim that flexible/base-isolated designs 'often outperform brute stiffness' is generally supported in structural engineering but is scenario-dependent (building type, soil, shaking frequency); present it as a strong design principle discovered through testing, not a universal law.

The original rated a 3D version 'strong' and also asserted it 'adds nothing' to the conceptual payload; that comparative verdict is not independently established. The 3D activity is retained as an optional spatial complement offering a different experience, neither claimed superior nor valueless, and carries no source because none supports a 3D-medium efficacy claim.

Original catalog guidance that dialogue 'cannot deliver' hands-on iteration and that a fixed cutaway 'cannot let the child test' was softened to narrow, observable scope limits (a fixed/recognition medium does not itself elicit test-and-iterate construction) rather than absolute incapacity claims.

probeDeeper: Your first tower fell — what one change did you make, and how did the re-test show it helped?
Is it better for a tall building to be totally rigid, or to be able to sway a little? Why?
How would people in a coastal town find out a tsunami is coming, and what should they do?
Why do communities practise earthquake and evacuation drills before anything happens?
assess.correctAnswer: The child builds and shake-tests a tower, then improves it with a real earthquake-resistant feature (wide/heavy base, cross-bracing, or a flexible base-isolated foundation) and shows from the re-test that it now sways or survives better; and explains a tsunami warning system detects the undersea quake and rising sea and alerts people to evacuate to high ground, with communities preparing via drills and evacuation routes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Makes the building as stiff and rigid as possible / clamps it down hard
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test it, then show a flexible base / base-isolation that lets the building move with the ground and sway safely.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Builds a rigid tower expecting stiffness alone to win; it cracks or topples.

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds tall and top-heavy on a narrow base
errorPatterns.nextMove: Widen and lower the base / add cross-bracing, then re-test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Centre of mass high on a narrow footing; it falls in the shake.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds features without testing or comparing — no evidence which helped
errorPatterns.nextMove: Isolate one change at a time and re-test to see its effect.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Changes the tower but doesn't re-shake or compare before/after.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses a tsunami warning with the earthquake itself, or thinks there's no way to warn people
errorPatterns.nextMove: Undersea quake detected → sea-level sensors → alert to evacuate to high ground.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't say how a tsunami is detected or how the alert reaches people.

responseLevels.gap: Builds without testing, or a rigid/top-heavy tower that fails; can't describe a resistant feature or a warning system.
responseLevels.full: Runs a build-test-improve loop, demonstrates a real resistant feature (wide base / bracing / base isolation) with evidence it helped, and explains tsunami detection → alert → evacuate plus community drills.
responseLevels.partial: Builds, tests and adds a feature but doesn't iterate or show which change helped, or explains buildings without the warning/preparation half.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are building materials and a tray you can shake like an earthquake. Build a tower that can survive the shaking, then test it, improve it, and show me which changes helped — and tell me how a coastal town would get warning of a tsunami and what people would do.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can 'know' buildings should be strong yet build a rigid, top-heavy tower that topples, or add material without testing. Watching the build-test-improve loop — and whether they discover that flexibility/base isolation beats rigid stiffness — separates reciting features from performing the design process.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Joints, Tendons & Ligaments

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Skeletal & muscular systems):** "biomechanics – the interaction between skeleton and muscles, including the measurement of force exerted by different muscles" and "the function of muscles and examples of antagonistic muscles."

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS1-3):** the muscular/skeletal system as an interacting subsystem; joint-level biomechanics detail is UK-led.

- **Operational details:** Children distinguish TENDONS (attach muscle to bone) from LIGAMENTS (attach bone to bone) and give each function, describe how a synovial joint (e.g. knee or elbow) works — cartilage cushioning bone ends, synovial fluid lubricating, ligaments holding the joint together — and explain how force is TRANSMITTED from a contracting muscle, through the tendon, to the bone, producing movement about the joint acting as a lever/pivot. The move that matters is mechanical: a muscle's pull is delivered along a tendon to move a bone around a joint — a linked chain of parts, each with a distinct job.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B→C. Builds on skeletal structure; directly sets up antagonistic muscle pairs. A child is secure when they can say what tendons vs ligaments connect, describe a synovial joint, and trace how muscle force becomes movement at a joint.
bestPractices: Teach the joint as a mechanical linkage (muscle→tendon→bone→movement) so each part's role is understood by its place in the chain.
Use a memorable discriminator for the two connectives (Tendon = muscle-To-bone; Ligament = Links bone-to-bone).
Describe synovial-joint features (cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments) by the problem each solves (cushioning, lubrication, stability).
Connect force to movement (the 'measurement of force' clause) so biomechanics is quantitative, not just labelling.
Bridge forward to antagonistic pairs by noting a muscle pulls the bone one way only.
keyRepresentations: Synovial-joint cross-section (cartilage, synovial fluid, ligament, tendon)
Muscle→tendon→bone force-path diagram about a joint pivot
Tendon vs ligament comparison (what each connects)
Lever model of a joint (effort, pivot, load)
commonMisconceptions: Swapping tendons and ligaments (which connects muscle-to-bone vs bone-to-bone).
Thinking joints are rigid connections rather than lubricated, movable structures.
Believing muscles attach directly to bone without tendons.
Thinking the joint itself generates force, rather than transmitting muscle force.
Assuming all joints move the same way (ignoring hinge vs ball-and-socket differences).

learn.summary: Learners (ages 11–13) learn to treat a joint as a mechanical linkage: a muscle's pull travels along a tendon to a bone, swinging it about the joint, which acts as the pivot of a lever (the muscle's pull is the effort, the joint is the pivot, the bone is the lever arm, and the load is the weight of the limb plus anything held). They distinguish tendons (attach muscle to bone, transmit force) from ligaments (attach bone to bone, hold the joint stable), and describe synovial-joint features — cartilage cushioning the bone ends, synovial fluid lubricating, ligaments providing stability — by the problem each solves. A force measurement in a simplified model shows how hard the muscle must pull to move the limb against a given load, addressing the biomechanics 'measurement of force' requirement, and prepares learners for antagonistic muscle pairs.

activities.title: Operate a working elbow/knee model and trace the force path
feedback: If the learner leaves the tendon out of the chain, point to the disabled-tendon moment: the muscle contracted but nothing moved, so the tendon is the link that delivers force to the bone.
If the learner says the joint 'makes' the force, re-run the contract control: force comes from the contracting muscle and is transmitted through the tendon; the joint is the pivot, not the source.
When the loosened ligament makes the joint wobble, connect it to the word: ligaments LINK bone to bone and give stability.
Reinforce the discriminator: Tendon = muscle-To-bone; Ligament = Links bone-to-bone.
activities.rationale: Biomechanics is about force being transmitted along a chain, so a model the learner operates — with engineered 'disable the tendon' and 'loosen the ligament' moments — may make the role of each part concrete and causal rather than a memorised label. A force readout ties contraction to movement, addressing the curriculum's measurement-of-force requirement. This is a research-informed proposal; the live model is one medium that may serve this, not the only way to teach the chain, and a clear diagram or verbal tracing can also convey it.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Biology requires teaching 'biomechanics – the interaction between skeleton and muscles, including the measurement of force exerted by different muscles' and 'the function of muscles and examples of antagonistic muscles'.

Tendons attach muscle to bone and ligaments attach bone to bone; synovial joints have cartilage and synovial fluid to reduce friction, and muscle contraction transmits force via the tendon to move the bone about the joint.
learnerActions: Operate a working joint model (elbow or knee): slide or trigger a 'contract' control on a muscle and watch the tendon tauten and pull the bone so the joint hinges about its pivot.
Identify, as the model moves, where cartilage cushions the bone ends, where synovial fluid lubricates, and where ligaments strap the two bones together.
Read the force gauge/readout as the load changes, and describe in your own words how hard the muscle must pull before the bone moves (remembering this is a simplified model).
Disable or 'cut' the tendon, then contract the muscle again: observe that the muscle bunches but the bone does not move, and state why.
Loosen a ligament and flex the joint: observe the joint wobbling and gapping, and state why.

In a sentence, trace the force from muscle → tendon → bone → movement at the joint, naming the muscle's pull as the effort, the joint as the pivot, the bone as the lever, and the weight of the forearm or lower leg (plus anything held) as the load.
activities.intendedInsight: A joint is a linked chain of parts each with a distinct job: the tendon delivers the muscle's pull to the bone, the ligament holds the bones together, and cartilage/synovial fluid let the surfaces glide. The joint transmits force; it does not generate it.

activities.title: Name the parts on a joint cross-section
feedback: If tendon and ligament are swapped, reinforce: Tendon = muscle-To-bone; Ligament = Links bone-to-bone.
If the learner describes the joint as bare bone-on-bone, point to cartilage cushioning and synovial fluid lubricating so surfaces glide rather than grind.
activities.rationale: A tappable cross-section is an efficient naming/discrimination scaffold and directly addresses the common tendon/ligament confusion. It names the parts but, being static, does not itself show force-transmission dynamics, so it complements rather than replaces a dynamic model or learner explanation.
sourceClaims: Tendons attach muscle to bone and ligaments attach bone to bone; synovial joints have cartilage and synovial fluid to reduce friction, and muscle contraction transmits force via the tendon to move the bone about the joint.
learnerActions: On a labelled synovial-joint cross-section, tap or point to each part and state its job: tendon → 'attaches muscle to bone'; ligament → 'attaches bone to bone'; cartilage → 'smooth cushion at bone ends'; synovial fluid → 'lubricates the joint'.
Answer a lift-the-flap style check: 'Tendon or ligament — which joins two bones?' → 'Ligament.'
Explain why cartilage and synovial fluid stop the bone ends grinding.
activities.intendedInsight: Each named structure in a synovial joint solves a specific problem: cushioning, lubrication, stability, or force transmission.

activities.title: Explore the joint in three dimensions
feedback: If the learner thinks all joints move the same way, compare the hinge motion of the knee/elbow with a ball-and-socket joint's rotation.
Connect the wrapping ligaments to their stabilising job: they hold the bones together through the full range of motion.
activities.rationale: A manipulable 3D joint supports spatial understanding of how surfaces meet and how ligaments wrap the joint. The muscle→tendon→bone force chain can be conveyed just as well in 2D, so 3D is offered for its spatial affordance, not as a universally necessary medium.
learnerActions: Rotate and flex a 3D model of a knee or elbow.
Observe how the cartilage surfaces meet, how ligaments wrap around the joint, and how the hinge moves in space.
Describe how the joint surfaces glide against each other as the bone rotates about the pivot.
activities.intendedInsight: A synovial joint is a genuinely three-dimensional structure: ligaments wrap it and surfaces meet and rotate in space, which a flat diagram foreshortens.

activities.title: Sort, match and sequence to check understanding
feedback: If a learner sorts correctly but can't predict failure consequences, revisit the model's disable moments: cut tendon → no force transmitted, bone won't move; torn ligament → joint unstable/loose but still powered.
Watch for the distractor 'tendons and ligaments both join muscles to bones' — correct to tendon = muscle-to-bone, ligament = bone-to-bone.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, matching and sequencing are clean items for checking naming and ordering, and a two-tier failure-prediction prompt helps discriminate genuine understanding from memorised words. Sorting and matching check recall and discrimination; they do not by themselves elicit independent explanation, so pair them with the learner stating the force path and failure reasoning in their own words.
learnerActions: Categorise roles as tendon vs ligament (e.g. 'moves the bone' vs 'stabilises the joint', 'muscle-to-bone' vs 'bone-to-bone').
Match each joint part to its function (cartilage → cushions; synovial fluid → lubricates; ligament → stabilises; tendon → transmits force).
Put the force path in order: muscle → tendon → bone → movement.
Answer a two-tier failure-prediction prompt: which would stop a muscle moving a bone at all — a cut tendon or a torn ligament — and why?
activities.intendedInsight: Secure understanding means mapping each connector to its function AND predicting the consequence when it fails.

constraints: The tappable cross-section is a naming scaffold: it names parts and busts tendon/ligament confusion but, being static, does not itself show force-transmission dynamics — pair it with a dynamic model or learner explanation.

The 3D model supports spatial understanding of how surfaces meet and ligaments wrap; it is offered for that affordance, not as a claim that the force chain can only be learned in 3D (2D conveys the chain equally well).
Sorting/matching/sequencing items check recall and ordering; they do not on their own require the learner to construct an explanation or predict failure consequences — include open prompts for that.

Distinguish the idealised model from a real joint: a rig or screen model simplifies the biomechanics and omits detail (multiple muscles, joint capsule, nerve control). State this simplification to learners, not only in review.

Key discriminator to maintain throughout: Tendon = muscle-To-bone (transmits force, moves the bone); Ligament = Links bone-to-bone (stabilises). Keep the joint framed as transmitting, not generating, force.

The original row rated a discussion/conversation format 'poor' ('best manipulated, not discussed'). A linkage is well suited to manipulation, but spoken explanation and failure-prediction questioning remain valuable for eliciting reasoning; do not treat discussion as having no teaching value.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles/content, not the tested efficacy of any specific activity.

The second source (BBC Bitesize) is marked verified:false in the row; the tendon/ligament/synovial-joint claims are drawn from it and should be confirmed against the curriculum/standard before relying on specific wording.

The original row asserted a static label diagram 'cannot' make the mechanical chain felt and that a linkage is 'best manipulated, not discussed'. These are catalog-preference claims not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to affordance/limit framing. A fixed diagram can still teach the chain, and discussion can elicit reasoning.

NGSS MS-LS1-3 treats the muscular/skeletal system as an interacting subsystem; the joint-level biomechanics detail (tendons/ligaments, synovial joint, force transmission) is UK (KS3)-led, so US alignment is partial.

The DfE claim was removed from the assessment activity's sourceClaims because it supports the biomechanics topic/content, not the assessment-design principle stated in that activity's rationale. The DfE claim is retained only in the working-model activity, where the force-gauge element directly implements the measurement-of-force requirement; the BBC claim is retained where it grounds the definitions being taught. Both are content grounding, not evidence that any specific medium is effective.
The original 'lever model (effort, pivot, load)' representation is only lightly carried; effort/pivot/load naming has been added to the summary and the first activity but could be developed further.

probeDeeper: Trace the path of the pull from a contracting muscle to the bone that moves — what does it pass through?
If a footballer 'tears a ligament' in the knee, why does the joint feel wobbly rather than paralysed?
Why don't the bones in your knee wear away from rubbing every time you walk?
Which would stop a muscle moving a bone at all — a cut tendon or a torn ligament — and why?
assess.correctAnswer: A tendon connects muscle to bone and transmits the muscle's pull to move the bone; a ligament connects bone to bone and holds the joint stable. Cut a tendon and the muscle can no longer move that bone (no force is transmitted). Tear a ligament and the joint becomes unstable/loose because the bones are no longer held firmly together.

errorPatterns.pattern: Tendons and ligaments are the same thing / interchangeable
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix the two links firmly: tendon = muscle-to-bone (moves the bone), ligament = bone-to-bone (stabilises the joint). Use an elbow model and trace each.
errorPatterns.distractor: Tendons and ligaments both join muscles to bones.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Swaps the definitions or says both join muscle to bone

errorPatterns.pattern: Muscles grip bones directly, with no tendon in between
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the chain muscle → tendon → bone; the tendon is the rope that carries the pull. Point to a tendon at the wrist or heel.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the muscle attaching straight to the bone, leaving the tendon out of the force path

errorPatterns.pattern: In a joint, bones touch and rub directly against each other
errorPatterns.nextMove: A synovial joint has cartilage cushioning the bone ends and synovial fluid lubricating them, so they glide rather than grind.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the synovial joint as bare bone-on-bone with nothing between

responseLevels.gap: Confuses tendon and ligament or leaves connective tissue out of how a joint works.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes tendon (muscle-to-bone, transmits force) from ligament (bone-to-bone, stabilises), explains the muscle→tendon→bone force path, and describes how a synovial joint cushions and lubricates the bones.
responseLevels.partial: States the two definitions correctly but can't predict the consequence of each failing, or omits cartilage/fluid in the joint.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: At your elbow there are tendons and ligaments, and they're easy to mix up: one connects a muscle to a bone, the other connects a bone to another bone. Which is which — and what would go wrong at the joint if a tendon were cut, compared with a ligament being torn?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands joint mechanics maps each connector to its role and predicts the right failure. A child who has only memorised the words swaps them, or can't say what each failure would cause, revealing the definitions aren't tied to function.

pedagogy.summary: An equation with two unknowns (a + b = 12, or 2x + y = 20) does NOT have a single answer — it has many solution pairs. The child generates such pairs and, within the stated constraints (whole numbers, positive, a range), lists them SYSTEMATICALLY so none is missed and none repeated. Fixing one unknown and stepping it through its possible values in order, computing the partner each time, makes the search exhaustive and reveals the pattern. It is a Year 6 precursor to simultaneous equations, where a SECOND equation pins the pair down to one.

Fix one unknown and step it through its permitted values in order (a = 1 → b = 11, a = 2 → b = 10, …), computing the partner each time so the list is complete and ordered
Record pairs in a two-column table so completeness is visible and answer 'how do you know you've found them all?'

Link to 'what two numbers can add up to' puzzles and to plotting the pairs as points on a line

A 'fix one unknown and step it' systematic list
Bar / part-whole model for a + b = 12
The pairs as points on a straight line (bridge to graphs and simultaneous equations)

learn.summary: Year 6 learners discover that an equation with two unknowns (e.g. a + b = 12, or 2x + y = 20) has MANY solution pairs, not one. They generate these pairs systematically by fixing one unknown and stepping it through its permitted values in order, computing the partner each time, so no pair is missed or repeated. Stated constraints (such as whole numbers, positive, or within a range) decide which pairs are valid; when values must be whole numbers within limits, the number of pairs is finite and can be counted. This is a precursor to simultaneous equations, where a second equation can usually pin the pair down to one answer.

activities.title: Build the pair-finder: sweep one unknown and watch the pairs appear
feedback: If the learner gives one pair as 'the answer' and stops: ask 'Is there another pair that works? And another?' Then fix a and step it through its values to reveal them all.
If the search is random with gaps or repeats: have them step one unknown through its values in order and record in a table — 'I know I have them all because I worked systematically.'
If they cannot say whether the list is complete: point to the ordered column of a-values and ask which values of a have not yet been tried.

Full solution for a + b = 12 (whole, > 0): (1,11), (2,10), (3,9), (4,8), (5,7), (6,6), (7,5), (8,4), (9,3), (10,2), (11,1) — 11 pairs, complete because every value of a from 1 to 11 has been tried in order.
activities.rationale: The Year 6 objective is to find pairs satisfying a two-unknown equation, framed as generating MULTIPLE pairs. Working randomly first hides which cases are missing; ordering and systematising exposes gaps and answers 'how do you know you've found them all?'. Fixing one unknown and stepping it makes the search exhaustive and reveals the linear pattern.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should 'find pairs of numbers that satisfy an equation with 2 unknowns'; the non-statutory guidance includes number puzzles such as 'what 2 numbers can add up to', framing the task as generating multiple pairs.

When children are asked to find all possibilities they first work randomly and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting and ordering their attempts exposes the gaps, and having a system is what ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
learnerActions: Before starting, compare a + b = 12 with a + 7 = 12: how many answers does each have? Notice that the one-variable equation has a single answer but the two-unknown equation has many.
Start with a + b = 12 (whole numbers, greater than 0). Set a = 1 and work out b; record (1, 11). Set a = 2 and work out b; record (2, 10). Continue in order: a = 3 → b = 9, a = 4 → b = 8, and so on.
Record each pair in an ordered two-column table (a | b) so completeness is visible.
After listing, answer: 'How many pairs are there? How do you know you have found them ALL?' State the justification: 'I tried every value of a from 1 to 11 in order.'

Optional interactive version: drag a slider for a that moves in whole-number steps from 1 to 11 and watch b recompute live so a + b = 12 always holds; each pair drops into the ordered table AND lights a point on a grid. Sweeping the slider fills the table in order while the separate points line up along a straight line — showing at once that there are many solutions and that stepping a through every permitted value catches them all.
activities.intendedInsight: An equation with two unknowns has a whole family of solution pairs; stepping one unknown through its permitted values in order generates every pair and lets you prove the list is complete.

activities.title: Let the constraints bound the count
feedback: If pairs like (0, 12), (13, −1), or decimals appear despite a 'whole, greater than 0' condition: reread the constraint together; it fixes which values of a are permitted and therefore how many pairs there are.
If allowing 0 or any whole number changes the count, ask the learner to re-list in order under the new rule and recount.
activities.rationale: Ignoring constraints produces invalid pairs and an incorrect count. Attending to the stated conditions makes the search both correct and finite, and shows why the number of pairs is what it is.
learnerActions: Reread the stated condition (whole numbers, positive, within a range) and decide which values of a are allowed before listing.
For a + b = 12 with 'whole, greater than 0', check: is (0, 12) allowed? Is (13, −1) allowed? Are decimals allowed? Explain why each is excluded by the condition.
Try a different constraint, e.g. 'a and b are whole numbers from 0 to 10 inclusive', and work out how the list of valid pairs changes and how many remain (a can now only be 2 to 10, so 9 pairs).

Optional interactive version: a constraints toggle ('whole numbers only', 'positive only', 'between 0 and 10') greys out the pairs that break the rule, so the learner SEES how the constraint bounds how many pairs exist.
activities.intendedInsight: The constraints bound which values of the stepped unknown are allowed, and therefore exactly how many valid pairs exist.

activities.title: Respect the coefficient: 2x + y = 20
feedback: If the learner offers (3, 17) for 2x + y = 20: have them substitute the numbers — 2×3 + 17 = 23 ≠ 20. The pair satisfies x + y = 20, not 2x + y = 20.
Prompt: substitute the chosen x and compute y = 20 − 2x explicitly rather than guessing a partner that sums to 20.
activities.rationale: Mishandling the coefficient (treating 2x + y as x + y) is a common error. Substituting and computing y = 20 − 2x each time makes the coefficient's role concrete and transfers the systematic method to a new two-unknown equation.
learnerActions: For 2x + y = 20, choose a value for x, then compute y = 20 − 2x explicitly — the 2 doubles x BEFORE y is added.
Find three valid pairs, e.g. x = 1 → y = 18 giving (1,18); x = 2 → y = 16 giving (2,16); x = 3 → y = 14 giving (3,14).
Check a tempting wrong pair: does (3, 17) satisfy 2x + y = 20? Substitute: 2×3 + 17 = 23, not 20. Note that (3, 17) fits x + y = 20, a different equation.
Explain in your own words how 2x + y = 20 differs from x + y = 20.
Optional interactive version: a 2x + y = 20 preset shows y recomputing as 20 − 2x as x changes, making the coefficient's effect visible.
activities.intendedInsight: A coefficient changes the partner computation: for 2x + y = 20 the partner is y = 20 − 2x, which is not the same as x + y = 20.

constraints: Establish FIRST that there are many pairs, not one — contrast a + b = 12 with a one-variable equation like a + 7 = 12.
The ordered two-column table (or a 'fix one unknown and step it' list) is essential for judging completeness; recording pairs out of order defeats the purpose.

Recognition-only or fill-in-the-blank items (complete-the-pair, categorise valid vs invalid, 'how many pairs?') can check the skill but do NOT by themselves build the systematic, exhaustive search; the learner must generate and order the pairs independently.

A static completed table beside the line of points can display the full solution set, but it does the discovery for the learner — they do not generate the pairs or test completeness themselves. Treat it as a reveal/illustration, not as the generating activity.
Plotting the pairs as points on a straight line is a bridge to graphs and simultaneous equations; keep it linked to the ordered table so the pattern connects back to the stepping method.

Interactive slider/toggle/point-lighting features named above are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; the underlying learning (stepping one unknown in order, computing the partner, justifying completeness) can also be done with pencil, paper, and a hand-drawn table.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: a + b = 12 (whole, >0) yields exactly 11 pairs (a from 1 to 11) — verified. For 2x + y = 20, y = 20 − 2x: (1,18), (2,16), (3,14) all satisfy 2x + y = 20 — verified. (3,17) gives 2×3+17 = 23 ≠ 20 and satisfies x + y = 20 instead — the distractor is correctly characterised.

The legacy row's claim that 3D and in-role dialogue formats 'add nothing' / 'cannot build' the skill was not established by the cited sources and has been removed rather than asserted as a universal law; the point retained is the narrowly scoped one that recognition-only responses do not elicit independent systematic generation.

The source claims cited in Activity 1 support the general teaching principle (generate multiple pairs; work systematically to prove completeness). No cited source directly supports the constraint-bounding principle (Activity 2) or the coefficient-handling principle (Activity 3), so those carry empty sourceClaims and remain qualified proposals.
The bar/part-whole model from the original keyRepresentations is not instantiated in these activities; it is left as an optional representation, apt for a + b = 12 but less natural for 2x + y = 20.

probeDeeper: You found one pair. Is there another that works? How many are there altogether — and how can you be sure you haven't missed any?
Why is a + b = 12 different from a + 7 = 12 — how many answers does each have?
For 2x + y = 20, does (3, 17) work? Check it by putting the numbers in.
If a and b were allowed to be any whole numbers including 0, how would your list change?
assess.correctAnswer: a + b = 12 (whole, > 0): (1,11), (2,10), (3,9), (4,8), (5,7), (6,6), (7,5), (8,4), (9,3), (10,2), (11,1) — 11 pairs, found by stepping a from 1 to 11; complete because every value of a has been tried in order. For 2x + y = 20: any three pairs with y = 20 − 2x, e.g. (1,18), (2,16), (3,14).

errorPatterns.nextMove: Show it is a whole family of solutions — 'is there another pair? and another?'; fix a and step it through its values to reveal them all
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Offers one pair as 'the answer' and is surprised that others also work

errorPatterns.pattern: Searches unsystematically — jumps around, so pairs are missed or duplicated and completeness cannot be judged

errorPatterns.nextMove: Reread the constraint; it fixes which values of a are allowed and therefore how many pairs there are
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists pairs such as (0, 12) or (13, −1) or decimals despite the 'whole, greater than 0' condition

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the coefficient in 2x + y = 20, treating it as x + y = 20

responseLevels.gap: Finds one pair or none; no system; cannot say how many pairs there are or whether the list is complete; for 2x + y ignores the coefficient.
responseLevels.full: Generates all valid pairs by stepping one unknown through its permitted values in order, records them in a table, justifies completeness ('every value of a from 1 to 11'), respects the constraints, and handles 2x + y = 20 by computing y = 20 − 2x — transferring the systematic method to a new two-unknown equation.
responseLevels.partial: Finds several pairs and knows there is more than one, but searches unsystematically (misses or repeats), cannot justify completeness, or slips on the constraints or the coefficient — has some pairs but not the ordered, exhaustive method.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is an equation: a + b = 12, where a and b are whole numbers greater than 0. Find ALL the pairs of numbers that work, and show me how you know you have every one. Then find three different pairs that satisfy 2x + y = 20.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands generates MANY ordered pairs and justifies completeness by 'I went through every value of a in order'; a child treating it as a single-answer equation gives one pair and stops, or searches randomly and cannot tell whether the list is complete. For 2x + y = 20, respecting the coefficient (y = 20 − 2x, e.g. (3, 14)) versus offering pairs that only fit x + y = 20 (like (3, 17)) separates coefficient understanding.

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils should 'find pairs of numbers that satisfy an equation with 2 unknowns'; the non-statutory guidance includes number puzzles such as 'what 2 numbers can add up to', framing the task as generating multiple pairs.

sources.claim: When children are asked to find all possibilities they first work randomly and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting and ordering their attempts exposes the gaps, and having a system is what ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
