pedagogy.summary: This is the step from NAMING shapes to DESCRIBING them by their parts — the van Hiele shift from the visual level (a shape is recognised by its overall look) to the descriptive/analytic level (a shape is understood by countable attributes: sides and corners of 2-D shapes; faces, edges and corners of solids). At age 5-6 the language stays informal, but the mathematical work is that children attend to component attributes rather than the holistic silhouette, and can compare two shapes by a single countable property. It is best taught with real, handleable shapes that children touch and count, comparing many varied examples so attention shifts from appearance to structure, and drawing the crucial distinction that each flat face of a solid is itself a 2-D shape.
bestPractices: Give children physical 2-D tiles and 3-D solids to hold; count sides, corners and faces by touching and MARKING each one (sticker/pen) so none is double-counted or missed.

Compare pairs of shapes on ONE countable property at a time ('which has more sides?'), deliberately varying size and orientation so children learn the property is independent of how big or which way up the shape is drawn.
Model precise-but-informal language ('this face is a square', 'this shape has 3 straight sides and 3 corners') and have children echo it while pointing.
Draw out the distinction between a flat 2-D shape and the flat FACE of a 3-D solid — each face of a solid is itself a 2-D shape; use the 'can you pick it up? is it flat or solid?' test.
Use atypical, 'wonky' exemplars (long thin triangles, tilted rectangles) and non-examples to break reliance on a single prototypical picture.
keyRepresentations: Handleable wooden/plastic 2-D shape tiles and 3-D solids (cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone)
Geoboards / pin-boards for making and counting the sides of a 2-D shape
Feely-bag: describe a solid by touch alone (forces attention to faces/edges/corners, not colour)
A 'peel-off' image of a solid whose faces lift away as separate 2-D shapes
commonMisconceptions: Judges a shape by its overall look or size rather than counting its sides/corners (the bigger-drawn shape 'has more').
Counts only the sides/corners/faces that are visible in a picture or facing them, missing the hidden ones.
Uses everyday words loosely — 'corner' and 'side' blur the difference between a solid's face, edge and vertex.
Treats a 3-D solid as if it were the 2-D shape of one of its faces (calls a cube 'a square').

learn.summary: Help 5-6 year olds move from naming shapes by their overall look to describing them by countable parts: sides and corners for flat (2-D) shapes; flat faces, edges and corners for solids (3-D). The central work is attending to component attributes rather than the holistic silhouette, comparing two shapes on a single countable property, and grasping that each flat face of a solid is itself a 2-D shape. Best taught with real, handleable shapes children touch and count, with varied examples so attention shifts from appearance to structure. Corner/face counting is clearest with flat-faced solids such as cubes and cuboids; curved solids (sphere, cylinder, cone) are described by their curved surfaces. On-screen rotatable models may add value by exposing hidden back features and peeling faces, but complement rather than replace physical handling.

activities.title: Count by touching and marking every part
feedback: If a child gives a cube 4 corners or 3 faces (only the ones facing them), hand them the solid to turn and count by touch, marking each corner as it is counted; then recount from a different face to confirm the total of 8 corners is stable.
Praise counting that tracks hidden parts: 'You turned it to find the corners round the back — that's how we know there are 8.'
activities.rationale: Marking each part as it is counted prevents double-counting and omission; recounting from a new starting point builds confidence that the count is a property of the shape, not of the view. Physical handling lets children find hidden faces/corners that a single picture conceals. Keeping the corner/face count to polyhedra avoids the ill-defined case of counting 'faces' or 'corners' on a sphere.
sourceClaims: Each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling and manipulating solids while looking at images helps children count faces, edges and vertices.

Students represent only the visible side of a 3-D figure and under-count parts that are not directly visible, reflecting difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure — grounds the hidden-feature under-count when counting corners/faces from a picture.
learnerActions: Hold a physical 2-D tile to count its sides and corners, or a flat-faced solid such as a cube or cuboid to count its corners and flat faces (curved solids like a sphere, cylinder or cone have curved surfaces rather than a full set of flat faces and corners, so describe those separately).
Count each side, corner or flat face by touching it and placing a sticker or pen mark on each one as it is counted, so none is double-counted or missed.
For a flat-faced solid (cube, cuboid), turn it over and count again from a different starting face to check the total stays the same.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's number of sides/corners/flat faces is found by systematically counting all of them, including the ones round the back, not by guessing from the front view.

activities.title: Compare two shapes on one countable property
feedback: If a child picks the larger triangle as having 'more sides' because it is bigger, count each side together by touching and marking; the rectangle's 4 sides against the triangle's 3 make counting win over size.
Reinforce: 'The triangle is bigger, but the rectangle has more sides — 4 against 3. We counted them.'
activities.rationale: Deliberately drawing the triangle larger than the rectangle sets size and side-count in conflict, forcing children to rely on counting. Varying size and orientation across many examples teaches that the property does not depend on how big or which way up a shape is drawn.
sourceClaims: Common early-years errors: children treat only regular triangles/brick-like rectangles as shapes (shape defined by its typical image) and only accept squares with a horizontal base (defined by orientation); the remedy is to attend to properties (sides/corners for 2-D; edges/faces/vertices for 3-D), handle real objects, and use varied orientations, sizes and materials.
learnerActions: Look at a triangle drawn large and a rectangle drawn small, placed side by side.
Decide which has more sides, and count each side by touching and marking it.
Say which has more sides and how you know, using the count rather than the size.
activities.intendedInsight: Which shape has more sides is decided by counting, not by which is drawn bigger: the count is independent of size and orientation.

activities.title: Each face is a 2-D shape; flat vs solid
feedback: If a child names the solid by a 2-D face ('it's a square'), place a single thin tile next to the cube and talk about how the tile is flat (one 2-D shape) while the cube has depth with six square faces; name each square as one of the six faces, not the whole solid.
Affirm precise-but-informal language: 'This face is a square, and the cube has six of them.'
activities.rationale: Naming each face as a 2-D shape ON the solid, while contrasting a flat tile (one 2-D shape) with the solid's depth and six faces, targets the 2-D-name-for-a-solid confusion directly. Ask children about the mathematical shape represented; a physical tile or card has slight thickness and can be picked up, so 'can you pick it up?' is not a reliable flat-vs-solid test and is avoided here.
sourceClaims: Children often name a solid by a 2-D shape (e.g. a coin called a 'circle'); the flat-vs-solid 'can you pick it up?' test and everyday twins (ball=sphere, box=cuboid, can=cylinder) help separate a 3-D object from a 2-D shape.

Each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling and manipulating solids while looking at images helps children count faces, edges and vertices.
learnerActions: Point to one face of a cube and name its 2-D shape ('this face is a square').
Check whether all the faces are the same 2-D shape.

Compare a single thin tile with the whole cube: the tile is almost flat and shows one 2-D shape, while the cube has depth and six flat faces. Note that a real tile or card has a little thickness but stands for an ideal flat shape, so talk about the shape it represents rather than whether you can pick it up.
Match everyday objects to solids and, where they have them, their flat faces (ball = sphere, no flat faces; box = cuboid, rectangle faces; can = cylinder, two circle faces and a curved surface).
activities.intendedInsight: A flat-faced solid such as a cube has flat faces that are 2-D shapes, but the solid is not the same as one of those faces: a cube is not 'a square'. Curved solids such as a sphere have curved surfaces instead of, or as well as, flat faces.

activities.title: Predict then count a cube's corners
feedback: Children who look without analysing may predict only the corners they can see from one view (for example 4 when looking straight at one face). Use the gap between the prediction and the counted 8, and their reaction to the corners 'round the back', to open a discussion about hidden features.
Encourage the realisation 'there are more round the back!' as the key moment that breaks visible-only counting.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-count structure makes the visible-only under-count visible to the child as a surprise, which motivates systematic turning-and-counting. This is a teaching use of a prediction prompt, not only an end-of-lesson check.
sourceClaims: Students represent only the visible side of a 3-D figure and under-count parts that are not directly visible, reflecting difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure — grounds the hidden-feature under-count when counting corners/faces from a picture.
learnerActions: Before counting, predict out loud how many corners the cube has altogether and say the number.
Turn and mark every corner together, counting the ones round the back.
Compare the predicted number with the counted total of 8, and talk about the corners that were hidden.
activities.intendedInsight: Looking at the front of a solid under-counts its parts; turning it reveals hidden corners, so a solid has features all the way round.

activities.title: Explore hidden structure with a rotatable solid model (optional complement)
feedback: When back corners swing into view, prompt 'there are more round the back!' and count up to the full total.
When a face peels away, ask what 2-D shape it is and whether all the faces are the same, linking the screen model back to the solid in the child's hands.
activities.rationale: Persistent glowing tags prevent double-counting, rotation surfaces hidden corners, and peel-off faces make 'each face is a 2-D shape' literally visible. These interaction examples are optional illustrations of the mechanism; a rotatable screen model may show hidden structure but is a complement to, not a replacement for, physical handling, and comparative efficacy over flat media is not established by the cited sources. A static labelled image can still teach the vocabulary even though it does not let the child count or discover hidden faces.
sourceClaims: Students represent only the visible side of a 3-D figure and under-count parts that are not directly visible, reflecting difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure — grounds the hidden-feature under-count when counting corners/faces from a picture.

Each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling and manipulating solids while looking at images helps children count faces, edges and vertices.
learnerActions: On screen, spin a solid-coloured (non-see-through) cube and tap each corner you can see; each tagged corner keeps a glowing dot that stays, so none is double-counted.
Keep turning the cube until the untagged corners from the back swing into view, and tag those too.
Tap a face so it peels off as a flat square that floats into a '2-D shapes' tray, separating the flat square from the solid block.
Alongside the screen, handle real wooden solids and count their corners and faces by touch.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid has features all the way round, and each flat face is a 2-D shape that can be seen apart from the solid; a model that persists tags and peels faces makes both ideas concrete.

activities.title: Break the prototype with wonky and atypical shapes
feedback: If a child rejects a tilted square or a long thin triangle, count the sides and corners together (and for the square, check the sides are equal and the corners are square) to confirm it still fits.
Confirm property-based reasoning: 'It has 3 straight sides and 3 corners, so it is still a triangle even though it is long and thin.'
activities.rationale: Atypical exemplars and non-examples break reliance on a single prototypical image and on fixed orientation, which are documented early-years errors. Varying the examples pushes attention to structure. A sort can check property-based classification but does not itself elicit the handling or explanation, so pair it with counting and talk.
sourceClaims: Common early-years errors: children treat only regular triangles/brick-like rectangles as shapes (shape defined by its typical image) and only accept squares with a horizontal base (defined by orientation); the remedy is to attend to properties (sides/corners for 2-D; edges/faces/vertices for 3-D), handle real objects, and use varied orientations, sizes and materials.
learnerActions: Examine long thin triangles, tilted rectangles, and squares with a non-horizontal base.

Count the sides and corners of each; for squares and rectangles also check that the corners are square corners (and, for a square, that all sides are the same length); then decide whether it is still the named shape.

Sort examples from non-examples, explaining the decision by the shape's sides and corners (how many, and for squares and rectangles whether the corners are square and the sides equal) rather than by how typical the shape looks.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape is defined by its properties (number and kind of sides/corners), not by matching a single typical picture or a particular orientation.

constraints: Keep language informal at this age: 'corners' for vertices is acceptable; the mathematical work is attending to countable parts, not formal terminology.

Physical, handleable shapes that children touch, turn and mark are central; screen models are a complement that may expose hidden structure and peeling faces, not a substitute for handling real solids.

A static labelled image or a scored quiz can teach vocabulary or check counts, but neither elicits the independent counting, handling and discovery of hidden features that this topic targets; use them as support or end-checks, not as the main learning experience.
A feely-bag (describe a solid by touch alone) usefully forces attention to faces/edges/corners rather than colour, and geoboards let children make and count sides of a 2-D shape.
When comparing two shapes, compare one countable property at a time and vary size and orientation so children learn the property is independent of appearance.

Paper and card cutouts have real thickness and can be picked up, so 'can you pick it up?' does not reliably separate flat from solid; use cutouts as approximations for ideal flat faces and ask about the flat shape represented versus the solid it is a face of.
Use a genuinely cube-shaped object when naming something a cube, and a cuboid for a general box.

Confine systematic corner/flat-face counting to polyhedra such as cubes and cuboids; describe curved solids (sphere, cylinder, cone) by their curved surfaces — e.g. a sphere has no flat faces, edges or corners — rather than force-fitting them to a corner/face count.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The Oxford Owl source's 'can you pick it up? is it flat or solid?' test is unreliable: flat tiles and card cutouts can also be picked up and have slight thickness. It was replaced in learner-facing text with a flatness/depth and face-count comparison and a question about the shape represented; the original claim is retained verbatim only as a sourceClaim, not as a learner instruction.

Corner/face counting was scoped to polyhedra (cube, cuboid). Curved solids do not carry a full set of countable flat faces/corners; this scoping is an editorial correction and is not drawn from a specific cited claim.

One cited source (Sudirman et al., 2023, on the visible-only under-count) used a junior-high sample and documents the general obstacle, not age 5-6 specifically; treat its application to young learners as an informed extrapolation.

The legacy claim that peeling faces and hidden-corner discovery can be achieved 'in a way no flat medium can' was softened: a rotatable model is proposed as a useful complement with a stated affordance (showing hidden structure), not as uniquely necessary. Comparative efficacy over flat media is not established by the cited sources.

The legacy framing that a static image is 'passive exposure, not analysis', that a quiz 'only checks', and that an in-role conversation 'adds no pedagogical value' were softened to scoped observable limits; these are not established as universal pedagogical laws by the sources.
Assessment and pedagogy source fields were not altered; only learning guidance and this audit were produced.

assess.poeTask: Hold up the cube. 'Predict: how many corners do you think this cube has altogether? Say your number before we count.' Most children who look without analysing predict 3 or 4 (the corners they see). Then turn and mark every corner together. The gap between their predicted count and the counted 8 — and their reaction to the corners 'round the back' — is the diagnostic: it exposes whether they were reasoning about the whole solid or only its visible face.
probeDeeper: Here is a triangle drawn big and a rectangle drawn small. Which has more sides, and how do you know?
Show me one face of the cube. What 2-D shape is it? Are all the faces the same shape?
How is this cube different from a square you draw on paper?
Roll the cube so a different face is on top. Does it still have the same number of corners? How can you be sure without recounting from scratch?
assess.correctAnswer: The faces are squares; the cube has 8 corners (vertices). Crucially, the child counts systematically — turning the cube or accounting for the corners they cannot see — rather than counting only the ones facing them. Informal 'corners' for vertices is fine at this age.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names the solid by one of its 2-D faces — 'it's a square' — not distinguishing the flat face from the 3-D block ('a cube is a square').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the solid with a single flat tile: 'can you pick it up? is it flat or solid?' Then name each face as a 2-D shape ON the solid, so the square is one of six faces, not the whole thing.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's a square.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked what the shape is, gives a 2-D name (square, circle) for the solid, or agrees the cube 'is a square'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts only the visible faces/corners and misses the hidden ones — gives a cube 3 faces or 4 corners (the number facing them).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand them the solid to turn and count by touch, sticking a marker on each corner as it is counted so none is missed or double-counted; then count again from a different starting face to confirm the total is stable.
errorPatterns.distractor: 4 corners.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States 4 corners or 3 faces for a cube; the second tier reveals they 'just looked' at the front rather than turning it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges 'more sides/corners' by overall size or the shape's typical look rather than by counting — picks the bigger-drawn shape as having more.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count each side by touching and marking it, with the triangle drawn deliberately larger than the rectangle so size and side-count disagree and counting has to win.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the triangle-vs-rectangle comparison (with the triangle drawn larger), names the triangle as having 'more sides' because it is bigger.

responseLevels.gap: Judges shapes by overall appearance or size, or gives a 2-D name for the solid ('it's a square'); cannot count sides/corners reliably or counts only the visible ones.
responseLevels.full: Uses a counted property to compare two shapes ('the rectangle has more sides — 4 against 3') independently of size and orientation, distinguishes the flat 2-D face from the 3-D solid, and accounts for hidden faces/corners when counting (SOLO relational, with transfer to a new case).
responseLevels.partial: Counts the sides, corners and faces correctly for a shape in front of them and can name a face's 2-D shape, but lists these attributes without using them to compare, or reverts to appearance when the size/orientation is varied (SOLO multistructural — lists the parts).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a real cube in the child's hands. Ask: 'What shape are the flat faces of this cube, and how many corners does it have? Tell me how you worked out the number of corners.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has moved from looking to analysing names the 2-D square face and counts all 8 corners by tracking the hidden ones; a child still at the visual level either calls the whole solid 'a square' (2-D/3-D conflation) or counts only the 3-4 corners facing them. The second tier — 'how did you work it out' — separates a real count from a guess: the analytic child describes turning/marking, the visual child says 'I just looked'.

sources.claim: Each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling and manipulating solids while looking at images helps children count faces, edges and vertices.
sources.source: Oak National Academy — Describe and name 3D shapes (KS1 / Year 2 Maths), key learning points and teacher tip

sources.claim: Students represent only the visible side of a 3-D figure and under-count parts that are not directly visible, reflecting difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure — grounds the hidden-feature under-count when counting corners/faces from a picture.
sources.source: Sudirman, Runisah, Kusumah & Martadiputra (2023), 'Epistemological Obstacle in 3D Geometry Thinking', Pegem Journal of Education and Instruction 13(4) (note: junior-high sample; documents the general obstacle, not age 5-6 specifically)

sources.claim: Common early-years errors: children treat only regular triangles/brick-like rectangles as shapes (shape defined by its typical image) and only accept squares with a horizontal base (defined by orientation); the remedy is to attend to properties (sides/corners for 2-D; edges/faces/vertices for 3-D), handle real objects, and use varied orientations, sizes and materials.
sources.source: NCETM — Early Years Shape and Space (common errors and approaches)

sources.claim: Children often name a solid by a 2-D shape (e.g. a coin called a 'circle'); the flat-vs-solid 'can you pick it up?' test and everyday twins (ball=sphere, box=cuboid, can=cylinder) help separate a 3-D object from a 2-D shape.
sources.source: Oxford Owl (Oxford University Press) — Geometry & shapes, Year 1 (age 5-6)

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Rocks and soil

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Science, Year 3 Rocks):** Pupils recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-ESS supports; soils as weathered Earth materials):** Recognise soil as broken-down rock plus decayed living matter, and that different soils have different properties.

- **Operational details:** The load-bearing idea is that soil is a MIXTURE — tiny broken-down rock particles plus decomposed organic matter (humus) — not a single 'brown stuff'. Children compare soil types (sandy, clay, loam) by observable and testable properties: particle size, how gritty or sticky it feels, and especially how fast water drains through (a percolation test). A second big idea is TIME: rock breaks down into soil incredibly slowly, over very long periods. Build understanding through hands-on investigation — examine soils with a lens, do a settling jar (particles sort into layers) and a drainage comparison — then link back to prior rock-property work: soil starts as rock.
bestPractices: Teach soil as a MIXTURE of broken rock + organic matter; separate the two components explicitly (a settling jar shows sand/silt/clay layers with humus floating on top).
Compare soil types (sandy vs clay vs loam) by testable properties, especially a fair drainage/percolation test with equal water and time.
Use hands-on investigation with hand lenses and jars — soil properties are felt and observed, not told.
Connect to prior rock work: soil begins as rock that has been broken down, and this takes a very long time.
Draw out why soil type matters (drainage affects which plants grow) to make the properties meaningful.
keyRepresentations: A settling jar showing soil separating into layers (stones, sand, silt, clay, floating humus).
A drainage/percolation comparison of sandy vs clay vs loam soils.
A soil-profile / cutaway diagram (organic layer over broken rock over bedrock).
A soil-property comparison table (gritty/sticky, drains fast/slow, colour).
commonMisconceptions: 'Soil is just dirt / one single substance' — not seeing it as a mixture of rock particles and organic matter.
'Soil has nothing to do with rock' — missing that soil is broken-down rock.
'All soils are the same' — not distinguishing sandy, clay and loam by property.
'Soil forms quickly' — underestimating the very long time rock takes to break down.
'Clay soil is best because it holds water' or 'sandy is best because it drains' — treating one soil as universally superior rather than suited to different conditions.

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds: soil is a MIXTURE of broken-down rock particles (sand, silt, clay) plus decomposed organic matter (humus), not a single 'brown stuff'. Children investigate by hand — a settling jar separates soil into layers, a fair drainage test compares soil types, and a hand lens reveals rock grains and leaf bits. A second big idea is TIME: rock breaks down into soil very slowly. Hands-on investigation with real local soil is the core experience; cutaway diagrams, profiles and sorting tasks support vocabulary and classification.

activities.title: Settling jar: watch soil pull apart into its parts
feedback: If a learner says 'it's all just dirt', point to the separated layers: 'The stones and sand that sank are broken-down rock; the dark floating bits are rotted plants — that's two different things mixed together.'
If a learner denies any link to rock, direct attention to the gritty sand and stones at the bottom: 'Those grains are tiny pieces of rock.'
Praise naming each layer and saying where it came from, not just listing colours.
activities.rationale: Separating the components physically makes the abstract 'mixture' idea observable, addressing the misconception that soil is a single substance and the misconception that soil has nothing to do with rock.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter.
Soil is a mixture of weathered rock particles (sand/silt/clay) and decomposed organic matter (humus); soil types differ in particle size and drainage; soil formation is very slow.
learnerActions: Scoop soil into a clear jar and fill with water, leaving space at the top.
Put the lid on, shake well, then set the jar down and leave it to settle.

Watch and record what settles first, what settles last, and what floats — you will typically see heavy stones and sand sink first, finer silt next, cloudy clay settle slowly on top, and dark bits of rotted leaf (humus) float; write down what you actually observe, as real soils vary.
Draw and label the layers you see, naming which are broken-down rock and which are once-living matter.
Use a hand lens on a pinch of dry soil to spot rock grains and small pieces of plant material up close.
activities.intendedInsight: Soil is a mixture: it separates into broken-down rock particles (sand/silt/clay) plus decomposed plant matter (humus), so it is not one single substance.

activities.title: Fair drainage race: sandy vs clay vs loam
feedback: If a learner says 'all soils are the same', contrast the drainage times they actually measured, for example: 'Look how much faster the water came through the sandy one than the clay one.' (Use the class's real results; dry, cracked clay can sometimes let water through quickly at first.)
If a learner claims one soil is simply best, ask 'best for what?' — clay holds water, sand drains quickly; each suits different conditions.
Reinforce the fair-test idea: 'We used the same amount of soil, the same amount of water, the same-sized funnels and the same timing, so the difference is most likely caused by the type of soil.'
activities.rationale: A controlled comparison lets children distinguish soil types by measurable properties and challenges both the 'all soils are the same' and 'one soil is universally best' misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Soil is a mixture of weathered rock particles (sand/silt/clay) and decomposed organic matter (humus); soil types differ in particle size and drainage; soil formation is very slow.
learnerActions: Set up three funnels or pots, one with sandy soil, one with clay soil, one with loam, each with the same amount of soil.
Pour the SAME amount of water into each at the same time to make it a fair test.
Watch and time how fast water drains through each, and record which is fastest and slowest.
Feel each soil (with permission) and note whether it is gritty or sticky.
Describe how the soils differ and suggest why a plant might prefer one soil over another.
activities.intendedInsight: Different soils have different, testable properties: water drains fast through sandy soil and slowly through clay, and these differences matter for which plants grow well — no single soil is universally 'best'.

activities.title: Soil profile and the slow story of soil
feedback: If a learner thinks soil 'was always there', connect to the profile: 'The solid rock at the bottom slowly crumbles into the loose soil above — it took a very long time.'
If a learner thinks soil forms quickly, emphasise the long timescale: rock breaks down over very many years, not overnight.
Reward answers that name both the rock origin and the once-living (humus) origin.
activities.rationale: A labelled profile gives vocabulary and a spatial story that supports the time/formation idea; it is a scaffold for the hands-on tests, not a replacement for them.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 3 Rocks: pupils recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter.
Soil is a mixture of weathered rock particles (sand/silt/clay) and decomposed organic matter (humus); soil types differ in particle size and drainage; soil formation is very slow.
learnerActions: Examine a soil-profile cutaway (organic layer on top, broken rock below, solid bedrock at the bottom) and label each layer.
For each layer, say what it is and where it came from.
Discuss or write how the solid rock below slowly breaks apart over a very long time to make the loose particles above it.
Use a lift-the-flap or 'what is soil made of?' task to recall the two main ingredients: broken rock and humus.
activities.intendedInsight: Soil forms slowly as rock gradually breaks apart over very long periods into particles that mix with decomposed living matter; in a profile like this one, the layers show that journey from solid bedrock up to soil (some soils instead form from rock pieces carried in by rivers, ice or wind).

activities.title: Sort and match soils by property
feedback: If a learner picks only 'rock' or only 'dead plants' as what soil is made of, remind them it is BOTH mixed together.
If a learner mismatches drainage, link back to the drainage race results.
Note: sorting and matching check recall and classification; they do not by themselves show a learner can run or reason through an investigation — pair them with the hands-on benches.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and matching give clean practice and checking of vocabulary and classification, complementing the investigative work. Recognition tasks can confirm classification but do not on their own elicit a learner independently constructing an explanation.
sourceClaims: Soil is a mixture of weathered rock particles (sand/silt/clay) and decomposed organic matter (humus); soil types differ in particle size and drainage; soil formation is very slow.
learnerActions: Sort soil cards or samples into gritty vs sticky groups.
Match each soil type (sandy, clay, loam) to its drainage speed (fast, slow, in between).
Answer: 'What is soil made of?' choosing the answer that names both broken-down rock and decomposed organic matter.
For plants: discuss why a soil's drainage might help or hinder certain plants.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can classify soils by observable properties and articulate that soil's two core ingredients are broken rock and humus.

constraints: Use real jars of local soil and a real percolation test as the essential hands-on complement; on-screen settling jars and drainage races are simulations that preview or review, consistent with the KS2 practical-science expectation for felt, observed investigation.
Keep the drainage comparison a fair test: equal soil amounts, equal water, equal time — otherwise differences cannot be attributed to the soil type.

A soil-profile diagram or on-screen cutaway supports vocabulary and the formation story but cannot deliver the drainage comparison that distinguishes soil types; use it alongside, not instead of, the tests.
Sorting/matching/multiple-choice tasks check recall and classification; they do not require learners to construct or run an investigation.
Avoid teaching any one soil as universally 'best' — frame clay (holds water) and sand (drains fast) as suited to different conditions.
Correct the 'plants eat soil' idea where it arises: plants take water and minerals from soil and make their own food by photosynthesis; soil is not consumed as food.
A dig-down 3D soil pit can give a spatial sense of horizons but is optional; the learning target is composition, drainage and formation time, which a labelled cutaway can also convey.
reviewNotes: Independent re-review: both prior corrections were verified present — activities[2].intendedInsight no longer states 'top down' and is consistent with its feedback (bedrock below crumbles upward), and activities[0] records observation rather than prescribing the outcome. No new critical learner-facing errors found.

This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims about soil composition, drainage differences by particle size, and slow formation come from DfE KS2 and USDA NRCS; these support the general principles but do not establish efficacy of any specific activity above.

Settling-jar layer order (stones/sand sink, silt, then clay; humus floats) reflects the row's description. Real-world results vary with soil composition and how long it is left; treat observed layers as approximate rather than guaranteed, and let children record what they actually see.

The original row asserts '3D adds little' and that dialogue 'can't run the tests'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; softened to scoped notes about affordances rather than universal claims.
Hand-lens/jar interactivity examples (zoom to reveal grains, shake-and-settle, timed funnels) are retained as concrete learning mechanisms, not mandated implementations.

probeDeeper: If you rubbed two rocks together for a very long time, how could that help make soil?
Are all soils the same? How do sandy soil and clay soil behave differently with water?
Do plants eat the soil? What do they actually get from it?
assess.correctAnswer: Soil is made over a very long time as rock gradually breaks down into tiny particles, mixed with decomposed plant and animal matter (humus). So soil comes partly from broken-down rock and partly from once-living things — it didn't just appear.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Soil has always just been there and isn't made of anything'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Soil forms as rock weathers and organisms decompose, over a very long time.
errorPatterns.distractor: Soil has always been there; it isn't made from anything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: gives no origin for soil

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Soil has nothing to do with rock'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Look at the sand and grit in soil — those are broken-down rock particles.
errorPatterns.distractor: Soil has nothing to do with rock.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies the broken-down-rock component

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Plants eat the soil / soil is the plant's food'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Soil gives water, minerals and support; plants make their own food by photosynthesis.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats soil as food that is consumed

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All soil is the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare sandy, clay and loam soils — how they feel and drain water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: no sense that soils differ

responseLevels.gap: Thinks soil was always there or has no link to rock.
responseLevels.full: Explains that soil forms slowly from broken-down rock mixed with decomposed organic matter, compares soil types by their properties, and knows plants take water and minerals from soil rather than eating it.
responseLevels.partial: Says soil comes from rock OR contains dead plants but not both, or thinks all soils are alike.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Where does soil come from — has it always just been there, or is it made from something? And what is soil actually made of?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks soil is just dirt that was always there, or who sees no link to rock, differs from one who knows soil forms from broken-down rock plus organic matter over a long time.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Tables, charts, and graphs

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Working Scientifically — 'analysis'):** Pupils should be taught to apply mathematical concepts and calculate results; present observations and data using appropriate methods, including tables and graphs; interpret observations and data, including identifying patterns and using observations, measurements and data to draw conclusions; and understand that scientific methods and theories develop as earlier explanations are modified. The programme of study also requires correct use of SI units and, in mathematics, plotting graphs of two variables, drawing a line of best fit through data points and finding its gradient.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 5 Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking, grades 6–8):** Students create algorithms/organise data to reveal patterns, and use digital tools and mathematical representations (e.g. graphs, tables) to describe and support scientific claims; SEP 4 (Analyzing and Interpreting Data, 6–8) requires constructing, analysing and interpreting graphical displays to identify linear and nonlinear relationships. The move from KS2/grade-5 is naming and using the correct display for the data type and beginning to quantify the relationship (gradient of a straight-line graph).

- **Operational details:** This is the representational capstone of the data spine: the child must (a) build a data table whose column headings carry both the quantity and its SI unit written as a ratio, e.g. 'Mass / g' or 'Time / s', with values to a consistent number of decimal places/significant figures; (b) choose the correct graph type from the data structure — bar chart for a categoric independent variable, line graph for a continuous IV, scatter graph for two co-varying continuous measures — and plot points accurately on labelled, evenly-scaled axes that use a sensible fraction of the grid; (c) draw a single straight line of best fit that balances points either side (not a dot-to-dot), and (d) read the gradient from two well-separated points on the LINE (not raw data points), expressing it with the compound unit (rise-unit ÷ run-unit). The IV conventionally goes on the x-axis, the DV on the y-axis.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/quantitative). This is where recording data stops being 'tidy presentation' and becomes quantitative analysis: the graph is a computation, and the gradient is a physical quantity extracted from it. Success = given a set of paired continuous measurements, independently produces a correctly headed table, selects and plots the right graph with sensible scales, draws a genuine line of best fit and calculates its gradient with the right unit — the platform on which the age-12+ conclusions/error-analysis topic then builds.
bestPractices: Teach the data structure first, then the display: decide whether the independent variable is categoric (→ bar chart) or continuous (→ line/scatter) BEFORE drawing anything, so graph choice is a reasoned decision not a habit.
Require the ratio-form unit in every heading and on every axis (e.g. 'Mass / g'), so the numbers in cells and on axes are pure and unambiguous — model it explicitly and mark it every time.

Explicitly teach scale choice as a design decision: axes should use at least half the available grid with a sensible interval (1, 2, 5, 10), and demonstrate side-by-side how a squashed or awkward scale hides a trend.

Contrast a line of best fit with a dot-to-dot join: show that best fit summarises the trend and averages out scatter, deliberately need NOT pass through every point (or the origin), and enables reading between data.
Read the gradient from two widely-separated points ON the line, not from raw data, and always attach the compound unit — practise the rise÷run with the units carried through the calculation.
Use real experimental data the child has a stake in (e.g. spring extension vs mass, cooling curves) so the gradient means something physical rather than being an abstract exercise.
keyRepresentations: Headed data table with ratio-form units, e.g. column 'Mass / g' | 'Extension / mm'
The graph-type decision tree: categoric IV → bar chart; continuous IV → line graph; two continuous measures → scatter graph
Labelled, evenly-scaled x–y axes (IV on x, DV on y) with a 'sensible scale' fraction-of-grid heuristic
Line of best fit balancing points above and below, with a right-angled 'rise/run' triangle drawn on it
Gradient as rise ÷ run carrying compound units (e.g. mm/g), read from two points on the line
commonMisconceptions: Joining data points dot-to-dot and calling it a line graph, instead of drawing a single best-fit line.
Believing the line of best fit must pass through every point or always through the origin.
Reading the gradient from raw data points rather than from two points on the drawn line.
Choosing a bar chart when both variables are continuous (so the trend/relationship is lost).
Omitting units from table headings and axis labels, or writing them inside every cell instead of in the heading.
Using a non-uniform, cramped or origin-forced scale that distorts or hides the pattern.
Quoting a gradient as a bare number with no unit, treating it as dimensionless.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13, learners work both directions on paired continuous data: they interpret what a line shows (a straight line indicates a constant-rate/linear relationship, and one through the origin — as in this spring data — is additionally proportional) AND construct the representation — a headed data table with ratio-form SI units, a graph type chosen from the data structure, accurately plotted points on evenly-scaled labelled axes, a single line of best fit, and a gradient read from two points on that line with its compound unit. The load-bearing work is construction with feedback at each step; recognition and value-reading tasks test the skill but do not themselves have the learner construct a table and graph from scratch. A spring extension vs load dataset makes the gradient a meaningful physical quantity (extension per unit load, in cm/N; this is the inverse of the spring's stiffness, which is load ÷ extension in N/cm).

activities.title: Graphing Studio: from raw data to a gradient
feedback: Heading without a unit is flagged amber until the ratio-form unit is added ('Load / N' accepted, 'Load' flagged); this keeps the numbers in cells pure and unambiguous.
Choosing a bar chart for two continuous variables leaves the axis in discrete blocks so the trend cannot show, making the mismatch visible rather than only marked wrong.

A squashed or awkward scale triggers a 'wasted grid' signal and clusters the points, showing how a poor scale hides a trend; a good scale uses at least about half the grid in equal steps with a sensible interval (1, 2, 5, 10).
A residual indicator shows points tugging above/below the dragged line until it balances, illustrating that best fit summarises the trend and averages out scatter rather than joining dots.

If the relationship is read incorrectly, prompt: a straight line shows a constant-rate (linear) relationship, and here, because it passes through the origin, extension is proportional to load — not merely a neat picture.
If a gradient is computed from one point or from raw data dots, prompt: use two well-separated points that lie ON the best-fit line and take the differences.
If the gradient is given as a bare number, prompt for its compound unit and its physical meaning (here cm/N = extension per unit load, the inverse of the spring's stiffness).
activities.rationale: Each sub-skill — heading with units, graph-type choice, scale design, line of best fit, interpreting the line, gradient from the line — is an act of construction or interpretation, so building with step-by-step feedback lets the learner feel why each convention matters and recompute as the representation changes. Using data the learner has a stake in makes the gradient a physical quantity rather than an abstract exercise.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Working Scientifically requires pupils to present observations and data using appropriate methods including tables and graphs, apply mathematical concepts and calculate results, and use SI units.
The mathematics national curriculum requires plotting graphs of two variables, drawing a line of best fit through data points, and finding its gradient.

NGSS SEP 5 (Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking) for grades 6–8 has students organise data and use mathematical representations such as graphs and tables to describe and support scientific claims; SEP 4 (Analyzing and Interpreting Data, 6–8) has them construct and interpret graphical displays to identify linear and nonlinear relationships.
learnerActions: Start from a real paired dataset, e.g. spring extension vs load (Load / N: 1, 2, 3; Extension / cm: 3, 6, 9).
Type table column headings; a heading of 'Load' (or 'Mass') alone is flagged until you add the unit as a ratio, e.g. 'Load / N' or 'Mass / g', at which point the column is accepted.

Choose a graph type for the data: if you pick a bar chart for two continuous measures, the x-axis stays in discrete blocks and the trend cannot appear, prompting you to switch to a line/scatter graph so the axis becomes continuous.

Set the axis scales; a cramped scale (e.g. an axis running to 100 when the extensions only reach 9 cm) lights a 'wasted grid' meter and the points huddle in one corner, so you re-space in equal steps until the data fills at least about half the available grid using a sensible interval (1, 2, 5, 10).

Drag a single straight line through the point cloud; a live residual indicator shows points pulling above and below until the pulls balance, and the line deliberately does NOT have to pass through every point (nor be forced through the origin).

Interpret the line itself: a straight line shows a constant-rate (linear) relationship between extension and load, and because this data passes through the origin it is additionally proportional; the steepness tells you how much extension you get per unit load.

Click two well-separated points that lie ON the line (not raw data dots); the studio marks the rise and run, computes rise ÷ run, and asks you to write the gradient with its compound unit (e.g. cm/N, or mm/g for a mass-based setup).
State what the gradient means physically, e.g. extension per unit load (cm/N); a stiffer spring gives a smaller gradient, because stiffness is load ÷ extension (N/cm), the inverse of this gradient.
activities.intendedInsight: Each table/graph convention exists to make data readable and computable: the graph is not decoration but a machine for extracting a physical quantity, and the gradient is that quantity carried with its unit — while the shape of the line tells you about the relationship (a straight line means a constant rate, and through the origin it is proportional).

activities.title: Decide the display before you draw
feedback: If a line graph is chosen for categoric data like favourite colours, prompt: a continuous line implies in-between values that do not exist between categories, so a bar chart is appropriate.
If a bar chart is chosen for two continuous measures, point out the trend/relationship is lost and a line or scatter graph is needed.
If the IV and DV are placed on the wrong axes, restate the convention: IV on x, DV on y.
activities.rationale: Deciding data structure first makes the display a justified choice and directly targets the common error of picking a bar chart for continuous data; naming the correct display and beginning to quantify the relationship is the step-up expected at this stage.
sourceClaims: NGSS SEP 5 (Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking) for grades 6–8 has students organise data and use mathematical representations such as graphs and tables to describe and support scientific claims; SEP 4 (Analyzing and Interpreting Data, 6–8) has them construct and interpret graphical displays to identify linear and nonlinear relationships.
learnerActions: Given a described dataset, classify the independent variable as categoric (e.g. favourite colours) or continuous (e.g. load in newtons) BEFORE choosing any display.
Match: categoric IV → bar chart; continuous IV → line graph; two co-varying continuous measures → scatter graph.
Sort the two variables onto the correct axes: independent variable on the x-axis, dependent variable on the y-axis.
Explain for each case why the chosen display reveals (or a wrong one hides) the pattern.
activities.intendedInsight: Graph choice is a reasoned decision driven by the data structure, not a drawing habit; the right display preserves the relationship you want to read.

activities.title: Test your graphing: targeted question set
feedback: For the gradient step, if points are taken from raw data rather than the drawn line, flag it as the classic error and require two points on the line.
If a gradient is given without its compound unit, mark it incomplete and ask for the unit.
For the distractor graph-type item, explain why the continuous-continuous data needs a line/scatter, not bars.
activities.rationale: Each component judgement maps cleanly onto a check, so a structured question set rigorously tests whether the skill transfers, especially under classic error-provoking distractors. It assesses application rather than providing the construct-and-recompute feedback of building a graph, so it works best alongside or after construction practice.
learnerActions: Pick the correct graph type for a described dataset, including a distractor case where a bar chart is tempting but wrong because both variables are continuous.
Complete a table heading by supplying the correct SI unit in ratio form.
Sort given variables onto x- vs y-axis (IV vs DV).
Read a value off a plotted line of best fit using a slider/marker.
Sketch a line of best fit through a plotted point cloud.
Calculate a two-point gradient, reading points from the LINE not the raw data, and supply the compound unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirm that each convention — unit in heading, correct graph type, axis assignment, reading off the line, gradient with units — can be applied independently and under the classic error conditions.

activities.title: Good-vs-bad graph: annotated exemplar reference
feedback: Each callout confirms the convention and why it matters; the flawed comparison names the specific fault (e.g. 'a dot-to-dot join cannot be read for a single gradient', 'a squashed scale hides the trend').
Prompt learners to apply the same checks to their own constructed graph.
activities.rationale: An annotated worked example supports comparison and self-correction. It is a reference and scaffold: because the learner reads about good practice rather than constructing and correcting their own, it is best paired with hands-on construction rather than used as the only activity.
learnerActions: Study a correctly built table-and-graph with tap-to-reveal callouts: 'this heading shows the unit as a ratio', 'best-fit line balances points above and below', 'gradient = rise/run read from two points on the line'.
Compare it side by side with a flawed version (missing units, cramped/uneven scale, dot-to-dot join, gradient from a single raw point) and name each fault.
Use the exemplar as a reference while constructing your own graph.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked exemplar makes the conventions and their rationale explicit and provides a reference standard for self-checking.

constraints: The exemplar/annotated-image activity is a reference scaffold: it shows good practice but does not have the learner construct or correct a graph, so it should accompany construction practice, not replace it.

The question set tests whether conventions are applied correctly but does not provide the step-by-step recompute-as-you-go feedback of building a graph; recognition and value-reading responses do not themselves elicit independent construction of a table and graph from scratch.
A line of best fit summarises a trend and need not pass through every point or through the origin; teach it as a balance of points above and below, explicitly contrasted with a dot-to-dot join.

Always read the gradient from two well-separated points that lie ON the drawn line, not from raw data points, and attach the compound unit (rise-unit ÷ run-unit); a gradient is not a bare dimensionless number.

Units belong in the table heading and axis label in ratio form (e.g. 'Mass / g'), not repeated inside every cell; axis scales must rise in equal steps and use at least about half the available grid with a sensible interval (1, 2, 5, 10).

Use a dataset the learner has a stake in (e.g. spring extension vs load) so the gradient is a meaningful physical quantity, and require them to state what it means (e.g. extension per unit load in cm/N, the inverse of the spring's stiffness in N/cm) and to interpret the line's shape (a straight line = a constant-rate/linear relationship, proportional only when it passes through the origin, as this data does).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Listed sources[].claim entries carry verified:false in the original row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'conversation' and '3D' entries claimed dialogue 'cannot let the child build a graph' and that a third dimension 'adds nothing'; these are narrowed here to affordance observations (the construction skill is visual-manual and lives on the grid; a dialogue can discuss reasoning but not substitute for building, and 2D tables/graphs are planar so an added spatial dimension does not serve the x–y structure). No comparative-efficacy or necessity claim is asserted beyond what sources support.

Arithmetic check: the diagnostic dataset (1,2,3 N → 3,6,9 cm) is proportional, so a genuine two-point calculation on the line (e.g. (1,3) and (3,9)) gives (9−3)/(3−1)=6/2=3 cm/N. The original correctAnswer writes this as '9 ÷ 3 = 3 cm/N', which is only valid because the proportional line passes through the origin; the activities require two well-separated points on the line and must not be read as endorsing a single-point y÷x method for non-proportional data.

Proportionality nuance: the original describes the straight line as 'proportional'. This holds for this through-origin dataset, but a straight line in general is linear/constant-rate without necessarily being proportional; the activities state this distinction explicitly rather than reproducing the overgeneralisation.

The pedagogy keyRepresentations example uses mm/g while the assessment uses cm/N — both are valid compound units for different setups and are not contradictory; the activities keep units tied to the actual dataset used.

The 'wasted grid' / 'scale efficiency' meter, residual shimmer, draggable points and unit validator are preserved as optional interaction examples that make the learning mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory mechanisms and could be realised with other construction-and-feedback media (including paper plotting with teacher checking).

probeDeeper: What does the straightness of the line tell you about the relationship between load and extension?
Your gradient is 3 — 3 what? What does that number mean for the spring?
If the data were the favourite colours of the class, would a line graph still be right? Why or why not?
Why must the axis scales go up in equal steps?
assess.correctAnswer: Interpretation: the straight line means extension is proportional to load (a constant relationship); the gradient (steepness) is how much extension you get per newton — here 3 cm/N — the spring's stiffness. Translation: the child writes headings with quantity AND unit (Load / N, Extension / cm), chooses a line graph (continuous numerical data), plots with labelled, evenly-scaled axes, draws the best-fit line, and calculates gradient = change in extension ÷ change in load = 9 ÷ 3 = 3 cm/N, stating what it means.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gradient as a bare number: calculates 3 but can't say it is cm per newton / the spring's stiffness.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x, carrying units — here extension per unit load; say what it means for the spring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The gradient is computed with no physical interpretation attached.

errorPatterns.pattern: Headings/axes without units: labels columns 'Load' and 'Extension' with no /N or /cm; axes unlabelled or unevenly scaled.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Every heading and axis needs quantity AND unit; scales must rise in equal steps.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The constructed table or graph omits units or uses an uneven scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong graph type: draws a bar chart for continuous numerical data.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Continuous numerical data → line or scatter graph; bars are for discrete categories.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Graph choice doesn't match the data type.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gradient from a single point or off-line points: computes y÷x of one data point, or uses points not on the best-fit line.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use two well-separated points that lie ON the best-fit line and take the differences.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The gradient method uses one point or raw data rather than two points on the line.

responseLevels.gap: Reads off single points but can't state the relationship; builds tables/graphs without units, with uneven scales, or picks the wrong graph type.
responseLevels.full: Interprets the line (proportional relationship; gradient = extension per newton = stiffness) AND constructs the representation correctly — units in headings, appropriate graph type, even labelled scales, best-fit line, gradient from two points with its meaning — translating fluently both ways.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets the trend and constructs a broadly correct graph, but omits units in headings/axes, or calculates the gradient without saying what it represents.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a line graph of a spring's extension against load, with a straight best-fit line through the points. First, tell me what the line is telling us — what does its straightness and its steepness (gradient) mean about the spring? Then, from this results table (Load / N: 1, 2, 3; Extension / cm: 3, 6, 9) set up the table properly with headings and units, choose and start the right graph, and work out the gradient of the line — telling me what the gradient represents.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two-way move is the discriminator: a student may read a graph yet not build one correctly (missing units in headings, uneven scales, wrong graph type), or plot competently yet not say what the gradient MEANS. Requiring both interpret and construct exposes whichever direction is weak, and the 'gradient = per-newton rate' meaning separates rote plotting from understanding.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1). Solve addition and subtraction WORD PROBLEMS within 10 using objects or drawings — applying the combining/taking-away concepts to real situations by modelling them concretely.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'solve one-step problems that involve addition and subtraction, using concrete objects and pictorial representations, and missing number problems'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.2 'solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10… by using objects or drawings'; the CGI problem taxonomy (add-to, take-from, put-together/take-apart, compare — with the unknown in various positions) frames difficulty.
• Operational details — The core skill is MODELLING: read/hear the situation, represent it with objects or a drawing, then read the answer off the model. Vary the problem STRUCTURE (result-unknown is easiest; change-unknown and start-unknown are harder) and the unknown POSITION, not just the numbers. Discourage keyword-matching ('altogether = add'); instead have children act out or draw what is happening. Keep totals within 10 so the count is manageable.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): solve a result-unknown add-to or take-from story with counters. Tier B (age 5): choose objects/drawing to model a put-together or take-apart problem and state the answer. Tier C (age 5-6): model a change-unknown or simple compare problem and explain how the drawing matches the story.
bestPractices: Teach modelling, not keyword-spotting: children act out or draw the SITUATION and read the answer from it, so 'altogether'/'left' don't become false triggers for +/−.
Systematically vary problem structure and unknown position (result-, change-, start-unknown; compare) so children build a robust sense of the operations, not one rote pattern.
Use consistent representations (counters, part-whole, bar/tape) so the model itself carries meaning across problems.
Have children retell the problem in their own words and point to each quantity in their model, tying language to representation to answer.
Start with result-unknown, keep numbers within 10, and introduce missing-number/compare forms only once modelling of simple problems is secure.
keyRepresentations: Counters/cubes acted on to match the story
Children's drawings/jottings (dots, crossing-out) of the situation
Part-part-whole model mapping story quantities to parts and whole
Simple bar/tape model for compare problems ('how many more')
Five-frame/ten-frame to organise the objects being combined or removed
commonMisconceptions: Keyword-matching ('altogether'→add, 'left'→subtract) instead of modelling the situation, which fails on compare and change/start-unknown problems.
Modelling only result-unknown structures and being stuck when the unknown is the change or the start.
Grabbing the two numbers in the problem and combining them regardless of what the story describes.
Miscounting the objects when acting out, or not matching the drawing to the actual quantities in the story.
For compare problems, adding the two amounts instead of finding the difference.

learn.summary: Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1): solve one-step addition and subtraction word problems within 10 by MODELLING the situation with objects or drawings, then reading the answer off the model. The core skill is representing what the story describes (things arriving, leaving, two groups combined, two groups compared, or a mystery start), not keyword-matching. Systematically vary problem structure and unknown position; keep totals within 10 so counting stays manageable.

activities.title: Story-modelling with counters and a mat
feedback: Check that the model matches the STORY, not just that the number is right: ask 'show me with the counters what happens to the apples.'
If the child combines both numbers (answers 8 for the apples, i.e. 6+2), have them act the take-away story out step by step with counters before counting, tying it to the removing action.
For the joining story, ask 'did the number get bigger or smaller — why?' to connect the action to the operation.
If the set-up is correct but the count slips, scaffold one-to-one counting; the modelling is sound, so do not reteach it.
activities.rationale: At this age, word-problem solving IS modelling: reading/hearing the situation, representing it concretely, and reading the result off the representation. Acting out the situation avoids the keyword-matching that fails on harder structures.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems, including missing-number problems, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
K.OA.2: solve addition and subtraction word problems within 10 using objects or drawings.
Problem difficulty is governed by situation structure and unknown position (Cognitively Guided Instruction taxonomy); teaching modelling rather than keyword-matching improves problem solving.
learnerActions: Listen to or look at a short situation, e.g. 'There are 6 apples on the tree; the wind blows 2 down.'
Take 6 apple counters and place them on a mat to match the start of the story.
Act out what happens — move the 2 fallen apples to the ground, or cross them out on a drawing.
Count what is left on the tree and say the answer aloud (4).
Retell the story in your own words and point to each quantity (the 6, the 2, what's left) in your model.
Repeat with a joining story, e.g. 'Sam has 3 marbles and gets 4 more — how many now?', adding counters to match and reading off the total (7).
activities.intendedInsight: You don't need a rule to decide 'add' or 'subtract' — you build what actually happened in the story with objects, and the answer is simply what you can then see and count.

activities.title: Part-whole and compare: beyond result-unknown
feedback: If the child adds the two numbers for the part-unknown (4 + 7 = 11), build the whole (7) and the known part (4) with counters so the gap becomes visible; use a part-whole or bar layout.
For compare problems, if the child adds the two amounts, line the groups up and point to the extra ones to show the difference is what's being asked.
Ask 'how many altogether, and how many do you already know?' to surface which quantity is missing.
Praise a correct layout even before the count, then support careful counting if needed.
activities.rationale: Difficulty is strongly influenced by situation structure and unknown position (as well as number size); missing-part, change-unknown, start-unknown and compare problems defeat keyword rules and rote result-unknown patterns, so they are introduced and modelled explicitly once simple problems are secure.
sourceClaims: Problem difficulty is governed by situation structure and unknown position (Cognitively Guided Instruction taxonomy); teaching modelling rather than keyword-matching improves problem solving.
Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems, including missing-number problems, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
learnerActions: Model a put-together problem with a missing part, e.g. 'There are 4 red counters and some blue ones, 7 altogether — how many are blue?'
Build the whole (7) and lay out the known part (4) using a part-part-whole frame.
Find the gap — the blue counters needed to fill the whole — and count them to give the answer (3).
Model a simple compare problem, e.g. 'how many more', by lining up two groups side by side (a bar/tape layout) and finding the difference.
For each problem, say whether it is a putting-together story or a comparing story, and explain how your drawing matches the words.
activities.intendedInsight: When the unknown is a part or a difference, you still build the situation — lay out what you know and find what's missing — rather than just combining the two numbers you can see.

activities.title: Narrate and show (talk alongside the model)
feedback: Prompt the child to connect language to representation: 'show me the part where things leave.'
If narration drifts from the model, pause and re-anchor each spoken quantity to a group of objects.

Keep the talk tied to acting on objects: the age-appropriate expectation is work with concrete objects and pictorial representations, so narration is intended to accompany modelling rather than replace it.
activities.rationale: Retelling the problem and pointing to each quantity ties language to representation to answer. Dialogue can develop sense-making; because the curriculum for this age expects work with concrete objects and drawings, talk is intended to accompany acting on objects, and its standalone efficacy is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Tell an adult or peer what is happening in the story in your own words.
As you narrate, show each step on the objects or drawing ('first there were six… then two fell…').
Answer prompts such as 'which part do you already know?' and 'what are we trying to find?' while pointing to the model.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the story into your own words and linking each phrase to a quantity in your model builds sense-making, so the words guide the action rather than triggering a reflex operation.

constraints: Teach modelling, not keyword-spotting: 'altogether'/'left'/'more' must not become fixed triggers for + or −, because they fail on compare, change-unknown and start-unknown problems.
Keep totals within 10 so counting is manageable; start with result-unknown and introduce missing-number and compare forms only once simple modelling is secure.
Systematically vary problem structure (add-to, take-from, put-together/take-apart, compare) and unknown position (result-, change-, start-unknown), not just the numbers.

A fixed single-story illustration (tap to count, reveal the answer) can anchor one problem's modelling but cannot let the child model varied structures or make their own drawing; treat it as a scaffold, not the whole skill.

Picture-based multiple-choice items can check whether a child recognises/applies the right operation, but a scored recognition format does not itself elicit the child building a model and can be answered by keyword-matching; if used, pair each item with a picture and avoid phrasing answerable by keyword alone.
Use consistent representations (counters/cubes, part-part-whole, bar/tape, five-/ten-frame) so the model itself carries meaning across problems.

Interactive affordances are optional illustrations, not requirements: e.g. dragging objects onto a mat, crossing out, a part-whole/bar frame to organise quantities, narrated scenes, auto-varying the problem type. These make the mechanism concrete but need not all be present.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed a scored recognition format 'can't develop the modelling process' and that talk alone is a 'weak' route; these are plausible but not established as universal laws by the cited sources. They have been narrowed to observable affordances / curriculum-grounded qualifications with 'may'/'intended' framing.

The legacy row rated a 3D interactive as adding nothing ('no spatial dimension to exploit'); this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been dropped rather than asserted. Physical manipulatives (counters/cubes) remain central and are themselves tactile.

Self-audit of the diagnostic arithmetic: (1) 6 apples, 2 eaten → 4 left; (2) 3 marbles + 4 → 7; (3) 4 red, 7 total → 3 blue. All correct. The error trace 'answers 8 for the apples' corresponds to 6+2 (combining regardless of story) and 'answers 11' corresponds to 4+7 (adding instead of finding the missing part) — both coherent misconception traces, retained as feedback cues.
Internal prerequisite/reteach reference codes from the original row were not migrated into learner-facing content.

probeDeeper: Show me with the counters what happens to the apples.
For the marbles, did the number get bigger or smaller — why?
How many counters altogether in the last one, and how many do you already know?
Which of these was a taking-away story and which was a putting-together story?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) 4; (2) 7; (3) 3 — with the situation modelled on the counters (take-away, join, and part-unknown respectively).

errorPatterns.pattern: Combines both numbers whatever the story — adds 6 and 2 for the take-away problem, or applies one default operation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act the story out with counters step by step before counting; link it to the take-away representation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 8 for the apples problem.

errorPatterns.pattern: Part-unknown problem solved by adding the two numbers (4 red, 7 total → 4 + 7 = 11) rather than finding the missing part.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the whole (7) and the known part (4) with counters and see the gap; use a part-whole / bar layout.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 11 for the blue counters.

errorPatterns.pattern: Right representation but miscounts the objects.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold one-to-one counting; the modelling is sound, so do not reteach it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct set-up (removes / joins / finds the gap) but the count slips.

responseLevels.gap: Applies one default operation regardless of the story; cannot model the situation.
responseLevels.full: Models each situation with objects and solves take-away, join, and part-unknown problems within 10 correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Solves result-unknown add and take-away by modelling, but the part-unknown problem defaults to adding the two numbers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Use the counters to solve these. (1) There are 6 apples and 2 are eaten — how many are left? (2) Sam has 3 marbles and gets 4 more — how many now? (3) There are 4 red counters and some blue ones, 7 altogether — how many are blue?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The result-unknown take-away and join (1, 2) are straightforward; the put-together-with-part-unknown (3) is harder and reveals whether the child models the situation or just operates on the two visible numbers. Watch whether they act the story out with counters (as the topic requires) or grab the numbers and apply a default operation.
