pedagogy.summary: This is the conceptual heart of the strand: understanding that a ratio expresses a MULTIPLICATIVE relationship between two quantities — one is always a constant number of times the other — and that this same relationship can be written as a ratio (a:b), as a fraction (a/b), and as a linear function (y = (a/b)x) whose graph is a straight line through the origin. The learning goal is to see these as one idea in three costumes, and above all to distinguish a multiplicative relationship (constant ratio) from an additive one (constant difference). Teaching should surface the invariant — what stays the same as the quantities grow — using ratio tables, double number lines and graphs, and should repeatedly contrast 'so many times as' against 'so much more than'.
bestPractices: Foreground the invariant: as both quantities scale, the DIFFERENCE changes but the MULTIPLE stays constant — make 'how many times' the thing children look for.
Move fluently between the three representations on one example: ratio 1:3, fraction 1/3 (or 3 times), and y = 3x graphed as a line through the origin — name them as the same relationship.
Use a ratio table and read it both ways: down the columns (scaling, the multiplier) and across (the constant a:b relationship / the y = kx rule).
Directly contrast multiplicative and additive tables side by side (one where y = 3x, one where y = x + 4) and ask which is a ratio relationship and why.
Connect the straight-line-through-the-origin graph to proportionality: doubling x doubles y only when the line passes through (0,0).
Ground the abstraction in a perceptible constant-ratio context (paint shade, concentration, speed) so 'same relationship' is something the child can see or taste, not just assert.
keyRepresentations: Ratio table with the constant multiplier visible down the columns and the a:b relationship across
Double number line aligned at 0 (equal ratios line up)
Straight-line graph through the origin (y = kx) with gradient = the ratio
The triple 1:3 = 1/3-relationship = y = 3x shown together
Paired multiplicative vs additive tables for contrast (y = 3x vs y = x + 4)
commonMisconceptions: Reads a relationship additively — fixes on the difference between a pair of values ('y is 4 more than x') instead of the constant multiple
Sees the constant multiplier for whole-number rows but cannot express it as a ratio, fraction, or y = kx
Confuses the part-to-part ratio a:b with the fraction a/b of the whole
Thinks any straight-line graph shows proportionality, not noticing it must pass through the origin

learn.summary: Learners come to see a ratio as a MULTIPLICATIVE relationship — one quantity is always a constant number of times the other — and to recognise this same relationship in three forms: a ratio a:b, a fraction a/b (x is a/b of y), and a linear function y=kx whose constant multiple k is the gradient and whose graph is a straight line through the origin. For the worked ratio 1:3 (x:y), x is 1/3 of y and y=3x, where the gradient 3 is y÷x. The central work is distinguishing a multiplicative relationship (constant ratio/multiple) from an additive one (constant difference). Vary the quantities, surface what stays the same (the multiple), and read the invariant across ratio tables, double number lines, graphs and a perceptible context such as paint shade. Keep part-to-part ratio a:b (x is 1/3 OF y) distinct from part-to-whole fraction (x out of the total x+y).

activities.title: One ratio, three costumes — and what breaks under 'add 4'
feedback: If a learner says the bigger batch is darker because there is 'more red', have them test y÷x on each row: it is always 3, so the proportion of red is unchanged — only the total amount grew.

If a learner fixes on a single pair's difference (e.g. '2 to 6 is +4'), have them test +4 on the next rows: 9 would have to be 7 and 12 would have to be 8, so +4 fails — the difference is not constant.
When the additive toggle is on, point to the line lifting off (0,0) and the shifting shade as the visible signs that the relationship is no longer a constant ratio.
Confirm that '×3', '1:3', 'x is 1/3 of y' and 'y=3x' are all names for the same relationship, and that the straight line passes through the origin because when x=0, y=0.
activities.rationale: The defining feature of this concept is an invariant that is felt by varying the quantities and watching what stays the same; linking a table, a graph and a perceptible mixture lets the constant multiple, the fraction and the gradient move together under scaling and break together under an additive rule. Linked panels with live recolouring and a rule toggle are offered as one concrete way to make the mechanism visible, not as the only means; this is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: At KS3 pupils 'understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio or a fraction' and 'relate the language of ratios and the associated calculations to the arithmetic of fractions and to linear functions'.

NCETM names as a central misconception that 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative', considering the difference a−b rather than the ratio a:b (e.g. assuming a ratio 2:5 means one share is always £3 more than the other). It presents the one structure x×k=y expressible as ratio, fraction and the linear function y=mx (a straight line through the origin), and distinguishes scalar from functional multipliers using ratio tables and double number lines (which must both start at aligned zeros).
learnerActions: Work with the ratio 1:3 (e.g. red:yellow paint) and extend a ratio table: 1:3, 2:6, 3:9, 4:12, scaling both quantities together.
For each new row, plot the point (x,y) on a coordinate graph and note that the points fall on a straight line passing through the origin (0,0).
Observe a perceptible constant-ratio context alongside: in an idealised, thoroughly mixed model, a paint swatch mixed in that ratio keeps the same orange shade as the batch grows.
Name the same relationship in three forms on this one example: ratio 1:3, fraction/multiple (y is 3 times x; x is 1/3 of y), and linear function y=3x with gradient 3 (the gradient equals y÷x).

Switch the rule from multiplicative (y=3x) to additive (y=x+4) and watch what changes: the graph's line no longer passes through the origin, the plotted points leave the straight proportional line, and the swatch shade shifts row by row.
State in your own words which quantity stays constant in each case — the MULTIPLE stays fixed for a ratio relationship, while the DIFFERENCE stays fixed for an additive one.
activities.intendedInsight: A ratio is a single multiplicative idea wearing three costumes (ratio a:b, fraction a/b, straight line y=kx through the origin); its signature is a constant multiple, not a constant difference. When the quantities scale, the difference changes but the multiple — and the colour, the ratio and the gradient — stay the same. An additive rule breaks the line-through-origin and changes the shade, which is what separates it from a ratio.

activities.title: Read the ratio table both ways
feedback: If a learner extends row by row to reach x=10, prompt them to use the ×3 multiplier directly: 10×3=30.
If a learner writes the fraction using the total as denominator (e.g. 2/8 for x:y=2:6), separate the readings: the ratio compares x to y (x is 1/3 of y); part-to-whole would compare x to x+y=8.
Confirm a double number line only shows equal ratios when both lines start at aligned zeros.
activities.rationale: Reading a ratio table down (scalar) and across (functional), with an aligned double number line, is the representation NCETM uses to distinguish scalar from functional multipliers; keeping part-to-part separate from part-to-whole addresses a documented confusion. These are proposed uses of standard representations, not tested interventions.
sourceClaims: NCETM names as a central misconception that 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative', considering the difference a−b rather than the ratio a:b (e.g. assuming a ratio 2:5 means one share is always £3 more than the other). It presents the one structure x×k=y expressible as ratio, fraction and the linear function y=mx (a straight line through the origin), and distinguishes scalar from functional multipliers using ratio tables and double number lines (which must both start at aligned zeros).
learnerActions: Take a ratio table and read DOWN the columns to find the scalar multiplier (how each row scales from the previous).
Read ACROSS the rows to find the constant functional relationship a:b / the y=kx rule between the two quantities.
Use a double number line aligned at 0 so that equal ratios line up, and check that both lines start at aligned zeros.
Given x=10 for a 1:3 relationship, work out y directly using the multiplier (×3) rather than extending the table row by row.

Distinguish 'x is 1/3 OF y' (part-to-part, the correct multiplicative reading) from 'x is a fraction of the whole x+y' (part-to-whole); for example, with 2 red : 5 blue beads, red is 2/5 of the blue count (part-to-part) but 2 out of 7 total beads (part-to-whole), anchoring each reading to its own picture.
activities.intendedInsight: A ratio table encodes both a scalar multiplier (down columns) and a functional multiplier (across, the y=kx rule); the multiple can be used directly to predict any value. A double number line aligned at zero shows equal ratios lining up. Part-to-part and part-to-whole are different comparisons.

activities.title: Sort and match: is it a ratio relationship?
feedback: For the x=2,y=5 / x=4,y=7 table, if a learner calls it a ratio, have them compute 5÷2=2.5 and 7÷4=1.75: the multiple is not constant, so it is additive (+3), not a ratio.
If a learner picks any straight line as proportional, ask where it crosses the y-axis: only a line through (0,0) represents y=kx.
When a learner matches 1:3 to y=3x, ask them to confirm the gradient of the line equals the multiple (3).
activities.rationale: Distinguishing multiplicative from additive tables and translating between forms can be checked with sorting, matching and prediction tasks using additive distractors. A sort can check classification and translation but does not itself require the learner to construct the invariant by varying quantities, so pair it with the manipulation activity above.
sourceClaims: At KS3 pupils 'understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio or a fraction' and 'relate the language of ratios and the associated calculations to the arithmetic of fractions and to linear functions'.
learnerActions: Sort several tables of values into 'ratio relationship' vs 'not a ratio relationship', justifying each by whether y÷x is constant.
Match equivalent forms: connect 1:3 with y=3x and with a straight line through the origin.
Predict y for a new x in a given table, with an additive answer offered as a tempting but wrong option, and explain why the additive choice fails.
Given two graphs, identify which shows proportionality and explain that it must pass through the origin.
Test a tricky table — x=2,y=5 and x=4,y=7 — and decide whether it is a ratio relationship (it is additive: +3 each time, but 5÷2 ≠ 7÷4, so no constant multiple).
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting and matching across forms, with deliberate additive distractors, can check whether a learner can translate among ratio, fraction and linear form and can reject an additive table as not proportional. A straight-line graph only shows proportionality when it passes through the origin.

activities.title: Justify it: times or more than?
feedback: If the learner reasons 'more red so darker' or 'different amounts so different', treat this as additive/absolute-amount reasoning and have them predict then check against y÷x.
Accept a full explanation only when it names the constant multiple AND notes that the difference is not constant.
Use the predict-observe-explain paint task so the reason stated before mixing is the diagnostic part.
activities.rationale: A Socratic challenge with a scaled counter-case targets the additive-vs-multiplicative distinction directly. Verbal justification can complement seeing the invariant across linked representations; use it alongside the manipulation activity rather than in place of it.
sourceClaims: NCETM names as a central misconception that 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative', considering the difference a−b rather than the ratio a:b (e.g. assuming a ratio 2:5 means one share is always £3 more than the other). It presents the one structure x×k=y expressible as ratio, fraction and the linear function y=mx (a straight line through the origin), and distinguishes scalar from functional multipliers using ratio tables and double number lines (which must both start at aligned zeros).
learnerActions: Face a mentor who presents tables and asks for each: 'is it times, or more than? How do you know?'
Defend your classification by pointing to the constant multiple and showing that the difference changes down the table.
Respond to a scaled counter-case when you give an additive answer — e.g. 'you said +4; check the next row, does +4 still work?'
Explain, before mixing any paint, whether a 2:6 batch will be darker, lighter or the same shade as a 1:3 batch, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Being pressed to justify whether a relationship is multiplicative or additive, and to meet a scaled counter-case, brings the reasoning into the open and can check whether the learner gives the right answer for the right reason.

constraints: Target age 12–14 (KS3); this is a conceptual objective about ratio notation and multiplicative relationships.
Ground the abstraction in at least one perceptible constant-ratio context (paint shade, concentration, speed) so 'same relationship' can be seen, not merely asserted.

The invariant is best surfaced by varying values and watching what stays fixed; a static annotated triple (table, ratio, graph) can summarise and reference the connections but does not itself let the learner vary quantities, so use it as a summary rather than the sole discovery activity.

Sorting, matching and prediction tasks can check and consolidate translation between forms but are recognition-level; they do not by themselves require independent construction of the invariant, so pair them with activities where the learner scales the quantities and states the relationship.

Express the linear form as y=kx where k (the gradient) is the constant multiple y÷x; for ratio 1:3 that is y=3x. Do not write the gradient as a/b (which for 1:3 would give the incorrect 1/3); a/b=1/3 is the separate fraction reading 'x is 1/3 of y'.
Keep part-to-part ratio a:b ('x is 1/3 OF y') distinct from part-to-whole fraction (x out of total x+y); do not let learners write the fraction with the total as denominator.
Double number lines must start at aligned zeros for equal ratios to line up; a ratio table does not need a 0:0 row, though including one can show the link to the origin on the graph.
A straight-line graph shows proportionality only when it passes through the origin; a line not through (0,0) represents y=kx+c, not a ratio relationship.

Live recolouring, a rule toggle (y=3x vs y=x+4), draggable/extendable table rows and linked plotting are offered as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are examples of interaction, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row expressed the linear function both as 'y=(a/b)x' and as the triple '1:3 = y=3x'. These are inconsistent: for the ratio a:b = 1:3 (x:y), the gradient is y÷x = b/a = 3, so y=3x, whereas y=(a/b)x gives the incorrect y=(1/3)x. The guidance has been corrected to state y=kx with gradient = y÷x; the original formula is recorded as an error, not offered to learners.

The legacy row rated a 3D artefact 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing'. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped; the relationship is primarily numeric/graphical, a reasonable scoping note, but no universal medium superiority is implied.
The legacy framing that the linked-panel tool is uniquely able to teach the concept has been softened: linked panels are one concrete way to expose the invariant, not the only way.

Arithmetic self-audit: for the counter-case table x=2,y=5 and x=4,y=7 the differences are +3 (5−2 and 7−4); the ratios 5÷2=2.5 and 7÷4=1.75 are unequal, confirming it is additive, not a ratio. For the 1:3 relationship, rows 2:6, 3:9, 4:12 give y÷x=3 throughout with differences 4,6,8 (not constant), confirming multiplicative. x=10 gives y=30. For the bead example 2 red : 5 blue, the total is 7, so part-to-whole red is 2/7, distinct from the part-to-part reading 2/5.

The original assess 'additive' distractor 'y is always 4 more than x' refers to the first pair 2→6 (difference 4); it is retained only as a diagnostic distractor to be challenged, never taught as correct.
The original part-to-whole distractor 'x is 2 out of the whole 8, so the relationship is 2/8' is retained only as a misconception to separate and correct, not as a valid reading.
Whether any of these proposed activities improve learning is untested; sources support the curriculum content and the additive misconception, not the specific interventions.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a jar of orange paint made from 1 spoon red and 3 spoons yellow, and a second, bigger batch you will make from 2 spoons red and 6 spoons yellow. PREDICT before mixing: will the bigger batch be a darker orange, a lighter orange, or exactly the same shade — and WHY? (A child reasoning 'more red, so darker' or 'different amounts, so different' is reasoning additively/by absolute amount; the reason stated before mixing is the diagnostic part.) OBSERVE: mix both — the shades match exactly. EXPLAIN: because 2:6 is the same ratio as 1:3 (both parts multiplied by 2), the multiplicative relationship — and so the colour — is unchanged; adding different amounts to each part is what would change the shade.
probeDeeper: 'Write this relationship as a ratio x:y, and as y = ? × x' — checks the translation among ratio, fraction and linear form.

Counterexample: 'Another table has x = 2, y = 5 and x = 4, y = 7. Is THAT a ratio relationship? How do you know?' — this one is additive (+3, but 5÷2 ≠ 7÷4); a child with the concept identifies it as 'add', NOT a constant ratio.
'If x = 10, what is y — and how do you know without extending the table row by row?' — tests whether the multiplier is used directly.
'If we plotted these points, what would the graph look like, and why does it go through (0,0)?' — links proportionality to the line through the origin.
assess.correctAnswer: y is always the same number of TIMES x — y is 3 times x (y = 3x). You can tell because the AMOUNT bigger changes (6 is 4 more than 2, 9 is 6 more, 15 is 10 more) so it is not a constant 'more than', but y ÷ x is always 3, a constant multiple — this is the multiplicative relationship, the ratio x:y = 1:3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive: fixes on the difference in the first pair ('y is 4 more than x, because 2 and 6') and treats the relationship as constant addition
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child test '+4' on every row (9 would need to be 7; 15 would need to be 9) — the difference is not constant. Then find y÷x for each row (all 3) to surface the constant multiple. Documented additive-strategy interference.
errorPatterns.distractor: y is always 4 more than x
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives '+4' (or another single-row difference) and does not check it against the other rows, where it fails

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the part-to-part ratio with a part-to-whole fraction: reads x:y = 2:6 and says 'so x is 2/6... 1/3 of the whole' misapplying the fraction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two readings: the ratio compares x to y (x is 1/3 of y); part-to-whole would compare x to x+y. Anchor each to its own picture.
errorPatterns.distractor: x is 2 out of the whole 8, so the relationship is 2/8
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child mixes up 'x is 1/3 OF y' (correct multiplicative reading) with 'x is 1/3 of the whole' (part-to-whole), or writes the fraction with the total 8 as denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees the ×3 for the whole-number rows but cannot express the relationship as a ratio, a fraction, or y = 3x
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach the concept — scaffold the notation link: 'times 3' = ratio 1:3 = y = 3x; connect to the straight-line-through-origin graph. The idea is present; the representations need joining.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says 'times 3' correctly but cannot write it as 1:3 or y = 3x when asked

responseLevels.gap: Reads the relationship additively (a constant 'more than') and cannot see that the difference changes; treats one pair's difference as the rule.
responseLevels.full: States that y is a constant number of times x, justifies it by the changing difference vs constant multiple, expresses the relationship as 1:3, 1/3 and y = 3x, links it to a straight line through the origin, and correctly rejects an additive table as not a ratio relationship.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the constant multiple (×3) for the given rows but cannot yet express it as a ratio/fraction/linear function, or slips between part-to-part and part-to-whole, or does not connect it to the line through the origin — knows the pieces without coordinating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a table of matching values. When x = 2, y = 6; when x = 3, y = 9; when x = 5, y = 15. I want two things. First: is y always the same AMOUNT bigger than x, or always the same number of TIMES x? Second, and most important: how can you tell from the table which one it is?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for the REASON (tier two), not just the classification, is what separates genuine multiplicative understanding from a guess. A child reasoning multiplicatively points to the constant multiple (3) and notes the difference is NOT constant; a child reasoning additively latches onto one pair's difference (2 to 6 is +4) and cannot see that the +4 fails on the next row. Because the 'amount bigger' visibly changes down the table while the multiple stays fixed, a correct answer is hard to give for the wrong reason and a wrong answer is hard to give for the right reason.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Matter Is Made of Particles

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry 'The particulate nature of matter'):** The properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model. (Introduced as a bridge at upper-KS2; formalised at KS3.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-PS1-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-1].

- **Operational details:** This is the model-INTRODUCING node: the big idea that all matter is made of tiny particles too small to see, and that this single idea EXPLAINS the observable behaviour of solids, liquids and gases. The move is from observation to inference — the child cannot see particles, so the model is justified by what it accounts for: why a gas can be squashed (particles far apart with empty space), why a solid holds its shape (particles packed and fixed), why sugar dissolves without adding volume (particles fit into gaps), why a smell spreads across a room (particles move and mix). Use discrepant events that only the particle model explains (compressing a gas syringe; dissolving with no volume increase; diffusion of a scent). Keep it QUALITATIVE and inferential — no kinetic-energy quantities yet. Guard the two cardinal errors: particles don't take on the material's macroscopic properties, and there is empty space (not air) between them.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). The child states [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-1] see and uses that model to EXPLAIN at least two different observations (e.g. gas compressibility and dissolving), recognising the model is inferred from evidence rather than seen.
bestPractices: Introduce the model through phenomena it EXPLAINS (compressing a gas, dissolving with no volume rise, a spreading smell), so it is inferred from evidence, not asserted.
Make the observation→model move explicit: we can't see particles, but they account for what we do see.
Keep it qualitative at this stage — no kinetic-energy numbers; reserve quantitative kinetic theory for KS3.
Explicitly guard against particles having macroscopic properties and against 'air' filling the gaps.
Use a macro-to-particle zoom so the invisible scale is felt concretely.
keyRepresentations: A macro/particle zoom toggle (object → the particles it's made of)
A gas syringe showing empty gaps closing on compression
A dissolving glass where sugar particles tuck into water's gaps (no volume rise)
A diffusion scene showing particles drifting and mixing
commonMisconceptions: Individual particles carry the material's properties (a particle of ice is cold/hard).
The space between particles is filled with air or something, not empty.
Matter is continuous, not particulate ('it's solid all the way through').
A dissolved or evaporated substance stops existing because you can't see it.
Gas has no particles / no mass because it's invisible.

learn.summary: Introduce the particle model of matter (ages 10–11) as an inference justified by what it explains, not asserted as fact. Learners run three tell-tale phenomena — compressing a sealed gas syringe, mixing liquids (e.g. 50 ml water + 50 ml alcohol) to a total volume a little less than the sum of the parts, and a spreading smell — then zoom from each visible event down to a particle-level picture that accounts for it. The teaching objective is the observation→model move: because we cannot see particles, the model earns belief by explaining why a gas squashes, why some mixtures end up with less volume than the parts added together, and why scents spread. Keep it qualitative (no kinetic-energy numbers). Guard two cardinal errors: individual particles do not carry the material's bulk properties, and the space between particles is empty, not filled with air or other material.

activities.title: Why we believe in particles: a three-phenomenon bench
feedback: If a learner predicts the gas cannot be squashed, point out it did compress, then ask what could possibly close up inside a sealed tube — lead to empty gaps between particles.
If a learner predicts 50 ml + 50 ml = exactly 100 ml, show the real observed result is less and ask what the smaller particles could be slotting into.

If a learner says the smell spreads because 'air pushes it', agree that air currents do help carry smells in a real room, then add that even in still air the scent's own particles move, drifting and mixing among the air particles.
Reinforce the key move: 'You never saw a particle — so why believe in them?' Answer: because they explain what you did see.
activities.rationale: The concept is an inference, so it is best introduced through the phenomena it explains and an explicit observation→model step, keeping the treatment qualitative at this stage. A predict-act-zoom loop makes the invisible scale and the reasoning concrete. (Efficacy of this specific sequence is proposed, not empirically validated here; the directly supporting phenomena-first claim comes from an unverified source.)
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-PS1-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-1]
The particle model should be introduced via phenomena it explains (compressibility, dissolving without volume change, diffusion); common errors are macroscopic particles and air-between-particles
learnerActions: Push a sealed gas syringe with a blocked nozzle and notice it compresses surprisingly far; predict first whether and why it should squash.
Then examine (or toggle to) a particle view: the plunger moves because widely-spaced particles close the empty gaps between them.

Mix 50 ml water with 50 ml alcohol (e.g. methylated spirit handled by an adult) in a measuring cylinder, or dissolve salt in a measured volume of water, and observe that the combined volume is a little less than the expected total; predict the final level and WHY beforehand.
Zoom to the particle view: smaller particles tuck into the spaces between larger particles, so less volume is added than expected.

Release a scent in one corner and track how long it takes to reach the far side, noting that in a real room draughts and air currents also help carry it; zoom in to see the scent particles moving, drifting and mixing among the air particles. For a slower view without draughts, watch a drop of food colouring spread in still water.
State in your own words the single hidden idea that explains all three puzzles: matter is made of tiny, constantly moving particles too small to see, with empty space between them.
activities.intendedInsight: We accept invisible particles because one idea — tiny, moving particles with empty space between them — explains three otherwise puzzling observations (compressibility, a mixed volume less than the sum of the parts, diffusion). The model is inferred from evidence, not seen.

activities.title: Zoom into a block: feeling the too-small-to-see scale
feedback: If a learner thinks particles only appear once matter is ground up, stress the intact block is ALREADY particles packed together; grinding separates them, it does not create them.

If a learner says a gas has no particles because it is invisible, revisit the diffusion phenomenon as evidence gas particles are present and moving, and point back to the sealed jar whose unseen air is still made of particles.
activities.rationale: A macro-to-particle zoom makes the invisible scale concrete and serves as a reference and intuition-builder. This is a companion scaffold: a static or reveal-only illustration shows arrangement but does not let the learner run the discrepant events that justify inferring particles, so it supports but does not replace the phenomenon bench.
learnerActions: Start from an everyday object — a block of metal, a cup of water, or a sealed jar that contains air — and use a tap-to-reveal or zoom to move from the whole object down to the particles it is made of; note that the air, though unseen, is also made of particles.

For each state, read a short flap explaining the arrangement: particles packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating in fixed positions (solid); still close together but irregularly arranged and able to slide past each other (liquid); spread far apart and moving freely in all directions (gas).
Describe aloud roughly how much smaller than the object a single particle is, to register that particles are too small to see.
activities.intendedInsight: All matter — including a solid metal bar and invisible gas — is made of enormous numbers of particles far too small to see; the three states differ in how those particles are arranged and spaced.

activities.title: Do properties belong to one particle or to the many? (predict, then explain, with probes)
feedback: If a learner says 'a copper particle is a tiny bit of copper, so it's orange and hard', ask what single colour one particle could even be, and what is between particles — shift to properties arising from many particles arranged together.

If a learner says air or 'more stuff' fills the gaps, clarify that the gaps between particles are empty (even in air itself there is nothing between the air particles); contrast with drawings where children instinctively fill the space.
Full understanding requires the 'properties belong to the many, not the one' reasoning, and transferring it across copper, water and ice — not just a yes/no answer.

Partial understanding looks like saying the particle isn't orange but being unable to say where bulk properties come from, or holding the model for copper but reverting to 'tiny copies' for ice or water.
A gap response says the single particle carries the bulk properties (orange/hard/wet) or fills the gaps with matter — particles treated as tiny copies of the material.
activities.rationale: This targets a widely documented particle-model error — attributing bulk properties to individual particles — and the related error that gaps are filled with air. A predict-then-explain structure makes the pre-observation reason the diagnostic part. The volume event from the phenomenon bench (50 ml water + 50 ml alcohol giving slightly less than 100 ml) is a concrete discrepant observation that the particle model explains.
sourceClaims: The particle model should be introduced via phenomena it explains (compressibility, dissolving without volume change, diffusion); common errors are macroscopic particles and air-between-particles
learnerActions: Consider a single particle of copper on its own: predict whether it is orange, hard and shiny like the whole bar, and explain WHY before any reveal.
Answer the probing questions: What is in the space between two copper particles? Is a single water particle wet and runny? If the bar were ice instead, is one ice particle cold?
State where the bar's colour, hardness and state actually come from if not from each particle.
activities.intendedInsight: Properties like colour, hardness and state are bulk properties that emerge from how huge numbers of particles are arranged and held together — they are not stamped on each individual particle. The gaps between particles are empty, not filled with air or more material.

constraints: Keep the whole treatment qualitative: no kinetic-energy quantities or numeric energy; reserve quantitative kinetic theory for later (KS3).

Guard the two cardinal errors throughout: individual particles do not carry the material's macroscopic properties, and the space between particles is empty, not air. This is also true in gases such as air and in mixtures: other particles may sit among them, but there is still empty space between all the particles.

The zoom/reveal illustration is a scaffold: it builds intuition and reference but does not supply the discrepant events (compress, dissolve, diffuse) that justify inferring particles, so it should accompany rather than replace the phenomenon work.

Recognition/matching tasks (e.g. matching phenomena to explanations, multiple-choice on 'why can a gas be squashed') can check classification or recall but do not elicit the independent predict-act-explain reasoning that makes the invisible model persuasive.
A discussion/dialogue format alone does not supply the discrepant evidence learners need to run and interpret; pair any discussion with the actual phenomena.

The 50 ml water + 50 ml alcohol result is slightly less than 100 ml. In the particle model this is explained by particles of one substance fitting into gaps between particles of the other. Present it as a real observed outcome using water+alcohol (or salt dissolved in a measured volume of water), where the effect is reliably observable. Do not state it as universal across all mixtures or solutes (dissolving sugar, for example, shrinks the volume very little), and do not imply the solute is always the smaller particle.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row marked one source (AAAS Project 2061 / BEST particle-model research) as verified:false; claims drawn from it about introducing the model via phenomena and about common errors should be treated as unverified.

Legacy entries asserted a linear quiz 'cannot' deliver the predict-act-zoom loop and that 3D 'adds nothing' because the reasoning is inferential. These were catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy claims; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limitation statements (recognition tasks don't elicit independent construction; a spatial 3D view offers packing intuition but at added cost for an inferential objective).

The mixing/dissolving 'no rise to the expected total volume' depends on the chosen substances and quantities; water+alcohol gives a clear volume contraction, while some solute/water combinations are less dramatic. Choose materials where the effect is observable and avoid overstating it as universal.
The diffusion timing of a scent depends on air currents and room conditions; treat 'slowly reaches the far side' as a typical qualitative outcome, not a fixed result.

sourceClaims were re-scoped: the DfE topic/standard claim was removed from the phenomena activity because it grounds the topic but not the phenomena-first teaching principle; the NGSS claim was retained because the activity enacts the model-development practice it names, while the (unverified) BEST phenomena claim is the only one directly supporting the phenomena-first teaching principle.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: mark a beaker at 50 ml water. Ask the child to predict the level after stirring in 50 ml of a fine solute (or mixing 50 ml water + 50 ml alcohol) — exactly 100 ml, or less, and WHY. A child with no particle model predicts exactly 100. The result is LESS than 100 (smaller particles slot into gaps between larger ones). The pre-observation reason — particles with spaces between them — is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If one particle isn't orange, how can a whole bar of them be orange? Where does the colour come from?
What is in the space between two particles of copper?
Water is wet and runny. Is a single water particle wet and runny? Why or why not?
If it had been a block of ice instead of copper — is one ice particle cold? What would you say to someone who says yes?
assess.correctAnswer: A single copper particle is NOT itself orange, hard, or shiny — those are properties of the whole bar, arising from how enormous numbers of particles are arranged and held together. Properties like colour, hardness and state are bulk properties of the collection, not carried by one particle. (Full marks require this 'properties belong to the many, not the one' reasoning, not just yes/no.)

errorPatterns.pattern: each particle has the bulk material's properties ('a copper particle is orange and hard'; 'water particles are wet')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what colour a single particle could even be, and what's between particles — shift them to properties as arising from many particles arranged together, not stamped on each one.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — a copper particle is a tiny bit of copper, so it's orange and hard too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: tier-two answer says the single particle is coloured/hard/wet like the bulk

errorPatterns.pattern: there is other matter (air, dust, more copper) filling the space between particles
errorPatterns.nextMove: In a pure substance the gaps are empty — there is nothing between the particles. Contrast with drawing where children fill the space.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — but the copper between the particles is what's orange.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the gaps are full of air or 'more stuff' rather than empty

errorPatterns.pattern: particles only exist/appear once matter is broken up, not in a continuous solid
errorPatterns.nextMove: The intact bar is ALREADY particles packed together — grinding doesn't create them, it just separates what's there. Use the packed-grid diagram.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: thinks a solid bar is continuous 'stuff' and particles are what you'd get by grinding it

responseLevels.gap: Says the single particle carries the bulk properties (orange/hard/wet), or fills the gaps with matter — particles as tiny copies of the material.
responseLevels.full: States properties like colour, hardness and state are bulk properties emerging from how many particles are arranged, not carried by one particle; treats gaps as empty; transfers the reasoning across substances (copper, water, ice).
responseLevels.partial: Says the particle isn't orange/hard but can't yet explain where the bulk properties come from, or holds the model for one case but reverts to 'tiny copies' for another (ice, water) — states the idea without the emergent reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: We say everything is made of tiny particles too small to see — a bar of copper, a cup of water, the air. Take one single particle of copper, on its own. Is it orange, hard and shiny like the bar? Then the important part: explain your answer — where do the copper bar's properties come from if not from each particle?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason exposes the most documented particle-model error: attributing bulk properties to individual particles ('particles of ice are cold and hard'). A child who thinks each particle is a tiny copy of the material answers 'yes, it's orange and hard' and cannot locate where properties come from; a child with the model says the properties emerge from arrangement.

pedagogy.summary: At 6-8, sorting matures into ORGANISING and RECORDING data: given a question, sort items into 2-3 categories, count each, and capture the result as a simple table or list of category-names-with-counts, then order the categories. The shift from the 5-6 skill is that the count is now written down as a record that can be read back to answer the question — the beginning of GAISE's data sense (data are information about a context). Teaching should start from a genuine question ('which packed-lunch fruit is most popular?'), collect and tally, transfer to a table, and always return to the question so the table is a tool, not a decoration.
bestPractices: Begin with a statistical question worth asking, so the organised data has a purpose to answer
Model the tally-then-table pipeline: sort/tally the raw data, then write each category name beside its count in a table or list
Keep category totals reconciling with the whole set ('7 + 5 + 4 = 16, and we had 16 cards') to build a self-check habit
Read the table back to answer the question and to order the categories most-to-fewest
keyRepresentations: Simple frequency table / list (category name + count)
Tally chart feeding the table
Sorted objects or cards arranged in rows as the concrete source
Ordered list of categories from most to fewest
commonMisconceptions: Records counts that don't line up with their categories (rows misaligned in the table)
Organises the data but cannot read it back to answer the original question (table treated as decoration)
Miscounts categories or the totals don't reconcile with the full set
Forces every item into the given categories (or invents overlaps) when some items fit none

learn.summary: For ages 6-8, sorting matures into organising AND recording categorical data: starting from a genuine statistical question, children sort items into 2-3 categories, count each, write each category name beside its count in a simple table or list, and order the categories by quantity. The new skill beyond the 5-6 level is that the count becomes a written record that can be read back to answer the question — the table is a tool, not a decoration. Teaching should begin from a real question (e.g. 'which packed-lunch fruit is most popular?'), collect and tally, transfer to a table with totals that reconcile against the whole set, and always return to the question.

activities.title: Survey organiser: from response cards to a table that answers the question
feedback: If row counts don't add up to the number of cards, a card may have been lost or double-counted — recount by moving each card aside as it is tallied, and check the parts sum to the whole
If asked 'which does the class like best?' and the child re-counts cards instead of reading the table, model reading it: 'the biggest number is beside…' and return to the question
If a card fits none of the given categories, don't force it into a pile — allow an 'other' category if genuinely needed
Point to each pile and its matching table row together as the number is written, so counts and labels stay correctly paired
activities.rationale: Organising categorical data is a procedural build-it task: sorting raw cards and watching a table populate makes the tally-then-table pipeline concrete and gives immediate feedback. Ordering the rows makes the answer surface, reinforcing that data are collected to answer a question about a context.
sourceClaims: At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable using tables and picture/bar graphs and develop 'data sense' — that data are information collected to answer a statistical investigative question about a context
Year 2 pupils interpret and construct simple tables and sort categories by quantity, asking and answering questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
learnerActions: Start from a real question the class cares about, e.g. 'which of these three snacks is most popular?' or 'which of these three fruits does our class like best?'
Take a shuffled stack of class response cards and sort each card into one of 2-3 categories, building a tally as you go
Write each category name beside its count in a simple table or list
Check that the row counts add up to the number of cards you started with (e.g. '7 + 5 + 4 = 16, and we had 16 cards')
Order the categories from most to fewest so the category with the biggest count rises to the top (if two categories have the same biggest count, say that they are tied rather than naming one winner)
Read the table back aloud to state which category answers the question

Test the table as a live record: if two more children chose one fruit, update that count, check that the new total is 2 more than before (e.g. 18 instead of 16), and see whether the ordered answer changes
activities.intendedInsight: An organised table is a tool that ANSWERS a question, not just a store of numbers: once ordered, the record visibly shows the most popular category, the totals should reconcile with the whole set, and updating a count updates the answer.

activities.title: Interactive reconcile-and-order check (optional self-check mechanism)
feedback: A reconcile flag when totals don't match the card count makes a lost or double-counted response visible — treat it as a prompt to recount, not a failure
When 'order' is pressed the rows re-rank most-to-fewest so the most popular category rises to the top, showing the answer emerging from the data itself
activities.rationale: Optional interactive mechanisms (drag-to-sort, a tally that builds, a count cell that checks against the raw data, an 'order' control) make the recording-and-reconciling of a constructed table concrete and give feedback as each count is entered. These are illustrative affordances, not required tools — the same pipeline of constructing a table and sorting categories by quantity works with physical cards and a paper table.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils interpret and construct simple tables and sort categories by quantity, asking and answering questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
learnerActions: Drag each response card to a category pile and watch a tally build
Type each count into a table's cells
Notice when the row counts are flagged for not reconciling with the number of cards, and fix the lost or double-counted response
Press an 'order' control and watch the rows rank themselves most-to-fewest, lifting the winning category to the top
Answer a final question — which category answers our question?
activities.intendedInsight: A live record stays trustworthy only when its parts reconcile with the whole; ordering the rows turns the record into a visible answer.

activities.title: Read a completed table to say what it means (annotation scaffold)
feedback: If the child reads a count without naming its category, re-pair the label and number together
This reference-only reading supports interpretation but does not itself practise organising raw data — pair it with a hands-on sort so the child also builds the table
activities.rationale: A labelled, static table can teach interpretation (what each row means, which is largest) as a reference scaffold. It is a complement to, not a replacement for, the build-it task, because it does not let the child organise raw data into a table.
sourceClaims: At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable using tables and picture/bar graphs and develop 'data sense' — that data are information collected to answer a statistical investigative question about a context
learnerActions: Look at a completed, labelled frequency table of category names and counts
Point to each row and say what it means ('this row says 5 children chose banana')
Say which row has the biggest count and what question that answers
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a table back — pairing each label with its count and identifying the largest — is a necessary step toward using data to answer a question.

constraints: Begin from a genuine statistical question so the organised data has a purpose to answer; always return to the question so the table is a tool, not a decoration
Model the full tally-then-table pipeline: sort/tally raw data, then write each category name beside its count
Build a reconcile habit: category totals should sum back to the whole set, and this self-check should be modelled explicitly
Limit to 2-3 categories with counts within young children's secure cardinality

Allow an 'other' category for items that fit none of the given categories, rather than forcing or double-placing them; keep the total number of categories, including 'other', within the 2-3 category limit (e.g. two named categories plus 'other')
The reading/annotation scaffold assesses and supports interpretation but does not elicit independent construction of a table from raw data; pair it with hands-on organising
Interactive reconcile/order controls are illustrative affordances; the same learning can occur with physical cards and a paper table — do not treat the digital tool as mandatory

Prerequisite reteach links from the source (secure cardinality; clean non-overlapping sorting) are noted here as teaching dependencies but are not learner-facing citations.
The arithmetic example '7 + 5 + 4 = 16' checks out and is retained as a reconcile illustration.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Our question is: which of these three fruits does our class like best? Here are everyone's choice cards. Organise them so we can answer the question, and show me the counts in a table. (Set the task and WATCH how they organise and record.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Observing the organising-and-recording shows what a verbal answer hides. A child with the skill produces a table whose counts are correctly paired and reconcile, and reads it back to answer the question; a child without it mis-pairs counts, loses cards, or organises the data yet cannot use it to answer 'which best'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Sexual Selection, Kin Selection & Game Theory (ages 12–13): sexual selection as a form of natural selection acting on mating success (runaway selection for peacock tails, bird-of-paradise displays, frog calls), kin selection and altruism (worker bees, meerkat sentinels) via Hamilton's rule and inclusive fitness, game theory in behaviour (hawk-dove/ESS), and cognitive ethology (evidence for animal emotion, play, culture).
• Standards — UK (DfE KS3): extends natural selection and variation into WHY apparently costly or self-sacrificing traits evolve; a working-scientifically strand on constructing evidence-based explanations of behaviour.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS4-4 (natural selection and differential reproductive success); HS-LS4 horizon; complements MS-LS2-2 interactions — here selection acts through mating and kinship.
• Operational details: the unifying move is that fitness = REPRODUCTIVE success, so a trait that lowers survival can still spread if it raises mating success (peacock tail) or if it helps copies of one's genes in relatives (Hamilton's rule: rB > C). Teach sexual selection (female choice / male-male competition; runaway and handicap/honest-signal ideas), kin selection/inclusive fitness (why sterile workers and self-endangering sentinels evolve), and game theory (hawk-dove, evolutionarily stable strategy — the best move depends on what everyone else does). Touch cognitive ethology carefully as an evidence question. Resolve the apparent paradox 'why would evolution favour a costly tail or self-sacrifice?'.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~12): explain how a costly ornament like a peacock's tail can be favoured (mating advantage). B (transitional, ~12–13): state Hamilton's rule in words and use it to explain altruism toward relatives. C (formal, ~13): explain an evolutionarily stable strategy with the hawk-dove game — why the best behaviour depends on the frequency of others' strategies.
bestPractices: Redefine fitness explicitly as reproductive success (not survival or strength), so the peacock's survival-costly tail stops being paradoxical.
Teach Hamilton's rule (rB > C) with worked relatedness numbers (helping a full sibling, r=0.5) so altruism becomes a quantitative gene's-eye prediction, not a vague 'for the good of the group'.
Use the hawk-dove game with payoffs the student can compute so an evolutionarily stable strategy emerges as frequency-dependent — the best move depends on what everyone else does.
Actively dismantle 'for the good of the species' group-selection thinking, replacing it with individual/gene-level reasoning.
keyRepresentations: A female-choice / handicap diagram: ornament size vs both survival cost and mating benefit, with the net-fitness optimum.
A relatedness tree with r-values annotated, feeding Hamilton's rule rB > C.
A hawk-dove payoff matrix with a frequency slider showing the stable mix (ESS).
A 'fitness = reproductive success' concept map linking survival, mating, and helping relatives to gene copies in the next generation.
commonMisconceptions: 'Animals do things for the good of the species/group' — selection favours traits raising the individual's (or its genes') reproductive success; group-selection explanations are usually wrong.
'The fittest = the strongest or longest-lived' — fitness is reproductive success; a short-lived, showy male can be fitter than a drab survivor.
'Costly ornaments are just decoration with no function' — they can be honest signals of quality or products of runaway female choice.
'Altruism disproves natural selection / animals are just being nice' — kin selection (helping relatives who share genes) explains apparent self-sacrifice quantitatively.
'There's always one single best behaviour' — the best strategy can be frequency-dependent (an ESS is a mix, not a lone winner).

learn.summary: Learners explore why apparently costly or self-sacrificing traits evolve by redefining fitness as reproductive success. Three linked models drive the ideas: a sexual-selection trade-off (ornament cost vs mating benefit), Hamilton's rule for kin-selected altruism (rB > C), and the hawk-dove game showing a frequency-dependent evolutionarily stable strategy. A concept check and an optional debate extension cover the definition of fitness, computing rB vs C, reading payoff matrices, and the evidence question of cognitive ethology.

activities.title: Peacock's tail: when a survival cost pays off
feedback: If a learner predicts the tail should disappear because it only hurts survival: they are treating survival as the whole of fitness. Point to the mating-success curve — more offspring from showier males can outweigh the survival cost.

If a learner says the peacock grows a big tail 'on purpose' to look good: recast it as selection over many generations on heritable variation in tail size via peahen preference, not a choice made within one individual's lifetime.
If a learner picks the smallest tail as 'best': ask them to read the NET curve, not the survival curve alone — the fitness optimum is where mating benefit minus survival cost is greatest.
activities.rationale: Making the two competing curves manipulable lets the paradox dissolve through the learner's own trade-off reasoning rather than assertion; a live female-preference control connects runaway selection to the shifting optimum. A labelled static ornament diagram can introduce the trade-off but cannot let learners locate the net-fitness peak by adjusting the variables.
sourceClaims: Sexual selection (female choice, male-male competition, runaway and handicap/honest-signal models) explains costly ornaments; kin selection via Hamilton's rule (rB > C) and inclusive fitness explains altruism toward relatives.
Natural selection acts through differential reproductive success and changes trait distributions over generations.
learnerActions: Vary the size of a peacock's ornament and read off two quantities that change with it: a rising survival cost (slower, easier for predators to catch) and a rising mating success (peahens choose showier males).

Combine the two into a net reproductive-success curve and find where it peaks. With the model's settings, notice the peak can sit at a large, 'wasteful'-looking tail rather than a small survival-safe one.

Increase the strength of female preference and observe how the optimum tail size shifts larger. In runaway selection, the preference and the tail evolve together over generations because offspring inherit both, so this pressure can keep strengthening.

Relate the same cost-versus-mating trade-off to other sexually selected traits — bird-of-paradise courtship displays and loud frog mating calls — and note that the mating advantage can arise through female choice OR through male-male competition.
State in your own words why natural selection has NOT removed the costly tail.
activities.intendedInsight: Fitness means reproductive success, not survival or strength: a trait that lowers survival can still spread if it raises mating success enough. The same logic covers other sexually selected traits (bird-of-paradise displays, frog calls) and both routes to mating success — female choice and male-male competition. Ornaments can be honest signals of quality or products of runaway female choice, not mere decoration.

activities.title: Hamilton's rule: why a sterile worker or a sentinel helps
feedback: If a learner explains the worker bee's sacrifice as 'for the good of the species': introduce inclusive fitness — helping close relatives propagates shared genes, so the sacrifice favours copies of the helper's own genes carried in kin.
If a learner uses r for distant kin as if it were 0.5: have them check the relatedness value; the lower r shrinks rB and raises the bar for helping to pay off.
If a learner concludes altruism disproves natural selection: show that the rule PREDICTS when helping is favoured, so apparent niceness is consistent with gene-level selection.
activities.rationale: Letting learners set r, B and C and watch the rB-versus-C threshold decide the gene's fate turns altruism into a quantitative prediction with worked relatedness numbers, directly targeting the group-selection misconception. A written statement of the rule alone leaves the threshold abstract.
sourceClaims: Sexual selection (female choice, male-male competition, runaway and handicap/honest-signal models) explains costly ornaments; kin selection via Hamilton's rule (rB > C) and inclusive fitness explains altruism toward relatives.
KS3 natural selection and variation provide the basis for explaining why costly or self-sacrificing traits evolve.
learnerActions: Set a relatedness value r for the helper and the helped (e.g. full sibling r = 0.5), a benefit B to the relative, and a cost C to the helper.
Compute rB and compare it with C; decide whether the altruism gene should spread (rB > C) or die out (rB < C).

Work a model case: treat a meerkat sentinel as paying a cost C to warn relatives (benefit B shared among kin). Vary r, B and C and find the threshold where helping becomes favoured. Note that field studies suggest sentinels may face little extra risk and may also benefit themselves (for example, they often spot danger and reach cover first), so real sentinel behaviour may not be pure kin-selected altruism.
Explain why this is a gene's-eye prediction — helping copies of one's own genes carried in relatives — rather than 'for the good of the species'.
activities.intendedInsight: Apparent self-sacrifice toward relatives is a calculable prediction of inclusive fitness: an altruism gene spreads when rB > C. This replaces vague group-benefit reasoning with quantitative individual/gene-level reasoning.

activities.title: Hawk-dove game: no single best move
feedback: If a learner expects pure aggression always to win: with injury cost greater than resource value, have them seed a population of almost all hawks plus a few doves (or add a few dove mutants to an all-hawk population) and watch hawks' average payoff fall as they keep fighting each other; the rare doves then do better than the hawks and increase. A population with no doves at all cannot be invaded by doves until some doves appear. (If injury cost is not greater than resource value the balance shifts toward hawks, so the payoffs matter.)

If a learner expects a single best strategy: point to the stable MIX the population converges on under these payoffs, and show how changing the payoffs moves that mix — or tips it to pure hawk — rather than crowning one fixed winner.

If a learner thinks the equilibrium is set by the starting mix: have them try several different starting mixes that each contain both hawks and doves, keeping the payoffs fixed, and notice they converge toward the same stable proportion.
activities.rationale: A population that the learner seeds and watches converge makes frequency dependence self-evident; live payoff controls let the equilibrium shift under the learner's hand. Reading a matrix alone can assess the idea but does not show the equilibrium settling itself.
sourceClaims: The hawk-dove game illustrates an evolutionarily stable strategy: the best behaviour is frequency-dependent, yielding a stable mix rather than a single winner.
learnerActions: Read a hawk-dove payoff matrix and work out what a hawk and a dove each gain when they meet a hawk and when they meet a dove.

Seed a population with a chosen starting mix of hawks and doves and let it play repeated contests. With the default payoffs set so injury cost exceeds resource value, watch the proportions settle toward a stable mixed equilibrium (the evolutionarily stable strategy).

Change the payoffs (e.g. the cost of injury in a hawk-hawk fight) and observe how the equilibrium moves — a mixed ESS when injury cost exceeds resource value, shifting toward pure hawk when it does not.

With injury cost set higher than the resource value, predict what happens when a few doves are added to a population that is almost all hawks, then test it: explain why pure aggression stops winning once almost everyone is a hawk.
activities.intendedInsight: The best behaviour can be frequency-dependent: with injury cost exceeding resource value an ESS is a stable mix, not a lone winner. 'Survival of the fittest' does not mean the strongest or most aggressive always wins — the best move depends on what everyone else is playing and on the payoff values (with a low injury cost, pure hawk can instead be favoured).

activities.title: Knowledge check: fitness, Hamilton's rule and payoffs
feedback: For a fitness item answered as 'survives longest' or 'strongest': restate fitness as reproductive success and cite the showy short-lived male who out-reproduces a drab survivor.
For an rB-vs-C error: have the learner recompute rB and line it up against C before deciding.
A recognition check confirms recall but does not show whether the learner can explore the trade-offs and equilibria themselves — pair it with the models above.
activities.rationale: A targeted check verifies the computational and definitional pieces that underpin the three models: the definition of fitness, the arithmetic of Hamilton's rule, and reading a payoff matrix. It is a complement to, not a substitute for, operating the models, since it does not elicit exploration of trade-offs or equilibria.
sourceClaims: Sexual selection (female choice, male-male competition, runaway and handicap/honest-signal models) explains costly ornaments; kin selection via Hamilton's rule (rB > C) and inclusive fitness explains altruism toward relatives.
Natural selection acts through differential reproductive success and changes trait distributions over generations.
The hawk-dove game illustrates an evolutionarily stable strategy: the best behaviour is frequency-dependent, yielding a stable mix rather than a single winner.
learnerActions: Answer what 'fittest' means in evolution (reproductive success, not longest survival or greatest strength).
Given r, B and C values, compute rB and state whether rB > C, and hence whether helping is favoured.
Read a hawk-dove payoff matrix and identify which strategy pays better against a given opponent.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the definition of fitness, the arithmetic of Hamilton's rule, and reading a payoff matrix as checkable knowledge.

activities.title: Optional debate: noble meerkat, or Hamilton's rule? (cognitive ethology extension)
feedback: If a learner settles 'nobility' as fact: ask what observation would distinguish a noble motive from a kin-selected one, and whether either is directly measurable.
If a learner accepts an animal-culture claim uncritically: have them separate the behaviour observed from the inferred inner state, and name the evidence needed.
Keep this as discussion: the quantitative models above are best operated, while this extension builds the working-scientifically skill of constructing evidence-based explanations.
activities.rationale: A Socratic debate develops the skill of constructing evidence-based explanations and probes the group-selection misconception, while cognitive ethology is genuinely an evidence/interpretation question suited to discussion. No cited source directly addresses cognitive ethology, so no source claim is mapped here.
learnerActions: Argue the possible explanations for 'is the meerkat sentinel being noble, is it Hamilton's rule, or is it simply looking after itself?' and decide which explanations make testable predictions.
Examine a claim about animal emotion, play or culture and separate the evidence from the interpretation — state what observation would support or weaken the claim.
Challenge a 'for the good of the species' statement and reframe it at the individual/gene level.
activities.intendedInsight: Behavioural explanations must be evidence-based; cognitive-ethology claims about animal emotion or culture are open evidence questions, and group-benefit language can usually be recast in individual/gene-level terms.

constraints: Redefine fitness explicitly as reproductive success (not survival, strength or longevity) before introducing any of the three models, or the peacock's tail stays paradoxical.
Hamilton's rule should be taught with concrete relatedness numbers (e.g. full sibling r = 0.5) so altruism is a quantitative gene's-eye prediction, not a vague appeal to 'the good of the group'.
Actively dismantle 'for the good of the species' group-selection thinking; replace it with individual/gene-level reasoning across all activities.

A static labelled diagram can introduce the ornament trade-off and a quiz can check rB vs C and matrix reading, but neither lets learners locate the net-fitness peak or watch an equilibrium settle; treat them as scaffolds/checks alongside the manipulable models.

The hawk-dove population result depends on the payoff values chosen; the mixed ESS holds when injury cost exceeds resource value, while a low injury cost can favour pure hawk, so avoid teaching one fixed mix as a universal answer.
Cognitive-ethology claims (animal emotion, play, culture) are evidence questions; present them as open and distinguish observation from interpretation rather than asserting conclusions.

Frequency sliders, live-converging populations and payoff-matrix controls are illustrative mechanisms to make the models concrete, not mandatory implementations; equivalent manipulable representations are acceptable.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all sources[].claim entries remain verified:false and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Bird-of-paradise displays, frog calls and male-male competition were restored to the sexual-selection activity from the source description/claim, having been dropped in an earlier draft.

Self-audit of arithmetic/logic: Hamilton's rule rB > C is stated correctly and the full-sibling r = 0.5 example is standard; the net-fitness peak requires mating benefit to rise faster than survival cost over the relevant range, which the model should ensure. No numerical errors were found in the source to correct.

The source's original artefact ratings asserted a static image 'cannot' carry the models and that 3D 'adds no conceptual value'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordance statements (static/quiz as scaffolds and checks).
Runaway vs handicap/honest-signal are presented together as explanations for costly ornaments; these are distinct mechanisms — ensure learners are not told the sim proves one over the other.

The claim that an all-hawk population 'does badly' and the specific stable mix depend on the chosen payoff matrix (injury cost relative to resource value); set payoffs so the ESS is a genuinely mixed outcome before presenting it as such, and note low-cost regimes can favour pure hawk. Hawk-dove learner actions were reworded so the mixed-ESS outcome is stated as a consequence of injury cost exceeding resource value rather than a universal result.

probeDeeper: What does 'fittest' actually mean in evolution — surviving longest, or something else?
Why might a peahen benefit from choosing a male with an outrageously costly tail?
A worker bee is sterile and dies defending the hive. How can 'selfish genes' produce such self-sacrifice?
If being a pure aggressive 'hawk' always won, what would happen once nearly everyone is a hawk?
assess.correctAnswer: Because survival isn't all that counts — evolutionarily what matters is passing on genes, which needs both surviving AND mating. Peahens prefer males with big, showy tails (a costly tail can signal a healthy, high-quality male), so bigger-tailed males mate more and leave more offspring. That extra mating success outweighs the survival cost, so the trait spreads and can even run away to extremes. This is sexual selection — a form of natural selection in which mating advantage, not just survival, drives the trait.

errorPatterns.pattern: Natural selection keeps only traits that aid survival, so a costly tail should be eliminated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redefine fitness as reproductive success — a trait that lowers survival can still spread if it raises mating success enough.
errorPatterns.distractor: Natural selection should have removed the tail, because it only hurts the peacock's survival.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the tail should vanish; treats survival as the whole of fitness.

errorPatterns.pattern: The peacock grows a big tail on purpose to attract mates, or because it wants to look good
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recast as selection over generations on heritable variation in tail size via female preference, not an individual's choice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Frames the tail as a strategy chosen by the individual within its lifetime.

errorPatterns.pattern: Self-sacrifice (a worker bee dying for the hive) evolves 'for the good of the species'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce inclusive fitness and Hamilton's rule — helping close relatives propagates shared genes, so the bee's sacrifice favours copies of its own genes in kin.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains altruism as being for the survival of the species as a whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Survival of the fittest' means the strongest or most aggressive individual always wins
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the hawk-dove model — an all-hawk population does badly; the best strategy is frequency-dependent (an evolutionarily stable strategy).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes pure aggression is always the best strategy.

responseLevels.gap: Equates fitness with individual survival; says the costly tail should disappear and treats altruism as impossible or simply 'for the good of the species'.
responseLevels.full: Explains fitness as reproductive success, resolves the peacock paradox through a mating-versus-survival trade-off and female choice/signalling (including runaway selection), accounts for altruism via kin selection and inclusive fitness, and recognises that the best behavioural strategy is frequency-dependent (hawk-dove / ESS).
responseLevels.partial: Knows sexual selection favours mating and states 'peahens like big tails', but can't connect it to fitness as reproductive success, and handles altruism and game-theoretic strategy only loosely — listing the ideas without integrating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A peacock's huge, heavy tail makes it slower and easier for predators to catch — it is bad for survival. So why hasn't natural selection got rid of it? Why do peacocks still grow these extravagant tails?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who equates fitness with survival alone says the tail 'should' disappear or can't explain it. A student who understands fitness as reproductive success explains the mating-versus-survival trade-off and names female choice or signalling. Resolving the apparent paradox through reproduction is the discriminator.

sources.claim: Natural selection acts through differential reproductive success and changes trait distributions over generations.
sources.source: NGSS MS-LS4-4

sources.claim: Sexual selection (female choice, male-male competition, runaway and handicap/honest-signal models) explains costly ornaments; kin selection via Hamilton's rule (rB > C) and inclusive fitness explains altruism toward relatives.
sources.source: Behavioural-ecology reference (Darwin sexual selection; Hamilton 1964 inclusive fitness; Zahavi handicap principle)
