pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Plant & Animal Reproduction (sexual vs asexual)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y5 'Living things and their habitats'):** pupils describe the life process of reproduction in some plants and animals.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-LS1-1 context / MS-LS3-2 foreshadow):** organisms reproduce as part of their life cycle; sexual reproduction produces offspring with variation while asexual reproduction produces identical offspring (the KS2 seed of the later MS-LS3-2 idea).

- **Operational details:** Two contrasts. In PLANTS: sexual reproduction (pollination → fertilisation → seed, involving two parents' genetic material) versus asexual reproduction (runners in strawberries, bulbs, cuttings — one parent, offspring are clones). In ANIMALS: egg-laying (oviparous — birds, frogs, insects, most fish/reptiles) versus live-bearing (viviparous — most mammals). The load-bearing idea, kept age-appropriate: sexual reproduction needs two parents and mixes their features so offspring VARY; asexual needs one parent and makes identical copies. Pupils describe each process, give examples, and compare egg-laying with live-bearing. This plants the seed for KS3 variation and inheritance.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (relational). Pupils relate parent-number to offspring variation (two parents → varied; one parent → identical) and compare reproductive strategies across plants and animals. Success = describes sexual and asexual plant reproduction with examples and explains why asexual offspring are identical.
bestPractices: Contrast the two plant routes directly — seed (two parents) vs runner/cutting (one parent) — so the parent-number-to-variation link is visible.
Keep genetics implicit and age-appropriate: 'mixes both parents' features' vs 'an exact copy', without alleles or DNA.
Use familiar, concrete asexual examples (strawberry runners, potato/onion bulbs, geranium cuttings) that children can picture or grow.
Compare egg-laying and live-bearing across real animals, avoiding the misconception that only mammals reproduce or that egg-layers don't have parents involved.
Foreshadow KS3 variation lightly: identical clones vs varied siblings is the hook, not the destination.
keyRepresentations: Flower cross-section (stamen, stigma, ovary) with the pollination→fertilisation→seed sequence
Asexual method cards: strawberry runner, bulb, cutting — each producing a clone
Offspring-variation gallery: varied seed-siblings vs identical clones
Egg-laying vs live-bearing comparison across animal groups
commonMisconceptions: Thinking all plants reproduce only from seeds, not knowing about runners, bulbs and cuttings (asexual reproduction).
Believing offspring from a cutting or runner are the plant's 'children' that will differ, rather than identical clones.
Assuming only mammals reproduce, or that egg-laying animals aren't really reproducing.
Confusing pollination with fertilisation, or thinking a seed forms without pollen from another flower in sexual reproduction.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year-olds, contrast sexual plant reproduction (pollination → fertilisation → seed, usually two parents, varied offspring) with asexual reproduction (runners, bulbs, cuttings, one parent, clones), and compare egg-laying with live-bearing animals. The load-bearing idea, kept age-appropriate without genes or alleles: the type of reproduction decides whether inherited features vary. Sexual reproduction mixes features, usually from two parents, so seed-grown offspring differ. Asexual reproduction copies one parent, so the offspring share the same inherited features. They may still differ in size or health because of growing conditions. This seeds KS3 variation and inheritance.

activities.title: Run both plant routes and compare the offspring
feedback: If a learner expects the runner or cutting plant to differ from its parent 'the way children differ', point to the gallery. One parent produces a clone with the same inherited features, so there is nothing to mix. Any size differences come from growing conditions.
If a learner says the runner is 'just the plant growing bigger, not reproduction', note that the new plant is separate and complete — that IS reproduction, the asexual kind.

If a learner treats pollination as the moment the seed forms, separate the steps: pollination transfers pollen to the stigma; fertilisation is the later joining of cells inside the ovule that actually forms the seed.
activities.rationale: Doing both routes and comparing several resulting offspring under the same conditions makes the link between type of reproduction and variation observable rather than asserted, and keeps genetics implicit. Fertilisation itself cannot be seen and must be modelled. If using an interactive model, optional mechanisms that make this concrete include dragging pollen between flowers, a step that shows fertilisation inside the ovule, and a side-by-side offspring gallery; these are illustrative, not required. The gallery is where the contrast is seen.
sourceClaims: Sexual reproduction in plants (pollination, fertilisation, seed) involves two parents and produces varied offspring; asexual reproduction (runners, bulbs, cuttings) involves one parent and produces genetically identical offspring (clones).
learnerActions: Carry out the sexual route: move pollen from a flower on one plant to a flower on a different plant of the same kind (pollination). Use a diagram or model to follow the later, invisible step where cells join inside the ovule (fertilisation), which leads to seeds forming. Then grow the seeds into several sibling plants.

Carry out an asexual route from a SINGLE parent: peg down several runners from one strawberry plant, take several cuttings from one geranium, or plant offset bulbs split from one parent bulb. Grow the new plants alongside the parent in the same conditions.
Place the two sets of offspring side by side in a gallery: a row of seed-grown siblings versus a row of runner/cutting-grown plants.

Describe out loud or in writing what differs, focusing on inherited features such as leaf shape, leaf pattern or flower colour. Seed-siblings may vary in these features, while runner/cutting plants should match their parent. Size or health differences in either row can come from growing conditions.

State the rule the comparison reveals: sexual reproduction (usually two parents) → offspring with mixed, varied features; asexual reproduction (one parent) → offspring with the same inherited features as the parent (clones).
activities.intendedInsight: Whether offspring vary in inherited features depends on the type of reproduction. Sexual reproduction, usually with two parents, mixes features and produces variation. Asexual reproduction from one parent produces a copy with the same inherited features, though growing conditions can still change size or health. Genes are not needed to explain this.

activities.title: Label the flower and sequence the sexual route (reference / pre-teach)
feedback: If the sequence is reversed or collapsed, re-separate pollination (pollen arrives at the stigma) from fertilisation (cells join inside the ovule) and from seed formation.
If an asexual card is misfiled, ask whether a new plant grows straight from part of one parent without flowers or seeds. If it does, it is a clone.
activities.rationale: A labelled, tappable diagram and ordered sequence build vocabulary and the step order efficiently as reference or pre-teaching. On its own this fixes the processes and names but does not let a learner generate offspring and see the resulting variation, so pair it with the comparison activity.
sourceClaims: Sexual reproduction in plants (pollination, fertilisation, seed) involves two parents and produces varied offspring; asexual reproduction (runners, bulbs, cuttings) involves one parent and produces genetically identical offspring (clones).
learnerActions: Identify and label stamen, stigma and ovary on a flower cross-section.
Put the sexual-reproduction steps in order: pollination → fertilisation → seed.
Sort example cards into asexual methods: strawberry runner, bulb, geranium cutting — naming each as producing a clone from one parent.
activities.intendedInsight: The processes and vocabulary of plant reproduction become crisp: the parts of a flower, the ordered pollination→fertilisation→seed sequence, and the familiar asexual methods.

activities.title: Compare egg-laying and live-bearing animals
feedback: If a learner thinks only mammals reproduce, point to birds and frogs: laying and hatching an egg is reproduction too.
If a learner thinks egg-layers 'aren't really reproducing', clarify that producing a new individual is reproduction regardless of egg or live birth.
activities.rationale: Comparing real animals across both strategies rounds out the reproductive strategies the standard names and directly confronts the 'only mammals reproduce' misconception.
sourceClaims: Animals reproduce by egg-laying (oviparous — birds, frogs) or live-bearing (viviparous — most mammals); this is the KS2 comparison of reproductive strategies.
learnerActions: Follow an egg-laying example (bird, frog, many insects): lay and hatch an egg.
Follow a live-bearing example (most mammals): a live birth.
Sort familiar animals into egg-laying vs live-bearing groups.
Answer: is one of these 'more' reproduction than the other? (No — producing a new individual is reproduction whether by egg or live birth.)
activities.intendedInsight: Animals reproduce in different ways — egg-laying and live-bearing — and both are genuine reproduction; it is not only mammals that reproduce.

activities.title: Check and apply: why do gardeners take cuttings?
feedback: If a learner says a cutting plant will differ from its parent, revisit: a cutting from one parent → clone with the same inherited features (only growing conditions change it); sexual reproduction, usually two parents → mixed features → variation.
If a learner is unsure why a gardener chooses cuttings, connect it to the gallery: cuttings give a plant with the same inherited features as the parent, while seeds can give variety.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and a short explanation check whether the type-of-reproduction to variation link holds, while the gardener question gives an authentic application. This activity checks and extends; it is not the first place the core contrast is built.
sourceClaims: Sexual reproduction in plants (pollination, fertilisation, seed) involves two parents and produces varied offspring; asexual reproduction (runners, bulbs, cuttings) involves one parent and produces genetically identical offspring (clones).
learnerActions: Match examples to type: strawberry runner → asexual; apple seed → sexual.
Answer which offspring are identical to the parent, and explain why cuttings are clones.
Discuss or explain: a gardener takes a cutting to get a plant exactly like this one — why choose a cutting over a seed if you want two identical plants?
activities.intendedInsight: Applying the parent-number rule to a real purpose (cuttings for identical plants, seeds for variation) consolidates and extends the core idea.

constraints: Keep genetics implicit and age-appropriate: say 'mixes both parents' features' vs 'an exact copy'; do not introduce alleles or DNA at this stage.

Pollination and fertilisation are distinct steps: pollination is pollen reaching the stigma; fertilisation is the later joining of cells inside the ovule that forms the seed. Do not treat them as the same moment.

A labelled diagram or sequence builds vocabulary and step order but does not let learners generate offspring and observe variation; treat it as reference/pre-teach and pair it with the hands-on comparison.
A sorting/matching check assesses categorisation and reasoning; it does not by itself elicit the independent act of running the two routes and observing the offspring gallery.
Use familiar, concrete asexual examples children can picture or grow (strawberry runners, potato tubers, onion or daffodil bulbs that form new offset bulbs, geranium cuttings).

Say 'most mammals' are live-bearing (some mammals lay eggs) and 'many insects' lay eggs rather than all; do not state all egg-laying animals have two parents, since this is not needed and not uniformly true at this level.

To show variation and copying, grow several offspring in each route under the same conditions. Then compare inherited features such as leaf shape or flower colour. Seed-grown siblings can show variation in these features, and clones should match their parent. Expect some size differences from growing conditions in both rows. A single specimen cannot demonstrate the contrast.

Interactive mechanisms (dragging pollen, a fertilisation step, a side-by-side gallery, egg-laying vs live-birth panels) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory requirements; the same contrast can be built with real plants, diagrams, or classroom demonstration.
Frame KS3 variation/inheritance as a light foreshadowing hook (identical clones vs varied siblings), not the destination of this lesson.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All three cited sources were recorded as verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source row rated 3D as 'poor' with the claim '3D adds no explanatory value.' This is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it has been dropped rather than restated as a universal limit. Reproduction here is well served by process-and-comparison tasks, but no claim is made that spatial/3D representation could never help.

The source row's 'ideal' framing asserts the contrast 'is felt by running each process' and that static art 'can't let the child run the cross.' Retained the genuine objective limit (a fixed diagram does not let a learner generate offspring to observe variation) while removing the implied claim that only the interactive lab can teach this.

Botanical note for reviewers: the row's assessment states a seed-grown strawberry/apple 'varies from its parents.' This is correct for sexual reproduction in general (apple seeds in particular do not come true to type); left as stated since it supports the two-parents→variation idea at an age-appropriate level.
The DfE curriculum claim was removed from Activity 1's sourceClaims because it attests a topic requirement, not the specific teaching principle (parent-number→variation) built in that activity.

Insects are predominantly oviparous but some are viviparous or parthenogenetic; the examples now say 'many insects' to preserve the original example without asserting a universal, which is beyond what the cited claim supports.

Clones are genetically identical to the parent; observable phenotype can still vary slightly with growing conditions. This is left implicit as age-appropriate, with the gallery comparison showing the clear contrast with seed-grown siblings.

probeDeeper: If there was no second parent, where do the runner plant's features come from?
How is growing a plant from a cutting like the strawberry runner?
A bird lays an egg and a dog gives birth to live pups — is one of these 'more' reproduction than the other?
If you wanted two plants exactly alike, would you grow them from seed or from cuttings? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — it is asexual reproduction: a new individual made from one parent without seeds or pollination. The runner plant is genetically identical to the parent (a clone). A seed-grown plant comes from sexual reproduction — pollination then fertilisation joins cells from two parents — so it varies from its parents.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It's not reproduction without a seed / two parents — the plant is just growing bigger.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define reproduction as producing a new individual; the runner plant is separate and complete — that is reproduction, just the asexual kind.
errorPatterns.distractor: That's not really reproduction — there's no seed, so it's just the plant growing bigger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the runner is reproduction; treats it as the parent expanding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates pollination with fertilisation — treats 'pollination' as the moment a seed is made.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two steps: pollination = pollen transferred to the stigma; fertilisation = the later joining of cells inside the ovule that actually forms the seed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says pollination alone makes the seed, or uses the two words interchangeably.

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't link variation to reproduction type — thinks the runner plant will differ from the parent (or that seed-grown plants are identical copies).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie the outcome to the mechanism: one parent → clone (identical); two parents → mixed inheritance → variation.
errorPatterns.distractor: The new runner plant will be a bit different from the parent, the way children differ from their parents.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the runner plant is 'a bit different', or that seedlings are exact copies of the parent.

responseLevels.gap: Denies asexual reproduction is reproduction; conflates pollination and fertilisation; thinks offspring are all identical or all different regardless of type.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes sexual (two parents, pollination then fertilisation, variation) from asexual (one parent, clones), gives correct examples, and reasons about egg-laying vs live-bearing and the cuttings application.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts both sexual and asexual reproduction with examples, but cannot connect reproduction type to variation, or still muddles pollination and fertilisation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'A strawberry plant sends out a runner that grows into a whole new strawberry plant — no flower, no seed involved. Is that really reproduction? And will the new plant be identical to the parent or a bit different — how does that compare with a plant grown from a seed?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 'Is that really reproduction?' separates a child who believes reproduction requires seeds or two parents from one who accepts asexual reproduction. The identical-vs-different tier separates a child who thinks all offspring vary (or all are copies) from one who links the TYPE of reproduction to whether offspring vary.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–8 years

- **Topic:** Light & Sound Vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE Science programmes of study, KS1–KS2 'working scientifically' / language):** read, spell and use scientific vocabulary correctly and with confidence when describing observations — here the domain terms drawn from Year 1 materials (transparent, opaque), Year 3 Light (light source, reflect, shadow, transparent, translucent, opaque) and Year 4 Sound (vibration, pitch, volume).

- **Standards — US (NGSS / CCSS-ELA):** NGSS has no stand-alone vocabulary performance expectation — the Framework expects academic vocabulary to EMERGE from doing science (terms introduced to label phenomena pupils investigate, e.g. under 1-PS4 Waves and the SEP 'Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information'); the matching explicit standards are CCSS-ELA Language L.1.6 / L.2.6 / L.3.6 ('acquire and use accurately… grade-appropriate… words and phrases, including those that signal…').

- **Operational details:** This is a LANGUAGE topic: the goal is that children NAME and correctly APPLY the words while describing real observations, not recite definitions. Teach each term in the context of the phenomenon it labels — introduce 'translucent' while torch-testing tracing paper, 'vibration' while watching rice dance on a drum — so the word is hung on an experience. Give a precise child-definition plus EXAMPLES and NON-EXAMPLES (Frayer-style), especially to prise apart near-neighbours (transparent vs translucent). Pre-empt everyday-vs-scientific clashes head-on: 'volume' means loudness here, not amount of space; 'pitch' is how high/low, not how loud; 'reflect' means light bouncing, not thinking. Build in many repeated exposures and demand productive use — children must SAY and WRITE the words in full sentences about their results (Oak's evidence: classify materials and explain a shadow 'using the words opaque and light source correctly'). Anchor with active testing and classifying (darkened-room torch test; sound-source sorts).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). At 6–8 success is applying each term accurately to a concrete observation — classifying materials as transparent/translucent/opaque, explaining a shadow with 'opaque' and 'light source', describing pitch/volume changes with vibration words. The threshold is precision: resolving the everyday meanings that interfere (loud≠high; reflect≠think) and recognising the translucent 'middle' category rather than a see-through/not binary. This vocabulary is a HARD prerequisite for eight downstream light and sound topics, so accuracy here pays forward.
bestPractices: Teach each term in the context of the phenomenon it names (introduce 'translucent' during the torch test, 'vibration' while rice dances on a drum) so the word attaches to a witnessed experience rather than a definition list — consistent with NGSS's 'vocabulary emerges from doing science'.
Give a precise child-friendly definition with EXAMPLES and NON-EXAMPLES (Frayer-style), especially to separate near-neighbours transparent vs translucent.
Pre-empt everyday-vs-scientific meaning clashes explicitly: name that 'volume' = loudness not amount, 'pitch' = high/low not loud, 'reflect' = light bouncing not thinking.
Provide many repeated exposures and require PRODUCTIVE use — children say and write the words in full sentences describing their own results, not just match definitions.
Anchor terms with active testing and classifying (darkened-room torch test for transparent/translucent/opaque; sorting sound sources) so the word labels something the child did.
Use formative probes/short sorts to catch where an everyday meaning is still interfering, and revisit — conceptual/linguistic precision develops gradually.
keyRepresentations: Frayer-style word map: definition, example, non-example and a picture for each term
Classification sort with a torch in a darkened scene: materials grouped into transparent / translucent / opaque
A word wall / labelled diagram pairing each term to the phenomenon it names (light source, shadow, reflect, vibration)
Sentence frames / talk stems ('A shadow forms when an ___ object blocks the light from a ___')
Paired pitch and volume displays kept visibly separate (a string changing tightness vs a sound changing loudness)
commonMisconceptions: 'All materials that let light through them are transparent' — collapsing the translucent middle category into transparent (Oak-named).
Treating transparent vs opaque as a strict binary, with no partial 'some light through' case.
Everyday meaning of 'volume' (amount of space/stuff) overriding the scientific meaning (loudness).
Confusing pitch with volume — hearing 'higher' and 'louder' as the same thing.
Using 'reflect' in its everyday sense (to think about) rather than light bouncing off a surface.
Calling any bright or shiny thing a 'light source' (e.g. a mirror or the Moon) rather than only objects that make their own light.

learn.summary: Help 6–8 year-olds NAME and correctly APPLY light and sound vocabulary (light source, transparent, translucent, opaque, shadow, reflect, vibration, pitch, volume) while describing real observations — not reciting definitions. The hardest work is prising apart words that look alike (transparent vs translucent) or clash with everyday meaning (volume=loudness not amount; pitch=high/low not loud; reflect=light bouncing not thinking) and reserving the translucent 'middle' category instead of a see-through/not binary. Anchor each term to a witnessed phenomenon, demand productive use in full sentences, and probe for lingering everyday meanings.

activities.title: Two-bench word workshop: light-sort and the split pitch/volume controls
feedback: If a frosted/blurry material is called transparent: 'You can see light but not a clear picture through it — that is translucent. Transparent is the clear window where you see the object clearly.'
If 'high volume' is said for loud or 'loud pitch' for high: 'Pitch is how HIGH or LOW; volume is how LOUD or QUIET. Tighten the string to change pitch; make the sound bigger to change volume.'
When a correct in-use sentence is produced, affirm the specific word use: 'Yes — the OPAQUE book blocks all the light, which is exactly why a shadow appears.'
activities.rationale: Keeping pitch and volume on separate controls that each change one witnessed effect lets the child discover they are independent, directly addressing the confusable pair. Showing a clear image vs a blur vs nothing makes translucent a concrete observed category. Optional live controls (sliders, dragging materials into the beam) make the mechanism concrete but are illustrative, not the only route — physical drums and torch tests can teach the same distinction.
sourceClaims: Oak Year 3 defines opaque (light cannot pass through), transparent (completely see-through, objects clearly seen) and translucent (some light passes but not clearly see-through); names the misconception 'all materials that let light through them are transparent'; uses a darkened-room torch test and a classify-into-groups activity; evidence includes classifying materials and explaining a shadow using the correct terms.

Light misconceptions form partly from the difference between scientific and everyday language; teaching the vocabulary (transparent, translucent, opaque, reflection, refraction) should pair words with investigating how materials interact with light; misconceptions are tenacious, so use formative assessment and repeated hands-on activities.
learnerActions: On a LIGHT bench, place materials (glass, tracing paper, a book) into a torch beam in a darkened scene and sort them into TRANSPARENT / TRANSLUCENT / OPAQUE groups.

Notice what you actually see: a clear image through glass (transparent), a fuzzy blur through tracing paper (translucent), nothing through the book (opaque) — so 'translucent' lands as a witnessed middle case, not a memorised word.

On a SOUND bench, use TWO deliberately separate controls. Move the PITCH control and watch a cartoon string tighten so the note squeaks higher — but NOT louder. Move the VOLUME control and the same note swells louder while staying the same height.
Say a full sentence for each placement, e.g. 'The OPAQUE book blocks the light, so a SHADOW forms,' and 'Tightening the string raises the PITCH; it does not change the VOLUME.'
activities.intendedInsight: Each term attaches to a distinct, witnessed effect. Pitch and volume change different things, so the two words pupils keep swapping finally pull apart; translucent is a real third category, not 'nearly transparent'.

activities.title: Frayer word maps anchored to the phenomenon
feedback: If a mirror or the Moon is listed as a light source: 'Those are bright because they BOUNCE light. A light source makes its own light — like the Sun or a torch.'

If the non-example box is empty: 'Picking something the word does NOT describe is how we fence off its edges — what lets light through but is NOT transparent, because you cannot see a clear picture through it? (frosted glass).'
activities.rationale: Explicit definition-plus-example-and-non-example instruction with the word tied to a phenomenon the child investigated is a well-established vocabulary approach and directly separates confusable Tier 3 terms.
sourceClaims: Effective vocabulary instruction teaches words explicitly in meaningful context with definitions, examples and non-examples and repeated exposures, and prioritises productive use; domain-specific (Tier 3) science terms are best developed alongside the phenomena rather than as decontextualised word lists.
learnerActions: For each target word build a map with four parts: a child-friendly definition, an EXAMPLE, a NON-EXAMPLE, and a picture.

Draw the example and non-example from something you actually tested or observed — e.g. for 'light source' the example is a torch or the Sun (makes its own light), the non-example is a mirror or the Moon (only reflects light).
For the near-neighbours, put transparent and translucent side by side so the definitions and pictures contrast directly (clear window vs frosted glass).
Add the everyday-meaning trap for the clashing words, e.g. for volume write 'HERE it means loudness, NOT amount of space.'
activities.intendedInsight: A precise definition paired with example and non-example separates near-neighbours and pins each scientific word apart from its everyday twin.

activities.title: Narrate the playground scene (productive use check)
feedback: If 'volume' is used for amount/size ('the volume of the box'): 'Here volume means how LOUD the sound is. The amount-of-space meaning is a different, maths meaning of the same word.'
If 'reflect' is used for thinking: 'In this topic reflect means light BOUNCES off a surface — like off the shiny slide or a puddle.'
If terms are dropped or swapped under the pressure of narrating, prompt for the missing/confused word rather than supplying the whole sentence, so the child produces it.
activities.rationale: Listening for use in a genuine description, not 'define opaque', surfaces exactly the everyday-vs-scientific clashes and the translucent middle, which rote definitions hide. Oak's evidence statements are themselves use-in-context (classify materials; explain a shadow using the correct terms).
sourceClaims: Oak Year 3 defines opaque (light cannot pass through), transparent (completely see-through, objects clearly seen) and translucent (some light passes but not clearly see-through); names the misconception 'all materials that let light through them are transparent'; uses a darkened-room torch test and a classify-into-groups activity; evidence includes classifying materials and explaining a shadow using the correct terms.

Effective vocabulary instruction teaches words explicitly in meaningful context with definitions, examples and non-examples and repeated exposures, and prioritises productive use; domain-specific (Tier 3) science terms are best developed alongside the phenomena rather than as decontextualised word lists.
learnerActions: Look at a picture of a sunny playground: a tree casting a shadow, a clear school window, a frosted-glass door, a shiny metal slide, and a child banging a drum.
Tell the whole story of the light and the sound, using as many target words as you can, correctly: light source, opaque, transparent, translucent, shadow, reflect, vibration, pitch, volume.

Aim for in-use sentences, e.g. 'The Sun is the light source; the tree is opaque so it blocks the light and makes a shadow; the window is transparent so light passes through; the shiny slide reflects light; the drum skin vibrates to make the sound; hitting it harder makes a bigger vibration and a louder volume; a tighter or smaller drum would have a higher pitch.'

Answer follow-up probes: 'Which word tells us WHY the tree can block the light?' 'The drum got louder — is that pitch or volume, and what would change the pitch instead?' 'Point to something transparent and something opaque and say each word.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to USE each term accurately inside a real description — keeping confusable pairs distinct and reserving translucent — is the actual goal, and it catches a child who can recite a definition but misapplies the word.

activities.title: Term–application sort and sentence completion (anchoring check)
feedback: Recognition and matching confirm the child can select the right word; follow a correct match with a request to USE the word in a sentence so production, not just recognition, is exercised.

If 'higher PITCH' is chosen for the harder hit: 'Harder hitting changes how LOUD the sound is — that is volume. Pitch is how high or low, and it changes when the string or drum is tighter or smaller.'
activities.rationale: Short sorts and fill-in sentences directly exercise correct application of the words and make a convenient formative probe for lingering interference. They assess selection well but should follow, not replace, productive use.
sourceClaims: Oak Year 3 defines opaque (light cannot pass through), transparent (completely see-through, objects clearly seen) and translucent (some light passes but not clearly see-through); names the misconception 'all materials that let light through them are transparent'; uses a darkened-room torch test and a classify-into-groups activity; evidence includes classifying materials and explaining a shadow using the correct terms.
learnerActions: Sort a set of materials or sound-source cards and match each to its term (transparent/translucent/opaque; what changes pitch vs what changes volume).
Complete sentence frames, e.g. 'A shadow forms when an ___ object blocks the light from a ___ ,' and 'Tightening the string makes the sound a higher ___ .'
Choose between the confusable pair in a forced choice: 'The child hit the drum harder — the sound got higher PITCH / louder VOLUME.'
activities.intendedInsight: Once the terms are anchored by observation and used in sentences, matching and completion checks confirm correct application and flag any term still being misused.

constraints: This is a LANGUAGE goal: success is naming and correctly APPLYING each word to a concrete observation, not reciting definitions. Require productive use — children SAY and WRITE the words in full sentences about their own results.
Matching, sorting and forced-choice tasks assess recognition/selection; they do not on their own elicit independent production, so pair them with a spoken or written use-in-context task.

A labelled glossary scene (tap an element to reveal term, definition, example/non-example) is a useful reference but is receptive — it presents words rather than requiring the child to resolve translucent-vs-transparent or pitch-vs-volume, so use it to support, not replace, active sorting and narration.

A 'word coach' persona the child explains observations to can serve productive use and gently correct a misused term ('you said louder — did you mean higher?'), but it cannot show the referent and can slip into simply telling the child the word; keep the witnessed phenomenon central.
Keep pitch and volume on visibly separate controls/displays so changing one does not change the other; do not conflate 'higher' with 'louder'.

Distinguish an idealised on-screen model (e.g. a cartoon string, a thin screen scene) from a real darkened-room torch test; both are useful and offer different experiences — neither is presented as the only way to learn.
Reserve 'light source' for objects that make their own light (Sun, torch); a mirror or the Moon only reflects light and is a non-example.
Everyday meanings to pre-empt by name: volume=loudness (not amount of space), pitch=how high/low (not loud), reflect=light bouncing (not thinking).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The EEF/Reading Rockets vocabulary source is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as un-reverified and do not overstate evidence strength.

Neither cited source directly addresses the SOUND terms (pitch/volume); the source claims support the light-vocabulary anchoring principle, while the pitch/volume separation is an unvalidated pedagogical proposal (though consistent with the pedagogy's own misconception list).

Self-audit: the original recommendation's claim that only a live interactive can 'pull pitch and volume apart' was softened — separate controls make the distinction concrete, but the pedagogical principle is independent of any one medium; static maps, physical drums and torch tests can also teach it.

Self-audit: 'volume' as loudness vs mathematical volume (amount of space) are genuinely different meanings of one word — correctly framed as an everyday/scientific clash, not an error, and both senses are retained.
Self-audit: 'light source' examples exclude mirror/Moon, consistent with the pedagogy's own misconception list, so no activity labels a reflective object as a source.

Self-audit: the forced-choice feedback in the anchoring-check activity targets the actual wrong option ('higher PITCH'); the correction (harder hit = louder = volume; pitch changes with a tighter/smaller string or drum) is physically accurate and coherent with the item.

Physical setups (torch, tracing paper, drum, rice) are approximations with real thickness and imperfections; the on-screen clear/blur/nothing demonstration is an idealised model of the same phenomenon.

probeDeeper: You said the tree makes a shadow — which word tells us WHY it can block the light?
The child hits the drum harder and it gets louder — which word is that, pitch or volume? And what would change the pitch instead?
Point to something transparent and something opaque in the room, and say each word as you point.
assess.correctAnswer: In narrating the scene the child USES the terms correctly — e.g. 'the Sun is the light source; the tree is opaque so it blocks the light and makes a shadow; the window is transparent so light passes through; the shiny slide reflects light; the drum skin vibrates to make the sound; hitting it harder makes a bigger vibration and a louder volume; a smaller or tighter drum would have a higher pitch.' The words are USED in context, not merely defined.

errorPatterns.pattern: Everyday 'volume': uses volume to mean amount or size rather than loudness ('the volume of the box')
errorPatterns.nextMove: In the sound context, volume = how loud; explicitly contrast it with the maths 'volume' (amount of space) so the two meanings don't collide.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies 'volume' to the quantity/space of an object rather than to how loud the sound is

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Reflect' means think: uses reflect for pondering, not for light bouncing
errorPatterns.nextMove: In this context reflect = light bounces off a surface; give the mirror/puddle referent to anchor the scientific meaning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses 'reflect' non-scientifically, or can't apply it to the shiny slide/light

errorPatterns.pattern: Pitch/volume swap: says 'high volume' for loud or 'loud pitch' for high — the confusable pair
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pitch = how high/low; volume = how loud/quiet; pin each to a separate change (tighten the string vs hit harder).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Swaps the two words when describing the drum

errorPatterns.pattern: Translucent collapsed into transparent: calls a frosted, see-through-but-blurry object transparent
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reserve translucent for 'light through but no clear image' — the clear window (transparent) versus frosted glass (translucent).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses 'transparent' for a translucent object when narrating

responseLevels.gap: Avoids the terms or uses them wrongly — volume for amount, reflect for thinking, pitch and volume swapped, or translucent things called transparent.
responseLevels.full: Narrates the scene using the terms accurately and appropriately, keeps the confusable pairs distinct and reserves translucent, and can point each word to its referent on request.
responseLevels.partial: Uses several terms correctly in the description but drops or misuses the confusable ones (pitch versus volume, or the translucent middle) under the pressure of narrating.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at this picture of a sunny playground: a tree casting a shadow, a window in the school, a shiny metal slide, and a child banging a drum. Tell me the whole story of what's happening with the light and the sound — use as many of these words as you can, in the right way: light source, opaque, transparent, shadow, reflect, vibration, pitch, volume.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Listening for USE in a real description (not 'define opaque') catches the child who can recite a definition but misapplies the word. The everyday-versus-scientific clashes surface here: 'volume' for loudness (not amount), 'reflect' for light bouncing (not thinking), pitch kept distinct from volume, and the translucent middle correctly reserved. A child with only rote definitions drops or swaps terms when actually narrating.

sources.claim: Oak Year 3 defines opaque (light cannot pass through), transparent (completely see-through, objects clearly seen) and translucent (some light passes but not clearly see-through); names the misconception 'all materials that let light through them are transparent'; uses a darkened-room torch test and a classify-into-groups activity; evidence includes classifying materials and explaining a shadow using the correct terms.

sources.claim: Light misconceptions form partly from the difference between scientific and everyday language; teaching the vocabulary (transparent, translucent, opaque, reflection, refraction) should pair words with investigating how materials interact with light; misconceptions are tenacious, so use formative assessment and repeated hands-on activities.

sources.claim: Effective vocabulary instruction teaches words explicitly in meaningful context with definitions, examples and non-examples and repeated exposures, and prioritises productive use; domain-specific (Tier 3) science terms are best developed alongside the phenomena rather than as decontextualised word lists.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1). COUNTING OBJECTS TO 20 — applying one-to-one correspondence AND cardinality to answer 'how many?' for sets up to 20 in any arrangement (line, array, circle, scattered), and counting out a given number (give-N). Where the counting principles become a reliable procedure.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals' and 'read and write numbers from 1 to 20 in numerals and words'. Underpinned by EYFS object counting; teen numbers (11–19) as 'ten and some more' bridge to place value.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.5 verbatim — 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
• Operational details: Combine one-to-one (tag each once) with cardinality (last word = total). Arrangement matters: line/array/circle are easier (a natural order exists); SCATTERED is hardest — the child must impose tracking (move counted items aside, or count round systematically). Give-N (count out exactly N) is the stronger check. Use the TEN-FRAME so teens read as a full ten + extras ('ten and three' = 13), seeding place value.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) counts a line of up to 20 accurately and counts ≤10 scattered by organising them. Tier B (5–6) counts 20 in any arrangement and gives-N up to 20. Tier C (6) counts a scattered 20 with a self-chosen tracking strategy and reads a teen set on a ten-frame as 'ten and __'.
bestPractices: Insist on a tracking strategy for scattered sets — move each counted object aside, or count along a consistent path — so nothing is missed or double-counted.
Use give-N ('count out 13') as the strongest assessment — harder than 'how many?' and it exposes shaky cardinality.
Introduce the ten-frame for teens: fill a ten, then extras, so 14 is seen as 'ten and four' (early place value, not a mystery word).
Vary the arrangement deliberately (line → array → circle → scattered) so counting is robust to layout and the 'different arrangement = different number' error is defeated.
Keep objects moveable and connect the count to the written numeral and the spoken 'altogether'.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames (one full + a partial for teens).
Moveable counters + a 'counted' tray.
Sets shown in line / array / circle / scattered (a deliberate arrangement ladder).
A numeral card matched to the counted set.
commonMisconceptions: Losing track on scattered sets → skips or double-counts (no tracking strategy).
Recounting when asked 'how many?' (cardinality not secure) or miscounting across the teens.
Treating teen numbers as unanalysable words rather than 'ten and some ones'.
Believing a rearranged set has a different total (conservation).

learn.summary: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1) counting objects to 20: coordinating one-to-one correspondence (tag each item exactly once) with cardinality (the last count word is the total) to answer 'how many?' for sets in any arrangement — line, array, circle, or scattered — and to count out a given number (give-N). Scattered sets are hardest because the child must impose a tracking strategy; give-N is the strongest check of cardinality. Ten-frames help teen numbers read as 'ten and some more', seeding place value. (The cited standard specifies scattered configurations up to 10 and ordered arrangements up to 20.)

activities.title: Organise and count a scattered set
feedback: If repeat counts give different totals, something went wrong in at least one count. Often counted and uncounted items got mixed up, but a number word may also have been skipped, or the words and pointing may have got out of step. Listen to the number sequence, and try physically moving each one aside as you count: 'move each one over here as you count it.'
If asked 'how many?' and the child recounts from the start, prompt: 'You just counted — what was the last number? That tells us how many.'
Ask: 'How could you count the scattered ones so you don't lose your place?' to prompt a self-chosen strategy rather than supplying one every time.
Rearrange the same counters and ask how many now — the total should not change because nothing was added or removed.
activities.rationale: One-to-one and cardinal principles must be coordinated to enumerate reliably, and moveable objects let a child physically track counted versus uncounted. Scattered arrangements demand a self-imposed strategy, which develops with practice rather than reteaching the count. The standard specifies scattered sets to 10; counting ~20 scattered is a harder extension drawn from the original Tier C.
sourceClaims: K.CC.5 verbatim: 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
One-one plus cardinal principles must be coordinated to reliably enumerate a set; tangible moveable objects help track counted vs uncounted.
learnerActions: Start with a small scattered pile (up to 10) of moveable counters or buttons spread randomly.
Count them by moving each counted item aside into a 'counted' tray (or sliding it along a consistent path) so counted and uncounted are clearly separated.
Say how many there are altogether, then recount and check you get the same number.
Repeat with a larger scattered set of up to 20 counters (a harder extension), choosing your own tracking path.
Match a numeral card to the final count.
activities.intendedInsight: A chaotic scatter becomes reliably countable by imposing order — moving each item as you count it so nothing is skipped or counted twice — and the last number you say is how many there are, no matter how the objects are arranged.

activities.title: Count out exactly N (give-N)
feedback: If the child counts past the target or hands over the whole pile, they are not yet using the number as a stop signal — state the target, count into a cupped hand, and do a stop-and-check: 'how many do we need? tell me when to stop.'
Follow up with 'Give me 4 more — now how many?' to link counting-on to the running total.
Praise stopping at exactly the right item, not just producing counters.
activities.rationale: Give-N is harder than 'how many?' because it requires holding a target while counting; it exposes shaky cardinality that a plain count can hide. Stopping at the target rebuilds the last-word-as-total link.
sourceClaims: K.CC.5 verbatim: 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
learnerActions: From a large pile, count out exactly a requested number (e.g. 'give me 13') into a cupped hand or small tray.
Say the target first, then count one item at a time, stopping when you reach it.
Check: 'How many did we need? Tell me when to stop' — point and count together to confirm you stopped at the target.
Try a round with a teen target such as 16, then compare counting out from different-sized piles.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting out a specific quantity means using the target number as a stop signal — you hold the goal in mind while counting, which is cardinality in action and a stronger test than simply reporting 'how many'.

activities.title: Vary the arrangement to make counting robust
feedback: If a child expects a different total after rearranging, slowly rearrange in front of them and recount together: nothing was added or taken away, so it stays the same.
Ask: 'If you started counting the line from the other end, how many?' to challenge the idea that direction changes the total.

Lines and arrays have a natural order to follow. Circles have an order too, but no natural start or end, so the child must mark or remember where they began to avoid counting items twice. Scattered sets need a strategy the child imposes. Name these differences so the child knows when extra care is needed.
activities.rationale: Deliberately varying arrangement makes counting robust to layout and challenges the belief that a different arrangement means a different number. Lines and arrays offer a natural order. A circle offers an order but no natural starting point, so the start must be marked. Scattered sets require imposed tracking. The conservation point — same total after rearranging — is a reasonable curricular inference and is not directly asserted by the cited standard.
sourceClaims: K.CC.5 verbatim: 'Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–20, count out that many objects.'
learnerActions: Count the same quantity shown four ways in turn: a line, a rectangular array, a circle, and scattered.
After counting a neat line, count it again starting from the other end and check the total is the same.
Count an array along rows, then along columns, and confirm the total does not change.
State each total aloud with 'altogether' and match it to the written numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: The total depends only on the objects, not on how they are laid out or which end you start from — a rearranged set still has the same number.

activities.title: Read teen numbers on a ten-frame as 'ten and some more'
feedback: If a teen is treated as an unanalysable word, point to the full frame and the extras: 'a full ten, and three more — thirteen.'
If the count across the teens slips, slow down and fill one frame completely before starting the extras.
Connect the spoken 'ten and four', the filled ten-frame, and the numeral 14 so all three line up.
activities.rationale: Ten-frames show teen numbers as ten-and-ones, which seeds place value and helps a child stop treating teens as random words. Note: the ten-frame source for this claim is marked unverified in the row and was not re-verified in this rewrite.
sourceClaims: Ten-frames represent teen numbers as ten-and-ones, seeding place value.
learnerActions: Count a teen quantity (11–19) by filling a ten-frame completely first, then placing the extras in a second frame.
Say the number as 'ten and three… thirteen' so the full ten and the extras are both visible.
Match the ten-frame picture to the written numeral (e.g. 13).
Repeat with other teen numbers, each time noticing the full ten plus a few more.
activities.intendedInsight: A teen number is not a mysterious word — it is a full ten with a few more ones, which is the beginning of place value.

activities.title: Spot and fix a miscount (optional Socratic check)
feedback: If the child misses the error, slow the demonstration down and point at the item that was skipped or double-counted.
Encourage them to name the fix ('move each one over as you count') rather than only saying 'it's wrong'.
activities.rationale: Fixing another's miscount may have mild Socratic value for articulating counting principles, but the core skill is an enacted count, so this supplements rather than replaces hands-on counting. Its efficacy is proposed, not validated.
sourceClaims: One-one plus cardinal principles must be coordinated to reliably enumerate a set; tangible moveable objects help track counted vs uncounted.
learnerActions: Watch (or listen to) a puppet or partner count a scattered pile, deliberately skipping one item or counting one twice.
Decide whether the count was right, explain what went wrong, and show how to count it correctly using a tracking strategy.
Suggest what the puppet should do differently next time (e.g. move each item aside).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to catch and explain a counting slip shows you understand why one-to-one tagging and tracking matter — not just how to recite numbers.

constraints: The core objective is an enacted count: the child must physically tag, track, and count out objects. Recognition-only tasks (choosing 'how many?' from options, judging a shown count) can assess or supplement but do not by themselves elicit the independent counting and give-N that is the point.
A labelled, already-counted set can serve as a reference example but cannot enact the count or the give-N task; use it only as a scaffold.
Give-N (count out exactly N) is a stronger check of cardinality than 'how many?' — include it, not just set-reporting.
Scattered-set tracking is a developing habit: if a child loses track, model a strategy (move each item aside) rather than reteaching counting as though the concept is absent.
Keep objects moveable and connect each count to the spoken total ('altogether') and the written numeral.

If an on-screen version is used, features like tap-to-count lockout (a counted item cannot be tapped again), a 'tidy into a line/ten-frame' helper, a drag-out give-N mode, and a persistent total badge can make the mechanism concrete — these are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms, and should not replace hands-on counting with physical objects.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The ten-frame/place-value source (NCETM early number guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; its claim is used cautiously and the uncertainty is noted in the ten-frame activity.
The conservation point in the arrangement-variation activity (rearranged set has the same total) is a reasonable curricular inference but is not directly asserted by any cited source claim.

The cited K.CC.5 standard specifies scattered configurations up to 10 and ordered arrangements (line/array/circle) up to 20. Activity 1's scattered set of up to 20 is a harder extension carried over from the original row's Tier C checkpoint, not a standard requirement.
The original prerequisite links (e.g. for point/say coordination and count-out overrun) are assessment-row metadata not reproduced as learner-facing content; retained conceptually as feedback moves.
No arithmetic or conceptual errors were found in the source counting examples (13 as a full ten plus three, 14 as 'ten and four', 17 in a line, counting out 16); these were preserved as given.

probeDeeper: How many did you get? Count them again — do you get the same?
How could you count the scattered ones so you don't lose your place?
Give me 4 more — now how many?
If you started counting the line from the other end, how many?
assess.correctAnswer: Tags each object once, keeps track of counted versus uncounted in the scattered set (moving or organising them), answers 'how many' with the last count word, and stops at exactly 13 when counting out.

errorPatterns.pattern: loses track on scattered sets — recounts or skips objects because counted and uncounted aren't separated
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT reteach counting as if the concept were missing — model a strategy: 'move each one over here as you count it', which is a tracking habit that develops with practice
errorPatterns.revealedBy: different totals on repeat counts of the scattered set; no strategy to keep place

errorPatterns.pattern: point/say coordination slip — number words come faster or slower than the pointing, so tags don't line up one-to-one
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill — slow to one touch per word, sliding each item aside; the coordination tightens with the move-it scaffold
errorPatterns.revealedBy: fingers and words out of sync, giving an over- or under-count

errorPatterns.pattern: count-out overrun — asked for exactly 13, counts past it or hands over the whole pile; doesn't use 13 as a stop signal
errorPatterns.nextMove: state the target, count into a cupped hand, and stop-and-check — 'how many do we need? tell me when to stop'; this rebuilds the last-word-as-total link
errorPatterns.revealedBy: keeps counting beyond 13 or gives all the counters

responseLevels.gap: Miscounts through skipping or double-counting, especially when scattered; cannot count out a requested quantity (keeps going past it).
responseLevels.full: Counts lines and scattered sets to 20 accurately with a tracking strategy, and counts out an exact requested quantity, stopping at the target.
responseLevels.partial: Counts a neat line to 20 accurately but loses track on scattered sets, or counts out a target only with support — the tracking strategy is not yet automatic.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 17 counters in a line — count them and tell me how many. Now here are 10 counters scattered on the table — count these. Last, here's a big pile: count out exactly 13 for me. (Watch the one-to-one tagging, whether they organise the scattered set, and whether they stop at 13.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A neat line hides what the scattered set and the count-out reveal. The line tests tagging; the scattered set tests keeping track (the child must impose order or move items); counting out exactly 13 tests holding a target while counting (cardinality in action). A child weak in one-to-one double-counts or skips especially when scattered; a child weak in cardinality counts out but doesn't stop at 13.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Solids, Liquids & Gases

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'States of matter'):** Pupils should be taught to "compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases." Non-statutory guidance: "develop simple descriptions of the states of matter (solids hold their shape; liquids form a pool not a pile; gases escape from an unsealed container)" and group/classify a variety of materials.

- **Standards — US (NGSS, honest gap):** NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to classifying the three states; the nearest is 2-PS1-1 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]', grade 2) and DCI PS1.A. State classification as a distinct topic is UK-led; the US treats it through observable-properties classification and later particle ideas (MS-PS1).

- **Operational details:** Move from naming to systematic classification by BEHAVIOUR, using three reliable tests: does it keep its own shape (solid), does it take the shape of its container and form a level surface (liquid), does it spread out to fill all the available space (gas)? Apply the tests to eight-plus everyday materials and, crucially, work the tricky cases that break naive rules: sand and other powders (they pour like a liquid but each grain is a solid that keeps its shape — a solid); steam (a gas, but the visible white cloud is actually tiny condensed water droplets, not the vapour itself); gels, foams, honey. Make the invisible-gas point concrete (air fills a bag; bubbles are gas). Keep it observational — do not yet require the particle model — but the behaviour patterns lay its groundwork.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (concrete→classifying). The child can define each state by its behaviour, sort eight or more everyday materials with a behaviour justification, and correctly resolve at least one tricky case (sand is a solid; steam is a gas) rather than sorting by appearance.
bestPractices: Classify by three behaviour tests (keeps shape / takes container shape / fills the space), not by look or feel alone.
Deliberately teach the tricky cases — sand and powders (pour but are solids), steam (gas vs visible droplets) — because they expose and correct the naive rules.
Make gases tangible: trap air in a bag, watch bubbles, feel a puff, so 'gas is real stuff' is evidenced, not asserted.
Test a liquid in different-shaped containers to show it takes the container's shape while keeping the same amount — the defining liquid behaviour.
Use consistent sorting criteria and record reasons, extending the classify-from-evidence skill from earlier grouping work.
Keep explanations observational at KS2; treat any particle talk as a light bridge, not a requirement (per DfE guidance).
keyRepresentations: A three-behaviour test chart (keeps shape / fills container / fills all space)
A same-liquid-in-different-containers demonstration (shape changes, amount stays)
Tricky-case cards: sand/powder (pours but solid), steam (gas vs droplets), honey, foam
A trapped-air bag / bubble demo making a gas observable
An eight-plus material sort with behaviour justifications
commonMisconceptions: Sorting by appearance — anything that pours (sand, salt, powder) is called a liquid, missing that each grain is a solid.
Gases are not matter / are weightless / are 'nothing', because they are usually invisible ('seeing is believing').
Believing the visible white cloud of 'steam' IS the water vapour, rather than tiny condensed droplets (the true vapour is invisible).
Thinking a liquid changes amount when it changes container shape (confusing shape with quantity).
Assuming very thick liquids (honey, gel) or very light solids (foam) can't be classified, or classifying them by feel rather than behaviour.

learn.summary: For children aged 8–9 classifying materials as solids, liquids or gases. The core objective is to sort by BEHAVIOUR rather than appearance, using three reliable tests: does it keep its own shape (solid), does it take the shape of its container and form a level surface (liquid), does it spread out to fill all available space (gas)? Learners apply these tests to eight or more everyday materials and work the tricky cases that break naive rules: sand and powders (they pour but each grain is a solid that keeps its shape), steam (a gas, but the visible white cloud is condensed water droplets, not the invisible vapour), plus gels, foams and honey. Gases are made observable and tangible so 'gas is real stuff' is evidenced, not asserted. Explanations stay observational; the particle model is a light bridge, not a requirement at this stage.

activities.title: Test the state bench: pour, seal, observe, sort
feedback: If a learner calls sand a liquid because it pours, direct attention to one grain: is that single grain hard with a fixed shape, or runny? Contrast the pouring PILE with the fixed GRAIN.
If a learner thinks water becomes 'less' or 'more' when it changes container shape, line up the same amount poured back and forth: the shape changes, the quantity does not.
If a learner sorts by feel or looks, ask them to say which of the three behaviour tests they actually observed before placing the item.
activities.rationale: Classification by behaviour is built by acting on substances and watching them respond; pouring into varied containers and observing makes the defining liquid behaviour (takes shape, keeps amount) and the sand case concrete. A hands-on bench or an interactive lets learners generate the evidence rather than being told the conclusion. A physical tray of real substances and jars serves the same purpose; a screen bench is one way to allow safe, repeatable manipulation (e.g. tilt/seal the jar, zoom to show solid grains), and a simulation is a safe way to show a gas visibly filling a container — a pre-prepared sealed demonstration works too.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'States of matter' statutory: 'compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases'; non-statutory 'solids hold their shape; liquids form a pool not a pile; gases escape from an unsealed container'.

Elementary misconceptions: sorting by appearance (powders as liquids), gas as non-matter, and the visible white 'steam' being mistaken for the water vapour rather than condensed droplets; conceptual change needs hands-on repeated observation.
learnerActions: Take each mystery substance and pour or place it into jars of different shapes; observe and record what happens.

Note which items keep the same shape in every jar (e.g. a wooden block) and which pool flat and take each jar's shape (e.g. water); then observe a gas swelling to fill a whole sealed jar (shown via a simulation/animation or a pre-prepared safe sealed demonstration — not a real coloured gas released in class), and see in the simulation that an open container would let the gas escape.
For the water, pour the same amount into several differently-shaped containers; confirm the shape changes while the amount stays the same.
Drop each tested item into a solid / liquid / gas bin and attach a short behaviour tag stating WHY (e.g. 'keeps its own shape', 'takes the jar's shape and lies flat', 'fills the whole space').

Test sand deliberately: pour it (it pours a bit like a liquid, but it heaps into a sloping pile instead of lying flat like water), then look closely at a single grain — note that each grain is hard and keeps its own shape, so classify sand as a solid because the GRAINS keep shape even though the pile pours.
activities.intendedInsight: A material's state is decided by how the material itself behaves (does it keep its own shape, take a container's shape, or fill all the space), not by whether it pours or how it looks. Sand pours but is a solid because each grain keeps its shape.

activities.title: Steam vs the white cloud
feedback: If a learner points to the white cloud as 'the gas', point out the clear gap just above the spout — that gap is the invisible vapour; the cloud further up is where it cooled into droplets.
If a learner says the cold plate 'made' new water, explain the plate cooled the vapour so it turned back into liquid droplets you can now see.
Connect to breath on a cold day: the visible mist is also tiny droplets, not the gas.
activities.rationale: The kettle cloud is a canonical tricky case that exposes the 'seeing is believing' misconception about gases. A predict-then-observe sequence forces the belief into the open before the demonstration corrects it. This activity needs a real (adult-handled) or faithfully simulated demonstration because the resolution comes from seeing the clear gap and the condensing droplets.
sourceClaims: Elementary misconceptions: sorting by appearance (powders as liquids), gas as non-matter, and the visible white 'steam' being mistaken for the water vapour rather than condensed droplets; conceptual change needs hands-on repeated observation.
learnerActions: With an adult handling the kettle safely, watch a boiling kettle and look for the small CLEAR gap right at the spout before the white cloud begins.
Before any reveal, predict which part is the actual gas (the real steam) and explain why.
Watch an adult hold a cold plate or spoon in the plume: observe droplets of liquid water forming on it.
State in your own words: the invisible part near the spout is the gas (water vapour); the white cloud higher up is tiny liquid droplets that have cooled and condensed.
activities.intendedInsight: True water vapour (steam) is an invisible gas; the visible white cloud above a kettle is tiny condensed liquid droplets, not the gas itself. 'I can see it, so that's the gas' is the belief to correct.

activities.title: Gas is real stuff
feedback: If a learner says a sealed 'empty' bottle contains nothing, have them squeeze it and feel the trapped air push back.

If a learner says gas weighs nothing, note the invisibility is why it feels that way; weighing a ball pumped up hard and then the same ball when soft, on a sensitive balance, can provide counter-evidence (a balloon blown up by mouth usually shows no measurable difference).
activities.rationale: Because gases are usually invisible, learners often treat them as 'nothing' or weightless. Making gas tangible through trapped air and bubbles provides direct evidence that gas is matter. Note: claims about the exact mass of air (e.g. a specific grams-per-litre figure) come from a source not marked verified and are not asserted here as a precise value.
sourceClaims: Elementary misconceptions: sorting by appearance (powders as liquids), gas as non-matter, and the visible white 'steam' being mistaken for the water vapour rather than condensed droplets; conceptual change needs hands-on repeated observation.
learnerActions: Trap air by sealing a bag or squeezing a capped bottle; feel the resistance and note the gas takes up space.
Blow bubbles or feel a puff of air on your hand to sense that the invisible gas is really there.

Compare a ball pumped up hard (e.g. a football inflated with a pump) with the same ball when soft. If a sensitive balance is available, weigh it both ways: the hard-pumped ball should weigh slightly more because extra air has been squeezed in. Discuss whether the gas has mass. (A balloon blown up by mouth is not a good test: the air inside is barely squeezed, so a classroom balance will show little or no difference.)
Answer: can you see the air in this room? Is it still a gas even though it's invisible?
activities.intendedInsight: Gases are real matter: they take up space and have mass, even though they are usually invisible. An 'empty' sealed bottle is actually full of air.

activities.title: Classify and check: the eight-plus material sort
feedback: If a learner is stuck on honey because it is 'in between', ask whether it keeps its own shape or slowly takes the jar's shape and forms a level surface over time (liquid behaviour).
If a learner classifies foam by how light it feels, redirect to the behaviour test: does it keep its own shape?
A recognition-only sort can show the final answer; ask the learner to state the behavioural evidence as well, so you can check the reasoning and not just the conclusion.
activities.rationale: Consolidating classification across many materials, including borderline cases, extends the classify-from-evidence skill and tests whether behaviour reasoning has replaced appearance reasoning. Sorting/matching tasks check the conclusion; pairing each choice with a stated behaviour reason keeps the focus on reasoning. This can be done with physical materials, picture cards, or an interactive sort.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'States of matter' statutory: 'compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases'; non-statutory 'solids hold their shape; liquids form a pool not a pile; gases escape from an unsealed container'.
learnerActions: Sort at least eight everyday materials into solid, liquid or gas, writing the behaviour reason for each.

Include genuinely tricky items — honey, jelly/gel, toothpaste, a solid foam such as a sponge — and decide each by behaviour rather than by how thick or light it feels; if an item shows both solid-like and liquid-like behaviour (e.g. toothpaste or shaving foam), record that it is a tricky mixture and describe what it does.
For each item answer 'which behaviour proves it?' by matching it to one of the three tests.
Explain aloud why sand is a solid and why the kettle cloud is not the gas.
activities.intendedInsight: Consistent behaviour-based criteria help classify awkward materials: very thick liquids (honey) and very light solids (solid foams such as a sponge or polystyrene) are judged by whether they keep their own shape, take a container's shape, or fill the space. Some materials, such as shaving foam, toothpaste or jelly, are mixtures that show some solid-like and some liquid-like behaviour, so it is fine to say they do not fit neatly.

constraints: Keep explanations observational at this age; do not require the particle model. Behaviour patterns lay its groundwork but particle talk should be a light bridge only (per DfE non-statutory guidance).
Any activity involving a boiling kettle or hot steam must be adult-handled; children observe only.
When showing a gas visibly filling a container, use a simulation/animation or an already-safe sealed gas; do not release coloured or hazardous gases around children.

A tap-to-reveal chart or annotated image can consolidate the three tests and label examples, but being fixed it cannot let the learner pour, seal or observe behaviour; use it as a scaffold alongside, not instead of, investigation of the tricky cases.

Quiz/sorting formats assess whether the learner reaches the right classification but do not by themselves elicit the behavioural evidence; pair them with a 'which behaviour proves it?' step and use them to check, not replace, hands-on observation.

Do not assert a precise mass-per-litre value for air to learners; the supporting source for that figure is not marked verified. The qualitative point (gas has mass and takes up space) is well supported by the tangible demonstrations.
Sand being a solid depends on recognising each grain keeps its shape; ensure learners look at an individual grain, not just the pouring pile.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claim that '~1 litre of air ≈ 1 g' comes from a source marked verified:false. It is not stated as a precise fact in the learner activities; only the qualitative 'gas has mass and takes up space' is used. Reviewers should confirm any numeric figure before presenting it.

The original row framed a screen bench as uniquely able to deliver the evidence and claimed 3D and dialogue formats add little; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to format-neutral guidance (real materials, cards, or interactives can all work, each with trade-offs).

The NGSS gap noted in pedagogy (no dedicated US performance expectation for three-state classification; nearest is 2-PS1-1 / PS1.A, with particle ideas at MS-PS1) is an honest curriculum-coverage limitation, retained here for reviewer awareness.

The coloured-gas-filling example was re-scoped to a simulation/animation or a pre-prepared safe sealed demonstration because releasing a real coloured gas around young children is unsafe; the 'escapes an open container' contrast is framed as the simulated illustration, since a sealed demo cannot show escape. The conceptual point (a gas expands to fill its container) is unchanged.

assess.poeTask: With the teacher handling a kettle safely, boil it and point out the small CLEAR gap right at the spout before the white cloud begins. Ask the child to PREDICT which part is the actual gas (the steam) and WHY, before revealing. Most point at the white cloud. Then hold a cold plate in the plume: droplets form, showing the 'gas' turning back to liquid water. The pre-reveal reasoning is diagnostic — 'I can see it so that's the gas' exposes the belief that gases are visible.
probeDeeper: One grain of sand under a magnifier — is that grain hard, or runny?
Can you see the air in this room? Is it still a gas even though it's invisible?
Is jelly a solid or a liquid? What about honey, or toothpaste?
Exactly where is the steam above the kettle — the clear bit near the spout, or the cloudy bit higher up?
assess.correctAnswer: Sand is a SOLID: it's made of many tiny solid grains, each keeping its shape; the pile pours only because the grains slide over one another. The white cloud above a kettle is NOT the gas — true steam (water vapour) is invisible; the white cloud is tiny liquid droplets that have condensed as the vapour cooled.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Pours means liquid' — classifies powders and grains as liquids because they flow.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Examine one grain under a magnifier — a hard solid with a fixed shape; contrast the pouring PILE with the fixed GRAIN.
errorPatterns.distractor: Sand is a liquid because it pours and takes the shape of the bucket.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls sand, sugar or salt a liquid.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The visible white cloud is the gas' — mistakes condensed droplets for the vapour; believes you can see a gas.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Note the clear gap just above the spout (that's the invisible vapour); the white cloud further up is where it has cooled into tiny liquid droplets.
errorPatterns.distractor: The white cloud above the kettle is the gas — that's what steam looks like.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points at the kettle plume (or breath on a cold day) as 'the gas'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gas is not matter — an 'empty' bottle has nothing in it; a gas weighs nothing and isn't a real substance.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fan the air, squeeze a sealed bottle, weigh an inflated vs deflated ball — gases are real matter that take up space and have mass.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a gas isn't a material, or that a sealed 'empty' bottle contains nothing.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by a single surface behaviour (pours = liquid, visible = gas); gets the tricky cases wrong; denies gases are matter.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by what the material IS, resolving the tricky cases — sand is solid grains, the kettle cloud is condensed droplets not the invisible gas — and treats gases as real matter.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts clear-cut solids, liquids and gases correctly and defines them by behaviour, but mishandles the tricky cases (sand, steam) using surface appearance.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Sand pours out of a bucket just like water does. Is sand a solid, a liquid, or something in between — and why?' Then: 'Now think about the white cloud you see above a boiling kettle. Is that cloud the gas (the steam itself), or is it something else?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Sand and the kettle-cloud are the canonical tricky cases. A child reasoning from surface behaviour ('it pours, so liquid'; 'I can see it, so that's the gas') gets both wrong; a child reasoning from what the material IS (solid grains; invisible vapour) gets both right. Tier-2 forces that reasoning into the open.
