pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Conduction, convection, and radiation

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum):** KS3 Physics, 'Energy: Energy changes and transfers' — statutory wording: 'Heating and thermal equilibrium: temperature difference between 2 objects leading to energy transfer from the hotter to the cooler one, through contact (conduction) or radiation; such transfers tending to reduce the temperature difference; use of insulators' (verified by fetch). NOTE — the KS3 statutory statement names ONLY conduction and radiation; CONVECTION is not named in this Energy statement, though it is conventionally taught and is supported by the KS3 'Matter / Energy in matter' content ('changes with temperature in motion and spacing of particles').

- **Standards — US National (NGSS):** MS-PS3 Energy — MS-PS3-3 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS3-3]' (insulated box / solar cooker / Styrofoam cup), underpinned by DCI PS3.A 'Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles of matter' and PS3.B 'Energy is spontaneously transferred out of hotter regions or objects and into colder ones' (verified by fetch). Both tiers place this content at lower-secondary / middle school and qualitative; quantitative heat-transfer is deferred (KS4 / HS).

- **Operational details:** This topic asks them to use particles to EXPLAIN three distinct mechanisms qualitatively — no equations yet. The organising idea is that a TEMPERATURE DIFFERENCE drives energy from hotter to cooler until the difference is gone (thermal equilibrium), and the three mechanisms are three different WAYS that happens: conduction (energy passed along by vibrating/colliding particles, fastest in metals via free electrons — the material does NOT move), convection (the heated FLUID itself becomes less dense, rises, and circulates — the material moves in a loop), and radiation (infrared emitted across empty space, needing no particles at all). The single most important teaching move is to make the child say WHAT is moving in each case (energy along stationary particles vs. the bulk fluid vs. an EM wave), because almost every misconception comes from blurring those. Pair each mechanism with its canonical particle picture and a real example, and tie rate to temperature difference.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional / early-formal, ~12–13). The child already has the particle model and the energy stores/pathways framework (prereqs).
bestPractices: Frame everything under ONE rule first — energy moves from hotter to cooler until the temperature difference disappears (thermal equilibrium) — then present the three mechanisms as three different ways that rule is carried out.

For EACH mechanism, make the child state explicitly WHAT moves: conduction = energy passed along by particles that stay put; convection = the heated fluid itself physically circulates; radiation = an infrared wave crosses a gap with no particles needed. This single distinction pre-empts most errors.

Use particle diagrams as the backbone: vibrating, fixed particles handing energy to neighbours (conduction, with free electrons drawn in metals to explain why metals are fast); a convection loop showing warmed fluid expanding, rising, cooling, sinking; radiation as wavy IR arrows across empty space.

Confront the 'cold flows in' idea head-on with the hotter-to-cooler rule: cold is not a substance that travels; a cold object simply gains energy and the warm one loses it. Use a draught / ice example and ask 'is cold coming in, or is warmth leaving?'

Use the metal-vs-wood 'feel' demonstration: two objects at the SAME room temperature feel different because metal conducts energy away from your warm hand faster — separating temperature from rate of conduction, and feeling from temperature.

Teach radiation as universal: ALL objects emit and absorb infrared (not just hot or 'dangerous' things); use thermal-imaging examples and the matt-black-vs-shiny surface result (dark, dull surfaces are better emitters and absorbers).

Link rate to temperature difference quantitatively-in-words: a bigger temperature difference means a faster transfer, and the rate falls as the difference shrinks — connect to why a hot drink cools fast at first then slowly.

Sort everyday examples by mechanism and by 'what moves' (radiator warms a room mostly by convection despite its name; the Sun reaches us by radiation through empty space; a metal spoon in soup by conduction) to force application of the model.
keyRepresentations: Particle diagram of conduction — a row of fixed, vibrating particles passing energy along to neighbours; free electrons added for metals to show why metals conduct fastest.

Convection-current loop — a cross-section (beaker or room) with arrows showing warmed fluid expanding, becoming less dense, rising, cooling and sinking; the MATERIAL circulates, the heat does not 'pass through' stationary fluid.
Infrared radiation arrows across a gap / vacuum — wavy IR emitted and absorbed with no medium; thermal-imaging (false-colour) photos.
The metal-vs-wood 'same temperature, different feel' demo — separating temperature from rate of conduction and from sensation.
Leslie cube / surface-colour comparison — matt black vs shiny silver faces emitting/absorbing IR at different rates.
A temperature-difference → rate dial: bigger difference = faster transfer; the cooling curve that steepens with a larger gap and flattens as equilibrium nears.
commonMisconceptions: 'Cold flows / cold gets in' — treating cold as a substance that travels. Energy only ever moves from hotter to cooler; a cold object gains energy, it does not emit cold.
'Heat rises' — over-generalised. It is warmed FLUID (less dense air/water) that rises in convection; heat itself has no inherent upward direction, and conduction/radiation are not 'up'.
Confusing temperature with heat / thermal energy — temperature measures average particle kinetic energy; a large warm object can hold more thermal energy than a small hot one.
'Metal is colder than wood' — objects in the same room are at the same temperature; metal merely conducts energy away from the hand faster, so it FEELS colder.
'Convection is heat moving through the liquid/gas' — in convection the fluid itself physically circulates; the energy is carried by moving matter, not passed through stationary matter.
'Radiation means nuclear / is only from very hot or dangerous things' — all objects emit and absorb infrared radiation at all times; it needs no medium and is not inherently harmful.
'Wool / a blanket / a coat gives out heat or warms things up' — insulators slow energy transfer; they do not generate heat (a blanket round ice keeps it cold).
Believing the rate of transfer is constant — it depends on the temperature difference, so a hot object cools quickly at first and ever more slowly as it nears equilibrium.
Assuming metals are the only conductors / that 'good conductor' and 'gets hot easily' are the same — conduction is about how fast energy passes through, not how hot a thing gets.

learn.summary: Learners aged 12–13 explain conduction, convection and radiation qualitatively using the particle model, organised under one rule: a temperature difference drives energy from hotter to cooler until the difference disappears (thermal equilibrium). The central move is making the learner state explicitly WHAT moves in each case — energy handed along particles that vibrate about fixed positions (conduction), the bulk fluid physically circulating (convection), and an infrared wave that needs no medium and can cross even a vacuum (radiation) — and tying the rate of transfer to the size of the temperature difference. Activities span an interactive particle sandbox, a sorting/assessment check, a reference triptych, a Socratic misconception dialogue, and a spatial loop view, each with a distinct purpose.

activities.title: Particle-level heat sandbox: what is moving in each mechanism?
feedback: If the learner says 'the heat travels up through the water', point to the dyed blob of actual water rising and ask what is moving — the matter or the heat.

When the learner predicts the vacuum will stop radiation, run the toggle: the IR arrows still cross, so this mechanism needs no particles (the perfect vacuum is an idealised model of 'no medium', not an achievable classroom condition).

If the learner calls metal 'colder', show the feel panel with metal and wood at equal temperature, both cooler than the hand, and reframe: the metal conducts energy away from the hand faster, so the hand cools faster.
Prompt the learner to connect the cooling curve that is steep at first and then flattens to a hot drink cooling fast at first and slowly later as the temperature gap shrinks.
On the Leslie cube / surface comparison, reinforce that dull, dark (matt-black) surfaces are better emitters and absorbers of infrared than shiny ones.
activities.rationale: The whole difficulty of this three-mechanism comparison is 'what is moving?'. Live particle motion lets a learner set a temperature difference, watch the rate respond, and see the key dissociations (stationary particles passing energy vs. circulating fluid vs. a wave crossing a vacuum) directly rather than being told. A fixed diagram can name these but cannot be manipulated to show the motion or the rate responding, so dynamic manipulation is proposed here for that specific affordance; efficacy is not independently tested.
sourceClaims: Persistent heat-transfer misconceptions — 'cold flows in', conflating heat with temperature, 'metal is colder than wood', insulators 'giving out' heat, and treating convection as heat passing through stationary fluid — are documented and are best addressed by making explicit what moves in each mechanism and applying the hotter-to-cooler principle.
learnerActions: In a conduction mode, heat one end of a bar of fixed, jiggling particles and watch vibration energy pass along to neighbours; toggle 'metal' to add free electrons that carry energy far faster and compare how quickly the far end of a metal vs wooden bar warms.

In a convection mode, heat the bottom of a beaker or room of free fluid particles; follow a dyed blob or arrows as warmed fluid expands (its particles move further apart), becomes less dense and rises, then cools at the top, becomes denser and sinks, tracing a visible loop — then state in words whether the fluid itself moves or the heat passes through still fluid.

In a radiation mode, emit infrared arrows from a hot object across a gap, then use a 'remove the air / vacuum' toggle (an idealised model) and check whether the target still warms; compare a matt-black vs shiny target (the same surface types compared on a Leslie cube, which is usually used to show emission) and see that the matt-black target absorbs infrared faster.
Move one shared 'temperature difference' slider across all three modes and describe how the transfer rate changes as the gap widens and as the two sides drift toward equilibrium.

Use a side 'feel' panel: when metal and wood are at the SAME temperature and both are cooler than the hand, the hand loses warmth faster to the metal — put into words how sensation, temperature and rate differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Each mechanism is a different way the hotter-to-cooler rule is carried out, distinguished by what actually moves: energy along stationary particles, the circulating bulk fluid, or an EM wave needing no medium; transfer rate grows with the temperature difference and falls toward equilibrium.

activities.title: Sort and challenge: which mechanism, and what moves?
feedback: For 'cold coming in', reinforce that cold is not a substance that travels; the warmer food loses energy to the colder freezer interior (and energy from the warmer room leaks into the freezer, not out of it).

For the metal-vs-wood item, use the approximately equal thermometer readings to restate that both are at about the same room temperature, cooler than the hand, and metal simply conducts energy from the hand faster, so it feels colder.
If the radiator is sorted as conduction by its name, note it warms a room mostly by convection despite the name.
activities.rationale: Once the mechanisms are taught, sorting by mechanism and by 'what moves', the predict-and-measure thermometer check, and targeted items on the named misconceptions make a well-defined check that targets errors directly. This is a consolidation/assessment step, not a first encounter; a sort can check classification but recognition-style items do not by themselves elicit independent construction of explanations.
sourceClaims: Persistent heat-transfer misconceptions — 'cold flows in', conflating heat with temperature, 'metal is colder than wood', insulators 'giving out' heat, and treating convection as heat passing through stationary fluid — are documented and are best addressed by making explicit what moves in each mechanism and applying the hotter-to-cooler principle.
learnerActions: Drag everyday examples into conduction / convection / radiation: metal spoon in soup, Sun warming skin, hot-air balloon, radiator warming a room, sea breeze — and for each state what is moving.

Predict what a thermometer (or thermal strip) reads on a metal spoon and a wooden spoon that have sat in the same room long enough to reach room temperature, then measure to check: the readings should be approximately the same, within measurement error.
Answer: 'Food in a freezer gets colder — is cold going into the food, or is energy leaving the food?' and justify using the hotter-to-cooler rule.
Explain why the metal spoon feels colder than the wooden one even though the measurements show approximately equal temperatures (both cooler than your hand).
Complete: 'energy travels from ___ to ___ until the temperature difference is ___'.
Order a cooling drink's transfer rate from fast to slow as the temperature gap shrinks.
activities.intendedInsight: The mechanism distinctions and the hotter-to-cooler rule can be applied to novel everyday cases; approximately equal readings show both spoons are at about the same (room) temperature, and the common cold-flows / heat-rises / metal-is-colder errors can be caught and corrected.

activities.title: Reference triptych: three mechanisms on tap
feedback: Where a learner is unsure which mechanism a situation uses, direct them back to the 'what moves' label for that panel.
Reinforce that all objects emit and absorb infrared, and that matt-black surfaces are better emitters and absorbers than shiny ones.
activities.rationale: A static labelled triptych names the mechanisms and surfaces facts and examples, which is useful for vocabulary and reference. It cannot be manipulated to show particles passing energy, fluid circulating, or rate responding, so it supports rather than carries the core 'what moves' insight and is best paired with the sandbox.
learnerActions: Open three labelled panels (conduction / convection / radiation) and tap a region in each to reveal 'what moves' and a real example.
Use a flap that contrasts shiny vs matt surfaces (as on a Leslie cube) for emitting and absorbing infrared.
Return to this glossary while working in the sandbox to check a term or example.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary, canonical pictures and real examples for each mechanism can be recalled and used as a reference layer.

activities.title: Thermal-imaging engineer: predict and justify
feedback: When the learner attributes feeling to the object's temperature, ask them to separate the object's temperature from the rate and direction energy leaves or enters the hand.

For the hot-railing counterexample, point out the railing is now hotter than the hand, so energy flows railing→hand quickly through the good conductor — fast conduction explains 'feels hot' just as it explained 'feels cold' when the metal was cooler than the hand.
When 'heat rises' appears, prompt for density: the heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler denser fluid sinks.
If the learner says the duvet 'gives out heat', reframe: insulators only slow energy transfer; a duvet around ice keeps it cold.
activities.rationale: Socratic dialogue is well suited to eliciting and challenging misconceptions by asking the learner to predict and justify. The payoff in this topic is largely visual and dynamic, so dialogue complements the sandbox as a misconception-eliciting warm-up or debrief rather than conveying the motion itself.
sourceClaims: Persistent heat-transfer misconceptions — 'cold flows in', conflating heat with temperature, 'metal is colder than wood', insulators 'giving out' heat, and treating convection as heat passing through stationary fluid — are documented and are best addressed by making explicit what moves in each mechanism and applying the hotter-to-cooler principle.
learnerActions: Respond to an in-role engineer who asks for predictions and reasons: 'Will the vacuum stop the heat? Why?', 'Why does the metal feel colder?', 'You said cold gets in — what is actually moving?'

Tackle the engineer's counterexample: on a hot day a metal railing (hotter than your hand) feels HOT, not cold — explain why the same good conductor now feels hot, separating the object's temperature from the DIRECTION energy flows.
State and defend a prediction, then revise the explanation in terms of what moves after seeing or reasoning through the outcome.
Trace how conduction, convection and radiation each play a part in a radiator heating a room.
Explain why a duvet keeps you warm even though it produces no heat of its own.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and defending predictions out loud surfaces the stubborn errors (cold flows in, metal is colder, radiation needs a medium, insulators give out heat) so they can be reframed around what actually moves and in which direction energy flows.

activities.title: Spatial convection loop and radiant spread
feedback: If orientation is confusing, return to the 2D cross-section where the loop direction is clearer.
Reinforce that in convection the circulating fluid carries the energy with it; this is much faster than energy passing slowly through still fluid by conduction.
activities.rationale: A spatial view adds a little for the convection loop and radiant spread, which are genuinely three-dimensional. The canonical classroom representations are 2D cross-sections and particle rows, which convey the core 'what moves' idea clearly, so the spatial version is an optional enrichment rather than the primary vehicle.
learnerActions: Explore a room-scale convection loop you can orbit, following warmed, less-dense fluid rising and cooler fluid sinking.
Watch radiant infrared spreading outward from a source through space.
Compare this spatial view with the 2D cross-section and describe what each makes clearer.
activities.intendedInsight: Convection has a genuinely spatial circulating loop and radiation spreads outward in space; seeing this at room scale can make the circulation and spread feel natural.

constraints: KS3 (DfE) statutory Energy wording names only conduction and radiation; convection is conventionally taught and is supported by the KS3 Matter / Energy in matter content on particle motion and spacing changing with temperature — present convection as curriculum-supported but note it is not in the Energy statement.
Keep the treatment qualitative with no equations; quantitative heat-transfer is deferred to KS4 / HS. Tie rate to temperature difference in words, not formulae.
Prerequisites: learners should already have the particle model and the energy stores/pathways framework.

The sorting/quiz check is a consolidation and recognition step; it can check classification but does not by itself elicit independent construction of explanations, so pair it with the sandbox and the dialogue where learners state reasoning in their own words.
The reference triptych is a glossary/scaffold: it names mechanisms and examples but cannot show motion or rate response, so it should not be the first or only encounter.
Insulators slow energy transfer and do not generate heat (a blanket or duvet around ice keeps it cold); keep this explicit when discussing coats, wool and duvets.
Radiation is universal and not inherently nuclear or harmful: all objects emit and absorb infrared at all times.

The 'remove the air / vacuum' toggle and the metal-feels-colder 'feel' panel are idealised models: a real classroom cannot make a perfect vacuum, and metal only feels colder when it is cooler than the hand (a hotter-than-hand metal surface feels hot) — keep these qualifications visible.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The IOP Spark source backing the misconception claims is marked verified:false in the row, and is the only backing for the misconception-targeting rationale; treat the efficacy framing (including the sourceClaims attached to activities 1, 2 and 4) as informed but not independently confirmed here.

Self-audit of science content: energy transfers from hotter to cooler (not 'cold flowing in'); in convection the less-dense heated fluid rises and carries energy (heat has no inherent upward direction); metal feels colder than wood at equal temperature because it conducts energy from the hand faster, not because it is a 'cold material', and when the metal is hotter than the hand it feels hot for the same fast-conduction reason.

Claims that a static image or 3D view 'cannot teach' / 'adds nothing' were rewritten as narrowly scoped affordance statements: a fixed diagram can teach vocabulary and canonical pictures but cannot be manipulated to show motion or rate response; a spatial view aids the genuinely 3D loop/spread but is not required.
The 'remove the air / vacuum' toggle is an idealised model; present it as demonstrating that no medium is needed, not as a literal achievable classroom vacuum.

The hot-railing counterexample, the duvet/insulator probe, the Leslie cube surface comparison, and the predict-then-measure thermometer reveal were drawn from the source assessment/representations into the activities to preserve those concrete examples; whether to use the hot-railing as core or extension is left to the teacher for this Tier B cohort.

assess.poeTask: Put out a metal spoon and a wooden spoon that have shared the same room. Ask the child to predict what a thermometer (or thermal strip) will read on each — different or the same — AND why. The 'metal is colder' child predicts a lower reading on the metal; the conduction child predicts equal readings. Then measure both to reveal they are identical.
probeDeeper: Predict the thermometer reading on each spoon before you measure. What do you expect, and why?
Counterexample: on a hot day (hotter than your body) a metal railing feels HOT, not cold. Why does the same 'good conductor' now feel hot?
Why does a duvet keep you warm if it doesn't produce any heat itself?
A radiator heats a room. Trace how conduction, convection and radiation each play a part.
assess.correctAnswer: No — both are at the same room temperature. The metal feels colder because it's a good conductor: it conducts heat away from your warm hand quickly, so your hand cools fast and feels the loss. Wood is a poor conductor, so it draws heat from your hand slowly and feels warmer. Feeling is about the RATE heat leaves your hand, not the object's temperature.

errorPatterns.pattern: Metal is naturally colder than wood, or metal 'holds/attracts cold' ('metal is a cold material').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Measure both with a thermometer — same temperature; reframe the feeling as heat leaving the hand fast through a good conductor.
errorPatterns.distractor: The metal spoon really is colder than the wooden one, because metal is a cold material.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the two objects are at different temperatures, or that metal contains cold.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cold flows INTO the hand from the metal ('the cold moves into you') — cold as a transferred substance.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Only energy (heat) moves, always hot→cold; 'cold' isn't a thing that flows — your hand loses heat to the metal.
errorPatterns.distractor: The cold flows out of the metal and into your hand, which is why it feels cold.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes cold travelling into the hand rather than heat leaving it.

errorPatterns.pattern: In convection, heat itself rises ('heat rises') rather than hot fluid rising because it's less dense.
errorPatterns.nextMove: The heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler denser fluid sinks — it's the fluid that moves, carrying energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains a convection current as 'heat goes up', with no mention of density or fluid movement.

responseLevels.gap: Says the spoons are at different temperatures, or that cold flows into the hand; explains convection as 'heat rises' with no density.
responseLevels.full: Explains that feeling depends on the RATE heat leaves the hand (conduction), that only heat (not cold) is transferred hot→cold, convection as less-dense heated fluid rising, and that rate rises with temperature difference; handles the hot-railing counterexample.
responseLevels.partial: Explains metal conducts heat faster but still slips into 'cold flowing' language, or explains convection without density, or can't handle the hot-day counterexample.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have sat in the same room all day. The metal one feels colder to your hand. Are they actually at different temperatures? Explain why the metal feels colder even though both have been in the same room.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks metal is 'naturally colder' or 'holds cold' answers differently from one who explains the conduction rate from the hand. The reason tier separates 'metal is colder / attracts cold' from 'metal conducts heat away from my hand faster'.

sources.claim: KS3 Physics 'Energy: Energy changes and transfers' statutory wording covers heating and thermal equilibrium, energy transfer from hotter to cooler by contact (conduction) or radiation, transfers reducing the temperature difference, and use of insulators; convection is NOT explicitly named in this Energy statement (the particle-motion/spacing-with-temperature content sits under KS3 'Matter / Energy in matter').

sources.claim: NGSS MS-PS3-3 asks students [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS3-3] minimizes or maximizes thermal energy transfer; DCI PS3.A states temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles of matter, and PS3.B states energy is spontaneously transferred out of hotter regions into colder ones.

sources.claim: Persistent heat-transfer misconceptions — 'cold flows in', conflating heat with temperature, 'metal is colder than wood', insulators 'giving out' heat, and treating convection as heat passing through stationary fluid — are documented and are best addressed by making explicit what moves in each mechanism and applying the hotter-to-cooler principle.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Nutrient Transport in Animals

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y6 'Animals, including humans'):** "describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans".

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE at this band):** transport by the circulatory subsystem is treated at MS-LS1-3 (body as interacting subsystems); no US elementary PE. Treat as UK-led.

- **Operational details:** This topic JOINS two systems the child has met separately: digestion (which breaks food into nutrients) and circulation (which carries them). The organising idea is a DELIVERY NETWORK: food is digested → nutrients (and water) are absorbed into the blood at the small intestine → the heart pumps blood through vessels → nutrients and water (and oxygen) are delivered to every cell in the body, and waste is carried away. The key conceptual move is that the blood is a TRANSPORT system connecting digestion to the whole body — nutrients don't just 'stay in the gut', they travel in the blood to where they're needed. Keep it at whole-system level (absorb→carry→deliver); capillary-level diffusion detail is KS3.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional, integrative). A Y6 child can describe each system alone; the target here is INTEGRATING them — tracing a nutrient from food, into the blood, and out to a working cell — which is the transitional, systems-thinking step.
bestPractices: Explicitly CONNECT the digestive and circulatory systems the child learned separately — this topic's whole value is the integration, so teach the hand-off at the small intestine.
Trace a concrete journey (a nutrient from a meal to a working cell) rather than describing transport abstractly, so the delivery network is followed step by step.
Stress that nutrients and water are ABSORBED INTO THE BLOOD and carried onward, correcting the idea that they stay in the gut.
Include water and oxygen as co-passengers and waste as the return cargo, so blood is understood as a two-way transport system.
Keep it whole-system (absorb→carry→deliver); defer capillary diffusion and active transport to KS3.
Use the correct vocabulary (blood vessels, artery/vein, nutrient, absorb) consolidated from the linked topics.
keyRepresentations: A linked digestive+circulatory diagram connected at the small intestine
A 'follow the nutrient' journey path from food → gut → blood → body cell
A close-up of nutrients/water crossing the intestine wall into a blood vessel
A whole-body delivery-network schematic (heart pumps, vessels branch, cells receive)
A two-way cargo diagram (nutrients/water/oxygen out, waste back)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking nutrients stay in the stomach or gut, rather than being absorbed into the blood and delivered around the body.
Treating digestion and circulation as unrelated systems, missing that circulation delivers what digestion releases.
Believing blood only carries oxygen, overlooking nutrients and water as cargo.
Assuming food 'becomes energy' directly in the gut, skipping the transport of nutrients to cells that then use them.
Thinking transport is one-way (delivery only), missing that blood also carries waste away from cells.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11 (UK DfE Y6 'Animals, including humans', statutory requirement to 'describe the ways in which nutrients and water are transported within animals, including humans'): the whole value of this topic is INTEGRATING two systems the child has met separately — digestion (breaks food into nutrients) and circulation (carries them). The organising idea is a delivery network: food is digested → nutrients and most water are absorbed into the blood at the small-intestine wall (the large intestine absorbs some more water) → the heart pumps blood through vessels → nutrients, water and oxygen are delivered to every cell, and waste is carried away. The key conceptual move is that nutrients do not stay in the gut — they travel in the blood to where they are needed. Keep it at whole-system level (absorb→carry→deliver); capillary diffusion and active transport are KS3.

activities.title: Follow one nutrient from a meal to a working cell
feedback: If a learner says food travels through tubes straight to the leg muscle, point to the small-intestine wall: nutrients are absorbed INTO the blood there; the blood, not the gut, delivers them to cells.
If a learner places absorption in the stomach, clarify that most absorption happens in the small intestine (its folded, villi-covered surface is huge); the stomach mainly digests.
If a learner treats the two systems as unconnected, highlight the handover point at the intestine wall: digestion prepares soluble nutrients, circulation distributes them.
If a learner thinks blood only carries oxygen, remind them nutrients and water are also cargo, and waste is the return load.
activities.rationale: Tracing one concrete journey step by step makes the absorb→carry→deliver network followable rather than abstract, and foregrounds the hand-off at the small intestine that is the actual integration target for this Tier B transitional checkpoint.
sourceClaims: For KS2: nutrients and water absorbed from digested food enter the blood and are carried by the circulatory system to cells throughout the body, linking the digestive and circulatory systems.
learnerActions: Pick a mouthful of food and trace what happens to it as it is digested along the gut.
At the small-intestine wall, identify the pivotal moment: the nutrient crosses OUT of the gut tube and INTO a blood vessel (absorption).
Follow the nutrient as the heart pumps blood carrying it through the vessels out to a working muscle cell (e.g. a leg muscle) that grabs and uses it.
Note the co-passengers — water and oxygen riding along in the blood too — and the waste picked up for the return trip, so blood is understood as two-way transport.
Name each hand-off aloud or in writing: digested in the gut → absorbed into blood at the small intestine → carried by the circulatory system → delivered to the cell.
activities.intendedInsight: The digestive and circulatory systems the child learned separately are one connected delivery network: the food you eat is absorbed into the blood and travels to every cell in your body.

activities.title: Trace the journey on a body outline
feedback: If the traced line skips from gut straight to muscle, ask where the nutrient entered the blood — the path must cross the small-intestine wall into a vessel first.
If no return path is drawn, prompt: what happens to the waste the cell produces? Blood carries it away too.
activities.rationale: Constructing and verbalising the route (rather than selecting from options) elicits independent explanation and surfaces whether the learner can locate the absorption hand-off; recognition tasks alone do not elicit this production.
sourceClaims: For KS2: nutrients and water absorbed from digested food enter the blood and are carried by the circulatory system to cells throughout the body, linking the digestive and circulatory systems.
learnerActions: On a body outline, draw a meal in the gut and a target muscle (e.g. in the leg or toes).
Use a finger or a drawn/coloured line to trace the path from the drawn meal, through the gut, across the small-intestine wall into a blood vessel, through the pumping heart, and out to the muscle.
Narrate each hand-off between systems as you go ('here it's absorbed into the blood', 'here the heart pumps it on', 'here the cell uses it').
Add arrows showing waste returning from the cell back into the blood to show two-way transport.
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing and narrating the whole path on a body makes the delivery network a route the learner can reconstruct and explain, not just recognise.

activities.title: Explain the diagnostic 'how do nutrients reach a leg muscle?' question
feedback: A complete explanation says: digested nutrients are absorbed through the small-intestine wall into the blood; the circulatory system then carries the dissolved nutrients to every cell, including the leg muscle. The gut absorbs, the blood transports — they work together.
If the learner describes food reaching the leg through pipes with no absorption into blood, reteach the hand-off at the small intestine explicitly.
If the learner is vague about where absorption happens, point to the small intestine and its villi/surface area; the stomach mainly digests.

A vague answer that knows blood carries nutrients but cannot say where absorption happens or how the systems connect needs the absorption hand-off made explicit before it counts as a full explanation.
activities.rationale: A two-tier question that contrasts a tube-only story with the absorption-into-blood route discriminates genuine systems integration from surface recall and directly targets the known misconceptions.
learnerActions: Consider: after you digest your dinner, nutrients need to reach a muscle in your leg. A student says the food just travels down through your intestines and straight into the leg.
Explain how the nutrients actually get from gut to leg muscle: what carries them, and where do they cross over?

Answer the probing follow-ups: At which organ do nutrients pass out of the gut into the blood? Why does it help that the small intestine has a huge, folded inner surface? If the circulatory system stopped, why would a leg muscle starve even though there's food in the gut? How do the digestive and circulatory systems depend on each other to nourish a cell?
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who understands transport routes nutrients via absorption into the blood; one without it imagines food travelling bodily through the gut to its destination, with no role for blood.

constraints: Keep it whole-system (absorb→carry→deliver); defer capillary-level diffusion and active transport to KS3.
Use correct vocabulary consolidated from the linked topics: blood vessels, artery/vein, nutrient, absorb.

Address the core misconceptions directly: nutrients do not stay in the stomach/gut; blood carries nutrients and water (not just oxygen); food does not 'become energy' in the gut — nutrients are transported to cells that then use them; transport is two-way (waste returns).

An ordering/matching/multiple-choice check can consolidate the integrated pathway and is a useful assessment, but recognition-only responses do not themselves elicit the independent explanation that tracing and narrating a journey do; pair recognition checks with a construction task to build and show understanding.

A static labelled figure (gut connected to blood, tappable stages revealing 'absorbed here' / 'carried in blood' / 'delivered to cells', with myth-buster flaps like 'do nutrients stay in your tummy?') can teach the network and is a strong scaffold; it shows the linked systems rather than letting the learner trace the journey themselves, so pair it with a tracing or narration task.

An in-role framing ('be a nutrient' / 'interview a red blood cell about its delivery route') can motivate the journey narrative; keep it anchored to the actual anatomical route so the integration objective is met.

Interactive affordances (glowing particle crossing, learner-pumped heart, split connected-systems view, tappable stages, flaps) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms; a finger-trace or drawn path can serve the same integration goal.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels one interactive format 'ideal' and claims the particle-crossing is felt 'in a way no static image can'; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the cited sources. It has been softened to a concrete tracing activity (which may be realised as an interactive, finger-trace, or drawn path) with the static-figure alternative preserved as a strong scaffold rather than an inferior option.
The source rates 3D as 'poor' because the network is flow-based; this is a format preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been dropped rather than asserted as a universal limitation.

Two of three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row (BBC Bitesize and NGSS); the DfE statutory requirement is the only verified claim. The DfE requirement is carried as objective context in the summary rather than cited as pedagogical support, because it establishes the curriculum topic, not the teaching principle behind these activities.

The BBC Bitesize claim is cited on the first two activities because it describes the absorb→carry→deliver content and the absorption hand-off those activities trace; it is not evidence that the tracing/narration method is more effective than other media, which remains untested.

Interactive affordances mentioned in the source (glowing particle, learner-pumped heart, split view of the two systems, tappable stages, myth-buster flaps) are preserved as OPTIONAL concreteness, not mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: At which organ do the nutrients actually pass out of the gut and into the blood?
Why does it make sense that the small intestine has a huge, folded inner surface?
If the circulatory system stopped, why would a leg muscle starve even though there's food in the gut?
How do the digestive and circulatory systems depend on each other to nourish a cell?
assess.correctAnswer: The digested nutrients are absorbed through the wall of the small intestine into the blood; the circulatory system then carries the dissolved nutrients in the blood to every cell, including the leg muscle. The digestive and circulatory systems work together — the gut absorbs, the blood transports.

errorPatterns.pattern: Food travels through the gut and tubes straight to where it's needed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Nutrients are absorbed into the blood at the small intestine wall; the blood, not the gut, delivers them to cells. Link the two systems explicitly.
errorPatterns.distractor: The food travels through tubes straight to the leg muscle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes food reaching the leg through pipes, with no absorption into blood

errorPatterns.pattern: Nutrients are absorbed in the stomach
errorPatterns.nextMove: Most absorption is in the small intestine, whose villi give a huge surface area; the stomach mainly digests, not absorbs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places absorption into the blood in the stomach rather than the small intestine

errorPatterns.pattern: The digestive and circulatory systems are completely separate
errorPatterns.nextMove: They interface at the intestine wall: digestion prepares soluble nutrients, and circulation distributes them. Show the handover point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the two systems as unconnected and can't say where they meet

responseLevels.gap: Imagines food travelling through the gut directly to its destination; no role for blood or absorption.
responseLevels.full: Explains nutrients are absorbed through the small-intestine wall into the blood and carried by the circulatory system to all cells, describing the two systems working together.

A student says the food just travels down through your intestines and somehow straight into the leg. How do the nutrients actually get from your gut to a leg muscle — what carries them, and where do they cross over?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 — recognise that the ocean holds an amazing variety of animals, from tiny seahorses and clownfish to enormous whales and sharks, differing hugely in shape and size.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS1): Y1 'identify and name a variety of common animals'; Y2 'notice that animals have offspring' and describe how habitats provide for the basic needs of different animals — the ocean as a habitat teeming with kinds of life.
• Standards — US (NGSS): builds toward K-ESS3-1 (organisms live in places that meet their needs) and 2-LS4-1 (observe and [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1]) — variety/biodiversity is the explicit K–2 anchor.
• Operational details: this is a NAMING + WONDER topic, not a mechanism. Success = name ≥5 ocean animals, articulate the size range (seahorse ↔ blue whale), and express curiosity. Anchor to real photographs at true relative scale; a child-vs-blue-whale silhouette makes 'enormous' concrete. Group by look (has-a-shell, has-fins, has-tentacles) informally — do not push formal classification (that is the 7–9 dependent).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete, ~5–6): names several familiar ocean animals from pictures; Tier B (transitional, ~6–7): orders a few by size and names one tiny + one huge; Tier C (~7): begins sorting by an observable feature, priming the later fish/mammal/invertebrate split.
bestPractices: Anchor in real photographs and short video clips of living animals in the sea, not cartoons — young children build accurate mental images from real referents and the wonder is the hook.
Make scale physical: show a human silhouette beside a blue whale, a coin beside a seahorse, so 'tiny' and 'enormous' are felt, not just labelled.
Elicit and name the child's own observations ('it has stripes', 'it has eight arms') to seed later feature-based grouping without imposing taxonomy yet.
Provide rich naming vocabulary in context (seahorse, clownfish, octopus, ray, shark, whale) and revisit across sessions for retention.
Connect to prior habitat knowledge: these animals all live in the same big salty home but look completely different — variety within one habitat.
keyRepresentations: A photographic 'gallery of the sea' spanning the size range from plankton-tiny to whale-huge
A relative-scale line-up (seahorse → clownfish → turtle → shark → whale) beside a child silhouette
Informal sorting mats by observable feature (fins / shell / tentacles / flippers) — a bridge, not a taxonomy
Simple labelled call-outs naming each animal and one memorable fact
commonMisconceptions: 'Everything that lives in the sea is a fish' — whales, octopuses, crabs and jellyfish are all lumped as fish (the misconception the whale/dolphin and classifying topics later dismantle).
'Big animals eat, tiny ones don't matter' — size is confused with importance; tiny animals (plankton, krill) are easy to overlook.
'Sea animals are scary/dangerous' — sharks and 'monsters' dominate; the true variety (gentle giants, tiny beauties) is missed.
Confusing very different animals that share a colour or shape (e.g. calling a dolphin a shark) because fine features aren't yet attended to.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, help children recognise that the ocean holds an amazing variety of animals — from tiny seahorses and clownfish to enormous whales and sharks — that differ hugely in shape and size. This is a naming-and-wonder topic: success means naming at least five ocean animals, articulating the size range (seahorse to blue whale), and expressing curiosity. Anchor to real photographs at true relative scale and seed informal grouping by observable features without imposing formal classification yet.

activities.title: Dive into the ocean: a photographic gallery at true scale
feedback: When a child names an animal, confirm and extend: 'Yes, that's a clownfish — see its orange and white stripes.'
If a child names only big, famous animals, point to the tiny ones: 'A seahorse, a shrimp, krill and tiny animal plankton are ocean animals too — the ocean's variety includes the very small.'
At the whale-vs-child silhouette moment, prompt wonder: 'They ALL live in the ocean, and they come in so many different shapes and sizes.'
activities.rationale: Young children build accurate mental images from real referents, and making scale physical (a human silhouette beside a blue whale, a coin beside a seahorse) lets 'tiny' and 'enormous' be felt rather than just labelled. The gallery delivers the core payload — names, images and relative scale — directly.
sourceClaims: UK KS1 science requires pupils to identify and name a variety of common animals and to describe how habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals.
The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, and its heart is roughly the size of a small car — a vivid scale anchor for 'enormous'.
learnerActions: Explore a continuous seascape (or printed gallery) that runs from the sunlit shallows down into the deep, showing real photographs of living sea animals — not cartoons.
Pick any creature that catches your eye (a darting clownfish, a drifting jellyfish, a shark, a seahorse, an octopus, a ray, a crab) and say or hear its name.
See each animal held at true relative scale: a pygmy seahorse about the size of a fingernail, a blue whale filling the whole view.
Lift a flap or turn to a note to discover one memorable fact about an animal (e.g. 'a blue whale's heart is about as big as a bumper car and weighs more than two grown-ups').
Compare a fingernail-sized pygmy seahorse and an enormous blue whale shown beside a child-sized silhouette, and say which is tiniest and which is most enormous.
activities.intendedInsight: The ocean is one big salty home, yet the animals in it are very different from one another in shape and size — and the size range, from tiny to enormous, is huge.

activities.title: Order by size and sort by what you see
feedback: Give encouraging confirmation when an ordering snaps into place smallest-to-largest; if an animal is misplaced, compare it directly to its neighbour: 'Is the shark bigger or smaller than the turtle?'
When a child groups by feature, name the feature back to them ('these all have tentacles or arms') without labelling it as a formal animal class.
If a child treats all the animals as basically the same, ask 'how is this one's body different from that one's?' to draw out shape and size contrasts.
activities.rationale: Eliciting and naming the child's own observations seeds later feature-based grouping without imposing taxonomy, and active ordering lightly primes grouping. This is a bridge, not a taxonomy — formal fish/mammal/invertebrate classification is a later dependent for ages 7–9.
sourceClaims: NGSS K–2 anchors biodiversity via 2-LS4-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1].
learnerActions: Arrange a set of specific animals shown at true scale (pygmy seahorse, clownfish, green sea turtle, great white shark, blue whale) into a line from smallest to largest.
Place animals onto informal sorting mats by one observable feature you choose: has fins, has a shell (for example a crab), has tentacles or arms (for example an octopus), has flippers.
Say aloud one observation about an animal as you sort it ('it has stripes', 'it has eight arms').
Name which animal you ordered as tiniest and which as biggest.
activities.intendedInsight: Ocean animals can be compared by size and grouped by features you can actually see — a first, informal step toward noticing that they are genuinely different kinds of animal.

activities.title: Quick check: name them and rank them
feedback: For a correct match or ordering, confirm warmly and name the animal again for retention.
For an error, return to the photograph and the scale comparison rather than just marking it wrong: 'Look again — which fills more of the picture?'
activities.rationale: A low-stakes matching and size-sequence check is a natural companion to the gallery for the two evidence goals (naming five or more and describing the size range). Note this format checks recognition and recall; it does not on its own elicit the child's own spoken wonder or extended description.
sourceClaims: UK KS1 science requires pupils to identify and name a variety of common animals and to describe how habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals.
learnerActions: Match an animal's name to its photograph.
Answer which animal in a set is the biggest and which is the smallest.
Put a few animals in order by size.
Name at least five different ocean animals from memory or from pictures.
activities.intendedInsight: I can name several ocean animals and place them along the tiny-to-enormous size range.

activities.title: Talk about the ocean's biggest and smallest (optional spark)
feedback: Answer each question with a real photograph and the animal's name, then invite a follow-up question.
Encourage the child to voice wonder and repeat back the animal names they use.
activities.rationale: Open conversation can spark curiosity, but at 5–7 the core goal is recognising and naming from images, and free dialogue is harder to steer to reliable naming outcomes and leans on stronger reading and speaking. Use it as a supporting spark alongside the gallery, not the main route.
learnerActions: Ask a grown-up, teacher, or a friendly 'marine biologist' or 'dolphin' character questions like 'what's the biggest animal?' and 'what's the smallest?'
Look at a photograph for each answer and say the animal's name.
Describe in your own words why one animal surprised you.
activities.intendedInsight: Curiosity drives questions, and asking about extremes (biggest, smallest) reveals just how much variety the ocean holds.

constraints: Use real photographs and short video clips of living animals, not cartoons, so children build accurate mental images.
Keep grouping informal (has-a-shell, has-fins, has-tentacles/arms); do not push formal fish/mammal/invertebrate classification — that is a later 7–9 objective.
Sorting mats are a bridge to classification, not a taxonomy; present features as things the child can see, not as fixed animal categories.
The matching/size quiz checks recognition and recall; it does not by itself elicit the child's independent spoken description or expressed wonder, so pair it with the gallery and talk activities.

Relative-scale representations must be honest (a pygmy seahorse fingernail-sized, most other seahorses roughly finger- to hand-sized, blue whale filling the view beside a child silhouette) so 'tiny' and 'enormous' are accurately felt.
A conversation activity depends on reading/speaking strength and is harder to steer to reliable naming; treat it as an optional spark, not evidence that dialogue is inferior for all learners.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All listed sources carry verified:false in the original row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The common misconception 'everything that lives in the sea is a fish' and the confusion of size with importance are drawn from the pedagogy and assessment fields; the gallery, sorting, and 'tiny animals count too' feedback aim to surface and prime these ideas, though full dismantling (whale as mammal, octopus/crab as invertebrate) is reserved for later 7–9 topics per the stated age scope.

NGSS 2-LS4-1 concerns comparing diversity across DIFFERENT habitats; because the objective here is variety within one habitat, that source is kept only on the observation/comparison-grouping activity and not attached to the single-habitat gallery, and even there the match is partial (observe-to-compare principle aligns, habitat-contrast does not).

The original row rated a 3D swim-through as adding cost/navigation load 'without deepening the core idea' and framed the conversation format as weaker; these are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy findings. A guided 3D drift (gentle drift past creatures with tap-to-name) or dialogue could still support naming and scale for some learners. The size-ordering and quiz formats were originally secondary to the illustrated gallery; alternatives are preserved here for their distinct purposes (active ordering, low-stakes check, curiosity spark).

probeDeeper: 'You named a whale and a crab. How is a crab's body really different from a whale's?'
'Is an octopus a fish? What about it is not fish-like?' (counterexample forcing the distinction)
'Name me the tiniest ocean animal you can think of, and the biggest.'
'If they're not all fish, what different KINDS of ocean animal can you think of?'
assess.correctAnswer: It's not right — the ocean is home to a huge VARIETY of very different animals, and they are not all fish. A clownfish and a seahorse are fish, but an octopus and a crab have no backbone (they're invertebrates), and a whale is a mammal. Ocean animals come in many shapes and sizes, from tiny (seahorse, shrimp) to enormous (whales, sharks).

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks every animal that lives in the sea is a fish ('they all swim in water, so they're all fish')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort a few by an obvious difference: a crab has a shell and legs, an octopus has 8 arms and no bones, a whale breathes air. Living in the sea doesn't make them all one kind.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — they all live in the sea and swim, so they're all fish
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees they're all fish; groups whale, octopus, crab as fish

errorPatterns.pattern: Only counts the big, famous animals (whale, shark) as 'ocean animals' and overlooks tiny ones
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the size range from tiny plankton/seahorses to giant whales — all ocean animals. Variety includes the very small, not just the spectacular.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names only large animals; surprised a seahorse or shrimp counts

errorPatterns.pattern: Can name animals but treats them as basically the same, missing how different their body shapes are
errorPatterns.nextMove: For two named animals, ask 'how is this one's body different from that one's?' — draw out shape/size contrasts to make 'variety' concrete.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists five names but can't describe any real difference in shape/size between them

responseLevels.gap: Says all sea animals are fish, or can name almost none; no sense of variety.
responseLevels.full: Names five+ clearly different ocean animals, recognises they are NOT all fish (some are mammals/invertebrates), and describes real differences in shape and size across the range — showing variety as different kinds, not just different fish.
responseLevels.partial: Names several ocean animals and senses they differ, but slips into calling them all fish, or notices only size and not that they are genuinely different kinds of animal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Think about a clownfish, an octopus, a whale, a crab, and a seahorse — all live in the sea. A child says: 'They're all just fish, because they all live in the sea and swim.' Is that right? Tell me some very different kinds of ocean animal, and whether they really are all fish.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who appreciates the variety names several genuinely different kinds and resists 'all fish'. A child with the common 'everything in the sea is a fish' idea agrees they're all fish because they swim in water. The second tier (name different kinds / are they all fish) reveals whether 'variety' means truly different animal types or just different-looking fish.

pedagogy.summary: Solving one- and two-step word problems within 100 with unknowns in all positions is fundamentally about MODELLING the situation, not about the arithmetic. Children must read what is happening (joining, separating, comparing), identify the unknown's position (result, change, or start), represent it — ideally with a bar model and an equation using a symbol for the unknown — and only then compute. The research-critical point is that keyword strategies fail, and problem difficulty is governed by semantic structure: start-unknown and compare problems are far harder than result-unknown.
bestPractices: Model before calculating: draw a bar model / part-whole and write an equation with a symbol for the unknown, then solve
Explicitly teach all problem structures — join/separate with result, change, or start unknown, and compare (how many more/fewer) — not just result-unknown
Do NOT teach keyword shortcuts ('more'→add); they break on compare and start-unknown problems
For two-step problems, name and hold the intermediate result before the second step
Use the DfE additive vocabulary (total, difference, more/less, change) tied to the situation, and connect comparison to 'difference'
keyRepresentations: Bar model (part-whole, comparison, two-step)
Part-whole diagram
Equation with a symbol/box for the unknown (e.g. 28 = □ − 15)
Number line (count-on for difference/change)
Cubes/counters to act out the situation
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy: choosing the operation from a cue word rather than the situation (fails on compare/start-unknown)
Start-unknown problems solved as if result-unknown (doing the stated operation forwards instead of its inverse)
Doing only the first step of a two-step problem
Compare problems: subtracting the wrong way or not seeing 'difference' as subtraction
Writing the equation to mirror word order rather than structure

learn.summary: Children aged 7–8 solve one- and two-step word problems within 100 with the unknown in any position (result, change, or start) and including comparison. The core skill is MODELLING the situation — reading whether it is joining, separating, or comparing; locating where the unknown sits; representing it with a bar model and an equation using a symbol for the unknown — and only then computing. Keyword shortcuts ('more'→add) are explicitly discredited because they break on compare and start-unknown problems, which are the hardest structures.

activities.title: Build the bar model, then write the equation (start-unknown focus)
feedback: If the learner subtracts (28 − 15) on the start-unknown story: ask 'which part are we trying to find — is it a part or the whole?' With a part-whole bar, the start is the whole; we know the two parts (15 who got off and 28 who remain), so we add them back to find the start (15 + 28 = 43). Act it out in reverse with counters.
If the learner's equation box sits where the answer 'usually' goes: ask 'does your box go where the answer usually goes, or somewhere else?' — reposition it to match the structure of the story.

If, on a two-step story, the learner stops after the first step: point to the labelled intermediate bar and ask 'is this the final answer, or is there more to do?' This may be a tracking lapse rather than a conceptual gap — underline both actions.
activities.rationale: Representing a problem's underlying structure with a strip/bar diagram before writing an equation, and attending to structure rather than surface story features, is supported as a problem-solving practice. Start-unknown is among the hardest structures and is precisely where keyword strategies fail, so it is a strong discriminating context for building genuine modelling and for writing an equation with a symbol for the unknown.
sourceClaims: Problem solving 'is not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; teaching students to represent a problem's underlying STRUCTURE with visual/schematic representations (strip diagrams — i.e. bar models) BEFORE writing an equation makes them more effective problem solvers, and teachers should attend to structure rather than surface story features. This recommendation carries a STRONG evidence rating (six studies).

Year 2 pupils solve problems with addition and subtraction involving numbers, quantities and measures, and use a symbol for an unknown in missing-number problems (e.g. 7 = □ − 9); comparison uses the language of difference.

Problem difficulty follows semantic structure: result-unknown is easiest, while start-unknown (change/start unknown) and compare structures are substantially harder; keyword strategies break down on precisely these structures.
learnerActions: Read a start-unknown story such as: 'Some children were on the bus. 15 got off. Now there are 28. How many were there at the start?'
Build a bar model: place the known parts (15 and 28) and leave the start as a labelled empty segment — decide whether the unknown is a part or the whole
Recognise that here the START is the whole, so the empty bar is found by adding the known parts 15 and 28
Write a matching equation using a symbol for the unknown, e.g. 28 + 15 = □ (equivalently □ − 15 = 28), so the picture and equation agree
Compute and check the equation and diagram tell the same story
For a two-step story, build a labelled intermediate bar and name that middle amount before doing the second step
activities.intendedInsight: The structure of the situation — not a cue word — determines the operation. 'Got off' suggests subtraction to a keyword solver, but when the start is the unknown whole and the two parts are known, you add. Seeing the diagram contradict the cue word is the moment modelling beats keyword-hunting.

activities.title: Model across all structures with a drag-to-build bar tool
feedback: If a comparison problem is subtracted the wrong way or the learner cannot start: show a comparison bar with the two quantities aligned; the overhang IS the difference. When the difference is unknown, find it by subtracting the smaller from the larger, or by counting on along a number line from the smaller to the larger. When the difference is known and one quantity is unknown, use the bar to decide whether to add or subtract.
If the written equation mirrors word order rather than structure: rebuild the bar first and let the equation follow the diagram.

OPTIONAL interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete (not mandatory): dragging segments to size them, a labelled empty segment for the unknown, and the tool live-writing the matching equation as the bar changes. A labelled intermediate bar can be revealed for two-step stories.
activities.rationale: Explicitly teaching all problem structures (not just result-unknown) and connecting comparison to 'difference' follows the semantic-structure hierarchy and the curriculum's use of a symbol for the unknown. A drag-to-build diagram supports construction and practice volume, which a static reference cannot.
sourceClaims: Problem difficulty follows semantic structure: result-unknown is easiest, while start-unknown (change/start unknown) and compare structures are substantially harder; keyword strategies break down on precisely these structures.

Year 2 pupils solve problems with addition and subtraction involving numbers, quantities and measures, and use a symbol for an unknown in missing-number problems (e.g. 7 = □ − 9); comparison uses the language of difference.

Problem solving 'is not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; teaching students to represent a problem's underlying STRUCTURE with visual/schematic representations (strip diagrams — i.e. bar models) BEFORE writing an equation makes them more effective problem solvers, and teachers should attend to structure rather than surface story features. This recommendation carries a STRONG evidence rating (six studies).
learnerActions: Work through stories spanning every structure: join and separate with the result, change, OR start unknown, and compare (how many more/fewer)
For each, drag bars to represent the known quantities and leave the unknown as a labelled empty segment
Let the tool write the matching equation with a symbol as you build, so you check that the equation mirrors the STRUCTURE, not the word order

Tackle deliberately chosen compare problems where a cue word would mislead — e.g. 'Sam has 34 stickers. That is 12 fewer than Ana. How many does Ana have?' The word 'fewer' tempts subtraction, but the comparison bar shows Ana's amount is the longer bar, so the answer is found by adding (34 + 12 = 46), decided by the structure and NOT by the word 'fewer'
For comparison stories, set the two quantities side by side so the extra length IS the difference
For a difference or change, you can also use a number line: count on from the smaller quantity up to the larger to find how many more/fewer
Use the DfE additive vocabulary — total, difference, more/less, change — tied to what is happening in the situation
activities.intendedInsight: Problems that look similar in words can have very different structures, and the position of the unknown changes which operation is needed. A manipulable bar (and a number line for difference) lets the learner construct and compare structures rather than match surface cues.

activities.title: Check understanding: match stories to equations and name the intermediate result
feedback: If the keyword-trap option is chosen: return to a bar model of the story and ask which quantity is unknown and whether it is a part or whole.
If only the intermediate result is given on a two-step item: prompt 'is that the final answer, or is there more to do?'
activities.rationale: Selection and matching tasks across all structures efficiently surface keyword-strategy and start-unknown errors. This format checks and reinforces recognition and justification rather than eliciting independent construction of a fresh model, so it complements — does not replace — the build activities above.
sourceClaims: Problem difficulty follows semantic structure: result-unknown is easiest, while start-unknown (change/start unknown) and compare structures are substantially harder; keyword strategies break down on precisely these structures.
learnerActions: Match stories to equations where the unknown sits in different positions (result, change, start)
On a compare story, choose among equations that include a keyword-trap option (a tempting equation that matches a cue word but not the structure), and justify the choice by the structure
On a two-step fill-in-the-blank, state the intermediate result explicitly before giving the final answer
Explain in words why each chosen operation fits the situation
activities.intendedInsight: When a learner can both pick the correct equation for each structure and say WHY — especially explaining why the keyword-trap option is wrong — that spoken/written justification shows structure, not a cue word, is driving the choice.

activities.title: Talk through the situation: what's happening, what do we know, what are we finding?
feedback: Elicit the structure and both steps from the learner; do NOT hand over the operation — ask questions that lead them to decide it from the situation.
Follow talk with an actual diagram and equation so modelling is completed, not left verbal.
activities.rationale: Discussion that foregrounds structure supports the modelling goal, but on its own lacks the manipulable diagram and practice volume; pair it with building and solving.
sourceClaims: Problem solving 'is not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; teaching students to represent a problem's underlying STRUCTURE with visual/schematic representations (strip diagrams — i.e. bar models) BEFORE writing an equation makes them more effective problem solvers, and teachers should attend to structure rather than surface story features. This recommendation carries a STRONG evidence rating (six studies).
learnerActions: Before computing, say what is happening in the story (joining, separating, comparing)
State what is known and what is being found, and where the unknown sits
For two-step stories, name both steps and the intermediate amount out loud
Then represent with a bar/equation and solve
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the situation first helps separate structure from surface wording and prevents jumping straight to an operation.

constraints: Do NOT teach keyword shortcuts ('more'→add, 'eaten'→subtract, 'fewer'→subtract); they break on compare and start-unknown problems. Use problems where a cue word misleads to discredit the shortcut.
Model before calculating: draw a bar/part-whole and write an equation with a symbol for the unknown, then solve.
Teach all problem structures — join/separate with result, change, or start unknown, and compare — not just result-unknown.
For two-step problems, name and hold the intermediate result before the second step.
Use DfE additive vocabulary (total, difference, more/less, change) tied to the situation; connect comparison to 'difference'.
A static worked bar model is useful as a reference for structure but cannot let the child model a fresh problem; treat it as a scaffold, not the goal.
Matching/selection tasks check and reinforce recognition and justification; they do not elicit independent construction of a model, so use them alongside build-and-solve activities.
Interaction examples (dragging, live equation writing, labelled intermediate bars) are illustrative of the learning mechanism, not required features.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified this session. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit of arithmetic in the source diagnostic problems: (1) 34+18=52, then 52−9=43 ✓; (2) compare 52−38=14 ✓; (3) start-unknown 28+15=43 ✓. All checked and consistent.

The semantic-structure difficulty hierarchy (result-unknown easiest; start-unknown and compare hardest) is attributed to Cognitively Guided Instruction / Carpenter & Moser and is marked unverified (not fetched this session). The bar-model/structure-before-equation practice is cited with a STRONG rating; the start-unknown example here is a proposal informed by it, not a separately tested intervention.
The source states the equivalence '28 + 15 = □ (or □ − 15 = 28)'. These are mathematically equivalent (28+15=43 and 43−15=28); both are retained as valid ways to express the start-unknown structure.
Restored the original keyRepresentation 'number line (count-on for difference/change)', which an earlier candidate had dropped; it is offered as an option, not a required method.
Reworded the compare example so subtraction is justified by the comparison bar/structure, explicitly not by the word 'fewer', to avoid accidentally reinstating a keyword rule.

probeDeeper: Show me this story as a bar model — which part are we trying to find, and is it a part or the whole?
For the apples problem, why did you add when it says 'eaten'? Could a 'taking away' story ever need adding?
You got 52 for Maya — is that the final answer, or is there more to do?
Write an equation with a box for the unknown — does your box go where the answer usually goes, or somewhere else?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) 43 — two steps: 34+18=52, then 52−9=43. (2) 14 — compare: 52−38. (3) 43 — start-unknown: 28+15 (the inverse of the stated 'eaten').

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy — picks the operation from a cue word rather than the situation ('eaten'/'fewer'→subtract)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Require a bar model first so the structure, not the word, drives the operation; use start-unknown and compare problems where the keyword misleads to discredit the shortcut.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the start-unknown problem the child does 28−15; in the compare problem they wait for a keyword that never comes

errorPatterns.pattern: Start-unknown solved as result-unknown — performs the stated operation forwards instead of its inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model with a part-whole bar: the START is the whole here, and we know a part and the result, so we add back. Act it out in reverse with counters.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For problem (3) the child subtracts the change from the current amount rather than recognising the start is the whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops after the first step of a two-step problem — answers (1) with 52
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: underline both actions and use a bar model where the intermediate result is visibly not the final answer. This is a tracking lapse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child computes 34+18 and gives 52, ignoring 'then lost 9'

errorPatterns.pattern: Compare problem subtracted the wrong way, or 'difference' not seen as subtraction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a comparison bar model showing the two quantities side by side; the extra length IS the difference, found by subtraction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For (2) the child adds, or subtracts the larger from... gives a nonsensical value, or cannot start

responseLevels.gap: Chooses operations by keyword, treats start-unknown as result-unknown, or stops after one step; cannot represent the structure.
responseLevels.full: Models every structure with a bar/equation (unknown in any position), carries out both steps tracking the intermediate result, handles compare and start-unknown, and explains why each operation fits the situation.
responseLevels.partial: Solves result-unknown and straightforward two-step problems and can model with support, but stumbles on compare or start-unknown, or mirrors word order in the equation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three problems and watch the child solve each, encouraging a drawing or equation: (1) 'Maya had 34 marbles, won 18, then lost 9 — how many now?' (2) 'Tom has 52 stickers. Anna has 38. How many fewer does Anna have?' (3) 'Some apples were in a bowl. 15 were eaten. Now there are 28. How many at the start?' Watch how they decide operations and whether they finish two-step problems.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Problem (1) tests whether both steps are carried out and the intermediate 52 is tracked. Problem (2) is a compare problem — a keyword solver hunting for 'take away' has no cue and may stall or add. Problem (3) is start-unknown — the hardest structure — where a keyword solver subtracts (28−15) because 'eaten' says take away, but the situation requires addition. Together they separate a structure-modeller from a keyword-matcher.
