pedagogy.summary: Estimating angles is the sense-making partner of protractor measuring: the child judges an angle's size in degrees WITHOUT a tool, by comparing it against internalised benchmark angles (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). The pedagogical goal is a stable mental image of a right angle and a half/three-quarter turn, so that any angle can be placed relative to them ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°'). This extends the acute/obtuse vocabulary to REFLEX angles (between 180° and 360°), which children meet here for the first time and which the semicircular protractor cannot directly read. Estimation is what makes measuring self-correcting: a child who expects 'about 130°' will not accept a protractor read of 50°.
bestPractices: Anchor a small set of benchmark angles as physical/mental images first — the right angle (corner, quarter turn), the straight angle (180°), 45° as half a right angle, 270° as three right angles — then estimate everything by comparison to the nearest benchmark.
Always estimate BEFORE measuring, then measure to check; treat a big estimate-vs-measure gap as a signal to recheck placement, not to discard the estimate.
Introduce reflex angles explicitly as 'more than a straight line, less than a full turn' and estimate them as 360° minus the smaller angle, since a semicircular protractor reads only to 180°.
Order/compare several angles by eye before any measuring, so relative judgement (which is bigger) is trained alongside absolute estimation (how many degrees).
Use bodily and everyday referents — clock hands, opening doors, ramps, turns — to build the benchmark images.
keyRepresentations: Benchmark angles as mental anchors: 45°, 90° (right angle), 180° (straight), 270°, 360°
The right angle as the master reference ('a bit more / a bit less than a corner')
Reflex angle as 360° minus its companion angle (turn imagery)
Clock hands / opening door as dynamic referents for angle size
commonMisconceptions: Judges size by ray length rather than opening, so estimates a wide-but-short angle as smaller than a narrow-but-long one (arm-length carryover).
Has no reflex concept — sees a 270° reflex angle and reads/estimates the smaller 90° companion instead.
Anchors only to 90° and 180°, so estimates cluster at right angles and straight lines with poor resolution in between (e.g. calls everything obtuse '120°').
Treats 'estimate' as 'measure without care' and expects an exact answer rather than a reasoned approximate range.

learn.summary: Teach angle estimation as the sense-making partner of protractor measuring: the child judges an angle's size in degrees WITHOUT a tool by comparing it to internalised benchmarks (45°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). The goal is a stable mental image of a right angle, a straight angle and a three-quarter turn, so any angle can be placed relative to them ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°'). This extends acute/obtuse vocabulary to REFLEX angles (between 180° and 360°), met here for the first time and not directly readable on a semicircular protractor. Estimation makes measuring self-correcting: a child who expects 'about 130°' will not accept a protractor read of 50°.

activities.title: Predict-then-reveal angle estimation trainer
feedback: Reward closeness within a tolerance band rather than exactness, so an estimate stays a reasoned range, not a failed exact answer.

When a child guesses '90-ish' for a clearly reflex angle, reveal the turn swinging past the straight line and show its true size as 360° minus the companion angle (for example about 270° when the companion is about 90°), so reflex stops being invisible.

When a child under-estimates wide-but-short-armed angles, let the error score flag the pattern, then overlay the two angles vertex-to-vertex so their openings compare directly regardless of arm length, and extend the short arms and re-order to show the size is unchanged.
Treat a big estimate-vs-measure gap as a signal to recheck both the protractor reading (placement and scale) and the estimate, not simply to discard the estimate.
activities.rationale: Estimation is a perceptual-numerical skill proposed to be built by repeated visual trials with feedback: a predict-then-reveal loop over many varied angles commits the child to an estimate, then feeds back the error, intended to calibrate the benchmark sense. Varying ray length independently of opening directly targets the documented arm-length misconception; including reflex angles forces the '360 minus companion' reasoning that a semicircular protractor cannot read directly.
sourceClaims: Angle size is measured with reference to a circle whose whole is 360°; benchmark fractions of a turn (right angle = 90°, straight = 180°) anchor degree understanding, and an n-one-degree-angle turn measures n degrees (4.MD.5).

The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
Judging angle size by the length of the arms rather than the amount of opening is a persistent, documented misconception.
learnerActions: Look at an angle shown in a random orientation and, BEFORE any measuring, commit an estimate of its size in degrees (set a slider or type a number).
In ordering rounds, drag four angles into order from smallest to largest by eye before anything is measured.
Reveal the true measure and your error; when offered, fade in a faint benchmark 'ghost' (right-angle corner, or 180° straight line) over the angle to see how your estimate compared.
Meet angles whose ray (arm) lengths are varied at random so a wide angle sometimes has short arms — estimate by the opening, not the line length.
Meet reflex angles that swing past the straight line, and estimate them as 360° minus the smaller companion angle.
activities.intendedInsight: Any angle can be placed relative to a small set of benchmarks, and reflex angles (between 180° and 360°) are real angles estimated as 360° minus their companion — not the smaller angle on the other side.

activities.title: Scored estimation and classification practice
feedback: Score the slider estimate against a tolerance band so a near miss counts as success.
Flag an arm-length error when ordering tracks ray length rather than opening, and prompt direct comparison of the openings.
If the child mis-classifies the reflex angle as acute or right, show that it opens past the straight line.
activities.rationale: Estimation maps cleanly onto scored response formats (slider estimate, ordering, classification choice), giving varied practice and checking. A response-format task may give less rapid many-trial feedback than a live predict-reveal loop, so it is proposed as a complement rather than a replacement. Including a short-ray wide-angle item targets the arm-length misconception.
sourceClaims: Judging angle size by the length of the arms rather than the amount of opening is a persistent, documented misconception.

The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
learnerActions: Use a slider to estimate a shown angle's degrees, aiming to land within a tolerance band.
Order four angles smallest-to-largest by eye as an ordering task before any measure is shown.
Classify shown angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex, and pick out the reflex angle in a diagram.
Tackle at least one deliberately short-armed, wide-opening item designed to catch the arm-length habit.
activities.intendedInsight: Relative judgement (which is bigger), absolute estimation (how many degrees) and classification (acute/obtuse/reflex) are distinct skills that can each be practised and checked.

activities.title: Benchmark-angle gallery with everyday referents
feedback: Confirm the benchmark image and name when revealed, and connect it to its everyday referent.
When the child decides 'more or less than a right angle', show the angle against the corner image to confirm.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal gallery can seed estimation by anchoring the benchmark set as stable mental images with everyday referents. It is a scaffold: it may establish the anchors but does not itself run the estimate-check loop that calibrates estimation, so it is intended to precede, not replace, repeated estimation practice.
sourceClaims: Angle size is measured with reference to a circle whose whole is 360°; benchmark fractions of a turn (right angle = 90°, straight = 180°) anchor degree understanding, and an n-one-degree-angle turn measures n degrees (4.MD.5).
learnerActions: Tap or reveal each benchmark in turn — 45° (half a right angle), 90° (right angle/corner/quarter turn), 180° (straight), 270° (three right angles), 360° (full turn) — and link it to a reference image.
Connect each benchmark to a bodily or everyday referent: clock hands, an opening door, a ramp, a turn.
Use a lift-the-flap or 'more or less than a right angle?' layer to decide, for a shown angle, whether it is above or below the corner benchmark.
activities.intendedInsight: A small set of benchmark angles, anchored as physical and mental images, is the master reference set against which every other angle is judged ('a bit more / a bit less than a corner').

activities.title: Add intermediate anchors to sharpen resolution
feedback: If estimates snap only to 90° or 180°, point out the gap and introduce an intermediate anchor the angle sits near.
Accept a reasoned range stated against two anchors rather than demanding one exact number.
activities.rationale: When benchmark resolution is too coarse, estimates cluster at right angles and straight lines; this is a sparse-anchor-deployment issue, not a concept failure, so the fix is to bring in and practise intermediate anchors rather than reteach the concept of angle.
sourceClaims: The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
learnerActions: For a learner whose estimates snap only to 90° and 180°, bring in the half-right-angle (45°) and 'a right angle plus a third of a right angle' (120°) as working anchors alongside the secure 90° and 180° images.
Estimate angles that deliberately sit BETWEEN benchmarks, such as 60°, 110° or 130°, naming the two anchors each one falls between.
Justify at least one estimate aloud with benchmark language ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°').
activities.intendedInsight: Anchoring only to 90° and 180° makes estimates cluster there with poor resolution in between; deploying intermediate anchors gives the mental ruler finer gradations.

constraints: Always estimate BEFORE measuring, then measure to check; a large estimate-vs-measure gap signals that both should be rechecked (protractor placement and which scale was read, and the estimate itself), not that the estimate was worthless.
Reward closeness within a tolerance band, not exactness: an estimate is a reasoned approximate range, not a failed exact answer. An estimate of 120° when the protractor reads 128° is a good estimate.
A semicircular protractor reads only to 180°, so reflex angles must be reasoned as 360° minus the smaller companion angle; do not treat the smaller companion as the answer.

The benchmark gallery is a scaffold that anchors reference images; it may seed estimation but does not build the skill on its own, which requires repeated estimate-then-check trials. It is a useful precursor, not a universal requirement.

Classification and ordering response items check relative and absolute angle sense but, used alone, may give less rapid many-trial feedback than a live predict-reveal loop; combine formats rather than claiming any one medium is required.
Vary ray length independently of opening deliberately: wide-but-short-armed angles are the key trap for the arm-length misconception and should be included on purpose.

45° is part of the target benchmark set; the resolution-sharpening activity only re-deploys it for learners who have anchored to 90°/180° alone, and does not imply 45° is an optional extra for everyone.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The ±15° tolerance band and the specific benchmark set (45°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°) come from the legacy assessment and pedagogy fields; they are reasonable for ages 9–10 but are design choices, not values established by the cited sources.

The original pedagogy summary additionally lists 30° and 60° as benchmark angles, which its own keyRepresentations omits. This rewrite follows keyRepresentations: 30° is not carried through, and 60° appears only as an intermediate anchor in the resolution-sharpening activity. The inconsistency is inherited from the source and is not resolved by the cited references.

Legacy catalog rationales claiming a 3D environment 'adds spatial overhead without improving' estimation, that a character 'cannot show hundreds of angles', and that a static image 'cannot run the estimate-check loop' were medium-comparison statements; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, not asserted as universal pedagogical laws. A fixed image can still teach the benchmark set.

The sources support benchmark-degree reasoning and the arm-length misconception; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific interactive medium or the stated tolerance band. Efficacy-flavoured comparisons are stated with proposed/may wording only.

probeDeeper: Point to the short-armed wide angle and a long-armed narrow one: 'You said this one is smaller — what if I made its lines just as long as the other's? Would it still be smaller?' (counterexample: arm length is irrelevant.)
'How did you decide this one was about 130° — what did you compare it to?' — listen for a benchmark (right angle) rather than a guess.
'This reflex angle — how could you use the smaller angle next to it to work out its size?' (probes 360°-minus-companion reasoning.)
'Your estimate was 120° and the protractor says 128° — is your estimate wrong?' — checks the child understands an estimate is a reasoned range, not a failed exact answer.
assess.correctAnswer: Orders the four correctly by opening (not by arm length), estimates each within roughly ±15° of its true size, classifies the ~270° one as reflex (over a straight line, under a full turn) rather than reading its 90° companion, and uses benchmark language ('a bit more than a right angle') to justify at least one estimate.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders by arm length not opening — puts the short-armed wide angle earlier (smaller) than a long-armed narrow one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the two angles vertex-to-vertex so the openings compare directly regardless of arm length; extend the short arms and re-order to show the size is unchanged.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ordering tracks ray length rather than degrees; the child may point to the longer lines as the reason it's 'bigger'.

errorPatterns.pattern: No reflex concept — estimates the ~270° reflex angle as its ~90° companion, or as 'about 90°', reading the wrong side of the opening.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the turn dynamically past the straight line; estimate reflex as 360° minus the companion; explicitly name 'reflex: more than 180°, less than 360°'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the reflex angle acute/right or gives a sub-180° number; treats the reflex mark as if it were the smaller angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Benchmark resolution too coarse — snaps every estimate to 90° or 180°, so a 130° angle is called '90' or '180' with nothing in between.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the half-right-angle (45°) and 'a bit past a right angle' (~120°) as extra anchors; practise estimating angles that sit between benchmarks. No reteaching of concept — the anchor set is just sparse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Estimates cluster only at right angles and straight lines; no use of 45°/60°/120° as intermediate anchors.

responseLevels.gap: Estimates bear little relation to actual size and ordering follows arm length or orientation; no benchmark reasoning and no reflex concept (reads reflex as its companion).
responseLevels.full: Orders all four by opening regardless of arm length, estimates each within about ±15° using benchmark comparisons including intermediate anchors, correctly identifies and estimates the reflex angle via 360°-minus-companion, and treats the estimate as a reasoned range confirmed (not replaced) by measuring.
responseLevels.partial: Estimates acute and obtuse angles reasonably against 90°/180° and orders standard angles correctly, but is caught by at least one of: the short-arm wide angle (orders by length), the reflex angle (no over-180° concept), or coarse resolution (snaps to 90/180). Can name benchmarks but not deploy intermediate ones.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out four angles the child can see but not measure — include one clearly acute (~40°), one obtuse (~130°), one drawn with short arms but a wide opening, and one reflex (~270°), with ray lengths deliberately uneven. Say: 'Without measuring, put these in order from smallest to largest, and tell me roughly how many degrees each one is.' Then let them measure to check. Watch the ordering and the estimates — do not coach.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The uneven ray lengths separate opening-based judgement from arm-length judgement; the short-arm wide angle is the trap. The reflex angle separates a child who has extended their concept past 180° from one who collapses it back to the acute companion. Ordering plus numeric estimate together expose both relative and absolute angle sense in one two-minute task.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Toxins Building Up (Bioaccumulation & Biomagnification)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 'Interactions and interdependencies'):** how organisms affect and are affected by their environment, including the accumulation of toxic materials — the named curriculum hook for this topic.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS2-4):** construct an argument [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-4] — a persistent toxin is exactly such a change, and its concentration up the chain drives population effects.

- **Operational details:** Two linked ideas pupils must separate and then combine. BIOACCUMULATION: a persistent toxin (one the body cannot break down or excrete, e.g. DDT, mercury) builds up in a single organism over its lifetime because intake exceeds removal. BIOMAGNIFICATION: because a predator eats MANY contaminated prey, and the toxin stays in the body, concentration MULTIPLIES at each step up the chain — so top predators carry the highest dose even when the water/producers hold only a trace. The classic case: DDT → plankton → fish → birds of prey (peregrine/osprey), eggshell thinning, population collapse (Silent Spring). Key: it is the PERSISTENCE plus the many-prey-per-predator ratio that causes the multiplication, mirroring — and contrasting with — energy LOSS up the chain (energy falls, toxin rises).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (quantitative/formal). Pupils reason quantitatively about concentration multiplying up levels and explain WHY top predators are most at risk. Success = predicts that a top predator carries the highest concentration and justifies it via persistence + accumulation across many prey.
bestPractices: Separate the two mechanisms explicitly: accumulation within ONE organism over time, then magnification ACROSS levels because predators eat many prey — pupils blur them.
Make persistence the pivotal variable: contrast a toxin that breaks down/is excreted (no build-up) with one that doesn't (build-up) so pupils see persistence is the precondition.
Anchor in the DDT/peregrine case with real ppm figures so the multiplication is evidenced, not asserted, and connects to a real population collapse.
Draw the deliberate mirror with energy transfer: energy DECREASES up the chain, persistent toxin INCREASES — teaching them together sharpens both.
Have pupils construct an evidence-based argument (MS-LS2-4) for why the top predator is worst hit, not just recite the pattern.
keyRepresentations: Food-chain concentration ladder with rising ppm figures (plankton 0.04 → small fish 0.5 → large fish 2 → osprey 25)
Per-organism toxin 'meters' that climb as feeding proceeds
Many-prey-per-predator visual: a predator absorbing the combined load of a pile of prey
Peregrine egg with thinned shell — the population-level consequence
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the toxin is most concentrated where it enters (the water/producers) rather than at the top of the chain.
Assuming the toxin harms all organisms equally, missing that concentration multiplies up the levels so top predators suffer most.
Believing the toxin 'wears off' or is excreted — not grasping that persistence (no breakdown/removal) is what allows build-up.
Conflating toxin magnification with energy transfer — not seeing that energy falls up the chain while persistent toxin rises.

learn.summary: For ages 12-13, teach bioaccumulation and biomagnification by separating two linked ideas: (1) a persistent toxin builds up WITHIN one organism over its lifetime because intake exceeds removal, and (2) concentration MULTIPLIES ACROSS levels because each predator eats many contaminated prey and retains their toxin, while most of the eaten mass is used up for energy rather than added to its body. Anchor in the classic DDT -> plankton -> small fish -> large fish -> bird-of-prey case with real ppm figures, make persistence the pivotal variable, draw the deliberate mirror with energy transfer (energy falls up the chain, persistent toxin rises), and have learners construct an evidence-based argument for why top predators are worst hit.

activities.title: Run the feeding chain and watch concentration climb
feedback: If a learner expects the toxin to spread out and weaken upward, point out the meters sum rather than divide: a predator inherits the toxin of everything it eats.
If a learner thinks only the water concentration matters, route the toxin through food, not drinking: it enters at the bottom and is concentrated by feeding up the chain.
When the persistence toggle is flipped to 'breaks down quickly' and magnification vanishes, prompt: 'What single property of the toxin made the build-up possible?' (persistence/non-removal).
Use the energy overlay to check the key discrimination: energy decreases, persistent toxin increases.
activities.rationale: Biomagnification is a counting-and-concentration story that is more convincing when learners make the concentration climb themselves and can isolate persistence as the cause via a counterfactual toggle. Live per-organism meters and the many-prey-per-predator visual make the multiplication mechanism concrete rather than asserted. These interactive elements are offered as examples of how to make the mechanism visible, not as a required technology; the same mechanism can be reasoned through from figures.
sourceClaims: Biomagnification: persistent toxins (DDT, mercury) accumulate in organisms and multiply in concentration up the food chain, so top predators carry the highest dose; DDT caused eggshell thinning and population declines in birds of prey (peregrine/osprey).
learnerActions: Seed the water/plankton with a tiny dose of a persistent toxin, then step through the four-level chain: each small fish eats ten plankton, each large fish eats ten small fish, and each bird eats ten large fish — with every organism keeping all the toxin from everything it eats.

Track a per-organism toxin meter that climbs 1 -> 10 -> 100 -> 1000 units as you feed each successive level. This is a simplified model of toxin load. Concentration also rises in real food chains: most of the eaten food's mass is used up for energy (respiration), but the toxin is kept, so it ends up in much less body mass than the food it came from.
Compare the near-clean water reading with the top predator's high reading, and link the high dose to a visible outcome (osprey/peregrine eggshell thinning and egg failure).
State in your own words why a harmless-looking trace in the water becomes a dangerous dose at the top.
Flip a persistence toggle so the toxin 'breaks down quickly' and observe that the magnification collapses; explain what that shows about the cause.
Toggle an energy-pyramid overlay and describe the mirror: energy shrinks up the chain while persistent toxin grows.
activities.intendedInsight: A trace of a persistent toxin can become a harmful dose in a top predator because the toxin is not broken down or excreted AND each predator takes in the combined load of many prey, while most of that food's mass is used up for energy, so the toxin is concentrated into less body mass; this contrasts with energy, which falls up the chain.

activities.title: Read the real DDT concentration ladder
feedback: If a learner says the figures just increase 'by chance', relink each rise to many-prey-per-predator plus retention.
Confirm the key fact: the environment can hold only a trace while the top of the chain carries a dangerous, potentially lethal dose.

Note that this ladder shows the pattern and case history but is a fixed example: it does not let you vary the dose or test the persistence counterfactual, so pair it with the feeding activity for the mechanism.
Note that the real figures do not rise by exactly ten each step (roughly x12.5, x4, x12.5), so treat the 1/10/100/1000 model as a simplified illustration of the same upward multiplication.
activities.rationale: A static annotated DDT chain with real ppm figures teaches the pattern and case history crisply and works well as pre-teaching or reference. A fixed example cannot be manipulated by the learner, but it still conveys the quantitative pattern and historical evidence.
sourceClaims: Biomagnification: persistent toxins (DDT, mercury) accumulate in organisms and multiply in concentration up the food chain, so top predators carry the highest dose; DDT caused eggshell thinning and population declines in birds of prey (peregrine/osprey).
learnerActions: Study a DDT food-chain ladder with real ppm figures at each level: plankton 0.04 ppm -> small fish 0.5 -> large fish 2 -> osprey 25.
For each level, answer 'why is this one higher than the one below it?' and specifically 'why is the osprey's so high?'

Examine the peregrine/osprey egg case and connect the high top-predator concentration to eggshell thinning and population collapse (Silent Spring, 1962, raised alarm about pesticide harm to birds; the eggshell-thinning link was established by later research).
Calculate or estimate roughly how many times more concentrated the osprey is than the plankton (about 25 / 0.04, i.e. ~625x), and state what that means for risk.
activities.intendedInsight: Real measured concentrations show the toxin is lowest where it enters (water/producers) and highest in the top predator, evidencing the multiplication pattern and its real population-level consequences.

activities.title: Build and argue the case for the top predator
feedback: If a learner says 'the small fish are worst affected because the poison gets weaker higher up', reverse the intuition: the toxin is retained and summed, so it concentrates upward.
If a learner says 'the osprey is big and strong so it copes best', point out body size does not clear a persistent toxin; the top predator receives the summed dose and is most, not least, at risk.
If a learner says 'the osprey must be drinking lots of the water', redirect to the feeding route: the toxin enters at the bottom and is concentrated by feeding up the chain.

A full answer names the top predator as most at risk, cites a real case, and reasons about the counterfactual; a partial answer knows toxins are 'worse at the top' and names an example but omits the persistence-plus-many-prey cause.
activities.rationale: The standard calls for constructing an argument, not reciting a pattern, so learners should produce explanation and reasoning including a counterfactual. A conversational history debrief supports argument and context after the mechanism is understood.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-LS2-4: construct an argument [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS2-4] — a persistent toxin is such a change.
DfE KS3 'Interactions and interdependencies' requires how organisms affect and are affected by their environment, including the accumulation of toxic materials.
learnerActions: Respond to the diagnostic scenario: 'A pesticide washes into a lake at a tiny concentration that is harmless in the water itself. Yet the fish-eating ospreys at the top get sick and their eggs fail. How can the poison be harmless in the water but dangerous in the osprey — and why is it the top predator, not the small fish, that suffers most?'
Construct a short written or spoken argument naming the top predator as most at risk and justifying it via persistence plus accumulation across many prey (MS-LS2-4).
Trace the pathway: show how DDT got from farm crops (via runoff into water) all the way into an osprey at the top of the lake food chain.
Answer the counterfactual: 'If the toxin DID break down quickly inside the body, would it still build up the chain? Why not?'
Explain how bioaccumulation differs from a predator simply eating one very poisonous meal.
Discuss the history using a Rachel Carson / Silent Spring debrief as a prompt for argument and context.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can independently construct an evidence-based argument that the top predator carries the summed dose of the whole chain because the toxin persists and predators eat many prey — and can reason about the break-down counterfactual.

activities.title: Check the reasoning (including the energy-vs-toxin discrimination)
feedback: If a learner confuses toxin with energy, re-run the energy overlay: energy decreases with each step, persistent toxin increases.
Recognition and calculation checks confirm the pattern but do not by themselves elicit a full constructed argument; use them alongside the argument activity.
For the habitat-change evidence point, prompt a concrete worked example (earthworms, beavers) since the toxin case centres on bioaccumulation, not habitat engineering.
activities.rationale: A check is a legitimate way to verify the quantitative reasoning and the key discrimination. The learning objective also includes how organisms change their habitat, which the toxin case alone does not cover, so this is flagged for explicit teaching.
learnerActions: Predict the concentration in the top predator given figures lower down, and sequence organisms by toxin load.
Answer 'why is the water low but the eagle high?' and perform a calculation multiplying concentration up the levels.
Answer a discrimination question contrasting toxin (rises up the chain) with energy (falls up the chain).
Separately, explain how organisms can change their habitat (e.g. earthworms aerating soil, beavers creating wetlands) to address the full 'affect their environment' objective.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure the quantitative pattern and the crucial discrimination that persistent toxin rises while energy falls up the food chain, plus the broader idea that organisms both affect and are affected by their environment.

constraints: Explicitly separate the two mechanisms: accumulation WITHIN one organism over time, then magnification ACROSS levels because predators eat many prey — learners commonly blur them.
Make persistence the pivotal variable: contrast a toxin that breaks down/is excreted (no build-up) with one that does not (build-up) so learners see persistence is the precondition.

Use real ppm figures (plankton 0.04 -> small fish 0.5 -> large fish 2 -> osprey 25) so the multiplication is evidenced, not asserted; present the 1/10/100/1000 model as a simplified illustration since the real figures do not rise by exactly ten each step.

A static ladder or infographic is a reference/pre-teach scaffold: it does not let learners vary the dose, toggle persistence, or watch the multiplication happen, so pair it with a feeding activity for the mechanism.
Recognition and calculation checks confirm the pattern but do not by themselves elicit an independently constructed argument, which the standard (MS-LS2-4) requires.
The toxin travels through food, not primarily drinking water; keep the feeding pathway central to avoid the 'drinking the water' misconception.
The objective includes how organisms change their habitat (earthworms, beavers); the toxin case does not cover this, so teach it separately.

Interactive examples (meters, persistence toggle, energy overlay, pile-of-prey visual) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory technology; the same learning can use paper ladders, worked calculations, and spoken/written argument.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, the DfE KS3 claim is marked verified in the source row; the two NGSS/background claims are marked verified:false. Treat the ppm figures and population-collapse details as unverified in this rewrite.

The specific ppm figures (0.04, 0.5, 2, 25) and the exact '10 prey per predator / 1 -> 10 -> 100 -> 1000' ratios are illustrative teaching numbers from the source row, not independently checked against measured field data; the real ladder does not multiply by exactly ten at each step (roughly x12.5, x4, x12.5).

The source-row feeding narrative described only plankton->fish->bird while asserting a four-step 1/10/100/1000 climb; the chain has been stated as four levels (plankton, small fish, large fish, bird) so the meter readings are internally consistent with the ppm ladder.

The source row characterised a 3D environment as adding 'navigation without illuminating the multiplication'; this is retained only as a design rationale for choosing a concentration-focused representation, not as a universal claim that 3D cannot teach the concept.
Source-row language implying biomagnification 'must be watched multiplying to be believed' has been softened; a learner can also reason it through from figures and argument.
Error-pattern wording about toxins being 'diluted/spread thinner' is preserved as a misconception to correct, not as a fact.

probeDeeper: Why does it matter that this toxin doesn't break down or get excreted?
How is bioaccumulation different from a predator just eating one very poisonous meal?
DDT thinned peregrine eggshells — trace how DDT got from farm crops all the way into a falcon.
If the toxin DID break down quickly inside the body, would it still build up the chain? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The toxin does not break down and is not excreted, so it stays in each organism's body. Each animal eats many contaminated prey and keeps all of their toxin, so the concentration MULTIPLIES at each step up the chain (bioaccumulation/biomagnification). The osprey has effectively taken in the accumulated toxin of many fish, each of which ate many smaller organisms — so it carries the highest dose, even though the water is dilute.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The poison gets diluted / spread thinner as it goes up the chain.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reverse the intuition: the toxin doesn't disperse, it is retained and summed — a predator inherits the toxin of everything it eats, so it concentrates upward.
errorPatterns.distractor: The small fish are worst affected — the poison spreads out and gets weaker further up the chain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the small fish are worst hit because the toxin 'weakens' higher up.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Top predators are big and strong, so they cope best / are least affected.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Body size doesn't clear a persistent toxin; the top predator receives the summed dose of the whole chain, so it is most, not least, at risk.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the osprey should be safest because it is the largest, most powerful animal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the toxin only matters if the water concentration is high — misses accumulation over many meals and over time.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Route the toxin through food, not water: it enters at the bottom and is concentrated by feeding up the chain; reteach the feeding-relationship pathway.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the osprey 'must be drinking lots of the water', ignoring the feeding route.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the toxin dilutes upward or that top predators are safest; explains the sickness by the water concentration alone.
responseLevels.full: Explains bioaccumulation as a persistent, non-excreted toxin multiplying because each predator eats many contaminated prey, names the top predator as most at risk, supports it with a real case, and reasons about the break-down counterfactual.
responseLevels.partial: Knows toxins are 'worse at the top' and can name an example (DDT, mercury), but cannot explain the mechanism — states the fact without the persistence-plus-many-prey cause.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'A pesticide washes into a lake at a tiny concentration that is harmless in the water itself. Yet the fish-eating ospreys at the top of the food chain get sick and their eggs fail. How can the poison be harmless in the water but dangerous in the osprey — and why is it the top predator, not the small fish, that suffers most?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the toxin 'spreads out and weakens' or that big predators cope best predicts the small fish suffer most, or everyone equally. Correct reasoning invokes non-breakdown plus eating many prey → multiplication up the levels, putting the top predator at greatest risk.

pedagogy.summary: Extending the standard columnar algorithm to whole numbers with more than four digits. The procedure is identical to four-digit work — align by place value, compose on carrying, decompose on borrowing — but scale raises the stakes: subtraction from large round numbers (500,000 - 234,178) forces an exchange that ripples across many zeros, and adding three or more five-digit numbers produces carries greater than one. Estimation-first and inverse checking remain essential because a single misaligned digit is now worth thousands.
bestPractices: Reinforce that nothing new is happening — same exchange rule, just more columns — to prevent 'big numbers are different' anxiety
Estimate by rounding before computing so a place-value slip in the thousands/ten-thousands is caught
Deliberately include a subtraction from a round number with several zeros (the extended borrow-across-zero)
When adding three or more numbers, make the >1 carry explicit ('13 ones = 3, carry 1 ten... but this column totals 24, carry 2')
Use place-value headers / squared paper so five- and six-digit numbers stay aligned
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with headers to hundred-thousands
Base-ten / place-value counters for the exchange rationale
Empty number line for the estimate and for counting-up subtraction
Part-whole bar for multi-addend structure
commonMisconceptions: Extended borrow-across-zero fails — cannot cascade an exchange through several zeros (500,000 - 234,178)
Smaller-from-larger bug persists at larger scale
Misaligns digits when numbers have different lengths
When a column totals 20+ (three addends), carries only 1 instead of 2
Checks by redoing rather than estimating or using the inverse

learn.summary: Extend the standard columnar algorithm to whole numbers with more than four digits. The procedure is identical to four-digit work (align by place value, compose when carrying, decompose when borrowing), but larger scale raises the stakes: subtracting from a large round number such as 500,000 − 234,178 forces an exchange that cascades across several zeros, and adding three or more five-digit numbers can produce carries greater than one. Estimation-first and inverse checking matter more because a single misaligned digit is now worth thousands.

activities.title: Borrowing across a row of zeros (500,000 − 234,178)
feedback: If the child stalls at the zeros or does not carry the exchange through every column (e.g. 265,832, where the tens was left as 10 instead of 9, or 275,822, where the ten-thousands was left as 10 instead of 9), model with place-value counters: exchange one hundred-thousand and walk it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 with a ten passed on until the ones hold 10.
If a smaller digit is subtracted from a larger one regardless of position, do a concrete exchange on the failing column and reassert that you cannot take more than is there without borrowing.
If the child checks only by redoing the same subtraction, scaffold the estimate (round both numbers) and the inverse addition, or a counting-up number line, instead of reteaching the algorithm.
activities.rationale: Borrow-from-zero is a well-documented systematic subtraction bug that intensifies when a minuend has several adjacent zeros, so a deliberate round-number case targets the most-failed large-number hazard. A live place-value/counters model can animate the exchange as the child performs it; physical counters, squared paper, or a counting-up number line serve the same rationale without requiring a specific tool.
sourceClaims: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug (Brown & Burton, 1325 students, 107 occurrences): the student changes a 0 to 9 but fails to continue borrowing leftward. When a minuend has several adjacent zeros (e.g. 500,000) the exchange must cascade through them, and this zero-borrow bug intensifies; smaller-from-larger (54 students) persists at scale. These are stable procedural bugs — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour — not carelessness.
Composing/decomposing (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm regardless of digit count; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods.

Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Set out 500,000 − 234,178 in columns aligned by place value, from the ones on the right.
Before computing, estimate by rounding (about 500,000 − 234,000 = 266,000) and note the expected size of the answer.

At the ones there is nothing to take 8 from, and every column to the left is 0; work the exchange by taking one hundred-thousand and walking it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 as a ten is passed along, until the ones finally hold 10.
Complete the subtraction to get 265,822.
Check with the inverse: 265,822 + 234,178 should return 500,000, and compare to your estimate (~266,000).
Optionally model the same subtraction as counting up on an empty number line — jump from 234,178 up to 500,000 and total the jumps — as an independent alternative that should also give 265,822.
Optionally repeat with an easier round-number case such as 500,000 − 234,000 and discuss why that borrow is simpler.
activities.intendedInsight: A single exchange can cascade through a row of zeros — each zero becomes a 9 as the ten is passed along, and the ones finally hold 10 — so a wall of zeros is not a dead end.

activities.title: Adding three numbers of up to five digits: when the carry is more than one
feedback: If the child carries only 1 from a column totalling 20 or more (e.g. 9 + 8 + 7 = 24), total the column aloud, separate it into 4 ones and 2 tens, and make the size of the carry explicit.

If a three-number sum is too small by exactly one (or more) in the column just above a heavy column (e.g. 10 too small when the ones totalled 24 but only 1 was carried), this may point to an undersized carry. Recount that column and check how many tens it holds.
If numbers of different lengths are misaligned so place values don't line up, use squared paper or place-value headers anchored from the ones on the right.
activities.rationale: A child drilled only on two-addend sums tends to assume a carry is always 1; a three-addend column that totals into the twenties surfaces and corrects that assumption. The original diagnostic problem does not actually create such a column, so a correctly chosen example is used for the larger carry while the given problem still serves alignment and repeated-carry practice. A part-whole bar can make the multi-addend structure explicit. A fill-in-the-blank format on carried digits plus a rounded estimate can assess this at scale but cannot verify handwritten alignment, so paper setup should also be observed.
sourceClaims: Composing/decomposing (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm regardless of digit count; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods.

Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Set out 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 in a single column layout, aligning by place value from the ones on the right (numbers of different lengths must still line up); optionally show the three addends as parts of a part-whole bar whose whole is the total.
Add the ones column aloud and name the full total (0 + 6 + 8 = 14): write 4, carry 1.

Work through the rest of this sum: note that every carry here is only 1 (column totals including carries: tens 10, hundreds 11, thousands 16; the ten-thousands totals 3 with no carry), finishing at 36,104. This is good practice at keeping three different-length addends aligned and tracking repeated carries.

Now tackle a case that genuinely produces a larger carry, e.g. 36,489 + 27,858 + 15,937: the ones column totals 9 + 8 + 7 = 24, so write 4 and carry 2 (not 1); completing it gives 80,284, with several columns (ones, hundreds and thousands) carrying 2.
Compute 34,567 + 28,945 = 63,512 as a clean two-addend check that the basic algorithm is intact.
Estimate by rounding before computing so a place-value slip in the thousands or ten-thousands is caught.
activities.intendedInsight: When a column of three or more addends totals 20 or more, the carry can be 2 (or more), not automatically 1. (Not every three-addend sum reaches that — 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 only ever carries 1 — so a case whose column actually totals into the twenties is needed to surface the larger carry.)

activities.title: Worked-example reference and estimate-then-check routine
feedback: If the child's answer is far from the estimate, that gap is the signal to recheck alignment and exchanges (and quickly confirm the rounding in the estimate itself). Do not simply change the estimate to match the answer.
A revealed worked example is reference only; the child should then set out and solve a fresh case themselves on paper.
Praise specifically when the child catches their own error via estimate or inverse, reinforcing why that beats redoing the sum.
activities.rationale: Rounding-to-check is a statutory expectation and a reliable guard against single-digit place-value slips at scale; the inverse operation is independent of the original method, so it catches errors a re-run would reproduce. A revealed worked example is a useful static reference but exercises recognition rather than independent construction, so it must be paired with the child doing the work.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Study a tap-to-reveal or step-by-step worked example of the across-many-zeros borrow, revealing each 0-becomes-9 exchange in turn to see the cascade clearly.
For every large calculation, first write a rounded estimate, then compute, then compare the answer to the estimate.
Check subtractions with the inverse addition (or a counting-up number line) and additions with an estimate rather than by redoing the same calculation.

Answer prompts: roughly how big should 500,000 − 234,178 be before working it out? Why did all those zeros turn into 9s? Would 500,000 − 234,000 be easier to borrow, and why? Why carry 2 and not 1 when a three-addend column totals into the twenties?
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating first and checking by the inverse catch place-value slips that are now worth thousands; redoing the same method just reproduces the same error.

constraints: This is a doing-on-paper procedural skill: the child must actually set out and compute the algorithm, not only recognise or describe correct steps.
Reinforce that nothing new is happening — same exchange rule, just more columns — to prevent 'big numbers are different' anxiety.

Deliberately include at least one subtraction from a round number with several zeros (the extended borrow-across-zero) and at least one three-or-more-addend sum whose column genuinely totals 20 or more (so a carry of 2 actually occurs).
Use place-value headers or squared paper so five- and six-digit numbers of different lengths stay aligned from the ones on the right.
A fill-in-the-blank or slider-based quiz can check carried/borrowed digits and estimates but cannot verify handwritten alignment, so observe paper setup directly.
A tap-to-reveal worked example is a static scaffold exercising recognition; it supports but does not replace independent construction on paper.

Base-ten counters, an empty number line, and on-screen place-value models offer different experiences of the exchange; any can make the cascade or the structure concrete, and none is strictly required.
Checking must use estimation or the inverse operation (or an independent counting-up method), not a re-run of the same calculation.

ORIGINAL ERROR CORRECTED: the row's assess.correctAnswer/diagnostic states the three-addend sum 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 'carries 2 where a column totals 20+', but no column of this sum reaches 20 even with incoming carries (column totals 14, 10, 11, 16, 3) — it carries only 1 throughout. To actually demonstrate a carry of 2, an agent-proposed example 36,489 + 27,858 + 15,937 = 80,284 is used (ones 9+8+7=24, write 4 carry 2; self-audit: 36,489+27,858=64,347, 64,347+15,937=80,284; columns carrying 2 are ones, hundreds and thousands). This replacement example is an unvalidated agent proposal and was not independently verified.

Representations restored: the original row's empty number line (estimate / counting-up subtraction) and part-whole bar (multi-addend structure) were only implicit in the earlier draft and are now offered as explicit optional representations.

The original catalog rationale claimed a conversation 'cannot exercise' a written algorithm and that a third dimension 'adds nothing'. These are fit judgements, not pedagogical laws; softened to narrow affordances/limits (dialogue supports but does not substitute for doing it on paper; the task is planar, so a 3D model offers no clear added value here).
One source (NRICH place-value material; DfE Appendix 1) is marked verified:false / not fetched this session; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: Roughly how big should the answer to 500,000 - 234,178 be, before you work it out?
Why did all those zeros turn into 9s when you subtracted?
What if it had been 500,000 - 234,000 - would the borrowing be any easier?
When you added the three numbers, why did you carry 2 and not 1 from the ones column?
assess.correctAnswer: 34,567 + 28,945 = 63,512 (composes through the columns). 500,000 - 234,178 = 265,822, cascading one exchange through the zeros. The three-addend sum = 36,104, carrying 2 where a column totals 20+. Estimate for the subtraction approx 500,000 - 234,000 = 266,000, close to 265,822; inverse 265,822 + 234,178 = 500,000.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot cascade an exchange through several zeros in 500,000 - 234,178 - stalls, or borrows only one column and leaves the rest as 0/9 wrongly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model with place-value counters: exchange one hundred-thousand and walk it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 with a ten passed on.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Wrong middle digits (e.g. 265,882, 275,822) or the child freezes at the wall of zeros

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position (smaller-from-larger bug) at five-digit scale
errorPatterns.nextMove: Concrete exchange on the failing column; reassert you cannot take more than is there without borrowing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Columns 'flipped' wherever the top digit is smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: When the three-addend column totals 20 or more, carries only 1 instead of 2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Total the column aloud (13 + 8 + 6 = 24), separate into 4 ones and 2 tens; make the size of the carry explicit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The three-number sum is out by a multiple of ten in the next column up

errorPatterns.pattern: Misaligns digits when the numbers differ in length, so place values do not line up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Squared paper / place-value headers, anchored from the ones on the right.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Column setup on paper

errorPatterns.pattern: Checks by redoing the same subtraction rather than estimating or using the inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the estimate (round both) and the inverse addition; do not reteach the algorithm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The check reproduces the original method

responseLevels.gap: Misaligns, or breaks down at the row of zeros; carries only 1 from a 20+ column; no sense of the answer's size.
responseLevels.full: Solves all three including the zero-cascade subtraction and the double carry, aligns correctly, AND verifies with an estimate and the inverse; transfers to a similar round-number subtraction.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the clean addition and can describe the steps, but fails the across-many-zeros exchange or the >1 carry, or checks only by redoing and never estimates.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three to set out and solve on paper, watching alignment and exchange: 34,567 + 28,945; 500,000 - 234,178; and add these three in one column: 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058. Then ask them to check the subtraction by estimating and by the inverse.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 500,000 - 234,178 forces an exchange through five zeros - the extended borrow-across-zero, the most-failed large-number case. The three-addend column forces a carry greater than one, which a child drilled only on two-addend sums mishandles. The clean addition confirms the basic algorithm is intact, so failures localise to the scale-specific hazards.

sources.claim: Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 5, Number — addition and subtraction)

sources.claim: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug (Brown & Burton, 1325 students, 107 occurrences): the student changes a 0 to 9 but fails to continue borrowing leftward. When a minuend has several adjacent zeros (e.g. 500,000) the exchange must cascade through them, and this zero-borrow bug intensifies; smaller-from-larger (54 students) persists at scale. These are stable procedural bugs — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour — not carelessness.
sources.source: Brown & Burton, 'Diagnostic Models for Procedural Bugs in Basic Mathematical Skills', Cognitive Science 2(2), 1978 (full text: ERIC ED159036)

sources.claim: Composing/decomposing (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm regardless of digit count; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods.
sources.source: NRICH place-value / unitising material; DfE Mathematics Appendix 1 (not fetched this session)

pedagogy.summary: Estimating from a graph means reading a value the graph gives: an output y for a given input x, an approximate solution where a curve or line meets the x-axis or another graph, or a contextual quantity from a real-world graph. It is inherently APPROXIMATE — read to the nearest sensible interval, using the axis scale. It is best taught with an explicit 'up-and-across' reading routine, always stating the scale first, and treating crossing points (with the x-axis, or between two graphs) as solutions to be read and then checked.
bestPractices: Teach a consistent reading routine: find the given value on one axis, travel to the graph, then across to the other axis, drawing the path so it can be checked.
State the scale of each axis before reading, and read to the nearest sensible fraction of a grid square — an estimate, not false precision.
Treat x-axis crossings as approximate solutions of 'f(x) = 0', and the intersection of two graphs as values satisfying both.
For a parabola, look for TWO crossings (or one, or none) rather than stopping at the first.
Sense-check every read-off value against the context — its units and a realistic range.
keyRepresentations: 'Up and across' reading lines drawn onto the graph
x-axis crossings as roots/solutions; intersection of two graphs as a common solution
Real-world axes (distance-time, cost) with a clearly labelled scale
A read-off shown as a band ('between 2 and 2.5, about 2.25') rather than a single false-precise figure
commonMisconceptions: Reads against the wrong scale (assumes each square is one unit) or reads off the wrong axis.
Gives a single false-precise value instead of an estimate to a sensible interval.
Stops at the first x-axis crossing, missing a parabola's second root.
Confuses where a single line crosses an AXIS with where two graphs intersect each other.

learn.summary: Learners estimate values from plotted linear and quadratic graphs using a consistent 'up-and-across' reading routine: state the axis scale first, find the given value on one axis, travel to the graph, then across to read the other axis. Reading is inherently approximate — report to a sensible interval, not false precision. Treat x-axis crossings as approximate solutions of f(x)=0 (a parabola has two, one, or none), and the intersection of two graphs as a value satisfying both. Real-world graphs (distance–time, cost) are read for contextual quantities with attention to units and realistic range.

activities.title: Up-and-across reading with the scale stated first
feedback: If read-off values are halved or doubled relative to the labelled axis, state the scale aloud and count grid units deliberately before reading.
If a learner writes 'y = 2' as if exact, or an over-precise 'y = 2.247', model reading a band: 'between 2 and 2.5, so about 2.25' — the goal is a sensible estimate.
Ask: 'If the axis went up in 2s instead of 1s, would your answer change? Why?' to surface scale-dependence.
activities.rationale: Misinterpreting the axis scale (not noticing the interval each grid line represents) is a documented graph-reading difficulty, and giving false-precise values is a commonly reported (though, in this row, unverified) error; an explicit scale-first routine and an estimate-as-band habit are proposed to target both directly.
sourceClaims: Reading values from a graph and misinterpreting the axis scale (failing to notice the interval each grid line represents) are documented student difficulties, and real-world (distance-time) graphs must be read for contextual quantities.
KS3 pupils should 'use linear and quadratic graphs to estimate values of y for given values of x and vice versa and to find approximate solutions of simultaneous linear equations'.
learnerActions: Before reading anything, state aloud what one grid square represents on each axis (e.g. 'each square is 1 unit' or 'each square is 2 units').
For a plotted curve, draw a line up from a given x-value to the curve, then across to the y-axis, and record the estimated y.
Read a value to the nearest sensible fraction of a grid square, writing it as a band (e.g. 'between 2 and 2.5, about 2.25') rather than a single over-precise figure.
Re-read the same physical point after the grid interval changes (e.g. squares now worth 2) and note how the number changes while the point does not.
activities.intendedInsight: A read-off value depends on the axis scale, so checking the scale comes before trusting any number; a value between grid lines is an estimate given to a sensible interval, not an exact figure.

activities.title: Finding both roots of a parabola
feedback: If a learner gives only one x for 'y = 0', point to the other branch — 'does the curve meet the x-axis anywhere else?' — and use the symmetry; scaffold rather than reteach.
If a learner answers 'y = 0' with −4 or (0, −4) (the y-intercept), clarify: 'y = 0 means the height is zero — where does the curve actually meet the x-axis?' and mark that axis.
For y = 5, check both symmetric branches are given (e.g. x ≈ 3 and x ≈ −3).
activities.rationale: Missing a parabola's second symmetric root and confusing axis crossings are reported errors (the supporting source is marked unverified in the row); explicit symmetry prompts and a y=0-versus-y-intercept distinction are proposed to address them.
sourceClaims: Missing a parabola's second (symmetric) root when reading solutions, and giving false-precise single values instead of estimates, are common graph-reading errors.
KS3 pupils should 'use linear and quadratic graphs to estimate values of y for given values of x and vice versa and to find approximate solutions of simultaneous linear equations'.
learnerActions: On a parabola such as y = x² − 4, find every x-value where the curve meets the x-axis (where height = 0), not just the first one encountered.

Use the symmetry of the curve: after finding one crossing, look on the opposite branch for its partner (a parabola that only touches the x-axis at its vertex has just one, and one that never reaches the x-axis has none).
Given a target height (e.g. y = 5), find both symmetric x-values that reach it, and read each as an estimate.
Distinguish 'y = 0' (where the curve meets the x-axis) from the y-intercept (where the curve meets the y-axis, here −4).
activities.intendedInsight: 'Find where y = 0' can have two answers for a parabola, located symmetrically; stopping at the first crossing misses a root, and the x-axis crossings are different from the y-intercept.

activities.title: Intersections as shared solutions, and checking read-offs
feedback: If a learner confuses an axis crossing with a graph–graph intersection, label each explicitly on the diagram and ask which question each answers.
Prompt: 'If I asked where this curve meets the line y = x, how would you find that from the graph?' then check the substitution.
For real-world graphs, ask whether the answer's units and magnitude are realistic for the situation.
activities.rationale: Treating an intersection as the common solution and checking a read-off against the equation (because poor scale or unlabelled axes yield wrong reads) are documented practices; real-world interpretation is a stated curriculum aim.
sourceClaims: The intersection of two plotted graphs is read as the solution satisfying both; an inaccurately plotted graph (poor scale, unlabelled axes) yields a wrong read-off, so a read solution should be checked (Mia's graphical sample response).

Reading values from a graph and misinterpreting the axis scale (failing to notice the interval each grid line represents) are documented student difficulties, and real-world (distance-time) graphs must be read for contextual quantities.
learnerActions: Read the intersection point of two plotted graphs (e.g. a curve and the line y = x) as the value(s) satisfying both.
Distinguish where a single line crosses an axis from where two graphs cross each other.

After reading a solution from a graph, substitute it back to check that it approximately satisfies the equation(s) (both sides come out close, not necessarily exactly equal), especially when the plot may be inaccurately drawn.
Interpret a real-world graph (e.g. distance–time) to answer a contextual question, stating units and sense-checking against a realistic range.
activities.intendedInsight: An intersection of two graphs gives the value(s) common to both; a graphical read-off is approximate and can be wrong if the plot is inaccurate, so solutions should be checked and sense-checked against context.

constraints: Report read-offs as estimates to a sensible interval (a band), not false-precise single values; the task is approximation using the axis scale.
State each axis scale before reading; do not assume one square equals one unit.

A static graph with pre-drawn read-off lines can demonstrate the routine but does not let the learner perform the reading across many different values, so pair any worked reference with active reading practice.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. multiple-choice on 'how many solutions') can check understanding of root count but do not by themselves elicit the learner drawing and executing the up-and-across reading; include tasks where the learner produces the reading lines and values.

An interactive draggable marker is one way to rehearse the routine and make dual roots salient; it is an optional scaffold, not a requirement — the same routine can be taught with pencil-and-paper reading lines on a printed graph.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched this session, and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claim about missing a parabola's second root and false-precise values is marked verified:false in the row; treat it as a plausible but unconfirmed documented error (used in activities 1 and 2) and do not overstate its evidentiary strength.

The legacy row asserted '3D adds nothing' and that 'an open dialogue cannot rehearse the act of reading off a graph'; these are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened — reading plotted graphs is a planar task well served by 2D representations, while discussion can still support reasoning about scale, symmetry and checking, even though it does not itself execute the reading.
Self-audit of worked values for y = x² − 4: at x = 2.5, y = 2.25 (6.25 − 4), consistent with 'about 2.2–2.3'; y = 0 at x = ±2; y = 5 at x = ±3 (9 − 4). These are arithmetically correct and retained.

The KS3 claim supports both estimating y for a given x (activity 1) and reading x for a given y — including y = 0 roots and y = 5 — through its explicit 'and vice versa' wording, so its retention in activities 1 and 2 is on-principle, not merely topical.
The interactive 'live highlighting of crossing points' and 'scale toggle' are preserved as optional mechanism examples, not mandated features.

probeDeeper: You read y at x = 2.5. If the axis went up in 2s instead of 1s, would your answer change? Why?
You found x = 2 gives y = 0. Is there another x that also gives y = 0? How does the shape of the curve tell you?
How sure are you of that value — could you write it as a range rather than a single number?
If I asked you where this curve meets the line y = x, how would you find that from the graph?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) y ≈ 2.25 (read up from x = 2.5 to the curve, then across — about 2.2–2.3). (b) x = −2 AND x = 2 — both crossings of the x-axis. (c) x ≈ 3 and x ≈ −3 — the curve reaches height 5 on both branches. Values are read as estimates to a sensible interval, using the stated scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops at the first crossing, missing the second root ('y = 0 when x = 2')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the other branch — 'does the curve sit on the x-axis anywhere else?' — and use the symmetry; scaffold rather than reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives only x = 2 for part (b), or only one x for part (c), ignoring the symmetric partner.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads against the wrong scale, treating each square as one unit when the axis says otherwise
errorPatterns.nextMove: State the scale aloud before each read and count grid units deliberately.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Read-off values are inconsistent with the labelled axis — e.g. halved or doubled.

errorPatterns.pattern: Insists on a single exact value, refusing to give an estimate or a range for a point between grid lines
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model reading a band ('between 2 and 2.5, so about 2.25'); the goal is a sensible estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 'y = 2' as if exact, or an over-precise 'y = 2.247', ignoring that the reading lies between grid lines.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads off the wrong axis / crossing: for 'y = 0' gives the y-intercept (−4, where the curve meets the y-axis) instead of the x-axis crossings
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify 'y = 0 means the height is zero — where does the curve actually sit ON the x-axis?'; mark that axis.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers part (b) with −4 or (0, −4) rather than x = ±2.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot execute the up-and-across reading, reads the wrong axis, or ignores the scale; gives one root only.
responseLevels.full: Reads outputs to a sensible estimate on the correct scale, finds BOTH roots using symmetry, can read an intersection/solution, and states appropriate precision — transferring the reading routine to a new value and to an intersection of two graphs.
responseLevels.partial: Reads single output values correctly using the scale, but stops at one root or treats an estimate as exact — performs individual reads without coordinating symmetry or approximation across the whole task.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is the graph of y = x² − 4, drawn on axes where each square is one unit. Using the graph and showing your reading lines each time: (a) what is y when x = 2.5? (b) for which values of x is y = 0? (c) roughly what is x when y = 5?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Part (a) shows whether the child reads up-and-across on the correct scale; part (b) separates those who give BOTH roots from those who stop at one; part (c) exposes whether they recognise two symmetric x-values and offer an estimate rather than a false-precise number. Watching the reading lines, not asking about the method, is what reveals the procedure.

sources.source: Mathematics Assessment Project, 'Solving Linear Equations in Two Variables' — teacher guide (Mia sample response)
