pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 7–9 — the ocean floor is not flat: it has mountains, ridges, valleys and the deepest trenches on Earth; the deepest point (Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench) is deeper than Mount Everest is tall.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 geography physical features and the water/landscape strand; complements Y3 rocks and KS2 mountains/volcanoes.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 2-ESS2-2 / 4-ESS2-2 (map land and water features, including the shapes and kinds of land and ocean-floor features) — the seafloor has varied terrain like the land.
• Operational details: two ideas — (1) the seafloor has VARIED terrain (underwater mountains/ridges, plains, and deep trenches), mirroring dry land; (2) a jaw-dropping SCALE anchor: the Mariana Trench's Challenger Deep (~10,935 m per NOAA) is deeper than Everest (8,848 m) is tall — drop Everest into the trench and its peak still sits ~2 km underwater. The scale comparison is the memorable hook; the varied-terrain idea corrects 'the seabed is a flat sandy bottom'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7–8): states the seafloor has mountains and deep trenches, not just flat sand; Tier B (~8–9): names the Mariana Trench as the deepest point; Tier C (~9): uses a scale comparison (Everest would still be underwater) to convey how deep it is.
bestPractices: Correct the flat-seabed image directly with a to-scale seafloor profile showing ridges, plains and a plunging trench.
Anchor the extreme depth with a concrete, verifiable comparison children can picture: Everest (8,848 m) placed in Challenger Deep (~10,935 m) is still ~2 km short of the surface.
Draw the land–sea parallel: the seafloor has the same kinds of features as dry land (mountains, valleys) — it's just hidden under water.
Use accurate NOAA depth figures while noting measurement is hard (numbers vary slightly) — a light lesson that science measurements carry uncertainty.
Connect forward: this varied, deep terrain is where deep-sea creatures live and why exploring it is so hard (links to the 9–11 topics).
keyRepresentations: A to-scale seafloor cross-section: continental shelf → slope → abyssal plain → ridge → trench
A vertical scale comparison: Mount Everest inverted inside the Mariana Trench
Labelled feature call-outs (ridge, seamount, trench, plain)
A depth ruler in metres marking the sunlight zone at top vs Challenger Deep at bottom
commonMisconceptions: 'The ocean floor is a flat, sandy bottom' — missing its mountains, ridges and trenches.
'The ocean is the same depth everywhere' — not knowing depth varies enormously.
'Mount Everest is the biggest vertical feature on Earth' — the Mariana Trench is deeper than Everest is tall.
Confusing the deep TRENCH (a narrow gash) with the ocean being uniformly that deep everywhere.
'Nothing could be under that much water' — not yet knowing life exists even in the deepest trenches (sets up deep-sea topics).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: the ocean floor is not a flat sandy bottom but a hidden landscape of mountains, mid-ocean ridges, flat abyssal plains, tall seamounts and deep trenches — resembling kinds of features also found on dry land. The memorable scale anchor is that the Mariana Trench's Challenger Deep (~10,935 m per NOAA) is deeper than Mount Everest (8,848 m) is tall, so Everest dropped into the trench would still have its summit roughly 2 km underwater. Learners should finish able to state the seafloor has varied terrain, name the Mariana Trench as the deepest point, and use the Everest comparison to convey how deep that is.

activities.title: Tap across a to-scale seafloor profile
feedback: If a learner predicts a flat or gently sloping 'bathtub' floor, trace the real profile with them: shallow shelf, then deep plain, then a ridge rising in the middle, with the deepest trenches off to the sides near edges and island arcs.
If a learner thinks the deepest part is right in the middle, point out that the mid-ocean RIDGE is actually shallower and the deepest trenches lie away from the centre.
Reinforce correct feature-naming by linking each one to its land counterpart (seamount ≈ volcanic mountain, trench ≈ deep narrow valley).
activities.rationale: Countering the flat-seabed image with a labelled to-scale profile lets children see and name the varied terrain, which is the first evidence goal. A tap-to-name interaction may make the land–sea resemblance concrete but is not evidenced as superior to other formats. An optional 'drop Everest in' control (see next activity) and feature call-outs make the scale tangible without being required. The land–sea equivalence rests on a source marked unverified, so it is presented as resemblance rather than strict equivalence.
sourceClaims: The ocean floor is not flat — it has mid-ocean ridges, mountains (seamounts), abyssal plains and deep trenches, mirroring the kinds of features found on land.
learnerActions: Before seeing the profile, predict aloud what the bare seabed would look like if all the water drained away — flat and smooth, or varied? Then study a wide to-scale cross-section running from the shore outward across an ocean basin: continental shelf → slope → abyssal plain with seamounts → mid-ocean ridge → abyssal plain → a deep trench near the far edge, beside an island arc.
Tap or point to each feature in turn (ridge, seamount, abyssal plain, trench) and say its name and one fact about it.
Check your earlier prediction against the profile: is the bare seabed flat and smooth, or varied? Say what surprised you.
Compare each undersea feature to a land feature it resembles (undersea mountain range, deep valley) and state that the seafloor has similar kinds of features to dry land, just hidden underwater.
activities.intendedInsight: The ocean floor has varied terrain — mountains, ridges, plains and deep trenches — not a uniform flat sandy bottom, and these resemble landforms found on land.

activities.title: Drop Everest into the trench
feedback: If a learner underestimates the scale (guessing the trench is a few hundred metres, or that undersea mountains are little bumps), use the overlay: Everest's whole height disappears into the trench with about 2 km to spare.
If a learner confuses the narrow trench with the whole ocean being that deep everywhere, clarify that the trench is a narrow gash — most of the seafloor is far shallower, with vast plains and ridges.
Note that measuring such depth is hard, so the exact numbers vary slightly between sources — a gentle reminder that science measurements carry uncertainty.
activities.rationale: A to-scale vertical comparison delivers the scale insight as a single memorable image and supports the depth-comparison evidence goal. The depth ruler and inverted-Everest overlay are concrete examples that make the quantity visible; they are offered as examples, not mandated.
sourceClaims: The deepest known point in the ocean is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, at approximately 10,935 metres (35,876 ft) below sea level (NOAA, citing Greenaway et al. 2021).
The Challenger Deep is deeper than Mount Everest (8,848 m) is tall — by roughly 2 km — so Everest placed in the trench would have its summit about 2 km underwater.
learnerActions: Look at a vertical depth ruler marked in metres, with the sunlit surface zone at top and Challenger Deep at the bottom.
Place (or trigger a 'drop Everest in' control that places) Mount Everest upright, with its base on the floor of Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, beside the ruler.
Read where Everest's summit stops and state that it is still roughly 2 km below the surface — the mountain is fully drowned.
Answer: which is greater, Everest's height (8,848 m) or the trench's depth (~10,935 m)? Then say the deepest point of the ocean is deeper than the highest mountain is tall.
Name the Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep) as the deepest point on Earth.
activities.intendedInsight: Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench (~10,935 m) is deeper than Mount Everest (8,848 m) is tall, so Everest would still sit about 2 km underwater — a memorable way to grasp how deep the ocean's deepest point is.

activities.title: Fly or dive to the deepest point (enrichment)
feedback: If the learner loses track of scale, pause at the 8,848 m marker and note the trench floor is still ~2 km further down.
Tie the journey back to the whole-profile view so the single vertical drop is understood as one narrow part of a varied landscape.
activities.rationale: A spatial flythrough or dive offers a three-dimensional view of relief and depth that a flat profile shows less directly, and the descent dramatises the Everest milestone. This is enrichment because the core facts are already met by the cross-section and depth comparison; a single vertical dive shows depth well, while a whole-profile view better shows terrain variety. Efficacy of the 3D medium over the profile is not established by the listed sources.
learnerActions: Travel along the seafloor in a flythrough or a descending submersible: skim an underwater mountain range, cross the flat abyssal plain, then plunge into the Mariana Trench.
Watch a live depth readout and call out when it passes 8,848 m — the 'Everest height' milestone — on the way down to ~10,935 m at the trench floor.
Describe aloud how the relief and depth change along the journey, and how far past the Everest milestone the descent continues.
activities.intendedInsight: Seafloor terrain is genuinely three-dimensional; travelling over ridges and down into the trench can convey relief and the depth of the descent, reinforcing the varied-terrain and scale ideas.

activities.title: Check and explain the seafloor
feedback: A gap response pictures a flat or simple-bowl seabed and names no features — reteach with the cross-section and feature names.
A partial response names features (ridge, trench, shelf) as a list but can't say how big they are or why they're there — prompt for scale and shaping process.

A full response describes a varied floor, grasps that the Mariana Trench is deeper than Everest is tall, and appeals to Earth processes (volcanoes, moving crust) to explain the relief, even predicting where deep or shallow zones lie.
activities.rationale: Short questions check all three evidence goals (terrain variety, naming the trench, scale comparison), and the 'why is it shaped that way' prompt separates 'water settles flat' from 'the crust itself is mountainous'. Recognition items confirm the facts but do not by themselves elicit an independent explanation, so the construct-an-explanation and drained-ocean prompts are included.
learnerActions: Answer: is the seafloor flat, or does it have varied terrain? Give at least one feature to support your answer.
Name the deepest point on Earth (the Mariana Trench / Challenger Deep).
Compare: which is greater, Mount Everest's height or the Mariana Trench's depth?

Explain WHY the seabed is shaped this way — its mountains, ridges and trenches are made and moved by the same Earth forces (moving crust, volcanoes) that build mountains and volcanoes on land. Water does not level the whole floor flat, though mud slowly settling on the bottom does help make the abyssal plains flat.
Respond to the drained-ocean prompt: 'A child says the bare seabed would be flat and smooth like a giant bathtub, maybe sloping a bit. Do you agree? What would we actually walk over, and why?'
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state the seafloor has varied terrain, name the Mariana Trench as the deepest point, use the Everest comparison, and begin to explain the relief as the result of Earth's crustal and volcanic processes rather than water levelling.

constraints: Use accurate figures (Challenger Deep ~10,935 m per NOAA; Everest ~8,848 m, officially 8,848.86 m since 2020) and note openly that deep-ocean measurement is hard, so figures vary slightly between sources.
Distinguish the narrow deep TRENCH from the ocean being uniformly that deep everywhere — most of the seafloor is far shallower, with plains and ridges.
A to-scale cross-section is a flat picture representing a 3D undersea landscape; keep the land–sea resemblance explicit so learners read it as terrain, not decoration.

Recognition/multiple-choice items confirm the three facts but do not on their own show the learner can independently explain WHY the seabed is shaped that way; include at least one construct-an-explanation task.

The 'why' explanation (crustal/volcanic processes) reaches beyond simply naming features and depends on prerequisite ideas about how mountains and volcanoes form; treat it as a stretch for the oldest/most ready learners.
Keeping the deepest-life idea (that creatures live even in the deepest trenches) available sets up later deep-sea topics, but is a forward link rather than a required outcome here.
Do not assert that any one medium (profile, 3D flythrough, dive or dialogue) uniquely teaches this content; the 3D options are qualified enrichment, not evidenced as superior.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of figures: Everest 8,848 m vs Challenger Deep ~10,935 m gives a difference of ~2,087 m ≈ 2 km, consistent with the 'summit about 2 km underwater' claim. The comparison question (which is greater: Everest's height or the trench's depth?) is correct with the trench being deeper.

The source claim that the seafloor mirrors land features is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited in activity 1 to support terrain variety and used only as resemblance. Strict land–sea equivalence should be confirmed before asserting it, and the summary was softened to 'resembling' for consistency.

The 'shaping process' explanation (crust/volcanoes build the seabed, not water levelling) appears in the assessment fields but is not directly backed by the listed sources; it is pedagogically sound but included as a stretch and flagged for source confirmation.

Non-preferred alternatives (3D flythrough, 2D dive-the-sub) are preserved as enrichment with their stated limitation that a single vertical descent shows depth well but terrain variety is better shown by a whole-profile view; their medium efficacy relative to the profile is not source-supported, so their rationale is qualified and sourceClaims left [].

probeDeeper: If the seabed had mountains and valleys, why can't we usually see them from a boat on the surface?
What could build a mountain range or a deep trench down on the seabed, where there's no rain or rivers?
The Mariana Trench is about 11 km deep and Everest is about 8.8 km tall. If you dropped Everest into the trench, would its peak stick out of the water?
Why is the middle of the Atlantic actually shallower (a ridge) rather than deepest?
assess.correctAnswer: The ocean floor is not flat — it has the biggest mountains, deepest valleys and longest ranges on Earth: gently sloping continental shelves near land, vast flat plains, huge undersea mountain chains (mid-ocean ridges), tall volcanic seamounts, and deep narrow trenches. The Mariana Trench is deeper than Mount Everest is tall. It's shaped this way because the seabed is made and moved by the same forces that build mountains and volcanoes on land, not by water settling flat.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The seabed is flat and smooth like a bathtub bottom' — assumes water covers a level surface.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a shaded-relief map or a cross-section profile of an ocean basin; point out a ridge, a trench and a seamount and compare their heights to land mountains.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the bottom would be flat and smooth, maybe sloping gently, like an empty bathtub.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a smooth floor; cannot name ridges, trenches or seamounts; may say it just slopes gently down and stays flat.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The deepest part is right in the middle' or 'gets steadily deeper the further out you go' — treats depth as a simple bowl.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace a real profile: shallow shelf, then deep plain, then a ridge rising in the middle, with the deepest trenches off to the sides.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — it just gets deeper and deeper toward the middle, like a bowl.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the middle of the ocean is deepest; surprised that a mid-ocean RIDGE is shallow and that the deepest trenches are near edges/island arcs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Underestimates the scale — thinks undersea features are small compared with land ones.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay Everest inside the Mariana Trench to show the trench is deeper than Everest is tall; the mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Guesses the deepest trench is a few hundred metres, or that undersea mountains are little bumps.

responseLevels.gap: Pictures a flat, smooth or simple-bowl seabed; names no features and gives no shaping process.
responseLevels.full: Describes a varied floor (shelf, plain, ridge, seamount, trench), grasps the scale (Mariana deeper than Everest is tall), and explains the relief as made by Earth's crustal/volcanic processes — transferring to predict where deep or shallow zones lie.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the seabed has features and can name some (ridge, trench, shelf) but treats them as a list and can't explain why they're there or how big they are.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Imagine we drained all the water out of the ocean and could walk across the bare seabed. A child says 'it would be flat and smooth, like the bottom of a giant bathtub, maybe sloping down a bit'. Do you think that's what we'd find — and if not, what would we walk over, and why is it shaped that way?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the bathtub picture predicts a smooth featureless floor and has no landforms to name; a child with the concept names varied features and appeals to Earth processes (volcanoes, moving crust) rather than to water levelling everything out. Asking WHY it's shaped that way separates 'water settles flat' from 'the crust itself is mountainous'.

sources.claim: The deepest known point in the ocean is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, at approximately 10,935 metres (35,876 ft) below sea level (NOAA, citing Greenaway et al. 2021).
sources.source: NOAA National Ocean Service — How deep is the ocean? (page fetched and confirmed)

sources.claim: The Challenger Deep is deeper than Mount Everest (8,848 m) is tall — by roughly 2 km — so Everest placed in the trench would have its summit about 2 km underwater.
sources.source: Greenaway et al. 2021 (NOAA-cited peer-reviewed study) / NOAA comparison (fetched and confirmed)

sources.claim: The ocean floor is not flat — it has mid-ocean ridges, mountains (seamounts), abyssal plains and deep trenches, mirroring the kinds of features found on land.
sources.source: NOAA Ocean Exploration — seafloor features / NGSS 4-ESS2-2

pedagogy.summary: Generating sequences at KS3 extends the KS2 term-to-term idea to a second, more powerful engine: the position-to-term (nth-term) rule, which gives any term directly from its position. The concept is best taught by contrasting the two rules on the same sequence — term-to-term chains from the previous term, position-to-term substitutes the position number into a formula such as 3n−2 — and by classifying sequences as arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or neither by explicitly testing the differences and the ratios.
bestPractices: Generate the same sequence two ways (term-to-term and position-to-term) so pupils see they describe the same numbers, and that position-to-term reaches the 50th term without listing the first 49.
Require pupils to generate a position-to-term rule by substituting n = 1, 2, 3, … , not by treating the formula as a term-to-term instruction.
Classify by writing the successive differences AND the successive ratios underneath: a constant difference means arithmetic, a constant ratio means geometric, neither means 'other'.
Explicitly contrast 'multiples of 3' (3n) with 'increases by 3' (e.g. 3n−2) so pupils see a sequence that increases by 3 need not contain multiples of 3.
Use a varied diet — increasing, decreasing, decimal, geometric and 'neither' — to prevent an only-increasing over-generalisation.
keyRepresentations: Position-to-term table (positions n=1,2,3,4 above; terms below)
Dual display: term-to-term arrows vs position-to-term substitution
Differences row and ratios row written under a sequence
Graph of terms against position (constant difference = constant steepness)
commonMisconceptions: Treating a position-to-term rule as a term-to-term instruction (reading 3n−2 as 'start at 3, subtract 2'), so the first term is wrong.
Classifying by 'it goes up' alone, failing to distinguish arithmetic from geometric or to spot a non-constant difference (1, 4, 9, 16).
Confusing 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3'.
Assuming a later term can be reached by multiplying an earlier one (10th term = 2 × 5th term).

learn.summary: KS3 pupils extend the KS2 term-to-term idea to the position-to-term (nth-term) rule, which gives any term directly from its position. The core moves: generate the SAME sequence two ways (chaining from the previous term vs substituting n=1,2,3,… into a formula like 3n−2); and classify sequences as arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or other by explicitly writing the successive differences AND successive ratios. Key pitfalls to address: reading 3n−2 as a term-to-term instruction ('start at 3, subtract 2'), classifying by 'it goes up' alone, and confusing 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3'.

activities.title: Dual-engine generator: the same sequence built two ways
feedback: If a position rule is being applied term-to-term, flag the first-term mismatch: write n=1 explicitly and substitute into 3n−2 to show the first term should be 1 (3×1−2=1), not 3.
When the learner jumps to the 50th term, contrast the instant position-to-term result with the slow term-to-term chain to make the efficiency concrete.
When the coefficient is dragged, show the inter-term step updating live so 'coefficient = common difference' is visible rather than asserted.
activities.rationale: Generating the same sequence two ways and contrasting the cost of reaching a distant term targets the statutory 'generate terms from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule' and is intended to address the misconception of reading a position rule as a term-to-term instruction. A position→term table and live coefficient linking are intended to make the mechanism concrete. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory Algebra: 'generate terms of a sequence from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule'; 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term'; 'recognise geometric sequences and appreciate other sequences that arise'.

The nth term is new learning at KS3; a sequence can be generated by a term-to-term OR a position-to-term rule and pupils should progress from one to the other. Pupils confuse 'multiples of three' with 'numbers which increase by three' (Example 6), and must be taught to attend to the position of a term rather than the term-to-term rule (Example 7b/7c — 'Liam' claims −5, 0, 5, 10, 15 is '5n' because it increases by 5). An arithmetic sequence adds/subtracts a constant amount; the coefficient of n equals the common difference.
learnerActions: Build a sequence term-to-term: set a start value and an operation (e.g. start at 1, add 3) and generate the chain one step at a time.
Build the same sequence position-to-term: type a rule such as 3n−2 and substitute n=1,2,3,4,5 to light up each term under its position.
Switch a sequence between the two modes and confirm the numbers are identical.
Press 'jump to the 50th term': in position-to-term mode the answer for 3n−2 appears at once; in term-to-term mode the machine visibly grinds through the 49 predecessors first.
Drag the coefficient of n in 3n−2 and watch the inter-term step change to match, so the coefficient is seen to equal the common difference.
activities.intendedInsight: A term-to-term rule chains from the previous term; a position-to-term rule substitutes the position number into a formula and so reaches any term (e.g. the 50th) directly without listing the earlier ones. In a linear rule such as 3n−2 (of the form an + b), the coefficient of n equals the common difference.

activities.title: Classify by writing differences AND ratios
feedback: If a learner calls 1, 4, 9, 16 arithmetic, point to its differences 3, 5, 7 — not constant — and to its non-constant ratios, so it is 'other'.
Reveal the differences and ratios rows on demand so the row that stays constant names the type.
If the learner checks only differences, prompt them to also write the ratios before deciding geometric vs other.
When the learner builds their own sequence, ask them to show which row stays constant so the type they claim is evidenced.
activities.rationale: Requiring both a differences row and a ratios row operationalises classification and is intended to counter the 'classify by direction' misconception and the failure to separate arithmetic from geometric. The 1, 4, 9, 16 example makes a changing difference visible on the differences row, and asking for a constructed example practises the production skill named in the assessment.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory Algebra: 'generate terms of a sequence from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule'; 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term'; 'recognise geometric sequences and appreciate other sequences that arise'.
learnerActions: For each sequence, write the row of successive differences and the row of successive ratios underneath it.
Sort sequences into arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or other (neither constant).
Work the worked set: 5, 8, 11, 14 (arithmetic, difference +3); 2, 6, 18, 54 (geometric, ratio ×3); 1, 4, 9, 16 (other — differences 3, 5, 7 not constant, ratios not constant).
State explicitly which row you checked to make each decision, so classification is a test rather than a guess.

Construct your own sequence of a requested type (for example a geometric sequence that starts at 5, with a ratio other than 1) and verify it with the differences and ratios rows. Note that a constant sequence such as 5, 5, 5 has both a constant difference (0) and a constant ratio (1), so it is both arithmetic and geometric.
activities.intendedInsight: A sequence is arithmetic when the successive differences are constant and geometric when the successive ratios are constant; 'it goes up' is not enough, because 1, 4, 9, 16 increases but has a changing difference. The same differences/ratios test can be used to build and check a sequence of a requested type.

activities.title: 'Multiples of 3' versus 'increases by 3'
feedback: If the learner expects 3n−2 to produce multiples of 3, line up 3n and 3n−2 so both increase by 3 but only one hits the multiples.
If they are surprised 1, 4, 7, 10 contains no multiples of 3, confirm the common difference is still +3.
activities.rationale: Side-by-side generation of 3n and 3n−2 targets the specific documented confusion between 'multiples of three' and 'numbers which increase by three'.
sourceClaims: The nth term is new learning at KS3; a sequence can be generated by a term-to-term OR a position-to-term rule and pupils should progress from one to the other. Pupils confuse 'multiples of three' with 'numbers which increase by three' (Example 6), and must be taught to attend to the position of a term rather than the term-to-term rule (Example 7b/7c — 'Liam' claims −5, 0, 5, 10, 15 is '5n' because it increases by 5). An arithmetic sequence adds/subtracts a constant amount; the coefficient of n equals the common difference.
learnerActions: Generate 3n (3, 6, 9, 12, …) and 3n−2 (1, 4, 7, 10, …) side by side.
Check each sequence against the 3-times table and record which terms are multiples of 3.
Explain why 1, 4, 7, 10 increases by 3 yet contains no multiples of 3.
activities.intendedInsight: A sequence that increases by 3 need not be the multiples-of-3 sequence; the constant difference (+3) and membership of the 3-times table are different properties.

activities.title: Which rule reaches the 50th term faster, and why? (discussion)
feedback: If a learner claims the 10th term is twice the 5th, have them generate both terms of, say, 3n−2 and compare: 3×5−2=13 and 3×10−2=28, which is not 2×13=26.
Surface the efficiency argument by comparing the work needed for each method to reach term 50.
activities.rationale: A Socratic efficiency discussion can surface why the nth-term rule matters and is intended to address the misconception that later terms are simple multiples of earlier ones. This is a complement to the generator, which demonstrates the efficiency directly.
learnerActions: Discuss with a partner (or a questioning prompt): to find the 50th term of 3n−2, which rule gets you there faster — term-to-term or position-to-term — and why?
Articulate that substitution reaches any term directly while chaining requires all earlier terms.

Challenge the claim '10th term = 2 × 5th term' and test it against an actual arithmetic sequence with a nonzero constant term, such as 3n−2. Then notice that it does happen to hold for 3n, so one example that works does not prove the general claim.
activities.intendedInsight: The position-to-term rule is powerful because it gives any term directly; you cannot in general reach a later term by multiplying an earlier one (doubling the 5th term does not in general give the 10th: it fails for 3n−2, although it happens to work for rules with no constant term, such as 3n).

activities.title: Practice set: generate, fill and match
feedback: Mark substitution errors by checking against n=1,2,3; a wrong first term may flag a term-to-term misreading (e.g. giving 3 as the first term of 3n−2), but it could also be a simple arithmetic slip.
For sorting errors, prompt the learner back to the differences/ratios rows.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, fill-in and matching map cleanly onto the required procedures and give retrieval practice. This set scores answers and supports fluency, but on its own it does not build the two-engines insight, which the generator and discussion are intended to build.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory Algebra: 'generate terms of a sequence from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule'; 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term'; 'recognise geometric sequences and appreciate other sequences that arise'.
learnerActions: Generate the first five terms of a position-to-term rule such as 3n−2 by substitution (fill in the blanks).
Sort a mixed set of sequences into arithmetic / geometric / other.
Match each nth-term rule to the sequence it produces.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency in substituting positions into a rule and in categorising sequences by the correct test.

constraints: Use a varied diet — increasing, decreasing, decimal, geometric and 'neither' sequences — to prevent an only-increasing over-generalisation.
Require pupils to generate a position-to-term rule by substituting n=1,2,3,… , not by treating the formula as a term-to-term instruction.
The practice/quiz set gives retrieval practice and scoring but does not by itself build the position-vs-term-to-term insight; pair it with generation and discussion.
A static side-by-side reference of the two rule types is a useful worked example but cannot recompute for a learner's own rule; treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main generative task.
Interaction examples (mode switching, jump-to-50th button, coefficient dragging, live differences/ratios rows) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched and 'verified':true is legacy. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy is untested.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic checks): 3n−2 for n=1..5 gives 1,4,7,10,13 — consistent across the row. 2,6,18,54 has ratio ×3 — correct. 1,4,9,16 has differences 3,5,7 (non-constant) and non-constant ratios — correctly classified as 'other'. The claim '10th term = 2 × 5th term' is a listed misconception; it is used only as something to challenge/disprove (for 3n−2: 5th=13, 10th=28, and 2×13=26≠28) and never as a valid rule.

Residual untested-efficacy wording in activities[4].rationale ('which the generator and discussion provide') and activities[3].rationale ('addresses the misconception') was softened to 'intended to build'/'intended to address' for consistency with the proposal (not validated) framing.

The source line 'a 3D rendering adds nothing' was treated as a catalog preference, not a universal law; the 3D alternative was omitted (sequence generation is non-spatial, so 3D is not required here) rather than propagated as a pedagogical rule.
The original 'scoring answers does not build the two-engines insight' was scoped to 'supports fluency but not, on its own, the insight' rather than an absolute 'a quiz only assesses' claim.

A construct-a-sequence-of-requested-type action was added to the classification activity to preserve the assessed production skill (responseLevels.full / probeDeeper); recognition and generation alone do not elicit this production.

Activity 2 cites only the statutory recognise-claim; the NCETM 'arithmetic adds/subtracts a constant amount; coefficient of n equals the common difference' claim also supports its differences test, but was not copied there to avoid importing unrelated content. Reviewers may add it if a tighter citation is wanted.
The pedagogy keyRepresentation 'graph of terms against position (constant difference = constant steepness)' was not carried into an activity and could optionally be added.

probeDeeper: For 3n − 2, what is the 10th term — and did you have to write out all ten to get it?
Your sequence 5, 8, 11, 14 — is it arithmetic or geometric, and what exactly did you check to decide?
1, 4, 9, 16 goes up by more each time. Does 'it goes up' make it arithmetic? What is different about it compared with 5, 8, 11, 14?
Give me a geometric sequence that starts with 5 — how did you build it?
assess.correctAnswer: 3n−2 gives 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 (substituting n = 1,2,3,4,5). 5, 8, 11, 14 is arithmetic (constant difference +3); 2, 6, 18, 54 is geometric (constant ratio ×3); 1, 4, 9, 16 is neither (differences 3, 5, 7 — not constant; ratios not constant). The child decides by checking the successive differences and the successive ratios.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies the position rule as a term-to-term instruction — reads 3n−2 as 'start at 3, subtract 2' and writes 3, 1, −1, … instead of substituting n.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Write n = 1, 2, 3 explicitly and substitute each into 3n−2 under its position; use a position→term table so the formula is read as 'multiply the position by 3, then subtract 2'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The first term is not 1; the terms do not match a substitution check for n = 1, 2, 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies by 'it goes up' alone — calls 1, 4, 9, 16 arithmetic because it increases, or cannot tell geometric from arithmetic.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child write the differences row and the ratios row under each sequence; the row that stays constant names the type, and if neither is constant it is 'other'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sorts by direction rather than by a constant difference vs a constant ratio; misses that 1, 4, 9, 16 has a changing difference (3, 5, 7).

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3' — expects 3n−2 to produce multiples of 3, or expects any '+3' sequence to be the 3-times table.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Generate 3n (3, 6, 9, …) and 3n−2 (1, 4, 7, …) side by side; both increase by 3 but only one is the multiples sequence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Checks terms against the 3-times table, or is surprised that 1, 4, 7, 10 increases by 3 yet contains no multiples of 3.

responseLevels.gap: Generates 3n−2 wrongly (applies it term-to-term or gets the first term wrong) and sorts sequences by 'goes up/down' without checking a difference or a ratio.
responseLevels.full: Generates by substitution, classifies all three by explicitly testing constant difference against constant ratio, articulates the position-to-term versus term-to-term distinction, and can construct a new sequence of a requested type.
responseLevels.partial: Substitutes correctly to generate the five terms and identifies arithmetic by a constant difference, but cannot reliably distinguish geometric (checks difference only, not ratio) or mislabels 1, 4, 9, 16 — has the parts but not the unifying difference-vs-ratio test.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Generate the first five terms of the sequence whose rule is 3n − 2. Then look at these three sequences — 5, 8, 11, 14, …; 2, 6, 18, 54, …; 1, 4, 9, 16, … — and sort each as arithmetic, geometric or neither, showing me how you decide.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Substituting the position numbers into 3n−2 (rather than treating it as a term-to-term instruction) reveals position-to-term fluency; classifying by testing BOTH constant difference and constant ratio (rather than 'it goes up') reveals the arithmetic/geometric structure. A child who conflates the two rule types produces the wrong first term, and a child who classifies by direction alone mis-sorts 1, 4, 9, 16 — so watching what they generate and sort discriminates without asking them to describe the method.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Savanna & Grassland Animals (ages 7–9): open, grassy habitats with few trees where survival turns on being seen from far off — driving herding, speed, and predator-prey dynamics.
• Standards — UK (DfE): extends KS1 'Living things and their habitats' and Y4 adaptation; introduces the idea that a habitat's OPENNESS shapes behaviour (herds, watchfulness) not just body features.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 2-LS4-1 (diversity across habitats); 3-LS4-3 (survive well/less well in a habitat) — and seeds the predator-prey survival relationship developed later.
• Operational details: anchor on the African savanna cast (zebra, wildebeest, gazelle, elephant, giraffe as prey/grazers; lion, cheetah, hyena as predators) and the key ideas — safety in numbers (herds/dazzle), speed and endurance, many eyes watching, and grazing that tracks seasonal grass and water (migration). Establish that open grassland gives little cover, so both hunters and hunted rely on speed, distance, and group behaviour.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~7–8): name savanna grazers and predators and say who eats whom. B (transitional, ~8–9): explain one way a herd helps prey survive (many eyes, confusion, dilution). C (formal, ~9): explain how open habitat drives both speed AND grouping, and link grazing movement to seasonal grass/water.
bestPractices: Root the habitat's demands in its openness — no trees to hide behind — so pupils derive herding, watchfulness and speed rather than memorising them.
Introduce 'safety in numbers' with concrete mechanisms (more eyes to spot danger; confusion of a moving mass; each individual less likely to be the one caught) instead of a slogan.
Frame predator vs prey as a fair two-sided problem (the cheetah must be fast AND close; the gazelle must be fast AND alert) to prepare the later arms-race idea without over-claiming.
Link grazing herds to seasonal grass and water so pupils see behaviour responding to a changing habitat, connecting to migration.
keyRepresentations: An open savanna scene with a grazing herd and a stalking predator at a distance — emphasising sightlines across open ground.
A 'many eyes' diagram showing a herd's overlapping fields of view vs a lone animal's blind spots.
A predator-prey chase pairing speed/stamina bars for cheetah vs gazelle.
A seasonal map showing herds moving to follow green grass and water.
commonMisconceptions: 'Predators always catch their prey' — most hunts fail; prey defences and group living work often.
'Being in a big group makes you an easier target' — herding usually lowers each individual's risk (dilution, confusion, shared vigilance).
'Savanna is a jungle/forest' — it is open grassland with scattered trees, and that openness is the point.
'The fastest animal always wins' — endurance, alertness, timing and cover matter as much as top speed.
'Grazers wander randomly' — herd movements track seasonal grass and water.

learn.summary: Savanna and grassland animals (ages 7–9): help pupils see that OPEN grassland with few trees for cover — where animals are visible from far off — favours herding, watchfulness and speed, while seasonal rains that change where grass and water are found drive seasonal movement. The anchor cast is African savanna herbivores/plant-eaters (zebra, wildebeest, gazelle, elephant, giraffe) and predators (lion, cheetah, hyena), with American grassland parallels (bison, prairie dogs). The central, hard-to-fake idea is that grouping changes survival ODDS: in a big, alert herd many eyes spot danger early, the moving mass confuses a hunter, and each individual is less likely to be the one caught (dilution). The preferred approach lets children operate this as a probability system; alternatives (sortable scene, matching/categorisation checks, outdoor tag game, guide-in-role hook) target naming, assessment, and curiosity. Address the misconceptions that predators always win, that a big group is an easier target, that savanna is a jungle, that the fastest always wins, and that plant-eaters wander randomly.

activities.title: Run the hunt: a safety-in-numbers simulation
feedback: When a learner leaves one gazelle alone and it is caught, prompt: what could a herd have done that this lone animal could not? (spot the predator sooner; make it hard to single out one target).
If a learner expects the big group to be caught more easily, point to the survival-rate meter across several runs and ask them to compare lone vs herd outcomes.
When they buff the predator and survival drops, ask what the prey could change (larger herd, higher vigilance) to show the problem is two-sided.
After the season toggle, ask why the herd had to move, linking grazing to following green grass and water.
activities.rationale: Survival odds are a dynamic, probabilistic system; letting children vary herd size and vigilance and observe changing catch rates over repeated runs is intended to make 'many eyes', confusion and dilution concrete rather than a memorised phrase. Optional interaction details (sliders, a survival-rate meter, a season toggle) are illustrative examples of the mechanism, not mandatory mechanisms, and the displayed survival numbers are illustrative rather than measured real-world probabilities.
sourceClaims: Group living reduces individual predation risk via increased vigilance ('many eyes'), the confusion effect, and dilution; most predator hunts fail.
Savanna is open grassland with scattered trees; large grazers migrate seasonally to follow grass growth and water (e.g. Serengeti wildebeest).
Open-habitat behaviour (herding, vigilance) extends KS1/KS2 habitat-and-adaptation content to behavioural adaptation.
learnerActions: Set a prey herd's size (from a lone animal up to a large herd) and how alert/watchful the animals are, then release a predator (lion or cheetah) and watch the chase play out.

Run repeated hunts and read a survival-rate meter that updates across runs, comparing a lone dozing gazelle (caught almost every time) with the same gazelle in a big, watchful herd (spotted early, the mass scatters, most hunts fail).
Make the hunt two-sided: increase the predator's speed or stamina and discover the prey must group tighter and stay more alert to keep surviving.
Use a season toggle that moves grass and water so the herd must relocate to keep feeding, connecting behaviour to seasonal migration.
activities.intendedInsight: Safety in numbers is not a slogan but a reduction in each individual's risk — from more eyes watching, confusion of a moving mass, and dilution — and open habitat with little cover is WHY large hoofed prey such as zebras and gazelles rely mainly on grouping, alertness and speed rather than hiding (burrowers like prairie dogs can still hide underground).

activities.title: Outdoor tag: does a crowd protect the target?
feedback: If a learner predicted the crowd would make the target easier to catch, compare the two timed runs and ask what the milling crowd did to the lion's chase.
If a learner says the zebras win by ganging up on the lion, note that in the game nobody tags the lion back — any protection came from being hard to single out, not from fighting.
Ask the probe questions to deepen: what must the herd do first, before any running? Would one zebra alone be safer or in more danger? Is the lion 'bad' for hunting, and why does it hunt?
Ask the open-habitat contrast: if there were thick trees everywhere instead of open grass, would a big herd still help in the same way?
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–compare body activity is offered to surface and test the 'a crowd is easy to catch in' misconception using children's own movement, making the confusion effect (difficulty singling out one target) observable. Because the lion must chase one named child, the game does not test dilution (the chance that someone else is the one caught); that idea is explored in the simulation. This is one concrete classroom enactment, not the only route to the idea.
sourceClaims: Group living reduces individual predation risk via increased vigilance ('many eyes'), the confusion effect, and dilution; most predator hunts fail.
learnerActions: Play a tag game outside. Name one child the 'target zebra'; a 'lion' must tag only that named child.
Before running, predict whether the lion catches the named zebra faster when the whole herd stays clumped and milling around that child, or when that child stands alone.
Run both versions and compare how quickly the lion catches the target each time.
Discuss what the clumped, moving crowd did and, if it was harder for the lion to catch the target, why it was harder to pick out and chase one child.
activities.intendedInsight: Running both versions is intended to let children observe whether a moving, clumped crowd protects the named target, challenging the naive guess that a crowd is easy to be caught in; where the crowd does protect the target, it is because a single individual becomes hard to single out.

activities.title: Explain how the herd helps
feedback: If a learner explains the herd only by friendship or family, reframe around the hunting lion: what does the group do the moment danger appears? Introduce 'more eyes' and 'harder to catch just one'.
If a learner says the herd stays together to gang up and fight the lion off, note that most prey flee rather than fight, and emphasise early warning and being hard to single out over combat.
If a learner calls the lion cruel or evil, establish that predators hunt to eat and survive — predator and prey is a natural relationship, not good-versus-bad.
If a learner only says 'safety in numbers' as a slogan, press for what the numbers actually do: early warning, and being harder to single out.
activities.rationale: Naming what the numbers actually do against a predator is hard to fake, so a social answer ('friends/family') and a mechanistic answer diverge clearly, discriminating genuine understanding from a memorised phrase. Requiring the learner to construct the explanation elicits produced reasoning rather than recognition; recognition alone would not elicit this produced explanation.
sourceClaims: Group living reduces individual predation risk via increased vigilance ('many eyes'), the confusion effect, and dilution; most predator hunts fail.
learnerActions: Read or listen to the scene: on the African savanna, zebras live together in big herds instead of wandering alone, and a lion is hunting nearby.
Write or say how being in a big group helps a single zebra stay safe — stating what the numbers actually DO against the predator.
Say whether the lion is a bad animal for hunting, and explain why the lion hunts at all.
Explain what it is about open grassland, rather than forest, that makes seeing danger early possible.
activities.intendedInsight: A full explanation names a mechanism — many eyes spot the predator early, or the moving crowd makes any one animal hard to single out — and treats predator–prey as feeding and survival, not malice; it links open ground to spotting danger from a distance.

activities.title: Name the cast and match who eats whom
feedback: If a learner sorts a predator as a plant-eater, ask what that animal eats and whether it hunts other animals.
If questions reveal the belief that predators always catch their prey, point out that most hunts fail and prey defences often work.
If a learner thinks a big group is an easier target, revisit the simulation or tag outcomes showing lower individual risk in a herd.
Confirm the habitat idea: savanna is open grassland with scattered trees, not a jungle or forest.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorisation and short questions assess the naming and relationship ideas and can surface the 'predators always win' and 'big group = easier target' errors; these check and consolidate knowledge but test rather than build the probabilistic intuition, so they work best alongside the simulation or body activity.
sourceClaims: Diversity of life across habitats and differential survival within a habitat; seeds predator-prey relationships.
Group living reduces individual predation risk via increased vigilance ('many eyes'), the confusion effect, and dilution; most predator hunts fail.
learnerActions: Name at least five grassland/savanna animals (e.g. zebra, wildebeest, gazelle, elephant, giraffe, lion, cheetah, hyena; bison and prairie dogs in American grasslands).
Sort the animals into plant-eaters and hunters/predators, noting that adult elephants and adult giraffes are rarely hunted, though their young can be.
Match each predator to prey it hunts (e.g. lion → zebra) to build a simple food chain.
Answer short questions on why herds help prey and on whether most hunts succeed or fail.
activities.intendedInsight: Pupils can name the savanna cast, tell apart plant-eaters and predators, describe who eats whom, and begin to flag that most hunts fail and that a big group is not an easier target.

activities.title: Open-ground scene and optional safari-guide hook
feedback: Prompt comparison between the herd's overlapping fields of view and the lone animal's blind spots: who spots the predator first, and why?
If a learner thinks plant-eaters wander randomly, use the seasonal map to show herds following grass growth and water.
If the guide's story raises a claim (e.g. 'the fastest always wins'), redirect to a run of the simulation to check whether endurance, alertness and timing also matter.

Reinforce that the open setting, with few trees or bushes for cover, is the point — it is why large hoofed animals like zebras and gazelles cannot rely on hiding (though burrowers like prairie dogs can dive underground).
activities.rationale: A tappable scene and a guide-in-role add context, emphasise sightlines across open ground, and motivate the topic, but on their own they carry the behavioural payoff weakly; they are framed here as scaffolds feeding the operational and explanation activities rather than substitutes for them.
sourceClaims: Savanna is open grassland with scattered trees; large grazers migrate seasonally to follow grass growth and water (e.g. Serengeti wildebeest).
Open-habitat behaviour (herding, vigilance) extends KS1/KS2 habitat-and-adaptation content to behavioural adaptation.
learnerActions: Explore a savanna scene with a grazing herd and a stalking predator at a distance; tap predator and prey roles to reveal who eats whom.
Compare a 'many eyes' picture of a herd's overlapping fields of view with a lone animal's blind spots, and discuss what the herd can see that the lone animal cannot.
Look at a seasonal map showing herds moving to follow green grass and water, and say why the herds keep moving.
Optionally, hear a safari-guide-in-role describe the scene as a curiosity hook, then return to the simulation or explanation task to test the ideas raised.
activities.intendedInsight: Open sightlines across grassland with only scattered trees, overlapping herd vigilance, and seasonal movement are visible features that set up the deeper survival logic; the scene and guide spark interest but the probabilistic payoff is explored in the other activities.

constraints: Ground the habitat's demands in its OPENNESS — few trees or bushes to hide behind — so pupils derive herding, watchfulness and speed rather than memorising them.
Teach 'safety in numbers' with concrete mechanisms (more eyes to spot danger; confusion of a moving mass; each individual less likely to be the one caught) rather than as a slogan.

Frame predator vs prey as a fair two-sided problem (the cheetah must be fast AND close; the gazelle must be fast AND alert) to prepare the later arms-race idea without over-claiming evolutionary conclusions for this age band.

Address misconceptions explicitly: predators do NOT always catch prey (most hunts fail); a big group usually lowers individual risk rather than raising it; savanna is open grassland with scattered trees, not jungle; top speed alone does not decide outcomes (endurance, alertness, timing, cover matter); herbivore movement tracks seasonal grass and water, it is not random.

A tap-to-reveal scene and a guide-in-role chat are context and motivation scaffolds; on their own they do not let a child operate the survival-odds system, so pair them with the simulation or the body activity — this is a scoped limit, not a claim that such formats can teach nothing.

Matching/categorisation and short-answer questions assess and consolidate; by themselves they check classification rather than build the probabilistic intuition, and recognition-only responses do not elicit the learner's own constructed explanation.

The simulation's survival-rate meter should reflect that most hunts fail and that herding/vigilance lower each individual's risk; its numbers are illustrative, not measured real-world probabilities. Avoid implying predators nearly always catch prey or that larger groups are easier to catch.

Use accurate feeding labels: giraffes browse leaves and elephants are mixed feeders, so sort herbivores as 'plant-eaters' rather than calling the whole cast 'grazers'; note that adult elephants and adult giraffes are rarely hunted (their young are more at risk), so not every plant-eater is equally likely to be prey.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; all four sources carry verified:false in the row, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Sources were not re-fetched; sourceClaims are exact copies of this row's claims and support the stated teaching principles only, not the empirical effectiveness of any specific activity.

The 'many eyes', confusion and dilution mechanisms and 'most hunts fail' come from an unverified behavioural-ecology reference; the simulation's numeric survival rates must be presented as illustrative, since no quantitative source is cited.
Keep the two-sided framing honest: the row seeds but does not establish a predator-prey 'arms race', so avoid over-claiming evolutionary conclusions with ages 7–9.

The legacy row framed the simulation as the only way the behavioural payoff can be 'felt' and dismissed 3D and quiz formats as merely testing; this has been softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than universal claims about what a format can or cannot teach.

The original row labels giraffe and elephant as 'grazers'; giraffes browse leaves and elephants are mixed feeders. The sort was reframed as 'plant-eaters (prey) vs predators' and the summary updated so no learner-facing text hinges on the inaccurate 'grazer' label; the original simplification is recorded here only.

assess.poeTask: Play a tag game outside. Name one child the 'target zebra'; a 'lion' must tag only that child. Children predict whether the lion will catch the named zebra faster when the whole herd stays clumped and milling around that child, or when that child stands out alone. Run both and compare — the clumped, moving crowd protects the target, violating the naive 'a crowd is easy to catch in' guess.
probeDeeper: What is the very first thing the herd needs to do to stay safe — before any running?
Would one zebra alone be safer, or in more danger, than a zebra inside a herd? Why?
Is the lion a bad animal for hunting the zebra? Why does the lion hunt at all?
What if there were thick trees everywhere instead of open grass — would a big herd still help in the same way?
assess.correctAnswer: In a big herd there are many eyes and ears to spot the lion early and warn the others, and when they all run any one zebra is less likely to be the one caught — the moving crowd makes it hard for the lion to pick out and chase a single target. Safety comes from numbers, shared lookout and confusion, not from the zebras fighting the lion off.

errorPatterns.pattern: They stay in a herd because they're friends or it's their family, like people
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe around the hunting lion — ask what the group does the moment danger appears; introduce 'more eyes' and 'harder to catch just one'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Because the zebras are all friends and like to be together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the herd by companionship with no link to the lion or to danger.

errorPatterns.pattern: The herd stays together so they can gang up and fight the lion off
errorPatterns.nextMove: Note that most prey flee rather than fight; emphasise early warning and being harder to single out over combat.
errorPatterns.distractor: So they can all attack the lion together and chase it away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes zebras attacking or scaring the lion as the main benefit of the group.

errorPatterns.pattern: Lions are bad or mean animals that kill for fun
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish predators hunt to eat and survive; predator and prey is a natural relationship, not good-versus-bad.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the lion cruel or evil; doesn't connect hunting to feeding and survival.

responseLevels.gap: Names savanna animals but explains herding only socially ('they're friends/family') with no link to predators.
responseLevels.full: Explains a mechanism — many eyes spot the predator early and any individual is less likely to be the one caught, or the moving crowd confuses the hunter — recognises predator–prey as feeding not malice, and links open grassland to being able to see danger coming.
responseLevels.partial: Connects the herd to the lion and says 'safety in numbers', but only as a slogan — can't say what the numbers actually do (early warning, harder to single out one), or thinks the benefit is ganging up to fight.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On the African savanna, zebras live together in big herds instead of wandering alone. A lion is hunting nearby. How does being in a big group help a single zebra stay safe?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with a social idea explains the herd by friendship or family and gives no survival mechanism. A child who understands names a mechanism — more eyes watching, or being harder to single out. Naming what the numbers actually DO against a predator is hard to fake, so the two answers diverge clearly.

pedagogy.summary: Tenths are the first structured step into fractions born from dividing ONE whole into ten equal parts — the bridge from fractions to decimal place value. The load-bearing ideas: ten equal tenths recompose exactly one whole (10/10 = 1), each tenth is small (it takes ten to rebuild the whole), and 3/10 is the same as 3÷10 (three wholes shared among ten). Teach with strips, tens-frames-as-lengths and number lines so counting in tenths lands cleanly at one whole rather than becoming 'ten'.
bestPractices: Count up and down in tenths on a number line and a strip, stopping deliberately at 10/10 = one whole to break the 'ten-tenths is ten' bias
Insist on ten EQUAL parts of one whole (not any ten pieces) using a partitioned strip
Connect 3/10 to 3÷10 by sharing three whole strips across ten places
Compare a tenth with a half (5/10 = 1/2) so children feel a tenth is far smaller than a half
Keep the whole visible and constant so a tenth of a bigger whole is seen to be a bigger piece with the same name
keyRepresentations: Whole strip partitioned into ten equal tenths (recomposes to one whole)
0-to-1 number line marked in tenths
Sharing model: three wholes shared among ten to show 3/10 = 3÷10
Overlay of tenths against a half (5/10 = 1/2)
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — reads ten-tenths as 'ten', or thinks a tenth is big 'because 10 is a big number'
Larger denominator = larger part (a tenth 'bigger than a half because 10 > 2')
Accepts any ten pieces as tenths, ignoring that the parts must be equal
Sees no connection between 3/10 and 3÷10 ('3 ÷ 10 can't be done, 3 is smaller than 10')
Thinks a tenth of a large whole and a tenth of a small whole are the same size

learn.summary: Tenths build on earlier work with fractions such as halves and quarters: dividing ONE whole into ten equal parts, and the bridge toward decimal place value. The load-bearing ideas are that ten equal tenths recompose exactly one whole (10/10 = 1), that each tenth is small because it takes ten of them to rebuild the whole, and that 3/10 is the same as 3÷10 (three wholes shared among ten). Partitioned strips, length-based number lines, and sharing models let counting in tenths land cleanly at one whole rather than drifting into 'ten'.

activities.title: Collect the tenths back into one whole
feedback: If the learner says ten-tenths is 'ten', physically recompose the ten tenths against the original whole: the row is the same length as one whole, not longer.
If the learner says a tenth is bigger than a half 'because 10 is more than 2', overlay five tenths onto one half so they see it takes five tenths just to make one half.
Reinforce that the denominator names how many equal parts make ONE whole, so with the same whole more parts means each part is smaller.
activities.rationale: A counting-and-recomposing sequence that deliberately stops at 10/10 = one whole is intended to address whole-number bias (reading fractions by their digits) and to build the magnitude sense Year 3 pupils are expected to develop when counting up and down in tenths; its effectiveness here is proposed rather than tested.
sourceClaims: Students commonly show whole-number bias, viewing fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), and must be helped to see fractions as single numbers with magnitude; equal-partitioning (parts must be equal) is a documented roadblock.
Year 3 pupils count up and down in tenths, recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into ten equal parts, and connect tenths to dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10.
learnerActions: Start with a single whole bar or strip and partition it into ten equal segments.
Collect the segments one at a time while counting aloud: one-tenth, two-tenths, three-tenths … up to ten-tenths.
At the tenth count, reassemble the ten segments end-to-end against the original whole and check that they match exactly, labelling the result '10/10 = 1 whole'.
Lay a piece covering exactly five tenths over one half of the whole and confirm that 5/10 = 1/2, so a single tenth is plainly far smaller than a half.
activities.intendedInsight: Ten equal tenths put back together remake exactly one whole, so 10/10 = 1 (not 'ten'), and each tenth is small because it takes ten of them to rebuild the whole — far smaller than a half.

activities.title: Share three wholes among ten to see 3/10 = 3÷10
feedback: If the learner says '3 ÷ 10 can't be done because 3 is smaller than 10', carry out the sharing concretely so they watch each place receive three tenths.
Name the completed share out loud: 'three shared among ten gives three tenths each, so 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10.'
If they write 10/3, re-link the notation: three of the ten equal pieces of one whole is 3/10.
activities.rationale: Connecting the fraction notation to an equal-sharing division is intended to address the misconception that 3/10 and 3÷10 are unrelated and matches the Year 3 expectation to connect tenths with dividing quantities by 10.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils count up and down in tenths, recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into ten equal parts, and connect tenths to dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10.
learnerActions: Set out three identical whole bars and ten plates (or ten places) to share them among.
Partition each whole into tenths and deal the tenths out equally, one at a time, until each of the ten places has received the same amount.
State how much each place received (three tenths) and write the sharing as 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10.
Discuss why this works even though 3 is smaller than 10: you share the three wholes into smaller pieces rather than giving whole bars each.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction such as 3/10 is the result of sharing three wholes equally among ten, so 3/10 = 3÷10; dividing by a number larger than the dividend is possible and gives a fraction less than one.

activities.title: Equal parts only, and the same whole
feedback: If the learner accepts unequal pieces as tenths, contrast the equal and unequal splits and ask which one is made of ten pieces that are all the same size.
If the learner thinks a tenth is always the same absolute size, place the two different-sized wholes side by side so the two tenths can be compared directly.
Emphasise that the name 'tenth' tells you the number of equal parts in its whole, not a fixed length.
activities.rationale: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock, and the relative nature of a fraction (the piece that is a tenth of a bigger whole is bigger when both wholes are visible) is a known source of confusion; contrasting cases and keeping the whole visible make the condition explicit.
sourceClaims: Students commonly show whole-number bias, viewing fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), and must be helped to see fractions as single numbers with magnitude; equal-partitioning (parts must be equal) is a documented roadblock.
learnerActions: Compare a whole split into ten EQUAL pieces with a whole split into ten UNEQUAL pieces.
Decide which one shows tenths and explain why (the ten parts must be the same size).
Check by trying to recompose each set back into the whole and noticing which one tiles the whole with matching equal pieces.

Then compare a tenth of a small whole bar with a tenth of a larger whole bar, keeping both wholes visible, and describe how the two tenths differ in physical size even though both are called 'a tenth'.
activities.intendedInsight: Only ten EQUAL parts of one whole count as tenths; and because a tenth is defined relative to its whole, the physical piece that is a tenth of a larger whole is larger than a tenth of a smaller whole when both wholes are shown, though both pieces share the name 'a tenth' and name the same fraction of their own whole.

activities.title: Place and name tenths on a number line
feedback: If a learner places 5/10 anywhere other than halfway, relate the point to the half-overlay from the first activity.
If they answer 'ten' for 10/10, point to where the tenth tenth lands — exactly at 1, the end of the whole.
Encourage reading each mark as a quantity, not just as a count of ticks.
activities.rationale: Positioning tenths on a line as single numbers with magnitude reinforces the magnitude understanding that counters whole-number bias; placing and naming on a line checks and consolidates this understanding rather than building the recompose-to-one-whole insight, and recognising a correct position does not by itself confirm the learner can produce the reasoning, so use it after the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: Students commonly show whole-number bias, viewing fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), and must be helped to see fractions as single numbers with magnitude; equal-partitioning (parts must be equal) is a documented roadblock.
learnerActions: Use a 0-to-1 number line marked in tenths.
Count up and down the line in tenths, naming each mark.
Place given tenths (for example 3/10) at the correct point and identify which point equals one half (5/10).
Fill in missing values such as 'ten-tenths = __' and justify with the recomposition idea rather than by counting ticks.
activities.intendedInsight: Tenths are single numbers with a fixed position and magnitude between 0 and 1, with 10/10 sitting exactly at one and 5/10 exactly at one half.

constraints: Keep the whole visible throughout, and keep it the same size except when deliberately comparing tenths of different-sized wholes, so that a tenth is always understood relative to its own whole.
Insist on ten EQUAL parts of one whole; any ten pieces are not tenths unless they are the same size.
Deliberately pause counting at 10/10 and reassemble to one whole, rather than letting the count slide into 'ten'.

Placing, naming, matching, and fill-in tasks (e.g. on a number line) check and consolidate understanding but do not by themselves build the recompose-to-one-whole insight; use them after the hands-on partitioning and sharing work.

A static labelled tenths strip can show the facts (this is 3/10; these ten make one whole; 5/10 = one half) but cannot itself enact the moment ten tenths fuse back into one whole; pair it with a recomposition the learner performs.

Partitioning and recomposing a visible whole provides the concrete experience of ten tenths reforming one whole; spoken discussion can support the reasoning about why a tenth is small but does not itself supply that partitioning and recomposition, so include the hands-on work rather than relying on discussion to provide it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and their efficacy is untested.

Self-audit of the magnitude claims: 10/10 = 1, 5/10 = 1/2, and 3÷10 = 3/10 are correct; a tenth is correctly described as far smaller than a half (five tenths make one half). No arithmetic errors found.
The original assessment correctly reads the denominator as the number of equal parts in one whole; this was preserved, and no conceptual corrections to the source were required.

As a number, one-tenth is always the same fraction; the 'bigger/smaller piece' point concerns the physical portion of a particular whole and holds only when both wholes are shown together, so it is retained with the explicit 'keep both wholes visible' condition.
The original's stronger comparative wording about dialogue adding little and 3D being decorative was softened to scoped affordances; comparative efficacy of media is untested and not asserted.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a whole strip. Ask: 'If I cut this into ten equal pieces and then lay all ten back end-to-end in a row, will the row be shorter than, the same length as, or LONGER than the whole strip? Predict, and say why.' A whole-number-biased child predicts 'longer, because now there are ten of them.' Then lay the ten tenths against the original whole — they match exactly. The pre-observation reason ('ten pieces so more') is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: How many tenths make one whole? And how many tenths is one half?
I have a bigger bar, also cut into ten equal pieces. Is one piece of that bar also called a tenth? Is it the same size as a tenth of the small bar?
Which is more, 3 tenths or 3 halves? Why?
Why do we write 3/10 and not 10/3 for three of the ten pieces?
assess.correctAnswer: Ten-tenths equals 1 (one whole), because ten equal tenths put back together make the whole bar again. Each tenth is much smaller than a half, because it takes ten tenths to make a whole but only two halves — so a tenth is far smaller (five tenths make one half).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — ten-tenths read as 'ten', and a tenth judged bigger than a half 'because 10 is more than 2'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recompose ten tenths into one whole in front of the child; overlay five tenths on one half; reteach the denominator as parts-of-one-whole
errorPatterns.distractor: Ten-tenths is 10, because I counted ten pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'ten' for 10/10, or says a single tenth is bigger than a half

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal-parts ignored — thinks 'tenths' just means ten pieces, regardless of whether they are the same size
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast an equal ten-split with an unequal one; only equal parts can be called tenths; check by recomposing to one whole
errorPatterns.distractor: Any bar broken into ten pieces shows tenths, even if the pieces are different sizes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts a bar broken into ten UNEQUAL pieces as showing tenths

errorPatterns.pattern: Fraction disconnected from division — does not see 3/10 as 3÷10 ('you can't do 3 ÷ 10, three is smaller than ten')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Share three whole strips across ten places so each place gets 3/10; name the share as 3÷10 = 3/10
errorPatterns.distractor: 3 ÷ 10 can't be done, because 3 is smaller than 10.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 3÷10 is impossible or 0, and treats 3/10 as unrelated to sharing three wholes among ten

responseLevels.gap: Says ten-tenths equals ten; judges a tenth bigger than a half because 10 > 2; accepts unequal pieces as tenths.
responseLevels.full: States ten-tenths = 1 and justifies by recomposition, orders a tenth as far smaller than a half by the ten-vs-two-parts argument, connects 3/10 with 3÷10, and transfers (a tenth of a different-sized whole is correspondingly bigger or smaller).
responseLevels.partial: Counts in tenths and states 10/10 makes one whole and that tenths are ten equal parts, but lists these facts without connecting them — cannot explain a tenth is small BECAUSE ten rebuild the whole, cannot link 3/10 to 3÷10, and stumbles on a tenth of a different-sized whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A chocolate bar is one whole. It is snapped into ten equal pieces. I eat the pieces one at a time and count: one-tenth, two-tenths, three-tenths… When I have eaten all of them, I have eaten ten-tenths. What number does ten-tenths equal, and why? And is each single piece bigger or smaller than a half — how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-biased child says ten-tenths is 'ten' (treating 10/10 as the count) and/or says a tenth is big 'because 10 is a big number'. Correct reasoning requires reading the denominator as the number of equal parts in ONE whole, so 10/10 rebuilds one and each part is small — the reason (tier 2) exposes the bias even when a rehearsed child guesses 'one'.

sources.claim: Students commonly show whole-number bias, viewing fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), and must be helped to see fractions as single numbers with magnitude; equal-partitioning (parts must be equal) is a documented roadblock.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide 'Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K-8' (Siegler et al. 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils count up and down in tenths, recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into ten equal parts, and connect tenths to dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10.
