pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Atoms, Elements & Compounds

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry 'Atoms, elements and compounds'):** A simple (Dalton) atomic model; the differences between atoms, elements and compounds; chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds. (The sub-atomic structure — nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons in shells — is commonly introduced at KS3 and formalised at GCSE/KS4.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-1].

- **Operational details:** The organising distinction is a hierarchy: atoms are the building blocks; an ELEMENT is one kind of atom; a COMPOUND is two or more kinds chemically joined in fixed ratio; a MIXTURE is substances together but not joined. Teach with models the child assembles — snap identical atoms to make an element, different atoms to make a compound, and read the formula off (H2O = two hydrogen + one oxygen). Introduce the simple atomic picture (a tiny central nucleus with electrons around it) to give atoms internal structure, and chemical symbols as the shorthand. The critical conceptual move: a compound has DIFFERENT properties from its elements (sodium + chlorine, both dangerous, make edible salt) and cannot be separated physically — unlike a mixture. Keep sub-atomic detail light (shells/electron arrangement is deepened at KS4).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child classifies a given particle diagram/formula as element, compound or mixture, writes/reads a simple formula, and explains that a compound's properties differ from the elements that formed it.
bestPractices: Build the element/compound/mixture distinction by assembling atoms into models rather than defining the terms verbally.
Read formulae directly off built models so symbols and subscripts mean 'how many of each atom'.
Make the key move that a compound has NEW properties unlike its elements (Na + Cl2 → edible salt).
Contrast a compound (chemically joined, fixed ratio, not physically separable) with a mixture (just together, separable).
Keep sub-atomic detail light at KS3 (nucleus + electrons); defer electron shells/arrangement to KS4.
keyRepresentations: Atom-snap models for element, compound and mixture
Live chemical formula readout (e.g. H2O) tied to the model
A simple atom diagram (nucleus + surrounding electrons + symbol)
A 'try to separate' test distinguishing mixture (separable) from compound (not)
commonMisconceptions: A compound is just a mixture of its elements and keeps their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by physical means (filtering, etc.).
The subscript in a formula multiplies the whole formula rather than the preceding atom.
Elements and atoms are the same thing (confusing the substance with its building block).
A molecule of an element (e.g. O2) must be a compound because it has two atoms.

learn.summary: Learners build the atom 	a2192 element 	a2192 compound 	a2192 mixture hierarchy by assembling atoms rather than memorising definitions. The core conceptual moves: an element is one kind of atom; a compound is two or more kinds chemically joined in a fixed ratio and has NEW properties unlike its elements; a mixture is substances together but physically separable. Learners also read simple formulae as 'how many of each atom', match chemical symbols, and meet a light introduction to atomic structure: a central nucleus containing protons and neutrons with electrons in shells around it. Detailed electron-shell arrangement is kept light at this stage.

activities.title: Atom workshop: build and classify
feedback: If a learner labels a two-atom element molecule (e.g. O2) a compound, point out both atoms are the SAME kind 	a2014 it is still an element; a compound needs different kinds of atoms.
If a learner reads the subscript in H2O as doubling the whole formula, clarify the subscript counts only the atom it immediately follows: H2O is 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.

If a learner expects to physically separate a compound, show the 'try to separate' test refusing the compound while cleanly splitting the mixture, and note a compound needs a chemical change to break apart, whereas a mixture separates by physical means.
activities.rationale: Constructing and classifying particles turns the hierarchy into an action rather than a verbal definition, and directly engages the common confusion between compounds and mixtures. A live formula readout and symbol key tie the shorthand to what was built. Interactive snapping, live formula updates and a separability test are illustrative mechanisms, not the only way to teach this; equivalent construction with physical atom models or paper cut-outs can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: simple (Dalton) atomic model; differences between atoms, elements and compounds; chemical symbols and formulae
NGSS MS-PS1-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-1]
Students confuse compounds with mixtures and expect a compound to retain its elements' properties; building and testing separability targets this
learnerActions: Drag atoms from a palette and snap identical atoms together (e.g. two blue atoms) 	a2014 observe the classifier label the result 'element'.
Snap different atoms together (e.g. two blue + one red) and watch a formula box write the compound's formula while the classifier flips to 'compound'.

Scatter a jumble of two or more DIFFERENT kinds of separate particles that are not joined to each other (e.g. some blue–blue molecules alongside some separate red atoms) and observe the classifier read 'mixture'; note that a jumble of identical molecules is still one pure substance, not a mixture.
Use a 'try to separate' tool: pull a mixture cleanly into its parts, then try the same on a compound and find it cannot be pulled apart physically.
State in your own words why the built thing is an element, a compound, or a mixture, and read the formula off your model as a count of each kind of atom.
activities.intendedInsight: Element, compound and mixture are distinguished by how atoms are arranged: one kind of atom (element), different kinds chemically joined in a fixed ratio (compound), or substances merely together and separable (mixture). A formula records how many of each atom are joined.

activities.title: New properties: a compound is not its elements
feedback: If a learner predicts the magnet still pulls iron from iron sulfide, that signals treating the compound as a mixture 	a2014 the pre-observation reasoning is the key diagnostic; reteach compound vs mixture at the particle level.

If a learner says water should help things burn 'because oxygen is in it', contrast with salt: sodium reacts violently in water and chlorine is poisonous, yet salt is edible 	a2014 bonding creates new properties. Likewise, the oxygen in water is chemically joined to hydrogen, so water does not behave like oxygen gas and does not support burning; it is often used to put out ordinary fires (though not every fire, e.g. oil or burning-metal fires).
Full understanding: 'a compound's properties are new, unlike a mixture where each part keeps its own.'
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain contrast (iron+sulfur mixture vs iron sulfide compound) and the sodium+chlorine	a2192salt case make the 'new properties' move concrete and target the classic misconception that a compound keeps its elements' properties. The reasoning before observation is what reveals the misconception.
sourceClaims: Students confuse compounds with mixtures and expect a compound to retain its elements' properties; building and testing separability targets this
learnerActions: Compare the properties of reactive sodium metal and poisonous chlorine gas, then observe (via demonstration or described reaction) that combined they form ordinary edible table salt (NaCl).
State what changed: the compound has its OWN properties, different from both elements.
Predict for iron filings mixed with sulfur powder: can a magnet still pull out the iron, and does it still look like iron + sulfur? (Yes 	a2014 it is a mixture; each part keeps its own properties.)

Then consider a fresh portion heated to form dark grey iron sulfide and predict whether the magnet still pulls out iron (No, if all the iron has reacted: a new compound has formed. In real demonstrations leftover unreacted iron may still be attracted, so any pull comes from leftover iron, not from the compound).
Explain the difference between the two iron/sulfur results in terms of 'just together' versus 'chemically joined'.
activities.intendedInsight: When elements chemically combine into a compound, the compound has genuinely new properties, unlike a mixture where each component keeps its own properties and can be separated physically.

activities.title: Atom structure and symbol reference
feedback: If a learner confuses 'atom' and 'element', clarify an element is a substance made of ONE kind of atom (many of them), while an atom is the single building block.
When reading CO2, confirm 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms, and that it is a compound because it contains different kinds of atoms.
Reinforce reading the subscript as the count of the preceding atom only.
activities.rationale: A reference/vocabulary anchor supports the structure and symbol targets named in the objective (nucleus with protons/neutrons, electrons in shells). A fixed diagram and symbol key cannot let a learner build formulae or test separability, so this activity is best paired with the building activities rather than used alone. Keep detailed electron-shell arrangement light at this stage; it is deepened later.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: simple (Dalton) atomic model; differences between atoms, elements and compounds; chemical symbols and formulae
learnerActions: Explore a labelled atom diagram showing a tiny central nucleus 	a2014 containing protons and neutrons 	a2014 with electrons arranged around it in shells, together with the element's chemical symbol (the electron-shell detail is kept light at this stage).
Match chemical symbols to their elements using a symbol key.

Read given formulae (e.g. H2O, CO2, NaCl) aloud, naming each element and how many atoms of each are present (for NaCl, which is not made of separate molecules, read the formula as a 1:1 ratio of sodium to chlorine).
Decide for each example whether it is an element or a compound and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: Atoms have internal structure 	a2014 a central nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons arranged in shells around it 	a2014 and chemical symbols are a shorthand; a formula names the elements present and the number of atoms of each. Detailed electron arrangement is kept light at this stage.

activities.title: Classify and build: check understanding
feedback: Matching and selecting check classification but do not by themselves show a learner can independently construct a formula 	a2014 include a build/fill-in step so learners produce, not just select.

If a learner cannot explain WHY water does not burn (only that it does not), that is a partial response: definitions without the bonding mechanism; prompt them to explain in terms of chemically joined atoms making a new substance.
activities.rationale: Classifying, matching and formula construction assess exactly the targeted outcomes and are best used after the building and properties activities. Including a construction step guards against mistaking recognition for independent production; recognition alone does not elicit production.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: simple (Dalton) atomic model; differences between atoms, elements and compounds; chemical symbols and formulae
NGSS MS-PS1-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-1]
learnerActions: Classify given particle diagrams as element, compound or mixture and justify each choice.
Match chemical symbols to their elements.
Build or complete a formula by filling in how many of each atom for a described molecule.
Transfer to fresh cases: water, carbon dioxide (CO2), sodium chloride (NaCl), and iron sulfide.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can apply the element/compound/mixture distinction, read and write simple formulae, and transfer the 'new properties / not physically separable' idea to new substances.

constraints: Appropriate for ages 11	a201312 (UK KS3 / US NGSS MS-PS1-1 introductory level).

Keep sub-atomic detail light: the objective names a simple model with a nucleus of protons and neutrons and electrons in shells 	a2014 introduce these, but keep the DETAILED electron-shell arrangement light and defer it to a later stage. Do not label the nuclear picture a 'Dalton' model (Dalton's model has no internal structure).

At this introductory level the element/compound/mixture logic and formulae are fully conveyed with 2D models and physical materials; detailed 3D molecular geometry is reserved for later molecular-shape work.
A static atom diagram and symbol gallery are reference/vocabulary scaffolds 	a2014 they cannot let a learner build formulae or test separability, so pair them with construction activities.
Recognition and matching tasks assess classification but do not elicit independent formula construction; include a build/fill-in step for production.

The 'try to separate' demonstration and sodium+chlorine	a2192salt demo are illustrative mechanisms; equivalent physical atom-model or paper-based construction can serve the same teaching purpose. Any physical enactment of the sodium+chlorine or iron+sulfur reactions requires appropriate safety controls, which the source does not detail.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row marks some citations unverified (NGSS MS-PS1-1 and the AAAS/BEST diagnostics claim, verified:false); only the DfE KS3 claim was marked verified. Treat comparative/effectiveness implications cautiously.

The original 'poor fit' claim that an in-role dialogue cannot teach this was softened: dialogue is less suited to constructive building/testing tasks, but this is a narrowly scoped suitability note, not an established universal limit.

Model inconsistency in the source: the pedagogy summary references a 'simple (Dalton) atomic model' (historically a structure-less solid sphere) while the node description and evidence require a 'simple Bohr model' (nucleus with protons/neutrons, electrons in shells). The corrected activities follow the objective, describe the nuclear structure without naming it 'Dalton', and keep detailed arrangement light. Reviewer should confirm the intended model and expected depth.

The sodium+chlorine	a2192salt and iron/sulfur reactions are demonstrations involving hazardous substances; any physical enactment requires appropriate safety controls, which the source does not detail.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: show iron filings and yellow sulfur powder mixed in a dish. Ask the child to predict — can a magnet still pull the iron out, and will it still look like iron + sulfur? (Yes: it's a mixture.) Then heat a fresh portion to form grey iron sulfide and ask the same. A child conflating mixture and compound predicts the magnet still works. It doesn't — a new compound formed. The pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Sodium is a metal that explodes in water; chlorine is a poison gas. Together they make table salt you eat. How can that be?
Is water a mixture or a compound? How would you get the hydrogen and oxygen back — could you just filter or evaporate?
In the formula CO₂, how many atoms of each element are there, and is it an element or a compound?
If you mixed iron filings and sulfur powder versus heated them into iron sulfide — what's different about the two results?
assess.correctAnswer: No — water does neither; it puts fires out. When elements combine into a COMPOUND, the compound has completely NEW properties, not the properties of the elements it came from. Hydrogen and oxygen are chemically bonded in water and no longer behave as the separate elements. Full marks need 'a compound's properties are new, unlike a mixture where each part keeps its own'.

errorPatterns.pattern: a compound keeps the properties of its elements ('water has oxygen in it so it helps burning')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a compound (sodium + chlorine → edible salt, though sodium explodes in water and chlorine is poisonous) with a mixture — bonding creates new properties. Reteach compound-vs-mixture at particle level.
errorPatterns.distractor: It would help things burn, because oxygen is part of it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts water burns or feeds fire because of the hydrogen/oxygen in it

errorPatterns.pattern: compound and mixture are the same thing ('water is just hydrogen mixed with oxygen')
errorPatterns.nextMove: A mixture separates by physical means and keeps each part's properties; a compound needs a chemical reaction to break and has new properties. Draw both at particle level.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, because it's really just hydrogen and oxygen mixed together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes H₂O as a mixture that could be un-mixed physically, not a bonded compound

errorPatterns.pattern: an element is a single atom, so 'oxygen' means one O atom
errorPatterns.nextMove: An element is a substance made of ONE kind of atom (many of them); a molecule is atoms joined; read H₂O as 2 H atoms + 1 O atom bonded. Separate the three terms explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: conflates atom, element and molecule when reading H₂O or O₂

responseLevels.gap: Predicts water burns/feeds fire from its elements; treats compound as a mixture or muddles atom/element/molecule.
responseLevels.full: Explains that a compound has new properties unlike its elements because they are chemically bonded, distinguishes compound from mixture (separation, particle picture), and reads formulae correctly — transferring to fresh cases (NaCl, CO₂, iron sulfide).
responseLevels.partial: Says water doesn't burn and names it a compound, but can't explain that bonding gives NEW properties or reliably distinguish compound from mixture at the particle level — definitions without the mechanism.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Water has the formula H₂O — it's made from hydrogen and oxygen. Hydrogen burns and oxygen is the gas fires need. So would you expect water to burn, or to help things burn? Then the important part: explain why water behaves the way it does, given what it's made of.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason exposes the classic atoms/compounds error: expecting a compound to inherit its elements' properties (and, underneath, confusing a compound with a mixture). A child who thinks water should burn treats H₂O as hydrogen-and-oxygen sitting together; a child who understands compounds says the bonding makes something new.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–11 years

- **Topic:** Simple Design Problems

- **Standards — UK (DfE Design & Technology KS2, Design):** pupils "use research and develop design criteria to inform the design of innovative, functional, appealing products that are fit for purpose, aimed at particular individuals or groups."

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-5-ETS1-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1]."

- **Operational details:** The move at this age is from "make something" to DEFINING the problem before making: naming who it is for, what would count as success (criteria), and what limits the work (constraints on materials, time, cost, size). Children learn to phrase a problem so that you could tell whether a solution worked — turning vague wishes ("make it good") into testable criteria ("the cup must hold 200 ml without leaking for one minute") and to distinguish a criterion (a goal the solution must meet) from a constraint (a limit on how you may reach it). Teach with real, bounded briefs and require the criteria to be measurable before any building.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). The child can, given a need, write two or more measurable success criteria and name at least one materials/time/cost constraint, and can sort mixed statements into criteria vs constraints. Not yet expected: formally weighting or trading off competing criteria (that is the next topic).
bestPractices: Start from an authentic, bounded need with a named user ("a younger child needs a way to carry three library books across the playground in the rain") so criteria and constraints have a real referent.
Insist criteria be TESTABLE before any building: rewrite "make it strong" as "holds 500 g without bending" — model the rewrite aloud and have children spot untestable wording.
Explicitly contrast criterion (what success looks like) with constraint (a limit you must work within); use a two-column sort of mixed statements to build the distinction.
Give constraints teeth: a real materials budget / part list / time limit so children feel that a constraint rules options out, not just describes them.
Defer solutions — spend a whole session only defining the problem, so children learn problem-definition is a distinct step, not a preamble to building.
keyRepresentations: Design brief card: NEED / USER / CRITERIA (measurable) / CONSTRAINTS (materials, time, cost) laid out as fillable slots.
Two-column criteria-vs-constraints sorter.
A 'testable?' check applied to each criterion — a thumb/tick that only turns green when the statement names a measurable outcome.
Constraint chips (allowed materials, £ budget, minutes) that visibly rule options in or out.
commonMisconceptions: Treating vague wishes as criteria ("make it nice/good/strong") instead of measurable outcomes.
Confusing criteria (goals) with constraints (limits) — e.g. listing 'use only card' as a success criterion.
Jumping straight to a favourite solution and back-filling the problem to fit it.
Thinking there is one 'right' problem statement, rather than a defensible one that makes success checkable.
Ignoring the user — writing criteria for what the maker wants, not what the named user needs.

learn.summary: For learners aged 8–11, teach the shift from 'make something' to DEFINING a design problem before building: name the user, state measurable success criteria, and list real constraints (materials, time, cost, size). The core skills are (1) rewriting vague wishes ('make it good/strong') into testable criteria ('holds 500 g without bending'; 'the cup holds 200 ml without leaking for one minute'), (2) distinguishing a criterion (a goal the solution must meet) from a constraint (a limit on how you may reach it), and (3) keeping in problem-space instead of jumping to a favourite solution. There is no single 'right' brief — a good brief is a defensible one that makes success checkable. The main activity has learners author a full design brief for an authentic, bounded need; supporting activities sort and sharpen individual statements; alternatives use annotated worked briefs and in-role client interviews to elicit and explain these distinctions.

activities.title: Author a design brief for a real, named user
feedback: If a criterion has no checkable condition (e.g. 'make it nice'), prompt: 'How would we CHECK it's nice? What would we see or measure?' and rewrite it together as an observable condition.

If the learner names an object to build before stating need/criteria/constraints, bracket it: 'That might be one answer — but first, what does ANY good answer have to achieve?' Redirect to problem and criteria.
If no limits are listed, ask 'What have we actually got? How long? How much can we spend?' and make listing at least one constraint a required step.
If a constraint is listed as a success goal (e.g. 'use only card' under criteria), point out that this is a limit on HOW you work, not what success looks like, and move it.

If the learner worries there is one 'right' answer, reassure that several different briefs can be valid — what matters is that the need, criteria, and constraints make success checkable, not that they match a fixed solution.

If the reading-corner glare scenario is chosen, test each criterion the same way: e.g. 'How would we check at 2 pm whether the screens are readable?' — by looking at the screens and desk surface, NEVER by looking toward the sun or holding any cover up to the eyes. Also probe 'Could a solution make the corner too dark to read a book?' so a sensible upper limit becomes a criterion too.
activities.rationale: At this age the learning objective is problem-definition as a separate step, so the task must require the child to WRITE a full brief for a named user, not just recognise good wording. Authentic bounded needs give criteria and constraints a real referent, and self-checking against 'could you test a solution with this?' makes measurability concrete.
sourceClaims: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1] [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1].
KS2 pupils use research and develop design criteria to inform the design of functional, appealing products fit for purpose and aimed at particular individuals or groups.
learnerActions: Choose a bounded, authentic need with a named user — for example 'a younger child needs to carry three library books across the playground in the rain', or 'the reading corner gets so bright in the afternoon that children can't read the tablet screens' — and write the NEED in problem terms.

Write at least two SUCCESS CRITERIA, phrased so you could actually check them. For each, ask 'How would we SEE or MEASURE this?' Rewrite 'make it strong' as 'holds 500 g without bending' and 'make it good' as an observable condition.
List at least one real CONSTRAINT on materials, time, or cost (e.g. 'only card and tape', 'one afternoon', 'under £2'), and say what option that constraint rules out.
Spend the whole session only defining the problem — do NOT design or build a solution yet.
Check your own brief: could someone use it to judge whether a finished solution worked? If a criterion can't be checked, rewrite it.
activities.intendedInsight: Defining a problem is itself a distinct act of construction: a good brief turns a vague wish into something whose success you could actually check, names who it is for, and states the limits you must work within — before any building begins. There is no single correct brief, only a defensible one that makes success checkable.

activities.title: Sort statements: criterion or constraint?
feedback: If 'use only card' or a budget is placed under criteria, note it describes a limit on means, not an outcome to achieve.
If a vague goal like 'make it good' is sorted confidently, flag that even as a criterion it isn't yet testable and would need rewriting before it could judge a solution.
activities.rationale: The criterion/constraint distinction is a crisp, judgeable one that a two-column sort builds directly. This supports the main brief-authoring task by isolating one sub-skill, though it exercises sorting rather than full authoring.
sourceClaims: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1] [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1].
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of about eight statements (some success goals, some limits on materials/time/cost) and sort each into two columns: CRITERIA (what success looks like) vs CONSTRAINTS (a limit you must work within).
For each placement, say in one sentence why it belongs there — e.g. 'use only card' is a limit on how you work, so it's a constraint.
For any statement you got wrong on a first pass, explain what made it easy to mix up.
activities.intendedInsight: A criterion is a goal the solution must meet; a constraint is a limit on how you may reach it. The same brief needs both, and they play different roles.

activities.title: Make it testable: rewrite vague criteria and set a threshold
feedback: If a rewrite still has no observable/measurable element, ask what you would physically see, weigh, or time to decide success.
If a chosen threshold is unreasonable for the need (far too easy or impossible), ask what the named user actually requires and adjust.
activities.rationale: Turning untestable wording into measurable conditions is the specific skill that makes a brief judgeable. Short targeted rewrites give fast practice; this checks the skill rather than having the child author a whole brief, so pair it with the authoring task.
sourceClaims: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1] [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-1].
learnerActions: Given a vague criterion such as 'make it strong', rewrite it as a measurable statement (e.g. 'holds 500 g without bending').
Given a need, choose a reasonable success threshold and justify it (e.g. 'the cup must hold 200 ml without leaking for one minute').
Given two phrasings of the same criterion, pick the one you could actually check and say why the other can't be tested.
activities.intendedInsight: A criterion is only useful if someone could observe or measure whether it was met; naming a quantity, time, or observable condition is what makes a wish testable. (The source requires criteria to be 'specified'; making them observable is how we meet that at this age.)

activities.title: Interview the client to sharpen the brief
feedback: If the learner writes criteria for what the maker wants rather than the user, have the client say 'but I need…' to refocus on the named user's need.
If a criterion stays vague after the conversation, have the client ask once more 'how will we test that?' before it is accepted.
activities.rationale: A spoken, responsive interview suits the elicitation side of problem-definition and models the 'how would we know?' habit. On its own it does not require the structured written brief, so use it to feed into the authoring task rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: KS2 pupils use research and develop design criteria to inform the design of functional, appealing products fit for purpose and aimed at particular individuals or groups.
learnerActions: Take on the role of a designer talking to the named user (the 'client') about their need.
Ask the client questions and let the client keep pushing back with 'How would we KNOW it worked?' until each proposed criterion becomes measurable.
After the conversation, write down the agreed need, two or more measurable criteria, and at least one constraint the client named (budget, time, or materials).
activities.intendedInsight: Problem-definition is a questioning stance: good criteria emerge by repeatedly asking how success would be checked and listening to what the user actually needs.

activities.title: Unpack a worked design brief
feedback: If an explanation of 'why measurable' just restates the criterion, press for the specific observation or measurement involved.
If the added criterion is vague or the added constraint doesn't actually rule anything out, send it back for a checkable/limiting rewrite.
activities.rationale: An annotated worked example is good exposition for the criterion/constraint and testable/vague distinctions. Because reading an example does not itself require the child to author or sort their own statements, the added-criterion step is included so it leads into production rather than staying at recognition.
learnerActions: Read a complete, well-formed design brief for a named user (need, user, criteria, constraints).
For each criterion, explain why it is measurable — what you could observe or measure to check it.
For each constraint, explain what option it rules out of the solution space.
Then write one new criterion and one new constraint you think the brief is missing, keeping them testable and real.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a strong brief dissected shows what 'measurable' and 'limiting' look like concretely, giving a model to imitate when writing your own — and the brief you add to is one defensible version, not the only possible one.

constraints: The main objective is for the child to AUTHOR a brief (need, measurable criteria, constraints) for a named user; sorting tasks and multiple-choice/rewrite exercises check sub-skills but do not substitute for full authoring.
Reading or tapping through a pre-authored annotated brief explains the distinctions but does not require the child to write or sort their own statements; treat it as a model, not the assessment.
An in-role client interview elicits and sharpens criteria but should still end in a written, structured brief; it supplements rather than replaces authoring.
Defer solutions: spend a session only defining the problem so children experience problem-definition as a distinct step, not a preamble to building.
Constraints need teeth — use a real materials list, budget, or time limit so children feel a constraint rules options out, not merely describes them.
There is no single 'right' problem statement; accept any defensible brief whose criteria and constraints make success checkable, rather than marking against one fixed answer.

If the reading-corner glare example is used, any check of light/readability must inspect the screens, desk, or the patch of light on the surface — never ask a child to look at or through a cover toward the sun.
Not yet expected at this level: formally weighting or trading off competing criteria (that belongs to a later topic).

Interactive feedback ideas (e.g. a live 'testable?' indicator that only turns green when a criterion names a measurable outcome; dragging statements into criteria/constraint columns with mis-sorts bouncing back; constraint chips that visibly grey out disallowed items in a mock parts tray) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both cited sources carry verified:false in the source row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source framed a screen-based 'Design Brief Builder' as uniquely 'ideal' and dismissed 3D/spatial media as adding nothing; these catalog-fit claims have been reframed as one proposal with stated affordances and optional interaction examples, not a universal necessity claim.

The diagnostic scenario (afternoon glare on reading-corner tablet screens) and its probe questions are now included as one OPTIONAL example brief within the authoring activity; it is one defensible framing, not the only correct brief, and its observation method is explicitly limited to checking the screens/surface, not looking toward the sun.

probeDeeper: You wrote 'block the light' — how would we check, at 2 pm, whether a solution had done that?
Is there such a thing as blocking TOO much light here? Should that be one of your criteria?
If we only had paper and tape and one afternoon, which of your criteria would be hardest to meet?
assess.correctAnswer: The child states the need in problem terms (reduce glare on the screens in the reading corner), specifies at least two success criteria phrased so you could check them (e.g. 'the screen is readable at 2 pm', 'it doesn't make the corner too dark to read a book'), and identifies real constraints — available materials, time, cost, or that it mustn't block the walkway — all WITHOUT jumping to a particular solution.

errorPatterns.pattern: Jumps straight to a solution instead of defining the problem ('we should just get blinds').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bracket the solution: 'That might be one answer — but first, what does ANY good answer have to achieve?' Redirect to problem and criteria before solutions.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names a specific object to build before stating any need, criteria, or constraints.

errorPatterns.pattern: Criteria are vague and unmeasurable ('make it good', 'make it nice') so you couldn't tell whether a solution worked.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Turn each vague criterion into a test: 'How would we CHECK it's good? What would we see or measure?' Rewrite together as observable conditions.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Success criteria contain no checkable condition — nothing you could observe or measure to decide success.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits constraints — treats materials, time, and cost as unlimited.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce constraints as part of every design brief: 'What have we actually got? How long? How much can we spend?' Make listing limits a required step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists needs and criteria but names no limits on resources; solution space is treated as boundless.

responseLevels.gap: States a solution rather than a problem, or gives only a vague aim with no checkable criteria and no constraints.
responseLevels.full: Defines the need, gives two or more observable/checkable success criteria, and identifies real constraints — producing a brief against which competing solutions could actually be tested.
responseLevels.partial: Frames the problem and offers criteria or constraints, but the criteria aren't all measurable or the constraints are thin — the brief couldn't yet be used to judge a solution cleanly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The reading corner gets so bright in the afternoon that children can't see the tablet screens. Before anyone builds anything, I want you to define the design problem: write down what need it addresses, at least two things a good solution must do (so we could tell if it worked), and what would limit us — like materials, time, or money. (Set the scenario and watch how the child frames it; do not supply the criteria yourself.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the framing reveals the habit asking can't: a child who understands stays in problem-space and writes checkable criteria, while a child who doesn't leaps straight to 'let's put up a curtain' and never separates the problem from one solution. Whether criteria are measurable only shows when the child writes them down.

pedagogy.summary: Algebraic modelling means translating a situation into an algebraic expression or formula, building a table of values from the rule, and plotting and interpreting the graph — moving fluently among words, symbols, tables and graphs. The load-bearing difficulty is the translation from words to symbols: children must define each variable as a NUMBER (a quantity), not a label, and capture the relationship's structure rather than mirroring the word order. It is best taught by insisting variables name quantities ('let n = the NUMBER of …'), checking every translation with numbers, and travelling the full word→symbol→table→graph loop.
bestPractices: Define variables as quantities, not labels: 'let s = the number of students', never 's = students'.
Check every worded translation against actual numbers before trusting it (substitute a case and see if it makes sense).
Build the structure from the relationship, not the word order — resist writing symbols in the order the words happen to appear.
Travel the whole loop: words → expression/formula → table of values → graph → interpret back in context.
Interpret the graph's features (intercept, gradient, shape) in the terms of the situation.
keyRepresentations: The four-way link: word problem ↔ expression/formula ↔ table of values ↔ graph
'Let [letter] = the number of …' variable definitions
A numeric check of a proposed translation
Graph features (through-origin, gradient) read back into the context
commonMisconceptions: Reversal error: translates 'six students per professor' as 6S = P (mirroring the word order) instead of S = 6P.
Letter-as-label: treats the letter as the object ('s = students') rather than the number of them.
Mirrors the word order rather than the relationship's structure (e.g. 'add 5 then double' → 2n + 5 instead of 2(n + 5)).
Reads a table or graph as isolated points without interpreting the relationship in context.

learn.summary: Algebraic modelling means translating a situation into an algebraic expression or formula, building a table of values from the rule, and plotting and interpreting the graph — moving fluently among words, symbols, tables and graphs. The hardest move is the words-to-symbols translation: each variable must name a NUMBER (a quantity), not an object or label, and the symbols must capture the relationship's structure rather than mirror the order of the words. Teach it by insisting variables name quantities ('let n = the NUMBER of …'), checking every translation by substituting real numbers, and travelling the full word→symbol→table→graph loop, then interpreting graph features back in context.

activities.title: Build and number-check an equation from a worded situation
feedback: If the learner writes 6S = T, prompt: 'Put T = 2 into your equation — how many students does it give? Does 2 teachers and only a third of a student match six students per teacher?' The contradiction drives the flip to S = 6T.

If the learner treats S as 'students' rather than 'the number of students' and stalls on substituting a value, redefine together: 'S = the NUMBER of students', then substitute a number so the letter behaves as a quantity.
When S = 6T is confirmed, the table should read T=1→S=6, T=2→S=12, T=3→S=18, and the graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient 6 — S rises by 6 for each extra teacher.
activities.rationale: Documented reversal errors arise from syntactic left-to-right word matching and from treating letters as labels rather than numbers; a numeric substitution check exposes the reversal because the reversed equation yields impossible (fractional) values for small cases such as T = 2, and even its whole-number values give fewer students than teachers, which a correct model never produces.
sourceClaims: Students systematically REVERSE a worded multiplicative relationship when translating to algebra — e.g. 'six students for every professor' becomes 6S = P instead of S = 6P — driven by word-order matching (syntactic left-to-right translation) and by treating letters as labels/objects rather than numbers (static comparison).
learnerActions: Read a worded situation such as 'there are six students for every teacher at a school'.
Define each variable as a quantity: 'let S = the NUMBER of students' and 'let T = the NUMBER of teachers'.
Assemble an equation from the letters, numbers and operations that links S and T.
Test the equation by substituting a real case: put T = 2 into your equation and work out S. Ask whether the answer is sensible for the situation.

If the equation gives an impossible result (for example 6S = T gives S = 1/3 of a student at T = 2, and fractional values 1/6, 1/3, 1/2 … for T = 1, 2, 3; even when it gives a whole number, such as S = 1 at T = 6, that means fewer students than teachers), revise it so it models the relationship, not the word order.
Once the equation checks out, fill a table for T = 1, 2, 3 and plot S against T.
activities.intendedInsight: An equation must model the RELATIONSHIP between quantities, not the left-to-right order of the words. Writing 6S = T for 'six students per teacher' copies the word order; substituting T = 2 then demands S = 1/3 of a student, which is impossible. Flipping to S = 6T models 'six times as many students as teachers' and produces a sensible, growing table.

activities.title: Travel the full loop: words → formula → table → graph → interpret
feedback: If the learner fills the table but cannot describe the line, prompt them to join consecutive points, state the constant rate of increase, and say what that rate means in students-per-teacher terms.

Contrast the two rules explicitly: S = 6T passes through the origin with gradient 6; S = T + 6 crosses the S-axis at 6 with gradient 1. Checking each with T = 2 (12 vs 8) confirms they are different relationships.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects pupils to move freely between numerical, algebraic, graphical and diagrammatic representations and to interpret graphs in context; coordinating all four and interpreting graph features is what separates fluent modelling from completing single isolated translations.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'model situations or procedures by translating them into algebraic expressions or formulae and by using graphs', and 'move freely between different numerical, algebraic, graphical and diagrammatic representations'.
learnerActions: Starting from a confirmed equation such as S = 6T, construct a table of values for several T values.

Plot the points and describe the pattern: the points lie on a straight line through the origin. A line may be drawn to show the trend, but only whole-number points are meaningful, because you cannot have part of a teacher or student.
State the gradient and read it back in context: 'the line rises by 6 students for every extra teacher — six students per teacher'.
Explain what the through-origin feature means in the situation (no teachers, no students).

Translate a changed relationship to test structure: if instead there were six students MORE than teachers (S = T + 6), rebuild the table and describe how the graph differs (line no longer through the origin; crosses the S-axis at 6; gradient 1).
activities.intendedInsight: A table and graph are not isolated points but a picture of a relationship. Reading the gradient and intercept back into the situation completes the modelling loop and distinguishes a multiplicative rule (per) from an additive one (more than).

activities.title: Spot the reversal and the misplaced structure
feedback: For 'add 5 then double', 2n + 5 actually means 'double then add 5', but 2(n + 5) follows the meaning; testing n = 3 gives 16 for the intended rule and 11 for 2n + 5, exposing the difference.
If a reversal option is chosen, substitute a value into both candidates and compare against the situation to reveal which is impossible (6S = T demands a fractional student at T = 2).
activities.rationale: Selecting among candidates and filling blanks checks whether the learner can identify a correct translation and reject the common reversal, but recognition alone does not require the learner to originate and self-correct a translation, so pair it with construction tasks.
sourceClaims: Students systematically REVERSE a worded multiplicative relationship when translating to algebra — e.g. 'six students for every professor' becomes 6S = P instead of S = 6P — driven by word-order matching (syntactic left-to-right translation) and by treating letters as labels/objects rather than numbers (static comparison).
learnerActions: Given a sentence, choose between the correct equation (S = 6T) and the reversed one (6S = T), and justify the choice with a numeric test.
Match worded situations to their matching expressions or formulae.
Fill the blank in a formula drawn from a sentence.
For 'add 5 then double', decide between 2n + 5 and 2(n + 5), then check with a number (e.g. n = 3: the intended rule gives 16, not 11).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and rejecting the reversed equation, and using brackets so the written expression carries out the operations in the order the situation describes (rather than relying on the default order of operations), consolidates structural translation.

constraints: Variables must be defined as quantities — 'let S = the NUMBER of students' — never as labels ('S = students'); a letter that names an object cannot be substituted with a value.
Every proposed translation must be checked by substituting at least one concrete case before it is trusted.

A side-by-side display of situation, equation, table and graph can illustrate the links but does not require the learner to perform the translation or expose a reversal; use it as a reference, not as the main task.

Recognition and matching tasks check whether a learner can identify a correct translation but do not elicit independent construction and self-correction; include at least one task where the learner builds an equation from scratch.

A live checker that substitutes a case and flags contradictions (e.g. demanding a fraction of a student), an auto-filling table and an auto-plotting graph are useful optional supports that make the loop self-correcting; they are illustrations of the mechanism, not required tooling, and the same numeric check can be done by hand on paper.
Distinguish multiplicative 'six per' relationships (S = 6T, through origin) from additive 'six more than' relationships (S = T + 6, intercept at 6); do not conflate them.

Describe the reversed equation's failure accurately: 6S = T yields growing student counts that are fractional for most teacher numbers (1/6, 1/3, 1/2 … for T = 1, 2, 3), and fractional students are impossible. Even its whole-number results (T = 6 gives S = 1) contradict the situation, because they give one student for every six teachers instead of six students per teacher. The numbers do not shrink.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent fresh audit: for S = 6T, T=1→6, T=2→12, T=3→18 and gradient 6 through the origin are correct; the reversed 6S = T gives S=1/6, 1/3, 1/2 at T=1,2,3 — impossible (fractional) counts that GROW rather than shrink, so the pedagogical point (fractional students) holds and is stated consistently across actions, feedback and constraints.

Corrected an inherited error: the original errorPatterns.revealedBy described the reversal as giving 'fractional or shrinking student numbers'; 6S = T does not produce shrinking values, so 'shrinking' is excluded from all learner-facing text and the impossibility is stated as fractional students.
Fresh check of the 'add 5 then double' example: the intended rule is 2(n+5); at n=3 this is 16, while the word-order mirror 2n+5 gives 11.
Fresh check of the additive contrast: S = T + 6 at T=2 gives 8 versus S = 6T giving 12; through-origin vs intercept-6 and gradients 6 vs 1 are consistent.

The original framed a text/chat format as unable to expose a reversal 'as sharply' and a third dimension as adding 'nothing'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been reframed in affordance terms (a numeric substitution check is the decisive move; discussion can still support reasoning; a static or 3D display can illustrate but not force the translation).
The source citations support the general principles of the reversal error and the curriculum expectation; they do not establish that these specific activity designs were tested for efficacy.

probeDeeper: Test your equation: if there are 2 teachers, how many students does it give? Does that match 'six students per teacher'?
A pupil wrote 6S = T. Put T = 3 into it — how many students? Is that sensible?
What does the steepness of your S-against-T graph tell you about the school?
If instead there were six students MORE than teachers (not six per teacher), how would the equation change?
assess.correctAnswer: S = 6T (six times as many students as teachers). Table: T = 1 → S = 6, T = 2 → S = 12, T = 3 → S = 18. The graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient 6 — S goes up by 6 for each extra teacher.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal error (word-order mirroring) — writes 6S = T, placing the multiplier on the wrong variable so the words' order is copied rather than the relationship
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test with numbers — 'if there are 2 teachers, how many students? Does your equation give 12?' — the contradiction drives the flip to S = 6T.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The equation is 6S = T (or 6S = P); the table then gives fractional or shrinking student numbers.

errorPatterns.pattern: Letter-as-label — treats S as 'students' and T as 'teachers' (objects) rather than the NUMBER of each, so cannot substitute a value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redefine as 'S = the NUMBER of students' and substitute a value to make the letter a quantity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'S stands for students' and stalls when asked to put a number in; cannot fill the table.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mirrors word order over structure — builds the expression in the order the words appear regardless of meaning (e.g. 'add 5 then double' → 2n + 5 instead of 2(n + 5))
errorPatterns.nextMove: Parse the relationship's structure and bracket accordingly; check the result with a number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Missing or misplaced brackets; the structure follows the sentence, not the operations' order.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the table/graph as isolated points, not a relationship — fills values but cannot describe the line or its meaning
errorPatterns.nextMove: Join consecutive points, describe the constant rate, and interpret the gradient in context (students per teacher).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Completes the table but cannot say the graph is a straight line through the origin or what its steepness means.

responseLevels.gap: Writes the reversed equation (6S = T) or treats the letters as labels; cannot build a consistent table.
responseLevels.full: Writes S = 6T, verifies it with numbers, fills the table, and describes the graph as a line through the origin with gradient 6 meaning six students per teacher — translating fluently across all four representations and to a new relationship.
responseLevels.partial: Writes a plausible equation and fills the table, but cannot justify it with a numeric check or interpret the graph's features in context — completes single translations without coordinating words, symbols, table and graph.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: At a school there are six students for every teacher. First: write an equation linking the number of students (S) and the number of teachers (T). Then: here is a table with T = 1, 2, 3 — fill in S for each, and tell me what the graph of S against T would look like.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who models the RELATIONSHIP writes S = 6T and the table grows in sixes; a child making the reversal error writes 6S = T (mirroring 'six students per teacher' left to right), which the table exposes — at T = 1 it demands S = 1/6, an impossibility a correct model never produces. The words→symbol→table chain makes the reversal visible.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** The Rock Cycle — rocks slowly change from one type to another over millions of years: igneous weathers into sediment, sediment compacts into sedimentary rock, heat and pressure make metamorphic rock, and melting starts the cycle again — a continuous process with no beginning or end.

- **Standards — UK (KS2→KS3 bridge):** In England the rock cycle and '[curriculum wording omitted; reference ON-SCI-2022-G4-E2.1]' are DfE **KS3 Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere**. At KS2 the statutory groundwork is Y3 **Rocks** (compare/group rocks, fossils, soils) and Y4 weathering/erosion contexts. So this topic teaches KS3 content and should be framed as building on Y3 Rocks — note the placement honestly.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** The full rock cycle is **MS-ESS2-1** ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-1, MS-ESS2-4, MS-LS2-3]…'). The nearest elementary anchor is **4-ESS1-1** (evidence from rock layers/fossils for landscape change over time) and 4-ESS2 (weathering/erosion). This topic bridges into MS. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisites 'Types of Rock' and 'Earth's Layers'. The three types are already known; the NEW idea is that they INTERCONVERT via processes (weathering/erosion → deposition/compaction → heat & pressure → melting & cooling) and that the cycle is continuous — no start, no end, and NOT a fixed one-way sequence. The load-bearing insight is that a single rock can take many different PATHS around (and across) the cycle over deep time.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (early-formal, cyclic-systems + deep-time reasoning). Children can trace a loop but tend to memorise one fixed order and struggle with 'millions of years' and shortcut paths. Success = trace at least one complete path, name the process at each step, and state the cycle is continuous over vast time.
bestPractices: Teach it as PROCESSES connecting the three known types, not a new list — each arrow is an event (weathering, compaction, heat/pressure, melting, cooling).
Break the 'one fixed order' misconception by having children trace MULTIPLE valid paths, including shortcuts (e.g. any rock can be melted, or uplifted and weathered) so the cycle isn't a single loop.
Anchor the timescale explicitly — millions of years — and contrast with the human/quick events elsewhere in the domain so 'slow' is felt against 'fast'.
Use a concrete follow-one-grain narrative (a mineral grain journeys from a lava flow, to a beach, to a buried layer, to a squeezed metamorphic band, to melt) to make the abstract cycle a story.
Connect drivers to the rest of the domain: Earth's internal heat (melting), weathering/erosion at the surface, and burial/pressure — the cycle is powered by the same forces already met.
keyRepresentations: The classic rock-cycle diagram (three types as nodes; processes as labelled arrows, including cross-cutting shortcuts)
Follow-one-grain journey narrative around the cycle
Process cards: weathering/erosion, deposition/compaction, heat & pressure, melting, cooling/crystallising
A deep-time ribbon (millions of years) alongside the cycle to scale the pace
commonMisconceptions: The rock cycle is a fixed one-way sequence igneous→sedimentary→metamorphic (there are many paths and shortcuts; any type can become any other).
The cycle has a beginning and an end (it is continuous, with no start or finish).
Rocks change quickly / you could watch it happen (changes take thousands to millions of years).
Only volcanoes change rocks (surface weathering/erosion, burial pressure, and deep heat all drive the cycle).
Once a rock is metamorphic (or any type) it stays that way forever (it can be weathered, melted, or re-formed into another type).

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, teach the rock cycle as a set of PROCESSES connecting the three already-known rock types (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic), not as a new list to memorise. The load-bearing insight is that a single rock can take many different PATHS around and across the cycle — including shortcuts — over millions of years, with no fixed one-way order and no beginning or end. The strongest activity lets learners pick a rock, apply a process (weather/erode, deposit/compact, heat & pressure, melt, cool), watch it transform, and deliberately take different routes on repeat runs; a diagram and a consolidation task support naming, sequencing and reinforcement. Note: in England this is KS3 content building on Y3 Rocks; in the US it maps to NGSS MS-ESS2-1 with 4-ESS1-1 as the elementary anchor.

activities.title: Operate a rock-cycle machine: apply processes and change the path
feedback: When a learner only ever repeats igneous→sedimentary→metamorphic, prompt: 'Could you melt this sedimentary rock right now? What would it become?' to surface a shortcut.
When a learner takes a new route, affirm: 'You just skipped a step — a metamorphic rock went straight to sediment by weathering. That shows there's no fixed order.'

If a learner expects the change to be fast, point to the deep-time counter: 'Notice how much time the slow steps added, like weathering, burial and squeezing. A whole journey around the cycle usually takes millions of years, far longer than a lifetime, even though some steps, like lava cooling, can happen fast.'
If a learner thinks only volcanoes change rocks, highlight the weathering/erosion and burial/pressure actions: 'Surface weathering and burial change rocks too, not just melting.'
activities.rationale: A cycle of interconverting states with multiple paths is a system learners can drive; applying processes and watching transformations is intended to make the many-route, continuous nature experiential rather than a memorised diagram. Repeated runs with different routes target the 'fixed one-way order' misconception, and a per-step time counter anchors the deep-time scale. The source supports the taught model (continuous cycle with multiple pathways); the driveable-medium efficacy is an agent proposal, not source-established.
sourceClaims: The rock cycle is a continuous process with multiple pathways in which igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks interconvert via weathering/erosion, compaction, heat and pressure, and melting.
learnerActions: Pick a starting rock (e.g. a chunk of igneous rock).

Choose an action to apply: weather and erode it into sediment; bury and compact sediment into sedimentary rock; bake and squeeze a rock into metamorphic rock; or melt a rock and let it cool into igneous rock.

Watch the rock visibly transform with each action, and read the deep-time counter that adds time for each step. Most steps, like weathering, burial and metamorphism, take thousands to millions of years. Some, like lava cooling, can be quick, but a full journey usually takes millions of years.
Run the cycle again and deliberately take a DIFFERENT route — e.g. melt a sedimentary rock directly into igneous, or weather a metamorphic rock directly into sediment.
State out loud, after several runs, whether there is a fixed order or a finish line, and why.

Optionally switch to a 'follow one grain' story mode that narrates the long journey of the material in a single mineral grain (lava flow → beach sediment → buried layer → squeezed metamorphic band → melt, where the grain itself is destroyed and its material joins new magma).
activities.intendedInsight: The rock cycle is a continuous web of transformations: any rock type can become any other depending on which process acts, there are shortcuts, and the whole thing unfolds over millions of years with no start and no end.

activities.title: Rock-cycle diagram with reveal-on-arrow and shortcut flaps
feedback: If a learner names only the standard loop, ask them to find and trace one shortcut arrow and name its process.
Confirm correct naming: 'Yes — that arrow is weathering and erosion, turning rock into sediment.'
If a learner treats the diagram as a strict circle, draw attention to the shortcut flap so they see the extra paths.
activities.rationale: A labelled diagram is useful reference and supports naming the steps and timescales. A fixed diagram does not let learners drive transformations the way the operable machine can, so a learner may read it as a single loop; adding reveal-on-arrow and explicit shortcut highlighting keeps the many-paths idea visible. This supports, rather than replaces, hands-on tracing of multiple routes. Relative medium limits here are a proposal, not source-established.
learnerActions: Study a rock-cycle diagram showing the three types as nodes and processes as labelled arrows.
Tap or examine each arrow to reveal the process it represents and its approximate timescale.
Open an 'Is there only one way round?' prompt that highlights cross-cutting shortcut paths (e.g. melting from any type, uplift-and-weather from any type).
Drill into 'heat & pressure' to see how metamorphism forms.
Trace with a finger at least two different valid paths through the diagram and name the process at each step.
activities.intendedInsight: Each arrow in the cycle is a named event, and the diagram contains more than one legitimate route — including shortcuts — rather than a single loop.

activities.title: Consolidate: sequence, match and judge valid paths
feedback: For a correct shortcut choice: 'Right — a sedimentary rock can be melted and cool into igneous without passing through metamorphic first.'
For 'the cycle ends' answers: prompt 'What happens to a rock after it melts and cools? Could it change type again?' to reinstate the no-end idea.
For a mismatched process, pair it back: 'Compaction squeezes loose sediment together — which rock type does that make?'
activities.rationale: The processes and paths give clean, orderable and selectable structure: sequencing, matching and judging valid paths consolidate naming and reinforce that shortcuts are allowed. A recognition/selection task verifies and strengthens the model but does not by itself elicit a learner's independent construction of a full journey, so it works best after the operable and diagram activities.
learnerActions: Order a valid path around the cycle from a scrambled set of steps.
Match each process to the rock type it produces (e.g. heat & pressure without melting → metamorphic; compaction and cementation of sediment → sedimentary; cooling of molten rock → igneous).
Choose which of several offered paths is a valid rock-cycle path, including an option that uses a shortcut.
Answer whether the cycle has an end, and justify the answer in a sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can name processes, produce a correct sequence, recognise that shortcut paths are legitimate, and articulate that the cycle is continuous.

constraints: Prerequisites: learners should already know the three rock types ('Types of Rock') and Earth's layers; the NEW idea here is that the types interconvert via processes and that the cycle is continuous.

Frame placement honestly: this is KS3 content (DfE KS3 Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere) built on Y3 Rocks in England; in the US it bridges toward NGSS MS-ESS2-1, with 4-ESS1-1 (rock-record change over time) and 4-ESS2 (weathering/erosion) as the nearest elementary anchors.
Teach arrows as events (weathering/erosion, deposition/compaction, heat & pressure, melting, cooling/crystallising), not as a new vocabulary list.
Deliberately require multiple paths and shortcuts so learners do not fossilise a single igneous→sedimentary→metamorphic order.
Anchor the timescale explicitly in millions of years; contrast with faster surface events so 'slow' is felt against 'fast'.
The diagram activity is a reference scaffold: a fixed diagram can still teach naming and routes, but it does not let learners drive transformations, so pair it with hands-on path-tracing.

The sequence/match/judge tasks are recognition-and-ordering responses; they consolidate and check but do not by themselves elicit a learner's independent construction of a full journey — use the operable machine or an explanation prompt for that.

Success criteria: trace at least one complete path, name the process at each step, and state that the cycle is continuous over vast time; stronger success is explaining that any type can become any other via different paths and shortcuts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row (NGSS mapping and the USGS/BGS rock-cycle description); the DfE curriculum citation is verified:true. Treat standards mappings and the continuous-multiple-pathways description as legacy, unverified claims.

sourceClaims were scoped to where the source directly backs the claim: the USGS/BGS continuous-multiple-pathways description underpins activity 1's taught model, but it does not establish the pedagogical efficacy of a diagram or a consolidation/selection task, so those carry []. Activity 1's source citation supports only the factual model it teaches, not the driveable-medium efficacy. No source attests medium superiority or activity effectiveness.

The legacy row's 'poor fit' entries claimed a 3D environment 'adds no relevant insight' and a conversation has 'no in-role persona central'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; omitted as boilerplate rather than asserted as limits. A 3D or dialogue treatment is not inherently valueless, but no distinct activity was specified for them here.

The legacy claim that a static image 'tends to reinforce a single fixed loop' is a relative tendency, not an absolute limit; softened to note a fixed diagram does not let learners drive transformations while still teaching naming and routes.

Checked for internal consistency: the transformations (weathering→sediment, compaction→sedimentary, heat & pressure→metamorphic, melting+cooling→igneous) and the shortcut examples (metamorphic→sediment; sedimentary→melt→igneous) are coherent with the stated continuous-cycle model; no arithmetic or force/motion claims present to audit.

The assessment's diagnostic (friend draws a single fixed circle) and probe questions were preserved in spirit as feedback prompts; the fixed-circle misconception is treated as the error to correct, never offered as a valid learner answer. Assessment fields themselves were not modified.

probeDeeper: Can a metamorphic rock turn straight into sediment without becoming igneous first? How?
What process would turn a sedimentary rock into an igneous one?
Roughly how long does it take a rock to change type — years, or much longer?
Is there a 'first' rock or a 'start' to the cycle? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: No — it isn't a fixed one-way loop. A rock can take many different paths and shortcuts: any type can become any other. For example, a metamorphic rock can be weathered straight into sediment (skipping 'back to igneous'), or a sedimentary rock can be melted and cool into igneous. Weathering, pressure, heat and melting can act in different orders, all over millions of years.

errorPatterns.pattern: The rock cycle is a fixed one-way circle — always igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → igneous in that order
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show multiple pathways — metamorphic weathering to sediment, or sedimentary melting to igneous.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it's a fixed circle that always goes in that one order.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists on one strict sequence; denies shortcuts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rocks change quickly — you could watch a rock go round the cycle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise deep time; the processes are extremely slow.
errorPatterns.distractor: The cycle happens quickly — a rock goes round in a short time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No sense of the millions-of-years timescale.

errorPatterns.pattern: A rock can only move 'forwards', never skip or reverse a step
errorPatterns.nextMove: Any type can turn into any other depending on which process acts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies e.g. metamorphic turning directly into sediment.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the rock cycle as a fixed one-way circle, or thinks rocks change quickly.
responseLevels.full: Explains any rock type can become any other by different paths and shortcuts (e.g. metamorphic→sediment, sedimentary→melt→igneous), driven by weathering/pressure/heat/melting over millions of years — a web, not a single loop.
responseLevels.partial: Names the types and processes and can trace the standard loop but insists the order is fixed / denies shortcuts.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A friend draws the rock cycle as a single circle: igneous always turns into sedimentary, then always into metamorphic, then back to igneous — always in that one order. Is the rock cycle really a fixed one-way loop like that? Explain what can actually happen to a rock.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can recite the three types and a circle diagram yet believe the order is fixed. Asking whether it's really a one-way loop forces the many-paths insight; a child holding the single-loop model insists on the strict sequence.
