pedagogy.summary: Children move from comparing mass to QUANTIFYING it: expressing mass as a number of units — first non-standard (this book balances 5 cubes), then standard (grams, kilograms) — and reading a simple dial/scale. The balance gives equivalence (the object balances N identical units); reading a graduated scale means valuing the intervals, not counting marks.
bestPractices: Use a balance to find how many IDENTICAL units balance the object (equivalence), recording as number + unit ('5 cubes', '200 g')
Insist units are identical — mixing cube sizes breaks the count (the unit-size principle: a larger unit gives a smaller count)
When reading a dial/scale, first work out what one interval is worth, then count intervals (spaces) to the pointer, not the marks
Estimate first, then check by measuring
Keep it practical; wait for the balance beam to settle before reading
keyRepresentations: Balance with identical unit-weights on one pan
Dial / kitchen scale with graduations
The number-line-like scale of graduations
The record: '5 cubes' or '200 g'
commonMisconceptions: Uses non-identical units yet counts 'more units = heavier' (unit-size ignorance)
Reads a scale by counting marks rather than valuing intervals; misreads a pointer between graduations
Thinks the count itself is the mass regardless of which unit was used
Reads before the balance settles / uses a mix of unit sizes

learn.summary: Children move from comparing mass to quantifying it: expressing mass as a number of units — first non-standard (this book balances 5 cubes), then standard (grams, kilograms) — and reading a simple dial or scale. A balance shows equivalence (the object balances N identical units); reading a graduated scale means valuing the intervals, not counting marks. The key insight is that a larger unit gives a smaller count for the same object.

activities.title: Balance it with identical units
feedback: If a count is reported while the beam is still moving, prompt: wait for the beam to settle, then read. If it settles tipped to one side, it is not balanced, so add or remove a cube; if no whole number of cubes levels it exactly, record 'about' or 'between' two counts.
If cubes of mixed sizes were used, point out that the count only means something when every unit is identical; redo with one size.
If the estimate was far off, that is fine — the point is to compare your estimate with the measured count and notice the gap.
activities.rationale: Equivalence via balancing is a concrete route into quantifying mass and underpins later standard-unit work. Recording as number-plus-unit anchors the idea that the unit matters.
sourceClaims: NCETM mastery tasks assess mass via balance equivalence ('this box weighs 10 kg, how much does each tin weigh?') and via reading dial/kitchen scales to compare masses ('what is the mass of two red bags? which is heavier, red or green? explain'); the Year 1 Big Idea introduces equivalence ('how many cubes are equivalent to the mass of the teddy?').
learnerActions: Place a book (or other object) on one pan of a balance.

Add identical unit-weights (e.g. interlocking cubes) one at a time to the other pan until the beam levels, or is as near level as you can get; if one more cube tips it the other way, the object is between two counts.

Wait for the beam to settle before reading, then count the cubes and record the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes', or 'about 8 cubes' / 'between 8 and 9 cubes' if it never quite levels.
Before you start adding cubes, check every cube is the same size; set aside any odd-sized ones.
Before adding any cubes, estimate how many you expect; after measuring, compare your estimate with the measured count.
activities.intendedInsight: Mass can be quantified as a number of identical units that balance the object; the record is a number plus a unit, not just a number.

activities.title: Same book, different unit size
feedback: If the child says the smaller big-cube count means the book is now lighter or has changed, show one big cube balancing several small cubes, so one big = many small; then the smaller count for the same book makes sense.
If the child claims 15 small cubes is heavier than 10 big cubes just because 15 > 10, compare the actual units directly on the balance: you cannot compare counts made with different-sized units.
Correct reasoning to reinforce: 'bigger cubes are heavier, so fewer of them balance the same book'.
activities.rationale: Directly targets unit-size ignorance by letting the child watch the count drop for an unchanged object. The inverse relationship between unit size and count is a core measurement idea, and discrete counting can otherwise convince children that unit size is irrelevant.
sourceClaims: The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement (inverse relationship between unit size and count); counting discrete items can wrongly convince children that unit size doesn't matter, when in measurement it is critical.
learnerActions: Measure the SAME book again, this time using larger unit-weights.
Count how many large units balance the book and compare with the earlier count of small units.
Say aloud why the number is different even though the book has not changed.
Discuss: can both counts be right at the same time — for example '5 big cubes' and '12 small cubes' for the same book? Explain how.
Place one large unit on one pan and add small units on the other until it balances, or is as close as possible — count about how many small units equal one large unit.
Answer: if you used really tiny units instead, would the number be bigger or smaller? Why?
activities.intendedInsight: A larger unit means fewer units are needed to balance the same object; the count changes because the unit changed, not because the mass changed. Conversely, smaller units give a larger count.

activities.title: Read the dial by valuing the intervals
feedback: If the child counts the lines/marks to get the number, show that the value lives in the spaces between marks: count intervals, not lines.
If the child is stuck when the pointer is between marks, read to the nearest graduation and name the interval value first.
Prompt to check: how did you decide one interval is worth 100 g? Look at the labelled numbers on the scale.
activities.rationale: Scale-reading errors from counting marks instead of valuing intervals are structurally the same slip as misreading a ruler; establishing interval value first prevents it.
sourceClaims: NCETM mastery tasks assess mass via balance equivalence ('this box weighs 10 kg, how much does each tin weigh?') and via reading dial/kitchen scales to compare masses ('what is the mass of two red bags? which is heavier, red or green? explain'); the Year 1 Big Idea introduces equivalence ('how many cubes are equivalent to the mass of the teddy?').
learnerActions: Look at a dial or kitchen scale marked at regular intervals (e.g. a mark every 100 g).
First work out what ONE interval is worth, e.g. the gap between two marks is 100 g.
Count the intervals (the spaces) from zero up to the pointer, not the marks, to find the mass — e.g. three intervals of 100 g means 300 g.
Read to the nearest graduation when the pointer falls between two marks.
Explain how you knew each mark meant 100 g and not 1 g.
activities.intendedInsight: A graduated scale is read like a number line: establish the value of one interval, then count intervals to the pointer — this is the same skill as reading a ruler.

activities.title: Compare and order masses from readings
feedback: If the child tries to compare counts taken with different-sized units, remind them comparisons only work when the units match.
If ordering is reversed, line up the recorded numbers and check which is larger, then match the symbol.
Encourage a spoken reason for each comparison, not just the symbol.
activities.rationale: Comparing and ordering with >, <, = is an explicit curriculum expectation and consolidates quantification into relational reasoning.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure mass (kg/g) to the nearest appropriate unit using scales, and compare/order mass recording with >, <, =.
learnerActions: Weigh or read several objects and record each mass with its unit.
Decide which is heavier and which is lighter, and put the objects in order by mass.
Record comparisons using the symbols >, < and = (e.g. 300 g > 200 g).
Explain a comparison aloud, e.g. 'the red bag is heavier because 300 g is more than 200 g'.
activities.intendedInsight: Once masses are quantified in the same unit, objects can be compared and ordered numerically and recorded with comparison symbols.

constraints: Units must be identical when counting; mixing unit sizes breaks the count and must be caught before reading.
Wait for the balance beam to settle before reading — a tipping beam is not yet balanced.
Reading a scale means valuing the interval first, then counting intervals (spaces) to the pointer; read to the nearest graduation when the pointer is between marks.
Comparisons and ordering are only valid when the same unit is used throughout.

A short selected-response check (read-the-dial, fill in 'the book = ___ cubes', spot the 'more cubes must be heavier' error, order objects by reading) can check whether the ideas have landed, but it does not by itself provide the hands-on balancing and unit-swap experience; use it alongside, not instead of, actual measuring.

A static labelled dial with a reveal of 'each mark = 100 g' can support interval-reading practice, but it cannot show the live balancing or the count changing when the unit is swapped; reserve the dynamic unit-swap for a setting where the same object can be re-measured.
Estimate before measuring so the measured count can be compared against a prediction.
Standard-unit (g/kg) and symbol-comparison work reflects Year 2 expectations above the stated 5–6 age band; treat it as an extension built on the non-standard balancing foundation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row asserted that a 3D balance 'adds nothing' over a 2D one and that 'dialogue cannot supply' the practice. These are catalog-preference claims not established by the cited sources; they have been removed. A physical (tactile) balance and a screen model offer different experiences, and discussion can support reasoning about why the count changes — only the measure-and-read practice specifically needs an actual balance and scale.

The inverse relationship (larger unit → fewer units) and the marks-vs-intervals reading principle are supported by the cited progression and curriculum documents at the level of general principle, not as evidence that these specific tasks were tested.

Note on terminology: the topic title pairs 'mass' and 'weight'. For these age 5–6 activities the quantity measured and balanced is mass; 'weight' is used colloquially as children often say it. No change was made to the pedagogy/assessment fields.

The Year 2 standard-units/comparison claim was removed from the non-standard cube-balancing activity and from the dial-reading activity because it supports standard-unit choice, estimation and symbol comparison (activity 4), not those activities' specific equivalence and interval-valuing principles; the NCETM dial/scale-reading claim is retained on the reading activity as support for the convention of reading graduated scales.

probeDeeper: 'You said the book is 5 big cubes but 12 small cubes — can both be right? How?'
'If you measured with really TINY cubes, would the number be bigger or smaller? Why?' (inverse relationship, fresh case)
'On the dial, how did you know this mark means 100 g and not 1 g?'
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Balances the book against identical, consistently-placed cubes and reports 'N cubes' with the unit. (2) Explains bigger cubes are heavier, so FEWER of them balance the same book — the count changed because the unit changed, not the book. (3) Values each interval (100 g) and counts intervals to the pointer, e.g. 300 g, rather than counting marks.

errorPatterns.pattern: Unit-size ignorance — counts units without regard to their size ('15 small cubes is heavier than 10 big cubes because 15 > 10')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Balance one big cube against several small cubes so the child sees one big = many small; insist on identical units; connect to 'larger unit → fewer units'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 2 claims the bigger-cube count means a heavier/different book, or compares objects using different-sized cubes

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a scale by counting marks rather than valuing intervals; can't read a pointer that falls between graduations
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish what ONE interval is worth first, then count intervals (spaces) not marks to the pointer — exactly as with a ruler; read to the nearest graduation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 3 counts the lines to get the number, or is stuck when the pointer is between marks

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't balance cleanly — reads before the beam settles, or unwittingly mixes unit sizes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Wait for the beam to level; check every unit is the same before counting — a procedural prompt, not a concept reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports a count while the balance is still tipping, or grabs a mix of cube sizes without noticing

responseLevels.gap: Counts units ignoring their size and/or reads a scale by counting marks; treats more units as always heavier.
responseLevels.full: Quantifies mass with identical units, explains that a larger unit gives a smaller count for the same object, and reads a graduated scale by valuing the intervals and counting them to the pointer.
responseLevels.partial: Measures with identical units and reads simple labelled scales, but is thrown when the unit changes (can't explain the different count) or when the pointer falls between graduations.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a balance, identical cubes, a set of larger cubes, a book, and a dial scale marked every 100 g. Watch how they work: (1) 'Use the balance and these cubes to find how many cubes this book weighs.' (2) 'Sam measured the same book with these bigger cubes and got a different number — why?' (3) 'Read the dial — what is the mass of this bag?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Item 2 catches unit-size ignorance — the child who thinks more cubes always means heavier can't explain the different count; item 3 catches the marks-vs-intervals scale-reading error, structurally the same slip as reading a ruler.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; use ×÷ within 100 to solve word problems involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'solve problems, including missing number problems, involving multiplication and division, including positive integer scaling problems and correspondence problems'; measurement contexts across Y3–Y4.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.3 — 'use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g. by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown.'
• Operational details — the objective is CHOOSING and representing the operation from the problem's structure, not computing (computation is prerequisite). Children must recognise the three situation types (equal groups, arrays/area, measurement e.g. length/mass) and both division structures (sharing vs measurement/quotitive: 'how many 4-cm pieces from 28 cm'). Teach the bar model and drawing-plus-equation with a symbol for the unknown as the core sense-making tools; resist key-word strategies (they fail on multi-structure problems). Measurement-quotient problems ('how many Xs fit') are a common blind spot.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): solve a one-step equal-groups × problem with a drawing. Tier B (age 8–9): solve a measurement-division problem ('how many 4-cm pieces from 28 cm') and write the equation with a symbol for the unknown. Tier C (age 9): choose the operation for a mixed set and justify each with a bar model.
bestPractices: Teach children to identify the situation STRUCTURE (equal groups / array-area / measurement) and represent it with a bar model or drawing before choosing an operation — not by scanning for key words.
Include measurement-quotient problems ('how many 4-cm pieces from 28 cm') explicitly, as grouping division is often neglected relative to sharing.
Require an equation with a symbol for the unknown, connecting the drawing to abstract notation and to the unknown-factor idea.
Mix multiplication and division (and both division structures) in the same set so children must decide rather than repeat one operation.
Use estimation and a sense-check ('is this answer reasonable for the context?') especially with measurement units.
keyRepresentations: Bar model — the unifying tool for equal-groups, array and measurement problems
Array/area drawing — for row/column and area contexts
Number line — measurement/grouping division (repeated 4-cm hops along 28 cm)
Equation with a symbol for the unknown (28 ÷ 4 = □) linking drawing to notation
commonMisconceptions: Key-word matching ('altogether'→add, 'each'→divide) leading to the wrong operation in multi-structure problems.
Recognising only sharing division and mis-handling measurement/grouping problems.
Choosing the operation by the size of the numbers rather than the situation.
Not attending to units in measurement problems (mixing cm and pieces).
Solving multi-step problems in one step, or ignoring a remainder's meaning in context.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: using multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in equal-groups, array/area, and measurement situations. The learning objective is CHOOSING and representing the operation from a problem's structure (computation is prerequisite), recognising the three situation types and both division structures — sharing/partitive ('28 shared among 4') versus measurement/quotitive ('how many 4-cm pieces from 28 cm'). The bar model, drawing-plus-equation with a symbol for the unknown, and reasonableness checks are the core sense-making tools; key-word strategies are discouraged because they fail on multi-structure problems.

activities.title: Build and partition a bar model to match the story
feedback: If the model doesn't match the story, name what each part of the bar should represent before choosing an operation — the drawing should dictate the operation, not the two numbers.
When the ribbon and sweets problems both give 7, prompt: 'What does the 7 count each time — pieces, or sweets per child?' to surface the quotitive/partitive distinction.

If the child is surprised both division stories give 7, model both with the same 28 counters: once grouping into 4s and counting the groups, once dealing into 4 piles and counting one pile — both are 28 ÷ 4.
Encourage a reasonableness check: sharing 28 among 4 must give fewer than 28; if the answer is larger, the operation is likely wrong.
Confirm by inverse where useful: does 7 × 4 = 28?
activities.rationale: Constructing and partitioning a model against a specific story, then writing the equation with a symbol for the unknown, builds the situation-to-operation mapping that is the actual objective. Mixing both division structures with the same numbers (28 and 4) forces genuine structure reading rather than repeating one operation. A live modeller where the child drags cut-marks and counts the segments makes the quotitive action concrete, but the same work can be done with drawn bars, number lines, or physical counters and ribbon, which should not be treated as inferior.
sourceClaims: Y3 pupils solve problems involving ×÷ including scaling and correspondence, using drawings and missing-number equations, across measurement contexts.
3.OA.3 requires solving ×÷ word problems within 100 in equal-groups, array and measurement situations using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown.
Bar models and structure-based problem parsing (not key words) support correct operation choice; measurement/quotitive division needs explicit attention.
learnerActions: Read a word problem such as 'A 28-cm ribbon is cut into 4-cm pieces — how many pieces?' and decide which quantity is unknown: the whole, the group size, or the number of groups.
Draw or build a bar representing the whole (28 cm), then mark the cut lines to make 4-cm segments, and count how many segments result (7).
Write the matching equation using a symbol for the unknown, e.g. 28 ÷ 4 = □, and say in words what the answer counts (pieces, not centimetres).

Repeat with a mixed set of stories — an equal-groups problem (e.g. '6 bags of 8 apples'), an array/area problem, a measurement/quotitive division, and a sharing/partitive division — building a model for each before choosing the operation.

For the sharing story ('28 sweets shared equally among 4 children'), model dealing the whole into 4 equal parts and count the size of one part (7), then compare to the measurement story that also used 28 and 4.
activities.intendedInsight: The operation comes from the structure of the situation, not from the numbers or a scanned key word. 'How many 4-cm pieces fit in 28 cm' is a division even though nothing is shared out — the quotitive/measurement meaning — and both division meanings can share the same equation (28 ÷ 4 = 7) while describing different actions.

activities.title: Sort and match problems by structure
feedback: When a key-word-based wrong option is chosen, point back to the structure: what is being combined, arranged in rows, or measured out?
After matching, ask the child to explain why the paired equation fits the story's structure, not just that it uses the same numbers.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and story-to-equation matching are efficient for surfacing and checking structure-recognition and key-word errors. This supports and checks the recognition side; recognising a match does not by itself build the habit of constructing a model for a brand-new story, so it is best paired with the modelling activity.
sourceClaims: Bar models and structure-based problem parsing (not key words) support correct operation choice; measurement/quotitive division needs explicit attention.
learnerActions: Sort a set of word stories into equal-groups, array/area, and measurement categories (a consolidation and checking task).
Match each story to the equation that represents it, including a symbol for the unknown.
Choose, from options, the model (bar, array, or number-line of repeated hops) that fits a given story, with wrong options reflecting key-word traps (e.g. 'altogether' nudging toward addition).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising situation type and matching it to equation and model consolidates the difference between the three structures and exposes key-word matching as unreliable.

activities.title: Reference gallery of the three structures
feedback: Prompt the learner to predict the model before revealing it, then compare their prediction with the exemplar and name any difference.
Use the gallery as a reference during modelling, not as a substitute for parsing new stories.
activities.rationale: A worked, reveal-on-tap gallery is a useful reference and prediction prompt. A fixed gallery does not itself present new stories to parse, so it scaffolds reference and prediction but does not replace the learner building models for novel problems.
learnerActions: Study one annotated worked example per structure (equal-groups, array/area, measurement), each showing the bar model and its equation with a symbol for the unknown.
Reveal the equation after first predicting which quantity is unknown and how the bar should be partitioned.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the three situation types side by side with their models and equations gives a reference for how structure maps to representation.

activities.title: Socratic problem-posing dialogue
feedback: If the learner names an operation before the structure, redirect to 'what is unknown here?' first.
Have the learner explain what the answer represents in the story's context.
activities.rationale: A 'what do we know, what are we finding?' dialogue develops the parsing step of word-problem solving and lets a character pose contextual problems. It should be combined with a drawn or built model, since spoken dialogue alone does not itself produce the manipulable bar.
learnerActions: Respond to a character (e.g. a shopkeeper or craftsperson) posing equal-groups and measurement problems by answering 'What do we know?' and 'What are we finding?' before computing.
State which quantity is unknown and why the chosen operation fits the situation.
Make up and pose an equal-groups problem of your own, then solve it.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating knowns, unknowns, and the reason for an operation builds problem-parsing and guards against grabbing numbers.

constraints: The objective is choosing and representing the operation from the problem's structure; computation within 100 is a prerequisite, not the focus.

Children must meet both division structures: sharing/partitive ('28 shared among 4 → 7 each') and measurement/quotitive ('how many 4-cm pieces from 28 cm → 7 pieces'). Measurement/grouping division is a common blind spot and must be included explicitly.
Discourage key-word strategies ('altogether'→add, 'each'→divide); they fail on multi-structure problems. Require structure-based parsing and a model.
Require an equation with a symbol for the unknown to link the drawing to abstract notation and the unknown-factor idea.
Mix multiplication and division (and both division structures) in the same set so the child must decide rather than repeat one operation.
Attend to units in measurement problems (distinguish cm from pieces) and use a reasonableness check (e.g. sharing 28 among 4 must give fewer than 28).

Sort/match tasks and reveal-on-tap galleries check and reference structure recognition but do not by themselves build the habit of constructing a model for a new story; pair them with construction work.
A dialogue supports problem-parsing but does not produce a manipulable bar model; it supplements rather than leads.

Interactive drag-to-cut and live model-checking are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; drawn bars, number lines, physical counters, or cut ribbon achieve the same modelling and must not be treated as inferior substitutes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source citations: the DfE claim is marked verified in the row; the CCSS 3.OA.3 and NCETM/IES claims are marked not verified. Do not treat cited standards as evidence that any specific activity here was tested for efficacy.

The legacy entry asserted that 3D 'adds no representational value' for this planar modelling work; this is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, and has been dropped rather than propagated as universal.
Arithmetic audit: 6×8=48, 28÷4=7, 7×4=28 all check out; the two division stories correctly share numbers 28 and 4 while differing in structure.
The quotitive vs partitive distinction is genuine and preserved; care was taken not to imply the two meanings require different equations — both are 28 ÷ 4, differing in what the quotient represents.
Quiz/catalog vocabulary (e.g. 'distractor', 'quiz-style') was removed from learner-facing text and audit descriptions and replaced with plain language.

The gallery rationale was narrowed from an absolute 'cannot be re-parsed' claim to a scoped affordance (a fixed gallery does not itself present new stories), aligning the text with the uncertainty note.

probeDeeper: What does your answer to the ribbon problem count — pieces, or centimetres?
The ribbon and the sweets both used 28 and 4. Why do they both come to 7?
Should sharing 28 sweets among 4 give more than 28 or fewer? Why?
Make up your own equal-groups problem and solve it.
assess.correctAnswer: 48 apples (6×8); 7 pieces (28÷4, quotitive — how many groups of 4); 7 sweets each (28÷4, partitive — size of each of 4 groups). The teacher watches for multiplication on the equal-groups problem and division on both division problems, with the child modelling the situation rather than grabbing the numbers and guessing an operation.

errorPatterns.pattern: number-grabs and guesses the operation — uses the two numbers with whatever operation comes to mind (adds 6+8, or multiplies 28×4)
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist on drawing the situation (6 bags, 8 in each) before choosing an operation, so the model dictates the operation, not the numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: operation chosen has no relation to the situation; child cannot say what the answer represents

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses the two meanings of division — cannot tell 'how many groups of 4' (quotitive) from 'shared among 4' (partitive), or thinks they must be different sums
errorPatterns.nextMove: model both with the same 28 counters — once making groups of 4 and counting the groups, once dealing into 4 piles and counting a pile — to show both are 28÷4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child is surprised both give 7, or uses different (wrong) operations for the two division problems

errorPatterns.pattern: multiplies when the problem requires division (or vice versa) because a keyword misled them
errorPatterns.nextMove: teach checking reasonableness — should the answer be bigger or smaller than the numbers given? Sharing 28 among 4 must give fewer than 28.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: e.g. sees 'each' or 'altogether' and applies a fixed operation regardless of structure

errorPatterns.pattern: chooses the right operation but makes a computation slip
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach problem-type; have the child recompute or check with the inverse (7×4 = 28?).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct set-up, wrong product/quotient

responseLevels.gap: number-grabs, chooses operations by keyword, or cannot say what the answer represents.
responseLevels.full: models each situation, selects the correct operation, distinguishes the two division meanings, checks reasonableness, and states what each answer represents.
responseLevels.partial: solves the equal-groups multiplication and one division type but confuses quotitive with partitive, or needs support to choose between multiply and divide.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small set of word problems within 100 to solve, watching which operation they set up for each: an equal-groups problem ('6 bags of 8 apples — how many apples?'), a measurement/quotitive division ('How many 4-cm pieces from a 28-cm ribbon?'), and a sharing/partitive division ('28 sweets shared equally among 4 children — how many each?'). Watch how they decide multiply vs divide, and which kind of division.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two division problems use the SAME numbers (28 and 4) but different structures; watching whether the child distinguishes 'how many groups' from 'how many in each' reveals genuine situation-modelling versus number-grabbing. Choosing to add or subtract, or multiplying when division is needed, exposes shallow keyword reading.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Living Things Vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y2 Living things and their habitats):** "explore and compare the differences between things that are living, dead, and things that have never been alive." The seven life processes / MRS GREN mnemonic itself is NON-STATUTORY in England — it appears in guidance, not the statutory programme of study — so it is taught as supporting language for the statutory living/dead/never-alive comparison, not as a required list.

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-LS1-1, nearest anchor):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-LS1-1]." NGSS has no discrete K–2 performance expectation that asks children to name the life processes; the vocabulary is developed as the language children use to describe living things and their needs.

- **Operational details:** This is a LANGUAGE topic: the goal is that children acquire and USE the words — living, dead, never been alive, and the life-process words (movement, nutrition/feeding, growth, reproduction, sensitivity, excretion) — as tools for giving REASONS, not as a list to recite. Teach it through sorting real and pictured objects into living / dead / never-alive and requiring a spoken reason using a life-process word ("the tree is living because it grows and makes seeds"). Deliberately include tricky contrast cases — fire, a toy dog, a seed, a shell, a fallen leaf — because these force children off the intuitive "it moves so it's alive" rule and onto the multiple-criteria definition. Attach each life-process word to a PLANT as well as an animal (a plant moves sap, respires, senses light, grows, makes seeds) so the vocabulary generalises beyond moving animals.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can name at least five life-process words and use one to justify a living/dead/never-alive sorting decision. Developmentally, under-sixes have little concept of 'living' and early KS1 children equate 'living' with movement; expect fire-is-alive and plant-is-not-alive errors and treat surfacing them as the point of the lesson, not a failure. Full self-movement-based reasoning and abstract definitions come later (≈9–11); here the target is correct WORD USE grounded in observation.
bestPractices: Anchor every life-process word to a concrete, observable example on a real or pictured organism, and require children to use the word in a spoken reason ("living because it grows") rather than recite a list.
Deliberately include tricky contrast cases in every sort — fire, a wind-up toy, a seed, a shell, a fallen leaf — to surface and then challenge the intuitive 'moves = alive' rule.
Apply each life-process word to a PLANT as well as an animal (sap movement, respiration, growth, seed-making, turning to light) so the vocabulary is not tied to moving animals.
Use three explicit bins — living / dead / never-been-alive — so children distinguish 'dead' (once alive) from 'never alive', a distinction teachers report pupils routinely confuse.
Begin with familiar organisms in the child's own environment before edge cases, building from the concrete outward.
keyRepresentations: Three-way sorting bench: living / dead / never been alive, with picture and real-object cards.
MRS GREN as a supporting mnemonic (Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition) — introduced as helper language, flagged non-statutory.
A labelled organism scene where each life-process word maps to a visible feature (roots feeding, leaves sensing light, seeds for reproduction).
Word–picture matching cards pairing each life-process term with a photograph that shows it.
commonMisconceptions: 'It moves so it's alive' — children over-generalise movement, judging fire, the sun, a clock or a boat to be living.
'Plants (and seeds and fungi) are not alive' — because they are not obviously active or moving; seeds especially are judged non-living.
Confusing 'dead' with 'never been alive' — e.g. treating a rock and a fallen leaf as the same category.
Attributing intentional, animal-like purpose to plants (a plant grows to the light because it 'wants' to), rather than describing sensitivity as a response.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach 'living things' vocabulary as language children USE to give reasons, not a list to recite. Children acquire and apply the words living, dead, never been alive, and the life-process words (movement, nutrition/feeding, growth, reproduction, sensitivity, excretion) by binding each word to a visible feature on a real organism and by sorting real and pictured objects into three bins while stating a spoken reason. Deliberately include tricky contrast cases (fire, a wind-up toy, a seed, a shell, a fallen leaf) to surface and challenge the intuitive 'it moves so it's alive' rule, and attach each life-process word to a PLANT as well as an animal so the vocabulary generalises beyond moving animals. The UK KS1 Y2 statutory focus is comparing living / dead / never-been-alive; the seven life processes (MRS GREN) are supporting, non-statutory language in England, and this lesson uses six of them, leaving out respiration (the R) as too abstract for this age. Developmentally, early KS1 children equate living with movement; surfacing fire-is-alive and plant-is-not-alive errors is the point of the lesson, not a failure.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal 'what makes it living' scene
feedback: When the child taps a word, show the exact matching evidence on the organism so the word is welded to a seen feature.

If the child is surprised the tree 'moves', confirm that plants move parts of themselves, such as leaves turning toward light or flowers opening and closing, usually too slowly to notice, and that plants are living even though they do not walk about.

When the leaves turn to the sun under 'sensitivity', describe it as the plant RESPONDING to light (and the bird responding to sound), not the plant 'wanting' to turn — sensitivity means responding to the surroundings, not having animal-like intentions.

For the fire flap, walk through the criteria one by one rather than just saying 'no': it burns fuel but does not feed and use food to grow its own body, it does not sense and respond, and it spreads but does not have young that grow up.
Prompt the child to use the word in a full reason: 'the tree is living because it grows and makes seeds'.
activities.rationale: This is a LANGUAGE/naming target, and binding each word to a visible feature on a real organism supports children in using the vocabulary to give reasons. Showing each process on a plant as well as an animal counters the documented tendency to judge plants and seeds as non-living, and the fire case targets the 'moves = alive' overgeneralisation. Framing sensitivity as a response guards against the documented tendency to attribute intention to plants. The live-reveal (leaves turning toward light, shown speeded up) is one proposed way to make the mapping concrete, not a required or validated mechanism.
sourceClaims: Children's criteria for 'living' develop in stages: under-sixes have little concept of living, then associate living with activity, then with movement, and only around 9–11 with self-movement; fire is commonly classified as living because it moves, and plants/fungi/seeds are often judged non-living because they are not obviously active.

MRS GREN's seven characteristics can each be applied to a plant (movement of sap, respiration, sensitivity to light/gravity, growth incl. repair, reproduction by seeds, excretion of oxygen, nutrition), which supports teaching life-process vocabulary as applying to plants and not only moving animals.
learnerActions: Look at a single rich scene containing a tree, a bird, a child, a seed, a fallen leaf, a rock, a toy, and a campfire.

Tap or point to a life-process word (movement, nutrition/feeding, growth, reproduction, sensitivity) and find the evidence for it on the organism: tap 'growth' and a seedling thickens and adds a leaf; tap 'nutrition' and the tree's roots take in water while its leaves use sunlight to make the tree's food, and the bird pecks a berry; tap 'reproduction' and the tree's seeds highlight; tap 'sensitivity' and the leaves slowly turn toward the light (shown speeded up) and the bird turns its head to a sound.

Tap 'movement' expecting only the bird to respond, and notice that parts of the tree move too, shown speeded up: its leaves slowly turn toward the light and its flowers open and close — a plant moves parts of itself even though it cannot walk about.
For each word, say it aloud applied to BOTH a plant and an animal (e.g. 'the tree grows and the bird grows').

Open the campfire flap: 'The fire flickers and grows — is it living?' and talk through how it differs from living things: it burns fuel but does not feed and use food to build its own body, it cannot sense and respond to its surroundings, and it can spread but does not have young that grow up.
activities.intendedInsight: Each life-process word maps to a feature you can see on a real organism, and plants show these processes too — so movement alone does not decide what is living.

activities.title: Three-way sort with a spoken reason
feedback: If a child places fire or a toy in 'living' because it moves, ask which other life processes it does: does it feed, grow by itself, sense, reproduce?
If a child places a seed or plant in 'never been alive' or a non-living bin, use growth, nutrition and reproduction to show it is living.
If a child calls the wooden chair 'never alive', trace the wood back to a tree so they re-sort it as 'dead / once alive'.
Accept a correct sort only when paired with a life-process reason; a bare right answer is not yet the target.
activities.rationale: Using three explicit bins makes children distinguish 'dead' (once alive) from 'never alive', a distinction teachers report pupils routinely confuse, and the required spoken reason makes the vocabulary do work rather than be recited. Including deliberate tricky cases surfaces the movement misconception so it can be challenged. This sort exercises classification; pair it with word-to-feature work so the language goal is also served.
sourceClaims: Children's criteria for 'living' develop in stages: under-sixes have little concept of living, then associate living with activity, then with movement, and only around 9–11 with self-movement; fire is commonly classified as living because it moves, and plants/fungi/seeds are often judged non-living because they are not obviously active.
DfE KS1 Year 2 statutory content requires pupils to 'explore and compare the differences between things that are living, dead, and things that have never been alive'.
learnerActions: Sort real and pictured objects into three bins: living / dead / never been alive.
Start with familiar organisms from the child's own environment (a growing plant, a pet, a person) before moving to edge cases.
Include the tricky contrast cases: fire, a wind-up or toy dog, a seed, a shell, a fallen leaf, a wooden chair, a rock.
After placing each object, pick the life-process word that justifies the choice and say the reason aloud ('the shell is dead because it was part of a living snail').
For 'dead' versus 'never been alive', trace the material to its origin: wood came from a tree and wool from a sheep (dead / once alive), while plastic and metal were never alive.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding living / dead / never-been-alive means checking several life processes and, for non-living things, whether they were ever part of something alive — not just whether they move.

activities.title: Word-to-picture matching and a check sort
feedback: If a word is matched to the wrong picture, point to the feature in the correct picture that shows that process.
If fire is sorted as living, revisit which processes it fails; if the seed is sorted as non-living, show growth and reproduction as evidence it is living.
Encourage naming at least five life-process words and using one to justify a sort.
activities.rationale: A matching and categorization task is a well-aligned check of whether the vocabulary has stuck and whether children can attach the right word to the right feature. It measures recognition and application but does not by itself elicit the child's own spoken reasoning, so use it alongside, not instead of, the reveal and sorting activities.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2 statutory content requires pupils to 'explore and compare the differences between things that are living, dead, and things that have never been alive'.
learnerActions: Match each clearly observable life-process word (movement, nutrition, growth, reproduction, sensitivity) to a photograph that shows it, and treat excretion as 'getting rid of waste' with an everyday example (such as an animal producing waste) rather than requiring an unambiguous single photo.
Sort six items into living / dead / never been alive, with fire and a seed included as deliberate contrast items.
For each decision, name a life-process word that justifies it.
activities.intendedInsight: I can recognise which word names which life process and use the right word when I classify an object.

activities.title: 'Is it alive?' questioning exchange
feedback: When the child leans on movement, redirect to the full set of processes: a car (or river, or toy robot) moves, but it does not feed and grow its own body, sense and respond like a living thing, or have young.
Model the life-process term for a vague idea the child expresses ('it gets big' → 'yes, it grows') until the child adopts the word; do not treat the everyday word as simply wrong.
Confirm a correct answer only when it includes a life-process reason.
activities.rationale: A tightly focused Socratic exchange can elicit and challenge the movement rule by forcing multi-criteria reasoning on moving-but-non-living cases (car, river, toy robot). For 5–7s the vocabulary set is fixed, so keep the questioning targeted; open dialogue complements rather than replaces the word-to-feature work.
sourceClaims: Children's criteria for 'living' develop in stages: under-sixes have little concept of living, then associate living with activity, then with movement, and only around 9–11 with self-movement; fire is commonly classified as living because it moves, and plants/fungi/seeds are often judged non-living because they are not obviously active.
learnerActions: Respond when a curious character holds up an object and asks 'Is it alive? Why?', naming a life-process reason.

Answer the probes when the character pushes back: 'But a car moves — is a car alive?', 'The river moves too — but does it grow, feed or reproduce?', and 'A toy robot walks and beeps — is it living? Why not?'
Give two life-process words that show a sunflower is alive, and say why a wooden chair is dead (once alive) rather than never alive.
activities.intendedInsight: Movement alone does not make something living; I must check the other life processes to decide and explain, so I do not simply swap 'it moves' for one other single rule.

constraints: This is a LANGUAGE topic: the goal is correct WORD USE grounded in observation (naming at least five life-process words and using one to justify a living/dead/never-alive decision), not reciting a list.

In England, the seven life processes / MRS GREN mnemonic are NON-STATUTORY supporting language; the statutory KS1 Y2 target is comparing living, dead, and never-been-alive. NGSS has no discrete K–2 performance expectation that asks children to name the life processes.

Expect and welcome 'fire-is-alive' and 'plant-is-not-alive' errors at this age; surfacing them is the point of the lesson. Full self-movement-based reasoning and abstract definitions come later (≈9–11).
Every life-process word must be anchored to a concrete, observable example and applied to a PLANT as well as an animal so the vocabulary is not tied to moving animals.

Frame sensitivity as a plant RESPONDING to its surroundings (light, gravity, touch, water), not as the plant 'wanting' something, to avoid reinforcing the misconception that plants act with animal-like intention.
Pair any on-screen reveal with hands-on sorting of real objects; the screen's job is to weld each word to a seen feature, and it does not replace handling real and pictured materials.

Matching/categorization and recognition tasks check whether vocabulary has stuck but do not by themselves elicit the child's own spoken reasoning; require a spoken life-process reason as the target evidence.
A manipulable 3D environment is not needed here, as the concept is not spatial; this is a scoping note, not a claim that 3D cannot ever help.
When challenging 'moves = alive', ensure children check multiple life processes rather than simply replacing movement with one other single rule.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed 'excretion of oxygen' for plants under MRS GREN; plant gas exchange is more nuanced (plants both take in and release oxygen and carbon dioxide depending on respiration and photosynthesis). For 5–7s, excretion as 'getting rid of waste' is sufficient; do not assert 'plants excrete oxygen' to learners. The source claim is preserved verbatim only in sourceClaims.
The NGSS source claim (K-LS1-1) was marked verified:false in the source row; treat the NGSS alignment as unconfirmed.

The original artefact-fit narrative ranked an interactive image as 'ideal' over sorting and dialogue partly on 'moment-of-insight' grounds; comparative efficacy is not established by the sources, so alternatives are preserved as complementary activities rather than inferior options.

The diagnostic examples (river, car, toy robot) are moving-but-non-living cases; any prompt using them should push children to check several life processes so they do not swap 'moves' for another single rule.

The 'attributing intention to plants' misconception from the original pedagogy is now addressed in activity[0] feedback and a constraint by framing sensitivity as a response; this was a documented misconception not previously handled in the learner-facing content.

probeDeeper: Is a river alive? It moves — but does it do the other life processes?
The wooden chair — was it ever part of something living? What?
Give me two 'life process' words that show a sunflower is alive.
A toy robot walks and beeps. Is it living? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The sunflower is living — it grows, needs nutrition and reproduces (life-process words). The wooden chair was once part of a living tree, so it is dead (once alive). The car has never been alive — it moves, but it doesn't grow, feed or reproduce; movement alone doesn't make something living. The child gives a life-process reason for each.

errorPatterns.pattern: things that move are alive and things that don't are not ('the car is alive because it moves; the plant isn't because it doesn't')
errorPatterns.nextMove: shift the test from movement to the full set of life processes; a car moves but doesn't grow, feed or reproduce, while a plant does
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls the car living and/or the sunflower non-living, using movement as the test

errorPatterns.pattern: plants aren't living (only animals are)
errorPatterns.nextMove: use growth, nutrition and reproduction to show that a plant is alive
errorPatterns.revealedBy: classifies the sunflower as not living

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses 'dead' with 'never been alive' (calls the wooden chair 'never alive')
errorPatterns.nextMove: trace materials to their origin — wood, wool and leather came from living things, so 'dead / once alive'; plastic and metal were never alive
errorPatterns.revealedBy: labels the chair never-alive, missing that wood came from a tree

errorPatterns.pattern: uses everyday words instead of life-process vocabulary ('it's alive because it's real / because it gets big')
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not treat as wrong; model the life-process term for the idea the child expresses, until they adopt it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reaches for vague words rather than 'growth', 'nutrition' or 'reproduction'

responseLevels.gap: Uses movement as the test — calls a car living or a plant non-living; cannot give a life-process reason.
responseLevels.full: Classifies living, dead and never-been-alive correctly, justifies each with the right life-process vocabulary, and explains that a plant is alive using at least two life processes, rejecting movement as the sole test.
responseLevels.partial: Classifies some items correctly and names a life process or two, but applies them inconsistently — still leaning on movement, or muddling 'dead' with 'never alive'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell me whether each of these is living, dead, or never been alive, and use a 'life process' word to say why: a sunflower growing in a pot, a wooden chair, and a car driving down the road.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This is the classic 'moving = alive' discriminator. A young child using movement as the test calls the car living and the sunflower not; a child using life-process reasoning classifies all three correctly and justifies each with the right word. The car and the sunflower together are the discriminator.

sources.claim: Children's criteria for 'living' develop in stages: under-sixes have little concept of living, then associate living with activity, then with movement, and only around 9–11 with self-movement; fire is commonly classified as living because it moves, and plants/fungi/seeds are often judged non-living because they are not obviously active.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Recording data

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils are taught to use "gathering and recording data to help in answering questions", alongside "observing closely, using simple equipment" and "identifying and classifying". This is the child's first structured capture of what they notice into a usable form.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 8 / SEP 4, grades K–2):** the K–2 progressions include "record information (observations, thoughts, and ideas)" and "record and share observations" and "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-1, K-ESS2-1, K-LS1-1]". Recording data into simple tables, tallies and drawings is the K–2 entry point to handling data.

- **Operational details:** Builds on performing simple tests (prerequisite mt_Wa44s-f8Ws). Three moves: (1) record observations/measurements in a simple TABLE or TALLY CHART; (2) use DRAWINGS or labelled diagrams to record what was seen; and (3) explain how the record helps ANSWER the question. The key idea for this age is that recording is not decoration — it captures information so it can be looked back at and used, and memory alone is unreliable. Feeds forward to presenting data in charts/keys and analysing design tests (dependents mt_7IFpDVNsmt, mt_nNYo5A-7Bl).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). A learner who can record observations in a simple table or tally, use a labelled drawing to record what they saw, and say how the record helps answer the question has met the bar. Choosing between graph types comes later (mt_7IFpDVNsmt, mt_rDjtmDogJr).
bestPractices: Give a genuine reason to record — collect so much or over such a time that memory obviously fails (e.g. tally minibeasts found, weather each day for a week) — so pupils feel WHY we write it down.
Model the tally as counting-as-you-go (the fifth stroke crossing the gate) so recording keeps pace with observing rather than being reconstructed afterwards.
Pair a labelled drawing with a table so pupils see two complementary record types — pictures for what it looked like, tables/tallies for how many.
Always close the loop: after recording, return to the question and ask 'what does our record tell us?' — recording exists to answer questions.
Keep headings and categories decided BEFORE collecting so the table is ready to fill, modelling a tiny bit of planning.
keyRepresentations: A simple two-column table (thing observed | count/measurement)
A tally chart with gated fives
A labelled observational drawing
A weather/nature 'over time' record strip (one entry per day)
A question → record → 'what it tells us' loop card
commonMisconceptions: Thinking you can just remember it — not seeing why data must be written down as you go.
Recording after the fact from memory rather than in the moment, losing accuracy.
Treating the drawing/table as the end product ('finished!') rather than something to READ to answer the question.
Muddled tallies (miscounting, not gating fives) that can't be read back.
Inventing categories or changing headings mid-collection so the record can't be totalled.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach recording data as an active skill: capture observations in simple tables, tally charts, and labelled drawings while events happen, then READ the record back to answer the original question. The core insight is that recording is not decoration — it captures information so it can be used later, because memory alone is unreliable. Includes a live capture activity, a read-back-and-choose practice set, and a reference scaffold, each with a distinct pedagogical purpose.

activities.title: Live tally-and-table capture
feedback: If you try to just watch and remember, the creatures dart off and the count slips away — mark a tally stroke for each one so you keep pace.
If your tally is muddled (fives not gated, strokes miscounted), it can't be read back — count as you go and cross the gate on every fifth stroke.
After recording, return to the question: 'What does our record tell us? Which has the biggest total?'
If you change a heading partway through, the counts may not match up and are hard to total — decide categories before you start.
activities.rationale: Recording is a doing skill: the child must capture observations as events unfold and then read the record back. A scene that produces events in real time is intended to give a felt reason to record live — if the child relies on memory, the count is easily lost — addressing the core misconception that you can 'just remember it'. Pairing a drawing with a table/tally models two of the simple record types named in the objective (tables, tally charts and drawings). A live on-screen tool is one suitable medium; an equivalent real-world collection (tallying minibeasts in the playground, logging weather daily, or rolling toy cars and recording distances) meets the same objective and should be used where practical.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires gathering and recording data to help in answering questions.
NGSS SEP 4 and SEP 8 at grades K-2 include recording information and observations and using observations to describe patterns.
learnerActions: Before collecting, agree the table headings and categories (e.g. one row per minibeast type, or one row per kind of weather with one mark added each day of the week) so the record is ready to fill.

Watch a scene where events keep happening — minibeasts scuttle across a garden, or the weather changes each day for a week — and mark a tally stroke for each thing as it happens, counting as you go (cross the gate on the fifth stroke).
Add a labelled observational drawing of one thing you saw, alongside the counting table, so you have two complementary record types — a picture for what it looked like and a table/tally for how many.
When the question drops in ('which minibeast did we see most?' / 'which kind of weather did we have on the most days?'), read the answer directly off your own totals.
Say out loud how your record helps answer the question.
activities.intendedInsight: Writing it down as it happens is what makes the question answerable later; a record is something you READ to find an answer, not just something you made and finished.

activities.title: Read the record and choose how to record
feedback: If you pick the wrong total, re-count the tally gate by gate — each full gate is five.
For 'which was most', find the row with the biggest count, not the first or last row.
A drawing is good for what something looked like; a tally/table is good for how many — match the record to what you need to know.
activities.rationale: Reading a tally/table to answer a question and choosing an appropriate record type consolidate the read-back half of the skill, and can be used during teaching as well as to check understanding. This format exercises reading-back but does not require capture-in-the-moment, so it complements rather than replaces the live activity.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires gathering and recording data to help in answering questions.
learnerActions: Look at a completed tally or table and answer questions from it: 'which was seen most?', 'how many altogether?', 'which day had no rain?'
Given a set of results to collect (e.g. counts of three kinds of leaf), choose which simple record would suit it — a tally chart, a two-column count table, or a labelled drawing — and say why.
Match given data to the best simple record type.
activities.intendedInsight: A record only works if it can be read back to answer the question, and different simple records suit different kinds of information.

activities.title: Parts of a tally chart (reference scaffold)
feedback: Notice the fifth stroke crosses the other four to make a gate — this lets you count in fives.
Every row has a label so you always know which count belongs to which thing.
activities.rationale: A fixed labelled example gives the child a model of what a well-structured record looks like. This is a support only: a reference image shows the structure but does not require the child to perform the active capture, so it should accompany, not substitute for, the live recording task.
learnerActions: Explore a labelled example tally chart and table: tap to reveal what each part is for — the heading row, one line per category, the gated group of five, the total.
Use this as a reference while setting up your own record in the capture activity.
activities.intendedInsight: A readable record has clear headings, one category per row, and tallies grouped in fives so they can be counted quickly.

constraints: Checkpoint is Tier A (concrete/observational): the bar is recording observations in a simple table or tally, using a labelled drawing, and saying how the record helps answer the question. Choosing between graph types comes later.
Builds on performing simple tests as a prerequisite and feeds forward to presenting data in charts/keys and analysing design tests.
Decide headings and categories BEFORE collecting so the table is ready to fill; avoid changing headings mid-collection, because the counts may no longer match up and become hard to total and compare.
Always close the loop: after recording, return to the question and ask what the record tells us.

The read-back/matching practice checks reading a record but does not elicit capture-in-the-moment; the reference image shows structure but does not require the child to construct a record. Both are scaffolds around the live capture task, not replacements for it.

Live on-screen scenes are one medium; equivalent real-world collection (tallying minibeasts, logging daily weather, rolling toy cars and recording distances) meets the same objective and should be used where practical.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NGSS Appendix F source (SEP 4/SEP 8, K-2) was marked verified:false in the source row; treat that citation's confirmation status as unverified even though the claim supports the recording principle.

The diagnostic 'which car rolls furthest' task in the source assessment uses distance, which involves measurement/comparison; for the youngest learners a count-based scene (how many of each minibeast, which day was rainiest) may be a gentler entry to recording. Both are retained as context; neither is asserted as superior.

The source rated conversation and 3D artefacts as 'poor'/'no spatial dimension' and framed a static image as unable to 'require' active capture. These are presented here as narrowly scoped affordance notes (a reference image supports but does not require construction), not as universal claims that other media cannot teach recording.

probeDeeper: How does your record show which result belongs to which car?
Why write it down as you go instead of at the end?
Looking at your record, which car won? How can you tell?
If you'd just remembered the results, could you be sure? What might go wrong?
assess.correctAnswer: The child creates a simple organised record — a table or chart pairing each car with its distance (or a labelled tally/drawing) — records each result as they go, and can read from it to answer which car rolled furthest. The record is organised enough that the results can be compared.

errorPatterns.pattern: Disorganised or unlabelled record: writes numbers with no indication of which car they belong to.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair each result with its car — a row or column per car so the record is readable later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The record is ambiguous — results can't be matched to cars afterwards.

errorPatterns.pattern: Relies on memory: does all the rolls first, then tries to remember the results to write down.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Record each result as it happens, so nothing is forgotten or mixed up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No recording happens during the activity itself.

errorPatterns.pattern: Record not linked to the question: makes marks but can't use them to say which car won.
errorPatterns.nextMove: 'Look at your record — which car has the biggest number?' Tie the record back to the question.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child can't read an answer off their own record.

responseLevels.gap: Records nothing until the end, or writes marks with no labels that can't be interpreted afterwards.
responseLevels.full: Sets up a simple organised record (table, tally, or labelled drawing) pairing each item with its result, records as the activity happens, and reads the answer to the question directly off the record.
responseLevels.partial: Records results in a mostly organised way but needs prompting to label clearly or to link the record back to the question.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: We want to find out which of these three toy cars rolls the furthest. You'll roll each car and need to keep a record so we don't forget the results. Set up a way to write down what happens, then do the rolls and record them. Afterwards, tell me how your record helps answer which car won. I'll watch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates a child who records systematically (a structure pairing each car with its result) from one who writes numbers with no labels, records nothing until the end (relying on memory), or makes marks they can't later interpret. The tell is whether the record can actually be used to answer the question.
