pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2). Understand that the multiples of 10 (10, 20, 30 … 90) each represent a whole number of TENS and ZERO ones: 30 means 3 tens and 0 ones. A special, high-frequency case of two-digit place value where the ones column is empty.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones)'; 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in tens from any number, forward and backward'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.2c 'the numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones)'.
• Operational details — Build each decade with tens rods only (no unit cubes) and place them in the tens column with an explicit 0 written in the ones column, so the empty ones place is SEEN, not omitted. Tie to skip-counting in tens (10, 20, 30 …) so the spoken sequence and the tens count line up. Contrast a decade (40 = 4 tens, 0 ones) with a nearby non-decade (43 = 4 tens, 3 ones) to fix the role of the zero.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): skip-count 10, 20, 30 … 90 and build 30 with three rods. Tier B (age 6-7): say '30 is 3 tens and 0 ones' and write 30 = 30 + 0 / 3 tens. Tier C (age 7): match any decade to its tens representation and explain why the 0 is needed (place-holder in the ones).
bestPractices: Build decades with tens rods ONLY and write a 0 in the ones column so the child sees the ones place is filled by zero, not absent — this is the seed of the place-holder idea.
Anchor to skip-counting in tens on a bead string or number track so '3 tens' and 'thirty' and the third stop line up as the same thing.
Contrast a decade with an adjacent non-decade (40 vs 43) so the 0 earns its meaning as 'no ones', not 'nothing'.
Name the decade words carefully (thirty, forty, fifty) and connect the '-ty' to 'tens', flagging the thirteen/thirty and fifteen/fifty confusions.
Use the tens|ones chart to show that reading only the tens column gives the decade name — reinforcing column-based reading of two-digit numbers.
keyRepresentations: Tens rods alone in the tens column with a visible 0 in the ones column
Bead string / number track marked in tens for skip-counting
0-100 number line with decade stops highlighted
Tens|ones place-value chart showing 'n tens, 0 ones'
Gattegno/place-value chart row of decades (10, 20 … 90) linking each to n×10
commonMisconceptions: Treating the 0 in a decade as meaningless ('nothing there') rather than as a place-holder marking zero ones.
Reading the tens digit as its face value — saying 30 is 'three' rather than 'three tens/thirty'.
Decade-word confusion — mixing thirteen with thirty, fifteen with fifty, because the '-teen' and '-ty' endings sound alike.
Believing decades are a separate kind of number unrelated to ordinary two-digit numbers, rather than the ones-is-zero case of tens-and-ones.
Miscounting the rods and losing track that each rod is worth ten, not one, when skip-counting.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y2), help children understand that the multiples of 10 (10, 20, 30 … 90) each represent a whole number of tens with zero ones — e.g. 30 is 3 tens and 0 ones. The key insight is that the 0 in a decade is an active place-holder marking the empty ones column, not 'nothing', and that decades are simply the 'whole tens, no ones' case of ordinary two-digit place value. Build quantities with tens rods, anchor to skip-counting in tens, and contrast a decade with a nearby non-decade so the 0 earns its meaning.

activities.title: Building decades with tens rods and a visible zero
feedback: If the child says the 0 'means nothing', rebuild 30 with rods and no cubes and point to the empty ones spot: that empty spot IS the zero — zero ones. Contrast 3 and 30 to show the 0 keeps the 3 in the tens place (and, if ready, 300, where two zeros hold the 3 in the hundreds place) — zeros act as place-holders in their own place.
If the child reads the 3 at face value ('three'), count the ones inside the three rods (30) and say '3 in the tens place = 3 tens = 30'.
When the child adds the loose cube and 30 becomes 31, affirm: the 0 was doing real work holding the ones place empty; once a one is there, the ones digit reads 1.
Praise explanations that state both parts: '3 tens AND 0 ones'.
activities.rationale: Making the quantity drive the numeral while the zero is held visibly in place lets children connect the spoken sequence, the tens count, and the written form, and distinguishes a decade from a non-decade. Building with tens rods and skip-counting supports recognition of decade numbers as whole tens.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones) and count in tens from any number forward and backward.
1.NBT.2c: the numbers 10, 20 … 90 refer to one to nine tens (and 0 ones).
Skip-counting in tens and grouping with tens rods support recognition of decade numbers as whole tens.
learnerActions: Set up a tens|ones chart (drawn or physical) with two columns.
Add tens rods one at a time into the tens column, placing no unit cubes; after each rod, say the count aloud: 'ten, twenty, thirty …' and write the numeral (10, 20, 30).
Each time, write a 0 in the ones column so the empty ones place is seen, not left blank.
Build 30 with three rods and say '30 is 3 tens and 0 ones'; build 50 with five rods and say '50 is 5 tens and 0 ones'.
Rebuild 30 with three rods, then add a single loose ones cube and read what you have: 30 becomes 31. Describe what the 0 was doing before you added the cube.
Optionally mark each decade on a 0-100 number line or bead string so the spoken word, the tens count, and the position all line up.
activities.intendedInsight: A decade is a whole number of tens with the ones column filled by zero; the 0 is a place-holder that keeps the tens digit in the tens place and marks that there are no ones. Decades are not a separate kind of number — they are the ones-is-zero case of tens-and-ones.

activities.title: Decade reference chart — tap, reveal, and lift the flap
feedback: If the child names the wrong number of rods, recount the rods with them and match the count to the tens digit.
Reinforce the connection between '-ty' endings and 'tens' (thirty = three tens).
activities.rationale: A labelled reference anchors the pattern and vocabulary of decades as counts of tens. This is a reference/anchor: it names and displays the pattern but does not itself have the child build up the sequence and watch the ones column stay empty, so pair it with the hands-on building activity.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones) and count in tens from any number forward and backward.
learnerActions: Work from a chart of the nine decades (10, 20 … 90).
For a chosen decade (e.g. 30), reveal its three tens rods, the words '3 tens, 0 ones', and the spoken name 'thirty'.
Use a 'where did the ones go?' prompt (e.g. a lift-the-flap or cover) to answer: there are zero ones, and the 0 marks that.
Read across several decades to notice that reading only the tens column gives the decade name.
activities.intendedInsight: Each decade numeral maps to a count of tens, a decade name (ten, or a '-ty' word from twenty to ninety), and a zero in the ones column; the tens digit tells you which decade it is.

activities.title: Consolidation: sequence, match, and justify the zero
feedback: For thirteen/thirty and fifteen/fifty mix-ups, build 13 (one ten and three ones) beside 30 (three tens, zero ones) so the structural difference is visible, and stress the ending sounds.
For a face-value or 'means nothing' answer about the 0, return to building the decade with rods and the empty ones column.
activities.rationale: Mixed practice with deliberate decade-word distractors probes the common thirteen/thirty and fifteen/fifty confusion and checks whether the 0 is understood. This consolidates and checks the pattern but does not itself have the child construct the underlying grouping, so use it after hands-on work.
sourceClaims: 1.NBT.2c: the numbers 10, 20 … 90 refer to one to nine tens (and 0 ones).
learnerActions: Put the decade numerals in order smallest to largest (10, 20 … 90).
Match each decade numeral to a picture of the correct number of tens rods.
Fill in blanks such as '30 = __ tens' and '50 = 5 tens and __ ones'.
Choose and explain the meaning of the 0 in a decade (zero ones / place-holder), not 'nothing'.
Distinguish sound-alike pairs: thirteen vs thirty, fifteen vs fifty — say which is 'teen' (ten and some) and which is 'ty' (whole tens).
activities.intendedInsight: Children can recognise and justify decades across different representations, and can avoid confusing '-teen' words with '-ty' words.

activities.title: 'Convince me the zero matters' discussion
feedback: Accept answers that connect the 0 to 'zero ones' and to keeping the 3 in the tens place; gently redirect answers that treat the 0 as decorative.
If talk alone stalls, hand over rods so the argument can be grounded in a build.
activities.rationale: A short reasoning task can surface and articulate the place-holder idea. Because this is fundamentally a build-and-see pattern, discussion is proposed as a follow-up to manipulating rods rather than as the primary route to the insight; it articulates reasoning but does not itself have the child build the grouping.
learnerActions: Discuss the question: 'Why does 30 need a zero? What would happen if we just wrote 3?'
Use rods or a chart to argue your case: show that without the 0, the 3 would sit in the ones place and mean three.
Explain to a partner or adult why 30 is not the same as 3, and what the 0 is holding.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the reason makes the place-holder role of the 0 explicit: it keeps the 3 in the tens place and marks zero ones.

constraints: Keep the ones column empty of cubes when building decades, but always write the 0 so the empty ones place is seen, not omitted — this is the seed of the place-holder idea.
Tie the build to skip-counting in tens so 'thirty', 'three tens', and the third stop on the number line line up as the same thing.
Always contrast a decade with an adjacent non-decade (40 vs 43; 30 vs 31) so the 0 means 'no ones', not 'nothing'.
Each rod is worth ten, not one; watch for miscounting that loses track of the ten-value during skip-counting.
When extending the place-holder idea to larger numbers (e.g. 300), state the digit's actual place (hundreds) rather than carrying 'tens place' across every example.

The reference chart and the sequence/match/justify practice consolidate or check the pattern but do not have the child build the underlying grouping on their own; precede them with hands-on rod building.
Recognition and matching tasks check the pattern but do not require the child to construct the grouping independently; include building and verbal explanation for that.
Discussion can surface and articulate the reasoning; for this build-and-see insight it is proposed as a follow-up to manipulating rods rather than as a substitute for building.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims for CCSS-M 1.NBT.2c and the NCETM materials are marked unverified in the original row; only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified. Do not treat the unverified claims as confirmed.

The original rated a 2D interactive bench as 'ideal', asserted 'a static picture cannot' make the quantity drive the numeral with the zero held in place, and dismissed 3D as adding nothing. These are catalog-fit modality preferences, not established pedagogical laws; the live-ticking numeral, hopping marker, and highlighted 0 are retained as optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not as a mandatory or uniquely effective medium.
1.NBT.2c is a US Grade 1 standard while the topic is pitched at UK Y2 (ages 6-7); the age mapping across jurisdictions is approximate.

The original error-pattern phrasing 'contrast 3 vs 30 vs 300 to show the 0 keeps the 3 in the tens place' was imprecise for 300 (the 3 is in the hundreds place there); corrected in feedback and constraints to describe zeros as place-holders in their actual place.
Comparative efficacy of discussion-as-follow-up versus other sequencings is untested; stated only as a qualified proposal.

probeDeeper: Build 50 with tens rods — how many single ones is that, and how many ones cubes did you use?
Why isn't 30 the same as 3?
If I add one more ten to 30, what do I have and how is it written?
assess.correctAnswer: The 3 means 3 tens; the 0 means there are 0 ones. So 30 is 3 tens and 0 ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the 0 as meaningless rather than as zero ones holding the place: 'the 0 doesn't mean anything'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 30 with tens rods and no unit cubes; the empty ones spot IS the zero. Contrast 3 vs 30 vs 300 to show the 0 keeps the 3 in the tens place.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 0 means nothing — it's just there.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the 0 is 'just there' or 'means nothing'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the digits at face value: 'the 3 means three'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Represent with 3 tens rods and count the ones inside (30). Say '3 in the tens place = 3 tens = 30'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 3 means three.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the 3 stands for three ones/things rather than three tens.

responseLevels.gap: Reads the 3 as three ones or calls the 0 meaningless; no tens-and-ones structure.
responseLevels.full: States 3 tens and 0 ones, and explains the 0 marks the empty ones place so the 3 stays in the tens position.
responseLevels.partial: Says '3 tens' but is unsure what the 0 contributes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 30. Point to the 3, then the 0. Ask: 'What is the 3 telling us, and what is the 0 telling us? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with decade place value says '3 tens, 0 ones'; a face-value thinker says the 3 means three (things) and the 0 'means nothing'. The reason tier reveals whether the 0 is understood as marking an empty ones place or dismissed as meaningless.

pedagogy.summary: This topic builds an argument from evidence: the Sun looks far brighter than every other star only because it is by far the closest star to Earth, not because it is the biggest or most powerful. Children learn the crucial distinction between apparent brightness (how bright something looks from here) and actual brightness, using the everyday torch analogy (a torch looks bright up close and dim far away), and argue that differences in stars' apparent brightness are mainly due to their different distances. Assessment stays with relative distances, not sizes or other stellar factors.
bestPractices: Lead with the torch/light-source-at-different-distances analogy so children feel that the SAME light looks dimmer when farther away.
Make apparent vs actual brightness explicit — 'how bright it looks from Earth' vs 'how much light it really gives out' — as the central distinction.
Frame it as engaging in argument from evidence: pupils support the claim (brightness difference is mainly distance) with the analogy and data.
Establish that the Sun IS a star, just the nearest one — directly countering 'the Sun is special/not a star'.
Keep to relative distances, not star sizes or masses/age (assessment boundary) — do not let 'bigger = brighter' creep in.
Use a strong scale contrast — the Sun is right next door while other stars are enormously farther — to motivate why it dominates our sky.
keyRepresentations: A torch moved near/far, dimming with distance while its true output is unchanged.
An apparent-vs-actual brightness pairing: how bright it looks vs how much light it gives.
A distance line placing the Sun very close and other stars vastly farther.
Two stars where the brighter-looking one turns out to be the closer, weaker one.
commonMisconceptions: A brighter-looking star must be bigger, closer AND more powerful — conflating apparent brightness with size/output.
The Sun is not a star, or is a special kind of object different from stars.
Brightness depends only on a star's size.
All stars are the same distance from Earth (a 'dome of stars').
The Sun is the biggest or intrinsically brightest star in the universe.

learn.summary: Children build an argument from evidence that the Sun looks far brighter than every other star mainly because it is by far the closest star to Earth, not because it is the biggest or most powerful. The central distinction is apparent brightness (how bright a light looks from here) versus actual brightness (how much light it truly gives out), developed through the torch-at-different-distances analogy. Work stays with relative distances, not star sizes, masses, or ages.

activities.title: The sliding torch: same light, different look
feedback: If the child says the bulb got weaker: nothing changed about the torch — you never touched the switch. Only the distance changed, so only how bright it LOOKS changed.

If the child says the light 'ran out' or 'got tired': the light is not used up; it spreads over a larger area the further it travels, so less enters your eye. Carry the torch to two or three set distances and compare.
Reinforce: 'how bright it looks from here' and 'how much light it really gives out' are two different things — name which one changed.
activities.rationale: Leading with a single manipulable light source lets children feel that distance alone changes apparent brightness while actual output is fixed, grounding the core evidence before stars are introduced. The spreading-light explanation directly addresses the 'light runs out' misconception.
sourceClaims: DCI ESS1.A: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-1]' — the conceptual basis for teaching apparent brightness via distance and the torch analogy.
learnerActions: In a dim room, hold a torch close and notice how bright it looks, then have someone slowly carry it far away (still pointing at you) and watch it look smaller and dimmer.
State aloud whether the torch bulb itself got weaker when you walked away (it did not — the switch and bulb are unchanged).
Explain in your own words why the SAME light looks dimmer: its light spreads out over more space the further it travels, so less of it reaches your eye.
Keep a note or imagined 'true brightness' label fixed on the torch while only its apparent brightness changes with distance.
activities.intendedInsight: A light's apparent brightness falls with distance even though its actual (true) output stays exactly the same; dimness from distance is about spreading light, not a weakening bulb.

activities.title: Two lights, two distances: which is really stronger?
feedback: A child who predicts 'the brighter-looking one must be more powerful' is conflating apparent with actual brightness — exactly the star-brightness misconception. After revealing, contrast: the lamp was always stronger; it only looked dim because it was far.
If correct: good — you separated 'looks bright from here' from 'is powerful', and you named distance as the reason they can disagree.
activities.rationale: Requiring a committed prediction with a reason BEFORE observing surfaces the apparent-vs-actual conflation as a diagnostic, and the reveal gives immediate corrective evidence. This mirrors the two-tier assessment's predict-observe-explain design.
sourceClaims: A dominant student misconception is that a brighter-looking star must be bigger or more powerful (confusing apparent with actual brightness), and that the Sun is not a star — the assessment boundary explicitly guards against attributing apparent brightness to size.
learnerActions: Set out a small dim torch and a much brighter lamp in a dim room. Hold the weak torch close to you and place the bright lamp far across the room; if the lamp still looks brighter, move it further away until the weak torch looks brighter from where you stand.
Before moving anything, predict WITH A REASON: which light is actually the more powerful — the one that looks brighter from where you stand? Commit to your answer out loud.
Now place both lights at the same distance from you and compare: if the lamp really gives out more light, it now looks brighter, even though it looked dimmer when it was far away.
Say which light looked brighter and which was actually more powerful, and explain what caused the mismatch.
activities.intendedInsight: The brighter-LOOKING light is not necessarily the more powerful one; a weak light held close can outshine a strong light placed far away. Apparent brightness depends heavily on distance.

activities.title: From torches to stars: build the argument
feedback: If the child says the Sun is the biggest/most powerful star because it looks brightest: a weak light held close outshines a strong light far away — the same is true for stars. The Sun looks brightest because it is nearest, which does not tell us it is the biggest.
If the child says the Sun isn't really a star: the Sun is an ordinary star seen close up; the stars in the night sky are distant suns.

If the child says distant stars are simply small or weak: how faint a star looks cannot by itself tell us how much light it gives out — some stars give out far more light than the Sun yet look faint because they are so far away.

Probe transfer: 'If we moved the Sun ten times further away, would it still look the brightest star in our sky? Why?' (Yes — it would look much dimmer, but it would still be far closer than any other star, so still by far the brightest.) And consider: could a star that gives out much more light than the Sun still look fainter to us? How?
activities.rationale: Transferring the torch evidence to stars and testing the 'move the Sun further' case lets children construct the argument-from-evidence the standard asks for, and directly counters the conflation of apparent brightness with size and the 'Sun is not a star' category error.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-ESS1-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-1]' — [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-1], and does not include other factors affecting apparent brightness (stellar mass, age, stage).
DCI ESS1.A: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-ESS1-1]' — the conceptual basis for teaching apparent brightness via distance and the torch analogy.
learnerActions: Meet two stars: one blazing brightly in the sky and one a faint speck. Predict which star actually gives out more light.
Check the given facts: in this example the bright-LOOKING star is nearby and actually gives out less light, while the faint speck gives out far more light but is enormously far away.

Order a set of stars by the distance facts given (not by how bright they look), compare that order with how bright each looks, and state the argument: how far away a star is strongly affects how bright it looks, and the Sun looks so much brighter than every other star mainly because it is so much closer.
Imagine dragging our own Sun out to the same distance as the other stars and describe what happens — it shrinks to just another faint dot.
State the conclusion the evidence supports: the Sun rules our sky only because it is the star next door, not because it is special, biggest, or most powerful.
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun is an ordinary star that looks far brighter than all others chiefly because it is the closest; some stars actually give out much more light than the Sun but look faint because of their vast distance.

activities.title: Argue it in role
feedback: If the explanation leans on size or power, redirect to the torch: how bright something looks from here depends on how far away it is as well as how much light it gives out, and the Sun looks brightest mainly because it is so close.
Prompt the learner to cite the two-light comparison as their evidence rather than just asserting the conclusion.
activities.rationale: A responsive dialogue may let the child rehearse and defend the argument aloud, which is proposed to surface lingering conflations; it is intended to complement, not replace, the hands-on light evidence that supplies the data for the argument. Its added value over the hands-on work is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Take the role of an astronomer explaining to a friend why the Sun is not a special object but an ordinary, nearby star.
Respond to the friend's challenge: 'But the Sun is obviously the brightest star there is!' — use the torch evidence to argue back.
Finish by distinguishing, in your own words, apparent brightness from actual brightness and naming distance as the main reason the Sun looks brightest.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the reasoning into spoken argument is intended to help consolidate the apparent-vs-actual distinction and the claim that the Sun's dominance in our sky is about proximity; this consolidation benefit is proposed, not demonstrated.

constraints: Keep to relative distances only — do not let star sizes, masses, ages, or stages enter the explanation; the assessment boundary excludes these and 'bigger = brighter' must not creep in.
Establish explicitly that the Sun IS a star, just the nearest one, to counter the 'Sun is special / not a star' category error.
Explain faint distant stars as light spreading over a larger area with distance, NOT as light being used up or 'running out'.

A hands-on or on-screen light whose distance the child can vary makes the apparent-vs-actual relationship concrete; a static compare-the-stars diagram with tap-to-reveal facts can serve as a reference but does not let the child vary distance and watch apparent brightness change, so it supports recall rather than this particular evidence-building.
A role-play or spoken argument can reinforce the conclusion but relies on evidence gathered elsewhere; use it to consolidate, not to supply the data.

A fly-out showing the vast relative distances (Sun right here, others light-years away) can convey scale, but the distance–brightness argument itself can be made with a simple near/far light demonstration; keep any 3D view within the relative-distance boundary.

Source claims are reproduced verbatim from the row; their cited verification status is legacy and was not independently re-checked here.

The scaffold with a 'fixed true-brightness gauge' alongside a moved light is retained as an optional interaction example to make the actual-vs-apparent distinction visible; it is one possible mechanism, not a required one.

The role-play activity carries no sourceClaims because no cited claim directly supports the efficacy of the dialogue format; it is a qualified proposal. The misconception claim cited in Activity 2 characterises the target misconception, not the efficacy of the predict-observe-explain format, which also remains untested.

The NGSS treatment of apparent brightness as 'mainly' distance-driven is a curriculum simplification (intrinsic luminosity also varies widely); it is preserved as stated by the standard, and Activity 3 keeps the nuance that faint-looking stars may be distant giants.

Self-audit: the physics was checked. Apparent brightness decreasing with distance is attributable to light spreading over a larger area (inverse-square intuition), not to the source weakening or light being consumed — the 'light runs out' framing is corrected into the activity feedback. No arithmetic, force/motion, fraction, or shade/solar claims are present. No conceptual errors needing correction were found beyond ensuring size/power are never used to explain apparent brightness.

assess.poeTask: Set out a small dim torch and a much brighter lamp in a dim room. Hold the weak torch close to the child and place the bright lamp far across the room. Ask them to PREDICT with a reason: which light is actually the more powerful — the one that looks brighter from here? Have them commit. Then bring the far lamp close (or carry the torch away) to reveal the distant lamp is far stronger despite looking dimmer at range. The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part: a child who says 'the brighter-looking one must be more powerful' is conflating apparent with actual brightness — exactly the star-brightness misconception.
probeDeeper: Could a star that is really much bigger and brighter than the Sun still look fainter to us? How?
Why does a torch look dimmer the further away it is — what is happening to its light?
If we moved the Sun ten times further away, would it still look the brightest star in our sky? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: The Sun looks brightest mainly because it is by far the CLOSEST star to us — not because it is the biggest or most powerful. Many stars are actually larger and more luminous but look faint because they are enormously far away. How bright a star LOOKS (apparent brightness) is chiefly set by its distance, which is different from how powerful it actually is.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the brightest-looking star must be the biggest or most powerful one' (apparent–actual brightness conflation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Torch-vs-floodlight: a weak light held close outshines a strong light far away; separate 'looks bright' from 'is powerful.'
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the Sun looks brightest because it is the biggest, most powerful star.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the Sun is the biggest/most powerful star because it looks the brightest

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Sun isn't really a star' (category error)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Sun is an ordinary star seen close up; the night stars are distant suns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies the Sun is a star at all

errorPatterns.pattern: 'far-off stars are dim because their light runs out / gets tired before reaching us' (light-as-exhaustion)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Light spreads over a larger area the further it travels, so less enters your eye — it isn't used up; show a torch at increasing distances.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains faintness by light 'running out' rather than spreading out over distance

responseLevels.gap: Equates looking-brightest with being biggest/most powerful, or denies the Sun is a star.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes apparent from actual brightness, argues the Sun looks brightest chiefly because it is the nearest star, and explains faint stars as distant (light spreading with distance) not weak; transfers with the 'move the Sun further' case.
responseLevels.partial: Says the Sun looks brightest because it's closest, but can't separate apparent from actual brightness, or thinks distant stars are simply small/weak rather than far.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The Sun looks far brighter than any other star. Is that because the Sun is bigger or more powerful than all other stars, or is there another reason? … Explain how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who conflates apparent with actual brightness answers 'yes, the Sun must be the biggest/most powerful.' A child reasoning correctly separates the two and names closeness/distance as the reason the Sun looks brightest. The 'or is there another reason?' framing plus the why-tier forces the distinction that a bare 'why is the Sun bright?' would let them dodge.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Classifying Materials

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." Clarification: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." DCI PS1.A: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations. CCC: Patterns.

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Working Scientifically, LKS2 Y3/4):** No specific content statement, but the enquiry type is statutory: "gathering, recording, classifying and presenting data in a variety of ways to help in answering questions" and "identifying differences, similarities or changes related to simple scientific ideas and processes." Builds on the KS1 'compare and group' objective and feeds the Y5 comparative/fair-test work.

- **Operational details:** This is the step up from casual sorting to a planned investigation. Have children choose ONE observable property to test (e.g. flexibility, hardness, magnetism), decide how they will test it the same way for every material, TEST several materials systematically, record each result in a table, and only THEN classify by the pattern of results. The discipline is consistency: the same test applied to every material, and the classification driven by recorded evidence rather than a first impression. Surface the Patterns crosscutting concept — which materials share the property? — and revisit that the same set classifies differently under a different property. Keep the property observable/testable at this age (not conductivity or solubility yet, which come in Y4–Y5).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (procedural). The child can plan a simple consistent test for one property, carry it out across several materials, record results in a table, and classify the materials into groups justified by the recorded evidence — recognising the shared-property pattern.
bestPractices: Insist on ONE chosen property tested the SAME way for every material — consistency is what makes it an investigation rather than casual sorting.
Record each result in a table BEFORE classifying, so groups are driven by evidence not first impressions.
Make the Patterns concept explicit: ask which materials share the property and name the group by the shared property.
Revisit rule-dependence — re-run with a different property and watch the same materials regroup — reinforcing that classification depends on the criterion.
Keep properties observable and testable for the age (hardness, flexibility, magnetism, texture); defer conductivity/solubility to Y4–Y5.
Model the plan→test→record→classify sequence so children internalise the investigation structure, not just the outcome.
keyRepresentations: A plan→test→record→classify investigation frame
A results table (materials down the side, the tested property across the top)
Sorting rings/branching (Carroll or simple tree) filled FROM the recorded results
A 'shared property' pattern highlight (which materials clustered together and why)
A re-classify prompt: the same materials sorted under a second property
commonMisconceptions: Classifying by an untested surface feature (colour, size) or first impression rather than by a systematically tested property.
Applying the test inconsistently across materials, so the comparison and resulting classes are invalid.
Treating classification as a fixed property of the object, not realising the groups depend on the chosen criterion.
Skipping the record-then-classify discipline — grouping from memory or expectation instead of from the data table.
Confusing 'classify' (assign to groups by a rule) with merely 'describe' or with running a fair test for a purpose (a different enquiry type).

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds learning to classify materials by observable properties, the core objective is a planned investigation (not casual sorting): choose ONE observable property, apply the SAME test to each material, record every result in a table, and only then classify from the recorded evidence — surfacing the pattern of which materials share the property, and seeing the same set regroup under a different property. The primary approach is a hands-on (or on-screen) investigation bench with live results logging; supporting approaches check the procedure with ordering/matching tasks and an annotated worked investigation.

activities.title: Investigation bench: pick a property, test the same way, record, then classify
feedback: If a group does not match the recorded table, highlight the mismatched material and ask the learner to re-check their own result before regrouping.

When a learner predicts or records 'yes' for a non-magnetic metal (aluminium foil, a piece of copper pipe or wire), have them slowly bring the magnet and watch nothing happen: the recorded 'no' is the fact — not all metals are magnetic. Only a few metals, such as iron, nickel and most steels, are attracted (some stainless steels are not). If a 'copper' coin sticks to the magnet, accept that result too: many such coins are copper-plated steel.
If the test is applied differently to different items, reset to one fixed testing action and have them repeat it identically on every material.
After a 'switch property' re-sort, prompt: 'The same materials, different groups — what changed? The materials, or the question we asked?'
Highlight the shared-property cluster and ask the learner to name the group by the property it shares.
activities.rationale: The target skill is procedural and multi-step: plan → test → record → classify. Live state can enforce the discipline (same test for all; classify from the record) and stage the re-classify-by-a-new-property realisation, making the criterion-dependence of classification concrete. A physical tray and magnet give a parallel hands-on enactment of the same procedure.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-PS1-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]'; clarification color/texture/hardness/flexibility and shared-property patterns; DCI PS1.A; CCC Patterns.
DfE KS2 Working Scientifically (LKS2): 'gathering, recording, classifying and presenting data in a variety of ways'; 'identifying differences, similarities or changes'.
Classification misconceptions: sorting by untested surface features, inconsistent testing, treating class as fixed rather than criterion-dependent.
learnerActions: Choose ONE observable property to test (e.g. 'is it magnetic?', hardness, or flexibility) from an offered set of age-appropriate, testable properties.
Commit to a single fixed test action and apply it identically to every material in turn (e.g. bring the same magnet to each material the same way).

Record each result as it happens in a table with materials down the side and the tested property across the top — e.g. steel paperclip yes, piece of copper pipe or wire no, wooden peg no, steel key yes. (Avoid using a coin as the 'copper' example: many 'copper' coins, such as UK 1p and 2p coins made since 1992, are copper-plated steel and are attracted to a magnet.)
Only after the table is complete, sort the materials into groups (e.g. 'magnetic' / 'not magnetic') and check that each group matches the recorded data.

Press a 'switch property' option to re-test the exact same materials under a second property (e.g. hardness) and watch them regroup — e.g. the steel key and a glass marble now share a group they did not before.
Name the shared-property group: say which materials clustered together and why.
Pair the screen work with a real tray of materials and a magnet to carry out the physical investigation alongside.
activities.intendedInsight: A classification is not a fixed fact about a material; it is the answer to the particular question you chose to test. Consistency of the test and grouping from recorded evidence (not first impressions) are what make it an investigation.

activities.title: Spot the flaw and order the steps (procedure checks)
feedback: For the inconsistent-test item, point to exactly which material was tested differently and why that invalidates the comparison.
For a wrong grouping, show the row in the table that contradicts the chosen group.
If the step order is wrong, emphasise that recording must come before classifying so groups are driven by evidence, not memory.
activities.rationale: Ordering and matching tasks can check whether a learner recognises the procedure and detects an invalid (inconsistent) test. Use as a check or reinforcement; such a task does not itself let the learner generate the evidence, so pair it with the investigation.
sourceClaims: Classification misconceptions: sorting by untested surface features, inconsistent testing, treating class as fixed rather than criterion-dependent.
learnerActions: Put the stages of a classifying investigation into the correct order: plan the test → test each material the same way → record results in a table → classify from the results.
Given a short scenario, identify an inconsistent (unfair) test used within a classification — where one material was tested differently from the others.
Given a completed results table, pick the classification (grouping) that genuinely matches the recorded data.
Sort stated materials into groups by a named property.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the correct investigation sequence, consistent testing, and evidence-matching groups reinforces the structure of the skill — though recognising it is not the same as carrying it out.

activities.title: Walk through a completed investigation (annotated model)
feedback: When a learner reveals a group, confirm whether their stated reason matches the recorded evidence for that group.
After the re-sort flap, ask which materials swapped groups and why, to check they attribute the change to the chosen property, not the materials.
If the learner treats the groups as fixed, point back to the second grouping as a counter-example.
activities.rationale: A guided annotated example reinforces the investigation structure and the shared-property pattern. It is a worked model that supports — but does not itself provide — the learner conducting and recording their own test.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-PS1-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]'; clarification color/texture/hardness/flexibility and shared-property patterns; DCI PS1.A; CCC Patterns.
learnerActions: Examine a finished investigation showing the results table, the groups formed, and the shared-property pattern.
Reveal the reasoning behind each part: tap the table, the single test method, and each group to see why the materials were placed there.
Open a flap/panel that re-sorts the same materials under a second property and compare the two groupings.
Explain in your own words why the same materials ended up in different groups.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a fully worked, correctly structured investigation can make the plan→test→record→classify sequence and the criterion-dependence of groups explicit before or after doing one yourself.

constraints: Keep properties observable and testable at this age (hardness, flexibility, magnetism, texture); defer conductivity and solubility to later years (Y4–Y5).
Insist on ONE chosen property tested the SAME way for every material; consistency is what distinguishes an investigation from casual sorting.
Require recording in a table BEFORE classifying, so groups are driven by evidence rather than first impressions.

Correct the specific misconception 'all metals are magnetic': aluminium and copper are metals but are not attracted to a magnet, and a recorded 'no' must be accepted even when it contradicts expectation. Only ferromagnetic materials (e.g. iron, nickel, cobalt and most steels) are noticeably attracted. Some stainless steels are not, and some 'copper' coins are copper-plated steel and are attracted. Do not let learners override a tested result in either direction.
Distinguish 'classify' (assign to groups by a rule) from merely 'describe', and from running a fair test for a purpose (a different enquiry type).

Ordering/matching tasks and annotated worked examples can check or reinforce the procedure but do not themselves elicit the learner planning and running the test that generates the evidence; use them alongside, not instead of, an actual investigation.

An in-role dialogue does not itself supply the physical testing or a populated data table, and children this age are unlikely to drive such an open conversation to a valid classification; keep the activity grounded in doing and recording.

Because classifying by observable properties is not inherently spatial, a clean 2D bench is sufficient and a real tray gives genuine tactile enactment; a 3D model's depth/physics offer no particular spatial affordance this classification task requires and add handling overhead.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated or tested interventions.

Self-audit of the magnetism example: the source row's correct-answer and probe content correctly treat aluminium and copper as non-magnetic metals and steel paperclip/steel key as magnetic — this is accurate (ferromagnetism). The 'all metals are magnetic' belief is flagged as a misconception to correct, not propagated, and the activity feedback explicitly resolves it rather than only caveating it.

One source (STEM Learning misconceptions) is marked unverified (verified:false) in the row; claims about specific misconception patterns rest on it. Treated as a supporting principle, not as evidence that any activity here was tested.
'Switch property' re-sort and shared-property highlight are retained as concrete interaction examples of the learning mechanism, offered as options, not mandated implementations.
Medium-limitation statements for conversation and 3D are retained only as narrow observable affordances / age-suitability notes, not as categorical claims that those media cannot teach the procedure.

probeDeeper: Your chart says the aluminium foil isn't magnetic even though it's metal — does that surprise you? What does it tell us?
Did you test every material in exactly the same way?
If we chose a different property instead of magnetism, would the groups be the same?
Is this copper coin magnetic? Test it — were you right beforehand?
assess.correctAnswer: Brings the magnet to each material the same way, records a yes/no for each in a chart, and sorts into magnetic / non-magnetic groups strictly from the recorded results — finding that only the steel paperclip is attracted, and that the other metals (aluminium, copper) are NOT.

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies from assumption, not results — 'all metals are magnetic', so groups metals together without genuinely testing, or overrides a 'no' from the aluminium.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them slowly bring the magnet to the aluminium foil and copper coin and watch nothing happen; the recorded 'no' is the fact — not all metals are magnetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Records or predicts 'yes' for a non-magnetic metal without a real test, or dismisses the actual result.

errorPatterns.pattern: Inconsistent test or no record — tests each material differently, or keeps results in their head, so the grouping can't be justified.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a record-as-you-go chart and one fixed testing action; this is a procedure gap — reconnect to grouping-by-property rather than reteaching magnetism.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No chart; groups produced from memory or feel; the magnet is used differently on different items.

errorPatterns.pattern: Tests several properties at once — muddles 'magnetic' with 'shiny' or 'heavy' and sorts by a blend.
errorPatterns.nextMove: 'One property at a time' — fix the single test (does the magnet pull it?) before sorting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Groupings track shininess/weight as much as magnetism.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by assumption or appearance without a consistent test or any record.
responseLevels.full: Applies one consistent test to every material, records results in a chart, and classifies strictly from the recorded data — accepting a result that contradicts expectation.
responseLevels.partial: Runs a test and records some results, but lets prior belief (all metals are magnetic) override a surprising result, or applies the test unevenly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out five materials (steel paperclip, aluminium foil, copper coin, plastic counter, wooden bead) and a magnet. Say: 'Plan and carry out a test to find which are magnetic. Test each the same way, record what you find in a chart, then sort them into groups from your results.' Watch them plan, test and record.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The aluminium and copper cases are deliberate traps for 'all metals are magnetic'. Watching shows whether the grouping is DRIVEN by the recorded test results or by assumption, whether the test is applied consistently, and whether results are actually recorded rather than remembered.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5-7 (KS1/Grades K-2): minibeast habitats and micro-habitats — the specific damp, dark, sheltered or sunny places different minibeasts live (under a log, in the soil, under stones, in leaf litter, in a pond, among flowers) and WHY each creature is found there.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' — identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited; identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including MICRO-HABITATS. Working-scientifically: observing closely, identifying and classifying.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 2-LS4-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1]).
• Operational details — the key idea is MATCH between creature and place: woodlice and worms need damp/dark (they dry out in sun); pond skaters need water; butterflies need flowers. Children PREDICT what lives in a place, then check by lifting/looking. Emphasise returning creatures and habitats to how they were found (care links to the 'caring for minibeasts' topic).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): names one place a given minibeast lives (worm → soil). Tier B (age 6): predicts what will be found under a log/stone before looking and checks. Tier C (age 7): explains the match with a reason ('woodlice live under logs because it's damp and dark and they'd dry out in the sun').
bestPractices: Frame every habitat as a MATCH with a reason — 'suited to' means the place gives the creature what it needs (damp, dark, food, water), not just 'that's where it is'.
Use predict-then-check: children guess what lives under the log/stone before lifting, making their thinking visible and memorable.
Ground it in a real micro-habitat hunt and model care — lift gently, look, return the log exactly as found.
Contrast micro-habitats side by side (damp under-log vs dry sunny wall) so the difference in residents is obvious.
Draw out the consequence of a mismatch (a woodlouse in the sun dries out) to cement why creatures stay in their suited place.
keyRepresentations: A garden cross-section showing layered micro-habitats from pond to soil to canopy, each with its residents.
Predict-then-check reveal (guess → lift the log → see who's there).
Creature-to-habitat matching board.
A simple 'what it needs' card (damp / dark / water / flowers) linking creature to place.
commonMisconceptions: 'Animals can live anywhere' — children don't yet see that a creature needs a place that suits it; a woodlouse can't thrive on a sunny wall.
'Habitat means the whole garden/wood' — the micro-habitat idea (the specific under-log, the specific pond edge) is the new precision at KS1.
'Dark, damp places are just where dirty bugs hide' — reframing: damp/dark IS the resource these creatures need.
'If I move it somewhere nicer it'll be happier' — moving a creature out of its suited micro-habitat can harm it.
Confusing a habitat (where it lives) with what it eats — related but distinct ideas.

learn.summary: For ages 5-7 (KS1 Y2 / Grades K-2), children learn that minibeasts live in specific micro-habitats suited to their needs: woodlice, worms and slugs in damp dark places (under logs, stones, leaf litter, in soil), pond skaters and dragonfly nymphs in water, aphids, caterpillars and ladybirds on sunny leaves, and butterflies among flowers. The core idea is the MATCH between creature and place, with a reason ('damp and dark so a woodlouse won't dry out'), learned through predict-then-check hunting and by reasoning about the consequence of a mismatch. Children should also practise careful handling — lifting gently and returning logs and stones exactly as found, and never placing a creature where it could come to harm.

activities.title: Bug detective: predict then check a micro-habitat
feedback: If the right creatures appear where predicted, confirm: 'Yes — woodlice under the damp log, because they need it damp and dark.'
If a guess was wrong, name the actual residents and their need: 'Pond skaters need water to walk on, so you find them on the pond, not under the log.'
Praise careful returning of the log: 'You put the home back the way you found it — that keeps the minibeasts safe.'
activities.rationale: Predict-then-check makes children's thinking visible and memorable, and grounding it in a real micro-habitat hunt with careful handling is described as standard KS1 practice that builds the observe/identify/classify working-scientifically skills.
sourceClaims: KS1 Y2 requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and to identify and name animals in their habitats, including micro-habitats.
Micro-habitat hunts (under logs, stones, leaf litter) grounded in prediction and careful return of creatures are standard effective KS1 practice.
learnerActions: Before looking, choose a micro-habitat (under a log, under a stone, in leaf litter, in the soil, at the pond edge, among flowers) and say out loud or tap picture-guesses for what you think lives there.
Lift the log/stone gently or look closely at the pond or flowerbed to check, and compare what you found against your guess.
For each creature found, say why it is there using a 'what it needs' idea (damp / dark / water / flowers / leaves).
Put every log and stone back exactly the way you found it before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Different micro-habitats hold different creatures because each creature needs the conditions that place provides — 'suited to its habitat' means the place gives the creature what it needs, not just 'that's where it happens to be'. Damp and dark are not where 'dirty bugs hide'; they are the resource these creatures need.

activities.title: Take me home: the consequence of a mismatch
feedback: Reinforce the reason: 'Out in the sun a woodlouse would dry out — that's why it needs the damp dark under the log.'
If a child says the creature 'wants' or 'chooses' the dark, recast it: 'It survives best where it's damp — the damp keeps it from drying out.'
Stress care: 'Because moving a creature to the wrong place can hurt it, we never put one in the sun and we always return it to where it lives.'
activities.rationale: Reasoning through, or watching a modelled, consequence of a bad match helps cement why creatures stay in suited places and addresses the 'animals can live anywhere' and 'move it somewhere nicer' misconceptions. A screen simulation showing a creature struggling in the wrong place and settling in the right one can give immediate why-feedback without risking a real animal.
sourceClaims: KS1 Y2 requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and to identify and name animals in their habitats, including micro-habitats.
learnerActions: Using a screen simulation, a drawing, or spoken reasoning — never a real creature — think about a given creature in two places: a damp shaded spot versus a dry sunny patch.

Predict what would happen in each: a worm or woodlouse left on hot dry pavement would dry out and struggle, while under a damp log it settles. Never actually place a real creature in the sun to test this.
Explain in your own words why the creature needs its damp dark place to survive.
activities.intendedInsight: A creature is not free to live anywhere: moving it out of its suited micro-habitat can harm it, which is why 'suited to' matters — the need is about survival, not preference or choice.

activities.title: Compare two places side by side
feedback: Correct answer to model: 'Mostly different ones — damp-loving creatures under the log, sun-liking ones on the leaf, because each survives best in different conditions.'
If a child expects the same minibeasts everywhere, pair each creature to its conditions so place predicts creature.

If a child misreads conditions ('under a log it's dry and bright'), have them feel and observe the actual conditions under a real log, which are usually damper, darker and cooler than the open ground nearby, though this varies with weather and setting.
activities.rationale: Contrasting micro-habitats side by side makes the difference in residents obvious and is the diagnostic that separates children who think any minibeast lives anywhere from those who grasp habitat preference.
sourceClaims: Grade 2 students [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1] (2-LS4-1).
Micro-habitat hunts (under logs, stones, leaf litter) grounded in prediction and careful return of creatures are standard effective KS1 practice.
learnerActions: Look at two contrasting micro-habitats at once — a damp shaded under-log spot and a dry sunny wall or leaf.
Predict whether you'd find the SAME minibeasts in both, or different ones, and say why before checking.
List who you'd expect in each: damp-loving woodlice, worms, slugs under the log; sun-liking aphids, caterpillars, ladybirds on the sunny leaf.
Match each creature to the conditions it does best in (damp, dark, sunny, leafy).
activities.intendedInsight: Because different creatures need different conditions, the place helps predict which creatures you are likely to find — where you look changes what you find.

activities.title: Garden cross-section: where everyone lives
feedback: Confirm correct placements and names zone by zone.
If a child treats the whole garden as one habitat, point to the specific under-log or pond-edge spot and its particular residents.
Prompt the reason if only the 'where' is given: 'Yes, worms in the soil — and why the soil? Because it's damp and dark.'
activities.rationale: A cross-section teaches the spatial WHERE and the precision of the micro-habitat idea well, though on its own it shows location rather than running a prediction or the consequence of a mismatch; it works best as a companion to the hunt and mismatch activities. A tap-to-reveal 'why here?' flap per zone can make the reasoning interactive.
sourceClaims: KS1 Y2 requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and to identify and name animals in their habitats, including micro-habitats.
learnerActions: Study a garden cross-section from pond to soil to leaf litter to canopy.
For each zone, name a creature that lives there and say one reason why ('why here?').
Add or draw a 'what it needs' card (damp / dark / water / flowers) linking each creature to its place.
activities.intendedInsight: A single garden contains many layered micro-habitats, each with residents suited to it — habitat means the specific place, not the whole garden.

activities.title: Sort and match creatures to habitats (check)
feedback: For a correct match, restate the reason to reinforce the 'suited to' link.
For an error, return to the conditions: 'Pond skaters need water — which group needs water?'
Watch for habitat/food confusion; clarify that where it lives and what it eats are related but different.
activities.rationale: A matching and sorting check can assess the creature–place pairing cleanly as a companion to active exploration; note it mainly confirms recognition of known pairings and does not by itself elicit independent prediction or explanation.
sourceClaims: KS1 Y2 requires pupils to identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and to identify and name animals in their habitats, including micro-habitats.
learnerActions: Sort a set of minibeast cards into micro-habitats: pond / soil / under-log / sunny leaf; some creatures (like worms or slugs) can fit more than one damp place, so say why you chose.
Match each creature to its habitat.
Answer 'why do woodlice hide under logs?' choosing or saying the reason (damp and dark, so they don't dry out).
activities.intendedInsight: Children can reliably link each minibeast to the conditions its habitat provides.

activities.title: Ask the minibeast (optional light intro)
feedback: Confirm the need named by the creature and connect it back to a real place to look.
Encourage the child to then go and check a real micro-habitat rather than stop at the story.
activities.rationale: A character dialogue can give a charming, accessible entry point to the concept; it is best used alongside exploring and matching, so treat it as an optional introduction rather than the main learning.
learnerActions: Pose a question to a minibeast character — 'Where do you live and why?' — and listen to or read its reply ('I live under logs because it's damp and I'd dry out in the sun').
Follow up by predicting where a different creature would say it lives.
activities.intendedInsight: Each creature's home is tied to a need it can explain, offering a friendly way into the 'suited to' idea.

constraints: Always frame a habitat as a MATCH with a reason — 'suited to' means the place gives the creature what it needs (damp, dark, food, water), not merely 'that's where it is'.
Model and require care: lift gently, look, and return logs and stones exactly as found; stress that moving a creature to the 'wrong' place can harm it.
Never demonstrate a mismatch by placing a real creature in harmful conditions (e.g. a sunny patch to watch it dry out); use a screen simulation, drawing, or predicted reasoning instead.
Recast 'the creature chooses/wants the dark' as 'it survives best where it's damp' — avoid implying conscious choice.
Keep habitat (where it lives) distinct from diet (what it eats) — related but separate ideas.

Matching/sorting and cross-section tap-to-reveal activities mainly check or display pairings; they do not by themselves elicit a prediction or the felt consequence of a mismatch, so pair them with active hunting.

Screen simulations of a creature 'shrivelling' in the sun are simplified representations of real survival pressure; present them as a model and, where possible, connect to real observation of conditions.
Specific conditions (how damp or dark a particular log is) vary with weather, material and setting — have children observe and feel actual conditions rather than assume a fixed result.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all sources[].claim entries remain unverified (verified:false) and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Activity 2's 'take me home' is a screen simulation, drawing or predicted-reasoning exercise and must never direct a child to place a real creature in harmful conditions, consistent with the care constraints.

The legacy entry asserted that a static cross-section 'can't run the predict-then-check' and that the concept 'is best learned by exploring... not by dialogue'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources, so they have been softened to scoped affordances and limits.
The shrivelling consequence is a simplification; it is pedagogically reasonable for the age but is a model of a survival effect, not a measured outcome — flagged for reviewer awareness.
Source claims about NGSS, DfE and general minibeast-education practice describe curriculum requirements/standard practice, not empirical efficacy of any specific activity here.

assess.poeTask: Before lifting a shaded, damp log, ask the child to predict which minibeasts (if any) are underneath and whether they'll match those on a nearby sunny leaf — and to say WHY. Then lift the log together and compare. The reason given before looking ('nothing / the same as everywhere' versus 'damp-loving ones like woodlice and worms') is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Why do woodlice and worms hide under logs instead of sitting on a sunny path?
If a place is wet and dark, what might you find there? What about dry and sunny?
What would happen to a worm left out on a hot, dry pavement?
assess.correctAnswer: Different ones. Minibeasts that like damp, dark places — woodlice, worms, slugs — live under the log, while ones that like sun and leaves — aphids, caterpillars, ladybirds — are on the leaf. Different creatures prefer different conditions, so where you look changes what you find.

errorPatterns.pattern: The same minibeasts live everywhere — 'you'd find the same ones in both places.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair each creature to its conditions — damp/dark for woodlice, sunny leaves for aphids — so place predicts creature.
errorPatterns.distractor: You'd find the same minibeasts in both places, because they live all over the garden.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects identical creatures under the log and on the leaf, with no notion of preference.

errorPatterns.pattern: Minibeasts think about and choose where to live, like picking a house.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recast preference as where they survive best — damp keeps a woodlouse from drying out — rather than a conscious choice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the woodlouse 'decides' it wants the dark.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the conditions — 'under a log it's dry and bright.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child feel and observe the actual conditions under a log — damp, dark, cool.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a shaded log as a dry, sunny place.

responseLevels.gap: Expects the same minibeasts everywhere, with no idea of habitat preference.
responseLevels.full: Predicts by matching creature to conditions and explains the preference, transferring the reasoning to a new micro-habitat such as a pond or soil.
responseLevels.partial: Predicts different creatures in the two places but can't link the difference to conditions (damp/dark versus sunny).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You lift up a damp log in the shade, and you also look on a sunny leaf. Would you expect to find the SAME minibeasts in both places, or different ones? Why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks any minibeast lives anywhere says 'the same.' A child who grasps habitat preference predicts different creatures and ties it to the conditions.
