1-PS4-4 is engineering-integrated and cross-links to the K–2 engineering-design PEs: K-2-ETS1-1 (define a simple problem), K-2-ETS1-2 (develop a simple sketch/drawing/physical model), K-2-ETS1-3 (analyse data from tests of two objects to compare strengths and weaknesses). The design process is iterative (define → design/build → test → improve), not linear. DCI PS4.C: people use a variety of devices to communicate over long distances.
learnerActions: Name the problem out loud: 'I need to send a message to a friend who is across the room and can't hear me speak.'
Sketch or describe a plan for a device before building it — choose light (a torch signaller), or sound (a cup-and-string telephone or a drum beat pattern).
Build the device from real tools and materials.
Agree a simple shared code with your partner BEFORE sending, e.g. one flash = 'yes', two flashes = 'no', or a drumbeat pattern for an agreed word.
Send the message and check with your partner whether they received the intended meaning correctly.

If it fails, work out WHY before changing something: if the meaning was wrong, fix or clarify the agreed code; if the signal could not be seen or heard at all (e.g. a slack string, or a flash too dim across a wide, bright room), pull the string taut, make the flash brighter, or shorten the gap.
Measure how far apart you can stand and still have the message arrive correctly.
Build or test a second device and compare the two: which carries the message further, and what are the strengths and weaknesses of each?
activities.intendedInsight: A device communicates only when an agreed code AND a well-built device work together to carry a real message over the distance — communication is sending information, not just producing light or noise.

activities.title: Define and brainstorm the problem with an inventor
feedback: If the child proposes only 'make a light' or 'make a noise', push on meaning: 'How will your friend know what it means?'
Reward ideas that name both a device AND an agreed code.

Treat this as a planning primer — the ideas here should be built and tested for real afterwards; the dialogue can prompt the define/brainstorm phase but does not itself produce a built, tested device.
activities.rationale: A spoken, in-role dialogue genuinely suits the DEFINE and BRAINSTORM phases at the front of the design process, prompting children to articulate the problem and the idea of a code before building. It is a design-thinking primer and should hand off to a physical build rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: 1-PS4-4 is engineering-integrated and cross-links to the K–2 engineering-design PEs: K-2-ETS1-1 (define a simple problem), K-2-ETS1-2 (develop a simple sketch/drawing/physical model), K-2-ETS1-3 (analyse data from tests of two objects to compare strengths and weaknesses). The design process is iterative (define → design/build → test → improve), not linear. DCI PS4.C: people use a variety of devices to communicate over long distances.
learnerActions: Take on a real scenario: an inventor needs to signal a ship at sea, or send a message to a friend across a valley.
Answer the inventor's questions: What problem are we solving? Who needs to receive the message, and why can't we just walk over or shout?
Brainstorm ways light or sound could carry the message — flashes, drumbeats, a string line between two cups.
Answer the pushback: 'How will they know what your flash MEANS?' — propose a code.
Hand off your best idea to the building stage and actually make it.
activities.intendedInsight: Good design starts by clearly defining the problem and the audience, and by planning how the signal will carry a meaning — not just how to make a signal.

activities.title: Explore real communication devices and their codes
feedback: Prompt children to name the code each device uses, not just what it looks like.
Connect each example back to the child's own build: 'Which of these gives you an idea for sending your message?'
Use this as idea-priming background; it shows examples but has no build-and-test loop, so it supports rather than replaces the hands-on making task.
activities.rationale: Seeing real communication technologies supports the background idea that people use devices to send information over distance (DCI PS4.C) and sparks design ideas. It has no build-and-test loop, so it supports but does not replace the hands-on design task.
sourceClaims: 1-PS4-4 is engineering-integrated and cross-links to the K–2 engineering-design PEs: K-2-ETS1-1 (define a simple problem), K-2-ETS1-2 (develop a simple sketch/drawing/physical model), K-2-ETS1-3 (analyse data from tests of two objects to compare strengths and weaknesses). The design process is iterative (define → design/build → test → improve), not linear. DCI PS4.C: people use a variety of devices to communicate over long distances.
learnerActions: Look at real communication devices one at a time: cup-and-string telephone, lighthouse, drum, semaphore flags, bell.
For each, work out how it sends a signal far away and what 'code' it uses — flashes, beats, flag positions, rings.
Play a 'what message is this sending?' guessing game for a given signal.
Use the examples to spark ideas for your own device and code.
activities.intendedInsight: People across history use many different devices to send information over distance, and each relies on an agreed code — giving ideas for your own design.

activities.title: Quick check on design steps and signal types
feedback: Confirm that a string telephone works with a TAUT string; a slack string does not carry the vibration.
If the design steps are ordered wrong, re-run the sequence pointing back to the last build the child actually did, and note that after 'improve' you often loop back to test again.

Treat this as a light knowledge check: it can confirm recognition of the step order and light-vs-sound sorting, but it does not elicit the independent construction of a working device, so it supplements rather than replaces building and testing.
activities.rationale: A short ordering/sorting check can confirm adjacent knowledge (step order, light-vs-sound, taut-string fact), but it assesses recognition and cannot produce the working device the standard requires, so it supplements rather than carries the design-build task.
sourceClaims: NGSS 1-PS4-4: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4, K-PS3-2]. Clarification examples: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4]', a pattern of drum beats. Assessment boundary: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-4].
learnerActions: Put the design steps in order: define → plan → build → test → improve.
Sort devices into 'uses light' versus 'uses sound'.
Answer: 'What makes a string telephone work — a taut string or a slack string?' (Correct answer: taut.)
activities.intendedInsight: The design process has a usual working order and is iterative (you loop back to improve), and different devices rely on light or on sound to carry a signal.

constraints: The deepest version of this learning is an actual physical build with real tools and materials, tested over a real distance — hands-on making, the taut-string fix, and iterative redesign are central to the standard's verb 'design and build'.
Keep focus on whether the signal and its meaning get across; do not require children to explain the underlying physics of why light or sound carries the signal (deferred to later years).
Agreeing a shared code in advance is essential: without it, producing light or noise transmits no information and the task is not complete.
Normalise redesign — the first attempt is expected to need improvement; do not treat design as one-shot.

Judge success by whether the receiver decodes the intended message correctly over the distance, not by how bright or loud the signal is. Note that a genuinely too-dim or too-distant signal can still be a legitimate thing to improve; the point is that brightness/loudness alone is not the measure of successful communication.

A screen-based signal activity can rehearse the define-design-build-test-improve loop and the encode-a-message-over-distance idea, but it is a rehearsal of the design thinking, not the physical build the standard calls for; use it as a fallback or supplement, not a replacement.
Spoken brainstorming and device-example exploration support only the define/brainstorm and idea-priming phases and must hand off to a real build.
Recognition checks (ordering steps, sorting light vs sound) assess adjacent knowledge and do not elicit independent construction of a working device.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three source claims were marked unverified in the original row (the K–2 engineering-design cross-links and the England DfE curriculum placement); treat their specifics as unconfirmed.

The original material in places implied a screen/2D model was the 'best available' vehicle only because a true physical maker option was absent (a noted catalog gap); this rewrite restores the physical build as the primary activity and treats on-screen versions as fallbacks.

Corrected a potential learner error carried from the original: 'louder/brighter' is NOT a general fix for a misunderstood message — when meaning fails to arrive, the fix is usually the agreed code or clarity; however, a genuinely too-dim or too-distant signal can legitimately be improved by brightness or a shorter gap. The actions, feedback and constraint now distinguish these cases in learner-facing text, not only here.

Claims that a static image 'cannot teach' the design loop, or that 3D 'adds nothing', were softened to scoped statements about what each medium does and does not rehearse; no comparative efficacy is asserted beyond the source claims.

The NGSS 1-PS4-4 build-requirement claim is attached to the recognition-check rationale because it establishes the build the check cannot satisfy; whether this counts as direct support is borderline and noted in the preservation audit.

probeDeeper: How did your friend know what your flashes MEANT — what did you agree before you started?
It didn't work the first time — what did you change, and why did that help?
Would shouting or flashing brighter have fixed it, or was it something about the code?
assess.correctAnswer: The child designs a device/method AND agrees a shared CODE with the partner (e.g. one flash = yes, two = no; or taps for letters), keeps a cup-string phone TAUT, sends the message, checks whether the partner decodes it correctly, and — if it fails — diagnoses why and changes something before retrying. Success = the friend correctly receives the intended message.

errorPatterns.pattern: Communication = just making a signal: flashes the torch or makes a noise with no agreed meaning
errorPatterns.nextMove: Information transfer needs a shared code agreed in advance; judge success by whether the message arrives, not by whether a light or sound was produced.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sends signals without first agreeing what they mean; the partner can't decode the message

errorPatterns.pattern: One-shot design: treats the first attempt as finished, with no testing or improving
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the design cycle — test, find the fault, change one thing, retry; design is iterative, not one-shot. Don't reteach light/sound, just prompt the cycle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Builds once and stops; doesn't test or iterate even when it fails

errorPatterns.pattern: Slack string / brighter-is-better: leaves the string slack, or 'fixes' a failed message by just being louder or brighter
errorPatterns.nextMove: A cup-string phone needs a TAUT string to carry the vibrations; if the message comes through wrong, it's the CODE or clarity to fix, not the loudness.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expects a slack string to carry the message, or responds to a decoding failure by increasing volume/brightness rather than fixing the code

responseLevels.gap: Produces light/sound with no agreed code, or stops after one attempt; the message doesn't arrive and isn't diagnosed.
responseLevels.full: Designs a method with an agreed code, keeps the device working (taut string / clear signal), tests whether the partner decodes the intended message, and iterates on failure by changing something specific — explaining how the light or sound carried the information.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees a basic code and sends a message, but doesn't check whether it arrived correctly, or doesn't improve the design when it fails.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Your job: send a short secret message to a friend across the room without speaking or walking over. Using a torch (or a cup-and-string phone), design a way to do it, agree with your friend how it works, then send the message and see if they get it right. If it doesn't work, change something and try again.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This is watched, not asked about. A child who grasps communication sets up an AGREED code and tests whether the message actually ARRIVES (is decoded correctly), then iterates on failure. A child who doesn't just makes light or noise with no shared code, calls it done after one try, or thinks brighter/louder is the fix. The give-away is whether they check that the friend understood.

pedagogy.summary: These are word problems that apply like-denominator addition and subtraction of fractions and mixed numbers in context — juice poured from a jug (separate, subtract), ribbon lengths joined (combine, add). The mathematics is already secured; the new demand is READING the situation to decide join versus separate, modelling it, computing, and interpreting the answer back in context (including regrouping a fraction sum that crosses a whole, e.g. 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 4). Teach by drawing the story on a bar or number line before writing symbols, holding the denominator as a fixed unit, and estimating with whole numbers to sanity-check.
bestPractices: Model the story on a bar/number line before writing the equation — draw the jug emptying or the ribbons joining
Decide join (+) vs separate (−) from the situation, and say which quantity is being removed or combined
Hold the denominator as a fixed unit (eighths stay eighths) to block add-across
Estimate with whole numbers first, then check the exact answer against it
Interpret the result in context and regroup a crossing sum (8/8 → 1 whole)
keyRepresentations: Bar model of the jug (part poured out shaded) or the ribbons laid end to end
Number line for combining/removing lengths
Story ↔ equation ↔ picture triple
Regroup of a fraction sum crossing a whole (8/8 = 1)
commonMisconceptions: Adds across denominators when combining (2 3/8 + 1 5/8 → 3 8/16)
Chooses the wrong operation — adds when the story separates, or vice versa
Leaves a crossing sum unregrouped (3 8/8 rather than 4)
Misreads which quantity is removed or kept in the context

learn.summary: Learners apply like-denominator addition and subtraction of fractions and mixed numbers to word problems (juice poured from a jug = separate/subtract; ribbons joined end to end = combine/add). The computation is already secured; the new demand is READING the situation to choose join versus separate, drawing a matching model, computing with the denominator held as a fixed unit, regrouping a fraction sum that crosses a whole (e.g. 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 4), and interpreting the result back in context. Core approach: draw the story on a bar or number line before writing symbols, keep eighths as eighths to block adding across, and estimate with whole numbers to sanity-check.

activities.title: Model the story before you compute
feedback: If a learner adds across (2 3/8 + 1 5/8 → 3 8/16), re-anchor eighths as a fixed unit on the bar: three eighths and five eighths is eight eighths. The denominator counts the size of the pieces and does not change when you combine them.

If a learner picks the wrong operation (answers 5/4 for the jug, or subtracts the ribbons), draw the action first — juice leaving the jug, or ribbons laid together — and name 'take away' or 'combine' before writing the symbol.
If a learner reports 3 8/8 for the ribbons, prompt 'how much is 8/8? then add it to the whole part' — the addition was correct and only needs tidying into 4.
Estimate first: the ribbons are about 2 + 2 = 4 inches, so a 3-something answer is a warning sign.
activities.rationale: Adding across denominators is the central documented error in fraction addition/subtraction, and visual models that hold the unit constant with 'which is bigger / more or fewer than you started' reasoning support correct joining and separating. Drawing the story before symbolising, and estimating with whole numbers, targets operation-choice and the crossing-sum regroup directly.
sourceClaims: The add-across misconception is the central documented error in fraction addition/subtraction; visual fraction models that hold the unit constant and 'which is bigger' reasoning support correct joining/separating
Same-denominator addition is answered correctly by the large majority of pupils, but a minority add both numerator and denominator; concrete materials and estimation aid remediation
Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and with like denominators, using visual fraction models and equations
learnerActions: Read: 'A jug holds 3/4 of a litre of juice; 2/4 of a litre is poured out — how much is left?' Draw a bar showing 3/4, shade the 2/4 poured away, and read the remaining 1/4 off your picture.
Read: 'Two ribbons are 2 3/8 inches and 1 5/8 inches long — what is their total length?' Draw the two ribbons laid end to end on a bar marked in eighths.
Before writing any symbols, say aloud whether the story is a 'take away' or a 'combine', and name which quantity is removed or joined.
Write the matching equation, keeping the denominator fixed (quarters stay quarters, eighths stay eighths): 3/4 − 2/4 = 1/4; 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 3 + 8/8 = 4.
When the fraction parts reach 8/8, regroup that whole into the whole-number count so the total reads 4 inches, not 3 8/8.
activities.intendedInsight: The story tells you the operation; a picture drawn first makes join-versus-separate visible, and holding the denominator as a fixed unit means combining 3/8 and 5/8 gives 8/8 = one whole, never 8/16.

activities.title: Act out pouring and joining with a locked-unit model
feedback: If the learner expects 3-something for the ribbons, point to the moment 8/8 fuses into a whole: 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 4. 3 8/16 is wrong, while 3 8/8 has the right value but should be regrouped as 4.
If the learner is unsure which operation a story needs, use the 'more or fewer than you started?' check: pouring out leaves fewer, joining makes more.
activities.rationale: Choosing the operation and modelling the story is the target skill, and an interactive surface where units stay locked lets a learner act out pouring/joining and see the equation update. Note: an interactive model is proposed as one concrete way to make the mechanism visible; a drawn bar or number line can achieve the same modelling without the live surface, so the medium is not uniquely required.
sourceClaims: The add-across misconception is the central documented error in fraction addition/subtraction; visual fraction models that hold the unit constant and 'which is bigger' reasoning support correct joining/separating
Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and with like denominators, using visual fraction models and equations
learnerActions: In a story workspace, pick the jug context and pour 2/4 out of a 3/4-litre jug; watch the removed part grey out, leaving 1/4, and read 'take away' straight off the picture.
Switch to the ribbon context and drag two ribbons (marked in eighths) end to end; watch the eighths auto-count as they join.
Notice that when 3/8 and 5/8 meet at 8/8 the eighths fuse into one whole inch and the total snaps to 4 inches.
Read the matching ± equation that the picture produces, and use a 'more or fewer than you started with?' check to confirm the direction of the operation.
activities.intendedInsight: Combining the fraction parts can make a whole appear in the whole-number count (8/8 → 1 whole), and when the pieces are kept as fixed eighths, adding across into sixteenths is not even a possible move.

activities.title: Study then classify the two story structures
feedback: If a story is misclassified, re-read for the action and what is unknown: words like 'poured out', 'left', 'remains' often go with separating and 'total', 'altogether', 'joined' often go with combining, but check the situation rather than relying on the word (e.g. '1/4 L was left after 2/4 L was poured out; how much was there at first?' needs addition).
If a matched equation changes the denominator (e.g. 8/16), flag it: the piece size stays the same when like fractions are combined.

Sorting and matching check whether the operation choice is secure, but do not by themselves elicit independent drawing of a new story; follow with drawing or modelling a fresh story so the learner also builds the reading, not only recognises it.
activities.rationale: Operation-choice and the add-across/unregrouped errors are cleanly surfaced by distractors built from those exact mistakes. Recognition and sorting tasks can diagnose the choice efficiently, but they do not by themselves elicit independent reading-and-modelling of a new story, so pair them with construction.
sourceClaims: Same-denominator addition is answered correctly by the large majority of pupils, but a minority add both numerator and denominator; concrete materials and estimation aid remediation
Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and with like denominators, using visual fraction models and equations
learnerActions: Study a worked pour-out (jug: 3/4 − 2/4 = 1/4) and a worked join (ribbons: 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 4), revealing the shaded/combined model and then the answer for each.
Answer 'what does 8/8 make?' for the ribbon total and explain where that whole goes in the answer.
Sort a set of new stories into 'combine' versus 'take away', then match each story to the ± equation that solves it.
Fill in a missing answer that requires a regroup step, and explain the regroup in words.
activities.intendedInsight: Pour-out stories separate (subtract) and joining stories combine (add); naming the structure first makes the correct operation and any crossing-sum regroup predictable.

activities.title: Talk through pour and join stories with a context character
feedback: If the learner names the wrong operation, slow down on the action word and run the 'more or fewer?' check before touching any number.
When the talk reaches 8/8, ask the learner to draw or point to where that whole joins the whole-number count (giving 4), since the conversation alone does not show the regroup happening.
activities.rationale: An in-role character can pose and vary stories and probe direction, which is proposed as one way to rehearse the reading of join versus separate. No cited source establishes the efficacy of the conversational medium itself; the source support attaches to the paired drawn bar/number line and estimation the activity pairs with. Its observable limit is that a conversation does not supply a visual surface where fraction parts combine, so it is paired with a drawn model; this is not evidence that dialogue is required or superior.
sourceClaims: Same-denominator addition is answered correctly by the large majority of pupils, but a minority add both numerator and denominator; concrete materials and estimation aid remediation
Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and with like denominators, using visual fraction models and equations
learnerActions: An in-role kitchen/craft character poses a pour-out story and a join story and varies the numbers; before any calculation, restate whether each story is 'take away' or 'combine' and name which quantity is removed or joined.
Answer the character's 'more or fewer than you started?' probe for each story to confirm the operation direction.

Explain your reasoning aloud; where the fraction parts need to be seen combining (e.g. 3/8 + 5/8 reaching 8/8), draw a bar or number line alongside the talk and point to where the whole joins the whole-number count (→ 4).
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through a story and naming its structure can rehearse operation-choice and direction, but a spoken exchange does not itself display the fraction parts fusing, so it is paired with a drawn model when the crossing-sum regroup needs to be seen.

constraints: All fractions in a problem must refer to the same whole and share a like denominator; these tasks do not cover unlike-denominator addition.
Hold the denominator as a fixed unit: combining 3/8 and 5/8 gives 8/8 = 1 whole, never 8/16. The denominator names the piece size and does not change when like fractions are joined.
Regroup any crossing sum: 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 = 3 + 8/8 = 4; 3 8/8 has the same value but has not been regrouped, so write the final answer as 4.

Sorting, matching and multiple-choice tasks assess operation-choice but do not elicit independent drawing/modelling of a new story; use construction tasks (draw the model, write and solve the equation) to build that skill.
A tap-to-reveal worked pair illustrates the two structures but does not let a learner model a fresh story — treat it as a scaffold, then move to learner-constructed models.

An interactive locked-unit model, a hand-drawn bar/number line, and an in-role conversation can each support the reading/modelling in different ways; none is uniquely necessary, so do not require a particular medium.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The Common Core 4.NF.3d source is marked verified:false in the row; treat its citation as a standards/topic reference, not as evidence of effectiveness.

No cited source establishes comparative efficacy between the interactive, drawn, conversational, or static media, nor that any medium is required or superior; such claims were softened to scoped, observable scaffold limits. The original row's statements that a 3D/interactive-image format 'cannot let the child model a new story', that 3D 'adds nothing', and that a conversation 'wants a visual surface' were not retained as universal laws.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3/4 − 2/4 = 1/4 (correct); 2 3/8 + 1 5/8: fraction parts 3/8 + 5/8 = 8/8 = 1, plus 2 + 1 = 3, total = 4 (correct). The add-across distractor 3 8/16 and the unregrouped form 3 8/8 are presented only as error patterns to diagnose, never as correct answers.

probeDeeper: In (b), the eighths added to exactly 8/8 — what does that make?
In (a), which part of the jug is gone and which is left — show me on your picture.
Estimate (b) first — about how many inches, before you compute exactly?
If the jug had 3/4 and you ADDED 2/4 instead of pouring it out, what would the answer be, and how is that different?

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across when combining: 2 3/8 + 1 5/8 → 3 8/16 (adds numerators and denominators of the fraction parts)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor eighths as a fixed unit on a locked bar — three eighths and five eighths is eight eighths — before regrouping to a whole
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The fraction part of the total has a changed denominator (8/16); whole numbers may be added correctly

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong operation: adds when the story says pour out (a), or subtracts when it says combine (b) — the situation is not read as join vs separate
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the action first — juice leaving the jug, or ribbons laid together — and name 'take away' or 'combine' before writing the operation
errorPatterns.revealedBy: (a) answered 5/4 (added), or (b) answered by subtracting; the picture, if drawn, does not match the words

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the crossing sum unregrouped: reports 3 8/8 for (b) rather than 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — 'how much is 8/8? then add it to the whole part' — the child added correctly and only needs to tidy
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 3 8/8 (a whole worth of eighths left in the fraction slot); the addition is otherwise correct

responseLevels.gap: Adds across, or picks the wrong operation, and cannot draw a matching model.
responseLevels.full: Reads join vs separate correctly, models it, computes with the denominator held fixed, regroups the crossing sum (to 4 inches), estimates, and transfers to a new like-denominator context.
responseLevels.partial: Chooses the right operation and computes, but leaves a crossing sum unregrouped (3 8/8) or cannot produce a picture that matches the story.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these, showing your working and a picture for each: (a) A jug holds 3/4 of a litre of juice; 2/4 of a litre is poured out — how much is left? (b) Two pieces of ribbon are 2 3/8 inches and 1 5/8 inches long — what is their total length?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The pair separates operation-choice from computation: (a) is a take-away (a child who adds gives 5/4), (b) is a combine whose fraction parts land on exactly 8/8, so a child who does not regroup reports 3 8/8 and one who adds across reports 3 8/16. Watching the working and the picture shows whether the story was read correctly and whether the crossing sum was regrouped — both invisible in a bare number.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Photosynthesis

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Nutrition & digestion / Photosynthesis):** the statutory programme requires pupils learn "photosynthesis as the key process for food production and therefore biomass for life", the "reactants in, and products of, photosynthesis, and a word summary for photosynthesis", the "dependence of almost all life on Earth on the ability of photosynthetic organisms, such as plants and algae, to use sunlight in photosynthesis to build organic molecules that are an essential energy store and to maintain levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere", and the "adaptations of leaves for photosynthesis".

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS1-6):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-1, MS-LS1-5, MS-LS1-6, MS-LS2-3]." The clarification statement emphasises tracing matter and energy; the assessment boundary excludes the biochemical mechanism of the sub-steps. Complemented by MS-LS1-7 (matter reorganised through chemical reactions) for the food/glucose link.

- **Operational details:** Build on the KS2 root that plants need light, water, air and nutrients (prerequisite mt_lutxvMlkwS) and the cell-biology prerequisite that chloroplasts are unique to plant cells (mt_fhqBH9scsU). Establish the word equation carbon dioxide + water → (light/chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen, sourcing each input to its origin: CO₂ from the air via stomata, water and minerals from the soil via roots, light captured by chlorophyll. Distinguish the raw materials (reactants) from the products, and stress that glucose is the plant's food/energy store — the source of biomass — not something absorbed ready-made. Foreshadow the dependent Carbon Cycle (mt_Be1A88GUpu): photosynthesis is the biological route by which CO₂ leaves the atmosphere.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). A learner who can write and explain the word equation, correctly source each reactant (air vs soil vs light), name the products, and articulate why nearly all life depends on photosynthesis for both food and atmospheric oxygen has met the bar. Balanced chemical/symbol equations and limiting-factor rate graphs are Tier C (GCSE) extensions, not required here.
bestPractices: Anchor to the word equation but always source the inputs: use a labelled plant with arrows showing CO₂ entering leaves, water/minerals rising from roots, and light striking chlorophyll — this directly targets the evidence statement 'distinguishes what plants get from air, soil and light'.

Confront the dominant 'plants get food from the soil' misconception head-on with the classic evidence: van Helmont's willow experiment (mass gained came from air and water, not soil) makes the counter-intuitive idea that plants build themselves largely from an invisible gas concrete and memorable.
Teach photosynthesis and respiration as a paired opposition once the equation is secure — plants do both — to pre-empt the misconception that plants only photosynthesise and animals only respire.

Use a real observable phenomenon (pondweed/Elodea bubbling oxygen under a lamp, or a destarched leaf turning blue-black with iodine only where light reached) so the abstract equation is grounded in something the child sees.

Emphasise energy transfer language: light energy is captured by chlorophyll and stored in glucose. Avoid saying plants 'make energy' — they transform and store it, mirroring the NGSS flow-of-energy framing.
keyRepresentations: The word equation laid out as a process (carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light and chlorophyll over the arrow) rather than a static line
A cross-section leaf diagram showing stomata (gas in/out), chloroplasts, and veins bringing water — the 'factory' model of the leaf
A whole-plant sourcing diagram: air (CO₂) to leaves, soil (water + minerals) to roots, sunlight to the canopy
An input–output 'balance' visual pairing photosynthesis with respiration (the reverse arrows) to show the gas exchange coupling
A rate response: brighter light / more CO₂ → faster bubbling, previewing limiting factors without quantifying them
commonMisconceptions: Believing plants get their food from the soil, or that soil minerals ARE the plant's food — minerals are needed in tiny amounts for making proteins/chlorophyll; the bulk food (glucose) is built from CO₂ and water.
Thinking plants photosynthesise instead of respiring, or that they only respire at night — plants respire continuously; photosynthesis is additional and light-dependent.
Assuming chlorophyll is a reactant that gets used up, rather than a catalyst-like pigment that captures light and is not consumed.
Confusing which gas is taken in and which is given out (mixing up the CO₂-in / O₂-out of photosynthesis with the reverse in respiration).
Thinking glucose is stored and used as glucose only — not realising it is converted to starch for storage and used to build the plant's biomass (cellulose, proteins).

learn.summary: Photosynthesis for 11–12 year-olds: establish the word equation (carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, driven by light energy captured by chlorophyll), source each input to its origin (CO₂ from air via stomata, water and minerals from soil via roots, light to the canopy), distinguish reactants from products, and explain why nearly all life depends on photosynthesis for food/biomass and atmospheric oxygen. Core misconception to confront: that plants get their food/mass from the soil. Also establish that plants both photosynthesise and respire. The target teaching objective is an input→output process where learners vary each raw material and observe the plant's response; labelling/sorting and reading-based experiment work are complementary scaffolds and assessments.

activities.title: Feed the plant: vary each input and watch the response
feedback: If a learner expects food to keep being made with the light off: highlight that photosynthetic oxygen release stops (in a real setup, bubbling may tail off over a short time) and no new glucose is made — light energy is required to drive the reaction, so no light means no food however much water and CO₂ are present.

If a learner treats light as an ingredient built into glucose: clarify that light is the energy source captured by chlorophyll, not a material that becomes part of the sugar; the materials built into glucose are carbon dioxide and water.
If a learner says the plant stops using oxygen in the dark: point out the plant still uses oxygen — it respires continuously; photosynthesis is the additional, light-dependent process.

If a learner raises a single input and expects the rate to climb without limit: note that once one input is plentiful, another input or condition becomes the limiting factor and the rate levels off (qualitatively, without quantifying). Separately, if any single necessary input is at zero the process stalls entirely — all are needed together.
activities.rationale: Photosynthesis is a process with inputs, a rate and products; letting learners manipulate each supply and see the plant respond is intended to make the sourcing (air vs soil vs light) and the input→output dependence more concrete than memorising, and to target the evidence statement about distinguishing what a plant gets from air, soil and light. A live/demonstrated response can show rate changes and the effect of removing an input, which a static diagram cannot; a static diagram remains a useful support for naming and sourcing. This interaction is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 statutory programme requires the reactants and products of photosynthesis, a word summary, the dependence of almost all life on photosynthetic organisms, and adaptations of leaves for photosynthesis.
learnerActions: Work with a plant model (physical bench setup, a simulation, or a teacher-run demonstration) that has three controllable supplies: a light source (brightness), air/CO₂, and water from the soil.

Starting with all three supplies on, raise each one in turn and observe and record what happens to the rate of oxygen bubbling (and, in a simulation, the displayed amount of glucose being built; glucose cannot be watched directly on a real bench).
Set water and CO₂ to maximum, then switch the light OFF. Predict first, then observe: does the plant keep making food? Write down what this tells you about which input drives the process.

In the simulation or model, switch each remaining input to zero one at a time and record whether photosynthesis stalls, concluding which inputs are necessary (in a real plant, cutting off water or CO₂ slows photosynthesis gradually rather than switching it off instantly).
Leave the plant in the dark and reveal/consider the plant's own use of oxygen; state in a sentence why this shows plants also respire, not only photosynthesise.
activities.intendedInsight: Light energy is the driver of photosynthesis and each of CO₂, water and light is necessary; glucose is built by the plant from air and water, and plants respire (use oxygen) as well as photosynthesise.

activities.title: van Helmont's willow: predict where the mass comes from
feedback: If a learner predicts the soil loses roughly the mass the tree gained: this reveals the 'soil feeds the plant' misconception — use the result (soil barely changed) to show the mass cannot come from soil, and establish that the carbon comes from CO₂ in the air.

If a learner says the mass comes mostly from water through the roots: distinguish what roots supply (water and minerals) from where the carbon and energy come from (air and light); the carbon atoms of glucose and wood come from atmospheric CO₂.
If a learner cannot say why a plant in darkness stops growing: connect to the earlier activity — without light energy there is no photosynthesis, so no new glucose is built.

If a learner is unsure about the sealed greenhouse: guide them that during the day photosynthesis draws CO₂ out of the air, so the measured CO₂ would be expected to fall in good light, as long as photosynthesis is faster than the CO₂ released by respiration of the plants and other organisms.

Target full explanation: light energy captured by chlorophyll combines CO₂ (from air) with water (from soil) to make glucose (carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen); the tree's dry mass is built mostly from carbon dioxide taken from the air, together with water.
activities.rationale: This is the classic discriminator for the 'food from soil' misconception: it is hard to answer 'the air' for the wrong reason, so the predicted reason is diagnostic of whether the learner holds the photosynthesis idea. Confronting the dominant misconception with memorable evidence is intended to help make the counter-intuitive idea (plants build themselves largely from an invisible gas) concrete. Note the van Helmont historical specifics are the widely-taught account and were not re-verified here.
sourceClaims: Van Helmont's willow-tree experiment showed a plant's mass increase came from water and air rather than the soil, evidencing that plants build food from CO2 and water.
learnerActions: Read/consider the classic experiment: a small willow is planted in a weighed pot of soil and watered for about five years until it gains many kilograms, while the soil loses only a tiny fraction of that (in the usual account, about 2 ounces, roughly 57 g).
Before the result is revealed, predict how much soil mass will be lost and, importantly, explain WHY.
Compare your predicted reason with the result: the soil barely changed, so the tree's large mass gain cannot have come mainly from the soil.

State in your own words where nearly all the extra mass (the wood) actually comes from. Explain that the experiment shows it did not come mainly from the soil (van Helmont himself concluded it came from water), and that later evidence showed the carbon comes from carbon dioxide in the air.
Answer follow-up probes: What happens to a well-watered plant kept in total darkness and why? Which part of the carbon dioxide ends up in the wood? Does a plant need oxygen, and when?
Extend to a sealed sunny greenhouse: predict what would happen to the measured CO₂ inside during the day, and explain why.
activities.intendedInsight: Almost all of a plant's extra mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air combined with water, using light energy; soil supplies water and small amounts of minerals, not the bulk of the mass.

activities.title: Name and source the parts: leaf anatomy and input origins
feedback: If a learner puts glucose or oxygen among the reactants: remind them these are products — what the plant makes — while CO₂ and water are the raw materials taken in.
If a learner sources CO₂ to the soil or water to the air: re-link to the leaf/root diagram — CO₂ enters leaves through stomata from the air, water rises from the soil through the roots.
If a learner says minerals are the plant's food: clarify minerals are needed in tiny amounts (for making proteins/chlorophyll); the bulk food, glucose, is built from CO₂ and water.
activities.rationale: Naming and sourcing are labelling and categorisation tasks that a tap-to-reveal illustration or paper diagram handles cleanly and that can give evidence of the sourcing statements. This supports recall and vocabulary but is a scaffold: being static, it cannot show rate or the effect of removing an input, and a sort can check classification but does not by itself elicit an explanation — so pair it with the manipulation activity to build causal intuition.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 statutory programme requires the reactants and products of photosynthesis, a word summary, the dependence of almost all life on photosynthetic organisms, and adaptations of leaves for photosynthesis.
learnerActions: On a whole-plant diagram, draw or place arrows showing CO₂ entering leaves, water and minerals rising from roots, and light striking the leaf canopy.
Label a leaf cross-section with stomata (gas in/out), chloroplasts (where light is captured), and veins (bringing water).

Sort a set of items — {carbon dioxide, water, minerals, glucose, oxygen} — into reactants of photosynthesis, products of photosynthesis, or neither (minerals are needed by the plant but are not reactants in the photosynthesis word equation). Then sort only the materials the plant takes in (carbon dioxide, water, minerals) into from-air vs from-soil, noting that glucose and oxygen are made by the plant.

Explain, in a lift-the-flap or written response, the myth 'the plant eats the soil': state that the plant builds its food from carbon dioxide from the air and water, using light energy, and that the soil supplies water and small amounts of minerals, not the bulk of the food.
activities.intendedInsight: The leaf is the 'factory' where carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil are turned into glucose and oxygen using light energy captured by chlorophyll; reactants and products can be named and correctly attributed to their origin.

activities.title: Pairing photosynthesis with respiration
feedback: If a learner says plants only respire at night: correct that plants respire continuously; in good light, photosynthesis also occurs and typically exceeds respiration (so the plant is a net oxygen producer while well lit).

If a learner says plants don't respire at all ('photosynthesis is plant breathing'): establish that plants respire like all organisms — photosynthesis is an additional, separate, light-dependent process.
If a learner says plants 'make energy': reframe as transforming and storing energy — light energy is captured and stored in glucose, mirroring energy-flow language.
activities.rationale: Teaching the pair once the equation is secure pre-empts the common misconception that plants only photosynthesise and animals only respire, and supports the NGSS framing of matter cycling and energy flow. Emphasising 'capture and store' rather than 'make' energy aligns language with the flow-of-energy idea.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-LS1-6 requires constructing [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS1-6, MS-LS2-3].
learnerActions: After the word equation is secure, write photosynthesis and respiration as paired processes, noting respiration broadly reverses the gas exchange (uses oxygen, releases carbon dioxide).
Explain when each happens: photosynthesis only in light; respiration continuously, day and night.
Answer: does a plant respire at night? Does it respire during the day? Justify your answer.

Connect to the wider picture: explain in a sentence why nearly all life on Earth depends on photosynthetic organisms for food/biomass and for maintaining atmospheric oxygen, foreshadowing the carbon cycle (photosynthesis is a route by which CO₂ leaves the atmosphere).
activities.intendedInsight: Plants both photosynthesise and respire; photosynthesis builds glucose and releases oxygen, respiration releases glucose's stored energy and uses oxygen, and together these underpin life's dependence on photosynthesis.

activities.title: Observe a real phenomenon: oxygen from pondweed and the starch test
feedback: If a learner expects equal bubbling regardless of light: point to the observation that brighter light generally gives faster bubbling, previewing that rate depends on conditions (without needing to quantify).
If a learner thinks the whole leaf should turn blue-black: connect back to the covered region — starch forms only where light reached, so only lit areas test positive.

If a learner concludes a fixed numeric result for any setup: note that observed rates and outcomes depend on the actual materials and conditions, so report what was measured under fair conditions rather than a guaranteed outcome.
activities.rationale: Grounding the equation in a phenomenon the learner can see (oxygen bubbling, the iodine starch test) connects the abstract process to real evidence and supports evidence-based explanation. Rate changes are shown qualitatively, previewing limiting factors without quantifying them, which is appropriate below GCSE.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-LS1-6 requires constructing [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS1-6, MS-LS2-3].
learnerActions: Observe pondweed (such as Elodea) under a lamp: count or compare the rate of gas bubbles (mostly oxygen) rising as the lamp is moved closer or further away, keeping the water temperature steady (e.g. use an LED lamp or a heat shield) so that light is the only factor changed.
Describe what happens to the bubbling as the light gets brighter, and relate it to the word equation (oxygen is a product).

Consider or observe a destarched leaf tested with iodine after partial covering: the leaf turns blue-black only where light reached, showing starch (made from glucose) formed only where photosynthesis occurred — which also shows glucose is stored as starch rather than kept only as glucose.
Write a short conclusion linking each observation to which input was being varied and what it shows.
activities.intendedInsight: The abstract equation is grounded in observable evidence: oxygen is released as a product and its rate responds to light, and the products of photosynthesis (stored as starch) appear only where light reached.

constraints: Target level (transitional/early-formal): learners should write and explain the word equation, correctly source each reactant (air vs soil vs light), name the products, and articulate why nearly all life depends on photosynthesis for food and oxygen. Balanced chemical/symbol equations and quantitative limiting-factor rate graphs are a later (GCSE) extension, not required here.
Builds on prerequisites: plants need light, water, air and nutrients, and chloroplasts are found in plant cells.
Light is the energy source captured by chlorophyll, not a material ingredient built into glucose — keep this distinction explicit in any activity listing the inputs.
Chlorophyll captures light and is not used up as a reactant; do not present it as consumed.
Use 'capture, transform and store energy' language, not 'plants make energy'.

Labelling/sorting diagrams and recall-style sorting are scaffolds and assessments: being static, they cannot show rate or the effect of removing an input, and a sort can check classification but does not by itself elicit independent construction of an explanation — pair them with manipulation and written/spoken explanation.

Rate and starch-test outcomes depend on the actual materials, setup and measured conditions; report observed results under fair conditions rather than asserting a guaranteed numeric or absolute outcome.

A 3D leaf-interior tour is at most supplementary for showing tissue layers and stomata; the core concept (inputs→products and rate) is not inherently spatial. A persona/interview framing is a niche engagement device and does not by itself demonstrate the manipulable input–output dependency that the live model shows.
Comparative claims about which medium teaches best are design judgements, not established by the cited sources; use proposed/may/intended wording for efficacy.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles or required content rather than proving any activity was tested.

The van Helmont source is marked unverified in the original row; treat the historical specifics (planted in a weighed pot, watered for years, soil losing only a few grams) as the widely-taught account rather than a precisely verified measurement.

Source claim about leaf adaptations is retained from the standards citation; the activities touch leaf anatomy but a fuller treatment of leaf adaptations for photosynthesis may be worth expanding to fully meet the DfE strand.

Original materials framed some medium comparisons strongly (e.g. a 2D model as 'ideal', dialogue as 'poor', 3D as adding little). These have been softened to scoped affordances/limits; comparative efficacy or necessity is not established by the source claims.
The claim that photosynthesis typically exceeds respiration in light is stated qualitatively in feedback; if precise net gas-exchange framing is needed, confirm wording with the teaching team.
Definite 'makes it concrete' phrasing in rationales has been softened to 'is intended to / can help', since the specific activity efficacy is untested.

assess.poeTask: Present van Helmont's experiment: a small willow planted in a weighed pot of soil, watered for years, grows into a large tree while the soil loses only a few grams. Before revealing the result, ask the child to predict how much soil mass will be lost and WHY. The predicted reason is diagnostic: a child expecting the soil to lose roughly the mass the tree gained holds the soil-food misconception; a child predicting the soil barely changes because the mass comes from air and water shows the photosynthesis idea.
probeDeeper: If a plant is kept well-watered in rich soil but in total darkness, what happens and why?
You said carbon dioxide from the air — what part of that gas actually ends up in the wood?
Does a plant need oxygen at all? If so, when, and what for?
What if we grew the tree in a sealed sunny greenhouse and measured the CO2 — what would happen to it during the day?
assess.correctAnswer: Almost all the extra mass comes from carbon dioxide taken from the AIR, combined with water, using light energy captured by chlorophyll to make glucose (carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen); the soil supplies water and small amounts of mineral nutrients, not the bulk of the mass.

errorPatterns.pattern: plants get their food and mass from the soil ('the soil feeds the plant / plants eat soil')
errorPatterns.nextMove: use van Helmont's result — the soil mass barely changed — to show the mass cannot come from soil; establish carbon comes from CO2 in the air
errorPatterns.distractor: It comes from the nutrients and food in the soil that the roots suck up
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reason names soil as the source of the tree's mass

errorPatterns.pattern: plants get their food/mass from water alone or from the roots
errorPatterns.nextMove: distinguish what roots supply (water and minerals) from where the carbon and energy come from (air and light)
errorPatterns.distractor: It comes mostly from all the water the tree drinks up through its roots
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names water or the roots as the food source, omitting CO2 and light

errorPatterns.pattern: photosynthesis is the plant's version of breathing; plants don't respire
errorPatterns.nextMove: establish plants BOTH photosynthesise and respire; photosynthesis makes glucose, respiration releases its energy
errorPatterns.revealedBy: surfaces on the probe — says plants only photosynthesise and never respire, or calls photosynthesis 'plant breathing'

errorPatterns.pattern: light is a raw material that gets used up and becomes part of the glucose
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify light is the ENERGY source captured by chlorophyll, not a material ingredient of glucose
errorPatterns.revealedBy: lists light alongside CO2 and water as a material built into the sugar

responseLevels.gap: Says the plant's mass or food comes from soil or water; cannot write the equation, or names light as a material ingredient.
responseLevels.full: Explains photosynthesis capturing light energy via chlorophyll to combine CO2 (air) and water (soil) into glucose, correctly attributes the tree's mass to atmospheric carbon, and separates the roles of air, soil and light — transferring to darkness or sealed-greenhouse cases.
responseLevels.partial: Writes carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen and can list raw materials and products, but treats them as separate facts — cannot say the bulk of the mass comes from air-borne CO2, confuses light (energy) with a raw material, or cannot separate the roles of air, soil and light.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A tree grows from a tiny seed into something that weighs many tonnes. Where does nearly all of that extra material — the wood, the mass — actually come from? Explain how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This is the classic van Helmont discriminator. A child holding 'plants eat soil / get food from soil' names soil as the source of the mass; a child with photosynthesis says the carbon comes from CO2 in the air. It is very hard to answer 'the air' for the wrong reason.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11; understand that the future of rainforests depends on BALANCING competing needs — economic development for local communities, indigenous peoples' rights to ancestral land, global biodiversity, and climate stability — with NO simple answer, requiring cooperation between governments, businesses, scientists, indigenous leaders and consumers.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (sustainability, economic activity, human/physical interaction) and citizenship (weighing viewpoints, informed debate); a synthesis capstone drawing on the whole domain.
• Standards — US: NGSS MS-ESS3-4 (human impact and resource trade-offs) and social-studies civic-reasoning; ties to arguing-from-evidence.
• Operational details — this is the domain's VALUES/synthesis node: the goal is not a right answer but disciplined reasoning about a genuine dilemma. Make the trade-offs REAL by voicing the stakeholders — a farmer who needs income, an indigenous leader defending ancestral land, a conservation scientist, a government official balancing development and debt, a business, a consumer — each with a legitimate stake. Teach that these interests genuinely CONFLICT (a soy farm feeds a family but clears forest) and that solutions must weigh, not erase, competing goods. Draw on prior nodes (deforestation drivers, conservation toolkit, climate, supply chains). Insist pupils steel-man each side before proposing a course, and that different groups each hold a lever.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (9): name three competing interests. Tier B (10): explain why there is no single simple solution. Tier C (11): propose how governments, businesses, consumers and scientists could EACH contribute, acknowledging a trade-off their proposal accepts.
bestPractices: Treat it as a values/synthesis capstone: the aim is disciplined reasoning about a genuine dilemma, not a single right answer.
Voice real stakeholders so trade-offs are felt as legitimate conflicts, not cartoon goodies vs baddies.
Require pupils to steel-man each side before proposing any course of action.
Draw explicitly on prior nodes (deforestation drivers, conservation toolkit, climate, supply chains) so the debate is evidence-based.
Show that each group (government, business, consumer, scientist, indigenous leader) holds a different lever — solutions are shared.
keyRepresentations: A stakeholder panel/map: each group with its interest and what it stands to lose.
A trade-off dashboard (economy, biodiversity, climate, indigenous rights) where no option wins on all axes.
A decision scenario grounded in a real region (e.g. an Amazon state weighing a road/soy expansion).
A 'who holds which lever' chart linking each actor to an action.
commonMisconceptions: 'Just ban all logging/farming and the problem is solved' — that ignores people who depend on the forest for a living.
'There's one correct answer if people weren't greedy' — the interests genuinely conflict even among well-meaning people.
'Only governments (or only consumers) can fix it' — every actor holds a partial lever; solutions are shared.
'Protecting the forest and helping local people are opposites' — some approaches (indigenous title, sustainable certification) serve both.
'Someone far away will sort it out' — consumer choices and global cooperation are part of the outcome.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: understand that the future of rainforests depends on balancing genuinely competing but legitimate interests — local livelihoods and economic development, indigenous peoples' rights to ancestral land, global biodiversity, and climate stability — with no single right answer. Pupils reason under real tension by holding several legitimate perspectives at once, steel-manning each before proposing a course, and recognising that governments, businesses, scientists, indigenous leaders and consumers each hold a different lever. The core objective is disciplined ethical/geographic reasoning about a real dilemma, not winning a debate or finding the 'correct' policy.

activities.title: In-role stakeholder interview: reason through the dilemma from the inside
feedback: If a pupil proposes a blanket ban, respond in the voice of a stakeholder it harms (the farmer's livelihood, the country's debt) and ask who would make the ban and how it would be enforced, whether by outsiders who cannot enforce laws in another country or by a national government policing huge, remote forests.

If a pupil frames it as greedy villains vs good heroes, introduce a sympathetic case — a family farming cleared land to eat, a poor country needing income — so they see competing needs, not just greed.

If a pupil assigns responsibility to only one group (e.g. 'the rainforest countries'), connect distant consumer demand, global climate benefits and regional rainfall benefits back to the choice, showing why a fair solution shares both responsibility and cost.
Praise answers that acknowledge a trade-off their own proposal accepts, rather than claiming a solution where everyone is completely happy.
activities.rationale: The learning here is irreducible, conflicting values held by real people, which an unscripted in-role dialogue is intended to surface by having each persona answer from a genuine stake, question the child back, and refuse to collapse into a tidy answer. Grounding each persona in prior learning (deforestation drivers, conservation options, climate, supply chains) keeps the debate evidence-based.
sourceClaims: Rainforest futures involve genuine trade-offs between economic development, indigenous land rights, biodiversity conservation and climate stability, requiring cooperation among governments, businesses, scientists, indigenous leaders and consumers
KS2 geography and citizenship require pupils to consider sustainability, weigh competing viewpoints and reason about human impact on environments
learnerActions: Interview, one after another, the people whose lives ride on a specific rainforest region: a smallholder farmer, an indigenous leader, a conservation scientist, a government minister weighing jobs and national debt, and a business buyer who sells cheap commodities linked to that region (e.g. soy or beef from the Amazon, or palm oil from Southeast Asia).

For each person, write down what they want and what they stand to lose — e.g. the farmer: 'This soy field is how my children eat'; the indigenous leader: 'The land is not for sale and has been defended for a thousand years'; the scientist naming species and carbon at stake; the minister weighing a REDD+ offer from abroad against development and debt.
Before proposing anything, steel-man each side: state the strongest, most sympathetic version of each person's position in your own words.

Propose a course of action, then face a push-back from at least one stakeholder — e.g. if you say 'just protect it all', answer the farmer who asks how their family eats, the point that one country cannot enforce its laws inside another country's borders, and the point that even a national ban is hard to enforce across huge, remote forests.
Name which lever each actor holds (government policy, business sourcing, consumer demand, scientific evidence, indigenous land title) and defend the specific trade-off your proposal accepts.
activities.intendedInsight: Every side has a genuine, legitimate claim; no solution leaves everyone whole; a workable future is a negotiated balance in which each actor gives something and each holds a partial lever — not a clever trick or a single ban.

activities.title: Govern the region: a trade-off decision simulation
feedback: If a pupil chases a 'high score', remind them the meters represent people's lives and competing goods, so the aim is a justified balance, not a maximum.
Prompt pupils to state which trade-off they accepted and whose interest they set lower, and to defend that choice.
activities.rationale: A coupled trade-off simulation is intended to make the structure of the dilemma tangible and let pupils quantify the stakes they argued verbally. Best used after the dialogue so the quantities attach to real debated positions; on its own it can imply an optimisable answer, which this topic does not have.
sourceClaims: Rainforest futures involve genuine trade-offs between economic development, indigenous land rights, biodiversity conservation and climate stability, requiring cooperation among governments, businesses, scientists, indigenous leaders and consumers
learnerActions: Take on the role of decision-maker for a real-grounded region (e.g. an Amazon state weighing a road or soy expansion) and allocate land and policy across development, forest protection, indigenous land title, and carbon/REDD+ deals.

Watch coupled meters — income/economy, biodiversity, climate/carbon, and community/indigenous rights — respond to each decision; the simulation is built with coupled trade-offs so no option scores highest on every axis at once.
Try to find an all-win solution, then explain in writing why you could not, and which values (not just numbers) you chose to prioritise and why.
Return to the stakeholder interview and quantify what you debated: show which person each meter change helps or hurts.
activities.intendedInsight: The no-free-lunch structure is intended to be felt directly: gains on one axis cost another, and the tension is between legitimate values, not merely a number to optimise.

activities.title: Stakeholder map primer: who is involved and what they'd lose
feedback: Check that at least three distinct competing interests are named (e.g. livelihoods, indigenous rights, biodiversity, global climate).
If two groups are listed as simply 'good vs bad', ask the pupil to name a legitimate reason each has for its position.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal map builds the factual scaffold of who is involved before the live reasoning. As a pre-brief, static cards orient the pupil to the stakeholders but do not themselves create the live tension or require defending a position under push-back, so it supports rather than replaces the dialogue.
learnerActions: Reveal each group in turn (smallholder farmer, indigenous community, conservation scientist, government, business, consumer) and record for each their main interest and what they stand to lose.
Draw a 'who holds which lever' chart linking each actor to one concrete action they could take (policy, sourcing standards, buying choices, evidence, defending land title).
Pair two groups and write one sentence on how what one wants could clash with what the other wants.
activities.intendedInsight: Who the stakeholders are and that each holds a different partial lever — a factual foundation for the reasoning work.

activities.title: Recall check: the competing interests and why no single answer
feedback: Accept any three of: economic development/livelihoods, indigenous rights, biodiversity, climate/rainfall, consumer demand.

A full answer cites enforcement/sovereignty and poverty as real obstacles and argues for balancing and cooperation; a partial answer lists interests as good-vs-bad without explaining how they genuinely conflict.
activities.rationale: A short recall task checks the factual prerequisites (naming interests, stating why no single solution). Because the topic is open-ended with no single right answer, use this for the recall scaffold alongside the reasoning work; recognition-style items alone do not elicit the independent, open-ended reasoning that is the core of this topic.
sourceClaims: KS2 geography and citizenship require pupils to consider sustainability, weigh competing viewpoints and reason about human impact on environments
learnerActions: Name at least three competing interests at stake in rainforest futures.
Explain in a sentence or two why there is no single simple solution.
For a fresh dilemma, transfer the reasoning: name the conflicting interests and why one law would not satisfy them all.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure the factual scaffold — the interests and the reason no single ban works — so it can anchor open reasoning.

constraints: The objective is disciplined reasoning about a genuine dilemma, not a single correct policy; do not reward pupils for 'solving' it or claiming a solution where everyone is completely happy.
Voice stakeholders as legitimate conflicting interests, not cartoon goodies vs baddies; require steel-manning each side before any proposal.
Ground every persona and argument in prior learning (deforestation drivers, conservation toolkit, climate, supply chains) so debate is evidence-based.
The decision simulation should not present an all-win or 'high-score' outcome; its role is to show that values, not just numbers, are in tension, and it works best after the dialogue.
The stakeholder map is a scaffold/primer: it orients pupils to who is involved but does not itself require defending a position under push-back.
The recall check verifies factual prerequisites; recognition-style items alone do not elicit the independent, open-ended reasoning that is the core of this topic.

Address misconceptions explicitly: a blanket ban cannot be enforced by one country inside another's borders, is hard to enforce even nationally across vast forests, and harms dependents without alternatives; the conflict is between legitimate needs, not just greed; responsibility is shared (consumer demand and global climate benefit implicate everyone); protecting forest and helping local people are not always opposites (indigenous title, sustainable certification can serve both).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both source claims are marked verified:false in the row; treat their support as provisional.

The original rated dialogue 'ideal' and asserted the simulation and quiz 'cannot' deliver the core learning; these comparative-necessity/superiority claims have been softened to scoped affordances and limits, since catalog ratings do not establish that other media cannot teach this.
Efficacy wording in activity rationales/insights has been changed to intended/proposed phrasing because none of the activities has been empirically tested.

Specific real-world mechanisms (REDD+ payments, sustainable certification, indigenous land title) are presented as examples to debate; pupils should treat their effectiveness as contested, not settled, as the sources do not establish comparative efficacy.

probeDeeper: Pick two of the groups who care about a rainforest and explain how what one wants could clash with what the other wants.
Is it fair to ask a poor country to protect a forest that benefits the whole world? What would make it fairer?
What if protecting the forest meant a local family lost the only land they can farm — how would you weigh that?
Can there be a solution that everyone is completely happy with? If not, how should people decide?
assess.correctAnswer: Because deforestation sits at the meeting point of several legitimate but competing interests, and one law can't satisfy them all. Local families and poor countries often depend on the land or its products for income and food; indigenous communities have rights to their territory and a say in its future; conservationists want biodiversity protected; the whole world benefits from the carbon and rainfall the forest provides; and businesses and consumers everywhere create demand for beef, soy, palm oil and timber. These interests genuinely conflict — protecting the forest can cost someone their livelihood, and no country can enforce a law inside another's borders. So the realistic path is balancing and negotiating between interests — international cooperation, payments to keep forests standing, sustainable production, and respecting local and indigenous rights — rather than one perfect ban. There is no single 'right answer' that makes every trade-off disappear.

errorPatterns.pattern: just ban it — one law would fix everything ('the government should make deforestation illegal and it would stop')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Role-play the stakeholders — a smallholder, an indigenous leader, a government, a consumer — and show whose needs a blanket ban would ignore and why it couldn't be enforced across borders.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the world could just pass one law banning all deforestation and the problem would be solved.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child proposes a single ban as the obvious solution and cannot see the livelihoods, rights or sovereignty problems it would create

errorPatterns.pattern: it's simply greedy people versus good people ('if everyone just stopped being greedy there'd be no problem')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce a sympathetic case — a family that farms cleared land to eat, a country that needs the income — so the child sees competing NEEDS, not just greed.
errorPatterns.distractor: The only reason forests are cut is that some people are greedy; there's no real dilemma.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child frames the whole issue as villains vs heroes and cannot name any legitimate reason a person might clear forest

errorPatterns.pattern: it's only one group's problem to solve ('it's the rainforest countries' job, nothing to do with the rest of us')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect distant consumer demand and worldwide climate benefit back to the choice; show why a fair solution shares both responsibility and cost.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's entirely up to the countries that have the rainforests — the rest of the world has no part in it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child assigns responsibility solely to the countries where forests grow and overlooks global demand and shared climate/rainfall benefits

responseLevels.gap: Says a single ban would work, or reduces the whole issue to greed — sees no competing legitimate interests.
responseLevels.full: Explains that several legitimate interests — livelihoods, indigenous rights, biodiversity, global climate/rainfall, consumer demand — pull against each other so no single answer satisfies all, cites enforcement/sovereignty and poverty as real obstacles, and argues for balancing and cooperation, transferring the trade-off reasoning to a fresh dilemma.
responseLevels.partial: Names more than one interest (e.g. money vs environment) but treats them as good-vs-bad or lists them without explaining how they genuinely conflict or why that makes one law unworkable.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: If cutting down rainforests causes so many problems, why can't the world's countries simply pass one law that bans all deforestation everywhere? Tell me WHY it isn't that simple.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who sees the issue as good-vs-bad ('greedy people won't stop') thinks one ban would work if only people were nicer. A child who understands trade-offs explains that the conflict is between legitimate interests — livelihoods, rights, biodiversity, climate, demand — that cannot all be maximised at once, and that sovereignty and poverty make a single global ban unworkable. The 'why' tier reveals whether they hold real competing values or a simple villains story.

pedagogy.summary: A percentage is a proportion expressed as parts per hundred: 40% means 40 out of every 100, so it is naturally 40/100 and 0.40, and 100% is the whole while 50% is half of it. The decisive idea — and the one children most often miss — is that a percentage is an OPERATOR ON A BASE, not a plain number: 50% is not 'fifty', it is half of whatever the whole is, so 50% of 20 is 10 while 50% of 200 is 100. Because a percentage is inherently 'out of 100', its size relative to the whole is fixed but its actual amount depends entirely on the base. Teach it on the hundred square (40 of 100 shaded) tied to the fraction n/100, the decimal, and a 0%–100% number line, and confront base-neglect head-on.
bestPractices: Anchor 'per cent = parts per hundred' on a 10×10 hundred square: shade 40 squares to show 40%, and read off 40/100 and 0.40 from the same picture.

Foreground the base from the outset: a percentage is a proportion OF a whole, so always ask '% of what?'; show that 50% of a small set and 50% of a large set are the same proportion but different amounts.
Link the three forms explicitly — 40% = 40/100 = 0.40 — and simplify where natural (40/100 = 2/5) so percentage sits inside the fraction–decimal web.
Establish landmarks: 100% = the whole, 50% = a half, 25% = a quarter, 10% = a tenth, 1% = a hundredth; and seed that percentages can exceed 100%.
Confront base-neglect with deliberate comparisons (10% of 500 = 50 versus 90% of 60 = 48) so children see a smaller percentage of a bigger base can be the larger amount.

Four-way link: percentage + fraction n/100 + decimal + 0%–100% number line
Bar model of a whole partitioned to show a percentage of it
Landmark strip (0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) against fractions/decimals
Two different-sized wholes each showing '50%' to expose the role of the base

Reading a percentage as a fraction with the number as denominator ('24% means 1/24', '40% means 1/40').
Percentage–decimal placeholder error: writing 9% as 0.9 instead of 0.09.
