pedagogy.summary: Upper-KS2 respiratory understanding has two intertwined strands children must not conflate: the AIR PATHWAY (nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli) branching like an upside-down tree into millions of tiny air sacs, and the MECHANICS of how air is moved (the diaphragm — a muscle sheet below the lungs — contracts and flattens to pull air in, relaxes and domes up to push air out; the lungs do not inflate themselves). The payoff sits at the alveoli: their huge combined surface and one-cell-thick walls, wrapped in capillaries, are WHERE gas exchange happens — oxygen crosses into the blood, carbon dioxide crosses out. Teach breathing as a pump-and-exchange system, keeping 'how air gets in' (diaphragm) separate from 'what the air is for' (exchange at the alveoli), because children routinely merge the two or think the chest muscles alone do the work.
bestPractices: Build the branching air pathway as a journey a breath takes, naming each narrowing tube in order (trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli), so the tree structure — not a list of words — is what sticks.

Make the diaphragm mechanism physical: a bell-jar / balloon-in-a-bottle model, or hands on the belly feeling it push out on the in-breath, so children feel that a muscle BELOW the lungs drives breathing (correcting 'lungs inflate by themselves').

Zoom in on a single alveolus wrapped in a capillary to show exchange as a two-way swap at a one-cell-thick wall — oxygen out of the air into blood, carbon dioxide out of blood into the air — not a one-way 'breathing in oxygen'.
Explain WHY alveoli are tiny and numerous: huge surface area in a small space. A 'if you spread them flat they'd cover a tennis court' comparison makes the surface-area idea concrete.
Keep the two strands on separate passes — first trace the pathway, then run the diaphragm pump, then connect them — rather than presenting one busy diagram that blurs structure and mechanism.
keyRepresentations: Branching 'upside-down tree' of the airways (trachea trunk → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli clusters)
Balloon-in-a-bottle / bell-jar model of the diaphragm (pull the sheet down → balloons inflate; release → deflate)
Single-alveolus-plus-capillary zoom showing the O2/CO2 two-way exchange across a thin wall
Diaphragm cross-section: flattens on inhale (chest volume up), domes on exhale (chest volume down)
Surface-area comparison (millions of sacs ≈ a tennis court) for why exchange is so efficient
commonMisconceptions: 'Lungs inflate themselves / the chest muscles just squeeze' — missing that the diaphragm below the lungs is the main driver, changing chest volume so air is pushed in by pressure.

'We breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide' as if the air swaps completely — in reality it is the same air mixture; only some oxygen is absorbed and some carbon dioxide added (carried from the KS1 breathing misconception).
'Air goes to the lungs and just sits there' — missing that the point is exchange with the blood at the alveoli.
'The lungs are two empty balloons' — missing the dense branching structure ending in millions of tiny sacs.
'Alveoli are the same as the tubes' — not distinguishing the delivery pipes (bronchioles) from the exchange sacs (alveoli).
'Air is pulled in by the nose sucking' — locating the pump in the wrong place; the driver is the diaphragm and chest volume.

learn.summary: Upper-KS2 learners (ages 9–11) build an understanding of the respiratory system as a pump-and-exchange system, keeping two strands distinct: (1) the AIR PATHWAY branching like an upside-down tree (nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli) and (2) the MECHANICS of how air is moved (the diaphragm, a muscle sheet below the lungs, contracts and flattens to enlarge the chest so the pressure inside drops and outside air is pushed in, then relaxes and domes up so the space shrinks and air flows out). The payoff is at the alveoli, where huge combined surface area and one-cell-thick walls wrapped in capillaries let oxygen cross into the blood and carbon dioxide cross out. Keep 'how air gets in' (diaphragm) separate from 'what the air is for' (exchange), because children routinely merge the two or think the lungs inflate themselves.

activities.title: Drive the breathing pump
feedback: If a learner says the lungs suck air in on their own, re-pair carefully: diaphragm contracts → chest space bigger → pressure inside drops → outside air flows in.
If a learner pairs 'diaphragm contracts' with breathing OUT, correct the pairing: contract = flatten = bigger space = air IN; relax = dome up = smaller space = air OUT.
Reinforce: breathing out is the reverse of breathing in — the diaphragm relaxes, the space shrinks, and air is pushed out.
activities.rationale: Making the diaphragm mechanism physical and driveable (a balloon-in-a-bottle / bell-jar model, or hands on the belly) may help learners feel that a muscle below the lungs drives breathing, addressing the common 'lungs inflate themselves' and 'nose sucks air in' misconceptions. A live model lets learners act on the diaphragm and observe the volume change; a hands-on jar model offers the same causal structure through touch. Efficacy of either medium is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Air travels via the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out; the diaphragm contracts and relaxes to move air in and out.
learnerActions: Operate a model where you pull the diaphragm sheet down and watch air stream in through the branching trachea → bronchi → bronchioles and fill the alveoli; release it and watch the diaphragm dome up and air flow out.
Say aloud, for each move, whether the chest space is getting bigger or smaller, and whether air is going in or out.
Explain in your own words why air rushes IN when the space gets bigger (pressure inside drops below the outside air, which pushes in), not because the lungs pull it in by themselves.
Optionally feel this on your own body: place hands on your belly and notice it push outward as you breathe in.
activities.intendedInsight: YOU cause the breath by moving a muscle BELOW the lungs, which enlarges the chest volume so the pressure inside drops and outside air is pushed in — the lungs do not inflate themselves.

activities.title: Zoom into a single alveolus
feedback: If a learner says oxygen just stays in the air sacs and fills the lungs, focus on the alveolus–capillary boundary: oxygen crosses the thin wall INTO the blood, carbon dioxide crosses OUT, and the blood delivers the oxygen onward.
If a learner describes the air as being completely swapped, clarify that it is the same air mixture — only some oxygen is absorbed and some carbon dioxide added.
activities.rationale: Zooming in on a single alveolus-plus-capillary shows exchange as a two-way swap at a thin wall, targeting the misconceptions that 'air just sits in the lungs' and that we 'breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide' as a complete swap. The thin-wall probe makes the structure–function link explicit.
sourceClaims: Air travels via the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out; the diaphragm contracts and relaxes to move air in and out.
learnerActions: Look closely at one air sac wrapped in a red capillary and trace what happens to each gas: oxygen crosses the thin wall out of the air and into the blood; carbon dioxide crosses the other way out of the blood and into the air.
Explain where the oxygen goes NEXT — the blood carries it onward to the body.
Answer: if the sac walls were thick instead of extremely thin (far thinner than paper), why would that make getting oxygen into the blood harder?
activities.intendedInsight: Exchange is a two-way swap across very thin walls (the alveolus wall and the capillary wall are each only one cell thick) — not a one-way 'breathing in oxygen', and the air is only partly traded, not fully swapped. The point of reaching the alveoli is exchange with the blood.

activities.title: Trace and name the airway tree
feedback: If a learner lists words without order, re-trace the breath's journey from widest tube to the sacs so the tree structure sticks, not a word list.
If a learner treats the lungs as two empty balloons, highlight the dense branching ending in millions of tiny sacs.
If a learner conflates bronchioles with alveoli, distinguish delivery pipes from exchange sacs.
activities.rationale: Building the pathway as a journey and explaining WHY the sacs are tiny and numerous addresses 'lungs are empty balloons' and 'alveoli are the same as the tubes'. The surface-area comparison (roughly half a tennis court) is an approximate figure, and estimates vary. This anatomy strand supports but does not replace the pump and exchange ideas.
sourceClaims: Air travels via the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out; the diaphragm contracts and relaxes to move air in and out.
learnerActions: Trace the journey a single breath takes, naming each part in order as the tubes narrow and finally end in sacs: nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Drill down from an 'alveoli cluster' into a single alveolus-and-capillary to see where the pipes end and the exchange sacs begin.

Explain why the lungs branch into millions of tiny sacs rather than being two big empty bags, using a surface-area idea (spread flat, the sacs would cover a very large area, often estimated at around 50–100 square metres, roughly half a tennis court).
Point to the difference between the delivery pipes (bronchioles) and the exchange sacs (alveoli).
activities.intendedInsight: The airways form a branching tree ending in millions of tiny sacs; their huge combined surface area in a small space is a key reason gas exchange is so efficient (along with very thin walls and a rich blood supply), and the sacs are different from the pipes that deliver air to them.

activities.title: Consolidate: sequence, direction, and mechanism
feedback: Recall-style tasks can confirm the facts are in place but do not by themselves build the pump intuition — follow a wrong answer by returning to the driveable model or jar model.
If exchange direction is confused, revisit the single-alveolus zoom before re-checking.
activities.rationale: After the model and zoom have built understanding, a mix of sequencing, matching, and sorting can consolidate the pathway order and exchange direction. A sort or match can check that the classification facts are in place, but it does not itself elicit the pressure/volume reasoning or a spoken explanation, so it is positioned as a follow-up, not the core.
learnerActions: Put the airway stages in the correct order from nose/mouth to alveoli.
Match each part to its job (diaphragm → drives breathing; alveoli → gas exchange; bronchioles → delivery pipes).
Sort statements into 'breathing in' vs 'breathing out' (diaphragm contracts/flattens, space bigger, air in — vs relaxes/domes, space smaller, air out).
Decide, for a 'what happens at the alveoli' question, which description shows oxygen crossing into the blood rather than merely filling the lungs.
activities.intendedInsight: The pathway order, the diaphragm in/out mechanism, and the exchange direction can be recalled and distinguished once the model has built the underlying intuition.

constraints: Keep the two strands on separate passes — first trace the pathway, then run the diaphragm pump, then connect them — rather than one busy diagram that blurs structure and mechanism.

Recall/matching/sorting tasks can check that facts and classifications are in place; they do not by themselves elicit the pressure/volume pump reasoning, which is better supported by an acted-on model or a physical investigation.

A balloon-in-a-bottle or bell-jar model is an approximation: the rubber sheet stands for the diaphragm and the balloons for the lungs; name what each part represents so learners do not take the model literally.

A static diagram can present and label the structure, but to observe the volume-change mechanism learners benefit from acting on a model (drag, pull, or a physical jar) and watching air move; a 3D chest tour is a nice-to-have for spatial orientation, not required to teach the pump or exchange.
Pitch for ages 9–11 (upper KS2, Years 5–6): connect to the circulatory system (blood carries oxygen onward) without requiring molecular-level detail.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source (Asthma + Lung UK) is marked verified:false in the row and underpins Activities 1–3; treat its claim as unconfirmed pending review. Its claim grounds the factual mechanism/pathway being taught, not the pedagogical efficacy of any medium.

The legacy row asserted that '3D adds no conceptual gain' and that 'a static image cannot' teach the mechanism. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to affordance-based statements; the original strong claims are noted here for review.

The 'oxygen delivered' meter linked to breaths-per-minute (previewing exercise) is retained only as an optional motivational preview, not a validated quantitative model, and should not be presented as measuring real oxygen delivery.
The tennis-court surface-area comparison is a commonly used approximation; exact figures vary by source and were not re-verified here.
The Y6 curriculum claim was not cited in any activity's sourceClaims because it supports topic/curriculum placement rather than a specific activity's teaching principle.

The source assessment correctAnswer credits the rib/intercostal muscles as helping the diaphragm enlarge the chest. The guidance centres the diaphragm alone as the main driver (consistent with the stated pedagogy and age band); the rib muscles' supporting role is a documented detail omitted deliberately and could be added as enrichment.

probeDeeper: In a model with a balloon inside a jar and a rubber sheet across the bottom, pulling the sheet down inflates the balloon. What in your body is the rubber sheet, and why does pulling it down fill the 'lung'?
If the walls of the air sacs were thick instead of paper-thin, why would that be a problem for getting oxygen into the blood?
Why do the lungs branch into millions of tiny sacs instead of being two big empty bags?
assess.correctAnswer: The diaphragm (with the rib muscles) contracts and moves down and out, making the chest space bigger; this lowers the air pressure inside the lungs, so air rushes in from outside to fill the space. Breathing out is the reverse — the diaphragm relaxes, the space shrinks, air is pushed out. At the alveoli, oxygen passes through the thin walls into the blood in the capillaries, and carbon dioxide passes the other way out of the blood; the blood then carries the oxygen to the body.

errorPatterns.pattern: The lungs suck the air in by themselves, like a balloon that inflates on its own — no diaphragm or pressure involved.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce the diaphragm as the driver: it enlarges the chest, pressure drops, air flows in. Use the balloon-in-a-jar model to make it felt.
errorPatterns.distractor: The lungs squeeze and suck the air in by themselves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes intake to the lungs actively pulling, with no role for the diaphragm or a pressure change.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the mechanism — thinks the diaphragm contracts to push air OUT.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-pair carefully: contract = bigger space = air in; relax = smaller space = air out. Demonstrate with the model.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Pairs 'diaphragm contracts' with breathing out (and relaxes with breathing in).

errorPatterns.pattern: Oxygen just fills the lungs and stays there — it doesn't cross into the blood.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Focus on the alveoli–capillary boundary: oxygen crosses the thin wall into the blood, carbon dioxide crosses out; link to the blood delivering oxygen onward.
errorPatterns.distractor: The oxygen stays in the air sacs and just fills the lungs up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ends the story at the air sacs; no gas exchange into the bloodstream.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the lungs inflate themselves or reverses the diaphragm, and treats oxygen as merely filling the lungs with no crossing into blood.
responseLevels.full: Explains breathing as a pressure/volume mechanism driven by the diaphragm AND gas exchange as oxygen crossing the thin alveoli walls into the blood (carbon dioxide out) — connecting mechanism and exchange into a working system.
responseLevels.partial: Traces the air pathway and mentions the diaphragm and gas exchange as separate facts, but can't explain the pressure mechanism (bigger space, lower pressure, air in) or clearly link the alveoli to the blood.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Air isn't pumped into your lungs the way the heart pumps blood — yet air still rushes in when you breathe in. What actually makes the air go IN? And once air reaches the tiny air sacs deep in the lungs, what happens to the oxygen — where does it go next, and how?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who says the lungs 'suck air in by themselves', or reverses the diaphragm, or thinks oxygen just fills the lungs, exposes the gap. Only the child who links a volume/pressure change to airflow AND oxygen crossing into the blood has the mechanism. The tier-two 'how does the oxygen get on' blocks a lucky pathway-recitation.

sources.claim: Y6 pupils study animals including humans; the respiratory system (air pathway, lungs, gas exchange) is taught as part of how the human body functions and links to the circulatory system.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Science programmes of study (KS2, Year 6, Animals including humans)

sources.claim: Air travels via the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out; the diaphragm contracts and relaxes to move air in and out.

pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic (META / nature of science):** Monitoring Volcanoes — how volcanologists watch for warning signs (gas emissions, ground swelling, small earthquakes), combine multiple kinds of evidence to assess risk, and why prediction involves EVIDENCE and UNCERTAINTY, not certainty.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement):** KS2 **Geography** (volcanoes/hazards) plus the 'working scientifically' spirit of KS2 science (gathering and interpreting evidence). The nature-of-science 'evidence with uncertainty' theme runs across the DfE science curriculum rather than a single statement. Frame as how scientists know, and how sure they can be.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** **4-ESS3-2**'s clarification explicitly names 'improving monitoring of volcanic activity' as an example solution — the direct anchor. The topic also embodies NGSS Nature-of-Science themes (science is based on evidence; scientific knowledge is open to revision; models have limits). State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisites 'Inside a Volcano' and 'Active/Dormant/Extinct'. Two payloads: (1) the SIGNS — rising gas, ground bulging as magma moves up, swarms of small earthquakes; and (2) the META lesson — no single sign is proof; scientists weigh several together, give probabilities/alert levels, and can be wrong (false alarms and missed calls both happen). The load-bearing idea is that good science here means reasoning under uncertainty from converging evidence — not a crystal ball.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (early-formal; nature-of-science reasoning). Children can list warning signs but expect science to give certain yes/no predictions and read a false alarm as 'the scientists failed'. Success = name warning signs, explain that scientists combine evidence, and articulate that prediction is uncertain — probabilities and alert levels, not guarantees.
bestPractices: Teach the warning signs as CONVERGING evidence: any one sign is ambiguous, but several together raise concern — model 'weight of evidence' reasoning.
Make uncertainty a feature, not a failure: introduce alert levels/probabilities and discuss that both false alarms and missed eruptions carry costs — scientists must judge under risk.
Connect each sign to the mechanism (magma rising → gas out, ground bulges, small quakes) so the signs are understood, not just listed.
Use real decisions (an evacuation call before an eruption) to show the human stakes of acting on uncertain evidence.
Explicitly name this as how science works generally — evidence-based, probabilistic, revisable — transferring beyond volcanoes.
keyRepresentations: A monitoring dashboard: gas sensor, ground-tilt/deformation, seismometer swarm — several signals rising together
'Weight of evidence' balance: multiple ambiguous signs combining into a risk level
Alert-level ladder (e.g. green→amber→red) as a probabilistic, not certain, judgement
Magma rising diagram linked to each surface sign (gas, bulge, small quakes)
commonMisconceptions: Scientists can predict the exact day/time of an eruption (they estimate risk/probability from evidence; timing is uncertain).
One warning sign means an eruption is certain (single signs are ambiguous; scientists combine several).
A false alarm means the scientists were wrong/bad at their job (acting under uncertainty means some false alarms and missed calls are unavoidable).
Monitoring stops eruptions (it can warn and reduce impacts, but cannot prevent the eruption).
If nothing has happened yet, the warnings were pointless (a non-eruption after warnings can be a correct low-probability outcome, not a mistake).

learn.summary: For ages 9-11, a META / nature-of-science unit on monitoring volcanoes: learners name the warning signs volcanologists watch (rising gas emissions, ground swelling/bulging as magma moves up, swarms of small earthquakes), link each sign to the mechanism of rising magma, and grasp that eruption prediction combines several converging signs into a risk level or alert - it is evidence-based and probabilistic, not a guarantee of exact timing. The load-bearing insight is that good science here means reasoning under uncertainty: a false alarm, or a quiet volcano after a warning, can still reflect a sound decision rather than failure.

activities.title: In role with a volcanologist on duty
feedback: When a learner leans on one sign alone, ask why a single signal might mislead and what a second or third independent sign would add.

When a learner treats the quiet-volcano evacuation as proof the scientist was wrong, prompt: what were the costs of evacuating versus not evacuating if it HAD erupted? Guide toward 'good decision under uncertainty'.
When a learner demands an exact date, contrast 'likely soon' with 'will definitely erupt Tuesday' and ask which a hidden, variable volcano interior could actually support.
Affirm reasoning that names converging evidence AND acknowledges remaining uncertainty.
activities.rationale: The nature-of-science content - weighing ambiguous evidence and living with uncertainty - may be well served by dialogue, where a learner can ask real questions and an expert reasons aloud about combining signs, issuing an alert, and shouldering a false alarm. This is a proposed fit, not an efficacy finding established here. Keep the persona age-appropriate and steer a hesitant child through signs -> weighing -> uncertainty.
sourceClaims: Volcanologists monitor gas emissions, ground deformation (swelling), and seismicity (small-earthquake swarms), combining signals into alert levels; eruption prediction is probabilistic and uncertain, not exact.
Nature-of-science: scientific knowledge is based on evidence and is open to revision; models and predictions have limits — themes embedded across NGSS.
learnerActions: Ask an in-role volcanologist the questions you really want answered: 'How do you know a volcano is about to erupt?', 'Can you tell me the exact day?', 'How sure are you?'

Have her show and explain the three main things she watches - gas emissions creeping up, the ground slowly bulging as magma pushes in, and swarms of tiny earthquakes - and why no single one is proof on its own.
Work through a Socratic challenge she poses, e.g. 'If only the gas rose but the ground stayed still, would you evacuate a town?' - give your reasoning out loud before she responds.
Discuss a real-type scenario: she once urged a town to evacuate and the volcano went quiet. Decide and argue whether that was a failure, then compare your view with her reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Prediction here means weighing several ambiguous signs together to judge a risk level - scientists act on the best evidence under uncertainty, so a false alarm can still be the right call.

activities.title: Make the call: an observatory monitoring panel
feedback: When signals disagree (two point to eruption, one doesn't), prompt the learner to say how that lowers certainty rather than forcing a yes/no.
After a false alarm, reinforce that acting on strong converging evidence can be correct even when no eruption follows.
After a missed sign, discuss what extra monitoring or cross-checking might catch it next time, and why perfect prediction isn't possible.
activities.rationale: A decision-making panel may let learners practise reasoning under uncertainty experientially, making the abstract 'weight of evidence' idea concrete through choices and consequences. Optional gauges, alert-level controls and outcome feedback are illustrative, not required. Proposed design, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Volcanologists monitor gas emissions, ground deformation (swelling), and seismicity (small-earthquake swarms), combining signals into alert levels; eruption prediction is probabilistic and uncertain, not exact.
learnerActions: Watch a set of gauges - gas level, ground tilt/deformation, and earthquake (seismicity) activity - change over a scenario.
Decide whether to raise or lower an alert level (e.g. green -> amber -> red) as the signals rise together or disagree.
Play through outcomes that include a false alarm and a missed sign, and read feedback framed as 'good decision under the evidence available', not simply right/wrong.
Explain afterwards which signals drove your call and how confident you could reasonably be.
activities.intendedInsight: Experiencing signals that rise together, conflict, or surprise you is intended to show that risk judgement draws on converging evidence and that uncertainty is built in, not a flaw.

activities.title: Explore and label a monitoring scene
feedback: Confirm correct instrument-to-sign matches and restate the magma-rising cause for each.
If a learner says one revealed sign proves an eruption, point back to the 'judge the risk from all the signs' message.
If a learner asks about other signals (e.g. temperature), confirm these can add evidence but still do not give certainty on their own.
activities.rationale: A labelled, reveal-based scene conveys WHAT is monitored and connects each sign to its mechanism. As a scaffold it can build knowledge but does not by itself exercise the probabilistic decision-making at the heart of the topic, so pair it with dialogue or a decision scenario. Proposed, not validated here.
sourceClaims: Volcanologists monitor gas emissions, ground deformation (swelling), and seismicity (small-earthquake swarms), combining signals into alert levels; eruption prediction is probabilistic and uncertain, not exact.
learnerActions: Examine a labelled observatory/volcano scene and tap or point to each instrument - gas sensor, tiltmeter, seismometer - to reveal what it detects and why it matters.
For each sign, state how it links to magma rising (magma pushing up -> more gas escapes, ground bulges, and small quakes occur).
Optionally note that scientists may also watch other signals, such as temperature changes, as extra evidence - without treating any single one as proof.
Answer a lift-the-flap style question - 'Can scientists be sure it will erupt?' - and check the response: 'No - they judge the risk from all the signs together.'
activities.intendedInsight: Builds the vocabulary and mechanism (what each instrument detects and why) as a foundation for the harder reasoning about combining evidence and uncertainty.

activities.title: Check understanding: signs, causes and what an alert means
feedback: For the 'certain' distractor, re-explain that a red alert issued before an eruption expresses a judged high risk from combined evidence, not a guarantee of an eruption.
For a correct match, restate the underlying mechanism briefly to reinforce understanding over rote recall.
activities.rationale: Recognition items efficiently check the warning signs and the uncertainty message. Because selected-response formats do not require learners to construct and defend reasoning, use this to confirm facts, not to assess the core nature-of-science reasoning - and note the slight tension in scoring a topic whose lesson is that certainty isn't available.
sourceClaims: Volcanologists monitor gas emissions, ground deformation (swelling), and seismicity (small-earthquake swarms), combining signals into alert levels; eruption prediction is probabilistic and uncertain, not exact.
learnerActions: Match each warning sign to what it can indicate (rising gas emissions / ground swelling / earthquake swarms -> possibly magma moving up, though each can have other causes).

Answer selected-response questions such as 'In this activity's alert scale, what does a red alert issued before any eruption mean?', choosing 'the risk is judged high from the combined evidence' and rejecting the tempting distractor 'an eruption is certain'. (In some real alert systems, red can also be used once an eruption is already happening.)
activities.intendedInsight: A quick recognition check can confirm learners hold the key facts and the crucial distinction that a high alert issued before an eruption means high judged risk, not certainty.

constraints: Prerequisites: a basic understanding of what is inside a volcano and the active/dormant/extinct distinction.
Teach the warning signs as converging evidence: any one sign is ambiguous; several together raise concern - model 'weight of evidence' reasoning rather than listing signs.
Make uncertainty a feature, not a failure: introduce alert levels/probabilities and discuss that both false alarms and missed eruptions carry costs.
Connect each sign to its mechanism (magma rising -> gas out, ground bulges, small quakes) so signs are understood, not memorised.

Correct these misconceptions explicitly, treating each as false: that exact-day prediction is achievable; that one sign is enough to be sure; that a false alarm means the scientists failed; that monitoring stops eruptions (it warns and reduces impact but cannot prevent them); that a non-eruption after warnings proves the warnings were pointless.

The labelled reveal scene and the recognition check are scaffolds: they build vocabulary and confirm facts but do not by themselves exercise independent reasoning under uncertainty, which needs discussion or decision-making.
Name this as how science works generally - evidence-based, probabilistic, revisable - so the lesson transfers beyond volcanoes.

A spatial/3D treatment is less suited for this evidence-weighing concept than for topics about physical structure; this is a reviewer judgement about fit for this topic, not an observed or tested finding, and not a universal rule.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three source claims (USGS monitoring/alert levels; NGSS Nature-of-Science appendix) are marked unverified in the source row; only the 4-ESS3-2 clarification claim was marked verified, and it supports curriculum placement rather than any activity's pedagogical efficacy. Source claims attached to activities support content substance only, not medium or scaffold efficacy.

The 'ideal/strong/possible/poor' preference ordering from the source has been removed; relative claims that dialogue is 'most powerful' or that a static image 'struggles' to carry the concept are presented as scoped affordances/limits only, not established efficacy findings.

The diagnostic probe mentions temperature as a monitored signal, while the main sign list names gas, ground deformation and seismicity; temperature is flagged only as an optional additional signal so it is preserved without being promoted into the canonical three-sign set.

probeDeeper: If two warning signs point to an eruption but a third doesn't, what should scientists do?
Is a scientist who orders an evacuation that turns out to be a false alarm wrong to have done it? Why or why not?
How is saying an eruption is 'likely' different from saying it 'will definitely happen on Tuesday'?
What could scientists learn from how this volcano behaved before its last eruption?
assess.correctAnswer: (Open — an epistemic probe, not a right/wrong answer.) A strong response surfaces: scientists gather several kinds of evidence (small earthquakes, ground swelling, gas emissions, temperature) and combine them, comparing with how this volcano and others behaved before past eruptions; but the inside of a volcano is hidden and every volcano behaves differently, so the signs make an eruption more or less LIKELY without fixing the exact time — prediction is about evidence and probability, not certainty.

errorPatterns.pattern: Scientists can/should predict the exact day — if they can't, they're just guessing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss how converging evidence raises confidence without giving certainty; forecasting isn't fortune-telling.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats any uncertainty as failure or as mere guessing.

errorPatterns.pattern: One warning sign is enough to know for sure
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss why scientists combine several independent signs and cross-check them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Relies on a single sign to decide.

errorPatterns.pattern: Nothing can be known in advance — eruptions are totally random and unknowable
errorPatterns.nextMove: Surface real cases where monitoring gave useful warnings and saved lives.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that any evidence tells us anything useful.

responseLevels.gap: Treats prediction as either certain knowledge or pure guessing; names no real evidence.
responseLevels.full: Describes combining multiple lines of evidence and comparing with past behaviour, and explains prediction gives evidence-based likelihood (not certainty) because the volcano's interior is hidden and each behaves differently — discussing the value of acting under uncertainty.
responseLevels.partial: Names warning signs but frames prediction as aiming for exact certainty, or relies on a single sign; doesn't articulate why uncertainty is inherent.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Volcanologists watch a volcano and say an eruption is 'likely soon' — but they can't say exactly when. How do they get evidence about what a volcano might do, and why can't they ever be completely certain about the day it will erupt?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A naive view treats prediction as either 'scientists just know' or 'it's only guessing'. A strong response holds the middle — evidence-based likelihood under real uncertainty, drawing on several converging signs rather than one — and can say WHY certainty isn't possible.

pedagogy.summary: At age 12-14 pupils learn the classical ruler-and-compass constructions — perpendicular bisector of a segment, perpendicular to a line from/at a point, and angle bisector — using ONLY compasses and a straight edge, with no measuring of lengths or angles. The essential shift is from DRAWING (find a midpoint with a ruler, judge a right angle by eye or protractor) to CONSTRUCTING (produce the result from geometric properties). The unifying property is the rhombus: equal-radius arcs from two points create four equal lengths, so the figure is a rhombus, whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect each other and bisect their angles. Taught this way, every construction is a deduction, and the commonest error — changing the compass radius between the two endpoints — is instantly diagnosable: unequal radii give a KITE (diagonals perpendicular but NOT bisecting), so the line is perpendicular but misses the midpoint. Because compasses are usually new at KS3, motor coordination is a real, separable hurdle; developing the concept first with dynamic geometry lets pupils reason about 'perfect' circles before wrestling the physical tool.
bestPractices: Teach the draw-vs-construct distinction explicitly: a construction uses geometric properties (equidistance), not measurement; require pupils to leave their construction arcs as evidence of method
Anchor every construction in the rhombus/isosceles-triangle property (equal radii → rhombus → diagonals perpendicularly bisect and bisect the angle), so steps are deductions, not a memorised routine
Make the equal-radius rule meaningful via the kite counter-case: unequal arcs build a kite whose diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so the midpoint is missed
Ensure the compass opening exceeds half the segment so the arcs intersect above and below; discuss why a smaller radius fails and a huge one is just wasteful

Present non-standard (diagonal, rotated) segments and angles, not only horizontal/vertical prototypes, and give time to build compass dexterity — ideally after establishing the idea with dynamic geometry
keyRepresentations: Two equal-radius circles/arcs from the segment ends and the rhombus they define
The rhombus-around-a-diagonal image (segment as one diagonal; the construction produces the other)
Kite counter-example (unequal radii) showing perpendicular-but-not-bisecting diagonals
Isosceles triangle whose altitude bisects the base at right angles and bisects the apex angle
Dynamic-geometry compass/straightedge for concept-before-dexterity
commonMisconceptions: Changing the compass radius between the two endpoints, constructing a kite instead of a rhombus, so the line is perpendicular but does not pass through the midpoint
Drawing rather than constructing — using a ruler to find the midpoint and a protractor/eye for the right angle — and leaving no construction marks
Opening the compasses to less than half the segment, so the arcs never intersect
Memorising the steps as an isolated routine with no link to the properties of circles and rhombuses
Treating the construction as valid only for horizontal/vertical segments (prototype-orientation bias)

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12–14 construct a perpendicular bisector, a perpendicular to a line from a point off it or at a point on it, and an angle bisector using compasses and an unmarked straight edge. Explain the equal-distance and congruent-triangle properties, leaving arcs visible rather than finding positions by measurement. Equal-radius circles centred at segment endpoints yield a perpendicular bisector; unequal radii can still give a perpendicular common chord, but it misses the segment midpoint. Optional dynamic geometry can separate reasoning from tool dexterity; physical compass practice remains part of the proposed tasks. Verification by measurement may check accuracy afterwards, but it does not justify the construction.

activities.title: Construct the perpendicular bisector with compasses and straight edge
feedback: If the line does not cross PQ at its midpoint, check whether the two sets of arcs have equal radii: unequal radii make a KITE (the line is perpendicular to PQ but does not bisect it), equal radii make a rhombus (the line is perpendicular to PQ AND bisects it).

If equal-radius arcs do not cross at two points, check the opening: below half PQ they do not meet; at exactly half they touch only at the midpoint. Use an opening greater than half PQ and allow enough space on the page.

If there are no arcs on the page and the midpoint was found with a ruler or the angle judged by eye, that is drawing, not constructing: redo it so every point of the line is equidistant from P and Q, shown by equal arcs.
Keeping the compass width unchanged between P and Q is the whole point — it is what forces the rhombus.
activities.rationale: Constructing is a doing-and-reasoning skill: pupils must physically execute equal-radius arcs and justify them from the rhombus/equidistance property. A finished static picture cannot be manipulated and does not require the pupil to perform the arcs or articulate the reasoning, so it serves at most as a labelled reference for the rhombus property. Leaving arcs visible makes the method inspectable and distinguishes construction from measurement.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.

A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Take a line segment PQ drawn diagonally (not horizontal or vertical), a pair of compasses and a straight edge — no ruler measuring and no protractor.
Open the compasses to MORE than half of PQ; discuss why an opening of half or less means the arcs only touch or never meet, and why an enormous opening just wastes space.
Place the compass point on P and sweep an arc above and below the segment; WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on Q and sweep again so the arcs cross at two points.
Rule the straight line through the two crossing points, leaving all construction arcs visible as evidence of method.
Explain why the line passes through the midpoint at 90°: the four equal radii form a rhombus, whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect each other.
Repeat on segments at several different orientations, not only horizontal/vertical ones.
activities.intendedInsight: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from P and Q. Equal-radius arcs locate two such points, and the straight line through them is the perpendicular bisector; visible arcs make the method inspectable, though arcs alone do not prove they were placed correctly.

activities.title: Bisect an angle using the same equal-arc idea
feedback: If the line does not appear to split the angle equally, check that the two inner arcs were drawn with the same radius from each arm-crossing point.

Leave your arcs visible — they show you constructed the bisector from equal lengths rather than measuring halves with a protractor. (The congruent halves follow from the equal arcs, so no measuring is needed to justify it.)
activities.rationale: Equal lengths and congruent triangles provide the justification for the angle bisector. After constructing, measuring both angles can be an optional check of drawing accuracy; it is not the construction method or a proof. This is a proposed property-based activity, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.

A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Take a marked angle (try one at a non-standard orientation), compasses and a straight edge.
Place the compass point at the vertex and sweep an arc that crosses both arms of the angle at two points.
WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on each of those two crossing points in turn and sweep equal arcs that meet inside the angle.
Rule the line from the vertex through that meeting point, leaving the arcs visible.
Explain how this reuses the equal-radius property: equal lengths from the vertex and equal arcs from the arm-crossings force the two halves to be congruent, so the line bisects the angle.
activities.intendedInsight: The same equidistance principle that bisects a segment also bisects an angle — one property, reused, rather than a second memorised routine.

activities.title: See the rhombus break into a kite with a dynamic compass (concept-before-dexterity scaffold)
feedback: When the figure flips to KITE, note exactly where the line crosses PQ relative to the midpoint — that gap is why unequal radii fail.
If you can state why the rhombus's crossing line bisects PQ but the kite's does not, you are reasoning from the property; move on to building the same construction by hand.
activities.rationale: A dynamic-geometry tool can separate the concept (equidistance locus, rhombus-vs-kite) from manual dexterity, and may let pupils reason about ideal 'perfect' circles before coping with the practical difficulties of real compasses, which some pupils may still find hard to control. The live slider and label flip are intended to make the failure mode concrete. This is a proposed scaffold: it does not develop the manual construction skill, which must be practised separately on paper, and its effectiveness over other media is untested.
sourceClaims: A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Use an on-screen compass whose radius locks once set: plant it on P and sweep an arc, then on Q and sweep an equal arc so the two equal circles cross at two points.
Rule the line through the crossings and observe the highlighted locus showing every point on it is equidistant from P and Q.

Now drag a slider that shrinks the second circle's radius (keeping it large enough that the two circles still cross); watch the crossing points drift, the line slide sideways while staying perpendicular to PQ, and the label flip from RHOMBUS to KITE — the line visibly misses the midpoint.
Articulate in your own words why 'keep the compass fixed' is a consequence of the rhombus property, not an arbitrary rule.
Transfer to real compasses and paper once the concept is secure.
activities.intendedInsight: When two circles cross, their common chord is perpendicular to the line through their centres. With equal radii, that chord also bisects PQ; with unequal radii it does not. Keep both circles crossing during the comparison, and explain the equal-radius rule rather than memorising it.

activities.title: Diagnose: construction or drawing? Which radius? Which shape failed?
feedback: For the 8 cm segment, any opening at or below 4 cm leaves arcs that cannot cross on both sides (at exactly 4 cm they only touch at the midpoint); the opening must exceed half the length.
The diagram with no arcs cannot be shown to be a construction — without equal arcs there is no evidence the equidistance property was used.
Unequal arcs give a kite: perpendicular, yes, but the line through the crossings does not bisect PQ (only PQ bisects it), so the line misses the midpoint.
activities.rationale: Questions of this kind assess the reasoning behind the construction and surface the specific misconceptions (radius too small, kite error, drawing vs constructing). They complement but cannot replace the performance task, since recognising a correct diagram is not the same as producing one.
sourceClaims: A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: For an 8 cm segment, choose which compass opening will work for the perpendicular bisector (more than 4 cm) and say why openings of 4 cm or less fail.

Compare a diagram with visible equal-radius construction arcs with a bare line. Explain which supplies evidence of the method and which does not; a bare line alone does not reveal whether someone constructed it and erased the arcs or drew it by measurement.

Given a diagram where the line is perpendicular to PQ but misses the midpoint, name the shape that was built (a kite) and explain why the line through the arc crossings does not bisect PQ, even though PQ bisects that line.

Answer: Why must the compass stay the same width from both P and Q, and what shape are you really making? How does the same equal-arc idea bisect an angle? Why would a ruler-and-protractor method not count as a construction?
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to diagnose the radius condition, the kite failure, and construction-vs-drawing demonstrates understanding of the underlying properties — though recognising a correct diagram does not substitute for executing the construction by hand.

activities.title: Construct a perpendicular from a point off a line
feedback: If the circle centred at A only touches l or misses it, increase the radius until it meets l twice. A single touch does not provide distinct B and C for this construction.
If an arc crossing coincides with A, use the other crossing, or adjust the common radius so D is distinct from A; two distinct points are needed to draw AD.
If the perpendicular does not pass through A, return to the given point and the equidistance argument. A perpendicular somewhere else on the line does not meet this task.
activities.rationale: This editorially added construction covers the explicit curriculum objective missing from the saved activities. It reuses the perpendicular-bisector equidistance reasoning; the specific procedure is a proposed task rather than an empirically tested design.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.
learnerActions: Draw a line l and a point A not on it. With centre A, choose a compass radius large enough for a circle to cross l at two distinct points B and C; extend l with the straight edge if needed.
Using equal radii from B and C, each greater than half BC, draw crossing arcs to locate a point D off l and distinct from A. Draw the straight line through A and D, keeping the arcs visible.
Explain why AB = AC and DB = DC place both A and D on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Since B and C lie on l, AD is perpendicular to l. Mark the foot H where AD meets l.
Explain that AH is the shortest distance from A to l. Repeat with a rotated line and A on the other side.
activities.intendedInsight: A point equidistant from B and C lies on their perpendicular bisector. Finding a second distinct equidistant point locates a perpendicular through the given off-line point without measuring a right angle.

activities.title: Construct a perpendicular at a point on a line
feedback: If B and C are not equally far from A, redraw them using the same circle centred at A; estimating their positions by eye does not establish that A is the midpoint.
If the arcs from B and C fail to cross away from l, increase their common radius beyond half BC.
A measured 90° angle can be an accuracy check, but explain the equal distances to justify why the construction works.
activities.rationale: This editorial addition covers the at-a-point case of the named objective and connects it to the already taught perpendicular bisector. It does not claim measured educational effectiveness.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.
learnerActions: Draw a line l with a given point A on it. Draw a circle centred at A to mark B and C on l, on opposite sides of A, so AB = AC.
Without changing the compass opening between B and C, draw equal-radius arcs from them, using a radius greater than half BC, to meet at D off l.
Rule AD and leave the arcs visible. Explain that A is the midpoint of BC and both A and D are equidistant from B and C, so AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC and is perpendicular to l at A.

Try a sloping line and then explain how this task differs from constructing a perpendicular through a point off the line. After the construction, a protractor can check practical accuracy without replacing the property-based justification.
activities.intendedInsight: The given point on the line can be made the midpoint of a constructed segment BC, so its perpendicular bisector passes through that point.

constraints: Use compasses and an unmarked straight edge to locate the required points and lines from geometric properties, rather than by measuring. A ruler or protractor may check practical accuracy afterwards; such checks do not prove or replace the construction.
Require pupils to leave their construction arcs visible as evidence that the equidistance/rhombus property, not measurement, produced the result.
Keep the compass width unchanged between the two endpoints, and open it to more than half the segment so the arcs intersect above and below.
Present segments and angles at non-standard (diagonal, rotated) orientations, not only horizontal/vertical prototypes.

A dynamic-geometry compass is a concept-building scaffold: it may help pupils reason about equidistance and the rhombus-vs-kite distinction but does not develop the manual dexterity, which must be practised with real compasses afterwards.
Recognition/multiple-choice items assess the reasoning only; they do not evidence the pupil actually executing the construction, which is the performance target.

Treat tolerances such as ±2 mm / ±2° as accuracy targets for the manual skill, distinguishing a dexterity lapse (correct method, slipped arcs) from a conceptual error (unequal radii, measuring instead of constructing).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a static picture and 3D as 'poor' and asserted '3D adds nothing' and that a static picture 'cannot build' the reasoning. These universal comparative claims are replaced here with narrow affordances (a fixed image cannot be manipulated and does not elicit the pupil executing arcs; recognition items do not elicit independent construction). These constructions are planar, so a 3D medium is simply not needed for the 2D locus reasoning; a labelled reference image can still support recall of the rhombus property.

Geometry self-audit: the rhombus/kite reasoning is internally consistent — equal radii from both endpoints give four equal sides (a rhombus) whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect; unequal radii give a kite (axis of symmetry PQ) with perpendicular diagonals, where PQ bisects the constructed line but the constructed line does NOT bisect PQ, so it misses the segment's midpoint. No arithmetic or force/motion content to correct. The 8 cm example (opening must exceed 4 cm, and exactly 4 cm only touches at the midpoint) is correct.

Paper diagrams are flat representations of ideal plane constructions; no solid-shape idealisation issue arises here, but treat drawn arcs as physical approximations of ideal circles when discussing tolerance.

The saved activities omitted perpendiculars from or at a given point even though the objective names them. Two conservative editorial activities now cover these cases using the perpendicular-bisector equidistance property. Original pedagogy and assessment remain unchanged.

The original evidence suggests measuring the two angle halves. This is compatible with a post-construction accuracy check; the construction itself and its justification use equal lengths and congruent triangles, not measurement.

Useful factual-audit repairs retain the common-chord perpendicular direction, correct the kite diagonal scope, and keep circles intersecting in the slider activity. Source claims remain verbatim even where their compressed kite wording needs the qualification given in the activities. No fresh source verification was performed.

probeDeeper: Why must the compass stay open to the same width from both P and Q — what shape are you really making?
If someone changed the compass width and got a line perpendicular to PQ that isn't the bisector, what shape did they make, and why doesn't it bisect?
Could you do this with a ruler and protractor instead? Why would that not count as a construction?
How does the same equal-arc idea let you bisect an ANGLE?
assess.correctAnswer: Opens the compasses to more than half PQ and, WITHOUT changing the radius, draws equal arcs from P and from Q that intersect above and below, then rules the line through the two intersections — leaving the arcs visible; the line passes through the midpoint at 90° (within about ±2 mm / ±2°). For the angle, draws an arc from the vertex crossing both arms, then equal arcs from those two points, and rules the vertex-to-intersection line. Relies on the equal-radius (rhombus) property, not measurement.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the compass radius between the two endpoints, constructing a kite instead of a rhombus — so the line is perpendicular to PQ but does not pass through the midpoint (does not bisect)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground on the rhombus property — four equal radii make a rhombus whose diagonals bisect; a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect — and insist the compass width is unchanged between endpoints
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The arcs from P and from Q have visibly different radii, and the resulting line does not cross PQ at its midpoint

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws rather than constructs — uses a ruler to find the midpoint and a protractor or eye for the right angle — and leaves no construction arcs
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach the draw-vs-construct distinction: a construction produces the result from geometric properties (equidistance), not measurement; require visible construction marks
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Measures PQ to mark its midpoint, judges 90° by eye/protractor, and the page shows a bare line with no arcs

errorPatterns.pattern: Opens the compasses to less than half the segment, so the arcs from P and Q never intersect
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect on both sides; connect to the equidistant-locus reason
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The arcs fail to meet above and/or below the segment, leaving no crossing points to rule through

errorPatterns.pattern: Compass dexterity lapse — the method is right but the arcs slip or are placed imprecisely, so the construction falls outside tolerance
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: give practice time with the equipment (this is usually new at KS3) and consider establishing the concept first with dynamic geometry
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equal radii and visible arcs, but the point/needle slipped and the result is off by more than ±2 mm / ±2°

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce the construction from properties — measures the midpoint, judges the angle by eye, or changes the radius so it fails — with no sense of why it should work.
responseLevels.full: Constructs the perpendicular bisector and angle bisector from the equidistance/rhombus property — radius equal and more than half, arcs left visible, at any orientation — and explains why equal radii force a rhombus whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect.
responseLevels.partial: Executes the memorised steps and often gets a correct-looking bisector, but cannot explain why the equal radii are needed or link it to the rhombus/equidistance property — slips to a kite or to measuring when the orientation is unfamiliar.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a pair of compasses, a straight edge, and a line segment PQ drawn diagonally (not horizontal), plus a marked angle. Say: 'Construct the perpendicular bisector of PQ using only the compasses and straight edge — no ruler measuring and no protractor. Then construct the bisector of this angle.' Watch whether they keep the compass radius equal from both endpoints, open it to more than half PQ, leave their construction arcs, and work from properties rather than measuring.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The finished construction is the evidence: equal-radius arcs and a line through the midpoint show the child used the rhombus/equidistance property; unequal arcs (a kite whose line misses the midpoint), or a ruler-found midpoint with an eyeballed right angle and no arcs, show drawing rather than constructing. A correct property-based construction cannot be produced by measuring.
