pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–14 years

- **Topic:** The Reactivity Series

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Chemical reactions):** pupils are taught "the use of the reactivity series to predict the outcome of displacement reactions" and the reactions of metals with acids, and are expected to represent reactions by word equations; the reactivity series and reduction of metal oxides with carbon underpin metal extraction.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-2):** analyse and interpret data on the properties of reactants and products to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred — displacement is evidenced by colour change, temperature change and a deposited metal.

- **Operational details:** Establish the ordered list of common metals (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold) as a ranking of how strongly each metal holds on to — or grabs — electrons/oxygen. Ground the order in observed evidence: vigour of reaction with water and with acid. Then teach the two big payoffs: (1) displacement — a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its compound (e.g. iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper, with the tell-tale orange copper coating); (2) extraction — carbon sits partway up the series, so it can reduce oxides of metals BELOW it (iron) but not those ABOVE it (aluminium, which needs electrolysis). Tie the order to history: gold found native, iron smelted with carbon since antiquity, aluminium only isolated once electricity was available.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early to formal). Given two metals or a metal and a metal-salt solution, the child predicts whether displacement happens and explains, using position in the series, why carbon extracts iron but not aluminium.
bestPractices: Build the series from evidence — have pupils rank metals by observed vigour with water and acid — rather than issuing the order as a mnemonic to memorise.
Teach displacement as the operational meaning of 'more reactive': a metal higher in the series pushes a lower one out of its compound, seen as a deposited metal and a colour change.
Use the position of carbon in the series to explain the industrial dividing line — carbon reduces oxides below it (iron) but metals above it (aluminium) need electrolysis.
Connect the series to the historical timeline of metal use (gold native, iron smelted, aluminium electrolytic) so the abstract order carries a concrete story.
Keep representation at word-equation level and reason qualitatively; save electrode half-equations and quantitative electrolysis for KS4.
keyRepresentations: The vertical reactivity ladder from potassium (top) to gold (bottom), with carbon and hydrogen marked as reference points.
A displacement grid (metal strips × metal-salt solutions) showing which pairings react.
Word equations for displacement, e.g. iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper.
A reaction-vigour bar chart from metal + water/acid tests.
A historical timeline linking extraction difficulty to when each metal came into use.
commonMisconceptions: Treating the series as an arbitrary list to memorise rather than an ordering by measurable reactivity.
Thinking any metal can displace any other, rather than only a more reactive metal displacing a less reactive one.
Believing carbon can extract all metals, missing that metals above carbon (e.g. aluminium) need electrolysis.
Confusing 'reactive' with 'strong' or 'heavy' — assuming gold or iron must be very reactive because they are hard or dense.
Assuming the deposited copper in a displacement reaction is a coating of the original metal rather than newly formed copper metal.

learn.summary: Learners build the reactivity series of common metals (potassium down to gold) from observed evidence rather than memorising a mnemonic, then use positions in the series to predict displacement reactions and to explain why carbon can extract some metals (iron) but not others (aluminium, which needs electrolysis). Representation stays at the word-equation, qualitative level appropriate for ages 12–14; electrode half-equations and quantitative electrolysis are deferred to later study.

activities.title: Rank the metals by observed vigour
feedback: If a learner places a metal by its hardness, weight, or value, point them back to the recorded reaction evidence: soft, light sodium reacts far more vigorously than dense, heavy, valuable gold. Ranking follows how eagerly it reacts, not how strong or heavy it is.
If the order is handed back as a memorised string with no justification, ask them to point to the specific observation (fizz rate, temperature change) that supports one pair's ordering.
Confirm correct placements by connecting them to the observation: 'Yes — copper did nothing with acid, so it sits low.'
activities.rationale: Deriving the series from comparative observation targets the core misconception that the list is arbitrary and anchors 'reactive' in observable behaviour rather than physical properties. Building order from evidence matches the KS3 expectation to use the reactivity series and study reactions of metals with acids, and the NGSS emphasis on interpreting data to determine whether a reaction occurred. The most vigorous metals are kept to simulation/demonstration on safety grounds.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the reactivity series to predict the outcome of displacement reactions and study reactions of metals with acids.
Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Observe each of several metals reacting with water and, separately, with dilute acid, recording what happens: fizzing rate, bubbles, any temperature rise, whether anything happens at all. The most reactive metals (potassium, sodium) are never handled by learners: their reactions with water are shown by simulation or teacher demonstration only, and their reactions with acid are far too violent to demonstrate, so these are shown by simulation only. Safer metals (e.g. magnesium, zinc, iron, copper) can be tested hands-on where feasible.

Use the observations to arrange the metals into an ordered list from most reactive to least reactive. For example, note from the demonstration/simulation that potassium reacts violently, that magnesium fizzes strongly in acid, and that copper shows essentially no reaction.
Mark where carbon and hydrogen sit as reference points once the metal order is established from the evidence.
Write a short justification for the placement of two chosen metals, citing the specific observation (e.g. 'magnesium is above zinc because it fizzed faster in the same acid').
activities.intendedInsight: The reactivity series is an ordering by measurable reactivity — how vigorously a metal reacts with water and acid — not an arbitrary list to recite. Position reflects evidence.

activities.title: Displacement grid — more reactive pushes out less reactive
feedback: If a learner predicts that any two metals/solution pairings react, show the empty cells: copper in magnesium sulfate does nothing. Displacement runs one direction only — more reactive displaces less reactive.
If a learner says the orange solid is a coating of the iron, clarify that iron has dissolved into solution (forming iron sulfate) while copper has come out of solution as new copper metal.
Reinforce correct predictions by tying them to series position: 'Magnesium is above copper, so it displaces it — exactly what you saw.'
activities.rationale: A comparison grid makes the directionality of displacement visible and directly confronts the 'any two metals react' and 'coating is the original metal' misconceptions. Word equations keep representation at the appropriate KS3 level. Running comparative reactions and interpreting the outcomes matches both the UK displacement standard and the NGSS data-interpretation emphasis.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the reactivity series to predict the outcome of displacement reactions and study reactions of metals with acids.
Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Lower each metal strip (e.g. iron nail, zinc, magnesium, copper) into each of several metal-salt solutions (e.g. copper sulfate, magnesium sulfate, zinc sulfate) and record which pairings react and which do nothing.
Observe the tell-tale signs of displacement: an iron nail in blue copper sulfate grows an orange copper coating while the blue colour fades.
For each cell of the grid, state before testing whether you expect a reaction based on the series, then compare with what happens.
Write the word equation for a reaction that occurred, e.g. iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper.
Explain whether the orange solid on the nail is the original metal or newly formed copper.
activities.intendedInsight: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound, and the reaction runs only one way. The deposited metal (e.g. copper) is newly formed, not a transferred coating of the original metal.

activities.title: Extraction bench — why carbon works for iron but not aluminium
feedback: If a learner thinks carbon can extract all metals, revisit carbon's position: metals above it (aluminium) resist reduction by carbon and need electrolysis.

If a learner says gold is unreactive because it is rare or precious, flip the causation: gold is found native and never tarnishes because it is unreactive; iron and aluminium are harder to extract because they are more reactive.
Confirm sound reasoning that connects position → extraction method → historical order.
activities.rationale: Using carbon's position to explain the industrial dividing line is a direct KS3/RSC objective and targets the misconception that carbon extracts all metals and the reversed cause–effect about gold's rarity. The historical strand gives the abstract order a concrete narrative. RSC resources state carbon's extraction limit as a chemistry principle; the activity presents it qualitatively.
sourceClaims: Carbon can reduce the oxides of metals less reactive than itself (e.g. iron) but not more reactive metals (e.g. aluminium), which require electrolysis.
learnerActions: Watch a teacher demonstration or simulation of heating a metal oxide with carbon and record the result: iron oxide is reduced to iron, while aluminium oxide is not reduced. (This is a high-temperature reaction, so it is demonstrated or simulated, not run hands-on by learners.)
Locate carbon's position in the series and identify which metal oxides lie below it (can be reduced by carbon) and which lie above it (cannot).
State the method needed to extract aluminium (electrolysis) and explain why carbon alone is not enough.

Build a short timeline linking extraction difficulty to history: gold found native (unreactive), iron smelted with carbon since antiquity, aluminium first isolated only in the 1820s (using an even more reactive metal, not carbon) and made cheaply in bulk only after industrial electrolysis began in the 1880s.
Explain the direction of cause and effect: gold is found as pure nuggets because it is unreactive — its rarity does not cause its low reactivity.
activities.intendedInsight: Carbon can reduce oxides of metals below it in the series (e.g. iron) but not those above it (e.g. aluminium), which require electrolysis. Reactivity causes the extraction difficulty and the historical timeline, not the other way round.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: the paired beakers
feedback: 'Copper wins because it is tougher/stronger' → separate chemical reactivity from physical strength: magnesium is more reactive than copper regardless of hardness, so magnesium displaces copper.
'Both react' → displacement runs one way only; copper is below magnesium, so copper cannot displace magnesium.
Full credit depends on predicting the single correct reaction and giving the direction before observing, using series position — not on which metal looks stronger or heavier.
For the chained case: magnesium is above zinc, which is above iron, so magnesium displaces iron from iron sulfate — high confidence from the transitive ordering.
activities.rationale: The paired setup discriminates between a reactivity-based model and strength/weight/'always reacts' models, because only the correct model predicts exactly one reaction and its direction. Predict-before-observe surfaces the learner's reasoning rather than letting the observation do the work. This mirrors the diagnostic assessment design for the topic.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the reactivity series to predict the outcome of displacement reactions and study reactions of metals with acids.
Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Before anything is mixed, look at two setups: a strip of magnesium going into blue copper sulfate, and a strip of copper going into colourless magnesium sulfate. Predict which one reacts and WHY.
Commit your reasoning in writing before observing — this prediction is the point of the task.
Observe: only the magnesium-in-copper-sulfate reacts (blue fades, copper deposits on the strip); copper in magnesium sulfate does nothing.
Explain the result using reactivity order, then extend: if magnesium displaces zinc and zinc displaces iron, predict what magnesium does to iron sulfate and how confident you are.
Answer the challenge: why won't ranking metals by how heavy they are predict displacement?
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering metals by reactivity predicts exactly one reaction and names its direction. A model based on 'stronger/heavier/tougher wins' or 'any two metals react' mispredicts. The reasoning, not just the observation, shows understanding.

activities.title: Reactivity ladder reference with history cards
feedback: If a learner leans on the ladder to answer prediction questions without reasoning, prompt them to justify from the relative positions rather than reading off a memorised rank.
Encourage cross-checking: 'Does the reaction you observed match where this metal sits on the ladder?'
activities.rationale: A static annotated ladder is a useful consolidation and reference aid for vocabulary, extraction methods, and the historical strand. Its limit: it does not let a learner generate the order from evidence or test predictions, which is where conceptual understanding forms, so it supports rather than replaces the investigative activities.
learnerActions: Consult a labelled vertical reactivity ladder from potassium (top) to gold (bottom), with carbon and hydrogen marked as reference points, to check vocabulary and ordering.
For a chosen metal, review its reaction with water and acid, its extraction method, and a short history note (gold found native, iron smelted, aluminium electrolytic).
Use the ladder as a lookup aid while doing the prediction and extraction tasks — not as the primary way to first learn the order.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference ladder consolidates vocabulary and the agreed order and links each position to extraction method and history.

constraints: Keep representation at word-equation level and reason qualitatively; defer electrode half-equations and quantitative electrolysis to later (KS4) study.
Build the series from observed evidence (vigour with water and acid) rather than issuing the order as a mnemonic to memorise.

Reactions of the most reactive metals (potassium, sodium) with water must be simulation or teacher demonstration only; learners never handle alkali metals. Limit hands-on pupil work to safer metals (e.g. magnesium, zinc, iron, copper).
Heating metal oxides with carbon is a high-temperature teacher demonstration or simulation, not an open pupil-run task.

The annotated reference ladder is a consolidation and lookup scaffold; on its own it does not let learners derive the order from evidence or test displacement predictions, so pair it with investigative tasks.

Recognition and lookup tasks (reading a ladder, selecting an answer) check ordering and vocabulary but do not elicit independent prediction and explanation; include tasks where the learner states a prediction and its reason before observing.

Use real hands-on displacement work (e.g. an iron nail in copper sulfate) where safe and feasible; a simulated bench is a complement, not a required substitute, and claims about any particular medium being uniquely necessary are not established here.

The historical timeline (native gold, carbon-smelted iron, electrolytic aluminium) is enrichment that illustrates the series; present reactivity as the cause of extraction difficulty, not the reverse.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the teaching principle, not the efficacy of any specific activity.

Two of the three sources (NGSS MS-PS1-2 and the RSC extraction resource) were marked unverified in the source row; the carbon-extraction limit and the NGSS data-interpretation framing are carried over on that basis and should be re-checked.

Safety: Activity 1 keeps the most reactive metals (potassium, sodium) to simulation/teacher demonstration only, with hands-on learner work restricted to safer metals; Activity 3's carbon reduction is likewise demonstration/simulation only because of the high temperatures involved. Matching constraints are included.

Attribution correction this pass: Activity 3's sourceClaims was reduced to the RSC carbon-extraction claim only; the DfE displacement/acids claim was removed there because it supports the topic generally but not the specific carbon-reduction principle of that activity.

Self-audit: the displacement direction logic (more reactive displaces less reactive; reverse does nothing) and the transitive chain (magnesium > zinc > copper ⇒ magnesium displaces copper) are internally consistent and were retained. The reversed cause–effect error about gold (rarity causing low reactivity) was corrected in the activity, not merely caveated.

Self-audit: the claim that carbon reduces oxides below it but not above it is a standard qualitative teaching model, presented qualitatively; aluminium-requires-electrolysis is kept at that level without asserting mechanism beyond KS3 scope. Zinc, lying below carbon, can be carbon-reduced — left to the general principle rather than enumerated.

Original source material framed a dialogue/conversation format and a 3D environment as adding 'nothing' or being unable to substitute; these universal-necessity claims were dropped and replaced with scoped notes on affordances and limits.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: show the two beakers (magnesium in copper sulfate; copper in magnesium sulfate). Ask the child to predict which changes and WHY before dropping the metals in. A 'toughest wins' or 'both react' model mispredicts. Only the magnesium beaker reacts (blue fades, copper deposits). The pre-observation reasoning by reactivity order is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Why can carbon extract iron from iron oxide but NOT aluminium from aluminium oxide?
Gold is found as pure nuggets in rivers but iron is always in rocks as ore — what does that tell you about their reactivity?
If zinc displaces copper, and magnesium displaces zinc, what does magnesium do to copper sulfate — and how sure are you?
Someone ranks metals by how heavy they are. Why won't that predict displacement?
assess.correctAnswer: Only magnesium-in-copper-sulfate reacts: magnesium is MORE reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution (blue fades, copper coats the strip). Copper-in-magnesium-sulfate does nothing because copper is LESS reactive than magnesium and can't displace it. The rule: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound. Full marks turn on ordering by reactivity, not on which looks stronger/heavier.

errorPatterns.pattern: reactivity means how hard/strong/heavy or how dangerous a metal is ('copper is tougher so it wins')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate chemical reactivity from physical strength — soft, light sodium is far MORE reactive than hard, dense gold. Rank by how eagerly each reacts, not by hardness.
errorPatterns.distractor: Copper reacts, because copper is a tougher, stronger metal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts the reaction by physical toughness or density rather than position in the reactivity series

errorPatterns.pattern: any two metals will react if you put them together ('metals always react with each other')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Displacement only runs one way — more reactive displaces less reactive; the reverse does nothing. Line up several pairs and predict each using the series.
errorPatterns.distractor: Both react, because whenever you mix two metals something happens.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts both mixtures react, with no notion of direction

errorPatterns.pattern: gold is unreactive because it is rare/precious (cause and effect reversed)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Flip it: gold is found as pure nuggets and never tarnishes BECAUSE it's unreactive; iron must be smelted and aluminium needs electrolysis because they're more reactive. Reactivity explains extraction history.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains gold's low reactivity by its rarity/value rather than the other way round

responseLevels.gap: Predicts by strength/weight/rarity or says any two metals react; can't name which of the pair reacts or why.
responseLevels.full: Orders metals by reactivity, predicts displacement direction for any pair, explains extraction method by position (native gold, carbon-smelted iron, electrolysed aluminium), and reasons that reactivity CAUSES the extraction difficulty — not the reverse.
responseLevels.partial: Predicts the magnesium case correctly and cites 'more reactive displaces less reactive', but can't extend to extraction (carbon/aluminium) or chain multiple displacements — the rule without its reach.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I drop a strip of magnesium into blue copper sulfate solution, and separately a strip of copper into colourless magnesium sulfate solution. In ONE of them a reaction happens and in the other nothing does. Which one reacts — and the important part, WHY that one and not the other?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The paired setup is the discriminator: a child who orders metals by reactivity predicts exactly one reaction and names the direction; a child who thinks 'the stronger/harder/heavier metal wins' or that any two metals react cannot say which, or predicts both. The reason, not the observation, reveals the model.

pedagogy.summary: Calculating simple probability is the procedural skill of applying P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes to equally-likely situations and giving the answer as a fraction in simplest form. The work is fluent, accurate execution across contexts (dice, bags, spinners): counting the favourable outcomes, counting the TOTAL (which includes the favourable ones), forming the fraction, checking the outcomes are equally likely, and simplifying.
bestPractices: Rehearse the same three-step routine across varied contexts — count favourable, count total, write and simplify — so it transfers beyond dice
Make explicit that the total is the WHOLE set of outcomes (favourable included), heading off the part-part error
Require a check that outcomes are equally likely BEFORE applying the formula
Connect 'more favourable outcomes → larger probability' by varying a bag's composition and watching the fraction grow
Always express in simplest form and confirm the simplified fraction names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale
keyRepresentations: P(event) = favourable/total written under the situation
Bags, dice, spinners with countable equally-likely outcomes
Simplified-fraction equivalence (2/8 = 1/4) on the 0-to-1 scale
Part-whole diagram of the outcome set
commonMisconceptions: Writing favourable-to-unfavourable (part-part) instead of favourable-over-total — e.g. 3/7 rather than 3/10 for 3 blue among 10
Applying the formula to situations whose outcomes are not equally likely (an uneven spinner, a weighted die)
Failing to simplify, or simplifying incorrectly
Miscounting the total — forgetting to include the favourable outcomes in the denominator

learn.summary: Learners build fluency with P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes for equally-likely situations, giving answers as fractions in simplest form. The core routine is: check the outcomes are equally likely, count favourable outcomes, count the TOTAL (which includes the favourable ones), form the fraction, and simplify. Practice should span varied contexts (dice, bags, spinners) and target the part-part error (favourable-to-unfavourable) and the misapplication of the formula to unequal outcomes.

activities.title: Varied probability ladder with simplest form
feedback: If a learner writes 3/7 for the bag, recount the whole set aloud including the favourable outcomes: everything that could be drawn is 10, so 10 goes on the bottom, giving 3/10.

If a learner applies the formula to an uneven spinner, prompt the equally-likely check first: when sections are different sizes the colour counts are not counts of equally-likely outcomes, so the simple formula does not apply.

If a learner leaves 2/8 unsimplified or reduces it wrongly, scaffold the simplifying step and confirm 1/4 sits at the same point on the 0-to-1 scale \u2014 simplifying does not change the actual chance.
If a learner combines numbers arbitrarily with no favourable-over-total structure, return to counting favourable, then total, then writing the fraction.
activities.rationale: The objective is fluent, accurate execution of favourable/total across contexts with simplest-form answers. Varied contexts support transfer beyond dice, and items built from the exact errors (part-part, unsimplified, formula on an uneven spinner) make the common mistakes surface and get corrected.
sourceClaims: The probability of an equally-likely event is favourable outcomes over total outcomes, written and simplified as a fraction; e.g. P(blue) for 3 blue among a total of counters is favourable/total.

Children tend to use additive/part-part comparisons and give the raw frequencies of outcomes rather than the part-whole proportion, so favourable-over-total must be taught explicitly against the part-part error.
learnerActions: Work a short series of problems, each a probability to be formed and then simplified: (a) a bag of 3 blue and 7 red marbles \u2014 find P(blue); (b) a fair six-sided die \u2014 find P(rolling a 4); (c) a spinner with 8 equal sections, 2 of them gold \u2014 find P(gold).
For each item, first confirm the outcomes are equally likely, then count the favourable outcomes, then count the WHOLE set of possible outcomes (including the favourable ones) for the denominator.
Write each probability as a fraction and simplify where possible (e.g. 2/8 \u2192 1/4).
On the bag item, if you write 3/7, stop and recount: the denominator is all 10 marbles, including the 3 blue ones, so the answer is 3/10.
Encounter at least one unequal-outcome situation (e.g. an uneven spinner with different-sized sections) and decide whether the simple formula applies before using it.
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator is the whole set of equally-likely outcomes, favourable included \u2014 so P(blue) among 3 blue and 7 red is 3/10, not 3/7. The simple favourable/total formula only applies when outcomes are equally likely, and simplifying (2/8 = 1/4) names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale.

activities.title: Editable bag: watch the fraction form and simplify
feedback: If a learner expects only the numerator to matter, vary the non-favourable counts and show that the denominator (whole set) and the scale marker both respond \u2014 e.g. adding red marbles enlarges the total, so P(blue) falls (as long as the bag has at least one blue; with no blue it stays 0).
Confirm that the simplified fraction lands on the same point of the 0-to-1 line as the unsimplified one \u2014 the chance is unchanged.
activities.rationale: A live model that forms favourable/total as the child edits the bag, shows simplification, and marks the scale can reinforce WHY the denominator is the whole set and how composition drives the value. This may support conceptual understanding alongside the procedural fluency. The interactive updating (live fraction, scale marker) is an optional illustrative mechanism, not required equipment.
sourceClaims: The probability of an equally-likely event is favourable outcomes over total outcomes, written and simplified as a fraction; e.g. P(blue) for 3 blue among a total of counters is favourable/total.
learnerActions: Edit the composition of a bag (e.g. add or remove blue and red counters) and read the probability fraction as it forms.
Identify the WHOLE set as the denominator each time the bag changes, confirming favourable counters are part of that total.
Watch the simplified form of the fraction and a marker on a 0-to-1 line move as the composition changes.
Predict: 'If I add 5 more red marbles, which number in the fraction changes, and does P(blue) go up or down?' then check against the live display.
activities.intendedInsight: More favourable outcomes relative to the whole set raise the probability; the denominator is always the whole outcome set. Seeing the fraction and its position on the scale update as the bag changes connects composition to the value of the probability.

activities.title: Worked example and Socratic 'out of how many?' check
feedback: If a learner gives odds (part-part, e.g. 3 to 7), re-pose 'and out of how many altogether?' until they name 10 as the whole set.
Confirm the worked fraction is in simplest form before moving on.
activities.rationale: A worked example plus targeted questioning models the routine and can surface the part-part misconception through explanation. This may build understanding but, on its own, does not supply the repeated varied practice that fluency needs \u2014 pair it with the practice ladder.
sourceClaims: Children tend to use additive/part-part comparisons and give the raw frequencies of outcomes rather than the part-whole proportion, so favourable-over-total must be taught explicitly against the part-part error.
learnerActions: Study a worked die or bag example: identify the favourable outcomes, then the whole set, then reveal the simplified fraction.
When asked 'and out of how many altogether?', state the full count of possible outcomes, not just the non-favourable ones.
Explain in your own words why the total includes the favourable outcomes.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the total as the whole set (favourable included) catches the part-part slip before it becomes a habit and makes the structure of the formula explicit.

constraints: Require an equally-likely check BEFORE applying favourable/total; the simple formula does not apply to uneven spinners, weighted dice, or other unequal-outcome situations.
Make explicit that the total is the WHOLE set of outcomes, with favourable outcomes included \u2014 this heads off the part-part (favourable-to-unfavourable) error.
Always express answers in simplest form and confirm the simplified fraction names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale.
A worked example with tap-to-reveal counts models the routine but cannot by itself provide the repeated, varied practice fluency requires; use it as an introduction alongside practice.

A single final answer does not reveal whether the learner counted the whole set, checked equal-likelihood, or simplified; favour formats that require constructing and simplifying the fraction across varied contexts.
The editable-bag live fraction, simplification display, and 0-to-1 scale marker are optional illustrative supports, not mandatory mechanisms or specific products.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked values: P(blue) with 3 blue of 10 total = 3/10; P(4) on a fair six-sided die = 1/6; P(gold) with 2 of 8 equal sections = 2/8 = 1/4. These are internally consistent across the source fields.
The part-part value 3/7 (3 blue to 7 red) is intentionally retained only as an error to be corrected, never presented as a valid answer.

Source claims support the favourable/total principle and the need to teach against the part-part error; they do not establish comparative efficacy of any particular activity format (quiz vs interactive vs dialogue). Any 'only a quiz drills this' or '3D adds nothing' framing has been reduced to scoped statements about observable affordances.

The legacy pedagogy summary listed the equally-likely check after forming the fraction, while its best-practice guidance placed the check before applying the formula; the corrected routine places the check first, consistent with the stated best practice.

probeDeeper: In 3/10, where does the 10 come from — is blue part of it?
You wrote P(gold) = 2/8. Can you write that more simply? Does simplifying change the actual chance?
If I added 5 more red marbles, which number in your fraction changes, and does P(blue) go up or down?
Would this formula still work if the spinner's sections were different sizes? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: (a) P(blue) = 3/10 — three favourable out of ten counters altogether, blue included in the total; (b) P(4) = 1/6; (c) P(gold) = 2/8 = 1/4 simplified. The child forms favourable/TOTAL each time, puts the whole set in the denominator, and simplifies where possible.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes favourable-to-unfavourable (part-part) instead of favourable-over-total — e.g. 3/7 for 3 blue among 10
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recount the whole set aloud including the favourable outcomes; the total is everything that could be drawn, so 10 not 7 goes on the bottom
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The denominator is the count of the OTHER outcomes rather than the whole set

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies favourable/total to a situation whose outcomes are not equally likely
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the equally-likely check first; if sections are unequal the colour counts are not counts of equally likely outcomes and the simple formula does not apply
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses the formula straight onto an uneven spinner or weighted device without checking the sections/outcomes are equal

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to simplify, or simplifies incorrectly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the simplifying step and confirm the simplified fraction sits at the same point on the scale; this is an execution lapse, not a conceptual gap
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Leaves 2/8 unsimplified or reduces it wrongly

responseLevels.gap: Cannot form the fraction or combines numbers arbitrarily; no favourable-over-total structure
responseLevels.full: Computes favourable/total across all three contexts with the whole set in the denominator, checks the outcomes are equally likely, and gives each answer in simplest form
responseLevels.partial: Forms favourable/total for the easy die case but writes part-part for the bag, forgets or botches simplifying, or applies the formula without checking equal-likelihood

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three problems on cards with paper: (a) a bag of 3 blue and 7 red marbles — find P(blue); (b) a fair six-sided die — find P(rolling a 4); (c) a spinner with 8 equal sections, 2 of them gold — find P(gold). Say: 'Work out each probability and write it as a fraction in its simplest form.' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they count the TOTAL correctly, whether they check the outcomes are equally likely, and whether they simplify.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching reveals whether the denominator is the whole set (3/10) or the leftovers (3/7), whether they check equal-likelihood before applying the formula, and whether they simplify — none of which a single final answer would expose.

sources.claim: Children tend to use additive/part-part comparisons and give the raw frequencies of outcomes rather than the part-whole proportion, so favourable-over-total must be taught explicitly against the part-part error.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1). Understand SUBTRACTION as taking away / separating from a group to find how many remain. The single most central node in the domain (centrality 0.65) — partner concept to addition-as-combining and the root of all later subtraction work.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'read, write and interpret mathematical statements involving… subtraction (−)…'; 'solve one-step problems that involve… subtraction, using concrete objects and pictorial representations, and missing number problems such as 7 = ? − 9'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.1/2 represent subtraction and solve take-from problems within 10; take-from (result unknown) is the canonical entry semantics.
• Operational details — Introduce take-away/separate first (remove objects, count what's left), but flag early that subtraction ALSO answers 'how many more/difference' and 'missing part' — these comparison and unknown-part meanings are where children later struggle if only 'take away' is taught. Model the physical removal, narrate it, then count the remainder. Keep within 5-10 with objects the child physically removes.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): physically remove some objects and count how many remain. Tier B (age 5): act out a take-from story ('5 biscuits, eat 2') and say how many are left. Tier C (age 5-6): explain subtraction as finding what's left, and recognise a simple 'how many more' difference situation as also being subtraction.
bestPractices: Start with take-away/separate (physically remove and count the remainder) because it is the most concrete meaning, but do NOT stop there — deliberately introduce comparison ('how many more') and missing-part meanings so subtraction isn't permanently equated with 'take away'.
Keep the removed part visible then hidden: showing what was taken and what remains helps the child see the whole splitting into part-taken and part-left (links to part-part-whole).
Narrate action then result ('5 biscuits, take away 2… 3 are left') so 'how many left/remain' attaches to the remaining quantity.
Use the same manipulatives and stories as addition, then contrast: combining makes more, separating leaves fewer — building addition and subtraction as inverse actions from the very start.
Ground the missing-number form (7 = ? − 9 style, or 5 − ? = 3) in acting out, so subtraction-as-unknown-part has an early concrete seed for later formalisation.
keyRepresentations: A group of physical objects with some physically removed/covered (take-away)
Ten-frame with counters removed, remainder visible
Part-part-whole model: whole splits into part-taken and part-left
Two rows of objects lined up for 'how many more' comparison (difference)
Act-out story scenes and drawings with a crossing-out to show removal
commonMisconceptions: Equating subtraction ONLY with 'take away', so comparison ('how many more') and missing-part problems aren't recognised as subtraction — the classic long-run difficulty.
Trying to 'take away' the larger from the smaller in a comparison and getting confused, or reversing to keep it 'takeable'.
Recounting the whole rather than the remainder, or counting the removed objects instead of what's left.
Believing subtraction always makes a number 'small' and being surprised that 8 − 1 is still large.
Reading 7 − 3 left-to-right as an instruction with no sense that it asks 'how many remain', so missing-number forms feel impossible.

learn.summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), build subtraction as taking away / separating from a group to find how many remain — physically removing objects and counting what is left — while deliberately seeding the comparison ('how many more'/difference) and missing-part meanings so subtraction is not permanently equated only with 'take away'. Keep quantities within 5-10 with objects the child physically handles. Introduce take-away first because it is the most concrete meaning, then contrast with addition-as-combining so the two are felt as inverse actions from the start.

activities.title: Take-away mat: remove and read what's left
feedback: If the child reports 2 (how many eaten): physically separate the 2, then point to the remaining group and ask 'how many are LEFT?'; name the difference between the result and the action.
If the child answers 7 (adds the numbers): act the story out — start with 5 and physically take 2 away — so the situation, not the two numbers, drives the operation.

If the child recounts the whole remaining set slowly from one instead of counting back: accept it. Let them recount the remainder; counting-back matures later and slow recounting is not an error here.
Probe: 'Show me with the biscuits what eating 2 does to the pile.' 'Which biscuits are the answer — the ones you ate or the ones still there?'
activities.rationale: Take-away/separate is the most concrete entry meaning; letting the child perform the removal and attend to the remainder targets the common errors of reporting the amount taken, reporting the original whole instead of what is left, or adding. Keeping the removed part briefly visible then hidden helps the child see the whole splitting into part-taken and part-left (part-part-whole).
sourceClaims: K.OA.1/2: represent subtraction with objects/drawings and solve take-from word problems within 10.
Y1 pupils read/write/interpret statements involving − and solve one-step subtraction and missing-number problems (e.g. 7 = ? − 9) with concrete objects and pictorial representations.
learnerActions: Start with 5 biscuits on a plate; physically remove (drag/take) 2 into a bin.
Watch or track the remaining count fall as you remove: 5 → 4 → 3.
Say and, if ready, assemble the statement '5 − 2 = 3'.
Point to which biscuits are the answer — the ones still on the plate, not the ones taken.
Narrate the action then the result: '5 biscuits, take away 2… 3 are left.'
activities.intendedInsight: The starting group splits into 'gone' and 'left', and the answer to a take-away is what remains — subtraction felt as a physical removal, with 'how many left' attached to the remaining quantity.

activities.title: Difference mode: 'how many more?' as subtraction
feedback: If the child tries to 'take away' the larger from the smaller or reverses the rows to keep it 'takeable': re-align the two rows one-to-one and point only to the unmatched tail as the answer.
Reinforce by lining the rows up physically so the matched pairs and the leftover tail are visually clear.
activities.rationale: Comparison and missing-part meanings are where children later struggle if only 'take away' is taught; aligning two rows makes the difference visible and concrete. This extends, rather than replaces, the take-away activity.
sourceClaims: Subtraction should be taught across take-away, comparison (difference) and missing-part meanings, not take-away alone, to prevent long-run difficulty.
learnerActions: Line up two rows of objects, one under the other, matching them one-to-one.
Find the unmatched tail — the objects in the longer row with no partner.
Count that leftover tail to answer 'how many more does this row have?'
Connect it back: this 'how many more' is also a subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction also answers comparison/difference questions ('how many more'), not only 'take away'. Meeting difference early is intended to help prevent the long-run difficulty of not recognising comparison problems as subtraction.

activities.title: Mystery removed: reason back to the missing part
feedback: If the child is stuck, let them act it out with real objects: start from the whole, remove groups, and check which removal leaves the remaining amount.
Keep the missing-number idea grounded in action rather than as abstract symbol manipulation at this age.
activities.rationale: Grounding the missing-number form in acting out gives subtraction-as-unknown-part an early concrete seed for later formalisation and links to inverse/unknown-addend thinking; it also addresses the misconception that a subtraction statement is just an instruction to perform rather than a relationship between a whole and its parts, where any one part can be the unknown.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils read/write/interpret statements involving − and solve one-step subtraction and missing-number problems (e.g. 7 = ? − 9) with concrete objects and pictorial representations.
Subtraction should be taught across take-away, comparison (difference) and missing-part meanings, not take-away alone, to prevent long-run difficulty.
learnerActions: See the starting group (e.g. 5) and the remaining group (e.g. 3), with the taken pile hidden or covered.
Work out how many must have been removed to leave what's there.
Act out or check by uncovering the hidden pile.
Say it as a missing-part sentence, e.g. '5 − ? = 3'.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction can ask for the unknown part that was taken away — an early concrete seed for missing-number forms (e.g. 5 − ? = 3, or 3 = 5 − ?) and for subtraction-and-addition as inverse actions. Acting it out also counters reading a written statement as a bare left-to-right instruction with no sense of the quantities involved.

activities.title: Still-scene anchor and take-from stories
feedback: Use the scene to confirm the remainder, but move to objects the child removes so they perform the action rather than only recognise the aftermath.
When talking, keep real objects present so reasoning is grounded, not reliant on still-forming language alone.
Ask: 'If you ate 3 instead of 2, would more or fewer be left? Why?' 'A friend says 5 take away 2 is 7 — what would you tell them?'
activities.rationale: A static crossed-out scene and tap-to-reveal anchor the take-away meaning and are useful supports; spoken co-play surfaces reasoning. These are anchors/scaffolds rather than the primary builder because the concept is about acting on objects, and recognising a revealed answer does not itself elicit the child's own removal.
sourceClaims: K.OA.1/2: represent subtraction with objects/drawings and solve take-from word problems within 10.
learnerActions: Look at a take-from scene (e.g. 5 biscuits, 2 with a bite taken or crossed out) and tap/lift a flap to reveal 'how many left?'.
Act out take-from stories aloud with real objects: '5 biscuits, eat 2 — how many are left?'
Alongside a parent or partner, talk through 'we ate some — how many are left?' while handling the actual objects.
Use the same manipulatives and stories used for addition, then contrast: combining makes more, separating leaves fewer.
activities.intendedInsight: A still take-from picture and spoken stories anchor the take-away meaning and language; contrasting with addition builds subtraction and addition as inverse actions.

constraints: Keep quantities within 5-10 and use objects the child can physically remove.

Do not stop at 'take away': deliberately introduce comparison (difference) and missing-part meanings. The evidence base identifies that if only 'take away' is taught, children tend to stop recognising comparison and missing-part problems as subtraction — the classic long-run difficulty.

A still take-from picture (crossed-out/bite scene with tap-to-reveal) anchors the take-away meaning but does not let the child perform the removal or explore comparison/missing-part meanings; treat it as a scaffold, not the sole teacher.

Talk-only prompts lean on still-forming language at this age; pair any 'how many are left?' conversation with real objects rather than using it alone. This does not mean talk cannot support reasoning.
Do not insist on counting-back or mark slow recounting of the remainder as wrong; counting-back matures later. Removing objects and recounting the remainder is acceptable.

Scored, linear picture quizzes are developmentally weak for ages 4-6; a small picture item may check recognition of 'how many left' but does not itself elicit the child's own physical removal, so keep any such item minor and not the primary route for building the concept.

Watch for 'subtraction always makes a number small': show that taking away leaves fewer than the start but not necessarily a small amount (e.g. 8 − 1 = 7, still a lot), so the child isn't surprised by it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three listed sources, the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified; the Common Core (K.OA) and NCETM/CGI comparison-structures claims are marked unverified in the source row — the comparative/structural guidance they support (including the 'guards against long-run difficulty' rationale) should be treated as informed practice, not confirmed efficacy.

The 'live remainder counter' and automatic sentence assembly are optional interaction examples that make the removal mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory. The core learning works with any physically removable objects.

Original row framed a static image as showing 'only the aftermath' and 3D as adding 'nothing'/only handling cost; these are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy claims, and are not asserted here. A still scene can still anchor the meaning; different media simply offer different experiences.
The audit retains the genuine objective limit that still pictures and recognition/reveal formats do not elicit the child's own physical removal, without claiming any medium is universally necessary.

The original misconception of reading a subtraction statement as a bare left-to-right instruction (so missing-number forms feel impossible) is addressed explicitly in the 'mystery removed' activity by grounding the symbolic form in acting out.

probeDeeper: Show me with the biscuits what 'eating 2' does to the pile.
If you ate 3 instead of 2, would more or fewer be left? Why?
Which biscuits are the answer — the ones you ate or the ones still there?
A friend says 5 take away 2 is 7. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: 3 — by removing 2 from the 5 and attending to what REMAINS (counting the leftover, or counting back 5 → 4 → 3), not by counting the ones taken away or by combining.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the amount TAKEN AWAY (2) instead of what is left — attends to the action, not the result.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically separate the 2, then draw attention to the remaining group and ask 'how many are LEFT'; label result vs action.
errorPatterns.distractor: 2 — that's how many you ate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 2 and points to the eaten biscuits.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back from one / recounts the whole set rather than counting back, or loses track counting back.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT insist on counting-back or mark slow recounting as wrong — remove the objects and let the child recount the remainder; counting-back matures later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child recounts the remaining biscuits slowly from one, or cannot count back reliably.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the two numbers instead of taking away — treats any two quantities as 'put together'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act the story out — start with 5, physically take 2 away — so the situation drives the operation rather than the numbers.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7 — you put them together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 7.

responseLevels.gap: Reports the amount taken away, or adds the numbers, or cannot find what remains.
responseLevels.full: Removes the part and reads the remainder (or counts back), and explains subtraction as finding how many are left.
responseLevels.partial: Finds 3 by physically removing and recounting the whole set from one; take-away enacted but not yet counting back or recalling.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You have 5 biscuits and you eat 2 of them. How many biscuits are left? How do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands subtraction as taking away removes 2 and focuses on the remainder; a child who does not may report how many were eaten (2), add the numbers (7), or lose track. The reason reveals whether 'take away' is understood as separating a part and reading the rest.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to recognise and DRAW shapes that satisfy a specified attribute (e.g. exactly five sides, a given number of angles) and to identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons and hexagons within a mixed set. The procedural work is building or selecting to a property — a pentagon is any closed figure with five straight sides — rather than reproducing a memorised prototype. The central obstacle is the prototype effect: children draw and accept only the regular, symmetrical, 'textbook' version and miss irregular or rotated members of the class. Best taught by generating many varied and irregular examples, defining each class by its attribute, and hunting for ALL members (including non-prototypical ones) in mixed sets.
bestPractices: Define each shape class by its attribute (a hexagon is ANY closed shape with 6 straight sides / 6 vertices) and check drawn shapes against it.
Demand and celebrate IRREGULAR and rotated examples — 'draw a different pentagon that doesn't look like that one' — to break the single-prototype image.
Give mixed 'find them all' sets that include irregular, tilted and near-miss shapes so identifying a class means applying the attribute, not matching a picture.
Model counting and marking each side/vertex once when drawing or checking, so the side-count is accurate.
Use dotted paper, geoboards or a peg grid to support accurate drawing of straight-sided closed figures.
keyRepresentations: Geoboard / pegboard and dotted paper for constructing polygons to a target side-count
Mixed shape sets containing regular, irregular, tilted and near-miss examples plus non-examples
Side/vertex tally marks made while counting
Side-by-side regular vs irregular pentagon/hexagon to show both satisfy the attribute
commonMisconceptions: Draws or accepts only the prototypical regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base example and misses irregular or rotated members of a class.
Miscounts sides or vertices when drawing or identifying (draws six sides when asked for five; loses track counting an irregular shape).
Draws a non-closed figure or one with curved sides, not attending to 'closed' and 'straight-sided'.
Judges class membership by the name/look ('that's not a quadrilateral, it's a diamond') rather than by counting the sides.

learn.summary: Children learn to draw and identify polygons by their defining attribute — a pentagon is ANY closed figure with five straight sides whose sides do not cross each other, not one memorised 'textbook' shape. The core obstacle is the prototype effect: learners draw and accept only the regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base version and miss irregular, tilted or rotated members of a class. Guidance centres on generating many varied and irregular examples, defining each class by its attribute (side/vertex count, closed, straight-sided, sides not crossing), and hunting for ALL members in mixed sets that include non-prototypical and near-miss shapes. Accurate side/vertex counting is scaffolded by marking each once.

activities.title: Build a polygon to a target side-count
feedback: If the shape has the wrong number of sides, recount together, marking each side exactly once from a clear start point; dotted paper or pegs keep sides straight.
If only a regular/symmetrical version is produced, prompt: 'Make one that is squished, tilted, or spiky but still has five straight sides' and affirm that it counts just as much.
If the figure has a gap or a curved/bulging edge, check it against the attributes aloud: is it closed? is every side straight?
Celebrate an irregular valid solution explicitly so the learner sees it is as correct as the neat one.
activities.rationale: Constructing to an attribute is an active production task that confronts the prototype effect directly; demanding varied and irregular examples is intended to break the single-image definition. Counting sides, checking closure (whether by the learner, an adult, or an optional live side-counter) and visibly accepting ANY valid (including irregular) shape are intended to make the defining attribute the thing being rewarded.
sourceClaims: A polygon is a 2-D shape made of three or more straight sides that meet at vertices; children are taught to identify and sort polygons by number of sides/vertices, using varied examples (all sides/vertices the same, some the same, all different). A common misconception is inaccurate counting of sides/vertices from losing track of the start point; remedy is to mark each side/vertex once as it is counted.

The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.
learnerActions: Given an instruction such as 'build a shape with exactly five straight sides', construct the figure on dotted paper, a geoboard, or a peg/rubber-band grid.
Count and mark each side (and vertex) once as it is drawn, so the total is checked rather than guessed.
Ensure the figure CLOSES and that every side is straight before declaring it finished.
When one valid shape is made, draw 'a different pentagon that does NOT look like the first one' — a long, spiky, or irregular one.
Compare a regular and an irregular example of the same class side by side and state why both satisfy the attribute.
activities.intendedInsight: A polygon class is defined by its attribute (number of straight sides meeting at vertices, closed figure with sides that do not cross), invariant to size, orientation and regularity — not by matching a single remembered prototype.

activities.title: Find them all in a mixed set
feedback: If an irregular or tilted member is skipped, draw attention to it and recount its sides together; attending to the awkward four-sided shape is intended to loosen the prototype grip as the learner sees the squished one also counts.
If a shape is included or excluded by its name/look alone (e.g. 'that's a diamond, not a quadrilateral'), redirect to counting the four straight sides.
If counting on an irregular shape loses track, model starting at one vertex and marking each side once around the figure.
activities.rationale: A 'find them all' set that deliberately contains non-prototypical and near-miss shapes is designed to require attribute-based classification and to surface the prototype misconception; it is hard to fake because the regular example alone is insufficient to complete the task.
sourceClaims: Young children over-rely on a prototypical exemplar: 93-96% identify a prototypical (equilateral, horizontal-base) triangle but far fewer accept atypical types (only ~30.5% identified all three of scalene/right/isosceles) or rotated versions; a non-formal attribute matching the prototype (e.g. horizontal base) is treated as defining ('imposed attribute'). Remedy: typical + atypical examples and non-examples.

The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.
learnerActions: From a mixed set that includes regular, irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples, mark EVERY member of a named class (e.g. 'circle all the quadrilaterals').
For each shape marked or skipped, justify by counting sides/vertices and checking closed + straight-sided, not by its name or look.
Deliberately inspect the awkward shapes — a long thin tilted four-sided shape, a dented pentagon — and decide membership by the attribute.
Explain why a square is a quadrilateral, and why a 'diamond' is also a quadrilateral regardless of its orientation.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying a class means applying its attribute to every candidate, including irregular and rotated ones, rather than recognising a familiar picture.

activities.title: Name, draw and justify by attribute
feedback: If the count is wrong, recount marking each side/vertex once; dotted paper keeps the sides straight.
If both drawings look the same, ask for a genuinely different-looking version with the same number of sides.
Accept and praise any closed, straight-sided figure with the correct count regardless of regularity.
activities.rationale: Requiring a spoken/written justification by attribute, plus a deliberately varied second example, checks that the class is defined by count rather than appearance.
sourceClaims: The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.

A polygon is a 2-D shape made of three or more straight sides that meet at vertices; children are taught to identify and sort polygons by number of sides/vertices, using varied examples (all sides/vertices the same, some the same, all different). A common misconception is inaccurate counting of sides/vertices from losing track of the start point; remedy is to mark each side/vertex once as it is counted.
learnerActions: Draw a named polygon (e.g. a hexagon) and explain how you know it is one by counting its six straight sides and six vertices/angles.
Produce a second example of the same name that looks clearly different from the first.
State the defining attributes in your own words ('a hexagon is any closed shape with six straight sides that do not cross each other').
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying class membership by the attribute count — and producing a non-prototypical second example — demonstrates the definition is understood, not just a remembered shape.

constraints: Tasks must require active drawing/construction and selection, not tap-to-reveal recognition: a static labelled picture can show examples but does not itself let the learner build or choose, and active production and selection are where the prototype misconception can surface.
Mixed 'find them all' sets must include irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples; a set of only regular shapes cannot discriminate attribute-use from picture-matching.

Any 'draw a pentagon' response format should be paired with a side-count check (counting/marking by the learner or an adult), since free drawing alone does not reliably verify the exact number of straight sides.

A fixed single-answer format under-rewards the many-different-valid-answers goal; whatever format is used, multiple distinct correct shapes (including irregular ones) must be treated as equally valid.

A live side-counter, closure check, and visible acceptance of any valid shape (e.g. a highlight on a correct irregular pentagon, a pulse on a missed tilted quadrilateral) are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete, but are optional illustrations, not required technology.

The topic is primarily 2-D polygon drawing and identification; the single 'cubes' reference does not require a 3-D spatial environment. If cube identification is added, ask about the mathematical solid REPRESENTED on a thin card (which itself has slight thickness and can be held), not whether the physical card can be picked up.
Scaffolds (dotted paper, geoboards, peg grids) support accurate straight sides and counting but should not become the only medium; plain drawing and physical shape sorting are also valid.

The Stanford DREME source is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed, and read its use in sourceClaims as topical/principle support only, not validated evidence.

The parentTitle field ('Angles in triangles (age 7+)') does not match the microTopic content (recognise/draw polygons by attribute); the description and evidence govern this guidance. Flagged for review as a possible labelling mismatch.

Original artefact-fit language asserting that a static image 'cannot teach' and that a quiz 'cannot reward' varied answers has been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; the comparative-necessity framing is not established by the cited sources.

probeDeeper: You drew this five-sided shape. Count the sides with me — is it exactly five?
Is THIS a quadrilateral? [show a long, thin, tilted, irregular four-sided shape] How do you know?
Could you draw a completely different pentagon — one that doesn't look like the first?
Is a square a quadrilateral? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Draws any closed figure with exactly five straight sides — need not be a regular pentagon. (2) Circles every four-sided shape, including irregular and rotated ones, and no others. (3) Draws a six-sided closed figure and justifies by counting six sides (and six vertices/angles). The attribute is satisfied by the count, not by matching a prototype.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws or accepts only the prototype — a regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base example — and misses irregular or rotated members of the class.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define the class by its attribute (a quadrilateral is ANY closed shape with four straight sides), then present many varied and irregular examples with non-examples to sort, and ask for a 'different one that doesn't look like that'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the quadrilateral hunt, skips irregular or tilted four-sided shapes; when asked to draw, produces only the textbook-regular version.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts sides or vertices when drawing or identifying — draws six sides when asked for five, or loses track counting an irregular shape.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: model numbering/marking each side as it is drawn or counted so each is counted exactly once; use dotted paper for accurate straight sides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn shape has the wrong number of sides; a recount gives a different total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws a non-closed figure or one with curved sides, not attending to 'closed' and 'straight-sided'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: State and check the defining attributes — closed, straight sides — against each drawn shape, using the 'is it / is it not a polygon' test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn polygon has a gap or a bulging/curved side.

responseLevels.gap: Draws or selects only the prototypical regular example, draws the wrong number of sides, or draws non-closed/curved figures — attends to the picture, not the attribute.
responseLevels.full: Draws any closed figure with the exact specified number of straight sides in varied/irregular forms, identifies ALL members of a class including irregular and rotated ones while excluding non-members, and justifies by the defining attribute (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Draws a correct example and identifies prototypical members, but misses irregular or rotated instances (circles the square but not an irregular quadrilateral) or occasionally miscounts sides (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three short tasks and watch how the child works: (1) 'Draw me a shape with exactly five straight sides.' (2) Hand them a mixed set of shapes (including irregular and tilted ones): 'Circle all the quadrilaterals.' (3) 'Draw a hexagon, and show me how you know it is a hexagon.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child draw and select reveals whether they build to the specified attribute or reach for a memorised prototype. The quadrilateral hunt deliberately includes irregular and tilted four-sided shapes: a child who circles only the square/rectangle is matching a picture, while one who circles the awkward ones is applying 'four straight sides'. This is hard to fake because the mixed set contains non-prototypical members.
