pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Naming Common Animals

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 Animals including humans):** "identify and name a variety of common animals including fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals." This is a UK-primary node: naming the five vertebrate groups and giving at least one defining feature of each is explicitly statutory in England.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no direct PE; nearest anchor 1-LS1-1 / DCI LS1.A):** NGSS does NOT ask children to name the five vertebrate classes; it emphasises external parts and their function ('all organisms have external parts... use their body parts to survive'). The naming task is UK-driven; the US connection is structure–function (feathers, gills, scales as parts that help an animal live in its environment).

- **Operational details:** Teach classification by OBSERVABLE PHYSICAL FEATURES, not by habitat or movement — this is the single most important framing, because children default to sorting by where an animal lives or how it moves. Give each group a small, memorable feature set (mammals: fur/hair, warm-blooded, live young, milk; birds: feathers, beak, eggs; fish: gills, fins, scales, live in water; reptiles: dry scaly skin, eggs; amphibians: moist skin, live on land and water). Let children free-sort a pile of animal pictures by their own criteria FIRST, then introduce the scientific groups, so they feel why a shared rule is useful. Deliberately teach the 'tricky' animals — whale and dolphin (mammals, not fish), bat (mammal, not bird), penguin (bird that can't fly), frog (amphibian, not fish) — as the cases that prove features beat habitat/movement.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–6, KS1 Y1). Children can name at least two animals in each of the five groups, sort pictures into the groups, and state one feature per group. Appropriate: observable external features, familiar exemplars. NOT appropriate yet: invertebrates, formal taxonomy/keys, cold- vs warm-blooded as a deep principle (introduce the words only lightly). Expect and directly address habitat-based ('lives in water = fish') and movement-based ('flies = bird') sorting errors.
bestPractices: Teach the rule that animals are grouped by OBSERVABLE PHYSICAL FEATURES, not by habitat or how they move — state it explicitly and return to it on every tricky case.
Let children free-sort animal pictures by their own criteria before introducing the scientific five, so a shared classification rule feels useful rather than arbitrary.
Give each group a short, memorable feature set and anchor it to two familiar exemplars, then add one tricky member (e.g. dolphin for mammals) to test the feature not the habitat.
Use hands-on picture-card sorting with self-checking (e.g. colour-coded card backs) so children verify their own grouping and get immediate feedback.
Pair sorting with fiction/nonfiction read-alouds to build the naming vocabulary and 'same and different' comparison language.
keyRepresentations: Five labelled sorting pens/columns: mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians, with animal picture cards.
A group→feature chart (fur–mammal, feathers–bird, gills/scales–fish, dry scales–reptile, moist skin–amphibian).
'Tricky animal' cards (whale, dolphin, bat, penguin, frog) used as decisive test cases.
Body-covering matching (cat–fur, blackbird–feathers, clownfish–scales, crocodile–dry scaly skin, frog–moist skin).
commonMisconceptions: 'Lives in water = fish' — sorting whales, dolphins and other sea mammals as fish by habitat.
'Flies = bird' — classifying bats as birds, or assuming all birds fly (penguins, ostriches).
Grouping by size, number of legs, or 'scary/friendly' rather than by biological features.
Believing insects/spiders are among the five groups — not yet distinguishing vertebrates from invertebrates.

learn.summary: Teach 5–6 year-olds to name and sort common animals into the five vertebrate groups (mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians) by OBSERVABLE BODY FEATURES, not by where an animal lives or how it moves. The central move is to let children free-sort animal pictures by their own criteria first, then introduce the scientists' five groups so a shared rule feels earned, and to use 'tricky' animals (dolphin, whale, bat, penguin, frog) as decisive cases where features beat habitat/movement. Children should be able to name two animals per group, sort pictures, and state one feature per group.

activities.title: Free-sort, then the scientists' five pens
feedback: When a child drops the dolphin with the fish, don't just mark it wrong — reveal the decisive feature: no gills but lungs and a blowhole, smooth skin not scales, a calf drinking milk. Then re-ask the group.
For a bat called a bird: 'A bat flies, but check its body covering — it has fur, not feathers, so it is a mammal. Feathers make a bird.'
For a penguin excluded from birds: 'A penguin can't fly, but it has feathers and a beak and lays eggs — so it is still a bird. Flying is not something ALL birds do.'

For a frog called a reptile: 'Amphibians like the frog have moist skin and young (tadpoles) that live in water; reptiles like the crocodile have dry, scaly skin, and most lay eggs with tough shells on land.'
Praise reasoning that names a feature ('right — gills, so fish') rather than just a correct label.
activities.rationale: Children often default to sorting by habitat or movement, so letting them experience their own rules first is intended to make a shared, feature-based rule feel useful; the tricky animals are chosen precisely to show features beat habitat/movement. A sorting task asks the child to commit a decision and be corrected, which is where the misconception surfaces.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common animals including fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals' and to describe and compare their structure.

The five vertebrate groups are defined by physical features (mammal: warm-blooded, live young, hair/fur; fish: cold-blooded, fins/tail, gills; bird: warm-blooded, hard-shelled eggs, feathers; reptile: cold-blooded, eggs, dry scaly skin; amphibian: cold-blooded, moist skin, land and water), and pupils should be taught that animals are classified by physical features NOT by where they live or how they move.

A documented pupil misconception is that all sea-dwelling animals are fish or that only birds can fly; tricky examples (dolphin/whale as mammals, penguin as a flightless bird, frog as an amphibian) are used to correct it.

Sorting and categorizing objects (including toy animals) into groups by observable attributes is a foundational early-learning skill best built through hands-on sorting and paired fiction/nonfiction read-alouds.
learnerActions: Give the child a pile of animal picture cards and ask them to sort them into groups any way they like, then say out loud the rule they used (e.g. 'these all live in water', 'these all have legs').

Introduce five labelled pens or columns — mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians — and the short feature set for each: mammals (fur/hair, feed babies milk, usually live young), birds (feathers, beak, eggs), fish (gills, fins, usually scales), reptiles (dry scaly skin, most lay eggs), amphibians (moist skin, young live in water).
Re-sort the same cards into the five pens, and for each card say which body feature put it there ('the cat has fur, so mammal').

Seed the deck with tricky cards — dolphin, whale, bat, penguin, frog — and talk through each: the dolphin lives in the sea but has no gills, breathes air with lungs, and feeds its babies milk, so it is a mammal.
Match each group to a body covering: cat–fur, blackbird–feathers, clownfish–scales, crocodile–dry scaly skin, frog–moist skin.
activities.intendedInsight: You decide an animal's group from its body features (covering, how it breathes, how its young are born/fed), not from where it lives or how it moves.

activities.title: Interactive sorting bench with live correction (optional digital scaffold)
feedback: On a mis-sort, zoom to the feature that decides it (blowhole/lungs, fur, feathers) rather than only marking it incorrect.
Reinforce the generalisation after each tricky card: the same 'check the body feature' rule just worked again.
activities.rationale: A drag-to-group interaction with live recompute lets each tricky animal do its teaching work by prompting a commitment and then revealing the decisive feature; the free-sort-first mode mirrors the hands-on approach. This is presented as one optional medium — a physical card sort may achieve the same learning and is the baseline activity, so the digital bench is not required.
sourceClaims: A documented pupil misconception is that all sea-dwelling animals are fish or that only birds can fly; tricky examples (dolphin/whale as mammals, penguin as a flightless bird, frog as an amphibian) are used to correct it.

Sorting and categorizing objects (including toy animals) into groups by observable attributes is a foundational early-learning skill best built through hands-on sorting and paired fiction/nonfiction read-alouds.
learnerActions: On a drag-to-group bench, drag each animal card into one of five labelled pens; on each drop, answer 'which feature?' so the choice is tied to a body feature.

Deliberately encounter a habitat-based mis-sort (dolphin → fish): the pen signals a problem and the card flips to a cutaway zoomed on the decisive feature (no gills / lungs and blowhole / calf drinking milk).
Start in a free-sort mode where you invent your own groups, then switch to the labelled-pens mode to see the scientists' five.
Repeat with bat (flies, but fur and milk → mammal) and penguin (a bird that can't fly) so the rule generalises beyond one case.
activities.intendedInsight: Committing a sort and then seeing the deciding body feature is meant to help the child shift from a 'where it lives' rule to a 'what its body is like' rule.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal feature chart for vocabulary
feedback: Confirm the feature link each time: 'Yes — the dolphin and the dog both feed their babies milk, so both are mammals, even though one lives in the sea.'
If a child relies on a familiar picture only, point to the tricky member to show the feature travels across habitats.
activities.rationale: A reveal chart can build the group→feature vocabulary cleanly before or alongside sorting. It teaches the features but does not itself require the child to commit and correct a sorting decision, so it works best paired with the sorting activity rather than used alone.
sourceClaims: The five vertebrate groups are defined by physical features (mammal: warm-blooded, live young, hair/fur; fish: cold-blooded, fins/tail, gills; bird: warm-blooded, hard-shelled eggs, feathers; reptile: cold-blooded, eggs, dry scaly skin; amphibian: cold-blooded, moist skin, land and water), and pupils should be taught that animals are classified by physical features NOT by where they live or how they move.
learnerActions: Explore a group→feature chart: tap a mammal to highlight its fur and reveal 'has hair, feeds milk'; tap a bird to highlight feathers; and so on across all five groups.

For each group, see one familiar representative AND one tricky member together (mammal: dog AND dolphin) so the SHARED feature, not the habitat, is what is highlighted — for the dog and dolphin, highlight feeding babies milk and breathing air, because a dolphin has almost no hair.
Say the feature aloud for each group to build the naming vocabulary: feathers–bird, gills–fish, fur–mammal, dry scales–reptile, moist skin–amphibian.
activities.intendedInsight: Each group has a short, memorable set of body features, and even animals that live in different places share the same group feature.

activities.title: Riddle animal: name the group from features
feedback: If the child answers from the habitat clue, redirect: 'You heard "the sea" — but which BODY clue did I give? Breathes air and feeds milk — that's a mammal.'
Reward answers that name the deciding feature.
activities.rationale: A spoken riddle/dialogue can spotlight the feature-vs-habitat tension by deliberately mixing a habitat clue with feature clues. It is a useful variation; for naming these five bounded, picture-anchored groups with 5–6 year-olds, direct picture sorting is a practical first-teaching route, with the riddle used as a complement. Relative efficiency across these media is not established by the available sources.
sourceClaims: A documented pupil misconception is that all sea-dwelling animals are fish or that only birds can fly; tricky examples (dolphin/whale as mammals, penguin as a flightless bird, frog as an amphibian) are used to correct it.
learnerActions: Listen to an in-role animal describe only its body features, not its home: 'I live in the sea but I breathe air and feed my babies milk — what group am I?'
Name the group and say which feature gave it away.

Answer probing follow-ups: 'How does the dolphin get its oxygen, and how is that different from a fish?'; 'How are a dolphin's babies born and fed compared with a fish's?'; 'A bat can fly — does that make it a bird? What would you check instead?'; 'Name one body feature that tells you an animal is a bird, and one that tells you it's a fish.'
Make up your own riddle for a classmate using only features.
activities.intendedInsight: The features in a description — not the place mentioned — decide the group.

activities.title: Check and read-aloud: naming and 'which is NOT' questions
feedback: For 'which is NOT a mammal', confirm via features: 'The frog has moist skin, and its young (tadpoles) live in water — amphibian, not mammal.'
If the child reverts to habitat/movement on a tricky item, return to the body-feature rule (body covering, how it breathes, how its babies are born and fed) before moving on.
activities.rationale: Matching and categorisation with tricky distractors faithfully assess this exact objective. This activity mainly checks naming and sorting, so it is best placed after the sorting and chart work that develop the feature-reasoning; read-alouds support the naming vocabulary.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 statutory content requires pupils to 'identify and name a variety of common animals including fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals' and to describe and compare their structure.

Sorting and categorizing objects (including toy animals) into groups by observable attributes is a foundational early-learning skill best built through hands-on sorting and paired fiction/nonfiction read-alouds.
learnerActions: Sort six animals into the five groups and match each group to its defining feature.
Answer discriminating questions: 'Which is NOT a mammal?' (frog, among bat, dolphin, fox) and 'Is flying something ALL birds can do?' (penguin shows no).
Pair the sorting with a fiction and a nonfiction read-aloud about animals to build naming vocabulary and 'same and different' comparison language.
activities.intendedInsight: I can name animals in each group, sort them, and justify each with a feature, including the tricky counter-examples.

constraints: Checkpoint is concrete/observational (≈5–6, KS1 Y1): children name at least two animals per group, sort pictures, and state one feature per group. Keep to observable external features and familiar exemplars.

Not appropriate yet: invertebrates (insects/spiders are not among the five groups), formal taxonomy or classification keys, and cold- vs warm-blooded as a deep principle — introduce those words only lightly.

Expect and directly address habitat-based ('lives in water = fish') and movement-based ('flies = bird') sorting errors on every tricky case; also watch for grouping by size, number of legs, or 'scary/friendly'.

The tap-to-reveal chart and the riddle dialogue teach/strengthen features but do not themselves require the child to commit and correct a sorting decision, where the misconception is most directly challenged; use them alongside an actual sort, not instead of one.
The final check mainly confirms whether a child can sort and name; use it after the teaching activities rather than relying on it alone to develop feature-reasoning.

Digital drag-to-group, cutaway reveals, and tap-to-reveal are optional media; a physical card sort with self-checking (e.g. colour-coded card backs), real specimen handling, or a zoo visit can achieve the same learning and provides a tactile complement.
A 3D model of an individual animal is not needed to teach classification by external features; clear 2D images suffice, and the extra interaction cost may not add classification insight for this age.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The pedagogy/sources describe the five groups partly with cold- vs warm-blooded language for correctness, but the checkpoint says to introduce warm/cold-blooded only lightly at this age; activities foreground observable coverings and breathing/young instead to stay age-appropriate.

Minor biological nuance: 'amphibians live on land and water' is simplified; amphibians typically have aquatic larvae and moister skin — stated as 'young live in water' to avoid implying all amphibians split time evenly. Reviewers may wish to confirm wording for exemplars like the frog.
One source (Reading Rockets, 'Patterns and Categorizing') is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

The original artefact comparison asserted a static picture 'cannot' let tricky animals teach, that 3D 'adds no insight', and that sorting 'teaches more efficiently' than dialogue; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

probeDeeper: How does the dolphin get its oxygen — and how is that different from a fish?
How are a dolphin's babies born and fed compared with a fish's?
A bat can fly — does that make it a bird? What would you check instead?
Name one body feature that tells you an animal is a bird, and one that tells you it's a fish.
assess.correctAnswer: The dolphin is a mammal: it breathes air (comes to the surface, has lungs not gills), gives birth to live young that drink milk, and is warm-blooded with a little hair — whereas fish breathe with gills and mostly lay eggs. You group by body features, not by where it lives.

errorPatterns.pattern: If it lives in water it's a fish ('the dolphin swims in the sea, so it's a fish')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Focus on features: it surfaces to breathe air and feeds its babies milk. Group by body characteristics, not where the animal lives.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's a fish because it lives in the sea and swims.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places dolphins or whales in the fish group because of habitat and swimming

errorPatterns.pattern: If it flies it's a bird ('a bat flies, so it's a bird')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Body covering decides the group: the bat has fur, so it's a mammal. Feathers make a bird.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls a bat a bird, grouping by how the animal moves

errorPatterns.pattern: Frogs and lizards are the same group ('a frog is a reptile')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Amphibians have moist skin and young that live in water (tadpoles); reptiles have dry scales and lay shelled eggs on land.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Confuses amphibians and reptiles, calling a frog a reptile

responseLevels.gap: Sorts animals by habitat or movement (in water→fish, flies→bird) and can't give a defining body feature for a group.
responseLevels.full: Assigns animals to the five groups using body features (feathers, fur, gills, moist vs dry skin) and correctly handles counter-examples such as an aquatic mammal or a flying mammal.
responseLevels.partial: Names features for familiar groups but reverts to habitat/behaviour for tricky animals like dolphins or bats.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A dolphin lives in the sea and swims just like a fish — but it isn't a fish, it's a mammal. What could you find out about the dolphin's body or its babies that would prove it belongs with the mammals and not the fish?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who groups by features cites breathing air, milk or live young. A child who groups by habitat says 'it lives in the sea and swims, so it's a fish' — the classic where-it-lives error that this sea-dwelling mammal is designed to expose.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7–9; understand the rainforest water cycle — trees absorb water through roots and release it through leaves (TRANSPIRATION), the moisture rises and forms clouds above the canopy, and rain falls back into the forest — a self-sustaining loop that generates much of the forest's own rain.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Y4 'States of matter' (evaporation/condensation in the water cycle) and Y3/Y4 'Plants' (water transport in plants); geography water-cycle strand.
• Standards — US: NGSS 5-ESS2-1 (interactions of geosphere/biosphere/hydrosphere/atmosphere) and 2-ESS2 water-in-the-world flavour; MS-ESS2-4 (water cycle driven by energy).
• Operational details — build on the general water cycle but add the BIOLOGICAL pump: it's not just oceans evaporating — the trees themselves breathe out water vapour (transpiration), so much that the forest largely rains on itself. Sequence it as a loop with arrows: roots absorb → leaves transpire → vapour rises → cools/condenses into cloud → rain → back to roots. Stress the SELF-SUSTAINING/feedback nature (fewer trees → less transpiration → less rain), the hook for the later deforestation topic.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (7): put the stages in order. Tier B (8): use 'transpiration' correctly for water leaving via leaves. Tier C (9): explain why the forest makes much of its own rain and predict what happens to rainfall if many trees are removed.
bestPractices: Build on the general water cycle, then ADD the biological pump — transpiration from leaves — as the rainforest's distinctive twist.
Draw it as a closed LOOP with directional arrows so the self-sustaining nature is visible.
Use the precise term 'transpiration' and tie it concretely to water escaping through leaves.
Stress the feedback: more trees → more transpiration → more rain; fewer trees → less rain — the hook for deforestation.
Anchor to the tropical-climate prerequisite (constant heat drives fast evaporation and lush transpiring growth).
keyRepresentations: A circular water-cycle loop diagram over a forest cross-section (roots→leaves→cloud→rain→roots).
A close-up of a leaf releasing vapour, labelled 'transpiration'.
A trees-vs-rainfall relationship (more forest, bigger clouds).
A single droplet's traceable journey around the loop.
commonMisconceptions: 'All the rain comes from the sea/sky' — the forest itself generates much of its own rain via transpiration.
'Plants only drink water, they don't release it' — leaves transpire large amounts of water vapour.
'Transpiration is the same as respiration/breathing out CO2' — it is water vapour leaving through leaf pores.
'Cutting trees won't change the rain' — fewer trees means less transpiration and less rainfall.
'Clouds form for no reason' — rising vapour cools and condenses into cloud.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach the rainforest water cycle as a loop that the trees help keep going, powered by the Sun's heat: roots absorb water, leaves release it as vapour (transpiration), the vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds above the canopy, and much of the rain falls back onto the forest, while moisture blowing in from the sea also adds rain. The distinctive idea beyond the general water cycle is the biological 'pump': the forest makes much of its own rain. Add the feedback that fewer trees mean less transpiration and can mean less rain, which seeds the later deforestation topic. Use precise vocabulary ('transpiration') and make the cause-and-effect visible and manipulable.

activities.title: Run and perturb the forest's rain loop
feedback: If a learner expects nothing to change when trees are removed: point out that with fewer leaves transpiring, there is less vapour, so the clouds shrink and the rain falls off — the loop is weakened.

If a learner says all the rain blows in from the sea: agree that some moisture does come from the sea, then show that the leaves themselves also release vapour that rises and condenses here, so the forest recycles much of its own water.
Reinforce the term: 'The water leaving the leaves as vapour is called transpiration.'
When the learner restores trees and the rain returns, confirm: 'The forest makes much of its own rain — the trees are part of the pump.'
activities.rationale: A manipulable loop lets the child see the self-sustaining and fragile nature of the cycle, because cloud density and rainfall recompute live from the tree count, which a static sequence cannot make felt in the same way. The optional tree-count control, single-droplet step-through, and a clear-the-forest action make the cause-and-effect concrete and seed the deforestation topic. Proposed as a research-informed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Rainforests generate much of their own rainfall through transpiration: trees release water vapour from their leaves, which forms clouds and precipitates back over the forest (moisture recycling)
learnerActions: Watch a forest cross-section where water climbs the trunks from the roots, puffs out of the leaves as vapour, gathers into clouds above the canopy, and falls back as rain onto the same forest.
Follow a single droplet all the way around the loop (roots → leaf → vapour → cloud → rain → roots), stepping through one stage at a time.
Use a 'how many trees?' control to reduce the number of trees, and observe what happens to the vapour, the clouds, and the rain.
Add trees back and describe, in your own words, what happens to the clouds and rainfall.
State the rule you discovered in the model: more trees → more transpiration → more rain; fewer trees → less transpiration → less rain.
activities.intendedInsight: The rainforest is not just receiving rain — the trees release water vapour through their leaves (transpiration), which helps form clouds and rain over the forest, so removing trees weakens the rain. This is a feedback loop, not only a one-way supply from the sea.

activities.title: Label the loop and name each stage
feedback: If a learner confuses transpiration with breathing out CO2: clarify that transpiration is water vapour leaving through tiny pores in the leaf, not the gas exchange of respiration.
If a learner thinks the clouds appear for no reason: point to the rising-vapour stage — the vapour cools higher up and condenses into cloud.
If a learner draws a straight line sea → cloud → rain: keep the sea arrow but redirect them to close the loop back to the roots, because much of the rain falls on the forest and is drawn up again.
Confirm correct use: 'Yes — transpiration is water leaving the leaf as vapour.'
activities.rationale: A labelled loop with selectable stages teaches the sequence and the precise vocabulary clearly. It does not let the child see the feedback between tree numbers and rainfall, so it works best alongside the manipulable loop above.
sourceClaims: KS2 pupils learn evaporation and condensation in the water cycle (Y4 States of matter) and water transport in plants (Y3 Plants)
Rainforests generate much of their own rainfall through transpiration: trees release water vapour from their leaves, which forms clouds and precipitates back over the forest (moisture recycling)
learnerActions: Study a circular diagram of the forest water cycle with directional arrows connecting roots → leaves → rising vapour → cloud → rain → back to roots.
Select the leaf and state what happens there, using the word 'transpiration' (water escapes from the leaf as vapour).
For each stage, say in one line what is happening (e.g. 'here the vapour cools and condenses into cloud').
Explain why the arrows form a closed loop rather than a straight line.
activities.intendedInsight: The water cycle in a rainforest is a closed loop with named stages, and transpiration is the specific step where water leaves the plant through its leaves as vapour.

activities.title: Predict, test and explain: the bag-on-a-branch investigation
feedback: The expected naive prediction ('no — where would water come from, it hasn't rained?') is the useful diagnostic: it reveals the belief that plants only drink water. Reveal the droplets and name transpiration.
If a learner says clearing forest only removes shade: connect losing trees to losing transpiration → fewer clouds → less rain; the loop is weakened.

Target explanation: 'The forest makes much of its own rain. Trees pull up water through their roots and release it from their leaves as water vapour (transpiration); that moisture rises, cools into clouds, and much of it falls back as rain onto the forest. So not all the rain blows in from the sea — the forest recycles much of its own water, which is why cutting the trees can reduce the rainfall.'
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain investigation surfaces the 'plants only drink water' and 'all rain comes from the sea' misconceptions directly, then lets real droplets provide the correction. The reason-tier forces the transpiration → cloud → rain chain rather than mere recall. Note that one bagged branch shows transpiration from a single plant but does not itself demonstrate forest-scale recycling, which must be explained.
sourceClaims: Rainforests generate much of their own rainfall through transpiration: trees release water vapour from their leaves, which forms clouds and precipitates back over the forest (moisture recycling)
learnerActions: Before testing, predict with a reason: if you seal a clear plastic bag over a leafy branch of a living plant and leave it in the light, will any water appear inside? Write down your reason.
Carry out (or watch) the investigation and return later to observe the inside of the bag.
Explain where the droplets came from, using the word 'transpiration'.
Answer: Where do the clouds above a rainforest come from, if not only from the sea?
Predict what might happen to the rain if half the forest were cut down, and give your reason.
Predict: if the trees could not transpire at all, how would the forest's rainfall change?
activities.intendedInsight: Plants release large amounts of water through their leaves (transpiration); this same process feeds the rainforest's clouds, so losing trees reduces the forest's own rainfall.

activities.title: Order the stages and use the key word
feedback: If the order is wrong, point back to the loop diagram and trace one droplet's journey.
If the learner picks 'all rain blows in from the sea', remind them the leaves release vapour that forms clouds here.
Confirm the correct fill: 'transpiration'.
activities.rationale: Short ordering and fill-in tasks check the sequence and vocabulary cleanly. These are recognition-and-recall checks: they confirm the learner can reproduce the loop but do not by themselves elicit the independent reasoning that the investigation and manipulable loop develop.
learnerActions: Put the five stages of the loop in the correct order: roots absorb water; leaves transpire; vapour rises; vapour cools and condenses into cloud; rain falls back to the roots.
Complete: 'Water leaves the leaf as vapour by a process called ____.' (transpiration)
Choose and justify the better statement: (a) all the rainforest's rain blows in from the sea; (b) the forest makes much of its own rain through transpiration.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the sequence, the term 'transpiration', and the self-rain idea so they can be recalled and explained.

constraints: Build on the general water cycle first, then add the biological pump (transpiration from leaves) as the rainforest's distinctive feature; do not present it as a fresh, unconnected idea.
Draw and discuss the cycle as a closed loop with directional arrows so the self-sustaining nature is visible, not a one-way sea → rain path.
Use the precise term 'transpiration' and tie it concretely to water escaping through leaf pores; distinguish it from respiration/breathing out CO2.
Anchor to the tropical-climate prerequisite: constant heat drives fast evaporation and lush, transpiring growth.

Ordering and fill-in-the-blank checks confirm recall and vocabulary only; they do not elicit independent explanation or let the child see the tree-count feedback, so pair them with the investigation and the manipulable loop.

A paper or screen diagram shows the stages but cannot recompute clouds and rainfall from tree numbers; the manipulable loop is what makes the feedback visible. The investigation shows transpiration from one real plant but does not by itself show the forest-scale recycling, which must be explained.
Age-appropriate simplification: the forest generates much of its own rain, not necessarily all of it; keep the 'much of its own rain' wording and avoid overclaiming.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two listed sources were not re-fetched and both carry verified:false in the original row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The quantitative share of rainfall the forest recycles is not specified in the sources; keep the hedged 'much of its own rain' claim and avoid stating a precise percentage.

The link 'fewer trees → less rain' is presented as a conceptual hook appropriate for this age; real-world rainfall depends on many factors (regional circulation, scale, geography). Treat the simplified feedback as a teaching model, not a quantitative prediction.

assess.poeTask: Seal a clear plastic bag over a leafy branch of a living plant (leave it in the light) and ask the child to predict, WITH A REASON, whether any water will appear inside. The naive prediction ('no — where would water come from, it hasn't rained?') is the diagnostic part. Return later to find droplets on the inside of the bag — water the leaves released by transpiration, the same process that helps make the forest's clouds.
probeDeeper: Use the word 'transpiration' to describe what a leaf does.
Where do the clouds above a rainforest come from, if not only the sea?
What might happen to the rain if half the forest were cut down? Why?
What if the trees couldn't transpire at all — how would the forest's rainfall change?
assess.correctAnswer: The forest makes much of its own rain. Trees pull up water through their roots and release it from their leaves as water vapour (transpiration); that moisture rises above the canopy, cools into clouds, and falls back as rain onto the same forest — a self-sustaining loop. So not all the rain blows in from the sea; the forest recycles its own water. That's why cutting down the trees can reduce the rainfall.

errorPatterns.pattern: all rain blows in from the sea/sky — the forest is a passive place that just gets rained on
errorPatterns.nextMove: introduce transpiration; the forest releases moisture that becomes its own clouds and rain
errorPatterns.distractor: All of it blows in from the sea as clouds
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says every drop comes from ocean clouds, with no role for the trees

errorPatterns.pattern: trees only take in water, never give it out — misses transpiration from leaves
errorPatterns.nextMove: water exits the leaves as vapour (transpiration), feeding the clouds
errorPatterns.revealedBy: describes roots drinking water but nothing leaving the leaves

errorPatterns.pattern: cutting trees only removes shade — doesn't connect losing forest to losing rain
errorPatterns.nextMove: fewer trees means less transpiration, fewer clouds, less rain; the loop breaks
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says clearing forest wouldn't change the rainfall

responseLevels.gap: Thinks all rain comes from the sea; trees play no part.
responseLevels.full: Explains the self-sustaining loop — roots draw water, leaves transpire vapour, clouds form, rain falls back — uses 'transpiration' correctly, and predicts that losing trees reduces the forest's own rainfall.
responseLevels.partial: Knows trees release some water or names transpiration, but can't join the full loop (leaf vapour → cloud → rain → same forest) or link it to deforestation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Rainforests are the rainiest places on Earth. Does ALL that rain blow in from the sea as clouds, or does the forest itself help make its own rain? Tell me which, and then tell me HOW the trees could make rain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks all rain comes from the sea/sky misses transpiration; the concept child explains the forest recycling its own water through the trees. The reason-tier forces the transpiration → cloud → rain loop.

sources.claim: KS2 pupils learn evaporation and condensation in the water cycle (Y4 States of matter) and water transport in plants (Y3 Plants)
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England — Science programmes of study, Y3 and Y4

sources.claim: Rainforests generate much of their own rainfall through transpiration: trees release water vapour from their leaves, which forms clouds and precipitates back over the forest (moisture recycling)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Add three one-digit numbers, using strategies including looking for a pair that makes 10 (e.g. 5 + 7 + 3 → 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15). Ages 6–7, procedural application of associativity/commutativity plus bonds to 10.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'add numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally, including... three one-digit numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.2 fluency and 1.OA.3 strategy use; 'add three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20' with make-ten grouping as the exemplar strategy.
• Operational details: the point is strategic grouping — scan the three addends for a bond to 10 (or a double), add that pair first, then add the third. Depends on quick recall of bonds to 10 and the freedom (commutative/associative) to reorder. Teach scanning explicitly rather than defaulting to left-to-right.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds three one-digit numbers correctly by any method. Tier B (age 7) — for 5 + 7 + 3 chooses 7 + 3 first because it makes ten. Tier C (age 7+) — reliably scans any three addends for the most useful pair (ten or double) and explains the choice.
bestPractices: Teach an explicit 'scan for a pair that makes ten (or a double)' habit before adding.
Rehearse bonds to 10 to fluency so the make-ten pair is spotted instantly.
Use rearrangeable counters/tiles so children physically move the useful pair together.
Contrast a make-ten route with a left-to-right route on the same triple to show the efficiency gain.
Keep sums within 20 initially so the third addition crosses ten at most once.
keyRepresentations: Three movable number tiles that can be reordered
Ten-frame that fills to ten from the chosen pair, then takes the third
Empty number line with a jump to ten then on
Bar/part-whole with three parts
Bonds-to-10 pairs chart as a scanning aid
commonMisconceptions: Always adding left-to-right and never scanning for a make-ten pair.
Not recognising a pair that makes ten because bonds to 10 aren't fluent.
Losing or double-counting the third addend after making ten.
Thinking the numbers must be added in the written order.
Miscounting when crossing ten while adding the third number by ones.

learn.summary: Teaches ages 6–7 to add three one-digit numbers efficiently by scanning for a pair that makes ten (or a double), adding that pair first, then adding on the third number — e.g. 5 + 7 + 3 → 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15. The objective is the strategic habit of scanning and reordering (supported by commutativity/associativity and fluent bonds to 10), not merely getting a correct total. Includes a hands-on manipulative core, fluency/strategy-choice practice, a narration conversation, and a worked anchor, with each scaffold's role made explicit. Interactive and efficacy details are proposed, not validated.

activities.title: Drag a pair to make ten on the ten-frame
feedback: When a chosen pair makes exactly ten, the two tiles fuse into a '10' and the frame fills (e.g. with a glow/click) — immediate confirmation that these two tiles make exactly ten, the pair the make-ten strategy looks for.

When the triple contains a make-ten pair but the chosen pair does not make ten (it goes past ten, e.g. 5 + 7 = 12, or falls short), the frame does not land cleanly on ten, showing why that pairing is less tidy here. The total can still be found, just by a longer route. For triples built around a double (e.g. 6 + 6 + 3, which has no make-ten pair), the double is the useful pair even though it does not fill the frame to exactly ten, so do not mark it as less tidy.
A live-updating running total tile lets the child check the sum as each tile is added.
If the third addend is lost or double-counted, prompt: set the third tile aside and bring it in last, then recount.
activities.rationale: The target is a strategic move — scan, pair, regroup — so physically reordering tiles and seeing a pair snap to ten is intended to train the scanning habit and to make the regrouping concrete through handling. Live recolouring/overflow feedback is intended to show whether a chosen pair makes ten. These interactive details are illustrative of the mechanism, proposed and not validated or required implementations.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils add three one-digit numbers using concrete, pictorial and mental methods.
Applying properties of operations as strategies (1.OA.3) includes grouping addends to make ten; 2.OA.2 targets fluency of such sums within 20.
Looking for pairs that make ten is a key mental-calculation strategy taught in early KS1.
learnerActions: Start with three movable number tiles above a ten-frame, e.g. 5, 7 and 3.
Scan the three tiles and decide which two you would add first: a pair that makes exactly ten, or, if there is no such pair, a double.
Drag two tiles together; if they make ten the frame fills completely and leaves a simpler 'ten and a bit' (here 5 + 10).
Deliberately try a less useful pairing first (e.g. 5 + 7 = 12) and notice the frame does not land on a clean ten, then find the better pair — it still gives a correct total, just by a slower route.
Repeat with triples that reward a make-ten pair, and with at least one triple that rewards a double instead.
Add the remaining third tile on last and read the running total.
activities.intendedInsight: Spotting the pair that makes ten (or a double) first turns an awkward three-number sum into an easier one: a make-ten pair leaves 'ten and a bit', and a double gives a known fact to add on to. The written order is not fixed, you are free to reorder, and any ordering still gives the same total.

activities.title: Which pair makes it easiest? — fluency and strategy choice
feedback: Confirm the efficient pair (e.g. 7 + 3) and point out that it is not the first two numbers written.
If the child selects the first two numbers by default, ask 'can you see two that make ten?' and rehearse the relevant bond.
Keep any timing light and supportive so it builds automaticity rather than anxiety.
activities.rationale: Practice with strategy-choice and quick retrieval is intended to build the automaticity that makes scanning easier. Recognition/selection items check whether the child chooses the efficient pair; they complement, but do not by themselves elicit, the hands-on reordering where the child freely moves the tiles and feels the ten form.
sourceClaims: Applying properties of operations as strategies (1.OA.3) includes grouping addends to make ten; 2.OA.2 targets fluency of such sums within 20.
Looking for pairs that make ten is a key mental-calculation strategy taught in early KS1.
learnerActions: Given a triple such as 5 + 7 + 3, choose which two numbers you would add first and say why.
Complete fill-in-the-blank totals for a set of triples, each containing a make-ten pair that is not the first two written.
Do a short, light timed set of spotting make-ten pairs to build quick recall of bonds to 10.
For each item, state the pair chosen and the leftover number before giving the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of bonds to 10 lets you spot the useful pair quickly; deliberately choosing a make-ten pair can make the addition quicker and less error-prone than always adding left-to-right.

activities.title: Narrate the pair you chose
feedback: If the child narrates adding the first two written numbers every time, highlight the ten pair and rehearse the scan-first habit — the skill, not the concept, is what's missing.
If the child insists numbers must be added in written order, demonstrate that reordering keeps the total the same (any two may be added first).
When a pair makes ten but the third number is lost or doubled, bring the third number in last and recount.
activities.rationale: Narration can reveal the underlying strategy and prompt reflection on order and choice, though a conversation alone does not have the child physically handle and reorder the addends. Best used alongside doing and watching the procedure rather than as a substitute for hands-on practice.
learnerActions: A tutor poses triples such as 5 + 7 + 3, 8 + 2 + 6 and 4 + 9 + 1.
For each, work out the total and say which two numbers you added first and why that choice helps.
Answer follow-ups: 'Is there a pair here that makes exactly ten?', 'Would you get the same total in a different order?', 'For 4 + 9 + 1, which pair makes ten and which number is left to add on?'
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the chosen pair makes the scanning strategy explicit and surfaces whether the child is truly scanning or just adding in written order.

activities.title: Worked anchor: see the make-ten pair highlighted
feedback: Point to the highlighted pair and the resulting 'ten and a bit' to anchor the method.
Note that this is an example to study: it shows the method but does not give feedback on the child's own attempts, so follow it with hands-on practice.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example cannot be manipulated and gives no feedback on the learner's own pairings, but it can provide a useful reference model of the two-step strategy. Treat it as a scaffold that precedes, not replaces, active practice.
learnerActions: Study a worked triple, e.g. 5 + 7 + 3, with the 7 + 3 pair highlighted as it makes ten.
Follow the two steps: pair to ten (7 + 3 = 10), then add the third (5 + 10 = 15).
Describe in your own words how the pair was chosen before moving to practice items.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear model of the scan-pair-add sequence gives a reference point for the strategy before independent practice.

constraints: Keep sums within 20 initially so adding the third number crosses ten at most once.
Depends on quick recall of bonds to 10; rehearse these to fluency so the make-ten pair is spotted readily.
Offer triples where the make-ten pair is NOT the first two numbers written, so the task genuinely requires scanning and reordering.
Include some triples that reward a double rather than a ten, so the habit generalises to 'useful pair', not only 'exactly ten'.

Recognition/selection items (choosing which pair is easiest) check strategy choice but do not by themselves elicit the child freely reordering and feeling the ten form; pair them with hands-on or spoken production.
The worked example is a reference anchor only: it provides no feedback on the child's attempts.
Watch for losing or double-counting the third addend after making ten; bring it in last and recount rather than reteaching the whole strategy.
A correct total alone is not evidence of the strategy — ask which two were added first to distinguish scanning from left-to-right adding.
A less useful pairing (e.g. 5 + 7 first) still reaches the correct total; frame it as slower/less tidy, not as wrong.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the interactive/efficacy details are untested.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 5+7+3=15, 8+2+6=16, 4+9+1=14 (matches the source answer key); make-ten pairs are 7+3, 8+2, 9+1 respectively — all consistent.
The claim that the make-ten route is 'faster and less error-prone' than left-to-right is taken from the row's discriminate note, not from independent empirical validation; it is kept qualified.

The source claim that '3D adds nothing' to adding three small numbers was removed as an unsupported categorical universal; the kept point is only that this task is planar/non-spatial, so a 3D model offers no particular affordance here.
One source (CCSS-M 1.OA.3/2.OA.2) and the NCETM guidance are marked verified:false in the row; treat their claims as unconfirmed.
The source describes timed/speeded retrieval; kept but framed as light and supportive to avoid implying speed pressure is required.
Pedagogy listed further representations (empty number line, bar/part-whole, bonds-to-10 chart) not developed into activities here; they remain legitimate scaffolds if elaborated.

probeDeeper: Which two did you add first, and why did you choose those?
Is there a pair here that makes exactly ten?
Would you get the same total if you added them in a different order?
For 4 + 9 + 1, which pair makes ten — and which number is left to add on?
assess.correctAnswer: 15, 16, 14. Watch for the child spotting and adding the make-ten pair first (7+3, then 8+2, then 9+1) and adding the remaining number on — rather than ploughing left-to-right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds strictly left-to-right, never scanning for a make-ten pair (5 + 7 = 12, then + 3).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'can you see two that make ten?'; highlight bonds to 10 and rehearse the scan-first habit — the skill, not the concept, is missing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Narrates adding the first two written numbers every time; ignores the ten pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You have to add them in the order they're written' — refuses to reorder to pair the ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Remind that any two may be added first (associative/commutative); demonstrate reordering keeps the total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Resists adding 7 + 3 first because 5 comes first on the page.

errorPatterns.pattern: Makes ten with a pair but then loses or double-counts the third addend.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically set the third tile aside and bring it in last; check the count. Don't reteach the strategy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches ten then forgets to add the leftover number, or adds it twice.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably total three one-digit numbers, or loses an addend when combining.
responseLevels.full: Scans the three addends, pairs the one that makes ten (or a double) first, adds the third on, and totals accurately and efficiently — explaining the choice.
responseLevels.partial: Totals correctly but always left-to-right, not spotting or using the make-ten pair.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, and each time tell me which two numbers you added first: 5 + 7 + 3; 8 + 2 + 6; 4 + 9 + 1.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Each triple contains an obvious make-ten pair that is NOT the first two numbers written. A child using the target strategy reorders to pair the ten; a child adding left-to-right can still get the totals but reveals no scanning, and is slower and more error-prone. Asking 'which two first?' exposes the strategy directly, so it discriminates even when totals are correct.

pedagogy.summary: This topic asks children to JUSTIFY why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations — the step from doing a strategy to explaining it. Two justifications are central: partitioning ('add tens and ones separately, then recombine') works because a number is composed of tens and ones and addends may be split, reordered and regrouped without changing the total (commutativity/associativity); and compensation ('add 100 for 99, then take 1 away') works as an equivalent transformation — you adjusted by a known amount and undo it. The goal is reasoning voiced in place-value language, not more correct answers.
bestPractices: Ask 'why does that work?' routinely, and press for reasons beyond 'that's the rule' — model place-value language back to the child
Ground justification in materials first (base-ten shows the whole is conserved when partitioned) then move to verbal argument
Make the properties explicit: order and grouping of addends don't change the total; use this to justify partitioning
For compensation, track the adjustment quantitatively — 'I added one too many, so I subtract one' — and why the direction is forced
Use talk moves (revoice, 'do you agree and why?', counterexamples) so explanations are built collaboratively
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (whole conserved under partitioning)
Number line (compensation: overshoot then step back)
Part-whole diagram (the number as tens + ones)
Worked strategy with each step annotated by its reason
Bar model (equivalent transformations preserve the total)
commonMisconceptions: Restating the procedure or citing authority ('the teacher said') instead of giving a reason
Doubting that splitting/reordering preserves the total (fearing something is lost when a number is broken up)
Compensation direction error: adding 100 for 99 then adding 1 (not seeing 100 is one too many)
Explaining WHAT was done but not WHY it is valid

learn.summary: Children justify WHY addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations — the step from executing a strategy to explaining it. Two justifications are central: partitioning ('add tens and ones separately, then recombine') is valid because a number is composed of tens and ones and addends may be split, reordered and regrouped without changing the total (commutativity/associativity); and compensation ('add 100 for 99, then subtract 1') is an equivalent transformation — you adjusted by a known amount and undo the surplus. The target is reasoning voiced in place-value language, not more correct answers. A dialogic 'prove-it' routine is well-suited as the primary vehicle because producing a justification requires the child to articulate their reasoning, which an open spoken exchange is well-suited to elicit; written annotation, manipulatives and spot-the-flaw tasks serve as complementary scaffolds and probes.

activities.title: Talk with a 'prove-it' partner who never accepts a bare rule
feedback: When the child only restates the steps, press 'but why doesn't splitting change the total?' — revoice any seed of a reason and build on it rather than supplying the full answer.
Model place-value language back: 'so 46 IS 40 and 6, and putting them back together gives the whole.'
For a compensation direction slip (adding 1 instead of subtracting), ask 'how much more is 100 than 99?' so the child tracks the surplus of one.
If the child thinks a different split (35 + 2) might break the method, have them add the parts and recombine to confirm the whole is unchanged.

Accept any genuine answer; the only thing not accepted is 'that's the rule' or 'the teacher said' — keep asking for the reason. Surface the reasoning for discussion rather than scoring it right/wrong.
activities.rationale: The objective is producing a justification, which requires the child to articulate their reasoning; an open 'why?' prompt that accepts answers but never a bare rule is well-suited to pushing the child to explain why splitting and compensation are valid. Talk moves (revoicing, pressing for reasoning, agree/disagree, counterexamples) move children from asserting to justifying, and justifying order/grouping of addends rests on commutativity/associativity.
sourceClaims: Productive mathematical discussion is built through talk moves (revoicing, pressing for reasoning, agree/disagree, counterexamples) that push children from asserting to justifying.

Year 2 pupils show that addition can be done in any order (commutative) but subtraction cannot, use the inverse relationship, and check by adding numbers in a different order — establishing commutativity and associativity; recording in columns supports place-value reasoning.
learnerActions: Solve 46 + 37 by adding tens and ones separately (40 + 30 = 70, 6 + 7 = 13, 70 + 13 = 83), then say the answer aloud.

When your partner (teacher, peer, or an in-role character) asks 'but why doesn't breaking 46 into 40 and 6 lose anything?', explain in your own words why splitting and recombining keeps the same total.
Try splitting 37 a different way — e.g. 35 + 2 instead of 30 + 7 — and explain whether the method still works and why, to show the reasoning transfers to a new split.
Solve 46 + 99 by adding 100 and then adjusting; when asked 'why take one BACK rather than add one?', explain how much too much 100 is compared with 99 and why the surplus must be removed.
Respond to a counterexample your partner offers (e.g. a friend who split 46 into 40 + 6 but only added the 40 and forgot the 6) and say whether that mistake means splitting itself is unreliable.
activities.intendedInsight: A remembered procedure becomes an owned explanation: the number IS its tens and ones, so like parts can be added and recombined without loss, and this holds whichever way you split; adding 100 for 99 adds exactly one too many, so you subtract one to land on adding exactly 99.

activities.title: Show the whole is conserved: partition with materials, compensate on a number line
feedback: If the child fears something is lost when a number is split, recombine the base-ten pieces in front of them to show the whole is conserved.
If the overshoot step-back is unclear, mark 99 and 100 on the line and point out 100 is one step beyond 99.
Prompt the child to voice the reason — the materials make the conserved whole visible and seed the explanation, but the child still needs to say why it is valid.
activities.rationale: Grounding justification in materials first lets the child see the whole conserved under partitioning and see compensation as overshoot-then-step-back, giving concrete footing before the verbal argument. These representations seed the explanation but do not by themselves make the child voice the reason, so pair them with the 'why?' prompt.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils show that addition can be done in any order (commutative) but subtraction cannot, use the inverse relationship, and check by adding numbers in a different order — establishing commutativity and associativity; recording in columns supports place-value reasoning.
learnerActions: Using base-ten blocks, a part-whole diagram, or a bar model, split 46 into 40 + 6 and check that the pieces still make 46 — nothing is lost when you break it up.
Rearrange the order and grouping of the parts (e.g. 6 + 40, or group the tens first) and confirm the total is unchanged.
On a number line, add 46 + 99 by jumping 100 forward, then step back 1; highlight the extra +1 you overshot by.
Say out loud why you step back rather than forward.
activities.intendedInsight: Partitioning preserves the total because the parts still compose the same whole and any order/grouping of addends gives the same sum; compensation is 'overshoot then step back' by the known surplus.

activities.title: Annotate a worked strategy with the reason for each step
feedback: If a label only restates the action ('added the tens'), ask 'why is that step valid?' and look for the place-value reason.
A static annotated strategy is useful reference, but reading a finished annotation does not by itself show the child can reason — follow it with the child explaining a fresh example aloud.
activities.rationale: A worked strategy with each step annotated by its reason makes the hidden place-value logic visible and gives a model for what a justification contains, while making clear that reading a finished annotation is a scaffold rather than independent reasoning.
learnerActions: Take a written worked method for 46 + 37 (40 + 30 = 70; 6 + 7 = 13; 70 + 13 = 83).
Label each step with WHY it is allowed, not just what was done (e.g. '46 is 40 and 6', 'the order of adding the parts doesn't change the total', 'recombining the parts gives the whole').
Do the same for a compensation method (46 + 99 = 46 + 100 − 1) and name the surplus of one and its undoing.
activities.intendedInsight: Every step of a strategy has a place-value reason; a justification names those reasons, not just the actions.

activities.title: Spot the flawed reasoning / pick the valid justification
feedback: After a selection, always ask the child to explain why the chosen justification is valid — recognising the right answer does not on its own show they can produce the reasoning.
For the 'add 1' error in the chain, re-anchor on 100 being one more than 99, so one must be taken back off.
activities.rationale: Choosing the valid justification or spotting the flaw in a reasoning chain can probe understanding of justification and target the common compensation-direction error. Selection tasks cannot capture an open explanation, so use them to probe and surface errors, then move to the child constructing their own reason.
learnerActions: Read two or three explanations of a compensation step and choose the one that correctly justifies subtracting 1 after adding 100.
Find the error in a written reasoning chain (e.g. one that adds 1 instead of subtracting it) and say what has gone wrong.
Explain in your own words why the correct justification is correct.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising valid versus invalid reasoning sharpens the child's sense of what counts as a justification, especially the forced direction of the compensation adjustment.

constraints: The goal is reasoning voiced in place-value language, not more correct answers; do not score the discussion right/wrong — surface reasoning for discussion.

Manipulatives, number lines, bar models and annotated strategies seed and model the explanation but do not themselves make the child articulate WHY — pair them with an explicit request for the child's reason.
Justification can be produced in speech or in writing; the dialogic routine is well-suited to eliciting it but is not the only valid medium.

Selection tasks (choose the valid justification, spot the flaw) assess and probe recognition; recognising a correct justification does not elicit independent construction of one, so follow them with the child explaining in their own words.
Compensation direction must be tracked quantitatively: 100 is one MORE than 99, so adding 100 adds exactly one too many and one must be subtracted; watch for the error of adding 1.
The compensation direction error (adding 1 instead of subtracting) should appear only as a flaw to be identified, never presented as a valid option.

Prerequisites to revisit if reasoning is shaky: three-digit place value / composition of number (if the child doubts splitting preserves the total), and the compensation strategy itself (if the compensation logic is absent).
Subtraction is not commutative even though addition is — do not let 'any order works' be over-generalised to subtraction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels one source (National Curriculum, KS1 Year 2) as verified and one (Michaels & O'Connor accountable talk moves) as verified:false; the talk-moves claim's evidence status is unconfirmed here.

In Activity 1 the National Curriculum claim supports the mathematical content being justified (commutativity/associativity of addends), while the Michaels talk-moves claim supports the dialogic-elicitation principle; these are distinct supports attached to the same activity.

The original entry asserts 'only the dialogue makes them articulate WHY it's allowed', that the task is 'inherently dialogic'/that justification 'must be spoken', and that a non-spatial 3D interactive 'adds nothing'. These comparative/necessity/modality claims are not established by the sources; softened to narrowly scoped affordances (a dialogic exchange is well-suited to eliciting articulated justification, which can also be written; other representations serve as scaffolds).
The bar-model representation from the original keyRepresentations was restored as an optional representation in Activity 2.
The source targets age 7+ but cites KS1 Year 2 curriculum (typically age 6-7); note this age/stage span when selecting number sizes.

probeDeeper: Does it matter whether you add the tens or the ones first? Why not?
You added 100 instead of 99 — exactly how much too much did you add, and how do you undo it?
Would splitting still work if you split 37 into 35 + 2 instead of 30 + 7? Explain why.
If a friend split 46 into 40 + 6 but then added only the 40 and forgot the 6, what went wrong — and does that mean splitting itself is unreliable?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning: splitting works because 46 is 40+6 and 37 is 30+7, and addends can be split, reordered and regrouped without changing the total, so adding like parts and recombining gives the same whole. Compensation works because 100 is one more than 99, so adding 100 adds one too many and you subtract one to get back to adding exactly 99 — an equivalent transformation.

errorPatterns.pattern: Restates the procedure or appeals to authority ('that's how you do it', 'the teacher said') with no reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: In discussion, press 'but why doesn't splitting change the total?'; revoice any seed of a reason and build on it. Do not score — keep drawing out the justification.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child describes the steps again when asked WHY, or defers to a rule without explaining

errorPatterns.pattern: Doubts that splitting/reordering preserves the total — worries breaking the number up loses something
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss with base-ten showing the whole is conserved under partitioning and that any order/grouping of addends gives the same total; reteach three-digit place value if the composition idea is shaky.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child is unsure the partitioned method must give the same answer, or thinks order could matter

errorPatterns.pattern: Compensation direction error — says add 100 for 99 then ADD 1, or can't justify the 'take 1 away'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss on a number line: 100 is one MORE than 99, so one step must come back off; track the surplus explicitly. Reteach the strategy if the compensation logic is absent.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child adjusts the wrong way, or cannot say how much too much was added

responseLevels.gap: Restates the steps or cites authority; gives no reason, or believes splitting could change the total.
responseLevels.full: Justifies with place value AND the properties — the number is composed of tens and ones so like parts add and any order/grouping works; compensation is an equivalent transformation (added too many, subtract the surplus) — and transfers the reasoning to a new split or number.
responseLevels.partial: Offers a partial reason — e.g. 'because 46 is 40 and 6' — but cannot yet justify why recombining the parts is valid, or gets the compensation direction without explaining it (lists the parts without explaining how operating on them preserves the total).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Discuss, don't mark: 'When you add 46 + 37 by working out 40 + 30 = 70 and 6 + 7 = 13 and then combining, why is it OK to break the numbers up like that and still get the right total?' Then: 'To add 46 + 99, someone adds 100 and then takes 1 away — why is that allowed, and how do they know to take 1 away rather than add it?' Listen for place-value and properties reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe separates a child who can JUSTIFY (invoking place-value composition and the properties, and tracking the compensation adjustment) from one who merely restates the steps or cites a rule. The partial-to-full boundary is exactly the move from listing the parts ('46 is 40 and 6') to explaining why operating on the parts and recombining is valid. Surfaced for discussion, not scored right/wrong.

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils show that addition can be done in any order (commutative) but subtraction cannot, use the inverse relationship, and check by adding numbers in a different order — establishing commutativity and associativity; recording in columns supports place-value reasoning.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1, Year 2)

sources.claim: Productive mathematical discussion is built through talk moves (revoicing, pressing for reasoning, agree/disagree, counterexamples) that push children from asserting to justifying.
sources.source: Michaels & O'Connor, Academically Productive Talk / accountable talk moves
